Government forces besieged Chóngqìng,
and recaptured it.
In the sixth month, on the day Wùchén,
Xú Hóngrú captured Zōuxiàn and Téngxiàn.
Jī Wényìn, Magistrate of Téngxiàn, died there.
Máo Wénlóng was promoted to Regional Commander.
Zhāng Yànfāng, Regional Commander of Guìzhōu, was appointed Pacification Regional Commander,
to suppress the Shuǐxī rebels under巡撫(Xúnfǔ) Wáng Sānshàn.
On the day Jǐsì,
Former Regional Commander Yáng Zhàojī and Mobile Corps Commander Chén Jiǔdé led troops to suppress the Shāndōng rebels.
In autumn, in the seventh month, on the *jiǎchén* day,
Lǐ Zhōngchén (李忠臣), Vice Commander of Sōngpān (松潘), and Commander-in-Chief Yáng Yùmào (楊愈懋) plotted to retake Yǒngníng (永寧),
but were unsuccessful
and both died.
The rebels attacked Dàbà (大壩);
Gōng Wànlù (龔萬祿), the Mobile Corps Commander, died in battle,
and Zūnyì (遵義) subsequently fell.
On the *guǐchǒu* day,
Shěn Xiè (沈[⿰⻖𠃘]) retired from office.
On the *yǐmǎo* day,
Emperor Shénzōng's (神宗) spirit tablet was enshrined in the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
On the *gēngshēn* day,
the relief troops for Qián (黔) were routed at Xīntiān (新添).
On the *guǐhài* day,
the Wǔyì (武邑) rebel Yú Hóngzhì (于弘志) rose in revolt,
but was soon executed.
In the eighth month, on the *gēngchén* day,
Sūn Chéngzōng (孫承宗), in his original official capacity, was appointed Superintendent of Military Affairs for Shānhǎiguān (山海關) and Jì (薊), Liáo (遼), Tiānjīn (天津), Dēng (登), and Lái (萊).
In the ninth month, on the first day, *jiǎwǔ*,
Emperor Guāngzōng's (光宗) spirit tablet was enshrined in the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
On the *rénchén* day,
Censor Féng Yīng (馮英) requested the establishment of county and prefectural militias,
with provisions to be supplied according to land acreage;
this was approved.
On the *yǐmǎo* day,
the Imperial brother Yóujiǎn (由檢) was enfeoffed as Prince Xìn (信).
Executions were suspended.
In winter, in the tenth month, on the *xīnwèi* day,
the Shuǐxī (水西) rebels invaded Yúnnán (雲南),
but were defeated by government troops.
On the *xīnsì* day,
government troops retook Zōuxiàn (鄒縣),
captured Xú Hóngrú (徐鴻儒) and others,
and the Shandong (山東) rebellion was quelled.
On the *rénwǔ* day,
Commander-in-Chief Lǔ Qīn (魯欽) replaced Dù Wénhuàn (杜文煥) as General Superintendent,
to aid Guìzhōu (貴州).
In the eleventh month, on the *guǐchǒu* day,
Zhū Xièyuán (朱燮元) was appointed Governor-General of Sichuan (四川) military affairs.
In the twelfth month, on the *jǐsì* day,
Wáng Sānshàn (王三善) and Vice Commander-in-Chief Liú Chāo (劉超) defeated the rebels at Lónglǐ (龍里),
and the siege of Guìyáng (貴陽) was lifted.
In this year,
Siam offered tribute.
In the third year, in spring, in the first month, on the *jǐyǒu* day,
Zhū Guózhēn (朱國zhēn), Vice Minister of Rites,
Gù Bǐngqiān (顧秉謙), Minister of Rites,
Zhū Yánxǐ (朱延禧) and Wèi Guǎngwēi (魏廣微), Vice Ministers of Rites,
were all appointed Minister of Rites and Grand Secretary of the Dōnggé (東閣),
and participated in military affairs.
On the *yǐmǎo* day,
the "Red-haired Barbarians" (Dutch) occupied Pénghú (澎湖).
Government troops from Guìzhōu (貴州) advanced in three columns to suppress Shuǐxī (水西);
Vice Commander-in-Chief Liú Chāo (劉超) was defeated at Lùguǎnghé (陸廣河).
In the second month, on the *yǐyǒu* day,
posthumous honors and stipends were granted to Mèng Chéngguāng (孟承光), the Scholar who died in Zōuxiàn (鄒縣), his mother Kǒng (孔) clan,
and his son Hónglüè (弘略).
In this month,
the presentation of fresh produce from Nánjīng (南京) was suspended.
In the third month, on the *guǐmǎo* day,
Joseon deposed its ruler, Lǐ Hún (李琿).
In this spring,
relief was provided to the prefectures and counties in Shāndōng (山東) that had suffered from military conflict.
In summer, in the fourth month, on the first day, *gēngshēn*,
there was an earthquake in the capital.
On the *jǐsì* day,
Zhū Guózuò (朱國祚) retired from office.
In the fifth month, on the *xīnchǒu* day,
Sichuan (四川) government troops defeated the rebels at Yǒngníng (永寧);
Shē Chóngmíng (奢崇明) fled to Hóngyá (紅崖).
In autumn, in the seventh month, on the *xīnmǎo* day,
there was a disaster in the Nánjīng (南京) imperial palace.
On the *rénchén* day,
Shē Chóngmíng (奢崇明) fled to Lóngchǎng (龍場),
and joined Ān Bāngyàn (安邦彥).
On the *dīngyǒu* day,
Annam (安南) raided Guǎngxī (廣西);
Hé Shìjìn (何士晉), the Grand Coordinator and Censor-in-Chief, repelled them.
On the *jǐhài* day,
Shǐ Jìxié (史繼偕) retired from office.
In the ninth month, on the *guǐsì* day,
Chén Liángxùn (陳良訓), a Supervising Censor, submitted a memorial outlining four matters for preventing hidden dangers,
and was sent to the prison of the Zhnfǔsī (鎮撫司).
In winter, in the tenth month, on the *yǐhài* day,
there was an earthquake in the capital.
On the *dīngchǒu* day,
executions were suspended.
In the intercalary month, on the *rénnǐ* day,
because of the birth of an imperial prince,
an imperial edict pardoned the empire.
In this month,
Wáng Sānshàn (王三善) suppressed Shuǐxī (水西),
repeatedly defeating the rebels,
and reached Dàfāng (大方).
In the eleventh month, on the first day, *dīngsì*,
sacrifices were offered to Heaven in the southern suburbs.
In the twelfth month, on the *guǐsì* day,
Lǐ Zōng (李倧) was enfeoffed as King of Joseon (朝鮮).
On the *wùxū* day,
there was an earthquake in the capital.
On the *gēngxū* day,
Wèi Zhōngxián (魏忠賢) was appointed Grand Director of the Eastern Depot.
In this year,
Siam and Ryūkyū offered tribute.
In the fourth year, in spring, in the first month, on the first day, *bǐngchén*,
Wú Yěqiáo (吳野樵), a commoner from Chángxīng (長興), killed the County Magistrate Shí Yǒuhéng (石有恆) and the Chief Clerk Xú Kěxíng (徐可行),
and was soon executed.
On the *yǐchǒu* day,
Wáng Sānshàn (王三善), returning from Dàfāng (大方), encountered an ambush,
was captured and died,
and all the officers and generals also died.
On the *gēngwǔ* day,
Hé Zōngyàn (何宗彥) died.
In the second month, on the *dīngyǒu* day,
there were earthquakes in Jìzhōu (薊州), Yǒngpíng (永平), and Shānhǎiguān (山海關),
damaging city walls and houses.
On the *jiǎyín* day,
there was an earthquake in the capital;
palaces shook and made sounds.
The Emperor was unwell.
In the third month, on the *dīngsì* day,
his illness improved.
On the *gēngshēn* day,
there was a military mutiny in Hángzhōu (杭州).
In this month,
there were repeated earthquakes in the capital.
In summer, in the fifth month, on the first day, *jiǎyín*,
there was a military mutiny in Fúníng (福寧);
the officials pacified it.
In the sixth month, on the *guǐwèi* day,
Yáng Lián (楊漣), Left Vice Censor-in-Chief, impeached Wèi Zhōngxián (魏忠賢) on twenty-four major charges.
Southern and northern officials who criticized Zhōngxián (忠賢) followed one after another,
but none were accepted.
On the *bǐngshēn* day,
there was heavy rain and hail.
Wàn Zǎo (萬燝), a Bureau Director in the Ministry of Works, was beaten to death with a staff;
Censor Lín Rǔzhù (林汝翥) was arrested and beaten with a staff.
In autumn, in the seventh month, on the *xīnyǒu* day,
Yè Xiànggāo (葉向高) retired from office.
On the *guǐhài* day,
the Yellow River burst its banks at Xúzhōu (徐州).
Relief was provided to the famine-stricken areas of Shāndōng (山東).
In winter, in the tenth month,
Chén Yútíng (陳于廷), Vice Minister of Personnel, Yáng Lián (楊漣), Vice Censor-in-Chief, and Zuǒ Guāngdòu (左光斗), Investigating Censor, were stripped of their official registers.
In the eleventh month, on the *jǐsì* day,
Hán Kuàng (韓爌) retired from office.
In this month,
Guìzhōu (貴州) government troops defeated the rebels at Pǔdìng (普定),
advanced to Zhījīn (織金),
and conquered it.
In the twelfth month, on the *xīnsì* day,
Wāng Wényán (汪文言), a Secretary of the Grand Secretariat, was arrested and sent to the prison of the Zhnfǔsī (鎮撫司).
On the *bǐngshēn* day,
Zhū Guózhēn (朱國zhēn) retired from office.
On the *guǐmǎo* day,
there was an earthquake in Nánjīng (南京), like thunder.
In this month,
the people of Liǎngdāng (兩當) rebelled,
killing the County Magistrate Niú Déyòng (牛得用).
In the fifth year, in spring, in the first month, on the *guǐhài* day,
the Later Jīn (大清) troops took Lüshùn (旅順).
On the *wùyín* day,
because the construction of Qìnglíng (慶陵) was completed,
Wèi Zhōngxián (魏忠賢) and others were granted hereditary official positions and rewards.
In this month,
Superintendent Lǔ Qīn (魯欽) and Liú Chāo (劉 Chāo) and others, returning from Zhījīn (織金),
were ambushed by the rebels,
and all the troops in the camps were routed.
In the third month, on the *jiǎyín* day,
a ceremony was held for the veneration of Confucius (孔子), the forebear of teachers.
On the *bǐngyín* day,
Yú Huáng (余煌) and others were granted the *jìnshì* (進士) degree, with varying ranks.
On the *jiǎxū* day,
Zhū Xièyuán (朱燮元) was appointed Governor-General of military affairs for Yúnnán (雲南), Guìzhōu (貴州), Sìchuān (四川), Húguǎng (湖廣), and Guǎngxī (廣西),
to suppress Ān Bāngyàn (安邦彥).
On the *dīngchǒu* day,
Wāng Wényán's (汪文言) case was tried,
and Yáng Lián (楊漣), Zuǒ Guāngdòu (左光斗), Yuán Huàzhōng (袁化中), Wèi Dàzhōng (魏大中), Zhōu Cháoruì (周朝瑞), and Gù Dàzhāng (顧大章) were arrested;
Zhào Nánxīng (趙南星), Minister of Personnel, and others were stripped of their official registers.
Soon after,
Lián (漣) and others were arrested and brought
to the prison of the Zhnfǔsī (鎮撫司),
and successively died in prison.
In summer, in the fourth month, on the *jǐhài* day,
Liú Yīzhǔ (劉一燝), Grand Secretary, was stripped of his official register.
In the fifth month, on the *guǐhài* day,
Yáng Suǒxiū (楊所修), a Supervising Censor, requested that
the "Staff Attack" (*Tǐngjí*) (梃擊),
the "Red Pill" (*Hóngwán*) (紅丸),
and the "Palace Relocation" (*Yígōng*) (移宮)
three cases be compiled into a book;
this was approved.
On the *yǐchǒu* day,
sacrifices were offered to Earth in the northern suburbs.
On the *gēngwǔ* day,
the law limiting the salaries of imperial clan members was implemented.
In the sixth month, on the *bǐngxū* day,
Zhū Yánxǐ (朱延禧) retired from office.
In the seventh month of autumn, on the day of Rénxū,
Shǒushàn Shūyuàn was destroyed.
On the day of Rénshēn,
Hán Kuàng was stripped of his status.
On the day of Jiǎxū,
the three Imperial Inspections of the Wànlì reign in the years Xīnhài, Dīngsì, and Guǐhài were retroactively criticized,
and Grand Secretaries Lǐ Sāncái and Gù Xiànchéng, among others, were stripped of their status.
In the eighth month, on the day of Rénwǔ,
Dōnglín academies for lecturing and study throughout the realm were destroyed.
Grand Secretary Sūn Shènxíng and others were stripped of their status.
On the day of Wùzǐ,
Zhōu Rúpán, Minister of Rites, was concurrently appointed Grand Secretary of the Dōnggé Pavilion.
Vice Ministers Dīng Shàoshì and Huáng Lìjí became Ministers of Rites.
Féng Quán, Junior Supervisor of the Imperial Household, became Vice Minister of Rites (Right).
All were concurrently appointed Grand Secretaries of the Dōnggé Pavilion,
and participated in military affairs.
On the day of Jǐhài,
Wèi Guǎngwēi was dismissed.
On the day of Rényín,
Xióng Tíngbì was executed in the marketplace,
and his head was sent to the Nine Frontiers.
In the ninth month, on the day of Rénzǐ,
Lǔ Zhījiǎ, Vice Regional Commander of Liáodōng, was defeated and killed at Liǔhé.
In the tenth month of winter, on the day of Jǐmǎo,
Gāo Dì, Minister of War, was appointed Grand Coordinator of military affairs for Liáo, Jì, Dēng, Lái, and Tiānjīn.
On the day of Bǐngxū,
executions were suspended.
On the day of Gēngyín,
Sūn Chéngzōng retired.
On the day of Bǐngshēn,
Wú Huáixián, an Imperial Secretary, was arrested and imprisoned in the Zhènfǔsī prison,
and beaten to death.
On the day of Gēngzǐ,
due to the birth of an imperial prince,
an imperial edict pardoned the realm.
In the eleventh month, on the day of Rénzǐ,
Zhōu Rúpán retired.
In the twelfth month, on the day of Yǐyǒu,
a list of Dōnglín faction members' names was posted,
and promulgated throughout the realm.
On the day of Wùzǐ,
former Grand Secretary Zhào Nánxīng was banished to the frontier.
In this year,
Liúqiú and Wūsīzàng paid tribute.
In the first month of spring of the sixth year, on the day of Wùwǔ,
the "Sāncháo Yàodiǎn" was compiled.
On the day of Dīngmǎo,
the Dà Qīng army besieged Níngyuǎn.
Commander-in-Chief Mǎn Guì and Níngqián Circuit Surveillance Commissioner Yuán Chónghuàn held out firmly.
On the day of Jǐsì,
the siege was lifted.
In the second month, on the day of Yǐhài,
Yuán Chónghuàn was appointed Assistant Censor-in-Chief,
exclusively in charge of military affairs,
and remained stationed at Níngyuǎn.
On the day of Wùxū,
following a memorial from Lǐ Shí, the eunuch in charge of weaving in Sūzhōu and Hángzhōu,
former Governor of Yìngtiān Zhōu Qǐyuán,
Chief Secretary of the Ministry of Personnel Zhōu Shùnchāng,
Left Censor-in-Chief Gāo Pānlóng,
Imperial Tutor Miào Chāngqī,
and Censors Lǐ Yìngshēng, Zhōu Zōngjiàn, and Huáng Zūnsu were arrested.
Gāo Pānlóng drowned himself.
Zhōu Qǐyuán and the others were imprisoned in the Zhènfǔsī prison,
and successively died in prison.
On the day of Jǐhài,
a sacrifice to the sun was held in the eastern suburbs.
In the third month, on the day of Dīngwèi,
eunuchs were appointed as army supervisors in various border garrisons.
Eunuch Liú Yìngkūn was stationed as defender of Shānhǎiguān.
Grand Secretary Dīng Shàoshì, Minister of War Wáng Yǒngguāng, and others repeatedly admonished against this but were not heeded.
For the merit of lifting the siege of Níngyuǎn,
Wèi Liángqīng, Wèi Zhōngxián's nephew, was enfeoffed as Earl of Sùníng.
On the day of Gēngxū,
Ān Bāngyàn attacked Guìzhōu.
The government army was defeated,
and Commander-in-Chief Lǔ Qīn died.
On the day of Rénzǐ,
Yuán Chónghuàn was appointed Governor of Liáodōng and Shānhǎi.
In the fourth month of summer, on the day of Dīngchǒu,

The eulogy states: After Shìzōng,
the Ming dynasty's administration daily declined,
and by the late years of Shénzōng,
it was utterly ruined.
Even a resolute and sagacious, heroic and martial ruler

But in addition, the Emperor was mediocre and weak,
women and eunuchs usurped power,
rewards and punishments were indiscriminately applied,
loyal and good officials suffered tragic fates,
and the myriad people became disaffected.
Though one might wish it not to perish,
how could it have been otherwise?

"If all officials truly applied themselves to their duties,
why would I need such people?"
On the day *jǐhài*,
the bandit Luó Rǔcái attacked Shānxī.
In the intercalary month, on the day *yǐchǒu*,
the surrendered bandits in Shǎnxī rebelled again,
capturing Gānquán
and killing Assistant Minister Zhāng Yǔndēng.
On the day *dīngmǎo*,
Dēngzhōu Mobile Corps Commander Kǒng Yǒudé led his troops to reinforce Liáo,
but mutinied at Wúqiáo,
capturing Língxiàn,
and successively capturing Línyì, Shānghé, and Qídōng,
and massacring Xīnchéng.
In the twelfth month, on the day *bǐngzǐ*,
the government troops from Jǐnán engaged the bandits at Ruǎnchéngdiàn,
and were defeated.
On the day *dīngchǒu*,
on the grounds that the construction of Dàlíng city provoked trouble,
Sūn Chéngzōng was stripped of his office.
That winter,
there was heavy snow in Yán'ān and Qìngyáng,
the people suffered from famine,
and banditry became even more rampant.
In the fifth year, in spring, in the first month, on the day *xīnchǒu*,
Kǒng Yǒudé captured Dēngzhōu,
Mobile Corps Commander Chén Liángmó died in battle,
and Commander-in-Chief Zhāng Kědà also died.
Governor-General Sūn Yuánhuà, Vice Envoy Sòng Guānglán, and others were captured,
and later released.
On the day *xīnhài*,
Kǒng Yǒudé captured Huángxiàn.
On the day *bǐngyín*,
Commanders-in-Chief Yáng Yùfán and Wáng Hóng led troops to suppress Kǒng Yǒudé,
and were defeated at Xīnchéngzhèn.
In the second month, on the day *jǐsì* (the first day of the month),
Kǒng Yǒudé besieged Láizhōu,
but Governor-General Xú Cóngzhì held his ground firmly.
On the day *xīnsì*,
Kǒng Yǒudé captured Píngdù.
In the third month, on the day *rényín*,
Vice Minister of War Liú Yǔliè was appointed to oversee military affairs in Shāndōng
to suppress Kǒng Yǒudé.
In summer, in the fourth month, on the day *jiǎxū*,
Liú Yǔliè was defeated at Shāhé.
On the day *guǐwèi*,
Xú Cóngzhì died from injuries.
That month,
Commanders-in-Chief Cáo Wénzhào and Yáng Jiāmó repeatedly defeated the bandits at Lǒng'ān and Jìngníng,
whereupon the bandits fled to Shuǐluòchéng,
and hungry people from Píngliáng and Zhuānglàng joined them,
and their power grew again.
In the fifth month, on the day *bǐngwǔ*,
Assistant Minister Zhū Dàdiǎn was appointed Censor-in-Chief,
and Governor of Shāndōng.
On the day *xīnhài*,
Minister of Rites Zhèng Yǐwěi and Xú Guāngqǐ were both concurrently appointed Grand Secretaries of the Dōnggé,
participating in military and political affairs.
In the sixth month,
the capital suffered heavy rain and floods.
On the day *rénshēn*,
the Yellow River burst its banks at Mèngjīn.
In autumn, in the seventh month, on the day *xīnchǒu*,
Eunuch Cáo Huàchún was appointed Director-General of military administration in the capital's camps.
On the day *guǐmǎo*,
Kǒng Yǒudé feigned surrender,
and enticed and captured Dēnglái Governor-General Xiè Lián;
Láizhōu Prefect Zhū Wànnián died.
On the day *jǐwèi*,
Sūn Yuánhuà was executed in the marketplace.
Liú Yǔliè was arrested and imprisoned,
and sentenced to frontier exile.
In the eighth month, on the day *jiǎxū*,
Hóng Chéngchóu defeated the bandits at Gānquán,
and bandit leader Bái Guǎng'ēn surrendered.
On the day *jiǎshēn*,
Zhū Dàdiǎn led troops to relieve Láizhōu,
and Vanguard Colonel Zǔ Kuān defeated the bandits at Shāhé.
On the day *yǐyǒu*,
the siege of Láizhōu was lifted.
On the day *guǐsì*,
the government troops decisively defeated Kǒng Yǒudé at Huángxiàn,
and then besieged Dēngzhōu.
In the ninth month, on the day *dīngyǒu*,
the sea pirate Liú Xiāng raided Fújiàn.
That autumn,
bandits from Shǎnxī entered Shānxī,
successively capturing Dàníng, Zézhōu, and Shòuyáng,
then branched out to Héběi,
attacked Huáiqìng,
and captured Xiūwǔ.
In winter, in the eleventh month, on the day *wùxū*,
Liú Xiāng raided Zhèjiāng.
In the sixth year, in spring, in the first month, on the day *guǐmǎo*,
Cáo Wénzhào was given command over the generals of Shān and Shǎn to suppress the bandits.
On the day *dīngwèi*,
Vice General Zuǒ Liángyù defeated the bandits at Shèxiàn,
whereupon the bandits fled into the mountains of Línxiàn,
and starving people eagerly joined them.
On the day *gēngshēn*,
envoys were dispatched to supervise the collection of overdue taxes in the capital province and other provinces.
That month,
Cáo Wénzhào attacked the Shānxī bandits
and repeatedly defeated them.
In the second month, on the day *rénshēn*,
Wang Zhìdào, the Left Vice Censor-in-Chief, was stripped of his official status.
On the day *guǐyǒu*,
roving bandits attacked Jīnán.
On the day *wùzǐ*,
Commander-in-Chief Chén Hóngfàn and others captured the water city of Dēngzhōu.
On the day *xīnmǎo*,
Kǒng Yǒudé fled by sea,
and Shāndōng was pacified.
In the third month, on the day *guǐsì*,
an imperial edict ordered Cáo Wénzhào and other generals to pacify the bandits within three months.
In summer, in the fourth month, on the day *jǐsì*,
the old and new Liaodong taxes in Yán'ān, Qìngyáng, and Píngliáng were remitted.
On the day *rénshēn*,
Commanders-in-Chief Dèng [?] and Zuǒ Liángyù suppressed the Hénán bandits.
In the fifth month, on the day *yǐsì*,
Eunuch Chén Dàjīn and others were assigned to supervise the armies of Cáo Wénzhào, Zhāng Yìngchāng, Zuǒ Liángyù, and Dèng [?].
On the day *rénzǐ*,
Kǒng Yǒudé and his associates Gěng Zhòngmíng and others sailed across the sea and surrendered to our Great Qīng.
On the day *guǐchǒu*,
the Hétáo tribes attacked Níngxià,
and Commander-in-Chief Hè Hǔchén died in battle.
In the sixth month, on the day *xīnyǒu* (the first day of the month),
Eunuch Gāo Qǐqián was assigned to supervise military provisions in Níng and Jǐn.
On the day *yǐchǒu*,
Zhèng Yǐwěi died.
On the day *gēngchén*,
Zhōu Yánrú retired from office.
On the day *jiǎshēn*,
Yánsuī Vice General Lǐ Bēi was sent to reinforce the suppression in Hénán.
On the day *gēngyín*,
Eunuch Zhāng Yíxiàn requested to press for the collection of over 17 million units of overdue taxes;
Investigating Censor Fàn Shútài remonstrated,
but his advice was not taken.
In autumn, in the seventh month, on the day *jiǎchén*,
the Great Qīng army captured Lǚshùn,
and Commander-in-Chief Huáng Lóng died.
On the day *guǐchǒu*,
Cáo Wénzhào was transferred to garrison Dàtóng;
Shānxī Governor-General Xǔ Dǐngchén requested to retain Cáo Wénzhào to suppress the bandits,
but was not permitted.
In the eighth month, on the day *jǐsì*,
Cáo Wénzhào defeated the bandits at Jìyuán,
and again defeated them at Huáiqìng.
In the ninth month, on the day *gēngxū*,
Nánjīng Vice Minister of Rites Qián Shìshēng was appointed Minister of Rites and concurrently Grand Secretary of the Dōnggé,
participating in military and political affairs.
In winter, in the tenth month, on the day *wùchén*,
Xú Guāngqǐ died.
In the eleventh month, on the day *guǐsì*,
Vice Ministers of Rites Wáng Yìngxióng and Hé Wúzhōu were both appointed Minister of Rites and concurrently Grand Secretaries of the Dōnggé,
participating in military and political affairs.
On the day *xīnhài*,
an imperial edict ordered Bǎodìng, Hénán, and Shānxī to unite their forces to suppress the bandits.
On the day *rénzǐ*,
the bandits crossed the Yellow River.
On the day *yǐmǎo*,
they captured Miǎnchí.
In the twelfth month,
they successively captured Yīyáng and Lúshì,
then branched out to attack Nányáng and Rǔníng,
and then pressed towards Húguǎng.
That year,
Ānnán offered tribute.
In the seventh year, spring, first month, on the *jǐchǒu* day,
Shàng Kěxǐ (尚可喜), the vice-general of Guǎnggù Dǎo (廣鹿島), surrendered to Our Great Qīng (大清).
A Grand Coordinator (Zǒngdū) was established for the five provinces of Hénán (河南), Shān (山), Shǎn (陝), Chuān (川), and Hú (湖).
Chén Qíyú (陳奇瑜), the Pacification Commissioner (Xúnfǔ) of Yánsuí (延綏), concurrently served as Vice Minister of War (Bīngbù Shìláng) for this role.
On the *gēngyín* day,
Grand General (Zǒngbīngguān) Zhāng Yìngchāng (張應昌) crossed the river
and defeated the rebels at Língbǎo (靈寶).
On the *rénchén* day,
the rebels crossed the Hàn (漢) River from Yún Yáng (鄖陽).
On the *guǐsì* day,
they attacked Xiāngyáng (襄陽),
then successively captured Zǐyáng (紫陽), Pínglì (平利), and Báihé (白河),
and entered Sìchuān (四川) to the south.
In the second month, on the *wùyín* day,
Kuízhōu (夔州) was captured,
and all the counties of Dàníng (大寧) were lost.
On the *jiǎshēn* day,
the ceremonial plowing of the emperor's field (jìtián) was performed.
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
Zhāng Xiànzhōng (張獻忠) unexpectedly attacked Shāng (商) and Luò (雒),
and all thirteen camps flowed into Hànnán (漢南).
In this month,
famine relief was provided in Dēng (登) and Lái (萊),
and overdue taxes were remitted.
In the third month, on the *dīnghài* day (the first day of the month),
there was a solar eclipse.
On the *jiǎchén* day,
Liú Lǐshùn (劉理順) and others were granted the titles of *jìnshì jízhì* (進士及第) and *chūshēn* (出身) with various distinctions.
On the *yǐsì* day,
Zhāng Yìngchāng (張應昌) engaged the rebels at Wǔlíng Shān (五嶺山),
and suffered a defeat.
On the *gēngxū* day,
the rebels fled from Sìchuān (四川) to Húguǎng (湖廣),
and Vice-General Yáng Shì'ēn (楊世恩) pursued and defeated them at Shíhékǒu (石河口).
From the previous year until this month, there had been no rain in Shānxī (山西),
and the people suffered a great famine.
Summer, fourth month,
the rebels fled from Húguǎng (湖廣) to Lúshì (盧氏) and Língbǎo (靈寶).
On the *guǐyǒu* day,
funds from the imperial treasury were disbursed for famine relief in Shǎnxī (陝西) and Shānxī (山西).
Fifth month, on the *bǐngshēn* day,
Vice-General Hè Rénlóng (賀人龍) and others defeated the rebels at Lántián (藍田).
Sixth month, on the *xīnwèi* day,

Grand Coordinator (Zǒngdū) and Vice Minister (Shìláng) Chén Qíyú (陳奇瑜), and Pacification Commissioner (Fǔzhì) and Censor-in-Chief (Dūyùshǐ) of Yún Yáng (鄖陽) Lú Xiàngshēng (盧象昇) joined forces at Shàngjīn (上津)
to suppress the Húguǎng (湖廣) rebels.
On the *jiǎxū* day,
the river burst its banks at Pèixiàn (沛縣).
In this summer,
the government army besieged rebels Gāo Yíngxiáng (高迎祥) and Lǐ Zìchéng (李自成) at Chēxiāng Xiá (車箱峽) in Xīng'ān (興安) for two months.
The rebels ran out of food
and feigned surrender.
Chén Qíyú (陳奇瑜) accepted it
and allowed them to escape the perilous pass.
They rebelled again
and captured the prefectures and counties they passed through.
Zhāng Yìngchāng (張應昌) pursued the rebels from Qīngshuǐ (清水),
and suffered a defeat.
Autumn, seventh month, on the *rénchén* day,
the Great Qīng (大清) army entered Shàngfāngbǎo (上方堡)
and reached Xuānfǔ (宣府).
On the *yǐwèi* day,
an imperial edict ordered Grand General (Zǒngbīngguān) Chén Hóngfàn (陳洪範) to guard Jūyōng (居庸),
and Pacification Commissioner (Xúnfǔ) of Bǎodìng (保定) and Censor-in-Chief (Dūyùshǐ) Dīng Kuíchǔ (丁魁楚) and others to guard Zǐjīng (紫荊) and Yànmén (雁門).
On the *xīnchǒu* day,
the capital was placed under strict alert.
On the *gēngxū* day,
the Great Qīng (大清) army captured Bǎo'ān (保安),
and many fortresses along the border were lost.
Eighth month,
Grand General (Zǒngbīngguān) Yóu Shìwēi (尤世威) and others were dispatched to reinforce the border.
On the *wùchén* day,
the Grand Coordinator (Zǒngdū) and Vice Minister (Shìláng) of Xuāndà (宣大), Zhāng Zōnghéng (張宗衡), was given command over the reinforcing troops from various garrisons.
Leap month, on the *jiǎshēn* day,
the rebels captured Lóngdé (隆德) and Gùyuán (固原),
and Councillor (Cānyì) Lù Mènglóng (陸夢龍) went to reinforce them
but was defeated and killed.
On the *dīnghài* day,
the Great Qīng (大清) army captured Wànquán Zuǒwèi (萬全左衞).
On the *gēngyín* day,
they returned to their garrisons and left the frontier.
On the *rényín* day,
Lǐ Zìchéng (李自成) besieged Hè Rénlóng (賀人龍) at Lǒngzhōu (隴州).
Ninth month, on the *gēngshēn* day,
the armor factory suffered a fire.
〔一０〕On the *gēngchén* day,
Hóng Chéngchóu (洪承疇) lifted the siege of Lǒngzhōu (隴zhou).
On the *jiǎxū* day,
because the rebels were concentrated in Shǎnxī (陝西),
an edict ordered Hénán (河南) troops to enter Tóng (潼) and Huá (華),
Húguǎng (湖廣) troops to enter Shāng (商) and Luò (雒),
Sìchuān (四川) troops via Xīng (興) and Hàn (漢),
and Shānxī (山西) troops to exit Púzhōu (蒲州) and Hánchéng (韓城),
to converge and suppress them.
Winter, tenth month, on the *gēngxū* day,
Húguǎng (湖廣) troops reinforced Hànzhōng (漢中),
and Vice-General Yáng Zhèngfāng (楊正芳) died in battle.
Eleventh month, on the *gēngchén* day,
Chén Qíyú (陳奇瑜) was arrested and imprisoned,
and sentenced to exile.
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
Hóng Chéngchóu (洪承疇) concurrently took charge of military affairs in the five provinces.
In this winter,
the Shǎnxī (陝西) rebels divided and attacked Húguǎng (湖廣) and Hénán (河南),
and Lǐ Zìchéng (李自成) captured Chénzhōu (陳州).
In this year,
Xiāmluó (暹羅) paid tribute.
In the eighth year, spring, first month, on the *yǐmǎo* day,
the rebels captured Shàngcài (上蔡),
then successively captured Sìshuǐ (汜水), Xíngyáng (滎陽), and Gùshǐ (固始).
On the *jǐwèi* day,
Hóng Chéngchóu (洪 Chéngchóu) exited the pass to suppress the rebels.
On the *xīnyǒu* day,
Zhāng Xiànzhōng (張獻忠) captured Yǐngzhōu (潁州).
On the *bǐngyín* day,
Fèngyáng (鳳陽) was captured,
and the imperial mausoleum's halls and pavilions were burned.
The Resident Official (Liúshǒu) Zhū Guóxiāng (朱國xiang) and others died in battle.
On the *rénshēn* day,
reinforcements from Xúzhōu (徐州) arrived at Fèngyáng (鳳陽).
Zhāng Xiànzhōng (張獻忠) attacked Lúzhōu (廬州),
and soon captured Lújiāng (廬江) and Wúwéi (無為).
Lǐ Zìchéng (李 Zìchéng) fled to Guīdé (歸德),
and with Luó Rǔcái (羅汝才), re-entered Shǎnxī (陝西).
Second month,
Zhāng Xiànzhōng (張獻忠) captured Qiánshān (潛山), Luótián (羅田), Tàihú (太湖), and Xīncài (新蔡),
but the Pacification Commissioner (Xúnfǔ) of Yìngtiān (應天) and Censor-in-Chief (Dūyùshǐ) Zhāng Guówéi (張國維) repelled him.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
due to the loss of the imperial mausoleum,
Grand Coordinator (Zǒngdū) of Canal Transport (Cáoyùn) and Minister (Shàngshū) Yáng Yīpéng (楊一鵬) was arrested and imprisoned,
and soon executed in the marketplace.
On the *dīngyǒu* day,
Grand General (Zǒngbīngguān) Dèng (鄧) defeated the rebels at Luóshān (羅山).
In this month,
Cáo Wénzhào (曹文詔) defeated the rebels at Suízhōu (隨州).
〔一一〕
Summer, fourth month,
Zhāng Xiànzhōng (張獻忠) again fled to Hànzhōng (漢中),
and attacked Píngliáng (平涼) and Fèngxiáng (鳳翔).
On the *dīnghài* day,
Zhèng Zhīlóng (鄭芝龍) defeated the sea pirate Liú Xiāng (劉香),
Xiāng (香) committed suicide,
and his followers all surrendered.
On the *xīnmǎo* day,
Hóng Chéngchóu (洪承疇) assembled his forces at Rǔzhōu (汝州),
and divided his generals to defend strategic points in Yù (豫) and Chǔ (楚).
On the *yǐsì* day,
the Sìchuān (四川) soldiers mutinied at Fánchéng (樊城),
〔一二〕and Dèng (鄧) committed suicide.
On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
Hóng Chéngchóu (洪承疇) returned west
and stationed his troops at Língbǎo (靈寶).
Fifth month, on the *yǐhài* day,
Wú Zōngdá (吳宗達) retired from office.
Sixth month, on the *jǐchǒu* day,
the government army encountered the rebels at Luànmǎ Chuān (亂馬川),
and suffered a defeat.
On the *rénchén* day,
Vice-Generals Ài Wànnián (艾萬年) and Liǔ Guózhèn (柳國鎮) attacked Lǐ Zìchéng (李 Zìchéng) at Xiānglè (襄樂) in Níngzhōu (寧州),
〔一三〕and were killed in battle.
On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
Cáo Wénzhào (曹文詔) pursued the rebels to Qiūtóu Zhèn (湫頭鎮) in Zhēnníng (真寧),
encountered an ambush,
fought valiantly, and died.
Autumn, seventh month, on the *jiǎxū* day,

Junior Supervisor (Shǎozhànshì) Wén Zhènmèng (文震孟) and Vice Minister of Justice (Xíngbù Shìláng) Zhāng Zhìfā (張至發) both became Vice Ministers of Rites (Lǐbù Shìláng) and concurrently Grand Academicians of the Dōnggé (東閣大學士),
participating in state affairs.
In this month,
Zhāng Xiànzhōng (張獻忠) unexpectedly attacked Zhūyáng Guān (朱陽關),
Grand General (Zǒngbīngguān) Yóu Shìwēi (尤世威) was defeated,
and the rebels again fled to Hénán (河南).
Eighth month,
Lǐ Zìchéng (李 Zìchéng) captured Xiányáng (咸陽),
and rebel general Gāo Jié (高傑) surrendered.
On the *rénchén* day,
an imperial edict ordered the撤撤of supervising eunuchs,
〔一四〕except for those in the imperial garrisons (Jīngyíng) and at Guān (關) and Níng (寧).
On the *xīnchǒu* day,
Lú Xiàngshēng (盧象昇) was made General Administrator of military affairs in Zhílì (直隸), Hénán (河南), Shāndōng (山東), Húguǎng (湖廣), and Sìchuān (四川).
Ninth month, on the *xīnhài* day,
Hóng Chéngchóu (洪承疇) led Vice-General Cáo Biànjiāo (曹變蛟) and others to defeat the rebels at Guānshān Zhèn (關山鎮).
Lǐ Zìchéng (李 Zìchéng) fled east
and joined with Zhāng Xiànzhōng (張獻忠).
On the *rénxū* day,
the government army was defeated at Wǎdiàn (瓦店) in Shěnqiū (沈丘),
and Grand General (Zǒngbīngguān) Zhāng Quánchāng (張全昌) was captured.
On the *rénshēn* day,
Wáng Yìngxióng (王應熊) retired from office.
In winter, in the tenth month, on the *gēngchén* day,
an imperial edict was issued, blaming himself.
He retired to the Wǔyīng Diàn,
reduced his meals, stopped the music,
showing that he would share hardships with his generals and soldiers.
On the *bǐngxū* day,
Hùbù Shàngshū Hóu Xún requested strict collection of old and new outstanding taxes.
This was approved.
On the *xīnmǎo* day,
Lǐ Zìchéng captured Shǎnzhōu.
In the eleventh month, on the *gēngxū* day,
Hé Wúzóu and Wén Zhènmèng were dismissed.
On the *gēngshēn* day,
sacrifices were offered to Heaven in the southern suburbs.
Zǒngbīngguān Zǔ Kuān defeated the bandits in Rǔzhōu.
In the twelfth month, on the *wùyín* day,
Fèngyáng was fortified.
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
Lú Xiàngshēng and Zǔ Kuān defeated Lǐ Zìchéng at Quèshān.
On the *wùzǐ* day,
Zuǒ Liángyù defeated the bandits at Wénxiāng.
On the *guǐsì* day,
the bandits attacked Jiāngběi,
and besieged Chúzhōu.
On the *yǐsì* day,
Lǎo Huíhuí and other bandits attacked Shǎnxī from Hénán.
Hóng Chéngchóu defeated them at Líntóng.
In this year,
Ānnán, Xiāmluó, and Liúqiú paid tribute.
In the ninth year, in spring, in the first month, on the *jiǎyín* day,
Zǒnglǐ Shìláng Lú Xiàngshēng and Zǔ Kuān relieved Chúzhōu,
and greatly defeated the bandits at Zhūlóngqiáo.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
former Lǐbù Shìláng Lín Hàn was appointed Dōnggé Dàxuéshì concurrently with his original official post,
participating in state affairs.
In the second month,

In summer, in the fourth month, on the *wùzǐ* day,

Lǐ Zìchéng attacked Yúlín,

the court officials were instructed to contribute to military expenses.

In this month,

In the eighth month, on the *guǐyǒu* day,

On the *jiǎshēn* day,

On the *bǐngshēn* day,

In the eleventh month, on the *dīngwèi* day,
outstanding taxes from five years ago or earlier in Shāndōng were exempted.

In this year,
Hóng Chéngchóu defeated the bandits at Lǒngzhōu,

In the tenth year, in spring, in the first month, on the *xīnchǒu* day, the first day of the month,

Lǎo Huíhuí and other bandits advanced to Jiāngběi,

In the second month, on the *jiǎxū* day,
envoys were dispatched to supervise the collection of outstanding taxes in the Zhíshěng.
On the *dīngyǒu* day,
the bandits attacked Qiánshān,
Zǒngbīngguān Zuǒ Liángyù and Fùshǐ Shǐ Kěfǎ defeated them at Fēngxiāngyì.

In the third month, on the *xīnhài* day,

On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
the imperial army relieved Ānqìng,

Fù Zǒngbīng Jīn Rìguān fought bravely and died,

On the *guǐsì* day,
there was a drought,

In this month,
Hóng Chéngchóu suppressed the bandits in Hànnán.

Bandits from Jiāngběi divided and attacked Hénán,
Zǒngdū Liǎngguǎng Dūyùshǐ Xióng Wéncàn was appointed Bīngbù Shàngshū,

Lǐ Zìchéng attacked Sìchuān from Qínzhōu.
In the sixth month, on the *wùshēn* day,
Wēn Tǐrén retired.
In this summer,
both Jī and Shānxī suffered a severe drought.
In autumn, in the seventh month,
Shāndōng and Hénán suffered from locusts,

In the eighth month, on the *jǐyǒu* day,
Lìbù Shìláng Liú Yǔliàng and Lǐbù Shìláng Fù Guān were both appointed Lǐbù Shàngshū,
Qiāndū Yùshǐ Xuē Guóguān was appointed Lǐbù Shìláng,
and all concurrently served as Dōnggé Dàxuéshì,
participating in state affairs.
On the *gēngshēn* day,
the city walls were inspected.
In the ninth month, on the *bǐngzǐ* day,
Zuǒ Liángyù defeated the bandits at Hóngxiàn.
On the *xīnmǎo* day,
Hóng Chéngchóu defeated the bandits at Hànzhōng.
On the *guǐsì* day,
Lǐ Zìchéng captured Níngqiáng.
In winter, in the tenth month, on the day Bǐngshēn,
Zìchéng entered Xīchuān from Qīpán Guān.
On the day Rén'yín,
Zhāohuà, Jiànzhōu, and Zǐtóng fell.

On the day Gēngxū,
Chéngdū was threatened.
In the eleventh month, on the day Gēngchén,
due to unusual celestial phenomena, self-reflection and correction were ordered,
and honest counsel was sought.
In the twelfth month, on the day Guǐmǎo,
Huáng Shìjùn retired from office.
Hóng Chéngchóu and Cáo Biànjiāo reinforced Sìchuān,
On the day Guǐhài,
This year,

Collation Notes
Annals, Chapter 24, Zhuāngliè Dì II
In the eleventh year, in spring, in the first month, on the day Dīngchǒu,

redundant officials in Nánjīng were dismissed.

Hè Féngshèng retired from office.
This month,
Lǐ Zìchéng emerged from Táo zhōu into the barbarian lands,

In summer, in the fourth month, on the day Xīnchǒu,

Zhāng Zhìfā retired from office.
On the day Jǐyǒu,
Yínghuò (Mars) moved in retrograde,
and court officials were admonished to reflect and correct themselves.
In the fifth month, on the day Guǐhài, the first day of the month,
officials were tested and selected at Zhōngzuǒmén.
In the sixth month, on the day Guǐsì,
there was a disaster at Ānmín Factory,
damaging the city walls
and injuring over ten thousand people.
On the day Rén'yín,
Kǒng Zhēnyùn retired from office.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
Yáng Sìchāng, Minister of War, Chéng Guóxiáng, Minister of Revenue, Fāng Féngnián, Vice Minister of Rites, and Cài Guóyòng, Vice Minister of Works, were all appointed Minister of Rites.
Fàn Fùcuì, Assistant Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, was appointed Vice Minister of Rites,
and concurrently Grand Secretary of the Dōnggé,
participating in state affairs.
Sìchāng continued to manage the Ministry of War.
This month,
the Two Capital Regions, Shāndōng, and Hénán suffered severe drought and locust plagues.

In the eighth month, on the day Wùxū,
due to repeated appearances of calamities and anomalies,

admonishing court officials to reflect and correct themselves.
On the day Guǐchǒu,
Fù Guān retired from office.

executions were suspended.
Bandit chief Luó Rúcaí and others attacked Xiāngyáng from Shǎnzhōu.

horses were requisitioned.

Hóng Chéngchóu and Cáo Biànjiāo heavily defeated the bandits on the southern plain of Tóngguān,

Luó Rúcaí surrendered.

Fāng Féngnián was dismissed.

This year,
Tǔlǔfān and Liúqiú paid tribute.
In the twelfth year, in spring, in the first month, on the day Jǐwèi, the first day of the month,
due to the many difficulties of the times,
the court officials' congratulations were declined.

In summer, in the fourth month, on the day Wùshēn,

Zuǒ Liángyù attacked and subjugated bandit leader Lǐ Wànqìng.
In the fifth month, on the day Jiǎzǐ,
Yáo Mínggōng and Zhāng Sìzhī, Vice Ministers of Rites,

Sūn Chuántíng was stripped of his status,

In the sixth month,
the Capital Region, Shāndōng, Hénán, and Shānxī suffered drought and locust plagues.
On the day Jǐyǒu,

In autumn, in the seventh month, on the day Rénshēn,

Xióng Wéncàn was stripped of his status,
and soon after arrested and imprisoned.
In the eighth month, on the day Guǐsì,

On the day Jǐhài,

On the day Rénzǐ,
Grand Secretary Yáng Sìchāng was appointed supreme commander to suppress the bandits,

In winter, in the tenth month, on the day Jiǎshēn, the first day of the month,

This year,

sacrifices were offered to the earth in the northern suburbs.

An appraisal says: The Emperor, succeeding Shénzōng and Xīzōng,
had a resolute ambition to achieve something.
At the beginning of his reign,
he showed profound sagacity and independent judgment,
eliminating treacherous and perverse elements.
The empire hoped for peace and order.
Alas, the general situation was already in decline,
and accumulated habits were hard to reverse.
At court, factional disputes abounded.
On the frontiers, generals were arrogant and soldiers lazy.
War and famine were reported from all four directions,
and roving bandits spread.
This eventually led to a complete collapse beyond salvation,
which can be called truly unfortunate.
However, during his seventeen years on the throne,
he did not indulge in pleasures of sight and sound.
He was diligent, vigilant, and earnest,
devoting his heart to governance.
He often sighed profoundly in court,
resolutely wishing to find extraordinary talents,
but he did not employ the right people,
which further exacerbated matters.
Moreover, he again trusted eunuchs,
deploying them in key positions,
his measures were inappropriate,
and his strategies were misguided.
As the dynasty's fate ended and its fortune shifted,
he suffered misfortune and calamity.
How could this not be due to the workings of fate?
By the time the great mandate found its new master,
and the demonic miasma was swept away,
the Emperor received a posthumous title and his mausoleum was established,
with generous rites.
This shows that the sagacious dynasty's supreme virtue surpasses a thousand ages,
and it also makes it known that the Emperor, though he suffered misfortune, did not disgrace himself,
and was a righteous and heroic figure of a fallen nation.

historians of successive dynasties have all made records of astronomy.
However, the history of Liáo (遼史) alone did not,
stating that celestial phenomena are manifest and enduring,
unchanging through a thousand ages.
Since solar eclipses and celestial anomalies were already recorded in the Basic Annals (Běnjì 本紀),
the Astronomical Monograph (Tiānwén Zhì 天文志) was deemed almost superfluous.
This argument is quite sound.
As for works like *Zhōubì* (周髀) and *Xuānyè* (宣夜),
the theories of Ān Tiān (安天), Qióng Tiān (窮天), and Xīn Tiān (昕天),
and the prognostication theories of the star officials,
they were already detailed in the *Jìn Shǐ* (晉史)
and also appeared in the *Suí Zhì* (隋志).
How can one say they are not superfluous?
Critics argue that the Astronomical Monograph (Tiānwén Zhì 天文志) of *Jìn* (晉) and *Suí* (隋) is considered the foremost,
yet it still suffers from this flaw;
the others can be imagined.
However, to therefore abolish the recording of astronomy
is also incorrect.
Although celestial phenomena show no difference between ancient and modern times,
the celestial scholars
and astronomical instruments
often improve with time.
Without a way to record them,
the significance of a generation's innovations would be lost and untransmitted,
which is also a defect in historical methodology.
As for comets, meteors,
halos, coronas, and inverted rainbows,
which are celestial warnings,
they cannot all be fully recorded in the Basic Annals (Běnjì 本紀);
how can they not be separately chronicled?
During the reign of Míng Shénzōng (明神宗),
Westerners such as Lì Mǎdòu (利瑪竇) entered China.
They were skilled in astronomy and calendrical calculations,
unveiling obscurities,
and developing calculations and instruments
that had never existed before.
Here, we extract their essentials
and record them in this chapter.
As for the celestial phenomena and star changes recorded in the veritable records (shílù 實錄), they are too numerous to be fully written;
we select the most extraordinary ones to preserve.
Solar eclipses are fully recorded in the Basic Annals (Běnjì 本紀),
therefore they are not repeated here.

Two Primary Forces (Liǎngyí 兩儀)
The *Chǔ Cí* (楚詞) states:
"The circle is ninefold,
who measured and planned it?"
The proponents of the armillary sphere (húntiānjiā 渾天家) say:
"Heaven envelops the Earth like an egg's yolk."
Thus, that Heaven has nine layers
and the Earth is spherical
was already spoken of by the ancients.
The Western theory
neither contradicts the ancients
nor lacks verification from the heavens;
therefore, it is presented here.
Regarding its description of the nine layers of heaven,
it says the uppermost is the Primum Mobile (Zōngdòngtiān 宗動天),
which has no stars.
Every day, it carries the other layers of heaven,
revolving once from east to west in a counter-clockwise direction.
Next is the heaven of Fixed Stars (Lièxiùtiān 列宿天),
then the heaven of Saturn (Tiánxīngtiān 填星天),
then the heaven of Jupiter (Suìxīngtiān 歲星天),
then the heaven of Mars (Yínghuòtiān 熒惑天),
then the heaven of the Sun (Tàiyángtiān 太陽天),
then the heaven of Venus (Jīnxīngtiān 金星天),
then the heaven of Mercury (Shuǐxīngtiān 水星天),
and the lowest is the heaven of the Moon (Tàiyīntiān 太陰天).
From the heaven of stars downwards, the eight layers of heaven
all rotate counter-clockwise with the Primum Mobile (Zōngdòngtiān 宗動天).
However, each heaven also has a degree of clockwise rotation,
from west to east,
which is consistent with the analogy of an ant walking on a millstone.
Although the degree of this clockwise rotation
has changed slightly compared to ancient times,
there is no major difference.
Only the movement of the stars
is the ancient degree of precession.
The ancients said that stars are immutable through a thousand ages,
but the solstices and equinoxes of the ecliptic recede westward each year.
They, however, say that the ecliptic is eternally fixed,
and the stars move eastward each year.
From current observation,
stars indeed move;
their theory is not mistaken.
As for dividing the celestial circumference into 360 degrees,
and assigning 96 *kè* (刻) to a day,
so that each hour gets exactly eight *kè* without fractions,
using this for calculations and instrument making
is very convenient.
Regarding their statement that the Earth is round,
they say the Earth is at the center of the heavens,
its body is spherical,
corresponding to the celestial degrees.
China is north of the equator,
thus the North Pole is always visible,
and the South Pole is always hidden.
Traveling 250 *lǐ* (里) south, the North Pole declines by one degree;
traveling 250 *lǐ* (里) north, the North Pole rises by one degree.
The same applies to east and west.
(Also 250 *lǐ* (里) difference for one degree.)
Calculating by the degrees of the celestial circumference,
the Earth's total circumference is known to be 90,000 *lǐ* (里).
Using the ratio of circumference to diameter,
the Earth's total diameter is found to be 28,647 *lǐ* (里) and 8/9ths of a *lǐ* (里).
Furthermore, north and south latitudes determine the vertical extent of the world.
Wherever the degree of the North Pole above the horizon is the same,
the four seasons and temperatures are identical.
If the degree of the South Pole above the horizon is the same as the degree of the North Pole above the horizon,
then their day and night lengths are identical.
Only the seasons are opposite:
spring here is autumn there,
and summer here is winter there.
East and west longitudes determine the horizontal extent of the world;
if two places are separated by 30 degrees of longitude,
the time difference is one *chén* (辰).
If they are separated by 180 degrees,
then day and night are reversed.
This theory is slightly similar to the spherical Earth concept of Zhámǎlǔdīng (札馬魯丁) in the *Yuán Shǐ* (元史).
Seven Regulators (Qīzhèng 七政)
The Sun, Moon, and five planets each have a layer of heaven;
these heavens are not concentric with the Earth,
thus their distance from Earth varies between high and low.
Their highest and lowest values
are all measured by the Earth's radius.
The Sun's highest distance from Earth is 1,182 times the Earth's radius,
and its lowest is 1,102 times.
The Moon's highest is 58,
and its lowest is 52.
Saturn's highest is 12,932,
and its lowest is 9,175.
Jupiter's highest is 6,190,
and its lowest is 5,919.
Mars's highest is 2,998,
and its lowest is 222.
Venus's highest is 1,985,
and its lowest is 300.
Mercury's highest is 1,659,
and its lowest is 625.
If one wishes to obtain the distance in *lǐ* (里) of the Seven Regulators (Qīzhèng 七政) from Earth,
then multiply by the Earth's radius of 12,324 *lǐ* (里).
It also states that Saturn is shaped like a melon,
with two small stars like ears on its sides.
Jupiter has four small stars around it,
revolving very rapidly.
The light of Venus waxes and wanes,
like the Moon's phases.
Using a telescope,
all can be clearly seen.
Further details are in the Calendrical Monograph (Lì Zhì 曆志).
Stars (Xīng 星)
In the early Chóngzhēn (崇禎) reign,
Xú Guāngqǐ (徐光啟), the Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū 禮部尚書), supervised the revision of the calendar
and presented the comprehensive star map within boundaries.
He believed that the *Huíhuí Lìchéng* (回回立成) only contained 278 stars with ecliptic longitudes and latitudes,
and its star charts only depicted 17 constellations with 94 stars,
lacking equatorial longitudes and latitudes.
Now, all are based on measurements from the first year of Chóngzhēn (崇禎),
with both ecliptic and equatorial longitudes and latitudes fully complete.
Later, he also presented two comprehensive star maps of the equator.
His argument states that the boundary between constantly visible and constantly hidden stars
varies with the altitude of the North Pole,
and thus cannot be confined by a map.
Moreover, celestial degrees become gradually narrower near the poles,
but the map of visible boundaries, starting from south of the equator,
has degrees that are conversely wider,
making the depicted constellations not conform to actual observation.
Therefore, the armillary sphere was cut in half along the equator,
one with the North Pole as its center,
and the other with the South Pole as its center.
From the center to the circumference,
all are 90 degrees,
summing to 180 degrees, which are equatorial latitudes.
The circumference divided into 360 degrees
are equatorial longitudes.
Then, based on the longitudes and latitudes of each star,
they are plotted,
so their distances, positions, and configurations all match celestial phenomena.
As for stars following the ecliptic in clockwise motion,
only ecliptic latitudes show no ancient-modern difference,
while equatorial longitudes and latitudes vary year by year.
However, there are also cases where both ecliptic and equatorial positions differ,
even to the extent of reversing their order.
For instance, the principal star of the constellation Zuī Xiù (觜宿)
was measured in the Táng (唐) dynasty to be 3 degrees before Shēn Xiù (參宿);
in the Yuán (元) dynasty, it was 5 *fēn* (分) before Shēn Xiù (參宿);
now, it has encroached upon Shēn Xiù (參宿).
Thus, the old method placed Zuī Xiù (觜宿) before Shēn Xiù (參宿),
but now Shēn Xiù (參宿) must be placed before Zuī Xiù (觜宿);
this cannot be forced.
There are also cases where there were many in ancient times but few now,
or where they existed in ancient times but are absent now.
For instance, among the six *jiǎ* (甲) and six stars in the Zǐwēi Yuán (紫微垣), there is now only one.
Of the sixteen stars of Huágài (華蓋), there are now only four.
Of the nine stars of Chuánshè (傳舍), there are now five.
Of the six stars of Tiānchú (天廚), there are now five.
Of the six stars of Tiānláo (天牢), there are now two.
Also, Tiānlǐ (天理), Sìshì (四勢), Wǔdì Nèizuò (五帝內座), Tiānzhù (天柱), Tiān (天), Dà Zànfǔ (大贊府), Dàlǐ (大理), Nǚyù (女御), Nèichú (內廚)
are all completely absent.
Of the six stars of Shìlóu (市樓) in the Tiānshì Yuán (天市垣), there are now two.
Of the seven stars of Chángchén (常陳) in the Tàiwēi Yuán (太微垣), there are now three.
Of the fifteen stars of Lángwèi (郎位), there are now ten.
Of the four stars of Chángyuán (長垣), there are now two.
The five stars of Wǔzhūhóu (五諸侯) are all completely absent.
Of the ten stars of Kùlóu (庫樓) in the Jiǎosù (角宿), there are now eight.
The seven stars of Zhéwēi (折威) in the Kàngsù (亢宿) are now absent.
Of the six stars of Kàngchí (亢池) in the Dǐsù (氐宿), there are now four.
The three stars of Dìxí (帝席) are now absent.
Of the five stars of Tiānguī (天龜) in the Wěisù (尾宿), there are now four.
Of the fourteen stars of Biē (鼈) in the Dǒusù (斗宿), there are now thirteen.
Tiānyuè (天籥) and Nóngzhàngrén (農丈人) are both absent.
Of the three stars of Luóyàn (羅堰) in the Niúsù (牛宿), there are now two.
The nine stars of Tiāntián (天田) are all absent.
Of the two stars each of Zhào (趙), Zhōu (周), Qín (秦), and Dài (代) in the Nǚsù (女宿), there is now one of each.
Of the seven stars of Fúkuāng (扶匡), there are now four.
The five stars of Lízhū (離珠) are now absent.
Of the two stars each of Sīwēi (司危) and Sīlù (司祿) in the Xūsù (虛宿), there is now one of each.
Of the four stars of Bàijiù (敗臼), there are now two.
Of the three stars of Líyú (離瑜), there are now two.
Of the thirteen stars of Tiānlěichéng (天壘城), there are now five.
Of the five stars of Rén (人) in the Wēisù (危宿), there are now three.
Of the three stars of Chǔ (杵), there is now one.
Of the four stars of Jiù (臼), there are now three.
Of the seven stars of Chēfǔ (車府), there are now five.
Of the nine stars of Tiāngōu (天鈎), there are now six.
Of the ten stars of Tiānchāo (天鈔), there are now four.
Of the two stars of Gàiwū (蓋屋), there is now one.
Of the forty-five stars of Yǔlínjūn (羽林軍) in the Shìsù (室宿), there are now twenty-six.
Of the twenty-two stars of Téngshé (螣蛇), there are now fifteen.
The nine stars of Bākuí (八魁) are now absent.
Of the ten stars of Tiān (天) in the Bìsù (壁宿), there are now three.
Of the seven stars of Tiānhùn (天溷) in the Kuísù (奎宿), there are now four.
Of the eight stars of Tiānjié (天節) in the Bìsù (畢宿), there are now seven.
The three stars of Xiánchí (咸池) are now absent.
Of the nine stars of Zuòqí (座旗) in the Zīsù (觜宿), there are now five.
Of the thirteen stars of Jūnjǐng (軍井) in the Jǐngsù (井宿), there are now five.
Of the six stars of Wàichú (外廚) in the Guǐsù (鬼宿), there are now five.
The fourteen stars of Tiānmiào (天廟) in the Zhāngsù (張宿) are now absent.
The five stars of Dōngōu (東甌) in the Yìsù (翼宿) are now absent.
Of the seven stars of Qīngqiū (青丘) in the Zhěnsù (軫宿), there are now three.
Its Jūnmén (軍門), Tǔsīkōng (土司空), and Qìfǔ (器府) are all absent.
There are also cases where they were absent in ancient times but exist now.
Next to Cèxīng (策星), there appeared a guest star,
which first emerged in the first year of the Wànlì (萬曆) reign (1573),
being large at first and then diminishing.
The stars of the South Pole,
unknown in ancient times,
have been frequently observed by those who have recently sailed to the south of the equator,
and consequently,
their longitudes and latitudes have been measured.
Many other stars have been added,
all detailed in the star chart.
Regarding the Milky Way (Yúnhàn, 雲漢),
it starts from Wěisù (尾宿)
and branches into two streams.
One passes through Tiānjiāng (天江), Nánhǎi (南海), Shìlóu (市樓),
past Zōngrén (宗人) and Zōngxīng (宗星),
crosses Tiānjīn (天津) to Téngshé (螣蛇).
The other goes from Jī (箕), Dǒu (斗), Tiānbàn (天弁), Hégǔ (河鼓), Zuǒyòuqí (左右旗),
crosses Tiānjīn (天津) to Chēfǔ (車府), then converges at Téngshé (螣蛇),
passes Zàofù (造父),
and proceeds directly to Fùlù (附路), Gédào (閣道), Dàlíng (大陵), Tiānchuán (天船),
gradually descending and moving south,
passing through Wǔchē (五車), Tiānguān (天關), Sīguài (司怪), Shuǐfǔ (水府),
alongside Dōngjǐng (東井),
entering Sìdú (四瀆),
passing the ruins of Quēqiū (闕丘), Húshǐ (弧矢), Tiāngǒu (天狗),
reaching the south of Tiānshè (天社) and Hǎishí (海石),
crossing Nánchuán (南船),
along Hǎishān (海山),
through the Cross and the Bee,
alongside Mǎfù (馬腹),
passing Nánmén (南門),
around Sānjiǎo (三角), Guī (龜), and Chǔ (杵),
and belonging to Wěisù (尾宿),
thus completing a circuit of the heavens.
Reasoning from this,
the hidden realms should naturally have a Milky Way,
and what they saw should not be false.
It is also said that the Milky Way consists of countless small stars,
and similarly, the accumulated corpses (Jīshī, 積尸) in Dàlíng (大陵) and Guǐsù (鬼宿) are also like this.
Examining the Tiānguān Shū (天官書), which states that the stars and the Milky Way are both scattered *qì* (氣) of metal,
then the stars and the Milky Way are fundamentally of the same kind,
which can be corroborated by this.
It is also said that Mǎosù (昴宿) has thirty-six stars,
all observed through a telescope.
In total, one thousand three hundred and forty-seven stars were measured and entered into the chart;
tiny and unnamed ones were not included.
Their magnitudes are divided into six classes: Class 1 has sixteen stars,
Class 2 has sixty-seven stars,
Class 3 has two hundred and seven stars,
Class 4 has five hundred and three stars,
Class 5 has three hundred and thirty-eight stars,
and Class 6 has two hundred and sixteen stars.
All have their longitudes and latitudes for both the ecliptic and equatorial paths.
Two volumes of tables
are included in the Chóngzhēn Lìshū (崇禎曆書) compiled by Guāngqǐ (光啟).
Here, the *jùxīng* (距星) of the twenty-eight lunar mansions and some first and second magnitude stars are preserved;
among the smaller, named ones,
a few are taken,
and listed on the left.

Ecliptic and Equatorial Degrees of the Lunar Mansions
The measurements of the twenty-eight lunar lodges' ecliptic and equatorial degrees and minutes taken in the first year of Chóngzhēn (1628)
all do not match the ancient records.
Since stars move along the ecliptic,
and the equator and ecliptic intersect obliquely,
it is
natural that their degrees cannot be without increase or decrease.
However, that the ecliptic degrees also show increases and decreases,
it is perhaps due to gains or losses in observation and calculation,
or perhaps the stars themselves have varying speeds.
We respectfully list their numbers
for reference.

Ecliptic and Equatorial Zodiacal Divisions
The names of the twelve zodiacal palaces are found in the Èryǎ,
and they are mostly determined according to the lunar lodges.
(For example, Lóu and Kuí constitute Jiànglóu,
Xīn is Dàhuǒ,
and the seven lodges of Zhūniǎo are Qúnshǒu, Qúnwěi, and so on.)
Thus, palaces have fixed lodges,
and lodges have fixed palaces;
this tradition has a long history.
After the Táng dynasty, precession began to be used,
but even then, the sky was treated as itself,
the year as itself,
and the palaces and stars remained unchanged.
In the Western method,
the mid-solar terms determine the crossing into a palace,
(such as the sun passing the Winter Solstice being considered entering the Xīngjì Palace.)
However, since stars have a difference in annual advancement due to precession,
the palaces thus have no fixed lodges,
and lodges can successively occupy various palaces.
This is a major departure from the ancient methods.
Here, the ecliptic and equatorial degrees of the lodges at their crossing into palaces in the first year of Chóngzhēn are
listed on the left
to mark this new beginning.

Astronomical Instruments
The Xuánjī Yùhéng was the origin of astronomical instruments,
but it was not seen in use during the Three Dynasties (Sāndài).
The Zhōulǐ mentions guībiǎo and húlòu,
but not jīhéng,
so its design cannot be investigated.
The Hàn people created the Húntiānyí,
claiming it was a remnant of the jīhéng system;
could this be true?
Thereafter, creations were made in successive generations.
Generally, those assembled with the liùhé, sāncén, sìyóu, and chónghuán
were called Húntiānyí;
those that were solid spheres,
with ecliptic and equatorial longitudes and latitudes drawn on them,
or adorned with constellations,
were called Húntiānxiàng.
Although their designs varied in detail,
they were essentially variations of each other.
Beyond these,
there were only guībiǎo and húlòu.
It was not until the Yuán dynasty created instruments like the Jiǎnyí, Yǎngyí, Kuījǐ, and Jǐngfú
that instrument making became truly refined and detailed.
When Míng Tàizǔ pacified the Yuán,
the Sìtiānjiān presented a crystal water clock (kèlòu),
which had two wooden puppets inside
that could automatically strike gongs and drums according to the time.
Tàizǔ, deeming it useless, smashed it.
In the 17th year of Hóngwǔ, a Guānxīngpán was made.
In the 18th year,
an observation platform (Guānxiàngtái) was established on Jīmíngshān.
In the 24th year, a Húntiānyí was cast.
In the 2nd year of Zhèngtǒng,
Huángfǔ Zhònghé, the director of the Xíngzài Qīntiānjiān, memorialized, saying:
"The observatory in Nánjīng has a Húntiānyí, Jiǎnyí, and guībiǎo for observing and measuring the movements of the Seven Luminaries (Qīzhèng),
but Běijīng only observes from atop the Chēnghuàmén city wall,
without instruments.
I beg to order officials from this bureau to go to Nánjīng,
make wooden models,
bring them to Běijīng,
to compare and verify the height of the celestial North Pole above the horizon,
and then cast them anew in bronze,
so that astrological predictions may have a basis."
This was granted.
In the winter of the following year,
bronze Húntiānyí and Jiǎnyí were cast in Běijīng.
An imperial inscription for the Guāntiānqì was composed.
Its text reads:
"In ancient times, the great sages,
governed by embodying the ways of Heaven,
revered Heaven with their hearts,
and observed Heaven with instruments.
What were these instruments?
The Xuánjī Yùhéng.
The jī represented the celestial body,
the héng examined the celestial movements.
Through generations,
spanning four thousand years,
modifications to the system were made,
its design becoming increasingly complete.
Observing with the instrument,
the outer sphere (liùhé) had instruments,
with solar longitudes and lunar latitudes,
where positions could be verified.
The middle sphere (sāncén) had the two paths of the Yellow and Red (Huáng Chì èrdào),
the sun, moon, and stars,
whose movements could be investigated.
The inner sphere (sìyóu) had horizontal pipes (héngxiāo) piercing through the center,
north, south, east, west,
allowing for elevation, depression, and rotation.
The creation of the Jiǎnyí
replaced the jīhéng,
its design compact yet precise in use,
simple yet refined.
Outside was the Húnhsiàng,
by turning to observe it,
with upper compass and lower square,
degrees, numbers, and cardinal points.
There was also a vertical gnomon (zhíbiao),
eight feet tall,
for the solstices, equinoxes, and seasonal divisions,
shadows could all be obtained.
Celestial phenomena are in Heaven,
the making of instruments is by humans,
measurements and calculations,
not erring by a hair's breadth.
What was made in the past is recorded now,
the craftsmanship of the design is increasingly superb,
both clear and comprehensive,
its use will be endless.
Heaven works diligently for the people,
serving Heaven is the primary task,
if the people do not lose their peace,
Heaven will indeed look after them.
When government is pure in benevolence,
the way of Heaven will be rectified,
this inscription is carved on this instrument,
to stimulate my reverence."
In the 11th year,
the officials of the bureau said:
"The Jiǎnyí has not been engraved with degrees,
and its foundation is low,
observing the sun and stars
is obstructed by buildings on all four sides.
The guībiǎo placed on the exposed platform
has light scattering in all directions,
and the shadow lacks a fixed rule.
The húlòu house is low,
the 'night sky pond' is narrow,
making it difficult to inject water to adjust the time.
We request a proper repair and construction."
This was approved.
In the winter of the following year,
Director Péng Déqīng further stated:
"In Běijīng,
the degree of the celestial North Pole above the horizon and the times of sunrise and sunset differ from Nánjīng,
and the varying lengths of day and night in winter and summer are also different.
Currently, the water clock arrows (lòujiàn) in the palace and government offices are all of the old Nánjīng style,
and cannot be used."
An imperial edict ordered the Nội Guānjiān to remake them.
In the 6th year of Jǐngtài, a Jiǎnyí for the inner observatory and a bronze pot were also made.
During the Chénghuà reign,
Shàngshū Zhōu Hóngmó again requested the construction of a Xuánjī Yùhéng,
and Xiànzōng ordered him to make it himself and present it.
In the 14th year,
the officials of the bureau requested to repair the Guǐyǐngtáng (Shadow Hall),
which was granted.
In the 2nd year of Hóngzhì,
Director Wú Hào said:
"According to verification of the sun's degrees at the four cardinal points,
the two paths of the ecliptic and equator should intersect at Bì and Zhěn.
However, the old Húnyí system at the observatory
shows the intersection of the two paths at Kuí and Zhěn,
which does not match the celestial phenomena.
Its north and south axes do not match the degrees of the poles' rise and set,
and the peep tube does not align with the sun's rise and set,
thus, although installed, it is not used.
The Jiǎnyí that is used is a remnant of Guō Shǒujìng's design,
but the 'North Pole cloud pillar' (Běijí Yúnzhù) is too short,
so when measuring fixed stars' distance from the pole,
it cannot be without error.
I request modification or new construction,
to establish a design for this dynasty."
The matter was sent to the Lǐbù,
which deliberated and ordered Vice Director Zhāng Shēn to make a wooden model
for testing,
and permitted the modification of the ecliptic degree.
In the 16th year of Zhèngdé,
Lòukè Bóshì Zhū Yù again stated:
"The dimensions of the guǐbiǎo are inconsistent,
making accurate measurement difficult,
and calculating the calendar uses Nánjīng's sunrise minutes and seconds,
which seems contradictory.
I request an imperial order for a high-ranking minister to oversee this matter,
to cast and erect bronze gnomons,
and verify the shadow at midday during the four seasons.
Furthermore, to inspect the old earth gnomon (tǔguī) erected in Yángchéng, Hénán,
to match it with today's guǐ,
and to establish guībiǎo in various places like Shāndōng, Húguǎng, Shǎnxī, Dàmíng,
to measure shadows in all four directions.
Then, by cross-referencing and comparing the new and old almanacs with the internal and external gnomon shadows,
a definitive method can be compiled,
so that celestial movements align and eclipses are not erroneous."
The memorial was submitted but not reported on.
In the 2nd year of Jiājìng, the Xiāngfēnggān and the two instruments, Jiǎn and Hún, were repaired.
In the 7th year, a forty-foot wooden gnomon was erected to measure sundial shadows
and determine the solar terms and new moons.
From then on, the various types of instruments from the Qīntiānjiān—Lìyùnyí, Zhèng'àn'àn, Xuánguǐ, Piānguǐ, Pánguǐ—were all available at the observatory,
all based on the Yuán dynasty methods.
During the Wànlì reign,
the Westerner Lì Mǎdòu (Matteo Ricci) created instruments such as the Húnyí, celestial globe, and terrestrial globe.
Lǐ Zhīzǎo from Rénhé wrote the Húntiānyíshuō,
explaining the methods of manufacturing and application,
the text being too long to include here.
Its design did not deviate from the methods of liùhé, sāncén, and sìyóu.
However, the ancient method cast the North Pole's height above the horizon
as a fixed degree,
whereas this one had a meridian arm (zǐwǔ tíguī)
that could adjust the height according to the locality,
which was more convenient for use.
In the second year of Chóngzhēn's reign (1629),
Xú Guāngqǐ, a Vice Minister of the Board of Rites, concurrently managed calendrical computations.
He requested the construction of six large quadrant instruments,
three large arc-limit instruments,
three suspended armillary spheres,
one eclipse instrument,
one celestial sphere for the longitudes and latitudes of the constellations,
one terrestrial globe for the longitudes and latitudes of all nations,
three horizontal sundials,
three rotating astrolabes,
three timekeeping clocks,
and three telescopes.
The request was approved.
Later,
he further stated: Regarding methods for determining time,
there are five matters to be discussed: first, the clepsydra;
second, the south-pointing needle;
third, the gnomon and its marker (biǎo niè);
fourth, instruments;
and fifth, sundials.
With clepsydras,
the water, being new or old, smooth or viscous, causes variations in speed;
the outlet tube, sometimes blocked or sometimes worn, causes variations in flow rate.
At the beginning of setting the clepsydra,
it must be done at the exact
first *kè* of noon.
If this *kè* is mistaken,
everything will be mistaken.
Therefore, the clepsydra is primarily used to supplement what instruments, sundials, and gnomons cannot do during dawn, dusk, and cloudy days,
and is not the
fundamental method for determining time.
The south-pointing needle
is used by technicians to determine north and south;
all determinations of direction and position derive their principles from it.
However, the needle does not point to the true meridian (proper *zǐwǔ*);
it has been said previously that it often deviates towards *bǐngwǔ*.
Upon examination by method,
it varies in different locations.
In the capital, it deviates eastward by five degrees and forty minutes.
If one were to rely on it to construct sundials,
at true noon on the winter solstice, it would be off by
one *kè* and forty-four minutes and some odd seconds early;
at true noon on the summer solstice, it would be off by fifty-one minutes and some odd seconds early.
As for the gnomon and its marker,
this is the method of ancient artisans for placing a gnomon,
observing the shadows cast by the sun's rising and setting,
and comparing them with the shadow at midday
to determine the correct cardinal directions.
The current method
places a small gnomon on a horizontal plane,
repeatedly measures the sun's shadow before and after true noon,
to find two equal-length shadows that define east and west,
thereby obtaining the shortest shadow in the middle as the
true meridian (*zhèng zǐwǔ*).
This technique is very simple.
As for instruments,
the Imperial Observatory already possessed an existing *Lìyùn Yí* (sphere for calculating motion),
used to measure the altitudes of the seven luminaries.
Your servant used it to verify the meridian,
repeatedly measuring the sun's altitude before noon,
and from the highest altitude,
obtained the shortest shadow,
which marks the true north-south line.
Once the true lines of *zǐwǔ* (north-south) and *mǎoyǒu* (east-west) are determined,
the time divisions are distributed according to method,
and various lines for the solar terms are added,
thus forming a horizontal sundial.
Furthermore, the currently
used inclined circular stone sundial is an equatorial sundial,
also calibrated using the derived true meridian line.
Both these sundials can provide the true time of day,
used for measuring
the sun by day.
As for the sundial for measuring stars,
it is essentially the method from the *Zhōu Lǐ* for observing the pole star at night.
However, in ancient times, the North Star was exactly at the stationary point,
but over time it has gradually
shifted,
now being more than three degrees away from the stationary point,
so the old method can no longer be used.
Therefore, a double-plate astrolabe is used,
with time marked on the upper plate
and solar terms on the lower plate.
By looking up and observing
two stars near the pole, the time is obtained,
which is called measuring stars at night.
In the seventh year,
Lǐ Tiānjīng, the Assistant Administrator supervising calendrical reform, stated: Minister Xú Guāngqǐ spoke of methods for determining time;
in ancient times there were clepsydras,
and more recently, wheel clocks.
Both of these rely on human adjustment,
which is not as good as seeking precision from the sun
and stars,
matching heaven with heaven,
which is the fundamental method.
He specifically requested the manufacture of sundials, astrolabes, and telescopes.
Your servant, having been ordered to take charge,
dares to briefly describe them.
As for the sundial,
it is a flat stone,
etched with thirteen lines for the solar terms,
including one line each for the winter and summer solstices,
while the remaining solar terms, where the sun's movement is equal,
share a single line for every two solar terms.
Around the plane are marked lines for the hours,
bounded by the times of sunrise and sunset for each solar term.
Furthermore, according to the
altitude of the North Pole above the horizon in the capital,
a triangular bronze gnomon is cast and placed in the center.
The full shadow of the gnomon indicates the hour,
while the sharp shadow within the gnomon indicates the solar term.
This is a general
description of the sundial.
As for the astrolabe,
it is made of a bronze pillar,
on top of which two concentric plates are mounted.
The inner plate is engraved with celestial degrees,
dividing the year into twelve palaces for the solar terms,
while the outer plate is engraved with the
hours.
A horizontal slit is carved in the middle,
used for observing stars.
The method is to align the first *kè* of *zǐ* (midnight) on the outer plate with a solar term on the inner plate,
then rotate the bronze plates to look north towards the Emperor Star (*Dì Xīng*)
and the great stars of *Gōuchén*,
so that both stars are seen in the slit.
Then, one looks at what the sharp pointer on the plate indicates,
which is the true time.
This is a general description of the astrolabe.
As for the telescope,
also called a peeping tube (*kuī tǒng*),
its construction involves nested, sliding tubes,
allowing for expansion and contraction.
Both ends use glass,
and its length is adjusted according to the distance
of the object being viewed.
Not only can it observe celestial phenomena,
but it can also bring objects several *lǐ* away into view as if they were close at hand,
and can be used to spot enemies and direct cannon fire,
thus having great
utility.
As for the sundials and astrolabes, to be placed correctly,
a platform must be built
to facilitate their placement.
The Emperor ordered eunuchs Lú Wéiníng and Wèi Guózhēng to the bureau to test their use.
The following year,
Lǐ Tiānjīng again requested the construction of a sand clepsydra.
In the early Míng dynasty,
Zhān Xīyuán noted that water clepsydras would freeze in severe cold and cease to function,
so he replaced water with sand.
However, the sand flowed too quickly,
not harmonizing with celestial movements. Therefore, in addition to the bucket wheel, he added four more wheels,
all with thirty-six teeth.
Later, Zhōu Shùxué found fault with its aperture being too small
and easily blocked by sand.
He then redesigned it with six wheels,
five of which had thirty teeth,
and slightly widened the aperture,
whereupon its operation began to align with sundials.
Lǐ Tiānjīng's request
probably carried on this legacy.
Indeed, constructing instruments and modeling celestial phenomena
is the primary duty of astronomers.
However, those skilled in the art can create by ingenuity.
Thus, the celestial instruments of the Westerners,
whose names are too numerous to list,
include the *Húngài Yí* (Armillary Sphere) and the *Jiǎnpíng Yí* (Simplified Armillary) as the most precise.
Their descriptions are fully contained in the complete book,
and are not recorded here.
Extreme Gnomon Shadows
Méi Wéndǐng of Xuānchéng said: The extreme gnomon shadows are always interdependent.
Knowing the altitude of the North Pole above the horizon
allows one to know the midday shadow for each solar term.
Conversely, measuring the midday shadow for each solar term
also allows one to know the altitude of the North Pole.
However, this technique is not easy.
In the method of the *guībiǎo*,
if the gnomon is short, distinguishing minutes and seconds is difficult;
if the gnomon is long, the shadow is faint
and indistinct.
This is why Guō Shǒujìng erected a forty-foot gnomon
and used a shadow-marker to observe it.
The sun's disc is very large;
a vertical gnomon measures the shadow of the sun's upper edge,
and a horizontal gnomon measures the shadow of the sun's lower edge,
neither of which is the number for the center.
This is why Guō Shǒujìng placed a horizontal beam at the top of the gnomon to measure it,
and his method can be called excellent.
However, his shadow-marker,
made of a copper plate with a pinhole the size of a mustard seed,
although tilted forward and backward to face the sun,
still the sun's
The height varies daily,
so how can the tilt of the bronze plate always be perfectly aligned?
If not aligned,
then light will not pass through,
and by the time one makes temporary adjustments, the sun will have already moved west.
One
must replace the bronze plate with a round wooden rod,
supported on both sides by two boards,
like an axle,
making it very easy to rotate.
Furthermore, replace the round hole with a straight slit,
and its use will become much more convenient.
However, the shadow marker can only remedy the defect of faintness,
and is not its fundamental solution.
One must correct its Gǔi biǎo,
level its Gǔi,
and standardize its Dù;
if any one of these three is
lacking, the shadow cannot be obtained.
Even if these three are obtained,
people's minds vary in their meticulousness,
eyesight in its sharpness,
and execution of tasks in its sincerity;
one cannot but choose carefully.
Understanding
this,
it is then possible to obtain the sundial shadow.
Western methods have made further advancements.
They state that the radius of the Earth is more than one thousandth of the radius of the sun-heaven system,
thus the observed altitude of the sun from the ground
must
be less than its true altitude from the Earth's center;
hence there is an addition for the Earth's radius difference.
Near the Earth there is a clear misty atmosphere [Qīngméng qì],
which can elevate low objects to appear high,
thus the sun's altitude deduced from the sundial shadow
may be greater than its true altitude in the heavens;
hence there is a subtraction for the clear misty atmosphere difference [Qīngméng chā].
These two differences
are both greater near the Earth and gradually decrease as the altitude increases,
until they become zero.
The Earth's radius difference is zero at the zenith,
and the clear misty atmosphere difference [Qīngméng chā] is zero at forty-five degrees.
In the early Chóngzhēn reign,
Westerners measured the altitude of the North Star above the horizon for various capital cities and provinces: Běijīng forty degrees,
(a full circle is three hundred sixty degrees,
degrees are calculated in sixty minutes,
same below.) Nánjīng thirty-two and a half degrees,
Shāndōng thirty-seven degrees,
Shānxī thirty-eight degrees,
Shǎnxī thirty-six degrees,
Hénán thirty-five degrees,
Zhèjiāng thirty degrees,
Jiāngxī twenty-nine degrees,
Húguǎng thirty-one degrees,
Sìchuān twenty-nine degrees,
Guǎngdōng twenty-three degrees,
Fújiàn twenty-six degrees,
Guǎngxī twenty-five degrees,
Yúnnán twenty-two degrees,
Guìzhōu twenty-four degrees.
(Regarding the above polar altitudes,
only those for the two capitals, Jiāngxī, and Guǎngdōng were actually measured;
the rest were approximated from maps.)
Furthermore, using a twelve-Dù sixty-minute table, the midday sun's shadow for various solar terms in Jīngshī was measured: Summer Solstice three degrees thirty-three minutes,
Mángzhòng and Xiǎoshǔ three degrees forty-two minutes,
Xiǎomǎn and Dàshǔ four degrees fifteen minutes,
Lìxià and Lìqiū five degrees six minutes,
Gǔyǔ and Chǔshǔ six degrees twenty-three minutes,
