Now, taking the Wànlì era as the epoch,
the Xīnsì year of the ninth year happens to be the period for 'Dòu Lì to change its constitution,'
and it also accords with the meaning of 'Qián Yuán uses nine' (a phrase from the Yì Jīng implying the completion of a cycle),
thus the calendar epoch is precisely here.
I once compared the Dàtǒng and Shòu Shí calendars;
by studying ancient records,
the solar terms differ by three days,
and by calculating the present,
the time differs by nine ke (quarters of an hour).
Although the difference is only nine ke,
when it occurs around midnight,
the difference becomes a full day.
If the solar terms differ by one day,
then the intercalation of a leap month differs by one month.
If the leap month differs by one month,
then the season differs by one quarter.
If the season differs by one quarter,
then the year differs by one year.
How can such errors be considered small?
This is because the Shòu Shí calendar's subtraction of fractions was too severe,
erring on the side of 'pre-heaven';
the Dàtǒng calendar made no subtractions,
erring on the side of 'post-heaven'.
Therefore, by harmonizing the two schools
and adopting an intermediate value,
a new rate was established,
and compiled into a book.
The main principles derive from Xǔ Héng,
but it differs from Xǔ Héng's calendar.
The yellow bell pitch (Huáng Zhōng) is the origin of the pitch-pipe and calendar system,
but the old calendars rarely mentioned it.
The new method begins with calculating the pitch-pipes, musical notes, and hexagrams.
In the time of Yáo, the winter solstice sun passed through a certain stellar position.
Hé Chéngtiān calculated it to be around 10 degrees in the constellations Xū and Nǚ (Aquarius and Capricornus).
Yī Xíng calculated it to be between Nǚ and Xū.
The Yuán dynasty calendar treatise also stated it was at the junction of Nǚ and Xū.
However, the Shòu Shí calendar examined it
and found it to be at 2 degrees in the constellation Niú (Capricornus).
The Dàtǒng calendar examined it
and found it to be at 1 degree in the constellation Wēi (Aquarius).
A difference of twenty-six degrees,
none of which aligns with the Yáo Diǎn (Canon of Yáo).
The new method, examining the Jiǎchén year of the first year of Yáo,
found that at the summer solstice at noon,
the sun was around 12 degrees in the constellation Liǔ (Hydra).
At the winter solstice at noon,
the sun was around 10 degrees in the constellation Nǚ (Capricornus).
The constellations Xīn and Mǎo (Scorpius and Taurus) were centered at dusk and dawn respectively,
each not exceeding half a stellar position from the exact noon position,
which aligns with the theories of Hé Chéngtiān and Yī Xíng.
These are the major differences from the old calendar;
the rest are detailed in the calendar treatise.
I hope that an imperial edict will instruct high officials and renowned scholars to review and adopt it."
The first part of his method is called "calculating convergence and divergence" (bù fāliǎn).
It takes the Jiājìng Jiǎyín year
The epochal cycle is 4560,
the period of full years is 1461.
The precession of the equinoxes is 1 second and 75 hu (fractions of a second).
The annual rate of solar terms has no fixed value,
but is determined and applied according to the annual precession.
The pitch-pipe resonance (that is, solar term resonance) is 55 days, 60 ke, and 89 fen.
The total pitch-pipe cycle is 60 days per xún (ten-day period).
Next is "calculating new moons and intercalary months" (bù shuòrùn).
The rates for new moon, full moon, and quarter moons are the same as in the Shòu Shí calendar.
The intercalary month resonance is 19 days, 36 ke, and 19 fen.
Next is "calculating the sun's path" (bù rìchán).
The sun's average daily motion is 1 degree.
The orbital period (that is, the celestial cycle) is 365 degrees and 25 fen.
The middle of the orbit is half of this.
The image cycle is also half of that.
The earthly branch cycle is one-twelfth of the orbital period.
The annual precession of the yellow and red (equatorial) paths,
the initial limit of increase and final limit of decrease,
and the initial limit of decrease and final limit of increase
are all the same as in the Shòu Shí calendar.
The circumferential resonance (zhōu yìng) is 238 degrees, 22 fen, and 39 miao.
(Note: The Shòu Shí calendar's method for finding the sun's degree
adds the accumulated degrees to the circumferential resonance,
starting from 7 degrees in Xū.
Its circumferential resonance is the number of degrees from 7 degrees in Xū to 10 degrees in Jī.
The Wàn Nián Lì Fǎ subtracts the accumulated degrees from the circumferential resonance,
starting from the beginning of Jiǎo.
Its circumferential resonance is the number of degrees from 10 degrees in Jī to the beginning of Jiǎo,
which should be 286 degrees and 45 fen.
The current number does not match,
which seems to be an error.)
Next is "calculating sundial shadows and clepsydra drips" (bù guǐlòu).
The degree of elevation of the North Pole,
the constant number of sundial shadows at the winter and summer solstices,
and the number of ke for the duration of day and night at the two solstices
are all based on the capital (Běijīng).
Reference is also made to Mount Yuè's platform,
to show the number of regional differences in li (distance).
Next is "calculating the moon's position" (bù yuèlì).
The moon's average motion, orbital period, and middle of orbit
are the same as in the Shòu Shí calendar.
The position cycle (that is, the period of speed and slowness limits) is 336 limits, 16 fen, and 60 miao.
The middle of the position is half of this.
The image of the position is also half of that.
The rotation difference is 1 day, 97 ke, and 60 fen.
The rotation resonance is 7 days, 50 ke, and 34 fen.
Next is "calculating the nodes" (bù jiāodào).
The true node and mean node are the same as in the Shòu Shí calendar.
The distance from the node is 14 degrees, 66 fen, and 66 miao.
The nodal cycle, mean node, and nodal difference
are the same as in the Shòu Shí calendar.
The nodal resonance is 20 days, 47 ke, and 34 fen.
Next is "calculating eclipses" (bù jiāoshí).
The outer limit for a solar eclipse is 6 degrees,
with a fixed method of 61.
The inner limit is 8 degrees,
with a fixed method of 81.
The fixed method for the lunar eclipse limit is the same as in the Shòu Shí calendar.
Next is "calculating the five planets" (bù wǔwěi).
The conjunction resonance (hé yìng) for Saturn is 262 days and 3026 fen;
for Jupiter, 310 days and 1837 fen;
for Mars, 343 days and 5176 fen;
for Venus, 203 days and 8347 fen;
for Mercury, 91 days and 7628 fen.
The calendrical resonance (lì yìng) for Saturn is 8604 days and 5338 fen;
for Jupiter, 4018 days and 6073 fen;
for Mars, 314 days and 49 fen;
for Venus, 60 days and 1975 fen;
for Mercury, 253 days and 7497 fen.
The cycle rates, degree rates, and degrees of appearance and disappearance at dawn and dusk
are all the same as in the Shòu Shí calendar.
After discussing it for over a year,
he said:
"The principle of the waxing and waning of Yīn and Yáng
accumulates gradually,
and there has never been anything that didn't start from a fraction of a second.
When calculating time and examining ancient records,
to suddenly add a fen at the centenary mark
is not reasonable.
For example, in the third year of Lǔ Yǐnggōng, the Xīnyǒu year,
down to the Zhìyuán Xīnsì year, which is two thousand years,
if calculated by the original Shòushí calendar method,
twenty fen should be added to the actual year,
resulting in the sixth kè of the Gēngwǔ day,
as the Winter Solstice of the Tiānzhèng system for that year.
In the following year, the Rénxū year,
down to the Zhìyuán Xīnsì year, which is one thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine years,
nineteen fen should be added according to the original method,
resulting in the fifty kè and forty-four fen of the Yǐhài day,
as the Winter Solstice of the Tiānzhèng system for that year.
Subtracting the two Winter Solstices,
we get a difference of three hundred and sixty-five days, forty-four kè, and forty-four fen.
This means that the surplus of the year is four-ninths of a day,
not one-quarter of a day.
No calendrical error
is more egregious than this.
The new method, after careful consideration,
postulates that if two seconds are added or subtracted each year,
and one extrapolates backwards,
then the Jiǎchǒu year of Zhāogōng is missed;
if one or one and a half seconds are added or subtracted,
then the Xīnhài year of Xīgōng is missed.
Now, taking an approximate mean,
the method sets a fixed distance and multiplies it by itself.
Seven times eight gives fifty-six, which is rounded up to the nearest hundred,
yielding one hundred.
Converting this to fen,
we get one second and seventy-five hū.
Then both Xīnhài and Jiǎchǒu are obtained."
Regarding the sun's ecliptic motion,
he said:
"Among the ancient calendars found in the Six Classics,
what can be clearly verified are none other than the sun's ecliptic motion and the culminating stars.
However, few astronomers have truly understood them,
probably because they do not know the difference between the Xià calendar and the Zhōu calendar.
Generally, the Xià calendar focuses on the jiéqì (solar terms),
while the Zhōu calendar focuses on the zhōngqì (intermediate solar terms).
Hé Chéngtiān took the first day of the first month, jiǎzǐ, at midnight, with the new moon and Yǔshuǐ (Rain Water) solar term coinciding, as the shàngyuán (beginning of the grand cycle).
This was inconsistent with the Xià calendar's new moon
and not in line with the Zhōu calendar's orthography.
Therefore, modern calculations of the yuèlíng (monthly ordinances) and xiǎozhèng (minor rectifications)
all do not align with ancient records.
Once, using the annual precession of the new method,
I examined the culminating stars in the Yáodiǎn,
and found that the so-called 'four mid-months'
refer to the culminating stars within thirty days, from the beginning of a jiéqì to the end of a zhōngqì.
Later generations' insistence on the two equinoxes and two solstices
is also an error."
Regarding observing the pole,
he said:
"From the Hàn to Qí and Liáng dynasties,
everyone believed that the Niǔ star was the immovable point.
Only Zǔgài's measurements showed that the Niǔ star was more than one degree from the pole.
From the Táng to the Sòng dynasties,
it was again measured that the Niǔ star was more than three degrees from the pole.
The Yuán Shǐ followed the three-degree measurement,
indicating that there was no definitive conclusion.
The new method does not measure the Niǔ star.
Instead, it uses the sun's shadow for verification.
On a gnomon board,
within the degrees of the celestial sphere, one degree is designated as the North Pole.
Starting from this degree, rotating clockwise,
count to sixty-seven degrees and forty-one fen,
which is the position of the sun's ecliptic at the Summer Solstice.
Then, count to one hundred and fifteen degrees and twenty-one fen,
which is the position of the sun's ecliptic at the Winter Solstice.
Rotating counter-clockwise,
the count is similar.
These four points, plus the center, make a total of five points,
each marked with a needle.
At midday on the two solstice days,
the board is stood upright, facing south, to cast a shadow.
When the shadows of the three needles coincide,
a string is then suspended to mark the center line,
and then crossed with a perpendicular line.
The distance from the horizontal line to the polar degree and fen is observed,
which is the degree and fen of the pole's altitude above the horizon."
Regarding the gnomon shadow,
he said:
"Hé Chéngtiān erected a gnomon to measure shadows,
and only then did he realize that since the Hàn dynasty,
the Winter Solstice always occurred three days later than calculated.
Therefore, calculating the gnomon shadow
is essential for calendrical reform.
The Shòushí calendar also relies on gnomon shadows as its basis,
but the calendrical treatises do not record the method for calculating gnomon shadows,
which is a deficiency.
Now, using the altitude of the North Pole,
combined with the two methods of arc and sagitta, to derive it,
we can perhaps fully explore its origins.
Furthermore, differences are established according to the varying topography, to account for all changes,
which was unprecedented before this."
He also said:

"The Shòushí calendar's discussion takes the first day of the first month, jiǎyín, and the winter solstice at dawn, in the fifteenth year of Lǔ Xiàngōng, the wùyín year, mentioned in the Former Hàn Shì,
as its starting point.
However, the fifteenth year of Xiàngōng is one hundred and sixty-one years after the first year of Yǐngōng, the jǐwèi year,
so it is clearly not within the Spring and Autumn period.
Yet the Yuán Shǐ states, 'Since Xiàngōng of the Spring and Autumn period,'
and also says, 'Zhāogōng's Winter Solstice
is proof of the sun's lost movement,'
which is an error.
The Xiàngōng jiǎyín Winter Solstice
has no other basis
except what Liú Xīn stated in his Sāntǒng Lì.
Can it be that the Zuǒ Zhuàn is not trustworthy,
but Xīn is?
The Winter Solstice in the first year of Tàichū was in the xīnyǒu year,
but Xīn took it as jiǎzǐ,
a difference of three days.
If he couldn't even know that,
how could he foresee hundreds of years before and after?
Therefore, for the thousand years around the Spring and Autumn period,
the conjunctions of qi and moon, and eclipses,
calculated by the Chánglì and Dàyǎn calendars are nearly correct,
while what Liú Xīn and Bān Gù said is entirely incorrect."
He also said:
"The Dàyǎn calendar discussion states that on the jiǎxū day of the eleventh month in the thirteenth year of Yuánjiā of the Sòng dynasty,
the length of the shadow changed due to the sun's varying motion.
The Shòushí calendar discussion also says this,
but I consider it an overstatement.
If the sun's motion were truly astray,
it should, like the precession,
shift gradually.
If it doesn't match this year,
how could it possibly match again next year?
Perhaps what previous generations measured
was not precise enough.
The Winter Solstice shadow is more than one zhàng long.
If the gnomon is tall and the shadow is long,
the shadow appears faint and indistinct.
Sometimes, sighting tubes, auxiliary gnomons, or shadow markers are used to find the true shadow.
However, a sighting tube might be slightly raised or lowered,
an auxiliary gnomon or shadow marker might be slightly moved forward or backward,
the gnomon itself might be slightly tilted,
or the guī surface might be slightly askew.
The shadows a few days before and after the two solstices
only shift by a hair's breadth,
making them difficult to distinguish.
Moreover, the entrusted personnel
may not know if they are correct.
Given the vast distances of the Nine Provinces,
it is not observed firsthand;
how can the reported gnomon shadows
be trustworthy?"
Regarding the clepsydra,
he said:
"The rising and setting of the sun and moon with eclipses, and the morning and evening appearances and disappearances of the five planets,
all calendrical methods are based on gnomons and clepsydrae.
However, gnomons and clepsydrae vary according to the north-south direction of the terrain
and the altitude of the celestial pole.
The Yuán people established their capital in Yān,
and their Shòushí calendar's early or late rising and setting of the seven luminaries,
and the long and short days and nights of the four seasons,
were all based on the gnomon and clepsydra of Dàdū.
In the early days of our dynasty, the capital was established in Jīnlíng.
The Dàtǒng calendar's gnomon and clepsydra were changed to follow Nánjīng,
with a difference of more than three kè between the summer and winter solstices.
Now, when calculating the minutes and seconds of eclipses,
the north-south and east-west differences, and the fixed disappearances and appearances of the five planets,
all follow the old methods of the Yuán people,
but only the clepsydra is changed,
which leads to mutual contradictions.
Therefore, the new method's gnomon and clepsydra
adhere to the old Yuán system."
Regarding his discussion of solar eclipses,
he said:
"There are two points where the sun's path and the moon's path intersect.
If they meet exactly at an intersection,
then the eclipse is total.
If they are merely close to an intersection, either before or after it,
then the eclipse is partial.
This is the celestial limit of intersection.
There is also a human limit of intersection.
For example, if a total eclipse occurs in Zhōngguó,
under the direct view of the sun,
the deficit is only half.
In regions beyond civilization,
they will be in the intersection path but not experience the eclipse.
If one views it from a different location,
the same applies.
Why is this?
The sun is like a large red ball,
and the moon is like a small black ball,
both suspended on a single line.
If the sun is above and the moon is below,
and one looks directly up from below them,
the black ball will certainly obscure the red ball,
appearing as a total eclipse.
However, when viewed from the side, there is a difference in distance,
thus varying the magnitude of the eclipse.
After the spring equinox,
the sun travels along the northern side of the celestial equator;
the eclipse magnitude is greater beyond the intersection point
and smaller within the intersection point.
After the autumn equinox,
the sun travels along the southern side of the celestial equator;
the eclipse magnitude is smaller beyond the intersection point
and greater within the intersection point.
This is why there is a north-south difference.
After the winter solstice,
the sun travels along the eastern side of the ecliptic;
the eclipse magnitude is greater before noon
and smaller after noon.
After the summer solstice,
the sun travels along the western side of the ecliptic;
the eclipse magnitude is smaller before noon
and greater after noon.
This is why there is an east-west difference.
When looking up at noon, the sun appears high;
when viewed level at dawn or dusk, it appears low.
This is why there is a difference from noon.
An eclipse occurring before noon is seen earlier;
an eclipse occurring after noon is seen later.
This is why there is a time difference.
All these differences
are found only in solar eclipses;
lunar eclipses do not have them.
Therefore, calculating solar eclipses
is quite difficult.
To calculate the variations across the jiǔfú,
one must rely on each specific location,
examine the length of sundial shadows,
and measure the height of the celestial pole,
and then one might succeed.
The numbers calculated in the calendar classics
are merely based on observations made in Yāndū.
It was formerly said: 'When the moon travels on the inner path,
eclipses are often verified.
When the moon travels on the outer path,
eclipses are often not verified.'
It was also said: 'Even if the celestial limit of intersection
is related to the inner path,
if it is outside the human limit of intersection,
it is similar to the outer path,
and the sun will not be eclipsed.'
This explanation seems plausible,
but it is not exhaustive.
For example, if a solar eclipse occurs around the summer solstice,
between yín, mǎo, yǒu, and xū (寅卯酉戌) hours,
and people observe it from the northeast or northwest,
then the eclipse magnitude on the outer path will actually be greater than on the inner path.
The sun's body is larger than the moon's;
the moon cannot completely obscure it.
Even during a total eclipse,
the sunlight radiates outwards,
forming a golden ring.
Therefore, there is no such thing as a 100% (ten-tenths) solar eclipse.
Even when total,
it is only 9 fen and 80 miao (9.8 tenths).
For solar eclipses in the Shòushí Lì,
the positive calendar limit is 6 degrees,
with a constant divisor of 60.
The negative calendar limit is 8 degrees,
with a constant divisor of 80.
Each limit is set,
and when divided by its constant divisor,
each yields ten-tenths.
Now, by adding a number to each of these constant divisors
and then dividing the limits,
one obtains 9 fen and more than 80 miao."
Regarding his discussion of lunar eclipses,
he said:
"The 'dark void'
is the shadow.
The obscuration of the moon by the shadow
has no differences in early or late, high or low,
nor distinctions across the four seasons or jiǔfú.
It is like suspending a black ball in a dark room,
with a lit candle to its left
and a white ball suspended to its right.
If the candlelight is blocked by the black ball,
then the white ball will not receive its light.
People observing from all sides
will see the same thing.
Therefore, there is no theory of a 'time difference' for lunar eclipses.
The Jìyuán Lì arbitrarily established a time difference,
and the Shòushí Lì followed it,
which was a mistake."
Regarding his discussion of the five planets (wǔwěi),
he said:
"Ancient methods for calculating the wǔwěi
did not account for the addition or subtraction of variable quantities.
Zhāng Zǐxìn of Běi Qí, through prolonged observation,
understood that the wǔwěi undergo expansion and contraction,
and that these variations should be added or subtracted to determine their daily positions.
This is because the wǔwěi travel inside and outside the ecliptic,
each having its own path,
and their speed varies depending on their distance from the sun.
The addition and subtraction of these variable quantities
are like the straight, oblique, or curved paths of a road.
A person from the Sòng dynasty said: 'The movement of the five planets
shows the greatest discrepancies particularly during their stationary and retrograde periods.
Those that advance from the inner side
must retrograde outwards.
Those that advance from the outer side
must retrograde inwards.
Their paths resemble the shape of a willow leaf,
sharper at the two ends than in the middle,
with the inbound and outbound paths quite far apart.
Therefore, the planets move slightly slower at the ends of their paths
because they are moving obliquely.
They move slightly faster in the middle of their paths
because they are moving directly.'
Previous generations, when revising calendars,
only adjusted or modified old methods;
they never truly examined celestial degrees.
Their method requires measuring the degrees and minutes of the moon and the five planets
every night at dusk, dawn, and midnight,
and recording them in a ledger.
After five full years,
excluding the days of cloudy weather and daytime observations,
one can obtain three years of actual movements,
and only then can they be connected by mathematical calculations."
In a memorial,
Fàn Qiān (范謙), Minister of Rítbù (禮部), reported:
“Regarding the method of the precessional difference (suìchā zhī fǎ 歲差之法),
since Yú Xǐ (虞喜),
each dynasty has had discussions about difference methods,
but there has been no unified rule.
The ways in which this has been sought
are roughly three: examining the middle stars of the lunar calendar (yuèlìng zhī zhōngxīng 月令之中星),
measuring the sun's shadow at the two solstices (èrzhì zhī rìjǐng 二至之日景),
and verifying the minutes and seconds of eclipses (jiāoshí zhī fēnmiǎo 交食之分秒).
Examining with a sighting tube (héngguǎn 衡管),
measuring with a gnomon (nièbiǎo 臬表),
and verifying with a clepsydra (lòukè 漏刻) —
these might even achieve accidental accuracy.
Astronomers (lìjiā 曆家) take the circumference of the heavens as 365 and a quarter degrees
to record the movements of the seven luminaries (qīzhèng 七政),
and further divide a degree into a hundred minutes,
and a minute into a hundred seconds,
which can be called precise.
However, the body of the armillary sphere (húnxiàng zhī tǐ 渾象之體)
has a diameter of only a few *chǐ* (尺),
and when the degrees of the heavens are laid out,
each degree is less than the width of a finger.
How can one place minutes and seconds there?
As for the gnomon, its height is no more than a few *chǐ* (尺),
and the marks on the clepsydra do not exceed a few *cùn* (寸).
With the sky being so high and vast,
to seek its minute details with objects measured in *chǐ* (尺) and *cùn* (寸),
to wish it to be absolutely flawless in its subtleties,
is that not difficult?
Therefore, when the difference is within minutes and seconds,
there is nothing to verify it with;
only when it exceeds one degree
can it be perceived, as if through a tube.
Is this why the wisdom and ingenuity of ancient and modern times
cannot fully encompass its changes?
For instance, as the Imperial Prince (shìzǐ 世子) said,
comparing the Dàtǒng (大統) and Shòushí (授時) calendars,
ancient calculations show a difference of three days in qi,
while modern extrapolations show a difference of nine *kè* (刻) in time.
Now, a time difference of nine *kè* (刻)
means a shift of one day between the hours of Hài (亥) and Zǐ (子),
and a shift of one month at the transition between the new moon (huì 晦) and the first crescent (shuò 朔).
This can be verified in the near future.
If it shifts earlier,
the new moon would appear on the evening of the second day;
if it shifts later,
the new moon would appear on the evening of the fourth day.
Currently, it does not seem to have reached this point.
His memorial should be sent to Qīntiānjiān (欽天監) for consultation, revision, and testing.
The Imperial Prince (shìzǐ 世子) is dedicated to calendrical studies,
broadly conversant with ancient and modern knowledge,
and should be granted an imperial edict of commendation and encouragement.”
This was granted.
Xíng Yúnlù (邢雲路), a jiānshì (僉事) of Hénán (河南), submitted a memorial stating:
“The essentials of calendrical governance
are none other than observing celestial phenomena, measuring shadows, awaiting auspicious times, and calculating with tallies (guānxiàng, cèjǐng, hòushí, chóucè 觀象、測景、候時、籌策) — these four matters.
Now, on the winter solstice of the year Bǐngshēn (丙申),
I measured it as one *kè* (刻) after noon on the day Yǐwèi (乙未),
while the Dàtǒng (大統) calendar calculated it as two *kè* (刻) after noon on the day Shēn (申),
a difference of nine *kè* (刻).
Moreover, this year, Lìchūn (立春), Xiàzhì (夏至), and Lìdōng (立冬) all happened to fall exactly at the midpoint of the Zǐ (子) hour.
I calculated Lìchūn (立春) as Yǐhài (乙亥),
while Dàtǒng (大統) calculated it as Bǐngzǐ (丙子);
Xiàzhì (夏至) as Rénchén (壬辰),
while Dàtǒng (大統) calculated it as Guǐsì (癸巳);
Lìdōng (立冬) as Jǐyǒu (己酉),
while Dàtǒng (大統) calculated it as Gēngxū (庚戌).
All were separated by one day.
If, by chance, the first day (yuánrì 元日) falls at the midpoint of the Zǐ (子) hour,
then the beginning of the year's ritual (lǚduān 履端) should be moved to the end of the month,
and the grand ceremony of imperial congratulations would be on the second day of the first month.
Is this a minor matter?
On the new moon of the intercalary eighth month,
there was a solar eclipse.
The Dàtǒng (大統) calendar calculated the initial obscuration at two *kè* (刻) after noon on the day Sì (巳),
with almost a total eclipse,
while I observed the initial obscuration at one *kè* (刻) after noon on the day Sì (巳),
with the eclipse stopping at just over seven fen (分).
The Dàtǒng (大統) calendar was nearly two *kè* (刻) behind the actual celestial event,
so the intercalations (rùn 閏), and the transitions (zhuǎnyìng 轉應) and conjunctions (jiāoyìng 交應) should all be adjusted accordingly.”
The Qīntiānjiān (欽天監), upon seeing Yúnlù's (雲路) memorial,
was greatly displeased.
Jiānjìng (監正) Zhāng Yìnghóu (張應侯) memorialized to criticize him,
calling his actions presumptuous, reckless, and misleading to the world.
Fàn Qiān (范謙), Minister of Rítbù (禮部), then stated:
“The calendar is a major national affair,
which scholars should diligently study,
not something for calendar officials to monopolize.
The laws prohibit
only those who speak wildly of omens and portents (yāoxiáng 妖祥).
The observatory officials (jiānguān 監官) adhere rigidly to established methods
and cannot revise them to match the heavens.
Fortunately, there are such people,
and we should work together with them in harmony,
not be jealous.
I request that Yúnlù (雲路) be appointed as Tídū Qīntiānjiān Shì (提督欽天監事),
to supervise the officials and staff,
and to meticulously observe and measure,
so as to complete this great work.”
The deliberation was submitted,
but not acted upon.
In the thirty-eighth year,
the observatory's prediction of the solar eclipse's minutes, seconds, and degree of obscuration on the new moon of the eleventh month, day Rén Yín (壬寅),
was refuted as erroneous by Zhífāng Láng (職方郎) Fàn Shǒujǐ (范守己) in a memorial.
The ritual officials (lǐguān 禮官) then requested that scholars proficient in calendrical studies be broadly sought,
to work with the observatory officials day and night in calculation,
hoping that the calendrical methods would be flawless.
Thereupon, Wǔguānzhèng (五官正) Zhōu Zǐyú (周子愚) said:
“The naturalized foreign subjects from Dàxīyáng (大西洋), Pángdí (龐迪) and Xióng Sānbá (熊三拔),
have brought with them calendrical methods from their country
that are mostly not found in Chinese classics.
I request that, following the precedent of translating the Xīyù (西域) calendrical methods during the Hóngwǔ (洪武) era,
scholars knowledgeable in calendrical science be appointed, along with observatory officials,
to translate all these books,
to fill the gaps in our classics.”
Earlier,
the Dàxīyáng (大西洋) man Lì Mǎdòu (利瑪竇) had presented local tribute items,
and then Dí (迪), Sānbá (三拔), Lóng Huámín (龍華民), Dèng Yùhán (鄧玉函), and Tāng Ruòwàng (湯若望) arrived one after another,
all profoundly skilled in astronomy and calendrical studies.
The Rítbù (禮部) then memorialized:
“Those who are proficient in calendrical methods,
such as Yúnlù (雲路) and Shǒujǐ (守己), who are highly regarded at this time,
should be promoted to Jīngqīng (京卿)
to jointly manage calendrical affairs.
Xú Guāngqǐ (徐光啟), Jiǎntǎo (檢討) of Hánlín Yuàn (翰林院), and Lǐ Zhīzǎo (李之藻), Yuánwàiláng (員外郎) of Nánjīng Gōngbù (南京工部), are also meticulous in calendrical principles
and can translate Western methods together with Dí (迪) and Sānbá (三拔),
so that Yúnlù (雲lù) and others can participate in editing and revising.
However, the accuracy and detail of calendrical methods
are most clearly revealed during eclipses,
so to propose calendrical reform,
it is essential to re-emphasize observation and testing.
I request an imperial edict to the relevant department to repair and manage instruments
to facilitate this work.”
The memorial was submitted,
but shelved.
Soon after, Yúnlù (雲路) and Zhīzǎo (之藻) were both summoned to the capital
to participate in calendrical matters.
Yúnlù (雲路) based his work on his own studies,
while Zhīzǎo (之藻) took Western methods as his primary source.
In the forty-first year,
Zhīzǎo (之藻), now holding the title of Nánjīng Tàipú Shàoqīng (南京太僕少卿),
memorialized the Western calendrical methods,
briefly mentioning the errors in the Bureau of Astronomy's (Táijiān 台監) calculations of the times and magnitudes of solar and lunar eclipses.
He strongly recommended Dí (迪), Sānbá (三拔), Huámín (華民), and Yáng Mǎnuò (陽瑪諾),
stating:
“Their discussions of astronomy and calendrical calculations
include matters not reached by former Chinese sages;
they do not merely discuss degrees and numbers,
but can also clarify the underlying principles.
The instruments they have created for observing the heavens and the sun (kuītian, kuīri zhī qì 窺天、窺日之器)
are all exquisitely precise.
Now, as Dí (迪) and others are advancing in age,
I request an imperial edict for the Rítbù (禮部) to establish a bureau
to acquire their calendrical methods
and translate them into books.”
Yáo Yǒngjì (姚永濟) of the Lǐkē (禮科) also made a similar statement.
At that time, due to delays in general affairs,
there was no leisure to establish a bureau.
In the forty-fourth year,
Yúnlù (雲路) presented his Qīzhèng Zhēnshù (七政真數),
stating:
“The method of calendrical calculation
must rely on the opposition of the two nodes.
When the two nodes are correctly aligned,
the degrees of minutes and seconds for the intermediate times
can be precisely determined.
Solar and lunar eclipses,
and the transits of the five planets (wǔxīng zhī língfàn 五星之凌犯),
are all conjunctions of the sun, moon, and five planets.
When the two nodes are in opposition,
they illuminate each other,
and the task of the seven luminaries is completed.”
In the spring of Tiānqǐ (天啟) first year,
Yúnlù (雲路) again elaborated on several historical and contemporary solar and lunar eclipses
to demonstrate the looseness of the Shòushí (授時) calendar
and prove the precision of the new method.
His memorial was sent to the Rítbù (禮部).
On the new moon of the fourth month, day Rénshēn (壬申), there was a solar eclipse,
and the eclipse magnitude and time predicted by Yúnlù (雲路)
differed from those predicted by the Qīntiānjiān (欽天監).
He himself claimed his new method was extremely precise,
but when tested at the appointed time,
all were found to be inconsistent with the celestial events.
Yúnlù (雲Lù) also once argued that the boundaries of the Dàtǒng (大統) calendar's celestial mansions (gōngdù jiāojiè 宮度交界)
should be determined by suìchā (歲差),
and not continue to use the numbers measured by the Shòushí (授時) calendar three hundred years prior.
Furthermore, the monthly divisions (yuèjiàn 月建) are not determined by the direction of the Big Dipper's handle (dǒubiāo 斗杓);
the Big Dipper's handle has suìchā (歲差),
but the monthly divisions do not shift.
These were all profound arguments.
On the *yǐyǒu* day of the fifth month in the second year of Chóngzhēn (1629), there was a solar eclipse.
According to Western methods, Xú Guāngqǐ, a Vice Minister of the Board of Rites, predicted
that Shùntiān Prefecture would see an eclipse of two *fēn* and some fraction,
Qióngzhōu would experience a total eclipse,
and north of Dàníng, there would be no eclipse.
The predictions of the Dàtǒng and Huíhuí calendars
for the eclipse *fēn* and time in Shùntiān
differed from Xú Guāngqǐ’s.
Eventually, Xú Guāngqǐ’s method was verified,
while the others were erroneous.
The Emperor severely reprimanded the supervising officials.
At that time, Gē Fēngnián, Chief of the Bureau of Astronomy, and others said:
“The Dàtǒng calendar was established at the beginning of the dynasty,
and it is essentially Guō Shǒujìng’s Shòushí calendar.
For two hundred and sixty years, not a single detail has been added or removed.
From the creation of the calendar in the eighteenth year of Zhìyuán (1281),
eighteen years later, in the eighth month of the third year of Dàdé (1299),
an expected eclipse did not occur.
In the sixth month of the sixth year, an eclipse occurred but was missed by prediction.
At that time, Guō Shǒujìng was managing the institute,
and even he had no recourse.
How much more so for those who rigidly adhere to the old methods?
If we continue to follow the old ways now,
there will inevitably be discrepancies in the future.”
Thereupon, the Board of Rites proposed establishing a bureau to revise it.
Xú Guāngqǐ was then appointed to oversee the revision of the calendar.
Xú Guāngqǐ said:
“Among recent scholars who discuss calendars,
most follow Guō Shǒujìng’s methods.
However, concepts such as the precession of the equinoxes,
the variation in the tropical year,
celestial latitude,
terrestrial longitude,
the proper motion of the constellations,
the epicycles of the moon and the five planets,
and the true and apparent conjunctions of the sun and moon
were unheard of in ancient times.
Only Western calendars possess them.
Without these methods,
eclipses and planetary transits
can never be precisely matched.
It is advisable to adopt their methods for comparative study and verification,
so that they can be integrated with the Dàtǒng calendar and unified.”
Later, Xú Guāngqǐ submitted ten proposals for calendar revision: First,
discuss the precession of the equinoxes,
the gradual increase and decrease in the eastward movement each year,
to correct the varying statements from ancient times regarding the lengths of one hundred, fifty, or sixty years.
Second,
discuss the small remainder of the tropical year,
which was more in the past and less now,
and the gradual changes,
as well as the reasons for the annual variation in the length of daylight,
to determine the winter solstice,
and to correct the solar terms and lunar phases.
Third,
daily measurement of the sun’s celestial longitude,
to determine the true rate of its acceleration and deceleration,
and the differences in its east-west, north-south, and high-low positions,
to calculate the sun’s path.
Fourth,
nightly measurement of the moon’s celestial longitude and latitude,
to determine the true rate of its varying speed,
and the differences in its east-west, north-south, and high-low positions,
to calculate the moon’s position.
Fifth,
precise measurement of the constellations’ celestial longitude and latitude,
to determine the rates of acceleration and deceleration, direct and retrograde motion, opposition and conjunction, and proximity and distance of the seven luminaries.
Sixth,
precise measurement of the five planets’ celestial longitude and latitude,
to determine the rates of acceleration and deceleration, retrograde motion, and visibility of their epicycles,
and the differences in their east-west, north-south, and high-low positions,
to calculate transits.
Seventh,
calculate the varying widths of the ecliptic and equatorial paths,
precisely measure the distance between the two paths,
and the distances of the moon and five planets from the ecliptic,
to determine their nodes.
Eighth,
discuss the proximity of the sun and moon to their nodes and the reasons for true and apparent conjunctions,
to determine the true rate of the difference from noon,
to correct eclipses.
Ninth,
measure the sun’s path,
and determine the degrees of the two poles' visibility above and below the horizon,
to determine the celestial latitudes,
to align the seven luminaries.
Through lunar eclipses, determine the terrestrial longitude between east and west,
to determine the exact time of eclipses.
Tenth,
following the methods of the Táng and Yuán dynasties,
measure the degrees of the two poles' visibility above and below the horizon locally,
and terrestrial longitude and latitude,
to find the varying lengths of day and night, dawn and dusk,
to correct the presence or absence, timing, and extent of eclipses.
He then recommended Lǐ Zhīzǎo, Vice Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud in Nánjīng, and the Westerners Lóng Huámín and Dèng Yùhán.
The proposal was approved.
In the ninth month, on the *guǐmǎo* day, the Calendar Bureau was opened.
In the third year (1630),
Dèng Yùhán died,
and the Westerners Tāng Ruòwàng and Luó Yǎgǔ were again invited to translate books and perform calculations.
Xú Guāngqǐ was promoted to Minister of the Board,
and continued to oversee the revision of the calendar.
At that time, Mǎ Rújiāo, a Circuit Censor for Sìchuān, recommended Léng Shǒuzhōng, a student from Zīxiàn, for his expertise in calendrical studies,
and sent his submitted calendar book to the bureau.
Xú Guāngqǐ strongly refuted its errors,
and also predicted the timing of the lunar eclipse in Sìchuān for the following April,
instructing him to compare measurements at that time.
In the first month of the fourth year (1631),
Xú Guāngqǐ submitted twenty-four volumes of calendar books.
In the summer, on the *wùwǔ* day of the fourth month,
a lunar eclipse was observed at night.
Xú Guāngqǐ predicted the *fēn*, *miǎo*, time, and direction.
He reported:
“A solar eclipse varies by location,
so the terrestrial latitude is used to calculate its extent,
and terrestrial longitude is used to calculate the added time (earlier or later).
The *fēn* and *miǎo* of a lunar eclipse
are the same throughout the empire,
and only terrestrial longitude is used to calculate the timing.
I have roughly calculated from the geographical map,
listing the initial obscuration *dù* and *fēn* for each Provincial Administration Commission.
Since the extent of the eclipse is the same everywhere,
the remaining rates can be deduced by analogy,
unlike a solar eclipse where latitude and longitude differ,
which requires detailed preparation.
Furthermore, the moon’s body is fifteen *fēn*,
so when it is completely immersed in the shadow, it is also fifteen *fēn*.
The current prediction of twenty-six *fēn* and sixty *miǎo*
is because the shadow’s body is larger than the moon.
If the eclipse occurs somewhat far from the node,
the moon’s body cannot entirely enter the shadow,
and its *fēn* are calculated solely based on the moon’s body.
This evening’s eclipse
is extremely close to the node,
so the moon entering fifteen *fēn* into the shadow constitutes totality.
It then advances another eleven *fēn* and a fraction
before light begins to return,
thus it is twenty-six *fēn* and a fraction.
The Huíhuí calendar's prediction of eighteen *fēn* and forty-seven *miǎo*
is roughly similar to this method.”
Later, Sìchuān reported that Léng Shǒuzhōng’s predicted lunar eclipse was two hours off,
while the new method was precisely accurate.
Xú Guāngqǐ again submitted twenty-one volumes of calendar books.
In the winter, on the *xīnchǒu* day of the tenth month, the new moon saw a solar eclipse.
The new method predicted that Shùntiān would see an eclipse of two *fēn* and twelve *miǎo*,
south of Yìngtiān would see no eclipse,
and north of the Great Desert would experience a total eclipse.
According to regulations, if the eclipse seen in the capital was less than three *fēn*,
no rescue rituals were performed.
Xú Guāngqǐ said: “Lunar eclipses occur at night,
so the precise timing (earlier or later) is difficult to ascertain.
However, solar eclipses are timed by gnomon,
leaving no room for discrepancy.
Therefore, the accuracy of calendrical methods
is
definitively
proven by this.
We are compiling the new method,
and it is gradually taking shape.
However, future eclipses are still far off,
and we will not witness them together with the supervising officials.
After the calendar is completed,
how
will its credibility be verified?
Moreover, there is another reason why this eclipse must be observed and measured.
According to the old method, if an eclipse occurs at true noon,
there is no time difference.
Now, this eclipse occurs at solar noon,
yet the new method still shows a time difference.
This is because the movements of the seven luminaries
all follow the ecliptic,
not the equator.
The ‘noon’ in the old method
refers to the noon on the equator,
not the true noon on the ecliptic.
Between the ecliptic and the equator,
only at the summer and winter solstices does the added time coincide with true noon,
thus aligning in degree.
Now, the tenth month new moon is still far from the winter solstice degree,
and the difference between the two noons
is twenty-three degrees and a fraction.
How can we not add or subtract simply because the added time is near noon?
This particular day,
at this particular time,
is sufficient to verify the correct calculation of time difference – that is one reason.
If the true rate of terrestrial longitude for this region
is not obtained,
then the added time is difficult to determine.
This method must be verified by measuring it several times during eclipses,
only then can it be compared and
unified.
Now, if this eclipse is measured according to the new method,
its added time and *fēn*
might not match before and after. It should be adjusted by taking into account the previously recorded terrestrial longitude and *fēn*, and deliberating on the changes.
fix,
this can be used to accurately determine the true rate of *lǐchā*,
this is the second point.
Regarding the method of *shíchā*,
one only knows that there is no addition or subtraction in the center,
but does not know that the *huángchì* is divided in the center.
Now, having seen it with one's own eyes,
everyone knows that the addition of time is due to the ecliptic.
Inferring that from this,
all other techniques are similar,
which is sufficient to know that learning is very easy,
this is the third point.
Even if the fraction is very small,
it is advisable to conduct detailed observations
to seek clear verification.
The Emperor approved his words.
At the appointed time,
Guāngqǐ led the supervising officials to pre-set the sundial,
adjust the water clock,
and use a goniometer to measure the altitude of the sundial at the peak of the eclipse.
They also opened a slanted slit in a secret room,
placed a peep tube and a telescope to measure the degree of obscuration,
and drew diagrams of the sun's fractional body to determine the magnitude of the eclipse.
The time and altitude were all consistent,
but the magnitude of the eclipse at its peak was less than two parts.
Thereupon, Guāngqǐ said:
"Since the degree and magnitude of the eclipse at its peak are in close agreement,
there is no need to trouble oneself with re-determining the *jīngdù lǐchā*.
Only the magnitude of the eclipse did not match.
The original calculator probably assumed that due to the great brightness of the sun's light,
it could diminish the moon's shadow,
and that only when the eclipse reached four or five parts or more,
would it match the original calculation.
However, this measurement,
using a peep tube in a secret room,
was able to obtain this fractional value.
If one relied solely on eyesight,
or reflection in a basin of water,
then it would be dazzling and unstable,
and the small difference might not stop at this."
At that time, there was a commoner from Mǎnchéng, Wèi Wénkuí,
who authored two books, *Lìyuán* and *Lìcè*.
He ordered his son, Xiànggān, to present *Lìyuán* to the court,
and the Tōngzhèngsī sent it to the bureau for examination.
Guāngqǐ pointed out seven matters that were highly critical: First,
the tropical year (suìshí) has shown a decreasing difference since the Hàn dynasty.
By the time of *Shòushí*, it had decreased to 24 minutes and 25 seconds.
According to Guō's method, it decreases by one per hundred years,
so it should now be 21 seconds and a fraction.
However, *Lìyuán* uses Zhào Zhīwēi's 36 seconds,
which is a sudden increase.
Second,
to find the chord and sagitta from the arc,
the accurate ratio (mìlǜ) should be used.
Yet, *Lìcè* still uses the method of "diameter one, circumference three",
which does not conform to the true numbers for arcs and chords.
Third,
the limits of the sun's varying speed (yíngsuō)
are not at the winter and summer solstices,
but rather six degrees after the winter and summer solstices.
Now, examining the sun's movement,
from the spring equinox to the summer solstice,
and from the summer solstice to the autumn equinox,
within these two limits,
the sun's hourly divisions are unequal.
Also, from the Beginning of Spring to the Beginning of Summer,
and from the Beginning of Autumn to the Beginning of Winter,
within these two limits,
the sun's hourly divisions are also unequal.
This can be seen through measurement.
Fourth,
it is stated that the moon is fastest when highest,
and slowest when lowest,
and that this is obtained by measuring with a *guībiǎo*.
This is incorrect.
The moon's varying speed (táiyīn chíjí) is an internal matter of its rotation,
while measuring height with a *biǎo* is an internal matter of its intersection.
How can they be conflated?
Moreover, the moon revolves above its orbit,
and also retrogrades,
so when highest, it moves extremely slowly westward,
and when lowest, it moves extremely quickly eastward.
The old method is exactly the opposite.
Fifth,
it is stated that there is no *shíchā* during a solar eclipse at noon.
This is incorrect.
*Shíchā* refers to the distance,
not the noon point equidistant from the equator,
but the center of the ecliptic limit, ninety degrees east and west.
Within the ecliptic limit,
some points are more than twenty degrees before or after noon.
If one only adds or subtracts based on noon,
how can it necessarily match?
Sixth,
it is stated that the fixed limit for eclipses (jiāoshí dìngxiàn)
is eight degrees for the lunar calendar and six degrees for the solar calendar.
This is incorrect.
For a solar eclipse,
it should be seventeen degrees in the lunar calendar
and eight degrees in the solar calendar.
For a lunar eclipse, it is twelve degrees for both lunar and solar calendars.
Seventh,
*Lìcè* states:
"In the sixth year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Wén of Sòng, in the eleventh month, on the *jǐchǒu* new moon,
there was a solar eclipse that was not 'hook-like' (bùjìn rúgōu),
and stars were seen during the day.
Now, calculating it with *Shòushí*,
it only eclipsed by six parts and ninety-six seconds,
thus Guō's calendar is erroneous."
Indeed, lunar eclipses are the same everywhere,
but solar eclipses vary in different regions.
The Southern Sòng capital was in Jīnlíng,
while Guō's calendar was compiled in Yāndì.
The difference in the elevation of the north pole is eight degrees.
Given that it was in the eleventh month, the eclipse difference should be slightly less than two parts.
What he meant by
"not 'hook-like'"
would be around nine parts.
Guō's calendar calculated it to be slightly less than seven parts,
which is a close match,
not an error.
Our bureau now determines solar eclipse magnitudes,
first by the *jiāo* (node),
then by the *dì* (location),
then by the *shí* (time);
none can be omitted.
Subsequently, Wénkuí repeatedly argued and raised difficulties,
so Guāngqǐ further elaborated on his previous statements,
compiling them into *Xuélì Xiǎobiàn*.
His discussions on the fractional remainder of the tropical year (*suìshí xiǎoyú*) and the variation of solar eclipses (*rìshí biànchā*) are particularly clear.
He stated:
"The fractional remainder of the tropical year
gradually decreased from the Hàn dynasty to the Yuán dynasty.
Now, the new method uses a tropical year
even shorter than that of the Yuán.
Those who do not understand will surely believe that it is not only earlier than Xiāntiān,
but even earlier than Dàtǒng.
However, calculating the winter solstice of *rénshēn*,
Dàtǒng yields the first *kè* of the *yínzhèng* hour on *jǐhài*,
while the new method yields the first *kè* and eighteen *fēn* of the *chénchū* hour.
Why is this?
Because the true year and the moon's *bùyuèlí* are similar;
the winter solstice has no fixed rate,
just as the fixed new moon (*dìngshuò*) and fixed full moon (*dìngwàng*) have no fixed rate.
Since the new moon and full moon have no fixed rate,
they should be adjusted by adding or subtracting from the mean new moon and full moon.
Since the winter solstice has no fixed rate,
it should be adjusted by adding or subtracting from the mean year.
Therefore, although the mean winter solstice of the new method
is earlier than Dàtǒng,
the fixed winter solstice is consistently later than Dàtǒng."
He also said:
"In the second year of Tiānshèng of Emperor Rénzōng of Sòng, the *jiǎzǐ* year,
on the *dīnghài* new moon in the fifth month,
the calendar officials calculated that there would be no eclipse,
while all other calendars predicted an eclipse.
According to the rules, there indeed should have been an eclipse,
but in reality, there was no eclipse at that time.
How can this be explained now?
This is because solar eclipses have a *biànchā* (variation) method.
When the moon is in the lunar calendar,
more than ten degrees from the node,
according to the rules, an eclipse should occur.
However, at this specific day and location, the north-south difference
transforms into an east-west difference.
Therefore, when discussing celestial motion,
the Earth's center is indeed aligned with the sun and moon,
so an eclipse is certainly not missed.
But from what human eyes see,
the sun and moon, which were previously close, appear to become distant,
so no eclipse is actually observed.
This was only the case in Biànjīng.
If one were several thousand *lǐ* east of Biàn,
an eclipse would gradually be seen,
and several tens of thousands of *lǐ* to the northeast,
a total eclipse would be seen.
Indeed, *biànchā* varies constantly;
sometimes much changes to little,
sometimes little changes to much,
sometimes existence changes to non-existence,
and sometimes non-existence changes to existence.
The difficulty in calendar calculation
lies entirely in these matters."
Soon after,
Guāngqǐ entered the Grand Secretariat (Nèigé).
On the fifteenth day of the ninth month of the fifth year,
there was a lunar eclipse.
The Astronomical Bureau calculated the initial phase (chūkū) to be at the first ke of mǎo hour.
Guāngqǐ and others calculated it to be at the third ke of mǎo hour.
The Huíhuí (Islamic) method calculated it to be at the first ke of chén hour.
The three methods differed,
leading to an imperial inquiry.
On the appointed day, observations were made,
but due to cloudy skies, nothing could be seen,
and thus there was no way to verify them.
Guāngqǐ then fully explained the reasons for the differences among the three methods,
stating: "The addition and subtraction of time (shíkè)
are due to the two errors of yíngsuō and chídá.
As for the yíngsuō error,
the old method starts from the winter and summer solstices,
while the new method starts from the highest point (zuìgāo).
The highest point
has a varying degree of movement (xíngfēn).
Only during the Shàoxīng era of the Sòng dynasty was it at the same degree as the summer solstice.
Guō Shǒujìng, a century after this,
was off by a degree and a fraction,
which was not yet noticed.
Now the highest point
is six degrees after the summer solstice.
This is why the yíngsuō errors of these two methods differ.
As for the chídá error,
the old method only uses one full cycle (zhuǎnzhōu),
which the new method calls the zìxínglún.
Beyond the zìxíng,
there are also two additional cycles (liǎngcìlún).
This is why the chídá errors of these two methods differ.
As for the Huíhuí calendar being different,
it might be
due to the sìyìng,
or due to the lǐchā.
Your servant truly does not understand the reason.
In summary,
all three schools follow their original methods for astronomical calculations
and cannot change their methods to accommodate each other.
In the future, there are two matters that should be thoroughly investigated: Firstly, the extent of the eclipse (shífēn duōguǎ).
During a solar eclipse,
the sun's bright light
often makes the eclipse appear before it is actually seen.
During a lunar eclipse,
the encroaching atmospheric disturbances
often make the eclipse appear to be seen before it actually occurs.
The difference can be more than one fen.
Now, to clearly observe the true extent of the eclipse,
there is the recently created kuī tǒng.
During a solar eclipse,
its light and image can be captured in a dark room,
projected onto a white silk screen.
From the initial phase (chūkū) to the full recovery (fùyuán),
the fractions will be truly accurate,
clearly without error.
For a lunar eclipse,
it can be used to observe the moments of convergence and divergence of the two celestial bodies from below,
making the outlines clear.
This is distinctly different from visual estimation.
This is the method for determining the extent.
Secondly, the timing of additions (jiāshí zǎowǎn).
For the technique of determining time,
the water clock (húlòu) is the old method,
and the wheeled clock (lúnzhōng) is the new method.
However, neither is as good as seeking accuracy from the sun and stars.
By day, use the sun;
by night, use any star.
Both
are measured for their longitude and latitude with instruments
and then calculated.
This is the method for determining time.
Once these two methods are established,
then the precision and errors of all techniques,
even to the minutest detail,
will not escape detection.
Ancient and modern lunar eclipses are not recorded in any histories.
As for solar eclipses,
from the Hàn to the Suí dynasties,
there were two hundred ninety-three in total,
of which seventy-seven occurred on the last day of the month (huì),
three on the day before the huì,
and three on the second day of the month.
Such was the inaccuracy.
From the Táng to the Five Dynasties, there were one hundred ten in total,
of which one occurred on the huì,
one on the second day of the month,
and one on the third day of the month.
This was slightly more accurate.
The Sòng dynasty had one hundred forty-eight in total,
with none on the huì,
which was even more accurate.
However, there were still thirteen
cases where an eclipse was predicted but did not occur.
The Yuán dynasty had forty-five in total,
also with none on the huì.
There was still one case where an eclipse was predicted but did not occur,
one where an eclipse occurred but was not predicted,
and one where a night eclipse was recorded as a day eclipse.
As for time differences reaching four or five ke,
this was already the case at that time.
It can be seen that for matters of infinite scope and depth,
it requires accumulated time and generations
to gradually perceive their beginnings
and subtle details.
Therefore, from the Hàn dynasty until now, seventeen hundred years have passed,
and thirteen schools have established methods.
Even Guō Shǒujìng, who was the most excellent,
still could not avoid a difference of several ke.
How, then,
can those who cling to old methods
be expected to be precise?"
In that year,
Guāngqǐ further submitted thirty volumes of almanacs.
In the tenth month of winter the following year,
Guāngqǐ resigned from calendrical duties due to illness,
and Lǐ Tiānjīng, the Shan̄dōng Vice-Administrator, replaced him.
A month later, Guāngqǐ passed away.
In the seventh year,
Wèi Wénkuí submitted a memorial,
stating that the calendrical officials' predictions for eclipses and solar terms were all incorrect.
Thereupon, Wénkuí was ordered to enter the capital for verification.
At that time, there were four schools discussing the calendar:
besides Dàtǒng and Huíhuí,
the Western (Xīyáng) method was established as the Western Bureau (Xījú),
and Wénkuí's method as the Eastern Bureau (Dōngjú).
Each person's statement was different,
confusing like a multitude of lawsuits.
Tiānjīng meticulously submitted twenty-nine volumes of almanacs,
along with a star screen (xīngpíng).
Both had been made under the supervision of the late assistant Guāngqǐ, who directed the Westerners.
Tiānjīng pre-calculated the conjunctions, oppositions, and movements of the five planets,
stating:
"On the twenty-fourth day of the intercalary eighth month,
Jupiter will infringe upon the Jīshīqì asterism.
On the fourth day of the ninth month, at early dusk,
Mars and Saturn will be at the same degree.
On the seventh day, at mǎo zhèng,
Venus and Saturn will be at the same degree.
On the eleventh day, at early dusk,
Venus and Mars will be at the same degree.
The old method predicts Mars and Saturn to be at the same degree
on the seventh,
which is three days later.
Venus and Mars at the same degree on the third,
which is eight days earlier."
However, Wénkuí stated
that Tiānjīng's report
of Jupiter infringing upon Jīshī was incorrect.
Tiānjīng further stated:
"On the night of the twenty-fifth day of the intercalary eighth month and the night of the first day of the ninth month,
I, along with Minister of Rites Chén Liùgē and others,
used a kuīguǎn (telescope) for measurement.
Jīshī was observed to be a cluster of dozens of small stars,
and Jupiter and Jīshī
were both visible within the kuīguǎn.
The circular diameter of the kuīguǎn is about an inch;
only if two stars are within thirty fēn of each other
can they be seen together.
For example, the three stars of the Zīxiù constellation are thirty-seven fēn apart,
thus they cannot be seen together.
However, Wénkuí merely bases his statements on conjecture,
without actual measurement.
He claims that on the second day, Jupiter was already in front of Liǔxiù.
How, then, could it have crossed Guǐxiù and flown over previously?"
Tiānjīng further calculated Jupiter's retrograde and prograde motions,
passing through Guǐxiù twice.
Its degrees, minutes, and time measurements
were later all verified.
Consequently, Wénkuí's argument was refuted.
Tiānjīng then submitted another thirty-two volumes of almanacs,
along with various instruments such as the sundial (rìguǐ), star dial (xīngguǐ), and kuī tǒng.
In the fourth month of the eighth year,
he again submitted the almanac for the movements of the Seven Luminaries (Qīzhèng) for the Yǐhài and Bǐngzǐ years, as well as twenty-six articles on reviewing and amending calendrical methods.
Its discussion of the seven *zhèng* [the sun, moon, and five planets] in the seven *gōngshuō* [public discussions] is as follows: First, the responses of the various luminaries should be reformed.
The root calculation for the parallel movements of the sun, moon, and five planets determines their responses,
which are the numbers of a certain luminary at a certain day and hour occupying a certain palace-lodge.
Now, the new method has reformed and set these responses,
all starting from the *wùchén* year of *Chóngzhēn* 1
after the Winter Solstice,
at midnight on the *jǐmǎo* day.
Second, to measure the movements of the various luminaries,
the ecliptic instrument [celestial globe] should be used.
The sun travels along the ecliptic,
and the moon and planets each have their own paths,
moving in and out of the ecliptic,
not along the celestial equator.
If measured with an equatorial instrument,
the obtained degrees of longitude and latitude
must be converted using the ecliptic-equator conversion table;
it is not as convenient as using the ecliptic instrument
to directly obtain the intrinsic degrees of the seven *zhèng*.
Third, the movements of the seven *zhèng* vary in different places.
The times of eclipses of the sun and moon, seen from east and west,
are inherently different,
which is beyond doubt.
Thus, how can the sun's passage through the twenty-four solar terms,
and the occultations, eclipses, and transgressions of the moon and five planets,
not follow the same principle as eclipses?
Therefore, although the new method's tables are based on
Shùntiānfǔ,
there are distinct methods for calculating
the movements in various other places.
Fourth, the additive and subtractive corrections for the various luminaries,
using the three-difference method of flat, standing, and fixed,
are still insufficient.
Calculating intrinsic motion by adding and subtracting parallel values
is a crucial task for calendrical experts.
However, the heavens are truly spherical,
and different from parallel [linear] types;
the old three-difference method,
all derived from *gōugǔ* [right-angled triangles] parallel definitions,
does not align with the celestial bodies.
Therefore, the true values of
various increases, decreases, gains, and losses
could not be obtained.
Now, the new method's additive and subtractive tables,
by aligning circles with circles,
can finally match the heavens.
Fifth, the longitude of the various luminaries can be determined at any time and place.
The old method, to find the longitude of a certain luminary on a certain day,
first required calculating the palace-lodge degrees and stellar positions of each luminary on the Winter Solstice,
and only then, by ratio-calculating the daily movements of each segment, could it be obtained.
The current method is not restricted by time, day, or location;
one simply consults the relevant table for calculation.
Sixth, "diameter one, circumference three" [π=3] is not the true method of arcs and chords.
Ancient calendrical experts measured circles with straight lines,
calling it the arc-and-chord method,
but calculating with "diameter one, circumference three"
is erroneous.
Now, the table of eight functions of circular division [trigonometric table] has been established;
its use is simple yet profound.
Arcs and chords,
and other lines,
can be obtained with just one multiplication or division.
Seventh, spherical triangles with three arcs
cannot be fully described by *gōugǔ*.
Ancient methods for measuring the heavens were based on *gōugǔ*,
but *gōugǔ* can handle right angles
but not oblique angles.
Moreover, the heavens are a sphere,
and on its surface, intersections with various paths generate many three-arc shapes,
*gōugǔ* is insufficient to fully describe them.
The discussion of stars in four points: First, the proper motion of fixed stars,
which is what is called precession,
is calculated from the ecliptic pole.
The degrees of each star from the celestial equator pole
differ between ancient and modern times.
Their distance inside or outside the celestial equator
also differs between ancient and modern times.
However, their distance from the ecliptic pole or their position inside or outside the ecliptic
remains constant throughout history,
which indicates that the sun, moon, and five planets all travel along the ecliptic.
Therefore, the proper motion of fixed stars
should be calculated from the ecliptic pole,
to determine the rate of precession.
Second, the stellar degrees of various lodges differ between ancient and modern times.
Fixed stars have the ecliptic pole as their pole;
therefore, the degrees of movement of each lodge star
are sometimes near and sometimes far from the celestial equator pole.
As they move closer to the pole,
the lines of the celestial equator passing through the lodge star become denser,
and the equatorial arc of that lodge is smaller.
As they move further from the pole,
the lines passing through the lodge star become sparser,
and the equatorial arc of that lodge is larger.
This is due to the difference between the two paths and two poles,
not because the lodge stars have different motions
or have changed positions.
For example, the *Zīsù* lodge star:
the Hàn [Dynasty] measured its distance from *Shēnsù* at two degrees,
the Táng [Dynasty] at one degree,
the Sòng [Dynasty] during *Chóngníng* at half a degree,
and Yuán [Dynasty]'s Guō Shǒujìng at five *fēn*.
Now, when measured,
it is not only without *fēn* [minutes],
but it has even encroached upon *Shēnsù* by twenty-four *fēn*.
Is this not a proof?
Third, determining time by measuring stars at night.
The sun moves left [westward] along the celestial equator,
fifteen degrees for every hour.
Now, measure the degrees of any star before or after the meridian circle,
then add or subtract its ecliptic longitude from the sun's ecliptic longitude,
to obtain the sun's degrees from the meridian circle,
thereby converting it into true time.
Fourth, the twelve zodiacal palaces defined during the Sòng [Dynasty],
at certain lodge degrees,
cannot now be defined at those same lodge degrees.
This is because fixed stars have proper motion,
and the lodge degrees have shifted to the right.
The discussion of the sun in four points: First, the limits of the sun's increase and decrease [of apparent speed]
are not the Winter and Summer Solstices,
nor what are called the highest and highest oppositions.
These limits shift to the right annually,
and have now passed six degrees and some more beyond the solstices.
Second, measuring the Winter and Summer Solstices with a *guībiǎo* [gnomon]
is not a good method.
Around the solstices, the sun's north-south movement
is very slight;
for a *biǎo* [pole] of one *zhàng*,
the daily shadow difference is no more than one *fēn* and thirty *miǎo*,
meaning one *miǎo* yields more than six *kè*.
If there is a measurement error of two or three *miǎo*,
it results in an error of nearly twenty *kè*.
How can accuracy be achieved?
The current method exclusively uses the Spring and Autumn Equinoxes,
because at these times, the sun travels twenty-four *fēn* north-south in one day,
and the daily shadow difference is one *cùn* and two *fēn*.
Thus, an error of one or two *miǎo* in measurement
results in less than one *kè* of calculation error,
which is most precise compared to the solstices.
Third, the times of sunrise and sunset
should be calculated from Shùntiānfǔ.
Because the elevation of the North Pole differs in various places,
the times of dawn and dusk also vary accordingly.
The *Dàtǒng* [calendar] calculated based on Yìngtiānfǔ,
therefore, the lengths of day and night
and the east-west bands of lunar and solar eclipses
it predicted were inaccurate.
Now, it is reformed based on Shùntiānfǔ.
Fourth, the "equal solar terms"
are not the true celestial solar terms.
The old method's solar term periods
were one twenty-fourth of a year's circumference.
However, the sun's movement
has increases and decreases,
and cannot be equally divided.
If equally divided,
then after the Spring Equinox, it would be two days later [than observed],
and before the Autumn Equinox, two days earlier.
Now, all are reformed.
The discussion of the moon in four points: First, besides the New and Full Moons,
there are separate increase and decrease corrections;
one single addition or subtraction is insufficient to cover them all.
The old method defined the moon's parallel motion,
calculating New and Full Moon corrections,
roughly five degrees and some more.
However, the amount at the two quarter-phases varies;
even the *Shòushí* [calendar] states that outside of New and Full Moons,
the parallel values are not fixed,
indicating the principle was clear but the method not fully specified.
Now, in addition to the primary correction,
a secondary correction is used,
called the "second and third mean values."
Second, the latitude cannot be fixed at five degrees;
it varies at different times.
Ancient and modern calendrical experts, using eclipse fractions and intersection ranges,
determined the distance between the ecliptic and lunar path to be approximately five degrees.
However, outside of New and Full Moons, the distance between the two paths
has increases and decreases,
the greatest distance being one-third of five degrees.
If there are two eclipses in a month,
and one seeks the distance from the ecliptic as five degrees at the quarter phases using an instrument,
it will not align with the heavens.
Third, the nodal movement has increase and decrease corrections.
The *Luó* and *Jìdū* [ascending and descending nodes] are the true and mean nodal movements,
which in ancient and modern times were considered parallel.
Now, upon careful measurement,
the moon is sometimes on the node;
if calculated as parallel,
it will certainly not match the calculations.
Therefore, an addition/subtraction [correction] is established,
as the mean value for nodal movement.
Fourth, there is no *Zǐqì* [Purple Qi] in celestial movements.
It was previously said to originate from intercalary surpluses,
and also to be the residual qi of wood.
Now, upon careful examination of the various luminaries,
no observable phenomenon confirms it,
thus it is known to be a baseless addition.
Four proposals regarding eclipses: Firstly, the angular diameters of the Sun and Moon are not constant.
This is because the Sun and Moon sometimes appear at their highest,
and sometimes at their lowest,
so their distance from Earth varies,
and their apparent sizes vary.
Also, due to varying distances, the Moon's shadow
is sometimes thicker, sometimes thinner,
which is why their angular diameters cannot be treated as constant.
Secondly, the precise mid-point of a solar eclipse is not determined by noon (午正),
but by the 90-degree point on the ecliptic.
Since the north-south and east-west deviations are all based on the ecliptic,
how can the time difference not be determined by the beginning and end points on the ecliptic when seeking the mid-point?
Moreover, where the ecliptic emerges above the horizon,
its two quadrants naturally have their own heights,
and also their own mid-points.
If this principle is not clear,
what should be added might be subtracted,
and what should be subtracted might be added.
All instances where additions of time do not match are due to this.
Thirdly, the duration from the initial contact to the final restoration of a solar eclipse
is always unequal,
and does not conform to the "two times halved" theory.
Since parallax can transform true motion into apparent motion,
when comparing the moments before and after the greatest eclipse using parallax,
it is rare for them not to be discrepant.
If the parallax is not constant before and after the greatest eclipse,
how can the apparent motion be constant before and after?
Now, if we use apparent motion to calculate the transformed times,
it is clear that the initial contact and final restoration
cannot be equal.
Fourthly, all regions should calculate the times and magnitudes of solar eclipses according to their terrestrial longitudes.
This is because the Sun and Moon are seen to rise and set at different times in different places on the Earth's surface,
due to their east-west positions.
Consequently, the times obtained are also different.
Therefore, although the eclipse phenomenon is one, the times observed vary.
This principle applies to both solar and lunar eclipses.
However, in the case of a solar eclipse, because the parallax varies with location,
the apparent distance of the Moon varies,
and thus the observed magnitude of the eclipse also varies.
Three proposals regarding the five planets: Firstly, the five planets should use the Sun's apparent motion,
and not be fixed by intervals.
This is because the five planets are all centered on the Sun:
they move faster when in conjunction with the Sun,
and retrograde when in opposition.
Furthermore, the Sun's motion varies in speed,
so the number of days for the conjunctions and occultations of the five planets
is sometimes fewer, sometimes more.
It is therefore impossible to fix their degrees and minutes by intervals.
Secondly, the five planets should have latitudinal motion added.
This is because the five planets have specific degrees of distance when they enter and exit the ecliptic.
Moreover, the three planets Mùxīng (木星), Tǔxīng (土星), and Huǒxīng (火星) have
large ecliptic latitudes when in opposition to the Sun,
and small ecliptic latitudes when in conjunction with the Sun.
The two planets Jīnxīng (金星) and Shuǐxīng (水星) have small latitudes when moving direct or occulted,
and large latitudes when moving retrograde or occulted.
Thirdly, when observing the five planets,
stars should be used as the standard.
Beyond using an ecliptic instrument for stellar observations,
instruments like the arc-and-arrow (弧矢) should be used.
By measuring the apparent distance of the observed planet from two stars in degrees and minutes,
and calculating according to the method,
the true longitude and latitude of the star can be obtained.
Alternatively, drawing a chart can also obviate the need for calculation.
At this time, the new methods, books, and instruments were all complete,
and repeated observations of eclipses and planetary transits consistently matched closely.
However, Wèi Wénkuí (魏文魁) and others obstructed them in many ways,
and the court eunuchs indeed controlled the situation.
Because of this, the emperor's will could not be decided.
He decreed that Tiānjīng (天經) and the Directorate of Astronomy (監局) should sincerely and thoroughly investigate,
and strive for a unified agreement.
That year,
Tiānjīng's predictions for the reappearance and disappearance of Shuǐxīng and the position of Mùxīng
all differed from the Dàtǒng (大統) system,
but the new method matched.
He also predicted that on the 27th day of the eighth month, at the second *ke* (刻) of *yínzhèng* (寅正),
Mùxīng, Huǒxīng, and the Moon (三曜) would all be at 6 degrees of Zhāng (張) constellation.
However, the Dàtǒng system predicted Mùxīng at 4 degrees of Zhāng,
and Huǒxīng and the Moon at 3 degrees of Zhāng.
On the appointed date,
they were indeed all at 6 degrees of Zhāng.
On the *Xīnyǒu* (辛酉) day, the 15th day of the first month of the ninth year,
a lunar eclipse was observed at dawn.
Tiānjīng, Dàtǒng, Huíhuí (回回), and the Eastern Bureau (東局) each separately predicted the times in minutes and seconds for the initial contact, greatest eclipse, and final restoration.
Tiānjīng, fearing that clouds might obscure the view on the appointed day,
calculated the times observed in Hénán (河南) and Shānxī (山西) based on longitudinal difference,
and petitioned to send officials to these places for verification.
On that day,

Tiānjīng, along with Luó Yǎgǔ (羅雅谷), Tāng Ruòwàng (湯若望), Dàlǐ Píngshì Wáng Yìnglín (大理評事王應遴), ritual official Lǐ Chàng (李焻), and directorate officials Shǒu Dēng (守登) and Wénkuí (文魁), went to the observation platform for verification.
Only Tiānjīng's predictions matched uniquely.
Afterwards,
the reports from Hénán fully matched the original predictions,
while in Shānxī, clouds obscured the eclipse, making verification impossible.
The Emperor, seeing that the new method was closer for predicting the lunar eclipse,
but that the 15th day was *yǔshuǐ* (雨水) (Rain Water),
while Tiānjīng had predicted the 13th day for *yǔshuǐ*,
ordered him to clarify the matter again.
Tiānjīng replied:
There are two methods for calculating solar terms: one is the equal solar term (平節氣),
and the other is the fixed solar term (定節氣).
For the equal solar term,
the actual length of a year
is divided equally into twenty-four parts,
where each part
is roughly fifteen days
and represents one solar term.
Therefore, starting from the winter solstice before the New Year,
it must pass 60 days and 87 *ke* and a fraction to reach
*yǔshuǐ*.
This is what the old method predicted as the second *ke* of *zǐzhèng* (子正) on the 15th day.
For the fixed solar term,
360 degrees are taken as the circumference of the heavens,
and also divided equally into twenty-four parts,
where each part
is fifteen degrees and represents one solar term.
Starting from the winter solstice before the New Year,
after 59 days and 2 *ke* and a fraction,
the Sun's
passage of 60 degrees marks *yǔshuǐ*.
This is what the new method predicted as the second *ke* and eight *fen* (分) of *mǎozhū* (卯初) on the 13th day.
The Sun's motion waxes and wanes;
if not adjusted by methods of addition and subtraction,
it will not conform to the heavens.
How can the actual length of a year be equally divided for solar terms?
If we prove this with the spring equinox,
the principle becomes even clearer.
The equinox
is the
point where the ecliptic and celestial equator intersect.
When the Sun reaches this point,
day and night are exactly equal.
The old method, on the 14th day of the second month,
noted that day was 50 *ke* and night was 50 *ke*.
This is correct.
If day and night are already equal on the 14th day,
then the new method's prediction of the spring equinox on the 14th day matches the heavens,
while the old method's prediction of the 16th day
is two days
behind the heavens.
Knowing the spring equinox,
then the autumn equinox and all other solar terms can be known,
and there will be no doubt about *yǔshuǐ*.
Afterwards, as the spring equinox approached, Tiānjīng
went to the observation platform every noon to measure the Sun's altitude at noon.
On the 14th day of the second month, the altitude was 50 degrees and 8 *fen*;
on the 15th day, it was 50 degrees and 33 *fen*.
Tiānjīng then said: The celestial North Pole in the capital (Jīngshī 經師) is 39 degrees and 55 *fen* above the horizon,
so the celestial equator should be 50 degrees and 5 *fen* high.
On the day of the spring equinox, the Sun is exactly on the celestial
equator,
and its noon altitude is equal to the altitude of the celestial equator.
Beyond this, the Sun's altitude must gradually increase.
Now, if we take the altitude measured on the 14th day,
and add
the terrestrial radius difference of 2 *fen*,
it is already 5 *fen* more than the celestial equator.
This is because the original prediction placed the spring equinox slightly after 2 *ke* and 5 *fen* of *mǎozhèng* (卯正).
At that time, the daily latitudinal motion was slightly less than 24 *fen*,
and the time difference was 21 *ke* and 5 *fen*,
so the latitudinal motion should be increased by slightly more than 5 *fen*.
By the 15th day,
including the terrestrial radius, the altitude compared to the celestial equator
was already 30 *fen* more.
How much more on the 16th day?
Therefore, the spring equinox should be on the 14th,
not on the 16th.
The autumn equinox is also similar.
He also presented a solar term diagram saying:
The inner circle, divided into 365 and a quarter degrees,
represents solar degrees.
