The outer circle, divided into 360 degrees,
represents celestial degrees.
Starting
from the winter solstice,
after 91 days, 31 *ke*, and 6 *fen*,
the spring equinox is reached.
This is limited by solar days,
but in terms of celestial degrees, it has already exceeded two degrees
and more.
And after 273 days, 93 *ke*,
and 19 *fen*,
the autumn equinox is immediately reached.
This is also limited by solar days,
but in terms of celestial degrees,
it is less than two degrees and more.
Is it not the case that the old method is two days behind the heavens for the spring equinox,
and two days ahead of the heavens for the autumn equinox?
In the first month, *xīnchǒu* day, of the tenth year,
there was a solar eclipse.
The *Tiānjīng* and others had predicted that in the capital, one *fēn* and ten seconds of the eclipse would be visible.
In *Yìngtiān* and other provinces, the *fēn* and seconds varied,
with only Yúnnán and Tàiyuán not experiencing the eclipse at all.
The times of initial contact, maximum eclipse, and last contact also differed.
The *Dàtǒng* predicted one *fēn* and sixty-three seconds of eclipse,
the *Huíhuí* predicted three *fēn* and seventy seconds,
while the Eastern Bureau's prediction was only over thirty seconds of obscured light due to a 'wandering vapor'.
However, when the eclipse occurred,
only the *Tiānjīng* prediction was accurate.
At this time, there was a move to abolish the *Dàtǒng* [calendar]
and adopt new methods.
Thereupon, Guō Zhèngzhōng (郭正中), the Zhīzhōu (知州) of Dàizhōu (代州) who managed the calendar affairs of the other bureau, said:
"The Chinese calendar absolutely cannot be entirely abolished,
and the Western calendar absolutely cannot be exclusively implemented.
Each of the four calendars has its strengths and weaknesses;
we should combine the various schools,
and also adopt Western methods."
In the first month of the eleventh year,
an imperial edict was issued to continue using the *Dàtǒng* calendar.
However, for phenomena like solar and lunar eclipses,
and the new, full, and crescent moons,
which, due to the passage of many years, showed discrepancies,
new methods and *Huíhuí* (回回) calculations were to be widely sought and referenced, and allowed to coexist.
That year,
*Tiānjīng* (天經) was promoted to Guānglùsì Qīng (光祿寺卿),
still managing calendar affairs.
In the twelfth month of the fourteenth year,
*Tiānjīng* stated:
"The *Dàtǒng* method for inserting an intercalary month [leap month] only considers months without a 'middle qi' (*zhōngqì*),
while the new method especially considers the timing of the conjunctions (*héshuò*) before and after.
In the new calendar for the fifteenth year that has been submitted,
the 'middle qi' for the tenth and twelfth months
happens to occur before the moment of the next month's conjunction.
Therefore, although there is no 'middle qi' within these months,
they are not actually intercalary months.
This is because if the 'qi' occurs before the conjunction,
then this 'qi' still belongs to the last day of the preceding month.
As for the second month of the sixteenth year, it only has the 'Jīngzhé' (*jīngzhé*) solar term.
However, the 'Chūnfēn' (*chūnfēn*) 'middle qi'
occurs after the conjunction of the third month.
Thus, the second month is an intercalary first month,
and the third month is undoubtedly the second month."
At that time, the Emperor was already deeply aware of the precision of Western methods.
By the *yǐchǒu* day in the third month of the sixteenth year, when there was a solar eclipse,
the prediction again proved uniquely accurate.
In the eighth month,
an imperial edict declared that Western methods were indeed precise,
and it was to be immediately adopted as the *Dàtǒng* calendar method
and circulated throughout the empire.
Not long after, there was a national change,
and it was ultimately not implemented.
Our present dynasty adopted it
as the *Shíxiànlì* (時憲曆).
According to the Míng (明) system,
calendar officials were hereditary positions.
During the Chénghuá (成化) and Hóngzhì (弘治) eras, they could still propose revisions and reforms,
but after the Wànlì (萬曆) era, they merely clung to their old ways and preserved outdated practices.
Among those who were not calendar officials but understood the calendar,
besides Zhèng Shìzǐ (鄭世子),
Táng Shùnzhī (唐順之), Zhōu Shùxué (周述學), Chén Rǎng (陳壤), Yuán Huáng (袁黃), and Léi Zōng (雷宗) all had writings.
Táng Shùnzhī did not have a complete book,
but his discussions are scattered in Zhōu Shùxué's *Lìzōng Tōngyì* (曆宗通議) and *Lìzōng Zhōngjīng* (曆宗中經).
Yuán Huáng authored *Lìfǎ Xīnshū* (曆法新書),
and its 'three origins' of heaven, earth, and man
were based on Chén Rǎng.
Léi Zōng also authored *Hébì Liánzhū Lìfǎ* (合璧連珠曆法).
All of them integrated the *Huíhuí* calendar into the *Shòushí* (授時) [calendar],
and although they could not achieve the subtlety of Zhèng Shìzǐ,
they also made discoveries
regarding the principles of both Chinese and Western calendars.
Xíng Yúnlù's (邢雲路) *Gǔjīn Lǜlì Kǎo* (古今律曆考)
is said by some to have originally come from the hand of Wèi Wénkuí (魏文魁).
Wèi Wénkuí's scholarship was fundamentally superficial,
so it's no wonder that his commentary on the *Shòushí* calendar
failed to grasp its essence.
Those Westerners who came to China
all called themselves Europeans.
Their calendar methods were similar to the *Huíhuí* [calendar],
but more precise.
It has been observed in previous dynasties that
most people from distant lands who discussed calendar methods were from the Western Regions,
while none were heard from the east, south, or north.
(The Táng (唐) dynasty's *Jiǔzhí Lì* (九執曆),
the Yuán (元) dynasty's *Wànnián Lì* (萬年曆),
and the *Huíhuí* calendar translated during the Hóngwǔ (洪武) era
were all from the Western Regions.)
Perhaps when Yáo (堯) commanded Xī (羲), Hé (和), Zhòng (仲), and Shū (叔) to reside in the four directions,
Xī Zhòng (羲仲), Xī Shū (羲叔), and Hé Shū (和叔) were limited to Yúyí (嵎夷), Nánjiāo (南交), and Shuòfāng (朔方) respectively.
Only Hé Zhòng was simply told to
"reside in the west,"
without a geographical limit.
Was this not because the influence of civilization had spread far to the west at that time?
By the end of the Zhōu (周) dynasty,
the descendants of astronomers were dispersed.
The Western Regions, Tiānfāng (天方) and other countries,
bordered the western frontier.
They were not obstructed by a vast sea like the east and south,
nor did they fear the extreme cold of the far north.
Thus, carrying books and instruments and venturing west
was naturally convenient for them.
Europe is west of the *Huíhuí* lands.
Their customs are similar,
but their habit of curiosity, love of novelty, and competitive spirit surpasses them.
Therefore, their calendar methods share the same origin as the *Huíhuí*,
but they have been improved from generation to generation,
thus surpassing what the *Huíhuí* could achieve.
This is also due to their competitive customs.
Since Xī and Hé lost their traditional duties,
among the ancient texts that can still be seen,
only *Zhōubì* (周髀) remains.
However, the Westerners' armillary sphere and equatorial mounting instruments,
the theory of five climatic zones (hot and cold),
the principle of a spherical earth,
and the methods of right triangles
all fall within the scope of the *Zhōubì*.
This also shows the origin and lineage of their knowledge.
Indeed, extensively seeking and broadly collecting to continue the lost traditions of a thousand years
is also in the spirit of "when ritual is lost, seek it in the wilds."
Therefore, this detailed discussion is presented.
Collation Notes
Gazetteer 8, Calendar 2, *Dàtǒng Lìfǎ* (大統曆法) 1, Part I (*Fǎyuán*) (法原)
Each calendar maker has an original basis,
which should be thoroughly recorded in the histories
to allow later generations to examine it.
For example, the *tàichū* (太初) calendar's derivation from pitch pipes and musical intervals,
and the *dàyǎn* (大衍) calendar's commencement with divination stalks,
are all detailed in this gazetteer.
The *Shòushí* calendar prioritizes astronomical observation and mathematical calculation,
seeking only to align with the heavens,
without being constrained by pitch pipes or hexagrams.
However, the principles on which its methods were established,
the derivation of its numbers,
as well as gnomon shadows and stellar positions,
are all contained in complete books.
In the biographies of Guō Shǒujìng (郭守敬) and Qí Lǚqiān (齊履謙),
there are book titles that can be examined.
The *Yuán Shǐ* (元史) (History of the Yuán Dynasty) indiscriminately compiled information,
only preserving Lǐ Qiān's (李謙) discourse records and the initial draft of the *Lìjīng* (曆經).
Its subsequent revisions of the 'three ratios' and the 'tables of computation',
as well as the methods of circle segmentation and arc-and-chord,
and the origins of the three-error corrections (level, standing, fixed),
were all completely omitted and not recorded.
This caused the subtle intentions of the authors to be lost,
to the regret of those who understood.
Now, based on the *Dàtǒng Lì Tōngguǐ* (大統曆通軌) and various *Lìcǎo* (曆草) books,
we have somewhat organized it,
starting with 'Principles of Calculation' (*Fǎyuán*),
followed by 'Tables of Computation' (*Lìchéng*),
and then 'Astronomical Computation' (*Tuībù*).
The 'Principles of Calculation' section has seven subheadings: "Gnomon and Observation of Distances" (*Jùgǔ Cèwàng*),
"Arc and Chord for Circle Segmentation" (*Húshǐ Gēyuán*),
"Difference between Ecliptic and Equator" (*Huángchìdào Chà*),
"Interior and Exterior Degrees of Ecliptic and Equator" (*Huángchìdào Nèiwài Dù*),
"Intersection of Lunar Path and Cycle" (*Báidào Jiāozhōu*),
"Three Corrections for Sun, Moon, and Five Planets (level, standing, fixed)" (*Rìyuè Wǔxīng Pínglìdìng Sānchà*),
and "Distance Difference and Clepsydra" (*Lǐchà Kèlòu*).
Gnomon and Observation of Distances (*Jùgǔ Cèwàng*)
In Běijīng (北京), a gnomon of four *zhàng* was erected.
At noon on the winter solstice,
the shadow length was measured to be seven *zhàng*, nine *chǐ*, eight *cùn*, and five *fēn*.
Subsequently, using a simplified armillary sphere, the Sun's position south of the horizon was measured at twenty-six degrees, forty-six and a half minutes,
which is half of the back arc.
The arrow length (*shǐdù*) was found to be
five degrees, ninety-one and a half minutes.
Placing the radius of the celestial sphere,
the remainder of the arrow length, fifty-four degrees, ninety-six minutes, is taken as the *gǔ* (leg),
which is the degree of this locality from the point directly beneath the Sun.
Using the method for finding the *jù* (base) from the hypotenuse and *gǔ*,
the *jù* was found to be twenty-six degrees, seventeen minutes, and sixty-six seconds,
which is half the chord of the arc of the Sun's emergence from the earth.
In Běijīng, a gnomon of four *zhàng* was erected.
At noon on the summer solstice,
the shadow length was measured to be one *zhàng*, one *chǐ*, seven *cùn*, and one *fēn*.
Subsequently, using a simplified armillary sphere, the Sun's position south of the horizon was measured at seventy-four degrees, twenty-six and a half minutes,
which is half of the back arc.
The arrow length was found to be
forty-three degrees, slightly less than seventy-four minutes.
Placing the radius of the celestial sphere,
the remainder of the arrow length, seventeen degrees, thirteen minutes, and twenty-five seconds, is taken as the *jù*,
which is the degree of this locality from the point directly beneath the Sun.
Using the method for finding the *gǔ* from the *jù* and hypotenuse,
the *gǔ* was found to be fifty-eight degrees, forty-five and a half minutes,
which is half the chord of the arc of the Sun's emergence from the earth.
By combining the degrees of the two solstices,
one hundred degrees and seventy-three minutes are obtained.
Halving this yields fifty degrees and thirty-six and a half minutes,
which is the degree of Běijīng's equator above the horizon.
Subtracting the degree of the equator above the horizon from one-fourth of the celestial circle [360 degrees],
the remainder is forty degrees, ninety-four minutes, ninety-three seconds, and seventy-five *wēi*,
which is the degree of Běijīng's North Pole above the horizon.
Arc and Chord for Circle Segmentation (*Húshǐ Gēyuán*)
The circumference of the celestial sphere is one hundred twenty-one dù and seventy-five fēn, less [a fraction].
(The "less" is not used.)
The radius is six hundred dù and eighty-seven and a half fēn.
(This is also the great chord of the ecliptic and equatorial planes.)
The inner and outer semi-arcs of the ecliptic and equatorial planes at the two solstices are twenty-four dù.
(The measurements are rounded to whole numbers.)
The arc-sagitta of the ecliptic and equatorial planes at the two solstices is four dù, eighty-four fēn, and eighty-two miǎo.
The great gōu of the ecliptic and equatorial planes is twenty-three dù, eighty fēn, and seventy miǎo.
The great gǔ of the ecliptic and equatorial planes is fifty-six dù, zero two fēn, and sixty-eight miǎo.
(Subtract the number of the sagitta from the radius.)
Method for Calculating the Sagitta by Circle Segmentation: Place the degrees of the semi-arc-back and multiply it by itself,
this is the square of the semi-arc-back.
Multiply the circumference of the celestial sphere by itself,
this is the upper term (上廉, shànglián).
Multiply the upper term by the square of the semi-arc-back,
this is the true dividend (正實, zhèngshí).
Multiply the upper term by the diameter,
this is the augmenting coefficient of the square (益從方, yìcóngfāng).
Double the semi-arc-back,
multiply it by the diameter,
this is the lower term (下廉, xiàlián).
Multiply the initial quotient by the upper term,
subtract the result from the augmenting coefficient of the square,
the remainder is the coefficient of the square (從方, cóngfāng).
Place the initial quotient and multiply it by itself, then subtract it from the lower term,
multiply the remainder by the initial quotient,
this is the coefficient of the lower term (從廉, cónglián).
Add the coefficient of the square and the coefficient of the lower term together,
this is the divisor (下法, xiàfǎ).
Multiply the divisor by the initial quotient,
subtract it from the true dividend;
if the dividend is insufficient to subtract,
adjust the initial quotient.
If there is a remainder,
divide it by subsequent quotients in order.
Double the initial quotient,
add it to the subsequent quotient and multiply by the upper term,
subtract the result from the augmenting coefficient of the square,
the remainder is the coefficient of the square.
Add the initial quotient and the subsequent quotient and multiply by itself,
also multiply the initial quotient by itself,
add these two numbers and subtract from the lower term,
multiply the remainder by the doubled initial quotient plus the subsequent quotient,
this is the coefficient of the lower term.
Add the coefficient of the square and the coefficient of the lower term together,
this is the divisor.
Multiply the divisor by the subsequent quotient,
subtract it from the remaining dividend,
and determine the subsequent quotient.
If there is a remainder,
divide it according to the method,
all the obtained quotients are the number of degrees of the sagitta.
(The ecliptic and equatorial planes use the same method.)
For example, to find the sagitta for one dù of the semi-arc-back:
The method says: Place one dù of the semi-arc-back and multiply it by itself,
you get one dù,
this is the square of the semi-arc-back.
Place the circumference of the celestial sphere, one hundred twenty-one dù, and multiply it by itself,
you get fourteen thousand eight hundred twenty-three dù, zero six fēn, and twenty-five miǎo,
this is the upper term.
Multiply the upper term by the square of the semi-arc-back,
you get fourteen thousand eight hundred twenty-three dù, zero six fēn, and twenty-five [miǎo],
this is the true dividend.
Multiply the upper term again by the diameter,
you get eighteen million four thousand seven hundred seven dù, eighty-five fēn, ninety-three miǎo, and seventy-five [sub-miǎo],
this is the augmenting coefficient of the square.
Double one dù of the semi-arc-back,
you get two dù,
multiply this by the diameter to get two hundred forty-three dù and fifty fēn,
this is the lower term.
The initial quotient is eighty miǎo.
Place the initial quotient, eighty miǎo, and multiply it by the upper term, fourteen thousand eight hundred twenty-three dù, zero six [fēn] twenty-five [miǎo],
you get one hundred eighteen dù and five thousand eight hundred forty-five [miǎo],
subtract this from the augmenting coefficient of the square, eighteen million four thousand seven hundred seven dù, eighty-five [fēn] ninety-three [miǎo] seventy-five [sub-miǎo],
the remainder is eighteen million four thousand five hundred eighty-nine dù, twenty-seven [fēn] forty-eight [miǎo] seventy-five [sub-miǎo],
this is the coefficient of the square.
Now place the initial quotient, eighty miǎo, and multiply it by itself,
you get sixty-four wēi,
subtract this from the lower term,
the remainder is two hundred forty-three dù, forty-nine fēn, ninety-nine miǎo, and thirty-six wēi.
Multiply this by eighty miǎo,
you get one dù, ninety-four fēn, seventy-nine miǎo, ninety-nine hundredths, and four hundred eighty-eight thousandths [of a miǎo],
this is the coefficient of the lower term.
Add the coefficient of the lower term and the coefficient of the square,
you get a total of eighteen million four thousand five hundred ninety-one dù, twenty-two fēn, twenty-eight miǎo, seventy-four hundredths, and four hundred eighty-eight thousandths [of a miǎo],
this is the divisor.
Multiply the divisor by the initial quotient,
you get fourteen thousand four hundred thirty-six dù, seventy-two fēn, ninety-seven miǎo, eighty-two hundredths, and ninety-nine thousandths [of a miǎo],
subtract this from the true dividend,
the remaining dividend is three hundred eighty-six dù, thirty-three fēn, twenty-seven miǎo, seventeen hundredths, and zero zero four zero nine six thousandths [of a miǎo].
The subsequent quotient is two miǎo.
Double the initial quotient, eighty miǎo,
you get one fēn and sixty miǎo.
Add the subsequent quotient, two miǎo,
you get one fēn and sixty-two miǎo,
multiply this by the upper term, fourteen thousand eight hundred twenty-three dù, zero six [fēn] twenty-five [miǎo],
you get two hundred forty dù, thirteen fēn, thirty-six miǎo, and one hundred twenty-five thousandths [of a miǎo],
subtract this from the augmenting coefficient of the square,
the remainder is eighteen million four thousand four hundred sixty-seven dù, seventy-two fēn, fifty-seven miǎo, and six hundred twenty-five thousandths [of a miǎo],
this is the coefficient of the square.
Now place the combined initial and subsequent quotient, eighty-two miǎo, and multiply it by itself,
you get sixty-seven wēi.
Add the number obtained by multiplying the initial quotient, eighty miǎo, by itself,
you get one miǎo and thirty-one wēi,
subtract this from the lower term,
the remainder is two hundred forty-three dù, forty-nine fēn, ninety-eight miǎo, and sixty-nine wēi.
Multiply this by the previously obtained one fēn and sixty-two miǎo,
you get three dù, ninety-four fēn, forty-six miǎo, and ninety-seven hundredths, seventy-eight thousandths [of a miǎo],
this is the coefficient of the lower term.
Add the coefficient of the lower term and the coefficient of the square,
you get eighteen million four thousand four hundred seventy-one dù, sixty-seven fēn, zero four miǎo, and six hundred thirty-seven hundred thousandths, seven hundred eighty thousandths [of a miǎo],
this is the divisor.
Multiply the divisor by the subsequent quotient,
you get three hundred sixty dù, eighty-nine fēn, forty-three miǎo, and three hundred thirty-four hundred thousandths, zero nine two zero seven five five six millionths [of a miǎo],
subtract this from the remaining dividend,
there is still a remainder of twenty-five dù, forty-three fēn, eighty-three miǎo, and eight hundred twenty-nine hundred thousandths, one two zero two zero four four millionths [of a miǎo].
(If it is less than one miǎo, discard it;
the same applies below.)
The sagitta found is eighty-two miǎo;
for the remaining degrees, use the method above
to find the sagitta,
which is the root for finding the relationships between the ecliptic and equatorial planes and their inner and outer degrees.
(Numbers are detailed later.)
Difference Between Ecliptic and Equatorial Planes
Method for Calculating the Accumulated Degrees of the Equator Under Each Degree of the Ecliptic:
Subtract the sagitta of the ecliptic from the celestial radius,
the remainder is the minor chord of the ecliptic and equatorial planes.
Place the minor chord of the ecliptic and equatorial planes,
multiply it by the great gǔ of the ecliptic and equatorial planes (the great gǔ is found in Circle Segmentation) to get the dividend.
The great chord of the ecliptic and equatorial planes (the radius) is the divisor.
Divide the dividend by the divisor,
this is the minor gǔ of the ecliptic and equatorial planes.
Place the sagitta of the ecliptic and multiply it by itself to get the dividend,
take the full celestial diameter as the divisor,
divide the dividend by the divisor,
this is the difference in the semi-back chord of the ecliptic.
Subtract this difference from the accumulated degrees of the ecliptic,
(that is, the semi-arc-back of the ecliptic.)
The remainder is the semi-arc chord of the ecliptic.
Place the semi-arc chord of the ecliptic and multiply it by itself to get the square of the gǔ,
place the minor gǔ of the ecliptic and equatorial planes and multiply it by itself to get the square of the gōu,
add these two squares,
extract the square root,
this is the minor chord of the equator.
Place the semi-arc chord of the ecliptic,
multiply it by the celestial radius (which is also the great chord of the equator) to get the dividend,
divide by the minor chord of the equator,
this is the semi-arc chord of the equator.
Place the minor gǔ of the ecliptic and equatorial planes,
(which is also the transverse minor gōu of the equator.)
multiply it by the great chord of the equator (i.e., the radius) to get the dividend,
divide by the minor chord of the equator,
this is the transverse great gōu of the equator,
subtract this from the radius,
the remainder is the transverse arc sagitta of the equator.
Multiply the transverse arc sagitta by itself to get the dividend,
take the full diameter as the divisor,
divide the dividend by the divisor,
this is the difference in the semi-back chord of the equator.
Add this difference to the semi-arc chord of the equator,
Given the ecliptic’s half-arc back one degree,
to find the equator’s accumulated degrees.
The method says: Set the radius at 60 degrees, 87 minutes, 50 seconds,
(which is the great chord of the ecliptic-equator.)
Subtract the ecliptic’s sagitta of 82 seconds from it, the remainder is 60 degrees, 86 minutes, 68 seconds.
This is the small chord of the ecliptic-equator.
Set the small chord of the ecliptic-equator.
Multiply it by the great leg of the ecliptic-equator, 56 degrees, 02 minutes, 68 seconds.
This obtains 3410 degrees, 17 minutes, 20 seconds, 30 millionths, 24 ten-millionths as the product (dividend).
Use the great chord of the ecliptic-equator, 60 degrees, 87 minutes, 50 seconds, as the divisor.
Divide the product by the divisor.
This obtains 56 degrees, 01 minute, 92 seconds.
This is the small leg of the ecliptic-equator.
(Also known as the small base of the equator.)
Set the sagitta of 82 seconds and square it.
This obtains 67 millionths.
Use the diameter of 121 degrees, 75 minutes, as the divisor.
Divide it, obtaining 55 ten-thousandths.
This is the difference in the ecliptic’s half-back chord.
Set the ecliptic’s half-arc back one degree.
Subtract the difference in the ecliptic’s half-back chord.
The remainder is the half-arc chord.
Since the difference is below millionths, it is not subtracted.
So, use one degree as the half-arc chord.
Set the ecliptic’s half-arc chord of one degree and square it.
This obtains one degree as the square of the leg.
Square the small leg of the ecliptic-equator, 56 degrees, 01 minute, 92 seconds.
This obtains 3138 degrees, 15 minutes, 07 seconds, 68 millionths, 64 ten-millionths as the square of the base.
Adding the two squares together obtains 3139 degrees, 15 minutes, 07 seconds, 68 millionths, 64 ten-millionths as the product of the chord.
Take the square root.
This obtains 56 degrees, 02 minutes, 81 seconds.
This is the small chord of the equator.
Set the ecliptic’s half-arc chord of one degree.
Multiply it by the radius (which is the great chord of the equator).
This obtains 60 degrees, 87 minutes, 50 seconds as the product (dividend).
Divide by the small chord of the equator, 56 degrees, 02 minutes, 81 seconds, as the divisor.
This obtains 1 degree, 08 minutes, 65 seconds.
This is the half-arc chord of the equator.
Set the small leg of the ecliptic-equator, 56 degrees, 01 minute, 92 seconds,
(Also known as the small base of the equator.)
Multiply it by the great chord of the equator (radius), 60 degrees, 87 minutes, 50 seconds.
This obtains 3410 degrees, 16 minutes, 88 seconds as the product (dividend).
Divide by the small chord of the equator as the divisor.
This obtains 60 degrees, 86 minutes, 53 seconds.
This is the equatorial transverse great base.
Set the radius of 60 degrees, 87 minutes, 50 seconds.
Subtract the equatorial great base of 60 degrees, 86 minutes, 53 seconds.
The remainder is 97 seconds.
This is the equatorial transverse arc’s sagitta.
Set the equatorial transverse arc’s sagitta of 97 seconds and square it.
This obtains 94.09 millionths.
Divide by the diameter as the divisor.
This obtains 77 ten-thousandths.
This is the difference in the equator’s back chord.
Set the equator’s half-arc chord of 1 degree, 08 minutes, 65 seconds.
Add the difference in the equator’s back chord.
This is the accumulated degrees of the equator.
Now, since the difference is below millionths, it is not added.
So, use the half-arc chord as the accumulated degrees.
Generally, the accumulated degrees of the equator obtained are 1 degree, 08 minutes, 65 seconds.
For other degrees, follow the above method.
To find the accumulated degrees of the equator for each ecliptic degree.
Subtract the two numbers.
This gives the ecliptic-equator difference.

According to Guō Shǒujìng's five principles of method creation, the first is the difference between the ecliptic and the equator.
This is its fundamental rate.
The old method involved subtraction and multiplication by one hundred and one degrees.
The Shòushí calendar established methods,
using gougu (right triangles), arc and arrow, square and circle, and oblique and straight lines to contain,
to find their differences,
which conforms to the principles of the armillary sphere,
and is more precise than ancient methods.
However, the records in the
Yuán calendar scriptures are very brief,
and mistakenly take the ecliptic's 'arrow degree' as the accumulated difference,
and the ecliptic's 'arrow difference' as the rate of difference.
Now, we correct it.
Diagram of cutting a circle into arcs and arrows (Image data not available yet)
When a complete circle is bisected,
it becomes a flat circle.
Cutting any part of a flat circle
forms an arc and arrow shape,
all having an arc back,
an arc string (chord),
and an arrow (sagitta).
Bisecting the arc and arrow shape,
it then has a half arc back,
a half arc string,
and an arrow.
From the string and arrow, a gougu shape is formed.
Taking the half arc string as the 'gou',
the remainder of the arrow minus the radius as the 'gu',
and the radius as the 'string' (hypotenuse).
Within the gougu, a smaller gougu is formed,
with a small 'gou', small 'gu', and small 'string'.
Thus, large and small can be mutually sought,
and flat and side views can be mutually used.
The principles of the armillary sphere,
are thus closely observed.
Side view diagram (Image data not available yet)
The flat one is the equator.
The oblique one is the ecliptic.
From the distance between the two solstices and the ecliptic and equator,
a large gougu is produced.
From the distance between the ecliptic and equator at each degree,
a small gougu is produced.
Plan view diagram (Image data not available yet)
The outer large circle is the equator.
When viewed from the North Pole,
the ecliptic is within the equator.
There are various degrees of the equator,
each having its own half arc string,
which produces a large gougu.
Also, each has its corresponding ecliptic half arc string,
which produces a small gougu.
These two can both be mutually sought.
According to old histories, there are no diagrams,
but a table is also a type of diagram.
Today's method of gougu, cutting a circle, and arcs and arrows,
is truly the basis for calendar makers' calculations.
Without diagrams,
it would be unclear,
hence we preserve the essential points.
Ecliptic-equator inner and outer degrees
Method for calculating the ecliptic degrees, its distance from the inner and outer equator, and its distance from the poles.
Subtract the small equatorial chord from the radius.
The remainder is the difference between the two equatorial chords.
(This is also the small arc and arrow of the ecliptic-equator,
also the inner and outer arrow,
also the difference between the 'gu' and the 'string'.)
Subtract the ecliptic's 'arrow degree' from the radius.
The remainder is the small chord of the ecliptic-equator.
Multiply this by the inner and outer half arc string of the ecliptic-equator at the two solstices to get the dividend.
Divide it by the large chord of the ecliptic-equator (which is the radius) to get the small arc chord of the ecliptic-equator.
(This is the inner and outer half arc string of the ecliptic-equator,
and also the small 'gou' of the ecliptic-equator.)
Square the small arc arrow of the ecliptic-equator (which is the difference between the two equatorial chords) to get the dividend.
Divide it by the entire diameter to get the half back string difference.
Add this difference to the small arc chord of the ecliptic-equator to get the half back of the small arc of the ecliptic-equator,
which is the inner and outer degree of the ecliptic-equator.
For the inner and outer degrees of the ecliptic-equator,
add them if within the initial period of increase and end of decrease,
subtract them if within the initial period of decrease and end of increase,
and in all cases, add or subtract the quadrant degree,
to obtain the Sun's distance from the North Pole in degrees and minutes.
For example, forty-four degrees after the winter solstice,
to find the Sun's distance from the inner and outer equator and its distance from the pole.
The method states: Set the radius at 60 degrees, 87 and a half minutes.
Subtract from it the small equatorial chord for 44 degrees of the ecliptic, which is 58 degrees, 35 minutes, 69 seconds.
The remainder is 2 degrees, 51 minutes, 81 seconds,
which is the small arc arrow of the ecliptic-equator (i.e., the inner and outer arrow).
Set the radius at 60 degrees, 875 (parts).
Subtract from it the ecliptic's 'arrow' for 44 degrees, which is 16 degrees, 56 minutes, 82 seconds.
The remainder is 44 degrees, 30 minutes, 68 seconds,
which is the small chord of the ecliptic-equator.
Take the small chord of the ecliptic-equator,
multiply it by the inner and outer half arc string of the ecliptic-equator at the two solstices, which is 23 degrees, 71 minutes.
This gives 1050 degrees, 51 minutes, 4238 as the dividend.
Divide this by the large chord of the ecliptic-equator, which is 600 degrees, 875 (parts),
resulting in 17 degrees, 25 minutes, 69 seconds, which is the small arc chord of the ecliptic-equator.
(This is the inner and outer half arc string.)
Square the small arc arrow of the ecliptic-equator, 2 degrees, 51 minutes, 81 seconds, to get the dividend.
Divide it by the entire diameter, 121 degrees, 75 minutes,
resulting in 5 minutes, 21 seconds, which is the back string difference.
Add this difference to the small arc chord of the ecliptic-equator, 17 degrees, 25 minutes, 69 seconds,
resulting in 17 degrees, 30 minutes, 89 seconds.
This is the Sun's inner and outer distance from the equator at 44 degrees before or after the two solstices.
Set the quadrant at 91 degrees, 31 minutes, 43.75 seconds.
Add to it the inner and outer degree, 17 degrees, 3089 (parts).
This gives 108 degrees, 62 minutes, 32.75 seconds,
which is the Sun's distance from the North Pole 44 degrees after the winter solstice.

Explanation of the Yíng Suō Zhāo Chā Tú
The methods of Yíngsuō Zhāochā (盈縮招差, "excess and deficit interpolation")
originally constitute a single quadrant method.
(For example, in the Yíng calendar, eighty-eight days and ninety-one kè constitute a quadrant;
in the Suō calendar, ninety-three days and seventy-one kè constitute a quadrant.)
Now, only nine limits are used,
taking this as an example.
The blank nine rows represent the base numbers of the Dìngchā (定差, "fixed difference"),
which are the "dividend" (shí 實).
The numbers of Píngchā (平差, "level difference") and Lìchā (立差, "standing difference") above the diagonal line
are the "divisor" (fǎ 法).
The Dìngchā (定差) in the blank spaces below the diagonal line
are the "remainder of the dividend" (yú shí 餘實).
Suppose the Dìngchā (定差) is ten thousand,
the Píngchā (平差) is one hundred,
and the Lìchā (立差) is one.
Now, to calculate the nine-limit method:
multiply the Dìngchā (定差) by the nine limits to get ninety thousand as the dividend.
Set aside the Píngchā (平差),
and multiply it by the nine limits twice,
to get eight thousand one hundred.
Set aside the Lìchā (立差),
and multiply it by the nine limits three times,
to get seven hundred twenty-nine.
Add these two numbers to get eight thousand eight hundred twenty-nine as the divisor.
Subtract the divisor from the dividend,
leaving eighty-one thousand one hundred seventy-one,
which is the nine-limit product.
Another method for the divisor:
multiply the Píngchā (平差) by the nine limits to get nine hundred,
then multiply the Lìchā (立差) by the nine limits twice to get eighty-one,
and add these two numbers to get nine hundred eighty-one as the divisor.
With the Dìngchā (定差) of ten thousand as the dividend,
subtract the divisor from the dividend,
leaving nine thousand nineteen,
which is the Dìngchā (定差) written in the last position of the nine limits.
Then, multiply the remainder of the dividend by the nine limits,
to get eighty-one thousand one hundred seventy-one,
which is the nine-limit product,
the same as previously obtained.
The former method first multiplies and then subtracts,
while the latter method first subtracts and then multiplies;
the principle is the same.
According to the Shòushí Lì (授時曆), for the excesses and deficits of the Qīzhèng (七政, "seven luminaries"),
calculations are established using Duòjī Zhāochā (垛積招差, "stacked-product interpolation").
This method cleverly matches the movements of the heavens,
and its approach is
different from the Western method of calculating with epicycles,
but leads to the same result.
However, the books of the Jiǔzhāng (九章, "Nine Chapters") transmitted in the world
do not record this technique. The Lìcǎo (曆草, "Draft of the Calendar") records the technique
but does not explain its rationale.
Méi Wéndǐng (梅文鼎) of Xuānchéng
provided a diagrammatic explanation for it,
and regarding the principles of Píngchā (平差) and Lìchā (立差),
and the method of Duòjī (垛積, "stacked product"),
he elucidated their underlying reasons.
There are dedicated books circulating in the world,
which cannot
be fully recorded here.
Therefore, the Zhāochā Túshuō (招差圖說, "Illustrated Explanation of Interpolation") is respectfully recorded,
to clarify the general idea of establishing the method.
For all arrangements of Lìchéng (立成, "established tables"):
Yíngchū Suōmò (盈初縮末, "beginning of excess, end of deficit"):
Set the Lìchā (立差) at thirty-one wēi (微, "microns").
Multiply by six,
to get one second and eighty-six wēi (微),
which is the Jiāfēn Lìchā (加分立差, "added-part standing difference").
Set the Píngchā (平差) at two fēn (分, "minutes") and forty-six seconds.
Double it,
to get four fēn (分) and ninety-two seconds.
Add it to the Jiāfēn Lìchā (加分立差),
to get four fēn (分), ninety-three seconds, and eighty-six wēi (微), which is the Pínglì Héchā (平立合差, "combined level and standing difference").
Set the Dìngchā (定差) at five hundred thirteen fēn (分) and thirty-two seconds.
Subtract the Píngchā (平差) of two fēn (分) and forty-six seconds from it,
then subtract the Lìchā (立差) of thirty-one wēi (微).
The remainder is five hundred ten fēn (分), eighty-five seconds, and sixty-nine wēi (微),
which is the Jiāfēn (加分, "added part").
Suōchū Yíngmò (縮初盈末, "beginning of deficit, end of excess"):
Set the Lìchā (立差) at twenty-seven wēi (微).
Multiply by six,
to get one second and sixty-two wēi (微),
which is the Jiāfēn Lìchā (加分立差).
Set the Píngchā (平差) at two fēn (分) and twenty-one seconds.
Double it,
to get four fēn (分) and forty-two seconds.
Add it to the Jiāfēn Lìchā (加分立差),
to get four fēn (分), forty-three seconds, and sixty-two wēi (微), which is the Pínglì Héchā (平立合差).
Set the Dìngchā (定差) at four hundred eighty-seven fēn (分) and six seconds.
Subtract the Píngchā (平差) of two fēn (分) and twenty-one seconds from it,
then subtract the Lìchā (立差) of twenty-seven wēi (微).
The remainder is four hundred eighty-four fēn (分), eighty-four seconds, and seventy-three wēi (微),
which is the Jiāfēn (加分).
All calculations above
are for the first day's numbers.
To calculate for the next day,
the Jiāfēn Lìchā (加分立差) is
cumulatively added to the Pínglì Héchā (平立合差),
to get the next day's Pínglì Héchā (平立合差).
Subtract the Pínglì Héchā (平立合差) from that day's Jiāfēn (加分),
to get the next day's Jiāfēn (加分).
The same applies to both Yíng (盈, "excess") and Suō (縮, "deficit").
When these Jiāfēn (加分) are accumulated,
they become the Yíngsuō Jī (盈縮積, "excess and deficit product"),
and these numbers are all found in the Lìchéng (立成).
Origin of the three differences (Píng, Lì, Dìng) for the tardiness and swiftness of the Moon
The Moon's orbital period is twenty-seven days, fifty-five kè (刻), and forty-six (parts).
Its divisions are measured into four xiàng (象, "phases"),
each xiàng (象) having seven sections.
The four xiàng (象) thus have twenty-eight sections.
Each section has twelve limits,
each xiàng (象) eighty-four limits,
totaling three hundred thirty-six limits,
completing one cycle of the four xiàng (象).
Using the four xiàng (象) as the divisor,
divide the orbital days,
to get six days, eight hundred eighty-eight and sixty-five (ten-thousandths) per xiàng (象).
Divided into seven sections,
each section's actually measured numbers for the Moon's tardiness and swiftness
are compared with the parallel movement,
to find the Jīchā (積差, "accumulated difference").

Set the Yīchā (一差),
and subtract it from the next section's Yīchā (一差) to get the Èrchā (二差, "second difference").

Set the Píngchā (平差) of the first section's limit, one fēn (分), zero zero seconds, seven two six (Wēi), as Fànpíngjī (汎平積, "general level product").
Set the Yīchā (一差) of the first section, forty-seven seconds, seven six (Wēi).
Subtract the Èrchā (二差) of the first section, nine seconds, three six (Wēi), from it,
leaving thirty-eight seconds, forty wēi (微),
which is the Fànpíng Jīchā (汎平積差, "general level accumulated difference").
Separately, set half of the Èrchā (二差) of the first section, nine seconds, thirty-six wēi (微),
to get four seconds, sixty-eight wēi (微),
which is the Fànlì Jīchā (汎立積差, "general standing accumulated difference").
Add the Fànpíng Jīchā (汎平積差) of thirty-eight seconds, forty wēi (微),
to the Fànpíngjī (汎平積) of one fēn (分), zero zero seconds, seven two six (Wēi),
to get eleven fēn (分), eleven seconds.
This is the Dìngchā (定差).
Set the Fànpíng Jīchā (汎平積差) of thirty-eight seconds, forty wēi (微).
Subtract the Fànlì Jīchā (汎立積差) of four seconds, sixty-eight wēi (微) from it,
leaving thirty-three seconds, seventy-two wēi (微) as the dividend.
Divide it by the twelve limits as the divisor,
to get two seconds, eighty-one wēi (微),
which is the Píngchā (平差).
Set the Fànlì Jīchā (汎立積差) of four seconds, sixty-eight wēi (微) as the dividend.
Using twelve limits as the divisor,
divide twice,
to get three wēi (微), twenty-five xiān (纖, "hairs"),
which is the Lìchā (立差).
To find tardiness and swiftness,
always multiply the calendar day by twelve limits and twenty fēn (分),
taking the beginning as below eighty-four limits,
and for those above, subtract one hundred sixty-eight limits to get the end.
Multiply each initial and final limit by the Lìchā (立差),
add the result to the Píngchā (平差),
then multiply by the initial and final limit again,
subtract the result from the Dìngchā (定差),
and multiply the remainder by the initial and final limit,
to get the tardiness and swiftness product.
The initial limit is from the point of greatest tardiness or swiftness, pushed forward,
and the final limit is from the point of greatest tardiness or swiftness, traced backward.
Their distances from the point of greatest tardiness or swiftness are the same,
thus their accumulated degrees are the same.
(The method for the Moon and the Sun is the same,
but the Sun establishes limits based on Dìngqì (定氣, "fixed qi-points"),
hence the differing numbers for Yíngsuō (盈縮).
The Moon establishes limits based on parallel movement,
hence the same origin for tardiness and swiftness.)
To establish the method: Set the *lì chā* (mean anomaly rate difference) at 3 *wēi* (minutes) and 25 *xiān* (fractions),
multiply it by 6,
and obtain 19 *wēi* and 50 *xiān*.
This is the *sǔn yì lì chā* (gain/loss mean anomaly rate difference).
Set the *píng chā* (equation of center) at 2 *miǎo* (seconds) and 81 *wēi*,
double it,
and obtain 5 *miǎo* and 62 *wēi*.
Then add the *sǔn yì lì chā* of 19 *wēi* and 50 *xiān*,
for a total of 5 *miǎo* and 81 *wēi*.
This is the *chū xiàn píng lì hé chā* (first limit combined mean anomaly rate difference).
From this, successively add
the *sǔn yì lì chā*
to get the *měi xiàn píng lì hé chā* (combined mean anomaly rate difference for each limit).
By the 80th limit,
the cumulative total reaches 21 *miǎo* and 415 *wēi*.
This is the maximum of the *píng lì hé chā*.
The difference at the 81st limit is 1 *miǎo* and 7809 *xiān*,
at the 82nd limit it is 1 *miǎo* and 7808 *xiān*,
and by the 83rd limit,
the *píng lì hé chā*
is equal to the middle division of the *yì fēn* (gain portion),
marking the end of the *yì fēn*.
The difference at the 84th limit
is also equal to the middle division of the *sǔn fēn* (loss portion),
marking the beginning of the *sǔn fēn*.
By the 86th limit, the difference
is also 21 *miǎo* and 415 *wēi*.
From this point, successively subtract the *sǔn yì lì chā*
to get the *měi xiàn píng lì hé chā* for each limit,
until the last limit, which is the same as the first limit.
Set the *dìng chā* (constant difference) at 11 *fēn* (parts) and 11 *miǎo*.
Subtract the *píng chā* of 2 *miǎo* and 81 *wēi*,
then subtract the *lì chā* of 3 *wēi* and 25 *xiān*.
The remainder is 11 *fēn*, 8 *miǎo*, 15 *wēi*, and 75 *xiān*.
This is the *jiā fēn dìng chā* (additive constant difference),
which is the initial *sǔn yì fēn* (gain/loss portion).
Set the *sǔn yì fēn*.
By adding it when gaining and subtracting it when losing, based on the *měi xiàn píng lì hé chā* for that limit,
you get the *cì xiàn sǔn yì fēn* (next limit's gain/loss portion).
Accumulate the *yì fēn*,
and subtract the *sǔn fēn*.
This gives the *chí jí dù* (rate of slowness and quickness) below it.
Take 820 *fēn* as the daily rate for one limit,
and successively add 820 *fēn* for the daily rate of each limit.
(All the above details are elaborated in the *Lì Chéng*.)
The origins of the three constants, *píng*, *lì*, and *dìng chā*, for the Five Planets: For each of the Five Planets, based on actual measurements,
divide its movement into eight segments
to find the accumulated difference,
roughly following the methods for the Sun and Moon.
For Mùxīng (Jupiter): (*lì chā* is added,
*píng chā* is subtracted).

The method is similar to that for Jīnxīng (Venus).
The fixed difference obtained is 3 fēn, 87 miǎo, 90 wēi.
The adjusted difference is 21 wēi, 65 xiān.
The vertical difference is 1 wēi, 41 xiān.
The above constitutes the origin of the three differences (adjusted, vertical, and fixed) for Shuǐxīng (Mercury).
For the five planets listed on the right,
the vertical difference is taken as miǎo (seconds),
the adjusted difference as běn (base),
and the fixed difference as zǒng (total).
Each of the five planets multiplies its segment number by miǎo.
For Mùxīng (Jupiter), Tǔxīng (Saturn), Jīnxīng (Venus), and Shuǐxīng (Mercury), they are combined with běn.
Only Huǒxīng (Mars) is compared with běn.
Each is accumulated by the accumulated days.
All five planets are compared with zǒng,
and then each is multiplied by the accumulated days,
to obtain their respective measured degrees and minutes.
For the accumulated days of the five planets,
the daily rate is used
to divide the number of days in a year, yielding 365 degrees, 25 minutes, tài.
Each is divided by four to obtain the quadrant.
Only for Huǒxīng (Mars) is one-third of the quadrant used.
Subtracting the quadrant gives the beginning of increasing and end of decreasing limits.
Adding the quadrant gives the beginning of decreasing and end of increasing limits.
The reason why the assigned degrees are days
is for the convenience of multiplying and dividing the increasing and decreasing calendars.
In reality, the number of accumulated days
is the accumulated degrees.
Lí Chā Kè Lòu (Difference in Hours and Clepsydra)
to find the difference between the two solstices and the ingress/egress difference.
The method states: Set the measured height of the North Pole above the horizon as 40 degrees, 95 minutes, as the semi-arc complement (半弧背).
Using the previous method of intersecting circle arcs and sines,
calculate the semi-arc sine above the horizon as 39 degrees, 26 minutes,
which is the middle leg (中股) of the large right triangle (大三斜).
Set the measured inner and outer degrees of the ecliptic and equator at the two solstices as 23 degrees, 90 minutes, as the semi-arc complement.
Using the previous method, calculate the inner and outer semi-arc sine as 23 degrees, 71 minutes.
(This is also the great segment of the ecliptic and equator,
and also the short sine of the small right triangle.)
Square the inner and outer semi-arc sine to get gōumì (句冪, the square of the base).
Square the radius to get xiánmì (弦冪, the square of the hypotenuse).
Subtract the two squares,
take the square root to get gǔ (股, the leg).
Subtract gǔ from the radius,
the remainder, 4 degrees, 81 minutes, is the ingress/egress sagitta (出入矢) for the two solstices,
which is the inner and outer sagitta of the ecliptic and equator.
On the summer solstice,
the southern limit to the horizon is 74 degrees, 26.5 minutes, as the semi-arc complement.
The semi-arc sine of the sun below the horizon is found to be 58 degrees, 45 minutes.
The radius is 600 degrees, 87.5 minutes,
which is the middle hypotenuse (中弦) of the great right triangle.
Set the middle leg of the great right triangle as 39 degrees, 26 minutes,
multiply it by the inner and outer semi-arc sine of the two solstices, 23 degrees, 71 minutes, to get the product (實).
Divide it by the radius, 600 degrees, 87.5 minutes,
to get 15 degrees, 29 minutes,
which is the middle leg of the small right triangle.
(This is also the small leg.)
Set the middle leg of the small right triangle as 15 degrees, 29 minutes.
Subtract it from the semi-arc sine of the sun below the horizon, 58 degrees, 45 minutes.
The remainder, 43 degrees, 16 minutes,
is the great leg.
Subtract the ingress/egress sagitta, 4 degrees, 81 minutes,
from the radius, 600 degrees, 87.5 minutes.
The remainder, 56 degrees, 06.5 minutes,
is the great hypotenuse (大股弦).
Set the great hypotenuse.
Multiply it by the small leg, 15 degrees, 29 minutes, to get the product.
Divide it by the great leg, 43 degrees, 16 minutes,
to get 19 degrees, 87 minutes, which is the small hypotenuse (小弦).
This is the semi-arc sine of the ingress/egress difference at the two solstices.
Set the semi-arc sine of the ingress/egress difference at the two solstices.
According to the method, find the semi-arc complement of the ingress/egress difference at the two solstices as 19 degrees, 96 minutes, 14 seconds.
Set the semi-arc complement of the ingress/egress difference at the two solstices as 19 degrees, 96 minutes, 14 seconds.
Divide it by the inner and outer semi-arc sine of the ecliptic and equator at the two solstices, 23 degrees, 71 minutes,
to get 84 minutes, 19 seconds,
which is the degree difference (度差分).
To find the daytime and nighttime kè (刻) for each degree of the ecliptic.
The method states: Set the desired inner and outer semi-arc sine of the ecliptic and equator for each degree.
Multiply it by the semi-arc complement of the ingress/egress difference at the two solstices to get the product.
Divide it by the inner and outer semi-arc sine of the ecliptic and equator at the two solstices,
to get the semi-arc complement of the ingress/egress difference for each degree.
(Another method: Set the inner and outer semi-arc sine of the ecliptic and equator.
Multiply it by the degree difference, 84 minutes, 19 seconds,
and you will also get the semi-arc complement of the ingress/egress difference.)
Subtract the inner and outer sagitta of the ecliptic and equator from the radius.
(This is the difference between the two sines of the equator,
seen in the previous table.)
Double the remainder.
Then multiply it by three.
Add one degree to the result.
This is the daily travel in 100 kè degrees.
(Another method: Double the inner and outer sagitta of the ecliptic and equator.
Subtract it from the full radius.
Multiply the remainder by three and add one degree.
This is the daily travel in 100 kè degrees,
also the same.)
Set the semi-arc complement of the ingress/egress difference for each degree.
Multiply it by 100 kè to get the product.
Divide it by the daily travel in 100 kè degrees.
The result is the ingress/egress difference in kè.
Set 25 kè.
Observe the ingress/egress difference in kè with respect to the ecliptic.
If it is inside the equator, add it.
If it is outside the equator, subtract it.
The result is the half-day kè.
Double it to get the daytime kè.
Subtract it from 100 kè
to get the nighttime kè.
For example, to find the daytime and nighttime kè for 44 degrees after the winter solstice.
The method states: Set the inner and outer semi-arc sine of the ecliptic and equator at 44 degrees after the winter solstice as 17 degrees, 25 minutes, 69 seconds.
(This is also the small arc sine of the ecliptic and equator,
taken from the previous table.)
Multiply it by the semi-arc complement of the ingress/egress difference at the two solstices, 19 degrees, 96 minutes, 14 seconds, to get the product.
Divide it by the inner and outer semi-arc sine of the ecliptic and equator at the two solstices, 23 degrees, 71 minutes,
to get 14 degrees, 52 minutes, 85 seconds,
which is the semi-arc complement of the ingress/egress difference.
(Another method: Set the inner and outer semi-arc sine of the ecliptic and equator as 17 degrees, 25 minutes, 69 seconds.
Multiply it by the degree difference, 0 degrees, 84 minutes, 19 seconds,
and you will also get 14 degrees, 52 minutes, 85 seconds,
which is the semi-arc complement of the ingress/egress difference.)
Set the radius as 600 degrees, 87.5 minutes.
Subtract the inner and outer sagitta of the ecliptic and equator at 44 degrees, 2 degrees, 51 minutes, 81 seconds (this is also the difference between the two sines of the equator,
taken from the previous table).
The remainder is 58 degrees, 35 minutes, 69 seconds.
(This is the small sine of the equator.)
Double it,
to get 116 degrees, 71 minutes, 38 seconds.
Multiply it by three,
add one degree,
to get 351 degrees, 14 minutes, 14 seconds,
which is the daily travel in 100 kè degrees.
(Another method: Double the inner and outer sagitta of the ecliptic and equator to get 5 degrees, 03 minutes, 62 seconds.
Subtract it from the full radius, 121 degrees, 75 minutes.
You also get 116 degrees, 71 minutes, 38 seconds.
Multiply by three and add one degree.
This is the daily travel in 100 kè degrees,
also the same.)
Set the semi-arc complement of the ingress/egress difference as 14 degrees, 52 minutes, 85 seconds.
Multiply it by 100 kè to get the product.
Divide it by the daily travel in 100 kè degrees, 351 degrees, 14 minutes, 14 seconds,
to get 4 kè, 13 minutes, 75 seconds,
which is the ingress/egress difference in kè.
Set 25 kè.
Subtract the ingress/egress difference in kè, 4 kè, 13 minutes, 75 seconds,
(because at 44 degrees after the winter solstice,
the ecliptic is outside the equator,
so subtract).
The remainder is 20 kè, 86 minutes, 25 seconds,
which is the half-day kè.
Double it to get 41 kè, 72.5 minutes,
which is the daytime kè.
Subtract the daytime kè from 100 kè.
The remainder is 58 kè, 27.5 minutes,
which is the nighttime kè.
(Another method: Set the ingress/egress difference in kè, 4 kè, 13 minutes, 75 seconds.
Double it,
to get 8 kè, 27.5 minutes.
Subtract it from the daytime and nighttime 50 kè at the spring and autumn equinoxes,
to get 41 kè, 72.5 minutes,
which is the daytime kè.
Add the doubled kè to 50 kè,
to get 58 kè, 27.5 minutes,
which is the nighttime kè.
If daytime decreases, nighttime increases,
and so on.)

are for the gǔi lòu (sundial and clepsydra) of Dàdū (大都, i.e., Yānjīng).
At summer, daytime is extremely long, 61 kè, 84 fēn.

When the Míng (明) dynasty moved its capital to Yān (燕),

Only in the Jǐsì (己巳) year of the Zhèngtǒng (正統) reign was a decree issued to adopt 61 kè for the calendar,

Treatise 10, Calendar 4, Dàtǒng Lìfǎ 2 (Tables)
The establishment of tables (lìchéng)
is to pre-arrange and fix the numbers of the waxing and waning and slow and fast motions of the sun, moon, and five planets
in advance,
to facilitate calculation and use.
The Yuán Zhì (元志) and the Lì Jīng Bù Qī Zhèng Yíng Suō Chí Jí (曆經步七政盈縮遲疾, "Calendrical Classic for Computing the Waxing and Waning, Slow and Fast Motions of the Seven Luminaries")
all have two methods.
One method uses the "three differences" to set up calculations,
which is the method for constructing the lìchéng.
The other method states:
multiply the waxing/waning parts below
by the limit parts (rù xiàn fēn) and divide by ten thousand (wàn yuē zhī),
then add the waxing/waning accumulated value below;
this is used for the lìchéng method.
However, the remaining lìchéng were not recorded,
making it impossible to perform calculations.
Now, they are fully recorded according to the Dà Tǒng Lì Tōng Guǐ (大統曆通軌).
There are four categories: the Sun's Waxing and Waning,
the Morning and Evening Divisions,
the Moon's Slow and Fast Motions,
and the Five Planets' Waxing and Waning.
(For more details, refer to the Fǎ Yuán (法原) and Tuī Bù Juǎn (推步卷) chapters.)
According to the Yuán Shǐ (元史),
the Shòu Shí Lì (授時曆) was completed in the 17th year of Zhìzhèng (至正 seventeen nián).
Wáng Xún (王恂) died in the 19th year.
Although the Shòu Shí Lì (授時曆) was promulgated at that time,
the numbers for the lìchéng had not yet been definitively drafted.
Guō Shǒujìng (郭守敬) classified and arranged them by analogy,
standardizing the minutes and seconds (fēn miǎo),
and compiling them into two volumes.
However, the current Qīn Tiān Jiān (欽天監) version
states that it was "Commissioned by Imperial Decree and Compiled by Your Servant Wáng Xún (王恂), Grand Master for Consultation (Jiāyì Dàfū), and Director of the Imperial Observatory (Tàishǐ Lìng)."
Does this imply that Wáng (王) had an earlier draft,
and Guō (郭) completed it?

Treatise 11: Calendar 5, The Dàtǒng Calendar Method, Part 3, Section 1 (Astronomical Calculations)
The Dàtǒng (Dàtǒng) astronomical calculations,
are all based on the Shòushí (Shòushí) Calendar,
only removing the waxing and waning.
However, the general rules for various quick methods,
are indeed necessary for computations.
Their sequence of steps,
also has slight differences from the calendar classics.
For example, the variations in solar terms and new moons,
the Shòushí (Shòushí) Calendar originally divided into two chapters,
now combined into one.
In the Shòushí (Shòushí) Calendar, the anomaly difference lies in the solar longitude,
the speed difference lies in the lunar apogee/perigee,
the true new moon and mean new moon are separated into two sections.
Now, after the mean new moon,
the true new moon is immediately calculated,
which is especially convenient for practical use.
There are seven categories: namely solar terms and new moons,
namely solar longitude,
namely lunar apogee/perigee,
namely meridian stars,
namely eclipses,
namely the five planets,
namely the four auxiliaries.
Calculating Solar Terms and New Moons (Variations Included)
The 17th year of Hóngwǔ (Hóngwǔ), the Jiǎzǐ (Jiǎzǐ) year, is taken as the epoch.
(The interval above to the Xīnsì (Xīnsì) year of Zhìyuán (Zhìyuán) is 104 calculation units.
The length of the year is 3,652,425 parts,
(measured without variations).
Half of this is the year cycle,
one-fourth of this is a solar term quadrant,
one twenty-fourth of this is a solar term calculation unit.
A day is 10,000 [parts].
(This is 100 *kè*,
a *kè* has 100 *fēn*,
a *fēn* has 100 *miǎo*,
and finer divisions like *wēi* and *xiān*
are all analyzed by multiples of 100.
The *qì* correspondence is 550,375 *fēn*.
Set the *jùsuàn* as 104,
and the obtained intermediate product is 376,199,775 *fēn*.
Add the *Xīnsì* *qì*
correspondence of 550,060 *fēn*,
to get a total product of 376,750,375 *fēn*.
Subtract the *Jìfǎ* of 60
from it,
the remainder is the *Dàtǒng qìyìng*.
The *rùnyìng* is 182,170 *fēn* and 18 *miǎo*.
Set the intermediate product,
add the *Xīnsì* *rùnyìng* of 2,020,050 *fēn*,
to get a *rùnjī* of 376,401,825 *fēn*.
Subtract the *Shuòshí* when full,
the remainder is the *Dàtǒng rùnyìng*.

To calculate *Tiānzhèng Dōngzhì*:
Set the accumulated years from *Hóngwǔ Jiǎzǐ* minus one,
multiply it by the *suìzhōu* to get the intermediate product,
add the *qìyìng* to get the total product,
subtract the *jìfǎ* when full.
The remaining number, if less than full,
is the *Tiānzhèng Dōngzhì*.
With 10,000 as a day,
designate the *jiǎzǐsuàn* outside
as the day and hour of the winter solstice.
Successively add the *tōngyú*,
and you will get the *Tiānzhèng Dōngzhì* for the following year.
To calculate *Tiānzhèng Rùnyú*:
Set the intermediate product,
add the *rùnyìng*,
subtract the *shuòcè* when full.
The remaining number, if less than full,
is the *Tiānzhèng Rùnyú*.
Successively add the *tōngrùn*, and you will get the *Tiānzhèng Rùnyú* for the following year.
To calculate *Tiānzhèng Jīngshuò*:
Set the *Dōngzhì*,
subtract the *rùnyú*.
If insufficient for subtraction, add the *jìfǎ* and then subtract,
which gives the *Tiānzhèng Jīngshuò*.
If there is no intercalary month,
add 543,671 *fēn* and 16 *miǎo*.
(Twelve *shuòcè* minus *jìfǎ*.)
If there is an intercalary month,
add 238,977 *fēn* and 09 *miǎo*.
(Thirteen *shuòshí* minus *jìfǎ*.)
If it reaches a full *jìfǎ*, subtract it again,
and you will get the *Tiānzhèng Jīngshuò* for the following year.
If the *Tiānzhèng Rùnyú* is above the *rùnxiàn*,
that year has an intercalary month.
To calculate *Tiānzhèng Yíngsuō*:
Set half a *suìzhōu*,
subtract the full *rùnyú* of that year from it.
The remainder is the *Tiānzhèng Suōlì* sought.
If you directly seek that of the following year,
subtract the *tōngrùn* from the *Tiānzhèng Suōlì*, and you will get it.
After subtraction,
if it is below 153 days and 09 [parts],
add the *shuòshí* again
to get the *Tiānzhèng Suōlì* for the following year.
To calculate *Tiānzhèng Chídá*:
Set the intermediate product,
add the *zhuănyìng*,
subtract the full *rùnyú* of that year.
If the remainder is a full *zhuănzhōng*, subtract it, and that is the *Tiānzhèng Rùzhuăn*.
If it is below *zhuănzhōng*, it is a *chídá lì*;
if it is above, subtract it to get a *chídá lì*.
If you directly seek that of the following year,
add 237,119 *fēn* and 16 *miǎo*.
(The accumulated sum of twelve *zhuăncā*.)
If there is an intercalary month, add the *zhuăncā* again.
In all cases, subtract the *zhuănzhōng* when full,
and the *chídá* remains as before.
If the *zhuănzhōng* is subtracted when full,
it indicates a change in *chídá*.
To calculate *Tiānzhèng Rùjiāo*:
Set the intermediate product,
subtract the *rùnyú*,
add the *jiāoyìng*.
Subtract the *jiāozhōng* when full, which gives the general day for *Tiānzhèng Rùjiāo*.
If you directly seek that of the following year,
add 6,082 *fēn* and 04 *miǎo*.
(Twelve *jiāocā* minus *jiāozhōng*.)
If there is an intercalary month, add 29,265 *fēn* and 73 *miǎo*.
(Thirteen *jiāocā* minus *jiāozhōng*.)
In all cases, subtract the *jiāozhōng* again when full,
and you will get it.
To calculate the *Jīngshuò* and *Xiánwàng* for each month:
Set the *Tiānzhèng Jīngshuò*,
add two *shuòcè*.
Subtract the *jìfǎ* when full, and you will get the *Jīngshuò* for the first month.
Successively add the *xiáncè*,
subtract the *jìfǎ*,
and you will get the *xiánwàng* and the next *shuò*.
To calculate each *qì*:
Set the *Tiānzhèng Dōngzhì*,
add three *qìcè*.
Subtract the *jìfǎ* when full, and you will get the day of *Lìchūn*.
Successively add the *qìcè*,
subtract the *jìfǎ*,
and you will get the days of the 24 *qì*.
To determine in which month an intercalary month occurs: Set up the *shuò* (new moon) calculation,
subtract the remaining *rùn* (intercalation) from the year with an intercalary month,
the remainder is the *shí* (dividend),
use the monthly *rùn* (intercalation) as the *fǎ* (divisor) and divide,
the number obtained indicates that starting from the month following the *tiānzhèng* (Heavenly Equinox) month, counting outwards,
you get the month where the intercalation occurs.
Intercalations may advance or recede,
this is still determined by having no *zhōngqì* (central solar term) in the *dìngshuò* (fixed new moon).
(If the remainder to be subtracted is less than the monthly *rùn*,
or just enough for one monthly *rùn*,
this means the intercalation occurred in the previous year.)
To calculate the *yíngsuō lì* (calendar of waxing and waning) for each month: Set up the *tiānzhèng suōlì* (Heavenly Equinox waning calendar),
add two *shuòcè* (new moon periods),
subtract half a *suìzhōu* (yearly cycle),
this gives the *yínglì* (waxing calendar) for the *jīngshuò* (mean new moon) of the first month.
Accumulatively add the *xiáncè* (half-moon periods),
this gives the *xiánwàng* (first and last quarters and full moon) and the next *shuò*.
If it reaches half a *suìzhōu*, subtract it for *jiāosuō* (crossing into waning);
if it again reaches half a *suìzhōu*, subtract it for *fùjiāoyíng* (returning to crossing into waxing).
To determine the *chūmò xiàn* (initial and final limits): If the *yínglì* is below the *yíngchū suōmò xiàn* (initial waxing and final waning limit),
and the *suōlì* is below the *suōchū yíngmò xiàn* (initial waning and final waxing limit),
each is considered the *chū* (initial).
Above this, subtract half a *suìzhōu* to get the *mò* (final).
To calculate the *yíngsuō chā* (waxing and waning difference): Set up the *chūmò lì xiǎoyú* (small remainder of the initial and final calendar),
multiply it by the *yíngsuō jiāfēn* (waxing and waning increment) from the *lìchéng* (pre-calculated tables) to get the *shí*,
divide it by the *rìzhōu wàn* (10,000 units of the daily cycle) as the *fǎ*,
add the resulting number to the *yíngsuō jī* (accumulated waxing and waning) below it,
this is the *yíngsuō chā*.
To calculate the *chídí lì* (calendar of slowness and swiftness) for each month: Set up the *tiānzhèng jīngshuò chídí lì* (Heavenly Equinox mean new moon slowness and swiftness calendar),
add two *zhuǎnchā* (turning differences),
this gives the *chídí lì* for the *jīngshuò* of the first month.
Accumulatively add the *xiáncè*,
this gives the *xiánwàng* and the next *shuò*.
If it reaches *zhuǎnzhōng* (mid-cycle turning), subtract it,
this is *chídí xiāngdài* (slowness and swiftness alternating).
To determine the *chídí xiàn* (slowness and swiftness limits): Set up each *chídí lì*,
multiply it by the *rìzhuǎn xiàn* (daily turning limit),
this gives the *xiànshù* (limit number).
Accumulatively add the *xiánzhuǎn xiàn* (half-moon turning limit),
if it reaches *zhuǎnzhōng xiàn* (mid-cycle turning limit), subtract it,
this gives the limits for each *xiánwàng* and the next *shuò*.
If directly seeking the next month,
add the *shuòzhuǎn xiàn* (new moon turning limit),
and if it reaches *zhuǎnzhōng*, subtract it,
this gives the result.
(Another method: Observe the *rìlǜ* (daily rate) in the *lìchéng*,
if there is one that is smaller than and close to the *chídí lì*, subtract it,
if the remainder is below 820,
this is the limit to be used.)
To find the *chídí chā* (slowness and swiftness difference): Set up the *chídí lì*,
subtract the *lìchéng rìlǜ* (calendar table daily rate) from it,
(If insufficient to subtract,
then shift one place back.)
Multiply the remainder by the *sǔnyì fēn* (gain and loss fraction) below it to get the *shí*,
divide it by 820 as the *fǎ*,
add the resulting number to the *chídí jī* (accumulated slowness and swiftness) below it,
this is the *chídí chā*.
To calculate the *jiājiǎn chā* (addition and subtraction difference): Observe the *yíngsuō chā* and *chídí chā* obtained for the *jīngshuò* and *xiánwàng*.
When *yíng* (waxing) meets *chí* (slow) or *suō* (waning) meets *jí* (swift), they are of the same kind and added together.
When *yíng* meets *jí* or *suō* meets *chí*, they are of different kinds and compared.
Multiply each by 820 to get the *shí*.
Then subtract 820 from the *chídí xiàn xíngdù* (slowness and swiftness limit degree)
to get the *dìngxiàndù* (fixed limit degree) as the *fǎ*.
Divide the *shí* by the *fǎ* to get the *jiājiǎn chā*.
*Yíngchí* (waxing slow) is addition,
*suōjí* (waning swift) is subtraction.
For different kinds compared:
if *yíng* is greater than *jí*, it's addition;
if *jí* is greater than *yíng*, it's subtraction.
If *suō* is greater than *chí*, it's subtraction;
if *chí* is greater than *suō*, it's addition.
To determine the *dìngshuò xiánwàng* (fixed new moon, first and last quarters, and full moon): Set up each *jīngshuò xiánwàng*,
add or subtract the *jiājiǎn chā* to or from it,
this gives the *dìng rì* (fixed day).
Observe the *dìngshuò gānmíng* (heavenly stem name of the fixed new moon).
If it is the same as the next *shuò*, the month is *dàyuè* (long month);
if different, the month is *xiǎoyuè* (short month).
A month without a *zhōngqì* is an *rùnyuè* (intercalary month).
If the *xiánwàng* falls below the *rìchū fēn* (sunrise fraction) for the corresponding day in the *lìchéng*,
then shift it back one day.

To calculate the *rùjiāo fànrì* (general day of nodal entry) for each month: Set up the *tiānzhèng jīngshuò rùjiāo fànrì* (Heavenly Equinox mean new moon general day of nodal entry) and add two *jiāochā* (nodal differences),
this gives the *rùjiāo fànrì* for the *jīngshuò* of the first month.
Accumulatively add the *jiāowàng* (nodal full moon),
if it reaches *jiāozhōng* (nodal end), subtract it,
this gives the *rùjiāo fànrì* for each month.
To directly find the next month,
add the *jiāochā* to get the result.
To determine the *tǔwáng yòngshì* (period of Earth's ascendance): Set up the *gǔyǔ*, *dàshǔ*, *shuāngjiàng*, and *dàhán* *qìrì* (solar term days),
subtract the *tǔwáng cè* (Earth's ascendance period).
If insufficient to subtract,
add the *jìfǎ* (epoch method) and subtract,
this gives the *tǔwáng yòngshì rì* for each.
To calculate the *fāliǎn jiāshí* (additional time for expansion and contraction): Set up the *xiǎoyú* (small remainder) of each determined *dìngshuò xiánwàng* and *qì* (solar term),
multiply it by 12,
if it reaches 10,000, it becomes a *shí* (hour),
starting from *zǐzhèng* (midnight).
If it reaches 5,000,
advance one more *shí*,
starting from *zǐchū* (beginning of midnight).
If the *shí* obtained from the calculation is incomplete,
divide it by 1,200 to get *kè* (quarter-hours),
starting from the first *kè*.
The *kè* of the *chūzhèng shí* (initial and proper hours)
are sequenced as *chūyī*, *èr*, *sān*, *sì* (first, second, third, fourth),
named externally to the calculation.
(The fourth *kè* is an odd fraction,
it accounts for one-third of the *kèfǎ* (quarter-hour unit).
Every three *shí* (hours) make one *kè*,
to complete the number of 12 *shí* and 100 *kè*.)
According to ancient calendars and *shòushí* (calendar transmission),
*fāliǎn* (expansion and contraction) was a single chapter.
*Fāliǎn* refers to
the detailed numbers of the sun's path expanding south and contracting north.
The *jiāshí* (additional time) is appended
to it,
which is used to record the *chénkè* (hours and quarter-hours) of *fāliǎn*,
hence it is called *fāliǎn jiāshí*.
The *dàtǒng* (Grand Unification) calendar adopted this for calculation convenience,
thus combining *fāliǎn* with *qìshuò* (solar terms and new moons) into
one chapter.
Some use multiplication and division to explain *fāliǎn*,
which is not its true essence.
To calculate the *yíngrì* (waxing day): Observe the *qì xiǎoyú* (small remainder of the solar term).
If it is above the *mòxiàn* (ending limit),
it is a *qì* with *yíng* (waxing).
Set up the *cèyú yīwàn líng yīqiān sìbǎi wǔshíliù diǎn èrwu* (period remainder 10,145.625),
(dividing the *qìcè* (solar term period) by 15 days.)
Subtract the *xiǎoyú* of the *qì* with *yíng* from it.
Multiply the remainder by *liùshíbā fēn liùliù* (68.66) (dividing 15 days by *qìyíng* (solar term waxing)).
Add the resulting number to the *qì dàyú* (large remainder of the solar term).
If it reaches the *jìfǎ*, subtract it.
Starting from *jiǎzǐ* (the first in the sexagenary cycle) outside the calculation,
this gives the *yíngrì*.
To find the next *yíng*: Set up the *yíngrì* and its *fēnmiǎo* (fractions of minutes and seconds).
Add the *yíngcè* (waxing period) to it,
then subtract the *jìfǎ*,
this gives the result.
To calculate the *xūrì* (waning day): Observe the *jīngshuò xiǎoyú* (small remainder of the mean new moon).
If it is below the *shuòxū* (new moon waning),
it is a *shuò* with *xū* (waning).
Set up the *xiǎoyú* of the *shuò* with *xū*.
Multiply it by *liùshísān fēn jiǔyī* (63.91) (dividing 30 days by *shuòxū* (new moon waning)).
Add the resulting number to the *jīngshuò dàyú* (large remainder of the mean new moon).
If it reaches the *jìfǎ*, subtract it.
Starting from *jiǎzǐ* outside the calculation, this gives the *xūrì*.
To find the next *xū*: Set up the *xūrì* and its *fēnmiǎo*.
Add the *xūcè* (waning period) to it,
then subtract the *jìfǎ*,
this gives the result.
To calculate the *zhísù* (lunar lodge at culmination): Set up the *tōngjī* (total accumulation),
(adding the *qìyìng* (solar term response) to the *zhōngjī* (central accumulation)).
Subtract the *rùnyìng* (intercalation response).
Accumulatively subtract *sùhuì èrshíbā wàn* (280,000 units of lodge reunion).
Starting from the *Yìxiù* (Wings lodge) outside the calculation, the remainder gives
the *tiānzhèng jīngshuò zhísù*.
Set up the *tiānzhèng jīngsù zhísù*,
add two *sùcè* (lodge periods),
this gives the *jīngshuò zhísù* for the first month.
Accumulatively add the *sùcè*,
this gives the *jīngshuò zhísù* for each month.
Then add or subtract the *jiājiǎn chā* below the *shuò* of each month,
this gives the *dìngshuò zhísù*.
To compute the *rìchán* (sun's ecliptic longitude):
A *zhōutiān* (full circle) is 365 degrees, 25 minutes, 75 seconds.
Half of that is a *bànzhōutiān* (half circle),
and half of that is a *xiàngxiàn* (quadrant).
The *suìchā* (precession) is 1 minute 50 seconds.
The *zhōuyìng* (response of the full circle) is 315 degrees, 10 minutes, 75 seconds.
Note that this *zhōuyìng* is for the *Zhìyuán Xīnsì* year (1281 CE),
it is the number from *Xūqī dù* (Void 7 degrees) to *Jīshí dù* (Sieve 10 degrees).
The *Hóngwǔ Jiǎzǐ* year (1384 CE) is 104 years apart,
the *suìchā* has already receded by 1 degree, 54 minutes, 50 seconds.
Yet the *zhōuyìng* still uses the old number,
which is likely a mistake in transmission.
To calculate the *tiānzhèng dōngzhì rìchán chìdào sùcì* (Heavenly Equinox Winter Solstice sun's ecliptic longitude on the equator in terms of lodge order): Set up the *zhōngjī*,
add the *zhōuyìng*,
(It should subtract the *suìchā* from the calendar epoch *jiǎzǐ*.)
If it reaches *zhōutiān*, subtract it.
If not exhausted,
starting from *Xūqī dù* (Void 7 degrees),
subtract it according to the order of each lodge,
this gives the *dōngzhì jiāshí chìdào rìdù* (Winter Solstice added time equinoctial sun degree).
If seeking the next year,
cumulatively subtract the *suìchā*,
this gives the result.

Calculating the Yellow Path Lunar Lodge Position of the Winter Solstice Day at the Proper Celestial Time. Set the Sun's equatorial degree for the Winter Solstice plus time.
Subtract from it the accumulated equatorial degrees after the solstice.
Multiply the remainder by the Yellow Path rate.
Divide by the equatorial rate.
Add the resulting number to the accumulated Yellow Path degrees.
This is the Sun's Yellow Path degree for the Winter Solstice plus time.
(The accumulated degrees and degree rates for both the Yellow Path and the equator
are all found in the original methodology.)
