Shēn twelve point eight, Jǐng thirty one point zero three, Guǐ two point one one, Liǔ thirteen, Xīng six point three one, Zhāng seventeen point seven nine, Yì twenty point zero nine, Zhěn eighteen point seven five, Jiǎo twelve point eight seven, Kàng nine point five six, Dī sixteen point four zero, Fáng five point four eight, Xīn six point two seven, Wěi seventeen point nine five.
Determining the Fixed Quadrant Degrees. Subtract the Sun's equatorial degree for the Winter Solstice plus time
from the Sun's Yellow Path degree for the Winter Solstice plus time.
This is the difference between the Yellow Path and the equator.
Subtract this year's Yellow Path-equator difference
from next year's Yellow Path-equator difference.
Divide the remainder by four.
Add it to the qi-quadrant.
This is the fixed quadrant degree.
Calculating the Fixed Qi Days for the Four Cardinal Points. Set the calculated Winter Solstice division.
This is the fixed qi for the winter cardinal point.
Add the initial盈 (yíng) [surplus] and final縮 (suō) [deficit] limits.
Subtract the full紀法 (jìfǎ) [cycle rule].
The remainder is the fixed qi for the spring cardinal point.
Add the initial縮 (suō) and final盈 (yíng) limits.
Subtract the紀法 (jìfǎ).
The remainder is the fixed qi for the summer cardinal point.
Add the initial縮 (suō) and final盈 (yíng) limits.
Subtract the紀法 (jìfǎ).
The remainder is the fixed qi for the autumn cardinal point.
Add the initial盈 (yíng) and final縮 (suō) limits.
Subtract the紀法 (jìfǎ).
The remainder is the fixed qi for the winter cardinal point of the following year.
Calculating the Days Separating the Four Cardinal Points. Subtract the greater remainder of the fixed qi of the previous cardinal point
from the greater remainder of the fixed qi of the next cardinal point.
Add sixty days.
This gives the number of days separating them.
If the next cardinal point's qi is insufficient for subtraction,
add sixty days and then subtract.
Then add another sixty days.
This is the number of days separating them.
Calculating the Accumulated Yellow Path Degrees for the Four Cardinal Points plus time. Set the Sun's Yellow Path degree for the Winter Solstice plus time.
Cumulatively add the fixed quadrant degrees.
Each obtains the accumulated Yellow Path degrees for the four cardinal points plus time.
Calculating the Subtraction Amount for the Four Cardinal Points plus time. Set the smaller remainder of the fixed qi for the four cardinal points.
Multiply it by its initial daily motion degree.
Divide by the day's circumference.
This is the subtraction amount for each cardinal point plus time.
The winter cardinal point moves one degree zero five one zero eight five.
The spring cardinal point is separated from the summer cardinal point by ninety-three days,
moving zero degrees nine nine nine seven zero three;
separated by ninety-four days, it moves one degree.
The summer cardinal point moves zero degrees nine five one five one six.
The autumn cardinal point is separated from the winter cardinal point by eighty-eight days,
moving one degree zero zero zero five zero five;
separated by eighty-nine days, it moves one degree.
Calculating the Accumulated Degrees for the Four Cardinal Points at Midnight. Set the accumulated Yellow Path degrees for the four cardinal points plus time.
Subtract their subtraction amount for plus time.
This is obtained.
Calculating the Yellow Path Lunar Lodge Positions for the Four Cardinal Points at Midnight. Set the accumulated Yellow Path degrees for the four cardinal points at midnight.
Subtract the full Yellow Path lunar lodge degrees.
This is obtained.
Calculating the Degrees Separating the Four Cardinal Points at Midnight. Set the accumulated Yellow Path degrees of the next cardinal point at midnight.
Subtract the accumulated Yellow Path degrees of the previous cardinal point at midnight.
The remainder is the degrees separating the two cardinal points.
If it is insufficient for subtraction,
add a full circumference (360 degrees) and then subtract.
Calculating the Daily Difference for the Four Cardinal Points' Movement Degree Adjustments. Subtract the accumulated degrees of motion for the separating days from the separating degrees.
Divide the remainder by the separating days.
This is the daily difference.
If the accumulated degrees of motion are subtracted from the separating degrees, it is an addition (加).
If the separating degrees are subtracted from the accumulated degrees of motion, it is a subtraction (減).
The autumn cardinal point is separated from the winter solstice.
The winter solstice is separated from the spring cardinal point by eighty-eight days,
with accumulated motion of ninety degrees point four zero zero nine.
For eighty-nine days, accumulated motion is ninety-one degrees point four zero one four.
The spring cardinal point is separated from the summer solstice.
The summer solstice is separated from the autumn cardinal point by ninety-three days,
with accumulated motion of ninety degrees point five nine nine zero.
For ninety-four days, accumulated motion is ninety-one degrees point five nine eight seven.
Calculating the Sun's Daily Degree at Midnight. Set the daily motion degree after each of the four cardinal points.
(Found in the "Lìchéng" [completed calculation table].)
Add or subtract the daily difference.
This is the fixed daily motion degree.
Set the Sun's daily degree for the four cardinal points at midnight.
Add the fixed daily motion degree each day.
Subtract the full Yellow Path lunar lodge degrees.
This is the Sun's daily degree at midnight.
Yellow Path Twelve Divisions Lunar Lodge Degrees: Wēi twelve degrees point six four nine one,
enters Jūzī (娵訾),
Chén (辰) is in Hài (亥).
Kuí one degree point seven three six two,
enters Jiànglóu (降婁),
Chén is in Xū (戌).
Wèi three degrees point seven four five six,
enters Dàliáng (大梁),
Chén is in Yǒu (酉).
Bì six degrees point eight eight zero five,
enters Shíshěn (實沈),
Chén is in Shēn (申).
Jǐng eight degrees point three four nine four,
enters Qúnshǒu (鶉首),
Chén is in Wèi (未).
Liǔ three degrees point eight six eight zero,
enters Qúnhuǒ (鶉火),
Chén is in Wǔ (午).
Zhāng fifteen degrees point two six zero six,
enters Qúnwěi (鶉尾),
Chén is in Sì (巳).
Zhěn ten degrees point zero seven nine seven,
enters Shòuxīng (壽星),
Chén is in Chén (辰).
Dī one degree point one four five two,
enters Dàhuǒ (大火),
Chén is in Mǎo (卯).
Wěi three degrees point zero one one five,
enters Xīmù (析木),
Chén is in Yín (寅).
Dǒu three degrees point seven six eight five,
enters Xīngjì (星紀),
Chén is in Chǒu (丑).
Nǚ two degrees point zero six three eight,
enters Xuánxiāo (玄枵),
Chén is in Zǐ (子).
Calculating the Time when the Sun Enters the Twelve Yellow Path Divisions. Set the entering lunar lodge degree.
Subtract the Sun's midnight degree for the day of entry.
Multiply the remainder by the day's circumference.
(One fen is made into one hundred fen.)
This is the dividend (實).
Subtract the Sun's midnight degree for the day of entry
from the Sun's midnight degree for the next day.
The remainder is the divisor (法).
Divide the dividend by the divisor.
The resulting number,
when calculated with the "fāliǎn jiā shí" (發斂加時) [convergence and divergence plus time method],
is the time of entry.
Calculating the Moon's Position.
Moon's mean daily motion: thirteen degrees, thirty-six fen, eighty-seven and a half seconds.
Circumference limit: three hundred thirty-six.
Half of it is the middle limit.
Half of that is the initial limit.
Limit's mean motion: one degree, zero nine fen, sixty-two seconds.
Sun's limit motion: eight fen, twenty seconds.
First Quarter (upper string): ninety-one degrees, thirty-one fen, forty-three seconds (greater).
Full Moon (wàng): one hundred eighty-two degrees, sixty-two fen, eighty-seven and a half seconds.
Last Quarter (lower string): two hundred seventy-three degrees, ninety-four fen, thirty-one seconds (lesser).
End of Nodal Passage: three hundred sixty-three degrees, seventy-nine fen, thirty-four point one nine six seconds.
New Moon (Shuò) mean motion: three hundred ninety-four degrees, seventy-eight fen, seven one one five one six eight seven five seconds.
Calculating the Mean Nodal Passage Day after the New Moon. Set the nodal passage end fen.
(Found in the "Qìshuò Lì" [Calendar of Qi and New Moons].)
Subtract the Tīanzhèng Jīngshuò Jiāofànfēn (天正經朔交汎分) [celestial standard's true new moon's nodal passage general fen].
This is the mean nodal passage day after the new moon.
To calculate for the next month,
cumulatively subtract the nodal passage difference of two point three one eight three six nine days.
This gives the next month's mean nodal passage day after the new moon.
If it is insufficient to subtract the nodal passage difference,
add the nodal passage end and then subtract.
If the nodal passage also occurs in this month,
it is the mean nodal passage day after the new moon for a month with a double nodal passage.
(There is bound to be a month with a double nodal passage every year.)
Calculating the Entry of Mean Nodal Passage into the Slow/Fast Calendar. Set the Jīngshuò Slow/Fast Calendar.
Add the mean nodal passage day after the new moon to get the mean nodal passage entry into rotation.
Below the midpoint of the rotation,
its slow/fast corresponds to the Jīngshuò.
Above it, subtract "rotation midpoint fast nodal passage slow" (轉中疾交遲),
and "slow nodal passage fast" (遲交疾).
To calculate for the next month,
cumulatively subtract the nodal passage rotation difference of three thousand four hundred twenty-three point seven six fen.
(Subtract the rotation difference from the nodal passage difference.)
This is obtained.
If it is insufficient for subtraction,
add the rotation midpoint and then subtract.
The slow and fast also alternate.
Calculating the Slow/Fast Difference for Mean Nodal Passage Entry into Limit. Set the Slow/Fast Calendar for Mean Nodal Passage Entry into Rotation.
According to the "Bù Qìshuò" [Method for Calculating Qi and New Moons],
calculate the slow/fast limit and slow/fast difference.
This is obtained.
Calculating the Fixed Difference for Mean Nodal Passage Addition/Subtraction. Set the Slow/Fast Difference for Mean Nodal Passage Entry into Limit.
Multiply it by the daily rate of eight hundred twenty fen.
Divide by the degree of motion below the slow/fast limit of entry.
This is obtained.
If it is slow, it is added (加);
if it is fast, it is subtracted (減).
Calculating the Middle Accumulation for True New Moon plus time. Set the Jīngshuò盈縮曆 (yíngsuō lì) [Surplus/Deficit Calendar for True New Moon].
(Found in the "Bù Qìshuò".)
If it is in the盈曆 (yínglì) [surplus calendar], it is the middle accumulation for plus time.
If it is in the縮曆 (suōlì) [deficit calendar], add half a year's circumference.
To calculate for the next month,
cumulatively add the Shuòcè (朔策) [New Moon strategy/reckoning].
Subtract the full year's circumference.
This is the middle accumulation for plus time for each new moon.
Call the day a degree.
(If there are two nodal passages in a month,
the later nodal passage uses the middle accumulation for plus time of the previous nodal passage's true new moon.)

Calculating the True Ecliptic Cumulative Degrees and Lunar Lodge Positions for Equinox-Solstice Added-Time by Reference to the Equinox-Solstice Distance. Place the date of the mean syzygy after the new moon.
Multiply it by the mean lunar motion to get the degrees past the equinox-solstice.
Add it to the cumulative value for the added-time of the preceding new moon.
This gives the true ecliptic cumulative degrees for the added-time from the equinox-solstice for each month.
Add the ecliptic daily degrees for the added-time from the winter solstice.
(See Rìchén.)
Subtract from this the ecliptic cumulative degrees in the table,
until it is less than a lunar lodge position.
This is then the true syzygy’s lunar position.
To calculate for the next month,
repeatedly subtract 1.463102 degrees, which is the difference between the mean syzygy and new moon.
(Subtract the ending degree of the syzygy from the circumference of the heavens.
This value should be 1.464080 degrees.)
If a month has a repeated syzygy,
it uses the same new moon.
(The following follows this pattern.)

Calculating the Date, Hour, and Minute of the True Syzygy. Place the date of the mean syzygy after the new moon.
Add the preceding new moon.
Remove the cycle divisor.
Add or subtract the difference in the mean syzygy.
Its date is calculated outside of the Jiǎzǐ cycle.
The fractional remainder is found by the method of increasing and decreasing added-time.
This gives the date, hour, and minute of the true syzygy.
To calculate for the next month,
repeatedly add the ending syzygy.
When it reaches the cycle divisor, remove it.
If there is a repeated syzygy,
add the ending syzygy again.
Calculating the Four Cardinal Ecliptic Lunar Lodge Positions. Place the ecliptic daily degrees of the winter solstice.
Repeatedly add the seasonal quadrant.
When it reaches the ecliptic cumulative degrees in the table, remove it.
This gives the ecliptic daily degrees for the added-time of the four cardinal points.
Ecliptic cumulative degrees table: Jī 10.4 degrees Dǒu 35.6 degrees Niú 42.8 degrees Nǚ 54.15 degrees Xū 63.1075 degrees Wēi 78.5075 degrees Shì 95.6075 degrees Bì 104.2075 degrees

Kuí 120.8075 degrees Lóu 132.6075 degrees Wèi 148.2075 degrees Mǎo 159.5075 degrees Bì 176.9075 degrees Zī 176.9575 degrees Shēn 188.0575 degrees Jǐng 221.3575 degrees Guǐ 223.5575 degrees Liǔ 236.8575 degrees Xīng 243.1575 degrees Zhāng 260.4075 degrees Yì 279.1575 degrees Zhěn 296.4575 degrees Jiǎo 308.5575 degrees Kàng 317.7575 degrees Dī 334.0575 degrees Fáng 339.6575 degrees Xīn 346.1575 degrees Wěi 365.2575 degrees
Calculating the Initial and Final Limits of the True Ecliptic After the Two Solstices. Place the true ecliptic cumulative degrees for the added-time from the winter solstice.
If it is below a half-year cycle, it is "after the winter solstice."
If it is above, subtract the half-year cycle.
The remainder is "after the summer solstice."
Also, observe the degrees and fractions after the two solstices.
If it is below the seasonal quadrant, it is the "initial limit."
If it is above, subtract the half-year cycle.
The remainder is the "final limit."
For calculating the next month,
if the current month is the initial limit,
then repeatedly subtract the mean syzygy-new moon difference.
The remainder is the initial limit of the next month.
If it cannot be subtracted,
then subtract the mean syzygy-new moon difference in reverse.
The remainder is the final limit of the next month.
If the current month is the final limit,
then repeatedly add the mean syzygy-new moon difference.
This is the final limit of the next month.
When it reaches the full seasonal quadrant,
subtract the half-year cycle.
The remainder is the initial limit of the next month.
Determining the Fixed Difference Degrees. Place the initial and final limits.
Multiply them by the total difference of the extreme images, 0.1605508.
This gives the fixed difference degrees.
(The total difference of the extreme images
is the extreme difference divided by the quadrant.
This value should be 0.1605442.)
To calculate the initial limit of the next month, repeatedly subtract.
For the final limit, repeatedly add.
Both are adjusted by adding or subtracting the mean extreme difference, 0.234902.
(The mean extreme difference
is the mean syzygy-new moon difference
multiplied by the total difference of the extreme images.
This value should be 0.235049.)
Calculating the Distance Difference Degrees. Place the extreme difference, 14.66 degrees.
Subtract the fixed difference degrees.
This gives the result.
To find the next month,
add or subtract the mean extreme difference.
(Add for the initial limit,
subtract for the final limit.)
Determining the Fixed Limit Degrees. Place the fixed difference degrees.
Multiply them by the total fixed extreme difference, 1.637107.
(The total fixed extreme difference
is 24 degrees divided by the extreme difference.
This value should be 1.637107.)
The result,
if the true syzygy is after the winter solstice, is subtracted.
If it is after the summer solstice, it is added.
In both cases, add or subtract 98 degrees.
This gives the result.
place the spring true ecliptic cumulative degrees.
Add the initial limit of the distance difference degrees and subtract the final limit.
If it is after the summer solstice,
place the autumn true ecliptic cumulative degrees.
Subtract the initial limit of the distance difference and add the final limit.
The result,
when full, is removed by the ecliptic cumulative degrees table.
This gives the result.

Calculating the Lunar Path's True Equinox-Solstice Subsequent Cumulative Degrees and Entering the Initial and Final Limits. Observe which lunar lodge position the lunar path's true equinox-solstice enters.
Then place the total ecliptic degrees of that lunar lodge.
Subtract the lunar path's true equinox-solstice lodge degrees.
The remainder is the subsequent cumulative degrees of the true equinox-solstice.
Repeatedly add the total ecliptic degrees of each lunar lodge.
When it reaches the full seasonal quadrant, remove it.
This is "after the half-syzygy."
When it reaches full again and is removed,
this is "after the central syzygy."
When it reaches full again and is removed,
this is "after the half-syzygy."
Observe the cumulative degrees of each syzygy.
If it is below a half-quadrant, it is the "initial limit."
If it is above, subtract the quadrant again.
The remainder is the "final limit."
Determining the Fixed Difference. Place the fixed limit degrees for each syzygy.
Subtract and multiply them by the initial and final limits.
The result,
divided by one thousand, gives the degrees.
This is the result.
(Add for after the true syzygy and central syzygy.
Subtract for after the half-syzygy.)
Calculating the Lunar Path's Fixed Cumulative Degrees and Lunar Lodge Positions. Place the cumulative degrees for each lunar lodge after each syzygy of the lunar path and ecliptic.
Add or subtract the fixed difference.
This gives the lunar path's cumulative degrees for each syzygy.
Add the lunar path's and ecliptic's true syzygy's fixed lodge degrees.
The total is the lodge degrees after the true syzygy.
Subtract the previous lodge's fixed cumulative degrees.
This gives the lunar path's lodge positions for each syzygy.
Calculating the Active Quadrant (rule). Place the lodge position after the true syzygy.
Add the fixed cumulative degrees of the final lodge of the preceding half-syzygy.
This is the active quadrant.
If the lodge degrees after the true syzygy are small,
and adding the preceding
syzygy's value is insufficient,
then place the lodge position after the true syzygy and add the seasonal quadrant. This is it.
If a month has a changing syzygy,
place the lodge position after the true syzygy.
Add the fixed cumulative degrees of the final lodge of the half-syzygy before the preceding syzygy.
This is the active quadrant for the changing syzygy.
For example, if the preceding true syzygy was Zhěn,
and the subsequent true syzygy is Jiǎo,
then the preceding syzygy lacks
one Zhěn.
To find the active quadrant,
place the lodge position after the true syzygy,
do not take the fixed cumulative degrees from Yì below and add them,
but still take the fixed cumulative degrees from Zhěn below.
Another example:
If the preceding true syzygy was Zhěn,
and the subsequent true syzygy is Yì,
then the preceding syzygy has one more Yì.
To find the active quadrant,
place the lodge position after the true syzygy,
do not take
the fixed cumulative degrees from Yì below and add them,
but still take the fixed cumulative degrees from Zhāng below.
Calculating the Days of Separation. Place the major remainder of the fixed first quarter.
Subtract the major remainder of the fixed new moon.
This gives the result.
From first quarter to full moon, from full moon to last quarter,
and from last quarter to new moon, follow this pattern.
If it cannot be subtracted,
add the cycle divisor and subtract.

Determining the Fixed New Moon, Quarter, and Full Moon Entered into the Expanding/Contracting Calendar and the Expanding/Contracting Fixed Difference. Place each month's new moon, quarter, and full moon entered into the expanding/contracting calendar.
Add or subtract the new moon, quarter, and full moon adjustment difference.
(All within the seasonal new moon calculation.)
This gives the fixed expanding/contracting calendar.
Observe the expanding calendar. If it is below the initial limit of expansion, it is the "initial limit of expansion."
If it is above, subtract the half-year cycle.
The remainder is the "final limit of expansion."
Observe the contracting calendar. If it is below the initial limit of contraction, it is the "initial limit of contraction."
If it is above, subtract the half-year cycle.
The remainder is the "final limit of contraction."
Find the expanding/contracting difference according to the seasonal new moon calculation.
This is the expanding/contracting fixed difference.
Determining the Cumulative Added-Time for the Fixed New Moon, Quarter, and Full Moon. Place the fixed expanding/contracting calendar.
If it is an expanding calendar at the new moon,
it is the cumulative added-time.
At the first quarter, add the seasonal quadrant.
At the full moon, add the half-year cycle.
At the last quarter, add three seasonal quadrants.
If it is a contracting calendar at the new moon,
add the half-year cycle.
At the first quarter, add three seasonal quadrants.
At the full moon, it is the cumulative added-time.
At the last quarter, add the seasonal quadrant.
After adding, if it is a full circumference of the heavens, remove it.
Calculating the Ecliptic Fixed Cumulative Degrees for Added-Time. Place the cumulative added-time for the fixed new moon, quarter, and full moon.
Add the expanding fixed difference below it if expanding, and subtract if contracting.
This gives the result.
Calculating the [Chìdào] Jia-Shi Fixed Accumulated Degrees and Lunar Lodge Positions. Set the [Huángdào] Jia-Shi fixed accumulated degrees.
If it is below the quadrant of the [Zhōutiān] phenomenon, it is "Zhìhòu" (after the extreme point).
If it is above and then subtracted, it is "Fēnhòu" (after the dividing point).
If it completes two quadrants and is then subtracted, it is "Zhìhòu".
If it completes three quadrants and is then subtracted, it is "Fēnhòu".
Set the [Fēnzhìhòu] [Huángdào] accumulated degrees.
Subtract from it the [Fēnzhìhòu] accumulated degrees within the [Lìchéng] table.
Multiply the remainder by the rate of [Chìdào] degrees below it.
Divide by the rate of [Huángdào] degrees.
Add the resulting number to the [Fēnzhìhòu] accumulated degrees.
Then add the subtracted quadrants.
This is the [Chìdào] Jia-Shi fixed accumulated degrees.
Set the [Chìdào] Jia-Shi fixed accumulated degrees.
Add the [Tiānzhèng Dōngzhì] Jia-Shi [Chìdào] daily degrees.
If it reaches the full [Chìdào] accumulated degrees, subtract it.
This gives the fixed [Shuò Xián Wàng] [Chìdào] Jia-Shi lunar lodge positions.
Calculating the [Zhèngbàn Zhōngjiāo] Hou-Jidu. Set the fixed [Shuò Xián Wàng] Jia-Shi [Chìdào] lunar lodge positions.
Observe after which [Jiāo] the [Shuò Xián Wàng] falls.
([Zhèngbàn],
[Zhōngbàn]).
Then, for the accumulated degrees after the [Jiāo],
add it to the lodge one before the [Shuò Wàng] Jia-Shi [Chìdào] lodge.
This is the [Zhèngbàn Zhōngjiāo] Hou-Jidu.
If it completes a [Qì] quadrant, subtract it.
This is the [Zhèngbàn Zhōng Huànjiāo].
Calculating the [Chūmò Xiàn]. Observe the [Zhèngbàn Zhōngjiāo] Hou-Jidu.
If it is below half a quadrant, it is the [Chūxiàn].
If it is above, subtract the [Qì] quadrant again.
The remainder is the [Mòxiàn].
Calculating the Fixed Difference between the Lunar Path and the Equator. Set the fixed limiting degrees of its [Jiāo].
Subtract and multiply it with the [Chūmò Xiàn].
The result,
divided by a thousand, is in degrees.
This is the fixed difference.
At the [Zhèngjiāo] and [Zhōngjiāo], it is added.
At the [Bànjiāo], it is subtracted.
Calculating the [Zhèngbàn Zhōngjiāo] Jia-Shi fixed accumulated degrees of the Lunar Path. Set the [Zhèngbàn Zhōngjiāo] Hou-Jidu.
Add or subtract the fixed difference from it.
This is the [Shuò Xián Wàng] Jia-Shi fixed accumulated degrees of the Lunar Path.
Calculating the fixed [Shuò Xián Wàng] Jia-Shi lunar lodge positions of the Lunar Path. Set the fixed [Shuò Xián Wàng] Jia-Shi fixed accumulated degrees of the Lunar Path.
Take the accumulated degrees of the Lunar Path after the [Jiāo].
Subtract it from the lodge one before the set lodge.
This is the result.
If a change of [Jiāo] occurs, the preceding accumulated degrees are greater,
and the set accumulated degrees are too small to subtract.
If transitioning from [Bàn] to [Zhèng],
add its [Jiāo] [Huó] quadrant and subtract.
If transitioning from [Zhèng] to [Bàn],
from [Bàn] to [Zhōng],
or from [Zhōng] to [Bàn],
always add the [Qì] quadrant and subtract.
Calculating the Midnight [Rùzhuǎnrì]. Set the [Jīng Shuò Xián Wàng] [Chízhi] calendar.
Add or subtract the fixed [Shuò Xián Wàng] addition/subtraction difference.
In the [Zhíli] (fast calendar),
it directly becomes the fixed [Shuò Xián Wàng] Jia-Shi [Rùzhuǎnrì].
In the [Chíli] (slow calendar), use the [Jiāzhuǎn Zhōngzhì] fixed [Shuò Xián Wàng] Jia-Shi [Rùzhuǎnrì].
Subtract the fixed [Shuò Xián Wàng] small remainder.
This is the midnight [Rùzhuǎnrì].
If the [Rùzhuǎnrì] is too small to subtract,
add the [Zhuǎnzōng] and subtract.
Calculating the Jia-Shi [Rùzhuǎndù]. Set the fixed [Shuò Xián Wàng] small remainder.
Remove the seconds.
Multiply by the fixed [Zhuǎndù] below the midnight [Rùzhuǎnrì].
Divide by ten thousand to get the minutes.
This is the result.

Calculating the fixed [Shuò Xián Wàng] midnight [Rùzhuǎn] accumulated degrees and lunar lodge positions. Set the fixed [Shuò Xián Wàng] Jia-Shi fixed accumulated degrees of the Lunar Path.
Subtract the Jia-Shi [Rùzhuǎndù].
This is the midnight accumulated degrees.
If the [Shuò Xián Wàng] Jia-Shi fixed accumulated degrees initially changes [Jiāo],
and is insufficient for subtraction,
when [Bàn] and [Zhèng] connect,
use the [Huó] quadrant.
When [Zhèngbàn] and [Zhōngbàn] connect,
add the [Qì] quadrant.
Then subtract the Jia-Shi [Rùzhuǎndù].
Then [Zhèng] becomes the latter half,
the latter half becomes [Zhōng],
[Zhōng] becomes the former half,
and the former half becomes [Zhèng].
Set the [Shuò Xián Wàng] midnight fixed accumulated degrees of the Lunar Path.
Subtract it according to the method for calculating the fixed [Shuò Xián Wàng] Jia-Shi lunar lodge positions of the Lunar Path.
This is the midnight lunar lodge position.
Calculating the dawn/dusk [Rùzhuǎnrì] and [Zhuǎndù]. Set the midnight [Rùzhuǎnrì].
Add the dawn minutes below the [Lìchéng] day, checked by the fixed [Yíngsuō] calendar.
This is the dawn [Rùzhuǎnrì].
(If it reaches the full [Zhuǎnzōng], subtract it.)
Set the dawn minutes of that day.
Multiply by the fixed [Zhuǎndù] below the midnight [Rùzhuǎnrì].
Divide by ten thousand for minutes.
This is the dawn [Zhuǎndù].
If calculating the dusk [Zhuǎndù],
check the dusk minutes below the day according to the method.
This is the result.
Calculating the dawn/dusk [Zhuǎn] accumulated degrees and lunar lodge positions. Set the [Shuò Xián Wàng] midnight fixed accumulated degrees of the Lunar Path.
Add the dawn [Zhuǎndù].
This is the dawn [Zhuǎn] accumulated degrees.
If calculating the dusk [Zhuǎn] accumulated degrees,
add the dusk [Zhuǎndù].
If it completes a [Qì] quadrant, subtract it.
Then the [Jiāo] changes.
(If, when calculating the midnight accumulated degrees,
due to the [Shuò Xián Wàng] Jia-Shi fixed accumulated degrees being insufficient to subtract the [Zhuǎndù],
and [Bàn] and [Zhèng] connected,
and the [Huó] quadrant was added and subtracted,
now it changes to [Zhèngjiāo] again,
then subtract the [Huó] quadrant.)
Set the dawn [Zhuǎn] accumulated degrees.
Subtract it according to the previous method.
This is the dawn minutes lunar lodge position.
Set the dusk [Zhuǎn] accumulated degrees.
Subtract it according to the method.
This is the dusk minutes lunar lodge position.
Calculating the relative degrees. The distance between [Shuò] and the first quarter,
and the distance between the first quarter and [Wàng],
use the dusk [Zhuǎn] accumulated degrees.
The distance between [Wàng] and the last quarter,
and the distance between the last quarter and [Shuò],
use the dawn [Zhuǎn] accumulated degrees.
Set the latter segment's dawn/dusk [Zhuǎn] accumulated degrees.
If it has the same [Jiāo] as the former segment,
then subtract the former segment's dawn/dusk [Zhuǎn] accumulated degrees.
The remainder is the relative degrees.
If the latter segment connects to two [Jiāo] with the former segment,
transitioning from [Zhèng] to [Bàn],
from [Bàn] to [Zhōng],
or from [Zhōng] to [Bàn],
add the [Qì] quadrant.
Transitioning from [Bàn] to [Zhèng],
add the [Huó] quadrant.
Then subtract the former segment's dawn/dusk [Zhuǎn] accumulated degrees.
If the latter segment connects to three [Jiāo] with the former segment,
if there is no transition from [Bàn] to [Zhèng] within it,
then add two [Qì] quadrants.
If there is a transition from [Bàn] to [Zhèng] within it,
then add one [Huó] quadrant
and one [Qì] quadrant.
Subtract the former segment's dawn/dusk [Zhuǎn] accumulated degrees.
Calculating the fixed [Zhuǎn] accumulated degrees. Set the dawn/dusk [Rùzhuǎnrì].
(From [Shuò] to [Xián],
from [Xián] to [Wàng],
use dusk.
From [Wàng] to [Xián],
from [Xián] to [Shuò],
use dawn.)
Subtract the latter segment from the former segment.
If insufficient for subtraction,
add twenty-eight days and subtract.
This is the dawn/dusk relative days.
From the former segment,
in the table, check for the same dawn/dusk relative days.
Take its fixed [Zhuǎn] accumulated degrees.
If the [Shuò Xián Wàng] relative days are one day less than the dawn/dusk relative days,
then for the same dawn/dusk relative days,
take its [Zhuǎn] accumulated degrees
and subtract the fixed [Zhuǎnjí] difference of 14.7154 degrees.
The remainder is the fixed [Zhuǎn] accumulated degrees from the former segment to the latter segment.

Calculating the Addition/Subtraction Difference. The difference between the relative degrees and the fixed [Zhuǎn] accumulated degrees is the true value.
Divide it by the [Shuò Xián Wàng] relative days.
If the relative degrees are greater, the result is an addition difference.
If smaller, it is a subtraction difference.
Calculating the Daily Fixed Degrees of the Moon's Travel. Set the [Shuò Xián Wàng] dawn/dusk [Rùzhuǎnrì].
Observe the fixed [Zhuǎndù] below the day in the [Chízhi] [Zhuǎndù] table.
Accumulate the days, adding or subtracting the addition/subtraction difference.
Stop at the relative day.
This is the result.
Calculating the Daily Lunar Lodge Positions at Dawn/Dusk. Set the [Shuò Xián Wàng] dawn/dusk lunar lodge positions.
Add the daily degrees of the Moon's travel.
If it completes the lunar path lodge positions, subtract it.
This is the result.

The Twelve Zodiacal Lodges of the Equator: [Hài] [Wēi]: 12.2615 degrees; [Xū] [Kuí]: 1.5996 degrees; [Yǒu] [Wèi]: 3.6378 degrees; [Shēn] [Bì]: 7.1579 degrees; [Wèi] [Jǐng]: 9.0640 degrees; [Wǔ] [Liǔ]: 4.0021 degrees; [Sì] [Zhāng]: 14.8403 degrees; [Chén] [Zhěn]: 9.2784 degrees; [Mǎo] [Dǐ]: 1.1165 degrees; [Yín] [Wěi]: 3.1546 degrees; [Chǒu] [Dǒu]: 4.0528 degrees; [Zǐ] [Nǚ]: 2.1309 degrees.
Calculating the Accumulated Degrees of the Zodiacal Lodges after the Moon's Path and the Equator's [Zhèngjiāo]. Observe after the [Zhèngjiāo] of the Moon's path and the Equator.
If a certain lunar lodge position is later in the accumulated degrees of each lodge,
then add it.
This becomes the accumulated degrees of the lodge after the [Zhèngjiāo] below that Zodiacal [Gōng].
To find the next [Gōng],
cumulatively add the [Gōnglǜ] 30.4381 degrees.
If it completes a [Qì] quadrant, subtract it.
Each gives the accumulated degrees of the lodge after the [Bànjiāo] and [Zhōngjiāo] below that Zodiacal [Gōng].
Calculating the precise positional degree of the palace boundary: Observe the positional degree of the palace boundary; if it is below a semi-quadrant, it is the initial limit;
if above, subtract the qi (氣) quadrant;
the remainder is the final limit.
Set its intersection's determined limit,
and subtract or multiply it with the initial and final limits.
The result,
divided by one thousand, gives the degrees.
For a direct intersection (zhèngjiāo 正交) or a central intersection (zhōngjiāo 中交), it is an added difference;
for a semi-intersection (bànjiāo 半交), it is a subtracted difference.
Set the accumulated degree of the palace boundary after the direct, semi-, or central intersection,
and add or subtract the determined difference from it,
to obtain the precise positional degree of the palace boundary.
Calculating the xìu (宿) sequence of the palace boundary: Set the precise positional degree of the palace boundary,
and from the moon's path, subtract the xìu (宿) that precedes the set position.
If it is insufficient for subtraction,
add the qi (氣) quadrant and subtract it.
Calculating the moment of the moon's entry into the palace below for each month and day: Set the xìu (宿) sequence of the palace boundary for each month,
and subtract the xìu (宿) sequence of the moon's position at dawn or dusk on the day of entry into the palace.
If it is insufficient for subtraction,
add the degree of the xìu (宿) preceding the palace boundary's xìu (宿) sequence and subtract.
Multiply the remainder by the day's circumference,
and divide by the determined daily travel degree of the Great Yin (Tàiyīn 太陰).
The resulting number,
then referring to the calendar of expansion and contraction (yíngsuōlì 盈縮曆), add the established dawn or dusk minutes for that day.
(Add dawn minutes for dawn,
add dusk minutes for dusk.)
If the full daily circumference indicates entry into the palace on the next day,
if not full, it is on the current day.
Calculate according to the convergence and divergence,
which is the moment of entry into the palace.
Calculating the Culminating Stars
Calculating the right ascension at midnight daily: Set the calculated daily midnight ecliptic,
(see sun's apparent path).
According to the method, subtract the accumulated ecliptic degree from it.
The remainder, divided by the ecliptic rate,
is added to the accumulated equatorial degree.
Then add the equatorial degree of the winter solstice (dōngzhì 冬至) according to the celestial prime (tiānzhèng 天正).
If it is after the spring prime (chūnzhèng 春正), add one quadrant.
After the summer solstice (xiàzhì 夏至), add half a circumference.
After the autumn prime (qiūzhèng 秋正), add three quadrants.
This gives the accumulated equatorial degree at midnight daily.
Calculating the xìu (宿) degree of the equatorial at midnight: Set the accumulated equatorial degree at midnight,
and subtract the equatorial xìu (宿) degrees one by one,
to obtain the equatorial xìu (宿) degree at midnight for the current day.
Calculating the dawn interval degree and the watch difference degree: Set the daily dawn minutes from the established calendar,
multiply by 366 degrees 25 minutes 75 seconds to get the dividend.
Divide by the daily circumference to get the dawn interval degree.
Double the dawn interval degree,
and divide by five to get the watch difference degree.
Calculating the culminating star at midnight daily: Set the calculated daily midnight equatorial xìu (宿) degree,
add half a circumference,
which is the accumulated degree of the culminating star at midnight.
Subtract the equatorial xìu (宿) degrees one by one,
to get the xìu (宿) degree of the culminating star at midnight.
Calculating the culminating star at dusk and dawn: Set the accumulated degree of the culminating star at midnight,
subtract the dawn interval degree,
which is the accumulated degree of the culminating star at dusk.
Accumulatively add the watch difference degree,
to get the accumulated degree of the culminating star for each watch and at dawn.
If it reaches a full equatorial xìu (宿) degree, remove it,
and that is the result.
One-fifth of the dawn minutes,
doubled, is the watch rate.
One-fifth of the watch rate is the point rate.
For all dusk minutes,
that is one watch and one point.
Accumulatively add the watch rate for each watch.
For all watch changes, that is one point.
Accumulatively add the point rate for each point.
Annals, Volume 12: Six Great Unified Calendar Methods, Part 3 (Calculations)
Calculating Eclipses
Eclipse cycle: 27 days 21 kè (刻) 2224.
Halve this for the central day of the eclipse.
Eclipse terminal degree: 363 degrees 7934196.
Halve this for the central degree of the eclipse.
Direct intersection degree (zhèngjiāo dù 正交度): 357 degrees 64.
Central intersection degree (zhōngjiāo dù 中交度): 188 degrees 05.
Anterior limit (qiánzhǔn 前準): 166 degrees 3968.
Posterior limit (hòuzhǔn 後準): 15 degrees 5.
Eclipse difference: 2 days 318369.
Eclipse opposition (jiāowàng 交望): 14 days 7652965.
Solar eclipse yang (yáng 陽) calendar limit: 6 degrees.
Fixed rule: 60.
Solar eclipse yin (yīn 陰) calendar limit: 8 degrees.
Fixed rule: 80.
Lunar eclipse limit: 13 degrees 5 minutes.
Fixed rule: 87.
Yang (yáng 陽) eclipse limit: (Observe the determined new moon entering the intersection.)
0 days 60 or below, 13 days 10 or above, on the 14th day,
regardless of the remainder, all enter the eclipse limit.
15 days 20 or below, 25 days 60 or above, on the 26th, 27th day,
regardless of the remainder,
all enter the eclipse limit.
Yin (yīn 陰) eclipse limit: (Observe the determined full moon entering the intersection.)
1 day 20 or below, 12 days 40 or above, on the 0th, 13th day,
regardless of the remainder,
all enter the eclipse limit.
14 days 80 or below, 26 days 05 or above, on the 27th day,
regardless of the remainder,
all enter the eclipse limit.
Furthermore, if the remainder of the determined new moon is 20 minutes or more before sunrise or after sunset,
the solar eclipse occurs at night.
If the remainder of the determined full moon is 8 kè (刻) 20 minutes or more before sunset or after sunrise,
the lunar eclipse occurs during the day.
In these cases, no calculation is necessary.

Calculating numbers for solar eclipses: Synodic month (jīngshuò 經朔), expansion and contraction calendar (yíngsuōlì 盈縮曆), expansion and contraction difference (yíngsuōchā 盈縮差), slow and fast calendar (chízílì 遲疾曆), slow and fast difference (chízíchā 遲疾差), added and subtracted difference (jiājiǎnchā 加減差), determined new moon (dìngshuò 定朔), general fraction of entry into intersection (rùjiāofànfēn 入交汎分) (All of the above are fully recorded.)
Determined entry into slow and fast calendar (dìngrùchízílì 定入遲疾曆) (Add and subtract the added and subtracted difference from the slow and fast difference to get this.)
Slow and fast determined limit (chízídìngxìan 遲疾定限) (Set the determined entry into the slow and fast calendar,
multiply by the daily rotation limit of 12 limits 20 minutes,
ignore the remainder.)
Determined limit travel degree (dìngxìanhángdù 定限行度) (Use the determined limit,
take the travel degree from the established calendar,
use slow for slow,
fast for fast,
subtract 8 minutes 20 seconds of daily travel minutes,
and obtain it.)
Sunrise minutes (rìchūfēn 日出分) (Use the expansion and contraction calendar,
take from the established calendar;
same below.)
Sunset minutes (rìrùfēn 日入分), half-day minutes (bànhzhòufēn 半晝分) (Take the dusk minutes from the established calendar,
subtract 5250 minutes,
and obtain it.)
Ecliptic xìu (宿) sequence with added time before the winter solstice (dōngzhì 冬至) in the year.
Calculating the constant degree of intersection (jiāochángdù 交常度): Set the general fraction of entry into intersection (rùjiāofànfēn 入交汎分) for the new moon with an eclipse,
multiply by the moon's mean motion degree,
and that is the result.
Calculating the determined degree of intersection (jiāodìngdù 交定度): Set the constant degree of intersection,
and for the new moon, add the expansion part and subtract the contraction part of the expansion and contraction difference (yíngsuōchā 盈縮差),
and that is the result.

Calculating the solar eclipse direct intersection (zhèngjiāo 正交) and central intersection (zhōngjiāo 中交) limits: Observe the determined degree of intersection; if it is below 7 degrees or above 342 degrees,
the eclipse is a direct intersection.
If it is above 175 degrees or below 202 degrees,
the eclipse is a central intersection.
If not within the limits, there is no eclipse.
Calculating the minutes before and after the middle: Observe the remainder of the determined new moon;
if it is below half a daily circumference,
subtract it from half a daily circumference;
the remainder is the minutes before the middle.
If it is above half a daily circumference,
subtract half a daily circumference;
the remainder is the minutes after the middle.
Calculating the time difference: Set half a daily circumference,
subtract the minutes before or after the middle.
Multiply the remainder by the minutes before or after the middle.
The result, divided by 9600, is the time difference.
For before the middle, it is subtracted;
for after the middle, it is added.
Calculating the determined minutes of maximum eclipse: Set the remainder of the determined new moon,
add or subtract the time difference,
and that is the result.
Calculating the determined minutes from noon: Set the minutes before or after the middle,
add the time difference, and that is the result.
(Only add, do not subtract.)
Calculating the maximum eclipse entry into the expansion and contraction calendar (yíngsuōlì 盈縮曆): Set the original expansion and contraction calendar,
add the major remainder of the determined new moon and the determined minutes of maximum eclipse,
and that is the result.
Calculating the maximum eclipse expansion and contraction difference (yíngsuōchā 盈縮差): Calculate according to the method for qi (氣) new moon.

Calculating the determined travel degree of maximum eclipse entry into the expansion and contraction calendar (yíngsuōlì 盈縮曆): Set the maximum eclipse entry into the expansion and contraction calendar,
and for the expansion and contraction difference (yíngsuōchā 盈縮差), add for expansion and subtract for contraction,
and that is the result.
Calculating the north-south general difference: Observe the determined travel degree of maximum eclipse entry into the expansion and contraction calendar;
if it is below a quadrant of the celestial circumference, it is the initial limit;
if above, subtract from half a sidereal year circumference to get the final limit.
Multiply the initial and final limits by themselves,
and divide by 1870 degrees.
The resulting number,
subtract from 4 degrees 46 minutes;
the remainder is the north-south general difference.
Calculating the north-south determined difference: Set the north-south general difference,
multiply by the determined minutes from noon.
Divide by half-day minutes,
and subtract from the general difference;
the remainder is the north-south determined difference.
If the general difference is a smaller number,
then reverse the subtraction.
For initial expansion and final contraction, if the eclipse is at a direct intersection (zhèngjiāo 正交), it is subtraction;
if at a central intersection (zhōngjiāo 中交), it is addition.
For initial contraction and final expansion,
if the eclipse is at a direct intersection (zhèngjiāo 正交), it is addition;
if at a central intersection (zhōngjiāo 中交), it is subtraction.
If it is obtained by reversing the subtraction of the general difference,
then the addition and subtraction are reversed.
Calculating the east-west general difference: Set half a sidereal year circumference,
subtract the determined travel degree of maximum eclipse entry into the expansion and contraction calendar.
Multiply the remainder by the determined travel degree of maximum eclipse entry into the expansion and contraction calendar.
Divide by 1870 to get the degrees,
which is the east-west general difference.
To determine the fixed difference for east and west: Place the general east and west difference.
Multiply it by the minute value determined by the distance to noon.
If it is two thousand five hundred *dù* for one *dù*,
and the resulting number is less than the general east and west difference,
then it is the fixed east and west difference.
If it is greater than the general difference,
subtract it from double the general difference;
the remainder is the fixed difference.
When the *Yíng Lì* (Prosperous Calendar) is before the mid-point,
and the *Suō Lì* (Contracting Calendar) is after the mid-point,
add for the *zhèng jiāo* (direct intersection) and subtract for the *zhōng jiāo* (middle intersection).
When the *Yíng Lì* is after the mid-point,
and the *Suō Lì* is before the mid-point,
add for the *zhèng jiāo* and subtract for the *zhōng jiāo*.
To determine the fixed limit *dù* for the *zhèng jiāo* and *zhōng jiāo*: If the solar eclipse occurs at the *zhèng jiāo*, place the *zhèng jiāo dù*;
if it occurs at the *zhōng jiāo*, place the *zhōng jiāo dù*.
Add or subtract the two fixed differences, north-south and east-west,
and you will obtain it.

To determine the *dù* of the solar eclipse into the *yīn* and *yáng* calendars, before and after the intersection: If the fixed intersection *dù* is less than the fixed limit *dù* of the *zhèng jiāo*,
subtract the fixed intersection *dù*;
the remainder is the *yīn lì* (yin calendar) *dù* before the intersection.
If it is greater,
subtract the fixed limit *dù* of the *zhèng jiāo*;
the remainder is the *yáng lì* (yang calendar) *dù* after the intersection.
If it is less than the fixed limit *dù* of the *zhōng jiāo*,
subtract the fixed intersection *dù*;
the remainder is the *yáng lì* *dù* before the intersection.
If it is greater,
subtract the fixed limit *dù* of the *zhōng jiāo*;
the remainder is the *yīn lì* *dù* after the intersection.
If the fixed intersection *dù* is less than seven *dù*, add the final intersection *dù*,
subtract the fixed limit *dù* of the *zhèng jiāo*;
the remainder is the *yáng lì* *dù* after the intersection.
To determine the minutes and seconds of a solar eclipse: For the *yáng lì*,
place the *yáng shí xiàn* (yang eclipse limit) of six *dù*,
subtract the *yáng lì* *dù* before and after the intersection.
(If it cannot be subtracted,
there is no eclipse.
The same applies to the *yīn lì*.)
Divide the remainder by the constant six *dù* for one *dù*.
For the *yīn lì*,
place the *yīn shí xiàn* (yin eclipse limit) of eight *dù*,
subtract the *yīn lì* *dù* before and after the intersection.
Divide the remainder by the constant eighty *dù* for one *dù*,
and you will obtain it.
To determine the fixed useful minute: Place the minutes and seconds of the solar eclipse and subtract and multiply by twenty minutes,
to get the square root product.
Extract its square root using the square root method,
to get the square root number.
Multiply it by five thousand seven hundred forty minutes (which is seven times eight hundred twenty minutes).
Divide it by the fixed limit travel *dù* for one *dù*,
and you will obtain it.
To determine the times of initial contact and final clearance of a solar eclipse: Place the fixed minutes of the greatest eclipse.
Subtract the fixed useful minutes for initial contact,
and add them for final clearance.
Add hours according to the *fā liǎn* (spread and convergence),
and you will obtain the exact times.
To determine the initial and final directions of a solar eclipse: For the *yáng lì*, initial contact is in the southwest,
greatest eclipse is in the due south,
and final clearance is in the southeast.
For the *yīn lì*, initial contact is in the northwest,
greatest eclipse is in the due north,
and final clearance is in the northeast.
If the eclipse is eight parts or more,
regardless of *yīn* or *yáng lì*, initial contact is in the due west,
and final clearance is in the due east.
(This is discussed based on the noon position.)
To determine the *huáng dào sù cì* (zodiacal lunar mansion) of the sun's track at the greatest eclipse: Place the fixed *dù* of the greatest eclipse entering the *Yíng Suō Lì*.
If it is in *yíng*, it is the fixed accumulated *dù*.
If it is in *suō*, add half a year's cycle to get the fixed accumulated *dù*.
Place the fixed accumulated *dù*.
Add the sun's *dù* on the *huáng dào* (ecliptic) at the added time of the winter solstice before the year.
If it exceeds the accumulated *dù* of the *huáng dào*, subtract it.
Up to the *sù cì* (lunar mansion) that is not full,
that is the sun's track at the greatest eclipse.
To determine a partial solar eclipse: Observe the minutes of initial contact and greatest eclipse.
If they are less than the minutes of sunrise,
it is a partial eclipse at dawn.
Observe the minutes of greatest eclipse and final clearance.
If they are greater than the minutes of sunset,
it is a partial eclipse at dusk.
At dawn, place the minutes of sunrise.
At dusk, place the minutes of sunset.
In both cases, subtract the minutes of the greatest eclipse from them.
The remainder is the partial eclipse difference.
Place the partial eclipse difference.
Multiply it by the minutes and seconds of the solar eclipse.
Divide it by the fixed useful minutes for one *dù*.
Subtract the result from the minutes and seconds of the solar eclipse.
The remainder is the visible minutes and seconds of the partial eclipse.

To determine the numbers used for lunar eclipses: *Yíng Suō Lì* (Prosperous and Contracting Calendars) *Yíng Suō Chā* (Prosperous and Contracting Differences) *Chí Jí Lì* (Slow and Fast Calendars) *Chí Jí Chā* (Slow and Fast Differences) *Jiā Jiǎn Chā* (Addition and Subtraction Differences) *Dìng Wàng* (Fixed Full Moon) *Rù Jiāo Fàn Fēn Dìng Rù Chí Jí Lì* (General minutes of intersection entering the slow and fast calendars) *Dìng Xiàn* (Fixed Limit) *Dìng Xiàn Xíng Dù* (Fixed Limit Travel *Dù*) *Chén Fēn Rì Chū Fēn* (Dawn minutes, sunrise minutes) *Hūn Fēn* (Dusk minutes) *Rì Rù Fēn* (Sunset minutes) *Xiàn Shù Suì Qián Dōng Zhì Jiā Shí Huáng Dào Sù Cì* (Limit number, zodiacal lunar mansion at the added time of the winter solstice before the year).
To determine the constant *dù* of the intersection: Place the general minutes of intersection below the full moon.
Multiply by the moon's parallel motion,
following the method for solar eclipses.
To determine the fixed *dù* of the intersection: Place the constant *dù* of the intersection.
Add the *Yíng Suō Chā* below the full moon if *yíng*, subtract if *suō*, and you will obtain it.
If it cannot be subtracted,
add the final intersection *dù* and then subtract.
To determine the fixed minutes of the greatest eclipse: Do not use the time difference.
Take the fixed minutes of the full moon as the minutes of the greatest eclipse.
To determine the fixed *dù* of the greatest eclipse entering the *Yíng Suō Lì*: The method is the same as for solar eclipses.
To determine the lunar eclipse entering the *yīn* and *yáng* calendars: If the fixed intersection *dù* is less than the mid-intersection *dù*, it is the *yáng lì*.
If it is greater, subtract the mid-intersection *dù*;
the remainder is the *yīn lì*.
To determine the *dù* before and after the intersection: Observe the result entering the *yīn* and *yáng* calendars.
If it is below the posterior standard, it is after the intersection.
If it is above the anterior standard, place the mid-intersection *dù* and subtract it;
the remainder is before the intersection.
To determine the minutes and seconds of a lunar eclipse: Place the lunar eclipse limit of thirteen *dù* and zero five.
Subtract the *dù* before and after the intersection.
(If it cannot be subtracted, there is no eclipse.)
Divide the remainder by the constant eighty-seven minutes for one *dù*,
and you will obtain it.
To determine the fixed useful minutes of a lunar eclipse: Place thirty minutes.
Subtract and multiply by the minutes and seconds of the lunar eclipse,
to get the square root product.
Extract its square root using the square root method,
to get the square root number.
Then multiply it by four thousand nine hundred twenty minutes (which is six times eight hundred twenty minutes).
Divide it by the fixed limit travel *dù* for one *dù*,
and you will obtain it.
To determine the times of the three phases of a lunar eclipse (initial contact, greatest eclipse, final clearance):
Place the fixed minutes of the greatest eclipse.
Subtract the fixed useful minutes for initial contact,
and add them for final clearance.
Obtain the times according to the *fā liǎn*, as for solar eclipses.
To determine the times of the five phases of a lunar eclipse: For a lunar eclipse of ten parts or more,
use the five phases:
initial contact, totality, greatest eclipse, reappearance of light, and final clearance.
Place the minutes and seconds of the lunar eclipse.
Subtract ten parts.
Subtract and multiply the remainder by ten parts,
to get the square root product.
Extract its square root,
to get the square root number.
Then multiply it by four thousand nine hundred twenty minutes.
Divide it by the fixed limit travel *dù* for one *dù* to get the inner minute of totality.
Subtract this from the fixed useful minutes;
the remainder is the outer minute of totality.
Place the fixed minutes of the greatest eclipse.
Subtract the inner minute of totality for the minute of totality.
Then subtract the outer minute of totality for the minute of initial contact.
Again, place the fixed minutes of the greatest eclipse.
Add the inner minute of totality for the minute of reappearance of light.
Then add the outer minute of totality for the minute of final clearance.
Obtain the times according to the *fā liǎn*.
To determine the *gēng diǎn* (night watches and hours): Double the dawn minutes.
Divide by five for the *gēng* (watch) method.
Divide by five again for the *diǎn* (hour) method.
To determine the lunar eclipse in *gēng diǎn*: Place each of the three or five phases.
If it is after the dusk minutes, subtract the dusk minutes.
If it is before the dawn minutes, add the dawn minutes.
If it is less than the *gēng* method, it is the first *gēng*.
If it is less than the *diǎn* method, it is one *diǎn*.
Calculate in sequence,
and you will obtain the number of *gēng diǎn* for each.
To determine the initial and final directions of a lunar eclipse: For the *yáng lì*, initial contact is in the northeast,
greatest eclipse is in the due north,
and final clearance is in the northwest.
For the *yīn lì*, initial contact is in the southeast,
greatest eclipse is in the due south,
and final clearance is in the southwest.
If the eclipse is eight parts or more,
initial contact is always in the due east,
and final clearance is in the due west.
To determine the *huáng dào sù cì* (zodiacal lunar mansion) of the moon's departure at the greatest eclipse: Place the fixed *dù* of the greatest eclipse entering the *Yíng Suō Lì*.
If it is in *yíng*, add half a celestial circle.
If it is in *suō*, subtract seventy-five seconds to get the fixed accumulated *dù*.
Place the fixed accumulated *dù*.
Add the sun's *dù* on the *huáng dào* (ecliptic) at the added time of the winter solstice before the year.
Subtract the accumulated *dù* of the *huáng dào*.
And you will obtain it.
To determine a partial lunar eclipse: Observe the minutes of initial contact, greatest eclipse, and final clearance.
If they are less than the minutes of sunset,
it is a partial eclipse at dusk.
If they are greater than the minutes of sunrise,
it is a partial eclipse at dawn.
(The calculation method is the same as for solar eclipses.)

Calculating the five planets' anterior and posterior conjunctions: Set the intermediate product.
Add the conjunction response.
Subtract the full circumference rate.
The remainder is the anterior conjunction.
Then, set the circumference rate again.
Subtract the anterior conjunction from it.
The remainder is the posterior conjunction.
If it reaches the full *suìzhōu* (yearly cycle) and is subtracted,
then that year has no portion of the posterior conjunction.
Calculating the five planets' intermediate product of days and degrees of the intermediate star: Set each planet's posterior conjunction.
This becomes the intermediate product of days and degrees of the intermediate star under the conjunction-obscuration (合伏, héfú) phase.
(If it is designated as a day,
it is called the intermediate product of days.
If it is designated as a degree,
it is called the intermediate star.
Cumulatively add the phase days to obtain the intermediate product for each phase.
(Subtract the full *suìzhōu* in all cases.)
Using the mean degree below each phase,
cumulatively add the mean degree below each phase.
(Subtract the full *suìzhōu*.)
If retrograde, subtract it.
(If it is not enough to subtract,
add a *suìzhōu* and then subtract.)
Then, cumulatively add again.
This gives the intermediate star for each phase.
Calculating the five planets' advance-and-retreat calendar: Set the intermediate product.
Add the calendaric response and the posterior conjunction.
Subtract the full calendaric rate.
The remainder, divided by the degree rate, gives the degree.
If it is below the calendar midpoint, it is advance (盈, yíng).
If it is above, subtract from the calendar midpoint to get retreat (縮, suō).
Set the advance-and-retreat calendar under each planet's conjunction-obscuration (合伏, héfú) phase.
Cumulatively add the limited degree below each phase.
Subtract the full calendar midpoint.
Advance exchanges with retreat,
and retreat exchanges with advance.
This gives the advance-and-retreat calendar for each phase.
Calculating the five planets' advance-and-retreat difference: Set the advance-and-retreat calendar for each phase.
Divide it by the calendar *cè* (measure) to get the *cè* number.
The remainder, if any,
is the *cè* remainder.
Multiply it by the gain-and-loss fraction below it (see the calculation table).
Divide by the calendar *cè*.
The resulting gain is added, and the loss is subtracted from the advance-and-retreat integral.
This is the advance-and-retreat difference.
For Jīnxīng (Venus), double it.
For Shuǐxīng (Mercury), triple it.
Determining the fixed accumulated days: Set the intermediate product for each phase.
Add for advance (盈) and subtract for retreat (縮) using its phase's advance-and-retreat difference.
This gives the result.
(Subtract the full *suìzhōu*.
If the intermediate product is not enough to subtract,
add a *suìzhōu* and then subtract.)
If the current phase originally has no difference,
borrow the difference from the preceding phase, adding for advance and subtracting for retreat.
For Jīnxīng (Venus) and Shuǐxīng (Mercury),
only use the obtained advance-and-retreat difference.
Do not triple or double it.
Calculating the added time fixed days: Set the fixed accumulated days.
Add the winter solstice fraction of the year's *tiānzhèng* (principal start).
Subtract the full *jìfǎ* (epoch method).
The remainder, designated as outside the *jiǎzǐ* calculation,
is the fixed day.
(If the fixed accumulated days had been subtracted by a full *suìzhōu*,
use the winter solstice of the current year.
If it had been added by a *suìzhōu* and then subtracted,
use the winter solstice of the preceding year.)
Calculating the entered month and day: Set the fixed accumulated days under the conjunction-obscuration (合伏, héfú) phase.
Add the *tiānzhèng* intercalary remainder. Divide by the full *shuòcè* (new moon rate) to get the number of months.
Starting from the eleventh month of the preceding year,
the portion not reaching the *shuòcè*
is the fraction of days already entered into the month.
Observe the fixed new moon *jiǎzǐ* for that month,
and compare it to the added time fixed day *jiǎzǐ*.
This gives the day of conjunction-obscuration.
Cumulatively add the number of days of separation.
Subtract the full number of days for each month, large or small.
This gives the entered month and day for each phase.
Determining the fixed star position: Set the intermediate star for each phase.
Following the method for determining the fixed accumulated days,
add or subtract the advance-and-retreat difference.
Calculating the added time fixed star position: Set the fixed star position.
Add the ecliptic daily degree of the winter solstice added time from the preceding year.
Subtract the full circumference.
If the fixed accumulated days had been added by a *suìzhōu*,
use the ecliptic daily degree from the preceding year.
If it encountered a *suìzhōu* subtraction,
use the ecliptic daily degree of the current year.
If there was originally no intermediate star degree,
then the phase also has no fixed star position or added time fixed star degree fraction below it.
Calculating the added/subtracted fixed fraction: Set the fixed day's small remainder.
Multiply it by the initial daily rate of its phase.
If it reaches 10,000, it becomes a fraction.
The obtained fractions for various phases are subtracted fractions.
For retrograde phases, they are added fractions.
Calculating the fixed star position at midnight and the *sùcì* (lunar lodge sequence): Set the added time fixed star position.
Add or subtract the added/subtracted fixed fraction.
This is the fixed star position at midnight.
Subtract the accumulated ecliptic degrees from the *jīndù* (pivot degree).
This is the *sùcì* at midnight.
For stationary phases, simply use the added time fixed star position as the fixed star position at midnight.
Calculating the Daily Rate and Degree Rate: Set the fixed days of each segment.
Subtract the fixed days of the next segment from them to get the daily rate.
If the next segment is insufficient for subtraction,
add the Jìfǎ and subtract.
Set the fixed stars at midnight for each segment.
Subtract the fixed stars at midnight for the next segment from them to get the degree rate.
If the next segment is insufficient for subtraction,
add the Zhōutiān and subtract.
For all segments near a stationary point,
always use the fixed stars at the additional time of the stationary segment,
and subtract the fixed stars at midnight of the current segment.
If the star's degree is retrograde,
subtract the previous segment from the following segment
to obtain each degree rate.
Calculating the Parallel Division: Set the degree rate.
Divide it by the daily rate
to obtain the parallel division.
Calculating the Fànchā, the Increase/Decrease Total Difference, and the Daily Difference: Subtract the parallel divisions of the preceding and succeeding parts of the current segment
to get the Fànchā for this segment.
(All segments of the five planets that are in occultation, or are slow near a stationary point, or are retrograde,
have no Fànchā.)
Double the Fànchā,
and shift one position to the right to get the Increase/Decrease Difference.
Double the Increase/Decrease Difference to get the Total Difference.
Set the Total Difference.
Divide it by the daily rate minus one to get the Daily Difference.
(If the initial daily motion is greater,
it is a Decrease Difference.
If the final daily motion is greater,
it is an Increase Difference.)
Calculating the Initial Daily Motion and Final Daily Motion: Add or subtract the Increase/Decrease Difference to or from the parallel division of the segment
to get the initial and final daily motions.
Compare the parallel division of the current segment with the parallel division of the next segment.
If the former is greater and the latter is smaller,
add it for the initial,
and subtract it for the final.
If the former is smaller and the latter is greater,
subtract it for the initial,
and add it for the final.
Calculating the Increase/Decrease Difference, Total Difference, and Daily Difference for Segments Without Fànchā: For segments in conjunction (héfú),
set the initial daily motion of the next segment.
Add half of its daily difference
(which is also the daily difference of the next segment)
to get the final daily motion.
For segments of morning occultation (chénfú) or evening occultation (xīfú),
set the final daily motion of the preceding segment (before the current segment).
Add half of its daily difference
(which is also the daily difference of the preceding segment)
to get the initial daily motion of the two occultations.
Subtract the initial and final daily motions obtained for the occultation segment
from the parallel division of the current segment.
The remainder is the Increase/Decrease Difference.
Then add or subtract the Increase/Decrease Difference to or from the parallel division
to get the initial and final daily motions.
Compare the final daily motion of the conjunction (héfú) with the parallel division.
If it is smaller, add;
if it is larger, subtract
to get the initial daily motion.
Compare the initial daily motion of the morning occultation (chénfú) or evening occultation (xīfú) with the parallel division.
Similarly, if it is smaller, add; if it is larger, subtract
to get the final daily motion.
For the end of morning slowness (chénchí mò) of Mùxīng and Huǒxīng,
the morning slowness (chénchí) of Tǔxīng,
the end of evening slowness (xīchí mò) of Jīnxīng,
and the evening slowness (xīchí) of Shuǐxīng,
set the final daily motion of the preceding segment.
Double its daily difference and subtract it.
(This is the daily difference of the preceding segment.)
The remainder is the initial daily motion.
For the beginning of prolonged slowness (jiǔchí chū) of Mùxīng and Huǒxīng,
the evening slowness (xīchí) of Tǔxīng,
the beginning of morning slowness (chénchí chū) of Jīnxīng,
and the morning slowness (chénchí) of Shuǐxīng,
set the initial daily motion of the succeeding segment.
Double its daily difference and subtract it.
(This is the daily difference of the succeeding segment.)
The remainder is the final daily motion.
For the evening occultation (xīfú) of Mùxīng, Huǒxīng, and Tǔxīng,
and the morning occultation (chénfú) of Jīnxīng and Shuǐxīng,
set the final daily motion of the preceding segment.
Internally add half of the daily difference of the preceding segment
to get the initial daily motion of the occultation segment.
Subtract them all from the parallel division.
The remainder is the Increase/Decrease Difference.
For the morning retrograde (chéntuì) and evening retrograde (xītuì) of Mùxīng and Huǒxīng,
set their parallel division.
Shift one position to the right,
multiply by six
to get the Increase/Decrease Difference.
For morning retrograde (chéntuì), subtract for the initial,
add for the final.
For evening retrograde (xītuì), add for the initial,
subtract for the final.
Morning adds, evening subtracts,
the two segments compare themselves.
For the evening retrograde-occultation (xītuìfú) and conjunction-retrograde-occultation (hé-tuìfú) of Jīnxīng,
set its parallel division.
Shift one position to the right,
multiply by three and halve it.
For the evening retrograde-occultation (xītuìfú) and conjunction-retrograde-occultation (hé-tuìfú) of Shuǐxīng,
halve the parallel division,
each serving as the Increase/Decrease Difference.
For the evening retrograde (xītuì) of Jīnxīng,
set the initial daily motion of the succeeding segment.
Subtract the daily difference
(the daily difference of the succeeding segment)
to get the final daily motion.
For the morning retrograde (chéntuì) of Jīnxīng,
set the final daily motion of the preceding segment.
Subtract the daily difference
(the daily difference of the preceding segment)
to get the initial daily motion.
Subtract all from the parallel division.
The remainder is the Increase/Decrease Difference.
For any Increase/Decrease Difference,
double it to get the Total Difference.
Divide it by the daily rate minus one
to get the Daily Difference.
If only one of the initial or final daily motions is available,
add or subtract the Increase/Decrease Difference
to find the other one,
following the method for occultation segments.
The rest is increased or decreased according to the comparison of preceding and succeeding parallel divisions.
For the end of evening slowness (xīchí mò) and beginning of morning slowness (chénchí chū) of Jīnxīng and Huǒxīng,
set the parallel division of the segment.
Multiply it by the "irregular division" of the intervening daily rate below.
(The seconds of the "irregular division"
correspond to the divisions of the parallel division.)
This is the Increase/Decrease Difference.
Set the parallel division.
For evening, use the Increase/Decrease Difference,
add it for the initial daily motion,
subtract it for the final daily motion.
For morning, it is the reverse.
Irregular Division (For the end of evening slowness (xīchí mò) and beginning of morning slowness (chénchí chū) of Jīnxīng and Huǒxīng,
if their Increase/Decrease Difference
is greater than the parallel division,
it is an irregular division.)
Seventeen days: 88.885 seconds; Sixteen days: 88.231 seconds; Fifteen days: 87.496 seconds; Fourteen days: 86.761 seconds.
Calculating the Detailed Daily Motion of the Five Planets: Set the fixed position of the constellation at midnight for each segment.
Add or subtract the initial daily motion sequentially
to get the constellation position for the next day.
Then add or subtract the daily difference to or from the initial daily motion
to get the daily motion.
Also add or subtract it sequentially to or from the constellation position for the next day.
If it exceeds the constellation positions of the ecliptic, remove the excess.
Continue until the constellation position of the next segment is reached,
which is the constellation position at midnight for each day.
Calculating the Time of Conjunction with Zodiacal Mansions for the Five Planets in Direct or Retrograde Motion: Observe the detailed daily motion of the five planets.
When it matches the name of a constellation position at the boundary of the twelve zodiacal mansions
and their degrees/minutes are close, subtract them.
Observe the remaining minutes.
If it is less than the current day's motion,
then the conjunction with the mansion occurs on this day.
For direct motion,
subtract the mansion boundary degrees/minutes from the star's motion degrees/minutes at midnight of this day.
For retrograde motion,
subtract the star's motion degrees/minutes at midnight of this day from the mansion boundary degrees/minutes.
Multiply each by the daily circle to get the dividend.
Use the daily motion of this day as the divisor.
Divide the dividend by the divisor.
The result,
according to the method of adding time for convergence/divergence,
gives the time of conjunction with the mansion.
Calculating the Occultation and Visibility of the Five Planets: To determine occultation and visibility,
for occultation (fú), the planet must be below the Sun;
for visibility (jiàn), the planet must be above the Sun.
For morning visibility (chénjiàn) and morning occultation (chénfú),
set the Sun's daily motion
and subtract the motion of each planet from it.
For evening visibility (xījiàn) and evening occultation (xīfú),
set the daily motion of each planet
and subtract the Sun's motion from it.
This gives the morning/evening occultation/visibility degrees for that day.
Set the current day's occultation/visibility degrees.
Subtract the next day's occultation/visibility degrees from them.
Divide the remainder by four
to get the morning/evening occultation/visibility minutes.
Observe if the current day's occultation/visibility degrees are greater than the next day's; if so, subtract;
if less, add.
For morning,
set the current day's occultation/visibility degrees.
Add or subtract the occultation/visibility minutes to or from them
to get the morning occultation/visibility degrees.
For evening,
multiply the occultation/visibility minutes by three.
Add or subtract them to or from the occultation/visibility degrees
to get the evening occultation/visibility degrees.
Observe whether it is above or below the occultation/visibility degrees of each planet.

To calculate the four “yú” (remainders) to the posterior tally: Set the current accumulated total,
add each “yú” to the posterior tally,
subtract the full cycle if it exceeds,
then you get it.
To calculate the four “yú” cycle’s posterior tally: Take the accumulated position to the posterior tally,
subtract the accumulated days of the initial and final degrees of each mansion in the established table,
then you get it.
To calculate the four “yú” entering each mansion’s subsequent initial and final degrees’ accumulated days: Set each “yú” cycle’s posterior tally,
add the winter solstice fen (minutes) of that year,
subtract the full jǐfǎ (cycle method) if it exceeds,
then you get each “yú” initial and final degrees’ accumulated days.
Zǐqì (Jupiter) and Yuèbèi (Moon Apogee) are the initial degrees of each mansion.
Luóhóu (Ascending Node) and Jìdū (Descending Node) are the final degrees of each mansion.
Qìbèi (Jupiter and Moon Apogee) move forward (direct motion).
Luójì (Lunar Nodes) move backward (retrograde motion).
To calculate the month and day of the four “yú” initial and final degrees’ accumulated days: Set each “yú” cycle’s posterior tally,
add Tiānzhèng (Heavenly Prime) intercalary excess and subtract the full shuòcè (new moon tally),
starting from the eleventh month up to the incomplete shuòcè (new moon tally),
then you get the month of entry.
Its initial and final degrees’ accumulated days,
(which is after subtracting the full jǐfǎ),
outside of the Jiǎzǐ (sexagenary cycle) calculation,
are the remaining days and hours.
Use fāliǎn (expansion and contraction method) to find the time.
By observing the Jiǎzǐ (sexagenary cycle) of the fixed new moon,
you will know the number of days since its entry into the month.
To calculate the four “yú” daily motion degree: Set each “yú” initial and final degrees’ accumulated days.
For Qìbèi (Jupiter and Moon Apogee), add the daily motion rate repeatedly,
up to the final degree, add its mansion’s residual days and fen (minutes),
then it is the initial degree of the next mansion.
For Luójì (Lunar Nodes), first add its mansion’s residual days and fen (minutes),
then add the daily motion rate repeatedly,
then it is the final degree of the next mansion.
For each, use its greater remainder,
outside of the Jiǎzǐ (sexagenary cycle) calculation, as the day and hour.
For its crossing into the next mansion,
use the smaller remainder with fāliǎn (expansion and contraction method) for the time.
To calculate the four “yú” crossing into a palace: Subtract each mansion’s accumulated days of crossing into a palace from the accumulated position to the posterior tally,
the remainder is the accumulated days of entry into a certain palace.
Add Tiānzhèng (Heavenly Prime) intercalary excess,
subtract the full shuòcè (new moon tally) if it exceeds,
starting from the eleventh month up to the incomplete shuòcè (new moon tally),
then you get the month of entry.
Also, set the accumulated days of entry into the palace,
add the winter solstice fen (minutes),
subtract the full jǐfǎ (cycle method) if it exceeds,
as the day and hour,
use the smaller remainder with fāliǎn (expansion and contraction method) for the time.
By observing the Jiǎzǐ (sexagenary cycle) of the fixed new moon,
you will know the crossing into the palace and the time.
