Treatise 13: Calendar 7, Huíhuí Calendar Method 1
The Huíhuí calendar method
was created by Mahāma, the king of the Western Regions country of Madīnah.
The elevation of the North Pole in that land is twenty-four and a half degrees,
and the longitude is 107 degrees west,
approximately eight thousand *lǐ* west of Yúnnán.
Its calendar epoch began in the *jǐwèi* year of the Kāihuáng reign period of the Suí dynasty,
which was the year of its founding.
In the early Hongwu reign period,
its book was obtained from Yuándū.
In the autumn of the fifteenth year,
Tàizǔ said that the Western Regions were most precise in observing celestial phenomena,
and their planetary latitudes were also unknown in China.
He ordered Hanlin scholar Lǐ Chōng and Wú Bózōng, along with Huíhuí grand masters Mǎ Shāyìhēi and others, to translate the book.
This method does not use intercalary months,
and takes three hundred and sixty-five days as one year.
A year has twelve palaces,
and palaces have intercalary days.
In one hundred and twenty-eight years, the palaces accumulate thirty-one intercalary days.
Three hundred and fifty-four days make one cycle,
a cycle has twelve months,
and months have intercalary days.
In thirty years, the months accumulate eleven intercalary days.
After 1941 years,
the palaces, months, days, and hours reconvene.
This is the general outline of its calendrical system.
According to historical records, the calendrical techniques of the Western Regions
include the Jiǔzhí Lì during the Táng dynasty
and Zhámǎlǔdīng’s Wànnián Lì during the Yuán dynasty.
The Jiǔzhí Lì was very coarse,
and the Wànnián Lì was not implemented for long.
Only the Huíhuí Lì established a department
affiliated with the Qīntiānlán (Imperial Astronomical Bureau),
and was used in conjunction with the Dàtǒng calendar for over two hundred and seventy years.
Although there were occasional discrepancies
in the presence or absence and depth of solar and lunar eclipses,
it was far superior to the Jiǔzhí and Wànnián calendars.
However, its books contained many omissions and errors.
This is because those who served as officials in the Bureau
mostly performed calculations using a sand table,
still relying on their own country's books.
And those in the Míng dynasty who studied its methods,
such as Táng Shùnzhī, Chén Rǎng, Yuán Huáng, and their like,
developed their own theories.
Therefore, the translated versions did not circulate widely,
and their incompleteness is understandable.
Now, we extensively consulted specialists among their descendants,
researched their original texts,
to fill in the omissions,
correct the errors,
and thus compile the Huíhuí Lìfǎ,
to be recorded in this chapter.
Accumulated years: From the year of Ālābǐ (Arabia) in the Western Regions,
(the *jǐwèi* year of Kāihuáng of the Suí dynasty),
down to the *jiǎzǐ* year of Hóngwǔ,
there are seven hundred and eighty-six years.
Numbers used: Heavenly cycle degrees: three hundred and sixty.
(Each degree has sixty *fen* (minutes).
Each *fen* (minute) has sixty seconds.
Below this, up to minute fibers, all follow this standard.)
Palaces: twelve.
(Each palace has thirty degrees.)
Daily cycle *fen* (minutes): one thousand four hundred and forty.
Hours: twenty-four.
(Each hour has sixty *fen* (minutes).)
*Kè* (quarters of an hour): ninety-six.
(Each *kè* (quarter of an hour) has fifteen *fen* (minutes).)
Palace degrees begin with Báiyáng (Aries).
Solar terms begin with Chūnfēn (Vernal Equinox).
The designated time begins at Wǔzhèng (noon).
(The first four *kè* (quarters of an hour) of Wǔ (noon) belong to the previous day.)
Number of the Qīyào: Sūn (Sun) one,
Yuè (Moon) two,
Huǒ (Mars) three,
Shuǐ (Mercury) four,
Mù (Jupiter) five,
Jīn (Venus) six,
Tǔ (Saturn) seven.
(The Qīyào are used to record days, not the Jiǎzǐ cyclical characters.)
Number of the Gōng (Zodiacal Palaces): Báiyáng (Aries) initial,
Jīnniú (Taurus) one,
Yīnyáng (Gemini) two,
Jùxiè (Cancer) three,
Shīzi (Leo) four,
Shuāngnǚ (Virgo) five,
Tiānpíng (Libra) six,
Tiānxī (Scorpio) seven,
Rénmǎ (Sagittarius) eight,
Mójíe (Capricorn) nine,
Bǎopíng (Aquarius) ten,
Shuāngyú (Pisces) eleven.
Days in the Gōng: Báiyáng Xū Gōng has thirty-one days.
Jīnniú Yǒu Gōng has thirty-one days.
Yīnyáng Shēn Gōng has thirty-one days.
Jùxiè Wèi Gōng has thirty-two days.
Shīzi Wǔ Gōng has thirty-one days.
Shuāngnǚ Sì Gōng has thirty-one days.
Tiānpíng Chén Gōng has thirty days.
Tiānxī Mǎo Gōng has thirty days.
Rénmǎ Yín Gōng has twenty-nine days.
Mójíe Chǒu Gōng has twenty-nine days.
Bǎopíng Zǐ Gōng has thirty days.
Shuāngyú Hài Gōng has thirty days.
(The twelve palaces above
are what are called the "fixed months,"
totaling three hundred sixty-five days,
which is the number of days in a year cycle.
If a leap year occurs in the Gōngfēn,
one day is added to the Shuāngyú Gōng,
totaling three hundred sixty-six days.)
Sizes of the Yuèfēn (Lunar Months): Odd months are long,
even months are short.
(These are the twelve months,
what are called the "moving months."
Long months have thirty days,
short months have twenty-nine days,
totaling three hundred fifty-four days,
which is the number of days in twelve months.
If a leap year occurs in the Yuèfēn,
one day is added to the twelfth month,
totaling three hundred fifty-five days.)
Highest longitudes of the Sun and the Five Planets (measured in the Jǐwèi year of the Suí dynasty):
Sun: two Gōng, twenty-nine dù, twenty-one fēn.
Saturn: eight Gōng, fourteen dù, forty-eight fēn.
Jupiter: six Gōng, initial dù, eight fēn.
Mars: four Gōng, fifteen dù, four fēn.
Venus: two Gōng, seventeen dù, six fēn.
Mercury: seven Gōng, six dù, seventeen fēn.
To find the leap day for the Gōngfēn (the remaining day of "ài"):
Set aside the accumulated years before the Western Regions' year,
subtract one,
and multiply by one hundred fifty-nine.
(Within one hundred twenty-eight years,
there are thirty-one leap days,
so multiply by the total number.) Add fifteen
internally
(for the leap correspondence).
Repeatedly subtract one hundred twenty-eight;
if the remainder is not full,
and it is ninety-seven or more,
(this is the leap limit),
that year has a leap day in the Gōngfēn;
otherwise, it has no leap day.
Add five to the quotient obtained from the division
(because the Gōngfēn table starts at Huǒ three,
it is necessary to add five).
If it reaches seven, remove it;
the remainder is the Qīyào for the first day of the Báiyáng Gōng for the desired year.
(If there is a leap, add one day;
the same applies later.)
To find the leap day for the Yuèfēn (the remaining day of "shuò"):
Set aside the accumulated years before the Western Regions' year,
subtract one,
and multiply by one hundred thirty-one
(multiply by the total number).
Add one hundred ninety-four
internally
(for the leap correspondence).
Repeatedly divide by thirty;
if the remainder is nineteen or more,
(this is the leap limit),
that year has a leap day in the Yuèfēn;
otherwise, it has none.
For the quotient obtained from the division,
if it reaches seven, remove it; the remainder is the Qīyào for the first day of the first month for the desired year.
Method for adding order: Set aside the accumulated days
(the total accumulation, including the Gōng leap days).
Subtract the month leap days,
and internally add three hundred thirty-one days
(the days before the Spring Equinox of the Jǐwèi year).
Divide by three hundred fifty-four (the number of days in one year).
From the remainder, subtract the added three hundred thirty-one,
then subtract twenty-three
(to complete the number of days in one year),
then subtract twenty-four
(the addition order of Hóngwǔ Jiǎzǐ),
then subtract one
(the one day lost due to the correction).
The resulting number is the actual elapsed years (from Jǐwèi to the present).
Another method: From the accumulated "Qì" (Gōng leap days combined with general leap days are the accumulated "Qì"),
subtract the month leap days
(set aside eleven,
multiply by the elapsed years,
add fourteen externally,
divide by thirty to get the number of month leap days).
Divide by three hundred fifty-four.
From the remainder, subtract the Hóngwǔ addition order of twenty-four,
then subtract the compensating day twenty-three,
then subtract the one day lost due to the correction.
The resulting number is as before.
(To find the general leap,
set aside eleven days and multiply by the elapsed years.
To find the Gōng leap, see above.)
Sun's longitude.
To find the highest total longitude: Set aside the accumulated years before the Western Regions' year,
enter them into the table of total years, months, and days,
and take the highest longitudes from the previous year, previous month, and previous day, and add them together.
(For example, if seeking ten years, take those for nine years.
This is because the longitudes in the table
are all for the full number of days of the current year and current month.
If seeking ten years, you would be exceeding the number if you took the tenth year directly.
The principle for months and days is the same.
Follow this rule hereafter.)
To find the highest longitude: Take the found highest total longitude,
add the measured highest longitude of the Sun
(two Gōng, twenty-nine dù, twenty-one fēn),
which is the highest longitude for the Báiyáng Gōng for the desired year.
If seeking the next Gōng,
successively add five miǎo and zero-six wēi.
If seeking the next month,
add four miǎo and fifty-six wēi.
To find the central longitude (daily parallel longitude):
Set aside the accumulated years, enter them into the table of total years, months, and days,
and add together the daily central longitudes
(the method for taking them is as before).
Internally subtract one fēn and four miǎo,
which is the central longitude for the first day of the Báiyáng Gōng for the desired year.
To find the longitudes for each Gōng, month, and day,
successively add the daily longitude (fifty-nine fēn and eight miǎo).
(The internal subtraction of one fēn and four miǎo
is sometimes said to be the difference in distance between the Western Regions and China,
but this is incorrect;
it refers to the longitude correspondence for the last day of the Gōngfēn in the Jǐwèi year.)
To find the proper longitude:
Take the central longitude for that day,
subtract the highest longitude for its Gōng,
and that is it.
(This is the longitude for entering the Yíngsuō calendar.)
To find the addition/subtraction difference (i.e., the Yíngsuō difference):
Use the proper Gōng longitude as the argument,
enter it into the Sun's addition/subtraction table,
and take the addition/subtraction difference according to the argument's Gōng longitude.
(This is called the undecided difference.)
For the small remainder below the dù,
use the proportional method:
subtract the addition/subtraction difference of the current dù
from the addition/subtraction difference of the next dù;
convert the remainder into miǎo
(e.g., one fēn is sixty miǎo);
multiply by the small remainder of the argument (also converted to miǎo)
to get a xiān
(miǎo multiplied by miǎo yields xiān).
Divide by sixty
to get wēi, then miǎo, then fēn.
(If the number is large,
first divide by sixty to get wēi,
then by sixty to get miǎo,
then by sixty to get fēn.)
Compare it with the previously obtained undecided addition/subtraction difference;
if it is less than the latter number (the addition/subtraction difference of the next dù),
add it;
if it is more than the latter number,
subtract it. This is the determined addition/subtraction difference in fēn.
(If there is no small remainder,
use the undecided difference directly as the determined difference.
Follow this rule hereafter.)
To find the longitude (ecliptic longitude
): Place its daily mean motion.
Add or subtract the fixed difference to or from it.
(Observe the argument of the fixed difference from the planet's own palace degree.
From the 1st to the 5th palace, it is a subtraction difference.
From the 6th to the 11th palace, it is an addition difference.
)The result is obtained.
To find the Qīyào (Seven Luminaries): Place the accumulated years into the Lìchéng table.
Take the Qīyào numbers under the total years, odd years, months, and days, and combine them.
Repeatedly subtract 7.
The remainder is the Qīyào for the first day of the Báiyánggōng (Aries Palace) in the desired year.
If finding for the next palace,
add the Qīyào numbers of each palace.
If finding for each successive day,
repeatedly add 1.
When it reaches 7, subtract it.
(Finding the Qīyào for Tàiyīn (Moon), the Wǔxīng (Five Planets), Luóhóu and Jìdū (Rāhu and Ketu), all follow this method.)
Tàiyīn's (Moon's) Motion
To find the mean motion: Place the accumulated years into the Lìchéng table.
Combine the mean motion numbers under the total years, odd years, months, and days.
The number obtained,
subtract 14 fen from it,
(Yǐwèi year should be turned back.)
is the mean motion for the first day of the Báiyánggōng (Aries Palace) in the desired year.
If finding for each successive day,
repeatedly add the daily motion.
To find the doubled distance (lunar body's motion in the small epicycle,
after the conjunction, it is the distance from the sun.)
: Place the accumulated years into the Lìchéng table.
Combine the doubled distance numbers under the total years, odd years, months, and days.
Subtract 26 fen from it.
This is the degree for the first day of the Báiyánggōng (Aries Palace) that is sought.
If finding for each successive day,
repeatedly add the daily motion of the doubled distance.
half of it
is the number of the small epicycle's center from the Sun.)
To find the motion of the primary epicycle (i.e., the Moon's revolution degree.)
: Place the accumulated years into the Lìchéng table.
Combine the primary epicycle motion numbers under the total years, odd years, months, and days.
Subtract 14 fen from it.
This is the degree for the first day of the Báiyánggōng (Aries Palace) that is sought.
If finding for each successive day,
repeatedly add the daily motion of the primary epicycle.
To find the first addition/subtraction difference (also called doubled distance difference.)
: Use the doubled distance palace degree as the argument.
Enter it into the Tàiyīn's first addition/subtraction Lìchéng table.
Obtain the addition/subtraction difference.
(Not a fixed difference yet.)
Then subtract it from the lower difference.
Multiply the remainder by the small remainder of the argument.
The result is in seconds.
(Fen multiplied by fen.)
Divide by 60 to convert it to fen.
Use this to add or subtract the unfixed difference.
(If the latter difference is greater, add; if smaller, subtract.
Same as for the Sun.)
This gives the first difference fen.
To find the fixed motion of the primary epicycle: Place its daily primary epicycle motion.
Add or subtract the first difference fen.
(Observe the doubled distance degree.
Add for the first six palaces.
Subtract for the latter six palaces.)
To find the second addition/subtraction difference: Use the fixed motion of the primary epicycle as the argument.
Enter it into the Tàiyīn's second addition/subtraction Lìchéng table.
Obtain the unfixed difference.
According to the proportional method,
(Same as before.)
find the zero number and add or subtract it to get the second addition/subtraction difference fen.
(Observe the argument.
For the first six palaces, it is a subtraction difference.
For the latter, it is an addition difference.)
To find the bǐfūfen (ratio-spread minutes): Use the doubled distance palace degree.
Enter it into the first addition/subtraction Lìchéng table.
Obtain the bǐfūfen.
If the zero minutes of the doubled distance are above 30 minutes,
take the bǐfūfen of the lower degree.
To find the yuǎnjìndù (distance degree): Use the fixed palace degree of the primary epicycle as the argument.
Enter it into the Tàiyīn's second addition/subtraction Lìchéng table.
Obtain the yuǎnjìndù fen.
Its argument's zero minutes are also obtained using the proportional method.
To find the fànchā dìngchā (general difference and fixed difference): Place the bǐfūfen.
Multiply it by the common denominator of the yuǎnjìndù.
Divide by 60 to convert it to fen.
This is the fànchā.
Add the fànchā to the second addition/subtraction difference.
This is the dìngchā (fixed difference).
To find the longitude: Place its daily Tàiyīn's mean motion.
Add or subtract the dìngchā from it.
This is the Tàiyīn's longitude.
(Observe the fixed motion of the primary epicycle.
Subtract for the first six palaces.
Add for the latter six palaces.)
Tàiyīn's Latitude
To find the distance between Jìdū and the Moon (i.e., the degree of entry into the nodes.)
: Place its daily Tàiyīn's longitude.
Subtract its daily Jìdū's motion
(i.e., Luóhóu and Jìdū's mean degree.)
This is the distance in degrees and minutes between Jìdū and the Moon.
To find the latitude: Use the palace degree of the distance between Jìdū and the Moon as the argument.
Enter it into the Tàiyīn's latitude Lìchéng table.
(For the upper palaces, use rightward direct degrees.
For the lower palaces, use leftward retrograde degrees.)
Obtain its degrees and minutes.
Using the proportional method, find the zero minutes and add or subtract them.
(Add for the first six palaces.
Subtract for the latter six palaces.)
This gives the latitude in degrees and minutes.
(If the argument is in the first six palaces, it is north of the ecliptic.
If after the sixth palace, it is south of the ecliptic.)
To find Luóhóu and Jìdū's motion: Place the accumulated years into the Lìchéng table for total years, odd years, months, and days.
Combine the Luóhóu and Jìdū's mean motion.
This is the daily motion for the Báiyánggōng (Aries Palace) in that year.
To find for each palace's first day,
add each palace's daily motion.
Subtract from 12 palaces.
The remainder is the daily motion of Jìdū for the desired palace.
If finding the detailed daily motion of Jìdū,
subtract the motion of the two preceding and succeeding segments.
Divide the remainder by the number of days between them.
This is the daily difference.
Then place the Jìdū motion of the preceding segment.
Repeatedly subtract the daily difference.
If finding Luóhóu's motion,
add six palaces to its daily Jìdū motion.
Wǔxīng's (Five Planets') Longitude
To find the highest total degree: The numbers are the same as for the Sun.
Follow the previous solar method to find it.
To find the highest motion: Place the highest total degree of the desired planet.
Add the measured highest motion of this planet.
(See above.)
This is the highest motion for the Báiyánggōng (Aries Palace) in that year.
To find for each palace and each day,
add each palace's daily motion.
To find the daily mean motion: Follow the solar method to find it.
To find the planet's own motion: Place the accumulated years into the Lìchéng table under total years, odd years, months, and days.
Combine each planet's own motion.
This gives the daily own motion for the Báiyánggōng (Aries Palace) in that year.
For Sīng (Saturn), Mùxīng (Jupiter), and Jīnxīng (Venus), subtract 1 fen.
For Shuǐxīng (Mercury), subtract 3 fen.
For Huǒxīng (Mars), do not subtract.
If finding for each palace and each day,
repeatedly add the planet's own daily motion accordingly.
For Shuǐxīng (Mercury), if its own motion encounters the first degree of the 3rd palace,
calculate it in 5-day segments.
Upon reaching the first degree of the 9th palace,
calculate it in 10-day segments.
The latitude is calculated similarly.
To find the mean motion of the small epicycle's center (i.e., the Wǔxīng's primary epicycle entered in the calendar.)
: For Tǔxīng (Saturn), Mùxīng (Jupiter), and Huǒxīng (Mars),
place the Sun's mean motion.
Subtract the planet's own motion.
This is the mean motion for these three planets.
Then subtract the highest motion from it.
This is the small epicycle's center motion for these three planets.
For Jīnxīng (Venus) and Shuǐxīng (Mercury),
their mean motion is the Sun's mean motion.
Subtract their highest motion from it.
The remainder is their small epicycle's center motion.
(If insufficient for subtraction,
add 12 palaces and then subtract.)
To find the first addition/subtraction difference (Yíngsuōchā, "increase/decrease difference.")
: Use the palace degree of the planet's small epicycle center as the argument.
Enter it into the planet's first addition/subtraction Lìchéng table.
Find it using the proportional method.
(Method same as for the Sun and Tàiyīn (Moon).)
To find the fixed own motion and the fixed small epicycle center motion: Observe the argument of the first addition/subtraction difference.
If in the 1st to 5th palaces,
use the addition/subtraction difference,
add to the own motion,
subtract from the small epicycle center motion.
Each becomes a fixed motion.
If in the 6th to 11th palaces,
use the addition/subtraction difference,
subtract from the own motion,
add to the small epicycle center motion.
Each becomes a fixed motion.
To find the second addition/subtraction difference: Use the planet's fixed own motion.
Enter it into the planet's second addition/subtraction Lìchéng table.
Obtain its degrees and minutes.
Use the proportional method to add or subtract.
(Same as before.)
To find the *bǐfūfēn* (ratio and distribution): For Sātār (Saturn), Mùxīng (Jupiter), Jīnxīng (Venus), Shuǐxīng (Mercury),
determine the *gōngdù* (degree of the zodiacal palace) by the center of the epicycle of the star.
Enter this into the first *jiājiǎn lìchéng* (addition and subtraction table).
Take the *bǐfūfēn*.
If the remainder of the *yǐnshù* (leading number) is 30 minutes or more,
take the *bǐfūfēn* of the subsequent row.
For Huǒxīng (Mars),
it is necessary to use the method of proportion to find it.
To find the *yuǎnjìndù* (apogee and perigee degree): Determine the *gōngdù* by the star's own motion.
Enter this into the second *jiājiǎn lìchéng*.
Take the *yuǎnjìndù*.
Find it according to the method of proportion.
To find the *fànchā* (general variation) and *dìngchā* (fixed variation): The method is the same as for Tàiyīn (the Moon).
To find the *jīngdù* (longitude): Place the fixed degree of the center of the epicycle.
Add or subtract the *dìngchā*.
(Observe the *yǐnshù*'s own fixed degree:
add if it is before the 6th *gōng* (palace),
subtract if after.)
Then add the highest travel degree of that star.
To find the *liúdùn* (stationary segment): Use the *gōngdù* determined by the center of the epicycle of its *liúdùn*
as the *yǐnshù*.
(This is the fixed limit for each star in the *lìchéng* to enter the calendar.)
Enter this into the *Wǔxīng shùntuìliú lìchéng* (Five Stars direct, retrograde, and stationary table).
At the close degree of the same *gōng*,
take the star's degree and minute,
and subtract it from the preceding and succeeding rows.
(If it falls between the 1st and 6th *gōng*,
subtract the current row from the succeeding row.
If it falls between the 6th and 1st *gōng*,
subtract the current row from the preceding row.)
Also, subtract the *gōngdù* of the *yǐnshù*
from the close degree of the same *gōng* in the *lìchéng*.
Multiply the remainders of the two subtractions (common fraction).
Divide by 6 degrees.
(Each interval in the *lìchéng* is 6 degrees.)
Convert to minutes by multiplying by 60.
Add directly and subtract inversely to the previously taken degree and minute.
If the obtained number is the same as the fixed degree of its own motion for that day,
then it is the stationary point for that day.
If its own fixed degree is greater, the stationary day has passed.
If it is smaller, the stationary day has not yet arrived.
To get a precise rate,
subtract the obtained number from its own fixed degree for that day.
Divide the remainder by the daily motion degree of each star.
(For example, Sātār's daily motion is 57 minutes and a fraction.)
This gives the number of days before or after the current day for the stationary day.
(Sātār is stationary for 7 days;
the three days before and three days after the stationary day
are all considered the same as the stationary day's number.
Mùxīng is stationary for 5 days;
the two days before and two days after the stationary day
are considered the same as the stationary day's number.
Huǒxīng, Jīnxīng, and Shuǐxīng do not have stationary periods;
they immediately move forward after retrograding and immediately retrograde after moving forward.
However, the point where the motion is extremely slow is considered the stationary point.)
To find the *xìxíngfēn* (detailed daily motion): For Sātār, Mùxīng, Jīnxīng, and Huǒxīng,
subtract the longitudes of the preceding and succeeding segments.
Divide the result by the number of intervening days to get the daily motion.
For Shuǐxīng, subtract the longitude of the first day of the *Báiyánggōng* (Aries Palace)
from the longitude of the previous day.
The remainder is the daily motion for the first day.
Also, subtract the longitudes of the preceding and succeeding segments.
Divide the remainder by the number of intervening days to get the parallel daily motion.
Add or subtract from the first day's motion.
Double it.
Divide by the number of intervening days between the day before the preceding segment and the succeeding segment
to get the daily difference.
Add or subtract this from the first day's motion.
(Add if the first day's motion is less than the parallel motion;
subtract if greater.)
This gives the daily motion.
For the five stars, place the longitude of the preceding segment.
Add the daily motion directly and subtract inversely,
to get the daily longitude of each star.
To find the *fújiàn* (conjunction/occultation and reappearance): Observe the fixed degree of each star's own motion.
If it is above the limit degree in the *Fújiàn lìchéng*,
then it is the morning and evening *fújiàn* of the five stars.
Five Stars Latitude: (To find the highest total motion, center motion, proper motion, and epicycle center degree,
all follow the method for the longitude of the five stars.)
To find the *zìxíng dìngdù* (fixed degree of proper motion): Place the *gōngdùfēn* (degree and minute of the palace) of the proper motion.
Multiply the *gōng* by 10 to get the degree.
(For example, for the 1st *gōng*, multiply by 10 to get 10 degrees.
This uses an approximate conversion method to create the latitude *lìchéng*.)
Multiply the degree by 20 to get the minute;
convert every 60 to a degree.
Multiply the minute by 20 to get the second;
convert every 60 to a minute.
Add them up to get the result.
To find the *xiǎolúnxīn dìngdù* (fixed degree of the epicycle center): Place the *gōngdùfēn* of the epicycle center.
Multiply the *gōng* by 5 to get the degree.
(For example, for the 1st *gōng*, multiply by 5 to get 5 degrees.)
Multiply the degree by 10 to get the minute;
convert every 60 to a degree.
Multiply the minute by 10 to get the second;
convert every 60 to a minute.
Add them up to get the result.
To find the *wěidù* (latitude): Use the *xiǎolúnxīn dìngdù* and *zìxíng dìngdù*
and enter them into the star's latitude *lìchéng* to take two values.
(One vertical, one horizontal.)
Subtract the obtained number from the succeeding row.
(If it crosses the *Huángdào* (ecliptic), add it to the succeeding row.)
Also, subtract the *xiǎolúnxīn dìngdù*
from the *xiǎolúnxīn dìngdù* at the top of the *lìchéng*.
(Top horizontal row.)
Multiply the remainders of the two subtractions.
Divide by the accumulated sum of *xiǎolúnxīn dù* at the top of the *lìchéng*.
(For example, for Sātār, the *xiǎolúnxīn dù* in the top horizontal row is spaced every 3 degrees; for Huǒxīng, every 2 degrees.)
Convert to minutes by multiplying by 60.
Use this to add or subtract from the two previously taken numbers.
(Subtract if greater than the succeeding row;
add if less.
If it crosses the *Huángdào*, subtract even if the succeeding row number is greater.)
Store it on the left.
Again, subtract the *zìxíng dìngdù* from the *zìxíng dìngdù* at the top of the *lìchéng*.
(First vertical row.)
Also, subtract the two taken numbers
from the lower row.
(If it crosses the *Huángdào*, add it to the lower row.)
Multiply the remainders of the two subtractions.
Divide by the accumulated sum of *zìxíng dù* at the top of the *lìchéng*.
(For example, for Sātār's vertical row, the *zìxíng dù* is spaced every 10 degrees; for Huǒxīng, every 4 degrees.)
Convert to minutes by multiplying by 60.
Add or subtract this from the number stored on the left.
(For example, if the two taken numbers are greater than the lower row, subtract;
if less, add.
If it crosses the *Huángdào*, and the obtained minute is greater than the number stored on the left,
subtract the stored number from the obtained minute.
The remainder is the north-south minute after crossing the *Huángdào*.)
This gives the fixed north-south latitude in minutes relative to the *Huángdào*.
To find the *wěidù xìxíngfēn* (detailed daily latitude motion): Place the preceding segment's latitude of the star.
Subtract it from the succeeding segment's latitude.
Divide the remainder by the number of intervening days to get the daily difference.
Place the preceding segment's latitude.
Add the daily difference directly and subtract inversely to get the daily latitude in minutes.
(Note: If the preceding segment's latitude is less than the succeeding segment's,
add the daily difference directly and subtract inversely.
If the preceding segment's latitude is greater than the succeeding segment's,
subtract the daily difference directly and add inversely.
This cannot be generalized.
If the north-south positions of the preceding and succeeding segments are different,
add the latitudes of the preceding and succeeding segments of the star.
Divide by the number of intervening days to get the daily difference.
Place the preceding segment's latitude.
Subtract the daily difference cumulatively until it cannot be subtracted further.
Subtract the remainder from the daily difference.
Add the remainder cumulatively to get the daily latitude.)
Method for Calculating Solar Eclipses: (For solar eclipse numbers,
if the new moon (conjunction) occurs before noon,
use the numbers from the previous day for calculation.
If it occurs after noon, use the numbers from the next day for calculation.)
To determine the *rìshí xiàndù* (solar eclipse limit): Observe the latitude of Tàiyīn at the new moon.
If it is below 45 minutes south of the *Huángdào*,
or below 90 minutes north of the *Huángdào*,
there will be an eclipse.
If the new moon occurs during the daytime,
the eclipse will be fully visible.
If the new moon occurs within three hours before sunrise and within 15 minutes after sunset,
(one quarter of an *shí*),
there will be a partial eclipse.
If the new moon occurs during the nighttime, it is not counted.
To find the *shíshènfànshí* (general time of maximum eclipse, i.e., conjunction): Place the degrees Tàiyīn has moved past the Sun at noon.
(The method for finding this is given later under "Tàiyīn's Hourly Movement Past the Sun for Lunar Eclipses.")
Convert to seconds.
Multiply by 24 to get the *shí* (dividend).
Place Tàiyīn's daily motion degree.
Subtract Sānyáng's daily motion degree.
Convert to seconds to get the *fǎ* (divisor).
Divide to get the hour.
Convert the fractional part of the hour to minutes by multiplying by 60.
Convert the fractional part of the minute to seconds by multiplying by 60.
30 seconds or more are rounded up to one minute.
60 minutes are rounded up to one hour.
The total is the *shíshènfànshí*.
To find the solar longitude at the time of conjunction: Convert the universal time of greatest eclipse into fractions.
Multiply it by the Sun's daily motion in degrees (converted to seconds).
Divide by twenty-four to get "wei" (微).
If it reaches sixty, reduce it to "miao" (秒) and "fen" (分).
Then add or subtract it from the Sun's longitude at noon (午正)
(subtract if the conjunction is before noon,
add if after noon).
This gives the Sun's longitude at the time of conjunction.
(This is the ecliptic longitude of the Sun on the day of greatest eclipse.)
To find the "jiājiǎn fēn" (加減分) (addition/subtraction fractions): Refer to the Sun's zodiacal palace at the time of conjunction.
Look it up in the table of day and night additions/subtractions (晝夜加減立成).
Obtain the "jiājiǎn fēn",
calculated using the method of proportion.
To find the hours, minutes, and seconds from midnight (子正) to the time of conjunction: Take the universal time of greatest eclipse.
Add or subtract the "jiājiǎn fēn"
(subtract for conjunctions before noon,
add for those after noon).
Then add or subtract twelve hours
(subtract twelve hours for conjunctions before noon,
add twelve hours for those after noon).
This gives the hours, minutes, and seconds from midnight to the time of conjunction.
(Note: The calculation starts from midnight.
This method has been altered to conform to the Dàtǒng (大統) system,
and is not the original method.)
To find the first east-west difference (longitude difference): Refer to the time of conjunction.
If the Sun's palace is in the right seven palaces of the "lìchéng" (立成) (table of longitude and latitude time additions/subtractions), take the upward-moving time
(順行, prograde motion).
If it is in the left seven palaces, take the downward-moving time
(逆行, retrograde motion).
For the time from midnight to conjunction,
find the longitude difference,
using the method of proportion.
(Only use the remainder below the hour for calculation.
The same applies below.)
This is the first east-west difference.
To find the second east-west difference: Refer to the Sun's palace at the time of conjunction in the "lìchéng"
(same as above).
Take the longitude difference for the next palace from midnight to the time of conjunction,
calculated using the method of proportion.
This is the second east-west difference.
To find the first north-south difference (latitude difference): For the time of conjunction,
use the Sun's palace and the time from midnight
to the conjunction in the "lìchéng"
(same as above).
Take the latitude difference,
calculated using the method of proportion.
This is the first north-south difference.
To find the second north-south difference: Using the Sun's palace at conjunction,
take the latitude difference for the next palace from midnight to the conjunction,
calculated using the method of proportion.
This is the second north-south difference.
To find the first time difference: Using the Sun's palace at conjunction and the time from midnight to conjunction,
look up the time difference in the "lìchéng",
calculated using the method of proportion.
To find the second time difference: Using the Sun's palace at conjunction,
take the time difference for the next palace from midnight to conjunction,
calculated using the method of proportion.
To find the east-west difference at the time of conjunction: Subtract the second east-west difference from the first east-west difference.
Convert the remainder to seconds.
Multiply it by the Sun's longitude in degrees and minutes at the time of conjunction
(also converted to seconds).
Divide by thirty degrees to get "xiān" (纖).
Reduce it by sixty to get "wei", "miao", and "fen".
Add or subtract this from the first east-west difference
(if the first east-west difference is less than the second, add;
if greater, subtract;
the same applies below).
This is the east-west difference at the time of conjunction.
To find the north-south difference at the time of conjunction: Subtract the second north-south difference from the first north-south difference.
Convert the remainder to seconds.
Multiply it by the Sun's longitude in degrees and minutes.
Divide by thirty to get "xiān".
Reduce it by sixty to get "wei", "miao", and "fen".
Add or subtract this from the first north-south difference.
This is the north-south difference at the time of conjunction.
To find the time difference at the time of conjunction: Subtract the second time difference from the first time difference.
Multiply by the Sun's longitude in degrees and minutes.
Divide by thirty.
Reduce it according to the rule.
Add or subtract this from the first time difference.
This is the time difference at the time of conjunction.
To find the epicycle motion at the time of conjunction: Convert the epicycle's daily motion (thirteen degrees and four minutes) into fractions.
Multiply it by the universal time of greatest eclipse
(also converted to fractions).
Divide by twenty-four to get "miao".
Reduce it according to the rule to get "fen" and "du" (度).
Add or subtract it from the epicycle's motion at noon
(subtract before noon,
add after noon).
This is the epicycle motion at the time of conjunction.
To find the ratio fractions: Use the epicycle motion as an argument
in the "lìchéng" (table of Sun and Moon's day and night time motion and apparent diameter fractions).
Take the Moon's ratio fractions for the nearest degree in the same palace,
calculated using the method of proportion.
To find the fixed east-west difference: Take the east-west difference at the time of conjunction, converted to seconds.
Multiply it by the ratio fractions, converted to seconds, to get "xiān".
Reduce it by sixty to get "wei", "miao", and "fen".
Add this to the east-west difference at conjunction
(add if present,
do not subtract if absent).
This is the fixed difference.
To find the fixed north-south difference: The method is the same as for the fixed east-west difference.
To find the fixed time of greatest eclipse (i.e., fixed minutes of greatest eclipse): On the day of conjunction,
if the Sun's longitude is in the left seven palaces of the "lìchéng" (table of longitude and latitude time additions/subtractions),
for its time difference,
subtract for black characters,
add for white characters.
If in the right seven palaces,
subtract for white characters,
add for black characters.
All these are added to or subtracted from the time from midnight to conjunction.
The result is then subtracted from the time starting from midnight.
This gives the "chūzhèng" (初正) time.
Convert the remainder to seconds.
Multiply by one thousand.
Divide by one hundred forty-four
(sixty minutes make one hour;
there are one thousand four hundred forty minutes in a day;
therefore, multiply by one thousand,
then divide by one hundred forty-four).
Reduce by sixty.
One hundred makes one "kè" (刻).
This is the fixed time of greatest eclipse.
To find the Moon's longitude at greatest eclipse: To the Sun's longitude at conjunction,
add or subtract the fixed east-west difference.
This gives the Moon's longitude at greatest eclipse.
(The addition/subtraction depends on the addition/subtraction of the time difference at the fixed time of greatest eclipse.)
To find the longitude of Jìdū (計都) at conjunction: Take the universal time of greatest eclipse, converted to fractions.
Multiply by Jìdū's daily motion (three minutes and eleven seconds), converted to seconds.
Divide by twenty-four to get "wei".
If it reaches sixty, reduce it to "miao" and "fen".
Add or subtract this from Jìdū's motion at noon on that day
(Luóhóu (羅喉) and Jìdū (計都) move in retrograde;
add for conjunctions before noon,
subtract for those after noon).
This is Jìdū's longitude at the time of conjunction.
To find the Moon's latitude at conjunction: At the time of greatest eclipse,
add or subtract the longitude of Jìdū at conjunction from the Moon's longitude.
The remainder is the separation between Jìdū and the Moon.
Look it up in the Moon's latitude "lìchéng".
To find the Moon's latitude at greatest eclipse: To the fixed north-south difference,
add or subtract the Moon's latitude at conjunction
(add if south of the ecliptic,
subtract if north).
This gives the latitude at greatest eclipse.
To find the Sun's proper motion at conjunction: Convert the Sun's daily motion (fifty-nine minutes and eight seconds) to seconds.
Multiply by the universal time of greatest eclipse
(also converted to fractions).
Divide by twenty-four.
The result is "wei".
If it reaches sixty, reduce it to "miao" and "fen".
Add or subtract this from its proper motion at noon on that day
(subtract for conjunctions before noon,
add for those after noon).
This gives the proper motion at conjunction.
To find the Sun's apparent diameter fractions: Use the Sun's proper motion at conjunction as the argument
in the "lìchéng" (table of apparent diameter fractions) for the nearest degree in the same palace.
Take the Sun's apparent diameter fractions,
calculated using the method of proportion.
To find the Moon's apparent diameter fractions: Use the epicycle motion at conjunction as the argument
in the "lìchéng" (same as above) to find the Moon's apparent diameter fractions for the nearest degree in the same palace,
calculated using the method of proportion.
To find the sum of the two radii fractions: Add the Sun's and Moon's apparent diameter fractions,
then halve the sum.
To find the Sun's eclipse limit fractions: Take the sum of the two radii fractions.
Subtract the Moon's latitude at greatest eclipse from it.
The remainder is the Sun's eclipse limit.
(If it is not enough to subtract, there is no eclipse.
If the Moon has no latitude,
it is a total eclipse.
If the Moon has no latitude and the Sun's diameter is greater than the Moon's diameter,
there is an annular eclipse.)
To find the Sun's fixed eclipse magnitude at greatest eclipse: Convert the Sun's eclipse limit fractions to seconds.
Multiply by one thousand as the dividend.
Divide by the Sun's apparent diameter fractions, converted to seconds, as the divisor.
Reduce by one hundred to get "fen".
This is the Sun's fixed eclipse magnitude at greatest eclipse.
To find the time difference (i.e., fixed usage minutes):
Square the Moon's latitude at greatest eclipse, converted to seconds.
Square the sum of the two radii fractions, also converted to seconds.
Subtract the two squared numbers.
Take the square root of the remainder.
Multiply by twenty-four as the dividend.
Divide by the Moon's daily motion minus the Sun's daily motion, both converted to fractions, as the divisor.
Divide the dividend by the divisor.
The result is in "fen".
Sixty "fen" make one hour.
This is the time difference.
To calculate the beginning of the eclipse (chūkuī): Set the determined time of the maximum eclipse (shíshèn dìngshí).
Subtract the time difference (shíchā).
Take the remaining time (yúshí) and convert it to the start of the zǐ (子) period (mìng qǐ zǐ zhèng), then subtract accordingly.
This gives the initial exact time (chū zhèng shí).
Convert the remaining minutes (yúfēn) to seconds.
Multiply by one thousand.
Divide by one hundred forty-four.
Reduce by sixty.
Every hundred becomes a kè (刻).
This is the time of the beginning of the eclipse (chūkuī shí kè).
To calculate the end of the eclipse (fùyuán): Set the determined time of the maximum eclipse.
Add the time difference.
Convert to the start of the zǐ period (mìng qǐ zǐ zhèng).
Follow the method for the beginning of the eclipse (rú chūkuī fǎ).
This gives the time of the end of the eclipse (fùyuán shí kè).
To calculate the directions for the beginning, maximum, and end of the eclipse: Same as the Dàtǒng fǎ.
Method for calculating lunar eclipses (yuèshí): (For various numbers related to lunar eclipses,
if the full moon (wàng) occurs before noon,
calculate using the previous day.
If the full moon occurs after noon,
calculate using the next day.)

To determine the limit of a lunar eclipse: Observe whether the moon's (tàiyīn) celestial longitude (jīngdù) on the full moon day (wàngrì) is within thirteen degrees of either Rāhu (luóhóu) or Ketu (jìdū) degrees.
And if the moon's celestial latitude (wěidù) is less than one degree and eight minutes.
If both conditions are met, there will be an eclipse (yǒushí).
Also, observe if the conjunction of the full moon (hé wàng) occurs within two hours before the moon rises
or two hours after it sets.
This limit implies an eclipse that is visible (dài shí).
Any occurrence beyond two hours is not considered (bù suàn).
To calculate the universal time of the maximum eclipse (shíshèn fàntí) (which is the mean time of the full moon (jīng wàng)):
Subtract six divisions (gōng) from the moon's celestial longitude for that day.
(If it is not enough to subtract,
add twelve divisions and then subtract.) Subtract the sun's (tàiyáng) degree at noon for that day to find the full moon before noon (qián wàng).
(If the sun's degree is not enough to subtract,
add six divisions and then subtract it to find the full moon after noon (hòu wàng).)
Convert the remaining difference (yúshù) to seconds.
Multiply by twenty-four to get the dividend (shí).
Take the moon's celestial longitude for that day.
Subtract the moon's celestial longitude for the previous day.
(If it is for a full moon after noon,
subtract the moon's celestial longitude for the following day.)
The remainder is the moon's daily motion (rìxíngdù).
Also, take the sun's degree at noon for that day.
Subtract the sun's degree at noon for the previous day.
(If it is for a full moon after noon,
subtract the sun's degree for the following day.)
The remainder is the sun's daily motion.
Subtract the two daily motions.
Convert the remainder to seconds to get the divisor (fǎ).
Divide the dividend by the divisor to get the hours (shí).
Convert the remainder of the hours to minutes (fēn) and seconds (miǎo) by multiplying by sixty.
This is the desired universal time of the maximum eclipse.
To calculate the moon's distance from the ecliptic (huángdào) at the maximum eclipse (shíshèn yuèlí huángdào gōngdù): Set the universal time of the maximum eclipse.
Convert both it and the sun's daily motion to seconds and multiply them.
Divide by twenty-four.
The result is xiān (纖).
Group every sixty to obtain wēi (微), seconds, and minutes.
Add or subtract this from the sun's degree at noon for that day.
(Subtract for a full moon before noon,
add for a full moon after noon.)
This gives the sun's degree at the time of the full moon (wàngshí tàiyángdù).
Add six divisions.
This is the desired value.
To calculate the day-night (zhòuyè) correction difference (jiājiǎnchā): Use the sun's degree at the time of the full moon as the argument (yǐnshù).
Input it into the table for day-night corrections (zhòuyè jiājiǎn lìchéng).
Obtain the addition/subtraction minutes (jiājiǎnfēn).
Calculate according to the proportionality method (bǐlì fǎ).
To calculate the determined time of the maximum eclipse (shíshèn dìngshí): Set the universal time of the maximum eclipse.
Add or subtract the day-night correction difference.
(Subtract for a full moon before noon,
add for after noon.)
Take the result.
Add or subtract twelve hours.
(If for a full moon after noon, add twelve; if for a full moon before noon, subtract from twelve hours.)
Convert to the start of the zǐ period.
This gives the initial exact time.
The small remainder (xiǎoyú)
is converted to kè according to the method (rú fǎ shōuwéi kè).
(The method is detailed in the solar eclipse (rìshí) section.)
This gives the determined time.
To calculate Ketu's degree at the time of the full moon (wàngshí jìdūdù): Convert the universal time of the maximum eclipse to seconds to get the dividend.
Multiply by Ketu's daily motion (three minutes and eleven seconds) converted to seconds.
Divide by twenty-four.
The result is xiān.
Group every sixty to obtain wēi, seconds, and minutes.
Add or subtract this from Ketu's motion at noon for that day.
(Rāhu (luóhóu) and Ketu move retrograde (nìxíng).
Add for a full moon before noon,
subtract for after noon.)
This gives the desired value.

To calculate the moon's celestial latitude at the time of the full moon (wàngshí tàiyīn wěidù): Subtract Ketu's degree at the time of the full moon from the moon's distance from the ecliptic at the maximum eclipse.
(If it is not enough to subtract,
add twelve divisions and then subtract.)
The remainder is the separation degree (xiānglídù) between Ketu and the moon.
Input this into the table for moon's celestial latitude (tàiyīn wěidù lìchéng) to obtain the value.
To calculate the moon's epicycle motion (běnlún xíngdù) at the time of the full moon (which is entered into the tardiness/swiftness calendar (chídílì)):
Take the moon's epicycle daily motion (thirteen degrees and four minutes).
Convert to minutes.
Multiply by the universal time of the maximum eclipse converted to seconds.
Divide by twenty-four to get wēi.
Group every sixty to obtain seconds, minutes, and degrees.
Add or subtract this from the epicycle motion at noon for that day.
(Subtract for a full moon before noon,
add for after noon.)
This gives the desired value.
To calculate the moon's diameter fraction (tàiyīn jìngfēn): Use the moon's epicycle motion in divisions and degrees at the time of the full moon.
Input it into the table for shadow and diameter fractions (yǐngjìngfēn lìchéng) to obtain the value.
(The method is detailed in the solar eclipse section.)
To calculate the moon's shadow diameter fraction (tàiyīn yǐngjìngfēn): Use the moon's epicycle motion in divisions and degrees at the time of the full moon.
Input it into the table for shadow and diameter fractions.
Obtain the value.

To calculate the sun's proper motion (tàiyáng zìxíngdù) at the time of the full moon: Multiply the sun's daily motion (fifty-nine minutes and eight seconds) and the universal time of the maximum eclipse, both converted to seconds.
Divide by twenty-four.
The result is xiān.
Group every sixty to obtain wēi, seconds, and minutes.
Add or subtract this from the sun's proper motion at noon for that day.
(The method is the same as calculating the sun's celestial longitude in the solar eclipse section.)
To calculate the shadow diameter reduction difference (yǐngjìng jiǎnchā): Use the sun's proper motion in divisions and degrees for that day as the argument.
Input it into the table for shadow diameter (yǐngjìng lìchéng).
In the same division (gōng) and near degree (jìndù), obtain the moon's shadow diameter difference (tàiyīn yǐngjìng chāfēn).
Calculate according to the proportionality method.
(The method is detailed earlier.)
To calculate the determined shadow diameter fraction (yǐngjìng dìngfēn): Subtract the shadow diameter reduction difference from the moon's shadow diameter fraction.
To calculate the two radii fractions (èrbànjìngfēn): Add the moon's diameter fraction and the determined shadow diameter fraction.
Divide by two.
To calculate the moon's eclipse limit (tàiyīn shíxiàn): Subtract the moon's celestial latitude at the time of the full moon from the two radii fractions.
(If it is not enough to subtract,
there is no eclipse.)
To calculate the determined fraction of the maximum eclipse (shíshèn dìngfēn): Convert the eclipse limit fraction to seconds.
Multiply by one thousand to get the dividend.
Convert the moon's diameter fraction to seconds to get the divisor.
Divide it.
Reduce by one hundred to get minutes.
This is the determined fraction of the maximum eclipse.

To calculate the moon's hourly motion past the sun (tàiyīn zhúshí xíngguò tàiyángfēn): Subtract the moon's celestial longitude for the previous day from the moon's celestial longitude at the time of the full moon.
Also, subtract the sun's proper motion for the previous day from the sun's proper motion at the time of the full moon.
Subtract the two remainders.
This is the moon's day-night motion past the sun (tàiyīn zhòuyè xíngguò tàiyángdù).
Convert to seconds and divide by twenty-four.
Group every sixty.
This gives the hourly motion past the sun.
To calculate the time difference (shíchā): Square the moon's celestial latitude fraction converted to seconds.
Also, square the two radii fractions converted to seconds.
Subtract the two numbers.
Take the square root of the remainder to get the dividend.
Divide by the moon's motion past the sun converted to seconds to get the divisor.
The result is the time difference.
(This is the determined fraction used from the beginning of the eclipse to the maximum eclipse.)
To calculate the times of the beginning and end of the eclipse (chūkuī fùyuán shí kè): Subtract the time difference from the determined time of the maximum eclipse.
This gives the time of the beginning of the eclipse.
Add it to the determined time of the maximum eclipse.
This gives the time of the end of the eclipse.
The method for converting times to kè
is the same as for a solar eclipse.
To calculate the time difference from totality to maximum eclipse (shíjì zhì shíshèn shíchā): Subtract the moon's diameter fraction from the two radii fractions.
Square the result converted to seconds.
Also, square the moon's celestial latitude converted to seconds.
Subtract these.
Take the square root to get the dividend.
Divide by the moon's hourly motion past the sun converted to seconds to get the divisor.
The result is the time difference.
To calculate the times of totality (shíjì) and first light (shēngguāng): Subtract the time difference from totality to maximum eclipse from the determined time of the maximum eclipse.
This is the time of totality.
Add it to the determined time of the maximum eclipse.
This is the time of first light.
To calculate the directions for the beginning, maximum, and end of the eclipse: Same as the Dàtǒng fǎ.
To find the times of sunrise and sunset: Use the sun's longitude at noon as the argument,
consult the table of day and night hours for the Western Regions,
take its degrees and minutes,
calculate by the proportional method,
this is the preliminary result in minutes.
Then, within the opposite mansion degree of the argument,
take its degrees and minutes,
(for example, if it's three degrees in the first mansion,
take it from three degrees in the sixth mansion.)
Also calculate by the proportional method,
this is the subsequent preliminary result in minutes.
Subtract the two preliminary results in minutes,
(if subtraction is not possible, add three hundred and sixty degrees and then subtract.)
The remainder in total seconds,
divide by fifteen,
group by sixty to get minutes and hours,
this yields the daylight hours, minutes, and seconds for the day.
Halve it to get the half-day hours, minutes, and seconds for the day.
Subtract the half-day hours, minutes, and seconds from twelve hours,
the remainder is the sunrise hours, minutes, and seconds.
Add twelve hours to get the sunset hours, minutes, and seconds.
To find the hours, minutes, and seconds of an eclipse at moonrise/moonset or sunrise/sunset: Observe whether the sunrise hours, minutes, and seconds,
and the sunset hours, minutes, and seconds for that day,
are greater than the hours, minutes, and seconds of first contact,
and less than the fixed hours, minutes, and seconds of greatest eclipse and last contact.
If so, there is an eclipse occurring.
Take the sunrise time or sunset time for that day,
and subtract the fixed hours, minutes, and seconds of greatest eclipse.
The remainder is the eclipse duration difference.
Set the fixed minutes of greatest solar/lunar eclipse,
multiply by the eclipse duration difference in total seconds,
divide by the time difference in total seconds,
the resulting number is the eclipse minutes.
Subtract the eclipse minutes from the fixed minutes of greatest eclipse,
the remainder is the observed minutes of the solar/lunar eclipse.
To find the night watch and dot times for a lunar eclipse: Set twenty-four hours,
subtract the daylight hours,
then subtract the twilight hours,
(seventy-two minutes,
which is the five *kè* weakness in the *Zhōnglì* calendar.)
The remainder is the nighttime hours.
Divide the total seconds by five to get the watch rule.
Five minutes of the watch rule is the dot rule.
If the eclipse is before midnight (*zǐzhèng*),
set the times for first contact, greatest eclipse, last contact, etc.,
subtract the sunset time,
then subtract half the twilight hours,
(thirty-six minutes.)
The remainder in total seconds,
subtract the watch rule from it to get the watch number.
If it's less than the watch rule,
subtract the dot rule from it to get the dot number.
If the eclipse is after midnight (*zǐzhèng*),
halve the nighttime hours,
add the times for first contact, greatest eclipse, last contact, etc.,
subtract the watch rule from it to get the watch number.
If it's less than the watch rule,
subtract the dot rule from it to get the dot number.
All are named starting from the first watch, first dot.
(When subtracting by the watch rule,
one subtraction is one watch.
If the remainder after subtraction is less than the rule,
it is also nominally called one watch.
The dot rule follows this principle.)
Transgression of *Tàiyīn* and the Five Planets
To find the daily motion of *Tàiyīn*: Subtract the longitude of the current day from the longitude of the next day,
the remainder is the daily motion for the current day.
To find the longitude of *Tàiyīn* at twilight: Take the longitude of *Tàiyīn* at noon on that day,
add the cumulative value (cumulative value for *Tàiyīn* rise/set and twilight addition/subtraction) for the twilight addition difference of that day,
this is the longitude of *Tàiyīn* at twilight for that day.
Take the longitude of *Tàiyīn* at noon on the next day,
subtract the cumulative value for the morning subtraction difference of that day,
this is the longitude of *Tàiyīn* at morning for that day.
To find the degrees of moonrise/moonset: Take the longitude of *Tàiyīn* at noon on that day,
add the cumulative value (which is the previous cumulative value) for the moonset addition difference of that day,
this is the longitude of *Tàiyīn* at moonset for that day.
Add the cumulative value for the moonrise addition difference of that day,
this is the longitude of *Tàiyīn* at moonrise for that day.
To find the constellation transgressed by *Tàiyīn*: After the new moon (*shuò*), observe the twilight longitude until the moonset longitude.
After the full moon (*wàng*), observe the moonrise longitude until the morning longitude.
Consult the cumulative table of constellations north and south of the ecliptic.
If the longitudes and latitudes are close, within one degree,
take them.
To find the exact time: Take the longitude of *Tàiyīn* at noon on that day,
subtract the longitude of each selected constellation,
convert to minutes,
multiply by twenty-four,
divide by the daily motion of *Tàiyīn* (also converted to minutes),
this gives the initial hours.
For the small remainder,
convert it to minutes by multiplying by sixty,
multiply by one thousand,
divide by one hundred and forty-four,
reduce by one hundred to get *kè* (quarter-hours),
this yields the desired exact time.
To find the vertical separation in minutes: Subtract the latitude of *Tàiyīn* from the latitude of the transgressed star,
the remainder is the vertical separation in minutes.
If the moon and star are both in the south,
if the moon's latitude is greater, it is lower separation;
if the moon's latitude is less, it is upper separation.
If both are in the north,
if the moon's latitude is greater, it is upper separation;
if less, it is lower separation.
If north and south are different,
if the moon is in the north, it is upper separation;
if in the south, it is lower separation.
To find the separation in minutes for the transgression of the Five Planets on various stars: Take the longitude and latitude of the Five Planets on that day,
consult the ecliptic cumulative table.
Observe the longitudes and latitudes of the inner and outer stars within each constellation.
If they are within one degree, take them.
Subtract the latitude of the Five Planets from the latitude of each star,
the remainder is the vertical separation in minutes.
To find the moon transgressing the Five Planets,
and the Five Planets transgressing each other: Observe the longitudes and latitudes of *Tàiyīn* and the Five Planets.
If they are close, within one degree,
take them.
Record Fourteenth, Calendar, Eighth, Islamic Calendar Method Two, Method for Creating Tables of the Central Motion of the Five Planets (Original: total years, zero years, months, days,
and the first day of the twelve mansions, making five tables in total.
Within each table,
the first column lists the year, month, day, and mansion numbers for that table.
The next column lists the Seven Luminaries.
The next lists the sun's central motion,
and the individual motions of Saturn (*Tǔxīng*), Jupiter (*Mùxīng*), Mars (*Huǒxīng*), Venus (*Jīnxīng*), and Mercury (*Shuǐxīng*), as well as the highest daily motion of the Five Planets.
The text is extensive and not recorded.
The method for creating the tables is recorded on the left.)
Table of the Sun's Central Motion by Day: One day's motion is fifty-nine minutes and eight seconds.
Accumulate this daily.
For a small month of twenty-nine days,
it yields twenty-eight degrees, thirty-five minutes, and two seconds.
For a large month of thirty days,
it yields twenty-nine degrees, thirty-four minutes, and ten seconds.
Table by Month.
Odd months are large,
even months are small.
An intercalary day is placed at the end.
For a large month, twenty-nine degrees, thirty-four minutes, ten seconds.
For a small month, twenty-eight degrees, thirty-five minutes, two seconds.
Accumulate this monthly.
Twelve months total eleven mansions, eighteen degrees, fifty-five minutes, nine seconds.
An intercalary day adds fifty-nine minutes and eight seconds.
Table of the First Day of Mansion Degrees.
Starting calculation from the first day of Aries (*Báiyáng Gōng*),
to the first day of Taurus (*Jīnniú Gōng*),
a total of thirty-one days,
it yields one mansion, one degree, thirty-three minutes, eighteen seconds.
(The accumulation of fifty-nine minutes and eight seconds.)
Observe the number of days in the mansion degrees,
(the number of days is shown previously.)
Accumulate this.
To the first day of Pisces (*Shuāngyú Gōng*),
it yields eleven mansions, one degree, eleven minutes, thirty-one seconds.
(The accumulation of three hundred and thirty-five days from Aries to here.)
Table of Zero Years.
Each year is eleven mansions, eighteen degrees, fifty-five minutes, nine seconds.
Every thirty years, there are eleven intercalary days.
Therefore, the second, fifth, seventh, tenth, thirteenth, sixteenth, eighteenth, twenty-first, twenty-fourth, twenty-sixth, and twenty-ninth years
all have an intercalary day added.
Approximation method: Each year subtracts eleven degrees, four minutes, fifty-one seconds.
An intercalary year subtracts ten degrees, five minutes, forty-three seconds.
Thirty years amount to one mansion, eight degrees, twenty-five minutes, thirty-one seconds.
Each year has three hundred and fifty-four days,
totaling ten thousand six hundred and twenty days.
Adding eleven intercalary days,
makes a total of ten thousand six hundred and thirty-one days.
Table of Total Years.
The first year is three mansions, twenty-six degrees, five minutes, eight seconds.
(This is the root number determined in the *Suí Jǐwèi* year,
one account says it is the number for the *Hóngwǔ Jiǎzǐ* year,
the calculations are already included.)
Six hundred years are five mansions, fourteen degrees, twenty-five minutes, nineteen seconds.
Every thirty years, add one mansion, eight degrees, twenty-five minutes, thirty-one seconds.
Up to one thousand four hundred and forty years,
it yields five mansions, fifteen minutes, thirty-three seconds.
Method for Creating Tables of the Individual Motion of the Five Planets
Table of Saturn's (*Tǔxīng*) Daily Motion: One day is fifty-seven minutes.
Accumulate this daily.
A small month is twenty-seven degrees, thirty-seven minutes.
A large month is twenty-eight degrees, thirty-four minutes.
The addition of one minute on the fifth, twelfth, twentieth, and twenty-eighth days
is due to the accumulation of seconds.
Table by Month.
A large month adds twenty-eight degrees, thirty-four minutes.
A small month adds twenty-seven degrees, thirty-seven minutes.
Accumulate this monthly.
Twelve months total eleven mansions, seven degrees, four minutes.
An intercalary day adds fifty-seven minutes.
Table of the First Day of Mansion Degrees.
The first day of Taurus (*Jīnniú Gōng*) is twenty-nine degrees, thirty-one minutes.
(The accumulation of thirty-one days of individual motion.
The other four planets follow this principle.)
Observe the number of days in the mansion degrees and accumulate this.
To the first day of Pisces (*Shuāngyú Gōng*) it is ten mansions, eighteen degrees, fifty-eight minutes.
Zero-year established calculations.
Each year, eleven gōng, seven dù, four fēn.
Whether there is an intercalary day
depends on the sun's mean motion.
In a zero-year, add the daily motion of the principal star (fēn).
(The following four stars follow this rule.)
Up to thirty years,
it totals one gōng, twelve dù, sixteen fēn.
Total-year established calculations.
The first year: eleven gōng, twenty-nine dù, eighteen fēn.
(This is the root number determined by the Suí Dynasty in the Jǐwèi year,
one account says it is the year number of Hóngwǔ Jiǎzǐ,
with additions incorporated.
The following four stars follow this rule.)

Zǒng Língnián Gōng Yuè Rì Qīyào Lìchéng Zàofǎ (Method for Compiling Tables of Total, Fractional Years, Months, Days, and the Seven Luminaries)
For the Zǒngnián Lìchéng:
The 1st year starts with Jīn (Venus) as the 6th luminary.
The 600th year starts with Rì (Sun) as the 1st luminary.
Every 30 years, add 5 to the number.
For the Língnián Lìchéng:
Starts with Shuǐ (Mercury) as the 4th luminary.
For the Gōngfēn Lìchéng (Constellation/Degree Calculations):
The Jīnniúgōng (Taurus) starts with Huǒ (Mars) as the 3rd luminary.
For the Yuèfēn Lìchéng:
Starts with Yuè (Moon) as the 2nd luminary.
For the Rìqī Lìchéng (Date Calculations):
Starts with Rì (Sun) as the 1st luminary.
(Method: If there is an intercalary day (rùn rì),
For a full year, use the qīyào of the year.
For an incomplete year,
Use the qīyào of the month.
Combine them,
To get the qīyào of the last day of each month.)
Tàiyáng Jiājiǎn Lìchéng (Solar Correction Table). (Uses the planet's own xiàng-dù as the argument.
Originally, the xiàng column was the first vertical column,
And the dù column was the top horizontal row.
Every three xiàng, 30 dù were distributed in sequence.
Inside, the addition/subtraction differences were listed.
And also the addition/subtraction fēn.
These addition/subtraction fēn
Are the differences between the addition/subtraction difference of the current dù and that of the next dù.
Now, they are removed,
Only the addition/subtraction difference values are listed.
The argument's xiàng are listed in the top horizontal row,
And the dù are listed in the first vertical column.
Look it up in forward and reverse,
The results are the same,
But it is simpler and quicker.
The Yuè (Moon) and Wǔxīng (Five Planets) correction tables
Follow this standard.)

Gāngwéi bùzhì,

Calculating the initial borders of the Ming
dynasty, they stretched eastward to Cháoxiǎn,
westward to occupy Tǔbō,
southward to encompass Ānnán,
and northward to border the Great Desert (Dàqí).
From east to west, it was eleven thousand seven hundred and fifty *lǐ*;
from north to south, ten thousand ninety-four *lǐ*.
From the time Chéngzǔ abandoned Dàníng
and moved Dōngshèng,
Xuānzōng relocated Kāipíng to Dúshí,
and during Shìzōng’s reign, Hāmì and Hétáo were abandoned again,
the borders then stretched eastward to Liáohǎi,
westward to Jiāyù,
southward to Qióngyá,
and northward to Yúnshuò.
From east to west, it was over ten thousand *lǐ*;
from north to south, ten thousand *lǐ*.
As for the regions where its influence and teachings reached,
which presented tribute annually,
but were not assigned officials to register them,
or kept under the control of marquises and commandants,
these are not included in this count.
Oh, how grand it was!
Commentators assert that the abandonment of Jiāozhǐ
was not a strategic error,
but the recent relocation of Kāipíng
weakened the defenses even further.
Even the establishment of the Wànquán Regional Military Commission (Wànquán Dūzhǐhuī Shǐsī)
was insufficient to suppress and pacify the various tribes beyond the mountains.
Thus, two reigns later, there was the change at Tǔmù.
However, Ruìhuáng considered his defeat and capture (méngchén) to be due to military indiscipline,
not the inadequacy of the established system.
Jǐngdì appointed capable individuals,
and improved defenses,
the national situation did not shift,
and the imperial carriage was soon recovered.
From this perspective,
the three *wèi* (garrisons)
were a narrow corner,
and indeed irrelevant to the grand strategy.
Towards its later period,
roving bandits initiated calamity on the western frontier,
gradually spreading,
and the Central Plains (Zhōngyuán) were devastated by them.
The solidity of its "metal walls and soup moats" (jīntāng zhī gù) was insufficient to control a collapse,
and the vastness of its territory (fányǔ zhī guǎng) was insufficient to form a pincer movement.
The borders were not diminished from former times,
and the strategic advantages were not impaired from the initial prosperity,
yet the disparity in strength was vast,
and the rise and fall were of a different order.
This was due to heaven sending down chaos and calamities,
and internal strife among the corrupt and foolish,
a failure of human affairs,
and not a loss of geographical advantage.
The saying goes,
“It lies in virtue, not in strategic strongholds” (zài dé bù zài xiǎn).
Is this not indeed true?
Now, examining the differences in its ascendance and decline,
and the reasons for its evolution,
they are fully recorded in this chapter.
A Treatise on Geography (Dìlǐzhì).
Jīngshī (Capital) Nánjīng (Southern Capital)
Jīngshī: The territory of the three prefectures of Jì, Yǎn, and Yù mentioned in the *Yǔgòng*.
Under the direct administration of the Yuán dynasty's Central Secretariat (Zhōngshūshěng).
In the first year of Hóngwǔ (1368), fourth month, it was divided and assigned to the Hénán and Shāndōng Branch Central Secretariats (Xíng Zhōngshūshěng).
In the second year, third month, the Běipíng and other places Branch Central Secretariat was established,
(governed from Běipíng Fǔ).
Those previously belonging to Shāndōng and Hénán were all restored to their original status.
It administered eight prefectures (fǔ),
thirty-seven subprefectures (zhōu),
and one hundred and thirty-six counties (xiàn).
In the eighth month, the Yànshān Regional Military Commission (Yànshān Dūwèi) was established.
(It was co-administered with the Branch Central Secretariat).
In the eighth year, tenth month, the Regional Military Commission was reformed into the Běipíng Regional Military Commission (Běipíng Dūzhǐhuī Shǐsī).
In the ninth year, sixth month, the Branch Central Secretariat was reformed into the Bùzhèngshǐsī (Administration Commission).
In the first year of Yǒnglè (1403), first month, Běijīng was established in Shùntiān Fǔ,
and referred to as
"Xíngzài" (Temporary Imperial Residence).
In the second month, the Běipíng Administration Commission was abolished,
and its administered territories were directly under the Běijīng Xíngbù (Branch Department).
The Běipíng Regional Military Commission was abolished,
and its administered territories were directly under the Běijīng Liúshǒu Xíng Hòujūn Dūdūfǔ (Běijīng Garrison Branch Rear Army Chief Military Commission).
In the nineteenth year, first month, Běijīng was renamed Jīngshī (Capital).
The Běijīng Liúshǒu Xíng Hòujūn Dūdūfǔ was abolished,
and directly under the Hòujūn Dūdūfǔ (Rear Army Chief Military Commission).
(Garrison *wèi* that had actual territory are appended;
those without actual territory are not included).
The Běijīng Xíngbù was abolished,
and directly under the Six Ministries (Liùbù).
In the early Hóngxī reign,
it was still called Xíngzài.
In the sixth year of Zhèngtǒng (1441), eleventh month, the designation Xíngzài was abolished,
and it was officially established as Jīngshī.
It administered eight prefectures (fǔ),
two directly administered subprefectures (zhílìzhōu),
seventeen dependent subprefectures (shǔzhōu),
and one hundred and sixteen counties (xiàn).
(Comprising three thousand two hundred and thirty odd *lǐ* (village units).
The establishment and evolution of prefectures, subprefectures, and counties
all begin from the Yuán dynasty.
Their evolutionary changes and dates already seen in the *Yuán Shǐ Dìlǐzhì* (Treatise on Geography of the History of the Yuán Dynasty)
are not recorded here.
Those not seen in the *Yuán Shǐ Dìlǐzhì*, or those changed from the Yuán dynasty by the Ming,
as well as those newly added or newly abolished,
are all documented.
