Collation Notes
Treatise 23: Rites 1 (Auspicious Rites 1)
The Rites of Zhōu and the Book of Etiquette and Ceremonial are still extant,
but the texts are incomplete and contain missing slips,
so the causes of their evolution and reform are not fully known.
Since the Hàn historians compiled treatises on rites,
later generations followed suit,
and the systems of each dynasty could thus be clearly investigated.
Ōuyáng Shì said:
"Since the Three Dynasties,
governance has emerged from two sources,
but rites and music have become mere empty names."
However, their application in suburban altars, ancestral temples, and courts,
down to villages and local communities,
was never without points of interest.
Only by cultivating, clarifying, and expounding them,
and acting with sincere intent throughout,
can one inspire superiors and inferiors, move ghosts and spirits,
and thereby achieve moral transformation.
How can it be said that the rites of later generations
cannot possibly trace back to the Three Dynasties?
At the beginning of his reign, Míng Tàizǔ, though pressed by other matters,
first established two bureaus for rites and music,
broadly recruited esteemed scholars,
and divided them into groups to thoroughly research the matter.
In the 1st year of Hóngwǔ, he ordered the Zhōngshū Shěng, along with the Hànlín Yuàn and Tàicháng Sī,
to determine and propose the sacrificial canon.
Thus, they reviewed the history of changes,
deliberated and set forth proposals for the suburban altars and ancestral temples.
The officials of rites and various Confucian scholars then compiled rituals for suburban altars, ancestral temples, mountains, rivers, etc.,
which contained instances of ancient emperors' sacrifices that evoked responses and served as warnings and examples,
naming it Cúnxīn Lù.
In the 2nd year, an imperial edict ordered the Confucian scholars to revise the book of rites.
The following year it was completed,
and given the name Dàmíng Jílǐ.
This book conformed to the Five Rites but also added sections on caps and robes, carriages, ceremonial guards, imperial retinues, lexicography, and music,
detailing all ceremonial procedures,
systems, names, and numbers,
in minute detail.

He also repeatedly commanded the deliberating officials of rites Lǐ Shàncháng, Fù Huán, Sòng Lián, Zhān Tóng, Táo Ān, Liú Jī, Wèi Guān, Cuī Liàng, Niú Liàng, Táo Kǎi, Zhū Shēng, Lè Sháofèng, Lǐ Yuánmíng, etc.,
to compile it into a collection.

Furthermore, an imperial edict ordered commanderies and counties to select virtuous and erudite scholars Xu Yīkuí, Liáng Yín, Zhōu Zǐliàng, Hú Xíngjiǎn, Liú Zōngbì, Dǒng Yí, Cài Shēn, Téng Gōngyǎn, to come to the capital,
to jointly revise the book of rites.
During his reign of over thirty years,
the books he authored that can be verified
include: Xiàocí Lù,
Hóngwǔ Lǐzhì,
Lǐyí Dìngshì,
Zhūsī Zhízhǎng,
Jīqǔ Dìngzhì,
Guózhāo Zhìzuò,
Dàlǐ Yàoyì,
Huángcháo Lǐzhì,
Dàmíng Lǐzhì,
Hóngwǔ Lǐfǎ,
Lǐzhì Jíyào,
Lǐzhì Jiéwén,
Tàicháng Jílǐ,
and Lǐshū.
As for rectifying the sacrificial canon,
all categories such as Tiānhuáng, Tàiyǐ, Liùtiān, and Wǔdì
were abolished,
and the titles of all deities
were changed back to their original names,
completely cleansing the deceptive and vulgar practices;
its transcendence over Hàn and Táng was indeed profound.
He also decreed the establishment of national mourning rites:
for parents, both wore the most severe mourning (zhǎncui),
while for the eldest son, it was reduced to one year (qīnián);
principal and secondary mourning attire followed a graduated reduction,
which, by weighing ancient and modern practices,
achieved a balanced mean.
During the Yǒnglè reign,
Zhū Xī's Family Rituals was promulgated throughout the empire,
and systems for imperial tours, regency, and daily lectures at the imperial study were also established.
The abolition of immolation of concubines in the imperial harem
began with Yīngzōng.
The distinction between嫡 (dì, principal wife's son) and 庶 (shù, concubine's son) in imperial tombs and ancestral temples
was rectified by Xiàozōng.
As for Shìzōng,
he took it upon himself to formulate rites and compose music.
The major changes he made,
such as separate sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
restoring morning sacrifices to the sun and evening sacrifices to the moon in the eastern and western suburbs,
abolishing the joint enshrinement of the two founding ancestors,
as well as prayers for harvest and grand rain sacrifices,
sacrifices to the empress who introduced sericulture,
sacrifices to the Most Sagely Teacher (Confucius),
and changing the title of the Most Sagely Foremost Teacher,
all demonstrated an ability to strike a balance with antiquity.
However, he alone, against all opinions,
enshrined Ruìzōng in the imperial ancestral temple above Wǔzōng,
favoring his birth father and violating the great succession principle,
beginning with clarity and ending with indulgence.
At that time, sycophantic officials
each offered their explanations.
Among those still extant,
such as Mínglún Dàdiǎn,
it was promulgated with an imperial preface;
Sìyí Chéngdiǎn
was compiled by Lǐ Shí and others under imperial command;
and Jiāosì Kǎoyì
was presented by Zhāng Fúqìng.
As for Dàmíng Huìdiǎn,
compiled since the reign of Xiàozōng,
it is particularly detailed regarding ritual systems.
During the reigns of Shìzōng and Shénzōng,
it was repeatedly augmented,
and the established laws of the dynasty are broadly contained therein.
Now, following the order of the Five Rites,
they are classified into categories,
and modifications made over time
are compiled under their respective types,
to document their evolution.

System of Altars and Sacred Enclosures; Number of Spirit Tablets, Sacrificial Vessels, Jade and Silk Offerings, Sacrificial Animals, Prayer Scrolls; Contents of Baskets and Platters; Various Discussions on Sacrificial Rites; Sacrificial Dates; Ritual Practice; Fasting and Purification; Dispatching Officials for Sacrifices, Subordinate Offerings, and Accompanying Sacrifices.
The Five Rites.
The first is the Auspicious Rites (Jí Lǐ).
All sacrificial affairs were managed by the Tàicháng Sì and belonged to the Lǐbù.
In the early Míng dynasty, the Yuánqiū, Fāngzé, Zōngmiào, Shèjì, Cháorì, Xīyuè, and Xiānnóng were designated as Grand Sacrifices (Dàsì).
The Tàisuì, Xīngchén, Fēngyúnléiyǔ, Yuèzhèn, Hǎidú, Shānchuān, Lìdài Dìwáng, Xiānshī, Qídú, Sīzhōng, Sīmìng, Sīmín, Sīlù, and Shòuxīng were designated as Middle Sacrifices (Zhōngsì).
All other gods were designated as Minor Sacrifices (Xiǎosì).
Later, Xiānnóng, Cháorì, and Xīyuè were reclassified as Middle Sacrifices.
Those personally sacrificed by the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) were
Heaven and Earth (Tiāndì), Ancestral Temples (Zōngmiào), Altars of Land and Grain (Shèjì), and Mountains and Rivers (Shānchuān).
If the country had major affairs,
then officials were ordered to offer sacrifices and make announcements.
For the Middle Sacrifices and Minor Sacrifices,
officials were dispatched to offer sacrifices,
and for the imperial mausoleums (Dìwáng Língmiào) and Confucius Temples (Kǒngzǐ Miào),
special emissaries were dispatched by imperial decree.
Those regularly performed each year were:

thirteen Grand Sacrifices: the prayer for grain on the first Xīn day of the first month, the great rain prayer (dàyú) in mid-summer, the great feast (dàxiǎng) in late autumn, and the winter solstice sacrifice at the Yuánqiū, all dedicated to Hào Tiān Shàngdì;
the summer solstice sacrifice at the Fāngqiū dedicated to Huáng Dìqí;
the spring equinox sacrifice to the Morning Sun (Cháorì) in the eastern suburbs;
the autumn equinox sacrifice to the Evening Moon (Xīyuè) in the western suburbs;
the offering at the Tàimiào in the four mid-seasons and late winter;
and the sacrifice to Tàishè and Tàijì on the first Wù day of mid-spring and mid-autumn.
There were twenty-five Middle Sacrifices: the sacrifice to Dìshè and Dìjì on the day after the first Wù day of mid-spring and mid-autumn;
in mid-autumn, sacrifices to the Tàisuì, Fēngyúnléiyǔ, the generals of the four seasonal months (Sìjì Yuèjiàng), as well as the Yuèzhèn, Hǎidú, Shānchuān, and Chénghuáng;
on the day of frost's descent (Shuāngjiàng), a sacrifice to Qídú at the drill ground (jiàocháng);
in mid-autumn, a sacrifice at the Qídú Temple south of the city;
in mid-spring, a sacrifice to Xiānnóng;
in mid-autumn, sacrifices to the gods of Heaven and Earth (Tiānshén Dìqí) at the Shānchuān Tán;
in mid-spring and mid-autumn, sacrifices at the Lìdài Dìwáng Miào;
and on the first Dīng day of the mid-month of spring and autumn, sacrifices to the Xiānshī Kǒngzǐ.
There were eight Minor Sacrifices: in early spring, a sacrifice to Sīhù;
in early summer, a sacrifice to Sīzào;
in late summer, a sacrifice to Zhōngliú;
in early autumn, a sacrifice to Sīmén;
in early winter, a sacrifice to Sījǐng;
in mid-spring, a sacrifice to the god of Sīmǎ;
on Qīngmíng and the first day of the tenth month, sacrifices to Tàilì;
and also on the first and fifteenth days of each month, sacrifices to the gods of fire and thunder (huǒléi zhī shén).
As for the ten temples in the capital (Jīngshī)
and fifteen temples in Nánjīng,
officials were dispatched to offer sacrifices at their respective seasonal times.
Those that were not regular sacrifices but were occasionally performed
included the new Son of Heaven plowing the ceremonial field (gēngjí) and offering to Xiānnóng,
and visiting schools to perform the Shìdiàn ceremony.
During the Jiājìng era,
the Empress offered sacrifices to Xiāncán
and Gāoméi,
all of which were specially performed as occasion demanded.
The sacrifices offered by the kingdoms (Wángguó) included:
Tàimiào, Shèjì, Fēngyúnléiyǔ, Shānchuān within the feudal territory (fēngnèi shānchuān), Chénghuáng, Qídú, Wǔsì, and Lìtán.
The sacrifices offered by prefectures (fǔ), departments (zhōu), and counties (xiàn) included:
Shèjì, Fēngyúnléiyǔ, Shānchuān, Lìtán, Xiānshī Miào, and the local Dìwáng Língmiào.
Each guard (wèi) also sacrificed to Xiānshī.
As for commoners (shùrén),
they were also permitted to sacrifice to the village altar (lǐshè), the god of grain (gǔshén), as well as to grandparents and parents, and to sacrifice to the kitchen god (Sīzào),
all recorded in the Book of Sacrifices (Sìdiǎn).
Although there were minor changes over time,
their general outline could not be surpassed.
As for the regulations for altars and enclosures (tánwěi zhī zhì),
the number of spirit tablets (shénwèi), sacrificial vessels (jìqì), jade and silk (yùbó), sacrificial animals (shēngláo), and prayer scrolls (zhùcè),
the contents of the bīn and dòu vessels,
and the names of the sacrificial wines,
differentiating their similarities and differences,
and reviewing their initial and final additions and deletions,
are listed in the introductory section,
and briefly mentioned in this current section,
so that there will be no omissions
and also to avoid redundancy.
Regulations for Altars and Enclosures (Tánwěi zhī zhì).
In the early Míng dynasty,
the Yuánqiū was built outside Zhèngyángmén,
on the south side of Zhōngshān,
and the Fāngqiū was built outside Tàipíngmén,
on the north side of Zhōngshān.
The Yuánqiū altar had two tiers.
The upper tier was seven zhàng wide,
eight chǐ and one cùn high,
with four ascending steps leading out in each direction,
each with nine steps.
The main south steps were nine chǐ and five cùn wide,
and the east, west, and north steps were eight chǐ and one cùn wide.
The lower tier's surrounding altar surface
was five zhàng wide both longitudinally and horizontally,
its height was proportional to the upper tier,
all steps had nine levels.
The main south steps were one zhàng, two chǐ, and five cùn wide,
while the east, west, and north steps were five cùn and five fēn narrower.
The brick paving and railings
were all made of glazed tiles (liúlí).
The enclosure (wěi) was fifteen zhàng from the altar,
eight chǐ and one cùn high,
with four Língxīng Mén on each side,
three on the south,
and one each on the east, west, and north.
The outer wall (wài yuán) was fifteen zhàng from the enclosure,
with the same gate design.
The altar for all gods of Heaven and Earth (Tiānxià Shénqí Tán) was outside the East Gate.
The spirit storehouse (shénkù) had five bays,
located north of the outer wall,
facing south.
The kitchen (chúfáng) had five bays,
located northeast of the outer altar,
facing west.
The storehouse (kùfáng) had five bays,
facing south.
The slaughterhouse (zǎishēngfáng) had three bays,
and a celestial pond (tiānchí)
was also located north of the outer storehouse.
The residential quarters for functionaries (zhíshì zhāishè)
were southeast of the outer wall of the altar.
There were two archways (fāng),
located east and west of the transversal covered walkway (héng yǒngdào) outside the outer gate.
The burning altar (liáotán) was southeast of the inner enclosure, in the bǐng direction,
nine chǐ high,
seven chǐ wide,
with an opening to the south at the top.
The Fāngqiū altar had two tiers.
The upper tier
was six zhàng wide,
six chǐ high,
with four ascending steps leading out in each direction,
the south one being one zhàng,
and the east, west, and north ones eight chǐ,
all with eight steps.
The lower tier
was two zhàng and four chǐ wide on each side,
six chǐ high,
with four ascending steps leading out in each direction,
the south one being one zhàng and two chǐ,
and the east, west, and north ones one zhàng,
all with eight steps.
The enclosure was fifteen zhàng from the altar,
six chǐ high.
The outer wall was sixty-four zhàng on each side,
the rest of the design was the same.
To the south of the suburbs, there was a bathhouse (yùshì),
and the burial pit (yìkǎn) was within the inner enclosure, in the rén direction.
In the fourth year of Hóngwǔ (1371), the Yuánqiū was rebuilt.
The upper tier was four zhàng and five chǐ wide,
five chǐ and two cùn high.
The lower tier was one zhàng, six chǐ, and five cùn wide on each side,
four chǐ and nine cùn high.
The total diameter of the two tiers was seven zhàng and eight chǐ.
From the altar to the inner enclosure wall,
it was nine zhàng, eight chǐ, and five cùn on each of the four sides.
From the inner enclosure wall to the outer enclosure wall,
it was thirteen zhàng, nine chǐ, and four cùn on the south,
eleven zhàng on the north,
and eleven zhàng and seven chǐ on the east and west.
For the Fāngqiū,
the upper tier was three zhàng, nine chǐ, and four cùn wide,
three chǐ and nine cùn high.
The lower tier was one zhàng, five chǐ, and five cùn wide on each side,
three chǐ and eight cùn high,
with a total diameter of seven zhàng and four cùn.
From the altar to the inner enclosure wall,
it was eight zhàng, nine chǐ, and five cùn on all four sides.
From the inner enclosure wall to the outer enclosure wall,
it was eight zhàng and two chǐ on all four sides.
In the tenth year (1377), the regulations for combined sacrifices were revised.
Following the old design of the Yuánqiū,
it was covered with a roof,
named Dàsì Diàn,
with a total of twelve bays.
On the central stone platform, seats for Shàngdì and Huáng Dìqí were arranged.
The east and west sides were thirty-two bays wide.
The main south Dàsì Mén had six bays,
connected by a covered corridor (bùláng),
communicating with the main hall (diàn) and its side corridors (wǔ).
Behind the hall was Tiānkù with six bays.
The tiles were all yellow liúlí.
The kitchen and storehouse were northeast of the hall,
the slaughtering pavilion and well were northeast of the kitchen,
all connected to the two side corridors of the hall by covered corridors,
and enclosed by a surrounding wall at the back.
To the south were three stone arched gates leading to the Dàsì Mén,
which was called the inner altar (nèi tán).
The outer surrounding wall was nine lǐ and thirty steps long,
and south of the three stone arched gates were three covered walkways (yǒngdào),
the central one being the Spirit Path (Shéndào),
the left the Imperial Path (Yùdào),
and the right the King's Path (Wángdào).
The areas on both sides of the paths were slightly lower,
designated for attending officials.
The Palace of Abstinence (Zhāigōng) was southwest inside the outer wall,
facing east.
Later, the tiles of the hall were changed to blue liúlí.
In the twenty-first year (1388), the altars and enclosures were further repaired.
Pines and cypresses were planted behind the altar,
and twenty ponds were dug southeast of the outer enclosure,
where ice was harvested in winter and stored in an icehouse (língyīn)
for use in summer and autumn sacrifices.
Chéngzǔ moved the capital to Běijīng and replicated this system.
In the ninth year of Jiājìng, the sacrificial rites were again separated.
The Huánqiū Tán was built about five lǐ outside Zhèngyángmén,
south of the Dàsì Diàn,
and the Fāngzé Tán was built east of Āndìngmén.
The Huánqiū had two tiers,
its platform surface and railings were all of blue glazed tiles,
with corners made of white jade stone.
Its height and breadth dimensions all followed the ancestral system,
but the sacred path was made longer.
There were four inner gates.
Outside the south gate were the liáolú (burning furnace) and máoxiěchí (hair and blood pool),
and to the southwest, the wàngliáotái (viewing platform for burning).
There were also four outer gates.
Outside the south gate to the left was the jùfútái (robe changing platform),
outside the east gate were the shénkù (divine storehouse), shénchú (divine kitchen), jìqìkù (ritual implement storehouse), and zǎishēngtíng (slaughter pavilion).
Outside the north gate, directly north, was the Tàishéndiàn.
The main hall was for storing the spirit tablets of Shàngdì and Tàizǔ,
and the side halls were for storing the spirit tablets of the accompanying deities.
Outside, four Heavenly Gates were built.
The east one was called Tàiyuán,
the south one Zhāohēng,
and the west one Guǎnglì.
Further west was the luánjiàkù (imperial carriage storehouse),
and further west the xīshēngsuǒ (sacrifice preparation area),
with the Shénlèguān to its north.
The north gate was called Chéngzhēn.
Northwest outside the north gate was the Zhāigōng (Abstinence Palace),
and stretching to the west was the tányún (altar gate).
North of the altar,
was the old Tiāndì Tán,
which was the Dàsì Diàn.
In the seventeenth year, it was demolished,
and the Tàishéndiàn was renamed Huángqióngyǔ.
In the twenty-fourth year, the Dàxiǎngdiàn was built
on the site of the former Dàsì Diàn.
The Fāngzé also had two tiers,
its platform surface was of yellow glazed tiles,
the steps were increased to nine levels,
using white stone enclosed by square ditches.
Inside,
outside the north gate to the west was the yìwèi (burying place),
to the east the dēngtái (lamp stand),
and outside the south gate was the Huángqíshì.
Outside,
outside the west gate, stretching to the west, were the shénkù, shénchú, zǎishēngtíng, and jìqìkù.
Outside the north gate to the northwest was the Zhāigōng.
Further out, four Heavenly Gates were built;
outside the west gate to the north were the luánjiàkù, qiǎnguānfáng (sending official's room), and nèipéicìguānfáng (inner accompanying official's room).
Further out was the tányún (altar gate),
and outside the gate was the Tàizhéjiē Páifāng,
protecting an altar area of over 1,400 mǔ.
The Tàishèjì Tán
was southwest of the palace city,
aligned east-west,
built in the early Míng dynasty.
It was five zhàng wide,
five chǐ high,
with four sets of descending steps,
all with five levels.
The altar earth was five colors according to direction,
covered with yellow earth.
The altars were five zhàng apart,
and south of the altars were planted pines.
The two altars shared one enclosure,
thirty zhàng square,
five chǐ high,
paved with bricks,
with gates decorated in colors corresponding to their directions.
The surrounding wall had four gates;
the south Língxīngmén had three,
the north Jǐmén had five,
and the east and west Jǐmén each had three.
Each Jǐmén had twenty-four halberds arranged.
In the tenth year of Hóngwǔ, the altar was moved to the right of the Wǔmén.
Shè and Jì shared one altar,
divided into two tiers.
The upper tier was five zhàng wide,
the lower tier five zhàng three chǐ wide,
and five chǐ high.
The outer enclosure was five chǐ high,
and each side was nineteen zhàng and a fraction.
The outer wall was sixty-six zhàng and a fraction east-west,
and eighty-six zhàng and a fraction north-south.
North of the wall were three gates,
outside the gates was the jìdiàn (sacrificial hall),
and north of that was the bàidiàn (bowing hall).
Outside that were again three gates,
and the wall had one gate each to the east, west, and south.
During the Yǒnglè reign,
altars were built in Běijīng
following this system.
The Dìshèjì Tán was in Xīyuàn,
its altar base six cùn high,
two zhàng five chǐ square,
paved with fine bricks,
filled with clean earth.
North of the altar were two archways,
called Shèjiē.
The Wángguóshèjì Tán was smaller than the Tàishèjì by three-tenths in height and breadth.
The Fǔ, Zhōu, Xiàn Shèjì Tán
was smaller by five-tenths in breadth,
and four-tenths in height,
with three levels of steps.
Later, it was all decided to combine sacrifices on the same altar,
as in the capital.
The Cháorì and Xīyuè Tán
were built in the third year of Hóngwǔ.
The Cháorì Tán was eight chǐ high,
the Xīyuè Tán six chǐ high,
both four zhàng square.
There were two enclosures,
each twenty-five bù.
In the twenty-first year, they were abolished.
In the ninth year of Jiājìng, they were rebuilt,
each altar having one tier.
The Cháorì Tán was of red glazed tiles,
the Xīyuè Tán used white.
The Cháorì Tán had nine levels of steps,
the Xīyuè Tán six levels,
all of white stone.
Each had two Heavenly Gates built.
The Xiānnóng Tán
was five chǐ high,
five zhàng wide,
with four sets of descending steps.
The Yùgēngjíbǐ (Imperial Plowing Field Position)
was three chǐ high,
two zhàng five chǐ wide,
with four sets of descending steps.
The Shānchuān Tán
was built in the ninth year of Hóngwǔ.
It had a main hall and a bowing hall, each with eight bays,
and east and west side corridors with twenty-four bays.
To the southwest was the Xiānnóng Tán,
to the southeast the Jùfú Diàn,
south of the hall was the Jítián Tán,
to the east the Qídú Miào,
and behind it was the Shéncāng.
The surrounding wall was over seven hundred zhàng long,
and the land within the wall was cultivated annually with grains and vegetables,
for sacrificial purposes.
In the tenth year of Jiājìng,
it was renamed Tiānshéndìqí Tán,
and arranged separately to the left and right.
The Tàisuì Tán was the same as the Yuèdú.
The Yuèzhèn Hàidú Shānchuān Chénghuáng Tán
was built on a high mound,
facing south,
two chǐ five cùn high,
ten times wider (than height),
with four sets of descending steps,
five levels facing south,
and three levels facing east, west, and north.
The Wángguó Shānchuān Tán
was four chǐ high,
with four sets of descending steps,
and three zhàng five chǐ square.
The Tiānxià Shānchuān Suǒzài Tán (Altars for Mountains and Rivers Everywhere under Heaven)
was three chǐ high,
with four sets of descending steps,
three levels,
and two zhàng five chǐ square.
The numbers of divine tablets, sacrificial vessels, jade and silk, sacrificial animals, and prayer tablets. Divine tablets:
Huánqiū.
On the Winter Solstice of the first year of Hóngwǔ,
on the first tier of the main altar,
Hàotiān Shàngdì faced south.
On the second tier,
Dàmíng was to the east,
followed by the stars,
Yèmíng to the west,
followed by Tàisuì.
In the second year, Rénzǔ was enshrined as a co-sacrificed deity,
positioned on the first tier,
facing west.
In the third year,
within the inner enclosure below the altar,
sacrifices to Fēngyún Léiyǔ were added.
In the seventh year, it was reorganized;
within the inner enclosure,
there were three altars each to the east and west.
The two altars for the Stars
were set up separately to the east and west.
Next,
to the east were Tàisuì and the Wǔyuè (Five Sacred Mountains),
to the west were Fēngyún Léiyǔ (Wind, Cloud, Thunder, Rain) and the Wǔzhèn (Five Guarding Mountains).
Outside the inner enclosure,
there were two altars each to the east and west.
To the east were the Sìhǎi (Four Seas),
to the west the Sìdú (Four Rivers).
Next were the Tiānxià Shénqí Tán (Altars for Deities Everywhere under Heaven),
set up separately to the east and west.
Fāngqiū.
In the second year of Hóngwǔ (1369), at the summer solstice,
the first tier of the main altar was dedicated to
Huángdìzhī,
facing south.
The second tier was dedicated to
the Wǔyuè (Five Sacred Mountains) in the east,
followed by the Sìhǎi (Four Seas);
the Wǔzhèn (Five Guarding Mountains) in the west,
followed by the Sìdú (Four Great Rivers).
In the third year (1370), Rénzǔ was added as a consort,
positioned on the first tier,
facing west.
Within the enclosure below the altar,
additional sacrifices were offered to the mountains and rivers of the realm.
In the seventh year (1374), a revision was made:
within the inner enclosure,
there were two altars each to the east and west.
The east altars were for the Sìhǎi (Four Seas),
and the west altars for the Sìdú (Four Great Rivers).
Next to these were two altars
for the mountains and rivers of the realm.
Outside the inner enclosure,
one altar for the gods and spirits of the realm was established to the east and one to the west.
In the twelfth year (1379), in the first month, a combined sacrifice was offered at the Dàsì Diàn (Great Sacrifice Hall).
In the main hall, there were three altars:
Shàngdì and Huángdìzhī both faced south.
Rénzǔ's consort position was to the east,
facing west.
There were fourteen altars for the subordinate sacrifices.
On the eastern side of the imperial steps was one altar called Dàmíng,
and on the western side, one altar called Yèmíng.
There were six altars in each of the two side corridors: two altars for the Xīngchén (Stars and Constellations);
next to the east,
Tàisuì, Wǔyuè, and Sìhǎi;
next to the west,
Fēngyún Léiyǔ (Wind, Clouds, Thunder, and Rain), Wǔzhèn, and two altars for Sìdú;
and next to these, two altars for the mountains and rivers and gods and spirits of the realm.
All faced east or west.
In the twenty-first year (1388), four stone platforms were added within the Dānchí (Vermillion Pavement):
one each for Dàmíng and Yèmíng,
and two for the Xīngchén.
Outside the inner enclosure were twenty stone platforms: ten altars to the east
for the Běiyuè, Běizhèn, Dōngyuè, Dōngzhèn, Dōnghǎi, Tàisuì, Dìwáng, mountains and rivers, gods and spirits, and Sìdú;
and ten altars to the west
for the Běihǎi, Xīyuè, Xīzhèn, Xīhǎi, Zhōngyuè, Zhōngzhèn, Fēngyún Léiyǔ, Nányuè, Nánzhèn,
and Nánhǎi.
All faced east or west.
The platforms were a little over three chǐ high,
surrounded by stone railings,
with ramps for ascent and descent.
Stone niches were carved on the platforms
to place the spirit tablets.
During the Jiànwén reign (1399-1402),
Rénzǔ was removed,
and Tàizǔ was enshrined as consort instead,
positioned on the first tier,
facing west.
In the first year of Hóngxī (1425), Wénhuángdì was added below Tàizǔ.
In the ninth year of Jiājìng (1530), the separate sacrifice rites were restored.
For the Huánqiū (Altar of Heaven), Dàmíng was to the east,
and Yèmíng to the west.
Next to the east were
the Èrshíbāxiù (Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions), Wǔxīng (Five Planets), and Zhōutiān Xīngchén (Stars of the Entire Heaven).
Next to the west was
Fēngyún Léiyǔ.
This made a total of four altars.
For the Fāngqiū (Altar of Earth), the Wǔyuè were to the east,
along with the three mountains Jīyùn, Yìshèng, and Shénliè;
the Wǔzhèn were to the west,
along with the two mountains Tiānshòu and Chúndé.
Next to the east were the Sìhǎi,
and next to the west, the Sìdú.
Both the southern and northern suburbs exclusively enshrined Tàizǔ as consort.
The consort position for the Tàishèjì is described elsewhere.
The main position for Xiānnóng faced south,
and the consort position for Hòujì faced west.
As for all spirit tablets,
those for Heaven, Earth, and Ancestors were called
"shénbǎn" (spirit boards),
while the rest were called
"shénpái" (spirit plaques).
The shénbǎn for the Huánqiū were two chǐ five cùn long,
five cùn wide,
one cùn thick,
with a five-cùn high base,
made of chestnut wood.
The main position's inscription read "Hàotiān Shàngdì,"
and the consort position's inscription read "Mǒu Zǔ Mǒu Huángdì,"
both with yellow background and gold characters.
The spirit boards for the subordinate sacrifices of Fēngyún Léiyǔ
had a red background and gold characters.
For the divine seats,
Shàngdì used a dragon chair and dragon table,
with a brocade cushion placed on top;
the consort position was similar.
For the subordinate sacrifices,
the positions were placed on tables,
without seats.
The main position at Fāngqiū was called Huángdìzhī;
the consort and subordinate sacrifices
had the same specifications as for the Huánqiū.
The ancestral tablets of emperors and empresses in the Fèngxiān Diàn were one chǐ two cùn high,
four cùn wide,
with a two-cùn high base,
made of wood,
adorned with gold,
and carved with blue characters.
The niches were two chǐ high,
two chǐ wide,
with a four-cùn high base,
lacquered red and carved with golden dragon, phoenix, and flower patterns,
with two windows opening,
fitted with red gauze,
with golden bronze rings on the sides,
and gold-woven brocade inside as a cushion.
For the Shèjì (Altars of Land and Grain),
the Shèzhǔ (tablet of the God of Land) was made of stone,
five chǐ high,
five chǐ wide,
slightly pointed at the top.
It stood on the altar,
half buried in the earth,
facing roughly north-south;
Jì (God of Grain) did not use a tablet.
In the tenth year of Hóngwǔ (1377), all were fitted with wooden tablets,
lacquered vermillion.
After the sacrifice,
they were stored in the treasury,
and the stone tablets were still buried in the altar,
with only their tips slightly exposed.
Later, for the ancestral consort, her tablet was made into a gilt plaque stand,
resembling the cases used for the former sages.
In the Jiājìng period (1522-1566),
they were kept in the imperial ancestral temple.
The imperial Shèjì spirit tablets were made of wood,
one chǐ eight cùn high,
three cùn wide,
with a vermillion lacquer background and gold writing.
A stone niche was placed south of the altar
to store the spirit tablets.
The Shèzhǔ for princely courts, prefectures, and counties were all made of stone,
two chǐ five cùn long,
one chǐ five cùn wide.
The spirit tablets for the Rìyuè Tán (Altars of Sun and Moon)
were made of pine and cypress,
two chǐ five cùn long,
five cùn wide,
with a five-cùn high base.
They had vermillion lacquer and gold characters;
others followed this pattern.
Sacrificial Vessels
for the Nánjiāo (Southern Suburb Altar).
In the first year of Hóngwǔ (1368), it was decreed that
for the main position,
one Dēng (sacrificial vessel),
twelve Biàndòu (bamboo and wooden sacrificial vessels) each,
two Fúguǐ (square and round grain vessels) each,
and three Jué (wine cups);
on the altar,
two Tàizūn (large wine vessels),
one Zhùzūn, one Xīzūn, and one Shānlèi each;
below the altar,
one Tàizūn,
and two Shānlèi.
For the subordinate sacrifice positions,
one Dēng,
ten Biàndòu each,
two Fúguǐ each,
and two Zhùzūn and two Xīzūn each were placed to the east and west.
The Běijiāo (Northern Suburb Altar) was the same.
In the seventh year (1374), for the subordinate sacrifices at the Huánqiū,
a total of six Jiǔzūn (wine vessels) were placed to the west of the altar,
three for the Dàmíng position and three for the Yèmíng position.
For the gods and spirits of the realm,
three Xíng (meat broth vessels),
eight Biàndòu each,
two Fúguǐ each,
and three Jiǔzūn each were placed to the east and west, both inside and outside the enclosure,
with three Jué for each position.
For Fāngqiū and the Yuèzhèn,
three Jiǔzūn were placed for each,
three Jiǔzūn each were placed to the east and west inside the enclosure,
and three Jiǔzūn each were placed to the east and west outside the enclosure,
with three Jué for each position.
The gods and spirits were the same as for the Huánqiū.
In the eighth year (1375),
for the subordinate sacrifices at the Huánqiū,
one Dēng and two Xíng were added.
For each position,
additional Jiǔjiǎ (wine goblets) were provided:
thirty each for Xīngchén and the gods and spirits of the realm,
and fifteen each for Tàisuì, Fēngyún Léiyǔ, Yuèzhèn, and Hǎidú.
Fāngqiū's
subordinate sacrifices were the same.
In the tenth year (1377), the rites for combined sacrifices were established;
the arrangements for each altar remained as before,
except that Tàisuì and Fēngyún Léiyǔ each had ten Jiǔzhǎn (wine cups),
and a total of three Jiǔzūn and eighteen Jué were placed to the south of the altar in both the eastern and western corridors.
In the twenty-first year, revised:
On the main hall, three altars.
For each altar,
one *dēng*
and twelve *biāndòu* each;
two *fǔguǐ* each.
A total of six *jiǔzūn* and nine *jué* were set up southeast of the hall,
facing west.
Inside the vermillion steps, four altars.
For Dàmíng and Yèmíng, one *dēng* each;
ten *biāndòu*;
two *fǔguǐ*;
three *jiǔzūn*;
three *jué*.
For the Star Constellations, two altars.
For each, one *dēng*;
two *xíng*;
thirty wine cups.
The rest were the same as Dàmíng.
Outside the perimeter wall, twenty altars.
For each, one *dēng*;
two *xíng*;
ten *biāndòu* each;
two *fǔguǐ* each;
ten wine cups;
three *jiǔzūn*;
three *jué*.
For the Shénqí altars,
three *xíng*;
eight *biāndòu* each.
For the altars of Emperors and Kings, Mountains and Rivers, Four Great Rivers, Central Sacred Mountains, and Gods of Wind, Clouds, Thunder, and Rain,
thirty wine cups each.
The rest were all the same as the Sacred Mountains and River Deities.
Regular sacrifices at the Tàimiào.
Established in the first year of Hóngwǔ:
For each temple, one *dēng*;
three *xíng*;
twelve *biāndòu* each;
two *fǔguǐ* each.
A total of three *jiǔzūn*, eight gold *jué*, and sixteen porcelain *jué* were set up in the east and west of the hall, facing north.
In the twenty-first year, revised:
For each temple, two *dēng*;
two *xíng*.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
nine *jiǔzūn* were universally set up for the nine temples,
with one added for the *xiáp* sacrifice;
seventeen gold *jué*,
with two added for the *xiáp* sacrifice;
thirty-four porcelain *jué*,
with four added for the *xiáp* sacrifice.
Princes participating in the sacrifice.
Established in the third year of Hóngwǔ:
Three *dēng* and three *xíng* each;
twelve *biāndòu* each;
two *fǔguǐ* each;
three *jiǔzūn*;
two *jiǔzhù*.
In the twenty-first year, revised:
One *dēng* and one *xíng* each;
three *jué* each;
ten *biāndòu* each;
two *fǔguǐ* each.
A total of three *jiǔzūn* were used east of the hall.
Meritorious officials participating in the sacrifice.
Established in the second year of Hóngwǔ:
For each position, two *biāndòu* each;
two *fǔguǐ* each.
In the second year, an addition was established:
A total of two *jiǔzūn* were used;
two *jiǔzhù*.
In the twenty-first year, revised:
Ten altars.
For each altar, one *xíng*;
two *biāndòu* each;
one *fǔguǐ* each;
three *jué*.
A total of three *jiǔzūn* were used west of the hall.
Tàishèjì.
Established in the first year of Hóngwǔ:
Three *xíng*;
ten *biāndòu* each;
two *fǔguǐ* each.
The same for the secondary positions.
For the main and secondary positions, three *jiǔzūn* were all set up east of the altar.
In the eleventh year, revised:
For each position, one *dēng*;
two *xíng*;
twelve *biāndòu*.
For the main and secondary positions, a total of three *jiǔzūn* were set up;
nine *jué*.
Later, when Tàizǔ and Chéngzǔ were both included in the sacrifice,
one *jiǔzūn* was added;
three *jué*.
For the Prefectural, Sub-prefectural, and County Shèjì:
One *xíng*;
four *biāndòu*;
two *fǔguǐ*.
Sacrifice to the Morning Sun and Evening Moon.
Established in the third year of Hóngwǔ:
Two *tàizūn*, two *zhùzūn*, and two *shānléi* each,
located in the southeast corner on the altar,
facing north.
Two *xiàngzūn*, two *húzūn*, and two *shānléi* each,
located below the altar.
Ten *biāndòu* each;
two *fǔguǐ* each;
three *dēng* and three *xíng* each.
Xiānnóng.
Same as Shèjì,
with one *dēng* added,
and two *biāndòu* reduced.
Shénqí.
Established in the second year of Hóngwǔ:
For each altar, four *biāndòu* each;
one *fǔguǐ*, *dēng*, and *jué* each.
In the ninth year, revised:
In the main hall, a total of three *jiǔzūn* were set up;
seven *jué*.
In each of the two side halls, three *jiǔzūn* were set up;
three *jué*.
The rest were as before.
In the twenty-first year, revised:
For each altar, one *dēng*;
two *xíng*;
ten *biāndòu* each;
two *fǔguǐ* each;
thirty wine cups.
Star Constellations.
In the center of the main hall, one *dēng*;
two *xíng*.
For the other nine altars,
two *xíng*.
For each altar, ten *biāndòu*;
one *fǔguǐ* each;
thirty wine cups;
one *jué*.
A total of three *jiǔzūn* were set up.
Tàisuì and various other gods.
Eight *biāndòu* each;
two *fǔguǐ* each;
three *jiǔzūn*.
Same for Sacred Mountains, Rivers, Mountains, and Streams.
Successive Emperors and Kings.
Established in the fourth year of Hóngwǔ:
One *dēng*;
two *xíng*;
eight *biāndòu* each;
one *fǔguǐ* each;
one *zǔ*;
three *jué*;
three *zūn*.
In the seventh year, revised:
One *dēng*, *xíng*, and *fǔguǐ* each;
ten *biāndòu* each;
three *jué* each.
A total of five *jiǔzūn* were set up on the west steps of the hall,
and three *jiǔzūn* on the east steps of the hall.
In the twenty-first year, an addition was established:
For each position, two *xíng*;
two *fǔguǐ* each.
For the five chambers, a total of three *jiǔzūn* were set up;
forty-eight *jué*.
For the secondary positions, for each altar, two *biāndòu* each;
one *fǔguǐ* each;
one *kuìpán*.
For each position, one *xíng*;
three wine cups.
Three Sovereigns.
Eight *biāndòu* each;
two *fǔguǐ* each;
two *dēng* and two *xíng* each;
three *jué*;
one *xīzūn*, one *xiàngzūn*, and one *shānléi* each.
Secondary positions.
Four *biāndòu* each;
two *fǔguǐ* each;
one *xíng*;
three *jué*;
one *xīzūn* and one *xiàngzūn* each.
For the Zhìshèng Xiānshī:
In the first year of Hóngwǔ (1368), it was decreed that there should be
six biāndòu each,
two fǔguǐ each,
one dēng,
two xíng,
and one xīzūn, xiàngzūn, and shānlěi each.
For the Sīpèi seats,
four biāndòu each,
one fǔguǐ each,
and one dēng.
For the Shízhé
and the Liǎngwǔ,
two biāndòu.
In the fourth year (1371), it was further decreed that
for the principal seat,
ten biāndòu each,
three jiǔzūn,
three jué,
the rest as before.
For the Sīpèi,
one jiǔzūn per seat,
the rest the same as the principal seat.
For the Shízhé,
one jué for the east and west respectively,
four biāndòu each per seat,
one fǔguǐ each,
one xíng,
and one jiǔzhǎn.
For the Liǎngwǔ,
thirteen altars each for the east and west,
one jué each for the east and west,
four biāndòu each per altar,
one fǔguǐ each,
and four jiǔzhǎn.
In the fifteenth year (1382), it was further decreed that
for the principal seat,
one jiǔzūn,
three jué,
one dēng,
two xíng,
eight biāndòu each,
and two fǔguǐ each.
For the Sīpèi seats,
a total of one jiǔzūn,
three jué each,
one dēng,
two xíng,
six biāndòu each,
and one fǔguǐ each.
For the Shízhé,
a total of one jiǔzūn,
five jué each for the east and west,
one xíng,
four biāndòu each,
and one fǔguǐ each.
For the Dōngxī Wǔ,
four jué for every four seats,
two biāndòu each,
and one fǔguǐ each.
In the sixth year of Jǐngtài (1455), the Liǎngwǔ were increased by two biāndòu each
and one fǔguǐ each.
In the twelfth year of Chénghuà (1476),
the principal seat's biāndòu were increased to twelve.
In the ninth year of Jiājìng (1530), they were again reduced to ten.
The qíqú
were the same as for the Xiānnóng.
For the Mǎshén,
four biāndòu each,
and one fǔguǐ, dēng, xiàngzūn, and húzūn each.
Jade, silk, and sacrificial animals
There were three grades of jade: for the Shàngdì,
azure bì;
for the Huángdìqí,
yellow cóng;
for the Tàishè and Tàijì,
two guī with bases;
for the Zhāorì and Xīyuè,
guī and bì of five cùn.
There were five grades of silk: called the silk for jiāosì rituals,
used for the principal accompanying seats in jiāosì.
For the Shàngdì,
azure;
for the Dìqí,
yellow;
for the accompanying seats,
white.
Called the silk for ritual offerings to deities,
used for Shèjì and below.
For Shèjì,
black;
for the Dàmíng,
red;
for the Yèmíng, xīngchén, Tàisuì, fēngyúnléiyǔ, and all Tiānxià Shénqí, all white;
for the Wǔxīng,
five colors;
for the Yuèzhèn, Sìhǎi, and Língshān, the color appropriate to their direction;
for the Sìdú,
black;
for the Xiānnóng,
principal and accompanying all green;
for the Qúnshén,
white;
for the Dìwáng Xiānshī, all white.
For the qíqú,
in the first year of Hóngwǔ (1368), black was used;
in the seventh year (1374), it was changed to red;
in the ninth year (1376), it was fixed at two black and five white.
Called the silk for Fèngxiān rituals,
used in the Tàimiào,
two per temple.
Called the silk for Zhǎnqīn rituals,
used for imperial princes who receive secondary sacrifices.
Called the silk for Bàogōng rituals,
used for meritorious officials who receive secondary sacrifices.
All white.
One for each seat.
Only at the Yuánqiú,
in the ninth year of Jiājìng (1530), twelve were used,
while for the Zhōutiān Xīngchén, a total of ten were used;
for the Kǒngmiào Shízhé and Liǎngwǔ, one each for east and west, it is said.
Furthermore, in the eleventh year of Hóngwǔ (1378),
the emperor considered the use of paper money in minor sacrifices as improper.
The ritual officials deliberated and decreed that
in the capital,
Dàsì and Zhōngsì should use prescribed silks,
with baskets.
Outside the capital,
kingdoms, prefectures, departments, and counties should also follow this.
Minor sacrifices should only use sacrificial animals and liquor.
Sacrificial animals are of three grades:
calves,
sheep,
and pigs. The preferred color is
reddish-brown, or sometimes black. For
Grand Sacrifices,
they are purified for ninety days; for
Middle Sacrifices,
thirty days; for
Minor Sacrifices,
ten days. On the first day of the month, one month before a
Grand Sacrifice,
the emperor personally goes to the sacrificial animal enclosure to inspect the animals.
Each day, one high-ranking minister goes to inspect them. In the
second year of Hóngwǔ,
the emperor felt that inspecting the sacrificial animals
too close to the altar
was unsettling for the people.
Thus, he established the ritual for inspecting sacrificial animals,
placing it two hundred paces from the altar. In the
seventh year, a regulation was established: for
Grand Sacrifices,
the emperor personally inspects the animals; for
Middle and Minor Sacrifices,
an official is dispatched. In the
eleventh year of Jiājìng, it was revised: for the
winter and summer solstices
and prayers for grain,
the emperor personally inspects five days before the sacrifice;
afterwards, ministers are dispatched.
For the Yuánqiū,
tawny calves; for the
Fāngqiū,
yellow calves; for
accompanying deities,
each pure calf. In the
seventh year of Hóngwǔ, accompanying deities for the Yuánqiū were added. For
celestial bodies,
one ox,
three sheep and pigs. For
Tàisuì,
one ox, sheep, and pig. For
wind, clouds, thunder, rain, and all deities under heaven,
five sheep and five pigs each. For
Fāngbīng accompanying deities and
all mountains and rivers under heaven,
one ox,
three sheep and pigs each. For the
dì sacrifice at the Tàimiào,
the principal and accompanying deities all receive tàiláo;
for the xiá sacrifice, all receive tàiláo.
For seasonal offerings, each temple receives one calf, one sheep, and one pig.
For accompanying deities of imperial princes,
established in the third year of Hóngwǔ,
a total of one ox, one sheep, and one pig.
In the twenty-first year, it was revised:
each altar receives one calf, one sheep, and one pig.
For accompanying deities of meritorious officials,
established in the second year of Hóngwǔ,
each deity receives one sheep and one pig body.
In the twenty-first year, it was revised:
each altar receives one sheep and one pig.
For Tàishèjì,
one calf, one sheep, and one pig each;
accompanying deities are the same.
For the shèjì of prefectures, departments, and counties,
the principal and accompanying deities
receive a total of one sheep and one pig.
In the seventh year of Hóngwǔ, it was added that
each receives one sheep and one pig.
For Rìzhāo and Yuèxī,
one calf, one sheep, and one pig each.
Xiānnóng is the same as Tàishèjì.
For shénqí,
established in the second year of Hóngwǔ,
six sheep and six pigs.
In the twenty-first year, it was revised:
each altar receives one calf, one sheep, and one pig.
In the tenth year of Jiājìng,
for heavenly deities on the left
and earthly deities on the right,
five sacrificial animals each.
For celestial bodies,
each altar receives one sheep and one pig.
For Língxīng and various deities,
each deity receives one sheep and one pig,
and a total of one ox.
For Tàisuì and various deities,
all receive tàiláo.
For the deities of Yuèzhèn Hǎidú,
one calf, one sheep, and one pig.
For emperors,
each chamber receives one calf, one sheep, and one pig;
for accompanying deities,
each altar receives one sheep and one pig.
For Xiānshī, it is like emperors;
for the Four Associates, it is like accompanying deities;
for the Ten Sages, one pig body divided into five parts each for east and west;
for the two corridors, one pig each for east and west,
later increased to three.
For the Xiānshī of prefectural, departmental, and county schools,
one sheep and one pig.
For the Four Associates,
a total of one sheep and one pig,
carved into four bodies.
For the Ten Sages, one pig each for east and west,
carved into five bodies.
For the two corridors, one pig,
carved into one hundred and eight parts.
For qí dáo,
established in the ninth year of Hóngwǔ, calves, sheep, and pigs were used;
after Yǒnglè,
calves were removed.
Kingdoms and guard-stations are the same.
For the Five Sacrifices and horse deities, only sheep and pigs are used.
Prayer Scrolls
The prayer tablets for the southern and northern suburbs are one chi and one fen long,
eight cun wide,
and two fen thick,
made of catalpa wood.
For ancestral temples,
they are one chi and two cun long,
nine cun wide,
and one fen thick,
made of catalpa wood,
covered with paper mulberry.
All deities, emperors, and Xiānshī
have prayers,
the texts of which are numerous and not recorded here.
The prayer stand is set up in the west.
Contents of Biān and Dòu
For all the contents of the biān and dòu,
when twelve items are used,
the biān contain shaped salt, dried fish, jujubes, chestnuts, hazelnuts, water caltrops, foxnuts, deer jerky, white cakes, black cakes, parched grains, and glutinous rice cakes.

The dòu contain pickled leeks, minced meat in vinegar, pickled celery, pickled mustard greens, minced rabbit meat, pickled bamboo shoots, minced fish, spleen slices, pork belly, cooked rice, and millet mixed with meat.
When ten items are used,
the biān omit parched grains and glutinous rice cakes,
and the dòu omit cooked rice and millet mixed with meat.
When eight items are used,
the biān further omit white and black cakes,
and the dòu further omit spleen slices and pork belly.
When four items are used,
the biān are filled only with shaped salt, dried fish, jujubes, and chestnuts,
and the dòu are filled only with pickled celery, minced rabbit meat, pickled mustard greens, and minced deer meat.
When two items each are used,
the biān contain chestnuts and deer jerky,
and the dòu contain pickled mustard greens and minced deer meat.
When two fǔ and two guǐ are used,
they are filled with millet and glutinous millet, and rice and foxtail millet.
When one each is used,
they are filled with millet and foxtail millet.
The dēng contains tàigēng,
and the xíng contains hégēng.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ,
the Ministry of Rites stated:
"The Lǐjì, Jiāotèshēng says,
'For the sacrifice in the suburbs,'
'earthenware and gourds are used as vessels,'
valuing simplicity.
The Zhōulǐ, Biēnrén states,
'For all sacrifices, provide the contents of fǔ and guǐ.'
The commentary says,
'earthen fǔ are used for outer sacrifices.'
Today, porcelain is used for sacrifices,
which aligns with ancient intent.
However, the likes of pán and yú differ in form from the ancient fǔ, guǐ, dēng, and xíng.
Now we propose that all sacrificial vessels be made of porcelain,
their forms imitating ancient fǔ, guǐ, dēng, and dòu,
but biān should be made of bamboo."
An imperial edict approved this.
Wine offerings follow the Zhōu system,
using new and old fermented grains
to prepare the five qís and three jiǔs.
Their actual names and quantities in the zūn
vary.
Miscellaneous Discussions and Rituals for Sacrifices
Regarding miscellaneous discussions and rituals for sacrifices:
for all spirit tablets,
the emperor's tablet is
one chi and two cun square,
three cun thick,
red with gold characters.
The crown prince's tablet is
nine cun square,
two cun thick,
red with blue characters.
Tablets for accompanying officials
are all white with black characters.
Kneeling mats.
Initially crimson was used.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, a regulation was established:
mats for the suburban altars have grass mats as the cover
and rushes as the padding.
For ancestral temples, shèjì, Xiānnóng, and mountains and rivers,
red patterned silk is used as the cover,
and red cotton cloth as the padding.
Chanting and Singing.
Whenever the Emperor personally conducted sacrifices,
when entering and taking his place,
the Tàicháng Sì would announce “Zhōngyán” (inner solemnity),
and announce “Wàibàn” (outer preparation).
Washing, ascending the altar, drinking the blessed wine, receiving the sacrificial meat—
for each, a eulogy would be offered.
Also, for all sacrifices,
a position for washing goblets would be set up,
for rinsing and wiping the goblets.
Upon first ascending the altar,
“Zàibài” (bow twice) would be chanted,
and upon pouring the libation,
“Cìfúzuò” (bestow blessings and sacrificial meat) would be chanted.
In the 7th year of Hóngwǔ,
the Lǐbù memorialized that this was too cumbersome and tedious,
and it was all deleted.
Incense Offering Ritual.
In the early Míng dynasty, this was performed for all sacrifices.
In the 7th year of Hóngwǔ, it was abolished based on the words of Hàlín Zhān Tóng.
In the 9th year of Jiājìng, it was restored.
Bowing Ritual.
Initially,
every section involved two bows.
In the 9th year of Hóngwǔ,
the ritual officials memorialized:
“The texts of Yīxiàn, Sānxiàn, Wǔxiàn, and Qīxiàn in the Lǐjì
do not record bowing rituals.
During the Tang and Song dynasties, for suburban sacrifices,
two bows were performed for each ritual section.
However, for the Yàxiàn and Zhōngxiàn,
the Son of Heaven did not perform the ritual,
but had his ministers perform it.
Now we propose that for grand sacrifices and medium sacrifices,
from welcoming the deities to drinking the blessed wine and sending off the deities,
the ritual of two bows should be performed for each section.”
The Emperor ordered that each section comprise twelve bows,
with four bows each for welcoming the deities, drinking the blessed wine and receiving the sacrificial meat, and sending off the deities.
Ascending the Altar and Removing Sandals.
Initially, this was not practiced.
In the 8th year of Hóngwǔ, an edict instructed the officials of the Hàlín Yuàn to determine the ritual of removing sandals when ascending the altar for grand sacrifices.
The xuéshì Yuè Sháofèng, after consulting various records on court and sacrificial ceremonies from the Hàn and Wèi dynasties onwards,
proposed that on the day before the suburban sacrifices and temple offerings,
the appropriate authorities should prepare mats on the ground,
set up an imperial screen outside the southeastern gate of the altar,
and set up a place for the attending officials to remove their footwear on the west side of the altar gate.
On the day of the sacrifice,
the imperial carriage would enter the screen area,
remove sandals, and ascend the altar.
Those ascending the altar as attendants, carriage guides, ritual chanters, prayer readers, as well as the sub-offering and accompanying sacrificial officials,
would all remove their sandals outside,
and in turn ascend the altar to perform their duties.
The xiélǜláng and yue Wǔshēng would, as before, take their places barefoot in socks.
After the sacrifice,
they would descend the altar and put on their sandals.
This was followed.
In the 17th year of Jiājìng, this ritual was abolished.
Sacrifice Dates.
Selected by the Qīntiān Jiān,
the Tàicháng Sì would submit a memorial to the Fèngtiān Diàn on the first day of the 12th month.
This was because ancient divinatory methods no longer existed,
and the selection of auspicious gānzhī days was used as a substitute for divination.
In the 7th year of Hóngwǔ, the Tàicháng Qīng was ordered to deliberate on sacrifice dates,
record them on a tablet,
and perform sacrifices according to the times,
establishing this as a regulation.
On the day of the sacrifice,
officials would be dispatched to oversee the ceremony,
and those showing disrespect or impropriety would be punished.
Ritual Practice.
For all sacrifices,
three days and two days beforehand,
all officials would practice the rituals at the Cháotiān Gōng.
In the 9th year of Jiājìng, it was revised:
for the Winter Solstice suburban sacrifice,
ritual practice would be seven days and six days beforehand.
Fasting and Purification.
In the 2nd year of Hóngwǔ,
the xuéshì Zhū Shēng and others, by imperial command, drafted the “Text on Fasting and Purification,” which stated:
“ ‘Jie’ (purification) means
to prohibit external actions.
‘Zhāi’ (fasting) means
to regulate one’s inner being.
Bathing and changing clothes,
residing in an outer lodging,
abstaining from alcohol,
abstaining from pungent foods,
not inquiring about illnesses,
not attending funerals,
not listening to music,
not handling legal cases—
this is purification.
Concentrating one’s mind,
being strictly reverent and cautious;
if one has any thoughts,
one immediately thinks of the deity being sacrificed to,
as if it is above,
as if it is by one’s left and right,
with pure and sincere devotion,
without a moment’s lapse—
this is fasting.
For grand sacrifices, seven days:
the first four days are purification,
the last three days are fasting.”
Tàizǔ said:
“For all sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, the deities of the land and grain, ancestral temples, mountains and rivers, etc.,
to pray for blessings for the empire,
an order should be issued for all officials to fast and purify themselves.
However, if it is for one’s own prayers to Heaven and Earth and all deities,
unrelated to the affairs of the people,
no such order should be issued.”
He also said:
“To fast for five or seven days
is too long;
people’s hearts are easily slackened.
Only for the impending sacrifice,
fast and purify for three days,
and strive for utmost sincerity and concentration,
then it might reach the divine. ”
Thus, this was established as a regulation.
That year, following the memorial of Lǐbù Shàngshū Cuī Liàng,
seven days before a grand sacrifice,
accompanying sacrificial officials would go to the Zhōngshū Shěng to receive their oath and admonition.
Each would perform their duty,
not sharing responsibilities,
lest they incur the standing laws of the state.
For ancestral temples and the deities of the land and grain,
three days of fasting would be observed,
without an oath and admonition.
In the 3rd year, he instructed Lǐbù Shàngshū Táo Kǎi, saying:
“The human heart is inconstant in its resolve;
it must be constantly warned
to prevent it from straying.”
Thus, he ordered the Lǐbù to cast a bronze figure,
one foot five inches tall,
holding an ivory tablet.
For grand sacrifices, “three days of fasting” would be written on the tablet;
for medium sacrifices, “two days of fasting” would be written on the tablet.
The Tàicháng Sì would present it and place it in the fasting place.
In the 4th year, it was stipulated that for the Son of Heaven’s personal sacrifices, fasting would be five days;
for sacrifices performed by dispatched officials, three days;
and for sending down incense, one day.
In the 5th year, he ordered all yámen to each set up a wooden plaque
to warn against irreverence,
with the inscription:
“The state has its standing laws,
and the deities observe them.”
For all sacrifices,
these would be displayed.
Also, following Táo Kǎi’s memorial,
for all personal sacrifices,
the Huáng Tàizǐ would remain in the palace,
and the Qīnwáng would attend in military attire.
Even if the Huáng Tàizǐ and Qīnwáng did not participate in the sacrifice,
they were to observe fasting and purification equally.
In the 6th year, fasting quarters for accompanying sacrificial officials were built southwest of the northern suburban fasting palace,
and the ritual of fasting and purification was re-established.
For all sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
after noon, five days before the main sacrifice,
one would bathe and change clothes,
and reside in an outer room.
The next morning,
all officials would view the oath and admonition plaque at the Fèngtiān Mén.
The day after that,
they would make a report at the Rénzǔ Miào,
then retire to the fasting palace,
and observe three days of fasting.
For ancestral temple offerings,
after noon, four days before the main sacrifice,
one would bathe and change clothes,
and reside in an outer room.
Starting the next day,
three days of fasting would be observed.

For sacrifices to the deities of the land and grain, the morning sun, the evening moon, the circumpolar stars, Tàisuì, wind, clouds, thunder, and rain, the Five Sacred Mountains and Four Great Rivers, and other mountains and rivers,
two days of fasting would be observed,
following the previous procedure.
For all imperial edicts to send down incense,
or for officials dispatched to perform sacrifices on behalf of the Emperor,
one day beforehand, one would bathe and change clothes,
and reside in an outer room.
The next day, the official would be dispatched.
In the 7th year, a regulation was established:
four days before a grand sacrifice,
the Tàicháng Qīng would go to the Tiānxià Shénqí Tán to perform a ceremonial announcement,
and the Zhōngshū Céngxiàng would go to the Jīngshī Chénghuáng Miào to issue a dispatch.
The next day,
the Emperor would go to the Rénzǔ Miào to request co-worship.
In the 21st year, a regulation was established:
two days before fasting and purification,
officials of the Tàicháng Sì would lodge at their yámen.
The next day,
they would memorialize to request the commencement of fasting.
The day after that,
the bronze figure would be presented,
and an imperial edict would be issued instructing all civil and military officials to fast and purify themselves.
On this day,
officials of the Lǐbù and Tàicháng Sì would issue a proclamation to the Chénghuáng god,
requesting all deities to be worshipped throughout the empire,
and burn incense at their respective temples for three days.
In the 26th year, the ritual for transmitting edicts, administering oaths, and giving prohibitions was established.
Three days before any Grand Sacrifice,
all officials would proceed to the imperial palace,
following the etiquette of a Grand Court Assembly.
The official transmitting the edict would proclaim,
"On such and such a date,
a sacrifice will be performed at such and such a place.
You, civil and military officials,
starting from such and such a day,
shall observe a three-day fast.
You must be reverent and cautious."
After the edict was transmitted,
four prostrations were made,
and the completion of the ritual was reported.
In the 7th year of Xuāndé, during the Grand Sacrifice to the Southern Suburbs,
the emperor resided in the fasting palace.
He ordered that any palace eunuchs or attendants who drank alcohol, ate meat, entered the altar, or spat on the ground
should all be punished.
Those in the Sīlǐ Jiān who tolerated such behavior would receive the same punishment.
On the day of fasting,
the imperial censors would inspect each official at their fasting quarters.
This was also enforced in Nánjīng,
where all observed the fast in the same manner.
In the 5th year of Hóngzhì,
Lǐ Suì, a junior minister of the Hónglú Temple, stated,
"Officials performing sub-sacrifices and accompanying sacrifices
are borrowing rooms and beds from Daoist priests, leading to a mix of noble and common,
which is inconvenient for summons.
I request
that fasting rooms be built
in the vacant land at the altar site,
following the style of the audience chambers at Tiānshòu Shān."
This was granted.
In the 9th year of Jiājìng, it was stipulated that three days prior,
the emperor would proceed to the Fèngtiān Diàn,
and all officials, in court attire, would listen to the oath and prohibitions.
In the 11th month of the 4th year of Wànlì,
the Board of Rites reported that the winter solstice sacrifice to Heaven was on the 23rd,
the memorial of sacrifice should be presented on the 18th,
and all officials should receive the oath and prohibitions on the 19th.
On that day,
it was the empress dowager's birthday,
and officials should wear auspicious attire to offer congratulations.
Since two rituals coincided on the same day,
with different dress codes,
they requested that both the memorial of sacrifice and the oath/prohibitions be moved to the day before.
The emperor ordered that the memorial of sacrifice and the oath/prohibitions proceed as before,
and the congratulatory ceremony be held on the 18th.
Dispatching Officials for Sacrifices
In the 26th year of Hóngwǔ, the ritual for transmitting edicts and specially dispatching officials was established.
On that day,
the emperor would ascend the throne as per normal ritual,
and all officials would make one prostration.
After the ritual,
the sacrificing official would proceed to the prostration position and make four prostrations.
The official transmitting the edict would come out from before the emperor and proclaim the edict.
For example, when sacrificing to Kǒngzǐ,
it would say:
"On such and such a date,
a sacrifice is made to the Former Teacher Kǒngzǐ, Dàchéng Zhìshèng Wénxuān Wáng.
I command you, official, to perform the rites."
When sacrificing to successive emperors,
it would say:
"On such and such a date,
a sacrifice is made to the Former Sages, successive emperors.
I command you, official, to perform the rites."
They would prostrate themselves,
rise,
make four prostrations,
and then depart after the ritual.
The ritual for dispatching officials to present incense.
Early morning, one day before the sacrifice,
the emperor, in a leather cap and court robe,
would ascend the Fèngtiān Diàn.
The incense bearer would hand the incense to the sacrificing official.
The sacrificing official would hold it and descend from the central steps, proceeding along the central path.
Upon reaching outside the Wǔ Mén,
the incense would be placed inside a dragon palanquin.
The honor guard and musicians
would escort it to the sacrificial site.
Later, it was stipulated that on the day of the sacrifice,
the presentation of incense would follow the usual ritual,
with strict readiness.
After the sacrificing official completed the sacrifice and reported back,
the restrictions would be lifted, and they would return to the palace.
In the 9th year of Jiājìng, it was stipulated that officials dispatched for grand sacrifices
would not partake in the "blessing wine" ceremony.
Sub-sacrifices and Accompanying Sacrifices
For all officials performing sub-sacrifices,
the Tàicháng Temple would request an imperial decree in advance.
In the 7th year of Hóngwǔ,
Tàizǔ said to Scholar Zhān Tóng,
"During grand sacrifices,
performing sub-sacrifices only at the final offering
is improper."
Zhān Tóng then discussed it with Scholar Sòng Lián and reported to the emperor,
that as soon as the initial offering and presentation of jade and silk were almost complete,
the sub-sacrificing officials should immediately perform their initial offering.
The secondary and final offerings would follow the same pattern.
In the 9th year of Jiājìng, when the four suburban altars were completed,
the emperor instructed the Tàicháng Temple, saying,
"For grand sacrifices,
sub-sacrificing officials must be designated in advance
so they can practice the rituals."
Therefore, Grand Secretaries like Zhāng Cōng were used for the altars of Dàmíng, Yèmíng, Xīngchén, and Fēngyún Léiyǔ.
According to the old system,
twenty-four civil and military ministers and close attendants were used for sub-sacrifices.
Now, it was set at four people.
Officials of the judicial departments were still excluded, following the old custom.
For all accompanying sacrifices,
in the 4th year of Hóngwǔ,
the Tàicháng Temple, citing the rites of Zhōu and the system of Táng,
proposed using military officials of the fourth rank and civil officials of the fifth rank or higher.
Those who were old, sick, had skin diseases, were crippled, bereaved, or had bodily infirmities were excluded.
This was followed.
Later, it was stipulated that for suburban sacrifices,
all supervising secretaries of the Six Offices would participate in accompanying sacrifices,
but not in other sacrifices.
It was also stipulated that for all Northern and Southern Suburban sacrifices,
beforehand, accompanying officials and service personnel would be bestowed with plain robes of coarse cloth,
and musicians and dancers would each be given new clothes.
A system of ivory tablets for accompanying officials entering the altar was established.
Whenever the Son of Heaven personally performed a sacrifice,
they would wear these to enter.
There were two types:
round ones for sacrificing officials,
and square ones for service personnel.
Both were stored in the imperial treasury.
They would be issued for sacrifices,
and those without them were not allowed to enter the altar.
In the 29th year of Hóngwǔ, when sacrifices to mountains, rivers, and all deities were first performed,
ranked officials wore sacrificial robes,
while unranked officials wore public service robes.
In the 29th year of Hóngwǔ, following the suggestion of ritual ministers,
unranked officials,
for all sacrifices, would wear sacrificial robes,
the same as those of the ninth rank.

Suburban Sacrifice Paired Deities.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ,
sacrifices were first offered at the southern suburb.
The officials discussed paired sacrifices.
Tàizǔ humbly refused,
personally composing a proclamation to the Tàimiào stating:
"Those who have possessed the realm throughout history
have all paired their ancestors with Heaven.
I alone dare not,
because my achievements are not yet complete,
and my governance has deficiencies.
Last year, Heaven sent a warning,
with sounds in the southeast,
thunder and fire burning boats and striking the eaves of the hall.
Morning and evening, I am fearful,
afraid that I cannot uphold the virtue of Shàngdì who cherishes life.
Therefore, I dare not presumptuously offer my ancestor to be paired.
Only the ancestral spirit communicates with Heaven.
If Shàngdì questions,
I wish that what I have done be reported before the Emperor,
good and evil without concealment.
After the southern suburban sacrifice is completed,
I will lead all officials reverently to the ancestral temple,
to announce the completion of the great ritual,
and together share the blessings bestowed by Shàngdì."
The following year, on the summer solstice, when the Fāngqiū was to be sacrificed to,
the officials again requested it.
Tàizǔ firmly refused to approve.
They pressed their request.
He then said,
"Wait until Qìngyáng is pacified,
then we will discuss it."
In the eighth month,
Qìngyáng was pacified.
In the eleventh month, on the winter solstice,
the officials again pressed their request.
Thereupon, Huángkǎo Rénzǔ Chún Huángdì was enshrined with Heaven at the Yuánqiū.
The following year, the Fāngqiū sacrifice
was conducted similarly.
In the first year of Jiànwén, Tàizǔ was enshrined instead.
Upon the change of the era name to Hóngxī,
an imperial edict stated:
"Tàizǔ received the mandate from Heaven,
inaugurating the imperial enterprise.
Tàizōng revitalized the imperial ancestral temple and altars of state,
establishing peace again throughout the realm.
Their sacred virtues and divine achievements
are equally paired with Heaven and Earth.
The *Yì* says,
'Offer to Shàngdì,
pairing with ancestral spirits.'
I revere my ancestors
and will forever maintain this single mind.
On the fifteenth day of the first month, during the great sacrifice to the spirits of Heaven and Earth,
Huángzǔ and Huángkǎo will be enshrined as paired deities."
Thus, before the suburban sacrifices, a proclamation was made to the Tàimiào and the altars of spirits,
requesting that Tàizǔ and Tàizōng both be paired.
In the ninth year of Jiājìng,
Gěishìzhōng Xià Yán submitted a memorial, stating:
"Both Tàizǔ and Tàizōng are honored as consorts,
with father and son arrayed together.
Examining the principles of the classics,
this cannot but raise doubts.
Your servant believes that the people of Zhōu worshipped Hòujì in the suburb sacrifice to consort with Heaven,
and Tàizǔ is fully worthy of this.
They worshipped Wénwáng in the Míngtáng to consort with Shàngdì,
and Tàizōng is fully worthy of this."
The ritual officials convened a discussion,
believing that the two ancestors had been worshipped as consorts
for over a hundred years,
and it was not appropriate to lightly change it suddenly.
The Emperor issued an edict,
wishing to offer Tàizǔ as consort in the southern and northern suburbs on the winter and summer solstice days,
and to offer Tàizōng as consort with Shàngdì in the Dàsìdiàn at the beginning of the year.
Thereupon, Grand Secretaries Zhāng Cōng, Zhái Luán, and others stated
that the distribution of the two ancestors
was not in accord with righteousness.
Furthermore, they presented the edict and temple prayers written by Rénzōng.
The Emperor again ordered a collective discussion in the Dōnggé.
All believed:
"In the worship at the Tàimiào,
the successive emperors are arranged facing each other according to their generation,
so there is no objection to their being arrayed together.
Moreover, Tàizǔ and Tàizōng
both enjoyed great merits and virtues.
The Yuánqiú and Dàsìdiàn are both places of worship,
and both are considered Heaven.
Therefore, when worshipping the ancestor who consorts with Heaven,
not one should be omitted.
Your servants privately propose that in the southern and northern suburbs and the Dàsìdiàn,
in every sacrifice, both ancestors should be honored as consorts."
The Emperor ultimately considered the joint consortion to be against ritual,
and instructed the Grand Secretaries to study it further.
Cōng and others stated:
"The Rites say: 'When it is established,
no one dares abolish it.'
All sacrifices are like this,
let alone the grand ceremony of ancestral consortion?
Moreover, in ancient times, the suburb sacrifice and the Míngtáng were in different locations,
hence they could be distributed.
Now the Yuánqiú and Dàsìdiàn are on the same ground as the southern suburb.
If the winter solstice ceremony is held in the bào and Tàizōng is not present,
and the early spring ceremony is held in the qí and Tàizǔ is not present,
our hearts are truly uneasy."
The Emperor replied again:
"All things originate from Heaven,
and humans originate from their ancestors.
Heaven is but one Heaven,
and ancestors are also but one ancestor.
Therefore, in the great sacrifice to Heaven,
only Gāohuángdì should be honored as consort.
Are Wénhuángdì's merits and virtues
not worthy of consorting with Heaven?
But the establishment of the heavenly mandate
was originally initiated by Gāohuángdì.
For example, in the royal enterprise of Zhōu,
King Wǔ indeed accomplished it,
but Hòujì alone consorted with Heaven,
and Wénwáng alone consorted with Shàngdì.
At that time, no one heard of disputes over merits and virtues."
Consequently, he ordered the discussion to be shelved.
Shortly after, Xià Yán again submitted a memorial, stating:
"The suburb sacrifices of Yú, Xià, Yīn, and Zhōu
only had one ancestor as consort.
Later Confucians forced interpretations,
dividing the suburban altars into two,
and misinterpreted the meaning of 'consorting with the deceased father' in the Dàyì and 'revering the father' in the Xiàojīng.
This led to the Tang and Song dynasties changing ancient practices,
resulting in two ancestors being jointly honored,
and three emperors being jointly consorted.
We hope you will make a definitive decision from your imperial heart,
following the previous edict."
The Emperor replied:
"The ritual officials previously cited that the Tàimiào does not object to being in one hall.
However, worshipping the Emperor and honoring ancestors are different.
This argument is irrelevant."
He still ordered further discussion.
Thereupon, the ritual officials again submitted their proposal:
"Although the southern and northern suburbs are called ancestral institutions,
they are in fact a new creation today.
We request to follow your sacred edict,
and offer Tàizǔ alone as consort in both.
As for the Dàsìdiàn, it was established by Tàizǔ.
Now, if he is not allowed to receive sacrificial offerings there,
we fear that Tàizōng might not be at ease.
It is appropriate to continue offering both ancestors as consorts."
This proposal was then followed.
(Jiaosi Yizhu)
In the winter solstice of Hóngwǔ First Year (1368),
the Emperor sacrificed to Hàotiān Shàngdì at the Huánqiū.
Prior to this,
the Emperor observed scattered fasting for four days,
and strict fasting for three days.
Two days before the sacrifice,
the Emperor, wearing the Tōngtiān Guān and scarlet gauze robes, inspected the sacrificial animals and vessels.
The next day,
the officials in charge arranged the settings.
On the day of the sacrifice,
in the early morning, the imperial carriage arrived at the Dàcì.
The Tàicháng Qīng announced the "Zhōngyán" (middle solemnity),
and the Emperor put on the Gǔnmiǎn (imperial ceremonial robes and crown).
The "Wàibàn" (outer preparations) was announced,
and the Emperor entered and took his position.
The Zhànlǐ (master of ceremonies) chanted "Yíngshén" (welcoming the deities).
The Xiélǜ Láng raised his banner and played the Zhōnghé music.
The Zhànlǐ chanted "Fánchái" (burning wood).
The Jiāoshè Lìng ascended to the altar and offered incense,
burning a whole calf on the Liáotán.
The Zhànlǐ chanted "Qǐng Xínglǐ" (requesting to proceed with the ritual).
The Tàicháng Qīng reported, "The officials have respectfully prepared everything,
please proceed with the rites."
The Emperor bowed twice.
The Huáng Tàizǐ and all officials present also bowed twice.
The Zhànlǐ chanted "Diànyùbó" (presenting jade and silk).
The Emperor proceeded to the washing station.
The Tàicháng Qīng praised, saying:
"Having fasted and abstained in the preceding days,
this morning we present the sacrifice.
By increasing its purity,
we face the divine spirits."
The Emperor inserted his guī-tablet into his belt,
washed his hands,
and wiped them dry.
He removed the guī-tablet,
and ascended the altar.
The Tàicháng Qīng praised, saying:
"The divine spirits are above,
let us be solemn and dignified."
He ascended from the Wǔbì (south steps).
The Xiélǜ Láng raised his banner and played the Sùhé music.
The Emperor proceeded to the divine seat of Hàotiān Shàngdì, knelt,
inserted his guī-tablet,
offered incense three times,
presented jade and silk,
removed his guī-tablet,
bowed twice, and returned to his position.
The Zhànlǐ chanted "Jìnzǔ" (presenting the sacrificial food).
The Xiélǜ Láng raised his banner and played the Nínghé music.
The Emperor proceeded to the divine seat,
inserted his guī-tablet,
presented the sacrificial food,
removed his guī-tablet,
and returned to his position.
The Zhànlǐ chanted "Xíng Chūxiànlǐ" (performing the First Offering ritual).
The Emperor proceeded to the wine-washing station,
inserted his guī-tablet,
washed the wine cup,
wiped the wine cup,
handed the cup to the attendant,
and removed his guī-tablet.
He proceeded to the wine vessel,
inserted his guī-tablet,
held the cup,
received the fànqí (clear wine),
handed the cup to the attendant,
and removed his guī-tablet.
The Xiélǜ Láng raised his banner and played the Shòuhé music and performed the Wǔgōng dance.
The Emperor proceeded to the divine seat, knelt,
inserted his guī-tablet,
offered incense,
poured sacrificial wine,
presented the wine cup,
and removed his guī-tablet.
The Dúzhù Guān held the prayer tablet and knelt to read it.
After reading, the Emperor prostrated himself,
rose,
bowed twice,
and returned to his position.
For the Second Offering,
lǐqí (sweet wine) was poured,
and the Yuhe music and Wéndé dance were performed.
For the Final Offering,
àngqí (turbid wine) was poured,
and the Xīhé music and Wéndé dance were performed.
The ceremonies were the same as the First Offering,
but without reading the prayer tablet.
The Zhànlǐ chanted "Yǐnfú Shòuzò" (drinking the blessed wine and receiving the blessed meat).
The Emperor ascended the altar,
arrived at the Yǐnfú position,
bowed twice,
knelt,
and inserted his guī-tablet.
The Fèngjué Guān poured the blessed wine and knelt to present it.
The Tàicháng Qīng praised, saying:
"This wine and meat,
given by the deities,
bestows blessings and good fortune,
which all the myriad people share."
The Emperor received the cup,
offered a libation of wine,
drank the blessed wine,
and placed the cup on the diàn (stand).
The Fèngzò Guān presented the blessed meat while kneeling.
The Emperor received the meat,
handed it to the attendant,
removed his guī-tablet,
prostrated himself,
rose,
bowed twice,
and returned to his position.
The Huáng Tàizǐ and all officials present below him
all bowed twice.
The Zhànlǐ chanted "Chèdòu" (removing the sacrificial vessels).
The Xiélǜ Láng raised his banner and played the Yōnghé music.
The Zhǎngjì Guān removed the sacrificial vessels.
The Zhànlǐ chanted "Sòngshén" (sending off the deities).
The Xiélǜ Láng raised his banner and played the Ānhé music.
The Emperor bowed twice.
The Huáng Tàizǐ and all officials present below him also bowed twice.
The Zhànlǐ chanted for the Dúzhù Guān to present the prayer tablet,
the Fèngbì Guān to present the silk,
and the Zhǎngjì Guān to take the food and wine cups.
Each proceeded to the liáo (burning pit) location.
The "Wàngliáo" (gazing at the burning) was chanted.
The Emperor arrived at the Wàngliáo position.
When half of the offerings had been burned,
the Tàicháng Qīng reported that the rites were complete.
The Emperor returned to the Dàcì,
and the solemnity was lifted.
In the summer solstice of Second Year (1369),
the Emperor sacrificed to Huángdìqí at the Fāngqiū,
and the ceremony was entirely the same.
However, after welcoming the deities, the hair and blood were buried.
After the sacrifice,
the sacrificial animals, silk, prayer tablets, and food were buried,
which differed from the Jiāotiān (heavenly sacrifice).
In that winter,
Rénzǔ was enshrined to accompany Heaven at the Southern Suburb,
and the ceremony was the same as in First Year.
For presenting jade and silk, presenting sacrificial food, and the three offerings,
the Emperor always first proceeded before the divine seat of Shàngdì,
then before the divine seat of Rénzǔ,
and performed the rites similarly,
but without using jade.
In Fourth Year (1371), it was stipulated that
six days before the sacrifice,
all officials should bathe and stay in their government offices.
The next day,
they should proceed in court attire to the Dānchí of Fèngtiān Diàn,
and receive the oath and admonition.
The Chéngxiàng (Chancellor) announced the sacrificial date to all deities,
then proceeded to various temples to offer incense for three days.
The following day,
the imperial carriage proceeded to Rénzǔ Miào,
to announce the request for co-worship.
After the ceremony was complete,
the Emperor returned to the Zhāigōng (fasting palace).
In Seventh Year (1374), the elaborate procedures of "Zhōngyán," "Wàibàn," and chanting the offering of incense were removed.
