The "Shí'èr Bài Lǐ" (twelve bows ritual) was established.
In Tenth Year (1377), the system of combined sacrifice was changed.
For presenting jade and silk, presenting sacrificial food, and the three offerings,
the Emperor first proceeded before the divine seat of Shàngdì,
then Huángdìqí,
then Rénzǔ,
while all other procedures remained as before.
In Jiājìng Eighth Year (1529), the ritual of burning incense at various temples was abolished.
In Ninth Year (1530), the system of separate sacrifices was restored.
The Lǐbù (Ministry of Rites) submitted the detailed procedures for the Grand Sacrifice at the Huánqiū.
Ten days prior,
the Tàicháng Sì submitted a request to inspect the sacrificial animals.
Next, three high officials were requested to inspect the animals,
and four were to assist in the offerings.
Five days prior,
the Jǐnyī Wèi prepared the imperial carriage.
The Emperor proceeded to the sacrificial animal grounds to inspect the animals.
The day before that,
he wore ordinary clothes and made an announcement at the ancestral temple.
Four days prior,
the Emperor ascended the Fèngtiān Diàn.
The Tàicháng Sì presented the bronze effigy as was the customary rite.
The Tàicháng Bóshì requested the ancestral tablet of Tàizǔ at the Wénhuá Diàn,
awaiting the Emperor to personally fill in his imperial name before it was brought out.
Three days prior,
the Emperor donned sacrificial robes,
and with dried meat, minced meat, wine, and fruits, he proceeded to the Tàimiào
to invite Tàizǔ to be the principal deity.
The Emperor returned and changed his clothes,
then ascended the Fèngtiān Diàn,
where all officials in court attire received the solemn admonition.
Two days prior,
the Tàicháng Guānglù Qīng reported on the inspection of the sacrificial animals.
The Emperor went to the Fèngtiān Diàn to personally fill in the prayer tablet.
The day before, court was suspended.
The Jǐnyī Wèi prepared the ceremonial carriage,
and placed the imperial sedan at the Fèngtiānmén.
Wearing ordinary clothes, he made an announcement at the temple,
and rode in the imperial carriage to the Nánjiāo.
Entering through the Xītiānmén,
he dismounted the carriage outside the Zhāohēngmén.
Officials from the Lǐbù and Tàicháng guided him through the left gate
into the inner enclosure.
The Tàicháng Qīng guided him to the Huánqiū,
where he reverently inspected the altar and its positions.
Next, he went to the Shénkù to inspect the bamboo and wooden vessels,
and to the Shénchú to inspect the sacrificial animals.
After completing this, he exited through the left gate,
ascended the carriage, and proceeded to the Zhāigōng.
The assistant offering officials and accompanying sacrificial officials prostrated.
Officials from the Lǐbù and Tàicháng went to the Huángqióngyǔ
to retrieve the spirit tablet of Huángtiān Shàngdì, the ancestral tablet of Tàizǔ, and the spirit tablets of the accompanying deities,
and reverently placed them on the altar seats.
On the day of the sacrifice,
at the third drum,
the Emperor rode in his carriage from the Zhāigōng to the west of the spirit path in the outer enclosure,
then dismounted and proceeded to the grand waiting area east of the spirit path.
Officials from the Lǐbù and Tàicháng Sì who had carried the spirit tablets reported their completion,
and withdrew.
All officials lined up on the east and west sides of the spirit path to await.
The Emperor emerged in sacrificial robes.
The guiding official led him through the left Língxīngmén into the interior.
The chanters and guiding officials led him to the inner enclosure.
The ceremonial master announced the musicians and dancers to take their positions,
and the officiating officers each performed their duties.
The Emperor arrived at the imperial prostration position.
From the burning of firewood and welcoming of the spirits to the completion of the rites,
all rituals were conducted as before.
He went to the grand waiting area to change clothes.
Officials from the Lǐbù and Tàicháng reverently placed the spirit tablets in the Huángqióngyǔ.
He returned to the Zhāigōng,
and rested briefly.
The imperial carriage returned.
After proceeding to the temple and offering veneration,
he returned to the palace.
The edict was issued as proposed.
The following year,
the rites for the Fāngzé were established.
One day prior,
the Tàicháng Qīng requested the ancestral tablet of Tàizǔ for its position,
and reverently placed it in the Huángqí Shì.
On the appointed day,
officials from the Lǐbù and Tàicháng together requested the spirit tablet of Huángdì Qí, the ancestral tablet of Tàizǔ, and the spirit tablets of the accompanying deities,
and reverently placed them on the altar seats.
After the sacrifice,
the Tàicháng reverently placed the spirit tablets and spirit plaques in the Huángqí Shì,
and reverently returned the ancestral tablet to the ancestral temple chamber.
All other procedures were as per the Huánqiū rites.
In the tenth month of that year,
the Emperor was about to perform the Jìjiāo sacrifice,
and issued an edict to the Lǐbù Shàngshū Xià Yán, expressing his desire to personally perform the ritual of reverent placement.
Xià Yán then drafted the ceremonial notes and submitted them.
In advance, eleven officiating officers were selected to carry the ancestral tablets,
two high officials were selected to assist in offerings at the side halls,
the prayer text was drafted,
and dried meat, minced meat, wine, fruits, silk fabric, incense, and candles were prepared.
The day before, the ritual of announcing to the ancestral temple was performed.
The divine sedan and incense table were set up in the Fèngtiān Diàn,
two divine tables in the Tàishén Diàn,
two divine tables in the east and west side halls,
and one incense table in the center of the Dānchí.
A grand waiting area was set up outside the left gate of the Huánqiū.
At dawn that day,
the Emperor, in ordinary clothes, proceeded to the Fèngtiān Diàn
and performed one prostration and three kowtows.
The officiating officers then successively carried the ancestral tablets of Hàotiān Shàngdì, Tàizǔ Gāohuángdì, and the accompanying deities,
and reverently placed each in a sedan,
bringing them to outside the gate of the Huánqiū Tàishén Diàn.
The Emperor rode in his carriage to the Zhāohēngmén.
The ritual officials guided him to the Dānchí of the Tàishén Diàn.
The officiating officers then took the ancestral tablets from the divine sedans and carried them up to the stone seats,
reverently placing them in the shrines.
The Emperor then proceeded to the front of the incense table
and performed the three-offering rite as prescribed.
After the ritual,
he exited to the grand waiting area and took his seat.
All officials performed one prostration and three kowtows.
After completion, they returned to the palace.
The Emperor followed this,
and ordered that sacrificial robes be worn for the ritual,
and that one official from the Tàicháng Sì serve as guide,
along with four high-ranking officials from the Lǐbù.
In the winter solstice of the eleventh year,
the Shàngshū reported,
“Previously, during rites at the Nánjiāo,
the cold wind was unbearable.”
Therefore, drawing upon the ritual texts that mention the Son of Heaven establishing grand and minor waiting areas for the sacrifice to Heaven,
he requested
“to construct a small waiting area with a yellow felt imperial tent.
For every grand sacrifice,
the relevant department shall provide it.
In case of wind and snow,
it shall be set up below the Huánqiū,
where the Emperor can perform the ritual facing the altar from within the tent,
while the ascending, descending, placing, and offering rites are performed by officiating officials of the Tàicháng.”
It was ordered that this be made a regulation.
The Qígǔ
rite was not practiced in the early Míng dynasty.
During the reign of Shìzōng,
the rite of distributing offerings to the two ancestors was revised.
Due to insistent requests from various officials,
he then permitted the Qígǔ rite at the Dàsì Diàn,
with the two ancestors as principal deities.
In the tenth year of Jiājìng, on the first Xīn day of the first spring month,
the Qígǔ rite was first performed at the Dàsì Diàn.
After the ritual,
the Emperor still felt it was inappropriate in his heart,
and instructed Zhāng Cōng, saying:
“From ancient times, only one ancestor was paired with Heaven.
Now, with two ancestors paired together,
it is absolutely not to be followed by later generations.
Henceforth, for the Dàbào and Qígǔ,
only Tàizǔ shall be the principal deity.”
Soon after, he personally composed the prayer text,
revised the ceremonial notes,
changed the date to the Jīngzhé solar term,
made the rite slightly less grand than the Dàsì,
reduced the silk offerings by one-tenth,
did not set up accompanying altars,
and did not burn firewood,
establishing this as the fixed format.
On the Jīngzhé solar term of the eleventh year,
the Emperor was ill
and could not attend personally,
so he ordered Wǔdìng Hóu Guō Xūn to deputize.
The Jìshì Zhōng Yè Hóng said:
“Qígǔ and Dàbào,
though their names differ,
both are sacrifices to Heaven in the suburbs.
No ancestors ever failed to personally perform the suburban sacrifice.
During the Chénghuà and Hóngzhì eras,
if there was a reason,
it would rather be postponed until the third month.
This is because the suburban sacrifice is a grave rite
and should not be deputized by a minister.
I request that once His Imperial Majesty recovers,
another auspicious day be chosen for the ritual.”
This was not followed.
In the eighteenth year, it was changed to be performed in the Xuánjí Bǎodiàn within the inner palace,
without accompanying deities,
thus becoming a fixed practice.
In the first year of Lóngqìng,
the ritual officials stated:
“The personal sacrifice to the Xīannóng,
followed by plowing the ceremonial field, is in the spirit of the Qígǔ.
Now, with these two sacrifices both performed in spring,
it is inevitably cumbersome and frequent.
Moreover, the Xuánjí Bǎodiàn
is in a restricted area,
and for all officials to attend the sacrifice,
entry and exit are inconvenient.
It is advisable to abolish the Qígǔ
and only perform the rites at the Xīannóng Tán.”
This was adopted.
Dàyú
In the early Míng dynasty,
whenever there were droughts, floods, disasters, or extraordinary anomalies,
the emperor would either personally pray,
or make a public declaration in the palace,
or at the steps of the Fèngtiān Diàn.

Alternatively, officials would be dispatched to offer sacrifices and make announcements at the imperial ancestral temples, mausoleums, and altars of the land and grain, as well as to the mountains and rivers.
There was no fixed ceremony.
In the eighth year of Jiājìng (1529), when prayers were offered for rain in spring
and for snow in winter,
the emperor personally composed the sacrificial texts
and personally officiated at the sacrifices at the southern suburb and the Altars of Mountains and Rivers.
The next day,
sacrifices were offered at the Altars of Land and Grain.
Light-colored robes and caps were worn,
the imperial equipage was not displayed,
the imperial road was not cleared,
no co-sacrifices were set up,
and no music was played.
In the ninth year (1530),
the emperor wished to perform the Grand Yú (Rain) Ceremony on the vermilion steps of the Fèngtiān Diàn.
Xià Yán said:
"According to the Zuǒ Zhuàn, 'When the Dragon star appears, the Yú sacrifice is performed.'
This means that in the Sì month, when all things begin to flourish
and await rain to grow large,
sacrifices are made to Heaven to pray for nourishing rain for all grains.
The Yuè Lìng states: 'For the Yú sacrifice to Dì, grand music is used,
and then all counties are ordered to perform Yú sacrifices,
sacrificing to all lords, ministers, and officials who have benefited the people,
to pray for abundant harvests.'
The Tōng Diǎn says: 'In the Sì month, the five directional Dì are sacrificed to in the Yú sacrifice;
its altar is called Yú,
and the Yíng sacrifice is performed beside the southern suburb.'
Former minister Qiū Jùn also stated: 'The Son of Heaven, in addition to the suburban sacrifices to Heaven,
should establish a separate altar for praying for rain.
In later generations, this ritual was not transmitted,
and whenever there was a drought,
people would resort to heterodox practitioners for prayers,
not striving to move (Heaven) with sincerity,
but trying to coerce it with magical arts,
which is indeed a great deception.'
Qiū Jùn's intention was to select a site beside the suburb for a Yú altar,
and perform the ritual after the first month of summer.
Your servant believes that since the prayer for grain has already been performed in early spring,
if from the second to the fourth month,
the rain and sun are timely,
then the Grand Yú sacrifice
can be performed by dispatched officials.
However, if the rains are delayed,
Your Majesty should personally perform the prayers."
Thus, the Chóngyú Tán (Grand Rain Altar) was built to the east of the Tàiyuán Mén, outside the Huánqiú Tán (Circular Mound Altar),
establishing a fixed system.
In years of drought, prayers would be offered,
with Tàizǔ (Emperor Hóngwǔ) as co-sacrificed.
In the twelfth year (1533),
Xià Yán and others said:
"In ancient times, for the Grand Yú sacrifice,
the Music Master was ordered to practice grand music and the Huáng Wǔ (Imperial Dance).
This was to utilize the harmony of sounds and forms
to express the energies of Yīn and Yáng.
We request that after the three libations are completed,
and when the nine musical movements cease,
the Yúnmén dance be performed.
Furthermore, we request that Confucian ministers select lines from the 'Yún Hàn' poem
to compose a Yúnmén piece,
so that civil and military dancers can perform the dance together and sing it.
For Yúnmén,
the music of Dì Yáo,
was used by the Zhōu officials to sacrifice to the gods of Heaven,
taking the meaning that clouds come from the energy of Heaven
and rain comes from the energy of Earth.
We also request to increase the number of drum and wind instrument sections,
and train one hundred child dancers,
dressed in green and holding feathers,
to circle the altar singing and dancing to the Yúnmén tune,
with nine movements in total."
Consequently, they presented the ceremony,
modeled after the Prayer for Grain ceremony.
They further stated:
"The Grand Yú is a sacrifice to Heaven to pray for rain;
whenever there is a severe drought,
the Ministry of Rites shall request its performance in late spring."
The emperor agreed to their proposal.
In the seventeenth year (1538), he personally prayed at the altar,
wearing green robes,
using one ox,
and offering cooked food.
Grand Feast Ceremony
In the early Míng dynasty, there was no Míngtáng (Bright Hall) system.
In the sixth month of the seventeenth year of Jiājìng (1538),
Fēng Fāng, a retired assistant prefect of Yángzhōu Prefecture, submitted a memorial stating:
"There is no greater filial piety than honoring one's father,
and no greater way to honor one's father than to make him co-sacrificed with Heaven.
We request to restore the ancient rites
and build a Míngtáng.
We further request to elevate the temple name of the deceased Imperial Father, Xiàn Huángdì, to include 'Zōng' (ancestor),
so he may be co-sacrificed with Shàngdì."
This was sent to the Ministry of Rites for discussion.
Minister Yán Sōng and others said: "In ancient times, Fúxī and Shénnóng first sacrificed to Shàngdì,
or established the Míngtáng.
Thereafter, the Xià dynasty had its Shìshì (Ancestral Chamber),
the Yīn people had their Chóngwū (Double-roofed Building),
and the Zhōu people established the Míngtáng system,
which was
more detailed than that of Xià and Yīn.
For the sagely kings served Heaven
as a son serves his father,
with reverence in status and intimacy in affection.
Therefore, a system of annual sacrificial rites was established:
the Winter Solstice at the
Huánqiú,
the Prayer for Grain in early spring,
the Yú Altar in early summer,
and the Míngtáng in late autumn,
all of which were to show reverence.
At the Míngtáng, the emperor offered a grand feast,
which was also to show intimacy.
Now,
as a new system is being created,
ancient methods are difficult to ascertain;
the essential point is to follow the intent of the former kings.
The Míngtáng and Huánqiú
are both for serving Heaven.
The current Dàsì Diàn (Grand Sacrifice Hall) is north of the Huánqiú,
southeast of the Forbidden City,
which perfectly corresponds to the ancient orientation.
Therefore, the autumn feast at the Míngtáng
should appropriately be performed at the Dàsì Diàn.
Regarding the rite of co-sacrifice,
Zhōu Gōng (Duke of Zhou) in ancient times honored Wén Wáng with ancestral sacrifices at the Míngtáng.
The Shī Zhuàn (Commentary on the Book of Odes) states that just as things are formed by Dì,
so too are humans formed by their fathers.
Therefore, in late autumn, Dì is sacrificed to at the Míngtáng,
and the father is co-sacrificed with him,
taking the time when things are accomplished.
During the Míngtáng feast of Hàn Xiàowǔ (Emperor Wu of Han),
Jǐng Dì was co-sacrificed;
Xiàozhāng (Emperor Zhang) co-sacrificed
Guāngwǔ (Emperor Guangwu);
Táng Zhōngzōng co-sacrificed Gāozōng;
Mínghuáng (Emperor Xuanzong) co-sacrificed Ruìzōng;
Dàizōng co-sacrificed Sùzōng;
Sòng Zhēnzōng co-sacrificed Tàizōng;
Rénzōng co-sacrificed Zhēn
zōng;
Yīngzōng co-sacrificed Rénzōng.
These were all successive co-sacrifices from generation to generation;
this emphasized kinship.
Sòng Qián Gōngfǔ said:
'For the suburban sacrifice,
the founding
ancestor who had the achievements of a sage is co-sacrificed.
For the Míngtáng sacrifice,
the succeeding ruler who possessed the virtues of a sage is co-sacrificed.'
At that time, Sīmǎ Guāng
and Sūn Biàn debated this in court,
while the great scholars Chéng and Zhū advocated it below.
This emphasized the merits and virtues of ancestors.
Now that the ancient Míngtáng Grand Feast
system is being restored,
the Dì to be co-sacrificed
can only be decided by these two theories.
If based on merit and virtue,
then Tàizōng (Emperor Yǒnglè) rebuilt the country,
his merits matching those of Tàizǔ (Emperor Hóngwǔ),
so he should be co-sacrificed
with Tàizōng.
If based on kinship,
then Xiàn Huángdì (Emperor Xiàn),
from whom Your Majesty originates,
Your Majesty's merits and virtues
are precisely the merits and virtues of the Imperial Father,
so he should be co-sacrificed with
Xiàn Huángdì.
As for the proposal to add 'Zōng' to the title,
your servants dare not make arbitrary recommendations."
The emperor issued an edict:
"The Grand Autumn Sacrificial Rite at the Míngtáng
shall be performed at the Fèngtiān Diàn.
Regarding the co-sacrificed Dì, a unified theory must be sought.
Why should the Imperial Father not be given the title 'Zōng'?
Reconvene and report."
Thereupon, Táng Zhòu, an Assistant Minister of the Ministry of Revenue, submitted a memorial stating: "Among the rites of the Three Dynasties,
none were as complete as those of Zhōu.
The Xiàojīng (Classic of Filial Piety) says:
'Sacrifice to Hòujì in the suburbs to make him co-sacrificed with Heaven,
and offer ancestral sacrifices to Wén Wáng at the Míngtáng to make him co-sacrificed with Shàngdì.'
It
also says:
'There is no greater way to honor one's father than to make him co-sacrificed with Heaven,'
referring to Zhōu Gōng.
Commentators say that Zhōu Gōng possessed the virtues of a sage,
created rites and music,
and Wén Wáng was just
His father,
therefore, was cited to prove the filial piety of the Sage,
and it was merely an answer to Zēngzǐ’s question.
It does not mean that those who possess the empire
must all have their fathers match Heaven
to be considered filial.
Otherwise,
when Duke of Zhōu (Zhōu Gōng) assisted King Chéng in ascending the throne,
the rites were probably established for King Chéng,
and for Duke of Zhōu, it was the "strict father,"
but for King Chéng, it would be the "strict ancestor."
However, after Duke of Zhōu returned governance,
we have not heard of King Chéng, on account of the "strict father,"
abolishing the sacrifice of King Wén matching Heaven
and transferring it to King Wǔ.
Later generations who sacrificed in the Míngtáng
all had their fathers match,
which is a misinterpretation of the meaning of the Classic of Filial Piety (Xiàojīng)
and a violation of the rites of the former kings.
Once, someone asked Zhū Xī, saying:
“After Duke of Zhōu,
should King Wén be matched,
or should the current king’s father be matched?”
Xī said:
“Only King Wén should be matched.”
He further said:
“What about the successors of Zhōu?”
Xī said:
“Only ancestors with merit should be matched.
Later generations were merely confused and misled by the doctrine of the ‘strict father’.”
From this perspective,
it is clear that the matching in the Míngtáng
is not exclusively for the father.
Now, the ritual officials are unable to discern the error of the "strict father,"
nor do they cite the grandeur of Wén, Wǔ, Chéng, Kāng.
Instead, they indiscriminately quote the inadequate examples of the Hàn, Táng, and Sòng dynasties.
What can be said of this!
Nevertheless,
Fēng Fáng’s proposal regarding the Míngtáng,
though not yet to be followed,
the rite of the Míngtáng
must not be abolished.
Now, both the Southern and Northern suburbs primarily emphasize honoring the venerable,
but only with a grand offering to Dì in late autumn
can the principle of cherishing kin be fulfilled.
Since the Three Dynasties (Sān Dài),
the suburban sacrifice and the Míngtáng each had their respective Dì to match.
Tàizǔ and Tàizōng both had flourishing merits and virtues.
Compared to Zhōu,
Tàizǔ is like Hòujì,
and Tàizōng is like King Wén.
Now, both suburban sacrifices and the prayer for grain
all honor and match Tàizǔ,
but Tàizōng alone has no match,
which is a significant omission.
Therefore, the great offering ceremony in the Fèngtiān Diàn
must honor and match Tàizōng;
only then will the ritual system of our dynasty be complete.
The emperor was enraged,
and sent Zhòu to the imperial prison.
Sōng then re-convened the court officials
to first discuss the rite of matching the emperor,
stating:
“Considering the aim of completing things in late autumn,
and the text of the ‘strict father’ matching Heaven,
it is appropriate to honor and offer the Xiàn Huángdì to match Dì and partake of the meal.”
Consequently, he requested to honor the Wén Huángdì and sacrifice to him during the prayer for grain in early spring.
The emperor accepted the request for Xiàn Huáng to match Dì,
but rejected the proposal for Wén Huáng, which was not carried out.
Later, regarding the rite of conferring a dynastic temple title (chēng zōng),
he gathered civil and military ministers in the Dōng Gé to deliberate,
stating:
“The rites say: ‘
An ancestor (zǔ) has merit; a founder (zōng) has virtue.’
Commentators say: ‘Zǔ
means beginning.
Zōng
means revered.’
The commentary to the Book of Hàn (Hàn Shū) says: ‘The term zǔ refers to the beginning,
meaning the beginning of receiving the mandate.
The term zōng refers to the revered,
meaning having virtue worthy of reverence.’
The Classic of Filial Piety says: ‘One sacrifices to King Wén in the Míngtáng,
to match Shàngdì.’
Wáng Sù’s commentary says: ‘For Duke of Zhōu towards King Wén,
it was to revere and sacrifice to him.’
This is the explanation of zōng as revered.
In ancient times,
the Son of Heaven had seven ancestral temples (qī miào).
Liú Xīn said: ‘Seven is the proper rule,
but if there is merit and virtue, then one is honored as zōng;
one cannot pre-set a number.
If zōng is not within the number,
zōng is a change.’
Zhū Xī also considered Xīn’s view to be correct.
Chén Shì’s Book of Rites (Chén Shì Lǐ Shū) says: ‘Father in the zhāo position and son in the mù position,
and having a fixed number,
is ritual.
Ancestor’s merit and founder’s virtue,
and having no fixed rule,
is righteousness.’
This is the theory that zōng has no number,
and rites arise from righteousness.
Now, citing ancient righteousness
and inferring human sentiment,
the late emperor’s (Huáng Kǎo) supreme virtue is widely known,
secretly assisting Heaven.
It is permissible to honor him as zōng for his virtue.
His sacred sons and divine grandsons
pass down boundless succession;
all are propagated by Huáng Kǎo alone.
It is also permissible to honor him as zōng for his lineage.
It is fitting to add the title zōng to Huáng Kǎo,
to match Dì in the Míngtáng,
and forever be a temple of enduring virtue.”
The emperor, because the memorial did not mention incorporating into the ancestral temple (fù miào),
kept it within the palace and did not issue it.
Then, he fabricated a text of questions and answers from his officials,
writing "Questions on the Míngtáng" (Míngtáng Huòwèn),
to show to his assisting ministers.
The general idea was:
“Wén Huáng is a distant ancestor,
and does not conform to the principle of a ‘strict father.’
It is proper to match with the father.
Although there is no fixed theory for conferring a dynastic temple title (chēng zōng),
revering one’s parents and honoring one’s superiors
is what righteousness dictates.
Since he is given the title zōng,
he should be incorporated into the ancestral temple.
How can there be a rite where the four closest kin are not complete in the Grand Ancestral Temple (Tài Miào)?”
Since the emperor rejected the correct deliberations
and favored his private kin,
and thinking in his heart that Tàizōng would never have a matching sacrifice,
and having no way to apologize to his court officials,
he then decided that Xiàn Huáng would match Dì and receive the title zōng,
and changed Tàizōng’s title to Chéngzǔ.
At that time, the Míngtáng had not yet been built.
As late autumn was pressing,
he then performed a grand offering to Shàngdì in the Xuánjí Bǎodiàn,
honoring Ruìzōng Xiàn Huángdì as the match.
The hall was in the northwest corner (qián yú) on the right side of the palace,
formerly named Qīn'ān Diàn.
After the ceremony was completed,
the Ministry of Rites requested the emperor to ascend the hall,
and all officials offered congratulations,
following the ceremony of celebrating the completion of suburban sacrifices.
The emperor, because it was the first grand offering,
ordered a banquet for all officials in the Jǐnshēn Diàn.
However, due to a foot ailment, he did not preside over the hall,
and ordered the officials not to perform the congratulatory rites.
The ritual officials reported this,
and the banquet was also canceled,
and the Guānglù Sì was ordered to distribute the provisions.
In the twenty-first year, an imperial edict was issued to the Ministry of Rites:
“The grand offering in the Míngtáng in late autumn,
a ritual典 from the prosperous Zhōu,
runs concurrently with the suburban sacrifices.
Previously, as the location for the offering was not yet determined,
a special sacrifice was held in the Xuánjí Bǎodiàn,
which I sincerely felt was incomplete.
The old hall in the Southern Suburb,
originally for major sacrifices,
was ordered by the relevant authorities to be demolished last year.
I personally designed the structure,
erected it as a hall,
and respectfully named it Tàixiǎng,
to manifest the intention of reverently serving Shàngdì.”
Thus, it was decided that a grand offering to Shàngdì would be held annually in autumn,
with the late emperor Ruìzōng honored as the match.
The ceremony would follow that of the Southern Suburb,
and the arrangements would be like the prayer for grain.
The following year,
the Minister of Rites, Fèi Cǎi, with the construction of the Grand Offering Hall nearing completion,
requested the emperor to name the hall’s gate.
The gate was named Dàxiǎng,
and the hall was named Huángqián.
When the hall was completed,
the grand offering continued to be held in the Xuánjí Bǎodiàn,
with officials regularly sent to perform the rites.
In the first year of Lóngqìng,
the ritual officials stated:
“The grand offering ritual of our dynasty,
initiated by Huáng Kǎo,
was to posthumously honor Ruìzōng,
to manifest the filial piety of the ‘strict father’ matching Heaven.
From the perspective of His Majesty,
Ruìzōng is the imperial ancestor,
not conforming to the meaning of the Zhōu people sacrificing to King Wén in the Míngtáng.”
Thereupon, the emperor acceded to their request,
abolished the grand offering ritual,
and ordered the Xuánjí Bǎodiàn to be renamed Qīn'ān Diàn again.
On auspicious days, bowing to Heaven.
At the beginning of the Jiājìng reign,
following the old rituals of previous dynasties,
the Heaven-Worshiping Rite was performed daily within the palace.
Later, deeming it to be disrespectful,
it was abolished.
On New Year's Day (Zhèngdàn), Winter Solstice (Dōngzhì), and the Emperor's Birthday (Shèngdàn Jié),
the rites were performed on the imperial steps (dānbì) of the Fèngtiān Diàn.
After the suburban sacrifices (jiāosì) were established,
the Winter Solstice rite was then abolished.
Only on New Year's Day and the Emperor's Birthday were rites performed at the Xuánjí Bǎodiàn.
On New Year's Day in the first year of the Lóngqìng reign,
it was decreed that Heaven be worshiped in the palace,
without external functionaries being used,
and sacrificial offerings were also not procured from the Tàicháng Temple.
Collation Notes

Monograph (Zhì) Twenty-Five: Rites (Lǐ) Three (Auspicious Rites Three) - Altars of Soil and Grain (Shèjì), Sacrifices to the Sun in the Morning and Moon in the Evening (Cháorì Xīyuè), Former Agricultural Deity (Xiānnóng), Former Sericultural Deity (Xiāncán), Deity of Fertility (Gāoméi), Sacrifices for Proclamation (Jìgào), Sacrifices for Prayer and Repayment (Qíbào), Deities (Shénqí), Stars and Constellations (Xīngchén Língxīng Shòuxīng) (Sīzhōng Sīmìng Sīmín Sīlù), Grand Year Star (Tàisuì), Monthly Generals (Yuèjiāng), Wind, Clouds, Thunder, and Rain (Fēngyún Léiyǔ), Sacred Peaks, Sea Deities, Mountains, and Rivers (Yuèzhèn Hǎidú Shānchuān), City Gods (Chénghuáng)
Altars of Soil and Grain (Shèjì)
The sacrifices to Shèjì,
from the capital (Jīngshī) to the various kingdoms, prefectures (fǔ), sub-prefectures (zhōu), and counties (xiàn), all possessed them.
Those altars located southwest of the imperial city
were called Tàishèjì.
In the early Míng dynasty, the Tàishè was built to the east,
and the Tàijì to the west,
with both altars facing north.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ,
the officials of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shěng) reached a consensus:
"According to the Zhōu system,
the Junior Clan Master (Xiǎozōngbó) was in charge of establishing the divine altars of the state,
with the Shèjì to the right,
and the ancestral temple (zōngmiào) to the left.
The sacrifices to Shèjì
were performed on an open altar, not in a covered building.
Their arrangement was outside the central gate (zhōngmén)
but inside the outer gate (wàimén).
They were revered and intimately cherished,
on par with ancestors.
However, the Son of Heaven had three altars to the Soil (shè).
That established for the various surnames was called Tàishè.
That established for himself was called Wángshè.
Furthermore, the altars of the vanquished states were covered,
preserved even after the state's demise,
to show respect for the deities.
Later generations of Sons of Heaven only established the Tàishè and Tàijì.
Hàn Gāozǔ established official Tàishè and Tàijì,
with sacrifices twice a year for each.
Guāngwǔ established the Tàishèjì to the right of the Luòyáng ancestral temple,
with sacrifices three times a year: in the second month of spring and autumn, and in the twelfth month (là).
The Táng dynasty followed the Suí system,
building the Shèjì altars together to the right of the Hánguāng Mén,
with sacrifices on the Wù day of the second month of spring and autumn.
Xuánzōng elevated the Shèjì to a great sacrifice,
and ordered sacrifices to be offered in all four seasons.
The Sòng system was like that of the Eastern Hàn.
Yuán Shìzǔ built the Shèjì altars inside the Héyì Mén,
with sacrifices on the first Wù day of the second month of spring and autumn.
It is now fitting to offer sacrifices on the first Wù day of the second month of spring and autumn."
In the second month of that year,
Tàizǔ personally sacrificed to the Tàishè and Tàijì.
Shè was accompanied by Hòutǔ,
facing west.
Jì was accompanied by Hòujì,
facing east.
The Emperor wore a Píbiànfú,
inspected the sacrificial animals;
then wore a Tōngtiānguān and Jiàngshāpáo,
and performed the three libation rites.
Initially,
the Emperor ordered the Central Secretariat and Hànlín Yuàn to discuss constructing a shelter
to protect against wind and rain.
Scholar Táo Ān said:
"The Son of Heaven's Tàishè must receive wind, rain, frost, and dew.
The altars of vanquished states, however, are roofed,
as they do not receive the sun's yang.
Building a roof is not appropriate.
If wind and rain are encountered,
then an offering should be made from afar at the fasting palace (zhāigōng)."
This was followed.
In the third year,
five sacrificial halls were built north of the altar,
and further north, five bowing halls were built,
to provide shelter from wind and rain.
In the tenth year,
Tàizǔ, considering the separate sacrifices to Shèjì and the inappropriateness of the accompanying deities,
submitted the matter to the ritual officials for deliberation.
Minister Zhāng Chóu stated: "According to the Tōngdiǎn,
Zhuānxū sacrificed to Gònggōng's son, Jùlóng, as Hòutǔ.
Hòutǔ
is Shè.
Lìeshān's son, Zhù, was Jì.
Jì
is the official in charge of fields (tiánzhèng).
Táng, Yú, and Xià followed this.
This is how Shèjì began.
During a drought, Shāng Tāng moved the Shè,
replacing Zhù with Hòujì.
He wished to move Jùlóng,
but there was no one
to succeed him,
so he stopped.
However, Wáng Sù believed that Shè sacrificed to Jùlóng,
and Jì sacrificed to Hòujì,
both being human ghosts,
not earth deities.
And Chén's Lǐshū also states that Shè sacrifices to the spirits of the five soils,
and Jì sacrifices to the gods of the five grains.
Zhèng Kāngchéng also said that Shè is the general god of the five soils,
and Jì is the god of plains and lowlands.
Jùlóng had the merit of leveling water and soil,
so he accompanied Shè;
Hòujì had the merit of sowing seeds,
so he accompanied Jì.
These two theories differ.
In the Yuánshǐ reign of Hàn,
Xià Yǔ accompanied the official Shè,
and Hòujì accompanied the official Jì.
The Táng, Sòng, and Yuán dynasties again used Jùlóng to accompany Shè,
and Zhōu Qì to accompany Jì.
There has never been a fixed conclusion
regarding the system of accompanying deities.
As for the profound meaning of the separation and combination of Shèjì,
the Shū Jǐzhàogào states:
'establish the Shè in the new city,'
and Kǒng's commentary says:
'Shèjì share the same sacrificial animals.'
The Zhōulǐ
says: 'The Fēngrén is in charge of establishing the King's Shè enclosure,'
and the commentary says:
'Not mentioning Jì means that when Shè is mentioned, Jì follows it.'
Chén's Lǐshū says:
'Without soil, grain cannot grow;
without grain, the soil cannot demonstrate its life-giving effect.
Therefore, when sacrificing to Shè, Jì must also be included.'
Shāntáng Kǎosuǒ says:
and Jì is the chief of the five grains.
Jì grows from the soil,
so Shè and Jì are indeed inseparable.'
Their combined sacrifice
has clear ancient evidence.
I request that Shèjì be made into a single altar.
As for Jùlóng,
he was the son of Gōngshì (Gònggōng),
and sacrificing to him is without justification.
Shāng Tāng wished to move him but failed.
The Hàn dynasty once replaced him with Xià Yǔ,
but Xià Yǔ is now already enshrined among the imperial ancestors.
Qì (Hòujì) is also associated with Xiānnóng.
I request that Jùlóng and Qì be removed from their accompanying positions,
and that Rénzǔ Chún Huángdì be respectfully enshrined as the accompanying deity,
thus completing a grand ceremony of our dynasty."
Consequently, the altar was rebuilt to the right of the Wǔmén,
with Shèjì combined into a single altar.
Initially,
Shèjì was categorized as a middle sacrifice,
but upon Rénzǔ being enshrined as accompanying deity,
it was elevated to a great sacrifice.
Sacrifices were performed in court robes (miǎnfú),
and the rite of respectful enshrinement was carried out.
In the spring of the eleventh year,
the new ritual for sacrificing to Shèjì was implemented.
The rites of welcoming the spirits, receiving blessings, and sending off the spirits involved twelve bows in total,
the rest remaining as before.
During the Jiànwén reign,
Tàizǔ was instead enshrined as the accompanying deity.
During the Yǒnglè reign,
the Běijīng Shèjì Tán was completed,
with its system mirroring that of Nánjīng.
After Hóngxī,
Tàizǔ and Tàizōng were both enshrined as accompanying deities.
According to the old system,
on the first Dīng day, sacrifices were made to Kǒngzǐ,
and on the following first Wù day, sacrifices were made to Shèjì.
In the eighth month of the seventeenth year of Hóngzhì,
the first Dīng day was the tenth,
and the first Wù day was the first (of the month).
The ritual officials requested to sacrifice to Shèjì on the eleventh day.
Censor Jīn Hóng impeached them,
stating that this would make it a middle Wù day,
not a first Wù day.
The Ministry of Rites replied in a memorial, saying:
"In the twentieth year of Hóngwǔ, the eleventh day was once taken as the first Wù day,
so this is not a new mistake."
An imperial decree ordered adherence to the old system,
still using the first Wù day.
In the ninth year of Jiājìng, an edict was issued to the Ministry of Rites:
"Heaven and Earth are most revered,
followed by the ancestral temples,
and then the altars of the gods of soil and grain.
Now, our ancestor is enshrined with Heaven,
and also enshrined with the god of soil.
This is an error of the ritual officials.
It should be changed to follow the old system of the imperial ancestors:
Tài Shè (Grand Altar of Soil) should be paired with Jùlóng,
and Tài Jì (Grand Altar of Grain) with Hòujì."
Thereupon, the rites for the配位 (pèi wèi, paired deities) at the altars of the gods of soil and grain were corrected,
and this was announced to the Tài Miào and the altars of the gods of soil and grain.
The two paired deities were then stored in the寝廟 (qǐn miào, sleeping temple),
and the ceremony of eight prostrations was newly established.
The altar located west of the Bīnfēng Tíng in the Xīyuàn
was called Dì Shèjì (Imperial Altars of Soil and Grain).
The Dì Shè (Imperial Altar of Soil) was to the east,
and the Dì Jì (Imperial Altar of Grain) to the west,
both facing north.
Initially, it was named Xīyuàn Tǔgǔ Tán (Western Garden Altar of Soil and Grain).
In the tenth year of Jiājìng,
the emperor said, "The Tǔgǔ Tán is also Shèjì.
Why is it distinguished from the Tài Shèjì?"
Zhāng Cōng and others said:
"In ancient times, the Son of Heaven was called Wáng (King).
If we now call it Wáng Shè and Wáng Jì,
the name would be the same as the Shèjì of a princely establishment.
The divine tablet previously designated as 'Gods of the Five Soils and Grains'
is most appropriate in its meaning."
The emperor adopted the meaning of Dì Jì (Imperial Plowing Ceremony),
and changed the name to Dì Shè (Imperial Altar of Soil) and Dì Jì (Imperial Altar of Grain),
to be sacrificed on the day after the first Wù day (戊日, wù rì) of the month.
Later, it was changed to the second Wù day.
If the second Wù day was after the full moon,
then the Shàngsì (上巳, shàngsì) festival was still used.
The spring announcement and autumn report became the established system.
In the first year of Lóngqìng,
the Ministry of Rites said:
"The name Dì Shèjì
has no precedent from ancient times,
and is suspected of being redundant.
It should be abolished."
This was approved.
Zhōngdū also had a Tài Shè Tán,
built in the fourth year of Hóngwǔ.
It was constructed using soil from five directions.
Zhílì and Hénán supplied yellow earth,
Zhèjiāng, Fújiàn, Guǎngdōng, and Guǎngxī supplied red earth,
Jiāngxī, Húguǎng, and Shǎnxī supplied white earth,
Shāndōng supplied blue earth,
and Běipíng supplied black earth.
From over 1,300 prefectures and counties across the realm,
each contributed one hundred jīn of earth,
taken from famous mountains and high, dry places.
The Shèjì of kingdoms was established in the fourth year of Hóngwǔ.
In the eleventh year,
a ritual official said:
"Since the Tài Shèjì are worshipped together on the same altar,
the various prefectures, departments, and counties of the kingdoms should also use a single altar,
called 'Gods of the State Soil and State Grain,'
without paired deities."
The edict approved this.
In the ninth month of the thirteenth year, it was again established that there should be two altars with one surrounding wall, as in the original style.
In the eighteenth year, the ceremonies for the worship of Shèjì, mountains, rivers, etc., by kingdoms were established,
involving twelve prostrations.
For the Shèjì of prefectures, departments, and counties,
in the first year of Hóngwǔ, the altar system was promulgated to all commanderies and counties nationwide.
All were to be established in the northwest of their respective cities,
with the Altar of Soil on the right and the Altar of Grain on the left.
In the eleventh year,
it was established that they should be worshipped together on the same altar, like in the capital.
The chief offering official was a military officer responsible for defense,
and civil officials were the secondary and final offering officials.
In the thirteenth year,
when Líshuǐ County sacrificed to Shèjì,
beef hash was used instead of deer hash.
The Ministry of Rites said:
"According to established regulations,
if ritual items are lacking, they may be substituted with other items."
The emperor said:
"What is meant by 'lacking' refers to items not produced in that locality.
Líshuǐ does indeed have deer;
this means the local officials deliberately acted in a perfunctory manner.
The reason all officials can manage their duties and fulfill their responsibilities to the people
is because they always maintain a respectful and apprehensive heart.
If they can neglect the gods,
then what fear would they have regarding human affairs?"
He ordered them to be judged according to the law.
He then ordered the Ministry of Rites to instruct all commanderies and counties nationwide
that for all sacrifices, the ritual items must be prepared.
If they are not local products and cannot be purchased,
then their absence is permitted.
In the fourteenth year, it was ordered that all three offering officials should be civil officials,
and military officials should not participate.
For Lǐ Shè (village altars of soil),
one altar was established for every hundred households in a village,
to worship the gods of the five soils and five grains.
Worship of the Rising Sun and Setting Moon
In the third year of Hóngwǔ,
the Ministry of Rites said: In ancient times, there were six rites for worshipping the sun and moon.
The Jiāo Tè Shēng (郊特牲) says,
"At the suburban sacrifice,
a great report is made to Heaven, with the sun as the principal deity,
and the moon as its consort."
This is the first.
The Yù
Zǎo (玉藻) says,
"Worship the rising sun outside the eastern gate."
The Jì Yì (祭義) says,
"Sacrifice to the sun in the eastern suburb,
sacrifice to the moon in the western suburb."
This is the second.
The Xiǎo Zōngbó (小宗伯) says,
"Perform
the Sī Lèi (肆類) sacrifice in the four suburbs,
mark out the altar for the sun in the eastern suburb,
mark out the altar for the moon in the western suburb."
This is the third.
The Yuè Lìng (月令) for the first month of winter says
"Pray for the coming year to the Celestial Ancestors."
Celestial Ancestors
refer to the sun and moon
and the like.
This is the fourth.
The Jìn Lǐ (覲禮) says,
"Bow to the sun outside the eastern gate,
then return to worship Fāngmíng.
Perform the rite to the sun outside the southern gate,
perform the rite to the moon outside the northern gate."
This is the fifth.
"If frost, snow, wind, or rain are untimely,
then perform the Yíng (禜) sacrifice to the sun and moon."
This is the sixth.
Commentators say that worshipping them due to the suburban sacrifice
is not a principal sacrifice.
Worshipping them through the Lèi Yíng (類禜) sacrifice,
or performing rites to them when receiving feudal lords,
are not regular sacrifices.
Only worshipping the rising sun outside the eastern gate at the spring equinox,
and the setting moon outside the western gate at the autumn equinox
are
the principal and regular sacrifices.
Indeed, Heaven and Earth are most revered,
so their beginning points are used for sacrifices at the two solstices.
The sun and moon are secondary to Heaven and Earth.
At the spring equinox, the yang qi is just growing,
and at the autumn equinox, the yin qi is about to increase,
so sacrifices are made at the two equinoxes,
which captures the meaning of yin and yang.
From the Qín dynasty, eight gods were worshipped,
the sixth being the Lord of the Moon,
the seventh the Lord of the Sun.
Yōng (雍) also had temples for the sun and moon.
The Hàn dynasty sacrificed to Tàiyǐ in the suburbs,
and changed the Zhōu methods for worshipping the rising sun and setting moon.
They often sacrificed at the suburban Tàizhì (泰畤),
and at dawn, went out from the temporary palace,
bowed to the sun facing east,
bowed to the moon facing west,
and then bowed to the sun and moon below the hall, east and west.
Emperor Xuān worshipped the sun at Shénshān Cí
and
the moon at Láishān Cí.
Emperor Míng of Wèi first worshipped the rising sun in the eastern suburb
and the setting moon in the western suburb.
The Táng dynasty, on the two equinox days,
worshipped the rising sun and setting moon to the east and west of the imperial city.
The Sòng
people followed this,
elevating it to a great sacrifice.
During the Yuán dynasty, the sun and moon were secondary deities at the suburban altar.
As for worshipping the rising sun and setting moon at the two equinoxes,
it was discussed to establish this during the Huángqìng era, but not implemented.
Now, we should examine ancient records and correct the rituals of sacrifice,
establishing separate altars for their exclusive worship.
The altar for the rising sun should be built outside the eastern gate of the city,
and the altar for the setting moon should be built outside the western gate
of the city.
The rising sun should be worshipped at the spring equinox,
and the setting moon at the autumn equinox.
The stars should be included in the sacrifices at the moon altar.
This was approved.
Their sacrificial rites were the same as those for Shèjì.
In the twenty-first year,
the emperor, considering that Dàmíng and Yèmíng were already secondary deities,
abolished the sacrifices to the rising sun and setting moon.
In the ninth year of Jiājìng
the emperor said,
“When performing the grand sacrifice to Heaven, the sun is honored as the primary deity,
and the moon as its consort.
The Dàmíng Tán (Altar of Great Brightness) should be different from the Yèmíng Tán (Altar of Night Brightness).
Moreover, the sun and moon shine upon us,
their功 (contributions) are immense.
Gods like Tàisuì
receive two sacrifices a year,
but the sun, moon, and stars are merely worshipped as secondary deities in one sacrifice.
This is morally unsettling.”
Grand Secretary Zhāng Cōng also deemed it an incomplete institution.
Therefore, it was decided that the spring and autumn equinox sacrifices would continue as before,
but the Cháorì Tán (Altar for Sacrificing to the Morning Sun) would be built outside Cháoyáng Mén,
facing west;
and the Xīyuè Tán (Altar for Sacrificing to the Evening Moon) outside Fùchéng Mén,
facing east.
The altar designs would have varying degrees of grandeur to distinguish them.
For Cháorì,
one hundred *mǔ* of land would be protected for the altar;
for Xīyuè,
thirty-six *mǔ* of land would be protected for the altar.
Cháorì would have no secondary deities.
Xīyuè would share one altar with the Five Planets, the Twenty-eight Lunar Mansions, and all the stars of the heavens,
affiliated facing south.
For the spring sacrifice,
the time would be *yín* (3-5 AM),
to welcome the sunrise.
For the autumn sacrifice,
the time would be *hài* (9-11 PM),
to welcome the moonrise.
In the tenth year,
the Ministry of Rites presented the rituals for Cháorì and Xīyuè: for Cháorì, four bows when welcoming the spirits,
two bows when receiving blessings and sacrificial meat,
and four bows when sending off the spirits;
for Xīyuè, two bows for welcoming spirits, receiving blessings and sacrificial meat, and sending off spirits, in each case.
Other matters were as per the old rituals.
In the first year of Lóngqìng,
the Ministry of Rites deliberated and decided that
the emperor would personally perform sacrifices in the eastern suburbs in the *jiǎ*, *bǐng*, *wù*, *gēng*, and *rén* years,
and in the western suburbs in the *chǒu*, *chén*, *wèi*, and *xū* years.
In other years, civil officials would be dispatched to perform the substitute sacrifice at the Cháorì Tán,
and military officials at the Xīyuè Tán.
In the third year,
the Ministry of Rites presented the ritual for Cháorì,
stating:
“If the main sacrifice encounters wind and rain,
a temporary shelter should be set up in front of the altar,
and the imperial carriage will proceed to the shelter to perform the rites.
The ascending, descending, offering, and presenting of sacrifices
will all be carried out by officials from the Tàicháng Sì.”
An imperial edict said,
“Granted.”
Concerning Xiānnóng,
in the first year of Hóngwǔ, an edict was issued to court officials to hold the *jìtián* (plowing field) ceremony in the coming spring.
Thereupon, ritual officials Qián Yòngrén and others stated:
“Zhèng Xuán of Hàn said that the royal *shè* (altar of soil and grain) was in the *jìtián*.
Zhù Qīnmíng of Táng said: ‘Xiānnóng is *shè*.’
Chén Xiángdào of Sòng said: ‘*Shè* is *shè*,
Xiānnóng is Xiānnóng.
What is sacrificed at *jìtián* is Xiānnóng,
not *shè*.’
As for performing the sacrifice to Xiānnóng on the same day as personally plowing,
there is no clear text in the Rites.
Only *Zhōu Yǔ* says: ‘The Minister of Agriculture arranges the *jì* ceremony.’
And Wéi Zhāo’s commentary says: ‘Sacrificing to its deity is to pray for agriculture.’
It was in the Hàn dynasty that Xiānnóng was sacrificed on the day of the *jìtián*,
and its rites became established.
From Jìn to Táng and Sòng, this was continued without abolition.
During the Zhènghé reign,
officials were ordered to sacrifice to Xiānnóng,
and only the ritual of personal plowing was performed.
After the southern migration,
personal sacrifices were resumed.
Although Yuán deliberated on plowing the *jìtián*,
the emperor ultimately did not perform it personally.
For the sacrifice to Xiānnóng,
officials were ordered to act as substitutes.
Now it is proposed that on the day of plowing the *jìtián*,
the emperor will personally sacrifice to Xiānnóng.
After the rites,
he will personally plow the *jìtián*.
This will be done on a selected day in mid-spring.”
This was adopted.
In the second month of the second year,
the emperor built the Xiānnóng Tán in the southern suburbs,
north of the *jìtián*.
He personally performed the sacrifice,
with Hòujì as the consort deity.
The vessels and sacrificial rites were the same as those for *shèjì*.
After the sacrifice,
the *gēngjì* (plowing and offering) rite was performed.
Two sets of imperial plows and hoes,
wrapped in blue silk,
and four imperial plowing oxen,
covered in blue cloth, were used.
After the ceremony,
he returned to the great tent.
The Prefect of Yìngtiān Fǔ and the magistrates of Shàngyuán and Jiāngníng counties led commoners to complete the plowing of the field.
On this day, officials and elders were feasted and honored at the altar site.
In the second month of the tenth year, an official was dispatched to sacrifice to Xiānnóng,
and the officials of Yìngtiān Fǔ were ordered to lead farmers and elders to participate in the sacrifice.
In the twenty-first year, the ritual for sacrificing to Xiānnóng was revised;
no consort deity was set up.
During the Yǒnglè reign, an altar was built in the capital,
following the Nanjing system,
southwest of the Tàisuì Tán.
It had nine stone steps.
To the west was the burial mound,
to the east the fasting palace and imperial carriage depot,
to the northeast the divine granary,
to the southeast the Hall for Donning Robes,
and in front of the hall was the viewing area for plowing.
Six hundred *mǔ* of land were protected for the altar,
and over ninety *mǔ* were for supplying millet and presenting new produce.
Every year, on the *shàngwǔ* day of mid-spring,
the Prefect of Shùntiān Fǔ would perform the sacrifice.
Later, whenever a new emperor ascended the throne,
the *gēngjì* rite would be performed,
and the emperor would personally sacrifice.
In the first year of Hóngzhì, the *gēngjì* ritual was formalized.
Days before, all officials would observe fasting.
Officials from Shùntiān Fǔ would present plows, hoes, and various seeds,
which inner court officials would then bring out and hand over,
exiting through the left side of Wǔ Mén,
placed on a decorated carriage,
with drums and music,
and sent to the *jìtián* site.
On the appointed day,
the emperor, in a *yìshàn guān* (winged-front cap) and yellow robe,
would proceed to the Hall for Donning Robes at the altar site,
don the *gǔnmiǎn* (ceremonial robe and crown),
and sacrifice to Xiānnóng.
After completing this,
he would return,
and change back into the *yìshàn guān* and yellow robe.
The Tàicháng Qīng would guide him to the *gēngjì* position,
standing facing south.
The Sāngōng and others would take their respective places.
The Hùbù Shàngshū would kneel facing north and present the plow and hoe.
Officials from Shùntiān Fǔ would kneel facing north and present the whip.
The emperor would grasp the plow,
and complete three pushes and three returns.
The Hùbù Shàngshū would kneel and receive the plow and hoe.
Officials from Shùntiān Fǔ would kneel and receive the whip.
The Tàicháng Qīng would request the emperor to return to his position.
The Prefect would carry a blue box and sow the seeds, then cover them.
The emperor would go to the outer gate,
sit facing south,
and observe the Sāngōng performing five pushes,
and the Shàngshū and Jiǔqīng performing nine pushes.
The Tàicháng Qīng would announce that the plowing was completed.
The emperor would return to the Hall for Donning Robes,
and ascend the throne.
The Prefect, leading the magistrates of the two counties and the elders, would perform the rites.
Then ten each of superior, middle, and inferior farmers
would be introduced, holding farming tools for an audience,
and ordered to complete the plowing of the field.
All officials would perform the congratulatory ceremony,
and wine and food would be bestowed.
Officials of the third rank and above would sit east and west on the imperial steps;
those of the fourth rank and below would sit below the platform.
Elders would also be feasted and honored beside the altar.
After the banquet,
the imperial carriage would return to the palace.
Grand music and drums would play vigorously,
and each farmer would be granted one bolt of cloth.
In the tenth year of Jiājìng,
the Emperor, considering the rituals to be overly cumbersome,
ordered the Ministry of Rites to revise them.
The welcoming and sending off of the gods were limited to two bows.
Two days prior,
the Shùntiān Fǔyǐn would place ploughs, hoes, and various seeds in a decorated palanquin,
and proceed to the plowing grounds.
All officials' congratulations were also abolished.
Later, it was further debated to construct a "plough-root carriage" (gēnggēn chē) to carry the ploughs and hoes.
After the Fǔyǐn presented them on the day of the sacrifice,
the ploughs and hoes, carried inside the carriage, would precede the imperial carriage (yùlù).
As for the Emperor observing the plowing from the Wǔmén Gate,
the ground was low and inconvenient,
so it was proposed to build an observation platform (guāngēng tái).
An imperial edict approved all these proposals.
Later, it was further ordered to reclaim idle land in the Xīyuàn (Western Garden) for cultivation.
A hall was built and named Wúyì (Carefree),
and pavilions were named Bīnfēng (Airs of Bīn),
Shěnggēng (Inspecting Plowing),
and Shěngliǎn (Inspecting Harvesting).
A granary was named Yù (Abundant).
The Ministry of Rites submitted the numbers for the provision of sacrificial grains (zīshèng) for the suburban altars and ancestral temples,
and then stated:
"The Emperor’s three pushes at the plowing field (jìtián) in the Southern Suburb,
where high officials and ministers each exert their efforts,
are more significant than those in the Xīyuàn.
Although the Xīyuàn is overseen by agricultural officials,
the Emperor frequently inspects the plowing and harvesting there,
making it more diligent than the plowing field.
We request that the produce from the plowing field
be stored in the Yuánlǐn Shéncāng (Round Granary for Gods) in the Southern Suburb,
to supply the sacrifices at the Yuánhuán Qiū (Altar of Heaven), Qígǔ (Prayer for Grain), Xiānnóng (First Farmer), Shénqítán (Altar of Heaven and Earth), Chánglíng and other imperial tombs,
and for the successive emperors and myriad gods.
The produce from the Xīyuàn
should be stored in the Yùcāng (Abundant Granary),

to supply the sacrifices at Fāngzé (Altar of Earth), Cháorì (Morning Sun), Xīyuè (Evening Moon), Tàimiào (Imperial Ancestral Temple), Shìmiào (Family Ancestral Temple), Tàishèjì (Grand Altars of Land and Grain), Dìshèjì (Imperial Altars of Land and Grain), Dìxiá (Great Joint Sacrifice), Xiāncán (First Sericulturalist), and to Master Kǒngzǐ (Confucius)."
This was approved.
In the sixteenth year, an edict stated that whenever the Emperor personally plowed,
the Hùbù Shàngshū (Minister of Revenue) should first sacrifice to Xiānnóng.
When the Emperor arrived,
he would perform only the three-push ritual.
In the thirty-eighth year, personal plowing was abolished,
and only an official was dispatched to sacrifice to Xiānnóng.
In the forty-first year, it was further ordered that the relevant department should no longer submit reports.
In the first year of Lóngqìng, the cultivation and various sacrifices in the Xīyuàn were abolished,
and all supplies were taken from the plowing field.
Xiāncán
was not included in the sacrificial canon at the beginning of the Míng dynasty.
During the Jiājìng era,
the Dōugěishìzhōng (Chief Supervising Secretary) Xià Yán requested to convert the imperial estates and fields into imperial silkworm factories and mulberry gardens.
He ordered officials to plant mulberries and other trees,
to prepare for sericulture within the palace.
In the ninth year, he again submitted a memorial, stating
that the rituals of plowing and sericulture
should not be neglected unequally.
The Emperor then issued an edict to the Ministry of Rites:
"In ancient times, the Son of Heaven personally plowed,
and the Empress personally reared silkworms,
to encourage all under heaven.
Starting this year,
I will personally sacrifice to Xiānnóng,
and the Empress will personally rear silkworms.
Investigate the ancient systems,
and present the complete rituals for approval."
Grand Secretary Zhāng Cōng and others requested to build the Xiāncán Tán (Altar of the First Sericulturalist) outside Āndìngmén Gate.
Jìanshì Huò Tāo argued against it due to the long distance.
The Ministry of Revenue also stated:
"The area near Āndìngmén Gate to the west
lacks sufficient water sources,
and there is no place for bathing silkworms.
Within the Imperial City, the Xīyuàn has the waters of Tàiyè and Qióngdǎo.
According to the Táng dynasty system, it was within the imperial garden,
and the Sòng dynasty also had it within the palace.
It is appropriate to follow this precedent."
The Emperor said that the Táng people acted out of convenience and ease,
which should not be emulated.
Thereupon, the Lǐbù Shàngshū (Minister of Rites) Lǐ Shí and others stated:
"The distance from Dàmíngmén Gate to Āndìngmén Gate is long,
so please let the Empress's carriage (fèngniǎn) exit through Dōnghuá and Xuánwǔ Gates."
They then listed four matters: one, the ritual for processing cocoons;
two, the orientation of the altar enclosure;
three, the tools for picking mulberry leaves;
four, the officials in charge of the altar.
The Emperor accepted their suggestions,
ordering the exit to be from Xuánwǔ Mén Gate.
Inner palace eunuchs arranged the imperial guard (yíwèi),
ten thousand soldiers,
five thousand to surround the altar area,
five thousand to guard the road,
and the rest as deliberated.
In the second month,
the Ministry of Works submitted the plans for the Xiāncán Tán,
〔一０〕and the Emperor personally finalized its design.
The altar was twenty-six *chǐ* (feet) square,
stacked in two tiers,
two *chǐ* and six *cùn* (inches) high,
with four flights of steps projecting outwards.
Mulberry trees and other trees were planted to the west, east, and north.
Inside, the Cán Gōng Lìng Shǔ (Office of the Sericulture Palace Director) was established.
The mulberry-picking platform (cǎisāng tái) was one *chǐ* and four *cùn* high,
ten times its width in area,
with three flights of steps projecting outwards.
There were five rooms for the Luánjià Kù (Imperial Carriage Storage).
Behind it, the Zhītáng (Weaving Hall) was built.
The altar enclosure was eighty *zhàng* (rods) square.
The Ministry of Rites submitted the Empress's personal sericulture ritual.
When the silkworms were about to hatch,
the Qīntiān Jiān (Imperial Observatory) would select an auspicious *jǐsì* day and report it.
The Shùntiān Fǔ would provide the names and numbers of the "silkworm mothers" (cánmǔ) and send them to the Northern Suburb.
The Ministry of Works would provide the silkworm mothers with hooks, screens, baskets, frames, and other implements.
The Shùntiān Fǔ would present silkworm eggs and a hook-basket.
Inner palace officials would hold them out
and then hand them back.
They would exit through the right gate of Xuánwǔ Mén,
place them in a decorated palanquin,
and with drums and music, escort them to the silkworm chamber.
The silkworm mothers would receive the silkworm eggs,
bathe and feed them, and wait.
Noblewomen of civil fourth rank, military third rank and above, would all accompany the sacrifice,
each bringing a maidservant holding a hook-basket.
The Empress would fast for three days,
while all inner palace attendants, along with the master of ceremonies (sīzàn), the six female officials of the Shàng Bureau (liùshàng), and those who were to enter the altar,
would fast for one day.
The day before,
the Tàicháng Sì (Court of Imperial Sacrifices) would prepare the sacrificial tablet (zhùbǎn),
sacrificial offerings,
six each of sheep, pigs, *biāndòu* (bamboo and wooden sacrificial vessels),
〔一一〕and black silk, and send them to the Cán Gōng Lìng (Director of the Sericulture Palace).
On that day,
they would be distributed to the female officials in charge of the ritual.
Before dawn,
the imperial guard would arrange military preparations.
The female musicians and the Supervisor of Palace Arrangements (sīshè jiān) would prepare the ceremonial guards and the heavy *zhái* carriage (zhòngzháichē),
all awaiting outside Xuánwǔ Mén.
As dawn approached,
an inner palace attendant would go to Kūnníng Gōng Palace to request the Empress's presence.
The Empress, in her everyday attire,
guided by the female officials, would exit the palace gate,
mount a shoulder palanquin,
and proceed to Xuánwǔ Mén.
The inner palace attendant would request her to descend from the palanquin
and ascend the heavy *zhái* carriage.
The imperial guards, ceremonial guards, and female musicians would lead the way,
exiting through Běi'ānmén Gate,
shielded by portable curtains,
and arriving at the eastern gate of the altar's inner enclosure.
The inner palace attendant would request her to descend from the carriage
and mount a shoulder palanquin.
The imperial guards and ceremonial guards would stop outside the eastern gate.
The Empress would enter the Jùfú Diàn (Hall for Donning Robes),
change into ritual attire,
exit,
and proceed to the altar.
The master of ceremonies would announce her to take her position.
Princesses and noblewomen from both within and outside the palace would each take their bowing positions.
The sacrifice to Xiāncán would be performed,
with three offerings (sānxiàn lǐ),
and the female officials would perform their duties as prescribed.
Four bows would be made to welcome the gods,
two bows for receiving blessings and sacrificial meat (fúzhuò),
and four bows to send off the gods.
For all bowing, kneeling, and rising,
the princesses and noblewomen from both within and outside the palace would do the same.
After the ritual was complete,
the Empress would return to the Jùfú Diàn,
and change back into her everyday attire.
The Director of Protocol (Sī Bīn) led the external imperial ladies (wài mìngfù) first to the eastern steps (bìxià) of the Mulberry Gathering Altar (Cǎisāng Tán),
facing north and south.
The Director of Ceremonial (Shàng Yí) announced the request,
and the Empress (Huánghòu) proceeded to the mulberry gathering position,
facing east.
Princesses (Gōngzhǔ) and those below them stood to the east of the Empress's position,
also facing north and south,
with west being the place of honor.
Those holding hooks knelt to present the hooks,
and those holding baskets knelt to offer the baskets and receive the mulberries.
The Empress gathered three strips of mulberry leaves,
then returned to sit at the ceremonial gate (yímén) south of the altar,
observing the imperial ladies gathering mulberries.
The imperial ladies of the Three Dukes (Sān Gōng) gathered five strips,
and the imperial ladies of the Marquises (Liè Hóu) and Nine Ministers (Jiǔ Qīng) gathered nine strips.
When finished,
each handed them to a female attendant (nǚshì).
The Director of Protocol (Sī Bīn) led one internal imperial lady (nèi mìngfù)
to the Mulberry Chamber (Sāng Shì),
with the Director of Works (Shàng Gōng) leading those holding hooks and baskets following.
The Director of Works (Shàng Gōng) presented the mulberries to the silkworm mother (cánmǔ).
The silkworm mother (cánmǔ) received the mulberries,
shredded and finely cut them,
and handed them to the internal imperial lady (nèi mìngfù).
The internal imperial lady (nèi mìngfù) fed the silkworms,
and after sprinkling one tray (bó),
returned.
The Director of Ceremonial (Shàng Yí) announced the completion of the rites,
and the Empress (Huánghòu) returned to sit in the Robe Preparation Hall (Jùfú Diàn).
The Director of Protocol (Sī Bīn) led the silkworm mothers (cánmǔ) and others to prostrate themselves,
after which the Director of Chants (Sī Zàn) called for order.
The external imperial ladies (wài mìngfù) stood in their proper positions,
and the Director of Ceremonial (Shàng Yí) delivered an address saying:
"Since the Sericulture Ritual (Qīncán) is completed,
it is appropriate to offer congratulations."
After performing four bows,
an banquet was bestowed upon the imperial ladies (mìngfù),
and wine and food were also bestowed upon the silkworm mothers (cánmǔ).
Princesses (Gōngzhǔ) and internal imperial ladies (nèi mìngfù) were in the hall,
while external imperial ladies (wài mìngfù) of civil and military second rank and above were on the terrace (tái),
and those of third rank and below were in the vermillion courtyard (dānchí).
The Director of Imperial Meals (Shàng Shí) presented the dishes.
The Jiaofang Division (Jiàofāng Sī) female musicians played music.
After the banquet,
Princesses (Gōngzhǔ) and those below them each returned to their ranks and performed four bows.
Upon completion of the rites,
the Empress (Huánghòu) returned to her palace,
with an escort as before.
The imperial edict was as proposed.
In the fourth month,
the silkworm affairs were declared complete,
and the Cocoon Processing Ceremony (Zhìjiǎn Lǐ) was performed.
Ten silkworm women skilled in reeling silk and ten weavers were selected.
[一二] An auspicious day was divined,
and the Empress (Huánghòu) left the palace,
with an escort as per usual ceremony,
arriving at the Weaving Hall (Zhī Táng).
One internal imperial lady (nèi mìngfù) performed the "three basins of water" rite (sān pán shǒu lǐ),
distributing it among the weavers,
to conclude the event.
The Director of the Silkworm Palace (Cán Gōng Lìng) sent the materials to the Bureau of Weaving and Dyeing for Imperial Robes (Shàng Yī Zhī Rǎn Jiān Jú) to make sacrificial robes.
For the worship of the Ancestral Silkworm (Xiān Cán),
only music was used,
not dance.
The female musicians' caps and robes were all black.
In the second month of the tenth year,
the ritual officials (lǐchén) said:
"Last year, the Empress (Huánghòu) personally performed the mulberry gathering,
which was sufficient to inspire and encourage the empire.
Now, the construction of the Ancestral Silkworm Altar and Hall (Xiān Cán Tán Diàn) is not yet complete,
so it is appropriate to send an official to perform the rites for now."
The Emperor (Dì) initially disagreed,
ordering it to be performed as before.
Later, deeming the Empress's (Huánghòu) entry and exit inconvenient,
he ordered the Ancestral Silkworm Altar (Xiān Cán Tán) to be rebuilt in the Western Park (Xīyuàn).
To the east of the altar was the Mulberry Gathering Terrace (Cǎisāng Tái),
to the east of the terrace was the Robe Preparation Hall (Jùfú Diàn),
to the north was the Silkworm Chamber (Cán Shì),
with wing rooms (xiāngfáng) on either side,
and behind it were ancillary chambers (cóngshì),
for the residence of the silkworm women (cánfù).
The Silkworm Palace Bureau (Cán Gōng Shǔ) was established to the left of the palace,
with one director (lìng)
and two assistants (chéng),
chosen from among diligent and cautious internal eunuchs (nèichén).
In the fourth month,
the Empress (Huánghòu) performed the Sericulture Ritual (Qīncán Lǐ) in the Inner Park (Nèiyuàn).
The Emperor (Dì) said that since there were no congratulations for the personal plowing (qīngēng),
why should there be congratulations for this?
Only the kowtow rite (kòutóu lǐ) should be performed,
and the female musicians should only provide entertainment for the banquet,
not lead the procession.
In the thirty-eighth year, the Sericulture Ritual (Qīncán Lǐ) was abolished.
In the forty-first year, the proposals from the responsible offices were also abolished.
Gāoméi
In the ninth year of Jiājìng,
Lǐ Shíyáng, a scholar from Qīngzhōu, requested to sacrifice to Gāoméi
to pray for an imperial heir (shèngsì).
The ritual officials (lǐguān) reported it.
The Emperor (Dì) said:
"Although Gāoméi is an ancient rite,
it is indeed difficult to perform now."
So the proposal was shelved.
Later, the rites for sacrificing to Gāoméi were established.
A wooden platform (mùtái) was set up east of the imperial city (Huángchéng),
north of Yǒng'ān Mén,
in the Zhèn (east-northeast) direction.
On the platform,
the August Heaven Supreme Emperor (Huángtiān Shàngdì) faced south,
with a red calf (xīngdú)
and a dark jade bi (cāngbì).
The Emperor Xiàn (Xiàn Huángdì) was enshrined as a co-sacrificed deity (pèi),
facing west,
with one ox, one sheep, and one pig.
Gāoméi was below the altar, facing west,
with the same number of sacrificial animals.
The rite involved three offerings.
The Emperor (Huángdì) was positioned below the altar, facing north,
while the Empresses and Consorts (Hòufēi) were several tens of zhang to the south, facing north,
using screens (wéi).
Below the altar, bows and arrows (gōngshǐ) and quivers (gōngdú) were arranged in numbers corresponding to the Empresses and Consorts (Hòufēi Pín).
After the sacrifice,
female officials (nǚguān) guided the Empresses and Consorts (Hòufēi Pín) to Gāoméi,
knelt to take the bows and arrows and handed them to the Empresses and Consorts (Hòufēi Pín),
who received them and placed them in their quivers.
Sacrificial Proclamations (Jìgào)
According to the Míng system,

for all events such as ascending the throne (dēngjí), imperial tours (xúnxìng), bestowing posthumous titles (shàng shì), burying in mausoleums (zàng líng), enthroning empresses or crown princes (cè lì), enfeoffing nobles (cè fēng), capping ceremonies (guān), and weddings (hūn),
sacrifices and proclamations were made to Heaven and Earth (Tiāndì), the Ancestral Temples (Zōngmiào), and the Altars of Land and Grain (Shèjì).
For all construction of palaces (gōngshì),
and ordering generals to lead armies (mìng jiàng chū shī),
or for annual droughts and floods (suìshí hànlǎo),
sacrifices and proclamations were made to Heaven and Earth (Tiāndì), Mountains and Rivers (Shānchuān), the Grand Ancestral Temple (Tàimiào), the Altars of Land and Grain (Shèjì), and Hòutǔ.
At the beginning of an reign,
sacrifices and proclamations were also made to the Confucius Temple (Kǒngmiào) in Quèlǐ and the imperial tombs (língqín) of past dynasties.
In the second year of Hóngwǔ, following the memorial by Cūi Liàng, the Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū),
for the Round Altar (Huánqiū), Square Altar (Fāngqiū), and Grand Sacrifices (Dàsì),
a personal proclamation was made to the Grand Ancestral Temple (Tàimiào) in advance,
and envoys were also sent to proclaim to all deities at the Altars of All Deities (Tiānxià Shénqí Tán).
In the sixth year,
Niú Liàng, the Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū), memorialized that
for the Grand Duke Jupiter (Tàisuì) and other deities,
whenever prayers or thanks were offered,
fifteen altars were set up.
When there were matters requiring sacrificial proclamations,
twenty-eight altars with deity tablets were set up.
In the center,
for the Grand Duke Jupiter (Tàisuì), Wind, Clouds, Thunder, and Rain (Fēng Yún Léi Yǔ), the Five Sacred Mountains (Wǔ Yuè), the Five Guardian Mountains (Wǔ Zhèn), and the Four Seas (Sì Hǎi),
there were five altars in total.
To the east,
for the Four Rivers (Sì Dú), the Capital Region (Jīngjī), Húguǎng, Shāndōng, Hénán, Běipíng, Guǎngxī, Sìchuān, and Gānsù Mountains and Rivers,
the monthly generals (yuèjiàng) for the summer and winter seasons,
and the Capital City God (Jīngdū Chénghuáng),
there were twelve altars in total.
To the west,
for Zhōngshān,
Jiāngxī, Zhèjiāng, Fújiàn, Shānxī, Shǎnxī, Guǎngdōng, and Liáodōng Mountains and Rivers,
the monthly generals (yuèjiàng) for the spring and autumn seasons,
and the deities of military banners (qídú) and warships (zhànchuán),
there were eleven altars in total.
If the Emperor (Huángdì) personally performed the sacrifice,
he wore a leather cap and performed the one-offering rite (yī xiàn lǐ),
performing the rite once for every three altars.
In the eighth year,
the Emperor (Dì) resided in the Central Capital (Zhōngdū),
and made sacrificial proclamations to Heaven and Earth (Tiāndì) at the Round Altar (Huánqiū) of the Central Capital (Zhōngdū).
In the ninth year,
as the various princes (zhū wáng) were about to depart for their fiefdoms (fān),

they made separate day sacrifices and proclamations to the Grand Ancestral Temple (Tàimiào), the Altars of Land and Grain (Shèjì), the Sacred Mountains (Yuè), Guardian Mountains (Zhèn), Seas (Hǎi), and Rivers (Dú),
as well as the famous mountains and great rivers of the empire,
and again sacrificed and proclaimed to Heaven and Earth (Tiāndì) at the Round Altar (Huánqiū).
Initially,
when the various princes (zhū wáng) came to court and returned to their fiefdoms,
they sacrificed to Zhēnwǔ and other deities at the Duānmén,
using nine pigs, nine sheep, and silk fabrics.
Sacrifices to the guardian military banners (hùwèi qídú) at the Chéngtiān Mén
were also done in the same way.
In the twenty-sixth year,
the Emperor (Dì), deeming the rites too complex,
established the custom of using one pig and one sheep,
without silk fabrics.
Soon after, the sacrifices at the Duānmén were abolished, and only two altars, one for meat and one for vegetarian offerings, were used for sacrifices outside the Chéngtiān Mén.
In the 7th year of Yǒnglè
he offered sacrifices and reported to Heaven and Earth, the Ancestral Temple, and the Altars of Land and Grain.
In the autumn of the 8th year of Jiājìng
since he would personally offer sacrifices to the various gods of mountains and rivers,
he ordered that it was not necessary to dispatch officials to report to the Tàimiào in advance.
Whenever he entered or exited,
he would personally report to his ancestors in the inner hall.
On the day before the Imperial Birthday,
he would report with wine and fruits to the successive emperors and empresses in the Fèngxiān Diàn.
On the day itself,
he would report with wine and dried meat to Huángtiān Shàngdì in the Xuánjí Bǎodiàn.
He dispatched officials to offer sacrifices with sacrificial animals and liquor to the various mountain mausoleums of Shénliè, Tiānshòu, and Chúndé,
as well as Dōngyuè and the Dūchénghuáng.
He offered vegetarian sacrifices to Zhēnwǔ and the Língjì Gōng.
He also reported that a fast was being observed for Dàojí Qībǎo Dìzūn.
In the 3rd year of Lóngqìng
since he would personally offer sacrifices at the Cháorì Tán,
he reported in advance to the Fèngxiān, Hóngxiào, and Shénxiāo Diàn.
Prayers and Reports
In the 2nd year of Hóngwǔ
Tàizǔ prayed and reported to the various deities
because there had been no rain for a long spring.

In the center, five altars were set up for the gods of Wind, Clouds, Thunder, Rain, the Five Sacred Mountains (Yuè), the Five Preserving Mountains (Zhèn), the Four Seas, and the Four Great Rivers (Dú).
Altogether there were five altars.

To the east, seven altars were set up for the gods of Zhōngshān, the two Huái River regions, Jiāngxī, the two Guǎng regions, the northern part of Hǎinán, Shāndōng, the mountains and rivers of Yānnán and Yānjì, and the military banners and pennants.
Altogether there were seven altars.

To the west, six altars were set up for the gods of Jiāngdōng, the two Zhè River regions, Fújiàn, Húguǎng, Jīngxiāng, Hénánběi, Hédōng, the mountains and rivers of Huázhōu, and the Chénghuáng of the imperial capital.
Altogether there were six altars.
Silks were presented at the five central altars.
For the initial offering,
the Emperor personally performed the rites,
and officials were ordered to make separate offerings in the two side halls.
In the summer of the 3rd year
there was a drought.
On the 1st day of the 6th month,
the Emperor, in plain clothes and straw sandals,
walked and prayed at the Shānchuān Tán.
He sat on a straw mat in the open,
exposed to the sun by day,
and sleeping on the ground by night,
for three days.
In the 6th year
following the words of Níu Liàng, Minister of the Board of Rites,
for the various gods of Tàisuì,
spring prayers and autumn reports were made,
totaling fifteen altars.
In the center were
Tàisuì, Wind, Clouds, Thunder, Rain, the Five Yuè, the Five Zhèn, and the Four Seas.
To the east were
the Four Dú, the mountains and rivers of the imperial domain,
the monthly generals of the spring and autumn seasons,
and the Chénghuáng of various prefectures in the capital.
To the west were
Zhōngshān, the mountains and rivers of Gānsù,
the monthly generals of the summer and winter seasons,
and the gods of military banners, pennants, and warships.
Each had five altars.
At that time, Gānsù had recently submitted,
so its mountain and river sacrifices were included with those of the capital.
The rites for personal sacrifices were the same as those for reporting sacrifices.
In the 3rd month of the 9th year of Zhèngtǒng
rain and snow were overdue,
so officials were dispatched to sacrifice to Heaven, Earth, the Altars of Land and Grain, Tàisuì, Wind, Clouds, Thunder, Rain, the Yuè, Zhèn, Hǎi, and Dú.
In the 17th year of Hóngzhì
there was a prolonged drought in the imperial domain and Shāndōng.
Officials were ordered to sacrifice and report to Tiānshòu Shān,
and various巡撫 were separately ordered to sacrifice and report to Běiyuè, Běiyuè, Dōngyuè, Dōngzhèn, and Dōnghǎi.
In the spring of the 8th year of Jiājìng
the Emperor issued an edict to the Board of Rites:
"Last winter there was little snow,
and now it is time for spring cultivation,
