but the rain has not fallen.
I should personally sacrifice at the Southern Suburb, the Altars of Land and Grain, and the mountains and rivers."
Shàngshū Fāng Xiànfū and others said:
"The 'Dàzōngbó' chapter of the Zhōu Lǐ states: 'Perform the rites of wilderness in times of mourning, misfortune, and plague.'
Commentators explain: 'When the ruler's meals are not served,
the imperial roads are not cleared,
and sacrificial utensils are not hung,
all these are meant to show a sense of deprecation and reduction.'
It also says: 'When the state has great misfortunes,
then report to Shàngdì and the Four Directions.'
Commentators say: 'Misfortune refers to calamities.
Lǚ means
to arrange.
To arrange sacrifices to pray for them,
the ritual is not as complete as a regular sacrifice.'
Now His Majesty pities and toils for the myriad people,
personally going out to pray.
The rituals should be simple and brief,
to respond to the warning from Heaven.
All officials attending court shall follow,
jointly expressing sincerity in reflecting on errors and making petitions."
Thereupon, the ritual procedures were drawn up and submitted.
In the 2nd month, he personally prayed at the Southern Suburb,
and to the mountains and rivers on the same day.
The Altars of Land and Grain were used on the following day,
and the roads were not cleared.
The caps and robes were of light colors,
and all officials wore the same.
Civil officials of the fifth rank and above, and military officials of the fourth rank and above, stood outside the Dàsì Mén,
while other officials stood outside the Nántiān Mén,
taking their places to assist in the sacrifice.
That autumn,
the Emperor wished to personally sacrifice to the various gods of mountains and rivers.
Lǐ Shí, Minister of the Board of Rites, said:
"According to old practice for sacrifices to mountains and rivers,
the rites were performed at midnight,
with the Emperor leaving the capital to fast and lodge in the suburbs the day before.
After the sacrifice,
the imperial carriage would return in the early morning.
Completing the event over two days
made the ritual too onerous.
It would be appropriate to follow the example of the Xiānnóng Tán,
performing the rites at dawn."
Thereupon, the procedures were prepared and submitted.
The edict was approved.
A leather cap was worn for the sacrificial attire,
and two bows were made for welcoming and sending off the gods.
In the 11th year
Grand Secretary Lǐ Shí and others, as no imperial heir had yet been born,
requested court officials to go to the Yuè Zhèn and famous mountains to pray.
The Emperor wished to send out Daoist priests,
carrying incense and silk,
ordering the local guardians to perform the rites,
and the court ministers to separately go to the Dìqí Tán to pray and report.
Thereupon, Xià Yán, Minister of the Board of Rites, said:
"Our dynasty established the Dìqí Tán,
appeasing all from the Yuè, Zhèn, Hǎi, Dú, to distant and near famous mountains and great rivers.
To pray here
is exactly in line with the ancient meaning of 'wàng yǎn'
(praying from a distance).
However, the辅臣 (Assistant Ministers)'s request
was limited to the Yuè Zhèn.
I humbly believe that mountains, rivers, seas, and lakes
manifest auspiciousness and divine efficacy,
sharing the same merit as the Yuè Zhèn.
Moreover, the mountains of Jīyùn, Yìshèng, Shénliè, Tiānshòu, and Chúndé
are also places where the ancestral spirits rest peacefully,
and the rites of prayer for all these cannot be omitted."
So, ministers were ordered to go to the altars for separate sacrifices.
Dìqí Tán
In the second year of Hóngwǔ, following the suggestion of Cūi Liàng, the Minister of Rites,
altars for all the celestial and terrestrial deities were constructed to the east of the outer enclosure of the Yuánqiū,
and to the west of the outer enclosure of the Fāngqiū.
On the day before the suburban sacrifice,
the Emperor personally went to the altars,
set up the divine tablets,
facing west,
and offered sacrifices with wine and dried meat.
On the day of the suburban sacrifice,
after the secondary sacrifices and accompanying sacrifices were almost complete,
he would proceed to the altars to offer sacrifices.
Later, it was decided that an official would be dispatched to give prior notice.
Furthermore, a Mountain and River Altar was built to the west of the Heaven and Earth Altar outside Zhèngyángmén,
to collectively sacrifice to various deities.
In total, nineteen altars were established:
the Grand Astrological God of the Year (Tàisuì) and the monthly generals for the four seasons (spring, summer, autumn, winter) came first;
next, the deities of wind, clouds, thunder, and rain;
next, the Five Sacred Mountains (Wǔyuè);
next, the Five Defensive Peaks (Wǔzhèn);
next, the Four Seas (Sìhǎi);
next, the Four Great Rivers (Sìdú);
next, the capital's Zhōngshān;
next, Jiāngdōng;
next, Jiāngxī;
next, Húguǎng;
next, Huáidōng and Huáixī;
next, Zhèdōng, Zhèxī, and Fújiàn;
next, Guǎngdōng, Guǎngxī, Hǎinán, and Hǎiběi;
next, Shāndōng, Shānxī, Hénán, and Héběi;
next, Běipíng and Shǎnxī;
next, Zuǒjiāng and Yòujiāng;
next, the mountains and rivers of various nations such as Ānnán, Gāolí, and Zhànchéng;
next, the city god of the capital (Jīngdū Chénghuáng);

next, the Six Great Banners (Liùdáo Dàshén), the Great Generals of the Banner (Qídáo Dàjiàng), the Banner Gods of the Five Directions (Wǔfāng Qíshén), war boats, metal drums, cannons, bows and crossbows, flying spears, flying stones, and all the deities before and behind the battle array.
For all these, the Emperor personally performed the rites.
Before the sacrifice,
the official of rites announced:
"For the sacrificial texts,
from the Grand Astrological God of the Year (Tàisuì) down to the Four Seas (Sìhǎi),
a total of five altars,
for those where the Emperor refers to himself as 'your subject,' His Majesty should personally sign his imperial name.
For the deities of Zhōngshān and other gods,
where the Emperor refers to himself as 'I,' please have an official of rites sign on His Majesty's behalf."
The Emperor said:
"Even for correspondence between friends,
one still personally signs their name,
let alone for divine beings?"
Thus, he added his personal signature.
Later, it was further decided that three days after the Jīngzhé and Qiūfēn solar terms,
officials would be dispatched to offer sacrifices at the Mountain and River Altars to the various deities.
In the seventh year, it was ordered that in the first ten days of the middle month of spring and autumn,
a day should be chosen for the sacrifice.
In the ninth year, the system for the Mountain and River Altars was re-established,
with a total of thirteen altars.

In the main hall were seven altars: the Grand Astrological God of the Year (Tàisuì), wind, clouds, thunder, and rain, the Five Sacred Mountains (Wǔyuè), the Five Defensive Peaks (Wǔzhèn), the Four Seas (Sìhǎi), the Four Great Rivers (Sìdú), and Zhōngshān.
The east and west corridors each had three altars.
In the east:
the mountains and rivers of the capital region (Jīngjī Shānchuān), and the monthly generals for summer and winter.
In the west:
the monthly generals for spring and autumn, and the city god of the capital (Jīngdū Chénghuáng).
In the tenth year, it was decided that for the seven altars in the main hall,
the Emperor would personally perform the rites,
while meritorious officials would be dispatched to make secondary offerings in the east and west corridors.
In the twenty-first year, the altars and enclosures for the various deities of the Great Sacrifice Hall were expanded and renovated.
An edict was then issued stating that the spring sacrifices for all thirteen altars and their deities were to be suspended,
and instead, a day in the middle ten days of the eighth month each year
would be chosen for the sacrifice.
The Ministry of Rites was ordered to revise the ceremony for sacrificing at the Mountain and River Altars,
to be consistent with those for the Altars of Land and Grain (Shèjì).
During the Yǒnglè reign,
the Mountain and River Altars constructed in the capital (Jīngshī) followed the same system as those in Nánjīng,
with the only difference being that to the right of Zhōngshān in the main hall,
the deity of Tiānshòushān was added.
In the eleventh year of Jiājìng, the Mountain and River Altar was renamed the Altar of Celestial and Terrestrial Deities (Tiānshén Dìqí Tán),
and the order of the Cloud Master (Yúnshī), Rain Master (Yǔshī), Wind Lord (Fēngbó), and Thunder Master (Léishī) was changed.
The Celestial Deities Altar was on the left,
facing south,
comprising the Cloud, Rain, Wind, and Thunder deities,
a total of four altars.
The Terrestrial Deities Altar was on the right,
facing north,
comprising the Five Sacred Mountains (Wǔyuè), the Five Defensive Peaks (Wǔzhèn), Jīyùn Yìshèng Shénliè Tiānshòu Chúndé Wǔlíngshān, the Four Seas (Sìhǎi), and the Four Great Rivers (Sìdú),
a total of five altars.
For the accompanying sacrifices:
the mountains and rivers of the capital region (Jīngjī Shānchuān)
faced west;
the mountains and rivers of the entire realm (Tiānxià Shānchuān)
faced east.
In the mid-autumn of years designated by Chén, Xū, Chǒu, and Wèi (earth branches),
the Emperor would personally perform the sacrifice,
while in other years, a high-ranking minister would be dispatched to preside over the sacrifice.
The Grand Astrological God of the Year (Tàisuì), monthly generals, banner deities, and city gods
were sacrificed to separately.
In the seventeenth year, the honorific title Huángtiān Shàngdì was added,
and a prior announcement was made to the deities.
Consequently, an altar was set up to the southeast of the outer enclosure of the Yuánqiū,
where the Emperor personally determined the positions of the divine tablets and
arranged the ceremonial procedures for the Altar of Celestial and Terrestrial Deities.
The Ministry of Rites stated:
"Since His Majesty personally offers at the Great Bright Altar (Dàmíng Tán),
the ministers making secondary offerings at the four altars
should not be arranged in parallel.
We request that after the Emperor has offered incense,
an official be ordered to make the offering on his behalf."
The Emperor decided that after offering incense, presenting silk, and offering wine, and returning to his position,
the officials making secondary offerings could then perform their rites.
For the second and final offerings,
the officiating officers would act on behalf of the Emperor,
while at other altars, the offering officials would perform all three offerings.
In the first year of Lóngqìng,
the officials of rites stated:
"Since the Celestial and Terrestrial Deities are already included in the sacrifices at the Northern and Southern Suburbs,
the mid-autumn sacrifice to the deities should not be performed again."
It was ordered to abolish it.
Star Altars (Xīngchén Tán)
In the third year of Hóngwǔ,
the Emperor said to the ministers of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shěng):
"The sun and moon each have dedicated altars for sacrifice,
yet the stars are merely attached to the moon altar sacrifice,
which is not in accordance with ritual."
The Ministry of Rites proposed that south of the city, in front of the altars for the various deities, facing directly south,
nine additional bays should be built,
where the morning sun and evening moon, and all the stars of the heavens, would be sacrificed to.
All rites would be performed there.
The morning sun and evening moon would still be sacrificed to during the spring and autumn equinoxes,
while the stars would be sacrificed to three days before the Emperor's birthday (Tiānshòujié).
This was followed.
In the ninth month of the fourth year,
the Emperor personally sacrificed to all the stars of the heavens.
The main hall had a total of ten altars,
with the position for all the stars of the heavens set up in the center,
with ceremonies similar to those for the morning sun.
In the twenty-first year, since the stars were already included in the sacrifices at the Southern Suburbs,
the sacrifice to avert evil from the stars (yíngxīng zhī jì) was abolished.
Lingxing and Other Deities (Língxīng Zhūshén)
In the first year of Hóngwǔ,
the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Sī) reported:
"The Rites of Zhōu state, 'Sacrifice to Sīzhōng, Sīmìng, the Wind Master, and the Rain Master by burning wood on a pyre.'
The Heavenly Storehouse (Tiānfǔ) states, 'If sacrificing to Heaven, then sacrifice to Sīmín and Sīlù,
and present the number of people and the amount of grain,
which are received and stored.'
Emperor Gāodì of Hàn ordered commanderies and kingdoms to establish shrines to Língxīng.
According to the Táng system,
Língxīng was sacrificed to on the chén day after the beginning of autumn (Lìqiū).
On the hài day after the beginning of winter (Lìdōng), officials were dispatched to sacrifice to Sīzhōng, Sīmìng, Sīmín, and Sīlù,
using a minor ox sacrifice (shǎoláo).
The Sòng sacrifices were like the Táng's,
but the Star of Longevity (Shòuxīng) was sacrificed to on the day of the autumn equinox.
We now propose to follow the Táng system,
sacrificing on separate days,
and to build altars south of the city."
This was approved.
In the second year, following the memorial of Cūi Liàng, the Minister of Rites,
the Star of Longevity (Shòuxīng) was sacrificed to on the Emperor's birthday (Shèngshòurì) each year,
and on the same day, Sīzhōng, Sīmìng, Sīmín, and Sīlù were sacrificed to,
to show that the people shared in these blessings.
Língxīng was sacrificed to on the fifteenth day of the eighth month.
Officials were dispatched to perform all these rites.
In the third year, the sacrifices to the Star of Longevity (Shòuxīng) and others were abolished.
Sacrifices to the Grand Astrological God of the Year (Tàisuì), Monthly Generals, Wind, Clouds, Thunder, and Rain
In antiquity, there were no altars for Tài-Suì or the Yuè-Jiàng.
The Míng dynasty was the first to give weight to their sacrifices.
The addition of the Yún-Shī (Cloud Master) after the Fēng-Shī (Wind Master)
also began in the Míng dynasty.
Tài-Zǔ already had the various Tài-Suì deities sacrifice alongside him at the Huán-Qiū,
and also offered joint sacrifices at the Qún-Sì-Tán (Altar of Group Sacrifices).
Afterward, he ordered the ritual officials to deliberate on a dedicated sacrificial altar.
The ritual officials stated:
“Tài-Suì
is the deity of the twelve earthly branches.
According to the Shuō-Wén,
the character '歲' (suì) is composed of '步' (bù) and '戌' (xū).
Jupiter travels once a year,
passing through the twelve earthly branches to complete a circuit,
much like walking.
According to Yin-Yang school theories,
there are also the twelve Yuè-Jiàng,
deities assigned to the ten days and twelve hours,
such as Tiān-Yǐ, Tiān-Gāng, Tài-Yǐ, Gōng-Cáo, and Tài-Chōng.
Though not seen in the classics,
successive dynasties have followed this practice.
The Yuán dynasty, whenever undertaking major construction,
sacrificed to Tài-Suì, Yuè-Jiàng, Rì-Zhí (Day Duty deity), and Shí-Zhí (Hour Duty deity) at the Tài-Shǐ-Yuàn (Bureau of the Grand Scribe).
As for the sacrifices to the Fēng-Shī and Yǔ-Shī (Rain Master),
they are mentioned in the Zhōu-Guān (Rites of Zhou),
and later generations all observed these sacrifices.
During the Tiān-Bǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
the Léi-Shī (Thunder Master) was added after the Yǔ-Shī.
The Sòng and Yuán dynasties followed this.
However, the Táng system sacrificed to each separately according to the season,
losing the original intention of joint worship.
It is appropriate to combine Tài-Suì and the various celestial deities of wind, cloud, thunder, and rain into one altar,
and all the terrestrial deities into another altar,
offering dedicated sacrifices in spring and autumn.”
Thus, it was decided to sacrifice to the various Tài-Suì deities on the days of Jīng-Zhí and Qiū-Fēn (Autumn Equinox) south of the city.
Three years later, because the various deities represented the singular essence of Yin and Yang,
flowing without interruption,
the two altars were combined into one,
and the Yuè-Jiàng of the four seasons were added.
The sacrificial dates were also changed
to three days after Jīng-Zhí and Qiū-Fēn for both the celestial and terrestrial deities.
In the tenth year of Jiā-Jìng, the Ministry of Rites was ordered to examine the Tài-Suì altar system.
The ritual officials stated:
“The deity Tài-Suì
is not recorded in the sacrificial canons of Táng or Sòng.
Although the Yuán dynasty had sacrifices,
there was no fixed canon.
The system of altars
has no basis in antiquity.
Tài-Suì, as a celestial deity,
should have an open-air altar for sacrifice,
modeled after the Shè-Jì-Tán (Altar of Land and Grain) but slightly smaller.”
This was followed.
Consequently, the Tài-Suì-Tán was built west of Zhèng-Yáng-Mén,
opposite the Tiān-Tán (Temple of Heaven).
In the center,
was the Tài-Suì-Diàn (Hall of Tài-Suì).
In the east wing,
were the two altars for the spring and autumn Yuè-Jiàng.
In the west wing,
were the two altars for the summer and winter Yuè-Jiàng.
The emperor personally offered sacrifices in the Bài-Diàn (Prostration Hall).
Every year in the first month of spring, when ancestral temples were honored,
and on the day of the annual collective sacrifice at year-end,
officials were dispatched to offer sacrifices.
The kingdoms, prefectures, and counties also sacrificed to the Fēng-Yún-Léi-Yǔ-Shī (Masters of Wind, Cloud, Thunder, and Rain),
and continued to build altars southwest of the city.
Sacrifices were offered on the days of Jīng-Zhí and Qiū-Fēn.
Sacrifices to the Yuè-Zhèn-Hǎi-Dú (Five Sacred Mountains, Five Guardian Mountains, Four Seas, and Four Rivers) and other mountains and rivers.
In the second year of Hóng-Wǔ,
Tài-Zǔ offered joint sacrifices to the various deities of the sacred mountains and rivers south of the city,
but there was no dedicated sacrifice.
Moreover, the places of worship
were houses, not altars,
which was not the way to honor the deities.
The ritual officials stated:
“Yú-Shùn sacrificed to the four sacred mountains,
and the term 'Wǔ-Yuè' (Five Sacred Mountains) first appeared in the Wáng-Zhì (Institutes of Kings).
In the Zhōu-Guān,
'sacrificed to the four directional deities in the four suburbs,'
Zhèng’s commentary states
that the four directional deities were the Wǔ-Yuè, the Four Guardian Mountains (Sì-Zhèn), and the Four Rivers (Sì-Dú).
The 'Shī-Xù' (Prefaces to the Odes) mentions imperial tours and rites to the four sacred mountains, rivers, and seas,
so there were also sacrifices to the Four Seas.
The emperor's acts of 'fang-wang' (looking afar and sacrificing)
were all-encompassing.
However, the sacred mountains, guardian mountains, and rivers,
being within the feudal territories of the feudal lords,
were each sacrificed to by them.
Qín abolished the feudal system,
and the sacred mountains and rivers were all under the jurisdiction of the sacrificial officials.
Hàn re-established the feudal lords,
so the marquises each sacrificed to the mountains and rivers within their own territories,
without imperial involvement.
During Emperor Wǔ's time,
some feudal states were divided or abolished, and
all Wǔ-Yuè were within the emperor's domain.
During Emperor Xuān's time,
the rite of sending envoys with credentials to sacrifice to the sacred mountains and rivers first began.
From Wèi to Suí,
shrines for the sacred mountains, guardian mountains, and rivers were established in their respective localities,
and officials were dispatched to offer sacrifices.
Under the Táng and Sòng systems,
there were sacrifices ordered to be performed by local governors and county magistrates,
sacrifices offered by looking afar during suburban sacrifices,
and also sacrifices performed by dispatched envoys.
The Yuán dynasty dispatched envoys to sacrifice to the sacred mountains, guardian mountains, and rivers,
dividing them into five routes: east, west, south, north, and central.
Now, it is fitting to combine the sacred mountains, guardian mountains, rivers, and all mountains, rivers, city gods, and other terrestrial deities throughout the realm into one altar,
equal to the celestial deities,
and offer dedicated sacrifices in spring and autumn.”
Thus, the sacrificial dates were set for Qīng-Míng and Shuāng-Jiàng.
One day before,
the emperor personally inspected the sacrificial animals.
On the day itself,
wearing the Tōng-Tiān-Guān (Heaven-Connecting Crown) and a crimson gauze robe,
he proceeded before the Yuè-Zhèn-Hǎi-Dú
and performed the three libations ritual.
For the mountains, rivers, and city gods,
separate sacrificial officials performed the rites.
That year, eighteen officials were appointed
to sacrifice to the deities of the sacred mountains, guardian mountains, and rivers throughout the realm.
The emperor, wearing a Pí-Biàn (deer-skin cap), presided in the Fèng-Tiān-Diàn (Hall of Honoring Heaven),
personally signed his imperial name,
and presented the incense and prayer text to the envoys.
All officials, in court attire,
saw them off to the Zhōng-Shū-Shěng (Central Secretariat),
and the envoys departed with the offerings.
A golden box held the incense,
two yellow brocade banners,
and twenty-five taels of silver were used to purchase sacrificial items.
Three years later, an edict定 established the divine titles for the Yuè-Zhèn-Hǎi-Dú deities.
It briefly stated:
“The way of governance
must be rooted in ritual.
The ennoblement of the sacred mountains, guardian mountains, and rivers
originated in Táng and Sòng.
Indeed, the essence of spiritual power
gathers to form deities,
who must receive their mandate from the Shang-Dì (Supreme Emperor).
How can national titles be bestowed upon them?
This disrespect for ritual is unprecedentedly severe.
Now, in accordance with ancient regulations,
all previously granted titles from earlier dynasties are to be removed.
The Wǔ-Yuè shall be called 'Deity of the Eastern Sacred Mountain Tài-Shān',
'Deity of the Southern Sacred Mountain Héng-Shān',
'Deity of the Central Sacred Mountain Sōng-Shān',
'Deity of the Western Sacred Mountain Huá-Shān',
and 'Deity of the Northern Sacred Mountain Héng-Shān'.
The Wǔ-Zhèn shall be called 'Deity of the Eastern Guardian Mountain Yí-Shān',
'Deity of the Southern Guardian Mountain Kuài-Jī-Shān',
'Deity of the Central Guardian Mountain Huò-Shān',
'Deity of the Western Guardian Mountain Wú-Shān',
and 'Deity of the Northern Guardian Mountain Yī-Wú-Lǘ-Shān'.
The Sì-Hǎi (Four Seas) shall be called 'Deity of the Eastern Sea',
'Deity of the Southern Sea',
'Deity of the Western Sea',
and 'Deity of the Northern Sea'.
The Sì-Dú shall be called 'Deity of the Eastern River Dà-Huái',
'Deity of the Southern River Dà-Jiāng',
'Deity of the Western River Dà-Hé',
and 'Deity of the Northern River Dà-Jì'. ”
The emperor personally signed his name on the prayer text
and dispatched officials to announce and sacrifice with the revised divine titles.
Six years later,
the ritual officials stated:
“As Sì-Chuān was not yet pacified,
sacrifices to the Jiāng-Dú (Yangtze River deity) were offered by looking afar from Xiá-Zhōu.
Now that Shǔ has been subdued,
an envoy should be dispatched to offer sacrifices to the Nán-Dú (Southern River) directly.”
This was followed.
In the tenth year, eighteen officials were appointed
to separately sacrifice to the Yuè-Zhèn-Hǎi-Dú,
and imperial decrees were bestowed upon them.
In the fourteenth year of Wàn-Lì,
the巡抚 (巡撫) Xún-Fǔ Hú Lái-Gòng requested that the sacrifice to the Běi-Yuè (Northern Sacred Mountain) be moved to Hún-Yuán-Zhōu.
The ritual officials stated:
“The Dà-Míng-Jí-Lǐ (Collected Rites of the Great Míng) records that
the sacrifices to the Běi-Yuè in Hán, Táng, and Sòng
were all held in Qǔ-Yáng-Xiàn, Dìng-Zhōu,
which aligns with historical records.
The designation of Hún-Yuán as Běi-Yuè
is only found in local gazetteers and stele inscriptions;
there is no verifiable evidence in the classics.
Therefore, continuing to sacrifice in Qǔ-Yáng is correct.”
Other Sacrifices to Mountains and Rivers.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, the emperor personally offered sacrifices to the gods in Biànliáng,
and still dispatched officials to sacrifice to the mountains and rivers within the borders.
In the second year,
all the mountains and rivers of the realm were included in the sacrifices at the Yuèdú (Peaks and Rivers) Altar.
The emperor also considered that Ānnán and Gāolí had both submitted as vassals,
and that their national mountains and rivers
should be sacrificed to in the same way as those of Zhōngguó.
He issued an edict to the Zhōngshū Shěng and the ritual officials to investigate this.
Ānnán had twenty-one mountains,
six rivers (jiāng),
and six rivers (shuǐ).
Gāolí had three mountains
and four rivers.
He commanded that these be recorded in the sacrificial canon,
and altars be set up for their sacrifices.
In the third year, envoys were sent to Ānnán, Gāolí, and Zhānchéng
to sacrifice to their national mountains and rivers.
The emperor fasted and purified himself,
and personally composed the sacrificial prayers.
He also sent officials to promulgate edicts regarding the rectification of the divine titles of mountains and rivers in Ānnán, Zhānchéng, and Gāolí.
In the sixth year,
the various states of Liúqiú had already paid tribute,
so sacrifices were offered to their national mountains and rivers.
In the eighth year,
Niú Liàng, Shàngshū of the Lǐbù, stated:
"Since sacrifices to the mountains and rivers of the realm in the capital have been abolished,
it is also not fitting for the Son of Heaven to personally sacrifice to the mountains and rivers of foreign countries."
The Zhōngshū Shěng and the ritual ministers requested that these be included in the sacrifices of the respective provinces,
and this was granted.
Guǎngxī included Ānnán, Zhānchéng, Zhēnlà, Xiāmluó, and Suǒlǐ in its sacrifices.
Guǎngdōng included Sānfóqí and Zhǎowā.
Fújiàn included Rìběn, Liúqiú, and Bóní.
Liáodōng included Gāolí.
Shǎnxī included Gānsù, Gān, and Wūsīzàng.
The capital no longer offered these sacrifices.
It was also decided, based on the ritual officials' suggestion,
that the mountains and rivers of the various provinces should face south from the center,
while those of foreign countries should face east and west,
and be sacrificed together on the same altar.
Regarding the sacrifices to the mountains and rivers of vassal kingdoms,
regulations were established in the thirteenth year of Hóngwǔ.
In the eighteenth year, it was stipulated that vassal kingdoms should sacrifice to mountains and rivers,
with ceremonies similar to those for Shèjì,
but without the burial texts.
For all sacred peaks, strategic mountains, sea deities, and other mountains and rivers,
the local officials were ordered to offer two sacrifices annually, during Qīngmíng and Shuāngjiàng.
Chénghuáng.
In the second year of Hóngwǔ,
the ritual officials stated:
"The origin of the sacrifice to Chénghuáng is obscure.
Former scholars believed that since there was already Shè,
there should not also be Chénghuáng.
Thus, Lǐ Yángbīng's record of the Jìn'yún Chénghuáng in the Táng dynasty stated: 'The sacrificial canon has no mention of it,
only Wú and Yuè have it.'
However, the Chénghuáng temple in Chéngdū was
built by Lǐ Déyù;
Zhāng Yuè had a text for sacrificing to Chénghuáng;
Dù Mù had a text for sacrificing to the Huángzhōu Chénghuáng.
So it was not unique to Wú and Yuè.
Moreover, the Wúhú Chénghuáng temple was built in the second year of Wú Chìwū.
Mùróng Yǎn of Gāo Qí and
the Prince of Wǔlíng of Liáng offered sacrifices to Chénghuáng,
all recorded in history,
so it was not unique to the Táng dynasty.
Since the Sòng dynasty, these temples were found throughout the realm.
Some were granted temple names,
some were bestowed noble titles,
and some even twisted and forced interpretations
to assign a specific person as the god's name.
According to Zhāng Jiǔlíng's text for sacrificing to the Hóngzhōu Chénghuáng, it says: '
Chénghuáng provides protection,
the common people depend on it.'
Thus, the intention of worshipping it in previous dynasties existed.
Now, it is appropriate to include it in the sacrifices at the altars of the Yuèdú gods."
Then, it was commanded that they be granted noble titles.
The capital's Chénghuáng was enfeoffed as Chéngtiān Jiànguó Sīmín Shēngfú Mínglíng Wáng.
Kāifēng, Línháo, Tàipíng, Hézhōu, and Chúzhōu were all enfeoffed as kings.
Other prefectures were enfeoffed as Jiànchá Sīmín Chénghuáng Wēilíng Gōng,
ranked second grade.
Departments were enfeoffed as Jiànchá Sīmín Chénghuáng Língyòu Hóu,
ranked third grade.
Counties were enfeoffed as Jiànchá Sīmín Chénghuáng Xiǎnyòu Bó,
ranked fourth grade.
Robes, crowns, and tassels all varied accordingly.
The literary officials were ordered to compose the imperial edicts for their promulgation.
In the third year, an edict abolished the noble titles,
stipulating that they be referred to simply as "the god of the Chénghuáng of such-and-such prefecture, department, or county."
It also ordered that other deities be removed from the temples.
Temple regulations were established,
with height and width similar to the official halls of government offices.
Wooden tablets were made as the main objects of worship;
sculpted images were destroyed and placed in water,
their clay used to plaster walls,
and painted with clouds and mountains.
In the sixth year, the spirit tablet for the Zhōngdū Chénghuáng was completed,
and officials were sent with incense and silk to install it.
Since the capital's Chénghuáng was already part of the mountain and river altar sacrifices,
in the twenty-first year, the temple was rebuilt.
Soon after, it was included in the sacrifices at the Grand Sacrificial Hall,
and the spring sacrifice at the mountain and river altar was abolished.
During the Yǒnglè reign,
a temple was built to the west of the capital city,
named Dàwēilíng Cí.
In the ninth year of Jiājìng, the inclusion of Chénghuáng in the mountain and river altar sacrifices was abolished.
Annually, on the day of the flag and banner sacrifice in the middle of autumn,
the god of the capital Chénghuáng was also sacrificed to.
On all imperial birthdays and on the eleventh day of the fifth month, the god's birthday,
officials of the Tàicháng Sì Tángshàng conducted the rituals.
If the nation suffered a great calamity, the temple was informed.
In vassal kingdoms, the king personally offered sacrifices;
in the various prefectures, departments, and counties, the governor or magistrate presided.

Collation Notes: Chapter 26, Rituals 4 (Auspicious Rituals 4): Imperial Tombs and Temples of Past Dynasties, The Three Sovereigns, The Sage Teacher, Our First Teacher Confucius, Flags and Banners, The Five Sacrifices, The Horse God, Nánjīng Temples of Spirits, Temples of Meritorious Officials, The Nine Temples of the Capital, Various Temples of Spirits, The Lì Altar.
Imperial Tombs and Temples of Past Dynasties.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, envoys were sent to visit the imperial tombs of previous dynasties,
and the various provinces were ordered to submit maps,
totaling seventy-nine.
The ritual officials investigated those with conspicuous achievements and virtues,
namely: Fúxī,
Shénnóng,
Huángdì,
Shǎohào,
Zhuānxù,
Táng Yáo,
Yú Shùn,
Xià Yǔ,
Shāng Tāng, Zhōngzōng, Gāozōng,
Zhōu Wénwáng, Wǔwáng, Chéngwáng, Kāngwáng,
Hàn Gāozǔ, Wéndì, Jǐngdì, Wǔdì, Xuāndì, Guāngwǔ, Míngdì, Zhāngdì,
Hòuwèi Wéndì,
Suí Gāozǔ,
Táng Gāozǔ, Tàizōng, Xiànzōng, Xuānzōng,
Zhōu Shìzōng,
Sòng Tàizǔ, Tàizōng, Zhēnzōng, Rénzōng, Xiàozōng, Lǐzōng,
totaling thirty-six.
Robes and crowns were made for each,
and incense and silk were sealed in boxes.
Táo Yì, Assistant Secretary of the Mìshū Jiān, and others were sent to repair and conduct the sacrificial rites,
and the emperor personally composed the sacrificial prayers and dispatched them.
For each tomb, twenty-five taels of white silver were provided for sacrificial offerings.
Tombs that had been opened were reburied;
those that were damaged were restored.
Temples that were dilapidated were repaired.
For those without temples, altars were set up for sacrifices.
Local officials were also ordered to prohibit logging and gathering.
Seasonal sacrifices were offered,
using a grand animal sacrifice (tàiláo).
In the fourth year,
the Lǐbù finalized its deliberation,
combining the sacrifices to thirty-five emperors.
Ten were in Hénán: Chén sacrificed to Fúxī and Shāng Gāozōng;
Mèngjīn to Hàn Guāngwǔ;
Luòyáng to Hàn Míngdì and Zhāngdì;
Zhèng to Zhōu Shìzōng;
Gǒng to Sòng Tàizǔ, Tàizōng, Zhēnzōng, and Rénzōng.
One in Shānxī: Yínghé sacrificed to Shāng Tāng.
Two in Shāndōng: Dōngpíng sacrificed to Táng Yáo;
Qūfù to Shǎohào.
Three in Běipíng: Nèihuáng sacrificed to Shāng Zhōngzōng;
Huá to Zhuānxù and Gāoxīn.
Two in Húguǎng: Líng sacrificed to Shénnóng;
Níngyuǎn to Yú Shùn.
Two in Zhèjiāng: Kuàijī sacrificed to Xià Yǔ and Sòng Xiàozōng.
Fifteen in Shǎnxī: Zhōngbù sacrificed to Huángdì;
Xiányáng to Zhōu Wénwáng, Wǔwáng, Chéngwáng, Kāngwáng, and Xuānwáng,
Hàn Gāodì, Jǐngdì;
Xiánníng to Hàn Wéndì;
Xīngpíng to Hàn Wǔdì;
Cháng'ān to Hàn Xuāndì;
Sānyuán to Táng Gāozǔ;
Lǐquán to Táng Tàizōng;
Púchéng to Táng Xiànzōng;
Jīngyáng to Táng Xuānzōng.
Annual sacrifices were held on the first day of the middle spring and middle autumn months.
Thereupon, envoys were sent to each tomb to offer sacrifices.
A stele was erected at each tomb,
inscribed with the sacrificial date and the number of animals and silks,
for the local officials to guard.
Later, local officials were ordered to carry out repairs and maintenance annually,
and two tomb guards were appointed to oversee them.
Every three years, furthermore,
sacrificial prayers, incense, and silk were issued,
and an imperial order dispatched musicians and dancers from the Tàicháng Sì to carry them to the respective locations,
where local officials were ordered to offer sacrifices.
Those sacrificed to were,
compared to the previous list, without Zhōu Xuānwáng,
Hàn Míngdì, and Zhāngdì;
but Wāhuáng was added in Zhàochéng,
Hòuwèi Wéndì in Fùpíng,
Yuán Shìzǔ in Shùntiān,
and Sòng Lǐzōng in Kuàijī,
totaling thirty-six emperors.
Later, Suí Gāozǔ was added in Fúfēng,
but Lǐzōng was again removed from the sacrifices.
Furthermore, officials in charge of imperial tombs and temples were ordered to choose a day in the first ten days of the middle spring and autumn months
to offer sacrifices.
In the sixth year,
the Emperor decreed that the founding monarchs of the Five Thearchs (Wǔdì), Three Sovereigns (Sānhuáng), as well as the Hàn, Táng, and Sòng dynasties,
should all have temples built in the capital for sacrifices.
Consequently, the Temple of Emperors and Kings of Successive Dynasties (Lìdài Dìwáng Miào) was built on the sunny side of Qīntiān Shān.
Following the system of "same hall, different chambers" of the Imperial Ancestral Temple (Tàimiào),
there were five main chambers: the central chamber for the Three Sovereigns (Sānhuáng);
the easternmost chamber for the Five Thearchs (Wǔdì);
the westernmost chamber for Yǔ (Yǔ) of Xià, Tāng (Tāng) of Shāng, and King Wén (Wénwáng) of Zhōu;
the next eastern chamber for King Wǔ (Wǔwáng) of Zhōu, Emperor Guāngwǔ (Guāngwǔ) of Hàn, and Emperor Tàizōng (Tàizōng) of Táng;
and the next western chamber for Emperor Gāozǔ (Gāozǔ) of Hàn, Emperor Gāozǔ (Gāozǔ) of Táng, Emperor Tàizǔ (Tàizǔ) of Sòng, and Emperor Shìzǔ (Shìzǔ) of Yuán.
Sacrifices were offered annually on the *jiǎ* day of the first ten days of the middle months of spring and autumn.
Later, as King Wén (Wénwáng) of Zhōu ultimately remained a subject,
and Emperor Gāozǔ (Gāozǔ) of Táng gained the empire through Tàizōng (Tàizōng),
their sacrifices were suspended.
Emperor Gāozǔ (Gāozǔ) of Suí was added to the sacrifices.
In the seventh year, an order was issued for all statues in the Temple of Emperors and Kings (Dìwáng Miào) to be sculpted wearing imperial robes and crowns (gǔnmiǎn zuòxiàng),
except for Fúxī (Fúxī) and Shénnóng (Shénnóng), who had no system of clothing at their time,
and thus did not need to wear crowns and robes.
In the eighth month,
the Emperor personally offered sacrifices at the new temple.
Later, the sacrifice to Emperor Gāozǔ (Gāozǔ) of Suí was abolished.
In the twenty-first year, it was ordered that during the annual suburban sacrifices (jiāosì),
the emperors and kings of successive dynasties should be additionally sacrificed to in the Grand Sacrificial Hall (Dàsì Diàn).
Moreover, in the middle ten days of the eighth month each year,
a day was chosen for an official to be dispatched to offer sacrifices at the original temple,
while the spring sacrifice was discontinued.
It was also decreed that in years when officials were dispatched to sacrifice at various imperial tombs (líng),
the temple sacrifices would be suspended.
In this year, an imperial edict allowed famous ministers of successive dynasties to be honored alongside.
The Minister of Rites (Lǐguān), Lǐ Yuánmíng, submitted a memorial proposing thirty-six individuals.
The Emperor deemed Sòng's Zhào Pǔ (Zhào Pǔ) disloyal to Emperor Tàizǔ (Tàizǔ)
and thus unsuitable to be honored alongside.
Among the four eminent ministers of Yuán,
Mùhuálí (Mùhuálí) was the foremost,
so it was inappropriate to sacrifice to the grandson while omitting his ancestor.
Mùhuálí (Mùhuálí) could be sacrificed to, and Āntóng (Āntóng) should be removed.
Since Bóyán (Bóyán) was sacrificed to,
Āshù (Āshù) need not be sacrificed to.
Chén Píng (Chén Píng) and Féng Yì (Féng Yì) of Hàn,
and Pān Měi (Pān Měi) of Sòng,
all had good beginnings and endings,
and could be sacrificed to.

Thus, it was determined that Fēng Hòu (Fēng Hòu), Lì Mù (Lì Mù), Gāoyáo (Gāoyáo), Kuí (Kuí), Lóng (Lóng), Bóyí (Bóyí), Bóyì (Bóyì), Yī Yǐn (Yī Yǐn), Fù Yuè (Fù Yuè), Zhōugōng Dàn (Zhōugōng Dàn), Zhàogōng Shì (Zhàogōng Shì), Tàigōng Wàng (Tàigōng Wàng), Zhào Hǔ (Zhào Hǔ), Fāng Shú (Fāng Shú), Zhāng Liáng (Zhāng Liáng), Xiāo Hé (Xiāo Hé), Cáo Cān (Cáo Cān), Chén Píng (Chén Píng), Zhōu Bó (Zhōu Bó), Dèng Yǔ (Dèng Yǔ), Féng Yì (Féng Yì), Zhūgě Liàng (Zhūgě Liàng), Fáng Xuánlíng (Fáng Xuánlíng), Dù Rúhuì (Dù Rúhuì), Lǐ Jìng (Lǐ Jìng), Guō Zǐyí (Guō Zǐyí), Lǐ Shèng (Lǐ Shèng), Cáo Bīn (Cáo Bīn), Pān Měi (Pān Měi), Hán Shìzhōng (Hán Shìzhōng), Yuè Fēi (Yuè Fēi), Zhāng Jùn (Zhāng Jùn), Mùhuálí (Mùhuálí), Bó'ěrhū (Bó'ěrhū), Bó'ěrshù (Bó'ěrshù), Chìlǎowēn (Chìlǎowēn), and Bóyán (Bóyán),
a total of thirty-seven individuals,
were honored alongside in the east and west side halls (wǔ),
with four altars.
Initially,
Tàigōng Wàng (Tàigōng Wàng) had a Temple of King Wǔchéng (Wǔchéngwáng Miào),
where officials were regularly dispatched to offer sacrifices following the ritual of *shìdiàn* (ceremony of presenting sacrificial offerings to Confucius).
By this time,
the temple sacrifices were abolished,
and the kingly title was removed.
During the Yongle (Yǒnglè) relocation of the capital,
officials from the Nanjing Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Nánjīng Tàicháng Sì)
were dispatched to perform the rituals at the Temple of Emperors and Kings (Dìwáng Miào).
In the ninth year of Jiajing (Jiājìng), the practice of honoring successive emperors and kings at the southern suburban sacrifices (nánjiāo) was abolished.
An order was issued to build the Temple of Emperors and Kings of Successive Dynasties (Lìdài Dìwáng Miào) to the west of the capital city,
with sacrifices offered annually in the middle months of spring and autumn.
Later, the temple sacrifices in Nanjing (Nánjīng) were also abolished.
In the second month of spring in the tenth year,
as the temple was not yet completed,
the Emperor personally offered sacrifices to the emperors and kings of successive dynasties in the Wénhuá Diàn,
with a total of five altars,
and four altars for famous ministers on the east and west sides of the imperial stairs (dānbì).
Lǐ Shí (Lǐ Shí), Minister of the Board of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū), stated:
"The old ritual contained a phrase 'bestow good fortune and sacrificial meat (cìfúzòu)'.
'Bestow' implies from superior to inferior.
This should only be used for suburban sacrifices, ancestral temples, and altars of soil and grain.
For emperors and kings of successive dynasties,
it should only say 'respond (dá)'."
The imperial edict approved this.
In the summer of the eleventh year,
the temple was completed
and named the Hall of Reverence for Virtue and Honoring Sages (Jǐngdé Chóngshèng zhī Diàn).
The hall had five chambers,
east and west side halls,
a repository for sacrificial vessels behind the main hall,
and Jǐngdé Mén (Jǐngdé Mén) at the front.
Outside the gate were the divine treasury (shénkù), divine kitchen (shénchú), slaughtering pavilion (zǎishēng tíng), and bell tower (zhōnglóu).
Two archways (fāng) stood east and west on the street,
called Jǐngdé Jiē.
On the *rénchén* day of the eighth month, the Emperor personally offered sacrifices.
The Emperor entered through the central gate,
bowing twice each when welcoming the spirits (yíngshén), receiving good fortune and sacrificial meat (shòufúzòu), and sending off the spirits (sòngshén).
Thereafter, one grand minister was dispatched annually to perform the rites,
with four others assisting in the offerings.
In years when sacrifices were made at imperial tombs (língqǐn), specifically the *zǐ*, *wǔ*, *mǎo*, and *yǒu* years,
the autumn sacrifice was suspended.
In the twenty-fourth year,
following the proposal of Chén Fěi (Chén Fěi) from the Bureau of Rites (Lǐkē),
the sacrifices to Emperor Shìzǔ (Shìzǔ) of Yuán at his tomb and temple,
and to Mùhuálí (Mùhuálí) and others honored alongside, were abolished.
Emperor Tàizōng (Tàizōng) of Táng and Emperor Tàizǔ (Tàizǔ) of Sòng were moved back to the same chamber.
There were fifteen emperors in total,
and thirty-two famous ministers honored alongside.
Three Sovereigns (Sānhuáng)
In the early Míng dynasty, following the Yuán system,
the Three Sovereigns (Sānhuáng) were jointly sacrificed to on the third day of the third month and the ninth day of the ninth month.
In the first year of Hongwu (Hóngwǔ), it was ordered that grand sacrificial animals (tàiláo) be used for the sacrifices.
In the second year, it was commanded that Gōumáng (Gōumáng), Zhùróng (Zhùróng), Fēng Hòu (Fēng Hòu), and Lì Mù (Lì Mù) be honored as left and right attendants,

and the ten great physicians Yú Fú (Yú Fú), Tóng Jūn (Tóng Jūn), Jiùdà Jì (Jiùdà Jì), Shàoshī (Shàoshī), Léigōng (Léigōng), Guǐyúqū (Guǐyúqū), Bógāo (Bógāo), Qíbó (Qíbó), Shàoyú (Shàoyú), and Gāoyáng (Gāoyáng) be honored alongside.
The ritual was similar to the *shìdiàn*.
In the fourth year,
the Emperor considered the widespread sacrifices to the Three Sovereigns (Sānhuáng) in all prefectures and counties to be disrespectful.
The ritual officials debated:
"Emperor Xuánzōng (Xuánzōng) of Táng once established temples for the Three Sovereigns (Sānhuáng) and Five Thearchs (Wǔdì) in the capital.
It was not until the time of Emperor Chéngzōng (Chéngzōng) of Yuán
that Three Sovereigns (Sānhuáng) temples were established in prefectures, subprefectures, and counties.
Joint sacrifices in spring and autumn,
with medicine as their focus,
is highly improper."
The Emperor said:
"The Three Sovereigns (Sānhuáng) succeeded Heaven and established the ultimate principles,
laying the foundation for education for ten thousand generations.
Is it acceptable for them to be debased by being associated with physicians?"
He ordered that no prefecture or county should offer disrespectful sacrifices.
In the eleventh year of Zhengde (Zhèngdé), a temple for Fúxīshì (Fúxīshì) was built in Qínzhōu (Qínzhōu).
Qínzhōu (Qínzhōu)
was the ancient land of Chéngjì (Chéngjì),
following the memorial of the巡按御史 (Xún'àn Yùshǐ, Imperial Inspector) Féng Shíxióng (Féng Shíxióng).
During the Jiajing (Jiājìng) era,
a Three Sovereigns Temple (Sānhuáng Miào) was built north of the Imperial Academy of Medicine (Tàiyīyuàn),
named Jǐnghuì Diàn.
The Three Sovereigns (Sānhuáng) and the Four Attendants (sìpèi) were enshrined in the center.
Among those honored alongside,

the east side hall contained Jiùdà Jì (Jiùdà Jì), Qíbó (Qíbó), Bógāo (Bógāo), Guǐyúqū (Guǐyúqū), Yú Fú (Yú Fú), Shàoyú (Shàoyú), Shàoshī (Shàoshī), Tóng Jūn (Tóng Jūn), Léigōng (Léigōng), Mǎ Shīhuáng (Mǎ Shīhuáng), Yī Yǐn (Yī Yǐn), Biǎn Què (Biǎn Què), Chúnyú Yì (Chúnyú Yì), and Zhāng Jī (Zhāng Jī), fourteen individuals.

The west side hall contained Huà Tuó (Huà Tuó), Wáng Shūhé (Wáng Shūhé), Huángfǔ Mì (Huángfǔ Mì), Gě Hóng (Gě Hóng), Cháo Yuánfāng (Cháo Yuánfāng), Sūn Sīmiǎo (Sūn Sīmiǎo), Wéi Cízàng (Wéi Cízàng), Wáng Bīng (Wáng Bīng), Qián Yǐ (Qián Yǐ), Zhū Gōng (Zhū Gōng), Lǐ Gǎo (Lǐ Gǎo), Liú Wánsù (Liú Wánsù), Zhāng Yuánsù (Zhāng Yuánsù), and Zhū Yánxiū (Zhū Yánxiū), fourteen individuals.
Annually, on the *shàngjiǎ* day of the middle months of spring and autumn,
the senior officials of the Board of Rites (Lǐbù Tángshàngguān) performed the rites,
with two senior officials of the Imperial Academy of Medicine (Tàiyīyuàn Tángshàngguān) assisting in the offerings,
using minor sacrificial animals (shàoláo).
Furthermore, a Shèngjì Diàn was built within,
to sacrifice to the ancient physicians,
presided over by imperial medical officials.
In the twenty-first year,
the Emperor considered the regulations to be too restrictive and cramped,
and ordered the temple to be expanded.
Sainted Teachers (Shèngshī)
The sacrifices to the Sainted Teachers (Shèngshī)
began with Emperor Shìzōng (Shìzōng).
The Imperial Teachers (Huángshī) Fúxīshì (Fúxīshì), Shénnóngshì (Shénnóngshì), and Xuānyuánshì (Xuānyuánshì);
the Thearch Teachers (Dìshī) Táotángshì (Táotángshì) and Yǒuyúshì (Yǒuyúshì);
and the Kingly Teachers (Wángshī) King Yǔ (Yǔ Wáng) of Xià, King Tāng (Tāng Wáng) of Shāng, and King Wén (Wén Wáng) and King Wǔ (Wǔ Wáng) of Zhōu,
these nine sages faced south.
On the left was the Former Sage (Xiānshèng) Zhōugōng (Zhōugōng),
and on the right was the Former Teacher (Xiānshī) Kǒngzǐ (Kǒngzǐ),
both facing east and west.
Annually, on the day before the spring and autumn imperial lectures,
the Emperor, wearing a leather cap (píbiàn),
would prostrate and kneel,
performing the *shìdiàn* ceremony.
Offerings of soup, wine, dried fruits, and silk were sacrificed in the eastern chamber of the Wénhuá Diàn.
Initially,
there was a Buddhist statue in the eastern chamber.
The Emperor considered it inappropriate,
removed it,
and then sacrificed to the Former Sage (Xiānshèng) and Former Teacher (Xiānshī).
He personally composed the sacrificial texts
and performed the ritual of enshrining the spirit tablets.
The assisting ministers, ritual officials, and lecturing officials waited until the ritual was completed
before entering to bow.
Previously, in the early Hongwu (Hóngwǔ) period,
Sòng Lián (Sòng Lián), the Associate Director of the Imperial Academy (Sīyè), proposed following the views of Xióngshì (Xióngshì) of Jiàn'ān (Jiàn'ān),
to establish Fúxī (Fúxī) as the patriarch of the Daoist orthodoxy (dàotǒng),
with Shénnóng (Shénnóng), Huángdì (Huángdì), Yáo (Yáo), Shùn (Shùn), Yǔ (Yǔ), Tāng (Tāng), Wén (Wén), and Wǔ (Wǔ) arranged in sequence.
To offer ranked sacrifices in the Emperor's academy (tiānzǐ zhī xué)
would further honor the Daoist orthodoxy (dàotǒng).
Emperor Tàizǔ (Tàizǔ) did not follow this.
By this time,
Emperor Shìzōng (Shìzōng) acted according to his intention.
In the sixteenth year, the sacrifices were moved to behind the Yǒngmíng Diàn,
with the rituals performed as before.
Thereafter, officials were often dispatched to offer sacrifices on behalf of the Emperor.
In the early Longqing (Lóngqìng) period,
the rites were again performed in the eastern chamber of the Wénhuá Diàn.
Temple Sacrifices to the Ultimate Sage and Former Teacher Kǒngzǐ (Zhìshèng Xiānshī Kǒngzǐ Miào Sì)
During the Hàn, Jìn, and Suí dynasties, he was sometimes referred to as Xiānshī (先師, Former Teacher),
or Xiānshèng (先聖, Former Sage), Xuánní (宣尼), or Xuánfù (宣父).
The Táng dynasty posthumously honored him as Wénxuān Wáng (文宣王, King of Culture and Proclamation).
The Sòng dynasty added the title Zhìshèng Hào (至聖號, Supreme Sage).
The Yuán dynasty further added the title Dàchéng (大成, Great Accomplishment).
Míng Tàizǔ (明太祖) entered Jiānghuái Fǔ (江淮府),
and first paid respects at Kǒngzǐ Miào (孔子廟, Confucius Temple).
In the second month of Hóngwǔ (洪武) first year, an imperial edict commanded that Kǒngzǐ (孔子) be sacrificed with the grand offering (tàiláo) at the Guóxué (國學, National Academy),
and also dispatched envoys to Qūfù (曲阜) to offer sacrifices.
Before they departed, he issued an instruction, saying:
"The Way of Zhòngní (仲尼)
is vast and enduring,
coexisting with Heaven and Earth.
Those who possess the realm unfailingly observe sacrificial rites with reverence.
As the lord of the realm, I
aspire to greatly illuminate education and transformation
to practice the Way of the Xiānshèng (先聖).
Now that the Shìdiàn (釋奠, Offering Ceremony) has been completed at Chéngjūn (成均, National Academy),
I still dispatch you to perform the sacrificial rites at Quèlǐ (闕里).
You should approach this with reverence."
Furthermore, a system was established:
every year, in the first Dīng day of the second spring and autumn months,
the emperor would offer incense,
and officials would be dispatched to offer sacrifices at the Guóxué.
The prime minister served as the first offerer,
the Hànlín Xuéshì (翰林學士, Hanlin Academy Scholar) as the second offerer,
and the Guózǐ Jìjiǔ (國子祭酒, Libationer of the National Academy) as the final offerer.
Before the ceremony,
the emperor would observe fasting and abstinence.
The offering officials, accompanying officials, and ritual attendants all observed scattered fasting for two days,
and concentrated fasting for one day.
One day before the sacrifice,
the emperor would wear the píbiànfú (皮弁服, leather cap and ritual robe)
and proceed to Fèngtiān Diàn (奉天殿) to offer incense.
On the day of the ceremony,
the offering officials performed the rites.
In the third year, an edict abolished the封號 (fēnghào, enfeoffment titles) of all deities,
but Kǒngzǐ's (孔子) enfeoffment title remained as before.
Moreover, it was commanded that for the Qūfù (曲阜) temple courtyard,
the government would annually provide sacrificial animals and silk,
so that the Yǎnshèng Gōng (衍聖公) could manage the sacrificial rites.
In the fourth year,
the Lǐbù (禮部, Ministry of Rites) submitted a memorial to determine the rituals and objects.
The original eight biāndòu (籩豆, ritual vessels for dried and liquid foods) were changed to ten,
and biān (籩) were to be made of bamboo.
The fǔguǐ (簠簋, ritual vessels for grains), dēngxíng (登鉶, ritual vessels for soup), and dòu (豆) that were initially made of wood,
were all replaced with porcelain.
The sacrificial animals were changed to cooked ones.
There were sixty music performers,
forty-eight dance performers,
and two dance leaders,
totaling one hundred and ten people.
The Lǐbù requested to select the most outstanding citizens from the capital to serve as music and dance performers.
Tàizǔ (太祖) said:
"Music and dance are matters for scholars,
moreover, the Shìdiàn (釋奠) is for exalting the teacher.
It is appropriate to select Guózǐ Shēng (國子生, students of the National Academy) and children of high officials who are studying,
and train them in advance."
In the fifth year, Mèngzǐ (孟子) was removed from co-worship.
The following year,
the emperor said:
"Mèngzǐ distinguished heterodox doctrines,
refuted perverse theories,
and elucidated Kǒngzǐ's (孔子) Way.
He shall be reinstated to co-worship as before."
In the second month of the seventh year,
as there was a solar eclipse on the first Dīng day,
the ceremony was changed to the middle Dīng day.
In the fifteenth year,
the newly constructed Tàixué (太學, Imperial Academy) was completed.
The temple was located to the east of the academy,
with the Dàchéng Diàn (大成殿, Hall of Great Accomplishment) in the center,
two wings (wǔ) to the left and right,
and Dàchéng Mén (大成門, Gate of Great Accomplishment) in front.
To the left and right of the gate, twenty-four halberds were arrayed.
Outside the gate, to the east was the Xīshēng Chú (犧牲廚, sacrificial animal kitchen),
to the west was the Jìqì Kù (祭器庫, ritual vessel storehouse),
and further in front was the Língxīng Mén (靈星門, Spirit Star Gate).
Since its inception,
the emperor had visited it numerous times to inspect.
Upon its completion,
officials were dispatched to offer sacrifices.
The emperor personally attended the Shìdiàn,
and also decreed that Kǒngzǐ (孔子) be universally worshipped throughout the realm,
and promulgated the Shìdiàn Yízhù (釋奠儀注, Procedures for the Offering Ceremony).
For the academies of prefectures, departments, and counties,
the biāndòu (籩豆) were eight,
and the ritual vessels, animals, and pens
were all diminished compared to those at the Guóxué.
The three offerings ritual was the same,
but the Ten Philosophers and the two wings received one offering.
For these sacrifices,
each was performed by its chief official;
if there was a Bùzhèng Sī (布政司, Provincial Administration Commission), then by a Bùzhèng Sī official;
separate offerings were performed by the Confucian scholars and respected elderly scholars of the local academy.
These ceremonies were performed on the first Dīng day of the middle months of spring and autumn each year.
Initially,
the Guózǐ Jìjiǔ was dispatched to preside over the sacrifice at the Guóxué.
Later, officials from the Hànlín Yuàn (翰林院, Hanlin Academy) were dispatched,
but the Guózǐ Jìjiǔ, upon first assuming office,
was always dispatched to perform one sacrifice.
In the seventeenth year, an imperial order commanded that on the first and fifteenth days of each month,
the Guózǐ Jìjiǔ and lower-ranking officials perform the Shìcài Lǐ (釋菜禮, Simple Offering Ceremony),
and the county magistrates and lower-ranking officials proceed to the academy to offer incense.
In the twenty-sixth year, the Dàchéng Yuè (大成樂, Music of Great Accomplishment) was promulgated throughout the realm.
In the twenty-eighth year, following the suggestion of Yáng Dǐ (楊砥), a vice director of the Xíngrén Sī (行人司, Bureau of Messengers),
Yáng Xióng (揚雄) of the Hàn dynasty was removed from co-worship,
and Dǒng Zhòngshū (董仲舒) was added.
In the thirtieth year, as the Kǒngzǐ Miào (孔子廟) at the Guóxué was too narrow,
the Gōngbù (工部, Ministry of Works) was ordered to renovate it,
and its design was all planned by the emperor.
The Dàchéng Diàn (大成殿) and its gate each had six pillars,
the Língxīng Mén (靈星門) had three,
the east and west wings had seventy-six pillars,
the Shénchú Kù (神廚庫, Spirit Kitchen and Storehouse) each had eight pillars,
and the Zǎishēng Suǒ (宰牲所, Slaughtering Place) had six pillars.
In the early Yǒnglè (永樂) reign,
a temple was built to the east of the Tàixué.
In Xuāndé (宣德) third year,
based on the words of Lǐ Yì (李譯), an instructor in Wàn Xiàn (萬縣),
the Lǐbù was ordered to review and correct the names and positions of the Xiānxián (先賢, Former Worthies) in co-worship,
and promulgate them throughout the realm.
In the tenth year,
Jiǎng Míng (蔣明), an instructor in Cílì (慈利), requested that Wú Chéng (吳澄), a Yuán (元) Confucian scholar, be worshipped.
The Grand Secretaries Yáng Shìqí (楊士奇) and others stated that he should be included in co-worship,
and it was approved.
In Zhèngtǒng (正統) second year,
Hú Ānguó (胡安國), Cài Shěn (蔡沈), and Zhēn Déxiù (真德秀), Sòng (宋) Confucian scholars, were included in co-worship.
In the third year, the worship of Kǒngzǐ (孔子) in Buddhist and Daoist temples was forbidden throughout the realm.
Péi Kǎn (裴侃), a professor and descendant of the Kǒng (孔), Yán (顏), and Mèng (孟) families, stated:
"In the Wénmiào (文廟, Temple of Literature) across the realm, only the transmission of the Way is discussed
to determine the order of positions.
In the family temple at Quèlǐ (闕里),
the father-son relationship should be correctly established
according to the cardinal human relations.
Yán Zǐ (顏子), Zēng Zǐ (曾子), and Zǐsī (子思)
are sons,
co-worshipped in the main hall.
Wú Yáo (無繇), Zǐ (子), and Bóyú (伯魚)
are fathers,
co-worshipped in the corridors and wings.
Not only is the hierarchy incorrect,
but it is also feared that the spirits are not at ease.
Moreover, Shúliáng Hég (叔梁紇) has already been posthumously enfeoffed as Qǐshèng Wáng (啟聖王),
and a hall was established to the west of the Dàchéng Diàn (大成殿) for his worship.
While the fathers of Yán (顏) and Mèng (孟) are both enfeoffed as dukes,
only Bóyú (伯魚) and Zǐ (子) remain marquises.
I request that they be posthumously enfeoffed as dukes,
and together with the fathers of Yán (顏) and Mèng (孟), be co-worshipped in the Qǐshèng Wáng Diàn (啟聖王殿)."
The emperor commanded the Lǐbù to implement this,
and also discuss adding enfeoffment titles for Bóyú (伯魚) and Zǐ (子).
In Chénghuà (成化) second year,
Dǒng Zhòngshū (董仲舒) was posthumously enfeoffed as Guǎngchuān Bó (廣川伯),
Hú Ānguó (胡安國) as Jiànníng Bó (建寧伯),
Cài Shěn (蔡沈) as Chóng'ān Bó (崇安伯),
and Zhēn Déxiù (真德秀) as Pǔchéng Bó (浦城伯).
In the twelfth year, following the suggestion of Guózǐ Jìjiǔ Zhōu Hóngmó (周洪謨),
the music and dance were increased to bāyì (八佾, eight rows),
and the biāndòu (籩豆) each to twelve.
In Hóngzhì (弘治) eighth year, Yáng Shí (楊時) was posthumously enfeoffed as Jiānglè Bó (將樂伯),
and included in co-worship,
in the position after Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光).
In the ninth year, the music and dance performers were increased to seventy-two people,
following the imperial system.
In the twelfth year,
the Kǒngmiào (孔廟, Confucius Temple) at Quèlǐ (闕里) was destroyed by fire,
and the relevant authorities were ordered to rebuild it.
In the seventeenth year,
the temple was completed,
and Grand Secretary Lǐ Dōngyáng (李東陽) was dispatched to offer sacrifices and announce its completion,
and an imperial inscription was erected.
In Zhèngdé (正德) sixteenth year, an edict commanded the relevant authorities to rebuild the Kǒng (孔) family temple in Qúzhōu (衢州),
with government funds provided,
to oversee the project.
Dr. Kǒng Chéngyì (孔承義) was ordered to preside over the sacrifices.
In the ninth year of the Jiājìng reign,
Grand Secretary Zhāng Cōng stated:
"There are matters in the sacrificial rites for the Former Master [Confucius]
that ought to be corrected.
Shūliáng Hū is the father of Kǒngzǐ.
Yán Lù, Zēng, and Kǒng Lǐ are the fathers of Yán [Huí], Zēng [Shēn], and Zǐsī respectively.
The three disciples are accorded sacrifices in the temple court,
while Hū and the other fathers are only given secondary sacrifices in the two side halls.
How can this accord with the original intentions of the sages?
I request that a separate chamber be erected behind the Dàchéng Hall
to sacrifice to Shūliáng Hū,
and that Yán Lù, Zēng, and Kǒng Lǐ be placed alongside him."
The emperor considered this to be correct.
He then said:
"The sage's veneration for Heaven and for his parents is the same.
Now, with twelve *biāndòu* (sacrificial vessels),
and a calf used as the sacrificial animal,
entirely following the rites for sacrificing to Heaven,
this is also not the correct ritual.
Their posthumous titles and ceremonial robes should all be reformed."
Zhāng Cōng, following the emperor's intention,
said:
"Kǒngzǐ should be referred to as 'Former Sage, Former Master' (Xiānshèng Xiānshī),
not as 'King.'
The sacrificial building should be called a 'temple' (miào),
not a 'hall' (diàn).
For the sacrifices, wooden tablets should be used,
and the statues should be destroyed.
Ten *biāndòu* should be used,
and the music should be with six ranks of dancers (liù yì).
The titles of Duke, Marquis, and Earl for those accorded sacrifices should be abolished,
and they should simply be referred to as 'Former Worthy' (Xiānxián) or 'Former Scholar' (Xiānrú).
The twelve secondary sacrificants, such as Shēn Dǎng, Gōngbó Liáo, and Qín Rǎn, should be dismissed.
Lín Fàng, Qú Yuàn, and six others should be sacrificed to in their respective hometowns.
Hòucāng, Wáng Tōng, Ōuyáng Xiū, Hú Yuàn, and Cài Yuándìng should be added to the secondary sacrificants."
The emperor commanded the Ministry of Rites to deliberate with the scholars of the Hànlín Academy.
Compiler Xú Jiē submitted a memorial arguing against changing the titles and destroying the statues.
The emperor was enraged,
and demoted Xú Jiē.
He then personally wrote "A Discourse on Rectifying the Sacrificial Rites for Kǒngzǐ" (Zhèng Kǒngzǐ Sìdiǎn Shuō),
which generally stated that Kǒngzǐ considered the usurpation of kingship by Lǔ to be wrong,
and would certainly not himself usurp the rites of the Son of Heaven.
He further wrote "An Additional Record on Rectifying the Sacrificial Rites for Kǒngzǐ" (Zhèng Kǒngzǐ Sìdiǎn Shēnjì),
both of which were sent to the Imperial Historiography Academy.
Zhāng Cōng then composed "A Question and Memorial on Rectifying the Sacrificial Rites for Kǒngzǐ's Temple" (Zhèng Kǒngzǐ Miàosìdiǎn Huòwèn) and presented it.
The emperor deemed the arguments detailed and correct,
and also ordered the Ministry of Rites to hold a collective discussion.
Thereupon, Censor Lí Guàn and others stated:
"When the sacred ancestor first rectified the sacrificial rites,
all the titles of the gods of mountains and rivers in the empire were removed,
only the Former Master Kǒngzǐ remained as before,
which indeed had a profound meaning.
Your Majesty suspects Kǒngzǐ's sacrifices
are too grand, resembling the rites for sacrificing to Heaven.
The Master's inaccessibility
is like Heaven's impossibility of being ascended step by step;
even if compared to Heaven,
it would not be excessive.
Since the Táng dynasty honored Kǒngzǐ as Wénxuān Wáng,
the imperial rites and music have been used.
Sòng Zhēnzōng once wanted to enfeoff Kǒngzǐ as an Emperor;
some said that the Zhōu only used the title of King,
and the title of Emperor should not be added.
However, Luó Cóngyàn's argument
held that adding the title of Emperor was also acceptable.
As for Zhōu Dūnyí, he believed that Kǒngzǐ would be a King for ten thousand generations without end,
and kings would sacrifice to Kǒngzǐ.
Shào Yōng, on the other hand, believed that Zhòngní would be a King for ten thousand generations.
Among those who argued that Kǒngzǐ should not be called King,
there was only Wú Chéng.
We humbly hope that a broad study of all opinions will be made,
to seek what is most appropriate."
At that time, Lí Guàn's memorial stated:
"None is more revered than Heaven and Earth,
and none is more revered than one's father and teacher.
Your Majesty reveres Heaven and honors parents,
and should not uniquely question Kǒngzǐ's title of King as an usurpation."
The emperor was greatly enraged by this,
suspecting Lí Guàn was using this to criticize his posthumous honoring of his imperial father,
denounced him as treacherous and wicked,
and handed him over to the judicial authorities for interrogation,
stripping him of his office.
Grand Secretary Wáng Rǔméi and others also strongly argued against removing the title of King;
the emperor dismissed all their arguments as fallacies.
Thereupon, the Ministry of Rites deliberated with the various officials:
"Humans consider the sage to be supreme,
and the sage considers Kǒngzǐ to be supreme.
Sòng Zhēnzōng called Kǒngzǐ 'Zhìshèng' (Utmost Sage),
which fully expressed this meaning.
Now, on Kǒngzǐ's spirit tablet, the inscription should be 'Zhìshèng Xiānshī Kǒngzǐ,'
removing the title of King and the appellations 'Dàchéng' and 'Wénxuān.'
The Dàchéng Hall should be renamed 'Former Master Temple' (Xiānshī Miào),
and the Dàchéng Gate should be renamed 'Temple Gate' (Miàomén).
The Four Disciples (sì pèi) should be called Fùshèng Yánzǐ, Zōngshèng Zēngzǐ, Shùshèng Zǐsīzǐ, and Yàshèng Mèngzǐ.
The Ten Philosophers (shí zhé) and all disciples below them
should all be referred to as 'Xiānxián Mǒuzǐ.'
From Zuǒ Qiūmíng downwards,
all should be referred to as 'Xiānrú Mǒuzǐ.'
They should no longer be called Duke, Marquis, or Earl.
Following the regulations first established by the sacred ancestor for the Nánjīng Guózǐjiān,
wooden spirit tablets should be made.
The sizes should also be determined
and established as a fixed pattern.
The statues should be immediately removed.
For the spring and autumn sacrifices,
the old system of the early dynasty should be followed,
with ten *biāndòu* and ten *dòu*.
All schools throughout the empire
should use eight *biāndòu* and eight *dòu*.
The musical dance should be limited to six ranks of dancers.
Each school should erect a separate shrine,
in the center of which Shūliáng Hū's spirit tablet should be inscribed 'Qǐshèng Gōng Kǒng Shì Shénwèi' (Spirit Tablet of Duke Qǐshèng, Mr. Kǒng),
with Yán Wúyáo, Zēng Diǎn, Kǒng Lǐ, and Mèngsūn Shì placed alongside him,
all referred to as 'Xiānxián Mǒushì.'
As for the worthies accorded secondary sacrifices,
their merits and demerits must be examined.
Shēn Dǎng is Shēn Chéng;
one of them should be removed.
Gōngbó Liáo, Qín Rǎn, Yán Hé, Xún Kuàng, Dài Shèng, Liú Xiàng, Jiǎ Kuí, Mǎ Róng, Hé Xiū, Wáng Sù, Wáng Bì, Dù Yù, Wú Chéng should be removed from the sacrifices.
Lín Fàng, Qú Yuàn, Lú Zhí, Zhèng Zhòng, Zhèng Xuán, Fú Qián, Fàn Níng should each be sacrificed to in their hometowns.
Hòucāng, Wáng Tōng, Ōuyáng Xiū, and Hú Yuàn should be added."
The emperor ordered that all these proposals be carried out.
Furthermore, following the suggestion of Attendant Usher Xuē Kǎn,
Lù Jiǔyuān was advanced to secondary sacrifice status.
Earlier,
during the Hóngwǔ reign,
Academician Sòng Lián requested that statues be removed and spirit tablets be used,
and many ritual and musical regulations be changed,
but Tàizǔ did not approve.
Between the Chénghuà and Hóngzhì reigns,
Junior Supervisor Chéng Mǐnzhèng once said that Mǎ Róng and eight others should be expelled.
Grand Secretary Zhāng Jiǔgōng elaborated on this,
and also requested the removal of Xún Kuàng, Gōngbó Liáo, Qú Yuàn, etc.,
and the advancement of Hòucāng, Wáng Tōng, and Hú Yuàn.
This was rejected by ritual official Zhōu Hóngmó and ceased.
Now, with Zhāng Cōng strongly advocating for it,
the others dared not object.
The destruction of statues largely followed Sòng Lián's proposal,
and the removal and retention of former worthies
generally aligned with Zhāng Jiǔgōng's suggestions.
The advancement of Ōuyáng Xiū
was due to the Púyì controversy.
The following year,
the Qǐshèng Gōng Shrine at the Guózǐjiān was completed.
Following the proposal of Minister Lǐ Shí,
the spring and autumn sacrifices
were held on the same day as those at the Wén Miào.
The *biāndòu* and sacrificial animals and silks were similar to those for the Four Disciples,
the East and West secondary positions were similar to those for the Ten Philosophers,
and the secondary sacrificants, scholars Chéng Shǎng, Zhū Sōng, and Cài Yuándìng, were similar to those in the two side halls.
When imperial assistants sacrificed at the Wén Miào,
the Libationer sacrificed at the Qǐshèng Shrine.
In Nánjīng,
the Libationer sacrificed at the Wén Miào,
and the Academician sacrificed at the Qǐshèng Shrine.
Thus, the regulations were established:
In the main hall, the Former Master faced south,
and the Four Disciples faced east and west.
Slightly behind were the Ten Philosophers: Mǐnzǐ Sǔn, Rǎnzǐ Yōng, Duānmùzǐ Cì, Zhòngzǐ Yóu, Bùzǐ Shāng, Rǎnzǐ Gēng, Zǎizǐ Yǔ, Rǎnzǐ Qiú, Yánzǐ Yǎn, and Zhuānsūn Zǐshī, all facing east and west.

The secondary sacrificants in the two side halls were: Former Worthies Tántái Miè míng, Mì Bùqí, Yuán Xiàn, Gōngyě Cháng, Nángōng Shì, Gāo Chái, Qīdiāo Kāi, Fán Xū, Sīmǎ Gēng, Gōngxī Chì, Yǒu Ruò, Qín Zhāng, Shēn Chéng, Chén Kàng, Wūmǎ Shī, Liáng Zhān, Gōng Āi, Shāng Qú, Rǎn Rú, Yán Xīn, Bó Qián, Cáo Xù, Rǎn Jì, Gōngsūn Lóng, Qīdiāo Duō, Qín Shāng, Qīdiāo Túfù, Yán Gāo, Shāng Zé, Rǎnsì Chì, Rèn Bùqí, Shízuò Shǔ, Gōngliáng Rú, Gōngxià Shǒu, Gōngjiān Dìng, Hòuchù, Quándān, Xīróng Diǎn, Hǎnfù Hēi, Yán Zǔ, Róng Qí, Qín Zǔ, Zuǒrén Yǐng, Jùjǐng Jiāng, Zhèng Guó, Gōngzǔ Jùcí, Yuán Kàng, Xiàn Chéng, Lián Jié, Yàn Jí, Shúzhòng Huì, Yán Zhīpú, Guī Xùn, Yuè Kài, Gōngxī Yúrú, Dí Hēi, Kǒng Zhōng, Gōngxī Diǎn, Bùshú Chéng, Shī Zhīcháng, Qín Fēi, Yán Kuài.

Former Scholars Zuǒ Qiūmíng, Gōngyáng Gāo, Gǔliáng Chì, Fú Shèng, Gāotáng Shēng, Kǒng Ānguó, Máo Cháng, Dǒng Zhòngshū, Hòucāng, Dù Zǐchūn, Wáng Tōng, Hán Yù, Hú Yuàn, Zhōu Dūnyí, Chéng Hào, Ōuyáng Xiū, Shào Yōng, Zhāng Zài, Sīmǎ Guāng, Chéng Yí, Yáng Shí, Hú Ānguó, Zhū Xī, Zhāng Shì, Lù Jiǔyuān, Lǚ Zǔqiān, Cài Shēn, Zhēn Déxiù, Xǔ Héng, totaling ninety-one people.
In the fifth year of Lóngqìng,
Xuē Xuān was added to the secondary sacrificants.
During the Wànlì reign,
Luó Cóngyàn and Lǐ Tóng were added to the secondary sacrificants.
In the twelfth year,
Chén Xiànzhāng, Hú Jūrrén, and Wáng Shǒurén were also added to the secondary sacrificants.
In the twenty-third year,
Zhōu Dūnyí's father, Fǔchéng, from the Sòng dynasty, was added to the secondary sacrificants in the Qǐshèng Shrine.
It was also decreed that every year on the first *dīng* day of mid-spring and mid-autumn,
the emperor would issue an edict in the hall,
dispatching high officials to sacrifice to the Former Master and those alongside him.
For the Ten Philosophers, two officials from the Hànlín Academy, and for the two side halls, two officials from the Guózǐjiān, would separately offer sacrifices.
On the first day of each month,
and for each cohort of successful *jìnshì* candidates, the *shìcài* ceremony was performed.
The supervising officials of prefectural, subprefectural, county, and military academy schools would conduct the rites.
A lesser ox was used as the sacrificial animal,
and the music was the same as at the Imperial Academy.
For metropolitan prefectures and attached county schools,
only the *shìcài* ceremony was performed.
In the fifteenth year of Chóngzhēn,
because Zuǒ Qiūmíng personally received instruction from the Sage,
his title was changed to 'Former Worthy.'
Furthermore, the six Sòng scholars Zhōu, the two Chéngs, Zhāng, Zhū, and Shào were also changed to 'Former Worthy,'
positioned below the Seventy Disciples
but above the scholars of Hàn and Táng.
However, this change was only implemented at the Imperial Academy;
the temple court at Quēlǐ and the schools throughout the empire had not yet been formally notified.
Banners and Flags
There are four sacrificial rites for the banners and standards.
The first:
In the first year of Hóngwǔ (1368),
the ritual officials memorialized:
"Regarding the banners and standards that should be sacrificed to when an army marches,
the 'banner' refers to the commander's banner (yáqí).
The 'Huángdì Chūjūn Jué' (Yellow Emperor's Military Edicts) states: 'The yáqí
is the essence of the general,
and a manifestation of the army's morale.
Whenever a yáqí is first erected,
it must be sacrificed to on an auspicious day (gāngrì).'
The 'standard' (dú)
refers to the banner top.
The 'Tàibái Yīnjīng' (Secret Classic of the Great White Planet) states: 'The great general erects the dú in the central camp.
The Son of Heaven has six armies,
hence six dú are used.
They are made of yak tails
and placed on the head of the left outer horse.'
The Táng, Sòng, and Yuán dynasties all had sacrifices for banners and standards.
It is now fitting to establish a temple in the capital,
and in spring, on the day of Jīngzhé,
and in autumn, on the day of Shuāngjiàng,
send officials to offer sacrifices."
Thereupon, an order was given to build a temple behind the office of the Dūdū Fǔ (Chief Military Commission),
with the Dūdū serving as the presenting official.
The spirit tablets were inscribed with "Spirit of the Army's Yáqí, Spirit of the Six Dú."

In the second month of the seventh year (1374), an imperial edict commanded the Crown Prince, accompanied by the various princes, to proceed to the Yuèwǔ Chǎng (Reviewing Ground) to sacrifice to the banners and standards.
Seven altars were erected,
and the three-offering ceremony was performed.
Later, the spring sacrifice was discontinued,
and sacrifices were only offered on Shuāngjiàng day at the Jiàochǎng (Drill Ground).
The second:
On the day of the year-endLàxiǎng (winter sacrifice) at the Tàimiào (Imperial Ancestral Temple),
sacrifices were offered to the banners and standards outside Chéngtiānmén.
The third:
The Banner and Standard Temple was located to the left of the Shānchuān Tán (Altar of Mountains and Rivers).
Originally,
the banners and standards were sacrificed together with the spirits of Tàisuì (Jupiter) at the south of the city.
In the ninth year (1376), a separate temple was built.
Every mid-autumn,
on the day the Son of Heaven personally sacrificed at the Shānchuān Tán,
an official from the Qíshǒuwèi (Banner Guard) was dispatched to perform the rites.

For the main sacrifice, the Spirit of the Great General of the Banners, the Spirit of the Great General of the Six Standards, the Spirits of the Five-Directional Banners, the Righteous Spirit that Governs Warships, the Spirits of the Golden Drums, Horns, Muskets, and Cannons, the Spirits of Bows, Crossbows, Flying Spears, and Flying Stones, and the multitude of Five Prosperity Deities before and behind the battle lines,
a total of seven deities,
shared one altar,
facing south.
The Emperor wore a leather cap (píbiàn)
and descended from Fèngtiāndiàn to offer incense.
The presenting official performed the ritual duties.
The sacrificial items were similar to those for the Xiānnóng (First Farmer),
with seven pieces of silk,
two black and five white.
The burial of hair and blood and the gazing at the bonfire (wàngliáo)
were the same as for the spirits of wind, clouds, thunder, and rain.
After the sacrifice,
six wine vessels were placed on the ground.
Six roosters were stabbed,
and their blood was sprinkled to anoint them.
The fourth:
After the Yǒnglè reign (1403-1424),
there was a sacrifice to the Divine Banner,
specifically for the spirits of fire and thunder.
On the first and fifteenth days of each month (shuò wàng),
the Tídū (Commander) of the Shénjīyíng (Divine Machine Camp) sacrificed at the Jiàochǎng.
The sacrificial animals were a shǎoláo (minor sacrifice, typically a pig and a sheep).
All banners and standards were stored in the Nèifǔ (Imperial Treasury),
and displayed only during sacrifices.
When a vassal state (wángguó) sacrificed to banners and standards,
military officials in military attire were dispatched to perform the rites.
All weìsuǒ (military garrisons) in the empire established temples behind their public offices,
with the Zhǐhuīshǐ (Commander) as the primary offering official,
and his subordinates as the secondary and final offering officials.
The ritual items were scaled down compared to the capital.
Five Sacrifices
In the second year of Hóngwǔ (1369), regulations were established
that at the year-end Làxiǎng,
all five sacrifices were offered outside the temple gate.
In the eighth year (1375),
the Ministry of Rites memorialized:
"The rites of the Five Sacrifices (wǔsì)
varied in the Zhōu, Hàn, Táng, and Sòng dynasties.
It is now proposed that in the first month of spring, the door (hù) be sacrificed to,
with an altar erected to the left of the imperial palace gate,
presided over by the Sīmén (Official in Charge of Gates).
In the first month of summer, the stove (zào) be sacrificed to,
with an altar erected in the imperial kitchen,
presided over by an official from the Guānglùsì (Court of Imperial Entertainments).
In the last month of summer, the central hearth (zhōngliú) be sacrificed to,
with an altar erected in the danchí (vermilion steps) of the Qiánqīnggōng,
presided over by an imperial eunuch (nèiguān).
In the first month of autumn, the outer door (mén) be sacrificed to,
with an altar erected to the left of the Wǔmén,
presided over by the Sīmén.
In the first month of winter, the well (jǐng) be sacrificed to,
with an altar erected in front of the great kitchen well within the palace,
presided over by an official from the Guānglùsì.
In the first months of the four seasons, on the day of the Tàimiào sacrifice,
and in the last month of summer, on the day when earth energy is strongest (tǔwàng zhī rì),
the sacrificial animals should be a shǎoláo."
The edict was approved.
It was then decreed that the zhōngliú sacrifice be established in front of the Wénlóu (Literary Tower) outside Fèngtiāndiàn.
Additionally, at the year's end, the Five Sacrifices were jointly offered in the western wing of the Tàimiào,
with officials from the Tàichángsì (Court of Imperial Sacrifices) performing the rites.
Horse God
In the second year of Hóngwǔ (1369), an order was given to sacrifice to the spirits of the Horse Ancestor (mǎzǔ), the First Shepherd (xiānmù), the Horse Altar (mǎshè), and the Horse and Foot (mǎbù),
and an altar was built at Hòuhú.
The ritual officials stated:
"The Zhōu officials sacrificed to the Mǎzǔ in spring,
which is the Tiānsì constellation;
in summer, they sacrificed to the Xiānmù,
who was the first to raise horses;
in autumn, they sacrificed to the Mǎshè,
who was the first to ride horses;
in winter, they sacrificed to the Mǎbù,
who was the spirit causing harm to horses.
The Suí dynasty adopted the Zhōu system,
sacrificing in the middle month of the four seasons.
The Táng and Sòng dynasties followed this.
It is now decreed that in the middle months of spring and autumn,
on jiǎ, wù, or gēng days,
officials be dispatched to offer sacrifices.
Four altars are to be built,
seasonal music (shílè) is to be used,
and the three-offering ceremony is to be performed."
In the fourth year (1371),
Shǔ Míngshēng presented ten fine horses,
one of which was white,
over ten feet tall,
and could not be saddled or bridled.
Tàizǔ said:
"Heaven gives birth to extraordinary creatures,
and there must be a spirit overseeing them."
He ordered the Tàicháng to sacrifice to the Mǎzǔ with a shǎoláo,
and to press the horse down with four hundred catties of sandbags,
and have men ride it in the imperial garden.
After a long time, it gradually became docile.
The Emperor rode it to offer the evening sacrifice to the moon (xīyuè) on Qīngliángshān.
Upon its return,
he was greatly pleased,
and named it Fēiyuèfēng.
He again ordered the Tàicháng to sacrifice to the Mǎzǔ.
In the fifth year (1372), all the spirits were combined into one altar,
and only the spring sacrifice was performed annually.
In the thirteenth year of Yǒnglè (1415), the Běijīng Mǎshéncí (Horse God Temple) was established at Liánhuachí.
For the Nánjīng Mǎshén (Horse God of Nanjing),
the Nán Tàipú (Southern Court of Imperial Stud) presided over the rites.
Nanjing Divine Temples
Initially called the Ten Temples.
For Běijí Zhēnwǔ (True Martial of the North Pole), on the third day of the third month and the ninth day of the ninth month;
for Dàolín Zhēnjué Pǔjì Chánshī Bǎozhì, on the eighteenth day of the third month;
for the Dū Chénghuáng (Capital City God), on the day after the sacrifice to emperors and kings in the eighth month;
for Císhān Guǎnghuì Zhāngwáng Bó, on the eighteenth day of the second month;
for Wǔxiǎn Língshùn, on the eighth day of the fourth month and the twenty-eighth day of the ninth month;
all were sacrificed to by officials from the Nánjīng Tàichángsì.
For Hàn Mòlíng Wèi Jiǎng Zhōngliè Gōngzǐ Wén, Jìn Chéngyáng Biàn Zhōngzhēn Gōng Hú,
Sòng Jìyáng Cáo Wǔhuì Wáng Bīn, Nán Táng Liú Zhōngsù Wáng Rénzhān, and Yuán Wèiguó Zhōngsù Gōng Fúshòu, all on the first day of the four seasonal first months (sìmèng shuò),
and at year-end,
officials from the Yìngtiān Fǔ (Yìngtiān Prefecture) sacrificed.
Only the Jiǎng Temple had an additional sacrifice on the twenty-sixth day of the fourth month.
Including the Temple of Meritorious Officials (Gōngchén Miào), there were eleven.
Later, four more were added: the Guān Gōng Miào (Temple of Guān Gōng),
built in the twenty-seventh year of Hóngwǔ (1394) on the south side of Jīlóngshān,
named Hàn Qián Jiāngjūn Shòutíng Hóu.
In the tenth year of Jiājìng (1531), its error was corrected,
and it was renamed Hàn Qián Jiāngjūn Hànshòutíng Hóu.
In the four first months of the seasons and at year-end,
officials from the Yìngtiān Fǔ sacrificed;
on the thirteenth day of the fifth month,
officials from the Nánjīng Tàichángsì sacrificed.
Tiānfēi (Heavenly Consort),
