enfeoffed in the seventh year of Yǒnglè (1409) as Hùguó Bìmín Miàolíng Zhāoyìng Hóngrén Pǔjì Tiānfēi,
on the fifteenth day of the first month and the twenty-third day of the third month,
officials from the Nánjīng Tàichángsì sacrificed.
For the Tàicāng Shénmiào (Grand Granary God Temple), on the full moon days of mid-spring and mid-autumn,
officials from the Nánjīng Hùbù (Southern Ministry of Revenue) sacrificed.
For the Sīmǎ, Mǎzǔ, Xiānmù Shénmiào (Temples of the Minister of War, Horse Ancestor, and First Shepherd),
in the middle ten days of the middle months of spring and autumn,
officials from the Nánjīng Tàipúsì (Southern Court of Imperial Stud) sacrificed on selected days.
All temples used a shǎoláo,
except Zhēnwǔ and Zhēnjué Chánshī, who received vegetarian offerings (sùxiū).
Temple of Meritorious Officials
Tàizǔ, having already arranged for meritorious officials to be enshrined in the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
also commanded the construction of a separate temple on Jīlóng Shān.
Twenty-one meritorious officials were ranked;
those who had died had statues made,
while for the living, their positions were left vacant.
Main Hall: Zhōngshān Wǔníng Wáng Xú Dá, Kāipíng Zhōngwǔ Wáng Cháng Yùchūn, Qíyáng Wǔjìng Wáng Lǐ Wénzhōng, Nínghé Wǔshùn Wáng Dèng Yù, Dōng'ōu Xiāngwǔ Wáng Tāng Hé, Qiánníng Zhāojìng Wáng Mù Yīng.
Two sheep,
two pigs.

Western Annex: Yuègúo Wǔzhuāng Gōng Hú Dàhǎi, Liánggúo Gōng Zhào Déshèng, Cháogúo Wǔzhuàng Gōng Huá Gāo, Guógúo Zhōngliè Gōng Yú Tōnghǎi, Jiānggúo Xiāngliè Gōng Wú Liáng, Āngúo Zhōngliè Gōng Cáo Liángchén, Qiángúo Wēiyì Gōng Wú Fù, Yànshān Zhōngmǐn Hóu Sūn Xīngzǔ.

Eastern Annex: Yǐnggúo Gōng Féng Guóyòng, Xīhǎi Wǔzhuāng Gōng Gěng Zàichéng, Jìgúo Gōng Dīng Déxīng, Càigúo Zhōngyì Gōng Zhāng Déshèng, Hǎigúo Xiāngyì Gōng Wú Zhēn, Qígúo Wǔyì Gōng Kāng Màocái, Dōnghǎi Jùngōng Máo Chéng.
Two sheep,
two pigs.
Each of the two wings had one tablet erected,
collectively inscribed with
"Spirits of Deceased Commanders, Thousand and Hundred Households, and Garrison Commanders."
Ten sheep,
ten pigs.
In the four last months of the year,
the imperial son-in-law and commandant was dispatched to offer sacrifices.
Initially,
when Hú Dàhǎi and others died,
Tàizǔ ordered their images to be placed in the temples of Biàn Hú and Jiǎng Zǐwén.
When the Temple of Meritorious Officials was completed,
they were moved there for worship.
In Yǒnglè 3, because Zhōngshān Wáng's achievements and virtues were paramount,

it was also ordered that on New Year's Day, Qīngmíng, Zhōngyuán, Mèngdōng, and Dōngzhì, officials from the Tàicháng Sì (Court of Imperial Sacrifices) be sent to offer sacrifices at the family temple of the Dàgōng Fāng,
using "shàoláo" (a lesser sacrifice, a pig and a sheep).
Nine Temples in the Capital
The nine temples worshipped in the capital.
The Zhēnwǔ Temple,
built in Yǒnglè 13,
to worship Běijí Yòushèng Zhēnjūn.
In Zhèngdé 2, it was renamed Língmíng Xiǎnyòu Gōng,
located east of Hǎizi Qiáo;
the sacrifice dates were the same as in Nánjīng.
The Dōngyuè Tàishān Temple,
outside Cháoyáng Mén,
sacrificed on the twenty-eighth day of the third month.
The Capital Chénghuáng Temple,
sacrificed on the eleventh day of the fifth month.
The Hànshòutíng Hóu Guān Gōng Temple,
built during the Yǒnglè reign.
In Chénghuà 13,
an imperial edict also commanded the construction of a temple east of Wǎnpíng Xiàn,
sacrificed on the thirteenth day of the fifth month.
All these sacrifices were conducted by officials from the Tàicháng Sì.
The Capital Tàicāng Shén Temple was built in Tàicāng,
sacrificed by officials from the Hùbù (Ministry of Revenue).
The Sīmǎ, Mǎzǔ, and Xiānmù Shén Temples,
sacrificed by officials from the Tàipú Sì (Court of Imperial Stud).
The Sòng Wénchéng Xiàng Temple,
in Yǒnglè 6, upon the request of Tàicháng Bóshì Liú Lǚjié,
was built west of the Shùntiān Fǔ School.
The Yuán Shìzǔ Temple,
abolished during the Jiājìng reign.
All were sacrificed by officials from Shùntiān Fǔ in mid-second and mid-eighth months.
Hóng'ēn Língjì Gōng,
worshipping Xú Zhīzhèng and Zhī'è.
In Yǒnglè 15,
a temple was established west of the Imperial City;
on New Year's Day, Winter Solstice, and imperial birthdays,
one official each from the Nèigé (Grand Secretariat), Lǐbù (Ministry of Rites), and the eunuchs offered sacrifices.
On their birthdays,
officials from the Lǐbù offered sacrifices.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
Grand Secretary Liú Jiàn and others requested that no Grand Secretaries be dispatched.
During the Jiājìng reign,
it was changed to sending officials from the Tàicháng Sì.
As for Rónggúo Gōng Yáo Guǎngxiào,
in Hóngxī 1, he was enshrined in the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
In Jiājìng 9, his temple worship was revoked,
and he was moved to Dàxīnglóng Sì,
in the northwest corner of the Imperial City.
Later, the temple burned down,
and he was again moved to Chónggúo Sì.
Dōngyuè and the Capital Chénghuáng used "tàiláo" (a grand sacrifice, an ox, a pig, and a sheep);
the five temples used "shàoláo";
Zhēnwǔ and Língjì Gōng used vegetarian offerings.
Various Temples of Deities
In Hóngwǔ 1, an order was issued to the Zhōngshū Shěng (Central Secretariat) to instruct prefectures and counties
to seek out deities deserving of worship.
Famous mountains and great rivers, sage emperors and enlightened kings, loyal ministers and martyrs,
all who had rendered service to the state and bestowed favor upon the people,
were to be recorded in the sacrificial canon,
and officials were ordered to offer sacrifices seasonally.
In Hóngwǔ 2, an edict was again issued to all deities under heaven,
who had consistently performed meritorious deeds for the people,
and whose deeds were clearly manifest,
even if not formally sacrificed to,
people were forbidden from destroying or demolishing their temples.
In Hóngwǔ 3, the封号 (titles) of various deities were set,
and all overly complimentary titles from later generations were removed.
Any temple of a deity under heaven not in compliance with the sacrificial canon
was considered an illicit temple,
and officials were not permitted to offer sacrifices there.
In Hóngzhì 1,
Zhāng Jiǔgōng of the Lǐkē (Office of Rites) stated:
"If the sacrificial canon is upright, then people's hearts will be upright.
Currently, besides the regular sacrifices of the court,
there are also offerings to Shìjiāmóuní Wénfó, Sānqīng Sānjìng Jiǔtiān Yìngyuán Léishēng Pǔhuà Tiānzūn, Jīnyùquè Zhēnjūn Yuánjūn,
Shénfù Shénmǔ,
and in various Daoist temples, there are also sacrifices to Shuǐguān Xīngjūn
and various deities and emperors,
which is not the way to set an example for the empire."
The emperor sent his memorial to the Lǐbù,
where Minister Zhōu Hóngmó and others stated: Shìjiāmóuní Wénfó was born in the Central Indian Kingdom of the West.
Those who follow his teachings
take the original nature as the Dharmakāya,
and the virtuous deeds as the Sambhogakāya,
combining the true body
into three,
but in reality, it is one person.
Daoists take Lǎozǐ as their master.
Zhū Xī once said:
"If Yùqīng Yuánshǐ Tiānzūn is not the Dharmakāya of Lǎozǐ,
and Shàngqīng
Tàishàng Dàojūn is not the Sambhogakāya of Lǎozǐ,
and if two images are established,
they are also not one with Lǎozǐ.
And Lǎozǐ himself is Tàishàng Lǎojūn of Shàngqīng;
this is imitating Buddhism but doing so erroneously."
From now on, whenever there are festivals like Wànshòu,
no auspicious fasting rituals should be constructed,
or in case of funeral rites,
no commendatory fasting rituals
should be constructed.
Sacrifices by dispatched officials to Dàxīnglóng Sì and Cháotiān Gōng are all to be halted.
As for Běijí Zhōngtiān Xīngzhǔ Zǐwēi Dàdì,
the five stars of the North Pole are within the Zǐwēi Yuán.
In the early Zhèngtǒng reign,
the Zǐwēi Diàn was built,
with statues erected for sacrifice and prayer.
Indeed, the *yōu yáo* (dark and distant) sacrifice to the stars
is an ancient rite.
But now to image it as a human,
and to call it an emperor,
when checked against the sacrificial canon,
it truly has no basis.
As for Léishēng Pǔhuà Tiānzūn,
Daoists consider him the general controller of the five thunders,
and also take the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month as the day of the Tiānzūn's manifestation.
Therefore, yearly
on this day, officials are dispatched to Xiǎnlíng Gōng to offer sacrifices.
However, wind, clouds, thunder, and rain
are worshipped together at the Southern Suburbs,
and the Altar of Mountains and Rivers also has autumn sacrifices,
so this sacrifice should also
be abolished.
As for Zǔshī Sāntiān Fújiào Fǔxuán Dàfǎshī Zhēnjūn,
records say:
"Zhāng Dàolíng of Hàn,
was skilled in curing illnesses with talismans.
During the Tiānbǎo reign of Táng,
and Xīníng and Dàguān periods of Sòng,
he was repeatedly honored as Zhèngyī Jìngyìng Zhēnjūn,
and his descendants also received titles.
The current dynasty still inherits the title of Zhèngyī Sìjiào Zhēnrén."
However,
Shào BóWēn of Sòng said:
"Zhāng Lǔ's ancestors, Líng and his father Héng,
transmitted talismanic methods to each other,
and called themselves 'Teacher Lords'."
Now, the fifteenth day of the first month is taken as Líng's birthday,
and officials are dispatched
on this day
to Xiǎnlíng Gōng to offer sacrifices and prayers,
which is also not part of the sacrificial canon.
As for the Dàxiǎo Qīnglóng Shén (Greater and Lesser Green Dragon Deities),
records say:
"There was a monk named Lú,
who resided on Xīshān.
Two young boys came to serve him.
At that time, there was a long drought,
and the boys entered the pond and transformed
into two green dragons,
whereupon rain was obtained.
Later, Lú was granted the title 'Gǎnyìng Chánshī,'
a temple was built and statues erected,
and a separate dragon shrine was established by the pond.
During the Xuāndé reign,
Dàyuántōng Sì
was built,
the two dragons were given additional titles,
and sacrifices were offered in spring and autumn."
Recently, there have been continuous droughts,
and prayers have gone unanswered,
so it is clear that they are not worthy of veneration.
As for Zǐtóng Dìjūn,
records say:
"The deity's surname was Zhāng, given name Yàzǐ,
residing on Qīqǔ Shān in Shǔ.
He served in Jìn and died in battle,
and people built a temple for him.
During Táng and Sòng, he was repeatedly
enfeoffed up to Yīngxiǎn Wáng.
Daoists say that the emperor commanded Zǐtóng to manage the affairs of Wénchāng Fǔ and human official salaries,
hence Yuán added the title 'Dìjūn,'
and all schools under heaven
There are also temples for sacrifices.
During the Jǐngtài reign,
the old temple in the capital was expanded and renovated.
Annually, on the third day of the second month, the god's birthday,
an envoy was dispatched to offer sacrifices."
Since Zǐtóng's spiritual power was manifested
in Shǔ,
it is appropriate for the temple to be situated in that area.
The six stars of Wénchāng are unrelated to him,
so it is fitting to order their abolition.
The temples dedicated to him in schools throughout the realm
should all be demolished.
The Běijí Yòushèng Zhēnjūn
is the Xuánwǔ seven mansions;
later generations considered him a Zhēnjūn [Perfected Lord],
and depicted turtles and snakes beneath him.
Sòng Zhēnzōng, to avoid a taboo name,
changed it to
Zhēnwǔ.
At the beginning of the Jìngkāng reign,
he was given the additional title Yòushèng Zhùshùn Língyìng Zhēnjūn.
The Gazetteer states:
"Zhēnwǔ was the crown prince of Jìnglè Wáng,
who cultivated himself on Wǔdāng Shān,
achieved功成飛昇 (perfection and ascended).
He was commanded by the Heavenly Emperor to guard the north.
With unbound hair and bare feet,
he raised a black standard and a dark banner."
This is an embellishment by Daoists.
The imperial stele of our dynasty
states that
Tàizǔ, in pacifying the realm,
received much unseen assistance,
and once built a temple in Nánjīng to worship him.
When Tàizōng quelled the troubles,
because the deity had shown manifest merit,
temples were also
rebuilt in the northeast corner of the capital city and on Wǔdāng Shān.
In both capitals, officials were dispatched on the first and fifteenth of each month to offer sacrifices,
and Wǔdāng Shān also had a dedicated official to oversee the sacrifices.
Xiànzōng once cast a gold image.
Now, it is requested that we only follow the precedent from the Hóngwǔ era,
offering vegetarian dishes on the third day of the third month and the ninth day of the ninth month each year,
with a Táicháng official
dispatched to offer sacrifices,
and all other practices be stopped and abolished.
As for Chóng'ēn Zhēnjūn and Lóng'ēn Zhēnjūn:
Daoists say Chóng'ēn's surname was Sà and given name Jiān,
a native of Xīshǔ,
who in Sòng Huīzōng's time studied magic from Wáng Shìchén, Lín
Língsù and others, with proven efficacy.
Lóng'ēn,
on the other hand, is Yùchú Huǒfǔ Tiānjiàng Wáng Língguān,
who also studied talismanic magic from Sà.
During the Yǒnglè reign,
because the Daoist
Zhōu Sīdé was skilled in transmitting Língguān's methods,
a Tiānjiàng Temple and an Ancestral Master Hall were built west of the Forbidden City.
During the Xuāndé reign,
it was renamed Dàdé Guàn
and the two Zhēnjūn were enfeoffed.
In the early Chénghuà reign, it was renamed Xiǎnlíng Gōng.
New robes were changed annually,
at no small expense.
Recently, prayers have gone unanswered,
so these should also be abolished.
As for Jīnquè Shàngdì and Yùquè Shàngdì:
the gazetteer states:
"The Língjì Gōng in Mǐnxiàn worshipped Xú Wēn's sons Zhīzhèng and Zhī'è from the Five Dynasties period.
The imperial
stele of our dynasty states that Tàizōng once suffered from illness,
prayed to the deities, and received an immediate response,
thus greatly renovating the temples in the Mǐn region
and offering sacrifices in spring and autumn.
He also established a temple in the capital,
and additionally enfeoffed them as Jīnquè
Zhēnjūn and Yùquè Zhēnjūn.
During the Zhèngtǒng and Chénghuà reigns,
they were repeatedly granted the title Shàngdì.
Officials were dispatched for sacrifices on the first and fifteenth of each month and on festive occasions,
and fresh offerings were made in due season,
with robes changed
four times a year."
The lineage and deeds of these deities
were not inherently extraordinary;
their usurped titles should be rectified,
and their extravagant expenses should also be curtailed.
As for Shénfù Shèngdì, Shénmǔ Yuán
jūn, and Jīn Yùquè Yuánjūn:
these are the parents of the two Xú,
and their consorts.
The Sòng dynasty enfeoffed their father, the King of Qí, as Zhōngwǔ Zhēnrén,
and their mother, Lady Tián, as Rén
shòu Xiānfēi,
with their consorts all becoming Xiānfēi.
From Yǒnglè to Chénghuà,
they were repeatedly granted their current titles,
which should also be stripped, and their worship abolished.
As for the deity of Dōngyuè Tàishān:
Tàishān is the chief of the Five Sacred Mountains,
and its temple is at the foot of the mountain in Tài'ān Zhōu.
Also, every year there are combined sacrifices at the Southern Suburb and the Mountain and River Altar.
Outside Cháoyáng Mén, there is an old Dōngyuè temple from the Yuán dynasty,
which our dynasty has maintained.
Since sacrifices are already offered exclusively within the domain,
and combined sacrifices are made at the suburban altars,
then the sacrifices at this
temple
are indeed redundant.
As for the deity of the Jīngshī Dūchénghuáng:
it was formerly located southwest of Shùntiān Fǔ.
The eleventh day of the fifth month was considered the deity's birthday,
so on this day and on festival occasions, officials were
dispatched to offer sacrifices.
However, the Chénghuáng deity
is not a human ghost;
how can it have a birthday?
Moreover, since the Southern Suburb autumn sacrifices already include it,
sacrifices on its birthday and festival occasions
are inappropriate.
All these should be abolished.
When the proposal was submitted,
an order was given for the construction of rituals (zhāijiào)
and the dispatch of officials for sacrificial announcements,
and the sacrifices at the Dōngyuè, Zhēnwǔ, Chénghuáng, and Língjì Gōng temples
were to remain as before.
The imperial titles of the two Xú Zhēnjūn and their parents and wives were revoked,
and they were restored to their old enfeoffments.
Their crowns, robes, and other items were to be returned and burned,
and the rest was to be carried out as proposed.
According to the sacrificial canons,

in Yìng Tiān, offerings were made to Chén Qiáo, Yáng Bāngyì, Yáo Xīng, and Wáng Huá;
in Chéng Dū, to Lǐ Bīng, Wén Wēng, and Zhāng Yǒng;

in Jiàn Níng, to Xiè Yífǔ;

During the reign of Xuān Zōng,

During the reign of Yīng Zōng,

During the reign of Xiàn Zōng,

During the reign of Xiào Zōng,

in Jiàn Níng, to Liú Zǐhuī;
in Wū Sà, to Tán Yuān;
in Lú Líng, to Wén Tiānxiáng;
in Wù Yuán, to Zhū Xī;
in Dū Chāng, to Chén Hào;
in Ráo Zhōu, to Jiāng Wànlǐ;
in Fú Zhōu, to Chén Wénlóng;

in Guǎngxī, to Mǎ Kǎi.
During the reign of Wǔ Zōng,
in Zhēn Dìng, offerings were made to Yán Gǎoqīng and Zhēn Qīng;
in Sháo Zhōu, additional offerings were made to Zhāng Jiǔlíng's son Zhěng;
in Yí Zhōu, to Zhū Gěliàng;
in Xiāo Shān, to Yóu Zuò and Luó Cóngyàn.
All were famous ministers of successive dynasties,
whose deeds were prominent.
After local officials petitioned,
ritual officials deliberated and reported,
and the events are recorded in the Veritable Records,
with verifiable dates.
As for the ministers of the Ming dynasty who rivaled those of previous histories,
whether for their achievements,
or their learning and conduct,
or their integrity,
or their sacrifice in death,
they are enumerated in local gazetteers,
and inscribed on steles;
there is no shortage of them.
Among the most significant:
the Loyal Ministers' Shrine at Pó Yáng Hú worshipped Dīng Pǔláng and thirty-four others;
the Loyal Ministers' Shrine at Nán Chāng worshipped Zhào Déshèng and thirteen others;
the Loyal Ministers' Temple at Tài Píng worshipped Huā Yún, Wáng Dǐng, and Xǔ Yuàn;
the Loyal Ministers' Shrine at Jīn Huá worshipped Hú Dàhǎi.
All these canons were personally established by Tài Zǔ.
Subsequently,
in Tōng Zhōu, offerings were made to Cháng Yùchūn;
at Shān Hǎi Guān, to Xú Dá;
in Sū Zhōu, to Xià Yuánjí and Zhōu Chén;
in Huái Ān, to Chén Xuān;
at Hǎi Zhōu Wèi, to Wèi Qīng and Xú Ānshēng;
in Gān Zhōu, to Máo Zhōng;
in Yú Lín, to Yú Zǐjùn;
in Háng Zhōu, to Yú Qiān;
in Xiāo Shān, to Wèi Jì;
in Tīng Zhōu, to Wáng Dé'rén;
in Guǎng Zhōu, to Yáng Xìnmín and Máo Jí;
in Yún Nán, to Mù Yīng and Mù Shèng;
in Guì Zhōu, to Gù Chéng;
in Lú Líng, to Liú Qiú and Lǐ Shímiǎn;
in Guǎng Xìn, to Dèng Yóng;
in Bǎo Qìng, to Hè Xīnglóng;
in Shàng Háng, to Wǔ Jì and Dīng Quán;
in Qìng Yuǎn, to Yè Zhēn;
in Yún Nán, to Wáng Yī and Wú Yún;
in Qīng Tián, to Liú Jī;
in Píng Yáng, to Xuē Xuān;
in Háng Zhōu, to Zōu Jì and Xú Shànshù;
in Jīn Huá, to Zhāng Mào.
All these are widely known
and clearly verifiable.
As for other spirits of mountains, rivers, and dragons in prefectures and counties, loyal and heroic individuals,
and those worshipped because prayers were answered,
the records in the Collected Statutes
are even more detailed.
The Lì Tán (Altars for Spirits of the Dead)
The Altars for the Grand Lì (Taì Lì Tán) are for sacrificing to unenshrined spirits.
The Spring and Autumn Annals says,
"When spirits have a place to return,
they will not become malevolent ghosts."
This is its meaning.
According to the sacrificial rites,
the Son of Heaven sacrifices to the Grand Lì,
feudal lords sacrifice to the Public Lì (Gōng Lì),
and grand masters sacrifice to the Clan Lì (Zú Lì).
The Rites for the Burial of a Scholar says,
"When ill, one prays to the Lì."
Zhèng's commentary states,
"During the Hàn dynasty, common folk all sacrificed to the Lì in autumn,"
which means this sacrifice reached both high and low.
However, later generations did not perform it.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ (1370), a system was established:
In the capital, the Grand Lì were sacrificed to.
An altar was set up in Xuánwǔ Hú.
Annually, on Qīngmíng and the first day of the tenth month, an official was dispatched to offer sacrifice.
Seven days prior,
a summons was issued to the City God of the capital.
On the day of the sacrifice,
the divine tablets of the City Gods of the capital and provinces were placed on the altar,
and the tablets of the unenshrined spirits were placed below the altar, to the east and west.
Three sheep,
three pigs,
and three *shi* of cooked rice were offered.
Kingdoms sacrificed to the Kingdom Lì (Guó Lì);
prefectures and departments sacrificed to the Commandery Lì (Jùn Lì);
counties sacrificed to the District Lì (Yì Lì).
All set up altars north of the city,
and performed two sacrifices a year, as in the capital.
Village communities sacrificed to the Village Lì (Xiāng Lì).
Later, it was stipulated that the Commandery Lì, District Lì, and Village Lì
all be sacrificed to on Qīngmíng, the fifteenth day of the seventh month, and the first day of the tenth month.
Collation Notes
Treatise Twenty-Seventh, Rites Five (Auspicious Rites Five), Temple System: Dì and Xiá Sacrifices, Seasonal Offerings, Presenting New Harvests, Adding Posthumous Titles, Temple Taboos.
System of Ancestral Temples
In the early Míng, four ancestral temples were built southeast of the imperial city,
each being a separate temple.
The Imperial Great-Great-Grandfather resided in the center;
the Imperial Great-Grandfather was first to the east;
the Imperial Grandfather was first to the west;
the Imperial Father was second to the east.
All faced south.
In the central chamber of each temple, the spirit tablet was enshrined.
There were two side chambers to the east and west,
and two covered corridors on the sides.
There were three gates,
with twenty-four halberds at each gate.
Outside was the main palace compound.
South of the main gate was the fasting chamber,
and west of that, the food preparation chamber,
both with five bays,
facing north.
East of the gate,
the divine kitchen had five bays,
facing west.
South of that was one animal slaughtering pond,
facing south.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ (1368), the Central Secretariat was ordered to gather Confucian ministers to deliberate on the sacrificial canons.
Lǐ Shàncháng and others stated: According to the Zhōu system,
the Son of Heaven had seven ancestral temples.
And the Shāng Shū says,
"The temple of the seventh generation
can be used to observe virtue,"
from which it is known that the Son of Heaven having seven temples
has existed since ancient times.
Tài Zǔ's temple would not be moved for a hundred generations.
The three *zhāo* and three *mù* were arranged by generational order,
and moved when kinship ended.
This was the regular rite for those who possessed the empire.
As for King Wén of Zhōu and King Wǔ of Zhōu,
though their kinship had ended and they should have been removed,
because of their merits, they deserved to be honored as patriarchs.
Therefore, a separate temple was established for each,
called the Wén 世室 (Ancestral Chamber of Wén) and Wǔ 世室 (Ancestral Chamber of Wǔ),
which also would not be moved for a hundred generations.
The Hàn dynasty established a temple for each emperor,
without ordering *zhāo* and *mù*,
and also had temples in commanderies and states, as well as funerary garden temples.
When Guāng Wǔ restored the dynasty,
he established the Gāo Miào in Luò Yáng,
sacrificing to
Gāo Zǔ and Emperors Wén, Wǔ, Xuān, and Yuán, five emperors in total.
Also, in the old Gāo Miào in Cháng'ān,
he sacrificed to Emperors Chéng, Āi, and Píng, three emperors.
Separately, four ancestral temples were established in Nán Yáng's
Chōng Líng,
sacrificing to his father, the Lord of Nán Dùn, and the four generations above him.
Up to Emperor Míng, his last will decreed that his spirit tablet be stored in a separate chamber where Empress Guāng Liè changed clothes.
Later emperors followed suit,
all
being stored in the temple of Shì Zǔ.
Hence, the system of 'same hall, different chambers'
persisted until the Yuán dynasty, without change.
Emperor Gāo Zǔ of Táng honored his great-great-grandfather, great-grandfather, and father,
establishing four temples in Cháng'ān.
Emperor Tài Zōng debated establishing seven temples,
leaving the chamber of the Great Ancestor vacant.
Emperor Xuán Zōng innovated the system,
establishing
nine chambers,
sacrificing to eight generations.
During the reign of Emperor Wén Zōng,
ritual officials stated that Emperor Jǐng, who received his enfeoffment from Táng,
and Emperors Gāo Zǔ and Tài Zōng, who founded the dynasty and received the Mandate,
should not be moved for a hundred generations.
When kinship ended
of the ruler.
Ritual demands periodic removal of ancestral tablets to a secondary shrine,
while at the Dì and Xiá sacrifices, they are all worshipped together as usual.
Subsequently, the three ancestral temples of Jìng, Wén, and Wǔ were considered one generation.
Therefore, throughout the Táng dynasty,
there were always
nine generations and eleven chambers.
From the Sòng dynasty, Tàizǔ posthumously honored the four ancestors Xī, Shùn, Yì, and Xuān.
Whenever a Dì sacrifice occurred,
the ancestral tablets were arranged according to zhāomù sequence,
leaving the east-facing position empty.
Shénzōng designated
Xīzǔ as the founding ancestor of the Tàimiào.
By the time of Huīzōng, the Tàimiào was expanded to ten chambers,
with five ancestors never being removed.
In the Chóngníng era,
Wáng Sù's theory was adopted, stating that the two removed ancestral tablets
were beyond the seventh generation,
and thus nine temples were built.
Gāozōng moved south,
sacrificing to nine generations.
By Níngzōng's reign,
a separate hall for the four ancestors was first built,
and Tàizǔ's east-facing
position was rectified.
Yuán Shìzǔ built the ancestral temple in Yānjīng,
with Tàizǔ placed in the center
as the unmoving ancestor.
By the Tàidìng era,
there were seven generations and ten chambers.
Now, it is requested to posthumously honor the four generations of great-great-grandfather, great-grandfather, grandfather, and father,
each with their own temple.
Thereupon, the deceased great-great-grandfather was posthumously titled Xuán Huángdì,
with the temple name Dézǔ,
and the deceased great-great-grandmother was titled Xuán Huánghòu.
The deceased great-grandfather was posthumously titled Huángdì,
with the temple name Yìzǔ,
and the deceased great-grandmother was titled Huánghòu.
The deceased grandfather was posthumously titled Yù Huángdì,
with the temple name Xīzǔ,
and the deceased grandmother was titled Yù Huánghòu.
The deceased father was posthumously titled Chún Huángdì,
with the temple name Rénzǔ,
and the deceased mother, Lady Chén, was titled Chún Huánghòu.
An imperial edict ordered the manufacture of Tàimiào sacrificial vessels.
Tàizǔ said:
"Ritual conforms to human sentiment
and can be initiated based on righteousness.
What is precious is to weigh and measure appropriately,
and to make adjustments according to the times.
In recent times, people rigidly adhere to antiquity,
fond of using ancient biāndòu and the like
to sacrifice to their ancestors.
Since these are not used when alive,
it is utterly meaningless
to use them for the dead.
Kǒngzǐ said: 'Serve the dead as if serving the living,
serve the absent as if serving the present.'
Therefore, the implements and attire for the ancestral temple
should all be according to the rites for serving the living."
Thereupon, silver vessels were made
and gilded with gold.
There were eight wine pots, bowls, and basins,
two hundred and forty vermilion lacquer plates and bowls,
and all the clothes racks, pillow mats, trunks, screens, and bathing rooms were prepared.
Later, an edict further commanded that vessels gilded with silver
should all be replaced with gold.
In the second year, an edict stated that the sacrificial texts for the Tàimiào should only refer to the emperor as "Filial Son Emperor" (Xiàozǐ Huángdì),
and not "subject."
Whenever the Heir Apparent was dispatched to perform the rites,
he should only be referred to as "the eldest son so-and-so" (mìng chángzǐ mǒu),
not "Heir Apparent."
Later, he was called "Filial Great-Grandson Emperor" (Xiàoxuánsūn Huángdì),
and then changed to "Filial Great-Grandson Successor Emperor" (Xiàozēngsūn Sì Huángdì).
Initially,
one piece of silk was used for each chamber in the Tàimiào.
In the second year, following the Ministry of Rites' deliberation,
two pieces of white silk were used.
Also, following the memorial of Minister Cuī Liàng,
guī and zàn scepters were made.
In the eighth year, the Tàimiào was rebuilt.
The main hall was at the front,
and the sleeping hall at the back.
Both halls and their wings had two side corridors.
The sleeping hall had nine bays,
each containing a chamber,
housing the ancestral tablets,
in the style of "same hall, different chambers."
In the tenth month of the ninth year,
the new Tàimiào was completed.
The central chamber housed Dézǔ,
the first eastern chamber housed Yìzǔ,
the first western chamber housed Xīzǔ,
and the second eastern chamber housed Rénzǔ,
all facing south.
In the fifteenth year,
the ancestral tablet of Empress Xiàocí was enshrined in the Tàimiào for worship,
and subsequent empress enshrinements followed this precedent.
Upon Jiànwén's ascension,
Tàizǔ's tablet was enshrined in the temple.
The divine seat in the main hall was next to Xīzǔ,
facing east.
The ancestral tablet in the sleeping hall was in the second western chamber,
facing south.
Chéngzǔ moved the capital
and built the temple according to the Nánjīng design.
In the seventh month of Xuāndé first year,
the Ministry of Rites presented the ceremony for enshrining Tàizōng's ancestral tablet.
One day beforehand,
an official was dispatched to the Tàimiào to perform the sacrificial announcement rite.
In the afternoon,
the Grand auspicious sacrifice was performed in the Jǐyán Hall.
At dawn the next day,
wine and fruits were laid out in the Jǐyán Hall,
and two imperial palanquins and four decorated pavilions for the imperial seal and patent were placed on the Dānbì in front of the hall.
The emperor, wearing light-colored robes,
completed the sacrificial announcement rite,
whereupon the Supervisor of Rituals knelt and requested the ancestral tablet to ascend the palanquin,
to be escorted to the Tàimiào for enshrinement.
Two eunuchs carried the ancestral tablet,
and four eunuchs carried the imperial seal and patent,
exiting through the central door of the hall,
and were placed in the imperial palanquins and decorated pavilions.
The emperor followed to the Sīshàn Gate,
changed into sacrificial robes,
and ascended the imperial carriage.
Outside the Wǔmén Gate,
ceremonial guards with umbrellas and fans led the way.
Inside the Miàojiē Gate,
the emperor descended from the imperial carriage.
The Supervisor led him to the imperial palanquin and reported,
kneeling to request the ancestral tablet to be enshrined in the Tàimiào,
then prostrated himself,
and rose.
Eunuchs carried the ancestral tablet, imperial seal, and patent,
and the emperor followed,
entering through the central gate,
to the third eastern chamber of the sleeping temple,
where it was enshrined facing south.
The emperor kowtowed,
and upon completion,
the sacrifice followed the regular sacrificial rites.
Civil and military officials wore sacrificial robes and performed the rites.
The divine seat in the main hall
was next to Rénzǔ's,
facing west.
In the fifth month of the second year,
Rénzōng's ancestral tablet was enshrined in the temple,
following the previous rites.
In the sleeping hall,
it was in the third western chamber,
facing south.
In the main hall,
it was next to Gāozǔ's,
facing east.
Subsequent enshrinements of deceased emperors followed
this precedent.
In the twelfth month of Zhèngtǒng seventh year, Empress Zhāo's ancestral tablet was enshrined in the temple.
The ancestral tablet proceeded to the divine seats of the previous emperors to pay respects.
After the rites were completed,
the Tàicháng Sì officials announced "bestow seat,"
and eunuchs carried her robes and crown,
placing them with Rénzōng's divine seat.
"Request Emperor Xuānzōng to pay respects" was announced.
Eunuchs carried Xuānzōng's robes and crown and placed them on a mat,
performed the four prostrations,
and then enshrined them on the seat.
When Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
Xiànzōng was to be enshrined in the ancestral temple.
At that time, the nine ancestral temples were already complete.
Those who debated the matter all said that the four temples of Dé, Yì, Xī, and Rén
should be successively moved to the side temple (tiao).
The ritual officials said:
"Since the state's Dédào upward,
one cannot determine the generational order,
so Dédào is like Hòujì of Zhōu,
and cannot be moved to the side temple.
When Xiànzōng is enshrined,
Yìzǔ should be moved to the side temple.
It is appropriate to build a separate side temple
behind the sleeping hall of the Grand Ancestral Temple,
following the ancient system of a 'jia shi' (attached room).
At the end of the year, the tablets of those moved to the side temple will be brought together for joint worship,
following the ancient ritual of 'xia ji' (joint sacrifice)."
Yáng Shǒuchén, an Attendant Minister of the Ministry of Personnel, said:
"According to ritual,
the Son of Heaven has seven ancestral temples,
honoring ancestors for their accomplishments and founders for their virtue.
Dédào can be compared to Bào Yǐ of Shāng and Yǎ Yǔ of Zhōu,
not to Qì or Hòujì.
The debaters are accustomed to seeing Sòng Confucians who adopted Wáng Ānshí's theory,
thus making it that the seven temples already have a founding ancestor
and also a Grand Ancestor.
The Grand Ancestor, having been associated with Heaven,
yet cannot occupy the main south-facing position,
which is not the correct ritual.
I now request to move Dédào, Yìzǔ, and Xīzǔ to the side temple simultaneously.
From Rénzǔ downward, there will be seven temples.
When all are moved to the side temple in due course,
then Tàizǔ will be likened to Qì and Hòujì,
and the tablets moved to the side temple will be stored in the rear sleeping hall,
while the 'xia' ritual will be performed in the front hall.
For seasonal sacrifices, Tàizǔ will be honored.
For the 'xia' sacrifice, Dédào will be honored.
Thus, accomplishments and virtue will both be exalted,
and grace and righteousness will also be complete."
The Emperor followed the ritual officials' suggestion,
building a side temple behind the sleeping hall,
and dispatched officials to offer sacrifices and announce it to the ancestral temples.
The Emperor wore plain clothes and announced to Xiànzōng's mat and cushion.
After the sacrifice,
Yìzǔ's spirit tablet and robes were reverently moved to the rear hall,
while the bed curtains, imperial seat, and ceremonial objects were stored in the spirit treasury.
Subsequent transfers to the side temple followed this example.
In the spring of the ninth year of Jiājìng (1530),
Shìzōng performed a special sacrifice.
He ordered that screens be set up inside the hall as in the nine temples,
with all the sagely emperors facing south,
each offering their sacrifices.
Three prayers were read,
and the rest remained as before.
In the first month of the tenth year (1531),
the Emperor, due to the revised temple sacrifices, announced it to the Grand Ancestral Temple, the World Temple, and the three tablets in the side temple.
He moved Dédào's spirit tablet to the side temple,
reverently placed Tàizǔ's spirit tablet in the center of the sleeping hall,
and then in order moved
the spirit tablets of the seven emperors.
On the dìngyǒu day,
the Emperor went to the Grand Ancestral Temple to perform a special sacrifice.
In the ninth month, he issued an edict to Grand Secretary Lǐ Shí and others, stating
that
"the system of ancestral temples,
where fathers and sons, and brothers, are in the same hall,
is not appropriate according to ritual.
From Tàizōng downward, separate temples should be established,
facing south."
Minister Xià Yán memorialized:
"There is little vacant land
on either side of the Grand Ancestral Temple.
Ancestral temple matters are weighty;
the initial planning should be cautious."
There was no reply.
Liáo Dàonán, a Central Administrator, said:
"From Tàizōng downward, separate temples should be built
in the wings.
There should be a central palace to unify the temples,
so there is no need for separate gates and walls.
There should be an attached room to store the tablets,
so there is no need for separate sleeping temples.
Only let each sagely emperor retain their full尊 (dignity).
The Emperor himself performs the rites at Tàizǔ's temple,
while the others dispatch close officials to offer sacrifices,
following the ancient ritual of feudal lords assisting in sacrifices."
The Emperor was pleased and
ordered a conference.
Yán and others said:
"The Grand Ancestral Temple has limited space,
and may not be able to accommodate them.
If the scale is reduced,
it would not conform to ancient rites.
Moreover, even if the separate temples are completed,
for Your Majesty to visit all the temples
would not only be physically arduous,
but also daily time would be insufficient.
The ancient text about the Zōngbó (Master of Ancestral Rites) performing the secondary sacrifice on behalf of the empress
refers to doing so within one temple.
We have not heard of a subject acting as the principal sacrificer for a whole temple.
Furthermore, ancient feudal lords were mostly vassals of the same surname.
Can those who attend the sacrifices today
be compared to the ancient feudal lords assisting in sacrifices?
The late minister Qiū Jùn suggested sacrificing at one temple every other day,
taking fourteen days to complete all.
This was likely said when there was no other solution,
and was forced.
If the nine temples are in one hall,
it risks being seen as mixed and undifferentiated.
We propose using wood to construct imperial yellow canopies,
like the system of the temple courtyard,
and setting them up according to the number of temples.
Also, set up screens within them,
so that the respect of special offerings can be shown."
The proposal was submitted,
but not replied to.
In the thirteenth year (1534),
the Nánjīng Grand Ancestral Temple suffered a fire.
Zhàn Ruòshuǐ, Minister of Rites, requested to temporarily combine the incense and fire of the Nánjīng Grand Ancestral Temple with the Nánjīng Fèngxiān Temple,
rebuild the Grand Ancestral Temple,
and make new spirit tablets for the sagely emperors.
The Emperor summoned Minister Yán and other officials for a collective discussion.
Yán, together with Grand Secretary Zhāng Fújìng and others, said:
"A state having two temples
began with Hàn Huì.
A deity having two spirit tablets
began with Qí Huán.
The three capital temples of Zhōu
were established when the state was moved,
and the tablets were carried when leaving the state;
these were not two temples and two tablets.
The bodies of descendants are what the ancestors rely on.
Since the sagely sons and divine grandsons personally perform sacrifices here,
then the ancestral spirits will naturally ascend and descend here.
Today is precisely the time to exclusively fix the temple system,
making this place the foundation.
Nánjīng originally had the Fèngxiān Temple;
its daily incense and fire
should be merged and offered as usual.
The former site of the Grand Ancestral Temple should follow the ancient intention of altars and platforms,
building high walls,
carefully managing opening and closing,
to show reverence and solemnity."
This was adopted.
At that time, the emperor wished to rebuild the Nine Temples.
Xià Yán then said:
"The ancestral temples in the capital,
are about to revert to the ancient system.
And the Nánjīng Tàimiào having suffered a sudden disaster,
is probably the silent assistance and auspicious guidance of Heaven and the venerable ancestors,
which cannot but be received with reverence."
The emperor was pleased,
and issued an edict for construction to begin in spring.
The officials deliberated that to the south of the Tàimiào,
to the left would be the three Zhāo temples,
which, with the Wénzǔ Shìshì, would make four;
to the right would be the three Mù temples.
Each of the temples would be over sixteen zhàng deep,
with the main hall and sleeping hall of the Shìshì slightly grander,
its length and width,
equal to the other temples.
The main gate of the array of temples would be parallel to the Tàimiào Jǐmén (Halberd Gate),
and the rear wall of the array of temples would be parallel to the rear wall of the Tàimiào Tiāomiào.
A diagram was presented.
The emperor, believing that the Shìshì should still be exceptionally grand,
ordered further deliberation.
Yán and others requested to expand the front hall of the Shìshì,
making it over four chi taller than the other temples,
and half again as deep and wide;
the sleeping hall would be over two chi taller than the other temples,
and its depth and width would be the same.
This was approved.
In the first month of the fourteenth year, an edict was issued to the cabinet ministers:
"Now that Wénzǔmiào is proposed to be built as the Shìshì,
the character for the Imperial Ancestor's Shìmiào should be avoided."
Zhāng Fújìng said:
"The Shìmiào has been recorded in the Mínglún Dàdiǎn,
and edicts have been issued to the four quarters,
so it cannot be changed.
The Wénshìshì should be called Tàizōngmiào.
For the other temples, the character zōng should not be used,
but rather their original temple names;
when they are moved in the future,
their name plaques can be changed."
This was followed.
In the second month, the old temples were completely demolished and rebuilt.
Each temple was to be a complete palace,
with its own hall and sleeping quarters.
Behind the Tàizǔmiào's sleeping quarters was a Tiāomiào,
where the ancestral tablets to be retired were enshrined.
The Tàimiào's gates and halls all faced south;
the gates of the other temples faced east and west,
but their inner gates, halls, and sleeping quarters all faced south.
In the twelfth month of the fifteenth year,
the new temples were completed,
and the Imperial Ancestor's temple was renamed Ruìzōng Xiànhuángdìmiào.
The emperor then enshrined the spirit tablets of the four ancestors, Dé, Yǐ, Xī, and Rén, in the Tiāomiào,
and the spirit tablet of Tàizǔ in the Tàimiào.
All officials participated in the sacrifice as prescribed.
The next day,
the spirit tablets from Tàizōng downwards were enshrined,
arranged in the various temples.
The nine high-ranking officials and high-ranking military nobles
were ordered to all proceed to the Tàizōngmiào to participate in the sacrifice.
Civil officials of the third rank and above,
and military officials of the fourth rank and above,
were assigned to proceed to the various temples to perform the rites.
On a chosen day, the emperor personally carried the spirit tablet of Tàizǔ,
and civil and military ministers carried the spirit tablets of the Seven Ancestors,
enshrining them in the Jǐngshéndiàn.
In the fourth month of the twentieth year,
the Tàimiào suffered a fire,
and the tablets of Chéngzǔ and Rénzōng were destroyed.
The tablets of the successive emperors were enshrined in the Jǐngshéndiàn.
Ministers were dispatched to Chánglíng and Xiànlíng to report the matter of the imperial and empress tablets,
which were also enshrined in the Jǐngshéndiàn.
In the tenth month of the twenty-second year,
as the old temple site was too narrow,
an order was given to survey and design the regulations.
The proposal was submitted three times,
but not approved.
After a long time,
an order was finally given to revert to the old system of "same hall, different chambers,"
and the temple system was finally established.
In the sixth month of the twenty-fourth year,
Fèi Cài, the Minister of Rites, and others, regarding the enshrinement of spirits in the Tàimiào,
requested to fix the order of precedence.
The emperor said:
"Since there are neither zhāo and mù divisions,
nor generational order,
only the ethical order should be followed.
Tàizǔ shall be in the center,
to his left in order shall be Chéng, Xuān, Xiàn, Ruì,
and to his right in order shall be Rén, Yīng, Xiào, Wǔ,
all facing south."
In the seventh month,
as the temple construction rites were completed,
all officials presented congratulations,
and an edict was issued to the empire.
The new temple remained to the left of the palace gate,
with a main hall of nine bays,
two side corridors in front,
and a southern Jǐmén.
To the left of the gate was the divine storehouse,
and to the right, the divine kitchen.
Further south was the temple gate,
outside which, to the southeast, was the slaughter pavilion,
to the south the divine palace supervisor's office,
and to the west the temple street gate.
Behind the main hall was the sleeping hall,
where the spirit tablets of the successive emperors were enshrined.
Further back was the Tiāomiào,
where the retired ancestral tablets were stored,
all facing south.
In the twenty-seventh year,
the emperor wished to enthrone Empress Xiàoliè Fāngshì in the Tàimiào,
and remove Rénzōng.
Grand Secretary Yán Sōng, Minister of Rites Xú Jiē, and others initially
all opposed it, but later could not maintain their argument.
In the eleventh month of the twenty-ninth year, Rénzōng was removed,
and Empress Xiàoliè was then enthroned in the fourth western chamber.
In the eighth month of the sixth year of Lóngqìng,
Mùzōng was about to be enthroned in the temple,
and the Minister of Rites was ordered to deliberate on which temple chamber should be retired.
Lù Shùdé of the Bureau of Rites said:
"Xuānzōng is only five generations removed from Mùzōng,
so I request to enthrone Ruìzōng in the Shìmiào as before,
and not remove Xuānzōng."
This memorial was sent to the Ministry of Rites,
which deliberated that Xuānzōng's generational position was still recent,
and removing him would be inappropriate.
They then stated:
"In ancient times, one generation constituted one temple,
not one emperor constituting one generation.
Thus, the temples of Jìn had eleven chambers but six generations,
and the temples of Táng had eleven chambers but nine generations.
From Sòng Tàizǔ upwards tracing four ancestors to Huīzōng,
the system of nine generations and eleven chambers was first established,
because Tàizǔ and Tàizōng were considered of the same generation.
Thereafter, Huīzōng was enthroned with Zhézōng in the same generation,
and Gāozōng was enthroned with Qīnzōng in the same generation,
none were removed.
When Guāngzōng was enthroned,
it increased to nine generations and twelve chambers.
Now, from Xuānzōng to Mùzōng there are six generations,
and adding the two ancestors above makes only eight generations.
According to the Sòng system, there is no need to remove anyone.
However, if one chamber is added to both the left and right of the sleeping hall,
then reverence for ancestors and respect for the lineage can proceed without conflict."
The emperor ordered to follow the old edict,
and Xuānzōng was consequently removed.
In the seventh month of the first year of Tiānqǐ,
Guāngzōng was about to be enthroned in the temple.
Hóng Wénhéng, the Tàichángqīng, requested not to remove Xiànzōng,
but to remove Ruìzōng.
This was not accepted.
Dìxiá
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, the collective sacrifice (xiá) was performed in the Tàimiào.
The spirit tablets of Dézǔ and the Imperial Ancestor's consorts were placed in the center,
facing south.
The spirit tablets of Yǐzǔ and the Imperial Ancestor's consorts were in the first position to the east,
facing west.
The spirit tablets of Xīzǔ and the Imperial Ancestor's consorts were in the first position to the west,
facing east.
The spirit tablets of Rénzǔ and the Imperial Ancestor's consorts were in the second position to the east,
facing west.
In the seventh year,
Dá Lùyǔquán, a censor, said:
"Seven years have passed since Your Majesty received the Mandate, yet the dì sacrifice has not been performed.
It is appropriate to consult ancient and modern practices
to establish a ritual for this dynasty."
The edict was sent to the Ministry of Rites, the Tàichángsī, and the Hànlínyuàn for deliberation.
They opined:
"In the Yú, Xià, Shāng, and Zhōu dynasties,
the lineages were clear,
hence the dì rite could be performed.
Since the Hàn and Táng dynasties,
no one has been able to clearly ascertain the origin of their founding ancestors.
What was then called the dì sacrifice
was merely a collective sacrifice (xiá) to the ancestors who had been removed from the main temple and worshipped,
which was the great xiá of ancient times,
not dì.
Sòng Shénzōng once said: 'Dì
is for carefully examining the origin of the ancestors.'
This means that if the origin of the ancestors is unknown,
the dì rite cannot be performed.
Now the state reveres four ancestral temples,
but the origin of the founding ancestor has not been investigated,
so dì cannot be performed hastily."
Tàizǔ agreed with their deliberation.
In the first year of Hóngzhì, it was decided that at the end of each year, the spirit seat of Yǐzǔ from the Tiāomiào would be moved to the left of the main hall,
placed above Xīzǔ,
and the rite of collective sacrifice (xiá) would be performed.
In the tenth year of the Jiājìng era
Shìzōng inquired of Grand Secretary Zhāng Cōng regarding the meaning of dì and xiá sacrifices,
ordering him to discuss it with Xià Yán.
Yán composed an essay on the meaning of dì and presented it,
the general idea being:
"From the Hàn dynasty onwards,
genealogies are difficult to ascertain.
To perform the dì sacrifice to Huángdì as in the Yú and Xià dynasties,
or to Dì Kù as in the Shāng and Zhōu dynasties,
cannot be fully reconciled.
Carefully clarifying the ancient classics
and selecting the subtle arguments of previous Confucians,
it is appropriate to establish a vacant position for the sacrifice."
The Emperor deeply approved of it.
At that time, Middle Compiler Liáo Dàonán stated that the Zhū clan was descended from Zhuānxù,
requesting that the Tàizǔ Shílù be used as evidence
to perform the dì sacrifice to Zhuānxù.
Thereupon, an edict was issued to the Ministry of Rites with the two memorials from Yán and Dàonán,
for officials to convene and deliberate in detail.
All the ministers said:
"Those who propose a vacant position
are vague and without basis;
those who honor Zhuānxù
are dealing with a distant age and difficult to verify.
Since the temple system has already designated the position of Gāohuángdì's original ancestor,
performing the dì sacrifice to Dézǔ is the correct approach."
The Emperor favored the vacant position
and ordered further deliberation.
Yán again submitted a memorial arguing that there were four points of doubt in performing the dì sacrifice to Dézǔ,
and moreover stated that Tàizǔ, as designated now, was the original ancestor within the Tàimiào,
not the original ancestor for a ruler establishing an original ancestor temple.
The Emperor sent down both his memorials.
The ministers then requested the establishment of a vacant position,
to perform the dì sacrifice to the imperial primordial ancestor (Huáng Chūzǔ),
facing south,
with Tàizǔ as co-sacrificed,
facing west.
The ritual officials then stated that
since the grand xiá sacrifice was performed annually,
they requested the grand dì sacrifice be performed every three years,
so that the frequency would be appropriate.
The Emperor personally composed a proclamation to the imperial ancestors,
stipulating that it be performed in the bǐng and xīn years,
and ordered the Ministry of Rites to prepare the rituals and select a date.
In the fourth month,
the Ministry of Rites submitted the ritual procedures for the grand dì sacrifice.
On the day before, a proclamation was made at the temple,
with three days of purification,
preparing incense, silk, sacrificial animals, and liquor according to the seasonal sacrifice procedures.
The Jǐnyī Wèi set up an honor guard;
the Tàicháng Qīng placed the spirit tablet of the imperial primordial ancestor and the spirit tablet of Tàizǔ in the main hall of the Tàimiào,
arranged according to the diagram.
On the day, the ceremony was performed
according to the procedures for the grand sacrifice at the Yuánqiū.
When deliberating on removing Dézǔ from the ancestral tablets in the main temple [to a side temple] and
abolishing the New Year's Eve sacrifice,
it was decided to perform the grand xiá sacrifice in the middle ten days of winter.
The Tàicháng Sì placed the spirit tablet of Dézǔ in the center of the main hall of the Tàimiào,
facing south.
Yìzǔ and below
were arranged in order facing east and west.
In the fifteenth year
At the Beginning of Spring (Lìchūn), a special sacrifice was offered (zhìxiǎng),
with each tablet brought out to the hall.
At the Beginning of Summer (Lìxià), Beginning of Autumn (Lìqiū), and Beginning of Winter (Lìdōng), the tablets of Tàizǔ, Chéngzǔ, and the seven other ancestors were brought out,
and sacrifices were offered in Tàizǔ's hall,
constituting a seasonal xiá sacrifice.
In the middle ten days of the last month of winter,
a date was divined to bring out the tablets of the four ancestors and Tàizǔ, Chéngzǔ, and the seven other ancestors,
and sacrifices were offered in Tàizǔ's hall,
constituting a grand xiá sacrifice.
After the sacrifice,
each tablet was returned to its chamber.
In the seventeenth year
with the full posthumous titles of emperors and empresses of the nine temples written out.
For seasonal xiá sacrifices, only "Emperor Mǒu Zǔ Mǒu Zōng" was written.
The date for the grand xiá sacrifice in the last month of winter was changed again,
with Dézǔ, Yìzǔ, Xīzǔ, Rénzǔ, and Tàizǔ in their separate chambers all facing south;
Chéngzǔ facing west and to the north;
and Rénzōng and the seven subsequent ancestors facing each other east and west.
The ritual involved three offerings,
six renditions of music,
and an eight-row dance.
The Emperor offered to Dézǔ and his empress,
twelve ministers offered separately to the various emperors,
and twelve eunuchs offered separately to the various empresses.
In the eleventh month of the twentieth year
ritual officials deliberated:
"For the year-end grand xiá sacrifice, the removed tablets should be displayed,
but the Jǐngshén Diàn is narrow.
We request that the four ancestors be temporarily sacrificed in the rear chamber,
using joined tables,
and displaying the ceremonial vessels,
to facilitate movement."
An imperial edict approved this.
It was approved.
In the twenty-second year
the rituals of bringing out the tablets, offering incense, and pouring libations were abolished.
When the time came, the emperor's robes and crowns were brought out and put away,
with officials from the Tàicháng Sì and Shéngōng Jiān performing the duties.
In the twenty-fourth year
and the announcement sacrifice was also abolished.
Instead, the grand xiá sacrifice was performed on New Year's Eve,
with rituals similar to the seasonal sacrifices.
In the twenty-eighth year
When Mùzōng ascended the throne,
the Ministry of Rites, due to the mourning period for the late emperor not yet being over,
requested to follow the precedent of the eighteenth year of Hóngzhì
that for the year-end grand xiá sacrifice and the early spring seasonal sacrifice,
officials be dispatched to perform the duties.
Music would be set up but not played.
The Emperor would perform purification at the mourning place,
and participating officials, being within the twenty-seven-day period,
should be temporarily exempted.
This was followed.
Seasonal Sacrifices
In the first year of Hóngwǔ
Every year, during the first months of the four seasons and on New Year's Eve,
there were five sacrifices in total.
Scholars Táo Ān and others said:
"In ancient times, for the four seasonal sacrifices,
three sacrifices were jointly offered in the ancestral temple,
while only the spring sacrifice was performed in individual temples.
From the Hàn dynasty onwards,
all temples had a common hall but separate chambers,
so all four seasons had joint sacrifices.
Now, it is appropriate to imitate the recent system
and perform joint sacrifices in the first temple,
so as to conform to ritual propriety
and avoid excessive repetition."
Tàizǔ ordered that the early spring sacrifice be a special sacrifice in individual temples,
while the three other seasons and New Year's Eve would have joint sacrifices in Dézǔ's temple.
In the second year
spring on Qīngmíng,
summer on Duānwǔ,
autumn on Zhōngyuán,
winter on Dōngzhì,
and New Year's Eve as before.
In the third year
Minister of Rites Cuī Liàng said:
"The first month of a season
is the beginning of the four seasons.
Following seasonal changes
and expressing filial piety,
therefore three sacrificial animals, millet, and various items are prepared for the sacrifice.
As for the middle and last months of a season,
it is merely offering new produce.
Since the suburban sacrifices are already performed,
it is difficult to conduct temple sacrifices.
It is appropriate to revert to the old system.
For festivals such as Qīngmíng,
various seasonal items should be prepared for offering."
This was followed.
In the ninth year
For all seasonal sacrifices,
the spirit seats of Dézǔ and his empress were placed in the main hall,
facing south.
Yìzǔ was on the left,
Xīzǔ on the right,
facing east and west.
Rénzǔ was next to Yìzǔ.
For all spirit seats, no spirit tablets were enshrined,
only robes and crowns were placed.
After the ritual,
they were stored away.
For early spring, a day in the first ten days was chosen;
for the three other first months and New Year's Eve, the first day of the month was used,
and all were joint sacrifices.
From then on, all five sacrifices abolished special sacrifices
and adopted the ritual of joint worship.
In the twenty-first year
Changing the previous system,
there were four bows to welcome the spirits,
four bows to drink the blessings,
and four bows after the ritual.
In the twenty-fifth year
If there was a national mourning event,
music would be set up but not played.
In the first month of the third year of Zhèngtǒng
The Ministry of Rites stated:
"According to custom,
three days beforehand, the Tàicháng Sì would present a memorial for the sacrifice,
and the Emperor would receive it in the main hall.
This day
is the death anniversary of Emperor Xuānzōng,
so normally bells and drums are not sounded.
The Emperor should only conduct affairs at the western side gate.
The Emperor, however, considered the sacrifice a grave matter,
and still should ascend the hall.
All other matters should follow the precedents from the Yǒnglè era."
It was performed accordingly.
In the sixth year of Tiānshùn
cabinet ministers, due to the mourning of the Empress Dowager,
requested to change the seasonal sacrifice of early winter to after the mourning period.
This was followed.
In the fourth year of Chénghuà
the Ministry of Rites, due to the mourning of Empress Dowager Cíyì,
requested to change the seasonal sacrifice of early autumn to the seventh day.
This was not followed.
In the eleventh year of Jiājìng,
Grand Secretary Zhāng Fú-jìng and others stated:
“For the sacrifices in the Tàimiào,
only the ceremonial robes and hats are displayed.
His Majesty’s reform to bring out the spirit tablets for the rites
is truly in accordance with ancient rituals.
However, personally visiting all the temples
to retrieve and place the tablets
is inevitably overly arduous.
We now request that His Majesty
personally place the spirit tablet of Tàizǔ.
For the spirit tablets of the emperors and empresses in the other temples,
this task should be assigned to the officials responsible for holding the tablets, both inside and outside the court.”
The Emperor acceded to their request.
In the seventeenth year, the Xiǎng and Xiá rites were established.
For the special Xiǎng sacrifice on Lìchūn,
the Emperor personally sacrificed to Tàizǔ,
while eight high officials were dispatched to offer sacrifices to the other emperors,
and eight eunuchs (inner officials) offered sacrifices to the empresses.
For the seasonal Xiá sacrifice on Lìxià,
all the spirit tablets were brought out to the Tàimiào.
Tàizǔ faced south,
Chéngzǔ faced west,
ranked above the seven other ancestral spirits,
with Rén, Xuān, Yīng, Xiàn, Xiào, Ruì, and Wǔzōng facing each other from the east and west.
For the seasonal Xiá sacrifices in autumn and winter,
the rites were the same as those for summer.
In the twenty-fourth year,
when the new temple was completed,
it was again decreed that for the Xiǎng and Xiá sacrifices, only the ceremonial robes and hats would be displayed,
and the spirit tablets would not be brought out.
In the first year of Lóngqìng,
for the seasonal Xiǎng sacrifice in Mèngxià,
as Shìzōng's ceremonial table and cushion had not yet been removed,
following the precedent of the first year of Zhèngdé,
the day before,
the Emperor, in ordinary attire, offered sacrifices and prayers at the ceremonial table and cushion,
reverently requesting the performances of the Xiǎng sacrifices in all temples.
Thereafter,
all seasonal Xiǎng and Xiá sacrifices falling within the period of the great mourning (Dàxiáng)
followed this practice.
Presenting New Offerings (Jiànxīn)
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, the ritual items for presenting new offerings on the first day of each month in the Tàimiào were established.
In the first month:
chives, shepherd's purse, fresh vegetables, chicken eggs, duck eggs.
In the second month:
water celery, wormwood, heart of palm, goslings.
In the third month:
tea, bamboo shoots, carp, Chinese herring.
In the fourth month:
cherries, plums, apricots, Reeves's shad, pheasants.
In the fifth month:
new wheat, snake gourd, peaches, plums, crabapples, tender chickens.
In the sixth month:
watermelons, muskmelons, lotus seeds, winter melons.
In the seventh month:
water caltrops, pears, red dates, grapes.
In the eighth month:
gorgon fruit, new rice, lotus roots, wild rice stems, ginger, mandarin fish.
In the ninth month:
adzuki beans, chestnuts, persimmons, oranges, crabs, bream.
In the tenth month:
papayas, tangerines, oranges, radishes, rabbits, wild geese.
In the eleventh month:
buckwheat, sugarcane, swans, cormorants, deer.
In the twelfth month:
mustard greens, spinach, white fish, crucian carp.
All these rites were personally performed by the Emperor.
Not long after,
they were assigned to the Tàicháng (Court of Imperial Sacrifices).
In the second year, an imperial edict stated,
that for all seasonal produce,
the Tàicháng should first offer them to the ancestral temples,
and only then present them to the Emperor.
In the third year, the presentation of new offerings on the first day of the month was established.
For each temple, there was one sheep, one pig, eight baskets and dishes (biāndòu), two each of square and round vessels (fǔguǐ, dēngxíng), three wine vessels (zūn),
as well as the regular fare of goose stew and rice.
The Tàicháng Qīng (Minister of Imperial Sacrifices) and the participating sacrificing officials performed the rites in ceremonial robes.
For the Wàng sacrifice (on the fifteenth day),
only the regular fare of goose stew and rice was offered,
and the rites were performed in ordinary attire.
There was also the ceremony of Xiànxīn (presenting offerings),
whereby any special new items presented from the four directions,
beyond the monthly Jiànxīn,
were presented by the Tàicháng Qīng and the inner palace officials in ordinary attire at the Tàimiào,
without performing formal rites.
Thereafter, the sacrifices on the first and fifteenth days of the month,
as well as Jiànxīn and Xiànxīn,
were all conducted at the Fèngxiān Diàn.
Adding Posthumous Titles (Jiāshàng Shìhào)
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, posthumous titles were conferred upon the four ancestral temples (sì miào),
and the ceremonial tablets (cè) and seals (bǎo) were all made of jade.
The jade tablets were one chi two cun long,
one cun two fen wide,
and five fen thick.
The number of tablets depended on the length of the inscription.
They were joined with gold cords,
placed on brocade cushions,
and covered with a red silk brocade pa embellished with gold leaf.
The cè box
was lacquered in vermilion, carved with gold,
and decorated with dragon and phoenix patterns.
The bǎo (seal)
had seal script,
was four cun nine fen wide,
and one cun two fen thick.
It had a golden coiled dragon knob,
was tied with brocade ribbons,
wrapped in red brocade,
and covered with a pa, then placed in a lù (seal box),
which was adorned with gold.
The inscription on Dézǔ’s cè read:
“Your filial great-great-grandson, the succeeding emperor, your servant so-and-so,
bows twice and kowtows to make this report.
Your servant has heard that respecting one’s ancestors
is the deepest human emotion.
When ancestors obtained the world [empire],
they passed it on to their descendants;
when descendants obtained the world,
they posthumously honored their ancestors.
This is a universal principle throughout history.
Your servant encountered the uprising of armies across the land,
personally donned armor,
commanded troops,
pacified the four quarters,
to bring peace to the people,
and the land expanded daily,
all under the protection of the ancestors.
The officials and common people urged your servant to become emperor,
yet the esteemed parents of previous generations have no titles.
Therefore, respectfully, we confer upon the most reverend great-great-grandfather, the former ruler (fǔ-jūn), the honorable title of Xuán Huángdì,
with the temple name Dézǔ.
We humbly pray that your noble spirit
will witness this filial devotion.”
The inscription on the bǎo read
“Seal of Dézǔ Xuán Huángdì.”
For Xuán Huánghòu, Yìzǔ, and subsequent emperors and empresses,
the cè and bǎo were all similar.
During the Jiànwén reign,
the ceremonies for posthumously conferring titles and writing cè
were not recorded due to their abolition.
In the fifth month of the first year of Yǒnglè, the deliberation on the posthumous titles for Gāo Huángdì and Gāo Huánghòu was presented.
The day before,
a table for the deliberation on posthumous titles was set up in the Fèngtiān Diàn.
On that morning,
the Emperor ascended the throne in his ceremonial robe and crown,
following the usual protocol.
Civil and military officials in court attire bowed four times.
An official from the Lǐbù (Ministry of Rites) then announced the presentation of the deliberation on posthumous titles.
Two ceremonial ushers led the head of the officials to ascend the crimson steps (Dānbì).
The official holding the deliberation on posthumous titles handed the document to the head of the officials,
who entered through the central gate
and proceeded to the center of the hall.
An announcement was made to present the deliberation on posthumous titles.
The imperial carriage rose,
and moved towards the table with the deliberation document.
The head of the officials advanced and placed it on the table,
then knelt,
and all officials knelt.
After the Emperor had read it,
he returned to his seat.
The head of the officials and all officials prostrated themselves, rose,
returned to their positions,
and again performed four bows.
After the ceremony,
the Emperor personally picked up the deliberation on posthumous titles
and handed it to the officials of the Hànlín Yuàn (Hanlin Academy) to draft the ceremonial inscription (cè wén).
In the sixth month,
to confer an honorable posthumous title,
a fast and purification was observed in advance,
and officials were dispatched to make sacrifices and announce it to Heaven and Earth, the Imperial Ancestral Temple, and the Altars of Land and Grain.
The Hónglú Sì (Court of Imperial Entertainments) set up a censer table in the Fèngtiān Diàn (Hall of Receiving Heaven).
Early on that day,
the imperial attendants placed the imperial records (cè) and seals (bǎo) on the table.
The Tàicháng Sì (Court of Imperial Sacrifices) set up cè and bǎo tables outside the gate of the Tàimiào (Grand Ancestral Temple),
one before the divine tablet of the Deceased Emperor (Huángkǎo) and one before that of the Deceased Empress (Huángbǐ).
The Hónglú Sì set up the cè and bǎo palanquins outside the Fèngtiān Mén (Gate of Receiving Heaven),
with the imperial procession (lúbù) and musical instruments (yuèxuán) arranged as usual.
All officials, in sacrificial robes, proceeded to outside the Tàimiào gate and stood waiting.
The officiating officials and the officials designated to proclaim the cè and bǎo
first entered through the right gate of the Tàimiào,
and stood in order on the right side of the hall.
The Emperor, in his imperial robe (gǔnmiǎn), was in the Huágài Diàn (Hall of Auspicious Canopy).
Four officials, in sacrificial robes, entrusted with holding the cè and bǎo,
stood in order on the east and west sides of the Fèngtiān Diàn.
The Hónglú Sì requested that the ceremony proceed.
The Emperor came out to the front of the cè and bǎo table in the Fèngtiān Diàn.
The officials holding the cè and bǎo each held them and walked forward,
placing them inside the decorated palanquin (cǎiyú).
The imperial procession and grand music led the way.
The Emperor rode in his palanquin (yú),
following the decorated palanquin.
Upon reaching outside the Wǔmén (Meridian Gate), he descended from his palanquin,
and ascended the imperial carriage (lù).
He arrived at the Tàimiào gate.
All officials knelt, waiting for the decorated palanquin to pass,
then rose.
The Emperor descended from his carriage,
and followed the decorated palanquin to outside the middle gate of the Tàimiào.
The officials holding the cè and bǎo each held them and walked forward.
The Emperor followed,
reaching the upper level of the imperial steps (dānbì).
The cè and bǎo were placed on the tables.
The Master of Ceremonies (diǎnyí) intoned the commands as usual.
The Imperial Attendant (nèizàn) announced "Take positions."
The diǎnyí announced "Welcome the spirits, play music."
When the music stopped,
the nèizàn announced "The Emperor makes four bows."
All officials followed.
The diǎnyí announced "Present the cè and bǎo."
The officials holding the cè and bǎo walked forward.
The Emperor's procession entered through the left gate,
arrived in the midst of the temple,
and proceeded to before the divine tablet of the Deceased Emperor.
It was announced "Kneel,"
and "Insert the ceremonial tablet (guī)."
It was announced "Present the cè."
The official holding the cè knelt and presented it to the Emperor's left.
The Emperor received the cè and handed it to the officiating official,
who placed it on the left side of the table.
It was announced "Remove the guī."
The attendant (zàn) announced "Proclaim the cè."
The official proclaiming the cè knelt and proclaimed it to the Emperor's left.
The text of the cè read:
"On the first year of Yǒnglè,
the guǐwèi year,
the first day of the sixth month, dìngwèi,
on the eleventh day, dìngsì,
your filial son, the succeeding Emperor, your servant [name],
reverently bows and kowtows, saying:
Your servant has heard that eminent virtue praised Yáo,
and Chónghuá (Shùn) beautified Shùn.
Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ,
the sagely rulers succeeded one another,
their achievements and virtues both flourishing,
all receiving illustrious titles.
Reverently contemplating our Imperial Father, the Emperor,
who commanded heaven and initiated a new era,
rising from humble origins,
he quelled chaos and disorder,
transformed barbarians into Chinese,
and governed the world with filial piety.
For over forty years,
the people rejoiced in eternal peace.
Rites, music, and culture,
established laws for ten thousand generations.
His virtue matched Heaven and Earth,
his brightness equalled the sun and moon,
his achievements surpassed a thousand ages,
his Dao topped a hundred kings.
We reverently present this cè and bǎo,

and respectfully confer the posthumous title: Shèngshén Wénwǔ Qīnmíng Qǐyùn Jùndé Chénggōng Tǒngtiān Dàxiào Gāo Huángdì (Sagely Divine, Civil and Martial, Reverent and Brilliant, Who Initiated the Epoch, of Eminent Virtue and Accomplishment, Who Ruled Heaven, of Great Filial Piety, the Exalted Emperor),
with the temple name Tàizǔ (Grand Ancestor).
We humbly pray that the divine spirit ascends and descends,
silently blessing the common people,
his boundless protective cover
enduring forever with Heaven."
When the proclamation of the cè was finished,
it was announced "Insert the guī."
It was announced "Present the bǎo."
The official holding the bǎo knelt and presented it to the Emperor's left.
The Emperor received the bǎo,
and handed it to the officiating official,
who placed it on the right side of the table.
It was announced "Remove the guī."
The attendant announced "Proclaim the bǎo."
The official proclaiming the bǎo knelt and proclaimed it to the Emperor's right.
The text of the bǎo was the same as the posthumous title.
When the proclamation of the bǎo was finished,
it was announced "Prostrate,"
then "Rise."
The Emperor proceeded to before the divine tablet of the Deceased Empress,
and presented and proclaimed the cè and bǎo according to the preceding ceremony.
The text of the cè read:
"Your servant has heard that from ancient times, Empresses,
all inherited the family lineage.
The consort from Guīrù (Shùn's wife) initiated prosperity for the imperial house,
and Zhōu Jiāng (King Wén's wife) assisted in governance,
establishing the foundation for the state ruler.
Reverently contemplating our Imperial Mother, the Xiàocí Huánghòu (Empress Xiàocí), who with her sagely nature assisted the sage,
rising together from humble circumstances,
she greatly helped in times of difficulty,
transforming the family into a nation.
She was diligent and frugal,
reverent and sincere,
filial and benevolent,
thereby upholding the lineage of divine spirits,
and managing the affairs of all things appropriately.
She held the position of Central Palace (Empress) for fifteen years,
the family and state followed her example,
and the world returned to benevolence.
We reverently present this cè and bǎo,

and respectfully confer the posthumous title: Xiàocí Zhāoxiàn Zhìrén Wéndé Chéngtiān Shùnshèng Gāo Huánghòu (Filial, Benevolent, Luminous, Exemplary, Utterly Benevolent, Civil and Virtuous, Who Received Heaven and Followed the Sage, the Exalted Empress).
We humbly pray that the sagely spirit ascends and descends,
receiving benevolence and revealing her name,
her glory shining like the sun and moon,
illuminating eternal generations."
The text of the bǎo was the same as the posthumous title.
When the proclamation of the bǎo was finished,
the Emperor returned to his position.
It was announced "Four bows."
All officials followed.
The sacrificial ceremony proceeded as usual.
The next day,
an imperial edict was issued to the whole empire.
Upon the completion of the ceremony for conferring the posthumous title,
the officials participating in the sacrifice and officiating were granted a feast,
and other officials were granted one ingot of paper currency.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
in the ninth month,
the Lǐbù (Ministry of Rites) and various ministers submitted their proposal for the posthumous titles of the Deceased Emperor (Dàxíng Huángdì) and Rénxiào Huánghòu (Empress Rénxiào).
Rénzōng immediately received it,
and after reading it,
wept uncontrollably,
then sent it to the Hànlín Yuàn (Hanlin Academy) to draft the cè of posthumous titles.
The Lǐbù presented the ceremony for conferring posthumous titles.
A fast and purification was observed in advance, and sacrifices were dispatched as usual.
The imperial attendants placed the cè and bǎo palanquins outside the Fèngtiān Mén.
The next morning,
the cè and bǎo were placed in the palanquins.
The Emperor, in mourning attire, proceeded to the Fèngtiān Mén.
The imperial attendants lifted the cè and bǎo palanquins.
The Emperor followed behind the palanquins,
descended the steps,
and ascended his imperial carriage.
All officials stood south of the Jīnshuǐ Qiáo (Golden Water Bridge),
kneeling facing north.
After the palanquins passed,
they rose.
They followed to outside the Sīshàn Mén (Gate of Thinking Goodness),
stood in order,
facing north.
The Emperor descended from his imperial carriage.
The cè and bǎo palanquins entered through the middle gate,
and reached the upper level of the imperial steps of the Jǐyán Diàn (Hall of Ceremonial Arrangement).
The Emperor entered through the left gate,
and took his position for bowing on the imperial steps.
The officials holding the cè and bǎo entered through the left gate of the hall,
and reached before the ceremonial table.
The Master of Ceremonies announced "Four bows."
The Imperial Grandson (Huáng Tàisūn), imperial princes (qīnwáng), and imperial grandsons (huángsūn) accompanied the bows on the imperial steps.
All officials accompanied the bows outside the Sīshàn Mén.
The Emperor entered through the left gate of the hall,
proceeded to before the position of the Deceased Emperor,
and knelt to present the cè and bǎo.
When the officials proclaiming the cè and bǎo finished proclaiming,
it was announced "Prostrate," then "Rise."
The Emperor proceeded to before the divine tablet of Rénxiào Huánghòu,
the ceremony being the same.
It was announced "Return to position," and "Four bows."
The Imperial Grandson and those below him followed.
When the ceremony was finished,
the sacrificial ceremony proceeded.
On that day,
the divine tablet of Rénxiào Huánghòu was re-inscribed,
and an edict was issued to the whole empire.
Thereafter,
when conferring honorable posthumous titles on emperors, grand empress dowagers (tài huángtàihòu), and empress dowagers (huángtàihòu),
all followed this precedent.
In the seventeenth year of Jiājìng,
Shìzōng, acting on Fēng Fāng's memorial,
added a temple name to Xiàn Huángdì,
calling him Zōng and pairing him with the emperor.
Thus, Tàizōng was renamed Chéngzǔ.
He ordered the creation of divine tablets for the two sages in the Nángōng,
then proceeded to Jǐng Shén Diàn
to offer the imperial scrolls and seals.
Wén Huángdì was honored with the title Chéngzǔ Qǐtiān Hóngdào Gāomíng Zhàoyùn Shèngwǔ Shéngōng Chúnrén Zhìxiào Wén Huángdì.
Xiàn Huángdì was honored with the title Ruìzōng Zhītiān Shǒudào Hóngdé Yuānrén Kuānmù Chúnshèng Gōngjiǎn Jìngwén Xiàn Huángdì.
Additionally, the grand title of Huángtiān Shàngdì was conferred.
On the first day of the eleventh month,
the Emperor proceeded to the Nánjiāo
to respectfully present the imperial scrolls and memorials.
After the ceremony was completed,
he returned to the Tàimiào
to offer the imperial scrolls and seals.
Gāo Huángdì was additionally honored with the title Tàizǔ Kāitiān Xíngdào Zhàojì Lìjí Dàshèng Zhìshén Rénwén Yìwǔ Jùndé Chénggōng Gāo Huángdì.
Gāo Huánghòu was additionally honored with the title Xiàocí Zhēnhuà Zhéshùn Rénhuī Chéngtiān Yùshèng Zhìdé Gāo Huánghòu.
On this day,
the empress in the Zhōnggōng held the spirit tablet of Gāo Huánghòu,
assisting in the secondary offering ceremony.
Civil and military officials and their wives accompanied the sacrifice.
Another day was chosen to proceed to the Tàimiào
to perform the ceremony of renaming the spirit tablets.
Regarding temple taboos:
In the first month of the first year of Tiānqǐ, following a memorial from the Lǐbù,
all characters containing the radical "shuǐ" (water) with the character "gè" were
changed to
"luò."
All characters containing the radical "mù" (wood) with the character "jiāo" were
changed to
"jiào."
However, as the term "dūxué chēngjiào" was deemed inappropriate,
it was changed to "xuézhèng."
For all princely establishments and civil and military officials
who had committed temple taboos or imperial name taboos,
all were rectified.
Collation Notes:

Volume 28, Rites 6 (Auspicious Rites 6): Fèngxiān Diàn, Fèngcí Diàn, Xiàn Huángdì Miào, Princes participating in sacrifices, Meritorious officials participating in sacrifices, Royal ancestral temples, officials' family temples.
Fèngxiān Diàn.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ,
Tàizǔ, feeling that the regular sacrifices at the Tàimiào
were insufficient to express filial devotion,
also built the Fèngxiān Diàn to the east inside the palace gate.
The Tàimiào symbolized the outer court,
and the Fèngxiān Diàn symbolized the inner court.
The main hall had five bays,
facing south,
