and was two zhàng and five chǐ deep.
The front porch had five bays,
and was half that deep.
Divine tablets and effigies of four generations of emperors and empresses were made,
and the ceremonial items and prayer texts were standardized.
Every morning and evening,
the Emperor, Crown Prince, and various princes offered sacrifices twice a day.
The Empress, accompanied by concubines, daily presented meals.
Sacrifices were offered on various festivals,
and new seasonal items were presented on the first day of each month.
The types of items followed the regulations established in the first year.
However, in the third month, no shad (jǐyú) was used.
In the fourth month, the quantity of reeves shad (shíyú) was reduced,
and king gourd (wángguā) and pig (zhì) were added.
In the fifth month, eggplant (qié) was added.
In the ninth month, persimmons (shì) and crabs (xiè) were reduced.
In the tenth month, papaya (mùguā) and radish (lúbo) were reduced,
and yam (shānyào) was added.
In the eleventh month, swans (tiāné) and cormorants (cí●) were reduced,
and deer (zhāng) was added.
All these were reported by the Tàicháng
and sent to the Guānglù Sì for offering.
Whenever new seasonal items appeared,
the Tàicháng provided them.
Additionally, the memorial days of the Imperial Father and Mother were recorded,
and sacrifices were regularly offered seasonally.
When Chéngzǔ moved the capital to Běijīng,
he built it according to the existing system.
In the first year of Xuāndé, after Tàizōng was enshrined in the temple,
Zhèng Wáng Zhān Jùn was again sent to the Fèngxiān Diàn
to set up wine and fruits for a sacrificial announcement,
and to install the divine tablet.
In the seventh year of Tiānshùn, after Xiàogōng Huánghòu was enshrined in the temple,
the Emperor returned to perform the ceremony of installing the divine tablet,
which was slightly similar to the temple enshrinement ceremony.
In the seventeenth year of Hóngzhì,
Lìbù Shàngshū Mǎ Wénshēng stated:
"The boats transporting fresh goods from Nánjīng
were originally established for the Fèngxiān Diàn.
The number of boatmen reached a thousand,
and they extorted along the way.
Now Yáng and Xú are suffering from drought,
and I wish to follow the ancient spirit of reducing rites during famine years
to alleviate the people's hardship."
The relevant department was ordered to deliberate and implement it.
Upon Wǔzōng's ascension,
Xīzǔ's spirit tablet was removed.
The divine tablet in the Fèngxiān Diàn was also moved to the west of Dézǔ,
and its effigy, bed curtains, and ceremonial items were stored in the imperial storehouse.
In the fourteenth year of Jiājìng, the sacrifices and rites for the inner halls were established.
On Qīngmíng, Zhōngyuán, Shèngdàn, Dōngzhì, and Zhèngdàn,
there were prayer texts,
and music like banquet music.
On the birthdays of the two empresses, and the birthdays of the empress and concubines,
there were all sacrifices,
but no prayer texts or music.
On Lìchūn, Yuánxiāo, the eighth day of the fourth month, Duānyáng, Zhōngqiū, Chóngyáng, and the eighth day of the twelfth month,
there were all sacrifices,
using seasonal food.
Previously there were no prayer texts,
but now exhortations were added.
According to the old rituals,
one would only bow once per room.
Upon reaching the central room, after kneeling and chanting the prayer,
one would bow four more times
and burn the prayer silk.
Now, one would bow four times at one's position,
present silk and libations,
and after the prayer,
the empress and concubines would assist in the secondary offering,
and the officiating official would perform the final offering.
After the food was removed,
one would bow four more times.
For memorial sacrifices,
formerly one would wear formal attire and play music.
Now, one would change into lighter colored clothes
and omit the music.
All sacrifices to the altars of earth, sun, and moon,
departures and returns,
as well as enfeoffment announcements and sacrifices,
and rituals on the first and fifteenth of the month,
were all performed here.
In the fifteenth year,
Lǐbù Shàngshū Xià Yán and others memorialized:
"The spirit tablet of Dàolíng Huánghòu
was previously provisionally enshrined next to Xiàohuì Tàihòu in the Fèngcí Diàn, due to kinship.
Now that the spirit tablets of the three empresses are planned to be moved to the imperial mausoleum hall,
Dàolíng also ought to be provisionally moved to a side room in the Fèngxiān Diàn,
where sacrifices and announcements will be made,
and food offerings will be arranged uniformly."
This was approved.
In the first year of Lóngqìng,
the Lǐbù stated:
"According to the old system,
the Tàimiào had five sacrifices a year,
while seasonal and memorial day sacrifices
were performed in the Fèngxiān Diàn.
Now that Xiàojié Huánghòu has been enshrined in the Tàimiào,
it is also appropriate to enshrine her divine tablet in the Fèngxiān Diàn."
Thus, a divine seat and ceremonial items were set up in the ninth room,
and an official was sent to perform sacrifices and announcements as per the rites.
In the third year of Wànlì,
the Emperor desired to enshrine the divine tablets of Xiàoliè and Xiàokè empresses
in the Fèngxiān Diàn.
The ritual officials stated that during the time of Shìzōng,
discussions focused on enshrinement in the mausoleum,
not in the inner hall.
The Emperor said:
"The Fèngxiān Diàn already houses the divine tablets of Xiàosù, Xiàomù, and Xiàohuì empresses,
all established by the Imperial Ancestors,
and it is appropriate to follow this precedent for enshrinement."
It seems that at that time, although the three empresses were each enshrined in mausoleum temples,
they were still simultaneously sacrificed in the Fèngxiān Diàn,
but the outer court was unaware of this.
He ordered the Grand Secretary Zhāng Jūzhèng and others to inspect.
Zhāng Jūzhèng and others stated:
"The Fèngxiān Diàn enshrines the imperial ancestors,
and anyone honored as an empress
can be enshrined and receive sacrifices in the inner hall,
which differs from the Tàimiào's one emperor, one empress rule.
Therefore, it is also appropriate to enshrine them and offer sacrifices now."
This was approved.
Previously,
for enfeoffment and sacrificial announcements,
officials of the Tàicháng Sì (Court of Imperial Sacrifices) would preside over the rites,
and a request would still be submitted to dispatch an official.
By the first year of the Wànlì reign (1573),
the Emperor personally performed the rites,
and the request to dispatch an official was abolished.
In the second year (1574),
the Tàicháng Sì suggested that as the inner palace was a restricted area,
it would be more convenient to use eunuchs to serve the rites.
The Emperor approved their request.
For all Saints' Day (Shengjie), Mid-Yuan Festival (Zhōngyuán), Winter Solstice (Dōngzhì), and year-end (Suìmù) occasions,
in the early Jiājìng reign, all were announced and sacrificed at the Fèngxiān Diàn.
In the fifteenth year (1536), the Mid-Yuan Festival sacrifice was abolished.
In the forty-fifth year (1566), the year-end sacrifice was abolished.
In the first year of the Lóngqìng reign (1567), the Saints' Day and Winter Solstice sacrifices were abolished.
For the Fāngzé, offering sacrifices at dawn to the sun (Cháorì), and offering sacrifices at dusk to the moon (Xīyuè),
as well as going out to announce and returning to pay respects (chūgào huícān),
during the Jiājìng reign, these were performed at the Jǐngshén Diàn.
In the first year of the Lóngqìng reign (1567), they were again performed at the Fèngxiān Diàn.
For the death anniversaries (jìchén) of all Emperors and Empresses,
before the Jiājìng reign, they were performed at the Fèngxiān Diàn.
In the eighteenth year (1539), the death anniversaries of Gāohuángdì and his Empress were changed to the Jǐngshén Diàn,
and those of Wénhuángdì and his Empress and below were held at the Yǒngxiào Diàn.
In the twenty-fourth year (1545), they were again performed at the Fèngxiān Diàn.
For all sacrifices and announcements in the inner palace,
from the second year of the Wànlì reign (1574) onwards,
if the Emperor personally performed the sacrifice, the sacrificial offerings, announcement texts, and ritual officers
all came from the inner eunuchs.
If an official was dispatched to offer sacrifices on behalf of the Emperor,
all came from the Tàicháng Sì.
However, for items that required dried meat and minced meat sauces,
even for personal sacrifices, these all came from the Tàicháng Sì.
In the fourteenth year of the Wànlì reign (1586),
a ritual official stated:
"In recent years, for the enfeoffment of Imperial Noble Consorts (Huángguìfēi),
and sacrificial announcements at the Fèngxiān Diàn,
the sacrificial prayers and ritual officers came from the inner court,
while the sacrificial offerings were provided by the Tàicháng Sì,
creating an inconsistency in the rites.
The Tàicháng Sì is specifically in charge of sacrificial ceremonies,
while the Guānglù (Court of Imperial Entertainments) is in charge of food and drink.
Sacrificial announcements in the inner court
are based on the principle of offering food at meal times.
It is appropriate to follow the old system:
for all sacrificial announcements in the inner palace,
whether performed personally by the Emperor or by a dispatched official,
the sacrificial offerings should be provided by the Guānglù Sì;
only for the announcement texts and ritual officers,
if performed personally by the Emperor, they should be handled by the inner court;
if an official is dispatched, the Tàicháng Sì should temporarily handle them."
This was followed.
Fèngcí Diàn
Upon ascending the throne, Xiàozōng
posthumously bestowed the empress title Xiàomù Tàihòu on his birth mother, Consort Jì Shì,
and interred her with him in Màolíng.
Because she could not be enshrined in the ancestral temple,
the Fèngcí Diàn was specially built to the right of the Fèngxiān Diàn to worship her.
Five offerings were made annually,
and new offerings and death anniversary sacrifices
all followed the rituals of the Tàimiào Fèngxiān Diàn.
In the seventeenth year of the Hóngzhì reign (1504),
Xiàosù Zhōu Tàihòu passed away.
Previously, during the Chénghuà reign,
the arrangements for Empress Dowager Zhōu's interment and ancestral temple worship had been decided in advance.
Now, auxiliary officials were summoned to discuss the ritual of enshrinement in the ancestral temple.
Liú Jiàn and others said:
"The discussion indeed took place,
but the Tang and Song precedents cited at that time
were not customs from before the Han dynasty."
The Emperor believed that matters should follow ancient precedents,
and thus cited the separate worship of Empress Dowager Xiàomù in the Fèngcí Diàn,
and ordered court officials to deliberate.
Jiàn withdrew,
and then again submitted a memorial arguing the matter
to strengthen the Emperor's resolve.
Thereupon, Duke of Yīngguó Zhāng Mào, Minister of Personnel Mǎ Wénshēng, and others stated:
"The ritual of the ancestral temple
is a public consensus of the realm,
not something that descendants can privately decide.
The seven temples of Yin and Zhou,
where father is Zhāo and son is Mù,
each have a designated seat,
one emperor and one empress, which is the proper order of ritual.
The 'Chūnqiū' records 'the palace of Kǎo Zhòngzǐ,'
and Hú Ānguó's commentary says: 'Mèngzǐ entered the temple of Huìgōng,
but Zhòngzǐ had no place for sacrifices.'
From this, it can be seen that Lǔ upheld the Zhou rites,
and the system of former kings still existed,
because the ancestral temple did not have two consorts.
We respectfully note Emperor Xiànzōng's imperial decree,
which states, 'My heart is ultimately not at ease.'
We surmise that the late Emperor's deepest feelings,
due to his reluctance to disobey his benevolent mother's wishes,
led him to reluctantly agree to the discussion of co-enshrinement.
The officials, wishing to exercise discretion to resolve the matter,
also had no choice but to do this.
To manage according to ritual
and fully realize the late Emperor's posthumous wishes,
truly awaits this day.
Consulting the 'Zhōulǐ,'
there is a text about sacrificing to the former empress (xiānbǐ),
whose commentary says 'Jiāng Yuán,'
which is what the 'Shī' refers to as 'Bìgōng.'
The Tang and Song dynasties, in revering empresses dowager
who were not co-enshrined in the ancestral temple,
instead established separate halls to offer sacrifices to them,
also in line with the meaning of Bìgōng.
In our dynasty, from the ancestors until now, we have already exceeded nine temples,
and there have been no second co-enshrinements.
It is now appropriate to build a new temple outside the Fèngxiān Diàn,
like the Bìgōng in the 'Shī' and the separate halls of the Song,
where annual offerings can be made,
and she can still be referred to as Tàihuáng Tàihòu,
thus fulfilling both sentiment and ritual."
The proposal was submitted,
and Jiàn and others were again summoned to the plain tent.
The Emperor pulled out a diagram of the Fèngxiān Diàn from his sleeve,
pointed to a section on the west and said:
"This is the Fèngcí Diàn."
Then he pointed to a section on the east and said:
"This is the divine kitchen.
I wish to build a separate temple here,
move Empress Dowager Xiàomù's spirit tablet (shénzhǔ) here,
and worship both here."
Jiàn and the others all replied:
"Most appropriate."
Soon after, the Qīntiān Jiān (Imperial Astronomical Bureau) reported
that the year was not auspicious.
The court deliberated and decided to temporarily enshrine her in the center of the Fèngcí Diàn,
moving Empress Dowager Xiàomù to the left.
When Xiàozōng崩 (died),
Wǔzōng ascended the throne.
The Ministry of Rites then submitted the protocol for enshrining Xiàosù's spirit tablet.
Beforehand, there was a three-day fast,
with announcements made to the Fèngxiān Diàn and Xiàozōng's funeral altars.
On that day, in the early morning,
the Emperor wore a black yìshànguān, light-colored clothes, and a black xīdài,
and first went to Xiàomù's spirit seat.
After the ceremony,
the Emperor proceeded to the front of the spirit seat
and requested the spirit tablet to descend from its seat.
The Emperor held the tablet and stood,
while the inner attendants moved the spirit seat to the left chamber of the hall.
After the Emperor had enshrined it,
he performed the kòutóu禮 (bowing ceremony).
At noon,
the Emperor went to the Qīngníng Gōng to Xiàosù's funeral altar.
After performing the ceremony,
the inner attendants brought the spirit tablet sedan chair to the front of the hall,
and the ceremonial robes and crown sedan chair to the Dānbì (imperial steps).
The Emperor proceeded to the prostration position,
followed by the imperial princes in auspicious attire,
bowed four times,
and rose.
The Emperor held the spirit tablet and exited through the central gate of the hall,
enshrining it within the sedan chair.
The attendants carried the ceremonial robes and crown, placing them in the sedan chair to follow.
The Emperor led the imperial princes in walking behind.
Upon reaching outside the Bǎoshàn Mén,
the Empress Dowager Grand and the Empress Dowager led the palace consorts to welcome them inside the gate.
They first proceeded to the Fèngcí Diàn,
and stood in order on the west side of the hall.
The spirit tablet sedan chair arrived outside the Fèngxiān Diàn gate,
and paused briefly.
The Emperor went to the sedan chair and knelt,
requesting the spirit tablet to proceed to the Fèngxiān Diàn,
prostrated himself,
rose,
and held the spirit tablet, entering through the left gate of the hall
to the mat position inside the hall,
knelt,
and placed the spirit tablet.
After the Emperor performed the five bows and three kòutóu禮,
he held the spirit tablet,
again exiting through the left gate,
and placed it inside the sedan chair.
Upon reaching outside the Fèngcí Diàn gate,
the Emperor held the spirit tablet, entered through the central gate,
and after enshrining it on the spirit seat,
performed the ceremony for settling the spirit,
with three offerings as per the usual protocol.
The Empress Dowager Grand and those below her bowed four times.
After the ceremony,
the inner palace officers set up a mat position to the south of the center of the hall.
The Emperor went before the spirit seat of Xiàomù Huángtàihòu,
knelt and requested the spirit tablet to pay respects to Xiàosù Tàihuángtàihòu,
knelt and placed it on the mat position,
prostrated himself,
rose,
and performed the five bows and three kòutóu禮.
After this,
the Emperor held the tablet and rose,
again settling it on the spirit seat,
and performed the spirit-settling ceremony as before.
The Empress Dowager and those below her bowed four times.
In the first year of Jiājìng,
Shìzōng enshrined Xiàohuì Shào Tàihòu in the ancestral temple.
In the second month of the eighth year,
Fāng Xiànfū, Minister of Rites, and others stated:
"It is proper for Dàolíng Huánghòu to be enshrined in the Tàimiào (Grand Ancestral Temple),
but now the system of nine temples is complete.
Considering precedents from the Táng and Sòng dynasties,
if an Empress did not have her own chamber in the Tàimiào,
a separate temple was created.
Therefore, the Qǔtái Ritual mentions separate temples for Empresses
and the dì and xiá sacrifices in the Tàimiào.
Furthermore, the Lǐjì Sàngfú Xiǎojì states:
'A woman is enshrined with her ancestress,
if there are three ancestresses,
she is enshrined with the closest one.'
Commentators explain:
'The closest one refers to the birth mother of her husband's father.'
Now, since Xiàohuì Tàihuángtàihòu is truly the birth mother of the deceased Emperor Xiàn,
Dàolíng Huánghòu should be enshrined beside her."
An imperial decree assented.
In the third month,
the ceremony for enshrining her in the ancestral temple was performed.
Beforehand, sacrifices and announcements were made to all halls.
On the appointed day,
Dàolíng Hòu's tablet was requested to proceed to the Fèngcí Diàn for enshrinement.
Inner attendants held the spirit tablet, the posthumous title册 (scroll), and the ceremonial robes and crown, following the Emperor to the Fèngxiān Diàn for an audience.
The Emperor took his position
and performed the five bows and three kòutóu禮.
Next, he proceeded to the Chóngxiān Diàn,
then to the Fèngcí Diàn,
to pay respects to the three Empresses Dowager.
Inner attendants held the tablet and settled it on the spirit seat.
The imperial consorts and those below them bowed four times.
In the fifteenth year,
the Emperor, considering that the three Empresses Dowager were separately worshipped in the Fèngcí Diàn,
deemed it more appropriate to enshrine them in the mausoleum temple.
The court officials deliberated:
"In ancient times, the ancestral temples of the Son of Heaven
had only one emperor and one empress;
the birth mother was offered sacrifices in the sleeping quarters,
and this ceased upon her death.
The sacrifices in Xiàozōng's Fèngcí Diàn
were for a son to worship his birth mother,
to fulfill lifelong filial piety.
However, the Rites state, 'A concubine's mother is not worshipped perpetually' (bù shì jì),
with a commentary explaining:
'Not worshipped perpetually means the son sacrifices to her,
but it stops at the grandson.'
This clearly emphasizes the importance of the adopted ancestor,
and thus one does not again care for one's private grandmother.
Now, Your Majesty is a great-grandson to Xiàosù;
a grandson to Xiàomù;
and a grandson to Xiàohuì.
The Rites do not permit perpetual worship beyond the grandson,
so it is fitting that their tablets be moved.
Examining the precedent of the Sòng dynasty's Xīníng era, when the Fèngcí Miào was abolished,
it aligns with the present situation.
It is appropriate to move the tablets to the mausoleum temple,
and perform the ancestral sacrifices there annually as before."
The report was approved.
The Fèngcí Diàn was subsequently abolished.
Shìzōng's Xiàoliè Hòu
was worshipped in the Hóngxiào Diàn during the Lóngqìng era,
and moved to be enshrined in the Fèngxiān Diàn in the third year of Wànlì.
Mùzōng's mother, Xiàokè Huángtàihòu,
was worshipped in the Shénxiāo Diàn in the early Lóngqìng era,
and Xiàoyì Hòu was also enshrined beside her.
In the sixth year,
Xiàoyì was enshrined in the Tàimiào.
In the third year of Wànlì,
Xiàokè was moved to be enshrined in the Fèngxiān Diàn,
and both temples were abolished.
Xiàn Huángdì Miào
In the fourth month of the second year of Jiājìng, sacrifices for the ancestral temple of Emperor Xīngxiàn were first ordered,
with music using the eight-row dance.
Initially,
the ritual officials' deliberation on the temple system was unresolved.
The Imperial Academy student Hé Yuān submitted a memorial,
requesting the establishment of a "Perpetual Chamber" (shìshì) to the east of the Tàimiào.
Wāng Jùn, Minister of the Board of Rites, and others all deemed it impermissible.
The Emperor decreed that a separate chamber be established beside the Fèngxīandiàn
to fully express filial piety.
The ritual officials convened a discussion, stating:
"The establishment of the Fèngcí
was based by ritual ministers on the specific temple of Jiāng Yuán.
As for establishing a temple for one's biological father within the Imperial City,
this is unprecedented in antiquity.
Only Emperor Āi of Hàn established a temple in the capital for King Gòng of Dīngtáo,
which cannot serve as a precedent."
Shí Bǎo, Grand Secretary of the Grand Secretariat, and others also stated it was impermissible.
The Emperor did not listen.
The area behind the Fèngcídiàn was renovated as the Guāndédiàn to enshrine him.
In the fourth month of the fourth year,
Hé Yuān, who had already been appointed Assistant Administrator of the Court of Imperial Entertainments,
again submitted a memorial requesting the establishment of a "Perpetual Chamber"
to honor the Emperor's biological father (huángkǎo) in the Tàimiào.
Xí Shū, Minister of the Board of Rites, and others deliberated:
"The Son of Heaven has seven temples.
Emperors Wén and Wǔ of Zhōu both had merits and virtues,
hence the 'Perpetual Chambers' of Wén and Wǔ were established above the three zhāomù.
Emperor Xiàn was posthumously given the title of Emperor
but was not an actual Son of Heaven.
Hé Yuān's words are baseless flattery;
we request that his memorial be shelved."
The Emperor ordered a re-deliberation,
and Xí Shū and others stated:
"If the spirit tablet is placed above Emperor Wǔzōng,
then Wǔzōng is the sovereign,
and the distinction must not be usurped.
If placed below Emperor Wǔzōng,
then Emperor Xiàn is his uncle,
and the spirit would ultimately not be at peace."
At that time, among court officials, opinion on whether to refer to him as 'father' (kǎo) or 'elder uncle' (bó) was divided,
with roughly half on each side.
But when it came to discussing his enshrinement in the Tàimiào,
not a single person thought it permissible.
Academicians Zhāng Cōng and Guì È also all deemed it impermissible,
and Xí Shū again secretly submitted a memorial arguing against it.
The Emperor did not listen
and again ordered a conference.
It was then decided, following the precedent of Emperor Xuān of Hàn,
to establish a Nímào within the imperial city,
modeled after the Wénhuádiàn.
The ritual vessels, music, and dances
all followed the rites for the Son of Heaven.
The Emperor personally named it the Shìmào.
In the seventh month of the fifth year, the Emperor instructed the Board of Works that the Guāndédiàn was too narrow,
and he wished to build a separate one to the left of the Fèngtiāndiàn.
Zhào Huáng, Minister, deemed it impermissible,
but the Emperor did not listen.
Thus, it was built to the east of the Fèngxīan,
named Chóngxiāndiàn.
In the thirteenth year, he ordered the name of the Chéngtiān Ancestral Temple changed to Lóngqìngdiàn.
In the fifteenth year,
to avoid a channel,
the Shìmào was relocated
and renamed Xiàn Huángdì Miào.
The old Shìmào was then renamed Jǐngshéndiàn,
and the sleeping palace was named Yǒngxiàodiàn.
In the seventeenth year, at Fēng Fāng's request,
he was referred to as 'zōng' to be enshrined in the Míngtáng.
The ritual officials dared not disobey.
Those gathered for deliberation took a long time,
stating:
"In antiquity, father and son had different zhāomù,
while brothers were in the same generation.
Thus, the Yīn dynasty had four rulers of one generation sharing a temple,
and Emperor Tàizǔ and Emperor Tàizōng of Sòng both occupied the zhāo position.
Now, the Emperor's biological father and Emperor Xiàozōng should share one temple."
Thus, Emperor Xiàn was enshrined in the Tàimiào.
In the twenty-second year, the Tàimiào was renovated.
The court deliberated that Emperor Ruìzōng and Emperor Xiàozōng should both occupy one temple,
both as zhāo.
The Emperor rebuked his ministers for not serving with full loyalty
and shelved their proposal.
Soon after, Jiāng Rǔbì, Junior Supervisor of the Left, requested that the temple of the Emperor's biological father be moved to the foremost position of the Mùmào,
to serve as the future 'Perpetual Chamber,'
standing side-by-side with Emperor Chéngzǔ's temple.
Guō Xīyán, Right Remonstrance Official, further wished to establish only four close relatives' temples outside Emperor Tàizǔ's temple's 'Perpetual Chamber,'
and to transfer Emperors Xiàozōng and Wǔzōng out of the main temple.
The ritual ministers rejected his absurdity, and it was stopped.
In the sixth month of the twenty-fourth year,
the new Tàimiào was completed.
Emperor Ruìzōng was then enshrined in the fourth position to the left of the Tàimiào,
his order elevated above Emperor Wǔzōng,
and the sacrifices of the special temple were abolished.
In the forty-fourth year, as fungus grew on the pillars of the old temple,
it was renamed Yùzhīgōng,
and daily offerings and seasonal sacrifices were established.
At the beginning of Emperor Mùzōng's reign,
due to the request of ritual ministers,
the seasonal sacrifices and those on festivals, death anniversaries, and occasions requiring notification to the spirits were abolished,
with only daily offerings continuing.
In the first year of Lóngqìng,
Wáng Zhì of the Ministry of Rites requested the abolition of Emperor Xiàn's enshrinement in the Tàimiào,
and to consecrate him solely in the Shìmào.
The memorial was sent down to the relevant departments.
In the ninth year of Wànlì,
Dīng Rǔqiān of the Ministry of Rites requested to continue the exclusive sacrifices at Yùzhīgōng
and to restore the imperial robes and crowns of Emperor Xuānzōng and his Empress to the Tàimiào.
The Emperor rebuked Dīng Rǔqiān for his absurd proposal
and demoted him to an external post.
In the first year of Tiānqǐ,
Lǐ Zōngyán, Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, memorialized that the removal of ancestral tablets from the temple (tiāomiào) should be discussed,
stating:
"Emperor Ruìzōng's entry into the temple
was Emperor Shìzōng's endless filial piety.
However, from the perspective of His Majesty,
it is now distant.
When Emperor Guāngzōng is enshrined,
it could either follow the old practice of removal
or a new deliberation.
For a filial son, it is indeed to serve parents with affection,
but for a benevolent person, it is to lead ancestors with righteousness."
The memorial was sent down to the Board of Rites,
but ultimately could not be followed.
Princes Participating in Sacrifices
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, it was decreed that Emperor's Elder Uncle, Shòuchūn Wáng, and his wife, Lady Liú, would be on one altar;
Emperor's brothers, Nánchāng Wáng, Huòqiū Wáng, Xiàcài Wáng, Ānfēng Wáng, Huòqiū Wáng's wife, Lady Zhái, and Ānfēng Wáng's wife, Lady Zhào, on one altar;
Emperor's brothers, Méngchéng Wáng, Xūyí Wáng, Línhuái Wáng, and Línhuái Wáng's wife, Lady Liú, on one altar.
Later, it was decided that all wives would be referred to as Concubines (fēi).
Emperor's nephews, Bǎoyìng Wáng, Lù'ān Wáng, Láinán Wáng, Dūliáng Wáng, Yīngshān Wáng, Shānyáng Wáng, and Zhāoxìn Wáng, on one altar,
a total of nineteen individuals.
In spring and summer, sacrifices were held in the eastern corridor of Rénzǔ Miào;
in autumn, winter, and on New Year's Eve, in the eastern corridor of Dézǔ Miào.
The Emperor performed the initial offering (chūxiàn lǐ),
while other offering officials went to the spirit tablets to make their separate offerings.
In the fourth year, the princes were moved to the eastern wall inside the hall.
In the ninth year,
the new Tàimiào was completed,
and Méngchéng Wángfēi Tián Shì and Xūyí Wángfēi Táng Shì were added to the sacrifices.
During the Zhèngdé reign,
Censor Xú Wénhuá stated:
"For those in the clan who reach adulthood but have no descendants,
the sacrifice eventually falls to the grandsons of their brothers.
These princes are now five or six generations removed,
and should be removed from the main temple (yí tiāo)."
The ritual officials deliberated and deemed it impermissible.
During the Jiājìng period,
they continued to be arranged in order in the eastern corridor.
In the twenty-fourth year,
the newly built Tàimiào was completed.
They were again moved and arranged along the eastern wall,
and the separate offerings were abolished.
In the fourteenth year of Wànlì,
Péi Yìngzhāng, Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, stated:
"The princes were originally enshrined with their ancestors.
Now the temples of the four ancestors have been removed,
and the princes have nowhere to be enshrined.
The sacrifices should be abolished,
and they should be enshrined in the removed ancestral temple (tiāomiào)."
The Board of Rites stated:
"The tiāo is for storing the spirit tablets of abandoned temples,
intended for ancestors, not for descendants.
Rites have 'tiāo,'
but we have not heard of 'pei tiāo' (being enshrined in the removed temple).
We request to follow the initial system
and arrange them in order in the eastern corridor as the appropriate rite."
The report was approved.
Meritorious Officials Enshrined Together
In the second year of Hóngwǔ (1369), when sacrifices were offered at the Tàimiào,
Liáo Yǒng'ān, Yú Tōnghǎi, Zhāng Déshèng, Sāng Shìjié, Gěng Zàichéng, Hú Dàhǎi, and Zhào Déshèng were enshrined as co-sacrificers.
Six blue cloth screens were set up in the courtyard of the Tàimiào,
and officials were dispatched to offer sacrifices separately.
After the emperor’s secondary offering was about to conclude,
the rites were performed.
Each year, for the spring and autumn sacrifices at the temple,
they were enshrined for co-sacrifice in the east wing of Rénzǔ Temple.
In the third year, eight meritorious officials, including Cháng Yùchūn, were designated for co-sacrifice.
In spring and summer, they were placed in the west wing of Rénzǔ Temple,
and in autumn and winter, in the west wing of Dézǔ Temple.
Their spirit tablets were set facing east,
and the practice of using screens was then abolished.
The rites for the three offerings were redefined:
the emperor made the first offering,
and at that time, the sacrificing officials would proceed to perform their rites separately,
without bowing.
In the fourth year,
Tàizǔ said to the officials of the Zhōngshū Shěng:
"The sacrifices at the Tàimiào
include the arrangement of meritorious officials in the side wings.
Now that the combined sacrifice rites for the Tàimiào have been established,
I, with the ancestors fully present,
allow the deceased meritorious officials and old acquaintances to rely slightly on the divine spirits,
to share in the sacrifices.
This is not only a grand ceremony for the court's ancestral temple,
but also expresses my heart of not forgetting meritorious officials."
Thereupon, the ritual officials deliberated:
"During all combined sacrifices,
a yellow cloth pavilion should be erected,
with the spirit tablets of the paternal ancestors in the center,
and two walls on either side,
to offer sacrifices to the imperial princes and meritorious officials,
with senior ministers dispatched to offer sacrifices separately."
The edict approved this.
Soon after, an order was given to remove the cloth pavilion.
In the ninth year,
the new Tàimiào was completed.

Xú Dá, Cháng Yùchūn, Lǐ Wénzhōng, Dèng Yù, Tāng Hé, Mù Yīng, Yú Tōnghǎi, Zhāng Déshèng, Hú Dàhǎi, Zhào Déshèng, Gěng Zàichéng, and Sāng Shìjié, a total of twelve individuals, were enshrined in the west wing,
and Liáo Yǒng'ān was removed.
During the Jiànwén reign,
Sòng Lǐ, the Assistant Minister of the Lǐbù, stated:
"Meritorious officials have their own temple on Jīlóng Shān;
I request to abolish their co-sacrifice at the Tàimiào."
The emperor, considering it a custom set by the former emperor,
did not comply.
He also ordered that after the Tàimiào sacrifices were completed,
another official should be sent to offer sacrifices at their own temple.
In the first year of Hóngxī (1425), Zhāng Yù, Zhū Néng, and Yáo Guǎngxiào were enshrined for co-sacrifice at the Tàimiào.
Zhāng Fǔ, Zhū Yǒng, Wáng Tōng, and Yáo Jì, the Junior Supervisor of the Shàngbǎo, were dispatched to sacrifice to their respective fathers.
In the ninth year of Jiājìng (1530), based on Liáo Dàonán's suggestion,
Yáo Guǎngxiào was removed.
In the tenth year, based on the proposal of Lǐ Yú, the Director of the Xíngbù,
Liú Jī's position was advanced to rank above the Six Kings.
In the sixteenth year, based on the memorial of Wǔdìng Hóu Guō Xūn,
his ancestor Yīng was advanced.
Initially, the meritorious officials in the two temples
were ranked according to their noble titles.
When Jī's position was advanced above dukes and marquises,
it was then ordered again for the ritual officials to deliberate on the ranks of meritorious officials in the two temples.
Consequently, Yīng was placed above Sāng Shìjié,
Zhāng Yù and Zhū Néng below Mù Yīng,
and Jī below Shìjié.
In the twenty-fourth year, all co-sacrificers were moved to the west wall of the new Tàimiào,
and the separate offerings were abolished.
In the fourteenth year of Wànlì (1586),
Péi Yìngzhāng, the Tàicháng Qīng, stated:
"In the temple, the empresses are listed above;
it is appropriate for ministers of different surnames to be distinguished by proper ritual.
Moreover, when the most revered bows down below,
the spirits of the various ministers must also be uneasy."
An order was given to revert to the west wing,
and officials were dispatched to offer sacrifices separately.
In the first year of Tiānqǐ (1621),
Lǐ Zōngyán, the Tàicháng Shàocīng, stated:
"Previous dynasties all had civil officials participating in ancestral sacrifices;
our dynasty should not be the sole exception."
This was submitted to the Lǐbù for deliberation,
but it was not implemented.
Royal Ancestral Temples
In the fourth year of Hóngwǔ (1371),
Táo Kǎi, the Minister of the Lǐbù, and others, deliberated and decided that
within the palace walls of a royal domain,
the ancestral temple should be on the left,
and the Altar of Land and Grain on the right.
The temple's structure was:
a main hall of five bays,
a sleeping hall of the same size,
and a gate of three bays.
In the eighth year of Yǒnglè (1410), the Xiǎng Táng for Qín Mǐnwáng was built,
and it was ordered to follow the specifications of Jìn Gōngwáng's,
but elevated by one foot.
Consequently, the Xiǎng Táng was standardized to seven bays,
one hundred and nine feet five inches wide,
twenty-nine feet high,
and forty-three feet five inches deep.
In the thirteenth year of Hóngzhì (1500),
Níng Wáng Chénháo memorialized that the ritual music for temple sacrifices had no fixed form,
and requested its promulgation for observance.
The Lǐbù deliberated:
"In the first year of Hóngwǔ (1368),
Academician Sòng Lián and others memorialized to standardize the sacrificial rites and music for the various royal domains,
using 'qīng' characters,
but there were only names of tunes
without lyrics.
Please have each royal household investigate and compile them.
Thereupon, the Chief Scribe of Jìngjiāng Wáng submitted the musical scores,
and also stated that for the five sacrifices in the first ten days of the four seasonal months and on New Year's Eve, the items used,
sacrificial vessels, and ritual dances, all ritual protocols strictly followed the imperial regulations established at the beginning of the dynasty."
This was followed.
In the eighth year of Jiājìng (1529),
Qín Wáng Chōngyào stated:
"Dài Yìwáng should be enshrined in the temple,
but from the initial enfeoffment until now,
the number of five temples has already been filled.
I request to establish a system for transferring ancestral tablets."
The ritual officials stated:
"For imperial princes to transfer ancestral tablets,
there is no precedent in ancient systems.
It is appropriate to derive and scale down the rites of transferring and enshrining from the Tàimiào.
The first enfeoffed should be in the center,
never moved for a hundred generations,
and the subsequent four generations,
when kinship becomes distant, should be transferred.
However, as feudal lords do not have temples for transferred tablets,
the transferred tablets should be enshrined in the chamber of the founding ancestor,
placed in a cist and stored.
At the end of each year, the transferred tablets should be taken out for combined sacrifices."
The edict approved the proposal.
Family Temples of Officials
In the early Míng dynasty, there was no fixed system.
For the time being, the system of Zhū Zǐ's ancestral shrines was imitated,
enshrining the spirit tablets of the great-great-grandfather, great-grandfather, grandfather, and father for four generations,
and sacrificing to them in the middle month of each season,
with additional sacrifices on the day of the deceased's anniversary in the twelfth lunar month and offerings during seasonal folk festivals.
It was already enacted that commoners could offer sacrifices to their grandparents and parents.
This was established as a regulation.
Regarding the rites of seasonal offerings in the sleeping hall,
they were generally similar to the system of ancestral shrines for officials.
The hall had three bays,
with two sets of three-tiered steps,
and two gates, inner and outer.
The hall was equipped with four niches,
each niche holding a table.
The great-great-grandfather resided on the west,
and so on towards the east,
with the spirit tablets stored in cists.
Cabinets were placed against the two walls,
the west storing books and clothing,
the east storing sacrificial vessels.
Collateral relatives without descendants
were attached according to their seniority.
Commoners had no ancestral shrines;
they placed the spirit tablets of two generations in the middle of their living quarters,
without cists.
In the 6th year of Hóngwǔ (1373), the rites for ancestral temples for dukes, marquises, and below were established.
For all dukes, marquises, and ranking officials,
a separate ancestral shrine of three rooms shall be built to the east of their residence
to worship their gāozǔ (great-great-grandfather), zēngzǔ (great-grandfather), zǔ (grandfather), and kǎo (father),
and their consorts shall be enshrined alongside them.
If the ancestral shrine is not yet ready,
the spirit tablets shall be placed in the central hall for offerings and sacrifices.
For officials of the second rank and above,
one sheep and one pig shall be offered.
For officials of the fifth rank and above,
one sheep shall be offered.
For those below the fifth rank, one pig shall be offered.
All offerings shall be divided into four parts and presented cooked.
If one cannot provide sacrificial animals,
food offerings shall be prepared.
The vessels used
shall be appropriate to the official's rank
and the family's means.
Two days prior,
the chief worshipper shall inform the emperor
to be excused from morning court.
All sacrifices
shall be performed on an auspicious day of the four mid-months (the second month of each season),
or on the vernal or autumnal equinox,
or the winter or summer solstice.
The day before the sacrifice,
one shall bathe, fast, and change clothes,
and lodge in an outer dwelling.
At dawn,
the chief worshipper and his wife, leading those who will participate in the sacrifice, shall proceed to the ancestral shrine.
The chief worshipper shall carry the censer containing the principal and associated spirit tablets,
place it on a tray,
and have a junior family member carry it to the sacrificial area.
The chief worshipper shall open the censer
and take out the spirit tablets of each male ancestor.
The chief wife shall open the censer
and take out the spirit tablets of each female ancestor,
arranging them in order.
Junior family members shall carry the associated spirit tablets
and place them on the east and west walls.
Attendants shall present the food offerings.
One person shall read the prayer,
also assisting with the rites,
chosen from among junior family members and relatives.
After the spirit tablets are arranged,
everyone shall take their positions.
The chief worshipper shall stand to the east.
His paternal uncles and elder brothers shall stand slightly to his east and in front of him.
Other relatives shall stand behind him.
The chief wife shall stand to the west.
Her mother and other mothers shall stand slightly to her west and in front of her.
Other women shall stand behind her.
When the announcer calls for bowing,
all shall bow twice.
The chief worshipper shall go before the incense table, kneel,
offer incense three times,
and present and pour wine.
Attendants shall pour wine before the associated spirit tablets.
The prayer reader shall kneel and read the prayer.
When the announcer calls for bowing,
the chief worshipper shall return to his place,
and he and the chief wife shall both bow twice.
The second and final offerings shall follow the same procedure,
except no prayer is read.
For each offering,
attendants shall also make offerings before the associated spirit tablets.
After the rites are completed,
they shall bow twice,
burn the prayer and paper money in the central courtyard,
and return the spirit tablets to their censer.
In the 11th year of Chénghuà (1475),
the Libationer Zhōu Hóngmó said:
"For ancestral temples of officials and commoners, the spirit tablets
are all arranged from west to east.
Ancient times had no saying that the path of spirits favors the right.
It is only the temple system of our Tàizǔ (Emperor Hóngwǔ)
that accords with the ancient kings' principle of 'Zhāo on the left, Mù on the right.'
It should be ordered that officials from the first to ninth rank
shall all establish one temple,
with variations in height and width according to their rank.
For spirit tablets, gāozǔ shall be placed on the left,
zēngzǔ on the right,
zǔ next on the left,
and kǎo next on the right."
The Emperor ordered the ritual ministers to deliberate and revise the regulations.
In the 15th year of Jiājìng (1536),
the Minister of Rites, Xià Yán, said:
"According to the three dynasties, there were systems of five, three, two, or one ancestral temples,
depending on whether they were feudal lords, ministers, or high-ranking officials of upper, middle, or lower grades.
Later generations have different official positions and no hereditary enfeoffments and territories;
how can one be overly rigid in adhering to ancient practices?
It was only during the Sòng dynasty that the Confucian scholar Chéng Yí first simplified it to four generations.
From dukes and ministers to scholars and commoners,
none were an exception.
It is said that the system of five degrees of mourning
extends to gāozǔ (great-great-grandfather),
so sacrifices should also follow this.
Currently, it is stipulated that officials of the third rank and above shall establish five temples,
and those below shall all establish four temples.
Those with five temples
shall also follow the Táng system:
five bays and nine rafters,
with partition boards on the side providing five chambers.
The five-generation ancestor shall be enshrined in the middle,
and gāozǔ, zēngzǔ, zǔ, and nì (father) in the four side chambers.
Those with four temples
shall have three bays and five rafters,
with gāozǔ and zēngzǔ enshrined in the middle chamber,
and zǔ and nì in the two side chambers.
If the founding ancestor is to be worshipped,
then as Zhū Xī stated, during the sacrifice,
a paper tablet shall be made
and burned after the sacrifice.
For those of the third rank and above,
when the lineage generations reach their limit,
the current ancestor eligible for a temple shall become the perpetually worshipped ancestor
and shall not be moved.
For those of the fourth rank and below,
the four generations shall simply be moved in succession."
This was adopted.
Collated Notes

Gazetteer 29, Rites 7 (Auspicious Rites 1): Accession Ceremony, Grand Court Audience Ceremony, Regular Court Audience Ceremony, Crown Prince and Princes' Court Audience Ceremony, Princes' Arrival at Court Ceremony, Various Officials' Court Audience Ceremony, Empress's Court Audience Ceremony, Congratulatory Court Audience for the Crown Prince Ceremony, Grand Feast Ceremony, Ceremony for Conferring Honorable Titles and Emblems.
The second type is auspicious rites.
Those performed at court
are called court assemblies,
feasts,
conferring honorable titles and emblems,
investitures,
imperial lectures,
and memorials.
Those performed at the Píyōng (imperial academy)
are called inspection of learning.
Those extending from the Son of Heaven to commoners
are called capping ceremonies
and weddings.
Those performed throughout the realm
are called imperial tours,
imperial edicts and amnesties,
and village drinking rituals.
The major ones are recorded.
Similar rituals
are attached to their respective categories.
Accession Ceremony
When Hàn Gāodì ascended the throne on the north bank of the Fàn River,
the rites of humble beginnings were not yet complete.
From the Wèi and Jìn dynasties onwards,
accession often involved receiving the abdication and changing the reign title.
Yuán Shìzǔ had long held a respected position;
after unifying the realm,
he merely held a congratulatory court audience.
When the Míng dynasty arose,
Tàizǔ, in the 12th month of the 1st year of Wú (1367), was about to ascend the throne.
He ordered Left Chancellor Lǐ Shàncháng and others to prepare the ceremony.
Shàncháng, leading the ritual officials, presented the memorial.
On the day of accession,
the Emperor first offered sacrifices to Heaven and Earth.
After the rites were completed,
he ascended the imperial throne in the southern suburbs.
The Chancellor, leading officials and below, as well as the elders of the capital city,
bowed, congratulated, danced,
and cried 'Long live!' three times.
With imperial regalia and retinue,
he proceeded to the Tàimiào (Imperial Ancestral Temple),
presented the posthumous titles and imperial seals for his four generations of ancestors,
and offered sacrifices to the altars of the land and grain.
Upon returning,
he donned the imperial robe and crown,
ascended the Fèngtiān Diàn (Hall of Receiving Heaven),
and officials presented memorials of congratulations.
Earlier,
the Shìyí Sì (侍儀司) set up a table for memorials to the northwest of the inner path within the Dānchí (丹墀).
Positions for prostrating officials from the Chéngxiàng (丞相) downwards were set up to the east and west of the inner path.
Each rank had a different position,
arranged in rows facing north.
The officials holding, opening, and announcing the memorials were positioned to the west of the memorial table,
facing east.
Two Jūyí Yùshǐ (糾儀御史) were to the south of the memorial table,
facing east and west.
Two Sùwèi Zhènfǔ (宿衞鎮撫) were at the eastern and western sides of the steps,
and twenty-four Hùwèi Bǎihù (護衞百戶) were to their south,
slightly behind.
Two Zhībān (知班) were
to the north of the civil and military officials' prostration positions,
facing east and west.
The Tōngzàn (通贊) and Zànlǐ (贊禮), two officials, were to the north of the Zhībān,
the Tōngzàn to the west
and the Zànlǐ to the east.
Four Yǐn Wénwǔ Bān (引文武班) officials were to the north of the civil and military officials' prostration positions,
slightly behind,
facing east and west.
Two Yǐn Diànqián Bān (引殿前班) officials were to the south of the Yǐn Wénwǔ Bān.
Two officials carrying the memorial table were to the north of the Yǐn Wénwǔ Bān.
Two officials carrying the memorial table for the throne were at the western steps,
facing east.
On the Dānbì (丹陛), three Zhīhuī Sì (指揮司) officials of the Diànqián Bān (殿前班) were positioned,
facing east.
Three Xuānhuī Yuàn (宣徽院) officials were positioned,
facing west.
Yíluán Sì (儀鸞司) officials were to the left and right of the central gate of the hall,
and eight Hùwèi Qiānhù (護衞千戶) were at the east and west gates of the hall,
all facing east and west.
Four Míngbiān (鳴鞭) officials were to the south of the Diànqián Bān,
facing north.
Six Jiāngjūn (將軍) were to the left and right of the hall gates,
and four Tiānwǔ Jiāngjūn (天武將軍) were at the four corners of the steps,
all facing east and west.
Inside the hall,
the Shàngbǎo Sì (尚寶司) set up a treasure table in the center,
and the Shìyí Sì (侍儀司) set up a memorial table to the south of the treasure table.
Civil and military attendants of both classes were to the east and west in the hall,
including Wén Qǐjūzhù (文起居注), Jǐshìzhōng (給事中), Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ (殿中侍御史), Shàngbǎoqīng (尚寶卿),
and Wǔ Xuándāo Zhīhuī (武懸刀指揮),
facing east and west.
The official receiving the memorial was to the south of the civil attendants' class,
facing west.
Two Nèizàn (內贊) were to the south of the official receiving the memorial,
and two Juǎlián Jiāngjūn (捲簾將軍) were in front of the curtain,
all facing east and west.
On that day,
the Gǒngwèi Sì (拱衞司) displayed the imperial regalia (lǔbù),
arranged armed guards outside the Wǔmén (午門),
displayed flags and banners,
and set up the five imperial carriages (wǔlù) outside the Fèngtiān Mén (奉天門).
Two Shìyí Shèrén (侍儀舍人)
carried the memorial table in.
When the drum sounded for the first preparation (chūyán),
all officials in court attire stood outside the Wǔmén.
The Tōngzàn, Zànlǐ, Sùwèi officials, various attendants, and Shàngbǎoqīng attendants entered.
When the drum sounded for the third preparation (sānyán),
officials from the Chéngxiàng downwards entered.
The Huángdì (皇帝) ascended the throne in his ceremonial robes (gǔnmiǎn),
and the grand music and drum ensemble began to play.
When the music stopped,
the Jiāngjūn rolled up the curtain,
and the Shàngbǎoqīng placed the imperial seal (bǎo) on the table.
The Gǒngwèi Sì cracked the whip (míngbiān),
and the Yǐnbān led all officials into the Dānchí to their prostration positions.
When they first moved, music played;
when they reached their positions, the music stopped.
The Zhībān announced the classes,
and the Zànlǐ announced the prostration.
Music played,
four prostrations were made,
and they rose.
The music stopped.
Officials from the memorial-holder downwards entered through the west gate of the hall.
The Nèizàn announced the presentation of the memorial.
The official holding the memorial knelt and presented it.
The official receiving the memorial inserted his ceremonial tablet (hù),
knelt to receive it,
and placed it on the table.
He then withdrew his tablet,
rose,
and retreated to stand
facing east.
The Nèizàn announced the reading of the memorial.
The official reading the memorial came forward,
inserted his tablet,
and knelt.
The official opening the memorial inserted his tablet
and knelt with him.
After the reading,
the official opening the memorial withdrew his tablet,
returned the memorial to the table,
and both retreated.
The official reading the memorial prostrated and rose.
All exited through the west gate of the hall
and returned to their positions.
The Zànlǐ announced the prostration.
Music played,
four prostrations were made,
and the music stopped.
They inserted their tablets,
bowed three times,
and performed the ritual dance.
They clasped their hands above their foreheads,
and shouted "Wànsuì!" (萬歲!) three times.
They withdrew their tablets,
prostrated and rose.
Music played,
four prostrations were made,
and the congratulations concluded.
Thereupon, officials were dispatched to enfeoff the Huánghòu (皇后) with a document,
and to establish the Huáng Tàizǐ (皇太子),
and an edict of accession was proclaimed to the world.
As Chéngzǔ's (成祖) accession was sudden,
its deliberation was not detailed.
When Rénzōng (仁宗) acceded,
earlier,
the Sīshè Jiān (司設監) arranged the imperial throne at the Fèngtiān Mén.
The Qīntiān Jiān (欽天監) set up the timing drum,
the Shàngbǎo Sì (尚寶司) set up the treasure table,
and the Jiàofāng Sì (教坊司) prepared the Zhōnghé Sháolè (中和韶樂),
which was set up but not played.
On that morning,
officials were dispatched to report to Heaven, Earth, and the Imperial Ancestors,
and the Huángdì, in mourning attire, reported to the funerary couch and mat.
At the appointed time,
bells and drums sounded,
and the imperial regalia were displayed.
The Huángdì, in ceremonial robes,
proceeded to the Fèngtiān Mén.
All officials, in court attire,
entered the Wǔmén.
Honglú Sì (鴻臚寺) guided the attendant officials in performing the ceremony,
and requested the emperor to ascend the throne.
The Huángdì exited through the central gate,
ascended the throne,
and a whip was cracked.
All officials presented memorials,
performed the ceremony,
and issued edicts,
all according to the established rites.
After Xuānzōng (宣宗),
successions by the crown prince were all similar.
In the sixteenth year of Zhèngdé (正德),
Shìzōng (世宗) entered to inherit the great line of succession.
Earlier, a temporary palace (xíngdiàn) was built outside the Xuānwǔ Mén (宣武門),
facing south.
Curtains, canopies, and an imperial throne were set up,
and the Yìshàn Guān (翼善冠) and robes, as well as the imperial regalia (lǔbù dàjià), were prepared in wait.
At the appointed time,
all officials met the imperial carriage in the suburbs.
The imperial carriage entered the temporary palace,
and the four prostrations were performed.
The next day,
he entered through the Dàmíng Mén (大明門).
He reviewed the draft edict,
changed the reign title,
and, in plain clothes, proceeded to the funerary couch and mat of the deceased emperor (dàxíng jīyán) to make announcement.
Upon completion,
an incense table was set up on the Dānbì (丹陛) of the Fèngtiān Diàn (奉天殿).
The Huángdì, in ceremonial robes,
performed the ceremony of reporting to Heaven and Earth.
He proceeded to the Fèngxiān Diàn (奉先殿) and Fèngcí Diàn (奉慈殿) to make announcement,
and then proceeded again to the funerary couch and mat of the deceased emperor, the Císhòu Huáng Tàihòu (慈壽皇太后), and the Zhuāngsù Huánghòu (莊肅皇后) to perform ceremonies respectively,
then proceeded to the Huágài Diàn (華蓋殿).
All officials, in court attire, entered.
An imperial decree was issued to waive congratulations,
and five prostrations and three kowtows were performed.
The Honglú Sì officials requested the emperor to ascend the hall,
and the emperor exited through the central gate to preside in the Fèngtiān Diàn.
Whips were cracked,
prostrations were announced,
and edicts were issued,
all according to regulation.
Grand Court Ceremony
During the Hàn (漢) dynasty's grand court ceremony,
seven quarters of an hour before the end of the night watch,
bells rang for receiving congratulations.
Ministers (gōngqīng) and lower officials came to the court with gifts,
those of two thousand shí (石) rank and above ascended the hall,
shouted "Wànsuì!",
and then feasted.
The Jìn Xiánníng Zhù (晉咸寧注)
distinguished between morning congratulations and daytime gatherings.
Under the Táng (唐) system,
on New Year's Day (Zhèngdàn), Winter Solstice (Dōngzhì), the first day of the fifth month (Wǔyuè Shuò), and the Qiānqiū Jié (千秋節),
congratulations were always received at court.
The Sòng (宋) dynasty followed this.
In the ninth month of the first year of Hóngwǔ (洪wu) of Míng Tàizǔ (明太祖), the New Year's Day court assembly ceremony was established,
which was somewhat similar to the accession ceremony.
Thereafter, it was repeatedly changed by imperial edict,
and established as a standard system.
For New Year's Day (Zhēngdàn) and Winter Solstice (Dōngzhì),
the day before,
the Shàngbǎo Sì (Office of Imperial Seals) sets up the imperial throne in the Fèngtiān Diàn (Hall of Receiving Heaven),
and the imperial treasure table (Bǎo’àn) to the east of the throne,
and the incense table (Xiāng’àn) to the south of the Dānbì (Imperial Steps).
The Jiàofāng Sì (Office of Music) sets up the Zhōnghé Sháoyuè (Central Harmony and Splendor Music) inside the hall, to the east and west,
facing north.
The next morning,
the Jǐnyī Wèi (Brocade-Clad Guard) arrays the Lǔbù (imperial standard and paraphernalia) and Yízhàng (ceremonial guard) on the Dānbì and Dānchí (Imperial Courtyard),
sets up the míngshàn (display fans) inside the hall,
and arrays the lièchēlù (imperial carriages) in the Dānchí.
Four whip-crackers,
to the left and right, face north.
The Jiàofāng Sì arranges the dàyuè (grand music) on the Dānbì, to the east and west,
facing north.
The Yílǐ Sì (Office of Rites) sets up two tables, Tóngwén (Unified Culture) and Yùbó (Jade and Silk), to the east of the Dānbì.
The Jīnwú Wèi (Imperial Guard) stations hùwèi guān (guarding officials) inside the hall and on the Dānbì,
and arrays jiǎshì (armored warriors) from the Dānchí to outside the Wǔmén (Meridian Gate).
The Jǐnyī Wèi stations jiāngjūn (generals) from the Dānbì to outside the Fèngtiān Mén (Gate of Receiving Heaven),
and arrays qízhì (flags and banners) outside the Fèngtiān Mén,
all arranged to the east and west.
The Diǎnmù Suǒ (Directorate of Imperial Stables) arrays zhàngmǎ (ceremonial horses) and xīxiàng (rhinoceros and elephant) south of the Wénlóu and Wǔlóu (Civil and Martial Towers),
facing east and west.
The Sīchén Láng (Official in Charge of Announcing the Dawn) is positioned on the east side of the inner pathway,
near the north.
Two Jiūyí Yùshǐ (Censorate Officials Supervising Rites)
are positioned to the north of the Dānchí.
Two nèizàn (inner prompters)
are positioned inside the hall.
Two wàizàn (outer prompters)
are positioned to the north of the Dānchí.
Officials for Chuánzhì (Delivering Edicts) and Xuānbǎo (Reading Memorials) are positioned inside the hall,
all facing east and west.
At the first drum signal,
all officials don their court attire
and array outside the Wǔmén.
At the second signal,
they enter through the Left and Right Yèmén (Flanking Gates),
proceed to the east and west of the Dānchí,
and stand facing north.
At the third signal,
the Zhíshì Guān (Officials in Charge of Affairs) proceed to the Huágài Diàn (Hall of the Illustrious Canopy).
The Emperor, in gǔnmiǎn (imperial ceremonial robes and crown), ascends the throne,
and the sound of the bell ceases.
The Yílǐ Sì announces that the Zhíshì Guān should perform the ceremony.
The zàn (prompter) calls for five bows.
When finished,
it is announced that the Emperor should proceed to the hall.
As the imperial procession sets forth,
the Zhōnghé Yuè plays.
Shàngbǎo Sì officials carry the imperial seal and precede the procession,
while Dǎojià Guān (Guiding Officials) lead the way.
Fans open and curtains roll up.
The imperial seal is placed on the table,
and the music stops.
Whips crack to announce the time.
The duìzàn (answering prompter) calls for the formation of ranks.
When the ranks are in order,
the Zànlǐ (Prompter of Rites) calls for bowing.
The dàyuè plays.
The zàn calls for four bows.
They rise,
and the music stops.
The Diǎnyí (Master of Ceremonies) calls for the presentation of the memorial (jìnbǎo).
The music plays.
Two Jǐshì Zhōng (Supervising Secretaries)
proceed to the Tóngwén table.
The Xùbān (Arranger of Ranks) guides them to lift the table and enter through the eastern gate,
placing it in the center of the hall.
The music stops.
The nèizàn calls for the announcement of the memorial’s summary (xuānbǎomù).
The Xuānbǎomù Guān (Official Announcing the Summary) kneels,
announces it,
prostrates,
and rises.
The call to announce the memorial is made.
The Zhǎnbǎo Guān (Official Unfurling the Memorial) takes the memorial.
The Xuānbǎo Guān (Official Announcing the Memorial) approaches the curtain.
The wàizàn calls,
“All officials kneel.”
After the memorial is announced,
both inner and outer prompters call,
“Prostrate,
rise.”
The Xùbān lifts the memorial table to the east of the hall.
The wàizàn calls, “All officials kneel.”
The Dàizhìcí Guān (Official Delivering the Congratulatory Address) kneels in the center of the Dānbì,
and delivers the address, saying:
“Your humble servant [name],
on this occasion of New Year's Day,
when the three yang bring prosperity,
and all things are renewed.”
For the Winter Solstice, he says:
“The lǜ (pitch-pipe) responds to Huángzhōng,
and the day marks the longest night.”
“We reverently consider Your Majesty, the Emperor,
who receives blessings from Heaven,
and ensures eternal prosperity under Heaven.”
After the congratulations,
the wàizàn calls,
“All officials prostrate,
rise.”
The music plays.
Four bows,
rise.
The music stops.
The Chuánzhì Guān (Official Delivering Edicts) kneels and announces the delivery of the edict.
He exits through the eastern gate,
reaches the Dānbì,
stands facing east,
and declares, “There is an edict!”
The Zànlǐ calls,
“Kneel!”
The edict is announced.
For New Year’s Day, it says:
“The joy of the beginning of the year
is shared with you, my ministers.”
For the Winter Solstice, it says:
“The joy of the lengthening day
is shared with you, my ministers.”
For the Wànshòu Shèngjié (Emperor's Birthday), the address is:
“Your humble servant [name],
reverently meeting the auspicious day of Your Majesty the Emperor's birth,
sincerely leads all civil and military officials in respectfully wishing Your Majesty a thousand years of longevity.”
No edict is delivered.
The Zànlǐ calls, “Prostrate,
rise.”
The music stops.
The zàn calls for inserting the hù (tablet) into the belt,
bowing three times,
and performing the ritual dance.
The zàn calls for kneeling and performing the shānhū (mountain call, i.e., "Long Live!").
All officials clasp their hands and raise them to their foreheads, saying,
“Wànsuì!” (Long Live!).
The call for shānhū is made again,
and they say,
“Wànsuì!”
The call for a second shānhū is made,
and they say,
“Wànwànsuì!” (Ten Thousand Times Ten Thousand Years!).
Whenever "Wànsuì" is called,
the musicians and imperial guards respond in unison.
The zàn calls for removing the hù,
prostrating,
rising,
and the music plays.
The zàn calls for four bows,
rising,
and the music stops.
The Yílǐ Sì announces that the ceremony is completed.
The Zhōnghé Yuè plays.
Whips crack.
The imperial procession sets forth.
Shàngbǎo Guān (Officials of Imperial Seals) carry the imperial seal.
Dǎojià Guān lead the way.
Upon reaching the Huágài Diàn,
the music stops.
All officials exit in order.
In the 30th year of Hóngwǔ (1397), it was revised that the Tóngwén and Yùbó tables should both be moved into the center of the hall,
and after the memorial was announced, they should be lifted and placed south of the Bǎo’àn.
In the 16th year of Jiājìng (1537), it was revised that the Fāngwù Àn (tribute table) from the Fān Guó (Vassal States) should enter the middle path of the Dānbì from left and right.
The Shídìng Gǔ (Time-Setting Drum) was placed on the Wénlóu.
The dàyuè was arranged inside the Fèngtiān Mén, to the east and west,
facing north.
Other ceremonies also had minor additions or deletions.
On the day of Lìchūn, the spring offering is presented.
Officials from the Imperial City, prefectures, and counties bring the spring cases up the eastern steps
and place them kneeling in the middle of the imperial thoroughfare (dānbì).
They prostrate,
rise.
The master of ceremonies (zànbài) calls out,
music plays.
They bow four times,
rise,
music stops.
Civil and military officials stand facing north.
The official delivering the address goes to the east of the central thoroughfare,
kneels, and states:
"It is the auspicious day of the New Spring,
it is proper to offer congratulations."
The master of ceremonies calls out,
music plays.
They bow five times and kowtow three times,
rise,
music stops.
The Ministry of Rites (Yílǐ Sī) announces that the ceremony is complete.
In the eleventh year of Zhèngtǒng,
on New Year's Day (Zhèngdàn) which was also Lìchūn,
the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù) deliberated that after the officials of Shùntiān Fǔ presented the spring offering,
all officials should proceed to their ranks to perform the Zhèngdàn congratulatory ceremony.
According to old regulations,
the congratulatory ceremony was performed on the Winter Solstice (Dōngzhì).
In the ninth year of Jiājìng, the sacrifices to the Two Suburbs were separated.
On the Winter Solstice (Dōngzhì), the Grand Offering (Dàbào) was held,
and on that day, the Rite of Completion (Qìngchéng Lǐ) was performed.
The next day,
the Emperor would go to the inner palace (nèidiàn)
to perform the Seasonal Sacrifice (Jiéjì Lǐ).
He would then go before the Empress Dowager (mǔhòu) to perform the congratulatory ceremony,
after which he would proceed to Fèngtīan Diàn to receive congratulations.
Regular Court Audience (Chángcháo Yí)
According to ancient rites,
the Son of Heaven had outer court (wàicháo), inner court (nèicháo), and banquet court (yàncháo).
Emperor Xuān of Hàn held court once every five days.
During the Táng dynasty,
the Son of Heaven would daily proceed to Zǐchén Diàn to meet his officials, which was called "regular attendance" (chángcān).
On the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month, he would proceed to Xuānzhèng Diàn to meet his officials, which was called "entering the cabinet" (rùgé).
During the Sòng dynasty, attendant officials (shìcóng guān) would daily attend court at Chuígǒng (hall), which was called "regular attendance" (chángcān).
Officials from all departments would attend court at Zǐchén (hall) once every five days, which was called "six attendances" (liùcān).

Court officials in the capital would attend court at Zǐchén (hall) on the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month, which was called "first-day attendance" (shuòcān) and "fifteenth-day attendance" (wàngcān).
In the third year of Hóngwǔ of the Míng dynasty, regulations were established.
On the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month,
the Emperor, wearing a leather cap (píbìanfú), would proceed to Fèngtīan Diàn.
Officials in court attire would stand east and west on the imperial terrace (dānchí),
bowing twice.
The head of the ranks would go forward,
bowing with all the officials,
and proclaim
"Long live Your Majesty" (Shènggōng wànfú).
They would return to their positions,
all bowing twice,
then stand in divided ranks.
Officials from the provinces, prefectures, censorate (tái), and ministries (bù) who had memorials
would ascend the hall via the western steps.
After presenting their memorials, they would descend the steps,
and all officials would exit.
In the seventeenth year, the "first and fifteenth day greeting" (shuòwàng qǐjū lǐ) ceremony was abolished.
Later, it was revised.
On the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month, the Emperor would proceed to Fèngtīan Diàn.
Regular court officials would stand in order on the imperial terrace (dānchí),
facing east and west.
Officials expressing gratitude or requesting leave would stand in order outside Fèngtīan Mén,
facing north.
Music would play as the Emperor ascended the throne.
Regular court officials would bow once and kowtow three times.
Music would stop,
and they would return to their ranks.
Officials expressing gratitude or requesting leave, outside Fèngtīan Mén,
would bow five times and kowtow three times.
The Emperor would then depart.
Furthermore, for all early court audiences,
the Emperor would proceed to Huágài Diàn.
Civil and military officials would stand east and west outside the Lùdǐng gate.
Whips would crack,
and the ceremony would proceed in order.
Officials of the fourth rank and above would enter the hall to attend.
Officials of the fifth rank and below would remain standing facing north as before.
Those who had matters to present would step out of their ranks.
After presenting their matters, whips would crack, and they would exit in order.
If the Emperor proceeded to Fèngtīan Diàn,
the ceremony would first be performed at Huágài Diàn.
After the presentation of matters,
officials of the fifth rank and below would go to the imperial terrace (dānchí),
standing facing north.
Officials of the fifth rank and above, and those from the Hànlín Yuàn, Gěishìzhōng, and Yùshǐ, would await the cracking of whips outside the Central Left and Central Right gates,
then proceed into the hall to stand in order.
After the court audience, they would exit.
Whenever all officials were seated in attendance before the Emperor,
if an official presented a matter,
they must stand up,
and resume their seats after the presentation.
When following the Emperor walking on the imperial terrace (dānchí),
they must always face north,
not south,
and turn left and right without turning their backs to the north.
When the Emperor ascended Fèngtīan Mén and the imperial thoroughfare (dānbì),
attendant officials were not allowed to pass directly through the central path or the royal path (wángdào).

In the twenty-fourth year, the attendant officials were designated: to the east were the heads of the Six Ministries (Liù Bù) and the Censorate (Dūchá Yuàn), the seal-holding censors (zhǎngyìn yùshǐ) of the Thirteen Circuits (Shísān Dào), officials from Tōngzhèng Sī, Dàlǐ Sì, Tàicháng Sì, Tàipú Sì, Yìngtiān Fǔ, Hànlín Yuàn, Chūnfāng, Guānglù Sì, Qīntiān Jiān, Shàngbǎo Sī, Tàiyī Yuàn, the judges of the Five Military Commissions (Wǔjūn Duànshì), and officials of the capital counties.
To the west were the Five Chief Military Commissions (Wǔjūn Dūdū), commanders of the Imperial Guard (Jǐnyī Wèi Zhǐhuī), seal-holding commanders of various guards, Gěishìzhōng, and Zhōngshū Shèrén.
It was also ordered that the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù) prepare court plaques for all officials,
on which their ranks would be clearly written.
These would be placed on wooden railings to the left and right of the imperial terrace (dānchí),
for officials to stand by in order.
In the twenty-sixth year, it was ordered that all who entered the hall must wear proper shoes (lǚduì).
In the early years of Yǒnglè,
it was ordered that officials of the Grand Secretariat (Nèigé) stand east of the golden platform (jīntái) during court audiences,
while the Imperial Guard (Jǐnyī Wèi) stood to the west.
Later, they moved to the imperial path (yùdào),
standing opposite each other east and west.
In the fourth year, an edict was issued to the Six Ministries (Liù Bù) and close attendant officials, saying:
"Early court audiences often deal with matters memorialized from the four directions.
In the afternoon, matters are simpler,
and discussions between monarch and ministers can proceed leisurely.
From now on, all matters requiring deliberation
shall be addressed at the evening court audience."
In the seventh year, an edict was issued to the itinerant Ministry of Rites (Xíngzài Lǐbù), saying:
"The winter air in Běijīng is severe and freezing.
When officials attend early court and present matters,
standing for a long time is unbearable.
Henceforth, after the court audience,
matters shall be presented in the side hall (biàndiàn) inside Yòushùn Mén."
In the early years of Jǐngtài,
the afternoon court audience (wǔcháo) ceremony was established.
For all afternoon court audiences,
the Emperor would proceed to Zuǒshùn Mén,
where a precious desk (bǎo'àn) would be set up.
Officials holding office and presenting matters would await outside Zuǒyè Mén.
When the Emperor emerged,
they would enter in order.
Officials from the Grand Secretariat (Nèigé), Five Chief Military Commissions (Wǔ Fǔ), and Six Ministries (Liù Bù) presenting matters,
and attendant officials from the Six Offices of Scrutiny (Liù Kē),
would stand in order to the west of the desk.
Two attendant censors (shìbān yùshǐ),
two officials arranging ranks (xùbān),
and four generals (jiāngjūn)
would stand facing north to the south of the desk.
One herald (míngzàn)
would stand to the east of the desk,
facing west.
Imperial Guard (Jǐnyī Wèi) and officials from the Court of State Ceremonial (Hónglú Sì) would stand facing east.
Officials in charge of generals (guǎnjiāngjūn guān) and imperial guards (shìwèi guān) would stand to the west of the generals.
After officials from the Five Chief Military Commissions (Fǔ) and Six Ministries (Bù) finished presenting matters,
the desk would be removed,
and all officials would withdraw.
If there were confidential matters,
they would be presented before the Emperor.
In the ninth year of Jiājìng, it was ordered that after the regular court ceremony,
officials of the Grand Secretariat (Nèigé) would ascend via the eastern steps, and Imperial Guard (Jǐnyī Wèi) officials via the western steps,
standing to the east and west of the imperial throne (bǎozuò).
If there were imperial envoys (qīnchāi guān) or foreigners receiving imperial edicts (chì),
one official from the Imperial Printing Office (fāngjú guān) would hold the edict and stand behind the Grand Secretariat (Nèigé),
slightly forward.
After the officials receiving the edict paid their respects,
the official holding the edict would receive the imperial command and descend via the left steps,
following the imperial path (yùdào) to present it.
In the sixth year of Lóngqìng, an edict was issued to hold court audiences on the third, sixth, and ninth days of the month.
In the third year of Wànlì, it was ordered that four officials for recording daily activities (qǐjū guān) be designated for regular court audiences.
They would be placed above the Gěishìzhōng in the eastern ranks,
slightly forward,
to facilitate observation and listening.
For afternoon court audiences,
they would be placed to the west of the imperial throne (yùzuò),
slightly to the south.
Regarding the order of entry for all court audiences,
in the twenty-fourth year of Hóngwǔ, it was ordered that generals attending court (cháocān jiāngjūn) enter first,
followed by close attendants (jìnshì),
then Dukes (gōng), Marquises (hóu), Imperial Sons-in-law (fùmǎ), and Earls (bó),
then the Five Chief Military Commissions (Wǔ Fǔ) and Six Ministries (Liù Bù),
then officials of Yìngtiān Fǔ and various other capital offices.

In the fourteenth year of Chénghuà, it was ordered that successful candidates in the imperial examinations (jìnshì) stand behind incumbent officials, according to the order of their respective departments.
Court Audience Ceremony for the Crown Prince (Huángtàizǐ Qīncháo Yí)
Former histories mostly do not record this.
In the tenth month of the first year of Hóngwǔ of the Míng dynasty, regulations were established:
For major court audiences like New Year's Day,
the Huángdì would ascend the Fèngtiān Diàn.
First, the Huáng Tàizǐ and Qīnwáng would be seated in order at the Wénlóu.
Bowing positions and kneeling cushions would be set up precisely in the center on the Dānbì.
When the Huángdì ascended the throne,
the officials on duty in front of the hall would rise and complete their greetings.
The yínjìn would lead the Huáng Tàizǐ and Qīnwáng to enter through the East Gate of Fèngtiān,
and all officials would enter together.
Music would begin.
The Huáng Tàizǐ and Qīnwáng would ascend from the East Steps,
reaching their bowing positions on the Dānbì,
and the music would stop.
The zàn would call for four bows.
Music would begin.
They would rise.
Music would stop.
The yínjìn would guide them to enter through the East Gate of the hall.
Music would begin.
The nèizàn would lead them to the position in front of the imperial throne,
and the music would stop.
He would call "Kneel."
The Huáng Tàizǐ would kneel and offer congratulations, saying,
"I, your eldest son, (name),"
"now on this occasion of Lǚduān Jié" (for winter solstice, he would say
"Lǚcháng"),
"respectfully lead my younger brothers (names)
to reverently pay respects and offer congratulations to Fùhuáng Bìxià."
The imperial decree would be transmitted as before.
The zàn would call for prostration.
They would rise.
The Huáng Tàizǐ and all Wáng would exit through the East Gate.
Music would begin.
The yínjìn would lead them back to their bowing positions on the Dānbì,
and the music would stop.
The zàn would call for four bows.
Music would begin.
They would rise.
Music would stop.
They would descend from the East Steps.
Music would begin.
Upon reaching the Wénlóu,
the music would stop.
All officials would follow and offer congratulations.
For audiences with the Huánghòu,
these would be held at the Kūnníng Gōng,
broadly following the ritual for audiences with the Huángdì.
In the twenty-sixth year, the court audience was changed to be held at the Qiánqīng Gōng.
On that day,
the Huángdì and Huánghòu would ascend their thrones,
with attendants guiding them as per ritual.
The yǐnlǐ would lead the Huáng Tàizǐ and his Fēi, and the Qīnwáng and their Fēi to the positions in front of the upper seats.
The zànlǐ would call for four bows.
They would rise.
The zànlǐ would lead the Huáng Tàizǐ forward.
The zàn would call "Kneel."
The yǐnlǐ would have the Tàizǐ Fēi, all Wáng, and their Fēi all kneel.
The Huáng Tàizǐ would deliver an address,
as before,
but no imperial decree would be transmitted.
The zànlǐ would call for the Huáng Tàizǐ to prostrate.
He would rise.
The yǐnlǐ would call for all Wáng to prostrate.
They would rise.
The Tàizǐ Fēi and all Wáng Fēi would also rise.
The zànlǐ would lead the Huáng Tàizǐ back to his position.
The zàn would call for bows.
The Huáng Tàizǐ and those below him would all perform four bows.
When the ceremony was complete,
the yǐnlǐ would lead them to the front of the Huánghòu.
The subsequent calls for bowing
would all be as per the ritual for audiences with the Huángdì.
The address would refer to "Mǔhòu Diànxià."
When the ceremony was complete,
they would exit.
In the seventh year, it was further changed:
no congratulatory address would be made;
only the ceremony of eight bows would be performed.
The ritual for court audiences with the Huáng Tàihòu
was all the same.
Ritual for the Audience of Various Wáng
In ancient times,
feudal lords would have one audience every six years.
The Hàn system had a ritual of "four appearances."
The Wèi system dictated that Fānwáng were not permitted to enter for audiences.
In the Tàishǐ period of the Jìn dynasty,
it was ordered that for Wánggōng and those below who came for audience,
the four directions would each be divided into two turns.
After the Táng dynasty,
many Qīnfān did not go to their fiefs.
The Míng dynasty emulated ancient enfeoffment,
so Qīnwáng would not regularly come for audience from their fiefs.
When they did, they would be generously rewarded.
In the early Míng,
whenever they came for audience,
the imperial throne would be set up in the Fèngtiān Diàn in advance,
as per the usual ritual.
The various Wáng would be seated in the east side rooms outside Fèngtiān Mén.
After three drum rolls,
all officials would enter and take their standing positions.
The yǐnlǐ would guide the Wáng, dressed in gǔnmiǎn,
to enter through the East Gate,
ascend the East Steps,
and take their positions.
The Wángfǔ attendants would take positions on the Dānchí.
The zàn would call for bows.
Music would begin.
The Wáng and his attendants would all perform four bows.
They would rise.
Music would stop.
The Wáng would enter through the East Gate of the hall.
Music would begin.
The nèizàn would lead him to the front of the imperial presence.
Music would stop.
The Wáng would kneel.
All Wángfǔ officials would kneel.
The Wáng would deliver an address, saying:
"I, the (ordinal) son, Wáng (name),
now on this occasion of (time) enter for audience,
respectfully come to Fùhuáng Bìxià to pay respects."
The zàn would call for prostration.
He would rise.
The Wáng would exit through the East Gate.
Music would begin.
He would return to the bowing position.
Music would stop.
The zàn would call for bows.
The Wáng would rise.
The attendants would all perform four bows.
They would rise.
Music would begin.
The imperial procession would depart.
The Wáng and all officials would exit in sequence.
