In the twenty-sixth year of Hóngwǔ, it was stipulated:
For all grand audiences of the Wáng,
the ritual of eight bows would be performed.
For ordinary audiences,
one bow.
Whenever paternal uncles or elder brothers saw the Tiānzǐ,
in court, they would perform the ritual of sovereign and subject;
in the private palace, they would perform the ritual of family members.
Paternal uncles and elder brothers would sit facing west,
receiving four bows from the Tiānzǐ.
The Tiānzǐ would sit in the center, facing south,
to honor the principle of kinship,
while preserving the ritual of sovereign and subject.
For audiences of external relatives,
the Huánghòu's parents would perform the ritual of sovereign and subject when seeing the Dì;
the Hòu would perform the ritual of family members when seeing her parents.
When the Huáng Tàizǐ saw the Huánghòu's parents,
the Huánghòu's parents would stand facing west,
and the Huáng Tàizǐ would face east and perform four bows.
The Huánghòu's parents would stand to receive two bows,
and return two bows.
Ritual for the Audience of Various Departments
According to Míng regulations,
officials from across the realm would come for audience once every three years.
Starting from the sixteenth day of the twelfth month,
the Hónglú Sì would lead them in for audience in sequence.
After the twenty-fifth day,
daily, officials from the regional administration would follow the regular court officials to enter Fèngtiān Mén and perform the ritual.
Officials from prefectures, subprefectures, and counties, as well as head officials of various departments and native officials, would all perform the ritual outside Wǔmén.
After the grand New Year's Day audience,
regional officials would line up in front of the Fèngtiān Diàn;
those from Zhīfǔ and below
would line up south of the Jīnshuǐ Qiáo at Fèngtiān Mén,
as per the ordinary court audience ritual.
In the third year of Tiānshùn, it was ordered that all regional officials coming for audience
would be demoted one rank compared to capital officials.
In the fifth year of Wànlì, it was ordered that for all audiences,
the Nánjīng Fǔyǐn, the acting Tàipú Sì Yuànmǎ Sì Qīng, and the two Sī of Bù and Àn,
would all have their audience on the sixteenth day of the twelfth month,
performing the ritual with the outer court officials.
They would proceed from the Yòuyè Mén to the imperial presence,
led in sequence by Hónglú Sì officials.
As for officials from the Yányùn Sì and those from Zhīfǔ and below,
Zhèjiāng and Jiāngxī on the seventeenth day;
Shāndōng and Shānxī on the eighteenth day;
Hénán and Shǎnxī on the nineteenth day;
Húguǎng and Nánzhílì on the twentieth day;
Fújiàn and Sìchuān on the twenty-first day;
Guǎngdōng and Guǎngxī on the twenty-second day;
Yúnnán and Guìzhōu on the twenty-third day;
Běizhílì on the twenty-fourth day;
each would perform the ritual with the outer court officials,
and be led in for audience before the emperor.
If an audience was waived, it would be stopped,
but they would still await an imperial audience day to be led in.
For the New Year's Day audience,
all would enter the hall front to perform the ritual.
All officials coming for audience or to express gratitude
would wear formal attire;
on New Year's Day, they would wear court attire,
but not red shoes.
For ordinary audiences, all wore brocade.
Regulations for the Central Palace's Audience

Only the *Kāiyuán Lǐ* of the Táng dynasty had ceremonies for an audience with the Grand Empress Dowager and Empress receiving congratulations from all officials, and for the Empress meeting with external noblewomen.
The Míng dynasty system had no ceremony for the Empress receiving congratulations from all officials,
but as for the imperial consorts and below,
the audience and congratulatory ceremonies on New Year's Day (*zhèngdàn*) and Winter Solstice were
established by imperial decree in the ninth month of Hóngwǔ first year.
Whenever the Central Palace held an audience for congratulations,
the palace eunuchs would set up the Empress's throne in Kūnníng Gōng.
The imperial regalia on the vermillion steps
were held by palace eunuchs.
The imperial regalia in the hall
were held by palace maids.
Female musicians were arrayed outside the palace gate.
The imperial noble consort's tent was set up west of the palace gate,
near the north;
the princesses' tents were set up east of the palace gate,
a little to the south;
the external noblewomen's tents were set up south of the gate,
facing east and west.
The Empress, wearing her *wēiyī*, emerged from her chamber;
the retinue moved,
the music started.
She ascended the throne,
the music stopped.
The master of ceremonies guided the external noblewomen through the east gate into the inner path,
where they stood in eastern and western ranks,
and then stopped.
He guided the imperial noble consort and other consorts through the east gate,
to the kneeling position on the steps.
The announcer called for bows,
music started,
they bowed four times and rose,
music stopped.
He guided them through the east gate of the hall,
music started.
The inner announcer led them to the kneeling position in the hall,
music stopped.
The announcer called for kneeling,
all consorts knelt.
The imperial noble consort delivered an address saying,
"We, your handmaids [name] and others,
meet this auspicious occasion of the year's beginning" –
for the Winter Solstice it would say
"the longest day" –
"and respectfully come to Her Majesty the Empress's hall to offer congratulations."
After the address,
all prostrated themselves,
rose,
music started.
They returned to their positions,
music stopped.
The announcer called for bows,
music started,
they bowed four times and rose,
music stopped.
They descended the east steps and exited.
The master of ceremonies guided the princesses through the east gate,
to the kneeling position on the steps,
standing in order,
performing the ritual like the imperial consorts.
The master of ceremonies guided the external noblewomen to the kneeling position in the central path in front of the hall,
and the announcer called for bows as per the ritual.
The head of the rank ascended the west steps,
entered the west gate of the hall,
music started.
The inner announcer led them to the kneeling position in the hall,
the head of the rank and all noblewomen knelt.
The head of the rank delivered an address saying:
"We, your handmaids, Lady [title] [name] and others, offer congratulations."
After the congratulations,
they exited and returned to their positions.
The officer of pronouncements knelt to receive the imperial command,
exited through the central door of the hall,
stood east of the open platform,
facing south,
and announced that there was an imperial decree.
All noblewomen knelt,
and the officer of pronouncements proclaimed the decree saying:
"The joy of the year's beginning
is shared with you, ladies."
The announcer called for rising.
The officer of pronouncements reported that the decree had been proclaimed.
The Empress rose,
music started.
She entered the inner chamber gate,
music stopped.
All noblewomen exited.
The ceremonies for the Grand Empress Dowager and Empress Dowager receiving congratulations were the same.
In Hóngwǔ twenty-sixth year, the Central Palace's congratulatory audience ceremony was re-established.
On the day before,
female officials set up the throne and incense table.
On the day of, eunuchs set up the imperial regalia and arrayed female musicians east and west of the vermillion steps,
facing north,
and set up a writing desk at the east gate of the hall.
When the noblewomen arrived at the palace gate,
the master of ceremonies led them to their kneeling positions,
and female officials, fully dressed, attended to the ranks.
Officials like the *Shànggōng* and *Shàngyí* went inside to welcome her,
the Empress, fully dressed, emerged,
music played,
and the announcer called for bows as per the previous ritual.
Female officials carried the writing desk through the east gate of the hall,
music started.
When they reached the center of the hall,
music stopped.
The announcer called for kneeling,
all noblewomen knelt.
The announcer called for the proclamation of the memorial's headings,
the female official proclaimed them,
then the announcer called for unrolling the memorial,
the female official proclaiming the memorial went to the table,
unrolled and proclaimed it,
then moved the table to the east of the hall.
All noblewomen rose,
the master of ceremonies led the head of the rank up the east steps and into the east gate of the hall,
music started.
The inner announcer led them to the center of the hall,
music stopped.
The announcer called for kneeling,
the head of the rank and all noblewomen knelt.
After the head of the rank delivered the address,
all rose,
and exited through the west gate.
The announcer calling for bows and the officer of pronouncements proclaiming the decree
were all as per the ritual,
and the ceremony concluded.
For the *Qiānqiū Jié* (Empress's birthday), the address said:
"Meeting this auspicious *Qiānqiū* festival,
we respectfully come to Her Majesty the Empress's hall to offer congratulations."
No imperial decree was transmitted.
For the monthly audience on the first and fifteenth day of the lunar month (*shuòwàng*) for noblewomen,
on that day, the throne was set up in the palace,
and imperial regalia and female musicians were arrayed.
When the Empress ascended the throne,
the leading female official guided the noblewomen into their ranks,
civil officials' wives to the east, military officials' wives to the west,
each according to her husband's rank.
The announcer called for bows,
music started,
four bows.
The ceremony concluded,
they exited.
It was excused during rain, cold, or great heat.
Later, noblewomen's congratulatory audiences
were all held at Rénzhì Diàn.
The audience with the Eastern Palace consort followed a similar ritual to that with the Central Palace,
but no decree was transmitted.
Audience and Congratulatory Ceremonies for the Eastern Palace
There is no record of these before the Hàn dynasty.
During the reign of Suí Wéndì,
on the Winter Solstice, all officials offered audience to the Crown Prince,
with music played as he received congratulations.
According to Táng regulations,
palace officials paid their respects and offered congratulations to the Crown Prince,
all dancing and bowing.
In Kāiyuán, this ritual was abolished.
According to custom,
when all officials addressed the Crown Prince, they merely referred to him by name;
only palace officials referred to themselves as 'ministers'.
In Míng Hóngwǔ fourteenth year,
the supervising secretary Zhèng Xiāng (鄭相同) petitioned to revert to the ancient system,
and an imperial edict was issued for all officials to deliberate.
The compilers Wú Shěn (吳沈) and others deliberated saying:
"The Eastern Palace
is the great foundation of the state,
through which the sacred body is continued and the heavenly mandate inherited.
The respectful rites of subjects and sons
must not be divided.
We request that all who address the Eastern Palace
continue to refer to themselves as 'ministers' as before."
This was followed.
For all audiences with the Crown Prince,
in advance,
the Official of the Seal Administration (Diǎnxǐguān) would set up the Imperial Crown Prince's seat in the Wénhuá Hall (Wénhuá Diàn).
The Imperial Bodyguard (Jǐnyīwèi) would arrange ceremonial guards outside the hall.
The Imperial Music Bureau (Jiàofāng Sī) would display grand music instruments inside the Wénhuá Gate (Wénhuá Mén), to the east and west,
facing north.
The Army Headquarters Guard (Fǔjūn Wèi) would arrange armored soldiers and banners outside the gate.
The Imperial Bodyguard (Jǐnyīwèi) would station twelve generals outside the central gate of the hall and outside the Wénhuá Gate (Wénhuá Mén),
facing east and west.
Officials of the Protocol Bureau (Yílǐ Sī) would set up a writing desk outside the eastern gate of the hall,
and arrange positions for all officials to bow below the hall, to the east and west.
Officials for relaying orders and announcing memorials (chuánlìng xuānjiān děng guān) would be positioned inside the hall, to the east and west.
On that day,
all officials would proceed outside the Wénhuá Gate (Wénhuá Mén).
The usher (Dǎoyǐnguān) would announce the outer readiness.
The Imperial Crown Prince, in full ceremonial robes, would emerge,
and the music would begin.
He would ascend the seat,
and the music would stop.
All officials would enter,
the prostrations would be announced,
and the music would begin.
They would make four prostrations and rise,
and the music would stop.
The Chancellor (Chéngxiàng) would ascend from the western steps,
proceed to the bowing position inside the hall,
and all would kneel.
The Chancellor (Chéngxiàng) would offer an address, saying:
"We, your humble servants, now encounter the 'three yangs bringing prosperity' (sānyángkāitài),
with all things renewing.
We respectfully consider His Imperial Crown Prince,
who abundantly enjoys great fortune."
Upon completion,
they would prostrate themselves,
rise,
and return to their positions.
An attendant (Shèrén) would carry the writing desk into the hall.
The procedures for holding, unfolding, announcing, and relaying memorials (pěngjiān, zhǎnjiān, xuānjiān, chuánlìng)
were slightly similar to those for the Empress.
The order would state:
"As we tread upon these three yangs,
we wish to share in the auspicious celebrations."
The rest was as per ritual.
For the winter solstice address,
it would be changed to
"The律应 (lǜyìng) corresponds to huángzhōng (huángzhōng),
and the sun is at its longest."
The relayed order would be changed to
"the festival of treading upon the longest."
For the Thousand Autumns Festival (Qiānqiū Jié) address, it would say:
"We now encounter the birthday of His Imperial Crown Prince.
We respectfully lead the civil and military officials,
and respectfully wish a thousand years of longevity."
No order would be relayed.
For all new moons and full moons (shuòwàng),
after officials withdrew from the court audience,
they would proceed outside the Wénhuá Hall (Wénhuá Diàn) gate,
standing to the east and west.
The Imperial Crown Prince would ascend the hall,
and the music would begin.
All officials would perform one bow.
Officials expressing gratitude for favors (xièēn) and resigning (cíguān) would also perform the ritual.
In the twelfth month of the first year of Hóngwǔ (Hóngwǔ yuán nián),
the Emperor, considering that the tutors of the Crown Prince (Dōnggōng Shīfu) were all venerable and long-serving ministers,
who should be treated with exceptional courtesy,
ordered a discussion on the ceremony for the Three Grand Tutors (Sān Shī) to pay respects to the Crown Prince (Dōnggōng).
The officials of the Board of Rites (Lǐguān) deliberated, saying:
"According to the Táng (Táng) system,
when all officials paid respects to the Crown Prince (Dōnggōng),
they performed four bows,
and the Imperial Crown Prince would return the latter two bows.
When the Three Dukes (Sān Gōng) paid respects, he would return all bows, before and after.
In recent times, the custom of returning bows is not practiced,
but the ritual for the Three Grand Tutors (Sān Shī) cannot be disregarded.
Therefore, it is now proposed that for all grand court audiences,
the Imperial Crown Prince's seat be set up in the Dàběn Hall (Dàběn Táng).
A kneeling cushion for returning bows be set up in the center of the hall.
Positions for the Three Grand Tutors (Sān Shī), guests (bīnkè), and exhortation officials (yùdé) to bow be set up in front of the hall.
The Imperial Crown Prince, in everyday attire, would ascend the seat.
The Three Grand Tutors (Sān Shī) and guests, in everyday attire, would enter and take their positions,
standing facing north.
The Imperial Crown Prince would rise,
facing south.
Four bows would be announced,
and the Imperial Crown Prince would return the latter two bows."
In the sixth year, an edict ordered that when officials had an audience with the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ),
they should remove their ceremonial knee-covers (bìxī) and pendants (pèi) from their court attire.
In the twenty-ninth year, an edict ordered court ministers to discuss the ceremony for imperial princes (qīnwáng) to see the Crown Prince (Dōnggōng).
The officials of the Board of Rites (Lǐguān) deliberated:
When the various princes (Zhū Wáng) came for an audience,
the Imperial Crown Prince's position would be set up in the center of the main hall.
The various princes' (Zhū Wáng) bowing positions would be set up outside the hall gate and inside the hall.
The bowing positions for the princely household officials (Wángfǔguān) would be set up to the east and west of the path in the courtyard.
Positions for all officials to stand by would be set up in the courtyard,
facing east and west.
On the appointed day,
armored soldiers would be arrayed,
ceremonial guards displayed,
and music arranged as usual.
The various princes (Zhū Wáng) would proceed to the tent outside the Crown Prince's (Dōnggōng) gate.
The Imperial Crown Prince, in everyday attire, would emerge,
and the music would begin.
He would ascend the seat,
and the music would stop.
The usher (Yǐnlǐ) would guide the various princes (Zhū Wáng) to their positions outside the hall gate.
As they first proceeded,
music would begin;
when they took their positions,
music would stop.
They would be guided to enter through the eastern gate of the hall,
and music would begin.
An inner announcer would guide them to their positions,
standing facing north,
and the music would stop.
Kneeling would be announced,
and the princes (Wáng) and princely household officials (Wángfǔguān) would all kneel,
delivering an address, saying:
"We now encounter a certain festival,
and respectfully proceed to His Imperial Crown Prince."
Upon completion of the address,
the princes (Wáng) and princely household officials (Wángfǔguān) would all prostrate themselves,
rise,
and music would begin.
They would return to their positions,
and the music would stop.
Bowing would be announced,
music would begin,
and the princes (Wáng) and princely household officials (Wángfǔguān) would all perform four bows.
They would rise,
and the music would stop.
Upon completion of the ritual,
the princes (Wáng) and all officials would exit in order.
When the princes (Wáng) reached the rear hall,
it was a family ritual.
Both the Crown Prince (Dōnggōng) and the princes (Wáng) would wear everyday attire.
The princes (Wáng) would enter through the eastern gate of the Wénhuá Hall (Wénhuá Diàn),
and proceed to the rear hall.
The princes (Wáng) would face west,
and the Crown Prince (Dōnggōng) would face south.
Upon completion of the meeting ritual,
they would sit,
the Crown Prince (Dōnggōng) in the center,
facing south,
and the various princes (Zhū Wáng) arrayed to the east and west.
In the twenty-eighth year of Jiājìng (Jiājìng èrshíbā nián),
the Board of Rites (Lǐbù) submitted a memorial, stating:
"According to custom,
when the Imperial Crown Prince received congratulations,
his seat was set up in the Wénhuá Hall (Wénhuá Diàn).
Now that it has been changed to yellow tiles,
it seems appropriate to avoid this honorable place."
The Emperor said:
"When the Crown Prince (Dōnggōng) receives congratulations,
his position should be set up to the left of the Wénhuá Gate (Wénhuá Mén),
facing south.
However, the guards are not yet fully prepared,
so let it be so for now."
In the second year of Lóngqìng (Lóngqìng èr nián), when the Imperial Crown Prince was formally invested,
an edict ordered that his seat for receiving congratulations be set up in the eastern section of the Wénhuá Hall (Wénhuá Diàn) gate.
Grand Banquet Ceremony
In the Hàn (Hàn) grand court assembly,
all officials would ascend the hall,
proclaim 'long live the Emperor' (wànsuì),
and raise their wine cups.
All officials would receive bestowed banquets,
with grand music playing.
In the Táng (Táng) grand banquet,
there would be singing at the ascent,
or the Nine Ensembles (Jiǔ Bù Jì) would be set up in the palace courtyard.
The Sòng (Sòng) held grand banquets for all officials in the middle months of spring and autumn, and on the Thousand Autumns Festival (Qiānqiū Jié),
setting up elaborate "mountain-tower" stages (shānlóu páichǎng),
which were utterly luxurious and extravagant.
The Míng (Míng) system
had grand banquets (dà yàn), medium banquets (zhōng yàn),
regular banquets (cháng yàn), and small banquets (xiǎo yàn).
In the first year of the Hóngwǔ reign, a grand banquet for all officials was held in the Fèngtiān Diàn.
Officials of the third rank and above ascended to the hall,
while the rest arrayed themselves on the Dānchí.
Subsequently, the ritual for banquets on the New Year's Day and Winter Solstice sacred festivals in the Jǐnshēn Diàn was established.
In the twenty-sixth year, the ritual for grand banquets was re-established
and held in the Fèngtiān Diàn.
In the first year of the Yǒnglè reign,
a grand banquet was held
to celebrate the completion of the suburban sacrifices.
In the nineteenth year, a grand banquet was held
to celebrate the completion of the suburban altars, altars of soil and grain, ancestral temples, and palaces in Běijīng.
During the Xuāndé and Zhèngtǒng reigns,
officials who did not attend court were
given festival money.
For Lìchūn, Yuánxiāo, the eighth day of the fourth month, Duānwǔ, Chóngyáng, and Làngbā,
during the Yǒnglè reign,
banquets were all bestowed upon officials at Fèngtiānmén,
with music played.
Thereafter, banquets were all held outside Wǔmén,
without music.
On Lìchūn, spring pancakes were bestowed;
on Yuánxiāo, glutinous rice balls;
on the eighth day of the fourth month, Bùluòjiá (bean cakes).
(During the Jiājìng reign,
Bùluòjiá was changed to wheat cakes.)
On Duānwǔ, cool rice dumplings;
on Chóngyáng, cakes;
on Làngbā, noodles.
All were served outside Wǔmén,
with seating arranged by official rank.
In the winter of the fifth year of the Xuāndé reign,
there had been no snow for a long time,
then a heavy snow fell in the twelfth month.
The Emperor showed his officials a poem expressing joy at the snow,
and then bestowed a snow-viewing banquet.
The officials presented responding poems,
and the Emperor selected those with admonitory messages to record them
and wrote a preface for them.
On the Empress Dowager's birthday,
a banquet was bestowed outside Wǔmén in the fourth year of the Zhèngtǒng reign.
On the Crown Prince's birthday,
during the Yǒnglè reign,

a banquet was bestowed upon grandees of the ministries, officials of the Chūnfāng, censors and investigators, close attendants of the Jǐnyīwèi, and officials from across the realm who presented memorials,
held in the Wénhuá Diàn.
After the Xuāndé reign,
banquets were all held outside Wǔmén.
For sacrifices at the Yuánqiú, Fāngzé, prayers for grain, morning and evening worship of the sun and moon, the ceremonial plowing, daily lectures in the Jīngyán, and the Crown Prince's studies,
meals were always bestowed.
For the Empress's sericulture ritual,
meals were bestowed upon internal and external noblewomen.
For compiling and proofreading books,
upon opening the bureau and upon completion of the books,
banquets were always bestowed.
When Grand Secretaries completed their nine-year term,
a banquet was bestowed at the Lǐbù,
with the Nine Chief Ministers attending.
New jinshì graduates were bestowed a banquet called Ēnróng.
For all grand feasts,
the Shàngbǎo Sì set up the imperial seat in the Fèngtiān Diàn,
the Jǐnyīwèi set up yellow banners to the east and west outside the hall,
and the Jīnwú and other guards set up twenty-four escorting officials to the east and west of the hall.
The Jiàofāng Sì set up nine-part musical performances and songs inside the hall,
set up grand music outside the hall,
and arranged three dance and miscellaneous performance troupes below the hall.
The Guānglù Sì set up a wine pavilion to the west of the imperial seat,
a meal pavilion to the east of the imperial seat,
and pavilions for delicacies, vinegars, and sauces to the east and west of the wine and meal pavilions.
Imperial mats were set up to the east and west of the imperial seat,
and the Crown Prince's seat was set up to the east of the imperial seat,
facing west.
The seats for the various princes followed to the south,
facing east and west.
Officials of the fourth rank and above were seated inside the hall,
while those of the fifth rank and below were seated in the east and west side corridors.
The Sīhú, Shàngjiǔ, and Shàngshí each performed their duties.
At the appointed time,
the Yílǐ Sì requested the Emperor to ascend to his seat.
As the imperial carriage advanced,
grand music began.
Upon ascending to the seat,
the music stopped.
Whips cracked,
and the Crown Prince and imperial princes ascended to the hall.
Civil and military officials of the fourth rank and above entered through the east and west gates,
standing in the middle of the hall,
while those of the fifth rank and below stood on the Dānchí.
They performed obeisance as prescribed.
The Guānglù Sì presented the imperial meal,
and grand music began.
When it reached before the Emperor,
the music stopped.
Internal officials presented flowers.
The Guānglù Sì opened the goblets and poured wine,
proceeding before the Emperor
to present the first goblet.
The Jiàofāng Sì performed the tune Yánjīng zhī qǔ.
As the music began,
all internal and external officials knelt.
The Jiàofāng Sì knelt and presented wine.
After drinking,
the music stopped.
All officials prostrated themselves,
then rose,
and performed obeisance as prescribed.
Each took their seat.
The序班 (Xùbān, master of ceremonies) went to scatter flowers among the officials.
For the second goblet, the tune Huángfēng zhī qǔ was performed.
As the music began,
the Guānglù Sì poured wine before the Emperor,
and the Xùbān poured wine for the officials.
The Emperor raised his goblet,
and the officials also raised their goblets.
The music stopped.
Soup was presented,
with drum and wind instruments leading the procession, marking the beat.
When they reached outside the hall,
the drum and wind instruments stopped.
Music began in the hall.
Officials rose.
Guānglù Sì officials presented soup.
Officials resumed their seats.
The Xùbān served soup to the officials.
The Emperor raised his chopsticks,
and the officials also raised their chopsticks.
The completion of the meal was announced,
and the music stopped.
Martial dancers entered,
performing the dance Píngdìng Tiānxià zhī wǔ.
For the third goblet, the tune Juànhuángmíng zhī qǔ was performed.
As the music began,
wine was presented as before.
When the music stopped,
the dance Fǔ'ān Sìyí zhī wǔ was performed.
For the fourth goblet, the tune Tiāndào Chuán zhī qǔ was performed,
wine and soup were presented as before,
and the dance Chēshū Huìtóng zhī wǔ was performed.
For the fifth goblet, the tune Zhènhuánggāng zhī qǔ was performed,
wine was presented as before,
and the dance Bǎixì Chéngyìng zhī wǔ was performed.
For the sixth goblet, the tune Jīnlíng zhī qǔ was performed,
wine and soup were presented as before,
and the dance Bāmán Xiànbǎo zhī wǔ was performed.
For the seventh goblet, the tune Chángyáng zhī qǔ was performed,
wine was presented as before,
and the dance Cǎilián Duìzi zhī wǔ was performed.
For the eighth goblet, the tune Fānglǐ zhī qǔ was performed,
wine and soup were presented as before,
and the dance Yúyuè Yúyuān zhī wǔ was performed.
For the ninth goblet, the tune Jiàliùlóng zhī qǔ was performed,
and wine was presented as before.
The Guānglù Sì collected the imperial goblets,
and the Xùbān collected the officials' cups.
Soup was presented,
followed by the main meal.
Grand music began.
Officials rose.
After the presentation, they resumed their seats.
The Xùbān served food to the officials.
Upon completion,
the completion of the meal was announced,
and the music stopped.
The meal was removed,
and the dance Bǎihuā Duì zhī wǔ was performed.
The removal of the tables was announced.
The Guānglù Sì removed the imperial tables,
and the Xùbān removed the officials' tables.
The completion of the banquet was announced.
All officials vacated their seats,
and stood facing north.
Obeisance was performed as prescribed.
Officials stood divided into east and west sides.
The Yílǐ Sì announced the completion of the ritual.
As the imperial carriage departed,
the music stopped,
and they exited in order.
For the "middle banquet" (zhōngyàn), the banquet ritual was as above,
but only seven goblets were presented.
The "ordinary banquet" (chángyàn) was like the middle banquet,
but with one bow and three kowtows,
and wine was presented either three or five times before stopping.
For banquets for noblewomen,
ceremonial guards and female musicians were set up in Kūnníng Gōng.
The Empress, in her everyday attire, ascended to her seat.
Imperial consorts, the Crown Princess, princely consorts, and princesses, also in their everyday attire, followed out of their chambers
and took their seats.
Noblewomen of all ranks stood behind their seats.
The Prime Minister's wife led the noblewomen in presenting the imperial food trays.
The Prime Minister's wife carried longevity flowers.
Second-rank external noblewomen each carried food trays
before the imperial consorts, the Crown Princess, princely consorts, and princesses.
Noblewomen of all ranks took their seats.
Palace attendants distributed longevity flowers inside the hall and in the east and west side corridors.
Wine was poured seven times,
food was served five times.
The pouring of wine, presentation of soup, and music starting and stopping
were all according to ritual.
Ritual for Presenting August and Auspicious Titles
A son did not follow the Way of ennobling his father.
When Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn was moved by the words of the House Steward,
and honored his father, Tàigōng,
Xún Yuè criticized this.
When Emperor Āi of Jìn wanted to honor and exalt the Empress Dowager,
Jiāng Pàn believed that an announcement should be made to the ancestral temple of Xiǎnzōng,
to make it clear that the matter was not his personal decision.
The Sòng and Yuán records both include the ceremony for bestowing an honorific title upon the Empress Dowager,
but without making an announcement to the ancestral temple,
which was non-ritualistic.
According to the Míng system,
when the Emperor ascended the throne,
and honored his birth mother or a concubine as Empress Dowager,
an honorific title would be bestowed.
Later, if the Empress Dowager was exalted on account of a celebratory event,
two or four characters would be added to her honorific title (huīhào).
During the reign of Shìzōng,
for the two Empresses Dowager,
this was increased to eight characters.
When bestowing a huīhào, an address was given,
but for bestowing an honorific title (zūn hào), only the presentation of the imperial seal and book was performed.
The bestowal of a zūn hào
began with Xuānzōng's ascension to the throne and honoring the Empress Dowager.
Prior to this, officials were sent to offer sacrifices and make announcements to Heaven, Earth, and the altars of grain and soil.
The Emperor personally made announcements to the ancestral shrines of Emperor Tàizōng and the late Emperor.
On that day,
bells and drums were rung,
and all officials wore court attire.
At Fèngtiānmén, the imperial seal and book, a decorated palanquin, and a fragrant sedan were arranged.
Zhōnghé Sháolè and Dàlè music
were arranged but not played.
Eunuchs arranged the Empress Dowager's throne
and displayed imperial regalia in the palace.
The imperial seal and book table was placed in front of the throne,
the Emperor's bowing position was set in the center of the vermilion steps,
and the princes' bowing positions were within the vermilion courtyard.
Female musicians were arranged but did not play.
The Emperor, in his ceremonial robes, proceeded to Fèngtiānmén.
The officials carrying the imperial seal and book placed them in the palanquin,
eunuchs lifted the palanquin,
and the Emperor followed the palanquin, descending the steps and ascending his carriage.
All officials stood facing north
south of the Jīnshuǐqiáo,
and knelt when the palanquin arrived,
rising after it passed.
They then proceeded to the south of the bridge outside the Sīshànmén,
standing facing north.
The Emperor descended his carriage inside the Sīshànmén.
The Empress Dowager ascended her throne.
The palanquin reached the vermilion steps.
The Emperor entered through the left gate,
arrived at the right of the steps,
and stood facing north.
The princes, in their ceremonial robes, took their positions.
Four bows were announced,
and the Emperor, princes, and all below them performed four bows.
The officials carrying the imperial seal and book entered through the central gate of the hall,
and stood on the left.
The Emperor entered through the left gate of the hall,
knelt at his bowing position,
and all princes and officials knelt.
The insertion of the ceremonial tablet (guī) was announced,
followed by the presentation of the imperial book.
The official bearing the book knelt and presented it,
and the Emperor received and then offered it.
The attending official knelt to receive it
and placed it on the left of the table.
The presentation of the imperial seal was announced,
and the official bearing the seal knelt and presented it.
The Emperor received the seal,
offered it,
and the attending official knelt to receive it
and placed it on the right of the table.
The withdrawal of the ceremonial tablet was announced,
followed by the proclamation of the imperial book,
which an attending official knelt to read aloud.
The Emperor prostrated himself,
rose,
exited through the left gate,
and returned to his bowing position.
Four bows were announced,
and it was proclaimed that all officials should perform four bows together.
The ceremony concluded,
and the imperial procession departed.
On this day,
the Emperor, accompanied by the Empress Dowager, paid respects at the Fèngxiāndiàn and the ancestral shrines,
performing rites of homage and gratitude.
After the rites,
the Empress Dowager returned to her palace,
donned her informal court attire,
and ascended her throne.
The Emperor, leading the Empress, imperial consorts, princes, princesses, and female officials of the Six Bureaus,
performed congratulatory rites.
The next day,
female relatives of officials of the fourth rank and above
performed the rite of presenting memorials.
After Xuāndé,
the ceremonies were similar.
In the early Zhèngtǒng reign,
the ceremony for honoring the Grand Empress Dowager was similar.
In the second month of the eighth year of Tiānshùn, the address by the female relatives was augmented to say:
"We, so-and-so ladies and concubines,
respectfully observe that Your Majesty the Empress Dowager resides in the seat of maternal virtue,
and eternally receives blessings and longevity."
In the eighteenth year of Hóngzhì, when honorific titles were bestowed upon the two Empresses Dowager,
the Empress Dowager's address was changed to say:
"Residing in the compassionate inner quarters,
greatly enjoying blessings and longevity."
In the second month of the first year of Jiājìng, when honorific titles were bestowed,
due to the excessive exertion of the four palaces performing the rites,
it was divided into two days.
Also, because the mourning period for Wǔzōng was not yet complete,
Empress Zhuāngsù was exempted from the morning congratulations,
and the female relatives congratulated the three palaces,
also on separate days.
The bestowal of a huīhào
began in the first month of the second year of Tiānshùn, when it was bestowed upon the Empress Dowager.
The address said:
"Your Imperial Highness, the succeeding Emperor, your subject,
humbly observes that Your Majesty the Empress Dowager,
whose merits and virtues are equally profound,
is now honored with an exalted huīhào,
may you eternally enjoy blessings and longevity,
and may all under heaven rejoice."
The address by the female relatives presenting memorials and congratulations said:
"We, so-and-so ladies and concubines,
respectfully observe that Your Majesty the Empress Dowager's virtue is as profound as the earth,
and is truly fitting for this glorious title,
may your longevity and blessings be boundless,
and may public sentiment rejoice and support you."
Other parts followed the usual ceremony.
Later bestowals of huīhào and additions to huīhào
followed this pattern.
In the twenty-third year of Chénghuà,
the Ministry of Rites submitted the ceremony,
but the rites for the Crown Princess were omitted,
so a special order was given to add them.
COLLATED NOTES

Record Volume 30, Rites 8 (Auspicious Rites 2) Ceremony for Enfeoffing the Empress (with attached ceremony for enfeoffing consorts) Ceremony for Enfeoffing the Crown Prince and Crown Princess Ceremony for Enfeoffing Princes and Princess Consorts (with attached ceremony for enfeoffing princesses) Ceremony for the Emperor's Coming of Age Ceremony for the Capping of the Crown Prince and Imperial Princes Ceremony for the Capping of Officials Ceremony for the Capping of Commoners
Ceremony for Enfeoffing the Empress
In ancient times, there was no enfeoffment rite for establishing an empress.
It was not until Emperor Líng of Hàn established Lady Sòng Měirén as empress
that he first presided at the hall,
ordering the Grand Commandant to hold the imperial insignia (jié),
present the imperial seal and ribbon (xǐshòu),
and read the imperial book.
The empress faced north and referred to herself as a subject and concubine,
kneeling to receive them.
Thereafter, this became a fixed system,
but the ritual texts varied in each dynasty.
The Míng ritual notes largely drew upon and adopted the systems of the Táng and Sòng.
In the early period of Tàizǔ,
the system was established.
For all enfeoffments of empresses,
three days beforehand, fasting and abstinence were observed,
and officials were sent to offer sacrifices and make announcements to Heaven, Earth, and the ancestral temples.
The day before,
the Bureau of Ceremonial Protocol set up the imperial seal and book table in front of the Emperor's throne in the Fèngtiāndiàn,
arranged the position for the official holding the imperial insignia to the east of the book table,
the official in charge of the insignia to their left,
slightly to the rear,
and the position for the official receiving the imperial decree to their south,
all facing west.
The positions for the chief and deputy envoys receiving the decree were set up south of the transverse street,
facing north.
The positions for the officials receiving and proclaiming the decree were set up north of them,
and the positions for the officials bearing the imperial insignia, book, and seal were set up to their northeast,
all facing west.
The kneeling mats for the chief and deputy envoys receiving the imperial book and seal were set up north of the positions for receiving the decree,
facing north.
Two masters of ceremony stood on the vermilion steps, facing south,
two ritual assistants stood north of the chief and deputy envoys,
and two class managers stood south of the ritual assistants,
all facing each other east and west.
The positions for all officials and attendants
were as in the court ceremony.
That day in the morning,
the imperial procession was arrayed,
armored soldiers were deployed,
and music was performed as per ritual.
Inner palace officials set up the Empress’s enfeoffment and investiture document and imperial seal table in the palace,
an incense table in the main hall,
a temporary table for the enfeoffment document and imperial seal in front of the incense table,
and female musicians on the vermilion steps.
At dawn,
the chief and deputy envoys and all civil and military officials entered.
After three drum signals for strict attention,
the Huángdì, wearing a ceremonial robe and crown, ascended the Fèngtiān Diàn.
Officials from the Lǐbù presented the enfeoffment document and imperial seal,
placing each on its respective table.
All assisting officials,
each took their positions in the main hall.
The music began,
and they bowed four times.
They rose,
and the music stopped.
The Chéngzhìguān announced the issuance of the Empress’s enfeoffment document and imperial seal.
After the announcement,
they exited through the central gate,
descended the central steps,
went to the Xuānzhì position,
and declared,
"There is an imperial edict!"
The chief and deputy envoys knelt,
and the Chéngzhìguān proclaimed the edict, saying:
"Enfeoffing Consort Mǒu Shì as the Empress,
commanding you and others to hold the staff of authority and perform the rites."
After the proclamation,
they entered through the west gate of the hall.
The chief and deputy envoys prostrated themselves,
then rose.
The attendants lifted the enfeoffment document and imperial seal tables,
exited through the central gate,
and descended the central steps.
The Fèngjiéguān led the Zhǎngjiézhě as a vanguard,
proceeding to the chief and deputy envoys’ kneeling mats,
and placed the tables to the north.
The Zhǎngjiézhě removed the staff cover,
and presented the staff to the Fèngjiéguān.
The Fèngjiéguān then presented it to the chief envoy,
the chief envoy presented it to the Zhǎngjiézhě,
and the Zhǎngjiézhě knelt to receive it.
They rose,
and stood to the left of the chief envoy.
The Fèngjiéguān retired.
The Yǐnlǐ guided the chief envoy to the position for receiving the enfeoffment document.
The Fèngcèguān presented the enfeoffment document to the chief envoy,
the chief envoy knelt to receive it,
and placed it on the table.
They retired,
and returned to their positions.
The deputy envoy receiving the imperial seal proceeded likewise.
Music began,
and the chief and deputy envoys bowed four times.
They rose,
and the music stopped.
The chief envoy followed the enfeoffment document,
the deputy envoy followed the imperial seal,
the Zhǎngjiézhě led the way,
followed by those carrying the tables,
and the music began.
They exited the Fèngtiānmén,
and the music stopped.
The Shìyí announced that the rites were complete.
The imperial carriage departed,
and all civil and military officials exited.
The Zhǎngjiézhě added the staff cover,
the Fèngcèbǎoguān all inserted their tablets into their belts,
took the enfeoffment document and imperial seal and placed them inside the dragon palanquin.
The honor guard and grand music led the way,
to outside the Zhōnggōng gate,
and the music began.
The Empress, wearing the Jiǔlóng Sìfèngguān and
the Huīyī,
came out of her chamber,
to the main hall,
and stood facing south.
The music stopped,
and the chief and deputy envoys temporarily placed the enfeoffment document and imperial seal on the table set up outside the gate.
The Yǐnlǐ guided the chief and deputy envoys and the Nèishǐ Jiānlìng to their positions.
The chief envoy went before the Nèishǐ Jiānlìng,
announcing, "The envoy for the enfeoffment ceremony, Mǒu,
and deputy envoy Mǒu,
present the imperial edict to bestow the Empress’s enfeoffment document and imperial seal."
The Nèishǐ Jiānlìng entered to report to the Empress,
then came out,
and returned to his position.
The Yǐnlǐ guided the inner and outer ladies of the court to their positions.
The chief envoy presented the enfeoffment document to the Nèishǐ Jiānlìng,
the Nèishǐ Jiānlìng knelt to receive it,
and presented it to an inner palace official.
The deputy envoy presented the imperial seal likewise.
All returned to their positions.
The Nèishǐ Jiānlìng led the inner palace officials bearing the enfeoffment document and imperial seal to enter,
each placing them on their tables.
The Shàngyí guided the Empress down the steps,
to stand at the position in the courtyard.
Inner palace officials bearing the enfeoffment document and imperial seal stood to the east and west of the Empress.
The Nèishǐ Jiānlìng announced,
"There is an imperial edict!"
The Shàngyí announced, "Bow!"
The Empress bowed,
and music began.
She bowed four times and rose,
and the music stopped.
After the proclamation of the edict,
the inner palace official bearing the enfeoffment document presented it to the inner palace official who was to read it. After reading,
it was presented to the Nèishǐ Jiānlìng.
The Nèishǐ Jiānlìng knelt to present it to the Empress,
the Empress knelt to receive it,
and presented it to the Sīyán.
The presentation of the imperial seal was as before.
After receiving it,
it was presented to the Sībǎo.
The Shàngyí announced, "Bow!"
The Empress bowed as before.
The Nèishǐ Jiānlìng exited,
went before the chief and deputy envoys,
and announced,
"The Empress’s enfeoffment ceremony is complete."
The envoys retired to the south of the cross street of the Fèngtiān Diàn,
standing facing north, to the west and above.
The Jǐshìzhōng stood to the northeast of the chief and deputy envoys,
facing west.
The chief and deputy envoys bowed twice to report back, saying:
"The ceremony of enfeoffing the Empress by imperial edict is complete."
They bowed twice again.
The Jǐshìzhōng reported it,
then they retired.
After the Empress received the enfeoffment document and imperial seal,
she ascended her seat.
The Yǐnlǐ guided the head of the inner ladies of the court,
who went to the congratulatory position in the main hall and knelt,
offering a speech, saying:
"On this occasion, Your Royal Highness the Empress,
having received the enfeoffment document and imperial seal,
is now established in the central palace.
We are filled with boundless joy and celebration,
and respectfully offer our congratulations."
The Zhànbài announced, "Bow!"
Music began.
She bowed twice,
rose,
and the music stopped.
She retired,
and returned to her position.
Then the head of the outer ladies of the court was guided in,
to the congratulatory position in the main hall,
following the ritual for the inner ladies of the court.
After the rites, all exited.
The Empress descended from her seat,
music began.
She returned to her chamber,
and the music stopped.
The next day,
all the officials presented memorials of congratulations.
The emperor held court to receive congratulations,
as was customary.
Then a day was chosen
to perform the ancestral temple visit ceremony.
First, officials were dispatched to perform rituals with sacrificial animals,
announcing that the empress would soon pay her respects.
Before the appointed day,
the empress fasted for three days,
while inner and outer noblewomen and serving palace eunuchs fasted for one day.
A kneeling position for the empress was set up outside the temple gate and inside the temple;
kneeling positions for inner noblewomen participating in the sacrifice were set up south of the temple courtyard;
kneeling positions for outer noblewomen participating in the sacrifice were set up south of the inner noblewomen's positions.
The master of ceremonies (司贊, Sīzàn) stood east and west of the empress's kneeling position;
the master of guests (司賓, Sībīn) stood north of the inner noblewomen's positions;
the incense officer (司香, Sīxiāng) stood to the right of the incense table.
Washing implements were arranged east of the steps,
and the washing officer (司盥洗官, Sī Guànxǐguān) stood at that spot.
On the day,
inner and outer noblewomen, each in their pheasant-embroidered robes (翟衣, Díyī), gathered outside the inner gate of the central palace.
The empress wore a nine-dragon, four-phoenix crown
and an imperial ceremonial robe (褘衣, Huīyī).
She exited the inner palace gate,
ascended her sedan chair,
descended outside the outer gate,
and ascended the ceremonial pheasant-chariot (重翟車, Zhòngdí Chē).
The musical ensemble (鼓吹, Gǔchuī) was arranged but did not play.
The supervisor of ceremonies (尚儀, Shàngyí) arranged the honor guard,
followed by the outer noblewomen,
then the inner noblewomen,
all riding in chariots leading the procession.
Palace eunuchs (內使監, Nèishǐjiān) escorted,
and the imperial guard (宿衞, Sùwèi) with weapons led and followed.
When the empress arrived at the temple gate,
the master of guests led the noblewomen in first.
The empress descended from her chariot,
and the master of ceremonies guided her in through the left gate,
to her position,
standing facing north.
The noblewomen each took their positions,
standing facing north.
The master of ceremonies announced "bow,"
and the master of guests assisted in the bowing,
whereupon the empress and noblewomen all bowed twice,
and rose.
The master of ceremonies requested her to approach the washing station,
where she washed and dried her hands,
then ascended from the eastern steps,
to before the spirit tablets.
The master of ceremonies announced "offer incense three times,"
and the incense officer presented the incense on the right.
After the empress offered incense three times,
she was guided back to her position,
and the bowing was repeated as before.
The master of ceremonies announced "ceremony concluded."
The empress exited through the left gate of the temple,
followed by the noblewomen in order.
The empress ascended her chariot,
with the noblewomen leading,
as when they arrived.
After passing the temple,
the musical ensemble played with vigor,
and the empress entered the palace.
On that day,
the emperor feasted his officials in the Jǐnshēn Diàn (謹身殿),
and the empress feasted the inner and outer noblewomen in the Central Palace,
both following the ceremonial protocols for New Year's Day banquets.
When Chéngzǔ (成祖) ascended the throne
and enfeoffed Empress Xú (徐氏),
the regulations were slightly different.
The emperor, in his leather cap and ceremonial robes (皮弁服, Píbiànfú), was in the Huágài Diàn (華蓋殿).
Officials from the Hànlín Yuàn (翰林院) affixed the imperial seal to the edict,
after which he proceeded to the Fèngtiān Diàn (奉天殿)
to issue the decree for the empress to receive her enfeoffment.
After the ceremony,
the Hànlín officials presented the edict to the officials of the Lǐbù (禮部),
who then bore the edict to the Chéngtiān Mén (承天門) to read it aloud.
The emperor returned to the palace,
and, accompanied by the empress in full ceremonial attire, proceeded to the Fèngxiān Diàn (奉先殿) to announce the event.
The empress, in full ceremonial attire, waited in the inner hall
for the emperor to be seated.
The female usher (贊引女官, Zànyǐn Nǚguān) guided her to the kneeling position
to perform the ceremony of gratitude,
and music played.
She bowed eight times,
rose,
and the music stopped.
The ceremony was concluded.
The next day,
the emperor and empress received congratulations and held a banquet,
following the previous rituals.
In the eighth year of Tiānshùn (天順) (1464),
it was additionally stipulated that imperial princes should offer congratulations to the emperor first,
then proceed to offer congratulations to the empempersss Dowager,
and then perform the eight bows before the empress.
In the thirteenth year of Jiājìng (嘉靖) (1534), when Empress Fāng (方氏) was enfeoffed,
the ministers of rites presented the ceremonial protocols,
which included a ceremony of announcement in the inner hall (謁告內殿儀, Yègào Nèidiàn Yí),
but no ceremony of announcement at the Grand Ancestral Temple (太廟, Tàimiào) or the Dynastic Ancestral Temple (世廟, Shìmiào).
The emperor ordered a discussion on increasing it.
Thereupon, the ministers of rites submitted the revised protocols.
Fasting for three days beforehand,
the relevant department arranged the displays as for the seasonal collective sacrifice (時祫儀, Shíxiá Yí).
On the day,
the emperor rode in the imperial chariot (御輅, Yùlù),
and the empress and concubines rode in pheasant-chariots,
together proceeding to the Grand Ancestral Temple.
Appointed officials presented the spirit tablets of the seven ancestral temples to ascend the spirit seats.
The emperor held the spirit tablet of Gāo Huángdì (高皇帝),
and the empress held the spirit tablet of Gāo Huánghòu (高皇后),
and they ascended the spirit seats.
Receiving the spirits, offering incense, presenting silks, and performing libations and oblations,
with music playing and stopping,
all followed the customary procedures.
Then they proceeded to the Dynastic Ancestral Temple to perform the rites,
following the same procedures as above.
In the first year of Lóngqìng (隆慶) (1567), it was additionally stipulated that,
on the day following the issuance of the imperial edict,
the noblewomen should perform the ceremony of seeing the empress.
Regulations for enfeoffing imperial concubines.
From the third year of Hóngwǔ (洪武) (1370), when Sūn (孫氏) was enfeoffed as Guìfēi (貴妃),
it was stipulated that the emperor would not hold court,
and the official in charge of promulgating decrees would declare:
"Concubine so-and-so,
is specially enfeoffed as Imperial Concubine so-and-so.
I command you, ministers, to carry the staff of authority (節, jié) and perform the rites."
Only a scroll of enfeoffment (冊, cè) was presented,
without an imperial seal (寶, bǎo);
the rest was the same as the Central Palace rituals.
In the seventh year of Yǒnglè (永樂) (1409), the ceremony for enfeoffing concubines was established.
The emperor, in his leather cap and ceremonial robes, was in the Huágài Diàn,
issuing the decree.
It was not until Xuānzōng (宣宗) established Consort Sūn (孫貴妃)
that an imperial seal was first bestowed.
When Xiànzōng (憲宗) enfeoffed Consort Wàn (萬貴妃),
she was first referred to as "Imperial" (皇, huáng),
which was no longer the old Hóngwǔ custom.
In the tenth year of Jiājìng (1531),
the emperor enfeoffed nine嫔 (pín),
and the ritual officials submitted the ceremonial protocols.
The day before,
the relevant department arranged the ceremonial guards as for the new moon and full moon ceremonies.
On the appointed day,
the emperor, in his imperial robe (袞冕, Gǔnmiǎn),
after announcing the event at the Grand Ancestral Temple and Dynastic Ancestral Temple,
changed into his leather cap and ceremonial robes
and proceeded to the Huágài Diàn.
All officials, in their formal attire (公服, Gōngfú), entered to perform the rites.
The chief and deputy envoys (正、副使, Zhèng, Fùshǐ), in court robes, received the decree,
and carried the staff of authority and scroll of enfeoffment to the nine嬪's palaces.
The nine嬪 greeted them outside the palace gate
and then proceeded to the kneeling positions.
A female official read the scroll of enfeoffment,
the nine嬪 received the scroll,
and bowed eight times in succession.
The staff of authority was sent out of the palace gate to report completion.
The nine嬪 then waited in full ceremonial attire,
and the empress led them to the Fèngxiān Diàn to announce the event,
and then to the emperor and empress to express gratitude,
all following the ceremonial protocols for enfeoffing imperial concubines.
Only the ceremonial jade tablet (圭, guī) used secondary jade,
and the grain patterns (穀文, gǔwén) and silver scroll were slightly reduced by one-fifth compared to those for imperial concubines (皇妃, huángfēi).
In the twentieth year (1541), Consort Dé (德妃) Zhāng (張氏) was enfeoffed.
Because the consort was about to enter her chamber,
and the emperor was then resting quietly,
no decree was issued,
and no announcement was made in the inner hall;
the rest was as before.
Ceremonies for enfeoffing the Crown Prince and Crown Princess
The title of "Crown Prince" (皇太子, Huáng Tàizǐ) first appeared in the Hàn (漢) Dynasty.
Emperor Míng (明帝) first introduced the ceremony of "standing before the imperial presence to enfeoff" (臨軒、冊拜之儀, Línxuān, Cèbài zhī Yí).
In the Táng (唐) Dynasty, the older ones were enfeoffed before the imperial presence,
while younger ones had envoys sent to perform the enfeoffment inside.
The Sòng (宋) Dynasty only used the "standing before the imperial presence" method.
The Yuán (元) Dynasty only used the "enfeoffment inside" method,
regardless of age.
When the Míng dynasty established its regulations,
for the enfeoffment of the Crown Prince,
the arrangements made by the responsible officials were similar to those for enfeoffing an empress.
The Crown Prince's bowing position was set up on the dàn bì (vermilion steps).
During the "inner solemnity" phase,
the Huángdì, wearing his gǔnmiǎn (dragon robe and crown), took his seat in the Jǐnshēn Diàn.
The Crown Prince, in his miǎnfú (ceremonial robes and crown), waited at Fèntiān Mén.
During the "outer readiness" phase,
the Huángdì ascended to Fèntiān Diàn.
The master of ceremonies led the Crown Prince through Fèntiān Dōngmén.
The music began,
and he ascended via the eastern steps to his position on the dàn bì.
The music stopped.
All officials took their places in the dànchí (courtyard).
The music began,
the Crown Prince bowed twice,
stood up,
and the music stopped.
The officer conveying the decree exited through the central hall door,
stood outside the door,
and declared:
"A decree has been issued."
The Crown Prince knelt.
The decree was announced, saying:
"The eldest son [name] is hereby enfeoffed as Huángtàizǐ (Crown Prince)."
The Crown Prince prostrated himself,
stood up,
and the music began.
He bowed twice,
and the music stopped.
The master of ceremonies led the Crown Prince through the eastern hall door,
and the music began.
The inner attendant guided him to the front of the imperial seat,
and the music stopped.
The inner attendant prompted him to kneel,
and prompted the reading of the enfeoffment scroll.
After the reading,
he prompted the insertion of the guī (ceremonial jade tablet),
and prompted the presentation of the scroll.
The Crown Prince inserted the guī,
knelt to receive the scroll,
and handed it to an inner attendant.
He was then prompted to receive the seal,
following the same ceremony as receiving the scroll.
He was prompted to remove the guī,
the Crown Prince removed the guī,
prostrated himself,
stood up,
and exited through the eastern hall door.
The attending officials, holding the jiezé (scepter and scroll) and bǎo (seal), followed him out.
The Crown Prince returned to his position,
and the music began.
He bowed four times, stood up,
and the music stopped.
He descended via the eastern steps,
and the music began.
When he reached Fèntiān Mén,
the music stopped.
The honor guard and musicians escorted the scroll and seal to Wénhuá Diàn.
The official holding the jiezé reported back,
and the officials from the Lǐbù (Ministry of Rites) took the imperial edict to Wǔmén to read it aloud.
All officials welcomed the edict to Zhōngshū Shěng,
for promulgation.
The master of ceremonies announced the completion of the rites,
the emperor departed,
and returned to the palace.
The Crown Prince went to the inner palace,
waited for the Huánghòu (Empress) to be seated,
and performed the ceremony of morning gratitude,
bowing four times.
He respectfully thanked, saying:
"Your humble son [name],
having now received the enfeoffment decree,
respectfully comes to Your Majesty the Mother Empress to express gratitude."
He bowed four more times,
and the ceremony concluded.
The Qīnwáng (Princes of the Blood), Shìzǐ (heirs apparent of princes), and Jùnwáng (Commandery Princes) waited on the steps of Wénhuá Diàn.
The Crown Prince took his seat,
and the Qīnwáng and those below them ascended from the eastern steps,
took their bowing positions, and bowed four times.
The eldest Prince respectfully congratulated, saying:
"Your humble younger brother [name],
now that his elder brother the Crown Prince has gloriously received the enfeoffment scroll and seal,
is overcome with joy,
and respectfully leads all younger brothers to Your Highness to offer congratulations."
After the congratulations,
they all bowed four times.
The Crown Prince stood up,
and they exited in order.
All the princes went to the Zhōnggōng (Central Palace, i.e., the Empress's palace) and bowed four times.
After the eldest Prince delivered his address of congratulations,
they all bowed four times and exited.
On that day,
the Crown Prince went to Wǔyīng Diàn to see his paternal uncles,
performed the family ritual,
bowed four times,
and his uncles sat facing west to receive it.
He saw his elder brothers,
performed the family ritual,
bowed twice,
and his elder brothers stood facing west to receive it.
The next day,
all officials presented memorials and congratulations,
and inner and outer noblewomen offered congratulations to the Zhōnggōng,
as per usual custom.
Then a day was chosen
for the Crown Prince to visit the Tàimiào (Imperial Ancestral Temple).
In the 28th year of Hóngwǔ,
the Crown Prince and Qīnwáng were all given golden scrolls,
without seals.
In the 2nd year of Yǒnglè, it was stipulated that
three days prior, fasting and purification should be observed,
and officials sent to offer sacrifices to Heaven and Earth and the Zōngmiào.
After receiving the scroll and seal,
the Crown Prince would first go to the Tàimiào to report,
then proceed to Fèntiān Diàn to give thanks,
and then enter to thank the Zhōnggōng.
In the 10th month of the 22nd year of Yǒnglè, when the Eastern Palace was enfeoffed,
because the zǐgōng (coffin containing the deceased emperor) was in mourning,
music was arranged but not played.
After completing the rites at Fèngxiān Diàn,
he still went to the jǐyán (altar with the spirit tablet) to report.
In the 11th month of the 2nd year of Xuāndé,
when an imperial son was born,
the assembled officials submitted a memorial requesting the establishment of a Crown Prince.
In the 2nd month of the 3rd year, the ceremony was performed.
As the Crown Prince was still young,
the principal and deputy envoys were ordered to present the scroll and seal at Wénhuá Mén.
In the 11th year of Chénghuà, upon the successful completion of the ceremony for establishing the Crown Prince,
civil and military officials were divided into five ranks,
and varying amounts of brocade and silk were bestowed.
In the 2nd month of the 18th year of Jiājìng, when the Eastern Palace was enfeoffed,
the emperor went to Nánjiāo to report to Shàngdì,
and went to the Tàimiào to report to the imperial ancestors.
For Běijiāo and the temples of the successive emperors and ancestral shrines below, officials were dispatched.
At that time, the Crown Prince was only two years old,
and a wet nurse carried him.
He welcomed the scroll and seal at the gate of Wénhuá Diàn,
and went before the emperor to express gratitude.
The Huánghòu and Guìfēi (Noble Consort) performed eight bows on behalf of the Crown Prince.
Before the Huánghòu,
the Guìfēi performed eight bows on his behalf.
Before the Guìfēi,
the wet nurse performed four bows on his behalf.
The rest followed regular custom.
For the enfeoffment of the Huángtàizǐfēi (Crown Princess),
the decree was transmitted on the same day as the Crown Prince's.
When the jiezé and scroll were about to reach the inner palace,
the Princess descended from the eastern steps,
welcomed them, and placed them on a table.
She was prompted to take her bowing position,
prompted to kneel,
and the Princess knelt.
She was prompted to announce the scroll,
a female official knelt to take the scroll,
and stood to announce it.
She was prompted to receive the scroll,
and prompted to insert the guī.
The female official handed the scroll to the Princess,
the Princess inserted the guī,
received the scroll,
and handed it to the female official.
The female official knelt to receive it,
and stood holding it.
She was prompted to remove the guī,
stand up,
and bow four times.
After the ceremony,
the inner official holding the jiezé exited,
the Princess escorted him outside the hall,
and the principal and deputy envoys, holding the jiezé, reported back.
On that day,
the Princess, in full ceremonial attire, went to Fèngxiān Diàn to perform the reporting ceremony.
Then she went to the palace gate,
waited for the emperor and empress to be seated,
entered to give thanks,
and performed the eight-bow ceremony.
She also went before the imperial consorts in various palaces,
and performed the four-bow ceremony.
Returning to her palace,
she went before the Crown Prince,
and also bowed four times.
After the ceremony,
she took her seat,
and the Wángfēi (Princess Consorts), Gōngzhǔ (Princesses), Jùnzhǔ (Commandery Princesses), and outer noblewomen,
bowed in congratulation in the dànchí as per custom.
Ceremony for enfeoffing Qīnwáng and Wángfēi:
During the Hàn dynasty, Qīnwáng were enfeoffed at the ancestral temple.
During the Táng dynasty, enfeoffment was decreed from the palace veranda,
with extremely detailed and complete rituals.
During the Sòng dynasty, there were enfeoffment decrees,
but all were declined with memorials,
and only the welcoming official delivered the proclamation to the residence.
The Yuán dynasty also issued decrees for enfeoffment,
but did not perform the enfeoffment ceremony.
In the 3rd year of Hóngwǔ of the Míng dynasty, a system was established:
When enfeoffing a Qīnwáng,
the Zōngmiào was informed in advance,
and the arrangements made by the responsible officials were similar to those for enfeoffing the Eastern Palace.
On the appointed day,
the Huángdì 皇帝 proceeded to the Fèngtiān Diàn 奉天殿.
The Huáng Tàizǐ 皇太子 and qīnwáng 親王 entered through the Fèngtiān Dōngmén 奉天東門.
Music began,
and they ascended from the eastern steps.
The Huáng Tàizǐ 皇太子 entered through the eastern gate of the palace,
and an internal attendant guided him to before the imperial presence,
where he stood in attendance.
The qīnwáng 親王 entered to the prostration position on the dānqí 丹墀,
and the music ceased.
The master of ceremonies announced the prostration,
and music began.
They bowed a second time,
stood up,
and the music ceased.
The official in charge of imperial decrees carried out the decree as usual.
All the princes knelt,
and the decree was proclaimed, saying:
"So-and-so, a son of the emperor, is enfeoffed as King So-and-so;
So-and-so is enfeoffed as King So-and-so."
When the proclamation was finished,
all the princes prostrated themselves,
and stood up.
The master of ceremonies announced the prostration,
and music began.
They bowed a second time,
stood up,
and the music ceased.
The director of ceremonies guided the kings to enter through the outer eastern side of the palace,
and music began.
An internal attendant led them to the prostration position before the imperial throne,
and the music ceased.
The kings knelt.
The master of ceremonies announced the bestowal of the imperial patent.
The official holding the patent presented it to the official reading the patent.
After it was read,
it was presented to the chéngxiàng 丞相.
The chéngxiàng 丞相 presented it to the kings.
The kings inserted their guī 圭 tablets and received it,
then presented it to an internal eunuch.
The bestowal of the imperial seal followed the above ceremony.
When it was finished,
the kings removed their guī 圭 tablets,
prostrated themselves,
and stood up.
The director of ceremonies guided the kings out
and back to their positions.
In turn, all the other princes were led into the palace
and received their imperial patents and seals as usual.
When the internal eunuchs had placed the imperial patents and seals in the decorated palanquins,
the master of ceremonies announced the prostration,
and music began.
All the princes bowed four times,
stood up,
and the music ceased.
The internal eunuchs carried the palanquins forward.
The qīnwáng 親王 descended the eastern steps,
and music began.
They exited through the Fèngtiān Dōngmén 奉天東門,
and the music ceased.
The Lǐbù Shàngshū 禮部尚書 requested the imperial edict to be sealed,
and proceed to the Wǔmén 午門 to be publicly read.
When the ceremony was complete,
the Huángdì 皇帝 returned to the palace,
and the Huáng Tàizǐ 皇太子 departed.
If a king was young,
an official would be dispatched to deliver the imperial patent and seal to him.
The chéngxiàng 丞相 would proceed to the king's residence,
stand in the northeast,
face southwest,
and proclaim the decree.
For the youngest, the ceremony of holding and embracing was performed.
On this day,
the qīnwáng 親wáng paid respects to the Huánghòu 皇后 and Tàizǐ 太子,
which was similar to the Tàizǐ 太子 receiving the patent and paying respects.
The qīnwáng 親wáng each went to offer congratulations on their own.
The younger ones went to the older ones
and performed the four-bow ceremony.
All civil and military officials went to congratulate the qīnwáng 親wáng,
also performing the four-bow ceremony.
The chéngxiàng 丞相 knelt in the main hall,
while civil and military officials were in the courtyard.
The chéngxiàng 丞相 delivered an address, saying:
"We, officials So-and-so and others,
upon the occasion of Your Royal Highness, the qīnwáng 親wáng, gloriously receiving the imperial patent and seal,
and the completion of the enfeoffment ceremony,
are filled with boundless joy."
After the congratulations,
the chéngxiàng 丞xiàng and all officials bowed four times again.
The next day,
the Huáng Tàizǐ 皇太子, in ceremonial robes, paid court and offered congratulations to the Huángdì 皇帝 at the Fèngtiān Diàn 奉天殿.
The Tàizǐ 太子 delivered an address, saying:
"I, the eldest son So-and-so,
upon the occasion of my younger brothers So-and-so and others being enfeoffed and establishing their states,
respectfully come to Your Imperial Majesty, my Father-Emperor, to offer congratulations."
To offer congratulations to the Zhōnggōng 中宮 (Empress),
he delivered an address, saying:
"I respectfully come to Your Royal Highness, my Mother-Empress, to offer congratulations."
All civil and military officials presented memorials and petitions to congratulate the Huángdì 皇帝, the Zhōnggōng 中宮, and the Dōnggōng 東宮,
following the ceremony for the Dōnggōng 東宮 receiving the patent.
The imperial and external ladies of rank congratulated the Zhōnggōng 中宮,
delivering an address, saying:
"We, concubines So-and-so and others,
upon the occasion of the qīnwáng 親wáng being enfeoffed and establishing their states,
respectfully come to Your Royal Highness, the Huánghòu 皇后, to offer congratulations."
On this day,
all civil and military officials and ladies of rank were each granted a banquet.
On an chosen day,
all the kings visited the Tàimiào 太廟.
At that time, the five kings, Qín 秦, Jìn 晉, Yān 燕, Chǔ 楚, and Wú 吳, were all grown,
while the four kings, Qí 齊, Tán 潭, Zhào 趙, and Lǔ 魯, were still young.
Therefore, both sets of regulations were applied.
The Jìngjiāng Wáng 靖江王 was enfeoffed as a qīnwáng 親wáng,
thus his ceremony followed that of Qín 秦 and Jìn 晉.
In the 28th year, it was established that
the legitimate eldest son of a qīnwáng 親wáng,
when ten years old,
would be granted a golden patent and seal,
and established as a wáng shīzǐ 王世子 (heir apparent to a prince).
The next legitimate son and all concubine-born sons would all be enfeoffed as jùnwáng 郡王.
All wáng shīzǐ 王世子 must be the legitimate eldest son.
If a king was thirty years old,
and his principal consort had no legitimate son,
his sons would only be jùnwáng 郡王.
It was only when the king and his principal consort reached fifty years old without a legitimate son
that the eldest concubine-born son would be established as wáng shīzǐ 王世子,
and inherit the enfeoffment.
The imperial court would send an envoy to perform the ceremony of bestowing the patent.
At the end of the Chénghuà 成化 reign,
when the five kings, Xīng 興, Qí 岐, Yì 益, Héng 衡, and Yōng 雍, were enfeoffed,
the emperor personally announced it at the Fèngxiān Diàn 奉先殿,
and dispatched envoys to the respective princely residences to bestow the patents,
abolishing the ceremony before the imperial presence.
And for all princes who were to inherit their enfeoffment,
officials were dispatched to bestow the patents at the end of the year.
During the Jiājìng 嘉靖 reign,
this was changed to the first month of spring
and established as a regulation.
The ceremony for granting patents to princely consorts was the same as that for granting patents to the Tàizǐ Fēi 太子妃.
Ceremony for granting patents to gōngzhǔ 公主.
In the seventh month of the ninth year of Hóngwǔ 洪武, envoys were ordered to grant patents to gōngzhǔ 公主.
A patent table was set up southeast of the imperial throne in the Qiánqīng Gōng 乾清宮,
and the patent was made of silver characters gilded with gold.
The Huángdì 皇帝 and Huánghòu 皇后 ascended the throne,
and dispatched envoys to carry the patent and transmit the decree as usual.
The envoy reached the Huágài Diàn 華蓋殿,
where the gōngzhǔ 公主 bowed to receive it.
The ceremony was roughly similar to that for granting a patent to the Tàizǐ Fēi 太子妃.
All imperial grand-aunts were called dàzhǎnggōngzhǔ 大長公主;
imperial sisters were called zhǎnggōngzhǔ 長公主;
imperial daughters were called gōngzhǔ 公主;
daughters of qīnwáng 親wáng were called jùnzhǔ 郡主;
daughters of jùnwáng 郡wáng were called xiànzhǔ 縣主;
granddaughters were called jùnjūn 郡君;
great-granddaughters were called xiànjūn 縣君;
and great-great-granddaughters were called xiāngjūn 鄉君.
From jùnzhǔ 郡zhǔ downwards,
they received imperial decrees of enfeoffment
but not imperial patents.
Ceremony for the Huángdì 皇帝's coming-of-age cap ceremony.
In ancient times, the capping ceremony was always held in the ancestral temple, and
the Son of Heaven underwent four additions to his cap.
After the Wèi 魏 dynasty, the capping ceremony began to be held in the main hall.
Furthermore, as the Son of Heaven was of supreme reverence,
the ceremony involved only one addition,
a practice followed by successive dynasties.
The Míng 明 dynasty established regulations in the third year of Hóngwǔ 洪wu.
In advance,
the Tàishǐ Yuàn 太史院 divined a date,
the Gōngbù 工部 manufactured the ceremonial robes,
the Hànlín Yuàn 翰林院 drafted the prayers,
and the Lǐbù 禮部 prepared the ceremonial procedures.
The Zhōngshū Shěng 中書省 carried out the decree,
appointing an official to act as Tàishī 太師,
and another official to act as Tàiwèi 太尉.
After the date was divined,
officials were dispatched to inform Heaven and Earth and the ancestral temples.
The day before,
the internal eunuch supervisor ordered the ceremonial cap mat to be placed in the center of the Fèngtiān Diàn 奉天殿.
To its south were set up the ceremonial robe table, the incense table, and the treasure table.
The Shìyí Sī 侍儀司 set up the positions for the Tàishī 太師 and Tàiwèi 太尉 for bowing and standing south of the Wénlóu 文樓,
facing west.
The prostration positions were set up within the inner path of the dānchí 丹墀.
The waiting positions were set up west of the imperial mat in the hall.
The washing positions were set up west of the dānqí 丹墀.
The positions for all civil and military officials and various attendants were arranged as in the Grand Court Ceremony.
On this day, at dawn,
the drums were beaten three times as a signal,
and all officials entered.
The Huángdì wore a kōngdǐng cè, shuāngtóng jì, shuāngyù dǎo, and jiàngshā páo,
and came out in his imperial carriage.
The guards cleared the way, announcing his presence, and music was played as usual.
The Huángdì ascended his seat.
After the whip was cracked and the time announced,
the ushers directed each official to perform their duties.
The Tàishī and Tàiwèi entered first,
and took their places for bowing;
then all the other officials entered.
The usher announced the bows,
and music began.
They bowed four times,
then stood up,
and the music stopped.
The master of ceremonies guided the Tàishī first to the washing station,
where he inserted his hù, washed, and dried his hands;
then he removed his hù
and ascended via the western steps.
The inner usher received and guided him to the west of the imperial seat,
where he stood facing east.
The master of ceremonies then guided the Tàiwèi to wash and dry his hands,
after which he entered and stood south of the Tàishī.
The master of rites announced the request to perform the coming-of-age capping ceremony.
The Tàiwèi approached the Huángdì,
moved slightly to the right,
knelt, and inserted his hù.
He removed the kōngdǐng cè and handed it to the inner attendant,
who placed it in a box.
After presenting the comb and setting the xi,
he removed his hù,
stood up,
and retreated to stand on the west.
The Tàishī advanced
and stood facing north.
The inner attendant supervisor ordered someone to bring the miǎn and stand on the left,
and the Tàishī recited a祝 (zhù) [prayer/blessing], saying:
"On this auspicious day of the propitious month,
we first perform the capping ceremony.
May you enjoy a long and blessed life,
to usher in great fortune."
The inner attendant supervisor held the miǎn,
knelt, and presented it to the Tàishī.
The Tàishī inserted his hù,
knelt, and received the miǎn.
After the cap, pin, and tassel were added,
he removed his hù,
stood up,
and retreated to stand on the west.
The supervisor of the Imperial Household Administration requested the Huángdì to don the gǔnfú.
The Huángdì stood up
and donned the gǔnfú.
The master of rites requested him to take his imperial seat.
The inner usher announced the presentation of the sweet wine,
and music began.
The Tàishī approached the Huángdì, standing facing north.
The Guānglù Qīng presented the wine to the Tàishī.
The Tàishī inserted his hù and received the wine,
reciting a 祝 (zhù) [prayer/blessing], saying:
"This sweet wine is truly rich,
this excellent offering fragrant.
Receiving the blessings of Heaven,
may you enjoy a long life without forgetfulness."
After the recitation,
he knelt and handed it to the inner attendant.
The inner attendant knelt and received the wine,
then presented it.
The Huángdì received it,
offered a little,
sipped the wine,
and then handed the empty cup to the inner attendant,
and the music stopped.
The inner attendant received the cup and descended,
handing it to the Tàishī.
The Tàishī received the cup and stood up,
handing it to the Guānglù Qīng.
The Guānglù Qīng received the cup and retreated.
The Tàishī removed his hù,
retreated,
and returned to his position.
The inner usher guided the Tàishī and Tàiwèi out of the western gate of the hall,
music began,
and they descended from the western steps.
The master of ceremonies guided them to the bowing position in the dànchí,
and the music stopped.
The usher announced the bows,
and music began.
The Tàishī, Tàiwèi, and all civil and military officials bowed four times,
stood up,
and the music stopped.
They performed three dances,
shouted "shānhū",
prostrated themselves,
stood up,
and music began.
They bowed four more times,
and the music stopped.
With the ceremony concluded,
the Huángdì stood up,
the whip was cracked,
and music began.
He entered the palace,
and the music stopped.
All officials departed.
The Huángdì changed into a tōngtiān guān and jiàngshā páo,
and paid respects to the Tàihòu,
following the New Year's Day ceremony.
A day was chosen to pay respects at the Tàimiào,
which was the same as the seasonal sacrifice.
The next day,
all officials, in their formal attire, offered congratulations,
and a banquet was bestowed in the Jǐnshēn Diàn.
In the first month of the third year of Wànlì,
the emperor chose a day for his long-hair ceremony,
and ordered the Lǐbù to prepare the rituals.
Dàxuéshì Zhāng Jūzhèng and others said:
"Rituals of capping and marriage are highly valued.
His Majesty, when he was in the Dōnggōng, already underwent the capping ceremony,
performing the 'three additions' to honor his status,
and holding the goblet for the wine offering.
Since the grand ceremony has been completed,
the minor details can be omitted,
and there is no need to instruct the departmental officials to deliberate and propose.
Instead, notify the Fèngxiān Diàn, Hóngxiào Diàn, and Shénxiāo Diàn in advance of the long-hair ceremony.
After the ceremony,
go to the two imperial Tàihòu palaces
to perform the five bows and three kòutóu ritual,
and then proceed to the Qiánqīng Gōng to receive congratulations."
The emperor approved this,
and it was thus enacted as a regulation.
Capping Ceremony for Imperial Crown Prince and Imperial Princes
The Lǐ [Rites] state:
"The capping is performed at the eastern steps (zù),
to signify succession.
The wine offering (jiào) is made at the guest's position,
the 'three additions' progressively elevate status,
the additions being for accomplishment.
After capping, a courtesy name (zì) is given,
this being the way of adulthood."
"Even the eldest son of the Son of Heaven
is still treated as a scholar (shì)."
