This ritual was used throughout various dynasties.
For the Ming imperial crown prince's coming-of-age capping ceremony,
the ages for the capping ceremonies of Zhōu Wénwáng and Chéngwáng were referenced:
the earliest was twelve,
the latest fifteen.
In the twenty-fourth year of Jiājìng,
Mùzōng, then the Dōnggōng,
was only ten years old,
and there was a desire to perform the capping ceremony.
Dàxuéshì Yán Sōng and Shàngshū Fèi Cài initially both found it difficult,
but later succumbed to the imperial will, deeming it feasible,
and requested to simplify the cumbersome rituals slightly,
only retaining the essential parts of the ceremony.
The emperor, however, believed the capping should be a complete ceremony,
and it was not performed until the twenty-eighth year.
Its ceremony
was established in the first year of Hóngwǔ.
Beforehand,
the Tàishǐjiān divined an auspicious day,
the Gōngbù prepared the gǔn miǎn and other robes,
and the Hànlín Yuàn drafted the congratulatory texts.
The Zhōngshū Shěng, by imperial decree,
appointed one of its officials as the 'guest' (bīn) [presiding official],
and another official as the 'usher' (zàn).
After the day was divined,
officials were sent to announce it to Heaven, Earth, and the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
The day before,
the imperial seat and incense table were arranged in the Fèngtiān Diàn,
the imperial crown prince's changing room (cì) was set up in the eastern chamber of the hall,
and the guest and usher's changing rooms were outside the Wǔmén.
At dawn,
the attending officials placed the léixǐ at the eastern steps,
arranged the imperial crown prince's capping mat on the southeast of the hall,
facing west,
arranged the wine offering mat on the western steps,
facing south,
hung curtains within the eastern vestibule (xù),
placed a cushion inside the curtains,
and also hung curtains outside the vestibule.
The Yùyòngjiān displayed the robes to the east inside the curtains,
with the collar facing north.
The gǔnfú with nine embroidered symbols, yuǎnyóu guān, jiàngshā páo, zhéshàng jīn, zīxī, and xīzhān were south of the robes,
and the comb was even further south.
The director of ceremonies filled the sweet wine into the side zūn,
added a ladle and cover,
and placed it south of the wine offering mat.
A diàn was set up east of the zūn,
with two jué placed on it.
The food presenters filled the food,
and placed it north of the zūn.
All attending officials stood in their respective places.
The drum beats thrice with the "yán" cadence.
Civil and military officials enter.
The Huángdì, wearing the tōngtiān guān and jiàngshā páo,
ascends the throne as in the usual ceremony.
The Bīnzàn take their places.
Music plays.
They perform four bows and rise.
Music stops.
The Shìyí Sī kneels to receive the imperial decree,
descends to the eastern steps,
goes before the Bīn,
and announces, "There is an imperial edict."
The Bīnzàn and all officials present kneel.
The decree is proclaimed, saying:
"The Huáng Tàizǐ is to be capped.
You, my ministers, are commanded to perform the ceremony."
All prostrate themselves,
rise,
and perform four bows.
All civil and military attendants take their places inside the hall.
The Bīnzàn and officiating officials proceed to their positions below the eastern steps.
Officials of the Dōnggōng and the Tàicháng Bóshì proceed to the eastern chamber in front of the hall,
guide the Huáng Tàizǐ to the capping mat,
two inner palace attendants (nèi shì) attend at his sides,
Dōnggōng officials follow behind,
and music plays.
He takes his seat facing southwest,
and music stops.
The Bīnzàn, in order, proceed to the léixǐ.
Music plays.
They tuck in their hú,
wash and wipe their hands,
and take out their hú.
Music stops.
They ascend from the western steps.
The officiating person presents the zhéshàng jīn.
The Bīn descends one step to receive it.
Holding the back with the right hand,
and the front with the left,
he advances before the Tàizǐ's mat,
faces north, completes the blessing,
kneels and caps him.
Music plays.
The Bīn rises,
and stands facing north and south by the mat.
The Zànguānzhě advances before the mat,
kneels facing north,
straightens the cap,
rises,
and stands behind the Bīn.
A nèi shì kneels and presents the robes.
The Huáng Tàizǐ rises,
puts on the robes,
and music stops.
The Bīn bows to the Huáng Tàizǐ, inviting him to resume his seat.
The Bīnzàn descend,
proceed to the léixǐ,
then the Zàn advances and kneels,
removes the zhéshàng jīn,
places it in a box,
rises,
and hands it to a nèi shì.
The officiating person presents the yuǎnyóu guān.
The Bīn descends two steps to receive it.
Music plays.
The cap is presented as in the previous ceremony.
The Zàn advances,
kneels facing north,
and pins the cap and ties the strings.
A nèi shì kneels and presents the robes.
Music stops.
The Bīn bows to the Huáng Tàizǐ, inviting him to resume his seat.
He again proceeds to the léixǐ.
The Zàn removes the cap.
The officiating person presents the gǔnmiǎn.
The Bīn descends three steps to receive it.
Music plays.
The cap is presented and the strings tied.
A nèi shì kneels and presents the robes.
As in the previous ceremony,
music stops.
The Tàicháng Bóshì guides the Huáng Tàizǐ to descend from the eastern steps.
Music plays.
He ascends from the western steps,
takes his place at the lǐ xí,
sits facing south,
and music stops.
The Bīn proceeds to the léixǐ, washes and wipes his hands.
The Zànguānzhě takes the jué, washes and wipes the jué,
proceeds to the Sī Zūn's place to pour the lǐ,
and hands it to the Bīn.
The Bīn receives the jué,
kneels and presents it to the Huáng Tàizǐ.
After the blessing,
the Huáng Tàizǐ tucks in his guī,
kneels to receive the jué,
and music plays.
After drinking,
he places the jué down,
and holds the guī.
The food presenter offers food before him.
The Huáng Tàizǐ tucks in his guī,
eats,
holds the guī,
and rises.
Music stops.
The jué and food are removed.
The Bóshì guides the Huáng Tàizǐ to descend from the western steps,
goes to the eastern chamber of the hall,
changes into court robes,
and proceeds to the bowing position on the dānchí,
facing north.
All officials belonging to the Dōnggōng return to their bowing positions.
The Bīnzàn proceed slightly east of the Huáng Tàizǐ's position,
facing west.
The Bīn advances slightly and speaks the words of bestowing the courtesy name:
"By imperial decree, a courtesy name is bestowed as Mǒu."
The Huáng Tàizǐ bows twice,
kneels to listen to the proclamation of the decree.
He bows twice again,
and rises.
He advances before the Imperial presence, kneels and reports:
"Your servant is not nimble,
but how could I not respectfully accept?"
After reporting,
he returns to his position.
All attending officials descend from the hall and return to their positions.
After the four bows are completed,
the Huángdì rises.
An internal attendant (nèi gěishì) guides the Huáng Tàizǐ into the inner palace,
to see the Huánghòu,
as in the New Year's Day ceremony.
The next day, he visits the ancestral temple,
as in the seasonal offering rites.
The day after that,
all officials, in court robes, proceed to Fèngtiān Diàn to offer congratulations,
then withdraw and change into official attire,
proceed to the Dōnggōng to offer congratulations,
and are granted a banquet.
In the 14th year of Chénghuà, the capping ceremony for the Huáng Tàizǐ was further revised.
The day before,
a temporary tent (mùcì) is set up in the eastern gallery of Wénhuá Diàn.
A jié'àn, xiāng'àn, guānxí, lǐxí, guànxǐ, Sī Zūn suǒ, etc., are set up,
all as prescribed.
Nèi shì spread the curtains and hangings,
and arrange the páofú, píbiànfú, gǔnfú, guīdài, xì, yìshàn guān, píbiàn, and jiǔliú miǎn.
At dawn,
the Huángdì ascends to Fèngtiān Diàn to issue a decree,
sending an official with the jié.
The Huáng Tàizǐ greets him outside the Wénhuá Diàn gate,
carries it in,
places it on the table,
and withdraws.
Officials from the Lǐbù guide the Huáng Tàizǐ before the xiāng'àn.
Music plays.
He bows four times.
Music stops.
The first capping ceremony is performed.
A nèi shì presents the yìshàn guān.
The Bīn pronounces a blessing:
"On this auspicious month and propitious day,
you receive your first cap.
May you respectfully bear this,
and forever be blessed with great fortune."
Music plays.
The Bīn kneels to present the cap,
rises,
and music stops.
An official from the Lǐbù requests him to change robes.
The Huáng Tàizǐ enters the tent,
comes out wearing the páofú,
and is requested to resume his seat.
The second capping ceremony is performed.
A nèi shì presents the píbiàn.
The Bīn pronounces a blessing:
"The capping ceremony is performed again,
to perfect your noble virtue.
Be reverent and careful in your demeanor,
as a model for the people."
After capping,
he enters the tent,
comes out wearing the píbiànfú and xì,
and is requested to resume his seat.
The third capping ceremony is performed.
A nèi shì presents the miǎnliú.
The Bīn pronounces a blessing:
"With all ceremonial robes added,
be diligent and reverent.
May the imperial plan be eternally firm,
for ten thousand myriad years."
After capping,
he enters the tent,
comes out wearing the gǔnfú,
and is requested to resume his seat.
When the ritual of the capping ceremony was performed,
the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) proceeded to the wine mat,
and music began.
He then sat down,
and the music stopped.
Officials from the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Guānglù Sì) presented the wine table,
and music began.
The announcer poured and offered wine to the guest of honor (bīn),
who, holding the cup, went to the front of the mat,
and the music stopped.
The guest of honor (bīn) offered a prayer, saying:
"The excellent wine is profoundly fragrant,
offered again with renewed perfume.
May you receive the blessings of Heaven,
and prosper for ten thousand generations."
The guest of honor (bīn) knelt and presented the cup.
The Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) held his jade tablet (guī) inserted in his belt,
received the cup,
and placed it on the table.
The Imperial Music Bureau (Jiàofāng Sī) played music,
performing the "Joyful Thousand Springs" (Xǐqiānchūn)曲 melody.
Next, wine was presented.
The Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) raised the cup and finished drinking,
then placed the cup on the table,
and the music stopped.
Officials from the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Guānglù Sì) presented the meal,
and music began.
Upon reaching the table,
the music stopped.
After the meal,
the jade tablet (guī) was removed,
the table was cleared,
and the guest of honor (bīn) and announcer resumed their positions.
The officiating announcer (míngzàn) announced the reception of the imperial admonition (chìjiè).
The Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) descended the steps,
and music began.
Upon reaching the bowing position,
the music stopped.
The official who was to announce the imperial admonition (chìjiè) went slightly east of the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ),
stood facing west,
and said:
"There is an imperial decree!"
The Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) knelt,
and the imperial admonition (chìjiè) was proclaimed:
"Serve your sovereign and parents with filial piety,
and be friendly to your brothers.
Cherish the virtuous and love the people,
reside in benevolence and act by righteousness.
Be neither negligent nor arrogant,
and may you greatly prosper for ten thousand generations."
Music began.
He bowed four times and rose,
and the music stopped.
The official holding the ceremonial staff (jí) carried it out,
and music began.
The Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) escorted the ceremonial staff (jí) to outside the palace gate,
then returned to the east wing.
The inner attendants (nèishì) escorted him back to the palace,
and the music stopped.
The guest of honor (bīn), announcer (zàn), and other officials holding the ceremonial staff (jí) reported on their mission,
and the rest followed the old ritual.
On that day,
the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) went before the Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu), the Emperor (Huángdì), and the Empress (Huánghòu) to express gratitude,
performing the five bows and three kowtows ceremony,
with music.
The next day,
the Emperor (Huángdì) and the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) received congratulations from all officials,
as was customary.
The capping ceremony for imperial sons (Huángzǐ).
For the first capping (chūjiā),
a hair net (wǎngjīn) was presented,
and the祝詞 incantation said:
"This is an auspicious day,
capping for adulthood.
May you uphold filial piety and fraternity,
and may fortune and blessings come in abundance."
For the second capping (zàijiā),
the Winged-Uplifted Cap (Yìshàn Guān) was presented,
and the incantation said:
"This capping ceremony is performed,
truly for the cultivation of virtue.
Revere and be cautious in your demeanor,
as a model for the people."
For the third capping (sānjiā),
the imperial robe and crown (gǔnmiǎn) were presented,
and the incantation said:
"With the capping reaching the third addition,
your mandate and attire are manifest.
Revere spirits and serve your superiors,
and forever secure your feudatory."
When pouring the wine, the prayer said:
"Excellent wine and good offerings,
fragrant and perfumed.
Receive this great blessing,
and prosper for a hundred generations."
The admonition (chìjiè) text said:
"Be filial to your sovereign and parents,
and friendly to your brothers.
Cherish the virtuous and love the people,
and act according to ritual and righteousness.
Be neither excessive nor arrogant,
and forever preserve wealth and nobility."
The arrangement of items, duties, and the announcement of the decree and expression of gratitude,
were all the same as for the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ).
Initially,
on the day after the imperial son's (Huángzǐ) capping,
after all officials had offered congratulations,
they proceeded to the princely palace (wángfǔ) to perform the rites.
In the 23rd year of Chénghuà
on the second day after the imperial son's (Huángzǐ) capping,
each went to the east wing of the Gate of Fengtian (Fèngtiānmén) to sit in order,
and all officials, in their regular attire, performed four bows.
In the 29th year of Wànlì
Féng Qí, Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū), stated:
"According to the old system for the Crown Prince's (Huáng Tàizǐ) capping,
the capping mat and wine mat were set up inside the Hall of Literary Glory (Wénhuá Diàn).
Now the Hall of Literary Glory (Wénhuá Diàn) is where the Emperor (Huángshàng) presides and dispatches officials,
so the Crown Prince's (Huáng Tàizǐ) capping and wine mat
should be moved to the east wing of the hall.
Furthermore, for the capping of imperial princes (qīnwáng),
the mat was previously set up in the east wing of the Gate of Imperial Supremacy (Huángjí Mén).
Since the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) is moving his mat to the east wing of the hall,
the imperial princes (qīnwáng) should move their mats to the west wing of the hall."
This was followed.
In the 11th month of the 9th year of Yǒnglè
and his capping was performed in the Hall of Grand Canopy (Huágài Diàn),
with a ceremony identical to that of the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ).
Capping Ceremony for Officials (Pǐnguān Guānlǐ)
In ancient times, men were capped at twenty sui,
and Grand Masters (dàfū) were not granted peerage until fifty,
hence there was no capping ceremony for Grand Masters (dàfū).
According to the Táng system,
there were three cappings (sānjiā):
the son of a first-rank official wore the imperial robe and crown (gǔnmiǎn),
down to the son of a ninth-rank official who wore the Swallow-Tailed Cap (juébàn),
all imitating the scholar's (shì) ritual but with additions.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ
the first capping (shǐjiā) used the Black Cloth Cap (zī bùguān),
the second capping (zàijiā) used the Cap for Advancing the Worthy (jìnxián guān),
and the third capping (sānjiā) used the Swallow-Tailed Cap (juébàn).
The procedure was as follows:
a day was chosen beforehand,
the host informed the ancestral temple,
and then divined for the guest of honor (bīn).
Two days before,
the guest of honor (bīn) and the cap assistant (zànguān) were instructed.
The next day,
a temporary seat was set up to the right outside the main gate,
facing south.
On the day itself,
one rose early,
and set up the wash basin (xǐ) southeast of the eastern steps (zuòjiē),
with its east-west position aligned with the eastern eaves-drip (dōngliù),
or for officials of the sixth rank and below, aligned with the eastern main beam (dōngróng),
and its north-south position according to the depth of the hall.
The water jar (léi) was to the east of the basin (xǐ),
with a ladle and cover (sháomì).
The basket (fěi) was to the southwest of the basin (xǐ).
A ceremonial towel (jīn) was spread inside the basket (fěi),
and covered.
Mats were laid under the western window of the east room,
clothing was arranged to the east of the mats,
with the collar pointing north.
Four reed mats (guān yán) were laid,
with four rush mats (zǎoxí) on top,
to the south.
The standing wine vessel (zūn) and wine bottle (wǔlǐ) were to the north of the clothing,
with a ladle and cover (sháomì),
and a stand (diàn) was set up to the north of the wine vessel (zūn).
For officials of the fourth rank and below,
a basket (fěi) was set up but without a stand (diàn),
and food was arranged to the north of the stand (diàn).
A wash basin (xǐ) was set up in the east room,
near the north.
The water jar (léi) was to the west of the basin (xǐ),
the basket (fěi) was to the northeast of the basin (xǐ),
and a ceremonial towel (jīn) was placed inside.
At dawn,
the bìngzàn 賓贊 arrived outside the gate.
The zhǎngcìzhě 掌次者 led him to the antechamber.
The bìngzàn 賓贊 wore his ceremonial robes;
all those involved in the ritual wore their respective attire
and took their positions.
For each of the guànzě 冠者, there was a casket of headdresses.
A person held it,
attending to the west of the western steps,
facing east and positioned to the north.
The zhǔxí 主席 (principal seat) was set up above the zùjiē 阼階 (eastern steps),
facing west.
The bìnxí 賓席 (guest seat) was set up at the western steps,
facing east.
The guànzě 冠者’s seat was to the northeast of the zhǔzhě 主者 (principal person),
facing west.
The zhǔzhě 主者, in ceremonial robes, stood below the zùjiē 阼階,
opposite the eastern chamber,
facing west.
All the qīn 諸親 (relatives), in ceremonial robes, stood southeast of the léixǐ 罍洗 (ablution basin),
facing west and positioned to the north.
The zūnzhě 尊者 (honored elders) were in a separate room.
The bìnzhě 儐者 (usher), in ceremonial robes, stood inside the gate, to the east of the path,
facing north.
The guànzě 冠者 wore a double-bun hairstyle, an empty-topped cè 幘 (cap), twin jade dǎo 導 (hairpins), a colored pleated skirt, a brocade sash, and black leather shoes.
For those of the sixth rank and below,
the dǎo 導 was not of jade.
They stood inside the room,
facing south.
The zhǔzhě 主者 and the zànguànzhě 贊冠者 (assistant for the capping ceremony), in ceremonial robes, stood inside the room, to the east of the door,
facing west.
The bīn 賓 (guest) and zànguànzhě 贊冠者 came out of the antechamber
and stood to the west of the gate,
facing east and positioned to the north.
The bìnzhě 儐者 advanced to receive instructions,
then went to stand to the east of the gate,
facing west,
and said:
"I respectfully request instructions regarding the ritual."
The bīn 賓 said:
"So-and-so's son is having an auspicious ceremony;
I am commanded to officiate."
The bìnzhě 儐者 entered to report.
The zhǔzhě 主者 welcomed the bīn 賓 to the east outside the main gate,
facing west,
bowing twice.
The bīn 賓 returned the bows.
The zhǔzhě 主者 bowed to the zànguànzhě 贊冠者.
The zànguànzhě 贊冠者 returned the bow.
Then he bowed to the bīn 賓.
The bīn 賓 returned the bow.
The zhǔzhě 主者 entered.
The bīn 賓 and zàn 贊 (assistant) followed him in,
reaching the inner gate and the steps.
The zhǔzhě 主者 requested them to ascend.
The bīn 賓 declined three times
before ascending.
The zhǔzhě 主者 ascended from the zùjiē 阼階,
stood to the east of the seat,
facing west.
The bīn 賓 ascended from the western steps,
stood to the west of the seat,
facing east.
The bīn 賓 and zànguànzhě 贊冠者 reached the courtyard,
washed their hands at the xǐ 洗 (ablution basin),
ascended from the western steps,
entered the eastern room,
and stood to the south of the zhǔzànguànzhě 主贊冠者 (principal assistant for the capping ceremony),
facing west.
The zhǔzànguànzhě 主贊冠者 led the guànzě 冠者 to stand to the west outside the room,
facing south.
The bīn 賓 and zànguànzhě 贊冠者 took the sī 纚 (headband), zhí 櫛 (comb), and zān 簪 (hairpin),
knelt and placed them at the southern end of the yán 筵 (mat),
then retreated to stand to the north of the seat,
a little to the east,
facing west.
The bīn 賓 bowed to the guànzě 冠者.
The guànzě 冠者 advanced and ascended the seat,
sitting facing west.
The bīn 賓 and zànguànzhě 贊冠者 advanced to the front of the yán 筵,
knelt facing east,
removed the double-bun hairstyle,
finished combing,
put on the sī 纚,
rose,
and returned to their position.
The bīn 賓 descended to the léi 罍,
finished washing,
and proceeded to the western steps.
The zhǔzhě 主者 stood behind the seat, facing west.
The bīn 賓 stood on the western steps,
facing east.
The person holding the zībùguān 緇布冠 (black cloth cap) ascended.
The bīn 賓 descended one step to receive it,
holding the back with his right hand
and the front with his left,
then advanced to the front of the guànzě 冠者’s yán 筵,
standing facing east.
The zhù 祝 (invoker) recited the ritual invocation for a shīlǐ 士禮 (scholar’s capping ceremony).
After the invocation was complete,
he knelt and capped him.
He rose,
and returned to his position.
The bīn 賓 and zànguànzhě 贊冠者 advanced to the front of the yán 筵,
knelt facing east,
tied the yìng 纓 (chin strap),
rose,
and returned to their position.
The guànzě 冠者 rose.
The bīn 賓 bowed to him to go to the room.
Both the bīn 賓 and zhǔzhě 主者 sat down.
The guànzě 冠者, dressed in a qīngyī sùshang 青衣素裳 (green tunic and plain skirt), came out to the west of the door,
standing facing south.
Both the bīn 賓 and zhǔzhě 主者 rose.
The bīn 賓 bowed to the guànzě 冠者.
The guànzě 冠者 advanced and ascended the seat,
sitting facing west.
The bīn 賓 and zànguànzhě 贊冠者 knelt,
removed the zībùguān 緇布冠,
finished combing,
and put on the sī 纚.
The bīn 賓 presented the jìngxiánguān 進賢冠 (scholar's cap),
stood and invoked,
as in the first capping ritual.
(Changing
"wànnián 萬年"
to
"yǒngnián 永年,"
and changing
"húfú 胡福"
to
"xiáfú 遐福.")
After the invocation was complete,
he knelt and capped him,
rose,
and returned to his position.
The bīn 賓 and zànguànzhě 贊冠者 knelt,
removed the jìngxiánguān 進賢冠,
finished combing,
and put on the sī 纚.
The bīn 賓 presented the juébàn 爵弁 (magistrate's cap),
stood and invoked,
as in the second capping ritual.
The bīn 賓 and zànguànzhě 贊冠者
placed the zān 簪 (hairpin) and tied the yìng 纓 (chin strap) as before.
The guànzě 冠者 went to the room
and came out wearing the juébàn 爵弁 attire.
The zhǔzànguànzhě 主贊冠者 removed the sī 纚, zhí 櫛, and yán 筵,
and took them into the room.
Then another yán 筵 was set up to the west of the inner door,
facing south.
The guànzě 冠者 came out from the west of the room door,
standing facing south.
The zhǔzàn 贊 (principal assistant) washed the zhī 觶 (wine cup) in the room,
poured the lǐ 醴 (sweet wine), and came out,
standing facing south.
The bīn 賓 bowed to the guànzě 冠者 to go to the west of the yán 筵,
standing facing south.
The bīn 賓 received the lǐ 醴,
advanced to the front of the guànzě 冠者’s yán 筵,
standing facing north.
After the invocation was complete,
the guànzě 冠者 bowed to receive the zhī 觶.
The bīn 賓 returned to the western steps and returned the bow.
The person holding the zhuàn 饌 (food offerings) presented them at the yán 筵.
The guànzě 冠者 held the zhī 觶 in his left hand,
took the pú 脯 (dried meat) with his right,
and made an offering between the biāndòu 籩豆 (food vessels).
The zànzhě 贊者 (assistant) took a portion of the zǐ 胏 (ribs) and gave it to the guànzě 冠者,
who placed the zhī 觶 to the west of the jiàn 薦 (mat) to make an offering.
The guànzě 冠者 sat and took the zhī 觶,
made an offering of the lǐ 醴,
placed the zhī 觶 down,
bowed twice.
The bīn 賓 returned the bow.
The guànzě 冠者, holding the zhī 觶, rose.
Both the bīn 賓 and zhǔzhě 主者 sat down.
The guànzě 冠者 ascended the yán 筵,
knelt and placed the zhī 觶 to the east of the jiàn 薦.
He rose,
advanced,
knelt facing north and took the pú 脯,
then descended from the western steps.
He entered to see his mǔ 母 (mother),
advanced and placed the pú 脯 in front of her seat.
He retreated,
bowed twice, and exited.
If the mǔ 母 was not present,
he would send someone to receive the pú 脯 below the western steps.
Initially,
the crowned youth entered to see his mother.
The guest and host both rose.
The guest descended
and stood facing east in the western order of seats.
The host descended
and stood facing west in the eastern order of seats.
The crowned youth exited
and stood to the east of the western steps,
facing south.
The guest advanced slightly to bestow a courtesy name upon him,
declining according to the rites for a scholar.
The crowned youth bowed twice,
knelt, and said:
"I, Mǒu, am not clever;
morning and night I will respectfully comply."
The guest departed,
and the host escorted him outside the inner gate,
facing west,
and requested to honor his attendants.
The guest went to his lodging,
and the host entered.
Initially,
when the guest departed,
the crowned youth faced east to see his relatives.
The relatives bowed to him,
and the crowned youth returned the bow.
The crowned youth faced west to bow to the guest assistant (bīnzàn),
and the guest assistant also returned the bow.
He saw his elders in a separate room,
also in the same manner.
After the guest and host had removed their ceremonial attire,
they entered the sweet wine (lǐ) banquet.
After one round of libations was complete,
the guest and all the other guests left their places
and stood to the east of the gate,
facing west.
The host came out to bow to the guest,
and the guest returned the bow.
The host entered first,
followed by the guest and all the other guests.
Upon reaching the steps,
the guest stood on the western steps,
the host stood on the eastern steps,
and the other guests stood below the western steps.
The host handed the ceremonial silk basket (bìfěi) to the guest assistant,
returned to his position,
went back to the eastern steps,
and faced north to bow in farewell.
The guest assistant descended from the western steps.
The host escorted the guest outside the main gate,
facing west,
bowed twice, and entered.
If he was an orphan, then his paternal uncles (zhūfù) and elder brothers (zhūxiōng) would instruct the guest.
On the day of the capping,
the host, with his hair tied in a topknot (jì), welcomed the guest.
The capping took place below the eastern steps,
and the ceremony was also similar.
The next day, he paid respects at the ancestral temple.
The crowned youth, in court attire, entered through the south gate, along the western path of the central courtyard,
faced north, bowed twice, and exited.
Capping Rites for Commoners (Shùrén Guānlǐ)
Of the ancient capping rites that survive, only the rites for scholars (shì) remain.
Later generations all adapted and used them.
In the first year of Hongwǔ of the Ming dynasty, an edict established the capping rites,
extending to commoners (shùrén),
with every detail meticulously prepared.
However, from officials downwards,
few were able to perform them.
They were recorded by the Ministry of Rites
merely as historical precedents.
All males aged fifteen to twenty
could undergo capping.
Before capping,
the day was divined,
the guest was divined,
and the guest was instructed,
all according to the ceremony for officials (pǐnguān).
On this day,
rising early,
a tent was erected as a room to the east of the main hall,
all dressed in formal attire.
Washing implements were set up to the southeast below the eastern steps.
Clothes were arranged in the room below the western window.
Two mats were to the south,
and wine was placed next to the clothes to the north.
Pú tóu, jīn, and mào,
each placed on a tray,
were carried by three people.
They stood below the hall to the west of the western steps,
facing south, with the easternmost one in the highest position.
The host stood below the eastern steps,
the relatives stood to the east of the washing implements,
and the ushers stood outside the gate awaiting the guest.
The crowned youth, wearing a doubled topknot (shuāngjì) and a robe,
with a headband (lèbó) and white shoes, waited in the room.
When the guest arrived,
the host went out to welcome him,
bowed, and entered.
Once seated,
the crowned youth came out of the room.
The officiant requested to begin the ceremony.
The guest's assistant (zànzhě) took the comb (zhì), hair tie (zǒng), fine-toothed comb (bì), and headband (chāngtóu),
and placed them at the southern end of the mat.
The guest bowed to the crowned youth,
who immediately sat facing west on the mat.
The assistant combed his hair,
bound the topknot, applied the hair tie,
and added the headband.
The guest descended,
and the host also descended,
standing below the eastern steps.
The guest washed his hands;
the host bowed and yielded,
ascended from the western steps,
and returned to his position.
The officiant advanced the cap (jīn).
The guest descended one step to receive it,
approached the crowned youth's mat,
and faced east.
The祝詞 (zhùcí) was the same as for officials.
After the incantation,
he knelt and put on the cap.
He rose
and returned to his position.
The crowned youth rose,
the guest bowed to him, who then entered the room,
changed clothes,
into a deep robe (shēnyī) and large belt,
and came out to the capping mat.
The guest washed his hands as before.
The officiant advanced the hat (mào).
The guest descended two steps to receive it.
He advanced with the incantation (zhù),
knelt,
after capping,
rose,
and returned to his position.
He bowed to the crowned youth, who then entered the room,
changed clothes,
into a pleated robe (lánshān) and waist belt,
and came out to the capping mat.
The guest washed his hands as before.
The officiant advanced the pú tóu.
The guest descended three steps to receive it.
He advanced with the incantation,
knelt,
after capping,
rose,
and returned to his position.
He bowed to the crowned youth, who then entered the room
and came out in official attire (gōngfú).
The officiant removed the capping mat
and set up the sweet wine (lǐ) mat by the western steps,
facing south.
The assistant poured the sweet wine and came out of the room,
standing to the south of the crowned youth.
The guest bowed to the crowned youth, who immediately took his seat,
standing facing west.
The guest received the sweet wine,
approached the mat, and faced north to make an incantation.
The crowned youth bowed to receive it,
and the guest returned the bow.
The officiant advanced the food.
The crowned youth took his seat,
and after eating and drinking,
bowed twice.
The guest returned the bow.
The crowned youth left his seat
and stood to the east of the western steps,
facing south.
The guest bestowed a courtesy name upon him,
using the same words as for officials.
The crowned youth bowed,
and the guest returned the bow.
The crowned youth bowed to his parents,
and his parents rose for him.
He bowed to the most senior of his paternal uncles,
then went out to meet the local gentry (xiāngxiānshēng) and his father's close friends (zhíyǒu).
The gentry and close friends all returned the bow.
The guest retired,
and the host requested to honor the guest.
After persistent requests,
he entered
and set out wine and food.
After the guest retired,
the host toasted the guest assistant,
presenting silk as a gift.
After the rites were completed,
the host took the crowned youth to see the ancestral shrine,
where they bowed twice and exited.
Collation Notes (Jiàokānjì)

Volume Thirty-One (Zhì Dìsānshíyī), Rites Nine (Lǐ Jiǔ) (Auspicious Rites Three (Jiālǐ Sān)): Ceremony for the Emperor's Empress Investiture (Tiānzǐ Nàhòu Yí); Ceremony for the Crown Prince's Consort Investiture (Huángtàizǐ Nàfēi Yí); Marriage Rites for Imperial Princes (Qīnwáng Hūnlǐ); Marriage Rites for Princesses (Gōngzhǔ Hūnlǐ); Marriage Rites for Officials (Pǐnguān Hūnlǐ); Marriage Rites for Commoners (Shùrén Hūnlǐ); Ceremony for the Emperor's Inspection of Schools (Huángdì Shìxué Yí); Imperial Lectures (Jīngyán); Daily Lectures (Rìjiǎng); Ceremony for the Crown Prince Leaving the Palace to Give Lectures (Dōnggōng Chūgé Jiǎngxué Yí); Reading Ceremony for Imperial Princes (Zhūwáng Dúshū Yí).
Ceremony for the Emperor's Empress Investiture (Tiānzǐ Nàhòu Yí).
There are six rites of marriage.
For the Son of Heaven, there was no personal welcoming ceremony.
Since the Hàn and Jìn Dynasties,
envoys were always dispatched, bearing credentials, to welcome the bride.
The ceremonial gifts and procedures
were adjusted according to the times.
In the early Míng Dynasty,
all emperors performed the Investiture Ceremony after ascending the throne.
In the seventh year of Zhèngtǒng,
when Yīngzōng had his grand marriage,
the ceremonial procedures were finally standardized.
For the Nàcǎi (presenting betrothal gifts) and Wènmíng (asking the bride's name) rites,
an auspicious day was chosen beforehand,
and officials were sent to announce it to Heaven, Earth, and the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
On the appointed day,
the imperial throne, the decree table, the credential table, the imperial guard, the ornate carriage, and the Zhōnghé Grand Music were arranged as prescribed.
The Ministry of Rites displayed the gifts on the Dānbì (vermilion steps) and below the Wénlóu (literary tower).
At dawn,
the Emperor, in his ceremonial robes, ascended the throne.
After the civil and military officials, in their court robes, performed their salutations,
they returned to their positions.
The principal and副 (deputy) envoys, in their court robes, bowed four times.
The attendants carried the decree table and the credential table
out through the middle gate.
The gifts followed them,
all placed in the central path of the Dānbì.
The officer proclaiming the decree announced, saying:
"We have selected the daughter of such-and-such official to be the Empress.
We command you, sirs, to proceed with credentials to perform the Nàcǎi and Wènmíng rites."
The principal and deputy envoys bowed four times.
The imperial procession set forth.
The decree and credential tables were carried out through the middle gate of Fèngtiānmén.
The principal and deputy envoys took the credentials and the imperial decree and placed them in the ornate carriage.
The ceremonial guard and the grand music preceded them,
exiting through Dàmíngmén.
They removed their court robes,
rode on horseback,
and proceeded to the Empress's residence.
At the residence, a tent for the envoys was set up to the left outside the main gate,
facing south.
An incense table was set up in the main hall.
The decree and credential tables were set up to the south,
and another table was set up to the north.
When the envoys arrived,
the master of ceremonies led them into the tent.
Attending officials displayed the gifts in the main hall.
The envoys came out of the tent,
presenting the imperial decree on the table.
The ritual official entered first,
standing to the east;
the host of the marriage, in court robes, came out,
standing to the west.
The ritual official said:
"By imperial decree, an Empress is to be established,
and envoys have been dispatched to perform the Nàcǎi and Wènmíng rites."
He led the host out to welcome them.
The envoys held the imperial decree and the credentials.
The host followed them to the hall,
placing the imperial decree and credentials on the table.
The principal and deputy envoys stood on either side of the table.
The host bowed four times,
and knelt before the table.
The principal envoy took the Nàcǎi decree,
and announced, saying:
"We, inheriting the celestial order,
reverently succeed to the grand design.
The way to govern the nation
is rooted in ordering the family.
The relationship between husband and wife,
the principle of Heaven and Earth,
is indeed of utmost importance for sustaining reverence for ancestral sacrifices
and for coordinating sincerity in support and care.
That which it relies upon is truly weighty.
Respectfully following the command of the Holy Mother, the Empress Dowager,
We dispatch envoys with credentials,
to select with propriety."
After the announcement,
it was handed to the host.
The host handed it to the attendant,
who placed it on the north table, slightly to the left.
The deputy envoy took the Wènmíng decree,
and announced, saying:
"We consider the way of husband and wife to be
the foundation of the great relationships.
To establish the proper position within the inner court
must rely on a renowned family.
We specially dispatch envoys with credentials to inquire the name with propriety.
We await the forthcoming report."
After the announcement,
it was handed over as before,
and placed on the table, slightly to the right.
The host prostrated himself,
then rose.
The attendant presented the memorial table,
and handed the memorial to the host.
The host knelt and handed it to the principal envoy.
The memorial stated:
"Your servant, so-and-so,
humbly receives the auspicious command.
The principal envoy, such-and-such official, and others
have solemnly proclaimed the imperial decree and edict,
inquiring about your servant's name and lineage.
Your servant's daughter
was born of your servant and his wife,
is the great-granddaughter of the late official so-and-so,
the granddaughter of the late official so-and-so,
and the maternal granddaughter of the late official so-and-so.
Your servant's daughter is so many years old this year.
We respectfully present this for your information."
The host prostrated himself,
rose,
and retired, bowing four times.
The envoys exited,
placing the memorial in the ornate carriage.
The host stepped forward and said:
"Please allow the attendants to offer refreshment."
After the food and drink,
the host presented silk as a token of appreciation to the envoys.
The envoys exited.
The host escorted them to outside the main gate.
The envoys followed the ornate carriage through the left gate of Dàmíngmén,
and upon reaching outside Fèngtiānmén,
handed the memorial and credentials to the Directorate of Ceremonial,
reporting back on their mission.
Next were the Nàjí (presenting auspicious omens), Nàzhēng (presenting betrothal gifts), and Gàoqī (announcing the date) rites.
Imperial decrees were proclaimed, and envoys dispatched,
all following the previous procedures.
However, for the Nàzhēng, black and crimson silks, bundles of silk, six horses, a grain-patterned jade scepter, and other items were used.
The decree text stated:
"We hereby betroth the daughter of such-and-such official to be the Empress.
We command you, sirs, to proceed with credentials to perform the Nàjí, Nàzhēng, and Gàoqī rites."
At the Empress's residence,
the arrangements were as before,
except that an additional jade and silk table was set up.
When the envoys arrived,
they placed the imperial decree and the jade and silk on the table,
and the six horses were displayed in the courtyard below the hall.
Attendants first arranged the Empress's coronet, robes, and other items in the main hall.
The ritual official entered.
The host came out to welcome them.
Attendants carried the jade and silk table.
The principal envoy held the Nàjí and Nàzhēng decrees.
The deputy envoy held the Gàoqī decree.
The credential-bearer held the credentials.
They entered in order,
each placing their items on the table.
The host bowed four times,
and knelt before the table.
The principal envoy took the decree,
and announced, saying:
"For the divination of the grand marriage,
the tortoise shell, milfoil, and diviners have all concurred.
Respectfully following the ritual canons,
envoys are dispatched with credentials to announce the auspicious omen."
He further announced, saying:
"Your daughter possesses the virtue of chastity and tranquility,
qualifying her for the selection as a motherly model,
and is fitting to jointly serve Heaven, Earth, and the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
We specially dispatch envoys with credentials,
to present the betrothal gifts with propriety."
After the announcement,
it was handed to the host.
The principal and deputy envoys then presented the jade scepter and the black and crimson silks to the host,
all following the previous procedures.
The deputy envoy took the decree,
and announced, saying:
"The year is auspicious, the month good,
and the lucky day, so-and-so Jiǎzǐ,
is most suitable for the grand marriage.
We specially dispatch envoys with credentials,
to announce the date with propriety."
After the announcement,
it was handed over as before.
The host bowed four times.
The envoys exited with the credentials.
The host performed obeisance to the envoys.
The envoys returned,
reporting back on their mission as initially.
Next, when the册 (cè) (investiture book) is issued to welcome her,
the officials in charge set up the arrangements according to the previous ceremony.
The Lǐbù (禮部) (Ministry of Rites) displays wild geese and gifts on the Dānbì (丹陛) (imperial steps).
The Nèiguānjiān (內官監) (Directorate of Palace Attendants) displays the Empress's ceremonial entourage carriages outside the Fèngtīanmén (奉天門).
The imperial edict states:
"Now, We invest so-and-so's daughter as Empress.
We command you and others to hold the staff and present the 册 (cè) and 寶 (bǎo) (seal),
and perform the welcoming ceremony."
The principal and deputy envoys place the 册 (cè) and 寶 (bǎo) in a decorated palanquin,
and proceed to the Empress's residence.
Upon arriving at the gate,
they place the imperial edict, 册 (cè), and 寶 (bǎo) on a table.
The ritual officials enter first.
The person in charge of the marriage comes out, dressed in court attire, to greet them.
The ritual official says:
"By imperial decree, We are investing an Empress,
and have dispatched envoys holding staffs to present the 册 (cè) and 寶 (bǎo),
and perform the welcoming ceremony."
The person in charge of the marriage goes out to welcome them.
The attendants carry the table and lead the way.
The envoys carry the imperial edict and the staff.
The attendants follow with the geese and gifts.
Upon reaching the main hall,
each item is placed on a table.
The envoys stand to the left and right.
The person in charge of the marriage bows four times,
then retreats to stand in the southwest.
Female officials present the Jiǔlóng Sìfèngguān (九龍四鳳冠) (Nine-Dragon Four-Phoenix Crown) and Wēiyī (褘衣) (ceremonial robes) to the Empress.
Eunuchs arrange the ceremonial guards in front of the central hall,
and set up female musicians below the hall,
who perform and cease as in the usual ceremony.
The envoys hand the staff, 册 (cè), and 寶 (bǎo) to the official of the Sīlǐjiān (司禮監) (Directorate of Ceremonial).
The interior attendants lead the Empress into the central hall.
The Empress, fully robed, emerges from her chamber,
proceeds to the incense table,
stands facing the palace,
and bows four times.
An attendant proclaims the 册 (cè).
The Empress kneels.
After the official proclaiming the 册 (cè) finishes,
he hands it to the Empress.
The Empress inserts her jade tablet,
receives the 册 (cè),
and hands it to a female official.
The female official kneels to receive it,
and stands to the west.
An attendant proclaims the 寶 (bǎo),
following the ceremony for proclaiming the 册 (cè).
An attendant removes the jade tablet.
An attendant announces "Rise."
After bowing four times,
the Empress enters her chamber.
hands it to the envoys,
The official of the Sīlǐjiān (司禮監) exits holding the staff,
The person in charge of the marriage kneels before the table.
The principal envoy proclaims the welcoming imperial edict,
then hands it to the person in charge of the marriage.
The deputy envoy presents the geese and gifts.
The person in charge of the marriage kneels to receive them all,
as in the previous ceremony.
The person in charge of the marriage rises.
The envoys bow four times and exit.
The person in charge of the marriage bows to the envoys as before.
Female officials request the Empress to emerge from her chamber.
She descends from the eastern steps,
stands before the incense table,
and bows four times.
She ascends the hall,
and stands facing south.
The person in charge of the marriage advances to stand on the east,
facing west,
and says:
"Be cautious, be respectful,
day and night, do not transgress."
He retreats to stand by the eastern steps.
The mother advances,
stands on the west,
facing east,
ties the skirt and girdle,
and says:
"Strive, be respectful,
day and night, do not transgress."
She retreats to stand by the western steps.
The palace attendants request her to board the palanquin.
The Empress descends the steps and boards the palanquin.
The procession departs,
with the ceremonial guards and grand music leading the way,
followed by the decorated palanquin,
with the principal and deputy envoys following,
then the officials of the Sīlǐjiān (司禮監) escorting.
They enter through the central gate of the Dàmíngmén (大明門).
All officials, dressed in court attire, welcome them in ranks outside the Chéngtiānmén (承天門).
After the palanquin enters,
they withdraw.
When the Empress reaches outside the Wǔmén (午門),
bells and drums are sounded,
and the ceremonial entourage stops.
The principal and deputy envoys hand the staff to the Sīlǐjiān (司禮監),
and report completion of their mission.
The officials carrying the 册 (cè) and 寶 (bǎo) carry them,
with ceremonial guards and female musicians leading the way,
and proceed to the Fèngtīanmén (奉天門).
Upon reaching the inner courtyard's curtained chamber,
the Sīlǐjiān (司禮監) hands the 册 (cè) and 寶 (bǎo) to female officials.
The Empress exits the palanquin
and enters via the western steps.
The Emperor descends via the eastern steps to welcome her in the courtyard,
bows to the Empress, and they enter the inner palace.
The Emperor proceeds to the changing room
to don his imperial robes.
The Empress proceeds to the changing room
to change into ceremonial attire.
Together they proceed to the Fèngxīandiàn (奉先殿) (Hall for Worshipping Ancestors),
and perform the ancestral temple worship ceremony.
After the sacrifice,
they return to the palace.
For the marital wine ceremony,
the Emperor changes into his Píbìan (皮弁) (leather cap)
and ascends to the inner palace.
The Empress changes her clothes
and ascends after him.
Each takes their seat,
facing each other from east and west.
Attendants place food trays before them.
Female officials take four golden goblets,
pour wine, and present it.
After drinking,
food is presented.
After wine and rice are presented again,
female officials take two halves of a calabash, pour wine,
mix it, and present it.
After drinking,
and after the food is again presented,
they rise
and change into ordinary clothes.
The Emperor's attendants eat the Empress's leftover food,
and the Empress's attendants eat the Emperor's leftover food.
The next morning,
both the Emperor and Empress wear ceremonial attire,
awaiting the Empress Dowager to take her seat.
The Emperor and Empress advance before her seat.
Palace women stand to the Empress's left with a plate of dried meat.
Both the Emperor and Empress bow four times.
Attendants bring a table.
Palace women hand the plate of dried meat to the Empress.
The Empress holds it and places it on the table.
Female officials carry the table.
The Empress follows to stand before the Empress Dowager,
presents it,
and returns to her position.
Both the Emperor and Empress bow four times.
On the third morning,
the Emperor wears his imperial crown,
and the Empress wears her ceremonial attire.
Together they proceed to the Empress Dowager's palace
and perform the eight-bow ceremony.
Returning to the palace,
the Emperor wears his Píbìan (皮弁)
and takes his seat.
Female officials lead the Empress,
in ceremonial attire, to stand before the Emperor
and perform the eight-bow ceremony.
The Empress returns to her palace
and takes her seat.
The ritual usher guides the inner relatives and female officials of the Liùshàng (六尚) (Six Directorates),
who perform the eight-bow ceremony;
next, the eunuchs of the various directorates and bureaus
perform the eight-bow ceremony.
On this day,
the Emperor presides at the Fèngtīandiàn (奉天殿),
issuing an edict as in the usual ceremony.
On the fourth morning,
the Emperor wears his imperial robes and crown and presides at the Huágàidiàn (華蓋殿).
Princes bow eight times,
then the attending officials bow five times.
Then he ascends to the Fèngtīandiàn (奉天殿).
All officials present memorials
and perform the congratulatory ceremony.
On this day,
the Empress Dowager and the Empress each wear ceremonial attire and take their seats.
Princes enter,
bow eight times, and exit.
Next, inner and outer noblewomen offer congratulations, and outer noblewomen present memorials,
all as in the usual ceremony.
On the fifth day, the hand-washing and feeding ceremony is performed.
The Shàngshànjiān (尚膳監) (Directorate of Imperial Banquets) prepares the food.
The Empress, in ceremonial attire, proceeds before the Empress Dowager,
and bows four times.
The Shàngshí (尚食) (Director of Food) hands the food to the Empress.
The Empress holds the food and presents it on the table,
returns to her position,
bows four times,
and retreats to stand in the southwest.
After the meal is finished,
she is led out.
The ceremony for the Crown Prince taking a consort.
The system of previous dynasties was the same as taking a Queen.
After the Suí and Táng dynasties,
the groom began to personally receive his bride.
The Son of Heaven would preside over the jiào jiè (exhortation and admonition) ceremony from the imperial pavilion.
The Sòng dynasty first implemented the guàn kuì (washing and feeding) ritual,
and the Míng followed it.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, a system was established:
whenever a ritual was performed,
envoys would be dispatched bearing credentials,
just like the Emperor's grand wedding ceremony.
Nà Cǎi (presenting betrothal gifts) and Wèn Míng (inquiring about the name).
The imperial decree stated:
"By imperial decree, so-and-so's daughter is taken as the Crown Prince's consort.
You are commanded to perform the Nà Cǎi and Wèn Míng rites."
Upon arriving at the consort's residence,
the usher came out
and approached the envoy, saying:
"May I ask about the matter?"
The envoy said:
"The Crown Prince's consort
should belong to a virtuous family.
The state has its established regulations,
and I am sent to perform the Nà Cǎi rite."
The usher entered to report,
and the marriage sponsor said:
"My humble daughter
is ignorant of the rules of the inner chambers
and is insufficient to be chosen.
Humbly receiving the imperial command,
I dare not decline."
The usher came out to report,
the envoy entered,
displayed the ritual gifts in the courtyard,
and declared the imperial decree, saying:
"I have been commanded to select."
After the ritual of presenting the wild geese was completed,
the envoy exited.
The usher again approached the envoy, saying:
"May I ask about the matter?"
The envoy said:
"The selection of the Crown Prince's consort
has been agreeable.
Now, divination will be performed,
and by imperial decree, the name will be inquired about."
The usher entered to report,
and the marriage sponsor said:
"The imperial decree states that my humble daughter
can serve the Crown Prince's palace;
I dare not decline."
The usher came out to report.
The envoy re-entered,
displayed the gifts and presented the wild geese as prescribed,
and declared the imperial decree, saying:
"I have been commanded to inquire about the name
and will consult divination."
The marriage sponsor said:
"My humble X-th daughter,
born of so-and-so."
Next was Nà Jí (announcing the auspiciousness of the divination).
The usher inquired about the matter as before,
and the envoy said:
"Having consulted divination,
the augury is harmonious and favorable.
By imperial decree, I am sent to announce the auspiciousness."
The usher entered to report,
and the marriage sponsor said:
"My humble daughter is foolish
and I fear she may not be capable.
That the divination is auspicious
is indeed my good fortune.
I respectfully comply with the regulations and decree."
The usher came out to report.
The envoy entered,
displayed the gifts and presented the wild geese as prescribed,
and declared the imperial decree, saying:
"By imperial decree, I announce the auspiciousness."
Next was Nà Zhēng (presenting the major betrothal gifts).
The usher came out to report,
the envoy entered and displayed jade, silk, and other gifts,
but did not present the wild geese,
and declared the imperial decree, saying:
"I am sent by imperial decree to announce the completion."
Next was Qǐng Qī (requesting the wedding date).
The message was:
"Having consulted the tortoise and milfoil,
such and such a month and day are auspicious.
By imperial decree, I am sent to announce the date."
The marriage sponsor said:
"How dare I not comply with the command?"
The gifts were displayed and wild geese presented as prescribed.
Next was Gào Miào (informing the ancestral temple).
Dispatching envoys bearing credentials to bestow the imperial patent and seal, and the ceremonial instructions,
all as detailed previously.
Next was Jiào Jiè (exhortation and admonition).
The Emperor wore the Tōngtiān Guān (Celestial Crown) and the jiàng shā páo (crimson gauze robe),
and took his seat in the Fèngtiān Diàn (Hall of Honoring Heaven).
All officials stood in attendance.
The usher led the Crown Prince to the red steps,
where he performed four bows.
He entered the east gate of the hall and proceeded to his seat,
standing facing east.
The libation officer advanced with a cup,
the Crown Prince knelt,
inserted his ceremonial tablet (guī),
received the cup, and poured a libation.
The food officer advanced with food,
he knelt and received it in the same manner.
He rose,
went to his seat and sat down.
After eating and drinking,
he was led to kneel before the imperial seat.
The Emperor commanded him, saying:
"Go and welcome your consort,
to inherit the affairs of my ancestral temple,
and encourage leadership with reverence."
The Crown Prince said:
"I, your humble servant, respectfully obey the imperial decree."
He bowed deeply and rose.
He exited to the red steps,
completed four bows,
the Emperor returned to the palace,
and the Crown Prince departed.
Next was Qīn Yíng (personally receiving the bride).
The day before,
the relevant authorities set up the Crown Prince's temporary residence outside the consort's main gate,
facing south.
The Eastern Palace officials' temporary residence was to the south,
facing east and west respectively.
On the day itself, at dawn,
the Eastern Palace officials, in full court attire, displayed the imperial insignia, drums, and wind instruments outside the Eastern Palace gate.
The Crown Prince, in full ceremonial robes and crown, rode in his carriage and exited,
with bodyguards accompanying him as prescribed.
Upon reaching the palace gate,
he dismounted from the carriage and ascended the imperial chariot.
All Eastern Palace officials followed to the consort's residence.
The chariot turned to face south,
he dismounted from the chariot and ascended the carriage.
Upon reaching the temporary residence,
he dismounted from the carriage and entered the residence.
All Eastern Palace officials also proceeded to their residences.
Before this,
when the Crown Prince was about to arrive,
the marriage sponsor held a banquet for the bride.
At the appointed time,
the consort, wearing a yú dié (embroidered phoenix robe) and huā chāi (flower hairpin),
came out and stood facing south in the hall.
Her governess stood to her left and right.
The marriage sponsor, in full court attire, stood below the west steps.
The usher led the Crown Prince out of his temporary residence,
to stand east of the main gate,
facing west.
The usher, in court attire, came out
and stood east of the gate,
saying:
"May I ask about the matter?"
After the usher knelt and reported,
the Crown Prince said:
"I have been commanded to personally receive the bride."
The usher received the command, rose,
and relayed it to the usher.
The usher entered to report,
and led the marriage sponsor out to welcome the Crown Prince west of the main gate,
where he bowed twice facing east.
The Crown Prince returned the bow.
The usher led the Crown Prince to enter the gate and turn left,
with the wild goose bearer following.
The usher led the marriage sponsor to enter the gate and turn right.
The Crown Prince ascended the east steps and advanced,
standing before the hall entrance,
facing north.
The marriage sponsor ascended the west steps,
stood to the west,
facing east.
The usher announced the presentation of the wild goose,
and the wild goose bearer advanced with the goose.
The Crown Prince received the goose,
and handed it to the marriage sponsor.
The marriage sponsor knelt to receive it,
rose,
handed it to his attendants,
and retreated to stand to the west.
The Crown Prince bowed twice,
descended from the east steps,
and exited to his temporary residence to await.
The marriage sponsor did not descend to see him off.
Initially,
when the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) entered the gate,
the Consort's (Fēi) mother came out
and stood outside the inner gate (gémén),
west of the goose-offering place,
facing south.
After the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) bowed,
palace attendants (gōngrén) and governesses (fùmǔ) led the Consort (Fēi) out
to stand to her mother's left.
The presiding official for the marriage (zhǔhūnzhě) commanded them, saying:
"Be warned, be warned!
Be diligent and reverent day and night,
and do not disobey orders!"
The mother commanded her, saying:
"Strive, strive!
Your father has instructions:
go and receive them with utmost reverence!"
The concubine-mothers (shùmǔ) repeated to her, saying:
"Listen respectfully to your parents' words."
Palace attendants (gōngrén) and governesses (fùmǔ) held and guided her retinue.
The Consort (Fēi) rode in a palanquin out of the gate,
then dismounted from the palanquin
and rode in a phoenix sedan chair (fèngjiào).
After the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) raised the curtain,
he then ascended his imperial carriage (lù),
with attendants as when he arrived.
Upon reaching outside the gate of the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng),
he dismounted from the imperial carriage (lù) and rode in a palanquin.
Upon reaching the inner gate (gé),
he dismounted from the palanquin and entered,
waiting to the east outside the inner hall gate,
facing west.
The official in charge of the women's quarters (sīguī) guided the Consort (Fēi) to the west outside the inner hall gate,
facing east.
The Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) bowed to the Consort (Fēi) and entered,
performing the nuptial cup (héjǐn) ceremony,
following the ritual for the Empress (zhōnggōng).
Next was the morning audience.
On that day,
the Consort (Fēi) went to the steps of the inner hall
to await the Emperor's (Huángdì) ascension to his seat.
The official in charge of the women's quarters (sīguī) guided the Consort (Fēi) in,
to stand facing north,
to bow twice,
and to ascend from the west steps.
Palace attendants (gōngrén) presented a tray of dates and chestnuts,
advancing to the front of the imperial seat to hand it to the Consort (Fēi).
The Consort (Fēi) placed it before the Emperor (Yùqián),
then returned to her position
and bowed twice.
After the ceremony,
she went before the Empress (Huánghòu),
presenting a tray of dried meat (duànxiū),
as in the ceremony above.
Next was the offering of wine (lǐ Fēi) to the Consort (Fēi),
then the ritual washing and offering of food (guànkuì),
then the visit to the ancestral temple (yèmiào),
then the morning felicitations from officials (qúnchén) and noblewomen (mìngfù).
All followed the established rituals.
In the fourth year,
the daughter of Kàipíng Wáng Cháng Yùchūn was enfeoffed as Crown Prince Consort (Huáng Tàizǐ Fēi).
The Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù) submitted the ceremonial procedures (yízhù).
Tàizǔ reviewed them and said:
"For the betrothal gifts (zhìlǐ), do not use hairpins (jī),
but only golden plates.
For the pheonix chariot (diézhē), use a phoenix sedan chair (fèngjiào).
The geese should be made of jade.
Ancient rites include the groom personally welcoming the bride, holding the rope and managing the wheel.
Now, with the use of a sedan chair (jiào),
then raising the curtain is appropriate.
For the nuptial cup (héjǐn),
follow the ancient system of using gourds (páo).
When the Consort (Fēi) has her morning audience and
enters the palace,
she should ride in a small carriage,
covered by a curtain.
For the visit to the ancestral temple (yèmiào),
the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) should go together with her.
Three days after the ceremonies are completed,
a banquet should be given for the officials (qúnchén) and noblewomen (mìngfù)."
This was decreed as law.
In the 22nd year of Chénghuà, the marriage rites were revised.
All ceremonial tablets (jiécè) and other documents
were to exit through the Left Gate of Fèngtian (Fèngtian Zuǒmén).
The Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) personally welcomed the bride,
exiting through the East Cháng'ān Gate (Dōng Cháng'ānmén).
On the day of the personal welcome,
the Consort (Fēi) wore informal attire
and performed rituals at her parents' family temple.
Attendants prepared wine and food,
which the Consort (Fēi) then ate and drank.
Her parents sat in the main hall.
The Consort (Fēi) went before them and bowed four times to each.
Her father instructed her, saying:
"When you go to the Great Interior (Dànèi),
be diligent and careful day and night,
and never fail in filial piety and reverence."
Her mother instructed her, saying:
"Your father has given instructions;
you must respectfully receive them."
Before the nuptial cup (héjǐn),
bowing positions were set up separately in the Crown Prince's (Huáng Tàizǐ) inner hall.
The Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) bowed to the Consort (Fēi) and entered to take his position,
bowing twice.
The Consort (Fēi) bowed four times,
and then each ascended their seat.
After the temple visit (miàojiàn),
all officials (bǎiguān) offered morning felicitations,
delivering a speech that said:
"We, your officials (mǒu guān chén mǒu),
respectfully observe that the auspicious rites of the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) are completed,
thereby extending the long and prosperous fortune of the imperial ancestral temple (zōngshè).
We, your officials (chén mǒu), are overcome with joy and happiness,
and respectfully offer our congratulations."
The Emperor (Dì) bestowed a banquet, following the New Year's Day (Zhèngdàn) ceremony.
Noblewomen (mìngfù) went before the Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) and Empress (Huánghòu) to offer congratulations,
and were also granted a banquet,
delivering a speech that said:
"The auspicious betrothal rites of the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) are completed,
further extending the splendid fortune."
The rest generally followed the Hóngwǔ rites.
Marriage rites for Prince (Qīnwáng)
According to the Táng system,
when an imperial son took a consort,
a Prince (Qīnwáng) was appointed to preside over the marriage.
In Sòng, the Emperor (Huángdì) personally oversaw the admonitions and ceremonies from his elevated platform (línxuán jiàojiè),
which were roughly similar to those of the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ).
The Míng followed this.
The imperial edict (xuānzhì) stated:
"Enfeoff so-and-so (mǒu shì) as the Consort (wángfēi) of Prince so-and-so (mǒu wáng)."
For the presentation of betrothal gifts (nàcǎi),
the speech said:
"The consort (lì) of Prince so-and-so (mǒu wáng)
is of virtuous and refined character.
Therefore, I (mǒu) am sent to perform the betrothal gift (nàcǎi) ceremony."
For the asking of the name (wènmíng), the speech said:
"As so-and-so (mǒu) has received the imperial command,
the matter will be submitted to divination.
I am commanded to ask the name."
The presiding official for the marriage (zhǔhūnzhě) said:
"The imperial decree (zhì) states that the daughter of your servant so-and-so (chén mǒu)
can serve Prince so-and-so (mǒu wáng).
Your servant so-and-so (chén mǒu) dares not decline."
For the announcement of the auspicious prognostication (nàjí), the speech said:
"The divination (bǔshì) has been auspiciously confirmed,
so I (mǒu) am sent to announce the good fortune."
The presiding official for the marriage (zhǔhūnzhě) said:
"The daughter of your servant so-and-so (chén mǒu)
is foolish and not capable.
That the divination (bǔ) bestows good fortune (jí)
is a blessing for your servant,
and I respectfully abide by the established regulations."
For the presentation of formal gifts (nàzhēng), the speech said:
"For the consort (lì) of Prince so-and-so (mǒu wáng),
the divination (bǔ) has been auspiciously confirmed.
I (mǒu) am commanded to announce the completion with ceremonial objects."
The presiding official for the marriage (zhǔhūnzhě) said:
"The imperial decree (zhì) bestows upon your servant weighty gifts.
Your servant so-and-so (chén mǒu) respectfully abides by the established regulations."
For the request for the wedding date (qǐngqī), the speech said:
"On a certain month and day, an auspicious day (juānjí) has been chosen.
I (mǒu) am commanded to announce the date."
The presiding official for the marriage (zhǔhūnzhě) said:
"I respectfully obey the command."
For the admonition and ceremony (jiàojiè), the command said:
"Go forth and welcome your companion (xiàng),
to continue your household,
strive to lead with reverence."
His personal welcome of the bride (qīnyíng), the nuptial cup (héjǐn), the morning audience (cháojiàn), and the washing and offering of food (guànkuì)
were all as for the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ).
After the washing and offering of food (guànkuì),
the Prince (Wáng), in his ceremonial cap (píbànfú),
and the Consort (Fēi), in her pheasant robe (díyī),
went before the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng)
and performed the four-bow ritual.
The Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng) received it seated; the Eastern Palace Consort (Dōnggōng Fēi) stood to receive two bows
and returned two bows.
The Prince (Wáng) and Consort (Fēi) went to the Consort's (Fēi) family home.
The Consort's (Fēi) father came out to welcome them.
The Prince (Wáng) entered first,
followed by the Consort's (Fēi) father.
Upon reaching the hall,
the Prince (Wáng) stood to the east,
and the Consort's (Fēi) parents stood to the west.
The Prince (Wáng) bowed four times.
The Consort's (Fēi) parents stood to receive two bows
and returned two bows.
The Prince (Wáng) sat in the middle.
Other relatives saw the Prince (Wáng),
bowing four times,
and the Prince (Wáng) received all of them seated.
The Consort (Fēi) entered the central hall.
Her parents sat,
and the Consort (Fēi) bowed four times.
The rest
followed the family rites in order.
In the era of Tàizǔ,
the crown prince and imperial princes had two consorts.
In the eleventh month of the eighth year of Hóngwǔ, Dèng Yù, the Duke of Wèiguó, was ordered to give his daughter as a secondary consort to the Prince of Qín.
No imperial decree was transmitted,
no imperial册 (cè) was issued,
and the prince did not personally receive her.
A principal envoy and a deputy envoy performed the nàzhēng (納徵) ceremony.
Their caps and robes were modeled after the regulations for second-rank officials of the Táng and Sòng dynasties.
The ceremonial guard was slightly reduced compared to that of the principal consort.
On the day of the wedding,
the prince wore a píbiàn (皮弁) cap and robe,
and led the consort to pay respects at the Fèngxiān Diàn.
The prince was slightly ahead on the east side,
and the consort slightly behind on the west side.
After the ceremony, they entered the palace.
The prince and the principal consort sat upright,
and the secondary consort bowed four times before the prince,
then bowed four times again before the principal consort.
The secondary consort sat on the east side,
and the banquet completed the ceremony.
The next day, for the morning audience,
the bowing positions were the same as for visiting the Fèngxiān Diàn.
When visiting the Zhōnggōng (中宮),
jujubes, chestnuts, and dried meat were not used,
but the rest was the same.
Princesses' Weddings
In ancient times, when the Son of Heaven married off his daughters,
he did not personally preside over the wedding,
but had a feudal lord of the same surname preside over it,
hence the term gōngzhǔ (公主).
The Táng dynasty still had imperial princes preside over the weddings.
The Sòng dynasty ceased this practice,
only instructing the marriage officiator to present a memorial at the inner east gate,
whereupon the Son of Heaven himself presided.
The Míng dynasty followed this.
Whenever a princess was married off,
the nàcǎi wènmíng (納采問名) ceremony was performed.
The groom's family prepared gifts and a memorial at their family compound,
and bowed twice towards the imperial palace.
The marriage officiator presented it to the inner east gate,
and addressed the inner attendant, saying:
"By imperial grace, a residence is bestowed upon the son of a certain official,
who practices the rites of his ancestors.
Your servant so-and-so requests to perform nàcǎi."
He knelt and handed the memorial to the inner attendant.
The inner attendant knelt to receive it,
and presented it to the inner palace.
Those carrying geese and gifts followed him in.
The inner attendant came out,
and the marriage officiator said:
"Divination will be performed.
Your servant so-and-so requests to perform wènmíng."
He presented the memorial as before,
and the inner attendant came out and said:
"There is an imperial decree."
The marriage officiator knelt,
and the inner attendant proclaimed:
"The emperor's [number] daughter
is enfeoffed as Princess [name]."
The marriage officiator prostrated himself,
then rose.
He entered to rest,
and was granted a banquet before leaving.
The nàjí (納吉) ceremony was the same as nàcǎi.
The marriage officiator stated:
"Divination was performed,
and the omen said it was auspicious.
Your servant so-and-so respectfully dares to announce nàzhēng."
The groom's family prepared black and crimson silks, jade and silks, a carriage and horses, and a memorial as per the regulations.
The marriage officiator stated:
"By imperial grace, a residence is bestowed upon the son of a certain official,
who observes the rites of his ancestors.
Your servant so-and-so presents bundles of silk, a carriage, and horses as nàzhēng."
For the qǐngqī (請期) statement, it was said:
"Your servant so-and-so respectfully requests an auspicious date."
On the day of qīnyíng (親迎),
the groom, in court robes, reported to the ancestral temple, saying:
"By imperial grace, a residence is bestowed upon so-and-so.
On a certain day, qīnyíng will be performed.
I dare to report this."
As he was about to depart,
his father performed a libation in the hall,
and offered counsel as he wished.
The groom bowed twice and departed,
arriving within the inner east gate.
The inner attendant led him to the resting place,
and those carrying geese and gifts arranged them in the courtyard.
On that day,
the princess, in ceremonial robes, bade farewell at the Fèngxiān Diàn,
bowed four times before the emperor and empress,
and received a goblet.
The emperor and empress offered instructions and admonitions as they wished.
After receiving the mandate,
she bowed four more times.
Descending the steps,
inner court ladies escorted her to just outside the inner palace gate,
and the princess ascended her palanquin.
Upon reaching the inner east gate,
she descended from the palanquin.
The groom lifted the curtain,
and the princess ascended the sedan chair.
The groom exited to his resting place and stood.
The goose-bearer knelt and handed the goose to the groom.
The groom received the goose,
knelt, and presented it to the inner attendant.
The inner attendant knelt to receive it and handed it to his assistants.
The groom bowed twice,
departed first,
and returned on horseback.
The princess's ceremonial retinue of carriages and palanquins departed later.
Dukes, marquises, and all officials' wives escorted her to the residence.
The groom awaited her at the gate.
When the princess arrived,
the groom lifted the curtain.
The princess descended,
and together they went to the ancestral shrine.
The groom stood to the east,
the princess to the west,
and both bowed twice.
A goblet was presented,
a prayer was read,
and they bowed twice again.
They exited
and went to the bridal chamber.
The groom and princess faced each other and bowed twice,
then each took their seats,
the groom to the east,
the princess to the west.
Food was served and the héjǐn (合卺) ceremony performed as regulated,
then they again faced each other and bowed twice.
The next day,
they saw the groom's parents.
The groom's parents sat to the east,
facing west.
The princess stood to the west,
facing east,
and performed the four-bow ceremony.
The groom's parents returned two bows.
On the tenth day,
the fùmǎ (駙馬) paid respects to express gratitude at court,
performing the five-bow ceremony.
Initially,
in the ninth year of Hóngwǔ,
Tàizǔ appointed Lǐ Shàncháng's son, Qí, as Fùmǎ Dūwèi (駙馬都尉),
to marry Princess Lín'ān.
Prior to the appointed date, he announced it at the Fèngxiān Diàn.
Two days before the marriage,
he ordered envoys to grant the imperial册 (cè) to the princess.
The day after the册 (cè) was granted,
she visited the Fèngxiān Diàn.
Also, the ceremony for the fùmǎ (駙馬) to receive the imperial edict was established:
an official from the Lìbù (吏部) carried the imperial edict in a dragon pavilion
to the grand tutor's residence,
where the fùmǎ (駙馬), in court attire, bowed to receive it.
The next day,
Shàncháng and the fùmǎ (駙馬) expressed their gratitude.
Ten days later,
the wedding date was requested.
In the twenty-sixth year, the ceremonial procedures were slightly changed.
However, although the procedures existed,
the rites of bowing to the groom's parents and the mutual bowing between the princess and fùmǎ (駙馬)
were in fact never performed throughout the Míng dynasty.
The following year, the titles and wedding rites for princesses and commandery princesses,
as well as the ranks of fùmǎ (駙馬) and yíbīn (儀賓), were again revised.
In the second year of Hóngzhì, Rénhé Zhǎng Gōngzhǔ was enfeoffed,
and the wedding ceremony was re-established.
Upon entering the residence,
the princess and the consort together bowed to Heaven and Earth,
performing the eight-bow ceremony.
Inside the hall, the princess's seat was placed to the east,
facing west.
The consort's seat faced east,
and the rest followed the previous ceremony.
In the second year of Jiājìng,
Ān Pán and others, Censor of the Ministry of Works, stated:
"When the consort sees the princess,
he performs four bows,
and the princess sits and receives two bows.
Although noble and humble are inherently different,
the division between husband and wife is fixed;
this is not proper according to ritual."
This was not heeded.
In the first year of Chóngzhēn,
Chén Zhōngshèng, the director for instructing consorts, said:
"Your servant instructs the consort Gǒng Yǒnggù.
The consort bows four times at dawn on the moon terrace outside the palace gate,
and says that after three months,
he will go to the main hall, the main gate, and the spirit screen,
performing the rites as before.
Only then does he offer food to the princess,
while the princess eats above,
and the consort stands by her side.
After this,
then marriage is discussed.
The consort sends fruits and delicacies to your servant in writing,
and the princess reciprocates with a written reply,
all of which are a great breach of decorum.
Once the marriage cup is shared,
they are truly husband and wife.
How can there be kneeling and bowing for several months,
calling oneself a subject and attending to meals,
and only then getting married?
The Comprehensive Statutes stipulate four bows before the sharing of the marriage cup,
clearly indicating that there are no bowing rites after the sharing of the marriage cup.
Treating the emperor's son-in-law [like a subordinate],
akin to a servant,
how can this uphold the dignity of the court?"
The emperor approved his words,
and ordered Yǒnggù to choose a day to get married immediately.
For selecting consorts,
the Ministry of Rites posted notices for sons of officials, soldiers, and commoners in the capital, aged fourteen to sixteen,
who were well-featured, behaved with dignity, and were well-educated, to register.
Eunuchs from the Directorate of Ceremonial would conduct selections at the residences of various princes.
If no suitable candidates were found,
they would extensively search in the capital region, Shāndōng, and Hénán.
Three candidates would be selected,
one would be personally chosen by the emperor,
and the remaining two would be sent to their local Confucian schools
to become government-subsidized students.
From the Xuāndé reign,
consorts began to have instructors,
who were appointed from academic officials.
After the Zhèngtǒng reign,
consorts were ordered to study and practice rites at the Imperial Academy.
In the sixth year of Jiājìng, it was finally stipulated that one director from the Ministry of Rites
would be exclusively responsible for instructing in the consort's residence.
Marriage Rites for Officials
According to the Zhōu system,
all dukes, marquises, grandees, and scholars who married
used the six rites.
After the Táng dynasty,
the rituals and objects were often reduced or increased according to official rank.
In the fifth year of Hóngwǔ of the Míng dynasty, an imperial edict stated:
"Ancient marriage rites
united the joy of two families,
to emphasize human relations.
In recent times,
people only talk about betrothal gifts,
becoming accustomed to extravagance.
The ceremonial system should be promulgated
to promote frugality,
to improve customs."
Therefore, at that time, the details of the grades were clear,
all with restrictions,
but few adhered to them later.
According to the system,
for all officials marrying,
or arranging a marriage for their sons,
a matchmaker was used to exchange letters.
If the woman's family agreed,
an auspicious day was chosen for the 'Nàcǎi' (presenting betrothal gifts).
The principal of the wedding set up a guest table.
On the appointed day,
after preparing the prayer tablet and announcing it at the ancestral temple,
the guest arrived at the woman's residence.
The principal of the wedding, in official attire, came out to greet them,
bowing to the guest and the matchmaker, and invited them in.
Wild geese and gifts were arranged in the hall.
The guest was on the left, the host on the right,
the matchmaker stood south of the guest,
all bowed twice.
The guest approached the host and said:
"Such-and-such official, valuing the importance of a marital partner, bestows it upon such-and-such;
such-and-such follows the traditional rites,
and respectfully sends such-and-such to present the betrothal gifts."
The principal of the wedding said:
"Such-and-such's daughter has not been properly instructed by her mother;
having already been chosen,
how dare we not accept with gratitude?"
The guest and host sat facing each other, west and east.
After removing the geese and accepting the gifts,
the geese and the gifts for the 'Wènmíng' (asking the name) rite were displayed again.
The guest rose,
approached the principal of the wedding, and said:
"Such-and-such official, carefully considering the marriage,
intends to perform divination,
and requests the name."
The principal of the wedding replied:
"Such-and-such's such-and-such daughter,
born of such-and-such wife."
This was written on red silk,
or on gilded paper,
stating the daughter's birth order, age, and years.
The guest declined,
and the principal of the wedding invited the attendants to perform the rites.
After the rites,
the guest was seen off outside the gate.
'Nàjí' (announcing the auspiciousness) followed the 'Nàcǎi' ceremony.
The guest delivered a speech, saying:
