"Such-and-such official has received the auspicious command,
and having consulted divination,
the turtle and milfoil have both agreed,
sends such-and-such to announce the auspiciousness."
The principal of the wedding said:
"Such-and-such's untrained daughter,
since the auspiciousness has been announced,
how dare we decline?"
'Nàzhēng' (presenting the betrothal tribute) followed the 'Nàjí' ceremony,
adding black and crimson silks, a bundle of silks, and a written letter,
but without geese.
The guest delivered a speech, saying:
"Such-and-such official, valuing the importance of a marital partner,
bestows this favor upon such-and-such official,
and follows the traditional rites.
There is an unworthy tribute,
and we dare to request its acceptance as betrothal tribute."
The principal of the wedding said:
"Such-and-such official has bestowed such a grand tribute upon such-and-such,
how dare we not accept with gratitude?"
The guest handed the written letter to the principal of the wedding,
who also replied with a written letter.
'Qǐngqī' (requesting the date) also followed the 'Nàjí' ceremony.
On the day of the 'Qīnyíng' (personally greeting the bride),
the groom's father announced it at the ancestral temple.
The groom stood facing north, bowing twice.
His father commanded him, saying:
"Go yourself to welcome the auspicious partner,
to establish your household's internal governance."
The groom replied:
"How dare I not follow your command?"
He bowed twice.
The matchmaker led the groom to the bride's home.
On that day,
the bride's principal of the wedding announced it at the ancestral temple,
and offered ritual wine to the bride according to family rites.
The groom arrived at the gate,
dismounted,
and went to the waiting place outside the main gate.
The bride's attendants invited the bride, in ceremonial dress,
to a seat inside the bedroom door,
facing south.
The groom came out of the waiting place.
The principal of the wedding came out to greet him outside the gate,
bowed, and invited him in.
The principal of the wedding entered the gate and turned right.
The groom entered the gate and turned left,
with the wild goose bearer following,
and stood facing north in front of the bedroom door.
The principal of the wedding stood east of the door,
facing west.
The groom bowed twice,
presented the wild goose,
and returned to the waiting place.
The principal of the wedding did not descend to see him off.
After the groom left,
the bride's parents sat facing south.
The wet nurse guided the bride to bow four times.
Her father commanded her, saying:
"Go to your husband's family,
take obedience as the correct path,
and do not forget reverence and respect."
Her mother commanded her, saying:
"Be always respectful and cautious,
and do not violate the commands of your parents-in-law."
Her stepmother added:
"You must earnestly listen to these teachings,
and do not bring shame upon your parents."
The wet nurse and maidservants escorted the bride out of the gate,
and she ascended the carriage.
The honor guard led the way,
and the escorts rode behind the carriage.
The groom returned first to wait.
When the bride's carriage reached the gate,
he came out to greet her within the gate,
bowed to the bride, and led her in.
When they reached the inner chamber door,
the groom ascended the steps first,
followed by the bride.
Entering the chamber,
the groom washed his hands in the southeast of the room,
and the bride's attendants held a towel and offered water to pour over him.
The bride washed her hands in the northwest of the room,
and the groom's attendants held a towel and offered water to pour over her.
After washing,
each took their seat,
the groom to the east,
the bride to the west.
A food tray was presented,
wine was served,
and dishes were presented.
After the wine and food were finished,
they were served again as before.
Maids poured wine into a divided gourd cup (jǐn)
and presented it before the groom and bride.
After each drank,
they all rose
and stood to the south of their seats,
facing each other, east and west.
Both bowed twice.
The groom and bride entered the chamber
to change clothes.
The groom's attendants ate the bride's leftovers,
and the bride's attendants ate the groom's leftovers.
The next day, they paid respects at the ancestral temple.
The groom's father's bowing position was set below the eastern steps,
with the groom behind him.
The principal wife's bowing position was set below the western steps,
with the bride behind her.
All relatives stood in order according to their rank.
On that day, they rose early,
and the groom's father and those below him took their places,
bowing twice.
The officiant led the bride to the center of the courtyard,
where she stood facing north.
The groom's father ascended from the eastern steps,
approached the spirit tablet,
and knelt.
He offered incense three times,
made wine sacrifices three times,
read the prayer,
rose,
and stood to the west.
The bride bowed four times,
retired,
and returned to her position.
The groom's father descended from the western steps to his bowing position,
and the groom's father and all below him bowed twice,
completing the ritual.
Next, they paid respects to the father-in-law (jiù) and mother-in-law (gū).
On that day,
the bride stood below the hall
and, upon seeing her jiù and gū seated,
took her position and bowed four times.
The governess led the bride to ascend from the western steps,
approaching the jiù.
Attendants presented jujubes and chestnuts to the bride.
After the bride presented them,
she descended the steps and bowed four times.
She then approached the gū,
presented dried meat (duànxiū),
following the same ritual as before.
Next, the jiù and gū offered wine to the bride,
following family etiquette.
Next was the washing and feeding ceremony.
On that day,
the bride's family prepared dishes and brought them to the groom's house.
The jiù and gū took their seats,
and the bride bowed four times.
She ascended from the western steps
to approach the jiù.
Attendants raised the food tray and handed the dishes to the bride.
The bride presented the dishes,
and the attendants added a spoon and chopsticks.
She presented dishes to the gū
in the same manner.
After the meal,
the dishes were removed,
the bride descended the steps to her position,
bowed four times,
and the ritual was completed.
The jiù and gū again offered wine to the bride,
following the initial ritual.
Commoner Wedding Ceremony
The *Lǐ* (Rituals) says:
"Wedding rites extend downwards"
Thus, the performance of the six rites
is the same for noble and commoner.

Zhū Zǐ's *Jiālǐ* (Family Rituals) does not include "asking the name" (wènmíng) or "announcing the auspiciousness" (nàjí), only "presenting betrothal gifts" (nàcǎi), "presenting money" (nàbì), and "requesting the date" (qǐngqī).
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, this was set as the standard and used;
an order was issued prohibiting engagements by designating a child in the womb or by cutting off a piece of clothing (for an infant).
For all commoners marrying,
men aged sixteen
and women aged fourteen or older
were permitted to marry.
The groom wore ordinary clothes,
or sometimes borrowed a ninth-rank official's attire.
The bride wore a floral hairpin and large-sleeved dress.
The rites of nàcǎi, nàbì, and qǐngqī
roughly imitated the ceremonies for officials.
There was a matchmaker but no wedding guests (bīn),
and the speeches also differed slightly.
The day before the personal welcome,
the bride's family sent people to arrange and furnish the groom's bedchamber,
which was popularly called "pūfáng" (preparing the room).
As for the ceremonial announcement (gàocí), the wine libation for admonition (jiàojiè), presenting the wild goose (diànyàn), and the joining of the divided gourd cup (héjǐn),
all were as per the official's ceremony.
Paying respects to ancestors (zǔnǐ), jiù, and gū,
and the jiù and gū offering wine to the bride,
also roughly corresponded.
Emperor's Ritual of Visiting the School
The *Lǐ* (Rituals) states:
"Whenever a school is first established,
there must be a ritual offering to the Former Sages and Former Teachers."
During the decline of the Zhōu (周) Dynasty,
these rituals fell into disuse.
Emperor Míng of Hàn (漢明帝) first visited the Pìyōng (辟雍).
After the Táng (唐) Dynasty,
when the Son of Heaven visited the school,
a lecture platform was first set up.
In the fifteenth year of Hóngwǔ,
Tàizǔ (太祖) was about to visit the Guózǐjiān (國子監).
Those who discussed it said:
"Though Kǒngzǐ (孔子) is a sage,
he is still a subject.
It is proper for the ritual to include one offering and two bows."
Tàizǔ did not agree,
and ordered Lǐbù Shàngshū Liú Zhòngzhì (禮部尚書劉仲質) to establish the regulations.
Prior to the day, the imperial canopy was set up to the east of the Dàchéng Mén (大成門),
facing south,
and the imperial seat was placed in the Yílún Táng (彝倫堂).
On the day itself,
school officials led all students to welcome the imperial carriage to the left of the Chéngxián Jiē (成賢街).
The emperor entered the imperial canopy,
donned his píbiàn (皮弁) attire,
and proceeded to the spirit tablet of the Former Teacher,
bowing twice.
He offered a goblet,
and bowed twice again.
The Four Associates (sìpèi), Ten Philosophers (shízé), and two side halls (liǎngwǔ) made separate offerings,
following the usual ceremony.
The emperor entered the imperial canopy
and changed into ordinary clothes.
He ascended his palanquin,
proceeded to the Yílún Táng, and took his seat.
School officials and students bowed five times and kowtowed,
lining up in order, east and west, below the hall.
Officials of the third rank and above, and attendant officials,
entered the hall in sequence,
lining up in order, east and west.
An announcement was made for the lecture to begin.
The Jìjiǔ (祭酒), Sīyè (司業), Bóshì (博士), and Zhùjiào (助教), four people, entered through the western door,
reaching the center of the hall.
An announcement was made to present the scripture desk before the emperor.
An official from the Lǐbù (禮部) reported,
requesting to present the scripture to the lecturing official.
The Jìjiǔ knelt to receive it.
The lecturing official was granted a seat.
Then, placing the scripture on the lecture desk,
he kowtowed,
and sat on a couch-table in the southwest corner to lecture.
Ministers, members of the Hànlín Yuàn (翰林院), and scholars were granted seats.
They all kowtowed
and sat in order, east and west.
All students stood in a circle to listen.
After the lecture,
they kowtowed
and returned to their original positions.
The Sīyè, Bóshì, and Zhùjiào
each proceeded to lecture in turn.
They exited the hall door
and returned to their positions.
An announcement was made to proclaim the imperial decree.
School officials and students formed ranks, all kneeling facing north,
to listen to the proclamation,
bowing five times and kowtowing.
After the ceremony,
school officials and students went out to Chéngxián Jiē to send off the imperial carriage.
The next day,
the Jìjiǔ led the school officials to present a memorial expressing gratitude.
In the fourth year of the Yǒnglè reign,
Zhèng Cì, Minister of the Board of Rites, citing the Sòng dynasty system,
requested to wear boots and robes,
and perform a double prostration.
The Emperor did not comply,
and the four-prostration ceremony was still observed.
After the imperial lectures concluded,
tea was bestowed upon all officials.
The Board of Rites requested to erect a stele commemorating the Emperor's visit to the National University,
and the Emperor personally composed the text for it to be engraved on stone.
The Jìjiǔ and others submitted a memorial expressing gratitude.
The Emperor presided at Fèntiānmén,
bestowed a banquet upon all officials,
and also granted two sets of zhùsī silk gauze robes to the Jìjiǔ and Sīyè respectively,
one set of zhùsī silk robes to each of the thirty-five academic officials,
and five ding of paper currency to each of the more than three thousand jiānshēng.
In the ninth year of the Zhèngtǒng reign,
the Emperor visited the Guózǐjiān,
following the established ritual.
After the ceremony,

a banquet was granted to dukes, marquises, earls, imperial sons-in-law, military officials of the rank of Dūdū and above, civil officials of the third rank and above, as well as Hánlín Xuéshì down to Jiǎntǎo, and Guózǐjiān Jìjiǔ down to Xuélù.
Previously,
when the Emperor visited the university and offered sacrifices to the Former Teachers,
no sacrificial animals were provided,
nor was music played.
It was not until the first year of the Chénghuà reign
that sacrificial animals and music were first used.
On the day of the imperial visit,
music was set up but not performed.
After the ceremony,
all officials offered congratulations,
and clothes were bestowed,
and a banquet was granted,
all extended to the descendants of the three clans of Kǒng, Yán, and Mèng.
In the first year of the Hóngzhì reign, it was stipulated that fasting should precede by one day,
additional silk offerings should be made at the sacrifice,
sacrificial animals should be the Grand Sacrifice (tàiláo),
and the "officials for separate offerings" (fēnxiàn guān) were changed to "officials for separate presentations" (fēndiàn guān).
In the first year of the Jiājìng reign, it was stipulated that the Yǎnshènggōng, leading the descendants of the three clans,
and the Jìjiǔ, leading the academic officials and students,
should present a memorial of thanks,
and all should be granted a banquet at the Board of Rites.
In the twelfth year, as the sacrificial rites for the Former Teachers had been duly regularized,
when the Emperor again visited the university,
ministers were ordered to make offerings at the Qǐshènggōng Shrine.
In the fourth year of the Wànlì reign, it was stipulated that the congratulatory ceremony should take place on the following day,
rewards as before,
and the banquet be waived.
Originally,
Xìanzōng had summoned the descendants of the three clans to the capital to observe the ceremony,
and also ordered the Yǎnshènggōng to make separate offerings.
Later, Shìzōng ordered the Yǎnshènggōng and the two Bóshì of Yán and Mèng,
five elders of the Kǒng clan,
and two each from the Yán and Mèng clans,
to come to the capital to assist in the sacrifices.
Imperial Lectures (Jīngyán)
In the early Míng dynasty, there was no fixed day
nor fixed location.
In the early Zhèngtǒng reign,
it was first established as a regular ritual,
with lectures given three times a month on the second day of each ten-day period at the Wénhuádiàn,
three times a month,
with temporary exemptions during extreme heat and cold.
The system was as follows:
one meritorious minister acted as the Director of Imperial Lectures (Zhī Jīngyán Shì),
and a Grand Secretary of the Grand Secretariat (Nèigé Xuéshì) either directed or co-directed.
Ministers (Shàngshū), Censor-in-Chiefs (Dū Yùshǐ), Commissioners of the Office of Transmission (Tōngzhèng Shǐ), Grand Justices (Dàlǐ Qīng), and Grand Secretaries (Xuéshì) and others attended in rank,
two officials from the Hánlín Yuàn or Chūnfáng, and the Guózǐjiān Jìjiǔ, gave the lectures,
two officials from the Chūnfáng displayed the books,
two officials each from the Supervising Secretaries (Gěishìzhōng) and Censors (Yùshǐ) served as masters of ceremonies,
one senior official each from the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Hónglúsì) and the Embroidered-uniform Guard (Jǐnyīwèi) served,
one announcer (míngzàn) called out the ritual steps,
four ushers (xùbān) held the trays,
and one meritorious minister or imperial son-in-law led the generals and imperial bodyguards.
The Board of Rites selected an auspicious day and made the request.
In advance, the imperial throne was set up in the Wénhuádiàn,
the imperial desk was set to the east and slightly south of the throne,
and the lecture desk was set to the south and slightly east of the imperial desk.
On that day,
the Directorate of Ceremonial (Sīlǐjiān) first arranged one volume each of the Four Books, Classics, and Histories on the imperial desk,
and one volume each on the lecture desk—all with the Four Books to the east,
and the Classics and Histories to the west.
The lecturers each prepared their lecture notes and placed them inside the volumes.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
the Director of Imperial Lectures and the attending officials and others stood on the Dānbì (vermilion steps),
performing five prostrations and three kowtows.
(Later, for each lecture, only the kowtow ceremony was performed.)
They then ascended the hall in order,
standing in rows facing east and west.
Two ushers
moved the imperial desk to the front of the throne,
and two others moved the lecture desk to the south and directly in the center of the imperial desk.
The Hónglú officer announced the commencement of the lecture.
Two lecturers came out from the east and west ranks,
proceeded to the front of the lecture desk,
and stood side-by-side facing north.
The eastern and western book-displaying officials each went to the copper cranes south of the imperial desk,
and stood facing each other.
The Hónglú officer announced for the lecturers to bow,
and rise.
The eastern book-displaying official went to the front of the imperial desk,
knelt to display the Four Books,
and then retired to stand under the eastern crane.
The lecturer went to the front of the lecture desk,
reported the title of the book to be lectured,
and retired after lecturing.
The book-displaying official knelt to close the book,
and then retired to stand under the crane.
The western book-displaying official displayed the Classics or Histories,
the lecturer advanced to lecture,
and retired,
as before.
The Hónglú officer announced for the lecturers to bow,
and rise.
Each retired to their east or west rank,
the book-displaying officials followed them,
and the ushers removed the imperial and lecture desks.
After the ceremony,
wine and food were commanded to be bestowed.
All officials went out to the Dānbì,
performing the kowtow ceremony.
Upon reaching the Zuǒshùnmén,
after finishing the wine and food,
they entered and performed the kowtow ceremony.
In the first year of the Lóngqìng reign, it was stipulated that on the day before, an announcement should be made to the Fèngxiāndiàn,
and to the Jǐyán.
On the day itself,
the Emperor proceeded to the west chamber of the Wénhuádiàn,
to perform rites to the Former Sages and Former Teachers.
The lecture notes were to be presented for review two days in advance.
In the second year of the Wànlì reign, it was stipulated that spring lectures should begin on the twelfth day of the second month
and end on the second day of the fifth month,
and autumn lectures should begin on the twelfth day of the eighth month
and end on the second day of the tenth month,
without needing a special request.
Daily Lectures (Rìjiǎng)
For the daily lectures,
held in the Wénhuáchuāndiàn,
only the lecturing and reading officials and Grand Secretaries of the Grand Secretariat attended,
without the need for ceremonial officials and others.
There were either four or six lecturers.
At the beginning of the open reading,
formal attire was worn,
with five prostrations and three kowtows.
Later, ordinary attire was worn,
with one prostration and three kowtows.
The Grand Secretaries attended together inside the hall,
waiting for the Emperor to verbally announce,
"Sirs, come,"
then they all entered,
kowtowed,
and stood facing east and west.
The reader first bowed to the Emperor,
then went to the desk to display the book,
pressed it with a golden ruler,
and held an ivory bookmark.
After reading five times,
they closed the book, bowed once, and retired.
First the Four Books,
then the Classics,
then the Histories,
the lecture proceeded like the reading ritual.
After the attendant official for writing had finished supervising the writing,
they each kowtowed and retired.
Tea was bestowed in the Wénhuádiàn,
and wine and food were bestowed at the Wénhuámén.
Afternoon lectures
were established in the sixth year of the Lóngqìng reign.
Every day after the morning lecture,
the Emperor would proceed to the nuǎngé (warm chamber) to rest briefly,
and review memorials.
The Grand Secretaries and others would retire to the west side chambers.
After some time,
they would lead the lecturers to proceed again for the afternoon lecture,
lecturing on the Essential Abridgments of the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn (Tōngjiàn Jiéyào) and the Essentials of Governance of the Zhēngguān Reign (Zhēngguān Zhèngyào).
After the lecture,
the Emperor would return to the palace.
On the third, sixth, and ninth days, when the Emperor attended the morning court,
the lectures and readings were temporarily exempted.
Moreover, in the sixth year of Jiājìng, regulations were established.
On the third and eighth days of the month,
two officials for the jīngyán and rìjiǎng
would lecture on Dàxué Yǎnyì.
In the tenth year, the ceremony for lecturing at Wúyì Diàn was established.
At dawn,
the Emperor, in everyday attire, would ride his palanquin to the palace gate.
All officials would await him outside the gate.
The Emperor would alight from the palanquin,
and ride a sedge litter
to the palace and ascend his seat.
All officials would bow once and kowtow three times outside the palace gate,
then enter
and stand in rows to the east and west.
When the lecture was announced,
one Grand Secretary serving as the lecturing official would step forward and kowtow.
Upon being granted a seat,
he would kowtow once
and then sit.
When the lecture concluded,
the official displaying the book would kneel and close the lecture chapter,
and the lecturing official would kowtow and return to his position.
Then another academician, by imperial order, would sit and lecture,
completing the ritual as before.
All officials would proceed to Bīnfēng Tíng to await the imperial carriage.
A banquet would be bestowed inside the pavilion.
Ceremony for the Crown Prince to Lecture Outside the Palace.
Tàizǔ commanded Scholar Sòng Lián to instruct the Crown Prince and other princes in the Classics at Dàběn Táng.
Later, this was moved to the rear hall of Wénhuá Diàn.
Shìzōng changed it to a private hall,
and it was then moved to the east wing of the hall.
In the second year of Tiānshùn, the ceremony for lecturing outside the palace was established.
Early on that day,
the imperial guards and ceremonial attendants would be present as usual.
The officials in charge would bow four times at the rear hall of Wénhuá Diàn.
The Hónglú officials would invite the Crown Prince to ascend the hall,
and the Imperial Tutors and Protectors and other officials would bow four times on the danbi.
All officials would withdraw.
The inner attendants would guide the Crown Prince to the rear hall to ascend his seat,
and present a writing desk.
The attendant officials, Imperial Readers, and lecturing officials would enter,
dividing into rows to stand to the east and west.
The inner attendants would open the books,
and the Imperial Readers and lecturing officials would successively read and lecture,
kowtowing before withdrawing.
As for the daily lecture and reading ceremony,
after the morning audience,
the Crown Prince would proceed to his quarters and ascend his seat.
[一０]The imperial guards and other officials were not needed;
only the attendant officials, Imperial Readers, and lecturing officials would enter,
performing the kowtow ritual.
The inner attendants would open the books.
First, the Four Books would be read,
then the Imperial Reading official of the eastern row would step forward
and read along ten or more times,
then withdraw and return to his position.
Next, the Classics or Histories would be read,
with the official of the western row reading along,
similarly.
After reading,
all officials would withdraw.
At sì shí,
all officials would enter.
The inner attendants would open the books.
The lecturing officials would finish lecturing on the Four Books read earlier,
then withdraw from their positions.
The same would apply to lecturing on the Classics and Histories.
After lecturing,
the attendant scribe would assist in practicing calligraphy.
After writing,
all officials would kowtow and withdraw.
For all reading,
after three days, there would be a review,
memorizing until proficient.
On review days,
no new books would be taught.
For all calligraphy practice,
one hundred characters would be written in spring, summer, and autumn,
and fifty characters in winter.
On the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month, holidays, or during strong winds, heavy rain or snow, severe cold, or intense heat,
it would be temporarily suspended.
In the eleventh year of Hóngzhì, it was revised:
the Three Grand Tutors, Three Junior Tutors, and court officials would bow four times at the danbi,
then enter through the left and right palace gates,
standing to the east and west.
After the lecture and reading concluded,
they would kowtow and withdraw.
In the sixth year of Lóngqìng, the Crown Prince's seat was changed to the east wing of Wénhuá Diàn,
facing west in the center.
The officials for daily lecturing and reading
would first proceed to outside Wénhuá Mén, facing east and west,
and stand in rows.
After the Emperor concluded his daily lecture and jīngyán,
the Crown Prince would come out of his quarters and ascend his seat.
Whenever the Crown Prince began his lectures,
the Grand Secretaries would attend for five consecutive days.
Thereafter, they would attend once on the third and eighth days of each month,
first bowing and departing,
and then other officials would enter.
In the eleventh year of Chóngzhēn,
Gu Sīchóu, the academician acting as Minister of Rites, stated:
"The completion of the Crown Prince's grand ceremonies and the imperial grants over successive reigns are well-documented.
The Veritable Records state that in the fifteenth year of Chénghuà,
when the Crown Prince began lecturing,
the six ministers were all promoted to Grand Tutor or Grand Guardian.
In the tenth year of Hóngzhì,
when the Crown Prince began lecturing,
the four Grand Secretaries including Xú Pǔ,
and seven ministers including Mǎ Wénshēng,
were all promoted to Palace Guardian."
The Emperor ordered the matter to be deliberated and implemented.
Ceremony for Princes' Studies
The study hall was in the right wing of Huángjí Mén.
Lecturing officials were selected from ministerial officials or jinshi who were reappointed as Hanlin officials.
In the second year of Tiānshùn, it was established that
upon first entering the study hall,
early on that day,
the prince would arrive at the study hall north of Yòushùn Mén,
face east,
and sit in the center.
The director of lectures and readings and the lecturing officials would perform a four-bow ritual.
Inner attendants would place the books on the desk,
and sit to the left of the desk.
The lecturing official would advance and stand to the right of the desk,
read along ten times,
kowtow, and withdraw.
For daily lectures and readings,
early in the morning,
the prince would arrive at the study hall.
The lecturing official would perform the kowtow ritual,
read along ten times,
and exit.
After meals,
they would return to the hall to accompany and supervise writing.
After lecturing on the books,
they would still kowtow and withdraw.
In the sixth year of Wànlì, it was established that
a central seat would be placed in the study hall,
the reading desk on the left,
and the writing desk on the right.
The辅臣 (Fǔchén) would lead the lecturing and scribal officials to await outside the gate.
When the prince entered the study hall,
an imperial command would be announced:
"The teacher enters."
The Fǔchén would lead all officials in,
perform four bows,
and stand in their respective rows.
After the lecturing officials successively taught the books ten times each,
an imperial command would be announced:
"The teacher may take wine and food."
All officials would exit.
The prince would temporarily enter the south room of the hall for a short rest.
The Fǔchén would each lead officials in.
An imperial command would be announced:
"The teacher enters,"
whereupon they would enter and stand in their respective rows.
The attendant scribe would supervise writing, and after the lecturing officials successively completed their lectures,
all officials would bow once and exit.
Correction Notes
Treatise 32, Rites 10 (Auspicious Rites 4, Guest Rites) Imperial Tours,

Crown Prince as Regent, Imperial Grandson as Regent, Proclamation of Edicts Ceremony, Receiving Edicts and Pardons Ceremony, Presenting Books Ceremony, Presenting Memorials and Petitions Ceremony, Village Archery Ritual, Vassal States' Tribute Ritual, Envoy to Vassal States Ceremony, Vassal States' Envoy Presenting Memorials Ceremony, Protocol for Officials' Meetings, Protocol for Commoners' Meetings.
System of Imperial Tours.
In the sixth year of the Yǒnglè reign, the emperor conducted a northern tour.
The Ministry of Rites dispatched officials to the provinces.
All important matters, foreign tributes, and submission of memorials
were to be reported to the traveling court.
Minor matters were to be reported to the capital for Imperial consideration.
Before the Imperial carriage departed,
prayers were offered to Heaven and Earth, the Deities of the Soil and Grain, the Imperial Ancestral Temple, and Xiàolíng.
Sacrifices were made to the spirits of the great rivers and the standard.
A farewell sacrifice was performed at Chéngtiānmén.
Along the route, officials were dispatched
to perform sacrifices where required.
Upon approaching Běijīng,
an altar was erected to sacrifice to the mountains and rivers of Běijīng.
When the Imperial carriage arrived,
prayers were offered to Heaven and Earth,
and sacrifices were made to the mountains and rivers within the territory.
The retinue consisted of 50,000 cavalry and infantry.
Attending officials included:
one Dūdū from each of the Five Chief Military Commissions,
one senior official from each of the Ministries of Personnel, Revenue, War, and Justice,
two senior officials from each of the Ministries of Rites and Works,
one senior official from the Censorate,
twenty-four Censors,
nineteen Supervising Secretaries,

a total of twenty senior officials from the Grand Court of Appeal, the Grand Court of Judicial Review, the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, the Court of Imperial Entertainments, and the Court of State Ceremonial,
three officials from the Hanlin Academy and the Grand Secretariat,
six officials including lecturers, compilers, and archivists,
and a total of fifty-four directors from the Six Ministries.
Other officials are not listed here.
Before the Imperial carriage departed,
a banquet was held for all officials,
and banknotes were bestowed upon the accompanying officials and military officers.
Upon arrival in Běijīng,
a banquet was held for all officials and elders,
and banknotes were bestowed upon all officials and noblewomen.
In the commanderies and counties passed through,
officials, students, and elders paid respects.
Court officials were dispatched to investigate the competence of local magistrates and prefects,
and promotions or demotions were immediately enacted.
Supervising Secretaries and Censors visited the elderly,
bestowing silk, cloth, wine, and meat.
In the eighteenth year of the Jiājìng reign, the emperor traveled to Chéngtiān.
Beforehand, he personally offered prayers to the Supreme Emperor at Xuánjí Bǎodiàn.
On the same day,
prayers were offered to the Imperial Ancestors and at the Ruìzōng Temple.

Officials were dispatched to offer separate prayers at the Northern Suburb Altar and at the temples of Chéngzǔ and subsequent emperors, the Deities of Soil and Grain, the Sun and Moon, and various other deities.
The Imperial carriage exited Zhèngyángmén,
with the empress and imperial concubines following in their sedan chairs.
The Jǐnyīwèi set up an Imperial military formation for the carriage,
with eight thousand guardsmen
bearing the Imperial palanquin and litter
and holding ceremonial insignia.
A Commander of the Imperial Guards served as vanguard.
Two high-ranking military officials were left to guard the capital,
and the Minister of War was to advise on military and state affairs,
each granted an Imperial edict to carry out their duties.
High-ranking civil and military officials were separately dispatched
to oversee Xuāndà, Jìzhōu, and Shānhǎiguān,
and to tour the Nine Frontiers,
each also granted an Imperial edict.
At the gates of the Imperial City and the capital city,
one high-ranking civil or military official was assigned to guard each.
Six thousand guardsmen were established for security and escort.
When the Imperial carriage departed,
all officials in auspicious attire saw it off beyond Zhāngyìguān.
The number of accompanying officials and troops
was roughly similar to that during the Yǒnglè period.
Those who had already departed and were on the road were excused from court attendance,

except for the Ministries of Rites and War, the Court of State Ceremonial, the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, the Censorate, the officials responsible for ceremonial protocol, and the Court of Imperial Entertainments, who accompanied the emperor.
Passing through Zhēndìng,
a distant sacrifice was made to the Northern Peak.
The emperor wore informal attire,
while attending high officials and the Grand Censor in charge of inspection wore auspicious attire for the ceremony.
At Wèihuī,
an official was dispatched to sacrifice to Jìdú.
At Jūnzhōu,
a distant sacrifice was made to the Central Peak;
at Yíngzé,
a sacrifice was made to the Yellow River;
the ceremony was similar to that for the Northern Peak.
At Nányáng,
an official was dispatched to sacrifice to Wǔdāngshān.
Along the route, officials were dispatched to offer sacrifices
at the temples and tombs of ancient emperors, sages, loyal ministers, and martyrs.
The Grand Censors, Provincial Governors, and officials of the Three Judicial Offices welcomed the emperor at the border,
and presented themselves in auspicious attire at the temporary palace.
Students and elders
all welcomed the emperor from thirty *lǐ* away.
At the princely estates passed through,
the Imperial Princes waited for the Imperial carriage in informal attire,
then followed to the temporary palace,
and paid respects in ceremonial robes and crowns.
A banquet was bestowed,
but members of the Imperial clan were not permitted to leave.
Upon arrival in Chéngtiān,
the emperor proceeded to the temple of Xiàn Huángdì to offer prayers.
Four days later,
the ceremony of offering prayers to Heaven was performed on the Imperial steps of Lóngfēidiàn,
with Xiàn Huángdì as co-sacrificed.
Changing into a leather cap and ceremonial robes,
the emperor proceeded to the altars of the State Deities of Soil and Grain and the mountains and rivers to perform the rites.
The next day,
he visited Xiǎnlíng.
The following day,
the accompanying officials submitted memorials of congratulation,
and an Imperial edict was issued in due form.
Upon returning to the capital,
the emperor personally thanked the Supreme Emperor, the Imperial Ancestors, and his Imperial Father,
and dispatched officials to offer prayers at the suburban altars, ancestral temples, altars of Soil and Grain, and to all deities,
performing the rites as before.
Regency of the Crown Prince
According to ancient custom,
when the Crown Prince went out, it was called
"Supervising the Army" ;
when he remained in the capital, it was called
"Acting as Regent" .
From the Three Dynasties onwards,
only the Tang Crown Princes acted as Regents,
using a twin-dragon tally,
but the specific ceremonies are not well-documented.
In the seventh year of the Yǒnglè reign,
when the Imperial carriage traveled to Běijīng,
regulations were established.
For ordinary court sessions,
the Crown Prince presided over affairs to the left of Wǔmén.
The Imperial Guards and various officials submitted reports as usual.
If he held court in Wénhuàdiàn,
only those summoned by Imperial decree were allowed to enter.
All military and state secrets, as well as urgent matters concerning princely estates,
were to be reported for Imperial instruction.
In case of border alarms,
troops were to be immediately deployed for suppression and capture,
and a swift report sent to the traveling court.
The guards at the Imperial City and all its gates
were increased.
On Imperial birthdays, New Year's Day, and the Winter Solstice,
the Crown Prince led all officials to bow before Wénhuàdiàn to present memorials,
performing the twelve-bow ritual.
The memorial exited through the central gate,
and the Crown Prince saw it off through the left gate to Wǔmén,
then returned to his palace.
All officials escorted it to outside Cháng'ān Yòumén,
and civil officials of the fifth rank and above, military officials of the fourth rank and above,
as well as close attendants and Supervising Censors,
all rode horses to escort it to outside Sānshānmén,
where the memorial was handed over to the transmitting official.
On the appointed day,
prayers were offered to Heaven for longevity,
and the eight-bow ritual was performed.
On New Year's Day, Winter Solstice, and the Qīanqiū Festival,
all officials offered congratulations at Wénhuàdiàn as usual.
For sacrifices at the Imperial Ancestral Temple
and to the deities of Soil and Grain,
the Crown Prince was commanded beforehand to perform the sacrifices.
For other prescribed sacrifices to deities,
the Court of Imperial Sacrifices reported to the traveling court,
and officials were dispatched to perform the rites.
Whenever foreign envoys came to court,
a banquet was granted according to custom,
and the Ministry of Rites was ordered to send them to the traveling court.
Whenever Imperial edicts arrived,
a dragon pavilion, ceremonial insignia, and grand music were set up.
All officials in court robes
went out beyond Sānshānmén to welcome them.
The Crown Prince, in ceremonial robes and crown, welcomed them before Wǔmén.
Upon reaching Wénhuàdiàn,
the five-bow, three-kòutóu ritual was performed,
and the edict was unrolled and read in the hall.
The messenger held the edict and placed it in the dragon pavilion,
and the Crown Prince saw him off beyond Wǔmén.
Officials from the Ministry of Rites placed the edict in a cloud carriage,
and civil and military officials of the second rank and above welcomed it to Chéngtiānmén,
where it was read aloud as usual.
With drum and music, the messenger was escorted to Huìtóngguǎn.
When the messenger saw the Crown Prince,
he performed the four-bow ritual,
and a banquet was granted by the Ministry of Rites.
In the twelfth year, during the Northern Expedition,
regulations were again established.
Ordinary court sessions were held in Wénhuàdiàn,
and all reports from civil and military officials
were submitted to Běijīng.
In the eighteenth year of the Jiājìng reign, during the Southern Tour,
the Crown Prince was ordered to act as Regent.
As the Crown Prince was young at the time,
one Grand Secretary was appointed to remain in the capital,
and all military and state affairs were to be reported to him for action.
Regency of the Imperial Grandson
In the eighth year of the Yǒnglè reign,
the emperor embarked on a Northern Expedition from Běijīng.
At that time, the Crown Prince was already acting as Regent in the south.
Therefore, the Imperial Eldest Grandson was ordered to act as Regent in Běijīng.
At that time, Xuānzōng had not yet come of age,
and only after his capping ceremony was he referred to as the Imperial Grandson.
Its system was
that every day, the Imperial Eldest Grandson (Huángzhǎngsūn) would attend to matters at the left of Fèngtiānmén,
with guards as per usual ceremony.
When various offices had matters,
they would submit a memorial for implementation.
As for military secrets (jūnjī) and important matters of the princely establishments (wángfǔ),
one memorial would be submitted to the Imperial Crown Prince (Huángtàizǐ) for decision,
and one would be reported to the traveling court (xíngzàisuǒ).
On the Imperial Birthday (Shèngjié),
an incense table would be set up in Fèngtiāndiàn,
and ceremonies performed as usual.
Memorials (biǎowén) from all offices under Heaven would all go to Běijīng.
Tributes from the Four Barbarians (Sìyí) would all be sent to Nánjīng.
For military selections (wǔxuǎn) and offenses committed by officials or commoners,
major ones would be referred to the Imperial Crown Prince (Huángtàizǐ),
and minor ones handled by the Imperial Eldest Grandson (Huángzhǎngsūn).
For offenses by imperial relatives (huángqīn),
they would be referred to the Imperial Crown Prince (Huángtàizǐ).
If the offense was severe or involved rebellion,
the person would be immediately detained,
and imperial relatives (huángqīn) ordered to jointly interrogate them.
If they did not confess,

then dukes (gōng), marquises (hóu), earls (bó), the Five Chief Military Commissions (Wǔfǔ), the Six Ministries (Liùbù), the Censorate (Dūcháyuàn), and the Grand Court of Revision (Dàlǐsì) would be ordered to jointly interrogate them again with the imperial relatives (huángqīn),
and the matter reported to the Imperial Crown Prince (Huángtàizǐ),
awaiting the return of the imperial carriage to the capital (Jīng),
for a memorial requesting a decision.
Ceremony for Proclaiming Edicts
Whenever decrees were issued to the four directions,
there were imperial edicts (zhàoshū),
imperial pardons (shèshū),
imperial tallies (chìfú) and vermilion tallies (dānfú),
and imperial commands (zhìyù) and handwritten edicts (shǒuzhào).
Edicts and pardons (zhào shè)
were first proclaimed in the imperial court (quē tíng),
and then promulgated.
Imperial tallies (chìfú), etc.,
were carried by envoys and delivered to the appointed official,
kept secret and not to be opened.
The ceremonies for opening, reading, and receiving
differed.
In the 26th year of Hóngwǔ, the ceremony for proclaiming edicts was established.
An imperial throne (yùzuò) was set up in Fèngtiāndiàn,
a precious table (bǎo'àn) to the east of the hall,
the Zhōnghé Shaole music (Zhōnghé Shaole) performed within the hall,
grand music (dàyuè) set up outside Wǔmén and Chéngtiānmén,
and a reading table (xuāndú'àn) set up above Chéngtiānmén,
facing southwest.
In the early morning,
imperial guards (jiàowèi) held a cloud canopy (yúngài) in front of the curtains within the hall,
and all officials in court robes (cháofú) lined up outside Chéngtiānmén,
while dukes (gōng) and marquises (hóu) lined up outside Wǔmén,
facing east and west.
The Emperor, in a leather cap (píbiàn) and robes,
ascended the hall as per ceremony.
An official from the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù) held the imperial edict (zhàoshū) and proceeded to the table,
after applying the imperial seal (yòngbǎo),
placed it inside the cloud canopy (yúngài).
The imperial guards (jiàowèi) held the cloud canopy (yúngài)
and exited through the east gate of the hall.
Grand music (dàyuè) played,
descending from the eastern steps,
passing through Fèngtiānmén to the south of Jīnshuǐqiáo and outside Wǔmén.
Music played,
dukes (gōng) and marquises (hóu) led the way,
welcoming it to above Chéngtiānmén.
The crier (míngzàn) called for officials to line up (páibān),
civil and military officials took their positions,
and music played.
Four prostrations (sìbài) were performed,
and the music stopped.
The official responsible for proclaiming and unfolding the edict (xuāndú zhǎndú guān) ascended the table,
announced "There is an imperial command" (yǒu zhì),
and all officials knelt.
An official from the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù) held the imperial edict (zhàoshū),
and handed it to the proclaiming official (xuāndú guān).
After proclaiming it,
the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù) official held it and placed it within the cloud canopy (yúngài).
The ceremonial assistant (zànlǐ) called "Prostrate and rise" (fǔfú xīng),
and music played.
Four prostrations (sìbài) were performed,
and the music stopped.
Dancing and shouting "Long live!" (wǔdǎo shānhū) was performed,
followed by another four prostrations (sìbài).
The Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Yílǐsī) reported the completion of the ceremony,
and the imperial carriage (jià) departed.
An official from the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù) held the imperial edicts (zhàoshū) and distributed them to the envoys,
and all officials withdrew.
In the 6th year of Jiājìng, further regulations were established:
the Court of State Ceremonials (Hónglú) officials set up an edict table (zhào'àn),
the Imperial Bodyguard (Jǐnyīwèi) set up a cloud canopy tray (yúngài pán) inside Fèngtiāndiàn to the east,
another cloud tray (yún pán) was set up above Chéngtiānmén,
a decorated sedan chair (cǎiyú) was set up outside Wǔmén,
and the Court of State Ceremonials (Hónglú) officials set up a proclaiming table (xuāndú'àn) above Chéngtiānmén.
All officials entered and stood in the Dānchí,
and the Emperor, in his imperial crown (miǎnfú), ascended the throne,
as per court ceremony.
An official from the Hanlin Academy (Hànlín Yuàn) held the imperial edict (zhàoshū) and followed,
standing to the east in front of the throne.
All officials entered their ranks,
performed four prostrations (sìbài),
and exited to outside Chéngtiānmén.
The proclamation of the edict was announced,
the Hanlin Academy (Hànlín Yuàn) official held the imperial edict (zhàoshū) and handed it to the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù) official,
who held it to the cloud tray (yún pán) table.
The imperial guards (jiàowèi) held the cloud canopy (yúngài),
all exiting through the left gate of the hall,
to outside Wǔmén,
placing the edict in the decorated sedan chair (cǎiyú).
Dukes (gōng), marquises (hóu), and earls (bó) and officials of the third rank and above led the way,
welcoming it to above Chéngtiānmén,
where the proclamation and bowing were
all as per the above ceremony.
An official from the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù) held the imperial edict (zhàoshū) and handed it to an Imperial Bodyguard (Jǐnyīwèi) official,
who placed it in a cloud box (yúnxiá),
tied it with a colorful rope to a dragon pole (lónggān),
and sent it down.
An official from the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù) held it and placed it in a dragon pavilion (lóngtíng),
and with drums and music, it was escorted to the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù),
and handed to the envoys for promulgation.
In the 6th year of Lóngqìng,
when the edict reached Huángjímén,
the completion of the ceremony was reported,
and the imperial carriage (jià) returned.
Ceremony for Receiving Imperial Edicts and Pardons
Established during the Hóngwǔ period.
Whenever an envoy was dispatched to open and read an imperial edict or pardon,
local officials would prepare a dragon pavilion (lóngtíng), ceremonial guards (yízhàng), drums, and music,
and go out of the city to welcome it.
The envoy would dismount,
present the imperial edict (zhàoshū) and place it in the dragon pavilion (lóngtíng),
facing south,
and local officials in court robes (cháofú) would perform five bows (wǔbài lǐ).
All officials and the drums and music would lead the way,
the envoy would mount his horse and follow behind the dragon pavilion (lóngtíng),
to the gate of the public office (gōngjiē mén).
All officials would enter first,
civil and military officials standing in eastern and western rows,
awaiting the arrival of the dragon pavilion (lóngtíng),
then lining up and performing four bows (sìbài).
The envoy would present the edict (zhào) to the official responsible for unfolding and reading it (zhǎndú guān),
who would kneel and receive it,
and proceed to the reading table (kāidú'àn).
After proclaiming it,
the edict (zhào) would be presented to the imperial envoy (cháoshǐ),
and again placed in the dragon pavilion (lóngtíng).
All officials would perform four bows (sìbài),
perform dancing and shouting "Long live!" (wǔdǎo shānhū),
and then perform four more bows (sìbài).
The head of the ranks (bānshǒu) would proceed to the front of the dragon pavilion (lóngtíng),
kneel and ask for the Emperor's (huánggōng) well-being and ten thousand blessings (wànfú),
and the envoy would bow and reply:
"His Sacred Majesty (shènggōng) is blessed with ten thousand blessings (wànfú)."
All officials would withdraw,
change their clothes, meet the envoy,
and perform two bows (liǎngbài lǐ) together.
Then, with drums and music, the edict (zhào) would be escorted to the official pavilion (guāntíng).
If there were any visiting officials present,
the ceremony would first be performed by the local defense official (shǒuchén).
Ceremony for Presenting Books
Among ceremonies for presenting books, the Veritable Records (Shílù) were the most important.
The Emperor would wear a formal robe (gǔnmiǎn),
and all officials in court robes (cháofú)
would present memorials (biǎo) offering congratulations.
For other compiled and completed books,
they would be presented with memorials (biǎo).
For re-engraved books and the Imperial Genealogy (Yùdié),
they would simply be carried in.
This elaborately details the ceremony for presenting the Veritable Records (Shílù),
and others can be inferred from it.
During the Jiànwén reign,
the Veritable Records of Tàizǔ were completed,
but the ceremony for their presentation is unknown.
In the first year of Yǒnglè,
the revised Veritable Records of Tàizǔ were completed.
A censer table was placed in the center of the Dān Bì (vermilion steps) in Fèngtīan Diàn.
A memorial table was placed to the east of the Dān Bì.
A precious sedan chair was set up at Fèngtīan Mén.
Halberd bearers, imperial regalia, and grand music were arranged as per custom.
History officials placed the Veritable Records in the sedan chair.
The Emperor ascended the hall as in a grand court ceremony.
All officials stood to the left and right of the Dān Chí (vermilion steps leading to the throne).
The Hónglú officials led the precious sedan chair to the Dān Bì.
History officials placed the Veritable Records on the table,
then returned to their ranks.
The Hónglú officials announced the presentation of the Veritable Records.
The rank order officials carried the Veritable Records table,
entering in sequence through the central door of the hall,
with the head of the ranks entering through the left door.
The Emperor rose.
The rank order officials placed the Veritable Records table in the center of the hall.
The head of the ranks knelt before the table.
The usher announced for all history officials to kneel.
The rank order officials and inner palace officials carried the Veritable Records table into the Jǐnshēn Diàn,
placing it in the center.
The Emperor resumed his seat.
The usher announced "prostrate."
The head of the ranks prostrated,
then rose.
They returned to their positions.
The usher announced "four bows."
The usher announced the presentation of the memorial.
The rank order officials carried the memorial table,
entering through the left door,
and placing it in the center of the hall.
The usher announced the reading of the memorial.
The usher announced for all officials to kneel.
After the reading,
they prostrated,
rose,
and bowed four times.
The officials who presented the Veritable Records withdrew to the east ranks.
All officials returned to their ranks.
The Hónglú officials announced congratulations.
All officials bowed four times and rose.
The usher announced "there is an imperial decree."
The history officials returned to their ranks.
The usher announced "kneel."
The imperial decree was read, stating:
"The merits and virtues of Tàizǔ Gāohuángdì and Gāohuánghòu shine brilliantly,
and the compilation is detailed and accurate.
Our heart rejoices,
and We share this with you, Our ministers."
After the decree was read,
they prostrated and rose,
performed three ritual dances,
then bowed four times.
The ceremony concluded.
In the fifth year of Wànlì,
the Veritable Records of Shìzǔ were completed,
and the presentation ceremony was further established.
A precious sedan chair, an incense pavilion, and a memorial pavilion were set up in front of the History Academy.
The Emperor, in his ceremonial robe and crown, was at the Zhōngjí Diàn.
All officials attended in court attire.
The supervisors, chief compilers, and compilers,
in court attire, arrived in front of the academy.
The supervisor official held the memorial and placed it in the memorial pavilion.
The compiler official held the Veritable Records and placed them in the precious sedan chair.
The Hónglú officials led the procession.
Using drums, music, and parasols,
they descended the steps of Huìjí Mén,
reached the south of the bridge,
and proceeded along the central path.
The supervisor and chief compiler officials followed behind the memorial pavilion,
proceeding over the two bridges to Huángjí Mén.
The Veritable Records sedan chair entered through the central gate.
The memorial pavilion entered through the left gate,
arriving before the table on the Dān Chí.
The supervisor official held the memorial and placed it on the table.
The compiler official held the Veritable Records and placed them on the table.
Both stood attendant to the east of the stone Dān Chí.
After the officials in the inner hall performed the rituals,
the Emperor emerged and ascended to the Huángjí Diàn.
The supervisor and chief compiler officials entered.
The presentation of the Veritable Records and the memorial were both as per the Yǒnglè ceremony.
The next day,
the officials of the Directorate of Ceremonial sent the Veritable Records down from the inner hall,
again placing them in the precious sedan chair,
using parasols,
and together with the supervisor and chief compiler officials, sent them to the Huángshǐ Chéng for respectful storage.
Ceremony for Presenting Memorials and Edicts
According to the system established in the early Míng dynasty,
whenever a princely mansion observed a Sànt Jié (Emperor's birthday) or the Winter Solstice or New Year's Day,
arrangements would be completed in advance.
The prince, in his ceremonial crown and robe, would take his place and bow four times,
then proceed to the censer table and kneel.
After presenting the memorial,
he would return to his place,
bow four times,
perform three ritual dances,
shout "Long Live the Emperor,"
and bow four more times.
All officials, in court attire, followed in their ranks to perform the rites.
The ceremony for presenting an edict to the Empress was similar,
except there were no ritual dances or shouts of "Long Live."
When presenting an edict to the Crown Prince,
the prince wore a píbìan (leather cap) and
performed eight bows.
All officials, in court attire, followed in their ranks to perform the rites.
For all congratulatory memorials and edicts presented,
if an imperial son was enfeoffed as a prince,
he would refer to himself before the Emperor as
"Your Majesty's [ordinal number] son, Prince [name]."
He would refer to the Emperor as
"Father Emperor, Your Imperial Majesty,"
and to the Empress as
"Mother Empress, Your Royal Highness."
If he was a grandson,
he would refer to himself as
"Your Majesty's [ordinal number] grandson, Prince [name]."
He would refer to the Emperor as
"Grandfather Emperor, Your Imperial Majesty,"
and to the Empress as
"Grandmother Empress, Your Royal Highness."
If he was a younger brother,
he would refer to himself as
"Your Majesty's [ordinal number] younger brother, enfeoffed as [title]."
He would refer to the Emperor as
"Elder Brother Emperor, Your Imperial Majesty,"
and to the Empress as
"Respected Sister-in-law Empress, Your Royal Highness."
A nephew would refer to himself as
"Your Majesty's [ordinal number] nephew, enfeoffed as [title]."
He would refer to the Emperor as
"Paternal Uncle Emperor, Your Imperial Majesty,"
or "Maternal Uncle Emperor, Your Imperial Majesty,"
and to the Empress as
"Paternal Aunt Empress, Your Royal Highness,"
or "Maternal Aunt Empress, Your Royal Highness."
If he was of a senior relation,
he would refer to himself as
"Your Majesty's minister, enfeoffed as [title]."
He would refer to the Emperor as
"Emperor, Your Imperial Majesty,"
and to the Empress as
"Empress, Your Royal Highness."
If he was a grand-nephew or younger,
he would refer to himself as
"Grand-nephew, great-grand-nephew, great-great-grand-nephew, enfeoffed as [title]."
All would refer to the Emperor and Empress as
"Great-uncle Emperor, Your Imperial Majesty," or "Grand-uncle Emperor, Your Imperial Majesty,"
and "Great-aunt Empress, Your Royal Highness," or "Grand-aunt Empress, Your Royal Highness."
It was not until the Shìzōng reign
that all princely mansions were ordered to
use the imperial title in their memorials and edicts,
and not to use familial courtesy.
For all congratulatory memorials and edicts presented by officials outside the capital,
on the day before,
colorful decorations would be hung in their public offices and on the streets.
Civil and military officials would all cleanse themselves and fast,
lodging in their respective offices.
In the early morning,
a dragon pavilion would be set up in the courtyard.
Ceremonial guards, drums, and music would be arranged on the outdoor platform.
A memorial table would be set up in front of the dragon pavilion,
and a censer table in front of the memorial table.
The position for the official presenting the memorial would be to the east of the dragon pavilion.
When the first drum signal was given,
all officials would don their full attire.
At the second signal,
the head of the ranks, in full attire, would proceed to the censer table,
cleanse and use the seal,
place the memorial on the table,
and withdraw to stand behind the screen.
At the third signal,
all officials would enter their ranks and bow four times.
The head of the ranks would proceed to the censer table.
The usher announced "kneel."
All officials knelt.
The attendant reverently knelt and handed the memorial to the head of the ranks.
The head of the ranks reverently knelt and handed it to the official presenting the memorial.
The official presenting the memorial reverently knelt and received it,
placing it in the dragon pavilion.
The head of the ranks returned to his position.
All officials bowed four times,
performed three ritual dances,
shouted "Long Live the Emperor,"
and bowed four times.
Golden drums, ceremonial guards, drums, and music, with all officials as the vanguard,
preceded the official presenting the memorial, who was behind the dragon pavilion to the east.
Upon reaching the outskirts,
the dragon pavilion would be placed facing south.
The ceremonial guards, drums, and music would be arrayed as before.
Civil and military officials would stand attendant.
The head of the ranks would take the memorial and hand it to the official presenting the memorial.
The official presenting the memorial would receive the memorial while mounted,
and immediately depart.
All officials would withdraw.
The
Rites Record says:
"When the ceremony of district drinking is abandoned,
the lawsuits of disputes will multiply."
Therefore, among the rites recorded in the Yí Lǐ,
only the district drinking ceremony reached the common people.
From Zhōu to Míng,
alterations and additions varied through generations,
but this rite was never abandoned.
In the fifth year of Hóngwǔ, an imperial edict commanded the Ministry of Rites to deliberate and establish the ceremony of district drinking,
ordering officials and school instructors to lead the elderly scholar-officials
to perform it in schools,
and it was also performed in local communities among the people.
In the sixteenth year, an imperial edict circulated the illustrated regulations for the district drinking ceremony throughout the realm,
to be performed annually on the fifteenth day of the first lunar month and the first day of the tenth lunar month
in the Confucian schools.
The ceremony
was presided over by the chief administrator of the prefecture, department, or county.
One retired official from the district known for his virtue served as the honored guest (bīn),
a person of advanced age and virtue was chosen as the secondary guest (juàn bīn),
the next in rank was the associate guest (jiè),
then the three guests (sān bīn),
and finally the multitude of guests (zhòng bīn).
The educational officer served as the Master of Ceremonies (sī zhèng).
The announcer of rites (zàn lǐ), the usher (zàn yǐn), and the reader of regulations (dú lǜ),
were all to be skilled individuals.
Prior to the event,
the guest's seat was placed between the two pillars on the north side of the hall,
slightly to the west,
facing south;
the host's seat was on the eastern steps (zuò jiē),
facing west;
the associate guest's seat was on the western steps,
facing east;
the secondary guest's seat was to the east of the honored guest,
facing south;
the three guests' seats were to the west of the honored guest,
facing south.
All were separate seats, not connected.
For the multitude of guests aged sixty and above,
seats were placed in the western corridor (xī xù),
facing east, with the most senior to the north.
If there were many guests, seats were also set on the western steps,
facing north, with the most senior to the east;
the seats for subordinate officials were in the eastern corridor (dōng xù),
facing west, with the most senior to the north.
For the multitude of guests aged fifty and below,
positions were set below the hall, to the west of the western steps,
aligned with the corridor,
facing east, with the most senior to the north.
If there were many guests, positions were also set to the south of the western steps,
facing north, with the most senior to the east.
The Master of Ceremonies (sī zhèng) and the reader of regulations (dú lǜ)
were positioned below the hall, to the south of the eastern steps,
facing north, with the most senior to the west.
The host's aide (zhǔ zhī zàn zhě) was positioned to the east of the eastern steps,
facing west, with the most senior to the north.
The host and subordinate officials gathered in the eastern corridor,
the honored guest, associate guest, and multitude of guests gathered outside the school gate (xiáng mén),
and the secondary guest also gathered outside the gate.
Wine vessels (jiǔ zūn) were placed in the southeastern corner of the hall,
covered with ladles and cloths (sháo mì),
using kudzu cloth;
the cup-washing basin (jué xǐ) was below the eastern steps to the southeast;
a basket (fěi) was to the west of the cup-washing basin,
filled with cups (jué zhì);
the hand-washing basin (guàn xǐ) was to the east of the cup-washing basin.
Tables were set before the seats both above and below the hall,
with plates of food (dòu) arranged on them.
Those aged sixty received three plates,
seventy received four plates,
eighty received five plates,
ninety received six plates,
and those below the hall received two plates.
The host's plates were the same number as the honored guest's,
all filled with pickled vegetables and minced meat (zū hǎi).
On the appointed day,
as the honored guest approached the gate,
an attendant reported, saying:
"The honored guest has arrived."
The host, leading his subordinates, went out to welcome him outside the gate,
the host facing west,
the honored guest and those below him all facing east.
After three bows and three deferrals,
they ascended the hall,
bowed twice to each other,
and took their seats.
An attendant reported the arrival of the secondary guest (juàn),
who was welcomed and seated according to the previous ritual.
The announcer of rites (zàn lǐ) announced, "The Master of Ceremonies (sī zhèng) raises the cup (yáng zhì)."
The Master of Ceremonies proceeded to the hand-washing basin (guàn xǐ) position,
then to the cup-washing basin (jué xǐ) position,
took a cup (zhì) from the basket (fěi),
and washed the cup.
He ascended from the western steps,
went to the wine vessel (zūn suǒ) to pour wine,
then advanced between the two pillars,
standing facing north.
All those seated rose.
The Master of Ceremonies bowed,
and the secondary guest and those below him all returned the bow.
The Master of Ceremonies then raised the cup (jǔ zhì),
and spoke, saying:
"Humbly considering the imperial court,
which follows ancient statutes.
It values and promotes the ritual teachings,
and holds the district drinking ceremony,
not for mere eating and drinking.
All of us, young and old,
should mutually encourage each other.
As ministers, exhaust loyalty;
as sons, fulfill filial piety;
let there be order between elders and youngsters;
brothers be friendly and respectful.
Internally, harmonize clans;
externally, live peacefully with neighbors;
let nothing be abandoned or neglected,
so as not to disgrace one's parents."
When he finished speaking,
the announcer of rites announced, "The Master of Ceremonies drinks the wine."
After drinking,
the bow and return were as before.
The Master of Ceremonies returned to his position,
and the secondary guest and those below him all sat.
The announcer of rites announced, "Read the regulations."
Attendants brought the regulation table to the center of the hall.
The reader of regulations went to the table,
stood facing north and read,
all as in the raising of the cup ceremony.
All those who had committed transgressions came to the main seats to stand and listen,
and returned to their positions after the reading.
The announcer of rites announced, "Serve the food."
Attendants brought the food tables to the honored guest,
then to the secondary guest,
then to the associate guest,
then to the host,
and then to the three guests and all others in sequence.
The announcer of rites announced, "Present wine to the honored guest."
The host descended to the hand-washing and cup-washing positions,
washed the cup and poured wine,
went before the honored guest,
and placed it on the mat.
He withdrew slightly,
bowed twice,
and the honored guest returned the bow.
He then went before the secondary guest,
and did likewise.
The host withdrew and returned to his position.
The announcer of rites announced, "The honored guest returns the wine."
The honored guest rose,
the secondary guest followed him,
and they went to the hand-washing and cup-washing positions as prescribed.
They went before the host,
and placed the cup.
The honored guest, secondary guest, and host all bowed twice,
and each returned to his seat.
Attendants then poured wine for the associate guest, the three guests, and the multitude of guests in sequence.
The announcer of rites announced, "Drink wine,"
either three rounds
or five rounds.
After three kinds of soup were served.
The announcer of rites announced, "Clear the food."
All those seated rose.
The secondary guest, host, and subordinate officials stood on the east,
the honored guest, associate guest, three guests, and multitude of guests stood on the west,
all bowed twice.
The announcer of rites announced, "Escort the honored guest."
They descended the hall in sequence,
separating to go east and west,
still bowing three times before exiting the school gate and withdrawing.
The district drinking ceremony in the villages was largely similar.
In the twenty-second year,
it was ordered that all offenders should be seated in the outer rows,
with those of similar transgressions forming a section,
not permitted to mix among the good and virtuous,
which was established as a regulation.
Thirdly are guest rites (bīn lǐ),
for receiving rulers and envoys from tributary states (fān guó).
During the Zhènghé era of Sòng,
the Five Rites were elaborated and fixed.
Taking from the Zhōu Guān's Account of Ceremonial Officers (Sī Yí) who managed the nine ranks of guests and the ushers,
and the imperial edict for kings to face south when receiving feudal lords (zhū hóu) for court audiences,
the court audience rituals were therefore classified as guest rites.
According to ancient times, feudal lords
each ruled their own states,
cared for their people as children,
and it was appropriate to treat them with guest rites,
not to equate them with later generations of subordinate officials.
Therefore, this was changed to follow the old practice,
and the rites for interactions between all officials and common people were appended to it.
Tribute Rites for Tributary Kings
When tributary kings (fān wáng) came to court,
the rites for welcoming, honoring, feasting, and entertaining them
were most detailed in the Táng system.
In the Sòng period,
tributary states all sent envoys to present tribute,
and only the envoys were received.
In the second year of Hóngwǔ of the Míng dynasty, the regulations were established.
Whenever a vassal king (Fānwáng) arrived at Lóngjiāngyì,
two officials, a Shìyí and a Tōngzàn, were dispatched to accompany them.
The custodian would set up the Fānwáng's seat in the northwest of the hall,
facing east.
The Zhīfǔ of Yìngtiānfǔ would go out to greet them,
and set up a seat in the southeast of the hall,
facing west.
They would meet as guest and host.
After the banquet,
the Zhīfǔ would return,
and the Fānwáng would see him off outside the gate.
The next day,
the accompanying officials would escort the Fānwáng into the Huìtóngguǎn,
and the Lǐbù Shàngshū would immediately host a banquet there to entertain them.
When the Shàngshū arrived,
the Fānwáng would meet him dressed in their national attire.
The banquet, reception, and send-off were all as at Lóngjiāngyì.
When the wine was served,
music was played.
The next day,
the Zhōngshūshěng would report to the throne,
and an official would be appointed to visit the residence
and entertain them as before.
The Shìyísī would instruct the Fānwáng and their entourage to wear their full attire,
practice the ceremonies for three days at Tiānjièsì,
and then choose a day for the imperial audience.
The Fānwáng and their entourage would be stationed outside Wǔmén.
The Fānwáng's position for bowing would be in the middle of the Dānchí,
slightly to the west.
The entourage would be behind them.
Tables for tribute items (Fāngwù) would be set up on the east and west sides of the Dānchí.
There would be two Zhībān,
located to the north of the Fānwáng's bowing position.
Two Fānwáng Shèrén, who would guide the Fānwáng,
would be located to the north of the Fānwáng.
Two Fānwáng Cóngguān Shèrén, who would guide the Fānwáng's entourage,
would be located to the north of the Fānwáng's entourage,
all facing each other from east to west.
When the drums sounded "sān yán,"
all officials would enter to attend.
The attendants would carry the Fāngwù tables.
The Fānwáng would follow the tables, entering through the west gate,
to the west of the Dānchí in front of the palace,
and stand there awaiting.
The emperor, wearing a Tōngtiān Guān and Jiàngshā Páo, would ascend the throne.
The Fānwáng and their entourage would each take their bowing positions,
placing the Fāngwù tables in front of their bowing positions.
After the Zàn had announced the four bows,
the Yǐnbān would lead the Fānwáng to ascend the hall.
The Xuānfāngwùguān, with the Fāngwù certificate, would ascend via the west steps,
enter the west gate of the hall,
and be led by the Nèizàn to before the emperor.
The Zàn would announce the bow.
The Fānwáng would bow twice,
kneel,
and offer congratulations and a speech.
The Xuānfāngwùguān would read the certificate.
After the Chéngzhìguān had read the imperial decree,
the Fānwáng would prostrate themselves,
rise,
bow twice again,
exit through the west gate of the hall,
and return to their position.
The Zàn would announce the bow.
The Fānwáng and their entourage would all make four bows.
When the ceremony was complete,
the emperor would rise,
and the Fānwáng and those below would exit.
The starting and stopping of music would be as usual.
When meeting the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) in the main hall of the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng),
bowing positions would be set up outside the hall.
The Huáng Tàizǐ, wearing Píbànfú, would ascend the seat.
The Fānwáng would bow twice.
The Huáng Tàizǐ would stand to receive.
The Fānwáng would kneel to offer congratulations,
and after the speech,
return to their position and bow twice.
The Huáng Tàizǐ would return the bow.
When the Fānwáng exited,
their entourage would perform the four-bow ceremony.
When meeting a Prince (Qīnwáng),
they would face each other from east to west and bow twice.
The Prince would return the bow.
They would all take their seats,
with the Prince's seat slightly to the north.
After the ceremony,
they would salute and exit.
When meeting the Chancellor (Chéngxiàng), the Three Dukes (Sāngōng), the Grand Commander (Dà Dūdū), or the Censor-in-chief (Yùshǐ Dàfū), the rites were all equal.
When the Fānwáng requested leave,
the ceremony was as for the imperial audience,
but without the imperial decree being read out.
The Zhōngshūshěng, with officials from the Lǐbù, would escort them to Lóngjiāngyì,
and the banquet would be as at the beginning.
In the fourth month of the twenty-seventh year,
as the old rites were considered cumbersome,
an order was issued to revise them.
Whenever a vassal state came for an imperial audience,
officials from the Lǐbù would first be sent to entertain them at the Huìtóngguǎn.
The next day,
each would wear their national attire;
if they had been granted court attire before, they would wear court attire.
They would have an imperial audience at Fèngtiāndiàn.
After performing the eight-bow ceremony,
they would proceed to Wénhuádiàn to pay respects to the Huáng Tàizǐ,
performing the four-bow ceremony.
When meeting a Qīnwáng,
it was also similar;
the Prince would stand to receive,
and then return two bows.
The entourage would perform the rites following the Fānwáng.
Whenever there was a banquet,
the Fānwáng would sit below the Marquises (Hóu) and Earls (Bó).
Whenever a vassal state sent envoys (shǐzhě) for tribute,
upon arrival at the驿 (Yì),
a Tóngzhī from Yìngtiānfǔ would be dispatched to receive them with courtesy.
The next day, upon arrival at the Huìtóngguǎn,
the Zhōngshūshěng would report to the throne,
and a Lǐbù Shìláng would be ordered to receive them at the residence according to the rites.
After the banquet,
they would practice the ceremonies for three days,
and then choose a day for the imperial audience.
The display of ceremonial guards and the presentation of memorials
were all as prescribed.
The Chéngzhìguān would go before the envoy
and announce, "There is an imperial decree!"
The envoy would kneel,
and the decree would be read, saying:
"The Emperor asks, when the envoy arrived,
was your King well?"
After the envoy replied,
they would prostrate themselves,
rise,
and bow twice.
The Chéngzhìguān would announce, "There is a further decree!"
The envoy would kneel.
The decree would be read, saying:
"The Emperor further asks,
the envoy has traveled far and toiled."
The envoy would prostrate themselves,
rise,
and bow twice.
After the Chéngzhìguān had reported back,
the envoy would perform four bows again.
When the ceremony was complete,
the emperor would rise,
and the music would start and stop as prescribed.
When meeting the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng), they would bow four times.
After presenting the Fāngwù,
they would bow four times again.
When visiting the Chéngxiàng, Dà Dūdū, or Yùshǐ Dàfū,
they would bow twice.
After presenting a letter,
they would bow twice again.
When meeting the Lángzhōng of the Left Department (Zuǒ Sī Lángzhōng) and others, the rites were all equal.
For all imperial banquets,
the imperial seat is arranged in the Jǐnshēn Diàn.
The seat for the Heir Apparent (Huáng Tàizǐ) is set to the east of the imperial seat,
and the seats for the various princes (Zhū Wáng) below the Heir Apparent,
facing west.
Seats for the vassal kings (Fān Wáng) are set in the first row to the west of the hall,
facing east.
Seats for civil and military officials are set in the second and third rows,
facing east and west.
There are nine rounds of wine,
five servings of food,
and grand music (Dà Yuè) and chamber music (Xì Yuè) are played alternately,
with dance performances presented.
Attendant officials from vassal states sit under the west corridor (Wǔ),
with the same number of wine rounds and food items,
but no music is played.
When the Eastern Palace (Dōng Gōng) hosts a banquet for vassal kings,
the Heir Apparent’s seat is set in the center of the hall,
with seats for the various princes beside it,
facing east and west.
The vassal kings' seats are set in the western part,
below the various princes,
facing east.
The Three Mentors (Sān Shī), guests (Bīn Kè), and counselors (Yù Dé) are positioned in the second row in the hall,
facing east and west.
Attendant officials of the vassal kings and officials of the Eastern Palace are positioned in the west corridor,
facing east and ascending north.
The Hèshēng Láng arrange the music,
and the Guānglù Sì provide the wine and dishes,
all according to the protocol of the Jǐnshēn Diàn.
Alternatively, if a grand councilor (Zǎixiàng) requests an imperial decree to host a banquet to reward and comfort,
seats are arranged in the rear hall of the Zhōngshū Shěng,
with guests facing west and the host facing east.
Seats for the attendant officials of the vassal kings and officials of the Left and Right Bureaus (Zuǒ Yòu Sī) are set in the Left Bureau (Zuǒ Sī).
The Jiàofāng Sì arrange music in the hall and by the south pillars of the Left Bureau.
When the vassal king arrives outside the provincial gate (Shěng Mén),
provincial officials welcome him in,
and his attendant officials follow behind.
They ascend the steps and take their seats.
There are seven rounds of wine,
five types of food,
music is played,
and various performances are presented.
After the banquet,
provincial officials escort them to the gate.
Banquets held by the Dūdū Fǔ and Yùshǐ Tái are similar.
For banquets for foreign envoys (Fān Shǐ),
the Lǐbù, by imperial decree, hosts the banquet at the Huìtóng Guǎn.
The馆人 (Guǎnrén) arrange the seating and imperial wine table,
and the Jiàofāng Sì arrange music and dances.
Lǐbù officials arrange the dragon pavilion (Lóng Tíng) outside the Wǔ Mén.
Guānglù Sì officials request an imperial decree to fetch the imperial wine,
place it in the dragon pavilion,
and are led by an honor guard (Yízhàng) with drums and music.
Upon arrival at the馆 (Guǎn),
the foreign envoys come out to greet them outside the gate.
Attendants carry the wine through the central path,
placing it on the table.
The official bearing the imperial decree stands to the east of the table,
announces "there is an imperial decree" (yǒu zhì),
and the envoy kneels facing the palace.
After listening to the proclamation,
the aide (zàn) leads them in two bows.
The official bearing the imperial decree pours wine and hands it to the envoy,
who kneels facing north and drinks it. After finishing,
he bows twice again.
They then take their respective seats.
There are seven rounds of wine,
five types of soup (tāng),
and music and performances are presented as per protocol.
After the banquet,
the official bearing the imperial decree exits,
and the envoy escorts him to the gate.
When the Heir Apparent hosts an imperial banquet,
palace officials (gōngguān) are sent to treat them with courtesy.
Provincial (shěng), prefectural (fǔ), and Censorate (tái) offices also host banquets,
with five rounds of wine,
five types of food,
and music,
but no performances are presented.
Protocol for sending envoys to vassal states (Fān Guó)
The practice of sending envoys, bestowing seals and sashes (xǐshòu), and inquiring about well-being, offering congratulations, or expressing condolences,
began in the Hàn dynasty.
Envoys sent by the Táng dynasty to foreign countries
were called "envoys entering vassal lands" (Rù Fān Shǐ), and by the Sòng dynasty "state trust envoys" (Guó Xìn Shǐ).
After Míng Zǔ established control over the realm,
he dispatched envoys bearing imperial edicts (zhàoshū) to instruct various countries,
or to present incense and silk (xiāngbì) to sacrifice to their country's mountains and rivers.
His intention to pacify and soothe was very strong,
and it did not harm the dignity of the state (guótǐ),
which was considered more effective than previous dynasties.
Whenever an envoy is dispatched,
officials of the Hànlín Yuàn draft the edict.
At the appointed time,
arrangements are made according to standard protocol.
All officials attend,
