and the Emperor takes his seat in the Fèngtiān Diàn.
Lǐbù officials hold the imperial edict,
and the Shàngbǎo Sì requests the use of the imperial seal,
which is wrapped in a yellow gold-embroidered cloth (xiāojīn fú), placed on a tray,
and set on the table.
The envoy goes to the bowing position and performs four bows,
with music starting and stopping as per protocol.
The official bearing the imperial decree (chéngzhì guān) goes to the imperial steps (dānbì) and announces "there is an imperial decree,"
and the envoy kneels.
The decree is proclaimed, saying:
"The Emperor commands this envoy, [name], to proclaim this edict to [country's name].
You shall respectfully obey Our command."
After the proclamation,
the envoy prostrates,
rises,
and bows four times.
Lǐbù officials bear the edict down from the central steps (zhōngbì),
and present it to the envoy.
The envoy carries it out the Wǔ Mén,
and places it inside the dragon pavilion.
The imperial procession departs,
and all officials exit.
When the envoy enters the territory of a vassal state,
he first sends someone to report to the king,
who dispatches an envoy to meet them from afar.
In advance, tents are erected and decorations are hung with colorful silks outside the national gate at the public guest house,
a dragon pavilion and incense table are arranged,
and gongs, drums, honor guards, and grand music are prepared.
Colorful silks are also hung in the streets and alleys within the city,
a Quyếtíng is set up above the king's palace hall,
and an incense table in front of it.
The position for the official bearing the imperial edict (pěngzhào guān) is set to the northeast of the palace steps,
followed by the official proclaiming the edict (xuānzhào guān) and the official unfolding the edict (zhǎnzhào guān) to the south,
all facing west.
When the imperial envoy arrives,
he is welcomed into the guest house.
The king, along with his national officials and elders, comes out to greet him outside the national gate,
performing five bows.
The honor guard with drums and music leads the dragon pavilion in,
with the envoy following.
Upon reaching the palace hall,
the dragon pavilion is placed in the center.
The envoy stands to the east of the incense table,
and the vassal king positions himself in the center of the palace courtyard facing north,
with his officials following.
The envoy stands facing south,
announces "there is an imperial decree,"
and the vassal king and all below him perform four bows.
The vassal king ascends from the west steps,
goes before the incense table, and kneels.
He offers incense three times,
prostrates,
rises,
and all officials do the same.
The vassal king returns to his position.
The envoy goes before the dragon pavilion,
takes the imperial edict, and hands it to the official bearing the imperial edict.
The official bearing the imperial edict carries it to the reading table (kāidú àn),
and hands it to the official proclaiming the edict.
The official proclaiming the edict receives the edict,
and the official unfolding the edict unfolds it opposite him.
The vassal king and all below him kneel to listen.
After the proclamation,
the edict is again placed in the dragon pavilion.
The vassal king and all below him prostrate,
rise,
perform four bows,
perform three dances (sān wǔdǎo),
and then perform four bows again.
Music is played for all bows.
After the ceremony,
the envoy gives the imperial edict to the relevant department (suǒ sī) for promulgation.
The vassal king and the envoy exchange courtesies as guest and host.
When bestowing seals and sashes and gifts upon a vassal king,
the decree is proclaimed, saying:
"The Emperor commands this envoy, [name],
to present the seal and sash to the king of [country's name].
You shall respectfully obey Our command."
Upon arriving in the vassal state,
the decree is proclaimed, saying:
"The Emperor commands [envoy's name],
to carry the seal and bestow it upon your king, [name],
along with gifts."
The rest is as per protocol.
Protocol for vassal states sending envoys to present memorials
Established in the second year of Hóngwǔ.
The responsible offices would decorate the royal palace and the streets and alleys of the capital city with colorful silks,
setting up a quètíng in the exact center of the main hall.
In front of it, a table for memorials and dispatches was placed,
and further in front, an incense table.
The envoy was positioned to the east of the incense table,
and two officials holding the memorials and dispatches were to its west.
A lóngtíng was set up in the exact center of the palace courtyard to the south,
with ceremonial guards, drums, and music all prepared.
In the early morning,
the seal-keeper would place the seal table in the hall,
and after cleansing the seal,
would place both the memorials and dispatches, and the seal, on the table.
The King wore his ceremonial robes,
and all officials wore their court robes.
After proceeding to the table and applying the seal,
the memorial was wrapped in a yellow袱,
and the dispatch in a red袱,
each placed in its own box,
and then each wrapped again in a yellow袱.
The officials carrying the memorials and dispatches would place them on the table.
The master of ceremonies would lead the King to the exact center of the palace courtyard,
with all officials positioned behind him.
The prostration was announced,
and music began.
After two prostrations,
the music stopped.
The King proceeded to the incense table and knelt,
all officials also knelt,
and after three offerings of incense were completed.
The official carrying the memorial took it, knelt facing east, and presented it to the King.
The King received the memorial and presented it to the envoy.
The envoy knelt facing west to receive it,
rose,
and placed it on the table.
Standing was announced,
and the King returned to his position.
The prostration was announced,
music began,
and the King and all officials performed four prostrations.
Music stopped,
and the ceremony was complete.
The officials carrying the memorials and dispatches walked forward with the memorial,
placed it in the lóngtíng,
with gongs, drums, ceremonial guards, and music leading the procession.
The King escorted it to outside the palace gate
and then returned;
all officials in court robes escorted it to outside the national gate.
Only then did the envoy depart.
Protocol for Meetings Between Rank Officials
Regarding salutations and prostrations by officials,
established in the twentieth year of Hóngwǔ,
when gōng, hóu, and fùmǎ meet,
each performs two prostrations.
When a first-rank official meets a gōng, hóu, or fùmǎ,
the first-rank official stands on the right,
performs two prostrations,
and the gōng, hóu, or fùmǎ stands on the left,
returning the禮.
When a second-rank official meets a first-rank official,
the same applies.
Third-rank officials and below follow this pattern.
If a third-rank official meets a first-rank official,
or a fourth-rank official meets a second-rank official,
they perform two prostrations.
First and second-rank officials respond as appropriate,
and other ranks follow this pattern.
If there is a distinction of kinship and seniority,
private etiquette is followed.
An order in the thirtieth year stated that
all hundred officials distinguish seniority by their rank.
When officials of close rank perform salutations,
they stand facing each other from east and west,
with the junior to the west
and the senior to the east.
If their ranks differ by two or three grades,
the junior lowers himself,
and the senior rises.
If their ranks differ by four grades or more,
the junior prostrates himself,
and the senior receives it sitting,
and kneels to report if there is business.
When civil and military officials gather publicly,
they are seated according to their rank order.
If their qualifications and ranks are the same,
they are ordered according to their yámén's sequence.
When officials from princely establishments sit or stand with court officials,
they are positioned according to their rank,
but always after court officials.
Established in the fourteenth year of Chénghuà,
the seating order for zǒngbīng and xúnfǔ officials outside the capital:
zuǒyòu dūdū rank alongside zuǒyòu dùyùshǐ,
dūdū tóngzhī rank alongside fù dùyùshǐ,
and dūdū qiānshì rank alongside qiān dùyùshǐ,
with civil officials to the east and military officials to the west.
Those of bó rank or higher are seated to the left.
Re-established in the fifteenth year,
if a dùyùshǐ is a zǒngdū or a tídū jūnwù,
regardless of whether they are zuǒ, yòu, fù, or qiān,
they are all seated to the left.
Even if a zǒngbīngguān holds the rank of bó,
they are seated to the right.
Regarding avoidance when officials meet,
established in the thirtieth year of Hóngwǔ,
a fùmǎ encountering a gōng or hóu must take a different path.
First and second-rank officials encountering a gōng, hóu, or fùmǎ
lead their horse to the side
and wait for them to pass.
A second-rank official seeing a first-rank official
proceeds to the right to yield the way.
A third-rank official encountering a gōng, hóu, or fùmǎ
leads their horse away to avoid them,
encountering a first-rank official leads their horse to the side,
and encountering a second-rank official proceeds to the right to yield the way.
A fourth-rank official encountering an official of first rank or higher
leads their horse away to avoid them,
encountering a second-rank official leads their horse to the side,
and encountering a third-rank official proceeds to the right to yield the way.
Fifth-rank to ninth-rank officials
follow this pattern with corresponding differences.
Subsequently, this was not fully adhered to.
Even civil officials of the first rank and above
did not avoid gōng, hóu, xūnqī ministers;
and regarding mutual avoidance among themselves,
it was based on official position, not rank.
Regarding subordinate officials seeing their superiors,
established in the twentieth year of Hóngwǔ,
subordinate officials stand in order above the hall steps,
collectively perform one bow,
the superior cups their hands,
and the leading official returns the bow.
When meeting superior officials for public duties or at seasonal festivals,
they all perform two prostrations,
the chief official cups their hands,
and the leading official returns the禮.
Regarding officials on public duty,
established in the twentieth year of Hóngwǔ,
officials of all yámén, large and small,
perform a solemn bow each day during public duty.
Assistant officials bow to the chief official,
and the chief official returns the禮.
Leading officials bow to the chief official and assistant officials,
and the chief official and assistant officials cup their hands.
Protocol for Commoners Meeting
An order in the fifth year of Hóngwǔ stated that
in the countryside, seniority is determined by age.
For commoners such as scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants, for everyday meetings, and for visits and banquets during festivals,
the younger one bows first.
In seating arrangements,
the elder takes the superior position.
An order in the twelfth year stated that
when officials, both inner and outer, retire and reside in their hometowns,
they only observe distinctions of seniority within their clan and the families of their maternal grandparents and wives,
following family禮.
If there is a banquet,
a separate table is set for them,
and they are not permitted to sit below those without official positions.
When meeting with officials who also retired,
they are ordered by爵;
if their爵 are the same,
they are ordered by age.
When meeting with unrelated commoners,
they do not need to return the禮.
Commoners, however, visit them with official etiquette.
Those who insult them are punished according to the law.
Established in the twenty-sixth year,
when commoners' children, grandchildren, younger siblings, nephews, nieces, and sons-in-law meet elders,
students meet their teachers,
or servants meet the head of the household,
if they have been separated for a long time, they perform four prostrations;
if for a short time, they perform a bow.
For other relatives, regardless of seniority,
if separated for a long time, they perform two prostrations;
if for a short time, they perform a bow.
For peers, the same applies.
Collation Notes
Volume 33 of the Treatise on Rites, Part 11 (Military Rites): Imperial Expeditions,
Dispatching Generals, Májì, Receiving Surrender, Reporting Triumph and Presenting Captives,
Discussing Merits and Bestowing Rewards, Grand Review and Grand Archery, Rescuing the Sun and Beating Drums.
The fourth category is Military Rites.
Imperial Expeditions are foremost,
followed by Dispatching Generals.
When an army is dispatched,
there is the rite of Májì.
Upon return, there are the rites of Receiving Surrender, Reporting Triumph and Presenting Captives, and Discussing Merits and Bestowing Rewards.
During peacetime, there are the rites of Military Reviews and Grand Archery.
And the system of Rescuing the Sun and Beating Drums
is also appended by category.
Imperial Expeditions
In the intercalary seventh month of the first year of Hóngwǔ, an imperial edict established military rites.
Officials of the Zhōngshū Shěng, along with Confucian scholars, stated:
"In ancient times, the Son of Heaven personally led campaigns
to conform to Heaven and respond to the people,
to eliminate the wicked and remove the cruel,
and thereby bring peace to all under Heaven.
From Huángdì's practice of using weapons to conquer those who did not submit,
this was its beginning.
According to the Zhōu system,
when the Son of Heaven personally led a campaign,
he would perform a 'Lèi' (類) sacrifice to the Supreme Deity,
an 'Yí' (宜) sacrifice at the Grand Altar of Soil and Grain,
a 'Zào' (造) sacrifice at the ancestral temple,
a 'Mā' (禡) sacrifice at the place of the campaign,
and sacrifices to the mountains and rivers passed through.
When the army returned,
he would report victory and present captives at the temple and altar of soil and grain.
Later, the Northern Wèi had the system of 'Xuānlùbù' (宣露布, publishing an imperial edict).
The Táng continued the old practices,
and the Sòng also occasionally adopted them."
Thereupon, old regulations were thoroughly examined,
and the rites for imperial campaigns were established and reported.
Prior to the campaign,
a day was chosen to offer sacrifices to Heaven, Earth, the imperial ancestors, and the altars of soil and grain.
The emperor would wear a wǔbiàn (武弁) cap,
ride in a gé lù (革輅) carriage,
prepare the six armies,
provide sacrificial animals and silks,
and have music performed.
All performed the 'sānxiàn' (三獻, three offerings) rite,
the ceremony being the same as for grand sacrifices.
Also, a 'Mā' sacrifice was performed at the shrine south of the capital.
For all mountains, rivers, sacred peaks, and major waterways passed through, 'tàiláo' (太牢, grand offerings) were used;
for the next in importance, 'shàoláo' (少牢, lesser offerings);
and for others, 'tèshēng' (特牲, single animal offerings).
If the march was fast,
only wine and dried meat were used,
with one biāndòu (籩豆) vessel for each.
Prior to this,
fasting was observed for one day.
The emperor would wear a tōngtiānguān (通天冠) cap and a jiàngshāpáo (絳紗袍) robe,
inspect the sacrificial animals and clean vessels.
On the day of the sacrifice,
he would wear a wǔbiàn cap
and perform the 'yīxiàn' (一獻, single offering) rite.
Upon triumphant return,
sacrifices were offered to the ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain,
the rites being the same as for setting out.
Captives were presented at the temple and altar of soil and grain,
an imperial edict ('lùbù') was issued to all under Heaven,
and then merits were discussed and rewards distributed.
During the Yǒnglè, Xuāndé, and Zhèngtǒng reigns,
these were generally observed.
In the fourteenth year of Zhèngdé,
when the emperor personally led a campaign against Chén Háo,
the Lǐbù submitted sacrificial ritual instructions as before.
The emperor ordered that all sacrifices be performed by delegated officials.
When a memorial requested sending officials,
there was an imperial decree not to send them.
The issuance of edicts
also followed the old system.
In the eleventh month of the following year, when about to return triumphantly,
the ritual officials said:
"Chén Háo rebelled,
and Your Majesty personally led the six armies
to rectify his crimes,
which is similar to the precedent of the Xuāndé emperor's personal campaign against the commoner Hán, Gāo Xù.
However, all rites and ceremonies are impossible to verify.
We request that on the day of the army's return,
the sacred carriage enter through the Zhèngyángmén,
and officials be dispatched to offer thanks to Heaven, Earth, the temples, and altars of soil and grain.
The imperial carriage should proceed to the Fèngxiān Diàn and Jǐyán Diàn,
and after paying respects,
have an audience with the Empress Dowager.
Early the next day,
Your Majesty should ascend the Wǔmén Gate Tower,
where all officials will pay respects,
and the rite of presenting captives will be performed.
A day will be chosen to issue an imperial edict to all under Heaven."
In the twelfth month,
the emperor returned to the capital.
All officials welcomed him outside the Zhèngyángmén.
The emperor, dressed in military attire, entered on horseback.
Dispatching Generals
In the first year of Hóngwǔ,
officials of the Zhōngshū Shěng, meeting with other officials, deliberated and reported:
"When a ruler dispatches generals,
it is to punish the guilty
and eliminate harm to the people.
The Shū (Book of Documents) speaks of Dà Yǔ leading campaigns,
and the Shī (Book of Odes) praises Nán Zhòng for his swift campaigns.
The Shǐ Jì quotes a military text saying:
'When ancient rulers dispatched generals,
they knelt and pushed the axle (of the general's chariot).'
Hàn Gāo emperor appointed Hán Xìn as general,
setting up an altar and performing rites.
The Northern Qí personally bestowed the axe and 'yuè' (鉞, battle-axe).
The Táng announced it at the ancestral temple and altars of soil and grain,
and also at Tàigōng's temple.
The Sòng bestowed the banner and staff at the court hall,
then announced it at the temple and altars of soil and grain,
and also performed a 'Mā' sacrifice to Huángdì."
Now, the rite for dispatching generals is established:
The emperor, wearing a wǔbiàn cap,
presides at the Fèngtiān Diàn.
The Grand General enters and kneels on the dānchí (丹墀, red pavement),
performing four bows.
He ascends the hall from the western steps,
bows twice and kneels.
The official receiving the imperial decree announces it,
bestowing the 'jié' (節, staff of authority) and 'yuè' (battle-axe) upon the Grand General.
The Grand General receives them,
and hands them to the attendant.
He prostrates himself,
rises,
bows twice, and exits.
Descending the steps,
he returns to his position,
and performs four bows.
The imperial carriage returns to the palace,
and the Grand General exits.
Outside the Wǔmén Gate, he reviews his subordinate officers and soldiers,
erects flags and banners,
sounds gongs and drums,
straightens the ranks,
and carries the 'jié' and 'yuè'.
Music leads the procession,
and all officials send him off in order.
For the rites of sacrificing at the ancestral temple and altars of soil and grain,
the Grand General is immediately ordered to prepare sacrificial animals and silks,
and perform the 'yīxiàn' rite,
which is the same as the ceremony for officials dispatched to sacrifice at the temple and altars of soil and grain.
For the ceremony of announcing to Wǔchéng Wáng's temple,
two days prior,
the Grand General inspects the sacrificial animals.
On the day of the sacrifice,
the Grand General signs the prayer tablet at his tent,
enters and takes his place,
bowing twice.
He proceeds to the spirit tablet, offers incense, presents silks, and bows twice.
He presents the prepared wine offering,
reads the prayer,
and bows twice.
He returns to his position,
and bows twice.
He drinks the blessed wine and receives the sacrificial meat,
then bows twice again.
The 'dòu' (豆) vessels are removed,
and he gazes at the burning of the prayer tablet.
For the co-worshiping deities,
the Grand General also performs the rites.
For the accompanying sacrifices in the two side corridors,
the various generals make their respective offerings.
'Mā' sacrifice
During the period of the Emperor's personal expedition,
the Emperor, his grand general, and accompanying sacrificial officials all observed a day of fasting.
The day before,
the Emperor wore the Tōngtiānguān (通天冠)
and the Jiàngshāpáo (絳紗袍) to inspect the sacrificial animals,
proceeded to the divine kitchen,
and oversaw the cleaning of the cauldrons.
The officials in charge set up the jūn yá (軍牙) and six dàos (六纛) to the north of the temple,
with the jūn yá to the east,
the six dàos to the west,
twelve biāndòus (籩豆),
two fǔguǐs (簠簋) each,
and three xíngdēngzǔs (鉶登俎) each.
The yàn kǎn (瘞坎) was set up northwest of the divine seats,
with mats placed in front of the kǎn.
Upon them were placed five wine bowls,
five roosters,
and other offerings as usual.
On the day of the sacrifice,
the yá qí (牙旗) and six dàos were set up behind the divine seats.
The Emperor, wearing the Wǔbiàn (武弁),
entered through the left south gate.
Upon reaching the south of the temple courtyard,
he stood facing north in the exact center.
The grand general and accompanying sacrificial officials arranged themselves in civil and military ranks behind him.
They welcomed the gods,
bowed twice,
and presented the silks.
They performed the first offering ceremony,
first proceeding to the divine seats of the jūn yá,
then to the divine seats of the six dàos,
bowing twice at each.
The second and final offerings followed the same procedure.
However, during the first offering, the prayer was read.
He proceeded to the place for receiving blessings,
bowed twice, drank the blessing,
and received the sacrificial meat,
then bowed twice again.
The chief sacrificial official removed the dòu (豆),
the master of ceremonies chanted for the departure of the gods,
and they bowed twice again.
The officials in charge took the prayer texts and silks,
the chief sacrificial official took the food offerings to the burning place,
and the Tàicháng (太常) requested to observe the burning.
The officials in charge killed chickens,
dripped their blood into the wine bowls,
and sprinkled it for the gods.
When the burning was halfway,
it was announced that the ceremony was complete,
and the imperial carriage returned.
If a general was dispatched,
the three offering ceremonies would be performed at the Qídàomiàotán (旗纛廟壇).
The grand general performed the first offering,
and the other generals performed the second and final offerings.
Receiving Surrender
In the seventh month of the fourth year of Hóngwǔ (洪武),
the surrender memorial of Míng Shēng (明昇) from Shǔ Xià (蜀夏) arrived at the capital.
Tàizǔ (太祖) ordered the Zhōngshū (中書) to convene and deliberate on the ceremony for receiving surrender.
The ministries requested to follow the precedent of Sòng Tàizǔ (宋太祖) receiving the surrender of the Shǔ ruler Mèng Chǎng (孟昶),
proposing that on the day Míng Shēng was to have an audience,
the Emperor would preside at Fèngtiānmén (奉天門).
Shēng and his retinue would kneel outside Wǔmén (午門) to present their memorial requesting punishment.
The attendant minister of ceremonies would carry the memorial in,
the official proclaiming the memorial would read it aloud,
and the official conveying imperial decrees would emerge to transmit the decree.
Shēng and his group would all prostrate themselves on the ground.
The attendant secretary of ceremonies would help Shēng to rise,
and his subordinate officials would also rise,
kneeling to listen to the proclamation of the decree releasing them from their crimes.
Shēng and his group would bow five times,
and shout "Wànsuì!" (萬歲!) three times.
The official conveying imperial decrees would transmit the decree,
bestowing clothes, caps, and belts.
The attendant secretary of ceremonies would lead Shēng into the Dānchí (丹墀) to bow four times.
The attendant minister of ceremonies would transmit the imperial edict,
Shēng would kneel to listen to the imperial proclamation,
prostrate himself and bow four times,
shout "Wànsuì!" three times,
and then bow four times before departing.
The hundred officials would perform the congratulatory ceremony.
The Emperor, considering that Chǎng (昶) had solely governed the state,
and his actions were extravagant and indulgent,
but Shēng was young,
and affairs were handled by his subordinates,
waived the ceremony of kowtowing and prostrating on the ground to present a memorial requesting punishment.
He only ordered Shēng and his officials to have an audience,
and the hundred officials to offer imperial congratulations.
Reporting Victory and Presenting Captives
Whenever the Emperor personally led an expedition,
upon the army's return,
the Emperor would lead all the generals to arrange the victorious music and the captives and severed heads outside the south gate of the temple
and the north gate of the altar to the god of earth and grain.
They would offer sacrifices to the temple and the altar,
performing the three offering ceremonies,
similar to the rites of dispatching the army.
After the sacrifice,
the captives and severed heads would be handed over to the Xíngbù (刑部),
and the Xiélǜláng (協律郎) would lead the music in retreat.
The Emperor, wearing the Tōngtiānguān and Jiàngshāpáo,
would ascend the Wǔmén Tower
to issue an open proclamation to all under Heaven.
The hundred officials, wearing court attire, would listen,
the ceremony being the same as when an imperial edict or pardon was read aloud.
Ceremony for a Grand General Reporting Victory.
Beforehand,
the Dàdūdū (大都督) would report with an open proclamation.
The imperial palace eunuchs would arrange the imperial seat in the front hall of the Wǔmén Tower.
The position for the victorious music would be set up in front of the tower,
the Xiélǜláng positioned north of the victorious music,
and the Sīlè (司樂) positioned south of the Xiélǜláng.
The position for presenting captives would also be set up slightly south of the tower,
the generals and officers presenting captives positioned north of it,
and the Xíngbù Shàngshū (刑部尚書) positioned north of the generals and officers,
all facing north.
The Xíngbù Shàngshū's position for receiving captives would be set up west of the captive presentation position,
facing east.
The open proclamation table would be set up in the middle of the inner path,
facing south.
The position for receiving the open proclamation would be east of the table,
and the position for transmitting the decree would be northeast of the table,
both facing west.
The position for proclaiming the open proclamation would be south of the civil and military ranks,
facing north.
On the appointed day, in the early morning,
the victorious music, captives, and severed heads would first be arranged outside the gates of the temple and the altar to the god of earth and grain,
without playing songs.
After the sacrificial ceremony was completed,
the music would be rearranged in front of the Wǔmén Tower.
Generals and officers would lead the captives to stand outside the array of weapons,
and the hundred officials would take their standing positions.
The Emperor, in ordinary attire, would ascend the tower,
with his guards as usual.
The grand general would take his position in front of the tower,
bow four times.
The other generals would follow him,
then retreat
to their standing positions.
The victorious music would be announced.
The Xiélǜláng, holding a banner, would lead the musicians to their positions.
The Sīlè would kneel and request to play the victorious music.
The Xiélǜláng would raise the banner,
and the drums and wind instruments would begin to play,
performing the musical piece.
When the music stopped,
the proclamation of the open document would be announced.
The official conveying the decree would hand the open document to the official receiving it,
who would be led by the usher to kneel at the table to receive it,
then proceed south along the central path
to hand it to the official proclaiming the open document.
After the proclamation,
it would be given to the Zhōngshū Shěng (中書省) to be promulgated throughout the realm.
The generals and officers would lead the captives to their positions.
The Xíngbù Shàngshū would kneel and report:
"So-and-so official has presented captives from such-and-such place,
requesting them to be handed over to the relevant department."
After reporting,
he would return to his position.
Those destined for execution would stand in the west wing,
facing east,
to be handed over to the execution officials.
For those whose crimes were pardoned,
the official conveying the decree on the tower would proclaim the imperial edict,
which contained an order to release them from their bonds.
The imperial order would be conveyed below.
After their release,
the master of ceremonies would announce that the released captives should express gratitude,
all bowing four times and shouting three times.
The generals and officers would lead the released captives away.
If there were any grants to be given,
the imperial edict for the grants would be proclaimed then.
The grand general and those below him would proceed to their bowing positions,
performing the dance and mountain shouts as usual.
They would kneel slightly in front of the ranks,
offer congratulations and deliver their addresses.
The hundred officials would then bow four times again,
and after the ceremony, return to the palace.
In the sixth month of the third year of Hongwǔ,
Left Deputy General Lǐ Wénzhōng achieved a great victory in his northern campaign.
He dispatched officials to send the captured Yuán prince, Bǎidélibālā, and the imperial seal to the capital.
All officials requested to perform the captive presentation ceremony.
The Emperor disallowed it;
the details are recorded in the Imperial Annals.
He merely ordered them to wear their native attire.
After the audience,
they were granted Chinese clothing and headwear to express gratitude.
The Emperor further told the provincial ministers:
"As for the concubines of the former dynasty who had an audience with the sovereign,
the Yuán had this custom,
but there is no need to emulate it."
He also ordered them to wear their native attire,
be received by the Empress,
and be granted Chinese clothing to express gratitude.
In the eleventh month,
Grand General Xú Dá and Wénzhōng's armies returned.
The imperial carriage went out to welcome them on the riverbank.
The next day,
Xú Dá led the generals in presenting a memorial on pacifying the desert.
The Emperor presided in the Fèngtiān Hall,
attended by the Crown Prince and imperial princes.
All officials, in court attire, stood in attendance.
Xú Dá and Lǐ Wénzhōng presented the memorial and offered congratulations.
After the ceremony,
they withdrew via the west steps.
The Crown Prince and imperial princes entered to offer congratulations.
Later it was stipulated:
for all great victories,
a day would be chosen for the announcement.
On that day, no memorials were to be presented.
All officials would offer congratulations in ceremonial attire.
On the same day, officials would be dispatched to offer sacrifices and report to the suburban altars and imperial ancestral temples.
For moderate victories and below,
only the victory would be announced;
no sacrifices or celebrations would be held.
In the fourth year of Yǒnglè, it was stipulated:
for any victory,
officials from the Ministry of War would report it via an urgent dispatch.
If a great general was still in the army, officials carrying the urgent dispatch would perform the ceremony.
The next day, the reading ceremony would be held.
On the third day, the congratulatory ceremony would be held.
The rest would follow the previous rites.
When Wǔzōng returned from campaigning against Chénháo,
the Ministry of Rites presented the captive presentation ceremony protocol.
As the Emperor was indisposed at the time,
it was not carried out.
In the tenth month of the twenty-third year of Jiājìng,
the rebel Wáng Sān repeatedly led Jínáng to invade Dàtóng,
but the imperial army used a stratagem to capture them.
Officials were dispatched to give thanks at the northern and southern suburban altars, Jǐngshén Hall, and the Grand Altars of Soil and Grain.
A day was chosen to present the captives,
and all officials offered congratulations.
In the second year of Tiānqǐ,
Sìchuān presented the rebels Fán Yǒubāng and others,
and Shāndōng presented the rebels Xú Hóngrú and others.
Officials were dispatched to announce sacrifices at the suburban altars and imperial ancestral temples,
and the captives were presented from the imperial tower.
Discussing Merits and Bestowing Rewards
Whenever armies returned victorious,
the Central Secretariat would issue a document to the Grand Military Commission.
The Ministry of War would detail the merits of all generals.
The Ministry of Personnel would detail their ranks, titles, and positions.
The Ministries of Revenue and Rites would detail the reward standards.
The Central Secretariat would convene the six ministries to deliberate and determine the merits and rewards,
and then memorialize the Emperor for final decision.
One day prior,
the imperial seat and incense table would be set up in the Fèngtiān Hall.
The precious seal table and imperial edict table would be placed in the center of the hall.
The patent of appointment table would be placed north of the center of the imperial steps.
The announcement edict table would be placed north of the patent of appointment table.
The Ministers of Personnel, Revenue, and Rites would be positioned in the southeast of the hall.
The Grand Military Commissioner and Minister of War would be positioned in the southwest of the hall.
The officials to be rewarded would kneel and prostrate themselves in the center of the imperial courtyard.
Those awaiting their turn would stand in order in the southwest of the imperial courtyard.
The recipients of rewards would be positioned south of the patent of appointment table.
The attendants holding the rewards would be positioned west of the recipient officials' waiting position.
For each official, one person would carry the patent of appointment, and one person would carry the gift,
both facing north.
Other arrangements would follow the court ceremony.
On that day,
after three drum rolls,
the attending officials would take their places.
The Emperor, in imperial robes and crown, would ascend the throne.
The Crown Prince and various princes, in imperial robes and crowns,
would enter from the east gate of the hall to stand in attendance.
The officials to be rewarded would enter and take their prostration positions,
performing four bows.
The official receiving the edict would kneel to receive it,
exit through the central gate of the hall.
The Ministers of Personnel, Revenue, and Rites would exit through the west gate of the hall,
and stand east of the patent of appointment table.
The official receiving the edict, facing south, would announce "There is an imperial edict!"
All officials to be rewarded would kneel.
The edict would be proclaimed:
"We commend so-and-so for rendering service to the nation,
and it is fitting to bestow upon them noble ranks and rewards.
Now, they are appointed to such-and-such a position,
and granted such-and-such items.
Let them reverently receive Our command."
After the proclamation,
the officials to be rewarded would prostrate themselves,
rise,
and bow twice.
The bestowal of rewards would be announced.
The first official to be rewarded would proceed to the table and kneel.
The Minister of Personnel would hold the patent of appointment,
and the Minister of Revenue would hold the gift,
each presenting them to the official to be rewarded.
The official to be rewarded would hand them to the attendants on their left and right,
prostrate themselves,
rise,
and return to their position.
After the other officials had successively received their rewards,
the official receiving the edict, the Minister of Personnel, and others would all report back to the Emperor,
then withdraw to their positions.
All the rewarded officials would bow twice,
perform three ceremonial dances,
and utter "Long live!"
They would prostrate themselves,
rise,
and bow four more times.
Upon completion of the ceremony,
the Emperor would return to the palace.
All officials would exit,
and outside the Wǔmén Gate, they would place the patents of appointment and gifts in dragon pavilions.
With ceremonial guards, drums, and music, they would be escorted back to their respective residences.
The next day, they would present a memorial of thanks,
following the usual rites.
Grand Review
In the tenth month of the fourth year of Xuāndé,
the Emperor was about to review the military outside the city.
He commanded the Military Commission to array the troops.
One high-ranking civil official and one high-ranking military official from each ministry,
along with one subordinate official, were to accompany him.
During the Zhèngtǒng reign,
reviews were sometimes held in the near suburbs,
or in the Xīyuàn (Western Garden),
without fixed regulations.
In the second year of Lóngqìng,
Grand Secretary Zhāng Jūzhèng stated:
"During the time of the ancestors, there was a Grand Review ceremony.
I humbly request Your Majesty to personally oversee it."
The Ministry of War cited the precedents of Xuānzōng and Yīngzōng,
requesting its implementation.
It was ordered to be held in the eighth month of the following year.
When the time came,
the Ministry of Rites established the protocols.
One day prior,
the Emperor, in ordinary attire, would make an announcement in the inner palace,
performing four bows,
similar to the ceremony for leaving the city.
The Directorate of Palace Services would set up the imperial tent on the general's platform.
The Grand Minister Overseeing Military Affairs and the inspecting censors would supervise the generals and soldiers in preparing the drill ground in advance.
On the day itself,
early in the morning,
officials would be dispatched to the drill ground to sacrifice to the deities of the military banners.
The officers and soldiers of the three grand camps would be fully armed.
Four generals would command two thousand cavalry to escort the imperial carriage.

Civil officials, including high-ranking officials from each ministry, seal-holding officials of the supervising offices, officials from the two sections of Rites and Military, officials from the Ceremonial Department of the Ministry of Rites, officials from the four bureaus of the Ministry of War, censors for correcting ceremonies and supervising archery, and service officials from the Court of Imperial Entertainments,
and military officials, including those of military commissioner rank and above, high-ranking officials of the Jǐnyīwèi, and seal-holding and associate officials of the Southern Pacification Office,
all wearing crimson casual attire,
bearing their escort permits,
with ivory identification tablets suspended,
would first proceed to the drill ground.
On this day, court audience was exempted.
The Jǐnyīwèi would prepare the imperial honor guard.
The Emperor, in ordinary attire, would ride a palanquin out through the Cháng'ān Left Gate.
Imperial guards would lead and follow,
with gongs and drums resounding.
Exiting the Āndìng Gate,
they would arrive outside the Yuèwǔ Gate.
The Grand Minister Overseeing Military Affairs, leading senior and junior generals in military attire, would kneel to welcome them.
Entering below the general's platform,
they would stand in order facing north.
As the imperial carriage entered the Yuèwǔ Gate,
the inner central army would fire three signal cannons.
Gongs and drums would resound in all camps.
The escorting officials would stand in order outside the temporary imperial residence gate.
When the imperial carriage arrived at the gate,
the Emperor would descend from the palanquin.
Officials from the Ministry of War would lead him into the temporary imperial residence.
Gongs would sound to silence the drums,
awaiting his ascent to the seat.
The escorting officials would perform one bow,
and wine and food would be conveyed to them.
All officials would express thanks and exit,
standing in order east and west below the general's platform.
Officials from the Ministry of War would request the grand review.
Officials from the Ministry of War and the Court of Imperial Entertainments would lead the imperial carriage to ascend the platform,
firing three cannons.
After the officers and soldiers of the capital garrisons had kowtowed,
they would stand in attendance to the east and west.
The Grand Minister Overseeing Military Affairs would be arrayed north of the escorting officials,
and the various generals would be arrayed south of the escorting officials.
The Bīngbù Shàngshū (Minister of War) presented a memorial requesting that
all camps should organize their men and horses.
A horn was blown on the platform,
a yellow banner was waved,
and the Zǒngxié Róngzhèng (Grand Coordinator of Military Affairs) and all staff officers, etc., returned to their respective units.
The Bīngbù Shàngshū requested to review the formation,
and three cannons were fired.
The cavalry and infantry officers and soldiers performed the formation
according to the usual practice.
After the performance,
the horn was blown again,
the yellow banner was waved,
and all the officers and soldiers returned to their camps.
A moment later,
the Bīngbù Shàngshū requested to review the archery.
The Zǒngxié Róngzhèng and officials below him, as well as the Gōng, Hóu, Fùmǎ, Bó, Jǐnyīwèi and other officials who were to watch the archery,
all competed in archery below the platform.
Three arrows for horseback archery,
and six arrows for foot archery.
Those who hit the target were reported by drum beats,
and the Yùshǐ (Censor) and Bīngbù officials supervised and recorded.
For Bǎzǒng (Battalion Commander) and below, as well as family retainers and soldiers,
the Fǔbù Dàchén (Ministers of the Six Boards) and Yùshǐ and Bīngbù officials conducted the review in the east and west halls.
For skills such as spears, swords, and firearms,
the Zǒngxié Róngzhèng was authorized to select one company
to present for examination before the emperor.
The Bīngbù Shàngshū reported that the grand review was complete,
and a signal flag was raised below the platform.
The Zǒngxié Róngzhèng and all generals then proceeded to the platform,
standing in order facing north.
A Hónglúsì official announced the imperial decree,
and instructed them to kneel.
After the decree was read,
he instructed them to kowtow.
All officials retired first,
exited the gate,
and then the Hùcóng (attendant) officials performed the kowtow ceremony.
After the ceremony,
the imperial carriage returned to the temporary palace.
A short while later,
the Hùcóng officials hurried to stand inside the gate.
The Huángdì (Emperor) ascended his imperial carriage.
The Zhōngjūn (Central Army) fired three cannons,
all camps played military music,
and the Lúbù (imperial insignia) and cavalry escorted the carriage as it had arrived,
with gongs, drums, and grand music resounding in harmony.
The Zǒngxié Róngzhèng and those below him waited for the imperial carriage to arrive,
kowtowed, and withdrew.
The cavalry stopped outside Cháng'ān Zuǒmén (Left Gate of Enduring Peace).
The Lúbù and grand music stopped outside Wǔmén (Meridian Gate).
When the imperial carriage returned,
they proceeded to the inner palace to pay respects
as before.
Those officials who did not escort the carriage
stood in order in their ceremonial robes south of the bridge outside Chéngtiānmén (Gate of Accepting Heaven).
They respectfully sent off the carriage,
and when the carriage returned,
they greeted it as before.
The next day,
the Zǒngxié Róngzhèng and officials below him presented a memorial of thanks,
and all officials attended the class to perform the congratulatory ceremony,
as usual.
The Bīngbù reported on the strengths and weaknesses of the officers and soldiers, the number of arrows hitting the target, and their training levels.
Two days later,
the Huángdì held court at Huángjímén (Gate of Imperial Supremacy),
and issued an imperial edict to encourage the officers and soldiers.
The Zǒngxié Róngzhèng received it in a decorated sedan chair,
and the officers and soldiers welcomed and escorted it to the training ground,
where the edict was read and the ceremony performed as usual.
On this day,
rewards were given and punishments meted out with distinctions.
The next day,
the Zǒngxié Róngzhèng led his staff officers to again express gratitude.
An imperial edict was issued in accordance with the deliberations.
As the imperial carriage returned,
the music of Wǔchéng was played.
The grand review in Wànlì 9th year
followed the precedent of Lóngqìng.
Grand Archery
The ritual of grand archery
has not been practiced by later generations;
only the Sòng Shǐ (History of Song) lists it under auspicious rites.
In the Míng Jílǐ (Collected Rites of the Ming Dynasty), it is appended to military rites,
and the Huìdiǎn (Collected Statutes) also follows this.
Its system
was established in Hóngwǔ 3rd year.
For all sacrifices at the suburban altars and ancestral temples,
the grand archery ceremony was performed in advance,
and the Gōngbù (Ministry of Works) manufactured the targets (shèhóu) and other equipment.
There were seven types of archery targets (shègǔ).
The tiger target (hǔgǔ) with five colors
was used by the Tiānzǐ (Emperor).
The bear target (xiónggǔ) with five colors
was used by the Huángtàizǐ (Crown Prince).
The leopard target (bàogǔ) with five colors
was used by the Qīnwáng (Princes of the First Rank).
The leopard target (bàogǔ) with four colors
was used by civil and military officials of the first and second ranks.
The sǎn target (sǎngǔ) with three colors
was used by officials from the third to fifth ranks.
The fox target (húgǔ) with two colors
was used by officials from the sixth to ninth ranks.
The cloth target (bùgǔ) with no color
was used by the sons and brothers of civil and military officials and outstanding commoners.
During archery,
the fán (arrow stand) was placed to the right of the target.
The fán was also called róng,
seen in the Zhōulǐ (Rites of Zhou), Dàsīmǎ (Grand Minister of War), fúbùshì,
whose duty was to hold flags and wait for the successful archers to shield their bodies.
A bì and wéi (protective screens) were set up,
placed in front during archery
to align the arrows.
Five types of archery hitting devices (shèzhōng) were set up.
The leather tree hit (píshùzhōng)
was used for the emperor's grand archery.
The village hit (lǘzhōng)
was used for the emperor's feast archery.
The tiger hit (hǔzhōng)
was used for archery by the Huángtàizǐ and Qīnwáng.
The rhinoceros hit (sìzhōng)
was used by civil and military officials from the first to fifth ranks.
The deer hit (lùzhōng)
was commonly used by officials from the sixth to ninth ranks, and by sons and brothers of civil and military officials and outstanding commoners.
For the official duties,
two Sīzhèngguān (Chief Justice officials) were appointed,
responsible for examining the rank and status of the archers and the strength of their arms to determine pairs,
and recording whether they hit the target on tallies,
a duty of Bīngbù officials.
Two Sīshè (Archery Masters) were appointed,
responsible for first shooting a strong bow at the target to encourage others,
to rouse the spirits of the crowd,
a duty filled by military officials.
Two Sīshèqìguān (Archery Equipment Masters) were appointed,
responsible for distinguishing the strength of bows,
dividing them into three grades,
and assigning them based on the strength of the archer,
a duty of Gōngbù officials.
The Jǔjuézhě (Cup Bearer)
was responsible for offering mare's milk to the successful archers to drink,
a duty of Guānglùsì officials.
The Qǐngshèzhě (Archery Inviter)
was responsible for determining paired archery.
After archery,
they would again invite certain pairs to shoot,
a duty of the Shìyísī (Bureau of Ceremonial Etiquette).
The Dàihuòzhě (Arrow Gatherers) were responsible for collecting arrows and delivering them to the Sīshèqìzhě,
a service provided by servants and slaves.
Six Zhíqízhě (Flag Bearers)
were responsible for holding five-colored flags behind the róng.
If an archer hit the center,
a red flag was raised in response.
If they hit a color,
a colored flag was raised in response.
If it was too far west,
a white flag was raised.
If it was too far east,
a green flag was raised.
If it went over the target,
a yellow flag was raised.
If it fell short of the target,
a black flag was raised.
Two soldiers were responsible for this.
Two Yǐnlǐ (Ceremony Guides)
were responsible for guiding civil and military officials in their advance and retreat,
a duty of the Shèngrén (Secretaries) of the Shìyísī.
Tàizǔ also believed that the archery rites of the ancient kings had long been abandoned,
and the art of bow and arrow was exclusively practiced by military men,
while many literati did not understand it.
Therefore, he issued an edict that students of the Guóxué (National Academy) and prefectures and counties should all practice archery,
and distributed the ritual forms throughout the realm.
On the first and fifteenth day of each month, they practiced in public offices or vacant lots.
The archery rituals for official schools
roughly imitated the grand archery style but simplified its rites.
The initial archery position was thirty paces,
and was progressively increased to ninety paces from behind.
Four arrows were shot,
with two people forming a pair.
During the Yǒnglè period, there was the system of polo and willow shooting.
On the fifth day of the fifth month of the eleventh year, the emperor visited the Eastern Garden,
for polo and willow shooting,
allowing civil and military officials, envoys from the Four Barbarians, and resident elders in the capital to gather and observe.
The polo officials were divided into two teams,
and from the Huángtàisūn (Imperial Grandson) down, various princes and ministers in turn played polo and shot arrows,
and those who hit were rewarded with varying amounts of silk and cloth.
Saving the Sun and Beating Drums
In Hóngwǔ 6th year, second month, the ritual for saving a solar eclipse was established.
On that day,
the Huángdì wore ordinary clothes,
and did not sit in the main hall.
The Zhōngshūshěng (Central Secretariat) set up an incense table,
and all officials performed the ritual in court attire.
Drummers beat drums,
and only stopped when the sun returned to its full circle.
For a lunar eclipse,
the Dàdūdūfǔ (Chief Military Commission) set up an incense table,
and all officials performed the ritual in ordinary clothes,
without beating drums.
If it was raining, snowing, or cloudy, it was excused.
In the third month of the twenty-sixth year, the regulations were revised.
The Lǐbù set up an incense table on the open terrace,
facing the sun.
Golden drums were set up inside the Yímén,
and music was set up beneath the open terrace.
All officials took their positions on the open terrace to perform kowtows.
At the appointed time,
all officials entered in court attire,
the music began,
they performed four kowtows and rose,
the music stopped,
and they knelt.
The attendants held drums,
the head of the group struck the drum three times,
and all the drums sounded in unison.
After the drum sounds ceased and returned to silence,
they performed the four kowtows again.
For a lunar eclipse,
all officials in casual attire would go to the Dūdūfǔ to perform rescue ceremonies as usual.
For various offices outside the capital,
for a solar eclipse, they would go to the Bùzhèngshǐ Sī, fǔ, zhōu, and xiàn;
for a lunar eclipse, they would go to the Dūzhīhuīshǐ Sī and wèi suǒ,
as usual.
In the sixth year of Lóngqìng,
there was a great mourning.
Just as the mourning attire was completed,
a solar eclipse occurred.
All officials first mourned before the imperial spirit tablet,
then proceeded to the Lǐbù,
wearing plain white clothing and black horned belts.
They performed four kowtows facing the sun,
without drums or music.
Collation Notes
Chapter 34, Rites 12 (Inauspicious Rites 1): Imperial Mausoleums
The fifth section is Inauspicious Rites.
All matters concerning imperial mausoleums, ancestral temples, funerals, mourning periods, and the mourning regulations for scholars and commoners
are arranged by category.
The rites for visiting mausoleums and commemorating death anniversaries
are also appended.
Imperial Mausoleums
When Tài Zǔ ascended the throne,
he posthumously conferred imperial titles upon his four paternal generations.
His imperial paternal grandfather, Xī Zǔ,
was buried north of Bīnchéng in Sìzhōu, Fèngyáng Fǔ.
His posthumous temple name was Zǔlíng.
A Cí Jì Shǔ was established,
with one Fèngsì official appointed,
and two hundred ninety-three陵戶 (línghù, mausoleum households).
His imperial father, Rén Zǔ,
was buried in Tàipíng Xiāng, Fèngyáng Fǔ.
When Tài Zǔ arrived at Háo,
he once considered reburying him,
but it was not carried out.
Instead, more earth was added to build up the mound,
and twenty families, including the former residents Wāng Wén and Liú Yīng, were ordered to guard it.
In the second year of Hóngwǔ, it was given the posthumous temple name Líng,
later changed to Huánglíng.
The Huánglíng Wèi and Cí Jì Shǔ were established,
with one Fèngsì official and three Sī Chéng officials,
all of whom were hereditary from meritorious old families.
There were three thousand three hundred forty-two líinghù,
who took turns for night duty and sweeping.
There were twenty-four Lǐshēng.
In the fourth year, the Zǔlíng Miào was built.
Following the Tang and Song system of "same hall, different chambers,"
both the front hall and the sleeping hall had fifteen bays each,
with two on each side, east and west,
serving as side chambers,
as proposed by Jìn Wáng Sù.
The middle three bays were connected to form one chamber,
housing the spirit tablet of Dé Zǔ,
for joint sacrifices.
The eastern bay housed Yì Zǔ,
and the western bay housed Xī Zǔ.
In the nineteenth year, the heir apparent was ordered to Sìzhōu to repair the Zǔlíng
and bury the imperial crowns and robes of the three ancestral emperors and empresses.
In the thirty-first year,
Tài Zǔ passed away.
The Lǐbù determined that
on the day after imperial officials in the capital heard of the mourning,
they were to wear plain white clothes, black gauze caps, and black horned belts,
and proceed to the Nèifǔ to listen to the imperial will.
They would fast and lodge in their respective offices,
and at dawn and dusk, proceed to the jǐyán (imperial spirit tablet) to weep.
Three days later, they would don mourning attire,
and weep before the imperial spirit tablet at dawn and dusk,
until the burial.
The mourning period began on the day mourning attire was donned,
and ended on the twenty-seventh day.
Imperial ladies were to wear mourning attire,
remove their hair ornaments,
and enter through Xīhuámén to mourn before the imperial spirit tablet.
All princes, heirs apparent, princely consorts, commandery princesses, eunuchs, and palace women were to observe zhǎncuī (deepest mourning) for three years,
ending after twenty-seven months.
When attending court and conducting affairs,
they wore plain white clothes, black gauze caps, and black horned belts;
after court, they wore mourning attire.
All officials wore ramie-cloth round-collar shirts, ramie-cloth caps, ramie headbands, and ramie shoes.
Imperial ladies wore ramie-cloth large-sleeved long shirts,
and ramie-cloth head coverings.
Spirit articles were like the imperial equipage.
Spirit tablets were made of chestnut wood,
their system followed family rites.
Envoys distributed the imperial will throughout the realm.
For officials outside the capital,
on the day the imperial edict arrived,
they were to wear plain white clothes, black gauze caps, and black horned belts,
and perform four kowtows.
After listening to the proclamation,
they would express sorrow,
then perform four kowtows again.
Three days later, they would don mourning attire,
and set up an incense table to mourn before the imperial spirit tablet every morning,
ending after three days.
Each dispatched an official to the capital to offer sacrifices,
with sacrificial items prepared by the Lǐbù.
At Xiàolíng, a Shéngōng Jiān, Xiàolíng Wèi, and Cí Jì Shǔ were established.
Jiànwén Dì issued an edict for a three-year mourning period,
the details are in the Basic Annals.
Due to the usurpation and removal,
the system of mourning and burial was not transmitted.
