禮官請靈駕進發。
皇太子、親王以下哭送出Duānmén外，
行辭祖禮。
執事官設褥位於Tàimiào香案前。
皇太子易常服，
捧神帛，
由左門入，
至褥位跪，
置神帛於褥，
興，
正立於神帛後跪。
禮官跪於左，
奏Tàizōng Tǐtiān Hóngdào Gāomíng Guǎngyùn Shèngwǔ Shéngōng Chúnrén Zhìxiào Wén Huángdì謁辭。
皇太子俯伏，
興，
贊五拜三叩頭畢，
皇太子捧神帛興，
以授禮官。
禮官安輿中，
請靈駕進發。
皇太子仍喪服，
親王以下隨行。
梓宮由Dàmíng Zhōngmén出，
皇太子以下由左門出，
步送至Déshèng Mén外，
乘馬至陵，
在途朝夕哭奠臨。
諸王以下及百官、軍民耆老、四品以上命婦，
以序沿途設祭。
文武官不係山陵執事者悉還。
Upon reaching the mausoleum,
the officiants first arrayed the imperial coffin carriage outside the gate of the offering hall,
awaiting the arrival of the grand imperial carriage.
The ritual officials requested the spirit palanquin to descend from its carriage,
ascend the imperial coffin carriage,
and proceed to the offering hall.
The officiants respectfully carried the coffin inside.
The Huáng Tàizǐ and qīnwáng entered through the left gate.
Once the coffin was settled and respectfully placed,
the rite of settling the spirit was performed.
The Huáng Tàizǐ bowed four times,
rose,
poured libations,
and read the prayer.
He prostrated himself,
rose,
bowed four times,
and expressed lamentation.
The qīnwáng and those below them accompanied the bows,
following the usual ceremony.
An official was dispatched to offer sacrifices and make announcements to Hòutǔ and Tiānshòushān,
and the rite of temporary placement and offerings was performed,
as in the preceding ceremony.
When about to seal the xúangōng,
the Huáng Tàizǐ and those below him knelt before the coffin.
The inner attendants requested the spirit palanquin to proceed to the xúangōng,
and the officiants respectfully carried the coffin into the huángtáng.
The inner attendants presented the imperial seal and patent, placing them in front,
displayed the burial artifacts,
and performed the presentation rite.
The Huáng Tàizǐ bowed four times and rose,
poured libations,
and presented the offerings.
The officiants presented the jade and silk to the right,
the Huáng Tàizǐ received the offerings,
and handed them to the inner attendants,
who carried them into the huángtáng for placement.
He prostrated himself,
rose,
bowed four times,
expressed lamentation,
and then the xúangōng was sealed.
The banquet rite was performed,
as in the temporary placement and offerings ceremony.
An official was dispatched to offer sacrifices and thanks to Hòutǔ and Tiānshòushān.
An incense table was set up outside the xúangōng gate,
and a spirit tablet table was set up in front,
facing west.
The Huáng Tàizǐ's bowing position was set up in front,
facing north.
The inner attendants washed their hands, respectfully placed the spirit tablet on the table.
The official for inscribing the spirit tablet washed his hands and, facing west, completed the inscription.
The inner attendants respectfully placed the spirit tablet on the spirit seat,
and stored the silk box inside.
The inner attendants then formally requested the divine spirit of Tàizōng Wénhuángdì to ascend the spirit tablet.
The ceremonial master prompted four bows,
rising,
offering wine,
and reading the prayer.
Prostration,
rising,
four bows,
and expressing lamentation.
The inner attendants opened the casket and received the tablet,
then requested the spirit tablet to descend from its seat and ascend the palanquin.
Upon reaching the offering hall,
they formally requested the spirit tablet to descend from the palanquin and ascend the seat,
and performed the initial 'Yú' sacrifice.
The Huáng Tàizǐ bowed four times,
made the initial offering,
presented silk and wine,
read the prayer,
prostrated himself,
and rose.
For the secondary and final offerings,
he bowed four times,
expressed lamentation,
and gazed at the burial.
The imperial attendants carried the spirit silk box and buried it in front of the hall,
and burned the inauspicious artifacts in the wilderness.
The first 'Yú' sacrifice was on the day of the funeral,
the second 'Yú' on a "soft" day,
the third 'Yú' on a "hard" day.
Thereafter, one 'Yú' was performed every other day,
until the ninth 'Yú' was completed.
While on the journey,
the Huáng Tàizǐ performed the rites.
Upon returning to the capital,
the Huángdì performed the rites.
When the spirit tablet was about to return,
the inner attendants requested the spirit tablet to descend from its seat and ascend the palanquin,
with the honor guard and retinue as usual.
The Huáng Tàizǐ followed,
still performing morning and evening offerings.
Upon reaching the capital,
a temporary tent was first set up outside the city,
the honor guard was arrayed,
and the drum and wind instruments were prepared but not played.
All officials in mourning attire awaited outside the city.
When the spirit tablet entered the tent,
all officials arranged themselves and performed five bows and three kowtows.
When the spirit tablet moved,
all officials followed.
Upon reaching outside Wǔmén,
the Huángdì, in mourning attire, welcomed it inside Wǔmén,
expressed lamentation,
and led the spirit tablet on foot to ascend Jǐyándiàn.
The Huángdì stood on the hall,
the inner attendants requested the spirit tablet to descend from the palanquin and ascend the seat,
and the rite of settling the spirit was performed.
The Huángdì bowed four times,
rose,
poured libations,
and read the prayer.
Prostrated himself,
rose,
bowed four times,
and expressed lamentation.
The Huáng Tàizǐ and those below him accompanied the bows.
All officials performed the rites as usual outside Sīshànmén.
The next day,
all officials performed the consolation rite.
The cessation of weeping ('zúkū') was performed on the "hard" day after the 'Yú' sacrifice.
The rite was the same as the 'Yú' sacrifice,
and from then on, morning and evening offerings ceased.
The 'Fù' sacrifice was performed on the day after 'zúkū'.
Tàichángsì set up wine and food in Tàimiào,
as in the seasonal sacrifice ceremony,
with music prepared but not played.
The honor guard, umbrellas, and fans were arrayed outside Wǔmén,
the inner attendants brought the imperial sedan chair before Jǐyándiàn.
The Huángdì, in mourning attire, bowed four times,
and expressed lamentation.
He rose,
ceased lamenting,
and stood to the east of the bowing position,
facing west.
The inner attendants requested the spirit tablet to descend from its seat and ascend the sedan chair,
proceeding to Tàimiào for the 'Fù' sacrifice.
Upon reaching outside Sīshànmén,
the Huángdì changed into sacrificial attire,
ascended the imperial carriage,
followed to outside Wǔmén,
and knelt before the imperial sedan chair.
The Tàicháng Qīng formally requested the spirit tablet to descend from the sedan chair.
The Huángdì prostrated himself,
rose,
and carried the spirit tablet through the left gate,
ascending to the imperial steps.
The Master of Ceremonies announced
"Tàizōng Wénhuángdì visits the temple."
Upon reaching the front of the temple,
the inner attendants carried the spirit tablet to the mat position,
and the Huángdì performed the eight-bow rite behind it.
This was the same for every temple.
The inner attendants held the spirit tablet facing north,
the Tàicháng Qīng stood to the east of the altar,
facing west.
He announced
"Grant a seat."
The Huángdì inserted his ceremonial tablet,
respectfully placed the spirit tablet on the seat,
proceeded to the bowing position and performed the sacrificial rite,
as in the seasonal sacrifice ceremony.
The Tàicháng Qīng formally requested the spirit tablet to return to Jǐyán,
the Huángdì carried the spirit tablet out through the left gate of the temple,
and respectfully placed it on the imperial sedan chair.
The Huángdì ascended the imperial carriage and followed,
descended from the carriage at Sīshànmén,
changed into mourning attire,
and followed to before Jǐyándiàn.
The inner attendants requested the spirit tablet to descend from the sedan chair,
and ascend the seat.
The Huángdì entered through the left gate of the hall,
and after completing the rite of settling the spirit,
removed his mourning attire and returned to the palace.
The next day,
all officials in plain clothes performed the consolation rite.
For the Grand Mourning (Dàxiáng),
the spirit tablet was respectfully placed in Tàimiào,
the rites detailed in the temple regulations.
The Huángdì performed a sacrificial announcement at Jǐyándiàn.
The Huángtàihòu, Huánghòu, and those below each offered sacrifices at one altar.
The princely households dispatched officials to offer sacrifices at one altar.
The civil and military officials in the capital offered sacrifices at one altar.
As soon as the spirit tablet departed from Jǐyándiàn,
the inner attendants immediately removed the Jǐyán and curtains,
and burned them outside Sīshànmén.
For the 'Tàn' sacrifice,
a qīnwáng was dispatched to the mausoleum to perform the rites.
In the first year of Hóngxī
, Rénzōng passed away.
The Crown Prince returned from Nánjīng.
When he reached Liángxiāng
, the palace first announced the mourning
and proclaimed the imperial edict.
Civil and military officials in regular attire bowed four times outside the Wǔmén Gate.
After the proclamation,
they began to wail,
then bowed four more times.
They changed into plain clothes
and received the Crown Prince at Lúgōuqiáo.
South of the bridge, a temporary tent and an incense table were set up.
When the Crown Prince arrived,
in regular attire,
he proceeded to the tent and bowed four times.
He listened to the imperial edict being proclaimed,
then bowed four more times,
and wept to his utmost sorrow.
He changed into plain clothes and dismounted below the right gate of Cháng'ān
, then walked weeping to outside the palace gate.
He removed his hat and robes,
went with disheveled hair before the imperial coffin,
bowed five times and kowtowed three times,
and wept to his utmost sorrow.
Everyone in the palace, from the Empress downwards, wept with disheveled hair.
The Crown Prince went to the eastern part of the mourning place
to see his mother, the Empress Dowager.
After the imperial princes had successively seen the Crown Prince,
each went to their mourning places
to perform the sacrificial and announcement rites.
All mourning ceremonies were as before.
Only the crying and mourning in the capital, morning and evening, was changed to three days.
Afterwards, morning mourning was limited to seven days.
Outside the capital, crying and mourning, morning and evening, was limited to three days,
with no morning mourning ceremony.
Wives of civil and military officials from the first to fourth ranks were ordered to enter for mourning.
After the mourning period ended,
the ritual officials requested that the Emperor wear light-colored clothes, a black gauze yíshàngguān (winged cap), and a black jade belt
to attend to state affairs at Fèngtiānmén.
All officials wore light-colored clothes, black gauze hats, and black jade belts,
and attended court as per usual custom.
After court,
they would revert to the mourning attire for Tàizōng.
The Emperor said:
"How can My heart endure this?
Even an extra day is better than having already ceased."
He continued to wear plain clothes, sitting by the west corner gate,
with no bells or drums chiming,
ordering that the matter be discussed again after one hundred days.
After one hundred days,
the ritual officials again requested that he preside at Fèngtiānmén.
The Emperor ordered to wait until the construction of the imperial tomb was completed.
Previously,
an imperial edict had ordered the construction of Xiànlíng.
The Emperor summoned Shàngshū Jiǎn Yì and Xià Yuánjí and instructed them:
"The state, with the wealth of the four seas, buries its parents,
so how can it begrudge the labor and expense?
However, ancient sagely emperors and enlightened kings all followed principles of frugality.
A filial son, thinking to preserve the body and soul of his parent eternally,
also does not desire a lavish burial.
Moreover, the imperial father's last edict
is known to all under heaven;
it is appropriate to follow his former wishes."
Thereupon, a sleeping hall of five bays was constructed,
with five bays each for the left and right corridors and spirit kitchens,
and a three-bay gate tower.
Its scale was significantly reduced compared to Chánglíng,
and all was planned by the Emperor himself.
Lìbù Shàngshū Jiǎn Yì and others requested that after the enshrinement in the ancestral temple,
he wear plain clothes and attend to affairs at the west corner gate.
Until the late autumn and end of the year,
the seasonal banquet rites were performed.
Bells and drums chimed,
and he presided over court in a yellow robe at Fèngtiānmén.
After the dànjì (final mourning sacrifice),
he finally shed his plain clothes.
This was followed.
When Xuānzōng passed away,
the mourning and burial followed the precedents of Xiànlíng.
Only the mourning for wives of officials was changed
to those of the third rank and above.
When Yīngzōng passed away,
his dying wish was for the Crown Prince to marry after one hundred days
and not to have concubines buried alive with him.
When Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
after one hundred days, he presided over court at Fèngtiānmén,
and all rites and ceremonies used auspicious precedents.
When Xiànzōng passed away,
Xiàozōng, having already completed the mourning period, still wore a plain yíshàngguān, hemp clothes, and a waist cord for court,
with no bells or drums chiming.
All officials attended court in plain clothes,
and after one hundred days, things returned to normal.
On the first day of the first month of Hóngzhì first year
, as the xiǎoxiáng (first anniversary of death) had not yet arrived,
the Emperor wore a yellow robe and presided over court in the main hall.
The next day,
he still wore a black yíshàngguān,
light-colored clothes, and a rhinoceros horn belt.
When the dàxiáng (second anniversary of death) arrived,
the spirit tablets were enshrined in the Tàimiào and Fèngxiāndiàn.
At the dànjì,
court was suspended.
An auspicious day was chosen to dispatch officials to the imperial tomb to offer sacrifices.
When Xiàozōng passed away,
the Gōngbù stated:
"The late Emperor's last edict
earnestly took frugality and love for the people as its foundation.
We request that the various departments of the imperial household be ordered
to ensure that all burial ceremonies, funerary objects, and the imperial tomb's halls and buildings
are reduced and simplified."
The Lǐbù stated:
"The hundred-day period customarily calls for a change of attire,
but as the imperial coffin has not yet entered the imperial tomb,
we request that His Majesty continue to wear a plain yíshàngguān, hemp robes, and a waist cord
, and attend to affairs at the west corner gate,
with no bells or drums chiming,
and that all officials continue to attend court in plain clothes."
This was followed.
From the farewell to the spirit to the yúlǐ (consolation sacrifice and enshrinement),
Prince Róng was present in the accompanying ranks.
Later, the Prince requested exemption due to illness.
The Lǐbù requested that officials such as the Fùmǎ (imperial son-in-law) present silk at the ancestral worship.
The Emperor said:
"For the ancestral worship and presentation of silk,
I shall perform it Myself."
When the funeral procession departed,
the imperial princes only accompanied it to outside the Dàmíngmén Gate.
During the journey and upon arrival at the tomb for the libation ceremony,
all rites were performed by the escorting mourning officials.
This subsequently became the precedent.
When Shìzōng passed away,
an imperial decree exempted wives of officials from mourning.
In the first month of Lóngqìng first year
, before twenty-seven days had passed,
the Emperor, in mourning attire, presided at Xuānzhìmén Gate.
All officials, in plain clothes and with waist cords, offered condolences.
When the funeral procession departed,
the Emperor performed the farewell libation ceremony.
For the ancestral worship,
officials were dispatched to present silk and perform the rites.
When the imperial coffin arrived at Shùntiānfǔ,
imperial relatives, wives of officials, and wives of officials of the third rank and above offered sacrifices.
The rest followed the old system.
When Guāngzōng ascended the throne,
the Lǐbù stated:
"Mourning attire has had regulations throughout the generations,
but it was definitively set by Xiàozōng.
This is because Xiàozōng was devoted to his parents,
and his mourning rites were detailed and complete,
hence the three temples of Wǔ, Shì, and Mù all followed them.
Now, in accordance with the old system,
His Majesty shall wear mourning attire and attend to affairs at Wénhuámén,
with all officials attending court in plain clothes,
until the imperial coffin departs for burial, at which point the mourning attire shall be shed."
This was followed.
From Rénzōng's Xiànlíng onwards,
the regulations for the Ming dynasty were frugal.
When Shìzōng was buried at Yǒnglíng,
its scale began to become extravagant.
And when Shénzōng was buried at Dìnglíng,
Jìshìzhōng Huì Shìyáng and Yùshǐ Xuē Zhēn inspected the tomb construction,
and the cost was said to be over eight million.
Collation Notes

Monograph 35, Rites 13 (Inauspicious Rites 2): Mausolea of Empresses. Mausolea of Emperor Xīngzōng and Empresses. Mausolea of Emperor Ruìzōng and Empresses. Funerals of Imperial Consorts, etc. Funerals of Crown Princes and Consorts. Funerals of Imperial Princes, Princesses, and Consorts.
Mausolea of Empresses.
In the fifteenth year of Hóngwǔ,
Empress Mǎ shì passed away.
The Ministry of Rites requested the adoption of Sòng dynasty regulations.
Thus, an order was issued that civil and military officials in the capital, and those awaiting appointments,
should each be given one bolt of cloth
to make their own mourning garments.
They all wore zhǎncuī for twenty-seven days, after which they removed them,
and wore plain white clothes for one hundred days.
All officials in the capital,
after three days, wearing plain white clothes, proceeded to the outside of the Yòushùn Mén,
donned mourning attire to pay their respects,
then changed back to plain white clothes to perform the ritual of offering condolences,
which lasted for three days.
Wives of military officials of the fifth rank and above, and civil officials of the third rank and above,
also went in plain white clothes to the Qiánqīng Gōng on the fourth day to pay their respects.
They covered their heads with hemp cloth,
wore hemp shirts, skirts, and shoes,
and removed all ornaments and makeup.
The mourning regulations for
officials outside the capital were the same as for those in the capital.
Upon hearing the news, they donned mourning attire in their public offices;
the attire for their wives was also the same as for the wives of capital officials,
and was removed after three days.
Soldiers, civilians, men and women wore plain white clothes for three days.
Slaughtering was prohibited:
for forty-nine days in the capital,
and three days outside the capital.
Music and sacrifices were suspended for one hundred days.
Marriages:
officials suspended them for one hundred days,
soldiers and civilians for one month.
Before the funeral procession began,
a notification was made to the Tàimiào,
and officials were dispatched to sacrifice to the deities of Jīnshuǐ Qiáo, Wǔmén, and other places, as well as the deity of Zhōngshān.
The Emperor personally offered sacrifices at the jīyán.
All officials, in mourning attire, went outside Cháoyáng Mén to bid farewell.
On that day,
the coffin was interred in the Huángtáng.
The Crown Prince made an offering,
using xuánxūn jade bi discs,
and performed the farewell ceremony.
When the spirit tablet returned to the palace,
all officials in plain white clothes greeted it outside Cháoyáng Mén,
and again performed the ritual of offering condolences.
The Emperor again offered sacrifices of wine and food at the jīyán diàn,
and all subsequent yús from the second to the ninth
followed the same procedure.
Officials were dispatched to offer thanks to the deity of Zhōngshān.
Upon the completion of the sùkū (end of initial mourning period),
the spirit tablet was taken to the temple to perform the fùxiǎng ceremony.
After one hundred days of mourning,
the Emperor ceased court appearances,
and offered sacrifices at the jīyán diàn,
showing reverence but not bowing.
The Eastern Palace (Crown Prince) and those below him offered silk and wine;
all officials in plain white clothes performed the ritual of offering condolences.
The Crown Prince, Imperial Princes, Imperial Consorts, and Princesses offered livestock and wine sacrifices at Xiàolíng;
Dukes, Marquises, and others followed.
Wives of officials went to the jīyán diàn to make offerings.
Thereafter, during all seasonal festivals and memorial days,
the Crown Prince and Imperial Princes offered sacrifices at the jīyán and the mausoleum.
For xiǎoxiáng (first anniversary of death),
court was suspended for three days.
Music and slaughtering were prohibited in the capital.
Daoist jiao rituals were performed at Línggǔ Sì and Cháotiān Gōng for three days each.
The Emperor, leading the Crown Prince and those below him, went to the jīyán diàn to offer sacrifices.
All officials in plain white clothes
went to the palace gate.
After offering incense,
they went to the Hòu Yòumén to offer condolences.
Wives of officials outside the capital went to the jīyán diàn to offer incense.
The Crown Prince and Imperial Princes wore mourning caps of boiled cloth with nine layers of white ribbon,
Imperial Grandsons wore seven layers;
all removed the head gongs (headbands made of hemp),
and wore a "fùbǎn pìlǐng cuī" (a specific type of mourning garment).
When seeing the Emperor and officials, they wore plain white clothes, black gauze caps, and black rhinoceros horn belts.
Imperial Consorts, Princesses, and those below them,
covered their heads with boiled cloth,
and removed the waist gongs (waistbands made of hemp).
Members of the Imperial clan and Imperial Sons-in-law wore mourning caps of white ribbon,
and removed the head gongs.
The Nèi Shàngyī and Shàngguān (palace officials responsible for clothing and caps)
burned the removed garments in position bǐng in front of the jīyán diàn.
The Crown Prince and Imperial Princes returned to the mausoleum to perform the rites.
For dàxiáng (second anniversary of death),
the spirit tablet was enshrined in the Fèngxiān Diàn.
A pre-scheduled period of fasting and purification, and announcement to the ancestral temple, was observed.
After all officials had accompanied the sacrifice,
they performed the ritual of offering condolences.
When Emperor Chéngzǔ's Empress Xú shì passed away,
court was suspended from the next day,
and no bells or drums were rung.
The Emperor, in plain white clothes, was present at the Xījiǎo Mén.
All officials, in plain white clothes, went outside the Sīshàn Mén to mourn and pay respects,
after which they performed the ritual of offering condolences.
After three days, mourning attire was donned,
and the mourning and paying of respects followed the previous ceremony.
Starting from the next day,
all lodged and abstained in their public offices,
until twenty-seven days had passed.
Wives of civil and military officials of the fourth rank and above, starting from the day they donned mourning attire,
went inside the Sīshàn Mén to mourn and pay respects for three days.
Officials awaiting selection and handling affairs
all wore mourning attire.
Scholars from the Réncái Jiān, clerks, Buddhist monks and Daoist priests, and elders of wards and neighborhoods all wore plain white clothes.
Starting from the day mourning attire was donned,
they went to the Yìngtiān Fǔ to express grief for three days.
All other procedures followed the regulations from Empress Gāo's time.
Regulations were also set for the mourning attire of Imperial Princes, Princesses, etc.:
Imperial Heirs (shìzǐ) and Commandery Princes (jùnwáng) all wore qīcuī bùzhàngqī (mourning for one year without a staff).
Wives of Imperial Heirs and Commandery Princes, and Commandery Princesses all wore dàgōng (mourning for nine months).
The Imperial Princes of Zhōu and Chǔ, Ningguo Commandery Princesses, and sons of Commandery Princes all wore xiǎogōng (mourning for five months).
Eunuchs were dispatched to inform the Imperial Princes' residences.
Preparations were made for the fù (enshrinement of spirit tablet) and
a visit to the Tàimiào.
Sacrificial vessels, posthumous title scrolls, and posthumous title seals all used sandalwood.
Before the conferring of the scroll,
the Emperor personally informed Heaven and Earth on the imperial steps of the Fèngtiān Diàn.
At the Huágài Diàn,
officials from the Hónglú Sì led the officials who were to confer the scroll and seal to perform the ceremony,
and an imperial decree was proclaimed, saying:
"On the fourteenth day of the tenth month of the fifth year of Yǒnglè,
the posthumous title is conferred upon the late Empress.
You are ordered to perform the rite."
After four bows,
the official leading the ranks brought the scroll and seal cases to the imperial steps of the Fèngtiān Diàn,
placed them in a decorated carriage,
exited through the central path,
entered through the Yòushùn Mén to the jīyán diàn,
placed the scroll and seal on the table,
and retreated to wait outside the hall.
The female officer of court rites went before the incense table,
knelt, and reported:
"The Emperor has sent an official to confer the posthumous title upon the late Empress.
This is respectfully announced."
Then she announced the scroll.
A female officer held the scroll and proclaimed it to the right of the jīyán,
placed the scroll on the table,
and proclaimed the seal in the same manner.
After the officer of court rites announced the completion of the ceremony,
the female officer placed the scroll and seal cases to the left of the jīyán.
An inner palace official came out to report the completion of the ceremony,
and the officials who conferred the scroll and seal reported back.
After one hundred days,
the Ministry of Rites requested that the Emperor hold court at the main gate,
bells and drums be rung,
and officials change to light-colored garments.
The Emperor, stating that the coffin had not yet been buried,
did not consent.
At the end of the full year (period of mourning),
the Emperor, in plain white clothes, went to the jīyán to offer sacrifices.
All officials offered condolences at the Xījiǎo Mén,
and court was suspended for three days.
Music and slaughtering were prohibited in the capital for seven days.
Officials from the Ministry of Rites performed Daoist jiao rituals at Tiānxī Sì and Cháotiān Gōng.
The next day,
the Emperor, in auspicious attire, held court at the Fèngtiān Mén,
and bells and drums were rung.
All officials wore light-colored clothes, black gauze caps, and black horn belts.
After court, they returned to their offices and continued to wear plain white clothes.
On the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month,
court audiences and congratulatory rites were conducted as usual.
For sacrifices at the jīyán,
they wore mourning caps of boiled cloth.
When the funeral procession commenced,
fasting was observed for three days.
Officials were dispatched to announce the burial date to the altars of Heaven, Earth, and Grain.
The Emperor, in plain white clothes, offered sacrifices and reported to the jīyán.
The Crown Prince and those below him performed the rites in mourning attire.
Officials were dispatched to sacrifice to the deities of the bridges and gates along the route and all other gods specified in the sacrificial canon.
All officials and their wives, in plain white clothes,
offered sacrifices along the road in order.
When the coffin reached the riverbank,
all officials bade farewell at the riverbank.
The Crown Prince escorted it across the river.
Prince Hàn (Hàn Wáng) oversaw the journey,
mourning and offering sacrifices morning and evening along the way.
Officials and commoners who came to greet and offer sacrifices
all wore plain white clothes.
After the burial,
the escorting officers and soldiers, and the soldiers who carried the coffin, were granted varying amounts of paper money and rice.
During the Zhèngtǒng reign,
when Rénzōng's empress, née Zhāng, passed away,
the Ministry of Rites determined the funeral rites for the Grand Empress Dowager.
After the Emperor donned mourning attire for three days,
he resumed governance.
All sacrificial ceremonies were not to be suspended.
Princes and officials of all ranks, both within and outside the court, as well as their wives, were to perform ritual weeping as before.
Mourning attire was to be worn for twenty-seven days before being removed.
Soldiers, civilians, men, and women were to wear plain white clothes for thirteen days.
Princes were not to attend the funeral.
External officials were not to offer incense.
Subjects were not to be prohibited from enjoying music or performing marriages.
Upon the burial,
an official was dispatched to announce it to the Tàimiào.
The Emperor personally carried the empress dowager's clothes and headdress to pay respects at the spirit tablets of the successive emperors and empresses, and of Rénzōng.
He also carried Xuānzōng's clothes and headdress to pay respects at the empress dowager's spirit tablet.
These rites were observed according to the seasonal sacrifices.
During the Tiānshùn reign,
when Xuānzōng's empress, née Sūn, passed away,
the ceremonies followed precedent,
with the only change being that the ritual weeping was performed at the Qīngníngmén.
When Yīngzōng's empress, née Qián, passed away,
the rites were as before,
but the prohibition on slaughtering was limited to seven days,
and foreign envoys were exempted from ritual weeping.
In the first year of Zhèngdé (1506),
Jǐngdì's empress, née Wāng, passed away.
The Ministry of Rites convened with the ministers and suggested
that it should follow the precedent for an imperial concubine,
with the court suspended for three days,
and sacrifices offered at nine altars.
The Empress Dowager, the Empress, princes, civil and military officials below them, and their wives were all to offer sacrifices.
The decree was approved.
Xiànzōng's deposed empress, née Wú,
passed away in the fourth year of Zhèngdé (1509).
Based on the recommendations of Grand Secretary Lǐ Dōngyáng and others,
the rites followed the precedent for Yīngzōng's Consort Huì.
Xiànzōng's empress, née Wáng,
passed away in the thirteenth year of Zhèngdé (1518).
Three days later,
the Emperor arrived from Xuānfǔ,
and then the mourning was announced.
All officials wore plain white clothes
and listened to the announcement of the posthumous edict outside the Qīngnínggōng gate.
When the coffin was moved,
a temporary platform was constructed beforehand,
positioned across from the Shùntiānfǔ intersection.
In the morning, the Emperor went out the Běi'ānmén to meet it,
while the Empress Dowager and the Empress awaited the coffin on the platform.
They then returned to the Qīngnínggōng,
where the Emperor personally presented the coffin to pay respects to the ancestors.
All officials walked and escorted it outside the Déshèngmén,
but only the escorting officials rode on horseback.
The next day,
the Emperor carried the spirit tablet back to the capital,
and all officials met him at the Déshèngmén.
The Emperor, in plain white clothes and a hemp girdle, was at the Xījiǎomén,
and all officials offered condolences.
After the final wailing,
the mourning attire was removed.
Xiàozōng's mother, née Jì,
was a concubine of Xiànzōng.
She passed away during the Chénghuà reign,
and the court was suspended as per precedent.
From the initial mourning to the burial,
the Emperor, the Empress Dowager, the Empress, concubines, princesses, and imperial princes all offered sacrifices.
An imperial prince was dispatched to carry the prayer scroll and perform the rites.
The tomb site and funeral ceremonies were both treated with great honor.
Imperial relatives, all officials, and their wives participated in the funeral escort and offered sacrifices,
all according to proper protocol.
Shìzōng's grandmother, née Shào,
passed away in the first year of Jiājìng (1522).
After the mourning period ended,
Minister Máo Chéng and others petitioned to resume auspicious affairs immediately.
The proposal was submitted again,
and an order was given to consult the funeral rites for Empress Dowager Xiàosù.
Chéng and others stated:
"When Xiàosù passed away,
the burial date was not far off,
so mourning attire was temporarily worn
to await the completion of the imperial tomb construction,
which is different from the present situation.
Moreover, it is inappropriate to appear before all nations in plain white clothes
during the New Year's Day audience.
If filial piety is not forgotten,
it is sufficient to merely avoid entering the central gate
and not striking the bells and drums."
This was followed,
and the monthly court sessions on the first and fifteenth were still exempted.
Four days after the burial,
the Emperor went to the Fèntiānmén,
and all officials performed the condolence ceremony,
then auspicious affairs were resumed.
During the Jiājìng reign,
when Xiàozōng's empress, née Zhāng, passed away,
the ritual officials submitted the old regulations.
The Emperor deemed that the suburban sacrifices should not be profaned
and abolished the announcement sacrifices.
He also said that as for personally performing the various rites,
he had already previously issued an edict for a substitute,
so the temple visit rites were also abolished.
When the Tàichángsì proposed the ancestral worship and enshrinement in the temple,
requesting officials to carry the spirit tablets from each temple,
an edict stated that the tablets need not be brought out,
which was a reduction in ceremony.
Previously, when Wǔzōng's empress, née Xià, passed away,
the Ministry of Rites submitted a ritual protocol,
which included wearing plain hats, plain clothes, and hemp girdles for wailing, as well as a condolence ceremony for all ministers.
The Emperor said:
"I am not in mourning for my imperial brother's empress.
Moreover, I respectfully serve the two empress dowagers,
and the Empress Mother's birthday is approaching;
I cannot bear to use purely plain white.
I shall wear blue clothes for official duties;
all other ceremonies should be reconsidered."
Thereupon, Minister Shàngshū Xià Yán and others stated:
"Regarding the funeral rites for Empress Zhuāngsù,
there is no room for discussion among subjects.
However, as the Emperor, with the dignity of the Son of Heaven,
since the mourning period is over,
there is no need to be at the Xījiǎomén.
After all ministers have donned mourning attire,
they should not wear plain clothes for court audiences."
When the funeral and burial ceremonies were submitted,
the Emperor again decreed:
"The affairs of Empress Yì should be different from the primary empresses of previous dynasties.
Since there is no offering of tables and mats,
she should be immediately enshrined in the temple,
and the Empress should preside over affairs in the inner palace."
Yán and others deliberated:
"According to ritual,
the enshrinement announcement is made after the final wailing.
This is because when a new spirit tablet is to be brought in,
an old one is to be removed,
hence the prior announcement.
This applies to ordinary ceremonies,
but it is not applicable to today's circumstances.
Empress Yì's spirit tablet should indeed be immediately enshrined in the Tàimiào
to ensure the peace of her spirit,
and the enshrinement announcement rite should be exempted."
They then submitted the protocol.
The decree was approved.
In the seventh year of Jiājìng,
Empress Chén of Shìzōng died.
The Ministry of Rites submitted the funeral and sacrificial rites.
The Emperor suspected they were excessively lavish.
The proposal was submitted again,
and the Emperor personally revised and approved it,
generally reducing the scale,
intending to remove the mourning attire after nine days.
Grand Secretaries Zhāng Cōng and others said:
"The relationship between husband and wife
is established alongside the Three Cardinal Guides.
The sovereign is the master of the cardinal guides and constant virtues,
and thus must be especially cautious.
In the Zǔozhuàn, Duke Zhāo, fifteenth year, sixth month, day Yǐchǒu,
Prince Shòu of King Jǐng of Zhōu died.
In autumn, eighth month, day Wùyín,
Queen Mù died.
Shū Xiàng said: 'The King has two three-year mourning periods within one year.'
According to ancient rites,
a father mourned his son,
and a husband mourned his wife,
both for a three-year mourning period.
Later generations,
for a husband mourning his wife,
first instituted the Zhīcuī zhàngqī (one-year mourning with a staff) attire;
if parents were alive, no staff was used.
Mourning attire,
from a one-year period downwards,
was interrupted for feudal lords,
but that specifically referred to collateral one-year mourning.
As for a wife's mourning,
originally it was a three-year mourning period,
reduced to one year (qīnián),
so it was certainly never interrupted.
Now, Your Majesty is observing a one-year mourning period for the Empress,
but by substituting days for months,
it is only twelve days.
Your subjects observe a three-year mourning period for the sovereign's mother,
but by substituting days for months,
it is only twenty-seven days.
Compared to ancient rites,
this is already a significant reduction.
Your Majesty should observe the one-year mourning period for twelve days,
and your subjects should wear plain clothes
for a total of twenty-seven days.
Otherwise,
the bonds of grace and propriety will be unclear,
and the ceremonial rites will be amiss."
Minister of Rites Fāng Xiànfū also extensively quoted from chapters such as the Yílǐ and the "Mourning Attire" (Sāngfú),
arguing repeatedly,
and also citing the precedents recorded in the sacred edicts of the three dynasties regarding the death of Empress Rénxiào,
where Tàizōng, after wearing mourning attire,
still wore white clothes and caps for several months to prove his point.
The Emperor said:
"During Empress Wén's mourning,
there was no empress dowager above,
and the crown prince was below,
so it was appropriate to observe the full rites with greater solemnity.
Now I dare not fail to change this system."
Later,
Grand Secretary Huò Tāo said:
"Currently, when officials mourn their wives,
there is no rite of wearing mourning attire while attending to affairs.
This is because a wife's mourning is internal and not external,
as yin should not override yang.
The sacred edict states, 'wear plain clothes for ten days,
emulating the meaning of suspending court sessions,'
which is acceptable if practiced within the inner court.
However, when facing all officials,
presiding over myriad affairs,
occupying the position of yang,
wearing the attire of the inner palace is not permissible.
Officials wear mourning for the Empress
because she is the motherly exemplar of the realm.
According to the rites,
when a father is alive, one mourning one's mother
does not use a staff when ascending to the hall,
to show respect for the father.
Why should this be different in the imperial court?
Your servant requests that Your Majesty wear a black cap and plain clothes,
and hold court at the Xījiǎomén for ten days;
then wear a black cap and black clothes to hold court at Fèntiānmén,
while officials entering the Zǔoyèmén should wear black gauze caps and green robes to stand in their ranks.
When returning to their public offices and private chambers,
they should still wear plain clothes and white caps for twenty-seven days.
If it is said that this still does not fully satisfy the rites,
then it should be removed after the burial at the imperial tomb is completed."
The Emperor followed his advice.
Soon after, the ceremonies for bestowing the imperial title and posthumous name were set.
The Ministry of Rites deliberated:
"Before the appointed day,
the Emperor, in his ceremonial robe and crown, should announce it at the Fèngxiān Palace and Chóngxiān Palace.
On the appointed day,
the Emperor, in ordinary attire, should hold court at Fèntiānmén;
the chief and deputy envoys should be in ordinary attire;
and all officials should wear light-colored clothes and black horn belts,
entering their ranks to perform the rites as usual.
When the imperial decree and memorial come to the Yòushùnmén,
the inner eunuchs should carry them through the main gate,
placing them on the table before the spirit tablet.
The inner ritual attendant should prompt them to take their places and offer incense,
the official proclaiming the decree should stand and proclaim it,
then replace the decree on the table.
The inner eunuchs should carry the imperial envoy's staff out through the main gate,
handing the staff to the chief and deputy envoys,
reporting the completion of the rites,
and the chief and deputy envoys should return the staff and report back."
The next day,
the Ministry of Rites transcribed and issued the decree to the entire realm.
At this time, the funeral rites for the Empress, after Empress Wén,
were performed again for the first time.
During the Yǒnglè period, the ceremonial records were destroyed by fire,
and what was recorded in the Collected Statutes was brief,
so the Emperor made the decision himself,
establishing it as a regulation.
When the coffin was to be buried,
the Emperor personally set all the ceremonies,
also reducing them.
As the Sīshànmén was close to the Rénzhì Palace,
he ordered officials to mourn for only one day,
and also abolished the rite of bidding farewell to the ancestors,
with the coffin departing through the Zǔowángmén.
In the twenty-sixth year,
Empress Fāng died.
The funeral was announced on the same day,
and the Ministry of Rites was instructed:
"The Empress once saved me from danger;
examine and follow the funeral rites of the former empress."
The Ministry of Rites established the rites:
"The mourning attire should be donned on the fourth day.
Thereafter, wear a black cap and plain clothes.
After ten days, change to light-colored clothes,
and all court sessions should be held at the Xījiǎomén.
All officials should wear plain clothes and mourning bands for ten days,
and thereafter black gauze caps, black horn belts, and plain clothes,
for a total of twenty-seven days.
The Emperor should hold court in ordinary attire at the Fèntiānmén,
while officials wear light-colored clothes,
with bells and drums sounding and whips cracking as usual,
but no ascending to the main hall on the first and fifteenth of the month.
When the coffin departs for burial,
officials begin to wear ordinary attire.
The Emperor should perform rites at the Fèngxiān and other palaces,
all in ordinary attire.
For sacrifices before the spirit tablet,
he should wear the appropriate ceremonial attire.
On the day the mourning period ends,
inner officials should be commanded to perform the sacrifice on his behalf."
This was followed.
Soon after, an edict stated:
"Placing imperial concubines after the crown prince is against the rites;
this should be corrected."
When the burial took place,
the ministry officials requested the old rites.
An imperial decree ordered that the coffin should proceed along the central path,
and the Yújì (peace-offering sacrifice) should follow the prescribed nine repetitions.
The Xuángōng should be placed on the left,
and on another day, she would be enshrined and sacrificed to alongside the main consort.
The ministry officials again submitted ritual instructions,
changing the Xiédiàn (Temporary Hall) to Xíngxiǎngdiàn (Temporary Enjoyment Hall).
Also, because from the departure of Empress Xiàojié's coffin to the return of her spirit tablet to the capital took nearly half a year,
during which officials wore ordinary attire on festive days,
and now Empress Xiàoliè's coffin was departing on the tenth and returning on the fifteenth,
the circumstances and rites were different,
so they requested instructions regarding the mourning attire for officials.
The Emperor ordered that those who traveled with the funeral procession
should continue to wear mourning attire.
After the sacrifice, they should enter court wearing black gauze caps and plain clothes,
and conduct affairs wearing plain caps and plain clothes.
When receiving the spirit tablet, they should still wear mourning attire,
perform the peace-offering rite outside the Sīshànmén,
and then change to plain caps and plain clothes to attend to affairs.
Previously,
the Emperor had ordered Xiàoliè to be placed on the left,
and Xiàojié to be moved.
However, because Xiàojié had been peacefully interred for a long time,
it was deemed improper to disturb her,
so this was abandoned.
Instead, he ordered Xiàoliè to be placed on the right,
leaving the left side empty for himself.
Mùzōng's mother, Dù Shì,
passed away in the thirty-third year.
The Ministry of Rites stated:
"It is appropriate to follow the mourning regulations for Shūfēi Jì Shì during the Chénghuà reign.
Furthermore, Yù Wáng is already married,
so he should observe mourning and preside over the funeral,
accompanying the coffin out of the city."
It was then decided to suspend court for five days,
and Yù Wáng was to observe the Zhǎncūi three-year mourning period according to the Xiàocí Lù.
An imperial envoy was sent to enthrone the spirit tablet,
open the tomb chamber,
offer sacrifices to Hòutǔ in gratitude,
and officials from the Ministry of Works were also to be employed.
The number of attendants for the funeral procession and honor guard were all increased from the previous standard.
The emperor considered this not in accordance with proper rites,
and ordered a review of the precedent set by Xiánfēi Zhèng Shì.
Thereupon, Shàngshū Ōuyáng Dé and others resubmitted the ceremonial regulations:
court was suspended for two days,
and no bells or drums were sounded.
The emperor wore light-colored clothes,
and conducted affairs at Fèngtiān Mén.
All officials wore light-colored clothes, black gauze caps, and black rhinoceros horn belts for court attendance.
Yù Wáng was ordered to preside over the offering and libation rituals.
The Prince, accompanied by his consort, entered the palace,
dressed in plain white mourning clothes, wept with utmost sorrow,
performed four bows, and oversaw the encoffining.
After donning the mourning attire,
he wept and observed the mourning rites morning and evening for three days.
Thereafter, one offering was made daily,
ceasing after a total of twenty-seven days.
He was still to observe the full Zhǎncūi three-year mourning period in his private residence.
On the day of conferring the posthumous title and burning the yellow tablet,
sacrificial rites were arranged,
and Yù Wáng went before the spirit tablet to perform the rituals.
The funeral procession departed through Xuánwǔ Mén.
Yù Wáng walked alongside it to just outside the Imperial City gate,
and after the roadside offerings were completed,
he returned to the palace.
The emperor stated that burning the yellow tablet was an imperial decree,
not something the Prince could perform,
and thus it should follow the usual ceremony.
The Ministry of Rites submitted a memorial in reply:
"The ceremony for burning the yellow tablet for imperial consorts
has long been erroneously transmitted.
All involve bowing to offer wine
and kneeling to read the eulogy,
thereby adopting parts of the ceremony for bestowing a posthumous honorific title,
without considering that bestowing a posthumous title is an imperial decree.
The sacrificial text refers to 'the emperor dispatching a decree,'
which differs from bestowing an honorific title.
Now, acting on the imperial edict to proceed with common rites,
the bestowal of the posthumous title should be re-examined
and follow the ritual for bestowing sacrificial offerings.
Both reading the eulogy and proclaiming the decree should be performed standing, without bowing."
This was approved,
and established as a regulation.
Mùzōng's empress, Lǐ Shì,
was Yù Dǐ's primary consort.
She had passed away earlier
and was buried in Xīshān.
In the first year of Lóngqìng,
she was posthumously granted the title Xiàoyì Huánghòu,
and the announcement was personally made to Shìzōng's imperial tablet.
At Huángjí Mén,
a minister was dispatched with a scepter to present the imperial册 treasure to the mausoleum.
Shénzōng's mother, the Empress Dowager Lǐ Shì,
passed away in the forty-second year of Wànlì.
The emperor instructed the Ministry of Rites to arrange a ceremony of superior distinction.
The emperor himself wore mourning clothes and performed the offering and sacrificial rites.
All imperial consorts of Mù Miào, middle palace concubines, the Crown Prince, various princes, and princesses below them all donned mourning attire.
All officials went outside Cíníng Gōng gate to weep and mourn,
while official ladies entered the palace gate to weep and mourn.
All other aspects followed the grand funeral rites.
Xīngzōng Emperor and Empress' Mausoleum
In the twenty-fifth year of Hóngwǔ,
the Crown Prince passed away.
The Ministry of Rites was ordered to deliberate on the funeral rites.
Shìláng Zhāng Zhì and others proposed:
"According to mourning rites,
a father wears Qīcuī for one year for his eldest son.
Presently, the emperor should change days to months,
wear Qīcuī for twelve days,
and shed it after the sacrifices.
Inside the palace, civil and military officials should fast and lodge in their offices.
The next day,
they should wear plain white clothes and attend the mourning at Wénhuá Diàn,
and be issued mourning attire of rough hemp.
After three days, they don the full mourning attire
and gather at Chūnhé Mén to weep.
The next day,
they perform the condolence rites in plain white clothes.
Those who are to participate in sacrifices and the funeral procession
are still to wear mourning attire and headbands for the performance.
In the capital,
all major and minor sacrifices and music are suspended
until the day of burial.
Marriages are suspended for sixty days.
Outside the capital,
civil and military officials change their clothes
and express their sorrow at their offices.
The next day,
they don full mourning attire and perform the rites.
All major and minor sacrifices and music are suspended for thirteen days,
and marriages are suspended for thirty days."
For those officials inside and outside the capital who offered sacrifices,
the emperor ordered the Guānglù Sì to provide the items,
and officials merely expressed their sorrow and performed the rites.
When Jiànwén Dì ascended the throne,
he posthumously honored him as Xīngzōng Xiàokāng Huángdì.
The mausoleum name he proposed is not recorded.
His primary consort, Cháng Shì,
passed away before Xīngzōng.
Tàizǔ wore plain white clothes
and suspended court for three days.
The empress wore plain white clothes and sorrowfully observed the mourning,
and the Crown Prince wore Qīcuī.
After the burial,
they changed back to ordinary clothes.
The imperial grandson wore Zhǎncūi
for sacrifices and offerings.
Various princes and princesses wore mourning attire according to regulations.
In the early Jiànwén reign,
she was posthumously titled Xiàokāng Huánghòu.
In the early Yǒnglè reign,
both titles were posthumously rescinded.
When Fú Wáng ascended the throne in Nánjīng,
the former titles of the emperor and empress were restored.
Ruìzōng Emperor and Empress' Mausoleum
The mausoleum of Ruìzōng Emperor and Empress is in Ānlù Zhōu.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he posthumously honored him as Ruìzōng Xiàn Huángdì.
The mausoleum and temple were renovated,
and given the name Xiǎnlíng.
Later, followers of Xī Jìn repeatedly suggested that Xiàn Huángdì's coffin should be reburied at Tiānshòushān.
The emperor did not agree.
In the seventeenth year of Jiājìng,
the emperor's mother, Jiǎng Tàihòu, passed away.
The Ministry of Rites stated:
"On New Year's Eve,
the twenty-seven-day mourning period for the late Empress Dowager has ended.
Coincidentally, it is the New Year's Day;
we request that Your Majesty wear a black cap and light-colored clothes to receive court."
Before the memorial was sent down,
the emperor instructed Grand Secretary Xià Yán:
"On New Year's Day, I will worship Heaven at Xuánjí Diàn.
Should I still wear sacrificial robes,
or should I change clothes one day in advance?"
The Ministry of Rites requested
"that for worshipping Heaven and receiving court on New Year's Day,
and for the day before, Your Majesty wear blue clothes.
For the spring sacrifice,
Your Majesty should fast for three days prior,
wear blue clothes,
and your ministers should do the same.
All other aspects should follow the precedent of Xiàozhēn Huáng Tàihòu's funeral rites."
This was not followed.
Thus, it was decided
that on New Year's Eve, the emperor would change into auspicious black clothes;
on New Year's Day, he would wear sacrificial robes to perform the sacrificial rites at Xuánjí Diàn,
wear the Yìshànguān and yellow robe to ascend the throne;
all officials would wear their official robes and deliver eulogies;
bells and drums would be sounded, whips would be cracked,
and hall music would be played.
At this time, the debate about moving the coffin north or south for joint burial
remained unresolved for a long time.
The emperor personally visited Chéngtiān.
Upon his return,
it was decided that the coffin would be interred in the south.
The Ministry of Rites submitted the funeral regulations.
Beyond the usual ceremonies,

the emperor further added and stipulated farewells at Tàimiào, farewell libations at Chéngtiān Mén, dispatched libations at Cháoyáng Mén, descending and feasting the spirits after enthroning the spirit tablet,
and sacrifices when the coffin boarded a boat and ascended the bank.
When the coffin was led out,
the emperor wore mourning clothes and performed all rites as prescribed.
All officials walked alongside the procession to outside Cháoyáng Mén,
offered libations,
and had envoys perform the dispatched libation rites.
Upon reaching Tōngzhōu,
the official responsible for the spirit tablet reported back.
When the spirit tablet returned to the capital,
all officials welcomed it outside the gate.
The emperor, in mourning clothes, led the empress and others to weep and welcome it inside Wǔmén,
and it was enshrined in Jǐyán Diàn.
Wherever the coffin passed rivers, waterways, mountains, and deities,
sacrificial animals and wine were offered.
Meritorious officials, in blue clothes, performed the rites,
and the coffin was brought up to the Xí Diàn.
First, they proceeded to Ruìzōng's old mausoleum,
and moved the remains to Èn Diàn,
then brought the coffin to the temple again,
and buried it together in the new tomb.
Imperial Consorts' Funerals
In the ninth month of the seventh year of Hóngwǔ
, Guìfēi Sūnshì passed away.
Having no children,
Tàizǔ ordered Wú Wáng Sū to preside over the funeral arrangements
, wearing the mourning clothes of a compassionate mother (címǔ fú),
namely zhǎncuī for three years.
The Dōnggōng and all other princes wore qī mourning.
From this, the Xiàocí Lù was compiled.
During the Yǒnglè reign,
Guìfēi Wángshì passed away.
Court was suspended for five days,
the Emperor offered one sacrifice,
the Empress, imperial concubines, and Crown Prince each offered one sacrifice,
the princes collectively offered one sacrifice,
and the princesses collectively offered one sacrifice.
For the seven sevens, the hundred-day period, and the second anniversary,
sacrifices were offered and an imperial edict conferring a posthumous title was issued,
and the Fén Huáng ritual was performed.
The tomb area was opened,
and officials were dispatched to offer sacrifices to Hòutǔ.
On the eve of the funeral procession,
the farewell sacrifice to the spirit and the sacrificial altar were the same as for the initial mourning,
except that six Shàngsī departments and internal eunuchs (nèiguān) and attendants (nèishǐ) each had an additional altar.
For the Qǐdiàn, Zǔdiàn, and Qiǎndiàn, one sacrifice was offered for each.
On the day of the funeral procession,
all officials escorted the coffin to the roadside sacrificial place,
with imperial relatives and imperial sons-in-law (fùmǎ) sharing one altar,
dukes, marquises, and earls, both civil and military, sharing one altar,
and external imperial ladies sharing one altar.
At city gates along the route, sacrifices were performed;
for inner gates, internal eunuchs were dispatched;
for outer gates, officials from the Tàicháng Sì were dispatched.
Upon burial,
a Qiǎndiàn and a sacrifice were offered at one altar.
Upon covering the tomb,
officials were dispatched to offer sacrifices to Hòutǔ,
and the spirit sedan was welcomed to the memorial hall (xiǎng táng),
where the Ānshén ritual was performed,
and one sacrifice was offered.
In the seventh year of Tiānshùn,
Jìngfēi Liúshì passed away.
Court was suspended for five days.
The Emperor wore light yellow clothes and attended to state affairs at Fèntiānmén.
All officials wore light-colored clothes, black gauze caps (wūshā mào), and black rhinoceros horn belts (hēijiǎo dài) for court attendance.
The imperial edict (cèwén) was placed before the coffin,
and the Crown Prince and those below performed the Sānxiàn ritual.
The honor guard before the coffin included
twenty-four internal eunuch female musicians,
twenty women carrying floral banners and snow willows,
and eleven female generals.
From the initial mourning until the farewell sacrifice at the first anniversary,
an additional altar was set up for sacrifices beyond the regular ones.
In the fourteenth year of Hóngzhì,
Xiànmiào's Lìfēi Zhāngshì had her funeral procession.
Court was suspended for one day.
All imperial concubines buried with the emperor
were offered sacrifices in the main hall (diàn nèi) at seasonal times.
For those separately buried in Jīnshān and other places,
internal eunuchs were dispatched to perform the rites.
During the Jiājìng reign,
it was first decreed that they should all be incorporated into the imperial tombs (zhū líng),
and sacrifices offered on both sides of the Éndiàn,
with red paper tablets inscribed with
“The Seat of Emperor [X]'s [Y]-th Concubine.”
After the sacrifice,
they were burned.
Later, carved wooden plaques with names and titles were used instead.
In the thirteenth year of Jiājìng, an imperial edict was issued to the Ministries of Rites and Works:
“The Shìfù and Yùqī shall all use the number nine.
Nine concubines sharing one tomb,
and one memorial hall (xiǎngdiàn) for all,
is hereby established as the permanent system.”
Funeral and Burial Rites for the Crown Prince and Crown Princess
Since the Hóngwǔ reign,
after Yìwén Tàizǐ,
up to the eighth year of Chénghuà when Dàogōng Tàizǐ passed away,
who was only three years old.
The Emperor instructed the Ministry of Rites
that the rites should be simplified,
and princes' establishments (wángfǔ) and civil and military officials were all exempted from presenting incense and silk.
The Ministry of Rites submitted the protocol.
From the second day after the initial mourning,
court was suspended for three days.
The Emperor wore a Yìshàn crown and plain clothes,
which were removed after seven days.
After another three days,
he attended court at Xījiǎomén,
without the ringing of bells and drums,
and sacrifices used vegetarian food.
Civil and military officials,
wearing plain clothes, hemp cloth, mourning bands (diédài), hemp shoes, and gauze caps wrapped in cloth,
proceeded to Sīshànmén to wail in mourning (kū lín),
and this was lifted after one day.
On the fourth day,
they attended Xījiǎomén in plain clothes to offer condolences.
Princes' establishments and civil and military officials outside the capital
wailed in plain clothes,
and this was lifted after two days.
In the twenty-eighth year of Jiājìng,
Zhuāngjìng Tàizǐ passed away.
The Ministry of Rites submitted the funeral rites.
The Emperor said:
“The Son of Heaven is exempt from a specific mourning period (jué qī).
Moreover, three children passed away before the age of fifteen,
so my wearing of mourning is inappropriate.
Court will only be suspended for ten days.
All officials shall wear mourning clothes according to the system,
which will be removed after twelve days.
They shall proceed to the place where the coffin is interred
, and be exempted from wailing in mourning at the gate.
For the burial, relatives and trusted officials shall be dispatched to perform the rites.”
In the second month of the forty-seventh year of Wànlì,
Crown Prince's Cairen Wángshì passed away.
It was decreed that the precedent of Crown Princess Guōshì should be followed.
Court was suspended for five days,
and no bells or drums were rung.
The Emperor wore light-colored clothes,
and all officials wore plain blue clothes and black rhinoceros horn belts for court attendance.
The Imperial Grandson (huángzhǎngsūn) presided over the food offerings (kuìdiàn).
Funeral and Burial Rites for Princes and Princesses and their Consorts
In the twenty-eighth year of Hóngwǔ,
Qín Wáng Shuǎng passed away,
and an imperial edict established the funeral rites.
Rites Minister Rèn Hēngtài stated:
“According to the Sòng system,
court should be suspended for five days.
However, as it coincides with a seasonal sacrifice (shí xiǎng),
I request a temporary suspension for one day.
The mourning attire for the Emperor and below,
down to the imperial ladies of a princess (jùnzhǔ) and the Jìngjiāng Wáng's palace,
shall all be the same as for the Lǔ Wáng's funeral rites.
The Crown Prince shall wear qīcuī for the qī period,
which shall also be converted from months to days,
removed after twelve days,
and plain clothes worn for one year.”
This was approved.
The system was established: for the death of a prince (qīnwáng),
court was suspended for three days.
The Ministry of Rites proposed dispatching officials to manage the funeral and burial rites,
the Hánlín Yuàn to draft sacrificial texts, posthumous title edicts, and tomb epitaphs,
the Ministry of Works to make the banner (míngjīng),
officials to construct the tomb,
officials from the Qīntiānlán to select the burial date,
and eight students from the Guózǐjiān to report the訃告 (fùgào) to all princes' establishments.
There was one imperial sacrifice,
one each from the Empress Dowager, Empress, and Dōnggōng,
and one each from resident civil and military officials in the capital.
From the initial mourning until the removal of mourning clothes,
there were thirteen imperial sacrifices in total,
and one from resident civil and military officials within the prince's domain.
Regarding mourning attire,
the prince's consort (wángfēi), heir apparent (shìzǐ), all sons, and commander of a commandery (jùnwáng), and princess of a commandery (jùnzhǔ),
down to palace women,
wore zhǎncuī for three years.
Resident civil and military officials within the prince's domain wore qīcuī for three days,
and wailed in mourning for five days before removal.
City residents and soldiers wore plain clothes for five days.
Commandery princes, all sons, and commandery mistresses (jùnjūn)
wore qīcuī for one year for an elder brother, paternal uncle, or paternal grand-uncle;
the commandery princess wore xiǎogōng.
For the death of a prince's consort,
one imperial sacrifice was offered,
and one each from the Empress Dowager, Empress, Dōnggōng, and princesses.
The Bùzhèngsī commissioned officials to open the tomb and conduct the joint burial.
The sacrificial rites for a second consort (jìfēi) and a third consort (cìfēi) were the same.
For a fūrén, only one imperial sacrifice was offered.
All were buried in the same tomb.
For the death of a commandery prince,
court was suspended for one day.
The Xíngrénsī dispatched officials to manage the funeral and burial rites,
and most other arrangements were similar to those for a prince,
without sacrifices from the Empress Dowager or Empress.
The commandery princess's rites were the same as for a prince's consort,
without sacrifices from princesses.
The funeral rites for a second consort or third consort of a commandery prince buried jointly
were all the same as for the principal consort.
For the death of an heir apparent,
one imperial sacrifice was offered,
and one from the Dōnggōng.
For the seven-day intervals, the hundredth day, burial, first anniversary, and removal of mourning clothes,
one imperial sacrifice was offered for each.
For the funeral rites of an imperial grandson (shìsūn),
they were the same as for an heir apparent,
but omitting the seven-sevens and Dàxiáng sacrifices.
For a Zhènguó Jiāngjūn,
there were only three sacrifices: upon hearing the news, on the hundredth day, and at burial.
For a Fèngguó Jiāngjūn and below,
one imperial sacrifice was offered.
Initially,
in the fifth month of the ninth year of Hóngwǔ
Jìn Wángfēi Xiè Shì passed away.
An order was given to discuss the regulations for mourning attire.
Shìjiǎng Xuéshì Sòng Lián and others deliberated, saying:
“According to the Táng system,
the Emperor observes mourning for Imperial concubines and others.
According to the Sòng system,
the Emperor observes mourning for Imperial relatives.
Now, referring to and adapting the Táng and Sòng systems,
the Emperor and Zhōnggōng [Empress] shall wear dàgōng [heavy mourning],
all other concubines shall wear xiǎogōng [light mourning],
Nánchāng Huángfēi shall wear dàgōng,
Dōnggōng [Crown Prince], princesses, and other princes shall all wear xiǎogōng.
The Prince of Jìn shall wear qīcuī qī [mourning for one year with cut edges].
Jìngjiāng Wángfēi shall wear xiǎogōng.
The consort of a Prince shall wear sīmá [finest mourning].
Court shall be suspended for three days.
Once the mourning attire is put on,
the Emperor, in plain clothes, shall enter the mourning chamber,
and after fifteen days, the mourning cries shall commence.
All officials shall offer condolences.
The Emperor shall leave the chamber, remove the mourning attire,
and wear ordinary clothes.”
The decree stated:
“Agreed.”
Thereafter,
the mourning for princely consorts followed this precedent.
In the thirteenth year of Zhèngtǒng
with fifteen rooms.
For a Commander Prince, the burial ground was thirty mù,
with nine rooms.
For the son of a Commander Prince, the burial ground was twenty mù,
with three rooms.
For a Commander Princess or a County Princess, the burial ground was ten mù,
with three rooms.
In the second year of Tiānshùn
the Ministry of Rites memorialized and stipulated:
Princes and those below [in rank],
should follow the precedents for civil and military high officials.
If either the Prince or the consort dies first,
their crypt should be constructed together.
For those buried later,
the local officials concerned are merely to arrange the burial.
A succeeding consort shall be buried beside the former,
sharing the same ancestral hall.
In the second month of the eighth year of Chénghuà
Xīn Wáng Jiànzhì passed away.
On the day of the funeral procession,
the Emperor did not hold court.
At the time of burial,
court was suspended for one day.
In the thirteenth year
Péng Sháo, the Provincial Surveillance Commissioner of Sìchuān, said:
“When a Prince or Commander Prince passes away,
officials are dispatched to offer sacrifices, and envoys are numerous,
causing labor and disturbance to the populace.
Henceforth, only Princes shall follow the old custom;
for Commander Princes, an official shall be dispatched for one sacrifice at the initial mourning,
all others being dispatched by local officials.
For the mourning of a Kingdom's mother consort,
eunuchs shall be dispatched to offer sacrifices.
Currently, there are many Imperial kinswomen,
and where there are resident eunuchs serving as garrison commanders,
they should be dispatched to perform the rites.
Furthermore, in the burial grounds of Kingdoms,
husband and wife are interred in the same grave.
When first constructing it,
officials are dispatched to supervise the construction.
For opening the crypt for joint burial,
I request that only local officials be ordered [to oversee it].”
The Emperor assented to the Ministry of Rites’ report,
the sacrificial rites for princely consorts remained as before,
and the rest was carried out according to the proposal.
In the seventh month of the sixteenth year of Hóngzhì
Shēn Wáng Yòukǎi passed away.
The Ministry of Rites stated:
“The late Yí Mù Wáng [Prince Yímu] died
before leaving his mansion.
Shēn Wáng had left his mansion but had not yet proceeded to his fiefdom.
It is proposed that he be treated according to the precedent of Yí Mù Wáng,
referring to the example of Princes outside the capital.”
Regarding the burial grounds for princely consorts recorded in the Huìdiǎn [Collected Statutes],
in the early Míng, the ten Princes of Shòuchūn and others, along with their consorts, who were posthumously enfeoffed,
had their tombs located at Bái Tǎ, twenty-five lǐ northwest of Fèngyáng Fǔ,
with a Directorate for Sacrifices and Tomb Households established.
The five Princes of Nánchāng and others, along with their consorts, were interred in the Imperial Mausoleum at Fèngyáng,
and officials would offer sacrifices during seasonal rites,
all sharing in the offerings.
Many Princes below Huáixiàn Shìzǐ [Crown Prince Huáixiàn] who had not yet proceeded to their fiefdoms
were buried in the Western Hills,
with eunuchs dispatched annually to perform rites.
In the first month of the fifteenth year of Yǒnglè
Princess Yǒng'ān passed away.
At that time, a lantern banquet was just being held,
which was subsequently canceled.
Court was suspended for four days,
sacrifices were granted,
and the relevant officials were ordered to manage the funeral and burial.
In the second month [of the same year],
Fúqīng Gōngzhǔ, the eighth daughter of Tàizǔ, passed away.
Court was suspended for three days.
By decree,
whenever the death of a princess was announced,
court was suspended for one day.
From the initial mourning to the great mourning [third anniversary],
the Emperor made twelve sacrifices in total.
At the burial,
court was suspended for one day.
The ceremony was slightly less grand than that for Princes,
but the mourning regulations were the same,
except that officials did not wear mourning attire.
For those [princesses] not yet married who were buried in the Western Hills,
eunuchs were dispatched annually to perform rites.

Chapter 36, Rites 14 (Inauspicious Rites 3): Visits and Sacrifices to Mausoleums and Temples; Commemoration Days; Receiving Reports of Royal Deaths from Vassal States and Sacrificial Rites; Observing Mourning for Princes, Dukes, and High Officials; Attending Funerals of Princes, Dukes, and High Officials; The Empress Observing Mourning for Her Father and Grandparents; Dispatching Envoys for Condolences; Dispatching Envoys to Confer Titles on Princes, Dukes, and High Officials; Granting Sacrifices and Burials; Regulations for Mourning and Burial; Stele and Epitaphs and Conferring Posthumous Titles; Mourning Rites for Officials; Mourning Rites for Commoners; Periods of Mourning.
Visits and Sacrifices to Mausoleums and Temples
In the third month of the first year of Hóngwǔ
In the second year
Lǐbù Shàngshū Cuī Liàng requested that the Tàicháng Sī [Court of Imperial Sacrifices] conduct the sacrificial announcement ceremony.
Bóshì Sūn Wúyǔ said:
“The system of Imperial mausoleums
was most complete in the Hàn dynasty,
but initially, there was no ceremony of sacrificial announcement.
The temple name and mausoleum name are different.
The temple name replaces the name of the deceased Emperor,
and a册谥 [冊謚, memorialized posthumous title] must be bestowed,
and announced to the spirits.
The mausoleum name is merely for the subsequent Kings to distinguish the sequence [of their ancestors].
I wish for the sacrificial announcement at Yīng Líng to be abolished.”
Liàng said:
“Hàn Guāngwǔ added the name Chāng to ancestral mausoleums,
and Sòng Tàizǔ added Qīn, Kāng, Dìng, Ān to the mausoleums of his great-great-grandfather, great-grandfather, grandfather, and father.
Honoring ancestors means honoring their mausoleums,
and honoring their mausoleums necessarily involves an announcement.
Rites are based on human sentiment;
announcing it is correct.”
The court deliberations all agreed with Liàng.
It was followed.
At Xīzǔ Líng,
every year on the New Year’s Day, Qīngmíng, Zhōngyuán, Dōngzhì, and on the first and fifteenth days of each month,
officials from the local directorate would offer sacrifices and perform rites.
Also, from that location, distant sacrifices were offered to Dèzǔ and Yìzǔ mausoleums.
Yīng Líng was later renamed Huánglíng [Imperial Mausoleum],
with an additional sacrifice in the first month of winter,
all performed by officials from the directorate;
on the first and fifteenth days of the month,
officials from the Zhōngdū Liúshǒusī [Central Capital Guard Command] performed rites.
In the eighth year [of Hóngwǔ, 1375], an edict ordered the Hánlín Yuàn to discuss the rites for monthly, seasonal, and festival sacrifices at mausoleums.
Xuéshì Yuè Sháofèng and others said:
“The various ancestral temples and tomb parks of the Hàn dynasty had side halls,
with daily sacrifices at the sleeping quarters,
monthly sacrifices at the temple,
and seasonal sacrifices at the side hall.
Later, when the Eastern Hàn capital was Luòyáng,
due to the distant location of the various mausoleums in Guānxī,
only special sacrificial animals were used four times a year.
Whenever the Emperor traveled west,
he would personally visit.
After sacrificing at the suburban and ancestral temples in the first month of the year,
he would successively visit the various mausoleums in Luòyáng.
The system of Imperial tomb parks in the Táng dynasty
stipulated that for the mausoleums of Imperial ancestors and above,
food was offered on the first and fifteenth days of the month,
and one sacrifice each on Yuánrì [New Year’s Day], Dōngzhì [Winter Solstice], Hánshí [Cold Food Festival], Fúlà [Dog Days and Laba], and Shè [Spring and Autumn Equinoxes].
For the mausoleums of Imperial fathers,
food was offered on the first and fifteenth days of the month and on festival days,
and new harvest offerings were also presented to all mausoleums.
In the second year of Yǒnghuī
all required offerings of food.
During the Kāiyuán period [713-741], an imperial order stipulated that at the six mausoleums of Xiàn, Zhāo, Qián, Dìng, Qiáo, and Gōng,
food was offered on the first and fifteenth days of the month,
and a separate sacrifice was held on Dōngzhì and Hánshí.
In the Sòng dynasty, every spring and autumn in the middle month,
the Tàicháng Zōngzhèng Qīng [Ministers of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices and Court of Imperial Clan Affairs] were dispatched to pay respects to the various mausoleums.
Our dynasty’s old custom
was that every year on Yuándàn [New Year’s Day], Qīngmíng, the fifteenth day of the seventh month, the first day of the tenth month, and Dōngzhì,
tàiláo [grand sacrifice with an ox, pig, and sheep] was used,
and officials were dispatched to offer sacrifices.
At the two locations of Bái Tǎ,
shǎoláo [minor sacrifice with a pig and sheep] was used,
and eunuchs performed the rites.
Now it is proposed to follow the old customs,
adding the use of tàiláo on Xiàzhì [Summer Solstice].
For Fúlà, Shè, and the first and fifteenth days of each month,
a special sheep shall be used,
and officials from the Directorate for Sacrifices shall perform the rites.
If a festival coincides with the first or fifteenth day of the month, Fúlà, or Shè,
then the festival rites shall be used.”
This was followed.
In the sixteenth year,
the Hall of Xiàolíng was completed,
and the Huáng Tàizǐ was ordered to offer sacrifices with animals and wine.
In the early morning, after the sacrificial ceremonies were arranged,
the Huáng Tàizǐ and Qīnwáng entered through the East Gate,
and proceeded to their kneeling positions in the hall,
all bowing four times.
The Huáng Tàizǐ moved slightly forward,
offered incense three times,
poured libations,
and read the prayer which said:
"When the imperial mausoleum was first constructed,
the rituals for offerings and enjoyment were not yet complete.
Now that the ritual hall is finished,
and the spirit tablets are enshrined,
we respectfully make this announcement."
Then the rituals of Yàxiàn and Zhōngxiàn were performed,
and everyone from the Huáng Tàizǐ downwards bowed four times.
All those performing the rituals were Nèiguān.
In the twenty-sixth year, an order was issued that
when carriages and horses passed the mausoleum,
and for officials and commoners guarding the mausoleum entering it,
they must dismount a hundred paces away.
Violators would be judged for great disrespect.
In the early Jiànwén reign,
it was stipulated that at Xiàolíng annually on Zhèngdàn, Mèngdōng, Jìchén, and Shèngjié,
incense rituals would be performed.
On Qīngmíng, Zhōngyuán, and Dōngzhì,
sacrifices would be performed.
Veteran meritorious ministers performed the rituals,
while civil and military officials accompanied the sacrifices.
If a Qīnwáng went to his enfeoffment,
those passing through the Jīngshī would visit the mausoleum.
Officials arriving on public business,
those entering the city would visit the mausoleum,
and those leaving the city would bid farewell to the mausoleum.
If the state had important affairs,
officials would be dispatched to offer sacrifices and make announcements.
The Tomb of Yìwén Tàizǐ was to the left of Xiàolíng.
On Sìmèng, Qīngmíng, Zhōngyuán, Dōngzhì, Suìmù, and Jìchén,
there were a total of nine sacrifices.
In the first year of Yǒnglè,
the Gōngbù reported on the black tiles of the Zǔlíng in Sìzhōu.
The Emperor ordered them to be changed to yellow,
following the style of the Huánglíng.
When Xuānzōng ascended the throne,
he dispatched Zhèng Wáng to visit and offer sacrifices at Xiàolíng.
In the second year of Zhèngtǒng, an edict stated that
for the imperial tombs at Tiānshòushān,
those who cut down trees would be heavily punished.
The Dūcháyuàn would post prohibitions,
Jǐnyīwèi officials and guards would patrol,
and Gōngbù and Qīntiānjiān officials would establish boundaries around the mountain.
In the tenth year, when visiting Sānlíng,
an edict instructed all officials to wear light-colored clothes,
following the precedents of Hóngwǔ and Yǒnglè.
Chén Zǔguī, the Sīlǐ Tàijiān of Nánjīng, stated:
"Xú Fǔ, the Wèi Guógōng, when offering sacrifices at Xiàolíng,
always enters directly through the Red Ticket Gate
to perform rituals inside the hall,
which is presumptuous and should be changed."
Xú Fǔ replied:
"Entering through the Red Ticket Gate
is to emphasize the importance of the ancestral sacrifices
and to honor the Emperor's command.
Exiting through the small side gate
is to observe the proper distinction for a subject.
This practice has been followed
for nearly a hundred years,
how dare I arbitrarily change it?"
The matter was referred to the Lǐbù for deliberation,
which stated:
"At Chánglíng and Tàimiào,
when officials are dispatched to offer sacrifices,
the gates they use are the same in nature as those at Xiàolíng,
so it should remain as before."
This was followed.
In the first year of Hóngzhì, the Nèiguānjiān was dispatched to oversee the Huánglíng in Fèngyáng,
and all officials passing by on public business were to visit the mausoleum.
In the seventeenth year, the spirit seat at Yùlíng was altered.
Initially,
it was proposed that Empress Dowager Xiàosù Tàihuáng Tàihòu be interred with Yùlíng.
Officials had already been dispatched to inform the various mausoleums and Hòutǔ of Tiānshòushān,
but the Qīntiānjiān believed that the "year-slaughter" star was in the north,
and the direction was unfavorable.
The Nèiguānjiān also said that the imperial tomb of Yīngmiào
should not be lightly disturbed.
Thus, it was proposed to build a separate temple
to enshrine her spirit tablet.
The Emperor was not satisfied with this,
and finally moved Yīngmiào to the center,
Xiàozhuāng to the left,
and Xiàosù to her right.
During the Zhèngdé period,
it was decided that for Chánglíng and other mausoleums below it,
each would be provided with a Shéngōngjiān, a guard unit (wèi), and a Cíjièshǔ.
On Qīngmíng, Zhōngyuán, and Dōngzhì,
Fùmǎ Dūwèi would be separately dispatched to perform the rites,
