with civil and military officials accompanying the sacrifices.
On Jìchén, Zhèngdàn, Mèngdōng, and Shèngjié,
Fùmǎ Dūwèi would also be dispatched to perform the rites.
When Qīnwáng went to their enfeoffments,
they would visit the various mausoleums to bid farewell.
For the Tomb of Empress Gōngràngzhāng,
Nèiguān performed rites on Qīngmíng, Zhōngyuán, Dōngzhì, and Jìchén.
For the Mausoleum of Emperor Jǐng in Xīshān,
the sacrificial dates were as above,
and Yíbīn performed the rites.
Originally,
Chéngzǔ changed the name of Huángtǔshān to Tiānshòushān.
In the tenth year of Jiājìng, Zǔlíng was named Jīyùnshān,
Huánglíng was named Yìshèngshān,
Xiàolíng was named Shénlièshān,
Xiǎnlíng was named Chúndéshān,
and Tiānshòushān,
along with Fāngzé, were included in the sacrifices.
The local authorities in charge offered sacrifices and announced to the Shānzhī of each mausoleum.
The Lǐguān then submitted a memorial, stating:
"At the Shénzhītán, during the annual autumn sacrifice,
there are spirits of Zhōngshān and Tiānshòushān;
now Jīyùn děng shān should be added."
This was approved.
In the fourteenth year, an edict was issued to Xià Yán, the Lǐbù Shàngshū, stating:
"On Qīngmíng Festival, officials are already dispatched to visit the imperial tombs,
and then sacrifices are repeated in the inner hall,
which seems cumbersome and repetitive."
Xià Yán thereupon stated:
"Our dynasty's sacrificial rites,
such as Tèxiǎng, Shíxiǎng, Xiájì, and Dìjì,
fully conform to the classics
and can serve as a model for the ages.
However, the visits to the imperial tombs and Fèngxiāndiàn largely follow precedents from previous dynasties.
The sacrifices at the imperial tombs are performed three times annually: Qīngmíng, Zhōngyuán, and Dōngzhì.
Zhōngyuán is a folk festival,
its practice is not based on the classics.
Previously, the suburban sacrifice (Jiāosì) was paramount,
hence the visit to the imperial tombs on Dōngzhì,
which was to emphasize the beginning of the vital energy (yìqì)
and extend the meaning of repaying one's origins.
Now, since the grand rite of repaying Heaven (Dàbào Pèitiān) is performed on Dōngzhì,
the mausoleum rites become less significant.
Moreover, when there are affairs at Nánjiāo,
and accompanying sacrificial officials are excused
to travel far to the mountain mausoleums,
it may not fully express sincerity in honoring ancestors and matching Heaven.
Therefore, the Dōngzhì visit to the imperial tombs can be abolished,
and Zhōngyuán moved to Shuāngjiàng,
while Qīngmíng remains as before.
This is because the Qīngmíng rite is performed in spring,
where 'when the rain and dew have thoroughly moistened,
the gentleman steps upon it
with a sense of awe and apprehension.'
The Shuāngjiàng rite is performed in autumn,
where 'when the frost and dew have fallen,
the gentleman steps upon it
with a sense of sorrow and grief.'
Since officials are dispatched to the imperial tombs on these two festivals,
the sacrifices in the inner hall
should truly not be repeated."
This was then made into a standing order.
In the fifteenth year, an imperial edict stated:
"The ancestral temple is more important than the imperial mausoleum;
its rites are more stringent.
Therefore, within the temple, there is one emperor and one empress,
whereas in the mausoleum, two or three empresses may be buried with the emperor.
Now, to separately establish the Fèngcí Diàn (奉慈殿) [for the spirit tablets]
is not as fitting as enshrining the spirit tablets in the mausoleum hall.
Moreover, when the imperial coffin is interred together,
but the spirit tablet is separately placed,
it approaches the act of demotion,
not of showing filial affection."
Thereupon, the spirit tablets of the three empresses, Xiàosù (孝肅), Xiàomù (孝穆), and Xiàohuì (孝惠), were moved to the mausoleum hall.
Another imperial edict stated:
"The designations of Huáng Tàihòu (皇太后) and Tàihuáng Tàihòu (太皇太后) for the spirit tablets of the three empresses
are honorific titles bestowed by their descendants.
Now that they have been moved to the mausoleum hall,
the name and reality do not correspond."
Yán Děng (言等) deliberated and said:
"The spirit tablets of the three empresses,
whose rites do not permit them to be enshrined in the ancestral temple,
should by principle follow the rite of 'tiāo' (祧) [transferring to a distant ancestral temple or separate shrine].
Moving and enshrining them in the mausoleum hall
is deeply in accordance with the established rites.
As for the titles Huáng Tàihòu (皇太后) and Tàihuáng Tàihòu (太皇太òu),
these are honorific titles conferred by descendants.
Now that they have been moved and enshrined in the mausoleum,
we should follow the principle of husband and wife,
and change the inscription on the spirit tablet of Xiàosù (孝肅)
to exclude the character 'Ruì' (睿);
the spirit tablets of Xiàomù (孝穆) and Xiàohuì (孝惠)
should both exclude the character 'Chún' (純).
This way, the distinction between principal and secondary consorts is made,
and reverence for elders is simultaneously magnified."
The command was given to proceed as proposed.
Another edict stated: When offering sacrifices and making announcements at Cháng Líng (長陵) and the other seven mausoleums, [the emperor] should personally prostrate and bow;
at the mausoleums of Gōngràng Zhāng Huánghòu (恭讓章皇后) and Jǐng Huángdì (景皇帝), he should also offer a single prostration
to express feelings of remembrance and gratitude.
In the seventeenth year, the mausoleum hall was renamed Ēn Diàn (恩殿),
and its gate was named Ēn Mén (恩門).
Also, the Chéngzǔ Shènglì Tíng (成祖聖蹟亭) was completed on Píngtái Shān (平臺山),
and the emperor led his retinue in performing the sacrificial rites.
In the twenty-first year,
Gù Lín (顧璘), the Minister of Public Works (Gōngbù Shàngshū), requested that the imperial poems on the holy achievements of Xiǎnlíng (顯陵) be
set to music
for offerings at the mausoleum and temple.
The Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù) stated:
"At all the mausoleums in Tiānshòu Shān (天壽山),
music is not used for annual sacrifices."
Later, Fù Lín (傅霖), the eunuch serving as Garrison Commander (shǒubèi tàijiàn) of Chéngtiān Fǔ (承天府), requested an increase in the year-end sacrifice at Xiǎnlíng (顯陵).
The Ministry's deliberation stated:
"None of the mausoleums have regulations for year-end sacrifices."
An imperial edict ordered that both matters follow the Ministry's deliberation.
In the second year of Lóngqìng (隆慶),
the emperor went to Tiānshòu Shān (天壽山) for the spring sacrifice.
The day before, [he made announcements to] the jiàn (几筵) of Shìzōng (世宗) and the Fèngxiān (奉先), Hóngxiào (弘孝), and Shénxiāo (神霄) Diàn (殿).
The imperial carriage arrived at Hóng Mén (紅門) of Tiānshòu Shān (天壽山), where the emperor alighted from his sedan,
entered through the left gate,
re-entered his sedan,
and stopped at Gǎnsī Diàn (感思殿).
Two days later,
at dawn, the rites were performed.
The emperor, in a green robe,
rode in a plank sedan to outside the gate of Cháng Líng (長陵),
alighted from the sedan to the east,
entered through the left gate of the hall,
reached the bowing position,
offered incense,
and bowed four times.
Upon reaching the divine presence, he offered silk and wine, then
returned to his position.
For the second and final offerings,
he commanded the wine-pourers to act on his behalf,
and again bowed four times.
The rest followed the usual sacrificial ceremony.
He then proceeded to Yǒng Líng (永陵) to perform the rites.
On that day, six officials were dispatched,
all in green attire,
to perform sacrifices at the six mausoleums.
In the eighth year of Wànlì (萬曆),
the rites for visiting the mausoleums were as before.
In the eleventh year,
the emperor again visited the mausoleums.
The Ministry of Rites stated:
"It is fitting to follow the established regulations of Shìzōng (世宗),
and arrange for two days,
to visit and bow in sequence."
Thus, it was determined that at Cháng (長), Yǒng (永), and Zhāo (昭) Líng (陵),
incense would be offered,
eight bows made,
and silk personally presented.
For the first offering,
at the six mausoleums and two secondary mausoleums,
incense would be offered,
and four bows made.
For the presentation of silk for the three offerings,
all would be performed by attendant officials.
In the fourteenth year,
the Ministry of Rites stated:
"Regarding the imperial consorts buried in various places at Jīn Shān (金山),
during the Jiājìng (嘉靖) era, all were accorded sacrificial honors at the respective mausoleum halls,
and their separate tomb sacrifices were abolished.
Now, for the consorts of Shì Miào (世廟) interred in Xī Shān (西山),
this precedent should be followed.
As for the sacrificial offerings at the mausoleums,
at the nine imperial mausoleums and the mausoleums of Gōngràng (恭讓) and Gōngrén (恭仁), only wine and fruit are used,
while for Yuè (越) and Jìng (靖) princes and their consorts, there are also animals, fruits, and sacrificial prayers.
To follow the more lavish practice for the latter [seems contradictory],
because the emperors and empresses of the nine mausoleums
already receive combined year-end sacrifices at the temple,
and within ten days, there will also be the spring offering.
Therefore, at the mausoleum hall on New Year's Day, only wine and fruit are used,
which is not parsimonious;
for the princes and their consorts, who do not participate in either the combined or spring sacrifices,
the single New Year's Day sacrifice should not be simplified.
Thus, animals, silk, and sacrificial prayers are used,
which is not lavish.
However, since Gōngràng (恭讓) and Gōngrén (恭仁) do not participate in the combined offerings at the temple,
nor are animals and silk provided at their mausoleum halls,
this constitutes a deficiency in ritual,
and what is lacking should be added.
As for the sacrificial prayers for the princes and their consorts,
they still use those from the time of their interment,
which should be changed to reflect the meaning of dispatching officials at seasonal times,
so that sentiments are aligned and rites are settled."
The report was approved.
Regarding the regulations for the imperial mausoleums (shān líng),
there is a treasure city (bǎochéng);
Cháng Líng (長陵) is the largest, with a diameter of one hundred and one zhàng (丈) and eight chǐ (尺).
Next is Yǒng Líng (永陵), with a diameter of eighty-one zhàng (丈).
Each mausoleum differs in depth and width by zhàng (丈) and chǐ (尺).
Directly in front is the bright tower (mínglóu),
in which stands a stone tablet with the emperor's temple name and posthumous title,
and below it is the spiritual resting gate (língqǐn mén).
Only Yǒng Líng (永陵) has an arched gate (quànmén) inside.
To the left and right walls, there is one gate and one tower each.
In front of the bright tower is a stone altar (shí jǐyán),
and further in front are the Ēn Diàn (恩殿) and Ēn Mén (恩門).
Among the halls, only Cháng Líng (長陵) has a double-eaved, nine-bay hall,
with fifteen side halls on each side.
Yǒng Líng (永陵) has a double-eaved, seven-bay hall,
with nine side halls on each side.
All other mausoleums have five-bay halls,
and five-bay side halls.
Outside the gate, there is either one or two divine storehouses (shénkù),
a divine kitchen (shénchú), a slaughtering pavilion (zǎishēng tíng),
and a holy achievements stele pavilion (shènglì bēitíng).
All mausoleum steles are placed outside the gate,
and mostly have no inscription.
South of Cháng Líng (長陵) is the general spirit way (zǒng shéndào),
with stone bridges,
eighteen pairs of stone figures,
four sky-supporting pillars (qíngtiānzhù),
and two stone ornamental pillars (shí wàngzhù).
Cháng Líng (長陵) has a Stele of Divine Merit and Holy Virtue (Shéngōng Shèngdé Bēi),
personally composed by Rénzōng (仁宗),
located directly south of the spirit way.
To the south is Hóng Mén (紅門),
and outside the gate is a stone archway.
Inside the gate is Shízhì Diàn (時陟殿),
which serves as a changing room for the imperial carriage.
Slightly east of Yǒng Líng (永陵) is Gǎnsī Diàn (感思殿),
which serves as the imperial resting place.
East of the hall is the divine horse stable (shénmǎ chǎng).
Anniversary of Death (Jìchén):
In the fourth month of the eighth year of Hóngwǔ (洪武),
on the anniversary of Rénzǔ's (仁祖) death,
Tàizǔ (太祖) personally went to the imperial mausoleum to offer sacrifices.
In the first year of Yǒnglè (永樂),
Lǐ Zhìgāng (李至剛), Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū), and others submitted a memorial to establish that
two days before the anniversary of Gāo Huángdì's (高皇帝) death,
the emperor should wear light-colored clothing
and attend to affairs at the Xījiǎo Mén (西角門).
No bells or drums should be sounded,
no rewards or punishments issued,
no music played,
and slaughtering forbidden.
All officials should wear light-colored clothing and black horned belts for morning audience.
On the day itself,
the emperor should personally offer sacrifices at Fèngxiān Diàn (奉先殿),
and also lead all officials to Xiàolíng (孝陵) to offer sacrifices.
The anniversary of Gāo Huánghòu's (高皇后) death was to be observed similarly.
An order in the fourth year of Xuāndé (宣德) stipulated that
whenever an anniversary of death occurred,
the Tōngzhèng Sī (通政司), Lǐkē (禮科), and Bīngmǎ Sī (兵馬司) should not present prisoners for audience or report matters.
In the fifth year, an imperial edict instructed all officials to discontinue the audience and reporting ceremonies.
Upon Yīngzōng's (英宗) ascension,
he summoned officials from the Ministry of Rites and the Hànlín Yuàn (翰lín Yuàn) to deliberate on the rites for anniversaries of death.
Grand Academicians (Dàxuéshì) Yáng Shìqí (楊士奇) and Yáng Róng (楊榮),
and Academician (Xuéshì) Yáng Pǔ (楊溥) deliberated:
"Each year, on the anniversaries of Gāo Miào Dì Hòu (高廟帝后), Wén Miào Dì Hòu (文廟帝后), and Rénzōng (仁宗),
light-colored clothing should be worn,
no bells or drums sounded,
and affairs attended to at Fèngtiān Mén (奉天門).
On Xuānzōng's (宣宗) anniversary of death,
on the day of the lesser mourning (xiǎo xiáng),
affairs should be attended to at Xījiǎo Mén (西角門)."
This was adopted.
In the 14th year of Hóngzhì, an order was issued:
whenever an anniversary of death (jìchén) occurs,
officials attending court are not permitted to wear clothing made of zhùsī, shā, or luó.
On the death anniversaries of Emperor Jǐng and Empress Gōngràng,
if it coincides with a seasonal festival (jiélìng),
one should wear attire with blue silk patterns.
On Emperor Xuānzōng's death anniversary,
if it coincides with a sacrifice,
one should wear red.
In the 8th month of the 16th year,
Mǎ Wénshēng, Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū), stated:
"During the Xuāndé reign,
on Emperor Rénzōng's death anniversary,
all government offices (zhūsī) were exempted from presenting memorials.
From Emperor Tàizǔ to Emperor Rénzōng's birth and death anniversaries,
court was always suspended.
Later, at an unknown time,
on Emperor Rénzōng's death anniversary,
memorials continued to be presented as before.
Only on the death anniversaries from Emperor Tàizǔ to Emperor Xiànzōng,
all officials wore light-colored clothing and black horn belts.
The imperial court also held audiences,
bells and drums were sounded,
and memorials were presented.
I believe that from Rénzōng to Xiànzōng,
the generations have been near and far,
and the attire should reflect varying degrees of solemnity.
I request that on Emperor Rénzōng's death anniversary and Emperor Yīngzōng's birth anniversary,
court audiences be held,
and bells and drums be sounded.
If it coincides with Emperor Xiànzōng's or Empress Xiàomù's death anniversary,
no court audience should be held;
light-colored clothing should be worn,
plain meals should be consumed,
and no other matters should be attended to.
Alternatively, following the precedent from Emperor Xuānzōng's time,
from Emperor Tàizǔ to Emperor Xiànzōng's birth and death anniversaries,
court should be suspended for one day.
On Emperor Xiànzōng's and Empress Xiàomù's death anniversaries,
it should be as I have proposed."
The Emperor then referred the matter to the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù) for deliberation.
The ministry officials stated:
"According to the Classics and commentaries,
a 'jìrì' (death anniversary) is the day of a parent's death.
Thus, the day of death is the jì,
not the birth anniversary.
The saying 'jìrì bùyòng' (death anniversary not used)
means not to undertake other activities on this day.
The saying 'jìrì bùlè' (death anniversary not joyful)
means that auspicious events should not be held.
On this day, one should exclusively focus on mourning and remembrance of one's parents,
and all other matters should not be undertaken.
However, the precedents of previous dynasties
are still in effect,
and we dare not alter them."
The Emperor then made the decision to attend to affairs in light-colored attire.
In the 7th year of Jiājìng, an order was issued:
on a death anniversary, sacrifices should only be offered at the principal altar.
In the 18th year, an order was issued:
on the death anniversaries of Emperor Gāomiào and empresses, sacrifices should be offered at Jǐngshéndiàn.
On the death anniversaries of the successive emperors (lièshèng) and empresses, sacrifices should be offered at Yǒngxiàodiàn.
In the 24th year, an order was issued:
sacrifices should still be offered at Fèngxiāndiàn.
Protocol for the Emperor in His Imperial Carriage Receiving Funeral Announcements from Tributary Kings
Whenever a tributary king passes away,
and the envoy's funeral announcement arrives,
an imperial tent (yùwò) is set up in the ren-position (north-northwest) inside Xīhuámén Gate.
The Emperor, in plain attire, proceeds to the tent in his imperial carriage.
The Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng) announces:
"The heir apparent of [such-and-such] state has dispatched [such-and-such] official, his attendant,
to announce the passing of [such-and-such] king, his sovereign."
The official who conveys the imperial edict (chéngzhì guān) goes before the envoy and proclaims the edict, saying:
"The Emperor asks [such-and-such] king of your state,
'What illness caused your passing?'"
The envoy replies with the cause.
The general protocol is similar to that for attending the funeral of a prince, duke, or high minister,
but without expressing grief.
When funeral announcements arrive from dukes, governors, and other officials beyond the frontier,
during the Yǒnglè reign, an official was dispatched to offer incense and to read an imperial edict for the sacrifice.
Later, a regulation was established:
based on their request,
a memorial (biǎo) and a sacrificial text (zhàiwén) would be granted,
for them to take back and perform the sacrifice themselves.
For those who fell ill and died after coming to the capital,
an official would be dispatched to offer imperial sacrifice, or a coffin and burial would be bestowed.
Later, it was stipulated that at the end of the year, a collective memorial (lèizòu) would be presented,
and officials would be dispatched to perform sacrifices.
However, this rule does not apply to those who died in battle on the frontier.
For foreign envoys who fall ill and die,
the local officials are ordered to bestow a coffin and perform a sacrifice;
they may also return for burial if they wish.
Protocol for the Emperor in His Imperial Carriage Expressing Grief for Princes, Dukes, and High Ministers
In the 2nd year of Hóngwǔ, Cháng Yùchūn, Prince Kāipíng, died in the army.
When the news arrived,
the ritual officials requested to follow the precedent of Emperor Tàizōng of Sòng expressing grief for Zhào Pǔ.
Thus, a regulation was established:
whenever a prince or duke passes away,
the funeral announcement is reported to the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Sī),
which informs all officials.
An imperial tent (yùwò) is set up in the ren-position inside Xīhuámén Gate.
The imperial seat is arranged,
and a plain mat is placed.
The position for the funeral announcer (fùzhě) is set up in front,
and positions for all officials to accompany the crying are set facing east and west.
The position for conveying condolences (fèngwèi) is set north of the announcer's position,
facing north.
Two ritual officiants (zànlǐ) are positioned north of the announcer's position.
Two guides for the announcer (yǐnfùzhě) are positioned south of the ritual officiants.
Four guides for the officials (yǐnbǎiguān) are positioned north of the accompanying positions,
all facing east and west.
On that day,
the ceremonial guard is prepared at Fèntiānmén Gate to receive the imperial carriage.
The Emperor, in plain attire, proceeds to the tent in his imperial carriage.
Music is arranged south of the tent,
but not played.
The Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices announces:
"[Such-and-such] official has come with the funeral announcement.
On [such-and-such] date,
his humble servant, [such-and-such] official, passed away from [such-and-such] illness.
Please express grief."
The Emperor weeps,
and all officials weep.
The Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices announces to cease weeping.
After the officials offer condolences,
they stand in their respective ranks.
The announcer performs four bows and withdraws.
The Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices announces that the ceremony is concluded.
The imperial carriage returns to the palace,
and all officials depart.
The protocol for the Crown Prince (Dōnggōng) expressing grief for princes and dukes is the same,
except that the tent is set up outside the west gate of the Eastern Palace,
and those accompanying the crying are all subordinates of the Eastern Palace.
Protocol for the Emperor in His Imperial Carriage Attending the Funeral of Princes, Dukes, and High Ministers
Whenever a funeral announcement from a prince, duke, or high minister arrives,
the Directorate of Astronomy (Tàishǐ Jiān) selects a date for the Emperor to attend the funeral.
The Imperial Bodyguard (Gǒngwèi Sī) sets up a large pavilion (dàcì) outside the main gate of the bereaved family's residence,
and sets up the imperial seat in the main hall.
The responsible officials (yǒusī) set up positions for all officials to the left and right of the large pavilion.
The Ministry of Ceremonial (Shìyí Sī) sets up positions for all officials to stand in attendance to the left and right in front of the hall.
Four ritual guides (yǐnlǐ) are positioned north of the officials,
facing east and west.
Positions for the chief mourner and his subordinates to prostrate are set up in front of the hall.
Positions for the principal female mourner (zhǔfù) and her subordinates to weep are set up behind a curtain to the north of the coffin.
On that day,
the imperial carriage arrives at the large pavilion,
the ceremonial chariot (lù) is descended from,
the sedan chair (yú) is mounted,
and the Emperor enters to change into plain attire.
All officials also change their attire
and enter first to stand in their respective ranks in front of the hall.
The imperial sedan chair exits the pavilion.
The chief mourner and his subordinates remove their mourning sashes (dié) and staffs (zhàng),
in mourning attire,
and come out to welcome at the main gate.
Upon seeing the imperial carriage,
they cease weeping,
perform two bows,
and enter to the west inside the gate.
The imperial carriage enters the gate.
Four generals lead the way,
and four follow behind.
Upon entering the main hall,
the sedan chair is descended from,
and the Emperor ascends to the spirit altar.
All officials stand in ranks behind.
The Emperor weeps,
and all officials weep.
The Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices announces to cease weeping.
Three sticks of incense are offered,
and three libations of wine are poured.
The Emperor then exits to the imperial seat in the main hall.
The chief mourner and his subordinates proceed to the bowing positions below the hall
and perform two bows.
The official who conveys the imperial edict goes before the chief mourner and says,
"There is an imperial edict."
The chief mourner and his subordinates all kneel.
After the edict is proclaimed,
they all perform two bows
and withdraw to stand to the west of the hall.
The Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices announces that the ceremony is concluded.
The Emperor mounts the sedan chair
and exits to the large pavilion
to change attire.
When the imperial sedan chair exits,
the chief mourner and his subordinates come forward, perform two bows, and withdraw.
The Emperor descends from the sedan chair and mounts the ceremonial chariot.
The chief mourner weeps with his staff and enters.
Various ceremonial guards and announcers chant,
generally as usual.
Regulations for suspending court attendance for the funeral of a Gōng or Hóu,
established in the 23rd year of Hóngwǔ.
If a Gōng or Hóu dies at home,
upon hearing the news of the death, court is suspended for three days.
For the burial,
one day.
If they die away from home,
upon hearing the news,
one day.
When the coffin arrives in the capital,
three days.
For the burial,
still one day.
On days when court is suspended,
no bells or drums are sounded,
and all officials attend court in plain, light-colored clothes.
Initially, the rule was
that from a Dūdū down to a Dū Zhīhuī, if they died,
court would be suspended for two days.
After the Yǒnglè reign, this was revised,
so that only for Gōng, Hóu, Fùmǎ, Bó, and first-rank officials,
court would be suspended for one day.
Mourning rituals for the empress's father or ancestors.
If the empress's parents pass away,
the訃報 (fùbào) is sent to the Tàicháng Sì,
which then relays it to the Nèishǐ Jiān.
Before the appointed day,
a mat for offerings is set up beneath the east wall of a separate hall,
serving as the position for the empress to express her grief and for the inner court ladies and below to weep.
The empress goes out to this separate hall.
The Nèishǐ Jiān attendant announces,
"[Your] deceased father, such-and-such official, passed away on such-and-such month and day."
If it's the mother, it's announced as
"deceased mother, such-and-such夫人 (fūrén)."
The same applies for paternal grandparents.
The empress weeps,
and the inner court ladies and below all weep profusely.
The empress asks for the cause of death,
and again weeps profusely.
Then, dressed in plain clothes,
all inner court ladies also in plain clothes,
the weeping stops,
and she returns to the palace.
The Nèishǐ Jiān attendant then reports this.
An imperial edict is received:
"The empress shall attend the funeral."
At the mourning house, an offering mat is set up to the east of the mourning chamber,
with the attending inner court ladies weeping below it.
The chief mourner and below weep to the west of the mourning chamber,
and the principal female mourner and below weep beneath the curtain to the north of the mourning chamber.
On the appointed day,
the Nèishǐ Jiān presents a plain carriage,
with ceremonial guards to lead the way.
The empress, in plain clothes, leaves the palace,
ascends the palanquin,
which has white cloth curtains on three sides.
Upon reaching outside the gate,
she descends from the palanquin
and ascends the plain carriage.
Upon reaching inside the main gate of the mourning house,
she descends from the carriage, weeps, and enters,
still surrounded by the traveling curtains.
All those attending weep and enter.
The chief mourner and below
descend to stand and weep at the foot of the west steps.
The empress ascends from the east steps,
advances to the east of the corpse,
and leans on the corpse to weep.
All those attending weep.
The chief mourner ascends from the west steps,
and all weep to the west of the corpse.
When the empress reaches her weeping position,
the Nèishǐ Jiān attendant kneels and requests her to stop weeping.
Those who should offer condolences approach the empress,
and offer condolences according to the usual rites.
If the empress awaits the completion of the mourning attire,
then the attending ladies who should return, return first.
If the funeral is not attended immediately on that day,
then in the afternoon, weeping resumes in the separate hall.
The Shàngfú department prepares the empress's Qīcuī (齊衰) and the attending ladies' mourning clothes,
which are presented on the day the mourning family dons their attire.
She proceeds to the spirit altar, bows twice,
offers incense,
returns to her position,
and bows twice again.
If mourning for imperial princes' relatives,
it is still done in the separate hall, facing south,
without setting up an offering mat.
Ritual for sending envoys for condolences.
The Tàicháng Sī dispatches envoys by imperial decree for condolences.
Before the appointed day,
the position for announcing the imperial decree is set up to the north of the main hall of the mourning house,
facing south;
the position for the chief mourner to receive condolences is to the south,
facing north;
female mourners stand and weep beneath the curtain to the north of the coffin.
On that day,
the envoy arrives.
The chief mourner removes his staff,
takes off his hempen headband and mourning clothes,
stops weeping,
and goes out to the middle gate to greet the envoy.
He then enters first
and takes his bowing position in front of the hall.
Weeping stops inside and out.
The envoy enters
and, taking his position, announces "There is an imperial decree."
The chief mourner and below bow twice and kneel.
The decree is announced:
"The Emperor, upon hearing of the passing of such-and-such official,
sends his minister, so-and-so, to offer condolences."
The chief mourner and below bow twice again.
After the ceremony,
all inside and out weep.
The envoy departs.
The chief mourner goes to outside the middle gate,
bows in farewell,
and enters weeping with his staff.
If it is a palace envoy, it is announced as "There is an imperial order."
The rituals for sending envoys with posthumous gifts and offerings
are similar.
The standard posthumous gifts are:
for a first-rank official, sixty shí (石) of rice,
and sixty pǐ (匹) of hemp cloth.
For a second-rank official, it's five units less;
for third and fourth-rank, four units less;
for fifth and sixth-rank, three units less.
For Gōng and Hóu, it is one hundred.
After the Yǒnglè reign, a fixed system was established:
Gōng, Hóu, Fùmǎ, and Bó all receive gifts determined by imperial decision.
Those who die in battle receive the full amount.
Those who die of illness while guarding frontiers, on expeditions, or transporting grain by sea receive half.
Ritual for sending all officials to attend the funeral of a prince, Gōng, or high minister.
Before the appointed day,
the responsible department sets up seating arrangements at the mourning house.
On that day,
all officials who are to attend condolences arrive in plain clothes.
The chief mourner and below take their weeping positions at the east steps.
The principal female mourner and below take their weeping positions to the north of the coffin.
All officials enter,
take their positions in front of the coffin and weep.
The chief mourner and principal female mourner and below all weep.
Weeping stops,
they bow twice,
and the chief mourner and below return the bow.
The head of the group approaches the chief mourner to express condolences.
When finished, all officials depart.
The chief mourner bows in farewell,
and enters weeping with his staff.
The ritual for attending a burial is the same.
Ritual for sending envoys to confer posthumous titles on princes, Gōng, and high ministers.
Before the appointed day,
the Lǐbù requests the imperial decree for the册 (cè) document to be made.
The Hànlín Yuàn receives the imperial instruction to draft the text.
The Zhōngshū Shěng and Lǐbù request that a certain official be appointed as envoy.
On that day,
the Cí Jì Sī sets up a dragon pavilion and an incense pavilion in the center in front of the Wǔ Mén.
Attendants set up the official position for announcing the decree to the northeast of the main hall at the recipient's house,
facing south;
the chief mourner, acting on behalf of the recipient, takes position in front of the hall,
facing north.
An official from the Lǐbù seals the册 (cè) document,
places it in a gilded casket,
wraps it in a yellow cloth, and places it in the dragon pavilion.
Ceremonial guards and drum music lead the procession
to the house.
The representative recipient goes out to the main gate to greet them.
Attendants carry the dragon pavilion and place it in the center of the hall.
The envoy enters
and stands to the northeast.
The representative recipient takes his bowing position
and bows twice.
The envoy steps slightly forward
and announces,
"There is an imperial decree."
The representative recipient kneels.
The decree is announced:
"The Emperor sends his minister, so-and-so,
to confer posthumous titles on the late official, so-and-so, as such-and-such merit and such-and-such noble rank."
After the announcement,
the representative recipient bows twice again.
The envoy takes the册 (cè) document and presents it to him.
The representative recipient receives it and places it in front of the spirit tablet.
The envoy departs.
The representative recipient sees him off to outside the main gate.
If a册 (cè) document is not used,
the Lìbù uses a Gàomìng (誥命).
The mourning family prepares a yellow copy of the册 (cè) text,
and sets up a sacrificial ritual in front of the spirit tablet.
The representative recipient bows twice.
The attendant unfolds the yellow copy and reads it aloud to the left.
The chief mourner and below all bow twice,
and then burn the yellow copy.
Imperial gifts for sacrifice and burial.
In the ninth month of the fourteenth year of the Hóngwǔ reign (1381),
Yǎnshèng Gōng Kǒng Xīxué passed away.
An official was dispatched to offer sacrifices.
Thereafter,
regulations for the sacrifices and burials of all officials
were established.
The edicts for offering sacrifices to officials issued by Tài Zǔ
were often written with his imperial brush.
During the Jiājìng reign,
Shì Zōng personally composed sacrificial texts for the Minister of Rites, Xí Shū, and the Minister of War, Lǐ Chéngxūn.
These were all special favors,
not standard regulations.
In the twelfth month of the first year of the Lóngqìng reign (1567),
the Ministry of Rites debated and submitted articles on compassionate grants.
For the sacrifices and burials of all officials,
whether they were grand or humble,
all were to comply with the Huìdiǎn.
For special favors,

such as attendants who constantly assisted in lectures and readings, military officers who personally participated in battles and campaigns, and Eastern Palace officials who lectured in the palace with merit:
based on precedents from the Jiājìng reign,
sacrifices and burials were increased by one grade.
Those without sacrifices were granted one altar of sacrifice.
Those without burials were granted half a burial.
Those with half a burial were granted a full burial.
For lecturing officials of the fifth rank, they themselves received sacrifices.
For the fourth rank, their parents did.
For the third rank, their wives did.
For military officers of the fourth rank, they received sacrifices and burials.
For the third rank (if not yet full term), their parents did.
For those who had lectured for many years, provided much edification, died in military service, or had outstanding meritorious achievements,
the compassionate grants were increased generously,
and an imperial decree was to be requested at the time.
According to the Huìdiǎn,
all first-rank officials
received nine altars of sacrifice.
Additional sacrifices for parents and wives,
either two altars or one altar,
or for wives only one altar—
such favors were difficult to predetermine.
When a request was made,
a proposal was to be drafted and submitted.
Second-rank officials received
two altars.
If they were also one of the Three Junior Protectors of the Eastern Palace,
or concurrently Grand Academician and posthumously granted the first rank,
it increased to four altars.
Parents and wives each received one altar.
Retired officials who were also one of the Three Junior Protectors received an additional altar.
Those who were also Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince received an additional three altars.
If the wife had not been ennobled as a Fūrén, no sacrifice was offered.
Third-rank officials received sacrifices and burials.
Both serving and retired officials received one altar.
Those concurrently academicians and posthumously granted Minister of the Censorate received two altars.
Those who died of illness before completing their full term received half of one altar.
Funeral arrangements were all according to old precedents.
Fourth and fifth-rank officials could not receive double ennoblement.
Therefore, for fourth-rank officials promoted from the sixth or seventh rank,
their parents received sacrifices.
For those promoted from the fifth rank,
due to the rule against double ennoblement,
they subsequently did not receive sacrifices.
It is now decreed that for fourth-rank officials,
all who have completed their full term,
even if their parents were only granted the fifth-rank ennoblement,
also receive one altar of sacrifice.
For officials of the fourth rank and above,
favors for themselves and their parents
must be granted only after completing their full term.
However, some who held second and third-rank positions consecutively for four or five years,
and whose parents were not granted third-rank ennoblement,
ultimately received no sacrifices.
Their length of service should also be considered.
Officials who held second and third-rank positions consecutively for more than three years,
even if they had not completed their full term as third-rank officials,
both they themselves and their parents receive the sacrifices and burials of a third-rank official.
For those who held third and fourth-rank positions consecutively for more than three years,
even if they had not completed their full term as fourth-rank officials,
they themselves follow the precedent for third-rank officials who have not completed their full term,
receiving one and a half altars of sacrifice,
and their parents receive one altar of sacrifice for burial.
For those who were impeached and retired to idleness,
even if they received a general amnesty
and were reinstated to retirement,
they still do not receive sacrifices and burials.
For meritorious officials' sacrifices and burials,
and for imperial relatives, decisions are made by the emperor.
Fùmǎ Dūwèi received fifteen altars of sacrifice.

For Gōng, Hóu, and Bó who managed princely households and garrisoned camps internally, or served as regional commanders externally with outstanding achievements and were also granted Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince or above,
they were to comply with the Huìdiǎn.
Gōng and Hóu received sixteen altars,
Bó received fifteen altars.
Those who managed princely households, garrisoned camps, and were regional commanders with meritorious service received seven altars.
Those who managed princely households and garrisoned camps for long service received five altars.
Those who managed princely households and garrisoned camps but whose administrative achievements were not notable received four altars.
Those who oversaw affairs but were impeached, investigated, and confirmed to be retired to idleness received two altars.
Those who were impeached but not yet confirmed by investigation received one altar.
Those confirmed to have committed serious crimes
had their sacrifices and burials, which they would have otherwise received according to their rank, all rescinded.
Furthermore, during the Zhèngdé reign,
Gōng, Hóu, and Bó each received three altars of sacrifice as standard.
During the Jiājìng reign, it was two altars.
Now, the Jiājìng precedent is followed,
restoring the old system of the Huìdiǎn.
For military officials' sacrifices and burials,
the precedents of Zhèngdé and Jiājìng are followed.
Dūdū Tóngzhī, Qiānshì, and Jǐnyīwèi Zhǐhuī received three altars of sacrifice.
Acting Dūdū Tóngzhī and Qiānshì received one altar.
The rest were to be categorized similarly.
The emperor approved their proposal.
In the sixth year of the Wànlì reign (1578), it was further revised:
all officials who retired, were on sick leave, retired to care for parents, or were awaiting appointment,
their sacrifices and burials were the same as those of incumbent officials.
In the twelfth year (1584), it was further stipulated:
for officials who were impeached and requested retirement,
if, after a long period of deliberation, it was determined there was originally nothing objectionable,
they would still be given sacrifices and burials.
Their parents and wives would be differentiated according to their own rank.
The regulations for funerals
were established in the fifth year of Hóngwǔ (1372).
For shrouds,
officials of the third rank and above received three;
fourth and fifth rank, two;
sixth rank and below, one.
For rice and pearls in the mouth (fànhán),
fifth rank and above received millet and pearls;
ninth rank and above received rice and small pearls.
For funerary banners (míngjīng) and crimson silk streamers (jiàngbó),
the width was one strip.
Fourth rank and above, nine feet long;
sixth rank and above, eight feet;
ninth rank and above, seven feet.
For burial clothes,
officials received one set of court attire
and ten sets of regular attire,
and ten quilts.
A spirit tablet was placed in front of the coffin,
using white silk to tie a soul banner to which the spirit would attach.
For coffins and outer coffins (guānguǒ),
officials' coffins were made of oiled fir and painted vermilion,
and outer coffins were made of common fir.
For funeral wall screens (qiángshà),
Gōng and Hóu had six;
third rank and above, four;
fifth rank and above, two.
For burial objects (míngqì),
Gōng and Hóu had ninety items;
first and second rank, eighty items;
third and fourth rank, seventy items;
fifth rank, sixty items;
sixth and seventh rank, thirty items;
eighth and ninth rank, twenty items.
"Yǐn"
refers to the ropes for pulling the hearse.
"Pī"
refers to the crimson cloth,
tied to the four pillars of the hearse,
held by attendants on the sides
to prevent overturning.
"Duó"
refers to bronze bells,
used to regulate the funeral dirges.
Gōng and Hóu had four pulling ropes and six Pī cloths,
and eight Duó on each side.
First and second rank had three pulling ropes and four Pī cloths,
and six Duó on each side.
Third and fourth rank had two pulling ropes and two Pī cloths,
and four Duó on each side.
Fifth rank and below
had two pulling ropes and two Pī cloths,
and two Duó on each side.
Feather banners (yǔfān) had poles nine feet long.
Fifth rank and above,
one person held it to lead the coffin.
Sixth rank and below did not use them.
Rough hemp cloth (gōngbù)
was used by officials,
three feet long.
Fāngxiàng figures,
fourth rank and above had four eyes;
seventh rank and above, two eyes;
eighth rank and below did not use them.
The Willow Hearse (liǔchē) used bamboo latticework on top,
decorated with colorful knots.
Curtains were hung on the sides,
and heavy tassels at the four corners.
Two tomb tablets (zhìshí),
used by all officials.
One was the cover,
inscribed "Tomb of such-and-such official."
The other was the base,
inscribed with the name, hometown, three ancestral generations, birth year, death and burial dates, descendants, and burial location.
For women, it followed their husband and descendants' ennoblement.
The two stones faced each other,
bound with iron and buried in the tomb.
For sacrificial offerings,
fourth rank and above used sheep and pigs;
ninth rank and above used pigs.
Initially,
in the second year of Hóngwǔ, an imperial edict ordered the burial of Kāipíng Wáng Cháng Yùchūn on the northern slope of Zhōngshān,
and ninety sets of burial objects were provided
to be placed in the tomb.
Two gongs,
four drums,
two red flags and two whisks,
one red silk canopy, one saddle, and one cage,
two bows,
three arrows,
one stove, one cauldron, and one brazier,
all made of wood.
One water jar, one set of armor, one helmet, one cup stand, one _zhǎn_, one pot, one vase, one wine jar, one spittoon, one washbasin, and one incense burner,
two candle holders,
one incense box and one incense spoon,
two incense chopsticks,
one bottle for incense spoons and chopsticks, one tea bell, and one tea cup,
two chopsticks,
two spoons,
one bottle for spoons and chopsticks,
two bowls,
twelve plates,
two pouches,
all made of tin
and wrapped in gold.
One ceremonial sword, one _yá zhàng_,
one gold-wrapped standing melon,
two bone _gǔ suì_ and two rattling sections,
one folding chair, one footrest, and one horse stool,
six ceremonial horses,
one spear, one sword, one axe, one crossbow, one dining table, one bed, one screen, one staff, one chest, one folding bed, and one incense table,
two stools,
all made of wood.
Sixteen musicians,
twenty-four ceremonial guards,
six horse controllers,
ten maidservants,
four deities: Qīnglóng, Báihǔ, Zhūquè, Xuánwǔ,
two door gods,
ten warriors,
all made of wood,
each one _chǐ_ high.
Miscellaneous items:
six _shà_,
one _bì_,
one basket, one _sì_, one clothes hanger, one clothes rack, one _jīn_, and one _pán_,
two _bāo_,
two _shāo_,
two grain and beverage bottles,
one oil bottle,
one gauze curtain and one warm tent.
Three bolts of blue silk,
two bolts of scarlet silk,
each bolt eighteen _chǐ_ long.
Later, the regulations were set:
dukes and marquises with ninety items should follow this.
The rest were to be reduced in sequence.
Stele and Tablets
In the early Míng dynasty,
when civil and military ministers passed away,
it was customary to petition the emperor,
who would command a Hànlín official to compose an inscription
for a spirit-path stele.

Only during the reign of Tàizǔ for Zhōngshān Wáng Xú Dá, during the reign of Chéngzǔ for Róngguó Gōng Yáo Guǎngxiào, and during the Hóngzhì reign for Chāngguó Gōng Zhāng Luán, when they built their ancestral tombs,
were the inscriptions all personally written by the emperor.
The system for these
was established in the third year of Hóngwǔ.
Officials of the fifth rank and above used steles,
with a tortoise-base and a _chī_ head.
Officials of the sixth rank and below used tablets,
with a square base and a round head.
In the fifth year, the system was re-detailed.
For meritorious officials ennobled as kings after their death,
the _chī_ head was three _chǐ_ two _cùn_ high,
the stele body nine _chǐ_ high,
and three _chǐ_ six _cùn_ wide,
the tortoise-base three _chǐ_ eight _cùn_ high.
First rank: _chī_ head.
Second rank: Qílín and Fèng covering.
Third rank: Tiānlù and Bìxié covering.
Fourth to seventh ranks: square base.
The head, compared to those ennobled as kings after their death,
was progressively reduced by two _cùn_,
stopping at one _chǐ_ eight _cùn_.
The stele body was progressively reduced by five _cùn_,
stopping at five _chǐ_ five _cùn_.
Its width was progressively reduced by two _cùn_,
stopping at two _chǐ_ two _cùn_.
The base was progressively reduced by two _cùn_,
stopping at two _chǐ_ four _cùn_.
The system for tombs and graves
was also established in the third year of Hóngwǔ.
First rank:
the grave site circumference was ninety _bù_,
the tomb mound one _zhàng_ eight _chǐ_ high.
Second rank:
eighty _bù_,
one _zhàng_ four _chǐ_ high.
Third rank:
seventy _bù_,
one _zhàng_ two _chǐ_ high.
For these ranks, there were six stone beasts each.
Fourth rank:
forty _bù_.
Seventh rank and below: twenty _bù_,
six _chǐ_ high.
In the fifth year, it was re-established.
For meritorious officials ennobled as kings after their death,
the grave site circumference was one hundred _bù_,
the tomb mound two _zhàng_ high,
the surrounding tomb wall one _zhàng_ high,
four stone figures,
two civil and two military,
two stone tigers, sheep, horses, and two stone spirit-path pillars each.
For first to sixth ranks, the grave site was as per the old system,
the seventh rank added ten _bù_.
First rank tomb mound one _zhàng_ eight _chǐ_ high,
second to seventh ranks progressively reduced by two _chǐ_.
First rank tomb wall nine _chǐ_ high,
second to fourth ranks progressively reduced by one _chǐ_,
fifth rank four _chǐ_.
First and second ranks had two stone figures,
one civil and one military,
two tigers, sheep, horses, and spirit-path pillars each.
Third and fourth ranks had no stone figures,
fifth rank had no stone tigers,
sixth rank and below had none.
During the reign of Tàizǔ,
the tomb of Yáng Wáng in Xūyí was provided with two hundred and ten tomb guards,
the tomb of Xú Wáng in Sùzhōu with ninety-three tomb guards,
and the tomb of Chúyáng Wáng in Chúzhōu was also provided with tomb guards.
In the fourth year, meritorious officials Lǐ Shàncháng, Xú Dá, Cháng Mào, and Féng Shèng were granted one hundred and fifty tomb guards;
Dèng Yù, Táng Shèngzōng, Lù Zhònghēng, Huá Yúnlóng, Gù Shí, Chén Dé, Gěng Bǐngwén, Wú Zhēn, Sūn Kè, and Guō Xīng were granted one hundred tomb guards.
In the fifteenth year of Chénghuà,
the Nánjīng Ministry of Rites reported:
"The tombs of fourteen meritorious officials, including Cháng Yùchūn and Lǐ Wénzhōng,
are all outside the city of Nánjīng.
Lǐ Wénzhōng's great-grandson È and others
stated that they were in disrepair due to age,
and requested that workers be assigned for their repair."
The emperor approved their memorial,
and also ordered that for those without descendants,
one person should be assigned to guard the tomb.
Bestowal of Posthumous Titles
Princes (qīn wáng) generally used one character;
princes (jùn wáng) used two characters,
the same for civil and military ministers.
Whether to bestow or not
was decided by the emperor.
If an official's rank was not high but they had rendered service in attendance,
or if they had died diligently performing their duties,
a posthumous title was specially granted;
this was not the usual custom.
In the early Hóngwǔ reign,
for those who deserved a posthumous title,
the Ministry of Rites would request an imperial decree
and instruct the Hànlín Academy to draft a memorial.
In the fifteenth year of Hóngzhì, a system was established:
whenever a prince (qīn wáng) died,
the provincial governors (_fǔ_ and _àn_) would act;
when a prince (jùn wáng) died,
the prince of their own prefecture and the attendant chief secretary would act;
they would investigate and report to the throne,
and then deliberate on the posthumous title.
For civil and military ministers requesting posthumous titles,
the Ministry of Rites would seek an imperial decree,
and instruct the Ministry of Personnel and Ministry of War to verify their achievements.
The Ministry of Rites would classify them into three grades:
those with excellent conduct and achievements were superior,
those who were fairly good were medium,
and those with no commendable achievements were inferior;
these would be sent to the Hànlín Academy to propose a posthumous title.
If someone deserved a posthumous title but had not received it,
the _fǔ_ and _àn_ officials, as well as the Censorate officials, would report it.
According to the old system of the early Míng dynasty,
the rules for posthumous titles ranged from seventeen characters to one character,
each with its own distinctions.
However, throughout the reign of Gāo Dì,
civil officials never received posthumous titles,
and military officials could not receive them unless they were granted the titles of Hóu or Bó.
The two princes, Lǔ Wáng and Qín Wáng, were styled Hāng and Mǐn.
It was not until Jiànwén granted a posthumous title to Wáng Yī,
and Chéngzǔ granted one to Hú Guǎng,
that civil officials began to receive posthumous titles.
By the time of Shìzōng, this practice was extended indiscriminately even to Daoist alchemists,
and four-character titles were added.
According to established regulations,
officials of the third rank were eligible for posthumous titles,
and literary officials were titled
"Wén."
However, there were also cases where officials below the third rank received posthumous titles,
and where the title
"Wén"
was not exclusive to literary officials.
This was sometimes due to meritorious service,
sometimes due to integrity and righteousness,
or sometimes due to reputation and substance,
breaking with convention for distinguished commendation,
to serve as an encouragement.
There were also occasional instances of improper or excessive awards.
In the first year of Wànlì,
the Minister of Rites stated:
"For high officials who are eligible for posthumous titles,
it is fitting to widely consult and strictly examine their cases.
For those who are eligible but have not yet been petitioned for,
regardless of how long ago their deaths occurred,
the Fǔ, Àn, Kē, and Dào officials should propose them,
and after deliberation, they should be supplemented."
In the twelfth year,
the Minister of Rites stated:
"Posthumous titles for high officials
must be publicly acknowledged and accepted,
without any blemish,
and should be submitted for imperial decision.
If their conduct was ordinary,
even if their official rank was high,
they should not be granted indiscriminately."
The Emperor followed all these recommendations.
In the thirty-first year,
Guō Zhèngyù, a Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites, requested a strict enforcement of the posthumous title regulations.
He proposed revoking the titles of four individuals:
Xǔ Lùn,
Huáng Guāngshēng, Lǚ Běn, and Fàn Qiān;
one person whose title should be revoked but was altered instead:
Chén Zàn;
and seven to be supplemented:
Wǔ Wéndìng, Wú Tì, Lǔ Mù, Yáng Jìzōng, Zōu Zhì, Yáng Yuán, and Chén Yǒunián.
Grand Secretaries Shěn Yīguàn and Zhū Gēng strongly protected Lǚ Běn,
and his proposal was not followed.
Soon after,
Censor Zhāng Bāngjùn requested that Lǚ Nán be enshrined in the Confucius Temple,
and also discussed fourteen individuals who should be supplemented with posthumous titles, including
Yōng Tài and Wèi Xuézēng.
After long deliberation by the Ministry,
a total of seventy-four individuals were collectively proposed in separate submissions,
but they were kept by the emperor and not acted upon.
It was not until the first year of Tiānqǐ that an imperial decree finally approved them,
and ten more individuals who had been subsequently petitioned for were added,
but nine of Bāngjùn's original requests were not included.
Wǔ Wéndìng and others requested by Zhèngyù were also finally settled at this point.
In total, there were eighty-four individuals.
Among those of lower official rank who received posthumous titles,
Zōu Zhì, Liú Tái, Wèi Liángbì, Zhōu Tiānzuǒ, Yáng Yǔnshéng, Shěn Liàn, Yáng Yuán, Huáng Gǒng, Yáng Shèn, Zhōu Yí, Zhuāng Quán, and Féng Yìngjīng all received them for their forthright remonstrance;
Mèng Qiū, Zhāng Yuánbiàn, Cáo Duān, Hè Qīn, Chén Màoliè, Mǎ Lǐ, and Táo Wànglíng all for their scholarship and conduct;
Zhāng Quán for his loyalty and righteousness;
Lǐ Mèngyáng for his literary talent;
Lǔ Mù, Yáng Jìzōng, Zhāng Cháoruì, Zhū Guān, Fù Xīndé, and Zhāng Yǔnjì all for their integrity.
Yáng Shèn's posthumous title of Wénxiàn
and Zhuāng Quán's Wénjié
also encompassed their literary achievements.
In the third year,
Lín Yáoyú, Minister of the Ministry of Rites, stated:
"The posthumous title ceremony is held every five years.
Since the forty-fifth year of Wànlì until now,
for those who have received imperial benevolence but not yet a posthumous title,
the Nine Ministers and Censorates should meet and deliberate with my Ministry."
The Emperor approved.
However, at this time,
the timing was inconsistent.
In the sixth year,
Péng Rǔnán, a Supervising Censor of the Ministry of Rites, stated:
"What is observed nearby is truly remembered.
It is fitting not to exceed the five-year limit."
He also said:
"Officials of the third rank and above should be granted posthumous titles,
and the loyalty and righteousness of the Jiànwén officials,
the participation of Táo Ān and others in the military council,
and the martyrdom of Yè Chēn and others on the battlefield,
should all be supplemented with posthumous titles."
The matter was referred to the Ministry of Rites,
which deemed the Jiànwén officials not easy to lightly propose,
so it was not carried out.
It was not until the time of Fú Wáng
that, following the suggestion of Lǐ Qīng, a Supervising Censor of the Ministry of Works,
posthumous titles were posthumously granted to fourteen founding meritorious officials including Lǐ Shàncháng,
fourteen remonstrating officials of Zhèngdé including Jiǎng Qīn,
and nine tragically deceased officials of Tiānqǐ including Zuǒ Guāngdòu.
And the Jiànwén Emperor's younger brothers Yǔnchēng, Yǔnjī, and Yǔnqián,
and his son Wénkuí,
also received posthumous supplements due to clear memorials.
Funeral Rites for Officials
The funeral rites for officials recorded in the Jílǐ and Huìdiǎn
are based on the Yílǐ: Shì Sāng (Funeral Rites for Scholars),
referred to the Táng dynasty regulations,
and also incorporated the compilation of Zhūzǐ Jiālǐ,
making them generally understood and practiced.
Here, the main points are listed,
but the detailed rituals are not fully recorded.
Regarding the initial rites upon death:
when ill,
one is moved to the main chamber.
During the "testing with floss" ritual,
one waits until breathing has ceased before wailing.
The chief mourner (Sāng Zhǔ) and chief female mourner (Zhǔ Fù) are appointed,
with competent descendants serving as funeral guardians.
The coffin is prepared, and訃告 (obituaries) are sent out.
A corpse bed and draped hall are set up,
and a pit is dug.
Bathing implements are prepared;
four people bathe the deceased,
or three for those of the sixth rank and below,
then the mouth is filled.
An empty seat is placed,
a soul banner is tied,
and a funerary banner (míngjīng) is erected.
On the day after death, the small encoffining (xiǎoliǎn) takes place.
The day after that, the grand encoffining (dàliǎn) occurs,
the coffin is closed,
and a spirit bed is placed to the east of the coffin.
The day after that,
people of the five degrees of mourning all wear their respective mourning clothes,
and then mourn and offer condolences in the morning.
After mourning clothes are donned,
morning and evening offerings are made,
and after one hundred days, the initial wailing ceases (zúkū).
Then a burial site is chosen,
and after three months, the burial takes place.
The Hòutǔ is informed,
and then the burial pit is dug.
A memorial stone is carved,
burial objects (míngqì) are made,
a grand hearse is prepared,
and a spirit tablet (shénzhǔ) is made.
After the funeral procession departs,
upon arrival at the tomb,
the interment occurs.
The funerary banner and memorial stone are placed inside the pit,
the pit is covered and refilled with earth,
and then the Hòutǔ is worshipped at the tomb.
The spirit tablet is inscribed,
and reverently installed.
One ascends the carriage and returns home, wailing.
Regarding the Yú sacrifices:
on the day of the burial,
at midday, the first Yú sacrifice is performed.
On a "soft day" (róurì, an even-numbered day), a second Yú sacrifice,
and on a "hard day" (gāngrì, an odd-numbered day), a third Yú sacrifice.
If the distance from home requires an overnight stay or more,
the first Yú sacrifice is performed at the burial site.
If the tomb is far,
and a róurì is encountered en route,
it is also performed at the lodging place.
However, the third Yú sacrifice
must await arrival at home before being performed.
After the third Yú sacrifice,
on a gāngrì, the wailing ceases (zúkū).
The next day, the spirit tablet is enshrined in the family ancestral temple (fù jiāmiào).
After one year, the minor mourning ceremony (xiǎoxiáng) is held.
The mourning period up to this point is thirteen months,
not counting intercalary months.
Anciently, a day was divined for the sacrifice,
but now only the first death anniversary (chūjì) is used,
and the chief mourner changes into light mourning clothes (liànfú).
After two years, the major mourning ceremony (dàxiáng) is held.
The mourning period up to this point is twenty-five months,
and only the second death anniversary (dì'èrjìrì) is used for the sacrifice.
The light mourning clothes (dǎnfú) are displayed,
and the transfer is announced at the ancestral hall.
The spirit tablet is re-inscribed,
and moved progressively westward,
and the spirit tablet is reverently placed in the ancestral hall.
The spirit seat is removed,
and the spirit tablet is reverently moved and buried beside the tomb.
After the dàxiáng,
after an interval of one month, the dǎn sacrifice is performed.
The mourning period up to this point totals twenty-seven months.
On a chosen day,
the chief mourner, wearing dǎnfú, proceeds to the ancestral hall
to respectfully perform the dǎn ceremony.
Those who hear of a death from afar,
upon first hearing,
change their clothes,
cry, and set out.
Upon arriving home,
they lean on the coffin and weep,
and after four days complete the mourning attire.
If they are unable to set out yet,
then they set up a spirit tablet,
and after four days change their clothes.
If the burial has already taken place,
then they first weep at the tomb,
return home and weep before the spirit tablet,
and after four days complete the mourning attire.
Those observing mourning from Qīcuī downwards, upon hearing of a death,
set up a spirit tablet and weep.
If they rush to the funeral,
they complete the mourning attire upon arriving home.
If they do not rush to the funeral,
they complete the mourning attire after four days.
Whenever there is a reburial,
the xiàozǐ and below, as well as wives, concubines, and daughters,
all wear Sīmá mourning attire;
Zhōuqīn and below wear plain clothes.
There are no ancestral offerings,
no crying back (after burial),
no Fāngxiāngquítóu;
the rest follows the usual burial rites.
After the burial,
one observes the first Yú offering before the auspicious curtain and spirit tablet.
The xiàozǐ and below,
go out to a separate place,
remove their Sīmá mourning attire, wear plain clothes, and return.
In the fourth month of Hóngwǔ twenty-sixth year, the system of Qīfú rushing to funerals was abolished.
Previously, all officials, upon hearing of the deaths of their grandparents, paternal uncles, or brothers,
were allowed to rush to the funerals.
At this time, the Lìbù reported:
"Grandparents, paternal uncles, and brothers all observe Qīnián mourning.
If all are allowed to rush to funerals and observe mourning,
some might successively encounter five or six Qīnián deaths,
or the journey might be several thousand lǐ,
resulting in less time serving in office,
frequent changes,
and neglect of official duties.
From now on, except for parents and paternal grandparents who are the primary inheritors and observe Dīngyōu,
for other Qīnián deaths, rushing is not permitted;
only send someone to offer sacrifices."
This was adopted.
For the funeral rites of scholars and commoners,
as recorded in the Jílǐ and Huìdiǎn,
the general outline imitates the system for officials,
with minor additions or subtractions.
In Hóngwǔ first year,
Yùshǐ Gāo Yuánkǎn stated:
"The people of Jīngshī,
following old customs,
whenever there is a funeral,
hold banquets,
gather relatives and friends,
and perform music to entertain the deceased,
without any signs of grief or sorrow,
which is utterly inappropriate for governing.
I request that this be prohibited to strengthen moral customs."
Thereupon, the Lǐguān were ordered to establish regulations for commoners' mourning attire.
In the fifth year, an imperial edict stipulated:
"For commoners' burial clothes, one set is used,
consisting of one shēnyī, one dàdài, and one pair of shoes;
skirts, trousers, shirts, and socks are as they usually wear.
Rice for the mouth-filling ceremony uses liáng,
with three coins included.
The míngjīng uses five chì of red silk.
Burial shroud and relatives' gifts are as they possess.
〔一一〕The coffin should be made of sturdy wood,
with yóushān being superior,
bǎi next,
and túshān sōng next to that.
Black lacquer and gold lacquer are to be used;
vermilion red is not permitted.
One set of míngqì.
Three chì of white cloth are used for the gōngbù to draw the hearse.
〔一二〕The liǔchē covers the coffin with a quilt.
Two zhìshí tablets,
following the official ceremony.
The tomb mound should be eighteen bù in circumference.
Sacrifices use a pig,
according to what the family has."
Another edict stated:
"The ancient funeral rites
were based on grief and sorrow,
and the provisions for the funeral
were commensurate with the family's means.
In recent times,
the wealthy have indulged in excessive extravagance,
while those lacking means have borrowed money and goods,
boasting about the funeral procession.
Some are also misled by fēngshuǐ,
keeping coffins for years
without burial.
It should be ordered that the Zhōngshūshěng ministers convene to deliberate and establish regulations,
which are to be promulgated and observed.
Violators shall be punished."
It was also decreed to the Lǐbù:
"The ancients had the command to cover bones and bury corpses.
In recent times, people have become accustomed to the Yuán customs,
where the deceased are sometimes cremated by fire,
and their bones thrown into water.
Nothing is more damaging to affection and corrupting to customs than this.
This shall be prohibited.
If the poor have no land,
the local officials shall select spacious land for public cemeteries,
allowing them to be buried.
If there are those who served as officials far from home and cannot return for burial,
the officials shall provide funds for their return."
Mourning Periods
At the beginning of the Míng dynasty, the Dàmíng Lìng was promulgated,
and the various grades of mourning attire
largely followed those of previous dynasties.
In Hóngwǔ seventh year,
the Xiàocílù was completed,
and its illustrations were again included in the Dàmíng Lìng,
displayed both internally and externally.
Previously, when Guìfēi Sūnshì passed away,
an imperial edict commanded the Lǐguān to establish mourning regulations.
Lǐbù Shàngshū Niú Liàng and others reported:
"According to the Zhōu Yílǐ,
if the father is alive,
one observes Qīnián mourning for the mother,
but for a concubine mother, there is no mourning."
Tàizǔ said:
"The affection for parents is one,
yet the distinction is so great;
this is utterly unreasonable."
Thereupon, he commanded Hànlín Yuàn Xuéshì Sòng Lián and others, saying:
"Supporting the living and sending off the dead
are the great policies of sagely kings.
Avoiding talk of death and illness
are the vulgar customs of a decadent age.
The mourning rites of the Sāndài were lost during the decadent Zhōu,
and suppressed during the tyrannical Qín.
From Hàn and Táng onwards,
none could deliberate on this.
Human emotions are boundless,
but ritual makes them appropriate.
What the human heart finds peace in,
that is where heavenly principles reside.
You all shall thoroughly investigate and establish the mourning rites."
Consequently, Lián and others found that among those who discussed observing mourning for mothers, there were forty-two individuals;
twenty-eight wished to observe three years,
and fourteen wished to observe Qīnián.
Tàizǔ said:
"Three years of mourning
is a universal mourning period.
Observing those who wish to observe three years,
they are double those who wish to observe Qīnián.
Is this not what heavenly principles and human emotions find peace in?"
Thus, it was established as a fixed regulation.
A son for his parents,
a concubine's son for his biological mother,
all observe Zhǎncuī for three years.
A principal son and other sons for a concubine mother
all observe Qīcuī with a staff for Qīnián.
He further ordered that the Wǔfú mourning system
be compiled into a book,
for internal and external observance.
There are five types of mourning attire.
Zhǎncuī,
made of the coarsest hemp cloth,
with the lower edge unstitched.
Qīcuī,
made of slightly coarser hemp cloth,
with the lower edge stitched.
Dàgōng,
made of coarse cooked cloth.
Xiǎogōng,
made of slightly coarser cooked cloth.
Sīmá,
made of slightly finer cooked cloth.
There are eight categories of mourning.
Those who observe Zhǎncuī for three years include: a son for his parents,
a concubine's son for his biological mother,
a son for his stepmother;
a son for his Címǔ (referring to when the mother dies and the father orders another concubine to raise him),
a son for his foster mother (referring to one who was adopted out to others from a young age);
an unmarried daughter for her parents,
a married daughter who is divorced and returns home for her parents;
a principal grandson who is the primary inheritor for his grandparents and great-great-grandparents;
one who is adopted as heir for his adopted parents,
and who is the primary inheritor for his adopted grandparents;
if the husband is adopted as heir, the wife follows in mourning;
a wife for her husband's parents;
a concubine's son's wife for her husband's biological mother;
a wife or concubine for her husband.
Those who observe Qīcuī Zhàngqī mourning are: the legitimate son and other sons for their concubine mother;
the legitimate son's wife and other sons' wives for their husband's concubine mother,
for a remarried mother, a divorced mother, or a stepmother who remarried after the father's death and whom the child followed;
a husband for his wife.
Those who observe Qīcuī Bùzhàngqī mourning are: parents for their legitimate eldest son and other sons,
parents for their unmarried daughters,
a stepmother for the eldest son and other sons,
a foster mother for the eldest son and other sons;
a grandson for his paternal grandparents,
a granddaughter, even if married, does not reduce (her mourning grade),
and this applies to paternal great-grandparents and great-great-grandparents;
for paternal uncles and aunts;
a concubine for her husband's eldest son and other sons,
and for the son she bore;
for brothers,
for brothers' sons and brothers' unmarried daughters,
for paternal aunts and unmarried sisters;
a concubine for the principal wife;
a remarried mother or divorced mother for her sons;
an unmarried daughter, or a married daughter who has no husband or son,
for her brothers and brothers' sons;
a remarried stepmother for her former husband's sons who follow her;
for a stepfather with whom one cohabits, when neither has a Dàgōng or closer relationship to the other (from the original family);
a woman for her husband's brothers' sons,
a woman for her husband's brothers' unmarried children;
a married daughter for her parents;
a concubine for her parents;
one who has been adopted as heir for his (adoptive) parents;
a married daughter for her brothers who are successors to the father;
a paternal grandfather for his legitimate grandson;
parents for their eldest son's wife.
Those who observe Qīcuī Wǔyuè mourning are: for paternal great-grandparents.
Those who observe Qīcuī Sānyuè mourning are: for paternal great-great-grandparents,
for a stepfather with whom one formerly cohabited but now does not,
for a stepfather with whom one cohabits, but both have Dàgōng or closer relatives (of their own to mourn).
Those who observe Dàgōng Jiǔyuè mourning are: for paternal first cousins (brothers) and unmarried paternal first cousins (sisters),
for paternal aunts, sisters, and brothers' married daughters;
parents for the wives of their other sons,
and for their married daughters;
a paternal grandfather for his other grandsons;
for brothers' sons' wives;
a wife for her husband's paternal grandparents,
for her husband's paternal uncles and aunts,
for her husband's brothers' sons' wives,
for her husband's brothers' married daughters;
a married daughter for the paternal uncles and aunts of her natal clan,
and for her brothers and brothers' sons,
for paternal aunts, sisters, and brothers' unmarried daughters;
one who has been adopted as heir for his (adoptive) brothers and unmarried (adoptive) paternal aunts and sisters;
a wife for her husband's birth parents;
for brothers' sons who have been adopted as heirs (to other families).
Those who observe Xiǎogōng Wǔyuè mourning are: for paternal granduncles and grandaunts,
for paternal first cousins once removed,
for paternal second cousins (brothers) and unmarried paternal second cousins (sisters),
for sons of paternal first cousins,
for unmarried paternal grandaunts,
for unmarried sisters of paternal granduncles,
for unmarried daughters of paternal first cousins,
for brothers' wives;
one who has been adopted as heir for his (adoptive) paternal aunts and sisters who are married;
for a legitimate grandson's wife,
for married paternal first cousins (sisters),
for married granddaughters,
for brothers' grandsons and brothers' unmarried granddaughters,
for maternal grandparents,
for maternal uncles and aunts,
for half-siblings sharing the same mother but different fathers,
for sisters' sons;
a wife for her husband's paternal aunts and sisters,
for her husband's brothers and her husband's brothers' wives,
for her husband's brothers' grandsons and husband's brothers' unmarried granddaughters,
for her husband's paternal first cousins' sons and husband's paternal first cousins' unmarried daughters.
Those who observe Sīmá Sānyuè mourning are: for clan paternal great-grandparents,
for clan paternal granduncles and grandaunts,
for clan paternal uncles and aunts,
for clan paternal cousins (brothers) and unmarried clan paternal cousins (sisters),
for unmarried clan paternal great-grandaunts,
for unmarried clan paternal grandaunts and clan paternal aunts,
for brothers' great-grandsons,
and the same for their unmarried great-granddaughters,
for great-grandsons and great-great-grandsons,
for grandsons of paternal first cousins,
and the same for their unmarried granddaughters,
for sons of paternal second cousins,
and the same for their unmarried daughters,
for married paternal grandaunts, sisters of paternal granduncles, and paternal second cousins (sisters),
for brothers' married granddaughters,
for paternal first cousins' married daughters,
for a wet nurse,
for maternal cousins (sons of maternal uncles),
for paternal aunts' sons (cross-cousins),
for maternal aunts' sons (cross-cousins),
for maternal grandsons,
for a son-in-law,
for a wife's parents,
for brothers' grandsons' wives,
for paternal first cousins' sons' wives,
for paternal first cousins' wives,
for maternal grandsons' wives,
for nephews' wives;
a wife for her husband's paternal great-grandparents and great-great-grandparents,
for her husband's paternal granduncles and grandaunts,
for her husband's paternal first cousins once removed,
for her husband's brothers' great-grandsons,
for her husband's paternal first cousins,
for her husband's paternal first cousins' grandsons,
and the same for their granddaughters,
for her husband's paternal second cousins' sons,
for her husband's brothers' grandsons' wives,
for her husband's paternal first cousins' sons' wives,
for her husband's paternal first cousins' wives,
for her husband's paternal first cousins (sisters),
for her husband's maternal grandparents,
for her husband's maternal uncles and aunts,
for her husband's paternal grandaunts and husband's unmarried sisters of paternal granduncles;
a married daughter for the paternal granduncles and grandaunts of her natal clan,
for the paternal first cousins once removed of her natal clan,
for the children of paternal first cousins of her natal clan,
for the paternal grandaunts and unmarried sisters of paternal granduncles of her natal clan,
for the married paternal first cousins (sisters) of her natal clan;
one who has been adopted as heir for his birth maternal grandparents.
In the first month of the 18th year of the Jiājìng reign, an edict was issued to the Grand Secretaries:
"Recently, while observing mourning and recuperating from illness,
I perused the 'Tángōng' and other chapters of the Lǐjì.
The ritual systems and regulations recorded therein are not unified,
nor do they contain the complete rituals for the Tiānzǐ.
Although it states, 'The three-year mourning period
is universal for all ranks,'
there are also significant differences between antiquity and the present.
What the Imperial Ancestor (Tàizǔ) established,
does not have a complete text.
Whenever there is mourning for an emperor or empress,
it is unavoidable to still rely on old precedents for rituals.
As for caps, robes, and mourning attire,
the regulations of the responsible offices are inconsistent.
You are to consult with the officials of the Lǐbù to examine and finalize these.
From the beginning of mourning until the removal of mourning clothes,
the regulations for the various degrees of caps and robes should all be made into ceremonial procedures,
so that they may be made perfectly appropriate."
Thereupon, the Lǐbù discussed the various regulations for mourning attire and submitted a memorial.
The Emperor ordered them to be further examined and finalized,
with illustrations and annotations,
together with complete rituals for sacrifices and burials,
to be compiled into a book for reference.
Collated Notes
Treatise Thirty-Seven: Yuè One
The ancient sage-kings,
after establishing order and achieving success, composed music,
to harmonize with the nature of Heaven and Earth,
and to embody the emotions of all beings.
Heavenly spirits would descend, and the will of the people would be in harmony.
Indeed, music
is the voice of the heart.
If the ruler's heart is harmonious,
there is nothing within the universe that is not harmonious.
Therefore, when music is created by the ruler,
the people below are transformed.
From the Qín and Hàn dynasties onward,
this principle gradually diminished.
The way of music became disconnected from governance,
and the customs of the people daily inclined towards decadence.
When the Míng dynasty arose,
Emperor Tàizǔ was determined to revive elegant court music (Yǎyuè).
At that time,
Confucian ministers such as Lěng Qiān, Táo Kǎi, Zhān Tóng, Sòng Lián, and Yuè Sháofèng all understood phonology and rhythm,
and together they thoroughly investigated, corrected, and established (the music).
However, historical precedents were vague and incomplete,
and though they desired to restore ancient sounds,
there was no means to do so.
Emperor Tàizǔ, at that time, also considered the sentiments of the common people as frivolous,
and focused on severe punishments to restrain them.
As for the fundamental principle of maintaining moderation and embodying harmony,
he had no time to attend to it.
Emperor Wén inquired about the pitch of Huángzhōng,
but none of the officials or artisans could provide an answer.
During the reigns of Emperors Yīng, Jǐng, Xiàn, and Xiào,
the grand ceremonial music (gōngxuán) merely became an empty formality.
At banquets in the imperial court,
and sacrifices at the suburban altars,
the musicians from the imperial music bureau and Daoist performers
were irreverent and perfunctory.
Liú Xiáng and Hú Ruì deeply lamented this.
Emperor Shìzōng took it upon himself to compose music.
Zhāng È and Lǐ Wénchá gained imperial favor for their understanding of music,
but ultimately achieved nothing.
For the writings of scholars and officials could only discuss the theory,
but when applied to the five notes and six pitches, they often did not harmonize.
Music officials could record the sounds and movements but did not understand their deeper meaning.
Therefore, throughout generations, none could fully comprehend it.
Examining the musical creations of the Míng dynasty,
they mostly compiled from the old practices of the Hàn, Táng, Sòng, and Yuán dynasties,
and slightly changed their names.
All the sequences of sounds and forms,
and the complexity of instruments and numbers,
were indeed brilliantly and comprehensively implemented at that time,
but elegant and popular styles were mixed,
and there was no way to correct them.
Therefore, they are fully listed in this chapter,
for those who wish to study them.
Tàizǔ, upon first conquering Jīnlíng,
immediately established the office of Director of Music.
The following year, elegant music (yǎyuè) was instituted
to be used for the sacrifices at the suburban altars (jiāoshè).
In the first year of Wú, an order was issued that from this point forward, for court audiences,
