female musicians were not to be used.
Previously, an order had been given to select Daoist youths (dàotóng) to serve as music and dance performers (yuèwǔshēng),
and by this time, they had been assembled.
Tàizǔ was at the Jímén gate,
and summoned the scholars Zhū Shēng and Fàn Quán to lead the music and dance performers to an audience,
where he reviewed and tested them.
Tàizǔ personally struck a stone chime (shíqìng),
and ordered Shēng to identify the five notes (wǔyīn).
Shēng was unable to discern them,
mistaking the gōng note for the zhǐ note.
Tàizǔ smiled at his error,
and ordered the performers to sing one piece before dismissing them.
In this year, the Tàicháng Sī (Court of Imperial Sacrifices) was established,
with subordinate officials such as Xiélǜláng.
At the end of the Yuán dynasty, there was a person named Lěng Qiān,
who was knowledgeable in music
and skilled at playing the se (zither),
living as a Daoist recluse on Wúshān mountain.
He was summoned to be a Xiélǜláng,
and was ordered to standardize the musical scores and vocal notation for ceremonial music,
so that the performers could practice them.
Stones from Língbì were taken to make chimes,
and tung wood from Húzhōu was collected to make qín and se zithers.
He then verified and corrected the elegant music for the four ancestral temples (sìmiào),
and Tàizǔ ordered Qiān to calibrate the pitches and rhythms, and the bianzhong (bronze bells) and bianqing (stone chimes) instruments,
thus establishing the system for music and dance.
Daoist youths continued to be used as music performers,
while the dance performers were changed to handsome and intelligent sons of military and civilian families.
Furthermore, the Jiàofāng Sī (Office of Music and Entertainment) was established,
responsible for grand music at banquets.
It appointed officials such as Dàshǐ, Fùshǐ, and Héshēngláng,
and directors of the left and right Sháoyuè,
and left and right Sīyuè,
all staffed by professional musicians.
Later, Héshēngláng was renamed Fèngluán.
In the spring of the first year of Hóngwǔ, Tàizǔ personally sacrificed to Tàishè and Tàijì.
In the summer, the xiáxiang ceremony was held at the Tàimiào.
In that winter, sacrifices were offered to Hào Tiān Shàngdì at the Yuánqiū.
The following year, sacrifices were offered to Huángdìqí at the Fāngqiū,

and successively to Xiānnóng, the Sun and Moon, Tàisuì, Wind and Thunder, the Five Sacred Mountains and Four Great Rivers (yuèdú), the Stars of the Heavens, successive Emperors, and Zhìshèng Wénxuānwáng (Confucius).
For all of these, the number of musical and dance performances
and the names of the tunes to be played were determined.
At the Yuánqiū:
For welcoming the spirits,
the "Zhōnghé" tune was played.
For presenting jade and silk,
the "Sùhé" tune was played.
For presenting sacrificial animals,
the "Nínghé" tune was played.
For the first offering,
the "Shòuhé" tune was played,
along with the "Wǔgōng" dance.
For the second offering,
the "Yùhé" tune was played.
For the final offering,
the "Xīhé" tune was played,
both accompanied by the "Wéndé" dance.
For removing the sacrificial vessels,
the "Yōnghé" tune was played.
For sending off the spirits,
the "Ānhé" tune was played.
For observing the burnt offerings,
the "Shíhé" tune was played.
The Fāngqiū ceremonies were identical,
but the lyrics for the tunes differed,
and "observing the burnt offerings" was changed to "observing the buried offerings" (wàngyì).
For Tàishè and Tàijì,
the "welcoming the spirits" tune was changed to "Guǎnghé,"
the "presenting sacrificial animals" step was omitted,
the rest were the same as Fāngqiū,
but the lyrics for the tunes differed.
For Xiānnóng:
For welcoming the spirits and presenting silk,
the "Yǒnghé" tune was played.
For presenting the cooked meats,
the "Yōnghé" tune was played.
For the first offering and final offering,
the "Shòuhé" tune was played for both.
For removing the sacrificial vessels and sending off the spirits,
the "Yǒnghé" tune was played for both.
For observing the buried offerings,
the "Tàihé" tune was played.
For worshipping the Morning Sun (Zhāorì):
For welcoming the spirits,
the "Xīhé" tune was played.
For presenting jade and silk,
the "Bǎohé" tune was played.
For the first offering,
the "Ānhé" tune was played,
along with the "Wǔgōng" dance.
For the second offering,
the "Zhōnghé" tune was played.
For the final offering,
the "Sùhé" tune was played,
both accompanied by the "Wéndé" dance.
For removing the sacrificial vessels,
the "Nínghé" tune was played.
For sending off the spirits,
the "Shòuhé" tune was played.
For observing the burnt offerings,
the "Yùhé" tune was played.
For worshipping the Evening Moon (Xīyuè):
For welcoming the spirits, "Nínghé" was substituted,
from presenting silk onwards it was the same as Zhāorì,
but the lyrics for the tunes differed.
For Tàisuì, Wind and Thunder, and Yuèdú:
For welcoming the spirits,
the "Zhōnghé" tune was played.
For presenting silk,
the "Ānhé" tune was played.
For the first offering,
the "Bǎohé" tune was played.
For the second offering,
the "Sùhé" tune was played.
For the final offering,
the "Nínghé" tune was played.
For removing the sacrificial vessels,
the "Shòuhé" tune was played.
For sending off the spirits,
the "Yùhé" tune was played.
For observing the burnt offerings,
the "Xīhé" tune was played.
For the Stars of the Heavens (Zhōutiān Xīngchén),
initially offered alongside Xīyuè,
they were separately worshipped in the fourth year of Hóngwǔ.
For welcoming the spirits,
the "Nínghé" tune was played.
For presenting silk and the first offering,
the "Bǎohé" tune was played,
along with the "Wǔgōng" dance.
For the second offering,
the "Zhōnghé" tune was played.
For the final offering,
the "Sùhé" tune was played,
both accompanied by the "Wéndé" dance.
For removing the sacrificial vessels,
the "Yùhé" tune was played.
For sending off the spirits,
the "Yōnghé" tune was played.
At the Tàimiào:
For welcoming the spirits,
the "Tàihé" tune was played.
For presenting the imperial edict and seal,
the "Xīhé" tune was played.
For presenting the cooked meats,
the "Nínghé" tune was played.
For the first offering,
the "Shòuhé" tune was played,
along with the "Wǔgōng" dance.
For the second offering,
the "Yùhé" tune was played.
For the final offering,
the "Xīhé" tune was played,
both accompanied by the "Wéndé" dance.
For removing the sacrificial vessels,
the "Yōnghé" tune was played.
For sending off the spirits,
the "Ānhé" tune was played.
For the first offering, the Dédian, Yìdiàn, Xīdiàn, and Réndiàn each played their music and performed their dances,
while for the second and final offerings, the four temples shared them.
For the sacrifice to Confucius (Shìdiàn Kǒngzǐ),
initially the old "Dàchéng" ceremonial music was used.
In the sixth year of Hóngwǔ, Zhān Tóng, Yuè Sháofèng, and others were ordered to compose new musical pieces.
For welcoming the spirits,
the "Xiánhé" tune was played.
For presenting silk,
the "Nínghé" tune was played.
For the first offering,
the "Ānhé" tune was played.
For the second and final offerings,
the "Jǐnghé" tune was played.
For removing the food and sending off the spirits,
the "Xiánhé" tune was played.
For successive Emperors (Lìdài Dìwáng):
For welcoming the spirits,
the "Yōnghé" tune was played.
For presenting silk and the first offering,
the "Bǎohé" tune was played,
along with the "Wǔgōng" dance.
For the second offering,
the "Zhōnghé" tune was played.
For the final offering,
the "Sùhé" tune was played,
both accompanied by the "Wéndé" dance.
For removing the sacrificial vessels,
the "Nínghé" tune was played.
For sending off the spirits,
the "Shòuhé" tune was played.
For observing the buried offerings,
the "Yùhé" tune was played.
Also, the musical chapters for the state sacrifices were established.
When welcoming the deities,
the music of Tàiqīng was played.
For the first offering,
the music of Shòuqīng was played.
For the second offering,
the music of Yùqīng was played.
For the final offering,
the music of Xīqīng was played.
When clearing the food,
the music of Yōngqīng was played.
When sending off the deities,
the music of Ānqīng was played.
For the altars of the land and grain, mountains and rivers,
the welcoming music was changed to Guǎngqīng,
and the music for offering and burying was added, called Shíqīng.
These were the musical songs and rhythms for the sacrifices.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, the system for court assemblies and banquets was also established.
For all imperial birthdays, New Year's Day, Winter Solstice, and grand court audiences,
the Hèshēngláng arranged music on the crimson steps, south of the hundred officials' bowing positions,
facing north.
When the Emperor emerged,
the imperial guard stirred.
The Hèshēngláng raised the banner,
played the music of Fēilóng Yǐn,
the music began,
and the Emperor ascended the throne.
When the music stopped,
the banner was lowered.
When the hundred officials bowed,
the music of Fēngyúnhuì was played.
After bowing,
the music stopped.
The Prime Minister ascended the hall to deliver a speech,
playing the music of Qìnghuángdū.
After the speech,
the music stopped.
The hundred officials bowed again,
playing the music of Xǐshēngpíng.
After the bowing ceremony,
the music stopped.
When the Emperor rose,
the music of Hèshèngcháo was played.
Upon returning to the palace,
the music stopped.
When the hundred officials withdrew,
the Hèshēngláng and musicians exited in sequence.
For all banquets,
four Hèshēngláng oversaw the music and dance.
Two held banners,
standing on both sides in front of the musicians;
two supervised the music,
standing on both sides behind the musicians.
After the arrangements in the hall were complete,
the Hèshēngláng, holding banners, ascended via the two staircases,
standing to the left and right of the imperial wine table;
two led the singers and musicians to ascend via the two staircases,
standing on both sides of the crimson steps,
facing east and west.
Two dance masters, holding flags,
led the martial dancers to stand south of the west staircase;
another two, holding feathered fans,
led the civil dancers to stand south of the east staircase;
another two, holding banners,
led the dancers from the Four Barbarian Tribes to stand southwest of the martial dancers;
all faced north.
The martial dance was called the "Dance of Pacifying the World,"
symbolizing the use of majestic achievement to quell disaster and chaos;
the civil dance was called the "Dance of Carriages and Books Uniting,"
symbolizing the attainment of great peace through civil virtue;
the Four Barbarian Tribes dance was called the "Dance of Soothing and Securing the Four Barbarian Tribes,"
symbolizing the submission of distant peoples through [wǔ dé] virtue.
Two leaders of the grand music,
holding bamboo wands,
led the grand musicians to array themselves west of the crimson steps.
The musicians for the civil and martial dances were arrayed east of the crimson steps.
The musicians for the Four Barbarian Tribes were arrayed north of the Four Barbarian Tribes dance.
All faced north.
When the Emperor was about to emerge,
the imperial guard stirred,
and the grand music began.
Upon ascending the throne,
the music stopped.
When the first cup was presented,
the Hèshēngláng raised the banner,
and sang and played the music of Qǐ Línháo.
Two music leaders led the singers and musicians to the front of the wine table,
facing north,
and stood in two rows.
After the performance,
the banner was lowered,
and the music supervisors led the performers to withdraw.
For the second cup,
the music of Kāitàipíng was played.
For the third,
the music of Ānjiànyè was played.
For the fourth,
the music of Xuēqúnhóng was played.
For the fifth,
the music of Píngyōudū was played.
For the sixth,
the music of Fǔsìyí was played.
For the seventh,
the music of Dìngfēngshǎng was played.
For the eighth,
the music of Dàyītǒng was played.
For the ninth,
the music of Shǒuchéngpíng was played.
The raising and lowering of the banner,
and the advance and retreat of the singers and musicians,
were all according to the previous ritual.
When the first course of food was presented,
the Hèshēngláng raised the banner,
and sang and played the music of Fēilóng Yǐn,
and the grand music began.
After eating,
the music stopped,
and the banner was lowered.
For the second course,
the music of Fēngyúnhuì was played.
For the third,
the music of Qìnghuángdū was played.
For the fourth,
the Dance of Pacifying the World was performed.
For the fifth,
the music of Hèshèngcháo was played.
For the sixth,
the Dance of Soothing and Securing the Four Barbarian Tribes was performed.
For the seventh,
the music of Jiǔchónghuān was played.
For the eighth,
the Dance of Carriages and Books Uniting was performed.
For the ninth,
the music of Wànniánchūn was played.
The raising and lowering of the banner were according to the previous ritual.
After the nine musical pieces and three dances were completed,
the Emperor rose,
and the grand music began.
Upon entering the palace,
the music stopped,
and the Hèshēngláng, holding the banner, led the performers to exit in sequence.
The banquet music
was later changed twice.
Those established in the fourth year were:
first, "Origin of the Great Beginning,"
second, "Looking Up to the Great Brightness,"
third, "People's First Birth,"
fourth, "Myriad Things Flourish,"
fifth, "Riding the Six Dragons,"
sixth, "The Heavenly Steps are Level,"
seventh, "Ruler's Virtue Achieved,"
eighth, "Sage's Way Carried Out,"
ninth, "Music of Peace and Tranquility."
Their lyrics
were composed by Zhān Tóng and Táo Kǎi.
Those established in the fifteenth year were:
first, "Fiery Essence Opens the Era,"
second, "Imperial Wind,"
third, "Favored by the Imperial Brightness,"
fourth, "Way of Heaven Transmitted,"
fifth, "Reviving the Imperial Order,"
sixth, "Jīnlíng,"
seventh, "Chángyáng,"
eighth, "Fragrant Nectar,"
ninth, "Driving the Six Dragons."
For all grand court audiences,
the Jiàofāngsī arranged the Zhōnghé Sháolè music east and west of the hall,
facing north;
the grand dances were arranged east and west of the crimson steps,
also facing north.
When the Emperor rose,
the Zhōnghé Sháolè played the music of Shèng'ān.
Upon ascending the throne and presenting treasures,
the music stopped.
When the hundred officials bowed,
the grand music began.
After bowing,
the music stopped.
When memorials were presented,
the grand music began.
After completion of presentations,
the music stopped.
When the memorial summaries were announced,
and the congratulations finished,
the hundred officials prostrated,
and the grand music began.
After bowing,
the music stopped.
When the imperial decree was announced,
the hundred officials danced and cheered "Long live!"
and the grand music began.
After bowing,
the music stopped.
When the Emperor rose,
the Zhōnghé Sháolè played the music of Dìng'ān,
guiding the Emperor to the Huágài Diàn,
and the music stopped.
The hundred officials exited in sequence.
During grand banquets,
the Jiàofāngsī would set up the Zhōnghé Sháoyuè in the hall,
and the Dàyuè outside the hall.
Three mixed dance troupes would be arranged below the hall.
When the imperial carriage set off,
the Dàyuè would play.
Upon ascending the throne,
the music would stop.
Civil and military officials would enter and line up outside the hall,
bowing to the north,
and the Dàyuè would play.
After the bows were completed,
the music would stop.
When the imperial feast was presented,
the music would play.
When it was finished,
the music would stop.
When flowers were presented,
the music would play.
When they were finished,
the music would stop.
When the first cup was presented,
the Jiàofāngsī would perform the tune Yánjīng Kāiyùn,
and the music would play.
After the internal and external officials had bowed,
the music would stop.
When flowers were scattered,
the music would play.
When they were finished,
the music would stop.
For the second cup,
the Jiàofāngsī would perform the tune Huángfēng.
When the music stopped,
soup would be presented.
The Gǔchuī Xiǎngjié would lead the way to outside the hall.
When the Gǔchuī stopped,
the music in the hall would play.
When the officials had finished their soup and dishes,
the music would stop.
The martial dancers would enter,
and the Jiàofāngsī would request to perform the dance Píngdìng Tiānxià.
For the third cup,
the Jiàofāngsī would request to perform the tune Juàn Huángmíng,
and wine would be presented as before.
When the music stopped,
the Jiàofāngsī would request to perform the dance Fǔ'ān Sìyí.
For the fourth cup,
the tune Tiāndào Chuán would be played,
and wine and soup would be presented as before.
When the music stopped,
the dance Chēshū Huìtóng would be performed.
For the fifth cup,
the tune Zhèn Huánggāng would be played,
and wine would be presented as before.
When the music stopped,
the Bǎixì Chéngyìng would be performed.
For the sixth cup,
the tune Jīnlíng would be played,
and wine and soup would be presented as before.
When the music stopped,
the Bāmán Xiànbǎo Chéngyìng would be performed.
For the seventh cup,
the tune Chángyáng would be played,
and wine would be presented as before.
When the music stopped,
the Cǎilián Duìzi Chéngyìng would be performed.
For the eighth cup,
the tune Fānglǐ would be played,
and wine and soup would be presented as before.
When the music stopped,
the Yúyuè Yúyuān Chéngyìng would be performed.
For the ninth cup,
the tune Jiàliùlóng would be played,
and wine would be presented as before.
When the music stopped,
the cups would be cleared.
When soup was presented,
and the grand meal was presented,
the music would play.
After the officials had finished their rice and food,
the music would stop,
and the Bǎihuā Duìwǔ Chéngyìng would be performed.
The banquet would conclude, and the tables would be cleared.
The officials would take their leave,
bowing to the north,
and the music would play.
After the bows were completed,
the music would stop.
When the imperial carriage set off,
the Dàyuè would play, and whips would crack,
and all officials would exit in order.
These were the musical and rhythmic protocols for the imperial court's celebratory banquets.
Regarding the system of musical instruments,
for suburban altars, mounds, temples, and altars of state,
it was established in the first year of Hóngwǔ.
There were sixty-two musicians:
sixteen sets of biānzhōng and sixteen sets of biānqìng,
ten qín,
four sè,
four bófǔ,
one zhù and one yú each,
four xūn,
four chí,
eight xiāo,
eight shēng,
four dí,
and one yìnggǔ;
twelve vocalists;
one Xiélǜláng holding a banner to lead them.
In the seventh year, four yuè and
four fèngshēng were added,
the xūn were increased to six,
and the bófǔ reduced to two,
totaling seventy-two people.
For dances, there were sixty-two martial dancers,
with two lead dancers,
each holding a gān and a qī;
sixty-two civil dancers,
with two lead dancers,
each holding a yǔ and a yuè;
and two dance masters holding jié to lead them.
This totaled one hundred and thirty people.
However, for the Wénmiào, there were sixty musicians:
sixteen sets of biānzhōng and sixteen sets of biānqìng,
ten qín,
four sè,
four bófǔ,
one zhù and one yú each,
four xūn,
four chí,
eight xiāo,
eight shēng,
four dí,
and one dàgǔ;
ten vocalists.
In the sixth year, the Tàihé Zhōng was cast.
Its design
imitated the Sòng Jǐngzhōng.
Using the number nine times nine,
it was eight chi and one cùn high.
It was adorned with nine dragons,
supported by a lóngjù,
and a tower was built northeast of the Huánqiū Zhāigōng,
where it was hung.
During suburban sacrifices,
when the imperial carriage moved, the bell would chime.
Upon ascending the altar,
the bell would stop,
and all other instruments would play.
After the ceremony,
upon ascending the imperial palanquin,
the bell would chime.
It would stop only
when the music leading the imperial carriage began.
In the seventeenth year, it was recast,
and its size was reduced by four-tenths.
Court audiences.

four shēng,

four lóngdí,
four pípá,

four páixiāo,

ten qín,
four sè,
two biānzhōng,
two biānqìng,
two yìnggǔ,
one zhù,

For the grand music of the imperial steps: two xìzhú,
twelve xiāo,
twelve shēng,
twelve dí,
twelve tóuguǎn,
eight qín,
eight pípá,
eight twenty-stringed instruments,
two fāngxiǎng,
two gǔ,
eight pāibǎn,
twelve zhànggǔ.
For the court audience of noblewomen to the empress:
female musicians were arranged with two xìzhú,
fourteen xiāo,
fourteen shēng,
fourteen dí,
fourteen tóuguǎn,
ten qín,
eight pípá,
eight twenty-stringed instruments,
six fāngxiǎng,
five gǔ,
eight pāibǎn,
twelve zhànggǔ.
This was for the three festivals of Zhèngdàn, Dōngzhì, and Qiānqiū.
Thereafter, the Grand Empress Dowager and Empress Dowager also used it.
For朔wàng朝參: two xìzhú,
four xiāo,
four shēng,
four dí,
four tóuguǎn,
two qín,
two pípá,
two twenty-stringed instruments,
one fāngxiǎng,
one gǔ,
two pāibǎn,
six zhànggǔ.
Grand banquets.
In the 1st year of Hóngwǔ, the music for accompanying meals inside the hall was set: six xiāo,
six shēng,
four singers.
For the grand music of the imperial steps: two xìzhú,
four xiāo,
four shēng,
six pípá,
six qín,
four kōnghóu,
four fāngxiǎng,
four tóuguǎn,
four lóngdí,
twenty-four zhànggǔ,

two bǎn.
Musical instruments for the civil and martial dances: two shēng,
two héngguǎn,
two qín,
two zhànggǔ,
one dàgǔ,
one bǎn.
Music for the dances of the Four Barbarians: two yāogǔ,
two pípá,
two húqín,
two kōnghóu,
two tóuguǎn,
two qiāngdí,
two qín,

In the 26th year, the music for accompanying meals inside the hall was further set: one zhù,
one yú,
one bófǔ,
four qín,
two sè,
four xiāo,
four shēng,
four dí,
two xún,
two chí,
one páixiāo,
one zhōng,
one qìng,
one yìnggǔ.
For the grand music of the imperial steps: two xìzhú,
four xiāo,
four shēng,
two dí,
two tóuguǎn,
two pípá,
two qín,
two twenty-stringed instruments,
two fāngxiǎng,

Music for welcoming the meal: two xìzhú,
two shēng,
four dí,
two tóuguǎn,
two qín,
ten zhànggǔ,
one gǔ,

Music for presenting the meal: two shēng,
two dí,

Tàipíng Qīngyuè: four shēng,
four dí,

Regulations for the attire of musicians and dancers.
For suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples,
set in the 1st year of Hóngwǔ;
for court audiences,
set in the 3rd year of Hóngwǔ.
For the civil and martial dances: thirty-two martial dancers,
holding gān on the left and qī on the right,
in four rows,
eight people per row.
The dance movements included raising, stepping forcefully, sitting, rising, striking, and stabbing.
Two dance masters led them, holding jīng.
Thirty-two civil dancers,
holding yuè on the left and dí on the right,
in four rows,
eight people per row.
The dance movements included advancing, retreating, leisurely movements, bowing, yielding, ascending, and descending.
Two dance masters led them, holding dàochì.
For the dances of the Four Barbarians: sixteen dancers,
in four rows,
four people per row.
The dance movements included bowing, kneeling, paying respects, joyous leaping, and prostrating.
Two dance masters led them, holding chuáng.
These are the music, dances, instruments, and attire for sacrificial ceremonies and court audiences.
During Tàizǔ's time,
there were some additions and deletions前后.
As for the crude and vulgar musical pieces,
he ordered the scholarly officials to change their lyrics.
The compositions for the two suburban sacrifices
were personally made by Tàizǔ.
Later, when the sacrifices were combined,
their lyrics were changed again.
For the sacrifice to the Imperial Altar of Earth and Grain, with Rénzǔ as co-sacrificed,
seven new compositions were also made.
He once admonished the ritual officials, saying:
“The poetry of ancient music
is harmonious and proper.
The poetry of later generations
is licentious and boastful.
Therefore, all flattering and seductive lyrics are discarded and not adopted.”
He once ordered scholarly officials to compose songs for the imperial return journey,

including pieces such as "Divine Descent of Auspiciousness" (Shén Jiàng Xiáng), "Divine Bestowal" (Shén Kuàng), "Indulgent Wine" (Hānjǐu), "Lustful Wilderness" (Sè Huāng), and "Hunting Wilderness" (Qín Huāng),
totaling thirty-nine chapters.
They were named "Songs for the Imperial Luan" (Yù Luán Gē),
all embodying the intention of satire and admonition.
However, the composers of that time
only aimed for clarity and easy understanding,
and were not able to achieve the sonorous elegance and robustness
of the poetry from the Hàn and Jìn periods,
which could be recorded and recited.
The court music in the palace
had lyrics that came from the entertainers of the Jiàofāng,
and often deviated from the proper standards of elegance.
The twelve-month musical pieces,
performed according to the monthly pitches,
as well as pieces for presenting and welcoming meals,
all used Yuèfǔ, xiǎolìng, and zájù for entertainment.
The popular clamor
and licentious songs were unrestrained.
What Tàizǔ wished to discard
was instead set up in the palace halls and steps, without being deemed strange.
In the eighteenth year of Yǒnglè,
the altars and temples in Běijīng were completed.
The ritual music for combined sacrifices and offerings
followed the old system exactly.
The banquet music and dances were newly standardized: the first performance was the "Ten Thousand Years of Longevity" (Shàng Wànshòu) tune,
and the "Pacifying the World" (Píngdìng Tiānxià) dance;
the second performance was the "Thanking Heaven's Grace" (Yǎng Tiān'ēn) tune,
and the "Soothing the Four Barbarians" (Fǔ Sì Yí) dance;
the third performance was the "Feeling Earth's Virtue" (Gǎn Dìdé) tune,
and the "Carriages and Books Meeting in Unity" (Chē Shū Huì Tóng) dance;
the fourth performance was the "People Live Happily" (Mín Lè Shēng) tune,
and the "Setting Straight Ten Thousand States" (Biǎo Zhèng Wànbāng) dance;
the fifth performance was the "Feeling Imperial Grace" (Gǎn Huáng'ēn) tune,
and the "Heaven's Mandate for the Virtuous" (Tiānmìng Yǒudé) dance;
the sixth performance was the "Celebrating a Bountiful Year" (Qìng Fēngnián) tune;
the seventh performance was the "Gathering Auspicious Omens" (Jí Zhēn Yìng) tune;
the eighth performance was the "Eternal Imperial Blueprint" (Yǒng Huángtú) tune;
the ninth performance was the "Joy of Grand Peace" (Lè Tàipíng) tune.
The tunes were superficial,
and the dances were even more vulgar.
In the first year of Jǐngtài,
Assistant Instructor Liú Xiáng submitted a memorial pointing out these faults.
He requested an imperial edict for scholarly officials to elaborate on the meaning of morality and education,
and the joy shared between ruler and minister,
to compose poems and chapters,
and to harmonize them with pitch pipes,
like the ancient sounds of Língtái, Pìyōng, Qīngmiào, and Zhànlù,
to invigorate customs and education,
and to serve as a grand ceremony for the age.
At that time, because the existing practices had been used for a long time,
they ultimately could not be changed.
Afterward, the court music performed by the musicians of the Jiàofāngsī
often contained discords.
In the Chénghuà reign,
a ritual official once requested to triple their quota,
to extensively teach and selectively adopt.
In the early Hóngzhì reign,
Xiàozōng personally tilled the sacrificial field,
and the Jiàofāngsī performed zájù to serve,
interspersed with coarse language.
The Censor-in-Chief Mǎ Wénshēng sternly reprimanded and dismissed them.
The Supervising Secretary Hú Ruì once said:
“Receiving court in the palace
is a grand ceremony,
yet the court music in the palace is assigned to the Jiàofāngsī;
the sacrifices to the Five Sacred Mountains and the Four Great Rivers,
held every three years,
are entrusted to the musicians and dancers of the Shénlèguān.
This profanes the gods
and harms the general order.
I hope Your Majesty will order the court officials to deliberate,
that for the sacrifices to the mountains and rivers,
gentlemen should be involved.
For the court music,
children from common households should be selected for training,
and an official should be appointed to manage them.
After years,
they should be given appropriate official positions.”
The emperor considered that performing music for sacrifices
was an old national custom
and could not follow the suggestion.
When Mǎ Wénshēng was Minister,
he presented a memorial due to disasters,
one of which was
to seek out renowned scholars to rectify the elegant music.
The matter was passed down to the ritual officials.
The ritual officials stated:
“Gāohuángdì ordered scholarly officials to verify the eight tones,
manufacture musical instruments,
and deliberate on musical compositions.
Many of the lyrics for the ascending chants
were personally decided by him.
However, after more than one hundred and thirty years,
they have not been re-verified,
and the pitch and rhythm are erroneous;
rectification is urgently needed.
Moreover, the officials of the Tàicháng Temple may not be fully capable of the task of instrument making and pitch harmonization.
We request that an imperial edict be issued to various departments,
to widely seek out officials from within and outside the court, as well as recluses who are proficient in music,
and respectfully send them to the capital.
After the ritual officials thoroughly deliberate and reach a consensus,
then instruments can be made and pitches corrected,
perhaps thereby restoring the ancestral system
and achieving great harmony.”
The emperor approved their memorial.
In his later years, an edict was sent to Nánjīng and various princely establishments
to select those proficient in musical arts to come to the capital,
but it was again dismissed due to the words of the ritual officials.
In the third year of Zhèngdé,
Wǔzōng instructed Kāng Néng and others of the Neizhōnggǔsī, saying:
“The grand celebration banquet
is watched by both Chinese and foreign officials,
so grand music should be performed.
Recently, music has been neglected and incomplete,
unable to lend solemnity to the imperial court.”
The Ministry of Rites then requested to select strong young musicians from the three academies,
and strictly supervise their training,
and also to transfer skilled performers from various provincial departments to the capital for service.
However, those under their jurisdiction became increasingly mixed and disorderly,
with acrobatics and various performances becoming daily more prevalent in the Forbidden Palace.
Afterward, the prefectures of Héjiān and others, in compliance with the imperial edict, sent music households,
who were housed in new residences.
Once the musicians gained favor,
they frequently argued that those remaining outside should not be neglected,
so skilled performers sent by various provincial departments were again transferred to the Jiàofāng.
Thus, several hundred more people were given imperial transportation and provisions,
and the power of the entertainers greatly expanded.
Zāng Xián, a performer, was promoted,
and competed for favor and usurped power with other treacherous favorites.
In the first year of Jiājìng,
Censor Wāng Shān requested to ban all frivolous pastimes,
ordering the Jiàofāngsī not to present new tunes or clever techniques.
Shìzōng greatly approved and accepted this.
At this time, various ceremonies were being re-standardized,
and thus there was also an interest in music.
The Guāndédé Hall was built to worship Xiàndì,
and harmonizers were summoned to train music for the sacrificial rites.
Later, when the Shìmiào Temple was completed,
the hall was renamed Chóngxiān.
He then personally composed musical pieces,
and ordered Grand Secretary Fèi Hóng and others to revise the names of the tunes,
to distinguish them from those of the Tàimiào.
The tune for welcoming the spirits was called "Yǒnghé zhī Qǔ",
the first offering "Qīnghé zhī Qǔ",
the second offering "Kānghé zhī Qǔ",
the final offering "Chōnghé zhī Qǔ",
the removal of dishes "Tàihé zhī Qǔ",
and the sending off of the spirits "Nínghé zhī Qǔ".
Hóng and others further deliberated,
that since Xiàndì lived and grew up in a time of peace,
and did not value military achievements,
all three offerings should use civil virtue dances.
This was followed.
Later, the Tàicháng Temple again made a request,
so ritual officials were ordered to discuss with Zhāng Cōng.
Cōng said:
“Musical dances are graded by the number of rows of dancers,
not by a partial or complete use of civil and military aspects.
If the eight-row formation
uses its civil aspect but removes its military aspect,
then of the two rows in front of the steps,
the left side will be present but the right side missing.
This would mean His Majesty performs the ritual music of the Son of Heaven,
but degrades it himself.”
Thus, Cōng’s suggestion was followed, and both dances were still used.
In the second month of the ninth year, the Emperor first prayed for grain in the southern suburbs.
The Emperor personally composed the musical scores,
and ordered the Tàicháng to harmonize them with the musical notations.
In this year,
the Emperor first sacrificed to the Xīancán (First Silkworm Deity),
and instructed the officials of rites to discuss the music and dance.
The officials of rites stated:
"The sacrifice to the Xīancán,
was practiced by both the Zhōu and Hàn dynasties.
However, the rituals for its music and dance
are not recorded in the classics or histories.
The Kǎiyuán record of Xīancán rituals from the Táng dynasty states that
the Grand Master of Music set up a Gōngxuán (palace-style bell and chime stand) within the altar enclosure of the northern suburbs,
and all female artisans were arrayed behind it.
From this, it can be known that female musicians were used for the Xīancán sacrifice.
The Táng Liùdiǎn (Six Statutes of the Táng Dynasty) states that
the Gōngxuán dance involved eight ranks of dancers (bāyì),
and the Xuánxuán (grand-style bell and chime stand) dance involved six ranks of dancers (liùyì).
From this, it can also be known that eight ranks of dancers were used for the Xīancán sacrifice.
However, it only mentions the costumes of the male dancers (wǔshēng)
but not those of the female dancers (wǔnǚ).
Below the illustration of the Xīancán sacrifice in Chén Yáng's Yuèshū (Book of Music),
there is only a drawing of the Gōngjià Dēnggē (palace-frame ascending song),
but no mention of dance.
Although having both music and dance
is customary for sacrificial rites,
the Zhōu and Hàn systems are now indeterminable,
and the Sòng dynasty's Xīancán sacrifices,
performed by appointed officials,
cannot be relied upon either.
Only the Kǎiyuán era's practice is somewhat close to antiquity,
and Mr. Chén's Yuèshū also provides clear textual evidence.
Previously, when sacrificing to the Xīannóng (First Farmer),
due to an insufficient number of ranks of dancers,
eight ranks were reduced to six.
Therefore, for the current Xīancán sacrifice,
only vocal music should be used,
and no music or dance,
which would also conform to ancient practices.
Moreover, this would show a slight moderation of the Xīannóng ritual."
The Emperor, deeming dance not a woman's affair,
abolished its use.
He ordered a discussion on the costumes for the female musicians and for it to be reported.
The officials of rites stated:
"The northern suburbs represent the Yin direction,
and its color is appropriately black.
Sympathetic resonance of the same color
is the way to serve the deities.
The Hàn dynasty sacrificed to silkworms in the eastern suburbs,
and the Wèi dynasty in the western suburbs,
where the colors were all green,
which was not their proper color.
Therefore, the female musicians' costumes should be black."
So, six musical compositions were used,
and dance was omitted.
All the female musicians wore black robes and headwear,
thus establishing the Xīancán musical scores.
Furthermore, as the sacrificial rites were being revised for the northern and southern suburbs,
and the sacrifices to the sun at dawn and moon at dusk were restored,
the Emperor ordered his literary officials to retrieve the old musical scores from the Hóngwǔ era
and revise them completely.
The officials of rites then requested to broadly seek and inquire,
and if there were any like Hú Yuán and Lǐ Zhào of the Sòng dynasty,
their names should be reported.
They would be assigned to the Tàicháng
to examine and determine the yǎyuè (ritual music).
Shìzhōng Xià Yán then recommended Zhāng È, a retired Acting Vice Minister of the Grand Court of the Imperial Stud in Gānsù, in response to the summons.
The Emperor ordered him to be quickly summoned.
Upon his arrival,
Zhāng È said: "The rectification of grand music
first requires the determination of the yuánshēng (fundamental pitch).
The yuánshēng originates from the moment of awakening from profound oblivion,
at the juncture of hái and zǐ (the last and first earthly branches, representing midnight).
Accumulated silk threads form a háo,
accumulated
háo form a lí,
accumulated lí form a fēn.
One shí (two hours) has thirty fēn,
and one day has twelve shí.
Therefore, sound originates from the day,
and the lǜ (pitch standards) arise from the hours.
Qì (vital energy) precedes sound,
and sound
follows qì.
If one is constrained by instruments in seeking qì,
then qì cannot reach the instruments,
but instead becomes constrained by them.
How then can one determine Huángzhōng and establish the calendar's origin?
One must follow
Cài Yuándìng,
cut many bamboo pipes to simulate the Huángzhōng pitch,
with each differing by one fēn in length.
On the winter solstice, one should observe them according to the lǜ
and select them according to the method.
For example, if among the various pipes
the first to eject ash is found,
then the yuánqì is obtained.
Verify its time,
if it is at the second kè of the beginning of zǐ,
then the first kè of the beginning of zǐ has shifted to the second kè of the beginning of zǐ;
if it is at
the second kè of zǐzhèng (mid-zǐ),
then the first kè of zǐzhèng has shifted to the second kè of zǐzhèng.
I wish that one official knowledgeable in the calendar be ordered
to observe together with me,
so that the yuánshēng might be obtained,
and
ancient music restored.
He further said: 'The ancients made sixteen bianzhōng (sets of bronze bells),
not merely for aesthetic display,
but for the purpose of xuángōng (pitch modulation).
The lower eight bells are
Huángzhōng, Dàlǚ, Tàicù, Jiázhōng, Gūxǐ, Zhònglǚ, Ruíbīn, and Línzhōng;
the upper eight bells are
Yīzé, Nánlǚ, Wúshè, Yìngzhōng, Huángzhōng, Dàlǚ, Tàicù,
and Jiázhōng.
In recent times, only the Huángzhōng key is used,
and the sixteen bells are not fully equipped,
thus the ancient method of establishing music has been lost.
Moreover, the Tàicháng only notates music with
the characters wǔ, fán, gōng, chǐ, shàng, yī, sì, liù, gōu, and hé,
moving further and further from antiquity.
For example, while Huángzhōng being hé seems correct,
equating Dàlǚ
to xiàsì,
Tàicù to gāosì,
Jiázhōng to xiàyī,
Gūxǐ to gāoyī,
Yīzé to xiàgōng,
and Nánlǚ to gāogōng, and so on,
all assign
two lǜ to one character.
How can xuángōng derive the lǜ,
using only the Huángzhōng key?
Furthermore, Huángzhōng, Dàlǚ, Tàicù, and Jiázhōng are the four qīngshēng (clear tones) of the upper register.
Huángzhōng is the sovereign,
supremely peerless.
When Huángzhōng is the gōng (tonic),
then the eleven
other lǜ all follow and are controlled by it,
and no subject, commoner, or matter dares to transgress it.
As for Jiázhōng as the gōng,
then Wúshè is born below it as zhǐ,
Wúshè gives birth above to
Zhònglǚ as shāng,
and Zhònglǚ gives birth below to Huángzhōng as yǔ.
However, the main lǜ of Huángzhōng has a long sound,
not according to the one-third reduction sequence for Zhònglǚ as shāng.
Therefore, to use
Huángzhōng as yǔ,
one must use the zǐshēng (child tone),
which is the qīngshēng of shànghuángliù (upper Huángzhōng six),
precisely because one dares not use the full sound of Huángzhōng,
but only half of it.
The keys from
Gūxǐ downwards
are generally similar to this.
This is how these four qīngshēng are established.
The sixteen bianzhōng
operate on the same principle.
Hú Yuán of the Sòng dynasty understood this meaning,
therefore he made the circumferences of all four qīngshēng smaller to accommodate it.
However, although the sounds of Huángzhōng and Tàicù were correct,
those of Dàlǚ and Jiázhōng
were not,
thus causing all twelve lǜ and five sounds to be incorrect.
As for Lǐ Zhào and Fàn Zhèn, they only used the twelve lǜ,
and did not use the four qīngshēng,
so that
those that conformed to the三分損益 (sānfēn sǔnyì, "loss and gain by one-third") method were harmonious.
From Yīzé downwards,
how could their subjects, commoners, and matters
distinguish between noble and base,
and avoid transgression?
I have also examined the Zhōu Lǐ (Rites of Zhōu),
which discusses yuánzhōng, hánzhōng, and huángzhōng as the three gōng of heaven, earth, and man,
with music for presenting to the deities
and music for descending deities.
The music for presenting to the deities
is to play Huángzhōng,
sing Dàlǚ,
which corresponds to zǐ and chǒu,
and dance Yúnmén to sacrifice to the celestial deities.
Then play Tàicù,
sing Yìngzhōng,
which corresponds to yín and hài,
and dance Xiánchí to sacrifice to the terrestrial deities.
Then play Gūxǐ,
sing Nánlǚ,
which corresponds to chén and yǒu,
and dance Dàsháo to sacrifice to the four directions.
Then play Ruíbīn,"
They sang Línzhōng,
with wǔ and wèi combined,
and danced Dàxià to sacrifice to the mountains and rivers.
Then they played Yízé,
sang Xiǎolǚ,
with sì and shēn combined,
danced Dàwǔ to honor the ancestors,
and danced Dàhuò to honor the ancestresses.
The so-called music for invoking spirits
is as follows: at the Winter Solstice sacrifice to Heaven at the Yuánqiū,
Yuánzhōng is used as gōng,
Huángzhōng as jué,
Tàicù
as zhēng,
and Gūxǐ as yǔ.
These three yang lǜ follow each other consecutively.
This consecution
is the way of Heaven.
At the Summer Solstice sacrifice to Earth at the Dìfāngqiū,
Hánzhōng is used as
gōng,
Jiázhōng as jué,
Gūxǐ as zhēng,
and Nánlǚ as yǔ.
These three yin lǚ are mutually generative.
This mutual generation
is the accomplishment of Earth.
At sacrifices to the ancestral
temple,
Huángzhōng is used as gōng,
Dàlǚ as jué,
Tàicù as zhēng,
and Jiázhōng as yǔ.
These three lǜ and lǚ are mutually harmonized.
This mutual harmonization
is the
essence of humanity.
Moreover, Yuánzhōng
is also Jiázhōng.
It originates from the qi of Fángxīn,
serving as the bright hall of Heaven and Earth.
Sacrifices to Heaven commence gōng from this;
on the qín, it is the jué string's
tenth huī,
the mǎo position.
Hánzhōng
is also Línzhōng.
It originates from the qi of the kūn position,
outside Jǐngdōngyúguǐ.
It presides over earth deities;
sacrifices to Earth
commence gōng from this;
on the qín, it is the zhēng string's fifth huī,
the wèi position.
Huángzhōng
originates from the qi of Xūwēi,
serving the ancestral temple.
Sacrifices to human spirits commence gōng from this;
on the
qín, it is the gōng string's third huī,
the zǐ position.
As for six changes bringing down heavenly spirits,
eight changes summoning earth deities,
and nine changes appeasing human spirits,
there is no distinction
of difficulty or ease.
Indeed, yang numbers begin at zǐ and end at the shǎoyīn shēn.
Yin numbers begin at wǔ and end at the shǎoyáng yín.
Yuánzhōng is at mǎo;
from mǎo to
shēn is six counts,
hence six changes bring down heavenly spirits.
Hánzhōng is at wèi;
from wèi to yín is eight counts,
hence eight changes summon earth deities.
Huángzhōng is at zǐ;
from
zǐ to shēn is nine counts,
hence nine changes appease human spirits.
All of these use the sound of the original lǜ
to summon the spirit of its original position,
hence the principle of sympathetic resonance is swift.
Some
say that since the Hàn dynasty,
Heaven, Earth, spirits, and deities have become accustomed to new sounds,
so why bother with reform?
They do not realize that from a human perspective,
from Hàn until now is one thousand seven
hundred years;
from the perspective of Heaven and Earth,
it is but an instant.
If we rectify it now,
it is still achievable.
He also submitted two musical treatises he had authored.
One was titled Dàchéng Yuèwǔ Tú Pǔ,
which provided notation for each character of music, from the qín and sè downwards.
The other was titled Gǔyǎ Xīntán,
which displayed twelve diagrams symbolizing the twelve lǜ.
Each diagram had an explanation.
He also considered the qín as the correct sound
and the lineage of music.
For all major music in suburban temples,
he separately noted the qín strings and fixed huī positions,
each with its specific meaning.
He further claimed that what his heart alone truly understood,
the subtlety of this profound system, could not be expressed in words.
The memorial was referred to the Ministry of Rites.
The ritual officials stated:
"Musical pitch systems have long been neglected;
officials of the Tàicháng Sī follow and practice gōngchǐ notation,
no longer knowing about tunings like Huángzhōng.
We, your subjects, have recently been commanded to rehearse the newly established ceremonial music for suburban sacrifices,
and when asked about ancient regulations,
we were utterly unable to respond.
Now, È claims that the four pure sounds are what enable xuán'gōng,
and his notation of strings and fixed huī
demonstrates a deep understanding of the shortcomings of current music.
His desire to consult those knowledgeable in calendrical science
for mutual reference
is furthermore a discussion that delves into origins and traces sources.
It seems to be beyond what current music officials can achieve."
Consequently, È was appointed Tàicháng Sì Chéng
and ordered to proceed to the Tàihé Diàn to verify and establish the music and dances.
È then submitted a memorial, saying:
"The Zhōulǐ has music for suburban sacrifices
and music for ancestral sacrifices.
The distinction between honoring superiors and parents is clear,
and the pitches and rhythms are naturally different.
Your subject has respectfully listened to the imperial temple music,
and its lǜ begins with Línzhōng,
a tuning different from that of the Tàimiào.
Your subject secretly finds this strange.
The imperial temple and the Tàimiào share the same rites,
but Línzhōng and Huángzhōng are different musical systems.
Hánzhōng presides over sacrifices to earth deities,
its position is associated with the kūn direction,
its stars correspond to Jǐngguǐ,
and its music is played with eight changes,
to repay the功 of generating and sustaining life.
Therefore, Línzhōng is used to begin the melody,
and Línzhōng concludes the melody.
Huángzhōng presides over sacrifices to the ancestral temple,
its position is associated with the zǐ constellation,
its stars belong to Xūwēi,
and its music is played with nine completions,
to repay the virtue of the origin and source.
Therefore, Huángzhōng is used to begin the melody,
and Huángzhōng concludes the melody.
The principles and meanings each have their specific intentions,
and the sounds and numbers silently resonate.
Moreover, Heaven and Earth are the symbols of parents,
and the great sovereign is designated as the zōngzǐ.
Now, using the music for sacrificing to the mother
to play for sacrificing to the zōngzǐ,
I fear that the spirit of the imperial temple in Heaven
will certainly not be at peace or pleased.
I do not know what the composer of this music
saw.
Your subject has examined the old musical notation,
the characters use Huángzhōng,
and the sound is the same as the Tàimiào.
However, upon careful listening to the seven sounds,
one lǜ is missing in the middle;
I will now correct and supplement it.
If played according to the corrected format,
then ancestors and descendants will flow together in one qi,
and the two gōngs of Hánzhōng and Huángzhōng will not lose their harmonious tuning.
The distinction between honoring superiors and parents will both be achieved,
and the hearts of both gods and men will be pleased."
The edict was sent down to the ritual officials.
Lǐ Shí and others submitted a report,
deeming:
"What Zhāng È said
is deeply consistent
with what We have heard from various books on lǜlǚ (pitch pipes).
In the Huángzhōng mode,
Huángzhōng serves as gōng,
Tàicù as shāng,
Gūxǐ as jué,
Ruíbīn as biànzhǐ,
Línzhōng as zhǐ,
Nánlǚ as yǔ,
and Yìngzhōng as biàngōng.
The old musical scores used hé,
sì,
yī,
chǐ,
and gōng.
They removed the gōu sound of Ruíbīn
and skipped to use the lìu of the regenerated Huángzhōng.
This was a fault of the old musical scores.
If it were the Línzhōng mode,
then Línzhōng would be gōng,
Nánlǚ would be shāng,
Yìngzhōng would be jué,
the half-tone of Dàlǚ would be biànzhǐ,
the half-tone of Tàicù would be zhǐ,
the half-tone of Gūxǐ would be yǔ,
and the half-tone of Ruíbīn would be biàngōng.
Recently, Shěn Jūjìng revised the musical scores,
using chǐ,
hé,
sì,
yī,
gōng,
and lìu.
Now, hé
is Huángzhōng;
sì
is the fundamental tone of Tàicù;
yī
is the fundamental tone of Gūxǐ;
and lìu
is the subsidiary tone of Huángzhōng.
To take Línzhōng as gōng,
and yet the sounds used for jué, zhǐ, and yǔ
are all not of its own mode,
is a grave error.
Moreover, the Línzhōng mode
is not suitable for use in ancestral temples,
and the Tàimiào (Grand Ancestral Temple) and Shìmiào (Ancestral Temples of Subsequent Reigns)
should not have different modes.
Zhāng È’s insight is particularly sharp.
From now on, the old harmonized pitch standard should be used,
with the sole addition of the gōu sound of Ruíbīn,
the removal of the lìu of the regenerated Huángzhōng,
and the substitution of the fán of Yìngzhōng
〔一０〕to complete the Huángzhōng mode.
This would significantly improve
the meaning of inspiring communication with the spirits."
Thereupon, Zhāng È was ordered to re-establish the music for ancestral temple offerings,
and Shěn Jūjìng and others were arrested for investigation.
Zhāng È soon after compiled and finalized the sacrificial songs for the Emperor's She (altar of soil) and Jì (altar of grain) and submitted them.
An imperial edict praised his diligence,
promoted him to Shà qīng (Vice Minister)
and put him in charge of teaching elegant music.
Xià Yán again cited the ancient practice that when the constellation Dragon appears, a rain sacrifice (yú) is performed,
and the music master is ordered to practice grand music
and perform the Huángwǔ dance.
He requested to follow ancient rites
to establish the system for grand rain sacrifices.
After the completion of the three offerings,
and when the nine-fold music ceases,
the lyrics of the "Yúnhàn" poem should be adapted
to create a piece called "Yúnmén,"
to be performed by both civil and military dancers singing in unison.
The emperor approved his proposal.
At that time, the Qīmiào (Seven Ancestral Temples) had been established,
but the music system was not yet complete.
The ritual officials therefore requested to revise the elegant music for the ancestral temples,
stating:
"The four ancestors, Dé, Yì, Xī, and Rén, have long been moved to side temples,
and the old musical scores are no longer suitable.
Tàizǔ founded the dynasty,
Tàizōng stabilized the realm,
and the successive holy emperors maintained the achievements.
There should be songs of praise
to respond to those in heaven
and transmit them for ten thousand generations.
For special offerings,
or combined offerings (xiáxiǎng),
or grand combined offerings (dàxiá),
poems and songs of praise
should be commissioned from Confucian ministers
for imperial approval.
As for musical instruments and dances,
they should follow the established forms of the Tàimiào
and be fully regulated."
The edict approved.
Later, Xiàndì was honored as Ruìzōng
and enshrined in the Tàimiào.
Thereupon, the musical scores for the spring special offerings, the three seasonal combined offerings, and the grand combined offering in late winter for the Jiǔmiào (Nine Ancestral Temples)
were all revised.
In the eighteenth year, during the imperial tour to Xīngdū,
the emperor personally composed musical scores
to offer sacrifices to Shàngdì in Fēilóng Diàn,
with the deceased imperial father as co-sacrificer.
Subsequently,
when the Qīmiào caught fire,
the system of 'same hall' (tóngtáng) was restored,
and for the four seasonal combined offerings,
the musical scores and instruments remained as per the old system.
Initially, the number of music officials and dancers for the Qīmiào was increased.
From the four suburban altars and nine ancestral temples to the altars of Tàisuì and other deities,
the number of musicians and dancers reached 2,100.
Later, it was gradually reduced,
retaining half.
Zhāng È was promoted to Tàicháng Qīng (Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices),
and again put forward his previous arguments,
proposing three matters: first, to establish special bells (tèzhōng) and special chime stones (tèqìng) to mark musical sections;
second, to restore the gōngxuán (hanging system for bells and chimes) to conform to ancient standards;
third, to determine pitch pipes by observing the primal qi.
The matters were sent to the ritual officials,
who stated:
"Special bells and special chime stones should be part of the music ensemble.
In the temple courtyard,
moving them around would be inconvenient,
so they should not be newly crafted.
Only Huángzhōng is the origin of sound and qi.
The method of observing qi
is truly to seek the middle qi to determine the middle sound,
which is the most fundamental principle for composing music.
Its method,
if a heavy chamber is sealed,
and a pipe is cut and filled with ash,
covered with red silk,
according to the calendar, when the qi arrives, the ash flies,
verified by measuring with millet grains,
there are established methods to follow.
For this method,
a chamber should be built in the vacant land outside the outer wall of the Yuánqiū,
and calendrical observers should be selected to oversee the task.
Once some progress is made,
then officials should be entrusted to verify it."
This was adopted.
An edict was then issued to procure millet from Yángtóu Shān in Chángzǐ Xiàn, Shānxī,
five dòu each of large, medium, and small grades,
to prepare for observing qi and determining pitch.
From Míng Tàizǔ to Shìzōng,
musical scores were repeatedly changed,
yet the crucial matter of pitch pipes in their creation
had not been thoroughly elucidated.
Lǚ Huái, Liú Lián, Hán Bāngqí, Huáng Zuǒ, Wáng Bāngzhí, and others wrote extensively,
but their positions were not involved with ritual music,
so their words remained theoretical.
Although Zhāng È gained office through his knowledge of music,
observing qi ultimately proved elusive
and could not be used to accurately determine pitch.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
Lǐ Wénlì, a professor from Pútián,
wrote Lǜlǚ Yuánshēng,
exclusively advocating the theory of Huángzhōng being three cùn and nine fēn as found in Lǚ Lǎn (Lü's Spring and Autumn Annals).
In the early years of Shìzōng's reign,
Censor Fàn Yǒngluán submitted this book,
but its theories contradicted ancient ones,
and thus could not be adopted.
In the sixth month of Jiājìng seventeen,
Liaozhou Tongzhi Lǐ Wénchá presented four of his musical treatises.
The ritual officials stated that these contained many insights into musical theory and notation that previous scholars had not discovered.
Thereupon, Lǐ Wénchá was appointed Tàicháng Diǎnbù (Archivist of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices)
to commend and encourage him.
However, what he proposed,
"to determine the five tones based on human voice,"
was
impracticable.
During Shénzōng's reign,
Zhèng Shìzǐ Zài Yù authored Lǜlǚ Jīngyì, Lǜxué Xīnshuō, and Yuèwǔ Quánpǔ, totaling several volumes,
which he formally submitted.
In Chóngzhēn six,
Lǐbù Shàngshū (Minister of Rites) Huáng Rǔliáng presented Zhāodài Yuèlǜ Zhì.
It was consigned to the Imperial Historiography Academy
for reference and study,
but not yet implemented.

Invoking the Spirits, "Zhōnghé zhī Qǔ" (Music of Central Harmony):
Oh, the azure vault of Heaven, vast and encompassing,
Its immense canopy covers all with boundless grandeur.
The Yuánqiū is erected to the south of the capital,
Where all spirits gather and descend in unison.
We, like ants, are humble in our sincerity,
Unable to expect communication on our own.
We imagine the spirits arriving with countenances of gold and jade,
Riding dragons and phoenixes, borne by clouds and wind.
Behold the Southern Suburb, brightly manifesting,
Gazing upon the Supreme One, sublime and lofty.
Offering Jade and Silk.
Tune of Solemn Harmony: The August Spirit is majestic,
Reverently we gaze upon its awe-inspiring brilliance.
Jade and silk are presented,
Borne in baskets, they are brought forward.
Solemn and supremely revered,

With care, this ritual sacrifice is made,
Its efficacy testifies to the August One.
Presenting the Sacrificial Meat.
Tune of Concentrated Harmony: The sacrificial rites are reverently displayed,
The offerings are not valued for their grandeur.
We dare to use a pure calf,

Though these humble offerings,
May not be perfectly complete.
May the deity accept them,
To partake and observe.
First Offering.
Tune of Enduring Harmony: Humble and insignificant as I am,
How dare I implore the Nine Heavens,
And trouble the Imperial hearing.
Yet the Imperial heart is compassionate,
Responsive and receptive.
Now you descend upon the altar,
Spirits gather in profusion.
Though your servant is foolish and ignorant,
I rejoice and am gladdened,
For it is the progeny's intimate ancestor.
I pour the clear wine into the goblet,
And look up to the supreme virtue and profound merit.
Second Offering.
Tune of Peaceful Harmony: Graced by Heaven's favor,
You dwell graciously upon the Purple Altar.
My heart is filled with joy,
Officials and commoners alike rejoice.
Humbly I hasten to serve,
My mind is at ease.
A second offering before the Emperor,
In a ceremony of peace and tranquility.
Final Offering.
Tune of Bright Harmony: I, this humble son,
Rely solely on the grace of Father Heaven,
And depend solely on the compassion of Heaven,
With utmost diligence from within and without.
How shall I present it?
Offerings include fragrant millets,
And pure grains are laid out.
Overjoyed, I clap my hands,
Serving the deities with festive leisure.
Though the ritual concludes with three offerings,
The sentiment is long-lasting and far-reaching.
Removing the Offerings.
Tune of Harmonious Peace: The cooked offerings are now presented,
The sacrifices are completed.
The deities, in their positions,
Have both smelled and blessed.
All officials swiftly move,
To clear away these sacrificial vessels.
If the provisions were insufficient,
We still hope for divine forgiveness.
Escorting the Deities.
Tune of Tranquil Harmony: The deities depart, difficult to detain,
Their long sleeves flutter gracefully.
All spirits follow, one after another,
Guarding the divine chariot as it circles.
We bow our heads and gaze at the sky,
The cloudy path is distant and vast.
Watching the Burning.
Tune of Timely Harmony: The burning pyre on the altar,
Is brilliant and sparkling.
Silks, sacrificial animals, and millets,
Are hoped to reach the Celestial Capital.
Serving the deities in the realm of light,
The ritual is gloriously accomplished.
Solemnly we gaze upon it,
The Jade Palace shines brightly.
