"carriages and niǎn for inspection,"
and the "Shǔmiáo" poem says,
"I carry, I niǎn,"
indicating that conveyances ridden by officials and commoners were also called niǎn.
It was not until the Qín dynasty that their wheels were removed,
and their design was thus elevated.
It is clear that niǎn with wheels were drawn by horses
to distinguish them from bùniǎn.
Its dimensions are:
height one zhàng, two chǐ, five cùn, nine fēn;
width eight chǐ, nine cùn, five fēn;
shaft length two zhàng, five cùn, plus a fraction;
niǎnzuò height three chǐ, four cùn, plus a fraction;
the rest is the same as the dàlù.
The niǎntíng
is six chǐ, four cùn, plus a fraction high.
It has four pillars lacquered red,
each five chǐ, four cùn, plus a fraction long.
The kǎnzuò
is the same height as the lù.
Its sides are lacquered red with looped ribbon panels.
To the front, left, and right are doors,
five chǐ, plus a fraction high,
and two chǐ, four cùn, plus a fraction wide.
By the doors are two grilles each,
and at the back are three grilles and a míng●,
all lacquered red
and adorned with gold-wiped, bronze-chiseled flower-leaf attachments.
The centers of the grilles are woven with yellow thread ribbons.
The interior design of the tíng is the same as the dàlù,
except that the soft seat does not use a patterned carpet,
but a red carpet.
Outside the tíng are twelve red curtains.
The niǎndǐng and yuánpán together are two chǐ, six cùn, plus a fraction high,
both top and bottom lacquered red,
with a green adornment for the niǎngài.
Its bronze dragons, liánzuò, bǎogài, huángwū, and tiānlún, niǎntíng
are all of the same design as the dàlù.
The tàicháng qí, tātī, xíngmǎ, and similar items
are also the same as the dàlù.
It is drawn by eight horses,
equipped with saddles, saddlecloths, cruppers, reins, and bell-tassel ornaments.
The xiǎomǎniǎn
is one chǐ less in both height and width compared to the dàmǎniǎn.
The shaft length is one zhàng, nine chǐ, plus a fraction;
the rest is the same as the dàmǎniǎn.
The niǎntíng is five chǐ, five cùn, plus a fraction high.
It has four pillars lacquered red,
each five chǐ, four cùn, plus a fraction long.
The kǎnzuò
is lacquered red,
with looped ribbon panels around its sides.
To the front, left, and right are doors,
five chǐ high,
and two chǐ, two cùn, plus a fraction wide.
By the doors are two grilles each, and a míng●,
with a screen wall-panel at the back,
all lacquered red
and adorned with gold-wiped, bronze-chiseled flower-leaf attachments.
The bottom of the tíng is lacquered red,
with a red patterned carpet and a red brocade mattress.
Outside are four red curtains,
and it is drawn by four horses.
The rest is the same as the dàmǎniǎn.
The bùniǎn
was anciently pulled by foot.
According to the Míng system,
it is one zhàng, three chǐ, two cùn, plus a fraction high,
and eight chǐ, two cùn, plus a fraction wide.
The niǎnzuò is three chǐ, two cùn, plus a fraction high,
with twelve surrounding carved wooden, five-colored cloud and solid gold-leafed dragon panels,
interspersed with solid gold-leafed upward and downward liánzuò.
Below are twelve carved wooden, gold-lined, five-colored cloud panels.
There are four shafts,
lacquered red.
The two central shafts are three zhàng, five chǐ, nine cùn long;
the two left and right shafts are two zhàng, nine chǐ, five cùn, plus a fraction long,
all adorned with gilt-bronze dragon heads and tails.
The niǎntíng is six chǐ, three cùn, plus a fraction high,
with four pillars six chǐ, two cùn, plus a fraction long.
The kǎnzuò
is lacquered red,
with twelve surrounding carved wooden, agarwood-colored, gold-outlined fragrant herb panels,
adorned with gold-wiped, bronze-chiseled flower-leaf attachments.
To the front, left, and right are doors,
five chǐ, seven cùn, plus a fraction high,
and two chǐ, four cùn, plus a fraction wide.
By the doors are two red-lacquered cross-grille panels each,
carved and decorated with eight agarwood-colored, gold-outlined cloud-dragon panels,
with an equal number of cloud panels below.
At the back is a red-lacquered screen,
with five agarwood-colored, gold-outlined cloud-dragons carved on it.
Behind the screen are three carved agarwood-colored, gold-outlined cloud-dragon panels,
and an equal number of cloud panels.
All are adorned with gold-wiped, bronze-chiseled flower-leaf attachments.
The rest is the same as the mǎniǎn,
except that it uses ten red curtains.
The niǎndǐng and yuánpán together are two chǐ, six cùn, plus a fraction high.
Its liánzuò, niǎngài, tiānlún, xiǎnyī, and similar items
are all the same as the mǎniǎn.
The dàliáng bùniǎn
is one zhàng, two chǐ, five cùn, plus a fraction high,
and one zhàng, two chǐ, five cùn, plus a fraction wide.
Its four sides have red-lacquered frames,
decorated with twenty carved wooden, five-colored cloud panels,
interspersed with gold-leafed upward and downward liánzuò.
Below are red-lacquered rúyì looped ribbon panels,
in an equal number.
There are six red-lacquered shafts: the two central shafts are four zhàng, three chǐ, five cùn, plus a fraction long;
the two left and right shafts are four zhàng, plus a fraction long;
the two outer shafts are three zhàng, six chǐ, five cùn, plus a fraction long.
Both front and back are decorated with carved wooden, gold-leafed dragon heads and tails.
The niǎntíng is six chǐ, five cùn, plus a fraction high,
and eight chǐ, five cùn, plus a fraction wide,
with four red-lacquered pillars.
To the front, left, and right are doors,
five chǐ, eight cùn, plus a fraction high,
and two chǐ, five cùn, plus a fraction wide,
with twelve surrounding gold-outlined fragrant herb panels.
By the doors are two grilles each,
and at the back are three grilles and a míng●, all lacquered red,
woven with yellow thread ribbons.
The bottom of the tíng is covered with a felt cushion,
and topped with a red brocade mattress and mat.
There is one red-lacquered seat,
its sides carved wood in agarwood color,
with gold-outlined bǎoxiànghuā.
The backrest, mattress, skirt, and curtains are the same as the mǎniǎn.
Inside are two red-lacquered tables;
one red-lacquered railing incense table,
with four railings,
the pillar tops all carved wood with gold-leafed squatting dragons;
one gilt-bronze dragon-lidded incense burner,
with incense spoon, chopsticks, and bottle;
and two red brocade stools.
Outside are three red curtains.
The niǎndǐng is two chǐ, seven cùn, plus a fraction high,
and has a gilt-bronze bǎozhū atop,
with upward and downward liánzuò,
one chǐ, three cùn, plus a fraction high;
four yellow thread round ribbons hang from the top.
The top is painted vermillion,
covered with red felt,
and its four hanging sides are made of yellow felt shaped as rúyì clouds,
with yellow felt edging strips;
its four sides are adorned with three layers of yellow qǐ lìshuǐ,
each layer having one hundred and thirty-two pleats,
interspersed with embroidered five-colored cloud-dragon patterns.
Alternatively, a large red luó may cover the top,
with yellow luó for the rúyì cloud edging strips,
and the lìshuǐ also uses yellow luó.
Below the top, the four sides are draped with red felt curtains,
with yellow felt edging strips,
and four gilt-bronze clouds at the corners.
Inside the tíng, the bǎogài is embroidered with five dragons,
topped with a red-lacquered wooden frame,
covered with yellow qǐ as a huángwū,
with one embroidered cloud-dragon at the center of each of the four sides of the top.
From the four corners of the niǎntíng to the niǎnzuò,
four yellow thread round ribbons hang from the top,
along with gold-leafed wooden fish.
At the front left and right corners of the niǎntíng are two turning corner railings,
and at the back is one straight railing with turning corners,
all lacquered red,
carved wood with solid gold-leafed dragons,
interspersed with five-colored cloud panels.
Inside the railings, mats are spread all around.
The ornaments of its twelve railing pillars and items like the tātī
are all the same as the mǎniǎn.
A jiào (轎)
is a vehicle carried on shoulders.
After the Central Revival of the Sòng (宋) dynasty,
the Empress once rode in a lóng jiān yú (龍肩輿).
Due to military campaigns,
and the ruggedness of roads,
an edict commanded officials to ride in jiào (轎s),
named
“zhú jiào zi” (竹轎子),
also known as
“zhú yú” (竹輿).
The Yuán (元) emperor used elephant jiào (轎s),
drawn by two elephants.
The use of red board jiào (轎s)
began in the Míng (明) dynasty.
Their design
was six chí (尺) nine cùn (寸) and odd in height.
The top was painted red.
Near the top were round-framed lì fáng chuāng (蜊房窗) windows,
gilded bronze huǒ yàn bǎo (火焰寶),
with upright and inverted lotus pedestals,
and at the four corners, gilded bronze yún chà (雲𩽆).
There were two jiào (轎) poles,
fastened at the front and back with gilded bronze dragon heads and tails,
with yellow velvet tassels and ropes.
The four sides were red-painted boards,
with two doors on the left and right,
secured with gilded bronze nails and hinges.
Inside the jiào (轎) was one red-painted framed chair,
one fú shòu bǎn (福壽板) (fortune and longevity board) with a cushion.
Inside the chair was a yellow brocade-woven cushion for leaning and sitting,
with a skirt around the chair,
and a mat and foot cushion spread below.
There was one yellow silk jiào yī (轎衣) (sedan chair cover) and one oiled silk rain cover,
a blue felt cover,
and red felt-edged cloud patterns.
In the 13th year of Jiājìng (嘉靖) (1534), when visiting the temples,
the Emperor and the empresses and concubines all rode in jiān yú (肩輿s) out of the palace,
and dismounted at Fèngtiān Mén (奉天門) to ascend the lù (輅).
In the 4th year of Lóngqìng (隆慶) (1570), during the celebratory banquet for the suburban sacrifice,
the Emperor rode in a bǎn yú (板輿) out of Guījí Mén (歸極門),
entered Huángjí Mén (皇極門),
and dismounted at the main hall.
When the imperial carriage went out,
there was a jù fú wò diàn (具服幄殿) (portable dressing tent).
According to the Zhōu Guān (周官) (Rites of Zhou), the large and small secondary structures,
wooden frames and reed screens,
were surrounded above, below, and on four sides by awnings and covers,
to resemble palace chambers.
The Míng (明) imperial procession recorded a jù fú wò diàn (具服幄殿),
and the ceremonial guard had huáng zhàng fáng (黃帳房) (yellow tents),
which was still the Yuán (元) system.
The tents and curtains
were made of yellow cotton cloth.
Beast mouths were placed on top,
the poles were painted red,
the pole tops were decorated with colored squatting lions,
and had felt tops.
The gēng gēn chē (耕根車) (plowing vehicle)
was first built during the Shìzōng (世宗) reign.
The Hàn (漢) dynasty had gēng chē (耕車) (plowing carts),
the Jìn (晉) dynasty called them gēng gēn chē (耕根車),
all used by the emperor for personal plowing.
In the 10th year of Jiājìng (嘉靖) (1531),
when the Emperor was about to plow the jí tián (耤田) (sacred field),
an edict ordered the construction of a gēng gēn chē (耕根車).
The ritual officials reported:
“Consulting the Dà Míng Jí Lǐ (大明集禮) (Collected Rites of the Great Míng),
the plowing of the jí (耤) field followed the Sòng (宋) system,
riding the yù lù (玉輅) (jade chariot),
with the gēng gēn chē (耕根車) carrying the lěi sì (耒耜) (plow and spade) traveling alongside.
Now examining the ceremonial procedures,
the officials of Shùntiān Fǔ (順天府) (Shuntian Prefecture) present the lěi sì (耒耜) and early-sown seeds placed in a richly decorated carriage,
departing two days before the sacrifice.
Now using a gēng gēn chē (耕根車) to carry the lěi sì (耒耜),
it is appropriate to order the construction of the vehicle,
to be presented early on the day of the sacrifice,
with the lěi sì (耒耜) placed in it,
traveling ahead of the yù lù (玉輅).
However, examining the ritual texts,
there are only illustrations,
but no dimensions for height or width.
It should be made slightly smaller than the current chariot style,
and generally of a green color.”
This was approved.
The Empress's lù (輅),
one.
Height one zhàng (丈) one chí (尺) three cùn (寸) and odd,
with a flat platform.
Front and rear carriage supports and goose wings,
four hanging rú yì (如意) (scepter-shaped) drop-bead boards.
The shafts were one zhàng (丈) nine chí (尺) six cùn (寸) long,
all painted red.
The shafts were fastened with gilded bronze phoenix heads, phoenix tails, and phoenix feather-shaped leaves.
On the left and right of the flat platform hung mudguards and two wheels,
pierced by one axle.
Each wheel had eighteen spokes,
all painted red,
the felloes fastened with gilded and engraved bronze leaf-shaped plates.
The wheel hubs inside
were fastened with gilded bronze engraved lotus petal wheel plates,
and the axle contained a yellow velvet rope for harnessing the shafts.
The lù (輅) pavilion was five chí (尺) eight cùn (寸) and odd in height,
with four red-painted pillars.
Above the threshold base were twelve agarwood-colored boards with gold-outlined auspicious herbs.
There were doors on the front left and right,
four chí (尺) five cùn (寸) and odd in height,
two chí (尺) four cùn (寸) and odd in width.
Beside the doors were two agarwood-colored gold-lined rhomboid lattice panels each,
with tasseled ring boards below,
with bright patterns,
fastened with gilded bronze engraved leaf-shaped plates.
At the back was a red-painted five-mountain screen,
with gold-inlaid phoenix and cloud patterns,
above the screen was a red-painted board,
with gold-inlaid cloud patterns,
in the center was a carved wooden phoenix completely covered in gold.
Behind the screen were red-painted boards,
all fastened with gilded bronze engraved leaf-shaped plates.
The bottom of the pavilion was painted red,
with a red floral carpet and a red brocade cushion mat,
and one red-painted chair.
The backrest had a carved wooden phoenix outlined in gold and decorated with five colors,
with auspicious herb and cloud boards above and below,
and one red fú shòu bǎn (福壽板) with a cushion.
Inside the chair was a yellow brocade-woven cushion for leaning and sitting,
with a skirt around the chair,
and yellow brocade curtains.
(Or yellow patterned gauze.)
Outside were twelve red curtain panels.
The two front pillars
were inlaid with gold,
with precious flower patterns above,
phoenix and cloud patterns in the middle,
and tortoise shell patterns below.
The lù (輅) top had a round disc two chí (尺) and odd in height,
with a gilded bronze standing phoenix finial,
with upright and inverted lotus pedestals,
and four hanging yellow tasseled ropes from the top.
The top of the disc was painted red,
the bottom四周 (all around) agarwood-colored with gold-outlined cloud patterns,
inside with green ground five-colored cloud patterns,
with green adorning the lù (輅) canopy.
Inside was a precious canopy,
with a red-painted frame,
composed of eight sections,
covered with yellow brocade;
the center and four sides were embroidered with nine phoenixes,
and five-colored cloud patterns.
Three layers of tiān lún (天輪) (celestial wheels),
painted red,
above were seventy-two carved wooden gilded-edged radiant leaf panels,
inside decorated with three layers of green-ground carved wooden five-colored cloud phoenix patterns,
interspersed with seventy-two painted five-colored cloud backing panels.
Below, the four sides were fitted with yellow bronze,
above were three layers of yellow brocade water-drip strips,
interspersed with embroidered phoenix patterns.
Four hanging blue brocade sashes,
each embroidered with a phoenix.
The four corners of the round disc were connected to the lù (輅) baseboard
with four yellow tasseled ropes from the top.
The lù (輅) pavilion had two turning corner railings on the front and back left and right each,
with embedded tasseled ring boards,
all painted red;
totaling twelve pillars,
the pillar tops had carved wooden red lotus flowers,
with gold-outlined green and blue decorated lotus flower pillar embraces.
Its footrest and traveling horse accessories
were the same as those of the dà mǎ niǎn (大馬輦) (large horse carriage).
The Ān chē (安車) (comfortable carriage),
originally one of the five lù (輅s) for queens in the Zhōu Lǐ (周禮) (Rites of Zhou).
Yìng Shào's (應劭) Hàn Guān Lǔ Bù Tú (漢官鹵簿圖) (Illustration of Official Imperial Equipage of the Hàn) shows five-colored Ān chē (安車s).
The Jìn (晉) empress rode in a yún mǔ ān chē (雲母安車) (mica comfortable carriage).
The Táng (唐) empress's Ān chē (安車)
was made like the jīn lù (金輅) (golden chariot).
The Míng (明) empress's Ān chē (安車) was uniquely simple.
Its construction:
It is nine _chǐ_ and seven _cùn_ with some餘 (remainder) in height.
It has a flat platform,
with railings and swallow-wing boards both at the front and back.
There are two shafts,
each one _zhàng_ and six _chǐ_ and seven _cùn_ with some餘 (remainder) in length,
all lacquered red,
and adorned with gilt-bronze phoenix heads, phoenix tails, and phoenix feather-shaped leaves.
On both sides of the flat platform hang mudguards and two wheels,
connected by one axle.
Each wheel has eighteen spokes,
all lacquered red.
The central part of the axle is wrapped in imperial yellow felt, to which the shafts and various ropes are attached.
The carriage pavilion is four _chǐ_ and four _cùn_ high,
supported by four red-lacquered square pillars,
on top of which are mounted twelve colorful floral panels.
At the front on the left and right are doors,
three _chǐ_ and seven _cùn_ with some餘 (remainder) in height,
and two _chǐ_ and two _cùn_ with some餘 (remainder) in width.
Next to the doors are two red-lacquered cross-shaped trellises on each side.
At the back is a three-mountain screen,
and the wall panels behind the screen are all lacquered red,
adorned with gilt-bronze chiseled floral leaves.
The floor of the pavilion is a red-lacquered board,
covered with a red floral carpet and a red brocade cushion,
with yellow silk gauze curtains around all sides,
and four red outer curtains.
The carriage canopy has a red-lacquered gilt-bronze precious pearl finial,
with a lotus base,
six _cùn_ high.
At the four corners are gilt-bronze phoenix heads,
with four hanging tasseled ropes,
and red-lacquered wooden fish.
The canopy is covered with three layers of yellow silk gauze, serving as a drip-proof covering,
embroidered with gold-thread _luán_ and phoenix patterns,
with red silk tassels hanging below the phoenix heads.
Its footrest, outrider screen, and carriage cover are the same as those for the _lù_ (imperial carriage).
_Xíngzhàng_ (moving screens) and _zuòzhàng_ (sitting screens)
have existed since the Táng (唐) and Sòng (宋) dynasties.
Behind the Empress's _Zhòngdí_ (重翟) carriage,
there are six _xíngzhàng_
and three _zuòzhàng_,
held by palace maids on either side of the carriage.
However, the _Táng Shū_ (唐書) and _Sòng Shǐ_ (宋史) do not record their specifications.
According to the _Jīn Shǐ_ (金史),
a _xíngzhàng_ is eight _chǐ_ long
and six _chǐ_ high;
a _zuòzhàng_ is seven _chǐ_ long
and five _chǐ_ high.
The Míng (明) Empress used _xíngzhàng_ and _zuòzhàng_,
both made of red damask,
painted with ascending and descending _luán_ and phoenix cloud patterns;
the _xíngzhàng_ had auspicious grasses painted on its drip-proof covering,
and the _zuòzhàng_ had cloud patterns painted on its top.
The _lù_ (imperial carriage), _ānchē_ (comfortable carriage), _xíngzhàng_, and _zuòzhàng_ for the Tài Huáng Tàihòu (太皇太后) and Huáng Tàihòu (皇太后)
were of the same specifications as those for the Empress.
The carriage of an Imperial Concubine is called a _Fèngjiào_ (鳳轎),
a different name from previous dynasties.
Its construction:
It has a blue top,
with a gilt-bronze pearl finial on top,
and one gilt-bronze flying phoenix at each of the four corners,
from which hang silver globular incense burners, precious canopies, and colored knots.
The body of the sedan chair
is a red-lacquered wooden frame,
with woven bamboo matting on three sides,
painted with _dí_ (翟) patterns,
and adorned with gilt-bronze chiseled floral leaves.
The carrying poles are red-lacquered,
decorated with gilt-bronze phoenix heads and phoenix tails.
It has blue gold-thread brocade-edged red curtains and decorative bands,
and inside are a red folding chair and a sitting cushion.
There is one red gold-thread brocade sedan chair cover,
with a gold-thread precious pearl pattern;
the drip-proof covering
has a fragrant grass pattern;
the decorative bands and curtains
all have phoenix patterns.
There is one red oiled silk rain cover for the sedan chair.
From the Empress downwards,
all use two _xíngzhàng_
and one _zuòzhàng_,
distinguished only by their painted decorations.
The _xíngzhàng_ and _zuòzhàng_ of Imperial Concubines
are both made of red damask,
painted with cloud-phoenixes,
while the _xíngzhàng_'s drip-proof covering is painted with fragrant grasses.
The Crown Prince's _Jīnlù_ (金輅)
is one _zhàng_ two _chǐ_ and two _cùn_ with some餘 (remainder) in height,
and eight _chǐ_ and nine _cùn_ wide.
The shafts are one _zhàng_ nine _chǐ_ and five _cùn_ long.
The _lù_ seat is three _chǐ_ and two _cùn_ with some餘 (remainder) in height.
The flat platform, drip-bead boards, spokes, and felloes are all the same as those of the _Yùlù_ (玉輅).
The _lù_ pavilion is six _chǐ_ and four _cùn_ with some餘 (remainder) in height,
supported by four red-lacquered pillars,
five _chǐ_ and four _cùn_ long.
Around the seat platform are gold-lined multicolored fragrant grass panels.
At the front on the left and right are doors,
five _chǐ_ with some餘 (remainder) in height,
and two _chǐ_ and four _cùn_ with some餘 (remainder) in width.
Next to the doors are two trellises on each side,
woven with red tasseled ropes and bright beads,
all lacquered red.
At the back is a five-mountain screen,
with five carved wooden dragons overlaid with gold on a blue ground,
interspersed with multicolored cloud patterns.
The red-lacquered panels behind the screen
are all adorned with gilt-bronze chiseled floral leaves.
It has a red-lacquered frame soft seat,
with red felt hanging tassels,
four large ropes,
from which hang lotus-shaped stone pendants.
It is covered with a red carpet and a red brocade cushion.
There is one red-lacquered chair,
with one folding panel and cushion.
The chair has a red gold-woven brocade backrest and seat cushion,
with chair skirts around all sides,
and red silk gauze curtains,
edged with blue silk gauze on the outside.
There are twelve red curtains.
The chair is carved and overlaid with gold dragons and colorful clouds,
with one gold-lined colorful cloud panel below.
Inside the pavilion, red tasseled ropes are woven.
The _lù_ roof and circular platform
are two _chǐ_ and five _cùn_ with some餘 (remainder) in height,
with a gilded bronze precious pearl finial,
with an inverted and upright lotus base,
nine _cùn_ high,
from which hang four red tasseled ropes attached to the top.
The platform is vermillion-lacquered,
with cloud patterns painted on a blue ground both inside and outside below,
and the _lù_ canopy is adorned in blue.
Inside the pavilion, around the perimeter, are blue _dǒugǒng_ (bracket sets),
supported by vermillion-lacquered frames.
The precious canopy is assembled with eight sections,
covered with red silk gauze,
with a cloud-dragon embroidered in the center,
and the rest embroidered with multicolored cloud patterns.
The three layers of the celestial wheel are all red-lacquered,
with seventy-two carved wooden panels with gold-lined radiating leaves on top,
and three layers of carved wooden gold-overlaid cloud-dragon patterns on a blue ground inside,
interspersed with seventy-two multicolored cloud backing panels,
with brass nails all around.
On top are three layers of red silk gauze serving as a drip-proof covering,
each layer having seventy-two pleats,
interspersed with embroidered multicolored cloud-dragon patterns.
The decorations at the four corners are the same as those of the _Dàlù_ (大輅),
except that the round tassels are made of red thread.
At the front of the _lù_ pavilion is one straight railing,
at the back is one straight railing with a corner turn,
and on the left and right are two railings,
with multicolored cloud panels inlaid inside,
all vermillion-lacquered.
There are fourteen pillars in total,
the pillar capitals are of the same design as those of the _Dàlù_.
Behind the pavilion are two red flags,
made of red silk brocade,
with nine streamers.
Each streamer is embroidered with one ascending dragon inside and out.
The waist of the left flag is embroidered with the sun, moon, and Big Dipper,
and the pole has a gilt-bronze dragon head.
The waist of the right flag is embroidered with a _fú_ (黻) pattern,
and the pole has a gilt-bronze _jǐ_ (戟).
Two gilt-bronze bells are attached,
from which hang red tassels.
Its footrest, outrider screen, and similar items
are the same as those of the _Yùlù_.
The tent cover is made of blue cotton cloth,
the pole finials are blue-green crouching _ní_ (猊),
and the rest are the same as the Imperial Carriage's tent cover.
The Crown Prince Consort's carriage
is also called a _Fèngjiào_ or _Xiǎojiào_ (小轎),
and its specifications are the same as those of an Imperial Concubine.
The specifications for the _xíngzhàng_ and _zuòzhàng_ are also the same.
The Qīnwáng's Xiànglù (Elephant Chariot)
has its height reduced by six cùn compared to the Jīnlù (Gold Chariot),
and its width reduced by one chǐ.
The length of the shafts is reduced by one chǐ compared to the Dàlù (Grand Chariot).
The chariot seat is three chǐ and a fraction high,
and the rest of its decorations are the same as the Jīnlù.
The chariot pavilion is five chǐ two cùn and a fraction high,
with four red-lacquered pillars.
Around the top of the seat railing are red-lacquered striped環板 (huánbǎn, ring panels).
There are doors on the front, left, and right,
four chǐ five cùn and a fraction high,
and two chǐ two cùn and a fraction wide.
Beside the doors are two each of partition screens and bright-● (untranscribed character, likely part of a name or specific term), and a five-mountain screen at the rear,
all red-lacquered,
decorated with gilded copper engraved with floral and leaf patterns and nailed on.
The pavilion floor is red-lacquered,
with a red floral carpet and red brocade cushions.
The style of its chairs, backrests, seat cushions, curtains, and red blinds
are all the same as the Jīnlù.
The chariot roof and circular disc are two chǐ four cùn and a fraction high,
topped with a gilded copper precious pearl finial,
the rest being the same as the Jīnlù.
The three layers of the Tiānlún (Heavenly Wheel) are all red-lacquered,
carved with sixty-three wooden panels with gilded edges and radiating leaves,
with three layers of blue-ground carved wood with five-color cloud patterns inside,
interspersed with sixty-three painted five-color cloud backing panels,
and fastened with brass all around.
Three layers of red qi (gauze) drip guards are applied above,
each layer having eighty-one pleats,
embroidered with auspicious grass patterns.
In front hang two green qi (gauze) sashes,
both embroidered with rising dragons and five-color cloud patterns.
The four corners of the circular disc are connected to the chariot seat panels
with four red corded round sashes that climb to the top,
and red-lacquered wooden fish.
The front and rear railings of the pavilion are the same as the Jīnlù,
with one railing panel on each side,
inlaid with striped環板 (huánbǎn, ring panels),
all red-lacquered.
There are a total of fourteen pillars,
the pillar tops carved with red lotus flowers,
with gold lines and blue-green decorations on the lotus-holding pillars,
and a floral carpet laid inside the front railing.
Two red flags,
the same as those erected on the Jīnlù,
with only five red tassels hanging from the poles.
Its steps, outriders, and other appurtenances
are also the same as the Jīnlù.
The tent uses green chī (hornless dragon) heads,
the rest being the same as the Dōnggōng (Eastern Palace).
The Qīnwángfēi's (Princess Consort's) carriage
is also called a Fèngjiào (Phoenix Palanquin) or Xiǎojiào (Small Palanquin),
its construction being entirely the same as the Dōnggōngfēi's (Crown Princess's).
Only the Fèngjiào's covering uses plain red silk.
The Xiǎojiào has two coverings: one uses alum red plain ramie silk,
and the other uses plain red silk.
The xíngzhàng (travel screens) and zuòzhàng (seat screens)
are made in the same style as the Dōnggōngfēi's.
The Gōngzhǔ's (Princess's) carriage:
in the Sòng dynasty, the Yànzháichē (Pheasant Chariot) was used,
and the early Míng dynasty followed this.
Afterwards, it was standardized
that the Fèngjiào, xíngzhàng, and zuòzhàng
should be like those of the Qīnwángfēi.
The Huángsūn's (Imperial Grandson's) carriage:
during the Yǒnglè reign,
it was stipulated that the wedding procession and ceremonial guard of the Huángtàisūn (Imperial Grandson Heir Apparent) should be like that of a Qīnwáng,
one grade lower than the Huángtàizǐ (Crown Prince),
and an Xiànglù should be used.
A Jùnwáng (Prince of a Commandery) has no lù (chariot),
only a zhàngfáng (tent-carriage),
made in the same style as the Qīnwáng.
The Jùnwángfēi (Princess Consort of a Commandery) and Jùnzhǔ (Commandery Princess) both use a Zháijiào (Pheasant Palanquin),
made in the same style as the Huángfēi's (Imperial Consort's) Fèngjiào,
only replacing the phoenix with a pheasant.
The xíngzhàng and zuòzhàng are the same as the Qīnwángfēi's,
but painted with cloud-and-pheasant patterns.
Regulations for officials riding in carriages.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, an order was issued
that no carriage should be carved with dragon or phoenix patterns.
Officials of the first to third ranks
should use silver chī (hornless dragon) embroidered belts with gilded decoration,
and blue curtains.
Fourth and fifth ranks
should use plain lion head embroidered belts,
and blue curtains.
Sixth to ninth ranks
should use plain cloud-head blue belts,
and blue curtains.
Palanquins were made in the same style as carriages.
Commoners' carriages and palanquins
must all be black-lacquered,
with flat roofs,
black curtains,
and cloud-head patterns were forbidden.
In the sixth year, an order was issued
that all carriages and palanquins were forbidden to use vermilion lacquer,
and carriages for officials of the fifth rank and above could only use blue curtains.
Women were permitted to ride in palanquins,
and old and infirm officials and commoners could also use them.
In the fourth year of Jǐngtài, an order was issued
that officials of the third rank and above in the capital could ride in palanquins.
In the seventh year of Hóngzhì, an order was issued
that civil and military officials who were permitted to ride in palanquins
should have them borne by four bearers.
However, administrators of the Five Chief Military Commissions (Wǔfǔ),
internal and external garrison commanders (zhènshǒu, shǒubèi), as well as Gōng (Dukes), Hóu (Marquises), Bó (Counts), Dūdū (Chief Military Commissioners), etc.,
regardless of age,
were all forbidden to ride in palanquins.
Those who violated the rule by riding in palanquins or presumptuously used eight bearers
would be reported to the emperor.
This was because Tàizǔ (the Hongwu Emperor) did not want meritorious officials to neglect equestrian skills and archery;
even high-ranking Gōng,
when leaving, had to ride horses.
In the first year of Yǒnglè,
Fùmǎ Dūwèi Hú Guān (Imperial Son-in-Law and Commandant Hú Guān) violated regulations by riding in Jìn Wáng Jì Xī's (Prince of Jìn Jì Xī's) Zhūlǔ Zōngjiào (vermilion-lacquered palanquin made of coir),
and was impeached by Gěishìzhōng Zhōu Jǐng (Investigating Censor Zhōu Jǐng).
An imperial edict pardoned Hú Guān but sent a strongly worded letter to Jì Xī,
severely reprimanding him.
Only high-ranking civil officials rode in palanquins;
lower-ranking officials also rode horses.
Furthermore, all civil officials were permitted to ride in carriages,
and high-ranking officials could ride in Ānchē (comfortable carriages).
Later, this practice was long abandoned.
In the fourth year of Zhèngdé,
Lǐbù Shìláng Liú Jī (Vice Minister of Rites Liú Jī) stated
that according to the Dàmíng Jílǐ (Collected Rites of the Great Míng Dynasty),
Gōng, Qīng, and high-ranking officials could ride in Ānchē,
and thus requested to standardize the grades for palanquins, fans, and umbrellas/canopies.
The Emperor, noting that within the capital,
Ānchē and canopies had not been used for a long time,
rejected his request,
but ordered that palanquins and fans should be used according to existing regulations.
In the fifteenth year of Jiājìng,
Lǐbù Shàngshū Huò Tāo (Minister of Rites Huò Tāo) said:
"According to established ceremonial regulations,
capital officials of the third rank and above may ride in palanquins.
Recently, civil officials have all been using jiānyú (shoulder litters)
or riding in nǚjiào (women's palanquins).
I humbly request that the ritual regulations be reaffirmed
so that subordinates may have something to comply with."
Thereupon it was stipulated that officials of the fourth rank and below were not allowed to ride in palanquins,
nor were they permitted to use jiānyú.
In the second year of Lóngqìng,
Gěishìzhōng Xú Shàng (Investigating Censor Xú Shàng) impeached Yìngchéng Bó Sūn Wéndòng (Count of Yìngchéng Sūn Wéndòng) and others for riding in palanquins in and out,
acting arrogantly and improperly.
The Emperor ordered the forfeiture of Sūn Wéndòng's salary and others'.
Then an edict was issued that military officials in both capitals, unless by special imperial favor, were not allowed to ride in palanquins,
and civil officials of the fourth rank and below using wéijiào (curtained palanquins)
were prohibited as per regulations.

In the third year of Wànlì, it was stipulated by imperial decree that meritorious relatives and military officials were not allowed to use wéijiào, jiānyú, or jiāochuáng shàngmǎ (folding chairs for mounting horses).
As for exceptional special favors,
in the Xuāndé reign, Shàobǎo Huáng Huái (Grand Guardian Huáng Huái), when accompanying the emperor on a tour of the Xīyuàn (Western Garden),
once rode a jiānyú into the forbidden palace.
During the Jiājìng reign,
Yán Sōng (嚴嵩), by imperial edict, served in the imperial garden,
and being nearly eighty years old,
was permitted to ride a jiānyú in and out.
As for military officials, Guō Xūn (郭勛) and Zhū Xīzhōng (朱希忠) were specially commanded to ride jiānyú when accompanying the emperor on his southern inspection tour,
and later were granted the privilege of regular use.
All these were exceptions to the regulations.
Regulations for umbrellas and canopies.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ,
an order was issued that commoners were not allowed to use silk-gauze sun umbrellas,
but only oil-paper rain umbrellas.
In the third year, an order was issued that within the capital, officials of the first and second ranks could use umbrella-canopies,
while others used rain umbrellas.

In the sixteenth year, it was ordered that Shàngshū (Ministers), Shìláng (Vice Ministers), Zuǒyòu Dūyùshǐ (Left and Right Censors-in-Chief), Tōngzhèngshǐ (Chief Reviser of Memorials), Tàichángqīng (Grand Master of Ceremonies), Yìngtiān Fǔyǐn (Prefect of Yìngtiān Prefecture), Guózǐ Jìjiǔ (Libationer of the Imperial Academy), and Hànlín Xuéshì (Academicians of the Hànlín Academy) were permitted to display umbrella-canopies.
In the twenty-sixth year, it was stipulated that first and second-rank umbrellas should have silver fútú (stupa) finials,
and third and fourth-rank umbrellas should have red fútú finials,
all with black or dark brown silk-gauze covers,
red silk linings,
and three eaves;
rain umbrellas should use red oil-silk.
Fifth-rank umbrellas had red fútú finials,
blue silk-gauze covers,
red silk linings,
and two eaves;
rain umbrellas were the same.
Fourth-rank, and sixth to ninth-rank umbrellas
used red fútú finials,
blue silk covers,
red silk linings,
and two eaves;
all rain umbrellas used oil paper.
In the thirty-fifth year,
officials' umbrella-canopies were not allowed to use gold embroidery
or vermilion decoration.
Gōng (Dukes), Hóu (Marquises), Fùmǎ (Imperial Sons-in-Law), and Bó (Counts) were treated the same as first and second-rank officials.
In the ninth year of Chénghuà, an order was issued that officials in both capitals could use oil umbrellas when it rained,
but sun umbrellas were not allowed to be displayed within the capital.
Regulations for saddles and bridles.
In the 6th year of Hóngwǔ, it was decreed that commoners were not allowed to adorn with gold,
only copper and iron decorations.
In the 26th year, it was stipulated that Gōng, Hóu, officials of the 1st rank, and 2nd rank use silver-inlaid
iron fittings,
and apply silver painting.
Officials from the 3rd to 5th rank
use silver-inlaid
iron fittings,
and apply oil painting.
Officials from the 6th to 9th rank
use tin plating,
iron fittings,
and apply oil painting.
In the 35th year,
all officials and commoners were to use black tassels under their horses' jaws and black cruppers and bridles,
not allowing red tassels or decorations adorned with gold, inlaid with gold, sky blue, or vermilion.
Soldiers and commoners were to use iron fittings,
with black and green oil paint.
Collation Notes
Volume 42: Carriages and Apparel II - Emperor's Ceremonial Robes and Crown, Empress's and Consorts' Headwear and Robes, Crown Prince's and Princes' and below Headwear and Robes.
Emperor's Ceremonial Robes and Crown.
In the 1st year of Hóngwǔ,
scholar Táo Ān requested the creation of five crowns.
Tài Zǔ said:
"This ritual is too complex.
For sacrifices to Heaven and Earth and the ancestral temple,
wear the gǔnmiǎn.
For sacrifices to the altars of soil and grain and other ceremonies,
wear the tōngtiān guān [crown] and
scarlet gauze robes.
The rest are not needed."
In the 3rd year, it was further stipulated that for the New Year's Day, winter solstice, and emperor's birthday, the gǔnmiǎn should be worn,
and for sacrifices to the altars of soil and grain, first farmers, and investitures,
the same applied.
In the 16th year, the system for the gǔnmiǎn was established.
The miǎn [crown] was
round in front and square at the back,
black on the outside and reddish-yellow on the inside.
It had twelve strings of beads (liú) at both the front and back,
each string with twelve beads of five-colored jade.
The five-colored braids had twelve loops,
each loop separated by one cùn.
Red silk cord was used for the chin strap,
yellow floss for the earplugs (chōngěr),
and a jade hairpin (zān) served as a guide.
The gǔn [robe] consisted of
a black upper garment and a reddish-yellow lower garment,
with twelve embroidered symbols (shí'èrzhāng).
The sun, moon, stars, mountain, dragon, and magnificent bird (huáchóng) — six symbols — were woven onto the upper garment,
while the ancestral vessel (zōngyí), aquatic grass (zǎo), fire, rice grains (fěnmǐ), axe pattern (fǔ), and antithetical pattern (fú) — six symbols — were embroidered onto the lower garment.
A white plain silk sash (dàdài)
had a reddish-yellow lining.
The knee-cover (bìxī) matched the color of the lower garment,
embroidered with patterns of dragons, fire, and mountains.
A jade leather belt,
and jade pendants.
The large sash (dàshòu) had six colors:
red, yellow, black, white, light blue, and green.
There were three small sashes (xiǎoshòu),
their colors the same as the large sash.
Three jade rings were interspersed.
A white plain silk inner garment (zhōngdān),
with a fú pattern on the collar,
and a blue border.
Yellow socks,
yellow shoes (xī),
with gold ornamentation.
In the 26th year, it was revised:
The gǔnmiǎn had twelve symbols.
The miǎn's top board was one chǐ two cùn wide
and two chǐ four cùn long.
The crown had a cover,
black on the outside and vermilion on the inside;
the rest was as per the old system.
The guī [scepter] was one chǐ two cùn long.
The gǔn [robe] had
a black upper garment and a reddish-yellow lower garment,
with twelve symbols as per the old system.
The zhōngdān was made of plain gauze.
A red plain silk bìxī,
one chǐ wide at the top,
two chǐ wide at the bottom,
and three chǐ long,
woven with three symbols: fire, dragon, and mountain.
A leather belt with jade pendants,
three chǐ three cùn long.
The dàdài was plain on the outside with a vermilion lining,
with borders on both sides,
the upper part of vermilion brocade,
the lower part of green brocade.
The dàshòu was
woven in six colors (yellow, white, red, black, light blue, green),
with a purely black ground of five hundred shǒu.
(One single-strand yarn twisted together forms one xì,
four xì form one fú,
five fú form one shǒu.)
There were three xiǎoshòu,
their colors the same as the dàshòu.
Three jade rings were interwoven.
Vermilion socks,
red shoes (chìxī).
In the 3rd year of Yǒnglè, it was stipulated:
The miǎn guān (crown) was made of black gauze,
the cover on top was called yán,
with a paulownia wood base,
covered with damask,
black on the outside and vermilion on the inside,
round in front and square at the back.
A jade crossbar (yùhéng) held the crown,
and a jade hairpin (yùzān) passed through the knob.
The knob and the crown's base (wǔ) (the part below the front body is called wǔ,
the suī [tassel] is below the crown,
also called wǔ)
and the place where the chin straps were tied
were all decorated with gold.
The yán had yellow floss (tǒuhuáng) hanging down on both sides to plug the ears,
(using yellow jade.)
Tied with black silk cords (xuángǎn),
supported by white jade pendants (báiyù tián) and a vermilion chin strap (zhūhóng).
The rest was as per the old system.
The yùguī (jade scepter) was one chǐ two cùn long,
sharpened at the top,
carved with four mountains,
symbolizing the four boundary mountains (sìzhèn zhī shān).
This was in the style of the Zhōu dynasty's zhènguī,
different from the plain dàguī.
Its lower part was wrapped with yellow damask,
and separately encased in a pouch
with a golden dragon pattern.
The gǔn robe had twelve symbols.
The black upper garment had eight symbols:
sun, moon, and dragon on the shoulders,
stars and mountain on the back,
fire, huáchóng, and zōngyí on the sleeves,
(three on each sleeve.)
All were woven in their original colors on the collar, cuffs (biǎo), borders (chún), and hem (jū).
(Biǎo refers to the sleeve ends.
Chún refers to the garment borders.)
The reddish-yellow lower garment had four symbols:
two each of zǎo, fěnmǐ, fǔ, and fú woven onto it.
Three panels in front,
four panels at the back,
front and back not connected,
with a shared waistband,
having pleats,
and borders of the original color (fēi and tī).
(A border on the side of the lower garment is called fēi,
a border at the bottom of the lower garment is called tī.
Chún refers to borders.)
The zhōngdān was made of plain gauze.
It had a blue collar, cuffs, borders, and hem,
with thirteen fú patterns woven onto the collar.
The bìxī matched the color of the lower garment,
with four symbols,
two each of zǎo, fěnmǐ, fǔ, and fú.
It had borders of the original color,
with cords (xùn)
applied in the seams.
Two jade hooks.
Two jade pendants (yùpèi),
each using one yùhéng, one yǔ, two jū, one chōngyá, and two huáng;
below the yǔ hung one jade flower and two jade drops;
carved with cloud and dragon patterns outlined in gold.
From the héng downwards, five cords were tied,
threaded with jade beads.
When walking, the chōngyá, two drops, and huáng touched each other, making a sound.
Two gold hooks.
There were two xiǎoshòu,
six-colored (yellow, white, red, black, light blue, green) on a reddish-yellow ground.
The dàshòu was
six-colored (yellow, white, red, black, light blue, green) on a reddish-yellow ground.
Three xiǎoshòu had the same colors as the dàshòu.
Three jade rings were interspersed,
with dragon patterns,
all woven.
The socks and shoes (xī) were both red,
the shoes had black tips and borders (jūchún),
with yellow ornamentation on the shoe tips.
In the eighth year of Jiājìng, the emperor instructed Grand Secretary Zhāng Cōng:
“The formal robes (gǔnmiǎn) have a leather belt (gé dài);
why is it not used now?”
Zhāng Cōng replied:
“According to Chén Xiángdào’s Lǐ Shū (Book of Rites),
ancient leather belts (gé dài) and great belts (dà dài)
were all called pán.
The leather belt was used to attach the ceremonial apron (pèi fú),
and then the great belt was added over it.
The ceremonial tablet (hù) was inserted between the two belts.
Indeed, the leather belt was used to attach the ceremonial apron in front,
the sash (shòu) in back,
and the ornaments (pèi) on the sides.
It has been used with formal robes (miǎnbìan) since ancient times.
Now, only the leather belt is not used,
resulting in the front and back ornaments having nothing to be attached to.
They are then attached between the skirt (shāng) and the waist,
which deviates from the ancient system.”
The Emperor said:
“When wearing formal robes (miǎn fú) to offer sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
and to enjoy the ancestral spirits,
if the leather belt is missing,
it does not accord with the meaning of 'pure and bright grand attire' (qímíng shèng fú).
Also, I have observed that the Huìdiǎn records the ceremonial apron (bìxī) as being made of silk gauze (luó),
with three patterns—fire, mountain, and dragon—woven on it.
And the edging of the great belt (dà dài) uses brocade.
These all do not match what is currently worn.
You should meticulously investigate and draw diagrams for the style of the leather belt (gé dài) and how to attach the ceremonial apron (bìxī), ornaments (pèi), and sashes (shòu),
and submit them.”
He further said:
“The upper garment (yī) and skirt (shāng) are separated into upper and lower garments,
but now the upper garment covers the skirt.
The skirt was made like a curtain (wéi),
but now it has two panels.
My intention is that the upper garment should only be level with the bottom of the skirt's waist,
revealing the skirt’s six patterns.
What do you think?”
Later, he again instructed Zhāng Cōng, expressing doubt about altering ancestral systems.
Zhāng Cōng replied:
“I have investigated the rites,
and the upper garment not covering the skirt
is perfectly consistent with Your Majesty's intention.
Indeed, the upper garment has six patterns,
and the skirt has six patterns,
each with its own symbolic meaning.
Therefore, the upper garment naturally should not cover the skirt.
The Dà Míng Jí Lǐ and the Huìdiǎn are not different from the ancient system.
Currently, the upper garment has eight patterns,
and the skirt has four patterns,
so the upper garment often covers the skirt,
but this has no basis in classic texts.
The illustrated notes stored in the Grand Secretariat
are probably due to the weaving officials
following customary errors.
Now, by correcting this,
we are restoring the ancestral system,
not making changes.”
The Emperor's decision was then made.
He then further instructed Zhāng Cōng, saying:
“The upper garment has six patterns;
anciently they were painted,
but now they should be woven.
I command the Bureau of Weaving and Dyeing to investigate the formal robes (miǎn fú) from the beginning of our dynasty.
The sun and moon should each be five inches in diameter,
and this should be followed.
The skirt has six patterns;
anciently they were embroidered,
and this should also be followed.
Anciently, the colors used were black (xuán) and yellow (huáng),
symbolizing Heaven and Earth.
Now the skirt uses dark red (xūn),
which has no symbolic meaning.
The ancient practice should be followed.
The leather belt (gé dài) is the same as the sash belt (shù dài).
Jade should be used at the back,
with the ornaments (pèi) and sashes (shòu) tied below it.
The ceremonial apron (bìxī) should match the color of the skirt.
Its embroidery should have a dragon above and fire below;
the mountain pattern may be omitted.
You and the other Grand Secretaries should jointly investigate this.”
Thereupon, Yáng Yīqīng and others deliberated in detail:
“The formal robes (gǔnmiǎn)
since the time of Huáng Dì and Yǔ [Shùn] have been black (xuán) upper garments and yellow (huáng) skirts,
with twelve patterns.
Sun, Moon, Stars, Mountain, Dragon, and Flowery Pheasant
are, in order from top to bottom,
the six patterns of the upper garment;
Sacred Vessels (Zōng Yí), Algae (Zǎo), Fire (Huǒ), Grains of Rice (Fěnmǐ), Axe-head (Fǔ), and Back-to-back Bows (Fú)
are, in order from bottom to top,
the six patterns of the skirt.
After the Zhōu Dynasty, the system gradually changed,
to either eight or nine patterns,
already deviating from antiquity.
Our Grand Progenitor Emperor (Tài Zǔ Huángdì) re-established the twelve-pattern system,
but the manufacturing officials continued to follow erroneous practices,
which was not the original intention of the design.
We humbly implore Your Sacred Judgment without doubt.”
The Emperor then ordered a propitious day to be chosen to rectify the system.
The crown (guān) was a round frame covered with black silk gauze (wū shā).
The twelve strands of beads (liú) were adorned with seven-colored jade beads.
Blue floss (qīng kuàng) filled the ear-plugs (chōng ěr),
adorned with two jade beads.
The rest followed the old system.
The upper garment was black (xuán yī) and the skirt was yellow (huáng shāng),
with six patterns on each.
According to the old system during the Hóngwǔ reign,
the sun and moon were five inches in diameter,
the skirt was continuously connected front and back like a curtain (wéi),
and its six patterns were embroidered.
The ceremonial apron (bìxī) matched the color of the skirt,
made of silk gauze (luó).
One dragon was embroidered above,
and three flames below,
attached to the leather belt (gé dài).
The great belt (dà dài) was plain on the outside (sù biǎo) and crimson on the inside (zhū pèi),
edged with crimson above
and green below.
The leather belt (gé dài) had jade in front,
but no jade in back,
covered by the attached ornaments (pèi) and sashes (shòu).
The inner garment (zhōng dān) and ceremonial tablet (guī)
were all according to the Yǒnglè period system.
Crimson socks (zhū wà),
red slippers (chì xì),
and a yellow cord (huáng tāo) edged with a black tassel knot (xuán yīng jié).
Emperor's Tōngtiān Crown (Tōngtiān Guān) and Robes.
Established in the first year of Hóngwǔ.
For sacrifices at the suburbs and temples, inspecting sacrificial animals,
and the crownings, marriages, and Buddhist/Daoist rituals of the Crown Prince and various princes,
the Tōngtiān Crown and crimson gauze robes (jiàng shā páo) were worn.
The crown was adorned with a golden bóshān ornament,
twelve cicada ornaments,
and pearls and kingfisher feathers at the top.
It had a black headband (jiè zé),
a woven cord (zǔ yīng),
and a jade hairpin (yù zān dǎo).
The crimson gauze robes (jiàng shā páo)
were in the style of a deep garment (shēnyī).
A white gauze inner garment (bái shā nèi dān)
with black collar (zào lǐng), cuffs (biǎo), facings (chùn), and hem (jū).
A crimson gauze ceremonial apron (jiàng shā bìxī),
a white false belt (bái jiǎ dài),
and a square-fronted collar (fāngxīn qǔlǐng).
White socks (bái wà),
red slippers (chì xì).
The leather belt (gé dài) and ornaments/sashes (pèi shòu)
were the same as for the formal robes (gǔn fú).
Emperor's Píbìan Robes.

Worn for court audiences on the first and fifteenth of the month, issuing edicts, offering incense, submitting memorials, tributary visits from foreign states, court audiences for provincial officials, and imperial examinations.
After Jiājìng,
they were also worn for sacrifices to Tàisuì, mountains, rivers, and various deities.
Its system was established in the twenty-sixth year of Hóngwǔ.
The Píbìan was covered with black silk gauze (wū shā),
with twelve seams (fèng) front and back,
each seam adorned with twelve five-colored jade pieces.
It had a jade hairpin (yù zān dǎo)
and a red woven cord (hóng zǔ yīng).
The garment was a crimson gauze robe (jiàng shā yī),
with the ceremonial apron (bìxī) matching the color of the robe.
A white jade ornamented leather belt (bái yù pèi gé dài).
A jade hook (yù gōu) and a scarlet and white great belt (fēi bái dà dài).
White socks (bái wà),
black slippers (hēi xì).
Established in the third year of Yǒnglè.
The Píbìan was as in the old system,
but the seams (fèng), the crown base (guān wǔ), and the places where the hairpin (zān) was inserted and the cord (yīng) tied
were all decorated with gold and jade.
The ceremonial tablet (guī) was as long as that for the formal robes (miǎn fú),
with a ridge and double upright patterns.
The crimson gauze robe (jiàng shā páo)
had a collar, cuffs, facings, and hem in its original color.
A red skirt (hóng shāng),
but without woven patterns.
The inner garment (zhōng dān)
had a red collar, cuffs, facings, and hem.
The rest was all as regulated for the formal robes (miǎn fú).
The emperor's Wǔbiànfú (military cap and robe).
In the early Míng dynasty,
it was worn when the emperor personally led expeditions or dispatched generals.
In the eighth year of Jiājìng, an imperial edict was given to Grand Secretary Zhāng Cōng, saying:
"The Huìdiǎn records that for personal expeditions and the Lèimà (sacrifice before battle) ritual,
the Wǔbiànfú is always worn.
It must be prepared."
Cōng replied:
"The Zhōu Lǐ mentions the Wéibiàn (leather cap),
which means a cap made of crimson leather,
and also clothing.
Our present dynasty has made adjustments based on ancient practices,
giving rise to the Píbiàn (leather cap) system.
The current Wǔbiàn should be like the Píbiàn,
but while the Píbiàn is covered with black gauze,
the Wǔbiàn should be covered with crimson gauze."
He then presented a diagram.
The emperor responded:
"The diagram shows the form,
but there's no place to attach things.
The ancient cap's shape was pointed at the top,
whereas the current Píbiàn is round.
I believe that a sharp top conveys lightness and advantage,
so it should follow ancient practice.
Also, the robe, skirt, and shoes are all red,
why is this?
Furthermore, there are no pendants or sashes;
if used for sacrifice,
is this permissible?"
Cōng replied:
"Since ancient times, both miǎn (ceremonial crown) and biàn (cap) attire have used a leather belt,
to which the fú (apron) was attached in front,
and the shòu (sash) behind.
The Wéibiàn
is indeed attached to the leather belt.
Military affairs value might and splendor,
hence the pure use of red."
The emperor again responded to Cōng:
"The cap, robe, skirt, and shoes should all follow ancient practices,
adding a leather belt,
pendants, sashes, and a guī (ceremonial jade tablet)."
Thus the system was finalized:
the biàn was pointed at the top,
red in color,
with twelve seams on top,
adorned with five-colored jade in the middle,
scattered like stars.
The crimson robe, crimson skirt, and crimson apron
were all red.
The pèi (pendants), shòu (sash), and leather belt
followed the usual system.
The pèi, shòu, and crimson apron
were all attached to the leather belt at the top.
The shoes were the same color as the skirt.
The jade guī was slightly smaller than the Zhènguī (territorial jade tablet),
pointed at the top and square at the bottom,
with a seal script inscription reading
"Punish the guilty and pacify the people."
The emperor's everyday attire.
Established in the third year of Hóngwǔ:
a black gauze upward-folding-corner headcloth,
a round-collared, narrow-sleeved robe,
and a belt occasionally adorned with gold, amber, or transparent rhinoceros horn.
In the third year of Yǒnglè, it was revised:
the cap was covered with black gauze,
with upward-folding corners,
later named Yìshànguān (Winged Goodness Cap).
The robe was yellow,
with a round collar,
narrow sleeves,
and one coiled gold dragon woven on the front, back, and each shoulder.
The belt was made of jade,
and the boots were made of leather.
Previously,
in the twenty-fourth year of Hóngwǔ,
the emperor traveled incognito to the Shénlèguān (Temple of Divine Music),
and saw someone wearing a netted headscarf (wǎngjīn).
The next day,
he ordered a wǎngjīn to be brought,
and distributed it to the thirteen Bùzhèngsǐsī (Provincial Administration Commissions),
decreeing that all people, regardless of status,
should wear wǎngjīn.
Thus, the Son of Heaven also regularly wore a wǎngjīn.
Furthermore, the Huìdiǎn records the crown ceremony for the imperial grandson, stating,
"The cap-bearer kneels to add the wǎngjīn,"
yet the crown and robes for the emperor and crown prince
are missing and not recorded.
In the seventh year of Jiājìng, the Yànbìanfú (leisure cap and robe) was revised.
Initially,
the emperor, finding his leisure attire still following common customs,
instructed Zhāng Cōng to research the ancient imperial system for leisure ceremonial robes.
Cōng then extracted the descriptions of
"Xuánduān Shēnyī"
(dark-colored ceremonial robe and deep robe) from ritual texts,
and submitted them with diagrams and notes.
The emperor participated in finalizing the system
and instructed Cōng to discuss it in detail.
Cōng stated:
"In ancient times, besides the miǎn robes,
the Xuánduān and Shēnyī
were the most widely used.
The Xuánduān was worn by all from the Son of Heaven down to the scholars;
it was the formal attire of the state.
The Shēnyī was worn by all from the Son of Heaven down to commoners;
it was the ceremonial attire of sages and worthies.
Now, by adding embellishments to the Xuánduān,
without changing the old system,
and changing the Shēnyī to yellow,
while remaining an undergarment,
it truly embodies the imperial way of making opportune adjustments and modifications."
The emperor then decreed to the Ministry of Rites, saying:
"The ancient Xuánduān was universally used from top to bottom.
Today is not like ancient times;
even in leisure,
it is appropriate to distinguish ranks and statuses."
Therefore, based on ancient systems,
it was renamed
"Yànbìan,"
conveying the meaning of dwelling in the deep palace alone,
and taking ease and comfort as a warning.
Its system:
the cap frame was like that of the Píbiàn,
covered with black gauze,
divided into twelve segments,
each pressed with gold thread,
adorned in front with one five-colored jade cloud,
and with four mountains arranged at the back,
a crimson ribbon forming the grouped tassel,
and two jade hairpins.
The robe followed the ancient Xuánduān system,
dark in color,
with blue edges,
embroidered with the sun and moon on both shoulders,
one coiled round dragon in front,
two coiled square dragons at the back,
eighty-one dragon patterns added to the edges,
and fifty-nine dragon patterns on the collar and both sleeves combined.
The overlap was the same length as the front and back,
with thirty-six dragon patterns in total.
The lining followed the Shēnyī system,
yellow in color.
The sleeves were round, the cuffs square,
and the hem reached the ankles, with twelve panels.
A plain belt,
crimson lining with blue exterior,
green trimmed edges,
and nine jade dragons adorning the waist.
Black shoes,
with crimson edges, red tassels, and yellow knots.
White socks.
The empress's crown and robes.
Established in the third year of Hóngwǔ:
for receiving investiture, visiting temples, and court audiences,
the ceremonial robe was worn.
Its crown:
a round frame covered with kingfisher feathers,
adorned on top with nine dragons and four phoenixes,
twelve large flowers,
and an equal number of small flowers.
Two side-wings (bóbìn),
with twelve ornamental pins.
The Huīyī (embroidered phoenix robe)
was dark blue with painted pheasants,
a red ground,
with twelve grades of five colors.
A plain gauze inner garment,
with an fú (ax-pattern) collar,
and crimson silk gauze cuffs and hem.
The bìxī (knee-cover) matched the color of the robe,
with a brownish-black collar and border,
using three grades of pheasant patterns.
The great belt matched the color of the robe,
with crimson lining on the outside,
the upper part of crimson brocade,
the lower part of green brocade,
and the ties made of green cord.
A jade leather belt.
Blue socks and blue shoes,
adorned with gold.
In the third year of Yǒnglè (1405), the regulations were established.
The crown ornament featured nine jadeite dragons,
four gold phoenixes.
One central dragon held a large pearl in its mouth,
with a jadeite canopy above
and hanging pearl tassels below.
The rest all held pearl drops in their mouths.
There were forty pieces of pearl and jadeite cloud ornaments,
and the number of large and small pearl flower ornaments was as before.
Three *bó bìn* (temple ornaments)
were adorned with gold dragons and jadeite clouds,
all with hanging pearl drops.
A pair of jadeite mouth-rims,
adorned with twelve jeweled gold-filigree flowers,
with the same number of jadeite filigree.
A pair of gold-filigree mouth-rims for the *tuō jiān* (hair ornaments).
Five pieces of pearl and jadeite facial ornaments.
A pair of pearl rings.
A black gauze forehead band,
painted with gold dragon patterns,
using twenty-one pearls.
The *zhái yī* (phoenix robe)
was deep blue,
woven with twelve grades of *zhái* (pheasant) patterns,
interspersed with small wheel flowers.
The red collar, cuffs, and hem
were woven with gold cloud and dragon patterns.
The *zhōng dān* (inner robe)
was made of jade-colored gauze,
with a red collar, cuffs, and hem,
woven with thirteen *fú* (ax-head) patterns.
The *bì xī* (knee cover) was the same color as the robe,
woven with three grades of *zhái* (pheasant) as patterns,
interspersed with four small wheel flowers.
Its collar and trim were deep purple,
woven with gold cloud and dragon patterns.
The jade *gǔ guī* (valley tablet)
was seven inches long,
pointed at the top,
carved with valley patterns.
A yellow silk ribbon bound its lower part,
enclosed in a yellow pouch,
with gold dragon patterns.
The jade *gé dài* (leather belt)
was made of blue silk,
painted with gold cloud and dragon patterns,
with ten jade ornaments
and four gold ornaments.
The *dà dài* (great sash),
both outer and inner sides, were half blue and half red,
with a pure red end.
It hung down, woven with gold cloud and dragon patterns,
with a vermilion upper trim
and a green lower trim.
One blue silk auxiliary sash.
The *shòu* (sash) had five colors:
yellow, red, white, light blue, and green,
on a dark red ground,
interspersed with two jade rings,
all woven.
Three small sashes,
the same color as the great sash.
Two jade *pèi* (pendants),
each using one jade *héng* (crossbar), one *yǔ* (semi-circular pendant), two *jū* (square pendants), one *chōng yá* (teeth-like pendant), and two *huáng* (arc-shaped pendants).
Below the *yǔ* hung one jade flower and two jade drops.
They were carved with cloud and dragon patterns, painted with gold.
From the *héng* downwards,
five woven cords were attached,
threaded with jade beads.
When walking, the two *chōng yá* drops and two *huáng* would touch, producing sound.
At the top was a gold hook,
accompanied by a small sash of five colors,
on a dark red ground,
woven.
Blue socks and slippers,
adorned with painted gold cloud and dragon patterns,
with a black trim.
Each slipper's toe was augmented with five pearls.
Empress's everyday attire.
Established in the third year of Hóngwǔ (1370),
a double-phoenix-flanked-dragon crown,
head ornaments, bracelets, and bangles used gold, jade, pearls, and kingfisher feathers.
Various colored round-collared robes,
embroidered with gold dragon and phoenix patterns.
The belt used gold and jade.
Revised in the fourth year (1371),
a dragon and phoenix pearl and jadeite crown,
a true-red large-sleeved robe and *xiá pèi* (cape),
a red silk long skirt,
and a red *bèi zi* (jacket).
The crown's design was like a special topknot,
adorned with dragon and phoenix ornaments.
The robe used woven gold dragon and phoenix patterns,
with added embroidery.
Revised again in the third year of Yǒnglè (1405),
the crown used black gauze,
attached with jadeite *bó shān* (mountain-shaped ornament),
adorned with one gold dragon
flanked by pearls.
Two jadeite phoenixes,
all holding pearl drops in their mouths.
Two pearl peonies front and back,
with eight petals,
and thirty-six jadeite leaves.
Two pearl and jadeite *rǎng huā bìn* (flower-shaped temple ornaments),
twenty-one pearl and jadeite clouds,
one jadeite mouth-rim.
Nine gold jeweled filigree flowers,
adorned with pearls.
Two gold phoenixes,
holding pearl tassels in their mouths.
Three *bó bìn* (temple ornaments),
adorned with *luán* and phoenixes.
Twenty-four gold jeweled filigree ornaments,
with pearl drops hanging from the edges.
Two gold hairpins.
A pair of coral phoenix crown beaks.
The *dà shān* (large robe) and *xiá pèi* (cape):
the *shān* was yellow,
the *xiá pèi* was deep blue,
woven with gold cloud, mist, and dragon patterns,
or embroidered, or inlaid with jadeite and gold circles,
adorned with pearl and jade pendants,
carved with dragon patterns.
Four-paneled jacket,
(which is the *bèi zi*.)
Deep blue,
embroidered with gold round dragon patterns.
The *jū yī* (robe of ceremony) was red,
with gold cloud and dragon patterns woven front and back,
or embroidered, or inlaid with jadeite and gold circles,
adorned with pearls.
The *dà dài* (great sash) was made of red silk gauze,
with a border.
The rest was either blue or green,
each matching the color of the *jū yī*.
The bordered and trimmed jacket was
yellow,
with a red collar, cuffs, and hem,
all woven with gold multi-colored cloud and dragon patterns.
The bordered and trimmed skirt was
red,
with a green border and trim,
woven with gold multi-colored cloud and dragon patterns.
The jade belt
was as regulated for the inner part of the *zhái yī*,
only with one fewer gold ornament.
The jade flower multi-colored knotted sash was
made of red and green silk gauze for the knots,
with one jade sash flower,
carved with cloud and dragon patterns.
The sash belt had six jade drops,
four gold hanging flower petals,
and six small gold leaves.
One red silk gauze belt.
Two white jade cloud-patterned *dīng dāng* (tinkling pendants),
made according to the *pèi* (pendant) regulations,
with gold hooks,
one gold *rú yì* cloud canopy,
from which hung five red cords,
one gold square-hearted cloud plaque,
all engraved with cloud and dragon patterns,
backed with red silk,
from which hung four long-headed gold flowers,
one medium and small gold bell,
and finally, five white jade cloud-shaped *qín* (ornaments).
Blue socks and slippers
were the same as regulated for the inner part of the *zhái yī*.
Empress Consorts, Imperial Concubines, and Inner Court Ladies' Attire.
In the 3rd year of Hóngwǔ, it was stipulated that
Empress Consorts' ceremonial attire for receiving investiture, assisting in sacrifices, and attending court assemblies
included a coronet adorned with nine fěi pheasants, four fèng phoenixes, and nine branches of floral hairpins.
The number of small flowers was the same.
Two bòbìn sidepieces each had nine diàn ornaments.
The díyī robe
was of blue fabric embroidered with dí pheasants,
arranged in rows on the garment and skirt,
tiered into nine grades.
A plain blue gauze zhōngdān undergarment
had a fú collar,
and crimson silk cuffs, trim, and hem.
The bìxī apron matched the color of the skirt,
adorned with embroidered double zhì pheasants,
forming two grades of insignia,
with a zōu-colored collar edge.
The dàdài sash matched the color of the garment.
A jade gédài belt.
Blue stockings and xì shoes, with pèi and shòu pendants.
For everyday attire:
A luánfèngguān coronet,
with head ornaments, bracelets, and bangles made of gold, jade, pearls, jewels, and kingfisher feathers.
Round-collared gowns of various colors,
embroidered in gold with luánfèng phoenixes,
but not yellow.
Belts were made of gold, jade, or rhinoceros horn.
It was also stipulated that
a shānsōng tèjì topknot,
false sideburns with floral hairpins,
or a huāchāi fèngguān coronet were worn.
A true red dàxiùyī large-sleeved robe,
xiápèi stole,
red luó skirt,
and bèizi vest.
The garment was made of woven gold or embroidered with fěngwén phoenix patterns.
In the 3rd year of Yǒnglè, it was revised again:
For ceremonial attire:
Two jiǔdíguān coronets,
made of black silk gauze,
attached with a green bòshān ornament,
decorated with two large pearl dí pheasants,
three small pearl dí pheasants,
and four green dí pheasants,
all with pearls dripping from their mouths.
In the center of the coronet was one precious pearl seat
and one green cloud-top seat.
The pearl peonies, green rǎnghuā floral sidepieces, and other similar ornaments
were all according to the specifications of the Shuāngfèng Yìlóngguān coronet,
but with ten fewer green clouds.
Additionally, two green peony flowers, two rǎnghuā flowers,
four face flowers,
four plum blossom rings,
and two pearl rings each.
The dàshān robe, xiápèi stole, and yànjū pèifú leisure ornaments
were all the same as those of the Empress,
but the woven gold embroidery
was all with clouds, mist, and fěngwén phoenix patterns,
without clóud-dragon patterns.
Nine Concubines' Attire.
In the 10th year of Jiājìng, it was first stipulated that
the coronet used nine dí pheasants,
secondary to the Empress Consorts' fěng phoenixes.
The dàshān robe and jūyī garment
were according to the Empress Consorts' system.
The guī tablet used secondary jade grain patterns.
Inner Court Ladies' Attire.
In the 5th year of Hóngwǔ, it was stipulated that
those of the third rank and above wore huāchāi hairpins and díyī robes.
Those of the fourth and fifth ranks wore shānsōng tèjì topknots,
and a dàshān robe for ceremonial attire.
Guìrén ranked as third-grade,
using the Empress Consort's yànjū coronet and dàshān robe with xiápèi stole as ceremonial attire,
and a zhūcuì qìngyúnguān coronet,
jūyī robe, bèizi vest, and yuánchuàn àoqún collared and trimmed jacket and skirt as everyday attire.
Palace Maids' Attire
was the same as that of the Sòng dynasty.
Purple,
with a round collar,
narrow sleeves,
embroidered all over with small folded branch kuí flowers,
encircled with gold,
pearl-netted, with gold belts and red skirts.
Bow-shaped tuǒ shoes,
embroidered with small gold flowers on top.
A black gauze hat,
decorated with flowers,
with a round pearl attached to the brim.
Pearl-knotted sideburn combs.
Dangling pearl earrings.
Crown Prince's Attire.

For assisting in sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, the God of Grain, and the Ancestral Temple, and for grand court assemblies, receiving investiture, and taking a concubine, he wore a gǔnmiǎn robe and crown.
In the 26th year of Hóngwǔ, it was stipulated that
the gǔnmiǎn robe had nine embroidered symbols.
The miǎn crown had nine liú strings,
each string with nine jade beads.
A golden zān hairpin and dǎo string,
red zǔyīng tassels,
and two jade tiàn earplugs.
The guī tablet was nine cun and five fen long.
A black upper garment and crimson lower garment.
The upper garment had five symbols,
embroidered with mountains, dragons, huáchóng ornate insects, zōngyí sacrificial vessels, and fire.
The lower garment had four symbols,
embroidered with algae, powdered rice, fǔ axe-head, and fú bow-back.
A white gauze zhōngdān undergarment,
with a fú collar.
The bìxī apron matched the color of the lower garment,
embroidered with two symbols: fire and mountains.
A gédài leather belt,
with a golden hook and *pán* buckle,
and jade pèi pendants.
The shòu ribbons were woven in five colors (red, white, black, light blue, green),
with a pure red ground,
three hundred and thirty shǒu threads.
Three small shòu ribbons,
of the same colors.
Interspersed with three jade rings.
The dàdài large sash,
white on the outside and crimson on the inside,
edged with red at the top,
and green at the bottom.
White stockings,
and red xì shoes.
In the 3rd year of Yǒnglè, it was stipulated that
the miǎn crown
was black on the outside and crimson on the inside,
round in front and square in back,
with nine liú strings at both the front and back.
Each liú string had nine interwoven five-colored silken threads,
strung with nine five-colored jade beads,
red, white, cyan, yellow, and black in sequence.
A jade héng crossbar, golden zān hairpin,
black dǎn string with cyan kuàng cotton hanging down to fill the ears,
(using cyan jade.)
Supported by white jade tiàn earplugs,
and crimson huángyīng chin strap.
The jade guī tablet was nine cun and five fen long,
with brocade wrapped around its lower part,
and a sheath.
The gǔnfú robe had nine embroidered symbols.
The black upper garment had five symbols:
dragon on the shoulder,
mountain on the back,
fire, huáchóng ornate insects, and zōngyí sacrificial vessels on the sleeves,
(three on each sleeve.)
All were woven.
The collar, cuffs, trim, and hem were of the garment's original color.
The crimson lower garment had four symbols,
woven with two each of algae, powdered rice, fǔ axe-head, and fú bow-back.
Three panels in front,
four panels in back,
not connected,
joined at the waist,
with pleats,
and an original-colored bìxī apron lining.
The zhōngdān undergarment was made of plain gauze,
with a cyan collar, cuffs, trim, and hem,
the collar woven with eleven fú patterns.
〔一０〕The bìxī apron matched the color of the lower garment,
with four symbols,
woven with algae, powdered rice, fǔ axe-head, and fú bow-back.
It had an edge of its original color,
with a string,
applied in the seam.
Above it were two jade hooks.
Two jade pèi pendants,
each with one jade héng, one yǔ, one jū, one chōngyá, and two huáng;
〔一一〕below the yǔ hung one jade flower and two jade drops.
Carved with cloud-dragon patterns,
and traced in gold.
From the héng downwards,
five zǔ strings were attached,
strung with jade beads.
Above were golden hooks.
Four-colored (red, white, light blue, green) small shòu ribbons accompanied it,
with a crimson ground.
The dàdài large sash,
plain on the outside and crimson on the inside,
at the waist and hanging down,
all had stitching,
the upper stitching in crimson,
the lower stitching in green.
The buttons and ties used cyan zǔ strings.
The dàshòu large ribbon was four-colored,
(red, white, light blue, green.)
With a crimson ground.
The small shòu ribbon was three-colored.
Interspersed with two jade rings,
with dragon patterns,
all woven.
Stockings and xì shoes were all red,
the xì shoes had black qú trim,
and black ornaments on the toe of the xì shoes.

For the first and fifteenth day of each lunar month, during imperial audiences, when imperial edicts are issued, when incense is offered, when memorials are presented, or when foreign states pay tribute or present themselves in audience,
one wears a Píbiàn.
It was established in the third year of Yǒnglè (1405).
The Píbiàn
is covered with black gauze,
〔一二〕with nine seams front and back.
Each seam is adorned with nine five-colored jade pieces.
The seams, the crown's framework, and the points where the hairpin passes through and the tassel is tied
are all decorated with gold.
It has a gold hairpin and a vermilion tassel.
The jade Guī tablet
is made according to the inner regulations for the Miǎnfú.
A dark red gauze robe,
with a collar, cuffs, borders, and hem of its original color.
A red lower garment,
made according to the regulations for the inner lower garment of the Miǎnfú,
but without woven patterns.
The inner garment is made of plain gauze,
in the style of the Shēnyī.
It has a red collar, cuffs, borders, and hem,
with eleven fú patterns woven into the collar.
The ornamental apron matches the color of the lower garment,
with edges of its original color.
It has a woven cord
placed within the seam.
Above it are two jade hooks.
The jade pendants are made according to the inner regulations for the Miǎnfú,
but without cloud-dragon patterns.
There are four small ribbons of four colors attached to them.
The large sash, large ribbons, socks, and shoes are red,
all made according to the inner regulations for the Miǎnfú.
Regarding the informal attire (chángfú),
it was established in the first year of Hóngwǔ (1368) as
a black gauze 'folding-up' cap (zhéshàngjīn).
In the third year of Yǒnglè (1405), it was changed to
a black gauze 'folding-corner-upward' cap (zhéjiǎoxiàngshàngjīn),
(also called the Yìshànguān),
which was the same for imperial princes (qīnwáng), commandery princes (jùnwáng), and their heirs apparent (shìzǐ).
The robe is red,
with a round collar and narrow sleeves.
There is one gold-woven coiling dragon on the front, back, and each shoulder.
A jade belt and boots
are made of leather.
Crown Prince Consort's (Huángtàizǐfēi) crown and attire.
Established in the third year of Hóngwǔ (1370),
the ceremonial attire is the same as that of the Imperial Consort (Huángfēi).
In the third year of Yǒnglè (1405), it was revised.
A nine-huī four-fèng crown,
with a lacquered bamboo framework,
covered with kingfisher feathers.
It is adorned with nine kingfisher huī and four gold fèng,
all holding pearl drops in their mouths.
Forty cloud-shaped ornaments of pearls and kingfisher feathers,
nine large pearl flower trees,
and the number of small pearl flowers matches these.
A pair of double bòbìn (side ornaments),
decorated with luán and fèng,
all with dangling pearl drops.
A pair of kingfisher feather mouth-rings,
adorned with nine pearl and jewel diànhuā (ornamental flowers),
and kingfisher feather diàn (inlaid ornaments) in the same number.
A pair of gold mouth-rings supporting the hairpins.
Five face ornaments of pearls and kingfisher feathers.
A pair of pearl hair rings.
One black gauze forehead ornament with pearls,
with gold-painted fèng patterns,
using twenty-one pearls.
The Zháiyī (robe embroidered with pheasants) is
blue in color,
woven with nine grades of zhái patterns,
interspersed with small wheel-shaped flowers.
It has a red collar, cuffs, borders, and hem,
woven with gold cloud-dragon patterns.
The inner garment (zhōngdān)
is made of jade-colored gauze.
It has a red collar, cuffs, borders, and hem,
with eleven fú patterns woven into the collar.
The ornamental apron matches the color of the robe,
woven with two grades of zhái as patterns,
interspersed with three small wheel-shaped flowers.
It has a dark grey collar and edges,
woven with gold cloud-fèng patterns.
The regulations for her jade Guī, sash and ribbons, jade pendants, socks, and shoes
are all the same as for the Imperial Consort.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ (1370), the informal attire (chángfú) was again established.
A rhinoceros horn crown,
carved with floral fèng.
The head ornaments, bracelets, shirt, and belt are all the same as for the Imperial Consort.
In the fourth year (1371), it was established that
the crown is also the same as for the Imperial Consort.
In the third year of Yǒnglè (1405), a crown for informal wear (yànjūguān) was established.
It is made of black fine silk crepe,
attached with a kingfisher feather Bóshān ornament.
On top is one jewel mount,
flanked by two pearl-and-kingfisher fèng,
all holding pearl drops in their mouths.
Two pearl peonies at the front and back,
with eight petals each,
and thirty-six kingfisher feather leaves.
Two pearl-and-kingfisher feather ránghuā side ornaments.
Sixteen cloud-shaped ornaments of pearls and kingfisher feathers.
A pair of kingfisher feather mouth-rings.
Nine gold jewel diànhuā,
adorned with nine pearls each.
A pair of gold fèng,
holding pearl knots in their mouths.
Double bòbìn,
decorated with luán and fèng.
Eighteen gold jewel diàn,
with pearl drops hanging from the edges.
A pair of gold hairpins.
A pair of coral fèngguānzī (crown beaks).
The large robe (dàshān), iridescent shawl (xiápèi), and ornaments for informal wear
are all the same as for the Imperial Consort.
Imperial Prince's (Qīnwáng) crown and attire.
When assisting at sacrifices, visiting temples, offering congratulations at court, receiving investiture, or marrying a consort, one wears a Gǔnmiǎn.

For the first and fifteenth day of each lunar month, during imperial audiences, when imperial edicts are issued, when incense is offered, when memorials are presented, or when the Four Barbarians pay tribute or present themselves in audience, one wears a Píbiàn.
Established in the twenty-sixth year of Hóngwǔ (1393),
the Miǎnfú is entirely the same as for the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng, i.e., the Crown Prince),
except that the crown tassels (miǎnliú) use five colors.
The jade Guī tablet is nine cùn, two fēn, and five lí long.
