It has a blue robe and a dark red lower garment.
In the third year of Yǒnglè (1405), the regulations for the Miǎnfú and Píbiàn were again established
to be entirely the same as for the Dōnggōng.
Their informal attire (chángfú) is also the same as for the Dōnggōng.
In the seventh year of Jiājìng (1528), an edict was issued to the Ministry of Rites:
"I have emulated the ancient Xuánduān,
and designed an Yànbìan crown and attire for myself for informal wear,
and further designed the Zhōngjìngguān and attire,
bestowing it upon those of rank.
However, the regulations for the imperial clan (zōngshì) and various princes (zhūwáng) are not yet complete.
Now, I have considered the designs of the Yànbìan and Zhōngjìngguān,
and have again created a model with diagrams,
naming it the Bǎohéguān and attire.
For the eldest sons of commandery princes (jùnwáng zhǎngzǐ) and above,
its style is already clear.

For the Generals who Guard the State (Zhènguó Jiāngjūn) and below, down to the Commandant of the State by Grace (Fèngguó Zhōngwèi), and also the Chief Secretary (Zhǎngshǐ), Judicial Administrator (Shěnlǐ), Ritual Officer (Jìshàn), Professor (Jiàoshòu), and Companion Reader (Bàndú),
all shall wear the Zhōngjìngguān and attire,
according to their respective ranks.
Court officials (yíbīn) and other officials are not permitted to wear it generally.
The distinct style of the Zhōngjìngguān and attire
is to honor the worthy based on their grades.
The distinct style of the Bǎohéguān and attire
is to express affection for kin according to their diminishing status.
With grades and diminishing status clearly defined,
this ensures what ritual preserves.
What is preserved is harmony.
What is harmonious is secure.
This is the meaning of the bestowed name.
Let the diagrams and explanations be distributed to the various princely households (zhūwángfǔ),
and be obeyed as an imperial order."
The regulations for the Bǎohéguān:
It is based on the Yànbìan,
using nine black silk threads,
without the hairpin and five jade pieces.
The rear fan (hòushān) is one piece,
divided into four sections.
The robe
is blue with blue borders,
with square dragon insignias (fānglóngbǔ) on the front and back.
The body uses plain ground,
and the borders use cloud patterns.
The lining uses a Shēnyī,
jade-colored.
The belt has a blue outer surface, green lining, and green edges.
The shoes use black and green knots,
with white socks.
Imperial Prince Consort's (Qīnwángfēi) crown and attire.
When receiving investiture, assisting at sacrifices, or attending court assemblies, one wears ceremonial attire.
Established in the third year of Hóngwǔ (1370) as a nine-huī four-fèng crown.
In the third year of Yǒnglè (1405), a nine-zhái crown was again established,
with regulations the same as for the Imperial Consort.
Her large robe (dàshān), iridescent shawl (xiápèi), and ornaments for informal wear
are the same as for the Crown Prince Consort (Dōnggōngfēi),
except that one gold ornament is reduced.
The jade ribbons (yùshòu) have
carved treasure-phase flower patterns (bǎoxiànghuā wén).
The Princess's (Gōngzhǔ) crown and attire
are the same as for the Imperial Prince Consort,
except that no Guī tablet is used.
The ceremonial attire for the heir apparent of a Qīnwáng.
For Sòngjié, Qiānqiūjié, as well as Zhèngdàn, Dōngzhì, when presenting congratulatory memorials and during the Qīnwáng's birthday and other festivals,
all wore the gǔnmiǎn.
In the 26th year of Hóngwǔ (1393), it was stipulated:
The gǔnmiǎn has seven designs (zhāng).
The miǎn (crown) has three-color jade beads
and seven streamers (liú).
The guī (scepter) is nine cùn long.
The blue robe has three designs,
woven with huáchóng, huǒ, and zōngyí.
The crimson skirt has four designs,
woven with zǎo, fěnmǐ, fǔ, and fú.
A plain gauze zhōngdān (inner garment),
with a blue collar and cuffs,
and a red bìxī.
A leather belt,
adorned with white jade,
and a dark silk sash (shòu).
The shòu is purple,
woven with three colors (purple, yellow, and red),
interspersed with three white jade rings.
White socks
and red xì (sandals).
In the 3rd year of Yǒnglè (1405), it was revised:
The miǎn crown has eight streamers each in the front and back.
Each streamer has eight strands of five-color silk,
threaded with eight three-color jade beads,
in alternating red, white, and green colors.
The jade guī is nine cùn long.
The blue robe has three designs:
huǒ on the shoulders,
huáchóng and zōngyí on both sleeves,
all woven.
The collar, cuffs, and hem are of the garment's original color.
The crimson skirt, jade ornaments, belt, and sash
are all the same as those for a Qīnwáng,
except the collar has two fewer fú patterns.
The píbiàn (leather cap) is covered with black gauze.
It has eight seams each in the front and back,
with eight three-color jade pieces attached to each seam.
The rest of the regulations are the same as for a Qīnwáng.
The guī, ornaments, belt, sash, socks, and xì are as specified for the miǎnfú (ceremonial crown and robe).
The changfú (ordinary attire) is also the same as for a Qīnwáng.
In the 7th year of Jiājìng (1528), the Bǎohé Crown and Robe were established,
based on the yànbiàn (leisure cap).
It uses eight plumes,
without jade hairpins.
The back mountain (of the crown) is divided into four sections by a fan-shaped partition.
The attire is the same as for a Qīnwáng.
The ceremonial attire for the wife of the heir apparent of a Qīnwáng.
In the 3rd year of Yǒnglè (1405), it was stipulated:
Same as for the wife of a Qīnwáng,
except the crown uses seven pheasants (zhái).
The ceremonial attire for a Jùnwáng.
In the 3rd year of Yǒnglè (1405), it was stipulated:
The miǎn crown has seven streamers each in the front and back.
Each streamer has seven strands of five-color silk,
threaded with seven three-color jade beads.
The guī is nine cùn long.
The blue robe has three designs:
fěnmǐ on the shoulders,
zǎo and zōngyí on both sleeves,
all woven.
The crimson skirt has two designs,
woven with two fǔ and two fú each.
The zhōngdān (inner garment),
its collar woven with seven fú patterns,
the rest is the same as for the heir apparent of a Qīnwáng.
The píbiàn (leather cap)
has seven seams each in the front and back,
with seven three-color jade pieces attached to each seam.
The rest is the same as for the heir apparent of a Qīnwáng.
The guī, ornaments, belt, sash, socks, and xì are as specified for the miǎnfú.
The chángfú is also the same as for the heir apparent of a Qīnwáng.
In the 7th year of Jiājìng (1528), the Bǎohé Crown and Robe were established.
The crown uses seven plumes.
The attire is the same as for the heir apparent of a Qīnwáng.
The ceremonial attire for the wife of a Jùnwáng.
In the 3rd year of Yǒnglè (1405), it was stipulated:
The crown uses seven pheasants,
the same as for the wife of the heir apparent of a Qīnwáng.
The dàshān (grand robe), xiápèi (ornamental scarf), and yànjū (leisure) ornaments
are all the same as for the wife of a Qīnwáng,
except embroidered with cloud and pheasant patterns,
not coiled phoenix patterns.
The court attire for the eldest son of a Jùnwáng.
A seven-beam crown,
a plain crimson silk-gauze robe,
a plain white gauze zhōngdān,
a plain crimson silk-gauze skirt and bìxī,
a two-color dàdài (large belt) of plain crimson silk-gauze and plain white gauze,
〔一三〕a jade court belt,
a scarlet red floral brocade,
a golden pheasant sash,
a jade ornament,
an ivory hù (tablet),
white silk socks,
and black leather cloud-head shoes.
Public attire:
A black crêpe gauze fútóu (head-wrap),
a plain crimson silk robe,
and a jade leather belt.
Ordinary attire:
A black gauze cap,
a crimson silk robe woven with gold lions,
a round collar,
a jade sash,
and black leather shoes with copper threads.
The Bǎohé crown
is made in the style of the Zhōngjìng crown,
using five plumes;
the attire is the same as for a Jùnwáng,
with a square dragon woven in gold on the bùzi (rank badge).
The ceremonial attire for a Jùnzhǔ.
In the 3rd year of Yǒnglè (1405), it was stipulated:
The same as for the wife of a Jùnwáng,
but without a guī,
and with one pair of four-bead rings fewer.
The ceremonial attire for the wife of the eldest son of a Jùnwáng.
A five-pheasant crown adorned with pearls and kingfisher feathers,
a crimson silk dàshān,
a dark blue silk bèizi (sleeveless jacket) embroidered with golden pheasants,
a blue gauze xiápèi embroidered with golden pheasants,
and golden pendants.
The ceremonial attire for a Zhènguó Jiāngjūn.
The same as for the eldest son of a Jùnwáng.
The ceremonial attire for the wife of a Zhènguó Jiāngjūn.
The same as for the wife of the eldest son of a Jùnwáng.
The ceremonial attire for a Fǔguó Jiāngjūn.
The same as for a Zhènguó Jiāngjūn;
except the crown has six beams,
and the belt uses rhinoceros horn.
The ceremonial attire for the wife of a Fǔguó Jiāngjūn.
The same as for the wife of a Zhènguó Jiāngjūn;
except the crown uses four pheasants,
and the pendants are gilded silver.
The ceremonial attire for a Fèngguó Jiāngjūn.
The same as for a Fǔguó Jiāngjūn;
except the crown has five beams,
the belt uses gold-carved flowers,
and the chángfú has crimson woven with gold tigers and leopards.
The ceremonial attire for a Shūrén (wife of Fèngguó Jiāngjūn).
The same as for the wife of a Fǔguó Jiāngjūn;
except the bèizi and xiápèi
are embroidered with golden peacock patterns.
The ceremonial attire for a Zhènguó Zhōngwèi.
The same as for a Fèngguó Jiāngjūn;
except the crown has four beams,
the belt uses plain gold,
and the ornaments use yàoyù (imitation jade).
The ceremonial attire for a Gōngrén (wife of Zhènguó Zhōngwèi).
The same as for a Shūrén (wife of Fèngguó Jiāngjūn).
The ceremonial attire for a Fǔguó Zhōngwèi.
The same as for a Zhènguó Zhōngwèi;
except the crown has three beams,
the belt uses silver-carved flowers,
the sash uses a coiled eagle pattern,
the gōngfú uses dark blue plain silk-gauze,
and the chángfú has red woven with gold bears.
The ceremonial attire for a Yírén (wife of Fǔguó Zhōngwèi).
The same as for a Gōngrén (wife of Zhènguó Zhōngwèi);
except the crown uses three pheasants,
the bèizi and xiápèi
are embroidered with golden mandarin duck patterns,
and the pendants are silver.
The ceremonial attire for a Fèngguó Zhōngwèi.
The same as for a Fǔguó Zhōngwèi;
except the crown has two beams,
the belt uses plain silver,
the sash uses a magpie pattern,
the fútóu is black lacquer,
and the chángfú has red woven with gold tigers.
The ceremonial attire for an Ānrén (wife of Fèngguó Zhōngwèi).
The same as for a Yírén (wife of Fǔguó Zhōngwèi);
except the dàshān uses scarlet red,
and the bèizi and xiápèi are embroidered with golden magpie patterns.
The ceremonial attire for a Xiànzhǔ.
A five-pheasant crown adorned with pearls and kingfisher feathers,
a crimson silk dàshān,
a dark blue silk bèizi embroidered with golden peacocks,
a blue gauze xiápèi embroidered with golden peacocks,
and gilded silver pendants.
The ceremonial attire for a Jùnjūn.
The same as for a Xiànzhǔ;
except the crown uses four pheasants,
and the bèizi and xiápèi are embroidered with golden mandarin duck patterns.
The ceremonial attire for a Xiànjūn is the same as for a Jùnjūn;
except the crown uses three pheasants.
The ceremonial attire for a Xiāngjūn is the same as for a Xiànjūn;
except the dàshān uses scarlet red,
and the bèizi and xiápèi are embroidered with golden magpie patterns.
Collation Notes

Volume 43, Chapter on Carriages and Attire 3: Attire for Civil and Military Officials; Attire for Official Ladies; Attire for Relatives of Officials Inside and Outside the Court; Attire for Court Eunuchs and Below; Attire for Scholars and Commoners; Attire for Musicians; Attire for Soldiers and Servants; Attire for Foreign Vassals; Robe Colors for Monks and Daoists.
Official attire of ministers.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, formal attire and court attire were commanded to be instituted,
to be bestowed upon all officials.
At that time, the Lǐbù stated:
"Various officials were previously conferred titular official ranks,
which differed in rank from their currently held substantive offices.
For instance, Censor Dǒng Xīzhé was previously conferred the title of Cháoliè Dàfū and Zhīzhōu of Lǐzhōu,
but held a seventh-rank substantive office;
Director Sòng Miǎn of a ministry was previously conferred the title of Yàzhōng Dàfū and Zhīfǔ of Huángzhōu,
but held a fifth-rank substantive office.
Since titular ranks and currently held offices differ,
the attire and its colors cannot but differ.
We request that regulations for this be established."
Thereupon, an imperial edict commanded the ministers of the central ministries to deliberate and decide.
The Lǐbù again stated:
"According to the Táng Dynasty system,
attire and colors were all based on the titular official rank.
According to the Yuán Dynasty system,
titular ranks and substantive offices each followed the higher of the two,
and attire and colors were determined accordingly.
In the beginning of our dynasty, attire and colors followed the titular official rank,
which was similar to the Táng system."
Thereupon, it was decided that attire and colors would be based on the titular official rank,
not taking into account the current office.
Consequently, the bestowed robes and belts also all followed this rule.
In the third year,
the Lǐbù stated:
"Successive dynasties had different favored colors.
The Xià favored black,
the Shāng white,
the Zhōu red,
the Qín black,
the Hàn red,
the Táng attire was yellow,
and their banners and flags were red.
Now our state, succeeding after the Yuán Dynasty,
takes its model from the Zhōu, Hàn, Táng, and Sòng Dynasties.
For attire and colors, the favored color
red is appropriate."
This was approved.
Court attire for civil and military officials.
Established in the twenty-sixth year of Hóngwǔ:

For grand sacrifices, celebrations of completion, New Year's Day, Winter Solstice, the Emperor's birthday, as well as issuing imperial edicts, reading out edicts, presenting memorials, and transmitting imperial commands,
all used beamed caps,
red gauze upper garments,
white gauze inner garments,
with blue trim on the collar and borders,
red gauze lower garments,
with blue borders,
red gauze ceremonial aprons,
large sashes of red and white two-colored silk,
leather belts,
pendants and ribbons,
white socks and black shoes.
For ranks one to nine,
the distinction was made by the number of beams on the cap.
A Duke's cap had eight beams,
plus a lóngjīn sable cicada ornament,
a vertical ornament with five folds,
four pillars,
five sections of fragrant grass,
and jade cicadas front and back.
A Marquis's cap had seven beams,
a lóngjīn sable cicada ornament,
a vertical ornament with four folds,
four pillars,
four sections of fragrant grass,
and golden cicadas front and back.
An Earl's cap had seven beams,
a lóngjīn sable cicada ornament,
a vertical ornament with two folds,
four pillars,
two sections of fragrant grass,
and tortoiseshell cicadas front and back.
All these also had pheasant tails inserted.
A Fùmǎ was the same as a Marquis,
but did not use pheasant tails.
For the first rank,
the cap had seven beams,
did not use the lóngjīn sable cicada ornament,
the leather belt and pendant were both jade,
the ribbon was a yellow, green, red, and purple four-colored brocade woven with cloud-phoenix patterns,
tied below with a blue silk net,
and two jade ribbon rings.
For the second rank,
six beams,
a leather belt,
rhinoceros horn ribbon rings,
the rest was the same as the first rank.
For the third rank,
five beams,
a leather belt with gold plaques,
a jade pendant,
the ribbon was a yellow, green, red, and purple brocade woven with cloud-crane patterns,
tied below with a blue silk net,
and two gold ribbon rings.
For the fourth rank,
four beams,
a leather belt with gold plaques,
a 'medicine jade' pendant,
the rest was the same as the third rank.
For the fifth rank,
three beams,
a leather belt with silver plaques,
with carved patterns,
a 'medicine jade' pendant,
the ribbon was a yellow, green, red, and purple brocade woven with coiled-eagle patterns,
tied below with a blue silk net,
and two silver-gilt ribbon rings.
For ranks one to five,
the ceremonial tablets were all ivory.
For the sixth and seventh ranks,
two beams,
a leather belt with silver plaques,
a 'medicine jade' pendant,
the ribbon was a yellow, green, and red three-colored brocade woven with magpie patterns,
tied below with a blue silk net,
and two silver ribbon rings.
Only Censors wore the xièzhì (badge).
For the eighth and ninth ranks,
one beam,
a leather belt with black horn plaques,
a 'medicine jade' pendant,
the ribbon was a yellow and green two-colored brocade woven with xīchì patterns,
tied below with a blue silk net,
and two copper ribbon rings.
For ranks six to nine,
the ceremonial tablets were all huái wood.
As for military officials who were on guard duty,
they had separate attire and colors.
Miscellaneous officials not yet admitted into the ranks,
for grand court audiences and presenting memorials and performing rites, only used formal attire.
In the thirtieth year, it was ordered that they should be treated like ninth-rank officials,
and use court attire.
In the eighth year of Jiājìng, the regulations for court attire were re-established.
The beamed cap was as the old style,
the upper garment was red gauze with blue borders,
its length extending seven cūn below the waist,
not covering the lower garment.
The inner garment was white gauze with blue borders.
The lower garment had seven panels,
three in front and four in back,
with three pleats on each panel,
red gauze with blue borders.
The ceremonial apron was attached to the leather belt.
Ribbons,
each followed the patterns according to their rank.
Pendants and ribbons were worn behind the leather belt,
tied and covered by it.
Their rings also each followed the rank,
using jade, rhinoceros horn, gold, silver, or copper,
and were not woven into the ribbon.
The outer and inner surfaces of the large sash were both plain,
only its two ends and the hanging parts were bordered with green,
and it was bound by a blue cord.
Leather belts were all as the old style.
Jade pendants were exactly as the regulations described in the Shīzhuàn,
removing the double drops and two héng.
As for the third rank and above, they used jade,
the fourth rank and below used 'medicine jade',
and socks and shoes were all as the old style.
In the fifth year of Wànlì, it was ordered that all officials at the New Year's Day court audience,
must not presume to wear vermilion shoes.
According to custom,
in the eleventh month, all officials wore ear warmers.
That year, during court audiences, provincial officials, jǔrén, and jiànshēng,
were not permitted to wear ear warmers when entering court.
When personally offering sacrifices in the suburbs, at the ancestral temples, and to the gods of soil and grain,
civil and military officials who participate in the supplementary sacrifices
shall wear sacrificial robes.
In the 26th year of Hóngwǔ (1393), it was decreed that
officials from the first to the ninth rank
should wear robes of blue silk gauze,
with an inner garment of white sheer silk,
both with black collars and borders.
A skirt of red silk gauze,
with black borders.
A bǐxī (kneepad) of red silk gauze.
A fāngxīn qǔlǐng (square heart curved collar).
Their crowns, belts, pendants, and sashes varied by rank
and were the same as those for court robes.
It was also stipulated that officials' household sacrificial robes
for those of the third rank and above
should omit the fāngxīn qǔlǐng.
For those of the fourth rank and below,
the pendants and sashes were also omitted.
In the 8th year of Jiājìng (1529), the sacrificial robes for all officials were revised.
The upper garment was of blue silk gauze,
with black borders,
the same as the court robe.
The lower garment was of red silk gauze,
with black borders,
the same as the court robe.
The bǐxī, shòuhuán (sash ring), dàdài (large belt), gédài (leather belt), pèiyù (jade pendant), and wàlǚ (socks and shoes) were all the same as for the court robe.
For inspecting sacrificial animals, worshipping the sun and moon, performing the plowing ceremony, and sacrificing to successive emperors,
only the officials of the Jǐnyīwèi (Brocade-Clad Guard) in the main hall
wore large crimson python robes,
with flying fish patterns,
black gauze caps,
luándài (phoenix belts),
and carried xiùchūndāo (embroidered spring sabers).
When sacrificing at the Tàimiào (Grand Ancestral Temple) and to the gods of soil and grain,
they wore large crimson informal attire.
Civil and military officials' official uniforms.
Established in the 26th year of Hóngwǔ (1393).
These were worn for morning and evening court audiences to present memorials, stand guard, express gratitude, and bid farewell.
Outside civil and military officials
wore them daily for official duties.
Their style was:
a round-necked robe with a right lapel,
made of zhùsī (ramie silk), or shāluójuàn (gauze, thin silk, or fine silk),
with sleeves three chi wide.
First to fourth ranks wore
crimson robes;
fifth to seventh ranks wore
blue robes;
eighth and ninth ranks wore
green robes;
unranked minor officials
had robes, hu (tablets), and belts similar to those of the eighth rank and below.
The floral patterns for official uniforms: First rank,
large single-branch flowers,
five cùn in diameter;
Second rank,
small single-branch flowers,
three cùn in diameter;
Third rank,
scattered flowers without stems and leaves,
two cùn in diameter;
Fourth and fifth ranks,
small miscellaneous floral patterns,
one cùn and five fēn in diameter;
Sixth and seventh ranks,
small miscellaneous flowers,
one cùn in diameter;
Eighth rank and below had no patterns.
Pútóu (head-wraps): two types, lacquered and gauze,
with extended wings one chi and two cùn long;
Pútóu for minor officials
had hanging ribbons,
but later they were again ordered to have extended wings
and no hanging ribbons,
like those of ranked officials.
The hu were made according to the court robes.
Waist belts: First rank, jade,
either patterned or plain;
Second rank, rhinoceros horn;
Third and fourth ranks,
gold litchi pattern;
Fifth rank and below, black horn.
They used blue leather
and still had a whip-tail hanging below.
The boots were black.
Later,
for regular court audiences, only court robes were worn,
but on the first and fifteenth of the month, official uniforms were worn for court attendance.
All military officials who were on duty as guards
had separate clothing colors
and were not restricted by this regulation.
The clothing colors, floral patterns, and waist belts of gōng (dukes), hóu (marquises), fùmǎ (imperial sons-in-law), and bó (earls)
were the same as those of the first rank.
If the floral patterns for civil and military officials
could not be woven,
plain ones were used.
When officials attended court,
if it rained or snowed, they were permitted to wear raincoats.
When presenting memorials in the Fèngtiān, Huágài, and Wǔyīng halls,
one must wear soft-soled shoes;
violators would be impeached by the yùshǐ (Censor).
In the 5th year of Wànlì (1577), it was ordered that for regular court audiences,
all officials should wear their respective brocade and embroidered robes.
For officials attending court for audience or farewell, or to express gratitude,
regardless of whether they were ranked or unranked,
they should perform the rites in official uniform.
Civil and military officials' informal attire.
Established in the 3rd year of Hóngwǔ (1370),
for daily court audiences and official duties,
the black gauze cap, round-collared robe, and sash were considered the official uniform.
For the sashes:
First rank, jade;
Second rank, patterned rhinoceros horn;
Third rank, gold with carved patterns;
Fourth rank, plain gold;
Fifth rank, silver with carved patterns;
Sixth and seventh ranks, plain silver;
Eighth and ninth ranks, black horn.
For retired officials and those who resigned due to parental care,
they wore gauze caps and sashes.
Those who were demoted or dismissed for wrongdoing
wore attire similar to commoners.
In the 24th year (1391),
it was again decreed that gōng, hóu, bó, and fùmǎ should wear sashes similar to the first rank,
and minor officials similar to the eighth and ninth ranks.
The rules for court officials' informal attire (lǐxiè, ceremonial shoes)
were established in the 6th year of Hóngwǔ (1373).
Previously,
when officials entered court,
if it rained, they all wore nailed boots,
their sounds echoing throughout the halls and steps.
The Shìyísī (Bureau of Ceremonial Etiquette) requested a prohibition.
Tàizǔ (Emperor Hóngwǔ) said:
"In ancient times, people wore lǚ (shoes) when entering court;
boots only began to be used in the Táng Dynasty.
Let court officials make soft-soled leather xǐe
to be worn over their boots,
and removed upon leaving court."
The Lǐbù (Ministry of Rites) stated that this was extravagant and exceeded regulations.
An imperial edict was issued to reiterate the prohibition,
and to refer to the systems of the Hàn and Táng Dynasties
for promulgation and compliance.
For officials,
first and second ranks used multicolored patterned silks, damasks, brocades, and embroidered designs,
with jade for the cap crown and cap beads;
third to fifth ranks used multicolored patterned silks, damasks, and brocades,
with gold for the cap crown,
and for cap beads, other materials could be used
besides jade;
sixth to ninth ranks used multicolored patterned silks, damasks, and brocades,
with silver for the cap crown,
and agate, crystal, or fragrant wood for cap beads.
First to sixth ranks were permitted to wear four-clawed dragons
embroidered in gold.
The Lǐbù further deliberated:
"It is inappropriate for ranked officials to wear court official uniforms
when meeting elders,
according to principle.

They should wear specially made liángguān (beam caps), jiàngyī (crimson robes), jiàngshang (crimson skirts), gédài (leather belts), dàdài (large belts), dàbáiwà (large white socks), wūxī (black shoes), and pèishòu (pendants and sashes),
but their robes and skirts should have no borders or hems.
Those of the third rank and above wore pendants and sashes;
those of the third rank and below did not."
This was adopted.
In the 22nd year, it was decreed that civil and military officials should wear rain hats when it rained.
When on official duty outside, they should wear hats.
Entering the city was not permitted.
In the 23rd year, regulations were established:
The robes of civil officials, from collar to hem,
should be one cùn above the ground.
Sleeves should extend beyond the hands,
then return to the elbows.
Gōng, Hóu, and Fùmǎ were to follow the same rules as civil officials.
For military officials, robes should be five cùn above the ground,
and sleeves should extend seven cùn beyond the hands.
In the 24th year, it was decreed that
Gōng, Hóu, Fùmǎ, and Bó's robes
should be embroidered with Qílín and Báizé.
First-rank civil officials: Xiānhè;
second-rank: Jǐnjī;
third-rank: Kǒngquè;
fourth-rank: Yúnyàn;
fifth-rank: Báixián;
sixth-rank: Lùsī;
seventh-rank: Xīchìniǎo;
eighth-rank: Huánglí;
ninth-rank: Ānchún.
Miscellaneous officials: Liànquè;
Censors (Fēngxiàn Guān): Xièzhì.
First and second-rank military officials: Shīzi;
third and fourth-rank: Hǔbào;
fifth-rank: Xióngpí;
sixth and seventh-rank: Biāo;
eighth-rank: Xīniú;
ninth-rank: Hǎimǎ.
It was also decreed that ranked officials' everyday attire should use various colored zhùsī, língluó, and cǎixiù.
Official garments and curtains
were not permitted to use the three colors xuán, huáng, or zǐ,
nor were dragon and phoenix patterns to be woven or embroidered.
Violators would have their crime extend to the dyers and manufacturers.
Personnel attending court
were to wear colored clothing in all four seasons,
and pure plain white was not allowed.
In the 30th year, it was decreed that retired officials' (zhìshì guān) dress colors should be the same as those currently in office.
For court audiences, felicitations, expressing gratitude, or farewells,
they were all to wear full official dress.
In the 4th year of Jǐngtài, it was decreed that Jǐnyīwèi Commanders serving as imperial guards (shìwèi zhě)
were allowed to wear Qílín.
In the 2nd year of Tiānshùn, it was decreed that officials and commoners' clothing should not use mǎnglóng, fēiyú, dòuniú, dàpéng, xiàngshēng shīzi, sìbǎoxiānghuā, dàxīfānlián, dàyúnhuā patterns,
nor the colors xuán, huáng, zǐ, xuánsè, hēi, lǜ, liǔhuáng, jiānghuáng, or mínghuáng.
In the 13th year of Hóngzhì, it was officially decreed through memorial that
Gōng, Hóu, Bó, civil and military ministers, and those guarding frontiers (zhènshǒu), or serving as garrisons (shǒubèi),
who, contrary to regulations, memorialized to request mǎngyī or fēiyú clothing,
would be impeached by the kēdào
and punished with severe penalties.
In the 11th year of Zhèngdé, the Eastern and Western Official Halls (Dōng, Xī liǎng guāntīng) were established,
and all officers and soldiers wore yellow armored jackets (huáng zhàjiǎ).
This spread throughout the capital and provinces.
Even those in grand red and purple robes (jīnfēi shèngfú zhě)
would certainly add this on top.
Dūdū Jiāng Bīn and others, on their red hats worn in the sun,
attached indigo-dyed swan feathers,
considering them a noble decoration.
Nobles wore three feathers,
the next rank two feathers.
Bīngbù Shàngshū Wáng Qióng was bestowed one feather,
and wore it to the training grounds (jiàochǎng),
considering it a special favor.
Thereafter, wherever the imperial tour passed,
no Dūxiǎng Shíláng or Xúnfǔ Dūyùshǐ failed to wear an armored jacket when appearing before the Emperor.
In the 13th year,
when the imperial carriage returned to the capital,
an imperial decree was issued,
ordering those greeting the emperor to wear yèssā, large hats, and luán belts.
Soon after, all officials were granted one piece each of large red zhùsī, luósā.
Regarding their dress patterns:
first-rank Dòuniú,
second-rank Fēiyú,
third-rank Mǎng,
fourth and fifth-rank Qílín,
sixth and seventh-rank Hǔ, Biāo.
Members of the Hánlín Academy and Kēdào were granted these regardless of rank.
Only officials below fifth rank in the Bùcáo were not included.
At that time, civil officials' dress patterns also featured animals,
and the Qílín robe extended to fourth-rank officials,
which was a particularly unusual event.
In the 16th year,
when Shìzōng ascended the throne, an edict stated:
"Recently, there has been an abuse of jade belts
and mǎnglóng, fēiyú, dòuniú dress patterns.
These have all been improperly requested and obtained by various minor officials, miscellaneous personnel, and commanders from different regions.
Henceforth, none of these are allowed.
Inferior military officials who usurp the dress patterns of Gōng and Hóu
are also strictly forbidden from doing so."
In the 6th year of Jiājìng, a renewed prohibition was issued to officials both inside and outside the capital,
forbidding the unauthorized wearing of colorful decorated fabrics or forbidden colors.
In the 7th year, after the regulations for everyday formal wear (yànjū fǎfú) were established,
Grand Secretary (Géchéng) Zhāng Cōng remarked:
"There is no clear regulation for ranked officials' everyday wear (yànjū zhīfú).
Crafty and strange individuals
compete to create eccentric clothing, thereby disrupting the established order.
I humbly request that we revert to the ancient xuánduān
and create a simple, new system
to be widely promulgated throughout the empire,
so that the noble and the humble may have distinct ranks."
The Emperor then reinstated the design of the Zhōngjìng crown and robe (guānfú), distributing the illustrations to the Lǐbù,
and issued an imperial instruction stating:
"Our ancestors, after studying ancient precedents, established regulations
for ranked officials' court and sacrificial attire,
each with its specific distinctions.
However, it is human nature
to be diligent in public view
but lax in private.
The ancient sagely kings were mindful of this,
and established the xuánduān as everyday wear.
Recently, clothing has become eccentric,
with no distinction between high and low,
how can the people's aspirations be settled?
Therefore, I have deliberated on the ancient xuánduān system,
renaming it 'Zhōngjìng',
hoping that when one advances, one thinks of loyalty,
and when one retires, one thinks of rectifying errors.
I have already had it illustrated and described,
to be manufactured according to the pattern.
In the capital, officials of the seventh rank and above, and those of the eighth rank and above from the Hánlín Academy, Guózǐ Jiān, and Xíngrén Sī, are permitted to wear it.

In the provinces, regional officials (fāngmiàn guān), all prefectural chief officials (fǔ tángguān), zhou and xian magistrates (zhōuxiàn zhèngtáng), and Confucian school instructors (rúxué jiàoguān) are permitted to wear it.
Military officials are limited to Dūdū and above.
Others are not permitted to wear it indiscriminately."
The Lǐbù distributed the illustrations and descriptions throughout the empire,
to be carried out as instructed by the edict.
According to records, the Zhōngjìng crown imitated the ancient xuán guān;
the crown frame was as prescribed,
covered with black gauze (wūshā),
with both 'mountains' (liǎngshān) arranged at the back.
The crown top was still square in the middle and slightly raised,
with three beams (sānliáng) each pressed with gold thread,
and edged with gold.
For fourth-rank officials and below,
the gold was omitted,
and it was edged with light-colored silk thread.
The Zhōngjìng robe imitated the ancient xuánduān robe;
the color used was deep blue (shēnqīng),
made of zhùsī shāluó.
Third-rank and above had cloud patterns (yún),
fourth-rank and below were plain (sù),
edged with blue-green (lánqīng),
with patches (bǔzi) embroidered with patterns appropriate to their rank in front and back.
The inner robe (shēnyī) used jade color (yùsè).
A plain belt (sùdài),
similar to the belt system of ancient grand masters (dàfū),
blue on the outside with green edges and sashes (bì).
Plain shoes (sùlǚ),
with blue-green tassels (tāojié).
White socks.
In the 16th year,
when officials held court at the imperial residence (zhùbì suǒ),
Bīngbù Shàngshū Zhāng Zàn wore a mǎng robe.
The Emperor was angry,
and instructed Grand Secretary (Géchéng) Xià Yán, saying:
"A Shàngshū is second-rank,
why is he wearing a mǎng robe?"
Xià Yán replied:
"What Zhāng Zàn is wearing
is an imperially bestowed fēiyú robe;
it is just so bright that it resembles a mǎng."
The Emperor said:
"Why does a fēiyú have two horns?
Strictly forbid this."
Thereupon, the Lǐbù officially decreed
that civil and military officials were not permitted to arbitrarily wear mǎngyī, fēiyú, dòuniú, or other forbidden extravagant and exotic clothing colors.
As for large red zhùsī shāluó robes,
only officials of fourth rank and above, and in the capital, fifth-rank officials of the six boards (tángshàng guān) and imperial lecturers (jīngyán jiǎngguān) were permitted to wear them.
Fifth-rank officials and those attending imperial lectures but not as lecturers
were all to wear green embroidered brocade (qīnglǜ jǐnxiù).
For auspicious ceremonies (jíqǐlǐ),
they were only to wear red woolen cloth robes (hóngbùróng hè).
The patterns for ranked officials
were all to follow their respective ranks.
Jǐnyīwèi commanders
serving as imperial guards were still permitted to wear Qílín.
However, those on salary not serving as imperial guards,
and Qiān/Bǎihù even if serving as imperial guards,
were not permitted to usurp this privilege.
In various dynasties, imperial賜服 (cìfú, bestowed attire) were granted.
Among civil officials, there were those who had not yet reached the first rank but were granted jade belts;
this began with Xúeshì (Scholar) Luó Fùrén (羅復仁) during the Hóngwǔ (洪武) reign.

正二品 (zhèng èr pǐn, a principal second rank in the official hierarchy).
They wore robes embroidered with qílín (麒麟, mythical creature) and jade belts,
which were granted to them by the emperor when they attended court during the Jǐngtài (景泰) reign.
From then on, this became a regular practice.
Cabinet members were granted mǎngyī (蟒衣, python robes);
this began with Liú Jiàn (劉健) and Lǐ Dōngyáng (李東陽) during the Hóngzhì (弘治) reign.
Qílín (麒麟) robes were originally for gōng (公, dukes) and hóu (侯, marquises),
but cabinet members also wore them,
as Yán Sōng (嚴嵩) and Xú Jiē (徐階) both received such grants during the Jiājìng (嘉靖) reign.
Xiānhè (仙鶴, cranes)
were the attire for civil officials of the first rank.
During the Jiājìng (嘉靖) reign, Chéngguó Gōng (成國公) Zhū Xīzhōng (朱希忠) and Dūdū (Commander-in-Chief) Lù Bǐng (陸炳) wore them,
both for serving at the Xuántán (玄壇, Mysterious Altar).
And Xúeshì (Scholars) Yán Nà (嚴訥), Lǐ Chūnfāng (李春芳), and Dǒng Fèn (董份), though of the fifth rank, wrote qīngcí (青詞, Taoist invocations),
and were also granted xiānhè (仙鶴, crane robes).
Soon after, an edict stipulated that they should only be used when serving at the altar,
whereupon even shàngshū (尚書, ministers) dared not wear crane robes.
Later, an imperial edict ordered the Nánjīng (南京) weaving factory to produce shimmering yellow robes with qílín (麒麟) and xiānhè (仙鶴) patches,
and these were granted to Yán Sōng (嚴嵩);
shimmering yellow was a color reserved for imperial use.
Xú Jiē (徐階) was also granted robes with a "son ascending to heaven" mǎng (蟒, python) pattern.
During the Wànlì (萬曆) reign,
Zhāng Jūzhèng (張居正) was granted a "sitting python" robe.
Wǔqīng Hóu (武清侯) Lǐ Wěi (李偉), as the father of the empress dowager,
also received such a grant.
The court attire, formal attire, and everyday attire for yíbīn (儀賓, imperial sons-in-law)
were all determined by their rank,
and were the same as those for civil and military officials,
except that their hu (笏, ceremonial tablets) were all made of ivory;
the floral patterns of their robes were similar to those of military officials.
In the thirteenth year of Hóngzhì (弘治, 1500), it was decreed that
gùnjun yíbīn (郡君儀賓, sons-in-law of郡主 (gùnjǔ, princesses of the second rank)) wore gold belts with carved flowers,
and lions on their chest and back patches.
Xiànzhǔ yíbīn (縣主儀賓, sons-in-law of 縣主 (xiànzhǔ, princesses of the third rank)) wore gold belts with carved flowers.
Gùnjūn yíbīn (郡君儀賓, sons-in-law of郡君 (gùnjūn, princesses of the fourth rank)) wore plain gold belts,
with tigers and leopards on their chest and back patches.
Xiànjūn yíbīn (縣君儀賓, sons-in-law of縣君 (xiànjūn, princesses of the fifth rank)) wore silver belts with carved flowers.
Xiāngjūn yíbīn (鄉君儀賓, sons-in-law of鄉君 (xiāngjūn, princesses of the sixth rank)) wore plain silver belts,
with pīao (彪, smaller tigers) on their chest and back patches.
Those who misused them
would have their caps and belts removed,
wear a plain headscarf,
and study Confucian classics and rites in a Confucian school for three years.
The caps and robes of zhuàngyuán (狀元, top scholar) and other jìnshì (進士, successful candidates in the imperial examination).
The zhuàngyuán (狀元) cap had two梁 (liáng, beams),
a crimson silk round-collared robe,
a white silk zhōngdān (中單, inner garment),
a brocade sash,
a bìxī (蔽膝, knee cover),
a gauze cap,
a huái (槐, pagoda tree) wood hu (笏, ceremonial tablet),
a plain silver belt,
a yàoyù (藥玉, imitation jade) pendant,
court boots,
and socks.
All these were bestowed by the emperor,
and worn on the day of presenting a memorial to thank the emperor.
Jìnshì (進士) wore a headscarf like a wūshāmào (烏紗帽, black gauze cap),
slightly flat on top,
with expanded corners more than one cùn (寸) wide
and about five cùn (寸) long,
tied with hanging ribbons,
and made of black gauze.
A deep blue silk robe,
edged with green silk,
with wide sleeves that did not taper.
A huái (槐) wood hu (笏),
a leather belt and a green one,
decorated with black horn,
with a táwěi (撻尾, whip tail) hanging behind.
After the palace examination, they were distributed at the Guózǐjiàn (國子監, Imperial Academy),
and worn on the day of the chuánlú (傳臚, announcement of results).
After presenting a memorial to thank the emperor,
and after visiting the former masters and performing the shīcàilǐ (釋菜禮, vegetable offering ceremony),
they would change into everyday clothes,
and their caps and robes would be sent back to the Guózǐjiàn (國子監) for storage.
The caps and robes of mìngfù (命婦, noblewomen).
In the first year of Hóngwǔ (洪wu, 1368), it was decreed that
mìngfù (命婦) of the first rank
wore a crown with nine flower-hairpins.
Two bóbìn (博鬢, side ornaments),
and nine tián (鈿, metallic ornaments).
They wore díyī (翟衣, pheasant robes),
embroidered with nine layers of dí (翟, pheasants).
A plain gauze zhōngdān (中單, inner garment),
a fǔ (黼, axe-patterned) collar,
and red plain silk sleeves and hems.
The bìxī (蔽膝, knee cover) matched the color of the skirt,
with a zōu (緅, purplish-black) collar edge,
and adorned with embroidered double dí (翟) patterns,
forming two grades of insignia.
A jade belt.
Green socks and xi (舄, ceremonial shoes),
with a sash.
Second rank:
A crown with eight flower-hairpins.
Two bóbìn (博鬢),
and eight tián (鈿).
Díyī (翟衣) of eight grades,
rhinoceros horn belt,
the rest as for the first rank.
Third rank:
A crown with seven flower-hairpins.
Two bóbìn (博鬢),
and seven tián (鈿).
Díyī (翟衣) of seven grades,
gold leather belt,
the rest as for the second rank.
Fourth rank:
A crown with six flower-hairpins.
Two bóbìn (博鬢),
and six tián (鈿).
Díyī (翟衣) of six grades,
gold leather belt,
the rest as for the third rank.
Fifth rank:
A crown with five flower-hairpins.
Two bóbìn (博鬢),
and five tián (鈿).
Díyī (翟衣) of five grades,
black horn belt,
the rest as for the fourth rank.
Sixth rank:
A crown with four flower-hairpins.
Two bóbìn (博鬢),
and four tián (鈿).
Díyī (翟衣) of four grades,
black horn belt,
the rest as for the fifth rank.
Seventh rank:
A crown with three flower-hairpins.
Two bóbìn (博鬢),
and three tián (鈿).
Díyī (翟衣) of three grades,
black horn belt,
the rest as for the sixth rank.
From the first to the fifth rank,
the color of the robe followed the husband's purple.
For the sixth and seventh ranks,
the color of the robe followed the husband's crimson.
Their large belts were the same color as their robes.
In the fourth year (of Hóngwǔ, 1371), considering that ancient emperors and feudal lords wore gǔnmiǎn (袞冕, ceremonial robes and crowns),
and empresses and noblewomen also wore huījí (褘翟, ceremonial robes with pheasant patterns).
Now, as all officials used liángguān (梁冠, beamed caps) and jiàngyī (絳衣, crimson robes) as court attire,
and dared not use miǎn (冕, imperial crowns),
then external mìngfù (命婦) should also not wear díyī (翟衣) for court attendance.
The Ministry of Rites was ordered to deliberate on this.
After the deliberation and imperial approval,

it was decreed that mìngfù (命婦) wore a shānsōng tèjì (山松特髻, special hairstyle with mountain pine), false sideburns with flower ornaments, a true red large-sleeved robe, and a zhūcuì cùjīn xiápèi (珠翠蹙金霞帔, pearl and kingfisher feather gold-embroidered cape)
as court attire.
A zhūcuì jiǎoguān (朱翠角冠, red and kingfisher feather horned crown), gold and pearl flower-hairpins, and wide-sleeved robes with various colors edged in green,
were for informal wear.
First rank:
Wore a gold-embroidered patterned xiápèi (霞帔, cape),
decorated with gold, pearls, and kingfisher feathers,
and a jade pendant.
Second rank:
Wore a gold-embroidered cloud-shoulder large mixed-flower xiápèi (霞帔),
decorated with gold, pearls, and kingfisher feathers,
and a gold pendant.
Third rank:
Wore a gold-embroidered large mixed-flower xiápèi (霞帔),
decorated with pearls and kingfisher feathers,
and a gold pendant.
Fourth rank:
Wore an embroidered small mixed-flower xiápèi (霞帔),
decorated with kingfisher feathers,
and a gold pendant.
Fifth rank:
Wore a gold-threaded large mixed-flower xiápèi (霞帔),
decorated with painted silk flowers in original colors,
and a gold pendant.
Sixth and seventh ranks:
Wore a gold-threaded small mixed-flower xiápèi (霞帔),
decorated with painted silk flowers in original colors,
and a gilt silver pendant.
Eighth and ninth ranks:
Wore a plain dark red silk xiápèi (霞帔),
decorated with painted silk in original colors,
and a silver pendant.
For headwear:
First and second ranks:
Gold, jade, pearls, and kingfisher feathers.
Third and fourth ranks:
Gold, pearls, and kingfisher feathers.
Fifth rank:
Gold and kingfisher feathers.
Sixth rank and below:
Gilt silver interspersed with pearls.
In the fifth year (of Hóngwǔ, 1372), the caps and robes for officials' noblewomen were revised.
First rank (yī pǐn):
For ceremonial attire, use a mountain-pine-style special topknot (shān sōng tè jì),
five kingfishers (cuì sōng),
eight golden pheasants (jīn zhái),
each holding a pearl knot in its mouth.
On the front, one pearl-and-kingfisher pheasant (zhū cuì zhái),
four pearl-and-kingfisher flower ornaments (zhū cuì huā) in rows (gē),
three pearl-and-kingfisher cloud-and-joy flower ornaments (zhū cuì yún xǐ huā) in rows (gē);
on the back hair, one pearl shuttlecock (zhū suō qiú),
one pearl-and-kingfisher flying pheasant (zhū cuì fēi zhái),
four pearl-and-kingfisher combs (zhū cuì shū),
one gold cloud-head connected three-pronged hairpin (jīn yún tóu lián sān chāi),
one pearl curtain comb (zhū lián shū),
two golden hairpins (jīn zān);
one pair of pearl shuttlecock rings (zhū suō huán).
The large-sleeved gown (dà xiù shān)
is made of crimson red (zhēn hóng sè).
The shawl (xiá pèi) and jacket (bèi zi)
are both dark blue (shēn qīng sè).
Ramie silk (zhù sī), twilled silk (líng), gauze (luó), and fine silk (shā) are used as appropriate.
The shawl (xiá pèi) is embroidered with couched gold (cù jīn xiù) cloud, mist, and pheasant patterns (yún xiá zhái wén),
with chiseled gold pendants (zá huā jīn zhuì zi).
The jacket (bèi zi) is embroidered with gold (jīn xiù) cloud, mist, and pheasant patterns (yún xiá zhái wén).
For everyday wear, use a pearl-and-kingfisher auspicious cloud coronet (zhū cuì qìng yún guān),
three pearl-and-kingfisher pheasants (zhū cuì zhái),
one golden pheasant (jīn zhái),
each holding a pearl knot in its mouth;
at the temples, two pearl-and-kingfisher flowers (zhū cuì huā),
one pair of small pearl-and-kingfisher combs (xiǎo zhū cuì shū),
one gold cloud-head connected three-pronged hairpin (jīn yún tóu lián sān chāi),
two gold temple-pressing double-headed hairpins (jīn yā bìn shuāng tóu chāi),
one gold back-of-head comb (jīn nǎo shū),
two golden hairpins (jīn zān);
one pair of gold-footed pearl-and-kingfisher Buddha-face rings (jīn jiǎo zhū cuì fó miàn huán);
bracelets (zhuó chuàn) are all gold.
Long outer garments (cháng áo) and long skirts (cháng qún)
of various colored ramie silk (zhù sī), twilled silk (líng), gauze (luó), and fine silk (shā) are used as appropriate.
The borders (yuán chèn) of the long outer garment (cháng áo)
are either purple or green,
embroidered with couched gold (cù jīn xiù) cloud, mist, and pheasant patterns (yún xiá zhái wén).
For the sash (kān dài),
use red, green, or purple,
embroidered with couched gold (cù jīn xiù) cloud, mist, and pheasant patterns (yún xiá zhái wén).
The long skirt (cháng qún)
has horizontal and vertical gold-embroidered continuous vine-and-flower patterns (chán zhī huā wén).
Second rank (èr pǐn):
On the special topknot (tè jì), seven golden pheasants (jīn zhái),
each holding a pearl knot in its mouth,
the rest is the same as the first rank (yī pǐn).
Everyday wear is also the same as the first rank (yī pǐn).
Third rank (sān pǐn):
On the special topknot (tè jì), six golden peacocks (jīn kǒng què),
each holding a pearl knot in its mouth.
On the front, one pearl-and-kingfisher peacock (zhū cuì kǒng què),
on the back hair, two kingfisher peacocks (cuì kǒng què).
The shawl (xiá pèi) is embroidered with couched gold (cù jīn) cloud, mist, and peacock patterns (yún xiá kǒng què wén),
with chiseled gold pendants (zá huā jīn zhuì zi).
The jacket (bèi zi) is embroidered with gold (jīn xiù) cloud, mist, and peacock patterns (yún xiá kǒng què wén),
the rest is the same as the second rank (èr pǐn).
For everyday wear, on the coronet, three pearl-and-kingfisher peacocks (zhū cuì kǒng què),
two golden peacocks (jīn kǒng què),
each holding a pearl knot in its mouth.
The borders (yuán chèn) of the long outer garment (cháng áo).
For the sash (kān dài),
either purple or green,
both embroidered with cloud, mist, and peacock patterns (yún xiá kǒng què wén).
The long skirt (cháng qún)
has horizontal and vertical panels (héng shù lán) both embroidered with continuous vine-and-flower patterns (chán zhī huā wén),
the rest is the same as the second rank (èr pǐn).
Fourth rank (sì pǐn):
On the special topknot (tè jì), five golden peacocks (jīn kǒng què),
each holding a pearl knot in its mouth,
the rest is the same as the third rank (sān pǐn).
Everyday wear is also the same as the third rank (sān pǐn).
Fifth rank (wǔ pǐn):
On the special topknot (tè jì), four silver-gilt mandarin ducks (yín dù jīn yuān yāng),
each holding a pearl knot in its mouth.
On the front, one pearl-and-kingfisher mandarin duck (zhū cuì yuān yāng),
three small pearl-inlaid kingfisher cloud-and-joy flower ornaments (xiǎo zhū pù cuì yún xǐ huā) in rows (gē);
on the back hair, two kingfisher mandarin ducks (cuì yuān yāng),
one silver-gilt cloud-head connected three-pronged hairpin (yín dù jīn yún tóu lián sān chāi),
one small pearl curtain comb (xiǎo zhū lián shū),
two gilt silver hairpins (dù jīn yín zān);
one pair of small pearl comb rings (xiǎo zhū shū huán).
The shawl (xiá pèi) is embroidered with cloud, mist, and mandarin duck patterns (yún xiá yuān yāng wén),
with gilt silver chiseled flower pendants (dù jīn yín zá huā zhuì zi).
The jacket (bèi zi) is embroidered with cloud, mist, and mandarin duck patterns (yún xiá yuān yāng wén),
the rest is the same as the fourth rank (sì pǐn).
For everyday wear, on the coronet, three small pearl-and-kingfisher mandarin ducks (xiǎo zhū cuì yuān yāng),
two gilt silver mandarin ducks (dù jīn yín yuān yāng),
and a pearl-strung plaque (tiǎo zhū pái).
At the temples, two small pearl-and-kingfisher flowers (xiǎo zhū cuì huā) in rows (gē),
one cloud-head connected three-pronged hairpin (yún tóu lián sān chāi),
one comb (shū),
two temple-pressing double-headed hairpins (yā bìn shuāng tóu chāi),
two gilt hairpins (dù jīn zān);
one pair of silver-footed pearl-and-kingfisher Buddha-face rings (yín jiǎo zhū cuì fó miàn huán).
Bracelets (zhuó chuàn) are all silver-gilt.
The borders (yuán chèn) of the long outer garment (cháng áo)
are embroidered with cloud, mist, and mandarin duck patterns (yún xiá yuān yāng wén).
The long skirt (cháng qún)
has horizontal and vertical panels (héng shù lán) embroidered with continuous vine-and-flower patterns (chán zhī huā wén),
the rest is the same as the fourth rank (sì pǐn).
Sixth rank (liù pǐn):
On the special topknot (tè jì), three kingfishers (cuì sōng),
four silver-gilt paradise flycatchers (yín dù jīn liàn què),
each holding a pearl knot in its mouth.
On the front, one silver-gilt paradise flycatcher (yín dù jīn liàn què),
four small pearl-and-kingfisher flowers (xiǎo zhū cuì huā) in rows (gē);
on the back hair, one kingfisher shuttlecock (cuì suō qiú),
two kingfisher paradise flycatchers (cuì liàn què),
four kingfisher combs (cuì shū),
one silver cloud-head connected three-pronged hairpin (yín yún tóu lián sān chāi),
one pearl-bordered kingfisher curtain comb (zhū yuán cuì lián shū),
two silver hairpins (yín zān).
The large-sleeved gown (dà xiù shān)
is made of twilled silk (líng), gauze (luó), pongee (chóu), and fine plain silk (juàn) as appropriate.
The shawl (xiá pèi) is embroidered with cloud, mist, and paradise flycatcher patterns (yún xiá liàn què wén),
with chiseled silver pendants (zá huā yín zhuì zi).
The jacket (bèi zi) is embroidered with cloud, mist, and paradise flycatcher patterns (yún xiá liàn què wén),
the rest is the same as the fifth rank (wǔ pǐn).
For everyday wear, on the coronet, three gilt silver paradise flycatchers (dù jīn yín liàn què),
and two more gilt silver paradise flycatchers (dù jīn yín liàn què),
and a small pearl-strung plaque (tiǎo xiǎo zhū pái);
bracelets (zhuó chuàn) are all silver.
The borders (yuán chèn) of the long outer garment (cháng áo).
For the sash (kān dài),
either purple or green,
embroidered with cloud, mist, and paradise flycatcher patterns (yún xiá liàn què wén).
The long skirt (cháng qún)
has horizontal and vertical panels (héng shù lán) embroidered with continuous vine-and-flower patterns (chán zhī huā wén),
the rest is the same as the fifth rank (wǔ pǐn).
Seventh rank (qī pǐn):
Ceremonial attire and everyday wear
are both the same as the sixth rank (liù pǐn).
For the eighth rank (bā pǐn) and ninth rank (jiǔ pǐn) ceremonial attire,
only the large-sleeved gown (dà xiù shān), shawl (xiá pèi), and jacket (bèi zi) are used.
The large gown (dà shān) is the same as the seventh rank (qī pǐn).
The shawl (xiá pèi) is embroidered with continuous vine-and-flower patterns (chán zhī huā),
with chiseled silver pendants (zá huā yín zhuì zi).
The jacket (bèi zi) is embroidered with detached branch roundel flower patterns (zhāi zhī tuán huā).
A small pearl auspicious cloud coronet (xiǎo zhū qìng yún guān) is universally used.
Everyday wear also uses a small pearl auspicious cloud coronet (xiǎo zhū qìng yún guān),
three silver-interspersed gilt silver paradise flycatchers (yín jiān dù jīn yín liàn què),
and two more silver-interspersed gilt silver paradise flycatchers (yín jiān dù jīn yín liàn què),
and a small pearl-strung plaque (tiǎo xiǎo zhū pái);
one silver-interspersed gilt silver cloud-head connected three-pronged hairpin (yín jiān dù jīn yún tóu lián sān chāi),
two silver-interspersed gilt silver temple-pressing double-headed hairpins (yín jiān dù jīn yā bìn shuāng tóu chāi),
one silver-interspersed gilt silver back-of-head comb (yín jiān dù jīn nǎo shū),
two silver-interspersed gilt silver hairpins (yín jiān dù jīn zān).
The borders (yuán chèn) of the long outer garment (cháng áo) and the sash (kān dài) are both embroidered with continuous vine-and-flower patterns (chán zhī huā),
the rest is the same as the seventh rank (qī pǐn).
Also stipulated is the system for the round gown (tuán shān) of official women (mìng fù):
it is made of red gauze (hóng luó),
embroidered with multiple pheasants (zhòng zhì) according to rank.
First rank (yī pǐn) has nine pheasants,
second rank (èr pǐn) has eight,
third rank (sān pǐn) has seven,
fourth rank (sì pǐn) has six,
fifth rank (wǔ pǐn) has five,
sixth rank (liù pǐn) has four,
seventh rank (qī pǐn) has three,
the rest do not use embroidered pheasants.
In the 24th year, it was stipulated that
when official women (mìng fù) have an audience with the sovereign or empress,
or when at home they see their parents-in-law and husband, and for sacrificial rites, they wear ceremonial attire.
The wives of dukes (gōng), marquises (hóu), and counts (bó) are the same as the first rank (yī pǐn).
The large-sleeved gown (dà xiù shān)
is crimson red (zhēn hóng sè).
First rank (yī pǐn) to fifth rank (wǔ pǐn)
use ramie silk (zhù sī), twilled silk (líng), gauze (luó);
sixth rank (liù pǐn) to ninth rank (jiǔ pǐn)
use twilled silk (líng), gauze (luó), pongee (chóu), fine plain silk (juàn).
Shawls (xiá pèi) and jackets (bèi zi) are all dark blue satin (shēn qīng duàn).
Dukes (gōng), marquises (hóu), and first rank (yī pǐn), second rank (èr pǐn)
use gold-embroidered (jīn xiù) cloud, mist, and pheasant patterns (yún xiá zhái wén);
third rank (sān pǐn), fourth rank (sì pǐn)
use gold-embroidered (jīn xiù) cloud, mist, and peacock patterns (yún xiá kǒng què wén);
fifth rank (wǔ pǐn)
use embroidered cloud, mist, and mandarin duck patterns (yún xiá yuān yāng wén);
sixth rank (liù pǐn), seventh rank (qī pǐn)
use embroidered cloud, mist, and paradise flycatcher patterns (yún xiá liàn què wén).
The large-sleeved gown (dà xiù shān)
has a collar width of three inches,
the two collar flaps extend straight down one foot,
with three buttons (niǔ zi) fastened in between,
and two buttons (niǔ zi) fastened at the end.
The buttons (niǔ) are under the button flap (yǎn niǔ),
they are released when bowing.
There are two shawls (xiá pèi),
each embroidered with seven birds (qín),
used according to rank,
four in front and three in back.
The pendant (zhuì zi) has one chiseled bird (zá huā qín) in the center,
with cloud and mist patterns (yún xiá wén) on four sides,
the bird (qín) is like that on the shawl (xiá pèi),
used according to rank.
The ceremonial tablet (hù) is made of ivory.
In the 26th year, regulations were set.
For the first rank:
The crown used gold accessories.
Five pearl-adorned phoenixes,
two full-blooming pearl peonies,
three half-blooming pearl flowers,
twenty-four pieces of kingfisher-feather clouds,
eighteen pieces of kingfisher-feather peony leaves,
and one set of kingfisher-feather mouth-ring.
Above it, eight gold treasure-inlaid flowers,
two gold phoenixes,
and two pearl knots held in their mouths.
For the second to fourth ranks:
The crown used gold accessories.
Four pearl-adorned phoenixes,
two full-blooming pearl peonies,
four half-blooming pearl flowers,
twenty-four pieces of kingfisher-feather clouds,
eighteen pieces of kingfisher-feather peony leaves,
and one set of kingfisher-feather mouth-ring.
Above it, eight gold treasure-inlaid flowers,
two gold phoenixes,
and two pearl knots held in their mouths.
For the first and second ranks:
The xiápèi and bèizi both featured cloud and phoenix patterns,
with engraved gold pendants.
For the third and fourth ranks:
The xiápèi and bèizi both featured cloud and peacock patterns,
with engraved gold pendants.
For the fifth and sixth ranks:
The crown used gilt-silver accessories.
Three pearl-adorned phoenixes,
two full-blooming pearl peonies,
five half-blooming pearl flowers,
twenty-four pieces of kingfisher-feather clouds,
eighteen pieces of kingfisher-feather peony leaves,
and one set of kingfisher-feather mouth-ring.
Above it, eight gilt-silver treasure-inlaid flowers,
two gilt-silver phoenixes,
and two pearl knots held in their mouths.
For the fifth rank:
The xiápèi and bèizi both featured cloud and mandarin duck patterns,
with gilded engraved silver pendants.
For the sixth rank:
The xiápèi and bèizi both featured cloud and swift patterns,
with engraved silver pendants.
For the seventh to ninth ranks:
The crown used gilt-silver accessories.
Two pearl-adorned phoenixes,
two full-blooming pearl osmanthus flowers,
six half-blooming pearl flowers,
twenty-four pieces of kingfisher-feather clouds,
eighteen pieces of kingfisher-feather osmanthus leaves,
and one set of kingfisher-feather mouth-ring.
Above it, eight gilt-silver treasure-inlaid flowers,
two gilt-silver phoenixes,
and two pearl knots held in their mouths.
For the seventh rank:
The xiápèi, pendant, and bèizi
were the same as those for the sixth rank.
For the eighth and ninth ranks:
The xiápèi used embroidered intertwined floral patterns,
the pendant was the same as for the seventh rank,
and the bèizi was embroidered with detached floral medallions.
Court and provincial officials' relatives' crowns and robes.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ,
Lǐbù Shàngshū Cuī Liàng was commanded to deliberate and finalize the regulations.
The fathers, elder brothers, paternal uncles, younger brothers, nephews, sons, and grandsons of court and provincial officials used black gauze caps
with soft-footed hanging ribbons,
round-collared robes,
and black rhinoceros horn belts.
For the grandmothers and mothers of ranked officials, and the wives of their close younger brothers and nephews living together with their sons and grandsons, their ceremonial robes
were to match the rank of the official they resided with.
They universally used lacquered gauze, pearl, and kingfisher-feather qìngyún crowns,
robes of their respective rank,
xiápèi, bèizi,
and bordered-hem jackets and skirts.
However, the shānsōng special topknot
was only permitted for those who had received a seal or imperial edict.
Secondary wives of ranked officials
were permitted to use the pearl and kingfisher-feather qìngyún crown and bèizi of their husband's rank as ceremonial attire.
Gold-embroidered wide-collared, long jackets and long skirts served as their ordinary attire.
In the 25th year,
an order was issued allowing the fathers, elder brothers, paternal uncles, younger brothers, nephews, sons, and sons-in-law of civil and military officials
to all wear boots.
Eunuchs' crowns and robes.
In the early Míng dynasty, the Nèishǐjiān was established.
They wore black gauze caps with gold-painted curved-foot brims,
robes with floral medallions on the chest and back, round collars, and narrow sleeves,
black rhinoceros horn belts,
and boots with red fan-shaped uppers and black lower sections.
The huǒzhě of various palaces
wore clothes similar to commoners.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, an edict was issued to the prime ministers:
For those in the Nèishǐjiān who did not yet have an official title,
a special crown should be made
to distinguish them from jian officials.
The Lǐbù submitted a memorial and it was approved:
Whenever Nèishǐjiān officials attended court assemblies,
they were to perform the rites wearing court robes and official robes according to their rank.
Their ordinary attire included
round-collared shirts with sunflower medallions on the chest and back,
without restriction on color;
black gauze caps;
and rhinoceros horn belts.
Those without rank who were attendants
wore round-collared shirts as ordinary attire,
without chest or back medallions,
without restriction on color;
black rhinoceros horn belts;
and black gauze caps
with soft hanging ribbons.
Those under fifteen years of age
only wore small black gauze caps.
According to Dàzhèngjì,
after Yǒnglè,
eunuchs attending the emperor
always wore mǎngfú,
made like a yīsā,
with embroidered mǎng on both sides,
fastened with luán belts.
This was for informal occasions.
Next were fēiyú,
only used when entering to serve.
Those who were noble and held power
were bestowed mǎng,
which were difficult for even first-rank civil and military officials to obtain.
A single mǎng had its face always depicted obliquely,
while a seated mǎng had its face depicted frontally,
which was even more noble.
There were also those with knee-flounces,
also like a yīsā,
with mǎng insignia above,
and fine cloud mǎng woven horizontally at the knees.
This was for accompanying the emperor on southern suburban sacrifices and to imperial tombs,
making it convenient for riding horses.
Or when summoned for informal audiences,
both monarch and subjects would not wear robes,
but use these.
However, mǎng were divided into five-clawed and four-clawed,
and the flounces had distinctions of red and yellow.
In the first year of Hóngzhì,
Dū Yùshǐ Biān Yōng stated:
"Our dynasty has no system for mǎngyī for ranked officials.
Moreover, mǎng have no horns and no feet,
but now many eunuchs beg for mǎngyī,
which closely resembles the dragon form,
and is not according to the regulations."
Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued to prohibit it.
In the 17th year, an edict was issued to Grand Secretary Liú Jiàn, saying:
"Eunuchs' presumptuousness is particularly rampant."
Then he spoke of the colors that should be prohibited,
saying:
"Mǎng, lóng, fēiyú, and dòuniú
were originally prohibited,
and should not be privately woven.
If there are any that were bestowed,
and they have become worn out over time,
it is inappropriate to weave and use them again without permission.
Xuán, huáng, zǐ, and zào are strictly prohibited,
and even liǔhuáng, mínghuáng, and jiānghuáng colors
should also be prohibited."
Xiàozōng paid close attention to restraining them,
hence the repeated admonitions.
However, the eunuchs' arrogance and indulgence had been long-standing,
and the accumulated habits persisted,
making it impossible to stop them.
Initially,
Tàizǔ regulated eunuchs' attire,
making their gauze caps different from those of other officials,
and they had no court crowns or fútóu,
nor sacrificial robes.
In the early Wànlì reign,
when Mùzōng entered the Tàimiào,
the great eunuchs wore jìnxián crowns
and sacrificial robes to follow,
because the Nèifǔ sacrificed to the gods of the central eave, kitchen, and well,
and eunuchs were customarily dispatched.
Thus, they created their own sacrificial robes,
which was not decided by court deliberation.
Attire of the Shìyí Shèrén.
In the 2nd year of Hóngwǔ
the Board of Rites deliberated and decided.
For Shìyí Shèrén leading ceremonies,
following the Yuán dynasty system,
they wore a zhǎnjiǎo pútóu,
a narrow-sleeved purple robe,
a gilded belt,
and black patterned boots.
For everyday wear,
they wore a wūshā Tángmào,
collared robes of various colors,
a black horn belt,
and the robes were not to be yellow.
In the 4th year
the Zhōngshū Shěng deliberated and decided that
Shìyí Shèrén, along with the Zhībān of the Yùshǐ Tái,
when guiding rituals and performing duties,
should wear a Jìnxián guān
without beams,
a crimson-colored robe.
Their bìxī, shoes, socks, belt, and hù
were to be the same as those of a ninth-rank official,
but without the zhōngdān.
Attire of the Jiàowèi.
In the 3rd year of Hóngwǔ
soldiers bearing weapons
all wore a lǚjīn éjiāojiǎo pútóu as headwear.
Their attire included pìxié and bàoxiànghuā patterned skirts and jackets of various colors,
a copper kuíhuā belt,
and black patterned boots.
In the 6th year
Jiàowèi were ordered to wear zhǐsūn,
a belt,
a pútóu,
and boots.
Zhǐsūn,
also written as zhìsūn,
was originally a Yuán dynasty system,
meaning a monochrome robe.
In the 14th year
a black lacquered qiàngjīn lìzhī copper-studded style,
with five studs clustered together,
slightly raised edges and borders on all four sides,
and tightly bound with blue.
In the 22nd year
were ordered to regularly wear a headscarf or a kēnǎo.
In the 25th year
were ordered to wear boots when on duty,
but not when out and about.
Attire of the Kèqī.
The Sòng dynasty established kuàixíng qīncóngguān,
which in the early Míng were called Kèqī.
They wore a fāngdǐng jīn,
a robe with eagles and hawks on the chest and back,
a huāyāo,
a xiàn'ǎozi,
broad flat silk tassels of various colors,
a large carved ivory ring,
and walking leggings with eight straps.
In the 6th year of Hóngwǔ
only carved ivory tassel rings were used,
the rest being the same as commoners.
Headwear and robes of Rúshì, Shēngyuán, and Jiānsheng.
In the 3rd year of Hóngwǔ
In the 23rd year

they should be one cùn off the ground,
sleeves long enough to cover the hands,
and when folded back, three cùn short of the elbow.
In the 24th year
considering that the headwear and robes of scholars
were indistinguishable from those of clerks and yamen runners,
it was deemed appropriate to differentiate them.
The Gōngbù was ordered to devise styles for submission.
Tàizǔ personally inspected them,
and they were finalized after three changes.
Shēngyuán wore a lánshān
made of jade-colored plain cloth or silk,
with wide sleeves edged in black,
and a soft headscarf with black tassels and trailing ribbons.
Those who entered the Imperial Academy through imperial examinations
did not change their attire.
Towards the end of Hóngwǔ,
they were permitted to wear sun-shading hats,
which later became privately worn.
During the Hóngxī reign
the Emperor asked who the people in blue robes were,
and his attendants replied that they were jiānsheng.
The Emperor said:
"Wearing dark blue robes is better."
So they were changed to dark blue round-collared robes.
In the 22nd year of Jiājìng
the Lǐbù reported that the headwear and robes of scholars were strange,
including the Língyún jīn and others,
which were very contrary to ritual regulations,
and an edict was issued to the relevant authorities to prohibit them.
In the 2nd year of Wànlì
brocade-embroidered shoes, carrying umbrellas,
or wearing ear-warmers.
Violators would be sent by the Wǔchéng Yùshǐ for questioning.
Attire of commoners.
In the early Míng,
for commoners' weddings,
they were permitted to borrow the attire of a ninth-rank official.
In the 3rd year of Hóngwǔ
commoners initially wore a sìdài jīn,
which was changed to a sìfāng píngdìng jīn,
and collared robes of various colors,
but yellow was not permitted.
It was also ordered that men's and women's clothing
should not presumptuously use gold embroidery, brocade, zhùsī, or língluó,
but only allow chou, silk, or plain gauze.
Their boots were not allowed to be cut with patterns or decorated with gold thread.
Head ornaments, hairpins, and bracelets were not allowed to use gold, jade, pearls, or kingfisher feathers,
but only silver.
In the 6th year
Those not yet classified into ranks were subject to the same rule.
Commoners' hats
were not allowed to have a finial,
and hat beads were only permitted to be crystal or fragrant wood.
In the 14th year
merchants were only allowed to wear silk and cloth.
If a farming family had one person who was a merchant,
they were also not allowed to wear chou or gauze.
In the 22nd year
and their entry and exit from markets was not restricted;
those not engaged in agriculture were not permitted to wear them.
In the 23rd year
sleeves long enough to cover the hands,
and when folded back, three cùn short of the elbow;
commoners' robes were to be long,
five cùn off the ground,
sleeves six cùn longer than the hands,
sleeve width one chì,
and cuff opening five cùn.
In the 25th year
because commoners violated prohibitions,
their boots were cleverly cut with patterns,
inlaid with gold thread and blue stripes.
An edict was issued to the Lǐbù to strictly prohibit commoners from wearing boots,
only allowing them to wear leather zālù.
However, in the cold northern regions,
they were permitted to use straight-stitched cowhide boots.
In the 1st year of Zhèngdé
In the 16th year
those who wore them either within prohibited gates or roaming outside
would be apprehended by investigators.
Attire of scholars' and commoners' wives.
In the 3rd year of Hóngwǔ
scholars' and commoners' wives,
for head ornaments, used silver plated with gold;
earrings used gold and pearls;
bracelets used silver;
they wore light-colored round robes
made of zhùsī, língluó, chou, or silk.
In the 5th year
without gold embroidery.
Robes and jackets were limited to purple, green, peach-blossom red, and other light, pale colors,
and bright red, dark blue, or yellow were not permitted.
Belts were to be made of blue silk cloth.
Unmarried girls
wore three small buns,
gold hairpins,
pearl-headed hair ornaments,
and narrow-sleeved bèizi.
For all maids,
they wore high buns,
silk or cloth narrow-collared long jackets,
and long skirts.
Young maids
wore double buns,
long-sleeved short tops,
and long skirts.
In the 10th year of Chénghuà

In the 1st year of Zhèngdé
gemstone head ornaments, or bracelets.
Attire of Xiélǜ Láng and Yuèwǔ Shēng.
In the early Míng,
for suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples, yayue was used.
Xiélǜ Láng wore a pútóu,
a purple silk robe,
and a lìzhīdài;
yuèshēng wore a scarlet robe and a zhǎnjiǎo pútóu;
wǔshì wore a pútóu,
a red silk robe,
a lìzhīdài,
and black boots;
wénwǔshēng wore a red robe,
wǔwǔshēng wore a scarlet robe,
both with a zhǎnjiǎo pútóu,
a leather belt,
and black boots.
Grand Music for Court Assemblies, Nine Performances: Singers wore Zhōnghuá Yītǒng Jīn,
red silk robes with large sleeves,
embroidered with patterns of yellow orioles and parrots,
red raw silk undershirts,
brocade collars,
apricot red silk skirts,
white silk wide-leg trousers,
dark green silk cords,
white silk socks,
and dark brown boots.
The chorus leaders and music directors wore: black silk wide-band headscarves,
dark blue silk robes with large sleeves,
red raw silk undershirts,
brocade collars,
gilt belts,
and black boots.
The Three Dances:
First, the Martial Dance,
called the "Dance of Pacifying the World."
The dancers
all wore golden hair-bun crowns,
purple silk tassels,
dark blue silk narrow-sleeved shirts embroidered with patterns of dancing cranes,
white raw silk undershirts,
brocade collars, large red silk outer robes with gold embroidery,
red silk skirts with gold embroidery,
black raw silk borders with painted floral patterns,
white silk wide-leg trousers with gold embroidery,
dark blue silk borders with gold embroidery,
red silk neck wraps,
red knots,
red silk waistbands,
gilt belts,
dark blue silk large cords, brocade armbands,
and black boots with green cloud patterns.
The dance masters wore: golden hair-bun crowns,
purple silk tassels,
dark blue silk robes with large sleeves,
white silk undershirts,
brocade collars,
gilt belts,
and black boots with green cloud patterns.
Second, a Civil Dance,
called the "Dance of Unified Administration and Tribute."
The dancers
all wore black lacquered and gilded Fang Mountain crowns,
dark blue silk tassels,
red silk robes with large sleeves,
red raw silk undershirts,
brocade collars,
red silk neck wraps,
red knots,
gilt belts,
white silk wide-leg trousers,
white silk socks,
and dark brown boots.
The dance masters' crowns and robes were the same as the dancers,
except their large-sleeved robes were dark blue silk,
and they did not wear red silk neck wraps or red knots.
Third, a Civil Dance,
called the "Dance of Soothing the Four Barbarians."
The dancers:
Four Eastern Barbarians [Dōngyí]
wore hair coiled at the back,
tied with red gold-embroidered headbands,
red silk gold-embroidered forehead bands,
with a gilt Bóshān mountain ornament in the center,
and gilt hair rings on both sides,
bright gold earrings,
dark blue silk robes with large sleeves painted with floral patterns,
red raw silk collars and cuffs,
red silk gold-embroidered skirts,
dark blue gold-embroidered skirt borders,
red raw silk undershirts,
brocade collars,
gilt belts,
and black leather boots.
Four Western Barbarians [Xīróng]
wore patterned brocade headwraps,
bright gold earrings,
red ramie silk finely pleated jackets,
bright red silk cloud collars,
green raw silk borders,
dark blue silk wide-leg trousers with gold embroidery,
red gold-embroidered belts with combined pouch,
cross-shaped gold-painted prayer beads,
five-colored gold-embroidered silk incense pouches,
red silk neck wraps,
red knots,
and red leather boots.
Four Southern Barbarians [Nánmán]
wore "facing heaven" buns,
tied with red silk raw silk silver ingots,
red gold-embroidered forehead bands,
bright gold earrings,
red woven gold short jackets,
green woven gold finely pleated short skirts,
velvet brocade trousers,
patterned ramie silk handkerchiefs,
gold-painted forehead plaques,
gold and pearl necklaces with small gold bells,
brocade leg wraps,
gold-painted lion-barbarian belts,
green gold-embroidered neck wraps,
red knots,
and red leather boots.
Four Northern Barbarians [Běidí]
wore Chányú crowns,
sable fur brims,
double drooping buns,
red gold-embroidered headbands,
red silk gold-embroidered forehead bands,
various colored finely pleated jackets,
dark blue raw silk cloud collars,
red knots,
red gold-embroidered wide-leg trousers,
belts with combined pouch,
and black leather boots.
The dance masters
all wore white rolled-brim hats,
gilt hat tops,
single red tassels,
purple silk hat strings,
red and green gold-embroidered jackets,
white gold-embroidered wide-leg trousers,
dark blue gold-embroidered borders,
gilt belts,
green neck wraps,
red knots,
and red leather boots.
All the grand music performers and the performers for the two civil and martial dances
all wore curved-foot pútóu headwear,
red silk robes with large sleeves painted with floral patterns,
gilt belts,
red silk neck wraps,
red knots,
and black leather boots.
The musicians of the four barbarian tribes
all wore lotus hats,
various colored finely pleated jackets,
white gold-embroidered wide-leg trousers,
red gold-embroidered borders,
red and green silk waistbands,
red silk neck wraps,
red knots,
and patterned boots.
During the Yǒnglè period,
the ritual music for the Yòu Food ceremony within the palace was established.
For the "Pacifying the World" dance,
the lead dancers and musicians
all wore indigo-blue gauze scarves,
indigo-blue, red, green, or jade-colored gauze jackets with gold-embroidered front and back panels,
solid gold-colored copper belts,
red gauze waist sashes,
black boots with cloud-patterned toes,
and indigo-blue and green gauze hip covers with gold embroidery.
The dancers' attire was similar.
For the "Pacifying the Four Barbarians" dance: four Gāolí dancers,
all wore conical hats,
indigo-blue gauze jackets with gold-embroidered front and back panels,
copper belts,
and black boots;
four Liúqiú dancers,
all wore cotton fabric floral handkerchiefs,
indigo-blue gauze large-sleeved jackets,
copper belts,
white glossy silk striped踢袴 (tīkù) trousers,
and black leather boots;
four Běifān dancers,
all wore fox-fur hats,
indigo-blue and red ramie silk jackets with gold embroidery,
and copper belts;
four Wǔlǔsù Huíhuí dancers,
all wore indigo-blue gauze hats,
Bǐlǐhǎn cotton fabric floral handkerchiefs,
copper belts,
and black boots.
For the "Chēshū Huìtóng" dance,
all dancers wore black gauze headscarves,
indigo-blue, green, or jade-colored black-edged robes with lapels,
tea-brown cord sashes, and black leather four-seam boots.
For the "Manifesting Righteousness to All Nations" dance,
two lead dancers wore
indigo-blue gauze scarves,
red gauze neckerchiefs with gold embroidery,
red plain silk undershirts with brocade collars,
red plain silk full-sleeved jackets with gold embroidery,
indigo-blue cord copper belts,
brocade armlets,
black boots with cloud-patterned toes,
various colored hip covers with gold embroidery,
and red silk waist sashes.
The attire of the dancers and musicians
was the same as that of the lead dancers.
For the "Heaven's Mandate to the Virtuous" dance,
two lead dancers wore
indigo-blue covered gauze ruyi caps,
red plain silk undershirts with brocade collars,
red plain silk large-sleeved robes,
various colored silk painted wrapped belts,
black horn side belts,
blue silk brocade cloud-patterned black boots,
and white cloth socks.
The attire of the dancers and musicians
was the same as that of the lead dancers.
In the fifth year of Hóngwǔ, the caps and robes for Z̄hàiláng,
Yuèsheng,
and Wénwǔwǔshēng were established.
Z̄hàiláng wore
black Jièzé caps,
made of lacquered cloth,
without patterns;
red silk narrow-sleeved shirts,
with red plain silk for the𩹉 (xiàng);
black leather four-seam boots;
and black horn belts.
Wénwǔwǔshēng and Yuèsheng wore
black Jièzé caps,
made of lacquered cloth,
with painted gold cicadas on top;
red silk large brocade robes,
with painted intertwined square sunflower patterns on the front and back;
red plain silk for the𩹉 (xiàng),
with two brocade armlets added;
black leather four-seam boots;
and black horn belts.
Wǔwǔwǔshēng wore
military caps,
made of lacquered cloth,
with painted gold cicadas on top;
their attire, boots, and belts
were the same as those of the Wénwǔwǔshēng.
In the ninth year of Jiājìng, the attire for Wénwǔwǔshēng was established: for the Yuánqiū sacrifice, indigo-blue ramie silk robes;
for the Fāngzé sacrifice, black-green gauze robes;
for the Cháorìtán sacrifice, vermillion gauze robes;
and for the Xīyuètán sacrifice, jade-colored gauze robes.
Caps and robes for palace female musicians.
Established in the third year of Hóngwǔ.
All female musicians serving the empress and wives of officials such as Fènglúan
wore their hair in natural-colored buns,
and indigo-blue gauze round-collared robes.
Tídiào female musicians wore
black lacquered Tángjīn caps,
dark red gauze round-collared robes with gold-embroidered flowers,
gilt floral belts,
and black boots.
Gēzhāng female musicians wore
black lacquered Tángjīn caps,
dark red gauze skirts and jackets with gold embroidery,
breast sashes,
dark red gauze headbands,
indigo-blue and green gauze painted cloud collars,
and black boots with gold-painted peony flowers.
Zòuyuè female musicians
wore attire similar to that of Gēzhāng musicians.
