In the ninth year of Jiājìng, for the sacrifice to Xiāncán,
the caps and robes for female musicians were established.
Black crêpe gauze caps with gold-painted cicadas,
black silk tassels,
black plain gauze large-sleeved female robes with gold-embroidered sunflower patterns on the front and back,
black plain silk undershirts,
brocade collars,
gilded belts,
white socks,
and black flat shoes.
Caps and robes for the Jiàofāngsī.
Established in the third year of Hóngwǔ.
Jiàofāngsī musical performers wore
indigo-blue swastika-topped scarves,
and red and green waist sashes.
Female entertainers wore
clear horn caps,
and black Bèizi vests,
and were not allowed to wear the same as commoners' wives.
Páizhǎng serving before the emperor wore
drum and wind instrument caps,
red gauze small-sleeved robes with front and back panels,
red silk waist sashes,
and black boots.
Sèzhǎng wore
drum and wind instrument caps,
red and indigo-blue ramie silk robes with painted hundred flowers,
and red silk waist sashes.
Singers wore
military caps,
red gauze large-sleeved robes with gold-woven front and back panels,
red plain silk undershirts with brocade collars,
black horn belts,
red processed silk brocade-trimmed trousers,
black leather Qínlǚ (qínlǚ) shoes,
and white cotton interlined socks.
The attire of musicians
was the same as that of singers.
For Jiàofāngsī officials' everyday caps and belts,
they were the same as those of other officials;
when serving before the emperor,
they held powdered lacquer hu tablets,
wore black lacquered fútóu headwear,
black-green gauze large-sleeved robes with lapels,
black horn side belts,
and black boots.
Jiàofāngsī entertainers
wore green scarves as their everyday attire,
to distinguish them from the attire of gentry and commoners.
Musicians all wore drum and wind instrument caps,
without brocade cords,
only red waist sashes,
and their attire color was not restricted to red or green.
Jiàofāngsī women
were not allowed to wear caps
or Bèizi vests.
Musicians' clothing
was limited to bright green, peach blossom red, jade color, water red, and tea brown.
Pái and Sèzhǎng,
and musicians,
all wore black headscarves
and mixed-colored cords.
Caps and robes for princely estate musicians.
Established in the fifteenth year of Hóngwǔ.
For grand music and banquet ceremonies during court audiences,
the musicians for the seven musical performances
all wore red silk small-sleeved unlined robes with painted square floral patterns on the front and back,
decorated drum and wind instrument caps,
brocade armlets,
black boots,
red gauze painted headbands,
and red silk waist sashes.
The rest of
the musicians wore green silk small-sleeved unlined robes with painted square floral patterns on the front and back,
plain drum and wind instrument caps,
red silk painted headbands,
and red silk waist sashes.
Military Uniforms.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, an order was issued to make clothing,
with the inner and outer layers of contrasting colors.
It was called a Yuānyāng Zhàn'ǎo (Mandarin Duck Battle Jacket),
to designate the new army.
In the twenty-first year, it was stipulated that banner bearers, guard soldiers, and strongmen
all wore red Pàn'ǎo (waistcoats).
For other guard garrisons,
their Pàn'ǎo were the same.
All Pàn'ǎo
were knee-length
with narrow sleeves,
and padded with cotton inside.
In the twenty-sixth year, an order was issued for cavalry to wear front-opening jackets,
which were convenient for riding horses.
Those who wore them without authorization
were punished.
Uniforms for Yàolì (attendants) and Gōngrén (public servants).
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, it was stipulated that
Yàolì wore
round-topped caps
and black clothes.
In the fourth year, it was stipulated that
Yàolì and Gōngshǐrén (envoys) wore
black round-collared shirts,
flat-topped caps,
white dātè (sashes),
and carried tin plaques.
In the fourteenth year, an order was issued for the Zhī Jìn (attendants) of various yámén (government offices),
who originally wore black clothes,
to change to light blue.
In the twenty-fifth year,
Yàolì and Bàn Dāng (assistants)
were not allowed to wear boots,
only leather Zápáng (leggings).
Crowns and Robes for Foreign Rulers and Officials.
In the second year of Hóngwǔ,
Gāolí (Goryeo) envoys came to court,
requesting the system for sacrificial attire.
An order was given to manufacture and bestow it upon them.
In the twenty-seventh year, the protocol for tributary missions from Fān Guó (tributary states) was established:
when a king came to court,
he was to wear the court attire that had been previously bestowed upon him
for the audience.
In the thirty-first year, the King of Liúqiú (Ryukyu) and his officials were bestowed with crowns and robes.
During the Yǒnglè reign,
the King of Zhōngshān (Chūzan) of Liúqiú was bestowed with a Píbàn (leather cap),
a Yùguī (jade scepter),
a Línpáo (unicorn robe),
and a Xīdài (rhinoceros horn belt),
corresponding to a second-rank official's status.
In the third year of Xuāndé,
King Lǐ Pán of Cháoxiǎn (Joseon) stated:
"During the Hóngwǔ reign,
Your Majesty graciously bestowed upon the king a Miǎnfú Jiǔ Zhāng (crown and ceremonial robes with nine insignia),
and the accompanying officials' crowns and robes were two grades lower than those of the imperial court.
Therefore, the first-rank accompanying officials,
compared to the third-rank imperial court officials,
received the Wǔliáng Guānfú (five-beam crown and robes).
In the early Yǒnglè reign,
my late father Fāngyuǎn sent the crown prince Tí to court,
and he was graciously bestowed with a Wǔliáng Guānfú.
I humbly believe that the crown prince's crown and robes
should not merely be the same as a first-rank accompanying official's.
I beg Your Majesty to establish a special regulation."
Thereupon, an order was given to make a Liùliáng Guān (six-beam crown) and bestow it upon him.
In the sixth year of Jiājìng, an order was issued that foreign tribute bearers
were not allowed to arbitrarily use clothing that violated regulations.
If violated,
both sellers and buyers would be punished equally.
Monk and Daoist Robes.
In the fourteenth year of Hóngwǔ, it was stipulated that
Chán (Zen) monks wore
tea-brown regular robes
and jade-colored kāṣāya (monk's robes) with green sashes.
Jiǎng (sermon-giving) monks wore
jade-colored regular robes
and light red kāṣāya with green sashes.
Jiào (teaching) monks wore
black regular robes
and light red kāṣāya with black sashes.
Monk officials followed the same.
Only the officials of the Sēnglùsī (Office of Monastic Affairs)
had their kāṣāya
decorated with golden patterns and rings.
Dàoshì (Daoist priests) wore
blue Fǎfú (ceremonial robes) as regular attire,
and their court robes were all red.
Daoist officials also followed the same.
Only the officials of the Dàolùsī (Office of Daoist Affairs)
had their Fǎfú and court robes
decorated with golden patterns.
All Daoist officials in the capital wore
red Daoist robes,
Jīnlán (golden cassock),
and Mùjiǎn (wooden tablets).
Daoist officials outside the capital wore
red Daoist robes
and Mùjiǎn,
but did not use Jīnlán.
Dàoshì wore
blue Daoist robes
and Mùjiǎn.
Collation Notes

Gazetteer Volume Forty-Four: Carriages and Robes (4), Imperial Seals, Empress's Imperial Credentials and Seals, Imperial Consorts and Below's Credentials and Seals, Crown Prince's Imperial Credentials and Seals, Crown Prince's Consort's Imperial Credentials and Seals, Prince and Below's Imperial Credentials and Seals, Iron Certificates, Seals, Tallies and Tokens, Palace System, Official and Commoner Housing System, Implements
At the beginning of the Míng dynasty, there were seventeen imperial seals.
The large ones were called
"Huángdì Fèngtiān Zhī Bǎo" (Seal of the Emperor, Following Heaven's Mandate),
"Huángdì Zhī Bǎo" (Seal of the Emperor),
"Huángdì Xíng Bǎo" (Traveling Seal of the Emperor),
"Huángdì Xìn Bǎo" (Credential Seal of the Emperor),
"Tiānzǐ Zhī Bǎo" (Seal of the Son of Heaven),
"Tiānzǐ Xíng Bǎo" (Traveling Seal of the Son of Heaven),
"Tiānzǐ Xìn Bǎo" (Credential Seal of the Son of Heaven),
"Zhìgào Zhī Bǎo" (Seal for Edicts and Proclamations),
"Chìmìng Zhī Bǎo" (Seal for Imperial Orders),
"Guǎngyùn Zhī Bǎo" (Seal of Vast Fortune),
"Huángdì Zūnqīn Zhī Bǎo" (Seal of the Emperor Honoring Relatives),
"Huángdì Qīnqīn Zhī Bǎo" (Seal of the Emperor Cherishing Relatives),
"Jìngtiān Qínmín Zhī Bǎo" (Seal of Reverence for Heaven and Diligence for the People);
there were also
"Yùqián Zhī Bǎo" (Seal Before the Emperor's Presence),
"Biǎozhāng Jīngshǐ Zhī Bǎo" (Seal for Commending Classics and Histories)
and
"Qīnwén Zhī Xǐ" (Seal of Imperial Culture).
The red tallies were used to verify orders across the four directions.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, when the imperial seals were to be made,
a Persian merchant sailing across the sea presented beautiful jade,
saying:
"This comes from Yútián (Khotan),
passed down through my ancestors,
and is destined to become an imperial seal."
An order was then given to craft it into a seal,
but it is unknown which of the seventeen seals
was made from this jade.
Chéngzǔ (Emperor Yǒnglè) also made
"Huángdì Qīnqīn Zhī Bǎo",
"Huángdì Fèngtiān Zhī Bǎo",
"Gàomìng Zhī Bǎo" (Seal for Imperial Investitures),
and "Chìmìng Zhī Bǎo".
In the thirteenth year of Hóngzhì,
Máo Zhìxué, a commoner from Hùxiàn, found a jade seal by the Níhé River.
Its inscription read,
"Shòu Mìng Yú Tiān,
Jì Shòu Yǒngchāng" (Received Mandate from Heaven, Longevity and Eternal Prosperity).
Its color was white with a slight bluish tint, and it had a Chī (hornless dragon) knob.
Xióng Chōng, the Shǎnxī Provincial Governor, believed it to be the reappearance of the Qín seal,
and sent someone to present it.
Fù Hàn, the Minister of Rites, stated:
"Since the original Qín seal,
the records of its acquisition, loss, authenticity, and falsity throughout various dynasties are fully recorded in historical texts.
The one now presented, its seal script differs from the fish and bird seal script transcribed in works like Chuògēng Lù (Record of Retirement from Farming).
Its Chī knob also does not resemble the coiled five dragons, the missing corner of the Chī, or the Wei record carved on the side, as described in historical accounts.
The Qín seal has long been lost.
The one now presented, and those obtained during the Sòng and Yuán dynasties,
are all suspected to be imitations of the Qín seal carved by later generations.
I humbly believe that the purpose of a seal
is to identify documents and prevent fraud,
not to be treated as a treasured plaything.
Since Qín Shǐhuáng obtained Lántián (Lantian) jade to make his seal,
it was passed down and used after the Hàn dynasty.
From then on, there was cunning contention and forceful acquisition,
believing that possessing this seal was sufficient to receive the Mandate,
without realizing that the Mandate is received through virtue,
not through a seal.
Therefore, if they could not find it,
they would counterfeit it to deceive people;
if they obtained it,
the ruler and ministers would be visibly joyful,
to boast and display it to the world.
These are all matters that invite ridicule for a thousand generations.
Our Gāo Huángdì (Emperor Hóngwǔ) personally created a set of seals for our dynasty,
each inscription having its own meaning,
applied according to circumstances.
They are truly sufficient as symbols of receiving the Mandate for our dynasty,
and establish a legal precedent for ten thousand generations.
What need is there for this seal?"
The Emperor followed his advice,
rejected it, and did not use it.
In the 18th year of Jiājìng, seven new treasures were made:
"Bào" (seal) of the Emperor of Dà Míng, who received the mandate of Heaven and governs in accordance with it,"
"Bǎo of Dà Míng, who received the Mandate,"
"Bǎo for touring the world,"
"Bǎo for issuing instructions,"
"Bǎo for bestowing virtue,"
"Bǎo for punishing evildoers and pacifying the people,"
and
"Bǎo for rectifying the myriad people by imperial decree."
Together with the imperial seals from the beginning of the dynasty,
there were twenty-four imperial seals in total,
overseen by the officials of the Shàngbǎo Sì (Office of Imperial Seals).
For the Empress's ceremonial investiture document (cè),
two sheets of gold cè were used,
each one Zhōu chì long and two cùn wide,
five cùn wide,
and two fēn five lí thick.
The characters were divided into lines according to their number,
engraved in regular script (zhēnshū).
There were holes at the top and bottom,
connected by a red cord (tāo),
opening and closing like a book cover (shūzhì),
placed on a red brocade cushion (rù).
The cè box (cèlü) was made of wood,
decorated with pure gold embossed with coiling dragons (pánlóng) in the lìfěn technique,
lined with red ramie silk,
with the cè itself wrapped inside a small red silk brocade pouch (xiāojīn xiǎofú),
and then covered externally with a red silk brocade outer pouch (xiāojīn jiāfú),
secured externally with a five-colored small cord.
The imperial seal (bǎo) was made of gold,
with a tortoise-shaped knob (guīniǔ),
and bore the seal script (zhuànwén)
"Bǎo of the Empress."
It was five cùn nine fēn square according to the Zhōu chì,
and one cùn seven fēn thick.
The seal tray (bǎochí) was made of gold,
its width designed to accommodate the seal.
There were two sets of seal chests (bǎoquè):
one for the seal,
and one for the seal tray.
Each set had three layers: the outer chest was made of wood,
decorated with pure gold embossed with coiling dragons in the lìfěn technique,
and lined with red ramie silk;
the middle chest was made of gold engraved with coiling dragons;
the inner small chest was decorated like the outer chest,
and contained a seal stand (bǎozuò),
with coiling dragons carved at the four corners,
decorated with pure gold.
On the stand was a brocade cushion,
with the seal wrapped in a small red silk brocade pouch,
and each chest was covered externally with a large red silk brocade pouch.
On the day of the investiture,
both the cè and the bǎo were placed on a red lacquered sedan chair (yú'àn),
the top of which had a red silk hanging decoration (lìshuǐ),
carried by a litter (dānchuáng).
From the Imperial Noble Consort (Huáng Guìfēi) downwards,
there was a cè but no bǎo, only an印 (yìn, seal).
For a Consort (Fēi)'s cè,
two gilded silver sheets were used,
their length and width the same as the Empress's cè.
The cè box was decorated with pure gold embossed with coiling phoenixes (pánfèng) in the lìfěn technique.
Her seal (yìn) was made of gold,
with a tortoise-shaped knob,
its dimensions the same as the seals of the various princes (zhūwáng),
and bore the inscription
"Yìn of the Imperial Consort."
The chest was decorated with coiling phoenixes.
In the first year of Xuāndé,
the Emperor, considering Imperial Noble Consort Sūn's virtuous conduct,
specially requested the Empress Dowager
to have a golden bǎo made and bestowed upon her.
Soon after, she gave birth to an imperial heir.
From then on, bestowing a bǎo upon an Imperial Noble Consort
became a customary practice (gùshì).
In the tenth year of Jiājìng,
when the Nine Concubines (Jiǔpín) were established,
their cè were made of silver,
one-fifth smaller than the Imperial Consort's,
and decorated with gold.
For the Imperial Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ)'s cè and bǎo:
The cè was made of gold,
in two sheets,
its form and the decoration of its box and chests were the same as the Empress's cè.
The bǎo was made of gold,
with a tortoise-shaped knob,
bearing the seal script
"Bǎo of the Imperial Crown Prince."
Its form and the decoration of its tray and chests were the same as the Empress's bǎo.
For the Imperial Crown Princess (Huáng Tàizǐ Fēi)'s cè and bǎo:
Her cè was made of gold,
two sheets,
weighing one hundred liǎng,
each sheet one chì two cùn high,
and five cùn wide.
The cè was backed with brocade,
connected by a red silk cord,
cushioned with a brocade cushion,
and wrapped with a red silk brocade pouch.
Its box was decorated with pure gold embossed with cloud phoenixes (yúnfèng) in the lìfěn technique,
with silver flower nails and hinges inside,
inlaid with gold wire, iron tubes, and locks;
externally it was covered with a red silk brocade pouch.
The specifics of her golden bǎo were not detailed.
In the 28th year of Hóngwǔ, it was reformed,
and only a golden cè was bestowed,
no bǎo was used.
For the Imperial Prince (Qīnwáng)'s cè and bǎo:
The cè's form was the same as the Imperial Crown Prince's.
His bǎo was made of gold,
with a tortoise-shaped knob,
five cùn two fēn square according to the Zhōu chì,
and one cùn five fēn thick,
bearing the inscription
"Bǎo of [Name] Wáng."
The decoration of its tray and chests
was the same as the Imperial Crown Prince's bǎo.
The decoration of the bǎo box,
however, was carved with coiling chí (hornless dragons).
For the Imperial Princess Consort (Qīnwáng Fēi)'s cè and yìn:
Her golden cè was
one cùn shorter than the Crown Princess's cè,
but all other aspects were the same,
and the text of the cè was comparable to an Imperial Prince's.
The specifics of her golden yìn were not detailed.
In the 28th year of Hóngwǔ, it was reformed,
and only a golden cè was bestowed.
For the Princess (Gōngzhǔ)'s cè and yìn:
Two silver sheets for the cè,
with engraved characters gilded,
placed on a red brocade cushion.
The cè box was decorated with pure gold embossed with coiling chí in the lìfěn technique.
Her yìn was similar to the Sòng system,
made of gold,
with a tortoise-shaped knob,
bearing the inscription
"Yìn of the Princess of [Name] State."
It was five cùn two fēn square,
and one cùn five fēn thick.
The yìn tray was made of gold,
its width designed to accommodate the seal.
The outer yìn chest was made of wood,
decorated with pure gold embossed with coiling phoenixes in the lìfěn technique,
the middle chest was made of gold engraved with coiling phoenixes,
the inner small chest
was decorated like the outer chest.
For the Heir Apparent (Shìzǐ) of an Imperial Prince, a golden cè and golden bǎo were used.
For succession, only a golden cè was bestowed;
a golden bǎo was used for transmission.
The Heir Apparent Consort (Shìzǐ Fēi) also used a golden cè.
In the 23rd year of Hóngwǔ, an Heir Apparent Consort's yìn was cast,
its form similar to a Prince Consort's,
a golden yìn,
with a tortoise-shaped knob,
bearing the seal script
"Yìn of [Name] Shìzǐ Fēi."
For a Commandery Prince (Jùnwáng),
a gilded silver cè and a gilded silver yìn were used,
the cè text comparable to an Heir Apparent's.
His Consort only received a gilded silver cè.
Iron Certificates (Tiěquàn) for Meritorious Officials.
In the second year of Hóngwǔ,
Tàizǔ (Emperor Hóngwǔ) wished to enfeoff meritorious officials,
and considered making iron certificates,
but there was no established system yet.
Someone mentioned that a commoner from Táizhōu, Qián Yǔnyī, had in his family collection an iron certificate bestowed by the Táng dynasty upon Qián Liú, King of Wúyuè.
An envoy was then dispatched to retrieve it,
and its design was adopted, with modifications.
Its shape was like a tile,
divided into seven ranks.
For Gōng (Dukes), there were two ranks: one was one chì high,
one chì six cùn five fēn wide;
the other was nine cùn five fēn high,
one chì six cùn wide.
For Hóu (Marquises), there were three ranks: one was nine cùn high,
one chì five cùn five fēn wide;
another was eight cùn five fēn high,
one chì five cùn wide;
the third was eight cùn high,
one chì four cùn five fēn wide.
For Bó (Counts), there were two ranks: one was seven cùn five fēn high,
one chì three cùn five fēn wide;
the other was six cùn five fēn high,
one chì two cùn five fēn wide.
The outside was engraved with detailed records of their service and granted favors,
to commemorate their achievements;
the inside was inscribed with the number of pardons for crimes and reductions in salary,
to guard against their transgressions.
The characters were inlaid with gold.
There were ninety-seven pairs in total,
each divided into left and right halves:
the left half was issued to the meritorious official,
the right half was stored in the imperial treasury (nèifǔ),
and in case of an incident, they would be brought together
to verify authenticity.
In the third year, great enfeoffments were made to meritorious officials.
Six were made Gōng,
twenty-eight were made Hóu,
and all were granted iron certificates.
The Gōng were
Lǐ Shàncháng, Xú Dá, Lǐ Wénzhōng, Féng Shèng, Dèng Yù, and Cháng Mào.
The Hóu were

Tāng Hé, Táng Shèngzōng, Lù Zhònghēng, Zhōu Déxīng, Huá Yúnlóng, Gù Shí, Gěng Bǐngwén, Chén Dé, Guō Zǐxīng, Wáng Zhì, Zhèng Yùchūn, Fèi Jù, Wú Liáng, Wú Zhēn, Zhào Yōng, Liáo Yǒngzhōng, Yú Tōngyuán, Huá Gāo, Yáng Jǐng, Kāng Duó, Zhū Liàngzǔ, Fù Yǒudé, Hú Měi, Hán Zhèng, Huáng Bīn, Cáo Liángchén, Méi Sīzǔ, and Lù Jù.
In the twenty-fifth year, the system of iron certificates was revised.
They were granted to Gōng Fù Yǒudé,
Hóu Wáng Bì, Gěng Bǐngwén, Guō Yīng, and the late Gōng Xú Dá and Lǐ Wénzhōng,
and Hóu Wú Jié and Mù Yīng,
a total of eight families.
In the early Yǒnglè reign,
meritorious officials of the Jìngnàn campaign were also granted them.
Seals and credentials for all officials.
In the early Hóngwǔ reign,
the Seal Bureau cast seals for all central and provincial agencies.
For officials of the principal first rank (zhèng yīpǐn),
there were silver seals,
with three platforms (sāntái),
three cun and four fen square,
and one cun thick.
The Six Ministries (liùbù), the Censorate (dùcháyuan), and the various provincial military commissions (dū sī) were
all of the principal second rank (zhèng èrpǐn),
with silver seals with two platforms (èrtái),
three cun and two fen square,
and eight fen thick.
Other officials of the principal second rank and concurrent second rank (cóng èrpǐn)
had silver seals with two platforms,
three cun and one fen square,
and seven fen thick.
Only the Yǎnshèng Gōng, despite being of the principal second rank,
had a three-platform silver seal,
which was granted in the third year of Jǐngtài.
The two prefectures of Shùntiān and Yìngtiān were both of the principal third rank (zhèng sānpǐn),
with silver seals,
two cun and nine fen square,
and six fen and five lí thick.
Other officials of the principal third rank and concurrent third rank (cóng sānpǐn)
all had copper seals,
two cun and seven fen square,
and six fen thick.
Only the Grand Court of Imperial Stud (tàipú sì), the Court of Imperial Entertainments (guānglù sì), and the provincial Salt Transport Commissioners (yányùn sī)
were all of the concurrent third rank,
with copper seals,
one fen smaller in square dimension,
and five lí smaller in thickness.
For the principal fourth rank (zhèng sìpǐn) and concurrent fourth rank (cóng sìpǐn),
all had copper seals,
two cun and five fen square,
and five fen thick.
For the principal fifth rank (zhèng wǔpǐn) and concurrent fifth rank (cóng wǔpǐn),
all had copper seals,
two cun and four fen square,
and four fen and five lí thick.
Only the concurrent fifth rank officials of the various provincial prefectures (zhōu)
had copper seals,
one fen smaller in square dimension,
and five lí smaller in thickness.
For the principal sixth rank (zhèng liùpǐn) and concurrent sixth rank (cóng liùpǐn),
all had copper seals,
two cun and two fen square,
and three fen and five lí thick.
For the principal seventh rank (zhèng qīpǐn) and concurrent seventh rank (cóng qīpǐn),
copper seals,
two cun and one fen square,
and three fen thick.
For the principal and concurrent eighth ranks (zhèng cóng bāpǐn),
all had copper seals,
two cun square,
and two fen and five lí thick.
For the principal and concurrent ninth ranks (zhèng cóng jiǔpǐn),
all had copper seals,
one cun and nine fen square,
and two fen and two lí thick.
Those not in a ranked stream (wèi rù liú)
had copper "strip records" (tiáojì),
one cun and three fen wide,
two cun and five fen long,
and two fen and one lí thick.
All the above had straight knobs (zhíniǔ)
and Nine-Fold Seal Script (jiǔdié zhuànwén).
Initially,
miscellaneous officials (zázhí) also had square seals,
but this was changed to strip records in Hóngwǔ thirteen.
Among all official seals,
only the silver seal of the Wényuān Gé (Hall of Literary Brilliance),
with a straight knob,
one cun and seven fen square,
and six fen thick,
bore Jade-Chopstick Seal Script (yùzhù zhuànwén),
indicating its special importance.
Military officials entrusted with heavy responsibilities,
such as the generals for Punishing the West (zhēngxī), Guarding the North (zhènshuò), and Pacifying the Man (píngmán),
had silver seals,
with tiger knobs (hǔniǔ),
three cun and three fen square,
and nine fen thick,
bearing Willow-Leaf Seal Script (liǔyè zhuànwén).
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
high-ranking dukes (shànggōng) sometimes wore general's seals.
Later, dukes, marquises, earls (bó), and military governors (dūdū) were appointed as supreme commanders (zǒngbīng guān),
and were known as
"seal-bearing generals" (guàyìn jiāngjūn).
When there were military campaigns, the supreme commander was ordered to wear the seal and depart;
upon returning, he would present the seal he had worn to the court.
Apart from this,
only the supreme commander for grain transport (cáoyùn zǒngbīng)
had a seal like a general's.
The practice of supreme commanders and assistant generals (cānjiàng) wearing seals in the provincial garrisons
began in the first year of Hóngxī.
There were also civil officials who wore general's seals:
Wáng Jì, as Minister of War (bīngbù shàngshū), campaigned against the Miáo in Húguì
and wore the Seal of the General for Pacifying the Man;
Wáng Yuè, as Left Censor-in-Chief (zuǒ dūyùshǐ), defended Dàtóng
and wore the Seal of the General for Punishing the West.
Other civil and military ministers
who held weighty authority by imperial edict
were sometimes given copper "border passes" (guānfáng),
with straight knobs,
one cun and nine fen and five lí wide,
two cun and nine fen long,
and three fen thick,
bearing Nine-Fold Seal Script.
Even a grand councilor (zǎixiàng) on a frontier mission
would not have one different from a department official.
However, during the Zhèngdé reign,
Zhāng Yǒng's campaign against Prince Ānhuà
used a gold-cast one;
and during the Jiājìng reign,
Gù Dǐngchén, while in charge of the capital garrison,
used one carved from ivory.
These were all special grants.
Initially,
Tàizǔ valued the office of censor (yùshǐ),
dividing the country into thirteen circuits such as Hénán.
For each circuit, two seals were cast,
with the inscription
"Correcting Errors and Rectifying Faults" (shéngqiān jiūmiù).
The resident censor (shǒuyuàn yùshǐ) held one,
and the other was stored in the imperial treasury (nèifǔ).
When needed, it was issued for use and returned upon completion of the mission.
In Hóngwǔ twenty-three,
Censor-in-Chief Yuán Tài reported that the seals for the various circuits had similar inscriptions.
It was then ordered that they be remade as "Investigating Censor for such-and-such circuit" (mǒudào jiānchá yùshǐ).
For those on special assignment,
it was "Patrolling and Investigating Censor for such-and-such place" (xún'àn mǒuchù jiānchá yùshǐ),
a copper seal with a straight knob,
with an eyelet,
one cun and five fen square,
and three fen thick,
bearing Eight-Fold Seal Script (bādié zhuànwén).
When Chéngzǔ first visited Běijīng,
some officials held two or three seals.
Xià Yuánjí even managed the seals of the Nine Chief Ministers (jiǔqīng),
and all departments sought decisions from the court chambers,
indicating his weighty responsibility.
In the early Míng dynasty,
Gāolì was granted a gold seal,
with a turtle knob (guīniǔ),
three cun square,
inscribed
"Seal of the King of Gāolì."
Ānnán was granted a gilded silver seal,
with a camel knob (tuóniǔ),
three cun square,
inscribed
"Seal of the King of Ānnán."
Zhànchéng was granted a gilded silver seal,
with a camel knob,
three cun square,
inscribed
"Seal of the King of Zhànchéng."
Tǔbō was granted a gold seal,
with a camel knob,
five cun square,
inscribed
"Seal of the King of Báilán."
Tallies and Plaques.
Whenever a Prince of the First Rank (qīn wáng) was summoned,
an official would be dispatched bearing a golden tally (jīn fú) to deliver the message.

When Princes of the First Rank (qīn wáng) who were enfeoffed (zhī fān), or other officials such as those garrisoning (zhèn shǒu), pacifying (xún fǔ), or superintending (zhū guān) made a memorial requesting tallies (fú yàn),
all such requests were presented to the Ministry of War (Bīngbù),
which then instructed the Directorate of Imperial Seals (Shàngbǎo Sī) to issue them.
In the 26th year of Hóngwǔ (洪武) (1393), regulations were established: for all public errands (gōng chāi),
involving important military matters or those dispatched by imperial decree (fèng zhǐ chāi qiǎn) with post-horse privileges (gěi yì),
after the Ministry of War (Bīngbù) issued the verification certificate (kān hé),
they would proceed to the Imperial Household Department (Nèi fǔ),
to obtain the tallies (fú yàn),
and then depart with post-horse privileges (gěi yì).
Upon completion of the mission, these were to be returned.
In the 37th year of Jiājìng (嘉靖) (1558), regulations were established: the internal and external officials (nèi wài guān) guarding (shǒu bèi) Nánjīng (南京) and Fèngyáng (鳳陽),
as well as the Commanders-in-Chief (zǒng bīng) and Pacification Commissioners (xún fǔ) garrisoning (zhèn shǒu) various places,
and all internal and external guards (nèi wài shǒu bèi) who defended a single region (shǒu yī fāng) and were not subject to the control of the garrison commanders (zhèn shǒu),
were all to receive tallies (fú yàn) for presenting memorials.
However, Supervising Musketry (jiān qiāng), Rectifying Military Preparations (zhěng chì bīng bèi),
and the defending officials (shǒu bèi guān) of a single city or fortress,
were not permitted to obtain tallies (fú yàn).
As for their design,
the top was woven with images of boats and horses.
Those for dispatching horses used the "Horse" (mǎ) character designation.
Those for dispatching boats used the "Water" (shuǐ) character designation.
Those for dispatching double horses used the "Reach" (dá) character designation.
Those for dispatching single horses used the "Pass" (tōng) character designation.
Those for dispatching station boats used the "Trust" (xìn) character designation.
In the 4th year of Hóngwǔ (洪武) (1371), golden plaques (bǎo jīn pái) were first made and used.
For all military secret documents,
apart from the officials of the Chief Military Commission (Dūdū Fǔ) and the Grand Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shěng),
no one was permitted to memorialize arbitrarily.
When there was an imperial decree (zhào) to mobilize troops,
the Grand Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shěng) and the Chief Military Commission (Dūdū Fǔ) would jointly review and memorialize,
then each would produce their stored golden plaques (jīn pái),
and enter to request the use of the imperial seal.
Military mobilization tallies (tiáo fā fú pái) were also made for the army,
using iron,
five cùn long,
half that in width.
Engraved on the top were two flying dragons,
and on the bottom two qílín.
The top had a circular opening (yuán qiào),
through which a red silk cord (hóng sī tāo) was threaded.
Officials were once sent bearing golden plaques (jīn pái) and trust tallies (xìn fú) to the Western Barbarians (Xīfān),
to exchange tea for horses.
There were forty-one such plaques.
The upper half was kept in the Imperial Household Department (Nèi fǔ),
the lower half was issued to the various barbarians (gè fān).
The seal script read
"By Imperial Decree" (Huángdì Shèngzhǐ),
the left side read
"To Be Dispatched as Appropriate" (Hé Dāng Chāifā),
and the right side read
"Those Who Disobey Shall Be Beheaded" (Bù Xìn Zhě Zhǎn).
In the 22nd year (1389), golden plaques (jīn pái) and trust tallies (xìn fú) were again issued to the Western Barbarians (Xīfān).
Thereafter, when barbarian officials (fān guān) came to the frontier (fā sè),
they all brought the original issued plaques and tallies (pái fú).
In the 2nd year of Yǒnglè (永樂) (1404), trust tallies (xìn fú) and red plaques with golden characters (jīn zì hóng pái) were made and issued to the various barbarian tribes (zhū mán) of Yúnnán (雲南).
Whenever a new reign era (gǎi yuán) was proclaimed in successive dynasties,
the trust tallies (xìn fú) and golden plaques (jīn pái) issued to foreign countries
had to be re-cast with the new reign year (xīn nián hào) and issued.
These were the tallies and credentials (fú xìn) that reached the four distant regions (sì yì).
As for the golden plaques (jīn pái) worn by military officials (wǔ chén), they were made in the 4th year of Hóngwǔ (洪武) (1371).
They were two cùn wide,
one chǐ long.
Engraved on the top were twin dragons,
and on the bottom two recumbent tigers.
The ends of the plaque had circular openings (yuán qiào),
through which a red silk cord (hóng sī tāo) was threaded.
Commanders (zhǐhuī) wore golden plaques (jīn pái)
with twin cloud-dragons (shuāng yúnlóng)
and twin tiger-tallies (shuāng hǔ fú).
Battalion Commanders (qiānhù) wore gilded silver plaques (dù jīn yín pái)
with a single cloud-dragon (dú yúnlóng)
and a single tiger-tally (dú hǔ fú).
Company Commanders (bǎihù) wore plain cloud-silver plaques (sù yún yín pái) with tallies.
Tàizǔ (太祖) personally inscribed a text on them, which read:
"Heaven aids the people,
and I (zhèn) lead them and soothe them.
My might extends over the land of Huáxià (華夏),
truly relying on brave ministers (hǔ chén).
I bestow upon you these golden tallies (jīn fú),
to be eternally passed down to your descendants."
When the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) offered sacrifices at the suburban altars and ancestral temples (jiāo miào),
or inspected schools (shì xué), or personally ploughed the ceremonial field (jí tián),

the meritorious officials (xūn wèi) who escorted him, as well as dukes (gōng), marquises (hóu), counts (bó), imperial sons-in-law (fùmǎ), the daily duty officers (rì zhí) of the Five Chief Military Commissions (Wǔ Fǔ Dūdū), the duty officers of the Imperial Bodyguard (Jǐnyī Wèi Dāng Zhí),
and the commanders (dūdū) leading the commanders (zhū wèi qiān bǎi hù) of various guards (wèi) on night patrol of the Inner Imperial City (Nèi Huángchéng),
and the rotating officials (lún guān) of the various Imperial Insignia Guards (Jīnwú zhū wèi) who patrolled and inspected during court sessions,
were all issued golden plaques (jīn pái).
There were plaques with dragons, tigers, qílín, lions, or clouds,
differentiated according to rank.
As for the imperial escort golden-character silver plaques (hù jià jīn zì yín pái), they were made in the 6th year of Hóngwǔ (洪wu) (1373).
Later, they were changed to guard golden plaques (shǒu wèi jīn pái),
made of copper,
coated with gold.
They were one chǐ high,
three cùn wide,
divided into five character designations.
The "Benevolence" (Rén) designation,
engraved with a single dragon coiling among clouds and flowers,
was worn by dukes (gōng), marquises (hóu), counts (bó), and chief military commissioners (dūdū).
The "Righteousness" (Yì) designation,
engraved with a recumbent tiger among coiling clouds and flowers,
was worn by commanders (zhǐhuī).
The "Propriety" (Lǐ) designation,
engraved with a xièzhì among coiling clouds and flowers,
was worn by battalion commanders (qiānhù) and guard provosts (wèi zhèn fǔ).
The "Wisdom" (Zhì) designation,
engraved with a lion among coiling clouds and flowers,
was worn by company commanders (bǎihù) and provosts of sub-guards (suǒ zhèn fǔ).
The "Trust" (Xìn) designation,
engraved with coiling clouds and flowers,
was worn by generals (jiāng jūn).
Cast below the plaque were
the two seal characters
"Guard" (shǒu wèi).
Cast on the back were
"All guarding officers and soldiers wearing this plaque" (Fán shǒu wèi guān jūn xuán dài cǐ pái)
and twenty-four other characters.
The opening at the top of the plaque was threaded with a blue silk cord (qīng sī).
Provosts (zhèn fǔ) and generals (jiāng jūn) who were on duty and lodged in the imperial guard (sui jià zhí sù wèi) wore these.
When off duty, they were returned.
All night patrol officials (yè xún guān)
obtained command tallies (lìng pái) from the Directorate of Imperial Seals (Shàngbǎo Sī).
Commanders (zhǐhuī) and battalion commanders (qiānhù) of the various gates of the Forbidden City (Jìnchéng) and the Imperial Insignia Guards (Jīnwú děng wèi)
received plaques with the "Shen" (Shēn) character designation.
From one to four for the Meridian Gate (Wǔmén),
from five to eight for the Left and Right Gates of Cháng'ān (Cháng'ān Zuǒ Yòu Mén) and the East Glorious Gate (Dōnghuá Mén),
from nine to twelve for the West Glorious Gate (Xīhuá Mén),
and from thirteen to sixteen for the Mysterious Warrior Gate (Xuánwǔ Mén).
The commanders (zhǐhuī) of the Five City Military and Horse Divisions (Wǔ Chéng Bīngmǎ) also received command tallies (lìng pái) daily.
For the East, West, South, North, and Central cities,
they received plaques with the five character designations of "Wood" (mù), "Metal" (jīn), "Fire" (huǒ), "Water" (shuǐ), and "Earth" (tǔ).
The Left-Behind Five Guards (Liúshǒu Wǔ Wèi), city patrol officials (xún chéng guān), and guarding officials (shǒu wèi guān) of the Imperial Insignia Guards (Jīnwú děng wèi)
all received copper tallies (tóng fú).
The commanders (zhǐhuī) of the Left-Behind Guards (Liúshǒu Wèi) received plaques with the "Inherit" (Chéng) character designation and the East, West, and North character designations.
All of these had the left half of the character in raised (yáng wén) script,
for matching the left halves.
For the Imperial Insignia Guards (Jīnwú děng wèi),

the commanders (zhǐhuī) and battalion commanders (qiānhù) of the Upright Gate (Duānmén), the Gate of Receiving Heaven (Chéngtiānmén), and the East, West, and North Gates of Peace (Dōng, Xī, Běi Ānmén) received plaques with the "Inherit" (Chéng) character designation and the East, West, and North character designations.
All of these had the right half of the character in incised (yīn wén) script,
for matching the right halves.
Only when the character designations on the copper tallies (tóng fú) matched exactly
were patrols permitted.
When palace eunuchs (nèi guān) and palace servants (nèi shǐ) left,
they also had to have their copper tallies (tóng fú) matched by the gate-guarding officials (shǒu mén guān) before proceeding.
The guarding soldiers (shǒu wèi jūn) of the nine gates of the Imperial City (Huángchéng) and the palisade guards (wéi zǐ shǒu)
each received copper plaques with the "Courage" (Yǒng) character designation.
The Imperial Bodyguard (Jǐnyī) cavalrymen on duty (xiàowèi shàng zhí) and the clerks, scribes, and cooks of the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Guānglù Sì lì diǎn chú yì),
during grand sacrifices,
all wore twin-fish copper plaques (shuāng yú tóng pái).
In the 6th year of Yǒnglè (永樂) (1408), when the Emperor visited Běijīng (北京),
all accompanying officials wore ivory plaques (yá pái).

The Five Chief Military Commissions (Wǔ Fǔ), the Six Ministries (Liù Bù), the Censorate (Dùchá Yuàn), the Grand Court of Revision (Dàlǐ Sì), and the Imperial Bodyguard (Jǐnyī Wèi) each cast seals (yìn xìn).
The Office of Transmission (Tōngzhèng Sī) and the Court of State Ceremonials (Hónglú Sì) each cast border seals (guān fáng).
These were called the seals and border seals (yìn xìn guān fáng) of the traveling yamens (xíng zài yámén).
Later,
the Imperial Household Department (Nèi fǔ) was ordered to store them in the Seal and Ribbon Office (Yìnshòu Jiān).
In the 18th year of Jiājìng (嘉靖) (1539), during the Southern Tour,
the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù) retrieved them
to issue to those accompanying the Emperor.
For all sacrifices at the suburban altars and ancestral temples (jiāo miào), the officials assisting in the sacrifices and those performing duties,
all received ivory plaques (yá pái) upon entering the altar.
This began in the 8th year of Hóngwǔ (洪武) (1375).
Round floral plaques (yuán huā pái)
were received by officials assisting in the sacrifices.
Long floral plaques (cháng huā pái)
were received by officials performing duties.
Long plain plaques (cháng sù pái)
were received by those in charge of affairs.
They were also called sacrificial plaques (sì pái).
Whenever the Emperor visited imperial tombs (líng qǐn),
all accompanying officials received small ivory plaques (xiǎo yá pái) from the Directorate of Imperial Seals (Shàngbǎo Sī).
In the 9th year of Jiājìng (嘉靖) (1530),
when the Empress performed the ritual of sericulture (qīn cán lǐ),
the wives of civil officials of the fourth rank and above and military officials of the third rank and above, as well as their attendants (shǐ rén),
all received ivory plaques (yá pái) from the Directorate of Imperial Seals (Shàngbǎo Sī).
There were distinctions between cloud-flower round plaques (yún huā yuán pái)
and bird-shaped long plaques (niǎo xíng cháng pái).
All civil and military officials attending court, and Jǐnyīwèi (錦衣衞) officers on duty,
also received a *yápái*,
to prevent fraud and impersonation.
This began in the eleventh year of Hóngwǔ.
Its design
was made of ivory,
with the official's title and rank engraved upon it.
If one did not wear it, the gatekeepers would refuse entry.
Private lending and borrowing of *yápái* was punished according to the law.
The characters on the *yápái* were categorized as follows:
Gōng (公), Hóu (侯), Bó (伯) used the character *xūn* (勳);
Fùmǎ Dūwèi (駙馬都尉) used the character *qīn* (親);
civil officials used the character *wén* (文);
military officials used the character *wǔ* (武);
Jiàofāng (教坊) officials used the character *lè* (樂);
eunuchs entering the palace used the character *guān* (官).
In the sixteenth year of Zhèngdé,
Xíng Huán (邢寰) of the Ministry of Rites stated:
"*Yápái* should only be worn by regular court officials.
Recently, powerful traitors have usurped authority,
and those promoted by imperial decree have taken to wearing *yápái*.
It is fitting to clean this up and emphasize the importance of these symbols of status."
Therefore, it was decreed that civil officials who did not attend court
should not be indiscriminately issued *yápái*;
while military officials who advanced to attend the imperial retinue, carried swords, or held incense burners,
were to be issued them.
In the twenty-eighth year of Jiājìng,
artisans and military officials serving in the imperial household
all wore court attendance *yápái*.
An imperial decree had once abolished and revoked them,
but they were subsequently reissued.
Chén Bāngxiū (陳邦修), a Grand Secretariat supervising secretary, brought this to attention.
The Ministry of Rites replied in a memorial:
"The *Huìdiǎn* (會典) states
that civil and military officials entering and exiting the forbidden gates must wear *yápái*,
with distinctions for 'on duty' (zhíshì, 執事), 'serving' (gōngshì, 供事), and 'court attendance' (cháocān, 朝參).
Those 'on duty' or 'serving'
received them at appointed times
and returned them on schedule.
Only the court attendance *yápái*
could be worn day and night,
not merely as a means of security,
but also to show distinctions in rank and status.
Those with honorary titles and salaries, or those merely serving or on duty,
should not all receive them.
However, for entry and exit through the palace gates,
if all were abolished and revoked,
how would inspection and scrutiny be carried out?
The Shàngbǎosī (尚寶司) has several hundred old *pái* (牌) stored,
with the inscription 'entering the imperial household' (*rù nèifǔ*, 入內府).
Please issue these to them.
As for military officials of the guard units,
apart from those holding seals and serving as imperial guards,
those not belonging to court attendance or serving roles
should have all theirs abolished and revoked.
Those who purchased *yápái* by contributing grain, had them registered by deception, or who were dismissed or retired officials and failed to return the *yápái* they had received,
should all be arrested and interrogated."
This was approved.
In the fifteenth year of Hóngwǔ, the imperial envoy's staff was designed:
a yellow, three-tiered canopy,
two *chǐ* long,
enclosed in a yellow gauze bag.
Also, a cinnabar-lacquered stand was made,
upon which the staff was placed.
When an envoy received a mission,
they would carry it forth;
when the envoy returned,
they would hold it to report back.
In the twenty-third year, an edict ordered the examination and determination of the envoy's staff's design.
The Ministry of Rites memorialized:
"During the time of Hàn Guāngwǔ (漢光武),
bamboo was used for the staff,
the handle eight *chǐ* long,
with three layers of yak tail hair.
However, Huáng Gōngshào's (黃公紹) *Yùnhuì* (韻會) notes: The Hàn staff's handle was three *chǐ* long,
with three layers of yak tail hair,
made from yak tail.
The edict followed the three *chǐ* design.
Regarding the design of the palace buildings.
In the first year of Wú, a new inner palace was built.
The main hall was called Fèntiān Diàn (奉天殿),
behind it was Huágài Diàn (華蓋殿),
and further behind was Jǐnshēn Diàn (謹身殿),
all flanked by corridors.
Before Fèntiān Diàn was Fèntiānmén (奉天門).
To the left of the hall was Wénlóu (文樓),
to the right was Wǔlóu (武樓).
Behind Jǐnshēn Diàn was the palace,
the front called Qiánqīng (乾清),
the back Kūnníng (坤寧),
with the six palaces arranged in sequence.
Outside the palace buildings,
it was surrounded by the Imperial City (*Huángchéng*, 皇城).
The gates of the city were:
in the south Wǔmén (午門),
in the east Dōnghuá (東華),
in the west Xīhuá (西華),
in the north Xuánwǔ (玄武).
At that time, there were those who suggested that auspicious stones from Ruìzhōu (瑞州) could be used to pave the ground.
Tàizǔ (太祖) said:
"I strive to uphold frugality and simplicity,
yet I fear becoming accustomed to extravagance.
Are you leading me towards luxury and splendor?"
The speaker was ashamed and withdrew.
In the eighth year of Hóngwǔ, the grand inner palace buildings were rebuilt,
and completed in the tenth year.
The main gate was Wǔmén,
flanked by two towers.
The middle had three gates,
and to the east and west were Zuǒyèmén (左掖門) and Yòuyèmén (右掖門).
Inside Wǔmén was Fèntiānmén,
and inside Fèntiānmén was Fèntiān Diàn,
where the emperor received court felicitations.
To the left and right of the gate were the East and West Corner Gates.
To the left and right gates of Fèntiān Diàn,
the left was Zhōngzuǒ (中左),
the right was Zhōngyòu (中右).
Between the two corridors,
the left was Wénlóu,
the right was Wǔlóu.
Behind Fèntiān Diàn was Huágài Diàn,
and behind Huágài Diàn was Jǐnshēn Diàn,
behind which was the main gate of Qiánqīng Gōng (乾清宮).
Outside Fèntiānmén, between the two corridors, there were gates:
the left was Zuǒshùn (左順),
the right was Yòushùn (右順).
Outside Zuǒshùnmén was Wénhuá Diàn (文華殿),
which was where the Crown Prince handled affairs.
Outside Yòushùnmén was Wǔyīng Diàn (武英殿),
where the emperor resided during periods of fasting and purification.
The system remained as before,
but the scale was grander.
In the twenty-fifth year, the Jīnshuǐ Qiáo (金水橋) of the grand inner palace was rebuilt,
and Duānmén (端門) and Chéngtiānmén Lóu (承天門樓) were each built with five bays,
as well as the East and West Cháng'ān (長安) Gates.
In the fifteenth year of Yǒnglè, the Western Palace was built in Běijīng.
In the center was Fèntiān Diàn,
flanked by two halls, left and right.
To the south was Fèntiānmén,
flanked by East and West Corner Gates.
Further south was Wǔmén,
and yet further south was Chéngtiānmén.
To the north of the hall were the Rear Hall, Cool Hall, Warm Hall, and the palaces of Rénshòu (仁壽), Jǐngfú (景福), Rénhé (仁和), Wànchūn (萬春), Yǒngshòu (永壽), Chángchūn (長春), etc.,
totaling over 1,630 rooms.
In the eighteenth year, Běijīng was constructed.
All the regulations for the palaces, halls, and gates
were exactly like those in Nánjīng,
but even more magnificent.
The central court was called Fèngtiān Diàn.
In total, there were eight thousand three hundred and fifty bays of roofs.
To the left of the hall was Zhōngzuǒmén,
and to the right was Zhōngyòumén.
To the east of the red steps was Wénlóu,
to the west was Wǔlóu.
To the south was Fèngtiānmén,
which was used for regular audiences.
To the left was Dōngjiǎomén,
to the right was Xījiǎomén.
The eastern wing corridor was Zuǒshùnmén,
the western wing corridor was Yòushùnmén.
Directly to the south was Wǔmén.
It had three central gates,
flanked by two watchtowers.
Each watchtower had a pavilion.
To the left was Zuǒyèmén,
to the right was Yòuyèmén.
A little to the south of Wǔmén on the left
was Quēzuǒmén,
and Shénchúmén,
inside of which was Tàimiào.
A little to the south on the right
was Quēyòumén,
and Shèzuǒmén,
inside of which was Tàishèjì.
Further directly to the south was Duānmén.
To the east was Miàojiē mén,
which was the right gate of Tàimiào.
To the west was Shèjiēmén,
which was the south left gate of Tàishèjì Tán.
Further directly to the south was Chéngtiānmén.
Then, turning to the east, was Cháng'ānzuǒmén;
turning to the west, was Cháng'ānyòumén.
Behind the east was Dōng'ānmén,
behind the west was Xī'ānmén,
behind the north was Běi'ānmén.
Directly to the south was Dàmíngmén.
In the middle was the Imperial Way,
with long corridors stretching a thousand paces to the east and west.
Behind Fèngtiān Diàn was Huágài Diàn,
and further behind was Jǐnshēn Diàn.
To the left of Jǐnshēn Diàn was Hòuzuǒmén,
to the right was Hòuyòumén.
Directly to the north was Qiánqīngmén.
Inside was Qiánqīng Gōng,
which was the Emperor's private residence.
Behind it was Jiāotài Diàn.
Further behind was Kūnníng Gōng,
where the Empress resided.
To the east was Rénshòu Gōng,
to the west was Qīngníng Gōng,
to house the Empress Dowager.
To the east of Zuǒshùnmén was Wénhuá Diàn.
To the west of Yòushùnmén was Wǔyīng Diàn.
To the southeast of Wénhuá Diàn was Dōnghuámén,
to the southwest of Wǔyīng Diàn was Xīhuámén.
Behind Kūnníng Gōng was Kūnníngmén.
Behind that gate was Xuánwǔmén.
Other palaces and halls,
numerous in name,
cannot all be listed,
making up the so-called "thousand gates and ten thousand households."
Within the Imperial City and outside the Palace City,
there were twelve gates: Dōngshàngmén, Dōngshàngběimén, Dōngshàngnánmén, Dōngzhōngmén, Xīshàngmén, Xīshàngběimén, Xīshàngnánmén, Xīzhōngmén, Běishàngmén, Běishàngdōngmén, Běishàngxīmén, Běizhōngmén.
Furthermore, the Imperial Grandson's Palace was built to the southeast of the Imperial City.
Shíwáng Jiē was built to the southeast outside Dōng'ānmén.
Xuānzōng paid attention to refinement,
building Guǎnghán and Qīngshǔ two halls,
as well as Dōng and Xī Qióngdǎo.
Wherever he toured,
he placed scriptures and books.
In the sixth year of Zhèngtǒng, the three halls were rebuilt.
During the Jiājìng era,
Cíqìng Gōng was built on the ground behind Qīngníng Gōng,
and Cíníng Gōng was built on the former foundation of Rénshòu Gōng.
In the thirty-sixth year,
the three halls' gate-towers were destroyed by fire.
The Emperor, considering that the hall's name, Fèngtiān,
was not suitable for an inscription,
ordered the Ministry of Rites to discuss it.
The ministry officials collectively reported:
"When the Imperial Ancestor first established it,
naming it Fèngtiān
was to overtly show reverence.
Since it was named thus,
it implies that the vast Heaven is watching,
solemnly above.
When presiding over court,
sitting to conduct morning audiences
seems inappropriate.
Now that repairs are beginning,
it is fitting to change the name
to respond to Heaven's blessing."
The following year, Fèngtiānmén was rebuilt,
and its name was changed to Dàcháomén.
In the forty-first year, Fèngtiān Diàn was renamed Huángjí,
Huágài Diàn was renamed Zhōngjí,
Jǐnshēn Diàn was renamed Jiànjí,
Wénlóu was renamed Wénzhāo Gé,
Wǔlóu was renamed Wǔchéng Gé,
Zuǒshùnmén was renamed Huìjí,
Yòushùnmén was renamed Guījì,
Dàcháomén was renamed Huángjí,
Dōngjiǎomén was renamed Hóngzhèng,
and Xījiǎomén was renamed Xuānzhì.
Also, the small pavilion to the right of Qiánqīng Gōng was renamed Dàoxīn.
The left side gate was Rén'dàng,
and the right gate was Yìpíng.
At the beginning of Shìzōng's reign,
idle land in Xīyuàn was reclaimed for farming.
A hall was built called Wúyì,
and a pavilion called Bīnfēng.
Also, pavilions were built called Shěnggēng
and Shěngliǎn.
Every year during planting and harvest,
the Emperor would personally observe.
In the thirteenth year,
the pavilions by the river east in Xīyuàn were completed.
He personally named one Tiān'é Fáng,
the one to the north Fēi'ài Tíng.
Before Yíngcuì Diàn was Fúxiāng Tíng,
before Bǎoyuè Tíng was Qiūhuī Tíng,
before Zhāohé Diàn was Chéngyuān Tíng,
and behind it was Huáitái Pō.
Before Línyī Tíng was Shuǐyún Xiè.
Two pavilions outside Xīyuànmén were Zuǒlínhǎi Tíng and Yòulínhǎi Tíng.
At the northern sluice gate was Yǒngyù Tíng.
To the east of the river was Jùjǐng Tíng.
The pavilion at Lǚliáng Hóng was renamed Lǚliáng,
and before it was Yǐjīn Tíng.
Before Cuìyù Guǎn was Jiéxiù Tíng.
The system for Princely Mansions.
It was established in the fourth year of Hóngwǔ.
The city wall was twenty-nine feet high.
The main hall's foundation was six feet nine inches high.
The main gate, front and rear halls, and the four gate-towers
were decorated with blue-green and gilded points.
Corridors and rooms were decorated with blue-black.
The main gates of the four city walls
were painted with red lacquer,
with gilded copper nails.
The palace hall's bracket sets converged at the roof,
with coiled *chī* painted in the center,
decorated with gold,
and the edges painted with the Eight Auspicious Flowers.
The front and rear hall seats
used red lacquer with gilded coiled *chī*,
and curtains used red embroidered with gilded coiled *chī*.
The wall behind the seat was painted with coiled *chī* and colored clouds,
later changed to dragons.
Mountains, rivers, the Altars of Land and Grain, and the Ancestral Temple were established within the King's City.
In the seventh year, the names of the princely residences were established:
the front hall was Chéngyùn,
the middle hall Huányuán,
the rear hall Cúnxīn.
The four city gates were:
the south Duānlǐ,
the north Guǎngzhì,
the east Tǐrén,
the west Zūnyì.
Tàizǔ said:
"May the various princes, seeing the names, reflect on their meaning,
to serve as a protective screen for the Imperial House."
In the ninth year, it was established that princely palaces, gates, corridors, and city gate-towers
were all to be covered with blue glazed tiles.
He also ordered the officials of the Central Secretariat
that only princely palaces could be decorated with vermilion and dark blue-green;
other residences were only to be decorated with red and green.
In the twelfth year,
the various princely mansions were completed.
Their design specified:
the central hall, Chéngyùn Diàn, had eleven bays;
behind it was Huányuán Diàn,
next was Cúnxīn Diàn, each with nine bays.
The two wing corridors of Chéngyùn Diàn formed two side halls.
From Cúnxīn and Chéngyùn,
encompassing the two wing corridors,
up to Chéngyùnmén,
there were one hundred and thirty-eight bays of rooms.
Behind the hall were the front, middle, and rear three palaces,
each with nine bays.
The two wings of the palace gate and other rooms numbered ninety-nine bays.
Outside the King's City,
within the perimeter wall, four gates, halls, treasuries, and other rooms,
there were altogether more than eight hundred bays of palaces, halls, and rooms.
In the eighth year of Hóngzhì, the system for princely mansions was revised,
with some additions and deletions.
The system for Junwang (Princely) Mansions.
It was established in the fourth year of Tiānshùn.
Gate-towers, reception halls, kitchens, treasuries, granaries, etc.,
amounted to only several tens of rooms in total.
Princess's Residences.
In the fifth year of Hóngwǔ (1372),
the Ministry of Rites stated:
"During the Táng and Sòng dynasties, princesses were considered to be of the first senior rank (zhèng yī pǐn),
and their residences followed the system for the first senior rank.
Now, for the princess's residence,
we propose nine bays for the main hall,
with eleven purlins.
It should be adorned with patterned, zoomorphic ridges,
and the beams, columns, *dǒugǒng*, and eaves should be decorated with colorful paintings,
but without gold.
The main gate should have five bays,
with seven purlins.
The large gate
should be painted green
with bronze rings.
The stone plinths and wall bricks
should be intricately carved with delicate patterns."
This was approved.
Officials' Residences.
In the early Míng dynasty,
it was forbidden for officials and commoners to have houses
decorated with carvings of ancient emperors, empresses, sages, or figures of the sun, moon, dragons, phoenixes, *suānní*, *qílín*, rhinoceroses, or elephants.
For officials who retired after their term,
their status was the same as those currently in office.
If their fathers or grandfathers held office,
and they passed away,
their children and grandchildren were permitted to reside in their fathers' or grandfathers' houses.
In the twenty-sixth year of Hóngwǔ (1393), regulations were established:
officials building houses
were not allowed to use *xiēshān zhuǎnjiǎo* (hip-and-gable roof with corner brackets),
double eaves with multiple *dǒugǒng*,
or painted coffers (*zǎojǐng*),
except that double eaves were not prohibited for multi-story residences.
For dukes (gōng) and marquises (hóu),
the front hall had seven bays with two side chambers,
and nine purlins.
The central hall had seven bays,
and nine purlins.
The rear hall had seven bays,
and seven purlins.
The gate had three bays,
and five purlins,
and was to be finished with gold lacquer and zoomorphic tin rings.
The ancestral temple had three bays,
and five purlins.
It was to be covered with black tiles,
the ridge adorned with patterned tile beasts,
and the beams, columns, *dǒugǒng*, and eaves decorated with colorful paintings.
Doors, windows, purlins, and posts were to be finished with gold lacquer.
Corridors, side rooms, kitchens, and storehouses,
were not to exceed five bays
and seven purlins.
For officials of the first and second ranks,
the main hall had five bays,
and nine purlins,
the roof ridge used tile beasts,
and the beams, columns, *dǒugǒng*, and eaves were decorated with green and blue paintings.
The gate had three bays,
and five purlins,
painted green,
with zoomorphic tin rings.
For officials from the third to fifth ranks,
the main hall had five bays,
and seven purlins,
the roof ridge used tile beasts,
and the beams, columns, and eaves were decorated with green and blue paintings.
The gate had three bays,
and three purlins,
painted black,
with tin rings.
For officials from the sixth to ninth ranks,
the main hall had three bays,
and seven purlins,
and the beams and columns were decorated with earth yellow.
The gate had one bay,
and three purlins,
a black door,
with iron rings.
For officials' residences,
doors, windows, and lattices were not permitted to use vermilion lacquer.
Behind the residences of meritorious officials,
a vacant space of ten *zhàng* (33 meters) was to be left,
and five *zhàng* (16.5 meters) on both sides.
It was not permitted to relocate military personnel or commoners to reside there,
nor was it allowed to occupy excessive land in front, behind, or on the sides of the residence,
to construct pavilions and halls,
or to dig ponds,
for the purpose of sightseeing.
In the thirty-fifth year (1402), the prohibitions were reiterated:
main halls for first and third-rank officials each had seven bays,
and the beams and columns of main halls for sixth to ninth-rank officials were only to be decorated with light blue.
Commoners' Dwellings.
In the twenty-sixth year of Hóngwǔ (1393), regulations were established:
they were not to exceed three bays
and five purlins,
and *dǒugǒng* and colorful decoration were not permitted.
In the thirty-fifth year (1402), the prohibitions were reiterated:
it was not permitted to build houses with nine or five bays,
and even if a household had one or twenty houses,
depending on their financial means,
none were allowed to exceed three bays.
In the twelfth year of Zhèngtǒng (1447), a slightly more flexible order was issued:
commoners' houses with more purlins but fewer bays
were not subject to the prohibition.
Prohibitions on Utensils.
In the twenty-sixth year of Hóngwǔ (1393), it was stipulated:
For dukes (gōng), marquises (hóu), and first and second-rank officials,
wine pitchers and wine cups were to be gold,
and other items silver.
For third to fifth-rank officials,
wine pitchers were silver,
wine cups gold.
For sixth to ninth-rank officials,
wine pitchers and wine cups were silver,
and all other items were ceramic or lacquerware.
Wooden items were not permitted to be vermilion, or to be decorated with applied gold, painted gold, or carved with dragon patterns.
For commoners,
wine pitchers were tin,
wine cups silver,
and other items ceramic or lacquerware.
For all officials,
bed surfaces, screens, and partitions
were to be decorated with various colors of lacquer,
and were not permitted to be carved with dragon patterns
or decorated with gold on vermilion lacquer.
For military officers and soldiers,
bows and arrows were black lacquered,
and bow cases and quivers
were not permitted to be decorated with vermilion lacquer or painted gold.
In the fourth year of Jiànwén (1402), officials and commoners were admonished
not to presumptuously use gold wine goblets,
and chairs, tables, and wooden utensils were also not allowed to be vermilion or gold-decorated.
In the sixteenth year of Zhèngdé (1521), it was stipulated:
For first and second-rank officials,
utensils were not to be jade,
only gold was permitted.
Merchants and artisans were not permitted to use silver for their utensils.
Other regulations were the same as for commoners.
Collation Notes
Monograph Forty-Five: Examinations, Part One
There were four main methods of selection for office:
namely, schools (xuéxiào),
imperial examinations (kē mù),
recommendation (jiànjǔ),
and appointment by selection (quánxuǎn).
Schools were for education,
examinations for advancement,
recommendation for broad recruitment,
and selection for official deployment.
Through these, all talents of the realm were gathered.
Under the Míng system,
the imperial examinations were paramount,
with all ministers and grand secretaries emerging from them.
Schools served to cultivate talent for the imperial examinations.
Those who entered officialdom directly through schools
were also considered secondary to those who passed the examinations.
Beyond these were miscellaneous streams.
However, the three paths of *jìnshì*, *jǔgòng*, and miscellaneous streams were all used in parallel;
though one might be emphasized,
none were entirely abandoned.
Recommendation was prominent in the early days of the dynasty,
but later ceased due to the exclusive reliance on imperial examinations.
Appointment by selection was the beginning of entering officialdom;
without it, there was no other way.
These four methods are clearly and fully recorded from beginning to end,
and thus the reasons for the successes and failures in selecting scholars over the two hundred and seventy years can be seen.
To pass the imperial examinations (kējǔ) one had to go through schools (xuéxiào),
but one could establish a career from schools without necessarily passing the imperial examinations.
There were two types of schools:
the National Academy (Guóxué)
and the prefectural (fǔ), sub-prefectural (zhōu), and county (xiàn) schools. Students from prefectural, sub-prefectural, and county schools who entered the National Academy
could then obtain official positions;
those who did not enter could not.
Those who entered the National Academy
were generally called *jiānshēng*.
Those who passed the provincial examinations were called *jǔjiān*,
licensed scholars (*shēngyuán*) were called *gòngjiān*,
sons of officials were called *yìnnjiān*,
and those who donated money were called *lìjiān*.
Among *gòngjiān*,
there were *suìgòng* (annual tribute students),
there were *xuǎngòng* (selected tribute students),
there were *ēngòng* (grace tribute students),
and there were *nàgòng* (purchased tribute students).
Among *yìnjiān*,
there were *guānsheng* (official students),
and there were *ēnsheng* (grace students).
The establishment of the Guózǐxué began in the Yǐsì year of the early Míng dynasty.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, an edict commanded that sons of officials and bright, talented commoners proficient in literature
should all be enrolled as students.
More than ten individuals, including Guóqí and Wáng Pú, were selected
to attend to the Crown Prince's studies within the palace.
When they were summoned to the Jǐnshēndiàn to answer questions,
their demeanor was bright and clear,
and their replies were thorough and elegant.
Tàizǔ was pleased
and consequently bestowed generous gifts upon them.
After the realm was settled,
an imperial decree ordered the selection of students from prefectural, sub-prefectural, and county schools to enter the Guózǐxué.
Additionally, young Jǔrén like Zhào Wéiyī and Gòngshēng like Dǒng Mǒu were selected to study there.
They were given clothes and bedding
and ordered to first gain experience in clerical duties in various offices.
These were called Lìshì Jiānshēng.
The most intelligent and astute among them, such as Lǐ Kuò, were selected to narrate books in the Wénhuá and Wǔyīng Halls.
These were called Xiǎo Xiùcai.
Those whose talent and learning were superior, and who were intelligent and eminent,
were made to extensively read numerous books,
thoroughly explain the studies of morality and statecraft,
with the expectation of being greatly employed.
These were called Lǎo Xiùcai.
Initially,
the Yìngtiān Fǔxué was renamed Guózǐxué.
Later, it was rebuilt at the foot of Jīmíngshān.
Afterward, the school was changed to a Directorate (Jiān),
and officials such as Jìjiǔ, Sīyè, Jiānchéng, Bóshì, Zhùjiào, Xuézhèng, Xuélù, Diǎnjí, Zhǎngzhuàn, and Diǎnbù were established.
It was divided into six halls to accommodate the students:
namely, Shuàixìng, Xiūdào, Chéngxīn, Zhèngyì, Chóngzhì, and Guǎngyè.
Next to the school were quarters for students,
called Hàofáng.
They were generously provided with stipends,
and annually given cloth, silk, patterned brocade, and sets of clothing, caps, and shoes.
On New Year's Day, Lantern Festival, and other major festivals,
they were all awarded festival money.
Xiàocí Huánghòu accumulated grain in the Directorate,
establishing over twenty "Red Granaries" (Hóngcāng)
to support the wives and children of the students.
For Lìshìshēng who were unmarried,
money was granted for marriage proposals,
along with two sets of women's clothing
and two shí of rice monthly.
For students who had stayed in the capital for many years,
whose parents were alive,
or whose parents had passed away but grandparents or paternal uncles and aunts were alive,
they were all sent home to visit their relatives.
Each person was given a set of clothing
and five dìng of paper money
for travel expenses.
Such was the generosity and care shown to them.
As for the method of their instruction,
every morning,
the Jìjiǔ and Sīyè would sit in the hall,
with subordinate officials from the Jiānchéng downwards,
and the chief official, the Diǎnbù,
standing in order.
After the students bowed,
they were questioned on the Classics and Histories,
standing with folded hands awaiting instructions.
Only on the first and fifteenth of the month were holidays granted.
On other days, they ascended the hall for communal meals,
then held group discussions, repeated lectures, and recited texts,
taking turns with lessons as a regular practice.
What they studied, in addition to the Four Books and the principal classics,
also included Liú Xiàng's Shuōyuàn, as well as laws, statutes, calligraphy, mathematics, and the Imperial Proclamations (Yùzhì Dàgào).
Each month, they were tested on one topic from the classics and one from literary meaning,
and two topics from edicts, proclamations, memorials, policy essays, judgments, and internal examinations.
Daily, they practiced writing over two hundred characters,
using the models of the calligraphers the Two Wángs, Zhì Yǒng, Ōu, Yú, Yán, and Liǔ.
In each class, one person was selected as Zhāizhǎng
to supervise the students' studies.
Their attire, gait, and eating habits
had to be strictly corrected to be in moderation.
At night, they had to stay in the Directorate.
If they had a reason to go out, they had to inform their class's instructor,
who would then order the Zhāizhǎng to lead them to report to the Jìjiǔ.
The Jiānchéng kept a register of transgressions.
Those who did not comply were recorded.
Those who offended repeatedly were flogged.
Those who offended four times were even dismissed and banished.
The regulations and rules of the school
were repeatedly revised,
achieving a balance between leniency and strictness.
There were prohibitions regarding halls and dormitories,
dining and bathing.
For visiting relatives or returning home after marriage,
deadlines were set based on the distance.
Those who exceeded the deadline were demoted to serve as Diǎnshǐ in distant places,
and some were punished by being made clerks.
Officials responsible for instruction
had to be selected from among experienced elders.
Sòng Nà and Wú Yǒng were promoted from Confucian scholars to Jìjiǔ,
with Nà especially highly regarded as a renowned teacher.
Many Jinshì of successive examinations came from the Tàixué,
and in the Wùchén year, Rèn Héngtài ranked first in the palace examination.
Tàizǔ summoned Nà, praised and rewarded him,
commissioned a commemorative inscription,
and erected a stone tablet at the Directorate gate.
In the Xīnwèi year, Xǔ Guān
also received similar honors.
From then on, the Jinshì inscription tablets continued without interruption.
Each year, the Ànchásī across the realm selected Xīwènyuán aged twenty or above, who were steady and refined,
to be sent to the Directorate for assessment and retention.
Jǔrén who failed the Metropolitan Examination
entered the Directorate to complete their studies.
Furthermore, due to a memorial by Censor Guān Xián,
this was established as a fixed rule.
Prefectural, sub-prefectural, and county schools each annually contributed one Xīwènyuán.
The Hànlín Academy tested them on one topic from the classics, one from literary meaning,
and one legal judgment.
Those who passed were categorized: first-class entered the Guózǐjiān,
second-class were sent to Zhōngdū,
and those who failed were sent back.
The supervising instructors were penalized by having their stipends suspended.
Consequently, scholars from all directly administered provinces gathered at the capital.
Yúnnán and Sìchuān both had indigenous official students.
Japan, Ryukyu, and Siam also had official students who entered the Directorate to study.
They were invariably given generous gifts,
and their attendants were also provided for.
Between the Yǒnglè and Xuāndé eras,
they arrived one after another.
By the Chénghuà and Zhèngdé periods,
Ryukyuan students were still arriving.
The establishment of the national school in Zhōngdū
began in the eighth year of Hóngwǔ.
It was abolished in the twenty-sixth year,
and its teachers and students were all transferred to the capital.
In the first year of Yǒnglè, the Běijīng Guózǐjiān was first established.
In the eighteenth year, when the capital was relocated,
the capital's Guózǐjiān became the Nánjīng Guózǐjiān,
and thus the Tàixué students were divided into northern and southern directorates.
Tàizǔ, concerned that sons of military officials only learned military matters
and rarely pursued scholarship,
ordered the Dà Dūdū Fǔ to select them for the Guóxué.
Those in Fèngyáng immediately studied in Zhōngdū.
He ordered Hán Guógōng Lǐ Shàncháng and others to assess and determine the ranking of instructors and students,
dividing them into classes.
Cáo Guógōng Lǐ Wénzhōng oversaw the Directorate affairs to maintain discipline.
Thereafter, many sons of meritorious officials entered the Directorate to study.
In the first year of Jiājìng, Dukes, Marquises, and Earls who had not yet held office and were under thirty years old
were ordered to be sent to the Directorate to study.
Soon after, those who had already held office were also ordered to be sent,
and young meritorious relatives vied to enroll, considering it an honor.
The students of the six halls had a system of accumulating points.
The two Sīyè were divided into left and right,
each supervising three halls.
All who had mastered the Four Books but not yet the Classics
resided in Zhèngyì, Chóngzhì, and Guǎngyè.
After a year and a half or more,
those whose writing and reasoning were clear and articulate
were promoted to Xiūdào and Chéngxīn.
After another year and a half,
those proficient in both Classics and Histories, and excellent in both writing and reasoning,
were promoted to Shuàixìng.
Upon promotion to Shuàixìng,
points were accumulated.
The method was:
in the first month of each season, one essay on the meaning of the main classic was tested;
in the middle month, one essay on论 (lùn) was tested,
and one topic from edicts, proclamations, memorials, or internal examinations;
in the last month, one policy essay on classics and history was tested,
and two legal judgments.
For each test,
those excellent in both writing and reasoning received one point;
those excellent in reasoning but weak in writing received half a point;
and those with errors received no points.
Those who accumulated eight points within the year were considered qualified
and granted an official appointment.
Those who failed continued to study in the halls.
If there were exceptionally talented and learned individuals,
a memorial was submitted to the emperor for his decision.

In the twenty-sixth year of Hóngwǔ, all sixty-four Jiānshēng, including Liú Zhèng and Lóng Tán, were promoted to various official positions such as Bùzhèng and Ànchá envoys of provincial administrations,
and Cāncóng, Cānyì, Fùshǐ, and Qiānshì.
Such was the great importance placed on their employment at once.
The number of those who became high officials in various regions
was countless.
Lǐ Kuò and others were promoted from Wénhuá and Wǔyīng to Yùshǐ.
Kuò was later transferred to Gěishìzhōng and concurrently a clerk in the Qíxiàng Fǔ.
Indeed, selections for the Censorate and remonstrance officials also came from the Tàixué.
Those in regular appointments became officials of the sixth rank or below in prefectures, sub-prefectures, and counties.
Initially,
due to the chaos and destruction in the north,
few people were knowledgeable in scholarship.
Therefore, 366 *Guózǐshēng* (students of the Imperial Academy) including Lín Bóyún were dispatched to various commanderies to teach.
Later, this practice was extended to other provinces,
and those who were robust and skilled in writing were selected to serve as *jiàoyù* (instructors) and other officials.
Although Tàizǔ occasionally held imperial examinations,
most of the officials were a mix of *jiānsheng* (Imperial Academy students) and those recommended by others.
Hence, at that time, among those serving both inside and outside the capital,
*tàixuéshēng* (Imperial Academy students) were the most prominent.
After one or two generations,
the *jìnshì* (presented scholar) degree became increasingly important,
and the recommendation system was abolished.
Consequently, the *jǔ* (recommended scholar) and *gòng* (tribute student) statuses became increasingly diminished in prestige.
Although the system of accumulating points and gaining experience did not change from its initial method,
the Northern and Southern *Jìjiǔ* (Libationers) Chén Jìngzōng and Lǐ Shímǐan made great efforts to revive and rectify it,
but it gradually failed to live up to its beginning.
The general trend of public sentiment
was exclusively towards the *jiǎkē* (first class of the imperial examination).
Career advancement and decline
were determined on the day of the selection audience.
If *jiānsheng* could not achieve the highest rank,
even if they spurred themselves on with great effort,
they could not succeed.
Such was the momentum of this entrenched system.
When the precedent of "donating grain for status" (*nàsù*) was opened,
the social stratification gradually became confused.
Moreover, commoners could also use the precedent of *shēngyuán* (licentiates) to enter the Imperial Academy,
being called *mínshēng* (commoner students),
or *jùnxiù* (talented and outstanding individuals),
and the status of *jiānsheng* became even more diminished.
Thus, while residing in the same Imperial Academy,
*jǔ* and *gòng* students could become assistant officials of prefectures or regular officials of departments and counties;
*guānshēng* (official students) and *ēnshēng* (favored students) could be selected for minor capital positions in ministries, courts, prefectures, guards, bureaus, and temples,
which was still considered a legitimate career path.
However, *jiānsheng* who entered by precedent
could only be selected as assistant officials of departments and counties or chief officials of prefectures;
those assigned to capital positions
belonged to the *Guānglùsì* (Court of Imperial Entertainments) or *Shànglínyuàn* (Imperial Parks);
those who wished to go to distant places
were appointed as chief officials of military garrisons in Yúnnán, Guìzhōu, Guǎngxī, and various border provinces,
as well as vacancies for *wèixué* (garrison schools) and *wángfǔ jiàoshòu* (princely tutors),
and would remain on an irregular career path for life.
The entry of *jǔrén* (recommended men) into the Imperial Academy
began in the mid-Yǒnglè reign.
Those who failed the metropolitan examination
were often ordered by the *Hànlín Yuàn* (Hanlin Academy) to record their outstanding individuals,
allowing them to enter the Academy to await a later examination,
and they were given the salary of a *jiàoyù*.
At that time,
the metropolitan examination had a *fùbǎng* (supplementary list),
most of whom were appointed as *jiàoguān* (educational officials),
hence those ordered to enter the Academy also received this salary.
In the eighth year of Xuāndé, the Minister of Rites, Hú Yíng, along with Grand Secretaries Yáng Shìqí and Yáng Róng, were ordered to select 24 *jǔrén* from the *fùbǎng*, including Lóng Wén,
and send them to the Academy for advanced studies.
The *Hànlín Yuàn* assessed their writings every three months,
the same as *shùjíshì* (probationary Hanlin bachelors),
which showed considerable distinction.
Later, no separate examinations were held;
instead, *fùbǎng* members aged 25 or older were appointed to teaching positions,
while those younger
either relied on their relatives
or entered the Academy to study.
Subsequently, age was no longer a restriction,
and both relying on relatives and entering the Academy were permitted.
Those who relied on relatives
returned to their hometowns to study,
relying on their families to pursue their studies.
There were also cases of mourning for parents, marriage, visiting parents, and escorting young children,
all following the precedent of relying on relatives,
with a time limit for returning to class.
During the Zhèngtǒng reign,
there was a shortage of educational officials nationwide,
but *jǔrén* disliked their lowly and undesirable positions,
many being unwilling to take them.
In the thirteenth year,
Censor Wàn Jié requested an imperial decree for the Ministry of Rites to select more *fùbǎng* members
for teaching positions.
The ministerial officials stated that seven out of ten *jǔrén* wished to rely on relatives and enter the Academy,
while only three out of ten wished to take teaching positions.
They suggested that each should follow their own desire,
and thus rejected the request.
By the thirteenth year of Chénghuà,
Censor Hú Lín stated:
"Most educational officials nationwide are *suìgòng* (annual tribute students),
whose words, conduct, and writings are insufficient to serve as exemplars.
I request that more *jǔrén* be selected and appointed,
