and that *gòngshēng* (tribute students) be no longer selected."
The ministry deliberated and maintained the *suìgòng* system as before,
while *jǔrén* educational officials were still permitted to participate in the metropolitan examination.
From then on, those who took up teaching positions gradually increased.
During the Jiājìng reign,
both the Northern and Southern National Academies were empty.
It was proposed that all *jǔrén* who failed the examination should be sent to the Academy,
and a deadline be set to urge them.
However, *jǔrén* who were unwilling to enter the Academy
could not ultimately be forced.
Therefore, besides *shēngyuán* and *suìgòng*,
it became necessary to frequently hold *xuǎngòng* (selected tribute) examinations to fill the National Academies.
The entry of *gòngshēng* into the Academy
was initially determined by the selection of *shēngyuán*.
Later, each school was ordered to send one *gòng* student annually,
hence they were called *suìgòng*.
This system also underwent several changes.
In the twenty-first year of Hóngwǔ, it was stipulated that prefectural, departmental, and county schools would rotate every one, two, or three years.
In the twenty-fifth year, it was stipulated that prefectural schools would send two annually,
departmental schools three every two years,
and county schools one annually.
In the eighth year of Yǒnglè, it was stipulated that for departments and counties with fewer than five *lǐ* (households),
departments would send one annually,
and counties one every other year.
In the nineteenth year, the *suìgòng* system was ordered to follow the Hóngwǔ twenty-first year precedent.
In the seventh year of Xuāndé, it reverted to the Hóngwǔ twenty-fifth year precedent.
In the sixth year of Zhèngtǒng, it was revised again: one from prefectural schools annually,
two from departmental schools every three years,
and one from county schools every other year.
During the Hóngzhì and Jiājìng reigns,
it was again stipulated that prefectural schools send two annually,
departmental schools three every two years,
and county schools one annually,
which became a permanent system.
Later, for the three clans of Kǒng, Yán, and Mèng,
as well as capital schools, garrison schools, regional military commissions, native officials,
and the distant provinces of Sìchuān, Yúnnán, and Guìzhōu,
the annual tribute method
also saw occasional increases or decreases.
At the beginning of the *suìgòng* system,
candidates had to be assessed for upright conduct and superior literary understanding to be selected.
Later, only those who had received stipends for many years were chosen.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
Nánjīng *Jìjiǔ* Zhāng Mào stated:
"During the Hóngwǔ and Yǒnglè reigns,
students of the Imperial Academy numbered in the thousands.
Now, only over 600 *kēgòng* (tribute students who took examinations) remain in the Academy.
*Suìgòng* are promoted in sequence,
and eight or nine out of ten are infirm and uninspired.
*Jǔrén* residing in the Academy
are also often behind schedule.
There are not enough assigned,
and their education yields little effect.
In recent years, there has been an initiative to increase the number of tribute students,
but those selected are also individuals in sequence,
constrained by qualifications,
and many talented individuals are held back.
I request that, in addition to the regular tribute students, the *Tíxué* (Education Intendant) implements a *xuǎngòng* system,
without distinguishing between *lǐnshàn* (stipendiary) and *zēngguǎng shēngyuán* (increased quota licentiates),
conducting general examinations,
to earnestly seek those who excel in both conduct and scholarship, are young and vigorous, and have repeatedly achieved superior grades,
to fill the tribute quota.
In total, across the vastness of the empire,
approximately five to six hundred people should be selected.
If this is done every three to five years,
then talent can gradually return to former years."
This was then submitted to the ministry for deliberation and implementation.
This is how *xuǎngòng* began.
*Xuǎngòng* were mostly talented individuals; upon entering the Academy, they often achieved superior grades in lessons and examinations,
and those assigned to various bureaus also demonstrated capability.
*Suìgòng* grew old and declined,
their standing diminished day by day,
so they only wished to take teaching positions and not enter the Academy.
In the twenty-seventh year of Jiājìng,
*Jìjiǔ* Chéng Wéndé requested that among the *suìgòng* taking the court examination, only those immediately selected be kept at the ministry,
while all others be sent to the Academy.
This was approved.
The *suìgòng* students collectively submitted a memorial stating
that their families were poor and their parents old,
and they did not wish to enter the Academy.
The Ministry of Rites again requested to comply with their wishes
and instead send all *jǔrén* to the Academy.
This was also approved.
*Jǔrén* were unable to enter the Academy on time,
and Nánjīng *Jìjiǔ* Pān Shèng even requested severe penalties to compel their attendance.
Thus, the three categories of *jǔrén*, *xuǎngòng*, and *suìgòng* alternately flourished and declined,
and the fullness or emptiness of the National Academies
was never constant.
During the Wànlì reign,
Gāo Rúxīn of the Ministry of Works stated:
"*Xuǎngòng* is not an ancestral system.
It was initially intended to supplement the deficiency of *suìgòng*,
but later it obstructed the path of *suìgòng*.
I request its abolition."
Shénzōng considered this to be true.
By the Chóngzhēn reign,
it was practiced again.
*Ēngòng* (special tribute students) were those selected when the state had celebratory events or imperial edicts upon an emperor's enthronement.
They were considered immediately below *suìgòng*.
The *nàgòng* (donated tribute students) were slightly better than the *lìjiān* (by-precedent *jiānsheng*),
but in reality, they were similar.
The entry of [Yìnzi]荫子 into the Guózǐjiān国子监.
In the early Míng明 dynasty, due to the previous dynasty's system of [Rènzǐ]任子,
civil officials of the first to seventh ranks
were all permitted to nominate one son ([yìn yī zǐ]荫一子) to inherit their emoluments.
Later, this was gradually restricted,
so that only officials of the third rank and above in the capital could request such a nomination,
and these were called [Guānsheng]官生.
Those who entered through special imperial grace,
regardless of official rank,
were called [Ēnsheng]恩生.
Some were immediately granted official positions,
while others were sent to the Guózǐjiān国子监 to study.
[Guānsheng]官生 had to be sons of third-rank capital officials,
a rule established in the third year of Chénghuà成化 (1467) following the suggestion of Assistant Instructor [Lǐ Shēn]李伸.
At the time, Supervising Secretary [Lǐ Sēn]李森 opposed it.
The Emperor issued an edict,
reprimanding him for being harsh;
it merely stipulated that only those who had served for a long time and had outstanding administrative achievements
should not be subject to abuse (of this privilege).
Once nominated,
they were examined by the education commissioner and sent for a departmental examination,
similar to the system for [Gòngsheng]贡生,
and then admitted into the Guózǐjiān国子监.
At that time, [Lǚ Yuánzǐ]吕原子, a [Yìnjiān]荫监 student from the Grand Secretariat, was appointed a Secretary of the Central Secretariat,
and in the seventh year, [Xīnmǎo]辛卯 (1471), he requested to take the Shùntiān顺天 provincial examination.
The Board (of Rites) requested that this be permitted.
Supervising Secretary [Ruì Jī]芮畿 opposed it.
The Emperor granted [Lǚ]吕's request,
but stipulated it should not set a precedent.
However, subsequently,
those appointed as Secretaries through the [Yìn]荫 system
were all permitted to take the examinations.
After the Jiā嘉 and Lóng隆 eras,
some sons of Grand Secretaries were initially appointed as Assistant Ministers of the Imperial Seal Office,
then directly promoted to Vice Minister of that same office,
and advanced through the Guānglù寺 (Court of Imperial Entertainments) and Tàicháng寺 (Court of Imperial Sacrifices) to positions among the Nine Senior Officials.
There were also those who, through military merit, were nominated to the Imperial Bodyguard,
often bypassing the Imperial Academy.
Others were all admitted into the Guózǐjiān国子监.
The origin of [Ēnsheng]恩生 dates back to
the first year of Jiànwén建文 (1399), when [Wú Yún]吴云’s son, [Wú Fǔ]吴黼, was enrolled as a Guózǐjiān国子监 student,
because [Wú Yún]吴云 had died a martyr in Yúnnán云南.
In the sixteenth year of Zhèngdé正德 (1521), a regulation was established
that for all civil and military officials who died in loyal remonstrance,
one son would be admitted to the Guózǐjiān国子监.
Subsequently, frontier officials who died as martyrs also obtained the right to nominate a son.
Moreover, in the eighteenth year of Hóngzhì弘治 (1505), a regulation was established
that for attendants to the Crown Prince [Dōnggōng]东宫,
who had served for many years in lecturing and assisting with merit,
after their death,
if their sons and grandsons sought imperial grace,
the Ministry of Rites would memorialize and request the Emperor's decision.
In the first year of Zhèngdé正德 (1506), it was further stipulated
that if their grandfathers or fathers had served for three years,
one son would be immediately appointed as a probationary Secretary of the Central Secretariat to practice calligraphy;
if they had not served for three years,
one son would be sent to the Guózǐjiān国子监 to study.
In the eighth year (1513), it was further stipulated
that for officials attending the Crown Prince for three years,
one son would be admitted to the Guózǐjiān国子监.
Also, in the twelfth year of Wànlì万历 (1584), a regulation was established
that a third-rank lecturer ([rìjiǎngguān]日讲官),
even if his probationary period was not complete,
could have one son admitted to the Guózǐjiān国子监.
The [Lìjiān]例监 (regular students admitted through specific criteria) system began in the first year of Jǐngtài景泰 (1450),
due to the urgent border situation.
It ordered people nationwide who offered grain or horses to be admitted to the Guózǐjiān国子监 for study,
limited to one thousand people.
It was in effect for four years and then abolished.
In the second year of Chénghuà成化 (1466),
Nánjīng南京 suffered a great famine,
and the local officials suggested
that officials, military personnel, and commoners' sons and grandsons should offer grain to be admitted to the Guózǐjiān国子监.
Minister of Rites [Yáo Kuí]姚夔 said:
"The Imperial Academy is a place for nurturing talent.
Recently, the directly administered provinces have sent students over forty years old,
and those offering hay and horses number tens of thousands,
an unbearable excess.
Moreover, it would cause the world to value wealth over merit,
and the scholarly ethos would decline daily."
The Emperor agreed,
and rejected the local officials' proposal.
However, subsequently, whether in times of famine,
or due to border alarms,
or for large-scale construction projects,
this practice was often resumed by citing past precedents,
and ultimately could not be stopped.
These are the general origins and developments of the various types of Guózǐjiān国子监 students: [Jǔ]举 (recommended), [Gòng]贡 (tribute), [Yìn]荫 (nominated), and [Lì]例 (regular).
The system of Guózǐjiān国子监 students undertaking practical service began in the fifth year of Hóngwǔ洪武 (1372).
During the Jiànwén建文 era,
a system of assessment was established, divided into three grades: superior, medium, and inferior.
Those in the superior grade were selected for appointment,
while those in the medium and inferior grades had to serve another year and be re-assessed.
Those of superior grade were employed according to that grade,
those of medium grade were not restricted by rank
and were appointed according to their talents,
and those of inferior grade returned to the Guózǐjiān国子监 to study.
In the fifth year of Yǒnglè永乐 (1407), thirty-eight Guózǐjiān国子监 students were selected to be assigned to the Hànlín Yuàn翰林院
to practice translating texts from the four barbarian tribes.
In the ninth year, [Xīnmǎo]辛卯 (1411), [Zhōng Yīng]钟英 and five others passed the imperial examination,
all being appointed as probationary Hanlin academicians ([Shùjíshì]庶吉士).
After the [Rénchén]壬辰 (1412) and [Yǐwèi]乙未 (1415) examinations,
many of those involved in translation passed the metropolitan examinations,
and it became customary for them to be appointed as [Shùjíshì]庶吉士.
Students undertaking practical service became famous,
and the imperial favor they received was thus.
At the beginning of Rénzōng's仁宗 reign,
the Central Military Command presented a memorial stating that seven Guózǐjiān国子监 students had been diligent and careful in their official duties,
and requested that they be selected and appointed to official positions.
The Emperor did not permit it,
and instead ordered them to return to the academy
and advance through the imperial examinations.
Many other students undertaking practical service
were unwilling to return to the Guózǐjiān国子监.
So the Grand Court of Revision presented a memorial,
stating that twenty Guózǐjiān国子监 students working in the Six Offices of Scrutiny, upon completing their term,
were supposed to return to the Guózǐjiān国子监,
but wished to continue working in the offices.
The Emperor summoned these twenty people again,
and instructed them to return to their studies.
This was because at that time,
there were many vacancies for Supervising Secretaries in the Six Offices of Scrutiny,
and these students coveted those positions.
The Emperor perceived their intentions,
and therefore did not grant them official positions.
Xuānzōng宣宗, due to many vacancies for educational officials,
selected and employed three hundred and eighty Guózǐjiān国子监 students.
And [Chéng Fù]程富 and others, recommended by Censor-in-Chief [Gù Zuǒ]顾佐,
were sent to various circuits to serve for three months,
and then selected for appointment,
known as probationary censors ([shìyùshǐ]试御史).
The assignment of Guózǐjiān国子监 students to practical service
was initially based on the chronological order of their admission to the Guózǐjiān国子监.
For mourning a parent or attending ancestral sacrifices,
some would remain at home for seven or eight years,
and when they finally entered the Guózǐjiān国子监,
they would immediately be assigned.
[Chén Jìngzōng]陈敬宗 and [Lǐ Shímiǎn]李时勉 successively memorialized,
suggesting that the time spent physically in the Guózǐjiān国子监 should determine precedence.
Subsequently, the time spent caring for parents, managing capital storehouses, living with relatives, attending school, and being at home
was also counted as time spent in the academy.
Only sick leave and other accidents
were then considered as vacant periods.
Students disputed their seniority based on years and months,
each citing regulations.
In the fifth year of Chénghuà成化 (1469),
Libationer [Chén Jiàn]陈鉴 submitted two memorials fully explaining the situation,
requesting an imperial decree for the Ministry of Rites to deliberate and establish a moderate regulation,
but this was rejected by the Office of Scrutiny for Rites.
[Chén Jiàn]陈鉴 again memorialized,
arguing back and forth.
It was then sent to the Ministry for re-deliberation,
which requested meticulous verification of each case,
still considering the geographical distance, and the number of days of water travel as a standard.
However, the back-and-forth of official documents
was chaotic and cumbersome,
with arbitrary adjustments up and down,
leading to many abuses,
and ultimately no unified standard could be achieved.
Initially, Guózǐjiān国子监 students were ordered to advance from [Guǎngyè]广业 (Broad Industry) to [Shuàixìng]率性 (Following Nature) colleges
before they could accumulate points for official appointments.
Before Tiānshùn天顺 (1457-1464),
after more than ten years in the Guózǐjiān国子jian,
they were then assigned to various departments for practical service.
After three months of service,
they would remain for another year,
and then be sent to the Ministry of Personnel for selection.
Those who cleared the yellow registers for the Ministry of War or accompanied censors on tours
were subject to a three-year term.
Subsequently,
because many Guózǐjiān国子jian students were held up,
the time for assignment to practical service was frequently reduced to expedite the process.
Each year, during selection,
the outstanding ones were immediately assigned to practical service,
some even before completing a year.
In the eighth year of Hóngzhì,
the number of *jiànshēng* (Imperial College students) in residence was small,
but the Board of Civil Office (Lìbù) heard that over ten thousand people were awaiting selection,
some of whom had not obtained an official position for over ten years.
The Libationer (Jìjiǔ) Lín Hàn, seeing that few students were regularly attending,
and thus insufficient to be assigned to various duties,
requested that *kēgòng* (imperial examinations and selection) be opened.
Ní Yuè, the Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū), reported back in a memorial, saying,
“The quota for *kējǔ* (imperial examinations) is already fixed,
and cannot be increased.
However, I request an increase in the number of *suìgòng* (annual tribute students),
and that the various departments' assignments (*lìshì*) be regulated,
requiring that only after the full period of months and days is complete
can there be a rotation,
so that students remain in the Imperial College for a slightly longer period,
and the selection of officials will also not be stalled.”
By the tenth year of Jiājìng,
the *jiànshēng* in residence numbered fewer than four hundred,
while the annual quota for various departments’ assignments was in the thousands.
Lǐ Shí, the Minister of Rites, cited Ní Yuè’s previous proposal, saying:
“Yuè’s two expedient methods
were: first, to increase the annual quota to ensure sufficient students for regular attendance,
and second, to propose longer periods for assigned duties to ensure students remained for a longer time.
Thus, for prefectural, subprefectural, and county schools, the system of 'two tributes in one year, three tributes in two years, and one tribute in one year' was implemented as a difference,
and was carried out for four years before stopping.
As for the various departments’ assigned duties,
after three months of attendance evaluation,
another year of duty followed;
the remainder, such as document copying, was one year;
*qīnghuáng*, *xiěgào*, *qīngjūn*, and *qīngjiàng* were three years;
and assignments like imperial tours,
all followed the old regulations regarding days and months.
Now, the Imperial Academy (Guóxué) is even more short of people
than during the Hóngzhì period.
I request that the precedents mentioned above
be deliberated and implemented.”
This was generally followed,
but the tribute quota was not increased.
Not long after,
following requests from Libationer Xǔ Gào and Education Censor Hú Shíshàn,
an imperial edict increased the tribute quota,
as Ní Yuè and Lǐ Shí had previously proposed.
After the Lóngqìng and Wànlì reigns,
schools gradually declined,
and everything simply followed old practices.
In the second year of Chóngzhēn, following the advice of Vice-Libationer (Sīyè) Ní Jiāshàn,
the point system was reinstated.
In the eighth year, following the advice of Libationer Ní Yuánlù,
selection by tribute was designated as the main channel,
and selection by contribution (i.e., purchase of a student status) as a supplementary channel.
For selection by tribute, there was no limit on the assignment period,
with completion of the required points as the standard;
for selection by contribution, the original fixed assignment period was the standard.
Assigned duties were not divided into "main" and "miscellaneous,"
but rather the duration of the duty period was determined by the evaluation grade.
The various departments' duties for students
were not to be confused with common miscellaneous assignments.
Upon completion of the period,
their diligence and idleness were assessed,
and reported to the Board of Civil Office.
Those who failed to comply
were sent back to the Imperial College for further instruction.
At this time, the regulations of the Imperial College had long been decadent,
and could not be invigorated.
The *jiànshēng* assigned to various duties included:
Board of Civil Office, forty-one;
Board of Revenue (Hùbù), fifty-three;
Board of Rites, thirteen;
Grand Court of Revision (Dàlǐ Sì), twenty-eight;
Office of Transmission (Tōngzhèng Sī), five;
Office of Scrutiny for Personnel (Xíngrén Sī), four;
Five Chief Military Commissions (Wǔjūn Dūdū Fǔ), fifty;
these were called "main duties" (*zhènglì*).
The best among them were selected after three months,
with the number increasing or decreasing at the end of the period.
There were also document copying assignments for various departments:
Board of Revenue, ten;
Board of Rites, eighteen;
Board of War (Bīngbù), twenty;
Board of Punishments (Xíngbù), fourteen;
Board of Works (Gōngbù), eight;
Censorate (Dūchá Yuàn), fourteen;
Grand Court of Revision and Office of Transmission, four each;
accompanying Censors on tours, forty-two;
these were called "miscellaneous duties" (*zálì*).
The best among them were selected after one year.
There were also various general service assignments:
*qīnghuáng*, one hundred;
*xiěgào*, forty;
*xùhuáng*, fifty;
*qīngjūn*, forty;
Treasury of Heavenly Resources (Tiāncáikù), ten;
initially these were called "long assignments" (three years),
but later changed to one year for selection;
Treasury of Imperial Provision (Chéngyùnkù), fifteen;
Directorate of Ceremonial (Sīlǐ Jiān), sixteen;
Seal Office (Shàngbǎo Sī), six;
Six Offices of Scrutiny (Liù Kē), forty;
initially these were "short assignments,"
but later also fixed at one year for selection.
There were also those who accompanied Censors to review documents, one hundred seventy-eight;
Board of Works, *qīngjiàng*, sixty;
all were selected upon completion of their tasks.
There were also Board of Rites, *xiě mínqíng tiáolì*, seventy-two;
Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Guānglù Sì), document review, four;
ritual preparation, eight;
participating in memorials, twenty;
reporting訃 (obituaries), twenty;
distributing stipends, twelve;
Embroidered Uniform Guard (Jǐnyī Wèi), four;
Board of War, checking horse registers, thirty;
Board of Works, Timber Factory (Dàmùchǎng), twenty;
Rear Palace Bureau, accounting, ten;
Directorate of Imperial Stables (Yùmǎ Jiān), four;
Treasury of Heavenly Resources, four;
Zhèngyángmén, four;
Chóngwén, Xuānwǔ, Cháoyáng, and Dōngzhí gates, three each;
Fùchéng, Xīzhí, Āndìng, and Déshèng gates, two each;
these returned to the Imperial College after six months.
The schools of the commanderies and counties
were linked with the Imperial Academy (Tàixué),
their establishment began in the Táng dynasty.
The Sòng dynasty set up school officials in various circuits and prefectures,
and the Yuán dynasty largely followed this,
but their methods were not fully developed.
Until the Míng dynasty,
all prefectures, subprefectures, counties, and garrisons throughout the realm
established Confucian schools,
with over four thousand two hundred teaching officials,
and countless students.
The methods of teaching and nurturing were comprehensive.
In the second year of Hóngwǔ,
Emperor Tàizǔ first established the National Academy (Guóxué),
and issued an edict to the ministers of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shěng), saying:
“The abuses of school education
reached their extreme in the Yuán dynasty.
Between the upper and lower classes,
it was a tide of collapse and a gust of decline;
although schools were established,
they existed in name only.
Since the military uprisings,
people have practiced warfare,
knowing only weapons,
and ignorant of ritual vessels.
I believe that to govern the state, education and transformation must come first,
and for education and transformation, schools are fundamental.
Although there is an Imperial Academy in the capital,
schools throughout the realm have not yet flourished.
It is fitting to order all commanderies and counties to establish schools,
invite scholar-teachers,
instruct students,
and discuss the sagely Way,
so that people may gradually be transformed day by day and month by month,
to restore the traditions of the former kings.”
Thus, schools were extensively established:
prefectures had one Professor (Jiàoshòu),
subprefectures had one Director of Studies (Xuézhèng),
and counties had one Instructor (Jiàoyù),
each.
All had Tutors (Xùndǎo):
four for prefectures,
three for subprefectures,
and two for counties.
The number of students (*shēngyuán*) was:
forty for prefectural schools,
with subprefectural and county schools decreasing by ten in sequence.
Teachers and students received monthly stipends of grain,
six *dǒu* per person,
and local officials provided fish and meat.
School officials received varying monthly salaries.
Students specialized in one classic,
and were taught in subjects like ritual, music, archery, charioteering, calligraphy, and arithmetic.
Emphasis was placed on finding true talent,
and the stubborn and disobedient were expelled.
In the fifteenth year, school regulations were promulgated at the Directorate of Education (Guózǐ Jiān),
and twelve prohibitive articles were also promulgated throughout the realm,
engraved and erected on a stone tablet (wòbēi),
placed to the left of the Mínglún Táng (Hall of Human Relations).
Those who did not obey
were judged as violating regulations.
Indeed, there was no place without a school established,
and no person whom education did not reach.
The sounds of the *xiáng* (elementary schools) and the music of the *xù* (higher schools)
adhered strictly to rules and order,
without distinction between remote villages and distant frontiers,
mountain corners and sea shores.
This was the flourishing state of Míng dynasty schools,
unmatched by the Táng and Sòng dynasties.
Although the number of *shēngyuán* was fixed at the beginning of the dynasty,
it was not long before an order was given to increase their number (增廣, *zēngguǎng*),
without limitation.
During the Xuāndé reign,
the quota for *zēngguǎng* was set: sixty individuals for prefectural schools in the capital,
forty individuals for prefectural schools outside the capital,
and state and county schools reduced by ten in sequence.
During the Chénghuà reign,
regulations for military schools (衞學, *wèixué*) were established: eighty military students (*jūnshēng*) for four *wèi* and above,
sixty military students for three *wèi* and above,
forty military students for two *wèi* or one *wèi*,
and twenty military students for *yǒusī* Confucian schools.
Children of indigenous officials (*tǔguān*)
were permitted to enter nearby Confucian schools,
without a fixed quota.
As the number of *zēngguǎng* increased,
those initially provided with stipends were called *lǐnshàn shēngyuán*,
while the *zēngguǎng* were called *zēngguǎng shēngyuán*.
After a long time,
as talent grew even more abundant,
additional students were admitted beyond the quota,
attached to the end of the ranks of *zhūshēng*,
and called *fùxué shēngyuán*.
All those who initially entered school
were simply called *fùxué*,
while *lǐnshàn* and *zēngguǎng*
were filled by those who ranked higher in the biennial (*suìkē*) examinations.
Those who were not *lǐnshēng* for a long time were
not permitted to serve as *suìgòng*.
Scholars who had not yet entered school
were generally called *tóngshēng*.
During the year of the grand triennial examination (*dàbǐ*),
one or two exceptionally bright individuals were occasionally admitted,
who passed all three rounds,
allowing them to enter the examination hall together with the *zhūshēng*,
and were called *chōngchǎng rúshì*.
If they passed, they became *jǔrén*;
if they failed, they still had to await the *tíxuéguān*'s annual examination (*suìshì*),
and if they qualified,
they were then permitted to enter school.
The *tíxuéguān* served for three years
and examined the *zhūshēng* twice.
First, they assessed the merits and demerits of *zhūshēng* in six ranks,
which was called the annual assessment (*suìkǎo*).
Those at the top of the first rank,
if there were vacancies among the *lǐnshàn shēng*,
were sequentially promoted to fill them,
and the next in rank filled *zēngguǎng shēng* positions.
Those in the first and second ranks were all given rewards,
the third rank remained as normal,
the fourth rank received corporal punishment,
the fifth rank caused *lǐn* and *zēng* students to be demoted by one rank,
and *fùshēng* to be demoted to *qīngyī*;
the sixth rank resulted in expulsion.
Next, those in the first and second ranks were selected as *kējǔ shēngyuán*,
to take the provincial examination (*xiāngshì*),
which was called the examination for degrees (*kēkǎo*).
The appointments to *lǐn* and *zēng* and the awards
were all the same as for the *suìshì*.
The ranks were still divided into six,
but generally, many were placed in the third rank.
Those in the third rank could not take the *xiāngshì*,
and those who were flogged or expelled were merely one in a hundred,
or even none at all.
For scholar-students taking examinations,
for every *jǔrén*,
the rate was thirty *kējǔ* students.
As the quota for *jǔrén* was repeatedly expanded,
the number of *kējǔ* also increased daily.
When the number of those seeking *jǔrén* status increased,
additional candidates were often taken beyond the fixed quota,
to win the hearts of scholars.
All education supervisors acted similarly.
In the tenth year of the Jiājìng reign, an order was issued to reduce the number of *shēngyuán*,
but Censor Yáng Yí protested, and it was stopped.
During the Wànlì reign,
when Zhāng Jūzhèng was in power,
he thoroughly reduced the number of *shēngyuán* nationwide.
The education supervisors carried out the order excessively,
such that when *tóngshēng* entered school,
some prefectures or counties admitted only one person;
the reduction in *kējǔ* can be inferred from this.
Initially, *shēngyuán* were admitted to school by the Circuit Censor (*xún'àn yùshǐ*),
the two Provincial Administration Commissions (*Bù* and *Àn*), and prefectural, state, and county officials.
In the first year of Zhèngtǒng, a *tíxuéguān* was specially appointed,
specifically tasked with supervising educational administration (*xuézhèng*);
in the Southern and Northern Zhílì, these were all censors,
and in other provinces, Assistant Surveillance Commissioners (*fùshǐ*) and Vice Surveillance Commissioners (*qiānshì*) were employed concurrently.
In the first year of Jǐngtài, the *tíxuéguān* position was abolished.
In the sixth year of Tiānshùn, it was re-established,
and each was granted eighteen Imperial Edicts (*chìyù*)
to be followed.
Once *tíxuéguān* were established in the direct provinces,
some areas under their jurisdiction were too vast,
and some places were very remote,
which annual tours could not reach,
so appropriate adjustments were made.
Areas outside the passes, and various military commands (*Dūsī*), garrisons (*Wèisuǒ*), and indigenous officials were assigned to circuit supervisors (*fēnxún dàoyuán*);
Lú, Fèng, Huái, Yáng, Chú, Xú, and Hé in Zhílì were assigned to the Jiāngběi Circuit Censor;
Héng, Yǒng, and Chēn in Húguǎng were assigned to the Húnán Circuit;
Chén and Jìng were assigned to the Chén Yuán Circuit;
Qióngzhōu in Guǎngdōng was assigned to the Hǎinán Circuit;
and the *wèisuǒ* in Gānsù were assigned to the Circuit Censor (*xún'àn yùshǐ*);
all also acted under special edicts.
In the forty-first year of Wànlì,
Nán Zhílì was divided into upper and lower Jiāng,
and Húguǎng was divided into north and south,
each then adding one *tíxuéguān*.
The duty of the *tíxuéguān*
was solely to supervise schools,
not to handle judicial cases (*xíngmíng*).
Of the lawsuits they received,
serious ones were sent to the Provincial Surveillance Commission (*Ànchásī*),
and minor ones were sent to local officials (*yǒusī*);
in Zhílì, they were forwarded to the Circuit Censor (*xún'àn yùshǐ*).
Governors-General (*Dū*), Governors (*Fǔ*), Circuit Censors (*Xún'àn*), and the two Provincial Administration Commissions (*Bù* and *Àn*)
were also not allowed to infringe upon the duties of the *tíxuéguān*.
In the early Míng dynasty,
teachers and Confucian scholars were treated with courtesy;
education officials were promoted to Supervising Secretaries (*gěishì*) and Censors (*yùshǐ*),
and *zhūshēng* who became *suìgòng* easily obtained good offices.
However, discipline was also very strict.
During Tàizǔ's reign,
when education officials completed their term,
the number of *suìgòng shēngyuán* they produced was also scrutinized.
Later, *suìgòng* became a regular school practice.
In the twenty-sixth year, regulations for evaluating school officials were established,
with success in the civil service examinations (*kējǔ*) being the sole criterion for highest or lowest performance.
Upon completing a nine-year term,
the number of successful *jǔrén* was assessed:
nine for prefectural schools, six for state schools, and three for county schools was considered the highest.
If these education officials also passed an examination on the classics,
they were promoted.
Fewer *jǔrén* resulted in a 'middle' ranking,
and even passing the classics examination would not lead to promotion.
Very few or no *jǔrén* at all resulted in the 'lowest' ranking,
and if they also failed the classics examination,
they were dismissed or demoted.
Such was the strictness with which education officials were treated.
*Shēngyuán* who had been in school for ten years
without achieving anything,
and those who committed serious offenses,
were all sent to the Board to serve as clerks (*lì*),
and their stipends were confiscated.
In the fourteenth year of Zhèngtǒng, this system was reiterated and slightly modified.
Those who committed serious offenses such as bribery, rape, theft, fraudulent registration (*màojí*), frequenting prostitutes, or marrying while in mourning,
if in Zhílì, were sent to serve as cooks (*shànfū*) in the Guózǐjiàn;
in other provinces, they were sent to serve as cooks or attendants (*zhāifū*) in nearby Confucian schools,
and upon completion of their term, they became commoners,
all their stipends being confiscated.
Those who committed minor offenses and served as clerks
did not have their stipends confiscated.
Such was the strictness with which *zhūshēng* were treated.
However, subsequently, the demotion or dismissal of education officials
and the assignment or expulsion of *shēngyuán*
were all disregarded and not enforced,
and even the 'Sleeping Stele' (*wòbēi*) became merely a formality.
Among the *zhūshēng*,
the best passed the examinations,
the next became *lǐnshēng*,
and after many years, became *gòng*;
or were selected and promoted to *gòngshēng*.
Those who repeatedly failed examinations, were over fifty years old, and wished to retire
were granted official caps and belts (*guāndài*),
and their status was restored.
Later, there was a system of donating grain or horses to enter the Imperial Academy (*jiān*),
so *zhūshēng* could also enter the academy through this precedent.
In addition to examining essays during the *tíxuéguān*'s annual examinations,
education officials were ordered to recommend one or two *zhūshēng* of superior or inferior conduct,
to be rewarded or punished as an encouragement or warning.
This is the general outline.
The essays written by scholars taking examinations
are commonly called *jǔyè*.
There was one essay on the meaning of the Four Books,
over 200 characters long.
There was one essay on the meaning of the Classics,
over 300 characters long.
The focus was simply on clarity of the text's main idea,
not on flowery embellishment.
Later, new styles and novel interpretations were sought,
further departing from the original intention.
In the fifteenth year of Wànlì (1587),
the Ministry of Rites stated:
"Early Táng-era essays emphasized ornate beauty, leading scholars towards frivolousness;
early Sòng-era essays emphasized intricate obscurity, leading people towards devious complexity.
In the early years of our dynasty, *jǔyè* sometimes used phrases from the Six Classics;
later they quoted from *Zuǒzhuàn* and *Guóyǔ*;
then they quoted from *Shǐjì* and *Hànshū*.
When *Shǐjì* was exhausted, they used the Six Masters;
when the Six Masters were exhausted, they used the Hundred Schools;
eventually, even Buddhist scriptures and Daoist canons were excerpted and used.
Where would such harmful practices end?
In the early years of Hóngzhì, Zhèngdé, and Jiājìng,
the examination essays that passed were pure, authentic, and elegant.
It would be appropriate to select the best among them,
publish them for the academies,
so that scholars may know the correct direction."
Therefore, over 110 essays that had passed were selected,
and a memorial was submitted requesting their publication,
to serve as a standard.
At that time, novelty was highly esteemed,
and the traditional norms of our predecessors were scorned.
The preferences of the scholars were followed,
and the imperial directive was not obeyed.
Between Qǐ and Zhēn (Tiānqǐ and Chóngzhēn reigns),
the literary style changed even more.
Fluency in quoting from the Classics, Histories, and Hundred Schools was considered superior,
and those who indulged in unrestrained expression also became numerous.
Although prohibitions against bizarre, abstruse, and recondite styles were repeatedly issued,
the trend was too strong to reverse,
and ultimately, they could not be enforced.
Commentators liken the Míng *jǔyè* essays to Táng-era poetry:
the early years of the dynasty to Early Táng,
Chénghuà, Hóngzhì, Zhèngdé, and Jiājìng to High Táng,
Lóngqìng and Wànlì to Middle Táng,
and Qǐ and Zhēn to Late Táng.
Outside of Confucian schools (*rúxué*),
there were also Clan Schools (*zōngxué*), Community Schools (*shèxué*), and Military Academies (*wǔxué*).
For the establishment of Clan Schools,
the heir apparent, eldest sons, other sons, generals, and company commanders (*zhōngwèi*) who had not yet reached adulthood were all included.
Their teachers

were chosen from among the Prince's Household Administrative Officer (*wángfǔ zhǎngshǐ*), Court Gentleman for Encouraging Goodness (*jìshàn*), Reading Companion (*bàndú*), Professor (*jiàoshòu*), and other officials who excelled in learning and conduct.
During the Wànlì reign,
it was stipulated that all imperial clan members' sons aged ten and above
should enter the Clan Schools.
If there were many clan sons,
several teachers would be assigned,
or one person from the imperial clan would be recommended as the Clan Head (*zōngzhèng*)
to manage its affairs.
Students were instructed to recite and study books such as *Huáng Míng Zǔxùn*, *Xiàoshùn Shìshí*, and *Wéishàn Yīnzhi*,
while the Four Books, Five Classics, *Tōngjiàn*, and *Xìnglǐ* were also read concurrently.
Later, two assistant Clan Heads (*zōngfù*) were added.
Students who entered the schools
were examined annually by the Provincial Education Administrator (*tíxuéguān*),
and their attire was identical to that of regular *shēngyuán* (licentiates).
It was later decreed that they should also participate in the provincial examinations (*xiāngshì*),
and were permitted to pass.
Subsequently, Clan Schools gradually increased,
and there were quite a few who achieved success in both levels of the examinations (*liǎngbǎng*) and began their careers in the Hànlín Academy.
As for Community Schools (*shèxué*),
starting from the eighth year of Hóngwǔ (1375),
teachers were hired to educate the children of the common people,
who also read the *Yùzhì Dàgào* and the laws and statutes of the present dynasty.
During the Zhèngtǒng era,
they were permitted to become supplementary Confucian students (*rúxué shēngyuán*).
In the seventeenth year of Hóngzhì (1504), it was ordered that all prefectures (*fǔ*), subprefectures (*zhōu*), and counties (*xiàn*) establish Community Schools,
select excellent teachers,
and send common children under fifteen years old to study there,
where they would learn the rites of capping, marriage, funerals, and sacrifices.
However, this system was long abandoned,
and gradually ceased to be implemented.
Regarding the establishment of Military Academies (*wǔxué*),
from the Hóngwǔ era, Confucian Schools were established in garrisons (*wèi*) such as Dàníng,
to educate the children of military officers.
During the Zhèngtǒng era,
Chéngguó Gōng Zhū Yǒng memorialized, suggesting the selection of 51 brave and skilled commanders (*dūzhīhuī*) and other officers,
and 100 young officers proficient in horsemanship and archery.
Only then were Military Academies ordered to be built in the two capitals to instruct them.
Soon after, it was ordered that the sons of commanders of regional military commissions (*dūsī*) and garrisons (*wèisuǒ*) who were eligible to inherit positions and were ten years old or older,
should be selected and sent by the Provincial Education Administrator (*tíxuéguān*) to study in the Military Academies.
Those without Military Academies nearby were sent to Garrison Schools (*wèixué*) or nearby Confucian Schools.
During the Chénghuà era,
the supervising department was ordered to examine the military students (*wǔshēng*) admitted at the end of each year.
Those who had studied for ten years or more and were found to be untalented
would have their stipends revoked and positions returned,
and be sent to the camps for training.
During the Hóngzhì era,
following the advice of the Minister of War (*Bīngbù Shàngshū*) Mǎ Wénshēng,
the *Wǔjīng Qīshū* (Seven Military Classics) were printed and distributed to the Military Academies in the two capitals and to heirs-apparent to official positions.
During the Jiājìng era,
the Military Academy in the eastern part of the capital city was moved to a ruined temple in the western corner of the Imperial City,
so that the sons of senior and junior military officers, as well as newly ennobled nobles,
could pursue their studies there,
taught by prominent civil and military officials.
During the Wànlì era,
the Ministry of War stated,
“The Armaments Bureau (*Wǔkù Sī*) originally had a special Principal Official (*zhǔshì*) dedicated to managing the Military Academy,
but recently this position was eliminated.
We request that it be re-established.”
It was also requested that when an instructor ascends the dais,
even a commander (*dūzhīhuī*) should observe the etiquette of a disciple,
and that this be established as a formal procedure
in accordance with the precedents in the *Huìdiǎn* (Collected Statutes).
The emperor's edict agreed to all proposals.
In the tenth year of Chóngzhēn (1637), it was ordered that all prefectural, subprefectural, and county schools throughout the realm should establish military student positions (*wǔxué shēngyuán*),
and the Provincial Education Administrator (*tíxuéguān*) would uniformly recruit them.
Later, the precedents and examples from the *Huìdiǎn* were further reiterated,
regarding the recording of merits and capabilities,
and methods for exceptional promotion, demotion, assignment to training, rewards, punishments, and encouragement.
However, at that time, affairs were critical,
and it brought no benefit.
Collation Notes
Monograph 46, Elections 2
The examination system (*kējǔ*)
followed the old practices of the Táng and Sòng dynasties,
but slightly altered the method of testing scholars,

specifically basing examination questions on the Four Books and the Five Classics: *Yì* (Classic of Changes), *Shū* (Classic of Documents), *Shī* (Classic of Poetry), *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals), and *Lǐjì* (Book of Rites).
This was devised by Tàizǔ and Liú Jī.
The essays somewhat imitated Sòng-era classical essays (*jīngyì*),
but were written in the tone of ancient figures,
using parallel prose,
and were called *bāgǔ* (eight-legged essays),
commonly known as *zhìyì* (examination essays).
Every three years was a grand examination (*dàbǐ*),
where *shēngyuán* from the directly administered provinces were examined.
This was called the provincial examination (*xiāngshì*).
Those who passed were called *jǔrén*.
The following year,
*jǔrén* were examined in the capital.
This was called the metropolitan examination (*huìshì*).
Those who passed
were personally examined by the emperor in the court.
This was called the palace examination (*tíngshì*),
also known as the imperial examination (*diànshì*).
They were divided into three ranks (*jiǎ*) to determine the order of their standing.
The first rank had only three individuals,
who were called *zhuàngyuán*, *bǎngyǎn*, and *tànhuā*,
and were granted the title of *jìnshì jí dì*.
The second rank had a certain number of individuals,
who were granted the title of *jìnshì chūshēn*.
The third rank had a certain number of individuals,
who were granted the title of *tóng jìnshì chūshēn*.
The titles of *zhuàngyuán*, *bǎngyǎn*, and *tànhuā*
were established by the system.
And officials commonly referred to the first place in the provincial examination as *jièyuán*,
the first place in the metropolitan examination as *huìyuán*,
and the first place in the second and third ranks as *chuánlú*.
Provincial examinations (*xiāngshì*) were held in the years of Zǐ, Wǔ, Mǎo, Yǒu;
metropolitan examinations (*huìshì*) in the years of Chén, Xū, Chǒu, Wèi.
Provincial examinations were in the eighth month,
metropolitan examinations in the second month.
Both had the ninth day as the first session,
three days later as the second session,
and another three days later as the third session.
When the imperial examination system (*kējǔ*) was first established,
the first session tested two essays on the meaning of the Classics and
one essay on the meaning of the Four Books;
the second session,
one essay of discourse (*lùn*);
the third session,
one policy question (*cè*).
Ten days after passing the examinations,
they were again tested on five skills: horsemanship, archery, calligraphy, arithmetic, and law.
Later, a fixed format for the imperial examinations was promulgated.
The first session tested three essays on the meaning of the Four Books
and four essays on the meaning of the Classics.
For the Four Books, Zhū Zǐ's collected annotations (*Jízhù*) were primary.
For the *Yì*, Chéng Chuán and Zhū Zǐ's original meaning (*Běnyì*) were primary.
For the *Shū*, Cài Shì Chuán and ancient commentaries (*gǔzhùshū*) were primary.
For the *Shī*, Zhū Zǐ's collected commentaries (*Jízhuàn*) were primary.
For the *Chūnqiū*, the three commentaries—*Zuǒshì*, *Gōngyáng*, *Gǔliáng*—as well as Hú Ānguó's and Zhāng Qià's commentaries were primary.
For the *Lǐjì*, ancient commentaries were primary.
During the Yǒnglè era,
the *Sìshū Wǔjīng Dàquán* (Grand Compendium of the Four Books and Five Classics) was promulgated,
and commentaries and sub-commentaries were no longer used.
Subsequently,
Zhāng Qià's commentary for the *Chūnqiū* was also no longer used,
and for the *Lǐjì*, only Chén Hào's collected interpretations (*Jíshuō*) were used.
The second session tested one essay of discourse (*lùn*),
five judicial decisions (*pàn*),
and one document selected from imperial edicts (*zhào*), proclamations (*gào*), memorials (*biǎo*), or internal regulations (*nèikē*).
The third session tested five policy questions (*cè*) on current affairs related to the Classics and Histories.
The imperial examination
took place on the first day of the third month.
The provincial examination
was directly administered by the capital prefecture (Jīngfǔ),
and in other provinces by the provincial administration commissioner (Bùzhèngsī).
The metropolitan examination
was held at the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù).
For the chief examiners (zhǔkǎo),
there were two for both the provincial and metropolitan examinations.
For the associate examiners (tóngkǎo),
there were four for the provincial examination
and eight for the metropolitan examination.
There was one supervisor (tídiào),
who was a capital official (Jīngguān) when inside [the capital],
and a provincial administration commissioner (Bùzhèngsī guān) when outside [the capital].
For the metropolitan examination,
there were two supervising officials (jiānshì) from the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù guān),
an imperial censor (yùshǐ) when inside [the capital],
and a provincial judicial commissioner (Ànchásī guān) when outside [the capital].
For the metropolitan examination,
the imperial censor (yùshǐ) was responsible for the supply, collection, and safekeeping of the examination papers;
for sealing, transcription, proofreading, receiving papers, and patrolling and guarding the gates,
and for searching for concealed items.
All these duties had fixed personnel,
each performing their respective tasks.
Candidates (jǔzǐ)
included students from the Imperial Academy (Guózǐshēng) and from prefectural, sub-prefectural, and county schools who had completed their studies,
scholars (rúshì) who had not yet entered officialdom,
and officials who had not yet entered the mainstream bureaucracy.
All were recommended by the responsible authorities (yǒusī) as possessing honest and upright character, and commendable literary skills and conduct, to participate.
However, school instructors (xùndǎo) who specialized in teaching students,
retired officials,
families of entertainers (chāngyōu),
and those in mourning for their parents,
were all prohibited from taking the examination.
At the top of the examination paper,
the candidate was to write their name for three generations (sāndài xìngmíng), their ancestral home (jíguàn), age (niánjiǎ),
the classical text they specialized in (suǒ xí běnjīng),
and the seal mark of the supervising office (suǒsī yìnjì).
On the day of the examination, upon entering the examination hall,
discussions and impersonation were prohibited.
For those who had not submitted their papers by evening,
three candles were provided.
Within the text, candidates had to avoid imperial names (yùmíng) and temple names (miàohào),
and were not allowed to identify their own family background.
The sealing (mífēng) and numbering were done with three composite characters.
The papers written by the candidates used ink
The transcribed papers used vermilion ink
and were called "vermilion papers" (zhūjuàn).
The place where scholars were examined
was called the "examination compound" (Gòngyuàn).
The individual cubicles for students
were called "number rooms" (hàofáng).
The soldiers guarding each person
were called "number soldiers" (hàojūn).
When examination officials entered the compound,
the inner and outer gates were immediately sealed and locked.
The supervisors (tídiào), inspecting officials (jiānshì), etc., outside were called "outer curtain officials" (wàilián guān),
while the chief examiners (zhǔkǎo) and associate examiners (tóngkǎo) inside were called "inner curtain officials" (nèilián guān).
For the imperial examination, officials from the Hanlin Academy (Hànlín) and court officials (cháochén) known for their literary excellence
were appointed as "paper readers" (dújuànguān).
They jointly reviewed the policy essays (duìcè),
determined the rankings,
and awaited the emperor's arrival at the imperial hall (línxuān).
Sometimes the rankings were as initially proposed,
other times they were revised.
The imperial edict (chuánzhì) would then announce the successful candidates by rank (chàngdì).
The first-place scholar (zhuàngyuán) was appointed compiler (xiūzhuàn),
the second- and third-place scholars (bǎngyǎn, tànhuā) were appointed reviser (biānxiū),
and those selected as probationary bachelors (shùjíshì) from the second and third ranks
all became Hanlin officials (Hànlínguān).

Others might be appointed to positions such as supervising secretary (gěishì), imperial censor (yùshǐ), director (zhǔshì), scrivener (zhōngshū), messenger (xíngrén), judicial reviewer (píngshì), court ceremonialist (tàicháng), or academician of the Imperial Academy (Guózǐ bóshì),
or appointed as judicial commissioner of a prefecture (fǔ tuīguān), sub-prefect (zhīzhōu), or county magistrate (zhīxiàn), etc.
Provincial graduates (jǔrén) and imperial students (gòngshēng) who failed the examinations but entered the Imperial Academy (rùjiān) and were selected
might be appointed to minor capital positions,
or as prefectural assistants (fǔzuǒ) or principal officials of sub-prefectures and counties (zhōuxiàn zhèngguān),
or as educational officials (jiàozhí).
This is a general outline of the selection of officials during the Ming dynasty.
Throughout the Ming era,
civil administration was prioritized over military affairs (yòuwén zuǒwǔ).
However, military examinations (wǔkē) were also established to recruit military talent,
which can be appended here.
Initially,
when Tàizǔ (洪武帝) began his uprising,
he first gathered talented individuals.
In the first year of Wú (吳), an order was issued to establish both civil and military examinations to select scholars,
instructing officials to encourage talented scholars (xiùshì) and brave and intelligent individuals (zhìyǒng zhī rén) among the populace
to diligently study in due course,
and to present themselves as tributaries (gòng) to the capital
in the year examinations were held.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ (洪武), an imperial edict stated:
"The Hàn, Táng, and Sòng dynasties
each had their own established systems for selecting officials,
but they merely valued literary skill and did not seek individuals complete in both virtue and art.
The former Yuán dynasty treated scholars very well,
but powerful and influential individuals
often took in ambitious and competitive persons (bēnjìng zhī rén),
who, through connections and flattery,
would usurp official salaries.
Those with true talent and integrity
were ashamed to advance alongside them,
and willingly remained hidden in the mountains and forests rather than emerging.
The decline of customs
reached such a point.
Starting from the eighth month of this year,
a special civil service examination (kējǔ) will be established,

specifically to select those who are clear in their understanding of the classics, cultivate their conduct, are extensively knowledgeable in ancient and modern affairs, and whose fame matches their reality.
I shall personally examine them at court (qīn cè yú tíng),
rank them by their merit, and appoint them to office.
May all civil officials (wénchén) throughout the empire (zhōngwài) advance through the civil service examinations,
and those not from the examinations shall not be granted official positions."
Thereupon, each province (xíngshěng) in the capital region (Jīngshī) held provincial examinations: the quota for Zhílì (直隸) was one hundred persons,
Hénán (河南), Shāndōng (山東), Shānxī (山西), Shǎnxī (陝西), Běipíng (北平), Fújiàn (福建), Jiāngxī (江西), Zhèjiāng (浙江), and Húguǎng (湖廣) each had forty persons,
and Guǎngxī (廣西) and Guǎngdōng (廣東) each had twenty-five persons.
If there were many talents or if the number was not met,
the quota was not strictly adhered to.
Gāolí (高麗), Ānnán (安南), and Zhànchéng (占城)
were permitted by imperial edict for their scholars (guóshìzǐ) to take the provincial examinations in their own countries,
and then to contribute (gòng) to the capital.
The following year, the metropolitan examination
selected one hundred and twenty successful candidates.
The emperor personally composed the policy questions,
and the examination was held at the Fèngtiān Diàn (奉天殿).
Wú Bózōng (吳伯宗) was promoted to first place.
A yellow placard was hung outside the Wǔmén (午門),
the imperial edict was announced at the Fèngtiān Diàn (奉天殿),
and a banquet was bestowed at the Ministry of the Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shěng).
Bózōng was appointed junior director (yuánwàiláng) of the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù),
and the others were appointed to various offices according to their rank.
At that time, as the empire was newly settled,
each province (xíngshěng) was ordered to hold examinations for three consecutive years,
and because there were many vacant official positions,
all provincial graduates (jǔrén) were exempted from the metropolitan examination
and proceeded to the capital for selection.
Furthermore, young and exceptionally talented individuals like Zhāng Wéi (張唯) and Wáng Huī (王輝) were promoted to reviser (biānxiū) in the Hanlin Academy (Hànlín Yuàn),
and Xiāo Sháo (蕭韶) was appointed director (zhícháng) of the Secretariat (Mìshū Jiān).
They were ordered to enter the Wénhuá Táng (文華堂) within the forbidden city to study,
with Sòng Lián (宋濂), a grand tutor (zànshàn dàfū) to the crown prince, and others as their teachers.
In his leisure from governing, the emperor
would often visit the hall,
evaluate the merits and demerits of their writings,
and provide them with wine and food from the Imperial Household Department (Guānglù) daily.
For each meal,
the crown prince (Huángtàizǐ) and various imperial princes (qīnwáng) would take turns hosting them,
and bestowed upon them silver, bows and arrows, saddles and horses, and winter and summer clothing,
treating them with great favor.
Later, he felt that many of those selected were young men
who were few in number in applying what they had learned to practical affairs,
so he merely ordered officials to recommend talented individuals (xiáncái),
and abolished the civil service examination (kējǔ).
It was not until the fifteenth year
that it was reinstated.
In the seventeenth year, the format of the civil service examination (kējǔ) was finally established,
and the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù) was ordered to promulgate it to all provinces.
Thereafter, it became a permanent system,
and recommendations (jiànjǔ) gradually became less important,
and eventually fell into disuse.
In the eighteenth year, for the imperial examination,
the first-rank metropolitan graduates (jìnshì) Dīng Xiǎn (丁顯) and others were promoted to compiler (xiūzhuàn) in the Hanlin Academy (Hànlín Yuàn),
the second-rank candidates such as Mǎ Jīng (馬京) were appointed reviser (biānxiū),
and Wú Wén (吳文) was appointed editor (jiǎntǎo).
The entry of metropolitan graduates (jìnshì) into the Hanlin Academy (Hànlín)
began from this time.
Metropolitan graduates (jìnshì) were ordered to observe administration (guānzhèng) in various offices;
those in the Hanlin Academy (Hànlín), Imperial Edict Office (Chéngchì Jiān), and other yamen
were called probationary bachelors (shùjíshì).
The practice of metropolitan graduates (jìnshì) becoming probationary bachelors (shùjíshì)
also began from this time.
Those in the Six Ministries (Liùbù), Censorate (Dūchá Yuàn), Grand Court of Revision (Dàlǐ Sì), and other yamen were still called metropolitan graduates (jìnshì),
and the term "metropolitan graduate observing administration" (guānzhèng jìnshì) also began from this time.
Subsequently, there were increases and decreases in examination quotas (shì'é),
changes in regulations (tiáolì),
variations in the importance of inner and outer examiners (kǎoguān),
and successes and failures in examination affairs (wéishì).
Their minor details will not be discussed,
but those concerning national policy (guóshì) cannot be left unmentioned.
Regarding the quotas for the xiāngshì,
in the seventeenth year of Hóngwǔ, an imperial edict declared that the number was not to be restricted by quota,
but rather to be filled in accordance with actual contributions.
In the first year of Hóngxī, fixed quotas first appeared.
Thereafter, they gradually increased.
By the Zhèngtǒng reign,
Zhílì (North and South) was fixed at one hundred candidates,
Jiāngxī at sixty-five candidates,
while other provinces decreased from five,
down to Yúnnán with twenty candidates as the fewest.
During the Jiājìng reign,
it increased to forty,
and Guìzhōu also had twenty candidates.
During the Qìng, Lì, Qǐ, and Zhēn reigns,
the two Zhílì provinces further increased to over one hundred thirty candidates,
while other provinces gradually increased but none exceeded one hundred.
When Jiāozhǐ was first opened, ten candidates were set as the quota,
but this ceased when the territory was abandoned.
Regarding the quotas for the huìshì,
in the early days of the dynasty, there was no fixed number.
It could be as few as thirty-two people,
while at its most,
such as in the yìchǒu year of Hóngwǔ and the bǐngxū year of Yǒnglè,
it reached four hundred seventy-two people.
Thereafter, it was sometimes one hundred,
sometimes two hundred,
sometimes two hundred fifty,
sometimes three hundred fifty.
The increases and decreases were inconsistent,
and all were determined by memorializing the throne upon the approaching date.
After the yìwèi year of Chénghuà,
three hundred candidates were generally selected.
There were instances where, due to a specific request or an imperial edict of grace, an additional fifty or one hundred candidates were selected,
but this was not the regular system.
Initially,
the Ministry of Rites selected scholars
without distinction of North or South.
However, starting from the dīngchǒu year of Hóngwǔ,
among the fifty-two people selected by examiners Liú Sānwú and Bái Xìndǎo, including Sòng Cóng,
all were Southern scholars.
In the third month,
during the palace examination,
Chén ān was promoted to first place.
The Emperor was enraged by the biased selection,
and ordered twelve officials, including Attendant Reader Zhāng Xìn, to review the papers.
ān was also involved.
The Emperor's anger did not subside,
and he executed Xìndǎo, Xìn, ān, and others,
and exiled Sānwú to the border.
He personally reviewed the papers,
and selected sixty-one people, including Rèn Bóān.
In the sixth month, another palace examination was held,
with Hán Kèzhōng taking first place.
All were Northern scholars.
Nevertheless, until the Yǒnglè reign,
selection was never based on geographical division.
In the first year of Hóngxī,
Rénzōng ordered Yáng Shìqí and others to fix the quota for selecting scholars,
with sixteen for Southerners
and fourteen for Northerners.
During the Xuāndé and Zhèngtǒng reigns,
the papers were divided into Southern, Northern, and Central scrolls.
Taking one hundred as the standard,
fifty-five were selected from the South,
thirty-five from the North,
and ten from the Center.
In the early years of Jǐngtài,
an imperial edict instructed to follow the precedent of the Yǒnglè reign.
In the second year, xīnwèi,
the Ministry of Rites was about to implement it,
but Supervising Secretary Lǐ Kǎn contested it,
saying:
"The ministerial officials wish to rely solely on literary skill,
and select more Southerners."
Vice Minister of Justice Luó Qǐ also supported Kǎn's statement.
The matter was referred to the Ministry of Rites,
which reported back:
"Your servants are following an imperial edict,
not a private request."
Emperor Jǐng ordered compliance with the imperial edict,
and did not follow Kǎn's suggestion.
Before long,
Supervising Secretary Xú Tíngzhāng again requested to follow the precedent of the Zhèngtǒng reign.
In the fifth year, jiǎxū,
during the huìshì,
the Ministry of Rites memorialized for a final decision.
Thereupon, Tíngzhāng's suggestion was again adopted,
and papers were divided into Southern, Northern, and Central scrolls: The Southern scroll included
Yìngtiān and the prefectures of Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng,
Zhèjiāng, Jiāngxī, Fújiàn, Húguǎng, and Guǎngdōng.
The Northern scroll included
Shùntiān, Shāndōng, Shānxī, Hénán, and Shǎnxī.
The Central scroll included
Sìchuān, Guǎngxī, Yúnnán, Guìzhōu, and the two prefectures of Fèngyáng and Lúzhōu,
and the three subprefectures of Chúzhōu, Xúzhōu, and Hézhōu.
In the twenty-second year of Chénghuà,
when Wàn Ān was in power,
and Zhōu Hóngmó was Minister of Rites,
both being from Sìchuān,
they, following the request of Provincial Administration Commissioner Pān Zhěn,
reduced two quotas each from the North and South,
to increase the quota for the Center.
In the second year of Hóngzhì, the old system was reinstated.
Thereafter, this was followed without change.
Only in the third year of Zhèngdé,
Supervising Secretary Zhào Duó, acting under Liú Jǐn's instruction,
requested to expand the quotas for the xiāngshì in Hénán, Shǎnxī, and Shāndōng.
Thus, Shǎnxī was increased to one hundred,
Hénán to ninety-five,
and Shāndōng to ninety.
And considering the division of huìshì into Southern, Northern, and Central scrolls to be uneven,
the Sìchuān quota was increased by ten,
and included in the Southern scroll,
while the rest were included in the Northern scroll,
with both North and South taking one hundred fifty candidates evenly.
This was because Jǐn was from Shǎnxī,
and Grand Secretary Jiāo Fāng was from Hénán,
who colluded in drafting imperial decrees,
each serving their private interests.
When Jǐn and Fāng fell,
the old system was soon restored.
Initially,
for the xiāngshì in the two capitals,
the chief examiners were all Hánlín scholars.
For examiners in other provinces,
beforehand, learned and upright scholars and officials were appointed from among Confucian officials and scholars.
Therefore, there were those who were not in court and repeatedly held positions as examiners.
In the third year of Jǐngtài, an order was given that the two Provincial Administration Commissioners and Provincial Surveillance Commissioner
should jointly recommend incumbent educational officials,
aged between thirty and fifty, who were learned, honest, and prudent,
to be appointed as examiners.
Thus, educational officials serving as chief examiners
became a fixed rule.
Thereafter, local authorities acted with favoritism,
appointing unsuitable persons,
and supervising officials often encroached upon their duties.
In the fifteenth year of Chénghuà,
Censor Xǔ Jìn requested that all provinces should follow the example of the two capitals,
and specially appoint Hánlín scholars as chief examiners.
The Emperor instructed the Ministry of Rites to strictly curb private malpractices,
but did not grant his request.
Repeated warnings were issued to outside supervising officials not to usurp the chief examiner's authority,
and if an examiner was unsuitable,
the recommender would be implicated.
It was also ordered that the Education Intendant evaluate the grades of educational officials,
to be considered for appointment.
However, as this had been practiced for a long time,
ingrained habits were difficult to change.
In the fourteenth year of Hóngzhì,
Xiè Duó, who was in charge of the Guózǐjiàn, said:
"Examiners are all appointed by provincial censors,
their status being humble, they are instructed by them,
with outside supervising officials pre-determining selections.
This is called prevention and restraint,
but is in fact corruption,
and the examination system is ruined.
I beg that high officials in the two capitals be ordered
to each recommend subordinate officials with known literary reputations,
and send two officials to each province as chief examiners,
so that the previous abuses might be eradicated."
At that time, this could not be adopted.
In the seventh year of Jiājìng, following the suggestion of Vice Minister of War Zhāng Cōng,
all provincial chief examiners were dispatched from capital officials or jìnshì,
two for each province.
Initially,
the inner examiners for the two capitals also all consisted of educational officials.
By this time, it was ordered to add one official from the Supervising Secretariats or Bureaus,
who served as inner examiners for two examinations in the two capitals.
Then, the officials from Supervising Secretariats or Bureaus were again dismissed and not sent,
and capital officials were also not sent as chief examiners for the provinces.
Until the eleventh year of Wànlì,
an imperial edict established regulations for the examination halls.
The Ministry deliberated and again put forward Zhāng Cōng's proposal,
saying:
"At that time, due to a minor dispute over etiquette between the chief examiners and supervising officials,
it was implemented for two examinations and then stopped.
Now, it is appropriate to again dispatch court officials."
Thus, for Zhèjiāng, Jiāngxī, Fújiàn, and Húguǎng, compilers and revisers were used.
For other provinces, officials from the Supervising Secretariats and Bureaus were used,
and fellow examiners were also mostly jìnshì of the first class,
with only one or two educational officials included.
This was because, starting from the twenty-fifth year of Jiājìng, following the suggestion of Supervising Secretary Wàn Yúkǎi,
educational officials were carefully selected for the provincial xiāngshì.
If there were not enough, judges and county magistrates from other provinces were appointed to supplement them.
In the forty-third year, following a memorial from a Nanjing Censor,
for the inner examiners of the two capitals, capital officials who were jìnshì were used:
two each for the Yì, Shī, and Shū Classics,
and one each for the Chūnqiū and Lǐjì Classics,
while educational officials were only partially included for the rest.
In the fourth year of Wànlì, it was again discussed that old and infirm educational officials serving as inner examiners in the two capitals should be sent back.
For Běijīng, enough were drawn from probationary jìnshì and reserve first-class jìnshì.
For Nánjīng, they were drawn from nearby county magistrates and judges.
By this time, educational officials became even more diminished.
Initially established,
for the metropolitan examination, there were eight co-examiners.
Three were drawn from the Hànlín Academy,
and five from educational posts.
In Jǐngtài 5 (1454), following the request of Hú Yíng, the Minister of Rites,
all were drawn from the Hànlín Academy and various ministry bureaus.
Subsequently, the number of "room examiners" (fángkǎo) gradually increased.
By Zhèngdé 6 (1511),
seventeen people were appointed:
eleven from the Hànlín Academy,
and three each from the Supervising Secretariats and Six Ministries.
They were divided into five rooms for the Shī Jīng,
four each for the Yì Jīng and Shū Jīng,
and two each for the Chūn Qiū and Lǐ Jì.
In Jiājìng 11 (1532),
Xià Yán, the Minister of Rites, discussed three matters concerning the examination halls.
One of them concerned the co-examiners for the metropolitan examination.
He stated that typically eleven lecturers were used.
Now there were only eleven lecturers,
all of whom should enter the examination hall
to fulfill the duties.
He requested that three or four more people be selected from the ministries and Supervising Secretariats
to make up for the insufficiency of Hànlín scholars.
Shìzōng commanded that it be done as requested.
However, it was only implemented occasionally,
and then reverted to the old system.
In Wànlì 11 (1583),
due to the large number of Yì Jīng papers,
one examiner for the Shū Jīng was reduced and added to the Yì Jīng.
In Wànlì 14 (1586),
the number of Shū Jīng papers again increased,
so one Hànlín scholar was added
to make up for the lack of Shū Jīng examiners.
By Wànlì 44 (1616),
following a memorial by the Supervising Secretary Yú Màozī,
one room was added each for the Shī Jīng and Yì Jīng,
making a total of twenty rooms.
There were twelve Hànlín scholars,
and four each from the Supervising Secretariats and Ministries.
This system remained unchanged until the end of the Míng dynasty.
In the early Hóngwǔ reign,
a banquet was bestowed upon all successful jinshì scholars at the Central Secretariat.
In Xuāndé 5 (1430), a banquet was bestowed at the Central Military Commission.
In Xuāndé 8 (1433), a banquet was bestowed at the Ministry of Rites,
and from then on, this became a fixed regulation.
The selection of shùjíshì
began in Hóngwǔ Yǐchǒu (1385),
when jinshì scholars were chosen for the post,
and it was not exclusively assigned to the Hànlín Academy.
In Yǒnglè 2 (1404), after bestowing official posts upon the three first-rank scholars, Zēng Qǐ, Zhōu Shù, and Zhōu Mèngjiǎn,
it was further ordered that fifty people of superior literary talent, such as Yáng Xiāng, be selected from the second-rank scholars,
along with ten people skilled in calligraphy, such as Tāng Liú.
All of them became shùjíshì of the Hànlín Academy.
Thus, the position of shùjíshì became exclusively assigned to the Hànlín Academy.
It was also ordered that academicians such as Xiè Jìn select those with outstanding talent and sharp intellect,
to study at the Wényuāngé.
Jìn and others selected Zēng Qǐ (compiling editor),
Zhōu Shù (compiler), Zhōu Mèngjiǎn (compiler), Yáng Xiāng (shùjíshì), and others, totaling twenty-eight people,
to correspond to the number of the Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions.
The shùjíshì Zhōu Chén personally requested to study further, being young.
The emperor was pleased and granted his request,
increasing the number to twenty-nine people by adding Chén.
The Directorate of Ceremonial provided brushes, ink, and paper monthly.
The Court of Imperial Entertainments provided morning and evening meals.
The Ministry of Rites provided oil, candles, and paper money monthly,
three ingots per person.
The Ministry of Works selected residences for them near their homes.
The emperor occasionally visited the academy to conduct examinations.
They had one day off every five days,
and inner eunuchs were always ordered to accompany them,
and they were provided with attendants and escorts.
Among those selected that year—Wáng Yīng, Wáng Zhí, Duàn Mín, Zhōu Chén, Chén Jìngzōng, Lǐ Shímǐan, etc.—
no fewer than ten or more people
had their names passed down through later generations.
Subsequently, the number selected in each examination
varied without a fixed quota.
In Yǒnglè 13 (1415), sixty-two people were selected,
while in Xuāndé 2 (1427), there was only Xíng Gōng,
because he had been practicing translating books of the "Four Barbarians" in the Hànlín Academy for a long time,
and others were not allowed to participate.
In Hóngzhì 4 (1491),
the Supervising Secretary Tú Dàn, noting that shùjíshì had not been selected for several consecutive examinations,
requested that the ancestral system be followed.
Grand Secretary Xú Pǔ stated:
"Since Yǒnglè 2 (1404),
selections have sometimes occurred every other examination,
or consecutively for several examinations,
or not for several examinations,
or three examinations were combined for a single selection,
with no fixed limit.
Sometimes the Grand Secretariat selected them,
sometimes the Ministry of Rites sent selections,
sometimes they were selected jointly with the Ministry of Rites,
sometimes limited by age,
sometimes restricted by locality,
sometimes chosen based on reputation,
sometimes identified from the palace examination papers,
sometimes by setting separate examination questions,
also without a fixed system.
Since ancient times, emperors have reserved talents in academies for education and nurturing.
The method by which our dynasty cultivates and nurtures them,
apart from the successful jinshì scholars,
is solely through the path of shùjíshì,
yet sometimes they are selected, sometimes not.
Moreover, talented individuals are not necessarily all selected,
and those selected are not necessarily all talented.
If further restricted by locality and age,
then many already accomplished talents would be discarded and unused.
I request that from now on,
a fixed system be established:
once an examination is held,
a selection is made.
Let new jinshì scholars record their essays, policies, poems, rhapsodies, prefaces, notes, and other writings from daily life,
with a minimum of fifteen pieces,
and present them to the Ministry of Rites,
which will send them to the Hànlín Academy for evaluation.
Young people with five new works
are also permitted to submit them for trial at the Hànlín Academy.
Those whose rhetoric and literary quality are commendable will be selected according to their numerical order.
The Ministry of Rites, using anonymous examination papers,
will, along with the Grand Secretaries, set examination questions in the Eastern Cabinet.
If the examination papers are consistent with the submitted writings,
they will be included in the pre-selection.
No more than twenty people will be selected per examination,
and no more than three to five will be retained per selection.
Those who achieve success in the future will surely be reliable."
Xiàozōng agreed to his request,
ordering the Grand Secretariat to jointly select candidates with the Ministries of Personnel and Rites as a regular practice.
From Jiājìng Guǐwèi (1523) to Wànlì Gēngchén (1610),
there were nine examinations in between during which no selections were made.
Shénzōng often ordered selections every other examination.
Wú Dàonán, the Vice Minister of Rites, opposed this.
In Chóngzhēn Jiǎxū (1634) and Dīngchǒu (1637),
no selections were made again;
otherwise, the regulations were followed.
Those who were selected
were called "guǎn xuǎn" (academy selection).
One high-ranking and experienced official from the Hànlín or Jiān Academy would instruct them,
and this was called "jiàoxí" (teaching and practicing).
After three years of study,
the excellent ones were retained in the Hànlín Academy as compilers or revisers,
while the next best were sent out as Supervising Secretaries or Censors,
which was called "sàn guǎn" (dispersing from the academy).
Their status was distinctly different
from regularly appointed officials awaiting selection.
In the early years of Chéngzǔ's reign,
of the seven Grand Secretaries,
half were not from the Hànlín Academy.
Hànlín compilers were also drawn from various backgrounds.
From Tiānshùn 2 (1458),
Lǐ Xián memorialized to fix the rule that compilers must be exclusively selected from jinshì scholars.
From then on,
one could not enter the Hànlín Academy without being a jinshì,
nor enter the Grand Secretariat without being from the Hànlín Academy.
The Ministers and Vice Ministers of Rites for both the Northern and Southern Administrations,
and the Right Vice Minister of Personnel,
could not be appointed without being from the Hànlín Academy.
And when shùjíshì first entered,
they were already commonly regarded as "reserved grand secretaries."
In total, of the more than 170 Grand Secretaries throughout the Míng dynasty,
nineteen out of twenty were from the Hànlín Academy.
Indeed, the civil service examination system was more flourishing than in previous dynasties,
and the flourishing of the Hànlín Academy was unprecedented in earlier dynasties.
Few children of high-ranking officials
succeeded in the examinations in the early days of the dynasty.
In Jǐngtài 7 (1456),
Chén Xún and Wáng Wén, because their sons failed the Northern Provincial Examination,
strongly attacked the chief examiner Liú Yǎn.
The Censorate and ministries were greatly agitated and criticized their wrongdoing.
The emperor reluctantly acceded to their wishes,
ordering their sons to participate in the metropolitan examination,
but inwardly despised them.
In Zhèngdé 3 (1508),
Jiāo Fāng's son, Huángzhōng, passed the metropolitan examination.
Fāng recused himself from reading the papers.
However, Huángzhōng ranked first in the second class,
and Fāng was still not satisfied,
even demoting several Hànlín scholars to vent his anger.
In Zhèngdé 6 (1511),
Yáng Tínghé's son, Shèn, ranked first in the palace examination.
Tínghé also recused himself from reading the papers at that time.
Shèn succeeded due to his high talent,
and no one criticized him for it.
In the 23rd year of Jiājìng, during the imperial examination,
Zhái Luán's sons, Rǔjiǎn and Rǔxiào, were both among the candidates.
Shìzōng suspected the two of having improperly obtained the first-class ranking,
and suppressed the first-place candidate to third place,
placing the third-place candidate in the third class.
When the examination papers were unsealed,
the one originally ranked third
was indeed Rǔxiào.
The emperor was greatly suspicious.

The Supervising Secretaries Wáng Jiāo and Wáng Yáorì thereupon impeached the Chief Examiners for the metropolitan examination, Junior Supervising Secretary Jiāng Rǔbì and the examiners of the various bureaus, for colluding privately for bribes.
