They further pursued the case of the Shùntiān provincial examination examiners Qín Míngxià and Pǔ Yīngqí for flattering Luán,
and consequently, Rǔbì and others were imprisoned in the Jǐnyīwèi (鎮撫司) jail.
When the investigation was complete,
an edict ordered Rǔbì, Míngxià, and Yīngqí to be flogged,
and all were dismissed from their posts and sent to idle retirement.
Luán and his sons were forced to become commoners.
At the beginning of Shénzōng's reign,
Zhāng Jūzhèng was in power.
In the second year, Jiǎxū,
his son failed the examination at the Ministry of Rites.
Jūzhèng was displeased,
and consequently, no庶吉士 (shù jí shì) were selected.
By the fifth year,
his son Sìxiū successfully passed as the second person in the first class.
By the eighth year,
his son Màoxiū successfully passed as the first person in the first class.
And the sons of the Grand Secretaries Lǚ Diàoyáng, Zhāng Sìwéi, and Shēn Shíxíng
also successively became Jinshì.
Censor Wèi Yǔnzhēn submitted a memorial detailing current abuses,
stating that it was inappropriate for sons of grand secretaries to pass the examinations.
The emperor demoted Yǔnzhēn.
In the sixteenth year,
Assistant Minister of the Ministry of Rites Huáng Hóngxiàn presided over the Shùntiān examination,
and Wáng Xījué's son, Héng, topped the list.
Minister (郎中) of the Ministry of Rites Gāo Guì impeached the successful candidates (舉人) Lǐ Hóng and others,
and also included Héng,
stating:
"Since the sons of former grand secretaries were all promoted at the same time,
the sons of high officials have lost credibility among the people.
Now, the son of Grand Secretary Xījué, Héng,
is known for his great talent,
and it would not be difficult for him to achieve rapid advancement on his own.
Yet people remain half-doubtful and half-believing.
It is fitting to re-examine him along with everyone else,
to clarify the intentions of the high official."
Xījué was greatly angered,
and submitted a memorial to defend himself,
using overly strong language.
Principal of the Ministry of Justice Ráo Shēn again submitted a strong memorial arguing against it.
The emperor demoted Guì to an outside post,
imprisoned Shēn,
and stripped him of his office.
The impeached candidates were re-examined,
and Héng still placed first,
with not a single person being dismissed.
In the 20th year, during the metropolitan examination,
Lǐ Hóng passed.
Hóng
was the son-in-law of Grand Secretary Shēn Shíxíng.
Just before the results were announced,
a Supervising Secretary from the examination bureau held up his paper,
believing that the son-in-law of a grand secretary should not pass.
Chief Examiner Zhāng Wèi had the eighteen bureau examiners jointly review it,
and all said the writing was acceptable.
But the Supervising Secretary still insisted it was not.
Wèi angrily said:
"If the examination is not based on the writing,
then what will be the standard for fairness?
I am willing to take the blame."
Hóng was then allowed to pass.
After Wáng Héng was impeached,
while Xījué was in office,
Héng did not take the Ministry of Rites examination again.
In the 29th year, he finally passed as the second person in the first class.
From then on, when grand secretaries were in power,
none of their sons passed the examinations.
There were many abuses in the examination system,
leading to frequent discussions.
Since Tàizǔ severely punished Liú Sānwú and others,
during the Yǒnglè and Xuāndé periods, most people were submissive.
When Chén Xún and Wáng Wén tried to frame Liú Yǎn,
Gāo Gǔ protected him,
and Yǎn remained unharmed.
In the twelfth year of Hóngzhì, during the metropolitan examination,
Grand Secretary Lǐ Dōngyáng and Junior Supervising Secretary Chéng Mǐnzhèng served as examiners.
Supervising Secretary Huá Dǎng impeached Mǐnzhèng for selling examination questions to candidates Táng Yín and Xú Tài.
Lǐ Dōngyáng was then ordered to review the papers alone.
Supervising Secretary Lín Tíngyù further attacked Mǐnzhèng with six suspicious matters.
Mǐnzhèng was demoted,
and Yín and Tài were both dismissed and punished.
Yín,
a talented scholar from Jiangnan,
had placed first in the Nánwéi (southern examination) in the Wùmǐ year.
Many commentators lamented his fate.
In the sixteenth year of Jiājìng,
Minister of Rites Yán Sōng repeatedly pointed out satirical remarks in the examination records of Yìngtiān and Guǎngdōng,
provoking Shìzōng's anger.
The Chief Examiner of Yìngtiān and the Circuit Censor of Guǎngdōng were both arrested and interrogated.
In the twenty-second year,
the emperor personally criticized the Shāndōng examination records for being satirical,
leading to the arrest and flogging to death of Censor Yè Jīng outside the palace gate.
Officials from the Provincial Administration Commissioner (布政) down were all banished to distant posts.
This was also due to Sōng's malicious accusations.
In the 40th year,
Wú Qíng of Wúxī, a Supervising Secretary (中允) and Chief Examiner for Yìngtiān, selected thirteen candidates from his hometown.
He was impeached,
and both he and Deputy Examiner Hú Jié were demoted to outside posts.
Consequently, Hanlin scholars from Nánjī (southern capital) were no longer allowed to preside over the Yìngtiān examination.
In the fourth year of Wànlì,
Shùntiān Chief Examiner Gāo Rǔyú selected Zhāng Jūzhèng's sons Sìxiū and Màoxiū,
and Wáng Zhuàn's sons Zhīhéng and Zhīdǐng, who was a protégé of Jūzhèng and a Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel.
After Jūzhèng's death,
Censor Dīng Cǐlǚ re-examined these abuses,
and stated:
"Rǔyú used 'Shùn also appointed Yǔ'
as an examination question,
which was likely meant to flatter Jūzhèng by alluding to the abdication of a throne."
Those in power disliked Cǐlǚ,
and demoted him to an outside post,
but many critics sided against Rǔyú.
In the 38th year, during the metropolitan examination,
Assistant Minister (庶子) Tāng Bīnyǐn was a co-examiner,
and he exchanged examination papers with various bureaus,
involving a total of eighteen people.
The following year,
Censor Sūn Jūxiāng impeached Bīnyǐn for his private relationship with Hán Jìng,
and that all the exchanges were for Jìng's sake.
At that time, the Ministry of Personnel was conducting an evaluation.
Minister Sūn Pīyáng consequently included Bīnyǐn and Jìng in the evaluation's dismissals.
Jìng was quite renowned for his writing,
and many regretted his dismissal,
but because he was associated with the Xuān (Wei Zhongxian) faction,
they deemed his dismissal appropriate.
In the 44th year, during the metropolitan examination,
Shěn Tónghé of Wújiāng placed first,
and Zhào Míngyáng of the same district placed sixth.
Tónghé was notoriously poor at writing,
and much of his writing came from Míngyáng's hand.
When the matter was discovered,
both were demoted to military exile.
In the fourth year of Tiānqǐ,
examiners from Shāndōng, Jiāngxī, Húguǎng, and Fújiàn
were criticized and severely reprimanded by imperial edict
for satirical remarks in their policy questions.
Initially ordered to be demoted and transferred,
they were later dismissed.
Jiāngxī Chief Examiner Dīng Gānzǐ was even imprisoned and faced sentencing,
having provoked Wèi Zhōngxián's anger.
Earlier, in the second year, Xīnyǒu,
Supervising Secretary Qián Qiānyì presided over the Zhèjiāng examination.
The seven main essays in the paper of the successful candidate Qián Qiānqiū showed signs of manipulation.
After the list was announced,
he was denounced by others.
Qiānyì reported it himself,
and Qiānqiū was exiled to a military post.
Not long after,
he was pardoned and returned.
In the second year of Chóngzhēn, during the selection of Grand Secretaries,
Qiānyì, as Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites, was included,
but Minister Wēn Tǐrén was not.
Tǐrén brought up the Qiānqiū incident,
and submitted a memorial attacking Qiānyì.
Qiānyì was consequently dismissed,
and never rose again throughout the Ming dynasty.
Other criticisms of examination abuses
were numerous both before and after this,
often most severe in the Běiwéi (northern examination),
and less so in other provinces.
Bribes and connections, bringing in substitutes, cutting and passing papers, impersonation, and fraudulent registrations—
innumerable abuses emerged,
impossible to fully investigate,
with illicit connections being the most egregious.
Matters were obscure,
and sometimes accusations were made for revenge,
which indeed occurred.
Other minor successes and failures
are not worth mentioning.
Some events from previous examinations that were somewhat different:
At the beginning of Yǒnglè,
due to sudden military conflicts,
in the first year, Guǐwèi,
provincial examinations were first ordered in each province.
In the second year, Jiǎshēn, the metropolitan examination was held,
not following the old Wǔwèi calendar due to circumstances.
In the seventh year, Jǐchǒu, during the metropolitan examination,
Chén Suì and ninety-four others passed.
Chéngzǔ was then on a northern campaign,
and the Crown Prince ordered them to study at the Guózǐjiàn (Imperial Academy),
awaiting the return of the imperial carriage to the capital for the palace examination.
In the ninth year, Xīnmǎo, Xiāo Shízhōng was finally ranked first.
In the fifth year of Xuāndé (1430), *gēngxū*,
the Emperor personally presided over the imperial examination, concluding the policy questions.
He retired to the Wǔyīng Diàn
and said to the Hànlín scholars:
"When selecting scholars, I do not value empty rhetoric.
If there are those like Liú Fén and Sū Zhé who speak straightforwardly and argue forcefully,
I will surely promote them conspicuously."
He then composed the "Cèshì Gē" (Song for Examinees) to show the officials responsible for grading the papers,
but the top-ranking scholar he selected, Lín Zhèn,
also showed nothing remarkable.
In the eighth year, *guǐchǒu* (1433), the top-ranking scholar in the imperial examination was Cáo Nài,
who had qualified in the metropolitan examination from his position as a *diǎnshǐ* in Tàihé, Jiāngxī.
In the seventh year of Zhèngtǒng, *rénxū* (1442),
Nán Yù, a clerk from the Xíngbù, and Zhèng Wēn, a postmaster from Gōnglíng, also both passed the examination.
In the tenth year, *yǐchǒu* (1445),
both the metropolitan and imperial examinations' top scholar was Shāng Lù.
Lù,
a native of Chún'ān,
was the top scholar in the Zhèjiāng provincial examination in the *yǐmǎo* year (1435) at the end of Xuānzōng's reign.
He was first in all three examinations,
and scholars enthusiastically called him "Sānyuán" (Triple First).
In the Míng dynasty, Lù was the only one to achieve this.
The graders for the imperial examination were all *jiǎkē* (first-class graduates),
but that year Xú Xī, the Minister of War, and in the thirteenth year, Nài Héng, the Vice Minister of Revenue, were mere clerks.
In the first year of Tiānshùn, *dīngchǒu* (1457), Yáng Shàn, the Censor-in-Chief of the Left, who graded the papers, was a *yìzì shēng* (interpreter student).
At that time, there was not much strict adherence to social strata.
Later, however, there were no more miscellaneous officials participating in the metropolitan examination or serving as graders.
On the day of the examination in the seventh year, *guǐwèi* (1463),
a fire broke out in the examination hall,
killing over ninety people.
They were all posthumously granted the *jìnshì chūshēn* (equivalent to a *jìnshì* degree).
The metropolitan examination was rescheduled for the eighth month.
In the third month of the following year, *jiǎshēn* (1464),
the imperial examination finally took place.
At that time, Yīngzōng had already died,
and since Xiànzōng's accession was less than a year after a great mourning,
he presided over the examination at the Xījiǎomén (Western Corner Gate).
In the third year of Zhèngdé, *wùchén* (1508),
Eunuch Liú Jǐn recorded fifty names and showed them to the chief examiners,
thereby expanding the quota to fifty names.
In the fifteenth year, *gēngchén* (1520),
Wǔzōng was on a southern tour
and did not get to hold the imperial examination.
The following year,
Shìzōng ascended the throne,
and in the fifth month, he presided over the examination at the Xījiǎomén,
promoting Yáng Wéicōng to the first place.
Zhāng Cōng was also a *jìnshì* from that same examination list,
and within six or seven years,
he was in charge of state affairs,
his power equaling that of the sovereign.
In the eighth year of Jiājìng, *jǐchǒu* (1529),
the Emperor personally reviewed the imperial examination papers,
and with his own hand commented on the policy responses of Luó Hóngxiān, Yáng Míng, and Ōuyáng Dé in the first class,
and Táng Shùnzhī, Chén Shù, and Rèn Hàn in the second class, six people in total.
Each received an added commendation.
Grand Secretary Yáng Yīqīng and others then selected Shùnzhī, Shù, Hàn, and Hú Jīng, totaling twenty people, as *shùjíshì* (probationary Hànlín academicians).
They submitted their names
and requested that officials be appointed to instruct them.
Suddenly, an imperial edict was issued saying:
"The selection of *jíshì*
is indeed a good old system of our ancestors.
Recently, high-ranking officials have been selecting them for personal gain,
gaining favor and forming factions,
which is useless to the state.
From now on, there is no need to select and retain them.
As for Táng Shùnzhī and others, all appointments are to be made.
The Lìbù, Lǐbù, and Hànlín Yuàn are to meet and report on this."
Minister Fāng Xiànfū and others then appeased the imperial decree, saying that Shùnzhī and the others need not be retained,
and also limited the quota for the Hànlín Yuan:
three *shìdú*, three *shìjiǎng*, and three *xiūzhuàn*;
six *biānxiū* and six *jiǎntǎo*.
This was established as a regulation.
It is likely that Shùnzhī and others were disciples of Zhāng Cōng and Huò Tāo,
but they inwardly disagreed with the discussion of the Grand Rites
and refused to curry favor,
which Zhāng Cōng resented.
Zhāng Cōng also intended to undermine Yáng Yīqīng at the time,
thus he introduced the argument about forming factions,
and the old custom was thereby abolished.
By the eleventh year, *rénchén* (1532),
the selection for the Imperial Academy had been suspended,
but in the ninth month, it was reinstated.
In the fourteenth year, *yǐwèi* (1535),
the Emperor personally composed the policy questions
and graded them himself by hand,
promoting Hán Yìnglóng to the first place.
He issued an edict discussing the reasons for the ranking of the three in the first class and the first in the second class.
The Lǐbù consequently placed the imperial edict at the beginning of the *Dēngkē Lù* (Record of Successful Candidates),
and the policy responses of the twelve individuals
were all published in order.
In the twentieth year, *xīnchǒu* (1541),
the examination topics for selecting *shùjíshì* were
a prose essay titled "Yuán Zhèng" (Original Governance)
and a poem titled "Dú Dàmíng Lǜ" (Reading the Great Míng Code),
both personally decreed by the Emperor.
In the forty-fourth year, *yǐchǒu* (1565), during the imperial examination,
the Emperor no longer presided over the hall.
During Shénzōng's reign,
presiding over the hall became even rarer.
In the *rénxū* year (1622) of Tiānqǐ, during the metropolitan examination,
Grand Secretaries Hé Zōngyàn and Zhū Guózùo were appointed as chief examiners.
By custom,
cabinet ministers presided over examinations,
with one Hànlín or Jiànzhàn official assisting.
At that time, Gù Bǐngqiān, the Minister of Rites, had already been nominated,
but a special edict appointed Guózùo.
Guózùo humbly declined,
but the Emperor said:
"This year,
as it is my first examination,
I am specially using two assistant ministers to glorify this important ceremony.
You need not decline."
Thereafter, it became customary for two assistant ministers to preside over examinations.
That year, the Zōngkē (examination for imperial clan members) was opened,
and Zhū Shènduǒ became a *jìnshì*.
Following Zōngyàn and Guózùo's request,
he was immediately appointed *zhōngshū shèrén*.
In the fourth year of Chóngzhēn (1631),
Zhū Tǒngshì became a *jìnshì*
and was initially selected as a *shùjíshì*.
The Lìbù stated that since Tǒngshì was a member of the imperial clan,
it was not appropriate for him to serve in a position close to the Forbidden Palace,
and requested that he be reassigned as a *zhōngshū shèrén*.
Tǒngshì submitted a memorial arguing against this,
and an imperial order was issued to retain him as a *shùjíshì*.
In the seventh year, *jiǎxū* (1634),
Lín Hàn, the Vice Minister of Rites and a chief examiner, stated
that the candidate Yán Màoyóu had mastered the Five Classics
and had composed twenty-three interpretations.
The Emperor, impressed by his extensive knowledge,
permitted him to be sent to the inner examination (for direct consideration).
Màoyóu passed the *fùbǎng* (supplementary list),
and was specially granted the *jìnshì* degree.
His name was printed on a separate line,
before the first-place name in the examination record.
From then on, those who qualified through the Five Classics
followed one after another.
The martial examinations (*wǔkē*)
were established in the first year of Wú (1367).
In the twentieth year of Hóngwǔ (1387), Yú Lǐbù (Yu, Minister of Rites) requested
the establishment of martial schools
and the use of martial examinations.
Sons of military officials from various provinces were to take the examinations.

In the eighth year of Tiānshùn (1464), an order was issued for civil and military officials throughout the country to recommend those who were knowledgeable in military strategy and outstanding in courage and valor.
The provincial governors, inspecting censors, and three judicial commissioners
in each province, and the inspecting censors in Zhílì, were to conduct the examinations.
Those who passed would be tested in strategy by the Bīngbù (Ministry of War) together with the commander-in-chief in the marshal's residence,
and tested in archery from horseback and on foot in the training grounds.
Those who answered two strategy questions, hit four or more arrows while riding, and two or more arrows on foot, were considered successful.
Those who hit half of the required arrows while riding and on foot were ranked next.
In the fourteenth year of Chénghuà (1478), following the request of Eunuch Wāng Zhí,
martial provincial and metropolitan examinations were established,
all following the precedents of the civil examinations.
In the sixth year of Hóngzhì (1493), it was stipulated that martial examinations would be held every six years,
with strategy questions first,
followed by archery from horseback and on foot.
Those who failed the strategy questions were not allowed to proceed to archery.
In the seventeenth year (1504), it was changed to an examination every three years,
with the results posted and a banquet granted.
In the fourteenth year of Zhèngdé (1519), it was stipulated that
the first round would test archery from horseback,
with thirty-five paces as the standard;
the second round would test archery on foot,
with eighty paces as the standard;
and the third round would test one strategy question.
Provincial examinations were held in the *zǐ*, *wǔ*, *mǎo*, *yǒu* years (every three years, representing a fixed cycle).
In the early Jiājìng period,
a system was established:
those applying for the martial examinations in each province
were examined by the inspecting censor in the tenth month;
the martial schools in the two capitals selected candidates through the Bīngbù;
all were sent to the Bīngbù.
The metropolitan examination was held in the fourth month of the following year,
with two Hànlín officials as examiners
and four *gěishìzhōng* or *bùcáo* officials as associate examiners.
The dates for both provincial and metropolitan examinations were the 9th, 12th, and 15th of the month.
Dispatching for review,
supervising the examination, and posting the results
largely imitated the civil examinations but with reduced rigor.
Thereafter, it was sometimes suspended and sometimes reinstated.
It also imitated the civil examinations' Northern and Southern quotas,
dividing candidates into frontier regions (*biānfāng*) and interior regions (*fùzàng*).
For every ten successful candidates,
six were usually from the frontier and four from the interior.
In the thirty-eighth year of Wànlì (1610), the quota for the metropolitan examination was set,
with a general rate of one hundred *jìnshì* being selected.
Later, there were instances where thirty additional candidates were authorized by imperial decree,
but this was not a regular system.
During the reigns of Emperor Mùzōng and Emperor Shénzōng,
deliberators once said that military examinations should prioritize skill and bravery.
Towards the end of the Wànlì reign,
officials of the Ministry of Personnel again requested the special establishment of a military examination for general-calibre talents.
The first round would test horsemanship, archery on foot, spears, swords, sabers, halberds, boxing, and various martial arts techniques.
The second round would test encampment, landmines, gunpowder, war chariots, and similar items.
In the third round, candidates would speak on military strategy, astronomy, or geography, whichever they were most proficient in.
The proposal was approved but not implemented.
In the fourth year of Chóngzhēn,
when the results of the military metropolitan examination were announced,
critics were greatly displeased.
The Emperor ordered Zhōngyǔn Fāng Fēngnián and Ní Yuánlù to re-examine the candidates,
selecting 120 people including Wēng Yīng.
Fāng Fēngnián and Ní Yuánlù, considering that talent was urgently needed at the time,
submitted a memorial requesting a palace examination and the declaration of successful candidates,
following all the precedents for civil examinations.
Thereupon, Wáng Láipìn and others were granted the ranks of *Jìdì* and *Chūshēn* with varying distinctions.
The military palace examination began from this point.
In the fourteenth year, an edict was issued to the various ministers to specially establish the "Extraordinary Schemes and Remarkable Bravery" examination.
When the imperial decree was issued,
no one responded.
Textual Notes
Monograph Forty-Seven: Selection of Officials (3)
After Tàizǔ captured Jīnlíng,
he summoned the scholars Fàn Zǔgàn and Yè Yí.
After conquering Wùzhōu,
he summoned scholars Xǔ Yuán, Hú Hàn, and others to daily lecture on the classics, history, and the way of governance.
After conquering Chǔzhōu,
he conscripted the venerable scholars Sòng Lián, Líu Jī, Zhāng Yì, and Yè Chēn to Jiànkāng,
and established the "Hall for Honoring the Worthy" to accommodate them.
Sòng Lián was appointed as the Provincial Education Intendant for Jiāngnán and other areas.
Zhāng Yì and Yè Chēn were made Assistant Circuit Intendants for Field Management.
Líu Jī remained in the imperial counsel, participating in planning and deliberation.
In the third month of the *Jǐachén* year, an imperial edict was given to the Central Secretariat, stating:
"Now that Our territory is expanding daily,
both civil and military talents are needed.
How can there be no outstanding and extraordinary talents in the world?
Whether they are hidden in mountains and forests,
or concealed among the ranks of soldiers,
if those in authority do not guide and uplift them,
they will not be able to reveal themselves.
From now on, anyone who can submit a memorial, express their views, expound on the principles of governance, or display outstanding military strategy,
the Army Supervisor's Office and the Grand Military Governor's Office shall report their names.
Or, if one cannot write well but possesses valuable insights,
they are permitted to go to the palace to personally present their matters.
As for local officials aged fifty or above,
even if they are experienced and proficient in governmental affairs,
their energy has already declined.

It is appropriate to instruct the relevant officials to select talented and outstanding individuals from the populace, aged twenty-five or above, with bright dispositions, extensive learning, and administrative ability, to be summoned to the Central Secretariat,
to be employed alongside the elderly officials.
After ten years,
the old officials will retire,
and the young ones will already be proficient in their duties.
In this way, there will be no shortage of talent,
and officials will be well-chosen.
Let this intention be communicated
and announced to the subordinate offices."
Thereupon, prefectures and counties annually recommended worthy talents, as well as brave and resourceful military strategists, and scholars knowledgeable in astronomy,
sometimes including those also skilled in law.
Subsequently, strict prohibitions were imposed on recommendations,
and those who made excessive recommendations were prosecuted.
In the first year of the Wú era, the Imperial Diarists Wú Lín, Wèi Guān, and others were dispatched with silks and textiles to seek reclusive worthies throughout the land.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, worthy talents from all over the realm were summoned to the capital
and appointed as governors and magistrates.
In the winter of that same year,
Wén Yuánjí, Zhān Tóng, Wèi Guān, Wú Fǔ, Zhào Shòu, and others were again dispatched to travel throughout the land,
seeking out worthy talents,
each given silver and then sent away.
In the third year, an edict was issued to the court officials, stating:
"The Six Ministries oversee the affairs of the entire realm,
and only those with broad learning, extensive knowledge, and both talent and virtue
are fit to hold such positions.
Fearing that there might be those living in reclusion in the mountains and forests,
or serving in lower offices,
instruct the relevant officials to thoroughly investigate and seek them out."
In the sixth year, another edict was issued, stating:
"Worthy talents
are the treasure of the nation.
Ancient sage-kings toiled in seeking worthies.
Such as Emperor Gāozōng's seeking of Fù Yuè,
and King Wén's seeking of Lǚ Shàng.
Were those two rulers lacking in wisdom?
Rather, they anxiously sought out those among builders and butchers,
because without a full complement of worthy talents,
governance could not be achieved.
The *hónghú* (swans/geese) can fly far
because they have wings.
The *jiāolóng* (flood dragon) can soar
because it has scales and mane.
A ruler can achieve good governance
because he has worthy individuals to assist him.
As for scholars in the mountains and forests whose virtue, conduct, literature, and arts are commendable,
the relevant officials shall identify and recommend them,
respectfully send them to the capital,
and We shall employ them
to achieve supreme governance."
In this year,
the imperial examinations were consequently abolished,
and instead, the relevant officials were ordered to identify and recommend worthy talents,
taking virtue and conduct as the foundation,
and literary and artistic accomplishments as secondary.
The categories included:
"intelligent and upright,"
"worthy and upright,"
"filial, fraternal, and diligent in agriculture,"
"scholar,"
"filial and incorruptible,"
"cultivated talent,"
"talent,"
and "venerable citizen."
All were respectfully sent to the capital
and promoted without regard for sequence.
And tribute students from various provinces also advanced through the Imperial Academy.
Thereupon, the imperial examinations were abolished for ten years,
until the seventeenth year when they were re-instituted,
and the method of recommendation continued concurrently, without being abolished.
At that time, all civil and military officials, great and small, inside and outside the court, were permitted to recommend.
Even miscellaneous officials in granaries, treasuries, agencies, and bureaus
were ordered to recommend scholars of literary talent and administrative ability.
Those who were recommended and arrived
were then ordered to make further recommendations.
Therefore, from mountains, forests, caves, thatched huts, and impoverished residences,
none failed to make their way to the top,
and countless individuals rose from commoners to high officials.
Venerable scholars Bào Xún, Yú Quán, Quán Sīchéng, and Zhāng Chángnián, who were over ninety years old,
were summoned to the capital
and immediately appointed Grand Academicians of Wénhuá Hall.
Scholars Wáng Běn, Dù Jiào, Zhào Mínwàng, and Wú Yuán were specially appointed as Four Assistant Officials concurrently serving as Guests of the Crown Prince.
Worthy talent Guō Yǒudào,
cultivated talents Fàn Mǐn and Zēng Tài,
tax-paying talent Zhèng Yí,
and scholar Zhào Zhù were appointed Minister from their commoner status.
Scholars Zhāng Zǐyuán and Zhāng Zōngdé became Vice Ministers.
Venerable scholars Líu Yù and Guān Xián became Vice Censors-in-Chief.
Erudite scholars Zhāng Wéntōng and Ruǎn Zhòngzhì became Assistant Censors-in-Chief.
Talent Hè Cóngdào became Junior Minister of the Court of Judicial Review.
Filial and incorruptible Lǐ Dé became Prefect.
Scholar Wú Yǒng became Chancellor of the Imperial Academy.
Worthy talents Luán Shìyīng, Xú Jǐngshēng, and Lǐ Yánzhōng,
scholars Zhāng Suì and Wáng Lián became Provincial Administration Commissioners.
Filial and fraternal Lǐ Hǎochéng and Niè Shìjǔ,
worthy talents Jiǎng Ānsù, Xuē Zhèngyán, and Zhāng Duān,
and literary talent Sòng Liàng became Provincial Administration Vice Commissioners.
Scholars Zhèng Kǒnglín, Wáng Décháng, and Huáng Tóngshēng,
worthy talents Yú Yìngjǔ, Mǎ Wèi, Xǔ Ān, Fàn Mèngzōng, Hé Dézhōng, Sūn Zhòngxián, Wáng Fú, and Wáng Qīng,
and intelligent talents Zhāng Dàhéng and Jīn Sīcún became Regional Surveillance Commissioners.
These are examples of those notably promoted.
Those who gradually rose to noble official positions
were also countless.
It was once decreed to the Ministry of Rites:
"Scholars proficient in classics, cultivated in conduct, and experienced in current affairs
should be summoned to the capital.
Those aged sixty or above but below seventy
shall be placed in the Hanlin Academy to be available for consultation.
Those aged forty or above but below sixty
shall be employed in the Six Ministries and the two Provincial Administration and Surveillance Offices."
Indeed, at that time,
there was no other path to official advancement,
hence many often attained sudden nobility.
The Ministry of Personnel's reports recommending officials to be appointed
often reached over 3,700 people,
and even the lowest number was over 1,900.
Furthermore, wealthy households and venerable citizens were also allowed to have audience,
and if their replies pleased the emperor,
they were immediately given good official positions.
And the monk Guō Chuán from Kuàijī,
recommended by Sòng Lián, was promoted to Hanlin Attendant.
These are all verifiable examples.
When the imperial examinations were re-established,
both paths were used concurrently,
and neither was ever unduly prioritized or neglected.
During the Jiànwén and Yǒnglè eras,
those who rose through recommendation still had internal appointments to the Hanlin Academy or external appointments to provincial administration offices.
And Yáng Shìqí, as a recluse,
and Chén Jì, as a commoner,
were abruptly appointed Chief Compilers of the Veritable Records of Tàizǔ.
Their disregard for qualifications was also like this.
Subsequently, the imperial examinations gradually gained more importance,
and recommendations became increasingly less significant.
Literati generally considered it an honor to advance through the examination halls;
although officials frequently received imperial edicts to seek out worthy talents,
as talent declined,
they merely went through the motions as a matter of routine.
Xuānzōng once bestowed upon his ministers his imperial compositions, the *Yīlán Cāo* and the *Zhāoyǐn Shī*,
to encourage and inspire them.
However, few responded,
and public sentiment was generally dismissive.
In the first year of Zhèngtǒng,
the acting Ministry of Personnel stated:
"During the Xuāndé reign,

an edict was issued to the provincial administration and surveillance commissioners, and the prefectural, sub-prefectural, and county officials throughout the empire, to recommend one worthy and upright person each.
This recommendation process is still ongoing;
it should be halted."
The emperor believed that the court's search for talent should not cease.
Henceforth, those who came
were to be examined by the senior officials of the Six Ministries, the Censorate, and the Hànlín Yuàn.
Those who passed would be appointed,
and those who failed would be dismissed.
Recommendations subsequently became even rarer.
In the first year of Tiānshùn, an edict proclaimed:
"Among recluses,
if there are those whose learning spans heaven and man, whose talents are capable of governing the country, and who maintain a lofty detachment without seeking fame,
the relevant authorities shall report their cases truthfully."
Censor Chén Jì reported on the learning and conduct of the scholar Wú Yǔbì from Chóngrén.
Jiāngxī Grand Coordinator Hán Yǒng was ordered to respectfully invite him to the capital.
Upon his arrival, he was granted an audience
and appointed Zuo Yùdé.
Wú Yǔbì declined, citing illness.
The emperor again ordered Lǐ Xián to bring him for an audience at the Wénhuá Diàn,
and casually asked:
"I value your learning and conduct,
and have specially appointed you as a palace official,
burdening you with assisting the Crown Prince."
Wú Yǔbì firmly declined.
He was granted a banquet at the Wénhuá Diàn,
with Lǐ Xián ordered to attend,
and was given an imperial edict of praise and reward.
An imperial courier was dispatched to escort him home;
this was indeed a special honor.
By the nineteenth year of Chénghuà,
Chén Xiànzhāng, a *jǔrén* from Guǎngdōng, was recommended,
appointed Xiūzhuǎn of the Hànlín Yuàn,
but allowed to return home.
The ceremonial provisions were significantly reduced.
Later, during the Hóngzhì reign,
Pān Chén, a scholar from Zhèjiāng;
during the Jiājìng reign,
Wén Zhēngmíng, a *shēngyuán* from Nán Zhílì, and Yè Yòuxué, a scholar from Yǒngjiā,
were all recommended and appointed Dàizhào of the Hànlín Yuàn.
During the Wànlì reign,
Qú Jiǔsī, a *jǔrén* from Húguǎng, was also appointed Dàizhào;
Liú Yuánqīng, a *jǔrén* from Jiāngxī, was appointed Bóshì of the Guózǐjiān;
Zhāng Huáng, a recluse from Jiāngxī, was merely nominally appointed Xùndǎo of Shùntiān Fǔ.
And although Chén Jìrú, a recluse from Zhílì, and Yáng Sīxīn, a *jǔrén* from Sìchuān, were all recommended,
their cases were merely sent to the Ministry of Rites.
In the ninth year of Chóngzhēn,
the Ministry of Personnel again deliberated on recommending *xiàolián*,
stating:
"Our ancestors' courts only occasionally carried this out;
there was no fixed system.
Now, it should be implemented throughout the provinces.
Great care should be taken to search for
truly filial and incorruptible scholars, possessing talent and virtue, well-versed in classics and upright in conduct.
They should be reported by the provincial administration and surveillance commissioners to the circuit censors,
who will verify and memorialize,
then test and appoint them."
At that time, recommendations proliferated throughout the empire,
but they were all appointed to broken-down prefectures and counties,
ultimately without great effect.
By the seventeenth year,
an order was given that vacant positions in the fallen prefectures and counties of Yù [Hénán] and Chǔ [Húguǎng] could all be filled by the grand coordinators and circuit censors,
without restrictions on official rank, miscellaneous backgrounds, or *shēngyuán* status.
This was an urgent search for talent,
not the customary selection of scholars in times of peace.
As for the fourth year of Zhèngdé,
the high officials of Zhèjiāng recommended Zhōu Lǐ, Xú Zǐyuán, and Xǔ Lóng from Yúyáo,
and Xú Wénbiāo from Shàngyú.
Liú Jǐn, noting that all four were fellow townsmen of Xiè Qiān,
and that the imperial edict draft originated from Liú Jiàn,
falsely issued an edict sending Lǐ and others to the gendarmerie commands,
exiling them to frontier garrisons.

He compelled the provincial administration commissioners Lín Fú, Shào Bǎo, Lǐ Zàn, and nineteen other officials including administration vice commissioners, surveillance vice commissioners, prefectural, and county officials, to pay a fine of two hundred *shí* of rice.
Furthermore, he stripped Jiàn and Qiān of their offices,
and stipulated that
people from Yúyáo could not be selected as capital officials.
This was an instance where individuals suffered misfortune due to recommendations,
another variation.
Matters of official appointment
for civil officials belonged to the Ministry of Personnel, and for military officials to the Ministry of War,
with the Ministry of Personnel's responsibilities being particularly crucial.
The Ministry of Personnel had four bureaus,
of which the Bureau of Civil Appointments managed selections,
and the Bureau of Merit Evaluation managed appraisals;
their functions were especially vital.
Candidates for selection, besides *jìnshì*, *jǔrén*, and *gòngshēng*,
included
*guānshēng*, *ēnshēng*, *gōngshēng*, *jiànshēng*, and *rúshì*,
as well as miscellaneous personnel such as *lìyuán*, *chéngchāi*, *zhīyìn*, *shūsuàn*, *zhuànshū*, *yìzì*, and *tōngshì*.
*Jìnshì* constituted one path,
*jǔrén* and *gòngshēng* another,
and *lìyuán* and others another;
this was known as the simultaneous use of three paths.
Capital officials such as section chiefs of the Six Ministries, grand secretaries, imperial couriers, court reviewers, and academicians,
and outer officials such as prefects, judicial commissioners, and county magistrates,
were selected from *jìnshì*.
Outer officials such as judicial commissioners, county magistrates, and education officials
were selected from *jǔrén* and *gòngshēng*.
Capital officials such as heads of the Five Chief Military Commissions and the Six Ministries,
and subordinate officials of the Office of Transmission, the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, the Court of Imperial Entertainments, and the Palace of the Eastern Palace,
were selected from *guānshēng* (hereditary privileged students).
Subordinate officials of prefectures and counties,
and heads of the three provincial commissions (surveillance, administration, and judicial),
were selected from *jiànshēng*.
Heads of outer prefectures, outer guards, and salt administration offices,
and various miscellaneous officials both inside and outside the capital, both ranked and unranked,
were selected from *lìyuán*, *chéngchāi*, and similar roles.
This was the general overview.
The variations and differences
can be inferred.
Those initially appointed were called *tīngxuǎn*,
and those promoted were called *shēngqiān*.
The method of selecting officials
involved six evaluations and six selections by the Ministry of Personnel annually.
There were six direct selections,
six classified selections,
and two selections for distant regions.
For initial appointments and promotions/demotions determined by appraisal,
major selections occurred in even-numbered months, with their order decided in odd-numbered months.
For reassignments, demotions, mourning leave, and waiting for appointment,
urgent selections occurred in odd-numbered months.
The special selection
was held every three years.
Petitions for grace by *jǔrén*
and appointments of annual *gòngshēng* as education officials
had no fixed schedule.
All promotions
required a full evaluation period.
If a vacancy needed to be filled without waiting for the full term,
it was called *tuīshēng* (expedited promotion).
Grand Secretaries of the Grand Secretariat and Ministers of the Ministry of Personnel
were selected by court deliberation (*tíngtuī*) or imperial special decree.
Vice ministers and below, and chief instructors,
were selected by court deliberation involving the Ministry of Personnel and officials of the third rank and above.
Officials below the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices
were selected by the Ministry [of Personnel].
Officials below the Chief Minister of the Office of Transmission and the Vice Minister of Surveillance
were selected by the Ministry of Personnel at the Hóngzhèng Mén.
Grand Secretaries of the Palace of the Eastern Prince were selected by the Grand Secretariat;
other yamen officials were selected by their respective seal-holding heads.
Among outer officials,
only grand coordinators and provincial governors were selected by court deliberation,
with the Nine Chief Ministers jointly participating,
and the Ministry of Personnel presiding.
Vacancies for provincial administration and surveillance commissioners
were filled by joint recommendation of officials of the third rank and above.
For surveillance commissioners and administration vice commissioners,
they were promoted in sequence.
As for military commissioners for frontier defense and similar roles,
they were generally selected and recommended,
and issued imperial letters of appointment.
Frontier prefects and subordinate officials also received imperial letters.
Chāngpíng, Jìzhōu, and other places in Jì and Liáo;
Dàtóng, Héqǔ, Dàizhōu, and other places in Shānxī;
Gùyuán, Jìngníng, and sixty-one other places in Shǎnxī
were all considered frontier vacancies,
and their appointments were handled with extra caution.
Those with merit were promoted out of sequence,
while those who erred in managing frontier affairs were punished without pardon.
Inner-land surveillance and administration commissioners were generally promoted in sequence,
but later, many were promoted out of sequence without regard for seniority,
with some experiencing four or five promotions within a year, rising from assistant surveillance commissioner to administration vice commissioner.
Many surveillance and administration commissioners were additionally appointed outside the regular quota,
often establishing several additional titles beyond their regular responsibilities of guarding and touring,
making it impossible to standardize.
Outer prefects, sub-prefects, and county magistrates,
and inner subordinate officials of the various Nine Chief Ministries,
were all regular selection officials.
Their selection, appointment, promotion, and dismissal
were all handled by the Ministry of Personnel.
Initially, the lot-drawing method (*niānjiū fǎ*) was used,
which changed to drawing lots (*chèqiān*) during the Wànlì reign.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Ní Sīhuì, a supernumerary director of the Bureau of Civil Appointments, memorialized eighteen articles on selection policies,
one of which was to discuss drawing lots.
Minister Lǐ Dài proposed its implementation and it was approved,
and Sūn Pīyáng subsequently carried it out.
Although there were later criticisms of its shortcomings,
it was not changed again throughout the Míng dynasty.
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
the system of north-south rotation was established,
with southerners serving in the north,
and northerners serving in the south.
Later, as the official system gradually became fixed,
except for education officials,
one was not allowed to serve in one's home province,
but there were no restrictions on north or south.
Initially,
Tàizǔ once presided over the selection of officials at Fèngtiānmén,
and decreed that qualifications should not be strictly adhered to.
Some selected individuals were immediately appointed Shìláng,
and the Cān-Sī were the most numerous.
Jìnshì, Jiānshēng, and those recommended
were used interchangeably.
Gěishì and Yùshǐ,
were also equally divided between initial appointments and promotions.
After the Yǒnglè and Xuāndé eras,
qualifications were gradually followed,
but the Tái-Shěng still had many initial appointments.
By the Hóngzhì and Zhèngdé eras,
qualifications became strictly adhered to.
Although Jǔrén and Gòngshēng were referred to as "proper paths" alongside Jìnshì,
the disparity in their standing
was as vast as heaven and earth.
During the Lóngqìng reign,
Grand Secretary Gāo Gǒng stated:
"In the early years of the dynasty,
many Jǔrén who reached the Bāzuò became famous officials.
Later, Jìnshì became heavily favored,
while Jǔrén were greatly underestimated,
reaching an extreme by now.
I request that from the time of appointment,
only administrative achievements be considered,
without regard for their origin."
However, the accumulated momentum was too great,
and it could not be reversed.
During the Chóngzhēn reign,
petitioners repeatedly advocated
the idea of "employing all three paths equally."
Occasionally, one or two Jǔrén, such as Chén Xīnjiǎ and Sūn Yuánhuà,
were placed in crucial positions,
but ultimately led to their downfall.
Employing the military Jǔrén Chén Qǐxīn as a Gěishì
also led to his reputation collapsing.
Thus, the court again thought it better to adhere to qualifications.
However, those from the Jiǎbǎng who misguided the nation were also not few.
Gěishìzhōng and Yùshǐ were called Kē-Dào.
There were fifty Kē officials
and one hundred and twenty Dào officials.
From the early Míng dynasty until the Tiānshùn and Chénghuà eras,
Jìnshì, Jǔrén, Gòngshēng, and Jiānshēng could all be selected for appointment.
Those who were promoted,
besides Tuīguān and Zhīxiàn,
sometimes came from the ranks of academic officials.
Later, Jiānshēng and newly promoted Jìnshì were no longer allowed to participate.
Some were appointed after serving as Shùjíshì,
or were selected by examination after three years of service in internal or external departmental positions.
Internally, these included Zhǔshì of the Five Ministries in the two capitals, Zhōng, Háng, Píng, Bó,
Bóshì and Zhùjiào of the Guózǐjiān, etc.
Externally, they included Tuīguān and Zhīxiàn.
Those who entered from Tuīguān and Zhīxiàn positions
were called Xíngqǔ.
For those with special recommendations,
even if their term of service was not yet complete,
they could also participate.
The number of vacancies for Kē-Dào determined the number of candidates selected by examination,
there was no fixed quota.
For their appointments,
the Lìbù and Dūcháyùan collaborated in proposing candidates.
Gěishì were all formally appointed,
while Yùshǐ had to serve a probationary year before formal appointment,
except for Shùjíshì.
During the Jiājìng and Wànlì eras,
it was often decreed that ministerial officials were not allowed to transfer to Kē-Dào,
but this was also occasionally practiced later.
Jǔrén, Gòngshēng, Tuīguān, and Zhīxiàn
were generally allowed to participate in the selection examinations alongside Jìnshì,
but usually only one in four.
During the Jiājìng reign,
Jiānshēng were once allowed to participate in the selection.
This was later abolished.
During the Wànlì reign,
all administrative matters fell into disarray.
In the twenty-fifth year,
the number of new and old officials in the Tái-Shěng was less than half of the established quota.
In the thirty-sixth year,
there were only a few Kē officials,
and only two Dào officials.
A Nán Kē official served concurrently as nine officials for two years,
and there was also only one Nán Dào official.
With the internal bureaus empty,
external assignments were also lacking.
The巡àn for Huái, Yáng, Sū, Sōng, Jiāngxī, Shǎnxī, Guǎngdōng-Xī, Xuāndà, Gānsù, Liáodōng, as well as Shǎnxī's Chámǎ,
and Hédōng's Yánkè,
had vacancies for several years.
Gěishìzhōng Chén Zhì then requested urgent selection by examination,
but received no reply.
In the thirty-ninth year,
a memorial for selection by examination was submitted,
but was again held up in the palace and not acted upon.
Tuīguān and Zhīxiàn nominated for promotion to Tái-Shěng,
awaited orders at the court,
unable to freely leave or stay.
In the forty-sixth year,
Wáng Xiàngfù, the Yùshǐ in charge of Hénán Dào, again stated:
"Among the Yùshǐ of the thirteen Dào, only eight are in active service,
and among the Gěishì of the six Kē, only five are active.
Meanwhile, various assignments such as enfeoffment and examination supervision,
as well as those who have completed their external tours and reported illness or sought replacements, arrive in succession.
An urgent discussion on adaptable methods is needed."
Grand Secretary Fāng Cóngzhé also stated:
"The officials selected by examination
have waited for six years,
enduring many hardships.
The Lìbù's proposal to consult the Lǐbù and Dūcháyùan to assign them in order
is merely a stopgap measure.
It would be better to specifically approve the Lìbù's nominations,
so that these officials can now receive their appointments and perform their duties,
thereby maintaining the integrity of the administration."
Ultimately, none were acted upon.
It was not until the early reign of Guāngzōng
that all previous memorials for selection by examination were approved,
and the Tái-Shěng suddenly became densely staffed.
According to the examination selection regulations,
the excellent candidates were appointed Gěishìzhōng,
the next best as Yùshǐ,
and the next best were used as departmental officials.
Although there was an examination at the time,
there were pre-existing recommendation lists,
from the hands of the Jiǔqīng and Tái-Shěng officials,
which were often used to determine rankings.
In the third year of Chóngzhēn,
after the Lìbù completed its selections,
it memorialized to promote a certain number of Gěishì and Yùshǐ,
and for two Zhōngshū whose recommendation lists differed regarding their suitability,
a memorial was submitted for imperial decision.
The Emperor criticized them for evasion,
ordering a more definitive resolution,
but did not criticize the impropriety of the recommendation lists.
Beijing officials who were not Jìnshì could not be selected by examination,
while Tuīguān and Zhīxiàn, whether Jǔrén or Gòngshēng, all underwent Xíngqǔ.
However, among the prefects and magistrates nationwide,
Jìnshì accounted for thirteen,
and Jǔrén/Gòngshēng for seventeen;
whereas for Tuīguān and Zhīxiàn selected by Xíngqǔ,
Jìnshì accounted for nineteen,
and Jǔrén/Gòngshēng only eleven.
What Jǔrén/Gòngshēng obtained
was largely Tái positions but not Shěng positions,
and more in the south than in the north.
Yùshǐ Wáng Dàochún spoke of this.
The Emperor said that in employing people, talent should be considered,
and that it was not appropriate to adhere to qualifications,
and ordered the relevant departments to consider implementing it.
Initially,
for urgent vacancies in the censorate,
Xíngqǔ was conducted irregularly.
During the Shénzōng era,
it was set at once every three years,
but by this time, it was held annually.
The Emperor followed the request of Lìbù Shàngshū Mǐn Hóngxué
to return to a three-year cycle.
This is the general overview of selecting officials for the censorate and remonstrance.
Recommendations (Bǎojǔ)
were intended to supplement the shortcomings of the official selection system
and to share the power of the Lìbù.
This began in the seventeenth year of Hóngwǔ, when all officials attending court were ordered to recommend honest and capable subordinates.
In the first year of Yǒnglè, it was decreed that Beijing officials of civil rank seven and above,
and external officials down to county magistrates,
should each recommend one person they knew,
who would then be promoted according to their talent.
Later, if those recommended were found to be corrupt,
the recommenders were implicated,
and this law was also occasionally put into practice.
However, during the Hóngwǔ and Yǒnglè eras,
the selection of officials was still uniformly initiated by the ministries.
Early in the reign of Rénzōng,
all administrative affairs were reformed.
In the first year of Hóngxī, a special order for recommendation and promotion was issued.
Metropolitan officials of the fifth rank and above, as well as Censorate officials and Supervising Secretaries,

and external officials, namely the principal and assistant officers of the two provincial administrations (Bùzhèngshī and Ànchásī) and the principal officers of prefectures (fǔ), subprefectures (zhōu), and counties (xiàn),
were each to recommend those they knew.
However, incumbent principal and assistant officers of prefectures, subprefectures, and counties, and those who had committed crimes of embezzlement,
were not allowed to be recommended.
Other officials, or those who were relegated to lower ranks,
or military and civilian personnel who were honest, upright, and capable of governance,
were all to be reported by name.
At that time,
the power of metropolitan officials was not yet great.
When officials of the Censorate and the Six Ministries completed their terms of assessment,
they were promoted by the Ministry of Personnel to become regional prefects.
Later, a system was established
that whenever there was a vacancy in the two provincial administrations (Bùzhèngshī and Ànchásī) or for a prefect (zhīfǔ),
metropolitan officials of the third rank and above were to recommend candidates.
In the third year of Xuāndé,
Kuàng Zhōng, Zhào Yù, and others were appointed as prefects of Sūzhōu, Sōngjiāng, and other prefectures through recommendation,
and edicts were bestowed for them to take office.
In the tenth year, Guō Jì, Yáo Wén, and others were appointed as prefects,
also in the same manner.
Among those recommended and presented were
department directors (lángzhōng), assistant department directors (yuánwài), censors (yùshǐ), as well as secretaries (sīwù), couriers (xíngrén), and vice-abbots (sìfù),
which was not according to the usual regulations.
Many of them later had excellent administrative achievements.
Ministry clerks and censors,
recommended and introduced by their superior officials,
were mostly capable in their offices.
As for those who headed the Ministry of Personnel,
Jiǎn Yì and Guō Jǐn also received imperial edicts repeatedly.
The emperor also worried that his officials might be afraid of joint implication and thus would not recommend,
so he spoke to Grand Secretary Yáng Pǔ about the difficulty of finding complete talents,
saying:
"How can a single recommendation
guarantee their conduct for life?
To obtain virtuous talents,
it is even more important to strengthen the methods of education and cultivation."
Therefore, at that time, government administration flourished,
reaching its zenith.
This continued into the reign of Yīngzōng,
who fully adhered to the old ways.
However, as it was practiced for a long time,
it could not be without flaws.
Those recommended might be relatives from one's hometown, old acquaintances, or subordinates and protégés,
who had a history of private association.
Prominent regional officials such as Fāng Zhèng and Xiè Zhuāng were disgraced due to their recommendations.
And for those without official recommendations,
inside the court, censors,
and outside, prefects,
often remained unpromoted for nine years.
In the seventh year of Zhèngtǒng, the system of recommending county magistrates was abolished.
In the eleventh year,
Censor Huáng Shāng said:
"In the early days of the dynasty, Supervising Secretaries and Censors
were promoted by memorial to regional prefects.
In recent years, regional prefects are mostly promoted through recommendations by court officials.
Supervising Secretaries and Censors, whose duty is to impeach and censure,
how can they not displease someone?
I request that the Ministry of Personnel be ordered to continue to propose appointments and dismissals according to regulations."
The emperor agreed with his words
and ordered the ministry to discuss and implement it.
The following year,
Supervising Secretary Yú Biàn again pointed out that Fāng Zhèng and Xiè Zhuāng's affairs had failed,
and argued that the recommenders should be held accountable.
He also stated that when there was a vacancy for a regional prefect,
the Ministry of Personnel should propose it for the emperor's decision.
Minister Wáng Zhí, Duke of Yīngguó Zhāng Fǔ, and others stated
that many regional prefects appointed through recommendation
were competent,
and the system should not be rashly changed.
Yīngzōng still followed the advice of Zhāng Fǔ and Wáng Zhí,
but adopted Yú Biàn's memorial,
allowing censorial officials to impeach.
In the thirteenth year,
Censor Tú Qiān again submitted a memorial,
pointing out the malpractice of recommendees who became regional prefects immediately changing their previous conduct.
He requested to revert to the old Hóngwǔ system,
selecting and promoting officials from those within and outside the court who had completed their nine-year assessment,
or personally selecting court officials of talent and prestige to appoint.
The imperial edict approved this.
The system of high officials recommending officials
was thus abolished.
During the Jǐngtài reign,
recommendation was resumed.
Supervising Secretary Lín Cōng presented the disadvantages of rapid promotion through recommendation,
saying:
"Currently, there are over thirty vacancies for officials like Vice-Administrators (Cānzhèng).
I request that for now, officials of the third rank and above be allowed to recommend.
Thereafter, only officials of the third rank and above from the two provincial administrations (Bùzhèngshī and Ànchásī) should jointly recommend,
and all others should be left to the Ministry of Personnel."
The imperial edict agreed to both.
In the fifth year of Chénghuà,
censorial officials again requested recommendation for regional positions,
and the Ministry of Personnel included prefects as well.
The emperor followed the request of the censorial officials,
but ordered that vacancies for prefects still be handled by the Ministry of Personnel's recommendations.
A year later,
because many joint recommendations were found inappropriate,
even for regional officials, only two candidates were to be recommended by the Ministry of Personnel for imperial review,
and the order for recommendation was abolished.
Later, Censor-in-Chief Lǐ Bīn requested that metropolitan officials of the fifth rank and above who were in charge of affairs, as well as Supervising Secretaries and Censors,
each recommend those they knew for appointments in subprefectures and counties.
This was granted.
In the twelfth year of Hóngzhì, another edict ordered ministers of the ministries and censorial offices to each recommend regional prefects.

The Ministry of Personnel then requested to follow the precedents of previous years, such as Mǎ Wénshēng's promotion to Provincial Censor-in-Chief (Ànchásǐ) and Tú Xiōng's promotion to Vice Censor-in-Chief (Qiāndūyùshǐ),
to exceptionally promote one or two individuals
to encourage and incentivize,
and also to consider those not recommended by high officials.
All of their proposals were followed.
At that time,
Xiàozōng was keen on effective governance,
and ordered the Ministries of Personnel and War
to submit a detailed report of the careers of all metropolitan and regional civil and military officials in both capitals
every season for imperial review.
However, this was conducted in conjunction with the recommendation system,
not relying solely on it for governance.
After the Zhèngdé reign,
the system of submitting detailed reports gradually fell into disuse.
In the eighth year of Jiājìng,
Supervising Secretary Xià Yán again requested to follow the Hóngzhì precedent,
and also to briefly outline the recommendation and impeachment of worthy and unworthy officials.
In the first month of each season,
the ministers of the ministries were to send these to the censorial offices to be presented to the emperor.
It was decreed to establish this as a regulation.
However, the method of recommending regional prefects
was never revived for the rest of the Míng dynasty.
As for those dismissed from office due to involvement in incidents, or promoted for their urgent talents,
this was called 'restoration from dismissal.'
Those recalled from home and pre-appointed due to a need for vacancies
were called 'additional appointments.'
These were aspects of the personnel selection system that were not detailed,
but were occasionally implemented in the middle and later periods.
Term assessment (kǎomǎn) and performance evaluation (kǎochá)
were two methods that complemented each other.
Kǎomǎn
assessed an individual's salary history,
with three categories: competent (chēngzhí),
ordinary (píngcháng),
and incompetent (bùchēngzhí),
corresponding to upper, middle, and lower grades.
Kǎochá
evaluated all officials, both metropolitan and external, throughout the empire,
with eight categories: greedy (tān),
cruel (kù),
frivolous and impetuous (fúzao),
inadequate (bùjí),
old (lǎo),
sick (bìng),
retired or incompetent (bà),
and indiscreet (bùjǐn).
The kǎomǎn system
issued a certificate after three years,
called the first assessment (chūkǎo);
after six years, the second assessment (zàikǎo);
and after nine years, the comprehensive assessment (tōngkǎo).
Promotions and demotions were determined according to duties and regulations.
For those affiliated with the various ministries and temples,
initially they were only provisionally appointed;
they would only receive substantive appointments after completing their kǎomǎn.
External officials were generally assessed in stages awaiting review.
Miscellaneous assessments sometimes occurred after one or two years,
or three years, or nine years.
If the complexity of prefectures and counties did not match the official's capacity,
their positions would be interchanged,
known as 'transferring to a busy post' (diàofán) or 'transferring to a simple post' (diàojiǎn).
In the eleventh year of Hóngwǔ, the Ministry of Personnel was ordered to assess the merits and demerits of officials attending the imperial audience.
Those who were competent and without fault were rated as superior,
granted seats and invited to a banquet.
Those with faults but who were competent were rated as middle,
invited to a banquet but not granted seats.
Those with faults and who were incompetent were rated as inferior,
not invited to the banquet,
and stood in sequence at the gate.
Only after the banquet guests departed
were they allowed to leave.
This marked the beginning of the assessment of officials attending the imperial audience.
In the fourteenth year,
its regulations were gradually settled.
In the capital, officials of the Six Boards below the fifth rank
were subject to assessment of their conduct and ability by the principal officer of their own yámén,
who would also verify their diligence or idleness.
Officials of the fourth rank and above,
as well as all close attendants and censors (yùshǐ) who served as the eyes, ears, and enforcers of discipline,
and officials of the Tài Yī Yuàn, Qīn Tiān Jiān, and princely (wángfǔ) establishments who were not part of the regular selection,
were, upon completion of their terms, subject to promotion or demotion
at the emperor's discretion.
Principal officers and subordinate officials of the direct administration (zhílì)
were assessed by the principal officer of their own yámen,
and upon completion of their terms, re-assessed by an investigating censor (jiānchá yùshǐ).
Principal officers of the various Administration Commissions (bùzhèng shǐsī)
were all assessed by the Surveillance Commission (ànchá sī).

Principal officers of the Tea and Horse Commissions (chámǎ tíjǔ sī), Salt and Horse Commissions (yánmǎ tíjǔ sī), Salt Distribution Commissions (yányùn sī), Salt Revenue Commissions (yánkè tíjǔ sī), and military officers
were all assessed by the Administration Commission (bùzhèng sī),
and then sent to the Surveillance Commission (ànchá sī) for re-assessment.
Officials of the Administration Commission (bùzhèng sī) of the fourth rank and above,
and those of the Surveillance Commission (ànchá sī) and Salt Distribution Commission (yányùn sī) of the fifth rank and above,
were, upon completion of their terms, subject to promotion or demotion
at the emperor's discretion.
Internal and external officials entering the flow of promotion (rùliú) and miscellaneous officials (zá zhíguān),
upon completion of a nine-year term,
were issued a certificate to report to the Ministry of Personnel (lìbù) for assessment,
and were promoted or demoted according to established rules.
If there were any with exceptional merit or extraordinary abilities who surpassed their peers,
their cases were decided at the emperor's discretion.
Furthermore, the complexity or simplicity of their duties
and their performance (excellence or mediocrity) in previous official posts
were mutually considered and assessed
to determine their grade for promotion or demotion.
Regarding the criteria for complexity or simplicity:
in external prefectures (wàifǔ), those with land tax and grain revenue of 150,000 shí or more,
in departments (zhōu) with 70,000 shí or more,
in counties (xiàn) with 30,000 shí or more,
or those directly facing princely (wángfǔ) establishments, the three commissions (dūbùzhèng, ànchá sāisī),
or having military garrisons,
or located on an important post road,
or serving as a critical supply point on the frontier,
were all deemed to have complex duties.
Prefectures with grain revenue less than 150,000 shí,
departments less than 70,000 shí,
counties less than 30,000 shí,
and those in quiet, remote areas,
were all deemed to have simple duties.
All agencies in the capital
were uniformly subject to the "complex duties" category.
In the sixteenth year,
the system for assessing capital officials was slightly adjusted;
all were to be reported by their superiors to the Ministry for assessment.
In the eighteenth year,

the Ministry of Personnel (lìbù) reported that among the 4,117 officials from administration, surveillance, prefectural, departmental, and county yámen who presented themselves for imperial audience (cháojìn),
one-tenth were deemed competent,
seven-tenths were ordinary,
one-tenth were incompetent,
and another one-tenth were corrupt and mediocre.
The emperor ordered that those deemed competent be promoted,
the ordinary be reinstated,
the incompetent be demoted,
the corrupt be handed over to the judicial authorities for punishment,
and the mediocre be dismissed as commoners.
During the Yǒnglè and Xuāndé reigns,
officials, both inside and outside the capital, for whom no previous regulations existed,
were gradually incorporated into the system.
It was also agreed, according to the Ministry's proposal,
that if an official's first assessment was "competent," their second assessment was not yet conducted, and their current assessment was "competent,"
or if their first assessment was "ordinary," their second assessment was not yet conducted, and their current assessment was "competent,"
they would all be promoted according to the standard for "competent" officials.
From that time onward,
the old system was largely followed.
While the advantages and disadvantages during this period are too numerous to list,
the fundamental regulations remained largely unchanged.
Regarding the system of assessment (kǎochá),
capital officials were assessed every six years,
in the years of Jǐ and Hài.
Those of the fourth rank and above declared their own performance for the emperor's decision.
Those of the fifth rank and below were categorized differently for retirement (zhìshì), demotion (jiàngdiào), or dismissal as commoners (xiánzhù wéimín).
A roster was submitted for imperial approval,
and this was called Jīngchá (Capital Assessment).
From the Hóngzhì reign,
it was stipulated that external officials would have an imperial audience (cháojìn) every three years,
in the years of Chén, Xū, Chǒu, and Wèi.
The assessment (chádiǎn) followed this,
and was called Wàichá (External Assessment).
Departments and counties reported monthly to their respective prefectures;
prefectures summarized these assessments
and reported annually to the Administration Commission (bùzhèng sī).
After three years,
the Grand Coordinator (fǔ) and the Censor-in-Chief (àn) would jointly review the conduct of their subordinates,
prepare a roster for report,
and categorize them using the "Eight Methods" (bāfǎ).
There were four types of disciplinary actions for assessments,
the same as for capital officials.
Implemented in the early Míng dynasty,
it was continuously observed,
and was called Dàjì (Grand Reckoning).
Those who were punished by the reckoning
were never to be re-employed,
and this became a permanent system.
In the fourth year of Hóngwǔ, Zhū Shǒurén, Minister of Works (gōngbù shàngshū), was ordered to inspect the officials of Láizhōu and other commanderies in Shāndōng.

In the sixth year, the Censorate (yùshǐ tái) and the surveillance commissions (ànchá sī) of various circuits (dào) were ordered to investigate whether local officials (yǒusī guān) had committed any offenses,
and to report their findings for promotion or demotion.
This was the beginning of the assessment system (kǎochá).
During the Hóngxī reign,
censors (yùshǐ) were ordered to assess external officials.
Since those entrusted with the imperial mandate could not be entirely impartial,
Jiǎn Yì, Minister of Personnel (lìbù shàngshū), was instructed to strictly admonish them
to ensure utmost fairness.
In the second year of Jǐngtài,
the Ministry of Personnel (lìbù) and the Censorate (dūchá yuàn) assessed over 730 officials who were to be dismissed.
The emperor, fearing the decision might be inappropriate,
convened other high ministers to re-assess them,
and one-third were retained.
In the fifth year of Chénghuà,
Zhāng Lún, Right Vice Minister of Personnel of Nánjīng (nánjīng lìbù yòushìláng), and Gāo Míng, Right Vice Censor-in-Chief (dūchá yuàn yòumián dūyùshǐ), assessed probationary officials (shùguān).
The emperor, noting that the seal-holding officials of the various yámen did not all sign off,
suspected some impropriety,
and ordered Vice Minister Yè Shèng and Supervising Secretary Máo Hóng (dū gěishìzhōng) to conduct a public investigation,
which also resulted in some changes.
In the sixth year of Hóngzhì, a total of 1,400 officials were to be dismissed,
along with 1,135 miscellaneous officials.
The emperor decreed:
"For regional prefects (fāngmiàn zhīfǔ), there must be concrete evidence,
not vague or generalized statements,
to avoid wrongful accusations.
For officials below the prefectural and departmental levels who have served less than three years,
a comprehensive review should also be conducted and reported."
Minister Wáng Shù and others presented their arguments requesting this,
emphasizing that even if their tenure was short, corrupt and harmful prefectural, departmental, and county officials
must not be allowed to remain in office.
However, the emperor ultimately believed that talented individuals were hard to come by,
and issued repeated instructions,
granting many pardons.
Over ninety officials who were supposed to be dismissed were retained.
Supervising secretaries (gěishì) and censors (yùshǐ) again submitted memorials requesting the dismissal of those overlooked and those who should have retired but were retained.
The emperor again ordered the Ministry of Personnel (lìbù) to provide concrete evidence,
and Minister Shù submitted the evaluation reports of various officials and the Ministry's investigation results for imperial review.
The emperor ultimately considered the evaluation reports not entirely accurate,
and ordered a re-assessment.
Minister Shù, feeling his words were disregarded,
and suspecting foul play,
forcefully sought to resign.
By the fourteenth year,
Lín Hàn, Minister of Personnel of Nánjīng (nánjīng lìbù shàngshū), stated
that external officials below the level of bureau (sī) and prefecture (fǔ)
were assessed once every three years,
and military officials in both capitals and outside
were assessed and selected once every five years,
but officials of the fifth rank and below in both capitals
were assessed only once every ten years,
which was a major oversight in the system.
An imperial edict was issued,
and the Ministry of Personnel (lìbù) reiterated its request in line with Lín Hàn's words,
and thus the rule for assessing capital officials every six years was established.
In the year of the Jīngchá,
high ministers declared their own performance.
Once decisions for retention or dismissal were made,
if officials were found to have overlooked misconduct,
supervising secretaries (gěishì) and censors (yùshǐ) would impeach them,
a process called Shíyí (Picking up Omissions).
Those targeted by Shíyí
could not escape.
During the Hóngzhì, Zhèngdé, Jiājìng, and Lóngqìng reigns,
scholar-officials valued their integrity and reputation,
considering being subject to an assessment punishment (guà chádiǎn) a lifelong blemish.
By the Wànlì reign,
Grand Secretaries (gécén) sometimes showed favoritism,
occasionally retaining one or two officials to obstruct the assessment system.
Moreover, the intense factional disputes among officials,
most notably in the Xīnhài and Dīngsì years,
are detailed in their respective biographies.
Once factions were formed,
they retaliated against each other
until the fall of the dynasty.
The Ministry of War (Bīngbù) had four departments.
Among them, the Department of Military Appointments (Wǔxuǎn) managed appointments and dismissals,
and the Department of Provisions (Zhífāng) managed military administration.
Their duties were particularly important.
Regarding all military positions,
internally there were the Five Chief Military Commissions (Wǔfǔ) and the Guard Command (Liúshǒusī);
externally there were the various Regional Military Commissions (Dūsī), various Garrisons (Wèisuǒ), and the Three Pacification Commissions (Sānxuān) and Six Comfort Commissions (Liùwèi).
For regular officials, there were eight ranks: Grand Commissioner (Dūdū), Associate Grand Commissioner (Tóngzhī), and Assistant Grand Commissioner (Qiānshì);
Regional Commander (Dūzhǐhuīshǐ), Associate Regional Commander (Tóngzhī), and Assistant Regional Commander (Qiānshì);
and Chief and Associate Guard Commanders (Zhèng Fù Liúshǒu).
For hereditary officials, there were nine ranks: Commander (Zhǐhuīshǐ), Associate Commander (Tóngzhī), and Assistant Commander (Qiānshì);
Garrison Commander (Wèi Suǒ Zhènfǔ);
Chief and Associate Company Commanders (Zhèng Fù Qiānhù);
Centurion (Bǎihù);
and Provisional Centurion (Shìbǎihù).
There were twenty-one Regional Commanders (Dūzhǐhuīshǐ) in the directly administered provinces,
two Guard Commands (Liúshǒusī),
ninety-one Garrisons (Wèi),
and two hundred eleven battalions for defense, agricultural colonies, and pasture management (Shǒuyù Túntián Qúnmù Qiānhùsuǒ).
Beyond these were the native chieftaincies (Miao Man Tǔsī),
all subject to selection by the Ministry.
From the early years of the Yǒnglè era,
three major encampments (Sāndàyíng) were established,
each with drilling officers (Guǎncāoguān),
and each battalion (shào) had branch managers (fēnguǎn), camp officers (zuòyíngguān), and departmental officers (zuòsīguān).
During the Jǐngtài era,
ten regiment encampments (tuányíng) were established,
and two more were later added.
Each had its own camp officers (zuòyíngguān),
all specially appointed and supervised by trusted high officials,
and not subject to the Ministry of War's (Bīngbù) selection.
General selections (dàxuǎn) were based on:
ethnicity (sèmù),
appearance (zhuàngmào),
talent and conduct (cáixíng),
enfeoffment and bestowal (fēngzèng),
and inheritance and protection (xíyìn).
There were four paths (tú):
hereditary office (shìzhí),
military jinshi (wǔjǔ),
military service (hángwǔ),
and purchase of rank (nàjí).
Initially,
military positions were primarily held by those of merit and long service.
Emperor Tàizǔ, concerned about their lack of discipline,
issued the "Records of Training and Admonishing Military Officers" (Wǔshì Xùnjiè Lù) and the "Great Edict for Military Officials" (Dàgào Wǔchén Lù).
Later, military talent was also considered,
with triennial military jinshi examinations (sānsuì wǔjǔ),
sexennial metropolitan military examinations (liùsuì huìjǔ),
and annual recommendations (měisuì jiànjǔ),
all falling under the Ministry's appointments and dismissals.
Over time,
discipline deteriorated,
and selections became chaotic.
During the Zhèngdé era,
more than three thousand individuals falsely claimed achievements and were promoted.
During the Jiājìng era,
Grand Secretary Zhānshì Huò Tāo stated: "During the Chénghuà era,
the number of military positions from Emperor Tàizǔ's time quadrupled;
now it has increased several more times.
The Brocade-Clad Guard (Jǐnyīwèi) initially had a quota of 205 officers;
now it has reached 1,700
officers,
almost an eightfold increase.
In the early Hóngwǔ era,
the sons of those who inherited positions for military merit, aged twenty, were tested.
If they failed the initial test,
they inherited the position provisionally and received half pay.
After two
years, they were retested;
those who passed received full pay,
while those who still failed were banished to the military.
This system was extremely strict,
so positions were not redundant and salaries were easy to disburse.
Since the Yǒnglè era,
new officials
were exempt from testing,
and although old officials were still tested,
bribery ensured that no one failed.
This is why military positions have become increasingly excessive.
During the Yǒnglè campaign in Jiāozhǐ,
rewards were given without promotion.
Recently, not
only were those who captured enemy heads promoted,
but also those who reported and captured rebels and bandits were all promoted.
This is why military positions have become even more redundant.
It is appropriate to order high officials to follow the precedent of the 'Clear Register' (Qīnghuáng)
and examine all internal and external military positions, their ranks, and merits,
investigating the generational inheritance through ancestors,
and succession through uncles, nephews, and brothers.
Whether
their merit was from the Hóngwǔ or Yǒnglè eras,
or from after the Xuāndé era,
or an act of grace for imperial eunuchs' brothers and nephews,
or for the descendants of meritorious relatives and imperial sons-in-law,
or through passing the military jinshi examination,
they should be
ranked into various grades,
implicitly incorporating methods of reduction and streamlining.
Perhaps they may inherit hereditarily,
perhaps for life,
perhaps their descendants may succeed,
or perhaps not.
Detailed registers should be kept,
clearly displayed,
to
serve as encouragement and discouragement."
Consequently, officials like Supervising Secretary (Gěishìzhōng) Xià Yán were ordered to investigate false claims and redundancies.
Xià Yán and others pointed out the abuses,
stating:
"Garrison commanders (Zhènshǒuguān) previously reported only five attached personnel (zòudài),
but now it reaches three or four hundred.
There are cases where one person reports attached personnel in several places,
and cases where multiple places gain merit at the same time.
Others cleverly devise new names for merit,
and verification records are not thoroughly reviewed,
nor are selections subject to scrutiny and rejection.
Such practices as rectifying and re-promoting, or combining merits for additional conferment,
result in countless abuses.
All should be abolished to demonstrate divine judgment."
The Ministry reviewed and approved the proposal.
Those who gained positions through favoritism and were redundant
were reduced by several thousands,
clearing out long-standing parasites.
In the fifteenth year of the Wànlì era, an edict was again issued to strictly investigate.
Moreover, orders were given for the Regional Commanders (Tí-Zhèn) and Censorate (Kē Dào) to cooperate with the Ministry of War (Bīngbù)
to assess seniority by age,
evaluate skills,
and rank recommendations,
dividing them into three grades,
named "Public Selection" (Gōngxuǎn).
However, this was merely a superficial gesture,
ultimately yielding little practical effect.
Military officials' noble titles stopped at the sixth rank.
If an official died, his position was inherited;
if old or infirm, he was replaced.
If the lineage became extinct over time,
a collateral branch would succeed.
If one reached sixty years of age,
a son would replace him.
According to regulations set in the early Míng dynasty,
