the legitimate son inherited or replaced,
with priority given by age.
If the legitimate line died out,
the legitimate son's illegitimate son or grandson
would succeed;
if that line also died out,
a brother would succeed.
After the Yǒnglè era,
surviving military personnel (qíjūn yúdīng) from official families (guānshè) who had distinguished themselves in battle
were allowed to inherit or replace positions with their original salaries and responsibilities.
All followed this.
Their demoted descendants would still replace them in the demoted position.
During the Hóngzhì era,
collateral branches were allowed to inherit with a reduction in rank.
During the Zhèngdé era,
collateral branches were ordered to enter the general banner (zǒngqí).
During the Jiājìng era,
collateral branches without merit
were not allowed to be recommended.
All promoted officials from official families
held positions similar to their fathers'.
Those who died in battle and were granted hereditary succession
were given the first rank for regular officials.
All officials who inherited or replaced positions
were tested in horsemanship and archery.
Generally, hereditary positions were difficult to scrutinize,
hence the detailed regulations,
but they also bred numerous abuses and corrupt practices.
Nor were these few.
For high-ranking officials,
a joint recommendation was required.
For vacancies in the seal-holding positions of the Five Chief Military Commissions (Wǔjūn Dūdūfǔ),
one person was selected from among the incumbent Dukes (Gōng), Marquises (Hóu), and Earls (Bó).
For vacancies as Co-Administrators (Qiānshū),
two persons were recommended from among Dukes (Gōng), Marquises (Hóu), and Earls (Bó) receiving salaries, as well as Regional Commanders (Dūzhǐhuī) in the capital,
and Chief and Associate Grand Generals (Zhèng Fù Zǒngbīngguān) outside the capital.
For the high-ranking officials of the Brocade-Clad Guard (Jǐnyīwèi) and the seal-holding positions of the Vanguard Guard (Qiánwèi),
two persons were recommended following the precedent of the Five Chief Military Commissions (Wǔfǔ).
For Regional Commanders (Dūzhǐhuī) and Guard Commanders (Liúshǒu) and below,
one person was recommended.

In the sixteenth year of the Zhèngdé era, it was ordered that officials of the Five Chief Military Commissions (Wǔfǔ) and the Brocade-Clad Guard (Jǐnyīwèi) must be promoted from among Regional Commanders (Dūzhǐhuī) who had repeatedly demonstrated merit.
Officials of other Garrisons (Zhūwèi) were not hereditary,
only those of the Brocade-Clad Guard (Jǐnyīwèi) were hereditary.
The military governance
of military officers was like the investigation of civil officials.
In the second year of Chénghuà, it was decreed that an assessment be conducted every five years,
whereby all incumbent officials holding seals, those drawing salaries, those engaged in operational duties, and those newly inheriting office would be assessed as a whole.
In the thirteenth year, it was decreed that a general assessment be conducted in both capitals as a regular practice.
Ministers of the Five Chief Military Commissions and senior officials of the Jǐnyī Wèi would make self-reports pending imperial decree.
The regional commanders-in-chief of the directly administered provinces would do likewise.
Officials belonging to the Five Chief Military Commissions within the capital, as well as those in the garrisons of the directly administered provinces,
were all to be reported and recommended by the inspecting officials and Board officials.
Outside the capital, officials of the Regional Military Commissions and garrisons
were to have their rosters compiled by the Grand Coordinators and Censor-in-Chiefs and submitted to the Board.
For officials from Vice Assistant down
to Company Commander and above,

the Three Judicial Offices (Regional Military Commission, Provincial Administration Commission, and Provincial Surveillance Commission) would investigate, report, and submit them to the Grand Coordinator,
who would then consult the Board for assessment, recommendation, and memorialization to the throne.
Those in the Jǐnyī Wèi responsible for military affairs were to be assessed with extra rigor;
the Northern and Southern Commanders of the Jǐnyī Wèi were next in stringency.
The same applied by regulation to officials in various garrisons, local defense units, and all Regional Military Commissions subordinate to the Grand Coordinator.
However, those in charge of grain transport were exempt from the assessment.
Collation Notes
Records, Chapter 48: Officials (1)
The official system of the Míng Dynasty
followed the old systems of the Hàn and Táng Dynasties, with additions and deletions.
Since the thirteenth year of Hóngwǔ, when the position of Chancellor was abolished and not re-established,
the administration of the Central Secretariat was divided and transferred to the Six Boards.
The Ministers (shàngshū) were made responsible for all affairs of the realm,
with the Vice Ministers (shìláng) assisting them.
The Grand Secretaries of the Palace and Hall merely served as consultants.
When the emperor personally wielded the levers of power,
the Grand Secretaries rarely participated in decision-making.
Impeachment was the responsibility of the Censorate,
memorials were conveyed by the Office of Transmission,
and reversals of judgments were referred to the Grand Court of Revision.
This also reflected the lingering influence of the Hàn Dynasty's Nine Ministers.
The Grand Military Commission was divided into five,
and military levies and deployments were overseen by the Board of War.
Outside the capital, the Three Judicial Offices (Regional Military Commission, Provincial Administration Commission, and Provincial Surveillance Commission) were established,
responsible for military, judicial, financial, and grain matters,
while their assessments were left to the Chief Military Commissions and Boards.
At this time, the powers of the Boards of Civil Office, Revenue, and War were significant.
By the reigns of Rénzōng and Xuānzōng,
the Grand Secretaries, by virtue of their status as tutors to the crown prince,
were successively promoted to the Three Solitary Ones,
and their prestige grew further.
Xuānzōng, regardless of the importance of the internal affairs,
submitted all matters to Grand Secretaries Yáng Shìqí and others for their consideration and approval.
Although Jiǎn Yì of the Board of Civil Office and Xià Yuánjí of the Board of Revenue were occasionally summoned for audiences
and allowed to participate in the affairs of various Boards,
such opportunities were rare and their closeness did not compare to that of Shìqí and the others.
From then on,
the power of the Grand Secretariat grew daily.
Even if one or two heads of the Boards of Civil Office or War attempted to dispute right and wrong,
they would invariably fail.
By the middle of Shìzōng's reign,
Xià Yán and Yán Sōng successively held power,
thereby becoming truly prominent chancellors,
suppressing the Six Ministers.
However, the Grand Secretariat's drafting of edicts
could not be finalized without the imperial eunuchs' vermilion endorsements,
and thus the power of the chancellor was transferred to the palace eunuchs.
Consequently, the order of the imperial court,
and the advancement or retreat of virtuous scholar-officials,
were entirely manipulated by their hands.
The "companion eaters" (sycophants) were too busy conforming to their intentions,
and even if there were occasional virtuous assistants,
they could only watch helplessly and could not save the situation.
Initially,
those who led the Five Chief Military Commissions
were all distinguished meritorious officials and veteran generals,
and the military system was orderly.
During the Yǒnglè reign,
eunuchs were appointed to supervise military affairs,
but they still dared not be reckless.
After several generations of custom,
meritorious relatives and debauched scions managed military discipline,
which daily grew more lax and corrupt.
Eventually, more and more eunuchs were added,
with inspecting eunuchs at every frontier,
and supervising eunuchs for all major campaigns in the four directions.
Thus, frontier affairs deteriorated greatly,
and the Míng Dynasty's fate became unsustainable.
Tracing the causes of its rise and fall, its order and disorder,
how could it not lie in the success or failure of employing personnel!
As for the establishment of offices and division of duties,
the system of mutual support,
and the complete regulations,
they are detailed in the subsequent chapters.
Readers may examine them to understand.

Court of the Imperial Clan; Three Ducal Ministers and Three Solitary Ones; Three Grand Tutors and Three Junior Tutors to the Crown Prince; Grand Secretariat; Board of Civil Office; Board of Revenue (with the Director-General of Granaries and Storehouses attached); Board of Rites; Board of War (with the Assistant Administrator of Military Affairs for the Capital Garrisons attached); Board of Punishments; Board of Works (with the Supervisor of the Yìzhōu Mountain Factories attached)
Court of the Imperial Clan (Zōngrén Fǔ).
One Zōngrén Líng (Chief of the Imperial Clan),
one Left Zōngzhèng and one Right Zōngzhèng (Imperial Clan Director),
one Left Zōngrén and one Right Zōngrén (Imperial Clan Minister).
(All are Senior First Rank.)
They were in charge of the registers of the imperial nine clans,
periodically revising the imperial genealogy (yùdié),
recording matters concerning the legitimate and illegitimate children of the imperial clan, their names, enfeoffments, succession, births, deaths, marriages, posthumous titles, and burials.
Whenever members of the imperial clan submitted petitions,
these were reported to the emperor,
and their talents were presented,
and their transgressions recorded.
Initially,
in the third year of Hóngwǔ, the Grand Court of the Imperial Clan (Dàzōngzhèng Yuàn) was established.
In the twenty-second year, it was reorganized into the Court of the Imperial Clan (Zōngrén Fǔ),
and concurrently led by imperial princes.
(Qín Wáng Shǎng was the Líng;
Jìn Wáng Gāng and Yān Wáng Dì were the Left and Right Zōngzhèng;
Zhōu Wáng Sù and Chǔ Wáng Zhēn were the Left and Right Zōngrén.)
Thereafter,
meritorious relatives and high-ranking ministers provisionally managed the affairs of the Fǔ,
without holding permanent official titles,
and its responsibilities were entirely transferred to the Board of Rites.
Its subordinate office was
the Bureau of Records (Jīnglì Sī),
with one Jīnglì (Registrar).
(Senior Fifth Rank.)
Responsible for receiving and dispatching documents.
The Grand Preceptor (tàishī), Grand Tutor (tàifù), and Grand Guardian (tàibǎo) constituted the Three Ducal Ministers (Sān Gōng).
(Senior First Rank.)
The Junior Preceptor (shàoshī), Junior Tutor (shàofù), and Junior Guardian (shàobǎo) constituted the Three Solitary Ones (Sān Gū).
(Junior First Rank.)
They were responsible for assisting the Son of Heaven in managing yin and yang,
governing the state, and propagating enlightenment.
Their duties were extremely important.
There was no fixed number of appointees,
nor were they exclusively assigned.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, Lǐ Shàncháng was appointed Grand Preceptor,
and Xú Dá was appointed Grand Tutor.
(Previously,
Cháng Yùchūn had already been posthumously granted Grand Guardian.)
None of the Three Solitary Ones held concurrent positions.
During the Jiànwén and Yǒnglè periods, the offices of Ducal Ministers and Solitary Ones were abolished.
Rénzōng re-established them.
(In the eighth month of the twenty-second year of Yǒnglè, the Three Ducal Ministers and Three Solitary Ones were re-established.)
In the third year of Xuāndé, an imperial edict instructed Grand Preceptor and Duke of Yīng, Zhāng Fǔ;
Junior Preceptor and Minister of the Board of Civil Office, Jiǎn Yì;
Junior Tutor, Minister of the Board of War, and Grand Secretary of the Huágài Hall, Yáng Shìqí;
and Junior Guardian concurrently Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince and Minister of the Board of Revenue, Xià Yuánjí,
to each cease their existing responsibilities,
attend by the emperor's side,
and be consulted on matters of governance.
The offices of Ducal Ministers and Solitary Ones thus became almost exclusively assigned.
When Yì and Yuánjí died,
Shìqí returned to managing the affairs of the Grand Secretariat.
From then on,
the Ducal Ministers and Solitary Ones were merely honorary titles,
bestowed upon meritorious relatives and civil and military ministers as additional or posthumous appointments.
No civil official was appointed as a Living Ducal Minister;
it was only through posthumous grants that they could obtain such titles.
In the second year of Jiājìng, Yáng Tínghé was appointed Grand Tutor,
but he declined it.
Thereafter, the only civil official to be appointed a Ducal Minister
was Zhāng Jūzhèng, who was appointed Grand Tutor in the ninth year of Wànlì,
and Grand Preceptor in the tenth year.
The Grand Preceptor to the Crown Prince (tàizǐ tàishī), Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (tàizǐ tàifù), and Grand Guardian to the Crown Prince (tàizǐ tàibǎo)
(all Junior First Rank)
were responsible for assisting the Crown Prince with morality and virtue,
and diligently protecting him.
The Junior Preceptor to the Crown Prince (tàizǐ shàoshī), Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince (tàizǐ shàofù), and Junior Guardian to the Crown Prince (tàizǐ shàobǎo)
(all Senior Second Rank)
were responsible for attending the Crown Prince to observe the morality and virtue of the Three Ducal Ministers and instructing him.
The Guest to the Crown Prince (tàizǐ bīnkè)
(Senior Third Rank)
was responsible for attending the Crown Prince, assisting in rituals,
and admonishing him for errors.
All were high officials of the Eastern Palace (Crown Prince's establishment),
with no fixed number of appointees,
nor were they exclusively assigned.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ,
when Emperor Tàizǔ personally led an expedition,
fearing that the establishment of separate palace officials for the Crown Prince's regency might create discord,
he instead appointed court officials to concurrent palace positions: Lǐ Shàncháng concurrently as Junior Preceptor to the Crown Prince,
Xú Dá concurrently as Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince,
Cháng Yùchūn concurrently as Junior Guardian to the Crown Prince,
and the Registrar-Censor Wén Yuánjí and Fàn Xiǎnzǔ concurrently as Guests to the Crown Prince.
In the third year,
Minister of the Board of Rites Táo Kǎi requested that suitable individuals be selected to exclusively hold Eastern Palace positions,
and that concurrent appointments be abolished,
so that there could be clear responsibility for assisting and guiding the Crown Prince.
The emperor admonished him, stating that the affair of Jiāng Chōng served as a clear warning,
and that the system of concurrent appointments was not without reason.
Consequently,
the tutors and preceptors of the Eastern Palace
remained only concurrent, additional, or posthumous titles.
It was only during the Yǒnglè period,
when Emperor Chéngzǔ visited Běijīng,
that Yáo Guǎngxiào was exclusively appointed Junior Preceptor to the Crown Prince,
to remain and assist the Crown Prince.
Thereafter,
throughout the entire Míng Dynasty, these titles were purely honorary and had nothing to do with assisting and guiding the Crown Prince.
Grand Secretaries of the Zhōngjí Hall
(formerly the Huágài Hall),
Grand Secretaries of the Jiànjí Hall
(formerly the Jǐnshēn Hall),
Grand Secretaries of the Wénhuá Hall,
Grand Secretaries of the Wǔyīng Hall,
Grand Secretaries of the Wényuán Pavilion,
Grand Secretaries of the Dōng Pavilion,
(all of Principal Fifth Rank)
were in charge of recommending or rejecting proposals,
presenting advice and admonitions,
reviewing memorials,
and drafting rescripts and replies
to ensure fairness in all government affairs.
All communications from the emperor to his subordinates,
called zhào (edicts),
gào (proclamations),
zhì (decrees),
cèwén (investiture documents),
yù (imperial mandates),
shū (letters),
fú (tallies),
lìng (orders),
or xí (written orders),
were drafted and approved by them
before being issued to the various departments below.
All communications from subordinates to the emperor,
called tí (reports),
zòu (memorials),
biǎo (petitions),
jiǎngzhāng (lecture notes),
shūzhuàng (written statements),
wéncè (documents),
jiētiē (postings),
zhìduì (imperial replies),
lùbù (public announcements),
or yì (translations),
were reviewed, endorsed, and revised by them,
and only after ensuring fairness were they submitted.
Whenever the imperial carriage went out for suburban sacrifices or imperial tours, they would escort it.
When the emperor held imperial lectures (jīngyán),
they would serve as Chief Supervisors of the Jīngyán or Co-supervisors of the Jīngyán.
When the Crown Prince left the palace to study,
they would oversee the matter
and appoint officials
to instruct him.
For coronations and weddings,
they served as masters of ceremonies and envoys for presenting betrothal gifts.
When compiling the Veritable Records, historical records, and other books,
they served as Chief Editors.
For the Spring and Autumn sacrifices to Confucius on the first Dīng day,
they would act as officiants.
For the metropolitan examinations, they served as examiners;
for the palace examinations, they served as readers of the papers.
When presenting the names of successful candidates for the imperial examination,
one Grand Secretary would draft the inscription
to be carved on stone at the Imperial Academy (Tàixué).
For major ceremonies and important political matters,
after the Nine Ministers, Censorate, and Supervising Secretaries had deliberated and decided,
they would, based on the established codes
and adapting to circumstances,
assess the feasibility
and report their recommendations.
When issuing edicts, they would present them to the Ministry of Rites.
When requesting imperial decrees, they would review the relevant circumstances to make the request.
Requests for names or enfeoffment by members of the imperial clan
and requests for posthumous titles by officials
were all drafted and submitted by them.
Because they dined within the imperial palace
and constantly attended the emperor in the palace halls,
to avoid the title of prime minister,
they were also called the Nèigé (Grand Secretariat).
Previously,
Tàizǔ, inheriting the previous system,
established the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shěng)
and appointed Left and Right Chéngxiàng (Prime Ministers)
(Principal First Rank.
In the first month of jiǎchén,
Left and Right Xiàngguó (Grand Counselors) were first established.
Lǐ Shàncháng was appointed Right Xiàngguó,
Xú Dá was appointed Left Xiàngguó.
In the first year of Wú, all officials' rituals were to honor the left,
so Right Xiàngguó was changed to Left Xiàngguó,
and Left Xiàngguó was changed to Right Xiàngguó.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, they were changed to Left and Right Chéngxiàng.)
Also Píngzhāng Zhèngshì (Administrators of Governmental Affairs)
(From First Rank),
Left and Right Chéng (Vice Prime Ministers)
(Principal Second Rank),
and Cānzhī Zhèngshì (Participators in Governmental Affairs)
(From Second Rank)
to oversee all officials.
Subordinate officials were established:
Left and Right Divisions,
Lángzhōng (Director)
(Principal Fifth Rank),
Yuánwàiláng (Assistant Director)
(Principal Sixth Rank),
Dūshì (Registrar) and Jiǎnjiào (Reviewer)
(Principal Seventh Rank),
Zhàomó (Scribe) and Guǎngōu (Supervisor)
(From Seventh Rank).
The Cānyì Fǔ (Counselor's Office) had:
Cānyì (Counselor)
(Principal Third Rank),
Cānjūn (Staff Officer) and Duànshì Guān (Judicial Officer)
(From Third Rank),
Duànshì (Judge) and Jīnglì (Registrar)
(Principal Seventh Rank),
and Zhīshì (Secretary)
(Principal Eighth Rank).
The Dūzhènfǔ司 (Commandery Marshal's Office) had:
Dūzhènfǔ (Commandery Marshal)
(Principal Fifth Rank).
The Kǎogōng Suǒ (Merit Evaluation Office) had:
Kǎogōng Láng (Director of Merit Evaluation)
(Principal Seventh Rank).
In the tenth month of jiǎchén, the Dūzhènfǔ司 was subordinated to the Grand Military Command (Dà Dūdū Fǔ).
In the first year of Wú, the Cānyì Fǔ was abolished.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, the Kǎogōng Suǒ was abolished.
In the second year, the Zhàomó, Jiǎnjiào Suǒ, and Duànshì Guān were abolished.
In the seventh year, ten Zhíshěng Shèrén (Provincial Palace Secretaries) were established,
later changed to Zhōngshū Shèrén (Secretaries of the Central Secretariat).
In the ninth year of Hóngwǔ, the Píngzhāng Zhèngshì and Cānzhī Zhèngshì were eliminated.
In the first month of the thirteenth year, Chéngxiàng Hú Wéiyǒng was executed,
and subsequently the Central Secretariat was abolished.
(All its officials were dismissed,
except for the Zhōngshū Shèrén.)
In the ninth month, four Fǔguān (Assisting Officials) were established,
with Confucian scholars such as Wáng Běn appointed to these positions.
(The four Fǔguān were established and announced at the Imperial Ancestral Temple (Tàimiào).
Wáng Běn, Dù Yòu, and Gōng Xiào were appointed as Spring Officials.
Dù Xiào, Zhào Mínwàng, and Wú Yuán were appointed as Summer Officials,
also serving as Tàizǐ Bīnkè (Grand Mentors to the Crown Prince).
Vacancies for Autumn and Winter Officials
were temporarily filled by Wáng Běn and others.
Within a month, they were divided into three ten-day shifts for duties.
Their rank was below that of dukes, marquises, and military governors.
) They were also soon abolished.
In the fifteenth year, following the Sòng dynasty system,
Grand Secretaries of the Huágài Hall, Wǔyīng Hall, Wényuán Pavilion, and Dōng Pavilion were established.
(Shào Zhì, Minister of Rites, was appointed to Huágài;
Wú Bózōng, Reviewer, to Wǔyīng;
Sòng Nà, Hanlin Academician, to Wényuán;
Wú Chén, Archivist, to Dōng Pavilion.)
Additionally, Grand Secretaries of the Wénhuá Hall were established
(aged Confucian scholars like Bào Xún, Yú Quán, and Zhāng Chángnián were recruited for this)
to assist and guide the Crown Prince.
All were of Principal Fifth Rank.
In the twenty-eighth year, an imperial edict was issued to all officials:
"The state has abolished the prime minister,
and established various offices, ministries, censorates, and courts to manage all affairs,
a legislation that is extremely thorough and excellent.
Future emperors
must not consider re-establishing the prime minister.
Any official who petitions for its establishment
shall be punished with the ultimate penalty."
At that time,
the Hanlin Academy (Hànlín) and the Eastern Palace Secretariat (Chūnfáng)
were responsible for reviewing memorials from various departments
and concurrently handled dismissals and rebuttals.
The Grand Secretaries merely attended the emperor
to answer questions.
During the Jiànwén reign,
Grand Secretaries were renamed Academicians (Xuèshì).
All Grand Secretaries were dismissed,
and one Academician was appointed for each.
The Jǐnshēn Hall was also renamed Zhèngxīn Hall,
and a Zhèngxīn Hall Academician was established.
When Chéngzǔ ascended the throne,
he specially appointed Xiè Jìn, Hú Guǎng, Yáng Róng, and others to serve in the Wényuán Pavilion,
participating in state affairs.
The participation of Cabinet ministers in state affairs began from this point.
However, at that time,
those who entered the Nèigé were all officials from the Hanlin Academy (biān, jiǎn, jiǎngdú),
without subordinate officials,
and they could not independently control the various departments.
Nor could they interfere with the memorials from those departments.
Rénzōng promoted Yáng Shìqí and Yáng Róng, who were former officials of the Eastern Palace.
Shìqí was promoted to Lǐbù Shìláng兼Huágài Diàn Dàxuéshì,
and Róng was promoted to Tàicháng Qīng兼Jǐnshēn Diàn Dàxuéshì.
(The position of Jǐnshēn Diàn Dàxuéshì
was first established by Rénzōng.)
The power of the Grand Secretariat gradually increased.
Later, Shìqí, Róng, and others were all promoted to the position of Shàngshū.
Although they resided in the Grand Secretariat,
their official rank was invariably accorded higher esteem as Shàngshū.
During the Jǐngtài reign,
Wáng Wén was initially promoted from Zuǒ Dū Yùshǐ to Lìbù Shàngshū
and entered the Grand Secretariat.
Thereafter,
the Gàochì Fáng and Zhìchì Fáng both established Zhōngshū Shèrén.
The Six Ministries followed the Secretariat’s directives
in everything,
and the power of the Secretariat grew even heavier.
During Shìzōng’s reign,
the Three Halls were completed.
Huágài was renamed Zhōngjí,
and Jǐnshēn was renamed Jiànjí.
The titles of the Grand Secretaries were adjusted accordingly.
After the Jiājìng reign,
their positions in court rankings
were all placed above the Six Ministries.
Lìbù.
One Shàngshū
(Senior Second Rank),
one Left and one Right Shìláng each
(Senior Third Rank).
Its sub-offices:
Sīwù Tīng,
with two Sīwù
(Junior Ninth Rank).
The four bureaus of Wénxuǎn, Yànfēng, Jīxūn, and Kǎogōng each had
one Lángzhōng
(Senior Fifth Rank),
one Yuánwailáng
(Junior Fifth Rank),
and one Zhǔshì
(Senior Sixth Rank).
In the 31st year of Hóngwǔ, one Zhǔshì was added to the Wénxuǎn Sī.
In the 11th year of Zhèngtǒng, one Zhǔshì was added to the Kǎogōng Sī.
The Shàngshū was in charge of the regulations concerning the selection and appointment of officials, the conferment of titles and honors, and the evaluation of performance for the entire empire,
to identify talent
and assist the Son of Heaven in governing.
This was akin to the duties of the ancient Zǒngzǎi,
and was considered particularly important among the Five Ministries.
The Shìláng served as his deputies.
The Sīwù were in charge of urging, supervising, checking delays, canceling, and maintaining records.
(In the early Míng dynasty,
four Zhǔshì and four Sīwù were established,
serving as leading officials,
and possessing the seal of Zhǔshì.
In the 29th year of Hóngwǔ, Zhǔshì were reclassified as Sīguān,
and two Sīwù were abolished.
This was uniform across all ministries.)
The Wénxuǎn Sī was in charge of the ranking, promotion, and transfer of officials,
assisting the Shàngshū.
There were nine grades for civil officials,
each with a senior and junior subdivision,
making a total of eighteen ranks.
Those below the ninth grade were called “unranked” (wèi rù liú).
Regarding selections,
there were annual grand selections,
emergency selections,
selections for remote regions,
selections for annual tribute students appointed to education,
occasional selective appointments,
and selections for Jǔrén seeking imperial favor.
Selected individuals were all entered into the personnel roster,
their grades were categorized,
their appointments were impartially decided, and they were promoted in sequence.
All promotions required a full term of service evaluation.
If there was a vacancy that needed to be filled,
without waiting for the full term evaluation,
it was called “promotional recommendation.”
For classified recommendations, one person was advanced;
for singular recommendations, two people were advanced.
For officials of the third rank and above,
the Nine Ministers, as well as the Qiāndū Yùshǐ and Jìjiǔ,
two or three people were recommended by court selection.
For the Grand Secretariat
and the Shàngshū of the Lìbù and Bīngbù,
two people were recommended by court selection.
In general, princely officials were not transferred to external posts,
royal relatives were not appointed to internal posts,
and relatives of high ministers were not allowed to serve in the Censorate or Supervising Secretariats.
If subordinates were of the same clan as their superiors, they had to yield to the superior.
If the talent or locality of an external official was unsuitable,
they would be mutually exchanged based on the complexity or simplicity of the roles.
Those who received inherited promotions or sought promotions
were all allowed to make a direct plea.
Acting appointments, probationary appointments, and substantive appointments were used to establish seniority;
establishment, merger, and concurrent appointments were used to adapt to complexity or simplicity;
recommendations, reinstatement of the dismissed, and summons were used to invigorate the obscure and stagnant;
receiving emoluments without duties and supernumerary appointments were used to bestow imperial favor;
demotion and dismissal were used to deal with transgressions;
official regulations were used to supervise administration;
and leave of absence was used to understand human sentiments.
The Yànfēng Sī was in charge of conferring noble titles, inherited privileges, posthumous honors, and official calculations,
assisting the Shàngshū.
In general, titles could not be conferred without meritorious service to the state or military achievement,
and honorific titles could not be granted without a special imperial decree.
Whether hereditary
or non-hereditary,
all were issued with patents (gàojuàn).
The Yǎnshèng Gōng and those granted titles through imperial favor to imperial relatives
were not issued patents.
For all patents,
there was one left and one right copy.
The left was stored in the Imperial Household Department,
and the right was given to the family of the meritorious official.
For inherited titles, their patents were requested,
their merits and demerits were investigated,
and their lineage was verified,
to determine the degree of their hereditary transmission, demotion, or abolition.
For native officials, their eligibility for inheritance was investigated,
and a document was sent to the Wénxuǎn Sī for nomination.
(Xuānwèi, Xuānfǔ, Ānfǔ, and Zhǎngguān of various offices who commanded indigenous troops
were under the Bīngbù.)
Regarding inherited privileges,
in the early Míng dynasty,
from the first rank to the seventh rank,
all could grant one son an inherited position to perpetuate their emoluments.
(In the 16th year of Hóngwǔ, regulations for the inherited privileges of officials' sons were established.
A son of a Senior First Rank official
was appointed to a Senior Fifth Rank position.
A son of a Junior First Rank official
was appointed to a Junior Fifth Rank position.
A son of a Senior Second Rank official
was appointed to a Senior Sixth Rank position.
A son of a Junior Second Rank official
was appointed to a Junior Sixth Rank position.
A son of a Senior Third Rank official
was appointed to a Senior Seventh Rank position.
A son of a Junior Third Rank official
was appointed to a Junior Seventh Rank position.
A son of a Senior Fourth Rank official
was appointed to a Senior Eighth Rank position.
A son of a Junior Fourth Rank official
was appointed to a Junior Eighth Rank position.
A son of a Senior Fifth Rank official
was appointed to a Senior Ninth Rank position.
A son of a Junior Fifth Rank official
was appointed to a Junior Ninth Rank position.
A son of a Senior Sixth Rank official
was appointed to an upper-grade unranked position.
A son of a Junior Sixth Rank official
was appointed to a middle-grade unranked position.
A son of a Senior or Junior Seventh Rank official
was appointed to a lower-grade unranked position.)
Later,
restrictions were gradually imposed.
Only metropolitan officials of the third rank and above,
who had completed their terms and achieved meritorious service,
could initially grant one son an inherited position, called Guānsheng.
Those who gained it through special imperial grace were called Ēnshēng.
Regarding posthumous honors,
posthumous enfeoffments for Gōng, Hóu, and Bó
were all advanced by one grade.
Officials of the third rank and above who showed outstanding political achievements, or who died in remonstrance, died for their principles, or died in battle,
were all eligible for posthumous official titles.
For those currently in office, they were initially granted honorary titles.
Metropolitan officials who completed one term
and external officials who completed one term and were highly praised
were all granted patents for themselves.
Officials of the seventh rank and above could all extend imperial favor to their ancestors.
Officials of the fifth rank and above received imperial patents (gàomìng),
while those of the sixth rank and below received imperial mandates (chìmìng).
(For the First Rank,
three generations, four scrolls.
For the Second and Third Ranks,
two generations, three scrolls.
For the Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, and Seventh Ranks,
one generation, two scrolls.
For unranked officials below the Eighth Rank,
one scroll for themselves.
The scroll spindle for the First Rank was made of jade,
for the Second Rank of rhinoceros horn,
for the Third and Fourth Ranks of gilded metal,
and for the Fifth Rank and below of horn.)
Great-grandparents, grandparents, and parents all received titles corresponding to their sons' and grandsons' official ranks.
Gōng, Hóu, and Bó were treated as First Rank.
Internal and external noblewomen received ranks corresponding to their husband's or son's rank.
When alive, it was called "enfeoffment" (fēng);
when deceased, it was called "posthumous grant" (zèng).
If there were prior transgressions or condemnations, the grant would be suspended.
There are forty-two grades of civil officials’ honorary titles (sǎnjiē),
differentiated by their performance reviews (lìkǎo).
(For the first rank, principal grade (zhèng yī pǐn),
the initial appointment is Tèjìn Rónglù Dàfū,
and promotion is to Tèjìn Guānglù Dàfū.
For the first rank, secondary grade (cóng yī pǐn),
the initial appointment is Rónglù Dàfū,
and promotion is to Guānglù Dàfū.
For the second rank, principal grade (zhèng èr pǐn),
the initial appointment is Zīshàn Dàfū,
promotion is to Zīzhèng Dàfū,
and additional conferment is Zīdé Dàfū.
For the second rank, secondary grade (cóng èr pǐn),
the initial appointment is Zhōngfèng Dàfū,
promotion is to Tōngfèng Dàfū,
and additional conferment is Zhèngfèng Dàfū.
For the third rank, principal grade (zhèng sān pǐn),
the initial appointment is Jiāyì Dàfū,
promotion is to Tōngyì Dàfū,
and additional conferment is Zhèngyì Dàfū.
For the third rank, secondary grade (cóng sān pǐn),
the initial appointment is Yàzhōng Dàfū,
promotion is to Zhōng Dàfū,
and additional conferment is Dàzhōng Dàfū.
For the fourth rank, principal grade (zhèng sì pǐn),
the initial appointment is Zhōngshùn Dàfū,
promotion is to Zhōngxiàn Dàfū,
and additional conferment is Zhōngyì Dàfū.
For the fourth rank, secondary grade (cóng sì pǐn),
the initial appointment is Cháoliè Dàfū,
promotion is to Cháoyì Dàfū,
and additional conferment is Cháoqǐng Dàfū.
For the fifth rank, principal grade (zhèng wǔ pǐn),
the initial appointment is Fèngyì Dàfū,
and promotion is to Fèngzhèng Dàfū.
For the fifth rank, secondary grade (cóng wǔ pǐn),
the initial appointment is Fèngxùn Dàfū,
and promotion is to Fèngzhí Dàfū.
For the sixth rank, principal grade (zhèng liù pǐn),
the initial appointment is Chéngzhí Láng,
and promotion is to Chéngdé Láng.
For the sixth rank, secondary grade (cóng liù pǐn),
the initial appointment is Chéngwù Láng,
promotion is to Rúlín Láng,
and clerks with talent and ability are appointed Xuāndé Láng.
For the seventh rank, principal grade (zhèng qī pǐn),
the initial appointment is Chéngshì Láng,
promotion is to Wénlín Láng,
and clerks with talent and ability are appointed Xuānyì Láng.
For the seventh rank, secondary grade (cóng qī pǐn),
the initial appointment is Cóngshì Láng,
and promotion is to Zhēngshì Láng.
For the eighth rank, principal grade (zhèng bā pǐn),
the initial appointment is Gōngláng,
and promotion is to Xiūzhí Láng.
For the eighth rank, secondary grade (cóng bā pǐn),
the initial appointment is Gōngzuǒ Láng,
and promotion is to Xiūzhí Zuǒláng.
For the ninth rank, principal grade (zhèng jiǔ pǐn),
the initial appointment is Jiāngshì Láng,
and promotion is to Dēngshì Láng.
For the ninth rank, secondary grade (cóng jiǔ pǐn),
the initial appointment is Jiāngshì Zuǒláng,
and promotion is to Dēngshì Zuǒláng.
) There are nine titles for external noblewomen (wàimìngfù).
(A duke’s wife is called the wife of a certain state, i.e., "Mǒu Guó Fūrén."
A marquis’s wife is called "Mǒu Hóu Fūrén."
An earl’s wife is called "Mǒu Bó Fūrén."
A first-rank official’s wife is called Fūrén,
and later referred to as Yīpǐn Fūrén.
A second-rank official’s wife is called Fūrén.
A third-rank official’s wife is called Shūrén.
A fourth-rank official’s wife is called Gōngrén.
A fifth-rank official’s wife is called Yírén.
A sixth-rank official’s wife is called Ānrén.
A seventh-rank official’s wife is called Rúrén.
) If a woman is enfeoffed because of her son or grandson,
the character "tài" is added,
unless her husband is still alive.
The order of conferment and posthumous conferment is as follows:
once for seventh to sixth rank,
once for fifth rank,
(the initial system had a conferment once for fourth rank,
but this was later removed),
and once each for third, second, and first ranks.
Three mothers cannot be enfeoffed concurrently.
If there are two enfeoffments, the higher rank is taken.
If the father’s office is higher than the son’s,
he is advanced one grade.
If a father should have his stipend suspended,
or if a son becomes the heir of another,
they may all have their enfeoffment transferred.
If the principal wife is alive, the birth mother is not enfeoffed.
If the birth mother has not been enfeoffed, the wife is not enfeoffed first.
The enfeoffment of a wife
is limited to one principal wife (díqī) and one successor wife (jìqī).
If those who have been enfeoffed or posthumously enfeoffed later fail due to corruption,
their titles are stripped retrospectively.
The Bureau of Merits (Jīxūn) manages merit ranks, personnel registers, and matters of mourning and care for the elderly,
assisting the Minister (Shàngshū).
There are ten civil merit titles (wénxūn).
(For the first rank, principal grade,
Left and Right Pillar of the State (Zuǒ/Yòu Zhùguó).
For the first rank, secondary grade,
Pillar of the State (Zhùguó).
For the second rank, principal grade,
Principal Senior Administrator (Zhèngzhì Shàngqīng).
For the second rank, secondary grade,
Principal Administrator (Zhèngzhì Qīng).
For the third rank, principal grade,
Assistant Administrator (Zīzhì Yǐn).
For the third rank, secondary grade,
Assistant Junior Administrator (Zīzhì Shàoyǐn).
For the fourth rank, principal grade,
Aiding Administrator (Zànzhì Yǐn).
For the fourth rank, secondary grade,
Aiding Junior Administrator (Zànzhì Shàoyǐn).
For the fifth rank, principal grade,
Rectifier of Common Affairs (Xiūzhèng Shùyǐn).
For the fifth rank, secondary grade,
Assistant Rectifier of Common Affairs (Xiézhèng Shùyǐn).
) From the fifth rank and above,
a merit title is granted only after two performance reviews.
For all transfers, dismissals, and demotions of officials, their age, birthplace, and origin are written down.
Every year in the twelfth month, "yellow postings" (tiēhuáng) are made,
and "clear yellow postings" (qīnghuáng) in spring and autumn,
all submitted to the Imperial Household Department (Nèifǔ).
If there are reasons,
they are removed.
Officials whose parents are seventy years old
and who have no brothers
may resign to care for them.
For the three-year mourning period,
officials must resign their posts to observe the rites,
and those who evade, conceal, or shorten their mourning periods are exposed.
Only officials of the Imperial Astronomy Bureau (Qīntiānjiān)
return to their posts after three months of mourning leave.
The Bureau of Merits (Kǎogōng) manages the assessment and evaluation of officials, and their promotion and demotion,
assisting the Minister (Shàngshū).
All internal and external officials are given a letter of appointment (gěiyóu).
The initial review is after three years,
the second review after six years,
and a comprehensive review is conducted after nine years,
with a memorial requesting that officials be promoted or demoted based on whether they are competent, ordinary, or incompetent.
Promotion does not exceed two grades,
demotion does not exceed three grades,
and the most severe cases are dismissed or punished.
Capital officials are inspected once every six years,
in the years of Yǐ and Hài.
Officials below the fifth rank who are found incompetent are demoted or penalized accordingly;
officials above the fourth rank declare their own cases,
and their retention or removal is decided by imperial decree.
External officials make an imperial audience once every three years,
in the years of Chén, Xū, Chǒu, and Wèi.
Prior to this, the Surveillance and Provincial Administration Commissioners (Fǔ, Àn Guān) are informed,
and each compiles a record of the merits and demerits of their subordinates over the past three years, noting their performance reviews,
which are then sent for review and verification to determine promotions and demotions.
Officials of granaries, stables, and treasuries are reviewed annually,
patrol inspectors every three years,
and education officials every nine years.
The reviews of prefectural, sub-prefectural, and county officials
are differentiated based on the complexity of their assigned area.
The review of clerks is
after three or six years of service,
after which they are assigned by the Bureau of Appointments (Yànfēng Sī).
After nine years of service,
they are again tested and appointed as officials.
Only imperial princes’ officials, and officials of the Imperial Astronomy Bureau (Qīntiānjiān), Imperial Manufactories (Yùyòng Jiān), etc., are not reviewed.
For all impeachment memorials against internal and external officials,
their merits and demerits are investigated,
and a proposal for retention or removal is submitted for imperial decision.
For recommendations and retention,
their administrative achievements are verified and commended.
In the early Míng dynasty,
four departments were established within the Zhōngshū Shěng,
each responsible for matters of finance and grain, rites and ceremonies, criminal justice, and construction.
In Hóngwǔ first year (1368), the six ministries of Lìbù, Hùbù, Lǐbù, Bīngbù, Xíngbù, and Gōngbù were first established,
with a Shàngshū, Shìláng, Lángzhōng, Yuánwàiláng, and Zhǔshì.
(The Shàngshū was of principal third rank,
the Shìláng of principal fourth rank,
the Lángzhōng of principal fifth rank,
the Yuánwàiláng of principal sixth rank,
and the Zhǔshì of principal seventh rank.)
They remained subordinate to the Zhōngshū Shěng.
In the sixth year (1373),
each ministry was assigned two Shàngshū
and two Shìláng.
The Lìbù established three subordinate departments: Zǒngbù, Sīxūn, and Kǎogōng.
Each department had one Lángzhōng and one Yuánwàiláng,
and two Zhǔshì.
In the thirteenth year (1380), the Zhōngshū Shěng was abolished,
and following the system of the Six Qīng of the Zhōu officials,
the ranks of the Six Ministries were raised.
Each was assigned one Shàngshū and one Shìláng.
(Only the Hùbù had two Shìláng.)
Each ministry was divided into four subordinate departments,
with the Lìbù adding Sīfēng to its subordinate departments.
Each subordinate department had one Lángzhōng, one Yuánwàiláng, and one Zhǔshì.
Later, one Shìláng was added.
In the twenty-second year (1389), Zǒngbù was changed to Xuǎnbù.
In the twenty-ninth year (1396), it was fixed as the four bureaus of Wénxuǎn, Yànfēng, Jīxūn, and Kǎogōng, coexisting with the five subordinate departments.
All were called Qīnglì Sī.
During the Jiànwén reign (1399-1402),
the Shàngshū of the Six Ministries were changed to principal first rank,
and Zǔo and Yòu Shìzhōng (principal second rank) were established,
ranking above the Shìláng.
The character "Qīnglì" was removed from all bureaus.
In the early Chéngzǔ reign (1403),
all old systems were restored.
In Yǒnglè first year (1403),
Běipíng was designated Běijīng,
and two Běijīng Xíngbù Shàngshū
and four Shìláng were appointed.
Subordinate to them were the six Cáo Qīnglì Sī.
(For the Lì, Hù, Lǐ, Bīng, and Gōng five Cáo,
there was one Lángzhōng, one Yuánwàiláng, and one Zhǔshì each.
For the Xíng Cáo,
there was one Lángzhōng,
one Yuánwàiláng,
four Zhǔshì,
one Zhàozhí and one Jiǎnjiào each,
and one Sīyù.
Later, the Hù Cáo also added three Zhǔshì.)
Subsequently, the Six Ministries were again separately established,
each called Xíngzài [Ministry Name].
In the eighteenth year (1420), the capital was fixed in Běijīng,
the Xíngbù and the Six Cáo were abolished,
and the officials of the Six Ministries were moved to the north,
no longer using the term "Xíngzài."
For those remaining in Nánjīng,
the character
"Nánjīng"
was added.
In Hóngxī first year (1425), officials for each ministry were again established in Nánjīng,
removing the
"Nánjīng"
character,
and those in Běijīng had the character
"Xíngzài"
added.
The Xíngbù was also re-established.
In Xuāndé third year (1428), the Xíngbù was again abolished.
In Zhèngtǒng sixth year (1441),
the character
"Xíngzài"
was removed in Běijīng,
and
"Nánjīng"
was again added in Nánjīng,
thus becoming the established system.
During the Jǐngtài reign (1450-1457),
the Lìbù sometimes had two Shàngshū.
In the early Tiānshùn reign (1457),
one was again abolished.
Indeed, the Shàngshū of the Lìbù
was a role model for all officials,
responsible for the appointment and dismissal of various officials,
and a crucial position in personnel evaluation.
Their ceremonial status was uniquely different,
with none comparable.
In the early Yǒnglè reign (1403),
Hanlin officials were selected to serve in the Nèigé.
Later, Grand Secretaries like Yáng Shìqí reached the rank of Three Gū,
and concurrently held the title of Shàngshū.
However, their rank was still below that of Shàngshū Jiǎn Yì and Xià Yuánjí.
During the Jǐngtài reign,
Wáng Wén, the Left Dū Yùshǐ, was promoted to Shàngshū of the Lìbù,
concurrently holding the title of Xuéshì,
and entered the Nèigé.
His seating order was still determined by his original rank.
From the second month of Hóngzhì sixth year (1493),
at an imperial banquet,
Grand Secretary Qiū Jùn, with the titles of Tàizǐ Tàibǎo and Lǐbù Shàngshū,
was seated above Wáng Shù, who held the titles of Tàizǐ Tàibǎo and Lìbù Shàngshū.
Thereafter, those who entered the Nèigé from the ranks of Shìláng or Zhānshì
were all seated above the Six Ministries.
Board of Revenue.
One Minister [shàngshū] (of the Board of Revenue)
(Principal Second Rank).
One Left Vice-Minister [zuǒ shìláng] and one Right Vice-Minister [yòu shìláng]
(Principal Third Rank).
Its subordinate offices:
Department of General Affairs [Sīwù Tīng],
two Supervisors of General Affairs [sīwù]
(Collateral Ninth Rank).
The thirteen Bureaus of Accounts [Qīnglì Sī] for Zhèjiāng, Jiāngxī, Húguǎng, Shǎnxī, Guǎngdōng, Shāndōng, Fújiàn, Hénán, Shānxī, Sìchuān, Guǎngxī, Guìzhōu, and Yúnnán.
Each bureau has one Director [lángzhōng]
(Principal Fifth Rank).
After Xuāndé, three Directors were added for the Shānxī Bureau,
two Directors for each of the Shǎnxī, Guìzhōu, and Yúnnán Bureaus,
and one Director for the Shāndōng Bureau.
One Assistant Director [yuánwàiláng]
(Collateral Fifth Rank).
In the seventh year of Xuāndé, one Assistant Director was added for each of the Sìchuān and Yúnnán Bureaus,
but these were later abolished.
Two Secretaries [zhǔshì]
(Principal Sixth Rank).
After Xuāndé, seven Secretaries were added for the Yúnnán Bureau,

The Minister [shàngshū] manages the national policies on population, land tax, and levies.
The Vice-Ministers [shìláng] assist in this.
They review land registers, annual accounts, and the actual collection figures for taxes and labor services,
which are then passed down to the subordinate offices.
Every ten years, the Yellow Registers [huángcè] are compiled,
categorizing households into upper, lower, and odd/even grades [gēnyú zhī děng],
to keep abreast of their prosperity and decline.
Prohibitions are in place against the encroachment, donation, fraudulent lodging, or concealed transfer of land,
against the concealment, evasion, flight, fraudulent substitution, or fragmented division of households,
and against successions or marriages that do not comply with regulations.
All these are to be comprehensively examined and corrected.
When the Emperor plows the imperial field [gēngjí],
the Minister presents the ploughs and hoes.
They are to open up wasteland for the poor,
to register and settle migrants,
to limit landholdings to curb heretical populations,
to use maps and registers to suppress land monopolizers,
to evaluate agricultural officials based on cultivation,
to provide pasture land for horse ranches,
to call for tenants to maximize land utility,
to cancel arrears to clear burdens,
to allocate resources to extend imperial favor,
to grant exemptions for those bearing heavy burdens,
to use paper currency and silver ingots to manage rewards,
to educate officials and common people through laws,
to standardize weights and measures for market transactions,
to stabilize prices using market estimates,
to relieve the suffering of the people through policies of accumulation and storage,
to assist the nation with policies concerning mountains and wetlands, ponds and lakes, customs and markets, mines and foundries,
to supply military provisions,
to facilitate grain transport through rules of direct exchange and deferred exchange,
to show compassion for disaster-stricken areas through decrees of tax reduction, relief loans, price stabilization, and locust eradication,
to fill border granaries through methods of transport, garrison farming, purchasing, and collection,
and to manage the status of the noble and the common through the system of official salaries.
(In the twenty-fifth year of Hóngwǔ, the system of annual salaries for civil and military officials, both internal and external, was revised).

The thirteen departments each managed the affairs of their respective provinces.
They also concurrently oversaw the tribute and taxes from the two Capitals and the directly administered areas,
as well as the salaries and stipends of various offices and garrisons (wèi suǒ),
and the provisions for border garrisons (biān zhèn).
They also managed the salt tax and customs duties of various granaries, storehouses, and customs barriers.
(The Zhèjiāng Department concurrently managed the Yǔlín Yòu, Liúshǒu Zuǒ, Lónghǔ, Yìngtiān, Lóngxiáng, Yìyǒng Yòu, and Kānglíng seven garrisons in the Capital,
and the Shénjī Battalion.
The Jiāngxī Department concurrently managed the Qíshǒu, Jīnwú Qián, Jīnwú Hòu, Jīnwú Zuǒ, and Jìyáng five garrisons in the Capital.
The Húguǎng Department concurrently managed the Guózǐjiān and Jiàofāngsī,
the Yǔlín Qián, Tōngzhōu, Héyáng, Bàotāo, Yǒnglíng, and Zhāolíng six garrisons in the Capital,
and the Xīngdū Liúshǒusī.
The Fújiàn Department concurrently managed Shùntiān Fǔ,
the Yānshān Zuǒ, Wǔxiáng Zuǒ, Wǔxiáng Yòu, Xiāoqí Yòu, Hǔbēn Yòu, Liúshǒu Hòu, Wǔchéng Zhōng, and Màolíng eight garrisons in the Capital,
the Wǔjūn, Xún
bǔ, Yǒngshì, and Sīwèi various battalions,
and the Yǒngpíng, Bǎodìng, Héjiān, Zhēndìng, Shùndé, Guǎngpíng, and Dàmíng seven prefectures of Běizhílì,
the Yánqìng and Bǎo'ān two departments,
the Dàníng Dūsī and Wànquán Dūsī,
as well as all garrisons and stations under the jurisdiction of Běizhílì,
and the Shānkǒu, Yǒngyíng, and Tōngjì various granaries.
The Shāndōng Department concurrently managed the Jǐnyī, Dàníng Zhōng, and Dàníng Qián three garrisons in the Capital, and the Liáodōng Dūsī,
the Liǎnghuái, Liǎngzhè, Chánglú, Hédōng, Shāndōng, and Fújiàn various Salt Transportation Commissioner's Offices,
the Sìchuān,
Guǎngdōng, Hǎiběi, Yúnnán Hēiyánjǐng, Báiyánjǐng, Ānníng, and Wǔjǐng various Salt Tax Administration Offices,
the Shǎnxī Língzhōu Salt Tax Office,
and the Jiāngxī Nángàn Salt Tax.
The Shānxī Department concurrently managed the Yānshān Qián, Zhènnán, Xīngwǔ, Yǒngqīng Zuǒ, and Yǒngqīng Yòu five garrisons in the Capital,
and the Xuānfǔ, Dàtóng, and Shānxī various garrisons.
The Hénán Department concurrently managed the Fǔjūn Qián, Yānshān Yòu, Dàxīng Zuǒ, and Yùlíng four garrisons in the Capital,
the Mùmǎ Qiānhùsuǒ, and the Zhílì Tóngguān Wèi and Púzhōu Qiānhùsuǒ.
The Shǎnxī Department concurrently managed the Zōngrénfǔ, Wǔjūn Dūdūfǔ, Lìubù, Dùcháyuàn, Tōngzhèngsī, Dàlǐsì, Zhànshìfǔ, Hànlínyuàn, Tàipúsì, Hónglúsì, Shàngbǎosī,
Lìukē, Zhōngshū Shèrén, Xíngrénsī, Qīntiānjiān, Tàiyīyuàn, Wǔchéng Bīngmǎsī, Jīngwèi Wǔxué, Wénxīyuàn, Pízuòjú,
the Liúshǒu Yòu, Chánglíng, Xiànlíng, and Jǐnglíng four
garrisons in the Capital,

and the Yánsuí, Níngxià, Gānsù, and Gùyuán various garrisons.

garrisons, and Yìngtiān Fǔ and the forty-nine garrisons of Nánjīng,
the Ānqìng, Sūzhōu, Sōngjiāng, Chángzhōu, Zhènjiāng, Huīzhōu, Níngguó, Chízhōu, Tàipíng, Lúzhōu, Fèngyáng, Huái'ān, and Yángzhōu thir
teen prefectures of Nánzhílì,
the Xú, Chú, Hé, and Guǎngdé four departments,
the Zhōngdū Liúshǒusī, and all garrisons and stations under the jurisdiction of Nánzhílì.
The Guǎngdōng Department concurrently managed the Yǔlín Zuǒ, Liúshǒu Zhōng, Yīngyáng, Shénwǔ Zuǒ, Yìyǒng Qián, and Yìyǒng Hòu six garrisons,
and the Fānmù and Diànjìng two chiliarchy offices.

hé, and Wèizhōu Zuǒ five garrisons in the Capital,

and the Dàjūncāng, Huángchéng Sì Méncāng, and the external
Línqīng, Dézhōu, Xúzhōu, Huái'ān, and Tiānjīn various granaries.
The Guìzhōu Department concurrently managed the Shànglínyuànsī,
Bǎochāo Tíjíusī,
Dūshuìsī,
Zhèngyángmén and Zhāngjiāwān various Xuānkèsī,
Déshèngmén and Āndìngmén various Shuìkèsī,
Chóngwénmén Fēn
sī,
the Jìzhōu, Huìzhōu, and Fùyù three garrisons in the Capital,
and the Jìzhōu, Yǒngpíng, Mìyún, Chāngpíng, and Yìzhōu various garrisons,
and the Línqīng, Xǔshù, Jiǔjiāng, Huái'ān, Běixīn, Yángzhōu, and Héxīwù various
customs barriers.
)They were divided into four sections: the Mínkē,

which managed the geography, populace, gazetteers, historical evolution, mountain and river topography, soil fertility and extent, and the number of households, produce, and their increase or decrease for the subordinate prefectures, departments, and counties;
the Dùzhīkē,
which managed the accounting for summer tax, autumn grain, retention, transportation, as well as expenditure for rewards and stipends;
the Jīnkē,
which managed the market tax, fish and salt tax, tea and paper currency tax,
and the collection of fines and confiscations;
and the Cāngkē,
which managed grain transport, military provisions, and receipts and disbursements of rations.
There were three types of appointments.
Appointments selected by the Lìbù were called Zhùchāi.
Those nominated and requested from above were called Tíchāi.
Those appointed by official dispatch were called Bùchāi.
They were replaced either after three years,
one year,
or three months.
Initially,
the Hùbù was established in the first year of Hóngwǔ (1368).
In the sixth year (1373), two Shàngshū and
two Shìláng were appointed.
It was divided into five sections: Yīkē,
Èrkē,
Sānkē,
Sìkē,
and Zǒngkē.
Each section had one Lángzhōng and one Yuánwàiláng,
and four Zhǔshì.
Only the Zǒngkē had two Lángzhōng and two Yuánwàiláng,
and five Zhǔshì.
In the eighth year (1375), the Zhōngshūshěng reported that the Hù, Xíng, and Gōng ministries were too busy.
The Hùbù's five sections
each had one Shàngshū and one Shìláng,
two Lángzhōng and two Yuánwàiláng,
and five Zhǔshì.
Among them, the Nèihuì Zǒngkē had six Zhǔshì,
the Wàiqiānzhàokē had two Zhǔshì,
four Sījì,
two Zhàomó,
and one Guǎngōu.
The Zàijīng Xíngyòngkù was also established,
subordinate to the Hùbù.
(It had one Dàshǐ,
two Fùshǐ,
one Diǎnshǐ,
and two Dūjiān.)
In the thirteenth year (1380), the ministry's rank was elevated,
and one Shàngshū and
two Shìláng were fixed.
It was divided into four subordinate departments: Zǒngbù,
Dùzhībù,
Jīnbù,
and Cāngbù.
Each department had one Lángzhōng and one Yuánwàiláng.
The Zǒngbù had four Zhǔshì,
the Dùzhībù and Jīnbù each had three Zhǔshì,
and the Cāngbù had two Zhǔshì.
Soon after, the Zàijīng Xíngyòngkù was abolished.
In the twenty-second year (1389), the Zǒngbù was renamed Mínbù.

In the twenty-third year (1390), the four departments were again divided into twelve departments: Hénán, Běipíng, Shāndōng, Shānxī, Shǎnxī, Zhèjiāng, Jiāngxī, Húguǎng, Guǎngdōng, Guǎngxī, Sìchuān, and Fújiàn.
(The Sìchuān Department concurrently oversaw Yúnnán.)
Each department had one Lángzhōng and one Yuánwàiláng,
and two Zhǔshì,
each overseeing the households, finances, and other affairs of one Bùzhèngsī,
and, depending on the complexity,
concurrently managed the Capital region.
Each department was still subdivided into four sections for management.
Additionally, one Zhàomó and one Jiǎnxiào were appointed,
to audit the incoming and outgoing documents,
and to supervise them.
In the nineteenth year (1386), the Bǎochāo Tíjíusī was re-established.
(The Bǎochāo Tíjíusī was first established in the seventh year of Hóngwǔ (1374),
with one Tíjíu,
ranked Zheng Qīpǐn;
one Fùtíjíu,
ranked Cóng Qīpǐn;
and one Lìmù,
appointed by the province.
Its subordinate Chāozhǐ and Yìnchāo two bureaus
each had one Dàshǐ,
ranked Zhèng Bāpǐn;
one Fùshǐ,
ranked Zhèng Jiǔpǐn;
and one Diǎnshǐ,
appointed by the province.
The Bǎochāo and Xíngyòng two treasuries
each had two Dàshǐ,
ranked Zhèng Bāpǐn;
two Fùshǐ,
ranked Zhèng Jiǔpǐn;
and one Diǎnshǐ,
appointed by the province.
Later, the Tíjíu was promoted to Zhèng Sìpǐn.
It was abolished in the thirteenth year (1380),
and re-established in this year (1386),
ranked Zhèng Bāpǐn.)
In the twenty-sixth year (1393), people from Zhèjiāng, Jiāngxī, Sū, and Sōng were forbidden from serving in the Hùbù.
In the twenty-ninth year (1396), the twelve departments were renamed twelve Qīnglìsī.
During Jiànwén's reign,
they reverted to four departments.
(See the Lìbù for the rest.)
Chéngzǔ restored the old system.
In the first year of Yǒnglè (1403), the Běipíngsī was renamed Běijīngsī.
In the eighteenth year (1420), the Běijīngsī was abolished,
and the Yúnnán, Guìzhōu, and Jiāozhǐ three Qīnglìsī were established.
In the tenth year of Xuāndé (1435), the Jiāozhǐsī was abolished,
and it was fixed at thirteen departments.
Thereafter, their responsibilities were merged.
The Shǎnxī Department concurrently managed the stipends of imperial relatives, meritorious nobles, and civil and military officials.
The Fújiàn Department concurrently managed the prefectures, departments, and garrisons of Běizhílì.
The Sìchuān Department concurrently managed the prefectures, departments, and garrisons of Nánzhílì.
The Shāndōng Department concurrently managed the salt taxes of the entire realm.
The Guìzhōu Department concurrently managed customs duties.
The Yúnnán Department concurrently managed grain transport and the various granaries of Lín and Dé.
The Guǎngxī Department concurrently managed the imperial horse and elephant stables and various granaries.
Early in the Míng dynasty,
a Sīnóngsī (Directorate of Agriculture) was once established,
but it was soon abolished.
(In the first year of Wú, a Sīnóngsī was established.
Its Qīng,
a Principal Third Rank official;
its Shǎoqīng,
a Principal Fourth Rank official;
its Chéng,
a Principal Fifth Rank official;
the Lìng of the Yōngtiánshǔ (Bureau of Common Fields),
a Principal Fifth Rank official;
its Diǎnbù and Sījì (Registrar and Accountant),
Principal Seventh Rank officials.
It was abolished in the first year of Hóngwǔ.
In the third year, the Sīnóngsī was re-established,
with its administrative seat opened in Hénán.
It appointed one Qīng,
two Shǎoqīng,
four Chéng,
and two Zhǔbù and Lùshì each.
It was abolished again in the fourth year.)
Later, a Pànlùsī (Directorate of Judicial Records) was established,
but it was also abolished.
(In the thirteenth year of Hóngwǔ, a Pànlùsī was established,
responsible for the salaries, official documents, and credentials of officials in the capital.
It appointed one Pànlù,
a Principal Seventh Rank official;
and two Fùpàn,
Auxiliary Seventh Rank officials.
Soon, the Pànlù was renamed Sīzhèng,
and the Fùpàn were renamed Zuǒ and
Yòu Sīfù.
It was abolished in the eighteenth year.)
Neither of these was subordinate to the Hùbù (Board of Revenue).
One Zǒngdūcāngcháng (Director-General of Granaries and Storehouses)
was in charge of supervising the grain reserves in the granaries and storehouses in the capital and places like Tōngzhōu.
Early in Hóngwǔ,
twenty Jūnchúcāng (Military Granaries) were established,
each with officials to manage their affairs.
During Yǒnglè's reign,
the capital was moved to Běijīng,
and the Jīngcāng (Capital Granaries) and various Tōngzhōu granaries were established.
Officials from the Hùbù were assigned to manage them.
In the fifth year of Xuāndé, Lǐ Chǎng was first appointed Hùbù Shàngshū (Minister of Revenue),
specifically to supervise these matters,
which then became a fixed system.
Thereafter,
whether a Shàngshū
or a Shìláng (Vice Minister),
they did not manage the regular affairs of the Board.
In the fifteenth year of Jiājìng, they were also ordered to concurrently supervise agricultural affairs in Xīyuàn.
Early in Lóngqìng's reign,
this concurrent duty was abolished.
In the second year of Wànlì, an additional Hùbù Zhǔshì (Secretary of Revenue) was assigned to accompany the treasury,
to daily receive and disburse silver with the Zhǔshì in charge of the treasury,
and to rotate at the end of each quarter.
In the ninth year, this was abolished,
and the Shìláng of the Board were ordered to manage it in rotation.
It was re-established in the eleventh year.
In the twenty-fifth year, Yòu Shìláng (Right Vice Minister) Zhāng Yǎngméng was appointed to supervise the Liáoxiǎng (Liaodong military provisions).
In the forty-seventh year, an additional Dūxiǎng Shìláng (Vice Minister Supervising Provisions) was appointed.
(During Chóngzhēn's reign,
there were supervisors for Liáoxiǎng, Kòuxiǎng (Rebel suppression provisions), and Xuāndàxiǎng (Xuānfǔ and Dàtóng provisions),
adding three or four more individuals.)
In the fifth year of Tiānqǐ, another Dūlǐqiánfǎ Shìláng (Vice Minister Supervising Currency Regulations) was appointed.
Lǐbù (Board of Rites).
One Shàngshū,
(Principal Second Rank,)
and one Zuǒ Shìláng (Left Vice Minister) and one Yòu Shìláng (Right Vice Minister) each,
(Principal Third Rank.)
Its subordinate offices:
Sīwùtīng (Bureau of General Affairs),
with two Sīwù (Secretaries),
(Auxiliary Ninth Rank.)
Yízhì, Cíjì, Zhǔkè, Jīngshàn — four Qīnglìsī (Bureaus of Scrutiny),
each with one Lángzhōng (Director),
(Principal Fifth Rank,)
one Yuánwàiláng (Assistant Director),
(Auxiliary Fifth Rank,)
and one Zhǔshì (Secretary),
(Principal Sixth Rank.
In the sixth year of Zhèngtǒng, an additional Zhǔshì was appointed to each of the Yízhì and Cíjì bureaus.
Another Zhǔshì was added to the Yízhìsī,
to instruct imperial sons-in-law.
In the fifth year of Hóngzhì, an additional Zhǔshì was appointed to the Zhǔkèsī,
to supervise the Huìtóngguǎn (Hall of Joint Reception).)
Its jurisdiction included:
Zhùyìnjú (Bureau for Casting Seals),
with one Dàshǐ (Chief Commissioner)
and two Fùshǐ (Deputy Commissioners).
(In the ninth year of Wànlì, one was abolished.)
The Shàngshū was in charge of the regulations concerning rites, sacrifices, banquets, and imperial examinations throughout the empire.
The Shìláng assisted him.
The Yízhì division was specifically in charge of various rituals, imperial enfeoffments, imperial examinations, and schools.
When the Son of Heaven ascended the throne,
or underwent the capping ceremony or grand wedding,
or enfeoffed the crown prince, imperial concubines, or crown princess,
or bestowed honorific titles upon the empress dowager,
or held court audiences and greetings,
or grand feasts and banquets,
or grand archery contests and banquet archery,
it would present the various ceremonial protocols in memorials.

As for the Jīngyán (Imperial Lectures), rìjiǎng (daily lectures), gēngjí (ploughing ceremony), shìxué (inspection of schools), cèshì (imperial examinations), chuánlú (proclamation of examination results), xúnshòu (imperial tours), qīnzhēng (personal imperial campaigns), jìnlì (presenting the calendar), jìnchūn (presenting spring offerings), xiànfú (presenting captives), and zòujié (reporting victories);
as for the crown prince's coming of age and acting as regent;
as for imperial princes' studies and departure to their fiefs;
as for the birth and naming of imperial children;
as well as the rites for all officials and noblewomen to pay respects to the crown prince and empress;
and the rites for various kingdoms,
all ceremonial forms were promulgated to the various bureaus.
Whenever imperial edicts or patents of nobility were transmitted,
or imperial edicts, proclamations, memorials, and communications between officials were read aloud,
they were given the appropriate forms.
Each year, requests were made to enfeoff imperial clan members as princes, commandery princes, generals, commandants, consorts, princesses, and noble ladies,
each ranked according to their closeness of relation.
Officials, when addressing imperial princes,
used their official titles and names but did not declare themselves their subjects.
The princes' own subjects declared themselves subjects to their princes.
Whenever patents of nobility for imperial clan members, imperial sons-in-law, court ladies, and tributary kings were issued,
it was coordinated with the Lìbù (Board of Personnel) to request them.
As for the seals of various bureaus,
their regulations were observed.
