gold,
gilded, and silver.
If worn out, they were to be replaced.
For all auspicious omens,
identify their specific nature and object,
and do not request for Fengshàn sacrifices to sway the emperor's mind.
Through the administration of schools, educate the literati.
Through the system of tribute examinations, recruit talented individuals.
Through the village drinking ritual, teach humility and deference to age.
Through caring for the elderly, honor the aged.
Through regulations, establish ranks and authority.
Through relief for the poor, extend benevolent governance.
Through commendations and displays, encourage and motivate.
Through submitting proposals and holding discussions, fully ascertain advantages and disadvantages.
Through prohibiting self-castration, deter wicked people.
The Cí Jì (department) was responsible for all sacrificial rituals, as well as astronomy, national mourning, and taboos of the ancestral temple.
There are three types of sacrifices:
to the celestial deities, terrestrial deities, and human spirits.
Distinguish between the great sacrifices, medium sacrifices, and small sacrifices, and offer them respectfully.
Inspect and frequently review the altars, shrines, and imperial tombs.
Prepare the offerings of sacrificial animals and wine, jade and silk, cooked cereals and meat broth, and items for burial and burning on land and water.
Rank the importance of those accompanied, those offered secondary sacrifices, and the merits and virtues, and perform the rites accordingly.
For all celestial and terrestrial deities recorded in the sacrificial canon,
consult the imperial statutes,
inform the relevant officials,
and diligently perform the sacrificial rites in due season.
Supervise the imperial astrologers in distributing the calendar and celestial phenomena throughout the realm.
During solar and lunar eclipses,
notify all internal and external offices to perform rescue rituals.
Upon any disaster or anomaly, immediately report it,
and if severe, request sacrifices and self-reflection.
For all funerals and sacrifices,
there are gradations according to status,
all with established regulations that are promulgated.
For all posthumous titles (shì),
for emperors (seventeen characters),
empresses (thirteen characters),
consorts, crown princes, and crown princesses (both two characters),
and imperial princes (one character),
and princely commanders (two characters),
characters are used to differentiate.
For meritorious relatives, civil and military ministers requesting funeral and sacrificial rites, grants, and posthumous titles,
the relevant office must be notified,
their conduct and abilities thoroughly examined,
public opinion gathered,
and a decision made to report to the throne.
For those attendants who served diligently, offered loyal remonstrance, and died,
even if their official rank did not qualify for a posthumous title,
they may all be specially granted one.
For all commemorative rites for deceased emperors and empresses,
sacrifices are offered at their mausoleums,
and court is suspended but duties are not neglected.
All matters concerning astronomy, geography, medicine, divination, teachers and shamans, music, Buddhist and Daoist clergy,
are to be registered and overseen.
Those who initiate heretical or delusional practices shall be punished without pardon.
The Zhǔ Kè (department) was responsible for all matters concerning tributary missions from foreign states, their reception, and the granting of gifts.
When foreign states bring tribute,
distinguish the tributary route, envoys, and the quantity, distance, and abundance of the tribute items,
to determine the appropriate reception and escort by royal envoys, banquets, lodging, food provisions,
and differences in rewards and gifts.
All tribute must be inspected,
before being delivered to the imperial treasury.
If incidental goods are carried,
their value shall be paid.
If a foreign state requests investiture for succession,
an imperial edict and seal shall be sent to their country.
Upon the return of the envoy,
they shall report on the customs and local products of that region,
and the protocols for gifts and courtesies.
If any foreign state performs meritorious service in defending the borders,
an imperial decree and seal shall be granted for their investiture.
When envoys from various countries travel,
if they have an imperial edict, the edict shall be verified;
if they have an official travel pass, the pass shall be verified,
and they shall not be allowed to enter without authorization.
When indigenous officials bring tribute,
their travel pass shall also be verified.
Upon their return,
an imperial edict engraved in gold shall be issued for their journey,
which must match a bronze tally.
All matters concerning the examination of spoken words,
translation of written texts,
escorting and hosting guests,
and assessing the competence of interpreters and translators from the Sīyí Guǎn (Four Barbarian Bureaus),
as well as prohibiting their collusion and leakage of information, are managed here.
All imperial grants and gifts,
and tributes of local products from various provinces,
are under its charge.
The Department of Imperial Cuisine [Jīngshàn] was responsible for feasts and banquets [yànxiǎng], sacrificial animals and vessels [shēngdòu], and wines and meals [jiǔshàn].
All ceremonial food bestowed by the emperor upon officials,
whether called "banquets" [yàn],
or "wine and food" [jiǔfàn],
was divided into three grades: upper, middle, and lower,
according to their official rank [pǐnzhì].
Foreign envoys [fānshǐ] and indigenous officials [tǔguān] received banquets [yàn]
and routine provisions [xiàchéng].
(Banquets [yàn] could be single
or double,
and routine provisions [xiàchéng] could be standard
or imperially bestowed [qīncì].)
All these were differentiated by their grade.
When imperial princes [qīnwáng] departed for their fiefs,
or when princes [wáng], dukes [gōng], or generals [jiāngjūn] came to court,
and their envoys,
the same rules applied.
All delicacies [shànxiū], fine wines [jiǔlǐ], and ingredients [pǐnliào]
were supplied by the Court of Imperial Entertainments [Guānglù],
which tallied the quantities
and managed their expenditure and receipt.
All kitchen staff [chúyì]
were conscripted from the populace
to serve the Court of Imperial Sacrifices [Tàicháng] and the Court of Imperial Entertainments [Guānglù];
those who had served for many years
could be selected to fill the post of Director of Palace Cuisine [Wángfǔ Diǎnshàn] in a princely establishment.
Annually, for the storage and distribution of ice,
the responsible departments were instructed to ensure cleanliness.
Initially,
in the 1st year of the Hóngwǔ reign (1368), the Ministry of Rites [Lǐbù] was established.
In the 6th year, two Ministers [shàngshū]
and two Vice Ministers [shìláng] were appointed.
It was divided into four subordinate departments: the General Department [Zǒngbù],
the Department of Sacrifices [Cíbù],
the Department of Imperial Meals [Shànbù],
and the Department of Reception [Zhǔkèbù].
Each department had one Director [lángzhōng] and one Assistant Director [yuánwàiláng],
and three Secretaries [zhǔshì].
In the 13th year, the departmental rank was raised [shēngbùzhì].
One Minister [shàngshū] and one Vice Minister [shìláng] were appointed,
and each subordinate department had one Director [lángzhōng], one Assistant Director [yuánwàiláng], and one Secretary [zhǔshì].
Soon after, an additional Vice Minister [shìláng] was appointed.
In the 22nd year, the General Department [Zǒngbù] was changed to the Department of Ceremonies [Yíbù].

In the 29th year, the Department of Ceremonies [Yíbù], Department of Sacrifices [Cíbù], and Department of Imperial Meals [Shànbù] were changed to the Bureau of Ceremonies and Regulations [Yízhì], Bureau of Sacrifices [Cí jì], and Bureau of Imperial Cuisine [Jīngshàn], respectively;
only the Department of Reception [Zhǔkè] remained as it was,
and all were collectively referred to as Bureaus of Administration [Qīnglìsī].
According to historical records, although the Minister of Rites [Zhōu Zōngbó] in the Zhōu dynasty was in charge of national rites [bānglǐ],
and the Minister of Education [Sītú] was already in charge of national education [bāngjiào],
what was referred to as "rites"
then only comprised sacrifices to spirits and deities [guǐshén císì].
However, the integration of ceremonial music [diǎnyuè] and ceremonial education [diǎnjiào],
covering everything from the imperial clan and princely states [zōngfān] internally
to various foreign states [zhūfān] externally,
and from celestial officials [tiānguān] above
to physicians [yīshī], cooks [shànfū], and entertainers [língrén] below,
with nothing left out,
only began in the Míng dynasty.
After the Chénghuà and Hóngzhì reigns,
these duties were often performed by Hanlin academicians and Confucian scholars [Hànlín Rúchén].
Those who rose from this path to become Grand Dukes and Regents [gōnggū] in an assisting and guiding capacity
surpassed those from all other ministries.
Ministry of War [Bīngbù].
One Minister [shàngshū],
(Principal Rank 2,)
and one Left and one Right Vice Minister [shìláng] each
(Principal Rank 3).
Its subordinates included
the Secretariat Office [Sīwùtīng],
with two Secretaries [sīwù]
(Auxiliary Rank 9).

The four Bureaus of Administration [Qīnglìsī]—Bureau of Selections for Military Officials [Wǔxuǎn], Bureau of Military Survey [Zhífāng], Bureau of Ordnance and Transport [Chējià], and Bureau of Military Stores [Wǔkù]—
each had one Director [lángzhōng]
(Principal Rank 5.
In the 10th year of the Zhèngtǒng reign, one additional Director [lángzhōng] was appointed for the Bureaus of Selections for Military Officials [Wǔxuǎn] and Military Survey [Zhífāng] each.
In the 3rd year of the Chénghuà reign, one additional Director [lángzhōng] was appointed for the Bureau of Ordnance and Transport [Chējià].
In the 9th year of the Wànlì reign, all these additions were abolished.)
Each had one Assistant Director [yuánwàiláng]
(Auxiliary Rank 5.
In the 10th year of the Zhèngtǒng reign, one additional Assistant Director [yuánwàiláng] was appointed for the Bureau of Selections for Military Officials [Wǔxuǎn].
In the 9th year of the Hóngzhì reign, one additional Assistant Director [yuánwàiláng] was appointed for the Bureau of Military Stores [Wǔkù].
Later, all were abolished.
In the 12th year of the Jiājìng reign, one additional Assistant Director [yuánwàiláng] was appointed for the Bureau of Military Survey [Zhífāng].)
Two Secretaries [zhǔshì]
(Principal Rank 6.
During the Hóngwǔ and Xuāndé reigns,
three additional Secretaries [zhǔshì] were appointed for the Bureau of Selections for Military Officials [Wǔxuǎn],
and four for the Bureau of Military Survey [Zhífāng].
In the 14th year of the Zhèngtǒng reign, one additional Secretary [zhǔshì] was appointed for the Bureaus of Ordnance and Transport [Chējià] and Military Stores [Wǔkù] each.
Later, these were abolished.
In the 11th year of the Wànlì reign, one additional Secretary [zhǔshì] was again appointed for the Bureau of Ordnance and Transport [Chējià].)
Under its jurisdiction were
one Director [dàshǐ] of the Court of State Ceremonials [Huìtóngguǎn]
(Principal Rank 9),
and two Deputy Directors [fùshǐ] (Auxiliary Rank 9).
One Director [dàshǐ] and one Deputy Director [fùshǐ] each for Dàtōng Pass [Dàtōngguān]
(both unranked [wèirùliú]).
The Minister [shàngshū] was in charge of policies for the selection, appointment, inspection, and training of military officials and soldiers [wǔwèi guānjūn] throughout the empire.
The Vice Ministers [shìláng] assisted him.

The Bureau of Selections for Military Officials [Wǔxuǎn] was responsible for the selection, appointment, promotion, transfer, hereditary succession, and merits and rewards of indigenous officials [tǔguān] in the guard garrisons [wèisuǒ].
There were six ranks for military officials,
and twelve meritorious ranks [xūn].
(Principal Rank 1:
Left and Right Grand Pillars of State [zuǒ, yòu zhùguó].
Auxiliary Rank 1:
Pillar of State [zhùguó].
Principal Rank 2:
Superior Protector of the Army [shànghùjūn].
Auxiliary Rank 2:
Protector of the Army [hùjūn].
Principal Rank 3:
Superior Commandant of Light Chariots [shàngqīngchē dūwèi].
Auxiliary Rank 3:
Commandant of Light Chariots [qīngchē dūwèi].
Principal Rank 4:
Superior Commandant of Cavalry [shàngqídūwèi].
Auxiliary Rank 4:
Commandant of Cavalry [qídūwèi].
Principal Rank 5:
Valiant Cavalry Commandant [xiāoqíwèi].
Auxiliary Rank 5:
Flying Cavalry Commandant [fēiqíwèi].
Principal Rank 6:
Cloud Cavalry Commandant [yúnqíwèi].
Auxiliary Rank 6:
Martial Cavalry Commandant [wǔqíwèi].)
There were thirty honorary ranks [sǎnjiē].
(Principal Rank 1:
Initially appointed Grand Master of Glorious Happiness (Special Advance) [Tèjìn Rónglù Dàfū],
promoted to Grand Master of Brilliant Happiness (Special Advance) [Tèjìn Guānglù Dàfū].
Auxiliary Rank 1:
Initially appointed Grand Master of Glorious Happiness [Rónglù Dàfū],
promoted to Grand Master of Brilliant Happiness [Guānglù Dàfū].
Principal Rank 2:
Initially appointed General of Swift Cavalry [Piàojì Jiāngjūn],
promoted to General of the Golden Guard [Jīnwú Jiāngjūn],
additionally appointed General of Dragon and Tiger [Lónghǔ Jiāngjūn].
Auxiliary Rank 2:
Initially appointed General Who Guards the State [Zhènguó Jiāngjūn],
promoted to General Who Stabilizes the State [Dìnguó Jiāngjūn],
additionally appointed General Who Serves the State [Fèngguó Jiāngjūn].
Principal Rank 3:
Initially appointed General Who Manifests Bravery [Zhāoyǒng Jiāngjūn],
promoted to General Who Manifests Resolution [Zhāoyì Jiāngjūn],
additionally appointed General Who Manifests Martial Prowess [Zhāowǔ Jiāngjūn].
Auxiliary Rank 3:
Initially appointed General Who Cherishes Distant Lands [Huáiyuǎn Jiāngjūn],
promoted to General Who Pacifies Distant Lands [Dìngyuǎn Jiāngjūn],
additionally appointed General Who Brings Peace to Distant Lands [Ānyuǎn Jiāngjūn].
Principal Rank 4:
Initially appointed General of Manifested Might [Míngwēi Jiāngjūn],
promoted to General Who Proclaims Might [Xuānwēi Jiāngjūn],
additionally appointed General Who Extends Might [Guǎngwēi Jiāngjūn].
Auxiliary Rank 4:
Initially appointed General Who Proclaims Martial Prowess [Xuānwǔ Jiāngjūn],
promoted to General Who Displays Martial Prowess [Xiǎnwǔ Jiāngjūn],
additionally appointed General of Trustworthy Martial Prowess [Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn].
Principal Rank 5:
Initially appointed General of Martial Virtue [Wǔdé Jiāngjūn],
promoted to General of Martial Integrity [Wǔjié Jiāngjūn].
Auxiliary Rank 5:
Initially appointed General of Martial Strategy [Wǔlüè Jiāngjūn],
promoted to General of Martial Resolution [Wǔyì Jiāngjūn].
Principal Rank 6:
Initially appointed Commandant Who Manifests Trust [Zhāoxìn Xiàowèi],
promoted to Commandant Who Upholds Trust [Chéngxìn Xiàowèi].
Auxiliary Rank 6:
Initially appointed Commandant Who Displays Loyalty [Zhōngxiǎn Xiàowèi],
promoted to Commandant of Loyal Martial Prowess [Zhōngwǔ Xiàowèi].)
There were six selections every year.
There were hereditary officials (shìguān),
and there were non-hereditary officials (liúguān).
Hereditary officials were of nine ranks:
(zhǐhuīshǐ,
zhǐhuītóngzhī,
zhǐhuīqiānshì,
wèizhènfǔ,
zhèngqiānhù,
fùqiānhù,
bǎihù,
shìbǎihù,
suǒzhènfǔ).
All had inherited positions (xízhí)
and substitute positions (tìzhí).
When they were young,
they received generous allowances.
If they could not inherit the position,
there were reductions and abolitions (jiǎn gé),
or complete abolitions (tōng gé).
Non-hereditary officials were of eight ranks:
(zuǒyòudūdū,
dūdūtóngzhī,
dūdūqiānshì,
dūzhǐhuīshǐ,
dūzhǐhuītóngzhī,
dūzhǐhuīqiānshì,
zhèngliúshǒu,
fùliúshǒu).
They were promoted and appointed from hereditary officials,
or employed through military examinations (wǔjǔ).
None could inherit their positions.
If there were any who held hereditary positions,
it was by special grace.
Those not truly appointed were called acting officials (shǔzhí);
(Acting officials
had their original rank increased by one level, counted as half a level,
received no salary,
and, if not for military merit,
could not be formally appointed.)
or probationary officials (shìzhí);
(Probationary officials were counted as one level,
received half salary,
and were not granted imperial patents (gào).)
or contributed officials (nàzhí).
(Contributed officials received salary
but did not manage affairs.)
Battle merits were of two grades: extraordinary merit (qígōng) was the highest,
first merit (tóugōng) was secondary.
Head merits (shǒugōng) were of four grades: those from Yíbĕi were the greatest,
Liáodōng was secondary,
Xīfān and Miáomán were again secondary,
and internal rebel forces (nèidì fǎnkòu) were again secondary.
For all comparisons and assessments,
there were old officials (jiùguān)
(those before the 31st year of Hóngwǔ were old)
and new officials (xīnguān).
(Those from after Chéngzǔ were new.)
Regarding military administration (jūnzheng),
examinations and selections were held every five years.
Before the deadline, the pacification commissioner (fǔ) and surveillance commissioner (àn) would submit reports of merits and demerits,
which would be reviewed to decide retention or dismissal.
The commanders-in-chief (zǒngbīngguān) in the halls of the Five Chief Military Commissions (Wǔfǔ) and the Jǐnyī Wèi,
all made self-assessments,
and the emperor decided.
Two individuals were recommended for the highest ranks,
and one for ranks below Dūzhǐhuī.
All native chieftain officials (tǔsī zhīguān) were of nine ranks,
from junior third rank (cóngsānpǐn) to junior seventh rank (cóngqīpǐn),
and all received no annual salary.
Their sons, younger brothers, clan members, wives, daughters, as well as sons-in-law and nephews who inherited or substituted,
all followed their local customs.
Officials guarding the frontiers (fùsài zhīguān),
from Dūdū to Zhènfǔ,
a total of fourteen ranks,
all had their imperial patents (gàochì) checked to prevent imposture.
For posthumous appointments (zèngguān) for those who died in imperial service (wángshì),
two ranks were added;
for those who died in battle (zhànzhèn),
three ranks were added.
All appointments and dismissals originating from the imperial decree (zhōngzhǐ)
had to be reported again before being carried out.
Yellow slips were used to verify maps and reports (tú zhuàng);
initial achievements (chūjì) were used to issue imperial patents (gàochì);
effectiveness and merit (xiàogōng) were used to assess commanders (jiànglǐng);
competitions and trials (bǐshì) were used to train soldiers (zútú);
generous support (yōuyǎng) was used for those whose lines of grace (ēngù) were extinguished;
praise and compensation (bāoxù) were used to encourage those who fought to the death;
honorary positions (jìlù) were used to control those favored by grace (ēnxìng);
and laws regarding killing surrendered enemies, being besieged and lost, evading the enemy, and inciting rebellion were used to enforce military discipline (sùjūnjī);
and codes regarding legal punishments (diǎnxíng), moral depravity (bàilún), robbery (xíngjié), and retreating from battle (tuìzhèn) were used to cut off hereditary stipends (shìlù).

The Bureau of Military Provisions (Zhífāng) was in charge of maps (yútú), military regulations (jūnzhì), city defenses (chénghuáng), garrisons (zhènshù), selection and training (jiǎnlìan), and expeditions (zhēngtǎo).
All geographical features of the realm, including their dangers, ease, distances,
and borders between frontier and interior,
were recorded in maps and documents (túběn).
Reports were submitted every three years,
along with the numbers of officials, soldiers, chariots, and cavalry.
All military systems maintained internal and external cohesion;
military officials were not allowed to arbitrarily issue tallies to conscript or mobilize.
From the Dūdū Fǔ,
Dūzhǐhuī Sī,
Liúshǒu Sī,
to the interior and exterior Wei garrisons (wèishǒuyù), agricultural colonies (túntián), and various herd thousand-household offices (qúnmùqiānhùsuǒ),
ceremonial guard offices (yíwèisī),
native chieftain offices (tǔsī),
and various foreign Dū Sī and Wei garrisons,
each commanded its own officials, soldiers, and tribes,
to heed orders for conscription, defense, tribute, and frontier protection.
They were to repair and dredge their city moats and inspect them regularly.
There were five ranks of garrison officers (zhènshù jiàngxiào):
Zhènshǒu,
Xiéshǒu,
Fēnshǒu,
Shǒubèi,
and Bèiwō.
All were established as needed,
and troops were stationed in accordance with the strategic importance of the terrain.
All training of the Capital Garrisons (Jīngyíng)
was commanded by civil and military grandees,
and all Censorate (Kēdào) officials supervised them.
As for the training of general garrisons (jiāngjūn yíngliàn),
the Four Wei Garrisons (sìwèi yíngliàn),
and the garrisons of brave warriors (yǒngshì), young officials (yòuguān), palace attendants (shèrén), etc.,
they would examine their military supplies,
inspect their squads,
and observe their presence or absence, diligence or idleness,
to teach them the rhythm of sitting and standing, advancing and retreating, quickness and slowness, density and sparseness,
and the signals of drums and banners.
For expeditions, commanders were requested for deployment,
rewards and punishments were announced,
troops and provisions were mobilized,
and merits and demerits were recorded,
to promote or demote them.
Fortifications and barriers were used to defend the frontiers (biānjìao);
beacon fires were used to transmit messages;
passes and ferries were used to interrogate spies;
arrests were used to suppress bandits;
strong and able-bodied villagers were selected;
and methods of recall and release, recruitment and filling, selection and exemption, consolidation and relief, and release and care were used to organize the military ranks.
The Imperial Carriages (Chējià) department managed imperial equipage (lǔbù), ceremonial guards (yízhàng), imperial guards (jìnwèi), post stations (yìchuán), and horse pasturage (mù).
The grand imperial equipage (dàlǔbù)
was displayed for grand ceremonies and grand court assemblies;
the Dānbì carriage
was used for ordinary court sessions;
the Wǔchén carriage
was used during Shìzōng's southern tours.
All were categorized by their numbers,
and assigned to the relevant offices.
The imperial equipage of the Empress Dowager (Cígōng) and Empress (Zhōnggōng),
and the ceremonial guards of the Crown Prince (Dōnggōng) and imperial princes (zōngfān),
were also arranged similarly.
All palace guards (shìwèi)
were on full duty in the imperial hall,
and on rotational duty for ordinary court sessions.
The guard posts (shǒuwèi) and Imperial Bodyguard garrisons (qīnjūnwèi)
divided the front, back, left, and right four gates into four lines,
and patrolled them day and night.
(Guarding the Imperial City (Huángchéng):
the front Wǔmén formed one line,
the rear Xuánwǔmén formed one line,
the left Dōnghuámén formed one line,
and the right Xīhuámén formed one line.)
All post stations (yóuchuán)
in the capital were called Huìtóng Guǎn,
and outside the capital were called yì
or dìyùnsǔo.
All were operated with tally-vouchers (fúyàn guānquàn).
For all horse administration (mǎzhèng),
the specialized agencies were
the two directorates, Tàipú and Yuànmǎ.
They checked the registers
and regularly reported increases and decreases,
but the palace (nèi) did not participate.
The Imperial Armory (Wǔkù) was in charge of military weapons (róngqì), tallies and inspections (fúkàn), registers (chǐjí), military education (wǔxué), and firewood and servants (xīnlì).
Whenever internal or external officials and soldiers went on campaign,
the Ministry of Works (Gōngbù) was instructed to provide weapons and equipment.
Their numbers were recorded in registers.
Imperial decrees (zhìchì) were sent to various borders for conscription and mobilization.
When envoys left the passes,
their tallies (kànhé) had to be verified.
When military ranks were lacking,
orders were sent to the provinces, prefectures, and counties to recruit.
By methods of pursuit and arrest, record-keeping, household registration, appointments and dismissals, and suspension of recruitment,
they verified the numbers of recruited, assembled, condemned, exiled, and reassigned military households (yíngdīng chǐjí).
All young military officials (wǔzhí yòuguān)
and children of officials who had not yet inherited their positions
studied in military schools (wǔxué),
with one director (zhǔshì) supervising them.
The virtue or lack thereof of the school officials and the diligence or idleness of the students were reported.
Various offices and bureaus were supplied with firewood,
and their direct yamen had servants,
the number depending on the official's rank.
Initially,
in the first year of Hóngwǔ (1368), the Ministry of War (Bīngbù) was established.
In the sixth year (1373), one Minister (Shàngshū) was added,
and one Vice-Minister (Shìláng).
The Departments of General Administration (Zǒngbù), Imperial Carriages (Jiàbù), and Personnel (Zhífāng) were established,
with a Director (Lángzhōng), an Assistant Director (Yuánwàiláng), and a Secretary (Zhǔshì) for each,
matching the numbers in the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù).
In the thirteenth year (1380), the rank of the ministry was elevated,
and one Minister and one Vice-Minister were established.
Additionally, the Department of Armory (Kùbù) was added, making it four subordinate departments.
Each department had one Director, one Assistant Director, and one Secretary.
In the fourteenth year (1381), one probationary Vice-Minister was added.
〔一０〕In the twenty-second year (1389), the Department of General Administration was renamed the Department of Military Affairs (Sīmǎbù).

In the twenty-ninth year (1396), the four departments were definitively reorganized into the four Bureaus of Military Selection (Wǔxuǎn), Personnel (Zhífāng), Imperial Carriages (Chējià), and Armory (Wǔkù).
(Only the Bureau of Personnel retained its old name.)
During the Jǐngtài reign (1450-1456),
an additional Minister was appointed
to assist in the ministry's affairs,
but this position was abolished in the early Tiānshùn reign (1457).
In the fourth year of Lóngqìng (1570), two additional Vice-Ministers were appointed,
but they were soon abolished.
Towards the end of the Wànlì reign (c. 1620), the positions were re-established.
One assistant for managing military administration of the capital garrisons (Xiéli Jīngyíng Róngzhèng) was appointed,
(either a Minister,
a Vice-Minister,
or a Right Censor-in-Chief (Yòu Dū Yùshǐ)),
in charge of the training of the capital garrisons.
In the early Yǒnglè reign (c. 1403),
the three major garrisons were established,
all under military generals.
In the first year of Jǐngtài (1450), the position of Director of Garrison Training (Tídū Tuányíng) was first established,
and Minister Yú Qiān of the Ministry of War was appointed concurrently to lead it,
but it was later abolished.
In the third year of Chénghuà (1467), it was re-established,
usually held concurrently by a Minister of this ministry or a Censor-in-Chief.
In the twentieth year of Jiājìng (1541), Minister Liú Tiānhé was ordered to cease his ministerial duties,
given a separate seal (guānfáng),
and solely tasked with military administration.
In the twenty-ninth year (1550), the seal of
"Supreme Commander of Capital Garrison Military Administration" (Zǒngdū Jīngyíng Róngzhèng)
was given to Qiú Luán,
and a Vice-Minister of this ministry was instead appointed to assist in military administration,
without a separate seal.
In the ninth year of Wànlì (1581), it was abolished,
but re-established in the eleventh year (1583).
In the early Tiānqǐ reign (c. 1621),
one assistant was added,
but soon abolished.
In the second year of Chóngzhēn (1629), one more was added,
with Liú Zhīlún, a Shùjíshì (probationary Hanlin academician), appointed as Vice-Minister of War to fill the position.
Ministry of Justice (Xíngbù).

(Senior Second Rank),

In the first year of Chénghuà (1465), Sìchuān and Guǎngxī Bureaus each added one Secretary,

During the Wànlì reign (1573-1620),
one Secretary was abolished from each of the Húguǎng, Shǎnxī, Shāndōng, and Fújiàn Bureaus.

(Junior Ninth Rank).
The Minister
is in charge of judicial affairs, penal servitude, review of death sentences, and prison regulations across the empire.
The Vice-Ministers assist him.
Each of the thirteen bureaus is in charge of judicial affairs in its respective province, and concurrently manages the capital prefectures and directly administered areas assigned to it.

Dōngshèng Zuǒ (東勝左), Dōngshèng Yòu (東勝右), Fǔníng (撫寧), Mìyún Zhōng (密雲中), Mìyún Hòu (密雲後), Dàtóng Zhōngtún (大同中屯), Tóngguān (潼關), Yíngzhōu Wǔtún (營州五屯), Wànquán Zuǒ (萬全左), Wànquán Yòu (萬全右) Guards;
Kuānhé (寬河), Wǔdìng (武定), Púzhōu (蒲州) Qiān
hùsuǒ.
Guìzhōu (貴州) Department administered Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù);
Office of Scrutiny for Personnel (Lìkē);
Sīcài Jú (司菜局);
and Chánglú Yányùn Sī (長蘆鹽運司);
Dàníng Dūsī (大寧都司);
Wànquán Dūsī (萬全都司);
Zhílì Sūzhōu (蘇州), Bǎodìng (保定), Héjiān (河間), Zhēndìng (真定), Shùndé (順德) five
prefectures;
Sūzhōu (蘇州), Tàicāng (太倉), Jìzhōu (薊州), Zūnhuà (遵化), Zhènshuò (鎮朔), Xīngzhōu Wǔtún (興州五屯);
Zhōngyì Zhōng (忠義中), Zhuōlù (涿鹿), Héjiān (河間), Tiānjīn (天津), Tiānjīn Zuǒ (天津左), Tiānjīn Yòu (天津右), Dézhōu (德州), Xuānfǔ Zuǒ (宣府左), Xuānfǔ Yòu (宣府右), Kāi
píng (平), Bǎo'ān (保安), Wèizhōu (蔚州), Yǒngníng (永寧) Guards;
Liángchéng (梁城), Xīnghé (興和), Guǎngchāng (廣昌) Qiānhùsuǒ.
Zhàomó (照磨) and Jiǎnxiào (檢校) officials;
checked legal documents;
recorded stolen goods and redemptions.
The Prison Warden (Sīyù);
led prison officials;
managed prisoners.
For all military and civilian personnel, officials, as well as imperial clan members and meritorious relatives who violated the law,
they questioned their statements;
investigated the truth or falsehood of their circumstances;
applied laws and precedents to discuss the severity of their crimes and made recommendations.
Imperial edict prisons must be based on the original records;
they must not cater to the emperor's will.
All special decrees, separate imperial edicts, imperial precedents, or posted precedents,
unless they have been discussed and formally established as law,
must not be cited as comparisons.
For all death penalties,
whether immediate execution or execution after autumn,
all required three reviews.
The Two Capitals (Liǎng Jīng) and the Thirteen Provincial Administration Commissions (Shísān Bùzhèng Sī),
death row inmates were tried and settled annually.
Every five years, an imperial decree was requested to dispatch officials
to review and examine cases of injustice and delays.
After the first frost (shuāngjiàng), serious offenders were reviewed,
with officials from the Five Palaces (Wǔ Fǔ), Nine Ministers (Jiǔ Qīng), and Offices of Scrutiny and Censorate (Kē Dào Guān) jointly reviewing them.
Those with doubts were exiled to the frontier;
those with new statements were referred to the relevant department for re-interrogation;
those who fit the law were held for observation.
During the summer, hot weather reviews were conducted;
caning was waived;
exile and penal servitude were reduced;
light offenders were released.
In years of drought,
special imperial decrees for reviewing prisoners were also implemented similarly.
During major sacrifices, executions were halted.
For redemption from punishment,
according to the severity of the crime,
those sentenced to beheading (zhǎn), strangulation (jiǎo), miscellaneous offenses (záfàn), or the lowest grade of penal servitude (tú mò jiǎn zhě)
were allowed to redeem themselves.
Petitions must proceed from lower to higher levels;
if a matter was serious and urgent,
permission was granted to beat the Dengwen Drum (登聞鼓).
If there were major judicial cases in the four directions,
officials would receive orders to investigate them.
For executions in the four directions,
two departmental officials were dispatched to oversee them.
For all judicial rulings,
their names and numbers were reported annually,
called the "annual report" (suìbào);
the numbers of those detained, released, alive, and deceased were reported monthly,
called the "monthly report" (yuèbào).
Once a case was closed,
it was transferred to the Grand Court of Revision (Dàlǐ Sì) for review,
with fairness and impartiality being the imperative.
For all prison inspections,
one director (zhǔshì) was rotated monthly
to repair prisons;
ensure locks and keys were secure;
inspect for cruelty and abuse;
and provide clothing and food.
If a prisoner fell ill,
family members were allowed to visit,
and shackles were removed for medical treatment.
Records of captured prisoners,
and confiscated official and private slaves and maids,
were all kept for knowledge.
Officials with faults
were also recorded.
At the end of the year, a request was made to clear their records.
Names and categories were used to encompass statutes;
"eight characters" (bāzì) were used to summarize statements and discussions;
(yǐ, huái, jiē, gè, qí, jí, jí, ruò);
"five degrees of mourning" (wǔfú) were used to consider circumstances and law;
ink tattoos (mòniè) were used to identify thieves.
Confiscated property did not enter ancestral tombs;
confiscated wealth did not enter the treasury (dùzhī);
clan members were not immediately executed in the marketplace;
palace women were not immediately sent to prison;
the mourning, elderly, and infirm were not immediately interrogated.
(Detailed in the Treatise on Penal Law, Xíngfǎ Zhì.)
In the first year of Hóngwǔ (洪武), the Ministry of Justice (Xíngbù) was established.
In the sixth year, one Minister (Shàngshū) and one Vice Minister (Shìláng) were added.
The Zǒngbù (總部), Bǐbù (比部), Dūguānbù (都官部), Sīménbù (司門部) were established;
each department had two Director (Lángzhōng) and two Assistant Director (Yuánwàiláng) officials;
only the Dūguānbù had one of each.
The Zǒngbù and Bǐbù each had six Principal (Zhǔshì) officials;
the Dūguānbù and Sīménbù each had four Principal officials.
In the eighth year,
due to the vast and complex departmental affairs,
four sections (kē) were added;
each section had one Minister, one Vice Minister, and one Director;
two Assistant Directors;
and five Principal officials.
In the thirteenth year, the departmental ranks were elevated;
one Minister was established;
one Vice Minister;
still divided into four subordinate departments;
each department had one Director and one Assistant Director;
the Zǒngbù and Bǐbù each had four Principal officials;
the Dūguānbù and Sīménbù each had two Principal officials;
soon after, one more Vice Minister was added.
(This marked the beginning of distinguishing between Left and Right Vice Ministers.)
In the twenty-second year, the Zǒngbù was renamed Xiànbù (憲部).

In the twenty-third year, the four departments were divided into twelve departments: Hénán (河南), Běipíng (北平), Shāndōng (山東), Shānxī (山西), Shǎnxī (陝西), Zhèjiāng (浙江), Jiāngxī (江西), Húguǎng (湖廣), Guǎngdōng (廣東), Guǎngxī (廣西), Sìchuān (四川), Fújiàn (福建);
(the Zhèjiāng Department also administered Yúnnán);
each department had officials
according to the system of the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù).
In the twenty-ninth year, they were reformed into twelve Clear Offices (Qīnglì Sī).
In the first year of Yǒnglè (永樂), Běipíng was renamed Běijīng (北京).
In the eighteenth year, the Běijīng Department was abolished;
three departments, Yúnnán (雲南), Guìzhōu (貴州), and Jiāozhǐ (交阯), were added.

and it was then set at thirteen Clear Offices.

The Shàngshū was in charge of the regulations concerning all civil and military officials, and mountains and marshes throughout the empire.
The Shìláng assisted him.
The Yíngshàn Bureau was responsible for the management of construction and renovation projects.
This included all works related to palaces, imperial tombs, city walls, altars, ancestral temples, granaries, offices, barracks, and princely residences.
It gathered laborers and materials,
and supervised the timely completion of projects.
As for imperial regalia, ceremonial guards, and musical instruments,
they were transferred to the Neifǔ (Imperial Household Department) and the respective offices,
each managing them according to their duties,
and regularly inspecting their soundness and cleanliness,
and overseeing any defects or excesses.
All prison implements
had to conform to the law.
There were two types of artisans:
those on rotation (lúnbān), who served once every three years,
their service not exceeding three months,
after which they returned home;
and resident artisans (zhùzuò),
who worked for ten days a month
and received a small stipend.
There were two types of laborers:
those assigned to work as punishment for crimes,
called regular laborers (zhènggōng),
and miscellaneous laborers (zá gōng).
Three days of miscellaneous labor counted as one day of regular labor,
and these were assigned and adjusted according to the scale of the task.
As for the storage of materials:
the Shénmù Chǎng (Divine Timber Yard)
and Dàmù Chǎng (Great Timber Yard)
stored timber;
the Hēiyáo Chǎng (Black Kiln Yard)
and Liúlí Chǎng (Glazed Tile Yard)
produced pottery and tiles;
the Táijī Chǎng (Foundation Yard)
stored firewood and reeds.
All these were registered by their numbers for use in construction and repair.
The Yúhéng Bureau was responsible for harvesting from mountains and marshes, hunting, and smelting.
All meat, hides, bones, horns, feathers of birds and beasts
that could be used for sacrifices, guests, or food,
and for ceremonial vessels and military supplies,
were annually ordered from various offices for collection.
The water tax was eighteen birds and twelve beasts;
the land tax was eighteen beasts and twelve birds,
all collected in their respective seasons.
At the turn of winter and spring,
no nets or traps were to be set in rivers and marshes;
at the turn of spring and summer,
no poison was to be used in fields and plains.
Trampling was forbidden when crops were thriving,
and burning was forbidden when grains were harvested.
If a harmful beast was present,
it was permitted to catch it with traps,
and rewards varied.
The foothills of all imperial tombs
were not to be entered with axes, nor used for kilns or smelting, nor for graves.
For emperors, sages, loyal and righteous individuals, famous mountains, sacred peaks, imperial tombs, and ancestral temples that had rendered service and virtue to the people,
gathering firewood and pasturing were forbidden.
The benefits from mountain areas and gardens
were left for the people to collect, with light taxation.
All military uniforms and weapons
were ordered from the relevant offices for manufacture,
and inspected jointly with the Bīngbù (Ministry of War),
ensuring their strength and meticulousness.
As for pottery and ceramics,
there were annual supplies,
temporary supplies,
and reductions.
Their numbers were registered,
and their income tallied,
without light destruction to burden the people.
For all smelting works,
the materials were regulated,
the molds were carefully inspected,
and then handed over to the relevant officials.
Coins had to conform to the specified weight in zhū and liǎng,
submitted to the Neifǔ and then distributed.
Tablets, talismans, and firearms
were cast in the Neifǔ,
and it was forbidden to leak their designs to outsiders.
As for dyes,
if they were not local products, they were not to be taxed.
The Dūshuǐ 典 (director) manages matters concerning rivers and lakes, ponds, bridges and roads, boats and vehicles, weaving and manufacturing, contracts and deeds, and weights and measures.
Water conservancy is called zhuǎncáo (transportation of grain),
and irrigation of fields.
Annually, they store gold, stone, bamboo, and wood, and rolled fascines,
and repair gates and dams, shallow and deep sections, weirs and dikes, and embankments in a timely manner.
They carefully manage storage and discharge to prepare for drought and flood,
preventing damage to fields, houses, graves, and crops.
Those operating boats and mills shall not contend for profit with irrigation,
and those irrigating fields shall not contend for profit with zhuǎncáo.
For all important water junctions,
Jingcháo officials are dispatched to manage them specifically,
to supervise the officials in charge.
Conscripting common people must be done during agricultural slack seasons;
if it cannot wait until the slack season,
then the work is rushed to completion.
For all roads and ferries,
repairs and maintenance are carried out in a timely manner.
If there is an imperial tour or a grand mourning or grand ceremony,
they are repaired, cleared, and compared.
As for the systems of boats and vehicles,
there are huángchuán,
for imperial use;
zhēyángchuán,
for transporting grain by sea;
qiǎnchuán,
for transporting grain by river;
mǎchuán and fēngkuàichuán,
for transporting official goods;
bèi wō chuán and zhànchuán,
for repelling bandits and pirates.
There are dàchē,
dúyuánchē,
and zhànchē.
All their financial resources are gathered,
and they are equitably distributed according to their quantity, duration, and the labor involved.
For all weaving and manufacturing of ceremonial robes, imperial edicts, silk fabrics, sacrificial robes, clean clothes, and various cloths and fabrics,
orders are sent to the Nèifǔ, Nánjīng, Zhèjiāng, and other places,
to be fully aware of the numbers and to strictly economize.
For the iron certificates of Gōng, Hóu, and Bó,
their height and width are differentiated.
(The specific styles are detailed in the Lǐzhì.)
For all sacrificial vessels, imperial seals and registers, imperial carriages, tallies, and various artifacts, regulations are gathered at the Nèifǔ.
For all measurements, weights, and balances,
their calibration is carefully checked and then promulgated,
with standards displayed in the market,
and those who do not conform to the standards are punished.
The Túntián 典 (director) manages matters concerning garrison farming, tax collection, firewood and charcoal, corvée labor, and graves.
In places where military horses guard garrisons,
if transport is insufficient,
tuntian are established to augment military provisions.
This includes planning for construction, timber, city bricks, military camps, official residences, as well as combat clothing, equipment, draft oxen, and farming tools.
All tax collection from various merchants
varies according to their wealth.
For firewood and charcoal,
it is sourced from islands and shoals in the south, and from mountain foothills in the north.
Or it is levied from the common people,
either in kind or in cash,
and is budgeted according to its quantity.
Corvée labor for cutting and transporting firewood
is all hired labor.
For the system of graves, ancestral halls, steles, and stone beasts,
their differentiation is determined by the ranks of imperial clansmen, meritorious relatives, and civil and military officials.
(The system of graves
is detailed in the Lǐzhì.)
In the early Hóngwǔ era,
the Gōngbù and its officials were established,
with the Jiàngzuòsī subordinated to it.
(The Jiàngzuòsī was established in the Wú Yuánnián.
Qīng,
Zheng Sanpin;
Shàoqīng,
Zheng Sipin;
Chéng,
Zheng Wupin.
The Tíju of the Zuǒ and Yòu Tíjǔsī,
Zheng Liupin;
Tóng Tíjǔ,
Cong Liupin;
Sīchéng, Diǎnbù, Fù Tíjǔ,
Zheng Qipin.
The Dàshǐ of the Jūnxūkù,
Cong Bapin;
Fùshǐ,
Zheng Jiupin.
In Hóngwǔ Yuánnián, the Jiàngzuòsī was subordinated to the Gōngbù.)
In the sixth year, one Shàngshū and one Shìláng were added,
and the Zǒngbù, Yúbù, Shuǐbù, and Túntián were established as four subordinate departments.
The Zǒngbù had two Lángzhōng and two Yuánwàiláng;
the others each had one.
The Zǒngbù had eight Zhùshì;
the others each had four.
Furthermore, the Yíngzào Tíjǔsī was established.
(In Hóngwǔ Lìunián, the Jiàngzuòsī was reclassified as Zheng Liupin,
and its subordinate Tíjǔsī was reclassified as Zheng Qipin.
Soon after, the Yíngzào Tíjǔsī and Yíngzào Tíjǔ Fēnsī were established,
with each sī having one Zhèng Tíjǔ and two Fù Tíjǔ,
subordinated to the Jiàngzuòsī.)
In the eighth year, four divisions (kē) were added,
each with one Shàngshū, one Shìláng, and one Lángzhōng,
two Yuánwàiláng,
five Zhùshì,
and two Zhàomó.
In the tenth year, the Jiàngzuòsī was abolished.
In the thirteenth year, the official system was finalized,
establishing one Shàngshū,
one Shìláng,
and for the four subordinate departments (with the Túntián Bù becoming the Túnbù),
each had one Lángzhōng, one Yuánwàiláng,
and two Zhùshì.
In the fifteenth year, one Shìláng was added.
In the twenty-second year, the Zǒngbù was renamed Yíngbù.
In the twenty-fifth year, the Yíngshànsuǒ was established.
(The Jiàngzuòsī was renamed Yíngshànsuǒ,
with a rank of Zheng Qipin,
establishing two Suǒzhèng, two Suǒfù, and two Suǒchéng,
composed of skilled artisans.)
In the twenty-ninth year, the four subordinate departments were again renamed Yíngshàn, Yúhéng, Dūshuǐ, and Túntián, four Qīnglìsī.
After the Jiājìng era, one Shàngshū was added,
specifically to supervise large construction projects.
One Tídū of Yìzhōu Shānchǎng was appointed,
responsible for supervising matters concerning firewood and charcoal for imperial use.
In the early Míng dynasty,
firewood and charcoal were sourced from the reed marshes along the river and from the Lóngjiāng and Wǎxiè two fields.
During the Yǒnglè reign,
the capital was moved north,
so procurement was done from Báiyángkǒu, Huánghuāzhèn, Hóngluóshān, and other places.
In Xuāndé Lìunián, the Yìzhōu Shānchǎng was first established,
with a dedicated official in overall charge.
During the Jǐngtài reign,
it was moved to Píngshān,
and then to Mǎnchéng,
with successive supervision by a Shàngshū or Shìláng of this department.
In Tiānshùn Yuánnián, it was again moved to Yìzhōu.
In Jiājìng Bānián, it was abolished,
and its management was taken over by a Zhùshì.

Those serving outside the capital with the titles of Dūyùshǐ, Fùdūyùshǐ, or Qiāndūyùshǐ included:
Zǒngdū (Governor-General),
Tídū (Commander-in-Chief),
Xúnfǔ (Provincial Governor),
Zǒngdū jiān Xúnfǔ (Governor-General concurrently Provincial Governor),
Tídū jiān Xúnfǔ (Commander-in-Chief concurrently Provincial Governor),
and officials such as Jīnglüè (Administrator), Zǒnglǐ (Director-General), Zànlǐ (Assistant), Xúnshì (Inspector), and Fǔzhì (Pacification Commissioner).
(The title Xúnfǔ
originated from Yìwén Tàizǐ's circuit inspection of Shǎnxī.
In the 19th year of Yǒnglè (1421), twenty-six people, including Minister Jiǎn Yì, were dispatched to tour the empire
to pacify the military and civilian populace.
Thereafter, regardless of whether they were Ministers, Vice Ministers, Censors-in-Chief, or Junior Stewards,
they would report back upon completion of their duties,
or even be temporarily removed from their posts.
Initially called Xúnfǔ,
or Zhènshǒu (Defense Commander),
later, due to the lack of subordination between the Zhènshǒu Shìláng and the Xún'àn Yùshǐ,
leading to communication difficulties,
it was standardized as Dūyùshǐ.
Those Xúnfǔ who concurrently handled military affairs were given the title Tídū;
in areas with Zǒngbīng (Regional Commanders), they were given the title Zànlǐ or Cāncàn;
those with extensive jurisdiction and heavy responsibilities were given the title Zǒngdū.
Other titles such as Zhěngchì (Reorganizer), Fǔzhì (Pacifier), Xúnzhì (Circuit Administrator), Zǒnglǐ (Director-General) were
all specially established for specific matters.
Those who held the positions of Minister or Vice Minister while serving as Zǒngdū of military affairs
all concurrently held the title of Dūyùshǐ,
to facilitate their duties.)
The Dūyùshǐ's specific duties were to impeach all officials,
clarify injustices,
supervise the various circuits,
and serve as the Emperor's eyes, ears, and enforcer of discipline.
All corrupt high officials, petty individuals forming factions, and those abusing power to disturb governance,
were impeached.
All officials who were mediocre, greedy, or undermined official discipline,
were impeached.
All those with unorthodox scholarship, who submitted memorials proposing changes to established precedents, or sought advancement,
were impeached.
During imperial audiences and evaluations,
they collaborated with the Lìbù (Ministry of Personnel) in evaluating the competence and demotion or promotion of officials.
Major cases involving severe offenders were jointly tried at the outer court,
alongside the Xíngbù (Ministry of Punishments) and the Dàlǐ Sì (Grand Court of Judicial Review) to ensure fair judgment.
Those dispatched by imperial decree to the interior,
or to pacify outlying regions,
each acted according to their specific imperial mandate.
The Thirteen Circuits Jiānchá Yùshǐ
were primarily responsible for investigating and impeaching official corruption within and outside the capital,
either by openly presenting their accusations,
or by sealing and submitting their memorials.
Within the capital, they audited documents in the two capitals,
inspected the Imperial Garrisons,
supervised the rural and metropolitan examinations, and military examinations,
inspected the Guānglù Sì (Court of Imperial Entertainments),
inspected granaries and fields,
inspected the Imperial Treasury, Imperial City, and the Five City Divisions,
and took turns on duty at the Dēngwéngǔ (Drum of Appeals).
(Later changed to section members.)
Outside the capital, they served as Xún'àn (Circuit Inspectors),
(two for Běizhílì,
three for Nánzhílì,
one for Xuāndà,
one for Liáodōng,
one for Gānsù,
and one for each of the thirteen provinces).
They also cleaned up the army,
supervised schools,
(one for each of the two capitals;
in the late Wànlì era,
an additional one was established in Nánjīng).
They inspected salt administration,
(one for Liǎnghuái,
one for Liǎngzhè,
one for Chánglú,
one for Hédōng).
Tea and horses,
(Shǎnxī).
Canal transport inspection,
pass inspection,
(in the 4th year of Xuāndé (1429), Censors for toll stations were established,
and in the 10th year of Zhèngtǒng (1445), Chief Clerks were first dispatched).
Grain transport supervision,
horse branding,
and military agricultural colonies.
When the army was on campaign, they supervised military discipline and recorded merits,
each specializing in their specific supervisory duties.
The Xún'àn acted on behalf of the Emperor as imperial inspectors,
and their inspection, impeachment, and evaluation of vassal princes, high officials, prefectural, subprefectural, and county officials
were especially focused.
Major matters were reported for imperial decision,
while minor matters were decided on the spot.
Upon arrival at their inspection locations,
they first reviewed and recorded prisoners' cases,
and examined archived documents.
Those who had been wrongly imprisoned or released were investigated and rectified.
For all sacrificial altars and sites,
they inspected the walls, buildings, and sacrificial vessels.
They provided care for the orphaned and elderly,
inspected granaries,
audited finances,
encouraged schools,
praised virtuous individuals,
eliminated powerful corrupt officials,
to rectify customs
and strengthen governance.
In all imperial audiences, they corrected ritual infractions,
and in all sacrifices, they supervised the rites.
For all successes and failures in government,
and advantages and disadvantages for the military and populace,
they could speak frankly without evasion.
In the event of major policy decisions,
they gathered at the imperial court to deliberate.
While the Six Ministries were of utmost importance,
they had specialized functions,
but the Dūcháyuàn presided over the entire constitutional framework,
only having the power to investigate and rectify what they observed and heard.
When Censors impeached,
they had to clearly state the actual facts,
specify the dates,
and not resort to vague accusations
or trivial criticisms.
Upon returning from circuit inspection,
the Dūyùshǐ would review and impeach them, reporting their competence or incompetence.
If a Censor committed a crime,
their punishment was increased by three degrees,
and if bribery was involved, they were punished more severely.

Initially,
in the first year of Wú (Wú Yuánnián), the Censorate (Yùshǐ Tái) was established,
with a Censor-in-Chief Left (Zuǒ Yùshǐ Dàfū) and Right (Yòu Yùshǐ Dàfū),
(ranking 1a),
a Censor-in-Chief Assistant (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng),
(ranking 2a),
Supervising Censors (Shìyùshǐ),
(ranking 2b),
Censors for Drafting Documents (Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ),
(ranking 3a),
Palace Censors (Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ),
(ranking 5a),
Investigating Censors of the Inspection Bureau (Cháyuan Jiānchá Yùshǐ),
(ranking 7a),
an Executive Secretary (Jīnglì),
(ranking 5b),
a Director of Affairs (Dūshì),
(ranking 7a),
and Scrutiny Officers and Controllers (Zhàomó, Guǎngòu),
(ranking 8a).
Dèng Yù (Dèng Yù) and Tāng Hé (Tāng Hé) were appointed Censors-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Dàfū),
Liú Jī (Liú Jī) and Zhāng Yì (Zhāng Yì) were appointed Censor-in-Chief Assistants (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng),
and he instructed them, saying:
"The state establishes three grand offices:
the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū) oversees political affairs,
the Chief Military Commission (Dūdū) commands the military,
and the Censorate (Yùshǐ) is in charge of oversight and impeachment.
The discipline of the court entirely depends on these,
and the duties of the Censorate (Táichá) are especially clear and important.
You, my ministers, must rectify yourselves to lead your subordinates,
be loyal and diligent in serving your superiors,
do not be listless and follow old ways to indulge evil,
and do not use public office for private gain to harm the people."
In the ninth year of Hóngwǔ (Hóngwǔ Jiǔnián), Supervising Censors (Shìyùshǐ), Censors for Drafting Documents (Zhìshū), and Palace Censors (Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ) were abolished.
In the seventh month of the tenth year, an imperial edict dispatched Investigating Censors (Jiānchá Yùshǐ) to巡按 (xún'àn) the prefectures and counties.
In the thirteenth year, Left (Zuǒ) and Right (Yòu) Censor-in-Chief Assistants (Zhōngchéng) were specially established,
(ranking 2a),
and Left (Zuǒ) and Right (Yòu) Supervising Censors (Shìyùshǐ),
(ranking 4a).
Soon after, the Censorate (Yùshǐ Tái) was abolished.
In the fifteenth year, the Censorate (Dūchá Yuàn) was re-established,
with eight Investigating Censors-in-Chief (Jiānchá Dū Yùshǐ),
ranking 7a.

The Investigating Censors (Jiānchá Yùshǐ) were divided into twelve circuits: Zhèjiāng, Hénán, Shāndōng, Běipíng, Shānxī, Shǎnxī, Húguǎng, Fújiàn, Jiāngxī, Guǎngdōng, Guǎngxī, and Sìchuān (Zhèjiāng, Hénán, Shāndōng, Běipíng, Shānxī, Shǎnxī, Húguǎng, Fújiàn, Jiāngxī, Guǎngdōng, Guǎngxī, Sìchuān Shí'èrdào).
Each circuit had either five, or three or four Censors (Yùshǐ),
ranking 9a.
Each circuit cast two seals;
one was given to the most senior Censor (Yùshǐ) to keep,
and one was stored in the imperial household (Nèifǔ),
to be taken out when needed and returned when the task was completed,
inscribed with the characters
"Correcting faults and rectifying errors" (Shéngqiān Jiūmiù).
The scholars Lǐ Yuánmíng (Lǐ Yuánmíng) and Zhān Huī (Zhān Huī) were appointed Investigating Censors-in-Chief (Dū Yùshǐ),
and Wú Quán (Wú Quán) and others were appointed probationary Investigating Censors (Shì Jiānchá Yùshǐ).
(Probationary Censors (Shì Yùshǐ)
were formally appointed after one year.
There were also "Judicial Jinshi" (Lǐxíng Jìnshì)
and "Judicial Magistrates" (Lǐxíng Zhīxiàn) who managed legal cases in the Censorate (Dūcháyuan Xíngyù),
and were formally appointed after six months.
This was abolished during the Zhèngdé (Zhèngdé) reign.)
In the sixteenth year, the Censorate (Dūcháyuan) was promoted to rank 3a,
with one Left (Zuǒ) and one Right (Yòu) Censor-in-Chief (Dū Yùshǐ) each,
ranking 3a,
one Left (Zuǒ) and one Right (Yòu) Vice Censor-in-Chief (Fù Dū Yùshǐ) each,
ranking 4a,
two Left (Zuǒ) and two Right (Yòu) Assistant Censors-in-Chief (Qiān Dū Yùshǐ) each,
ranking 5a,
one Executive Secretary (Jīnglì),
ranking 7a,
and one Secretary of Affairs (Zhīshì),
ranking 8a.
In the seventeenth year, the Censor-in-Chief (Dū Yùshǐ) was promoted to rank 2a,
the Vice Censor-in-Chief (Fù Dū Yùshǐ) to rank 3a,
the Assistant Censor-in-Chief (Qiān Dū Yùshǐ) to rank 4a,
and the twelve circuit Investigating Censors (Jiānchá Yùshǐ) to rank 7a.
In the twenty-third year,
the Left Vice Censor-in-Chief (Zuǒ Fù Dū Yùshǐ) Yuán Tài (Yuán Tài) stated,
"The seals of the various circuits are identical,
raising concerns about fraud."
Thereupon, new seals were cast for the Investigating Censors (Jiānchá Yùshǐ) inscribed
"Seal of the Investigating Censor of [Circuit Name]" (Mǒudào Jiānchá Yùshǐ Yìn),
and their巡按 (xún'àn) seals were inscribed
"Seal of the Investigating Censor巡按 (xún'àn) [Place Name]" (Xún'àn Mǒuchù Jiānchá Yùshǐ Yìn).
In the first year of Jiànwén (Jiànwén Yuánnián), one Censor-in-Chief (Dū Yùshǐ) was established,
and the Assistant Censor-in-Chief (Qiān Dū Yùshǐ) was abolished.
In the second year, it was changed to the Censorate Grand Council (Yùshǐ Fǔ),
with a Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Dàfū),
and the twelve circuits were changed to Left (Zuǒ) and Right (Yòu) Courts (Liǎng Yuàn),
with only twenty-eight Censors (Yùshǐ).
Emperor Chéngzǔ (Chéngzǔ) restored the old system.
In the first year of the Yǒnglè reign, Běipíng Dào was changed to Běijīng Dào.
In the eighteenth year, Běijīng Dào was abolished.
Guìzhōu, Yúnnán, and Jiāozhǐ three circuits (dào) were newly established.
In the first year of the Hóngxī reign, it was referred to as Xíngzài Dūcháyuàn,
on par with the Six Ministries (Liù Bù).
It was also decided that circuit inspectors (xún'àn) would set out on their tours in the eighth month.
In the tenth year of the Xuāndé reign, Jiāozhǐ Dào was abolished,
and it was then set at thirteen circuits.
During the Zhèngtǒng reign,
the
character "Xíngzài"
was removed.
During the Jiājìng reign,
due to the clearing of military colonies (qīngtún),
three Assistant Censors-in-Chief (fù dūyùshǐ) were added,
but they were soon dismissed.
During the Lóngqìng reign,
due to the supervision of the Capital Garrisons (Jīngyíng),
three Right Censors-in-Chief (yòu dūyùshǐ) were added,
but they were also soon dismissed.
One Grand Coordinator of Grain Transport and concurrent Superintendent of Military Affairs and Grand Protector of Fèngyáng and other areas, concurrently managing river affairs.
In the time of Tàizǔ,
a Jīngjī Capital Grain Transport Bureau (Dū Cāoyùn Sī) was established,
and a Grain Transport Commissioner (cāoyùnshǐ) was set up.
(In the first year of Hóngwǔ, a Grain Transport Commissioner,
of 正四品 zhèngsìpǐn rank,
a Chief Clerk (zhīshì),
of 正八品 zhèngbāpǐn rank,
a Document Controller (tíkòng àndú),
of 從九品 cóngjiǔpǐn rank,
an affiliated official Supervisor of Transport (jiānyùn),
of 正九品 zhèngjiǔpǐn rank,
and a Grand Grain Master (dūgāng) were established.
The details are omitted.
They were abolished in the fourteenth year.)
During the Yǒnglè period,
a Grain Transport Commander-in-Chief (cāoyùn zǒngbīngguān) was established,
and Chén Xuān, the Earl of Píngjiāng, was in charge of grain transport.
During the Xuāndé reign,
Assistant Ministers (shìláng), Censors-in-Chief (dūyùshǐ), and Vice Ministers (shǎoqīng) and other officials were dispatched to supervise transport.
Up until the second year of Jǐngtài,
due to disruptions in grain transport,
Assistant Censor-in-Chief Wáng Hóng was first appointed Grand Coordinator,
and concurrently served as Grand Protector of the four prefectures of Huái, Yáng, Lú, and Fèng,
and the three subprefectures of Xú, Hé, Chú,
governing from Huái'ān.
In the eighth year of Chénghuà, one Grand Protector (xúnfǔ) and one Grand Coordinator of Grain Transport (zǒngcáo) were separately established.
In the ninth year, the old system was restored.
In the thirteenth year of Zhèngdé, they were again separately established.
In the sixteenth year, the old system was again restored.
In the thirty-sixth year of Jiājìng,
due to倭警 wōjǐng (Japanese pirate raids),
a Censor-in-Chief (dūyùshǐ) serving as Superintendent of Military Affairs and Grand Protector of Fèngyáng was added.
In the fortieth year, it was merged,
and changed to Grand Coordinator of Grain Transport and concurrent Superintendent of Military Affairs.
In the seventh year of Wànlì, the concurrent management of river affairs was added.
One Grand Coordinator of Military Affairs for Jìliáo, Bǎodìng and other areas, concurrently managing provisions.
Established in the twenty-ninth year of Jiājìng.
Previously,
when there were alarms in Jì and Liáo,
high-ranking officials were occasionally dispatched to inspect,
or were called Superintendents (tídū).
By this time, border troubles became even more severe,
so a Grand Coordinator (zǒngdū) was first established,
with his yamen at Mìyún,
and he oversaw the three Grand Protectors of Shùntiān, Bǎodìng, and Liáodōng,
and concurrently managed provisions.
In the ninth year of Wànlì, concurrent Grand Protector of Shùntiān and other areas was added.
In the eleventh year, the old system was restored.
In the first year of Tiānqǐ, a Liáodōng Military Commissioner (jīnglüè) was established.
(The title of Military Commissioner
began in the twentieth year of Wànlì with Sòng Yìngchāng and later Yáng Hào.
In the first year of Tiānqǐ,
Sūn Chéngzōng of the Grand Secretariat was again appointed to supervise the armies and administer Shānhǎiguān,
and was called Pivot of the Court (shūfǔ).)
In the fourth year of Chóngzhēn, it was merged into the Grand Coordinator.
In the eleventh year, another Grand Coordinator was established at Bǎodìng.
One Grand Coordinator of Military Affairs for Xuāndà, Shānxī and other areas, concurrently managing provisions.
In the first year of Zhèngtǒng, an Assistant Censor-in-Chief (qiān dūyùshǐ) was first dispatched to serve as Grand Protector of Xuāndà.
In the second year of Jǐngtài,
Grand Protectors were established in Xuānfǔ and Dàtóng respectively,
and Minister (shàngshū) Shí Pú was dispatched to manage military affairs.
During the Chénghuà and Hóngzhì reigns,
they were dispatched when there was an alarm.
In the eighth year of Zhèngdé, a Grand Controller (zǒngzhì) was established.
In the early Jiājìng reign,
he concurrently oversaw Piān and Bǎo.
In the twenty-ninth year, Piān and Bǎo were removed,
and the title of Grand Coordinator of Xuāndà, Shānxī and other areas was established.
In the thirty-eighth year, he was ordered to reside at Xuānfǔ during the autumn defense.
In the forty-third year, he moved his residence to Huáilái.
In the fourth year of Lóngqìng, he moved his residence to Yánghé.
One Grand Coordinator of Military Affairs for the Three Borders of Shǎnxī.
In the tenth year of Hóngzhì,
Huǒ Shāi invaded,
and it was debated to dispatch a high-ranking official as Grand Coordinator of Military Affairs for Shǎnxī, Gānsù, Yánsuí, and Níngxià.
Then Left Censor-in-Chief (zuǒ dūyùshǐ) Wáng Yuè was appointed to the post.
After the fifteenth year,
it was either established or abolished.
By the fourth year of Jiājìng,
it was finally established,
initially called Superintendent of Military Affairs.
In the seventh year, it was changed to Grand Controller.
In the nineteenth year, to avoid the character "zhì",
it was changed to Grand Coordinator,
with his yamen at Gùyuán,
and residing at Huāmǎchí during the autumn defense.
One Grand Coordinator of Military Affairs for the Two Guǎngs, concurrently managing provisions and salt administration, and concurrently Grand Protector of Guǎngdōng province.
In the second year of Yǒnglè, Grand Secretariat Drafter (gěishìzhōng) Léi Tián was dispatched as Grand Protector of Guǎngxī.
In the nineteenth year, Guō Xuān and Ài Guǎng were dispatched as Grand Protectors of Guǎngdōng.
In the third year of Jǐngtài,
Miao rebels arose,
and as the Two Guǎngs needed to coordinate assistance and support,
a Grand Coordinator was established.
In the first year of Chénghuà, he concurrently served as Grand Protector,
residing at Wúzhōu.
In the fourteenth year of Zhèngdé, Grand Coordinator was changed to Grand Controller,
and soon changed to Superintendent.
In the forty-fifth year of Jiājìng, a separate Grand Protector of Guǎngdōng was established,
and Superintendent was changed to Grand Coordinator,
only concurrently serving as Grand Protector of Guǎngxī,
residing at Zhàoqìng.
In the third year of Lóngqìng, a Grand Protector of Guǎngxī was again established,
removing the concurrent post.
In the fourth year, the Grand Protector of Guǎngdōng was abolished,
and changed to Superintendent of Military Affairs for the Two Guǎngs, concurrently managing provisions,
and Grand Protector of Guǎngdōng.
In the third year of Wànlì, it was again changed to Grand Coordinator,
with the addition of concurrent management of salt administration.
One Grand Coordinator of Military Affairs for Sìchuān, Shǎnxī, Hénán, Húguǎng and other areas.
Established in the fifth year of Zhèngdé,
and soon abolished.
In the twenty-seventh year of Jiājìng,
due to Miao troubles,
a Grand Coordinator of Military Affairs for Sìchuān, Húguǎng, Guìzhōu, Yúnnán and other areas was again established.
In the forty-second year, it was abolished.
In the first year of Tiānqǐ,
due to the rebellion of the aboriginal official Shē Chóngmíng,
a Grand Coordinator for the five provinces of Sìchuān, Húguǎng, Yúnnán, Guìzhōu, and Guǎngxī was again established.
In the fourth year, he concurrently served as Grand Protector of Guìzhōu.
One Grand Coordinator of Military Affairs for Zhèjiāng, Fújiàn, Jiāngnán and concurrent Controller of Jiāngxī.
Established in the thirty-third year of Jiājìng,
due to the Japanese pirate attack on Hángzhōu.
Abolished in the forty-first year.
One Grand Coordinator of Military Affairs for the five provinces of Shǎnxī, Shānxī, Hénán, Húguǎng, Sìchuān.
Established in the seventh year of Chóngzhēn,
sometimes concurrently for seven provinces.
After the twelfth year,
all were supervised by the Grand Secretariat.
One Grand Coordinator for Fèngyáng area and concurrent Controller of Military Affairs for Hénán and Húguǎng.
Established in the fourteenth year of Chóngzhēn.
One Grand Coordinator of Military Affairs for Bǎodìng area.
Established in the eleventh year of Chóngzhēn.
One Grand Coordinator of Military Affairs for Hénán and Húguǎng, concurrently Grand Protector of Hénán.
Established in the sixteenth year of Chóngzhēn.
One Grand Coordinator for Jiǔjiāng area and concurrent Controller of Military Affairs for Jiāngxī and Húguǎng.
Established in the sixteenth year of Chóngzhēn.
One Manager of Military Affairs for Southern Zhílì, Hénán, Shāndōng, Húguǎng, Sìchuān.
Established in the eighth year of Chóngzhēn,
with Lú Xiàngshēng as the incumbent,
who was either separate from or merged with the Grand Coordinator.
One Manager of River and Grain Transport and concurrent Superintendent of Military Affairs.
In the ninth year of Yǒnglè, a Minister (shàngshū) was dispatched to manage river affairs,
and thereafter Assistant Ministers (shìláng) and Censors-in-Chief (dūyùshǐ) were occasionally dispatched.
After Chénghuà,
the title Grand Coordinator of Riverways (zǒngdū hédào) began to be used.
In the fourth year of Zhèngdé, a Censor-in-Chief (dūyùshǐ) was permanently established.
In the twentieth year of Jiājìng, the Censor-in-Chief was given the concurrent official title of Minister of Works (gōngbù zhíxián),
as Superintendent of Riverways for Hénán, Shāndōng, and Zhílì.
In the fourth year of Lóngqìng, Superintendent of Military Affairs was added.
In the fifth year of Wànlì, it was changed to Manager of River and Grain Transport and concurrent Superintendent of Military Affairs.
Abolished in the eighth year.
One Manager of Grain Storage and Superintendent of Military Affairs, concurrently Grand Protector of Yìngtiān and other prefectures.
In the fifth year of Xuāndé, an Assistant Minister (shìláng) was first appointed as Grand Coordinator of Grain Storage and concurrent Grand Protector.
In the fourth year of Jǐngtài, it was decided to dispatch a Censor-in-Chief (dūyùshǐ).
In the thirty-third year of Jiājìng, due to alarms from the sea,
Superintendent of Military Affairs was added,
residing at Sūzhōu.
During the Wànlì reign,
he moved his residence to Jùróng,
but later moved back to Sūzhōu.
One Grand Protector of Zhèjiāng and other areas, concurrently Superintendent of Military Affairs.
In the early Yǒnglè reign,
a Minister (shàngshū) was dispatched to manage agricultural affairs in the Two Zhè (Liǎngzhè).
Thereafter, they either inspected or supervised salt administration,
and were dispatched when there were affairs.
In the twenty-sixth year of Jiājìng, due to alarms from the sea,
a Censor-in-Chief (dūyùshǐ) was first appointed as Grand Protector of Zhèjiāng,
concurrently managing the coastal areas of Fú, Xīng, Jiànníng, Zhāng, Quán in Fújiàn,
and Superintendent of Military Affairs.
In the twenty-seventh year, Grand Protector was changed to Inspector (xúnshì).
Abolished in the twenty-eighth year.
Re-established in the thirty-first year.
One Grand Protector of Fújiàn area, concurrently Superintendent of Military Affairs.
In the twenty-sixth year of Jiājìng, a Grand Protector of Zhèjiāng was established who concurrently oversaw Fú, Xīng, Zhāng, Quán and other areas.
In the thirty-fifth year, due to the long distance between Mǐn and Zhè,
a Censor-in-Chief (dūyùshǐ) serving as Superintendent of Military Affairs and concurrent Inspector of the coastal areas of Fú, Xīng, Zhāng, Quán, Fúníng was again established.
Later changed to Grand Protector of Fújiàn,
governing the entire province.
One Grand Coordinator (Xúnfǔ) for Shùntiān and other prefectures, concurrently regulating border defenses in Jìzhōu and other areas.
In the second year of Chénghuà (1466), a Censor-in-Chief (Dūyùshǐ) was specially appointed to assist in military affairs,
Grand Coordinator of Shùntiān and Yǒngpíng prefectures.
Soon after, he concurrently coordinated Héjiān, Zhēndìng, and Bǎodìng,
totaling five prefectures.
In the seventh year, he concurrently managed eight prefectures.
In the eighth year, due to the vastness of the Jīfǔ region,
it was divided in the middle by Jūyōng Pass,
and two Grand Coordinators were established.
The eastern one was the Grand Coordinator for Shùntiān and Yǒngpíng prefectures,
stationed in Zūnhuà.
In the second year of Chóngzhēn (1629), another Grand Coordinator was established for Yǒngpíng, concurrently serving as Military Commissioner (Tídū Jūnwù) for Shānhǎi Pass.
The former one only governed Shùntiān.
One Grand Coordinator for Bǎodìng and other prefectures, concurrently Military Commissioner for Zǐjīng and other passes, and managing river affairs.
In the eighth year of Chénghuà (1472), west of Jūyōng Pass,
another Grand Coordinator was established for Bǎodìng, Zhēndìng, Héjiān, Shùndé, Dàmíng, and Guǎngpíng six prefectures,
Military Commissioner for Zǐjīng, Dǎomǎ, Lóngquán and other passes,
stationed in Zhēndìng.
In the seventh year of Wànlì (1579), he concurrently managed river affairs.
One Grand Coordinator for Hénán and other areas, concurrently managing river affairs and Military Commissioner.
In the fifth year of Xuāndé (1430), Vice Minister of War (Bīngbù Shìláng) Yú Qiān was dispatched to be Grand Coordinator of Shānxī and Hénán.
In the fourteenth year of Zhèngtǒng (1449), Assistant Censor-in-Chief (Zuǒ Fùdū Yùshǐ) Wáng Lái was Grand Coordinator of Húguǎng and Hénán.
In the first year of Jǐngtài (1450), a Grand Coordinator for Hénán was specially established.
In the seventh year of Wànlì (1579), he concurrently managed river affairs.
In the eighth year, he was given the additional title of Military Commissioner.
One Grand Coordinator for Shānxī province, concurrently Military Commissioner for Yànmén and other passes.
In the fifth year of Xuāndé (1430), a Minister (Shìláng) was Grand Coordinator of Hénán and Shānxī.
In the thirteenth year of Zhèngtǒng (1448), a Censor-in-Chief (Dūyùshǐ) was first ordered to be solely Grand Coordinator of Shānxī,
and garrisoned Yànmén.
During the Tiānshùn and Chénghuà eras, it was temporarily abolished,
and soon re-established.
One Grand Coordinator for Shāndōng and other areas, supervising military-agricultural colonies, concurrently managing river affairs and Military Commissioner.
In the fifth year of Zhèngtǒng (1440), a Grand Coordinator was first established.
In the thirteenth year, it was decided to dispatch a Censor-in-Chief.
In the forty-second year of Jiājìng (1563), he was given the additional title of Supervising Military-Agricultural Colonies.
In the seventh year of Wànlì (1579), he concurrently managed river affairs.
In the eighth year, he was given the additional title of Military Commissioner.
One Grand Coordinator for Liáodōng, assisting in military affairs.
Established in the first year of Zhèngtǒng (1436).
Formerly stationed in Liáoyáng,
later, as the territory shrank daily,
moved to Guǎngníng,
stationed at Shānhǎi Pass,
then again stationed at Níngyuǎn.
One Grand Coordinator for Xuānfǔ, assisting in military affairs.
In the first year of Zhèngtǒng (1436), a Censor-in-Chief (Dūyùshǐ) was ordered to inspect north of the border,
and consequently proposed the establishment of a Grand Coordinator concurrently managing Dàtóng.
In the second year of Jǐngtài (1451), a separate Grand Coordinator for Dàtóng was established,
later merged into one again.
In the tenth year of Chénghuà (1474), it was again separated.
In the fourteenth year, the title of Assisting in Military Affairs was added.
One Grand Coordinator for Dàtóng, assisting in military affairs.
Initially, there was one Grand Coordinator for both Xuānfǔ and Dàtóng.
Later, it was either separated or merged.
In the tenth year of Chénghuà (1474), it was again specially established,
with the additional title of Assisting in Military Affairs.
One Grand Coordinator for Yánsuī and other areas, assisting in military affairs.
In the tenth year of Xuāndé (1435), a Censor-in-Chief (Dūyùshǐ) was dispatched to garrison.
In the first year of Jǐngtài (1450), a Grand Coordinator was specially established with the additional title of Participating in Military Affairs.
In the ninth year of Chénghuà (1473), the garrison was moved to Yúlín.
In the sixth year of Lóngqìng (1572), it was changed to Assisting in Military Affairs.
One Grand Coordinator for Níngxià, assisting in military affairs.
In the first year of Zhèngtǒng (1436), Right Assistant Censor-in-Chief (Yòu Qiāndū Yùshǐ) Guō Zhì was appointed to garrison Níngxià,
participating in military affairs.
In the first year of Tiānshùn (1457), it was abolished.
In the second year, it was re-established,
removing the "participating" title.
In the sixth year of Lóngqìng (1572), the title of Assisting in Military Affairs was added.
One Grand Coordinator for Gānsù and other areas, assisting in military affairs.
In the tenth year of Xuāndé (1435), a Minister (Shìláng) was ordered to garrison.
In the first year of Zhèngtǒng (1436),
as troops were used in Gān and Liáng,
a Minister (Shìláng) was ordered to participate in military affairs.
In the first year of Jǐngtài (1450), a Grand Coordinator Censor-in-Chief (Xúnfǔ Dūyùshǐ) was fixedly established.
In the sixth year of Lóngqìng (1572), it was changed to Assisting in Military Affairs.
One Grand Coordinator for Shǎnxī, assisting in military affairs.
In the early Xuāndé (1426) era,
a Minister (Shàngshū) or Vice Minister (Shìláng) was dispatched to garrison.
During the Zhèngtǒng (1436) era,
Right Censor-in-Chief (Yòu Dūyùshǐ) Chén Yì, Wáng Wén and others were ordered to serve in rotation.
In the early Jǐngtài (1450) era,
Gěng Jiǔchóu served as Vice Minister of Justice (Xíngbù Shìláng) to garrison.
Since official documents could not be directly sent to the Surveillance Commission (Ànchásī),
he was specially changed to Censor-in-Chief Grand Coordinator.
In the second year of Chénghuà (1466), the title of Military Commissioner was added,
later changed to Assisting (in military affairs),
stationed in Xī'ān,
and stationed in Gùyuán during autumn defense.
One Grand Coordinator for Sìchuān and other areas, concurrently Military Commissioner.
In the fifth year of Xuāndé (1430), a Censor-in-Chief (Dūyùshǐ) was ordered to garrison,
later this dispatch was suspended.
In the fourteenth year of Zhèngtǒng (1449), a Grand Coordinator was first established.
In the eleventh year of Wànlì (1583), the title of Military Commissioner was added.
One Grand Coordinator for Húguǎng and other areas, concurrently assisting in military affairs.
In the third year of Zhèngtǒng (1438), Censor-in-Chief (Dūyùshǐ) Jiǎ Liàng was ordered to garrison,
thereafter either a Vice Minister (Shìláng) or a Grand Judge (Dàlǐ Qīng) was dispatched to be Grand Coordinator.
In the first year of Jǐngtài (1450), a Grand Coordinator Censor-in-Chief (Xúnfǔ Dūyùshǐ) was fixedly established, concurrently assisting in military affairs.
In the eighth year of Wànlì (1580), it was changed to Military Commissioner.
In the twelfth year, it was restored to Assisting (in military affairs).
One Grand Coordinator for Jiāngxī, concurrently managing military affairs.
After Yǒnglè (1424),
Grand Coordinators were intermittently established to garrison.
After Chénghuà (1487),
it was fixed as Grand Coordinator,
though sometimes abolished.
In the sixth year of Jiājìng (1527), it was fixedly established.
In the fortieth year, the title of Concurrently Managing Military Affairs was added.
One Grand Coordinator for Nángàn, Tīng, Sháo and other areas, Military Commissioner.
In the tenth year of Hóngzhì (1497), a Grand Coordinator was first established.
In the eleventh year of Zhèngdé (1516), it was changed to Military Commissioner.
In the forty-fifth year of Jiājìng (1566), the title of Grand Coordinator was formalized,
with jurisdiction over Nán'ān, Gànzhōu, Nánxióng, Sháozhōu, Tīngzhōu, and Bīnzhōu,
stationed in Gànzhōu.
One Grand Coordinator for Guǎngdōng, concurrently assisting in military affairs.
In the middle of Yǒnglè (1403-1424),
a Grand Coordinator was established.
Later, the Governor-General (Zǒngdū) concurrently held the duties of Grand Coordinator,
so it was abolished and not established.
In the forty-fifth year of Jiājìng (1566), a Grand Coordinator was separately re-established,
with the additional title of Assisting in Military Affairs.
In the fourth year of Lóngqìng (1570), it was again abolished.
One Grand Coordinator for Guǎngxī.
Guǎngxī formerly had a Grand Coordinator,
whose evolution was not constant.
In the third year of Lóngqìng (1569), it was specially re-established.
One Grand Coordinator for Yúnnán, concurrently for Jiànchāng, Bìjié and other areas, assisting in military affairs, concurrently supervising provisions for Sìchuān and Guìzhōu.
In the ninth year of Zhèngtǒng (1444), a Minister (Shìláng) was ordered to participate in military affairs.
In the tenth year, a Garrison Commissioner (Zhènfǔ) was established.
In the first year of Tiānshùn (1457), it was abolished.
In the twelfth year of Chénghuà (1476), it was re-established.
In the thirtieth year of Jiājìng (1551), the title of Concurrently Managing Military Affairs was added.
In the forty-third year, it was changed to Assisting (in military affairs).
In the second year of Lóngqìng (1568), he concurrently coordinated Jiànchāng, Bìjié and other areas.
One Grand Coordinator for Guìzhōu, concurrently supervising Húběi, Chuāndōng and other areas, Military Commissioner.
In the fourteenth year of Zhèngtǒng (1449), due to the Miao rebellion, a Governor-General (Zǒngdū) was set up,
to garrison Guìzhōu, Húběi, Chuāndōng and other areas.
In the first year of Jǐngtài (1450), a separate Grand Coordinator for Guìzhōu was established.
In the eighth year of Chénghuà (1472), it was abolished.
In the eleventh year, it was re-established.
In the second year of Zhèngdé (1507), it was again abolished.
In the fifth year, it was again re-established.
In the forty-second year of Jiājìng (1563), the Governor-General (Zǒngdū) was abolished,
