and the Grand Coordinator was ordered to concurrently manage Húběi, Chuāndōng and other areas as Military Commissioner.
One Grand Coordinator for Tiānjīn, assisting in military affairs.
In the twenty-fifth year of Wànlì (1597), due to the Japanese invasion of Cháoxiān (Korea),
it was temporarily established,
and soon became a permanent institution.
One Grand Coordinator for Dēnglái, assisting in military affairs.
Established in the first year of Tiānqǐ (1621).
In the second year of Chóngzhēn (1629), it was abolished.
In the third year, it was re-established.
One Grand Coordinator for Ānlú, assisting in military affairs.
Established in the tenth year of Chóngzhēn (1637),
with Shǐ Kěfǎ appointed to the post.
In the sixteenth year, another Grand Coordinator for the four prefectures of Ān, Tài, Chí, and Lú was added.
One Grand Coordinator for Piān Yuán, assisting in military affairs.
In the twenty-seventh year of Wànlì (1599), it was temporarily established due to the expedition against Bō (Yang Yinglong),
and soon abolished.
After the second year of Tiānqǐ (1622),
it was either established or abolished.
In the second year of Chóngzhēn (1629), it was fixedly established.
One Grand Coordinator for Mìyún, assisting in military affairs.
Established in the eleventh year of Chóngzhēn (1638).
One Grand Coordinator for Huái Yáng, assisting in military affairs.
Established in the eleventh year of Chóngzhēn (1638).
One Grand Coordinator for Chéngtiān, assisting in military affairs.
Established in the sixteenth year of Chóngzhēn (1643).
One Governor (Fǔzhì) for Yúnyáng and other areas, concurrently Military Commissioner.
In the twelfth year of Chénghuà (1476), due to repeated rebellions by vagrants in Yún and Xiāng,
a Censor-in-Chief (Dūyùshǐ) was dispatched to pacify,
and consequently, a Governor (Fǔzhì) was proposed to govern them.
In the second year of Wànlì (1574), because the authority of the Governor was not exclusive,
the title of Military Commissioner concurrently Governor was added.
In the ninth year, it was abolished,
and in the eleventh year, re-established.
One Assistant for Military Affairs (Zànlǐ Jūnwù) for Sōngpān.
In the fourth year of Zhèngtǒng (1439), Wáng Kē was appointed to this post.
Office of Transmission (Tōngzhèngsǐ).
One Chief Transmission Officer (Tōngzhèngshǐ),
(Principal Third Rank),
one Left and one Right Transmission Officer (Tōngzhèng),
one Transmission Officer for Yellow Scrolls (Ténghuáng Yòu Tōngzhèng),
(Principal Fourth Rank),
one Left and one Right Director (Cānyì),
(Principal Fifth Rank).
Its subordinate department,
the Bureau of Administration (Jīnglìsǐ),
one Administrator (Jīnglì),
(Principal Seventh Rank),
one Secretary (Zhīshì),
(Principal Eighth Rank).
The Grand Court of Revisions (Tōngzhèng Sì 使) was in charge of receiving memorials from within and outside the capital, submitting them to the emperor, and rejecting or approving them.
Whenever people from all four directions made petitions or offered advice,
appealed against injustice,
or reported unlawful conduct,
the reasons for their petitions or accusations were copied into a ledger,
and the petitions were submitted to the emperor.
Whenever common people or officials from anywhere in the realm submitted sealed memorials,
they were immediately opened and examined in the public hall.
Excerpts were made into a duplicate copy,
and then they were reported to the emperor.
In the case of memorials from the Five Military Commands (Wǔjūn), Six Boards (Liùbù), Censorate (Dūchá Yuàn), and other yámén,
if they concerned matters of great secrecy and importance,
their submission to the emperor still required the seal of this office.
All official documents and verification tallies from various offices were meticulously checked and verified as correct.
They were then numbered and annotated.
Official documents were stamped with
the "Seal of Daily Illumination" (Rìzhào Zhī Jì),
and verification tallies with
the "Seal of Verification" (Yànzhèng Zhī Jì)
for security.
All proposals (tíběn) and memorials (zòuběn) from outside the capital,
and memorials (zòuběn) from within the capital,
were received,
compiled, and presented at the early morning audience.
Those who submitted them directly were reprimanded and rejected.
At the noon audience, officials and commoners who wished to speak on matters were introduced.
Secret matters were submitted at any time.
Any errors or delays were recorded and a collective request was made.
All copies issued, or rejections of official dispatches, verification tallies, litigation documents, numbers of arrests and summonses, and personnel assigned to duties,
were collectively reported at the end of the month,
and fully reported at the end of the year.
The Grand Court of Revisions (Tōngzhèng Sì) must participate
in deliberations on major policies, major judicial cases, and collective recommendations for civil and military high officials.
Initially,
in the 3rd year of Hóngwǔ (1370), the Office for Examining Petitions (Cháyán Sī) was established,
with two directors (sīlìng) appointed.
They were in charge of receiving memorials from all directions.
It was soon abolished.
In the 10th year (1377), the Grand Court of Revisions (Tōngzhèng Sì) was established.
Zēng Bǐngzhèng was appointed Grand Administrator of the Court of Revisions (Tōngzhèng Shǐ),
and Liú Rén was appointed Left Grand Administrator of the Court of Revisions (Zuǒ Tōngzhèng).
An imperial edict stated:
"Governance is like water;
it desires constant flow.
Therefore, the office is named 'Grand Court of Revisions' (Tōngzhèng)."
"You should carefully review commands to rectify all offices,
and convey hidden truths to facilitate all affairs.
Do not shy away from reporting matters to the emperor,
do not blindly follow when you should object and correct,
do not conceal when you should fully present,
and do not obstruct when you should arrange audiences."

In the 12th year (1379), supervising secretaries (jìshìzhōng) from the Directorate of Imperial Edicts (Chéngchì Jiān), the Office of Court Ceremonials (Diàntíng Yílǐ Sī), and the Translators' Office for Nine Passes (Jiǔguān Tōngshì Shǐ) were placed under its jurisdiction.
During the Jiànwén reign (1399-1402),
the Grand Court of Revisions (Tōngzhèng Sì) was renamed to Grand Court of Revisions (Tōngzhèng Sì),
the Grand Administrator (Tōngzhèng Shǐ) was renamed Grand Minister (Tōngzhèng Qīng),
and the Councilor of Revisions (Tōngzhèng Cānyì) was renamed Junior Minister (Shàqīng).
One Left Rectifier of Omissions (Zuǒ Bǔquē) and one Right Rectifier of Omissions (Yòu Bǔquē),
and one Left Remonstrator (Zuǒ Shíyí) and one Right Remonstrator (Yòu Shíyí) were added to the Court Secretariat (Sìchéng).
Emperor Chéngzǔ restored the old system.
In the 2nd year of Chénghuà (1466), a Supervisor of Imperial Rescripts and Right Grand Administrator (Tídū Ténghuáng Yòu Tōngzhèng) was established.
He did not manage the affairs of the court,
but recorded the details of military officers' inheritances in garrisons (wèisuǒ)
to aid in their selection and appointment.
It was abolished in the 9th year of Wànlì (1581).
Grand Court of Judicial Review (Dàlǐ Sì).
One Grand Minister (Qīng),
(senior third rank),
one Left Junior Minister (Zuǒ Shàqīng) and one Right Junior Minister (Yòu Shàqīng) each,
(senior fourth rank),
and one Left Court Secretary (Zuǒ Sìchéng) and one Right Court Secretary (Yòu Sìchéng) each,
(senior fifth rank).
Its subordinates were:
Secretariat Office (Sīwù Tīng),
with two Secretaries (Sīwù),
(junior ninth rank).
Left and Right Divisions (Zuǒ Yòu Èr Sì),
each with one Division Director (Sìzhèng),
(senior sixth rank),
two Assistant Division Directors (Sìfù),
(junior sixth rank;
later, one Right Assistant Division Director (Yòu Sìfù) was abolished).
Four Reviewers (Píngshì),
(senior seventh rank).
Initially, eight Right Reviewers (Yòu Píngshì) were established,
later four were abolished.
The Grand Minister (Qīng)
was in charge of reviewing and rectifying judicial cases.
The Junior Ministers (Shàqīng) and Court Secretaries (Sìchéng) assisted him.
The Left and Right Divisions (Zuǒ Yòu Èr Sì) separately handled criminal cases in the capital region and the thirteen provincial administration commissions (Bùzhèng Sī).
All legal cases interrogated by the Ministry of Justice (Xíngbù), the Censorate (Dūchá Yuàn), and the Five Military Command Punishments Officers (Wǔjūn Duànshì Guān)
were transferred with their case files,
and the prisoners were brought
to the court for detailed review and examination.
The Division Directors (Sìzhèng) of the Left and Right Divisions (Zuǒ Yòu Èr Sì)
each re-examined cases according to their jurisdiction.
After consulting the laws and regulations,
they had to re-examine the charges and statements.
Only when the facts were consistent and the guilt admitted
were they presented to the Grand Minister (Qīng) for approval and preparation of a memorial to the emperor.
Otherwise, they were returned for revision,
which was called "returning for re-examination" (zhàobó).
If the third revision was still inappropriate,
the interrogating official was impeached,
which was called "impeaching and rejecting" (cānbó).
If there were discrepancies with the law or erroneous inclusions,
the case was transferred to another division for re-interrogation,
which was called "transferring for different review" (fānyì).
If it was still unsatisfactory,
a request was made for the Nine Ministers (Jiǔ Qīng) to collectively examine it,
which was called "circular review" (yuánshěn).
If it had already been approved but the confession was unclear,
it was transferred for re-interrogation,
which was called "rejection for further inquiry" (zhuībó).
If repeated rejections still did not yield a suitable outcome,
an imperial edict was requested for a final decision,
which was called "imperial decision" (zhìjué).
Once a case was concluded,
no other office was allowed to issue a verdict
unless it had been approved by this court.
Any error would lead to impeachment.
Initially,
in the 1st year of Wú (1367), the Grand Minister of the Grand Court of Judicial Review (Dàlǐ Sì Qīng) was established,
with a rank of senior third grade.
It was abolished in the 1st year of Hóngwǔ (1368).
In the 3rd year (1370), the Office of Verification and Examination (Mókàn Sī) was established.
For all criminal cases and financial matters of various offices,
if there were instances of injustice, abuse, or concealment,
their merits and demerits were investigated and reported.
It was also soon abolished.
(In the 3rd year of Hóngwǔ (1370), the Office of Verification and Examination (Mókàn Sī) was established,
with a Director (sīlìng) and a Secretary (sīchéng).
In the 7th year (1374), one more Director (sīlìng) and five Secretaries (sīchéng) were added,
along with five chief officials (shǒulǐngguān),
divided into four sections.
It was abolished in the 10th year (1377).
In the 14th year (1381), the Office of Verification and Examination (Mókàn Sī) was re-established,
with one Director (sīlìng),
one Left Secretary (Zuǒ Sīchéng) and one Right Secretary (Yòu Sīchéng),
and one Left Assistant Secretary (Zuǒ Sīfù) and one Right Assistant Secretary (Yòu Sīfù).
It was abolished again in the 20th year (1387).
) In the 14th year (1381), the Grand Court of Judicial Review (Dàlǐ Sì) was re-established.
The Grand Minister (Qīng) was changed to senior fifth rank,
the Left and Right Junior Ministers (Zuǒ Yòu Shàqīng) to junior fifth rank,
and the Left and Right Court Secretaries (Zuǒ Yòu Sìchéng) to senior sixth rank.
Its subordinates included:
one Left Division Director (Zuǒ Sìzhèng) and one Right Division Director (Yòu Sìzhèng) each,
two Assistant Division Directors (Sìfù) each,
four Left Reviewers (Zuǒ Píngshì),
and eight Right Reviewers (Yòu Píngshì).
The Office of Criminal Review (Shěnxíng Sī) was also established,
to jointly rectify general judicial cases.
All criminal cases handled by the Grand Court of Judicial Review (Dàlǐ Sì)
were then reviewed in detail by the Office of Criminal Review (Shěnxíng Sī).
(The Office of Criminal Review (Shěnxíng Sī) had one Left Criminal Reviewer (Zuǒ Shěnxíng) and one Right Criminal Reviewer (Yòu Shěnxíng) each,
senior sixth rank;
and three Left Detailed Reviewers (Zuǒ Xiángyì) and three Right Detailed Reviewers (Yòu Xiángyì) each,
senior seventh rank.)

In the 17th year (1384), the Ministry of Justice (Xíngbù), the Censorate (Dūchá Yuàn), the Grand Court of Judicial Review (Dàlǐ Sì), the Office of Criminal Review (Shěnxíng Sī), and the Offices of Military Affairs (Wǔjūn Shìguānshǔ) were relocated outside Tàipíng Mén,
and the area was named Guànchéng.
In the 19th year (1386), the Office of Criminal Review (Shěnxíng Sī) was abolished.
In the 22nd year (1389), it was restored,
and the Grand Minister (Qīng) was of senior third rank.
(Two Junior Ministers (Shàqīng),
senior fourth rank,
three Secretaries (Chéng),
senior fifth rank.
Its Left and Right Division officers remained as before.)
In the 29th year (1396), it was abolished again,
and all case files were moved to Hòuhú.
It was re-established at the beginning of the Jiànwén reign (1399),
and the Left and Right Divisions (Zuǒ Yòu Sì) were renamed to Left and Right Bureaus (Zuǒ Yòu Sī),
the Division Director (Sìzhèng) was renamed Chief Reviewer (Dū Píngshì),
the Assistant Division Director (Sìfù) was renamed Deputy Chief Reviewer (Fù Dū Píngshì),
and the Secretary (Sīwù) was renamed Chief Registrar (Dū Diǎnbó).
(Secretaries (Sīwù) were established in the 26th year of Hóngwǔ (1393)).
In the early years of the Chéngzǔ reign,
the Dàlǐ Sì (Grand Court of Revision) was
still maintained. The officials of its Left and Right
Temples were again as in the Hóngwǔ period.
Due to the unequal number of evaluating officials (píngshì) in the two temples, Left and Right,
and the uneven complexity of the cases they handled,
the evaluating officials of the two temples were divided equally,
with six each for the Left and Right,
like the twelve divisions/circuits (sī dào) of the Xíngbù (Ministry of Justice) and Dūchá Yuàn (Censorate).
Each was assigned to oversee the review and adjudication of cases in the directly administered areas (zhílì).
(Initially,
Tàizǔ established four Left Píngshì,
responsible for criminal cases in the various yámen in the capital, and the wei-suǒ, fǔ, zhōu, and xiàn of the zhílì.
Eight Right Píngshì
were responsible for criminal cases in the thirteen bùzhèng sī, dū sī, wei-suǒ, fǔ, zhōu, and xiàn outside the capital.
)In Yǒnglè second year, the old system was restored.
Later, when the capital was moved to Běijīng,
the division of the temple's responsibilities was changed again.
(Criminal cases from the two capitals, five prefectures, six ministries, capital wei-suǒ and other yámen
belonged to the Left Temple.
Cases from Shùntiān and Yìngtiān Fǔ,
the wei-suǒ, fǔ, zhōu, and xiàn of the southern and northern zhílì, and the bùzhèng sī, dū sī, and wei-suǒ of Zhèjiāng and other provinces outside the capital,
belonged to the Right Temple.)
In Hóngzhì first year, four Right Píngshì were cut.
(At that time, the criminals throughout the realm
were generally not brought for review,
so the workload of the Right Temple was simpler than that of the Left Temple.)
In Wànlì ninth year,
the division of criminal cases throughout the realm between the Left and Right Temples was redefined.
The six sī dào of Zhèjiāng, Fújiàn, Shāndōng, Guǎngdōng, Sìchuān, and Guìzhōu
were handled by the Left Temple.
The seven sī dào of Jiāngxī, Shǎnxī, Hénán, Shānxī, Húguǎng, Guǎngxī, and Yúnnán
were handled by the Right Temple.
Those who could acquit or condemn according to the law were considered competent.
(The establishment of the Dàlǐ Sì
was for the purpose of exercising caution in punishments.
In the joint review by the Sān Fǎsī (Three Judicial Offices),
the initial review was led by the Xíngbù and Dūchá Yuàn,
while the appellate review
was led by this court.
In the early Míng dynasty,
torture instruments and prisons were still kept.
After Hóngzhì,
only case files were reviewed,
and prisoners were not brought to the court.)
The Sīwù (Manager) was in charge of the receipt and dispatch of documents.
Zhānshì Fǔ (Palace of the Heir Apparent's Household).
One Zhānshì,
(Principal Third Rank)
Two Shào Zhānshì,
(Principal Fourth Rank)
Two Fǔchéng,
(Principal Sixth Rank.)
Zhǔbù Tīng (Bureau of the Chief Scribe),
One Zhǔbù,
(Subordinate Seventh Rank)
Two Lùshì,
(Principal Ninth Rank)
Two Tōngshì Shèrén.
Zuǒ Chūnfāng (Left Spring Chamber),
One Dàxuéshì,
(Principal Fifth Rank)
One Zuǒ Shùzǐ,
(Principal Fifth Rank)
One Zuǒ Yùdé,
(Subordinate Fifth Rank)
Two Zuǒ Zhōngyùn,
(Principal Sixth Rank)
Two Zuǒ Zànshàn,
(Subordinate Sixth Rank)
Two Zuǒ Sīzhíláng,
(Subordinate Sixth Rank,
later not regularly established)
One Zuǒ Qīngjìláng,
(Subordinate Eighth Rank,
not regularly established)
Two Zuǒ Sījiàn,
(Subordinate Ninth Rank,
not regularly established.)
Yòu Chūnfāng (Right Spring Chamber),
likewise had the same positions.
Sījīng Jú (Bureau of Classic Texts),
One Xǐmǎ,
(Subordinate Fifth Rank)
Two Jiàoshū,
(Principal Ninth Rank)
Two Zhèngzì,
(Subordinate Ninth Rank.)
The Zhānshì was in charge of the affairs of the Fǔ, Fāng, and Jú,
assisting and guiding the Crown Prince.
The Shào Zhānshì assisted him.
Whenever attending the Crown Prince,
they, along with the Hanlin officials of the Fāng and Jú, took turns to give lectures on the Shàngshū, Chūnqiū, Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Dàxué Yǎnyì, Zhēnguān Zhèngyào, and other books.
Beforehand, they would compile chapters to be presented to the emperor,
and then proceed to Wénhuá Diàn to give lectures.
After the lectures,
they would lead their subordinates
to explain to the Crown Prince the important military and state affairs handled by the court,
and the benevolent and righteous treatment of foreign states.
For all court greetings,
they must first report to the court,
then prepare memorial-petitions to submit.
All officials of the Fǔ and the Fāng and Jú, as well as the Hanlin Yuàn,
could hold concurrent posts,
and participated in examinations and book compilation.
The Tōngshì Shèrén were in charge of the ceremonies for court audiences and farewells in the Eastern Palace (Crown Prince's Palace),
and the matters of conveying imperial inquiries and greetings.
When court officials offered congratulations, presented memorials, or presented spring and calendar gifts to the Crown Prince,
they would introduce them and present the offerings.
The Chūnfāng Dàxuéshì oversaw the Crown Prince's submission of memorials and petitions,
and the matters of lecturing and reading,
all of which they reviewed carefully and supervised.
The Shùzǐ, Yùdé, Zhōngyùn, and Zànshàn each carried out their duties accordingly.
Whenever the Eastern Palace acted as regent, commanded the army, went on hunts,
or attended court audiences,
they had to carefully review and sign
rebuttals and endorsements
before transferring them to the Zhānshì.
They had to report all auspicious and inauspicious omens.
They would advise and admonish on matters of internal and external administration that could serve as precedents,
as events arose.
If entertainers or servants introduced new songs or engaged in impropriety,
they would explain ancient principles,
reiterate established regulations,
correct them, and request their dismissal.
The Sīzhí and Qīngjìláng were in charge of impeaching palace officials
and rectifying official duties.
After lectures in Wénhuá Diàn,
when the officials dispersed,
if anyone remained behind to report matters or pay private visits,
they would jointly censure them.
The Sījiàn were in charge of admonitions and warnings,
to pick up omissions and mend faults.
Whenever there was a petition to the Eastern Palace,
they, with the Sīzhí and Qīngjì, would take up the brush to record the imperial directives,
and correct any falsehoods or errors.
The Xǐmǎ was in charge of classics, histories, philosophical works, collections, official documents,
and the compilation and publication of books and maps.
They established original, duplicate, and stored copies for imperial viewing.
All maps and registers from throughout the realm submitted to the Eastern Palace
were received and stored by them.
The Jiàoshū and Zhèngzì were in charge of copying, binding,
identifying errors, and adjusting pronunciations,
to assist the Xǐmǎ.
Previously,
in the early Hóngwǔ reign,
the Dàběntáng was established,
filled with ancient and modern books and maps,
and famous scholars from all over were summoned to instruct the Crown Prince and imperial princes.
These scholars specialized in classics, taught face-to-face,
and took turns on night duty.
Later,
when the Crown Prince resided in Wénhuá Táng,
the scholars attended him in rotation.
Talented and outstanding individuals were also selected to serve as companions for reading,
and were frequently granted banquets, composed poems,
discussed ancient and modern affairs,
and critiqued literature.
At that time,
the officials of the Eastern Palace,
apart from the Crown Prince's Shào Shī, Shào Fù, Shào Bǎo, and Bīnkè,
included the Left and Right Zhānshì,
Tóngzhī Zhānshì Yuàn Shì,
Fù Zhānshì,
Zhānshì Chéng,
Left and Right Shuàifǔ Shǐ,
Tóngzhī Zuǒ Yòu Shuàifǔ Shì,
Left and Right Shuàifǔ Fùshǐ,
Yùdé,
and Zànshàn Dàfū,
all of whom were concurrently held by veteran meritorious ministers.
There were also officials such as Wénxué, Zhōngshè, Zhèngzì, Shìzhèng, Xǐmǎ, Shùzǐ, and Zàndú.
In the fifteenth year, the officials of the Left and Right Chūnfāng were redefined,
each establishing Shùzǐ, Yùdé, Zhōngyùn, Zànshàn, and Sīzhíláng,
and each also setting up Dàxuéshì.
Soon after, the officials of the Sījīng Jú were established,
setting up Xǐmǎ, Jiàoshū, and Zhèngzì.
In the twenty-second year, due to the lack of overall organization among officials,
the Zhānshì Yuàn was first established.
In the twenty-fifth year, the Yuàn was changed to a Fǔ,
and the rank of Zhānshì was set at Principal Third Rank,
Chūnfāng Dàxuéshì at Principal Fifth Rank,
and Sījīng Jú Xǐmǎ at Subordinate Fifth Rank.
Although each had its own seal,
all matters were centralized under the Zhānshì Fǔ.
In the twenty-ninth year, Zuǒ Yòu Chūnfāng Qīngjìláng, Sījiàn, and Tōngshì Shèrén were added.
During the Jiànwén reign,
one Shàoníng and one Sìchéng were added,
along with two Bīnkè.
Also established were one Zīdé in the Zīdé Yuàn,
and two Zīshàn.
Its subordinates included
two Zàndú, two Zànshū, two Zhùzuòláng,
and one Zhǎng Diǎnjí each.
Chéngzǔ restored the old system.
In the early Yīngzōng reign,
the Dàxuéshì was ordered to oversee the lecturing officials.
It should be noted that the Grand Court of the Imperial Household (Zhānshì Fǔ 詹事府) was often concurrently managed by officials from other offices.
Before the Tiānshùn 天順 reign,
this was sometimes a Minister (Shàngshū 尚書), Vice Minister (Shìláng 侍郎), or Censor-in-Chief (Dūyùshǐ 都御史).
After the Chénghuà 成化 reign,
it was usually concurrently managed by a Minister or Vice Minister of the Board of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū 禮部尚書, Shìláng 侍郎) who had originated from the Hanlin Academy (Hànlín Yuàn 翰林院).
There was no fixed number of coordinating officials.
As for the Grand Academician (Dàxuéshì 大學士) of the Eastern Palace (Chūnfāng 春坊),
during the Jǐngtài 景泰 reign,
after Ní Qiān 倪謙 and Liú Dìngzhī 劉定之,
only Yáng Tínghé 楊廷和 served in this capacity,
and it was not re-established thereafter.
The Director of the Bureau of Rectification (Sīzhí 司直), Remonstrating Officer (Sījiàn 司諫), and Officer for Discipline (Qīngjì Láng 清紀郎) were also not regularly appointed.
Only in the eighteenth year of Jiājìng 嘉靖 were Lù Shēn 陸深 appointed Grand Supervisor (Zhānshì 詹事),
Cuī Xiǎn 崔 Xiǎn 少詹事 Junior Supervisor,
Wáng Jiào 王教, Luó Hóngxiān 羅洪先, Huá Chá 華察, and others appointed Academicians (Yùdé 諭德), Expositors (Zànshàn 贊善), and Equerries (Xǐmǎ 洗馬),
and Huángfǔ Xiào 皇甫涍, Táng Shùnzhī 唐順之, and others appointed Directors of the Bureau of Rectification and Remonstrating Officers.
All were renowned scholars of the empire.
Since Sòng Lián 宋濂 and others in the early Míng dynasty,
no court staff had been as distinguished as this.
Thereafter,
for lecturing and reading outside the palace,
other officials were often designated,
and the bureaus and offices of the Grand Court of the Imperial Household merely served as a stepping stone for Hanlin officials to be transferred and promoted.
Hanlin Academy (Hànlín Yuàn 翰林院).
One Academician (Xuéshì 學士),
(Principal Fifth Rank),
two Academicians of the Imperial Secretariat (Shìdú Xuéshì 侍讀學士) and two Lecturing Academicians (Shìjiǎng Xuéshì 侍講學士),
(both Concurrent Fifth Rank),
two Imperial Lecturers (Shìdú 侍讀) and two Lecturing Expositors (Shìjiǎng 侍講),
(both Principal Sixth Rank),
nine Erudites of the Five Classics (Wǔjīng Bóshì 五經博士),
(Principal Eighth Rank,
and hereditary,
separately noted),
two Archivists (Diǎnjí 典籍),
(Concurrent Eighth Rank),
two Imperial Calligraphers (Shìshū 侍書),
(Principal Ninth Rank,
later not regularly established),
six Attendants (Dàizhào 待詔),
(Concurrent Ninth Rank,
not regularly established),
one Chief Clerk (Kǒngmù 孔目),
(unranked).
History Compiler (Xiūzhuàn 修撰),
(Concurrent Sixth Rank),
Editor (Biānxiū 編修),
(Principal Seventh Rank),
Reviser (Jiǎntǎo 檢討),
(Concurrent Seventh Rank),
Supernumerary Hanlin (Shùjíshì 庶吉士),
no fixed number.
The Academician was in charge of imperial edicts, historical records, and literary compositions,
to deliberate on institutions,
review and rectify documents,
and serve as consultants to the Son of Heaven.
All imperial lectures (jīngyán rìjiǎng 經筵日講),
compilation of veriable records (shílù 實錄), jade registers (yùdié 玉牒), historical annals (shǐzhì 史志) and other books,
and compilation of memorials and reports from the Six Boards (Liù Cáo Zhāngzòu 六曹章奏),
were undertaken and supervised by imperial decree.
One Academician concurrently held the responsibility for imperial edicts and proclamations (gàochì 誥敕).
(During the Zhèngtǒng 正統 reign,
Wáng Zhí 王直 and Wáng Yīng 王英, as Vice Ministers of the Board of Rites, concurrently served as Academicians
and specialized in imperial edicts and proclamations,
but this was later abolished.
It was re-established in the seventh year of Hóngzhì 弘治.
During the Zhèngdé 正德 reign,
Bái Yuè 白鉞 and Fèi Hóng 費宏, as Ministers of the Board of Rites, entered the Eastern Cabinet (Dōnggé 東閣)
and specialized in imperial edicts and proclamations.
In the sixth year of Jiājìng,
this was again abolished,
and the Lecturers, Readers, Editors, and Revisers were put in charge.)
For major political affairs and grand ceremonies,
when ministers were gathered for discussion,
they would deliberate with various departments on the feasibility of matters.
When the imperial carriage visited the Imperial Academy (Tàixué 太學) for lectures,
and for all banquets celebrating suburban sacrifices (jiāosì qìngchéng 郊祀慶成),
the Academician would sit above the Principal Fourth Rank Capital Officials (sìpǐn jīngqīng 四品京卿).
The Imperial Lecturers and Lecturing Expositors were in charge of lecturing on classics and history.
The Erudites of the Five Classics,
initially five were established,
each in charge of lecturing on a specific classic.
Later, they were given preferential treatment as hereditary descendants of sages, worthies, and former scholars,
and did not manage academy affairs.
The History Compilers were in charge of compiling national history.
All major government affairs such as astronomy, geography, imperial clan, rites and music, military and penal matters,
as well as imperial edicts and proclamations, official documents,
and imperial responses,
were recorded and documented
to serve as material for the veritable records.
When the state had books to be compiled and written,
they would be assigned to research, compile, and compose.
They served as officers for unfolding scrolls during imperial lectures,
examiners for provincial examinations (xiāngshì 鄉試),
co-examiners for metropolitan examinations (huìshì 會試),
and collection officers for palace examinations (diànshì 殿試).
They were also responsible for recording daily imperial activities,
compiling memorials and reports from the Six Boards,
and transcribing yellow scrolls for enfeoffment, among other duties.
Supernumerary Hanlin studied in the Hanlin Academy,
with one Academician assigned to teach them.
The Imperial Calligraphers were in charge of providing calligraphy services using the six scripts.
The Attendants were in charge of responding to inquiries.
The Chief Clerks were in charge of official documents.
In the first year of Wú 吳,
the Hanlin Academy was first established,
ranked Principal Third Rank.
Academicians were set up,
(Principal Third Rank),
Lecturing Academicians,
(Principal Fourth Rank),
Directors of the Academy (Zhí Xuéshì 直學士),
(Principal Fifth Rank),
History Compilers and Registrars (Diǎnbù 典簿),
(Principal Seventh Rank),
Editors,
(Principal Eighth Rank).
In the second year of Hóngwǔ 洪wǔ, an Academician-in-Waiting (Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ 學士承旨) was established,
Principal Third Rank.
The Academician was re-designated,
Concurrent Third Rank.
(Lecturing Academicians,
Principal Fourth Rank,
Academicians of the Imperial Secretariat,
Concurrent Fourth Rank,
History Compilers,
Principal Sixth Rank).
Additional Wait-for-Call officials (Dàizhì 待制) were established,
(Concurrent Fifth Rank),
Attendants (Yìngfèng 應奉),
(Principal Seventh Rank),
Archivists,
(Concurrent Eighth Rank),
and other officials.
In the thirteenth year, an Inspector (Jiǎnyuè 檢閱) was added,
(Concurrent Ninth Rank).
In the fourteenth year, the Academician was set at Principal Fifth Rank.
The Academician-in-Waiting, Director of the Academy, Wait-for-Call officials, Attendants, Inspectors, and Registrars were abolished.
Chief Clerks, Erudites of the Five Classics, Imperial Calligraphers, Attendants, and Revisers were established.

Editors, Revisers, and Archivists, together with the Director of the Bureau of Rectification of the Left Eastern Palace (Zuǒ Chūnfāng Zuǒ Sīzhí Láng 左春坊左司直郎), Correctors (Zhèngzì 正字), and Expositers (Zàndú 贊讀), were ordered to review and reject memorials and reports from various departments.
If found fair and appropriate, their title would be signed as
"Such-and-such official of the Hanlin Academy concurrently handling the review and rejection of documents from various departments"
and their names listed.
In the eighteenth year, the ranks and officials were re-designated
(as listed previously,
but without Supernumerary Hanlin),
with Imperial Lecturers preceding Lecturing Expositors.
During the Jiànwén 建文 reign,
the Academician-in-Waiting was retained.
The two Academicians, Imperial Lecturers and Lecturing Expositors, were changed to Doctors of Letters (Wénxué Bóshì 文學博士).
Two academies, Wénhàn 文翰 (Literature) and Wénshǐ 文史 (History), were established.
Wénhàn housed Imperial Lecturers, Lecturing Expositors, Imperial Calligraphers, Erudites of the Five Classics, Archivists, and Attendants.
Wénshǐ housed History Compilers, Editors, and Revisers.
Chief Clerks were changed to Registrars.
Secretaries of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shèrén 中書舍人) were changed to Imperial Calligraphers
and attached to the Hanlin Academy.
Furthermore, Attendants of the Wényuān Pavilion (Wényuāngé Dàizhào 文淵閣待詔) and officials like Collectors of Omissions (Shíyí 拾遺) and Remonstrance Officers (Bǔquē 補闕) were established.
In the early Chéngzǔ 成祖 reign, the old system was restored.
In the ninth month of that year,
Lecturers, Readers, Editors, Revisers, and other officials were specially selected to participate in government affairs
(no fixed number was selected for service),
and this was called the Grand Secretariat (Nèigé 內閣).
However, even after Xiè Jìn 解縉, Hú Guǎng 胡廣, and others served in the Wényuān Pavilion,
they still successively signed academy affairs.
Only after Hóngxī 洪熙,
when Yáng Shìqí 楊士奇 and others were promoted to Grand Tutors (Shī Bǎo 師保),
and their courtesies surpassed all other officials,
did they no longer sign.
In the seventh year of Zhèngtǒng,
when the Hanlin Academy was completed,
Academician Qián Xílǐ 錢習禮 did not provide public seats for Yáng Shìqí and Yáng Pǔ 楊溥,
saying,
"This is not the office of the three dukes."
The two Yángs reported this.
Then the Board of Works (Gōngbù 工部) was ordered to prepare chairs and desks,
and the Board of Rites to determine seating arrangements,
because the Grand Secretariat was originally a function of the Hanlin Academy.
(Before Jiā Jīng 嘉靖 and Lóng Qìng 隆慶,
official documents and communications
were still referred to as from the Hanlin Academy;
thereafter, they were simply called from the Grand Secretariat.)
As for the Six Boards (Liù Bù 六部),
since the Chénghuà reign,
after Zhōu Hóngmó 周洪謨,
the Minister and Vice Minister of the Board of Rites had to be from the Hanlin Academy,
and one of the two Vice Ministers of the Board of Civil Office (Lìbù 吏部) had to be from the Hanlin Academy.
Those from the Hanlin Academy,
if Minister, also held the title of Academician
(this was true for all Six Boards);
if Vice Minister, also held the title of Academician of the Imperial Secretariat or Lecturing Academician.
As for officials in the Grand Court of the Imperial Household and the Eastern Palace offices,
depending on their rank,
they must carry a title from the Hanlin Academy.
(The Grand Supervisor and Junior Supervisor carried the title of Academician.
The Grand Academician of the Eastern Palace was not regularly established.

The Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent (Shùzǐ 庶子), Academician, Director of the Eastern Palace (Zhōngyǔn 中允), Expositor, Equerry, and others carried titles ranging from Academicians of the Imperial Secretariat/Lecturing Academicians down to Editor/Reviser.)
Historians:
From the fourteenth year of Hóngwǔ, three Xiūzhuàn were appointed,
four Biānxiū and four Jiǎntǎo each.
Thereafter, those appointed from the first-class *jìnshì*, as well as *shùjíshì* retained in the academies and given positions,
often exceeded the quota,
having no fixed number.
In the eighth year of Jiājìng, the numbers were again fixed at three Jiǎng, three Dú, and three Xiūzhuàn each,
six Biānxiū and six Jiǎntǎo each,
all recommended and appointed by the Lìbù,
following the precedent of other offices.
However, not long after,
due to a shortage of attendants,
an imperial edict commanded the selection of upright scholars with academic skills to fill these positions.
Consequently, seven individuals, including the Yùshǐ Hú Jīng, Yuánwàiláng Chén Shù, and Zhǔshì Táng Shùnzhī, were all redesignated as Biānxiū.
Afterward, the old practice was resumed,
with appointments made from *shùjíshì*,
ultimately without a fixed quota.
In the seventh year of Chóngzhēn, judicial officers and county magistrates were again selected and appointed as Biānxiū and Jiǎntǎo,
which was also an innovation,
not a permanent system.
*Shùjíshì*: From the early Hóngwǔ period, there were *shùjíshì* for the six departments.
In the eighteenth year, *jìnshì* serving as close attendants in the Hànlín Yuàn, Chéngchì Jiān, etc.,
were all referred to as *shùjíshì*.
In the second year of Yǒnglè, they were first designated as Hànlín Yuàn *shùjíshì*,
selecting *jìnshì* excellent in literature and skilled in calligraphy.
In the third year, they were tested.
Those retained,
if of the second class, were appointed Biānxiū;
if of the third class, they were appointed Jiǎntǎo.
Those not retained
became Gěishìzhōng or Yùshǐ,
or were sent out as Zhoūxiàn officials.
In the fifth year of Xuāndé, scholars were first ordered to provide instruction.
After Wànlì,
those in charge of instruction
were exclusively two Shìláng from the Lìbù and Lǐbù.
In the early Míng dynasty,
the Hóngwén Guǎn Xuéshì were once established,
(Established in the third year of Hóngwǔ, with Hú Xuàn as its Xuéshì, and Liú Jī, Wēi Sù, Wáng Běnzhōng, and Suī Jià also appointed concurrently as Hóngwén Guǎn Xuéshì,
but abolished shortly after.
During the Xuāndé period,
the Hóngwén Gé was re-established to the right of the Sīshàn Mén,
with Hànlín Xuéshì Yáng Pǔ in charge of the cabinet seal,
but soon merged into the Wényuān Gé.)
the Mìshū Jiān,
(Established in the third year of Hóngwǔ, with a rank of principal sixth grade.
One Jiānchéng and two Zhícháng were appointed.
Soon after, one Lìng, two Céng, and two Zhícháng were fixed,
managing books in the inner palace.
In the thirteenth year, it was merged into the Hànlín Yuàn Diǎnjí.)
and Qǐjūzhù,
(Established in the *jiǎchén* year.
In the first year of Wú, its rank was set at principal fifth grade.
In the fourth year of Hóngwǔ, it was corrected to principal seventh grade.
In the sixth year, it was promoted to subordinate sixth grade.
In the ninth year, two Qǐjūzhù were fixed,
but later abolished.
In the fourteenth year, it was re-established,
with a rank of subordinate seventh grade,
but soon abolished.
Until the Wànlì period,
Hànlín Yuàn officials were ordered to concurrently manage it.
It was later abolished again.)
but all were soon abolished.
Guózǐ Jiān:
One Jìjiǔ,
(subordinate fourth grade,)
one Sīyè,
(principal sixth grade.)
Its subordinates:
Shéngqiān Tīng:
one Jiānchéng,
(principal eighth grade.)
Bóshì Tīng:
five Wǔjīng Bóshì,
(subordinate eighth grade.)
The six halls of Shuàixìng, Xiūdào, Chéngxīn, Zhèngyì, Chóngzhì, and Guǎngyè:
fifteen Zhùjiào,
(subordinate eighth grade,)
ten Xuézhèng,
(principal ninth grade,)
seven Xuélù,
(subordinate ninth grade.)
Diǎnbù Tīng:
one Diǎnbù,
(subordinate eighth grade.)
Diǎnjí Tīng:
one Diǎnjí,
(subordinate ninth grade.)
Zhǎngzhuàn Tīng:
two Zhǎngzhuàn,
(unranked.)
The Jìjiǔ and Sīyè
were in charge of the regulations for instructing the students of the national academy.

All *jǔrén*, *gòngshēng*, official students, *ēnshēng*, *gōngshēng*, *lìshēng*, native officials, foreign students, young meritorious officials, and children of meritorious relatives and high ministers who entered the academy
were to observe the academy's rules and be instructed,
cultivated with knowledge that clarifies the essence and achieves practical application,
with filial piety and fraternal love, ritual propriety and righteousness, loyalty and trustworthiness, integrity and shame as their foundation,
and the Six Classics and various histories as their subject matter.
They were all required to uphold ethical relationships and good conduct,
diligently pursue their studies and enjoy social interaction,
to revive the teaching methods of the ancient music masters and academy instructors.
Those who did not comply
were disciplined with a rod;
if unrepentant,
they were banished.
Those who followed instructions
had a system of promotions based on accumulated points and exceptional merit.
Their coursework was presented quarterly to the Hànlín Yuàn for examination,
and the records were submitted to the emperor at the end of the year.
Every year in the middle spring and autumn, on the *dīng* day,
ministers were dispatched to sacrifice to the former sages,
and the Jìjiǔ oversaw the ceremonies.
When the imperial carriage visited the academy,
the Jìjiǔ held the classics and lectured.
When new *jìnshì* assumed their official robes,
the Jìjiǔ sat and received their bows.
The Jiānchéng was in charge of the affairs of the Shéngqiān Tīng,
participating in leading the academy's matters,
firmly establishing its regulations.
Any misdeeds by teachers or students, or unclean provisions,
were to be rectified and punished,
and recorded in the registry of transgressions.
The Bóshì were in charge of dividing the classics for instruction
and regularly evaluating the coursework.
For all classics,
namely *Yì*, *Shī*, *Shū*, *Chūnqiū*, and *Lǐjì*,
each person specialized in one classic,
while *Dàxué*, *Zhōngyōng*, *Lúnyǔ*, and *Mèngzǐ* were studied concurrently.
The Zhùjiào, Xuéshì, and Xuélù were in charge of teaching in the six halls.
Students pursuing their studies in their respective halls
were to be instructed in the meaning of the classics and texts,
and guided by rules and regulations.
The Diǎnbù managed official documents, money receipts, and expenditures.
The Diǎnjí managed books.
The Zhǎngzhuàn managed food and drink.
In the early Míng dynasty,
the Guózǐxué was established.
(In the ninth month of the Yǐsì year, the Guózǐxué was established,
using the former Jíqìng Lù School for this purpose.
In the 14th year of Hóngwǔ, the Guózǐxué was rebuilt at the foot of Jīmíng Shān.
)Officials such as Bóshì, Zhùjiào, Xuézhèng, Xuélù, Diǎnyuè, Diǎnshū, and Diǎnshàn were appointed.
In the first year of Wú, the official system for the Guózǐxué was formalized,
with the addition of Jìjiǔ, Sīyè, and Diǎnbù.
(Jìjiǔ,
Principal Fourth Rank;
Sīyè,
Principal Fifth Rank;
Bóshì,
Principal Seventh Rank;
Diǎnbù,
Principal Eighth Rank;
Zhùjiào,
Auxiliary Eighth Rank;
Xuézhèng,
Principal Ninth Rank;
Xuélù,
Auxiliary Ninth Rank;
Diǎnshàn,
see note.)
In the eighth year of Hóngwǔ, the Zhōngdū Guózǐxué was also established,
(ranked Principal Fourth Rank,)
and officials from the Guózǐxué were ordered to manage it.
In the 13th year, Diǎnshàn was changed to Zhǎngzhuàn.
In the 15th year, it was renamed Guózǐjiān,
with an Auxiliary Fourth Rank,
and appointed one Jìjiǔ,
one Sīyè,
one Jiānchéng and one Diǎnbù each,
three Bóshì,
sixteen Zhùjiào,
three Xuézhèng and three Xuélù each,
and one Zhǎngzhuàn.
(The ranks of these officials
are as previously listed.)
The system for the Zhōngdū Guózǐjiān was also similar.
In the 16th year, Sòng Nà was appointed Jìjiǔ,
and an imperial edict was issued to him, saying:
“The Grand Academy is the gateway for the worthy of the empire,
the source from which propriety and righteousness emerge,
and where talent arises.
You, sir, with your long-standing scholarship and revered virtue,
are specially appointed as Jìjiǔ.
May you embody Our intention of establishing education,
so that all students may achieve success,
scholarly customs be greatly transformed,
and the state thereby benefit.”
Lǐ Wénzhōng, Duke of Cáo, was also ordered to oversee the affairs of the academy,
and the emperor occasionally visited in his carriage.
(Consequently, academy officials were not allowed to sit in the central hall or pass through the central gate.)
In the 24th year, the ranks and number of officials in the Guózǐjiān were further revised.
(All
as previously listed.)
The Zhōngdū Guózǐjiān appointed one Jìjiǔ, Sīyè, Jiānchéng, Diǎnbù, Bóshì, Xuézhèng, Xuélù, and Zhǎngzhuàn each,
and two Zhùjiào,
with ranks identical to those in the capital.
In the 26th year, the Zhōngdū Guózǐjiān was abolished.
During the Jiànwén reign,
the Jiānchéng was promoted to a Hall Official,
and the Xuézhèng and Xuélù were abolished.
Chéngzǔ restored the old system.
In the first year of Yǒnglè, the Guózǐjiān was established in Běijīng,
appointing one Jìjiǔ, Sīyè, Jiānchéng, Diǎnbù, Bóshì, Xuézhèng, Xuélù, and Zhǎngzhuàn each,
and two Zhùjiào.
(Later, additional appointments were made irregularly,
with Zhùjiào reaching fifteen,
Xuézhèng eleven,
and Xuélù seven.
Later, two Zhùjiào,
four Xuézhèng,
and two Xuélù were abolished.
In the ninth year of Wànlì, four more Zhùjiào
and one Xuélù were abolished.)
In the ninth year of Xuāndé, the Sīyè position was eliminated.
In the 15th year of Hóngzhì, it was re-established.
In the early Míng dynasty,
Jìjiǔ and Sīyè were chosen from those with scholarly conduct;
later, all were transferred from officials of the Hànlín Yuàn.
The Yǎnshèng Gōng,
a hereditary title for the Kǒng clan,
(Principal Second Rank.
Robe, belt, imperial decree, and court rank of the First Rank.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, Kǒng Xīxué, the 56th generation descendant of Kǒngzǐ, was granted the hereditary title.)
Its subordinates included
one Zhǎngshū, Diǎnjí, Sīyuè, Zhīyìn, Zòuchāi, and Shūxiě each,
(all filled by temporary officials.)
The Zhīxiàn of Qūfù,
a hereditary post for the Kǒng clan.
(In the first year of Hóngwǔ, Kǒng Xīdà, a descendant of Kǒngzǐ, was granted the hereditary post of Zhīxiàn of Qūfù.)
Hereditary Wǔjīng Bóshì of the Hànlín Yuàn,
(Principal Eighth Rank,)
two from the Kǒng clan,
(In the first year of Zhèngdé, Kǒng Yánshéng, the 59th generation descendant of Kǒngzǐ, was appointed to oversee the temple sacrifice in Qúzhōu.
Kǒng Duānyǒu of the Sòng dynasty followed Gāozōng south across the river
and settled in Qúzhōu;
this is the Southern Branch of the Kǒng clan.
In the second year of Zhèngdé, Kǒng Wénlǐ was appointed to manage the temple sacrifice to Zǐsī.)
one from the Yán clan,
(In the third year of Jǐngtài, Yán Xīhuì, the 59th generation descendant of Yánzǐ, was appointed.)
one from the Zēng clan,
(In the 18th year of Jiājìng, Zēng Zhìcuì, the 60th generation descendant of Zēngzǐ, was appointed.)
one from the Zhòng clan,
(In the 15th year of Wànlì, Zhòng Lǚ, a descendant of Zǐlù, was appointed.)
one from the Mèng clan,
(In the third year of Jǐngtài, Mèng Xīwén, a descendant of Mèngzǐ, was appointed.)
one from the Zhōu clan,
(In the seventh year of Jǐngtài, Zhōu Miǎn, a descendant of the former scholar Zhōu Dūnyí, was appointed.)
two from the Chéng clan,
(In the sixth year of Jǐngtài, Chéng Kèrén, a descendant of the former scholar Chéng Yí, was appointed.
In the third year of Chóngzhēn, Chéng Jiēdào, a descendant of the former scholar Chéng Hào, was appointed.)
one from the Shào clan,
(In the third year of Chóngzhēn, Shào Jìzǔ, a descendant of the former scholar Shào Yōng, was appointed.)
one from the Zhāng clan,
(In the second year of Tiānqǐ, Zhāng Wényùn, a descendant of the former scholar Zhāng Zài, was made Bóshì.)
two from the Zhū clan,
(In the sixth year of Jǐngtài, Zhū Chán, a descendant of the former scholar Zhū Xī, was appointed.
In the second year of Jiājìng, Zhū Shù was also appointed Bóshì,
to oversee the temple sacrifice in Wùyuán.)
one from the Liú clan,
(In the seventh year of Jǐngtài, Liú Lù, the seventh generation descendant of Chéngyì Bó Liú Jī, was appointed;
later abolished.)
For the Jiàoshòu Division,
Jiàoshòu,
(Auxiliary Ninth Rank,)
Xuélu, and Xuésī,
(all unranked,)
one each for the Kǒng, Yán, Zēng, and Mèng clans.
Furthermore, at the Níshān and Zhūsì academies,
one Xuélù each.
Previously,
in the Yuán dynasty, descendants of Kǒngzǐ were enfeoffed as Yǎnshèng Gōng,
and bestowed with a third-rank seal.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ,
after Tàizǔ had already granted Kǒng Xīxué the hereditary title of Yǎnshèng Gōng,
he then addressed his ministers of ritual, saying:
“Kǒngzǐ is the teacher of emperors for ten thousand generations;
to treat his descendants
with a rank limited to the third
does not sufficiently honor and exalt them.
Therefore, bestow upon Xīxué the second rank,
and grant him a silver seal.”
He also ordered the exemption of descendants of the Kǒng, Yán, and Mèng clans from corvée labor.
In the 18th year, he issued an edict to the Ministry of Works to inquire
and release any descendants of sages and worthies who had been sentenced to penal servitude due to crimes.
In the 22nd year of Yǒnglè, the Yǎnshèng Gōng was granted a residence in the capital,
and an additional gold-woven robe of the first rank.
In the first year of Zhèngtǒng, an edict was issued to exempt all descendants of sages and worthies from corvée labor,
and to select intelligent and promising descendants of Zhōu, Chéng, Zhāng, and Zhū scholars suitable for education,
regardless of their number,
send them to local Confucian schools to study,
and provide them with stipends and meals.
In the first year of Chénghuà, academic seals were granted to the Kǒng, Yán, and Mèng clans,
ordering that one person with scholarly conduct be sent to the Guózǐjiān every three years.
In the sixth year, it was decreed that the newly succeeded Yǎnshèng Gōng should study in the academy for one year.
Collation Notes
Treatise 50, Bureaucracy 3: Tàicháng Sì (attached Tídū Sìyíguǎn),

Guānglù Sì, Tàipú Sì, Hónglú Sì, Shàngbǎo Sī, Liù Kē, Zhōngshū Shèrén, Xíngrén Sī, Qīntiān Jiān, Tàiyī Yuàn, Shànglín Yuàn Jiān, Wǔchéng Bīngmǎ Sī, Shùntiān Fǔ (attached Wǎnpíng and Dàxīng counties), Wǔxué, Sēngdào Lùsī, Jiàofāng Sī, Huàn guān, Nǚ guān.
Tàicháng Sì.
One Qīng,
(Principal Third Rank,)
two Shàoqīng,
(Principal Fourth Rank,)
two Sìchéng,
(Principal Sixth Rank.)
Its subordinates:
Diǎnbù Tīng,
two Diǎnbù,
(Principal Seventh Rank,)
two Bóshì,
(Principal Seventh Rank,)
two Xiélǜ Láng,
(Principal Eighth Rank,
increased to five during the Jiājìng reign.)
nine Zànlǐ Láng,
(Principal Ninth Rank,
increased to thirty-three during the Jiājìng reign,
later two abolished.)
twenty Sīyuè,
(Auxiliary Ninth Rank,
increased to thirty-nine during the Jiājìng reign,
later five abolished.)

For the shrines and sacrificial offices of Tiāntán, Dìtán, Zhāorì Tán, Xīyuè Tán, Xiānnóng Tán, Dìwáng Miào, Qígǔ Diàn, Chánglíng, Xiànlíng, Jǐnglíng, Yùlíng, Màolíng, Tàilíng, Xiǎnlíng, Kānglíng, Yǒnglíng, Zhāolíng,
each had one Fèngsì,
(Auxiliary Seventh Rank,)
and two Sìchéng,
(Auxiliary Eighth Rank.)
Xīshēng Suǒ,
one Lì mù,
(Auxiliary Ninth Rank.)
The Tàicháng Sì 掌 (Court of Imperial Sacrifices) was in charge of sacrificial rituals, ceremonies, and music.
It supervised all its officials and subordinates,
recorded their policies and decrees,
and reported to the Lǐbù (Ministry of Rites).
For all gods of heaven, deities of earth, and human spirits,
there were regular annual sacrifices.
Before the first day of the twelfth lunar month,
it would submit a memorial with the sacrificial dates for the coming year.
The Emperor would receive it at the Fèngtiān Diàn (Hall of Honoring Heaven),
and then it would be distributed to the various offices.
When the Emperor personally performed a sacrifice,
the Tàicháng Sì assisted with the rites and ceremonies.
When a high official acted on behalf of the Emperor,
the same applied.

Whenever the state had major ceremonies such as the enthronement of an empress or crown prince, investiture of a vassal, capping ceremony, wedding, construction, military expedition, or grand funeral,
or during annual droughts, floods, or major disasters,
the Tàicháng Sì would request permission from the Zōngmiào (Imperial Ancestral Temple) and Shèjì (Altars of Land and Grain).
For offering new produce, it would instruct the Guānglù Sì (Court of Imperial Entertainments) to supply the items.
Before a sacrifice, it would request an inspection of the sacrificial animals,
present the祝版 (prayer tablets) and 銅人 (bronze figurines),
ascend to the palace hall to request purification and fasting,
and have the Emperor personally sign his name.
The inspection of sacrificial animals was done jointly with the Guānglù Qīng (Minister of Imperial Entertainments).
Only for grand sacrifices would the Emperor personally inspect the animals;
for other sacrifices, high officials would inspect them daily.
For all sacrifices,
the washing of vessels, cooking, burying, incense, candles, jade, and silk,
and cleaning of the spirit canopy
had to be done with utmost reverence and cleanliness.

Those in charge of lighting the pyre, observing the pyre, reading prayers, performing rites, guiding the procession, managing incense, presenting offerings, raising banners, arranging displays, managing income and expenditure, leading the way, setting up positions, overseeing ceremonies, serving as master of ceremonies, presenting silk, holding wine cups, managing wine jars, and managing washing basins –
the Qīng, vice-ministers, and subordinates each took charge of their respective duties,
ensuring nothing was overlooked.
There were four grades of jade: namely, Cāngbì (azure jade disc),
(used for worshipping Heaven),
Huángcóng (yellow jade tube),
(used for worshipping Earth),
Chìzhāng (red jade tablet) and Báihǔ (white jade tiger),
(used for worshipping the sun and moon),
and Liǎngguī Yǒudǐ (two jade tablets with bases),
(used for sacrificing to the Tàishè and Tàijì).
There were five grades of silk: namely, Jiāosì Zhìbó (sacrificial silk for suburban altars),
(for worshipping Heaven and Earth),
Fèngxiān Zhìbó (sacrificial silk for honoring ancestors),
(for offering to ancestors),
Lǐshén Zhìbó (sacrificial silk for honoring gods),
(for sacrificing to Shèjì, various deities, emperors, and ancestral teachers),
Zhǎnqīn Zhìbó (sacrificial silk for showing kinship),
(for sacrificing to and honoring imperial princes),
and Bàogōng Zhìbó (sacrificial silk for rewarding merit),
(for sacrificing to and honoring meritorious officials).
There were four grades of sacrificial animals: namely, dú (calf),
niú (ox),
Tàiláo (grand sacrifice of ox, pig, and sheep),
and Shàoláo (lesser sacrifice of pig and sheep).
The preferred colors were red or black.
For grand sacrifices, animals were selected three months in advance;
for medium sacrifices, one month;
for minor sacrifices, ten days.
There were four grades of music: namely, Jiǔzòu (nine performances),
(used for worshipping Heaven and Earth),
Bāzòu (eight performances),
(for gods, deities, and Tàisuì),
Qīzòu (seven performances),
(for Dàmíng (Sun), Tàishè, Tàijì, and emperors),
and Liùzòu (six performances),
(for Yèmíng (Moon), Dìshè, Dìjì, Zōngmiào, and ancestral teachers).
There were two types of dances: namely, Wénwǔ (civil dance)
and Wǔwǔ (military dance).
Musical instruments were not to be moved.
Sacrifices at imperial mausoleums had no music.
At the end of the year, for the combined sacrifice to the five household deities,
the Shàokīng (Vice-Minister) would officiate.
Initially,
in the first year of Wú (1367), the Tàicháng Sī was established,
with a Qīng,
(rank 3a),
a Shàokīng,
(rank 4a),
a Chéng (secretary),
(rank 5a),
and Diǎnbù, Xiélǜláng, and Bóshì,
(rank 7a),
and Zànlǐláng,
(rank 8b).
In the early years of Hóngwǔ,
various Císì Shǔ (offices for sacrificial rituals) were established,
with a Shǔlìng and a Shǔchéng.
In the thirteenth year (1380), the official ranks of Xiélǜláng and others were redefined.
(Xiélǜláng was rank 8a,
Zànlǐláng was rank 9a,
and Sīyuè was rank 9b).
In the twenty-fourth year (1391), the various Shǔlìng were renamed Fèngsì,
and Shǔchéng were renamed Sìchéng.
In the thirtieth year (1397), the Sī was changed to Sì (Court),
but the official system remained the same.
(In the twenty-fifth year (1392), the Sìchéng had already been set at rank 6a).
During the Jiànwén reign,
two Zànlǐláng and
one Tàizhù (Grand Prayer-Reciter) were added,
and the various Císì Shǔ underwent reforms.
(The Tiāntán Císì Shǔ was changed to Nánjiāo Císì Shǔ,
the Sìzhōu Císì Shǔ to Sìbīn Císì Shǔ,
the Sùzhōu Císì Shǔ to Xīnfēng Císì Shǔ,
the Xiàolíng Mausoleum established the Zhōngshān Císì Shǔ,
and one Zhīguān was added for each Sīpǔsuǒ and Shénlèguān).
In the early years of Chéngzǔ,
only the Tiāntán was changed to Tiāndìtán (Altar of Heaven and Earth);
all others reverted to the Hóngwǔ era system.
(During the Jiànwén reign,
the Nánjiāo Císì Shǔ was changed to Jiāotán Císì Shǔ,
and then again to Tiāndìtán Císì Shǔ).
In the first year of Hóngxī (1425), the Xīshēng Suǒ (Office of Sacrificial Animals) was established,
with a Lìmù (clerk) in charge of documents.
(Before this,
in the third year of Hóngwǔ (1370), the Shénshēng Suǒ (Office of Divine Animals) was established,
with Lǐnshēnglìng, Dàshǐ, and Fùshǐ officials.
It was abolished in the fourth year (1371)).
During Shìzōng's reign, the sacrificial rites were reformed.
The Tiāndìtán was divided into Tiāntán and Dìtán.
The Shānchuāntán (Altar of Mountains and Rivers) and Jìtián Císì Shǔ (Office for Sacrifices at the Altar of Plowed Fields) were combined into the Shénqítán (Altar of Gods and Earth Spirits).
The Dàsì Diàn (Great Sacrifice Hall) was changed to Qígǔ Diàn (Hall of Prayers for Harvest).
Two new altars, Cháorì (Altar of Morning Sun) and Xīyuè (Altar of Evening Moon), were added,
each with its own Císì Shǔ.
Additionally, more Xiélǜláng, Zànlǐláng, and Sīyuè officials were added.
(In the third year of Lóngqìng (1569), forty-eight officials including Xiélǜláng were abolished.
In the sixth year of Wànlì (1578), they were re-established,
following the Jiājìng era system).
In the fourth year of Wànlì (1576), the Shénqítán was changed to Xiānnóngtán (Altar of the First Farmer).
The Tídū (Director) of the Sìyí Guǎn (Four Barbarian Bureaus).
One Shàokīng,
(rank 4a),
was in charge of translation matters.
From the fifth year of Yǒnglè (1407),
when foreign countries paid tribute,
eight bureaus were specially established: Ménggǔ (Mongolian), Nǚzhí (Jurchen), Xīfān (Tibetan), Xītiān (Indian), Huíhuí (Muslim), Bǎiyí (Bai people), Gāochāng (Kaochang), and Miǎndiàn (Burmese),
with Yìzìshēng (translators) and Tōngshì (interpreters).
(Tōngshì were initially subordinate to the Tōngzhèngshǐ Sī (Office of Transmission)).
They were responsible for translating spoken and written languages.
In the Zhèngdé reign,
the Bābǎi Guǎn was added.
(The country of Lánzhěgē from Bābǎi (modern-day Thailand/Laos region) paid tribute).
In the Wànlì reign,
the Xiāmluó Guǎn (Siamese Bureau) was also added.
Initially, the Sìyí Guǎn was subordinate to the Hànlín Yuàn (Hanlin Academy),
selecting Guózǐjiàn (Imperial Academy) students to learn translation.
In the first year of Xuāndé (1426), officials and commoners' children were also selected,
and entrusted with officials to teach them,
while Xuéshì (Academicians) reviewed their progress.
In the seventh year of Hóngzhì (1494), one Tàicháng Sì Qīng and one Shàokīng were added as Tídū,
and it was then transferred to the Tàicháng Sì.
In the Jiājìng reign,
the Qīng position was abolished,
leaving only one Shàokīng.
(Note that the Tàicháng Sì Qīng in Nánjīng
were often appointed through the imperial examination system.
In the Northern Court, from the Yǒnglè reign, music and dance performers were used,
who gradually rose through the ranks to become Sì Qīng,
and sometimes even received additional titles such as Lǐbù Shìláng (Vice Minister of Rites) or Shàngshū (Minister of Rites) to manage the Court,
a practice that was largely continued later.
It was not until the early Lóngqìng reign
that those with a Kējiǎ (examination background) were again primarily appointed.
Yìzìshēng
were highly regarded in the early Míng dynasty.
Those who passed the examination
were considered to have the same Kējiǎ background as those who passed the xiāngshì (provincial) and huìshì (metropolitan) examinations.
Later, they were relegated to a miscellaneous status.
Those in the bureaus,
when promoted or transferred, were all within the Hónglú Sì (Court of State Ceremonial)).
Guānglù Sì.
One Qīng,
(third rank, secondary),
two Shǎoqīng,
(fifth rank, principal),
two Sìchéng,
(sixth rank, secondary).
Its subordinate offices:
Diǎnbù Tīng,
two Diǎnbù,
(seventh rank, secondary),
one Lùshì,
(eighth rank, secondary).
The four Bureaus of Dàguān, Zhēnxiū, Liángyùn, and Zhǎnghǎi
each had one Zhèng,
(sixth rank, secondary),
four Shǔchéng,
(seventh rank, secondary),
and four Jiānshì,
(eighth rank, secondary).
Sīshēng Sī had
one Dàshǐ,
(ninth rank, secondary),
and one Fùshǐ,
(later abolished).
Sīmù Jú had
one Dàshǐ,
(ninth rank, secondary,
abolished in Jiājìng seventh year).
Yínkù had
one Dàshǐ.
The Qīng was in charge of sacrificial offerings, banquets, rewards, wines, and food.
He led the Shǎoqīng, Sìchéng, and other officials
to differentiate their names and numbers,
monitor their income and expenditure,
and assess their abundance or scarcity,
reporting to the Lǐbù.
For all sacrifices,
they would inspect the sacrificial animals with the Tàicháng.
When the Emperor personally offered sacrifices,
they would present the auspicious wine and receive the sacrificial meat.
For offering new harvests,
they would present the seasonal produce according to the monthly ordinances.
For funerals, they would provide offerings and meals.
The sacrificial animals, fruits, and vegetables used
were procured from the Shànglínyuàn.
If insufficient,
they were purchased from the common people,
at a price 10% above the market rate.
The cost of these purchases was paid quarterly from the Tiāncáikù.
They carefully received and stored fruit, fresh ingredients, and kitchen supplies contributed from the four directions.
The four directions contributed fruit, fresh ingredients, and kitchen supplies,
which were meticulously received and stored.
Vessels were transferred to the Gōngbù, and craftsmen were recruited to assist in their manufacture;
their success or failure was reviewed annually.
For all banquets, wine, and food, as well as foreign envoys and surrendered personnel,
they were categorized and supplied accordingly.
Imperial edicts and requests were recorded and reported back.
One Kēdào official was appointed to supervise,
monitoring their income and expenditure,
and rectifying malpractices.
From the fourth to the ninth month of each year,
all items for imperial use and sacrificial offerings were to use ice.
Dàguān supplied sacrificial items for palace meals, seasonal banquets, and feasts for foreign envoys.
Zhēnxiū supplied delicacies and dried fruits for palace meals.
Liángyùn supplied wines.
Zhǎnghǎi supplied malt sugar, oil, vinegar, sauce, plums, and salt.
Sīshēng raised sacrificial animals,
inspecting their fatness or leanness and purifying them.
Sīmù did likewise.
Initially,
in the first year of Wú, Xuānhuī Yuàn was established,
with a Yuànshǐ,
(third rank, principal),
a Tóngzhī,
(fourth rank, principal),
a Yuànpàn,
(fifth rank, principal),
and a Diǎnbù,
(seventh rank, principal).
The two Bureaus of Shàngshí and Shànglǐ were subordinated to it.
(Each Bureau had a Dàshǐ,
sixth rank, secondary,
and a Fùshǐ,
seventh rank, secondary).
In Hóngwǔ first year, it was renamed Guānglù Sì,
and a Guānglù Qīng,
(fourth rank, principal),
a Shǎoqīng,
(fifth rank, principal),
a Sìchéng,
(sixth rank, principal),
and a Zhǔbù,
(eighth rank, principal), were appointed.
The subordinate Shàngshí and other Bureaus,
and the Gōngxūkù of Tàicháng Sī were also subordinated to it.
(The ranks of the Bureau and Treasury officials remained unchanged).
In the second year, four Zhícháng were appointed.
When officials were granted food in the imperial presence,
they were ordered to serve.
In the fourth year, Fǎjiǔ Kù was established.
(It had an Nèijiǔfāng Dàshǐ,
eighth rank, secondary,
and a Fùshǐ,
ninth rank, secondary).
In the eighth year, the Sì was changed to a Sī,
and the Qīng's rank was raised,
(Qīng, third rank, secondary;
Shǎoqīng, fourth rank, secondary),
the Sìchéng became Sīchéng,
(sixth rank, secondary),
the Zhǔbù became Diǎnbù,
(seventh rank, secondary),
and a Lùshì was added,
(eighth rank, secondary).
Also, the four subordinate Bureaus of Dàguān, Zhēnxiū, Liángyùn, and Zhǎnghǎi were established,
each with one Lìng,
(sixth rank, secondary),
one Chéng,
(seventh rank, secondary),
and one Jiānshì,
(eighth rank, secondary).
Zīmù Suǒ had
one Dàshǐ,
(ninth rank, secondary),
and one Fùshǐ,
(unranked).
In the tenth year, the ranks of the non-official posts of Guānglù Sī were standardized.
(At that time, the officials serving in Guānglù Sī
were either palace officials,
or regular civil officials,
or cooks,
coming from different backgrounds,
all appointed to non-official posts.
At this time, it was decided
that those appointed from palace officials
would be given non-official ranks according to palace officials.
Those appointed from regular civil officials
would be given non-official ranks according to civil officials.
Those appointed from cooks,
the Qīng, third rank, secondary,
was granted Shàngshàn Dàfū;
the Shǎoqīng, fifth rank, principal,
was granted Fèngshàn Dàfū;
the Sīchéng, sixth rank, secondary,
was granted Sīshàn Láng;
the Chéng of each Bureau, seventh rank, secondary,
was granted Zhǎngshàn Láng;
the Jiānshì, eighth rank, secondary,
was granted Zhíshàn Láng).
Soon, all Bureaus and Treasuries were abolished,
and Sīshēng Sī was established.
Zīmù Suǒ was also changed to Sīmù Sī.
(Later it became Sīmù Jú).
In the thirtieth year, it was again changed to Guānglù Sì,
and the official system remained as before.
(The Shǎoqīng's rank was already fixed at fifth rank, principal).
During Jiànwén,
the ranks of Shǎoqīng and Sìchéng were raised.
(Shǎoqīng was raised to fourth rank,
Sìchéng was raised to fifth rank).
Sīpú Suǒ was added,
and Sīshēng Sī was changed to Zīshēng Suǒ,
(its rank was raised).
Chéngzǔ restored the old system.
In Zhèngtǒng sixth year, redundant officials in the four Bureaus were abolished.
(Previously,
Guānglù Qīng Nài Hēng, due to the complexity of supply matters,
requested an increase in officials for each Bureau.
At this time, a request was made to abolish them again.
Four Shǔzhèng,
five Shǔchéng,
and seven Jiānshì were abolished).
In Jiājìng seventh year, Sīmù Jú was abolished.
In Wànlì second year, one Yínkù Dàshǐ was added.
Tàipúsì (Court of the Imperial Stud).
One Qīng (Minister),
(Junior Third Rank),
two Shǎoqīng (Vice-Ministers),
(Principal Fourth Rank;
one additional person was added in the 11th year of Zhèngdé’s reign.)
Four Sìchéng (Secretaries),
(Principal Sixth Rank.)
Its subordinates:
Zhǔbùtīng (Bureau of the Chief Clerk),
one Zhǔbù (Chief Clerk),
(Junior Seventh Rank.)
Chángyíngkù (Ever-Full Granary),
one Dàshǐ (Director).
Under its jurisdiction:
various Mùjiān (Horse Pasture Agencies),
one Jiānzhèng (Chief Supervisor),
(Principal Ninth Rank),
one Jiānfù (Assistant Supervisor),
(Junior Ninth Rank),
one Lùshì (Registrar),
(later, the Jiānzhèng, Jiānfù, and Lùshì positions were all abolished.)
various Qún (Herds),
one Qúnzhǎng (Herd Leader),
(later abolished.)
The Qīng managed the regulations for horse husbandry,
reporting to the Bīngbù (Ministry of War).
One Shǎoqīng assisted in the affairs of the Court,
one supervised the horses in the military camps,
and one supervised the horses in the capital region.
The Sìchéng were responsible for managing the breeding and boarding of horses in the Jingwei (Capital Guards), Jīnnèi (Capital Region), and the six prefectures of Shāndōng and Hénán.
(Jǐnán, Yǎnzhōu, Dōngchāng, Kāifēng, Zhāngdé, Wèihuī.)
For all horses bred by the military and civilians,
stallions were distributed
according to the number of households and property.
Two tenths male,
eight tenths female,
constituted one herd.
(In the south, four mares and one stallion constituted a herd.)
Colts were collected annually,
known as "reserve horses,"
and their strength was standardized to supply the generals and soldiers.
If there were enough for the generals and soldiers,
the rest were boarded in the prefectures, departments, and counties within the capital region.
Their fatness, leanness, increase, and decrease
were registered by their coats and teeth, and they were inspected regularly.
Every three years, an Yùshǐ (Censor) would brand them,
selecting the strong and good, and culling the weak and inferior.
For grazing lands that had been reclaimed as fields,
their rent was collected annually.
In times of disaster or famine, these funds were used to assist in purchasing horses.
For compensation for losses,
horse money was levied and submitted to the Bīngbù.
The Zhǔbù handled the review of official documents.
The Dàshǐ managed the storage of horse money in the treasury.
Initially,
in the 4th year of Hóngwǔ’s reign, Qúnmùjiān (Herd Pasture Agencies) were established at the Dádáshīlǐying’s location.
Official offices were set up where water and grass were convenient,
dedicated to horse breeding.
In the 6th year, Qúnmùjiān was re-established in Chúzhōu,
and soon after renamed Tàipúsì,
with a rank of Junior Third Rank.
A Qīng, Shǎoqīng, and Sìchéng were appointed,
along with one Shǒulǐngguān Zhīshì (Chief Official Clerk) and one Zhǔbù.
In the 7th year, twenty-seven Mùjiān and Qún official posts were added,
subordinate to the Tàipúsì.
Soon after, the ranks of the Qúnmùjiān were fixed.
(Lìng (Prefect),
Principal Fifth Rank;
Céng (Assistant),
Principal Sixth Rank;
Zhènfǔ (Commander),
Junior Sixth Rank;
ten Qúntóu (Herd Supervisors) and one Lìmù (Clerical Scribe),
details omitted.)
In the 10th year, various Mùjiān such as Chúyáng and their affiliated Qún were further established.
The Mùjiān Lìng and Céng were renamed Jiānzhèng and Jiānfù.
(Jiānzhèng,
Junior Eighth Rank;
Jiānfù,
Principal Ninth Rank;
Yùliáng,
Junior Ninth Rank.
Later, Jiānzhèng was re-designated as Principal Ninth Rank.)
In the 22nd year, twelve Mùjiān, including Chúyáng, were established,
each with one Jiānzhèng,
two Jiānfù,
and one Lùshì.
One hundred twenty-seven Qún, including Lái'ān,
each with one Qúnzhǎng.
(Initially, two Qúnfù (Assistant Herd Leaders) were set up,
but these were abolished at this time.)
In the 23rd year, two additional Mùjiān, Jiāngdōng and Dāngtú, and their affiliated Qún were established.
Fifty-four Qún, including Wūyī, were abolished,
and seven Qún, including Yǒng'ān, were re-established,
fixing the number of Mùjiān at fourteen,
(Chúyáng, Dàxīng, Xiāngquán, Yízhēn, Dìngyuǎn, Tiāncháng, Chánghuái, Jiāngdū, Jùróng, Lìyáng, Jiāngdōng, Lìshuǐ, Dāngtú, Shūchéng.)
and Qún at ninety-seven.
(Dàshèngguān, Bǎizi, Liúxīng, Bǎoníng, Cǎotáng, five Qún,
subordinate to Chúyáng Jiān.
Yǒng'ān, Rúgāo, Yánhǎi, Bǎoquán, Cháoyáng, Yǒngchāng, Āndìng, seven Qún,
subordinate to Dàxīng Jiān.
Dàqián, Tóngchéng, Yǒngfēng, Lóngshèng, Lóngshān, Yǒngníng, Xīn'ān, Qìng'ān, Xiāng'ān, nine Qún,
subordinate to Xiāngquán Jiān.
Huáyáng, Shòuníng, Guǎnglíng, Shànyìng, four Qún,
subordinate to Yízhēn Jiān.
Lóngjiāng, Lóng'ān, Wànshèng, Lóngquán, four Qún,
subordinate to Dìngyuǎn Jiān.
Tiāncháng, Huáidé, Zhāoxìn, Déshèng, Wǔ'ān, five Qún,
subordinate to Tiāncháng Jiān.
Cháng'ān, Báishí, Jīngshān, Nánshān, Tuánshān, Cǎopíng, six Qún,
subordinate to Chánghuái Jiān.
Wànníng, Guǎngshēng, Wànjì, Shùndé, Dàxīng, Jìníng, Chóngdé, seven Qún,
subordinate to Jiāngdū Jiān.
Jùróng, Yìfēng, Réngxìn, Fúzǔ, Tōngdé, Chéngxiān, Shàngróng, Zhèngrén, Liàntáng, Shòu'ān, ten Qún,
subordinate to Jùróng Jiān.
Jǔfú, Cóngshān, Míngyì, Yǒngdìng, Fúxián, Chónglái, Yǒngchéng, Yǒngtài, Fèng'ān, nine Qún,
subordinate to Lìyáng Jiān.
Kāiníng, Quánshuǐ, Wéizhèng, Qīnghuà, Shénquán, Xīntíng, Chángtài, Guāngzé, eight Qún,
subordinate to Jiāngdōng Jiān.
Yífèng, Xiāntán, Lìxìn, Guīzhèng, Fēngqìng, Ānxīng, Yóushān, Yǒngníng, eight Qún,
subordinate to Lìshuǐ Jiān.
Shíchéng, Yǒngbǎo, Huàqià, Gūshú, Fánchāng, Duōfú, Dānyáng, Dézhèng, eight Qún,
subordinate to Dāngtú Jiān.
Zǎolín, Hǎitíng, Fúlóng, Lónghé, Huìlóng, Jiǔlóng, Wànlóng, seven Qún,
subordinate to Shūchéng Jiān.)
In the 28th year, all Qúnmùjiān were abolished,
and their horses were placed under the care of local officials.
In the 30th year, an Xíngtàipúsì (Traveling Court of the Imperial Stud) was established in Běipíng,
with the same rank as the Tàipúsì.
During the Jiànwén reign,
the rank of Sìchéng was promoted,
(formerly Sixth Rank,
promoted to Fifth Rank.)
Their chief official titles were also changed,
a Lùshì was added,
as well as the Diǎn and Diǎnmù two bureaus,
eighteen Qún including Sùxuán,
eight Mùjiān including Chúyáng,
and ninety-two Qún including Lóngshān.
Chéngzǔ restored the old system.
In the 1st year of Yǒnglè’s reign, the Běipíng Xíngtàipúsì was renamed Běijīng Xíngtàipúsì.
In the 18th year, the capital was established in Běijīng,
and thus the Xíngtàipúsì became the Tàipúsì.
In the 1st year of Hóngxī’s reign, it was again called Běijīng Xíngtàipúsì.
In the 6th year of Zhèngtǒng’s reign, it was fixed as Tàipúsì.
The old one in Chúzhōu
was changed to Nánjīng Tàipúsì.
(Sìchéng,
initially four were appointed.
During the Zhèngtǒng period,
eight more were added,
totaling twelve.
One was in charge of the Jingwei,
one in charge of the two prefectures of Shùndé and Guǎngpíng,
one in charge of the three prefectures of Kāifēng, Wèihuī, and Zhāngdé,
and nine were divided to manage the breeding and boarding of horses in the nine prefectures of Shùntiān, Bǎodìng, Zhēndìng, Héjiān, Yǒngpíng, Dàmíng, Jǐnán, Yǎnzhōu, and Dōngchāng.
In the 6th year of Hóngzhì’s reign, four were abolished.
In the 9th year of Zhèngdé’s reign, one more was added,
specifically to manage boarding matters.
In the 8th year of Jiājìng’s reign, three more were abolished,
leaving a total of six to manage,
rotating every three years,
and the boarding matters were handled concurrently by the prefectures, departments, and counties.
In the 3rd year of Lóngqìng’s reign, three more were abolished,
leaving only three.
One was appointed to supervise the treasury and assist in the capital and border regions,
and two were divided to manage horse administration on the eastern and western routes.)
Hónglúsì (Court of State Ceremonial).
One Qīng (Minister),
(Principal Fourth Rank),
one Zuǒshǎoqīng (Left Vice-Minister) and one Yòushǎoqīng (Right Vice-Minister),
(Junior Fifth Rank),
one Zuǒsìchéng (Left Secretary) and one Yòusìchéng (Right Secretary),
(Junior Sixth Rank.)
Its subordinates:
Zhǔbùtīng (Bureau of the Chief Clerk),
one Zhǔbù (Chief Clerk),
(Junior Eighth Rank.)
Sīyí (Ceremonial Affairs) and Sībīn (Guest Reception) two bureaus,
each bureau with one Shǔchéng (Bureau Secretary),
(Principal Ninth Rank),
four Míngzàn (Proclaimers of Ceremony),
(Junior Ninth Rank;
later five more were added.)
fifty Xùbān (Ceremonial Ushers),
(Junior Ninth Rank.
In the 36th year of Jiājìng’s reign, eight were abolished.
In the 11th year of Wànlì’s reign, six were re-established.)
The Hónglú Sì 鴻臚寺 managed affairs concerning court assemblies, guests, and auspicious and inauspicious rituals.
For all major national ceremonies, suburban sacrifices, ancestral temple rites, other sacrifices, court assemblies, banquets, imperial lectures (jīngyán 經筵), enfeoffments,
presentation of the calendar, presentation of spring, imperial edicts, and reports of victories, each performed its specific duty.
When external officials came for imperial audiences,
or various foreign states offered tribute,
as well as when officials and envoys reported on their missions or expressed gratitude,
whether for an audience or to make a departure,
the Hónglú Sì 鴻臚寺 officials introduced them.

On New Year's Day (zhèngdàn 正旦), the Lantern Festival (shàngyuán 上元), the Dragon Boat Festival (chóngwǔ 重午), the Double Ninth Festival (chóngjiǔ 重九), and the Winter Solstice (chángzhì 長至), when leave and banquets were granted,
and in the fourth month when character-fans (zìshàn 字扇) and longevity threads (shòulǚ 壽縷) were granted,
and in the eleventh month when warm ear coverings (nuǎněr 煖耳) were granted,
and after participating in sacrifices,
when sacrificial meat (zuò 胙) was distributed and gifts bestowed,
all officials were led to perform the rites.
The Sīyí 司儀 oversaw the arrangements and introductions.
When external officials arrived for an audience,
they first practiced the ceremonies at the temple.
The Sībīn 司賓 managed envoys from foreign states offering tribute,
distinguishing their ranks and instructing them on the etiquette of bowing and kneeling.
The Míngzàn 鳴贊 oversaw the chanting of ceremonial procedures.

All chamber announcers (nèizàn 內贊), general announcers (tōngzàn 通贊), counter announcers (duìzàn 對贊), reception announcers (jiēzàn 接贊), and transmitting announcers (chuánzàn 傳贊) were under their charge.
The Xùbān 序班 managed the attendance roster, lineup order, correction of ceremonies, and transmission of announcements.
Initially,
in the first year of Wú 吳 (1367), the Shìyí Sī 侍儀司 was established,
with a rank of junior fifth grade.
In the fourth year of Hóngwǔ 洪武 (1371), the positions of Shìyí Shǐ 侍儀使
(junior seventh grade),
Yǐnjìn Shǐ 引進使
(principal eighth grade),
Fèngbān Dūzhī 奉班都知
(principal ninth grade),
Tōngzàn 通贊, and Tōngshì Shèrén 通事舍人
(junior ninth grade) were established,
all being officials of the seventh grade and below.
In the ninth year (1376), it was renamed the Diàntíng Yílǐ Sī 殿庭儀禮司,
with one Shǐ 使
(principal seventh grade),
three Fù 副
(principal eighth grade),
one Chéngfèng 承奉
(junior eighth grade),
two Míngzàn 鳴贊
(principal ninth grade),
sixteen Xùbān 序班
(junior ninth grade),
one Jiǔguān Tōngshì Shǐ 九關通事使
(principal eighth grade),
and six Fù 副
(junior eighth grade).
In the thirteenth year (1380), the Shǐ 使 was changed to Sīzhèng 司正,
with one Zuǒ Sīfù 左司副 and one Yòu Sīfù 右司副 each,
the Xùbān 序班 were increased to forty-four,
the Chéngfèng 承奉 was abolished,
and four Sīyí 司儀 were added.
In the twenty-second year (1389), four Zuǒ Sīchéng 左司丞 and Yòu Sīchéng 右司丞 were added
(principal ninth grade).
In the thirtieth year (1397), it was finally renamed the Hónglú Sì 鴻臚寺,
its rank was elevated to principal fourth grade,
and sixty-two officials were established.
(The number and rank of officials from Qīng 卿 downwards were as previously listed.)
Moreover, foreign interpreters (wàiyí tōngshì 外夷通事) were established and subordinated to it.
During the Jiànwén 建文 reign (1399-1402),
the ranks of Shàocéng 少卿 and below were elevated.
(The Shàocéng 少卿 was elevated to principal fifth grade,
and the Sìchéng 寺丞 to principal sixth grade.
Also, the titles of its leading officials were changed,
and the Míngzàn 鳴贊 and Xùbān 序bān were all elevated in rank.)
The Sīyí 司儀 and Sībīn 司賓 bureaus were abolished,
and the Xíngrén 行人 were subordinated to the Hónglú Sì 鴻臚寺.
In the early years of Chéngzǔ 成祖's reign (early 15th century),
all old systems were restored.
The Shàngbǎo Sī 尚寶司.
One Qīng 卿
(principal fifth grade),
one Shàocéng 少卿
(junior fifth grade),
and three Sīchéng 司丞
(principal sixth grade).
(In the first year of Wú 吳 (1367), only one was established;
later two were added.)
It was in charge of imperial seals, tallies, and stamps,
and distinguished their proper use.
There were twenty-four seals.
Seventeen were old seals;
seven were newly made in the eighteenth year of Jiājìng 嘉靖 (1539).
The
"Huángdì Fèngtiān zhī Bǎo" 皇帝奉天之寶 (Seal of the Emperor who Reveres Heaven)
was a seal transmitted from the Táng 唐 and Sòng 宋 dynasties,
used for sacrifices to Heaven and Earth.
For imperial edicts and amnesties,
the
"Huángdì zhī Bǎo" 皇帝之寶 (Seal of the Emperor) was used;
for enfeoffments and granting rewards,
the
"Huángdì Xíngbǎo" 皇帝行寶 (Emperor's Traveling Seal) was used;
for issuing edicts to imperial princes and high officials, and for deploying troops,
the
"Huángdì Xìnbǎo" 皇帝信寶 (Emperor's Credential Seal) was used;
for bestowing honorific titles,
the
"Huángdì Zūnqīn zhī Bǎo" 皇帝尊親之寶 (Seal of the Emperor for Honoring Kin) was used;
for admonishing imperial princes,
the
"Huángdì Qīnqīn zhī Bǎo" 皇帝親親之寶 (Seal of the Emperor for Loving Kin) was used.
The
"Tiānzǐ zhī Bǎo" 天子之寶 (Seal of the Son of Heaven)
was for sacrifices to mountains, rivers, ghosts, and spirits;
the "Tiānzǐ Xíngbǎo" 天子行寶 (Son of Heaven's Traveling Seal)
was for enfeoffing foreign countries and granting rewards;
the "Tiānzǐ Xìnbǎo" 天子信寶 (Son of Heaven's Credential Seal)
was for summoning foreign tributaries and conscripting troops.
For imperial edicts, the
"Zhìgào zhī Bǎo" 制誥之寶 (Seal for Imperial Edicts) was used;
for imperial commands (chì 敕), the
"Chìmìng zhī Bǎo" 敕命之寶 (Seal for Imperial Commands) was used.
To reward officials and meritorious subjects,
the
"Guǎngyùn zhī Bǎo" 廣運之寶 (Seal of Vast Fortune) was used;
for imperial commands and instructions to officials attending court,
the
"Jìngtiān Qínmín zhī Bǎo" 敬天勤民之寶 (Seal for Reverence for Heaven and Diligence for the People) was used.
As for the
"Yùqián zhī Bǎo" 御前之寶 (Seal for Imperial Presence),
"Biǎozhāng Jīngshǐ zhī Bǎo" 表章經史之寶 (Seal for Commending Classics and Histories),
and "Qīnwén zhī Bǎo" 欽文之寶 (Seal for Respecting Culture),
these were used for documents such as literary works and historical records.
Shìzōng 世宗 (Jiajing Emperor) added seven seals:
the
"Fèngtiān Chéngyùn Dàmíng Tiānzǐ Bǎo" 奉天承運大明天子寶 (Seal of the Son of Heaven of Great Míng, who Receives Mandate by Reverence for Heaven),
the
"Dàmíng Shòumìng zhī Bǎo" 大明受命之寶 (Seal of Great Míng, who Received the Mandate),
the
"Xúnyòu Tiānxià zhī Bǎo" 巡狩天下之寶 (Seal for Imperial Tours of the Realm),
the
"Chuíxùn zhī Bǎo" 垂訓之寶 (Seal for Imparting Instructions),
the
"Mìngdé zhī Bǎo" 命德之寶 (Seal for Enjoining Virtue),
the
"Tǎozuì Ānmín zhī Bǎo" 討罪安民之寶 (Seal for Punishing Crimes and Bringing Peace to the People),
and the
"Chìzhèng Wànmín zhī Bǎo" 敕正萬民之寶 (Seal for Commanding and Rectifying the Myriad People).
