There was one seal for the Crown Prince,
named
"Huángtàizǐ zhī Bǎo" 皇太子之寶 (Seal of the Imperial Crown Prince).
The use of any seal
required an imperial petition and awaited issuance.
During every grand court assembly,
two officials from this office
would lead the imperial carriage with the seals.
After the emperor ascended the throne,
each placed a seal on the table,
standing in the hall in waiting.
When the ceremony was over,
they carried the seals out in order,
reaching the Zhōngjí Diàn 中極殿,
where they placed them on a table and exited.
When the imperial carriage left for an outing,
they followed, holding the seals.
At the end of the year,
the Qīntiān Jiān 欽天監 was informed,
and an auspicious day was chosen to immerse aromatic substances in water,
and the seals were washed at the Huángjí Mén 皇極門.
A register was kept detailing the number of times seals were used in a year.
All requests for seals, use of seals, carrying of seals, accompanying seals, washing of seals, and submission of seals
were conducted in conjunction with the eunuchs of the Shàngbǎo Jiān 尚寶監.
There were five types of gold plaques [jīnpái]
issued to imperial relatives, meritorious nobles, imperial guards’ retinue, those on duty, those on imperial inspection tours, and those on night watch: one was called Rén (仁),
its shape a dragon;
Dukes [gōng], Marquises [hóu], Earls [bó], and Imperial Sons-in-law [fùmǎ dūwèi] wore it.
One was called Yì (義),
its shape a tiger;
meritorious guards [xūnwèi] and commanders [zhǐhuī] wore it.
One was called Lǐ (禮),
its shape a qílín [qílín];
chiliarchs [qiānhù] wore it.
One was called Zhì (智),
its shape a lion;
centurions [bǎihù] wore it.
One was called Xìn (信),
its shape auspicious clouds;
generals [jiāngjūn] wore it.
There were four types of half-character copper tallies [bànzì tóngfú]
issued to patrol officers of the city temples and guards [xúnchéng sìwèi guān]: one was called Chéng (承),
one Dōng (東),
one Xī (西),
and one Běi (北).
The patroller held the left half,
the guard held the right half;
they matched them to verify.
There were six types of command tokens [lìngpái]: one was called Shēn (申),
issued to those on night警 duty in the Jīnwú (金吾) guards;
one Mù (木),
one Jīn (金),
one Tǔ (土),
one Huǒ (火),
and one Shuǐ (水),
issued to those on night警 duty in the five cities [wǔchéng].
There was one type of copper plaque [tóngpái]
for inspecting sentry soldiers,
called Yǒng (勇).
There were five types of ivory plaques [yápái]
for checking court attendance: Dukes [gōng], Marquises [hóu], and Earls [bó] used Xūn (勳);
Imperial Sons-in-law [fùmǎ dūwèi] used Qīn (親);
civil officials [wénguān] used Wén (文);
military officials [wǔguān] used Wǔ (武);
and the Bureau of Music [Jiàofāng Sī] used Yuè (樂).
In the Jiājìng (嘉靖) reign,
the comprehensive compilation was called 'official character [guānzì] [a certain] number';
those attending court wore them for entry and exit,
otherwise the gatekeepers would stop them.
Those who privately lent them [to others]
were punished according to the law.
If there was a reason,
they were returned to the Imperial Household Department [nèifǔ].
There were three types of sacrificial plaques [jìpái]: accompanying sacrifice officials [péisì guān] used Péi (陪);
service officials [gòngshì guān] used Gòng (供);
and attendants [zhíshì rén] used Zhí (執).
There were two types of double-fish copper plaques [shuāngyú tóngpái]: one was called Yán (嚴),
to enforce order among the Jǐnyī (錦衣) guards and school officers [xiàowèi] on duty;
one was called Shàn (善),
to distinguish the clerks and servants [xūyì] of the Court of Imperial Entertainments [Guānglù Sì] who performed services.
There were five types of tally tokens [fúyàn]: one was called Mǎ (馬),
one Shuǐ (水),
one Dá (達),
one Tōng (通),
and one Xìn (信).
(The system for tally tokens [fúyàn] was:
the upper part was woven with images of boats and horses.
For starting a horse journey,
the character "Mǎ"
was used.
For two horses,
the character "Dá"
was used.
For a single horse,
the character "Tōng"
was used.
For starting a boat journey,
the character "Shuǐ"
was used.
For a combined boat journey,
the character "Xìn"
was used.)

It was issued to imperial princes [qīnwáng] when they went to their enfeoffed territories [fān], and to civil and military officials [wénwǔ] dispatched to govern and pacify, and to envoys [xíngrén] sent on missions.
Censors [yùshǐ] on inspection tours were given seals;
when the task was completed,
all were verified and returned.
The inspection of entry and exit regulations,
and the management of their numbers,
made their responsibilities extremely close,
and their duties extremely important.
In the early years of Tàizǔ (太祖),
the Supervisor of Imperial Tallies and Seals [Fúxǐ Láng] was established,
with a rank of principal seventh grade.
In the first year of Wú (吳), it was changed to Minister of the Court of Imperial Accoutrements [Shàngbǎo Sī Qīng],
with a rank of principal fifth grade,
led by attendant scholarly officials [shìcóng rúchén] and meritorious guards [xūnwèi].

(For example, Gěng Xuān [Gěng Xuān] as Cavalier Attendant [Sǎnqí Shèrén], Huáng Guān [Huáng Guān] as Grand Councilor [Shìzhōng], and Yáng Róng [Yáng Róng] as Imperial Secretary [Shùzǐ] served as Ministers.)
Without talent, one could not be transferred [to this position].
Only sons and younger brothers of meritorious and guard ministers [xūnwèi dàchén] who received an imperial decree could be appointed Assistant Minister [chéng].
Later, many were appointed through imperial favor and sinecures,
without a fixed number of members.
The Six Offices of Scrutiny [Liù Kē] were: Personnel [Lì], Revenue [Hù], Rites [Lǐ], War [Bīng], Justice [Xíng], and Works [Gōng].
Each had one Chief Supervising Secretary [dū gěishìzhōng]
(principal seventh grade),
and one Left and Right Supervising Secretary [zuǒ, yòu gěishìzhōng] each
(subordinate seventh grade).
Supervising Secretaries [gěishìzhōng]:
four in the Personnel Office [Lì Kē],
eight in the Revenue Office [Hù Kē],
six in the Rites Office [Lǐ Kē],
ten in the War Office [Bīng Kē],
eight in the Justice Office [Xíng Kē],
and four in the Works Office [Gōng Kē]
(all subordinate seventh grade).
Later, the number of members increased or decreased inconsistently.
In the ninth year of Wànlì (萬曆), five from the War Office [Bīng Kē],
four each from the Revenue [Hù Kē] and Justice Offices [Xíng Kē], and two from the Rites Office [Lǐ Kē] were dismissed.
In the eleventh year, two each were re-established for the Revenue [Hù Kē], War [Bīng Kē], and Justice Offices [Xíng Kē],
and one for the Rites Office [Lǐ Kē].)
The Six Offices of Scrutiny [Liù Kē]
were in charge of attendance, remonstrance, correcting oversights, picking up omissions, and scrutinizing the affairs of the Six Boards [Liù Bù] and various bureaus.
For all imperial edicts and decrees that were promulgated,
major matters required re-reporting to the throne,
while minor matters were signed and issued;
if there was any error,
they would be sealed, returned, and reported [to the throne].
All memorials submitted by officials inside and outside the court,
after being classified and copied,
were scrutinized, signed, and forwarded to the appropriate Board,
and any errors were criticized and corrected.
The Personnel Office [Lì Kē]:
whenever the Ministry of Personnel [Lì Bù] conducted selections,
the Chief Supervising Secretary [zhǎng kē] (i.e., the Chief Supervising Secretary [dū gěishìzhōng],
so named because he held the seal of the current office [běnkē yìn];
the same applied to all Six Offices of Scrutiny [Liù Kē])
would collectively go before the emperor to request instructions.
All external officials receiving official documents [wénpíng]
first went to the Office to have them marked.
After internal and external officials were reviewed and made their self-declarations,
they would jointly present a memorial with the respective Offices.
They would pick up omissions and censure those who were derelict in their duties.
The Revenue Office [Hù Kē]:
supervised the annual income of gold and grain of the Court of Imperial Entertainments [Guānglù Sì],
and the money, paper currency, and miscellaneous items in the ten treasuries such as treasury 'Jiǎ' (甲).
Together with other Offices, they jointly supervised these;
this responsibility rotated every three months.
They would censure those within or outside the court who petitioned for land, or secretly occupied or encroached upon it.
The Rites Office [Lǐ Kē]:
supervised and revised the ceremonial regulations of the Ministry of Rites [Lǐ Bù].
Whenever a high-ranking official had been impeached, dismissed, or had their reputation tarnished,
this was recorded to verify the regulations for posthumous grants and titles.
The War Office [Bīng Kē]:
for all military officials' imperial decrees [tiēhuáng gàochì],
one person from this Office supervised.
The system for recommending selection and signing official documents [huàpíng]
was the same as the Personnel Office [Lì Kē].
The Justice Office [Xíng Kē]:
in the latter half of the second month of each year,
they would present the number of northern and southern prisoners from the previous year.
At the end of the year, they would collectively present the number of prisoners whose cases were still pending from the past year.
Every ten days, they would report the actual number of prisoners.
All these were based on reports transferred from the judicial authorities and presented to the emperor.
The Works Office [Gōng Kē]:
inspected and tested the Imperial Armory [Jūngì Jú],
and together with the Censors [yùshǐ], inspected the Ministry of Works Treasury [Jiéshèn Kù].
They also jointly scrutinized the Bureau of Coinage [Bǎoyuán Jú] with other Offices.
Regarding any deficiencies or errors in the emperor's virtue,
the gains and losses in court administration,
and the virtues and vices of the hundred officials,
each Office could submit individual memorials [dānshū zhuāndá],
or jointly sign public memorials [gōngshū liánshǔ zòuwén] to report them to the emperor.
(Although they were subordinate to the Six Offices of Scrutiny [Liù Kē],
for matters of great importance,
all Offices could report them jointly.
However, if a matter belonged to a particular Office,
that Office would be listed first.)
For all daily court audiences,
one official from the Six Offices rotates to stand on the left and right sides of the palace hall,
holding a brush to record imperial decrees.
For all memorials and petitions,
they are attached to the respective office's register daily,
and sent to the Nèi Gé every five days
for compilation.
Regarding matters processed by various offices according to imperial decrees,
they are canceled out every five days
to check for delays.
Imperial decrees conveyed by eunuchs must be reported back to the emperor,
and only after receiving further approval can they be implemented.
When acting as examining officials for the xiāngshì,
co-examining officials for the huìshì,
or卷-receiving officials for the diànshì.
When enfeoffing imperial relatives or foreign tributary states, or issuing pronouncements to foreign nations,
they serve as principal or deputy envoys.
For court attendance and door registers,
the Six Offices take turns managing them.
At the Dēngwén Gǔlóu,
one official is present daily,
all supervised by Jǐnyīwèi officers.
(In Hongwǔ first year, one Censor was assigned to supervise the Dēngwén Gǔ,
later the Six Offices and the Jǐnyīwèi took turns on duty.)
Upon receiving a petition,
they would draft a memorial and submit it sealed.
When prisoners were to be executed,
if someone submitted a petition to appeal an injustice,
the execution would be halted pending an imperial decree.
In all major court deliberations,
selection of high officials by court recommendation,
and major judicial interrogations by court trial,
the six chief officials of the offices were all involved.
In the early Míng dynasty,
Gěishìzhōng were generally established,
holding the principal fifth rank.
Later, their rank was changed several times
(the same as the Qǐjūzhù).
In Hongwǔ sixth year, twelve Gěishìzhōng were established,
holding the principal seventh rank.
They were initially divided into Six Offices,
with two officials per office.
One seal for the Gěishìzhōng was cast,
and the eldest official was chosen to manage it.
In the ninth year, the number of Gěishìzhōng was set at ten.
In the tenth year, they were subordinated to the Chéngchì Jiān.
In the twelfth year, they were re-subordinated to the Tōngzhèng Sī.
In the thirteenth year, the Jiàn Yuàn was established,
with one Zuǒ Sījìan and one Yòu Sījìan
(principal seventh rank),
and two Zuǒ Zhèngyán and two Yòu Zhèngyán
(subordinate seventh rank).
In the fifteenth year, Jiànyì Dàfū was also established
(with Bīngbù Shàngshū Táng Duó appointed to the position).
Soon all were abolished.
In the twenty-second year, Gěishìzhōng were renamed Yuánshì,
increasing to eighty-one individuals.
(Initially,
Wèi Mǐn, Zhuō Jìng, and eighty-one others served as Gěishìzhōng.
The emperor, finding this number coincidentally matched the ancient number of yuánshì,
changed their title to Yuánshì.
By this time,
he again considered the Six Offices to be the fundamental source of affairs,
and renamed them Yuánshì.)
Not long after,
they reverted to Gěishìzhōng.
In the twenty-fourth year, the staff of the offices were redefined:
one Dū Gěishìzhōng per office,
principal eighth rank;
two Zuǒ Gěishìzhōng and Yòu Gěishìzhōng,
subordinate eighth rank;
and a total of forty Gěishìzhōng,
principal ninth rank.
(The number of officials assigned to each office
was as previously listed.)
During the Jiànwén reign,
the Dū Gěishìzhōng was changed
to principal seventh rank,
and Gěishìzhōng
to subordinate seventh rank,
and the Zuǒ Gěishìzhōng and Yòu Gěishìzhōng were abolished.
Shíyí and Bǔquē were added.
At the beginning of the Chéngzǔ reign,
Shíyí and Bǔquē were abolished,
and Zuǒ Gěishìzhōng and Yòu Gěishìzhōng were re-established,
also holding the subordinate seventh rank.
Soon the Six Offices were reformed,
and their offices were moved to the duty rooms outside the Wǔ Mén to conduct affairs.
(The yámen of the Six Offices were formerly located west of the Shàngbǎo Sī inside the Brick Gate.
During the Yǒnglè reign, they were destroyed by fire,
and moved to the east and west outside the Wǔ Mén,
with one office on night duty each night.)
In Xuāndé eighth year, a Hùkē Gěishìzhōng was added,
specifically to manage the huángcè.
Zhōngshū Kē.
Twenty Zhōngshū Shèrén
(subordinate seventh rank).
Zhōngshū Shèrén on duty in the east rooms of Wénhuá Diàn,
Zhōngshū Shèrén on duty in the west rooms of Wǔyīng Diàn,
Zhōngshū Shèrén in the Nèi Gé Gàochì Fáng,
Zhōngshū Shèrén in the Zhìchì Fáng,
(all subordinate seventh rank,
without fixed numbers.)
The Zhōngshū Kē Shèrén were in charge of writing gàochì, zhìzhào, silver certificates, iron tallies, and other documents.
All drafts were requested from the Hànlín,
and seals from the imperial treasury.
The left halves of tallies and verification registers
were kept in the Gǔjīn Tōngjí Kù.
For gàochì
(gàomìng for dukes, marquises, earls, and officials of the first to fifth ranks; chìmìng for officials of the sixth to ninth ranks),
and verification registers,
initially the twenty-eight constellations were used,
later the Jíjiù Zhāng characters were used as designations.
The designations for gàochì
were Rén, Yì, Lǐ, Zhì,
used for dukes, marquises, earls, tributary kings, and officials of the first and second ranks;
the twelve earthly branches,
Wén, Xíng, Zhōng, Xìn,
used for civil officials of the third rank and below;
and the Qiānzìwén characters,
used for military officials and supplementary gàochì.
All were limited to a thousand designations,
after which they would restart.
Imperial princes' households and imperial sons-in-law were not assigned numbers.
Tǔguān were categorized by civil and military divisions.
For all grand court assemblies,
they would attend in their assigned ranks.
During festive court celebrations in the Eastern Palace,
they would escort the imperial carriage and attend in their ranks at the Wénhuá Diàn.
When enfeoffing imperial relatives,
they served as deputy envoys.
(For xiāngshì, huìshì, and diànshì,
they were occasionally dispatched
and assigned duties similar to those of office officials.)
During grand sacrifices at the Southern Suburb,
they would accompany the imperial carriage and perform their duties.
There were no principal or deputy members;
the seal was managed by the longest-serving member.
Wénhuá Diàn Shèrén
were responsible for writing books according to imperial decrees.
Wǔyīng Diàn Shèrén
were responsible for engraving imperial seals, books, maps, and albums according to imperial decrees.
Nèi Gé Gàochì Fáng Shèrén
were in charge of writing civil officials' gàochì,
translating imperial letters,
and foreign documents and petitions,
and the Bīngbù's records of merit and verification register drafts.
Zhìchì Fáng Shèrén

were in charge of writing zhìchì, imperial edicts, gàomìng, imperial certificates and memorials, imperial seals, jade genealogies, lecture notes, stele inscriptions, memorials, and petitions, and all confidential documents,
as well as the drafts of imperial tallies for various princely households.
In Hongwǔ seventh year, ten Zhíshěng Shèrén were initially established,
holding the subordinate eighth rank,
subordinated to the Zhōngshū Shěng.
In the ninth year, they became Zhōngshū Shèrén,
re-ranked to principal seventh rank,
and soon after changed to subordinate seventh rank.
In the tenth year,
they, along with the Gěishìzhōng, were all subordinated to the Chéngchì Jiān.
During the Jiànwén reign,
Zhōngshū Shèrén were abolished,
and renamed Shìshū,
promoted to principal seventh rank,
entered the Wénhàn Guǎn,
and subordinated to the Hànlín Yuàn.
Chéngzǔ restored the old system.
Soon, the Zhōngshū Kē office was set up outside the Wǔ Mén,
and twenty Zhōngshū Shèrén were permanently established.
(Those granted positions through favor or hereditary privilege who received salaries
were not included in the fixed quota.)
During the Xuāndé reign,
the Nèi Gé established the Gàochì Fáng and Zhìchì Fáng,
both staffed with Zhōngshū Shèrén.
In Jiājìng twentieth year, department directors (zhǔshì) from various ministries
and judicial review officials (píngshì) from Dàlǐ Sì were selected
to serve in the Gàochì Fáng and Zhìchì Fáng with their original titles.
In the forty-fourth year,
when there were vacancies in both rooms,
the Lìbù was ordered to examine and select candidates to become Zhōngshū Shèrén.
In Lóngqìng first year, officials serving in the two rooms were not allowed to be promoted to the rank of Jiǔqīng.
According to historical records, during the
Hóngwǔ reign, the Chéngchì Jiān (承敕監) was established. (Established in the ninth year of Hóngwǔ
It appointed one Lìng (令),
of Zheng liù pǐn (正六品) rank,
and two Chéng (丞),
of Cóng liù pǐn (從六品) rank.
Later, the Lìng was changed to Zheng qī pǐn (正七品),
and the Chéng to Zheng bā pǐn (正八品).
In the tenth year
with two appointees,
of Cóng qī pǐn (從七品) rank.
The Gěishì Zhōng (給事中) and Zhōngshū Shèrén (中書舍人) were all subordinate to it.
It was later abolished.) The Sīwén Jiān (司文監)
was established. (Established in the ninth year of Hóngwǔ
It appointed one Lìng,
of Zheng liù pǐn rank,
and two Chéng,
of Cóng liù pǐn rank.
Later, the Lìng was changed to Zheng qī pǐn,
and the Chéng to Zheng bā pǐn.
It was abolished in the tenth year
was established. (Established in the eighth year of Hóngwǔ
It appointed a Lìng and a Chéng.
In the ninth year
of Zheng liù pǐn rank,
and two Chéng,
of Cóng liù pǐn rank.
Later, the Lìng was changed to Zheng qī pǐn,
and the Chéng to Zheng bā pǐn.
It was abolished in the eighteenth year
These jointly managed the affairs of issuing imperial edicts and proclamations.
In the early Yǒnglè (永樂) reign,
the Nèigé Xuéshì (內閣學士) were ordered to preside over state affairs,
and all imperial edicts, proclamations, and decrees were assigned to them.
The copying and official transcription were handled by the Zhōngshū Shèrén who entered the office to perform these duties,
and would leave once the work was complete.
In the early Xuāndé (宣德) reign,
skilled calligraphers were first selected to work in a small room to the west of the cabinet,
which was called the Xī Zhìchì Fáng (西制敕房, Western Edict and Proclamation Room).
Meanwhile, the Xuéshì responsible for edicts and proclamations resided to the east of the cabinet,
drafted manuscripts, and handed them to the Zhōngshū for transcription and submission,
this was called the Dōng Gàochì Fáng (東誥敕房, Eastern Edict and Proclamation Room).
(This refers to the handling of official duties.
As for the title of Zhī Zhìgào (知制誥),
only Dàxuéshì (大學士) and other Xuéshì could hold it.)
After the Zhèngtǒng (正統) reign,
the Xuéshì were unable to oversee the edicts and proclamations,
so the Nèigé entirely entrusted these duties to officials such as the Zhōngshū, Xùbān (序班), and Yìzì (譯字).
Consequently, the Nèigé also had a Dōng Gàochì Fáng.
(This began because Liú Xuàn (劉鉉) did not eat with the Grand Secretaries.)
In the late Jiājìng (嘉靖) reign,
the Hànlín Shǐguān (翰林史官) were again tasked with external decrees,
while edicts for military officials continued to be handled by their subordinates.
However, imperial edicts, amnesties, revocations, and similar matters
had to go through the Gécén (閣臣),
and the Hànlín officials were not permitted to participate.
Those who were stationed at the Wénhuá (文華) and Wǔyīng (武英) Halls to handle imperial writings
were initially court eunuchs.
Later, the Zhōngshū were assigned to these posts in rotation,
and eventually, skilled calligraphers were exclusively appointed.
Broadly speaking, there were two paths for Shèrén.
Those selected by the Ministry through the Jìnshì (進士) examination
could be promoted to positions in the six ministries and censorate.
For Shèrén stationed in the two halls and two rooms,
it was not necessary to be selected by the Ministry;
anyone skilled in calligraphy from among Jiǎkē (甲科) graduates, Jiānshēng (監生), scholarly literati, or commoners
could serve in these positions.
Those who did not pass the imperial examinations
were initially appointed as Xùbān,
and then tested to become Zhōngshū Shèrén.
They could not be promoted to positions in the six ministries and censorate.
Even if they later received a higher title among the Jiǔliè (九列),
they still performed their duties while retaining their original title.
(Those from a Kǎishū (楷書) background
were sometimes granted the title of Tàicháng Qīng (太常卿).
Shěn Dù (沈度), Shěn Càn (沈粲), Pān Chén (潘辰), and others were even promoted to Hànlín Xuéshì and Lǐbù Shàngshū (禮部尚書).)
In the early Hóngwǔ reign,
there was also one Chéngtiānmén Dàizhào (承天門待詔),
four Géménshǐ (閤門使),
and ten Guānchásǐ (觀察使).
These were all later abolished.
The Xíngrén Sī (行人司).
One Sīzhèng (司正),
(Zheng qī pǐn rank),
one Zuǒ Sīfù (左司副) and one Yòu Sīfù (右司副) each,
(Cóng qī pǐn rank),
and thirty-seven Xíngrén (行人),
(Zheng bā pǐn rank.)
Their duties were solely to hold imperial credentials and serve as imperial envoys.
Whenever imperial edicts or amnesties were promulgated,
members of the imperial clan were enfeoffed,
various foreign states were appeased,
talented individuals were summoned and invited,
or there were awards, condolences, relief efforts, military matters, or sacrifices,
envoys were dispatched.
Each year during the imperial review of judicial cases,
the Xíngrén would carry imperial credentials to transmit decrees to the judicial authorities.
They would escort banished prisoners,
send them to the Wǔfǔ (五府) to fill in the detailed register,
and submit them for approval to the Nèifǔ (內府).
Initially,
the Xíngrén Sī was established in the thirteenth year of Hóngwǔ
appointing Xíngrén
of Zheng jiǔ pǐn (正九品) rank.
There were also Zuǒ Xíngrén (左行人) and Yòu Xíngrén (右行人)
of Cóng jiǔ pǐn (從九品) rank.
Later, the Xíngrén were changed to Sīzhèng,
and the Zuǒ Xíngrén and Yòu Xíngrén were changed to Zuǒ Sīfù and Yòu Sīfù respectively.
Three hundred forty-five Xíngrén were newly appointed.
In the twenty-seventh year
as many of the appointed Xíngrén were talented in filial piety and integrity,
but their service as envoys often failed to meet imperial expectations.
It was decided to establish forty Xíngrén Sī officials,
all to be chosen from Jìnshì graduates.
Without an imperial decree,
they could not be arbitrarily dispatched,
and the position of Xíngrén thereby became more significant.
During the Jiànwén (建文) reign,
the Xíngrén Sī was abolished,
and the Xíngrén were placed under the Hónglú Sì (鴻臚寺).
Emperor Chéngzǔ (成祖) restored the old system.
The Qīntiān Jiān (欽天監).
One Jiānzhèng (監正),
(Zheng wǔ pǐn (正五品) rank),
and two Jiānfù (監副),
(Zheng liù pǐn rank.)
Its subordinates included:
the Zhǔbù Tīng (主簿廳),
one Zhǔbù (主簿),
(Zheng bā pǐn rank),
one Gūanguān Zhèng (官正) for spring, summer, central, autumn, and winter each (five in total),
(Zheng liù pǐn rank),
eight Wǔguān Língtái Láng (五官靈臺郎),
(Cóng qī pǐn rank,
later four were abolished),
two Wǔguān Bǎozhāng Zhèng (五官保章正),
(Zheng bā pǐn rank,
later one was abolished),
two Wǔguān Qièhú Zhèng (五官挈壺正),
(Cóng bā pǐn (從八品) rank,
later one was abolished),
three Wǔguān Jiānhòu (五官監候),
(Zheng jiǔ pǐn rank,
later one was abolished),
two Wǔguān Sīlì (五官司曆),
(Zheng jiǔ pǐn rank),
eight Wǔguān Sīchén (五官司晨),
(Cóng jiǔ pǐn rank,
later six were abolished),
and six Lòukè Bóshì (漏刻博士),
(Cóng jiǔ pǐn rank,
later five were abolished).
The Director (jiānzhèng) and Deputy Director (fù) were in charge of observing celestial phenomena, determining the calendar and astronomical calculations, divination, and mathematical astronomy.
For all matters concerning the sun, moon, stars, wind, clouds, and atmospheric colors,
they led their subordinates in observation and measurement.
If there were any anomalies,
they were to secretly report them.
Professional training was divided into four branches:
astronomy (tiānwén),
clepsydra (lòukè),
Islamic astronomy (Huíhuí),
and calendar (lì).
From the Five Bureau Directors (wǔguān zhèng) down to the astronomy students (tiānwén shēng) and geomancers (yīnyáng rén),
each was assigned to a branch for study.
Annually on the Winter Solstice,
the Grand Calendar (Dàtǒng Lì) for the coming year was submitted for approval (in the 15th year of Chénghuà, the calendar for the coming year was promulgated on the first day of the tenth month),
and then transferred to the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù) for promulgation.

The Imperial Almanac (Yùlǎn Yuèlì Lì), the Calendar of the Seven Luminaries' Positions (Qīzhèng Chán Dù Lì), the Rén Dùn Jiǎ Calendar (Liùrén Dùnjiǎ Lì), and the Record of Seasonal Celestial Phenomena (Sìjì Tiānxìang Lù)
were all presented in advance.
Regarding calendar annotations,
the Imperial Calendar (Yùlì) had thirty annotations,
(such as those for sacrifices, issuing edicts, imperial tours, etc.),
the Civilian Calendar (Mínlì) had thirty-two annotations,
and the Rén Dùn Calendar (Rén Dùn Lì) had seventy-two annotations.
For sacrificial days,
selections were made and submitted the year before,
and the Ministry of Ceremonies (Tàicháng) was informed.
For matters of construction, military campaigns, capping ceremonies, weddings, and imperial tombs,
auspicious locations and dates were chosen.
At the beginning of spring (lìchūn),
the qi was observed in advance in the eastern suburbs.
During grand court audiences,
the time-telling drums and clepsydras were set up in the Hall of State (Wénlóu) to report the time;
the Supervisor of Dawn (Sīchén) and the "chicken callers" [were also present],
each performing their duties.
For solar and lunar eclipses,
the exact minute and second of the eclipse, its beginning and end, and its direction were calculated and reported in advance.
This was then sent down to the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù),
and circulated to all internal and external offices for rescue rituals,
with reports submitted based on divination texts.
(If an eclipse was less than one fen,
or if the Islamic calendar (Huíhuí Lì) predicted an eclipse of one fen or more,
it was reported but no rescue rituals were performed.)
Officials of the Directorate (jiān guān) were not permitted to change to other offices,
and their descendants were not allowed to switch to other professions.
If there was a shortage of personnel,
the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù) was notified to search for and test candidates.
The Five Bureau Directors (wǔguān zhèng) calculated the calendar,
and determined the four seasons.
The Supervisors of Calendars (sīlì) and Supervisors of Observation (jiānhòu) assisted them.
The Astronomer (língtái láng) differentiated the celestial positions and zodiacal divisions of the sun, moon, and stars,
in order to divine the changes in celestial phenomena.
On the four sides of the Astronomical Observatory (Guānxìangtái),
four astronomy students (tiānwén shēng) [were stationed],
rotating duties for observation and measurement.
The Diviner (bǎozhāng zhèng) specialized in celestial changes,
determining their auspiciousness or inauspiciousness.
The Clepsydra Officer (jiéhú zhèng) was in charge of the clepsydra.
The perforated pot was the clepsydra,
and the floating arrow was the indicator,
used to determine the positions of the culminating stars at dusk and dawn.
The Clepsydra Doctor (lòukè bóshì) determined the time using the clepsydra,
changed the time [display] with plaques,
reported the watches with drums,
and announced dawn and dusk with bells and drums.
The Supervisor of Dawn (Sīchén) assisted them.
In the early Míng dynasty,
the Directorate of the Grand Astrologer (Tàishǐ Jiān) was established,
with a Grand Astrologer (tàishǐ lìng),
an Associate Administrator (tōngpàn tàishǐ jiān shì),
an Assistant Administrator (qiānpàn tàishǐ jiān shì),
a Record-Keeping Officer (jiàoshì láng),
Five Bureau Directors (wǔguān zhèng),
Astronomers (língtái láng),
Diviners (bǎozhāng zhèng) and their deputies,
Clepsydra Officers (jiéhú zhèng),
Calendar Keepers (zhǎnglì),
and Overseers (guǎngōu) and other officials.
Liú Jī was appointed Grand Astrologer (tàishǐ lìng).
In the first year of Wú (1367), the Directorate (jiān) was changed to an Academy (yuàn),
ranked third principal grade.
(The Academy Head (yuànshǐ) was third principal grade,
the Vice Head (tóngzhī) was fourth principal grade,
the Academy Examiner (yuànpàn) was fifth principal grade,
the Five Bureau Directors (wǔguān zhèng) were sixth principal grade,
the Registrar (diǎnbù), Supervisors of Rain and Shine (yǔyáng sī), Time Officers (shíláng), and Record Keepers (jìhòu láng) were seventh principal grade,
the Astronomers (língtái láng) and Diviners (bǎozhāng zhèng) were eighth principal grade,
their deputies were eighth secondary grade,
and the Calendar Keepers (zhǎnglì) and Overseers (guǎngōu) were ninth secondary grade.)
In the first year of Hóngwǔ (1368), fourteen former Yuán dynasty Grand Astrologers (Tàishǐ) such as Zhāng Yòu and Zhāng Yí were summoned,
and the Grand Astrologer Academy (Tàishǐ Yuàn) was renamed the Directorate of Astronomy (Sītiān Jiān).
One Director (jiānlìng) was appointed,
(third principal grade),
two Deputy Directors (shǎojiān),
(fourth principal grade),
one Assistant Director (jiānchéng),
(sixth principal grade),
one Registrar (zhǔbù),
(seventh principal grade),
one Administrator (zhǔshì),
(eighth principal grade),
five Five Bureau Directors (wǔguān zhèng),
(fifth principal grade),
five Five Bureau Deputies (wǔguān fù),
(sixth principal grade),
two Astronomers (língtái láng),
(seventh principal grade),
two Diviners (bǎozhāng zhèng),
(seventh secondary grade),
three Supervisors of Observation (jiānhòu),
(eighth principal grade),
eight Supervisors of Dawn (sīchén),
(ninth principal grade),
and six Clepsydra Doctors (lòukè bóshì),
(ninth secondary grade).
Additionally, an Islamic Directorate of Astronomy (Huíhuí Sītiān Jiān) was established,
with one Director (jiānlìng),
(fourth principal grade),
two Deputy Directors (shǎojiān),
(fifth principal grade),
and two Assistant Directors (jiānchéng),
(sixth principal grade).
Zhèng Ālǐ and others from the former Yuán Islamic Directorate of Astronomy (Huíhuí Sītiān Jiān) were summoned to discuss the calendar.
In the third year (1370), the Directorate of Astronomy (Sītiān Jiān) was renamed the Directorate of Astronomy (Qīntiān Jiān).
In the fourth year (1371), an imperial edict decreed that officials of the Directorate (jiān guān) should specialize in astronomy,
and unless by special imperial decree, they were not to be promoted or transferred.
The honorary titles (sǎnguān) for Directorate officials were also set.
(Director (jiānlìng) was Zhèngyí Dàfū;
Deputy Director (shǎojiān) was Fēnshuò Dàfū;
Five Bureau Supervisors (wǔguān sī) was Sīxuán Dàfū;
Assistant Director (jiānchéng) was Língtái Láng;
Five Bureau Diviner (wǔguān bǎozhāng zhèng) was Píngzhì Láng;
Five Bureau Astronomer (wǔguān língtái láng) was Sīzhèng Láng;
and Five Bureau Clepsydra Officer (wǔguān jiéhú zhèng) was Jiéhú Láng.)
In the fourteenth year (1381), the Directorate of Astronomy (Qīntiān Jiān) was reclassified as fifth principal grade,
with one Director (lìng)
and one Assistant Director (chéng).
(The subordinate officials, from Five Bureau Directors (wǔguān zhèng) downwards,
had the same numbers as previously listed),
and were all granted civil honorary titles (wénzhí sǎnguān) according to their ranks.
In the twenty-second year (1389), the Director (lìng) was renamed Director (jiānzhèng),
and the Assistant Director (chéng) was renamed Deputy Director (jiānfù).
In the thirty-first year (1398), the Islamic Directorate of Astronomy (Huíhuí Qīntiān Jiān) was abolished,
and its calendrical methods were transferred to the main Directorate.
In the early Míng dynasty,
a Bureau of Doubt Resolution (Jīyí Sī) was also established
to manage divination,
but it was soon abolished.
(In the seventeenth year of Hóngwǔ (1384), the Bureau of Doubt Resolution (Jīyí Sī) was established,
with one Commander (sīlìng),
sixth principal grade,
and one Left and one Right Assistant Commander (zuǒ, yòu chéng),
sixth secondary grade.
Subordinate officials were Diviners (sīshì),
ninth principal grade,
with no fixed number.
It was soon abolished.)
The Imperial Academy of Medicine (Tàiyī Yuàn).
One Academy Head (yuànshǐ),
(fifth principal grade),
and two Academy Examiners (yuànpàn),
(sixth principal grade).
Its subordinates included
four Imperial Physicians (yùyī),
(eighth principal grade,
later increased to eighteen,
in the fifth year of Lóngqìng fixed at ten),
and one Clerk (lìmù),
(ninth secondary grade,
in the fifth year of Lóngqìng fixed at ten).
The Raw Medicine Storehouse (Shēngyàokù) and the People's Benevolent Pharmacy (Huìmín Yàojú)
each had one Grand Envoy (dàshǐ)
and one Deputy Envoy (fùshǐ).
The Tàiyīyuàn (太醫院) was in charge of medical treatment methods.
There were thirteen specialties in medical practice:
medical officers (yīguān 醫官), physicians (yīshēng 醫生), and medical students (yīshì 醫士)
specialized in different areas. These were: Dàfāngmài (大方脈, general medicine),
Xiǎofāngmài (小方脈, pediatrics),
Fùrén (婦人, gynecology),
Chuāngyáng (瘡瘍, surgery for sores and ulcers),
Zhēnjiǔ (鍼灸, acupuncture and moxibustion),
Yǎn (眼, ophthalmology),
Kǒuchǐ (口齒, dentistry),
Jiēgǔ (接骨, orthopedics for bone setting),
Shānghán (傷寒, febrile diseases),
Yānhóu (咽喉, ear, nose, and throat),
Jīnzú (金鏃, external injuries from metal objects/weapons),
Ànmó (按摩, massage),
and Zhùyóu (祝由, incantations and spiritual healing).
Children of medical families
were selected and taught by masters.
After three or five years, they underwent a first, second, and third examination,
and were then promoted or dismissed.
For all medicines,
their suitable soil was identified,
their quality (good or bad) selected,
and their preparation carefully controlled before use.
When medicinal ingredients were collected and submitted from all directions,
the Yùan (院) officials stored them in the raw medicine warehouse (shēngyàokù 生藥庫),
ensuring proper conditions regarding dryness and humidity.
A Lǐbù (禮部) official was delegated to inspect this.
When diagnosing the imperial pulse,
the emissaries (shǐ 使), administrators (pàn 判), and imperial physicians (yùyī 御醫) jointly examined and verified it.
They would meet with palace eunuchs (nèichén 內臣) to select medicines in the inner bureau (nèijú 內局),
seal and label the dosages with their combined names,
and then present a memorial detailing the medicinal properties and treatment methods.
When preparing imperial medicines,
Yùan officials and eunuchs supervised.
Every two doses were combined into one.
Once cooked,
it was divided into two vessels.
One was first tasted by an imperial physician and a eunuch,
and the other was presented to the emperor.
A ledger was also maintained,
stamped with the inner seal,
meticulously recording the year, month, and reasons,
for future reference and examination.
When a princely estate (wángfǔ 王府) requested a physician,
the Yùan (院) would dispatch an official or medical student by imperial decree.
If civil and military ministers or foreign rulers were ill,
officials were also sent by imperial decree to examine them.
Whether the treatment was appropriate or not,
a memorial was submitted to report back.
In the outer prefectures, subprefectures, and counties, Huìmínyàojú (惠民藥局, Bureaus of Benefiting the People with Medicine) were established.
In border garrisons (biānguān wèisuǒ 邊關衞所) and densely populated areas,
physicians (yīshēng 醫生), medical students (yīshì 醫士), or medical officers (yīguān 醫官) were set up,
all selected and dispatched after examination by the Yùan (院).
At the end of the year,
their merits and demerits were jointly assessed, and their performance ranked as 'most excellent' (diànzuì 殿最),
serving as a basis for promotion or demotion.
In the early reign of Tàizǔ (太祖),
the Yīxué Tíjué Sī (醫學提舉司, Directorate for Medical Education) was established.
A Tíjué (提舉) was appointed,
(of rank cōngwǔpǐn 從五品),
along with a Tóngtíjué (同提舉),
(of rank cóngliùpǐn 從六品),
a Fùtíjué (副提舉),
(of rank cóngqīpǐn 從七品),
a Yīxué Jiàoshòu (醫學教授, Professor of Medicine),
(of rank zhèngjiǔpǐn 正九品),
and Xuézhèng (學正), Guānyī (官醫), and Tílíng (提領),
(all of rank cóngjiǔpǐn 從九品).
Later, it was renamed Tàiyījīan (太醫監, Imperial Medical Superintendency).
A Shàojiān (少監) was appointed,
(of rank zhèngsìpǐn 正四品),
and a Jiānchéng (監丞),
(of rank zhèngliùpǐn 正六品).
In the first year of Wú (吳 Yuánnián 吳元年), the Jiān (監) was changed to a Yuàn (院).
A Yuànshǐ (院使) was appointed,
with the rank of zhèngsānpǐn (正三品),
a Tóngzhī (同知),
of zhèngsìpǐn (正四品),
a Yuànpàn (院判),
of zhèngwǔpǐn (正五品),
and a Diǎnbù (典簿),
of zhèngqīpǐn (正七品).
In the third year of Hóngwǔ (洪武), the Huìmínyàojú (惠民藥局) was established.
A Tílíng (提領) was appointed in prefectures,
and a Guānyī (官醫) in subprefectures and counties.
Medicine was provided
to poor and sick soldiers and commoners.
In the sixth year, the Yùyàojú (御藥局, Imperial Pharmacy) was established within the inner court (nèifǔ 內府),
and imperial physicians (yùyī 御醫) were appointed for the first time.
(The Yùyījú (御醫局)
was of rank zhèngliùpǐn (正六品).
Two Shàngyào (尚藥) and Fèngyù (奉御) were appointed,
two Zhícháng (直長),
and ten Yàotóng (藥童),
all filled by palace eunuchs (nèiguān 內官) and palace attendants (nèishǐ 內使).
Four imperial physicians (yùyī 御醫) were appointed,
filled by medical students (yīshì 醫士) from the Tàiyīyuàn (太醫院).
One Fèngyù (奉御) was in charge of
receiving famous medicinal contributions from all directions and storing medicinal products.
For all imperial medicines and tonics,
medical officers prepared them in the inner bureau (nèijú 內局),
and Tàiyīyuàn (太醫院) officials diagnosed.)
In the fourteenth year, the Tàiyīyuàn (太醫院) was downgraded to zhèngwǔpǐn (正五品).
One Lìng (令),
one Chéng (丞),
and one Lìmù (吏目) were appointed.
Four subordinate imperial physicians (yùyī 御醫)
were all granted honorary civil official titles.
In the twenty-second year, the Lìng (令) was again changed to Yuànshǐ (院使),
and the Chéng (丞) to Yuànpàn (院判).
In the fifteenth year of Jiājìng (嘉靖), the Yùyàofáng (御藥房, Imperial Dispensary) was changed to Shèngjìdiàn (聖濟殿, Hall of Sacred Healing),
and an Yùyàokù (御藥庫, Imperial Medicine Storehouse) was also established.
An imperial edict commanded imperial physicians (yùyī 御醫) to serve on rotation.
Shànglínyuàn Jiān (上林苑監, Imperial Parks and Gardens Superintendency).
One Zuǒ Jiānzhèng (左監正) and one Yòu Jiānzhèng (右監正) were appointed,
(both of rank zhèngwǔpǐn 正五品),
one Zuǒ Jiānfù (左監副) and one Yòu Jiānfù (右監副) were appointed,
(both of rank zhèngliùpǐn 正liùpǐn.
Jiānzhèng (監正) and Jiānfù (監副) were not always appointed later,
with a Jiānchéng (監丞) acting in their stead).
One Zuǒ Jiānchéng (左監丞) and one Yòu Jiānchéng (右監丞) were appointed,
(both of rank zhèngqīpǐn 正七品).
Its subordinates included
the Diǎnbù Tīng (典簿廳),
with one Diǎnbù (典簿),
(of rank zhèngjiǔpǐn 正九品).
There were four bureaus: Liángmù (良牧, Good Herding), Fānyù (蕃育, Breeding), Línhéng (林衡, Forest Management), and Jiāshū (嘉蔬, Fine Vegetables).
Each bureau had one Diǎnshǔ (典署),
(of rank zhèngqīpǐn 正七pǐn),
one Shǔchéng (署丞),
(of rank zhèngbāpǐn 正八pǐn),
and one Lùshì (錄事),
(of rank zhèngjiǔpǐn 正九pǐn).
The Jiānzhèng (監正) was in charge of parks, gardens, ponds, livestock, and tree planting.
For all birds and beasts, plants, vegetables, and fruits,
he directed his subordinates to supervise the herding and planting households,
managing their grazing and planting grounds according to the seasons,
to raise and cultivate them,
for sacrifices, guests, and meals for the imperial household (gōngfǔ 宮府).
The imperial parklands (yuàndì 苑地)
extended east to Báihé (白河),
west to Xīshān (西山),
south to Wǔqīng (武清),
north to Jūyōngguān (居庸關),
and southwest to Húnhé (渾河).
Hunting within these areas was forbidden.
Liángmù (良牧) oversaw cattle, sheep, and pigs.
Fānyù (蕃育) oversaw geese, ducks, and chickens.
The number of males and females of these animals was registered,
and their breeding and egg production were assessed.
Línhéng (林衡) managed fruits and flowers.
Jiāshū (嘉蔬) managed the cultivation of melons and vegetables.
The number of their plots and planted trees was counted,
and they were harvested and presented in due season.
In the twenty-fifth year of Hóngwǔ (洪武), a plan was discussed to open the Shànglínyuàn (上林院),
surveying land south of the city.
(From Niúshǒushān (牛首山) connecting to Fāngshān (方山),
and west along the riverbank).
When the maps were presented,
Tàizǔ (太祖) believed it would hinder the people's livelihoods,
and so it was stopped.
In the fifth year of Yǒnglè (永樂), the Shànglínyuàn Jiān (上林苑監) was first established,
with ten subordinate bureaus: Liángmù (良牧), Fānyù (蕃育), Jiāshū (嘉蔬), Línhéng (林衡), Chuānhéng (川衡), Bīngjiàn (冰鑑), and four Diǎnchá Zuǒ Yòu Qián Hòu (典察左右前後).
In the middle of Hóngxī (洪熙)'s reign,
they were merged into two bureaus: Fānyù (蕃育) and Jiāshū (嘉蔬).
(Liángmù (良牧) and Chuānhéng (川衡) were merged into Fānyù (蕃育);
Bīngjiàn (冰鑑) and Línhéng (林衡) were merged into Jiāshū (嘉蔬);
the four Diǎnchá (典察) bureaus were separately merged).
In the tenth year of Xuāndé (宣德), the four bureaus were finally fixed.
During the Zhèngdé (正德) period,
an additional ninety-nine supervising eunuchs were appointed.
In the first year of Jiājìng (嘉靖), eighty officials were cut,
and the Diǎnshǔ (典署) of the Fānyù (蕃育) and Jiāshū (嘉蔬) bureaus,
and the Lùshì (錄事) of the Línhéng (林衡) and Jiāshū (嘉蔬) bureaus were abolished.
Zhōng, Dōng, Xī, Nán, Běi Wǔchéng Bīngmǎ Zhǐhuī Sī (中、東、西、南、北五城兵馬指揮司, Commanderies of Infantry and Cavalry of the Five Wards: Central, East, West, South, North).
Each had one Zhǐhuī (指揮, Commander),
(of rank zhèngliùpǐn 正六品),
four Fùzhǐhuī (副指揮, Vice Commanders),
(of rank zhèngqīpǐn 正七品),
and one Lìmù (吏目).
The Zhǐhuī (指揮) was responsible for patrolling and arresting thieves,
clearing streets and ditches, and handling prisoners and fire prevention.
The capital city, both inner and outer, was divided into various districts for them to administer.
If there were vagrants or wicked people within their district, they were arrested and dealt with.
When the emperor personally visited the suburbs for sacrifices,
they led corvée laborers to serve.
(For fathers of empresses or princely consorts who held no official position,
if they were fathers of empresses, they were granted the title of Bīngmǎ Zhǐhuī (兵馬指揮);
if they were fathers of princely consorts, they were granted Fùzhǐhuī (副指揮);
but they did not actually handle affairs).
The Directorate of Daoists (Dàolù Sì).
Two Rectifiers-in-Chief of the Orthodox Unity (Zhèngyī) on the Left and Right,
(Rank 6a);
two Dharma Expounders on the Left and Right,
(Rank 6b);
two Spiritual Eminences on the Left and Right,
(Rank 8a);
two Profound Meanings on the Left and Right,
(Rank 8b);
one Supervisor of the Divine Music Temple (Shénlè Guān)
(Rank 6a);
one Temple Administrator
(Rank 8b;
abolished during the Jiājìng reign).
One Heavenly Master of the Orthodox Unity (Zhèngyī Zhēnrén) of Lónghǔ Shān
(Rank 2a.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ
Zhāng Zhèngcháng was summoned to court,
his title of Heavenly Master (Tiānshī) was removed,
he was enfeoffed as a Perfected Person (Zhēnrén),
and the title was hereditary.
During the Lóngqìng reign, the title of Perfected Person was abolished,
and they were merely called Supervisor.
It was restored at the beginning of the Wànlì reign.)
Two Dharma Officers (Fǎguān), two Assistant Instructors (Zànjiào), and two Scribes (Zhǎngshū).
One Spiritual Official (Língguān) each for Gézào Shān and Sānmáo Shān
(Rank 8a).
One Supervisor for Tàihé Shān.
The Directorates of Monks and Daoists (Sēng, Dào Lùsī) managed all monks and Daoists in the empire.
In the prefectures, subprefectures, and counties outside the capital, there were Directorates of Monks (Sēnggāng) and Daoists (Dàojì)
to manage these affairs,
all staffed by individuals skilled in classics and of upright conduct.
The Divine Music Temple (Shénlè Guān) managed music and dance
for the great sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, gods and spirits, and the ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain.
It was subordinate to the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Sì)
and had no administrative connection with the Directorate of Daoists.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ
They were abolished in the fourth year
In the fifth year
In the eleventh year
and positions for Supervisor and Temple Administrator were established.
(Initially,
the Supervisor was Rank 6b,
and the Temple Administrator was Rank 9b.
In the fifteenth year of Hóngwǔ
and the Temple Administrator to Rank 8b.
Whenever there was a court assembly,
the Supervisor was ranked below the Left Shànshì of the Directorate of Monks (Sēnglù Sì)
and above the Left Rectifier-in-Chief of the Directorate of Daoists.)
In the fifteenth year
(Each established officials as previously listed.)
Monks were divided into three classes: Chan (Chán),
Lecture (Jiǎng),
and Teaching (Jiào).
Daoists were divided into two classes: Complete Perfection (Quánzhēn)
and Orthodox Unity (Zhèngyī).
Officials were established without salaries
and were subordinate to the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù).
In the twenty-fourth year
limiting the issuance of ordination certificates to monks once every three years.
In all prefectures, subprefectures, and counties, monasteries and temples
were consolidated into one large establishment,
where all residents were to reside together.
The number of monks and Daoists
was limited to no more than forty in a prefecture,
thirty in a subprefecture,
and twenty in a county.
Commoners under forty years of age and women under fifty years of age
were not permitted to become monastics.
In the twenty-eighth year
those not proficient in the classics were dismissed.
Subsequently,
Buddhists received titles such as Dharma King (Fǎwáng), Son of Buddha (Fózǐ), and Grand National Preceptor (Dàguóshī),
while Daoists received titles such as Grand Perfected Person (Dà Zhēnrén) and High Scholar (Gāoshì).
They were bestowed with silver seals and python robes (mǎngyù),
and granted additional titles like Grand Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng), Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū), and Grand Guardian (Gōngbǎo),
some even being enfeoffed as Earls (Bójue).
These were all temporary favors,
not part of the regular system.
The Imperial Music Bureau (Jiàofāng Sì).
One Master of Imperial Carriages (Fèngluán)
(Rank 9a);
one Master of Right and Left Ceremonial Music (Sháowǔ) each,
one Master of Right and Left Music (Sīyuè) each
(both Rank 9b).
They were in charge of performing music and dance.
The staff consisted of hereditary musicians (yuèhù)
and were subordinate to the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù).
(During the Jiājìng reign,
the Imperial Music Bureau for Sacrifices at Xiǎnlíng was also established,
with one Master of Right and Left Music each.)
Eunuchs (Huànguān).
Twelve Directorates (Jiān).
(Each Directorate had one Grand Eunuch (Tàijiàn),
Rank 4a;
one Vice Grand Eunuch (Shàojiān) on the Left and Right each,
Rank 4b;
one Assistant Grand Eunuch (Jiānchéng) on the Left and Right each,
Rank 5a;
one Registrar (Diǎnbù),
Rank 6a;
an indefinite number of Attendants (Chángsuí) and Imperial Guards (Fèngyù),
Rank 6b.
This was the old system from Hóngwǔ.
Later, it was gradually reformed,
with details provided under each respective entry.)
The Directorate of Ceremonial (Sīlǐ Jiān).
(One Supervising Grand Eunuch (Tídū Tàijiàn),
one Grand Eunuch in Charge of Seals (Zhǎngyìn Tàijiàn),

an indefinite number of Grand Eunuchs for Drafting (Bǐngbǐ Tàijiàn), Grand Eunuchs on Duty (Suítáng Tàijiàn), Managers of various storehouses like Books and Famous Paintings, Managers of the Internal Writing Academy (Nèishūtáng), Managers of the Six Offices' Corridor (Liùkē Láng), and Registrars (Diǎnbù).
The Supervising Grand Eunuch oversaw all ceremonial rites, legal cases,
and the discipline of attendants, duty-bearers, and service personnel within the imperial city,
as well as the security of gates,
and the urging of supplies from the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Guānglù Sì), etc.
The Grand Eunuch in Charge of Seals managed internal and external memorials and imperial warrants (kānhé).
The Drafting and On-Duty Grand Eunuchs managed memorials and documents,
endorsing cabinet drafts with vermilion comments.
The Managers each oversaw their respective departments.
The Registrar recorded memorials and various receipts and expenditures ledgers.)
The Directorate of Palace Personnel (Nèiguān Jiān).
(One Grand Eunuch in Charge of Seals,
an indefinite number of General Managers (Zǒnglǐ), Managers (Guǎnlǐ), Scribes (Qiānshū), Registrars (Diǎnbù), Section Managers (Zhǎngsī), Copyists (Xiězì), and Overseers (Jiāngōng).
It managed the ten workshops: wood, stone, tile, earth, funerary materials, eastern travel, western travel, lacquer, weddings, and gunpowder,
as well as the Granary (Mǐyán Kù), Construction Storehouse (Yíngzào Kù), and Imperial Altars Storehouse (Huángtán Kù).
It handled all imperial construction of palaces and mausoleums,
as well as bronze and tin burial furnishings, utensils, and ice cellars.)
The Directorate of Imperial Accoutrements (Yùyòng Jiān).
(One Grand Eunuch in Charge of Seals,
two Chief Commanders (Bǎzǒng) for external surveillance,
an indefinite number of Registrars (Diǎnbù), Section Managers (Zhǎngsī), Copyists (Xiězì), and Overseers (Jiāngōng).
It manufactured all screens, beds, and other wooden articles for imperial use,
as well as zǐtán wood, ivory, ebony, mother-of-pearl inlay, and other curiosities.
It handled all manufacturing.
There was also one Overseer for the Rénzhì Diàn,
who managed books and painting albums written by the Grand Secretariat (Zhōngshū Chéngzhǐ) in the Wǔyīng Diàn,
which were presented to the emperor.)
The Directorate of Palace Furnishings (Sīshè Jiān).
(The staff was the same as the Directorate of Palace Personnel.
It managed imperial insignia, ceremonial guards, and curtains.)
The Directorate of Imperial Stables (Yùmǎ Jiān).
(One Grand Eunuch in Charge of Seals, one Grand Eunuch for Supervision, and one Grand Eunuch for Oversight.
Each of the four Tēngxiáng Guards camps had officials for supervision, section managers, registrars, copyists, and horse-takers.
The elephant house had section managers and other staff.)
The Directorate of Imperial Shrines (Shéngōng Jiān).
(One Grand Eunuch in Charge of Seals,
an indefinite number of Scribes, Section Managers, and Managers.
It managed the sweeping, incense, and lamps of the Imperial Ancestral Temple (Tàimiào) and other temples.)
The Directorate of Imperial Cuisine (Shàngshàn Jiān).
(One Grand Eunuch in Charge of Seals,
one Supervising Grand Eunuch for Imperial Entertainments (Guānglù Tàijiàn),
one General Manager,
an indefinite number of Managers, Scribes,
Section Managers, Copyists, Overseers, and Overseers for various cattle and sheep pens and factories.
It managed imperial meals, palace provisions, and banquets.)
The Directorate of Imperial Seals (Shàngbǎo Jiān).
(One Grand Eunuch in Charge of Seals,
an indefinite number of Scribes and Section Managers.
It managed imperial seals, imperial tallies (chìfú), and general's seals.
Whenever a seal was needed,
the external Ministry of Imperial Seals (Wài Shàngbǎo Sì) submitted a memorial to the Directorate to request imperial instruction.
It would then be collected from the female officials of the Ministry of Imperial Seals,
supervised during its use by the external office,
recorded in a ledger,
and returned.)
The Directorate of Records and Tallies (Yìnshòu Jiān).
(The staff was the same as the Directorate of Imperial Seals.
It managed the Library of Ancient and Modern Compilations (Gǔjīn Tōngjí Kù),
as well as iron charters (tiěquàn), imperial edicts (gàochì), official memoranda (tiēhuáng), seals, tallies (kānhé), warrants (fúyàn), and credentials (xìnfú).)
The Directorate of Hall Maintenance (Zhídiàn Jiān).
(The staff was the same as the above.
It managed the cleaning of various halls and corridors.)
The Directorate of Imperial Robes (Shàngyī Jiān).
(One Grand Eunuch in Charge of Seals,
an indefinite number of Managers, Scribes, Section Managers, and Overseers.
It managed imperial crowns, robes, shoes, and socks.)
The Directorate of General Affairs (Dūzhī Jiān).
(One Grand Eunuch in Charge of Seals,
an indefinite number of Scribes, Section Managers, Attendants, and Imperial Guards.
It formerly managed the transfer, notification, and verification of documents among various directorates.
Later, it only served as a vanguard and alarm-bearer when the emperor traveled.)
The Four Directorates (Sì Sī).
(Under the old system, each Directorate had one Directorate Commissioner (Sīzhèng),
of Principal Fifth Rank (zhèng wǔ pǐn);
and one Left and Right Deputy Commissioner (Zuǒ, Yòu Sīfù) each,
of Secondary Fifth Rank (cóng wǔ pǐn).
This was gradually changed later,
details below.)
The Directorate of Firewood Supply (Xīxīn Sī),
(with one Eunuch in Charge of Seals (Zhǎngyìn Tàijiàn),

a Director-General (Zǒnglǐ), Scriveners (Qiānshū), Managers of Dao (Zhǎngdào), Managers of Directorates (Zhǎngsī), Scribes (Xiězì), and Supervisors (Jiāngōng), as well as Scriveners (Qiānshū) and Supervisors (Jiāngōng) at the Outer Factory (Wàichǎng), Northern Factory (Běichǎng), Southern Factory (Nánchǎng), New Southern Factory (Xīnnánchǎng), and New Western Factory (Xīnxīchǎng), all without fixed numbers,
was in charge of matters concerning the firewood and charcoal used.)
The Directorate of Bells and Drums (Zhōnggǔ Sī),
(with one Eunuch in Charge of Seals (Zhǎngyìn Tàijiàn),
Scriveners (Qiānshū), Office Staff (Sīfáng), and Arts Officials (Xuéyìguān) without fixed numbers,
was in charge of the bells and drums for imperial audiences,
as well as court music, plays (chuánqí), "Passing the Brocade" (guòjǐn), "Beating the Rice" (dǎdào), and various other theatrical performances.)
The Directorate of Paper Money (Bǎochāo Sī),
(with one Eunuch in Charge of Seals (Zhǎngyìn Tàijiàn),
Scriveners (Qiānshū), managers, and Supervisors (Jiāngōng) without fixed numbers,
was in charge of manufacturing coarse and fine paper.)
The Directorate of Bathhouses (Hùntáng Sī),
(with one Eunuch in Charge of Seals (Zhǎngyìn Tàijiàn),
Scriveners (Qiānshū) and Supervisors (Jiāngōng) without fixed numbers,
was in charge of bathing matters.)
The Eight Bureaus (Bā Jú).
(Under the old system, each Bureau had one Commissioner (Dàshǐ),
of Principal Fifth Rank (zhèng wǔ pǐn);
and one Left and Right Deputy Commissioner (Zuǒ, Yòu Fùshǐ) each,
of Secondary Fifth Rank (cóng wǔ pǐn).)
The Bureau of Military Armaments (Bīngzhàng Jú),
(with one Eunuch in Charge of Seals (Zhǎngyìn Tàijiàn),
one Eunuch Overseer of the Imperial Armory (Tídū Jūnqì Kù Tàijiàn),
managers, Scriveners (Qiānshū), Directorate Managers (Zhǎngsī), Scribes (Xiězì), and Supervisors (Jiāngōng) without fixed numbers,
was in charge of manufacturing military armaments.
The Directorate of Gunpowder (Huǒyào Sī) was subordinate to it.)
The Bureau of Silver Crafts (Yínzuò Jú),
(with one Eunuch in Charge of Seals (Zhǎngyìn Tàijiàn),
managers, Scriveners (Qiānshū), Scribes (Xiězì), and Supervisors (Jiāngōng) without fixed numbers,
was in charge of crafting gold and silver ornaments.)
The Bureau of Laundry (Huànyī Jú),
(with one Eunuch in Charge of Seals (Zhǎngyìn Tàijiàn),
Scriveners (Qiānshū), and Supervisors (Jiāngōng) without fixed numbers.
All palace women who were old, dismissed, or retired,
were sent to this Bureau to reside.
However, this Bureau was not located within the Imperial City (Huángchéng).)
The Bureau of Headwear and Footwear (Jīnmào Jú),
(with one Eunuch in Charge of Seals (Zhǎngyìn Tàijiàn),
managers, Scriveners (Qiānshū), Directorate Managers (Zhǎngsī), and Supervisors (Jiāngōng) without fixed numbers,
was in charge of making hats and boots for palace staff,
caps and boots for Imperial Sons-in-law (Fùmǎ), and various caps and boots for banner guards of Feudatory Princes (Fānwáng) in their states.)
The Bureau of Needlework (Zhēngōng Jú),
(staffed similarly to the Bureau of Headwear and Footwear (Jīnmào Jú),
was in charge of making clothes for the palace.)
The Internal Bureau of Weaving and Dyeing (Nèi Zhīrǎn Jú),
(staffed similarly to the above,
was in charge of dyeing and manufacturing satin for imperial use and for palace application.
The Indigo Dyeing Factory (Lándiànchǎng) to the west of the city served as an external office for this bureau.)
The Bureau of Wine, Vinegar, and Noodles (Jiǔcùmiàn Jú),
(staffed similarly to the above,
was in charge of wine, vinegar, sauces, noodles, beans, and other foodstuffs for palace consumption.
It was not subordinate to the Imperial Winery (Yùjiǔfáng).)
The Bureau of Gardens (Sīyuàn Jú),
(staffed similarly to the above,
was in charge of vegetables, melons, and fruits.)
The Twelve Directorates (Shí'èr Jiān), Four Directorates (Sì Sī), and Eight Bureaus (Bā Jú)
are what were known as the Twenty-Four Yamen (Èrshísì Yámén).
Outside these are the Nèifǔ Gōngyòng Kù (Internal Household Supply Depot),
(One Pinyin Tàijiān as Director,
an indeterminate number of Zǒnglǐ, Guǎnlǐ, Zhǎnsī, Xiězì, and Jiāngōng.
They manage the rice for palace eunuchs and those in imperial tombs, as well as imperial yellow wax, white wax, agarwood, and other incenses.
All oil and wax depots are subordinate to it.
The old system stipulated that each depot should have officials similar to the Eight Bureaus.)
Sīyuè Kù (Key Management Depot),
(Staff as above,
managing the storage of copper coins for rewards and gifts.)
Nèichéngyùn Kù (Internal Transport Depot),
(One Pinyin Tàijiān as Director,
ten Jìnshì and Qiānshū Tàijiān,
an indeterminate number of Zhǎnsī, Xiězì, and Jiāngōng.
They manage the grand imperial treasury,
with all gold, silver, and various precious goods under its control.)
Ten Depots:
Jiǎzì (First Character Depot),
(Manages the storage of cinnabar, litharge, smoked plums, gamboge, mercury, and other items.)
Yǐzì (Second Character Depot),
(Manages the storage of memorial papers and padded jackets submitted by various provinces.)
Bǐngzì (Third Character Depot),
(Manages the storage of silk floss and cloth bolts.)
Dīngzì (Fourth Character Depot),
(Manages the storage of raw lacquer, tung oil, and other items.)
Wùzì (Fifth Character Depot),
(Manages the storage of bows, arrows, helmets, armor, and other items submitted.)
Chéngyùn (Transport Depot),
(Manages the storage of yellow and white raw silk.)
Guǎngyíng (Vast Abundance Depot),
(Manages the storage of gauze, damask, and various silk fabrics.)
Guǎnghuì (Vast Benevolence Depot),
(Manages the manufacturing and storage of scarves, combs, brushes, coin strings, and paper ingots.)
Zāngfá (Confiscated Goods Depot),
(Manages property confiscated by the government.
Each of the above depots has one Zhǎngkù official,
with an indeterminate number of Tiēkù and Qiānshū.)
Yùjiǔ Fáng (Imperial Wine Room),
(One Tídū Tàijiān,
with an indeterminate number of Qiānshū.
Manages the brewing of imperial wine.)
Yùyào Fáng (Imperial Pharmacy),
(Two Tídū Tàijiān, one chief and one deputy,
divided into two shifts.
An indeterminate number of Jìnshì and Yīguān.
Responsible for imperial medicines,
interacting with officials of the Tàiyī Yuàn.)
Yùchá Fáng (Imperial Tea Room),
(Two Tídū Tàijiān, one chief and one deputy,
divided into two shifts.
An indeterminate number of Jìnshì.
Responsible for serving tea, wine, fruits, and presenting imperial meals.)
Shēngkǒu Fáng (Livestock Room),
(One Tídū Tàijiān,
with an indeterminate number of Qiānshū.
Raises rare beasts and precious birds.)
Kèlòu Fáng (Clepsydra Room),
(One Zhǎngfáng official,
with an indeterminate number of Qiānshū.
Manages the daily time,
with Zhídiàn Jiānguān entering the palace to change time markers every hour,
and reporting water-clock readings at night.)
Gēnggǔ Fáng (Watch Drum Room),
(Eunuchs with minor offenses are in charge of this.)
Tiánshí Fáng (Sweet Food Room),
(One Zhǎngfáng official,
with an indeterminate number of Xiétóng.
Manages the making of "tiger-eye" and "woven-silk" candies and other sweets,
subordinate to the Yùyòng Jiān.)
Dànzǐ Fáng (Pellet Room),
(One Zhǎngfáng official,
with several Qiānshū.
Specifically prepares mud pellets.)
Língtái (Spirit Platform),
(One Pinyin Tàijiān as Director,
with an indeterminate number of Qiānshū Jìnshì and Kànshí Jìnshì.
Manages the observation of celestial bodies, weather, and clouds,
and predicts good or ill fortune.)
Táo Zuò (Cordage Workshop),
(One Zhǎngzuò official,
with an indeterminate number of Xiétóng.
Manages the manufacturing of various colors of velvet and various cords and sashes,
subordinate to the Yùyòng Jiān.)
Kuījiǎ Chǎng (Armor Factory),
(Formerly the Ànpèi Jú,
manages the manufacturing of military weapons.)
Ānmín Chǎng (Peaceful People Factory),
(Formerly Wánggōng Chǎng,
each factory has one Zhǎngchǎng Tàijiān,
with an indeterminate number of Tiēchǎng and Qiānshū.
Manages the manufacturing of firearms, gunpowder, and similar items.)
Wǔmén,
Dōnghuá Mén,
Xīhuá Mén,
Fèngtiān Mén,
Xuánwǔ Mén,
Zuǒ and Yòu Shùn Mén,
Zuǒ and Yòu Hóng Mén,
Huánggōng Mén,
Kūnníng Mén,
the left and right gates of the palace.
Dōnggōng Chūnhé Mén,
rear gate,
left and right gates,
and all gates inside and outside the imperial and capital cities,
(Each gate has one Zhèng official,
with an indeterminate number of Guǎnshì.
Responsible for opening and closing at dawn and dusk,
and controlling entry and exit.
Formerly, one Ménzhèng and one Ménfù were appointed for each.)
Tídū Dōngchǎng (Director of the Eastern Depot),
(One Pinyin Tàijiān as Director,
an indeterminate number of Zhǎngbān, Lǐngbān, and Sīfáng.
Two Tiēxíng officials
responsible for espionage, investigation, and judicial matters.
Formerly, one person from various directorates was chosen as Tídū,
but later it was exclusively the second or third person from the Sīlǐ and Bǐngbǐ.
The Tiēxíng officials,
were selected from the Jǐnyīwèi Qiānhù and Bǎihù.
Any Nèiguān who holds the Pinyin of Sīlǐ Jiān
has authority comparable to the chief grand secretary of the outer court;
one who directs the Dōngchǎng
has authority comparable to the chief censor.
Bǐngbǐ and Suítáng officials are comparable to various assistant grand secretaries.
Each sets up private officials such as Zhǎngjiā, Zhǎngbān, and Sīfáng.)
Tídū Xīchǎng (Director of the Western Depot),
(Not permanently established,
only Wāng Zhí and Gǔ Dàyòng established it.
Liú Jǐn also established the Xīnèichǎng.
Soon after, both were abolished.)
Tídū Jīngyíng (Director of the Capital Garrisons),
(Tídū Tàijiān,
Zuòyíng Tàijiān,
Jiānqiāng, Zhǎngsī, and Qiānshū all indeterminate in number.
Began in the first year of Jǐngtài.)
Wénshū Fáng (Documents Room),
(Ten Zhǎngfáng officials.
Manages the daily sealed memorials from the Tōngzhèng Sī,
and sealed memorials submitted by capital officials at Huìjí Mén and various princely establishments.
All cabinet drafts from outside,
and internal endorsement notes,
and all imperial edicts and rescripts,
are recorded in the Wénshū Fáng's ledger before being issued.
Anyone promoted to Sīlǐ
must have originated from the Wénshū Fáng,
like the Zhānshì Fǔ and Hànlín Yuàn officials in the outer court.)
Lǐyí Fáng (Ritual Room),
(One Tídū Tàijiān,
held concurrently by the Sīlǐ's Pinyin or Bǐngbǐ,
with an indeterminate number of Zhǎngsī, Xiězì, Guǎnshì, and Chángsuí.
Manages all auspicious rites such as selecting consorts, imperial sons-in-law, celebrating the birth of imperial princes and princesses, and choosing wet nurses.)
Zhōngshū Fáng (Secretariat Room),
(One Zhǎngfáng official,
with an indeterminate number of Sǎnguān.
Manages books, couplets, fan handles, and other items written by the Zhōngshū of Wénhuá Diàn,
receiving imperial orders to write them,
and presenting them upon completion.)
Yùqián Jìnshì (Imperial Attendants),
(Including Guǎnshì of Qiánqīng Gōng,
supervising various imperial affairs,
and Dǎmǎo Páizǐ,
who attend court holding swords,
both ranking below the Sīlǐ and Dōngchǎng Tídū Shǒubèi.
Also Yùqián Páizǐ,
Nuǎndiàn,
Guǎnguìzǐ,
Zànlǐ,
Dāyìng Chángsuí,
Dāngchāi Tīngshì,
Námǎ,
Shàngguān, Shàngyī, and Shànglǚ,
all are Jìnshì.)
Nánjīng Shǒubèi (Nánjīng Garrison Commander),
(One chief and one deputy Shǒubèi Tàijiān.
One official seal,
guarding the secondary capital,
an external assignment of the Sīlǐ Jiān.)
Tiānshòushān Shǒubèi (Tiānshòushān Garrison Commander),
(One Tàijiān.
Oversees the tomb-guarding Tàijiān of various imperial tombs,
responsible for protection.)
Húguǎng Chéngtiānfǔ Shǒubèi (Chéngtiānfǔ, Húguǎng Garrison Commander),
(One Tàijiān.
Administers the areas of Chéngdé, Jīng, and Xiāng,
guarding Xīngníng.)
Zhīzào (Textile Bureaus),
(One Tídū Tàijiān in Nánjīng,
one in Sūzhōu,
one in Hángzhōu.
Manages the weaving of imperial dragon robes.)
Zhènshǒu (Garrison Commissioners),
(Zhènshǒu Tàijiān began in Hóngxī,
and were widely established during Zhèngtǒng,
with every province and garrison having Zhènshǒu Tàijiān,
but they were abolished after the eighth year of Jiājìng.)
Shìbó (Maritime Trade Commissioners),
(Each of the three Shìbó Sī in Guǎngdōng, Fújiàn, and Zhèjiāng had a Tàijiān as Tídū,
later the Zhèjiāng and Fújiàn bureaus were abolished,
only the Guǎngdōng bureau remained.)
Jiāndū Cāngchǎng (Granary and Farm Supervisors),
(Each granary and farm had a Jiāndū Tàijiān.)
)The Shéngōngjiān for the various imperial tombs,
(each imperial tomb was moreover equipped with a Shéngōngjiān Tàijiàn to guard the tombs).
Beyond these, officials such as the Jiānjūn, Cǎibàn, Liángshuì, Kuàng, and Guān,
those who were not permanently established,
were too numerous to enumerate.
Initially,
in the first year of Wú, the Nèishǐjiān was established,
setting up a Jiānlìng
(principal rank 4),
a Chéng
(principal rank 5),
a Fèngyù
(subordinate rank 5),
a Nèishǐ
(principal rank 7),
and a Diǎnbù
(principal rank 8).
The Huángménguān established a Huángménshǐ
(principal rank 5),
and a Fù
(subordinate rank 5).
Later, it was reformed into the Nèishǐjiān and Yùyòngjiān,
each establishing one Lìng
(principal rank 3),
two Chéng
(subordinate rank 3),
a Fèngyù
(principal rank 6),
and a Diǎnbù
(principal rank 7).
The Huángménguān established a Ménzhèng
(principal rank 4),
and a Fù
(subordinate rank 4).
The Chūngōngménguān established a Zhèng
(principal rank 5),
and a Fù
(subordinate rank 5).
The Yùmǎsī established a Sīzhèng
(principal rank 5),
and a Fù
(subordinate rank 5).
The Shàngbǎo concurrently managed the Shǒudiàn, Shàngguān, Shàngyī, Shàngpèi, Shànglǚ, Shàngyào, Jìshì, and other Fèngyù,
(all principal rank 6).
In the second year of Hóngwǔ, it was stipulated to establish sixty Fèngyù in the Nèishǐjiān,
one Shàngbǎo,
seven Shàngguān,
ten Shàngyī,
nine Shàngpèi,
seven Shàngyào,
two Jìshì,
four Zhíshàn,
two Sīpú,
four Sīxiāng,
four Tàimiàosīxiāng,
and two Juānjié.
Four bureaus were established: Shàngjiǔ, Shàngcù, Shàngmiàn, and Shàngrǎn.
Each bureau established one Zhèng
and two Fù.
Two directorates were established: Yùmǎ and Yùyòng.
Each directorate established one Zhèng
and two Fù.
The Nèifǔkù established one Dàshǐ
and two Fùshǐ.
The Nèicāngjiān established one Lìng
and two Chéng.
Six bureaus were also established for the Dōnggōng: Diǎnxǐ, Diǎnhàn, Diǎnshàn, Diǎnfú, Diǎnyào, and Diǎnchéngbīng.
Each bureau established one Júlang
and one Chéng.
Additionally, gate officials were established.
For the Wǔmén and other thirteen gates,
each established one Ménzhèng
and one Fù.
For the Dōnggōng gate officials,
namely the Chūnhémén and other four gates,
each established one Ménzhèng
and one Fù.
In the third year, the Wángfǔ Chéngfèngsī was established.
(It established one Chéngfèng,
two Chéngfèngfù,
and three offices—Diǎnbǎo, Diǎnfú, and Diǎnshàn—
each establishing one Zhèng
and one Fù.
The gate officials established one Ménzhèng
and one Fù.)
The ranks of the Nèishǐjiān and Yùyòngjiān were all changed to subordinate rank 3.
(Lìng subordinate rank 3,
Chéng principal rank 4.)
The rank of the Huángménguān was subordinate rank 4.
(Ménzhèng subordinate rank 4,
Fù principal rank 5,
the Chūngōngménguān Zhèng and Fù were the same.)
In the fourth year, their ranks were again universally differentiated,
and they were bestowed with honorary titles.
Thus, the Nèishǐjiān was changed to principal rank 5,
and the Huángménguān to principal rank 6.
(In the fourth year of Hóngwǔ,
the honorary titles for palace officials were stipulated:
principal rank 4,
Zhōngzhèngdàfū;
subordinate rank 4,
Zhōngshìdàfū;
principal rank 5,
Zhōngwèidàfū;
subordinate rank 5,
Shìzhídàfū;
principal rank 6,
Nèishìláng;
subordinate rank 6,
Nèizhíláng;
principal rank 7,
Zhèngfèngláng;
subordinate rank 7,
Zhèngwèiláng;
principal rank 8,
Sīfèngláng;
subordinate rank 8,
Sīzhíláng.
Soon after, the Nèishǐjiān Lìng
was set at principal rank 5
and bestowed with the title Zhōngwèidàfū.
The Chéng,
subordinate rank 5,
was bestowed with the title Shìzhídàfū.
The Huángménzhèng, Júzhèng, Sīzhèng, Dōnggōngménzhèng, and Júzhèng
were all principal rank 6
and bestowed with the title Nèishìláng.
The Shàngbǎo, Fèngyù, Huángménfù, Júfù, Sīfù, Dōnggōngménfù, Júchéng,
Wángfǔchéngfèng, Ménzhèng, and Suǒzhèng
were all subordinate rank 6
and bestowed with the title Nèizhíláng.
The Shàngguān and other Fèngyù, Nèifǔkù Dàshǐ, Nèicāngjiān Lìng, Wángfǔchéngfèngfù, Ménfù, and Suǒfù
were all principal rank 7
and bestowed with the title Zhèngfèngláng.
The Kùfùshǐ and Cāngchéng
were all subordinate rank 7
and bestowed with the title Zhèngwèiláng.)
In the sixth year, the Yùyòngjiān was changed to Gòngfèngsī
(rank subordinate rank 7,
with five officials established).
The Nèicāngjiān was changed to Nèifǔcāng
(with the Jiānlìng becoming Dàshǐ
and the Jiānchéng becoming Fùshǐ).
The Nèifǔkù was changed to Chéngyùnkù
(still establishing Dàshǐ and Fùshǐ).
Soon after, the Jìshìsī was established,
with the eunuch Zhāng Yì as Sīzhèng
(rank principal rank 7).
Also, after examining the methods of impeaching palace officials from previous dynasties,
the Nèizhèngsī was established,
setting up one Sīzhèng
(principal rank 7)
and one Sīfù
(subordinate rank 7),
specifically to correct palace officials for impropriety and unlawful conduct.
It was then changed to Diǎnlǐsī,
and again changed to Diǎnlǐjìchásī,
raising its rank.
(The Sīzhèng was raised to principal rank 6,
and the Sīfù to subordinate rank 6.)
In the tenth year, the Shéngōng Nèishǐjiān was established,
setting up a Jiānlìng
(principal rank 5),
a Chéng
(subordinate rank 5),
a Sīxiāngfèngyù
(principal rank 7),
and a Diǎnbù
(subordinate rank 9).
The Tiāndìtán and Shéntán each had a Cíjìshǔ,
setting up a Shǔlìng
(principal rank 7),
a Chéng
(subordinate rank 7),
and a Sīxiāngfèngyù
(principal rank 8).
The five treasuries of Jiǎ, Yǐ, Bǐng, Dīng, and Wù
each established a Dàshǐ
(principal rank 7)
and a Fùshǐ
(subordinate rank 7).
For the Huángchéng gate officials, namely the Duānmén and other sixteen gates,
each established a Ménzhèng
(principal rank 7)
and a Fù
(subordinate rank 7).
In the twelfth year, the three directorates of Shàngyī, Shàngguān, and Shànglǚ were reorganized,
along with the three bureaus of Zhēngōng, Pízuò, and Jīnmào.
The Shàngpèijú was changed to Shàngpèijiān.
In the sixteenth year, the Nèifǔbǎochāo Guǎngyuán and Guǎnghuì two treasuries were established,
responsible for the collection and disbursement of paper currency.
Receipts were managed by the Guǎngyuánkù,
and disbursements by the Guǎnghuìkù.
(The Bǎochāo Guǎngyuánkù
established one Dàshǐ,
principal rank 9,
using a regular official;
and one Fùshǐ,
subordinate rank 9,
using a palace official.
The Bǎochāo Guǎnghuìkù
established two Dàshǐ,
principal rank 9;
and two Fùshǐ,
subordinate rank 9.)
Both civil officials and eunuch officials were employed.
In the 17th year, the ranks and duties of the various Directorates, Storehouses, and Bureaus for eunuch officials were revised.
For the Nèiguān Jiān,
one Lìng was established,
(Principal Rank 6),
two Chéng,
(Auxiliary Rank 6),
and one Diǎnbù,
(Principal Rank 9).
For the Shéngōng Jiān,
one Lìng was established,
(Principal Rank 7),
one Chéng,
(Auxiliary Rank 7),
and one Fèngyù,
(Principal Rank 8).
For the Shàngbǎo Jiān,
one Lìng was established,
(Principal Rank 7),
and one Chéng,
(Auxiliary Rank 7).
For the Shàngyī Jiān,
one Lìng was established,
(Principal Rank 7),
one Chéng,
(Auxiliary Rank 7),
and four Fèngyù,
(Principal Rank 8).
For the Shàngshàn Jiān,
one Lìng was established,
(Principal Rank 7),
and one Chéng,
(Auxiliary Rank 7).
For the Sīshè Jiān,
one Lìng was established,
(Principal Rank 7),
one Chéng,
(Auxiliary Rank 7),
and four Fèngyù,
(Principal Rank 8).
For the Sīlǐ Jiān,
one Lìng was established,
(Principal Rank 7),
and one Chéng,
(Auxiliary Rank 7).
For the Yùmǎ Jiān,
one Lìng was established,
(Principal Rank 7),
and one Chéng,
(Auxiliary Rank 7).
For the Zhídiàn Jiān,
one Lìng was established,
(Principal Rank 7),
four Chéng,
(Auxiliary Rank 7),
and fifteen Xiǎonèishǐ.
For the Gōngmén Chéngzhì,
five Fèngyù were established,
(Principal Rank 8).
For the Gōngmén Shǒuménguān,
one Ménzhèng was established,
(Principal Rank 8),
and four Fù,
(Auxiliary Rank 8).
For the Nèichéngyùn Kù,
one Dàshǐ was established,
(Principal Rank 9),
and two Fùshǐ,
(Auxiliary Rank 9).
For the Sīyào Kù,
one Dàshǐ was established,
(Principal Rank 9),
and four Fùshǐ,
(Auxiliary Rank 9).
For the Jīnmào Jú,
one Dàshǐ was established,
(Principal Rank 9),
and one Fùshǐ,
(Auxiliary Rank 9).
For the Zhēngōng Jú,
one Dàshǐ was established,
(Principal Rank 9),
and one Fùshǐ,
(Auxiliary Rank 9).
For the Zhīrǎn Jú,
one Dàshǐ was established,
(Principal Rank 9),
and one Fùshǐ,
(Auxiliary Rank 9).
For the Yánliào Jú,
one Dàshǐ was established,
(Principal Rank 9).
For the Sīyuàn Jú,
one Dàshǐ was established,
(Principal Rank 9).
For the Sīmù Jú,
one Dàshǐ was established,
(Principal Rank 9).
All were selected and appointed from among the eunuch officials.
In the twenty-eighth year, the offices, departments, stores, bureaus, and various gate officials of the Nèiguān Jiān (Directorate of Palace Eunuchs) were re-established,
along with the ranks and positions of the Dōnggōng Liù Jú (Six Bureaus of the Eastern Palace) and Wángfǔ Chéngfèng (Princely Establishment Attendants) officials.
There were eleven Nèiguān Jiān: namely,
Shéngōng Jiān,
Shàngbǎo Jiān,
Xiàolíng Shéngōng Jiān,
Shàngshàn Jiān,
Shàngyī Jiān,
Sīshè Jiān,
Nèiguān Jiān,
Sīlǐ Jiān,
Yùmǎ Jiān,
Yìnshòu Jiān,
and Zhídiàn Jiān. Each of these was staffed with one Tàijiān
(senior fourth rank),
one Zǔoshàojiān and one Yòushàojiān
(junior fourth rank),
one Zǔojiānchéng and one Yòujiānchéng
(senior fifth rank),
and one Diǎnbù
(senior sixth rank).
Additionally, Zhǎngsuí and Fèngyù were appointed
(senior sixth rank).
There were seven gate officials: Wǔmén, Dōnghuámén, Xīhuámén, Xuánwǔmén, Fèngtiānmén, Zǔoshùnmén, and Yòushùnmén.
Each was staffed with one Ménzhèng
(senior fourth rank)
and one Ménfù
(junior fourth rank).
There were two Sī:
Sīzhōnggǔ and
Xīxīn Sī. Each was staffed with one Sīzhèng
(senior fifth rank)
and one Zǔosīfù and one Yòusīfù
(junior fifth rank).
There were nine Júkù (Bureaus and Treasuries):
Bīngzhàng Jú,
Nèizhīrǎn Jú,
Zhēngōng Jú,
Jīnmào Jú,
Sīyuàn Jú,
Jiǔcùmiàn Jú,
Nèichéngyùn Kù,
Sīyào Kù,
and Nèifǔ Gōngyòng Kù. Each Júkù was staffed with one Dàshǐ
(senior fifth rank)
and one Zǔofùshǐ and one Yòufùshǐ
(junior fifth rank).
The six bureaus of the Eastern Palace, Diǎnxǐ, Diǎnyào, Diǎnshàn, Diǎnfú, Diǎnbīng, and Diǎnchéng,
each had one Júláng
(senior fifth rank)
and two Júchéng
(junior fifth rank).
Only the Diǎnxǐ Jú additionally had Jìshì and Fèngyù
(senior sixth rank).
The Qīnwángfǔ Chéngfèng Sī (Princely Establishment Attendant Department) had a Chéngfèngzhèng
(senior sixth rank)
and a Chéngfèngfù
(junior sixth rank).
There were three Suǒ:
Diǎnbǎo Suǒ,
staffed with one Diǎnbǎozhèng
(senior sixth rank)
and one Fù
(junior sixth rank);
Diǎnshàn Suǒ,
staffed with one Diǎnshànzhèng
(senior sixth rank)
and one Fù
(junior sixth rank);
and Diǎnfú Suǒ,
staffed with one Diǎnfúzhèng
(senior sixth rank)
and one Fù
(junior sixth rank).
The Mén'guān (Gate Officials)
were staffed with one Ménzhèng
(senior sixth rank)
and one Ménfù
(junior sixth rank).
Additionally, ten Nèishǐ (Palace Attendants) were appointed,
including one Sīguān,
three Sīyī,
one Sīpèi,
one Sīlǚ,

and two Sīshǐ.
For each Princess's establishment, a Zhōngshǐ Sī was set up,
with one Sīzhèng and one Sīfù.
In the thirtieth year, the Dūzhī Jiān was established,
staffed with one Tàijiān
(senior fourth rank),
one Zǔoshàojiān and one Yòushàojiān
(junior fourth rank),

(senior fifth rank),

(senior sixth rank).
The Yínzuò Jú (Silver Work Bureau) was also established,
