(senior fifth rank)
and one Fùshǐ
(junior fifth rank).
Tàizǔ once said to his attending ministers:
"I observe in the Zhōu Lǐ (Rites of Zhou) that
eunuchs did not number more than a hundred.
In later generations, they exceeded several thousands,
thus becoming the cause of disorder.
These people should only be used for cleaning and sweeping,
and for menial service.
Unless there is a specific assignment,
do not let their numbers grow excessively."
He also said:
"Among these people, the good ones are one or two in a thousand,
while the wicked ones are usually a thousand.
If used as eyes and ears,
then eyes and ears will be blinded;
if used as confidants,
then confidants will be afflicted.
The way to control them
is to make them fear the law,
not to allow them to achieve merit.
If they fear the law, they will be restrained;
if they achieve merit, they will become arrogant and lawless."
There was a palace attendant who had served the emperor for the longest time.
When he subtly touched upon political matters,
he was immediately dismissed
and never recalled for the rest of his life.
Consequently, a custom was established:
palace attendants were not allowed to be literate.
In the seventeenth year of Hóngwǔ, an iron plaque was cast
with the inscription:
"Eunuchs shall not interfere in government affairs;
violators will be executed."
It was placed in the palace gate.
An edict also ordered all departments not to communicate through documents with the Nèiguān Jiān.
However, in the twenty-fifth year, Niè Qìngtóng was ordered to go to Hézhōu to issue an imperial edict regarding tea and horses,
and this marked the beginning of eunuchs being sent on missions to conduct affairs.
Chéngzǔ also once said:
"I strictly follow Tàizǔ's instructions:
without an imperial seal and document,
even a single soldier or a single commoner
cannot be arbitrarily mobilized by a eunuch."
When someone privately employed artisans from Yìngtiān,
an immediate order was given to the Jǐnyī (Embroidered Uniform Guard) to arrest and punish them.
However, the widespread deployment of eunuchs
actually began during the Yǒnglè era.
In the first year,
Lǐ Xīng and others carried imperial edicts to commend the King of Xiānluó.
This was the beginning of eunuchs being sent on foreign missions.
In the third year, Zhèng Hé and others were ordered to lead twenty thousand troops
to bestow rewards upon the states of Gǔlǐ and Mǎnlà in the Western Ocean.
This was the beginning of eunuchs commanding troops.
In the eighth year, Wáng Ān and others were ordered to supervise the troops of Dūdu Tán Qīng and others,
and Mǎ Jìng was to inspect Gānsù.
This was the beginning of eunuchs acting as army supervisors and inspectors.
When Hóngxī's first year arrived,
Zhèng Hé was appointed to lead the expeditionary forces and officials to garrison Nánjīng,
and this practice was subsequently continued without change.
Wáng Ān was ordered to garrison Gānsù,
and thereafter, all provinces and garrisons had their own garrison eunuchs.
In the fourth year of Xuāndé, the Nèishū Táng (Inner Calligraphy Hall) was specially established,
and Grand Secretary Chén Shān was specifically ordered to teach literacy to young palace attendants.
Thus, Tàizǔ's regulation prohibiting literacy and reading for eunuchs
was abolished.
Wáng Jǐn and Jīn Yīng were bestowed with imperial seals,
placing them on par with high-ranking confidential ministers.
Jīn Yīng and Fàn Hóng were granted edicts exempting them from death,
which was no different from the iron certificates granted to meritorious officials.
During Yīngzōng's reign, Wáng Zhèn;
during Xiànzōng's, Wāng Zhí;
during Wǔzōng's, Liú Jǐn;
and during Xīzōng's, Wèi Zhōngxián—
they wielded supreme power,
and imperial authority and benevolence were transferred downwards.
Shénzōng's mining tax envoys
brought harm to every region.
The countless other cases of them relying on power to exert influence
cannot be fully recorded.
And the practice of granting official positions to younger brothers and nephews, and ennobling them as earls and dukes,
was the greatest disruption to the official system.
When Zhuāngliè Dì first eliminated the great villain,
both inside and outside the court praised the emperor.
However, afterwards, matters such as garrisoning, leading expeditions, supervising provisions, and establishing military camps
were all entrusted to eunuchs,
and thus the Míng Dynasty also perished.

In the fifth year of Hóngwǔ, they were fixed as six bureaus and one directorate.

and Gōngzhèng,

the twenty-four directorates were Rank 6a.

Rank 6a.
)In the twenty-second year, an imperial edict for palace officials was issued.
Those who served diligently,
for five or six years,
could return to their parents
and were allowed to marry.
Those of advanced age were permitted to return,
those who wished to stay were allowed to.
Those currently holding positions
were provided with stipends by the household.
In the twenty-seventh year, the ranks and positions were re-established.
(Twenty-four Diǎn were added,
Rank 7a.

Rank 7a.
From the six Shàng downwards,
the number of personnel remained as previously listed.
There were one hundred eighty-seven palace officials,
and ninety-six female scribes.
)Each of the six bureaus was granted a cast seal.

all duties were transferred to eunuchs.
Of the palace officials that remained,
only the four directorates of Shàngbǎo existed.

The
Zhǎngshǐ was in charge of the administration and decrees of the princely establishment,
assisting and admonishing to rectify the prince's faults,
leading the officials of the establishment to perform their respective duties,
and overseeing all miscellaneous affairs.
All requests for names, titles, marriages, favors, as well as expressions of gratitude, presentations of memorials and petitions, and letters,
were submitted by the Zhǎngshǐ on behalf of the prince.
If the prince committed a fault,
the Zhǎngshǐ would be interrogated.
Those who had previously committed offenses
were not to be selected for this position.
The Shěnlǐ was in charge of investigating and prosecuting criminal cases,
prohibiting and interrogating violent behavior,
without interfering with national laws.
The Diǎnshàn was in charge of sacrifices, entertaining guests,
and the meals of the prince and his consort.
The Fèngcǐ was in charge of sacrificial music and dance.
The Diǎnbǎo was in charge of the prince's seals, talismans, and plaques.
The Jìshàn was in charge of admonishing and guiding in ritual law,
explaining ancient principles,
and important points of national grace and righteousness,
to instruct the prince in goodness.
The Liángyī was in charge of medicine.
The Diǎnyí was in charge of arranging ceremonies.
The Gōngzhèng was in charge of construction, repair, and renovation of princely palaces and official residences.
The Bàndú was in charge of attending to the prince's daily life,
and arranging classics and histories.
The Jiàoshòu was in charge of instructing the prince in virtue and righteousness,
and proofreading classics.
All imperial kinsmen aged ten and above
entered the Zōngxué (Imperial Clan School),
where the Jiàoshòu and Jìshàn served as their teachers.
The Yǐnlǐ was in charge of receiving and dealing with guests,
and assisting in ceremonial decorum.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ (1370), the Wángxiàngfǔ (Prince's Chancellery) was established,
with one Zuǒxiàng (Left Chancellor) and one Yòuxiàng (Right Chancellor),
(both Senior Second Rank),
one Zuǒfù (Left Grand Tutor) and one Yòufù (Right Grand Tutor),
(both Junior Second Rank).
The Cānjūnfǔ (Counselor's Office) had
one Cānjūn (Counselor),
(Senior Fifth Rank),
two Lùshì (Registrars),
(Senior Seventh Rank),
and one Jìshàn (Moral Instructor),
(Senior Seventh Rank).
Their ranks were listed according to their respective official grades among the court officials.
Also established were the Diǎnqiān Sī (Document Verification Bureau) and Cèyìguān (Consultative Officials).
Soon after, as the military chancellors of the princely establishments were all meritorious ministers,
they were ordered to rank above the civil chancellors.
The officials of the Wángxiàngfǔ continued to be appointed alternately with court officials.
In this year, the Wángfǔ Jiàoshòu (Princely Preceptor) was established.
In the fourth year (1371), the official system was revised.

Cānjūn,

In the ninth year (1376), Cānjūn was changed to Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk),
and the Wángfùfǔ (Princely Grand Tutor's Office), Diǎnqiān Sī, and Cèyìguān were abolished.
Four Bànfú (Reading Companions) were added,
selected from among mature, learned, and prudent scholars.
Four Shìdú (Attendant Readers) were also appointed
to manage documents and records,
but if there were few, they were left unfilled.

Soon after, the principals of the Fèngcí (Sacrifices), Diǎnbǎo (Treasures), Diǎnshàn (Provisions), Liángyī (Medicine), and Gōngzhèng (Works) offices under the Wángxiàngfǔ, along with the Jìshàn, were all made Senior Eighth Rank,
and their Deputies
Junior Eighth Rank.
In the thirteenth year (1380), the Wángxiàngfǔ was completely abolished.
The Zhǎngshǐ Sī (Chief Clerk's Office) was promoted to Senior Fifth Rank,
and one Zuǒzhǎngshǐ (Left Chief Clerk) and one Yòuzhǎngshǐ (Right Chief Clerk) were appointed,
along with one Diǎnbù (Registrar).
Officials of the Wángfǔ Zīshēngsuǒ (Princely Livestock Office) and Cāngkù (Granaries and Treasuries) were all designated as miscellaneous officials.
In the twenty-eighth year (1395), the Jìngjiāng Wángfǔ Zīyìsuǒ (Consultative Office of the Prince of Jìngjiāng's Establishment) was established,
with one Zīyì (Consultant), one Jìshì (Secretary), and one Jiàoshòu (Preceptor).
During the Jiànwén reign (1399-1402),
two Qīnwáng Bīnfǔ (Princely Companions and Aides) were added,
one Bànfú (Reading Companion), one Bànjiǎng (Lecturing Companion), and one Bànshū (Writing Companion),
and three Zhǎngshǐ.
For commandery princes (Jùnwáng), two Bīnyǒu (Companions and Friends) were added,
one Jiàoshòu,
two Jìshì,
one Zhíshǐ (Attendant),
one Zuǒzhíshǐ (Left Attendant) and one Yòuzhíshǐ (Right Attendant),
one Lìmù (Clerk),
and one official each for the five offices of Diǎnyìn (Seal Keeper), Diǎncí (Sacrifices), Diǎnlǐ (Rites), Diǎnchuàn (Provisions), and Diǎnyào (Medicine),
two Diǎnyí (Masters of Ceremonies),
two Yǐnlǐ Shèrén (Masters of Ceremonies Attendants).
The Yízhàng Sī (Ceremonial Guard Office) had
one Lìmù.
When the Bīnfǔ, Sānbàn (Three Companions), Bīnyǒu, and Jiàoshòu had an audience,
they were permitted to sit,
addressed by name rather than as "subject,"
and treated with the courtesy due to guests and teachers.
At the beginning of the Chéngzǔ reign (1403),
the old system was restored,
and the Jìngjiāng Wángfǔ Zīyìsuǒ was changed to Zhǎngshǐ Sī.
During the Wànlì reign (1573-1620),
the Zhōu establishment (Zhōufǔ) appointed one Zōngzhèng (Director of Imperial Clan Affairs).
(Later, other establishments gradually adopted this too.)
Commandery princely establishments (Jùnwángfǔ) added one Jiàoshòu.
Also, in the seventh year of Hóngwǔ (1374),
a Gōngzhǔfǔ (Princess's Establishment) had one Jiālìng (House Steward),
(Senior Seventh Rank),
one Sīchéng (Deputy Steward),
(Senior Eighth Rank),
and one Lùshì (Registrar),
(Senior Ninth Rank).
In the twenty-third year (1390), the Jiālìng Sī was changed to Zhōngshǐ Sī (Eunuch Bureau),
staffed by eunuchs.
Chéngxuān Bùzhèngshǐ Sī (Provincial Administration Commission).
One Zuǒbùzhèngshǐ (Left Provincial Administrator) and one Yòubùzhèngshǐ (Right Provincial Administrator),
(both Junior Second Rank),
Zuǒcānzhèng (Left Policy Advisor) and Yòucānzhèng (Right Policy Advisor),
(both Junior Third Rank),
Zuǒcānyì (Left Consultative Councilor) and Yòucānyì (Right Consultative Councilor),
with no fixed number,
(both Junior Fourth Rank.
Cānzhèng and Cānyì were added as needed,
varying by province,
detailed in the various circuits.)
Jīnglì Sī (Secretariat),
one Jīnglì (Secretary),
(Junior Sixth Rank),
one Dūshì (Chief Clerk),
(Junior Seventh Rank).
Zhàomósuǒ (Document Review Office),
one Zhàomó (Document Reviewer),
(Junior Eighth Rank),
one Jiǎnjiào (Inspector),
(Senior Ninth Rank).
Lǐwènsuǒ (Interrogation Office),
one Lǐwèn (Interrogator),
(Junior Sixth Rank),
one Fùlǐwèn (Deputy Interrogator),
(Junior Seventh Rank),
one Tíkòng'àndú (Case Document Supervisor).
Sīyù Sī (Prison Office),
one Sīyù (Jail Warden),
(Junior Ninth Rank).
One Kùdàshǐ (Chief Granary/Treasury Administrator),
(Junior Ninth Rank),
one Fùshǐ (Deputy Administrator).
One Cāngdàshǐ (Chief Granary Administrator),
(Junior Ninth Rank),
one Fùshǐ (Deputy Administrator).
Zázàojú (Miscellaneous Manufactory Bureau), Jūngjìjú (Armaments Bureau), Bǎoquánjú (Coinage Bureau), ZhīRǎnjú (Weaving and Dyeing Bureau),
each with one Dàshǐ (Administrator),
(Junior Ninth Rank),
and one Fùshǐ (Deputy Administrator).
(The subordinate yámén (offices) varied by province,
detailed under miscellaneous officials.)
The Bùzhèngshǐ (Provincial Administrator) was in charge of the administration of a province.
When the imperial court issued decrees of benevolence or prohibitions,
they would receive and disseminate them,
passing them down to the local authorities.
When officials under their jurisdiction completed their terms,
they would assess their competence or incompetence,
rank their evaluations,
and report them to the Fǔ (Governor) and Àn (Provincial Surveillance Commissioner) to be forwarded to the Lìbù (Ministry of Personnel) and Dūcháyuàn (Censorate).
Every three years,
they would lead the chief officials of their prefectures, subprefectures, and counties
to an audience in the capital,
to be inspected.
Every ten years,
they would compile household registers to record the population and land area.
They would select and recommend talents (bīnxīng gòng),
managing the scholars of the entire province.
For members of the imperial clan (Zōngshì), officials, teachers and students, and military personnel,
they would periodically distribute their stipends and grain rations.
For sacrificial rituals to deities (Sìdiǎn Shénqí),
they would ensure timely observance.
They would provide for the poor, widowed, orphaned, and solitary among the people,
and commend the filial, brotherly, chaste, and upright.
In cases of floods, droughts, epidemics, or other disasters,
they would petition the emperor for remission and relief.
For all taxes, levies, and labor services,
they would assess the fertility and barrenness, and the density of the population and land in prefectures, subprefectures, and counties,
and then equalize the amounts.
For any major reforms or other administrative matters,
they would consult with the Dū (Military Commissioner) and Àn (Provincial Surveillance Commissioner) for discussion.
After planning and decision, they would request approval from the Fǔ and Àn, or the Zǒngdū (Governor-General).
For national celebrations or mourning,
they would dispatch deputies to offer congratulations or condolences in the capital.
When the emperor ascended the throne,
the Zuǒbùzhèngshǐ would personally attend.
The Cānzhèng and Cānyì were assigned to oversee various circuits (dào)
and were also tasked with managing grain storage, military farms, troop purification, courier stations, water conservancy, and pacifying the populace, among other duties,
and also assisted in co-managing the capital region (Jīngjī) through sub-offices.
(The two capitals did not establish Bùzhèngshǐ or Àncháshǐ offices,
nor did they have Cānzhèng, Cānyì, Fùshǐ, or Qiānshì,
thus nearby Bùzhèngshǐ and Àncháshǐ offices would manage them through sub-offices,
detailed in the various circuits.)
The Jīnglì and Dūshì
were responsible for receiving and issuing documents,
including detailed reports from the Xún'àn (Circuit Inspector) and Xúnyán Yùshǐ (Salt Censor),
using the Jīnglì's seal.
The Zhàomó and Jiǎnjiào were responsible for reviewing and verifying dossiers.
The Lǐwèn handled legal cases.
Initially,
Tàizǔ captured Jíqìng,
and personally led the Jiāngnán Mobile Secretariat (Xíng Zhōngshū Shěng).
In the Wùxū year,
a branch secretariat (Zhōngshū Fēnshěng) was established in Wùzhōu.
Thereafter, whenever an area was generally pacified,
a mobile secretariat (Xíngshěng) was established.
Its officials, from the Administrator (Píngzhāng Zhèngshì) downwards,
were largely the same as those of the Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shěng).
The mobile secretariat established the Administrator (Xíngshěng Píngzhāng Zhèngshì),
(ranked first grade, class 1a),
Left and Right Executive Assistant (Zuǒ, Yòu Chéng),
(ranked second grade, class 2a),
and Participant in Political Affairs (Cānzhī Zhèngshì),
(ranked second grade, class 2b).
In the Left and Right Bureaus (Zuǒ, Yòu Sī), there were
Director (Lángzhōng),
(ranked fifth grade, class 5b),
Assistant Director (Yuánwàiláng),
(ranked sixth grade, class 6b),
Chief Clerk (Dūshì) and Inspector (Jiǎnjiào),
(ranked seventh grade, class 7b),
Document Verifier (Zhàomó) and Superintendent (Guǎngōu),
(ranked eighth grade, class 8b).
In the Judicial Review Office (Lǐwèn Suǒ), there were
Chief Judicial Reviewer (Zhèng Lǐwèn),
(ranked fourth grade, class 4a),
Deputy Judicial Reviewer (Fù Lǐwèn),
(ranked fifth grade, class 5a),
and Manager (Zhīshì),
(ranked eighth grade, class 8b).
Later, Manager (Zhīshì) was changed to Controller of Cases and Documents (Tíkòng Àndú),
(referred to as Shěngzhù).

In the ninth year of Hóngwǔ, the mobile secretariats of Zhèjiāng, Jiāngxī, Fújiàn, Běipíng, Guǎngxī, Sìchuān, Shāndōng, Guǎngdōng, Hénán, Shǎnxī, Húguǎng, and Shānxī were all changed to Provincial Administration Commissions (Chéngxuān Bùzhèng Shǐsī).
The officials of Administrator (Xíngshěng Píngzhāng Zhèngshì),
Left and Right Executive Assistant (Zuǒ, Yòu Chéng) and others were abolished.
Participant in Political Affairs (Cānzhī Zhèngshì) was changed to Administration Commissioner (Bùzhèngshǐ),
ranked second grade, class 2a.
Left and Right Consultative Administrator (Zuǒ, Yòu Cāncè),
ranked second grade, class 2b.
Left and Right Bureaus (Zuǒ, Yòu Sī) were changed to Secretariat of the Provincial Administration Commission (Jīnglì Sī).
In the thirteenth year, the Administration Commissioner (Bùzhèngshǐ) was changed to
ranked third grade, class 3a,
and Consultative Administrator (Cāncè) to
ranked third grade, class 3b.
In the fourteenth year, Left and Right Counsellor (Zuǒ, Yòu Cānyì) were added,
ranked fourth grade, class 4a.
Soon after, one Left and one Right Administration Commissioner (Zuǒ, Yòu Bùzhèngshǐ) were each additionally appointed.
In the fifteenth year, the Yúnnán Provincial Administration Commission (Yúnnán Bùzhèngsī) was established.
In the twenty-second year, their rank was fixed at second grade, class 2b.
During the Jiànwén reign,
they were promoted to second grade, class 2a,
and one official was eliminated.
Chéngzǔ restored the old system.
In the first year of Yǒnglè, the Běipíng Provincial Administration Commission (Běipíng Bùzhèngsī) was made Běijīng.
In the fifth year, the Jiāozhǐ Provincial Administration Commission (Jiāozhǐ Bùzhèngsī) was established.
In the eleventh year, the Guìzhōu Provincial Administration Commission (Guìzhōu Bùzhèngsī) was established.
(Only one Commissioner was appointed,
other officials were as in other Provincial Administration Commissions.)
In the third year of Xuāndé, the Jiāozhǐ Provincial Administration Commission (Jiāozhǐ Bùzhèngsī) was abolished.
Excluding the two capitals,
the number was fixed at thirteen Provincial Administration Commissions.
When the Provincial Administration Commissions (Fānsī) were first established,
they held equal importance with the Six Ministries (Liùbù).
Administration Commissioners (Bùzhèngshǐ) could be appointed as Ministers (Shàngshū) or Vice Ministers (Shìláng).
A Deputy Censor-in-Chief (Fù Dūyùshǐ) was often sent out to serve as an Administration Commissioner (Bùzhèngshǐ).
This was still the case during the Xuāndé and Zhèngtǒng reigns,
but no longer thereafter.
Provincial Surveillance Commission (Tíxíng Ànchásǐsī).
One Surveillance Commissioner (Àncháshǐ),
(ranked third grade, class 3a),
Deputy Commissioner (Fùshǐ),
(ranked fourth grade, class 4a),
Assistant Commissioner (Qiānshì) with no fixed number,
(ranked fifth grade, class 5a.
See details under various Circuits.)
Secretariat (Jīnglì Sī),
one Secretary (Jīnglì),
(ranked seventh grade, class 7a),
one Manager (Zhīshì),
(ranked eighth grade, class 8a).
Document Verification Office (Zhàomó Suǒ),
one Document Verifier (Zhàomó),
(ranked ninth grade, class 9a),
one Inspector (Jiǎnjiào),
(ranked ninth grade, class 9b).
Prison Bureau (Sīyù Sī),
one Prison Warden (Sīyù),
(ranked ninth grade, class 9b).
The Surveillance Commissioner (Àncháshǐ) was in charge of judicial cases and impeachment within a province.
They corrected official misconduct,
restrained corruption and violence,
mediated lawsuits,
and redressed grievances,
thereby upholding moral discipline
and clarifying official administration.
Major matters were deliberated by the three commissions (Dū, Bù Èrsī) in council,
reported to the Governor (Fǔ) and Surveillance Commissioner (Àn),
and then submitted to the Ministry (Bù) and Censorate (Yuàn) for approval.
All rites of court audiences, congratulations, and condolences
were the same as those of the Provincial Administration Commission (Bùzhèngsī).
Deputy Commissioners (Fùshǐ) and Assistant Commissioners (Qiānshì)
were dispatched to patrol various circuits.

Matters such as military preparedness, education, civil administration, maritime patrols, military purification, post stations, water conservancy, military colonies, recruitment and training, and military supervision
were each handled by specially appointed officials,
who also were assigned to patrol and guard the capital region.
In the early Míng dynasty,
the Tíxíng Ànchásī (Provincial Surveillance Commission) was established.
In the first year of Wú, various Ànchásī circuits were established,
with an Àncháshǐ (Surveillance Commissioner),
principal third rank,
a Fùshǐ (Vice Commissioner),
principal fourth rank,
and a Qiānshì (Assistant Surveillance Commissioner),
principal fifth rank.
In the thirteenth year, the commissioner's rank was changed to principal fourth rank,
but it was soon abolished.
In the fourteenth year, it was re-established,
and various Ànchá Fēnsī (Branch Surveillance Offices) for each circuit were also established.
In the fifteenth year, Ànchá Fēnsī were again established for all prefectures, subprefectures, and counties in the realm.
Scholar-officials such as Wáng Cúnzhōng and 530 others were appointed as probationary Qiānshì,
each overseeing two counties.
They were empowered to investigate and impeach
any official for good or ill conduct, or any military or civilian for their benefits or harms.
In the sixteenth year, all probationary Qiānshì were abolished,
the Àncháshǐ was changed to junior third rank,
two Fùshǐ,
junior fourth rank,
and Qiānshì,
junior fifth rank,
with their numbers varying according to the number of circuits they oversaw.
In the twenty-second year, the Àncháshǐ was again set at principal third rank.
In the twenty-ninth year, the Ànchá Fēnsī were reorganized into forty-one circuits.

In the thirtieth year, the Yúnnán Ànchásī was first established.
(Previously,
the Bùzhèngsī was ordered to concurrently manage it.)
During the Jiànwén reign,
it was changed to the Shísān Dào Sùzhèng Ànchásī (Thirteen Circuit Rectification Surveillance Commission).
In the early reign of Chéngzǔ,
the old system was restored.
In the fifth year of Yǒnglè, the Jiāozhǐ Ànchásī was established,
and additional Qiānshì were added to various Ànchásī.
(Due to supervising military garrisons and grain,
one additional person each was added to Zhèjiāng, Jiāngxī, Guǎngdōng, Guǎngxī, Húguǎng, Hénán, Yúnnán, Sìchuān;
two each to Shǎnxī, Fújiàn, Shāndōng, Shānxī.
This was the beginning of the addition of Supervising Censors.)
In the twelfth year, the Guìzhōu Ànchásī was established.
In the fifth year of Xuāndé, the Jiāozhǐ Ànchásī was abolished.
(Excluding the two capitals where none were set up,
there were a total of thirteen Ànchásī.)
In the third year of Zhèngtǒng, additional Lǐcāng Fùshǐ (Vice Commissioners for Granary Management) and Qiānshì were established,
and one Qiānshì and one Bùzhèngsī Cānyì (Provincial Administration Commissioner's Councillor) were established in Gānsù
to supervise grain collection.
In the eighth year, additional Qiānshì were established,
specializing in managing tuntian (military agricultural colonies).
In the second year of Jǐngtài, additional Xúnhé Qiānshì (Assistant Surveillance Commissioners for River Patrol) were added.
Thereafter,
various provinces added new positions as needed,
some established, some abolished,
too numerous to count.

(stationed at Cízhōu).
In Húguǎng, the Wǔchāng Dào,
Jīngxī Dào,

Húběi Dào,

Yuán-Jìng Dào.

Fúníng Dào,
Xīng-Quán Dào,

Jiànnán Dào,

Wǔpíng Dào,
Zhāngnán Dào,

Jiànníng Dào,
Hǎidào,
(stationed at Zhāngzhōu),
Tíng-Zhāng Dào.
In Guǎngdōng, the Lǐngdōng Dào,
(stationed at Huìzhōu),
Lǐngxī Dào,

Lǐngnán Dào,
(stationed at the provincial capital),
Hǎiběi Dào,

Hǎinán Dào,

In Sìchuān, the Shàng Dōng Dào,

Xià Dōng Dào,

Chuānxī Dào,
Chuānběi Dào,

In Guǎngxī, the Fǔ-Jiāng Bīngxún Dào,

Guìlín Bīngxún Dào,

Cāngwú Bīngxún Dào,

Yòujiāng Bīngxún Dào,

Sī-Shí Dào,

Dū-Qīng Dào,

Kělán Dào.

Tóngguān Dào.
