The Dū Zhuǎnyùnshǐ (都轉運使) was in charge of salt affairs.
The Tóngzhī (同知) and Fùpàn (副判) administered them by separate departments.
There were six Dū Zhuǎnyùn Yánshǐ Sī (都轉運鹽使司) in total: namely, Liǎnghuái (兩淮),
Liǎngzhè (兩浙),
Chánglú (長蘆),
Hédōng (河東),
Shāndōng (山東),
and Fújiàn (福建).
There were fourteen separate departments: Tàizhōu (泰州), Huái'ān (淮安), and Tōngzhōu (通州) were subordinate to Liǎnghuái;
Jiāxīng (嘉興), Sōngjiāng (松江), Níngshào (寧紹), and Wēntái (溫台) were subordinate to Liǎngzhè;
Cāngzhōu (滄州) and Qīngzhōu (青州) were subordinate to Chánglú;
Jiāolái (膠萊) and Bīnlè (濱樂) were subordinate to Shāndōng;
Jiěyán Dōngchǎng (解鹽東場), Xīchǎng (西場), and Zhōngchǎng (中場) were subordinate to Hédōng.
Fùshǐ (副使) or Fùpàn (副判) administered them,
supervising the various salt fields, granaries, and salt tax bureaus,
all under the Dū Zhuǎnyùnshǐ (都轉運使),
jointly executing the decrees of the Xúnyán Yùshǐ (巡鹽御史) or Yánfǎ Dàochén (鹽法道臣).
(Fújiàn (福建) and Shāndōng (山東) had no Xúnyán Yùshǐ (巡鹽御史).
Further details are in the salt law section of the Shíhuò Zhì (食貨志).)
Yánkè Tíjiǔ Sī (鹽課提舉司).
One Tíjiǔ (提舉)
(from the fifth rank),
one Tóng Tíjiǔ (同提舉)
(from the sixth rank),
and an不定員 Fù Tíjiǔ (副提舉)
(from the seventh rank).
Its subordinates included
one Lìmù (吏目)
(from the ninth rank),
and one Kù Dàshǐ (庫大使) and Fùshǐ (副使).
Under its jurisdiction were
the Dàshǐ (大使) and Fùshǐ (副使) of each salt granary,
and the Dàshǐ (大使) and Fùshǐ (副使) of the salt tax bureaus of each field and well,
all one person each.
There were seven Tíjiǔ Sī (提舉司) in total: namely, Sìchuān (四川),
Guǎngdōng Hǎiběi (廣東海北)
(Liánzhōu (廉州)),
Hēiyánjǐng (黑鹽井)
(Chǔxióng (楚雄)),
Báiyánjǐng (白鹽井)
(Yáo'ān (姚安)),
Ānníng (安寧),
Wǔjǐng (五井)
(Dàlǐ (大理)),
and Cháhǎnnǎo'ér (察罕腦兒).
There was also the Liáodōng Jiānyán Tíjiǔ Sī (遼東煎鹽提舉司).
(The Tíjiǔ (提舉) was of the principal seventh rank,
the Tóng Tíjiǔ (同提舉) of the principal eighth rank,
and the Fù Tíjiǔ (副提舉) of the principal ninth rank.)
Its duties and responsibilities were all the same as those of the Dū Zhuǎnyùn Sī (都轉運司).
In the early Míng (明) dynasty,
a Dū Zhuǎnyùn Sī (都轉運司) was established in Liǎnghuái (兩淮).
In the first year of Wú (吳), the Liǎngzhè Dū Zhuǎnyùn Sī (兩浙都轉運司) was established in Hángzhōu (杭州).
The Dū Zhuǎnyùnshǐ (都轉運使) was fixed at the principal third rank,
and a Tóngzhī (同知)
(principal fourth rank),
Fùshǐ (副使)
(principal fifth rank),
Yùnpàn (運判)
(principal sixth rank),
Jīnglì (經歷)
(principal seventh rank),
Zhīshì (知事)
(principal eighth rank),
Zhàomó (照磨) and Gāngguān (綱官)
(principal ninth rank) were established.
Salt fields had Sīlìng (司令)
(from the seventh rank),
Sīchéng (司丞)
(from the eighth rank),
and Bǎifūzhǎng (百夫長)
(omitted in notes).
In the second year of Hóngwǔ (洪武), two Dū Zhuǎnyùn Sī (都轉運司) were established in Chánglú (長蘆) and Hédōng (河東),
as well as the Guǎngdōng Hǎiběi Yánkè Tíjiǔ Sī (廣東海北鹽課提舉司).
Soon after, two more Dū Zhuǎnyùn Sī (都轉運司) were established in Shāndōng (山東) and Fújiàn (福建).
In the third year, a Yánkè Tíjiǔ Sī (鹽課提舉司) was established in Cháhǎnnǎo'ér (察罕腦兒) in Shǎnxī (陝西).
Later, more were gradually added in various places.
During the Jiànwén (建文) reign,
the Guǎngdōng Tíjiǔ (廣東提舉) was changed to a Dū Zhuǎnyùn Sī (都轉運司).
In the early Yǒnglè (永樂) reign, it reverted to its former status.
In the fourteenth year, Censor Xúnyán (巡鹽) was first appointed.
In the third year of Jǐngtài (景泰), the Chánglú (長蘆) and Liǎnghuái (兩淮) Xúnyán Yùshǐ (巡鹽御史) were abolished,
and the Fǔ (撫) and Àn (按) officials were ordered to concurrently manage them.
Later, Censors were dispatched again.
Where there were no Censors,
the Ànchá Sī (按察司) managed them by separate divisions.
Also, during the Hóngwǔ (洪wu) reign,
a Cháyán Dū Zhuǎnyùn Sī (茶鹽都轉運司) was established in Sìchuān (四川)
(established in the fifth year of Hóngwǔ (洪wu),
with officials like those in the Dū Zhuǎnyùn Yánshǐ Sī (都轉運鹽使司).
Abolished in the tenth year).
Two Yánmǎ Sī (鹽馬司) were established in Nàxī (納溪) and Báidù (白渡)
(established in the fifth year of Hóngwǔ (洪wu),
with regularly selected officials as Sīlìng (司令)
and eunuchs as Sīchéng (司丞).
Abolished in the thirteenth year,
and soon re-established.
In the fifteenth year, they were changed to one Dàshǐ (大使) and one Fùshǐ (副使) each).
Later, all were abolished.
There was also the Shùnlóng Yánmǎ Sī (順龍鹽馬司),
which was also abolished.
Shìbó Tíjiǔ Sī (巿舶提舉司).
One Tíjiǔ (提舉)
(from the fifth rank),
and two Fù Tíjiǔ (副提舉)
(from the sixth rank).
Its subordinate was
one Lìmù (吏目)
(from the ninth rank).
It was in charge of tribute and trade with foreign countries overseas,
verifying the authenticity of envoys' credentials and tallies,
prohibiting communication with foreign countries,
levying duties on private goods,
equalizing trade,
restricting their entry and exit, and carefully providing for their accommodation.
In the first year of Wú (吳), a Shìbó Tíjiǔ Sī (巿舶提舉司) was established.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ (洪wu), the Tàicāng (太倉) and Huángdù (黃渡) Shìbó Sī (巿舶司) were abolished.
In the seventh year, the three Shìbó Sī (巿舶司) of Quánzhōu (泉州) in Fújiàn (福建), Míngzhōu (明州) in Zhèjiāng (浙江), and Guǎngzhōu (廣州) in Guǎngdōng (廣東) were abolished.
In the first year of Yǒnglè (永樂), they were re-established,
with officials set up according to the initial system of Hóngwǔ (洪wu),
and eunuchs were soon appointed to supervise them.
In the first year of Jiājìng (嘉靖),
Gěishìzhōng Xiàyán (給事中夏言) memorialized that the Japanese pirate problem arose from maritime trade,
and thus the two Shìbó Sī (巿舶司) of Fújiàn (福建) and Zhèjiāng (浙江) were abolished,
with only the Guǎngdōng Shìbó Sī (廣東巿舶司) remaining.
Chámǎ Sī (茶馬司).
One Dàshǐ (大使)
(principal ninth rank),
and one Fùshǐ (副使)
(from the ninth rank).
It was in charge of horse trade.
During the Hóngwǔ (洪wu) reign,
three Chámǎ Sī (茶馬司) were established in Táozhōu (洮州), Qínzhōu (秦州), and Hézhōu (河州),
with Sīlìng (司令) and Sīchéng (司丞) established.
In the fifteenth year, they were changed to one Dàshǐ (大使) and one Fùshǐ (副使) each.
Soon after, the Táozhōu Chámǎ Sī (洮州茶馬司) was abolished,
and the Hézhōu Chámǎ Sī (河州茶馬司) concurrently managed it.
In the thirtieth year, the Qínzhōu Chámǎ Sī (秦州茶馬司) was changed to Xīníng Chámǎ Sī (西寧茶馬司).
Also during the Hóngwǔ (洪wu) reign,
a Yǒngníng Chámǎ Sī (永寧茶馬司) was established in Sìchuān (四川),
later abolished,
and the Yǎzhōu Diāomén Chámǎ Sī (雅州碉門茶馬司) was re-established.
Also, in Guǎngxī (廣西), a Qìngyuǎn Yùmín Sī (慶遠裕民司) was established
(established in the seventh year of Hóngwǔ (洪wu),
with one Dàshǐ (大使) of the from eighth rank,
and one Fùshǐ (副使) of the principal ninth rank).
It traded for horses from the Bāfān Xī dòng (八番溪洞) region.
Later, it was also abolished.
Fǔ (府).
One Zhīfǔ (知府)
(principal fourth rank),
one Tóngzhī (同知)
(principal fifth rank),
and an不定員 Tōngpàn (通判)
(principal sixth rank),
and one Tuīguān (推官)
(principal seventh rank).
Its subordinates included
one Jīnglì (經歷) of the Jīnglì Sī (經歷司)
(principal eighth rank),
and one Zhīshì (知事)
(principal ninth rank).
The Zhàomó Suǒ (照磨所) had
one Zhàomó (照磨)
(from the ninth rank),
and one Jiǎnjiào (檢校).
The Sīyù Sī (司獄司) had
one Sīyù (司獄).
(Its jurisdiction is detailed elsewhere).
The Zhīfǔ presided over the administration of a prefecture.
They propagated culture and moral transformation,
resolved lawsuits,
and equalized taxes and labor services,
in order to educate and nourish the common people.
Every three years,
they investigated the competence of their subordinates,
ranking them up or down in their evaluations,
which were then sent to the province
and reported to the Lìbù.
For all imperial audiences, congratulatory ceremonies, mourning rituals, and memorial services,
they reported to the Bùzhèngshǐ Sī;
however, prefectures directly under the imperial court could report independently.
Whenever imperial edicts, amnesties, standard orders, or investigative tallies arrived,
they were to receive them respectfully
and transmit them to their subordinates for implementation.
The administration of all subordinates
was subject to the prefecture's control.
The Zhīfǔ weighed the importance of matters and issued orders accordingly.
Major issues were reported to the Fǔ, Àn, Bù, and Àn (Governors, Censors, Provincial Administration Commissioners, and Provincial Surveillance Commissioners),
and only acted upon after their approval.
They were in charge of all matters related to recommending candidates for the imperial examinations (bīnxīng kējìng),
supervising schools,
and maintaining sacrificial rituals.
All these were under their purview.

Although there were specialized officials for matters such as registers and accounts, military artisans, postal services, horse pasturage, bandits, granaries and warehouses, rivers and irrigation channels, dikes and defenses, and roads,
the Zhīfǔ
still generally oversaw and scrutinized them.

The Tóngzhī and Tōngpàn were responsible for various matters such as clearing troops, patrolling and arresting, managing grain, agricultural administration, water conservancy, garrison farms, and horse pasturage.
They had no fixed positions
(the responsibilities varied among prefectures;
for instance, the Tóngzhī of Yán'ān and Yánsuí also managed the people,
but not all such details are included here).
Nor did they have a fixed number of personnel.
(In border prefectures, the number of Tóngzhī could increase to six or seven.)
The Tuīguān handled judicial cases
and assisted with the assessment of officials.
(The position of Tuīguān in each prefecture
was first established in Hóngwǔ's third year.)
The Jīnglì, Zhàomó, and Jiǎnjiào received and dispatched official documents
and examined the comprehensive records of the six departments.
In the early Míng dynasty,
the various circuits (lù) were reorganized into prefectures.
In Hóngwǔ's sixth year, prefectures nationwide were divided into three classes: superior prefectures had a grain revenue of 200,000 shí or more,
their Zhīfǔ
held the rank of From the Third Grade;
middle prefectures had less than 200,000 shí,
their Zhīfǔ
held the rank of Regular Fourth Grade;
inferior prefectures had less than 100,000 shí,
their Zhīfǔ
held the rank of From the Fourth Grade.
Later,
all were uniformly set to Regular Fourth Grade.
In the seventh year, 308 officials in northern prefectures, subprefectures, and counties were reduced.
In the thirteenth year, twenty-four students from the Guózǐxié were selected to serve as officials in prefectures, subprefectures, and counties.
In the sixth month, the Zhàomó in various prefectures were abolished.
In the twenty-seventh year, they were re-established.
Since Xuāndé's third year, when the Jiāozhǐ Bùzhèngsǐ was abandoned,
there were a total of 159 prefectures nationwide.
Subprefectures (Zhōu).
One Zhīzhōu
(From the Fifth Grade),
one Tóngzhī
(From the Sixth Grade),
and an unfixed number of Pànguān
(From the Seventh Grade).
If a subprefecture covered less than thirty lǐ and had no subordinate counties,
the Tóngzhī and Pànguān were abolished.
If it had subordinate counties,
the Tóngzhī was abolished.
Its subordinate staff included
one Lìmù
(From the Ninth Grade).
Their specific jurisdictions are mentioned elsewhere.
The Zhīzhōu was in charge of the administration of a subprefecture.
There were two types of subprefectures:
subordinate subprefectures and
directly administered subprefectures.
Subordinate subprefectures were treated like counties,
while directly administered subprefectures were treated like prefectures,
though their official ranks were the same.
The Tóngzhī and Pànguān
performed their duties according to the complexity of the subprefecture's affairs.
There were a total of 234 subprefectures nationwide.
Counties (Xiàn).
One Zhīxiàn
(Regular Seventh Grade),
one Xiànchéng
(Regular Eighth Grade),
and one Zhǔbù
(Regular Ninth Grade).
Its subordinate staff included
one Diǎnshǐ.
(Their specific jurisdictions are mentioned elsewhere.)
The Zhīxiàn was in charge of the administration of a county.
For all taxes and labor services,
the actual collection was compiled annually,
and every ten years, yellow registers (huángcè) were created,
based on households and property for assessment.
Taxes included grain, silk and cloth, and various goods.
Labor services included physical labor, hired labor, and temporary requisitioned labor.
All were adjusted and equalized
based on the blessings or misfortunes of the seasons,
the fertility or depletion of the land,
and the wealth or poverty of the people.
In lean years, they would petition the prefecture or province to reduce or waive them.

The Zhīxiàn personally and diligently attended to all matters of caring for the elderly, offering sacrifices to deities, recommending scholars, expounding laws, commending the virtuous, assisting the poor, checking the bǎojiǎ system, strictly apprehending criminals, and hearing lawsuits.
All these were performed personally and with diligent care.
If products from mountains, seas, marshes, or lakes
were sufficient to support national expenditure,
they were to be collected and submitted as tribute according to the registers.
The Xiànchéng and Zhǔbù were responsible for managing grain and horses, and patrolling and apprehending.
The Diǎnshǐ managed the receipt and dispatch of official documents.
If there was no Xiànchéng
or no Zhǔbù,
they would divide the responsibilities of the Xiànchéng and Zhǔbù.
(The Xiànchéng and Zhǔbù positions
were subject to inconsistent additions and abolitions.
If a county had fewer than twenty lǐ of registered households, both were abolished.)
In Wú's first year, counties were divided into three classes: superior counties had a grain revenue of less than 100,000 shí,
their Zhīxiàn held the rank of From the Sixth Grade;
middle counties had less than 60,000 shí,
their Zhīxiàn held the rank of Regular Seventh Grade;
inferior counties had less than 30,000 shí,
their Zhīxiàn held the rank of From the Seventh Grade.
Later,
all were uniformly set to Regular Seventh Grade.
All newly appointed officials to prefectures and counties
were given travel expenses.
In Hóngwǔ's first year, talented individuals from across the empire were recruited for prefectural, subprefectural, and county positions.
Imperial edicts bestowed generous rewards
to encourage their integrity and sense of shame,
and imperial admonitions were issued repeatedly.
In the thirty-seventh year, eight regulations for prefectures, subprefectures, and counties were established,
promulgated throughout the empire,
to be eternally observed.
At that time,
for any honest, capable, and upright official in prefectures, subprefectures, or counties,
messengers (xíngrén) were invariably dispatched with imperial edicts to commend them,
increase their rank, and bestow gold.
This practice continued during the reigns of Rénzōng and Xuānzōng,
but became increasingly rare from Yīngzōng and Xiànzōng onwards.
Thereafter, the court increasingly valued internal affairs over external ones,
and this tradition completely vanished.
There were a total of 1,171 counties nationwide.
Confucian Schools (Rúxué).
For prefectures,
one Jiàoshòu
(From the Ninth Grade)
and four Xùndǎo.
For subprefectures,
one Xuézhèng
and three Xùndǎo.
For counties,
one Jiàoyù
and two Xùndǎo.
The Jiàoshòu, Xuézhèng, and Jiàoyù
were in charge of teaching and instructing the affiliated students (shēngyuán),
with the Xùndǎo assisting them.
For students receiving stipends and augmented grants (lǐnshàn zēngguǎng),
prefectural schools had forty students,
subprefectural schools had thirty students,
and county schools had twenty students,
with no fixed number for additional students.
Confucian school officials monthly assessed the students' academic performance and awarded them.
All school administration followed the "Wòbēi" (Prostrate Tablet) regulations,
and were subject to the supervision of the Tíxué Xiànchén.
Prefectural schools answered to the prefecture,
subprefectural schools to the subprefecture,
and county schools to the county.
Their ranking was determined by the number of successful candidates in the provincial examinations (xiāngjǔ).
In the early Míng dynasty,
the Rúxué Tíjǔ Sī (Bureau for the Recommendation of Confucian Scholars) was established.
In the second year of Hóngwǔ (1369), an imperial edict mandated that schools be established in all prefectures, subprefectures, and counties nationwide.
In the thirteenth year (1380), the rank of xuézhèng (school instructor) in various subprefectures was changed to "unranked" (wèirùliú).
(Previously, they were of rank nine, subordinate grade.)
In the twenty-fourth year (1391), the position of rúxué xùndǎo (Confucian instructor) was set above miscellaneous officials.
In the thirty-first year (1398), an edict ordered that all school officials nationwide be reassigned to adjacent prefectures, subprefectures, and counties.
In the first year of Zhèngtǒng (1436), the office of Tídū Xuéxiào Guān (Superintendent of Schools) was first established.
There were also Dūsī Rúxué (Confucian Schools of the Regional Military Commissions),
(established in the seventeenth year of Hóngwǔ
beginning with Liáodōng),
Xíng Dūsī Rúxué (Confucian Schools of the Provisional Regional Military Commissions),
(established in the twenty-third year of Hóngwǔ
beginning with Běipíng),
and Wèi Rúxué (Confucian Schools of the Guards),
(established in the seventeenth year of Hóngwǔ
starting with Mínzhōu Wèi;
and in the twenty-third year
starting with Dàníng and other guards).
These were to teach the children of military officials.
Each had one jiàoshòu (professor)
and two xùndǎo (instructors).
In Hédōng, a Dū Zhuǎnyùn Sī Rúxué (Confucian School of the Provincial Transport Commission) was also established,
structured like a prefecture.
Later, Xuānwèi (Pacification Commissioners), Ānfǔ (Comfort Commissioners), and other indigenous officials
all established Confucian schools.
Xúnjiǎn Sī (Patrol Inspectorates).
Xúnjiǎn (Patrol Inspector) and Fù Xúnjiǎn (Deputy Patrol Inspector),
(both of rank nine, subordinate grade),
were mainly responsible for apprehending bandits and thieves
and interrogating criminals and imposters.
They were established in all important passes and strategic points in prefectures, subprefectures, and counties outside the capital,
to lead corvée laborers and archers in guarding against unforeseen events.
Initially,
in the second year of Hóngwǔ (1369),
because Guǎngxī bordered Yáo and Tóng territories,
Xúnjiǎn Sī were first established at strategic passes and important locations
to guard against criminals and bandits.
Later, they were gradually added in other places.
In the second month of the thirteenth year (1380), a special imperial edict was issued concerning them.
Soon after, they were reclassified as miscellaneous officials.
Yì (Post Stations).
Yìchéng (Postmaster) managed postal transport and reception duties.
All boats, carriages, provisions, cooked meals, bedding, and tents
were to be carefully supplied
according to the rank of the guest
and the number of servants.
Expenses were paid by the prefecture, subprefecture, or county,
and records of income and expenditure were kept.
(The number of Xúnjiǎn and Yìchéng
varied among different prefectures, subprefectures, and counties.)
Shuìkè Sī (Tax Collection Bureaus).
(In prefectures, they were called Sī;
in counties, Jú.)
One Dàshǐ (Director),
(rank nine, subordinate grade),
managed tax affairs.
All merchants, brokers, butchers, and various markets
had regular levies,
which were collected periodically and their value remitted to the prefecture or county.
When common people traded land or houses,
they had to present contracts and request an official seal
to register the household,
whereupon three percent of the value was collected.
In the early Míng,
the official shops in the capital were renamed Xuānkè Sī (Proclamation Tax Bureaus),
and official shops in prefectures, subprefectures, and counties were renamed Tōngkè Sī (General Tax Bureaus).
Later, Tōngkè Sī were changed to Shuìkè Sī and Jú.
Cāng (Granaries).
One Dàshǐ (Director),
(rank nine, subordinate grade for prefectural granaries; unranked for subprefectural and county granaries),
one Fùshǐ (Deputy Director),
and one Kù Dàshǐ (Storehouse Director).
(Established in subprefectures and counties.)
Zhī Rǎn Zázào Jú (Bureau of Weaving, Dyeing, and Miscellaneous Manufacturing).
One Dàshǐ (Director),
(rank nine, subordinate grade; unranked for subprefectural weaving and dyeing bureaus),
and one Fùshǐ (Deputy Director).
Hépō Suǒ Guān (Officials of the River and Lake Stations)
were in charge of collecting fish taxes;
Zhágāu (Sluice Gate Officials) and Bàguān (Dam Officials)
were in charge of opening, closing, storing, and releasing water.
In the fifteenth year of Hóngwǔ (1382), it was decided that there would be a total of 252 Hépō Suǒ nationwide.
For those with an annual tax of 5,000 to 10,000 dàn of grain,
three officials were appointed;
for those with over 1,000 dàn, two officials;
and for those with over 300 dàn, one official.
Pīyàn Suǒ (Verification Offices).
One Dàshǐ (Director)
and one Fùshǐ (Deputy Director)
were in charge of verifying tea and salt permits.
Dìyùn Suǒ (Transport Relay Stations).
One Dàshǐ (Director)
and one Fùshǐ (Deputy Director)
were in charge of transporting grain and goods.
First established in the ninth year of Hóngwǔ (1376).
Previously,
outside the capital, garrison soldiers from wèisuǒ (military guards and battalions) were often used to transmit military prisoners.
Tàizǔ, considering this detrimental to their training and defense,
ordered the Ministry of War to establish more Dìyùn Suǒ in various places
to facilitate relaying.
One Dàshǐ and one Fùshǐ were appointed,
and based on the number of porters,
a Bǎifūzhǎng (Centurion) was appointed to lead them.
(Later, the Fùshǐ was eliminated,
and the Bǎifūzhǎng abolished.)
Tiěyě Suǒ (Iron Smelting Offices).
One Dàshǐ (Director)
and one Fùshǐ (Deputy Director).
First established in the seventh year of Hóngwǔ (1374).
There were thirteen such offices in total,
each with one Dàshǐ and one Fùshǐ.
(Initially,
the Dàshǐ was of rank eight, principal grade,
and the Fùshǐ of rank nine, principal grade;
later, both became unranked.)
Yīxué (Medical Schools).
For prefectures,
one Zhèngkē (Chief of Medical Studies),
(rank nine, subordinate grade).
For subprefectures,
one Diǎnkē (Registrar of Medical Studies).
For counties,
one Xùnkē (Instructor of Medical Studies).
Established in the seventeenth year of Hóngwǔ (1384),
officials appointed were not given salaries.
Yīnyángxué (Yin-Yang Schools).
For prefectures,
one Zhèngshù (Chief of Yin-Yang Arts),
(rank nine, subordinate grade).
For subprefectures,
one Diǎnshù (Registrar of Yin-Yang Arts).
For counties,
one Xùnshù (Instructor of Yin-Yang Arts).
Also established in the seventeenth year of Hóngwǔ (1384),
officials appointed were not given salaries.
Fǔ Sēnggāng Sī (Prefectural Monastic Registration Office),
one Dūgāng (Chief Monk Administrator),
(rank nine, subordinate grade),
and one Fù Dūgāng (Deputy Chief Monk Administrator).
Zhōu Sēngzhèng Sī (Subprefectural Monastic Rectification Office),
one Sēngzhèng (Monastic Rectifier).
Xiàn Sēnghuì Sī (County Monastic Association Office),
one Sēnghuì (Monastic Associate).
Fǔ Dàojì Sī (Prefectural Daoist Registration Office),
one Dūjì (Chief Daoist Administrator),
(rank nine, subordinate grade),
and one Fù Dūjì (Deputy Chief Daoist Administrator).
Zhōu Dàozhèng Sī (Subprefectural Daoist Rectification Office),
one Dàozhèng (Daoist Rectifier).
Xiàn Dàohuì Sī (County Daoist Association Office),
one Dàohuì (Daoist Associate).
All were established in the fifteenth year of Hóngwǔ (1382),
and officials appointed were not given salaries.
Collation Notes

Treatise 52: Officials 5: Gōng, Hóu, Bó; Fùmǎ Dūwèi (attached Yíbīn); Wǔjūn Dūdū Fǔ; Jīngyíng; Jīngwèi Jǐnyīwèi (attached Qíshǒu and other Wèi); Nánjīng Shǒubèi; Nánjīng Wǔjūn Dūdū Fǔ; Nánjīng Wèi; Wángfǔ Hùwèi (attached Yíwèi Sī); Zǒngbīngguān; Liúshǒusī Dūsī (attached Xíng Dūsī); various Wèi; various Suǒ; Xuānwèi Sī; Xuānfǔ Sī; Ānfǔ Sī; Zhāotǎo Sī; Zhǎngguān Sī (attached Mányí Zhǎngguān Sī); Jūnmín Fǔ (attached Tǔzhōu Tǔxiàn).
Gōng, Hóu, Bó were
three ranks
conferred upon meritorious ministers and imperial relatives by marriage.
All were hereditary
and transferable.
Meritorious ministers were given iron certificates.
There were four grades of titles:
those who assisted Tàizǔ in pacifying the empire were called "Kāiguó Fǔyùn Tuīchéng" (Founding and Assisting the Fortune, Promoting Sincerity);
those who followed Chéngzǔ in raising an army were called "Fèngtiān Jìngnàn Tuīchéng" (Serving Heaven, Pacifying Difficulties, Promoting Sincerity);
the rest were called "Fèngtiān Yìyùn Tuīchéng" (Serving Heaven, Assisting Fortune, Promoting Sincerity)
or "Fèngtiān Yìwèi Tuīchéng" (Serving Heaven, Assisting Protection, Promoting Sincerity).
Military officials were called "Xuānlì Wǔchén" (Manifesting Strength Military Ministers),
and civil officials were called "Shǒuzhèng Wénchén" (Upholding Rectitude Civil Ministers).
Annual salaries varied according to merit.
If one had already been ennobled and rendered further service,
the title was maintained or advanced,
and the salary increased.
Those who were talented and virtuous
were appointed as Zǒngdū (Grand Coordinators) of the Jīngyíng (Capital Garrisons),
or Zhǎng Qiānshū (Chief Registrars) in the Wǔjūn Dūdū Fǔ (Five Chief Military Commissions),
or Nánjīng Shǒubèi (Grand Defender of Nánjīng),
or dispatched as Zhènshǒu Zǒngbīngguān (Grand Commanders of Garrisons);
otherwise, they merely drew their salaries and attended court.
Those who inherited titles at a young age
all entered the Guózǐjiān (National Academy) to study.
In the eighth year of Jiājìng (1529), it was decreed that titles conferred upon imperial relatives by marriage
should not be hereditary;
any who were hereditary for one or two generations
were due to special imperial grace.
The Fùmǎ Dūwèi
ranked above a Bó.
All who married a Dà Zhǎng Gōngzhǔ, Zhǎng Gōngzhǔ, or Gōngzhǔ
were called Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
Those who married a Jùnzhǔ, Xiànzhǔ, Jùnjūn, Xiànjūn, or Xiāngjūn
were all called Yíbīn.
Their annual stipends varied,
and none were allowed to participate in government affairs.
In the early Míng dynasty,
Fùmǎ Dūwèi sometimes commanded troops stationed in garrisons or managed affairs of a prefecture or department.
During the Jiànwén era,
Méi Yīn served as the Zhènshǒu Zǒngbīngguān of Huái'ān,
and Lǐ Jiān as the Zuǒ Fù Jiāngjūn.
During the Chéngzǔ era,
Lǐ Ràng managed affairs for the Běijīng Xíng Bù.
Mù Xīn during the Rénzōng era,
and Sòng Hǔ during the Xuānzōng era,
both served as defenders of Nánjīng.
During the Yīngzōng era,
Zhào Huī managed affairs for the Nánjīng Zuǒ Fǔ.
The others were only responsible for offering sacrifices at Xiàolíng,
deputizing for ancestral temple sacrifices,
and assisting in the Zōngrén Fǔ affairs.
They were often given commands,
and fulfilled their duties once.
As for Ēnqīn Hóu Lǐ Zhēn,
Yǒngchūn Hóu Wáng Níng,
Jīngshān Hóu Cuī Yuán,
they were enfeoffed as marquises by imperial grace;
this was not according to regulation.
The Central, Left, Right, Front, and Rear Five Dūdū Fǔ
each had a Left and Right Dūdū
(rank 1a),
a Dūdū Tóngzhī
(rank 1b),
and a Dūdū Qiānshì
(rank 2a).
(These were honorary posts for meritorious service,
without fixed numbers.)
Their subordinates included
a Jīnglì Sī,
a Jīnglì
(rank 5b),
and a Dūshì
(rank 7b),
one of each.
The Dūdū Fǔ managed military affairs,
each overseeing its respective Dūsī and Wèisuǒ
(detailed in the Bīng Zhì, Wèisuǒ section),
and reporting to the Bīng Bù.
For all military officials—
hereditary officials, appointed officials, native officials succeeding to posts, those granted special care or allowances—
their subordinates reported to the Fǔ,
which then referred them to the Bīng Bù for selection.
Once selected,
they were referred back to the Fǔ,
which then sent them down to the Dūsī and Wèisuǒ.
Head officials were selected and appointed by the Lì Bù,
and their certificates were handled similarly.

All matters concerning military officials' imperial patents and edicts, stipends and rations, land and water infantry and cavalry drills, official residences and banner service examinations, military intelligence and reports, military recruitment and replacement, border and interior maps, documents, agricultural colonies, weaponry, boats and vehicles, and firewood and reeds
were referred to the relevant departments for overall management.
All Zhènshǒu Zǒngbīngguān and Fù Zǒngbīng in the various provinces and garrisons
were filled by Dūdū (actual or acting) of the three grades, or by Gōng, Hóu, or Bó.
In the event of a major expedition,
they were given the seals of Jiāngjūn, Dà Jiāngjūn, Qián Jiāngjūn, or Fù Jiāngjūn Zǒngbīng to lead the troops,
which were returned
after the mission.
The seal-holders and co-signers of each Fǔ
were generally Gōng, Hóu, or Bó.
(Occasionally, an old general who was genuinely a Dūdū would be among them,
but they were less than one in ten.)
Initially,
after Tàizǔ captured Jíqìng,
he immediately established the Xíng Shūmì Yuàn,
which he personally led.
He also established various Yì Tǒngjūn Yuánshuài Fǔ.
Soon, the Shūmì Yuàn was abolished,
and the Dà Dūdū Fǔ was established instead.
Zhū Wénzhèng was appointed Dà Dūdū,
to command all military affairs within and outside the capital,
and officials such as Sīmǎ, Cānjūn, Jīnglì, and Dūshì were established.
Additionally, Left and Right Dūdū,
Tóngzhī,
Fùshǐ,
Qiānshì,
and Zhàomó, one of each, were added,
along with a Duànshìguān.
According to the regulations,
the Dà Dūdū was rank 1b,
the Left and Right Dūdū rank 2a,
the Tóngzhī Dūdū rank 2b,
the Fù Dūdū rank 3a,
the Qiān Dūdū rank 3b,
the Jīnglì rank 5b,
and the Dūshì rank 7b.
For the Tǒngjūn Yuánshuài Fǔ, the Yuánshuài was rank 3a,
the Tóngzhī Yuánshuài rank 3b,
the Fùshǐ rank 4a,
the Jīnglì rank 7a,
the Zhīshì rank 8b,
and the Zhàomó rank 9a.
The Dū Zhènfǔ Sī was also made subordinate to the Dà Dūdū Fǔ
(previously it belonged to the Zhōngshū Shěng),
with a rank of 4b.
Soon, the Tǒngjūn Yuánshuài Fǔ was abolished.
In the first year of Wú, the official system was reformed;
the Dà Dūdū was abolished and not re-established.
The Left and Right Dūdū became the chief officials
(rank 1a),
the Tóngzhī Dūdū
(rank 1b),
the Fù Dūdū
(rank 2a),
and the Qiān Dūdū
(rank 2b),
all rising in rank.
Their subordinates included
a Cānyì
(rank 4a),
a Jīnglì,
a Duànshìguān
(rank 5b),
a Dūshì
(rank 7a),
and a Zhàomó
(rank 7b).
In the 9th year of Hóngwǔ, the Fù Dūdū was abolished,
and the Cānyì was renamed Zhǎngpànguān.
In the 12th year, the Dūdū Qiānshì was promoted to rank 2a,
and the Zhǎngpànguān to rank 3a.
In the 13th year, the Dūdū Fǔ was renamed the Wǔjūn Dūdū Fǔ,
which was divided to manage the various Wèisuǒ in the capital
(only Jǐnyī and other personal guards and Shangzhí Wèi were not subordinate to the Five Fǔ),
and the various Dūsī and Wèisuǒ outside the capital.
The Duànshìguān of the Zhōngjūn Dūdū Fǔ became the Wǔjūn Duànshìguān.
In the 15th year, the Wǔjūn Shíwèi Cānjūn Fǔ was established,
with Left and Right Cānjūn.
In the 17th year,
each of the Five Armies established two Left and Right Duànshì,
and one Tíkòng Àndú
(both rank 9b).
In the 23rd year, the Wǔjūn Duànshìguān was promoted to rank 5a,
with overall responsibility for the Five Armies' judicial affairs.
It was divided into five Sī,
each Sī establishing five officials: Jīrén, Jīyì, Jīlǐ, Jīzhì, and Jīxìn
(all rank 7a),
each handling the judicial affairs of their respective army.
In the 29th year, the Wǔjūn Zhàomó Suǒ was established,
exclusively responsible for documents.
During the Jiànwén era,
the Duànshì and the Five Sī officials were abolished.
In the 1st year of Yǒnglè, the Běijīng Liúshǒu Xíng Hòujūn Dūdū Fǔ was established,
with Left and Right Dūdū,
Dūdū Tóngzhī,
and Dūdū Qiānshì,
without fixed numbers,
and one Jīnglì and one Dūshì each.
Later, it was again divided into five Fǔ,
known as the Xíngzài Wǔjūn Dūdū Fǔ.
In the 18th year, the character
"Xíngzài"
was removed,
and for those in Yìngtiān, the character
"Nánjīng"
was added.
In the 1st year of Hóngxī, "Xíngzài" was reinstated,
and the Xíng Hòujūn Fǔ was also re-established.
In the 3rd year of Xuāndé, it was abolished again.
In the 6th year of Zhèngtǒng, the character
"Xíngzài"
was again removed.
The Capital Garrisons.
In the 22nd year of Yǒnglè (1424), three major camps were established,
namely the Wǔjūn Yíng (Five Military Camps),
the Shénjī Yíng (Divine Machine Camp),
and the Sānqiān Yíng (Three Thousand Camp).
The Wǔjūn Yíng and Shénjī Yíng each had a Zhōngjūn (Central Army), Zuǒyòushào (Left and Right Flanks), and Zuǒyòuyè (Left and Right Wings);
the Wǔjūn Yíng and Sānqiān Yíng each had five Sī (Divisions).
Two Xūnchén (meritorious officials) were selected for each camp to serve as Tídū (Commanders).
The officers managing the Shào and Yè of these camps
were called Zuòyíng (Camp Overseers)
and Zuòsī (Division Overseers).
(The officers of each Shào and Yè
were also largely appointed from among Xūnchén.)
Additionally, officers such as Bǎzǒng (Captain), Bǎsī (Squad Leader), and Bǎpái (Banner Bearer) were established.
(There were also camps such as the Wéizǐshǒu, Yòuguān, Shèrén, Dānzhōng, and Xiàoyì,
all attached to the Wǔjūn Yíng.)
In the 1st year of Jǐngtài (1450), elite troops from the three camps were chosen to form the Shítuányíng (Ten Regiment Camps),
commanded by Zǒngbīng (Commander-in-chief),
supervised by Zǒngdū (Governor-general),
and overseen by Nèichén (eunuchs).
The previously established camps
were referred to as Lǎoyíng (Old Camps).
(The three Lǎoyíng had a total of six Tídū,
two of whom were selected to lead the Tuányíng.)
In the 3rd year of Chénghuà (1467), the Tuányíng were divided into twelve.
Each camp was again subdivided, with the Wǔjūn Yíng and Sānqiān Yíng commanding cavalry,
and the Shénjī Yíng commanding firearms.
The commanders of these camps
were chosen from among Dūdū (Chief Military Commanders), Dūzhīhuī (Regional Commanders), or those with noble titles,
and were all under the unified command of a Zǒngdū.
During the Zhèngdé reign,
elite troops from the Tuányíng were again selected
to establish two Guāntīng (official offices), East and West,
with separate Zǒngbīng and Cānjìang (Assistant Commanders) appointed to lead them.
In the 29th year of Jiājìng (1550), the Tuányíng Guāntīng were abolished,
and the three major camps were reintegrated.
The Sānqiān Yíng was renamed Shénshū Yíng (Divine Hub Camp),
and officers such as Fù (Deputy), Cān (Assistant), Yóu (Patrol), Zuǒ (Aide), Zuòyíng, Hàotóu (Chief of Signal), Zhōngjūn, and Qiānbǎzǒng (Lieutenant-captain) were established.
(Wǔjūn Yíng: One Zànbīng Yíng (Combat Camp),
one Zuǒ Fùjiàng (Left Deputy General);
two Zànbīng Yíng,
one Liànyǒng Cānjìang (Drillmaster Assistant Commander);
three Chēbīng Yíng (Chariot Camps),
one Cānjìang;
four Chēbīng Yíng,
one Yóují Jiāngjūn (Patrol General);
five Chéngshǒu Yíng (City Defense Camps),
one Zuǒjí Jiāngjūn (Aid General);
six Zànbīng Yíng,
one Yòu Fùjiàng (Right Deputy General);
seven Zànbīng Yíng,
one Liànyǒng Cānjìang;
eight Chēbīng Yíng,
one Cānjìang;
nine Chēbīng Yíng,
one Yóují Jiāngjūn;
ten Chéngshǒu Yíng,
one Zuǒjí Jiāngjūn;
one Bèibīng Zuòyíng Guān (Reserve Camp Overseer),
one Dàhàotóu Guān (Grand Chief of Signal).
These were appointed by the Ministry.
One Jiānqiāng Hàotóu Guān (Supervising Weapons Chief of Signal),
eleven Zhōngjūn Guān,
four Suízhēng Qiānzǒng (Expeditionary Lieutenants),
twenty Suíyíng Qiānzǒng (Camp Lieutenants),
eight Xuǎnfēng Bǎzǒng (Vanguard Captains),
one hundred thirty-eight Bǎzǒng.
These were appointed by the camp.
Shénshū Yíng: One Zànbīng Yíng,
one Zuǒ Fùjiàng;
two Zànbīng Yíng,
one Liànyǒng Cānjìang;
three Chēbīng Yíng,
one Cānjìang;
four Chēbīng Yíng,
one Yóují Jiāngjūn;
five Chéngshǒu Yíng,
one Zuǒjí Jiāngjūn;
six Zànbīng Yíng,
one Yòu Fùjiàng;
seven Chēbīng Yíng,
one Liànyǒng Cānjìang;
eight Zhíshì Yíng (Service Camps),
one Cānjìang;
nine Chéngshǒu Yíng,
one Zuǒjí Jiāngjūn;
ten Chéngshǒu Yíng,
one Zuǒjí Jiāngjūn;
one Bèibīng Zuòyíng Guān,
one Dàhàotóu Guān.
These were appointed by the Ministry.
One Jiānqiāng Hàotóu Guān,
eleven Zhōngjūn Guān,
twenty Qiānzǒng,
six Xuǎnfēng Bǎzǒng,
one hundred fifty-seven Bǎzǒng.
These were appointed by the camp.
Shénjī Yíng: One Zànbīng Yíng,
one Zuǒ Fùjiàng;
two Zànbīng Yíng,
one Liànyǒng Cānjìang;
three Chēbīng Yíng,
one Yóují Jiāngjūn;
four Chēbīng Yíng,
one Zuǒjí Jiāngjūn;
five Chéngshǒu Yíng,
one Zuǒjí Jiāngjūn;
six Zànbīng Yíng,
one Yòu Fùjiàng;
seven Chēbīng Yíng,
one Liànyǒng Cānjìang;
eight Chéngshǒu Yíng,
one Zuǒjí Jiāngjūn;
nine Chéngshǒu Yíng,
one Zuǒjí Jiāngjūn;
ten Chéngshǒu Yíng,
one Zuǒjí Jiāngjūn;
one Bèibīng Zuòyíng Guān,
one Dàhàotóu Guān.
These were appointed by the Ministry.
One Jiānqiāng Hàotóu Guān,
eleven Zhōngjūn Guān,
twenty Qiānzǒng,
six Xuǎnfēng Bǎzǒng,
one hundred twenty-eight Bǎzǒng.
These were appointed by the camp.
In total, the three major camps
had five hundred eighty-six officers.)
All were commanded by one Tídū Zǒngbīng Guān (Commander-in-chief and Commander).
Later,
the title Tídū was changed to Zǒngdū,
and an imperial seal
"Zǒngdū Jīngyíng Róngzhèng" (Governor-general of Capital Garrison Military Affairs)
was cast,
which Qíu Luán was ordered to wear.
One Shìláng (Vice Minister) was additionally appointed
to assist in the military affairs of the Capital Garrisons.
It was stipulated that the Xúnshì Kēdào Guān (Inspecting Censorate Officials) would be replaced annually,
and all Nèishì Guān (eunuch officials) were abolished.
An Xúnshì Zhǔshì (Inspecting Principal Official) was added,
but was soon also abolished.
In the early Lóngqìng reign,
the Zǒngdū was again made the Tídū,
and the Xiélǐ (Assistant) was changed to Yuèshì (Reviewer),
and soon the Yuèshì was also changed to Tídū.
In the second month of the 4th year (1570), the Capital Garrison system was changed again.
Each of the three camps had a Tídū,
and additionally, one Yòu Dūyùshǐ (Right Censor-in-chief) was appointed to command them.
In the ninth month, the six Tídū were dismissed,
and the single Zǒngdū Róngzhèng was reinstated.
In the early Tiānqǐ reign,
one Xiélǐ was added,
but soon after,
that one person was again abolished.
In the early Chóngzhēn reign,
one person was again added.
The Capital Wèi Zhīhuīshǐ Sī (Capital Guard Commander's Office) had one Zhīhuīshǐ (Commander),
(principal third rank,)
two Zhīhuītóngzhī (Associate Commanders),
(auxiliary third rank,)
and four Zhīhuīqiānshì (Assistant Commanders),
(principal fourth rank.)
The Zhènfǔ Sī (Pacification Office) had
two Zhènfǔ (Pacification Commissioners),
(auxiliary fifth rank.)
Its subordinate offices included
the Jīnglì Sī (Registrar Office) with
a Jīnglì (Registrar),
(auxiliary seventh rank,)
a Zhīshì (Aide),
(principal eighth rank,)
a Lìmù (Clerk),
(auxiliary ninth rank,)
and one Cāng Dàshǐ (Grand Storage Commissioner) and one Fùshǐ (Deputy Commissioner) each.
The number of Qiānhùsuǒ (Thousand-Household Guard Units) under their jurisdiction
varied.
The Capital Guards (Jīngwèi) included the Imperial Bodyguards (Shàngzhíwèi)
and the Southern and Northern Capital Guards (Nán-Běijīngwèi).
Their ranks and emoluments were all the same.
Each had an official in charge of the seal (zhǎngyìn),
and a junior compiler (qiānshū).
Those appointed by imperial grace or hereditary privilege to receive stipends
had no fixed number.
There were twenty-six
Commands of the Imperial Bodyguards (Qīnjūn Zhǐhuīshǐ Sī) of the Imperial Bodyguards (Shàngzhíwèi).
These were: Jǐnyīwèi,
Qíshǒuwèi,
Jīnwú Qiánwèi,
Jīnwú Hòuwèi,
Yǔlín Zuǒwèi,
Yǔlín Yòuwèi,
Fǔjūnwèi,
Fǔjūn Zuǒwèi,
Fǔjūn Yòuwèi,
Fǔjūn Qiánwèi,
Fǔjūn Hòuwèi,
Hǔbēn Zuǒwèi.
(These were the twelve Upper Guards (Shàngshí'èrwèi),
established during the Hóngwǔ reign.)
Jīnwú Zuǒwèi,
Jīnwú Yòuwèi,
Yǔlín Qiánwèi,
Yānshān Zuǒwèi,
Yānshān Yòuwèi,
Yānshān Qiánwèi,
Dàxīng Zuǒwèi,
Jìyángwèi,
Jìzhōuwèi,
Tōngzhōuwèi.
(These were the ten Upper Guards (Shàngshíwèi),
established during the Yǒnglè reign.)
Téngxiáng Zuǒwèi,
Téngxiáng Yòuwèi,
Wǔxiáng Zuǒwèi,
Wǔxiáng Yòuwèi.
(Established in the eighth year of Xuāndé.)
The Imperial Bodyguards (Qīnjūn) who took turns on guard duty
were tasked with protecting the imperial palace
and were not subordinate to the Five Chief Military Commissions (Wǔ Dūdū Fǔ).
There were thirty-three
Capital Guards (Jīngwèi) that were subordinate to the Chief Military Commissions (Dūdū Fǔ).
These were: Liúshǒu Zuǒwèi,
Zhènnánwèi,
Xiāoqí Yòuwèi,
Lónghǔwèi,
Shěnyáng Zuǒwèi,
Shěnyáng Yòuwèi,
all subordinate to the Left Chief Military Commission (Zuǒjūn Dūdū Fǔ).
Liúshǒu Yòuwèi,
Hǔbēn Yòuwèi,
Wǔdéwèi,
all subordinate to the Right Chief Military Commission (Yòujūn Dūdū Fǔ).
Liúshǒu Zhōngwèi,
Shéncèwèi,
Yìngtiānwèi,
Héyángwèi, as well as the Commands of One Thousand Households for Horse Pastures (Mùmǎ Qiānhùsuǒ) and for Barbarian Herdsmen (Fānmù Qiānhùsuǒ),
all subordinate to the Central Chief Military Commission (Zhōngjūn Dūdū Fǔ).
Liúshǒu Qiánwèi,
Lóngxiángwèi,
Bàotāowèi,
all subordinate to the Front Chief Military Commission (Qiánjūn Dūdū Fǔ).
Liúshǒu Hòuwèi,
Yīngyángwèi,
Xīngwǔwèi,
Dàníng Zhōngwèi,
Dàníng Qiánwèi,
Huìzhōuwèi,
Fùyùwèi,
Kuānhéwèi,
Shénwǔ Zuǒwèi,
Zhōngyì Yòuwèi,
Zhōngyì Qiánwèi,
Zhōngyì Hòuwèi,
Yìyǒng Yòuwèi,
Yìyǒng Qiánwèi,
Yìyǒng Hòuwèi,
Wǔchéng Zhōngwèi,
Yùzhōu Zuǒwèi,
all subordinate to the Rear Chief Military Commission (Hòujūn Dūdū Fǔ).
Furthermore, there were fifteen
Capital Guards (Jīngwèi) that were not Imperial Bodyguards (Qīnjūn) and not subordinate to the Chief Military Commissions (Dūdū Fǔ).
These were: Wǔgōng Zhōngwèi,
Wǔgōng Zuǒwèi,
Wǔgōng Yòuwèi.
(The above three Guards were subordinate to the Ministry of Works (Gōngbù)
due to their artisans.)
Yǒngqīng Zuǒwèi,
Yǒngqīng Yòuwèi,
Péngchéngwèi,
Chánglíngwèi,
Xiànlíngwèi,
Jǐnglíngwèi,
Yùlíngwèi,
Màolíngwèi,
Tàilíngwèi,
Kānglíngwèi,
Yǒnglíngwèi,
Zhāolíngwèi.
In the early Míng dynasty,
the Commandery of the Imperial Bodyguards under the Emperor's Tent (Zhàngqián Zǒngzhì Qīnjūn Dūzhǐhuīshǐ Sī) was established,
with Féng Guóyòng as its Commissioner-in-Chief (Dūzhǐhuīshǐ).
Later, it was reorganized into the Command of Imperial Bodyguards of the Golden Halberd (Jīnwú Shìwèi Qīnjūn Dūhù Fǔ),
which had a Protector-General (Dūhù)
(senior second rank),
a Registrar (Jīnglì)
(principal sixth rank),
an Administrator (Zhīshì)
(junior seventh rank),
and an Inspector of Documents (Zhàomó)
(junior eighth rank).
In addition, Commands of Imperial Bodyguards (Qīnjūn Zhǐhuīshǐ Sī) were established for each Guard (Wèi),
with a Commissioner (Zhǐhuīshǐ)
(principal third rank),
an Associate Commissioner (Tóngzhī Zhǐhuīshǐ)
(junior third rank),
an Assistant Commissioner (Fùshǐ)
(principal fourth rank),
a Registrar (Jīnglì)
(principal seventh rank),
an Administrator (Zhīshì)
(junior eighth rank),
an Inspector of Documents (Zhàomó)
(principal ninth rank),
a Principal Commander of One Thousand Households (Zhèng Qiānhù) for the Commands of One Thousand Households (Qiānhùsuǒ)
(principal fifth rank),
an Assistant Commander of One Thousand Households (Fù Qiānhù)
(junior fifth rank),
a Garrison Commander (Zhènfǔ), and a Commander of One Hundred Households (Bǎihù)
(principal sixth rank).

Consequently, the seventeen Commands of Imperial Bodyguards (Qīnjūn Zhǐhuīshǐ Sī) of Wǔdé, Lóngxiáng, Bàotāo, Fēixióng, Wēiwǔ, Guǎngwǔ, Xīngwǔ, Yīngwǔ, Yīngyáng, Xiāoqí, Shénwǔ, Xióngwǔ, Fèngxiáng, Tiāncè, Zhènyǔ, Xuānwǔ, and Yǔlín were established.
This marked the beginning of the establishment of the Imperial Bodyguards (Qīnjūnwèi).
Soon after, the Command of Imperial Bodyguards of the Golden Halberd (Jīnwú Shìwèi Qīnjūn Dūhù Fǔ) was abolished.
Between the Hóngwǔ and Yǒnglè reigns,
additional Imperial Bodyguards (Qīnjūn) of various Guards (Wèi) were established,
known as the twenty-two Upper Guards (Shàng Èrshí'èrwèi),
which were divided to manage guard duties.
However, the Jǐnyīwèi was primarily responsible for surveillance, arrests, and managing imperial prisons,
led by a Commissioner-in-Chief (Dūdū) and a Commander-in-Chief (Dūzhǐhuī),
thus making it distinctly different from the other Guards (Wèi).
The Five Retainer Guards (Liúshǒu Wǔwèi)
were formerly the Chief Garrison Commands (Dūzhènfǔ Sī),
generally overseeing the palace guards.
Initially, they belonged to the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shěng),
then transferred to the Grand Chief Military Commission (Dà Dūdū Fǔ),
where a Chief Garrison Commander (Dūzhènfǔ)
(junior fourth rank),
an Assistant Garrison Commander (Fùzhènfǔ)
(junior fifth rank),
and an Administrator (Zhīshì)
(junior eighth rank) were appointed.
Soon after, it was reorganized into the Garrison Command of Imperial Bodyguards (Sùwèi Zhènfǔ Sī),
with a Garrison Commander of Imperial Bodyguards (Sùwèi Zhènfǔ) and an Administrator of Imperial Bodyguards (Sùwèi Zhīshì).
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, it was renamed the Command of Retainer Guards (Liúshǒuwèi Zhǐhuīshǐ Sī),
exclusively responsible for leading military horses to defend various city gates,
and for patrolling the Imperial City (Huángchéng) and managing the construction of city walls.
Later, it was promoted to the Grand Retainer Guard (Liúshǒu Dūwèi),
overseeing Tiāncè, Bàotāo, Fēixióng, Yīngyáng, Jiāngyīn, Guǎngyáng, Hénghǎi, Lóngjiāng, and the Left and Right Naval Guards (Shuǐjūn Zuǒ, Yòu), a total of ten Guards (Wèi).
In the eighth year,
it reverted to the Retainer Guard (Liúshǒuwèi),
and together with Tiāncè and eight other Guards (Wèi), became Commands of Imperial Bodyguards (Qīnjūn Zhǐhuīshǐ Sī).
(Only the Left and Right Naval Guards (Shuǐjūn Zuǒ, Yòu) were Commands (Zhǐhuīshǐ Sī).)
All were subordinate to the Grand Chief Military Commission (Dà Dūdū Fǔ).
In the eleventh year, it was reorganized into the Central Retainer Guard (Liúshǒu Zhōngwèi),
and the Left, Right, Front, and Rear Retainer Guards (Liúshǒu Zuǒ, Yòu, Qián, Hòu) were added,
remaining Imperial Bodyguards (Qīnjūn).
In the thirteenth year, they were finally divided and assigned to the Five Chief Military Commissions (Wǔ Dūdū Fǔ).
The Jǐnyīwèi
was responsible for imperial bodyguards, arrests, and judicial matters,
led by meritorious relatives and Commissioners-in-Chief (Dūdū); those receiving hereditary stipends were not fixed members.
For court assemblies and imperial tours,
they prepared the imperial equipage and ceremonial guard,
leading the Grand Han Generals (Dà Hàn Jiāngjūn)
(totaling 1,507 members) and others to escort the emperor.
For night watches, they took turns on duty.
For rituals such as worshipping the sun, sacrificing to the moon, ceremonial plowing, and inspecting sacrificial animals,
they wore "flying fish" robes (Fēiyúfú)
and carried embroidered spring swords (Xiùchūndāo),
attending the emperor's left and right.
They secretly investigated and regularly inspected bandits, villains,
streets, and drainage ditches.
Whenever imperial orders were received to interrogate prisoners and investigate cases,
they collaborated with the Three Judicial Offices (Sānfǎ Sī).
For military officers' spear-fighting competitions,
they supervised together with the Ministry of War (Bīngbù).
They commanded a total of seventeen offices.
The Central, Left, Right, Front, and Rear Five Offices (Zhōng, Zuǒ, Yòu, Qián, Hòu Wǔsuǒ)
commanded soldiers.

The Five Offices were divided into ten bureaus: Imperial Carriage (Luányú), Umbrella Bearers (Qínggài), Fan Bearers (Shànshǒu), Banner Bearers (Jīngjié), Streamer Bearers (Fānbāo), Sword Bearers (Bānjiàn), Axe and Yue Bearers (Fǔyuè), Ge and Ji Bearers (Gējǐ), Bow and Arrow Bearers (Gōngshǐ), and Elephant Trainers (Xùnmǎ),
each commanding generals and officers (jiāngjūn jiàowèi)
to prepare for imperial processions.
The Upper Central, Upper Left, Upper Right, Upper Front, Upper Rear, and Central Rear Six Imperial Bodyguard Offices (Shàngzhōng, Shàngzuǒ, Shàngyòu, Shàngqián, Shànghòu, Zhōnghòu Liù Qīnjūnsuǒ)
commanded generals, strongmen (lìshì), and military artisans.
The Elephant Training Office (Xùnxiàngsuǒ)
commanded elephant handlers to raise elephants,
for display at court assemblies, pulling imperial carriages, and carrying treasures.
In the early Míng dynasty,
the Gǒngwèi Sī was established.
Its rank was regular seventh grade,
managing and leading xiàowèi (military escorts)
and belonging to the Dūdū Fǔ (Chief Military Commission).
Later, it was changed to Gǒngwèi Zhǐhuīshǐ Sī (Commission of Guards for Military Escorts),
with a rank of regular third grade.
Soon after, it was again changed to Dūwèi Sī.
In Hóngwǔ third year (1370), it was changed to Qīnjūn Dūwèi Fǔ (Chief Military Commission of Imperial Guards),
managing the military personnel of the five Weì (Guards): Left, Right, Central, Front, and Rear.
The Yíluán Sī was also established under it.
In the fourth year (1371), the Yíluán Sī was designated regular fifth grade,
with one Dàshǐ (Grand Envoy)
and two Fùshǐ (Deputy Envoys).
In the fifteenth year (1382), the Yíluán Sī was abolished,
and the Jǐnyī Wèi (Brocade-Clad Guard) was established in its place,
with a rank of junior third grade.
Its subordinates included seven officers such as the Yùyǐ,
all of regular sixth grade.
It established the Jīnglì Sī (Bureau of Records),
in charge of the entry and exit of official documents;
and the Zhènfǔ Sī (Guard Commandant Bureau),
in charge of criminal cases within the Guard
and also managing military artisans.
In the seventeenth year (1384), the Jǐnyī Wèi Zhǐhuīshǐ was elevated to regular third grade.
In the twentieth year (1387), because many who administered the Jǐnyī Wèi acted illegally and tyrannically,
the instruments of torture were burned,
the prisoners were released,
and sent to the Xíngbù (Ministry of Justice) for trial and review.
An edict declared that all internal and external prisons would revert to the Sānfǎ Sī (Three Judicial Offices),
and the Jǐnyī prison was abolished.
During Chéngzǔ's reign, it was re-established.
Soon after, the Běi Zhènfǔ Sī (Northern Guard Commandant Bureau) was added,
specifically handling imperial edict prisons (Zhàoyù).
During the Chénghuà era (1465-1487),
a seal was carved and given to it,
allowing it to directly report completed cases
without involving the Jǐnyī,
and Jǐnyī officials were also forbidden from interfering.
The previously established one was designated the Nán Zhènfǔ Sī (Southern Guard Commandant Bureau),
exclusively managing military artisans.
The Qíshǒu Wèi (Standard-Bearer Guard)
was originally the Qíshǒu Qiānhù Suǒ (Standard-Bearer Chiliarchy),
reorganized in Hóngwǔ eighteenth year (1385).
It was in charge of the emperor's imperial drums and banners,
leading lìshì (strongmen) to accompany the emperor and guard his quarters.
(Xiàowèi and lìshì
were selected from strong young men among the populace.
Xiàowèi were specifically responsible for holding imperial regalia and ceremonial staffs,
and summoning officials before the emperor,
and being dispatched for duties,
subordinate to the Jǐnyī Wèi.
Lìshì were specifically in charge of imperial drums and banners,
accompanying the emperor in and out,
and guarding the four city gates,
subordinate to the Qíshǒu Wèi.)
For the annual sacrifice to the gods of the six banner chiefs (qítóu liùdáo),
in the eighth month at the altar,
and in the twelfth month outside Chéngtiānmén,
all were presided over by Weì officials.
It commanded five Suǒ (Battalions).
The Fǔjūnqián Wèi (Front Guard of the Palace Army)
was in charge of leading the youth army,
who took turns carrying swords and serving as imperial guards.
In the early Míng dynasty,
there were Dàidāo Shèrén (Sword-Bearing Gentlemen).
During the Hóngwǔ era,
Weìs like the Fǔjūn Wèi all had trained youth armies.
In Yǒnglè thirteenth year (1415), a youth army was specially selected for the imperial grandson,
and the Fǔjūnqián Wèi was established,
with its own officials,
(five Zhǐhuīshǐ,
ten Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī,
twenty Zhǐhuī Qiānshì,
ten Weì Zhènfǔ,
five Jīnglì),
commanding twenty-five Suǒ.
The Jīnwú, Yǔlín, and other nineteen Weìs
were responsible for guard duty and patrolling,
commanding a total of one hundred and two Suǒ.
The Téngxiáng and other four Weìs
were in charge of leading lìshì to stand guard and accompany the emperor,
commanding thirty-two Suǒ.
One Nánjīng Shǒubèi (Nanjing Defense Commissioner),
one Xié Tóngshǒubèi (Assistant Defense Commissioner).
In Nánjīng, the Shǒubèi and Cāncàn Jīwù (Adviser on Military Affairs) were important positions.
The Shǒubèi
was filled by a Gōng (Duke), Hóu (Marquis), or Bó (Earl),
also leading the affairs of the Zhōngjūn Dūdū Fǔ (Central Chief Military Commission).
The Xié Tóngshǒubèi
was filled by a Hóu, Bó, or Dūdū (Chief Military Commissioner),
leading the affairs of the five Fǔ.
The Cāncàn Jīwù
was led by the Nánjīng Bīngbù Shàngshū (Minister of War for Nanjing).
Its administrative seat was in the Zhōng Fǔ,
in charge of all retention, guard, and protection matters in Nándū (Nanjing).
In Yǒnglè nineteenth year (1421), the capital moved to Běijīng,
and an official from the Zhōng Fǔ in charge of its affairs was appointed to defend Nánjīng,
controlling all Weìsuǒ in Nánjīng.
In Hóngxī first year (1425), eunuchs began to serve as co-Shǒubèi.
In Jǐngtài third year (1452), one Xié Tóngshǒubèi was added.
The Nánjīng Wǔjūn Dūdū Fǔ (Nanjing Five Chief Military Commissions)
did not fully appoint Zuǒ Dūdū (Left Chief Military Commissioner), Yòu Dūdū (Right Chief Military Commissioner),
Dūdū Tóngzhī (Associate Chief Military Commissioner), or
Dūdū Qiānshì (Assistant Chief Military Commissioner).
It did not fully appoint them.
Its Zhǎngyìn (Seal Custodian) and Qiānshū (Document Signatory)
were all filled by meritorious nobles and third-rank Dūdū.
They were separately in charge of the Nánjīng Weìsuǒ,
reporting to the Nánjīng Bīngbù.
All matters concerning the management of the grand training grounds and riverine defense preparations, etc.,
were separately managed by the respective Fǔs under imperial decree.
The keys to the city gates
were exclusively managed by the Zhōng Fǔ.
(Initially, Chéngmén Láng were established,
abolished in Hóngwǔ eighteenth year (1385),
and the brass plates for gate access, locks, and keys
were put under the charge of the Zhōngjūn Dūdū Fǔ by imperial order.)
Its subordinates included
one Jīnglì and one Dūshì.
The Nánjīng Weì Zhǐhuīshǐ Sī
(officials detailed as for the Jīngwèi)
numbered forty-nine in total.
Thirty-two were subordinate to the five Dūdū Fǔs.
These were: Liúshǒuzuǒ Wèi (Left Retained Guard),
Zhènnán Wèi (Guard for Pacifying the South),
Shuǐjūnzuǒ Wèi (Left Naval Guard),
Xiāoqíyòu Wèi (Right Swift Cavalry Guard),
Lónghǔ Wèi (Dragon Tiger Guard),
Lónghǔzuǒ Wèi (Left Dragon Tiger Guard),
Yīngwǔ Wèi (Heroic Martial Guard),
Lóngjiāngyòu Wèi (Right Dragon River Guard),
Shěnyángzuǒ Wèi (Left Shenyang Guard),
Shěnyángyòu Wèi (Right Shenyang Guard),
subordinate to the Zuǒ Fǔ (Left Commission).
These were: Liúshǒuyòu Wèi (Right Retained Guard),
Hǔbēnyòu Wèi (Right Tiger Swift Guard),
Shuǐjūnyòu Wèi (Right Naval Guard),
Wǔdé Wèi (Martial Virtue Guard),
Guǎngwǔ Wèi (Vast Martial Guard),
subordinate to the Yòu Fǔ (Right Commission).
These were: Liúshǒuzhōng Wèi (Central Retained Guard),
Shéncè Wèi (Divine Strategy Guard),
Guǎngyáng Wèi (Vast Ocean Guard),
Guǎngtiān Wèi (Vast Heaven Guard),
and Héyáng Wèi, and the Mùmǎ Qiānhù Suǒ (Chiliarchy for Horse Herding),
subordinate to the Zhōng Fǔ (Central Commission).
These were: Liúshǒuqián Wèi (Front Retained Guard),
Lóngjiāngzuǒ Wèi (Left Dragon River Guard),
Lóngxiáng Wèi (Dragon Soaring Guard),
Fēixióng Wèi (Flying Bear Guard),
Tiāncè Wèi (Heavenly Strategy Guard),
Bàotáo Wèi (Leopard Strategy Guard),
Bàotáozuǒ Wèi (Left Leopard Strategy Guard),
subordinate to the Qián Fǔ (Front Commission).
These were: Liúshǒuhòu Wèi (Rear Retained Guard),
Hénghǎi Wèi (Traversing Sea Guard),
Yīngyáng Wèi (Eagle Soaring Guard),
Xīngwǔ Wèi (Prosperous Martial Guard),
Jiāngyīn Wèi (Jiangyin Guard),
subordinate to the Hòu Fǔ (Rear Commission).
There were also seventeen Qīnjūn Wèi Zhǐhuīshǐ Sīs: Jīnwúqián Wèi (Front Golden Crow Guard),
Jīnwúhòu Wèi (Rear Golden Crow Guard),
Jīnwúzuǒ Wèi (Left Golden Crow Guard),
Jīnwúyòu Wèi (Right Golden Crow Guard),
Yǔlínzuǒ Wèi (Left Feathered Forest Guard),
Yǔlínyòu Wèi (Right Feathered Forest Guard),
Yǔlínqián Wèi (Front Feathered Forest Guard),
Fǔjūn Wèi (Palace Army Guard),
Fǔjūnzuǒ Wèi (Left Palace Army Guard),
Fǔjūnyòu Wèi (Right Palace Army Guard),
Fǔjūnhòu Wèi (Rear Palace Army Guard),
Hǔbēnzuǒ Wèi (Left Tiger Swift Guard),
Jǐnyī Wèi (Brocade-Clad Guard),
Qíshǒu Wèi (Standard-Bearer Guard),
Jiānghuái Wèi (Jianghuai Guard),
Jìzhōu Wèi (Jizhou Guard),
Xiàolíng Wèi (Xiaoling Guard).
Together with the ten Weìs subordinate to the Zuǒ Fǔ,
the five Weìs subordinate to the Yòu Fǔ,
the seven Weìs subordinate to the Qián Fǔ,
and the five Weìs subordinate to the Hòu Fǔ,
all were subject to the control of the Zhōng Fǔ.
Each Weì commanded one hundred and eighteen Suǒ.
The Wángfǔ Hùwèi Zhǐhuīshǐ Sī (Commission of Guards for Princely Establishments)
had officials similar to those of the Jīngwèi (Capital Guards).
Wángfǔ Yíwèisī (Palace Guard Command).
One Yíwèizhèng (Commandant of Palace Guards),
(Principal Fifth Rank),
Two Yíwèifù (Deputy Commandants of Palace Guards),
(Auxiliary Fifth Rank),
Six Diǎnzhàng (Administrators of Ceremonial Weapons),
(Principal Sixth Rank).
The Yíwèi [officers]
were in charge of palace guards and ceremonial regalia.
The Hùwèi (Defenders)
were in charge of defending against extraordinary situations
and guarding the princely residence.
If there was a call for conscription or deployment,
they would obey the court's orders.
In the early Míng dynasty,
each princely residence established a Hùjūnfǔ (Guard Command).
In Hóngwǔ (洪武) 3rd year (1370), the Yíwèisī was established.
The Sī (Command) had one Zhèng (Commandant) and one Fù (Deputy),
their ranks equivalent to a Zhèng Qiānhù (Principal Commander of One Thousand Households) and Fù Qiānhù (Deputy Commander of One Thousand Households) respectively;
and six Sīzhàng (Administrators of Ceremonial Weapons),
their ranks equivalent to Bǎihù (Commander of One Hundred Households).
In the 4th year (1371), Sīzhàng was changed to Diǎnzhàng.
In the 5th year (1372), a Qīnwáng Hùwèi Zhǐhuīshǐsī (Commandery of Princely Guards) was established.
Each princely residence had three Hùwèi (Guards),
and each Wèi (Guard) had five Suǒ (Stations): Zuǒ (Left), Yòu (Right), Qián (Front), Hòu (Rear), and Zhōng (Center).
Each Suǒ had two Qiānhù (Commanders of One Thousand Households),
and ten Bǎihù (Commanders of One Hundred Households).
Additionally, two Wéizǐshǒu Suǒ (Outpost Guard Stations) were established,
each Suǒ with one Qiānhù.
In the 9th year (1376), the Hùjūnfǔ was abolished.
During the Jiànwén (建文) reign,
the Yíwèisī was renamed Yízhàngsī (Ceremonial Regalia Command),
and one Lìmù (Clerical Officer) was added.
At the beginning of the Chéngzǔ (成祖) reign, the old system was restored.

Zǒngbīngguān (Regional Commanders), Fùzǒngbīng (Deputy Regional Commanders), Cāncānjàng (Assistant Regional Commanders), Yóujī Jiāngjūn (Mobile Corps Generals), Shǒubèi (Garrison Commanders), and Bǎzǒng (Battalion Commanders),
had no fixed rank
and no fixed number of personnel.
Those who commanded an entire region were called Zhènshǒu (Garrison Commanders),
those who commanded a single route were called Fēnshǒu (Divisional Commanders),
those who each commanded a city or a fort were called Shǒubèi,
and those who jointly commanded a city with a principal general were called Xiéshǒu (Assistant Garrison Commanders).
There were also titles such as Tídū (Superintendent), Tídiào (Inspector), Xúnshì (Patroller), Bèiyù (Defender), Lǐngbān (Squad Leader), and Bèiwō (Coastal Defense Commander).
Generally, Zǒngbīng and Fùzǒngbīng
were often filled by nobles holding titles such as Gōng (Duke), Hóu (Marquis), Bó (Earl), or Dūdū (Chief Military Commissioner).
Those Zǒngbīng who held a seal and were called Jiāngjūn (General) included:
in Yúnnán (雲南), the Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the South);
in Dàtóng (大同), the Zhēngxī Qián Jiāngjūn (Front General Who Conquers the West);
in Húguǎng (湖廣), the Píngmán Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the Barbarians);
in Liǎngguǎng (兩廣), the Zhēngmán Jiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the Barbarians);
in Liáodōng (遼東), the Zhēnglǔ Qián Jiāngjūn (Front General Who Conquers the Barbarians);
in Xuānfǔ (宣府), the Zhènshuò Jiāngjūn (General Who Guards the North);
in Gānsù (甘肅), the Píngqiāng Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the Qiāng);
in Níngxià (寧夏), the Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the West);
in Jiāozhǐ (交阯), the Fùjiāngjūn (Deputy General);
and in Yánsuí (延綏), the Zhènxī Jiāngjūn (General Who Guards the West).
(All these seals
were established and issued in Hóngxī (洪熙) 1st year (1425).)
Those stationed in Jìzhèn (薊鎮), Guìzhōu (貴州), Húguǎng, Sìchuān (四川), and those supervising grain transport at Huái'ān (淮安)
were not allowed to be called Jiāngjūn or to hold a seal.
During the Xuāndé (宣德) reign,
two additional Zǒngbīng were established for Shānxī (山西) and Shǎnxī (陝西).
During the Jiājìng (嘉靖) reign,
the two Zǒngbīng for Guǎngdōng (廣東), Guǎngxī (廣西), Guìzhōu, and Húguǎng were divided into four.
The Fùzǒngbīng for Fújiàn (福建) and Bǎodìng (保定) were re-designated as Zǒngbīng,
and an additional Zǒngbīng for Zhèjiāng (浙江) was established.
During the Wànlì (萬曆) reign,
additional ones were established at Líntáo (臨洮) and Shānhǎi (山海).
During the Tiānqǐ (天啟) reign,
additional ones were established at Dēng (登) and Lái (萊).
By the Chóngzhēn (崇禎) era,
they became increasingly numerous and difficult to record,
and their authority and power were no longer what they had been in earlier times.
Indeed, in the early Míng,
even Cāncānjàng, Yóujī, and Bǎzǒng
were often filled by meritorious relatives, Dūdū, and other high-ranking officials,
but later this practice completely disappeared.
One Zhènshǒu Jìzhōu Zǒngbīngguān (Regional Commander of Jìzhōu),
previously established.
In Lóngqìng (隆慶) 2nd year (1568), he was redesignated as Zǒnglǐ Liànbīng Shìwù Jiān Zhènshǒu (Superintendent of Military Training Affairs and Concurrently Regional Commander),
stationed at Sāntúnyíng (三屯營).

stationed in Cháozhōu Fǔ.
One Assistant Grand Commander (Xiéshǒu Fùzǒngbīng),
(Cháozhāng Assistant Grand Commander (Cháozhāng Fùzǒngbīng),
added in the 3rd year of Wànlì,
stationed in Nán'ào.)
Seven Divisional Commanders (Fēnshǒu Cāncè),
(namely, the Cháozhōu Divisional Commander (Cháozhōu Cāncè),
the Qióngyá Divisional Commander (Qióngyá Cāncè),
the Léilián Divisional Commander (Léilián Cāncè),
the Dōngshān Divisional Commander (Dōngshān Cāncè),
the Xīshān Divisional Commander (Xīshān Cāncè),
the Divisional Commander (Cāncè) overseeing Guangzhou Maritime Defense (Guǎngzhōu Hǎifáng),
the Huìzhōu Divisional Commander (Huìzhōu Cāncè).)
One Training Patrol Commander (Liànbīng Yóujī Jiàngjūn),
five Garrison Commanders (Shǒubèi),
two Camp-dwelling Central Army Officers (Zuòyíng Zhōngjūnguān),
four Squad Leaders (Bǎzǒng).
One Grand Coordinator (Tídū) Vice Regional Commander (Fù Zǒngbīng) for Lángshān,
established in the 37th year of Jiājìng,
stationed in Tōngzhōu.
One Regional Commander (Zhènshǒu) Vice Regional Commander (Fù Zǒngbīng) for Jiāngnán,
formerly a Regional Commander-in-chief (Zǒngbīngguān),
stationed at Fúshān Harbor,
later moved to Zhènjiāng and Yízhēn.
Abolished in the 8th year of Jiājìng.
Reinstated in the 19th year.
Again abolished in the 29th year.
In the 32nd year,
it was changed to a Vice Regional Commander (Fù Zǒngbīng),
stationed at Jīnshān Wèi.
In the 43rd year, moved to Wúsōng.
Two Defense Area Assistant Commanders (Fēnshǒu Cānjìang),
(one named Xúzhōu Assistant Commander (Cānjìang),
one named Jīnshān Assistant Commander (Cānjìang)),
one Mobile Division Commander (Yóují Jiāngjūn),
six Garrison Commanders (Shǒubèi),
one Central Army Officer (Zhōngjūnguān) for Fèngyáng Military Affairs (Jūnmén),
thirteen Company Commanders (Bǎzǒng).
One Regional Commander-in-chief (Zǒngbīngguān) for Zhèjiāng,
established in the 34th year of Jiājìng,
overseeing the coastal defense of Zhèjiāng and Zhílì.
In the 35th year, changed to Regional Commander (Zhènshǒu) for Zhèjiāng and Zhílì.
In the 42nd year, changed to Regional Commander (Zhènshǒu) for Zhèjiāng.
Formerly stationed in Dìnghǎi County,
later moved to the provincial capital.
Four Defense Area Assistant Commanders (Fēnshǒu Cānjìang),
(one named Hángjiāhú Assistant Commander (Cānjìang),
one named Níngshào Assistant Commander (Cānjìang),
one named Wēnchǔ Assistant Commander (Cānjìang),
one named Táijīnyán Assistant Commander (Cānjìang)),
two Mobile Division Commanders (Yóují Jiāngjūn),
one Chief Investigator (Zǒngbǔ Dūsī),
seven Company Commanders (Bǎzǒng).
One Defense Area Assistant Commander (Fēnshǒu Cānjìang) for Jiāngxī,
(one named Nángàn Assistant Commander (Cānjìang),
established in the 43rd year of Jiājìng,
stationed in Huìchāng County).
Four Garrison Commanders (Shǒubèi),
six Company Commanders (Bǎzǒng).
One Regional Commander-in-chief (Zǒngbīngguān) for Fújiàn,
formerly a Vice Regional Commander (Fù Zǒngbīng),
established in the 42nd year of Jiājìng,
stationed in Fúníng Zhōu.
One Defense Area Assistant Commander (Fēnshǒu Cānjìang),
(one named Nánlù Assistant Commander (Cānjìang)),
three Garrison Commanders (Shǒubèi),
seven Company Commanders (Bǎzǒng),
one Camp Officer (Zuòyíngguān).
One Regional Commander-in-chief (Zǒngbīngguān) for Shāndōng,
augmented during the Tiānqǐ reign.
One Overall Administrator (Zǒngdū) of Coastal Defense (Bèi Wō Dūsī),
leading four Chief Investigators (Dūsī) of the Jìzhèn class.
Also three Garrison Commanders (Shǒubèi) for Hénán,
leading four Chief Investigators (Dūsī) of the Jìzhèn class.
One Regional Commander-in-chief (Zǒngbīngguān) for Grain Transport (Cáoyùn).
In the 2nd year of Yǒnglè, a Regional Commander-in-chief (Zǒngbīng) and a Vice Regional Commander (Fù Zǒngbīng) were established,
to command naval transport of military forces.
Later, naval transport ceased,
specializing in overseeing grain transport.
In the 1st year of Tiānshùn, they were also ordered to concurrently manage river administration.
One Assistant Commander (Cānjìang) for Joint Transport Supervision (Xiécóng Dūyùn),
(established in the 1st year of Tiānshùn),
twelve Company Commanders (Bǎzǒng),
(two in Nánjīng,
two in Jiāngnán Zhílì,
two in Jiāngběi Zhílì,
one in Zhōngdū,
two in Zhèjiāng,
one in Shāndōng,
one in Húguǎng,
one in Jiāngxī).
Left-behind Offices (Liúshǒu Sī).
One Chief Left-behind Official (Zhèng Liúshǒu),
(senior second rank),
one Deputy Left-behind Official (Fù Liúshǒu),
(senior third rank),
two Commander Concurrent Managers (Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī),
(junior third rank).
Its subordinates were:
Record Office (Jīnglì Sī),
Records Officer (Jīnglì),
(senior sixth rank),
Document Officer (Dūshì),
(senior seventh rank).
Judgment Office (Duànshì Sī),
Judge (Duànshì),
(senior sixth rank),
Deputy Judge (Fù Duànshì),
(senior seventh rank),
and one Clerk (Lìmù) for each.
They were in charge of the defense and protection of Zhōngdū and Xīngdū.
In the 2nd year of Hóngwǔ, an imperial edict designated Línháo as Zhōngdū,
establishing the Left-behind Guard Command Office (Liúshǒu Wèi Zhǐhuīshǐ Sī),
subordinate to the Fèngyáng Provisional Chief Military Commission (Xíng Dūdū Fǔ).
In the 14th year, the Zhōngdū Left-behind Office (Liúshǒu Sī) was first established,
commanding eight guards including Fèngyáng,
(Fèngyáng Wèi,
Fèngyáng Zhōng Wèi,
Fèngyáng Yòu Wèi,
Huánglíng Wèi,
Liúshǒu Zuǒ Wèi,
Liúshǒu Zhōng Wèi,
Chánghuái Wèi,
Huáiyuǎn Wèi),
protecting the Imperial Mausoleum (Huánglíng).
One Left-behind Official (Liúshǒu) was established,
and one Left and Right Deputy Left-behind Official (Fù Liúshǒu) each.
(Subordinate officials from Records Officer (Jīnglì) downwards
were as listed above).
In the 18th year of Jiājìng, Jīngzhōu Zuǒ Wèi was renamed Xiǎnlíng Wèi,
and the Xīngdū Left-behind Office (Liúshǒu Sī) was established,
commanding Xiǎnlíng and Chéngtiān Guards,
protecting Xiǎnlíng,
with officials established similar to those in Zhōngdū.
Chief Military Commission (Dūdū Zhǐhuīshǐ Sī).
One Chief Military Commissioner (Dūdū Zhǐhuīshǐ),
(senior second rank),
two Chief Military Commissioner Concurrent Managers (Dūdū Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī),
(junior second rank),
four Chief Military Commissioner Assistant Directors (Dūdū Zhǐhuī Qiānshì),
(senior third rank).
Its subordinates were:
Record Office (Jīnglì Sī),
Records Officer (Jīnglì),
(senior sixth rank),
Document Officer (Dūshì),
(senior seventh rank).
Judgment Office (Duànshì Sī),
Judge (Duànshì),
(senior sixth rank),
Deputy Judge (Fù Duànshì),
(senior seventh rank),
and one Clerk (Lìmù) for each.
Prison Office (Sīyù Sī),
Prison Warden (Sīyù),
(junior ninth rank).
Warehouses and fodder grounds,
one Director (Dàshǐ) and one Assistant Director (Fùshǐ) each.
Provisional Chief Military Commission (Xíng Dūdū Zhǐhuīshǐ Sī),
with officials established similar to the Chief Military Commission (Dūdū Zhǐhuīshǐ Sī).
The Chief Military Commission (Dūsī) managed the military administration of a region,
each leading its guards and subordinate to the Five Chief Military Commissions (Wǔ Fǔ),
and answerable to the Ministry of War (Bīngbù).
All Chief Military Commissioners (Dūsī) and civilian officials (liúguān),
or those holding hereditary offices,
were inspected annually by the Provincial Surveillance Commissioners (Xúnfǔ) and Provincial Judicial Commissioners (Ànchá) for their competence,
and evaluated every five years in military administration for dismissal or retention.
The Chief Military Commissioner (Dūdū Zhǐhuīshǐ) and Concurrent Managers (Tóngzhī) and Assistant Directors (Qiānshì)
would usually have one person in charge of the commission's affairs,
called "Seal Holder" (Zhǎngyìn),
one person for training troops,
one person for military colonies,
called "Document Reviewer" (Qiānshū).
Patrols,
military supplies, grain transport, capital maneuvers, defense, and various other duties
were also filled by selection,
otherwise they were called "Receiving Salary without Specific Duty" (Dàifèng).
Those acting as Chief Military Commissioners (Xíng Dūdū Zhǐhuīshǐ) for coastal defense or garrisons
were not allowed to set up their own headquarters or ascend the public dais.
For imperial court auspicious or inauspicious reports and memorials,
the titles of the Provincial Administration Commission (Bù) and Provincial Surveillance Commission (Àn) were listed above.
Records Officers (Jīnglì) and Document Officers (Dūshì)
handled official documents.
Judges (Duànshì)
managed legal cases and prisons.
In the early Míng dynasty,
Branch Regional Military Commissions (Xíng Dūdū Fǔ 行都督府) were established in various provinces.
Officials were appointed as in the Military Commissions (Dūdū Fǔ 都督府).
Also established were various Regional Guard Commanderies (Dū Wèi Zhǐhuīshǐ Sī 都衛指揮使司).
In the 4th year of Hóngwǔ 洪武 (1371), the Regional Guard Legal Offices (Dū Wèi Duànshì Sī 都衛斷事司) were established
to handle lawsuits involving military officers and soldiers.
Since Regional Guards (Dū Wèi 都衛) were also responsible for commanding various regions,
their duties were very important.
Officials were chosen and promoted from the imperial court;
hereditary succession was not permitted.
In the 7th year (1374), the Xī'ān 行都衛 Zhǐhuīshǐ Sī 西安行都衛指揮使司 was established in Hézhōu 河州.
In the 10th month of the 8th year (1375), an imperial edict mandated that all Regional Guards (Dū Wèi 都衛) be reorganized into Regional Military Commissions (Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ Sī 都指揮使司).
In total, thirteen Regional Military Commissions (Dūsī 都司) were reorganized and established:
(The Yānshān Dū Wèi 燕山都衛 became the Běipíng Dūsī 北平都司;
the Xī'ān Dū Wèi 西安都衛 became the Shǎnxī Dūsī 陝西都司;
the Tàiyuán Dū Wèi 太原都衛 became the Shānxī Dūsī 山西都司;
the Hángzhōu Dū Wèi 杭州都衛 became the Zhèjiāng Dūsī 浙江都司;
the Jiāngxī Dū Wèi 江西都衛 became the Jiāngxī Dūsī 江西都司;
the Qīngzhōu Dū Wèi 青州都衛 became the Shāndōng Dūsī 山東都司;
the Chéngdū Dū Wèi 成都都衛 became the Sìchuān Dūsī 四川都司;
the Fúzhōu Dū Wèi 福州都衛 became the Fújiàn Dūsī 福建都司;
the Wǔchāng Dū Wèi 武昌都衛 became the Húguǎng Dūsī 湖廣都司;
the Guǎngdōng Dū Wèi 廣東都衛 became the Guǎngdōng Dūsī 廣東都司;
the Guǎngxī Dū Wèi 廣西都衛 became the Guǎngxī Dūsī 廣西都司;
the Dìngliáo Dū Wèi 定遼都衛 became the Liáodōng Dūsī 遼東都司;
the Hénán Dū Wèi 河南都衛 became the Hénán Dūsī 河南都司.)
Three Branch Regional Military Commissions (Xíng Dūsī 行都司) were also established:
(The Xī'ān Xíng Dū Wèi 西安行都衛 became the Shǎnxī Xíng Dūsī 陝西行都司;
the Dàtóng Dū Wèi 大同都衛 became the Shānxī Xíng Dūsī 山西行都司;
the Jiànníng Dū Wèi 建寧都衛 became the Fújiàn Xíng Dūsī 福建行都司.)
In the 15th year (1382), the Guìzhōu 都司 and Yúnnán 都司 were added.
Later, the Běipíng Dūsī 北平都司 was made the Běipíng Xíng Dūsī 北平行都司.
In the 1st year of Yǒnglè 永樂 (1403), it was changed to the Dàníng Dūsī 大寧都司.
During the Xuāndé 宣德 reign,
the Wànquán Dūsī 萬全都司 was added.
In total, there were sixteen Regional Military Commissions (Dūsī 都司) in the empire.
(Beyond the thirteen provincial Dūsī,
there were the Liáodōng, Dàníng, and Wànquán Dūsī.)
Also, the Sìchuān Xíng Dūsī 四川行都司 was established in Jiànchāng,
and the Húguǎng Xíng Dūsī 湖廣行都司 in Yúnryáng.
In total, there were five Branch Regional Military Commissions (Xíng Dūsī) in the empire.
In the early Míng,
Commandaries of Inspection and Pacification (Dū Zhènfǔ Sī 都鎮撫司) were also established in various provinces,
with officials such as Commissioner of Inspection and Pacification (Dū Zhènfǔ 都鎮撫),
(ranking from grade 4b),
Assistant Commissioner of Inspection and Pacification (Fù Zhènfǔ 副鎮撫),
(from grade 5b),
and Manager (Zhīshì 知事),
(from grade 8b).
In the 1st year of Wú 吳 (1367), the Dū Zhènfǔ was changed to grade 5a,
the Fù Zhènfǔ to grade 6a,
and the Zhīshì was changed to Controller of Documents (Tíkòng Àndú 提控案牘),
and the notation "省注" (abbreviated/omitted notation) was added.
They were abolished in the 6th year of Hóngwǔ (1373).
The Guard Commanderies (Wèi Zhǐhuīshǐ Sī 衛指揮使司)
had officials appointed as in the Capital Guards (Jīng Wèi 京衛).
(Their ranks and grades were also the same.)
Outer Guards (Wài Wèi 外衛) were all commanded by Regional Military Commissions (Dūsī), Branch Regional Military Commissions (Xíng Dūsī), or Garrison Commandaries (Liúshǒu Sī 留守司).
They were mostly hereditary officials (shìguān 世官),
but some were appointed officials (liúguān 流官).
All matters regarding hereditary succession, promotion, appointment, generous provisions, retirement benefits, and military administration of their subordinates,
as well as the sealing and signing of reports, were submitted to the Regional Military Commission (Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ Sī),
forwarded to the affiliated Military Commission (Dūdū Fǔ),
and then sent to the Ministry of War (Bīngbù).
Annually,
the Grand Coordinators (Fǔ 撫) and Surveillance Commissioners (Ànchá 按察) would assess their competence;
every five years, military officials were evaluated,
and those found unsuitable were dismissed or replaced.
Regarding the management of Guard affairs,
only the officials responsible for sealing and signing were involved.
Regardless of whether they were Commanders (Zhǐhuīshǐ 指揮使), Assistant Commanders (Tóngzhī 同知), or Adjutants (Qiānshì 僉事),
competent individuals were selected to fill these roles.

They were responsible for managing various miscellaneous duties such as military farms (túntián 屯田), troop inspection (yànjūn 驗軍), camp drills (yíngcāo 營操), patrol and arrest (xún bǔ 巡捕), grain transport (cáoyùn 漕運), defense (bèiyù 備禦), outpost duty (chūshào 出哨), entering the guard (rù wèi 入衛), garrison duty (shùshǒu 戍守), and military equipment (jūnjì 軍器).
These were called "officials currently in charge" (jiànrèn guǎnshì 見任管事).
Those not performing duties but enrolled in a unit
were called "receiving salary and performing minor duties" (dàifèng chāocāo 帶俸差操).
When on campaign,
they would lead their subordinates
and follow the orders of the appointed commander-in-chief.
For the Battalion (Suǒ 所) and
Company of a Thousand Households (Qiānhù Suǒ 千戶所): one Commandant (Zhèng Qiānhù 正千戶),
(grade 5a),
two Assistant Commandants (Fù Qiānhù 副千戶),
(grade 5b),
and two Deputy Commandants (Zhènfǔ 鎮撫),
(grade 6b).
Its subordinates included
one Clerk (Lìmù 吏目).
A company of a thousand households (Qiānhù Suǒ 千戶所) had jurisdiction over ten companies of a hundred households (Bǎihù Suǒ 百戶所),
totaling ten Captains (Bǎihù 百戶),
(grade 6a).
Promotions, reassignments, and additions had no fixed quotas.
There were twenty Company Commanders (Zǒngqí 總旗)
and one hundred Platoon Leaders (Xiǎoqí 小旗).
The defensive companies of a thousand households (Shǒuyù Qiānhù Suǒ 守禦千戶所)
and military-civilian companies of a thousand households (Jūnmín Qiānhù Suǒ 軍民千戶所) had the same official appointments.
For all Captains (Qiānhù),
one person held the seal (zhǎngyìn 掌印),
and one person signed documents (qiānshū 僉書),
referred to as "managing the troops" (guǎnjūn 管軍).
Captains (Qiānhù) and Lieutenants (Bǎihù)
could be provisional (shì 試)
or formally appointed (shíshòu 實授).
For sealing documents,
one person could hold multiple seals.
In military administration,
the Guard (Wèi 衛) commanded the Battalion (Suǒ),
the Captain (Qiānhù) supervised the Lieutenant (Bǎihù),
the Lieutenant (Bǎihù) commanded the Company Commander (Zǒngqí) and Platoon Leader (Xiǎoqí),
who led their soldiers to obey orders.
If a Deputy Commandant (Zhènfǔ) had no legal cases,
they would manage the troops.
If a Lieutenant (Bǎihù) position was vacant,
they would fill it.
The defensive companies of a thousand households (Shǒuyù Qiānhù Suǒ)
were not subordinate to a Guard (Wèi)
but reported directly to the Regional Military Commission (Dūsī).
All Guards (Wèi) and Battalions (Suǒ) were subordinate to the Regional Military Commissions (Dūsī),
and the Regional Military Commissions (Dūsī) were further subordinate to the Five Chief Military Commissions (Wǔ Jūn Dūdū Fǔ 五軍都督府).
(The Zhèjiāng Dūsī, Shāndōng Dūsī, and Liáodōng Dūsī
were subordinate to the Left Chief Military Commission (Zuǒ Jūn Dūdū Fǔ 左軍都督府).
The Shǎnxī Dūsī, Shǎnxī Xíng Dūsī, Sìchuān Dūsī, Sìchuān Xíng Dūsī, Guǎngxī Dūsī, Yúnnán Dūsī, and Guìzhōu Dūsī
were subordinate to the Right Chief Military Commission (Yòu Jūn Dūdū Fǔ 右軍都督府).
The Zhōngdū Liúshǒu Sī 中都留守司 and Hénán Dūsī
were subordinate to the Central Chief Military Commission (Zhōng Jūn Dūdū Fǔ 中軍都督府).
The Xīngdū Liúshǒu Sī 興都留守司, Húguǎng Dūsī, Húguǎng Xíng Dūsī, Fújiàn Dūsī, Fújiàn Xíng Dūsī, Jiāngxī Dūsī, and Guǎngdōng Dūsī
were subordinate to the Front Chief Military Commission (Qián Jūn Dūdū Fǔ 前軍都督府).
The Dàníng Dūsī, Wànquán Dūsī, Shānxī Dūsī, and Shānxī Xíng Dūsī
were subordinate to the Rear Chief Military Commission (Hòu Jūn Dūdū Fǔ 後軍都督府).)
In the early Míng dynasty,
Companies of a Thousand Households (Qiānhù Suǒ) were established,
with a Commandant (Zhèng Qiānhù),
(grade 5a),
an Assistant Commandant (Fù Qiānhù),
(grade 5b),
a Deputy Commandant (Zhènfǔ), and a Captain (Bǎihù),
(grade 6a).
Also established were various Myriad Household Headquarters (Wànhù Fǔ 萬戶府),
with a Myriad Commandant (Zhèng Wànhù),
(grade 4a),
an Assistant Myriad Commandant (Fù Wànhù),
(grade 4b),
a Manager (Zhīshì),
(grade 8b),
and an Inspector (Zhàomó 照磨),
(grade 9a).
Soon after, these Myriad Household Headquarters (Wànhù Fǔ) were abolished
because the name did not match the reality,
and instead, officials like Commanders (Zhǐhuīshǐ) and Captains (Qiānhù) were established.
Those generals commanding 5,000 soldiers
were designated Commanders (Zhǐhuīshǐ);
those with 1,000 soldiers were Captains (Qiānhù);
those with 100 soldiers were Lieutenants (Bǎihù);
those with 50 soldiers were Company Commanders (Zǒngqí);
and those with 10 soldiers were Platoon Leaders (Xiǎoqí).
In the 2nd year of Hóngwǔ (1369), the Express Delivery Companies of a Hundred Households (Kèqī Bǎihù Suǒ 刻期百戶所) were established,
with 200 swift-footed individuals selected
and led by a Captain (Bǎihù).
In the 7th year (1374), the system of Guards (Wèi) and Battalions (Suǒ) was further defined.
