Previously,
for both inner and outer Guards and Battalions,
one Guard (Wèi) commanded ten Companies of a Thousand Households (Qiānhù Suǒ),
one Company of a Thousand Households (Qiānhù Suǒ) commanded ten Companies of a Hundred Households (Bǎihù Suǒ),
one Company of a Hundred Households (Bǎihù Suǒ) led two Company Commanders (Zǒngqí),
one Company Commander (Zǒngqí) led five Platoon Leaders (Xiǎoqí),
and one Platoon Leader (Xiǎoqí) led ten soldiers.
At this time, the system was revised:
each Guard (Wèi) established five Companies of a Thousand Households (Qiānhù Suǒ)—Front, Rear, Center, Left, and Right.
Generally, 5,600 men constituted one Guard (Wèi),
1,120 men constituted one Company of a Thousand Households (Qiānhù Suǒ),
and 112 men constituted one Company of a Hundred Households (Bǎihù Suǒ).
Each Company of a Hundred Households (Bǎihù Suǒ) established two Company Commanders (Zǒngqí)
and ten Platoon Leaders (Xiǎoqí).
In the 20th year (1387), it was first ordered that each Guard (Wèi) establish officials for sealing (zhǎngyìn) and signing (qiānshū),
with specialized duties for managing affairs,
where the Commander (Zhǐhuīshǐ) held the seal,
and Assistant Commanders (Tóngzhī) and Adjutants (Qiānshì) each commanded a battalion (suǒ).
If soldiers lacked martial skills or had unsharpened weapons,
the commanding officer was held accountable.
In the 23rd year (1390), Military-Civilian Commanderies (Jūnmín Zhǐhuīshǐ Sī 軍民指揮使司) and Military-Civilian Companies of a Thousand Households (Jūnmín Qiānhù Suǒ 軍民千戶所) were established.
In total, there were 547 inner and outer Guards (Wèi) in the empire,
and 2,593 Battalions (Suǒ).
From the Guard Commander (Wèi Zhǐhuī) downwards, most officials were hereditary,
and soldiers also succeeded their fathers,
establishing a fixed system for that era.
Indigenous officials (Tǔguān),
Enlightenment Commissioner’s Office (Xuānwèisǐ Sī):
One Enlightenment Commissioner (Xuānwèishǐ),
(Grade 3, junior);
one Assistant Administrator (Tóngzhī),
(Grade 4, senior);
one Deputy Commissioner (Fùshǐ),
(Grade 4, junior);
one Reviewing Secretary (Qiānshì),
(Grade 5, senior).
Registrar Office (Jīnglì Sī):
One Registrar (Jīnglì),
(Grade 7, junior);
one Chief Clerk (Dūshì),
(Grade 8, senior).
Pacification Commissioner’s Office (Xuānfǔ Sī):
One Pacification Commissioner (Xuānfǔshǐ),
(Grade 4, junior);
one Assistant Administrator (Tóngzhī),
(Grade 5, senior);
one Deputy Commissioner (Fùshǐ),
(Grade 5, junior);
one Reviewing Secretary (Qiānshì),
(Grade 6, senior).
Registrar Office (Jīnglì Sī):
One Registrar (Jīnglì),
(Grade 8, junior);
one Office Manager (Zhīshì),
(Grade 9, senior);
one Document Scrutinizer (Zhàomó),
(Grade 9, junior).
Pacification Office (Ānfǔ Sī):
One Pacification Commissioner (Ānfǔshǐ),
(Grade 5, junior);
one Assistant Administrator (Tóngzhī),
(Grade 6, senior);
one Deputy Commissioner (Fùshǐ),
(Grade 6, junior);
one Reviewing Secretary (Qiānshì),
(Grade 7, senior).
Its subordinate staff:
one Clerk (Lìmù),
(Grade 9, junior).
Recruitment Commissioner’s Office (Zhāotǎosǐ Sī):
One Recruitment Commissioner (Zhāotǎoshǐ),
(Grade 5, junior);
one Deputy Recruitment Commissioner (Fùzhāotǎo),
(Grade 6, senior).
Its subordinate staff:
one Clerk (Lìmù),
(Grade 9, junior).
Prefectural Magistrate’s Office (Zhǎngguānsǐ Sī):
One Prefectural Magistrate (Zhǎngguān),
(Grade 6, senior);
one Deputy Prefectural Magistrate (Fùzhǎngguān),
(Grade 7, junior).
Its subordinate staff:
one Clerk (Lìmù),
(unranked).
Barbarian Prefectural Magistrate’s Office (Mányí Zhǎngguānsǐ Sī):
One Prefectural Magistrate (Zhǎngguān) and one Deputy Prefectural Magistrate (Fùzhǎngguān) each,
(grades as above).
There were also barbarian officials (mányí guān), Miao people officials (miáomín guān), and chiliarchs (qiānfūzhǎng), deputy chiliarchs (fùqiānfūzhǎng), and other officials.
Military-Civilian Prefectures (Jūnmínfǔ), Indigenous Prefectures (Tǔzhōu), and Indigenous Counties (Tǔxiàn)
established officials like those in prefectures (fǔ), departments (zhōu), and counties (xiàn).
In the seventh year of Hóngwǔ
when the various barbarians in the southwest paid tribute,
most were appointed with their former Yuán dynasty titles.
They were given some regulations
and methods for collecting taxes, corvée, and levies were established.
Gradually, eleven became Enlightenment Commissioner’s Offices (Xuānwèisǐ Sī),
one became a Recruitment Commissioner’s Office (Zhāotǎosǐ Sī),
ten became Pacification Commissioner’s Offices (Xuānfǔsǐ Sī),
nineteen became Pacification Offices (Ānfǔsǐ Sī),
and one hundred and seventy-three became Prefectural Magistrate’s Offices (Zhǎngguānsǐ Sī).
Their principal and subordinate officials in prefectures, departments, and counties,
whether indigenous (tǔ) or regular (liú) officials,

(mostly, registrars (jīnglì) in Enlightenment Commissioner’s Offices (Xuānwèisǐ) and similar bureaus were regular officials (liúguān), and many assistant officials in prefectures, departments, and counties were regular officials (liúguān)),
all adhered to their local customs,
making them
cooperate in rallying the various barbarians,
diligently guarding the territory,
performing their duties of tribute,
and providing for levies and conscriptions,
without any disloyalty.
If there were feuds,
they were to memorialize and await the Son of Heaven’s (Tiānzǐ) command.
There were also three Barbarian Commander-in-Chief Offices (Fānyí Dūzhǐhuīshǐ Sī),
three hundred and eighty-five Guard Commander’s Offices (Wèizhǐhuīshǐ Sī),
three Enlightenment Commissioner’s Offices (Xuānwèisǐ Sī),
six Recruitment Commissioner’s Offices (Zhāotǎosǐ Sī),
four Myriarchates (Wànhùfǔ),
forty-one Chiliarchies (Qiānhùsuǒ),
seven stations (zhàn),
seven territories (dìmiàn),
and one stockade (zhài).
(Detailed information can be found in the treatise on military garrisons and posts in the Military Records (Bīng Zhì Wèisuǒ Zhōng)).
All these were for the barbarians (fānyí) attached to the stockades to govern their own lands.
Collation Notes
Treatise Fifty-Three on Food and Money, Part One
The record states:
"Wealth is derived from the land,
and methods from Heaven.
The foundation of a prosperous nation
lies in agriculture and sericulture."
In the early Míng dynasty,
following the old system of the Yuán,
cash currency was not widely circulated, and paper money was used.
The private use of silver for transactions was also prohibited,
which might seem inconvenient for the people.
However, during the Hóngwǔ (Hóngwǔ), Yǒnglè (Yǒnglè), Hóngxī (Hóngxī), and Xuāndé (Xuāndé) eras,
the common people were prosperous,
and the state treasuries overflowed.
This was because at that time,
agriculture was encouraged and reclamation was diligently pursued.
No land was left uncultivated,
and people dedicated themselves to their fundamental occupations.
Furthermore, military agricultural colonies (túntián) and salt monopolies (zhōngyán) were established to supply border troops,
so food provisions did not rely on local officials.
Thus, both the government and the people were sufficiently provided for,
and both soldiers and civilians were affluent.
Later,
the military agricultural colonies (túntián) were ruined by the annexation of powerful families,
and fiscal ministers (jìchén) altered the salt laws.
Consequently, border troops entirely depended on the Grand Granary (Tàicāng) for their sustenance,
and transport and supply often fell short.
After the Shìzōng emperor,
ways of squandering wealth multiplied,
and the state treasuries became depleted.
The Shénzōng emperor then increased taxes and levied heavy duties,
and mining taxes spread everywhere,
diverting regular revenues to fill the Left Treasury (Zuǒcáng).
Eunuchs (zhōngjuàn) and petty officials
extorted and embezzled indiscriminately.
Many people abandoned agriculture for commerce,
and fields became barren.
Officials were unable to care for the people
and instead oppressed them.
The entire realm was impoverished,
and reserves became even emptier.
Ignorant people often said that restoring paper money circulation could enrich the nation,
unaware that the prosperity of the early dynasty lay in diligent agriculture and sericulture,
not in the circulation of paper money.
Indeed, strengthening the foundation and economizing expenditure
are the essentials of financial management.
This chapter details the Míng dynasty’s financial administration,
explaining how it succeeded at first
and how it failed in the end,
outlining its causes and effects,
and presenting them in this treatise.
Population and Land System (Military Colonies (Túntián), Manorial Estates (Zhuāngtián))
Tài-Zǔ registered the households of the realm,
instituting household certificates (hùtiè) and household registers (hùjí).
These fully recorded names, ages, and places of residence.
The registers were submitted to the Hùbù (Board of Revenue),
and the certificates were issued to the people.
The officials annually calculated increases and decreases and reported them.
When the suburban sacrifices (jiāosì) occurred,
the Zhōngshū Shěng (Central Secretariat) presented the household registers at the altar,
recommending them to Heaven.
After the sacrifice, they were stored.
In the 14th year of Hóngwǔ (1381), an imperial edict commanded the compilation of the Yellow Registers (Huángcè) for all under heaven, for taxation and corvée.
One hundred and ten households formed one "lǐ" (village unit).
Of these, ten households with the most adult males (dīng) and grain (liáng) were designated as "zhǎng" (chiefs),
and the remaining one hundred households were divided into ten "jiǎ" (tithings),
with each "jiǎ" having ten people.
Annually, one lǐzhǎng and
one jiǎshǒu were appointed,
to oversee the affairs of their lǐ and jiǎ respectively.
Their turns were ordered according to the amount of dīng and liáng,
with a full cycle every ten years,
called "páinián" (annual rotation).
Within cities, these units were called "fāng",
near cities, "xiāng",
and in the countryside, "lǐ".
The lǐ were compiled into registers,
and the covers of these registers collectively formed a "yītú" (single diagram).
Those who were widowed, orphaned, solitary, or disabled and exempt from service
were appended after the ten jiǎ as "jīlíng" (odd remnants).
Monks and Daoists were issued ordination certificates (dùdié);
if they owned land, they were registered like commoners,
and those without land were also jīlíng.
Every ten years, officials revised these registers,
adjusting them based on increases or decreases in dīng and liáng.
There were four copies of the register: one was submitted to the Hùbù,
and the other three were kept by the Bùzhèng Sī (Provincial Administration Commission), fǔ (prefecture), and xiàn (county) respectively.
The one submitted to the Hùbù
had a yellow paper cover,
hence it was called the Huángcè (Yellow Register).
At the end of the year, it was presented
and sent to the East and West libraries of Hòuhú for storage.
Annually, one Hùkē Jìshìzhōng, two Yùshǐ, and four Hùbù Zhǔshì were appointed to correct errors.
Later, the Huángcè became merely a formality;
when officials collected taxes and arranged corvée,
they created a separate register for themselves,
called the Báicè (White Register).
All households were divided into three categories:
civilian (mín),
military (jūn),
and artisan (jiàng).
Civilian households included scholars (rú),
physicians (yī), and diviners (yīnyáng).
Military households included cavalrymen (jiàowèi),
strongmen (lìshì), archers (gōng), and post-station soldiers (pùbīng).
Artisan households included cooks (chúyì), tailors (cáiféng), and those involved in horses and boats (mǎchuán zhīlèi).
Along the coast were salt households (yánzào).
Buddhist temples had monks (sēng),
and Daoist temples had Daoist priests (dàoshì).
All were registered according to their profession.
Households were strictly defined by their register;
several surnames were prohibited from combining into one household.
Those who were unregistered or omitted from the household count
were allowed to register themselves.
In each lǐ, an "lǎorén" (elder) was appointed,
chosen from among the aged who were respected by the community,
to guide the people toward good
and mediate disputes in the village.
Households that evaded corvée were called "táohù" (fugitive households).
During famine or to escape war, those who moved elsewhere were called "liúmín" (migrant people).
Those who left for a specific reason and resided elsewhere were called "fùjí" (attached households).
Those moved by the court were called "yíxǐ" (resettled people).
For all táohù,
in the early Míng, they were compelled to return to their original registered place and resume their livelihoods,
granted one year's exemption from service.
The old and weak who could not return or were unwilling to return
were ordered to register in their current location,
given land, and required to pay taxes.
During the Zhèngtǒng reign,
a comprehensive register of táohù was compiled (táohù zhīzhī cè),
verifying their dīng and liáng.
For all liúmín,
Yīngzōng ordered an investigation of their registration,
assigning them to jiǎ for mutual guarantee,
and placing them under the jurisdiction of the local lǐzhǎng.
Auxiliary officials (fǔmín zuòèr guān) were appointed to pacify the people.
Those who returned to their original places
were encouraged, settled, and pacified,
given cattle, seeds, and rations.
Furthermore, following the advice of Yú Qiān, the Xúnfǔ of Hénán and Shānxī,
liúmín who resumed their livelihoods were exempted from taxes.
In the early Chénghuà reign,
the Jīng-Xiāng region was plagued by banditry,
with a million liúmín.
Xiàng Zhōng and Yáng Xuán, as Xúnfǔ of Húguǎng,
issued an order to expel them;
those who refused to comply were sent to the border for military service,
and countless died.
Jìjiǔ Zhōu Hóngmó wrote a treatise on liúmín,
citing the practice of "qiáozhì jùnxiàn" (establishing temporary prefectures and counties for migrants) from the Eastern Jìn dynasty,
so that those nearby could be registered locally, and those far away could have zhōu and xiàn established to pacify them.
Dū Yùshǐ Lǐ Bīn submitted this proposal.
Xiànzōng ordered Yuán Jié to go and pacify them,
recruiting 120,000 liúmín households,
allocating idle land,
establishing Yún'yáng Fǔ,
and setting up counties like Shàngjīn to govern them.
Hénán Xúnfǔ Zhāng Xuān also requested the resettlement of liúmín in the northwest.
The Emperor acceded to his request.
For those who were fùjí,
during the Zhèngtǒng reign,
family members of old and infirm officials who died in service,
if more than a thousand lǐ from their original registration, were allowed to be registered locally;
those less than a thousand lǐ away were sent back.
In the Jiǐngtài period,
civilian households (mínjí) were allowed to be registered locally;
military, artisan, and salt-worker households (jūn, jiàng, zàoyì) who falsely claimed civilian status were sent back.
As for those yíxǐ,
in the early Míng,
over four thousand landless households from Sūzhōu, Sōngjiāng, Jiāxīng, Húzhōu, and Hángzhōu were resettled
to cultivate land in Línháo,
provided with cattle, seeds, carts, and rations
for their journey,
and exempted from taxes for three years.
Xú Dá pacified the desert region,
resettling over 35,800 households from behind the mountains of Běipíng,
dispersing them among various prefectures and guards (wèi);
those registered as soldiers were given clothes and rations,
and civilians were given land.
Also, over 32,800 surviving households from the desert were settled to cultivate land in Běipíng,
establishing 254 garrisons (tún),
and opening up 1,343 qǐng of land.
Furthermore, 140,000 households from Jiāngnán were resettled in Fèngyáng.
Hùbù Lángzhōng Liú Jiǔgāo said:
"In ancient times, people from 'narrow counties' (xiáxiāng)
were permitted to move to 'broad counties' (kuānxiāng),
so that no land would be left unutilized,
and no one would lose their livelihood."
Tài-Zǔ adopted this suggestion,
relocating people from Zé and Lù in Shānxī to Hébĕi.
Later, people from western Zhèjiāng and Shānxī were repeatedly resettled in Chúzhōu, Hézhōu, Běipíng, Shāndōng, and Hénán.
People from Dēngzhōu, Láizhōu, and Qīngzhōu were also resettled in Dōngchāng and Yǎnzhōu.
Furthermore, 20,000 households from Zhílì and Zhèjiāng were resettled in the imperial capital (Jīngshī)
to serve as porters for granaries (cāngjiǎofū).
Tài-Zǔ's era saw the most resettlements,
with some being moved as punishment.
Jiànwén Dì ordered Wǔkāng Bó Xú Lǐ to go to Běipíng to survey land and settle them.
Chéngzǔ reviewed households in Tàiyuán, Píngyáng, Zézhōu, Lù'ān, Liáozhou, Qìnzhōu, and Fénzhōu with many dīng but little or no land,
dispersing their dīng and households to populate Běipíng.
After this,
resettlements became rare.
Initially,
Tài-Zǔ established the Yǎngjì Yuàn to care for the destitute,
providing monthly rations.
He established the Lòuzé Yuán to bury the poor.
Yìzhǒng (public graveyards) were established in prefectures, zhōu, and xiàn throughout the realm.
He also implemented policies for elder care,
granting titles to commoners aged eighty and above.
He further issued edicts to provide preferential relief to soldiers and civilians who suffered disasters.
However, in punishment for the powerful and wealthy who oppressed the poor and weak at the end of the Yuán dynasty,
many laws were made to favor the poor and suppress the rich.
He once ordered the Hùbù to register over 14,300 wealthy households from nine Bùzhèng Sī, including Zhèjiāng, and eighteen fǔ and zhōu of Yìngtiān,
summoning them in sequence,
and relocating their families to populate the Jīngshī,
calling them "fùhù" (rich households).
During Chéngzǔ's time,
3,000 wealthy households from Yìngtiān and Zhèjiāng were again selected
to serve as xiāngzhǎng in Wǎn and Dà counties of Běijīng,
registered in Jīngshī,
but still subject to corvée from their original registered places.
After prolonged provision of supplies,
they became impoverished and fled;
solid households from their original registered places were then chosen to replace them.
During the Xuāndé period, regulations were established:
fugitives were sent to the border for military service,
and officials, neighbors, and villages who concealed them were all punished.
In the fifth year of Hóngzhì (1492), the obligation to repatriate fugitive wealthy households was finally abolished;
instead, each household was levied three liǎng of silver
to assist xiāng civilians in their service.
During the Jiājìng period, this was reduced to two liǎng,
to be used for border military expenses.
Tài-Zǔ's intention in establishing these laws
was originally to emulate the Hàn dynasty's system of relocating wealthy households to populate Guānzhōng.
However, over time, abuses arose,
and it eventually became a source of hardship.
The number of households and individuals
varied in increase and decrease.
Those that can be investigated are:
in the 26th year of Hóngwǔ,
the empire had 10,652,870 households
and 60,545,812 individuals.
In the 4th year of Hóngzhì,
there were 9,113,446 households
and 53,281,158 individuals.
In the 6th year of Wànlì,
there were 10,621,436 households
and 60,692,856 individuals.
When Tài Zǔ reigned, after a period of warfare,
households and individuals were extremely prosperous.
Later, after a long period of peace,
they conversely did not reach that level.
When the Jingnán campaign began,
the area north of the Huái River was covered in luxuriant grass,
yet the population then actually increased compared to before.
Later, it gradually decreased,
reaching its lowest point during the Tiānshùn era.
During the Chénghuà and Hóngzhì eras, it prospered again,
but after Zhèngdé, it decreased once more.
As for why the population decreased,
Zhōu Chén said:
"They sought refuge with powerful families,
or falsely claimed to be artisans and fled to the two capitals,
or falsely claimed merchant licenses to trade in the four directions,
living with their entire families on boats,
leaving no trace."
But in essence,
the increase or decrease in households and individuals
was due to the strictness or laxity of government policies.
Thus, Xuān Zōng once discussed the population of past dynasties with his ministers,
believing that
"its prosperity
was based on rest and recuperation,
and its decline
was due to construction projects and military conflicts,"
which is indeed a profound observation.
The land system of the Míng dynasty
was generally of two types: called guāntián (official land)
and míntián (private land).
Initially,
guāntián all consisted of land that had become official property during the Sòng and Yuán dynasties.
Subsequently, there was land returned to the government,
confiscated land,
land awarded to the government by judgment,
xuétián (school land),
huángzhuāng (imperial estates),
mùmǎ cǎochǎng (horse pastures),
chéngruǎn mùxùdì (alfalfa fields within city walls),
shēngdì (sacrificial land),
yuánlíng féndì (garden, mausoleum, and tomb land),
gōngzhàn xìdì (publicly occupied vacant land),
zhuāngtián (estates granted to princes, princesses, imperial relatives, high ministers, eunuchs, and temples/monasteries),
bǎiguān zhítián (officials' stipendiary land),
biānchén yǎliántián (frontier officials' integrity-nurturing land),
jūn, mín, shāng túntián (military, civilian, and merchant屯田),
all collectively referred to as guāntián.
The rest was míntián.
During the chaos at the end of the Yuán dynasty,
most land registers were lost,
and land taxes lacked a standard.
When Míng Tài Zǔ ascended the throne,
he dispatched Zhōu Zhù and 163 others
to verify the land in Zhèxī
and fix its taxes.
He further ordered the Household Department to verify all land in the empire.
However, wealthy families in Liǎngzhè feared corvée labor,
and generally transferred their land to other households,
which was called tiějiǎo guìjì (iron-footed fraudulent registration).
In the 20th year of Hóngwǔ, he ordered students from the Guózǐ Jiàn, such as Wǔ Chún, to go to the prefectures and counties,
dividing areas according to grain production.
Each area was assigned four liángzhǎng (grain chiefs),
who measured the square or round shape of the fields,
then assigned character-based numbers,
recording the owner's name and the field's length and width,
compiling them into a register
shaped like fish scales,
called Yúlín Túcè (Fish-Scale Registers).
Before this,
an imperial edict ordered the compilation of huángcè (yellow registers) throughout the empire,
which took households as the main unit,
detailing the "old management, new acquisition, cancellation, and actual" numbers as a four-column format.
The Yúlín Túcè, however, took land as the main unit,
fully recording distinctions such as slopes, mounds, lowlands, fertile or barren lands, and saline flats.
The Yúlín Registers served as the warp,
for resolving land disputes.
The Huáng Registers served as the weft,
for establishing tax and corvée regulations.
When land was mortgaged or sold,
the tax and levies were fully recorded,
and officials registered it,
to prevent the land from being transferred while the tax remained with the original owner, causing harm to the people.
Also, because much land in the Central Plains was desolate,
he ordered provincial officials to discuss
and distribute land to the people based on their numbers.
A Sīnóng Sì was established,
which opened up and managed Hénán,
overseeing this matter.
The fields of Línháo were assessed based on manpower
and distributed by the mù (acre),
forbidding amalgamation.
In the north, land near cities was largely uncultivated,
so the people were summoned to cultivate it,
each person receiving 15 mù of land
and 2 mù of vegetable garden,
with three years of tax exemption.
Each year, the Zhōngshū Shěng reported the number of cultivated fields in the empire;
for smaller amounts, it was in the thousands of mù,
for larger amounts, it reached over 200,000.
For those who received cattle and farm tools from the government,
their taxes were collected,
but for those who reclaimed wasteland beyond the quota,
they were permanently exempt from levies.
In the 26th year, the land of the empire was verified,
totaling 8,507,623 qǐng,
indicating that little land was left fallow.
Generally, land near the city walls was considered superior,
and further away was medium or inferior.
Five chì made a bù,
240 bù made a mù,
and 100 mù made a qǐng.
Tài Zǔ continued the Yuán dynasty's lìshè system.
In the prefectures and counties north of the Yellow River, native residents were divided into lǐjiǎ by shè,
while relocated people in military colonies were divided into lǐjiǎ by tún.
Shè households initially occupied wider mù,
while tún households newly occupied narrower mù,
hence tún land was called xiǎomù (small mù),
and shè land was called guǎngmù (wide mù).
By the Xuāndé era,
wasteland that was permanently exempt from levies and low-lying, saline lands with no grain production
were all audited and included in the tax quota,
exceeding the old numbers.
Officials then used large mù to correspond to small mù to match the old quota,
with several mù sometimes treated as one mù.
The bù and chì measurements varied inconsistently,
allowing people to arbitrarily increase or decrease them,
leading to uneven land distribution,
especially in the north.
Guìzhōu had no records of qǐng, mù, or chì for land,
and all taxes were collected by local officials.
Over time, land records in various places
became quite confused
and did not match the Huáng Registers.
In the 15th year of Hóngzhì,
the total land in the empire was only 4,228,058 qǐng,
with guāntián being one-seventh of míntián.
In the 8th year of Jiājìng,
Huò Tāo, commissioned to revise the Huìdiǎn (Collected Statutes),
stated:
"From Hóngwǔ to Hóngzhì, 140 years,
the empire's registered land has decreased by more than half,
with Húguǎng, Hénán, and Guǎngdōng showing the greatest loss of registered land.
Either it was allocated to princely establishments,
or it was concealed by cunning commoners.
Guǎngdōng had no princely establishments,
so it was either concealed or abandoned to bandits.
Those who manage the national economy
must pay attention to this."
At this time,
Guì È, Guō Hónghuà, Táng Lóng, and Jiǎn Xiāo successively submitted memorials requesting a verification of land,
and Gù Dǐngchén requested on-site measurement of the land,
thus giving rise to the proposal for land measurement.
Ānfú in Jiāngxī and Yùzhōu in Hénán first implemented it,
but the method was not detailed enough,
and many people were suspicious and fearful.
Later, in the prefectures and counties of Fújiàn,
two registers, jīng (warp) and wěi (weft), were created,
and their method was quite detailed.
However, it was largely land-centric,
allowing those with much land to still manipulate the system.
In the early years of Shén Zōng's reign,
Xǔ Fúyuǎn, the Prefect of Jiànchāng, created a guīhùcè (household return register),
which assigned land according to people,
a method that was simple yet strict.
In the 6th year of Wànlì,
the emperor adopted the proposal of Grand Secretary Zhāng Jūzhèng,
ordering a general land survey throughout the empire,
to be completed within three years.
The "open square root method" was used,
using diameter and circumference for multiplication and division,
and supplementing irregular plots.
Thus, powerful and cunning individuals could not conceal land,
lǐjiǎ were spared from compensatory burdens,
and common people were free from fictitious grain taxes.
The total registered land was 7,013,976 qǐng,
an increase of three million qǐng compared to the Hóngzhì era.
However, Zhāng Jūzhèng was meticulous in his audits,
and somewhat considered exceeding the quota a merit.
Officials competed to modify the "small bow" (a measuring tool) to report more land,
or exploited existing land to fill fictitious quotas.
Consequently, Běizhílí, Húguǎng, Dàtóng, and Xuānfǔ
subsequently increased taxes based on the excess land reported.
The system of *Túntián*: was divided into
*Jūntún* (military *tún*) and *Míntún* (civilian *tún*).
In the early reign of Tàizǔ,
the *Mínbīng Wànhùfǔ* (Civilian Militia Myriad-Household Office) was established,
housing soldiers among farmers,
which was the best method.
He also ordered various generals to station troops at Lóngjiāng and other places;
only Kāng Máocái's achievements were the most outstanding,
so an edict was issued to commend him,
and this was used to admonish the generals and soldiers.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ,
the *Zhōngshūshěng* (Central Secretariat) requested to tax the *Túnzú* (stationed soldiers) of Tàiyuán and Shuòzhōu,
but it was ordered that they not be levied.
The next year,
the *Zhōngshūshěng* reported:
"For the *túntián* in Hénán, Shāndōng, Běipíng, Shǎnxī, Shānxī, and the various prefectures of Zhílì Huái'ān,
those where officials provided oxen and seeds should pay five-tenths tax,
while those who provided their own should pay three-tenths."
An imperial edict ordered that these not be levied for now,
but after three years, a rent of one *dòu* per *mǔ* would be collected.
In the sixth year,
*Tàipúchéng* Liáng Yěxiān Tiěmù'ěr reported:
"Within the territory of Níngxià, and from the southwest of Sìchuān to Chuánchéng,
and northeast to Tǎtān,
a distance of eight hundred *lǐ*,
the soil is fertile and rich,
suitable for attracting vagrants to settle and cultivate *túntián*."
This was followed.
At this time,
Dèng Yù, Tāng Hé, and other generals were dispatched to establish *túntián* in Shǎnxī, Zhāngdé, Rǔníng, Běipíng, and Yǒngpíng;
people from Zhēndìng in Shānxī were relocated to Fèngyáng for *míntún*.
Furthermore, because some died by drowning during sea transport of provisions to Liáo,
the *tún* policies were further discussed,
and all military and civilian personnel in the *wèisuǒ* (guard stations), prefectures, and counties across the realm engaged in reclamation.
Under this system,
migrants were moved to broad, sparsely populated areas,
and those recruited or exiled for crimes became *míntún*,
all under the jurisdiction of local officials.
The *jūntún* were under the jurisdiction of the *wèisuǒ*.
In border areas,
three-tenths of the troops guarded cities,
and seven-tenths cultivated fields.
In inland areas,
two-tenths guarded cities,
and eight-tenths cultivated fields.
Each soldier received fifty *mǔ* of land as one share,
was provided with plowing oxen and farm tools,
taught to plant trees,
exempted from rent and taxes,
and officials were dispatched to encourage cultivation,
while oppressive and violent officials were executed.
Initially, the tax was one *dòu* per *mǔ*.
In the thirty-fifth year, the standard for assessment was set: for one share of military land,
the regular grain was twelve *shí*,
stored in the *túncāng* (garrison granary),
to be drawn by the soldiers themselves,
with the surplus grain serving as stipends for the officials and soldiers of that *wèisuǒ*.
In the early years of Yǒnglè,
regulations for rewards and punishments of *túntián* soldiers and officers were established: in addition to the annual twelve *shí* of rice, a rate of six *shí* of surplus was set;
those who produced more were rewarded with paper currency,
and those who produced less were penalized by deductions from their stipends.
Also, as land fertility varied,
the law should differ accordingly,
so officials and soldiers were ordered to cultivate experimental plots of various types,
and their annual harvests were compared.
For the experimental plot cultivated by *Qiānhù* Chén Huái of Tàiyuán Zuǒwèi,
each soldier produced twenty-three *shí* of surplus grain;
the emperor ordered him to be heavily rewarded.
Hé Fú, the *Zǒngbīng* of Níngxià, accumulated particularly large amounts of grain,
and was granted an imperial edict of commendation.
*Hùbù Shàngshū* Yù Xīn reported:
"The various *wèi* in Húguǎng collect different types of grain;
I request that rice be used as the standard.
For every two *shí* of millet, grain, foxtail millet, broomcorn millet, barley, or buckwheat,
and two *shí* five *dòu* of rice paddy or glutinous rice,
and three *shí* of barnyard millet or wild rice,
all shall be equivalent to one *shí* of rice.
Wheat, sesame, and beans are equivalent to rice."
This was followed,
and enacted as law.
The numbers for *tún* and *shǒu* (garrisoning) were also revised.
In strategically important border areas,
*shǒu* outnumbered *tún*.
In remote areas and where grain transport was difficult,
*tún* outnumbered *shǒu*.
One hundred *tún* soldiers were assigned to a *Bǎihù*,
three hundred to a *Qiānhù*,
and five hundred or more to a *Zhǐhuī Tídū*.
Red plaques were set up in the *tún*,
listing the rules and regulations.
Those aged sixty, the disabled, and the young,
farmed for their own sustenance
and were not restricted by the regulations.
*Tún* soldiers whose farming duties were hindered by public affairs
were exempted from grain levies,
and *wèisuǒ* levies and assignments were prohibited.
At that time,
from Liáozuǒ in the east,
north to Xuān and Dà,
west to Gānsù,
south to Diān and Shǔ,
and as far as Jiāozhǐ,
and in the Central Plains, north and south of the Great River,
*tún* were established everywhere.
During Xuānzōng's reign,
various *tún* were repeatedly reviewed,
and for those where cultivation was halted due to campaigns and garrisons, or seized and concealed by powerful officials and gentry,
the surplus grain was reduced by half.
Those who returned from the north and settled in *tún*
were given carts, oxen, and farm tools.
The *tún* soldiers of various *wèi* in Liáodōng were divided into three grades:
those with both able-bodied men and oxen were upper grade,
those with either one were middle grade,
and those with neither were lower grade.
Yīngzōng exempted the regular grain from military land from being stored in granaries,
only levying the six *shí* of surplus grain.
Later, he also exempted the grain from officials and soldiers who opened up land along the border,
and reduced the grain from various border *túntián* by varying amounts.
During Jǐngdì's reign,
there were many incidents in border regions,
and troops were ordered to be divided into two shifts:
six days for drilling and guarding,
and six days for farming.
In the early years of Chénghuà,
Yè Shèng, the *Xúnfǔ* of Xuānfǔ, bought one thousand eight hundred government oxen,
and also acquired farm tools,
dispatched troops to cultivate *túntián*,
and exchanged harvested grain for silver
to compensate for the loss of government horses,
which the border people found convenient.
After Zhèngtǒng,
the *tún* policy gradually relaxed,
but *tún* grain still retained two-thirds of its former amount.
Later, much of the *túntián* was seized by eunuchs and military officers,
and the system was completely ruined.
During Xiànzōng's reign, there was considerable discussion about restoration,
but the income compared to the old one
was less than one-tenth.
During Hóngzhì,
*tún* grain became even lighter,
with some *mǔ* yielding only three *shēng*.
Extending to Zhèngdé,
the *túntián* in Liáodōng increased by over eighteen thousand *qǐng* compared to the Yǒnglè period,
but the grain production shrank by over forty-six thousand *shí*.
Initially,
during Yǒnglè,
*túntián* rice often exceeded by one-third,
and of the one hundred ninety thousand regular troops,
forty thousand *tún* soldiers provided for them.
Those who received provisions also cultivated their own land.
Troops outside the border had no monthly rations,
which ensured adequate border provisions.
By this time,
many *tún* soldiers had fled or died,
and the regular troops numbered only eighty thousand,
all relying on granaries for support.
Furthermore, border areas were frequently disturbed,
and farming was abandoned.
When Liú Jǐn monopolized power,
officials were dispatched to survey the land and collect arrears.
Those who sought to please Liú Jǐn
falsely inflated the land figures,
and their collection methods were cruel and harsh;
*Hùbù Shìláng* Hán Fú was particularly severe.
The soldiers in Liáo could not endure it,
and coerced the populace into rebellion,
which was only settled after pacification.
In the early Míng dynasty,
salt merchants were recruited to establish military-agricultural colonies (kāizhōng) in various border regions,
which were known as shāngtún.
By the middle of the Hóngzhì reign,
Yè Qí reformed the system,
and the kāizhōng system began to deteriorate.
All Huái merchants withdrew their businesses and returned home,
and many northwestern merchants also moved their families to the Huái region.
The borderlands became desolate,
a stone of rice cost five liǎng of silver,
and the border granaries were empty.
During the Shìzōng reign,
Yáng Yīqīng again requested the recruitment of merchants for kāizhōng,
and also requested to imitate the ancients in recruiting commoners to fill the frontier,
inviting people from Lǒngyòu and Guānxī to settle and cultivate the borderlands.
Afterwards, Zhōu Zé, Wáng Chónggǔ, Lín Fù, Chén Shìfǔ, Wáng Jī, Wáng Cháoyòng, Táng Shùnzhī, Wú Guìfāng, and others repeatedly discussed the tún farmland policy.
Páng Shàngpéng then took charge of the salt tún lands north of the Jiāng River,
and soon moved to the Jiǔbiān (Nine Border Garrisons),
where, together with Grand Coordinator Wáng Chónggǔ,
they meticulously planned the tún farmland policies.
However, at that time,
due to prolonged inertia,
it ultimately yielded little practical effect.
Investigating Censor Guǎn Huáilǐ stated:
"There are four main problems why tún farmland does not flourish.
Its problems are four.
Border regions are under emergency alert,
that is the first.
Oxen and seeds are not provided,
that is the second.
Able-bodied men flee and migrate,
that is the third.
Fields are outside the enemy's reach,
that is the fourth.
Given this situation, if those in charge of tún lands still wish to increase taxes based on registers,
they either deduct monthly rations,
or impose compensation on each tún soldier."
The lightness of tún grain taxes
reached its extreme during the Hóngzhì and Zhèngdé reigns;
it gradually increased during the Jiājìng reign,
and in the Lóngqìng era, it returned to a collection of one dòu per mù.
However, the number of tún soldiers fleeing increased even more.
The Director of Grain Supply did not inquire whether the tún lands existed,
and only disbursed half of the monthly rations.
Along the border, tún lands
sometimes transformed into saline-alkali land or sandy deserts,
yet the grain quota could not be reduced.
The Censor for Tún Lands also added extra "original" and "discounted" surcharges beyond the quota,
making the tún soldiers even more unable to bear the burden.
During the Wànlì reign,
the calculated area of tún lands was over 644,000 qǐng,
showing a deficit of over 249,000 qǐng compared to the Hóngwǔ reign.
Fields decreased daily, while taxes increased daily,
such were the problems.
At that time, Zhèng Rǔbì, the Provincial Governor of Shāndōng, requested the reclamation of fields on the islands of Dēngzhōu, Hǎiběi, and Chángshān.
Xǔ Fúyuǎn, the Provincial Governor of Fújiàn, successfully reclaimed fields on Mǐnhǎitánshān,
and again requested the reclamation of Nánrìshān and Pénghú;
he also said that the coastal mountains of Zhèjiāng,
such as Chénqián, Jīntáng, Pǔtuó, Yùhuán, and Nánjǐ,
could all be managed.
Wāng Yìngjiāo, the Provincial Governor of Tiānjīn, then requested the establishment of tún lands in Tiānjīn.
Some proposals were retained in the palace and not acted upon,
while others were soon abandoned.
During the reign of Xīzōng,
Investigating Censor Zhāng Shènyán again proposed tún lands in Tiānjīn.
And Censor Zuǒ Guāngdǒu ordered Lú Guānxìang, the Assistant Prefect in charge of river administration, to greatly promote the benefits of paddy fields.
Dǒng Yìngjǔ, the Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, followed up on this.
Guāngdǒu further established tún schools in Héjiān and Tiānjīn,
where he tested archery and horsemanship,
and granted one hundred mù of land to martial students.
Lǐ Jìzhēn, the Provincial Governor of Tiānjīn,
also worked diligently on tún affairs,
but there were still annual droughts and locust infestations,
preventing the achievement of substantial results.
During the Míng dynasty,
there were quite a few pastures,
which encroached upon commoners' livelihoods.
But those that were most detrimental to the people
were the imperial estates (huángzhuāng) and the estates of princes, imperial relatives, powerful nobles, and eunuchs (zhōngguān zhuāngtián).
Tàizǔ bestowed estates upon meritorious officials, dukes, marquises, and chancellors,
with the largest being a hundred qǐng;
princely estates were a thousand qǐng.
He also granted public fields to dukes, marquises, and military officials,
and also granted public fields to all civil officials,
using their rents to pay their salaries.
Commanders who died in battle were all granted public fields.
The tenants on the estates of meritorious officials
often relied on their influence to impose restrictions,
so the Emperor summoned his ministers to admonish them.
Later, dukes and marquises resumed their annual stipends,
and returned the bestowed fields to the state.
During the Rénzōng and Xuānzōng reigns,
requests for land gradually expanded,
and high officials were also able to request confiscated imperial estates and residences.
However, when Prince Níng, Zhū Quán, requested to irrigate a city to create grazing land for his庶zǐ (legitimate son of concubine),
the Emperor sent a letter,
citing ancestral regulations to refuse him.
By the time of Yīngzōng,
princes, imperial relatives, and eunuchs everywhere occupied official and private lands,
or even falsely accused commoners of occupation,
and requested investigation and punishment.
When the investigations confirmed the facts,
the Emperor ordered the return of land to the people on multiple occasions.
He then issued an edict prohibiting the seizure of commoners' land and petitions for land within the capital region.
However, the estates and ancestral burial grounds of powerful nobles and imperial clansmen,
whether bestowed or requested,
were countless.
The family of Liú Shùn, the Imperial Horse Supervisor, presented Jìzhōu pastures to the court;
this initiated the practice of presenting land.
Eunuch-owned lands
began with Yǐn Fèng and Xǐ Níng.
Initially,
during the Hóngxī reign,
there was the Rénshòugōngzhuāng (Rénshòu Palace Estate),
and later there were also the Qīngníng and Wèiyánggōngzhuāng estates.
In the third year of Tiānshùn (1459),
because the princes had not yet come of age
and their expenses were vast,
the Dōnggōng (Crown Prince), Dé Wáng, and Xiù Wáng estates were established.
When the two princes were enfeoffed,
the land reverted to the state.
When Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
he made the confiscated land of Cáo Jíxiáng into imperial estates for the palace,
and the name huángzhuāng (imperial estate) originated from this.
Thereafter, imperial estates spread throughout the prefectures and counties.
Investigating Censor Qí Zhuāng said:
"The Son of Heaven considers the four seas his home;
why must he establish estates
to compete for profit with poor commoners?"
This was not heeded.
In the second year of Hóngzhì (1489),
Lǐ Mǐn, the Minister of Revenue, and others submitted a memorial regarding natural disasters:
"There are five imperial estates within the capital region,
totaling over 12,800 qǐng of land;
there are 332 estates belonging to imperial relatives, powerful nobles, and eunuchs,
totaling over 33,000 qǐng of land.
The estate managers and officials recruit gangs of petty individuals,
calling themselves zhuāngtóu (estate heads) and bàndàng (attendants),
who occupy land,
extort wealth,
and defile women.
If anyone dares to dispute them,
they are immediately falsely accused in a memorial.
Estate officials and guards seize and bind people,
terrifying entire families.
The common people's hearts are deeply pained,
which is the origin of the natural disasters.
We humbly request the removal of these estate managers,
and that the land be returned to the common people for cultivation,
with a tax of three fēn of silver per mù,
to be used for the expenses of the various palaces."
The Emperor ordered the estate households to be admonished.
Also, based on a Censor's memorial,
he abolished the Rénshòugōngzhuāng,
returning it to pastureland,
and further ordered that all who had encroached upon grazing land
should return it to its original state.
A new regulation was also established,
that those who presented land to princely households would be exiled to the border garrisons.
When Zhào Xuān, a Palace Attendant, presented land in Xióngxiàn to be an imperial estate,
Zhōu Jīng, the Minister of Revenue, impeached him for violating the regulation,
and Xuān was sent to the imperial prison.
An imperial edict instructed the princely tutors
to punish any prince who instigated petitions.
However, at that time, presentations and petitions did not cease,
and requests became increasingly frequent.
The four princes of Huī, Xīng, Qí, and Héng
had lands totaling over 7,000 qǐng.
The three marquises of Huìchāng, Jiànchāng, and Qìngyún disputed land,
and the Emperor granted it to them.
When Wǔzōng ascended the throne,
within a month,
he established seven imperial estates,
which later increased to over 300 locations.
Princes and imperial relatives requesting or seizing commoners' land were countless.
he ordered Censor-in-chief Xià Yán and others to audit the imperial estates' land.
Xià Yán strongly stated that the imperial estates were oppressive to the people.
From then on, land that had been offered up or seized since the Zhèngdé reign,
was largely returned to the people.
However, the eunuchs and imperial relatives interfered again.
Hùbù Shàngshū Sūn Jiāo created a new register for imperial estates,
with a reduced quota compared to the old one.
The Emperor ordered an audit of the acreage from previous years to be reported,
renamed it "official land,"
no longer calling it "imperial estates,"
and decreed that the responsible offices collect silver and remit it to the board.
Nevertheless, much was embezzled by eunuchs,
with arrears accumulating to hundreds of thousands, becoming routine.
At this time,
petitions for land by meritorious nobles and imperial relatives, and land offerings by cunning commoners were forbidden.
Furthermore, requests for mountain fields and lakes by princely establishments were abolished.
Dé Wáng requested the idle lands in Dōngchāng and Yǎnzhōu inherited from the two commoners, Qí and Hàn,
and also lakes such as Báiyún.
Shāndōng Xúnfǔ Shào Xī rejected this according to the new regulations,
his words were very sharp.
Dé Wáng disputed it several times,
but the Emperor still followed the board's recommendation,
only retaining the estates initially requested for their enfeoffments.
Afterwards, any further petitions were not granted.
It was also stipulated,
that for all princesses' and dukes' estates,
those inherited over many generations would retain three-tenths.
In the 39th year of Jiājìng, Yùshǐ Shěn Yáng was dispatched to investigate and confiscate over 16,000 qǐng of concealed or usurped estates.
Mùzōng followed the suggestion of Yùshǐ Wáng Tíngzhān,
and re-established limits for generational reduction: meritorious officials' estates were limited to 200 qǐng for five generations,
and imperial relatives' estates ranged from 700 to 70 qǐng, varying by degree.
Initially,
during Shìzōng's time,
the six estates and two lakes in Chéngtiān, totaling over 8,300 qǐng,
were managed by eunuchs.
They also permitted school compounds to annex land,
adding 880 qǐng,
dividing it into twelve estates.
and land that had been annexed was returned to the people.
Furthermore, a decree was issued that if members of the imperial clan bought land without paying corvée, it would be confiscated by the state.
For lands belonging to imperial relatives, all were to be taxed by the responsible officials,
following the precedent of meritorious officials.
Although requests for grants were not uncommon,
the granted quotas were fixed,
and collections were regulated,
so the harm to the people somewhat diminished and ceased.
Shénzōng's grants were excessively extravagant,
and no request went unfulfilled.
Lù Wáng and Shòuyáng Gōngzhǔ received the most abundant favor.
And when Fú Wáng was enfeoffed,
he seized land in Hénán, Shāndōng, and Húguǎng to form his princely estates,
totaling up to 40,000 qǐng.
His officials strongly argued against it,
so it was reduced by half.
Princely officials and various eunuchs surveyed land and collected taxes,
crowding the roads.
Attendants and servants living off allowances numbered in the tens of thousands,
and their cruel and predatory extortions were unbearable to hear about.
Imperial warrants were used to arrest commoners,
and estate tenants were brutally killed.
Disturbance was widespread.
Censors-in-chief Guān Yìngzhèn, Yáo Zōngwén, and others repeatedly submitted remonstrances,
but none were acted upon.
At that time, the method for generational reduction of meritorious nobles' and imperial relatives' estates was revised again,
being somewhat more lenient than the old system.
Subsequently, those that should have been reduced through deliberation,
were often temporarily kept by imperial decree,
and could not be abolished.
During Xīzōng's reign,
the estates of the three kings, Guì Wáng, Huì Wáng, and Ruì Wáng, and the two princesses, Suìpíng Gōngzhǔ and Níngdé Gōngzhǔ,
While the household of Wèi Zhōngxián,
received even more extravagant illicit grants.
Indeed, from the mid-Míng dynasty onwards,
imperial estates encroached upon the common people's livelihoods,
and persisted until the end of the dynasty.
Collated Notes
Treatise 54, Economy and Finance 2, Taxation
Regarding the laws of taxation,
the rent, corvée, and tribute system of the Táng dynasty was still relatively ancient.
Since Yáng Yán established the Two-Tax System,
it was simple and easy to implement.
It was followed by successive dynasties,
and remained unchanged until the Míng dynasty.
When Tàizǔ was Wú Wáng,
taxes were one-tenth,
and the corvée system calculated labor based on land.
Counties were divided into three grades: upper, middle, and lower,
differentiated by taxes of 100,000, 60,000, and below 30,000 dàn respectively.
Prefectures also had three grades,
differentiated by taxes of around 200,000 and below 100,000 dàn.
At the beginning of his reign,
he established the taxation and corvée laws,
with the Yellow Registers as the sole standard.
The registers recorded households and land.
Households were liable for corvée,
and land was subject to rent.
Rents were called summer tax,
and autumn grain,
making two categories in total.
The summer tax was due no later than the eighth month,
and the autumn grain no later than the second month of the following year.
Households were classified as "adult households" (chéngdīng)
and "non-adult households" (wèichéngdīng),
making two categories in total.
When a person was born,
their name was registered as "not yet an adult household."
At sixteen, they became an "adult household."
An adult household was liable for corvée,
and exempted at sixty.
There were also those exempted from corvée due to official duties.
Corvée was categorized as lǐjiǎ,
jūnyáo,
and záfàn,
making three categories in total.
Corvée calculated by household was called jiǎyì;
by adult household was called yáoyì;
and extraordinary commands from above were called záyì.
All involved either physical labor,
or hired labor.
Prefectures, subprefectures, and counties verified the number of adult households in the registers,
and the extent of their property,
to distribute the burden equitably.
The Two Taxes:
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
the summer tax included rice and wheat,
coins and paper currency,
and silk.
The autumn grain included rice,
coins and paper currency,
and silk.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
the items for accounting included:
for summer tax: large and small rice and wheat,
wheat and buckwheat,
silk floss and waste silk,
tax silk,
silk floss commuted to silk fabric,
tax silk commuted to silk fabric,
actual silk,
agricultural silk commuted to silk fabric,
odd bits of agricultural silk,
household silk commuted to silk fabric,
revised tax silk fabric,
cotton commuted to cloth,
ramie cloth,
local ramie,
safflower,
hemp cloth,
paper currency,
rent in paper currency,
tax in paper currency,
original small silk fabric quota,
ceremonial silk fabric,
actual silk fabric,
silk fabric,
and commuted colored silk.
For autumn grain: rice,
rent in paper currency,
lease in paper currency,
mountain rent in paper currency,
rent in silk,
rent in silk fabric,
rent in coarse hemp cloth,
assessed cotton cloth,
rent in ramie cloth,
cow rent in rice and grain,
cotton lint per mu of land,
dates exchanged for rice,
date tree tax in rice,
assessed ramie commuted to rice,
cotton cloth,
fish tax in rice,
and revised tax silk commuted to rice.
During the Wànlì reign,
there were minor additions and reductions,
but generally, rice and wheat were primary,
with silk and paper currency secondary.
Summer tax in rice was collected only in Jiāngxī, Húguǎng, Guǎngdōng, and Guǎngxī;
wheat and buckwheat only in Guìzhōu;
agricultural silk was collected throughout the empire,
except in Chuān, Guǎng, Yún, and Guì;
other items varied according to local products.
Tàizǔ, upon establishing the nation, immediately issued an order:
For commoners with 5 to 10 mu of land,
they must plant half a mu each of mulberry, hemp, and cotton.
For those with over 10 mu, they must plant double that amount.
For each mu of hemp, 8 liǎng were taxed;
for each mu of cotton, 4 liǎng.
Mulberry cultivation was taxed starting from the fourth year.
If one did not plant mulberry,
one must provide one roll of silk fabric.
If one did not plant hemp or cotton,
one must provide one roll each of hemp cloth and cotton cloth.
This is how the agricultural silk and silk fabric taxes originated.
In the ninth year of Hóngwǔ
, throughout the empire, land tax
was ordered to be paid by the people in silver, paper money, coins, or silk.
One liǎng of silver, one thousand coins, or one guàn of paper money
were all equivalent to one dàn of rice.
For wheat, the value was reduced by two-tenths.
One pǐ of cotton or ramie cloth
was equivalent to six dǒu of rice,
or seven dǒu of wheat.
One pǐ of hemp cloth
was equivalent to four dǒu of rice,
or five dǒu of wheat.
Silk, fine silk, and other items were adjusted in value according to their weight and quality.
Those who wished to pay in grain were permitted.
In the seventeenth year,
Yúnnán substituted gold, silver, cowries, cloth, lacquer, cinnabar, and mercury for the autumn tax.
Thus, rice and wheat were called "principal goods" (běnsè),
while those who paid their taxes in other converted goods
were called "converted goods" (zhésè).
Two years later,
the Minister of Revenue, Yáng Jìng, was again ordered to audit the grain stored in granaries throughout the empire.
Any grain beyond two years' supply was to be collected as zhésè,
except for the various Administration Commissioners' Offices (Bùzhèng Sī) in the north, which needed grain to supply the border,
and were therefore still to receive millet.
In the thirtieth year, an imperial decree was issued to the Ministry of Revenue stating:
"Envoy Gāo Zhěn said
that Shǎnxī is struggling with unpaid taxes.
It is proposed that for all unpaid taxes throughout the empire
from the twenty-eighth year and before,
people be allowed to pay with whatever their locality produces,
accepting cloth, silk, cotton, and gold, silver, and other goods as payment.
Let this be made law."
Thereupon, the Ministry of Revenue stipulated: one dìng of paper money
was equivalent to one dàn of rice;
one liǎng of gold,
ten dàn;
one liǎng of silver,
two dàn;
one pǐ of silk,
one dàn and two dǒu;
one pǐ of cotton cloth,
one dàn;
one pǐ of ramie cloth,
seven dǒu;
and one jīn of cotton,
two dǒu.
The Emperor said:
"Collecting overdue taxes in converted goods
is intended to alleviate the people's hardship.
If the converted rates are this heavy,
it will only cause more distress to the people.
How can this be called compassion?
The conversion rate for gold and silver per liǎng should be doubled.
For paper money, only two guàn and five hundred wén should be equivalent to one dàn.
The rest shall follow what was proposed."
During the Yǒnglè reign,
after Jiāozhǐ was acquired,
its taxes were paid in silk,
lacquer,
sappanwood,
kingfisher feathers,
paper fans,
and various kinds of incense such as agarwood, eaglewood, and benzoin.
The Lí people of Qióngzhōu and the Yáo people of Zhàoqìng in Guǎngdōng submitted,
paying taxes at rates similar to the interior.
The empire's běnsè tax grain amounted to over thirty million dàn,
and silk, paper money, etc., to over twenty million [in equivalent value].
At that time,
the empire was prosperous and abundant,
with tax revenue overflowing.
Apart from several million dàn of rice and millet transported to the capital,
the granaries of the prefectures and counties accumulated so much
that it turned red and became inedible.
In lean years,
officials often first distributed grain for relief and loans
before reporting it.
Although annual tribute silver amounted to over three hundred thousand liǎng,
there were still strict prohibitions
against the use of silver for transactions among the populace.
Until the first year of Zhèngtǒng,
Vice Censor-in-chief Zhōu Quán stated:
"The stipends of officials in the various guards of the temporary capital are paid in rice from Nánjīng.
The long distance and high costs mean
that they often exchange rice for goods,
buying expensively and selling cheaply,
losing more than nine-tenths of their value.
The court thus wastes official salaries,
and officials receive no substantial benefit.
I request that in areas of Nánjī, Zhèjiāng, Jiāngxī, and Húguǎng where waterways are inaccessible,
taxes be collected in cloth, silk, and silver bullion
and sent to the capital to serve as stipends."
The Grand Coordinator of Jiāngxī, Zhào Xīn, also made a similar statement,
and Minister of Revenue Huáng Fú again petitioned with specific proposals.
The Emperor inquired with the Minister of Revenue of the temporary capital, Hú Yíng.
Hú Yíng replied that Tàizǔ had previously allowed converted tax payments in Shǎnxī and Zhèjiāng,
which the people found convenient.
So, following that system,
one dàn of rice or wheat
was converted to two qián and five fēn of silver.
In Nánjī, Zhèjiāng, Jiāngxī, Húguǎng, Fújiàn, Guǎngdōng, and Guǎngxī, a total of over four million dàn of rice and wheat
was converted into over one million liǎng of silver,
which was deposited into the Inner Court Treasury.
This was called "gold flower silver" (jīnhuāyín).
Subsequently, it was implemented throughout the empire.
Except for grain transported for military exchanges,
four dàn of grain were converted to one liǎng of silver and sent to the capital
as a permanent rule.
As various regions converted their revenue to silver,
the accumulation in granaries gradually decreased.
Initially,
Tàizǔ fixed the land tax for official and private lands throughout the empire.
For official land, the tax per *mǔ* was five *shēng*, three *hé*, five *sháo*.
For private land, it was reduced by two *shēng*.
For heavily-taxed land, it was eight *shēng*, five *hé*, five *sháo*.
For lands confiscated by the government, it was one *dǒu*, two *shēng*.
Only Sūzhōu, Sōngjiāng, Jiāxìng, and Húzhōu,
because he was angry that they had defended Zhāng Shìchéng,
had the lands of prominent families and wealthy commoners registered as official land,
and the tax quota was based on their private rent ledgers.
Moreover, Yáng Xiàn, the Minister of Agriculture, considering the fertile soil of Zhèxī,
increased its tax,
doubling the amount per *mǔ*.
Therefore, the official and private lands in Zhèxī were taxed twice as much as those in other regions,
with some *mǔ* taxed at two or three *shí*.
Generally, Sūzhōu was the most heavily taxed,
followed by Sōngjiāng, Jiāxìng, and Húzhōu,
and then Chángzhōu and Hángzhōu.
In the thirteenth year of Hóngwǔ, the Ministry of Revenue was ordered to adjust these quotas.
For *mǔ* taxed at seven *dǒu* five *shēng* down to four *dǒu* four *shēng*, the tax was reduced by two-tenths.
For those taxed at four *dǒu* three *shēng* down to three *dǒu* six *shēng*, the tax was uniformly collected at three *dǒu* five *shēng*.
For those below that, the old rate remained.
At that time, Sūzhōu Prefecture alone
had an autumn grain tax of over 2,746,000 *shí*.
Except for 150,000 *shí* of private grain,
all was official land grain.
The annual quota for official grain was comparable to that of the entire Zhèjiāng Province,
showing how heavy the burden was.
In the second year of Jiànwén, an imperial edict stated:
"The taxes in Jiāngnán and Zhèxī are uniquely heavy,
and in Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng, the tax collection is based on private rent,
which was solely to punish the unruly populace of that time.
How can this be made a fixed rule to severely burden one region?
It is proper to universally reduce and exempt it,
with no *mǔ* to be taxed over one *dǒu*."
Chéngzǔ completely abolished Jiànwén's policies,
and the tax burden on Zhèxī became heavy again.
When Xuānzōng ascended the throne,
Zhōu Gàn, the Provincial Administration Commissioner of Guǎngxī,
returned from inspecting the prefectures of Sūzhōu, Chángzhōu, Jiāxìng, and Húzhōu,
and reported:
"Many people in these prefectures have fled.
When I asked the elders,
they all said it was due to heavy taxes.
For example, the private land rent in Wújiāng and Kūnshān
was formerly five *shēng* per *mǔ*.
When commoners leased and cultivated land from wealthy families,
they paid one *shí* per *mǔ* as private rent.
Later, due to various incidents, these lands were confiscated by the government,
and the government would then collect the full amount as per the private rent rule.
Even collecting eight-tenths was unbearable for the people,
let alone collecting everything.
If everything is collected,
the people will surely freeze and starve;
it will be impossible for them not to flee.
In Rénhé, Hǎiníng, and Kūnshān, over 1,900 *qǐng* of official and private land were submerged by seawater.
Even after more than ten years,
the tax is still being collected.
With the land submerged in the sea,
where can the tax come from?
I request that the tax on confiscated lands and lands returned by dukes and marquises
be assessed according to the official land rates in those areas,
with a tax of six *dǒu* per *mǔ*.
For lands submerged by seawater,
their tax should be completely abolished.
This will prevent the land from becoming barren
and allow the common people to live in peace."
The Emperor ordered the Ministry to discuss and implement it.
In the second month of the fifth year of Xuāndé, an edict stated:
"For the old quota of official land rent,
lands taxed at one *dǒu* to four *dǒu* per *mǔ* shall each be reduced by two-tenths.
Those taxed at four *dǒu* one *shēng* to over one *shí* shall be reduced by three-tenths.
This is established as law."
Thereupon, Zhōu Chén, the Grand Coordinator of Jiāngnán, and Kuàng Zhōng, the Prefect of Sūzhōu,
cleverly calculated a reduction of over 700,000 *shí* in Sūzhōu's grain tax.
Other prefectures followed this example,
and the burden on the people of the southeast was somewhat alleviated.
Chén also ordered that official land in Sōngjiāng be taxed according to private land rates.
The Ministry of Revenue impeached him for altering established laws.
Although Xuānzōng did not punish him,
he also could not adopt the proposal.
However, the court repeatedly issued edicts
to remit taxes and levies.
Those in charge of calculations would secretly instruct officials
not to use the edicts as an excuse.
The Emperor spoke with Hú Yíng, the Minister, saying,
"The finance ministers are obstructing the imperial benevolence,"
but did not severely punish them.
In the first year of Zhèngtǒng, an order was issued that official land in Sūzhōu, Sōngjiāng, Zhèjiāng, and other places
should be taxed according to private land rates.
For autumn grain taxed at four *dǒu* one *shēng* to over two *shí*, it was reduced to three *dǒu*.
For those at two *dǒu* one *shēng* to four *dǒu*, it was reduced to two *dǒu*.
For those at one *dǒu* one *shēng* to two *dǒu*, it was reduced to one *dǒu*.
By the end of Xuāndé's reign,
Sūzhōu's accumulated unpaid grain tax reached 7,900,000 *shí*,
[一０] and the people were in extreme distress.
By this time,
they finally found some relief.
At the beginning of Yīngzōng's restoration,
Sūn Yuánzhēn, the Minister overseeing Zhèjiāng, and others were ordered to establish regulations for Hángzhōu, Jiāxìng, and Húzhōu.
[一一] It was decreed that those with heavy tax quotas should pay less *mǐ* (polished rice),
while those with light tax quotas should pay more *mǐ*.
Thus, it was stipulated that for official land with a *mǔ* quota of one *shí* or less,
and private land with a *mǔ* quota of seven *dǒu* or less,
one *shí* three *dǒu* of standard *mǐ* per *shí* of tax was to be collected annually.
For official and private land with a quota of four *dǒu* or less,
[一二] one *shí* five *dǒu* of standard *mǐ* per *shí* was to be collected annually.
For official land with a quota of two *dǒu* or less,
and private land with a quota of two *dǒu* seven *shēng* or less,
one *shí* seven *dǒu* of standard *mǐ* per *shí* was to be collected annually.
For official land with a quota of eight *shēng* or less,
and private land with a quota of seven *shēng* or less,
two *shí* two *dǒu* of standard *mǐ* per *shí* was to be collected annually.
In essence, heavy burdens were lightened,
and light burdens were made heavier,
with the aim of making the tax quotas fair.
However, the tax of one *shí* per *mǔ* was never reduced.
In the second year of Jiājìng,
Censor Lí Guàn stated:
"In the early years of the dynasty, the summer and autumn taxes amounted to over 4,700,000 *shí* of wheat,
now it is short by 90,000.
There were over 24,700,000 *shí* of rice,
now it is short by over 2,500,000.
Yet the proliferation of imperial relatives,
the redundancy of officials,
the large number of eunuchs,
and the increase in soldiers,
all draw their provisions from these funds.
Tax revenue is diminishing daily,
while expenditures are increasing daily.
I request a thorough review of the tax quotas established by the ancestors and the amounts of expenditures,
delineating each one.
Then it will be understood that revenue is limited,
and excessive spending cannot but be curtailed."
Thereupon, the Ministry of Revenue deliberated:
"Order all officials throughout the empire, upon completing their terms and being promoted,
to have their rent and tax collections within their tenure strictly reviewed.
Only if the full amount is collected and remitted
will they be permitted to receive their transfer documents.
We also humbly request the court to personally practice frugality
to set an example for the empire."
The Emperor accepted this.
Soon after, Gu Dingchén, the Tutor-in-waiting, submitted a memorial detailing four major long-standing problems concerning money and grain.
Firstly, to investigate and manage the old quotas for land and grain.
He requested that local officials be held responsible,
during the agricultural off-season,
to instruct the *Lǐjiǎ* (community self-governance units) to compile maps and registers
following the *Yúlín* (fish-scale) and *Fēngqí* (wind-banner) patterns of the Hóngwǔ and Zhèngtǒng eras.
These should meticulously list the original quotas for land and grain, the names of *zìwéi* (irrigation districts) and *zèhào* (tax numbers), parcel descriptions,
the numbers of collapsed, barren, and mature *bùkǒu* (land measurement units).
Officials should then re-examine them,
delineate
boundaries,
personally inspect, check, and measure the *mǔ*,
and clearly state the numbers of newly cultivated, corrected, and exempted areas.
These should be printed as books,
stored in official treasuries,
and distributed among the *Lǐ* (villages)
to serve permanently
as records for verification.
Furthermore, considering the convenient and practical precedents set by former Grand Coordinators Zhōu Chén and Wáng Shù,
fixed regulations should be established.
The numbers for actual annual collection, transportation, retention,
additional wastage, original form, converted form, as well as supplementary collection, temporary collection, combined collection, and suspended collection,
should be calculated and finalized,
then publicly posted for all to know.
This would prevent clerks and yamen runners
from perpetrating fraud,
and common people from suffering losses due to excessive levies and harassment.
Secondly, to expedite the annual collection of money and grain.
Before the Chénghuà and Hóngzhì reigns,
*Lǐjiǎ* urged collection,
households paid grain,
grain chiefs collected and remitted,
and prefectural and county officials supervised the collection.
Grain
chiefs dared not overcharge on the *húmiàn* (excess measured grain),
grain households dared not mix water, husk, and bran with the grain,
and officials and soldiers inspecting grain dared not obstruct or demand excessive amounts.
This benefited both public and private interests.
Recently,
officials no longer compare and urge the *Lǐjiǎ* and grain-bearing households.
Instead, they set deadlines and beat the grain chiefs,
ordering them to go down to the countryside to collect.
The powerful then use large *hú* to collect double,
demanding in many ways,
leaving places desolate.
The weak are bullied by the powerful,
delaying and deceiving,
and are forced to sell their property to make up for the payments.
Sometimes, old
corvées were in arrears,
newly appointed officials demanded repayment.
When one person defaulted on their debt,
their relatives were implicated,
and several hundred innocent people died from floggings, torture, or in prison.
Moreover,
in the past,
there were no more than two grain supervisors (正, 副) per district;
recently, there have been more than ten.
The actual amount of grain they collected and managed was small,
while the expenses for levies, payments, and
annual customary fees were large.
In one year, a prefecture or county
would typically ruin the livelihoods of a hundred middle-class families;
there was no greater harm.
It is advisable to order the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù) to deliberate and set precedents,
and then transmit them to the relevant offices,
to ensure that the selection and appointment of grain supervisors strictly adhere to old regulations.
If prefectural or county officials appoint too many grain supervisors,
allow them to indulge in abuses in the countryside,
or fail to entrust the village chiefs (lǐjiǎ) with urging collection,
and instead cruelly
torture grain supervisors by imposing deadlines for comparison,
they should be punished.
If this results in many deaths,
they should be investigated and prosecuted accordingly.
Secondly, there was a discussion about dispatching officials to comprehensively manage and restore the ever-normal granaries (yùbèicāng).
The memorial was submitted,
and the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù) stated:
"The points raised are all relevant to current abuses;
let the relevant offices implement them."
After several years of delay, nothing changed.
Grain supervisors (liángzhǎng),
during the reign of Tàizǔ,
were appointed from among those with extensive landholdings
to oversee the collection of taxes in their villages.
In the seventh month of each year,
prefectural and county officials would appoint an officer to travel to the capital (Jīng) together,
receive their credentials (kānhé), and proceed.
For every 10,000 shí of grain,
there would be one head supervisor and one assistant.
If the grain was delivered on time,
they would be granted an audience,
and if their words were agreeable,
they would often be promoted.
In his later years, regulations were revised,
and one head supervisor and one assistant were appointed to serve in rotation in each district.
During the Xuāndé reign,
they were again appointed permanently.
Levies and exactions became excessive,
and the people suffered greatly;
some even privately sold official grain for profit.
Those who were dismissed
due to losses in public revenue,
when the matter came to light,
would face ruin and death.
During the Jǐngtài reign,
grain supervisors were abolished,
but soon after, they were reinstated.
Since the system of official troops (guānjūn) transporting grain for exchange (duìyùn),
grain supervisors no longer had to transport grain to the capital (Jīngshī).
This caused considerable harm in the prefectures and villages (zhōulǐ),
which is why Dǐngchén addressed it.
Not long after,
Censor Guō Hónghuà and others also requested a universal land survey
to curb the abuses of contracting for losses and land engrossment.
The Emperor feared disorder
and did not consent.
Grand Secretary Xú Jùnmín said:
"The current land taxes
include those who received land from the government and
pay rent and taxes annually;
this is called official land (guāntián).
There are lands where rivers overflowed and submerged fields and ditches;
these are called 'collapsed-river' lands (tānjīang).
There are lands where people moved away or died without heirs, leaving fields abandoned but the grain tax still recorded;
these are called 'accident' lands (shìgù).
Poor people cultivate official land,
paying three dòu of rent per mù,
or in some cases five or six dòu, or even a shí or more.
For 'collapsed-river' and 'accident' lands with fictitious grain taxes,
the village chiefs (lǐjiǎ) bear the loss,
sometimes tens of shí or over a hundred shí.
The price of private land is ten times that of official land,
which poor people cannot afford.
However, the tax burden on official land is heavy,
often leading to difficulties in meeting quotas.
Compounded by the fictitious grain taxes on 'collapsed-river' and 'accident' lands,
which are then apportioned for payment,
there is constant harassment and flogging,
leaving no day of peace throughout the year.
Meanwhile, cunning wealthy individuals and corrupt clerks
employ deceptive registrations and transfers,
combining light tax burdens with heavy ones.
This is why the suffering of the common people
and the impoverishment of the villages
daily increase and worsen.
I request the establishment of regulations for equitable grain tax (jūnnliáng) and land limits (xiàntián).
'Collapsed-river' and 'accident' lands
should all be exempted.
Official and private lands should be combined into one system,
and taxes should be levied based on three grades—upper, middle, and lower—to equalize the grain tax.
Rich people should not own more than a thousand mù;
they are allowed to retain a hundred mù for their own use,
and any excess should incur additional frontier taxes (biānsùi).
If this is done,
there will be a limit to the amount (of land),
the burden will be appropriate,
the poor and rich will coexist peacefully,
and both public and private needs will be met."
The Ministry's (Bù) deliberation was:
"The geography and customs of different regions vary;
let the relevant offices carefully consider what is convenient."
It was not implemented.
Several years later,
following a memorial by the Grand Coordinator (xúnpǔ) of Yìngtiān, Hóu Wèi,
over ninety thousand shí of grain tax on collapsed coastal land (tānhǎitián) in Sūzhōu were exempted.
However, the abuses of transfer (nàyí) and arbitrary apportionment (fēisǎ)
persisted unchanged.
By the eighteenth year,
when Dǐngchén became Grand Secretary (Dàxuéshì),
he reiterated:
"The seven prefectures of Sū, Sōng, Cháng, Zhèn, Jiā, Hú, and Háng
contribute the most taxes in the empire,
but abuses by village clerks (lǐxū) and powerful gentry (háoyòu) are particularly severe.
It is advisable to thoroughly investigate and correct
all cases of concealed and abandoned land."
Thereupon, the Grand Coordinator (xúnpǔ) of Yìngtiān, Ōuyáng Duó, investigated over four thousand qǐng of desolate land,
〔一三〕calculated the rent to be over one hundred and ten thousand shí,
used over sixty thousand shí of concealed land tax to compensate,
and requested exemption for the remainder.
The Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù) ultimately refused to back down.
At that time, Zhào Yǐng, the Prefect (Zhīfǔ) of Jiāxīng, proposed:
"Land should not be divided into official and private,
nor taxes into different grades.
Everything should be taxed at a base rate of three dòu."
Duó then, with Wáng Yí, the Prefect (Zhīfǔ) of Sūzhōu, comprehensively assessed official and private land, combining and increasing the tax base.
They surveyed every mù of land,
and established grades.
The tax registers (jīngfùcè) they created
defined tax grain based on eight criteria: first, the original quota and its origin;
second, elimination of fictitious amounts due to accidents;
third, distinguishing different categories;
fourth, consolidating and rectifying actual amounts;
fifth, apportioning and transporting;
sixth, allocating surpluses from transport;
seventh, accounting for accumulated surpluses;
eighth, fixing a uniform quota (zhēngyī).
Eight criteria were also used to assess village chiefs (lǐjiǎ): first, household labor (dīngtián);
second, congratulatory expenses (qìnghè);
third, sacrificial rites (jìsì);
fourth, village banquets (xiāngyǐn);
fifth, congratulatory levies (kēhè);
sixth, relief for governance (xùzhèng);
seventh, public expenses (gōngfèi);
eighth, reserve funds (bèiyòng).
Three criteria were used to determine corvée (jūnyáo):
first, silver corvée (yínchāi);
second, labor corvée (lìchāi);
third, horse corvée (mǎchāi).
This was established as a precedent.
The "uniform quota" (zhēngyī)
was the total collection of silver and rice,
apportioned equitably by the mù of land.
For those with the heaviest and lightest tax burdens,
slight adjustments were made with regard to losses.
Those with heavy burdens could not entirely avoid losses,
but would gradually reduce the lost rice (hàomǐ),
and be assigned lighter burdens by deducting or offsetting them, secretly making it lighter.
Those with light burdens could not increase their gains;
they were required to pay in kind (běnsè),
and the lost rice (hàomǐ) would be progressively increased and multiplied,
secretly making it heavier.
The method of collection
used land as the "mother"
and households as the "children."
At that time, many powerful gentry obstructed this proposal,
but Dǐngchén alone considered it good,
saying:
"If this law is implemented,
my family will pay an additional thousand shí,
but the poor will pay a thousand shí less.
It must not be changed."
However, at that time,
the Emperor could not reduce the tax quota,
and officials who governed the people privately altered the system according to their own ideas.
Consequently, official land was not excessively burdened,
but the tax on private land instead increased.
At that time, there were also methods like "net silver" (gāngyín) and "one string of bells" (yīchuànlíng).
"Net silver" (gāngyín) meant
collecting the annual expenses for corvée service from the common people,
with 40% based on registered adults (dīng) and 60% on land (liáng),
which was easy to understand and not complicated,
like a net having a main rope (gāng).
"One string of bells" (yīchuànlíng)
was a method of joint collection and distribution.
From then on, common people paid taxes
only in kind (běnsè) or in converted silver (zhésè yín).
At that time, the empire's financial revenue,
entering the Tàicāng treasury annually, amounted to over two million liǎng.
The old system designated seventy percent for regular expenses,
and thirty percent was stored as reserves for military campaigns and famine,
this being the norm.
During the middle years of Shìzōng's reign,
border supply costs were heavy,
and with the addition of construction projects, sacrifices, and prayers,
