not a month passed without such activities,
leading to the depletion of the treasury.
The minister of finance tried every possible way to generate revenue,
even going so far as to sell temple lands
and redeem military offenses,
yet it was still insufficient.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Āndá invaded the capital.
Troops were increased and garrisons established,
and the military expenditure more than doubled.
In the thirtieth year,
annual expenditures for the capital and borders reached 5.95 million.
The Minister of Revenue, Sūn Yìngkuí, was greatly distressed and without a solution.
He then proposed an increase of 1.2 million in taxes in the southern Zhílí (Nánjī) and Zhèjiāng regions, among other prefectures and counties.
This was the beginning of the additional levies.
Thereafter,
the annual expenditures for the capital and borders,
at their highest, exceeded five million,
and at their lowest, were still over three million.
Annual revenue could not even cover half of the annual expenditure.
Consequently, revenue management became the primary method,

and methods such as extorting wealth and bribes, proposing additional levies, confiscating ill-gotten gains and ransoms, calculating deed taxes, commuting civilian labor service (mínzhuàng), *tíbiān*, *jūnyáo*, and expanding precedents came into being.
Initially, they relied on these to alleviate the scarcity,
but over time,
the funds flowing in diminished.
Moreover, there were many incidents in the four directions,
and officials often memorialized to retain or request exemption for their areas: Zhèjiāng and Zhílì for coastal defense against Japanese pirates,
Sìchuān and Guìzhōu for logging,
Shānxī, Shǎnxī, Xuāndà for military disasters and famine.
Not only were the levies imposed for military campaigns suspended,
but even the annual quota of two million
was deficient by one-third.
Yet, the awards and grants from the inner court,
the construction and maintenance of temples and palaces,
and a single piece of paper sent out from the palace in the middle of the night,
though the officials were pressed,
none dared to delay for a moment.
In the thirty-seventh year,
Dàtóng Yòuwèi reported an emergency.
Only seventy thousand [liǎng] of taxes entered the Tàicāng,
and the treasury reserves were generally less than one hundred thousand.
Minister of Revenue Fāng Dùn and others were worried and didn't know what to do.
They then seized the opportunity to fully report the state of the empty treasury,
and subsequently submitted seven opportune proposals for consideration.
Afterwards,
they also ordered all officials to propose financial management strategies.
Twenty-nine proposals were discussed and implemented,
but they were increasingly trivial
and not befitting the national system.
However, all arrears accumulated over many years were pursued and collected,
and outstanding taxes in kind from the south were also pursued and collected in silver.
At this time,
the southeast was afflicted by Japanese pirates.
Nánjī, Zhèjiāng, and Fújiàn had many additional *tíbiān* levies,
with Jiāngnán reaching four hundred thousand.
another name for an additional levy.
Its method
was to arrange ten households (jiǎ) based on their silver and labor capacity.
If one *jiǎ* was insufficient,
then a lower *jiǎ* would be "lifted" (*tí*) to supplement it,
hence it was called *tíbiān*.
After the Japanese pirate threat was pacified,
the巡撫(Xúnfǔ) of Yìngtiān, Zhōu Rúdǒu, begged for a reduction in the additional levies.
The investigating censor (Gěishìzhōng), Hé Kuí, also fully reported on the distress in Nánjī,
stating:
"The army commanders raising soldiers,
the Ministry of Works' material costs,
the river patrol recruiting soldiers,
the circuit intendants (Bīngbèidào)'s strongmen,
and the prefectural, sub-prefectural, and county local militias (xiāngbīng),
all become burdens on the people.
In severe cases, one tax is levied as ten.
I request that these be prohibited and abolished."
The emperor ordered action according to Hé Kuí's proposal,
but the *tíbiān* quota could not be reduced.
During the reigns of Lóngqìng and Wànlì,
the increased quotas remained as before,
and there were many irregular taxes,
leading to more outstanding grain taxes,
and increasingly clever tax evasion.
Some payments that had been remitted were overdue by more than ten years,
and some that had not been collected were reported as received,
with one county having as much as one hundred thousand [liǎng] in such discrepancies.
The amount of outstanding debt in each county reached several hundred thousand.
Fortunately, the Yītiáobiān law was implemented,
and there were no other disruptive levies,
so the people's resources were not greatly depleted.
The Yītiáobiān law
consolidated all taxes and services of a prefecture or county.
Land was measured and households counted,
and all land and poll taxes were paid to the officials.
For the year's labor service,
officials would recruit workers.
For labor service (lìchāi),
the cost of their wages and food was calculated and adjusted accordingly;
for silver service (yínchāi),
the cost of its payment was calculated
and an increment for wastage was added.
All regular assessments,
assigned tasks,
annual needs for the imperial treasury,
and retained funds,
as well as tribute in kind and local products,
were all consolidated into one item
and collected in silver based on acreage,
paid to officials,
hence it was called Yītiáobiān.
The legislation was quite simple and convenient.
During the Jiājìng era,
it was implemented and then stopped several times,
until the ninth year of Wànlì, when it was fully implemented.
Afterwards, the Three Great Campaigns followed one after another,
with some additional levies,
which were then removed once the matters were concluded.
By the forty-sixth year,
the Liáoxiǎng (Liaoning military provisions) suddenly increased by three million.
At that time, the inner treasury was full,
but the emperor was stingy and unwilling to release funds.
The Minister of Revenue, Lǐ Rúhuá, then cited the precedents of the campaigns against Japanese pirates and Bōzhōu,
adding three *lí* and five *háo* per *mǔ*,
increasing the empire's taxes by over two million.
The next year, another three *lí* and five *háo* were added.
The following year,
at the request of the Ministries of War and Works,
another two *lí* were added.
Combining the previous and latter additions, a total of nine *lí*
increased taxes by 5.2 million,
which then became an annual quota.
The only areas not affected were
the eight prefectures within the capital region (Jīnèi) and Guìzhōu.
In the first year of Tiānqǐ,
the investigating censor Zhēn Shū stated:
"The additional levies for Liáoxiǎng
are prone to unevenness.
For the empire, there are household tax silver,
poll tax silver,
and land tax silver.
When officials collect,
it is collectively called silver quota.
By imposing additional levies based on the silver quota,
the amount will not be missed.
The people in the east, west, south, and north
experience different conditions;
the methods for collecting cloth, silk, grain, and labor differ.
Only local officials truly understand these conditions
and can flexibly manage their collection.
Now, considering the suitability of people and land,
there will be no burden of partiality or exhaustion.
The method
should be to take the silver quota as the main basis,
while accommodating human sentiment
and considering local customs,
and issue proclamations to all provinces.
The annual retained and remitted silver amounts for each item,
with the added military provision quota,
should be apportioned according to the silver amounts,
and a total discount should be applied,
compensating the less burdened with the more burdened,
with the aim of not falling short of the military provision quota.
If this is done,
the common people will easily understand,
and the malpractice of corrupt clerks arbitrarily increasing or decreasing amounts can be prevented.
Furthermore, what the common people suffer from most
is paying grain tax without land
and poll tax without grain.
When land is sold to wealthy households,
the property is gone but the grain tax remains,
and they still pay the poll tax.
It is appropriate to take the quota for poll tax and grain tax,
and balance them to determine the amount.
So much grain should be associated with so many poll taxes.
Those who buy land
should collect the grain tax and also the poll tax,
so the county registers do not lose the poll tax quota,
the poor people are not burdened with losses,
and officials are also spared the problem of outstanding taxes."
It was sent to the Ministry for deliberation
and was adopted.
In the third year of Chóngzhēn (1630),
military campaigns began.
The Minister of War, Liáng Tíngdòng (梁廷棟), requested an increase in land taxes.
The Minister of Revenue, Bì Zìyán (畢自嚴), could not prevent it,
so an additional three *lí* (釐) per *mǔ* (畝) were levied on top of the original nine *lí*.
Only Shùntiān (順天) and Yǒngpíng (永平) Prefectures, having recently suffered from warfare, had no additional levy.
The remaining six prefectures were levied six *lí* per *mǔ*,
which was half of what other provinces paid.
The total increase in taxes amounted to over one million six hundred fifty-four thousand (1,654,000) units.
Five years later,
Grand Coordinator Lú Xiàngshēng (盧象昇) requested an additional one-tenth (1/10) tax on eunuch households' land taxes,
and the same for commoners' grain taxes exceeding ten *liǎng* (兩).
Later, a general levy of one *qián* (錢) per *liǎng* was imposed,
named "aid for military provisions" (助餉).
Two years after that,
the *jūnshū* (均輸) system was reinstated,
where taxes were paid based on grain.
Six *hé* (合) of rice were calculated per *mǔ*,
and one *shí* (石) of rice was commuted to eight *qián* (錢) of silver.
An additional one *fēn* (分) four *lí* (釐) and nine *sī* (絲) of silver per *mǔ* was levied.
Two years later,
Yáng Sìchāng (楊嗣昌) took charge as Grand Coordinator,
and one *fēn* (分) of silver per *mǔ* was added as "training provisions" (練餉).
Zhāng Ruòqí (張若麒), a Supervising Secretary in the Ministry of War, proposed that the remaining properties of deceased soldiers be collected and converted into official estates (*guān zhuāng*, 官莊),
divided into upper, middle, and lower grades.
Rent from eight *dǒu* (斗) down to two or three *dǒu* per *mǔ* was to be paid, varying by grade.
Censor Wèi Zhōuyìn (衞周胤) stated:
"Yáng Sìchāng's (楊嗣昌) poison has spread throughout the empire.
The 'suppression and training provisions' (剿練之餉) amount to as much as seven million.
How can the people's resentment be contained?"
Censor Hǎo Jìn (郝晉) also said:
"In the late Wànlì (萬曆) era,
the combined provisions for the Nine Border Garrisons (九邊餉) were only two million eight hundred thousand.
Now, the additional Líao provisions (遼餉) amount to nine million.
The 'suppression provisions' (剿餉) of three million three hundred thousand,
though already suspended,
were immediately replaced by 'training provisions' (練餉) of over seven million three hundred thousand.
Since ancient times, has there ever been a year where twenty million was collected and sent to the capital,
and then another twenty million was collected from the capital to send to the borders?"
Although these memorials were sharp and direct,
the situation at the time was critical,
and they could not be adopted.
The *yìfǎ* (役法) (corvée labor system) was established in the first year of Hóngwǔ (洪武) (1368).
For every one hundred *qǐng* (頃) of land, one able-bodied man was required.
If the land was less than one hundred *qǐng*, it was supplemented by other land to make up the quota,
called "equalized labor" (*jūngōngfū*, 均工夫).
Soon, the eighteen prefectures and subprefectures of Yìngtiān (應天),
and the three prefectures of Jiǔjiāng (九江), Ráozhōu (饒州), and Nánkāng (南康) in Jiāngxī (江西) had their *jūngōngfū* (均工夫) registers compiled.
Each year, during the agricultural off-season, laborers would go to the capital,
serve for thirty days, and then be sent home.
For households with much land but few able-bodied men,
tenants were used as laborers,
and the landlord provided one *shí* (石) of rice to cover their expenses.
For those who were not tenants but provided laborers based on the area of their land,
two *shēng* (升) five *hé* (合) of rice per *mǔ* was provided for expenses.
When the Yellow Registers (*Huángcè*, 黃冊) were completed,
one hundred and ten households formed a *lǐ* (里),
and each *lǐ* (里) was divided into ten *jiǎ* (甲), forming the *lǐjiǎ* (里甲) system.
Households were classified into upper, middle, and lower grades.
Labor service was equalized every five years,
and the registers were renewed every ten years.
Throughout the year, those subject to various miscellaneous labor duties
were ranked and equalized.
Silver or labor was chosen as convenient,
and this was called "equalized service" (*jūnyáo*, 均徭).
Other miscellaneous duties were called "miscellaneous general services" (*záfàn*, 雜泛).
All attendants (*zhīyìng*, 祗應), jailers (*jìnzǐ*, 禁子), and archers (*gōngbīng*, 弓兵)
were selected from common citizens;
grain-tax households were not to be drafted.
Anyone who illegally exacted an extra *qián* (錢) or drafted an extra laborer
was punished with exile.
Later, the law gradually relaxed.
Those who compiled the *yáoyì lǐjiǎ* (徭役里甲) (corvée labor *lǐjiǎ*)
based it on households,
exempting wealthy households while selecting only smaller ones.
Thus, commentators said that
the *jūnyáo* (均徭) system,
which was based on the registers of able-bodied men and grain,
with assets as the primary consideration,
and assessed the wealth of households,
was meant to accurately reflect their accumulated wealth.
However, examining the registers
meant that rich merchants and great traders were exempt,
while the local residents suffered.
Assessing households
meant that officials and local clerks could manipulate the system,
making the common people even poorer and more distressed.
Both approaches had their flaws.
However, an exclusive focus on able-bodied men and grain
was closer to the ancient ideal of *zū yōng diào* (租庸調) (land tax, labor service, textile tax).
So, it was ordered that the numbers for old labor-based service (*lìchāi*, 力差) and silver-based service (*yínchāi*, 銀差) be equated with the numbers for able-bodied men and grain,
striking a balance between difficulty and ease, lightness and heaviness.
Labor was used to meet quotas.
For the *lǐjiǎ* (里甲) system, apart from those who were due for service,
households were ranked by the amount of able-bodied men and grain, determining their order of service.
This was called the "rat's tail register" (*shǔwěicè*, 鼠尾冊),
and taxes were collected accordingly.
City dwellers and merchants who were prosperous but had no land
were allowed to declare themselves
to assist with silver-based service.
In the early Zhèngtǒng (正統) (1436-1449) era,
Commissioner Xià Shí (夏時) first implemented this in Jiāngxī (江西),
and other provinces followed suit,
making labor service somewhat fairer.
Thereafter, for all tributes paid to the court,
officials were responsible for allocation,
and for public and private needs of government offices,
the silver collected was again given to the *fānglǐ zhǎng* (坊里長) (ward and *lǐ* (里) chiefs),
who were held responsible for procurement.
What was given was not even one or two units,
while what was supplied could be ten or even a hundred.
Sometimes nothing was given at all,
except for the food and drink for the horses and attendants of the *lǐjiǎ* (里甲) who served for the year,
which greatly burdened the *lǐjiǎ* (里甲) households.
For all *jūnyáo* (均徭) services,
households delivering tribute to the court were designated "capital labor" (*jīngyáo*, 京徭).
When they delivered payments, they were deliberately obstructed by eunuchs,
making direct payment difficult.
Repeatedly going back and forth to exchange goods
often led to ruin.
The abuses of other demanding services
are too numerous to list.
In the early Míng (明) dynasty,
it was ordered that all local tributes to the court
had fixed quotas,
and rare and precious curiosities were not included.
Even if needed,
they were allocated to the *lǐjiǎ* (里甲)
who paid silver to purchase them.
However, the categories were redundant and fragmented,
providing loopholes for the cunning to exploit for profit.
Furthermore, large construction and repair projects,
and rituals conducted by shrine officials to pray for blessings,
led to excessive use of resources.
By the mid-Míng (明) dynasty,
Japanese pirates repeatedly invaded,
and the Yellow River burst its banks year after year,
exhausting national resources.
Consequently, the *lǐjiǎ* (里甲) and *jūnyáo* (均徭) services
exceeded their annual quotas.
For all civilian labor services,
besides the regular duties of the *lǐjiǎ* (里甲),

there were regular services like grain collectors (*liángzhǎng*, 糧長), tribute transporters (*jiěhù*, 解戶), horse and boat captains (*mǎchuántóu*, 馬船頭), innkeepers (*guǎnfū*, 館夫), attendants (*zhīhòu*, 祗候), archers (*gōngbīng*, 弓兵), yamen runners (*zàolì*, 皂隸), gatekeepers (*ménjìn*, 門禁), and cooks (*chúdǒu*, 廚斗).

Later, there were also services such as woodcutting (*zhuóxīn*, 斫薪), kindling collection (*yìchái*, 撎柴), river maintenance (*xiūhé*, 修河), granary repair (*xiūcāng*, 修倉), material transport (*yùnliào*, 運料), relay stations (*jiēdì*, 接遞), post stations (*zhànpù*, 站舖), and lock keepers (*zhápqiǎnfū*, 牐淺夫),
which were drafted as needed,
and increased each year.
After the Jiā (嘉) (1522-1566) and Lóng (隆) (1567-1572) eras,
the Single-Whip Reform (*Yītiáobiānfǎ*, 一條鞭法) was implemented,
calculating the total number of able-bodied men and grain for an entire province
and equally distributing the province's labor service.
Thus, *jūnyáo* (均徭) and *lǐjiǎ* (里甲) were combined with the Two Taxes (*liǎngshuì*, 兩稅) into one,
and the common people were less disturbed,
and matters were also easier to manage.
However, the grain chiefs (*liángzhǎng*, 糧長) and *lǐ* (里) chiefs (*lǐzhǎng*, 里長),
though nominally abolished, still existed in practice.
When various laborers were needed,
farmers were again drafted.
After the Single-Whip Reform (*Yītiáobiānfǎ*, 一條鞭法) had been in effect for more than ten years,
the regulations
became suddenly disordered and could not be fully followed.
During the Tiānqǐ (天啟) era (1621-1627),
Censor Lǐ Yìngshēng (李應昇) submitted a memorial detailing ten harms,

three of which critically pointed out the abuses of horse laborers (*mǎfū*, 馬夫), river laborers (*héyì*, 河役), grain *jiǎ* (糧甲), repair workers (*xiūbàn*, 修辦), and unofficial laborers (*báiyì*, 白役) in disturbing the people.
In the third year of Chóngzhēn (1630),
Fàn Jǐngwén (范景文), the Governor of Hénán (河南), said:
"What the people suffer from most
are the corvée duties (*chāiyì*, 差役).
For money and grain, there are collectors (*shōuhù*, 收戶) and transporters (*jiěhù*, 解戶).
For post stations, there are horse households (*mǎhù*, 馬戶).
For supplies, there are trading households (*hánghù*, 行戶).
All these are drafted from wealthy households,
known as 'great households' (*dàhù*, 大戶).
In reality,
those drafted are not truly wealthy citizens;
even households of moderate means are ruined by it.
Since the transformation into the Single-Whip Reform (*Yītiáobiānfǎ*, 一條鞭法),
which distributed the services within a region proportionally to the grain taxes within that region,
it should have provided some relief.
However, the common people still travel year after year,
exhausting their resources on subsidies.
This means that the Single-Whip Reform (*Yītiáobiānfǎ*, 一條鞭法) was implemented, but the 'great households' (*dàhù*, 大戶) were never truly abolished."
At that time, Supervising Secretary Liú Mào (劉懋) again memorialized to reduce the number of post station laborers (*yìfū*, 驛夫).
However, military requisitions and movements
were still imposed on registered households.
The post station laborers (*yìfū*, 驛夫) had no means of livelihood
and consequently joined the rebel bandits in causing unrest.
All military, artisan, and salt-making households
were permanently obligated to service.
If a military household member died or absconded,
replacements were conscripted from their original place of registration.
Artisan households were of two types: those who were permanently resident,
and those who served in rotation.
Resident artisans
worked ten days a month.
Those who did not report for their turn
had to pay a penalty silver of six qián per month,
hence they were called "paying a turn."
〔一七〕The officials in charge of supervisory bureaus
often appropriated artisans for their own use,
and also conscripted young artisans,
often by the thousands.
If they died or absconded,
replacements were conscripted as with military households.
Salt-making households were divided into upper, middle, and lower classes.
For each main adult male,
additional surplus males were assigned.
Upper and middle households, having more adult male labor,
might be assigned two or three additional males,
while lower households were generally granted exemptions.
Other categories included mausoleum households, garden households, coastal households, temple households, banner bearers, and storehouse attendants,
too numerous and trivial to count.
In the early Míng dynasty,
the proliferation of labor services
stemmed from the construction of ancestral temples, palaces, gates, and princely residences in both capitals.
Timber felling, brick making,
and the work of artisans and craftsmen
involved tens of millions of people.
Fortifications were built everywhere, and reservoirs were dredged;
a hundred kinds of tasks were undertaken.
Up to the Hóngwǔ and Xuāndé eras,
the suburban altars and granaries were still unfinished.
During the Zhèngtǒng and Tiānshùn periods,
the Three Palaces, the Two Courts, the Southern Imperial City, and the detached palaces
were successively built.
In the Hóngzhì era,
Grand Secretary Liú Jí said:
"In recent years, the labor services
have all been extracted from the imperial garrison soldiers.
Inside and outside military officials are forbidden from estimating the quantity of work or the number of people needed.
〔一八〕If five thousand people were actually needed,
the request would be for one or two tens of thousands,
without any oversight."
Ní Yuè, Minister of Rites, said:
"The expenses for various tasks amount to several hundreds of thousands,
and droughts follow one after another.
I beg that they be somewhat halted."
Tóng Xuān, Minister of Rites in Nánjīng, further reported on the hardships of labor services.
Lín Hàn, Minister of Personnel, also said:
"The two capitals have suffered successive disasters for years,
are distressed by a hundred tasks,
and filled with sorrow, resentment, and lament.
Shānxi and Shǎnxī provide for military expeditions.
Yúnnán and Guǎngdōng send troops for western campaigns to suppress rebels.
Shāndōng, Hénán, Húguǎng, Sìchuān, and Jiāngxī are building princely residences,
and their financial resources are insufficient.
Zhèjiāng and Fújiàn are procuring materials,
an amount that has increased compared to former days.
The treasuries are empty,
which cannot be disregarded."
The emperor accepted all their words,
but could not fully implement them.
During the Wǔzōng era,
the construction project for the Qiánqīnggōng was particularly large.
Because the original design of the Tàisùdiàn was simple and frugal,
it was renovated to be intricately carved and grand,
using over two million taels of silver,
employing over three thousand artisans,
and annually spending over thirteen thousand shí of grain for their wages and food.
Additionally, the Níngcuì, Zhāohé, Chóngzhì, and Guāngjì palaces were repaired,
and the Yùmǎjiān, Zhōnggǔsī, the Nánchéng Bàofáng's new rooms, and the Huǒyàokù were all completely rebuilt.
Powerful eunuchs' estates, ancestral temples, incense-burning Buddhist and Daoist temples,
the Ministry of Works also secretly used official silver to curry favor.
Zhāng Yuán, a Supervising Secretary, said:
"Artisans support their parents, wives, and children.
Soldiers on the roster defend against foreign invaders.
Imperial garrison troops guard the royal family.
How is it now that the people have no one to rely on,
soldiers are not in their ranks,
benefits go to private families,
and grievances accumulate in the public sphere?"
His memorial was submitted,
and he was demoted to Xīntiān Yìchéng in Guìzhōu.
Shìzōng undertook the most construction,
before his fifteenth year on the throne,
though it was nominally a period of reduction and frugality,
expenditures already reached six to seven million.
After that, they increased by ten to several tens of times,
with zhāigōng and secret halls rising simultaneously.
There were twenty to thirty workshops,
employing tens of thousands of artisans,
who were called soldiers,
with annual expenses of two to three million.
At that time, the Zōngmiào and Wànshòugōng suffered disasters,
but the emperor did not reflect on this;
repairs and constructions became even more urgent.
When funds were insufficient,
he ordered officials and commoners to make contributions;
when contributions were not enough,
he again instituted the sale of offices.
The toil of the people and the squandering of wealth
exceeded that of Wǔzōng.
After the Wànlì era,
construction and weaving projects
exceeded the prescribed limits by several times,
further compounded by conscriptions, levies, and mining,
leaving the people no respite.
When eunuchs threw the government into chaos,
they built residences and tombs,
〔一九〕exceeding all bounds of propriety,
and temples for their merit and private worship proliferated across the land.
For over two hundred years,
the people's strength had long been exhausted and depleted.
Among those who received exemptions due to their official duties,
some had one or two adult males exempted,
while others had as many as sixteen.
During the Wànlì era,
some had land exemptions amounting to two or three thousand.
As for the remission of taxes,
there were gracious remissions (恩蠲, Ēnjuān)
and disaster remissions (災蠲, Zāijuān).
Tàizǔ's (太祖) instructions were that
whenever there were floods or droughts in the four directions, taxes should be remitted.
In years of abundance without disaster or damage,
he would also select poor and barren areas for special remission.
Whenever there was a disaster in a year,
both taxes would be entirely remitted,
and rice would be lent;
in severe cases, rice, cloth, or paper currency would be granted.
He also established relief granaries (預備倉, Yùbèicāng),
ordering elderly people to exchange paper currency for rice to store grain.
When Jīng (荊) and Qí (蘄) suffered from floods,
he ordered Zhào Gān (趙乾), a principal in the Ministry of Revenue (戶部主事), to go and provide relief.
When Zhào Gān (趙乾) procrastinated for half a year,
he was angered and executed him.
When Qīngzhōu (青州) suffered from drought and locusts,
the officials concerned did not report it,
so he arrested and punished those officials.
When drought damaged prefectures and counties,
and the officials concerned did not report it,
he allowed elderly commoners to appeal,
and the officials were given the most severe punishment.
When Xiàogǎn (孝感) suffered from famine,
its magistrate requested to use the relief granaries for aid and loans.
The emperor ordered an imperial messenger (行人) to rush there by post-horse.
He also instructed the Ministry of Revenue (戶部), saying:
"From now on, whenever there is famine in a year,
first release grain from the granaries as loans,
and then report it.
This is hereby established as a regulation."
During his reign of over thirty years,
millions of cloth and paper currency were granted,
over a million *shi* (石) of rice,
and countless amounts of rent and taxes were remitted.
Chéngzǔ (成祖) heard that Hénán (河南) was suffering from famine,
but the officials concerned concealed it and did not report it,
so he arrested and punished them.
Consequently, he ordered the Censor-in-chief (都御史) Chén Yīng (陳瑛) to issue a public proclamation throughout the realm,
stating that officials who did not report flood, drought, or disaster damage
would not be pardoned for their crime.
He also decreed that the imperial court should dispatch inspecting officials annually,
and those who witnessed the people's hardships but did not report them
would all be arrested and imprisoned.
When Rénzōng (仁宗) was regent,
someone requested to issue relief.
He dispatched a messenger to rush and instruct them,
saying:
"The military and common people are in want,
crying out for sustenance.
Yet you still calmly initiate requests and await reports.
Can you not emulate Jí Àn (汲黯) of Hàn (漢)?"
During Xuānzōng's (宣宗) time,
the Ministry of Revenue (戶部) requested to verify the famine victims.
The emperor said:
"When the people are hungry and have no food,
providing aid should be like rescuing someone from drowning or a burning fire.
Why wait for verification?"
Indeed, during the reigns of the two ancestors (二祖), Rénzōng (仁宗), and Xuānzōng (宣宗),
benevolent governance was vigorously implemented.
In addition to the relief granaries (預備倉, Yùbèicāng),
they also frequently intercepted grain shipments (截起運)
and granted funds from the imperial treasury (內帑).
Where disaster-stricken areas had no stored grain,
rice from neighboring counties was dispatched to provide relief.
When locust nymphs first emerged,
people were invariably sent to catch and bury them.
For those who sold their children,
the government would redeem them.
They also ordered wealthy people to remit rent for their tenants.
Wealthy households lent grain to poor commoners,
exempting them from miscellaneous labor (雜役) as interest,
to be repaid in prosperous years.
Imperial estates (皇莊) and lakes (湖泊) were all de-restricted,
allowing commoners to gather resources.
Famine victims returning to their hometowns
were given rations.
Rice from the Jīng (京) and Tōng (通) granaries
was sold at a fair price.
They also preemptively disbursed official salaries and rations to suppress rice prices,
built official residences to house displaced people,
and provided food to collect abandoned infants.
Poor people in charity homes (養濟院) were all registered;
those without registration were housed and cared for at the Làzhú (蠟燭) and Fāngān (旛竿) two temples.
Such was their compassion for the people.
Shìzōng (世宗) and Shénzōng (神宗) were somewhat negligent in matters concerning the common people,
yet when disasters and famines occurred,
they would invariably grant remissions and relief,
not daring to violate the ancestral system.
The method of providing relief rice (振米之法) in the early Míng (明) dynasty was:
for adults, six *dou* (斗);
for minors, three *dou*;
children under five years old were not included.
After the Yǒnglè (永樂) era,
the amount was reduced.
As for those who donated rice for relief to redeem crimes,
during Jǐngdì's (景帝) time,
miscellaneous capital offenses required sixty *shi* (石) of rice;
exile or penal servitude were reduced by one-third,
and other punishments were progressively reduced accordingly.
The system of official contributions (捐納事例)
began with Xiànzōng (憲宗).
Scholars (生員) who donated one hundred *shi* (石) of rice or more
could enter the Guózǐjiān (國子監);
military and common people who donated two hundred fifty *shi* (石)
became unranked officials of the ninth rank (正九品散官);
an additional fifty *shi* (石)
increased their rank by two levels,
up to the seventh rank (正七品) at most.
[二０]During Wǔzōng's (武宗) time,
wealthy commoners who donated grain for relief,
one thousand *shi* (石) or more, had their gates specially honored;
those who donated nine hundred to two or three hundred *shi* (石)
were granted unranked official titles,
up to the sixth rank (從六品).
Shìzōng (世宗) ordered that righteous commoners who contributed twenty *shi* (石) of grain
be given official caps and belts (冠帶);
those who contributed more were granted official titles of the seventh rank (正七品);
those who reached five hundred *shi* (石)
would have commemorative arches (坊) erected by the authorities.
The method of providing relief porridge (振粥之法)
began with Shìzōng (世宗).
The method of reporting disasters (報災之法)
during the Hóngwǔ (洪武) era had no time limit.
In the middle of Hóngzhì (弘治),
it was first stipulated that summer disasters must be reported no later than the end of the fifth month,
and autumn disasters no later than the end of the ninth month.
During Wànlì (萬曆),
it was further divided:
nearby areas had limits of the fifth and seventh months,
and border areas the seventh and ninth months.
[二一]During the Hóngwǔ (洪武) era,
once disaster verification was confirmed,
total remission and exemption were granted.
In the middle of Hóngzhì (弘治),
it was first stipulated that a complete disaster (全災) would receive a seven-tenths exemption,
and from nine-tenths disaster downwards, it would be progressively reduced.
Furthermore, only the retained portion (存留) was remitted,
not the portion for transport (起運),
and this subsequently became a permanent regulation.
Collation Notes
Monograph Fifty-Five: Food and Money, Part Three: Grain Transport, Granaries
Since ancient times,
wherever grain transport (漕粟) was concentrated,
it was used to supply official granaries (官府廩食),
each according to the distance of the route.
When Tàizǔ (太祖) established his capital in Jīnlíng (金陵),
tributes and taxes from the four directions
reached the capital via the river,
the route being short and easy.
After Chéngzǔ (成祖) moved the capital to Yān (燕),
the route became long and distant,
and the method underwent three changes.
Initially, it was direct transport (支運);
then transfer transport (兌運) and direct transport (支運) were combined;
finally, all direct transport (支運) was changed to long-distance transport (長運), and the system was finalized.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ (洪武), during the northern expedition,
Zhèjiāng (浙江), Jiāngxī (江西), and the nine prefectures including Sūzhōu (蘇州) were ordered
to transport three million *shi* (石) of grain to Biànliáng (汴梁).
Later, Grand General Xú Dá (徐達) ordered the five prefectures of Xīn (忻), Guó (崞), Dài (代), Jiān (堅), and Tái (臺) to transport grain to Dàtóng (大同).
The Central Secretariat (中書省) issued a decree to the Shāndōng (山東) Provincial Administration Commission (行省),
recruiting hydraulic engineers to send supplies from the Yánghǎi (洋海) granary in Láizhōu (萊州) to Yǒngpíng Wèi (永平衞).
Thereafter, sea transport (海運) of supplies to Běipíng (北平) and Liáodōng (遼東) became a fixed system.
For the northwestern frontier, the Kāifēng (開封) canal was dredged to transport supplies to Shǎnxī (陝西);
from Shǎnxī (陝西), supplies were then transferred to Níngxià (寧夏) and Hézhōu (河州).
For the southwest, Sìchuān (四川) and Guìzhōu (貴州) were ordered to pay taxes in rice for salt (納米中鹽)
to save on long-distance transport.
At that time, all routes were supplied locally,
which was convenient.
In the first year of Yǒnglè (永樂), in response to the words of the Minister of Revenue (戶部尚書) Yù Xīn (郁新),
boats from Huái (淮) capable of carrying three hundred *shi* (石) or more were first used.
They would travel along the Huái (淮) River and Shāhé (沙河) to the Diēpō (跌坡) at Yǐngqí Kǒu (潁岐口) in Chénzhōu (陳州).
Separately, large boats would enter the Yellow River (黃河) to Bāliǔshù (八柳樹),
and then carts would transport the goods to the Wèihé (衞河) to be delivered to Běipíng (北平),
intermixed with sea transport.
At that time, the emperor frequently visited,
and all expenses depended on these supplies,
not just for frontier provisions.
There were two main transport routes, the Huái (淮) and the Sea (海);
and the Línqīng (臨清) granary stored grain from Hénán (河南) and Shāndōng (山東),
also for delivery to Běipíng (北平),
making a total of three routes when combined.
However, only sea transport used official troops;
the rest were all civilian transport.
After Jùn connected the Huìtōng Hé,
the emperor commanded the Grand Coordinator Jiǎ Yì and the Minister of Revenue Sòng Lǐ to transport goods by boat.
Lǐ found that the large sea-going vessels of 1,000 shí were often damaged due to poor craftsmanship,
so he built 500 shallow-draft boats
to transport one million shí of grain from Huái'ān, Yángzhōu, Xúzhōu, and Yǎnzhōu,
which was equivalent to the amount transported by sea.
The Earl of Píngjiāng, Chén Xuān, continued this
and gradually increased the number of boats to over 3,000.
At that time, there were granaries in Huái'ān, Xúzhōu, Línqīng, and Dézhōu.
People from Jiāngxī, Húguǎng, and Zhèjiāng transported grain to the Huái'ān granary,
where official troops were dispatched to transport it locally.
From Huái'ān to Xúzhōu, troops from Zhèjiāng and the directly-governed areas were used;
from Xúzhōu to Dézhōu, Imperial Guard troops were used;
and from Dézhōu to Tōngzhōu, troops from Shāndōng and Hénán were used.
They transported it in sequence,
four times a year,
totaling over three million shí,
and this was called zhīyùn (relay transport).
The method of zhīyùn was such that
those who transported
did not necessarily have to deliver the current year's grain;
and those who received
did not necessarily have to supply the current year's military provisions.
The numbers were pooled and balanced over several years,
with the goal of not falling short of the usual quota.
Consequently, both sea and land transport were abolished,
and only the zhēyáng boats remained.
Each year, at water stations such as Hénán, Shāndōng, and Xiǎotān,
300,000 shí of grain were exchanged.
Twelve-tenths were delivered to Tiānjīn,
and eighteen-tenths went from Zhígū into the sea and were delivered to Jìzhōu.
Within a few years,
many official troops were reassigned,
and so civilian transport was reinstated.
However, the long distances often caused delays.
In the fourth year of Xuāndé,
Xuān and Minister Huáng Fú suggested reinstating the zhīyùn method.
Thus, people from Jiāngxī, Húguǎng, and Zhèjiāng were ordered to transport 1.5 million shí of grain to the Huái'ān granary;
people from Sūzhōu, Sōngjiāng, Níngguó, Chízhōu, Lúzhōu, Ānqìng, and Guǎngdé were to transport 2.74 million shí of grain to the Xúzhōu granary;
and people from Yìngtiān, Chángzhōu, Zhènjiāng, Huái'ān, Yángzhōu, Fèngyáng, Tàicāng, Chúzhōu, Hézhōu, and Xúzhōu were to transport 2.2 million shí of grain to the Línqīng granary.
Official troops were then ordered to take over the transport to the Jīngcāng (Capital Granary) and Tōngcāng.
Since the civilian grain was delivered to nearby granaries,
their labor was greatly reduced.
Therefore, based on the distance of the location
and the amount of grain,
one-eleventh, one-third, or one-fifth of the civilian boats were requisitioned
for the official troops.
However, people from Shāndōng, Hénán, and Běizhílì (North Directly-governed areas) went directly to the Jīngcāng
and did not use zhīyùn.
Later, grain from Nányáng, Huáiqìng, and Rǔníng was ordered to be transported to the Línqīng granary,
and grain from Kāifēng, Zhāngdé, and Wèihuī was transported to the Dézhōu granary.
Subsequently, all grain from Shāndōng and Hénán was transported to the Dézhōu granary.
In the sixth year,
Xuān said:
"The people of Jiāngnán transporting grain to various granaries
take almost a year for a round trip,
which disrupts agriculture.
If the people transport it to Huái'ān and Guāzhōu,
and exchange it with the garrisons,
and the official troops transport it north,
being given travel expenses and additional rice for consumption,
then both the military and the people will benefit."
This was called duìyùn (exchange transport).
The emperor ordered his ministers to convene a meeting.
Jiǎn Yì and others from the Ministry of Personnel presented regulations for the official troops' duìyùn of civilian grain, including additional allowances based on distance.
For each shí,
Húguǎng received eight dǒu,
Jiāngxī and Zhèjiāng seven dǒu,
Nánzhílì (South Directly-governed areas) six dǒu,
and Běizhílì five dǒu.
If civilians transported grain to Huái'ān for exchange with military transport,
only four dǒu were added.
If the exchanged grain was not fully transported,
the civilians were still ordered to transport it themselves to the various granaries.
Those who did not wish to exchange
were also allowed to transport it themselves.
Since the troops received additional allowances
and were also given small sums of silver for expenses at floodgates and for transshipment,
and could carry other goods,
they were all happy to participate.
The people also found long-distance transport difficult.
Thus, there were many who opted for duìyùn,
and few for zhīyùn.
When the military exchanged rice with the people,
they often relied on their power to extort.
The emperor, aware of this abuse,
decreed to the Ministry of Revenue to appoint regular officials to supervise,
prohibiting private exchanges.
Later, the additional allowance of rice was somewhat reduced;
for distant areas, it was no more than six dǒu,
and for nearby areas, it was as little as two dǒu five shēng.
It was divided into three parts:
two parts were given as rice,
and one part was compensated with other goods.
The official grain measures were sharp on the surface (to ensure full measure),
while the additional grain measures were leveled.
Of the four million shí of grain transported,
four-tenths were stored in the Jīngcāng,
and six-tenths in the Tōngcāng.
For the three granaries of Línqīng, Xúzhōu, and Huái'ān, Censors were dispatched to supervise the collection.
In the early years of Zhèngtǒng,
the amount of grain transported was 4.5 million shí,
of which over 2.8 million shí were by duìyùn,
and only three or four-tenths were by zhīyùn at the four granaries of Huái'ān, Xúzhōu, Línqīng, and Dézhōu.
During the Tǔmù Incident,
all troops from Shāndōng and Zhílì were again kept for training and defense.
Grain transport for Sūzhōu, Sōngjiāng, and other prefectures was still the responsibility of the common people.
In the sixth year of Jǐngtài,
when the Wǎlà presented tribute,
military transport was reinstated.
At the end of Tiānshùn,
the duìyùn method had been in practice for a long time,
and granary officials coveted the surplus from the allowances,
often receiving exchanged grain with an overflowing measure
and demanding more,
which greatly distressed the troops.
Upon Emperor Xiànzōng's ascension,
the Assistant Commander of Grain Transport, Yuán Yòu, presented a memorial on expedient measures.
The emperor said:
"The laws clearly state
that when collecting grain, the households should measure it level,
and the additional allowance for each shí should not exceed five shēng.
Now the transport troops are willing to explicitly add more,
which shows that the granary officials' exploitation is excessive.
From now on, the troops shall measure it themselves,
adding five shēng per shí
without exceeding it.
Those who extort shall be punished."
Later, following the words of the supervising eunuch of the granaries,
the additional allowance was increased to eight shēng.
After some time,
it again exceeded the official amount as before,
and repeated prohibitions could not stop it.
Initially,
the amount of grain transported to the capital
had no fixed quota.
It was in the eighth year of Chénghuà that it was first set at four million shí,
and thereafter it became the norm.
755,600 shí were from the north,
and 3,244,400 shí were from the south.
Within this, 3.3 million shí were transported by duìyùn,
and 700,000 shí were changed from zhīyùn to duìyùn.
Among the duìyùn,
177,700 shí from Húguǎng, Shāndōng, and Hénán were paid in silver in lieu of grain.
In total, including duìyùn, changed duìyùn, and the additional rice delivered to the Jīngcāng and Tōngcāng,
it amounted to 5,189,700 shí.
Of this, Nánzhílì alone supplied 1.8 million shí of regular grain,
and Sūzhōu Prefecture alone 700,000 shí,
excluding the additional allowances.
The tax from Zhèjiāng was tens of thousands less than Sūzhōu.
Jiāngxī and Húguǎng were even further reduced.
Tiānjīn, Jìzhōu, Mìyún, and Chāngpíng
together supplied over 640,000 shí of rice,
all of which came from the duìyùn rice.
The Línqīng and Dézhōu granaries
stored over 190,000 shí of reserve rice,
which was filled with grain from Shāndōng and Hénán that had been changed to duìyùn.
In case of disasters,
rice from these two granaries was allocated to supplement the transport,
ensuring the four-million-shí quota was met
without any shortfall.
It was not until the seventh year of Chénghuà
that there was a proposal to change the system of exchange.
At that time, Téng Zhāo, the Grand Coordinator of Yìngtiān, ordered the transport soldiers to go to the waterside of Jiāngnán to make the exchange,
and in addition to the extra wastage,
an additional shí of rice was levied for every dǒu as a cross-river fee.
Several years later,
the Emperor then ordered the four granaries of Huái, Xú, Lín, and Dé to transport seventy myriad shí of rice,
all to be exchanged at the waterside.
From then on, all transport was changed to the exchange system,
and direct long-distance transport by official soldiers became a fixed institution.
However, at that time,
the granary officials often made excessive demands,
even imposing additional penalties,
so that the transport soldiers had to borrow repeatedly and could not cope.
In the first year of Hóngzhì,
Mǎ Wénshēng, the Censor-in-Chief, memorialized on the hardships of the transport soldiers,
saying:
"The transport boats from all the directly-administered provinces
are all paid for by the Ministry of Works,
which orders officials to supervise their construction.
Recently,
the Commander-in-Chief of Grain Transport requested to receive payment and build them himself, as the payments were not made on time.
However, the Ministry officials, fearing that the soldiers would not take good care of them,
proposed that the Ministry supply four-tenths of the materials,
the military garrisons be responsible for three-tenths,
and old boats account for three-tenths.
The military garrisons had no means to arrange this,
so all the soldiers sold their assets and their children to provide for it.
This is the hardship of shipbuilding.
The number of regular soldiers who have deserted is high,
but the quota is not reduced,
and all the remaining able-bodied men are conscripted to fill it,
with some households having three or four people serving.
Exchanging in spring and returning in autumn,
their hardships are myriad.
When the boats reach Zhāngjiāwān,
carts must be hired to transfer the goods,
and they often borrow to make ends meet.
This is the hardship of the journey.
As for what they borrow,
the transport officials use it for embezzlement,
demanding repayment at double interest.
And if soldiers carry local products to exchange for firewood and rice,
they are hindered by prohibitions
and often plundered.
Now, it is advisable to increase the shipbuilding cost by twenty liǎng of silver per vessel,
and to prohibit the abuses of transport officials and local authorities who impose levies, harm, and search,
so that the soldiers' distress may be somewhat alleviated."
An imperial edict approved his proposal.
In the fifth year,
Yè Qí, the Minister of Revenue, said:
"The prefectures of Sū and Sōng
have suffered continuous years of famine,
and the people buy grain transport rice
at two liǎng of silver per shí.
However, the provinces of Běi Zhílì, Shāndōng, and Hénán annually supply grain and fodder to the two borders of Xuān and Dà,
also at one liǎng of silver per shí.
Last year,
Sūzhōu already converted fifty myriad shí of grain transport to silver,
at one liǎng of silver per shí.
Now I request that this be extended to other prefectures,
with a slight adjustment in price.
For severely afflicted areas,
seven qián per shí;
for slightly less severe areas,
still one liǎng per shí.
All shall be remitted to the Ministry to be forwarded to the various borders,
to offset the annual supply quota of the three areas of Běi Zhílì,
while the original grain from these three areas will be collected and transported to the capital granaries,
thus saving costs and making affairs easier to manage."
This was approved.
Thereafter, in years of disaster,
it was often expedient to convert to silver,
with the amount being filled by grain transported from waterside granaries,
and the conversion price generally at six or seven qián,
never again reaching one liǎng.
Previously,
during the Chénghuà period, the long-distance transport system was implemented.
When grain was transported by the prefectures and counties of Jiāngnán to Nánjīng,
the official soldiers were ordered to exchange and distribute it at the waterside,
calculating the savings in extra wastage, transport, and towing fees,
resulting in an surplus of over one hundred thousand shí of rice,
which was stored in the reserve granaries for urgent use.
At this time,
the Grand Coordinator, Censor-in-Chief, requested that, due to abuses in the exchange and distribution system,
it be reverted to the old method of delivering to the granaries first before distribution.
The Ministry of Revenue said:
"The exchange and distribution method is good
and should not be changed."
An imperial edict approved the Ministry's proposal,
and the surplus was stored in the various guard granaries
for regular expenditure.
It was also approved, following the Ministry of Revenue's proposal, that the ninety thousand shí of grain converted for exchange in Shāndōng
should still be transported by the common people themselves to the Lín and Dé granaries,
and then distributed by official soldiers.
In the second year of Zhèngdé,
an official of the Grain Transport system requested to clear out the stores in the waterside granaries,
stating:
"In earlier times, the common people transported grain to the four granaries of Huái, Xú, Lín, and Dé
to await distribution by the guard soldiers.
Later, this was changed to exchange at the waterside in nearby prefectures and counties.
Subsequently, even the seventy myriad shí of transported grain was ordered to be converted for exchange.
However, beyond the seventy myriad shí,
there was still grain that had not been fully exchanged,
which the common people continued to transport to the four granaries,
where it remained undistributed for a long time,
leading to spoilage.
I request that the three hundred fifty thousand shí of grain from Zhèjiāng, Jiāngxī, and Húguǎng for regular exchange
be converted into silver and remitted to the capital,
and that the guard soldiers from these three provinces go to the Lín and Dé granaries,
to transport grain equivalent to the converted amount.
Then the grain in the various granaries will not rot,
and the transport soldiers of the three provinces will find it convenient to transport.
In addition to the annual grain transport quota,
an extra three hundred fifty thousand liǎng of silver will be obtained,
achieving several benefits with one action."
The Emperor ordered the Ministry officials to deliberate,
and it was granted as requested.
In the sixth year,
Shào Bǎo, the Vice Minister of Revenue, noting the delays in grain transport,
requested the re-establishment of the direct transport system.
The Ministry of Revenue deliberated,
saying that the direct transport system had been abolished for a long time
and could not be quickly reinstated,
so the matter was dropped.
The grain stored in the two granaries of Lín and Dé
amounted to one hundred ninety thousand [shí] in total,
which over ten years would be one hundred ninety myriad [shí].
From the beginning of Shìzōng's reign,
more and more allocations were made due to disasters and damages,
and Shāndōng and Hénán, due to annual poor harvests,
repeatedly requested reductions,
and moreover, much of the accumulated grain in the two granaries had rotted.
Consequently, proposals for conversion to silver frequently arose,
and the granary reserves gradually diminished.
In the first year of Jiājìng,
Yáng Hóng, the Commander-in-Chief of Grain Transport,
requested that the "light transport silver" be allowed to be directly disbursed by transport officials on the way,
to cover the costs of hiring boats and carts,
without the need for casing and sealing,
or calculating surpluses,
which would burden the transport soldiers.
Censors and supervising secretaries jointly rejected this.
The Ministry of Revenue said:
"The arguments of the supervising secretaries and censors
are primarily aimed at preventing corruption,
which is correct.
However, the 'light transport silver' was originally intended to fund transfer costs.
Now, fearing official soldiers' embezzlement and wastage, all the surplus is taken back to the Grand Granary,
thus treating transportation fees as regular grain,
which is not the original intention of the legislation."
Then it was decided that when transport boats reached Tōngzhōu,
the supervising censor of granaries would verify and inspect,
and allocate the actual amount needed,
establishing it as a fixed regulation.
Any surplus
would not be remitted to the Grand Granary,
but used to repair boats,
and officials and soldiers who embezzled would be severely punished.
Regarding the "light transport silver":
Xìanzōng, due to the conversion of various granaries,
provided travel expenses,
which initially included allowances for wastage;
for exchanged grain,
there was always a flat and a sharp measure,
hence the "sharp rice";
besides the four dǒu given per boat as transport allowance,
the remainder was converted to silver,
called "light transport silver."
This amounted to over four hundred forty-five thousand liǎng in total.
Later, much of it was remitted to the Grand Granary.
During the Lóngqìng era,
the transport route was difficult and obstructed,
and some suggested opening the Jiāolái River and resuming sea transport.
From Huái'ān, Qīngjiāng Pǔkǒu,
passing through Xīnbà and Mǎjiāháo to the Hǎicāngkǒu,
directly reaching Zhígū,
only following the coastal channels
without venturing into the open ocean.
The memorial was submitted,
and officials were dispatched to investigate and report,
but it was stopped due to the abundance of sandbanks in the water.
During the reign of Shénzōng,
the Grand Coordinator of Grain Transport, Shū Yìnglóng, stated:
"The state has two capitals established in parallel.
Huái, Xú, Lín, and Dé
are truly the north-south thoroughfares.
Since the long-standing practice of exchange transport,
Lín and Dé still have annual accumulations,
but the two granaries of Huái and Xú have not a single grain of rice.
I request that from now on, when Shāndōng and Hénán have a full harvest,
all the grains in kind be levied and deposited into the granaries.
Since Lín and Dé have already accumulated over 500,000 shí,
then these should be stored in the two granaries [Huái and Xú],
to accumulate 500,000 shí each and then stop."
This was approved.
At that time,
the conversion to silver gradually increased.
In the 30th year of Wànlì (1602),
the grain transport reaching the capital
was merely over 1.38 million shí.
However, the provincial governor proposed intercepting grain transport rice to aid river conservancy projects.
Zhào Shìqīng, a Supervising Secretary of Granaries and Fields, argued against this,
stating:
"The Grand Granary's income does not cover its outgoings.
In two years' time,
the six armies and myriad common people will be waiting for new grain transport to cook their meals.
If the delivery is delayed,
there will no longer be a capital city."
This was because in times of disaster and damage, converted silver
and grain transport in kind were originally used to pay the monthly stipends of the capital armies.
At that time, these were indiscriminately disbursed to provide for border garrisons,
which led to both silver and rice being depleted,
hence Shìqīng argued against it.
Thereafter, granary reserves gradually dwindled,
and grain transport administration also became increasingly lax.
By the time of Qǐ and Zhēn (Tiānqǐ and Chóngzhēn reigns),
the empire was in a state of desolation and burdened by expenses,
and annual supplies were even more insufficient to meet needs.
The number of transport ships,
from Yǒnglè to Jǐngtài,
varied greatly in size and
was numerous.
After Tiānshùn,
the number of ships was set at 11,770,
with 120,000 official soldiers.
They were permitted to carry local products as accompanying cargo,
exempt from taxes and duties.
During Xiàozōng's time, the limit was ten shí;
during Shénzōng's time, it reached sixty shí.
Xiànzōng set deadlines for transport ships to reach the capital:
for Běizhílì, Hénán, and Shāndōng, the first day of the fifth month;
for Nánzhílì, the first day of the seventh month.
For those crossing the river for exchange and transport,
it was extended by one month.
For Zhèjiāng, Jiāngxī, and Húguǎng, the first day of the ninth month.
After a three-year overall assessment,
those who violated the deadline
would have their transport officials demoted or penalized.
Wǔzōng listed waterway route maps,
requiring daily entries for travel progress and stopping stations.
Rice that missed the deadline was
stored in various granaries in Dézhōu,
called "temporary storage."
Shìzōng set deadlines for crossing the Huái River:
Jiāngběi by the twelfth month,
Jiāngnán by the first month,
Húguǎng, Zhèjiāng, and Jiāngxī by the third month.
During Shénzōng's time, this was changed to the second month.
Also, the deadline for reaching the capital, originally the fifth month,
was shortened by one month.
Those for the seventh, eighth, and ninth months
were successively shortened by two months.
Later, they were all shortened by one month.
At the beginning of Shénzōng's reign,
it was stipulated that collection into granaries should be in the tenth month,
and the exchange completed in the eleventh month.
For large counties, the limit for ships to arrive was ten days;
for small counties, five days.
In the twelfth month, loading began,
in the second month, they crossed the Huái,
and in the third month, they crossed Hóng and entered the locks.
All were required to present sample rice to the Ministry of Revenue in advance.
On the day the grain arrived,
it was collected only after verification proved it to be identical.
For all cases of disaster and damage for which conversion was requested and approved,
it must not exceed the seventh month.
For proposals submitted late or impromptu changes to proposals,
a record was made, and further review was exempted.
For grain lost to drifting,
it was to be compensated with edible rice.
Drifting in the Great River was a major problem,
while in the river channels it was a minor problem;
over 200 shí was a major problem,
under 200 shí was a minor problem.
Minor problems were reported by junior officers after investigation,
major problems were formally reported to the throne.
Afterwards, regardless of quantity,
all cases were reported to the throne for investigation.
Initially,
ships used nán (phoebe zhennan) and shān (fir) wood;
inferior ones used pine.
Minor repairs were done every three years,
major repairs every six years,
and new construction every ten years.
Each ship carried 472 shí of standard and attrition rice.
Later, due to a shortage of ships,
one ship carried 700 to 800 shí of rice.
Accompanying and smuggled cargo increased daily,
leading to delays and missed deadlines everywhere.
Upon encountering a river breach,
drifting immediately occurred,
and official soldiers took advantage of this for illicit gains.
Rice was converted to dry goods at the waterfront,
embezzled along the way,
falsely claimed as lost to fire or water,
and some even scuttled their own ships.
In the early Míng dynasty,
military officials were ordered to supervise sea transport,
and the office of Grand Canal Transport Commissioner was once established,
but soon abolished.
After Chéngzǔ, censors were used,
then Supervising Secretaries and Censors-in-Chief were used to urge and supervise,
while Department Directors and Assistant Department Directors were responsible for specific tasks,
and Directors of Bureaus supervised the exchange.
The system was not uniform.
In the second year of Jǐngtài (1451), the Grand Coordinator of Grain Transport was first established in Huái'ān,
working with the Regional Commander and Assistant Regional Commander on grain transport matters.
The Grain Transport Commissioner commanded twelve 'zǒng' (groups/units),
comprising 120,000 soldiers,
which corresponded to the twelve camps of capital garrison soldiers.
Initially,
Xuānzōng ordered the Regional Commanders for grain transport, Provincial Governors, and Supervising Secretaries to go to the capital every eighth month
to deliberate on the next year's grain transport matters.
When the Grand Coordinator of Grain Transport was established,
the Grand Coordinator was also ordered to go to the capital.
This practice was only abolished after the 18th year of Wànlì (1590).
Every first month of the year,
the Grand Coordinator of Grain Transport inspected Yángzhōu,
managing the passage through the locks at Guā and Huái.
The Regional Commander was stationed at Xú and Pī,
supervising the passage across Hóng and into the locks.
The Concurrent Director of Grain Transport Affairs escorted the grain to the capital.
For concentrated transport, there were Censors and Department Directors;
for escorting transport, there were Concurrent Directors of Grain Transport Affairs;
for supervising exchange, administering justice, managing Hóng, managing factories, managing locks, managing springs, and supervising granaries, there were Directors of Bureaus;
for Qīngjiāng and Wèihé, there were Surveillance Commissioners.
After the exchange and passage through Huái and Hóng,
the Provincial Governor, Grain Transport Commissioner, and River Conservancy Officials each reported according to their responsibilities.
If local officials did not have the rice ready,
or military garrisons did not have ships ready,
causing a delay in crossing the Huái,
the responsibility lay with the Provincial Governor.
If rice was ready and ships were available,
but not immediately inspected and released,
and it was not due to river obstruction but rather congestion and forced mooring,
causing a delay in crossing Hóng and subsequent drifting or freezing,
the responsibility lay with the Grain Transport Commissioner.
If ships and grain were on schedule,
but river channels were silted and shallow,
dredging was ineffective,
or lock gates were opened or closed at the wrong time,
preventing passage through Hóng or reaching the anchorage,
the responsibility lay with the River Conservancy Officials.
In the early Míng dynasty,
the grain transport administration often showed leniency and consideration.
Rénzōng and Xuānzōng prohibited impressment for grain boats
and pardoned those who delayed transport.
During Yīngzōng's time, ration deductions began to be equally distributed,
but the transport soldiers did not adhere to regulations and became a nuisance to the people.
Thereafter, grain transport administration became increasingly lax.
Soldiers exchanged attrition rice for private goods
and sold it along the way, causing delays.
Upon arrival,
they instead bought granary rice to make up for deficiencies,
often still falling short.
And the grain tribute heads often mixed sand and water into the rice,
especially in Hénán and Shāndōng,
which often resulted in rice that was steamed wet, moldy, and inedible.
Influential figures lent silver to transport soldiers for exorbitant profits,
even requesting customs duties be allocated for ship materials as compensation.
Grain transport junior officers were often appointed through bribery.
Granary and field administration extracted additional fees,
totaling up to 140,000 annually.
In the early reign of Shìzōng,
many abuses were reformed,
but the two abuses of drifting and exceeding deadlines
grew worse day by day.
After the mid-period,
they became even more inscrutable.
Beyond the grain collected for the Grand Canal transport system (cáoliáng),
the five prefectures of Sūzhōu, Sōngjiāng, Chángzhōu, Jiāxīng, and Húzhōu
transported over 170,040 shí of polished ordinary and glutinous rice for the imperial household (nèifǔ),
of which over 8,000 shí were commuted to silver payments.
The various prefectures also supplied over 44,000 shí of unpolished ordinary rice,
of which over 8,800 shí were commuted to silver payments.
The people were ordered to transport these,
and these were called "white grain boats" (báilíangchuán).
Since the long-distance transport (chángyùn) method was implemented,
all grain for the Grand Canal transport system was transported by soldiers,
but white grain continued to be transported by civilians as before.
During the reign of Mùzōng,
Lù Shùdé stated:
"Military transport serves to fill military stores,
while civilian transport serves to provide official salaries.
People know the hardship of military transport,
but they do not know that civilian transport is even more arduous.
The demands of boatmen,
the bullying by transport soldiers,
the waiting at major sluices,
and the entry into the capital and granaries—
all these generate countless abuses.
In the early Jiājìng period,
there were still families who could maintain their livelihoods through civilian transport,
but ten years later, none were left unbroken.
It would be very convenient to have soldiers take responsibility for the transport of white grain."
When the memorial was submitted,
it was sent to the ministries for deliberation.
It was not adopted.
For all granaries, there was a fixed quota to be supplied.
If some of this was diverted to other garrisons,
and grain was to be exchanged at a riverside depot (shuǐcì),
then the garrison soldiers assigned to receive the exchange were immediately ordered to be paid.
Local officials (zhōuxiànguān) supervised carters to transport it to distant granaries,
or were paid by the military and ordered to dispense the funds on the spot.
This was collectively called "digging transport" (wàyùn).
In the Nine Border Regions (Jiǔbiān zhī dì),
grain was mostly transported by cart.
During the Xuāndé period,
this was also the case for supplying Kāipíng.
However, in Lánzhōu, Gānsù, and Sōngpān,
the people were often made to carry loads on their backs.
In the Yǒnglè reign,
Guǎngdōng was once ordered to transport 200,000 shí of grain by sea to Jiāozhǐ.
In the early Míng dynasty,
there were military granaries (jūncāng) in the capital garrisons (jīngwèi).
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, their number was increased to twenty,
and Línháo and Línqīng granaries were also built to facilitate transshipment.
Each province (hángshěng) had granaries,
from which officials' salaries were drawn.
Border regions had granaries,
which received income from military agricultural colonies (túntián) to supply the troops.
Prefectures and counties (zhōuxiàn) set up relief granaries (yùbèicāng),
four in total—east, south, west, and north—
to provide relief in times of famine.
After the paper currency (chāofǎ) was implemented,
some of these were eliminated.
In the twenty-fourth year, 160,000 shí of grain were stored at Línqīng
to supply the cavalry training.
In the twenty-eighth year, four granaries were established at the gates of the Imperial City (huángchéng),
storing grain to supply the defending troops.
The number of granaries in the capital garrisons was increased to forty-one.
Furthermore, granaries were established in Běipíng, Mìyún, and other counties,
storing grain to support the northern expeditions.
During the Yǒnglè reign,
Tiānjīn and the Left Garrison Granary of Tōngzhōu (Tōngzhōu Zuǒwèicāng) were established,
and thirty-seven Beijing garrison granaries were also set up.
More prefectures and counties across the empire were ordered to establish granaries,
and the relief granaries located in the rural areas were moved into the cities.
When the Huìtōng River was completed,
granaries were first established at Xúzhōu, Huái'ān, and Dézhōu.
Línqīng, following the old Hóngwǔ system,
together with Tiānjīn Granary, made a total of five.
These were called "riverside granaries" (shuǐcìcāng)
to facilitate transshipment.
Later,
the Dézhōu Granary was moved to Yǒngqīngbà in Línqīng,
the Wǔqīng Garrison Granary was established at Héxīwù,
and the Tōngzhōu Garrison Granary was established at Zhāngjiāwān.
During the Xuāndé reign,
the Línqīng Granary was expanded to accommodate three million shí.
Beijing and Tōngzhōu granaries were also increased.

The capital granaries were patrolled quarterly by censors (yùshǐ), officials from the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù guān), and commanders of one thousand and one hundred households (qiānbǎihù) from the Brocade Guard (Jǐnyīwèi).

The outer granaries were supervised by the Provincial Administration Commission (Bùzhèng Shǐsī), Provincial Surveillance Commission (Ànchá Shǐsī), and Regional Military Commission (Dūsī) with their official seals.
For each granary gate,
two retired military officials,
leading ten old or young military laborers (jūndīng), guarded it,
changing every six months.
In the early Yīngzōng reign,
court officials were ordered to deliberate.
For all prefectures, subprefectures, and counties (sīfǔzhōuxiàn) across the empire,
those with granaries had the garrison granaries (wèisuǒcāng) attached to them;
those without granaries had garrison granaries re-assigned to their jurisdiction.
Only the garrisons in Liáodōng, Gānsù, Níngxià, Wànquán, and along the coast,
which had no prefectures, subprefectures, or counties, maintained their original arrangements.
During the Zhèngtǒng period,
seven more capital garrison granaries were established.
Since the exchange transport (duìyùn) method was implemented,
the amount dispensed by various granaries decreased,
and the Beijing and Tōngzhōu granaries could not hold all the grain.
Thus, one-third of the Línqīng, Dézhōu, and Héxīwù granaries were demolished
and converted into Beijing and Tōngzhōu granaries.
In the early Jǐngtài reign,
the Wǔqīng Garrison granaries were moved to Tōngzhōu.
In the early Chénghuà reign,
the relief granaries of Línqīng and Dézhōu located outside the city were abolished,
and empty granary stores inside the city were used to store relief rice.
The Línqīng one was named Chángyíng ("Ever-Full"),
and the Dézhōu one was named Chángfēng ("Ever-Abundant").
There were fifty-six capital granaries
and sixteen Tōngzhōu granaries.

Prefectures, subprefectures, and counties in the directly administered provinces (zhíshěng), princely establishments (fānfǔ), border passes (biān'ài), postal stations (bǎozhàn), and garrison agricultural colonies (wèisuǒ túntún) all had granaries.
Some had one or two,
while others had twenty or thirty.
When the relief granaries were first established,
Tàizǔ selected elders (qímín) to transport paper currency (chāo) to purchase rice
for relief purposes,
and entrusted them with their management.
Most prefectures and counties across the empire accumulated stores,
but later, these gradually fell into disuse.
Yú Qiān, as Grand Coordinator (Fǔwèishǐ) of Hénán and Shānxī,
restored this policy.
Zhōu Chén, as Grand Coordinator of Nánjī (Southern Capital Region),
established separate "granaries for aiding agriculture" (jìnóngcāng).
Others were unable to do so.
During the Zhèngtǒng period,
the crime of embezzlement was severely punished,
even to the extent of conscripting the wives of offenders into military service.
Furthermore, those who contributed 1,500 shí of grain
were awarded an imperial commendation as "righteous citizens" (yìmín)
and exempted from miscellaneous levies for their household.
For every shí of rice distributed for famine relief,
when there was a good harvest,
two shí and five dòu of unhusked rice were to be returned to the government.
In the third year of Hóngzhì, a limit was set for counties: those within ten lǐ had to accumulate 15,000 shí;
those within twenty lǐ, 20,000 shí.
For garrison companies (qiānhùsuǒ), 15,000 shí;
for platoons (bǎihùsuǒ), 300 shí.
At the end of their term (kǎomǎn),
their performance was assessed by the amount accumulated, determining their merit or demerit.
Those who failed to reach one-third of the quota had their salaries confiscated;
those who reached six-tenths or more were demoted.
In the eighteenth year, all fines and confiscations from pardoned criminals
were to be used to purchase grain for the granaries.
During the Zhèngdé reign,
prisoners were allowed to contribute paper,
and 80% of its value in rice was to be deposited in the granaries.
Military officers who committed offenses
could contribute grain in lieu of meritorious service.
Initially,
all relief granaries had granary officials (cāngguān).
By this time, these were abolished,
and county officials (zhōuxiànguān) and grain-supervising granary officials (guǎnlángcāngguān) took charge of their affairs.
In the early Jiājìng reign,
the Grand Academician (Yùdé) Gù Dǐngchén stated:
"During the Chénghuà and Hóngzhì periods,
the annual surplus rice was deposited into the relief granaries,
providing a reserve for emergencies.
Now, the autumn grain barely suffices for exchange transport,
and there is not a single grain in the relief granaries.
When disaster strikes,
memorials are immediately submitted to retain other grains or to persuade wealthy commoners to lend grain,
following past practices.
I beg that the relief granary grain be quickly restored to enrich the people."
The emperor then ordered the relevant authorities (yǒusī) to devise methods to accumulate more rice and grain,
still following the ancient ever-normal granary (chángpíng) system:
in spring, relieve the poor;
after the autumn harvest, return it to the government,
without charging interest.
The quotas were set at 10,000 shí for prefectures,
4,000-5,000 shí for subprefectures,
and 2,000-3,000 shí for counties.
Later,
it was further stipulated that for every ten lǐ, 15,000 shí should be accumulated,
increasing progressively upwards,
reaching 190,000 shí for areas within 800 lǐ.
Thereafter, accumulated grain was all sold at stable prices (píngtiào)
to aid the poor,
and reserves gradually diminished.
During the Lóngqìng reign,
prosperous prefectures had no more than 6,000 shí,
and small counties had only 1,000 shí.
Over time, the numbers further decreased,
and penalties for deficiencies also became lighter.
During the Wànlì reign,
even major prefectures and subprefectures reached a maximum of 3,000 shí,
while small counties sometimes had only 100 shí.
The authorities merely followed the forms (jùwén),
and though edicts were repeatedly issued to strictly admonish them,
they generally only deceived with false numbers.
In the Hongzhì reign,
Lín Jùn, the Grand Coordinator of Jiāngxī, once requested the establishment of ever-normal granaries and community granaries.
In the eighth year of Jiājìng, an order was issued for all Grand Coordinators and Provincial Censors to set up community granaries.
The people were ordered to form communities of twenty to thirty households each.
One person of substantial means and upright conduct was chosen from a wealthy family to be the community head (shèshǒu).
One person who was fair in handling affairs was chosen as the community chief (shèzhèng).
One person skilled in writing and calculation was chosen as the community deputy (shèfù).
They would gather on the first and fifteenth day of each month.
Households were classified as upper, middle, or lower.
They contributed between four dòu and one dòu of rice, with variations.
An additional five hé per dòu was collected as a surcharge.
Upper-class households managed these affairs.
In times of famine,
those upper-class households that were short were granted loans proportionally.
In years of good harvest, they returned to the granary.
Middle and lower-class households received grants according to need,
and did not need to return to the granary.
The officials kept registers and sent them to the Grand Coordinator and Provincial Censor.
They were inspected once a year.
If a granary was empty,
the shèshǒu was penalized by having to contribute one year's worth of rice.
The method was quite good,
but later it was not effectively implemented.
The treasuries and granaries in the two capitals
were established successively,
and their systems were generally similar.
The Imperial Household Department (Nèifǔ) had a total of ten treasuries.
The Nèi Chéngyùn Kù
stored silk fabrics, gold, silver, precious jade, ivory, horn, and feathers,
with "gold-flower silver" being the most significant,
with over one million liǎng contributed annually.
The Guǎngjī Kù
stored sulfur and saltpeter.
The Jiǎzì Kù
stored cloth and pigments.
The Yǐzì Kù
stored padded jackets, combat boots, and fur hats for soldiers.
The Bǐngzì Kù
stored cotton and raw silk.
The Dīngzì Kù
stored copper, iron, animal skins, and sappanwood.
The Wùzì Kù
stored armor and weapons.
The Zāngfá Kù
stored confiscated goods.
The Guǎnghuì Kù
stored cash and paper money.
The Guǎngyíng Kù
stored ramie and silk fabrics, gauze, damask, brocade, pongee, and fine silk.
Six of these treasuries belonged to the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù).
Only the Yǐzì Kù belonged to the Ministry of War (Bīngbù).
The Wùzì, Guǎngjī, and Guǎngyíng Kù belonged to the Ministry of Works (Gōngbù).
There was also the Tiāncái Kù,
also named the Sīyào Kù,
which stored the keys of various yámén [offices],
and also stored cash and paper money.
The Gōngyòng Kù
stored glutinous rice, husked rice, and tribute items.
The above were collectively called the Nèikù (Inner Treasuries).
Those within the palace
also included the Nèi Dōngyù Kù and Bǎozàng Kù,
called the Mìkù (Secret Treasuries).
All Mìkù were not subject to the jurisdiction of the authorities.
The various treasuries for porcelain located east of the Huìguī Mén
and Bǎoshàn Mén and in the southern city
were called the Wàikù (Outer Treasuries).
As for the various directorates, bureaus, and agencies within the Nèifǔ,
the Shénlè Táng,
the Xīshēng Suǒ,
the Tàicháng Sì, Guānglù Sì,
and Guózǐ Jiān
all stored their respective necessary items
according to their responsibilities.
The Tàipú Sì was where silver for horse purchases was kept.
In the early Míng dynasty,
circulating treasuries (xíngyòng kù) were established in the capital and various prefectures, departments, and counties
to receive worn and damaged paper money.
They were abolished during the Rénzōng Emperor's reign.
During the Yīngzōng Emperor's reign,
the Tàicāng Kù was first established.
Initially,
annual taxes were not collected in gold or silver,
except for the taxes on mining and metallurgy which yielded gold and silver
and were deposited into the Nèi Chéngyùn Kù.
Any annual taxes occasionally commuted into gold or silver
were all sent to Nánjīng to supply stipends for military officials.
When there were urgent needs on various borders,
funds were also drawn from there.
In the first year of Zhèngtǒng, the system of commuting grain tribute was reformed.
One million liǎng was set as the annual quota,
all of which was remitted to the Nèi Chéngyùn Kù
and no longer sent to Nánjīng.
Apart from the more than one hundred thousand liǎng allocated for military officials' stipends,
the rest was for imperial use.
This was known as "gold-flower silver."
In the seventh year, the Hùbù Tàicāng Kù was established.
Surplus wheat and rice from various direct provinces,
cotton, silk, silk fabrics, cloth, horse fodder, salt taxes, and customs duties from the ten treasuries—
all amounts commuted into silver—
were deposited into the Tàicāng Kù.
Confiscated family assets,
proceeds from selling land and properties,
recovered shop rents,
and funds submitted according to precedent
were also all deposited there.
It was exclusively for storing silver,
hence it was also called the Yínkù (Silver Treasury).
During the Hongzhì reign,
the Nèifǔ had numerous demands for supplies,
and often transferred silver from the Tàicāng Kù into the Nèikù.
A Nánjīng Yínkù was also established.
During the Zhèngdé reign,
the eunuchs in charge of the Nèi Chéngyùn Kù
repeatedly stated that the Nèifǔ's financial resources were insufficient
