and requested to draw silver from the Tàicāng Kù.
The Hùbù's remonstrances could not prevent this.
In the early Jiājìng reign,
the Nèifǔ's expenditures were comparable to those in the Hongzhì reign,
but later they doubled.
Initially,
the central vault of the Tàicāng Kù held over eight million liǎng of accumulated silver.
Subsequently received funds were stored in the two wings
for easy disbursement.
The central vault remained untouched,
and thus the central vault was designated the "old vault" (lǎokù),
and the two wings the "outer vault" (wàikù).
By this time,
the old vault contained only 1.2 million liǎng.
In the twenty-second year, a special order was issued that gold-flower silver and grain commutation silver, which were supposed to be remitted to the Nèikù,
should all be sent to the Tàicāng Kù for border defense use.
However, they later reverted to being deposited in the Nèikù.
In the thirty-seventh year, besides the one million liǎng of silver annually remitted to the Nèikù,
an additional amount was prepared for imperial requisition.
Later, another 400,000 liǎng of confiscated silver was taken into the Nèikù.
During the Lóngqìng reign,
silver was frequently drawn from the Tàicāng Kù into the Nèikù.
Eunuchs from the Chéngyùn Kù even sent blank requisitions to the Hùbù to take it.
Court officials submitted memorials of remonstrance,
but none were heeded.
Silver was also frequently drawn from the Guānglù Sì and Tàipú Sì.
Zhū Héng, the Minister of Works, remonstrated strongly,
but was not listened to.
Initially,
during the Shìzōng Emperor's reign,
the Tàicāng Kù's annual income was over two million liǎng.
By the sixth year of Wànlì of the Shénzōng Emperor's reign,
the Tàicāng Kù's annual income reached over 4.5 million liǎng.
However, in addition to the annual "gold-flower silver" supplied to the Nèikù,
an additional 200,000 liǎng of silver for purchases was added as a regular item.
Later, another 70,000 liǎng of silver for fodder for imperial training horses was added.
After a long period,
the silver in the Tàicāng Kù, Guānglù Sì, and Tàipú Sì
was almost entirely depleted through requisitions.
Rewards for military achievements on the border,
which were previously disbursed from the Nèikù,
were also taken from the Tàipú Sì.
For all the Jiǎzì and other treasuries,
the section chiefs (zhǔshì) inspected them jointly with the Censorate and Supervising Secretaries (kēdào).
The Tàicāng Kù
was led by the Assistant Director (yuánwàiláng) and Section Chief (zhǔshì),
with the Supervising Secretary (jǐshìzhōng) conducting inspections.
In the Jiājìng reign,
reports on receipts and disbursements were submitted every two months.
At that time, an old treasury of the Ministry of Works was repaired,
named the Jiéshèn Kù,
to store mined silver.
Wén Míng, the Minister, used it to pay workers.
The emperor questioned and reprimanded him,
ordering him to compensate with other silver.
From then on, it was exclusively used for imperial household expenditures.

In the various bùzhèngsī (provincial administration commissions), dūsī (regional military commissions), and zhíshěng fǔ, zhōu, xiàn, wèisuǒ (prefectures, sub-prefectures, counties, and guard stations of directly administered provinces) outside the capital,
all had treasuries
for storing gold, silver, paper money, silk, fines, and other confiscated items.
The xún'àn yùshǐ (inspecting censors) conducted audits once every three years.
All yùnsī (salt transportation commissions) also had treasuries for storing silver.
At the end of the year,
the xúnyán yùshǐ (inspecting salt censors) would dispatch officials to inspect them.
For all fǔ, zhōu, xiàn (prefectures, sub-prefectures, counties), shuìkèsī jú (tax bureaus), and hébósuǒ (fishery tax stations),
the annual land tax, commercial tax, fishery tax, yǐnyóu (salt certificates), qìběn (deed tax), and other levies,
Tàizǔ ordered the responsible officials to send them to the zhōu, xiàn, fǔsī (sub-prefectures, counties, prefectural offices),
and ultimately to the bù (ministries).
The bù would seal them in the treasury.
Their original seals
were not to be opened without authorization.
During the Yǒnglè reign,
it was first commissioned to conduct inspections.
In the middle
of the process, they would then be dispatched.
Upon reaching the bù, they would be re-inspected.
If found to be identical,
they would then be submitted for receipt.
During the Jiājìng reign,
a yànshìtīng (inspection hall) was established.
After passing inspection,
a certificate of submission would be issued for storage in the treasury.
On the ninth day of each month,
the xúnshì kùcáng kēdàoguān (supervising officials of the treasuries from the Censorate) would convene
to verify and receive them into the treasury.
Those found to be unfit would be rejected and replaced.
In the tenth year of Zhèngtǒng, the Tōngjìkù (Tongji Granary) was established in Tōngzhōu.
It was abolished during the Shìzōng reign.
In the early Lóngqìng reign,
treasuries were established in Mìyún, Jìzhōu, Chāngpíng, and other garrisons
to store the annual allowances for guest and main garrisons, public expenses for military commanders, and silver for pacification rewards and border repairs.
Among those who harmed the granaries and treasuries,
none were worse than the zhōngguān (eunuchs).
The supervisors of the various treasuries in the Nèifǔ (Imperial Household Department)
extorted without end.
During the Zhèngdé reign,
Chén Liáng, a zhǐhuī (commander) of the Táizhōu wèisuǒ, delivered military equipment.
It was delayed for eight years,
to the point that he had to beg for food in the market.
When the Nèifǔ received grain,
the increased wastage was often several times the rate.
Such was the extent of the problem.
Initially, no zhōngguān were appointed to the various granaries.
At the end of the Xuāndé reign,
a single zǒngdū zhōngguān (eunuch supervisor-general) was first appointed to the Jīng (Capital) and Tōng (Tongzhou) granaries.
Later, supervisors were also appointed to the Huái, Xú, Lín, Dé, and other granaries,
and the military and civilian personnel involved in grain transport suffered greatly from them.
Shìzōng, following the advice of Sūn Jiāo and Zhāng Fújìng,
removed all the zhōngguān,
but those supervising the various granaries remained as before.
After a long time,
following the advice of Gǔan Huáilǐ, a gěishìzhōng (remonstrance official),
they were finally abolished.
Initially,
the prefectural treasuries and granaries throughout the empire each had their own reserves.
Border provisions were not borrowed from the capital,
and the capital did not collect from outside.
During the Chénghuà reign,

Yáng Chéng, the xúnyán yùshǐ (inspecting salt censor), first requested that the fines and confiscated silver from the various yányùn tíjǔsī (salt transportation and control offices) be sent to the capital treasury.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
Zēng Áng, a gěishìzhōng (remonstrance official), requested that all public funds and accumulated surplus taxes from the bùzhèngsī (provincial administration commissions)
be entirely sent to the Tàicāng (Grand Granary).
Shàngshū Zhōu Jīng strongly argued against this,
believing that the reason for insufficient funds
was due to textile production, rewards, rituals, and construction projects,
and that to insist on collecting all wealth from the empire
was not in the spirit of storing wealth among the people.
When Liú Jǐn rose to power,
he then ordered all provincial treasuries and granaries to send their entire contents to the capital.
During the Shìzōng reign,
Mǐn (Fujian) and Guǎng (Guangdong) remitted surplus funds.
The Hùbù (Ministry of Revenue) requested that other provincial xún'àn (inspecting censors) be ordered
to submit annual reports as per regulation.
Furthermore, because the Tàicāng was depleted,
eight hundred thousand liǎng of silver from the Nán Hùbù (Southern Ministry of Revenue) treasury were transported to replenish it.
The Hùbù then submitted a proposal on financial management,
and two hundred thousand liǎng of accumulated silver from the Lín and Dé granaries
were recorded and transferred to the Tàicāng.
In the early Lóngqìng reign,
four yùshǐ (censors) were dispatched to travel throughout the empire
to search for and collect treasury silver.
During the Shénzōng reign,
Yùshǐ Xiāo Chóngwàng requested an audit of the annual silver quotas of the fǔ and xiàn to be submitted to the ministry,
but it was not reported.
Qiānhù Hé Qíxián requested an imperial edict for an inner official (eunuch) to supervise it with him.
The Emperor ultimately granted his request,
whereby the external reserves gradually diminished.
By the Tiānqǐ reign,
following the strategy of Fàn Jìshì, the Cāojiāng Xúnfǔ (River-Patrolling Governor),
an imperial edict was issued to supervise annual remittances,
and nothing was left uncollected.
The Nánjīng Nèikù (Nanjing Imperial Treasury) had quite a store of gold, silver, and precious treasures.
Wèi Zhōngxián forged an imperial decree to take them,
stealing them all, leaving it empty.
With both internal and external treasuries depleted,
it consequently led to ruin.
Jiàokānjì (Collation Notes)
Zhì (Treatise) Fifty-Six, Shíhuò (Food and Money) Four: Yánfǎ (Salt Administration), Cháfǎ (Tea Administration)
The profits from boiling seawater
were officially controlled by the state throughout the dynasties.
When Tàizǔ first rose,
he immediately established the Yánfǎ (Salt Administration),
setting up bureaus and appointing officials,
allowing merchants to trade it.
One-twentieth was collected
to fund military provisions.
Later, the tax was doubled,
but following Hú Shēn's advice,
the original system was restored.
In the year bǐngwǔ (1366),
salt officials were first established in Liǎnghuái.
In the first year of Wú (1367), Liǎngzhè was established.
In the early Hóngwǔ reign,
officials were successively established in various salt-producing areas.
There were six Dū Zhuǎnyùn Yánshǐsī (Chief Salt Transportation Commissions):
namely, Liǎnghuái,
Liǎngzhè,
Chánglú,
Shāndōng,
Fújiàn,
and Hédōng.
There were seven Yánkè Tíjǔsī (Salt Tax Control Offices): namely, Guǎngdōng,
Hǎiběi,
Sìchuān,
and Yúnnán.
The Yúnnán Tíjǔsī (Yunnan Control Office) had four (sub-offices),
namely, Hēiyánjǐng,
Báiyánjǐng,
Ānníng Yánjǐng,
and Wǔjǐng.
There was also one Shǎnxī Língzhōu Yánkèsī (Shaanxi Lingzhou Salt Tax Office).
Liǎnghuái had three subordinate fēnsī (branch offices):
namely, Táizhōu,
Huái'ān,
and Tōngzhōu.
There were two pīyànsuǒ (verification offices):
namely, Yízhēn
and Huái'ān.
There were thirty salt fields,
each with one Yánkèsī (Salt Tax Office).
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
the annual quota for large salt certificates was over 352,000.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
it was changed to small salt certificates,
and the amount was doubled.
It was the same during the Wànlì reign.
The salt was distributed to Yìngtiān, Níngguó, Tàipíng, Yángzhōu, Féngyáng,
Lúzhōu, Ānqìng, Chízhōu, and Huái'ān prefectures (nine prefectures) directly under the capital,
Chú and Hé sub-prefectures (two sub-prefectures),
the two bùzhèngsī (provincial administration commissions) of Jiāngxī and Húguǎng,
and Hénán, Rǔníng, Nányáng prefectures (three prefectures) and Chénzhōu sub-prefecture in Hénán.
In the middle of the Zhèngtǒng reign,
Guìzhōu also consumed Huái salt.
In the eighteenth year of Chénghuà,
Héngzhōu and Yǒngzhōu in Húguǎng switched to Hǎiběi salt.
In the second year of Zhèngdé,
Gànzhōu, Nán'ān, and Jí'ān in Jiāngxī switched to Guǎngdōng salt.
It was transported to the borders of
Gānsù, Yánsuí, Níngxià, Xuānfǔ, Dàtóng, Liáodōng, Gùyuán, and various forts in Shānxī Shénchí.
It was supplied to the Guānglùsì, Shéngōngjiān, and Nèiguānjiān.
The annual surplus salt silver paid into the Tàicāng was 600,000 liǎng.
Liǎngzhè had four subordinate fēnsī (branch offices):
namely, Jiāxīng,
Sōngjiāng,
Níngshào, and Wēntái.
There were four pīyànsuǒ (verification offices):
namely, Hángzhōu,
Shàoxīng,
Jiāxīng,
and Wēnzhōu.
There were thirty-five salt fields,
each with one Yánkèsī (Salt Tax Office).
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
the annual quota for large salt certificates was over 220,400.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
it was changed to small salt certificates,
and the amount was doubled.
It was the same during the Wànlì reign.
The salt was distributed to Zhèjiāng,
Sōngjiāng, Sūzhōu, Chángzhōu, Zhènjiāng, Huīzhōu prefectures (five prefectures) and Guǎngdézhōu sub-prefecture directly under the capital,
and Guǎngxìnfǔ prefecture in Jiāngxī.
It was transported to the borders of
Gānsù, Yánsuí, Níngxià, Gùyuán, and various forts in Shānxī Shénchí.
The annual surplus salt silver paid into the Tàicāng was 140,000 liǎng.
In the early Míng dynasty,
the Běipíng and Héjiān Salt Administration Offices were established;
later, they were renamed Héjiān Chánglú.
Under its jurisdiction were two sub-offices:
one called Cāngzhōu,
and one called Qīngzhōu;
two verification offices:
one called Chánglú,
and one called Xiǎozhígū;
twenty-four salt fields,
each with a salt tax office.
During the Hóngwǔ era,
the annual production was over 63,100 large salt certificates.
During the Hóngzhì era,
this was changed to over 180,800 small salt certificates.
The Wànlì era was the same.
Salt was distributed in Běizhílì,
and the prefectures of Zhāngdé and Wèihuī in Hénán.
It was supplied to the borders of
Xuānfǔ, Dàtóng, and Jìzhōu.
It was also supplied to the imperial court for sacrifices to the suburban altars and the hundred deities, for meals in the imperial household, and for distribution to all officials and departments.
Annually, over 120,000 liǎng of surplus salt silver entered the Tàicāng granary.
Shāndōng had two sub-offices under its jurisdiction:
one called Jiāolái,
and one called Bīnlè;
one verification office:
called Luòkǒu;
nineteen salt fields,
each with a salt tax office.
During the Hóngwǔ era,
the annual production was over 143,300 large salt certificates.
During the Hóngzhì era,
this was changed to small salt certificates,
double the amount.
During the Wànlì era,
it was over 96,100 certificates.
Salt was distributed in Shāndōng,
the three zhōu of Xú, Pī, and Sù in Zhílì,
and Kāifēng Fǔ in Hénán.
Later, Kāifēng changed to consuming Hédōng salt.
It was supplied to the borders of
Liáodōng and the various forts in Shénchí, Shānxī.
Annually, 50,000 liǎng of surplus salt silver entered the Tàicāng granary.
Fújiàn had seven salt fields under its jurisdiction,
each with a salt tax office.
During the Hóngwǔ era,
the annual production was over 104,500 large salt certificates.
During the Hóngzhì era,
this increased by over 700 certificates.
During the Wànlì era,
it decreased by 1,000 certificates.
These certificates were called Yīshān [mountain-dependent]
and Fùhǎi [sea-adjacent].
Yīshān paid in commuted silver.
Fùhǎi traded in actual salt,
but during Emperor Shénzōng's reign, it also changed to commuted silver.
Salt was distributed within the province.
Annually, over 22,000 liǎng of silver entered the Tàicāng granary.
The Hédōng salt under its jurisdiction,
initially had an eastern field sub-office established in Ānyì.
During Emperor Chéngzǔ's reign,
a western field was added in Jiězhōu,
but soon after, it was merged back with the eastern one.
In the sixth year of Zhèngtǒng, the western field sub-office was re-established.
In the second year of Hóngzhì, a central field sub-office was added.
During the Hóngwǔ era,
the annual production was 304,000 small salt certificates.
During the Hóngzhì era,
this increased by 80,000 certificates.
In the mid-Wànlì era,
it increased by another 200,000 certificates.
Salt was distributed in the four prefectures of Xī'ān, Hànzhōng, Yán'ān, and Fèngxiáng in Shǎnxī;
the five prefectures of Guīdé, Huáiqìng, Hénán, Rǔníng, and Nányáng, and Rǔzhōu in Hénán;
the two prefectures of Píngyáng and Lù'ān,
and the three zhōu of Zé, Qìn, and Liáo in Shānxī.
Areas listed in both regions
could purchase salt from both.
In the mid-Lóngqìng era,
Yán'ān changed to consuming Língzhōu well salt.
In the mid-Chóngzhēn era,
the two prefectures of Fèngxiáng and Hànzhōng also changed to consuming Língzhōu salt.
Annually, over 4,000 liǎng of silver entered the Tàicāng granary,
which was allocated for the pay and provisions of the Xuānfǔ Garrison and the Dàtóng Prince's establishment,
and to offset the people's grain tax silver in Shānxī,
totaling over 190,000 liǎng.
In Língzhōu, Shǎnxī, there were large and small salt lakes,
and also salt wells in Zhāngxiàn and Xīhé.
During the Hóngwǔ era,
the annual salt production was:
over 131,500 jīn from Xīhé,
over 515,600 jīn from Zhāngxiàn,
and over 2,867,400 jīn from Língzhōu.
The Hóngzhì era was the same.
During the Wànlì era,
the three locations together produced over 12,537,600 jīn.
Salt was distributed in the two prefectures of Gǒngchāng and Líntáo, and Hézhōu in Shǎnxī.
Annually, over 36,000 liǎng of silver was sent to Níngxià, Yánsuí, and Gùyuán for military provisions.
Guǎngdōng had fourteen salt fields under its jurisdiction,
Hǎiběi had fifteen salt fields under its jurisdiction,
each with a salt tax office.
During the Hóngwǔ era,
the annual production of large salt certificates was:
over 46,800 certificates from Guǎngdōng,
and over 27,000 certificates from Hǎiběi.
During the Hóngzhì era,
Guǎngdōng remained as before,
Hǎiběi produced over 19,400 certificates.
During the Wànlì era,
Guǎngdōng produced over 30,200 small raw salt certificates,
and over 34,600 small refined salt certificates;
Hǎiběi produced over 12,400 small standard/wastage salt certificates.
Salt came in raw and refined forms,
with refined being more expensive and raw cheaper.
Guǎngdōng salt was distributed in the six prefectures of Guǎngzhōu, Zhàoqìng, Huìzhōu, Sháozhōu, Nánxióng, and Cháozhōu.
Hǎiběi salt was distributed in the four prefectures of Léizhōu, Gāozhōu, Liánzhōu, and Qióngzhōu in Guǎngdōng;
the two zhōu of Guìyáng and Chēn in Húguǎng;
the ten prefectures of Guìlín, Liǔzhōu, Wúzhōu, Xúnzhōu, Qìngyuǎn, Nánníng, Pínglè, Tàipíng, Sīmíng, and Zhèn'ān in Guǎngxī;
and the five zhōu of Tián, Lóng, Sìchéng, Fèngyì, and Lì.
Annually, over 11,000 liǎng of salt tax silver entered the Tàicāng granary.
Sìchuān's salt wells had seventeen salt tax offices under their jurisdiction.
During the Hóngwǔ era,
the annual salt production was over 11,270,000 jīn.
During the Hóngzhì era,
it produced over 21,760,000 jīn.
In the mid-Wànlì era,
it produced over 9,861,000 jīn.
Salt was distributed in the five prefectures of Chéngdū, Zīzhōu, Shùnqìng, Bǎoníng, and Kuízhōu in Sìchuān;
and the five zhōu/xiàn of Tóngchuān, Jiādìng, Guǎng'ān, Yǎzhōu, and Guǎngyuán.
Annually, over 71,000 liǎng of salt tax silver was sent to the Shǎnxī garrisons.
Yúnnán's Hēiyánjǐng [Black Salt Well] had three salt tax offices under its jurisdiction,
Báiyánjǐng [White Salt Well] and Ānníngyánjǐng [Ānníng Salt Well] each had one salt tax office,
and the Five Wells had seven salt tax offices.
During the Hóngwǔ era,
the annual production of large salt certificates was over 17,800.
During the Hóngzhì era,
the amounts varied among the different wells.
The Wànlì era was the same as Hóngwǔ.
Salt was distributed within the province.
Annually, over 35,000 liǎng of salt tax silver entered the Tàicāng granary.
During Emperor Chéngzǔ's reign,
a Jiāozhǐ Supervisory Office was once established;
later, Jiāozhǐ was lost,
and so it was abolished.
In the Liáodōng salt fields, no officials were appointed;
military personnel and civilians boiled salt,
and merchants were invited to exchange grain for it to supply the army.
A large certificate was 400 jīn,
a small certificate was 200 jīn.
The origin of salt varied.
Salt from Jiězhōu
was formed by wind and water.
Salt from Níngxià
was scraped from the ground.
Salt from Huái and Zhè
was boiled from seawater.
Salt from Chuān and Diān
was drawn from wells.
Salt from Mǐn and Yuè
was accumulated brine.
Salt from Huáinán
was boiled.
Salt from Huáiběi
was sun-dried.
Salt from Shāndōng
was both boiled and sun-dried.
This is a general overview.
Among the Míng salt laws,
none was better than the kāizhōng system.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ,
the Shānxī provincial administration reported:
"Grain storage for Dàtóng,
transported from Língxiàn to Tàihélǐng,
is a long and costly journey.
We request that merchants be ordered to deposit one dàn of rice in the Dàtóng granary,
or one dàn and three dòu of rice in the Tàiyuán granary,
and be given one small certificate for Huái salt.
After merchants sell the salt,
they immediately present the original certificate to the local authorities for verification.
This way, transportation costs are reduced, and border reserves are replenished."
The emperor agreed.
Inviting merchants to transport grain in exchange for salt
was called kāizhōng.
Thereafter, in the border regions of various provinces,
merchants were often invited to participate in the salt trade for military provisions.
The salt law and border defense planning
operated in conjunction.
In the fourth year, the regulations for salt certificates (zhōngyán lì) were established.
Merchants were required to transport rice to the granaries of Línháo, Kāifēng, Chénqiáo, Xiāngyáng, Ānlù, Jīngzhōu, Guīzhōu, Dàtóng, Tàiyuán, Mèngjīn, Běipíng, Hénán Fǔ, Chénzhōu, and Běitōngzhōu.
Based on the distance of the journey,
the quantity varied from five dàn to one dàn.
Due to subsequent increases and decreases,
the regulations were not uniform.
Generally, they depended on the urgency of the times,
the price of rice,
and whether it was profitable for the certificate holders (zhōngnà zhě).
If the journey was long and the terrain treacherous,
the quantity was reduced and the burden lightened.
Certificates (kānhé) and ledgers (dǐbù) were compiled and placed,
then issued to various Administration Commissions (Bùzhèng Sī) and Regional Military Commissions (Dūsī), and garrisons (wèisuǒ).
After a merchant had paid the grain,
the amount of grain paid and the corresponding quantity of salt to be drawn were recorded.
The merchant would then take this to the various Salt Distribution Commissions (Zhuǎnyùn Tíju Sī) to draw the salt according to the number.
The Salt Distribution Commissions also had ledgers for verification.
If the certificate matched,
the salt was issued as per the quantity.
There were designated places for selling salt,
which were engraved on copper plates.
Those caught selling private salt (sīyán) were punished with death,
and those who forged salt certificates (yǐn) were punished similarly.
If salt and its certificate were separated,
it was treated as private salt.
When Chéngzǔ ascended the throne,
considering the scarcity of grain in the garrisons (wèi) of Běijīng,
all salt certificate transactions (zhōngyán) throughout the empire were suspended,
and they were exclusively opened for the capital's garrisons.
Only the Jīnchǐ Garrison (Jīnchǐ Wèi) and Chǔxióng Prefecture (Chǔxióng Fǔ) in Yúnnán,
the Yánjǐng Garrison (Yánjǐng Wèi) in Sìchuān,
and the Gānzhōu Garrison (Gānzhōu Wèi) in Shǎnxī
continued the salt certificate system as before.
Within a few years,
the grain in the capital's garrisons became abundant,
but the large army campaigning in Ānnán incurred heavy expenses,
the army provisions in Gānsù were insufficient,
and the common people were exhausted by transportation.
By the time Ānnán was newly annexed,
provisions became even more difficult to sustain.
Thus, various locations summoned merchants to engage in salt certificate transactions,
and other border areas gradually followed suit.
When Rénzōng was enthroned,
as the paper currency system (chāofǎ) was not functioning well,
a method to collect it was discussed.
The Minister of Revenue (Hùbù Shàngshū), Xià Yuánjí, requested that households possessing paper currency be allowed to purchase salt certificates (zhōngyán).
Consequently, regulations for salt certificates were established for various Salt Commissions (yánsī).
A certificate (yǐn) in Cāngzhōu was three hundred guàn,
half that in Hédōng and Shāndōng,
and one hundred guàn in Fújiàn and Guǎngdōng.
In the first year of Xuāndé, the system of purchasing certificates with paper currency (zhōngchāo lì) was suspended.
In the third year,
Yuánjí, citing the lack of provisions for officials, soldiers, and artisans in Běijīng,
submitted a proposal for a preparedness plan,
stating:
"The old salt certificate regulations are too burdensome, and few merchants come. I request that they be revised."
It was then decided that each certificate would require from two dòu and five shēng to one dòu and five shēng, varying according to circumstances,
and merchants were summoned to deliver rice to Běijīng.
The Minister of Revenue, Guō Dūn, said:
"Although the salt certificate regulations have been reduced,
few merchants are coming.
I request that, based on a total of ten parts,
six parts be allocated to those who deliver rice to the capital's granaries,
and four parts to those who have already delivered rice to Liáodōng, Yǒngpíng, Shānhǎi, Gānsù, Dàtóng, Xuānfǔ, and Wànquán.
All other salt certificate transactions (zhōngnà) are to be suspended."
He further said:
"In the Hóngwǔ era,
many merchants who held salt certificates for a long time died,
and those who claimed on their behalf often made fraudulent claims.
I request that for each certificate (yǐn), ten ingots of paper currency (chāo dìng) be issued."
The emperor agreed to all his requests,
and ordered that the paper currency be doubled.
As Gānsù, Níngxià, Dàtóng, Xuānfǔ, Dúshí, and Yǒngpíng were remote and dangerous,
few merchants were willing to go there for salt certificates.
It was permitted for resident officials and military households with grain to deliver rice and beans for salt certificates.
In the third year of Zhèngtǒng,
Shǐ Zhāo, the Grand General (zǒngbīng guān) of Níngxià, noting the shortage of horses in the border army
and that many officials, soldiers, and civilians in Yánqìng and Píngliáng raised horses,
requested permission to use horses for salt certificates.
One superior horse was equivalent to one hundred salt certificates (yǐn),
and an inferior horse to eighty certificates.
Later, in the various border garrisons, this was increased by twenty certificates.
Subsequently, for those who participated in horse-for-salt exchanges (zhōngnà) in Hézhōu,
a superior horse was twenty-five certificates,
and an inferior horse was five certificates less;
for those in Sōngpān,
a superior horse was thirty-five certificates,
and an inferior horse was five certificates less.
After a long time,
it reverted to the original system.
At the beginning of the horse-for-salt exchange system (zhōngmǎ zhī shǐ),
salt was issued after inspecting the horses.
Later, silver was paid to officials to purchase horses,
the silver went to the Administration Commissions (Bùzhèng Sī),
and was subsequently spent on imperial stipends (zōnglù), garrison provisions (túnliáng), border repairs (xiūbiān), and relief efforts (zhènjì),
with the silver being exhausted but no horses arriving,
and border provisions also became scarce from then on.
Consequently, merchants were summoned to exchange for Huái, Zhè, and Chánglú salt by delivering grain.
Those who exchanged for salt certificates in Gānsù were ordered to
receive seventeen parts Huái salt
and thirteen parts Zhè salt.
For Huái salt, only rice and wheat were accepted,
while for Zhè salt, peas and qīkē were also accepted.
Because Huái salt was more expensive,
many merchants favored it,
thus the arrangement of exchanging for both Huái and Zhè salt.
In the early Míng dynasty, the old systems of the Sòng and Yuán dynasties were maintained,
which were very generous in their compassion for salt households (hù).
They were given grasslands for gathering firewood,
and those suitable for cultivation were allowed to be reclaimed,
while also being exempt from miscellaneous corvée (zá yì).
They were also given starting capital in rice,
one dàn per certificate.
Granaries were established at the salt fields.
Annually, provisions from nearby prefectural and county granaries, and rice from garrison households (jūnyú mǐ) were allocated to be issued,
along with cash and paper currency,
based on the price of rice.
Soon, the amount of paper currency was fixed:
two guàn and five hundred wén for Huái and Zhè certificates,
and two guàn for Héjiān, Guǎngdōng, Hǎiběi, Shāndōng, Fújiàn, and Sìchuān certificates.
Salt households who committed miscellaneous crimes punishable by death or above were only punished with flogging,
by calculating the days of salt boiling as redemption.
Later, general collectors (zǒngcuī) were appointed,
who often exploited the salt households.
By the Zhèngtǒng era,
salt households were impoverished,
and many absconded,
with Sōngjiāng owing over six hundred thousand in taxes.
The people appealed to the court,
and Zhōu Chén, the Grand Coordinator (xúnfǔ) of Zhílì, was ordered to concurrently manage salt taxes.
Chén proposed four measures: casting iron cauldrons, showing compassion to brine workers (lǔdīng), selecting general collectors, and strictly prohibiting private trading,
and also requested that, in addition to the annual regular tax,
the arrears be collected.
The emperor granted his request.
It was ordered that the arrears be divided into six parts,
to be collected over six years.
At this time,
there were merchants who had been waiting to draw salt since the Yǒnglè era,
whose grandsons had taken over but still had not received it.
It was then decided to follow the precedent of the Hóngwǔ era,
and add paper currency ingots as compensation,
allowing those who wished to continue waiting to do so.
Moreover, because merchants had been waiting for a long time,
even with the reduction in the salt certificate requirements (kāizhōng), few were making new payments.
It was proposed that other Salt Commissions (yánsī) follow the old system,
while for Huái, Zhè, and Chánglú, using ten parts as a basis,
eight parts would be given to waiting merchants,
called 'regular shares' (chánggǔ),
and two parts would be stored by the government,
called 'reserve shares' (cúnjī).
Only when there was a border emergency
would merchants be summoned to purchase reserve shares.
The names 'regular shares' and 'reserve shares' originated from this.
Those who purchased regular shares paid a lower price,
while those who purchased reserve shares paid a higher price.
However, people found waiting very burdensome,
and eagerly sought reserve shares,
while regular shares became stagnant.
During the reign of Jǐngdì,
there were many incidents on the borders,
and reserve shares increased to six parts.
For border grain payments through salt certificates (zhōngnà biānliáng),
fodder and autumn green fodder were also accepted,
with three parts autumn green fodder equivalent to two parts fodder.
Guǎngdōng salt,
by regulation, was not to leave the province.
Merchants often bribed customs officials
to illegally sell it in Guǎngxī.
The Grand Coordinator, Yè Shèng, considered that allowing it would invalidate the law,
while prohibiting it would harm merchants.
He requested that they be allowed to pay rice to provision the border,
and then permitted it to leave the province,
benefiting both public and private interests.
In the early Chénghuà era,
there were successive years of disaster,
and the capital's reserves were insufficient.
Merchants were summoned to purchase salt certificates at the waterside granaries of Huái, Xú, and Dézhōu.
According to old regulations regarding salt,
the Ministry of Revenue would issue a public notice inviting merchants,
and there were no direct petitions.
However, wealthy individuals like Lǚ Míng, relying on their powerful connections, petitioned to secure the accumulated salt from Liǎnghuái.
An imperial decree approved this.
The Minister of Revenue, Mǎ Áng, was unable to uphold rectitude.
The decline of the salt administration began from this point.
Powerful magnates frequently got involved,
and merchants, having lost their profits,
along with military and civilian populations in Jiāngnán and the north, began constructing large ocean-going ships
equipped with weapons to smuggle salt.
Severe laws were then enacted,
stipulating that private traffickers and those who harbored them would all be sentenced to death,
their families exiled to frontier garrisons,
and those who secretly carried salt across borders conscripted into the army.
However, this failed to stop them.
In the nineteenth year, the quantity of accumulated salt was considerably reduced,
with regular shares at seventy percent
and accumulated shares at thirty percent.
Yet, merchants preferred to have visible salt,
and those who reported involvement in accumulated salt flocked to it,
so it was again increased to sixty percent.
Still, the salt from Huái and Zhè was insufficient,
so Lónglú and Shāndōng salt was allocated to supply it.
One person taking on allocations from several places,
and the long distances preventing personal attendance,
meant that frontier merchants frequently traded their salt permits with wealthy people in nearby areas.
From then on, there was a distinction between frontier merchants and interior merchants.
The salt of interior merchants could not be acquired quickly,
and the permits of frontier merchants were not sold cheaply,
leading to delays in reporting,
and the stagnation of accumulated salt became equivalent to that of regular shares.
Towards the end of Emperor Xiànzōng's reign,
eunuchs usurped power,
petitioning for unlimited amounts of Huái and Zhè salt.
The accumulated arrears in Liǎnghuái reached over five million permits,
and merchant permits became stagnant.
By the time of Emperor Xiàozōng,
the proposal to purchase surplus salt emerged.
Surplus salt referred to
the salt remaining to the salt-producing households after their regular tax contributions.
In the early Hóngwǔ era, a system was established
where merchants had designated salt fields for their allocations
and were not permitted to purchase supplementary salt beyond these fields;
diligent salt-producing households would send their surplus salt to the field office,
with two hundred *jin* constituting one permit,
for which one *shi* of rice would be given.
This salt was offered to merchants through the *kāizhōng* system,
without regard to their financial standing.
After the Chénghuà era,
merchants were ordered to purchase it,
and were encouraged to lend rice and wheat to support impoverished salt-producing households.
By this time, to reform the salt administration of Liǎnghuái,
Vice Minister Lǐ Sì requested that merchants be allowed to purchase surplus salt to supplement official permits,
and be exempted from the encouragement to lend,
and also that *kāizhōng* for all frontiers be suspended.
Once the tax arrears were cleared,
the government would sell the salt,
with one-third of the price
allocated to frontier reserves,
and one-third retained to compensate merchants for unpaid salt prices.
〔一０〕From this, surplus salt was used to supplement regular taxes,
and the salt administration underwent a minor change.
In the early Míng Dynasty,
merchants engaged in *kāizhōng* at various frontiers
recruited people to cultivate land
and built ramparts and forts for their self-protection,
so grains and beans in the frontier regions were never excessively expensive.
During the Chénghuà era,
payments in silver first appeared,
but this was never formally established as a regulation.
In the fifth year of Hóngzhì,
merchants were burdened by the need to guard and distribute salt.
Minister of Revenue Yè Qí requested that merchants be summoned to pay silver to the Transport Commission,
which would then be forwarded to the Grand Granary
and distributed to the various frontiers.
Each permit required three to four *qián* of silver, varying according to circumstances.
This was double the price of rice in the early days of the dynasty,
but merchants were spared the hardship of guarding and distributing salt.
For a time, the silver in the Grand Granary accumulated to over one million.
However, the *kāizhōng* system at the frontiers was abolished,
merchant garrisons were dismantled,
grains and beans became exorbitantly expensive,
and frontier reserves dwindled daily.
At the beginning of Emperor Wǔzōng's reign,
as the salt administration deteriorated day by day,
Ministers Wáng Qióng, Zhāng Xiàn, and others were ordered to clarify it along separate routes.
Meanwhile, Marquis of Qìngyún, Zhōu Shòu, and
Marquis of Shòuníng, Zhāng Hèlíng, each ordered their household members to petition for the purchase of Lónglú and Liǎnghuái salt permits.
An imperial decree granted permission.
The weaving eunuch Cuī Gǎo also petitioned for twelve thousand Lónglú salt permits.
The Ministry of Revenue granted half of these.
〔一二〕The emperor wished to grant them all.
Grand Secretary Liú Jiàn and others strongly argued against it,
with Lǐ Dōngyáng's words being particularly sharp.
The emperor was displeased.
Jiàn and others again submitted a memorial arguing their case,
and only then was the ministry's recommendation followed.
With powerful officials securing many *kāizhōng* permits,
and also being allowed to purchase surplus salt,
some permits were used for over ten years.
It was not until the second year of Zhèngdé that the order to clip the corners of old permits was reiterated,
a deadline was set for their recall,
and each permit required an increased payment for paper and a contribution of rice and wheat for relief.
The price of permits became heavy, but the obstruction of taxes remained the same.
Before this, in the early Chénghuà era,
Censor-in-Chief Hán Yōng established salt inspection stations in Zhàoqìng, Wúzhōu, Qīngyuǎn, and Nánxióng,
where one official salt permit incurred a tax of five *fēn* of silver,
and four additional surplus salt permits were allowed,
each taxed at one *qián* of silver.
Censor-in-Chief Zòu Hóng permitted an increase to six additional surplus salt permits,
taxed at six *qián* of silver.
By this time, it was increased to nine *qián*,
and the official permit was no longer taxed.
With the accumulation of stagnant permits,
private salt circulated freely.
Then, at the request of Ministry of Revenue Supervisor Dīng Zhìxiáng,
Zòu Hóng's old method was restored.
However, merchants from other places who smuggled surplus salt,
after being stopped and paying the price,
were only punished if the amount reached three hundred *jin*.
For Huái, Zhè, and Lónglú salt permits,
four-tenths were regular shares,
allocated to supply the main troops and for public works and relief at various frontiers;
six-tenths were accumulated shares,
not to be opened presumptuously
unless there was a major national event
or a frontier alarm.
When opened, it required a memorial from a frontier official,
reviewed and approved by the ministry,
and there was no instance of merchants arbitrarily petitioning or exclusively petitioning for Huái salt.
During the Hóngzhì era,
there was a large amount of accumulated salt.
During the Zhèngdé era,
powerful favorites then petitioned to open "residual salt,"
converting both accumulated and regular shares into regular taxes,
and all of it was to be commuted to silver.
Frontier officials had no provisions in times of urgency,
while influential figures monopolized the *kāizhōng* and sold their quotas,
increasing prices several-fold.
Merchants who paid eight *qián* of silver per permit
gained no profit
and many were unwilling to participate,
so tax revenue dwindled daily.
Cunning individuals engaged in smuggling and illicit schemes,
and a hundred abuses emerged.
Salt officials, under the influence of powerful eunuchs,
again listed various categories such as "scrap salt" and "station salt" to exploit the situation.
Upon Emperor Shìzōng's ascension, an edict
first ordered their abolition.
Not long after,
merchants like Lù Jùn, through connections with close favorites,
under the pretext of increasing prices,
petitioned to purchase "residual" and other salts.
Minister of Revenue Qín Jīn refused to approve.
The emperor specifically ordered that three hundred thousand permits of Huái salt be granted for Xuānfǔ through *kāizhōng*.
Qín Jīn stated:
"Treacherous individuals monopolize Huái salt *kāizhōng*,
selling their quotas and exploiting for profit,
causing Shāndōng and Lónglú salts to have no other distribution,
and accumulating them uselessly.
This severely depletes national expenditure
and jeopardizes frontier reserves."
Censor Gāo Shìkuí also argued against it.
An imperial decree reduced the Huái permits by one hundred thousand,
distributing Zhè and Lónglú salt instead.
Qín Jīn again stated:
"Xuān and Dà are both important garrisons,
and it is inappropriate to allow treacherous merchants to choose what is convenient for themselves,
but only to assign *kāizhōng* to Xuānfǔ."
The emperor agreed.
Later, however, Jùn and others requested that sixteen individuals be assigned *kāizhōng* for Xuānfǔ
and eleven for Dàtóng,
and their request was ultimately granted.
In the fifth year of Jiājìng, following the memorial of Investigating Censor Guǎn Lǜ,
the system of maintaining 4:6 shares of regular salt and accumulated salt was restored.
However, at that time,
excess salt (yúyán) was flourishing,
while regular salt (zhèngyán) for border provisions had been delayed for a long time,
so few merchants were willing to undertake it.
For excess salt, one only needed to obtain the official permit (kānhé),
and could immediately sell it,
so many merchants were willing to undertake it.
Since the Hóngzhì reign, excess salt had been used to supplement regular taxes.
Initially, it was to pay off arrears;
later, merchants were ordered to pay a price and transport it to the Ministry for border relief.
By the Jiājìng reign,
as there were military campaigns in Yánsuí
and a shortage of provisions in Liáozuǒ,
all 79,000-plus permits for excess salt from Liǎnghuái were issued for *kāizhōng* (border exchange) in the two frontier regions.
From then on, excess salt became widespread.
Initially, there was no fixed quota,
but soon after,
Liǎnghuái increased permits by over 1.4 million,
and each permit increased excess salt by 265 *jīn*.
The price per permit was
one *liǎng* nine *qián* of silver for Huáinán,
and one *liǎng* five *qián* for Huáiběi.
Furthermore, various fees for "disposal" and "penalties" were set up,
to exact harsh levies on merchant wealth.
Consequently, regular salt was not yet distributed,
but excess salt was estimated first,
causing hardship for both merchants and salt producers.
Cunning and devious individuals, under the pretext of officials buying excess salt,
illegally trafficked and privately produced salt.
Laws and prohibitions became ineffective,
and the salt administration (yánfǎ) greatly deteriorated.
In the thirteenth year,
Investigating Censor Guǎn Huáilǐ stated:
"The deterioration of the salt administration
has six major弊 (ills).
Border exchange (kāizhōng) is not timely,
and rice prices are soaring,
making it difficult to procure grain.
Powerful and influential families monopolize profit rights,
making it difficult to report salt transactions.
Officials levy fines,
and clerks extort,
making it difficult to pay taxes.
Distribution at the salt yards is delayed,
often for several years,
making it difficult to await distribution.
The fixed price is too high,
and interest cannot cover capital,
making it difficult to profit.
Private salt is everywhere,
and official salt is not selling,
making it difficult to trade.
With these six difficulties,
the regular tax (zhèngkè) is blocked.
Therefore, the treasury officials established excess salt to supplement it.
The profits from excess salt are high,
so merchants are certainly happy to participate.
However, it is not used for frontier exchange but for remittance to the Ministry,
so even if annual revenue reaches millions,
it does not benefit military provisions.
I have observed that during the time of our ancestors,
merchants paid very little for salt permits,
while salt producers received substantial capital for boiling salt.
Now, salt prices are ten times what they were before,
but the capital for production is not even one-tenth of what it was.
How can we prohibit private salt and prevent its circulation?
Therefore, to improve the salt administration,
we must first deal with excess salt.
To deal with excess salt,
we must significantly reduce the regular price.
Generally, if regular salt is cheap,
private trafficking will naturally cease.
Currently, it is appropriate to set the price:
five *qián* of silver per permit for regular salt,
and two *qián* five *fēn* for excess salt.
There is no need to remit it to Tàicāng,
but all should be cleared through *kāizhōng* and issued for border provisions.
The goal should be to collect all excess salt.
With the light price of regular salt,
merchants benefit;
with all excess salt collected,
salt producers also benefit.
There has never been a case where both merchants and salt producers benefited,
and the national revenue was not replenished."
The matter was referred to the relevant authorities,
and the Ministry of Revenue responded,
believing that the silver from excess salt should still be remitted to the Ministry as before,
otherwise the border provisions would be further depleted.
By the twentieth year,
the Emperor, believing that the disruption of the salt administration was due to excess salt,
issued an edict to abolish it.
Huái, Zhè, and Chánglú all reverted to the old system.
Those who smuggled salt were to have it confiscated,
and items to be sold were to be valued at current market prices.
Censor Wú Qióng also requested that all merchants who exchanged salt at the borders should pay in kind.
However, no sooner had the order been issued
than Minister of Personnel Xǔ Zàn immediately requested
to reopen excess salt to supply border needs.
The Ministry of Revenue responded in agreement,
and excess salt resumed circulation.
Previously,
in the sixteenth year, an order was issued for remote areas in Liǎngzhè
where official merchants did not operate:
mountain merchants would pay eight *fēn* of silver per hundred *jīn*
and be issued tickets to sell salt.
Later, this often infringed upon regular permits,
leading to a shortage in official merchant taxes,
and 2 million permits became stagnant,
requiring five or six years to be drawn.
Consequently, methods like pre-collection (yùzhēng), collateral (zhí dǐ), and seasonal drawing (jì chè) were implemented.
Pre-collection meant
paying taxes in advance,
without permission for private retention or withdrawal.
Collateral meant
pledging current salt transportation routes,
and holding one permit to offset another.
Seasonal drawing
was based on the order of tax payment,
with spring not delayed beyond summer,
and summer not exceeding spring.
However, ticket merchants could draw and sell upon paying taxes,
so the various pre-collection methods only burdened permit merchants.
Regarding the salt pond in Língzhōu,
ever since the proposal of Shǐ Zhāo to exchange salt for horses was implemented,
border provisions suffered shortages,
and the price of rice in Gānsù reached five *liǎng* of silver per *dàn*.
The Ministry of Revenue therefore memorialized to halt the horse exchange,
and summoned merchants to pay rice for salt.
In the twenty-seventh year, those involved in *kāizhōng* were ordered to pay only grain and fodder in kind.
In the thirty-second year, Hédōng was given a quota of 620,000 permits,
〔一三〕combining regular and excess salt into one,
and abolishing the name "excess salt."
At that time, Metropolitan Censor Wáng Shēn and Censor Huáng Guóyòng deliberated: for the excess salt of the salt producers in Liǎnghuái,
the officials would provide two *qián* of silver per permit
as production capital,
increasing the collection by 350,000 permits,
named "production capital salt" (gōngběnyán).
Merchants were ordered to exchange two permits of regular quota salt
and simultaneously exchange one permit of production capital salt,
which would cover the annual military expenditure of over 176,000 *liǎng*.
Their request was granted.
Initially,
the annual tax quota for Huái salt was 705,000 permits.
〔一四〕Those exchanged at the border were considered regular salt,
and later, excess salt was added, for which silver was paid and remitted to the Ministry.
By this time, the total quota, including the previous one, reached 1.05 million permits,
an increase of one-third of the original quota.
After several years of implementation, accumulated salt could not be sold,
and the salt administration became stagnant and ineffective.
Those who spoke on affairs repeatedly stated that production capital salt was a redundant appendage to the salt system.
The Ministry of Revenue, however, because national finances were currently constrained
and there was no other source for annual expenditures,
did not change it.
Jiāngxī province previously circulated 390,000 permits of Huái salt.
Later, Nán'ān, Gànzhōu, and Jí'ān changed to circulating Guǎng salt,
with only Nánchāng prefecture and other prefectures circulating 270,000 permits of Huái salt.
Soon after, private trafficking flourished,
and Yuánzhōu, Línjiāng, and Ruìzhōu privately consumed Guǎng salt,
while Fúzhōu and Jiànchāng privately consumed Fú salt.
Consequently, Huái salt circulated only 160,000 permits.
Within a few years,
national finances were greatly depleted.
Circuit Inspector Mǎ Sēn memorialized its harm,
requesting the construction of a bridge and establishment of a pass in Xiájiāng county
to control the vital thoroughfare between Mǐn and Guǎng,
to fully restore the Huái salt quota,
slightly increasing it to 470,000 permits.
Not long after, the bridge was destroyed,
and the increased quota of 200,000 permits was again abolished.
In the thirty-ninth year,
the emperor wished to reform the salt laws,
so he ordered Yān Màoqīng, Vice Censor-in-Chief, to take overall charge of the salt laws of Huái, Zhèjiāng, Shāndōng, and Chánglú.
Màoqīng
was a follower of Yán Sōng,
and received bribes every day.
The prescribed salt tax for the two Huái regions was over 610,000 liǎng of silver.
After the establishment of the gongběn salt system,
it increased by 900,000 liǎng.
Màoqīng further increased it,
so it reached one million liǎng.
It was to be remitted twice a year.
He also scoured the leftover salt from the four departments,
obtaining nearly two million liǎng of silver in total.
At the time, this was hailed as a great achievement.
He then established a method of strict deadlines,
where each salt patrolman
had a fixed quota of illegal salt to seize each quarter;
if he did not meet the quota,
his wages were cut.
Some patrolmen went a whole year without receiving a single coin,
so they jointly engaged in smuggling
to make huge profits.
They even robbed merchant ships
and falsely accused them of salt theft, then arrested them,
spreading poison throughout the coastal areas.
When Sōng lost power,
the Imperial Censor for Salt, Xú Kuàng, said:
"The salt laws of the two Huái regions,
referred to as chánggǔ,
cúnjī,
and shuǐxiāng,
total over 700,000 yín.
An yín is 200 jīn,
and an eight-fēn silver tax is paid.
After the Yǒnglè era,
an yín required two dòu five shēng of grain,
which was collected at the distribution centers,
and sold in various places,
with merchants profiting by five-tenths.
In recent years,
in addition to the regular salt,
there was surplus salt;
in addition to surplus salt,
there was also gongběn;
if gongběn was insufficient,
there were additional orders;
if additional orders were insufficient,
more yín were added.
Màoqīng pursued immediate profit
without considering the consequences,
which is the worst kind of mismanagement and political chaos.
Currently, disasters and famines are repeatedly reported,
and salt pans are submerged.
If we insist on reaching a million liǎng,
it will inevitably lead to people fleeing.
The string is pulled too tight and is about to break;
it cannot be made any more difficult than this."
Thereupon, all of Màoqīng's additions were abolished.
In the forty-fourth year,
Imperial Censor for Salt Zhū Bǐngrú memorialized to abolish the gongběn salt of the two Huái regions.
Since Yè Qí reformed the law,
border provisions often ran short.
After the eighth year of Jiājìng,
the kāizhōng system was somewhat restored,
with border merchants purchasing yín
and internal merchants waiting for distribution.
In the later years,
when gongběn salt became prevalent,
internal merchants were unable to draw salt for several years,
and thus were unwilling to buy yín.
Border merchants were also in distress,
so they sought to request the drawing of river salt.
River salt
was not stored in granaries,
but drawn directly from the river,
making it easier to distribute and yielding quicker profits.
When river salt became prevalent,
the stored cúnjī salt was held for longer,
and internal merchants also suffered,
making the price of yín even cheaper.
Consequently, unscrupulous individuals specialized in buying up border yín,
known as túnhù,
requesting river salt and
profiting handsomely.
At this time, it was again debated to attach surplus salt to regular salt
to cover the gongběn amount.
The túnhù were thus able to buy surplus salt cheaply and sell it expensively,
further distressing both border and internal merchants.
In the second year of Lóngqìng,
Páng Shàngpéng, Censor-in-Chief for Salt Administration, memorialized, saying:
"Border merchants reporting for exchange [of salt for provisions]
and internal merchants waiting for distribution
are inherently interdependent.
However, internal merchants sit idly while border merchants transport goods over long distances,
with uneven distribution of labor and ease,
which is why drawing river salt was meant to benefit border merchants.
However, once river salt became prevalent,
Huái salt was inevitably stagnant,
and internal merchants gained no profit,
meaning border merchants' yín would not sell.
It is now appropriate to halt the drawing of river salt,
but to separately price border merchants' yín.
From the self-issued yín and the beginning of the paper yín to the arrival of the yín at the department for verification,
it should be divided into three grades,
with a fixed amount of silver.
Once border merchants' warehouse notes have arrived,
internal merchants should not be allowed to delay.
Because if river salt is halted, Huái salt will circulate quickly,
and if the yín price is fixed, kāizhōng will naturally increase,
and both border and internal merchants will get what they desire."
The emperor agreed.
In the fourth year,
Imperial Censor Lǐ Xuéshī proposed to abolish the official purchase of surplus salt.
It was approved.
At this time, Gǔtián in Guǎngxī was pacified,
and Governor Yīn Zhèngmào requested the government to provide capital to buy Guǎngdōng salt,
which was then transported to Guìlín for sale.
Over 70,000 bags could yield a profit of more than 22,000 liǎng.
This was approved.
From the beginning of Jiājìng,
the system of four-tenths chánggǔ and six-tenths cúnjī was restored.
Later, due to various issues on the borders,
chánggǔ and cúnjī were both opened,
with the Huái quota of annual tax being over 705,000 yín,
and an additional 200,000 new yín per year for various borders.
During the Wànlì era,
due to major construction projects, over 600,000 yín of long-standing confiscated and defunct yín were sought out,
all outside the regular quota,
with no regular salt,
only allowing merchants to buy surplus salt as a supplement.
When the surplus salt was exhausted,
only heavy taxes based on yín were levied,
with added jiānfēi levies.
At that time, the price of Huái yín increased from over 1.2 million liǎng of silver to 1.45 million liǎng,
with new yín increasing daily,
and regular yín becoming increasingly stagnant.
Yǐn Yīng, a commander of a thousand households, requested to sell confiscated official salt by distribution,
which could yield 60,000 liǎng of silver.
Grand Secretaries Zhāng Wèi and others debated against this.
In the twenty-sixth year,
based on the memorial of Tián Yìngbì, Registrar of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
an imperial order
was issued appointing the eunuch Lǔ Bǎo to sell the confiscated official surplus salt of the two Huái regions.
Bāo Jiànjié, a Supervising Secretary, strongly presented the advantages and disadvantages.
It was not heeded.
Once Bǎo took office,
he then proposed to open the cúnjī salt.
Yáng Jùnmín, Minister of Revenue, said:
"The imperial decree clearly specifies confiscated official salt,
but cúnjī is not confiscated official salt.
Additional increases outside the quota
will certainly harm the regular tax.
Bǎo's proposal should not be followed."
Imperial Censor Mǎ Cóngchěng also debated against it.
Neither was heeded.
Bǎo then opened 80,000 yín of cúnjī,
with each yín weighing 570 jīn,
drawing it out of sequence and ahead of others,
stifling the regular salt from circulating.
Merchants and common people were greatly disturbed,
and unscrupulous individuals surged forth.
Dǒng Lián, Wú Yìngqí, and others argued about salt profits.
All tax supervisors in Shānxī, Fújiàn, and other places were already collecting salt taxes.
Gāo Shíxià, a commander of a hundred households, memorialized that the surplus salt in Zhèjiāng and Fújiàn could generate 300,000 liǎng in revenue annually,
but Governor Jīn Xuézéng's investigation memorialized that this was all false.
The memorial was submitted but not considered.
Consequently, Fújiàn remitted over 13,000 liǎng of silver,
and Zhèjiāng remitted over 37,000 liǎng of silver,
under the pretext of harsh levies,
causing merchants to suffer and yín to become stagnant.
Zhào Shìqīng, Minister of Revenue, pointed out that the harm was caused by Bǎo,
and then said:
"If one fēn more is collected outside the quota,
then one fēn less will be collected for the regular tax,
and the national treasury will become even more depleted.
I request that all unnamed floating levies be abolished."
There was no response.
From the summer of the thirty-fourth year to the spring of the following year,
the regular quota was in arrears by over one million liǎng.
Bǎo also became fearful
and requested the abolition of cúnjī yín salt.
Bǎo soon died.
An imperial decree was issued to abolish it,
but the weight of the yín could not be reduced.
Empress Dowager Lǐ hōng.
The emperor, following her dying instructions, abolished the "floating taxes" (fúkè) of various transport offices.
Merchants' difficulties eased slightly,
but old permits remained stagnant.
The Ministry of Revenue submitted ten proposals for salt administration.
These involved currently circulating permits,
and attaching old, accumulated permits to be sold off,
to clear the backlog.
Circuit Censor for Salt (Xúnyán Yùshǐ) Lóng Yùqí established a framework for salt administration,
where old permits were attached to circulating permits for use.
Huáinán was divided into ten frameworks (gāng),
and Huáiběi into fourteen frameworks.
It was estimated that within ten-plus years,
all old permits would be utilized.
This was adopted.
During the Tiānqǐ reign,
those focused on profit wantonly engaged in extortion and collection,
aiming to increase permits and seize control.
Wèi Zhōngxián's partisans, Guō Xìngzhì, Cuī Chéngxiù, and others,
skillfully devised pretexts to seize funds.
The revenue was immeasurable.
Commentators compared it to damming a river to fish.
In the Chóngzhēn period,
Grand Secretary (Gěishìzhōng) Huáng Chénghào presented a memorial on salt administration,
intending to make significant reforms.
At that time, military expenses were severely deficient,
so it could not be implemented.
Initially,
princes' households received salt from nearby sources.
Official and common households paid silver notes (chāo) according to the number of mouths for their salt,
and then collected it themselves.
However, officials and clerks often fraudulently inflated their household sizes,
with some officials drawing over two thousand catties,
and some clerks over five hundred catties.
Therefore, clerks were limited to no more than ten mouths,
and civil and military officials to no more than thirty mouths.
A large household paid twelve guàn (strings of cash) in silver notes and received twelve catties of salt;
a small household paid half.
In the third year of Jǐngtài, salt was first used to pay officials' salaries and rations,
with one hundred forty catties of salt equivalent to one shí (dan) of rice.
Beijing officials annually sent clerks to the salt fields,
where they wantonly engaged in illicit gains.
Jǐnyī Guards' clerks became even more oppressive,
often forming alliances with large ships to smuggle,
and local authorities could not investigate them.
The Circuit Censor for Salt then determined the amount of salt for various offices,
collected and distributed it to the clerks,
and prohibited them from going to the salt fields.
As the payment of silver notes and the cost of transport
had no source of funds,
many clerks absconded.
During the Jiājìng reign,
Secretary (Lángzhōng) Lù Guāngzǔ of the Ministry of Personnel spoke to Minister (Shàngshū) Yán Nà,
memorializing to abolish this practice.
Thereafter, various offices ceased to receive salt,
except for the Ministry of Revenue and the thirteen Circuits' censors, who continued to receive it annually as before.
For military and common households who paid silver notes according to the number of mouths,
Zhèjiāng paid three shēng of rice monthly
to buy one catty of salt.
Merchants would bring salt to officials,
who would collect and distribute it.
The urgency of this collection was greater than that of taxes.
During the Zhèngtǒng reign,
following the suggestion of Grand Secretary (Gěishìzhōng) Bào Huī,
the people were allowed to buy salt directly from merchants,
and the order to pay rice was abolished.
Furthermore, selling less than ten catties was not to be considered private salt.
However, the salt notes (yánchāo) were not abolished.
Later, when the Single-Whip Reform (Tiáobiānfǎ) was implemented,
it was incorporated into the regular tax.
Regarding officials supervising salt,
during the Hóngwǔ and Yǒnglè reigns,
censors were occasionally appointed to inspect salt taxes.
In the first year of Zhèngtǒng, Vice Minister (Shìláng) Hé Wényuān and Wáng Zuǒ,
and Vice Censor-in-Chief (Fù Dū Yùshǐ) Zhū Yǔyán were first appointed to supervise the salt taxes of Liǎnghuái, Chánglú, and Liǎngzhè.
Eunuchs and censors were also dispatched with them.
Soon after,
as the salt administration had been rectified,
an imperial edict recalled them.
Thereafter, censors were appointed to oversee salt,
following the example of circuit inspectors (xún'àn lì),
with annual rotation as a regular practice.
In the eleventh year, the various salt fields of Shāndōng were placed under the jurisdiction of the Chánglú Circuit Censor for Salt.
In the fourteenth year, Vice Censor-in-Chief Gěng Jiǔchóu was ordered to reform the salt administration of Liǎnghuái.
During the Chénghuà reign,
eunuch Wáng Yǔnzhōng and Assistant Censor-in-Chief (Qiān Dū Yùshǐ) Gāo Míng were specially dispatched to rectify the salt administration of Liǎnghuái.
Míng requested the addition of one Vice Commissioner (Fùshǐ) and two judicial officers (pànguān).
At the beginning of the Xiàozōng reign,
the salt administration was in disarray.
Minister (Shàngshū) Lǐ Mǐn of the Ministry of Revenue requested that upright officials be chosen to rectify it.
Thus, Vice Minister (Shìláng) Lǐ Sì of the Ministry of Revenue was assigned to Liǎnghuái,
and Vice Minister (Shìláng) Péng Sháo of the Ministry of Justice to Liǎngzhè,
both concurrently serving as Censor-in-Chief (Dū Yùshǐ),
and were granted imperial edicts for their dispatch.
In the fourteenth year of Hóngzhì,
Assistant Censor-in-Chief Wáng Jǐng supervised the salt administration of Liǎnghuái.
In the second year of Zhèngdé,
Assistant Censor-in-Chief Wáng Qióng was assigned to Liǎnghuái,
and Assistant Censor-in-Chief Zhāng Xiàn to Mǐn and Zhè.
Thereafter, only Liǎnghuái, due to its heavy taxes,
occasionally had high officials dispatched.
In the tenth year,
it was Vice Minister (Shìláng) Lán Zhāng of the Ministry of Justice.
In the seventh year of Jiājìng,
it was Vice Censor-in-Chief Huáng Chén.
In the thirty-second year,
it was Vice Censor-in-Chief Wáng Shēn.
By the thirty-ninth year,
Vice Censor-in-Chief Yān Màoqīng was specially appointed to oversee the four transport offices (yùnsī),
〔一七〕with particularly heavy authority.
From the second year of Lóngqìng, after Vice Censor-in-Chief Páng Shàngpéng oversaw the three transport offices of Liǎnghuái, Chánglú, and Shāndōng,
〔一八〕there were no more special dispatches of high officials.
The "barbarian" people (fānrén) were fond of dairy products.
If they did not get tea,
they would become ill.
Therefore, since the Táng and Sòng dynasties,
the method of exchanging tea for horses was practiced,
to control the Qiāng and Róng.
The Míng system was even more meticulous.
There was official tea (guānchá)
and commercial tea (shāngchá),
both stored at the border for exchange for horses.
Official tea was sometimes taxed with silver notes,
while commercial tea was taxed somewhat like the salt system.
Initially,
Tàizǔ ordered merchants to buy tea in tea-producing areas,
pay money, and request permits (yǐn).
For one hundred catties of permit tea,
two hundred (cash) was paid.
Amounts less than a permit were called "odd remnants" (jīlíng),
and were issued separate endorsement slips (yóutiē).
If there were no endorsement slips or permits, or if the tea permit was separated,
anyone could report it for capture,
and tea bureaus and verification offices were set up.
If the weight of tea and the permit did not match,
it was considered smuggled tea.
All those who violated the private tea laws
were punished with the same crime as private salt.
If private tea exited the border,
and the border passes did not interrogate it,
all involved were executed.
Later, it was further stipulated that for one tea permit,
one thousand (cash) was paid,
for one hundred catties of tea;
for one tea endorsement slip,
six hundred (cash) was paid,
for sixty catties of tea.
〔一九〕Subsequently,
it was also ordered to pay silver notes,
one guàn for each permit or endorsement slip.
In the early Hóngwǔ reign,
it was stipulated: In all tea-selling areas,
the Xuānkè Office would collect one-thirtieth.
In the fourth year,
the Ministry of Revenue reported:
“In the various counties of Shǎnxī, Hánzhōng, Jīnzhōu, Shíquán, Hànyīn, Pínglì, and Xīxiāng,
there are forty-five qǐng of tea gardens,
with over eighty-six thousand tea plants.
In Sìchuān, there are three hundred fifteen households of Bā tea producers,
〔二０〕with over two million three hundred eighty thousand tea plants.
It should be stipulated that for every ten plants, the government takes one.
For ownerless tea gardens,
soldiers should be ordered to weed and harvest,
taking eight out of ten,
〔二一〕to exchange for barbarian horses.”
This was adopted.
Thus, tea tax offices (chákèsī) were established in various tea-producing areas,
and tax quotas were set:
Shǎnxī, over twenty-six thousand catties;
Sìchuān, one million catties.
Tea and Horse Offices (Chámǎsī) were established in Qín, Táo, Hé, Yǎ, and other prefectures.
From Diāomén, Lí, Yǎ, extending to Gānsù, Wūsī Zàng,
the tea trade spanned over five thousand lǐ.
In Guīdé and other prefectures behind the mountains,
and among various tribes in the west,
all bought tea with horses.
The tea produced in Diāomén, Yǒngníng, Jūn, and Lián,
named "scissor [zhà] leaf,"
was exclusively used by the Western Barbarians,
and merchants never sold it beyond the border.
The Sìchuān Tea and Salt Transport Commissioner (Cháyán Dū Zhuǎnyùnshǐ) stated:
“It is advisable to establish separate tea bureaus,
collect their taxes,
and exchange them for red tassels, felt robes, rice, cloth, pepper, and wax to fund the state.
As for the tea harvested by residents,
following the method of issuing permits for sale in Jiāngnán,
it would benefit both public and private interests.”
Thus, tea bureaus were established in Yǒngníng, Chéngdū, Jūn, and Lián.
The people of Sìchuān therefore used tea to trade for wool blankets, wool tassels, and other items to pay their tea tax.
A fixed tax quota was set,
warehouses were established for storage,
and it was exclusively used for purchasing horses.
The people dared not privately gather tea,
and the tax quota was often undersupplied,
so the people frequently had to make up the difference.
The Sìchuān Bùzhèngsī reported on this situation,
and it was then allowed for the people to pick tea
and trade goods with the fān (Tibetans).
An imperial edict also exempted the people of the six fān Sī in Tiānquán
from corvée labor,
specifically ordering them to steam black tea for trading horses.
In the initial system,
fān merchants from Chánghéxī and other areas would enter Yǎzhōu with horses to trade for tea,
passing through Yánzhōuwèi in Sìchuān to Lízhōu before reaching their destination.
The Chámǎsī set the price:
one horse
for one thousand eight hundred catties of tea,
to be supplied at the Diāomén Chákèsī.
The fān merchants had a long and circuitous journey,
and the amount of tea given was too much.
Yánzhōuwèi reported on this situation,
requesting to establish a Chámǎsī at Yánzhōu
and to relocate the tea stored at Diāomén to that place,
and also to assess the quality of the horses to determine the amount of tea.
An edict ordered that the Chámǎsī remain as it was,
but fixed the rate: one top-grade horse
would be given one hundred and twenty catties of tea;
a medium-grade, seventy catties;
and a foal, fifty catties.
In the thirtieth year, the Qínzhōu Chámǎsī was relocated to Xīníng,
and an imperial decree was issued to the Yòujūn Dūdū, stating:
"Recently, private tea has been leaving the border,
and few people are engaging in mutual trade,
causing horses to become more expensive daily and tea cheaper daily,
which encourages the fān people's disrespect.
Dispatch orders to the Qín and Shǔ prefectures
to send Dūsī officials and soldiers to Sōngpān, Diāomén, Lízhōu, Yǎzhōu, Hézhōu, Líntáo, and outside the passes leading to the Western fān areas,
to patrol and prohibit private tea from leaving the border."
Furthermore, the Fùmǎ Dūwèi Xiè Dá was sent to convey to Shǔwáng Chūn:
"The state's monopoly on tea
is fundamentally for the purpose of trading for horses.
Border officials have failed to scrutinize,
allowing private traders to cross the border,
trading only for red tassels and miscellaneous items.
This allows the fān people to reap the profits,
while few horses enter China.
How can this be a way to control the Róngdí!
You should instruct the Bùzhèngsī and Dūsī
to enforce strict prohibitions
to prevent this loss of benefit."
At that time,
the Emperor was concerned about border defense,
using tea to trade for horses,
to secure the hearts of the fān people,
and also to strengthen China.
He once said to Hùbù Shàngshū Yù Xīn:
"Using three million catties of Hànzhōng tea from Shǎnxī
can procure thirty thousand horses,
and the Sōngmào tea from Sìchuān is similar.
The prohibition on private trading
must be strictly enforced."
For this reason, Qiāndū Yùshǐ Dèng Wénkēng and others were dispatched to investigate private tea in Chuān and Shǎn;
[二二] Fùmǎ Dūwèi Ōuyáng Lún was executed for private tea.
Gold牌信符 (gold plaques and tally tokens) were also made,
and the Cáo Guógōng Lǐ Jǐnglóng was ordered to carry them to the fān areas
to make agreements with the various fān tribes.
The seal script on the top read
"Huángdì Shèngzhǐ" (Imperial Edict),
on the left it read
"Hédāng Chāfā" (To be dispatched accordingly),
and on the right it read
"Bùxìnzhě Zhǎn" (Those who disbelieve shall be executed).
There were forty-one such plaques in total: for the Huǒbǎzàng, Sīnnángrì, and other tribes of Táozhōu,
four plaques were issued,
requiring them to submit three thousand fifty horses;
for the twenty-nine tribes of Bìlǐwèi Xīfān in Hézhōu,
[二三] twenty-one plaques were issued,
requiring them to submit seven thousand seven hundred five horses;
for the four Wèi of Qǔxiān, Āduān, Hǎndōng, and Āndìng in Xīníng,
and the Bāwā, Shēnzhōng, Shēnzàng, and other tribes,
sixteen plaques were issued,
requiring them to submit three thousand fifty horses.
The lower part of the gold plaques was issued to the various fān tribes,
and the upper part was stored in the Imperial Treasury as a token,
with officials dispatched every three years to verify the tallies.
There were two routes for transportation:
one from Hézhōu,
and one from Diāomén,
transporting over five hundred thousand catties of tea,
and obtaining thirteen thousand eight hundred horses.
Such was Tàizǔ's management of the fān.
During the Yǒnglè reign,
the Emperor, desiring to pacify distant peoples,
progressively increased the amount of tea given.
As a result, many traded for horses,
but tea became insufficient.
The tea prohibition also relaxed slightly,
with much private tea leaving the border.
The Diāomén Chámǎsī even used over eighty thousand catties of tea
to trade for only seventy horses,
and many were thin and weak.
Therefore, the tea prohibition was strictly re-enforced,
a Táozhōu Chámǎsī was established,
and a Gānsù Chámǎsī was also established in the territory of the Shǎnxī Xíng Dūsī.
In the thirteenth year, three Yùshǐ were specially dispatched to patrol and oversee the tea-horse trade in Shǎnxī.
Tàizǔ's prohibition of private tea
involved, from March to September,
dispatching four Xíngrén monthly
to patrol Hézhōu, Líntáo, Diāomén, Lízhōu, and Yǎzhōu.
Within half a year,
twenty-four officials were dispatched,
constantly coming and going.
In Xuāndé ten,
it was fixed that they would be dispatched once every three months.
The gold plaques and tally tokens had been stopped since the Yǒnglè era,
but were reissued at this time.
Not long after,
the fān people were plundered by the Běidí,
and moved to the interior,
and the gold plaques were lost.
And the Chásī, due to a shortage of tea,
only used Hànzhōng tea to trade for horses,
and no longer issued gold plaques,
merely allowing them to offer horses as tribute.
Before this,
at the end of Hóngwǔ,
four tea warehouses were established in Chéngdū, Chóngqìng, Bǎoníng, and Bōzhōu,
ordering merchants to submit rice in exchange for tea.
During the Xuāndé reign,
it was stipulated that for every hundred catties of official tea,
an additional one-tenth was levied as wastage.
Those who traded for tea
would send people to Gānzhōu and Xīníng,
and draw salt from Huái and Zhè to cover the expenses.
Merchants, relying on their documents, engaged in rampant private trading,
and official taxes were not fully collected for several years.
In the early Zhèngtǒng reign,
Dū Yùshǐ Luó Héngxìn reported on its abuses,
and the system of transporting tea and drawing salt was abolished,
with official transportation resuming as before,
managed by a capital official.
During the Jǐngtài reign,
the dispatch of Xíngrén was ceased.
In Chénghuà three, Yùshǐ were ordered to patrol the tea trade in Shǎnxī.
The fān people disliked the Yùshǐ,
and the number of horses arriving daily decreased.
So the Yùshǐ were recalled,
and Xíngrén were dispatched again,
and the Ànchásī was also ordered to patrol.
Later, the patrolling became unfocused,
and the Bīngbù reported its harm,
so Yùshǐ were dispatched again,
replaced annually,
making it a regulation.
Also, due to famine requiring relief,
merchants were again ordered to submit grain for tea,
and it was also ordered that one hundred catties of tea could be exchanged for five qián of silver.
The system of merchants paying tax in silver began from this point.
In Hóngzhì three,
Yùshǐ Lǐ Luán stated:
"The accumulated tea in the Chámǎsī is gradually decreasing,
horses on various borders are being depleted,
and Shǎnxī's various commanderies have had good harvests,
so there is no need to trade for grain.
I request that merchants be invited to trade for tea at the three Chámǎsī of Xīníng, Héxī, and Táozhōu,
with each *yǐn* not exceeding one hundred catties,
and each merchant not exceeding thirty *yǐn*.
The officials will collect four-tenths of it,
and the remainder will then be allowed for sale.
This could yield four hundred thousand catties of tea,
trading for four thousand horses,
and the process will stop once the number is sufficient."
This was followed.
In the twelfth year,
Yùshǐ Wáng Xiàn again stated:
"Since the opening of the tea trading prohibition,
private tea has become unstoppable,
and horse trading has become unfavorable.
I request to halt the grain-for-tea system.
In times of future
military conflict or famine,
we can then reconsider."
The Bù Fù followed his request.
The Sìchuān Chákèsī previously collected hundreds of thousands of catties for horse trade.
After Yǒnglè,
all fān horses came through the Shǎnxī route,
and much of the Sìchuān tea rotted.
Therefore, it was ordered to use a three-part ratio:
one part to be collected in kind (tea),
two parts to be converted to silver,
and the grain-for-tea system to be suspended for two years.
When Yánsuí experienced famine,
merchants were again invited to submit grain and fodder,
trading for four million catties.
Soon after, following the report by Yùshǐ Wáng Shào,
it was again prohibited,
and the system of inviting merchants to trade beyond the regular quota was also abolished.
In the sixteenth year, the position of Tea Censor was restored,
and Yáng Yīqīng, the Dū Yùshǐ overseeing horse administration, was appointed to concurrently manage it.
Yīqīng again proposed the *kāizhōng* (open exchange) system,
stating:
"If merchants are invited to buy tea,
and the government trades one-third of it,
then with five or six hundred thousand *jīn* of tea annually,
ten thousand horses can be obtained."
The Emperor assented to his request.
In the first year of Zhèngdé,
Yīqīng further suggested that
for merchants unwilling to receive payment,
half the tea should be given to them
to sell themselves.
This was then established as a permanent regulation.
Yīqīng also said that the system of gold tablets and tallies should be reinstated,
and requested the re-establishment of Inspecting Tea Censors to concurrently manage horse administration.
Consequently, Censors were dispatched again,
but the gold tablets, having long been abolished,
could ultimately not be reinstated.
Later, Emperor Wǔzōng favored Tibetan monks,
allowing people from the Western Regions to carry private tea exceptionally.
From then on, the tea laws deteriorated.
When the Tibetans traded for horses,
they could not distinguish weights and measures,
only specifying horses by the *bì* (bamboo scoop).
If the *bì* was large,
the officials suffered losses;
if small,
the merchants complained about the burden.
In the tenth year,
Inspecting Tea Censor Wáng Rǔzhōu devised a compromise,
In the third year of Jiājìng,
Censor Chén Jiǎng, finding merchant tea to be inferior and counterfeit,
mandated the collection of all dark tea.
As local production was limited,
tea was then categorized into two grades, superior and medium,
stamped on the *bì*,
with the merchant's name written and checked.
Soon, fifty thousand Sichuan tea permits were set,
twenty-six thousand for the interior (fùyǐn),
and twenty-four thousand for the border (biānyǐn).
Sprouted tea permits cost three *qián*,
and leaf tea permits cost two *qián*.
The amount of tea traded reached eight hundred thousand *jīn* and then stopped,
to prevent overabundance.
In the fifteenth year,
Censor Liú Liángqīng stated:
"The statutes say: 'Those who privately export tea across the border or officials who fail to detect it
shall both be put to a slow death by slicing.'
Indeed, among the frontier defenses in the west,
none are more critical than the various Tibetan tribes.
The Tibetans rely on tea for survival,
so strict laws are imposed to prohibit it,
and horses are exchanged as compensation,
to control the Tibetans' very lives,
strengthen China's frontiers,
