and sever the right arm of the Xiongnú.
This cannot be judged by ordinary laws.
In the early Hóngwǔ era, a regulation stipulated that
common people should not store more than a month's supply of tea.
In the middle of Hóngzhì,
merchants were summoned to trade tea,
sometimes to prepare for relief,
or to stock the border,
but internal consumption by the people was never forbidden.
Now, the punishment for communicating with Tibetans is reduced
merely to exile,
while tea in the interior is prohibited,
preventing people from consuming it,
and merchants are made to deliver their taxed tea
to the three Tea and Horse Administrations.
The Tea Administrations, being neighbors to the Tibetans,
facilitate private trade,
yet the prohibition is stricter in the interior prefectures.
This drives the people to private trading and provides them with capital.
As a result, major criminals escape the net,
while commoners carrying a *shēng* or *dǒu* are caught by the law.
Currently, the stores in the three Tea and Horse Administrations are calculated:
Táohé has enough for three years,
Xīníng for two years,
and merchant and taxed private tea continue to increase daily,
accumulating and rotting away uselessly.
The abuses of the tea law are thus.
Tibetan lands have many horses but no market,
and our tea is restricted and cannot circulate;
the situation will inevitably lead to mutual dependence,
and the initiative to control them is ours.
Now, residents of the Tea Administrations secretly exchange Tibetan horses for merchants to trade,
without a single day's pause in the year,
and by the time official exchanges occur,
the horses have already been depleted.
I request an edict to the three Tea and Horse Administrations
to retain only two years' supply,
and specify the amount of horses to be traded annually.
Apart from the official tea,
not an iota should be smuggled.
This will make tea prices soar,
subjugate the Tibetans,
and fine horses will become inexhaustible.
Moreover, greatly increase the open trade of merchant tea,
allow it to circulate in the interior,
with the government taxing half for military provisions,
while near-Tibetan areas like Hé, Lán, Jiē, and Mín
maintain the prohibition on sales as before,
and further intensify the punishment for communicating with Tibetans as per the statutes.
Táozhōu, Mínzhōu, and Hézhōu should be responsible for border defense,
Línláo and Lánzhōu for Lǒngyòu patrols,
and Xīníng for military preparedness,
with officials selected to guard each.
Those who fail to detect violations should be impeached for incompetence."
The memorial was submitted,
and approved.
Thereupon, the tea laws were somewhat rectified.
Censor Liú Lún, Grand Coordinator Wáng Yǐqí, and others,
requested the reinstatement of gold tablets and tallies for the various Tibetan tribes.
The Ministry of War deliberated,
saying: "Tibetan tribes are constantly deceitful,
and the northern barbarians plunder incessantly.
Gold tablets are quickly issued and quickly lost,
which greatly harms national dignity.
The Tibetans submit horses
with the intention of obtaining tea.
If the prohibition on private trade is strict,
then the Tibetans will naturally be compliant.
Even without issuing gold tablets,
horses can be collected.
If private trade flourishes,
we will have no means to secure their loyalty and control their fate.
Even if gold tablets are issued,
horses will not arrive."
It was then decided to issue *kānhé* (matching tallies) to them.
Afterwards, Shǎnxī suffered famine,
and tea households had no means of support,
accumulating considerable arrears in taxes.
In the thirty-sixth year,
the Ministry of Revenue, noting the disasters and earthquakes across Shǎnxī,
the urgent need for border provisions,
and the great deficit in national expenditure,
reported:
"Previously,
beyond the regular quota of tea for horse exchange,
much *kāizhōng* was opened to aid the public coffers,
sometimes reaching five million *jīn*.
Recently, Censor Liú Liángqīng also opened a million,
but later it was limited to the regular quota of eight hundred thousand *jīn*,
with taxed and private tea combined totaling merely over nine hundred thousand.
It is advisable to instruct the Inspecting Tea Censor to deliberate
and invite merchants for more *kāizhōng*."
Censor Yáng Měiyì stated:
"With yearly famines and impoverished people,
even the regular quota suffers losses;
how can there be surplus?
Now it is only appropriate to adhere to the annual rule of nine hundred thousand *jīn* for attracting Tibetans to exchange horses.
All measures like allowing circulation in the interior to curb private trade,
and increasing *kāizhōng* for famine relief,
should be suspended,
to prevent them from sharing profits with horse trade."
The Ministry of Revenue, with the treasury currently depleted,
requested to follow the precedent of the sixth year of Hóngzhì,
exchanging horses while also opening a million *jīn*
for recruitment in border garrisons to provide military provisions.
An imperial edict assented to this.
In the last years of Jiājìng,
Censor Pān Yīguì stated:
"Increased merchant tea in *kāizhōng*
is quite stagnant.
It should be reduced by fourteen or fifteen percent."
He also said:
"Sōngpān is close to Táozhōu and Hézhōu,
and private tea often slips out.
The Sōngpān permit quota should be suspended,
and the prohibition on entry into Tibetan areas strictly enforced."
All were approved.
As for the division of Sichuan tea permits into border and interior,
border tea was less and circulated easily,
while interior tea was abundant and often stagnant.
In the third year of Lóngqìng, twelve thousand permits were cut,
with thirty thousand assigned to Lízhōu and Yǎzhōu,
four thousand to Sōngpān and other border areas,
and four thousand retained for the interior,
with a total tax silver of over fourteen thousand *liǎng*
remitted to the Ministry to aid the border as a regular practice.
In the fifth year, Gānzhōu was ordered to emulate the precedents of Táozhōu, Hézhōu, and Xīníng,
opening *kāizhōng* every sixth month of the year,
exchanging eight hundred horses within two months.
Reward and punishment rules were established:
merchants whose permits were used up within one or two years received varying rewards,
while those who exceeded three years were punished
In the fifth year of Wànlì's reign (1577),
Āndá Blockaded the border,
requesting the opening of a tea market.
Censor Lǐ Shíchéng said:
"Tea is vital to the border tribes (fān).
If the northern barbarians (Dí) obtain it,
they could use it to control the tribes;
the tribes would then certainly follow the barbarians,
causing no small harm.
The Board discussed giving them over a hundred tea-baskets (bì),
but not permitting them to trade in the market."
From the time Liú Liángqīng relaxed the prohibitions in the interior,
Yáng Měiyì deemed it incorrect,
and later it was prohibited again.
In the thirteenth year (1585),
since Xī'ān, Fèngxiáng, and Hànzhōng were not adjacent to the tribes,
the prohibition was lifted there.
Merchants were invited and given permits (yǐn),
with thirteen parts (percent) levied for the government,
and the rest allowed for private sale.
Censor Zhōng Huàmín, observing that private tea was extensively smuggled out,
requested that responsibility be divided and assigned.
For Hànzhōng in Shǎnxī,
the Guānnán Circuit (dào) would oversee it,
with one prefectural assistant specifically stationed at Yúdùbà.
For Bǎoníng in Chuān (Sìchuān),
the Chuānběi Circuit (dào) would oversee it,
with one prefectural assistant specifically stationed at Jīhóubà.
They were to lead state and county officials and soldiers in defense."
This was adopted.
Tea was exchanged for horses,
solely in Hànzhōng and Bǎoníng.
However, Húnán produced tea,
and its price was cheap.
Merchants often crossed the border to smuggle it,
so those (permits) for Hànzhōng and Bǎoníng
were only one or twenty permits.
Tea households, wishing to meet their tax quotas,
frequently smuggled it out across the border.
The tribal peoples, benefiting from the cheap smuggled tea,
consequently refused to deliver horses.
In the twenty-third year (1595),
Censor Lǐ Nán requested a prohibition on Húnán tea,
stating:
"If Húnán tea circulates,
both the tea regulations and the horse administration will be harmed.
It should be ordered that the tea-inspecting Censor summon merchants to issue permits.
Those willing to report to Hàn (Hànzhōng), Xīng (Xīng'ān), Bǎo (Bǎoníng), and Kuí (Kuífǔ)
shall be approved for exchange.
Those crossing the border into Húnán
shall be prohibited.
Furthermore, Húnán has much fake tea;
consuming it pricks the mouth and damages the belly,
and the tribal people also suffer from its harm."
Afterward, Censor Xú Qiáo said:
"The tea from Hàn (Hànzhōng) and Chuān (Sìchuān) is scarce and expensive,
while Húnán tea is abundant and cheap.
The circulation of Húnán tea
does not impede Hànzhōng.
Hàn tea tastes sweet and mild,
while Húnán tea tastes bitter,
which is suitable with酥酪 (sūlào) – butter and cheese;
this also benefits the tribes.
However, laws should be established for strict scrutiny
to curb fake tea."
The Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù) reconciled their proposals,
making Hàn tea primary
and Húnán tea secondary.
Each merchant, upon receiving a permit,
would first be allocated Hàn and Chuān (tea) until completed,
then Húnán (tea).
If Hàn permits were insufficient,
they would be supplemented with Húnán permits.
This was approved.
In the twenty-ninth year (1601),
Shǎnxī's Provincial Censor (Xún'àn Yùshǐ) Bì Sāncái said:
"The collection of tea taxes and tribute
has a fixed annual quota.
Previously, due to a surplus of accumulated tea,
garden households faced difficulties in delivering and paying,
hence it was commuted to cash.
Now, merchants have vanished,
and
I request that the five states and counties of Hànzhōng resume paying in kind,
recruiting merchants to exchange five hundred permits annually,
which could yield over eleven thousand nine hundred horses."
The Ministry discussed,
that the six tea bureaus of Xīníng, Hé (Hézhōu), Táo (Táozhōu), Mín (Mínzhōu), Gān (Gānzhōu), and Zhuānglàng should collectively exchange nine thousand six hundred horses,
and this was made law.
During the Tiānqǐ reign,
an additional two thousand four hundred horses were exchanged.
At the beginning of the Míng dynasty, private smuggling was strictly prohibited,
but over time, corrupt practices daily arose.
By the latter period,
in addition to official permits, merchants
were often given reward tickets (shǎngyóupiào),
allowing them to engage in private trade.
The finest horses of the tribal people all went to corrupt merchants,
and what the tea bureaus purchased were only those of middle or lower quality.
The tribes, having obtained tea,
rebelled or submitted freely;
and military officials (jiānglì) also used private horses to replace tribal horses,
falsely claiming superior tea.
Thus, the tea regulations, horse administration, and border defense all deteriorated.
For other tea-producing regions:
Chángzhōu, Lúzhōu, Chízhōu, and Huīzhōu in Nánzhílì;
Húzhōu, Yánzhōu, Qúzhōu, and Shàoxīng in Zhèjiāng;
Nánchāng, Ráozhōu, Nánkāng, Jiǔjiāng, and Jí'ān in Jiāngxī;
Wǔchāng, Jīngzhōu, Chángshā, and Bǎoqìng in Húguǎng;
Chéngdū, Chóngqìng, Jiādìng, Kuízhōu, and Lúzhōu in Sìchuān;
merchants who exchanged permits would go to the three verification offices in Yìngtiān, Yíxīng, and Hángzhōu.
Tea taxes were collected at Jiāngdōng Guāfù in Yìngtiān.
From Sūzhōu, Chángzhōu, Zhènjiāng, Huīzhōu, Guǎngdé, and Zhèjiāng, Hénán, Guǎngxī, Guìzhōu, all levied paper currency (chāo).
Yúnnán, however, levied silver.
Regarding tribute tea (shànggòngchá):
The national tribute quota was over four thousand units.
The tribute from Jiànníng in Fújiàn was considered the finest quality,
with varieties such as Tànchūn, Xiānchūn, Cìchūn, Zǐsǔn, and Jiànxīn.
In the past, all were picked and ground,
pressed with silver plates,
to form large and small dragon-balls (lóngtuán).
Tàizǔ (Emperor Hóngwǔ), considering this burdensome to the people,
abolished its manufacture,
only ordering the collection of tea buds for submission,
and restored five hundred tribute-tea households.
All tribute tea
was supplied according to the quota
and not recorded in detail.
Collation Notes
Vol. 57, Food and Money 5: Money and Paper Currency, Mining and Metallurgy (with Iron Smelting and Copper Mines appended), Commercial Tax, Maritime Trade, Horse Markets
The rise of coinage
began with the "nine-palace circular system" (jiǔfǔ huánfǎ),
which was followed by successive dynasties.
Paper currency (chāo) originated with the "flying cash" (fēiqián) of the Táng,
the "exchange notes" (jiāohuì) of the Sòng,
and the "exchange certificates" (jiāochāo) of the Jīn.
From the Yuán dynasty onwards, paper currency was used throughout,
and coinage was almost abandoned.
Tàizǔ (Emperor Hóngwǔ) initially established the Bǎoyuán Bureau in Yìngtiān,
casting
"Dàzhōng Tōngbǎo"
coins,
which circulated alongside coins of previous dynasties.
Four hundred cash (wén) constituted one string (guàn),
forty cash one tael (liǎng),
and four cash one qián.
When Chén Yǒuliàng was pacified,
the Jiāngxī Provincial Administration (Xíngshěng) was ordered to establish the Huòquán Bureau,
issuing Dàzhōng Tōngbǎo coins,
in five sizes.
Upon his ascension to the throne,
he issued
"Hóngwǔ Tōngbǎo"
coins,
which were made in five denominations: called
"Dāng Shí" (worth ten),
"Dāng Wǔ" (worth five),
"Dāng Sān" (worth three),
"Dāng Èr" (worth two),
and
"Dāng Yī" (worth one).
The "Dāng Shí"
coin weighed one tael,
and the others decreased successively down to one qián.
All provincial administrations established Bǎoquán Bureaus,
casting coins alongside the Bǎoyuán Bureau,
and strictly prohibited private minting.
In the fourth year of Hóngwǔ (1371), the large Dàzhōng and Hóngwǔ Tōngbǎo coins were re-minted as small coins.
Initially,
the coins from the Bǎoyuán Bureau
bore the character "Jīng"
on their reverse.
Later, many were cast without it,
and those without the character "Jīng"
did not circulate among the common people,
hence the re-minting of small coins to facilitate circulation.
Soon after, privately cast coins were ordered to be treated as scrap copper and sent to the officials,
compensated with official coins.
At this time, officials compelled people to surrender copper,
leading people to destroy their utensils to submit to the government,
which was considered quite a hardship.
Meanwhile, merchants, following the old custom of the Yuán dynasty, used paper currency,
and many found it inconvenient to use coins.
In the seventh year,
the Emperor then established the Bǎochāo Tí jǔ Sī (Bureau for the Supervision of Precious Banknotes).
The following year, an imperial edict was issued to the Zhōng shū Shěng (Central Secretariat) to print Dà Míng Bǎochāo (Great Ming Precious Banknotes),
ordering their circulation among the populace.
Made from mulberry bark pulp,
their form was square,
one chì (foot) high,
six cùn (inches) wide,
bluish in color,
with a border of dragon patterns and flowers.
Across the top, it was inscribed
"Dà Míng Tōngxíng Bǎochāo" (Great Ming Circulating Precious Banknote).
Inside, on the upper two sides,
there were eight seal characters,
saying
"Dà Míng Bǎochāo,
Tiānxià Tōngxíng" (Great Ming Precious Banknote, Circulates Throughout the Realm).
In the middle was a diagram of strings of cash,
ten strings making one guàn (string of 1000 cash).
Below it stated:
"The Zhōng shū Shěng (Central Secretariat) has memorialized and been approved to print Dà Míng Bǎochāo to circulate alongside copper coins.
Counterfeiters shall be executed.
Informers who capture counterfeiters shall be rewarded with twenty-five liǎng (taels) of silver,
and also be given the property of the offender."
For a five hundred wén (cash) note, five strings of cash were depicted,
and other denominations followed the same design, diminishing in representation.
There were six denominations in total: one guàn,
five hundred wén, four hundred wén, three hundred wén, two hundred wén, and one hundred wén.
Each banknote of one guàn
was equivalent to a thousand wén of cash,
or one liǎng of silver;
four guàn were equivalent to one liǎng of gold.
The populace was forbidden from trading in gold, silver, or goods;
violators would be punished;
exchanging gold or silver for banknotes was permitted.
Consequently, the Bǎoyuán (Precious Source) and Bǎoquán (Precious Spring) Bureaus were abolished.
Two years later,
the Bǎoquán Bureau was re-established,
to cast small coins to circulate alongside the banknotes,
with denominations below one hundred wén to be paid only in coins.
Commercial taxes were collected in both coins and banknotes,
three parts coins to seven parts banknotes.
In the thirteenth year,
as the banknotes had become worn and dilapidated from long use,
a system for exchanging old banknotes was established,
ordering the creation of circulating treasuries in various locations,
allowing soldiers, civilians, merchants, and traders to deposit worn banknotes in the treasuries in exchange for new ones,
charging a small fee for materials and printing.
Coincidentally, the Zhōng shū Shěng (Central Secretariat) was abolished,
so the printing of banknotes was assigned to the Hù bù (Ministry of Revenue),
and the casting of coins to the Gōng bù (Ministry of Works).
The characters "Zhōng shū Shěng"
on the banknotes were changed
to "Hù bù"
and circulated alongside the old banknotes.
In the sixteenth year,
the Hù bù (Ministry of Revenue) established the Bǎochāo Guǎngyuán Kù (Precious Banknote Broad Source Treasury) and Guǎnghuì Kù (Broad Benefit Treasury);
the Guǎngyuán Kù managed inflows,
and the Guǎnghuì Kù managed outflows.
Soldiers in frontier garrisons
were given monthly salt rations in banknotes,
and various salt fields were given working capital in banknotes.
In the eighteenth year,
officials throughout the realm received their salaries and rice allowances in banknotes,
two guàn and five hundred wén being equivalent to one dàn (stone) of rice.
In the twenty-second year, an imperial edict reformulated the coin specifications: one jīn (catty) of raw copper
was to cast one hundred sixty small coins.
"Fold-two" coins were two and a half times that,
and "equal to three"
up to "equal to ten"
were scaled accordingly.
Smaller banknotes were also produced,
from ten wén to fifty wén.
In the twenty-fourth year, an edict instructed tax collectors
that any banknote with discernible characters and denominations,
regardless of wear and tear,
should be accepted and sent to the capital,
and those who coerced or falsely impersonated would be punished.
In the twenty-fifth year, a Bǎochāo Xíngyòng Kù (Precious Banknote Circulating Treasury) was established in the eastern market,
with a total of three treasuries,
each provided with thirty thousand dìng (ingots) of banknotes as capital,
to receive old banknotes and send them to the imperial treasury.
It was ordered that Dà Míng Bǎochāo should circulate alongside coins of previous dynasties,
with one guàn of banknote being equivalent to one thousand wén of cash.
The Tí jǔ Sī (Bureau for Supervision) was to print banknotes for three months,
stopping in the tenth month,
and the printed banknotes were to be sent to the imperial treasury for rewards and gifts.
The following year, the Xíngyòng Kù (Circulating Treasury) was abolished,
and the Bǎoquán Bureau was also abolished.
At this time, the people of Liǎngzhè (Zhejiang and parts of Jiangsu), Jiāngxī, Mǐn (Fujian), and Guǎng (Guangdong) valued coins heavily and banknotes lightly,
with some exchanging one hundred sixty wén of coins for one guàn of banknotes.
Consequently, commodity prices soared,
and the banknote system further deteriorated and became unworkable.
In the thirtieth year, the prohibition on trading with gold and silver was re-emphasized.
At the beginning of Chéngzǔ's reign,
violators were labeled as evil schemers,
but the making of ornaments and utensils
was exempt from the prohibition.
In the second year of Yǒnglè, an imperial edict pardoned offenders from death,
instead exiling their families to Xīngzhōu (a military garrison).
Zhāng Yù, an assistant commander of the Shǎnxī Dū Sī (Shaanxi Regional Military Commission),
was convicted for illicitly trading in official banknotes and sentenced to military exile.
A civilian in Jiāngxià, whose father had died,
used silver for burial preparations and was to be exiled to the frontier.
The Emperor, considering that he was compelled by the need to arrange the funeral
and not deliberately violating the law,
specifically showed compassion and pardoned him.
Dū Yùshǐ (Censor-in-Chief) Chén Yīng said:
"In recent years, the banknote system has not been effective,
all because the court has issued too many banknotes
and lacked a method for collecting them,
leading to heavy goods and light banknotes.
It would be better to temporarily implement the household salt distribution law.
The people of the realm number no less than ten million households,
and the government troops no less than two million families.
If we sincerely order them to pay banknotes for salt according to their household size,
we can collect over fifty million dìng."
The Emperor ordered the Hù bù (Ministry of Revenue) to convene all officials for a discussion.
Large households would consume one jīn of salt per month
and pay one guàn in banknotes;
small households would pay half that.
This proposal was adopted.
A Běijīng Bǎochāo Tí jǔ Sī (Beijing Bureau for the Supervision of Precious Banknotes) was established,
and all taxes, levies, fines, and penalties were to be collected in banknotes,
with their value reduced to one-tenth of what it was at the beginning of Hóngwǔ's reign.
Later, salt officials were also ordered to accept old banknotes for salt,

and the accumulated firewood from the Nánjīng Chōufēn Chǎng (Nanjing Extraction and Distribution Bureau) and bamboo and timber from the Lóngjiāng Tí jǔ Sī (Longjiang Bureau for Supervision) were sold to soldiers and civilians,
collecting banknotes in return.
Yìngtiān (Nanjing) was to procure reeds and firewood annually,
collecting eight-tenths in banknotes.
When the Emperor first ascended the throne,
Hù bù Shàngshū (Minister of Revenue) Xià Yuánjí requested to change the seal script on the banknote plates
to "Yǒnglè".
The Emperor ordered that the old design be retained.
From then on, throughout the Míng dynasty, the Hóngwǔ era name was used.
When Rénzōng was regent,
he ordered those who committed crimes punishable by flogging to pay banknotes.
Upon his ascension,
he inquired of Yuánjí why banknotes were not circulating.
Yuánjí replied:
"Many banknotes make them light (less valuable),
few make them heavy (more valuable).
Banknotes do not circulate among the people
because too many have been dispersed and too few collected.
A method for collecting them should be devised.
I propose that all taxes on market stalls and shops
be assessed by their size and importance,
and their levies increased.
When banknotes enter official coffers,
worn and soft ones collected by officials should all be destroyed.
From now on, fewer official banknotes should be issued,
making it difficult for the common people to obtain them,
and then they will naturally become more valuable."
An edict was then issued stating:
"The increased levies on market stalls will be restored to their original levels
once the banknote system is functioning.
Trade in gold, silver, cloth, and silk
is also temporarily prohibited."
However, at this time,
the people still valued banknotes lightly.
By the beginning of Xuāndé's reign,
one dàn of rice cost fifty guàn in banknotes,
so the prohibition on trading cloth, silk, rice, and wheat was relaxed.
Anyone trading in gold or silver or hoarding goods to raise prices was fined in banknotes.
For granaries in prefectures, counties, and garrisons with grain accumulated for over ten years,
all salt and grain taxes were collected in banknotes,
and autumn grain taxes were also converted to three-tenths banknotes.
Market stall taxes in banknotes were increased fivefold.
Boarding houses and inns paid five hundred guàn in banknotes monthly.
Orchards and carts
were also ordered to pay in banknotes.
The Hù bù (Ministry of Revenue) reported that the people only traded in gold and silver,
and banknotes remained stagnant and uncirculated.
Thus, the prohibition was made even stricter:
anyone trading with one qián (mace) of silver
would be fined one thousand guàn in banknotes;
corrupt officials who accepted one liǎng of silver
would have ten thousand guàn in banknotes confiscated,
and an additional amount equal to the fine for non-payment would be confiscated.
When Yīngzōng Ēngzōng ascended the throne,
there was an order to convert tax receipts of rice and wheat into silver.
Consequently, the number of those who paid in paper currency was reduced,
and rice, silver, and copper coins were used instead of paper currency.
The prohibition on using silver was relaxed.
Both the court and the common people largely used silver;
only for smaller transactions were copper coins used.
Only official salaries were paid in paper currency,
which became stagnant and did not circulate.
In the thirteenth year, the prohibition was reimposed,
and those who hindered the circulation of paper currency were to be prosecuted for one million *guàn* 貫,
and their entire families were to be exiled to the border.
During the Tiānshùn 天順 reign,
the prohibition was finally relaxed.
Xiànzōng 憲zōng ordered that both internal and external taxes and duties be collected in a combination of copper coins and paper currency,
and official salaries and military provisions were also paid in a combination of copper coins and paper currency.
At this time, one *guàn* 貫 of paper currency was worth less than one *wén* 文 of copper coin,
but when taxes were levied on the people in paper currency,
two *fēn* 分 and five *lí* 釐 of silver were collected for every *guàn* 貫.
This caused great hardship to the people.
In the first year of Hóngzhì 弘治,
the Tax and Duty Office in the capital,
and the household and salt taxes in Shùntiān 順天, Shāndōng 山東, and Hénán 河南,
all collected paper currency.
All customs barriers collected both copper coins and paper currency.
Later, these were all converted to silver payments.
However, the Hóngwǔ 洪武, Yǒnglè 永樂, and Xuāndé 宣德 coins had accumulated unused,
so an imperial edict was issued to circulate them,
ordering them to be used alongside coins from previous dynasties.
The Ministry of Revenue requested to resume minting,
and so the minting bureaus were reopened to cast coins.
For all payments of redemptions and collection of taxes,
coins from previous dynasties and *zhìqián* 制錢 were each accepted for half the amount;
if *zhìqián* 制錢 were unavailable, old coins were accepted,
with two old coins equivalent to one *zhìqián* 制錢.
*Zhìqián* 制錢 referred to
the coins of the current dynasty.
According to the old system,
coins minted by the Ministry of Works were deposited into the Tàicāng 太倉 and Sīyào 司鑰 treasuries;
customs duties collected in coins were also deposited into the Sīyào 司鑰 treasury.
Millions of coins were stored in total,
managed by eunuchs.
The autumn provisions for the 京衛 Jīngwèi armies were drawn from these,
with seven hundred coins equivalent to one *liǎng* 兩 of silver.
At the beginning of Wǔzōng's 武宗 reign,
officials of the ministry requested an investigation into embezzlement;
they also noted that when coins were used for salaries and provisions,
they only amounted to one-third of the silver value,
and requested that silver be disbursed from the Chéngyùn 承運 treasury.
At that time, eunuchs were in power,
and they did not listen to any of these requests.
Later, Páng Lì 龐瑮, a eunuch of the Sīyào 司鑰 treasury, said:
“Since the Hóngzhì 弘治 period, customs duties converted to silver have been deposited into the Chéngyùn 承運 treasury,
leading to a shortage of coins and paper currency.
Disbursements are insufficient,
so I request that the old Chénghuà 成化 system be followed,
where both coins and paper currency are accepted.”
This was adopted.
In the third year of Zhèngdé 正德,
accumulated coins from the Tàicāng 太倉 were used to pay official salaries,
at a ratio of ten parts,
one part coin and nine parts silver.
Following the suggestion of eunuch Zhāng Yǒng 張永,
coins from the Tiāncái 天財 treasury and the Ministry of Revenue’s and Provincial Administration Commission’s treasuries were disbursed,
collected at customs,
with seventy *wén* 文 of coin collected for one *qián* 錢 of silver,
and the prohibition on private minting was reiterated.
In the fourth year of Jiājìng 嘉靖,
the Xuānkè Fēnsī 宣課分司 was ordered to collect taxes,
with one *guàn* 貫 of paper currency equivalent to three *lí* 釐 of silver,
and seven *wén* 文 of copper coin equivalent to one *fēn* 分 of silver.
At this time, paper currency had long ceased to circulate,
and copper coins were also largely stagnant,
with silver becoming increasingly the sole currency.
In the early Míng 明, Hóngwǔ 洪武 coins were minted.
In the ninth year of Chéngzǔ 成祖, Yǒnglè 永樂 coins were minted.
In the ninth year of Xuāndé 宣德, Xuāndé 宣德 coins were minted.
After the sixteenth year of Hóngzhì 弘治,
Hóngzhì 弘治 coins were minted.
By the sixth year of Shìzōng’s 世宗 Jiājìng 嘉靖 reign,
Jiājìng 嘉靖 coins were extensively minted.
Each coin weighed one *qián* 錢 and three *fēn* 分,
and coins from previous dynasties that had not been minted were also supplemented.
In the thirty-second year, nine types of coins from Hóngwǔ 洪武 to Zhèngdé 正德 were minted,
a million *dìng* 錠 of each type,
and ten million *dìng* 錠 of Jiājìng 嘉靖 coins,
with each *dìng* 錠 containing five thousand *wén* 文.
And the various factories for tax and duty collection
exclusively accepted Jiājìng 嘉靖 coins.
The people suffered from a shortage of coins,
so eighty-one million *wén* 文 of new and old coins from the imperial treasury were disbursed for salaries and provisions.
It was also ordered that coins from all previous dynasties be in circulation.
Those who melted down new or old coins or used copper to make statues or implements
were to be punished as severely as those who privately minted coins.
Previously,
poor quality and debased coins circulated among the people,
typically with thirty or forty coins equivalent to one *fēn* 分 of silver.
Later, more lead and tin were mixed in,
making them thin, inferior, and without proper form,
until sixty or seventy *wén* 文 were equivalent to one *fēn* 分 of silver.
Shredded paper was inserted among them,
making them indistinguishable.
Based on the advice of Lǐ Yòngjìng 李用敬, a supervising secretary,
*zhìqián* 制錢 were allowed to circulate alongside miscellaneous coins from previous dynasties.
The best quality coins were all seven *wén* 文 for one *fēn* 分 of silver.
The rest were divided into three grades based on their quality,
with the lowest grade being twenty-one *wén* 文 for one *fēn* 分 of silver;
the private minting of debased and poor quality coins was strictly prohibited and made illegal,
and offenders were punished according to the law.
The small coins had been in circulation for a long time,
and their sudden abolition
caused considerable inconvenience to the people.
Coins from the imperial treasury were also disbursed to civil and military officials as salaries,
regardless of whether they were new or old, good or bad,
all calculated at seven *wén* 文.
Those who used their salary coins for trade
also coerced the people into accepting them at seven *wén* 文,
which also caused unrest among the people.
Coupled with continuous years of severe famine,
migrants from all directions flocked to the capital for food,
and the dead lay piled upon each other.
Commentators attributed this to the dysfunctional currency system.
Thereupon, Censor Hé Tíngyù 何廷鈺 presented a memorial,
requesting that the people be allowed to use small coins,
with sixty *wén* 文 equivalent to one *fēn* 分 of silver.
The Ministry of Revenue insisted on not complying.
Hé Tíngyù 何廷鈺 then impeached Minister Fāng Dùn 方鈍 and Director Liú Ěrmù 劉爾牧.
The Emperor was enraged,
dismissed Liú Ěrmù 劉爾牧,
adopted Hé Tíngyù's 何廷鈺’s proposal,
and ordered that the people's convenience be prioritized.
Furthermore, it was stipulated that seven *wén* 文 of Jiājìng 嘉靖 coins,
ten *wén* 文 of Hóngwǔ 洪武 and other coins,
and thirty *wén* 文 of coins from previous dynasties
were equivalent to one *fēn* 分 of silver.
However, the various debased and small coins,
due to the initial strict prohibition,
though occasionally allowed by imperial decree,
were ultimately not used again.
Instead, the common people competed to privately mint Jiājìng Tōngbǎo 嘉靖通寶 coins,
which circulated alongside official coins.
Supervising Secretary Yīn Zhèngmào 殷正茂 said:
“The price of copper in the two capitals is very high,
and minting coins does not cover the costs.
It is advisable to procure copper from Yúnnán 雲南,
transport it to Yuèzhōu 岳州 for minting.
This would cost thirty-nine thousand *liǎng* 兩 of silver in labor and capital,
and could produce six hundred and fifty million *wén* 文 of coins,
worth over nine hundred and thirty thousand *liǎng* 兩 of silver,
which would be enough to somewhat alleviate the nation's urgent needs.”
The Ministry of Revenue reviewed and replied:
“Yúnnán 雲南 is a remote and simple place,
so it is convenient to mint coins there.”
Accordingly, an imperial edict instructed the Governor to use twenty thousand *liǎng* 兩 of salt tax silver as capital.
Soon after,
Governor Wáng Bǐng 王昺 reported that expenses were high and income low,
and requested to stop minting.
The Emperor believed that small expenses should not be regretted,
and still ordered it to proceed.
Several years later,
Inspector Wáng Zhèng 王諍 again suggested stopping the minting.
The Ministry debated:
“The stagnation of the currency system
is due to the Xuānkè Sī 宣課司 collecting taxes at seven *wén* 文 for one *fēn* 分.
Cunning people take advantage of the opportunity to obstruct,
when there are many coins, they are debased and deceptive,
when there are few coins, they increase the value and exploit for profit.
Therefore, the more prohibitions there are, the more stagnant the currency becomes.
From now on, the conversion rate should be left to the convenience of the people,
without setting a fixed number of *wén* 文,
and taxes, duties, and official salaries should all use silver.”
Thus, minting in Yúnnán 雲南 was stopped,
and the Ministry of Revenue’s proposal was adopted.
At that time, the minted coins included those with *jīnbèi* 金背 (golden back),
those with *huǒqī* 火漆 (fire lacquer),
and those with *xuánbiān* 鏇邊 (spun edge).
Critics argued that coin minting was difficult,
and artisans were overworked and costly,
so they replaced the *xuánchē* 鏇車 (spinning wheel) with *lǜqiāo* 鑢鐋 (files).
Consequently, minters competed to mix in lead and tin for easier filing and polishing,
resulting in coarse and rough outlines,
and dull and dark color.
Counterfeiters imitated this,
and private minting became increasingly prevalent.
Even the *jīnbèi* 金背 coins were hindered and did not circulate.
Reports of capital crimes were daily,
but it could not be stopped.
The Emperor was troubled by this and
consulted Grand Secretary Xú Jiē 徐階.
Xú Jiē 徐階 presented five harms and
requested to stop coin minting at the Bǎoyuán Jú 寶源局,
and to give silver for all payments that should have been in coins.
The Emperor then investigated and punished artisans for embezzling materials and reducing labor,
and stopped minting.
Thereafter, taxes were collected in silver and not in coins.
Furthermore, the common people only used *zhìqián* 制錢,
not ancient coins,
and private minting became widespread.
The system of paper currency was abolished between the Hóngzhèng and Zhèngdé eras.
In the Tiānqǐ period,
Huì Shìyáng, a Supervising Secretary, again petitioned for its reintroduction.
In the late Chóngzhēn reign,
a person named Jiǎng Chén reiterated this proposal,
and was promoted to Secretary of the Ministry of Revenue.
Ní Yuánlù, who was then in charge of the Ministry,
strongly supported it,
but it ultimately proved unfeasible and was dropped.
Among the taxes on mines and smelters,
including gold, silver, copper, iron, lead, mercury, cinnabar, and malachite,
gold and silver mines were most harmful to the people.
When Xú Dá pacified Shāndōng,
a close minister requested the opening of silver mines.
Tàizǔ said that the disadvantages of silver mines
benefited the officials little,
but harmed the people greatly,
and therefore should not be opened.
Later, when someone requested the opening of silver mines in Shǎnzhōu,
the Emperor said:
"What the land produces
will eventually be exhausted.
The annual tax quotas are fixed,
but the demand for silver is endless.
Ministers who speak of profit
are all thieves who harm the people."
The Assistant Magistrate of Línzī begged to open the treasures of the mountains and seas to facilitate trade,
but the Emperor dismissed him.
Chéngzǔ reprimanded the common people of Héchí who spoke of mining.
Rénzōng and Xuānzōng continued the prohibition for generations,
filling up the pit shafts in Pānyú,
and halting mining at Báinígōu in Sōngxiàn.
However, in Yóuxī Xiàn, Fújiàn, at Yínpíngshān Silver Mine, there were forty-two smelting furnaces,
which began in the nineteenth year of Hóngwǔ.
In the seven counties of Wēnchù, Líshuǐ, Píngyáng, etc., in Zhèjiāng,
there were also mining establishments.
The annual tax from these was over two thousand liǎng.
During the Yǒnglè era,
eight silver pits were opened at Fènghuángshān in Shāngxiàn, Shǎnxī.
〔一０〕Officials were dispatched to Húguǎng and Guìzhōu to procure gold and silver for taxes,
and eunuchs and censors were again sent to verify it.
Three more pits were opened at Mǎ'ān and other locations in Púchéng Xiàn, Fújiàn,
and gold mining bureaus were established at Tàipíngxī and Jiāozhǐ Xuānguāng Zhèn in Guìzhōu,
along with the Géróngxī Silver Mining Bureau.
〔一一〕Silver smelting also occurred in Dàlǐ, Yúnnán.
Those places that did not produce gold or silver
were also repeatedly reformed or abolished.
Yet the annual quota for Fújiàn increased to over thirty thousand liǎng,
and for Zhèjiāng to over eighty thousand.
In the early Xuānzōng reign,
the Fújiàn tax was considerably reduced,
but later increased to over forty thousand,
and Zhèjiāng also increased to over ninety thousand.
Yīngzōng issued an edict to seal the mining pits,
and abolished the "zhálàn bàn" official system,
greatly relieving the people,
but the annual quota was not abolished.
The "suìbàn" (annual procurement)
was the old Hóngwǔ quota.
The "zhálàn bàn" (barrier procurement)
was what Yǒnglè and Xuānzōng had added.
Later, the "yǒngjiān" (perpetual smelting) was prohibited.
Treacherous commoners privately opened pits and engaged in mutual killing and injury,
which severe prohibitions could not stop.
An edict was issued to pardon them,
but they did not reform.
Proponents again requested the opening of silver mines,
so that profit would accrue to the government,
and thieves would have no place.
Thus, Vice Minister Wáng Zhì was ordered to manage them,
and establish annual quotas:
Fújiàn silver at over twenty thousand,
and Zhèjiāng double that.
Censors Cáo Xiáng and Féng Jié were also separately dispatched to supervise,
but their levies exceeded official taxes,
the people suffered, and thieves multiplied.
Followers of Dèng Màoqī and Yè Zōngliú plagued Zhèjiāng and Fújiàn,
and it was a long time before order was restored.
Jǐngdì once sealed them,
but soon, due to the large number of illegal miners,
Minister of War Sūn Yuánzhēn requested the opening of Zhèjiāng silver mines,
and consequently Fújiàn mines were also opened,
with the eunuch Dài Xìbǎo appointed to supervise them.
In the fourth year of Tiānshùn, the eunuch Luó Yǒng was dispatched to Zhèjiāng,
Luó Guī to Yúnnán,
Féng Ràng to Fújiàn,
and Hé Néng to Sìchuān.
The quotas for Zhèjiāng and Fújiàn were roughly as before,
Yúnnán had over one hundred thousand liǎng,
Sìchuān had over thirteen thousand,
totaling over one hundred eighty-three thousand liǎng.
In the Chénghuà era,
gold mines were opened in Húguǎng,
in Wǔlíng and twelve other counties, totaling twenty-one mines.
Annually, five hundred fifty thousand laborers were conscripted,
countless died,
and only thirty-five liǎng of gold were obtained.
〔一二〕Therefore, they were again closed.
Meanwhile, Zhèjiāng silver mines had their quotas reduced due to shortages,
and Yúnnán mines were repeatedly opened and stopped.
In the first year of Hóngzhì, Yúnnán's quota was reduced by twenty thousand liǎng,
Wēnchù by over ten thousand liǎng,
and the abandoned silver smelters in Púchéng were abolished.
By the thirteenth year,
Lǐ Shìshí, the Provincial Governor of Yúnnán, reported:
"Of Yúnnán's nine silver mines,
the mineral veins of four have long been exhausted.
I beg that their taxes be remitted."
This was approved.
Mining pits in Sìchuān and Shāndōng were also sealed one after another.
In the early Wǔzōng reign,
following the memorial of eunuch Qín Wén and others,
Zhèjiāng and Fújiàn silver mines were reopened.
Later, the Zhèjiāng local official reported that the mineral veins were exhausted,
so it was ordered that two thousand liǎng of silver be paid annually,
which ceased upon the execution of Liú Jǐn.
In the early Shìzōng reign,
the Dàlǐ mines were closed.
Later, in Jì, Yù, Qí, Jìn, Chuān, and Diān, gold and silver ore was submitted from various locations,
and its extraction was again debated
to assist with large construction projects.
After silver ore was obtained from Yùwàngyù,
the Emperor instructed the Grand Secretaries to widely promote mining.
Minister of Revenue Fāng Dùn and others requested that the Provincial Governors and Censors of Sìchuān, Shāndōng, and Hénán strictly supervise their subordinates
to search for mines one by one,
to fulfill the meaning of auspicious signs from heaven and earth.
Consequently, both public and private sectors eagerly pursued mining profits,
and illegal miners in Zhèjiāng and Jiāngxī even robbed Huīzhōu and Níngguó,
and troubles gradually multiplied across the realm.
In the early years of the Lóngqìng 隆慶 reign,
mining in the Jìzhèn 薊鎮 area was abolished.
In the southern central regions, all mining operations
were also forbidden by inscribed stone tablets.
In the twelfth year of the Wànlì 萬曆 reign (1584),
corrupt commoners repeatedly brought the profits of mining to the emperor's attention.
Many officials forcefully argued against its harm.
Although the emperor acquiesced,
he was displeased.
In the twenty-fourth year (1596),
Zhāng Wèi 張位 was in power,
and Zhòng Chūn 仲春, a chiliarch of the Former Guard, requested to open mines.
Zhāng Wèi 張位 could not stop it.
Once the door to mining was opened,
daily reports arrived from dismissed officers and commoners presenting new mines,
and thus, there was no place left unmined.
Eunuchs were dispatched in all directions: Wáng Zhōng 王忠 for Chāngpíng 昌平;
Wáng Hǔ 王虎 for Zhēn 真, Bǎo 保, Jì 薊, Yǒng 永, Fángshān 房山, and Wèizhōu 蔚州;
Tián Jìn 田進 for Chānglí 昌黎;
Lǔ Kūn 魯坤 for Kāifēng 開封, Zhāngdé 彰德, Wèihuī 衞輝, Huáiqìng 懷慶, Yèxiàn 葉縣, and Xìnyáng 信陽 in Hénán 河南;
Chén Zēng 陳增 for Jìnán 濟南, Qīngzhōu 青州, Jìníng 濟寧, Yízhōu 沂州, Téng 滕, Fèi 費, Pénglái 蓬萊, Fúshān 福山, Qīxiá 棲霞, Zhāoyuǎn 招遠, and Wéndēng 文登 in Shāndōng 山東;
Zhāng Zhōng 張忠 for Tàiyuán 太原, Píngyáng 平陽, and Lù'ān 潞安 in Shānxī 山西;
Hǎo Lóng 郝隆 and Líu Cháoyòng 劉朝用 for Níngguó 寧國 and Chízhōu 池州 in Nánzhí 南直;
Chén Fèng 陳奉 for Dé'ān 德安 in Húguǎng 湖廣;
Cáo Jīn 曹金 for Háng 杭, Yán 嚴, Jīn 金, Qú 衢, Xiàofēng 孝豐, and Zhūjì 諸暨 in Zhèjiāng 浙江;
later replaced by Líu Zhōng 劉忠;
Zhào Jiàn 趙鑒 and Zhào Qīn 趙欽 for Xī'ān 西安 in Shǎnxī 陝西;
Qīu Chéngyún 丘乘雲 for Sìchuān 四川;
Gāo Huái 高淮 for Liáodōng 遼東;
Lǐ Jìng 李敬 for Guǎngdōng 廣東;
Shěn Yǒngshòu 沈永壽 for Guǎngxī 廣xī;
Pān Xiāng 潘相 for Jiāngxī 江西;
Gāo Cǎi 高寀 for Fújiàn 福建;
Yáng Róng 楊榮 for Yúnnán 雲南.
All were granted credentials
and accompanied by the officials who had originally submitted the memorials.
If the mineral veins were too meager to yield anything,
the commoners were forced to compensate them.
Corrupt individuals, under the guise of mining,
used official transport to extort wealth from the people
and rode roughshod over prefectures and counties.
Officials who showed compassion for the people
were accused of obstruction
and arrested, interrogated, and dismissed.
At that time, many eunuchs were violent and overbearing,
but Chén Fèng 陳奉 was especially so.
Wealthy families and powerful clans were falsely accused of stealing minerals,
while fertile lands and beautiful residences were designated as having mineral veins beneath them.
He led his subordinates to surround and arrest people,
humiliated women,
and even cut off people's hands and feet and threw them into the river,
such was his cruelty.
The emperor indulged him and did not question him.
From the twenty-fifth year (1597) to the thirty-third year (1605),
the mining taxes submitted by these eunuchs amounted to nearly three million taels of silver.
Minor officials, leveraging their power, extorted
more than five times that amount,
leaving the people unable to make a living.
Wèi Yǔnzhēn 魏允貞, the Provincial Inspector of Shānxī 山西, memorialized:
“Currently, droughts and floods announce disaster,
heaven roars and earth quakes,
stars fall and qi shoots across the sky,
reported daily from all four directions.
There are military campaigns both internally and externally,
and the common people are exhausted.
Yet greedy petty individuals
exploit mining to indulge their gluttony.
If a conflict arises internally,
then the miners and supernumerary laborers will cause even greater calamity.
By that time,
it will be too late to implement the strategy of 'casting pearls and exchanging jade (to avert disaster).'”
Yáo Sīrén 姚思仁, the Circuit Censor for Hénán 河南, also stated:
“There are eight major concerns
regarding the harms of mining.
Miner bandits gather in groups,
easily inciting rebellion—this is the first.
Mine bosses are excessively burdened,
leading to a situation ripe for collapse—this is the second.
Miners are brutally harmed,
forced into displacement—this is the third.
Hired commoners lack grain,
crying out from hunger—this is the fourth.
Mine shafts are opened everywhere,
leading to wasteful expenditure with no benefit—this is the fifth.
The silver content in mineral sands is low,
and the people are forcibly made to buy them—this is the sixth.
All commoners are opening mines,
losing their agricultural and sericultural livelihoods—this is the seventh.
The reporting officials are overbearing,
with cruel punishments inciting revolt—this is the eighth.
Now, mine bosses die from accumulated losses,
common people die from forced purchases,
miners die from collapses
and from fighting.
If this is not stopped now,
even if the treasures of the imperial treasury are emptied
and the strength of the whole empire is exhausted,
it will do nothing to avert ruin.”
These memorials were submitted,
but none were heeded.
Those who understood the situation believed that the fall of the Míng 明 dynasty was already foreshadowed here.
Iron foundries were
established in the sixth year of Hóngwǔ 洪武 (1373).
There were thirteen such foundries in total:
Xián 賢, Xīnyù 新喻, Fēnyí 分宜 in Jiāngxī 江西;
Xīngguó 興國, Huángméi 黃梅 in Húguǎng 湖廣;
Láiwú 萊蕪 in Shāndōng 山東;
Yángshān 陽山 in Guǎngdōng 廣東;
Gǒngchāng 鞏昌 in Shǎnxī 陝西;
two in Jízhōu 吉州,
and one each in Tàiyuán 太原, Zé 澤, and Lù 潞 in Shānxī 山ī.
They annually produced over seven million four hundred and sixty thousand catties of iron.
Hénán 河南 and Sìchuān 四川 also had iron foundries.
In the twelfth year (1379), Chálíng 茶陵 was added.
In the fifteenth year (1382),
Wáng Yǔndào 王允道, an official from Guǎngpíng 廣平, said:
“Cízhōu 磁州 produces iron;
an official was established there in the Yuán 元 dynasty,
collecting over a million catties annually.
I request to restore the old system.”
The emperor, believing that the people's lives had just settled down
and that re-establishment would cause severe disturbance,
had him flogged and exiled overseas.
In the eighteenth year (1385), the iron foundries of the various Provincial Administration Commissions were abolished.
Later, the Ministry of Works stated:
“Jiāochéng 交城 in Shānxī 山西 produces Yúnzǐtiě 雲子鐵,
which was formerly a tribute of one hundred thousand catties,
used for repairing weapons,
and is not found elsewhere.”
Thus, it was re-established.
Subsequently, Wǔchāng 武昌 and Jízhōu 吉州 were successively restored.
In the final years,
based on the Ministry of Works' recommendation,
all were reopened,
allowing commoners to mine and smelt themselves,
with two parts out of thirty taken as tax.
During the Yǒnglè 永樂 era (1403-1424),
iron foundries were established in Lóngzhōu 龍州, Sìchuān 四chuān, and the Sānwànwèi 三萬衞 of the Liáodōng Dūsī 遼東都司.
During the Jǐngdì 景帝 era (1450-1457),
an official in charge of affairs requested to reopen iron mines in Shǎnxī 陝西 and Níngyuǎn 寧遠.
The Ministry of Works impeached him for violating regulations
and he was imprisoned.
The Supervising Secretary Zhāng Wénzhì 張文質 believed it was inappropriate to block free speech,
so he was released.
In the seventeenth year of Hóngzhì 弘治 (1504),
Guīshàn Xiàn 歸善縣 in Guǎngdōng 廣dōng requested to open iron foundries.
Local officials extorted bribes beyond the regular taxes,
leading to a rebellion by Táng Dàbìn 唐大鬢 and others.
The Censor-in-Chief Líu Dàxià 劉大夏 suppressed it.
In the fourteenth year of Zhèngdé 正德 (1519),
an iron factory was established in Guǎngzhōu 廣州,
managed by the Salt Revenue Department,
and private trading was prohibited, similar to salt laws.
In the thirty-fourth year of Jiājìng 嘉靖 (1555), iron foundries in the prefectures of Jiànníng 建寧 and Yánpíng 延平 were opened.
After the Lóngqìng 隆慶 and Wànlì 萬曆 reigns,
the old system was generally followed,
and special openings were not mentioned.
Copper mines,
in the early Míng 明 dynasty,
were only in Déxīng 德興 and Yánshān 鉛山 in Jiāngxī 江西.
Later, Líangshān 梁山 in Sìchuān 四chuān,
Wǔtái 五臺 in Shānxī 山xī,
Níngqiāng 寧羌 and Lüèyáng 略陽 in Shǎnxī 陝xī, and Yúnnán 雲nán
all mined mercury and malachite.
During Tàizǔ 太祖's reign (1368-1398),
the patrol inspector of Liánzhōu 廉州 stated:
“Jiēzhōu 階州 borders the Western Rong,
and has mercury mines and malachite and purple clay.
I wish to take the land by military force.”
The emperor refused.
Only the Dàwànshān 長官司 Great Wan Mountain Tusi of Guìzhōu 貴州 had mercury and cinnabar fields,
and the mountains of Huìchuān Wèi 會川衞 in Dōngchuān Fǔ 東川府, Sìchuān 四chuān, produced malachite, silver, and copper.
Because these bordered foreign territories,
fearing that soldiers and commoners might secretly extract minerals and cause trouble,
specific prohibitions were issued.
In the seventeenth year of Chénghuà 成化 (1481), the copper mines in Lùnán Zhōu 路南州, Yúnnán 雲nán, were sealed.
In the eighteenth year of Hóngzhì 弘治 (1505), the mercury fields of Bǎnbǎn Chǎngkēng 板板場坑 were abolished.
In the ninth year of Zhèngdé 正德 (1514),
the soldier Zhōu Dá 周達 requested to open various silver mines in Yúnnán 雲nán,
which also included copper, tin, and malachite.
The imperial edict approved it,
and mining was then progressively opened.
During the Jiājìng 嘉靖, Lóngqìng 隆慶, and Wànlì 萬曆 periods (1522-1620),
due to coinage demands,
copper mines in various places in Yúnnán 雲nán were repeatedly opened.
After a long time, the yield gradually decreased.
During the Chóngzhēn 崇禎 era (1628-1644),
ancient coins were then collected to supply the foundries.
In the early years of the Zhèngtǒng reign,
an imperial edict stipulated that all classes of door-front taxes and market stalls
should adhere to the old quotas of the Hóngwǔ era,
〔二一〕and should not be arbitrarily increased under the pretext of paper currency regulations.
Not long after,
following a memorial by Bīngbù Shìláng Yú Qiān,
the tax collection bureaus (shuìkèsī jú) in the directly administered provinces were abolished,
and their taxes were to be collected by the relevant local officials (yǒusī).
The ship material taxes (chuánliào chāo) in Jìníng, Xúzhōu, and Nánjīng Shàngxīnhé were suspended.
The tax gate (chāoguān) at Huòxiàn was moved to Héxīwù.
The ship material tax, which was to be paid at sixty guàn, was reduced to twenty guàn.
Merchants and common people found this convenient.
In the ninth year,
Wáng Zuǒ took charge of the Hùbù,
and official dwellings (guānfáng) were established at Zhāngyìmén
to collect commercial taxes and paper currency (shāngshuì kèchāo).
Tax collection officials (shuìkèsī guān) in the directly administered provinces were reinstated,
and taxation gradually became more complex.
In the first year of the Jǐngtài reign,
Yú Qiān held power,
and the ship material tax was further reduced to fifteen guàn.
Half of the taxes in Zhāngjiāwān and Liáoyáng were reduced.
Dàlǐ Qīng Xuē Xuān stated:
"For those who conceal and do not report the collection of taxes on firewood, charcoal, etc.,
to treat them as having committed the crime of a ship merchant concealing foreign goods,
and confiscate everything,
is too severe.
I request that they be treated under the law for concealing taxes."
The emperor assented.
In the seventh year of the Chénghuà reign, three additional Gōngbù officials were appointed in Wúhú, Jīngzhōu, and Hángzhōu.
Initially, the collection of taxes on bamboo and wood (chōufēn zhúmù)
only involved paper currency (chāo).
Later, it was replaced by silver,
and by this time, it gradually increased to tens of thousands of liǎng.
Soon after, imperial censors (Yùshǐ) were dispatched to collect taxes.
In the early years of Xiàozōng's reign,
Yùshǐ Chén Yáo stated:
"The tax monitoring officials at Chóngwénmén rely on extortion to show their capability,
which is not in line with the dignity of the state."
Consequently, it was ordered that, apart from merchant goods (kèhuò),
vehicles should not be searched and obstructed.
Also, following the advice of Gěishìzhōng Wáng Chǎng,
the tax-collecting imperial censors (chōufēn yùshǐ) in Wúhú, Jīngzhōu, and Hángzhōu were recalled,
and the second-rank subordinate officials of prefectures and subprefectures (fǔzhōu zuòèr guān) were made responsible for supervising the collection of their taxes.
In the thirteenth year, imperial censors were again dispatched.
In the eleventh year of the Zhèngdé reign, collection of incense money (xiāngqián) at the Bìxiá Yuánjūn Temple on Mount Tài was initiated,
following the suggestion of the garrison eunuch (zhènshǒu tàijiàn).
In the twelfth year,
Yùshǐ Hú Wénjìng requested the abolition of newly established tax collection stations (chōufēn chǎng).
Before a year had passed,
Eunuch Zhèng Xǐ requested their reinstatement in Shùndé and Guǎngpíng.
Gōngbù Shàngshū Lǐ Suì equivocated and held a neutral position,
and the practice of arbitrary taxation (héngzhēng) resumed.
Soon after, court eunuchs (zhōngguān) Lǐ Wén and Mǎ Jùn were ordered to the tax collection stations in Húguǎng and Zhèjiāng,
to share tax collection duties with the secretaries (zhǔshì).
In the early years of Shìzōng's reign,
many tax-collecting eunuchs and the tax collection bureaus (shuìkèsī jú) in Jiāngxī, Fújiàn, and Guǎngdōng were abolished.
Also, the eunuchs responsible for collecting taxes on stamped timber (chōuyìn mùzhí zhōngguān) in various prefectures of Zhēndìng were abolished.
The taxes from the nine gates of the capital city,
which in the early Hóngzhì reign amounted to over 660,000 guàn in paper currency
and over 2,880,000 wén in coins annually,
had greatly decreased
by the end of that reign.
From the seventh year of Zhèngdé onwards,
paper currency increased fourfold,
and coins increased by 300,000.
In the third year of Jiājìng,
an edict was issued to follow the precedent of the early Hóngzhì reign,
and the coins were still reduced by 300,000.
Provincial customs duties (guānshuì),
since Chénghuà,
were collected in silver.
Later, coins and paper currency were again collected.
In the eighth year, silver was collected again,
and this became the fixed regulation.
Initially, the paper currency customs (chāoguān) assessed ship materials to determine the tax.
Later, because assessing materials was difficult to verify,
the width of the ship's beam (liángtóu) was used as the standard,
ranging from five chǐ to thirty-six chǐ with variations.
The emperor ordered that a full chǐ be the limit,
and that fractions should not be taxed.
Eunuch Lǐ Néng requested to collect commercial taxes at Shānhǎiguān.
This was implemented for several years,
until Secretary Wū Yuè stated:
"Since there is already a market (quēchǎng) at Bālǐpù Qiántúnwèi in Guǎngníng,
it is not appropriate to levy taxes again."
It was then abolished.
Later, the Shānhǎiguān tax was reinstated,
and the Bālǐpù shop tax (diànqián) was abolished.
In the forty-second year, it was ordered that any surplus beyond the fixed annual quota for each customs gate
should all be deposited into the public treasury.
In the second year of Lóngqìng, the paper currency customs secretaries (chāoguān zhǔshì) were first issued seals of office (guānfáng chǐshū).
Soon after, it was ordered that for paper currency customs gates near a prefecture (fǔ),
the prefect (zhīfǔ) should collect and remit the taxes;
for those far from a prefecture,
the second-rank subordinate officials (zuòèr guān) should store them in the prefectural treasury (fǔkù),
and remit them to the board (bù) quarterly.
The secretary was responsible for verifying the quantity of goods reported by merchants to determine the tax amount,
and had no involvement in the collection or remittance.
In the early years of Shénzōng's reign,
it was ordered that for merchant goods entering the capital,
Héxīwù should issue a red manifest (hóngdān),
and upon arrival at Chóngwénmén, the three taxes (zhèng, tiáo, chuán) should be paid together.
For those not entering the capital,
Héxīwù would only collect the principal tax (zhèngshuì),
exempting the tiáo and chuán taxes.
In the eleventh year of Wànlì, all privately established and unnamed taxes throughout the realm were abolished.
However, since Lóngqìng,
the private imposition of taxes at bridges, roads, and passes (qiáoliáng, dàolù, guānjīn),
which enriched individuals and harmed the people,
could not be eliminated
despite repeated imperial edicts to investigate and abolish them.
By the time of the fire that destroyed the two palaces and three halls (liǎnggōng sāndiàn zāi),
the immense cost of reconstruction
led to the opening of mines and increased taxes.
And then there were the shop rents in Tiānjīn,
pearl taxes in Guǎngzhōu,
surplus salt from the two Huái regions,
provisions from Jīngkǒu,
maritime trade in Zhèjiāng,
salt and tea in Chéngdū,
famous timber in Chóngqìng,
boat taxes on Húkǒu and the Chángjiāng,
shop taxes in Jīngzhōu,
fish and reeds in Bǎodǐ, as well as door-front commercial taxes and oilcloth miscellaneous taxes.
Eunuchs were ubiquitous throughout the empire,
either collecting taxes or supervising mines,
coercing officials,
and striving to exploit the people.
During the reign of Wǔzōng,
the Supervising Eunuch of Maritime Trade, Bì Zhēn, stated:
"According to old regulations,
all ships sailing the seas
were exclusively managed by the Bureau of Maritime Trade.
Recently, they have been under the jurisdiction of the Regional Commanders, Grand Coordinators, and the Three Judicial Offices.
I beg that we return to the old convenient system."
The Ministry of Rites deliberated: The Bureau of Maritime Trade's duty is to handle tribute goods.
As for merchant ships sailing the seas and foreign ships anchored due to wind,
if not specified in an imperial edict,
they should not be involved by precedent.
An imperial decree ordered that it be handled according to the old precedent of Xióng Xuān.
Xuān had previously served as the Supervising Eunuch of Maritime Trade.
He had once, regarding not being involved in the collection of duties from foreign ships of various nations like Mǎlájiā,
petitioned to also manage it.
He was impeached by the Ministry of Rites and dismissed.
Liú Jǐn, privately favoring Zhēn,
mistakenly took this as a precedent.
In the second year of Jiājìng
Japanese envoys Zōngshè and Sòng Sùqīng came to offer tribute by separate routes,
contesting each other's authenticity.
The eunuch of maritime trade, Lài Ēn, accepted Sùqīng's bribe
and sided with Sùqīng.
Zōngshè then plundered Níngbō extensively.
The Censor, Xià Yán, stated that the Japanese problem originated from the maritime trade.
Consequently, it was abolished.
After the maritime trade was abolished,
Japanese sea merchants traveled back and forth freely.
Rogue local gentry on the coast colluded with them.
Laws and prohibitions could not be enforced,
and they turned into bandits.
In the twenty-sixth year
hundreds of Japanese pirate ships were anchored for a long time near Níngbō and Táizhōu.
Thousands of people landed, burned, and plundered.
Zhū Wán, the Grand Coordinator of Zhèjiāng, discovered that the ship owners were all high-ranking officials and powerful families.
They bought foreign goods at inflated prices,
reselling them for profit,
but the payments were not always timely,
which caused unrest.
So he strictly enforced the maritime prohibitions,
destroyed Yúhuáng,
and petitioned to issue an edict warning the powerful families,
but there was no reply.
In the twenty-eighth year
Wán again stated:
"The great heroes of Cháng'ào, such as Lín Gōng, have colluded with barbarian ships to cause trouble.
And powerful rogues communicate for profit,
acting as guides,
ravaging our coast.
They should be brought to justice."
The ministry's reply was not to approve.
However, Wán often executed on his own authority those powerful rogues who communicated with foreigners.
The Imperial Censor, Chén Jiǔdé, impeached Wán for inappropriate measures
and for causing trouble through arbitrary killings.
The emperor arrested Wán for investigation.
After Wán was dismissed,
the rogues became even more fearless.
Foreign collusion and internal strife
brewed into disaster.
Wāng Zhí, Xú Hǎi, Chén Dōng, Má Yè, and others rose,
and there was no peace on the seas.
In the thirty-fifth year
Japanese pirates plundered Fújiàn, Zhèjiāng, and the capital region extensively.
Hú Zōngxiàn, the Censor-in-Chief, sent his retainers Jiǎng Zhōu and Chén Kěyuàn as envoys to Japan to issue a proclamation.
Upon their return, they reported
that the Japanese desired to engage in tribute and trade.
The Ministry of War deliberated that it was not permissible,
so it was stopped.
In the thirty-ninth year
Táng Shùnzhī, the Grand Coordinator of Fèngyáng, proposed reinstating the three Bureaus of Maritime Trade.
The Ministry deliberated and agreed.
In the forty-fourth year
Zhèjiāng, based on the words of Grand Coordinator Liú Jī,
again abolished it.
Fújiàn opened and then was banned again.
During the Wànlì reign,
trade in Fújiàn was reopened,
but only the trade in saltpeter and sulfur was prohibited.
Eventually, both Bureaus of Maritime Trade were fully restored,
with eunuchs leading the positions as before.
During the Yǒnglè period,
three horse markets were established: one at the South Pass of Kāiyuán
to serve Haixī;
one five *lǐ* east of Kāiyuán city;
and one in Guǎngníng,
both to serve the Wúlánghǎisān Wèi (Uriankhai Three Guards).
Prices were set at four grades: top grade, eight bolts of silk
and twelve bolts of cloth;
the next grade, half that amount;
and the lower two grades each decreasing by one unit.
Later, the markets east of the city and in Guǎngníng were abolished,
with only the horse market at Kāiyuán South Pass remaining.
The Dàtóng horse market began in the third year of Zhèngtǒng
Grand Coordinator Lú Ruì requested that military and civilians be allowed to trade camels and horses at fair prices.
High-ranking officials and commanders like Lǐ Yuán communicated with interpreters,
and the trade of weapons and copper-iron was prohibited.
〔二四〕The emperor agreed.
In the fourteenth year
Censor-in-Chief Shěn Gù requested to use silver from the treasury of the Xīnjí Provisional Regional Military Commission to buy horses.
At that time, Yěxiān offered tribute horses for market trade.
The eunuch Wáng Zhèn arbitrarily cut the price of his horses.
Yěxiān launched a major invasion,
leading to the Tǔmù Incident.
In the fourteenth year of Chénghuà
Chén Yuè governed Liáodōng,
and reopened the horse markets for the Three Guards.
Interpreters Liú Hǎi and Yáo Ān indulged in rampant extortion,
causing resentment among the various Wúlánghǎi tribes.
They harassed Guǎngníng
and no longer came to the market.
Wáng Yuè, Minister of War, requested that one *cāncóng* (assistant commander) and one official from the Provincial Administration Commission supervise it,
to prevent any encroachment or exploitation.
Consequently, Hǎi and Ān were punished.
Soon after, it was ordered that Haixī and the Wúlánghǎi Three Guards enter the market;
Kāiyuán would have one market per month,
and Guǎngníng two markets per month,
with the taxes from the mutual trade used for rewards and subsidies.
During the Zhèngdé period,
it was ordered that those entering the market, once inspected,
must leave the territory by the deadline,
not carry bows and arrows,
and not approach the border wall
on days other than market days.
In the thirtieth year of Jiājìng
based on the words of Grand Commander Qiú Luán,
an imperial edict was issued to open horse markets in Xuānfǔ and Dàtóng.
Vice Minister Shǐ Dào was appointed to manage it.
Yáng Jìshèng, a Bureau Secretary of the Ministry of War, remonstrated.
It was not heeded.
Āndá soon invaded and plundered;
if the Dàtóng market was open, they raided Xuānfǔ;
if the Xuānfǔ market was open, they raided Dàtóng.
Before the currency had left the border,
the alarm reports arrived.
The emperor began to regret it
and recalled Dào.
However, the various tribes coveted the profits of the horse markets
and dared not openly declare a major invasion.
Border officials also often feared and deterred them
by enticing them with mutual trade.
The following year, the Dàtóng horse market was abolished.
Xuānfǔ's market had not yet been cut off,
and raids continued,
so it was also completely abolished.
In the fourth year of Lóngqìng
Āndá's grandson, Bǎhàn Nàjí, surrendered.
Thereupon, the discussion of tribute, enfeoffment, and mutual trade arose.
And the Xuānfǔ and Dàtóng mutual markets were reopened,
and the border became somewhat peaceful.
However, the rewards and subsidies were very generous.
The court saved on the provisions for guest soldiers and reduced patrol silver to fund them.
Rewards were increased year after year,
but demands grew even greater.
The officials in charge also secretly embezzled funds,
and border expenses consequently exceeded what was proper.
The Yìzhōu timber market in Liáodōng opened in the twenty-third year of Wànlì
Details are in the biography of Lǐ Huàlóng.
In the twenty-sixth year
it was abolished,
and the horse market was also abolished.
Later, Grand Commander Lǐ Chéngliáng strongly requested its restoration,
and Wàn Shìdé, the Grand Coordinator of Jìliáo, also memorialized the court.
In the twenty-ninth year
〔二五〕and thereafter became permanent.
Collation Notes

Volume 58, Food and Money 6, Palace Procurement and Manufacturing — Procurement and Manufacturing — Firewood and Charcoal — Timber Procurement — Pearl Fisheries — Textile Manufacturing — Porcelain Manufacturing — Salary and Account Management
The matters of procurement and manufacturing
varied in extravagance and frugality throughout successive dynasties.
Broadly speaking, it was lavish during Yīngzōng's reign,
followed by Xiànzōng and Wǔzōng,
reaching its peak during Shìzōng and Shénzōng.
Its itemized tasks were numerous and complicated,
and demands for resources were varied and confused.
The most massive and difficult
was timber procurement.
The largest annual productions
were textile manufacturing and porcelain manufacturing.
Wine, liquor, and fine dishes were managed by the Guānglù Sì.
Procurement and completion were handled by the Four Bureaus of the Ministry of Works, internal eunuch agencies, or dedicated special envoys.
Firewood and charcoal were managed by the Xīxīn Sì.
However, the greatest harm to the people
was often caused by eunuchs.
In the early Míng dynasty,
tributes presented to the court were simplified and reduced.
Prefectures and counties offered fragrant rice, ginseng, and grape wine,
but Tàizǔ considered this burdensome to the people
and rejected them.
In the early Rénzōng reign,
Guānglù Qīng Jǐng Quán memorialized,
saying it was an annual custom to dispatch a principal official to Nánjīng to procure civets with jade-like faces.
The Emperor rebuked him, saying:
"You petty man do not understand the principles of governance.
I have just issued an edict
to cease all non-urgent affairs to relieve the people.
How can I, for the trivial matter of food,
betray such a great trust!"
During Xuānzōng's reign,
the practice of government officials in Hézhōu buying dairy cows during the Yǒnglè period to produce ghee for court tribute was abolished,
and the cows were given to the garrison troops.
Two Imperial Censors were ordered to inspect the Guānglù Sì.
Any internal or external officials who overspent or made excessive demands
were to be reported.
In the early Yīngzōng administration,
the Sān Yáng held sway,
and the number of pastoral yellow cattle in the Southern Capital Region was reduced by forty thousand.
The amounts of molasses, fruits, dried meats, ghee, tea buds, glutinous rice, millet, and medicinal materials were all reduced by varying degrees.
Fishing officials in various locations were abolished.
Within a few months of his accession,
many things were economized.
There were over three hundred and seven thousand pieces of tableware for imperial use
made by the Nán Gōngbù,
including golden dragon and phoenix white porcelain wares
made in Ráozhōu,
vermilion food boxes and other wares
made by the Yíngshàn Suǒ
for delivering food to the palace.
The Shàngshàn Jiān often embezzled these.
The Emperor ordered an inventory to be prepared,
and the items were to be returned in full.
During the Jǐngdì reign,
following Yú Qiān's advice,
the practice of eunuchs in Zhēndìng and Héjiān procuring game and in Zhígū (Hai Kou) making dried fish was abolished.
In the eighth year of Tiānshùn (1464),
the Guānglù's fruit and material supplies totaled over one million two hundred and sixty-eight thousand catties,
an increase of one-fourth over the old quota.
In the early Chénghuà reign,
an edict decreed that the number of livestock in the Guānglù Sì should not exceed one hundred thousand.
The following year,
Lǐ Chūn, a minister of the Guānglù Sì, requested an increase.
Lǐbù Shàngshū Yáo Kuí said:
"During the Zhèngtǒng period,
the annual expenditure on chickens, geese, sheep, and pigs was thirty to forty thousand.
Since Tiānshùn, it has increased fourfold,
an excessive waste.
I request to follow the previous edict."
Two years later,
Jǐshì Zhōng Chén Yuè said:
"When the Guānglù purchases goods from the market,
it generally seizes them by force.
Vendors who encounter them
are like victims of robbery.
The supplies provided by the Guānglù
were formerly all sufficient.
That this is not the case now
is due to excessive demands
and misappropriation and wasteful spending."
Dàxuéshì Péng Shí also said:
"The Guānglù Sì employs scoundrels as purchasing agents,
who exploit public office for private gain,
depriving the people of all their profits.
I request that, according to the precedents of the Xuāndé and Zhèngtǒng periods,
the supplies be judiciously managed
and purchasing agents be prohibited."
Consequently, the annual quota for fish and fruits was reduced by one-tenth.
In the first year of Hóngzhì (1488), an order was issued to the Guānglù to reduce increased supplies.
Initially,
the Guānglù would advance official funds to purchase goods,
and the merchants and clerks would embezzle from this.
Later, when it was ordered that various trades first report and deliver goods before receiving payment,
idle people emerged, calling themselves 'reporting heads,'
who, under the pretext of supplying the court,
depressed prices and exacted double the amount,
filling their private pockets.
Yùshǐ Lǐ Luán reported this,
and the Emperor ordered it to be prohibited.
In the fifteenth year (1502),
Guānglù Qīng Wáng Héng
listed the numbers of wine and food for internal and external officials and servants, and fodder for animals kept,
totaling one hundred and twenty items.
An imperial decree was then issued,
stating that some items were to remain as before,
some were to be halved,
and some were to be stopped entirely.
Thus, the tigers at Gānmíng Mén, cats at Nánhǎizi, eagles and dogs at Xīhuá Mén, mountain monkeys at Yùmǎ Jiān, large pigeons at Xī'ān Mén, etc., were released,
and reductions were made in varying degrees,
while for those that remained, their feed was reduced.
Since the Chénghuà period,
over eighty 'sitting household' attendants were added,
and over one hundred and fifty eunuchs for conveying soup and rice were added by transmission.
The regular tributes from throughout the empire were insufficient,
so purchases were instead compelled from shops in the capital.
Payment was not made promptly,
burdening the merchants.
Bīngbù Shàngshū Liú Dàxià spoke of this due to an astrological omen,
and consequently, eunuchs were cut,
saving over eight hundred thousand taels of silver annually.
During Wǔzōng's reign,
daily and monthly provisions for various palaces
were several times greater than in the Tiānshùn period.
The number of kitchen staff,
which was only over six thousand three hundred during Rénzōng's time,
increased by one-fourth by Xiànzōng's time.
In the early Shìzōng reign,
it was reduced to four thousand one hundred,
and the annual silver quota was economized to thirteen thousand taels.
In middle age, it increased again to four hundred thousand.
When the assigned quota was insufficient,
funds were borrowed from the Tàicāng.
When the Tàicāng was also insufficient,
the original supplying prefectures and departments were ordered to increase their assignments proportionally.
Thus, the Emperor suspected embezzlement
and ordered the Lǐbù to investigate the situation,
requiring the Guānglù Sì to report the figures.
The Emperor again issued a decree of inquiry and reprimand.
Then, Imperial Censors were ordered to examine the monthly provision reports,
saving over twenty thousand taels of silver within two months.
From then on, this became a regular practice annually.
Previously, items for court tribute
were contributed according to local products
and called "annual provisions."
If these were insufficient,
officials would use money to purchase them,
which was called "procurement."
Later, both in-kind and monetary payments were accepted,
and procurement became increasingly frequent.
Consequently, merchants were summoned to buy goods,
but prices were often low,
and merchants disappeared.
In the twenty-seventh year (1548),
the Hùbù stated:
"In the capital, when merchants are summoned to deliver goods and receive payment,
wealthy merchants evade this,
and those who respond to the call are all poor and weak households.
We request a thorough census and review."
Jǐshì Zhōng Luó Chóngkuí said:
"The reason why various merchants are severely distressed
is that when prices are low, they are reduced,
but when prices are high, they dare not increase them.
Moreover, acceptance is not timely,
and if goods encounter wind and rain,
they become unusable,
often leading to losses.
After acceptance,
the responsible officials change frequently,
payment is not made immediately,
or even completely withheld.
Even if payment is fortunately made,
officials deduct from above,
and subordinate functionaries extort from below.
Although it is nominally an 'equal assessment,'
what is received is less than half.
If these abuses are eliminated,
merchants will willingly come forward.
Why is a census and review needed?"
Although the Emperor accepted his words,
a census and review were still conducted as proposed by the Hùbù.
During the reign of Mùzōng,
Lǐ Jiàn, the Junior Supervisor of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, submitted a memorial outlining ten matters.
The emperor approved it,
making significant reductions and curtailments: stopping the supply of Chéngtiān fragrant rice and rare birds and exotic beasts from foreign lands,
and abolishing the supply of fresh fish from Bǎodí.
All newly presented items
were to be managed by the Court of Imperial Entertainments,
without dispatching eunuchs.
He also agreed to the request of Grand Eunuch Lǐ Fāng,
stopping the levy of additional fine rice and white and green salt,
ordering that everything should follow the precedent set during the Chénghuá and Hóngzhì periods.
Censor Wáng Zōngzǎi requested the cessation of additional levies.
The Board's discussion decided to strictly adhere to the original quotas,
namely over 1,078,000 catties of fruit,
and over 58,000 taels of silver for livestock,
thus waiving over 20,000 taels of silver in additional levies.
Before this could be implemented,
Shénzōng ascended the throne
and issued an edict granting the waiver.
In the last years of Shìzōng’s reign,
annual expenditure was limited to 170,000 taels.
Mùzōng cut 20,000,
leaving a little over 150,000,
making administrative expenses quite economical.
In the early years of Wànlì,
it was further reduced to 130,000-140,000.
In the middle years, it gradually increased,
approaching 300,000,
and the burden on shopkeepers became even heavier.
At that time, eunuchs presented tribute and extorted bribes,
calling it "shop cushion money,"
an immeasurable expense.
The funds disbursed were insufficient to offset it,
and the people could not bear it,
fleeing and hiding en masse.
Therefore, wealthy households in the capital were conscripted as merchants.
When the order was issued,
those conscripted were like people going to their deaths,
bribing heavily to secure exemption.
Officials secretly apprehended them,
as if hunting for criminals.
Liú Yuēshū, the Magistrate of Wǎnpíng, stated:
"Once the capital's people are conscripted as merchants,
they are stripped of every last hair,
their capital entirely exhausted.
I request that advance payments be generously estimated and issued first,
to relieve the people's distress."
Censor Wáng Mèngzhèn denounced him for overstepping his authority,
and Yuēshū impeached himself and resigned.
By the time of Xīzōng,
the merchant burden became even heavier;
some supplied goods to the government but never received a single coin.
During the Hóngwǔ era,
when purchasing goods for the palace,
the price was usually increased by ten cash compared to market value,
thus benefiting the lower ranks at the expense of the higher.
In the early Yǒnglè period,
those who proposed collecting five-colored stones were reprimanded,
and because the tribute of alum from Wēnzhōu burdened the people,
the dyeing of cloth was abolished.
However, the dispatch of palace eunuchs
began at this time.
Construction projects flourished,
requisitions became more urgent,
and for items not native to the area,
people went bankrupt to procure them.
The demands for military equipment were especially innumerable.
During Rénzōng’s reign,
mountain fields, gardens, lakes and ponds, mines, fruit trees, and beeswax reserves, which had official guardians and prohibitions,
were all granted to the people.
Xuānzōng abolished the practice of obtaining gold and silver through barrier taxes.

Many other items, such as paper, indigo, ramie silk, gauze, pongee, satin, spices, vermillion, gold foil, safflower, madder,麂皮(jǐpí) deerskin, incense and wax, medicines, fruits, seafood, and cinnabar-red gilded dragon and phoenix artifacts,
were largely abolished or reduced.
Vice Censor-in-Chief Yì Qiān stated:
"The prices paid by officials for purchased materials
are less than one-tenth of their value;
