it is no different from taking them for free."
The emperor praised and accepted this,
ordering the Ministry of Works to investigate and punish.
Furthermore, acting on the words of Hǎo Zhì, the Ambassador of the Tài'ān Prefecture Tax Bureau,
all dispatched officials were recalled,
and an edict was issued that henceforth no unauthorized dispatches were permitted.
Except for military weapons and supplies,
all purchases were completely halted.
However, although edicts of leniency and exemption were repeatedly issued,
and eunuchs were repeatedly ordered to withdraw,
these commands were not genuinely implemented.
Eunuchs frequently claimed to be "procuring,"
oppressively extorting from the people.
Only after Yuán Qí, Ruǎn Jùduì, and over ten others were executed
did the problem somewhat subside.
Upon Yīngzōng’s ascension,
purchases from various places and the construction of ships for voyages to the Western Oceans were abolished,
and many superfluous expenses were ordered to be reduced.
In the eighth year of Zhèngtǒng (1443),
because procurement disturbed the people,
it was first ordered that payments be made by converting money and grain held in reserves,
and then transporting them to the two capitals nearby.
Previously, during Rénzōng’s time,
eunuchs were ordered to guard the border fortresses.
Yīngzōng again established eunuch garrisons in various provinces,
and there were also defense commanders and sub-commanders,
thus eunuchs were deployed throughout the empire.
This became even more severe during Xiànzōng’s reign;
envoys for purchasing books and collecting medicines
searched for rare treasures,
leaving nothing behind.
They suppressed the sale of salt certificates,
privately hunted birds,
squandered state funds,
and accepted private bribes,
often amounting to tens of thousands.
Precious incense from Tài Yuè and Tài Hé mountains,
which typically consumed 7,000 catties over three years,
was now doubled.
For Imperial Household materials,
prices increased five or sixfold.
Upon Xiàozōng’s ascension,
there were considerable reductions and curtailments.
Luó Míng, the Provincial Governor of Gānsù, stated:
"Garrison commanders and sub-commanders, both internal and external officials, compete in offering tribute.
They each dispatch envoys and subordinates to border garrisons to search for local products,
calling it 'procurement,'
but in reality, they deduct from soldiers' monthly rations and horse prices,
or cleverly extort strange treasures, dogs, and horses from foreign peoples.
They also establish various kitchens and dairies,
conscripting cooks to make butter and other items.
By the time of transport,
they cause disturbances along the way.
I beg that all these be abolished."
The report was approved.
However, thereafter, wasteful expenditures gradually increased.
When Wǔzōng appointed Liú Jǐn,
his profiteering knew no bounds.
Garrison eunuchs typically contributed tens of thousands of taels of silver.
There were various names for imperial shops,
and many annual requisitions were for non-local products.
When various Provincial Administration Commissioners came to court,
they each presented the harms of tribute collection,
but none were heeded.
In the early years of Shìzōng,
imperial household supplies were reduced by nine-tenths compared to the Zhèngdé period.
After the middle years,
construction for rituals and Daoist rites,
and the procurement of timber, incense,
jade, and precious stones,
kept officials and common people constantly busy.
The use of yellow and white wax reached over 300,000 catties.
There were also "summoned purchases"
and "conversion payments,"
which were three times the regular amount.
Agarwood, rosewood, and sea lacquer and other incenses amounted to over 100,000 catties.
They also dispatched people on various routes to buy ambergris,
but did not obtain it for over ten years.
The envoys then requested foreign ships to enter the harbor,
and finally obtained it after a long time.
For the Fāngzé and Rìcháotán altars,
red and yellow jade was used for sacrificial vessels.
When it could not be found,
it was purchased from the border regions of Shǎnxī.
Envoys were dispatched to search for it in Ādān (Aden),
two thousand li southwest of Tǔlǔfān (Turfan).
A considerable amount of silver from the Grand Granary
was taken into the Chéngyùn Treasury
to procure gold, jewels, and pearls.
Thus, cat's eye, emerald, malachite, sapphire, red jasper, northern river washed stones, diamonds, lapis lazuli, amethyst, and yellow jade
were all purchased.
Mùzōng inherited this situation
and pursued the purchase of jewels even more urgently.
Investigating Censors Lǐ Jǐ and Chén Wúdé submitted memorials remonstrating.
Lǐ Jǐ was imprisoned,
and Chén Wúdé was stripped of his official status.
From then on, provisions and requisitions greatly increased.
In the early years of Shénzōng,
Cuī Mǐn, the Grand Eunuch of the Imperial Chéngyùn Treasury, requested to buy gold and pearls.
Zhāng Jūzhèng sealed and returned Mǐn's memorial,
and the matter was consequently dropped.
After a long time,
the emperor grew increasingly avaricious,
and proposals for mining greatly flourished.
Expenses amounted to tens of thousands,
and the price of jewels increased twentyfold compared to previous times.
Chén Qú, Minister of the Ministry of Revenue, stated that the treasury was depleted
and advocated for greater frugality.
An imperial decree severely reprimanded him.
As for the Prefect of Shùntiān Prefecture, he was demoted
because his purchases of large pearls and dark green jade did not meet imperial specifications.
By the later years,
eunuchs were dispatched everywhere,
and procurement and manufacturing became even more frequent.
The Imperial Household reported a shortage,
even transferring silver intended for border defense to supply it.
Xīzōng entirely deferred to the eunuchs,
making procurement and manufacturing even more extensive.
Upon Zhuāngliè Dì’s ascension,
he finally began to rectify and economize,
but the treasury was already exhausted.
During the Yǒnglè reign,
the Rear Army Chief Military Commission (Hòujūn Dūdū Fǔ) sourced firewood and charcoal.
Soldiers from the seventeen garrisons (wèisuǒ) of Xuānfǔ were conscripted to collect it from the border regions.
In the early Xuānzōng reign,
considering that border timber could be used to impede enemy cavalry,
and that border troops should not be engaged in other duties,
an edict was issued to exempt them from felling and collecting,
ordering instead an annual payment of over twenty thousand liǎng of silver.
The Rear Army Chief Military Commission then summoned merchants to purchase and deliver it.
In the fourth year, a mountain factory was established in Yìzhōu,
and the Minister (shìláng) of the Ministry of Works (Gōngbù) was ordered to oversee it.
Civilians (mínfū) from the Northern Metropolitan Area (Běizhí), Shāndōng, and Shānxī were conscripted for transportation,
while the Rear Army Chief Military Commission continued to pay silver and summon merchants as before.
Initially,
the annual consumption of firewood was only over twenty million jīn.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
this increased to over forty million jīn.
As transportation became difficult,
Běizhí, Shāndōng, and Shānxī all began to pay silver to summon merchants.
During the Zhèngdé reign,
firewood consumption further increased,
raising the cost to over thirty thousand liǎng.
When receiving firewood and charcoal,
an additional surcharge of three-tenths was applied;
eunuchs (zhōngguān) often privately increased it several times over.
Arrears accumulated daily,
to the point where three years' worth of regular supply was used to cover one year's surcharge.
Minister (shàngshū) Lǐ Suì proposed
that the regular supply and surcharge should balance each other,
but the receivers again privately increased it,
treating forty thousand jīn as ten thousand jīn.
Furthermore, there were floating fees for payment and delivery,
which the people could not bear.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he appropriately reduced it.
In the sixth year of Lóngqìng,
the Rear Army Chief Military Commission found procurement and delivery difficult,
and it was reassigned to the Armory Department (Wǔkù Sī) of the Ministry of War (Bīngbù).
During the Wànlì reign,
the annual cost of firewood was estimated at three hundred thousand liǎng of silver.
Eunuchs were allowed to levy and demand payment from various merchants,
extracting it with cruel punishments,
and people said that the Department of Firewood Economy (Xīxīn Sī) was a trap.
The task of timber felling
began with Chéngzǔ's repairs and construction of the palaces in Běijīng.
In the fourth year of Yǒnglè, Minister Sòng Lǐ was sent to Sìchuān,
Minister Gǔ Pǔ to Jiāngxī,
Shī Kuí and Jīn Chún to Húguǎng,
Vice Censor-in-Chief (Fù Dū Yùshǐ) Liú Guān to Zhèjiāng,
and Assistant Censor-in-Chief (Qiān Dū Yùshǐ) Shǐ Zhòngchéng to Shānxī.
Lǐ reported that several large trees
floated themselves down a great valley into the river overnight.
The Son of Heaven considered it divine,
named the mountain Shénmù Shān (Divine Wood Mountain),
and sent officials to offer sacrifices.
In the tenth year, Lǐ was again ordered to fell timber in Sìchuān.
Upon Rénzōng's accession,
this task was abolished.
In the first year of Xuāndé, when renovating the altars and temples for Heaven, Earth, mountains, and rivers in Nánjīng,
Ministers Huáng Zōngzǎi and Wú Tíngyòng were again ordered to fell timber in Húguǎng.
Not long after,
due to a drought, it was stopped.
Soon after, large timber was again felled in Húguǎng,
and the Ministry of Works was instructed to make appropriate reductions,
but it was again suspended shortly thereafter.
In other places, felling was also started and stopped periodically.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
the imperial treasury (nèitǎng) was used to repair Qīngníng Gōng,
and timber felling in Sìchuān was halted.
During the Zhèngdé reign,
timber was felled in Húguǎng, Chuān, and Guì,
and Minister Liú Bǐng was ordered to oversee its transportation.
Eunuch Liú Yǎng impeached him for not selecting suitable timber for beams and pillars,
and Bǐng was ordered to submit a report,
while Minister of Works Lǐ Suì had his salary docked.
In the first year of Jiājìng, the Shénmù Qianhù Suǒ and its garrison soldiers were abolished.
In the twentieth year,
after a fire in the ancestral temple,
Minister of Works Pān Jiàn and Vice Censor-in-Chief Dài Jīn were sent to Húguǎng and Sìchuān to procure large timber.
In the twenty-sixth year, Minister of Works Liú Bóyuè was again sent to Sìchuān, Húguǎng, and Guìzhōu to fell timber,
with the Húguǎng province alone incurring expenses of over three million three hundred thirty-nine thousand liǎng.
Officials were also sent to investigate large timber left in other places.
County (jùnxiàn) officials (yǒusī) were arrested, prosecuted, and dismissed for delaying important works, not just once;
the counties along the Hé River suffered particularly.
During the Wànlì reign,
when construction of the three main halls (sān diàn) commenced,
nanmu and fir trees were felled in Húguǎng, Sìchuān, and Guìzhōu,
costing over nine million three hundred thousand liǎng of silver,
which was levied from the common people,
more than double the expenses of the Jiājìng years.
For the felling of Yingpíng and Tiaojiáo timber in Southern Zhílì and Zhèjiāng,
merchants' arrears reached two hundred fifty thousand.
Censors (kēchén) impeached the transport officials for delays and embezzlement,
but there was no response.
Public and private funds were squandered and embezzled,
leading to distress for all.
The pearl fisheries (zhūchí) in Guǎngdōng
were typically harvested once every few decades.
During the Xuānzōng reign,
someone requested that eunuchs be sent to harvest pearls from the Dōngguǎn pearl fishery;
he was imprisoned.
Yīngzōng first appointed eunuchs to supervise them,
and during the Tiānshùn period, a harvest was conducted once.
By the twelfth year of Hóngzhì,
as the pearls had aged for a long time,
the yield was the largest,
costing over ten thousand liǎng of silver,
and yielding twenty-eight thousand liǎng of pearls.
Consequently, the supervising eunuchs were dismissed.
In the ninth year of Zhèngdé, another harvest was conducted,
and in the fifth year of Jiājìng, another,
but the pearls were small and immature,
and very few.
In the eighth year, another edict ordered harvesting.
Lín Fù, the Grand Coordinator (xúnfǔ) of Liǎngguǎng, said:
"During the pearl harvesting in the fifth year,
over fifty people died,
and only eighty liǎng of pearls were obtained.
The world called it 'exchanging lives for pearls.'
I fear that even today, though we might exchange lives for pearls,
they might not be obtainable."
Investigating Censor (gěishìzhōng) Wáng Xīwén said:
"For the Léi and Lián pearl fisheries,
our ancestors established officials to supervise them,
merely to prevent disputes among the people.
During the Zhèngdé period,
the rebellious eunuchs were in power,
and they arbitrarily ordered harvesting,
spreading poison along the coast.
When Your Majesty ascended the throne,
you abolished the Pearl Fishery Vice Supervisor (Zhūchí Shàojiān),
but it was reinstated not long after.
Driving innocent people
into unforeseen dangers
to seek an uncertain object,
and demanding an impossible quota,
is not befitting a sagely reign."
Neither was he heeded.
In the sixth year of Lóngqìng, an edict ordered Yúnnán to contribute twenty thousand pieces of gemstones,
and Guǎngdōng to harvest eight thousand liǎng of pearls.
Upon Shénzōng's accession,
this was halted.
However, later, for presentations to the Empress Dowager,
and for the enfeoffment, investiture, and marriages of princes, imperial sons, and princesses,
annual provisions of gold, pearls, and gemstones were ordered.
Eunuchs Lǐ Jìng and Lǐ Fèng were again sent to Guǎngdōng to harvest over five thousand one hundred liǎng of pearls.
Investigating Censor Bāo Jiànjié strenuously remonstrated.
It was not accepted.
Harvesting was only stopped in the thirty-second year.
In the forty-first year,
based on the words of Commander (zhǐhuī) Ní Yīng,
it was reopened.
According to the Míng system,
weaving and dyeing in the two capitals (Liǎng Jīng),
both internal and external bureaus were established.
The internal bureaus were for imperial tribute,
the external bureaus for public use.
Nánjīng had the Shénbái Táng and Gōngyìng Jīfáng;
prefectures (fǔ) like Sūzhōu and Hángzhōu also had their own weaving and dyeing bureaus,
producing a fixed amount annually.
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
weaving and dyeing bureaus were established in provinces (xíngshěng) like Sìchuān and Shānxī,
and in Shàoxīng, Zhèjiāng.
Indigo dye establishments (lándìansuǒ) were also set up in Yízhēn and Liùhé,
cultivating indigo plants to supply dyeing needs.
Not long after, all were abolished.
The annual weaving of silk fabrics by local officials (yǒusī) across the realm was also abolished.
For rewards and grants,
silk was provided,
and a bureau was set up in Hòuhú for weaving.
During the Yǒnglè reign,
the Shèxiàn weaving and dyeing bureau was re-established.
Shǎnxī was ordered to weave camel hair fabrics.
During the Zhèngtǒng reign,
the Quánzhōu weaving bureau was established.
In the fourth year of Tiānshùn, eunuchs were sent to the five prefectures of Sūzhōu, Sōngjiāng, Hángzhōu, Jiāxīng, and Húzhōu,
to additionally produce seven thousand bolts of patterned silk beyond the regular quota.
Minister of Works Wēng Shìzī requested a reduction,
was imprisoned in the Jǐnyī Wèi prison,
and demoted to Prefect (zhīfǔ) of Héngzhōu.
The practice of assigned additional production began here.
Upon Xiàozōng's early accession,
weaving in Sūzhōu, Hángzhōu, Jiāxīng, Húzhōu, and Yìngtiān was suspended and exempted.
Later, it was re-established,
and eunuchs were given salt certificates (yányǐn),
to be sold in Huái for funding.
In the first year of Zhèngdé
(1506), the Shàngyījiān [Office of Imperial Robes] reported:
"The internal stores of various types of ramie silk, gauze, sheer silk, brocade, and shimmering fabrics,
embroidered with python-dragons, dòuniú, fēiyú, qílín, and lions on the sleeves and knee-panels,
as well as dòuniú, flying immortals, and celestial deer on the chest and back patches,
were all woven during the Tiānshùn
(1457-1464) era and have now been entirely depleted by imperial awards.
We request that the prefectures of Yìngtiān, Sūzhōu, and Hángzhōu be ordered to weave new ones according to the existing patterns."
The Emperor approved.
Consequently, over seventeen thousand bolts were manufactured.
During the Chénghuà
(1465-1487) and Hóngzhì
(1488-1505) eras, awards were granted very sparingly.
But from the time Liú Jǐn rose to power,
requests from favored eunuchs gradually expanded,
and those who had not even reached adulthood presumed to wear official robes and insignia,
leading to a daily increase in lavish awards.
Court eunuchs endlessly begged for salt warrants and customs passes,
and when supervising weaving,
they intimidated and coerced officials.
By the time of Shìzōng
(1521-1567), this scourge had not ceased.
Shortly after his accession, he ordered court eunuchs to supervise weaving in Nánjīng, Sūzhōu, Hángzhōu, and Shǎnxī.
When Mùzōng
(1567-1572) ascended the throne,
an edict was issued to withdraw the eunuchs,
but soon after, they were dispatched again.
In the seventh year of Wànlì
(1579), Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng suffered from floods,
and the Supervising Secretary Gù Jiǔsī and others requested the recall of the imperial eunuchs supervising weaving,
but the Emperor did not listen.
Grand Secretary Zhāng Jūzhèng strongly argued that with the famine and exhausted populace,
they could not endure the coercion,
and only then was it permitted.
However, soon after, eunuchs were dispatched again.
After Zhāng Jūzhèng died,
the amount of weaving gradually increased.
Beyond the annual production of the five prefectures of Sūzhōu, Hángzhōu, Sōngjiāng, Jiāxīng, and Húzhōu,
orders were also issued to Zhèjiāng, Fújiàn, Chángzhōu, Zhènjiāng, Huīzhōu, Níngguó, Yángzhōu, and Guǎngdé prefectures and subprefectures to produce,
adding over ten thousand bolts.
Shǎnxī produced over seventy-four thousand bolts of wool,
while Nánzhí [Nánzhílì] and Zhèjiāng produced ramie silk, gauze, sheer silk, damask, pongee, and ordinary silk fabric,
and Shānxī produced Lù Pongee,
all exceeding the old standards in length.
Within two or three years,
expenditures reached one million,
drawn from the Ministries of Revenue and Works,
draining the treasury,
and withholding funds needed for military and national affairs.
Ministerial and censorate officials repeatedly protested,
but none were heeded.
In his later years,
tax supervisors were again ordered to concurrently manage these affairs,
and corruption and abuses grew daily.
In the early Míng dynasty, the Northern and Southern Weaving and Dyeing Bureaus were established.
Nánjīng supplied looms,
and various provinces and direct-ruled areas annually produced goods for use,
while Sūzhōu and Hángzhōu weaving operations
were sometimes active, sometimes halted.
From the mid-Wànlì
era, frequent assignments were made,
reaching 150,000 bolts annually,
and this long-standing practice
became the norm.
Shǎnxī's production of wool robes
occurred occasionally during the Hóngzhì and Zhèngdé eras,
but during the Jiājìng and Lóngqìng eras, eunuchs were dispatched again,
and this too became a regular practice.
Regarding kiln production,
there was the Línqīng Brick Kiln outside,
and in the capital, the Glazed Tile and Black Tile Kilns,
all producing bricks and tiles
to supply construction and repair.
Xuānzōng
(1425-1435) first dispatched the eunuch Zhāng Shàn to Ráozhōu
to produce altars, seats, and ritual vessels of white porcelain with dragon and phoenix patterns for the Fèngxiāndiàn,
and Cízhōu produced ritual vessels for the Zhào princely household.
A year later,
Zhāng Shàn was executed for a crime,
and his assignment was terminated.
In the first year of Zhèngtǒng
(1436), the people of Fúliáng submitted over fifty thousand pieces of porcelain,
which were paid for with paper currency.
Private production of yellow, purple, red, green, blue, indigo, and white-ground blue-and-white porcelain was prohibited,
with violators punished by death.
Upon the completion of the imperial palaces,
orders were given to produce nine-dragon and nine-phoenix dining tables and other items,
and then later, blue dragon on white ground flower vases were also produced.
Wáng Zhèn deemed some to have cracks,
and dispatched a Jǐnyīwèi commander to flog the supervising official,
issuing an imperial edict for a eunuch to oversee the re-production.
During the Chénghuà
(1465-1487) era, eunuchs were dispatched to Jǐngdézhèn in Fúliáng
to fire imperial porcelain,
which was the most extensive and longest-lasting,
at immense cost.
In the early Xiàozōng
(1487-1505) era, the eunuchs were recalled,
but soon after, they were dispatched again.
In the fifteenth year of Hóngzhì (1502), they were recalled again.
By the end of Zhèngdé
(1521), they were dispatched again.
From the Hóngzhì era onwards,
over 300,000 pieces of porcelain remained unfinished.
In the early Jiājìng
(1522-1566) era, eunuchs were dispatched to supervise it.
Supervising Secretary Chén Gāomó stated that this caused great harm to the people
and requested its cessation.
The Emperor did not listen.
In the sixteenth year (1537), new ritual vessels for the Seven Imperial Tombs were made.
In the thirty-seventh year (1558), officials were dispatched to Jiāngxī
to produce thirty thousand pieces of porcelain for the inner palace's Daoist altars.
Later, a Ráozhōu Subprefect was additionally appointed
specifically to manage the firing at the imperial porcelain factory.
At this time, construction was most frequent,
with brick kilns near the capital and in Sūzhōu.
During the Lóngqìng
(1567-1572) era, an edict ordered the firing of over one hundred thousand pieces of porcelain in Jiāngxī.
In the nineteenth year of Wànlì (1591), an order was given to produce 159,000 pieces,
and then an additional 80,000 were added,
which was still unfinished by the thirty-eighth year (1610).
Thereafter, this task also gradually ceased.
Of the state's expenditures,
none were greater than emoluments and stipends.
In the ninth year of Hóngwǔ (1376), the annual provisions for imperial princes and princesses were stipulated.
A Qīnwáng [prince of the first rank] received:
50,000 *shí* of rice,
25,000 *guàn* of paper currency,
40 bolts of brocade,
300 bolts of ramie silk,
100 bolts each of gauze and sheer silk,
500 bolts of silk,
1,000 bolts each of winter and summer cloth,
2,000 *liǎng* of cotton,
200 salt warrants,
and 1,000 *jīn* of tea,
all disbursed annually.
For horse feed,
50 bolts of cloth were disbursed monthly.
For satin and silk fabrics,
materials were provided annually to artisans,
and delivered to the princely household for self-production.
The Jìngjiāngwáng [Prince of Jingjiang] received:
20,000 *shí* of rice,
10,000 *guàn* of paper currency,
half of the other items given to a Qīnwáng,
and 20 bolts of horse feed cloth.
An unfiefed Gōngzhǔ [princess] received:
10 bolts each of ramie silk, gauze, and sheer silk,
30 bolts each of silk, winter and summer cloth,
and 200 *liǎng* of cotton.
Once enfiefed,
she was granted an estate,
receiving 1,500 *shí* of grain annually,
and 2,000 *guàn* of paper currency.
An unfiefed son of a Qīnwáng
was treated the same as a Gōngzhǔ;
an unfiefed daughter received half of that.
A son already enfiefed as a Jùnwáng [prince of the second rank] received:
6,000 *shí* of rice,
2,800 *guàn* of paper currency,
10 bolts of brocade,
50 bolts of ramie silk,
half the amount of ramie silk for gauze and sheer silk,
100 bolts each of silk, winter and summer cloth,
500 *liǎng* of cotton,
50 salt warrants,
300 *jīn* of tea,
and 10 bolts of horse feed cloth.
A daughter already enfiefed or married
received: 1,000 *shí* of rice,
and 1,400 *guàn* of paper currency.
Her satin and silk fabrics were produced and supplied by the Qīnwáng's kingdom where she resided.
The secondary legitimate sons and concubine-born sons of the Crown Prince,
once enfiefed as Jùnwáng,
would only receive annual provisions after leaving the imperial household,
the same as a son of a Qīnwáng already enfiefed as a Jùnwáng.
Daughters would receive the same as a married daughter of a Qīnwáng after marriage.
In general, a Qīnwáng's heir apparent
was treated the same as an enfiefed Jùnwáng.
The legitimate eldest son of a Jùnwáng who inherited the title of Jùnwáng
received half of what an initial Jùnwáng received.
A daughter already enfiefed as a Xiànzhǔ [princess of a county] or married
received: 500 *shí* of rice,
500 *guàn* of paper currency,
and the other items were half of those given to an enfiefed daughter of a Qīnwáng.
When the sons of a Jùnwáng reached fifteen years of age,
each was granted sixty *qǐng* of land,
exempt from rent and taxes as an entailed estate,
which their descendants would perpetually guard.
In the 28th year, an imperial edict was issued, stating that as the emoluments of officials, civil servants, and military personnel were too vast,
the annual stipends of the various princes were to be reduced in quantity
to finance military and national expenditures.
Thus, the stipends were redefined: a qīnwáng was to receive 10,000 shí,
a jùnwáng 2,000 shí,
a zhènguó jiāngjūn 1,000 shí,
and a fǔguó jiāngjūn, fèngguó jiāngjūn, and zhènguó zhōngwèi would decrease by 200 shí respectively.
A fǔguó zhōngwèi and fèngguó zhōngwèi would decrease by 100 shí respectively.
A gōngzhǔ and fùmǎ would receive 2,000 shí,
a jùnwáng and yíbīn 800 shí,
a xiànzhǔ, jùnjūn, and yíbīn would decrease by 200 shí respectively,
and a xiànjūn, xiāngjūn, and yíbīn would decrease by 100 shí respectively.
Thereafter, this became a permanent system.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
he increased and decreased the annual stipends of the various princes,
which was not the usual practice.
At that time, the seven princes, namely Zhèng, Yuè, Xiāng, Jīng, Huái, Téng, and Liáng, had not yet been enfeoffed in their domains.
They were temporarily granted 3,000 shí of rice annually,
which then became a precedent.
In the 12th year of Zhèngtǒng, the stipends for princely establishments were set.
For jiāngjūn, it began from the day they were granted their name and enfeoffed.
For xiànzhǔ and yíbīn, it began from the day they married and left their family.
These stipends were to be allocated from the autumn grain taxes of nearby prefectures and counties.
In the 7th year of Jǐngtài, the stipends for jùnwáng, jiāngjūn, and those below them were set.
If they married earlier
and were enfeoffed later,
the start date was the day of enfeoffment.
If they were enfeoffed earlier
and married later,
the start date was the day of marriage.
Members of the imperial clan who were stripped of their titles due to crimes were called shùrén (commoners).
In the early reign of Yīngzōng,
they were generally granted grain.
During the Jiājìng era,
they received six shí of rice monthly.
During the Wànlì era, this was reduced to two shí or one shí.
Initially,
Tàizǔ greatly enfeoffed imperial relatives and vassals,
decreeing that they should all receive annual stipends for generations
and not be given official positions or duties,
showing immense familial affection.
However, as the imperial lineage grew daily,
the civil levies were limited.
Initially, stipends were entirely paid in kind.
Later, both in kind and paper money were used.
Some received half in kind,
some received more in kind than in paper money;
the rules varied.
Subsequently, the system became unsustainable,
and embezzlement and abuses only increased.
Countless corrupt practices emerged,
which could not be fully investigated.
Since the Hóngzhì era,
Ní Yuè, the Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū), had already petitioned for reductions
to lighten the burden on the people.
In the 41st year of Jiājìng,
Censor Lín Rùn stated:
“Among all affairs in the empire,
the most extremely corrupt and greatly worrying
is none other than the stipends for the imperial clan and vassals.
The empire annually supplies the capital with four million shí of grain,
while the total stipends for the various princely establishments amount to eight million five hundred thirty thousand shí.
Taking Shānxī as an example,
one million five hundred twenty thousand shí are retained,
while imperial stipends total three million one hundred twenty thousand shí.
Taking Hénán as an example,
eight hundred forty-three thousand shí are retained,
while imperial stipends total one million nine hundred twenty thousand shí.
The grain from these two provinces,
even if entirely submitted,
would not suffice to cover half of the stipends,
let alone the emoluments for officials and military provisions, which also come from it.
Therefore, from jùnwáng upwards,
they still enjoy ample provisions,
but from jiāngjūn downwards,
〔一０〕many cannot sustain themselves.
Hunger, cold, distress, and humiliation
are inevitable.
They often cry out on the streets
and gather to denounce officials.
Local officials
often fear rebellion.
Taxes cannot be increased,
yet the imperial clan continues to proliferate daily.
How can one not be disheartened?
It is fitting to order high-ranking officials and censors (kēdào) to convene a discussion at court,
and also to inform the various princes that the situation is critical and utterly corrupt,
making it imperative to adapt to change.
Order the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù) to calculate the tax quotas,
using a ten-year average,
and comprehensively account for remissions due to war and famine, retained amounts, and the numbers of newly enfeoffed princely establishments.
Together, propose excellent long-term solutions,
decided by Your Majesty's wisdom,
to establish an unchangeable rule for ten thousand generations.”
This was submitted to the ministry for further deliberation,
and it was approved.
By the 44th year, regulations for the imperial clan and vassals were finalized.
Jùnwáng and jiāngjūn received seventy percent in paper money.
Zhōngwèi received sixty percent in paper money.
Jùn-xiànzhǔ, jùn-xiànxiāngjūn, and yíbīn received eighty percent in paper money.
Many other cases of excessive or abusive grants were cut.
Consequently, the various princes also petitioned to renounce annual stipends,
some as little as 500 shí,
others as much as 2,000 shí.
Annual expenditures were slightly relieved,
but those from jiāngjūn downwards found it even harder to sustain themselves.
In the early Míng dynasty,
meritorious officials and imperial relatives were all granted official lands in lieu of regular stipends.
Later, they were ordered to return the land and be given rice stipends.
A gōng received 5,000 to 2,500 shí,
a hóu 1,500 to 1,000 shí,
a bó 1,000 to 700 shí.
Regarding the emoluments of all officials,
from the early Hóngwǔ era,
the annual stipends for chángxiàng, yùshǐ dàfū, and those below were set,
engraved on stone tablets in government offices,
and sourced from official lands in Jiāngnán.
In the 13th year, the system for annual rice stipends and paper money emoluments for civil and military officials, both internal and external, was redefined,
with miscellaneous clerks and functionaries included.
For officials of the first to fourth ranks (zhèng and cóng),
ranging from 1,000 shí to 300 shí,
each rank decreased by 100 shí,
all were given 300 guàn in paper money.
A zhèng wǔ pǐn official received 220 shí,
a cóng wǔ pǐn decreased by 50 shí,
and both received 150 guàn in paper money.
A zhèng liù pǐn official received 120 shí,
a cóng liù pǐn decreased by 10 shí,
and both received 90 guàn in paper money.
Zhèng and cóng qī pǐn officials received 10 shí less than cóng liù pǐn,
and both received 60 guàn in paper money.
A zhèng bā pǐn official received 75 shí,
a cóng bā pǐn decreased by 5 shí,
and both received 45 guàn in paper money.
Zhèng and cóng jiǔ pǐn officials received 5 shí less than cóng bā pǐn,
and both received 30 guàn in paper money.
These were inscribed on stone.
Monthly stipends for clerks:
For first and second-rank officials' offices, tíkòng and dūlì received 2 shí 5 dòu,
yuánshǐ and lìshǐ 2 shí 2 dòu,
zhīyìn, chéngchāi, lì, and diǎn 1 shí 2 dòu.
For third and fourth-rank officials' offices, lìshǐ, shūlì, and sīlì received 2 shí,
chéngchāi, lì, and diǎn received half of that.
For fifth-rank officials' offices, sīlì received 1 shí 2 dòu,
lì and diǎn 8 dòu.
For sixth-rank and below officials' offices, sīlì received 1 shí.
Clerks (lì and diǎn) of the Guānglù Sì and similar offices received 6 dòu.
Emoluments for educational officials (jiàoguān):
A zhōu xuézhèng received 2 shí 5 dòu of rice monthly.
A xiàn jiàoyù and fǔ zhōuxiàn xùndǎo received 2 shí of rice monthly.
Emoluments for leading officials (shǒulǐngguān):
All internal and external tíkòng, àndú, zhōu lìyì, and xiàn diǎnshǐ received 3 shí of rice monthly.
Emoluments for miscellaneous officials (zázhí):

All dàshǐ of granaries (cāng), treasuries (kù), passes (guān), fields (chǎng), bureaus (sī), departments (jú), ironworks (tiěyě), courier stations (dìyùn), and verification offices (pīyànsuǒ) received 3 shí monthly.
A fùshǐ received 2 shí 5 dòu monthly.
Officials of fishing stations (hépósuǒ) received 2 shí of rice monthly.
Officials of sluices and dams (zhábàguān) received 1 shí 5 dòu of rice monthly.
Teachers and students in schools throughout the empire received 1 shēng of rice per person daily for their provisions,
and items like fish, meat, salt, and vinegar were officially supplied.
Eunuch stipends:
1 shí of rice monthly.
In the 25th year, the emoluments for all officials were redefined.
A zhèng yī pǐn official received 87 shí of rice monthly.
From cóng yī pǐn to zhèng sān pǐn,
it decreased by 13 shí, down to 35 shí.
A cóng sān pǐn official received 26 shí.
A zhèng sì pǐn official received 24 shí.
A cóng sì pǐn official received 21 shí.
A zhèng wǔ pǐn official received 16 shí.
A cóng wǔ pǐn official received 14 shí.
A zhèng liù pǐn official received 10 shí.
A cóng liù pǐn official received 8 shí.
From zhèng qī pǐn to cóng jiǔ pǐn, it decreased by 5 dòu
until it stopped at 5 shí.
Thereafter, this became a permanent system.
During the Hóngwǔ 洪武 reign,
official salaries were entirely paid in rice,
sometimes supplemented with cash and paper currency.
One thousand cash,
or one string of paper currency,
was equivalent to one shí 石 of rice.
When Chéngzǔ 成祖 ascended the throne,
he ordered that all Gōng 公, Hóu 侯, and Bó 伯 (dukes, marquises, and earls) should receive their full salaries in rice.
However, the salaries of civil and military officials were to be paid partially in rice and partially in paper currency.
High-ranking officials received four or five tenths of their salaries in rice,
while low-ranking officials received six or eight tenths in rice.
[一一] Only those of the ninth rank, miscellaneous posts, clerks, petty officials, seal-keepers (zhīyìn 知印), total small banner-commanders (zǒngxiǎoqí 總小旗), and soldiers
all received their entire salaries in rice.
For those whose salaries were commuted to paper currency,
each shí 石 of rice was valued at ten guàn 貫 of paper currency.
In the second year of Yǒnglè 永樂 (1404), an order was issued for Gōng 公, Hóu 侯, and Bó 伯 to receive their salaries in a mix of rice and paper currency, similar to civil and military officials.
[no translation for this line]
When Rénzōng 仁宗 was enthroned,
official salaries were commuted to paper currency,
with each shí 石 reaching twenty-five guàn 貫.
In the eighth year of Xuāndé 宣德 (1433),
Hú Yíng 胡濙, the Shàngshū 尚書 (Minister) of the Lǐbù 禮部 (Ministry of Rites), was in charge of the Hùbù 戶部 (Ministry of Revenue).
He proposed reducing the value by ten guàn 貫 per shí 石,
and using ten parts as the standard,
with seven parts commuted to silk.
One pǐ 匹 of silk was equivalent to two hundred guàn 貫 of paper currency.
Shàoshī 少師 (Junior Preceptor) Jiǎn Yì 蹇義 and others believed that Rénzōng 仁宗 had been in the Spring Palace (Crown Prince's residence) for a long time,
and deeply pitied officials for their meager commuted salaries.
Therefore, upon his accession, he specifically increased them severalfold.
This was a benevolent policy,
how could it be violated?
Hú Yíng 胡濙 did not listen,
and proceeded to petition the emperor and implement it.
As a result, low-ranking officials found their daily needs unmet.
During the Zhèngtǒng 正統 reign,
officials of the fifth rank and above received two tenths in rice and eight tenths in paper currency;
those of the sixth rank and below received three tenths in rice and seven tenths in paper currency.
At that time, the value of paper currency depreciated daily.
What was fifteen guàn 貫 per shí 石 had gradually increased to twenty-five guàn 貫.
Yet, Wáng Zuǒ 王佐, the Shàngshū 尚書 of the Hùbù 戶部, again memorialized to reduce it to fifteen guàn 貫.
In the second year of Chénghuà 成化 (1466), following the request of Mǎ Áng 馬昂, the Shàngshū 尚書 of the Hùbù 戶部,
another five guàn 貫 were reduced.
According to old regulations,
civil and military officials in the two capitals whose salaries were commuted to goods
received paper currency in the first half of the year,
and sappanwood (sūmù 蘇木) and pepper (hújiāo 胡椒) in the second half.
In the seventh year, following the request of Yáng Dǐng 楊鼎, the Shàngshū 尚書 of the Hùbù 戶部,
cloth accumulated in the Jiǎzì Kù 甲字庫 (Jiǎ character storehouse) was valued and distributed.
One pǐ 匹 of cloth was considered equivalent to two hundred guàn 貫 of paper currency.
At this time, the paper currency system was not effective;
one guàn 貫 was worth merely two or three wén 文 of cash.
One shí 石 of rice commuted to ten guàn 貫 of paper currency
was worth only twenty or thirty wén 文 of cash.
Meanwhile, one pǐ 匹 of cloth was worth only two or three hundred wén 文 of cash.
If one pǐ 匹 of cloth was commuted to twenty shí 石 of rice,
then one shí 石 of rice was worth only fourteen or fifteen wén 文 of cash.
Since ancient times, official salaries had never been as meager as this.
[no translation for this line]
In the sixteenth year, it was again ordered to commute rice using sānsuōbù 三梭布 (three-shuttle cloth),
with each pǐ 匹 equivalent to thirty shí 石.
Later, coarse, wide cotton cloth was also equivalent to thirty shí 石.
The finest three-shuttle cloth was still worth two liǎng 兩 of silver,
while coarse cloth was worth only three or four qián 錢.
After a long time,
it was stipulated that one pǐ 匹 of cloth was equivalent to three qián 錢 of silver.
Thus, there were two categories of official emoluments: one was called Běnsè 本色 (primary form),
the other was called Zhésè 折色 (commuted form).
The Běnsè 本色 had three subcategories: one was Yuèmǐ 月米 (monthly rice),
one was Zhéjiànmǐ 折絹米 (silk-commuted rice),
and one was Zhéyínmǐ 折銀米 (silver-commuted rice).
For Yuèmǐ 月米,
regardless of the official's rank,
all received one shí 石.
For Zhéjiàn 折絹,
one pǐ 匹 of silk was equivalent to six qián 錢 of silver.
For Zhéyín 折銀,
six qián 錢 five fēn 分 of silver was equivalent to one shí 石 of rice.
The Zhésè 折色 had two subcategories: one was Běnsèchāo 本色鈔 (primary form paper currency),
and one was Jiànbù Zhéchāo 絹布折鈔 (silk and cloth commuted to paper currency).
Běnsèchāo 本色鈔, ten guàn 貫 were commuted to one shí 石 of rice;
later it increased to twenty guàn 貫.
For Jiànbù Zhéchāo 絹布折鈔,
each pǐ 匹 of silk was commuted to twenty shí 石 of rice,
and one pǐ 匹 of cloth was commuted to ten shí 石 of rice.
The stipends of Gōng 公 and Hóu 侯
were sometimes half Běnzhé 本折 (primary and commuted),
or with the commuted portion exceeding the primary, varying by case.
For civil and military officials' salaries,
those of the first principal rank
received only three tenths in Běnsè 本色,
progressively increasing to the ninth subordinate rank,
whose Běnsè 本色 was seven tenths.
For military officials of fǔwèi 府衞 (prefectural guard) units,
only the Běnsè 本色 rice commuted to silver was standardized,
at two qián 錢 five fēn 分 per shí 石,
which differed from civil officials;
all other aspects were the same.
The Fùjiàng 副將 (Brigade-Generals), Cānjiàng 參將 (Assistant Commanders), Yóujī 遊擊 (Mobile Corps Commanders), and Zuǒyuán 佐員 (Staff Officers) of the three major garrisons (sāndàyíng 三大營)
received five shí 石 of rice monthly.
The Tídū 提督 (Commander) and Cānjiàng 參將 of the Xúnkǎobīng Yíng 巡捕營 (Patrol and Arrest Camp) also received the same.
The Zhōngjūn 中軍 (Central Army Commander) and Bǎzǒng 把總 (Company Commander) of the patrol camp
received nine dòu 斗 of rations monthly,
and the Qípái Guān 旗牌官 (Banner and Tablet Officer) received half of that.
For the monthly rations of soldiers in garrisons (wèisuǒ 衞所) throughout the empire,
during the Hóngwǔ 洪武 reign,
it was ordered that cavalry soldiers in garrisons outside the capital should receive two shí 石 of rice monthly.
Infantry Zǒngqí 總旗 (Company Commanders) received one shí 石 five dòu 斗,
Xiǎoqí 小旗 (Squad Commanders) one shí 石 two dòu 斗,
and soldiers one shí 石.
Those defending cities received the full amount,
while those on military farms (túntián 屯田) received half.
Civilians and artisans conscripted into the army received eight dòu 斗.
Those in the Mùmǎ Qiānhùsuǒ 牧馬千戶所 (Horse Pasturing Qianhu Office) received one shí 石.
Civilian men drafted for military training received one shí 石.
Naval soldiers of the Jiāngyīn Hénghǎi Shuǐjūn 江陰橫海水軍 (Jiāngyīn Transverse Sea Navy) in rotation shifts (shāobān 稍班) and anchor-holders (dìngshǒu 碇手) received one shí 石 five dòu 斗.
For soldiers who died in battle or of illness, a funeral allowance of one shí 石 was given.
For those who died of illness in camp, half was given.
Those whose property was confiscated and were spared death by conscription into the army were called Ēnjūn 恩軍 (mercy soldiers).
Those with four or more family members received one shí 石,
those with three or fewer received six dòu 斗,
and those with no family members received four dòu 斗.
Additionally, soldiers were given monthly salt.
Those with family members received two jīn 斤,
those without one jīn 斤.
For soldiers in outer garrisons, this was converted to paper currency.
During the Yǒnglè 永樂 reign,
it was first ordered that in areas with abundant grain,
the monthly rations for banner soldiers (qíjūn 旗軍)
should be eight tenths in rice
and two tenths in paper currency.
Later, Shānxī 山西 and Shǎnxī 陝西 were both like this.
Fújiàn 福建, Liǎngguǎng 兩廣, and Sìchuān 四川 had seven tenths rice and three tenths paper currency.
Jiāngxī 江西 had half rice and half paper currency.
Only the capital army (Jīngjūn 京軍) and the Zhōngdū Liúshǒusī 中都留守司 (Central Capital Garrison Command),
as well as the armies of Hénán 河南, Zhèjiāng 浙江, and Húguǎng 湖廣,
continued to receive their entire rations in rice.
Later, a fixed system was established:
garrison soldiers with family dependents
received six dòu 斗 of rice monthly,
those without received four dòu 斗 five shēng 升,
and the remainder was commuted to paper currency.
All garrison soldiers transferred to the capital for training and duties, including labor,
received five dòu 斗 of rice.
Subsequently, there were various increases and decreases,
and the regulations for primary and commuted forms
varied in amount across different garrisons,
making it impossible to list them all.
[no translation for this line]
Regarding military provisions (bīngxiǎng 兵餉) for all garrisons,
there were Túliáng 屯糧 (farmed grain),
Mínyùn 民運 (civilian transport),
Yányǐn 鹽引 (salt permits),
Jīngyùn 京運 (capital transport),
Zhǔbīng Niánlì 主兵年例 (regular annual provisions for main troops),
and Kèbīng Niánlì 客兵年例 (annual provisions for guest troops).
As for Túliáng 屯糧,
at the beginning of the Míng 明 dynasty,
all garrisons had military farms (túntián 屯田).
The land cultivated by one army
was sufficient to supply the needs of that army.
The salaries and rations of garrison officials and clerks were all drawn from this.
Mínyùn 民運 meant that
when farmed grain was insufficient,
civilian grain was added.
Wheat, rice, beans, straw, cloth, paper currency, and cotton floss were transported to supply the frontier soldiers,
hence it was called Mínyùn 民運.
Later, it was mostly commuted to silver.
Yányǐn 鹽引 meant
attracting merchants to bring grain for the kāizhōng 開中 (salt exchange) system,
and merchants supplying grain from their depots (shāngtún 商屯),
which complemented military farms.
Later, silver was remitted to the Yùnsī 運司 (Transport Commissioner's Office),
so the name existed but the reality was lost.
Jīngyùn 京運 started
during the Zhèngtǒng 正統 reign.
Later, military farms and salt grain systems mostly fell into disuse,
and Jīngyùn 京運 increased daily.
Zhǔbīng 主兵 (main troops) had a fixed number,
while Kèbīng 客兵 (guest troops) had no fixed number.
Initially,
the main troops in each garrison were sufficient to guard their territory.
Later, they gradually became insufficient,
and recruited soldiers (mùbīng 募兵) were added.
When recruited soldiers were insufficient,
guest troops were added.
The more soldiers there were,
the more idle mouths to feed,
and annual provisions also increased daily.
The figures for Míng 明 land tax and expenditure income and outgo,
found in historical records,
can generally be investigated.
In the 26th year of Hóngwǔ
(1393), the total area of official and private fields was over 8,507,000 qǐng.
The summer tax included
over 4,717,000 dàn of rice and wheat,
over 39,000 dìng of paper currency, and
over 288,000 bolts of silk.
The autumn grain included
over 24,729,000 dàn of rice and
over 5,000 dìng of paper currency.
During the Hóngzhì
(1488-1505) era, the total area of official and private fields was over 6,228,000 qǐng.
The summer tax included
over 4,625,000 dàn of rice and wheat,
over 56,300 dìng of paper currency, and
over 202,000 bolts of silk.
The autumn grain included
over 22,166,000 dàn of rice and
over 21,900 dìng of paper currency.
During the Wànlì
(1573-1620) era, the total area of official and private fields was over 7,013,000 qǐng.
The summer tax included
a total of over 4,605,000 dàn of rice and wheat,
of which over 1,903,000 dàn were transported,
and the rest was kept locally;
over 57,900 dìng of paper currency; and
over 206,000 bolts of silk.
The autumn grain included
a total of over 22,033,000 dàn of rice,
of which over 13,362,000 dàn were transported,
and the rest was kept locally;
and over 23,600 dìng of paper currency.
Garrison fields totaled over 635,000 qǐng,
with over 1,900 flower gardens and granary foundations.
Grain collection amounted to over 4,584,000 dàn.
Grain and fodder converted to silver totaled over 85,000 liǎng,
cloth 50,000 bolts,
and paper currency over 50,000 guàn.
Various Salt Administrations (Yúnsī Tíjiǔ) levied over 2,228,000 salt licenses, both large and small.
The annual revenue figures included:
From the Nèi Chéngyùn Kù,
silver for Cíníng, Cíqìng, and Qiánqīng Three Palaces' grain
amounted to over 49,000 liǎng; golden flower silver over 1,012,000 liǎng;
and gold 2,000 liǎng.
From Guǎnghuì Kù, Héxīwù, and other seven paper currency passes (chāoguān),
paper currency amounted to over 29,280,000 guàn,
and copper coins over 59,770,000 wén.
Garrison field paper currency in the capital area (Jīngwèi) was over 56,000 guàn.
From Tiāncái Kù and the nine gates of the capital city, paper currency was over 665,000 guàn,
and copper coins over 2,430,000 wén.
From Jīng and Tōng Two Granaries,
including the grain transport for Jì and Mì garrisons, it was 4,000,000 dàn.
Garrison field beans in the capital area were over 23,000 dàn.
From the Tàicāng Silver Treasury,
the converted silver from surplus wheat and rice allocated from the Northern and Southern Zhílì, Zhèjiāng, Jiāngxī, Shāndōng, and Hénán provinces was over 257,000 liǎng.
Silk floss, tax silk, and agricultural silk converted to silver amounted to over 90,000 liǎng;
cotton and ramie cloth converted to silver amounted to over 38,000 liǎng.
Salaries of officials converted to silver amounted to over 26,000 liǎng.
Horse fodder converted to silver amounted to over 353,000 liǎng.
The five fodder fields in the capital converted to silver amounted to over 63,000 liǎng.
[一二] From various stables' granaries' wheat, beans, and fodder converted to silver, it was over 200,000 liǎng.
Household salt paper currency converted to silver amounted to over 46,000 liǎng.
From the six garrisons of Jì, Mì, Yǒng, Chāng, Yì, and Liáodōng,
civilian transport converted to silver amounted to over 853,000 liǎng.
From various Salt Administration Tíjiǔ's surplus salt, salt taxes, and salt duties, the silver amounted to over 1,003,000 liǎng.
Yellow and white wax converted to silver amounted to over 68,000 liǎng.
From Bà, Dà, and other stables' grain, the silver amounted to over 23,000 liǎng.
Frontier defense and newly added land area silver amounted to over 45,000 liǎng.
Garrison pasture land in the capital area increased silver by over 18,000 liǎng.
Chóngwénmén commercial tax and brokerage tax amounted to over 19,000 liǎng,
and copper coins over 18,000 guàn.
Zhāngjiāwān commercial tax amounted to over 2,000 liǎng,
and copper coins over 2,800 guàn.
Various paper currency passes converted to silver amounted to over 223,000 liǎng.
Tàishān incense tax amounted to over 20,000 liǎng.
Fines and confiscated property silver amounted to over 170,000 liǎng.
Commercial tax, fish tax, wealthy households, almanacs, able-bodied men, soldiers, and converted garrison provisions and converted monthly rations amounted to over 144,000 liǎng.
Northern Zhílì, Shāndōng, and Hénán transferred wheat, rice, beans, fodder, and salt paper currency to various frontier garrisons, converted to silver, amounting to over 842,000 liǎng.
Details of various miscellaneous items that are too numerous are not recorded.
The recorded annual revenue
only calculates what was transported to the capital and the frontiers,
and what was kept locally is not included.
The annual expenditure figures included:
Salaries for dukes (gōng), marquises (hóu), imperial sons-in-law (fùmǎ), and earls (bó), converted to silver, amounted to over 16,000 liǎng.
Salaries for officials and imperial academy students (jiànshēng) were over 40,000 dàn of rice.
Officials' converted salaries in silk, cloth, and silver amounted to over 44,000 liǎng,
and copper coins over 3,300 guàn.
For granaries, fodder fields, official treasuries, and armories (jiǎdǒu),
and various offices of Guānglù, Tàicháng, and the Nèifǔ bureaus, the actual payment for artisans and laborers was over 86,000 dàn of rice,
and converted to silver, over 13,000 liǎng.
For officials, flag-officers, soldiers, artisans, and laborers of the 78 garrisons including Jǐnyī, the actual payment was over 2,018,000 dàn of rice,
and converted to silver, over 206,000 liǎng.
Officials' converted salaries in silk, cloth, and silver amounted to over 268,000 liǎng.
Soldiers' winter clothes converted to cloth and silver amounted to over 82,000 liǎng.
For the generals and soldiers of the Wǔjūn, Shénshū, and Shénjī Three Great Camps, the actual payment was over 120,000 dàn of rice.
Winter clothes converted to cloth and silver amounted to over 2,000 liǎng.
For imperial troops' autumn defense rations for three months, it was over 43,000 dàn.
For horses in camp training, the actual fodder was over 24,000 dàn,
and grass over 800,000 bundles.

Collation Notes
Gazetteer Volume 59, Rivers and Canals 1, Yellow River Upstream
The Yellow River,
before the Táng Dynasty,
all flowed north into the sea.
During the Xīníng reign of the Sòng Dynasty,
it began to diverge southeast,
one branch joining the Sī River to enter the Huái River,
and another joining the Jǐ River to enter the sea.
During the Míngchāng reign of the Jīn Dynasty,
the northern flow ceased,
and the entire river entered the Huái River.
During the Yuán Dynasty, it frequently breached its banks,
and the suffering was particularly severe during the Zhìzhèng reign,
between Jìníng, Cáo, and Yùn,
over a thousand lǐ were submerged.
Jiǎ Lǔ was appointed Director-General,
and he directed it south,
converging with the Huái River to enter the sea.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ of the Míng Dynasty, the river breached at Shuānghékǒu in Cáozhōu,
flowing into Yútái.
Xú Dá was then campaigning in the north,
so he ordered the opening of the Tāchángkǒu,
diverting the river into the Sī River to facilitate transport,
and moved the seat of Cáozhōu to Ānlíng.
Tācháng refers to
the area west of Jìníng, south of Nàiláopō, stretching directly to Nányángdào in Yútái.
In the eighth year,
the river breached the Tàihuángsì embankment in Kāifēng.
An imperial edict ordered Ān Rán, the Assistant Commissioner of Hénán, to mobilize thirty thousand laborers to seal it.
In the fourteenth year, it breached Yuánwǔ, Xiángfú, and Zhōngmóu.
Officials requested construction.
The emperor considered it a natural disaster,
and only ordered the protection of the old embankments.
In the spring of the fifteenth year,
it breached Cháoyì.
In the seventh month, it breached Xíngzé and Yángwǔ.
In the seventeenth year, it breached the East Yuè Embankment in Kāifēng,
flowing horizontally for dozens of lǐ from Chénqiáo to Chénliú.
It also breached Shíxiàn,
flowing into the Bāhé River.
Officials were dispatched to seal the river,
and taxes were remitted for the affected areas.
In the twenty-second year,
the river submerged Yífēng,
and its seat was moved to Báilóucūn.
In the spring of the twenty-third year,
it breached the Fèngchíkǒu southeast of Guīdézhōu,
passing through Xiàyì and Yǒngchéng.
Soldiers from Xīngwǔ and ten other guards were dispatched,
to work with the people of Guīdé to build the embankment.
Officials who failed to report it were punished.
In the autumn of that year,
it breached Xīhuá and other counties of Kāifēng,
submerging homes.
Envoys were sent to provide relief to over fifteen thousand seven hundred households.
In the fourth month of the twenty-fourth year,
the river overflowed violently,
breaching Hēiyángshān in Yuánwǔ,
flowing east five lǐ north of the city of Kāifēng,
then southeast through Chénzhōu, Xiàngchéng, Tàihé, Yǐngzhōu, Yǐngshàng,
east to Zhèngyángzhèn in Shòuzhōu,
entirely entering the Huái River.
And the old course of the Jiǎ Lǔ River then silted up.
It also overflowed from the mouths of the two rivers in old Cáozhōu and Yùnchéng across Ānshān of Dōngpíng,
and the Yuán Dynasty's Huìtōnghé River also silted up.
The next year it breached Yángwǔ again,
inundating Chénzhōu, Zhōngmóu, Yuánwǔ, Fēngqiū, Xiángfú, Lányáng, Chénliú, Tōngxǔ, Tàikāng, Fúgōu, and another eleven prefectures and counties.
Officials presented maps to report it.
Civilian men and soldiers from Ānjí and seventeen other guards were mobilized for repair and construction.
In the winter of that year,
due to extreme cold,
the work was suspended.
In the eighth month of the thirtieth year, it breached Kāifēng,
with three sides of the city receiving water.
An imperial edict ordered the relocation of granaries to the high ground of Xíngyáng,
in preparation for unforeseen events.
In winter,
the Càihé River shifted to Chénzhōu.
Previously,
when the river breached,
it flowed north and east from Kāifēng.
By this time, its lower course was silted up,
and it breached again and turned south.
In the third year of the Yǒnglè reign,
the river breached the Wēn Xiàn embankment by forty zhàng.
The Jǐ and Láo rivers overflowed simultaneously,
submerging over forty lǐ of farmland.
Orders were given to repair the embankments.
In the fourth year, the breached bank of the Huáng Hé at Yángwǔ was repaired.
In the autumn of the eighth year,
the river breached at Kāifēng,
damaging over two hundred zhàng of the city wall.
Over fourteen thousand households were affected,
and over seven thousand five hundred qǐng of land were inundated.
The Emperor, considering Kāifēng a strategic buffer for the state,
specifically dispatched Grand Secretary Zhāng Xìn to inspect it.
Zhāng Xìn reported:
"From Yúwángkǒu in Xiángfú down to the lower Zhōngluán, a stretch of over twenty lǐ,
there is an old Huáng Hé bank
that is level with the current river surface.
If it is dredged and opened,
allowing the water to follow its old course,
then the force of the water can be reduced."
He then presented a map.
At this time, Minister Sòng Lǐ and Grand Secretary Jīn Chún were in the process of opening the Huìtōng Hé.
The Emperor then mobilized one hundred thousand civilian laborers
and ordered Earl Xú Hēng of Xìng'ān and Grand Secretary Jiǎng Tíngzàn to assist Jīn Chún in the work,
also tasking Sòng Lǐ to oversee the entire project.
In the seventh month of the ninth year,
the river returned to its old course,
from Jīnlóngkǒu in Fēngqiū,
down to Tāchǎng in Yútái,
where it met the Wèn Shuǐ,
and then entered the Huái River to the south via the two floods of Xú and Lǚ.
At this time,
the Huìtōng Hé had already been opened,
and the Huáng Hé merged with it,
greatly facilitating the grain transport route.
It was then proposed to cease sea transport,
and the water damage in Hénán also gradually subsided.
Subsequently, the Zhōngyán embankment at Yángwǔ breached,
inundating Zhōngmóu, Xiángfú, and Wèishì.
Lìn Fāng, a principal of the Ministry of Public Works, inspected the site
and reported:
"The embankment is at the impact point of a swift current.
During summer and autumn floods,
its force cannot be suddenly diminished.
It is advisable to roll earth and plant piles to defend it,
to prevent it from becoming a renewed disaster for the people."
He also said:
"Diverting the river at Zhōngluán
to let it follow its old course northward into the sea would indeed be a benefit for ten thousand generations.
However, the river embankments and dikes
are only made of reed ropes and mud grass,
and cannot last long.
It is advisable to weave wood into caissons,
fill them with stones,
which would reduce the water's force
and secure the embankments."
The Emperor's edict adopted all his suggestions.
In the fourteenth year, the river breached in fourteen prefectures and counties of Kāifēng,
passed through Huáiyuǎn,
and entered the Huái River via the Wō Hé.
In the twentieth year,
the Ministry of Public Works, seeing that the earth city embankments of Kāifēng frequently collapsed,
requested to dredge its eastern old course.
The request was approved.
In the first year of the Xuāndé reign, continuous rain
caused Kāifēng and ten counties to overflow.
In the third year,
due to river damage,
the Qiānhùsuǒ of Língzhōu was relocated to the east of the city.
In the sixth year, following the advice of the Hénán Provincial Administration Commissioner,
the silted channel from Xiángfú to Huánglínggāng in Yífēng, a stretch of four hundred and fifty lǐ, was dredged.
At this time,
Jīnlóngkǒu gradually silted up,
and the river frequently overflowed at Kāifēng again.
In the tenth year, following the advice of Censor Lǐ Mào,
Jīnlóngkǒu was dredged.
In the second year of the Zhèngtǒng reign, breached banks at Yángwǔ, Yuánwǔ, and Xíngzé were constructed.
The river also breached at Púzhōu and Fànxiàn.
In the third year,
the river breached again at Yángwǔ and Pīzhōu,
inundating Yútái, Jīnxiāng, and Jiāxiáng.
A few years later,
it breached again at Jīnlóngkǒu, the Yánggǔ embankment, and Zhāngjiā Hēilóngmiàokǒu.
The two floods of Xú and Lǚ also gradually became shallower,
and at the confluence of the Bā Hé at Tàihuángsì,
the water flow became very small.
In the thirteenth year, following the advice of Du Fú Tóngzhī Wǔ Xīng,
troops were mobilized to dredge it.
Meanwhile, the Chénliú water rose in summer,
breaching the Jīncūn embankment and the south bank of Hēitán.
Just as the construction was nearing completion,
it breached again.
In the autumn of that year,
Bāliǔshùkǒu in Xīnxiāng also breached,
inundating Cáo and Pú,
reaching Dōngchāng,
impacting Zhāngqiū,
breaching Shāwān in Shòuzhāng,
damaging the transport canal,
and entering the sea to the east.
The two floods of Xú and Lǚ thus became shallow and obstructed.
Minister Wáng Yǒnghé of the Ministry of Public Works was ordered to manage the matter.
Wáng Yǒnghé arrived in Shāndōng,
but the repair of Shāwān was not completed,
and work was suspended due to winter cold.
He also reported that the river breach originated from Wèihuī,
and it was advisable to instruct the Hénán defense officials to repair and seal it.
The Emperor sternly rebuked him,
ordering the three provincial administrations of Shāndōng to build Shāwān,
and urging Wáng Yǒnghé to seal Bāliǔshù in Hénán,
and dredge Jīnlóngkǒu,
to make the river follow its old course.
In the first month of the following year,
the river breached again at Liáochéng.
By the third month,
Wáng Yǒnghé dredged the Xīwān of Hēiyángshān,
diverting its water through Tàihuángsì to supply the Grand Canal.
He largely repaired and built the Shāwān embankment
but dared not fully seal it,
installing a diversion sluice gate,
and setting up three openings to discharge water,
which entered the sea from the Dàqīng Hé.
He also set up a two-opening diversion sluice gate on the west bank of Shāwān
to release upstream water,
and requested to suspend the Bāliǔshù project.
This was granted.
At this time,
the river was overflowing extensively,
and it diverted into the Dàqīng Hé,
not solely heading towards Xú and Lǚ.
Xú and Lǚ became increasingly shallow and obstructed,
and from Línqīng southward,
the transport route was difficult.
In the second year of the Jǐngtài reign, a special edict ordered Hóng Yīng and Wáng Xiān, the Touring Grand Censors of Shāndōng and Hénán respectively, to work together to govern,
ensuring that the water returned to the canal.
Wáng Xiān reported:
"West of Shǎnzhōu, the Huáng Hé
flows through mountain gorges,
and cannot cause harm;
east of Shǎnzhōu,
the terrain is flat and gentle,
and the water easily overflows,
thus causing much harm.
In the twenty-fourth year of Hóngwǔ, its course was changed.
The main Huáng Hé flowed about five lǐ north of Biànliáng,
entering the Huái River via Fèngyáng.
Its tributary that flowed out south of Xúzhōu was the Xiǎo Huáng Hé,
to facilitate grain transport.
Since the thirteenth year of Zhèngtǒng,
the river returned to its old course,
directly heading from behind Hēiyángshān to Shāwān and into the sea,
with only the Xiǎo Huáng Hé remaining to flow out from Xúzhōu.
The banks are high and the water is low;
it is dredged as it silts up, and sealed as it breaches,
which means the area south of Xúzhōu does not get enough water.
I have supervised the dredging by the three provincial administrations of Hénán
from the southeast of Hēiyángshān to Xúzhōu.
For the area south of Línqīng,
I request that Hóng Yīng be responsible."
Soon after,
Attendant Censor Zhāng Wénzhì impeached Wáng Xiān and Hóng Yīng for their lack of achievement in water control,
requesting to divert the Tāchǎng water to supply the two floods of Xú and Lǚ,
dredge the tributary north of Pānjiādù,
and reduce the force of the Shāwān water.
He also proposed to open the river mouth west of the Shāwān pontoon bridge,
build a sluice gate to divert water,
to irrigate Línqīng,
and appoint other officials to ensure its completion.
The Emperor's edict did not approve,
still ordering Wáng Xiān and Hóng Yīng to coordinate.
At that time, some argued:
"The land south of Shāwān is high,
so water cannot flow south into the Grand Canal.
We request to divert Nàiláopō water to irrigate the canal,
without letting it pass through Shāwān,
and open a separate river to avoid the force of its breaches."
Others again said:
"If Nàiláopō water is diverted south,
then the area north of it will become dry and obstructed."
Even more extreme voices said:
"The water at Shāwān is turbulent and swift,
and even stones and iron sink like feathers;
it is beyond human power.
It is advisable to set up rituals and spells to ward it off."
The Emperor was deeply worried,
and ordered Minister Shí Pú of the Ministry of Public Works to manage it,
and also bestowed an honorary title upon the River God.
Pú arrived.
Jùn deepened Hēiyángshān to Xúzhōu to facilitate grain transport,
but the breach at Shāwān remained as before.
Then, the court eunuchs Lí Xián and Ruǎn Luò were ordered,
along with Censor Péng Yì, to assist in the governance.
Pú and others built a stone dike at Shāwān
to prevent the river from bursting its banks,
and opened two Yuèhé canals,
diverting water to augment the Grand Canal,
and also to mitigate the force of the current.
In the fifth month of the third year,
the river gradually became shallower and narrower,
and the Shāwān dike was finally completed.
Pú was then promoted to Tàizǐ Tàibǎo,
and two new temples to the River God were built at Hēiyángshān and Shāwān,
with two sacrifices annually in spring and autumn.
In the sixth month,
heavy rains lasted for ten days,
and the north bank of Shāwān breached again,
drawing the Grand Canal's water eastward,
inundating all nearby land.
Yīng was ordered to oversee the repairs.
Again, the court eunuchs Lí Xián and Wǔ Gèn,
and Minister of Works Zhào Róng were dispatched to manage it.
In the first month of the fourth year,
the river breached again south of the Xīnsèkǒu,
and an imperial edict again conferred additional titles upon the River God.
By the fourth month,
the breach was finally plugged.
In the fifth month,
there was a great thunderstorm,
and the north bank of Shāwān breached again,
drawing Grand Canal water into the Yánhé,
completely obstructing grain barges.
The Emperor again ordered Pú to go.
Then, a new canal was dug,
three *lǐ* long,
to bypass the breach,
connecting to the Grand Canal upstream and downstream,
while the breach itself was dammed and blocked,
allowing both the new canal and the Grand Canal to be navigable.
The work was completed and reported to the Emperor.
Fearing it would not last long,
the Emperor ordered Pú to remain and manage the situation,
and appointed Yùdé Xú Yǒuzhēn as Qiāndū Yùshǐ specifically to manage Shāwān.
At this time, the flood disaster in Hénán was severe;
Yuánwǔ and Xīhuá both moved their county seats to avoid the water.
Patrolling Censor Xiān reported:
"The Yellow River formerly flowed from Kāifēng northward, then turned southeast into the Huái River,
causing no harm.
Since the thirteenth year of Zhèngtǒng, its course changed and split into two.
One branched off from Xīnxiāng's Bāliǔshù,
and flowed east along the old course through Yánjīn and Fēngqiū into Shāwān.
The other breached at Yíngzé,
overflowing into Yuánwǔ,
reaching Xiángfú, Fúgōu, Tōngxǔ, Wěichuān, Wèishì, Línyǐng, Yǎnchéng, Chénzhōu, Shāngshuǐ, Xīhuá, Xiàngchéng, and Tàikāng.
Hundreds of thousands of *qǐng* of fields were inundated,
and Kāifēng suffered especially severely.
Although large and small dikes were built west of the city,
each over thirty *lǐ* long,
the sandy soil was easily damaged,
breaching as soon as they were built.
The small dike was already submerged,
and the large dike was half ruined.
I request that soldiers and civilians be mobilized to assist in construction
to prevent future calamities."
The Emperor approved his memorial.
Huáng Shìjùn, a Junior Supervisor of the Imperial Stud, also said:
"The river divides into two branches;
one flows south from Yíngzé into Xiàngchéng,
the other flows north from Xīnxiāng's Bāliǔshù,
entering Zhāngqiū's Huìtōnghé,
passing through six or seven prefectures and counties,
approximately two thousand *lǐ*.
The people are all displaced and scattered,
yet officials still collect taxes from them.
I beg that the relevant authorities be ordered to review and remit these taxes."
The Emperor also approved his memorial.
Patrolling Censor of Hénán Zhāng Lán also said:
"On the east bank of the Yellow River at Yuánwǔ, two canals were once opened
to merge with the old Hēiyángshān river channel to supply water to Xú and Lǚ.
Now the river has changed course and breached to the north;
the two canals are silted up and impassable.
I fear Xú and Lǚ will lack water,
which will certainly hinder grain transport.
North of Hēiyángshān,
the river bends slightly.
I request that a new canal be dug at the breach to connect with the old channel,
to irrigate Xú and Lǚ."
The Emperor also agreed to this.
When Yǒuzhēn arrived at Shāwān,
he presented three strategies for river management:
"First, install sluice gates.
Your servant hears that the nature of water allows it to flow,
but not to be blocked.
Yǔ dug Lóngmén and
opened Yīquè,
which were measures for疏導 (dredging and guiding).
Thus, Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's attempt to block Hùzǐ ultimately failed,
while Emperor Míng of Hàn's dredging of the Biànhé showed results within a year.
Many people today discuss water control,
but only the method of controlling water gates described by Lèlàng Wáng Jǐng is worth adopting.
Since the soil at Shāwān is entirely sand,
it is prone to collapse and breach,
thus building dams or locks is not a good plan.
I request to modify Wáng Jǐng's method,
installing sluice gates in the water
and reinforcing their base,
making them five *chǐ* higher than the normal water level.
When the flow is small, it can be contained to aid transport;
when large, it can be released to flow to the sea,
thus having the benefit of free flow
without the problem of obstruction.
Second, open a diversion canal.
Generally, when water flow is large, it should be divided;
when small, it should be combined.
Currently, the Yellow River's powerful flow breaches its banks,
while the Grand Canal's flow is weak and shallow.
It is imperative to divide the Yellow River's water and combine it with the Grand Canal,
which will be beneficial without harm.
I request to assess suitable locations on the Yellow River for diversion,
and open a Guǎngjìhé canal,
passing over twenty *lǐ* through Púyáng, Bólíng, and the old Shāhé downstream,
and connecting upstream with Dōngyǐngtáng, Xīyǐngtáng, Xiǎolǐng and other places for several tens of *lǐ*.
Within this area, there is the ancient Dàjīntí which can be relied upon for solidity,
and outside, the eight-hundred-*lǐ* Liángshānpō can be depended on for drainage.
The two newly installed sluices are also quite sturdy,
and can regulate the flow,
so that when the Yellow River's water is high, it will not overflow and cause harm,
and when low, it will not become too shallow to obstruct grain transport."
The third is to deepen the Grand Canal.
The Emperor instructed Yǒuzhēn
to proceed according to his proposals.
Yǒuzhēn then crossed the Jì River and Wèn River,
followed the Wèi River and Qìn River,
traced the Great River,
and passed through Pú and Fàn,
surveying the terrain and water conditions.
He reported:
"The river flows from Yōng to Yù,
emerging from dangerous narrow sections into open plains,
where its force becomes unrestrained.
From Yù to Yǎn,
the soil becomes looser,
and the water's force even more unrestrained.
East of Shāwān,
the place called Dàhóngkǒu
is directly in its path,
and thus it breaches there,
seizing the path of the Jì and Wèn rivers to the sea and flowing away.
All other waters follow it to drain,
dikes collapse,
channels silt up,
it overflows when flooded,
and dries up when in drought,
thus obstructing the grain transport route.
However, if it is abruptly dammed,
the collapsed will collapse further,
and the silted will silt up more.
Now, I request to first dredge and guide the water;
when the water level is stable, then repair the breaches;
when the breaches are stopped, then dredge the silt."
Thereupon, channels were set up to dredge and guide it,
starting from the head of the Jīntí at Zhāngqiū,
extending southwest nine *lǐ* to Púyáng Luò,
then another nine *lǐ* to Bólíng Pō,
then another six *lǐ* to the Shāhé in Shòuzhāng,
then another eight *lǐ* to Dōngyǐngtáng and Xīyǐngtáng,
then another fifteen *lǐ* to Báilǐngwān,
then another three *lǐ* to Lǐhé,
a total of fifty *lǐ*.
From Lǐhé upstream twenty *lǐ* to Zhúkǒuliánhuāchí,
then another thirty *lǐ* to Dàzhūtán,
then crossing Fàn and Pú,
and further upstream to the west,
for several hundred *lǐ*,
passing through Chányuān to connect with the Hé and Qìn rivers,
nine weirs were built to prevent the river from spreading out laterally,
each ten thousand *zhàng* long,
filled with stone and bound with iron.
In the seventh month of the sixth year,
the project was completed,
and the canal was named Guǎngjì.
The breach at Shāwān had lasted nearly ten years,
and only then was it plugged.
This also coincided with the Yellow River flowing south into the Huái River,
whereupon Yǒuzhēn was able to successfully complete the work.
A total of tens of thousands of units of wood, iron, bamboo, and stone were expended,
with over fifty-eight thousand laborers,
and over five hundred fifty days of work.
From this point, the river water flowed north to assist grain transport,
and in the area between Ā, Juàn, Cáo, and Yùn,
hundreds of thousands of *qǐng* of fields that had been marshy
were recovered. Then, the grain transport canal was dredged,
from Shāwān north to Línqīng,
and south to Jìníng.
Eight sluices were again built at Dōngchāng,
using Wáng Jǐng's method of controlling water gates to stabilize the waterway,
and the river disasters in Shāndōng ceased.
In the seventh year, in the summer,
there were heavy rains in Hénán,
and the Huáng Hé burst its banks in Kāifēng, Hénán, and Zhāngdé.
That autumn,
there were heavy rains in Jīfǔ and Shāndōng.
All the rivers overflowed,
with water levels rising over a zhàng (about 3.3 meters) in high areas,
and many dikes and embankments were breached.
An imperial edict ordered Yǒu Zhēn to repair and construct them.
Not long after,
the work was completed,
and he returned to the capital to report.
He was greatly praised and rewarded,
and promoted to Vice Censor-in-Chief (fù dū yùshǐ).
In the first year of Tiānshùn (1457), the large protective dike of Xiángfú was repaired.
In the fifth year (1461), seventh month,
the Huáng Hé burst through Biànliáng's earthen wall,
and then through the brick wall.
The water level inside the city was over a zhàng,
and more than half of the official and civilian dwellings were destroyed.
The palace attendants of the Zhōu Prince's (Zhōu Wáng) mansion and all the local officials (shǒu tǔ guān) boarded boats and rafts to escape.
Countless soldiers and civilians drowned.
Xiāngchéng county town was also breached.
The Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shìláng), Xuē Yuǎn, was ordered to inspect the situation,
provide relief to disaster-stricken households, remit land taxes,
and repair official buildings and private residences in sequence.
In the second month of the following year,
Cáo Jiā Liū in Xiángfú was opened,
and the river's current gradually became calmer.
In the seventh year (1463), spring,
Jīn Jǐnghuī, the secretary (zhàozhōu) of the Hénán Provincial Administration Commission (Bùzhèng Sī), came to the capital upon completion of his term of office,
and memorialized, saying:
"In the early days of the dynasty,
the Yellow River was in Fēngqiū.
Later, it moved to Kāngwáng Mǎtóu,
thirty lǐ north of the city.
There were also two branch rivers: one flowed through Shāmén into the Grand Canal (Yùnhé),
and one flowed through Jīnlóngkǒu to Xúzhōu and Lǚxiàn into the sea.
In the Wùchén year of Zhèngtǒng (1448),
it burst its banks in Xíngzé,
then turned south of the city,
and merged into the Huái River.
The old river and its branches were all silted up,
and the漕河 (cáohé, grain transport canal) became shallow and stagnant as a result.
In the Guǐyǒu year of Jǐngtài (1453),
due to the water pressing against the city,
a dike forty lǐ long was built.
The labor and expense were excessive,
but the water would always burst forth and collapse it.
However, it had not yet reached the point of breaching the city moat and harming people.
By the Xīnsì year of Tiānshùn (1461),
the water arrived suddenly and violently,
and both the earthen wall and the brick wall collapsed.
The dikes built with the financial resources of seven prefectures
all became useless.
People were in a panic,
not knowing what would become of them.
The river does not follow its old course,
but merges into the Huái River;
this is its erratic behavior.
Now it is urgent to dredge and guide it to reduce its force.
If we only leave it to the Huái River
and consider dike protection as the long-term strategy,
I fear that Kāifēng will eventually become a habitat for fish and turtles.
I humbly request an imperial edict to the ministry and relevant authorities,
first to dredge and widen Jīnlóngkǒu to connect with the grain transport canal,
then to survey the old river or seek other places for water discharge,
to dig and dredge to quell the water disaster,
as a long-term plan."
The emperor ordered that his proposal be carried out.
In the seventh year of Chénghuà (1471), Wáng Shù was appointed Vice Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shìláng),
and ordered to take overall charge of river conservancy.
The establishment of the position of Grand River Administrator Vice Minister (Zǒnghé Shìláng) began with Shù.
At that time, the Huáng Hé was not a problem,
so Shù focused solely on the grain transport canal.
In the fourteenth year (1478),
the Huáng Hé burst its banks in Kāifēng,
destroying fifty zhàng of the protective city dike.
Lǐ Yǎn, the Censor-in-Chief (Dū Yùshǐ)巡撫 (xúnfǔ, grand coordinator) of Hénán, memorialized, saying:
"Hénán has repeatedly suffered from river disasters,
all caused by the blockage of the lower reaches.
It is advisable to dredge the area southwest of the new city of Kāifēng,
down to Liángjiāqiǎn's old river mouth, a seven-lǐ blockage,
to drain the upstream of Xìnghuāyíng.
Also, from Bājiǎohékǒu straight to Nándùn,
divert the scattered flow
to prevent disasters in Xiángfú, Yānlíng, Suīxiàn, Chénzhōu, and Guīdé.
An edict then ordered Yǎn to act upon it as he saw fit.
In the first month of the following year (1479),
the county seat of Xíngzé was moved to avoid the water,
but the Kāifēng dike soon became blocked again.
In the second year of Hóngzhì (1489), fifth month,
the Huáng Hé burst its banks in Kāifēng and Jīnlóngkǒu,
flowing into the Zhāngqiū Grand Canal.
It also burst through five places at Sàotóu into the Qìn River.
Many prefectures and counties were affected,
Biànliáng especially so.
Some even proposed moving Kāifēng city to avoid the disaster.
However, Xú Kè of the Provincial Administration Commission (Bùzhèng Sī) strongly opposed it,
and so it was stopped.
The authorities were ordered to mobilize a large number of soldiers to build dikes.
In the ninth month, Bái Áng was appointed Vice Minister of Revenue (Hùbù Shìláng),
to repair and manage the river channels.
He was granted a special imperial edict,
ordering him to consult with the three Grand Coordinators (xúnfǔ) of Shāndōng, Hénán, and Běizhílí,
to repair and build dikes as circumstances required, from the upstream breach to the Grand Canal.
In the first month of the third year (1490),
Áng memorialized, saying:
"Starting from the Huái River,
I surveyed the water situation down to Zhōngmóu and other counties in Hénán.
I saw that at the upstream breach,
thirteen parts of the water flowed into the south bank,
and seventeen parts into the north bank.
The southern breaches,
from Yángqiáo in Zhōngmóu to the border of Xiángfú, split into two branches:
one passed through Wèishì and other counties,
joined the Yǐng River,
flowed down Túshān,
and entered the Huái River;
the other passed through Tōngxǔ and other counties,
entered the Wō River,
flowed down Jīngshān,
and entered the Huái River.
Another branch went from Guīdé Zhōu through Bóxiàn in Fèngyáng,
also joining the Wō River and entering the Huái River.
The northern breaches,
from Yuánwǔ through Yángwǔ, Xiángfú, Fēngqiū, Lányáng, Yífēng, and Kǎochéng,
one branch flowed into Jīnlóng and other mouths,
reached Cáozhōu in Shāndōng,
and burst into the Zhāngqiū grain transport canal.
Last winter,
as the water receded and sand accumulated,
the breaches were already silted up,
thus merging into one large branch,
which flowed from Zháijiākǒu in Xiángfú, joined the Qìn River,
exited at Dīngjiādàokǒu,
and flowed down to Xúzhōu.
