This is the general trend of the river's north-south divergence.
For the two waters, Yǐng and Wō, joining the Huái River,
each has shoals and shallows,
and the water flow is quite weak,
so it is advisable to dredge them to reduce the river's force.
For the Qìn River joining the Xú River,
the river channel is shallow and narrow and cannot accommodate it,
thus there is a danger of flooding.
Moreover, although the upstream Jīnlóng and other mouths are temporarily silted,
they will eventually burst again.
It is advisable to build embankments in the seven counties through which the northern flow passes,
to protect Zhāngqiū.
However, the original edict concerned Shāndōng, Hénán, and Běizhílí,
but the Huái and Xú territories in Nánzhílí,
which are crucial areas through which the river flows,
are not yet under unified administration."
Therefore,
the responsibility was also assigned to Áng.
Áng appointed the Director (Lángzhōng) Lóu Xìng to assist in the management.
Then, with 250,000 laborers,
the long dike of Yángwǔ was built
to defend Zhāngqiū.
The breached river from Zhōngmóu was diverted out through Yángqiáo in Xíngzé
to reach the Huái River.
The ancient Biàn River in Sùzhōu was dredged to flow into the Sì River.
The Suī River was also dredged from Yǐnmǎchí in Guīdé,
passing through Fúlǐqiáo to Sùqiān to meet the grain transport canal.
Long dikes were built upstream,
and diversion gates were repaired downstream.
More than ten Yuè Hé channels were also dredged to discharge water,
and thirty-six breaches were sealed,
making the river flow into the Biàn River,
the Biàn into the Suī River,
the Suī into the Sì River,
and the Sì into the Huái River,
to reach the sea.
The water disaster gradually subsided.
Áng also stated that the Hénán section entering the Huái River was not the main channel,
fearing it might eventually be insufficient.
He then repaired the ancient long dikes at Yútái, Dézhōu, and Wúqiáo.
He also dug twelve small canals from northern Dōngpíng to Xīngjì,
which flowed into the Dàqīng River and the old Huáng Hé to enter the sea.
Stone weirs were built at each river mouth,
to be opened and closed as needed.
This was essentially a north-south separate governance,
while in the southeast, dredging was the primary focus.
In the second month of the sixth year, Liú Dàxià was appointed Vice Minister of War,
to manage the breached river at Zhāngqiū.
Previously,
the river had breached at Dàijiāmiào in Zhāngqiū,
diverting the Grand Canal to merge with the Wènshuǐ and flow north.
Chén Zhèng, an Assistant Minister of Works, was dispatched to oversee the repairs.
Chén Zhèng said:
"The Yellow River has two old courses: one is at Sūnjiādùkǒu in Yíngzé,
passing through Zhūxiānzhèn directly to Chénzhōu;
the other is at Yǐnmǎchí in Guīdézhōu,
connected to the Bózhōu area.
Both used to enter the Huái River,
but are now silted up,
causing the upstream flow to surge,
with its force heading entirely north.
From Sūnjiākǒu, Yángjiākǒu, Chēchuánkǒu in Xiángfú,
and Tóngwǎxiāng in Lányáng, the river breached into several channels,
all flowing into the Grand Canal.
Consequently, the situation above and below Zhāngqiū was extremely critical.
Many embankments from Tángyì to Jìníng collapsed,
and the Dàijiāmiào regulating sluice was too shallow and narrow to discharge water,
leading to breaches there as well.
I request dredging the old river course to reduce the force of the upstream flow,
and blocking the breached river to prevent downstream disaster."
Chén Zhèng was gradually implementing these repairs,
but died in office shortly thereafter.
The Emperor was deeply concerned,
and ordered his ministers to recommend someone competent for the task.
They all recommended Dàxià,
so he was granted an imperial decree to proceed.
In the twelfth month,
Tú Shēng, the Censor for Hénán, reported:
"The Yellow River is a scourge.
Breaching to the south troubles Hénán,
and breaching to the north troubles Shāndōng.
In the past, the Hàn Dynasty had breaches at Suānzǎo and
then at Hùzǐ;
the Sòng Dynasty had breaches at Guǎntáo and
then at Chánzhōu;
the Yuán Dynasty had breaches at Biànliáng and
then at Púkǒu.
However, the Hàn capital was in Guānzhōng,
and the Sòng capital was in Dàliáng.
The damage from river breaches
affected only a few prefectures bordering the river.
Now the capital relies entirely on the Huìtōng Hé, which transports millions of *shi* of grain annually.
If the river breaches to the north,
it will cause a great problem for grain transport.
I have extensively collected public opinion,
and there are four strategies for river management:
"Firstly, dredging.
East of Yíng and Zhèng, and west of the Five Rivers,
the Yǐnmǎ, Báilù and other rivers are all old courses of the Yellow River that flowed via the Guō into the Huái.
Subsequently, after flowing south for a long time,
either the river mouths became high with silt and could not discharge,
or the river channels became narrow and couldn't contain the water.
The water force had no way to be dispersed,
so it flooded and breached northward.
Now, if only the old courses to the southeast upstream are followed,
surveyed and dredged,
then the main flow will return to its channel,
and residual waters will find their way to valleys.
The downstream will be free from the disaster of collapse,
and the north bank will be free from the trouble of breaches.
Secondly, blocking.
After reducing the water force in the southeast,
embankments must be built in the northwest.
The old embankments above and below Huánglínggāng are damaged.
The downstream's northeast terrain must be surveyed,
considering the distance from the water,
to repair and build without omission,
forcing all hundred rivers back to the southeast,
to enter the sea via the Huái River.
Then Zhāngqiū will be safe,
and the Grand Canal can be secured."
Thirdly, appointing people,
recommending Zhāng Nài, the Assistant Prefect of Hénán.
Fourthly, long-term appointment,
asking to solely trust Dàxià,
and to build an office in Guīdé or Dōngchāng,
allowing him to make decisions from there.
The Emperor approved.
In the fifth month of the seventh year, he ordered Grand Eunuch Lǐ Xìng and Earl of Píngjiāng Chén Ruì to go and work with Dàxià to manage Zhāngqiū.
In the twelfth month, the work of blocking and filling the Zhāngqiū breach was completed.
Initially,
the river flow was turbulent and fierce,
and the breach was over ninety *zhang* wide.
Dàxià inspected it
and said:
"The downstream cannot be managed yet;
the upstream must be managed."
Thereupon, he opened a diversion channel about three *li* southwest of the breach,
so that grain transport could pass.
Then he dredged the old Jiǎlǔ River south of Huánglínggāng in Yífēng, over forty *li* long,
leading it from Cáo to Xú,
to reduce the water force.
He also dredged Sūnjiādùkǒu,
and separately dug a new river over seventy *li* long,
guiding it south,
to enter the Huái River eastward via Zhōngmóu and Yǐngchuān.
He also dredged the silted river at Sìfǔyíng in Xiángfú,
which divided into two from Chénliú to Guīdé.
One went via Xiǎo Hé Kǒu in Sùqiān,
the other via the Bóguō River,
both converging into the Huái.
Then, along both banks of Zhāngqiū,
platforms were built east and west,
markers were erected and ropes strung,
large ships were linked together and sunk to block it,
and filled with earth.
At the breach,
sunk ships were used to block it,
pressed down with large fascines,
both closing and breaching,
building as it breached,
working day and night without rest.
Once the breach was blocked,
it was encircled with a stone dike,
resembling a long rainbow, and the work was completed.
The Emperor sent an envoy with sheep and wine to commend him,
and renamed Zhāngqiū to Ānpíngzhèn.
Dàxià and others reported:
"The breach at Ānpíngzhèn has been blocked,
and the downstream river entering Dōngchāng and Línqīng to Tiānjīn and the sea has been opened.
However, the river mouth at Huánglínggāng must be built up,
to guide the upstream river south to Xú and Huái,
so that it may be a long-term plan for the safety of the transport route."
The court deliberated and agreed.
So, in the first month of the eighth year, seven places including Huánglínggāng and Jīnglóngkǒu were blocked and built up,
completing the work in fifteen days.
Huánglínggāng was upstream of Ānpíngzhèn,
its width over ninety *zhang*.
Jīnglóngkǒu and other mouths were even further upstream of Huánglínggāng,
their width over four hundred thirty *zhang*.
The river flow here was wide and rampant,
all critical strategic points.
With these mouths blocked,
the upstream river flow returned to Lányáng and Kǎochéng,
branching to pass through Xúzhōu, Guīdé, and Sùqiān,
flowing south into the Grand Canal,
joining the Huáishuǐ,
and eastward into the sea,
thus restoring the old southern course.
The long dike in Dàmíngfǔ,
starting from Zuòchéng,
passing through Huáxiàn, Chángyuán, Dōngmíng, Cáozhōu, Cáoxiàn to Yúchéng,
totaled three hundred sixty *li*.
The new dike at Jīnglóngkǒu and other mouths to the southwest
started from Yújiādiàn,
passing through Tóngwǎxiāng and Dōngqiáo to Xiǎosòngjí,
totaling one hundred sixty *li*.
The two dikes, large and small, reinforced each other,
and the stone dams were built up stoutly,
thus putting an end to the disaster of breaches.
The Emperor, seeing the completion of the Huánglínggāng river mouth,
decreed the construction of a Yellow River Temple to stabilize it,
granting it the plaque "Zhāoyìng."
That autumn,
Dàxià and others were summoned back to the capital.
Jīnglóng is Jīnlóng.
In the eleventh year,
the river breached at Guīdé.
Xiè Jí, an Assistant Director of Works in charge of river affairs, reported:
"One branch of the Yellow River
previously flowed from Xiǎofúqiáo east of Xúzhōu city into the Grand Canal,
reaching Pīzhōu and Sùqiān to the south.
Now the upstream Yellow River has breached at Xiǎobàzi and other places in Guīdézhōu,
merging with another branch of the Yellow River,
passing through Sùzhōu and Suīníng,
and flowing into the Grand Canal via Xiǎo Hé Kǒu in Sùqiān.
Consequently, the water flow from Xiǎo Hé Kǒu north to Xúzhōu gradually thinned,
and the river channel became shallow and obstructed.
Moreover, the two rapids of Xú and Lǚ
relied solely on the Qìnshuǐ for replenishment,
flowing from Qìnyuán, Hénèi, Guīdé to Xiǎofúqiáo in Xúzhōu.
Although it has a different source from the Yellow River,
in recent years, the flows of the River and Qìn have merged into one.
Now the Yellow River has breached south from Guīdé,
which might draw the Qìnshuǐ to flow south as well,
then the two rapids of Xú and Lǚ will surely become shallow and obstructed.
I request to immediately block the breach at Guīdé,
contain the Yellow River water into Xú to benefit grain transport,
and dredge the silted Qìnshuǐ,
allowing it to enter Xú to benefit Xú and Lǚ,
then the water will be deep and wide, and transport will be convenient."
The Emperor followed his request.
Not long after,
Zhāng Nài, the Vice Commissioner for River Management in Hénán, reported:
"I once requested to repair and build the broken dam at Hóujiātánkou,
to relieve the two floods at Xú and Lǚ.
Now, since June,
the river has overflowed its banks,
and the breach at Tánkou has deepened considerably,
requiring vast expenditures and labor,
making it difficult to succeed.
I have observed the water flow,
and the old river within the Jīnglóngkǒu dike connected to the Jiǎlǔhé,
running down to Xú and Huái via Dīngjiādàokǒu,
its traces are still present.
If a new canal were dug at Mùluándiàn in Wǔzhì, upstream,
connecting to the old river at Jīnglóngkǒu downstream,
waiting for the river to shift south,
then the water could be diverted into the canal,
hopefully allowing its mighty force to reach the two floods,
and grain transportation would not be obstructed."
The Emperor ordered this proposal to be submitted to Lǐ Huì, the Censor-in-Chief for Grand Canal Transport.
Two years later,
Gōng Hóng, the Prefect of Yǎnzhōu, reported:
"Vice Commissioner Nài, seeing the river tending southward,
wished to divert the Qìnshui from Jīnglóngkǒu into the Jiǎlǔhé,
and also to divert water from Wángpáikǒu, west of Guīdé, both upstream and downstream, also into the Jiǎlǔhé,
all passing through Dīngjiādàokǒu into Xúzhōu.
However, this autumn, the water flows east from Wángpáikǒu,
not southward through Dīngjiākǒu,
but counter-flows northeast to Huánglínggāng,
then enters Shàn from Cáoxiàn,
and connects to Yúchéng in the south.
I request that the responsible officials be ordered to promptly devise a plan for dredging and construction."
Thereupon, Zhèng Líng, the Provincial Censor-in-Chief of Hénán, reported:
"The two floods at Xú and Lǚ rely on the combined flow of the Hé and Qìn rivers eastward,
to provide mutual relief.
Now, there are twelve breaches in the dikes of the river above and below Dīngjiādàokǒu,
with a total width of over three hundred zhàng,
and the river is silted for over thirty lǐ.
If the upstream surges,
Cáoxiàn and Shànxiàn will suffer,
and Ānpíng will be at risk;
if the downstream overflows,
Xiāo and Dàng will be afflicted,
and canal transport will be impeded.
Dredging and construction are indeed urgent tasks."
The Ministry's reply approved it,
and so the dikes above and below Dīngjiākǒu were repaired.
Initially,
the Huánghé divided into three branches from Yuánwǔ and Xíngyáng: one went from Bózhōu and Fèngyáng to Qīnghékǒu,
connecting to the Huái River and then the sea;
one went from Guīdézhōu past Dīngjiādàokǒu,
reaching the Xiǎofúqiáo in Xúzhōu;
and one went from Wāníhé past Huánglínggāng,
also reaching the Xiǎofúqiáo in Xúzhōu,
which was the Jiǎlǔhé.
When the river breached at Huánglínggāng,
encroaching on Zhāngqiū,
and the northward flow diverted the漕 river,
Liú Dàxià went to block it,
and it still exited at Qīnghékǒu.
In the eighteenth year,
the river suddenly shifted north by three hundred lǐ,
to Xiǎohékǒu in Sùqiān.
In the third year of Zhèngdé, it again shifted north by three hundred lǐ,
to Xiǎofúqiáo in Xúzhōu.
In the sixth month of the fourth year, it shifted north again by one hundred and twenty lǐ,
to Fēiyúnqiáo in Pèixiàn,
all entering the canal.
At this time,
the old course of the southern river was silted up,
and the water only tended northward,
making the river narrow and overflowing between Shàn and Fēng,
breaching at Huánglínggāng, Shàngjiā, and other mouths,
submerging many fields and homes in Cáoxiàn and Shànxiàn,
even besieging the city walls of Fēngxiàn,
with the banks spread over a hundred lǐ wide.
The Director-General of Canal Transport and the provincial and patrolling officials of Shāndōng feared it would pass through the old courses of Jùyě and Yánggǔ,
thereby diverting the canal at Jìníng and Ānpíng,
and each submitted their views for consideration.
The deliberation was not settled.
In the ninth month of the following year,
the river again breached Huánglínggāng,
entering the Jiǎlǔhé,
overflowing and spreading,
directly reaching Fēng and Pèi.
Censor Lín Màodá also feared a northern breach at Ānpíngzhèn,
and requested to dredge the old courses upstream of Yífēng and Kǎochéng,
to divert the Hénán river southward to lessen its force,
and then block the breaches
and build the old dikes.
Cuī Yán, the Vice Minister of Works, was ordered to repair the Huánghé,
dredging Dǒngpénkǒu in Xiángfú and Sūnjiādù in Xíngzé,
and also dredging the Jiǎlǔhé and the old river in Bózhōu for several tens of lǐ,
and moreover building dikes at the breaches in various counties of Chángyuán, and the outer dike of Cáoxiàn, and the breaches at Liángjìng.
Before the work was completed, heavy rains came,
and the dikes burst.
Yán submitted a memorial stating:
"The river's momentum has become even more violent,
and it has flowed into the Wángzǐhé,
which is also an old course of the river.
If the upstream force is not significantly reduced,
the breaches will probably be difficult to block completely.
It would be better to build more dikes in Cáoxiàn, Shànxiàn, Fēngxiàn, and Pèixiàn,
to prevent it from moving north,
which might protect the canal."
He also requested that another high-ranking official knowledgeable in water conservancy be appointed for joint deliberation.
Thereupon, the Emperor blamed Yán for his ineffective management of the river,
and replaced him with Vice Minister Lǐ Táng.
Táng reported:
"The old courses of Lányáng, Yífēng, and Kǎochéng are silted up,
so all river flows enter the Jiǎlǔhé,
passing through Huánglínggāng to Cáoxiàn,
breaching at Liángjìng and Yángjiā.
Vice Minister Yán also tried to repair and dredge them,
but due to the high ground and river siltation,
as soon as it was dredged, it silted up again,
reducing little water,
and the breaches were difficult to build and block.
Now, observing the terrain below Liángjìng, it is the lowest,
thus all flows rush in to form a river,
directly reaching Pèixiàn.
Even if its mouth were built,
and there was no place to accommodate the entire flow,
it would certainly cause back-scouring of the Huánglínggāng dike,
and the transport route would be obstructed.
As for the old courses of the river,
those that are blocked cannot be reopened.
I request to build a dike from Sānchūnliǔ in Dàmíng to Fēiyúnqiáo in Pèixiàn,
over three hundred lǐ long,
to obstruct the river from shifting northward."
This was approved.
In the second month of the sixth year,
the work was not yet finished,
Táng reported:
"Chénqiáojí and Tóngwǎxiāng both need additional construction,
and I request that a vice commissioner be appointed to specialize in managing it."
Coincidentally, bandits arose in Hénán,
so Táng was summoned back to the capital,
and the Emperor ordered to cease the less urgent matters.
The task was then entrusted to the vice commissioner,
and thus the dike construction ceased.
In the sixth month of the eighth year,
the river again breached Huánglínggāng.
The Ministry deliberated that its location bordered Dàmíng, Shāndōng, and Hénán,
and the local officials lacked unified authority,
so they requested to specifically dispatch a high-ranking official.
Thus, Liú Kǎi, the Vice Censor-in-Chief for River Management, was appointed to concurrently manage the matter.
Kǎi reported,
leading the crowd to offer sacrifices and pray to the river god,
and two days later,
the river had already shifted south.
Minister Lǐ Suì then requested to offer sacrifices to the river,
and to bestow a sheep and wine upon Kǎi.
Kǎi had no plan for river management,
but merely attributed the success to the god.
The damage between Cáoxiàn and Shànxiàn worsened daily.
In the early years of Shìzōng's reign,
Gōng Hóng, the Vice Censor-in-Chief for River Management, reported:
"Since the early years of Zhèngdé,
the Huánghé has been constantly shifting,
gradually moving northward.
The waters of the great river combine into one stream,
and before reaching Huánglínggāng, they turn south,
exiting at Xúzhōu to enter the canal.
Huánglínggāng initially had three earthworks built,
two of which have already broken away,
fearing that the waters from the mountains and Shǎnxi would burst forth,
coupled with continuous heavy rains,
it would breach and rush to Zhāngqiū,
and return to the sea via the old course.
I once built a dike,
starting from Chángyuán,
passing through Huánglínggāng to Yángjiākǒu in Shāndōng,
extending over two hundred lǐ.
Now I propose to build another dike about ten lǐ away from the existing dike,
with the same length, height, and width.
Even if the river overflows the old dike,
flowing to ten lǐ away,
its speed will be slowed and its force diminished,
preventing a major breach."
This was approved.
Since the breach at Huánglínggāng,
there were no river disasters south of Kāifēng,
but the river in the northern prefectures and counties of Xú and Pèi shifted unpredictably.
In the fifth year of Jiājìng,
Gāo Yǒujī, the Censor-in-Chief for Grand Canal Transport, requested to dredge the Jiǎlǔhé in Shāndōng and Yuānyāngkǒu in Hénán,
to divert the water's force,
so as not to disproportionately harm one area.
The Ministry deliberated that it might harm Shāndōng and Hénán,
and disapproved.
That winter,
Zhāng Zhěng was appointed Vice Minister of Works and concurrently Vice Censor-in-Chief to manage the river.
Formerly,
Grand Secretary Fèi Hóng (費宏) said:
“East of where the Yellow River (黃河) enters Biànliáng (汴梁), it divides into three branches.
Although there may be breaches,
there is no great harm.
At the end of the Zhèngdé (正德) era,
the Guō Hé (渦河) and other rivers gradually became shallow and淤塞 (silted up),
and the main current of the Yellow River, having nothing to check its southward flow,
then flowed from Lányáng (蘭陽), Kǎochéng (考城), Cáo (曹), and Pú (濮) to the Fēiyún Qiáo (飛雲橋) in Pèi Xiàn (沛縣) and the Liūgōu (溜溝) in Xúzhōu (徐州),
all entering the Cáo Hé (漕河).
It overflowed and spread widely,
which was the river calamity of several years prior.
Recently,
the Shā Hé (沙河) at Pèi Xiàn (沛縣) was choked with surging sand,
and all official and civilian boats had to take the route through Zhāoyáng Hú (昭陽湖).
In late spring and early summer,
the lake surface becomes shallow and dry,
and the transport route is bound to be obstructed.
Therefore, the Guō Hé (渦河) and other rivers must be dredged urgently.”
Censor Dài Jīn (戴金) said:
“There are three routes for the Yellow River (黃河) to enter the Huái (淮) River: from Zhōngmóu (中牟) to Jīngshān (荊山), joining the long Huái (淮) River, it is called the Guō Hé (渦河);
from Kāifēng (開封) via Gégāng Xiǎobà (葛岡小壩), Dīngjiā Dàokǒu (丁家道口), Mǎmù Jí Yuānyang Kǒu (馬牧集鴛鴦口) to Xúzhōu Xiǎofúqiáo Kǒu (徐州小浮橋口), it is called the Biàn Hé (汴河);
from Xiǎobà (小壩) via Guīdé Chéngnán Yǐnmǎchí (歸德城南飲馬池) to Wénjiā Jí (文家集),
and via Xiàyì (夏邑) to Sùqiān (宿遷), it is called the Bái Hé (白河).
During the Hóngzhì (弘治) era,
the upper reaches of the Guō (渦) and Bái (白) Rivers became blocked,
and Xúzhōu (徐州) alone suffered the calamity.
It is appropriate to completely dredge
the small river from Xiǎobà (小壩) to Sùqiān (宿遷), along with the Jǐalǔ Hé (賈魯河), Yuānyang Kǒu (鴛鴦口), and Wénjiā Jí (文家集) at the blocked sections,
so that there will be more than one route for the water to flow towards the Huái (淮),
and Xúzhōu’s (徐州) water calamity will be alleviated.”
Censor Liú Luán (劉欒) said:
“On the south bank of Liángjìng Kǒu (梁靖口) in Cáo Xiàn (曹縣),
there was formerly the Jǐalǔ Hé (賈魯河).
Thirteen *lǐ* (里) south to Wǔjiā Kǒu (武家口),
it is silted up with yellow sand,
and must be dredged.
From Wǔjiā Kǒu (武家口) down to Mǎmù Jí Yuānyang Kǒu (馬牧集鴛鴦口), one hundred and seventeen *lǐ* (里),
which is the old channel of the Xiǎohuáng Hé (小黃河) leading to Xúzhōu (徐州),
the water has not yet dried up,
and it should also be dredged.”
The Governor-General of Grain Transport, Yáng Hóng (楊宏), also requested dredging of Guīdé Xiǎobà (歸德小壩), Dīngjiā Dàokǒu (丁家道口), Bózhōu Guō Hé (亳州渦河), and Sùqiān Xiǎohé (宿遷小河).
Yǒu Jī (友璣) and Zhěng (拯) also repeatedly made similar recommendations.
All these proposals were sent to the Ministry of Works for deliberation.
They considered that dredging the old channel of the Jǐalǔ Hé (賈魯河)
and opening the upper reaches of the Guō Hé (渦河)
would be a massive undertaking difficult to achieve,
and should not be lightly attempted.
Instead, they proposed building dikes to contain the water,
allowing it to flow into the main river only.
That year,
the upper reaches of the Yellow River (黃河) suddenly overflowed,
and in the northeast, at Miàodàokǒu (廟道口) in Pèi Xiàn (沛縣),
it cut across the Grand Canal,
poured into Jīmíngtái Kǒu (雞鳴臺口),
and entered Zhāoyáng Hú (昭陽湖).
The water flowing south from Wèn (汶) and Sì (泗) then went east,
while the river emerging from Fēiyún Qiáo (飛雲橋) overflowed northward,
silting up several tens of *lǐ* (里).
The river water submerged Fēng Xiàn (豐縣),
and its administration was relocated to avoid it.
The following year,
Zhěng (拯) said:
“Both Sūnjiā Dù (孫家渡) north of Xíngzé (滎澤) and
can divert water southward.
However, if these two rivers connect to the Guō (渦),
flow east into the Huái (淮),
and then further east to Fèngyáng Chánghuái Wèi (鳳陽長淮衛),
passing through the imperial tombs and gardens of Shòuchūn (壽春) princes,
the harm would be unpredictable.
Only the Bèn Hé (坌河) channel north of Nínglíng (寧陵),
which connects to Yǐnmǎchí (飲馬池)
and reaches Wénjiā Jí (文家集),
then passes through Xiàyì (夏邑) to Fúlí Qiáo (符離橋) in Sùzhōu (宿州),
and exits at Sùqiān Xiǎohékǒu (宿遷小河口) –
from Zhàopí Zhài (趙皮寨) to Wénjiā Jí (文家集),
a distance of over two hundred *lǐ* (里) –
if dredged and opened,
the force of the water would be easily reduced,
and the imperial gardens would be safe from harm.”
He then presented a diagram and explanation.
An order was given to set a date for starting the work.
However, the river breached at Cáo (曹)
and Shàn (單),
at Yángjiā (楊家) and Liángjìng (梁靖) two mouths in Chéngwǔ (城武), and at Wúshìjǔ Zhuāng (吳士舉莊),
rushing into Jīmíngtái (雞鳴臺),
diverting the Grand Canal.
The Pèi (沛) region was silted up for seven or eight *lǐ* (里),
and grain boats were blocked and could not proceed.
Censor Wú Zhòng (吳仲) reported this,
and then impeached Zhěng (拯) for his inability to manage river affairs,
requesting that a capable person be chosen to replace him.
That winter,
Shèng Yìngqī (盛應期) was appointed as Governor-General of River Conservancy with the title of Right Censor-in-Chief.
At this time,

Minor Supervisor of the Court of Imperial Entertainments Huáng Wǎn (黃綰), Academician-in-waiting Huò Tāo (霍韜), Left Censor-in-Chief Hú Shìníng (胡世寧), and Minister of War Lǐ Chéngxūn (李承勛) each presented their proposals for river management.
Huáng Wǎn (黃綰) said: “The Grand Canal relies on spring water from Shāndōng (山東),
and does not necessarily need water from the Yellow River (黃河).
It would be better to dredge the high and low lands between Yǎn (兗) and Jì (冀),
and channel the river northward,
to enter the sea
at Zhígū (直沽).”
Huò Tāo (霍韜) said: “Proponents wish to divert the river from Lányáng (蘭陽) to Sùqiān (宿遷).
If water overflows Xú (徐) and Pèi (沛),
there are still two dams to contain and defend it.
The mountains to the northeast stretch
like a wall,
providing a boundary.
If the river is diverted via Lányáng (蘭陽),
then Guīdé (歸德) and Fèngyáng (鳳陽) are flat lands for a thousand *lǐ* (里),
and the river would burst forth,
turning several commanderies into ravines.
The calamity would not be confined
to Xú (徐) and Pèi (沛) alone.
According to records, the Wèi Hé (衛河) flows from Wèihuī (衛輝) and Jí Xiàn (汲縣) to Tiānjīn (天津) into the sea,
which is still the ancient Yellow River (黃河).
It is now advisable to carefully inspect the terrain
between Héyīn (河陰), Yuánwǔ (原武), Huái (懷), and Mèng (孟),
and divert the river water into the Wèi Hé (衛河).
By the time it reaches Línqīng (臨清) and Tiānjīn (天津),
the water force at Xú (徐) and Pèi (沛) could be reduced by half.
Moreover, during the Yuán (元) dynasty, grain boats navigated the Jiāng (江) River to enter the Huái (淮),
then,
north of Fēngqiū (封丘),
they were transported overland for one hundred and eighty *lǐ* (里) to Qímén (淇門),
entering the Yù Hé (御河) to reach the capital.
The Yù Hé (御河)
is the Wèi Hé (衛河).
Now, diverting the river into the Wèi (衛),
in winter and spring, one can ascend the Wèi
River along Línqīng (臨清) to Tiānjīn (天津);
in summer and autumn, one can go via Xú (徐) and Pèi (沛).
This is one action that achieves both transport routes.”
Hú Shìníng (胡世寧) said: “Since the Yellow River (黃河) reached Biàn (汴),
it has divided into two southern channels: one exits west of Biàn (汴) city at Xíngzé (滎澤),
passes through Zhōngmóu (中牟), Chén (陳), and Yǐng (潁),
and enters the Huái (淮) at Shòuzhōu (壽州);
the other exits
east of Biàn (汴) city at Xiángfú (祥符),
passes through Chénliú (陳留) and Bózhōu (亳州),
and enters the Huái (淮) at Huáiyuǎn (懷遠).
Its southeastern channel flows from Guīdé (歸德) and Sùzhōu (宿州),
through Hóng Xiàn (虹縣) and Suīníng (睢寧),
and exits east
of Sùqiān (宿遷),
dividing into five routes: one from Chángyuán (長垣), Cáo (曹), and Yùn (鄆) to Yánggǔ (陽穀);
one from Shuānghékǒu (雙河口) in Cáozhōu (曹州) to Tāchángkǒu (塌場口) in Yútái (魚臺);
one from
Yífēng (儀封) and Guīdé (歸德) to Xiǎofúqiáo (小浮橋) in Xúzhōu (徐州);
one from Fēiyún Qiáo (飛雲橋) south of Pèi Xiàn (沛縣);
and one from the middle section of Xú (徐) and Pèi (沛), at Jìngshān (境山) and Běiliūgōu (北溜溝).
All six
channels enter the Grand Canal,
and converge with the Huái (淮) to the south.
Now, all these channels are blocked,
with only the Pèi Xiàn (沛縣) channel remaining.
When the currents merge, the water force is great,
and the riverbed is too narrow
to accommodate it,
hence it overflows and causes calamity.
Recently, it has also flooded into Zhāoyáng Hú (昭陽湖),
leading to slow flow and sand blockage.
It is advisable to use the old channels to divide its force.
West of Biàn (汴), dredge
from Sūnjiā Dù (孫家渡) to Shòuzhōu (壽州) to reduce the flow upstream.
For the channels southeast of Biàn (汴) exiting at Huáiyuǎn (懷遠), Sùqiān (宿遷), and the direct eastern routes of Xiǎofúqiáo (小浮橋) and Liūgōu (溜溝),
choose the most advantageous
one,
and dredge a channel
to discharge the downstream flow.
Alternatively, repair the abandoned dike south of Wǔchéng (武城),
extending to Fēng (豐) and Shàn (單) to connect to Miàodàokǒu (廟道口) north of Pèi (沛),
to prevent northward flow.
These are all urgent tasks
for river management.
As for the transport route,
a separate canal should be dug east of the lake, between Téng (滕), Pèi (沛), Yútái (魚臺), and Zōuxiàn (鄒縣), at Dúshān (獨山) and Xīn'ān Shèdì (新安社地),
connecting south
to Liúchéng (留城) and north to Shā Hé (沙河),
not more than a hundred *lǐ* (里).
Build a thick embankment on the west bank to serve as a lake barrier,
preventing the water from overflowing,
and use the lake as a zone for river overflow
and dispersal.
This is the best strategy.”
Lǐ Chéngxūn (李承勛) said: “The Yellow River (黃河) has six tributaries entering the Grand Canal.
Since the source of the Guō Hé (渦河) became blocked,
it then flowed north through Xiǎohuáng Hé (小黃河), Liūgōu (溜溝), and other places.
Within a few years, all these places became blocked,
and it then
converged and flowed out through Fēiyún Qiáo (飛雲橋).
Consequently, Fēng (豐) and Pèi (沛) suffered,
and the Jīngōu (金溝) transport route became silted up.
Fortunately, the eastern side is all mountains,
which still provide a barrier,
hence Zhāoyáng Hú (昭陽湖
got through with boats.
If it were to shift further north,
it would immediately rush into the sea.
The old route of Ānpíngzhèn would be concerning,
and the lives of millions of people in Shānxian and Gǔtíng would be at risk.
If it moved further north still,
then from Jìníng to Línqīng, all the waters of the transport route would flow together into the sea.
How could transport be maintained?
Your humble servant believes that, observing the
tendency of the six branching channels,
they should be guided southward
to prevent breaches.
Therefore, the lower reaches must be dredged.
To protect the people of Fēng, Pèi, Shānxian, and Gǔtíng,
it is necessary to build upon the old
dikes.
The dikes to their northwest must prevent overflow.
Therefore, the upper reaches must be embanked and guarded.
His argument for diverting water from Zhaoyánghú to the east for a transport route
was the same as Shìníng’s.
The matter was then sent to the Grand Ministers-Governor for discussion.
In the first month of the seventh year,
Yìngqī submitted his memorial,
following Shìníng’s plan,
requesting to convert the area east of Zhaoyánghú into a canal.
At that time, the river breached,
silting up over thirty *lǐ* at Miàodàokǒu.
Officials were then separately dispatched to dredge Zhàpízài,
Sūnjiādù,
and the Southern and Northern Liūgōu to reduce the flow in the upper reaches,
and to build dikes from Wǔchéng westward to the south of Pèixiàn
to prevent breaches to the north.
Due to a drought and subsequent self-correction,
those who spoke out requested the cessation of the new river project.
Yìngqī was then recalled to the capital,
and Pān Xīzēng, an Assistant Minister of Works, took his place.
Upon arriving at his post, Xīzēng
said:
“Recently, as the dredging of Zhàpízài has not yet opened up,
the Sūnjiādùkou should be dredged to reduce the river’s force.
I request an imperial decree for the Provincial Governor of Hénán, Pān Xūn, to supervise the Vice Commissioner of River Affairs
to ensure its timely completion.”
The Emperor granted his request.
Xīzēng further said:
“The reason why the Grand Canal below Miàodàokǒu has suddenly become silted for dozens of *lǐ*
is that the breached river comes from the west,冲撞 its mouth,
and also diverts the water of the Zháhér to the east into Zhaoyánghú,
causing the gate water not to flow south,
and the water from Fēiyúnqiáo sometimes overflows to the north.
Now, an eastern dike should be added between Jì and Pèi
to block the path into the lake,
and a western dike should be built to guard against the Yellow River’s impact.
Thus, the water will not disperse and slow down,
and Miàodàokǒu can be forever free from the worry of silting.”
The Emperor also agreed.
In the sixth month of the eighth year,
the long dike of Shān, Fēng, and Pèi counties was completed.
In the fifth month of the ninth year,
the river dike at Sūnjiādù was completed.
A month later,
the river breached at Cáoxiàn.
One breach started from the east of Húcūnsì,
flowing southeast to Jiǎjiābà into the ancient Yellow River,
and from Dīngjiādàokǒu to Xiǎofúqiáo into the Grand Canal.
Another started from the northeast of Húcūnsì,
dividing into two branches: one flowing southeast through Yúchéng to Dàngshān,
joining the ancient Yellow River to exit at Xúzhōu;
the other flowing northeast through the long dike of Shānxian to Yútái,
spreading into a slope water,
and entering the Grand Canal alongside Gǔtíng.
The long dikes of Shān, Fēng, and Pèi counties protected against it,
so it caused no harm.
Xīzēng memorialized:
“The Yellow River flowing from Guīdé to Xú and entering the canal
is its old route.
During the Yǒnglè reign,
a branch river in Kāifēng was dredged to reach Yútái and enter the canal to alleviate shallowness.
Since the Hóngzhì reign,
the Yellow River changed its course to flow from Shān and Fēng, exiting at Fēiyúnqiáo in Pèi,
and the old route of Guīdé became blocked,
as did the branch river at Yútái.
Now that the entire river has returned to its old route,
the severe disaster is far away,
and the branch flow reaches Yútái,
so there is no worry of shallowness or drying up.
This is beneficial for canal transport,
and a blessing for the nation.”
The Emperor was pleased,
and instructed the relevant authorities to be aware of it.
Xīzēng was then recalled to the capital.
From then on,
Fēng and Pèi gradually had no trouble,
but Yútái frequently overflowed.
In the eleventh year,
the Grand River Commissioner, Jiāndū Yùshǐ Dài Shízōng, requested to designate Yútái as a water reception area,
saying:
“The northern bank of the river is adjacent to the transport route.
As for those flowing southwest,
one exits via Sūnjiādù to Shòuzhōu,
one exits via Wōhékǒu to Huáiyuǎn,
one exits via Zhàpízài to Táoyuán,
and one exits via Liángjìngkǒu to Xiǎofúqiáo in Xúzhōu.
In previous years, all four channels were blocked,
and the entire river flowed south,
thus Fēng, Pèi, Cáo, Shān, and Yútái suffered in succession.
Now the disaster is solely concentrated on Yútái,
so it should be abandoned to receive water,
and then guided
to enter Zhaoyánghú,
pass through the New Canal,
and exit at Liúchéng, Jīngōu, and Jìngshān,
which would be easier to manage.
As for blocking the four river channels,
only the Wōhé passes by Zǔlíng,
and we dare not act rashly.
The other three branch rivers largely retain their old traces.
It is advisable to take advantage of Yútái’s blockage
to have the Kāifēng river workers roll fascines to fill the dikes,
forcing the river water to split,
then the water force at Yútái will gradually decrease.
Once the water recedes and the work is completed,
these three rivers, together with the former ones, will form four channels
to divert the water.
The river disaster can then be resolved.”
The next year,
Dū Yùshǐ Zhū Cháng replaced Shízōng,
and memorialized two matters concerning river control,
generally stating:
“The three major branch rivers should be opened as Shízōng planned,
and I request to block the岔口 (forked mouth) east of Liángjìngkǒu, which enters the Grand Canal via Yútái,
to defend against the Yellow River.
Then the silted area of over two hundred *lǐ* south of Gǔtíngzhèn can be dredged.
This is to block the mouth of the Yellow River to open the Grand Canal.
When the Yellow River turns into the Grand Canal at Gǔtíng,
flowing southward,
it reaches Xúzhōu in two days.
From Xúzhōu, flowing northward against the current,
it takes four days to reach Gǔtíng.
There is no greater benefit from the Yellow River water than this.
I fear the river might trend north,
perhaps overflowing Ānpíngzhèn via Yútái, Jīnxiāng, and Jìníng,
which would breach the dikes of the Grand Canal;
or if one of the three branches becomes blocked with silt,
then the Grand Canal south of Gǔtíng will also breach.
It is advisable to repair and build up the dikes,
confining the Yellow River into the Grand Canal.
This is to borrow the Yellow River’s water to supplement the Grand Canal.”
The Emperor decreed that Cháng should survey and manage the situation.
In the first month of the thirteenth year,
Cháng again memorialized: “Now Liángjìngkǒu and Zhàpízài are already open,
and Sūnjiādù is being dredged.
However, the Wōhé branch,
due to the silting of the main
river for over fifty *lǐ* at Yějīgāng in Suīzhōu downstream of Zhàpízài,
overflows onto the flat ground,
entering the Wōhé.
It is advisable to dredge it deep and wide,
guiding the overflowing water back into the main river,
and to build a long dike at Zhāngjiànkǒu in Suīzhōu
to Guōcūn in Guīdé,
a total of over a hundred *lǐ*,
to prevent floods.
Furthermore, the downstream of Liángjìngkǒu should be regularly dredged,
and the Yuèhé of Yífēng should be dredged to flow into it,
reaching
Xiǎofúqiáo,
which would reduce the water force on the north bank.
Indeed, as the river passes Yútái,
its flow gradually tends northward,
and there is a growing tendency for it to bypass Jìníng, head towards Ānpíng, and enter the sea to the east.
It was once proposed to block the mouth of the Chàhé to
secure the Grand Canal,
but with the raging water,
it may be difficult to block abruptly.
Even if blocked, there might still be horizontal breaches,
and places like Huánglínggāng and Lǐjūzhuāng might not be safe.
From Xúzhōu
upwards to Lǔqiáo, mud and sand accumulate,
and the spring water in Shandong is scarce,
so the transport route will inevitably be sluggish.
I request to construct a new, continuous great dike from Chéngwǔ to Jìníng, over a hundred and fifty
*lǐ* long,
to prevent overflow to the north.
And from Lǔqiáo to Pèixiàn, the eastern dike, over a hundred and fifty *lǐ* long, should be firmly and thickly built,
and reinforced with stones.
From Yútái to
Gǔtíng, the silted river should be opened,
diverting water into the canal,
to alleviate the troubles of Yútái and Chéngwǔ.
This follows the nature of water and does not contend with water for land.
The two branches of Sūnjiādù and Wōhé both flow out at Huáiyuǎn,
converging with the Huáihé flow at Fèngyáng,
passing through Huánglíng and Shòuchūn Wánglíng to Sìzhōu,
and through Zǔlíng.
Huánglíng is on high ground with no worries,
but Zǔlíng is bordered by the river on three sides,
and Shòuchūn Wánglíng is even closer.
Zǔlíng should have an earth dike built,
and Shòuchūn Wánglíng should have a stone embankment.
bank.
However, the matter was of great importance,
and they dared not act rashly.
The mouth of the Qīngjiāng Pǔ is directly at the confluence of the Huánghé and Huái Hé rivers.
When the waters of the two rivers rise, they flood into the river mouth,
causing
silting and obstructed transport.
It is advisable to dredge and widen it, and also to build dikes
to prevent flooding,
and construct dams to protect navigation.
None of these can be delayed.
In the past,
the Huái Hé river alone
flowed into the sea,
and at its mouth there were also tidal currents.
Upstream and downstream of Āndōng, there were various streams and ports like Jiànhé and Mǎluò to divert water into the sea.
Now, the Huánghé river converges into
the Huái Hé,
and the water's force is no longer as it was.
All these ports and tidal channels are now silted up,
unable to discharge quickly,
causing blockage downstream and overflow upstream,
obstructing the transport route.
It is advisable to progressively
dredge these channels and ports.
At the mouth of the sea, where there are sandy tidal flats,
many "dragon claw boats" should be deployed to repeatedly dredge and clear,
to widen the path into the sea.
This is what is called "killing its lower stream."
Although the diversion of the river from Yútái has been borrowed to facilitate grain transport,
it has never remained unchanged for several decades.
Should it shift elsewhere suddenly,
then Xúzhōu and Pèi Xiàn will surely dry up.
It is advisable to greatly dredge
the various springs in Shāndōng to converge into the Wèn Hé river,
then the channels of Xúzhōu and Pèi Xiàn will not suffer from drought,
and even if the Chàhé Kǒu is blocked, there will be no worries.
The Ministry of Works reported in agreement with his proposal,
and the Emperor approved its implementation.
Soon after,
Shāng (Cháng) left due to sorrow.
Liú Tiānhé was appointed Vice Censor-in-Chief and Superintendent of Rivers,
replacing Shāng (Cháng).
That year,
the river burst its banks at Zhàopízhài, entering the Huái Hé.
Gǔtíng became dry,
and Miàodàokǒu became silted up again.
Tiānhé employed 140,000 laborers to dredge it.
Subsequently,
the river suddenly broke through several openings from Dàqiū and Huícūn in Xiàyì,
turning northeast,
flowing through Xiāo Xiàn,
and then downstream to Xiǎofúqiáo in Xúzhōu.
Tiānhé stated:
"The Huánghé river has entered the Grand Canal from Yú Tái and Pèi Xiàn,
allowing smooth passage for transport boats for several decades,
but it has also silted up river channels, damaged sluice gates, obstructed spring flows, and widened the river course,
causing great harm.
Now that the Huánghé river has changed course and flows through Yúchéng, Xiāo Xiàn, and Dàngshān,
down to Xiǎofúqiáo,
while the two branches of Yúlínjí and Hóujiālín that used to divert water into the canal
are both silted and cut off,
the benefit is gone, and only the harm remains.
It is advisable to dredge the silted sections from Lǔqiáo to Xúzhōu, a distance of over two hundred *lǐ*."
The decree approved it.
In the fourteenth year, following Tiānhé's advice,
a *lǚshuǐ* dike to control the flow was built at the eastern branch of Chàhé Kǒu from Liángjìngkǒu in Cáo Xiàn.
Additionally, long dikes were built from Bālǐwān in Cáo Xiàn to Hóujiālín in Shàn Xiàn.
In the winter of that year,
Tiānhé submitted several proposals for river management,
which included:
"Regarding the eastern dike from Lǔqiáo to Pèi Xiàn,
it was formerly proposed to build it with stone to resist lateral currents.
Now that the Huánghé river has shifted southward,
it may not be necessary to build it.
At Sūnjiādù, the entire river shifted southward from the Zhèngtǒng reign,
but it became silted during the Hóngzhì period,
and despite repeated openings, it repeatedly silted up,
ultimately remaining impassable.
Now, the Zhàopízhài river is gradually widening.
If the ferry crossing were reopened,
and it merged with the Guō Hé river,
not only would the two floodwaters be obstructed,
but there might also be a risk to the imperial tombs.
It is advisable to leave it as it is and not attempt to manage it.
It was formerly proposed to add crescent dikes at Pánshí in Xiángfú, Tóngwǎxiāng in Lányáng, and Càijiākǒu in Kǎochéng.
I believe that among the parts of the Huánghé river that need defense, the north bank is the most important.
A great dike and a middle dike should be chosen where they are far from the river,
repaired and built up completely,
so that the seven or eight hundred *lǐ* stretch of the north bank is continuous, high, and thick.
Then, all the dikes previously surveyed for construction would be included within this,
and all could be abandoned and not built."
The Emperor also agreed.
In the fifteenth year,
Zhōu Jīn, the Censor-in-Chief overseeing grain transport, stated:
"Since the sixth year of Jiājìng,
the river flow has increasingly moved southward.
One branch flows directly down the Guō Hé river into the Chánghuái,
while the two branches of Liángjìngkǒu and Zhàopízhài each enter the Qīng Hé river,
converging at Xīnzhuāng Zhá,
and then irrigating the Guài Hé river.
As the water recedes, sand remains,
leading to daily silting.
The elders all say that the river originally came from Biàn, and was turbid,
while the Guō Hé, Huái Hé, and Sì Hé are clear.
Xīnzhuāng Zhá is directly at the confluence of the two waters.
Now that the Huánghé and Huái Hé have merged,
what was once a problem for Pèi Xiàn
has now shifted to Huái'ān.
Therefore, I request that another channel be established at Xīnzhuāng,
and a sluice gate be erected for water storage and discharge."
This was approved.
In the sixteenth year, in winter, following the advice of Yú Zhàn, Vice Censor-in-Chief and Superintendent of Rivers,
the upper reaches of Dìqiūdiàn and Yějīgāng were opened for over forty *lǐ*,
flowing from Táoyuánjí and Dīngjiàdàokǒu into the Old Huánghé river,
〔一三〕diverting Guō Hé water into the river to augment the flood flow.
In the eighteenth year,
Hú Zànzōng, Censor-in-Chief and Superintendent of Rivers, opened the Huánghé river branches at Sūn Jìkǒu and Sūn Lùkǒu in Kǎochéng,
to reduce the flood threat from the Guī Hé and Suī Hé rivers,
and also to irrigate Xúzhōu and Lǚ Xiàn.
He then built long dikes at these two mouths
and repaired the breach at Mǎmùjí.
In the fifth month of the twentieth year, Wáng Yǐqí, Vice Minister of War, was ordered to supervise river management,
and consult with Guō Chípíng, Vice Censor-in-Chief and Superintendent of Rivers.
〔一四〕A year earlier,
the Huánghé river had shifted south,
breaching at Yějīgāng,
and flowing through the Guō Hé river via Bózhōu into the Huái Hé.
The old breaches were all blocked.
The flow from Sūn Jìkǒu and Kǎochéng to Dīngjiàdàokǒu,
and then via Yúchéng into Xúzhōu and Lǚ Xiàn,
was also only two-tenths of its former volume.
Chípíng had managed it for a long time without effect,
and was demoted in salary and put on probation.
Upon Yǐqí's arrival,
he reported:
"At the beginning of the dynasty,
the Grand Canal only communicated with various springs and the Wèn Hé and Sì Hé rivers.
The Huánghé river was fierce and turbid,
constantly shifting.
Therefore, Xú Yǒuzhēn, Bái Áng, and Liú Dàxià strongly opposed
using it to facilitate transport.
Now, fortunately, the Huánghé river has shifted south,
and the various sluice gates have been restored.
It is advisable to dredge the various springs in Shāndōng into the newly opened channel at Yějīgāng,
to benefit Xúzhōu and Lǚ Xiàn;
and to build a long dike south of Pèi Xiàn,
collecting water as in the sluice river system,
solely to facilitate grain transport."
In the spring of the following year,
Chípíng requested to dredge the three rivers of Sūn Jìkǒu, Hùyùnkǒu, and Lǐjǐnggāokǒu,
so that they would flow east through Xiāo Xiàn and Dàngshān into Xúzhōu to facilitate transport.
That autumn,
following Yǐqí's advice,
a separate channel was opened outside Sūn Jìkǒu to discharge water,
to benefit Xúzhōu and Lǚ Xiàn.
After eight months,
the work on the three mouths was completed.
Yǐqí and Chípíng were both rewarded,
and Yǐqí was then recalled.
Soon after,
Lǐjǐnggāokǒu became silted up again.
Previously,
the river had burst its banks at Fēng Xiàn,
moving the county seat to Huàshān,
and only much later did it return to its former location.
When the river burst its banks at Mèngjīn and Xiàyì,
their cities were also moved.
And when Yějīgāng burst its banks,
many prefectures and counties along the Huái Hé in Fèngyáng suffered from floods.
It was then proposed to relocate Wǔhé and Méngchéng to avoid them.
However, Línhuái, being strategically located for the ancestral tombs, could not be moved.
Therefore, following the advice of Imperial Censor Jiǎ Tàihéng,
an imperial edict instructed the two officials overseeing river and land to urgently dredge the Dàngshān river channel,
and divert water into the two floods (likely referring to two flood channels),
to reduce the force of the southward flow.
In the autumn of the twenty-sixth year,
the river burst its banks at Cáo Xiàn,
water entering the city two *chǐ* deep,
and inundating Jīnxiāng, Yútái, Dìngtáo, and Chéngwǔ,
and breaching at Gǔtíng.
Zhān Hàn, Censor-in-Chief and Superintendent of Rivers, requested to dig more branch rivers at Zhàofǎlzhài and other mouths,
to divide the water flow.
The imperial edict approved.
In the ninth month of the thirty-first year,
the Yellow River breached its banks from Fángcūn Jí (房村集) in Xúzhōu (徐州) to Xīn'ān (新安) in Pīzhōu (邳州).
The transport waterway was choked for fifty *lǐ* (里).
Zēng Jūn (曾鈞), Vice Grand Censor-in-Chief of the General River Administration, submitted a strategy for river management.
〔一五〕It involved dredging from Fángcūn (房村) to Shuānggōu (雙溝) and Qǔtóu (曲頭),
and constructing a dyke from Gāomiào (高廟) in Xúzhōu (徐州) to the Yíhé (沂河) in Pīzhōu (邳zhou).
He further stated:
“The eighty *lǐ* (里) from Liúlíngtái (劉伶臺) to Chìyàn Miào (赤晏廟)
constitute the lower reaches of the Yellow River.
Accumulated sand has choked it,
so dredging should be prioritized.
Next is the old Yellow River mouth at Cǎowān (草灣),
where erosion and inundation have submerged the entire county of Āndōng (安東).
This also requires urgent construction,
with additional long dykes and jetties built to guard against erosion.
Furthermore, the new river mouth at Sānlǐgōu (三里溝) is six *chǐ* (尺) higher than the old mouth.
Opening the old mouth risks sand silting,
but the harm is relatively minor;
opening the new mouth inevitably brings the risk of inundation,
though it is quite convenient for grain transport boats.
It is advisable to temporarily close the new mouth,
construct a sluice gate,
and further reinforce the long dyke at Gāojiāyàn (高家堰),
while paving the various sluices at Xīnzhuāng (新莊) with stone to block lateral flows.”
The Emperor ordered Attendant Minister Wú Péng (吳鵬) to provide disaster relief to households,
and wholly adopted Jūn’s (鈞) proposals.
The new river at Sānlǐgōu (三里溝)
was opened by Yīng Jiǎ (應檟), Censor-in-Chief of Grain Transport, in a previous year, to connect the Qīnghé Kǒu (清河口) to the Yellow River water for transport.
Now, as the Yellow River enters the sea,
Jiànkǒu (澗口) and Āndōng (安東) in the lower reaches are both blocked by rising waters.
The river flow is obstructed and gradually rises,
spilling into Qīnghé Kǒu (清河口).
Sand accumulates easily,
and it silts up repeatedly after repeated dredging.
The ditch is located in the lower reaches of the Huái Shuǐ (淮水) before it joins the Yellow River.
Therefore, the Qīnghé Kǒu (清河口) was closed and this ditch was opened,
allowing boats to travel from Tōngjì Qiáo (通濟橋) upstream through the ditch to the Huái (淮),
reaching the Yellow River.
At this time, the dredging of Xú (徐) and Pī (邳) was nearing completion,
when overnight,
water surged and caused further silting.
The Emperor, following Yán Sōng’s (嚴嵩) advice,
dispatched an official to offer sacrifices to the river god.
Péng (鵬) and Jūn (鈞) then jointly submitted a request for urgent construction and dredging at Cǎowān (草灣) and Liúlíngtái (劉伶臺),
the construction of sluices at Sānlǐgōu (三里溝),
to divert the clear waters of the Sì Shuǐ (泗水);
and also to dredge one or two branch rivers from Xúzhōu (徐州) upstream to Kāifēng (開封),
to disperse the water flow.
That winter,
the work on the grain transport canal was completed, and Jūn (鈞) was promoted to the rank of Attendant Minister.
In the seventh month of the thirty-seventh year,
Xīnjí (新集) in Cáoxiàn (曹縣) silted up.
Xīnjí (新集) is adjacent to Liángjìng Kǒu (梁靖口),
and stretches through Xiàyì (夏邑), Dīngjiā Dàokǒu (丁家道口), Mǎmù Jí (馬牧集), Hánjiā Dàokǒu (韓家道口),
and Sījiā Dàokǒu (司家道口) to Jìmén (薊門) in Xiāoxiàn (蕭縣), exiting at Xiǎofúqiáo (小浮橋).
This was the old course of the Jiǎlǔ Hé (賈魯河).
Since the river calamity intensified,
branch rivers were separately opened from Xiǎohé (小河) to reduce the water force,
but the main river gradually became shallow.
By then, it breached,
flowing northeast towards Duànjiākǒu (段家口),
where it split into six branches:
Dàliúgōu (大溜溝), Xiǎoliúgōu (小溜溝), Qín'gōu (秦溝), Zhuóhé (濁河), Yānzhīgōu (胭脂溝), and Fēiyún Qiáo (飛雲橋).
All flowed via the Grand Canal to Xúhóng (徐洪).
Another branch split from Jiānchéng Jí (堅城集) in Dàngshān (碭山) down to Guōguànlóu (郭貫樓),
splitting into five branches:
Lónggōu (龍溝), Mǔhé (母河), Liánglóugōu (梁樓溝), Yángshìgōu (楊氏溝), and Húdiàngōu (胡店溝).
These also met Xúhóng (徐洪) via Xiǎofúqiáo (小浮橋),
and the old course of over two hundred fifty *lǐ* (里) from Xīnjí (新集) to Xiǎofúqiáo (小浮橋) was consequently silted and irrecoverable.
Thereafter,
the river veered east and west erratically,
without a fixed course.
For several years, the water dispersed,
preventing blockage and collapse.
However, excessive dispersion weakened the flow,
with shallow spots only two *chǐ* (尺) deep,
leading discerning observers to predict eventual silting.
By the seventh month of the forty-fourth year,
the river breached its banks in Pèixiàn (沛縣),
silting the transport waterway for over two hundred *lǐ* (里) upstream and downstream.
The entire river flowed against its current,
from Shāhé (沙河) north of Xúzhōu (徐州),
down to Tánglín Jí (棠林集) in Cáoxiàn (曹縣),
where it split into two branches to the north: the southern flow circled around Qīshān (戚山) and Yángjiā Jí (楊家集) in Pèixiàn (沛縣),
entering Qín'gōu (秦溝) to Xú (徐);
the northern flow circled around Húashān (華山) northeast of Fēngxiàn (豐縣), exiting through Sāntángjiào (三教堂) to Fēiyún Qiáo (飛雲橋).
It then further split into thirteen branches,
some cutting across,
some flowing against the current into the grain transport canal,
reaching Húlíng Chéngkǒu (湖陵城口),
spreading across the lake slopes,
reaching Xúzhōu (徐州),
vast and boundless,
and the river's transformation reached its extreme.
Consequently, Zhū Héng (朱衡) was appointed Minister of Works, concurrently managing river and grain transport,
and Pān Jìxún (潘季馴) was appointed Attendant Censor-in-Chief, overseeing river administration.
In the second month of the following year,
He Qǐmíng (何起鳴), Supervising Secretary of the Bureau of Works, was again dispatched to survey the river works.
Héng (衡) inspected the breaches;
the old channel had become land,
but the remains of the new river dug by Shèng Yìngqī (盛應期) were still visible.
The land was high,
and the river, after breaching, could not flow east beyond Zhāoyáng Hú (昭陽湖).
Thus, a plan for opening and dredging was decided.
However, Jìxún (季馴) argued that the new riverbed was shallow with gushing springs,
requiring immeasurable labor and expense,
and that the old course above Liúchéng (留城), being newly silted, could be restored.
Hence, a rift formed between the two men.
Qǐmíng (起鳴) reached Pèi (沛),
returned,
and reported:
“There are five difficulties in restoring the old river.
The complete diversion of the Yellow River would necessitate sacrificing the upper reaches;
Xīnjí (新集), Pángjiātún (龐家屯), and Zhàojiāquān (趙家圈) are all in the upper reaches.
To invest immeasurable wealth
into a long-abandoned river course
is practically impossible;
this is the first difficulty.
From Liúchéng (留城) to Pèi (沛),
it has become a vast expanse of water,
making construction impossible;
this is the second difficulty.
Spanning dozens of *lǐ* (里),
there is no path to cross,
and nowhere for a hundred thousand people to reside;
this is the third difficulty.
Dredging would lead to bogging,
and constructing banks would lack soil;
moreover, blocking the south would cause it to rush north;
this is the fourth difficulty.
In summer and autumn, prolonged flooding
makes it difficult to guarantee against silting;
this is the fifth difficulty.
The excavation of the new river is less costly,
and can prevent future breaches.
It is advisable to follow Héng’s (衡) suggestion to open the new river,
while also adopting Jìxún’s (季馴) suggestion
not to entirely abandon the old river.”
The court officials deliberated and decided,
and Héng (衡) then proceeded to open the new river.
At this time, Jìxún (季馴) advocated for restoring the old course,
and many court officials also agreed.
Consequently, they surveyed and discussed the upstream areas of Xīnjí (新集) and Guōguànlóu (郭貫樓).
Héng (衡) stated: If the river flows north of Jìngshān (境山),
the sluice canal will silt up;
if it flows south of Xúzhōu (徐州),
the two dams will dry up;
only within the forty-odd *lǐ* (里)
between Jìngshān (境山) and Xiǎofúqiáo (小浮橋)
is it beneficial without harm.
Since the Yellow River changed its course,
the branch rivers at Guōguànlóu (郭貫樓) in Dàngshān (碭山) have all silted up.
It has been rerouted from Húashān (華山), splitting into two branches, north and south:
the southern one exits at Qín'gōu (秦溝),
which is about five *lǐ* (里) south of Jìngshān (境山),
and the grain transport canal can benefit from it;
however, the northern one exits west of Pèixiàn (沛縣) and Fēiyún Qiáo (飛雲橋),
flowing upstream to Yútái (魚臺),
which
causes great harm.
The imperial court, unwilling to see the people suffer from floods,
earnestly desired the old course,
and ordered a survey of the upper reaches.
But I have reviewed the terrain and found five impossibilities.
From Xīnjí (新集) to Liǎnghékǒu (兩河口),
it is all flat plains and high ground,
with no trace of an old course to utilize;
while there is somewhat of a river shape from Guōguànlóu (郭貫樓) to Lónggōu (龍溝),
it is newly silted,
with no place to stand;
this
is the first impossibility.
Wherever the Yellow River passes,
it rarely fails to cause harm.
If it passes through Xīnjí (新集), Shāng (商), Yú (虞), and Xiàyì (夏邑) will suffer;
if it passes through Guōguànlóu (郭貫樓), Xiāo (蕭) and Dàng (碭) will suffer.
Now,
if the old course is restored,
the calamity of Yú (魚) and Pèi (沛) will shift back to Xiāo (蕭) and Dàng (碭);
this is the second impossibility.
The river flows west towards Húashān (華山),
with the force of water pouring down from a height.
To dig a canal through it,
to divert water southward,
one must construct a dam to block it horizontally,
stopping its eastward rush.
Amidst raging torrents and vast inundations,
building a dam several *lǐ* (里) long
is extremely difficult;
this
is the third impossibility.
Thirty thousand laborers,
prolonged work for a long time,
causing unrest in three provinces;
this is the fourth impossibility.
Great projects continually arise,
costing millions in expenses,
and if one fails
continuously,
all previous efforts would be ruined.
This is the fifth reason it is unfeasible.
Instead, we should widen the Qín Gōu,
allowing for smooth passage downstream,
and construct a long embankment on the south bank to prevent collapse.
This
can revive the people of Yú and Pèi who are submerged in misery.”
The proposal was accepted.
Héng then opened the Yútái Nányáng to Pèixiàn Liúchéng for over 140 *lǐ*,
and dredged the old river from Liúchéng downwards
to Jìng Shān and Cháchéng, a distance of over 50 *lǐ*.
From there, it joined the Huáng Hé.
He also built the Mǎjiāqiáo embankment, 35,280 *zhàng* long,
and a stone embankment 30 *lǐ* long,
to block the river that flowed out of Fēiyúnqiáo
and direct it into the Qín Gōu to enter Hóng.
Consequently, the Yellow River no longer encroached eastward,
the grain transport canal was opened, and the Pèi river dried up.
Before the work was completed,
the river again breached at Pèixiàn,
destroying the Mǎjiāqiáo embankment.
Critics submitted memorials requesting Héng's dismissal.
Soon after,
the work was finished.
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
and composed four poems to commemorate the success,
showing them to all officials on duty.
In the fifth month of the first year of Lóngqìng, Héng was promoted to Tàizǐ Shàobǎo.
Initially, when the river breached,
its branches spread widely across the land,
then flowed south into the Zhuó Hé.
When the new river was completed,
it all flowed into the Qín Gōu,
and all the northern and southern tributary rivers merged there.
However, the river's flow increased significantly.
In the seventh month of the third year, it breached at Pèixiàn,
and the areas from Kǎochéng, Yúchéng, Cáo, Dān, Fēng, Pèi to Xúzhōu all suffered damage.
Cháchéng was silted up,
and grain transport boats were blocked at Pīzhōu and could not proceed.
Although it was slightly opened later,
the Huáng Hé waters overflowed into the Pèi area,
and the Qín Gōu and Zhuó Hékǒu were alternately cleared and re-silted.
Zhū Héng had already been recalled,
and both the Ministry of Works and the Grand Censor-in-Chief of River Management, Wēng Dàlì, requested to open a new river south of Liáng Shān for grain transport,
to avoid the dangers of the Qín Gōu and Zhuó Hékǒu.
This was later known as the Jiā Hé.
An imperial edict ordered a survey of the terrain,
but it was not carried out.
In the autumn of the fourth year,
the Huáng Hé surged violently,
Cháchéng was again silted up,
and the Shā, Xuē, Wén, and Sì rivers in Shāndōng rapidly overflowed,
breaching the Zhòngjiāqiǎn transport canal,
flowing out from Liáng Shān to Qījiā Gǎng,
where they merged with the Huáng Hé.
Dàlì again requested to dredge it according to its momentum.
At this time,
the Huái Shuǐ also overflowed greatly,
silting up over ten *lǐ* from Tàishān Miào to Qīlǐ Gōu,
and the water flowed out from Zhūjiā Gōu
to Qīnghéxiàn Hénán Zhèn to merge with the Huáng Hé.
Dàlì further said:
"By opening the Xīnzhuāng Gate to allow boats to return,
and restoring Chén Xuān's old course,
the Huái River can be safe.
Only the Huáng Hé between Suīníng and Sùqiān shifts unpredictably,
and the imperial tombs in Sìzhōu are at risk.
I request to dredge the ancient Suī Hé,
passing from Sùqiān through Sùzhōu,
and exiting at Xiǎofúqiáo to discharge the waters of the two Hóng rivers.
Also, plan to restore the Qīnghé and Yúgōu bifurcated river section,
down to Cǎowān,
to avoid the danger of erosion and impact,
then the northern and southern transport routes can perhaps be secured."
At this time, Dàlì had already been transferred inward,
and was about to be replaced,
while Jì Xùn was reinstated as Grand Censor-in-Chief to oversee river management.
The Ministry deliberated and ordered a plan.
In the ninth month,
the river again breached at Pīzhōu,
from Suīníng Báilàngqiǎn to Sùqiān Xiǎohékǒu,
silting up 180 *lǐ*,
and grain vessels were blocked and could not proceed.
Dàlì said:
"Recently, the river disasters were not in Shāndōng, Hénán, Fēng, or Pèi,
but specifically in Xú and Pī.
Therefore, our prior desire to open the Jiā Hékǒu to divert the river's force, and to open the Xiāoxiàn River to reduce its flow,
was precisely because floating sand accumulated,
raising the riverbed,
as a precaution for the future.
Now, the autumn waters have surged continuously,
overflowing and causing disaster.
The expedient measure is to abandon the old course and follow the new breach;
the long-term strategy is to open the Jiā Hé to avoid floods."
He requested a decision between these two.
The Ministry's deliberation favored blocking the breach,
and ordered Dàlì to list the advantages and disadvantages for report.
Dàlì then presented three proposals simultaneously: opening the Jiā Hékǒu, following the new breach, and restoring the old course,
and also explained how their advantages and disadvantages were intertwined.
He happened to be dismissed,
and the proposals were not decided,
but Jì Xùn advocated restoring the old course.
At that time, from Cháchéng to Lǚ Liáng,
the Yellow River was constrained by the two banks,
〔一六〕 unable to flow downstream,
nor could it breach.
By the fourth month of the fifth year,
it breached from Língbì Shuānggōu downwards,
breaching three openings to the north
and eight to the south.
Branches overflowed,
the main current flowed down to Suīníng and out through Xiǎohé,
and the 80 *lǐ* of the main river at Chí Tóu Wān were completely silted up.
Jì Xùn employed 50,000 laborers
to block all eleven openings,
and dredged Chí Tóu Wān,
building over 30,000 *zhàng* of continuous embankments,
thus restoring the old course of Chí Tóu Wān.
Soon after, as many grain boats were lost and submerged while navigating the new currents,
Jì Xùn was dismissed.
In the spring of the sixth year, Shàngshū Héng was again appointed to manage the river works,
with Bīngbù Shìláng Wàn Gōng as the Grand Administrator of Riverways.
Upon their arrival,
they dismissed the Jiā Hé proposal,
and focused solely on the Xú-Pī River,
building long embankments
from Xúzhōu to Sùqiān Xiǎohékǒu, 370 *lǐ* long,
and repairing the large Huáng Hé embankment in Fēng and Pèi.
The main river flowed peacefully,
and the transport route was greatly opened.
Héng then submitted a memorial:
"Hénán has repeatedly suffered from river disasters,
and extensive embankments were built.
Now, it has enjoyed several decades of peace
due to strict defense and preparedness.
Xú and Pī are the main routes for grain transport,
and since much effort has been made to construct them,
much effort should also be made to protect them.
I request to employ ten laborers per *lǐ* for defense,
with one watch post every three *lǐ*,
and one elder supervising every four watch posts.
When the autumn waters rise,
they should ascend the embankments on the fifteenth day of the fifth month
and descend on the fifteenth day of the ninth month.
Those who wish to bring their families to reside there are permitted."
The imperial edict approved the proposal.
In the sixth month,
the Xú-Pī river embankment work was completed,
and Héng was ordered to return to his ministry,
with Héng and the Grand Administrator of Riverways, Grand Censor-in-Chief Wàn Gōng,
among others,
rewarded with varying amounts of silver and silk.
That year,
Censor Wú Cóngxiàn said:
"From Huái'ān upwards to Qīnghé downwards,
this is precisely where the Huái, Sì, Hé, and Hǎi rivers converge and clash.
River floods flow inward,
and sea tides surge upstream,
accumulating for a long time,
causing sand and mud to quickly gather,
thus leading to daily silting.
It is advisable to dredge and manage it during spring and summer,
then the downstream flow will be smooth,
and overflows will naturally subside."
The Emperor immediately ordered Héng and the grain transport officials to investigate and discuss.
And Chén Yīngjiàn, the Acting Langzhong overseeing river management,
recommended dredging the new river at the estuary,
which was over ten *lǐ* long,
five *zhàng* and five *chǐ* wide,
and one *zhàng* and seven *chǐ* deep,
employing over 6,400 laborers.
Guì Fāng said:
“The Huái River used to meet the Yellow River via the Qīng River and then flow into the sea.
Since the Yellow River breached at Cuī Zhèn last autumn,
the main Qīng Jiāng riverbed has become silted up,
and the mouth of the Huái River is blocked.
Consequently, the Huái River has weakened while the Yellow River has strengthened,
unable to reclaim its route into the sea via Cǎo Wān.
The entire Huái River has shifted south,
flooding the area between Shānyáng, Gāo, and Bǎo.
Previously, the lake water would not exceed five chǐ,
and the dikes were only seven chǐ high.
Now the dikes have been raised by twelve zhàng,
yet the water level surpasses them.
It is urgent to protect the lake dikes to reduce the water's force.”
The Ministry deliberated, believing that the dikes could only be protected
if the Huái River had an outlet.
They requested that Guì Fāng and others thoroughly plan this.
The report was approved.
Before the two proposals of opening a new river and protecting dikes were settled,
the river again breached at Cuī Zhèn.
Many sections on both banks of Sù, Pèi, Qīng, and Táo were destroyed.
The Yellow River became more and more silted each day.
The Huái River, pressed by the Yellow River,
shifted south.
This was the eighth month of the fifth year.
Xī Zhì proposed blocking the breach
and confining the water to the canal.
Guì Fāng wanted to scour it to form a river,
to serve as the old Yellow River's path to the sea.
The Emperor ordered the breach to be quickly sealed,
and after the water's force had somewhat stabilized,
he would follow Guì Fāng's suggestion.
At that time, Remonstrance Official Tāng Pìn'yǐn proposed diverting the Huái River into the Jiāng River to avoid the Yellow River.
Meanwhile, Guì Fāng reported:
“The Yellow River is flowing along its old course,
rushing downstream like a torrent.
The Huái River has taken advantage of the emptiness to surge into the old course at Qīngkǒu.
The water levels of the Huái and Yáng rivers are gradually subsiding.”
The Ministry deliberated on conducting an investigation,
but as the Yellow and Huái rivers had already merged,
the proposal was dropped.
Shī Tiānlín, Administrator of the Southern River Works, a Director in the Ministry of Public Works, said: The waters of the Huái and Sì rivers do not flow down to Qīngkǒu but rather to Shānyáng,
entering the sea from Huáng Pǔkǒu.
Huáng Pǔkǒu cannot drain all the water,
which inundates the lakes of Gāo, Bǎo, and Shàobó.
All the lake dikes are submerged,
but now they do.
The entry of the Huái and Sì rivers into the lakes
is also because Qīngkǒu was not
silted up before,
but now it is.
The silting of Qīngkǒu
is also because the Yellow River’s siltation level rises daily,
forcing the Huái River to yield to the Yellow River and shift south.
When the Huái River concentrates its strength to contend with the Yellow River,
the outcome might be evenly matched.
Since Gāojiāyàn was ruined,
the waters of the Huái River flowed
inward through Tōngjìqiáo
and Zhūjiā, etc., within Qīngkǒu.
Consequently, the strength of the Huái and Sì rivers was divided,
allowing the Yellow River to exert its full force to overcome their weakness.
This is why Qīngkǒu alone became so heavily silted this year.
Once the lower reaches
are silted,
the upper reaches must necessarily breach.
Every year, grain barges complete their transport by the fourth or fifth month,
and the dikes breach by the sixth or seventh month.
When the water rises, no effort can be made.
Only after the water recedes are plans made to block
the breaches.
As soon as early spring arrives,
transport operations are pressing again,
and only dike repairs are completed,
with no attention paid to the riverbed itself.
If the riverbed is not dredged, it will become even higher next year.
Breaches in the upper reaches
will inevitably affect Xú and Lǚ,
not just Pī and Qiān;
the drying up of the lower reaches
will extend completely to Pī and Qiān,
not just Qīng and Táo.
It is necessary to spare no effort
in grain transport for one year,
and spare tens of thousands in treasury funds,
to excavate and dredge the main river,
and allow ample time for completion,
thus achieving lasting peace.
As for Gāojiāyàn, Zhūjiā, and other outlets,
they should be promptly dammed and sealed,
so that the combined strength of the Huái and Sì rivers is sufficient to contend with the Yellow River.
Then the old course of the Huái River can be restored,
and the great danger to Gāo and Bǎo can be reduced.
If the sea outlets at Xīng and Yán are blocked,
they should also be greatly dredged.
And more large sluice gates should be built on the lake dikes,
with more tributary rivers
opened below the dikes.
Crucially, one cannot manage the Huái River without first managing the Yellow River,
nor can one consolidate the dikes without dredging the Huái River.
The matter was submitted to the various officials of the River and Canal Transport for deliberation.
The Huái River exited Qīngkǒu
because the Yellow River water rushed along the old Yellow River.
However, the old Yellow River had been heavily silted for a long time,
and it soon became blocked again,
causing the Huái River to still overflow.
Remonstrance Official Liú Xuán requested that the sea outlets be urgently opened
and that a high official be appointed to oversee the work with the river and canal transport officials.
Consequently, Guì Fāng was appointed Minister of Public Works, concurrently overseeing river and canal transport,
and the office of Grand Coordinator of River Works was abolished.
Guì Fāng died shortly after receiving the appointment.
In the summer of the sixth year,
Pān Jìxún succeeded him.
At that time, Remonstrance Official Lǐ Lái requested more dredging of the sea outlets
to guide the return of all waters.
Remonstrance Official Wáng Dàochéng, on the other hand, requested sealing the breach at Cuī Zhèn,
building a long dike at Táo and Sù,
repairing Gāojiāyàn,
and reopening the old Yellow River.
All these were submitted to the river officials for deliberation.
Jìxún and Assistant Minister for Canal Transport Jiāng Yīlín surveyed the water situation
and said that below the four branches of Yúntī Guān at the sea outlet,
it was seven or eight to more than ten lǐ wide,
and three or four zhàng deep.
If a separate plan for excavation was desired,
it must be of similar
depth and width
to allow discharge,
which would be extremely difficult.
Moreover, before reaching the sea outlet,
construction was still possible on dry land,
but in the area entering the sea,
with tides coming and going,
it would be
the same as the old outlet.
The old outlet was all accumulated sand,
which human effort could not dredge,
though water power could naturally scour it.
There is no principle for dredging the sea.
The only course is to guide the river
to the sea,
which is to use water to manage water,
and that is the strategy for dredging the sea.
The river also cannot be guided by human effort.
The only course is to repair the dikes
to prevent lateral breaches.
Then
the water will flow through the land,
and sand will follow the water,
which is the strategy for guiding the river.
For many years,
repairing dikes has been the task,
but they are low and weak and cannot withstand,
too close and cannot accommodate,
mixed with floating sand and cannot last.
This is why the river breached at Cuī Zhèn,
and much water spilled northward,
due to the absence of dikes.
The Huái River breached at Gāojiāyàn and Huáng Pǔkǒu,
and much water spilled eastward,
because the dikes were not strong.
Not
blaming the inadequacy of the protective measures,
but instead blaming dike building as an inferior strategy,
how can this be a sound argument!
With the upper reaches breaching laterally,
and the lower reaches bifurcated and divided,
its flow towards Yúntī
and the sea outlet
is like the spent force of a powerful crossbow.
The more the water's force is divided, the weaker it becomes.
How can it guide accumulated sand into the sea?
Therefore, the urgent task today for dredging the sea
must first be to block the breaches to guide the river,
and especially to strengthen the dikes to prevent breaches.
And to ensure the dikes do not breach,
they must be made of real earth and not
mixed with floating sand,
high and thick without sparing huge expenses,
set far back and not contend for land.
Only then can the dikes be made strong.
If the dikes along the river are strengthened,
and the Cuī Zhèn breach is sealed,
then
the Yellow River will not breach laterally, and its force will be concentrated on the canal.
If Gāojiāyàn is built
and Zhūjiā outlet is sealed,
then the Huái River will not breach laterally, and its force will be concentrated on joining the Yellow River.
Once the Huái and Yellow rivers merge,
they will
naturally have the momentum to control the sea.
Also, fearing their division and weakening,
the Qīngjiāngpǔ River must be temporarily blocked,
and strict control over opening and closing maintained to prevent internal surging.
For now, the Cǎo
Wānhé
and specifically rebuilt the 'cloud ladder' (梯) to restore its original course.
Then, continue to build a long dike for the new city of Huái'ān,
to prevent its downstream flow.
This ensures the full strength of the Huánghé and Huáihé Rivers,
with every
drop flowing to the sea.
Then the force will be strong and concentrated,
the accumulated sand downstream will naturally be removed,
the sea will be dredged without needing to be dug,
and the river will deepen without needing to be cleared.
This is what is meant by solidifying dikes to
guide the river,
and guiding the river to dredge the sea.
He also said: The Huánghé River enters Xúzhōu,
passes through Pīzhōu, Sùzhōu, Táoyuán, and Qīnghé,
meets the Huáihé River at Qīngkǒu, and then flows eastward into the sea.
The Huáihé River flows from Luòyáng to Fèngyáng,
passes through Xūyí and Sìzhōu,
meets the Huánghé River at Qīng
kǒu, and then flows eastward into the sea.
These are the original courses of the two rivers.
During the Yuán dynasty, grain was transported from Jiāngnán
by entering the sea directly from Miàowān in Yángzhōu,
never upstream via the Huáihé River.
Chén Xuān first built dikes around Gǔanjiā and other lakes,
connecting the Huáihé River as a transport route.
Fearing the Huáihé River might overflow,
he built the Gāojiāyàn dike to defend against it,
starting from Wǔjiādūn,
passing through
Dàjiàn and Xiǎojiàn to Fùnínghú,
so the Huáihé River would not encroach eastward.
Fearing the Huánghé River might also overflow,
he built dikes north of Xīnchéng to defend against it,
starting from Qīngjiāngpǔ,
along Pō
chíshān and Liǔpǔwān eastward,
so the Huánghé River would not encroach southward.
Later,
the dikes gradually tilted,
and water breached from Gāojiāyàn,
submerging the Huái prefecture like fish and turtles.
However, those in charge did not investigate the cause,
saying that the sea outlet was blocked
and that branch canals should be urgently dug.
Little did they know that once Cǎowān was opened,
the main river above Xīqiáo became silted up.
The new river was over twenty zhàng wide,
but only
about one zhàng deep,
which was only one-thirtieth of the original course.
How could it contain all the river's water?
With the downstream blocked,
the upstream naturally breached.
This is why the breaches at Cuīzhèn
occurred.
Now the new river is blocked again,
and the old river is gradually flowing through.
Although its depth and width are not yet one-tenth of the original river,
with both rivers flowing fully,
sand will be scoured by the water,
and it will not be difficult
to fully restore the river channel.
Once the river channel is restored,
it will be seven or eight lǐ wide at its broadest,
and no less than three or four hundred zhàng at its narrowest.
With its mighty flow eastward,
what water could it not contain?
Not only will it be unnecessary to dig elsewhere,
but Cǎowān can also be left undredged.
Therefore, for the present plan,
it is only necessary to repair Chén Xuān's old works,
construct high dikes on both the north and south,
to cut off the internal flooding from the two rivers,
which will prevent the inundation of Huái'ān and Yángzhōu.
Blocking the Huángpǔkǒu,
building the Bǎoyìng dike,
dredging the shallow areas like Dōngguān,
repairing the five sluices,
and restoring the five dams
will ensure the safety of the Huáinán transport route.
Firmly blocking the breaches at Cuīzhèn and other places below
Táoyuán
will allow the entire river to return to its original course.
With the Huánghé and Huáihé Rivers no longer branching off,
and both flowing into the sea,
sand will be scoured by the water,
the sea outlet will naturally recover,
and
the shallow obstructions at Táoyuan
and Qīnghé
will be insignificant.
This is the method of managing water with water.
As for the idea of dredging,
it is only applicable to sluice rivers.
Previous people repeatedly tried
without success,
merely wasting labor and materials.
Thereupon, he proposed six articles: first, to block breaches to reclaim the main river;
second, to build dikes to prevent breaches;
