third, to restore sluices and dams to protect the outer river;
fourth, to construct spillway dams to reinforce dikes;
fifth, to cease sea dredging projects to save expenses;
sixth, to abandon the proposal to open the old Huánghé River to maintain navigation.
The Emperor approved all his requests.
In the tenth month of the seventh year [of Wànlì],
the two river projects were completed.
Jì Xùn and Yī Lín were rewarded with silver and silk,
and Supervisor Yǐn Jǐn was dispatched to verify the completion.
In the spring of the eighth year, Jì Xùn was promoted to Crown Prince's Grand Guardian and Minister of Works,
and one of his sons was granted an official position.
Yī Lín and others were promoted accordingly.
In this campaign,
over sixty lǐ of the Gāojiāyàn dike were built,
over forty lǐ of the Guīrénjí dike,
over seventy lǐ of the Liǔpǔwān dike (east and west),
one hundred thirty breaches at Cuīzhèn and other places were blocked,
over fifty-six thousand zhàng of remote dikes were built along both banks of Xúzhōu, Suīyáng, Pīzhōu, Sùzhōu, Táoyuán, and Qīnghé,
one large dam each at Dàngshān and Fēngxiàn,
over one hundred forty lǐ of continuous dikes at Xúzhōu, Pèixiàn, Fēngxiàn, and Dàngshān,
four stone dams for reducing water flow were constructed at Cuīzhèn, Xú Shēng, Jì Tài, and Sānyì,
and the Tōngjì Sluice was moved to the south of Gānlóuchéng.
All dikes and dams between Huái'ān and Yángzhōu were repaired and built,
costing over five hundred sixty thousand taels of silver.
That autumn, Jì Xùn was promoted to Minister of War of Nánjīng.
Jì Xùn again requested the restoration of the old course from Xīnjí to Xiǎofúqiáo,
but Supervising Secretary Wáng Dàochéng and Henán Provincial Governor Zhōu Jiàn disagreed, and the proposal was dropped.
Since the time of Guì Fāng and Jì Xùn, the position of River Governor-General was abolished,
and thereafter, the Grand Coordinator of Grain Transport concurrently managed river affairs.
When Gāojiāyàn was first built,
Qīngkǒu was smooth,
and for several years,
there were no major problems with the river course.
By the fifteenth year [of Wànlì],
Fēngqiū, Yǎnshī, Dōngmíng, and Chángyuán were repeatedly breached.
Grand Secretary Shēn Shíxíng said:
"The breached areas are in three provinces.
If the local officials divide the repairs,
it will be easy to shirk responsibility.
The river course is not yet greatly damaged,
so there is no need to appoint a Censor-in-Chief.
A seasoned Supervising Secretary should be dispatched to inspect the river."
Thereupon, Cáng Jūjìng, a Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Works, was ordered to go.
Jūjìng requested the construction of a hundred-lǐ long dike from the east of Dàshèjí to Báimáojí.
This was approved.
Originally,
the Huánghé River entered the Grand Canal via Xiǎofúqiáo in Xúzhōu.
That river was deep and close to the main flood channel,
capable of scouring the flood channel to deepen the river,
which was beneficial for the transport route.
Later, it gradually shifted to Fēiyúnqiáo in Pèixiàn and the Dàliūgōu and Xiǎoliūgōu in Xúzhōu.
By the end of the Jiājìng era,
it breached at Shàojiākǒu,
exited at Qíngōu,
and entered the Grand Canal via Zhuóhékǒu.
The river was shallow,
approaching Cháchéng.
Cháchéng became silted up annually,
repeatedly harming the transport route.
In the winter of the fifth year of Wànlì,
the river again shifted southward,
exiting through the old course of Xiǎofúqiáo,
but was soon silted up again.
When Pān Jìxùn blocked Cuīzhèn,
he built thick dikes,
confining the water to the main channel.
Subsequently, when floods occurred,
river officials would add to the dikes,
and the river channel became progressively higher.
Therefore, Yáng Yīkuí, the Grand Coordinator of Grain Transport and Assistant Censor-in-Chief, wished to restore the old course of the Huánghé River,
requesting dredging from Dīngjiādàokǒu below Guīdé to Shíjiāngjūnmiao,
allowing the river to again exit via Xiǎofúqiáo.
He also said:
"Those skilled in water management
rely on dredging, not obstruction.
In recent years, dikes have been built upon dikes,
and the water level is so high it seems to hang in the air,
practically above one's forehead.
The cities and towns along the river
could be flooded by a breach.
It is advisable to measure the depth and shallowness of the river channel,
dredge wherever necessary,
and at the old courses where the Huánghé River branches,
set up stone sluices to relieve sudden floods."
Supervising Secretary Wáng Shìxìng, however, requested the restoration of the old course of the Lǎo Huánghé River.
He generally stated: From Xúzhōu downwards,
the river channel became progressively higher,
and dikes were built to confine it.
The dikes were level with Xúzhōu city.
The more tightly it was confined,
the swifter the flow,
exerting its full force on
the Huáihé River, which could not bear it.
Therefore, where the Huánghé and Huáihé Rivers once converged,
now the Huánghé is strong and the Huáihé has shrunk even more,
no longer converging.
When the Huánghé is strong and one opens the Tiānfēi and Tōngjì sluices,
Soon after, the Huái River burst its banks at the Zhāngfú Dī.
The Direct Zhílì Provincial Inspector Péng Yìngcān said:
"The Imperial Ancestral Tomb should be safe,
and since the east is currently preparing for Wō (Japanese pirate) alarms,
it is advisable to temporarily halt the river works."
The Ministry deliberated, ordering the river officials to carefully consider.
Yìnglóng and Zhēnguān said:
"For the long-term benefit of the Imperial Ancestral Tomb,
the branch river is indeed an unavoidable project.
We request that it be carried out when the Wō alarms cease next spring."
The matter was then shelved.
In the spring of the twenty-first year,
Zhēnguān reported back,
proposing to open the Xiǎohékǒu (Small River Mouth) connecting Guī and Xú,
to relieve the flooding in Xú and Pī;
and to divert the turbid river into the old course of Xiǎofúqiáo,
to alleviate the problem at Zhènkǒu.
This was submitted to the Grand River Administrator and other officials for collective deliberation,
but no decision was reached.
In the fifth month,
there was heavy rain,
and the river burst its banks at Huánggùkǒu in Dān Xiàn.
One branch flowed from Xúzhōu out through Xiǎofúqiáo,
and another flowed via the old river to Zhènkǒu Zhá (gate).
Pīchéng was submerged,
and countless dikes in the Gāo and Bǎo lakes burst.
The following year,
all the lake dikes were rebuilt and closed,
but the Yellow River rose greatly,
and the Qīngkǒu (Clear Mouth) became silted,
preventing the Huái River from flowing eastward.
Consequently, it carried the water from the upper reaches of Fùlíng and other lakes, along with mountain streams,
and violently flooded the Imperial Ancestral Tomb,
submerging Sìchéng.
In the twenty-third year,
the Gāoyóu Zhōngdī (Central Dike), Gāojiāyàn, and Gāoliángjiàn burst again,
and the water calamity became even more severe.
Previously,
Censor Chén Bāngkē had said:
"Consolidating dikes to confine the water has not yielded the benefit of scouring away sand,
but has instead led to breaches.
The method should be dredging,
and there are three ways.
When the water level is low in winter and spring,
order the shallow-water workers along the river to seize the opportunity to clear the shallows,
so that sand does not remain but is carried away –
this is the first.
For official and private boats traveling,
tie a harrow or plough to the stern of each boat,
and scour with the wind,
so that sand does not settle but is carried away –
this is the second.
Emulate the method of water mills and water pestles,
setting up wooden machines
to tumble with the water,
so that sand does not stay but is carried away –
this is the third.
The Huái River must inevitably meet the Yellow River,
so Gāoyàn (Gao Weir) absolutely cannot be abandoned.
Lake overflow will inevitably damage dikes,
so the breach at Zhōujiāqiáo absolutely cannot be opened.
Abandoned channels will inevitably silt up,
so the old Yellow River, Cǎowān, and other places absolutely cannot be restored."
The memorial was submitted to the relevant authorities for deliberation.
Hu Bù Láng (Secretary of the Ministry of Revenue) Huá Cúnlǐ, however, requested to restore the old course of the Yellow River,
and also to dredge Cǎowān.
At that time,
Yāopù had not yet been opened.
Gōng Bù Shìláng (Vice Minister of Works) Shěn Jiéfǔ said:
"Restoring the Yellow River should not be lightly discussed.
As for the other proposals, they are merely patching up deficiencies and remedying ills.
They should all be suspended."
Then Yìnglóng was recalled to the Ministry of Works.
This was in the ninth month of the twenty-second year.
Soon after, Jìshìzhōng (Supervising Secretary) Wú Yìngmíng said:
"Previously, due to the Yellow River's constantly shifting course,
the Yáo and Lǚ dikes were built to confine the water to the canal.
But after the water passed, sand settled,
and the riverbed grew higher day by day.
Residents below Xú and Pī were all submerged.
Now, outside Qīngkǒu, the yellow current is obstructed,
and inside Qīngkǒu, silt is piled up horizontally,
forcibly irrigating the upper reaches for about a hundred *lǐ*.
The Huái River merely flows as a superficial current over the sand,
and the water accumulated in Xū and Sì thus becomes a threat to the Imperial Ancestral Tomb.
Zhāng Zhēnguān's proposal to direct the Yāopù branch river to Cǎowān,
or to open another small river from the south bank of Qīng River to Luòjiāyíng, Mǎchǎng, and other places,
to meet the Grand River,
and to build gates for opening and closing,
so that whenever the transport canal becomes shallow,
this river can be used –
this is also a convenient strategy."
As for managing the Sì River,
there was a proposal to open Lǎozǐshān
to divert the Huái River into the Jiāng River.
It is advisable to install gates for timely opening and closing,
demolish the Zhāngfú Dī and dike Qīngkǒu,
to prevent the river water from flowing south.
The Ministry deliberated and sent officials from the river and transport systems for a joint investigation.
Zhílì Provincial Inspector Niú Yìngyuán, after visiting the Imperial Ancestral Tomb
and witnessing the river calamity firsthand,
submitted a drawing along with a memorial, saying:
"The Yellow River rising and blocking the Huái River
began in the late Jiājìng era when river officials excavated the huge rocks of the Xú and Lǚ dams,
causing sand to settle daily
and the riverbed to rise daily,
leading to breaches from
this point.
Those in charge had no way to remedy it.
Long dikes were built on both banks to confine it,
called the Lǚdī.
When the Lǚdī burst again,
heavy dikes were built a few *lǐ* away to
prevent further damage,
called the Yáodī.
Although they were repaired annually after bursting annually,
nothing could be done.
The confluence of the Yellow and Huái rivers
originally started from Luòjiāyíng, twenty *lǐ* north of the Qīng River,
then turned east to meet the Huái River at Dàhékǒu –
this is what was called the old Yellow River.
Chén Xuān, finding it winding,
opened a branch river from Luòjiāyíng,
which is the current river course,
and the old Yellow River silted up.
During the Wànlì era,
the Cǎowān
branch river was opened again,
and the Yellow River abandoned its old course to follow it,
leading to the confluence at Qīngkǒu,
where the two waters contended.
When the Huái River could not overcome the Yellow River,
it would escape into various gates.
The local people of Huái'ān
built an earthen ridge at each gate to prevent this.
Subsequently, the Yellow and Huái rivers surged violently,
and when the water receded, sand settled,
and Qīngkǒu consequently silted up.
This is now called Ménxiànshā (Threshold Sand).
Those in charge did not think of dredging Ménxiànshā,
but instead built the Gāoyàn (Gao Weir) alongside the earthen ridges,
stretching sixty *lǐ*.
They neglected the main channel of the entire Huái River
and further
built dikes to block Zhāngfúkǒu, which flowed into the Yellow River from the side.
Thus, the water flowed backward, becoming a problem for the Sìlíng (Sì Ancestral Tomb).
The year before last,
Bureau Secretary Zhēnguān proposed to open up Ménxiàn
shā and cut the Zhāngfú Dī.
What he emphasized was also the opening of the Yāopù branch river.
In summary,
if the silt in the entire mouth is not thoroughly dredged,
even if the Yāopù project is completed,
the Huái River water will not be able to flow out.
Moreover, the Bāo and Wáng mouths in the lower reaches have already burst,
making construction difficult.
How can this be compared to restoring the old course of the Yellow River
and thoroughly dredging the silt at Qīngkǒu, which is crucial?
Furthermore, clearing the upper reaches
is not as good as what Bureau Secretary Yìngmíng
proposed:
dredging the various breaches in the lower reaches of Cǎowān,
allowing it to return to Wǔgǎng via Āndōng,
or making measured clearings at Zhōujiāqiáo,
while urgently blocking Huánggùkǒu,
dredging
the Xiāo and Dàng canals,
and clearing the shallow obstructions at Fúlí.
As for the Xiǎohé (Small River) at Sùqiān, which is the main route for the Huái River into the Yellow River,
it should be urgently dredged
to give it an outlet."
Yìnglóng said:
"The Zhāngfú Dī has already burst for over a hundred *zhàng*,
and Qīngkǒu is currently being dredged,
but the opening of Yāopù cannot be abandoned."
Gōng Bù Shìláng (Vice Minister of Works) Shěn Sīxiào then said:
"The old Yellow River from Sānyì Zhèn to Yèjiā Chōng is only over eight thousand *zhàng*,
and its river shape still exists.
It should be urgently opened and dredged,
then the river will be divided into two:
one flowing from the old course to Yánjiāhé into the sea,
and one meeting the Huái River at Qīngkǒu,
and the calamity will naturally be alleviated.
I request that one official from the Fēnglì Division be dispatched
to formulate a unified plan with the river and transport officials."
Then Lǐ Kē Jìshìzhōng (Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Rites) Zhāng Qǐchéng was ordered to investigate.
But because the water calamity had persisted for years
without a conclusive plan,
and there was prolonged waste of resources,
Yìnglóng was dismissed from his post and returned to commoner status.
Cháng Jūjìng, Zhāng Zhēnguān, Péng Yìngcān, and others were all censured to varying degrees.
Censor Gāo Jǔ requested:
“Dredge Zhōujiāqiáo,
reduce Zhāngfú Dī,
open up Ménxiànshā,
and build rolling-water stone dams at Zhōujiāqiáo, Dàxiǎojiànkǒu, Wǔjiādūn, and above and below Lǜyánggōu.
Outside the dams, dredge rivers and build embankments,
allowing water to flow through the land.
Convert the twelve existing pond-dikes and sluices into dams,
to irrigate the twelve rivers outside the sluices,
thereby opening up a path to the sea.
Dredge the Mángdào Hé,
and build many more waterslides along the river,
to broaden the paths into the Jiāng.
However, as the mouth of the sea becomes increasingly blocked daily,
the river sand accumulates daily,
the riverbed rises daily,
and the Huái River will also be unable to flow smoothly.
There is Guànkǒu,
which appears considerably larger than the other mouths,
and the three mouths recently burst at Jiǎngjiā, Bāojiā, and Bìjiā directly align with it.
It is advisable to clear and dredge these into a river,
to allow water to enter the sea this way.”
Fán Zhàochéng, a junior minister in the Ministry of Public Works, also proposed opening up a sea mouth,
and said:
“The old sea mouth absolutely cannot be dredged.
We should dredge a new river from Bāojiāyíng to Wǔgǎngkǒu,
to allow water to enter the sea via Guànkǒu.”
Both proposals were sent to the Ministry of Public Works.
A request was made to jointly commission Qǐchéng to investigate and deliberate.
At this time,
Yáng Yīkuí, the Minister of Public Works and Director-General of Rivers, was impeached
and requested to be relieved of his duties,
saying:
“Qīngkǒu should be dredged,
the old course of the Huáng Hé should be restored,
the Gāoyàn does not need repair,
stone embankments do not need to be built,
and reduction sluice-dams do not need to be used.”
The emperor did not accept his resignation,
but instead issued an edict for him to devote himself to his duties.
Censor Xià Zhīchén then said:
“The sand at the sea mouth cannot be cleared,
Cǎowān Hé does not need dredging,
the forty-li new river at Yāopù does not need to be opened,
Yúntīguān does not need to be opened.
We must urgently open the Gāoyàn,
to save the ancestral tombs.”
He also said:
“Over the years,
the earth embankment at Gāoliángjiàn burst every time it encountered the summer and autumn floods,
and the stone embankment at Dàjiànkǒu collapsed every time it encountered turbulent waters.
When Gāoyàn exists,
it benefits Gāo and Bǎo little;
but if Gāoyàn bursts,
it causes great harm to Gāo and Bǎo.
Why not clearly deliberate and clearly open it,
so that people know to avoid it?”
Supervisor of the Ministry of Works Huáng Yùntài then further said:
“If the lower course of the Huáng Hé has not been discharged,
and we abruptly open Gāoyàn and Zhōujiāqiáo to discharge the Huái River water,
then as the Huái River flows south,
the Huáng Hé will certainly follow it,
the area between Gāo and Bǎo will become a swamp,
and the Grand Canal and the Yuèhé River will certainly burst.
It is better to dredge Wǔgǎngkǒu,
reach Guànkǒumén,
and let it enter the sea, which would be preferable.”
An edict was issued for both proposals to be investigated and deliberated.
Qǐchéng then memorialized, saying:
“Previously, the river did not pose a threat to the ancestral tombs.
Since the end of the Lóngqìng reign, when Gāo, Bǎo, Huái, and Yáng were in distress,
the officials then in charge were accustomed to immediate solutions.
After Qīngkǒu became silted up,
they built Gāoyàn to block it,
and constructed Zhāngfú to constrict it,
obstructing all the Huái River water to contend with the Huáng Hé,
without anticipating that its force was insufficient.
Later, stone was laid and built up,
the blockage became increasingly firm.
Of the water from the seventy-two streams that converged at the Sì River,
only a mouth a few zhang wide remained for it to exit.
One tenth exited,
nine tenths remained stagnant.
The riverbed rose daily,
the flow became increasingly blocked,
the Huái River found it increasingly difficult to exit,
and the accumulated water became increasingly deep.
How could it not flow backward and overflow, becoming a disaster for Sìlíng?
Now, proposals to dredge the Huái River to secure the ancestral tombs,
and to dredge the Huáng Hé to guide the Huái River,
are all different.
As for those who say Gāoyàn should be breached,
I believe it is an essential barrier for Huái and Yáng,
and can hardly be dispensed with.
It would be better to open Zhōujiāqiáo fifty li south of it to flow into Cǎozi Hú,
and greatly dredge it.
One branch would go through Jīnjiāwān into Mángdào Hé and flow into the Jiāng,
another branch would go through Zǐyīnggōu into Guǎngyáng Hú and reach the sea.
Then half of the upper Huái River water would have an outlet.
Fifteen li north of it, open Wǔjiādūn,
to flow into Yǒngjì Hé,
and exit through Yáowān Zhá directly to the Jīng Hé,
entering the sea from Shèyáng Hú.
Then half of the lower Huái River water would have a destination.
This is the primary urgent measure to save the ancestral tombs.”
At this time,
the accumulated water at the ancestral tombs had somewhat receded.
Yīkuí reported this,
and the emperor was greatly pleased,
again instructing all ministers to urgently discuss and agree upon discharge methods.
Thereupon, Qǐchéng and Yīkuí jointly proposed to divide and weaken the Huáng Hé flow to release the Huái River,
and separately dredge a sea mouth to guide the Huáng Hé.
However, Chǔ Fú, the Minister of Revenue overseeing grain transport, citing the annual famine north of the Jiāng,
and the people's inability to endure major public works,
wished to first discharge the Huái River and then gradually discuss dividing the Huáng Hé.
Censor Yìng Yuán reconciled their views,
saying:
“Guiding the Huái River is convenient and easy to accomplish,
dividing the Huáng Hé is a greater undertaking with long-term benefits.
However, the river officials' request is also for 680,000 *jīn* (taels of silver).
Why would the state be so stingy about this?”
Censor Chén Kuí, who had once governed Bǎoyīng,
feared that once Zhōujiāqiáo was opened,
Gāoyóu and Shàobó would become a basin,
and the Grand Canal, people's property, and salt fields would all suffer.
He memorialized to dispute this,
in very strong language.
His main point was:
Dividing the Huáng Hé should be prioritized, and the Huái River does not need deep treatment.
He also wished to open more paths to the sea,
allowing the waters of Gāo and Bǎo lakes to all flow eastward,
and then the waters of Zhōujiāqiáo and Wǔjiādūn could be discharged.
However, Mǎ Huàlóng, the prefect of Huái'ān, further presented five difficulties in dividing the Huáng Hé.
Lǐ Hóngdào, the military surveillance commissioner of Yǐngzhōu, then argued that Gāoyàn should be opened.
Fú then reported these to the emperor.
Supervisor of the Ministry of Works Lín Xīchūn refuted him,
saying:
“The Huái River is still the Huái River of old,
but the Huáng Hé is not the Huáng Hé of old.
Before, the riverbed was not high,
and the Huái River still flowed smoothly.
Now, the riverbed is already high,
and the Huái River suffers from backflow.
Therefore, guiding the Huái River is indeed for the Huái River,
and dividing the Huáng Hé is also for the Huái River.”
The Ministry of Public Works then reported again, saying:
“The previous proposal to open a branch river at Yāopù to divide the Huáng Hé flow
was suspended due to Japanese pirates and disaster damage,
thus leading to today's troubles.
If the work of dividing the Huáng Hé at Huángjiābà is again hindered,
and the Huái River blockage causes harm,
who will be responsible for the fault?
We request that the officials in charge of river conservancy guide the Huái River and divide the Huáng Hé,
and urgently proceed with the undertaking.”
The report was approved.
In the eighth month of the twenty-fourth year,
Yīkuí, whose project was not yet completed,
again listed ten matters concerning dividing the Huái River and guiding the Huáng Hé.
In the tenth month,
the river conservancy project was completed.
Jiǎng Chūnfāng, the Imperial Censor for Zhílì, reported this,
and again listed sixteen matters for follow-up.
Consequently, Yīkuí and others were rewarded with varying amounts.
In this undertaking,
200,000 laborers were employed.
A new river was opened at Táoyuán Huánghébà,
starting from Huángjiāzuǐ,
to Āndōng Wǔgǎng and Guànkǒu,
over 300 li long,
to divert the Huáng Hé water into the sea,
thereby curbing the strength of the Huáng Hé.
Seven li of sand at Qīngkǒu were cleared,
and stone sluices were built at Wǔjiādūn, Gāoliángjiàn, and Zhōujiāqiáo,
to discharge the Huái River water through three channels into the sea,
and also to draw its branches into the Jiāng.
Thus, the water disaster at Sìlíng was quelled,
and Huái and Yáng were safe.
However, at that time,
Yīkuí focused his efforts on the area between Táo and Qīng rivers, and between Huái and Sì rivers,
and believed that the breach at Huánggùkǒu in Dānxiàn, upstream,
did not necessarily need to be stopped.
Fū and Chūnfāng both requested that it be stopped.
The Supervising Secretary Lǐ Yìngcè said:
"The grain transport officials oversee transport,
and the river officials oversee engineering.
They each have their own views.
It is appropriate to have them discuss it again and analyze it."
Yīkuí said:
"One branch of the Huánggùkǒu flows through Yúchéng and Xiàyì, connecting to Dàngshān, Xiāoxiàn, and Sùzhōu, reaching Sùqiān,
and exits into the Báiyánghé.
A small branch separates at Liǎnghékǒu in Xiāoxiàn,
and exits at Xiǎofúqiáo in Xúzhōu.
The distance between them is less than forty *lǐ*.
It should be dredged to join the main river,
and the water from Zhènkǒuzhá and Jiāohú should be further channeled,
to meet the two waterways at Xiǎofúqiáo.
Then the Huánggùkǒu need not be stopped,
and the transport route will not be obstructed."
This was adopted.
Thereupon, it was proposed to dredge Xiǎofúqiáo, Yíhékǒu, and Xiǎohékǒu to aid the Xú and Pī transport routes,
to drain the overflowing waters of Dàng and Xiāo,
and to reinforce the Guīrén Dī to protect the imperial tombs.
At that time,
Xú and Pī once again found the transport route via Qīng and Sì rivers to be unfavorable,
and Fū remained concerned about this.
In the first month of the twenty-fifth year,
he again emphatically stated that if Huánggùkǒu was not stopped,
the entire Yellow River would shift south,
and the harm would be immediately apparent.
Many of the debaters also feared that it would erode Guīrén Dī downstream,
posing a threat to the two imperial tombs.
In the third month,
as the construction at Xiǎofúqiáo and other outlets was nearing completion,
Yīkuí said: "The transport route is unobstructed and flowing smoothly,
and the river's shift poses no interference;
there is already clear evidence.
However, the debaters are concerned about the ancestral tombs,
so I request that past events be cited to refute them.
In the fourteenth
year of Hóngwǔ (1381),
the Yellow River breached at Yuánwǔ,
flowing southeast to Shòuzhōu and entering the Huái River.
In the ninth year of Yǒnglè (1411),
the Yellow River flowed north into Yútái.
Soon after,
it breached again to the south,
flowing through the Guōhé
via Huáiyuǎn into the Huái River.
At that time, the two rivers converged,
passing through Fèng and Sì to exit at Qīngkǒu,
and no mention was made of it threatening the ancestral tombs.
In the thirteenth year of Zhèngtǒng (1448),
the Yellow River flowed north and impacted Zhāng
qiū.
During the Jǐngtài reign (1450-1457),
Xú Yǒuzhēn stopped it,
and it again flowed via the Guōhé into the Huái River.
In the second year of Hóngzhì (1489),
the Yellow River again flowed north,
Bái Áng and Liú Dàxià stopped it,
and it resumed its southern flow.
One branch went from Zhōngmóu to Yǐng and Shòu,
another from Bózhōu to the Guōhé and into the Huái River,
and another from Sùqiān's Xiǎohékǒu to meet the Sì River.
The general course of the Yellow River
crisscrossed between Yǐng, Bó, Fèng, and Sì,
overflowing downstream to Fúlí, Suī, and Sù.
No mention was made of concerns for the ancestral tombs,
nor of the embankment reaching Guīrén.
After the third year of Zhèngdé (1508),
the Yellow River gradually shifted north,
entering the Grand Canal through the three channels of Xiǎofúqiáo, Fēiyúnqiáo, and Gǔtíng,
all converging on Xú and Pī,
and exiting through Èrhóng.
Although the transport
route was facilitated,
the flooding was indeed severe.
In the eleventh year of Jiājìng (1532),
Zhū Shāng first spoke of a branch of the Guōhé passing through Fèngyáng Ancestral Tombs, which he dared not lightly touch.
However, at that time,
they still occasionally dredged Dǒngpénkǒu in Xiángfú, Wǔlǐpù in Nínglíng, Sūnjiādù in Xíngzé, and Zhàopízài in Lányáng,
or sometimes opened breaches
at Dìqiūdiàn, Jièpáikǒu, Yějīgāng in Suīzhōu,
and Yángcūnpù in Nínglíng.
All flowed into the old river,
then from Bó and Fèng into the Huái River.
The southern flow never ceased,
so
how could it have been a threat to the ancestral tombs?
After the twenty-fifth year of Jiājìng (1546),
the old southern course was finally completely stopped,
some flowing into the Grand Canal via Qín'gōu,
or via Zhuóhé.
For fifty
years, the entire Yellow River exited through Xú and Pī,
diverting the Sì River into the Huái River.
Yet those in charge were mistaking the guest for the host,
building embankments daily and constraining it,
which led to the river becoming increasingly blocked,
the Huái unable to resist
the Yellow,
retreating and pooling internally,
thus causing problems for the ancestral tombs at Xū and Sì.
This was truly due to the internal water's stagnation and obstruction,
not due to the external water's impact and erosion.
In the seventh
year of Wànlì (1579),
Pān Jìxùn first feared that the Yellow River's current would flow backward into Xiǎohé, Báiyáng, and other outlets,
carrying the waters of various rivers to impact the ancestral tombs.
Therefore, he built the Guīrén Dī as a protective measure,
and further exaggerated his argument,
claiming that the lifeblood of the ancestral tombs completely relied on this embankment.
Those who had habitually heard his argument
thus suspected that the breach at Huánggù would
erode Guīrén Dī downstream,
unaware that if Huánggù
breached,
the downstream would be easily drained,
and there would certainly be no fear of upstream backflow.
Furthermore, Xiǎohé will be completed soon,
and the feeder river will return to its old course,
moving even further from Guīrén Dī.
Why
bother with excessive worry?"
The report was approved.
Yīkuí then opened Xiǎofúqiáo,
built Yì'ānshān,
dredged Xiǎohékǒu,
and channeled water from Wǔyíquán to aid transport.
By April of that year,
the river again extensively breached at Huánggùkǒu,
overflowing Xiàyì and Yǒngchéng,
and flowed via Fúlíqiáo in Sùzhōu out through Xīnhékǒu in Sùqiān into the main river.
Half of it flowed via Xúzhōu into the old river to aid transport.
The upstream water dried up,
and the Yì'ān shùshuǐ héngbà (dam) was breached for over twenty *zhàng*,
the water flow at Xiǎofúqiáo became very shallow,
the two Hóng canals were reported dry,
and the transport route was obstructed.
Yīkuí then proposed dredging the two locations, Sàowān and Yùzuǐ, upstream of Huánggùkǒu,
and also extensively dredging Lǐjíkǒu to the north of Zhuóhé downstream,
to save the several tens of *lǐ* upstream of Xiǎofúqiáo from drying up.
He further reported:
"The Yellow River's southern turn at Hánjiādào, Pánchàhé, and Dīngjiāzhuāng,
all have banks over a hundred *zhàng* wide,
and are more than two *zhàng* deep.
This is the old course with a 'copper bottom and iron banks.'
At Liújiāwā,
it begins to flow strongly southward,
utilizing the Xīshānpō and Yǒnghúhú as reservoirs,
exiting at Xīkǒu and entering the Fúlíhé,
which is also an old course.
Only the Xú and Pī transport routes are shallow and dry,
which is why the opening of Xiǎofúqiáo was first proposed.
With further dredging and widening,
it will greatly benefit the transport route.
However, attempting to divert the entire river back from Huánggù
would require dredging four hundred *lǐ* of silted riverbed
and building a three-hundred-*lǐ*-long embankment on the south bank.
Not only would the cost be enormous,
but I fear there would be endless future troubles."
Censor Yáng Guāngxùn and others also proposed dredging the Sàowān straight channel,
extending the Zhuóhé for relief,
and building the Xīshānpō Guīrén Dī,
agreeing with Yīkuí.
Only Fū had a differing opinion.
The Emperor ordered that Yīkuí's proposal be followed.
In the spring of the thirty-first year,
the Governor of Shāndōng, Huáng Kèzǎn, said:
"Wángjiākǒu is the upper source of Méngshān.
Once the upper reaches are open,
the lower reaches cannot be allowed to drain sideways;
it is advisable to block the Méngshān mouth."
This was followed.
At that time, the Méngshān breach was over eighty zhàng wide,
and the new canal opened by Rúchūn in spring was not even half that width.
To block it and direct the water into it,
it was feared it could not bear the flow.
Someone offered a plan, saying:
"Once the river turns back,
its momentum will be like thunder;
using its force to scour it,
what is shallow can be deepened."
Rúchūn then ordered the water released.
The water was all mud and sand,
the flow slowed slightly,
and then it silted up.
In the fourth month of summer,
the water suddenly swelled,
impacting the area between Yú, Shàn, Fēng, and Pèi.
Rúchūn died of worry.
Thereupon, Lǐ Huàlóng was appointed Vice Minister of Works,
to take over his post.
Supervising Secretary Sòng Yīhán said:
"The old course of the Huáng Hé has been restored;
the imperial tombs and the Grand Canal are safe.
The breaches are feared to be difficult to block;
it is advisable to deeply dredge the shallow obstructions above Jiānchéng,
and to reinforce the banks of Xú and Pī,
so that the lower reaches have room to accommodate the water,
then the old river can be blocked."
Supervising Secretary Mèng Chéngjǐ said:
"Blocking the old river is urgent,
but dredging the new river is even more urgent."
As soon as Huàlóng arrived,
the river greatly breached at Sūjiāzhuāng in Shàn Xiàn and the Lǚ Dī in Cáo Xiàn,
and also breached the Tàiháng Dī at Sìpùkǒu in Pèi Xiàn,
inundating Zhāoyáng Hú,
entering Xiàzhèn,
and directly impacting the Grand Canal.
Huàlóng proposed opening the Jiā Hé,
connecting it to the Zhíhé in Pīzhōu,
to bypass the dangerous river section.
Supervising Secretary Hóu Qìngyuǎn then said:
"If the Jiā Hé is completed,
other projects can be gradually planned,
but the river must not be allowed to flow into the Huái.
If the Huái is managed well, the Hóngzé waters will recede,
and the imperial tombs will be safe."
In the first month of the thirty-second year,
the ministry reviewed Huàlóng's memorial,
broadly stating:
"From Guīdé downstream,
where the river joins the Grand Canal and flows into the sea,
there are three paths: one goes from Lányáng via Kǎochéng,
to Lǐjí Kǒu,
passes Jiānchéng Jí,
enters Liùzuòlóu,
exits Cháchéng and heads towards Xú and Pī;
this is called the Zhuóhé,
the central route.
Another goes from Cáo and Shàn, via Fēng and Pèi,
exits Fēiyún Qiáo,
overflows into Zhāoyáng Hú,
enters Lóngtáng,
exits Qíngōu and heads towards Xú and Pī;
this is called the Yínhé,
the northern route.
The third goes from Pānjiākǒu, passes Sījiādàokǒu,
reaches Héjiā Dī,
passes Fúlí,
goes via Suīníng,
enters Sùqiān,
enters the Grand Canal via Xiǎohékǒu;
this is called the Fúlí Hé,
the southern route.
The southern route is close to the imperial tombs,
the northern route is close to the Grand Canal;
only the central route is far from the imperial tombs,
and can also benefit the Grand Canal.
Previous river officials started projects which were not yet completed,
but the river course still exists."
Therefore, he memorialized that opening the Jiā would bring six benefits.
The Emperor followed his recommendation.
Minister of Works Yáo Jìkě said:
"The Huáng Hé shifts its course,
and river officials propose opening canals above Jiānchéng Jí to divert the river,
to clear the lower reaches,
and again divide the water into two routes at Liùzuòlóu and Yuànjiālóu to reduce its force.
This can both transfer the calamity from Fēng and Pèi,
and prevent the city of Dàngshān from being submerged.
Opening the Jiā and diverting the Huáng,
with both projects implemented concurrently,
I beg for swift release of funds to aid them."
This was approved.
In the eighth month,
Huàlóng memorialized that the Fēnshuǐ Hé was completed.
Details are in the Jiā Hé Zhì.
Huàlóng was promoted to Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent and Minister of War.
Coincidentally, Huàlóng was observing mourning for a parent and awaiting a replacement,
so Cáo Shípìn was appointed Vice Minister of Works,
to oversee river conservancy.
That autumn,
the river breached in Fēng Xiàn,
flowed through Zhāoyáng Hú, passed Lǐjiāgǎngkǒu,
exited Zhènkǒu,
and then inundated Nányáng upstream.
The breach in Shàn Xiàn collapsed again,
turning the flat land between Yútái and Jìníng into a lake.
In the spring of the thirty-third year,
Huàlóng said:
"The failure at Fēng
was due to lax patrol and defense,
and the failure at Shàn
was due to not deploying the brushwood dams early enough;
both were caused by the breach at Sūjiāzhuāng.
Southern Zhílì and Shāndōng blamed each other;
I request that the officials responsible for river defense in each area be penalized.
As for recent years, dyke maintenance has been neglected while urgent dredging was prioritized,
resulting in dyke breaches and overflowing water.
Instead of blaming the ineffective defense of the dykes,
they only attribute it to the insufficient depth of the dredged river.
Indeed, on the northern bank of the river, from Cáo Xiàn downwards, there is no path to enter Zhāngqiū;
on the southern bank, from Yúchéng downwards, there is no path to enter the Huái.
Only the route via Xú and Pī to Zhènkǒu serves as the Grand Canal.
Therefore, if the river breaches north of the river, between Cáo, Yùn, Fēng, and Pèi,
it will flow out through Zhāoyáng Hú via Lǐjiākǒu,
and the Grand Canal will overflow;
if it breaches south, between Yú, Xià, Xú, and Pī,
it will flow out via Xiǎohékǒu and Báiyáng Hé,
and the Grand Canal will dry up.
Now that the Jiā Hé is completed,
extending from the Zhíhé to Xiàzhèn,
it is separated from the Huáng Hé.
Between Shāndōng and Zhílì,
the river cannot control the fate of the Grand Canal.
However, above Zhūwàngkǒu,
if it breaches at Shàn, Shàn will be submerged;
if it breaches at Cáo, Cáo and Yú will be affected.
Fēng, Pèi, Xú, Pī, Yú, and Dàng all hang by a thread of dyke defense;
how can this be neglected?
As for Zhōngzhōu, Jīnglóngkǒu and Tóngwǎxiāng are all routes to enter Zhāngqiū;
Sūnjiādù, Yějīgāng, and Méngshān Sì are all routes to enter the Huái.
If one is not defended,
then in the north, the Grand Canal will be damaged,
and in the south, the imperial tombs will be threatened;
the harm is immense.
I request that from Kāifēng in the west,
to Xú and Pī in the east,
there should be no undefended areas.
From the Sīdào (provincial commissioners) above,
to the prefectures and counties below,
there should be no undefended personnel.
Only then can the river disaster perhaps be quelled."
The Emperor then issued an edict instructing Shípìn to reiterate this.
That autumn,
Shí Pìn stated:
"Since the decisive breach at Sū Zhuāng,
the entire area north of the Huái River has been submerged for three years.
Initially, it flooded Fēng and Pèi,
then submerged Shàn and Yú.
Chén Càn's efforts to block it failed,
and the dikes of Nányáng were completely destroyed.
Now it is about to inundate all of Jì,
and is encroaching upon the Grand Canal.
Your servant personally visited Cáo and Shàn,
observed the newly built dam at Wángjiākǒu upstream,
and observed the overflowing waters from the breach at Zhūwàngkǒu downstream.
I perceive three great concerns regarding the river,
and two opportunities that must not be missed.
The river has breached its dikes,
overflowing onto flat land.
Zhaōyáng is silting up daily,
and the downstream is accumulating sediment day by day.
The water flowing out of Lǐjiākǒu is gradually becoming weaker and slower,
making it inevitable that it will retreat and overflow upstream.
If it overflows to the south,
then Sūnjiādù and Yějīgāng will both enter the old course of the Huái River.
Do not say that Méngfāng is already blocked,
and have no worries about the imperial mausoleums.
If it overflows to the north,
then Zhīmazhuāng and Jīnglóngkǒu will both enter the old course of Zhāngqiū.
Do not say that the Jiā River project is already completed,
and have no worries about the Grand Canal.
Moreover, to the south, the lands of Xià and Shāng,
and to the north, those of Cáo and Pú,
are becoming lower,
their calamities more severe,
and their recovery more difficult.
Do not say that the disaster is limited to Yú and Jì,
and have no worries about the common people.
Consider the newly excavated river from Wángjiākǒu to Zhūwàng.
If its lower course is dredged to flow out at Xiǎofúqiáo,
then the three-hundred-li-long river will flow smoothly.
This is the first opportunity to seize.
From Xú downwards,
the Qīng River and Yellow River flow side-by-side.
Sand is being scoured by the water,
a phenomenon not seen for several decades.
If we therefore guide the water back to Xú,
there will be ample space to accommodate it.
This is the second opportunity to seize.
Your servant and other officials have carefully deliberated.
The central course of the river has two branches, north and south. The northern branch flows into the Zhuó River,
having been dredged and blocked twice.
However, the southern branch, which flows out at Xiǎofúqiáo,
has a low-lying terrain,
and its course is very favorable.
Its estimated length is over three myriad zhàng,
and the estimated cost is eight hundred thousand taels of silver.
The public treasury is depleted,
so I humbly request various methods for funding."
The memorial was submitted but withheld.
Shí Pìn then extensively excavated Zhūwàngkǒu.
Construction began in the eleventh month,
employing five hundred thousand laborers.
In the fourth month of the 34th year,
the project was completed.
From Zhūwàng to Xiǎofúqiáo, it stretched for 170 li.
The channel was wide and the dikes thick,
and the river returned to its old course.
In the sixth month,
the river breached at Guōnuǎnlóu Rénzìkǒu in Xiāoxiàn,
and the northern branch reached Cháchéng and Zhènkǒu.
In the 35th year,
it breached in Shànxiàn.
In the sixth month of the 39th year,
it breached at Lángshǐgōu in Xúzhōu.
In the ninth month of the 40th year,
it breached at Sānshān in Xúzhōu,
destroying 280 zhàng of lǚdī and
over 170 zhàng of yáodī.
The twenty li of main river downstream from Lílínpù were entirely turned into flat land,
and the waters of the Pī and Suī Rivers were exhausted.
Liú Shìzhōng, the Director-General of Rivers, opened a small channel outside Hánjiābà to draw water,
through which navigation east of the dam became possible.
In the 42nd year,
it breached at Chénpù in Língbì.
In the fifth month of the 44th year,
it again breached at Lángshǐgōu,
flowing through lakes like Hámán and Zhōuliǔ into the Jiā River,
exiting at Zhíkǒu,
and rejoining the Yellow River.
In the sixth month,
it breached at Táojiādiàn and Zhāngjiāwān in Kāifēng,
flowing under the Huìchéng Grand Dike to Chénliú,
and entering the Guō River in Bózhōu.
In the ninth month of the 47th year,
it breached at Píshāgāng in Yángwǔ,
flowing through Fēngqiū, Cáo, and Shàn to Kǎochéng,
and rejoining the old river course.
At this time, the imperial court's governance was increasingly lax,
and many reports from river officials were ignored.
In the 42nd year,
Liú Shìzhōng died,
and the post of Director-General of Rivers remained vacant for three years.
In the intercalary fourth month of the 46th year,
Wáng Zuǒ, Vice Minister of Works, was finally appointed to supervise the river administration.
River defenses deteriorated day by day,
and those in charge were unable to take effective action.
In the first year of Tiānqǐ (1621),
the river breached at Shuānggōu and Huángpù in Língbì,
flowing through Yǒngjī Hú out of Báiyáng and Xiǎohékǒu,
rejoining the Yellow River,
and the old course became silted and dry.
Chén Dàohéng, Vice Minister and Director-General of Rivers, employed laborers to build a dam.
At this time, Huái'ān experienced continuous heavy rains for several weeks,
and the Yellow River and Huái River surged several feet.
Breaches in the outer river of Shānyángfāng and the Qīng River combined to form a vast flood.
The water inundated Huáichéng,
and people climbed the city walls to live,
with boats navigating the streets.
It was finally blocked after a long time.
In the third year,
it breached at Qīngtián Dàlóngkǒu in Xúzhōu.
The Xú, Pī, Líng, and Suī Rivers all became silted.
The southern corner of Lǚliángchéng collapsed,
with sand accumulated more than a zhàng above ground level.
The Shuānggōu breach also filled up,
and 150 li both upstream and downstream became flat land.
In the sixth month of the fourth year,
it breached the Kuíshān Dike in Xúzhōu,
inundating the prefectural city from the northeast.
The water depth in the city reached one zhàng three chí.
One branch flowed from the south gate to Dà'ānqiáo northwest of Yúnlóngshān, entering Shígǒuhú.
The other flowed south from the old branch of the river to Dèng'èrzhuāng,
passed through Zūgōu southeast to reach Xiǎohé,
exited at Báiyáng,
and rejoined the Yellow River.
The people of Xú suffered from the flooding
and discussed pooling funds to relocate the city.
Lù Wénxiàn, a Supervising Secretary, presented six arguments against relocating Xúchéng.
But the situation left no choice,
so the prefectural seat was moved to Yúnlóng,
and river management was set aside without discussion.
In the seventh month of the sixth year,
the river breached at Huái'ān,
flowing backward into Luòmǎhú,
and inundating Pī and Sù.
In the thirteenth year, following the proposal of the Grand River Superintendent (Zǒngcáo Dū Yùshǐ) Lǐ Shìdá,
the Báoyīng Yuèhé was opened.
Báoyīng Fànguānghú,
among all lakes, was the most turbulent and treacherous,
spanning over one hundred and twenty *lǐ*.
Huáijiǎolóu stood in its center,
curved like a winnowing basket.
Wǎdiàn was to its south,
and Chènggōuwān to its north.
Westerly winds whipped up waves,
frequently capsizing boats.
Chén Xuān built a dike east of the lake,
storing water for the transport canal.
The upper reaches received water,
but the lower reaches had no outlet,
so it broke into eight shallows,
and gathered into six pools,
submerging all the salt fields of Xīng and Yán.
Moreover, the Huái River again overflowed from Zhōujiāqiáo,
drowning people
and harming river transport.
In the last years of Wǔzōng's reign,
the Langzhong Yáng Zuì requested to open the Yuèhé,
but the Board reviewed it and did not approve.
During the Jiājìng era,
the Gongbu Langzhong Chén Yùxián, Hubu Yuanwai Fàn Sháo, Yushi Wénrén Quán, and Yunliang Qiānhù Lǐ Xiǎn all spoke about it,
but the proposal was not implemented.
At this time,
the Gongbu Langzhong Xǔ Yìngkuí proposed a plan,
and Shìdá used his words in a memorial to the throne,
and it was then decided to proceed.
The river was dredged for over one thousand seven hundred *zhàng*,
three stone sluices were built,
two water-reducing sluices,
and dikes were built for over nine thousand *zhàng*,
one-third of which were stone dikes,
and secondary dikes for over five thousand *zhàng*.
When the work was completed,
it was bestowed the name Hóngjì.
Soon after, the stone sluices were changed to level-water sluices.
Yìngkuí also built the Gāoyóu protective city dike.
Subsequently,
at the northern and southern sluices of Hóngjì,
when the Huái River rose in summer and autumn,
it could not be controlled quickly enough,
and many boats capsized.
In the last years of Shénzōng's reign,
the Dūcáo Shìláng Chén Jiàn opened Yuèhé at both the north and south to mitigate the river's fury,
and only then did the current become stable.
In the fifteenth year,
the Dūcáo Shìláng Yáng Yīkuí requested to repair Gāojiāyàn to protect the upper reaches,
to pave Fànjiākǒu to prevent lateral breaches,
to clear Cǎowān to reduce the river's force,
and to repair Lǐbà to protect Xīnchéng.
An imperial decree approved his proposal.
Yīkuí also rebuilt Gǔhóngzhá.
Before this,
the waters of Wèn and Sì converged with the Yellow River via Cháchéng.
During the Lóngqìng era,
the turbid current flowed backward,
hindering transport boats.
The Langzhong Chén Yīng moved the Yellow River mouth eight *lǐ* east of Cháchéng,
building Gǔhóng and Nèihuá sluices,
and the transport canal exited from Gǔhóng.
Later, when the Yellow River flooded,
the silting became even worse.
After Yīkuí had rebuilt Gǔhóng,
the Emperor again followed the suggestion of the Jìshìzhōng Cháng Jūjìng,
ordering the additional construction of Zhènkǒuzhá outside Gǔhóng,
only eighty *zhàng* from the river.
This made water intake and discharge easier,
benefiting grain transport.
The Gongbu Shangshu Shí Xīng discussed Jì Xún's and Jū Jìng's memorials on follow-up matters,
requesting to assign responsibilities by area: extending the construction of Tǎshān Lǚtí and
Qīngjiāngpǔ Cǎobà;
initiating the construction of Báoyīng Xītí;
stone-paving Shàobóhútí;
dredging the silted Yúhé,
which should be undertaken in Huái and Yáng;
inspecting and restoring the four lakes of Nánwàng, Mǎtà, Shǔshān, and Mǎchǎng;
building Kǎnhé Gǔnshuǐbà;
adding Tōngjì and Yǒngtōng sluices;
and inspecting and restoring Ānshānhú land,
which should be undertaken in Shāndōng.
The Emperor approved his proposal.
Soon after,
all the works were completed.
In the nineteenth year,
Jì Xún said:
"South of Sùqiān, the terrain is low to the west.
I request to open a drainage dike to release water.
Sand will enter with the water,
and the land will rise with the sand.
This might eliminate the flood threat and save expenses."
He also requested to change the earth dike of Gāojiāyàn to stone,
and to build the Mǎnjiāzhá Western River-blocking Dam,
so that all the waters of Wèn and Sì would flow into the new river.
A water-reducing sluice was to be set up at Lǐjiākǒu
to discharge the accumulated water of Pèixiàn.
This was approved.
In the tenth month,
the Huái lakes greatly swelled,
and the stone dike at Jiāngdū Chúnjiāwān, Shàobó Nánbà, Gāoyóu Zhōngtí, Zhūjiādūn, and Qīngshuǐtán all breached.
The Langzhong Huáng Yuējǐn had just finished repairing the breaches
when the Shānyángdī also breached.
In the fifth month of the twenty-first year,
it rained.
The transport canal overflowed,
breaching the dikes around Jìníng and the Huái River.
The Zǒnghé Shangshu Shū Yìnglóng proposed: to build Gāngchéngbà
to block the Wèn River from the south,
and to open the Mǎtàhú Yuèhékǒu
to divert the Wèn River to the north.
To open Tōngjìzhá
and release the Yuèhé earthen dam to reduce the turbulent force.
His memorial was followed.
Within a few years,
the upper and lower reaches of the Huìtōng were unobstructed,
but the Yellow and Huái Rivers swelled simultaneously,
and Gāoyàn and the Gāoyóu dike repeatedly breached, harming transport.
Yìnglóng was eventually dismissed.
Suggestions poured in,
but nothing was decided.
Yáng Yīkuí replaced Yìnglóng as Zǒnghé Shangshu,
and strongly advocated for dividing the Yellow River and channeling the Huái River.
After more than a year of work,
as the project was nearing completion,
he again requested to release lake water to clear the transport canal,
saying:
"The lakes of Gāo and Bǎo were originally fertile land,
but since the Huái and Yellow Rivers backed up and blocked them,
they became waterlogged.
Now that the paths to the Yangtze River and the sea are dredged,
it is advisable to open and manage the sluices of Jīnghé, Zǐyīnggōu, Jīnwānhé, and the two sluices of Guā and Yí,
releasing large quantities of lake water,
and dredging canals within the lakes,
connecting them with the Gāo and Bǎo Yuèhé.
This would avoid the dangers of wind and waves on the transport route,
and when the water dries, the land can be used for farming,
provided to the people for cultivation,
and gradually a new tax can be levied,
which can cover river expenses."
The Emperor ordered it to be carried out as proposed.
At this time, as the lower reaches were cleared,
the Huái River gradually subsided,
but the Yellow River was breaching at Huánggū kǒu.
The Dūcáo Dū Yùshǐ Chǔ Fú feared too much leakage
and silting in Xú and Pī,
and strongly requested to block it.
Yīkuí insisted against it
and dredged the old channel from Liǎnghékǒu to Xiǎofúqiáo to facilitate transport.
However, the main course of the river shifted south,
and the transport channels at the two Hóng frequently dried up.
He again extensively dredged Lǐjíkǒu below Huánggū
to draw the Yellow River to supply it,
but it would silt up again before long.
Yīkuí then took charge of the Board.
In the twenty-sixth year,
Liú Dōngxīng succeeded him,
adhering to Yīkuí's old proposal,
and Lǐjíkǒu silted up even higher.
In the winter of that year,
a small river was opened at that location,
and in spring and summer, water was diverted into Xúzhōu.
This continued for three years,
but generally, it would silt up by autumn.
Thus, Zhàojiāquān was reopened to connect with the Yellow River,
and Kāihé was opened to aid transport.
Zhàojiāquān quickly silted up,
and Kāihé had not yet been restored,
when Dōngxīng died.
Then the Fèngyáng Xúnfǔ Dū Yùshǐ Lǐ Sāncái proposed to imitate the sluice-canal system from Zhènkǒuzhá to Mò'erzhuāng,
with one sluice every thirty *lǐ*,
building a total of six sluices in the river
to regulate the waters of Wèn and Jì,
merely to allow some transport.
Transport boats arriving in the capital
could no longer do so on schedule.
While Dōngxīng was in office,
he opened Shàobó Yuèhé,
eighteen *lǐ* long and over eighteen *zhàng* wide,
to avoid the dangers of the lake.
He also opened Jièshǒu Yuèhé,
over one thousand eight hundred *zhàng* long.
Two Golden Gate stone sluices were built at each,
benefiting transport boats.
In the 32nd year [of the reign],
Assistant Minister of River Conservancy, Lǐ Huàlóng, began to extensively open the Jiā Hé river.
From Zhí Hé to Lǐjiā Gǎng, over 260 lǐ,
it entirely avoided the dangers of the Huáng Hé.
When Huàlóng left office due to sorrow,
Assistant Minister of River Conservancy, Cáo Shípìn, completed his work.
Regarding the achievements of dredging the Jiā Hé,
he stated:
"Shū Yìnglóng first opened Hánjiā Zhuāng to drain lake waters,
and thus the route became passable.
Liú Dōngxīng extensively opened Liángchéng and Hóujiā Zhuāng to test the navigation,
and the route gradually widened.
Lǐ Huàlóng opened Lǐjiā Gǎng upstream,
excavated the Dūshuǐ Shí,
and opened Zhíhé Kǒu downstream,
dredging Tiánjiā Zhuāng.
He exerted all his effort in managing it,
and more than half of the transport was completed,
thus the route was opened.
Therefore, I was able to follow up and announce its completion."
He then submitted six proposals for post-completion arrangements,
and the transport route became greatly clear as a result.
Thereafter,
every year in the third month, the Jiā Hé dam was opened,
entering from Zhíhé Kǒu.
In the ninth month, the Zhàogōng dam was opened to enter the Huáng Hé.
Grain boats and official and private vessels all used this as the standard.
In the 44th year,
Censor for Grain Transport, Zhū Jiē, requested the repair of Quán Hú,
stating:
"Sòng Lǐ built the dam at Dàicūn,
diverting the two Wèn rivers from their path to the sea,
irrigating to form a river,
and then guiding the Zhū, Sī, Guāng, and Yí rivers to assist it.
Although the Wèn mobilized all its currents to fully support the grain transport,
it became exhausted after traveling a long distance,
already difficult to sustain.
Upon reaching Nánwàng,
it was again divided, with four-tenths going south to meet the Huái,
and six-tenths going north to Wèi,
making its force even weaker.
Moreover, this water rises in summer and autumn,
but dries up in winter and spring;
without rain, it dries up even in summer and autumn.
Lǐ anticipated that it could not be relied upon,
so he established sluice gates at various lakes along the river, such as Zhāoyáng, Nánwàng, Mǎtà, Shǔshān, and Ānshān,
naming them 'water cabinets' (shuǐguì).
When the grain transport river's water rose,
the overflow was stored in the lakes.
When the water subsided, it was released to irrigate the transport river.
Storage and release were regulated,
and unauthorized releases were punishable,
thus droughts and floods were no longer feared.
But as years passed and prohibitions slackened,
the lakes became shallow enough for cultivation,
and many were occupied by powerful gentry.
Zhāoyáng lake alone had become private farmland.
Recently, Shāndōng has had no rain for half a year,
and the springs are almost dry.
Searching for the water cabinets according to maps,
no one knows their location.
I beg that river officials be ordered to clear and verify them,
and urgently build embankments, dams, and sluice gates to widely store water."
The emperor granted his request.
While deliberating on dredging Quán Hú,
the river breached at Xúzhōu Lángshǐ Gōu,
entering the Jiā Hé through Háimán and other lakes,
and exiting at Zhíkǒu.
Transport boats faced danger and difficulty against the current.
Assistant Minister of River Conservancy, Chén Jiàn, opened Wǔ Hé and other outlets,
draining the water to calm the current.
Two years later,
the breach accumulated long silt,
and the river returned to its old course.
Assistant Minister of River Conservancy, Wáng Zuǒ, further built a moon dam to block it.
By the winter of Tàichāng first year,
Zuǒ stated:
"The water cabinets of the various lakes have been restored,
and Ānshān Hú has even been restored by 55 lǐ,
which truly benefits grain transport.
I request that the success or failure of the water cabinets be the primary criterion for evaluating river officials."
This was granted.
In Tiānqǐ first year,
the Huái and Huáng rivers overflowed,
breaching at Guī Hé Wánggōng Cí.
Sòng Tǒngyīn, Prefect of Huái'ān, and Liàn Guóshì, Magistrate of Shānyáng, worked hard to seal it.
In the autumn of the third year,
the outer river again breached in several places,
but was soon sealed.
In the winter of that year,
the Yǒngjì Xīn Hé was dredged.
Since Líng Yúnyì opened this river,
it was closed not long after.
Liu Shìzhōng, Grand Censor of River Conservancy, once opened the dam to aid transport,
but it was sealed again.
And the main river of Huái'ān had not been dredged for thirty years.
Therefore, it was proposed to first dredge the new river
to allow empty transport boats to return,
and then dredge the main river,
from Xǔjiā Zhá to Huìjì Cí, a length of over 1,400 zhàng.
A small sluice gate was also rebuilt at Tōngjì Yuè Hé.
All transport boats then used the main river,
and the new river was again closed.
At that time, the rapids at Wángjiā Jí and Mó'ér Zhuāng were becoming increasingly severe.
Zhū Guóshèng, Counsellor for Grain Transport, planned to dredge another river as a grain transport solution,
ordering Sòng Shìzhōng, Assistant Prefect, to survey from Jiākǒu eastward to Sùqiān Chéngōu Kǒu,
then upstream along Luòmǎ Hú,
up to Mǎjiá Hé,
making a round trip.
It was then proposed to open Mǎjiā Zhōu,
and also dredge the silted mouth of Mǎjiá Hé,
connecting upstream with the Jiā current,
and avoiding the danger of Liúkǒu downstream.
They also dredged 13 lǐ of sandy river at Sānchā Hé,
opened over a hundred zhàng of Tāozhuāng Hé,
deepened Xiǎo Hé by 20 lǐ,
and opened Wángnéng Zhuāng by 20 lǐ,
to connect to the mouth of Luòmǎ Hú.
Dozens of ditches like Zhāngjiā Gōu were filled and blocked,
to concentrate the water into the grain transport channel.
This river measured 57 lǐ,
and was named Tōngjì Xīn Hé.
In the fourth month of the fifth year,
the project was completed.
The transport route shifted to the new river,
free from the dangers of Liúkǒu and Mó'ér Zhuāng.
The following year,
Assistant Minister of River Conservancy, Lǐ Cóngxīn, opened 10 lǐ of land at Chéngōu
to complete the previous work.
In Chóngzhēn second year,
flooding farmland in Shān, Yán, Gāo, and Tài [prefectures].
In the fifth year,
the Jiànyì Běi Bà breached again.
Minister of River Conservancy, Zhū Guāngzuò, dredged Luòmǎ Hú,
avoiding thirteen dangerous sections of the river,
naming it Shùnjì Hé.
In the sixth year,
Liángchéng to Xútáng became silted into flat land,
delaying grain transport.
Guāngzuò was stripped of his office,
and Liú Róngsì succeeded him.
In the eighth year,
Luòmǎ Hú was blocked by silt.
Róngsì opened a river at Xú and Sù,
diverting Huáng Hé water into it.
He was impeached
and received a heavy sentence.
Assistant Minister Zhōu Dǐng succeeded him
and concentrated his efforts on the Jiā Hé.
He dredged the Màihé tributary,
built the dams before and after Wángmǔ Shān, the eastern embankment of Shèngyáng Shān, and the barrier dam at Mǎtí Yá Shízì Hé.
He dredged Liángchéng Zhá to Xútáng Kǒu, over six thousand zhàng.
In the summer of the ninth year,
Jiā Hé was reopened,
joining the main river at Sùqiān Chéngōu Kǒu.
Dǐng also repaired Gāojiā Yàn and the Xīngōu Yàngtián Yíng embankment,
reinforced the stone work of Tiānfēi Zhá,
removed the sand and gravel at Péngkǒu of Nánwàng Hú,
and dredged 160 lǐ from Liúlǚ Zhuāng to Huánglín Zhuāng.
However, at this time,
the Huáng and Huái rivers' overflows became increasingly severe,
back-flowing and harming grain transport.
Dǐng was in office for five years,
but ultimately lost his position due to obstructed transport.
His successor was Assistant Minister Zhāng Guówéi.
Immediately upon taking office,
he was reprimanded for dried-up grain transport.
In the fourteenth year,
Guówéi said:
"The Jìníng canal route, tracing upstream from the Zǎolín Sluice Gate past Shījiāzhuāng and Zhòngjiāqiǎn's two sluice gates,
suffers from silting up every year.
Each time, the Sì Hé is diverted via Lǔqiáo into the canal to relieve it.
During summer and autumn, when the water is high,
it is sufficient for easy navigation.
However, it carries sand into the river;
when the water recedes, sand accumulates.
The advantages and disadvantages are mixed.
Adjacent to it, the Báimǎ Hé collects various springs from Zōuxiàn,
and merges with the Sì Hé before flowing out at Lǔqiáo.
Its force is too weak to contend with the Sì Hé,
so the river channel is half silted up,
and is not usable for grain transport.
However, the wider section of its upper reaches is directly opposite the Zhòngjiāqiǎn Sluice Gate.
If directed to enter the canal from there,
the difference in elevation compared to Lǔqiáo is significant.
Moreover, it would transform a small stream into a torrent,
and also reduce the problem of sand seepage,
thereby relieving Zhòngjiāqiǎn, Shījiāzhuāng, and Zǎolín.
There would be three benefits."
He also said:
"Nánwàng is inherently a watershed,
relying solely on the spring sources from the eight prefectures/counties of Tài'ān, Xīntài, Láiwú, Níngyáng, Wènshàng, Dōngpíng, Píngyīn, and Féichéng,
which enter the canal via the Wèn Hé.
Thus, the Grand Canal can remain open.
Now, Dōngpíng, Píngyīn, and Féichéng are interrupted by silt.
I request that they be urgently dredged."
He again submitted a memorial with six strategies for the canal: one, to restore the Ānshān Hú reservoir to relieve the Běi Sluice Gate;
one, to alter and dredge the Cānglàng Hé's outlet from Wànnián Cāng to benefit the four sluice gates;
one, to extend dredging of the upper reaches of the Wèn Hé and Táo Hé to relieve the Pī Pài;
one, to divert the Yí Hé to exit at Xútángkǒu, thereby benefiting both Pī and Sù;
the remaining two were to clear the silt in the three prefectures/counties and to alter and dredge Báimǎ Hú.
All were ordered to be implemented as deemed appropriate.
Guówéi also dredged over 300 *lǐ* of the Huái-Yáng grain transport canal.
At that time,
river officials exerted all their efforts in repairs.
The Southern River was somewhat stable,
but the Northern River was frequently shallow and obstructed.
Meanwhile, the defending official of Hénán dammed the Huáng Hé to flood the bandits.
The river made a major breach at Kāifēng.
The downstream areas became increasingly silted day by day,
and river management further deteriorated.
Not long after, the Míng dynasty fell.
Collation Notes
Treatise 62, Rivers and Canals Four: Lower Canal and Sea Transport
The Jiāngnán Canal,
from the northern outskirts of Hángzhōu to the north of Xiècūn,
is Shí'èr Lǐ Yáng.
It passes Tángqī.
The waters of Déqīng flow into it.
Crossing Běilù Bridge, it enters the territory of Chóngdé.
Passing Sōnglǎo, it reaches Gāoxīn Bridge.
A branch river from Hǎiyán connects to it.
It winds around the south of Chóngdé City,
then turns northeast,
reaching the east of Xiǎogāoyáng Bridge.
Passing Shímén Táng,
it turns east,
becoming Wángwān.
Upon reaching Zàolín,
the water depth reaches a *zhàng*.
Passing Yǒngxīn,
it enters the territory of Xiùshuǐ.
Crossing Dǒumén Zhèn,
to its north is Fēnxiāng Pù.
Slightly to its east is Xiùtǎ.
Northward from the west of Jiāxīng City, it turns north,
exiting at the Shānqīng Three Sluice Gates.
Upon reaching Wángjiāngjīng Zhèn,
transport boats from Sōngjiāng come from the east to meet it.
To its north is Píngwàng Post Station.
To the east, it connects to Yīngdòu Hú.
Transport boats from Húzhōu exit Xīnxīng Bridge from the west to meet it.
Northward to Sōnglíng Post Station,
via Wújiāng to Sānlǐ Bridge.
To the north is Zhènzé Hú.
To the south is Huángtiāndàng.
The water force is turbulent.
Jiāpǔ Bridge has been repeatedly built.
Northward, it passes through Niányúkǒu to the east of Sūzhōu City.
Water from Yàtáng enters it.
Northward to Fēngqiáo,
via Shèdú, passing through Hǔshù Pass,
and Báihè Pù.
This is the boundary between Chángzhōu and Wúxī counties.
At Xīshān Post Station, the water is so shallow it can barely float tiles and gravel.
Passing Huángbù,
it reaches Luòshè Bridge.
The waters of the Jiǔlǐ Hé from Jiāngyīn connect to it.
To the northwest is Chángzhōu.
The grain transport canal formerly ran through the city.
It entered the Dōngshuǐmén,
and exited from the Xīshuǐmén.
At the end of the Jiājìng reign, to defend against *wō* (Japanese pirates),
its course was changed to follow the southern city moat.
At Jiāngyīn,
the waters of Shùntáng Hé flow from the east of the city to Dīngyàn.
Shāzǐ Hú is to its southwest.
The waters of Zhōngxī Stream from Yíxīng enter it.
Further west,
the waters of Zhídú enter it.
Further west are the Bēnniú and Lǚchéng Two Sluice Gates.
The boundary between Chángzhōu and Zhènjiāng is between them.
Both had Yuè Hé to assist in regulation and drainage,
but both were later abandoned.
To its south is Jīntán Hé.
The waters of Lìyáng and Gāochún flow out from there.
Twenty *lǐ* south of Dānyáng is Língkǒu.
Twenty-five *lǐ* north is Huángní Dam.
Both formerly had sluice gates.
Liànhú's water level is several *zhàng* higher than the grain transport canal.
One (channel) is via Sānsī Bridge,
and one is via Rénzhì Bridge.
Both enter the canal.
Northward, passing Dāntú Zhèn,
there is Zhūpó Tān, with much soft sand.
The canal route above Dāntú,
its water level (fullness or dryness) depends on the river tides.
Passing Zhènjiāng,
it exits Jīngkǒu Sluice Gate.
Outside the sluice gate, a sand blockage extends for twenty *zhàng*.
It can hide boats and shelter from the wind.
From here, one floats onto the Jiāng,
opposite Guābù.
From Běiguō (Hángzhōu) to Jīngkǒu, a total of over 800 *lǐ*,
all is calm water.
Passing through Jiāxīng and Sūzhōu,
where many waters gather.
West of Chángzhōu,
the land gradually rises.
The water is shallow and easily leaks.
The water level is inconsistent.
It is sometimes dredged and sometimes dammed.
Often, it also takes water from the Mèngdú and Déshèng Rivers.
It then floats eastward onto the Dàjiāng,
to reach Yángzhōu and Tàizhōu.
In the twenty-sixth year of Hóngwǔ, Chóngshān Hóu Lǐ Xīn was once ordered to dig the Yānzhī Hé in Lìshuǐ,
to open up the Zhèjiāng grain transport route.
This would avoid the need for transport and hauling at Dānyáng, and the dangers of wind and waves on the Dàjiāng.
However, grain from the Sān Wú region
still had to pass through Chángzhōu and Zhènjiāng.
In the thirty-first year, the river channels of the Bēnniú and Lǚchéng two dams were dredged.
During the Yǒnglè era,
the Liànhú Lake embankment was repaired.
The Tōngzhèng Zhāng Lián was ordered to mobilize 100,000 common laborers.
They dredged the Mèngdú Hé in Chángzhōu,
and also dredged Lánlíng Gōu.
Northward, it reached the Mèngdú Hé Sluice Gate,
over 6,000 *zhàng* long.
Southward, it reached Bēnniú Zhèn,
over 1,200 *zhàng* long.
And again, the three harbors of Jīngkǒu, Xīngǎng, and Gānlù in Zhènjiāng were dredged,
to reach the Jiāng.
Grain transport boats from Bēnniú went upstream to Jīngkǒu.
When the water was low, they changed course to follow Mèngdú, turning right towards Guāzhōu,
and reached Báitǎ.
This became the norm.
In the sixth year of Xuāndé, in response to a request from the people of Wǔjìn,
the Déshèng Xīnhé, forty *lǐ* long, was dredged.
In the eighth year,
the work was completed.
Grain transport boats from Déshèng entered the Jiāng northward,
directly to the Běixīnhé of Tàixīng.
Via Tàizhōu Dam, they reached Yángzǐ Wān and entered the grain transport canal.
This was even more convenient than Báitǎ.
Consequently, the grain transport canal and the Mèngdú and Déshèng Three Rivers were all open.
All could assist in transport.
In the first year of Zhèngtǒng,
court officials memorialized:
"From Xīngǎng to Bēnniú,
the grain transport canal is 150 *lǐ* long.
It formerly had water wheels to draw in the Jiāng tides for irrigation and infusion.
This allowed boats to pass and irrigated fields.
We request allocating government funds to install water wheels."
The imperial decree approved it.
However, the entrances of the three rivers into the Jiāng,
all varied in elevation.
Their water levels also alternated between rising and falling.
In the eighth year,
the people of Wǔjìn requested to dredge the Déshèng Hé and Běixīnhé.
The Zhèjiāng Military Commissioner Xiāo Huá, however, requested to dredge the Mèngdú.
Governor Zhōu Chén decided to dredge both rivers,
and abandon the construction of a dam on Běixīn.
The Dàqiáo Sluice Gate of Báitǎ Hé was opened and closed according to the season.
And the Chángzhōu and Zhènjiāng grain transport canals were also dredged.
During the Jǐngtài
period, the Cáohé again became silted,
so all grain boats were diverted to pass through the Mèngdú.
Three years later,
Censor Liàn Gāng said:
“Grain boats coming out to the Jiāng from Xiàgǎng and Mèngdú
have to travel against the current for three hundred *lǐ*
to reach Guāzhōu.
Déshèng is directly north of Xīn,
and Báitǎ is obliquely aligned with Mèngdú.
Crossing the river from these two banks is very short,
so it would be advisable to thoroughly dredge the silted areas.”
The emperor ordered Minister Shí Pú to manage the matter.
At that time, there was a proposal to dig the Qīlǐgǎng in Zhènjiāng,
to draw water from Jīnshān to flow through Dānyáng,
to avoid the dangers of the Mèngdú.
Zhènjiāng Prefect Lín È believed that it was a circuitous route with many rocks,
and would damage many commoners' fields and graves.
He suggested dredging Jīngkǒu Gate and Gānlù Dam,
as the distance would be shorter
and the effort less.
So, Lín È’s proposal was adopted.
Zhèjiāng Administration Commissioner Hú Qīng also wanted to remove the dams at Xīngǎng, Bēnniú, and other places,
and install stone sluices to store water.
This request was also granted.
However, the proposals to dredge the Déshèng River and dig the port were both shelved.
Although the stone sluices were built,
they could not store much water,
and grain boats still entered the Mèngdú.
In the first year of Tiānshùn,
Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices Líng Xìn stated that
it would be more convenient for grain vessels to pass through the Juéhé in Zhènjiāng.
The emperor agreed,
and ordered the Grand Coordinator of Grain Transport and Riverways, Lǐ Bǐng, to open the Qīlǐgǎng mouth,
and draw Jiāng water into it,
and also to dredge the silt at Bēnniú and Xīngǎng.
Provincial Governor Cuī Gōng further requested to add five more gates.
By the fourth year of Chénghuà,
the gate construction was finally completed.
From then on, all grain boats passed through the Juéhé;
those entering the other two rivers
were only empty return vessels and other boats.
By regulation,
the mouth of the Mèngdú River and various ports at Guā and Yí were to be dredged once every three years.
The Mèngdú was wide and did not silt up significantly,
but the Juéhé often dried up shortly after,
so it would then be changed back to the Mèngdú.
In the seventeenth year of Hóngzhì,
the ministers of the Board again reported the disadvantages of Xiàgǎng and Mèngdú being far from the Great Jiāng,
and requested urgent dredging of the silt at Jīngkǒu,
and drawing water from Liànhú to irrigate it.
An imperial edict ordered it to be carried out swiftly.
In the second year of Zhèngdé, the Báitǎ River and the four gates at Jiāngkǒu, Dàqiáo, Pānjiā, and Tōngjiāng were reopened.
In the fourteenth year, following the proposal of the Grand Coordinator of Grain Transport Zāng Fèng,
the upper and lower Juéhé in Chángzhōu were dredged,
and grain boats encountered no obstructions for over fifty years.
In the first year of Wànlì, it gradually dried up again,
and was dredged once more.
Tribute student Xǔ Rǔyú submitted a memorial saying:
“In the early days of the dynasty, four gates were established: named Jīngkǒu,
and Dāntú,
to prevent the three rivers from drying up;
named Lǚchéng,
and Bēnniú,
to prevent the five lakes from draining.
From Dānyáng to Zhènjiāng, three areas were impounded as lakes: named Liànhú,
Jiāozǐ,
and Dùshù.
Over the years,
residents encroached and cultivated,
and the two lakes, Jiāo and Dù, both dried up.
Only Liànhú remained,
which was also being encroached upon.
And all four gates were set up in vain.
I request to dredge the former sites of the three lakes to facilitate transport.”
The Governor-General of Rivers Fù Xīzhì said:
“Liànhú has already been dredged,
but Jiāozǐ and Dùshù have few sources and would be of no benefit.”
His proposal was therefore shelved.
Not long after,
Liànhú again became shallow due to silt.
In the fifth year,
Censors Guō Sījǐ and Chén Shìbǎo successively requested to restore Liànhú and
dredge Mèngdú.
And Supervising Secretary Tāng Pìnyǐn requested to build another gate next to Jīngkǒu,
to draw the Jiāng current inward;
when the tide rose, it would be opened,
and when it receded, it would be closed.
Censor Yǐn Liángrèn further said:
“Crossing the Jiāng from Mèngdú into Huángjiāgǎng,
although the water surface is wide, the Jiāng current is very calm.
From here to Tàixīng to reach Wāntóu and Gāoyóu is only over two hundred *lǐ*,
which can avoid unforeseen dangers at Guā and Yí.
As for crossing north of Jīngkǒu below Jīnshān,
encountering wind mid-stream carries the risk of being swept away or drowning.
It would be advisable to excavate the banks of Gānlùgǎng for over ten *lǐ* to create islands for mooring and turning.”
Censor Lín Yìngxùn further said:
“From Wànyuán Bridge to Mèngdú,
the two banks are steep and high,
easily collapsing with heavy rain and floods,
and the Jiāng tide brings sand,
making silting unavoidable.
It would be advisable to build gates at Wànyuán Bridge and Huángliánshù
to facilitate water storage and discharge.”
He also said:
“Liànhú, since the Western Jìn dynasty,
when Chén Mǐn dammed Mǎlín Stream
and drew water from eighty-four streams of Chángshān to irrigate Yúnyáng,
the embankment was named Liàntáng,
also called Liànhé,
for about forty *lǐ*.
Thirteen culverts were built around the lake.
During the Shàoxīng period of the Sòng dynasty,
a transverse dike was placed in the middle,
dividing it into upper and lower lakes,
and three gates were built: upper, middle, and lower.
The water from the eighty-four streams first flowed through Chénxī into the upper lake,
and then passed through the three gates into the lower lake.
During the Hóngwǔ period,
due to difficulties in the transport route,
three gates were built along the eastern embankment of the lower lake,
using lake water to aid transport,
but later they gradually became silted up.
Now, all encroachments should be abolished,
and it should be dredged again to become a lake.
The four boundaries of the upper lake are flanked by mounds,
and the northeast of the lower lake faces the river.
The original dike is intact;
only the gap in the middle needs to be repaired,
and the southwest should be further built up
to correspond with the northeast.
As for the three gates,
only the upper gate facing the lake remains as before.
It would be advisable to add middle and lower gates,
and further establish two overflow gates
between the middle and lower gates.
A total of over five thousand *mǔ* of fields should be reclaimed,
and privately installed culverts along the embankment should be blocked,
retaining only the original thirteen,
to regulate the discharge of lake water.
In winter and spring, they should be closed,
and not opened privately.
For Liànhú has no source,
relying solely on storage.
By increasing the dikes and opening the gates,
water will always be abundant,
and then it can aid transport.
I personally verified that the land of the upper lake is elevated,
where the water from the eighty-four streams originates,
and fear it may drain easily;
the lower lake land is flat and extensive,
only a few feet higher than the grain transport river,
and I often fear it will not fill.
If the water is truly plentiful and the dikes strong,
then it should be released as needed,
and the river will have full power.”
All these were submitted to the relevant authorities for deliberation.
In the thirteenth year,
Zhènjiāng Prefect Wú Huīqiān again said:
“The central dike of Liànhú should be ordered by officials to be repaired in early spring
to prevent breaches,
and powerful families should be prohibited from encroachment.”
This was followed.
In the seventeenth year, the Cáohé at Hénglín, Wǔjìn was dredged.
The Dàtōng Hé (Grand Canal)
was dug by Guō Shǒujìng of the Yuán dynasty.
From Dàtōng Qiáo, it flows eastward,
reaching Gāolí Zhuāng in Tōngzhōu,
where it joins the Báihé.
It then goes to Zhígū,
meets the Wèihé, and enters the sea,
stretching over one hundred and sixty *lǐ*.
There was one lock every ten *lǐ*
to store water for navigation,
and it was named Tōnghuì.
Also, as it was formed by the confluence of the Báihé, Yúhé, and Húnhé,
it was also called the Lùhé.
During the Hóngwǔ reign, it gradually fell into disuse.
In the eighth month of the fourth year of Yǒnglè (1406),
the imperial department in Běijīng reported:
"The banks of the three locks at Wǎnpíng, Chāngpíng, Xīhú, Jǐngdōng Niúlánzhuāng, and Qīnglóng Huájiā Wèngshān
have been breached by water."
The emperor ordered soldiers and civilians to repair them.
The following year, it was reported again:
"From Xīhú and Jǐngdōng to Tōngliú,
there are seven locks in total,
and the river channel is silted up.
From Báifú Cūn, southeast of Chāngpíng, to the confluence of Xīhú and Jǐngdōng Liúshuǐhé, a distance of one hundred *lǐ*,
twelve more locks should be added."
This was approved.
Before long,
all the locks were blocked,
and boats could no longer pass.
During the Chénghuà reign,
Yáng Mào, the Commander-in-Chief of Grain Transport, reported:
"Every year, from Zhāngjiāwān, boats are abandoned,
and goods are transferred by cart to the capital,
incurring immense hire costs.
The stone locks of the old Tōnghuìhé still exist,
about two *chǐ* deep.
By repairing the locks and impounding water,
using small boats for lighterage would be convenient."
There was also a proposal to dredge the river at Sānlǐhé, west of Yāndūn Qiáo in Zhāngjiāwān, for mooring boats.
and Shàngshū Yáng Dǐng and Shìláng Qiáo Yì were dispatched to investigate.
They reported:
"There were twenty-four old locks
for water passage and boat navigation.
However, in the Yuán dynasty, the water was outside the palace walls,
allowing boats to enter Hǎizǐ Wān inside the city.
Now the water exits from the Jīnshuǐhé of the imperial city,
so the old route cannot be used again.
Moreover, the Yuán dynasty diverted Báifú Quán (Spring) westward against the current,
which now passes through imperial tombs,
potentially disturbing the *dì mài* (earth's脉).
Also, Yīmǔ Quán (Spring) passes through Bái Yáng Kǒu Shāngōu (Mountain Gully),
and the two waters clash, making diversion difficult.
As for Sānlǐhé south of the city, it originally had no river source.
During the Zhèngtǒng reign, when the city moat was repaired,
fearing floods from heavy rains,
a channel was dug in the low-lying land southeast of Zhèngyáng Qiáo,
opening a moat entrance to drain the water,
which is how Sānlǐhé got its name.
Eight *lǐ* from the moat entrance,
it finally connects with the Húnhé.
The old channel banks are dotted with numerous houses and tombs,
the water is shallow, and the river is narrow.
Furthermore, it needs additional diversion of other streams to supplement it.
For instance, Xīhú Cǎoqiáo's source comes from Yùjiàng Jú, Mǎpǎo, and other places,
but the springs are not deep or extensive.
The Yuán people once used Jīnkǒu water,
which surged and submerged civilian houses,
so it was subsequently abandoned.
Only Yù Quán, Lóng Quán, and springs like Yuè'ér and Liǔshā
all originate in the northwest,
flowing along the mountain foothills,
and can be diverted into Xīhú.
