We request to dredge the source of Xīhú,
close the Fēnshuǐ Qīnglóng Zha (sluice),
divert all the spring waters from Gāoliáng Hé,
letting half of it exit through Jīnshuǐhé,
while the rest flows through the moat outside the capital,
converging east of Zhèngyángmén.
The city moat should also be closed,
preventing it from merging with Sānlǐhé.
The Dàtōng Qiáo locks and river should be opened and closed according to droughts and floods,
allowing boats to reach the granaries,
which would be very convenient."
The Emperor approved their proposal.
As 90,000 soldiers and laborers were being mobilized for dredging and repair,
due to an auspicious omen,
an imperial edict ordered all projects to cease.
The relevant department, considering the importance of grain transport,
then ordered 40,000 people to dredge the city moat,
while the rivers from Xīshān and Yù Quán to Zhāngjiāwān
would be gradually addressed.
Five years later,
Chén Ruì, Earl of Píngjiāng,
Lǐ Yù, Vice Minister of the Censorate,
and Shìláng Wēng Shìzī and Wáng Zhào were ordered to supervise the dredging of the Tōnghuìhé by grain transport soldiers,
following Dǐng's and Yì's previous proposal.
In the sixth month of the following year,
the work was completed.
From Dàtōng Qiáo to the mouth of the Húnhé at Zhāngjiāwān, a distance of over sixty *lǐ*,
three springs were dredged,
and four locks were added,
allowing grain boats to pass somewhat.
However, the three Chāngpíng springs diverted during the Yuán dynasty were all blocked and unusable,
and only Xīhú was diverted,
and even then, only half of its water,
making the river narrow and prone to filling up or drying out.
Within two years,
it was as sluggish as before.
In the second year of Zhèngdé (1507), it was once dredged,
and twelve locks and
forty-one dams from Dàtōng Qiáo to Tōngzhōu were repaired.
In the sixth year of Jiājìng (1527),
Censor Wú Zhòng reported:
"The Tōnghuìhé has been repeatedly repaired,
but always hampered by powerful figures.
However, the remains of the eight locks at Tōngliú and other places are still present;
if completed based on these,
it would be very easy to accomplish,
and over two hundred thousand *guàn* in cartage fees could be saved annually.
Moreover, throughout the dynasties, grain transport has always reached the capital,
and imperial provisions have never been stored fifty *lǐ* away."
The Emperor found this convincing
and ordered Shìláng Wáng Yuè, Hé Zhào, and Zhòng to investigate together.
Yuè and others reported:
"The terrain at Dàtōng Qiáo is over six *zhàng* higher than the Báihé.
If dredged to seven *zhàng*
to divert the Báihé to the capital,
all locks could be abolished,
but this is not easy to propose.
If we only dredge and repair the existing locks,
the Tōngliú Lock is within the old city of Tōngzhōu,
passing through two water gates,
and the Nánpǔ, Tǔqiáo, and Guǎnglì three locks are all in bustling markets and streets,
making transshipment inconvenient.
Only by the Báihé, west of the abandoned dam of the old small river,
less than one *lǐ* to the small dam that impounds water,
should it be repaired and built,
to allow passage to Pǔjì Zha,
which could save the effort of transshipping at four locks and two customs barriers."
However, Shàngshū Guì È argued that it was inconvenient
and requested to repair Sānlǐhé instead.
The Emperor sent his memorial to Grand Secretaries Yáng Yīqīng and Zhāng Cōng.
Yīqīng said:
"Using the old locks for transshipment
saves labor and expenses for the transport soldiers,
and should definitely be implemented."
Cōng also said:
"This is a plan for permanent peace after one effort,
while È's proposal involves extensive costs and difficult construction."
The Emperor then rejected È's proposal.
In the sixth month of the following year,
Zhòng reported the completion of the river
and presented five proposals,
stating:
"The terrain from Dàtōng Qiáo to Tōngzhōu Shíbà (Stone Dam) is four *zhàng* high,
and quicksand easily causes silting,
so it should be dredged and maintained regularly.
The official in charge of the river should be specially appointed
and not given other duties.
Officials and lock-keepers, having been cut back due to the cessation of transport,
should be restored to their original quotas.
The Qìngfēng Shàng Zha and Píngjīn Zhōng Zha are no longer in use,
and should be rebuilt outside the western water gate of Tōngzhōu.
Expenses for building small boats and annual maintenance and caulking
should all be deliberated and addressed."
The Emperor noted that previous inspections had not yielded immediate results,
and Zhòng and others completed the work in four months.
He issued an edict to reward them
and granted all their requests.
Zhòng also requested to keep Lángzhōng Hé Dòng, who supervised the work,
to specially manage the affair
as a long-term plan.
This was approved.
In the ninth year, Dòng was promoted to Yòutōngzhèng
and remained in charge of the Tōnghuìhé waterway.
At this time,
Zhòng was sent out as the Zhīfǔ of Chǔzhōu
and presented the *Tōnghuìhé Zhì* (Gazetteer of Tōnghuì River) he compiled.
The Emperor ordered it sent to the Historiography Academy
to be included in the *Huìdiǎn* (Collected Statutes)
and also commanded the Ministry of Works to publish it.
From then on, grain barges directly reached the capital
until the end of the Míng dynasty.
People remembered Zhòng's virtue
and built a shrine in Tōngzhōu to commemorate him.
The Jìzhōu River
was the supply route for the imperial army in Jìzhōu.
In the early Míng dynasty,
supplies for Jìzhōu were transported by sea.
In Tiānshùn second year (1458),
Mǐn Gōng, a hundred-household commander of Dàhé Guard, said:
"Nánjīng and the various guards in Zhílì
annually use banner soldiers to transport 30,000 shí of grain to the granaries of Jìzhōu and other guards.
This involves crossing more than seventy lǐ of open sea,
where winds and waves are treacherous.
The newly opened Gū River,
looking north towards Jìzhōu,
is directly aligned with the Shuǐtào and Gū River.
It is over forty lǐ long and direct,
and the water is deep.
The obstructions in between are only one-fourth of the total.
If a canal were dug for transport,
the dangers of the sea could be avoided."
This was referred to Grand General-in-Chief Dūdū Sòng Shèng and Inspecting Censor Lǐ Mǐn to investigate its feasibility.
Shèng and others deemed it convenient,
so the Zhígū River was opened.
It was five zhàng wide
and one zhàng five chǐ deep.
It was dredged once in Chénghuà second year (1466),
and again twenty years later,
along with dredging the Yāhóngqiáo waterway,
and a granary for sea-borne grain was built in Fēngrùn County.
In Zhèngdé sixteenth year (1521),
Wáng Zàn, a commander of grain transport, said:
"The new river northeast of Zhígū,
used for transporting supplies to Jìzhōu,
has shallow waters,
and boats can only navigate when the tide is in.
Border garrisons often face shortages of provisions.
It should be dredged to make it deeper and wider."
This was adopted.
Initially,
the new river was dredged once every three years.
In Jiājìng first year (1522), this was changed to once every two years,
becoming the norm.
In the seventeenth year (1538), the section from Yīnliúzhuāng Dàkǒu to Jiùcāngdiàn, measuring 116 lǐ, was dredged.
The section of Fēngrùn surrounding Xiānghé,
dredged since the Chénghuà era,
was used to transport over 100,000 shí of grain to supply the eastern route of Jìzhōu.
Later, it became silted and disused,
and the supplies were instead provided by Jìzhōu,
which was very inconvenient.
In Jiājìng forty-fifth year (1566), acting on the request of Censor Bāo Chéngyīn,
it was restored,
and three locks were built at Běijì, Zhāngguāntún, and Yāhóngqiáo to store water.
The Chāngpíng River
was the supply route for the imperial army guarding the various imperial tombs.
It started from Ānjì Bridge outside Gǒnghuá City
and reached Tōngzhōu ferry crossing.
It stretched 145 lǐ,
but thirty lǐ of it were silted and shallow, making navigation difficult.
In Lóngqìng sixth year (1572), it was extensively dredged,
allowing the transport of 40,000 shí of monthly grain rations for the imperial army of Chánglíng and other eight guards,
thus achieving smooth flow.
In Wànlì first year (1573), the old river outside Gǒnghuá City was again cleared.
Sea transport
began in the mid-Zhìyuán era of the Yuán dynasty.
Bó Yán used Zhū Qīng and Zhāng Xuān to transport grain to the capital,
totaling only over 40,000 shí.
Thereafter, it increased daily,
reaching over three million shí.
Initially,
the sea route was over thirteen thousand lǐ long,
and extremely treacherous.
Later, a new route was opened,
which was somewhat more direct.
Afterwards, Yīn Mínglüè again opened a new route,
which was even more convenient.
However, all routes went through the open ocean.
When the wind was favorable,
it took no more than ten days from western Zhèjiāng to the capital,
but many goods were lost to drifting.
In Hóngwǔ first year (1368),
Tài Zǔ ordered Tāng Hé to build ocean-going ships
to provision the soldiers on the northern expedition.
After the realm was settled,
skilled sailors were recruited to transport grain from the Yánghǎicāng granary in Láizhōu to supply Yǒngpíng.
Later, as military campaigns were frequently waged in Liáozuǒ and the regions north of it,
the Marquises Jìnghǎi Wú Zhēn, Yán'ān Táng Shèngzōng, Hánghǎi Zhāng Hè, and Zhúlú Zhū Shòu successively managed the transport of grain to Liáo,
making it a regular practice.
Over a hundred large ships of the army from the coastal guards of Jiāngnán and Zhèjiāng were supervised,
transporting hundreds of thousands of shí of grain.
Generals and officers below were awarded varying amounts of silk fabrics, pepper, sappanwood, cash, and banknotes,
while civilian laborers were exempted from corvée for one year,
and those who drowned received generous compensation.
In the thirtieth year (1397),
due to the surplus of military provisions in Liáodōng,
Liáo troops were simply ordered to cultivate the land there,
and sea transport was abolished.
In Yǒnglè first year (1403),
Earl Píngjiāng Chén Xuān supervised the transport of over 490,000 shí of grain by sea,
provisioning Běijīng and Liáodōng.
In the second year (1404),
since sea transport only reached Zhígū,
and small boats were separately used to transfer goods to the capital,
it was ordered that 1,400 open granaries be established in Tiānjīn
to expand storage capacity.
In the fourth year (1406), a system of combined sea and land transport was established.
Xuān transported a million shí of grain annually
and built the Bǎiwàncāng granary in Yǐn'érwānchéng, Zhígū.
Ten thousand registered soldiers from Tiānjīn Guard were stationed there for defense.
At this point,
it was ordered that grain from Jiāngnán be transported,
partly by sea,
and partly via the Huái and Huáng rivers,
then by land to the Wèihé River,
and into Tōngzhōu, becoming the norm.
Chén Xuān reported:
"Jiādìng is near the sea,
exposed to the impact of river currents.
The land is flat and extensive,
with no large mountains or high islands.
When sea vessels anchor,
they sometimes encounter winds and waves,
and are easily damaged if they strike hard objects or run aground in shallow water.
It is advisable to build an earthen mountain in Qīngpǔ
and erect beacons as markers,
so that boatmen know where to avoid hazards,
and the dangers of the sea will not be a problem."
An imperial edict approved this.
In the ninth month of the tenth year (1412),
the construction was completed.
It measured one hundred zhàng square
and was over thirty zhàng high.
It was named Bǎoshān.
The emperor personally composed an inscription to commemorate it.
In the fifth month of the thirteenth year (1415), sea transport was again abolished,
with only one general administration, Zhēyáng, remaining
to transport grain to Liáo and Jì.
In Zhèngtǒng thirteenth year (1448), the number of sea vessels for Dēngzhōu Guard was reduced from one hundred to eighteen,
with five ships transporting over 120,000 jīn of cloth, flowers, and paper money ingots from Qīng, Lái, and Dēng,
awarded annually to the Liáo army.
In Chénghuà twenty-third year (1487),
Vice Minister Qiū Jùn presented the Dàxué Yǎnyì Bǔ,
requesting the restoration of the old sea transport route to operate alongside river transport.
He generally stated:
"One sea vessel can carry a thousand shí,
equivalent to three river vessels, greatly reducing the number of soldiers needed.
River transport saves three-tenths of the cost compared to land transport,
and sea transport saves seven-tenths compared to land.
Although there is a risk of drifting and sinking,
it saves the labor of towing soldiers, the cost of lightering in shallow waters, and the need for sequential guarding,
so the advantages and disadvantages balance out.
Knowledgeable individuals familiar with sea routes should be sought out
to study and survey them."
His proposal was not adopted.
In Hóngzhì fifth year (1492),
the river burst its banks at Jīnlóngkǒu,
and there were calls to restore sea transport,
but the court did not agree.
In Jiājìng second year (1523),
the Zhēyáng administration lost 20,000 shí of grain to drifting,
and over fifty imperial soldiers drowned.
In the fifth year (1526), shipbuilding in Dēngzhōu was halted.
In the twentieth year (1541),
Commander-in-Chief of Rivers Wáng Yǐqí stated,
due to the obstruction and blockage of the river:
"Although sea transport is difficult,
there is a new north-south river between Píngdù Prefecture and the southeast.
In the Yuán dynasty, locks were built to directly reach Āndōng.
Both north and south routes proceeded through inland seas,
which were direct and without hazards.
This should be studied."
The emperor, considering the sea route too circuitous,
rejected his proposal.
In the thirty-eighth year (1559),
Hóu Rǔliàng, the Provincial Governor of Liáodōng, said:
"The route from Tiānjīn to Liáo,
from the sea mouth to Yòutúnhé Tōngbǎo, is less than 200 lǐ.
Cáo Pòdiàn, Yuètúo Sāng, Jiāngnǚfén, and Táohuādǎo along this route are all suitable for anchorage."
The Ministry reviewed and approved it.
In the forty-fifth year (1566),
Gěng Suícháo, the Provincial Governor of Shùntiān, surveyed the sea route:
from west of Yǒngpíng, entering the sea,
145 lǐ to Jìgèzhuāng,
and then another 426 lǐ to Tiānjīn,
all proceeding close to the shore.
In between, there was an open sea section of 120 lǐ,
and the Jiànhé, Liánghé, Xiǎogū, and Dàgū rivers could be used for shelter from wind.
His proposal was initially approved,
but was later thwarted and abandoned by a memorial from Censor Liú Xuān.
In that same year (1566),
acting on the proposal of Supervising Secretary Hú Yìngjiā,
the Zhēyáng administration was abolished.
In the fifth year of Lóngqìng's reign,
the Hé, Xú, and Pī rivers were silted up.
Following the suggestion of Gěishìzhōng Sòng Liángzuǒ,
the Zhēyáng Zǒng was re-established,
preserving the intention of maritime transport.
Liáng Mènglóng, the巡撫 (Xúnfǔ) of Shāndōng, strongly argued for the benefits of maritime transport,
saying:
"The sea route from Huái'ān in the south to Jiāozhōu,
and from Tiānjīn in the north to Hǎicāng,
is frequented by islanders and merchants.
I sent soldiers to transport rice and wheat from Huái and Jiāo to Tiānjīn,
and there were no disadvantages.
From Huái'ān to Tiānjīn is three thousand three hundred lǐ.
With a favorable wind,
it can be reached in two Xún (twenty days).
The boats sail along the near sea,
with islands providing continuous links,
so even in wind, shelter can be found.
This is much safer and more convenient than Yīn Mínglüè's old route.
Before the fifth month, the wind is favorable and gentle,
so sailing out at this time ensures no mishaps."
An order was given to allocate one hundred and twenty thousand dàn of grain from nearby漕糧 (cáoliáng)
for Mènglóng to implement.
In the sixth year,
Wáng Zōngmù supervised the漕 (cáo),
and requested the implementation of maritime transport.
An imperial edict ordered the transport of one hundred and twenty thousand dàn from Huái into the sea.
The route
was from Yúntīguān northeast, passing through Yīngyóushān, Āndōngwèi, Shíjiùsuǒ, Xiàhésuǒ, Qítángdǎo, Língshānwèi, Gǔzhèn, Jiāozhōu, Áoshānwèi, Dàsōngwèi, and Hángcūnzhài,
all on the open sea.
From Hǎiyángsuǒ, it passed through Zhúdǎo, Níngjīnsuǒ, and Jìnghǎiwèi,
then turned northeast to Chéngshānwèi, Liúgōngdǎo, and Wēihǎiwèi,
and west to Nínghǎiwèi,
all on the open sea.
From Zhīfúdǎo in Fúshān to Shāmén and other islands north of Dēngzhōuchéng's Xīnhǎikǒu,
it went west past Sāngdǎo and Jǐdǎo;
from Jǐdǎo west past Sānshāndǎo, Fúróngdǎo, Láizhōudàyáng, and Hǎicāngkǒu;
from Hǎicāng west past the Huáihé estuary and Yú'érpù,
then northwest past Hóuzhèndiàn and Tángtóusài;
from Hóuzhèn northwest past the estuaries of Dàqīnghé and Xiǎoqīnghé,
then along the Qǐgōuhé into Zhígū,
reaching Tiānjīnwèi.
In total, three thousand three hundred and ninety lǐ.
In the first year of Wànlì's reign,
seven grain transport vessels were wrecked off Jìmòfúshāndǎo,
several thousand dàn of rice were lost,
and fifteen military personnel drowned.
The Gěishì and Yùshǐ submitted memorials criticizing the failure,
and it was suspended and not resumed.
In the twenty-fifth year,
倭寇 (wōkòu) attacked,
and grain was transported from Dēngzhōu to supply the Korean army.
Yú Shìlián, the Fùshǐ of Shāndōng, again stated:
"For supplying Liáo, nothing is better than maritime transport;
and for maritime transport, nothing is better than Dēng and Lái.
From Dēng and Lái to Jīnzhōu is six or seven hundred lǐ,
and to Lǚshùnkǒu is only over five hundred lǐ.
With a favorable wind, a sail can reach it in one or two days.
Furthermore, there are islands like Shāmén, Tuójī, and Huángchéng in between,
serving as natural relay stations,
for stops and shelter from wind.
Only the two hundred lǐ from Huángchéng to Lǚshùn is somewhat far,
but with a convenient wind, it can be crossed in less than half a day.
If one travels from Tiānjīn to Liáo,
the open sea offers no anchorage;
from Huái'ān to Jiāozhōu,
though only three hundred lǐ,
from Jiāo to Dēng is a thousand lǐ away,
with reefs making passage difficult.
Only Dēng and Lái for supplying Liáo
is advantageous and easy."
At the time, this proposal was largely accepted,
but not implemented.
In the forty-sixth year,
Lǐ Chánggēng, the Xúnfǔ of Shāndōng, memorialized for the implementation of maritime transport,
and specifically appointed a Hùbù Shìláng to supervise it.
The details are found in Chánggēng's biography.
In the twelfth year of Chóngzhēn's reign,
Shěn Tíngyáng from Chóngmíng, serving as an Nèigé Zhōngshū,
again presented the advantages of maritime transport,
and compiled a five-volume work on maritime transport to submit.
An order was given to build sea vessels for trial.
Tíngyáng, with two vessels,
carrying several hundred dàn of rice,
departed from Huái'ān by sea on the first day of the sixth month of the thirteenth year,
and reached Tiānjīn on the full moon.
He waited for wind for five days,
the actual journey taking only one Xún (ten days).
The emperor was greatly pleased,
promoted Tíngyáng to Hùbù Lángzhōng,
and ordered him to Dēngzhōu to consult with Xú Rénlóng, the Xúnfǔ.
Huáng Yìn'ēn, the Fù Zǒngbīng of Shāndōng, also submitted nine proposals for maritime transport,
and the emperor immediately ordered him to supervise maritime transport.
Previously,
military provisions for Níngyuǎn were typically transported by Tiānjīn boats to Dēngzhōu,
then waited for a southeast wind to transfer grain to Tiānjīn,
and then waited for a southwest wind to transfer to Níngyuǎn.
Tíngyáng transported directly from Dēngzhōu to Níngyuǎn,
saving considerable expense.
Soon after, he was ordered to Huái'ān to manage maritime transport,
but was obstructed by Zhū Dàdiǎn, the Dūcáo Shìláng.
He was then ordered to relocate to Dēngzhōu
and take charge of Níngyuǎn's provisions.
In the sixteenth year, he was promoted to Guānglù Shàoníng.
During Fúwáng's reign,
Tíngyáng was ordered to use sea vessels to defend the Jiāng River,
and later was tasked with concurrently managing grain affairs.
After Nándū fell,
Tíngyáng struggled between the two princes, Táng and Lǔ,
and died for the cause.
In the mid-Jiājìng period,
court officials repeatedly discussed resuming maritime transport.
Wàn Biǎo, the Zǒngbīngguān of Cáoyùn, said:
"In the past, during maritime transport,
more than one hundred thousand (people) drowned annually.
Grain-carrying boats,
boatmen,
and supervising officials
all suffered unavoidable losses.
Those who now propose maritime transport often base their arguments on Qiū Jùn's theories,
but they are not well-versed in the actual circumstances."
Collation Notes
Record Sixty-Three: Rivers and Canals Five: Huáihé, Jiāhé, Wèihé, Zhānghé, Qìnhé, Hūtuóhé, Sānggānhé, Jiāoláihé.
The Huáihé River
originates from Tāizānshān in Píngshì, Hénán.
Passing through Tóngbó,
its flow begins to grow.
East to Gùshǐ,
it enters Yǐngzhōujìng in Nánjī,
where it merges with the Rǔ and Yǐng rivers and other waters to the east.
Passing north of Shòuzhōu,
the Féishuǐ enters it.
East of Huáiyuǎnchéng,
the Guōshuǐ enters it.
East through Fèngyáng and Línhuái,
the Háoshuǐ enters it.
Further east, south of Wǔhéxiàn,
it receives the Kuì, Tuó, Chōng, and Tóng rivers,
becoming powerful and swift.
Passing south of Sìzhōuchéng,
a little further east, the Biànshuǐ enters it.
Passing the foot of Guīshān,
it bends sharply northward,
meeting Hóngzé, Fùlíng, Nídūn, Wànjiā and other lakes.
Northeast to Qīnghé,
it merges with the Dàhé (Yellow River) to the south,
which is the ancient Sìmkǒu,
also known as Qīngkǒu;
this is the crucial confluence of the Huáng and Huái rivers.
On the south bank of the Huái,
the Cáohé river flows into it,
which is known as Qīngjiāngpǔkǒu.
Further east, it passes north of Huái'ān and southeast of Āndōng to reach the sea.
In the seventh year of Yǒnglè's reign,
it burst its banks at Shòuzhōu,
flooding Zhōngdū.
In the third year of Zhèngtǒng's reign,
it overflowed at Qīnghé.
In the fourth year of Tiānshùn's reign,
it overflowed at Fèngyáng.
All were repaired and built up in time,
causing no major harm.
In the twelfth year of Zhèngdé's reign,
the Cáodī embankment burst again,
inundating Sìzhōu.
Sìzhōu,
where the Imperial Ancestral Mausoleum was located,
was the lowest-lying area.
Initially,
the Huái River entered the sea from Yúntīguān in Āndōng,
without the problem of overflowing sideways.
However, when it met the Huáng River,
the Huáng River's flow was strong,
usurping the Huái River's path to the sea,
and the Huái River could not contend with the Huáng River,
often diverting to the east.
Chén Xuān dredged Qīngjiāngpǔ
and consequently built up the old embankment of Gāojiāyàn to block it.
Huái and Yáng relied on this to be free from fear,
but Fèng and Sì suffered repeated harm.
In the fourteenth year of Jiājìng's reign, based on the proposal of Dū Yùshǐ Liú Tiānhé,
an embankment was built to protect the imperial mausoleum,
and with the Gāoyàn embankment firmly in place,
the Huái River flowed freely out of Qīngkǒu,
ending the troubles of Fèng and Sì.
In the fourth year of Lóngqìng's reign,
Wēng Dàlì, the Zǒnghé Dū Yùshǐ, again reported the completion of the Huái River dredging project,
and the Huái River became even more tranquil.
In the third month of the third year of Wànlì
the Gāojiāyàn 高家堰 dam burst,
and Gāo 高, Bǎo 寶, Xīng 興, and Yán 鹽 were submerged in a great flood.
Meanwhile, the Yellow River's waters encroached upon the Huái River,
and gradually approached Fèng 鳳 and Sì 泗.
An imperial decree then ordered the construction of a stone embankment protecting the city of Sìlíng 泗陵, over two hundred *zhàng* 丈 long.
Sì 泗 gained some calm thanks to the stone embankment.
At this point,
Wú Guìfāng 吳桂芳, the Assistant Minister of the Grand Canal Transport, said:
"The river has burst at Cuīzhèn 崔鎮,
and the Qīnghé 清河 road is silted up.
The Yellow River is strong and the Huái River is weak,
moving south to inundate Shānyáng 山陽, Gāo 高, and Bǎo 寶.
I request urgent protection for the lake embankment."
The Emperor ordered a thorough consideration of its convenience.
Tāng Pìnyǐn 湯聘尹, a supervising secretary, proposed to divert the Huái River into the Yangtze River.
At that time, the Yellow River rushed from the Old Yellow River into the sea,
and the Huái River was able to take advantage of the emptiness to flow out through Qīngkǒu 清口.
Guìfāng 桂芳 reported this,
and the proposal was consequently shelved.
In the sixth year,
Pān Jìxún 潘季馴, the Censor-in-Chief of River Conservancy, stated:
"Gāoyàn 高堰
is the gateway to the Huái 淮 and Yáng 揚 regions,
and the key point for the Yellow and Huái Rivers.
If we wish to divert the Yellow River into the sea,
we must rely on the Huái River to scour the sand.
If the Huái River bursts southward,
then the turbid currents will become stagnant,
and Qīngkǒu 清口 will also be blocked.
The Yellow River will inevitably burst its banks and overflow,
and the upstream waters will flow over flat land,
and Pī 邳, Xú 徐, Fèng 鳳, and Sì 泗 will all be submerged in a great flood.
This means the Huái suffers, and the Yellow River suffers;
the Yellow River suffers, and the Grand Canal also suffers.
This is a situation where they are mutually dependent."
Consequently, the Gāoyàn 高堰 embankment was built,
starting from Wǔjiādūn 武家墩,
passing through Dàxiǎojiàn 大小澗, Fùlínghú 阜陵湖, Zhōuqíao 周橋, and Zháibà 翟壩,
eighty *lǐ* 里 long,
preventing the Huái River from flowing eastward.
Moreover, because there were two outlets, Wángjiǎn 王簡 and Zhāngfú 張福, on the north bank of the Huái River that discharged into the Yellow River,
dividing the water force,
Qīngkǒu 清口 was easily silted and shallowed,
and much of the Yellow River water also flowed back into the Huái River through these outlets.
Thus, embankments were built to protect against them.
This made the Huái River have no outlet,
and the Yellow River have no inlet,
so that all the Huái River water rushed to Qīngkǒu 清口,
joining the Great River to flow into the sea.
However, although the Huái River flowed out through Qīngkǒu 清口,
it also spilled westward into Fèng 鳳 and Sì 泗.
In the eighth year,
there was a flood,
and the Huái River lapped against the city of Sì 泗,
even reaching the steps of the ancestral mausoleum.
Yùshǐ 御史 Chén Yòngbīn 陳用賓 reported this.
Wáng Dàochéng 王道成, a supervising secretary, then said:
"The Yellow River has not yet risen,
but continuous rain happens to accumulate between the Huái 淮 and Sì 泗,
and Qīngkǒu 清口 can no longer discharge the water.
It is appropriate to order the river officials to dredge or block it."
Jìxún 季馴 said:
"The Yellow and Huái Rivers merge and flow eastward
with great speed.
Sìzhōu 四州 has undulating hills,
and the rainwater cannot drain,
thus causing the overflow.
If we wish to dredge,
the lower reaches are already deep,
with nothing to dredge;
if we wish to block,
the upper reaches cannot be blocked against the current."
Consequently, Jìxún 季馴 was ordered to assess the situation,
and in the end, his judgment was accepted.
In the sixteenth year,
Jìxún 季馴 again became the Censor-in-Chief of River Conservancy,
and several thousand *zhàng* 丈 were added to the embankments protecting Sìzhōu 四州,
all made of stone.
In the ninth month of the nineteenth year,
the Huái River overflowed Sìzhōu 四州,
rising above the city moat,
so the water gates were blocked to prevent internal flooding.
Consequently,
the accumulated water in the city could not drain,
nineteen out of twenty residents were drowned,
and it encroached upon the ancestral mausoleum.
The proposals for draining were inconsistent,
but Jìxún 季馴 believed it should be allowed to dissipate naturally.
Coincidentally, he coughed up blood and requested to return home,
and those who spoke out then requested that his departure be granted.
However, the Emperor sent Zhāng Zhēngguān 張貞觀, a supervising secretary, to investigate,
and Shū Yìnglóng 舒應龍, the Minister of River Conservancy, and others discussed in detail and reported to the throne,
but a plan had not yet been finalized.
For several consecutive years,
the Huái River burst eastward at Gāoliángjiàn 高良澗,
and flooded Sìlíng 泗陵 to the west.
The Emperor was furious,
dismissed Yìnglóng 應龍 from office,
and sent Zhāng Qǐchéng 張企程, a supervising secretary, to investigate.
Many of the discussants requested the demolition of Gāoyàn 高堰,
but Yáng Yīkuí 楊一魁, the Minister of River Conservancy, and Qǐchéng 企程 disagreed,
and strongly requested the division of the Yellow River and the diversion of the Huái River.
Thus, a sluice gate was built at Wǔjiādūn 武家墩,
to drain the Huái River water through the Yǒngjìhé 永濟河 to the Jīnghé 涇河,
thence to Shèyánghú 射陽湖 and into the sea.
They also built stone overflow gates at Gāoliángjiàn 高良澗 and Zhōuqíao 周橋,
to drain the Huái River water,
one through Chàhé 岔河 into Jīnghé 涇河,
and another through Cǎozihú 草子湖 and Bǎoyìnghú 寶應湖 down Zǐyīnggōu 子嬰溝,
all flowing into Guǎngyánghú 廣洋湖 and thence to the sea.
They also dredged the Máotánggǎng 茆塘港 at Gāoyóu 高郵,
connecting it to Shàobóhú 邵伯湖,
and opened Jīnjiāwān 金家灣,
flowing down Mángdàohé 芒稻河 into the Yangtze River,
to relieve the Huái River's overflow,
and the Huái River waters became calm.
Subsequently, the three sluices gradually became blocked.
During the Chóngzhēn 崇禎 period,
the Yellow and Huái Rivers overflowed,
and discussants again requested the opening of Gāoyàn 高堰.
Officials from Huái 淮 and Yáng 揚 in the court collectively submitted memorials and strongly argued against it,
and the proposal was consequently shelved.
However, at that time,
several outlets at Jiànyì 建義 frequently burst,
flooding Xīng 興 and Yán 鹽 downstream,
and the Huái River problem became more severe day by day.
The Jīahé 泇河 had
two sources.
One emerged from a valley south of Fèixiàn 費縣,
flowing southwest along Yízhōu 沂州,
and the other emerged from Jūnshān 君山 in Yìxiàn 嶧縣,
joining the Fèijīa 費泇 to the southeast,
known as the Eastern and Western Jīahé 泇河.
Southward, it met the Pénghé 彭河 water,
flowed east from Mǎjiāqiáo 馬家橋,
passed through lakes such as Wēishān 微山, Chìshān 赤山, and Lǚmèng 呂孟,
crossed Guǐxūlíng 葛墟嶺,
and then southward passed through Hóujiāwān 侯家灣 and Liángchéng 良城,
reaching Jīakǒuzhèn 泇口鎮,
where it joined lakes such as Gémán 蛤鰻 and Liánwāng 連汪.
Eastward, it met the Yíshuǐ 沂水,
flowed from Zhōuhú 周湖 and Liǔhú 柳湖,
connecting to the Dōngzhíhé 東直河 of Pīzhōu 邳州.
Southeastward, it reached Huángdūnhú 黃墩湖 and Luòmǎhú 駱馬湖 in Sùqiān 宿遷,
flowing through the Dǒng 陳 and Chén 陳 two canals into the Yellow River.
The proposal to divert the Sì 泗 River to join the Yí 沂 and Jì 濟 Rivers for the transport route,
to avoid the dangers of the Yellow River,
began with Wēng Dàlì 翁大立,
was continued by Fù Xīzhì 傅希摯,
and completed by Lǐ Huàlóng 李化龍 and Cáo Shípìn 曹時聘.
In the ninth month of the fourth year of Lóngqìng 隆慶,
the river burst at Pīzhōu 邳州,
silting up one hundred eighty *lǐ* 里 from Suīníng 睢寧 to Sùqiān 宿遷.
Wēng Dàlì 翁大立, Assistant Minister of River Conservancy, requested the opening of the Jīahé 泇河 to avoid the Yellow River water,
but it was not decided and then he was dismissed.
In the fourth month of the following year,
the river again burst at Pīzhōu 邳zhou,
and Luò Zūn 雒遵, a supervising secretary, was ordered to investigate.
Zhū Héng 朱衡, Minister of Works, requested that the proposal to open the Jīakǒuhé 泇口河 be submitted to the officials for thorough consideration.
The Emperor immediately ordered Zūn 遵 to jointly investigate.
Zūn 遵 said:
"Although the route of Jīakǒuhé 泇口河 is direct,
its construction is truly difficult.
Guǐxūlíng 葛墟嶺 is more than six *zhàng* 丈 higher than the river bed;
excavation only reached two *zhàng* 丈,
when springs gushed out from the bedrock.
Although Hóujiāwān 侯家灣 and Liángchéng 良城 have river-like formations,
there are many hidden rocks in the water,
making excavation difficult.
Even if excavated,
the rapids would make it impossible for transport boats.
Furthermore, in lakes such as Gémán 蛤鰻, Zhōuliǔ 周柳, etc.,
building embankments in the water
would incur immeasurable costs.
Although embankments can be built in lakes such as Wēishān 微山, Chìshān 赤山, and Lǚmèng 呂孟,
it would require excavating Guǐxūlíng 葛墟嶺 to drain the main channel
and opening the Dìbīngōu 地浜溝 to disperse the remaining flow,
only then could construction proceed."
He requested that the proposal be abandoned.
The imperial decree ordered Minister Zhū Héng 朱衡 to jointly reinvestigate with Wàn Gōng 萬恭, Censor-in-Chief of River Conservancy, and others.
Héng's 衡 memorial stated three difficulties,
generally in line with Zūn's 遵 points.
He also said that the Grand Canal was already open, and
the embankments between Xú 徐 and Pī 邳 were high and the water deep,
so there was no need for separate construction.
The proposal was then abandoned.
In the third year of the Wànlì 萬曆 reign,
Fù Xīzhì 傅希摯, Grand Censor-in-Chief of River Administration, stated:
"The proposal for the Jiāhé 泇河 was once made but then suspended,
citing three difficulties.
However, your minister dispatched drillers, surveyors, levelers, and draftsmen
to investigate these three difficult locations.
Starting from Quánhékǒu 泉河口,
and opening towards the southeast,
the difficulty of the starting point being low-lying
and the downstream trending high can be avoided.
Southwards, passing east of Xìngyìcūn 性義村,
the difficulty of Géxū Lǐng 葛墟嶺 being high and solid can be avoided.
Following Dǒugōuhé 陡溝河 through the flat area west of Guōcūn 郭村,
the hidden rocks of Liángchéng Hóujiāwān 良城侯家灣 can be avoided.
Approaching the Jiākǒu 泇口 area,
the depth of the river channel varies,
and the lakes and ponds are interconnected.
Though there are some gravel deposits,
they pose no obstacle to excavation.
Broadly speaking, it starts at Quánhékǒu 泉河口,
where the water enters,
and ends at Dàhékǒu 大河口,
where the water exits.
From northwest to southeast,
it is 530 *lǐ* (里) long,
nearly 80 *lǐ* (里) shorter than the Huánghé 黃河.
River channels and ponds constitute eighty to ninety percent of it.
With live water from the source,
the network is interconnected.
This is how Heaven provides for grain transport.
If we can sincerely donate the cost of ten years of river management
to complete the Jiāhé 泇河,
then there will be no worry of blockages or breaches in the Huánghé 黃河,
no worry of silting in Cháchéng 茶城,
no worry of difficulties or dangers at the Two Dams,
and no worry of damage to transport vessels.
The branch canal at Yángshān 洋山 need not be opened,
the sluice gates at Jìngshān 境山 need not be built,
the flood workers of Xú 圩 and Lǚ 呂 can be entirely saved,
and the dike work at Mǎjiāqiáo 馬家橋 can be suspended.
The immediate immeasurable cost
will be more than offset by future savings.
Your minister believes opening the Jiāhé 泇河 is beneficial."
Consequently, the emperor ordered Hóu Yúzhào 侯于趙, Grand Supervisor of the Department of Works, to meet with Xīzhì 希摯 and Liú Guāngguó 劉光國, Censor of River Transport,
to make a definite proposal and report.
Yúzhào 于趙 surveyed and reported on the matters concerning the Jiāhé 泇河:
"Within the 530 *lǐ* (里) from Quánhékǒu 泉河口 to Dàhékǒu 大河口,
from Zhíhé 直河 to Qīnghé 清河, over 300 *lǐ* (里)
do not rely on the Jiāhé 泇河,
and this work can be ceased.
However, from Xú 圩 and Lǚ 呂 to Zhíhé 直河, the upper and lower 200 *lǐ* (里),
if the river impacts Xiāo 蕭 and Dàng 碭, it will dry up the Two Dams;
if it impacts Suīníng 睢寧, it will silt up the Pīhé 邳河.
It is advisable to open it to avoid these harms,
which would cost approximately 1.5 million *jīn* (金) of silver.
However, the hidden rocks at Liángchéng 良城 are 550 *zhàng* (丈) long,
and the difficulty of excavation is hard to predict.
The Xìngyì Lǐng 性義嶺 and the Nányǔ Líng 南禹陵 both obstruct the river flow.
Once these two sections are opened,
the breaches of the Fēng 豐 and Pèi 沛 rivers
will inevitably flood in.
It is advisable to first excavate the rocks at Liángchéng 良城
and preemptively repair the dikes of Fēng 豐 and Pèi 沛.
Then the construction can be gradually discussed."
The Ministry reviewed and agreed with his words,
but stated that opening the Jiāhé 泇hé would take several years and would not be completed quickly,
and that river management should be prioritized.
The emperor was displeased,
accusing Yúzhào 于趙 of obstruction,
but the discussion was consequently shelved.
Twenty years later,
Shū Yìnglóng 舒應龍, Minister of River Administration, opened Hánzhuāng 韓莊 to drain lake water,
and the Jiāhé 泇hé route finally opened.
By the twenty-fifth year,
the Huánghé 黃河 breached at Huánggùkǒu 黃堌口 and shifted south,
almost cutting off flow below Xú 圩 and Lǚ 呂.
There was a discussion about opening Lǐjí Kǒu 李吉口, Xiǎofúqiáo 小浮橋, and below Zhènkǒu 鎮口,
building sluices to divert water for grain transport.
However, commentators argued this was not a permanent solution.
Thereupon,
Yáng Yìngwén 楊應文, Grand Supervisor of the Department of Works, and Yáng Tínglán 楊廷蘭, Grand Supervisor of the Department of Personnel, both advocated opening the Jiāhé 泇hé.
The Ministry of Works reviewed and approved the proposal.
The emperor ordered river and grain transport officials to survey and report,
but it was not carried out.
In the twenty-eighth year,
Censor Nài Qí 佴祺 again requested the opening of the Jiāhé 泇hé.
The Ministry of Works reported:
"Using the Huánghé 黃河 for grain transport has both advantages and disadvantages;
using the Jiāhé 泇hé for grain transport has advantages without disadvantages.
However, beyond the Jiāhé 泇hé,
passing through Wēishān 微山, Lǚméng 呂孟, Zhōuliǔ 周柳, and other lakes,
in autumn and winter, when the water rises, there are risks of wind and waves;
in winter and spring, when the water recedes, there are risks of shallows and obstructions.
Separate grain transport channels must be excavated upstream and downstream,
and sluice gates built to regulate water."
This was approved.
Liú Dōngxīng 劉東星, Minister of River Administration, oversaw the project,
but due to the sandy and rocky terrain,
the work was difficult and not completed.
Zhāng Wèndá 張問達, Grand Supervisor of the Department of Works, brought this up.
Censor Zhāng Yǎngzhì 張養志 again presented four points regarding the proposal to open the Jiāhé 泇hé: One is to open Huángníwān 黃泥灣 to connect to the Jiāhé 泇hé route.
Pīzhōu Yíhé Kǒu 邳州沂河口 is the gateway to the Jiāhé 泇hé.
Six or seven *lǐ* (里) into the entrance,
there is a lake called
Lián'èrwāng 連二汪,
whose water is shallow and wide,
with much silt downstream.
If one wishes to dredge it, there are no banks to repair;
if one wishes to build dams or fascines, there are no foundations to construct.
Outside the lake is
Huángníwān 黃泥灣,
not far from the lake,
where the land is quite low.
From Yíkǒu 沂口 to the northern cliff of the lake, about twenty *lǐ* (里),
a canal should be opened here to connect to Jiākǒu 泇口,
diverting lake
water into it.
Transport vessels could then directly reach Jiākǒu 泇口.
Another is to excavate Wànjiāzhuāng 萬家莊 to connect to the source of Jiākǒu 泇口.
Wànjiāzhuāng 萬家莊
is the area north of Jiākǒu 泇口.
Together with Táijiāzhuāng 臺家莊, Hóujiāwān 侯家灣, and Liángchéng 良城
and other places,
these are all high hills and mounds,
with many gravel stones,
making work extremely difficult.
Dōngxīng 東星 strenuously excavated and formed a river.
However, the river body is still shallow,
with only two or three *chǐ* (尺) of water.
It should be excavated four or five *chǐ* (尺) deeper,
so that the water from Hánzhuāng 韓莊 can connect downstream to Jiākǒu 泇口.
Then, transport vessels, regardless of size,
can easily reach their destination.
Another is to dredge the branch canal to avoid the dangers of Wēikǒu 微口.
Wēishānhú 微山湖 is west of Hánzhuāng 韓莊,
over thirty *lǐ* (里) long from upstream to downstream,
with water over one *zhàng* (丈) deep.
It is necessary to survey the depths
and shallows,
set up markers as guides,
and when the wind is favorable and sails are hoisted,
one can pass quickly.
However, if sudden strong winds are encountered,
damage and loss are unavoidable.
Currently, a branch canal of forty-five
*lǐ* (里) has been opened along the lake,
connecting upstream to Xīliǔzhuāng 西柳莊
and downstream to Hánzhuāng 韓莊,
providing a towing path.
It should be further dredged
to prevent the calamity of drifting and drowning.
The fourth point is that the Wànzhuāng 萬莊 area is high in elevation,
so the northward water flows southwards,
and its speed will increase there.
He requested that several sluice gates be built at that location
to store and release water as needed.
An imperial edict ordered a swift survey and implementation.
However, Dōngxīng 東星 fell ill and died.
Censor Gāo Jǔ 高舉 presented three strategies for river and grain transport,
again mentioning the Jiāhé 泇hé.
Yáng Yīkuí 楊一魁, Minister of Works, reported:
"The Jiāhé 泇hé passes through Liángchéng 良城, Pénghé 彭河, and Géxū Lǐng 葛墟嶺,
where the gravel is difficult to excavate.
Thus, the entrance is only one *zhàng* (丈) and six *chǐ* (尺) wide,
and its depth is similar.
It should be greatly dredged.
The Hánzhuāng Qú 韓莊渠 connects upstream to Wēishān 微山 and Lǚméng 呂孟.
It should be extensively dredged
to prevent silting and shallowness.
This will allow smooth flow into Mǎjiāqiáo 馬家橋 and Xiàzhèn 夏鎮,
serving as a supply route for grain transport."
Given the achievements already made on the Jiāhé 泇hé,
the emperor ordered river officials to further dredge it.
Thirty years later,
Yáo Jìkě (姚繼可), Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shàngshū), stated that the project on the Cái River (Cái Hé) should be stopped.
Thus, it was halted and not completed.
Not long after,
Lǐ Huàlóng (李化lóng), Vice Minister of River Conservancy (Zǒnghé Shìláng), again proposed opening the Cái River (Cái Hé),
connecting it to the Zhí River (Zhí Hé)
to avoid the dangers of the Yellow River.
Hóu Qìngyuǎn (侯慶遠), Investigating Censor of the Ministry of Works (Gōngkē Jǐshìzhōng), strongly supported this proposal,
but believed the estimated cost was too low
and the deadline too quick.
He requested a dedicated appointment and accountability for its completion.
In the first month of the thirty-second year,
the Ministry of Works (Gōngbù) responded to Huàlóng's (化lóng) memorial,
stating:
"Opening the Cái River (Cái Hé) has six benefits
and two undeniable advantages.
Once the Cái River (Cái Hé) is opened, transport will not rely on the Yellow River (Hé),
and the water levels of the Yellow River (Hé) can be ignored;
this is the first benefit.
Using the Cái River (Cái Hé), which is two hundred and sixty *lǐ* long,
to bypass three hundred and thirty *lǐ* of the Yellow River (Huáng Hé);
this is the second benefit.
If transport does not rely on the Yellow River (Hé),
then our governance can carefully observe the opportune conditions and manage it;
this is the third benefit.
The estimated cost is two hundred thousand *jīn* (gold),
to open a river two hundred and sixty *lǐ* long;
compared to Zhū Héng's (朱衡) new river project, this achieves twice the result with half the effort;
this is the fourth benefit.
Opening the river will necessarily involve recruitment;
when spring scarcity leads to work,
people disperse once wheat ripens,
the wealthy are undisturbed,
and the poor can sustain themselves;
this is the fifth benefit.
Grain boats crossing Hóng (洪)
must always wait until the end of spring,
fearing the Yellow River (Hé) rising.
With transport entering the Cái River (Cái Hé),
day and night pose no obstacle;
this is the sixth benefit.
It guards against dangers to the imperial tombs
and protects the people from disaster;
this is the first undeniable advantage.
Xúzhōu (徐州) has long suffered from floods;
once the Cái River (Cái Hé) is opened,
fewer people of Xú (徐) will become fish;
this is the second undeniable advantage."
The emperor deeply approved of this,
and ordered swift mobilization of labor for a long-term plan.
In the eighth month,
Huàlóng (化lóng) reported the completion of the Fēnshuǐ River (Fēnshuǐ Hé),
and two-thirds of grain boats were using the Cái River (Cái Hé).
Coincidentally, Huàlóng (化lóng) left due to mourning,
and Cáo Shípìn (曹時聘), Vice Minister of River Conservancy (Zǒnghé Shìláng), replaced him,
submitting a memorial praising Huàlóng's (化lóng) achievements.
However, at this time,
both guiding the Yellow River (Hé) and dredging the Cái River (Cái)
were undertaken concurrently,
and the work could not be completed.
Moreover, the Yellow River (Huáng Hé) repeatedly overflowed and damaged the Grand Canal (Cáoyún Qú).
Sòng Yīhán (宋一韓), Investigating Censor (Jǐshìzhōng), then criticized Huàlóng's (化lóng) error in opening the Cái River (Cái).
Huàlóng (化lóng) was indignant
and submitted a memorial to defend himself.
Shípìn (時聘) also vigorously argued that the Cái River (Cái) could be relied upon,
and thus outlined six measures for future improvement.
The Ministry (Bù) concurred with all his proposals.
It further stated:
"The Cái River (Cái) was opened during a time of obstructed transport,
so it is certainly not permissible to abandon the Yellow River (Huáng) because of the Cái River (Cái);
the canal benefited after the completion of the Cái River (Cái),
so it is also not permissible to abandon the Cái River (Cái) because of the Yellow River (Huáng).
With both benefits preserved,
it is hoped that they can be relied upon in times of urgency."
Therefore, he requested the construction of the Xīshān (郗山) embankment,
the leveling of Dùnzhuāngzuǐ (頓莊嘴),
the smoothing of the rapids at Dàfànkǒu (大泛口),
the dredging of shallow areas such as Māo'erwō (貓兒窩),
the construction of the Jùliáng Wúchōng (鉅梁吳衝) sluice gate,
and the expansion of the Sānshì Xútáng (三市徐塘) dam,
to complete the unfinished work on the Cái River (Cái Hé).
An imperial edict approved the proposal.
Several years later,
the Cái River (Cái) project remained unfinished,
and those overseeing transport again abandoned the Cái River (Cái) to use the Yellow River (Huáng).
Boats capsized,
and they were forced to move between the Yellow River (Huáng) and Cái River (Cái),
with transport deadlines far exceeded.
In the thirty-eighth year,
Sū Wéilín (蘇惟霖), Censor (Yùshǐ), memorialized on the advantages and disadvantages of the Yellow River (Huáng) and Cái River (Cái),
requesting exclusive focus on the Cái River (Cái).
He generally stated:
"The Yellow River (Huáng Hé) flows from Qīnghé (清河) through Táoyuán (桃源),
north to Zhíhékǒu (直河口),
a length of two hundred and forty *lǐ*.
This is downstream from the Cái River (Cái),
where the water is broad and level,
and transport boats only travel ten *lǐ* a day.
However, there is no other route,
so it must be used.
From Zhíhékǒu (直河口) upstream,
passing Pī (邳) and Xú (徐) to Zhènkǒu (鎮口),
a length of over two hundred and eighty *lǐ*;
this is called the Yellow River (Huáng Hé).
Another one hundred and twenty *lǐ*
then reaches Xiàzhèn (夏鎮).
To its east, from Māowō (貓窩) and Cáigōu (泇溝) to Xiàzhèn (夏鎮),
it is only over two hundred and sixty *lǐ*;
this is called the Cái River (Cái Hé).
East and west are opposite;
abandon one and choose the other.
The Yellow River (Huáng Hé) is as shallow as the Cái River (Cái) in March and April.
In early May,
its current is surging,
coming down from the sky,
making it impossible to move even a step.
Because its water carries sand,
the river mouth rises daily.
By early July,
it becomes ten times shallower and drier.
Overall,
there is no time when it can be traversed.
Drowning people and damaging boats,
its harm is extremely severe.
The Cái River (Cái Hé) can be traversed in a matter of days,
and rarely experiences storms.
If only we have officials who are sincere in their duties,
all deficiencies can be remedied in not more than three to five years,
providing benefits for hundreds of years."
Hé Shìjìn (何士晉), Investigating Censor of the Ministry of Works (Gōngkē Jǐshìzhōng), also stated:
"There is no more dangerous transport route than the Yellow River (Huáng Hé).
In earlier years, water from Zhaóyánghú (昭陽湖)
obstructed the transport route south of Xiàzhèn (夏鎮),
which is when the proposal to open the Cái River (Cái) was finally decided.
Avoiding the dangers of shallow, swift currents and two floods,
gathering various spring waters,
and opening and closing them as appropriate,
it allowed unobstructed passage for six years.
But now, suddenly, they want to abandon the Cái River (Cái) for the Yellow River (Huáng),
causing hurried damage to grain boats.
Sometimes they switch to the Dàfúqiáo (大浮橋),
but the river channel silts up,
and they return to the Cái River (Cái).
Consequently, transport arrives late,
and there is an anxious concern about being frozen in place;
the harm of using the Yellow River (Huáng) is thus somewhat evident.
However, the Cái River (Cái) project is unfinished,
with varying width, depth, and shallowness.
It should be widened and deepened
to be equivalent to the Huìtōng River (Huìtōng Hé).
Heavy transport and empty return journeys
will not obstruct each other,
and turns will not require avoidance.
The water will always be abundant,
and boats will not be delayed.
If tens of thousands of *jīn* are allocated annually from the water levy,
and supervised by honest and capable officials,
it can be completed in three years.
Then, following the northern bank of Luòmǎhú (駱馬湖),
extending east to Sùqiān (宿遷),
with extensive earthworks,
all dangers of the Yellow River (Huáng Hé) can be avoided,
and the matter of the Cái River (Cái Hé) will be concluded.
Some say that the spring sources are minute,
and if it's too wide and too deep,
there won't be enough water.
They do not realize that the source of the Cái River (Cái) extends far from Méng (蒙) and Yí (沂),
and nearby collects waters from Xútáng (徐塘), Xǔchí (許池), Wénwǔ (文武), and other spring rivers.
Its overall volume is roughly comparable to the Jìníng (濟寧) spring river.
Once the Lǚgōngtángkǒu (呂公堂口) is dammed,
all the waters of Shāndōng (山東) will be fully collected,
and with additional sluices, dams, and embankments,
what need be worried about insufficiency?
Others say that reaching Sùqiān (宿遷) directly is a circuitous and difficult task to complete.
This depends on employing the right people
and having effective methods for overall management."
The memorial was submitted,
but received no reply.
In the 31st year,
Gěishìzhōng Lǐ Yòngjìng stated:
“The new Jiāolái River is west of the old sea transport route.
Wáng Xiàn excavated the Mǎjiāháo,
diverting water from the Zhānglǔ, Bái, and Xiàn rivers to supplement it.
Now, boats from Huái can directly reach Máwān,
which is the southern mouth of the new river.
From Hǎicāng, they can directly reach Tiānjīn,
which is the northern mouth of the new river.
Over 300 *lǐ* long from north to south,
the tide water penetrates deep.
Within it are Jiǔxuéhú Lake and the Dàgū River,
all of which can be drawn upon to aid.
Only a little over 100 *lǐ* needs to be dredged,
so it should be opened urgently.”
Gěishìzhōng Hè Jìng and Yùshǐ Hé Tíngyù also requested this.
An imperial edict ordered Tíngyù to meet with the Shāndōng fǔ and àn officials to inspect it.
Later, due to the vast estimated cost,
the proposal was dropped.
In the 5th year of Lóngqìng,
Gěishìzhōng Lǐ Guìhé again requested its excavation and dredging.
An imperial edict dispatched Gěishìzhōng Hú Jiǎ to meet with the Shāndōng fǔ and àn officials to deliberate.
Jiǎ stated:
“The canal excavated by Xiàn,
where the shifting sand easily collapses,
and the fine currents of the Bái River drawn in are insufficient for irrigation.
Other rivers like Xiàn Hé, Xiǎojiāohé, Zhānglǔ Hé, Jiǔxué, and Dūpō are all shallow and narrow.
Though Jiāohé has a slight source,
its terrain slopes eastward,
preventing northward diversion.
None of these waters are sufficient.
The upper sources are dried springs,
with nothing to draw upon;
the lower reaches have shifting sand that easily breaks through,
and cannot last.
It would be a disturbance and expense without benefit.”
Xúnfǔ Liáng Mènglóng also stated:
“Xiàn mistakenly took a discarded canal from the Yuán dynasty as the old sea transport route,
unaware that the canal body is too long,
its springs dry up in spring and summer with no water to draw in,
and in autumn and winter, it floods without means to store or release.
The sand from the northern and southern seas easily blocks it,
making boat travel slow and impossible.”
So it was again reported as dropped.
In the 3rd year of Wànlì,
Nánjīng Gōngbù Shàngshū Liú Yìngjié and Shìláng Xú Shì again discussed sea transport,
stating:
“The difficulty of sea transport lies in the dangers of sailing on the open sea,
and the risk of capsizing and drowning.
Now, to eliminate these two problems,
from Jiāozhōu northward,
and Yángjiāquān southward,
dredge 100 *lǐ* of land.
There are no high mountains or long slopes to obstruct it,
and north of Yángjiāquān, it is all connected to the sea tides.
In summary,
the newly created sections are 50%,
the sections to be thoroughly dredged are 30%,
and those to be moderately dredged are 20%.
Probing with an auger,
there is no rock above or below,
so it can be opened without doubt.”
Thereupon, Shì was ordered to take charge of the matter.
Yìngjié’s proposal focused on connecting to the sea.
However, when Shì went to survey,
the land beside Jiāozhōu was high and steep,
preventing the tide from entering.
Only by drawing from spring sources could a river be formed,
but its route was over 250 *lǐ*,
requiring mountain excavation to draw water,
and embankment construction with sluice gates,
estimated to cost one million.
An imperial edict severely rebuked Shì,
saying he used difficult words to obstruct the accomplishment of the task.
At that time, Gěishìzhōng Guāng Mào memorialized to discuss it,
and further requested that Yìngjié be sent to investigate.
When Yìngjié arrived,
he stated that the water at both the northern and southern sea mouths was deep and wide,
and boats could ride the tide, detailing its conveniences in his report.
Shāndōng Xúnfǔ Lǐ Shìdá memorialized:
“North of the Nánhǎi Máwān,
Yìngjié said that sand accumulation was difficult to remove,
and proposed moving the old waterway 13 *lǐ* to avoid it.
He also worried that it connects south to Yālùgǎng,
and east to Lóngjiātún,
where sand accumulation is very high.
Once the canal mouth is opened,
sand will enter with the tide,
thus there was also a proposal to build gates to block the sand.
Your subject believes that if the gates are closed, how will the tide enter?
If the gates are open, how can the sand be blocked?
South of the Běihǎicāng mouth to the new river gate,
it is generally silted with shallow tides.
Yìngjié dredged two *lǐ* of the east bank,
only removing two *chǐ* of sand.
Once a large tide comes,
the sand will accumulate as before,
thus there was also a proposal to build embankments to restrict the water and block the sand.
Your subject believes that blocking the sand on both banks is feasible,
but if the tide rushes in the middle of the flow,
how can it be blocked?
The watershed is high and steep,
one section is only 20 *zhàng*,
but costs 1500 *jīn*.
Below there is much hard rock,
making water drawing very difficult.
Thus there was also a proposal to change the excavation to Wángjiāqiū.
Your subject believes that from Wújiākǒu to Tíngkǒu, the high and steep sections total 50 *lǐ*,
mostly containing hard rock.
What would be the cost?
And abandoning this, there is no other river to use.
Moreover, tidal patterns are regular;
the great tides, even if they reach slightly further,
only extend to Chéncūnzá and Yángjiāquān,
unable to advance further.
What's more, there are only two tides a day?
This reliability of tidal water is questionable.
The river course winds for 200 *lǐ*,
the three waters of Zhānglǔ, Bái, and Jiāo are tiny,
and the standing water of Dūpō
has already dried up.
Should a severe drought occur,
what springs can be drawn upon?
Drawing from springs is also unreliable.
The Yuán people excavated and dredged this river,
and historians said their labor and expenses were immeasurable,
but ultimately without success,
serving as a precedent.
Xún'àn Yùshǐ Shāng Wèizhèng also stated:
“Dredging below the watershed,
10 *zhàng* wide,
would require 1,000 laborers.
Just a few *chǐ* down is hard rock,
further down is all sand,
and further down is all black sand,
and further down, springs gush out.
Immediately after dredging, it silts up again,
only reaching a depth of 1 *zhàng* 2 *chǐ*.
If one absolutely wants to connect to the sea for boat travel,
another 1 *zhàng* depth must be dredged.
Even two million *liǎng* is
not enough to complete this.”
Gěishìzhōng Wáng Dàochéng also discussed its failures.
Gōngbù Shàngshū Guō Cháobīn again requested its suspension.
Consequently, Yìngjié and Shì were summoned back to the capital,
and the project was abandoned.
Thereafter, Zhōngshū Chéng Shǒuxùn,
Yùshǐ Gāo Jǔ and Yán Sīzhōng,
and Shàngshū Yáng Yīkuí successively discussed it,
but none were carried out.
In the 14th year of Chóngzhēn,
Shāndōng Xúnfǔ Zēng Yīng and Hùbù Zhǔshì Xíng Guóxǐ again reiterated the proposals of Wáng Xiàn and Liú Yìngjié.
100,000 *jīn* was allocated from the imperial treasury,
but before the work began,
Yīng left office.
In the summer of the 16th year,
Shàngshū Ní Yuánlù requested that grain tribute be diverted via the Jiāolái River for transport,
using small boats from the Jiāohékǒu to reach the watershed,
then using carts to cross the ridge for 40 *lǐ* to reach the Láihé,
and again using small boats to exit to the sea,
thus avoiding the danger of damage from reefs and islands.
Shāndōng Fùzǒngbīng Huáng Yìn'ēn’s proposal was similar.
None were carried out.
Collation Notes
Volume 64, Rivers and Canals 6, Water Conservancy in the Straight Provinces
The regulations for governing water and soil in the Three Dynasties were very detailed.
Since the abolition of the well-field system,
canals became blocked,
and water often could not be properly managed.
Thus, canals, ponds, wells, and reservoirs were dug
to provide irrigation.
In the early Míng dynasty,
Tàizǔ decreed that local officials,
when people submitted proposals for water conservancy,
should report them immediately.
Twenty-seven years later,
he specifically instructed the Ministry of Works (Gōngbù) that
ponds, reservoirs, lakes, and weirs that could store and release water for droughts and floods
should all be repaired according to their terrain.
Then, students from Guózǐjiàn and other talents were dispatched,
to go throughout the empire,
supervising water conservancy repairs.
The next winter,
commanderies and counties submitted reports.
A total of 40,987 ponds and weirs were opened,
which was greatly beneficial to the people.
Thereafter, when new construction occurred,
sometimes local labor was used,
sometimes resources from neighboring regions,
sometimes official materials were provided,
sometimes materials were collected from mountain areas,
sometimes labor was gathered during agricultural slack seasons,
sometimes tasks were organized as needed,
or sometimes a high minister was dispatched to oversee completion.
Throughout the Míng dynasty, water policies were repeatedly reformed,
and can be fully listed.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, the Tóngchéng Weir and Sluice in Hézhōu were repaired,
spanning over 200 *lǐ* in circumference.
In the fourth year, the Língqú Canal in Xīng'ān was repaired;
there were thirty-six steep sections of the canal.
The canal water originates from Hǎiyáng Shān,
and was dug during the Qín dynasty,
irrigating ten thousand *qǐng* of fields.
Mǎ Yuán repaired it,
but it later collapsed.
It was only then that it was restored.
In the sixth year, 20,000 laborers from Sōngjiāng and Jiāxīng were dispatched to open the Hújiāgǎng in Shànghǎi,
from the estuary to Cáojīng, over 1,200 *zhàng* in length,
to allow passage for sea vessels.
Additionally, Hǎiyán Gěnpǔ was dredged.
In the eighth year, the Pénglái Gé River in Dēngzhōu was opened.
Gěng Bǐngwén was ordered to dredge the Hóngqú Weir in Jīngyáng,
irrigating over 200 *lǐ* of fields in Jīngyáng, Sānyuán, Lǐquán, Gāolíng, and Líntóng.
In the ninth year, the Dūjiāngyàn Weir in Péngzhōu was repaired.
In the twelfth year,
Lǐ Wénzhōng said:
"Shǎnxī suffers from saline soil,
I request that a canal be dug within the city,
diverting water from the Lóngshǒu Canal to flow eastward."
His request was granted,
and it was lined with stone.
In the fourteenth year, the sea wall in Hǎiyán was constructed.
In the seventeenth year, the breached dike of the Zhānghé River in Cízhōu was repaired.
The Yuèshān Dam in Jīngzhōu was breached to irrigate common fields.
In the nineteenth year, the sea wall in Chánglè was constructed.
In the twenty-third year, breached dikes in Chóngmíng and Hǎimén, totaling over 23,900 *zhàng*, were repaired,
with 250,000 laborers employed.
The Pacification Commissioner of Yǒngníng in Sìchuān reported:
"Within our jurisdiction, there are 190 rapids,
and 82 major rapids at Jiāngmén,
all blocked by rocks."
An imperial edict ordered Jǐngchuān Hóu Cáo Zhèn to clear them.
In the twenty-fourth year, the Héngshānlǐng Sluice in Línhǎi was repaired,
along with the sea walls of Nínghǎi and Fènghuà, over 4,300 *zhàng* in length.
The sea wall in Shàngyú, 4,000 *zhàng* long, was constructed,
and stone sluices were rebuilt.
Dōngqián Hú in Dìnghǎi and Yín counties was dredged,
irrigating tens of thousands of *qǐng* of fields.
In the twenty-fifth year, the Yínshù Dōngbà River in Lìyáng was dug,
from Shízì Gǎng to Shāzǐhé Yānzhībà, over 4,300 *zhàng* long,
with over 359,000 laborers employed.
In the twenty-seventh year, the Zhījiāhé River in Shānyáng was dredged.
The people of Yùlín Zhōu said:
"The North and South Rivers of the prefecture are separated by over twenty *lǐ*,
we request them to be connected,
and stone sluices installed."
This was granted.
In the twenty-ninth year, the Luòdī embankment in Hénán was repaired.
The Língqú Canal in Xīng'ān was restored again.
At that time, the Minister Táng Duó arrived at the location due to military operations,
and reported on the canal's condition with a diagram.
He requested that it be deepened and widened,
to allow official boats to transport provisions for the army.
The Imperial Censor Yán Zhènzhí was ordered to blast and excavate the rocks in the steep ravines,
and the supply route was indeed opened.
In the thirty-first year,
the Hóngqú Weir collapsed,
and Gěng Bǐngwén was again ordered to repair it.
Additionally, over 103,000 *zhàng* of the canal were dredged.
In the fourth year of Jiànwén, the Wúsōng Jiāng River was dredged.
In the first year of Yǒnglè, the collapsed banks of the Hànshuǐ River in Ānlù and Jīngshān were repaired,
as well as the eastern embankment of the Tuòhé River in Zhāngqiū,
the breached banks in Gāomì and Wéi,
the river embankment in Ānyáng,
the breached protective city embankment in Fúshān,
the Zhēshān Jiāngtáng embankment in Zhèjiāng,
the Lóngkūtáng'àn embankment in Yúgàn,
the breach in the Chǔhé River in Línyǐng,
the Báilànghé River embankment in Wéixiàn,
the reservoirs and weirs in Qiánshān and Huáiníng,
the Qīngqí and Luópó Wéi embankments in Gāoyào,
the Xú Zào and Shí Lì ports in Tōngzhōu,
the Guǎngjì Canal in Píngyáo,
the Yángjiā Gǎng and Wáng Hànbà embankments in Jùróng,
the Yáotóugāng breached banks in Zhàoqìng and Fèngxiáng,
the Gāojiā and Túnnóu weirs in Nányáng, and the embankments of the Shā and Lǐ Rivers,
and the ancient river breach in Xiàxiàn spanning over 30 *lǐ*.
The Bǎodà and other embankments in Hézhōu, over 120 *lǐ* in length, were repaired and constructed,
with nine water-storage sluice gates.
Five river canals in Chāngyì were dredged,
Xiǎohénglì in Jiādìng was dug to connect the Qín and Zhào canals,
and the Húlú and other rivers in Kūnshān were dredged.
Xià Yuánjí was ordered to manage the water problems in Sūzhōu, Sōngjiāng, and Jiāxīng,
and to dredge the Yùnyán Hé River in Huátíng and Shànghǎi,
the sluice at Jīnshān Wèi, and the water-splitting port at Cáojīng.
Yuánjí stated:
"Among the prefectures west of Zhèjiāng,
Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng are in the lowest reaches,
while Jiāxīng, Húzhōu, and Chángzhōu are quite high,
surrounded by Tàihú Lake,
stretching over 500 *lǐ*.
It receives water from the streams and gullies of Hángzhōu, Húzhōu, Xuānchéng, and Shèxiàn,
which then disperses into the lakes such as Diànshān,
and flows into the Sānmǎo.
Recently, the ports have been silted up,
causing floods that harm crops.
The method of remedy
lies in dredging the Wúsōng ports.
The Wúsōng Jiāng River spans over 200 *lǐ*,
and is over 150 *zhàng* wide,
connecting to Tàihú Lake in the west,
and the sea in the east,
and was often dredged by previous dynasties.
However, due to the impact of tides,
it silts up soon after being dredged.
From Chángqiáo in Wújiāng to Xiàjiè Pǔ,
over 120 *lǐ*,
though the water flows,
it is actually narrow and shallow in many places.
From Pǔ to the entrance of Náncāng Pǔ in Shànghǎi,
over 130 *lǐ*,
tidal silting has
already turned it into flat land,
with accumulated sand and moving mud,
making construction difficult.
Liújiā Gǎng in Jiādìng is the ancient Lóujiāng River,
which flows directly into the sea.
Báimáo Gǎng in Chángshú flows directly into the [Yangtze] River.
Both are wide rivers with rapid currents.
It is advisable to dredge the north and south banks of Wúsōng, and ports like Āntíng,
to divert the waters from Tàihú Lake into the Liújiā and Báimáo ports,
to split their force.
Dàhuáng Pǔ in Sōngjiāng is a vital channel connecting to Wúsōng,
but its lower reaches are now blocked and difficult to dredge.
Next to it is Fànjiā Bāng,
which reaches the sea directly at the entrance of Náncāng Pǔ.
It should be dredged deep and wide.
Connecting to Dàhuáng Pǔ upstream,
it will carry the water from Mǎohú Lake,
and perhaps restore the old configuration of 'three rivers entering the sea'
from the *Yǔgòng*.
Once the waterways are clear,
we should survey the terrain
and install stone sluices in appropriate places,
to be opened and closed according to the seasons.
Every year when the water is low,
the圩 *wéi* embankments should be repaired in advance,
to prevent violent currents,
then the water problems can cease."
The Emperor ordered the dispatch of commoners to excavate and dredge.
Yuánjí walked day and night,
leading by example,
and the work was successfully completed.
In the second year, the river embankment in Táizhōu, 18,000 *zhàng* long, was repaired,
as well as the north and south dikes in Xīnghuà, the riverside *wéi* embankments in Táixīng, and the military colonies like Guābù in Liùhé.
The old Táicháo Jiāng River in Dāntú was dredged,
and the Jiāhú Táng'àn embankment in Xiàngshān was repaired,
as well as the Nàyǐn Pō and Diáolí port embankments in Hǎikāng and Xúwén counties,
fifteen sluices like Hùnshuǐ and six steep gates in Huángyán,
the river embankment in Mèngjīn,
the lake embankment in Fēnyí,
the Mátián Dī'àn embankment in Wǔzhí,
the Zhújìng Shuǐpō reservoir in Xiāngshān,
and the Fēnshuǐtáng reservoir in Xīng'ān was restored.
Xīng'ān has a river,
originating from Hǎiyáng Shān.
A stone weir was built across the river,
dividing it into north and south canals,
irrigating a wide area of common fields.
Stones were stacked on the weir like scales,
to prevent overflow.
Yán Zhènzhí removed stones and heightened the weir,
and the water had no outlet,
eroding the pond embankments,
all rushing into the north canal,
leaving the south canal shallow and sluggish,
causing the people to suffer losses.
By then, it was restored to its former state.
The people of Hǎimén requested that laborers from Huái'ān, Sūzhōu, and Chángzhōu assist in repairing the breached dikes of Zhāngdūn Gǎng and Dōngmíng Gǎng, over 100 *lǐ* long.
The Emperor said:
"The people of the three prefectures are currently suffering from water problems,
they should not be further burdened."
An official was dispatched to inspect,
and the people of Yángzhōu were ordered to assist in the construction.
The people of Dāngtú said:
"Cíhú Lake borders the [Yangtze] River,
connecting upstream to Xuānchéng and Shèxiàn,
east to Dānyáng Hú Lake,
and west to Wúhú.
Prolonged rains cause flooding,
and rising tides harm farmers,
it is advisable to send officials to survey and repair."
The Emperor granted their request,
and further instructed the Ministry of Works that
in Ānhuī, Ānhuī, Sūzhōu, Sōngjiāng, Zhèjiāng, Jiāngxī, and Húguǎng, wherever lakes and ponds were low-lying,
and *wéi* embankments dilapidated,
the local authorities should be urgently ordered to repair them.
Xià Yuánjí was again ordered to manage water in Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng,
clearing all old river ports.
He also dredged Qiāndūn Pǔ, Zhìhé Táng, Āntíng, Gù Pǔ, Lùjiǎo Pǔ, Yóujīng, and Huángjīng in Sūzhōu, totaling over 29,000 *zhàng*,
and Dàhuáng Pǔ, Chìyàn Pǔ, and Fànjiā Bāng in Sōngjiāng, totaling 12,000 *zhàng*,
to open up the lower reaches of Tàihú Lake.
Previously,
repairs were made to the Chóngyìyàn Weir in Hánshān.
Not long after,
the people of Hézhōu said:
"The Tóngchéngzhá sluice gate, which reaches Cháohú Lake upstream
and connects to the Yángzǐjiāng River downstream,
has caused over seventy breaches in the dikes,
we request repairs."
Its clerk Zhāng Liángxìng further stated:
"The water has flooded over fifty thousand qǐng of farmland in Má and Lǐng Lakes.
It is advisable to build dikes and embankments,
starting from Táohuāqiáo Bridge
and extending thirty lǐ to the border of Hánshān."
All requests were granted.
In the third year, the Cáozhéjiāng River embankment in Shàngyú was repaired,
along with over four thousand zhàng of dikes and weirs in Tuówùcūn Village, Wēnxiàn County,
the embankments of Liántáng in Nánhǎiwèi, Sìhuìxiàn County's Bòquèshuǐ, etc.,
and the riverbanks in Zhōuxìng and other townships in Wúwéizhōu, as well as the Wújiāngtún riverbanks in Yīngyángwèi.
Dikes were built for the breaches of Xiǎoqīnghé River in Chānglí and Lìchéng,
and for the northern bank of Xīnhékǒu in Yìngtiān,
extending three thousand three hundred zhàng from Dàshèngguān Pass to Jiāngdōngyì Post.
The old river in the north of Hǎizhōu was dredged,
connecting upstream to Gāoqiáo
and downstream to Línhóngchǎng and the Yùnyán hé River in Shānyáng for eighteen lǐ.
In the fourth year, repairs were made to the nineteen weirs in Xuānchéng,
the Mùhúwéi embankment in Fēngchéng,
the Wànshídī Dike along the river in Shíshǒu,
and the breached weir in Lìshuǐ.
Repairs were made to Dòutánhé River and Péngtānwéi embankment in Huáiníng,
Gù'ān in Shùntiān,
Jīngdài in Bǎodìng,
Lǔjiātào, Shèhékǒu in Lètíng, Liújiātáng, Yúnpō in Jíshuǐ,
and Liújiāwéigǎng port in Jiāngdū.
Riverbanks such as Wǔjiāxué in Guǎngjì, Húguǎng were built.
The Shítóugāngwéi embankment in Xīnjiàn and the river dike along the Jiāngpǔ were constructed.
The Yùnyánhé River in Tàizhōu, Qíntónghé River in Pǔdìng, and the three river mouths of Yíqiān in Xīxīnán were opened,
diverting water to the sea at the borders of Xīnghuà and Yánchéng.
The Fúshāntáng in Chángshú, thirty-six lǐ long, was dredged.
In the fifth year, repairs were made to the embankments in Chángzhōu, Wújiāng, Kūnshān, Huátíng, Qiántáng, Rénhé, and Jiāxīng,
the Nánhúbà Dam in Yúyáo,
and the breached dikes in Gāoyào Yíngāng, Jīnshān, etc.,
irrigating over five hundred qǐng of farmland.
The collapsed riverbanks in Hángzhōu were restored.
In the sixth year, the river in Píngyángxiàn County, Zhèjiāng was dredged.
In the seventh year, the breached bank of Xuànmǎtān in Ānlùzhōu and the stone dike in Hǎiyán were repaired,
and the Lánjiāngdī Dike in Tàixīng, over three thousand nine hundred zhàng long, was built.
Additionally, the northern淤hé River of Dàgǎng was dredged,
reaching south of the county,
and exiting into the Dàjiāng River,
over four thousand five hundred zhàng long.
In the eighth year, the Liànhútáng Dam in Dānyáng was repaired,
along with the Rǔhé River embankment in Rǔyáng,
the Yětángwéi and Bàngdàngbà dams in Nánlíng,
the Zhāngjiākēng and Héjiāzhōu embankments in Sōngzī,
one hundred and twelve breaches in Wéishuǐ and Fúkānghé River in Píngdùzhōu,
eight thousand zhàng of dikes and weirs,
and the Shítángguānlùqiáoliáng bridges in Wújiāng.
In the ninth year, repairs were made to Dīngpō and other dams and weirs in Ānfú,
Ráojiāpō in Ānrén, Shòuguāngdī Dike,
Jīngshān Jǐnglǐngwéi embankment in Ānlù,
Guāntáng in Chánglè,
the Shítǔtángqiáolù road from Chángzhōu to Jiāxīng, over seventy lǐ long,
one hundred and thirty-one spillways,
the Chēshuǐdī Dike in Jiānlì, over four thousand four hundred zhàng long,
the Huápōtúnpōdī Dike in Gāo'ān,
and over ten thousand zhàng of earth and stone embankments in Rénhé, Hǎiníng, and Hǎiyán.
The breached bank at Shùhékǒu in Yízhōu was built,
and the Shùhé River in Shùyáng was also dredged.
Breached dikes at Zhāngcūn and other mouths in Xīnchéng, Zhílì were built,
the Huángháotáng embankment in Rénhé, over three hundred zhàng long,
and Sūnjiāwéitáng embankment, over twenty lǐ long.
The Gāndānhé River in Wéixiàn and the old canal of Dìngxiāng, sixty-three lǐ long, were dredged,
and Hūtuó River water was drawn to irrigate over six hundred qǐng of farmland.
The Fúshānguānqú Canal was cleared,
the Qīngyánghédào waterway in Jiāngyīn was dredged,
and Báiláogōu River in Zōupíng, over thirty lǐ long.
The people of Líshuǐ said:
"There is the Tōngjìqú Canal in the county,
which diverts water from Sōngyáng, Suìchāng, and other streams into it.
With three sources, upper, middle, and lower,
it flows into forty-eight branches,
irrigating over two thousand qǐng of farmland.
The people at the upper source divert water for their own benefit,
causing the flow to cease at the lower source,
where sand clogs the canal.
We request the repair of the dikes and weirs to their former state."
The ministry discussed and approved it.
Zhāng Shēng, the magistrate of Qídōng, said:
"The floodwaters of Xiǎoqīnghé River have caused breaches,
submerging various salt fields and farmland in Qīngzhōu.
We request dredging the upper reaches
and repairing the long dike,
to make the water follow its old course."
The Crown Prince dispatched officials to manage it.
The people of Fūzhōu said:
"The Luòshuǐ River has breached westward,
collapsing the northeast corner of the prefectural city.
We request dredging the old course
and making it flow south along the eastern foothills of the prefecture."
This was granted.
In the tenth year, repairs were made to the tide-defending embankment in Píngyáng, Zhèjiāng,
over one hundred and twenty lǐ of breached riverbanks in Huángméi,
and the tide-defending dike in Hǎimén, one hundred and thirty lǐ long.
Over two thousand zhàng of embankment in Xīnhuì were built,
along with the Gōngjiǎn and other embankments in Xiànxiàn and Ráoyáng,
the breached bank of Hónghé River in Ānqíu,
eighty-nine breaches in Zhítíng and other rivers in Ānzhōu,
and forty-six breaches in Huáróng, Ānjīn, and other dikes.
The Pánlóngjiāng River in Shànghǎi and Báilànghé River in Wéixiàn were dredged.
Yáng Dǐ, the Acting Vice Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud in Běijīng, said:
"The military farms in Wúqiáo, Dōngguāng, Xīngjì, Jiāohé, and Tiānjīn suffered crop damage due to breached dikes from rainwater.
Twenty-five lǐ southeast of Liángdiànyì Post in Dézhōu, there is an old course of the Huánghé River,
which connects to the Tǔhé River south of the prefecture.
By digging a canal and setting up sluice gates,
the force of the water can be divided and mitigated,
greatly benefiting the people."
Servant-at-large Lìn Fāng was ordered to manage it.
In the eleventh year, repairs were made to Táoxīn and Zhènghé two weirs in Wúhú,
fifty-four breached riverbanks at the river mouths in Bǎodìng and Wén'ān two counties,
the Xīnhéwéi embankment in Yìngtiān,
Fúshèng and Qījiāzhuāng two dams in Tiāncháng,
and the Dàbīnhédī dike in Xíngzé.
The Tàipínghé River in Kūnshān was dredged.
In the twelfth year, sixteen sluice gates of the Ānfēngtáng Dam in Fèngyáng and the Niújiǎobà Dam, Xīncāngpù collapsed banks were repaired,
along with the Guōcūn and Mǎqǔ embankments in Wǔzhì,
the Lóngwānhé River in Liáochéng,
Hóngchuánkǒu in Púzhōu,
and the Cáocūnhédī embankment in Fànxiàn.
Breached dikes in Sānhé were built.
The Guānhé River in Hǎizhōu, two hundred and forty lǐ long, was dredged.
The people of Xièzhōu said:
"The Sùshuǐhé River in Línjìn flows against the current,
breaching the Yáoxiānqú weir,
entering sandy land,
flooding private fields,
and is about to reach the salt ponds."
Soon after, they further said:
"The nítáng pond water overflowed,
breaching the opening,
and entering the salt ponds."
Since the Sùshuǐqú and Yáoxiānqú canals flowed together,
officials were ordered to build according to their request.
In the thirteenth year, repairs were made to the breached bank in Xīngjì and the Diāojiāwéitúntiándī dike of Yǔlínyòuwèi in Nánjīng.
Lǐ Shēng, the county assistant of Wújiāngxiàn County, said:
"Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng suffer from severe water damage,
especially around Tàihú Lake,
it is urgent to release its downstream flow.
For example, the various ports of Báimáo in Chángshú,
Qiāndūn and other rivers in Kūnshān,
the十八都 ports and branches in Chángzhōu,
and the nearby lake waterways in Wúxiàn and Wúxī,
all should follow their old courses,
dredged and deepened.
The Càijīng and other sluice gates should also be repaired,
to open and close in time
with the coming and going of tides.
Then floods can be avoided,
and the people will benefit from cultivation."
This was granted.
In the fifteenth year, repairs were made to Sūnjiākǒu in Gù'ān and Gùzhǒng embankment in Línzhāng.
In the sixteenth year, repairs were made to the breached bank in Wèixiàn.
In the seventeenth year,
the people of Xiāoshān said:
"Within the county, there are forty-five lǐ of rivers and canals,
irrigating ten thousand qǐng of farmland,
but in recent years, they have been silted up.
We request dredging,
and also placing a sluice gate east of the Qiánqīngxiǎojiāngbà Dam,
so that there will be no worries about drought or flood."
The people of Xīnchéng, Shāndōng, said:
"The Zhènghuánggōu ditch east of the county originates from Zīchuān,
its downstream is obstructed and blocked,
and continuous rain impedes farming.
South of Chénjiāzhuāng, there is a dry river,
which connects to the ditch upstream
and to Wújiāng River downstream.
We request dredging and repair."
Both requests were granted.
In the eighteenth year,
the people of Hǎiníng and other counties said:
"The tide has submerged over two thousand six hundred zhàng of sea embankment,
extending to Wújiā and other dams."
Tōngzhèng Yuè Fú also said:
"Rénhé and Hǎiníng have damaged the Chángjiàng and other dams,
submerged by the sea for over one thousand five hundred zhàng.
The east bank's Zhěshān, Yánménshān, Shǔshān previously had sea routes,
but they have been silted up for a long time,
hence the tide is fiercer on the west bank.
We request military and civilians to carry out construction."
Both requests were granted.
The following year, the embankments in Hǎiníng and other counties were repaired.

In the 21st year, repairs were made to the Jiādìng embankments, and in Sōngjiāng, five thousand-plus zhàng of dikes damaged by the tide were repaired, and a breach of over a hundred zhàng in the dikes of the Shùnhuà Guard in Jiāozhǐ was also repaired.
The people of Wénshuǐ said:
"The Chángrěn Canal in Wéngǔ Mountain draws water from the Wéngǔ River.
It extends over thirty lǐ,
irrigating fields.
Now the river has burst its banks and the water is escaping."
Their petition was granted,
and it was repaired.
In the 22nd year, the Guǎngjì River gate in Línhǎi was repaired.
In Hóngxī元年, the coastal gate and dam in Huángyán were repaired.
Compared to early Yǒnglè,
an additional Assistant Prefect (Fǔpàn) was appointed,
specifically for this task.
The Gōngjiǎn Dike and the Yáodīkǒu in Xiànxiàn and Ráoyáng were repaired.
In Xuāndé二年, Huá Sōng, the Magistrate (Zhīxiàn) of Guī'ān in Zhèjiāng, stated:
"The Hóngqú Weir in Jīngyáng irrigates eight thousand four hundred-plus qǐng of fields in five counties.
During the Hóngwǔ era,
Gěng Bǐngwén, the Marquis of Chángxīng, repaired and dredged it multiple times,
but the weir was damaged not long after.
