During the Yǒnglè period,
the elder Xú Líng petitioned the court,
and an official was dispatched to build it,
but construction did not proceed.
I beg for a special mandate for a high minister to mobilize soldiers and laborers to cooperate in its repair."
This was granted.
In the 3rd year, forty-four weirs, including Dūjiāng, in Guànxiàn were repaired.
The people of Línhǎi said:
"The Húchán gates store water for irrigating fields,
but in recent years, the gates have been damaged,
causing the Jīnáo, Dàpǔ, Húlāi, and Jǔyǔ rivers, among others, to become blocked.
We beg for them to be opened and built."
The Emperor said:
"Water conservancy is an urgent matter.
For the people to have to appeal directly to the court,
this means the local officials are not capable."
He ordered the Ministry of Works to immediately instruct the prefectures and counties to begin work after the autumn harvest.
He also issued an edict to the whole empire:
"Wherever water conservancy projects are needed,
the local authorities shall proceed immediately,
without delay."
The Circuit Censor (Xún'àn Yùshǐ) for Jiāngxī, Xǔ Shèng, said:
"The banks of the Ruì River in Nánchāng are low-lying
and contain many fertile fields.
During the Hóngwǔ era, they were repaired and built,
and water was not a problem.
In recent years, the water has overflowed,
damaging the banks in over twenty places.
The Ānshā Shéngwān Weir in Fēngchéng, measuring over three thousand six hundred zhàng,
was swept away by water during the Yǒnglè period,
and a section of over one hundred thirty zhàng was rebuilt.
Recently, due to prolonged rain,
the river rose and the dike was damaged.
I beg that local authorities be ordered to recruit laborers for repairs."
Lù Bólún, a Secretariat Drafter (Zhōngshū Shèrén), said:
"The Qīpǔ Canal in Chángshú is a hundred lǐ long from east to west,
irrigating fields in Chángshú and Kūnshān,
yielding an annual rent of over two hundred thousand dàn of grain.
I beg to allow the people to dredge it themselves."
Both petitions were approved by imperial edict.
In the 4th year, the Liǔlínkǒu dike in Xiànxiàn was repaired.
The people of Qiánjiāng said:
"The Bànghú and Yánghú lakes both border the Xiāng River.
When the water rises, the banks burst,
causing immeasurable harm to the military and civilian屯田 (túntián) in the three guards of Jīngzhōu, Jīngmén, and various prefectures and counties in Jiānglíng.
We beg to dispatch soldiers and civilians for construction and repair."
This was granted.
The people of Fúqīng said:
"The official and civilian fields in Guāngxiánlǐ, numbering over a hundred qǐng,
are protected from seawater by dikes.
The dikes have been damaged for a long time,
and the fields are entirely desolate.
In the middle of Yǒnglè,
an order was given to repair them,
but it has not been carried out to this day,
preventing the people from farming."
The Emperor reprimanded the local authorities and ordered them to repair it promptly,
and instructed Minister Wú Zhōng to strictly order the prefectures and counties
to repair ponds, dikes, and weirs in a timely manner,
punishing those who were slow.
In the 5th year,
Chéng Jūn, the Touring Vice Minister (Xúnfǔ Shìláng), said:
"Hǎiyán is two lǐ from the sea.
Its stone-embedded earth embankment, over two thousand four hundred zhàng long,
has been eroded by water,
and all its stones are worn out.
It is proposed to build new stones inside the embankment,
keeping the old ones as an outer barrier.
I beg that, as in the Hóngwǔ era, the three prefectures of Jiāxīng, Yánzhou, and Shàoxīng be ordered to cooperate with laborers to undertake the project."
This was granted.
In the 6th year, dikes and weirs in Liúyáng and Guǎngjì counties were repaired,
as were the stone dike along the river northwest of Fēngchéng and the Qīwēi Dam southwest of it,
and the three dikes along the river in Shíshǒu.
The old river pond in Yúyáo was dredged.
Zhōu Chén, the Touring Vice Minister, said:
"The Yǒngfēng Weir in Lìshuǐ has a circumference of over eighty lǐ,
surrounded by lakes such as Dānyáng and Shíjiù.
Formerly, dikes and dams were built,
connecting to the Zhìmén Stone Pagoda,
which greatly benefited farmers.
Now they are dilapidated,
and I request their repair."
Jiàoyù (Instructor) Táng Mǐn said:
"The Gěngjīng Canal in Chángshú
connects to Méilǐ in the south,
communicates with Kūnchéng Lake,
and reaches the great river in the north.
During the Hóngwǔ era,
it was dredged to irrigate fields.
Now it is blocked,
and I request it be cleared."
Both were granted.
In the 7th year, the Xīnjīn Tōngjì Weir in Méizhōu was repaired.
The weir water flows from Péngshān,
dividing into sixteen channels,
irrigating over twenty-five thousand mù of fields.
The Salt Commissioner (Yányùnshǐ) of Hédōng said:
"The Yáoxiān River, near the salt lakes,
flows into Wǔxīng Lake and then into the Huángliú River.
Its banks are low-lying.
In recent years, due to heavy rains, the water overflowed,
surging to Xièzhōu.
The waves became more violent,
eventually breaching the south bank,
submerging over thirty lǐ of civilian fields,
and destroying all the salt lake protection dikes.
Furthermore, due to the high level of the downstream Sùshuǐ River,
silt accumulated and reversed the flow,
causing the Yáoxiān to burst.
I beg to mobilize civilian laborers for dredging."
This was granted.
Kuàng Zhōng, the Prefect (Zhīfǔ) of Sūzhōu, said:
"In Sūzhōu, Sōngjiāng, Jiāxīng, and Húzhōu, there are six lakes:
namely Tàihú, Pángshān, Yángchéng, Shāhú, Kūnchéng, and Shànghú.
In early Yǒnglè,
Xià Yuánjí dredged and channeled them,
but now they are silted up again.
I beg to dispatch a high minister to dredge them."
Thereupon, Zhōu Chén and Kuàng Zhōng were ordered to manage it.
That year,
the Fén River suddenly overflowed,
damaging the Tàiyuán dike.
The Garrison Commander (Zhènshǒu Dūsī) Lǐ Qiān and Circuit Censor (Xún'àn Yùshǐ) Xú Jié repaired it expediently,
and then submitted a swift report.
The Emperor commended them.
In the 8th year, the Gāopí Shídòng in Piānqiáo Guard, Húguǎng, was repaired,
as was the old river south of Wánxiàn's South Gate.
The Tóngchéng Weir Gate in Hézhōu was restored.
The Guǎnghuì Canal and others in Ānyáng were repaired,
as were the Fúyáng River and the Wǔzhuǎ Jìmín Canal in Cízhōu.
In the 9th year, the dikes along the river in Zhījiāng, Jiānglíng, were repaired.
Breached banks in Jìzhōu were built up.
Privately built dikes and weirs by the people of Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng were demolished.
In the 10th year, over one thousand five hundred zhàng of sea embankments in Hǎiyán, breached by tides, were built.
Shěn Zhōng, a Department Secretary (Zhǔshì), said:
"The Xǐaojiāng River in Shānyīn
connects upstream to Jīnhuá and Yánzhou,
and downstream to the three river mouths and the sea,
drawing water from Zhùjì, Pújiāng, and Yìwū lakes to allow navigation.
The river mouth is now silted up,
so it is advisable to build the Línpǔ Qī Weir to block the lake waters,
allowing them to continue flowing out through the Xiǎojiāng River."
The Ministry was ordered to review and decide.
In Zhèngtǒng元年, the dikes along the river in Jí'ān were repaired.
Breached dikes in Hǎiyáng, Dēngyún, Dūyún, Bùcūn, and other places were built up.
The Bàqiáo River in Xī'ān, Shǎnxī, was dredged.
In the 2nd year, breaches in Wángjiā and other places in Lǐxiàn were built up.
The dilapidated banks from Luántáishān to Wǎtángpǔ in Xīnhuì were repaired,
as were the breached dikes near the rivers in Jiānglíng, Sōngzī, Gōng'ān, Shíshǒu, Qiánjiāng, and Jiānlì.
Also, the Lǎolóng Dike in Húguǎng was repaired,
as it had been breached by the Hànshǔi River.
In the 3rd year, the three canals in Shùndé Township, Tàixīng, were cleared,
drawing lake water to irrigate fields;
and twenty-eight irrigation channels, including Yǒnglù, in Lùzhōu,
were connected to the Zhāng River.
In the 4th year, the Dùcūnkǒu dike in Róngchéng was repaired.
A diversion channel was set up outside Zhèngyángmén,
and internal city channels were also dredged.
The people of Jīngzhōu said:
"The river water west of the city is over ten zhàng higher than the city.
When prolonged rains damage the dike,
the water immediately floods the city.
We request repairs be made proactively."
Jīn Lián, the Grand Censor (Dū Yùshǐ) and Touring Censor (Xúnfǔ) of Níngxià, said:
"There are five canals in the garrison,
used for irrigation,
but now the Qīxīng, Hànbó, and Shīhuī canals in Míngshāzhōu have been blocked for a long time.
I request four ten thousand laborers be used to dredge them,
to irrigate over one thousand three hundred qǐng of uncultivated land."
Both were granted.
In the fifth year, dikes were repaired along Tàihú,
Hǎiyán coastline,
the upper, middle, and lower Xīnhé rivers in Nánjīng, and the waterproof dike at the Xīnjiāngkǒu of Jìchuān Wèi,
and various dikes in Huòxiàn and Nángōng.
Dikes were built in Shùntiān, Héjiān, and at Dùcūnkǒu and Lángjiākǒu in Róngchéng where breaches had occurred.
Breaches in the oyster rock dikes of Hǎiníng were sealed.
The canal connecting Wǔyòu and Xīnxīng Salt Fields in Yánchéng was dredged.
Initially,
in Lìshuǐ there was a town called Guǎngtōng.
To its west, Gùchéng Hú flowed into the Dàjiāng,
while to its east, Sāntǎ Yàn Hé flowed into Tàihú.
The distance between them was fifteen *lǐ*.
During the Hóngwǔ reign, a channel was dug to connect them for boats.
The county land was somewhat low-lying,
and the lake received waters from Níngguó and Guǎngdé,
so it would overflow during floods.
A dam was built at the town to resist this,
but the water from the weir could not reach below the dam.
That year,
the dam was rebuilt at Yèjiāqiáo.
Yānzhī Hé [River] was
a waterway leading into Qínhuái.
Boats from Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng all passed through it,
but it was obstructed by sand and stones.
Thus, it was dredged along with other waterways.
The Jīnghé dam in Shānyáng,
which connected to the Cáohé upstream
and reached Yánchéng downstream,
originally had a sluice gate for boats.
Over time, it had fallen into disrepair,
and there was also a fear of illicit water leakage.
So, the river mouth was blocked.
That year,
following the people's request,
the dam was repaired and the sluice gate reinstated.
In the sixth year, a bridge was built on the south bank of the river east of Xuānwǔmén.
The Yùhé Bridge and its dike in Jiāngmǐ Xiàng were repaired,
and the southwest river of the capital city was dredged.
Dikes were built along the various rivers of Fēngchéng Shāyuè, and a new embankment was constructed at Táoxīnxū in Wúhú.
The Guānhé river in Hǎiníng, along with Huātáng Hé and Jiáshíqiáo Tánghé, were dredged,
and two Wǎshí Yàn weirs were built.
Jiāngzhōu in Nánjīng was cleared,
reducing its water force,
to facilitate the repair and construction of collapsed banks.
Hán Jiǎn, the Zhīzhōu of Gāoyóu, stated:
"The two upper and lower sluices of the Guānhé river are both ruined,
and the river is also impassable.
Moreover, the Zǐyīng Gōu is blocked,
and the drainage culvert is closed,
leading to no relief for droughts or floods.
I request that they all be dredged and repaired."
An imperial edict ordered the Ministry to verify the facts and proceed.
In the seventh year, the Jiāngxī Guǎngchāng river bank, the Chángshānpǔ sea wall in Xiāoshān, and the Tōngjì Yàn in Péngshān were repaired.
Dikes were built at Pǔzikǒu and Dàshèngguān in Nánjīng,
and along the collapsed riverbanks of Jiǔjiāng and Wǔchāng.
Over thirty *lǐ* of silt in Jiānglíng, Jīngmén, and Qiánjiāng were dredged.
In the eighth year, the Xièqiáopǔkǒu dike in Lánxī and three Guānbēi weirs in Yìyáng were repaired.
The city moat of Nánjīng was dredged.
In the ninth year, the dikes and banks at Gěngjiāwān in Dézhōu and the Lí Gōu dike in Shíxiàn were repaired.
A breach in the Dùcūn dike in Róngchéng was built up.
The earthen dam at Línghú in Shàngyú was replaced with a stone sluice gate.
The Lǐgǔ, Sūtáng, Huágǎng, Shàngcūn, and Lǐzǒumǎtáng rivers in Wúxī were deepened,
connecting to Suzhōu Yuánshānhútáng in the southeast,
to the Yángzǐjiāng in the north,
and to the Xīnxīng Hé in the west,
to draw water for irrigating fields.
The old river at Niúmùgāng in Shíxiàn,
and the Tàipíng and Yǒngxīng rivers in Wǔjìn were dredged.
The Yǒng'ān Hé in Hǎiyán,
and the Xīnjīng and Táojīngtáng rivers in Cháoshìyuàn were cleared.
The Metropolitan Censor Chén Yì stated:
"Cháoyì is sandy,
making cultivation difficult.
The county seat's Luòhé river
connects with the Wèishuǐ river.
I request that a canal be dug to irrigate it."
The people of Xīn'ān stated:
"The Chánggōu Hé south of the city,
which connects to the Xú and Cáo rivers in the west,
and to the Zhígū in Xióngxiàn in the east,
is blocked by sand and earth.
We request that laborers be dispatched to dredge it."
The person Xiāo Yáo from Hǎiyáng stated:
"The county has a Chángxī stream,
whose source is at the foot of a mountain,
and it flows to the sea mouth.
It extends around Cháojùn,
so Gēnglóng and other *dū* (districts) all have ditches for irrigation.
However, the dry lands of Lóngjīn and other *dū* are without water,
and rely on nothing in times of drought.
We request that ditches be opened like in Gēnglóng."
Liú Yànliáng from Chánglè stated:
"Yánhú, over twenty *lǐ* long,
connects to Chóu'ānxī in the south
and to Dàoliúxī in the west,
and can be used for drought and flood control.
There are also Zhāngtánghán, Tángqiánhán, Dàtánghán, and Chéntánggǎng,
which are as beneficial as Yánhú.
We request that officials be ordered to dredge them."
The people of Guǎngjì stated:
"The county and its neighboring county, Huángméi,
transport thirty thousand *shí* of grain annually to Wàngniúdūn.
Small carts are laborious
and cannot withstand the toil.
The Liáojiākǒu port of Liánchéng Húgǎng has a ditch leading to the front of the *dūn*,
but it is too shallow for boats.
We request to cooperate with Huángméi to dredge it,
to facilitate water transport."
All requests were granted.
In the eleventh year, the Dòngtínghú dike was repaired.
Riverbanks in Dēngzhōu were built.
The Bālǐhé river in Jīnshāchǎng, Tōngzhōu, was dredged
to connect with the transport canal.
The people of Rènqiū stated:
"Língchénggǎng is twenty-five *lǐ* from the county.
Inside it is the Dìng'ānqiáo Hé river,
which flows north for eighteen *lǐ*,
but seven *lǐ* to the east is blocked by sand.
It should be dredged to connect with the port,
entering Zhāngjiāwān in Zhígū."
The Provincial Governor Zhōu Chén stated:
"Yìngtiān, Zhènjiāng, Tàipíng, and Níngguó prefectures
formerly had lakes like Shíjiù Hú.
The channels and ports within them
paid fish taxes annually.
The flat land and shallow beaches outside them
were open for people to graze livestock and collect water chestnuts and lotus roots,
but cultivation was prohibited.
Thus, when mountain streams swelled,
there was an outlet.
Recently, wealthy powerful families have built dikes to enclose fields,
obstructing lake waters,
so whenever there is a flood,
it harms the people.
This should all be strictly forbidden."
All requests were granted.
In the twelfth year, the Dàwānkǒu waterway in Píngdù Zhōu and the river outside the Gōng'ānmén in Jīngzhōu were cleared,
to facilitate transportation and payment for Gōng'ān and Shíshǒu counties.
Wáng Xìn, an official awaiting appointment in Zhèjiāng, stated:
"The Dōngxiǎojiāng river in Shàoxīng
connects to the seventy-two lakes of Zhùjì in the south
and to the Qiántángjiāng river in the west.
Recently, it has been blocked by tidal surges,
making the river level with the fields,
so boats cannot pass.
After prolonged rain, the water overflows,
and neighboring fields are often harmed.
We request that laborers be dispatched to dredge it."
This was granted.
In the thirteenth year, breaches in the Hàn and Táng dams in Níngxià were built up.
The Sùshuǐhé river in Shānxī and the Tōnghǎiquányuán in Nánhǎi County were cleared.
The city moat of Xuānfǔ was dug,
diverting mountain water from north of the city into the southern city's Dàhé river.
Wǔkāi Wèi in Húguǎng stated:
"The *wèi* borders the Miáo,
and the mountain roads are steep and dangerous.
Thirty *lǐ* from the *wèi* is a river connecting to Jìngzhōu Jiāng,
but it is full of rocks and sandbanks.
We request that it be cleared to facilitate transport."
Dèngchuān Zhōu in Yúnnán stated:
"The fields of our *zhōu* border the military fields of Dàlǐ Wèi along the lake.
Every year, rainwater and sand accumulate,
and crops are submerged.
We request that the *zhōu* and *wèi* military and civilians be ordered to clear and repair it."
All requests were granted.
In the fourteenth year, the Pānyǒng dike in Nánhǎi was dredged,
and a water gate was installed.
The people of Hézhōu stated:
"The *zhōu* has the Mǔzhèn Hé river,
which connects to the Má and Lǐ two lakes upstream
and to the Niútún Dàhé river downstream,
and is about seventy *lǐ* long
and eighty *zhàng* wide.
There is also Zhāngjiāgōu,
which connects to the Tóngchéng Zhá sluice gate,
leading to the Dàjiāng river.
It is half the length of Mǔzhèn,
and of similar width.
It irrigates over seventy *xū* (dike-protected fields) like Jiàngfú, and the military fields of various *wèi* in Nánjīng.
In recent years, the river has overflowed, and the sluice gates are ruined,
and most are silted up.
We request that work be undertaken to dredge it,
and that sluice gates be built at Mǔzhèn, Fēngshānzǔi, and Yègōngpō to prepare for droughts and floods."
This was granted.
In the first year of Jǐngtài (1450), dikes were built at Dānyáng, Gānlù, and other places.
In the second year (1451), the eastern and western embankments of the Yùhé River were repaired.
The city river east of the Āndìngmén Gate was dredged,
as were the rivers of the thirty-six Dū districts of Yǒngjiā,
and the Gùxīntáng pond in Chángshú,
which extended south to Dānghú,
and north to the Yángzǐjiāng River.
In the third year (1452), the Tàihé and Xìnfēng dikes were repaired.
Breached river sections were built up in Yán'ān and Suídé,
and the Xīchàhé River's banks leading to the Jiāng River in Miánzhōu were reinforced.
The Qīpǔtáng pond in Chángshú was dredged,
as was Hǎizi in Jiànzhōu.
Eleven streams and irrigation channels of the Mèngdúhé River were cleared.
The Ministry of Works reported:
“The Shítáng stone embankment in Hǎiyán, eighteen *lǐ* long,
is being breached by tidal waters.
Repairs made with loose earth
cannot last long.”
An imperial edict ordered the construction of a separate stone embankment to defend it.
In the fourth year (1453), more than ten *lǐ* of the Shùntánghé River in Jiāngyīn were dredged,
connecting east to the main river of Yǒnglì Cāng,
and west to Xiàgǎng and the Yángzǐjiāng River.
Mù Lín (沐璘), the Commander-in-Chief of Yúnnán, reported:
“East of the city, there is a river flowing south,
its source originating from Shàodiàn.
It merges with the ninety-nine springs to form one body,
and upon reaching Sōnghuābà, it divides into two branches: one encircles the foot of Jīnmǎshān Mountain
and enters Diānchí Lake;
the other flows from Hēiyáocūn Village to Yúnzéqiáo Bridge
and also enters Diānchí Lake.
Previously, a weir was built downstream
to irrigate hundreds of thousands of *qǐng* of military and civilian land,
but during heavy rains, there was no outlet for the floodwaters.
I request that households benefiting from this
be ordered to construct their own stone sluice gates,
to be opened and closed at appropriate times.”
The report was approved.
In the fifth year (1454), the Líyuánzhuāng Canal in Língbǎo was cleared,
connecting to Hónglújiàn,
irrigating ten thousand *qǐng* of land.
In the sixth year (1455), Dù Yù’s Canal in Huáróng was dredged,
allowing transport boats to enter the river,
avoiding the dangers of Dòngtíng.
Breached dikes at Dùcūnkǒu and Yángjiā and other places along the Báigōuhé River in Róngchéng and Gù'ān were repaired.
In the seventh year (1456),
Shàngshū Sūn Yuánzhēn (孫原貞) reported:
“There were formerly two sluice gates in the Xīhú Lake of Hángzhōu,
but they have recently collapsed,
and the lake has become silted up.
According to Sòng dynasty's Sū Shì (蘇軾): ‘Hángzhōu was originally a former coastal area,
where spring water was salty and bitter.
It was only after Lǐ Bì (李泌) of the Táng dynasty diverted lake water into the city for six wells
that the wells and towns gradually prospered,
and people should not be permitted to cultivate land here.’
Zhōu Cóng (周淙) also said: ‘Xīhú Lake values depth and breadth.’
Consequently, two hundred soldiers were recruited
specifically for dredging the lake.
Afterwards,
influential households again requested to cultivate land,
and the lake became increasingly filled with silt,
causing water to dry up during severe droughts.
An imperial edict ordered the Prefect Zhào Yǔmáo (趙與●) to dredge it,
removing all water caltrops, lotus, and reeds,
which benefited the people of Hángzhōu.
This is a brief account of the management of Xīhú Lake by previous generations.
Subsequently,
powerful families incessantly encroached upon it,
making the lake small and shallow,
and its sluice gates were damaged.
Now, civilian fields lack irrigation resources,
and official rivers are also obstructed.
I request an imperial order to the relevant authorities to initiate dredging
and prohibit encroachment to benefit the military and civilians.”
This was adopted.
In the second year of Tiānshùn (1458), the Wàngōngyàn weir in Péngxiàn was repaired,
irrigating over a thousand *qǐng* of land.
In the fifth year (1461),
Qiānshì Lǐ Guān (李觀) reported:
“The Jīngshuǐ River originates from the Zhòngshāngǔ Valley in Jīngyáng,
passes through Gāolíng,
and enters the Wèishǔi River at Lìyáng,
spanning two hundred *lǐ*.
The Hàn dynasty opened canals to irrigate fields,
and the Sòng and Yuán dynasties both appointed officials to manage them.
Although there are now the Hùkǒu, Zhèng, and Bái canals,
the dikes and weirs are damaged,
and the irrigation channels are blocked,
so the people do not benefit.”
Therefore, the relevant authorities were ordered to dredge them.
In the eighth year (1464),
the people of Yǒngpíng reported:
“The Qīhé River flows around the southwest of the city and enters the sea.
The city foundation is all rock,
so the water cannot breach it there.
Other sections are sandy and easily eroded.
Previous generations built an earth embankment in the northeast
and brick revetments in the southwest.
Now, with the passage of time, they have collapsed daily.
It is advisable to build a dike for the eastern flow,
and build a barrier across it to divert the water,
making it merge with the western flow,
so as to prevent the danger of erosion and collapse.”
Dū Yùshǐ Xiàng Zhōng (項忠) reported:
“The Hùkǒu, Zhèng, and Bái canals in Jīngyáng,
which draw water from the Jīngshuǐ River to irrigate tens of thousands of *qǐng* of fields,
still irrigated eight thousand *qǐng* during the Yuán dynasty.
Afterwards,
the canals became shallower day by day,
and their benefits were consequently lost.
In the early Xuāndé (1426-1435) era,
officials were dispatched to repair and dig them,
resulting in a harvest of three to four *shí* per *mǔ*.
Before long, they were blocked again,
and fields along the canals
became parched lands during droughts.
Jīngyáng, Lǐquán, Sānyuán, and Gāolíng all suffered from this.
Previously, I requested dredging on the left side of Lóngtán, the upper source of the Jīngshuǐ River,
down to the old canal mouth,
but it was subsequently halted due to an imperial edict.
Now, this work should be completed.
The well water west of Xī'ān city is salty and bitter,
and those who drink it often fall ill.
The Lóngshǒuqú Canal, which draws water for seventy *lǐ*,
is not easy to repair and build,
and its benefits only reach east of the city.
The Zàohé River, about one *shè* from the southwest of the city,
can be dug,
to divert its water to merge with the Lóngshǒuqú Canal,
which would benefit all residents.”
Pīzhōu Zhīzhōu Mèng Lín (孟琳) reported:
“The various communities of Yúxíng are all along the Yíhé River.
Due to prolonged rain, the banks have collapsed in twenty-eight places,
and all low-lying fields are submerged.
I request permission to repair and build them.”
Both requests were granted.
In the second year of Chénghuà (1466), the Ānfēngtáng pond in Shòuzhōu was repaired.
In the fourth year (1468), the city river of Shízhōu was cleared.
In the sixth year (1470), the Zhōujiājīng channel in Pínghú and the Dúshān seawall were repaired.
In the seventh year (1471),
tidal waters breached the banks of the Qiántángjiāng River and the areas of Shānyīn, Kuàijī, Xiāoshān, Shàngyú,
the two garrisons of Zhàpǔ and Lìhǎi,
and various salt fields of Qiánqīng.
Shìláng Lǐ Yǒng (李顒) was ordered to repair and build them.
In the eighth year (1472),
the breached banks of Xiāngyáng were diked.
In the tenth year (1474),
court officials met and discussed:
The old ditch of the Běichéngwéi polder in Jiāngpǔ
connects north to the Pǔzikǒu of the Chúhé River;
the old ditch of Hēishuǐquán east of the city
flows south into the Dàjiāng (Yangzi River).
The two ditches face each other,
separated by hills and ridges.
It is advisable to dig them through to form a river,
to draw water during drought and discharge it during floods.
This was adopted.
In the eleventh year (1475), the old canal of Qiántángmén Gate in Hángzhōu was dredged,
its left side connected to Yǒngjīnmén Gate,
and a bridge and sluice gate were built to store lake water.
Xúnfǔ Dū Yùshǐ Móu Fèng (牟俸) reported:
“Shāndōng's Xiǎoqīnghé River
connects upstream to the Báotū and other springs in Jǐnán,
and downstream to the Gāojiāgǎng salt fields along the coast of Lè'ān.
The Dàqīnghé River
connects upstream to the Kǎnhé and other springs in Dōngpíng,
and downstream to Hǎifēng and Lìjīn in Bīnzhōu,
and the rich Guó salt fields along the coast.
They are silted up
and suffer from extortion,
and rainfall also causes flooding.
Quànnóng Cāncèng Táng Yù (唐澞) dredged rivers and built sluice gates,
and I request that he also be in charge of water conservancy.”
The imperial edict approved this.
In the twelfth year (1476),
Xún'àn Yùshǐ Xǔ Jìn (許進) reported:
“The fifteen *wèi* (military guards) of Héxī,
extending from Zhuānglàng in the east
to Sùzhōu in the west,
stretch for nearly two thousand *lǐ*,
and their water resources are largely seized by powerful families.
It is advisable to establish a dedicated official to manage this.”
An imperial edict ordered the Túntián Qiānshì to take on this responsibility concurrently.
In the fourteenth year,
Fèng stated:
“The prefectures of Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng in Zhílì, and those in western Zhèjiāng,
have frequently suffered from droughts and floods for years.
This is because they encircle Tài Hú,
which is the lowest-lying area in the southeast,
and Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng are particularly in the lowest and most vulnerable spot.
Therefore, whenever there is prolonged rain,
all the waters rush and burst forth,
the lakes and marshes swell and overflow,
inundating boundless areas.
According to records, Tài Hú is the ancient Zhènzé,
receiving waters from the prefectures of Jiāxīng, Húzhōu, Xuānchéng, and Shèxiàn upstream,
and connecting to the three rivers of Lóu, Dōng, and Wúsōng downstream.
The Dōng Jiāng is no longer visible today,
but the old courses of Lóu and Wúsōng leading to the sea still exist.
Its topography, along with the two embankments of Fúshān and Báimáo in Chángshú, can guide the waters of Tài Hú into the rivers and sea,
saving the people from drowning,
and making the land arable.
Historical dynasties have established effective methods for dredging and excavating.
This dynasty has also often ordered officials to repair them,
but without grasping the essential points.
Meanwhile, wealthy families along the lake have profited by planting on the silted shoals.
Officials in charge of water management do not fully understand the benefits and harms;
they often place stone weirs at outlets,
build earth causeways,
or, fearing pirate boats,
drive in wooden palisades.
This has led to the obstruction of waterways,
causing distress to both public and private interests.
I request that a high official deeply knowledgeable in water conservancy be chosen to specialize in its management,
and that a Superintendent of Water Conservancy Sub-office be established to carry out repairs at all times,
then the water flow will be clear,
and the southeast will greatly benefit.”
The Emperor immediately ordered Fèng to concurrently lead water conservancy efforts,
allowing him to dredge and build as he saw fit.
Upon completion of the work,
a specialized sub-office was then established.
In the fifteenth year, the inner and outer waterways of Nánjīng were repaired.
In the eighteenth year, the eastern and western canals of Yúnnán were dredged,
from Sōnghuá Bà and Hēilóng Tán to Xīnán Liǔ Bà Nán Cūn,
irrigating tens of thousands of qǐng of fields.
The water gates, city arches, and forty-nine water gates at strategic passes of Jūyōng Guān were repaired,
along with one hundred and two watchtowers and beacon platforms.
In the twentieth year, the sea dikes of Jiāxīng and five other prefectures were repaired,
and specially selected京táng officials were sent to supervise them.
In the twenty-second year, the middle and lower two new rivers of Nánjīng were dredged.
In the third year of Hóngzhì,
following the suggestion of Grand Coordinator and Censor-in-Chief Qiū Nài,
an official was appointed to specifically manage the Dūjiāng Yàn in Guànxiàn.
In the sixth year, an imperial edict instructed Administrator Zhū Xuān to dredge the Yī and Luò rivers in Hénán,
the Gāopíng and Wànjīn canals in Zhāngdé,
the Guǎngjì canal in Huáiqìng,
and the Zhàogōng and other canals in Nányáng,
as well as the Táopī and other weirs in Rǔníng.
In the seventh year, the Tiān and Cháo rivers in Nánjīng were dredged,
to provide water for military garrisons'屯tián.
In July, Vice Minister Xú Guàn and Censor-in-Chief Hé Jiàn were ordered to manage water conservancy in western Zhèjiāng.
The work was completed in April of the following year.
When Guàn first received the imperial order,
he memorialized to have Secretary Zhù Cuì accompany him.
Cuì traveled in a small boat to thoroughly investigate the origins and courses.
Guàn then ordered Sūzhōu Sub-Prefect Zhāng Mín to clear the various rivers and waterways,
and store the water in a large dam.
He then opened the sandbar surface of Báimáo Gǎng,
and at low tide,
released the dammed water to scour it,
washing away all the sand and mud.
The tidal water surged and scoured,
making it wider and deeper day by day,
and the water reached the sea without obstruction.
He also ordered Zhèjiāng Administrator Zhōu Jìlín to repair over thirty lí of old dikes in Jiāxīng,
replacing them with stone,
and to reinforce and expand over seventy lí of embankments in Chángxīng, Húzhōu.
Guàn then reported:
“The southeast is where financial revenue originates,
but it suffers greatly from water calamities.
At the beginning of Yǒnglè,
Xià Yuánjí was ordered to dredge and clear.
At that time, due to the silting and swirling sand in the Wúsōng Jiāng,
construction could not be carried out.
Now, over ninety years later,
the ports and waterways are even more blocked.
I supervised officials to inspect the sites,
and dredged the Chángqiáo of Wújiāng,
guiding the scattered waters of Tài Hú into Diànshān, Yángchéng, Kūnchéng, and other lakes and marshes.
I also reopened the Wúsōng Jiāng and the Dàshí, Zhàotún, and other waterways,
to drain the waters of Diànshān Hú,
through the Wúsōng Jiāng to reach the sea.
I opened Báimáo Gǎng, Báiyú Hóng, and Niányú Kǒu,
to drain the waters of Kūnchéng Hú,
through Báimáo Gǎng to flow into the river.
I opened Xié Yàn, Qī Pù, Yántiě, and other ponds,
to drain the waters of Yángchéng Hú,
through Qīyā Gǎng to reach the sea.
The lower reaches are now clear,
no longer obstructed.
I then opened Lóujīng in Húzhōu,
to drain the waters from Xī Hú, Tiānmù, Ānjí, and other mountains,
flowing from the southwest into Tài Hú.
I opened Bǎidú in Chángzhōu,
to drain the waters from Lìyáng, Zhènjiāng, Liànhú,
flowing from the northwest into Tài Hú.
I also opened various sluice gates,
to drain the waters of the grain transport canal,
through Jiāngyīn to flow into the Dà Jiāng.
The upper reaches are also clear,
no longer stagnant.”
In this project,
one hundred and thirty-five rivers, ports, channels, ditches, lakes, ponds, sluice gates, and embankments were repaired and dredged.
Over two hundred thousand laborers were employed,
and Zhù Cuì contributed greatly to its success.
Grand Coordinator and Censor-in-Chief Wáng Xún said:
“The three ancient canals of Níngxià,
were open during the Eastern Hàn and Middle Táng dynasties.
However, the westernmost canal runs along the mountain,
over three hundred lí long,
and more than twenty zhàng wide.
Both banks are steep and dangerous,
and the old Hàn and Táng traces are all buried.
Soldiers should be dispatched to dredge and excavate it,
to divert water downstream.
And then earth should be used to build the eastern bank,
establishing barracks and garrisoning troops to block barbarian incursions.
I request thirty thousand taels of imperial silver,
along with six years of salt tax from Língzhōu,
to cover the expenses.”
He also requested to open a canal at Jīnjí Shān Hé Kǒu in Língzhōu,
to irrigate fields,
and allocate them to soldiers and civilians for tenancy and cultivation.
All requests were granted.
In the eighteenth year, the Chángshú Táng Bà was built and repaired,
from Shànghú Kǒu to the river,
and the Huáng, Sì, and other waterways,
and over thirty sandbars including Xīnzhuāng.
Xī Hú in Hángzhōu was dredged.
In the seventh year of Zhèngdé, the dikes at Fùyáng Hé Kǒu in Guǎngpíng were repaired.
In the fourteenth year, the right river at Xīnjiāng Kǒu in Nánjīng was dredged.
In the fifteenth year,
Censor Chéng Yīng said:
“The garrison fields of Yìngtiān and other guards located north of the Jiāng in Chúzhōu, Hézhōu, and Liùhé,
are low-lying,
and have repeatedly been damaged by water.
From Jīnchéng Gǎng to Zhuó Hé reaching Wū Jiāng, over thirty lí,
if dredged along the old course,
then the water flow will be relieved and the garrison fields will benefit.”
The imperial edict approved it.
In the first year of Jiājìng, the dikes and canals of Shùlù, Féixiāng, Xiàn, and Wèi were built and dredged.
Initially,
the waterways of Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng were all occupied by powerful families.
Grand Coordinator Lǐ Chōngsì divided the water into well-field areas,
demonstrating the method of excavation,
with each household occupying one section,
calculating the work and setting dates.
Dredging rakes were built,
using hundreds of large rafts,
pulling wooden teeth,
advancing and retreating with the tide,
striking and stirring up mud and sand.
Over a hundred small boats were placed,
trailing iron brooms to guide them.
Old courses were dredged,
new canals were dug,
and not a single large waterway or tributary
was left without irrigation.
The Emperor praised his efforts,
bestowing upon him silver and silk.
In the second year, the city walls and waterways east of Déshèng Mén and north of Cháoyáng Mén were repaired,
and five sections of official embankments in Yízhēn and Jiāngdū were built.
In the tenth year,
Bureau Director of the Ministry of Works Lù Shíyōng said:
“The Lúgōu Hé in Liángxiāng,
the Liúlí and Húliáng two rivers in Zhuōzhōu,
the Báigōu Hé in Xīnchéng and Xióngxiàn,
the Shā Hé in Héjiān,
and the Hūtuó Hé in Qīngxiàn,
all have silted lower reaches.
They should be dredged in a timely manner,
so that they can reach the sea.”
An imperial edict ordered the Grand Coordinator to deliberate on it.
In the eleventh year,
Tàipú Qīng Hé Dòng, after an inspection of the riverine flooding in the imperial domain, presented two points.
One concerned the Hūtuó Hé.
His first point stated:
“The three rivers of Zhēndìng—Yā Hé, Shā Hé, and Cí Hé—
all originate in Wǔtái.
They converge with various tributaries,
reach Lìnjiāquān on the Táng Hé,
and merge into the river at Héjiān.
Flowing southeast through Rènqiū, Bàzhōu, and Tiānjīn to the sea,
this is the old course.
The area southeast of Héjiān is high,
while the northeast is low.
Therefore, the water breached at Lìnjiākǒu,
and Sùníng and Xīn'ān both suffered its harm.
It is advisable to build up the breach
and dredge the old course.
The Húliáng Hé of Zhuōzhōu,
which branches off from the Jùmǎ Hé,
enters the Hún Hé east of the prefecture.
The Liúlí Hé of Liángxiāng,
originating in Cíjiāwù,
submerges underground,
and enters the Hún Hé east of Liángxiāng.
Recently, the Hún Hé has been obstructed,
and these two rivers do not flow.
However, the silt in the lower reaches is only four or five *lǐ* thick;
I request that it be dredged urgently.”
The Board responded, agreeing to proceed.
Lángzhōng Xú Yuánzhǐ was ordered to relieve the disaster,
and he memorialized:
“Rivers are meant to drain water,
but now they are instead blocked below;
marshes are meant to store water,
but now they are instead overflowing above.
Therefore, the imperial domain constantly suffers from water,
Shùntiān has half benefit and half harm,
Zhēndìng has more benefit than harm,
Bǎodìng has more harm than benefit,
and Héjiān suffers entirely.
During the Hóngzhì and Zhèngdé reigns,
long dikes were built,
and breaches were blocked,
but they quickly collapsed.
Now, only dredging can be implemented,
with six strategies in total.
First, dredge the main river,
to make its channel wider and deeper.
The Jiǔ Hé, coming from Shānxī,
should merge with the Hūtuó in the south without encroaching upon the prefectures of Zhēndìng,
and merge with the Báigōu in the north without encroaching upon the prefectures of Bǎodìng.
This is the primary principle.
Second, dredge the tributary rivers.
Let the flow of the Jiǔ Hé
pass through the Dàqīng Hé,
entering via the Zǐchéngkǒu;
pass through Wéndū Cūn,
entering via the Nièpánkǒu;
pass through Báiyáng Diàn,
entering via the Lìnjiākǒu;
pass through Zhānggē Wā,
entering via the Yángcūn Hé.
This will directly accommodate the small flows,
and the water force will be divided.
Third, dredge the breached rivers.
When the Jiǔ Hé flows peacefully,
the two tributary rivers can receive it,
but when it swells, the banks are breached in four directions.
It is advisable to retain one opening at each breach point,
and then dredge them to form a single channel,
to reduce the swiftness,
and prevent inundation.
Fourth, dredge the marsh rivers.
Connect the marshes to each other,
reaching the two main tributary rivers,
so that the lower areas have an outlet.
Fifth, dredge the silted rivers.
Let the Jiǔ Hé flow east
entirely through its old course,
making the high parts lower,
and the lower parts clear.
Those who occupy and obstruct the course
shall be punished.
Sixth, dredge the lower rivers.
One branch of the Jiǔ Hé exits at Qīng Xiàn,
another exits at Dīngzì Gū,
and the two flows meet at Yuànjiākǒu.
Therefore, construction must begin at Yuànjiākǒu,
and as effectiveness gradually appears,
then proceed in stages,
so as to reduce the water damage in the various prefectures.”
The Emperor praised and accepted his proposal.
The following year,
Guōjiāzhuāng in Xiānghé self-opened a new river channel,
one hundred and seventy *zhàng* long,
and fifty *zhàng* wide,
more than ten *lǐ* from the old river.
An imperial edict ordered the river officials to urgently repair it.
In the thirteenth year,
Xúnfǔ Dūyùshǐ Zhōu Jīn said:
“If the breach at Lìnjiāquān is blocked,
it will overflow to the east,
harming Héjiān;
if not blocked, the eastern flow will gradually silt up,
harming Bǎodìng.
It is advisable to keep the breach and dredge and widen the new river,
so that the water flows smoothly northeast,
without the worry of obstruction or drying up.”
This was followed.
In the twenty-fourth year, Nánjīng’s Hòuhú was dredged.
Initially,
Hú Tǐgān, when inspecting Wú,
seeing the flooding in Sōngjiāng,
proposed six strategies: namely, opening channels,
dredging lakes,
reducing the force of upstream flows,
breaching downstream gullies,
clearing tidal sand,
and establishing rules for land management.
In this year,
Lǚ Guāngxún, when inspecting Wú,
again memorialized five matters concerning the water conservancy of Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng: First, widely dredge to prepare for storage and drainage.
The land of Sānwú is a water country,
receiving waters from Tàihú and other marshes in the southwest,
where the water level is particularly low.
The northeast borders the sea,
and the hillocks
there
are particularly high compared to the southwest.
High areas suffer from drought,
and low areas suffer from floods.
In the past, people dug canals and ponds in the lower reaches,
guiding the waters of the various lakes north into the river,
and east into
the sea,
and also drew in river and tidal flows to spread outside the hillocks.
With proper storage and drainage,
there were no worries of flood or drought.
Recently, the numerous canals and ponds, both straight and intersecting,
have mostly been silted up and left untended;
only the Huángpǔ
and Liúhé rivers are somewhat clear.
However, the water sources of Tàihú are numerous and powerful,
and the two rivers are insufficient to drain them.
Moreover, many tributary rivers in the hillocks are obstructed,
leaving no
means for irrigation.
Thus, both high and low areas suffer,
and disasters are reported annually.
It is advisable to first survey the critical points,
and in areas like Diànshān where there are reeds,
guide the Tàihú waters to disperse into
Yángchéng, Kūnchéng, Sānmǎo, and other lakes.
Also, open the Wúsōng Jiāng and Dàshí, Zhàotún, and other *pǔ* (canals),
to drain the waters of Diànshān to the sea.
Dredge Báimáo
and Niányú and other outlets,
to drain the waters of Kūnchéng into the river.
Open Qīpǔ, Yántiě, and other *táng* (ponds/dikes),
to drain the waters of Yángchéng to the river.
Also, guide
the waters from the fields
entirely into smaller *pǔ*,
to feed into larger *pǔ*,
so that all flowing waters have a destination,
and all stored waters have an outlet.
Then the low-lying areas will be managed,
and there will be no
worry of floods.
Then dredge Àiqí and Tōngbō to irrigate Qīngpǔ,
dredge Gùpǔ and Wútáng to irrigate Jiādìng,
dredge Dàwǎ and other *pǔ* to irrigate the
eastern part of Kūnshān,
dredge Xǔpǔ and other *táng* to irrigate the northern part of Chángshú,
dredge Zāngcūn and other *gǎng* (harbors/channels) to irrigate Jīntán,
and dredge Zǎogǎng and other rivers to irrigate Wǔjìn.
All hillock
tributary rivers that are silted up and left untended
should be dredged deep and wide,
to restore them to their former state.
Then the upstream areas will also be managed,
and there will be no worry of drought.
This is the fundamental principle
of water conservancy for Sānwú.
Second, repair dikes and embankments to secure against lateral flows.
The southeast of Sūzhōu, Sōngjiāng, Chángzhōu, and Zhènjiāng is downstream,
and Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng are further downstream from Chángzhōu and Zhènjiāng,
making them prone to accumulation and difficult to drain.
Although rivers are guided and canals are dredged to divert water into the river and sea,
during autumn rains and floods,
when wind and waves collide,
the waters of the rivers and canals flow backwards into the fields,
causing erosion and damage.
In the Sòng Dynasty, Zhuǎnyùnshǐ Wáng Chúnchén once ordered Sūzhōu and Húzhōu to build field ridges to defend against water,
which the people found very convenient.
Sīnóngchéng Jiá Dàn also said:
“The regulation of rivers is rooted in the management of fields.”
The old folks all say,
twenty to thirty years ago,
the common people had abundant food.
With the surplus energy, they maintained the dikes,
and the fields became even more perfect.
Recently, all are impoverished,
with no time for repairs,
thus
the fields and dikes gradually deteriorated,
and there were many floods annually.
It is fitting to command the local officials to specialize in managing the dikes.
If the dikes are high, the fields will naturally be secure,
and even heavy rains and floods cannot cause harm.
Moreover, it is sufficient to control the waters of all the lakes to flow into the river estuaries,
then there will be no need for artificial breaches,
and the current will naturally be swift.
As for the hilly areas,
they too will benefit from the slightly higher river water,
and
gain irrigation from the *mǔyǐn* to provide water,
not only benefiting the low-lying fields.
One suggestion is to restore the sluice gates to prevent silting.
The waters of the river estuaries all flow from the plains into the rivers and seas.
With slow currents and strong tides,
sand surges with the waves,
and thus it easily silts up.
In the past, people, considering the convenience,
built sluice gates about ten *lǐ* from the rivers and seas, straddling the current.
They opened and closed them with the tides
to prevent silting.
In dry years, they would
keep them closed to store the flow,
and in flood years, they would keep them open to discharge the excess.
The so-called three benefits of setting up sluice gates
referred to this.
Recently, many have been blocked,
only the Fúshān
sluice gate in Chángshú still exists.
The old folks believe that if sluice gates were indeed installed at all river estuaries leading to the sea,
they would naturally remain unobstructed for a long time.
Another suggestion is to determine the urgency to allocate labor and expenses.
Another is to emphasize delegation of authority to ensure success.
The imperial edict agreed with all proposals.
Guāngxún then requested that Cúnfǔ Ōuyáng Bìjìn be specially appointed.
This was granted.
In the twenty-sixth year,
Gěishìzhōng Chén Fēi requested to imitate the irrigation methods for paddy fields in Jiāngnán,
to open ditches and channels north of the Jiāng River,
to alleviate water disasters,
and increase annual harvests.
The report was approved.
In the thirty-eighth year,
Zǒngdū Shàngshū Yáng Bó requested to develop water conservancy for the barren lands of Xuān and Dà.
This was granted.
Cúnfǔ Dūyùshǐ Wēng Dàlì stated:
"The water conservancy of Dōngwú,
since the dredging of Zhènzé's source to flow into the Jiāng River,
and the three rivers guided to flow into the sea,
along with the thirty-six estuaries of Sūzhōu,
the eight confluences of Sōngjiāng,
and the fourteen waterways of Pílíng,
all served to regulate floods and droughts.
Recently, due to conflicts with Japanese pirates,
at the intersections of branches and harbors,
many stakes and dikes were built for defense,
causing water flow to become stagnant,
and silt to accumulate daily.
Between the channels,
high ground became mounds.
Moreover, in the Jùqū, Húmǎo,
and those living alongside the water, planted reeds and rushes indiscriminately,
accumulating mud to form marshes.
The common people also frequently built their own dikes.
The upper reaches became weaker daily,
and the water flow diminished daily.
The waters of Huángpǔ and Lóujiāng were also occupied by naval forces,
and the lower reaches also silted up.
The sea tide was weak,
water conservancy was difficult to promote,
and the people's fields gradually became barren.
It is appropriate to construct stone sluice gates at Wúsōng, Báimáo, Qīpǔ, and other places,
opening and closing them seasonally.
Dredge and widen the grain transport canals of Zhènjiāng and Chángzhōu,
so that transport is unimpeded,
which is a benefit to both public and private interests."
The imperial edict approved.
In the forty-second year,
Gěishìzhōng Zhāng Xiànchén stated:
"The five prefectures of Sūzhōu, Sōngjiāng, Chángzhōu, Jiāxīng, and Húzhōu have repeatedly suffered from water disasters.
I request to dredge the branch rivers,
and open the tidal waters;
build dikes,
to resist turbulent flows.
Báimáogǎng, Liújiāhé, Qīpǔ, Yánglín, and all rivers, canals, and lakes that are blocked and marshy,
should all be dredged."
The emperor, considering that Jiāngnán had long suffered from Japanese pirate raids,
and the people should not be overburdened,
ordered to only selectively dredge the branch rivers.
In the forty-fifth year,
Cāncéng Líng Yúnyì requested the special appointment of a Yùshǐ to oversee water conservancy in Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng.
The imperial edict ordered the Xúnyán Yùshǐ to concurrently handle it.
In the third year of Lóngqìng, the Zhútǒnghé in Húguǎng was opened to drain the Hànjiāng River.
Cúnfǔ Dūyùshǐ Hǎi Ruì memorialized that the lower reaches of Wúsōngjiāng at Shànghǎi had silted up by more than fourteen thousand *zhàng*.
The river surface was formerly thirty *zhàng* wide,
and an additional fifteen *zhàng* was opened,
from Huángdù to Sòngjiāqiáo, a length of eighty *lǐ*.
The following spring,
Ruì stated:
"The routes of Sānwú to the sea
are bounded to the south by Wúsōng,
to the north by Báimáo,
and in the middle by Liúhé.
Liúhé is unobstructed,
while Wúsōng is still being dredged.
The local people request to open Báimáo,
estimated to involve dredging over five thousand *zhàng*,
with over one hundred and sixty-four thousand laborers."
He also said:
"The Wúsōng project is nearing completion,
only the two eastern and western dams have not been opened.
The elders all say that Kūnshān Xiàjiàkǒu, Wújiāng Chángqiáo, Chángzhōu Bǎodàiqiáo, Wúxiàn Xūkǒu, and all places that can allow flow into Wúsōng,
must be dredged one by one,
only then can the dams be opened."
Both requests were granted.
In that year, the seawall of Hǎiyán was built.
Four years later,
following the proposal of Cúnfǔ Shìláng Xú Shì,
the old river from Hǎiyán Qínzhùshān
south to Gǎnpǔ was reopened.
In the second year of Wànlì, the water holes of Jīngzhōu,
and the breached dikes at Chéngtiān Sìgǎng and Xièjiāwān were constructed.
The old dikes of Jīngzhōu and Yuèzhōu prefectures and the counties of Sōngzī were also rebuilt.
In the fourth year,
Cúnfǔ Dūyùshǐ Sòng Yíwàng stated:
"The waters of Sānwú,
from Jiāxīng and Xiùzhōu southeast along the coast northward,
all converge on Sōngjiāng,
and flow into the sea via Huángpǔ;
from Chángzhōu and Zhènjiāng northwest along the river eastward,
all converge on Jiāngyīn and Chángshú.
In between, Tàihú stores water,
forming a vast expanse,
flowing into Pángshān, Dúshù, Diànshān, Sānmǎo,
and Yángchéng lakes.
Then, by opening estuaries to draw from the lakes,
northward through Chángshú Qīpǔ, Báimáo and other ports into the river,
northeastward through Kūnshān, Tàicāng, passing through Liújiāhé,
southeastward through Wúsōngjiāng, Huángpǔ,
each entering the sea.
The various waters are interconnected,
surrounding and protecting on all sides,
like an inverted basin in the middle.
Hángzhōu, Jiāxīng, Húzhōu, Chángzhōu, and Zhènjiāng are situated around the four corners,
Sūzhōu is in the center,
and Sōngjiāng, receiving all the waters,
is in the lowest position.
I beg to specially appoint a Shuǐlì Qiánshì to assist the national economy."
The Ministry deliberated and decided to dispatch a Yùshǐ to supervise it.
In the sixth year,
Cúnfǔ Dūyùshǐ Hú Zhílǐ requested to first dredge Wúsōngjiāng Chángqiáo and Huángpǔ.
Prior to this,
Xún'àn Yùshǐ Lín Yìngxùn stated: "The water conservancy of Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng lies in opening the middle section of Wúsōngjiāng,
to facilitate its flow into the sea.
Tàihú has three routes to the sea: northeast via Liúhé,
which is
the old course of the ancient Lóujiāng;
southeast via Dàhuángpǔ,
which follows the intention of the ancient Dōngjiāng;
and in the middle is Wúsōngjiāng,
passing through Kūnshān, Jiādìng, Qīngpǔ, and Shànghǎi,
which is the main artery of Tàihú.
Now Liúhé and Huángpǔ are both open,
but why is the central river uniquely blocked?
It is because the river current meets the sea tide,
the sea tide is turbid,
relying on the river water
to swiftly scour it.
Liúhé solely receives the waters of Bā and Yáng lakes,
and also has Xīnyángjiāng and Xiàjiàpǔ flowing into it from the side;
Dàhuángpǔ receives the combined waters of Hángzhōu and Jiāxīng,
and also has Diànshān and Máodàng feeding it from upstream.
Therefore, the currents are all clear and swift,
sufficient to resist the tide,
and thus cannot silt up.
However, Wúsōngjiāng originates below Chángqiáo and Shítáng,
and enters after passing through Pángshān and Jiǔlǐ lakes.
Now Chángqiáo and Shítáng have been blocked,
and Pángshān and Jiǔlǐ
have again become shoals,
so its incoming flow is already weak.
Furthermore, Xīnyángjiāng and Xiàjiàpǔ divert its water to Liúhé,
making its force even weaker,
unable to overcome the sea tide."
the surging power to cleanse the muddy and turbid currents.
Over time,
the siltation left only a narrow channel.
The water lost its former path,
often leading to destructive floods.
Branch rivers and small ports
also became obstructed.
Previously cultivated fields
half became barren land.
The former Censor-in-Chief Hǎi Ruì (海瑞) strongly overcame numerous objections
and dredged the eighty *lǐ* (里) from Sòngjiāqiáo (宋家橋) at the Jiāngkǒu (江口) of Shànghǎi (上海) to Àiqí (艾祁) in Jiādìng (嘉定),
which fortunately remained navigable.
From
Àiqí (艾祁) to Mànshuǐgǎng (慢水港) in Kūnshān (崑山), over sixty *lǐ* (里),
all were elevated sandbanks.
It was urgently necessary to dredge them.
The plan was to deepen nine thousand five hundred *zhàng* (丈) and
widen to twenty *zhàng* (丈).
Once
this Jiāng (江) was opened,
Tàihú (太湖) would flow directly into the sea.
All the canals along the riverbanks could then draw water to irrigate fields,
and all the accumulated barren land in Qīngpǔ (青浦) could be reclaimed and cultivated.
This was also followed.
At this point,
the project was completed.
Yìng Xùn (應訓) further stated: "Wújiāng (吳江) County seat is situated directly east of Tàihú (太湖).
Lake water flows from here down the Wúsōng (吳淞) to the sea.
During the Sòng (宋) dynasty, where the transport route passed,
fearing wind obstructions and dangers,
long
bridges and stone embankments were built to facilitate towing.
The long bridge was one hundred thirty *zhàng* (丈) long,
with sixty-two arches.
The stone embankments had small openings if small,
and bridges if large.
The inner and outer *pǔjīng* (浦涇)
crisscrossed,
all designed for water discharge.
Half of the stone embankment's *jīngdòu* (涇竇) were silted up,
and both the inner and outer parts of the long bridge were ruined,
with only one or two arches allowing water through.
If not
dredged,
even if the lower Wúsōng (吳淞) were opened,
it would ultimately be useless.
It is advisable to open the Pángshānhúkǒu (龐山湖口)
from Chángqiáo (長橋) to Wújiāgǎng (吳家港).
Then the lake would have an outlet,
and the river would
have a destination,
ensuring an abundant source and a long flow,
which would be of great benefit."
The Dàhuángpǔ (大黃浦) of Sōngjiāng (松江) receives water from Háng (杭) and Jiā (嘉) in the southwest,
and water from Diàn (澱) and Mǎo (泖) and other wetlands in the northwest.
All converge in the Pǔ (浦).
The Xiùzhōutáng (秀州塘) and Shānjīnggǎng (山涇港) and other places are indeed the sources of the Huángpǔ (黃浦).
The channels from Diànshānhú (澱山湖) into the Huángpǔ (黃浦) are gradually becoming more silted and shallow.
It is advisable to dredge and clear them.
And from Huángpǔ (黃浦), Hénglào (橫澇), Zhūjīng (洙涇),
passing through Xiùzhōutáng (秀州塘) into Nánmǎo (南泖),
to Shānjīnggǎng (山涇港) and other places,
fourteen thousand *zhàng* (丈) and more,
awaiting dredging,
are especially urgent.
Other places, such as the Xīnjīng (茜涇), Yánglín (楊林), Báimáo (白茆), and Qīpǔ (七浦) ports in Sūzhōu (蘇),
the Púhuìtáng (蒲匯塘) and Guānshàotáng (官紹塘) in Sōngjiāng (松),
and the Zǎogǎng (澡港) and Jiǔqǔhé (九曲河) in Chángzhōu (常) and Zhènjiāng (鎮),
should
all be guided and opened up,
and gradually repaired.
In the eighth year, he further stated: "Sū (蘇) and Sōng (松) prefectures have hundreds of main rivers and branch canals.
The large ones discharge water into the sea,
the secondary ones connect lakes to rivers,
and the small ones draw water to irrigate fields.
Now Wúsōngjiāng (吳淞江), Báimáotáng (白茆塘), Xiùzhōutáng (秀州塘), Púhuìtáng (蒲匯塘), Mèngdúhé (孟瀆河), Shùnhé (舜河), and Qīngyánggǎng (青暘港) have all been completed.
Dozens of branch rivers
should all be
dredged and opened."
All his requests were granted.
After a long time,
based on Yí Wàng's (儀望) proposal,
a Vice-Commissioner for Water Conservancy of Sū (蘇) and Sōng (松) was specially appointed,
with Xǔ Yìngkuí (許應逵) in charge.
He then dredged over eighty *lǐ* (里) of Wúsōng (吳淞),
built over ninety embankments,
opened one hundred twenty-three new rivers,
dredged one hundred thirty-nine inner rivers,
and constructed eighteen *lǐ* (里) of coastline at Lǐjiāhóng Lǎoyāzuǐ (李家洪老鴉嘴) in Shànghǎi (上海),
spending two hundred thousand *tǎngjīn* (帑金).
Xǔ Yìngkuí (許應逵) completed half of the work with that amount.
Between the thirty-seventh and thirty-eighth years,
continuous heavy rains caused inundations,
and water disasters became increasingly severe.
Several years later,
Investigating Censor Guī Zǐgù (歸子顧) said:
"During the Sòng (宋) dynasty,
Wúsōngjiāng (吳淞江) was nine *lǐ* (里) wide.
It became silted up by the end of the Yuán (元) dynasty.
During the Zhèngtǒng (正統) reign,
Zhōu Chén (周忱) erected markers in the middle of the river
and cleared and dredged it.
Cuī Gōng (崔恭), Xú Guàn (徐貫), Lǐ Chōngsì (李充嗣), and Hǎi Ruì (海瑞) successively dredged it a total of five times.
Now, after more than forty years,
it has been abandoned and neglected.
It is advisable to make the river wide and the water swift,
and let the embankments, ports, and branch rivers flow in all four directions."
The memorial was withheld in the palace.
Investigating Censor Xuē Zhēn (薛貞) again requested its implementation,
but it was referred to the board for deliberation and not acted upon.
By the Tiānqǐ (天啟) reign,
Governor and Censor-in-Chief Zhōu Qǐyuán (周起元) again requested the dredging of Wúsōng (吳淞) and Báimáo (白茆).
In the early Chóngzhēn (崇禎) reign,
Director of a Bureau Cài Màodé (蔡懋德) and Governor and Censor-in-Chief Lǐ Dàiwèn (李待問) both made this request.
After a long time,
Governor and Censor-in-Chief Zhāng Guóweí (張國維) requested the dredging of the seventy-two channels of Wújiāng (吳江) Chángqiáo (長橋) and the caves of Jiǔlǐ (九里) and Shítáng (石塘).
Censor Lǐ Mó (李謨) again requested the dredging of Wúsōng (吳淞) and Báimáo (白茆).
All were referred to the board for deliberation,
but could not be implemented.
In the tenth year,
the Hóngdì (橫堤) in Xióngxiàn (雄縣) was extended by eight *lǐ* (里)
to guard against the floods of the Hūtúo (滹沱) River.
In the thirteenth year,
Xu Zhēnmíng (徐貞明), a junior minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, was concurrently appointed Imperial Censor
and head of the Land Reclamation Bureau.
As a supervising secretary, Zhēnmíng
had previously requested the development of water conservancy in the northwest, similar to the dike-fields system of the southerners,
to lead water to form fields.
The Ministry of Works deliberated and reported:
"In the various prefectures and counties of the capital region,
the waters from the fifteen rivers upstream drain into a single bay called Māo'ér (貓兒),
and the river mouth is extremely narrow and constricted.
Hence, the waters overflow everywhere.
It is imperative to open many branch rivers,
dredge the river mouth,
after which the water flow can be stabilized
and dredging can be implemented.
However, the project is enormous and the expenses are numerous.
And now, with the people weary and the treasury depleted,
we are focused on reducing expenditures.
We request that this proposal be dismissed."
It was then dropped.
Later, Zhēnmíng was demoted,
and he wrote a book called *Lùshuǐ Kètán* (潞水客譚),
discussing fourteen points on the necessity of water conservancy.
At that time, Governor Zhāng Guóyàn (張國彥) and Vice Commissioner Gù Yǎngqiān (顧養謙) were effectively implementing water conservancy projects in Jì (薊) and Yǒng (永) prefectures.
Thereupon, Supervising Secretary Wáng Jìngmín (王敬民) recommended Zhēnmíng,
who was specially recalled
and granted an imperial edict to inspect water conservancy.
Zhēnmíng then first managed the prefectures and counties east of the capital,
such as Mìyún Yànlè Zhuāng (密雲燕樂莊),
Pínggǔ Shuǐyù Sì (平谷水峪寺), Lóngjiāwù Zhuāng (龍家務莊),
Sānhé Tánghuì Zhuāng (三河塘會莊), and Shùnqìng Túndì (順慶屯地).
In Jìzhōu (薊州), there were Huángyá Yíng (黃厓營) north of the city,
Báimǎ Quán (白馬泉) and Zhènguó Zhuāng (鎮國莊) west of the city,
Mǎshēn Qiáo (馬伸橋) east of the city,
along Jíalín Hé (夾林河) down to Biéshān Pù (別山舖),
and along Yīnliú Hé (陰流河) down to Yīnliú (陰流).
In Zūnhuà (遵化), there were Píng'ān Chéng (平安城),
along the Grand Canal down to Shāhé Pù Xī (沙河舖西),
Tiěchǎng (鐵廠) south of the city, and from Yǒngzhū Hú (湧珠湖) down to Jǐucài Gōu (韭菜溝), Shàngsù Hé (上素河), and Xiàsù Hé (下素河) for over a hundred *lǐ*.
South of Fēngrùn (豐潤),
there were Dàzhài (大寨), Cìyútúo (剌榆坨), Shǐjiā Hé (史家河), and Dàwáng Zhuāng (大王莊);
to the east, Zhēnzǐ Zhèn (榛子鎮);
to the west, Yāhóng Qiáo (鴉紅橋),
along the river for over fifty *lǐ*.
In Yùtián (玉田), there were Qīngzhuāng Wù (青莊塢), Hòuhú Zhuāng (後湖莊), Sānlǐ Tún (三里屯), as well as Dàquán (大泉) and Xiǎoquán (小泉).
As for the coastal areas,
from Shuǐdào Gū Guān (水道沽關), Hēiyánzǐ Dūn (黑巖子墩) to Kāipíng Wèi Nán Sòngjiā Yíng (開平衞南宋家營),
it extended over a hundred *lǐ* east-west
and one hundred eighty *lǐ* north-south.
Over thirty-nine thousand *mǔ* of land were reclaimed.
When it came to Zhēndìng (真定), Zhēnmíng intended to manage the lands near the Hūtuó (滹沱) River.
Imperial Censor Wáng Zhīdòng (王之棟) said:
"The Hūtuó River cannot be managed by human effort;
it would only waste resources and trouble the people."
The emperor accepted his words
and intended to punish those who had proposed the plan.
Shēn Shíxíng (申時行) said:
"To call land reclamation for public benefit harmful to the people is
a very misguided opinion.
However, there are two reasons
for those who hold this view.
Firstly, the people of the north are idle and fond of leisure,
averse to strenuous labor.
Wet-rice farming involves the toil of plowing and weeding,
and the hardship of calloused hands,
which is inconvenient.
Secondly, powerful and influential families have encroached upon much land,
and without cultivation,
they collect profits from reeds, firewood, and fodder.
If these lands are reclaimed and cultivated into fields,
they will revert to rightful owners
and be managed by officials,
thereby eliminating their profits,
which is inconvenient.
However, when considering the grand strategy of the state,
the inconveniences are minor,
while the benefits are major.
It is only necessary to carefully consider the terrain,
and understand the people's sentiments.
Not all sandy areas need to be opened,
and there is no need to change the cultivation of millet and wheat.
If corvée labor is to be used,
it must be officially recruited,
without offending the people's feelings
or losing the benefits of the land.
This is a long-term strategy for the country."
Thereupon, Zhēnmíng was acquitted,
but the wet-rice farming project was ultimately abandoned.
Governor-General Liáng Wènmèng (梁問孟) built the border wall of Héngchéng Bǎo (橫城堡).
Concerned about the Yellow River problem in Níngxià (寧夏),
he requested to dike the Xīchà Hé (西岔河)
to obstruct the water from flowing eastward.
This was granted.
In the nineteenth year,
Zhou Hóngyuè (周弘禴), a minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, said:
"East of the river in Níngxià, there are the two dikes of Hàn (漢) and Qín (秦).
I request that they be built with stone, similar to the Hàn and Táng (唐) dikes west of the river.
And that a large canal be dredged outside the channels,
extending north to Yuānyāng (鴛鴦) and other lakes."
The imperial edict approved this.
In the twenty-third year,
the Yellow River and Huái (淮) River overflowed,
inundating Huái (淮) and Yáng (揚) prefectures.
Many suggested opening the Gāojiā Yàn (高家堰) to divert the Huái River.
Chén Kuí (陳煃), the magistrate of Bǎoyìng (寶應) and an Imperial Censor,
feared that opening Gāoyàn (高堰) would harm the people's salt fields.
He requested to dredge several rivers starting from Xīng (興) and Yán (鹽) eastward,
namely Báitú Hé (白塗河), Shíguǎ Kǒu (石●口), and Liáojiā Gǎng (廖家港),
to create multiple outlets to the sea.
Then, working from downstream to upstream,
dredge Qīngshuǐ (清水) and Zǐyīng (子嬰) two canals,
and also open more sluice gates at Guā (瓜) and Yí (儀) to discharge water.
Supervising Secretary Zhù Shìlù (祝世祿) also said:
"Those who suggest diverting the Huái River to enter the sea via Guǎngyáng (廣陽) and Shèyáng (射陽) two lakes
should note that Guǎngyáng is only eight *lǐ* wide,
and Shèyáng is only twenty-five *zhàng* wide.
They are called lakes,
but are actually rivers.
Moreover, they are three hundred *lǐ* from the sea,
winding and shallow and narrow.
The waters of the seven prefectures and counties of Gāo (高) and Bǎo (寶) rely solely on this one channel for discharge.
If the Huái River is also diverted into them,
the fields, homes, and salt fields
will surely not be spared.
East of Guǎngyáng Hú (廣陽湖) there is a large lake,
sixty *lǐ* square.
At the northern mouth of the lake, there is an old official canal,
from Guāndàng (官蕩) to Yánchéng Shíguǎ Kǒu (鹽城石●口),
only fifty-three *lǐ* to the sea.
This is a convenient way to guide the Huái River to the sea."
The Ministry and the river transport officials debated it,
but it was not implemented.
Soon after, Minister of River Conservancy Yáng Yīkuí (楊一魁) said:
"The Yellow River's backflow is precisely due to the obstruction at the river mouth.
Once the Yellow River diversion project is completed,
the river mouths at Shíguǎ Kǒu (石●口), Liáojiā Gǎng (廖家港), and Báijū Chǎng (白駒場),
along with Jīnwān (金灣) and Mángdào (芒稻) and other rivers,
should be urgently opened and dredged."
It was then ordered to proceed as per the proposal.
In the thirtieth year,
Governor-General Wāng Yìngjiāo (汪應蛟) of Bǎodìng (保定) said:
"The Yìshuǐ (易水) can irrigate Jīntái (金臺),
the Hūshuǐ (滹水) can irrigate Shān (山),
the Tángshuǐ (溏水) can irrigate Zhōngshān (中山),
the Fúshuǐ (滏水) can irrigate Xiāngguó (襄國),
and the Zhāngshuǐ (漳水) can irrigate Yèxià (鄴下).
And Yínghǎi (瀛海), being downstream of all rivers,
is thus called 'River Center,'
no different from the water country of Jiangnan.
As for the springs at the foot of the mountains
and the groundwater,
they are found everywhere.
It is advisable to set up dams and build sluices in each place,
open canals and build embankments.
Higher areas can be irrigated naturally,
while lower areas can be supplied by waterwheels.
Using the southern method of wet-rice farming,
within the six prefectures, tens of thousands of *qǐng* of wet-rice fields can be obtained.
The people of the capital region will henceforth be prosperous,
forever free from drought and flood disasters.
Should there unfortunately be an obstruction near the river,
it can also be compensated by exchanging grain from the south
and procuring it from the north.
This is an endless benefit for the state."
The report was approved.
Yìngjiāo then ordered the marine soldiers to cultivate military farms at Tiānjīn Gěgū (天津葛沽), Héjiā Quān (何家圈), Shuānggōu (雙溝), and Báitáng (白塘).
Each person was granted four *mǔ* of land,
totaling over five thousand *mǔ* cultivated,
with two thousand *mǔ* of wet rice.
The yield was abundant,
so he reported:
"If seven thousand *qǐng* of land are reclaimed,
over two million *shí* of grain can be obtained annually.
This is what has been implemented and proven effective."
In that year,
Guō Miǎn (郭勉), the prefect of Zhēndìng, dredged over forty springs, including Dàmíng (大鳴) and Xiǎomíng (小鳴),
irrigating a thousand *qǐng* of land.
In Xíngtái (邢臺), the Dáhúo (達活) and Yěhú (野狐) two springs flowed into the Niúwěi Hé (牛尾河),
and the Bǎiquán (百泉) flowed into the Lǐ Hé (澧河).
Twenty-one sluices and two embankments were built,
irrigating over five hundred *qǐng* of land.
In the first year of Tiānqǐ,
Censor Zuǒ Guāngdǒu adopted Yīng Jiāo's strategy,
re-establishing garrison fields in Tiānjīn,
and ordered Assistant Prefect Lú Guānxiàng to manage the water conservancy of the garrison fields.
The following year,
Touring Censor Zhāng Shènyán said:
“West of Zhīhé,
between Jìnghǎi and Xīngjì,
lie ten thousand qǐng of fertile land.
East of the river,
there are still places like Yánshuǐgū which are rich, fertile fields,
but unfortunately, all are barren and廢.
Now Lú Guānxiàng has opened up more than three thousand mǔ of land south of Kòujiākǒu.
The methods of irrigation ditches and reed ponds,
and the ways of planting and dredging,
are all well-established and systematic.
Why should people hesitate to do this?
There are generally five methods for opening and cultivating land.
One is official cultivation.
This means cattle, seeds, tools, cultivation, and hiring are all provided by the government,
and the government also collects all the income from the fields.
One is tenant cultivation.
This means people wish to reclaim land but lack the resources;
their cattle, seeds, and tools are supplied by the government,
and at harvest time,
the government takes four tenths of the yield.
One is civilian cultivation.
Those tenants with resources
volunteer to reclaim a certain amount of land;
once the wasteland is cultivated and productive,
it is assessed over several years to determine a constant yield,
from which one tenth is taken.
One is military cultivation.
This involves ordering the soldiers of the naval defense camps to cultivate the fields of Gěgū,
each person cultivating four mǔ,
and yielding two shí.
Because they receive travel and monthly rations,
the rent collected is heavier.
One is garrison cultivation.
Our ancestors'卫军 had garrison fields,
either fifty mǔ
or a hundred mǔ.
For soldiers who cultivated garrison land,
seventeen percent of the annual income went to the government,
and this income was then used for the annual expenses of the official army.
This was a well-devised system of integrating soldiers and farmers in the early days of the dynasty.
Four of these methods have been implemented;
however, for garrison cultivation, today soldiers and military are separated,
and the garrisons exist only in name.
We should select the surplus land from the various guards,
reclaim the fertile land of Jīnmén,
and implement it according to the official cultivation method.”
The memorial was sent to the relevant department,
and Tàipú Qīng Dǒng Yìngjǔ was ordered to manage the garrison fields from Tiānjīn to Shānhǎi.
After several years of planning,
one hundred eighty thousand mǔ of land were opened,
and countless grains were accumulated.
In the second year of Chóngzhēn,
Bīngbù Shìláng Shēn Yòngmào said:
“The waters of Yǒngpíng Luòhé and other rivers
are winding and wide,
and canals can be dredged to prevent drought and flood.
The gaps in the hillsides
are suitable for planting.
It is advisable to order the local officials to survey the land and examine the sources
to benefit the people.”
This was adopted.
JIAOKANJI
Volume 65, Military 1
The Míng dynasty established its rule by military prowess,
reforming the old Yuán system,
establishing guards and garrisons from the capital to the prefectures and counties.
Externally, they were commanded by Dū Sī,
internally by the Wǔjūn Dūdū Fǔ,
but the twelve guards above,
being the emperor's personal army, were not included.
For campaigns, generals were appointed as Zǒngbīng Guān,
leading the troops of the guards and garrisons;
once they returned, the generals surrendered their seals,
and the officers and soldiers each returned to their respective guards and garrisons.
This largely adopted the legacy of the Táng Fǔbīng system.
After Wénhuáng moved the capital north,
he strictly followed Tàizǔ's system,
but eunuchs observing the military
marked the beginning of trouble.
After Hóngwǔ and Xuāndé,
lulled by peace,
it wasn't long before the disaster of Tǔmù occurred.
Yú Qiān established the Tuányíng,
selecting elites,
unifying commands,
and fostering familiarity between soldiers and generals;
his method was quite good.
During the four reigns of Xiànzōng, Xiàozōng, Wǔzōng, and Shìzōng,
the camp system was repeatedly changed,
but its prestige only declined.
The soldiers of the guards and garrisons were exhausted by rotation duty,
and the troops in the capital were burdened by assigned tasks.
Eventually, in the late period,
the registers were long empty,
the ranks were depleted,
roving bandits arose like a swarm,
and the country crumbled.
Eunuchs surrendered at the pass,
the imperial guards collapsed below the city walls,
and thus the dynasty perished.
Now, we record the details of its system throughout the dynasty
and matters related to military administration
in this chapter.
Jīngyíng (Capital Garrison) Shìwèi Shàngzhí Jūn (Imperial City Guard, Capital City Patrol) Sìwèi Yíng (Four Guards Camp)
The capital army had three main camps:
one was the Wǔjūn,
one was the Sānqiān,
and one was the Shénjī.
Their systems were all established during the Yǒnglè era.
Initially,
Tàizǔ established the Tǒngjūn Yuánshuài Fǔ,
commanding military forces from various routes,
which was soon changed to Dà Dūdū Fǔ.
His nephew Wénzhèng was made Dà Dūdū,
exercising control over all armies both inside and outside the capital.
Two large and small training grounds were set up inside and outside the capital city,
dividing and training the soldiers of forty-eight guards.
Later,
it was further divided into the Five Military Commanderies of Front, Rear, Center, Left, and Right.
In the fourth year of Hóngwǔ,
the number of officers and soldiers was 207,800-plus.
Chéngzǔ increased the capital garrisons to seventy-two.
He then divided the infantry and cavalry into the Central Army (Zhōngjūn),
Left and Right Flanks (Zuǒyòu Yè),
and Left and Right Vanguards (Zuǒyòu Shào),
also known as the Five Armies (Wǔjūn).
Annually, he transferred soldiers from Zhōngdū, Shāndōng, Hénán, and Dàníng to the capital to be subordinate to them.
He appointed one supervising eunuch (tídū nèichén),
two military officials (wǔchén),
and two flag-bearing officers (zhǎnghàotóu guān);
one commander for the Grand Encampment (dàyíng zuòyíng guān),
and two battalion commanders (bǎzǒng);
one commander for the Central Encampment (zhōngyíng zuòyíng guān),
and one battalion commander each for the cavalry and infantry.
The officers for the Left and Right Flanks and Vanguards were similar.
There were also twelve camps (shíèryíng),
in charge of the cavalry guards accompanying the emperor,
with two battalion commanders appointed.
There was also the Perimeter Guards Camp (Wéizǐshǒuyíng),
in charge of training the imperial guards and spear-and-shield soldiers of the capital garrisons,
with one commander appointed,
who oversaw four divisions (sī),
designated as One, Two, Three, and Four,
each with two battalion commanders.
There was also the Junior Officials and Attendants Camp (Yòuguānshèrén Yíng),
in charge of training the junior officials and hereditary attendants of the capital garrisons,
with one commander,
and one battalion commander for each of the four divisions.
This was the organization of the Five Armies Camps.
Later,
three thousand surrendered soldiers from beyond the frontier were obtained,
and a camp was established, divided into five divisions.
One [division]

was in charge of imperial guards carrying the Grand Imperial Dragon Banner (dàjià lóngqí), precious banners (bǎodú), "Valiant" banners (yǒngzìqí), carrying the imperial seal (yùbǎo), and ordnance bureau (bīngzhàngjú) sundries.
One [division]
was in charge of imperial guards carrying the "Valiant" banners of the left and right twenty squads, and the banners, pennants, gongs, and drums of the imperial entourage.
One [division]

was in charge of imperial guards transmitting orders, camp flags and tokens, and the helmets, armor, imperial hats, imperial robes, and imperial footwear sundries from the Directorate of Imperial Accoutrements (Yùyòngjiān), Directorate of Imperial Hats (Shàngguān), Directorate of Imperial Robes (Shàngyī), and Directorate of Imperial Footwear (Shànglǚ).
One [division]
was in charge of imperial guards carrying the "Valiant" banners of the imperial entourage and the red-helmeted, directly-attached troops of the Five Armies.
One [division]

was in charge of imperial guards who were tiger-killers (shāhǔshǒu), carried imperial sedan chairs, and were from the forward vanguard cavalry camp, as well as the attendants from the Attendants Camp (Suíshìyíng) who served the crown prince, and returning soldiers from the Liáodōng Defense Force (Liáodōng Bèiyù).
Two supervising eunuchs were appointed,
two military officials,
two flag-bearing officers,
five division commanders (zuòsīguān),
thirty-four active battalion commanders,
sixteen imperial guard battalion commanders,
and four armored battalion commanders.
This was the organization of the Three Thousand Camp (Sānqiānyíng).
Later,
during the expedition to Jiāozhǐ,
the method of firearms was acquired,
and a camp was established for training.
The supervising eunuchs, military officials,
and flag-bearing officers
were all structured like those of the Three Thousand Camp,
and it was also divided into five armies.
For the Central Army,
there was one commander who was a eunuch,
and one military official.
Below them were four divisions,
each with one eunuch supervising firearms (jiānjīang nèichén),
one division commander (bǎsīguān),
and two battalion commanders.
The Left and Right Flanks and Vanguards were all similar.
Furthermore, after obtaining five thousand horses from Grand Commandant Tán Guǎng,
a camp was established called the Five Thousand Under (Wǔqiānxia),
in charge of drilling with firearms and the cavalry guards accompanying the emperor.
There was one commander who was a eunuch and one military official,
and below them were four divisions,
each with two division commanders.
This was the organization of the Divine Mechanism Camp (Shénjīyíng).
Ordinarily,
the Five Armies trained in encampment and formations,
the Three Thousand Camp trained in patrols and sentry duty,
and the Divine Mechanism Camp trained with firearms.
When the emperor went on expedition,
the Grand Encampment was in the center,
the Five Armies were stationed in different positions,
the infantry inside, the cavalry outside,
outside the cavalry was the Divine Mechanism Camp,
and outside the Divine Mechanism Camp was the long perimeter (chángwéi),
twenty *lǐ* in circumference,
for foraging within.
This was the system of the Three Great Camps (Sāndàyíng).
During the Hóngxī reign,
for the first time, one military official was appointed to oversee all camp administration.
In the fifth year of Xuāndé,
based on the words of Zhū Yǒng, Duke of Chéng,
select soldiers from the capital garrisons were assigned to the Five Armies for training.
The following year, officials from the Censorate (Kēdào) and the Embroidered Uniform Guard (Jǐnyī) were ordered to audit the numbers of soldiers in the various garrisons.
The emperor's campaigns against Gāoxù and his defeat of the Wùliánghā
were all won by the Capital Camps (Jīngyíng).
In the second year of Zhèngtǒng,
again due to Yǒng's recommendation, it was ordered that the soldiers of the Embroidered Uniform Guard and other garrisons, and the tomb-guarding garrisons should retain half [their number],
while their imperial guards and flag officers were attached to the Embroidered Uniform Guard for supervision and training,
and the rest were all assigned to the Three Great Camps.
During the Tǔmù Incident,
the capital army was almost completely annihilated.
Emperor Jǐng appointed Yú Qiān as Minister of War.
As Yú Qiān found that the Three Great Camps each had their own regulations,
and when it came to deployment,
the soldiers and generals were unfamiliar with each other,
he requested that one hundred thousand elite soldiers be selected from the various camps,
and divided into ten camps for unified training (tuánliàn).
Each camp had one grand commandant (dūdū),
one flag-bearing officer,
two regional military commissioners (dūzhīhuī),
ten battalion commanders,
one hundred squad leaders (lǐngduì),
and two hundred team commanders (guǎnduì).
