From the grand commandants of the Three Camps, one person was promoted to commander-in-chief (zǒngbīngguān),
supervised by a eunuch,
and the Minister of War or one Censor-in-Chief (Dūyùshǐ) served as supervisor.
The remaining soldiers returned to their original camps,
called "old home" (lǎojiā).
The system of the capital army underwent a transformation.
When Emperor Yīngzōng was restored to power,
Yú Qiān died,
and the unified training camps were abolished.
When Emperor Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
he reinstated them,
increasing them to twelve.
In the second year of Chénghuà, they were again abolished.
It was ordered that training be divided into first-class and second-class.
Soon, over one hundred and forty thousand first-class soldiers were selected.
Because the emperor considered the number too large,
he ordered them to be divided into twelve camps for unified training,
and distinguished their names:
there were four Martial Camps (Wǔyíng) – Fèn, Yào, Liàn, Xiǎn;
four Valiant Camps (Yǒngyíng) – Gǎn, Guǒ, Xiào, Gǔ;
and four Majestic Camps (Wēiyíng) – Lì, Shēn, Yáng, Zhèn.
Twelve marquises (hóu) were ordered to command them,
each assisted by a regional military commissioner,
supervised by a eunuch,
and overseen by a meritorious official (xūnchén).
These soldiers were named "Elite Vanguards" (Xuǎnfēng),
while those not chosen remained "old home" soldiers to perform labor,
and the method of unified training camps was slightly altered again.
In the twentieth year, the camps of Zhānzhōng and Xiàoyì were established;
they trained capital garrison attendants and surplus personnel.
These two camps,
established during the Yǒnglè period,
had later been abolished,
and were now re-established.
Before long,
they were abolished again as being useless.
The emperor reigned for a long time,
and paid special attention to the Capital Camps,
yet there were over seventy-five thousand missing soldiers,
largely concealed and occupied by powerful nobles.
Furthermore, Wāng Zhí was appointed supervisor of the unified training camps,
and the imperial guards were solely controlled by eunuchs,
which began with this emperor.
When Emperor Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
he appointed Censor-in-Chief Mǎ Wénshēng as supervisor.
At this time, the camp soldiers had long suffered from arduous labor.
At the end of Chénghuà,
Yú Zǐjùn had already spoken of it,
and Mǎ Wénshēng now strongly reiterated its unsuitability.
He also requested that two thousand elite cavalry and infantry be selected from each camp,
to be called upon in times of emergency.
Moreover, in accordance with the precedents of the Hóngwǔ and Yǒnglè reigns,
drills were to be held every five days,
with two days for maneuvering and setting up camp,
and three days for martial exercises.
This was approved.
At that time, Minister Liú Dàxià presented ten harmful practices,
and further memorialized to reduce the number of soldiers repairing the Qiánqīng Palace.
A eunuch said he was uncaring about the great project,
but Grand Secretary Liú Jiàn said:
"Cherishing soldiers
is the duty of a military official (sīmǎ)."
The emperor accepted this.
Coincidentally, Li Mèngyáng, a Household Department secretary, vehemently argued against the harm of employing soldiers for labor,
also implicating eunuchs who commanded troops.
Because his words offended Marquis of Shòuníng,
he was imprisoned,
and so the reforms were not implemented.
When Wǔzōng (武宗) ascended the throne,
the elite troops of the Twelve Camps numbered merely 60,500 men,
and the somewhat weaker ones were only 25,000.
Gě Sōng (葛嵩), a Supervising Secretary, requested that the elite of the Five Army Camps and the Three Thousand Camp be selected and returned to the Regimental Training Camps,
and that over 80,000 men remain in the camps to serve.
Hùirán Bó (惠安伯) Zhāng Wěi (張偉) erroneously cited old regulations to argue against it,
and the matter was dropped.
The hidden occupation remained as before.
When Zhì Pán (寘鐇) rebelled,
Grand Eunuch Zhāng Yǒng (張永) led the capital army to suppress him,
and the power of the eunuchs increased.
Later, when the wandering bandits arose,
border generals like Jiāng Bīn (江彬) gained favor
and requested the transfer of border troops to guard the capital.
Thereupon, tens of thousands of cavalry and household retainers from the Nine Borders were assembled in the capital,
named the Outer Four Families.
Two official halls were established.
Troops from the Regimental Camps, Valiant Warriors, and Four Guards were selected for training in the West Official Hall,
while the official army selected in the first year of Zhèngdé (正德) trained in the East Official Hall.
From then on, the troops of the two official halls became the vanguard,
while the Twelve Regimental Camps became the "old home" (i.e., less active, garrison troops).
After Wǔzōng (武宗) died,
the high officials, following his dying wish, disbanded them.
At that time,
construction work was vast and complex,
border generals held power,
and the military administration of the Capital Camps greatly deteriorated.
Supervising Secretary Wáng Liángzuǒ (王良佐), by imperial decree, selected troops.
According to the registers, there were over 380,000,
but fewer than 140,000 remained,
and only over 20,000 were selected.
When Shìzōng (世宗) ascended the throne,
after a long time,
following the advice of court officials,
one civilian official knowledgeable in military affairs was appointed to command the Capital Camps.
At this time, the fixed number of troops was over 107,000,
but only half remained.
Lǐ Chéngxūn (李承勛), the Minister of War exclusively in charge of the Capital Camps, requested to make up the number to 120,000.
The Board deliberated and followed the precedent from the Hóngzhì (弘治) era:
the old were to be replaced by strong recruits,
and in cases of desertion or death, the quartermasters were to replace them according to schedule.
This was adopted.
In the fifteenth year,
Wáng Tíngxiàng (王廷相), the Censor-in-Chief, supervised the Regimental Camps
and enumerated three abuses.
First,
soldiers were often assigned to miscellaneous duties,
working all year,
unable to participate in training.
Though nominally Regimental Camps ready for expedition,
they were in reality no different from field laborers.
Second,
when soldiers were replaced,
clerks and scribes demanded heavy bribes.
Poor soldiers could not afford them,
so the old and infirm were forced to serve,
while robust young men could not be recruited and trained.
Third,
wealthy soldiers, fearing camp training and conscription,
often bribed generals and officers to be listed among the "old home" (garrison) numbers.
The poor, even if old and exhausted,
were still constantly trained.
These words were quite pertinent.
Soon after, construction projects for the imperial ancestral temples and palaces in the two suburbs began,
and even more soldiers were pressed into service.
The Ministry of War requested to divide the rotations into two:
half would train,
half would be released to go home,
and their monthly stipends would be collected as payment for hired labor.
An imperial edict commanded this for one year.
Thereafter, when border alarms were urgent,
the Regimental Camps had few actual soldiers,
selecting only 30,000 cavalry,
still known as the East and West Official Halls.
The rest were all old and weak,
still privately employed by camp commanders and eunuchs.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Āndá (俺答) invaded,
and Dīng Rúkuí (丁汝夔), Minister of War, inspected the camps and found fewer than 50,000-60,000 men.
When driven out of the city gates,
they all wept, not daring to advance,
and the generals also looked at each other, their expressions changing.
Rúkuí (汝夔) was executed.
Grand Secretary Yán Sōng (嚴嵩)
then requested reforms to improve the situation.
Wáng Bāngruì (王邦瑞), Vice Minister of Personnel, acting as Minister of War,
then said:
"At the beginning of the dynasty,
the capital's elite forces numbered no less than 700,000-800,000,
and there was never a shortage of veteran generals.
Since the Three Great Camps were changed to the Twelve Regimental Camps,
and then to the Two Official Halls,
though gradually not as good as before,
the registered troops still numbered over 380,000.
Now, military preparedness has long been lax,
with only over 140,000 on the registers,
and no more than 50,000-60,000 undergoing training.
While provisions are distributed,
there are no troops for deployment.
When enemy cavalry penetrate deep,
both for battle and defense, there are no troops.
Even the existing soldiers are mostly old, weak, exhausted, or peddlers from the marketplace,
whose armor and weapons are supplied only at the last minute.
The problem lies not in desertion,
but in occupation of duties;
not in the soldiers,
but in the generals.
For the officials like Commanders, Garrison Officers, Headmen, and Battalion Commanders
are mostly noble scions and fops,
who ordinarily occupy the duties of camp soldiers,
drawing salaries for empty names.
When it's time for training, they simply gather market people,
making them dance and laugh.
In previous years,
Ministers Wáng Qióng (王瓊), Máo Bówēn (毛伯溫), and Liú Tiānhé (劉天hé) often intended to rectify this.
However, the generals, disliking anything that harmed their interests,
secretly plotted to obstruct,
and the soldiers, accustomed to arrogance and idleness,
competed to spread rumors,
so the matter was again halted,
leading to the harm we see today.
I beg Your Majesty to greatly assert your authority
and send officials to meticulously inspect."
The emperor approved his words
and ordered the Ministry of War to discuss reforms.
Thereupon, all Regimental Camps and Two Official Halls were abolished,
and the old system of the Three Great Camps was restored.
The Three Thousand Camp was renamed Shénshū (神樞).
Inner officials such as Supervising Directors and Supervising Weapons were abolished.
One military official was established,
named Commander-in-Chief of Capital Camp Military Affairs (Zǒngdū Jīngyíng Róngzhèng, 總督京營戎政),
with Xiánníng Hóu (咸寧侯) Qiú Luán (仇鸞) appointed to it;
and one civilian official,
named Assistant Administrator of Capital Camp Military Affairs (Xiélǐ Jīngyíng Róngzhèng, 協理京營戎政),
with Bāngruì (邦瑞) filling this position.
Below them, twenty-six subordinate officials, such as Vice Commanders and Assistant Commanders, were established.
Afterwards,
following the Board's deliberation,
the Four Military Camps were assigned to the central army of the Five Army Camp,
the Four Valiant Camps to the left and right vanguards,
and the Four Prestige Camps to the left and right flanks.
Each was assigned one Garrison Officer (zuòyíng guān, 坐營官)
as the main force,
responsible for city defense;
and two Assistant Generals (cānjìang, 參將)
for expeditions.
As the camp system was newly established, the emperor
announced it at the Imperial Ancestral Temple and implemented it.
He also dispatched four Censors to recruit soldiers in Jīfǔ (畿輔), Shāndōng (山東), Shānxī (山西), and Hénán (河南),
obtaining 40,000 men,
who were assigned to Shénshū (神樞) and Shénjī (神機).
Each was assigned one Vice General (fùjiàng, 副將),
and six additional combat generals were appointed
to separately command training.
The troops commanded by the Grand Generals of the Three Camps
were ordinarily called "Trained Braves" (liànyǒng, 練勇),
and their official titles were redefined when there was an incident.
Five Army Camp: one Grand General,
commanding 10,000 troops,
generally overseeing the Vice Commanders, Assistant Commanders, Guerrilla Commanders, Auxiliary Commanders, and Garrison Officers of the three camps;
two Vice Generals,
each commanding 7,000 troops;
four Assistant Generals for the left, right, front, and rear,
each 6,000;
four Guerrilla Commanders,
each 3,000.
Additionally, 66,660 reserve soldiers.
Shénshū (神樞) Camp: two Vice Generals,
each commanding 6,000 troops;
six Auxiliary Commanders,
each 3,000.
Additionally, 40,000 reserve soldiers.
The Shénjī (神機) Camp was similar.
Afterwards,
the number of officers in the Three Great Camps was determined: 196 in the Five Army Camp,
208 in the Shénshū (神樞) Camp,
and 182 in the Shénjī (神機) Camp,
totaling 586 officers.
All guards troops in the capital
were divided and assigned to the three camps.
Divided, they formed thirty camps;
combined, they were the Three Great Camps.
Throughout the emperor's reign,
this system was repeatedly changed.
Finally, the names of the central army, vanguards, and flanks were also abolished,
and they were simply referred to as battle and defense troops, simultaneously establishing a chariot camp.
In the past,
the Five Military Commands (Wǔjūn Fǔ) all established offices and issued seals,
managing military registers but not participating in training and maneuvers.
Officers for training and maneuvers were not issued seals.
The establishment of offices and seals for military administration (róngzhèng)
began with Chóu Luán.
As Chóu Luán was then favored and powerful,
he spoke to the emperor,
proposing to select 68,000 border troops
to take turns entering the capital for guard duty,
mixing and training with the capital forces.
He further ordered the commanders of the capital garrisons (Jīngyíng) to separately train the border troops,
thus bringing all border armies under the command of the capital.
When there was an alert at the frontier,
border generals could not mobilize their forces,
and border affairs further deteriorated.
After Chóu Luán died,
the officials of the Military Administration Bureau (Róngzhèng Tīng) that he had established were abolished,
but among the troops guarding the capital, only those from Gānsù were dismissed.
In the fourth year of Lóngqìng (1570),
Grand Secretary Zhào Zhēnjí requested to reclaim military authority
and reform the garrison system.
He strongly argued that the establishment of offices and casting of seals for military administration,
placing hundreds of thousands of men under one person's command,
was not the original intention of Tàizǔ and Chéngzǔ who divided command into separate commands and garrisons.
He requested to divide the 90,000 regular troops into five garrisons,
with each garrison selecting one general
to separately command and train them.
An imperial edict was issued for court officials to deliberate.
Minister Hò Ji
said, "The garrison system
was established after Shìzōng's careful consideration,
and should not be changed.
However, a grand general should not be solely established,
and military administration should not have seals.
I request to follow Zhēnjí's suggestion."
The imperial decree stated,
"Granted."
Consequently, each of the Three Great Garrisons (Sān Dà Yíng) appointed one Commander-in-Chief (Zǒngbīng)
and two Vice-Generals (Fùjiàng).
The assistant and subordinate officials
were adjusted in number,
each category totaling ten people.
The troops of the Five Military Commands (Wǔjūn Yíng)
were equally assigned to two garrisons,
each garrison having ten branches,
under the separate command of two Vice-Generals.
Marquises and Counts (Hóu Bó) served as Commanders-in-Chief,
later changed to Superintendents (Tídū).
Additionally, three civil officials were appointed,
also referred to as Superintendents.
After the establishment of six Superintendents,
each held their own opinions,
and matters often remained undecided for a month or more.
Censor Wēn Chún spoke of the drawbacks,
and so they were abolished,
with only two officials, the Governor-General (Zǒngdū) and Assistant (Xiélǐ), remaining.
In the second year of Wànlì (1574), following the request of Censor Ōuyáng Bó,
the military administration seal was reissued,
and two camp officers were eliminated.
In the fifth year (1577),
Censor Lín Jǐngyáng, who was inspecting the capital garrisons, requested extensive recruitment
and the establishment of elite vanguard forces (Xuǎnfēng).
At that time,
Zhāng Jūzhèng was in power,
scrutinizing names and actualities.
Many officials submitted proposals on military affairs,
with the main objectives being to ensure sufficient troops and select capable generals,
and garrison management was considerably improved.
After a long time,
the emperor tired of governance,
court officials gradually fell into factional disputes,
became accustomed to idleness and comfort,
and thus the system daily declined.
In the thirty-sixth year (1608),
Minister Lǐ Huàlóng managed military administration
and detailed the accumulated弊 (bì) in the capital garrisons.
An imperial edict was sent to the ministries for deliberation,
but ultimately nothing was revitalized.
When military incidents arose,
Zhào Shìxīn, the Governor-General of the capital garrisons, requested to relocate the training ground inside the city
for convenient drills.
Hú Láicháo, a Junior Supervisor of the Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Shàocīng), requested to transfer capital troops to garrison the borders,
which could transform weakness into strength.
Neither was of any practical use.
In the third year of Tiānqǐ (1623),
Assistant Minister Zhū Guāngzuò submitted a memorial to abolish the "old household troops" (lǎojiājūn)
and replace them with young and strong men.
The old household troops resented this,
throwing bricks and tiles at Zhū Guāngzuò,
and so the reform was not carried out.
At that time,
Wèi Zhōngxián was in power,
establishing internal training (nèicāo).
He also increased the number of eunuchs to serve as supervisors and minor eunuchs managing various posts (bǎpái),
and further recruited strong young men.
Many troops from various garrisons attached themselves to him.
When Emperor Zhuāngliè (Chóngzhēn) ascended the throne,
he dismissed the eunuchs,
but later reinstated them.
Lǐ Bānghuá, the Minister of Military Administration (Róngzhèng Shìláng), was indignant at the corruption of the capital garrisons.
He requested to eliminate the old, weak, and fraudulently listed soldiers,
and select capable and strong men to be the emperor's personal army.
The garrison soldiers were notoriously arrogant,
and some suspected this would lead to mutiny.
Meritorious relatives and palace eunuchs also hated Lǐ Bānghuá for harming their interests,
and daily rumors circulated.
The emperor dismissed Lǐ Bānghuá
and replaced him with Lù Wánxué,
who completely changed his methods.
Aside from the supervisors of the capital garrisons,
there were two officials in charge of overall policing,
and three officials in charge of supervising palace gates and inspecting and reviewing troops.
The emperor appointed eunuchs from the Directorate of Imperial Stables (Yùmǎjiān), Directorate of Ceremonial (Sīlǐjiān), and Secretariat (Wénshūfáng) to these positions,
thus bringing all garrison affairs under the control of eunuchs.
In the eighth month of the tenth year (1637),
the imperial carriage reviewed the city,
with armor and banners in grand display.
All officials followed, riding their horses with official belts.
The six armies, seeing the imperial carriage,
all shouted "Long Live the Emperor!"
The emperor was greatly pleased,
summoning Lù Wánxué into the imperial tent to commend and reward him,
offering him wine in a golden goblet.
However, it was merely a show for appearance's sake.
At this time, military affairs became increasingly urgent.
The emperor ordered capital troops to go out for defense and suppression,
all supervised by eunuchs.
Their provisions were generous,
and they were arrogant due to their power,
often seizing captives from others to claim merit,
and lightly humiliating various generals and soldiers,
causing the generals and soldiers to further lose cohesion.
Zhōu Yánrú re-entered the Grand Secretariat
and advised abolishing the internal training
and withdrawing all supervising eunuchs.
The capital troops returned to their garrisons.
At this time, the garrison generals and leading eunuch cronies
were ignorant of military matters.
Soldiers were merely registered to draw rations,
and the practice of hiring substitutes was rampant,
with one person in armor in the morning and another in the evening.
Although there were registers,
no one could identify them.
The emperor repeatedly issued edicts for training,
yet only two to three hundred people participated daily,
and they dispersed before dusk.
Countless capital garrison soldiers, numbering 100,000, escaped inspection and verification,
indulging in idleness and evading punishment.
The emperor once asked Minister of Military Administration Wáng Jiāyàn,
and Wáng Jiāyàn said,
"Today, only by strictly prohibiting the hiring of substitutes
and reforming the training methods can we perhaps save one in ten thousand,
but it is already too late."
The emperor was displeased and dismissed him.
In the sixteenth year (1643),
Lǐ Guózhēn, Earl of Xiāngchéng, took charge of military administration,
and eunuch Wáng Chéng'ēn supervised the capital garrisons.
The following year (1644),
rebel bandits entered Jūyōng Pass
and reached Shāhé.
The capital troops went out to resist,
but upon hearing the sound of cannons, they scattered and returned.
The bandits advanced unhindered to attack the imperial palace.
Only three thousand internal training troops guarded the ramparts,
and the capital thus fell.
Generally, the accumulated weakness of the capital army
was due to illicit occupation of posts and hiring of substitutes.
This malpractice truly originated from the effeminate garrison commanders
and the supervising eunuchs,
ultimately leading to the downfall of the dynasty.
As for the capital garrisons in the south,
after Yǒnglè's move north,
it was initially ordered that officials from the Central Office (Zhōngfǔ) managing its affairs should guard Nánjīng,
exercising control over the various guard stations (wèisuǒ) in the south.
In the early Hóngxī reign (1425),
eunuchs were appointed to concurrently serve as guardians.
In the late Xuāndé reign (1435),
officials for participating in military strategy (Cānzàn Jīwù Guān) were established.
During the Jǐngtài era (1450-1456),
assistant guardians (Xiétonng Shǒubèi Guān) were added.
In the late Chénghuà reign (1487),
the Minister of War of Nánjīng (Nánjīng Bīngbù Shàngshū) was ordered to participate in military strategy,
giving him exceptionally high regard among the five ministries.
Earlier,
the Divine Mechanism Camp (Shénjī Yíng) was established in the capital,
and one was also added in Nánjīng,
training together with the two large and small training grounds.
The soldiers drilled constantly without rest,
only excused during wind and rain.
For those who absconded from the roster,
Xiànzōng ordered censors (Nán Gěishì Yùshǐ) to periodically inspect the two training grounds.
Zhū Yí, Duke of Chéngguó, and eunuch Ān Níng found this inconvenient,
and deceitfully claimed that military affairs were secret,
and it was inappropriate for censors to question troop numbers.
The emperor punished the censors
and instead ordered the guardian and participating officials to conduct inspections,
making it a regulation.
During the Jiājìng reign,
officials repeatedly memorialized on the abuses of attrition and desertion in the Southern Camps.
In the winter of the 24th year, an imperial edict established the Zhènwǔ Camp,
staffing it with elite soldiers selected from various camps,
and supplementing them with agile and quick individuals from Huái and Yáng.
North of the Yangzi River, there was already the Chíhé Camp,
exclusively for garrisoning cities
and protecting imperial mausoleums.
Each of these two camps had three thousand soldiers,
commanded by meritorious ministers,
with separate training grounds established.
However, many of the soldiers in the Zhènwǔ Camp were ruffians.
When Supervising Minister of Revenue Huáng Màoguān curtailed their provisions,
they mutinied,
beating Màoguān to death.
An imperial edict ordered the execution of the ringleaders,
and appointed Minister of Revenue Jiāng Dōng as a Supervising Counselor.
Jiāng Dōng was excessively lenient,
which made the troops even more arrogant,
and they completely disregarded law and discipline.
Investigating Censor Wèi Yuánjí spoke about this,
and then recommended Vice Commander-in-Chief Liú Xiǎn from Zhè and Zhí to serve as the Grand Coordinator.
Before he arrived,
the Chíhé soldiers mutinied again,
beating Company Commander Wú Qīn.
An imperial edict ordered Liú Xiǎn to proceed immediately,
permitting him to bring five hundred Sichuan soldiers with him,
and only then was the situation stabilized.
In the first year of the Lóngqìng reign,
the Zhènwǔ Camp was abolished,
and its more than a thousand soldiers were reassigned to the two training grounds and the Shénjī Camp.
In the eleventh year of the Wànlì reign,
Supervising Counselor Pān Jìxún said:
"The original quota of training troops was one hundred and twenty thousand,
but now there are only a little over twenty thousand.
Ancestral troops and selected recruits are about half and half,
but selected recruits are not replaced as a rule,
which makes the camps empty.
I request that they be replenished like the ancestral troops."
Afterwards, Wáng Lín replaced Pān Jìxún
and said:
"The two training grounds, large and small,
have a total of over twenty-three thousand old and new officers and soldiers.
I request that, like the various frontier garrisons in Běijīng,
three thousand one hundred and twenty men form one contingent,
and each contingent be divided into central, left, and right platoons,
resulting in seven contingents.
The remainder should be placed under the flag and drum units,
to fill vacancies in various camps."
This was approved.
Supervising Censor Ruǎn Zǐxiào vehemently criticized the waste and abuses in the Southern Camps,
his words being very incisive,
yet ultimately no one rectified them.
Later,
following the request of Minister Wú Wénhuá,
the Supervising Counselor's authority over flags and warrants was increased,
allowing him to enforce military law
and also to exercise discretionary deployment.
In the thirty-first year, the Southern Central Army Standard Camp was established,
selecting over a thousand soldiers from the Grand Training Ground,
and appointing a Central Army Assistant Commander to train them.
Although the regulations were in place,
the times were accustomed to complacency,
and the state of affairs was as disorderly as in Běijīng.
By the Chóngzhēn reign,
when the roving bandits captured Lú and Fèng
and occupied the upper reaches of the river,
they had intentions of invading the secondary capital.
The officers and soldiers in the south were anxious day and night,
using the pretext of protecting imperial mausoleums and guarding the capital city,
merely hoping that the bandits would not move eastward.
Finally,
when Shǐ Kěfǎ served as Supervising Counselor and Minister,
he sought to revitalize the accumulated malpractices,
but he was dismissed before long,
so there is nothing further to say.
The system of Imperial Bodyguard Duty Guards.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne as King of Wú,
in the twelfth month of that year, the Gǒngwèi Division was established,
commanding marshals
and subordinate to the Capital Command.
In the second year of Hóngwǔ, it was renamed the Qīnjūn Dūwèi Command,
governing the Central, Left, Right, Front, and Rear Five Guard Armies,
and the Yíluán Division was subordinate to it.
In the sixth year, guard gold tablets were made,
fashioned from copper gilded with gold.
They were one foot long
and three inches wide.
They were marked with Rén, Yì, Lǐ, Zhì, Xìn as identification.
Both sides bore seal script: one said
"Guard,"
and the other said
"Accompanying the Emperor."
They were managed by the Shàngbǎo Division,
and guards wore them when on duty,
returning them when off duty.
In the fifteenth year, the command and division were abolished,
and the Jǐnyī Guard was established.
It had fourteen Northern and Southern Pacification Divisions,
subordinate to which were generals, strongmen, and marshals,
responsible for immediate imperial bodyguard duty, patrolling, and apprehending.
Later, the legitimate secondary sons of dukes, marquises, earls, grand commanders, and commanders were selected
to serve as meritorious guards and cavalry retainers,
while the Fǔjūn Qián Guard and the Qíshǒu and other twelve guards
each had blade-bearing officers.
The generals subordinate to the Jǐnyī Guard
were initially named Tiānwǔ,
later renamed Dàhàn Jiāngjūn,
totaling one thousand five hundred men.
They established company and battalion commanders,
and seven flag commanders.
Their troops formed a distinct army,
training off-duty as per regulations,
and were replenished only when vacancies reached fifty men.
Monthly provisions were two shí of grain,
and after accumulated service, they could be tested for promotion to company or battalion commander. If a commander died, his strapping and brave sons or younger brothers were allowed to replace him;
otherwise, common households were selected.
During the Yǒnglè reign,
the Five Armies and Three Thousand Camps were established.
Red Helmet and Bright Armor Generals were added, along with cross-bladed shield-bearers and similar personnel,
for imperial security.
Marshals and strongmen were conscripted from able-bodied commoners without serious illness or criminal record.
Strongmen were first subordinate to the Qíshǒu Guard,
later reassigned to the Jǐnyī and Téngxiáng Four Guards,
exclusively responsible for accompanying the emperor with drums and banners and guarding the four gates.
Marshals were originally subordinate to the Yíluán Division;
when the Division was changed to the Jǐnyī Guard,
they remained subordinate to it.
They were responsible for carrying the imperial regalia and ceremonial implements,
known as the Imperial Carriage,
Canopy Bearers,
Fan Bearers,
Banner and Staff Bearers,
Pennant and Streamer Bearers,
Sword Bearers,
Axe and Yue-Axe Bearers,
Ge-Halberd and Ji-Halberd Bearers,
Bow and Arrow Bearers,
and Horse Taming,
totaling ten divisions,
as well as imperial summons and dispatches before the carriage,
with duty rotations every three days.
Flag commanders and small flag commanders were established,
and led by meritorious imperial relatives.
There were six such officers in total: one commanding the Dàhàn Jiāngjūn, cavalry retainers, and blade-bearing officers of the Fǔjūn Qián Guard;
one commanding the cross-bladed shield-bearers of the Five Armies Camp;
and four commanding the Red Helmet Generals of the Shénshū Camp.
On imperial birthdays, New Year's Day, Winter Solstice, major sacrifices, oaths and prohibitions, enfeoffments, sacrificial missions, and issuing decrees, full duty was observed,
with three thousand men on duty;
otherwise, they rotated,
and their weapons, clothing, and positions were also slightly different.
For suburban sacrifices, imperial lectures, and imperial tours, attendance had specific regulations,
detailed in the Rites section.
Normally,
the duty generals waited outside the Wǔmén Gate morning and evening,
and at night they were responsible for the watches,
totaling one hundred men.
The cross-bladed officers and soldiers of the Five Armies
all lodged within the Imperial City.
The imperial bodyguard officers rotated duty,
one per day.
Only the generals commanding the Jǐnyī Guard and the cross-bladed shield-bearers
were on daily attendance.
The regulations for apprehension
and for those who abandoned their watch or left their post were particularly strict.
In total, there were one thousand five hundred and seven Dàhàn Jiāngjūn of the Jǐnyī Guard,
forty blade-bearing officers of the Fǔjūn Qián Guard,
two thousand five hundred Red Helmet Generals of the Shénshū Camp,
sixteen Battalion Commanders,
five hundred and two Bright Armor Generals,
two Battalion Commanders,
eight Dàhàn Jiāngjūn,
three thousand cross-bladed shield-bearers of the Five Armies Camp,
eight Battalion Commanders,
an unspecified number of meritorious guards and cavalry retainers,
and one hundred and eighty blade-bearing officers of the Qíshǒu and other guards.
This was a rough count of the imperial bodyguard personal armies.
After the Zhèngtǒng reign,
many sons and younger brothers of imperial consorts, princesses, dukes, marquises, and court eunuchs who received official appointments
were nominally registered in the Jǐnyī Guard.
During the Zhèngdé period,
those who memorialized for promotion or falsely claimed titles
also numbered no less than several hundred.
Wǔzōng enjoyed raising brave warriors,
and once assigned forty-seven company and battalion commanders
to be nominally Jǐnyī Guard officers receiving salaries and over one thousand one hundred others to serve as personal guards and brave warriors of the Imperial Stables Directorate,
receiving rations and training with cavalry.
He also ordered Dàhàn Jiāngjūn to be tested as provisional company commanders,
with full appointment after five years,
establishing this as a regulation.
As avenues for favor opened and imperial grace was over-extended,
the imperial security gradually became lax.
By the Wànlì era,
many guards evaded service or bought their way out of duty,
and these abuses were similar to those of the Three Great Camps.
Although a rule was established to strip those who left their posts of their monthly rations,
it could not be enforced.
When Tàizǔ established the Jǐnyīwèi,
it was solely responsible for ceremonial escorts.
At that time,
severe punishments were frequently used,
and offenders were often sent to the Jǐnyīwèi for interrogation and verification.
The Jǐnyīwèi's involvement in criminal investigations began from this point.
When Wénhuáng ascended the throne,
he relied on the Jǐnyīwèi as his close confidants.
Its subordinate Northern and Southern Commanderies (Zhènfǔsī)
—the Southern dealing with the Jǐnyīwèi's own criminal cases and military artisans,
while the Northern specialized in imperial prison cases—
would directly report on interrogations and submit petitions,
without informing the Jǐnyīwèi commander.
Their application of the law was harsh,
and the harm they caused was severe,
as detailed in the "Treatise on Penal Law."
Furthermore, the Jǐnyīwèi collected intelligence on the truth and falsehoods among the populace,
with "seal officials" (yìnguān) receiving imperial edicts to lead "officer-cadets" (guānxiào).
The eunuchs of the Dōngchǎng investigated affairs,
leading separate officer-cadets,
who were also allocated from the Jǐnyīwèi.
Because of this, they became entangled with the court eunuchs.
The defense of the Imperial City
used soldiers from twenty-two guards (wèi),
not just the Jǐnyīwèi army,
and gatekeeping was also overseen by the imperial guards on duty.
There were specialized officials for patrolling and policing the capital,
but Jǐnyīwèi officials were often ordered to assist.
Its proximity to power and influence
thus continued throughout the entire Míng dynasty.
Initially,
when Tàizǔ captured Wùzhōu,
he selected sons of wealthy families to serve as imperial guards,
calling them the "Imperial Central Army" (Yùzhōngjūn).
Later,
he established the "Commander-in-Chief of the Imperial Bodyguard" (Zhàngqián Zǒngzhì Qīnbīng Dūzhīhuǐshǐ).
Afterward, it was again abolished,
and a "Commander-in-Chief's Office" (Dūzhènfǔsī) was established,
subordinate to the Chief Military Commission (Dūdūfǔ),
managing the palace guards and patrols.
The ten guards—Jīnwú Front and Rear, Yǔlín Left and Right, Hǔbēn Left and Right, and Fǔjūn Left, Right, Front, and Rear—
would rotate on duty,
known as the "Imperial Guards" (Qīnjūn).
If they had a request,
they could directly report to the Ministry of War (Bù),
without involving the Chief Military Commission.
When the empire was pacified,
the Dūzhènfǔsī was renamed "Retained Guards" (Liúshǒu),
and five guards—Left, Right, Front, Rear, and Central—were established,
who were entrusted with the Inner Palace's bronze tallies.
Two men were dispatched daily for inspection,
and likewise at night,
these were the so-called "Imperial City Guard Officers and Soldiers."
In the 27th year, rules for Imperial City gatekeeping were further established.
For all court audiences,
when the gates first opened, the duty Dūdū, generals, and those with swords, commanders, chiliarchs, centurions, commandants, and palace attendants entered first,
then all officials entered in sequence.
The imperial guards on duty rotated every three days.
When eunuchs entered or exited, they had to match tallies and undergo strict searches.
Those exiting with gold and silks were inspected and their tallies verified,
while those entering with weapons or various medicines were arrested and dealt with.
Those who failed to notice were severely punished.
If commoners had matters to present,
they were not allowed to be forcibly stopped.
The Emperor, mindful of the guards' hardships,
ordered that if a family had unavoidable matters such as marriage, mourning, illness, or childbirth,
they could state their situation;
if a family had no other male adults,
and both parents were ill,
they were permitted leave to attend to them,
and return after recovery.
Before this,
when the new palace was completed,
an edict was issued to the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshūshěng) saying:
"Soldiers wounded or maimed in battle,
who cannot serve in the ranks,
can be housed in shelters built outside the palace walls,
working during the day
and patrolling at night."
Later,
it was decided that each of the twelve guards on imperial duty
would receive three hundred cash.
In the 28th year, shelters were again established at the four gates,
where "favored soldiers" (ēnjūn) were made to cook for the guards.
Favored soldiers were
those who had committed crimes and were spared death, and various surrendered soldiers.
During the Yǒnglè reign,
regulations were established:
each guard had its designated area.
From the Wǔmén to the left and right of the Chéngtiānmén,
extending to the left and right of the Cháng'ānmén,
and to the east and west of the Imperial City,
belonged to the Qíshǒu, Jìyáng, Jìchuān, Fǔjūn, Hǔbēn Right, Jīnwú Front, Yànshān Front, and Yǔlín Front eight guards.
From the left and right of the Dōnghuámén to the left and right of the Dōng'ānmén,
belonged to the Jīnwú, Yǔlín, Fǔjūn, and Yànshān four Left Guards.
From the left and right of the Xīhuámén to the left and right of the Xī'ānmén,
belonged to the four Right Guards.
From the left and right of the Xuánwǔmén to the left and right of the Běi'ānmén,
belonged to the Jīnwú, Fǔjūn Rear, Tōngzhōu, and Dàxīng four guards.
Each guard had a bronze tally,
issued by Tàizǔ.
They were named Chéng,
Dōng,
Xī,
and Běi,
each after its respective gate.
Patrollers held the left half,
and guardians held the right half.
When a guardian official met a patrol official,
they would match the tally and proceed with their duties.
The guard officials at each gate
would lead a patrol at night with bronze tallies and "Shēn" character plaques,
numbered from one to sixteen.
Inside the Imperial City were forty guard stations,
outside the Imperial City were seventy-two guard stations,
all equipped with bronze bells,
which were sounded in sequence.
Inside the Imperial City, there were one hundred "sitting watch generals" (zuògēng jiāngjūn) on the left and right,
twenty people per watch;
eight "running watch officials" (zǒugēng guān) at the four gates,
who would interchange and affix their seals to a register as verification.
One Dūdū, one sword-bearer, and one chiliarch or centurion each day
would lead the "Shēn" character plaques for night duty,
and inspect the soldiers at each gate.
Later, the Chief Military Commission was reformed,
and marquises (hóu) and earls (bó) were appointed to concurrently serve there.
In the early Hóngxī reign,
new hanging plaques for guards were made.
At that time, the imperial guards lacked sufficient personnel,
and guards could not be replaced.
The Emperor ordered the selection of soldiers from other guards to defend the Duān mén, Zhí mén, and other gates,
but Minister Lǐ Qìng deemed it inappropriate.
The Emperor said:
"A ruler cultivates virtue to win people's hearts.
If their hearts are won,
even if they are not favored confidants,
what is there to worry about?"
In the third year of Xuāndé, censors were ordered to inspect the guards.
During the Tiānshùn reign,
another supervising secretary (gěishìzhōng) was added.
In the tenth year of Chénghuà,
Minister Mǎ Wénshēng stated:
"Tàizǔ established the Imperial Guard Commanderies (Qīnjūn Zhīhuīshǐ Sī),
which were not subordinate to the Five Military Commissions.
Emperor Wén also re-established the twelve Imperial Guards,
and added several thousand 'Brave Warriors' (Yǒngshì),
who were subordinate to the Imperial Horse Bureau (Yùmǎjiān),
and were on imperial duty,
led by trusted confidant ministers.
Recently, they have become increasingly neglected and lax,
the Brave Warriors are no different from other camps,
within the Imperial City,
there are few military guards,
and the gatekeepers are particularly weak and infirm,
even unable to bear armor.
It is appropriate to instruct the officials of the Imperial Horse Bureau
to select and train the existing soldiers.
Furthermore, command the guard officials to always strictly maintain military order,
and diligently inspect those entering and exiting,
to prevent minor problems from escalating."
The Emperor agreed with his words,
but was unable to rectify the situation.
In the early Zhèngdé reign,
the patrols of the Imperial City's red outposts were strictly enforced,
with five commanders from the Liúshǒu guard ordered daily
to supervise the inner and outer night patrols.
One director (lángzhōng) and one secretary (zhǔshì) from the Ministry of War,
along with a censor and a Jǐnyīwèi official, would conduct inspections,
without undertaking other duties.
In the seventh year of Jiājìng, the clothing and rations for the on-duty officers and soldiers were increased,
issued once every five years.
In the eleventh year of Wànlì,
two "regional commanders" (bǎzǒng) were established inside and outside the Imperial City,
managing the east and west sections separately.
At that time, gate security became even more lax;
the guards were exploited by eunuchs,
often leaving their posts empty,
hiring street children or beggars to answer roll calls.
The "forked-knife" (chādāo) and "red-helmet" (hóngkuī) guards only reported for duty once the sun rose,
and their guardhouses were empty.
The sitting watch generals all paid monthly allowances to their subordinates.
All duties such as announcing names, patrolling the city, stamping registers, and running watches were abandoned.
In the fifteenth year, gate security was re-emphasized.
After a long time,
supervising secretary Wú Wénwěi requested the full restoration of the old system.
It was not granted.
In the last years,
there were cases of lost imperial tallies that were only discovered much later.
During the "Club Attack" incident (Tǐngjī zhī shì),
Zhāng Chà, a deluded man,
was able to intrude into the palace hall,
showing how deeply lax security had become.
Thereafter, affairs both within and outside the capital became numerous.
Although the Qǐ and Zhēn reigns repeatedly reiterated strictures,
they ultimately failed to reverse the decline,
which gradually led to the dynasty's demise.
The duties of the capital's patrol and arrest:
In the early Hóngwǔ reign,
the Bīngmǎ Sī was established,
to investigate fraud and treachery.
At night, patrol tallies were issued,
led by banner soldiers,
to inspect city gates, locks, and night travelers.
Later, zhènfǔguān of the Wèisuǒ were appointed,
and it was managed by the Zhōngjūn Dūdū Fǔ.
In the Yǒnglè reign,
the Wǔchéng Bīngmǎ Sī were added.
In the early Xuāndé reign,
as the Jīngshī suffered many robberies,
one hundred regular soldiers were added,
to assist the Wǔchéng in pursuing and arresting criminals.
Later,
an additional five hundred night patrol watchmen were added.
In the Chénghuà reign,
Jǐnyīguān were first ordered to supervise it together with censors.
In the last years of the reign,
two hundred troops from the training camps were allocated.
In Hóngzhì first year, four officers of zhǐhuī rank and below were selected from the Sānqiān Yíng,
to lead elite cavalry to patrol outside the Jīngchéng,
and five Jǐnyīguān,
and one wèiguān from the Qíshǒu and other Guards,
were assigned to different areas for patrolling and policing.
Patrol soldiers were issued tallies.
In the fifth year, bǎzǒng dūzhǐhuī were established,
specializing in patrol and arrest duties.
In the Zhèngdé reign,
additional bǎzǒng were established,
dividing the areas outside the Jīngchéng:
south to Hǎizi,
north to Jūyōng Guān,
west to Lúgōu Qiáo,
east to Tōngzhōu.
Two more officials were added within the city,
and supplemented by troops from the training camps,
and regulations for rewards and punishments for officers and soldiers were established.
In the last years of the reign,
the number of patrol soldiers increased to four thousand,
and cānjìang were specially appointed.
In Jiājìng first year, one more bǎzǒng was added for outside the city,
making a total of five, including the existing ones,
dividing jurisdiction over the two routes (east and west) within the city,
and the three routes (southwest, southeast, northeast) outside the city,
and the camp soldiers were increased to five thousand.
Furthermore, one in ten was selected,
establishing five hundred elite cavalry for scouting,
and their monthly stipends were increased.
Cānjìang were ordered to supervise their training,
and Bīngbù Láng supervised them.
At this time,
the Jīngjūn had long been corrupt and dilapidated,
and the patrol camps were no different.
In the thirty-fourth year,
there were only a little over three hundred soldiers.
Following the words of supervising secretary Qiū Yuè and others,
zhǐhuī Fán Jīng was stripped of his post,
and the private use of military horses for riding was prohibited.
In Wànlì twelfth year, following the deliberation of the Bīngbù,
if robberies occurred inside or outside the capital,
the Bīngmǎ Sī would be held responsible for incidents from mǎo (5-7 AM) to shēn (3-5 PM),
and patrol officers for incidents from yǒu (5-7 PM) to yín (3-5 AM);
if the bandits were numerous, they would cooperate to capture and suppress them.
After this,
the military quota doubled,
and when the emperor went out, or during court trials and prisoner registrations, they would form teams and station themselves at alley entrances.
Although the rosters were complete,
the soldiers and horses were actually depleted and insufficient for use.
There was one tídū for the patrol camps,
two cānjìang,
eighteen bǎzǒng,
eleven thousand patrol soldiers,
and five thousand horses.
Robbers ran rampant,
even stealing artifacts from within the palace.
Although their climbing ropes were found,
they could not be apprehended.
During the reign of Emperor Zhuāngliè,
the Bīngbù Zuǒ Shìláng was again appointed to special supervision.
However, half of the camp soldiers were ghost soldiers (drawing stipends without existing),
many horses were ridden by hired individuals,
and the strict limit for recovering stolen goods was only five days,
but soldiers continued to violate regulations as before.
As for the Sìwèi Yíng,
during the Yǒnglè reign,
returning soldiers who had fled to the north were used for horse-raising duties,
given grain and housing,
and called Yǒngshì.
Later, many were filled by those who presented horses,
and they were supervised and managed by officials from the Yùmǎ Jiān,
nominally belonging to the Yǔlín Guard,
but not actually under its direct command.
Soldiers falsely claimed identities,
and grain distribution could not be audited.
In Xuāndé sixth year, the Yǔlín Sānqiān Hùsuǒ was specially established to command them,
totaling over three thousand one hundred people.
Soon after, they were renamed Wǔxiáng and Téngxiáng Left and Right Guards,
known as the Sìwèi Jūn.
Four officers from these Guards were selected,
to serve as zuòyíng zhǐhuī,
supervised by eunuchs,
and trained separately from other camps,
known as "forbidden soldiers."
Their weapons and armor differed from other armies,
and they were stationed near the imperial carriage,
often embezzled by eunuch officials.
At the end of the Hóngzhì reign,
there were eleven thousand seven hundred eighty Yǒngshì,
and thirty thousand one hundred seventy banner soldiers,
with an annual expenditure of five hundred thousand piculs of grain.
Emperor Xiàozōng accepted the advice of court officials,
and audited them.
He also ordered that Yǒngshì presented by inner court officials,
must be verified and approved by the Bīngbù before being given stipends.
In the fifth year, their numbers were registered,
and this was made into a regulation.
This saved hundreds of thousands in annual expenditure.
When Emperor Wǔzōng ascended the throne,
the eunuch official Níng Jǐn requested to retain the number of people who had been eliminated.
Remonstrating officials and Minister Liú Dàxià argued against it,
but he did not listen.
Later, two offices were established,
and the Sìwèi Yǒngshì were selected to be subordinate to the Xīguāntīng,
managed by border general Jiāng Bīn, eunuch Zhāng Yǒng, and others.
When Emperor Shìzōng ascended the throne,
an imperial decree ordered that apart from the quota remaining from Hóngzhì eighteenth year,
all others should be cut,
and replacements must be investigated and approved by the Bīngbù.
As for the horses, cattle, and sheep of the Yùmǎ Jiān,
inspecting censorial officials were ordered to audit their numbers.
Soon after, an imperial edict exempted them from auditing,
and many horses were falsely added to the rolls.
A few years later,
the Yùmǎ Tàijiàn Mǐn Hóng again falsely issued an imperial decree to select Sìwèiguān.
Supervising secretary Zhèng Zìbì impeached him for deception and concealment,
but there was no response.
After a long time,
Bīngbù Shàngshū Lǐ Chéngxūn requested that the selection and audit should still be under the Ministry,
but the eunuch officials considered it inconvenient.
The emperor followed Lǐ Chéngxūn's advice.
In the sixteenth year, he again ordered the reinstatement of those who had been cut by the imperial edict upon his ascension,
totaling four thousand people.
Five years later,
an inner court official said,
that only over five thousand Yǒngshì remained,
and requested that sons and nephews be selected to fill the ranks,
to prepare for border alarms.
A Ministry official said:
"The original quota was five thousand three hundred thirty people.
In the eighth year, a clear audit,
already showed numbers exceeding the quota,
and moreover, this camp was not originally established for border defense."
The emperor followed the Ministry's deliberation.
However, abuses such as ghost enlistments, private employment, and false claims for grain continued as before.
In Wànlì second year, two zuòyíng guān were reduced.
Later,
it was again stipulated that vacancies for camp officers would be filled by selection from the Bīngbù.
Thereafter,
it was again obstructed by eunuch officials,
and still belonged to the Yùmǎ Jiān.
Many court officials commented on this,
but it could not be followed.
In the forty-second year,
supervising secretary Yáo Zōngwén inspected the camp,
saying:
"Of three thousand six hundred forty-seven guānyǒng,
only half were present.
Of one thousand forty-three horses,
none were present.
Of seven thousand two hundred forty official banner soldiers,
only over four thousand six hundred were present.
The same applied to their horses.
I request that this be handed over to the judicial offices for investigation and punishment."
The emperor could not investigate it.
At the end of the Tiānqǐ reign,
inspecting censor Gāo Hóngtú requested that following the example of the Sāndà Yíng,
they be divided into archers and crossbowmen, short-weapon soldiers, and firearms soldiers,
and be trained.
When Emperor Zhuāngliè was in power,
tídū inner court official Cáo Huàchún memorialized to rename it the Yǒngwèi Yíng,
appointing Zhōu Yùjí and Huáng Dégōng as commanders,
and it thus became a strong army,
which, when it went out to attack bandits,
always achieved success.
Huáng Dégōng's soldiers painted tiger heads on black cloth for their armor.
When bandits saw the Black Tiger Head Army,
most fled,
and it was said that their effectiveness surpassed that of the capital's main camps.
Collation Notes
Treatise Sixty-Six, Military Two: Wèisuǒ and Bānjūn.
Initially,
in the sixth year of Hóngwǔ (1373), Grand General Xú Dá and others were ordered to prepare defenses along the borders of Shānxī and Běipíng.
They were instructed to submit their respective strategic plans.
Following the advice of the Marquis of Huái'ān, Huá Yúnlóng,
from Yǒngpíng, Jìzhōu, and Mìyún westward for over two thousand Lǐ,
there were 129 passes and defiles,
all of which were garrisoned.
At Zǐjīngguān and Lúhuālǐng, chiliarchy commands (qiānhù suǒ) were established for defense.
An imperial edict also ordered the Shānxī Capital Garrison (dūwèi) to establish garrisons at Yànménguān, Tàihélǐng, and among the valleys of the Wǔ and Shuò mountains,
a total of seventy-three strategic passes,
all with stationed troops.
In the ninth year (1376), an imperial decree ordered the Yànshān Front, Rear, and other eleven garrisons (wèi)
to dispatch troops to guard 196 beacon towers at Gǔběikǒu, Jūyōngguān, Xǐfēngkǒu, and Sōngtíngguān,
using a mix of northern and southern soldiers.
In the fifteenth year (1382), an additional two hundred passes and defiles under the jurisdiction of the Běipíng Capital Command (dū sī)
were garrisoned by soldiers from various garrisons.
An edict commanded that the imperial princes near the frontier
were to
lead troops on border patrols every autumn.
In the seventeenth year (1384), Xú Dá was ordered to register the officers and soldiers in Běipíng.
He was further ordered to audit the officers and troops of the Liáodōng, Dìngliáo, and other nine garrisons.
Thereafter,
various dukes and marquises were regularly dispatched to inspect the frontier troops and horses
for registration.
In the twentieth year (1387), the Běipíng Provisional Capital Command (xíng dū sī) was established in Dàníng.
Its location was outside Xǐfēngkǒu,
the former Liáoxī Commandery,
and the Central Capital (zhōngjīng) Dàdìngfǔ of the Líao dynasty;
it was west of Dàtóng,
east of Liáoyáng,
and north of Běipíng.
When Féng Shèng defeated Nàhāchū
and returned with his army,
he fortified the city.
Consequently, a capital command and the Yíngzhōu Five Tún Garrisons were established,
and the imperial prince Quán was enfeoffed as the Prince of Níng.
Troops from various garrisons were transferred to guard it.
Earlier,
Lǐ Wénzhōng and others captured Yuán's Shàngdū,
establishing the Kāipíng Garrison and the Xīnghé and other chiliarchy commands;
there were four relay stations (yì) each to the east and west,
the east connecting to Dàníng,
and the west to Dúshí.
In the twenty-fifth year (1392), Dōngshèng City was built to the east of the Shòuxiáng City in Hézhōu,
and sixteen garrisons were established.
It faced Dàtóng,
and from Liáo westward,
the defense lines were interconnected for thousands of Lǐ.
In the first year of Jiànwén (1399),
Emperor Wén (Yǒnglè Emperor) raised an army
and attacked and captured Dàníng,
bringing the Prince of Níng, Quán, and all the armies back.
Upon his ascension to the throne,
the Prince of Níng was enfeoffed in Jiāngxī.
The Běipíng Provisional Capital Command was renamed the Dàníng Capital Command
and relocated to Bǎodìng.
The Yíngzhōu Five Tún Garrisons were transferred to Shùnyì, Jìzhōu, Pínggǔ, Xiānghé, and Sānhé,
and the Dàníng territory was ceded to the Wùliánghā.
From then on,
the mutual support between Liáodōng and Xuān-Dà was cut off.
Moreover, Dōngshèng was isolated and difficult to defend,
so the Left Garrison was relocated to Yǒngpíng,
and the Right Garrison to Zūnhuà,
leaving its original site deserted.
Earlier, Xīnghé was also abolished,
Kāipíng was moved to Dúshí,
and Xuānfǔ consequently became a major strategic town.
Nevertheless, the Emperor was very diligent in frontier defense.
From Xuānfǔ westward to Shānxī,
along the border, there were steep walls and deep moats everywhere,
with beacon towers connected.
Passes traversable by chariots and cavalry were guarded by one hundred households,
while those used by woodcutters and herdsmen were guarded by ten armored soldiers.
The Marquis of Wǔ'ān, Zhèng Hēng, served as the Grand Commander.
His imperial decree stated:
"All beacon mounds (yāndūn)
must be increased in height and thickness,
storing five months' provisions, firewood, medicine, and crossbows.
Wells should be dug next to the mounds,
and outside the wells, walls should be built level with the mounds,
appearing as one from the outside."
The intention of defending against raids with strong gates
was always paramount.
In the first year of Hóngxī (1425),
Bái Róng, a soldier from Shuòzhōu, requested the return of the Dōngshèng, Gāoshān, and other ten garrisons to their original locations.
Fàn Jì, a soldier from Xīngzhōu, also stated that
Shuòzhōu, Dàtóng, Kāipíng, Xuānfǔ, and Dàníng were crucial frontier strongholds.
Their land was arable,
and it was advisable to send generals with troops
to repair fortresses
and expand agricultural garrisons.
Neither proposal was adopted.
In the first year of Zhèngtǒng (1436),
Censor Zhū Chún requested the repair of the frontier wall.
Grand Commander Tán Guǎng said:
"From Lóngmén to Dúshí and Hēiyùkǒu, over 550 Lǐ,
the construction work is very difficult.
It would be better to increase beacon towers and watchtowers for observation."
Consequently, twenty-two beacon mounds were added to forts like Chìchéng.
Grand Commander Shǐ Zhāo of Níngxià said:
"The garrisons and forts under my jurisdiction
are all outside the river.
From the river eastward to Cháhǎnnáor,
reaching Suídézhōu,
the desert is vast and remote,
with no defenses whatsoever.
I request the construction of a scout cavalry camp at Huāmǎchí."
Grand Commander Fāng Zhèng of Dàtóng subsequently requested a cavalry camp,
intending to repair and rebuild a ruined camp at Bànlǐng Hóngsì'er.
Li Yí, the巡抚 (xúfǔ) and Chief Censor (dūyùshǐ) of Xuān-Dà, stating that Dàtóng was flat and open,
and scouting should be meticulous,
requested that a Vice Grand Commander be in charge of the eastern route,
and a Brigadier General (cānjīang) be in charge of the western route,
while the area to the north would belong to the Grand Commander and Chief Military Commissioner (dū zhīhuī).
All proposals were implemented as advised.
Three years later,
an edict ordered the blocking of various passes at Zǐjīngguān
and the increase of garrison troops.
At that time, the Wǎlà were gradually growing stronger,
and this followed the request of the Duke of Chéng, Zhū Yǒng.
Soon after, Yěxiān invaded the frontier,
and Emperor Yīngzōng was captured at Tǔmù.
Upon Emperor Jǐng's ascension to the throne,
over the next ten years,
border troubles increased daily.
Suǒlái, Máolǐhái, Āluóchū, and their kind
successively invaded,
leaving no peaceful year.
In the first year of Chénghuà (1465),
Grand Commander Zhāng Jié of Yánsuī said:
"The territories of Yánqìng and others span a thousand Lǐ,
with twenty-five camps and forts under jurisdiction,
each having only one or two hundred men,
making it difficult to resist the enemy.
It is advisable to select nine thousand elite troops to form six patrols,
stationing them in the two counties of Fǔgǔ and Shénmù,
the two cities of Lóngzhōu and Yúlín,
and the two forts of Gāojiā and Ānbiān,
so that there will be preparations for emergencies."
He also requested the deployment of over two thousand Fū and Qìng autumn defense troops to crucial points along the border.
This was adopted.
In the seventh year (1471),
Yú Zǐjùn, the Patrol Censor (xúnfǔ) and Chief Censor (dūyùshǐ) of Yánsuī, greatly built up the border city walls.
Earlier,
the Dōngshèng Garrison was located outside the river,
and Yúlín was administered from Suídé.
Later, Dōngshèng was moved inland,
losing its strategic advantage,
and the lands of Mǐzhī and Yúhé, nearly three hundred Lǐ, were abandoned.
During the Zhèngtǒng reign,
Garrison Commander Wáng Zhēn first built Yúlín City,
and established twenty-four camps and forts along the border.
Each year, troops from the Yán'ān, Suídé, and Qìngyáng Garrisons were dispatched for rotation.
During the Tiānshùn era,
Āluóchū entered Hétào and pastured there,
often leading various tribes to invade the interior.
At this point,
Yú Zǐjùn moved the administration to Yúlín.
From Huángfǔchuān westward to Dìngbiānyíng, for over 1200 Lǐ,
beacon towers and forts were visible everywhere,
horizontally blocking the Hétào entrance.
Inside, mountains were cut and valleys filled,
called Jiādào (gorge path),
extending east to Piāntóu,
and west to Níng and Gù.
The local conditions were harsh,
with brave generals and strong soldiers.
Northerners called it "Luòtuó Chéng" (Camel City).
In the twelfth year (1476),
Téng Zhāo, Vice Minister of War (bīngbù shìláng), and Zhāng Mào, Duke of Yīngguó, submitted a report on border defenses,
stating:
"Jūyōngguān, Huánghuāzhèn, Xǐfēngkǒu, Gǔběikǒu, and Yànhéyíng are guarded by fifteen thousand cavalry and infantry from the 'group camps' (tuányíng).
We request an additional five thousand troops
to be stationed in Yǒngpíng and Mìyún to support Liáodōng.
Liángzhōuzhèn Fānbān, Zhuānglàng, and the west of Hélánshān,
crossing the river from Xuěshān,
connecting south to Jìnglǔ,
all the way to Lín and Gǒng,
are all routes for enemy incursions.
We request the transfer of Shǎnxī official troops.
In addition, troops from Gān, Liáng, Lín, Gǒng, Qín, Píng, Hé, and Táo
should be stationed at Āndìng and Huìníng to intercept in case of alarm;
five thousand elite soldiers from Liángzhōu
should be stationed at strategic points
for mutual support."
The edict approved it.
In the twenty-first year (1485),
an imperial decree ordered all frontier soldiers
to conduct regular drills every year from September to March of the following year,
and to report on the drilled troops and horses,
as well as days excused due to wind and snow.
Border defenses were quite well maintained.
In the 14th year of Hóngzhì
Previously,
Gùyuán was considered inland territory,
with its defenses aimed only at Jìnglǔ.
When Huǒshāi entered and occupied Hétào,
it became a crucial front against the enemy.
Therefore, Kāichéng Xiàn of Píngliáng was reorganized as Gùyuán Zhōu,
to which four Wèi were subordinated.
A Zǒngzhì Fǔ was established,
to oversee the military affairs of Shǎnxī's three frontiers.
At this time, among the Shǎnxī frontiers, only Gānsù was relatively peaceful,
while Hāmì was repeatedly harassed by Tǔlǔfān.
Consequently, an imperial edict ordered the repair of Jiāyùguān.
In the spring of the 1st year of Zhèngdé
Yáng Yīqīng, the Zǒngzhì Sānbiān Dūyùshǐ, requested to re-establish a garrison at Dōngshèng,
"using the river as a defense,
connecting to Dàtóng in the east,
and Níngxià in the west,
so that the thousand-mile fertile land of Hétào
would return to our cultivation and pasture.
Then Shǎnyòu could find respite."
He also submitted six proposals, including the construction of Dìngbiān Yíng.
The emperor approved his memorial.
Soon after, he was dismissed for offending the eunuch Liú Jǐn,
and the constructed frontier wall extended only some forty *lǐ*.
Wǔzōng was fond of military matters,
and frontier generals such as Jiāng Bīn gained favor.
Many troops from the four garrisons of Liáodōng, Xuānfǔ, Dàtóng, and Yánsuī were transferred inland.
Additionally, 6,000 京軍 and 6,000 Xuānfǔ troops
were rotated in spring and autumn.
In the 13th year
Yánsuī would be subject to deployment by Xuān and Dà;
if they crossed the river,
Xuān and Dà would be subject to deployment by Yánsuī.
This followed the proposal of Wáng Qióng, the Bīngbù Shàngshū.
Initially,
when Dàníng was abandoned,
its territory was given to the Wūliánghǎ Sān Wèi (Wūyán, Fúyú, and Tàiníng),
who were originally attached to the court.
Before long,
they became unruly.
Xuānzōng once, while hunting,
personally led an army and defeated them.
From then on, they were awed and submissive.
Thus, Xǐfēng and Mìyún only had Dūzhīhuī stationed to guard them.
During the Tǔmù Incident,
it was widely rumored that the Sān Wèi had aided the rebels.
Later, officials such as Tàijiàn Cāncānjìang were added.
By this time,
Wūyán alone had become powerful,
and their intentions were unpredictable.
In the early Jiājìng period [1522-1566],
the Yùshǐ Qiū Yǎnghào requested to re-establish outposts like Xiǎohé on the outer frontier,
to control strategic points.
He also requested to cast more firearms,
distribute them to the border prefectures and counties,
recruit merchants to purchase grain,
and fill the stores of various frontier Wèi Suǒ.
The imperial edict ordered all these to be implemented.
Originally,
during Tàizǔ's time,
because the border armies' agricultural self-sufficiency was insufficient,
merchants were summoned to transport grain to the border and were given salt in return.
Wealthy merchants and powerful traders all contributed their own funds and labor,
recruiting people to cultivate land at the frontier.
Thus, border supplies were not depleted.
During the Hóngzhì period,
Yè Qí, the Hùbù Shàngshū, initiated a reform,
ordering merchants to deposit silver in the Tàicāng,
which was then distributed to various frontiers.
Merchants all abandoned their businesses and returned home,
border areas became desolate,
rice and grain prices soared,
and the border armies consequently suffered daily.
In the 11th year
Yùshǐ Xú Rǔguī submitted a memorial detailing frontier defense provisions,
stating that
"Yánsuī should transport grain from Shízhōu and Báodé,
traveling upstream along the Yellow River.
Húbú grain should go via Yúnyáng,
Biàn grain via Shǎn and Luò,
and Miǎn grain via Hànzhōng,
to reach Shǎnyòu.
Xuān and Dà produce two crops of wheat,
and should procure grain in various ways.
For Zǐjīng, Dàomǎ, Báiyáng, and other passes,
merchants should be recruited to hire carts for transport."
He also requested
"to station Xuānfǔ's mobile troops at Yòuwèi Huáilái,
to reinforce Dàtóng.
Select and appoint mobile troops at Shùnshèng Xīchéng for emergency reinforcement.
Mobile troops from Yǒngníng and other places should guard Xuānfǔ,
ready for deployment.
Eight prefectures of Zhílì should recruit brave militia for training,
to respond to urgent needs at the border, near and far.
Yúlín, Shān, and Shǎn mobile troops
should assist in their respective areas."
The report was approved,
but also could not be fully implemented.
In the 18th year
At this time,
Ándá and his tribes were strong and unruly,
repeatedly penetrating the territories of Dàtóng and Tàiyuán,
leaving the north and south of Jìnyáng desolate with smoke and fire.
Chén Jiǎng, the Xúnfǔ Dūyùshǐ, requested
"to station 6,000 troops at Chángyù, the eastern boundary of Lǎoyíngbǎo,
and to have Shānxī troops guard Dàtóng.
Regarding the strategic points of the Three Passes,
Níngwǔ is the central route,
most crucial at Shénchí;
Piāntóu is the western route,
most crucial at Lǎoyíngbǎo;
both should have Cānjìang appointed.
Yànmén is the eastern route,
most crucial at the various passes like Běilóu;
Bǎzǒng and Zhīhuī should be added.
And the Shénchí Shǒubèi should be moved to Lìmínbǎo,
the Lǎoyíngbǎo Yóují to Bājiǎosuǒ,
each with increased troops and equipment."
The emperor granted all his requests.
Although the plans were detailed,
the soldiers and generals were mostly timid and weak;
the capable ones could merely defend themselves.
In the 22nd year
According to old regulations,
the Zǒngbīng would be stationed in shifts at border forts during summer and autumn,
which was called 'dark ambush.'
By this time,
officials suggested
that all troops should go to the border in autumn,
divide their areas and defend,
and return after mid-ninth month,
rewarded with treasury silver.
After a long time,
this was abolished due to the labor and expense.
In the 24th year
Chén Háo, the Xún'àn Shānxī Yùshǐ, stated:
"The enemy has invaded Shānxī three times,
causing millions of casualties,
and spending six billion *liǎng* of silver in provisions,
yet achieved not an inch of merit.
I request to decide on a decisive battle,
and fully recover the Hétào territory."
The next year
the enemy attacked Yán'ān.
Zēng Xiǎn, the Zǒngdū Sānbiān Shìláng, strongly advocated for the recovery of Hétào,
and listed eighteen proposals.
The emperor praised him.
However, Dàxuéshì Yán Sōng, perceiving the emperor's reluctance for war,
and also wanting to kill the former cabinet minister Xià Yán,
impeached Zēng Xiǎn.
Both Zēng Xiǎn and Xià Yán were executed.
From then on, no one dared to speak about frontier affairs.
In the 29th year
Ándá attacked Gǔběikǒu,
entering through the secret path of Huángyúgōu,
and advanced directly to Dōngzhímén.
The generals dared not fight.
When the enemy retreated,
Dàjiàngjūn Qiú Luán strongly advocated for the proposal of tribute and market trade.
The next year
but raids and plundering continued as before.
The year after that
the horse market was abolished.
Initially,
border administration was strict and clear.
All imperial army soldiers had fixed duties.
The Zǒngbīngguān (Commander-in-Chief) commanding the army was the main force.
The Fù Zǒngbīng (Deputy Commander-in-Chief) led three thousand men as irregular forces.
The Yóují (Guerrilla Commander) led three thousand men for mobile defense as roving forces.
The Cānjiāng (Assistant Regional Commander) guarded various routes, providing East-West support as relief forces.
Camps, forts, and signal towers were classified as primary strategic points (jí chōng) or secondary strategic points (cì chōng),
determining the number of troops to be stationed.
During peacetime, drills, scouting, lookout duty, and clearing wild growth were all undertaken,
with no one daring to be negligent.
Even slight deviations from regulations
would result in punishment according to military law.
But afterwards, all these were abandoned and ruined.
Along the coast,
from Guǎngdōng's Lèhuì, bordering Ānnán,
five thousand lǐ to Mǐn,
then another two thousand lǐ to Zhè,
then another two thousand lǐ to Nán Zhílì,
then another eighteen hundred lǐ to Shāndōng,
then another twelve hundred lǐ past Bǎodǐ and Lúlóng to Liáodōng,
then another thirteen hundred lǐ to the Yālù Jiāng.
Island pirates and Japanese raiders
appeared and disappeared everywhere,
so coastal defense was also important.
In the first year of Wú (1367), following the suggestion of Lǐ Wénzhōng, Píngzhāng (Chancellor) of Zhèjiāng Xíngshěng (Branch Secretariat),
Jiāxīng, Hǎiyán, and Hǎiníng all had troops stationed for garrison duty.

In the twelfth month of the fourth year of Hóngwǔ (1371), Jinghai Hóu Wú Zhēn was ordered to register the soldiers from Wēn, Tái, and Qìngyuán prefectures who were part of Fāng Guózhēn's forces, as well as landless peasants from Lánxiù Shān,
totaling over one hundred and ten thousand people,
to be assigned to various Weì (guards) as soldiers.
It was also forbidden for coastal residents to privately go out to sea.
At that time, many remnants of Guózhēn and Zhāng Shìchéng's forces hid on islands,
colluding with Japanese raiders to become pirates.
In the fifth year (1372), Zhèjiāng and Fújiàn were ordered to build warships for defense against the Japanese.
The following year (1373), following the suggestion of Déqìng Hóu Liáo Yǒngzhōng,
the four Weì of Guǎngyáng, Jiāngyīn, Hénghǎi, and Shuǐjūn were ordered to add many multi-oared fast boats.
When there was no trouble, they would patrol;
when encountering pirates, large ships would engage in close combat,
and fast boats would pursue them.
An imperial edict appointed Zhēn as Zǒngbīngguān,
leading the troops of the four Weì,
and all imperial Weì and coastal Weì troops were subject to his command.
Every spring, a naval force would set out to sea,
patrolling various routes against the Japanese,
and returning in autumn.
In the seventeenth year (1384), Xìnguó Gōng Tāng Hé was ordered to inspect the coast
and build various coastal cities in Shāndōng, Jiāngnán, and Zhèjiāng East and West.
Three years later (1387), Jiāngxià Hóu Zhōu Déxīng was ordered to conscript one-third of the able-bodied men from the four prefectures of Fú, Xīng, Zhāng, and Quán in Fújiàn
to serve as coastal garrison troops,
obtaining fifteen thousand men.
Weìsuǒ (guard stations) were moved to strategic locations,
and sixteen cities were built.
Furthermore, the four Weì of Dìnghǎi, Pánshí, Jīnxiāng, and Hǎimén were re-established in Zhèjiāng,
Jīnshān Weì at Xiǎoguānchǎng in Sōngjiāng,
and the two Qiānhùsuǒ (thousand-household garrisons) of Qīngcūn and Nánhuìzuǐ City.
Línshān Weì was also established in Shàoxīng,
along with the Qiānhùsuǒ of Sānshān and Lìhǎi.
And in Níngbō, Wēn, and Tái and coastal areas,
eight Qiānhùsuǒ had already been established,
namely Píngyáng, Sānjiāng, Lóngshān, Kuò●, Dàsōng, Qiáncāng, Xīnhé, and Sōngmén,
all garrisoned with troops for defense.
In the twenty-first year (1388), Hé was again ordered to inspect Mǐn (Fújiàn) and Yuè (Guǎngdōng),
building cities and increasing troops.
Five Fújiàn Coastal Zhǐhuīshǐ Sī (Commanderies) were established,
named Fúníng, Zhèndōng, Pínghǎi, Yǒngníng, and Zhènhǎi.
They commanded twelve Qiānhùsuǒ,
named Dàjīn, Dìnghǎi, Méihuā, Wàn'ān, Púxǐ, Chóngwǔ, Fúquán, Jīnmén, Gāopǔ, Liù'áo, Tóngshān, and Xuánzhōng.
In the twenty-third year (1390), following the suggestion of Weì (guard) soldier Chén Rén,
sea vessels were built for Sūzhōu's Tàicāng Weì.
Soon after, coastal Weìsuǒ,
every Bǎihù (hundred-household unit) and Xúnjiǎnsī (patrol and inspection post) were ordered to each have two ships
to patrol the sea against pirates.
Later, following the suggestion of Shāndōng Dū Sī (Provincial Military Commissioner) Zhōu Yàn,
five Zǒngzhài (main garrisons) were built in Nínghǎi Weì,
which, with the eight Zǒngzhài of Láizhōu Weì,
jointly administered forty-eight Xiǎozhài (sub-garrisons).
Later,
venerable ministers and meritorious relatives like Wèiguó Gōng Xú Huīzǔ were again ordered to inspect the coast in separate groups.
The Emperor had always resented Japan's duplicity
and cut off their tribute envoys,
so there was no major trouble throughout the Hóngwǔ and Jiànwén reigns.
In the sixth year of Yǒnglè (1408), Fēngchéng Hóu Lǐ Bīn and others were ordered to suppress Japanese pirates along the coast,
and islanders, Tànhù (boat-dwelling households), merchants, and fishing families were again recruited as soldiers,
making defenses even stricter.
In the seventeenth year (1419),
Japanese pirates raided Liáodōng,
and Zǒngbīngguān Liú Jiāng annihilated them at Wànghǎiguō.
From then on, the Japanese were greatly intimidated,
and for over a hundred years,
there were no major invasions at sea.
The court merely ordered senior officials to patrol and inspect every few years.
By the mid-Jiājìng period (1522-1566),
Japanese pirate troubles gradually arose,
and a Xúnfǔ (Provincial Governor) for Zhèjiāng, concurrently overseeing Fújiàn's naval affairs as Tídū Jūnwù Dū Yùshǐ (Grand Censor Supervising Military Affairs), was first established.
Later,
the title Xúnfǔ was changed to Xúnshì (Inspector).
Before long,
Japanese piracy became even more rampant.
So, a Jīnshān Cānjiāng was added,
to guard the sea defenses of Sū and Sōng.
Soon after, this was changed to Fù Zǒngbīng,
and troops were transferred and recruited from Jiāngnán and Jiāngběi,
with officials and commoners from Xú and Pī filling the fighting and defending ranks.
Háng, Jiā, and Hú also saw the addition of Cānjiāng and Bīngbèi Dào (Military Preparedness Intendants).
In the thirty-third year (1554), Shāndōng militia and a thousand land and sea musketeers from Qīngzhōu were dispatched to Huái and Yáng,
to be at the disposal of Zǒngdū Nánzhí Jūnwù Dū Yùshǐ Zhāng Jīng.
At that time, the Japanese pillaged Háng, Jiā, Sū, and Sōng,
occupying Zhélín City as their base.
Both sides of the Great River were disturbed.
Jiānsī Rèn Huán defeated them,
and Jīng also achieved victory at Wángjiā Jìng.
The pirates then fled to sea,
and again attacked Sūzhōu.
Thereupon, Nánjīng Yùshǐ (Censor of Nanjing) Tú Zhònglǜ proposed five measures.
Regarding guarding sea entrances, he said:
"Guard Píngyáng Gǎng and Huánghuā'ào,
holding the strategic points of Hǎimén,
so that Wēn and Tái cannot be attacked.
Guard Nínghǎi Guān and Hútóu Wān, blocking the mouths of the Sānjiāng,
so that Níng and Shào cannot be spied upon.
Guard Biēzǐmén and Zhàpǔ Xiá,
so that Háng and Jiā cannot be approached.
Guard Wúsōng, Liújiā Hé, and Qīyā Gǎng,
so that Sū and Sōng cannot be ambushed.
Furthermore, naval vessels should be repaired and equipped,
of varying sizes,
with a hundred or fifty linked into one unit (●),
recruiting experienced sailors to command them,
and manning them with the original quota of naval soldiers,
placing defenses at various sea entrances according to urgency."
The Board approved his proposal.
Soon after,
the Ministry of War also stated:
"The area between Zhè, Zhí, Tōng, and Tài is most suitable for naval warfare.
In the past, sand-junks were often used to defeat pirates;
we request generous rewards to attract them.
For defense,
guarding the sea islands is paramount.
It is advisable to use sand-junks from Tàicāng, Chóngmíng, Jiādìng, and Shànghǎi, and ships from Fúcāng, Dōngguǎn, etc., to guard Pǔtuó and Dàqú.
Chénqián Shān is the beginning of the dividing line between Zhè and Zhí,
and Láng and Fú mountains control the head and tail,
connecting the river and the ocean,
also a crucial area.
It is advisable to urge the navy to firmly defend it."
The report was approved.
Later,
Yóubīng (Roving troops) were again ordered to be added to the five main garrisons of Zhílì's Wúsōng Jiāng, Liújiā Hé, Fúshān Gǎng, Zhènjiāng, and Chuí Shān,
under the command of the Jīnshān Fù Zǒngbīng.
At that time, Hú Zōngxiàn was Zǒngdū (Supreme Commander),
and he executed the sea pirates Xú Hǎi and Wāng Zhí.
Zhí's three thousand men again colluded with Japanese invaders,
and Mǐn and Guǎng were further disturbed.
In the thirty-seventh year (1558),
Dū Yùshǐ Wáng Xún requested
"to divide Fújiàn's Fú and Xīng into one route,
led by a Cānjiāng,
stationed at Fúníng,
with naval defenses from Liú Jiāng, Fēnghuǒ Mén, Yú Shān, and Xiǎochéng to Nánrì Shān;
Zhāng and Quán into one route,
led by a Cānjiāng,
stationed at Zhào'ān,
with naval defenses from Nánrì Shān to Wúyǔ, Tóngshān, Xuánzhōng, Zǒumǎ Xī, and Ānbiān Guǎn.
Both naval and land forces would be subject to their command.
Fújiàn's provincial capital is situated between north and south,
only fifty lǐ from the sea.
It is advisable to establish another Cānjiāng,
select and recruit elites to lead scouting vessels,
to support the main and auxiliary forces."
The Board replied and followed this.
Guǎngdōng's Huì and Cháo also saw the addition of a Cānjiāng,
stationed at Jiēyáng.
Fújiàn Xúnfǔ Dū Yùshǐ Yóu Zhèndé said:
"Zhèjiāng's Wēn and Chǔ border Fúníng,
where Japanese pirates appear and disappear.
It is advisable to promote Qī Jìguāng to Fù Zǒngbīng,
to guard it.
And add a Fúníng Shǒubèi (Defense Commander),
subordinate to Jìguāng.
A Shǒubèi should also be added at Zhāngzhōu's Yuègǎng,
subordinate to Zǒngbīngguān Yú Dàyóu.
Yán, Jiàn, and Shào are the upper reaches of the eight Mǐn regions,
and troops should be recruited to prepare for emergencies."
All were approved for implementation.
Later,
Zōngxiàn was arrested,
the Zǒngdū position was abolished,
and Zhèjiāng Xúnfǔ Zhào Bǐngrán concurrently managed military affairs.
Bǐngrán then requested that the Dìnghǎi Zǒngbīng be subordinate to Zhèjiāng,
the Jīnshān Zǒngbīng be subordinate to Nán Zhí,
both concurrently managing naval and land military affairs,
mutually supporting each other.
Afterwards,
the Japanese pirate invasion of Pútián was pacified,
and the old system of five naval camps was restored.
The Five Stockades were
Fúníng’s Fēnghuǒmén,
Fúzhōu’s Xiǎochéng’ào,
Xīnghuà’s Nánrìshān,
Quánzhōu’s Wúyǔ,
Zhāngzhōu’s Xīmén'ào,
also known as Tóngshān.
In the third year of Jǐngtài,
