the Minister of Garrison, Xuē Xīliǎn, proposed their establishment,
but they were later abolished.
At this point, Grand Coordinator Tán Lún submitted a memorial stating:
“The Five Stockades guard the outer sea,
a very thorough and comprehensive method,
and should be restored to their former state.
Fēnghuǒmén, Nánrì, and Wúyǔ three [missing character] should be designated as main troops,
while Tóngshān and Xiǎochéng two [missing character] should be designated as skirmishers.
Each stockade should have a Bǎzǒng,
divided patrol areas,
clear watchtowers,
and strict joint patrols.
The three-route Cāncéngs should be changed to Shǒubèi.
The newly recruited Zhè soldiers should be divided into two shifts,
each with nine thousand men,
rotating in spring and autumn.
The local militia from each county should all be supplemented with elite and fierce individuals,
with one military officer leading each prefecture,
and the Commissioner of Military Affairs inspecting them periodically.”
The Emperor approved all of it.
Lángshān originally had a Fù Zǒngbīng,
but at this time, it was changed to a Zhènshǒu Zǒngbīngguān,
concurrently overseeing the north and south of the great river.
By the early years of Lóngqìng,
Japanese pirates gradually ceased to be a major threat,
but various small bandits often appeared.
In the third year of Wànlì, a Guǎngdōng Nán'ào Zǒngbīngguān was established,
because it controlled the vital areas of Zhāng and Quán.
Japanese pirates invaded Cháoxiān,
and the imperial court dispatched a large army to assist,
for six years consecutively.
Consequently, a Xúnfǔ officer was established in Tiānjīn,
to defend the Jīdiàn.
More than ten years later,
following the suggestion of the Southern Zhílì Investigating Censor Yán Sīzhōng,
six hundred soldiers from the Huái'ān Grand Camp were deployed to guard Liáojiǎozuǐ.
Following the suggestion of Fújiàn Grand Coordinator Dīng Jìsì,
troops were stationed at Sānjiāng and Liú'ào, the entry points from Zhè into Mǐn,
and the local militia of Hǎichéng Tuánliàn Battalion were replaced with Zhè soldiers.
During the Tiānqǐ period,
a city was built on Pénghú,
with one Yóují,
two Bǎzǒngs,
commanding three thousand troops,
and炮towers were built for defense.
Previously,
during the Wànlì period,
Xǔ Fúyuǎn served as Grand Coordinator of Mǐn,
and proposed building a city on Fúzhōu’s Hǎitánshān,
which also involved the various islands of Pénghú,
and he also stated that the various mountains along the coast of eastern Zhè, such as Chénqián, Jīntáng, Yùhuán, and Nánjǐ, should all be managed.
Consequently, a Nánjǐ Fù Zǒngbīng was established,
but Pénghú was not attended to.
The place lay remotely in the sea,
winding like a long snake,
with many bifurcated harbors and scattered islands,
where the vast open spaces could hide large ships.
It was initially occupied by the "Red-haired" (Dutch),
but at this time, following the suggestion of Grand Coordinator Nán Jūyì,
it was retaken and garrisoned.
Since the Wōkòu incursions during the reign of Shìzōng,
major coastal cities
each established such officials as Zǒngdū, Xúnfǔ, Bīngbèi Fùshǐ, Zǒngbīngguān, Cāncéng, and Yóují.
As for the various defense arrangements,
in Guǎngdōng, it was divided into eastern, central, and western routes,
with three Cāncéngs established;
in Fújiàn, there were the Five Water Stockades;
in Zhè, there were Six Zǒngs:
one for Jīnxiāng and Pánshí two guards,
one for Sōngmén and Hǎimén two guards,
one for Chāngguó Guard and Qiáncāng, Juéxī, and other garrisons,
one for Dìnghǎi Guard and Kuò[missing character], Dàsōng, and other garrisons,
one for Guānhǎi and Línshān two guards,
one for Hǎiníng Guard,
all jointly commanded by four Cāncéngs;
in Southern Zhílì, east of Zhàpǔ,
a Cāncéng was established at Jīnshān Guard;
north of Huángpǔ,
a Zǒngbīng was established at Wúsōngjiāng Estuary;
in Huái and Yáng, the Zǒngbīng was stationed in Tōngzhōu,
and a Yóují was stationed in Miàowān,
and another land force Yóují was established in Yángzhōu,
awaiting deployment;
in Shāndōng, the three prefectures of Dēng, Lái, and Qīng had a Fùshǐ for inspecting maritime routes,
a Cāncéng for managing militia,
and a Dūzhīhuī Zǒngdū for coastal military defense against pirates;
in Jì and Liáo, the Dàgū estuary had heavily stationed troops,
led by a Fù Zǒngbīng,
with the two Yóujís of Mìyún and Yǒngpíng serving as reinforcements.
Outside Shānhǎiguān,
the troops of Guǎngníng Middle, Front, and other five garrisons guarded their respective patrol areas,
with the Níngqián Cāncéng as reinforcement,
and all the armies of Jīn, Fù, Hǎi, and Gài were responsible for maritime defense.
East of Sānchà,
outside Jiǔliánchéng, Zhènjiāng City was newly built,
with a Yóují established,
commanding one thousand seven hundred troops,
patrolling the sea,
connecting to the north with the land camp of the Kuāndiàn Cāncéng,
totaling seven garrisons in all,
with hundreds of Shǒubèi, Bǎzǒng, Fēnshǒu, and Xúnjiǎo (inspecting and jointly patrolling) officers.
The third, fourth, and fifth months were designated as major patrol periods,
and the ninth and tenth months as minor patrol periods.
Indeed, because the Wōkòu plague was so severe,
the defenses were also said to be the most extensive.
Japan's land mass faces Mǐn,
and Zhè's Zhāobǎoguān was on its tribute route,
thus Zhè and Mǐn were the most vulnerable points.
Southern incursions were from Guǎngdōng,
northern incursions were via the river to attack the secondary capital, Huái, and Yáng,
therefore, coastal defense
and river defense were of primary importance.
In the early Hóngwǔ era,
eight thousand naval soldiers were stationed at the Xīnjiāngkǒu south of the capital.
Later,
twelve thousand were gradually stationed,
and four hundred boats were built.
Land forces were also established at Pǔzikǒu on the north bank,
forming a pincer movement.
All the counties along the river under its jurisdiction,
from Jiǔjiāng, Guǎngjì, Huángméi upstream,
down to Sū, Sōng, Tōng, Tàii downstream,
encompassing Ānqìng, Chí, Hé, Tàipíng in the middle,
all bandits and private salt traffickers
were ordered to be pursued and arrested,
also serving to defend against Wōkòu.
During the Yǒnglè era,
meritorious officials were specially appointed as commanders to oversee river operations,
and later, Dū Yùshǐs were also employed.
In the fourth year of Chénghuà, following the suggestion of Jǐnyīwèi Qiānshì Féng Yáo,
river troops were ordered to establish defenses according to the terrain,
and generals were stationed at Guā, Yí, and Tàipíng to guard them.
Six years later,
Shǒubèi Dìngxīhóu Jiǎng Wǎn proposed transferring troops from Jiànyáng, Zhènjiāng, and other guards to fill vacancies in the river army.
In the thirteenth year, one military minister was chosen to be responsible for river operations,
without concurrently managing camp affairs.
Five years later,
following the suggestion of Nánjīng Dū Yùshǐ Bái Áng,
coastal garrison officials were instructed to provide mutual assistance,
and also given official seals.
This was enacted as a regulation.
During the Hóngzhì period,
the two shifts of troops at Xīnjiāngkǒu were ordered to follow the example of the Capital Camps,
with the first shift resting
and the next shift training immediately.
In the eighth year of Jiājìng,
the Jiāngyīn bandit Hóu Zhòngjīn and others rebelled,
and Supervising Secretary Xià Yán requested the establishment of a Zhènshǒu Jiāng, Huái Zǒngbīngguān.
Later, the bandits were suppressed,
and a Tídū was appointed to oversee the upper and lower reaches of the river.
Later, it was again abolished.
In the thirty-second year,
the Wōkòu threat intensified,
and a Fù Zǒngbīng was again established at Jīnshān Guard,
overseeing the coast up to Zhènjiāng,
to respond by land and water with the Lángshān Fù Zǒngbīng.
At that time, Jiāngběi was entirely overrun by Wōkòu,
so imperial troops from Jiǔjiāng and Ānqìng were quantitatively deployed to guard Jīngkǒu, Chuíshān, and other places.
After a long time,
Supervising Secretary Fàn Zōngwú stated:
“According to custom,
the Cāojiāng Dū Yùshǐ was responsible for river defense,
and the two Grand Coordinators of Yìng and Fèng were responsible for coastal defense.
Later, due to the Wōkòu alert,
Zhènjiāng downwards,
including Tōngcháng, Láng, Fú, and other places, were placed under the Cāojiāng,
thus the two Grand Coordinators could shirk their responsibilities.
The Cāojiāng, on the other hand, citing that these were not originally his troops,
found it difficult to command them remotely,
and also viewed them indifferently,
which was not the intention of entrusting responsibility.
It would be appropriate to designate Chuíshān and Sānjiānghuìkǒu as the boundary between the Cāojiāng and the Grand Coordinators.”
This was approved.
Thereafter, two Xúnshì Yùshǐs for the upper and lower Jiāng were added,
who could impeach officials and generals,
and the Nánjīng Qiān Dū Yùshǐ concurrently managed river operations,
without a separate appointment.
Initially,
an additional six thousand naval soldiers were recruited.
In the early years of Lóngqìng,
at the request of Dū Yùshǐ Wú Shílái,
one quarter was retained,
and the rest were all dismissed,
along with the abolition of the Zhōngjūn bǎzǒng and other officials.
Afterwards,
it was again ordered to establish garrisons in separate defense areas,
and they were held responsible for mutual support between upstream and downstream, and north and south.
It was also followed, based on the words of Dū Yùshǐ Sòng Yíwàng,
that all troops should be stationed along the river,
and not live in cities.
In the twentieth year of Wànlì,
due to the threat of Japanese pirates,
speakers requested the re-establishment of the Jīngkǒu Zǒngbīng.
Nánjīng Bīngbù Shàngshū Zhōng Zhēnjí and others argued that since there was already a Wúsōng Zǒngbīng,
it was not advisable to have two.
Therefore, a Bīngbèi Shǐzhě was established,
and every spring flood,
the Bèi Wō Dūdū was dispatched
to command the guard's naval and land forces to Zhènjiāng.
Seven years later,
Cāojiāng Gěng Dìnglì vigorously memorialized:
"The Yangtze River stretches over a thousand *lǐ*;
the upper river has five encampments
and three Bīngbèi officials;
the lower river has five encampments
and two Bīngbèi officials.
It is appropriate to entrust them with inspection and training,
and to consider the quality of their troops as the measure of their performance."
The Board discussed and agreed.
According to custom,
the northern and southern Zǒngshàoguān met every five days at a central location for a patrol,
and commanding officers also visited the river twice a month for patrols.
Thereafter, this was often not practiced.
During the Chóngzhēn reign,
again, meritorious officials were appointed as Cāojiāng,
and indolence became a habit;
patrols and inspections were mere formalities,
without substance.
Outside the Wèisuǒ,
prefectures and counties had Mínzhuàng,
and border prefectures had Tǔbīng.
Tàizǔ, when pacifying Jiāngdōng,
followed the Yuán system,
establishing Guǎnlǐng Mínbīng Wànhù Fǔ.
Later, following the advice of the Xīnxī Xíng Dū Sī,
border residents were allowed to provide their own weapons
and organize to defend the border.
Fújiàn and Zhèjiāng suffered from Japanese pirates,
and Zhǐhuī Fāng Qiān requested to register households with many male adults as soldiers.
Soon, this was deemed a problem for the local communities,
and an edict ordered mutual relocation between Fújiàn and Zhèjiāng.
At that time, militia were already in use,
but they were not recruited.
In the second year of Zhèngtǒng, recruitment began among retired soldiers and Mínzhuàng in various locations who were willing to serve,
and Shǎnxī gained 4,200 men.
Each person was given two bolts of cloth
and four *dǒu* of monthly grain.
In the early years of Jǐngtài,
envoys were sent to recruit Mínzhuàng separately in Zhílì, Shāndōng, Shānxī, and Hénán,
and Shānxī Yìyǒng were assigned to defend Dàtóng,
while the two passes of Zǐjīng and Dǎomǎ
also used militia for defense;
when the situation was resolved, they were discharged home.
In the second year of Chénghuà,
due to border alerts,
the militia at the two passes were reinstated.
An imperial edict ordered an Yùshǐ to go to Yán'ān and Qìngyáng to select able-bodied men for enrollment,
obtaining over five thousand men,
who were called Tǔbīng.
Because Yánsuí Xúnfǔ Lú Xiáng reported that border residents were fierce and courageous,
and could be trained as soldiers
to protect their fields, homes, wives, and children,
this order was issued.
In the seventh year of Hóngzhì, the method of Qiānmínzhuàng was established.
In prefectures and counties over seven or eight hundred *lǐ* away,
two men were selected per *lǐ*;
five hundred *lǐ*,
three;
three hundred *lǐ*,
four;
and over one hundred *lǐ*,
five.
Officials trained them,
and when an alert occurred, they were mobilized,
given travel provisions,
and the abuses of forced labor and selling exemptions were prohibited.
If wealthy commoners were unwilling,
they could pay a direct fee to the officials,
who would then recruit on their own.
Some were called Jībīng,
while those under Xúnjiǎnsī were called Gōngbīng.
Later, it was deemed impractical for them to cross borders to defend in winter,
so Dàtóng Xúnfǔ Liú Yǔ requested to exempt them from class training,
collecting silver and grain for Dàtóng,
and supplementing the service with Wēiyuǎn Túndīng, Shè, and Yúdīng.
Jǐshìzhōng Xióng Wěi also requested to enroll recruited commoners into nearby Wèisuǒ.
Both requests were granted.
In the fourteenth year,
because the Tǔbīng recruited in the northwestern border areas
were often fewer than five thousand,
envoys were sent with 200,000 *liǎng* of silver and 40,000 *liǎng* of silver for Taipu Temple's horse price to recruit.
Commanders of a thousand or a hundred households were promoted
based on the number of soldiers they recruited,
and those who had lost their positions could be reinstated,
then ordered to command the soldiers they recruited.
Subsequently, the Ministry of War deliberated and responded to Shìláng Lǐ Mèngyáng's memorial requesting to fill military ranks,
stating:
"The original quota of official soldiers in the Wèisuǒ throughout the empire was over 2.7 million,
but over the years, many have fled or died.
Previously, over 300,000 Mínzhuàng were selected,
and an additional 880,000 Shèrén and Yúdīng in the Wèisuǒ were verified,
while countless tens of thousands of Tǔbīng were recruited in the northwestern border areas.
We request, as suggested by Mèngyáng,
to investigate officials who fail to train Mínzhuàng or privately employ them for miscellaneous tasks,
and prosecute them as if they had unlawfully employed soldiers."
This was approved.
During the Zhèngdé reign,
roving bandits disturbed Shāndōng,
and Xúnfǔ Zhāng Fèng selected militia,
ordering them to buy their own horses and drill in groups,
which overwhelmed the common people.
Bīngbù Shìláng Yáng Tán spoke out about this.
The Mínzhuàng recruited by Dū Yùshǐ Níng Gǎo were mostly unreliable ruffians,
and he was impeached by Yùshǐ Zhāng Xuán.
In the twenty-second year of Jiājìng, the quota for Mínzhuàng in prefectures and counties was increased:
large ones to a thousand men,
medium ones to six or seven hundred,
and small ones to five hundred.
In the twenty-ninth year,
the capital was newly raided,
and it was decided to recruit militia,
at a rate of twenty thousand.
By the end of April each year,
they would go to the vicinity of the capital for defense.
Five years later,
Bīngbù Shàngshū Yáng Bó requested to eliminate the old and weak,
and retain the elite,
sending those outside the capital to various circuits as militia,
and those in the capital to be subordinate to the Xún Bǔ Cānjìang;
deserters would not be replaced.
The Emperor, seeing many phantom recruits
who consumed grain uselessly,
sent officials to investigate who should be dismissed and who should be reinstated, and to report.
During the Lóngqìng reign,
Zhāng Jūzhèng and Chén Yǐqín again requested to register militia in the capital region,
stating:
"The eight prefectures of Zhílì have many strong and fierce people;
by checking the household registers,
excluding only sons, the old, and the weak,
from three sons in a family, one son is registered;
from three brothers, one brother is registered.
A prefecture or large county can obtain 1,600 men,
and a small county can obtain 1,000 men.
They should be divided into regular soldiers and auxiliary soldiers,
their names recorded in registers,
and placed under the Fǔchén for training,
not exceeding three months a year,
and not exceeding three times a month.
After training, they are to return to farming,
and their status as commoners restored.
Outside of the annual training,
they are not to be dispatched for other purposes."
The responsible department was ordered to discuss and implement this.
However, since the Jiājìng reign,
the Shāndōng and Hénán militia garrisoning Jìmén
were generally required to pay silver to fund recruitment.
By the early Wànlì reign,
Shāndōng was levied up to 56,000 *liǎng* of silver,
greatly distressing the poor.
During the river management project,
Jǐshìzhōng Zhāng Zhēngguàn requested to recruit more Tǔbīng
to defend Huái, Yáng, Xú, and Pī.
When bandits arose in Jīnán,
Jǐshìzhōng Gěng Suílóng requested to reinstate the old system of Mínzhuàng,
specifically for capturing bandits.
During the Pōzhōu Rebellion,
Gōngbù Shìláng Zhào Kěhuái requested to train local residents,
and the Ministry of War therefore stated:
"It is not only Shǔ that lacks soldiers throughout the empire.
The official troops and Mínzhuàng in all provinces
should all dismiss the old and young,
and replace them with able-bodied soldiers.
Military drills should be under the Yìnguān and Cāoguān,
while civilian drills should be under the Zhèngguān and Bǔguān,
and the Jùnshǒu and Jiānsī should not interfere.
Camps should be established and units formed,
to facilitate mobilization."
All these proposals were discussed and implemented in succession.
In the late Ming Dynasty,
recruiting soldiers and raising funds became increasingly urgent.
Zōu Wéilián, a Director in the Ministry of War in Nánjīng, detailed the harms of conscription and recruitment.
Xú Jiǔhàn, a Provincial Administration Commissioner of Shānxī, particularly emphasized that civilian militias should not be mobilized.
During the Chóngzhēn reign,
banditry was rampant in the Central Plains.
Yáng Sìchāng, Minister of War, proposed that local prefectures and counties be ordered to train their indigenous population as soldiers.
Zhāng Shènyán, Vice Minister of Works, pointed out several inconveniences.
Moreover, Mǐ Shòutú, a Censor, outlined ten disadvantages,
arguing that it would be better to selectively train local militias,
increase the number of civilian strongmen and quick hands,
and prepare for local defense.
Later, after Yáng Sìchāng's death,
the training of soldiers also ceased.
Local militias
were recruited based on the strengths of their local customs and environment,
and mobilized to assist the military in times of need.
Those belonging to the military register were called Zhèbīng,
with Yìwū being the best,
Chù (Lishui) second,
Tái (Taizhou) and Níng (Ningbo) next.
They were skilled with the wolf-hook spear,
sometimes supplemented with forks and lances.
Qī Jìguāng developed the Yuānyāng Formation to defeat the Japanese pirates,
and was later famous for defending Jìmén.
There were also Chuānbīng and Liáobīng.
During the Chóngzhēn reign,
many were mobilized to suppress roving bandits.
Those not on the military register
were common in various places.
In Sōngxiàn, Hénán, they were called Máohúlu,
skilled in short weapons
and adept at mountain traversal.
In Sōng, Lúshì, Língbǎo, and Yǒngníng, there were many miner-soldiers,
called Jiǎonǎo
or Dǎshǒu.
Shāndōng had long-pole users.
Xúzhōu had archers.
Jǐngxíng had Mantis hands (Málángshǒu),
skilled in throwing stones,
which could reach over a hundred paces.
In Zhāng (Zhangzhou) and Quán (Quanzhou) of Mǐn (Fujian), they practiced darts and shields,
and were best at naval warfare.
People from Yǒngchūn, Quánzhōu, were skilled in martial arts.
During the Zhèngtǒng reign,
Guō Róngliù
gained merit by defeating the Shāyóu bandits.
Salt workers from salt-producing areas, who made their living from private sales,
were often strong and resolute.
In the early Chénghuà reign,
thousands of Hédōng salt workers,
equipped with their own cannons, powerful crossbows, and carts,
joined the official army to pursue bandits.
Salt workers from Cáojìng, Sōngjiāng,
during the Jiājìng reign,
pursued Japanese pirates to an island
and burned their boats.
Later, when Japanese pirates saw salt bags in civilian homes,
they would wave their hands and warn each other.
Guǎngdōng had mixed aboriginal people (mán), who were skilled in long shields and chopping swords,
with Xīnhuì and Dōngguǎn producing the strongest.
Yánsuí and Gùyuán had many indigenous people from outside the frontier,
skilled in riding and archery.
Yīngzōng ordered them to be selectively trained for autumn defense.
During the Dàténgxiá campaign,
Hán Yōng used them
to crush the Yáo and Zhuàng soldiers who used shield-knives.
The Lǔjiājūn of Zhuānglàng,
originally part of the imperial escort,
were, in the early Hóngxī reign,
placed under the command of indigenous commanders.
During the Wànlì reign,
ministers of the Board praised their bravery and strength,
saying they were feared by enemies,
and that they should be encouraged to be stored for frontier use.
Xīníng had eight hundred Ma households,
who often provided their own cavalry and equipment to face enemies.
Later, they were cut due to the request for tribute.
In the 19th year of Wànlì (1591),
the Grand Coordinator Zhèng Luò requested their reinstatement.
There were also monk soldiers,
from Shàolín, Fúniú, and Wǔtái.
During the Japanese pirate raids,
over forty Shàolín monks volunteered.
They also won many battles.
In the southwestern border regions, there were various native chieftain (tǔsī) soldiers.
The forces under the Tǔsī of Yǒngshùn and Bǎojìng in Húnán,
the Lángbīng from Dōnglán, Nàdì, Nándān, and Guīshùn in Guǎngxī,
and the Tǔsī of Yǒuyáng, the Qín clan of Shígǎzhu, and the Rǎn clan in Sìchuān
contributed the most.
In the late Ming Dynasty,
frontier affairs were urgent,
and officials specifically considered mobilizing the Tǔsī from the three provinces as the best strategy,
though its advantages and disadvantages were said to be equally balanced.
Collation Notes
Volume 68, Military Section 4: Clearing the Army Ranks, Training, Rewarding Merit, Firearms, Carts and Boats, Horse Administration.
In the early Míng Dynasty,
the conscription order was effectively implemented.
One able-bodied man from every household was conscripted into the army,
so there were no vacancies in the Wèisuǒ,
and even surplus men.
Not long after,
the Grand Military Command reported that
from the 10th month of the first year of Wú (1367)
to the 11th month of the third year of Hóngwǔ (1370),
over 47,900 soldiers had deserted.
Consequently, an order for their apprehension was issued,
and laws for punishment were established.
If a banner commander (xiǎoqí) had three deserters under his command,
he would be demoted to a common soldier.
From squadron commanders (zǒngqí) up to company commanders (bǎihù) and battalion commanders (qiānhù),
all were deprived of salary, demoted, or dismissed
depending on the number of deserters.
Punishments were even stricter for those on campaign away from their posts.
In the 16th year (1383), the Five Military Commissions ordered external Wèisuǒ
to promptly apprehend missing soldiers
and have the Supervising Secretaries Pān Yōng and others divide the responsibility for clearing the ranks.
The next year, following the advice of Yú Lún, Minister of War,
it was decreed that for Wèisuǒ households in the capital that had no heirs,
no one should falsely claim kinship with the same surname or a close relative of the same surname.
Officials were ordered to verify and make appointments,
and prefectural Wèisuǒ were not to send special envoys.
In the 21st year (1388), an edict ordered Wèisuǒ to verify their military ranks,
and it was forbidden
to conceal one's own son and substitute an adopted son.
That autumn,
Wèisuǒ were ordered to record the names and native places of soldiers in a register,
detailing the number of able-bodied men for easy replacement.
Military identity tallies (jūnjí kànhé) were also established,
distributed internally and externally,
to serve as verification for soldiers during inspections.
Upon the accession of Chéngzǔ,
Supervising Secretaries and other officials were dispatched to inspect the armies throughout the empire,
and the method for conscription and replacement of soldiers was revised.
Originally,
for households with three or more able-bodied men,
one was conscripted as a main soldier (zhèngjūn),
and there was a supplementary household (tiēhù)
whose able-bodied men would fill the vacancy
if the main soldier died.
At this time,
it was ordered that main soldiers and supplementary households would alternate service,
and single able-bodied men in supplementary households were exempted.
The families of soldiers were exempted from one able-bodied man's corvée.
In the first year of Hóngxī (1425),
Fàn Jì, a soldier of the Zuǒtúnwèi in Xīngzhōu, strongly criticized the disturbances caused by military recruitment.
Qián Xīng, a centurion of the Fùyùwèi, reported:
"My ancestor was a soldier of the Zhuōlùwèi.
After his death, my father succeeded him
and was granted the position of centurion for his merit.
I have already inherited my father's position,
yet my Wèisuǒ still considers my ancestor a deserter,
and repeatedly attempts to conscript him."
The Emperor said to Zhāng Běn, Minister of War:
"The military ranks are not clear,
and many abuses are like this."
Soon after Xuānzōng ascended the throne,
military abuses increased.
Cunning individuals often concealed their registers,
or falsely accused and forced good commoners into service.
The Emperor instructed the Ministry of War:
"The court treats soldiers and civilians
like a boat or a carriage carrying a load—
neither can be given undue weight.
Officials should carefully verify the facts
and not confuse them."
Then, Húang Zōngzài, Vice Minister of Personnel, and others were dispatched to clear the military Wèisuǒ throughout the empire.
In the third year (1428), an edict commanded Supervising Secretaries and Censors to clear the military,
establishing eleven regulations,
which were posted throughout the empire.
The next year, these were increased to twenty-two articles.
In the fifth year (1430), following Minister Zhāng Běn's request,
it was ordered that all officials and military banner commanders in the empire publicly investigate those recruited since the Hóngwǔ and Yǒnglè reigns who had no trace,
and exempt them.
In the sixth year (1431), it was ordered that if conscripted soldiers had elderly, sick, or only children as dependents,
they should be assigned to nearby areas.
Others who had fled from labor service were usually sent beyond the pass,
but this was changed to one year of penal labor,
to show compassion.
In the eighth year (1433), 159 people wrongly conscripted into the Sūzhōu Wèisuǒ were exempted,
and 1,239 people who had already received provisions were only required to serve for the rest of their lives.
Previously,
when military households in Sūzhōu and Chángzhōu had no heirs,
their relatives were implicated, often by the thousands.
Kuàng Zhōng, the Prefect, reported this to the court.
Moreover, commoners in Chángzhōu complained of 700-plus cases of being wrongly forced into military service.
Therefore, an edict specially commanded Vice Minister Zhōu Chén to clear the situation.
Early in the Zhèngtǒng reign,
an order was issued that households whose male family members liable for military service (gōujūn jiādīng) had all died
should be removed from the registers.
For runaway soldiers, those who had died, or those who had met with an accident,
or if a household was originally registered for military service
but happened to share the same name
and the local headman (lǐxū) maliciously reported them for revenge,
or if they had already been cleared but went to the Ministry (bù) to voice their grievances,
all were to be exempted.
It was a fixed rule
that all replacements for military ranks (bǔwǔ) were to be dispatched to the remote frontiers,
with people from the north and south interchanging.
Grand Secretary Yáng Shìqí (楊士奇) stated that the different climates (fēngtǔ) were unsuitable,
leading to premature deaths,
and requested that they be sent to garrisons (shù) in places suitable for them.
Acting Vice Minister of War Kuàng Yě (鄺埜) considered this to be a violation of ancestral institutions (zǔzhì)
and rejected it.
In the second year of Chénghuà (成化),
Lǐ Kǎn (李侃), the Provincial Governor (xúnfǔ) of Shānxī (山西), again requested that they be assigned to the Imperial Guard (jìnwèi),
and the proposal began to be implemented.
In the eleventh year, eleven Censors (yùshǐ) were ordered to clear the military registers (qīngjūn) in different routes,
with ten parts as the standard.
Those who achieved three parts were considered the best,
and those who fell short were ranked last.
At that time, those who had been demoted due to crimes and subsequently fled or died
also had their male family members liable for military service (jiādīng) conscripted.
Censor Jiāng Áng (江昂) said this was not
in line with the principle of "punishment does not extend to descendants" (fá fú jí sì),
and so it was prohibited.
Early in the Jiājìng reign,
the orders for capturing runaways became increasingly harsh,
with some cases involving dozens of implicated households
and conscriptions lasting for several decades.
Even when all male family members (dīngkǒu) had died out,
the circulars and reports continued endlessly.
Minister of War Hú Shìníng (胡世寧) requested that
"those who have been repeatedly reported as cleared be exempted from conscription (gōu).
Furthermore, those who evade service are certainly unreliable in times of urgency,
so they should be immediately reassigned to their original hometowns.
If a guard unit (wèisuǒ) has vacant ranks,
then other surplus personnel (shèyú) or criminals should be selected to fill them.
For those who commit serious offenses and are sent to frontier garrisons (biānwèi),
their family property should be forcibly sold,
and the entire household relocated,
to ensure they have no lingering thoughts (gùniàn).
This way, the garrison soldiers (wèizú) would all be natives,
and desertions would become fewer."
The emperor approved his words.
Later,
following the proposal of Vice Director (zhǔshì) Wáng Xuéyì (王學益),
conscription lists (gōudān) were created,
and laws were detailed and improved.
After a long time,
the dispatch of Censors (yùshǐ) for clearing military registers (qīngjūn) was suspended,
and the penalties for guarding and escorting runaway soldiers (táojūn) and for soldiers reporting to garrisons (wèi) beyond the deadline were relaxed.
The officials clearing military registers (qīngjūn guān) became increasingly idle,
and the documents faded.
Proponents then requested a renewed strict enforcement.
In the third year of Wànlì,
Investigating Censor (gěishìzhōng) Xú Zhēnmíng (徐貞明) stated:
"The conscription of soldiers (gōujūn) in the southeast
requires provisions and equipment from the registered households (hùdīng),
and transportation from local post stations (lǐdì),
costing no less than one hundred gold (bǎi jīn) per soldier.
This greatly burdens the people of the southeast
and ultimately does not improve military administration (jūnzheng).
It should be handled like the system for artisans (bānjiàng lì),
exempting them from escort and replacement,
but heavily collecting artisan silver (bānyín)
to fund recruitment,
so that the southeast is forever free from the disturbance of conscription and replacement,
and the ranks of the northwest are also filled."
Wáng Shìzhēn (王世貞), the Provincial Governor (xúnfǔ) of Yún Yáng (鄖陽), consequently spoke of four advantages: households subject to conscription
would be happy to be stationed nearby and would not seek to evade or hide,
this is the first advantage;
each would be accustomed to their local environment,
and would not be driven to desperation,
this is the second advantage;
if nearby, they would not flee,
and if they fled, they would be easy to pursue,
this is the third advantage;
the escorting households would not be ruined,
this is the fourth advantage.
However, the Ministry of War (bīngbù) ultimately rejected Zhēnmíng's proposal
and did not implement it.
Thirteen years later,
Guō Yìngpìn (郭應聘), the Minister of War (bīngbù shàngshū) in Nánjīng (南京), again requested that each be assigned to a nearby location,
and that the north and south be reorganized.
He also stated
"the soldiers to be conscripted (yìnggōu zhī jūn) in the Southern Zhílì (Nán Zhílì) number over sixty-six thousand,
implicating two to three hundred thousand people.
I request that all cases from before Tiānshùn (天順) be completely released and exempted."
This was approved,
and both near and far rejoiced.
However, after the order for reorganization was issued,
those seeking reorganization followed one after another.
The next year,
the Ministry of War (bīngbù) stated
"the military ranks (shíwǔ) are gradually depleting,
and soldiers in frontier garrisons (biānzhèn) are even hoping to escape service."
An imperial edict (zhǐ) was issued to revert to the old system,
and Yìngpìn's proposal was again not implemented.
All military garrisons (jūnwèi) were managed by the Bureau of Military Appointments (Zhífāng sī),
while conscription and clearing (gōuqīng) were under the charge of the Bureau of Military Equipment (Wǔkù sī).
When there was a conscription,
it was first reported by the guard unit (wèisuǒ),
and their native place and residence were verified.
The Imperial Household (Nèifǔ) issued a directive (pī),
and local officials (yǒusī) were ordered to apprehend the soldier himself,
which was called "following and apprehending" (gēnbǔ);
apprehending the male family member (jiādīng) was
called "conscripting and apprehending" (gōubǔ).
Occasionally, there were cases of exemption from military service (kāiwǔ) due to imperial grace.
In the twenty-third year of Hóngwǔ, an order was issued that students (shēngyuán) who should perform military service (jūnyì)
were to be sent home to complete their studies.
In the fourth year of Xuāndé,
Lǐ Zhìdào (李志道) from Shàngyú (上虞) was assigned to the Chǔxióng Guard (Chǔxióng Wèi).
He died,
and his grandson Zōnggāo (宗皐) was to succeed him.
At that time, he had already passed the provincial examination (xiāngshì).
Minister (shàngshū) Zhāng Běn (張本) reported this to the Emperor,
and he was exempted.
Such cases were extremely rare.
A household with military registration (jūnjí)
could only be removed from it if one attained the position of Minister of War (bīngbù shàngshū).
Soldiers who were to be escorted and dispatched
all had their wives registered.
There were expenses for stipends and military equipment, escorting soldiers' travel provisions, and soldiers' daily rations.
The compilation of these registers (cèdān) all followed a specific format.
Initially, three registers were established: household registration (hùkǒu), recruitment of soldiers (shōujūn), and clearing of military registers (qīngjūn).
In the thirty-first year of Jiājìng, four more registers were compiled,
named "military origin" (jūnguàn),
“base list” (dōudǐ),
“classified by guard unit” (lèiwèi), and "classified by surname" (lèixìng).
For conscripted soldiers, a separate military warrant (jūndān) was issued.
Throughout the Míng (明) dynasty,
the military registration (jūnjí) was extremely strict.
However, corrupt practices gradually accumulated,
and the disturbance to the populace became increasingly severe.
Míng Tàizǔ rose from commoner,
marshaled collective strength,
and conquered the realm.
After ascending the throne,
he repeatedly ordered his meritorious ministers and veteran generals to train troops in various routes,
but the system for this had not yet been established.
In the sixth year of Hóngwǔ, he ordered the Zhōngshū Shěng, the Dà Dūdū Fǔ, the Yùshǐ Tái, and the six ministries to deliberate on the "Statutes for Training Soldiers":
"Cavalrymen must be skilled in riding, archery, spears, and sabers.
Infantrymen must be skilled in bows, crossbows, and spears.
For archery, using half of twelve arrows,
the standard is to reach afar
and hit close targets.
To reach afar,
officers are at 160 paces and soldiers at 120 paces;
to hit close targets,
it is 50 paces.
For drawing a crossbow, using five of twelve arrows,
to reach afar,
for a foot-drawn crossbow, it is 80 paces;
for a cart-mounted crossbow, 150 paces.
To hit close targets,
for a foot-drawn crossbow, it is 40 paces;
for a cart-mounted crossbow, 60 paces.
Spears must be practiced skillfully in advancing and retreating.
For guards in the capital,
taking 5,000 men as a unit,
one-fifth of them,
led by officers from commander downwards, shall be brought before the emperor for examination.
The rest shall be tested in rotation.
For Regional Military Commissions and guards outside the capital,
each guard of 5,000 men,
one-fifth of them,
led by officers from chiliarch downwards, shall be brought to the capital for examination.
The rest shall be tested in rotation.
If soldiers are skilled in both infantry and cavalry,
the officers shall be rewarded according to their abilities;
otherwise, they shall be punished.
Soldiers shall be given 600 qián for travel expenses.
If for officers from commander downwards,
between three-tenths and six-tenths of the soldiers under their command fail,
their salaries shall be progressively docked;
if seven-tenths or more fail,
they shall be progressively demoted to the rank of common soldier.
If a Regional Military Commissioner has four-tenths or more of his soldiers fail,
his salary shall be docked for one year;
if six-tenths or more fail, he shall be dismissed from office."
Sixteen years later,
it was ordered that from all guards in the realm, skilled archers,
one in ten,
should be selected and sent to the capital in rotation during agricultural slack seasons for review,
with rewards and punishments for chiliarchs and centurions based on their performance.
Border troops were to be reviewed within their own guards.
In the twentieth year, the guard soldiers were ordered to practice archery at the Meridian Gate's crimson steps.
The following year, a further order stated:
"For cavalry and infantry soldiers of all guards in the realm,
they shall each be divided into ten classes.
Officers who have been promoted through seniority shall command them,
and they shall be reviewed and tested in the capital during the winter months.
Commanders, chiliarchs, and centurions
who are old and experienced in battle, or who are engaged in military farms, are exempt.
Training methods shall first be issued
for them to follow.
Those who do not follow the methods or are not skilled
shall be punished."
The following year, an imperial edict to the Five Military Commissions stated:
"Soldiers tested in competition shall be rewarded with paper currency in three grades.
They shall also each be given three ingots of paper currency for travel expenses.
Those who fail shall also be given this.
If in the following year's retest they still do not meet the standard,
the soldiers shall be banished to guard the frontiers in Yúnnán,
the officers shall be demoted to serve in campaigns,
and the battalion commander shall be demoted to a common soldier.
If the sons of military officials inheriting positions,
when tested in riding and archery, do not meet the standard,
they shall be ordered to return to their guard to manage affairs,
and be given half salary.
If after two years they are still found to be the same when retested,
they shall also be demoted to common soldiers."
When Wén Huáng ascended the throne,
he personally led five northern expeditions,
and the armies were often personally reviewed.
He also once ordered the Princes of Qín, Jìn, Zhōu, and Sù,
to each select 5,000 of their bodyguard troops,
and appoint officers to oversee them to Zhēndìng for training.
Commanding generals of Shǎnxī, Gānsù, Níngxià, Dàtóng, and Liáodōng,
as well as the Superintendent of the Central Capital and Regional Military Commissions like Hénán,
and guards like Xú and Sù,
were to send generals to lead cavalry and infantry to be stationed in Zhēndìng and Dézhōu for training,
awaiting their review in the capital.
In the early Jǐngtài period,
the Ten Regimental Camps were established.
The Supervising Secretary Dèng Lín presented the Xuānyuán Tú,
which was the ancient Eight Battle Formations method,
and this was then used to train the army.
During the Chénghuà period,
the Regimental Camps were increased to twelve,
and it was ordered that joint drills be held twice a month,
starting on the fifteenth day of the second spring month
and ending on the fifteenth day of the second summer month.
This also applied to autumn and winter.
In the ninth year of Hóngzhì,
Mǎ Wénshēng, the Minister of War, reaffirmed the Hóngwǔ and Yǒnglè training methods:
within five days,
two days for maneuvering formations and pitching camp,
three days for martial arts drills.
Wǔ Zōng was fond of martial arts,
and often ordered the supervising officers to drill the camps.
He also personally wielded the drum and gong to drill the soldiers of the four garrisons.
However, the main purpose was for unrestrained riding and amusement,
not for any practical effectiveness.
In the sixth year of Jiājìng, it was stipulated
that for pitching camp and deploying formations,
only the "Three-Layered Formation" and "Four-Gate Square Camp" were to be used.
It was also ordered that each camp select one or two skilled personnel for spears, sabers, arrows, shields, and firearms to serve as instructors,
who would then train others.
Later, the camp system was reformed,
dividing the troops into thirty branches,
establishing thirty generals,
each commanding 3,000 men for training.
The most elite among them were named "Select Vanguard,"
and their rewards for martial arts competition were generous.
The Grand Coordinator-Minister held four joint drills a month,
and on other days, the camp generals trained their respective units.
The Assistant Minister and inspecting supervising secretaries and censors could randomly enter a camp
to review, reward, or punish,
and thus select the "Select Vanguard."
The emperor also established an inner camp in the inner training ground
to train the imperial eunuchs.
In the early Lóngqìng period,
it was ordered that the promotion and demotion of generals in each camp be based on the number of points they received for training soldiers.
Those who fully trained their camp were promoted to Assistant Regional Military Commissioner,
with reductions for lesser achievements;
those who failed to train at all were demoted one rank from their inherited position
and dismissed from their post to return to their guard.
If training was successful within three years,
the coordinating minister of drills would commend and reward them with special favors;
those with no achievements would be deliberated for punishment.
Although regulations were established,
generals and soldiers were often lazy and lax,
and drills became mere formalities.
Earlier,
Qī Jìguāng, the Provincial Commander of Zhèjiāng, was renowned for his skill in training soldiers.
He once deployed local troops
and devised the "Mandarin Duck Formation" to defeat the Japanese pirates.
By this time,
he had become a Grand General.
Mù Zōng, following the request of Supervising Secretary Wú Shílái,
ordered Qī Jìguāng to train troops at Jìmén.
The Jìmén troops had been well-trained and orderly for several decades.
Qī Jìguāng once wrote the Liàn Bīng Shí Jì (Record of Practical Training) to instruct soldiers.
First was training the ranks,
starting with cavalry,
then infantry,
then chariots,
then baggage train;
first selecting the ranks,
then competing in skills,
all aimed at forming a cohesive camp.
Second was training courage,
making them understand the meaning of stopping and advancing, as well as superior-subordinate relationships, mutual friendship, and mutual assistance.
Third was training hearing and sight,
making them understand commands.
Fourth was training hands and feet,
making them skilled in techniques.
Fifth was training camps and formations,
detailing the deployment of formations, marching, pitching camp, and the standard and variations of engagement.
Finally, it concluded with training the generals.
Later, these methods were largely followed.
Regarding the system of rewarding merits,
during the reign of Tàizǔ,
great rewards were given for the pacification of the Central Plains, the southern campaigns, and the achievements in Yúnnán and Yuèzhōu.
Although the reward scales existed,
they were not explicitly legislated in advance.
Only in the twenty-ninth year was it ordered that for commanders, chiliarchs, and centurions of coastal guards who captured one Japanese pirate ship or bandits,
they would be promoted one rank,
rewarded with fifty taels of silver
and fifty ingots of paper currency.
For soldiers who captured or killed bandits by land or sea,
silver rewards varied.
In the early years of the Yǒnglè reign,
due to the long-standing efforts of generals and soldiers,
the Ministry of Rites was ordered to formulate a system based on the promotion and reward precedents set by Tàizǔ,
with adjustments.
Merits were divided into three grades: extraordinary merit (qígōng), first merit (shǒugōng), and secondary merit (cìgōng).
The weight and sequence of rewards
were generally determined by imperial decree on a case-by-case basis,
and no regulations were made in advance.
In the twelfth year, it was stipulated:
"Anyone who, during a battle,
breaks through to the enemy's rear and defeats the bandits,
who bravely enters the enemy formation to slay a general and capture a flag,
whose own unit has won while other units' outcomes are undecided but is able to provide rescue and defeat the enemy,
or who, having been commanded, can undertake a task and succeed in a surprising attack to defeat the bandits,
shall all be considered to have achieved extraordinary merit (qígōng).
Those who advance with concerted effort and are the first to defeat the bandits,
or whose vanguard is stalemated but whose rear unit pushes forward to defeat the bandits,
shall all be considered to have achieved first merit (shǒugōng).
Those who capture spies during military movements or within the camp
shall also be treated as having achieved first merit (shǒugōng).
All others shall be secondary merit (cìgōng)."
A merit reward certificate (gōngshǎng kànhé) was also established,
consisting of forty characters,
which read:
"Divine might, keen bravery and fierceness,
Strong, robust, firm heroes.
Victory coupled with swiftness,
Extraordinary merit, sharp vanguard exerted.
Wisdom and strategy declare marvelous plans,
Resolute and firm demonstrate loyalty.
Bold and decisive, able to bring stability,
Eminent fame, great achievements manifest."
These were numbered and stamped with the imperial seal,
stored at the Seal and Ribbon Office (Yìnshòu Jiān) within the imperial treasury (nèifǔ).
At that time,
the method for assessing merit was very strict.
In the fourteenth year of the Zhèngtǒng reign, merit reward plaques (shǎnggōng pái) were created,
with divisions for extraordinary merit (qígōng), head merit (tóugōng), and concerted effort (qílì),
managed by high officials.
Anyone who personally charged into the enemy formation to slay a general and seize a flag
was awarded an extraordinary merit plaque (qígōng pái).
Anyone who captured a Wǎlà (Oirat) alive or decapitated one enemy
was awarded a head merit plaque (tóugōng pái).
Even those without merit who were wounded
were awarded a concerted effort plaque (qílì pái).
These were specifically established for the Wǎlà (Oirat) incursions.
Thereafter,
the rewards for generals and soldiers were determined by the location of the merit,
and reported for implementation according to precedents.
The northern border was considered superior,
the northeastern border secondary,
Xīfān and Miáomán even further secondary,
and internal rebels in the interior even further secondary.
During the Shìzōng reign,
the suffering from Wō (Japanese pirates) was severe,
hence merits at sea were considered even superior to those at the northern border.
The northern border
extended from Gānsù eastward,
to Shānhǎiguān.
In the fourteenth year of the Chénghuà reign, it was stipulated:
"One person decapitating one enemy
is promoted one rank (yī zhì),
up to a maximum of three ranks.
If two people jointly decapitate an enemy,
the principal receives the same rank promotion.
Able-bodied males receive substantive appointments (shíshòu),
while young, weak individuals and women receive provisional appointments (shǔzhí).
Those who assisted or who decapitated four or more enemies
are all given rewards.
A commanding officer (lǐngjūn guān) with five hundred subordinates
who obtains five heads
is promoted one rank.
One who commands a thousand men
receives double this."
In the tenth year of the Zhèngdé reign, regulations were revised:
"One who single-handedly decapitates one enemy is promoted one rank.
If three people collaborate,
the principal is promoted provisionally one rank,
the assistants are given rewards.
If four, five, or six people collaborate,
the principal is given a reward,
the assistants are given appropriate rewards.
If two people jointly decapitate a young enemy,
the principal is treated according to the rule for three people,
the assistant is given an appropriate reward.
Those who do not wish to be promoted,
for each substantive rank (shíshòu),
are rewarded fifty taels of silver,
and for a provisional appointment (shǔzhí), twenty taels."
In the fifteenth year of the Jiājìng reign, it was stipulated that
commanding officers (lǐngjūn guān), qiānzǒng, and bǎzǒng
could be promoted up to three ranks only,
while dúzhīhuī (Regional Commanders) and above
could only be promoted provisionally two ranks,
the rest receiving additional rewards.
For the northeastern border,
it was initially stipulated that three heads equated to one at the northern border.
In the Wànlì reign,
this was changed to be equivalent to the northern border.
For Fān (ethnic minorities) bandits and Miáomán,
three heads also resulted in a promotion of one rank;
substantive (shíshòu) and provisional (shǔzhí) appointments
were handled as for the northern border.
Ten or more heads, as well as those falling short of the required number, received rewards.
In the third year of Wànlì, it was ordered that merits against Fān bandits in Shǎnxī
were to follow the Chénghuà precedents:
A military officer (jūnguān) or qiānzǒng commanding five hundred men,
whose subordinates decapitate thirty enemies,
or one commanding a thousand men who decapitates sixty enemies,
a bǎzǒng commanding five hundred men who decapitates ten enemies,
or one commanding a thousand men who decapitates thirty enemies,
all receive a one-rank promotion,
up to a maximum of three ranks.
For southern Mán (ethnic minorities) bandits,
the Xuāndé ninth year precedent stipulated that
three or more heads, and the capture or decapitation of the chief bandit,
all resulted in a one-rank promotion,
others receiving additional rewards.
In the sixteenth year of Zhèngdé, it was stipulated that a military officer whose subordinates decapitate one hundred enemies is promoted provisionally one rank,
three hundred enemies results in a substantive one-rank promotion,
four hundred enemies results in a one-rank promotion,
other merits receiving additional rewards.
For Wō (Japanese pirates),
the Jiājìng thirty-fifth year stipulated:
"Decapitating one Wō (Japanese pirate) chief
results in a three-rank substantive promotion;
those who decline are rewarded one hundred and fifty taels of silver.
Decapitating one pirate follower
results in a one-rank appointment.
Decapitating one Han Chinese coerced into collaboration
results in a one-rank provisional appointment.
Those who die in battle,
their own military rank and that of their son receive a one-rank substantive appointment.
Having merit in encountering bandits at sea
is uniformly considered extraordinary merit (qígōng)."
In the twelfth year of Wànlì, this was revised,
with slight changes from the old precedents,
making the difference in merit rewards dependent on the number of bandits and ships.
It was further stipulated that for naval engagements,
regardless of whether against Wōkòu (Japanese pirates) or sea bandits,
if confirmed as extraordinary merit (qígōng),
hereditary titles (shìxí) would be granted.
For Yí (ethnic minorities) bandits in Yúnnán,
the capture and decapitation merits were ranked similarly to those against Wō (Japanese pirates).
For internal rebels in the interior,
the Chénghuà fourteenth year precedent stipulated that
six heads resulted in a one-rank promotion,
up to a maximum of three ranks,
while young males, women, and those with nineteen or more heads, as well as those falling short of the required number, received rewards.
In the seventh year of Zhèngdé, the regulations for roving bandits (liúzéi) were set:
"Decapitating one famous bandit
results in a one-rank appointment,
which is hereditary;
followers are given rewards.
Decapitating one lesser bandit
results in a one-rank provisional appointment.
Decapitating three followers or dying in battle
all result in a one-rank appointment,
which is hereditary.
Those who return to camp with severe injuries and die
receive a one-rank provisional appointment."
Merit was also judged by the number of ears cut off,
with the highest achieving up to a two-rank promotion,
which was hereditary.
Previously,
the Níngxià campaign merit in the fifth year,
and later the Jiāngxī campaign merit in the first year of Jiājìng,
were both treated according to the roving bandit regulations.
During the Chóngzhēn reign,
Chuang and Xian were offered ten thousand taels of gold for their capture,
and ennoblement as marquises;
for other bandits, there were differences,
due to the severity of the bandit situation,
which changed the usual rules.
For captured people, livestock, and weapons,
the Chénghuà precedent stipulated that
they were all given to those who captured them.
Regarding merit-based rank promotions,
the Chénghuà fourteenth year precedent stipulated that
a soldier promoted one rank became a xiǎoqí (Junior Captain),
a shèrén (Palace Guard) promoted one rank was given an official's hat and belt,
and so on by analogy upwards.
In the forty-third year of Jiājìng, it was stipulated that
for officials such as dúdū (Chief Military Commissioners) for whom there were no further ranks to be promoted,
their sons eligible for inherited privilege (yìn) would receive an official's hat and belt.
In the thirteenth year of Wànlì, it was stipulated that
those dúzhīhuīshǐ (Regional Military Commissioners) who were promoted in rank
would not be appointed as dúdū (Chief Military Commissioners),
but would be rewarded fifty taels of silver,
and those whose salaries were increased would receive half of that.
For local civilian militias (yǒusī mín bīng),
the Lóngqìng sixth year stipulated that
they were to be treated according to the military regulations.
From the reigns of Hóngwǔ and Xuāndé onwards,
reward schemes were all predetermined based on the number of heads severed.
Regulations gradually multiplied,
and abuses daily emerged.
During the Zhèngdé reign,
Vice Commissioner Hú Shìníng stated:
"When two armies fight,
hands and eyes are instantaneous,
allowing no room for error;
how can there be leisure to sever heads?
Those who obtain heads may have killed surrendered soldiers,
or innocent civilians,
or happened to capture a lone bandit or a person who escaped from captivity –
these are not true merits.
It is advisable to select strong, clear-headed, upright officials
to serve as merit-recording officers
and severely punish this abuse."
At the time, this could not be implemented.
According to old practice,
guarding officials could recommend at most
five names for promotion.
Later, leading officers recommended as many as three or four hundred names,
who were not covered by the head-severing regulations.
Separate categories were established,
such as "transporting divine firearms,"
"carrying flags and tokens,"
"charging and breaking the enemy,"
"three times taking the lead,"
and "rendering service at the front."
The abuse of false claims
had reached its extreme by this point.
What the ancients called *pào* [cannon]
all launched stones by mechanical means.
In the early Yuán dynasty, after acquiring Western Region cannons,
fire was first used
to besiege the city of Càizhōu in Jīn.
However, the manufacturing method was not passed down,
and it was rarely used thereafter.
It was not until Míng Chéngzǔ pacified Jiāozhǐ
that the method for *shénjī qiāngpào* [divine machine firearms and cannons] was obtained,
and the Shénjī Yíng [Divine Machine Camp] was specially established for practice.
They were made using a mixture of raw and refined red copper.
For those made of iron,
the iron from Jiàn Tiěróu was the best,
followed by Western iron.
They varied in size.
Large ones were fired using carts;
medium and small ones used stands, stakes, or supports.
Large ones were very effective for defense,
small ones for battle;
they were used according to circumstances
as essential implements for military campaigns.
In the tenth year of Yǒnglè, an imperial edict ordered that from Kāipíng to Huáilái, Xuānfǔ, Wànquán, Xīnghé, and other mountain peaks,
five cannon mounts should be installed everywhere.
In the twentieth year, following Zhāng Fǔ's request,
additional ones were installed in the garrisons of Dàtóng, Tiānchéng, Yánghé, and Shuòzhōu in Shānxī to defend against enemies.
However, powerful weapons should not be shown to others,
and the imperial court also guarded them cautiously.
In the fifth year of Xuāndé, an imperial edict was given to Tán Guǎng, the commander-in-chief of Xuānfǔ:
"The divine musket is
highly valued by the state.
It should be supplied in appropriate quantities to border watchtowers and forts
to enhance military prestige,
but not given lightly."
In the sixth year of Zhèngtǒng,
border generals Huáng Zhēn and Yáng Hóng established a *shénchòng* bureau at Dúshí in Xuānfǔ.
The emperor, fearing that the outer manufacturing of firearms
might lead to the leakage of techniques,
issued an edict to stop it.
Towards the end of Zhèngtǒng,
border defenses became increasingly urgent.
Censor Yáng Shàn requested the casting of double-headed bronze muskets.
In the first year of Jǐngtài,
Circuit Supervising Secretary Jiāng Cháo stated:
"The Dūdu Píng'ān 'fire umbrella' stored in Zhēndìng
has iron spearheads on top,
surrounded by jingling bells,
with three gunpowder tubes.
When fired,
it can rout enemy horses.
Shī Áo, a commoner from Yìngzhōu, manufactured a musket
with a mechanism
that could fire three shots in an instant,
reaching over three hundred paces."
Both were tested.
In the eighth year of Tiānshùn,
Assistant Regional Commander Fáng Néng of Yánsuí reported that in breaking the bandits at Lùchuān,
the "Nine Dragon Tube" was used,
which, when ignited in one line, fired nine arrows simultaneously.
He requested that the design be distributed to all border areas.
It was not until the eighth year of Jiājìng
that, following the advice of Right Censor-in-chief Wāng Hóng,
the "Fo Láng Jī" cannon was manufactured,
called "Grand General,"
and distributed to various border garrisons.
"Fo Láng Jī"
is a country's name.
Towards the end of Zhèngdé,
ships from that country arrived in Guǎngdōng.
He Rú, a patrol inspector of Báishā, obtained its design
and made it of bronze,
five or six *chǐ* long.
The large ones weighed over a thousand *jīn*,
the small ones a hundred and fifty *jīn*.
They had a large belly and a long neck,
with a long opening in the belly.
Five *zǐchòng* [sub-cannons] were used,
filled with gunpowder and placed inside the belly.
They could fire over a hundred *zhàng*,
most effective in naval battles.
Mounted on "centipede ships,"
whatever they struck was shattered to pieces.
In the twenty-fifth year,
Governor-General of Military Affairs Wēng Wàndá submitted a memorial on the firearms he had manufactured.
The Ministry of War tested them
and reported:
"The 'Three-Shot Continuous Bead,' 'Hundred-Shot Vanguard,' and 'Iron Staff Thunder-Flight'
are all convenient to use.
The 'Mother-Child Fire Beasts' and 'Ground-Laying Landmine Cannons'
are only suitable for night raids on camps."
Censor Zhāng Duó also presented a "Ten-Eyed Bronze Cannon."
Large projectiles could fire up to seven hundred paces,
small projectiles a hundred paces;
the "Four-Eyed Iron Spear"
fired projectiles four hundred paces.
An imperial edict ordered the Ministry of Works to manufacture them.
During the Wànlì reign,
Assistant Prefect Huá Guāngdà submitted a memorial about the "Divine and Extraordinary Firearms" invented by his father.
The order was sent to the Ministry of War.
Later,
ships from the "Great West" arrived,
and a giant cannon,
called "Red Barbarian," was obtained.
It was over two *zhàng* long,
the heaviest weighing up to three thousand *jīn*.
It could pierce stone cities
and shake for dozens of *lǐ*.
During the Tiānqǐ reign,
it was bestowed the title of "Grand General,"
and officials were dispatched to make offerings to it.
During the Chóngzhēn reign,
Grand Secretary Xú Guāngqǐ requested that Westerners be employed to manufacture them
and distribute them to various garrisons.
However, many generals and commanders were incompetent,
city defenses were not solid,
and some abandoned them and left.
When the roaming bandits attacked the imperial capital,
the soldiers of the Three Great Camps fled without fighting,
and all the firearms and cannons fell into enemy hands,
which they then used to attack the city.
From the city walls, cannons were also fired at the bandits.
At that time, many palace eunuchs already harbored disloyal intentions;
they all filled empty weapons with powder
merely for the shock and noise.
The Míng dynasty established the Bīngzhàng [Arms] and Jūnqì [Military Equipment] bureaus,
which separately manufactured firearms.
Those called "General" ranged from "Great" to "Fifth."

There were also "Gate-Crushing Generals" in two sizes, "Divine Machine Cannons," "Xiāngyáng Cannons," "Zhan Kǒu Cannons" [cup-mouth cannons], "Wǎn Kǒu Cannons" [bowl-mouth cannons], "Whirlwind Cannons," "Meteor Cannons," "Tiger Tail Cannons," "Pomegranate Cannons," "Dragon Tiger Cannons," "Poison Fire Flying Cannons," "Continuous Bead Fo Láng Jī Cannons," "Signal Cannons," "Divine Cannons," "Pàoqián Cannons" [rampart cannon], "Ten-Eyed Bronze Cannons," "Three-Shot Continuous Bead Cannons," "Hundred-Shot Vanguard Cannons," "Iron Staff Thunder-Flight Cannons," "Fire Beast Ground-Laying Landmine Cannons," "Bowl-Mouth Bronze and Iron Muskets," "Handheld Bronze and Iron Muskets," "Divine Muskets," "Horse-Cutting Muskets," "One-Nest-of-Bees Divine Machine Arrow Muskets," "Large, Medium, and Small Fo Láng Jī Bronze Muskets," "Fo Láng Jī Iron Muskets," "Wooden Box Bronze Muskets," "Sinew-Wound Birch Skin Iron Muskets," "Invincible Hand Muskets," "Bird-Beak Muskets," "Seven-Eyed Bronze Muskets," "Thousand-Li Muskets," "Four-Eyed Iron Spears," "Various-Numbered Double-Headed Iron Spears," "Clasp-Handle Iron Handguns," "Rapid-Fire Guns," as well as "Fire Carts," "Fire Umbrellas," and "Nine Dragon Tubes,"
totaling several dozens of types.
Most were manufactured during the Zhèngdé and Jiājìng reigns.
Additionally, various border areas manufactured their own,
starting with Sìchuān in the fourteenth year of Zhèngtǒngtǒng.
Other items included swords, shields, bows, arrows, spears, crossbows, wolf-tooth staffs, caltrops, armor, and battle jackets.
Within the palace, there were the Bīngzhàng, Jūnqì, Zhēn Gōng [Needlework], and Ānpèi [Saddlery] bureaus,
belonging to the imperial storehouse
and managed by palace eunuchs.
Outside, there was the Kuījiǎ Chǎng [Helmet and Armor Factory],
belonging to the Ministry of War
and managed by bureau directors.
The capital and provincial administrative divisions, as well as the various garrisons,
also had their own miscellaneous manufacturing bureaus.
The names of military supplies and equipment are too numerous
to be fully recorded,
but firearms were scarce in previous eras,
hence they are particularly detailed here.
The Central Plains used chariot warfare,
while the Southeast benefited from boats and ships;
both were most crucial for military affairs.
Since the rise of cavalry,
the chariot system gradually fell into disuse.
In the fifth year of Hóngwǔ, single-shaft carts were manufactured:
a thousand for Běipíng and Shāndōng,
and eight hundred for Shānxī and Hénán.
In the eighth year of Yǒnglè, during the northern expedition,
thirty thousand *Wǔgāng* carts were used,
all solely for transporting provisions.
It was not until the twelfth year of the Zhèngtǒng reign that discussions began with the Grand Commander Zhū Miǎn.
They would use "fire chariots" (huǒchē) for battle preparations.
From then on, proposals for chariot warfare followed one after another.
In the fourteenth year,
Li Kǎn, an official of the Grand Secretariat (gěishìzhōng), requested a thousand "blind chariots" (mángchē),
linked with iron chains.
Cavalry would be positioned in the middle,
and each chariot would be flanked by five sword-and-shield bearers.
If the enemy attacked the formation,
the sword-and-shield bearers would strike them.
When the enemy retreated, the chains would be opened to release the cavalry.
The emperor ordered them to be built, consecrated, and then used.
Chariot designs were sent to the border regions,
using seven horses to pull them.
Níngxià had many ravines,
so Grand Commander Zhāng Tài requested the use of small chariots pulled by a single horse.
At the time, this was considered more convenient.
The arrow craftsman Zhōu Sìzhāng said
that the divine-mechanism gun (shénjīqiāng) could not be reloaded quickly after a single shot.
He requested chariots carrying twenty guns
and six hundred arrows.
Five gun racks would be placed at the front of each chariot,
with one person pushing,
two supporting,
and one responsible for cooking.
If the trial was successful,
they would be manufactured.
In the first year of the Jǐngtài reign,
the Earl of Dìngxiāng, Guō Dēng, requested the construction of "flanked chariots" (piānxiāngchē) based on ancient designs.
The shafts were thirteen feet long,
nine feet wide,
and seven feet five inches high.
The sides were made of thin leather
and fitted with cannons (chòng).
When moving, they would be linked side-to-side
and end-to-end,
connected by hooks and rings.
Each chariot carried clothing, provisions, weapons, and two "deer antlers" (lùjiǎo, a type of defensive barrier).
When encamped,
a barrier would be erected fifteen paces away.
Each chariot had a total of ten armed men (jiǎshì), including gunners, bombardiers, archers, crossbowmen, and sword-and-shield bearers.
When not in use, they would take turns pushing and pulling.
Outside, there were twenty long chariots
carrying large and small "general cannons" (jiāngjūnchòng).
There were five chariots for each direction.
Transport of firewood and foraging
were all conducted within the enclosure.
Also, one four-wheeled chariot
was used, displaying five-colored flags,
to direct based on the enemy's movements.
The court deliberated that these could be used for defense,
but were difficult for offense.
Guō Dēng was ordered to implement them at his discretion.
The Prefect of Lánzhōu, Lǐ Jìn, requested the creation of small, single-wheeled chariots.
A leather roof would be installed on top,
and a wooden board at the front,
painted with a beast face,
with holes for the mouth.
Four "bowl-mouthed cannons" (wǎn kǒu chòng),
four guns (qiāng),
and fourteen divine-mechanism arrows (shénjījiàn) would be placed there.
One flag would be raised.
When moving, they formed a battle array;
when stopped, they formed a camp.
In the second year,
Lǐ Xián, a director in the Ministry of Personnel (lìbù lángzhōng), requested the construction of battle chariots.
They were fifteen feet long
and six feet four inches high,
with four-sided panels,
perforated with holes for cannons.
Small windows were opened on top.
Each chariot occupied an area of five paces both front and rear.
Calculated at a thousand chariots,
they could cover sixteen li in each direction.
Fodder, provisions, weapons, and heavy baggage would all be supplied from within.
The emperor ordered immediate implementation.
In the second year of the Chénghuà reign, following Guō Dēng's proposal,
small army chariots were manufactured.
Each squad had six chariots,
each with nine men:
two to pull,
and seven taking turns.
A shield painted with a ni-head (ní shǒu) was placed at the front of each chariot,
making them appear like fortifications from afar.
In the eighth year,
Hé Jīng, a scholar from Níngdū, submitted a design for an enemy-repelling chariot (yùdíchē).
An iron net was installed on top,
with holes in the net for firing guns and crossbows.
When moving, it would be retracted.
Fifty chariots formed a team,
manned by three hundred seventy-five soldiers.
In the twelfth year,
the Censor-in-Chief of the Left (zuǒdūyùshǐ), Lǐ Bīn, requested the construction of flanked chariots (piānxiāngchē),
to be used in conjunction with deer antlers.
The Minister of War (bīngbù shàngshū), Xiàng Zhōng, requested an inspection.
Considering them inconvenient for climbing heights and traversing dangers,
he dismissed the idea.
In the thirteenth year, following the memorial of the Grand Commander of Gānsù, Wáng Xǐ,
fire-thunder chariots (léihuǒchē) were built.
A central pivot was installed,
allowing cannons to rotate and fire.
In the twentieth year,
Yú Zǐjùn, Governor-General of Xuāndà, organized five hundred chariots into one army.
Each chariot had ten soldiers,
and the gaps between chariots were filled with deer antlers.
Once built,
they were found to be too slow and heavy to be practical.
People at the time called them "Partridge Army" (zhègū jūn).
In the fifteenth year of the Hóngzhì reign,
Qín Hóng, Supreme Commander of Shǎnxī, requested the use of single-wheeled chariots,
named "Complete Victory" (quánshèng).
They were fourteen feet long,
with a total of six men above and below,
capable of charging enemy formations.
In the sixteenth year,
Fàn Jí, a retired prefect (xiánzhù zhīfǔ), presented his "Vanguard Thunderclap Chariot" (xiānfēng pīlìchē).
In the eleventh year of the Jiājìng reign,
Wáng Xīwén, an official of the Grand Secretariat (gěishìzhōng) in Nánjīng, requested the construction of chariots based on the designs of Guō Gù and Hán Qí.
These chariots would be built
sharp at the front and square at the rear.
Seven guns would be placed on top,
with a three-story turret,
each fitted with nine "divine ox crossbows" (jiǔniú shénnǔ).
Soldiers would flank them.
When moving, they carried armored soldiers;
when stopped, they formed a camp.
These were sent to the border garrisons for discretionary implementation.
In the fifteenth year,
the Supreme Commander (zǒngzhì) Liú Tiānhé again spoke of the convenience of the "Complete Victory" chariots,
but with some modifications.
Four men would push and pull them,
and the weight of firearms, bows, crossbows, and sword-and-shields carried would be standardized at one hundred fifty jīn.
The front of the box would be painted with a suānní (mythical beast),
and tiger shields would be arranged on the sides to protect the riders.
The emperor ordered that his design be followed.
In the forty-third year,
the responsible authorities approved a proposal
to train with four thousand chariots in the Capital Garrisons (jīngyíng).
Each chariot would have five infantrymen,
two divine guns (shénqiāng) and two "sandwich-shield guns" (jiāpǎ qiāng).
From the Zhèngtǒng reign onwards,
such were the proposals for chariot warfare,
yet they were never once used effectively against the enemy.
It was not until the Lóngqìng reign,
when Qī Jìguāng defended Jìmén,
that he memorialized to train seven battalions of chariots: four battalions under the Vice Grand Commanders of the Eastern and Western routes and the Governor-General's banner command,
stationed separately at Jiànchāng, Zūnhuà, Shíxiá, and Mìyún;
two battalions under the Grand Commanders of Jì and Liáo,
stationed at Sāntún;
and one battalion under the Grand Commander of Chāngpíng,
stationed at Chāngpíng.
Each battalion comprised one hundred fifty-six heavy chariots,
with an additional hundred light chariots,
four thousand infantrymen,
and three thousand cavalrymen.
Across two thousand li of the twelve routes,
with chariots and cavalry combined,
they could defend against tens of thousands of enemies.
Mùzōng approved this
and ordered the provision of construction costs.
However, they were specifically intended to block assaults
and deploy firearms,
and were also never actually used in battle.
Thereafter,
Wèi Xuézéng, the Provincial Governor (xúnfǔ) of Liáodōng, requested the establishment of a battle chariot battalion,
imitating the design of the flanked chariot.
Two "Frankish guns" (fólángjī) would be mounted on top,
and six "thunder-flying cannons" (léifēipào) and "rapid guns" (kuàiqiāng) below.
Each chariot would have twenty-five infantrymen.
At the end of the Wànlì reign,
the Grand Coordinator (jīnglüè), Xióng Tíngbì, requested the construction of double-wheeled battle chariots.
Each chariot would have two cannons,
flanked by ten soldiers,
all carrying firearms.
During the Tiānqǐ reign,

Yì Yìngchāng, the Circuit Censor (xún'àn yùshǐ) of Zhílì, presented designs for steel-wheeled chariots, small assault chariots, and other types, developed by Cáo Lǚjí, an official in the Ministry of Revenue (hùbù zhǔshì).
These were intended to repel enemies,
but were rarely put to use.
Generally, the terrain of the border regions was rugged
and unsuitable for chariot warfare.
The use of boats, however,
was suitable for the southeast.
Boat designs
varied between rivers and seas.
Tàizǔ established four hundred boats at Xīnjiāngkǒu.
In the early Yǒnglè reign,
the Fujian Regional Military Commission (Fújiàn dūsī) was ordered to build one hundred thirty-seven sea-going vessels.
Jiāng, Chǔ, the two Zhè districts, and the garrisons of Zhènjiāng prefectures were also ordered to build "sea-wind boats" (hǎifēngchuán).
In the early Chénghuà reign,
Yáng Qú of the Jìchuān Garrison (Jìchuān wèi) presented a diagram of oared boats.
These were all river boats.
Among seagoing vessels, those from Zhōushān’s Wūcáo were paramount.
The fúchuán were resilient against wind and waves,
and also fire-resistant.
In Zhèjiāng, the ten-masted vessels designated Ruǎnfēng and Cāngshān
were also good for pursuit.
Guǎngdōng ships,
made of iron-oak wood,
were even larger and sturdier than fúchuán.
They had two uses:
they could fire Fólángjī cannons,
and they could hurl fireballs.
The large fúchuán were similar,
able to carry a hundred people.
They were pointed at the bottom and broad at the top,
with a high prow and a high stern.
The rudder house had three levels,
there were two sails and masts,
and the sides were protected by planks.
Wooden battlements and gun carriages were installed on top.
The interior comprised four layers: the lowest was filled with earth and stones;
the next was for resting;
the third had six doors on the left and right,
with water tanks placed in the middle,
and all sail-hoisting and cooking took place there;
the topmost was like a viewing platform,
accessed by a ladder.
Winged planks were installed on the sides,
which could be relied upon for battle.
Arrows, stones, and firearms were all fired downwards.
They could travel with the wind.
The Hǎicāng was slightly smaller than the fúchuán.
The Kāilàngchuán could carry thirty to fifty people,
had a sharp bow,
four oars and one scull.
It moved like flying,
regardless of favorable or adverse winds or tides.
The Tóngchēchuán was even smaller than the Hǎicāng.
Cāngshān ships had broad bows and sterns,
using both sails and sculls.
Sculls were positioned near the rear along the sides of the ship,
five per side,
each scull having five "jumps" (oar positions),
with two men per "jump."
Planks were used to block off the "jumps" from above,
leaving their heads exposed outside.
Their construction had three layers:
the bottom filled with earth and stones,
the top for battle,
and the middle for sleeping.
Hoisting sails and dropping anchor
were all done on the upper layer.
Qī Jìguāng said:
"Wō ships are very small.
Once they enter shallow waters,
the large fúchuán and Hǎicāng cannot enter.
It is essential to use Cāngshuān ships to pursue them.
They are swift in engaging the enemy.
People in Wēnzhōu call them 'Cāngshān iron.'"
The Shā and Yīng ships
were used in conjunction.
The Shāchuán could engage in battle,
but lacked wing protection.
The Yīngchuán was sharp at both ends,
moving like flying, forwards and backwards.
Large mao bamboo was nailed to its sides,
and guns and arrows could be fired through windows between the bamboo.
People inside the windows and outside the hull were concealed to paddle.
These would first enter the enemy formation,
followed by the Shāchuán,
engaging in close-quarters combat,
and always winning.
Fishing boats were very small,
with three people per boat.
One held a cloth sail,
one an oar,
and one a niǎozuǐchòng (bird-beak gun).
Moving up and down with the waves,
they could surprise the enemy.
Wǎngsuōchuán,
found in Dìnghǎi, Línghǎi, and Xiàngshān,
were shaped like shuttles.
With bamboo masts and cloth sails,
they could only accommodate two or three people.
When encountering wind and waves, they could be carried into the foothills
and used for scouting.
Wúgōngchuán,
shaped like centipedes,
could carry Fólángjī cannons.
They were pointed at the bottom and broad on the surface,
with dozens of oars on both sides,
moving like flying.
Liǎngtóuchuán,
which turned on their rudders,
could travel swiftly with the wind in any direction.
No other ship could surpass their speed.
Since the Jiājìng era,
the southeast had daily preparations against the Wō,
hence the design of seagoing vessels
was particularly detailed and comprehensive.
According to the Míng system,
horses belonging to the inner court were managed by the Yùmǎjiān,
which was overseen by eunuchs.
Horses were pastured at Dàbà,
emulating the idea of the twelve stables in the Zhōu Rít.
Horses managed by officials
belonged to the Tàipúsì, Xíngtàipúsì, Yuànmǎsì, and various military guards,
reflecting the idea of the forty-eight inspectorates of the Táng dynasty.
Horses managed by the populace
were in the south, in prefectures directly administered by Yìngtiān, etc.,
and in the north, in directly administered prefectures and those of Shāndōng, Hénán, etc.
This was similar to the horse protection system of the Sòng dynasty.
The system of "bèiyǎngmǎ" (reserve horse breeding)
began at the end of the Zhèngtǒng era,
where selected horses were given to the frontier.
When frontier horses were sufficient,
the rest were pastured in the imperial domain.
Officially pastured horses were given to frontier garrisons,
and privately pastured horses to the capital army.
Both systems included breeding foals.
Lands for official pasturing were called cǎochǎng (grasslands),
or if leased to soldiers and civilians for farming, called shúdì (cultivated land).
Rent was collected annually to assist herdsmen in buying horses.
The herdsmen were called ēnjūn (favored soldiers),
duìjūn (squad soldiers),
gǎibiānjūn (reorganized soldiers),
