chōngfājūn (conscripted soldiers),
and chōufājūn (drafted soldiers).
Imperial parks for horses were divided into three grades:
the upper park had ten thousand,
the middle seven thousand,
and the lower four thousand.
One man tended ten horses,
and for every fifty men, one yǔzhǎng (stable master) was appointed.
The condition of all horses (fatness, leanness, increase, decrease)
was recorded by their hair and teeth, and regularly inspected.
Every three years, the Sìqīng, along with a Yùshǐ, branded them,
and sold the weak and inferior ones to acquire new stock.
The military horses for frontier guards, garrisons, prefectures, and counties, for soldiers and civilians, and for strong cavalry training,
were managed by the Xíngsìqīng.
When frontier needs were insufficient,
tea was exchanged with foreign tribes,
and goods were bought at the frontier.
For civilian pasturing, horses were allocated based on the number of able-bodied men and cultivated land.
Initially called hùmǎ (household horses),
they were later called zhǒngmǎ (breeding horses),
and foals were collected annually.
If a breeding horse died,
or if the number of foals was insufficient,
compensation had to be paid.
This was the general overview.
Initially,
when Tàizǔ established his capital in Jīnlíng,
he ordered the people of the six prefectures—Yìngtiān, Tàipíng, Zhènjiāng, Lúzhōu, Fèngyáng, and Yángzhōu—
and the two departments—Chú and Hé—to pasture horses.
In the sixth year of Hóngwǔ (1373), the Tàipúsì was established in Chúzhōu,
subordinate to the Bīngbù.
Later, five horse inspectorates were added in Chúyáng,
managing forty-eight herds.
Eventually,
there were forty inspectorates,
which were subsequently abolished,
leaving only three: Tiāncháng, Dàxìng, and Shūchéng.
Grasslands were set up in Tāngquán, Chúzhōu, and other places.
Furthermore, the three guards of Fēixióng, Guǎngwǔ, and Yīngwǔ
were ordered that for every five soldiers, one horse was to be kept.
Each horse was to produce a foal annually,
and the one-year-old foals were sent to the capital.
Later, the official pasturing was transferred to the relevant authorities,
and private pasturing was solely mandated.
In Jiāngnán, eleven households,
and in Jiāngběi, five households, were to raise one horse,
and they were exempted from other duties.
Tàipú officials supervised this.
From January to June each year, the "dìngjū" (established foals) were reported;
from July to October, the "xiǎnjū" (visible foals) were reported;
in November and December, the "zhòngjū" (heavy foals) were reported.
At the end of the year, horse administration was reviewed,
and officials of prefectures, departments, and counties were punished according to law.
A male horse was called ér,
and a female horse kòu.
One male and four females formed a qún (herd),
with one qúntóu (herd leader).
For every five herds,
there was one qúnzhǎng (herd chief).
In the thirtieth year, Xíngtàipúsì were established in Běipíng, Liáodōng, Shānxī, Shǎnxī, and Gānsù,
and grasslands for horse pasturing were designated.
In the early years of the Yǒnglè reign,
the Tàipú Sì was established in Běijīng,
administering Shùntiān, Shāndōng, and Hénán.
The previously established one became the Nán Tàipú Sì,
administering Yìngtiān and other six fǔ and two zhōu.
In the fourth year, the Yuànmǎ Sì was established in Shǎnxī and Gānsù,
controlling six jiān,
and each jiān controlling four yuàn.
The Běijīng and Liáodōng Yuànmǎ Sìs were also established,
their administration mirroring that of Shǎnxī and Gānsù.
In the twelfth year, the people of the Northern Jī were ordered to raise horses according to their household labor,
and officials in idle positions were selected to teach them animal husbandry.
Households with fifteen or fewer adult males were to raise one horse,
those with sixteen or more adult males, two horses.
For those dispatched for military service, seven households were to raise one horse,
and they would be exempted from punishment.
Soon after, based on the words of Tàipú Sì Qīng Yáng Dǐ,
households in the north with five adult males were to raise one,
and half of their land rent would be remitted.
From Jìzhōu eastward to the various wèi of Nánhǎi,
excluding garrison soldiers,
each soldier was to feed one breeding horse.
Regulations for horse rearing in the south were also set: Fèng, Lú, Yáng, Chú, and Hé were one horse per five adult males;
Yìngtiān and Tài, Zhèn were one horse per ten adult males.
Huái and Xú, when they first started raising horses,
also used adult males as the rate.
In the eighteenth year, the Běijīng Yuànmǎ Sì was abolished,
and all horses were pastured by the people.
In the first year of Hóngxī, the people were ordered to pasture horses, and a colt was levied every two years,
with half of the fodder and grain exempted.
From then on,
horses proliferated daily,
gradually spreading to neighboring provinces.
The people of Jǐnán, Yǎnzhōu, and Dōngchāng began raising horses
from the fourth year of Xuāndé.
The people of Zhāngdé, Wèihuī, and Kāifēng began raising horses
from the eleventh year of Zhèngtǒng.
Later, when Yěxiān invaded,
he seized twenty thousand horses,
which were kept near the capital,
to be used by the Tuányíng cavalry.
All the breeding horses from that time were given to prefectures like Yǒngpíng.
In the third year of Jǐngtài, stallions eighteen years and older and mares twenty years and older
were exempted from colt levies.
In the second year of Chénghuà,
since the southern lands did not produce horses,
it was changed to a silver levy.
In the fourth year, the Tàipú Sì Chángyíng Kù was first established,
to store silver for horses to be used as reserve.
At this time,
the people gradually found raising horses burdensome.
In the sixth year,
Lìbù Shìláng Yè Shèng said:
“Previously, when one colt was levied annually,
and the people were not disturbed,
it was because there was ample pasture land,
allowing the people to make a living.
Since the estates of powerful families gradually increased,
horse rearing gradually became insufficient.
In the early Hóngxī reign,
it was changed to one colt every two years.
In the early Chénghuà reign,
it was changed to one colt every three years.
The horses became thinner,
and the people became poorer.
However, horses are ultimately indispensable,
so the system of one colt every two years was reinstated,
which the people found even more unbearable.
I request an imperial edict for the border garrisons to adapt to local customs,
and to handle expediently all matters that can acquire horses to suffice the borders and
benefit both military and civilians.”
At that time, Mǎ Wénshēng was pacifying Shǎnxī,
and he also strongly argued about the burden of compensating for horses for the border army,
requesting that tūntián soldiers who had much land but few adult males and did not receive horses
pay one qián of silver annually,
to aid in compensation.
Although both were approved for implementation,
the people's hardship could not be relieved.
The successor to Mǎ Wénshēng in pacifying Shǎnxī was Xiāo Zhēn,
who requested to reduce the traveling Tàipú Sì.
The Bīngbù replied:
“During the Hóngwǔ and Yǒnglè eras,
traveling Tàipú Sìs and Yuànmǎ Sìs were established.
All tea horses and tribute horses from foreign peoples
were collected by the temples and pastured in the yuàn,
often numbering tens of thousands,
sufficient for border use.
After Zhèngtǒng,
northern enemies repeatedly raided and plundered,
and horses dwindled daily.
Those who spoke often requested their reduction or abolition,
which is to begrudge small expenses and forget grand plans.”
Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued to Xiāo Zhēn,
only instructing him to pay more attention to supervision.
Meanwhile, in the Northern Jī since Yǒnglè,
horses had multiplied daily,
and the people were invariably held responsible for pasturing them;
people aged fifteen would raise horses.
Tàipú Shàopīng Péng Lǐ noted that household adult males were limited,
while the colt levy was endless,
and requested to set a quota for breeding horses.
Coincidentally, Mǎ Wénshēng became Bīngbù Shàngshū,
and memorialized to implement Péng Lǐ's request.
Thus, the quota for breeding horses for the two capitals' Tàipú Sìs was set:
twenty-five thousand stallions,
and mares four times that number,
with colts to be delivered every two years.
This was enacted as a regulation.
This was in the sixth year of Hóngzhì.
In the winter of the fifteenth year,
Shàngshū Liú Dàxià recommended Nánjīng Tàicháng Qīng Yáng Yīqīng as Fù Dū Yùshǐ,
to oversee horse administration in Shǎnxī.
Yáng Yīqīng memorialized, saying:
“Our dynasty, considering Shǎnyòu suitable for pasturing,
established jiān and yuàn,
spanning over two thousand lǐ.
Later, all were abolished,
with only Chánglè and Língwǔ jiān remaining.
Now the pasture land is only a few hundred lǐ,
but it is still not insufficient for the western border,
the problem lies only in improper management of jiān and pastures,
and lack of methods for rearing.
Of the two jiān and six yuàn,
Kāichéng and Āndìng have convenient water sources,
and should be made upper yuàn,
to pasture ten thousand horses;
Guǎngníng and Wàn'ān as middle yuàn;
Hēishuǐ has narrow pastures,
Qīngpíng has limited land and barren soil,
to be lower yuàn.
Wàn'ān can hold five thousand,
Guǎngníng four thousand,
Qīngpíng two thousand,
and Hēishuǐ fifteen hundred.
Excluding those given to the army annually, the six yuàn
can regularly pasture thirty-two thousand five hundred horses,
sufficient for the three borders.
However, to greatly increase reproduction,
it is essential to accumulate more breeding horses.
It is advisable to increase them to a full ten thousand,
with one colt every two years,
and the previous number can be reached in five years.
I request to allocate forty-two thousand taels of Tàipú horse silver
to purchase seven thousand breeding horses in Píng, Qìng, Lín, and Gǒng.
Furthermore, the 'grace troops' (ēnjū) for horse rearing are insufficient.
I request to enroll displaced people and those sent back to their native places after questioning,
and treat them according to the example of ēnjūn.
All those sent to border garrisons as soldiers
should be reassigned to pasture horses in the various yuàn,
increasing their number to three thousand people.
I also request to survey the terrain,
build cities for trade,
plant elms and willows.
Horses would be pastured in spring and summer,
and returned in autumn and winter.
Thus, horses would be safe,
and could also be protected if enemies invade.”
Emperor Xiàozōng greatly valued border defense,
and Liú Dàxià was in charge of the Bīngbù.
Yáng Yīqīng’s proposals were invariably carried out.
He was promoted to Zǒngzhì, still overseeing horse administration.
The original quota of pasture land for the various jiān was over one hundred thirty-three thousand seven hundred qǐng,
but what remained was less than half.
Yáng Yīqīng verified it
and found over one hundred twenty-eight thousand qǐng of desolate land,
and also opened up over two thousand nine hundred qǐng of land in the Wǔ'ān Yuàn.
This was reported to the court in the second year of Zhèngdé.
However, after Yáng Yīqīng left office,
it was soon abolished again.
At that time, Yùshǐ Wáng Jì said:
“The people suffer from raising horses.
If a horse gives birth,
they often harm it.
Occasionally, when a colt is determined,
they bribe doctors to conceal it,
or openly cause the colt to fall and die.
A horse deficit only requires paying two taels of silver.
If a birth has been reported to the official
but the colt then dies,
it only requires paying three taels of silver.
If a born colt does not die, it starves.
Horses become thinner day by day,
and are of no practical use.
Now, for breeding horses, land, and adult males,
there is a fixed annual quota.
I request that the people be ordered to buy horses according to this quota,
and the breeding and birth of horses
be of no concern to local officials.”
The Bīngbù agreed with his words.
Thereafter,
whenever a report was made,
Wáng Jì’s words about local officials not being concerned with breeding horses
were always cited,
only demanding colts from the people,
abandoning the mother to seek the child.
Initially,
frontier officials requested horses,
and the Tàipúsì provided them from the existing horses.
After the change to collecting silver,
the number of horses dwindled daily,
but requests continued to pour in.
Ten thousand taels were disbursed
to purchase ten thousand horses.
Frontier officials were unable to procure good horses,
and many horses died.
Tàipúqīng Chǔ Qióng raised this as an issue,
requesting a return to the direct provision of horses.
He also pointed out the abuses of horse breeding, theft, and private borrowing in various border regions.
Although his words were keen,
they were not followed.
Meanwhile, the disbursements to border garrisons grew increasingly frequent.
For the thirty-six camps and forts in Yánsuí,
starting from Hóngzhì eleven,
over ten years,
twenty-eight thousand odd taels of Tàipú silver were disbursed
to buy and replace over forty-nine thousand horses.
Níngxià, Dàtóng, Jūyōngguān, and other places were not included in this count.
By Zhèngdé seven,
a regulation for receiving horses was established,
comprising twelve articles.
In Zhèngdé nine, the Tàipú again disbursed silver to purchase fifteen thousand horses from Shāndōng, Liáodōng, Hénán, and Fèngyáng and Bǎodìng prefectures.
In Jiājìng one,
Shǎnxī Yuànmǎ Shàoqīng Lú Bì submitted a memorial on horse administration,
requesting the collection of outstanding debts, clear branding, training in medicine, and equitable land service to address immediate concerns,
while expanding pastures for long-term planning.
The Emperor highly praised and adopted his proposals.
Thereafter, many spoke on horse affairs,
mostly devising solutions based on specific incidents,
merely providing temporary remedies.
In twenty-nine,
Āndá invaded,
and the Tàipú horses were lacking.
The Zhèngdé regulation for receiving horses was reinstated.
Later,
it was slightly augmented or reduced.
By forty-one,
a regulation was even introduced for donating horses in exchange for official positions.
In Lóngqìng two,
Tídū Sìyíguǎn Tàicháng Shàocīng Wǔ Jīn stated:
“The establishment of breeding horses
is solely for propagation and reserve.
Since reserve horses are now purchased separately,
breeding horses can be saved.
Currently, the reserve horses are sufficient at thirty thousand.
It is appropriate to order that for each horse, thirty taels of silver be paid
to the Tàipú.
All breeding horses should be sold,
with the proceeds remitted to the Bīngbù.
At ten taels per horse,
the one hundred twenty thousand horses in Zhílì, Shāndōng, and Hénán
could yield one million two hundred thousand taels of silver,
and also save two hundred forty thousand taels in fodder expenses.”
Censor Xiè Tíngjié argued:
“The ancestral system,
which concerns military affairs,
cannot be abolished.”
The Bīngbù agreed with Xiè Tíngjié.
However, at that time,
the imperial treasury was short of funds,
and envoys were being dispatched to collect outstanding taxes throughout the empire.
Mùzōng approved Wǔ Jīn’s memorial
and sent it to the ministries for deliberation.
The ministries requested that half be kept and half sold,
and this was followed.
The Tàipú began to hold silver
during the Chénghuà era,
but it was only a little over thirty thousand taels.
As breeding horses were sold,
the silver increasingly grew.
At that time,
the reserves from tributary trade were also meager.
When Zhāng Jūzhèng became Grand Secretary,
he strongly advocated for the complete sale.
Starting from Wànlì nine,
an upper price of eight taels per horse,
down to five taels,
was set, and fodder and land rent were also collected in silver,
further increasing the silver,
to supply the training camps with purchased horses and meet requests from various borders.
However, a gelding was often disbursed for thirty gold,
while prefectures and counties submitted inferior horses worth only a few gold.
Moreover, they were still boarded with horse-keeping households,
causing no less harm to the people than before.
Furthermore, when the state undertook construction projects or awarded bounties,
Tàipú silver was often borrowed,
further depleting the Tàipú treasury.
In fifteen,
Tàipúsì Qīng Luó Yìnghè requested a ban on borrowing.
In twenty-four, an imperial edict ordered the Tàipú to disburse silver for meritorious awards in Shǎnxī.
The Tàipúsì minister said:
“In previous years, the treasury accumulated over four million,
but since the two campaigns in the east and west,
only a quarter remains.
With the military campaign in Cháoxiǎn,
the accumulation of millions is completely gone.
What remains now
is only a little over one hundred thousand.
Moreover, this ministry’s annual quota for boarding horses is twenty thousand,
but this year, converted payments are accepted,
so the levy for horses is very small,
while the requisitions for the eastern campaign are particularly high.
If an alarm suddenly arises,
both horses and silver will be exhausted,
how can we respond?”
The memorial was sent to the ministries,
but no reforms could be made.
In the early years of Chóngzhēn,
an audit of the Hùbù, Bīngbù, and Gōngbù revealed
that Tàipú horse funds amounting to over thirteen million had been borrowed.
Indeed, since Wànlì,
the entire administration of the Tàipúsì had greatly deteriorated,
and frontier pasturage was neglected and abandoned,
making the situation beyond inquiry.
Later,
Yuán Chónghuàn, the Supreme Commander of Liáodōng, lacking horses,
requested that from the horses boarded by households in the two capitals’ prefectures and counties,
the value of three thousand horses be converted to silver to purchase horses from the western frontier.
Tàipúqīng Tú Guódǐng said:
“The imperial ancestors ordered the people to raise horses
specifically to supply the capital garrisons for cavalry training,
defending the capital city,
not for the frontiers.
Later, this was changed to commuted payments,
where in times of peace, horses were exchanged for silver,
and in times of alarm, silver was used to buy horses,
still with the intent of defending the capital.
Now, much of the commuted silver has already been disbursed to various garrisons.
If these horses are also completely converted,
what if an unforeseen event occurs?”
The Emperor approved his words
and rejected Yuán Chónghuàn’s request.
Concerning the Ming dynasty's Mǎzhèng (horse administration),
long-standing laws were beset by abuses.
The reasons for its initial flourishing and eventual decline
were largely due to the rise and fall of the pasture lands.
After Tàizǔ established pasture lands north and south of the Dàjiāng (Yangtze River),
he also designated pastoral lands in the northern frontier: from Dōngshèng westward to Níngxià, Héxī, Cháhǎnnǎor,
eastward to Dàtóng, Xuānfǔ, Kāipíng,
then southeast to Dàníng, Liáodōng,
reaching the Yālù Jiāng and a thousand *lǐ* to the north,
and southward to the territories defended by various *wèi*,
and also from Yànmén Guān westward to beyond the Huáng Hé,
eastward through Zǐjīng, Jūyōng, Gǔběi to Shānhǎi Wèi.
These desolate, open plains,
if not cultivated by soldiers or civilians,
were permitted for princes, imperial sons-in-law, and even soldiers and civilians near the border to gather firewood, forage, and graze their animals.
Frontier princely estates were not allowed to occupy them themselves.
During the Yǒnglè reign,
pasture lands were also established in the Jīdiàn (imperial domain).
Soon after, from Shùnshèng Chuān to the Sānggān Hé, a distance of over one hundred thirty *lǐ*,
where the water and grass were good,
it was ordered that a thousand cavalry from the Tàipú (Court of the Imperial Stud)
and one hundred soldiers from Huáilái Wèi should divide and graze them.
Later, the number increased to twelve thousand horses.
In the early Xuāndé reign,
nine more horse stables (mǎfāng) were established in Bǎo'ān Zhōu.
Thereupon, the Bīngbù (Ministry of War) reported
that horses were greatly multiplying,
and they were named according to their color.
There were twenty-five grades of coat color,
and three hundred sixty breeds.
Thereafter, cultivated estates increased daily,
pasture lands were daily reduced,
and both soldiers and civilians were burdened by breeding.
In the early Hóngzhì reign,
Tāng Miǎn, a *zhǔshì* (secretary) of the Bīngbù, Wáng Jì, *tàipúqīng* (Minister of the Imperial Stud), Hán Yòu, a *jǐshìzhōng* (supervising secretary), and Zhāng Chún, an *yùshǐ* (censor),
all requested a thorough investigation.
And Yòu said:
"The lands in Xiānghé and other counties are occupied by powerful families,
and in Bāzhōu and other places, there are imperial estates of the Rénshòu Gōng.
I request their abolition
to increase pasture land."
Although this was approved,
the occupation and tenancy had been long-standing,
and it ultimately could not be cleared.
The pasture lands for the various *wèi* in Nánjīng had also long been abandoned.
Zhāng Yíng, *shàngshū* (minister) of the Bīngbù, requested their restoration.
Hú Hǎi, an *yùshǐ*, said
he feared it would waste land resources,
and so it was stopped.
The ten thousand official horses of the Jīngshī Tuányíng (Capital Garrison)
and the official horses of the Qíshǒu and other *wèi* on duty
were all distributed among pasture lands.
At the end of spring each year,
horses not designated for use
were led by the *zuòyíng guān* (camp officials) to the fields for grazing.
Grass and beans were stopped as provisions,
and they returned at the end of autumn.
The *jǐshì yùshǐ* (supervising censor) would inspect and report any deceased horses or runaway soldiers.
Later, the horses on duty were not sent to pasture,
but the cavalry training horses were still sent out annually as usual.
In the sixth year of Jiājìng (1527),
Guō Xūn, the Wǔdìng Hóu (Marquis of Wǔdìng), citing border alarms,
petitioned to exempt them,
collecting rent from the various pastures to cover public expenses,
with the remainder stored in the Tàipú for purchasing horses.
Thereupon, the camp horses relied solely on the fodder provided by the Sīnóng (Ministry of Revenue),
at an annual cost of eighteen thousand *liǎng*,
which burdened the Hùbù (Ministry of Revenue),
and the pasture lands became even more derelict.
Debaters vied to profit from renting out land,
and by the time of Shénzōng,
the abuses were extreme.
The Chámǎ Sī (Tea-Horse Bureaus)
were established in Chuān and Shǎn (Sichuan and Shaanxi)
during the Hóngwǔ reign.
They allowed the Xīfān (Western Barbarians) to exchange horses for tea,
and were granted gold tallies and credentials
to prevent fraud.
Every three years,
court officials were dispatched to summon the various barbarian tribes to match tallies and trade,
giving one hundred twenty *jīn* of tea for a superior horse,
seventy *jīn* for a medium horse,
and fifty *jīn* for an inferior horse.
Those who privately exported tea were punished with death,
even meritorious relatives were not pardoned.
In the later years,
over thirteen thousand five hundred horses were exchanged.
During the Yǒnglè reign,
the prohibitions were slightly relaxed,
and fewer horses were exchanged.
Thus, it was ordered to strictly enforce the tea ban at the border passes,
and *yùshǐ* were sent to patrol and supervise.
At the end of Zhèngtǒng,
the gold tallies were abolished,
and *xíngrén* (envoys) were dispatched annually to inspect.
Many border residents violated the ban by engaging in private trade.
During the Chénghuà period,
it was decided to assign one *yùshǐ*
to specially manage the matter with an imperial edict.
During the Hóngzhì period,
Lǐ Dōngyáng, a *dàxuéshì* (grand secretary), said:
"With the abolition of the gold tally system,
private tea trade flourished,
and officials repeatedly deceived the barbarian tribes with inferior tea.
The barbarians felt resentment
and often offered emaciated horses in return.
It is advisable to strictly order the officials in Shǎnxī to post proclamations to inform them,
restore the gold tally system,
strictly collect good quality tea,
and moderately increase the price of horses,
then the acquisition of horses will surely be abundant."
When Yáng Yīqīng was appointed to supervise the Yùnmǎ (Imperial Stud),
he was then ordered to also manage salt and tea.
Yīqīng reinstated the old system,
prohibiting private trade and cultivating official tea.
Within four years, over nine thousand horses were exchanged,
and tea still accumulated over four hundred thousand *jīn*.
The salt tax from Língzhōu Salt Pond increased by fifty-nine thousand *liǎng*,
which was stored in the treasuries of Qìngyáng and Gùyuán
to buy horses for the frontier.
He also feared that without a dedicated official later,
the system would eventually be abolished.
Thus, in the early Zhèngdé reign,
he requested that the *xúnchá yùshǐ* (inspecting censor for tea) also manage the horse administration,
and that officials of the Tàipú and Yùnmǎ Sì (Imperial Stud) follow his directives,
which was approved.
*Yùshǐ* Zhái Táng annually collected over seven hundred eighty thousand *jīn* of tea
and exchanged over nine thousand horses.
Later, the system was again relaxed.
In the early Jiājìng reign,
the Hùbù requested to post proclamations prohibiting private tea.
All permits were to be issued with the seal of the Nán Hùbù (Southern Ministry of Revenue),
and prefectures, *zhōu*, and counties were not allowed to print them without authorization.
In the thirtieth year, an imperial edict granted credentials to barbarian tribes,
but the original system could not be restored.
The horse markets
began during the Yǒnglè reign.
Three markets were established in Liáodōng,
two in Kāiyuán,
and one in Guǎngníng,
each forty *lǐ* from the city.
During the Chénghuà reign,
Chén Yuè, the *xúnfǔ* (provincial governor), again memorialized to implement them.
They continued until the early Wànlì reign without abolition.
During the Jiājìng reign,
a horse market was opened in Dàtóng,
and the Shǎnbian Xuānzhèn (Xuānfu and Dàtóng garrisons on the Shaanxi border) subsequently followed suit.
In the fifth year of Lóngqìng (1571),
Āndá presented a memorial expressing submission and tribute.
Wáng Chónggǔ, the *zǒngdū* (grand coordinator), traded for over seven thousand horses,
at a value of over ninety-six thousand *liǎng*.
For their payment,
Liáodōng used rice, cloth, and silk,
while Xuān, Dà, and Shānxī used silver.
For those who presented tribute horses outside of market exchanges,
additional rewards of paper currency and silks were given.
Initially,
when Tàizǔ rose from Jiāngzuǒ (south of the Yangtze),
what he urgently needed were horses,
and he repeatedly sent envoys to market them in all directions.
On the Zhèngyuán Shòujié (Emperor's Birthday),
internal and external princes and generals all presented horses as tribute.
Foreign countries, local chieftains (*tǔsī*), and barbarian tribes regularly came to present tribute,
and the court always gave generous rewards,
doing everything possible to attract and pacify them.
Wéndì was diligent in distant strategies,
sending envoys to remote regions,
and many foreign countries came to court;
however, what he urgently needed was not horses.
Thereafter, accustomed to peace,
the power of control was lost,
and there was no external increase in horses,
relying solely on breeding and annual levies.
Compounded by the encroachment and exploitation by officials,
the horse administration became derelict,
and both soldiers and civilians were distressed.
Indeed, from Xuāndé onward in the Ming dynasty,
the ancestral system gradually fell into disuse,
especially so in military affairs,
and the Mǎzhèng was one such instance.
Collation Notes
Zhi Chapter Sixty-nine, Xíngfǎ One
Since the Hàn [Dynasty],
penal laws have undergone varied changes.
The Suí [Dynasty] revised the provisions for the Five Punishments,
and instituted the Three Memorials system.
The Táng [Dynasty] compiled laws and ordinances,
which were entirely based on ritual for their application.
The Sòng [Dynasty] adopted them,
but what was emphasized were imperial edicts,
and matters not covered by the statutes
were referred to edicts.
Thus, at times they were light, at times heavy,
with no consistent standard.
The Yuán [Dynasty] system
merely took contemporary exemplary cases as statutes and regulations.
In the early Míng [Dynasty],
Chancellor Lǐ Shàncháng and others stated:
"The laws of successive dynasties
all took the Hàn Nine Chapters as their foundation,
and were fully established by the Táng [Dynasty].
The current system should follow the old Táng model."
Tàizǔ followed their advice.
Initially,
Tàizǔ, chastened by the laxity of the Yuán [Dynasty]'s aftermath,
applied severe penalties.
However, these were decisions made specifically for a time,
not intended as permanent rules.
Later, he repeatedly issued edicts for clarification and correction,
and it was not until his thirtieth year that a unified system was enforced.
The deliberations for additions and subtractions
were meticulous and exhaustive,
intended for his descendants to uphold.
If any of his ministers dared to suggest changes,
they would be charged with the crime of altering ancestral decrees.
Yet, subsequent malpractices proliferated
because people did not understand the laws.
They mistakenly believed that the laws only provided broad outlines,
insufficient to cover the complexities of truth and falsehood.
Consequently, precedents were established based on laws,
and new precedents arose from existing ones.
The more numerous the precedents, the more endless the malpractices became.
Initially, edicts instructed internal and external censors
to examine officials
on their knowledge and study of laws and ordinances.
Those unable to comprehend them
were penalized accordingly.
It was hoped that people would understand the spirit of the law.
However, over time,
it became a mere formality.
As a result, corrupt officials bent the law,
arbitrarily applying light or heavy sentences.
For instance, some laws stipulated decisions by the emperor or temporary disposition,

established for cases involving the Eight Deliberations, which could not be summarily investigated, and for all suspicious cases with difficult-to-determine charges, or cases where the law had no explicit provision.
This did not mean the imperial court could arbitrarily grant life or death.
After the Yīngzōng and Xiànzōng reigns,
the spirit of compassion diminished,
and the trend of surveillance intensified.
Cases of major evildoers and heinous criminals
piled up like mountains,
yet imperial decrees from above
often let them off without question;
or, in cases where death was unwarranted,
a single document sent them to imperial prisons,
causing even more egregious harm.
Therefore, this general overview of Míng [Dynasty] penal law
concludes with the Factory and Guard organizations.
The names of the eunuchs from the Factories
are not fully recorded in traditional accounts,
so they are listed here
for reference.
When Míng Tàizǔ pacified Wǔchāng,
he immediately began discussing laws and ordinances.
In the tenth month of the winter of Wú Yuán year, he ordered Left Chancellor Lǐ Shàncháng to be the chief compiler of laws and ordinances.
Yang Xiàn, Fù Huán, who were Participators in the Administration of Governmental Affairs;
Liú Jī, the Censor-in-Chief;
Táo Ān, the Hanlin Academician, and twenty others were appointed as law discussion officials.
He instructed them, saying:
"Laws should be concise and appropriate,
making them easy for people to understand.
If the articles are numerous and complex,
or if a single matter has two interpretations,
allowing for light or heavy treatment,
officials can exploit this for corruption,
which is not the intent of the law.
Indeed, if the net is too fine, no big fish can be caught;
if the law is too strict, there will be no complete citizens in the country.
You all should meticulously deliberate and research,
and submit the articles of criminal law daily,
and I will personally review and discuss them."
Each time he visited the Western Tower,
he summoned his ministers, granted them seats,
and leisurely lectured on the meaning of the laws.
In the twelfth month,
the work was completed,
comprising one hundred and forty-five articles of ordinances
and two hundred and eighty-five articles of laws.
Fearing that common people might not fully know them,
he ordered Grand Judge Zhōu Zhēn and others to take the established laws and ordinances,
and apart from those concerning rites and music, institutions, taxes, and election methods,
all matters related to the daily lives of the common people,
were to be compiled by category,
their meanings explained,
and distributed to prefectures and counties.
It was named "Lǜlìng Zhíjiě" (Direct Explanation of Laws and Ordinances).
Tàizǔ, upon reading the book, rejoiced, saying:
"My people can now commit fewer transgressions."
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, he again ordered four Confucian scholars
to discuss the Táng [Dynasty] laws with judicial officials,
submitting twenty articles daily.
In the fifth year, prohibitions for eunuchs and laws for mutual concealment among relatives were established.
In the summer of the sixth year, the "Lǜlìng Xiàngāng" (Essentials of Laws and Ordinances) was published
and distributed to all government offices.
That winter,
he decreed that Liú Wéiqiān, the Minister of Justice, should thoroughly finalize the "Dàmíng Lǜ" (Great Míng Code).
Each time a chapter was presented,
he ordered it displayed in the two wings [of the palace],
and personally made revisions.
When it was completed,
Hànlín Academician Sòng Lián presented a memorial,
saying:
"Your servant received the edict in the eleventh month of the winter of the sixth year of Hóngwǔ,
and the work was completed in the second month of the following year.
The chapter titles are entirely based on the Táng [Code]: namely, 'Guarding and Prohibition,'
'Official System,'
'Household and Marriage,'
'Stables and Treasuries,'
'Unauthorized Levies,'
'Robbery and Theft,'
'Fighting and Litigation,'
'Fraud and Forgery,'
'Miscellaneous Laws,'
'Pursuit of Fugitives,'
'Adjudication of Cases,'
and 'General Principles.'
Two hundred and eighty-eight articles from the old laws were adopted,
one hundred and twenty-eight supplementary articles were added,
thirty-six articles from old ordinances were revised into laws,
thirty-one articles were created based on specific situations,
and one hundred and twenty-three articles were extracted from the Táng Code to fill gaps.
In total, there are six hundred and six articles,
divided into thirty volumes.
Whether reduced or augmented,
or retained in their original form,
they were all aimed at achieving appropriate severity or leniency."
In the ninth year,
Tàizǔ, reviewing the articles of the law, still found some unsuitable,
and ordered Chancellor Hú Wéiyōng, Grand Censor Wāng Guǎngyáng, and others to deliberate and clarify thirteen articles.
In the sixteenth year, he ordered Minister Kāi Jì to establish articles for fraud and forgery.
In the twenty-second year,
the Ministry of Justice reported:
"In recent years, the articles and precedents have been inconsistently augmented and subtracted,
leading to inappropriate judgments in cases.
We request that they be compiled and promulgated,
so that both those inside and outside the court know what to abide by."
Consequently, the Hanlin Academy was ordered to work with officials from the Ministry of Justice.
They took the additions made in recent years
and appended them by category.
The "Mínglì Lǜ" (Law on General Principles) was moved to the beginning of the compilation.
There were a total of thirty volumes,
with four hundred and sixty articles.
One volume of General Principles,
with forty-seven articles.
Two volumes of Official Laws,
namely 'Official System' with fifteen articles,
and 'Official Duties' with eighteen articles.
Seven volumes of Household Laws,
namely 'Households and Corvée' with fifteen articles,
'Fields and Dwellings' with eleven articles,
'Marriage' with eighteen articles,
'Granaries and Treasuries' with twenty-
four articles,
'Taxes and Levies' with nineteen articles,
'Money and Debts' with three articles,
and 'Markets and Shops' with five articles.
Two volumes of Ritual Laws,
namely 'Sacrifices' with six articles,
and 'Ceremonial System' with twenty
articles.
Five volumes of Military Laws,
namely 'Palace Guards' with nineteen articles,
'Military Administration' with twenty articles,
'Passes and Ferries' with seven articles,
'Stables and Herding' with eleven articles,
and 'Post Stations' with eighteen
articles.
Eleven volumes of Penal Laws,
namely 'Robbery and Theft' with twenty-eight articles,
'Homicide' with twenty articles,
'Fighting and Assault' with twenty-two articles,
'Verbal Abuse' with eight articles,
'Litigation' with twelve articles,
'Receiving Bribes' with eleven articles,
'Fraud and Forgery' with twelve articles,
'Sexual Offenses' with ten articles,
'Miscellaneous Offenses' with eleven articles,
and 'Pursuit of Fugitives' with eight
articles.
The second concerns twenty-nine articles on sentencing cases.
The 工律 (Gōnglǜ) is in two volumes,
the first on nine articles for construction,
the second on four articles for river defense.
There are two charts for the Five Punishments in total.
The first chart shows five:
笞 (chī) [light bamboo/cudgel],
杖 (zhàng) [heavy bamboo/cudgel],
徒 (tú) [penal servitude],
流 (liú) [exile],
死 (sǐ) [death].
There are five degrees of 笞 (chī) punishment,
ranging from ten to fifty blows;
with each ten blows being one degree for increase or decrease.
There are five degrees of 杖 (zhàng) punishment,
ranging from sixty to one hundred blows;
with each ten blows being one degree for increase or decrease.
There are five degrees of 徒 (tú) punishment:
one year of penal servitude with sixty blows of the杖 (zhàng),
one and a half years with seventy blows,
two years with eighty blows,
two and a half years with ninety blows,
and three years with one hundred blows;
with each ten blows of the杖 (zhàng) and half a year of penal servitude being one degree for increase or decrease.
There are three degrees of 流 (liú) punishment:
two thousand lì,
two thousand five hundred lì,
and three thousand lì,
all with one hundred blows of the杖 (zhàng);
with each five hundred lì being one degree for increase or decrease.
There are two forms of 死 (sǐ) punishment:
strangulation (絞, jiǎo)
and decapitation (斬, zhǎn).
Beyond the Five Punishments,
徒 (tú) includes a total of four years of penal servitude
(for those who receive a one-year reduction by precedent),
and five years of approved penal servitude
(for those whose sentences of decapitation, strangulation, or miscellaneous offenses are reduced).
流 (liú) includes resettlement (安置, ānzhì),
relocation
(遷徙, qiānxǐ)
(one thousand lì away from one's home village,
one hundred blows of the杖 (zhàng),
equivalent to two years of penal servitude),
and becoming a commoner outside the pass (口外為民, kǒuwài wéimín).
The heaviest is military exile (充軍, chōngjūn).
In the early Míng dynasty,
充軍 (chōngjūn) was solely for garrisoning and cultivating border lands.
Later,
the system was formalized,
divided into extreme borders, malaria-ridden regions, distant borders, border garrisons, coastal areas, and nearby regions.
Military exile could be for life (終身, zhōngshēn)
or perpetual (永遠, yǒngyuǎn).
Beyond the two forms of death punishment,
there was death by a thousand cuts (凌遲, língchí),
used
for those who committed crimes of great treason and sacrilege.
充軍 (Chōngjūn) and 凌遲 (língchí)
were not standard Five Punishments,
hence they were not listed in the charts.
For those who committed 徒 (tú) or 流 (liú) offenses a second time,
those sentenced to 流 (liú) were, at their original place of assignment,
to be
kept according to the method for artisans' and entertainers' households.
Triple 流 (liú) would result in one hundred blows of the杖 (zhàng)
and three years of forced labor (拘役, jūyì).
拘役 (Jūyì) meant that
while exiles were initially only resettled,
now forced
labor was added,
which was what the Táng and Sòng dynasties called "exile with added labor."
Those sentenced to 徒 (tú), at their original place of labor,
after serving the specified number of blows and years based on their offense,
were not to be made to labor for more than four years.
The second chart shows seven items:
笞 (chī),
杖 (zhàng),
訊杖 (xùnzhàng) [interrogation cudgel],
枷 (jiā) [cangue],
杻 (niǔ) [handcuffs],
索 (suǒ) [rope],
鐐 (liáo) [fetters].
The 笞 (chī) had a large end with a diameter of two分 (fēn) seven釐 (lí),
and a small end
reduced by one分 (fēn).
The 杖 (zhàng) had a large end with a diameter of three分 (fēn) two釐 (lí),
and a small end reduced by the same amount as the 笞 (chī).
Both 笞 (chī) and 杖 (zhàng) were made of荆條 (jīngtiáo) [chaste tree branches],
and were administered to the buttocks.
The 訊杖 (xùnzhàng) had a large end with a diameter of four分 (fēn) five釐 (lí),
and a small end reduced by the same amount as the 笞 (chī) and 杖 (zhàng).
It was made of 荆條 (jīngtiáo),
and was administered to the buttocks and thighs.
All 笞 (chī), 杖 (zhàng), and 訊 (xùn) [cudgels for interrogation]
were three feet five inches long.
They were to be
verified against official standards
and not fitted with
sinews, glue, or other materials for reinforcement.
Cangues (枷, jiā)
ranged from fifteen jīn to twenty-five jīn,
with their length and weight
marked on them.
They were five feet five inches long,
with a head width of one foot five inches.
Handcuffs (杻, niǔ) were one foot six inches long
and one inch thick.
They were used for male prisoners sentenced to death.
Ropes (索, suǒ)
were made of iron,
used to tie up those with minor offenses,
and were ten feet long.
Fetters (鐐, liáo)
were made of iron links,
used to bind the feet.
Those sentenced to penal servitude wore them while performing labor,
weighing three jīn.
There are also eight charts for mourning attire:
If a family member committed an offense, the severity of the punishment was determined by the degree of mourning attire.
Based on the principles of propriety,
foster mothers (養母, yǎngmǔ), stepmothers (繼母, jìmǔ),
and kind mothers (慈母, címǔ) all wore mourning for three years.
Assaulting and killing them
incurred the same penalty as assaulting and killing one's biological mother.
Brothers' wives all wore mourning for xiǎo gōng (小功, minor mourning).
Those who mutually concealed each other's crimes
would have their punishments
reduced.
Mourning for a husband's parents (舅姑, jiùgū) was all zhǎnzāi (斬衰, deepest mourning) for three years.
Those who assaulted, killed, or reviled them
were subject to the same laws as a husband who assaulted, killed, or reviled his parents.
Aunts' children, maternal uncles' children, and paternal aunts' children
all wore sī má (緦麻, lightest mourning).
These were called biǎo xiōngdì (表兄弟, maternal/paternal cousins)
and could not intermarry.
There are Ten Great Evils (大惡, dà'è):
謀反 (móufǎn) [rebellion],
謀大逆 (móudànì) [great treason],
謀叛 (móupàn) [treason],
惡逆 (ènì) [wickedness against superiors],
不道 (bùdào) [inhumanity],
大不敬 (dàbùjìng) [great disrespect],
不孝 (bùxiào) [lack of filial piety],
不睦 (bùmù) [disharmony],
不義 (bùyì) [unrighteousness],
內亂 (nèiluàn) [incest].
These were not pardoned even by general amnesty.
There are six categories of ill-gotten gains from corruption (貪墨之贓, tānmò zhī zāng):
監守盜 (jiānshǒudào) [theft by a guardian],
常人盜 (chángréndào) [theft by an ordinary person],
竊盜 (qièdào) [secret theft],
枉法 (wǎngfǎ) [bending the law],
不枉法 (bùwǎngfǎ) [not bending the law],
坐贓 (zuòzāng) [receiving bribes].
There are eight categories of persons whose cases are to be deliberated (當議者, dāngyìzhě):
議親 (yìqīn) [relatives of the emperor],
議故 (yìgù) [old acquaintances],
議功 (yìgōng) [those with merit],
議賢 (yìxián) [the virtuous],
議能 (yìnéng) [the capable],
議勤 (yìqín) [the diligent],
議貴 (yìguì) [the noble],
議賓 (yìbīn) [imperial guests].
Tài Zǔ (太祖) instructed the imperial grandson:
"This book first lists two punishment charts,
then eight propriety charts,
emphasizing propriety.
However, ignorant commoners,
if leniency orders were immediately annotated under the specific articles,
would surely easily commit crimes.
Therefore, with the intention of broad benevolence and cherishing life,
all these are generally listed within the Name and Precedent Law (名例律, Mínglìlǜ).
A good practitioner of the law will grasp its intent. "
The imperial grandson requested a revision of the five articles and above.
Tài Zǔ (太祖) reviewed and approved it.
The imperial grandson further requested:
"Clear punishments serve to aid moral education.
All matters related to the Five Relations (五倫, Wǔlún)
should ideally involve bending the law to extend sentiment."
Thereupon, he ordered seventy-three articles to be revised,
and further instructed him:
"I govern a turbulent age,
so punishments must necessarily be heavy.
You will govern an era of peace,
so punishments should naturally be light;
this is what is meant by 'punishments are heavy or light according to the age.'"
In the twenty-fifth year,
the Ministry of Punishments reported
that articles in the law that differed from the regulations should be revised.
Tài Zǔ (太祖) held that regulations (條例, tiáolì) were merely temporary
expedients,
and the established law (定律, dìnglǜ) could not be changed,
and did not consent.
In the thirtieth year, the Dà Míng Lǜ Gào (Great Ming Code and Edict) was completed.
At the Wǔmén Gate,
the Emperor instructed his officials, saying:
"I govern by imitating the ancients,
elucidating rites to guide the people,
and establishing laws to restrain the stubborn.
I published them as ordinances.
After they had been implemented for a long time,
there were still many transgressors.
Therefore, I composed the Dà Gào (Great Edict) to show the people,
so that they might know the way to seek good fortune and avoid misfortune.
The ancients called punishment 'auspicious punishment,'
was it not because they wished for all people to live together between heaven and earth?
However, the laws were in the hands of officials,
and the common people did not fully know them.
Therefore, I commanded the penal officials to extract articles from the Dà Gào,
summarize their essentials,
and append them to the laws.
All existing proclamations and prohibitions are hereby abolished.
Except for crimes of conspiracy against the throne and those already covered by the laws and edicts,
all miscellaneous offenses, whether major or minor,
shall be judged according to the regulations for commuting punishment with a fine.
These shall be compiled into a book,
published throughout the country,
so that all under heaven may know what to observe."
The Dà Gào was compiled because
Tài Zǔ was troubled that the people were accustomed to Yuán (Yuan Dynasty) practices,
prioritizing private interests over public good,
and becoming increasingly perverse.
In the eighteenth year, he collected various offenses of officials and common people,
and codified them into the Dà Gào.
Its ten categories were: 1. Tax evasion by collectors,
2. Improper transfer of guaranteed assets,
3. Deceptive concealment of land and grain,
4. Failure of common people to deliver entrusted goods,
5. Abandonment of land by scattering assignments,
6. Abusing the law for selfish gain,
7. False enlistment and desertion by soldiers,
8. Tattooed runaways,
9. Officials and jailers colluding to sell prisoners,
10. Scholars and officials nationwide refusing to serve the ruler.
The punishment for these crimes extended to confiscation of property.
The following year, a sequel and a third compilation were made,
all promulgated to academies for instructing scholars,
and schoolmasters were set up in villages to teach them.
Prisoners who possessed the Dà Gào
had their sentences reduced.
At that time,
over one hundred ninety thousand teachers and students who lectured on the Dà Gào came to court,
and were all given paper money and sent back.
Since the promulgation of the Lǜ Gào (Code and Edict),
the severe regulations contained in the Dà Gào were never lightly applied.
Later, criminals often invoked the Dà Gào to reduce their sentences,
and their possession of it was no longer even questioned.
Indeed, Tài Zǔ's legislative work
began in the first year of Wú,
was revised in the sixth year of Hóngwǔ,
standardized in the twenty-second year,
and finally promulgated throughout the empire in the thirtieth year.
Over time, the details were refined,
and the laws of the dynasty were finally established.
Judgments throughout the country
were uniformly based on what was promulgated in the thirtieth year.
As for the ordinances from the first year of Hóngwǔ,
if there were provisions not in the law but present in the ordinance,
the judicial authorities could invoke them as evidence,
requesting approval from the emperor before acting upon them.
Any violation of an ordinance was punishable by flogging.
For crimes specifically ordered by the emperor to be judged on a case-by-case basis
and not codified into laws or ordinances,
this rule did not apply.
If officials arbitrarily cited and compared them to laws,
resulting in discrepancies in the severity of punishment,
it was judged as deliberate misapplication of law.
If a crime had no explicit statute,
laws could be cited and compared to it,
a proposed sentence determined,
and submitted to the board for deliberation and memorialization to the throne.
If a judgment was made arbitrarily,
resulting in discrepancies in the crime or punishment,
it was judged as negligent misapplication of law.
Generally, the Míng (Ming Dynasty) laws were simpler and more concise than those of Táng (Tang Dynasty),
but less lenient than those of Sòng (Song Dynasty).
However, its spirit of compassion
is scattered throughout various articles,
and one can be used to infer the rest.
For example, if a crime warranted increased punishment,
it would only apply if the stolen goods reached the specified amount.
(For example, an embezzlement by a custodian was punishable by strangulation if the stolen goods amounted to forty strings of cash.
However, if it was only thirty-nine strings and ninety-nine coins,
lacking one coin, it would not be punished.)
The maximum increase in punishment was exile for three thousand *lǐ*,
with incremental increases in severity,
but never reaching the death penalty.
And for those whose sentences were reduced to exile,
it was a transition from death to life,
without distinction between strangulation or decapitation.
(This corresponds to the Táng (Tang Dynasty) law article on "aggravated punishment.")
A "day" was defined as one hundred *kè*.
A "year" was defined as three hundred and sixty days.
(For example, for deadlines concerning human life or various documents,
even if it was slightly short of one *kè* or one hour,
the offense could still not be penalized based on the limited number of months or years.
This corresponds to the Táng (Tang Dynasty) precedent of defining a day as one hundred *kè*.)
If a crime was committed by someone not yet old or infirm,
but the incident came to light when they were old or infirm,
it was judged according to the criteria for the old or infirm;
if a crime was committed by a minor,
but the incident came to light when they were adults,
it was judged according to the criteria for minors.
(This corresponds to the Táng (Tang Dynasty) law article on the old, young, and disabled.)
For capital crimes
not pardoned by general amnesty,
if the grandparents or parents were old and had no one to support them,
a memorial could be submitted for imperial decision.
For those sentenced to penal servitude or exile,
other lesser crimes could be commuted with a fine,
allowing them to remain and support their parents.
(This corresponds to the Táng (Tang Dynasty) law article on crimes not among the Ten Abominations.)
For meritorious officials and officials of the fifth rank or higher who were imprisoned,
close relatives were allowed to attend them,
and those sentenced to penal servitude or exile were permitted to have attendants accompany them;
violators would be punished by caning.
If cohabiting relatives committed crimes,
they could conceal each other.
(This corresponds to the Táng (Tang Dynasty) law article on mutual concealment among cohabiting relatives.)
Slaves were not allowed to denounce their masters.
In general, for those who accused others,
an accuser's grandparents or parents could not be cited as witnesses for their descendants,
a younger brother could not testify against an elder brother,
a wife could not testify against her husband,
and slaves could not testify against their masters.
Civil officials, whose duty was to uphold the law,
would not be subject to flogging for certain offenses.
Military officers, even if sentenced to penal servitude or exile,
could still be promoted based on their hereditary merits.
All such provisions,
some adopted from the Táng (Tang Dynasty) laws,
others newly established,
were meant to preserve the intimacy between father and son,
and establish the righteousness between ruler and minister, exercising discretion in their application.
When Jiànwén Dì ascended the throne,
he instructed the penal officials, saying:
"The Dà Míng Lǜ,
personally established by my Imperial Grandfather,
which he commanded me to examine carefully,
is often more severe than previous dynasties.
This is a code for governing a chaotic nation,
not a universal path for a hundred generations.
What I previously revised,
my Imperial Grandfather had already ordered to be implemented.
However, crimes that deserve compassion and doubt
are not limited to these.
Indeed, the law establishes major principles,
while rites accord with human nature.
To regulate the people with punishment
is not as good as regulating them with rites.
Therefore, instruct officials throughout the empire
to earnestly promote rites and education,
and pardon doubtful cases,
to manifest my benevolent intention towards all regions."
Chéng Zǔ decreed that judicial authorities interrogating prisoners
should deliberate strictly according to the Dà Míng Lǜ,
and not arbitrarily cite proclamations or regulations to create harsh penalties.
In the first year of Yǒnglè, the law against false accusations was established.
In the first year of Chénghuà, it was again ordered that those judging prisoners should strictly adhere to the main law,
abolishing all existing regulations.
In the fifteenth year,
Wáng Shù, the巡撫 (Xúnfǔ,巡撫) of Nán Zhílì, stated:
"After the Dà Míng Lǜ,
there are one hundred and eight 'jointly determined current laws' whose origin is unknown.
For example, the military laws frequently concern salary and provisions,
and the criminal laws concerning cursing an envoy or one's superior officer
all have disproportionate severities.
These are circulated everywhere,
misleading officials.
I request that their printing blocks be recalled and burned."
An order was immediately given to burn them.
Anyone who had convicted or acquitted people based on these laws
was to be judged for deliberate misapplication of law.
In the eighteenth year, the crime of extorting wealth through deception was established.
During the Hongzhì [Hóngzhì] reign,
a hundred years had passed since the establishment of the fixed laws,
and their enforcement became increasingly lax.
In the fifth year of Hongzhì [Hóngzhì],
the Minister of Justice, Péng Sháo [Péng Sháo], and others, at the request of the Grand Court Registrar, Lǐ Suì [Lǐ Suì],
compiled and revised the "Articles of Inquiry into Criminal Cases" (Wènxíng tiáolì [Wènxíng tiáolì]).
By the thirteenth year,
judicial officials again reported, saying:
"At the end of the Hongwǔ [Hóngwǔ] reign,
the Great Ming Code (Dà Míng Lǜ [Dà Míng Lǜ]) was established,
and later the Great Edict (Dà Gào [Dà Gào]) was further promulgated,
allowing for a reduction in punishment for crimes,
which has been followed by successive dynasties.
As for evading punishment outside the law,
the sage emperors, adapting to the times, extended the application, giving rise to precedents (lì [lì]).
Precedents are to assist the laws,
not to break them.
Yet, clever legal clerks, both inside and outside the court, sometimes exploit these precedents for personal gain,
causing the laws to be increasingly ignored and unused."
Thereupon, the Minister, Bái Áng [Bái Áng], and others were ordered to convene with the Nine Ministers [Jiǔ Qīng] to deliberate.
They added two hundred and ninety-seven articles from previous "Articles of Inquiry into Criminal Cases" that had proven effective over time.
The Emperor selected six of these matters,
ordering further deliberation and a report.
The Nine Ministers [Jiǔ Qīng] adhered to their initial recommendation,
so no changes were ultimately made.
However, from then on,
both laws (lǜ [lǜ]) and precedents (lì [lì]) were enforced concurrently,
and the legal net became somewhat tighter.
The six articles of prohibitions for princely establishments (wángfǔ jìnlì [wángfǔ jìnlì]),
which stipulated penalties for princes leaving the city without cause,
were particularly strict.
In the seventh year of Jiajìng [Jiājìng],
Wáng Yìngpéng [Wáng Yìngpéng], the巡撫 [Xúnfǔ] of Baodìng [Bǎodìng], said:
"During the Zhèngdé [Zhèngdé] era,
forty-four new articles were added to the 'Articles of Inquiry into Criminal Cases,'
which were deeply consistent with both reason and law, and all should be incorporated."
This was not followed.
Only an imperial edict stipulated that those who forged seals and those who committed theft three times could not apply for leniency.
The Minister of Justice, Hú Shìníng [Hú Shìníng], again requested the compilation of new precedents for judicial decisions (duànyù xīnlì [duànyù xīnlì]),
but it was also ordered that only the original legal texts and those officially sanctioned in the thirteenth year of Hongzhì [Hóngzhì] should be followed.
By the twenty-eighth year,
the Minister of Justice, Yù Máojiān [Yù Máojiān], said:
"Since the establishment of precedents during the Hongzhì [Hóngzhì] era,
nearly fifty years have passed.
I beg Your Majesty to order us, together with the Three Judicial Offices (sān fǎ sī [sān fǎ sī]),
to clarify the 'Articles of Inquiry into Criminal Cases' and the officially sanctioned precedents after the first year of Jiajìng [Jiājìng],
to be observed permanently.
As for the precedents between the thirteenth year of Hongzhì [Hóngzhì] and the first year of Jiajìng [Jiājìng],
although they were abolished by imperial edict,
there are some that were proposed in response to specific events,
and their reasoning was precise and worthy of adoption;
these should also be thoroughly examined.
If officials arbitrarily invoke precedents
to intentionally incriminate people,
they should be subject to discussion for demotion and punishment."
When Máojiān [Máojiān] left office,
an edict ordered Minister Gù Yìngxiáng [Gù Yìngxiáng] and others to finalize the deliberation,
increasing the articles to two hundred and forty-nine.
In the thirty-fourth year, based on the words of Minister Hé Áo [Hé Áo],
nine more matters were added.
During the Wanlì [Wànlì] reign,
the Censor Wū Shēng [Wū Shēng] requested a continued addition of articles.
By the thirteenth year,

the Minister of Justice, Shū Huà [Shū Huà], and others compiled the imperial edicts after the thirty-fourth year of Jiajìng [Jiājìng], as well as articles concerning the imperial clan and military administration (zōngfān jūngzhèng tiáolì [zōngfān jūngzhèng tiáolì]), regulations for apprehending bandits (bǔdào tiáogé [bǔdào tiáogé]), transport proposals (cáoyùn yìdān [cáoyùn yìdān]), and those related to criminal law (xíngmíng [xíngmíng]).
The laws were made the main text,
and the precedents (lì [lì]) were made footnotes,
totaling three hundred and eighty-two articles.
Many harsh regulations from the time of Emperor Shìzōng [Shìzōng] were deleted.
In the fourteenth year of Chóngzhēn [Chóngzhēn],
the Minister of Justice, Liú Zéshēn [Liú Zéshēn], again requested deliberation and finalization of the "Articles of Inquiry into Criminal Cases."
The Emperor believed that the laws (lǜ [lǜ]) should be strictly observed,
but precedents (lì [lì]) varied,
and for similar cases, there were two or three different precedents,
so it would be best to consolidate and unify them through revision.
However, at that time, enforcement was urgent,
and all offices were too busy correcting mistakes,
so the deliberation was not carried out.
When Tàizǔ [Tàizǔ] established the legal texts,
they were inherited by successive generations,
and none dared to lightly alter them.
Temporary adaptations,
whether by imperial edict
or proposed by court officials,
which related to the principles of governance
and whose recommendations were implemented,
cannot be without thorough detail.
In the first year of Hongwǔ [Hóngwǔ], an edict instructed provincial officials:
"When judging cases, be fair and lenient.
In ancient times, unless it was great treason or unfilial conduct,
punishment only extended to the individual.
If commoners committed crimes,
they should not be subject to guilt by association."
Minister Xià Shù [Xià Shù] once cited Hàn [Hàn] law,
requesting it be written into the code, that rebels should have their three paternal lines exterminated.
Tàizǔ [Tàizǔ] said:
"In ancient times,
the crimes of fathers, sons, and brothers did not affect one another.
Hàn [Hàn] continued Qín's [Qín] old ways,
and the law is too severe."
He rejected the memorial and did not implement it.
When a commoner's father was falsely arrested,
his son appealed to the Ministry of Justice,
but the judicial authorities charged him with overstepping the appeal process.
Tàizǔ [Tàizǔ] said:
"A son appealing his father's injustice
comes from the deepest filial affection;
he should not be punished."
When a son committed a crime and his father bribed for his exemption,
the Censor wanted to include the father in the judgment.
Tàizǔ [Tàizǔ] said:
"If a son is sentenced to death,
and his father tries to save him,
it is natural human emotion.
Only judge the son,
and pardon the father."
In the seventeenth year,
the Censor-in-Chief, Zhān Huī [Zhān Huī], reported that according to the law, a commoner who beat a pregnant woman to death
should be hanged,
and her son requested to take his place.
The Grand Justice, Zōu Jùn [Zōu Jùn], deliberated, saying:
"A son dying in place of his father is a pitiful act of affection.
However, the deceased woman involved two lives,
and the offender should be subject to a double death penalty.
Rather than preserving the offender,
it is better to spare the innocent son."
An edict followed Jùn's [Jùn] deliberation.
In the twentieth year,
Zhān Huī [Zhān Huī] said:
"A soldier who commits a crime should be caned.
This person has twice been punished and pardoned before;
the previous crimes should be brought up again,
and he should be executed."
Tàizǔ [Tàizǔ] said:
"If the previous crimes were already pardoned,
to bring them up again would be untrustworthy."
He was caned and sent away.
In the twenty-fourth year,
Páng Ān [Páng Ān], the Assistant Prefect of Jiāxīng [Jiāxīng], apprehended a seller of private salt and sent him to the capital,
and rewarded those who helped apprehend him with salt.
The Ministry of Revenue deemed this a violation of precedents,
fining him to compensate for the salt to the government,
and demanding an accounting of the crime.
Ān [Ān] said:
"Laws (lǜ [lǜ]) are the permanent statutes for ten thousand generations,
while precedents (lì [lì]) are temporary imperial decrees.
If one wishes to act according to precedent now,
then the words within the law that state no rewards should be given to those who apprehend criminals
would contradict themselves,
and trust would be lost throughout the realm."
Tàizǔ [Tàizǔ] approved his words
and issued an edict to follow the law (lǜ [lǜ]).
In the second year of Yonglè,
the Ministry of Justice reported that a commoner from Héjiān sued his mother,
and the authorities, in turn, proposed to sentence the mother.
An imperial edict ordered the son and the officials responsible to be arrested and punished.
In the third year, it was stipulated for civil officials, as well as military and civilian personnel of the guard posts both inside and outside the capital,
that for all grave offenses,
punishment should be meted out according to the statutes.
Lighter offenses would be exempt from flogging,
but recorded as crimes.
For matters involving undue encroachment or damage to others, or for offenses of a grave nature,
a special request should be submitted to the throne at the time.
In the sixteenth year, the prohibition against corrupt officials who commit bribery was strictly enforced.
Initially,
Tàizǔ severely punished corrupt officials,
decreeing that those who committed bribery would not be pardoned.
He further ordered the Ministry of Justice:
"Officials and clerks who accept bribes,
along with those who facilitated the bribery,
shall have their families resettled to the border.
This is to be established as a standing rule."
As time passed, the law became lax,
hence it was reiterated and strictly enforced again.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Dàlǐ Qīng Yú Qiān said:
"The law for fraud and deception
prescribes flogging and exile,
but now heads are being displayed,
which is not the intent of the imperial edict."
It was ordered that judgments be rendered according to the statutes.
In the second year of Xuāndé,
Jiāngxī Ànchásǐ Huáng Hàn said:
"Unregistered idlers among the populace
are fond of initiating lawsuits,
often compelling the old, young, infirm, and women to falsely accuse innocent people.
It is necessary to deliberate further on imposing additional penalties for such fabricated cases."
Thus, a regulation was established that old, young, infirm, and women who falsely accuse others would be fined paper money to redeem their crimes.
Later, during the reign of Xiàozōng,
in Nánjīng, those who falsely accused ten or more people
were, by rule, sent to the lands outside the passes to live as commoners.
However, for those over seventy years of age,
who by law should be allowed to redeem their crimes,
a further decree was issued,
stating that all individuals aged seventy and above, or fifteen and below, as well as the disabled,
should be judged according to the statutes.
Those who, by rule, should be assigned to frontier garrisons for scouting duties or sent outside the passes to live as commoners,
would still be dispatched according to the statutes.
If those aged eighty and above, or those suffering from chronic illnesses, committed offenses that warranted permanent exile,
their children and grandchildren would be dispatched instead;
and those whose offenses warranted assignment to military garrisons or lesser punishments would be exempted.
Initially, it was stipulated
that all officials and commoners who committed bribery with perversion of justice,
regardless of their origin (north or south),
would all be sent to the northern border garrisons for military service.
In the fifth year of Zhèngtǒng,
the three judicial offices in the provisional capital reported:
"When the laws were established during Hóngwǔ's reign,
paper money was valuable and goods were cheap.
Therefore, for bribery with perversion of justice amounting to 120 guàn,
execution by strangulation was commuted to military service.
Now, paper money is cheap and goods are expensive.
If the value of goods estimated in paper money for bribery with perversion of justice amounting to 120 guàn were all to be punished by military service,
the balance of severity would be lost.
Henceforth, for civil officials and other personnel
who accept bribes with perversion of justice which by law warrant execution by strangulation,
if the estimated paper money value is above 800 guàn,
they shall all be sent to the northern border garrisons for military service.
For those who accept bribes less than the aforementioned amount,
they shall be dealt with according to existing regulations."
This was approved.
In the eighth year,
the Dàlǐ Sì reported:
"The statutes state that for a first offense of theft, the right arm is tattooed;
for a second offense, the left arm is tattooed;
for a third offense, execution by strangulation.
Currently, thieves who commit a second offense after having received a pardon
are all treated as first offenders,
either still tattooing the right arm,
or not tattooing at all.
We request that this be standardized."
The memorial was sent to the three judicial offices for deliberation. They proposed:
"Those tattooed on the right arm who commit a second offense after a pardon shall be tattooed on the left arm.
Those tattooed on the left arm who commit another offense after a pardon shall not be tattooed,
and their case recorded.
Those who commit a third offense after a pardon shall be strangled."
The Emperor said:
"For thieves who have already been tattooed and commit a second offense after a pardon, they shall be dealt with according to the usual regulations,
regardless of the pardon,
and all their past and present offenses shall be fully reported to me."
Later, during the reign of Xiànzōng,
Dū Yùshǐ Lǐ Bǐng moved to abolish the old regulation.
Soon after, a thief in Nánjīng, Wáng Ātóng, was pardoned after five offenses.
Upon hearing this, the Emperor
decreed that the rule of three offenses, regardless of pardons before or after, should be reinstated.
By the reign of Shénzōng,
it was again proposed to revise the dispatching.
In the twelfth year, based on the words of Zhīxiàn Chén Mǐnzhèng,
if a commoner takes the daughter of his current wife's former husband as his son's wife,
or takes the son of his current wife's former husband as his daughter's husband,
they shall all be dealt with according to the law for half-siblings (different mothers, same father),
with a reduction in punishment degree.
In the first year of Chénghuà,
Liáodōng Xúnfǔ Téng Zhào said:
"The Dàmíng Lǜ is the established law of the dynasty,
yet for judging military officials,
rules are used instead of the statutes,
causing military officials to become increasingly unrestrained and undisciplined.
I request that all cases be handled according to the statutes."
An imperial edict approved this.
When military officials were dismissed or demoted,
they engaged in public slander and calumny.
The authorities, fearing trouble,
again memorialized to abolish this rule.
In the nineteenth year, the regulation for a third offense of theft was established.
The judicial authorities stated:
"In Nánjīng, for a third offense of theft,
if the value of the stolen goods reaches 100 guàn, the offender
should be executed by strangulation or decapitation.
Although the crimes are mixed,
the circumstances are quite serious.
A third previous offense
indicates a person who has accumulated evil and refuses to reform,
and thus cannot be judged by ordinary rules.
However, for offenses where the value is less than 100 guàn,
and the punishment is imprisonment or exile or lighter,
even if it is a third offense,
the actual circumstances are truly light,
and it is appropriate to treat them according to ordinary rules."
This proposal was submitted,
and approved.
In the sixth year of Hóngzhì,
Tàicháng Shǎoqīng Lǐ Dōngyáng said:
"The lightest of the Five Punishments are flogging with bamboo or light杖,
yet even these have specific measurements and varying numbers of strokes.
Nowadays, in various provincial offices,
punishments of flogging with bamboo or light杖 often result in death.
Even if the matter comes to light,
it is merely deemed to be 'due to official duties' and the official is reinstated.
By using the lightest of punishments,
people are put into a state from which they cannot return to life.
There are dozens,
even hundreds, of such cases,
with piled skeletons filling the prisons,
and blood staining the ground,
which is truly heartbreaking.
The law stipulates that those who unjustly interrogate commoners should pay with their lives,
and those who use illegal instruments of torture should be dismissed.
But if these are merely avoided,
it is then called 'official duty.'
Once given the name of 'official duty,'
no matter how many (deaths), it causes no harm.
This is a situation where the circumstances are grave but the law is light,
and it cannot go undiscussed.
I request that for all interrogations that lead to immediate death for minor offenses,
if accumulated to twenty or thirty or more persons,
in addition to the regular statutes,
a demotion or transfer be deliberated.
If a death from illness is not properly verified,
the doctor involved should also be punished."
This was then referred to the relevant offices for deliberation and action.
In the fifteenth year of Jiājìng,
there were cases where a person severely injured another with hands and feet,
and the victim died outside the stipulated period for accountability.
The Ministry proposed to sentence the offender to execution by strangulation for homicide due to fighting.
The Dàlǐ Sì, adhering to the regulation of the fourth year of Jiājìng,
argued that it should be judged as injury with flogging.
The ministers of the Ministry of Justice stated:
"The law sets a period of accountability,
and the regulations for criminal interrogation also state that for homicide due to fighting, where the circumstances and facts are clear,
even if death occurs outside the stipulated period,
a death sentence should still be proposed.
We request a definitive decision.
When our Ministry's proposals are submitted,
His Majesty often commutes the sentence to military service,
which, while not strictly upholding previous precedents,
is merely a slight reduction.
If a severe injury results in death outside the stipulated period,
and it is judged only by flogging,
this would be a lucky break for兇惡 criminals.
Moreover, if a person injures another with a dangerous weapon,
even if the victim recovers,
the rule is also military service.
How can it be that if a person actually beats another to death,
but the death happens to occur outside the stipulated period,
they should not bear the same guilt as injuring someone with a dangerous weapon?
Furthermore, the regulation of the fourth year has already been revoked.
We request that the central and local authorities be instructed to adhere to the regulations again."
The imperial edict followed the Ministry's deliberation.
Thereafter, for cases involving death outside the period of accountability,
all would be deliberated and proposed according to the statutes and regulations,
and submitted for a definitive imperial decision.
Above one hundred [strokes],
one must first receive one hundred strokes of the heavy bamboo,
only then is redemption permitted for the remaining offenses.
)Furthermore, for accidentally injuring a person,
it is judged according to the crime of fighting and injuring a person,
and redemption is permitted according to the statutes.
(For those resulting in death,
it is judged according to the redemption for various capital offenses (decapitation or strangulation),
with a payment of forty-two *guàn* of paper currency.
Eight tenths of this paper currency,
which amounts to thirty-three *guàn* and six hundred *wén*,
and two tenths in copper cash,
which amounts to eight thousand four hundred *wén*,
shall be given to the victim's family.
)If one has already served five years of penal servitude,
a repeat offense results in redemption from penal servitude.
(Thirty-six *guàn* of paper currency.)
If one commits an offense punishable by penal servitude or exile,
but is allowed to remain to support one's parents,
only one hundred strokes of the heavy bamboo are administered,
and the remaining offenses are redeemed.
(According to this law, one hundred strokes are actually administered,
not commutable by redemption,
and then the term of penal servitude or exile is calculated,
and redemption is permitted according to the rules for the elderly and young.
This statute was first implemented by imperial decree in the reign of Emperor Yīngzōng,
and later became a regulation.)
Astronomers and women who commit offenses punishable by penal servitude or exile,
receive one hundred strokes of the heavy bamboo,
and the remaining offenses are redeemed.
Even if the offense is only punishable by sixty strokes or
one year of penal servitude,
one hundred strokes are still administered.
This is what the statutes refer to as "those who should receive additional strokes."
In all cases, the original statutes are first consulted,
and the offenses of penal servitude or exile that have been committed
are reduced by imperial decree.
Upon the actual administration of the punishment,
it is determined whether someone is an astronomer
or a woman,
and according to the statutes, one hundred strokes of the heavy bamboo are administered,
with the remaining offenses redeemed.
The reason why all administered strokes must be one hundred
is to encompass the number for the five degrees of penal servitude.
However, this differs from the "surplus strokes" in cases of false accusation and redemption.
For those who redeem the remaining penal servitude, strokes are administered,
exile is commuted to penal servitude,
and penal servitude is commuted to strokes,
and redemption is based on the number of strokes.
The methods are different.
For women who commit offenses punishable by penal servitude or exile,
a regulation was established in the eighth year of Chénghuà:
excluding adultery, theft, unfilial conduct, and professional entertainers,
if it is determined that they have the means and are to receive strokes,
they may also pay paper currency to redeem their crimes.
(The rule is: for every ten strokes,
one *qián* of silver is commuted,
up to one hundred strokes,
which is commuted to one *liǎng* of silver.)
Whenever the statutes mention "redemption,"
it refers to the redemption of remaining offenses.
Whenever the regulations permit "redemption of crimes,"
it refers to the redemption from one hundred strokes of the heavy bamboo.
Penal servitude and strokes are categorized separately.
Except for women,
all other prisoners for penal servitude or exile receive strokes and do not redeem them.
Only in the thirteenth year of Hóngzhì
was it permitted for professional entertainers whose offenses were punishable by penal servitude, strokes, or light bamboo
to not actually receive the punishment.
This is the general outline of the statutes regarding paper currency.
The *lìchāo* (redemption according to regulations) was established in the twenty-ninth year of Jiājìng.
All military personnel, commoners, people of various occupations, and *shèyú* (rural gentry) who are deemed to have means,

along with civil and military officials, *jiānshēng* (Imperial Academy students), *shēngyuán* (licentiates), officials with official caps and belts, seal-keepers, dispatchers, *yīnyángshēng* (geomancers/diviners), doctors, elders, and *shèrén* (gentlemen-in-waiting),
regardless of whether their crimes are punishable by light bamboo, heavy bamboo, penal servitude, exile, or various capital offenses,
are all ordered to redeem their crimes by transporting lime, transporting charcoal, transporting bricks, delivering rice, delivering materials, etc.
(These above apply to those whose conduct is not flawed.)
If officials and others are to be removed from their positions according to regulations,
(These are those whose conduct is flawed.)
and if military personnel and commoners are deemed to have no means,
crimes punishable by light or heavy bamboo are actually administered.

Crimes punishable by penal servitude, exile, or various capital offenses are punished by various forms of labor, such as manning stations, performing patrol duty, or being assigned as ceremonial attendants.
For serious cases, they are assigned to salt boiling or iron smelting.
Capital offenses are commuted to five years,
exile to four years,
and penal servitude according to its term.
