For military personnel in the capital
who are not occupied with other duties, and those who are difficult to punish according to regulations,
light and heavy bamboo punishments are also commuted to labor.
According to the new regulations of the time,
those who commit adultery, theft, or receive stolen goods,
being persons with flawed conduct,
are generally not allowed to redeem their crimes.
However, military officers who are dismissed from their posts
are all assigned to transport charcoal, deliver rice, etc.,
without applying the actual punishment or assignment stipulated in the "Five Punishments" regulations.
This was to show leniency to military men
and hold civil officials to stricter account.
Therefore, in the capital, only five categories were implemented: performing labor, transporting prison provisions, etc.
Outside the capital, only two categories were implemented: "having means" and "having some means."
Thus, the laws became increasingly simple and direct.
In summary,
the *lǜchāo* (redemption according to statutes) was light,
while the *lìchāo* (redemption according to regulations) was heavy.
However, the *lǜchāo* was not originally light.
According to the ancestral system, one *wén* of paper currency
was equivalent to one *lí* of silver.
The statement that "ten strokes of light bamboo are commuted to six hundred *wén* of paper currency, equivalent to seven *lí* five *háo* of silver"
actually meant six *qián* of silver at that time.
The statement that "one hundred strokes of heavy bamboo are commuted to six *guàn* of paper currency, equivalent to seven *fēn* five *lí* of silver"
actually meant six *liǎng* of silver at that time.
With six *qián* of silver,
the *lìchāo* conversion was less than one *lí* of silver.
With one *liǎng* of silver,
the *lìchāo* conversion was less than one *fēn* of silver.
To expect this to deter criminals
was bound to be ineffective.
However, as the ancestral statutes could not be altered,
it was decided, out of necessity, to set the system at seven *lí* five *háo* and seven *fēn* five *lí*.
But in reality, the amount set
was still insufficient to match the severity of the crimes being redeemed.
It was then that the variations in regulations arose.
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
for officials, military personnel, and commoners who committed crimes and were allowed to redeem them,
the majority of the decrees involved penal labor,
such as being sent to Féngyáng for farming, to Chúzhōu to plant alfalfa, to perform labor in place of farmers, or to transport rice to the border to redeem crimes.
None of these involved payment in paper currency.
What is recorded in the statutes—
so many strokes of light bamboo,
so many *wén* of paper currency;
so many strokes of heavy bamboo,
so many *guàn* of paper currency—
established the law for an entire era.
However, according to imperial decrees from thirty years later,
criminals could redeem their crimes by transporting rice:
one hundred *shí* for capital offenses,
with lesser amounts for penal servitude and exile.
For those unable to perform the labor,
capital offenses required thirty *shí* of self-provided rice,
and penal servitude or exile fifteen *shí*.
All were to be transported and delivered to Gānzhōu and Wēilǔ,
where they would then be enlisted as soldiers.
Calculating the cost of the rice and the transport fees,
it was not significantly different from the amount in paper currency.
Thus, the system established for redemption by paper currency
was certainly not lighter than later regulations.
However, crimes are not fixed,
and over time, the paper currency system
became increasingly light day by day.
This was unforeseen at the time the statutes were established.
Taking the decree of the eleventh year of Yǒnglè as an example:
"Those whose decapitation offenses are light,
redeem with eight thousand *guàn* of paper currency;
strangulation and other capital offenses, six thousand *guàn*."
Eight thousand *guàn*
was eight thousand *liǎng* according to the statutes;
six thousand *guàn*
was six thousand *liǎng* according to the statutes.
Down to heavy bamboo offenses at one thousand *guàn*,
and light bamboo offenses at five hundred *guàn*,
these were also one thousand *liǎng* and five hundred *liǎng* respectively.
Although the enforcement was particularly strict during periods of reform,
how could it be that capital offenses required up to eight thousand *liǎng*,
and light and heavy bamboo offenses required up to one thousand *liǎng* or five hundred *liǎng*,
and still be enforceable?
This indicates that the flaws of the paper currency system,
by the early years of Yǒnglè,
were already more than ten times lighter than during the Hóngwǔ era.
During the Xuāndé period,
the prohibition on using silver for transactions was re-issued,
hoping to revitalize the paper currency system.
By the Hóngzhì period, paper currency became completely unusable,
leading to the establishment of the precedent allowing paper currency to be converted into silver.
When the new regulations were established in Jiājìng,
redemption for all crimes was categorized into "having means" and "having some means": "having means" meant fifty *dǒu* of rice,
equivalent to the six hundred *wén* of paper currency in the statutes;
"having some means" meant three *qián* in labor wages,
equivalent to one month of labor in the statutes.
Thus, the later *lìchāo*
was merely comparable to the initial *lǜchāo*.
Moreover, for the old, young, disabled, and infirm,
all those redeemed under the statutes for seven *lí* five *háo* of silver,
equivalent to six hundred *wén* of paper currency,
and seven *fēn* five *lí* of silver,
equivalent to six *guàn* of paper currency.
For all those referred to as *lǜshú* (redeemed by statutes),
compared to the initial *lǜchāo*,
how much more widely divergent were their actual values?
Only redemption for crimes like transporting charcoal or stone was somewhat heavier in the regulations,
because these crimes
originally all required personal attendance for the labor,
and one would return home after completing the task,
with no precedent for monetary redemption.
Later, the laws became increasingly lenient,
allowing for commutation by payment,
and the estimated value of the labor
was also roughly equivalent,
which truly posed no problem.
Broadly speaking, there were two types of commutation for punishment: one was forced labor,
the other was paying a fine in paper currency.
And the regulations changed three times.
Forced laborers
later mostly commuted their labor value by paying paper currency.
When the paper currency system broke down,
it changed to paying in silver or grain.
However, the terms "transporting ash," "transporting charcoal," "transporting stone," "transporting bricks," and "transporting broken bricks" still remained.
By the mid-Wànlì period,
throughout the country, the two categories of "able-bodied" (yǒulì) and "somewhat able-bodied" (shāoyǒulì) were in common use.
In the capital, various regulations
were not observed,
and the law increasingly became uniform.
This is what is meant by "adapting to changes without deviating from ancient principles."
Initially,
criminals were allowed to redeem their crimes through forced labor: death sentence criminals were confined for life,
exile and penal servitude criminals were assigned according to their term limits,
and cudgeling and flogging were calculated by days and months.
Whether building,
or cultivating land,
or boiling salt and smelting iron,
they were released after their term was full.
Those who were released
were led to the Imperial Bridge (Yùqiáo),
where they kowtowed,
and then were sent to Yìngtiān Fǔ
to be given a permit to return home.
Those who were to be assigned to military garrisons (chōngjūn)
were sent to the Shǎnxī Division (Shǎnxī Sī)
and dispatched according to their household registration.
Later, all were commuted to paying labor wages,
only the journey to the bridge remained as before.
In the second year of Xuāndé,
Censor Zhèng Dàoníng said:
"Commuting crimes by paying grain
is a lenient measure by the imperial court.
However, the military granary (jūncāng) is detaining prisoners
who have no grain to pay.
Since February last year,
ninety-six people have died."
Yú Shìjí, a secretary in the Ministry of Punishments (Xíngbù Láng), once memorialized:
"For prisoners without grain,
please collect it from their original registered domicile.
Artisans should still perform their labor,
and soldiers should still prepare for training.
If they are neither soldiers nor artisans,
then send them back to their subordinate prefectures and counties to collect it."
An imperial edict approved his memorial.
The initial system had three grades of exile (liúzuì),
depending on the distance of the location,
and military assignment (chōngjūn) to border garrisons had fixed destinations.
This was considered one degree below the death penalty,
with only exile and military assignment being severe.
However, the "Regulations on Names and Examples" (Mínglìlǜ) stated that "two deaths" and "three exiles" were each considered one reduction.
For example, if "two deaths" encountered an imperial pardon and were reduced by one degree,
it meant exile three thousand *lǐ*.
If "three exiles" were reduced by one degree by the Great Edict (Dàgào),
all became five years of penal servitude (tú).
Those who committed crimes of exile
were invariably reduced to penal servitude.
Therefore, the "three exiles" were always stipulated but not used.
And the regulation of military assignment (chōngjūn) was uniquely severe.
There were forty-six articles on military assignment in the statutes (lǜ),
and twenty-two articles in the "Duties and Responsibilities of Various Offices" (Zhūsī Zhízhǎng).
Thus, the regulations from the Hóngwǔ period were all not recorded in the statutes.
The regulations of the twenty-ninth year of Jiājìng
listed two hundred thirteen articles on military assignment,
which were largely similar to those set in the thirteenth year of Wànlì.
In the twenty-sixth year of Hóngwǔ, it was stipulated that
those who were to be assigned to military garrisons,
after judgment by the Dàlǐ Sì,
were handed over to the Shǎnxī Division.
This ministry established registers,
noting names, ages, native places, and ancestral domiciles,
and compiled them into two volumes, arranged by northern and southern registers,
one to be submitted to the Imperial Household (Nèifǔ),
and one to be given to the supervising commander of one hundred households (bǎihù)
who would take them to their military assignment.
For example, people from Zhèjiāng,
Hénán,
Shāndōng,
Shǎnxī,
Shānxī,
Běipíng,
Fújiàn,
and the directly administered prefectures of Yìngtiān, Lúzhōu, Fèngyáng, Huái'ān, Yángzhōu, Sūzhōu, Sōngjiāng, Chángzhōu, Hézhōu, Chúzhōu, and Xúzhōu,
were sent to garrisons belonging to Yúnnán and Sìchuān.
People from Jiāngxī,
Húguǎng,
Sìchuān,
Guǎngdōng,
Guǎngxī,
and the directly administered prefectures of Tàipíng, Níngguó, Chízhōu, Huīzhōu, Guǎngdé, and Ānqìng,
were sent to garrisons belonging to Běipíng, Dàníng, and Liáodōng.
If there were escapes or deaths,
replacements were enlisted according to the registers.
Later regulations included dispatching them to malarial regions and remote coastal areas,
with different regulations for each.
And military service could be for life (zhōngshēn)
or perpetual (yǒngyuǎn).
Perpetual service
extended to descendants
and was imposed on those who had genuinely committed capital crimes and had their sentences reduced.
The laws in the early Míng Dynasty were strict.
The number of military households (jūnhù) was in the thousands,
and after several generations,
it reached the tens of thousands.
There were cases where all male adults (dīng) had died and the household was extinct,
with only military property remaining,
or even no military property at all,
but the household name had not been removed.
The imperial court annually dispatched censors (yùshǐ) to "clear out the army" (qīngjūn),
and any vacancies had to be filled.
Whenever enlistment was enforced,
family members and local headmen (lǐzhǎng) were arrested,
extending to other *jiǎ* (tithings),
causing unrest even to chickens and dogs.
Critics said that although the death penalty was reduced by one degree,
the punishment was worse than dismemberment (dāojù).
For example, the banished individuals who were removed
were still on the military register even after the fall of the dynasty (guówáng),
a more tragic punishment than any other.
During the Jiājìng period,
someone requested to open a regulation for commuting military service.
Shìzōng said:
"The statutes allow commutation
only for minor crimes below penal servitude (tú) and cudgeling (zhàng).
Capital crimes, when there is compassion or doubt,
are reduced to banishment or dispatch,
and cannot be commuted."
Censor Zhōu Shíliàng again requested to expand the commutation regulations.
The ministry deliberated that those who were "able-bodied" (yǒulì) could pay ten *liǎng* of silver
to commute penal servitude of three years or more to one year,
and those who were "somewhat able-bodied" (shāoyǒulì) paid half of that.
But the proposal for commuting military service was ultimately rejected.
Censor Hú Zōngxiàn said:
"People from the south are not suited for military service.
Those who are sent to border garrisons
should be allowed to redeem themselves by paying silver."
The ministry agreed.
Therefore, a proposal for a payment regulation was submitted.
The emperor said:
"How can such a regulation be set in advance,
to await criminals?"
And again, he did not approve.
In the second year of Wànlì, the annual dispatch of censors to "clear out the army" was abolished,
and the task was combined with that of the touring censors (xún'àn),
bringing some relief to the people.
Investigating Censor Xú Huán said:
"Those who commit capital crimes with miscellaneous offenses and are allowed to serve in military garrisons
should follow their existing regulations."
Investigating Censor Yán Yònghé requested that those who were deemed pitiable during a general review
be exempted from perpetual military service.
Both requests were denied.
However, the legal authorities (Fǎsī) were ordered to establish a regulation:
"For the descendants of rebellious families and relatives ordered to be dispatched by special imperial decree,
replacements shall only be sought from the immediate branches of the original offender.
If they are completely extinct, they shall be cleared.
If they die of illness before being dispatched,
their replacement shall be waived.
For those who committed capital crimes and were exempted from death to serve in military garrisons,
their descendants born after they were registered in the military shall replace them in service,
and no descendants from their original registered domicile shall be conscripted.
Other military assignments and those dispatched beyond the passes (kǒuwài)
shall all be for life only."
In the eleventh year of Chóngzhēn, an edict was issued to the Ministry of War (Bīngbù):
"Regarding matters of enlistment and dispatch,
one thousand *lǐ* shall be considered 'nearby,'
two thousand five hundred *lǐ* shall be 'border garrisons,'
and beyond three thousand *lǐ* shall be 'remote border regions.'
For extremely remote malarial regions, four thousand *lǐ* and beyond shall be the standard.
Only the principal wife shall be detained;
if there is no wife, then so be it.
Unauthorized conscription of relatives and neighbors is forbidden.
If they are frail, infirm, old, or ill,
they shall be permitted to be dispatched beyond the passes as commoners."
In the fifteenth year, another edict stated:
"Those who are to be assigned to military garrisons according to existing regulations
shall be permitted to commute their crimes."
By this time, the empire was already in chaos,
and the proposal was ultimately not implemented.
The Míng system of military assignment was the strictest,
and offenders suffered the most.
Their relatives were subject to levies for military equipment,
and local couriers (lǐdì) were troubled by long-distance escorts.
Upon reaching their assigned garrison,
the garrison officers (wèiguān) would invariably demand customary fees.
However, benefiting from their escape,
they could embezzle the rations,
and often secretly released them.
Later, the laws gradually relaxed,
and fewer than one in ten of those dispatched and escorted actually arrived.
For those dispatched to the extreme borders,
the chief escorts would often bribe the Ministry of War,
and bringing their official permits to the garrisons,
would falsely record their reception,
while the military convicts were actually at home resting, so it was said.
Collation Notes
Monograph Seventy, Penal Law II
The regulations for joint trials concerning judicial relief outside the capital
were established during the Chénghuà reign.
Initially,
Tàizǔ was concerned that prisons were overcrowded,
so he dispatched censors Lín Yuàn, Shí Héng, and others to manage prisoners in various circuits,
and issued an imperial edict to them.
Xuānzōng, reading the Zhōu Guān Lì Zhèng at night, said:
"Respectfully attend to your prisons,
to secure the longevity of Our kingdom."
He sighed with emotion,
believing that the foundation of establishing the nation lay therein.
Thereupon, he issued an edict to the Sān Fǎ Sī, saying:
"We embody the Supreme Emperor's benevolent heart,
and prioritize compassion in judicial matters.
We order you to review thoroughly all major prisons in the realm.
If offenders are thousands of *lǐ* away,
and await execution,
how can there be no injustices?"
Consequently, he dispatched officials to review and record cases.
In the fourth month of the sixth year of Zhèngtǒng,
due to frequent appearance of omens of disaster,
an imperial edict was issued dispatching officials of the Sān Fǎ Sī to thoroughly review all doubtful cases in the realm.
Thus, censor Zhāng Jì, ministry of justice *láng* Lín Hòu, Grand Court of Revision *zhèng* Lǐ Cóngzhì, and thirteen others jointly received the imperial edict and departed.

Furthermore, Vice Minister of Justice Hé Wényuān, Grand Court of Revision *qīng* Wáng Wén, Vice Minister for Circuit Administration Zhōu Chén, and Minister of Scrutiny for the Ministry of Justice Guō Jǐn were dispatched to review the penal cases in the two capitals,
also with an imperial edict.
Later, judge Mǎ Yù said:
"I, your minister, have received an imperial edict to review penal cases.
I secretly observed that in various places, bandits who were arrested
were often implicated by enemies,
and their cases concluded through torture.
Without waiting for a detailed report,
many died or were injured.
Henceforth, false accusations should not be heard.
If there are indeed material evidences,
the censor and the Surveillance Commission should conduct a joint trial,
only then should a verdict be allowed.
If anyone dies or is injured before the review and recording,
they shall not be rewarded or promoted according to precedent."
In that year,
countless prisoners, including those sentenced to death, were released.
In the ninth year,
Vice Surveillance Commissioner of Shāndōng Wáng Yù said:
"Prison cases should be jointly reviewed,
but the censor and officials of the Sān Fǎ Sī sometimes only hold a joint session once a year,
and many prisoners die of illness in custody.
Previously, censors were often dispatched to conduct thorough reviews with the Surveillance Commission,
and many were released.
Now, it would be better to abolish the system of joint trials
and implement the method of thorough review,
dispatching one official from the Surveillance Commission
to specialize in reviewing all prisons."
The ministry insisted that the old system could not be abolished.
The emperor ordered that the review regulations remain as before,
and further, following the precedent of thorough review,
one official from the Surveillance Commission should be selected to conduct the review jointly with the Grand Coordinator Censor.
Those erroneously released should not be questioned for the time being,
but those involved in bribery and private interests should be investigated according to the law.
In the first year of Chénghuà,
Vice Minister of the Nanjing Ministry of Justice Chén Yì, due to disaster omens, again requested to follow the Zhèngtǒng precedent.
The ministry deliberated that there were many issues in various regions,
so it was not implemented.
In the eighth year,
officials such as Ministry of Justice *lángzhōng* Liú Zhì, and fourteen others, were dispatched to conduct reviews jointly with Grand Coordinator Censors and officials of the Sān Fǎ Sī,
and they were sent off with solemn imperial decrees.
In the twelfth year,
Grand Secretary Shāng Lù said:
"Since officials were dispatched in the eighth year,
five years have passed.
I request that it be carried out again according to precedent."
The emperor acceded to his request.
By the seventeenth year,
it was decided to conduct a major review in the capital every five years.
In that same year, officials from the ministries and judicial courts were dispatched to various parts of the realm,
to act in conjunction with Grand Coordinator Censors.
When those administering judicial relief arrived,
many were released.
In the forty-third year of Jiājìng, it was decided that if the amount of misappropriated property did not exceed one hundred *liǎng*,
and the property was completely exhausted, the person would be exempted from imprisonment for recovery.
In the fourth year of Wànlì, an imperial edict stipulated that those condemned to death for miscellaneous crimes, whose sentences were commutable to five years of penal servitude,
and those who committed two offenses warranting a total of four years of penal servitude,
should each have their sentences reduced by one year.
Other sentences such as penal servitude and exile were also reduced in grade.
All these were enacted based on memorials from officials advocating for judicial relief,
thus, even more lives were spared and preserved.
Initially,
in the eleventh year of Zhèngtǒng, Ministry of Justice *lángzhōng* Guō Xún and *yuánwàiláng* Lù Yú were dispatched to review prisoners in Nán Zhílì and Běi Zhílì.
If civil officials of the fifth rank and below committed crimes,
they were allowed to be arrested and interrogated.
During the Jiājìng period, a system was established
where, once a review official had completed their duties in a province,
the total number of cases submitted before and after would be counted,
and the number of approved changes and rejections would be examined,
and a general evaluation would be conducted.
Those with a high number of changed or rejected cases would be subject to impeachment.
Therefore, the power of judicial relief was significant,
and the responsibility was also not light.
This is the general overview of the review and recording by judicial officials within and outside the capital.
For all prisoners whose cases were adjudicated and sent forth by the Ministry of Justice,
the relevant offices would compile the total number of prisoners whose cases were heard,
regardless of the severity of the charges,
dividing them into a certain number of northern and southern individuals,
and send them to the Shāndōng bureau,
to be presented to the court and reported,
which was called the annual report.
Each month, the number of prisoners currently in custody was reported to the emperor,
which was called the monthly report.
For items such as labor and charcoal transportation,
every five days a report was sent to the Ministry of Works,
to be filled into the detailed registry,
and at the end of the month, it was reported in rotation by the Six Ministries.
All judicial officials in handling prisoners
had established procedures.
When bringing people in for questioning,
they must carry detailed official warrants.
For officials within or outside the capital of the fifth rank or above who committed an offense, a report must be submitted to the emperor for instructions,
and they could not be arbitrarily summoned for questioning and punishment.
For those belonging to the Eight Deliberations,
a sealed memorial was submitted to the emperor.
Civil lawsuits among the populace,
unless transmitted to the ministry by the Transmission Office,
the Ministry of Justice could not hear.
Those who made false accusations were punished in return,
those who bypassed proper channels for complaints were flogged,
and those who struck the Dengwen Drum without valid cause were beaten with a staff.
Accusations against interrogating officials
had to be verified before arrest and interrogation.
Furthermore, there were fixed dates for transferring prisoners after they were beaten until their bones were broken,
fixed instruments for torture,
fixed months and days for suspending punishments,
fixed methods for examining corpses and injuries,
fixed regulations for showing compassion to prisoners,
and fixed items for confiscation.
Only for acts of revenge was there no explicit regulation.
In the first year of Hóngzhì,
Minister of Justice Hé Qiáoxīn said:
"According to the old system for summoning people,
the local authorities must verify the detailed official warrant
and ensure it matches the tally,
before dispatching the person.
This was the profound intention of the imperial ancestors to nip evil in the bud and prevent subtle problems.
Recently, when summoning people inside and outside the capital,
they only rely on imperial warrants (*jiàtiě*).
Since no tallies are used,
true and false cannot be distinguished.
If cunning individuals falsely issue commands,
how can they be resisted?
I request that official warrants be issued as before."
The emperor said:
"This old precedent of the imperial ancestors cannot be abolished."
He ordered it to be reinstated.
However, *qíxiào* (military guards) who summoned people
usually carried *jiàtiě*.
In the first year of Jiājìng,
*qiānhù* Bái Shòu and others of the Jǐnyīwèi carried *jiàtiě* to the ministries.
Minister of Scrutiny Liú Jì argued that the original imperial endorsement should be sent to the ministries,
so that they would know the matter.
The two argued intensely,
and the emperor ordered an examination of the precedents from Chénghuà and Hóngzhì reigns to be reported.
Jì further stated
that the precedent had been this way since the Tiānshùn era.
The emperor adopted Shòu's argument,
and rebuked Jì for his statement,
but did not punish him for any crime.
During the Tiānqǐ period,
Wèi Zhōngxián used *jiàtiě* to summon Zhōu Shùnchāng and others,
which eventually triggered the Sūzhōu incident.
For executions in the two metropolitan areas,
detailed official warrants must also be verified.
In the twenty-first year of Jiājìng,
principal secretaries of judicial relief Dài Pián, Wú Yuánbì, Lǚ Yǒng, and others failed to verify the urgent internal tallies with the external tallies.
When they arrived,
they did not match the original external tallies,
and were impeached by the Grand Coordinator Censor,
and after paying a ransom, were reinstated to their posts.
For all prisoners whose cases have been examined and recorded,
those awaiting final judgment are limited to three days.
Those to be dispatched [to another jurisdiction] are limited to ten days.
Exceeding the limit will incur caning based on the number of overdue days.
Officials who allow prisoners to be detained until death will be punished with penal servitude.
This is the old regulation.
In the sixth year of Jiājìng,
Grand Supervisor Zhōu Láng said:
"Recently, prison officials have been harsh.
Regardless of the gravity of the offense,
all are indiscriminately imprisoned.
Regardless of whether a case is new or old,
they readily prolong it for months or even years.
Between the mere hint and the acceptance of a bribe,
before the memorial is even completed,
the prisoner's bones have already turned to dust.
Moreover, in remote prefectures and humble districts,
where supervision is lacking,
corrupt officials and brutal soldiers turn the prison into a marketplace.
They may restrict their food and drink to weaken them,
or move them to filthy pits to torment them,
inflicting all sorts of pain and suffering,
such that not one in ten survives.
I observe that the laws and ordinances state:
for all arrested and detained prisoners,
the elderly and infirm must be released or housed separately,
and the severe and minor cases must be categorized accordingly.
Cangues, fetters, and mats must be regularly inspected,
and cool drinks and warm enclosures must be provided in season.
Those without homes should be given clothes,
and those with illness should be given medicine.
There are specific rules for prolonged detention,
and imperial edicts for swift resolution.
These are the good laws and benevolent intentions of our ancestors.
It is proper to instruct all officials to uphold them.
The dates of arrest and detention, as well as whether cases are completed or not, and the conditions of illness and death,
should all be recorded in registers
and reported to the senior officials.
The speed of case resolution
and the number of illnesses and deaths should be compared
to determine merit or demerit for promotion or demotion."
The Emperor deeply agreed with his words,
and also ordered that any official, domestic or foreign, who applied the law with excessive harshness,
leading to the death of common people,
should immediately be dismissed as a commoner.
Even if their talent and integrity were commendable,
they were not to be recommended.
For all judicial officials, domestic and foreign,
only for capital crimes and serious theft offenses
was torture permitted for interrogation.
Other cases were limited to whipping and other regular punishments.
Cruel officials who used wooden rods, leg crushers, head clamps, branding irons, as well as "one-sealed letter," "rat's harp," "horse-blocking stick," "swallow's flight,"
or force-feeding water through the nose, or nailing fingers,
using blunt rods an inch in diameter, or bamboo strips with unremoved nodes and splinters,
or whipping the back or both ankles to cause injury and above,
all such cases must be reported for imperial approval,
and the offenders would be punished with military exile.
The months during which executions were suspended
were from after Lìchūn [Start of Spring]
until before Chūnfēn [Spring Equinox].
The days on which executions were suspended
were the 1st, 8th, 14th, 15th, 18th, 23rd, 24th, 28th, 29th, and 30th [of each month],
a total of ten days.
For inspecting corpses and injuries,
the Zhàomó Sì [Bureau of Scrutiny] would obtain a copy of the official corpse diagram from the ministry,
and entrust the Wǔchéng Bīngmǎ Sì [Five-City Military and Horse Division] to inspect it according to regulations.
In prefectures, the Tōngpàn [Assistant Prefect] and Tuīguān [Judicial Officer],
and in sub-prefectures and counties, the chief officials themselves would conduct the inspection,
and should not delegate it to subordinate officials.
For prisoners too poor to support themselves,
in the fifteenth year of Hóngwǔ, it was stipulated
that each person would receive one shēng of rice per day.
In the twenty-fourth year, this was abolished.
In the second year of Zhèngtǒng,
due to the words of Assistant Minister Hé Wényuān,
an edict was issued to restore the old practice,
and also to allow for the distribution of clothes obtained from seized property.
In the twelfth year of Chénghuà, an order was issued for officials to purchase medicines and send them to the ministry,
and also to establish more Huìmín Yàojú [Benevolent People's Pharmacies]
to treat prisoners.
By the fourteenth year of Zhèngdé,
fixed amounts of silver were allocated for prisoners' coal, oil, and medicines.
In the sixth year of Jiājìng,
strong criminal prisoners assigned to tasks such as transporting charcoal
were allowed to commute their labor to purchase rice,
which was then sent to the ministry's granary.
Approximately five hundred dàn [a unit of volume, usually for grain] per year,
and then the collection [of their labor] was suspended.
In winter, each prisoner was given a set of cotton clothes and trousers,
which the Tíláo Zhǔshì [Prison Warden] would verify and distribute.
For criminals whose property was confiscated,
in the first year of Hóngwǔ, it was stipulated
that, except for rebellion,
for other offenses, only land and livestock would be confiscated.
In the twenty-first year, an edict stated that for those plotting treasonous conspiracy and those counterfeiting banknotes,
their property and household members would be confiscated,
but agricultural tools and plowing oxen would be returned to them.
Those who should have their property and household members confiscated
were called "treasonous conspirators,"
those involved in "plotting rebellion and great treason,"
those in "evil treasonous conspiracies,"
those "counterfeiting banknotes,"
those "killing three people of one family,"
and those "leading the dismemberment and carving up of living people."
The ten articles stipulated in the Dàgào [Great Proclamation]
were never used afterwards.
Regarding revenge,
only the article concerning assault on grandparents was seen,
stating:
"If grandparents or parents are killed by others,
and the descendants unauthorizedly kill the perpetrator,
they shall be caned sixty strokes.
If they kill the perpetrator immediately, it shall not be discussed.
If other relatives are killed by others and one unauthorizedly kills the perpetrator,
they shall be caned one hundred strokes."
According to the law, if a criminal deserves death
and has already been apprehended,
if the captor unauthorizedly kills him,
the punishment is also limited to this.
Thus, the term "family members and others"
naturally includes siblings,
and the principle can be analogously applied.
For all executions,
after the annual autumn review,
the judicial authorities would request an imperial decree for capital offenses.
The Xíngkē [Office of Scrutiny for Punishments] would memorialize three times,
and upon receiving the decree, the execution would be carried out.
For those in outer provinces, a memorial requesting execution would be submitted before the winter solstice,
and a joint review and execution would be held.
In the first year of Zhèngtǒng, an order stipulated that after serious offenders had been memorialized three times,
an imperial warrant should still be requested
and given to the Jǐnyīwèi [Embroidered Uniform Guard] supervising execution officials,
who would lead the imperial guards to the judicial authorities
to take the prisoners to the execution ground.
It was also enacted that,
if a prisoner about to be executed claimed injustice,
they could directly beat the drum for grievances, and the Grand Supervisor would take down their statement and seal it for submission.
The warrant would then be handed to the imperial guard,
who would rush to the execution ground
to temporarily suspend the execution.
In the first year of Jiājìng,
Grand Supervisors Liú Jì and others, seeing that prisoners Liáo Péng and his son, Wáng Qīn, Táo Jié, and others had considerable internal backing,
feared that the emperor would not make a decision,
and therefore said:
"In previous years, after the three memorials were submitted,
by the time the imperial warrant was awaited, it was already noon.
After the drum for grievances was beaten, complaints were still received,
and by the time the report arrived, it was almost Wèi-Shēn [1-5 PM].
By the time a second request was made for execution,
it was already past Yǒu [5-7 PM].
This is utterly contrary to the intention of executing criminals in the marketplace
and having the public abandon them.
We request that from now on, when executing prisoners,
the matter be completed before Wèi [1-3 PM]."
This was adopted.
In the seventh year, it was decided
that if a serious offender claimed injustice,
their family could beat the drum on the day before the execution.
If the verdict was handed down before noon the next day,
the execution would proceed after noon,
without another review.
For executions in Nánjīng,
there was no precedent for review by the Xíngkē.
In the eighteenth year of Hóngzhì,
the Nán Xíngbù [Southern Ministry of Punishments] memorialized for the execution of three individuals without awaiting the proper time.
The Dàlǐ Sì [Grand Court of Revisions] had already reviewed and approved it.
It was then sent to the judicial authorities for deliberation,
who stated:
"Among serious offenders in the capital,
there are occasionally those executed without awaiting the proper time.
After review, approval, and memorialization,
and the Xíngkē's three memorials,
they might still receive imperial grace and be held for joint review.
Nánjīng has no precedent for review by the Xíngkē.
We request that after the autumn review,
these cases be collectively memorialized for final decision.
If there are exceptionally heinous criminals
who cannot be handled according to normal procedures,
a separate memorial should be submitted for their execution,
and this should be established as a regulation."
The imperial edict approved this.
For executions in various provinces,
in the first year of Yǒnglè, it was stipulated
that if there were more than one hundred death row prisoners,
an Imperial Censor would be dispatched to review and decide.
In the thirteenth year of Hóngzhì, it was stipulated that officials dispatched annually to review and decide serious cases
should all arrive after Shuāngjiàng [Frost's Descent]
and return within the prescribed period.
In cases of great celebrations and disasters, general amnesties were granted.
However, there were regular amnesties,
cases not eligible for amnesty,
and special amnesties.
Those guilty of the Ten Abominations (shí’è) and repeat offenders were not pardoned.
The legal text states:
"For amnesties, the crimes to be pardoned are determined at the time.
Special exemptions, or reductions and leniency,
are not subject to this restriction."
Among the Ten Abominations,
lack of familial harmony (bùmù) was also included in the examples of cases that could be pardoned under a general amnesty.
Thus, even those not usually pardoned could be forgiven.
If an imperial decree announced a general amnesty
without specifically designating the crimes,
then it would still follow the regular amnesty rules for non-pardonable offenses.
From the time Rénzōng (仁宗) established 35 amnesty articles,
all drafted by Yáng Shìqí (楊士奇),
the oppressive policies of the Yǒnglè (永樂) reign were completely abolished,
and subsequent generations followed them.
Whenever anything from previous reigns was inconvenient for the people,
it was removed by invoking an imperial testament or upon the emperor's ascension.
Anyone who reported a person for crimes committed before an amnesty
would immediately be charged with the crime they reported.
In the first year of Hóngzhì (弘治) (1488),
four commoners, including Lǚ Liángshān (呂梁山),
were sentenced to death for theft and murder
and encountered an amnesty.
The Grand Censor (dūyùshǐ) Mǎ Wénshēng (馬文升) requested their pardon from death and exile to the frontier.
The emperor specifically ordered them to be beheaded according to the law.
Shìzōng (世宗), though he repeatedly suspended executions,
was especially cautious about granting amnesties.
When court officials repeatedly invoked amnesty decrees
to pardon the officials involved in the Grand Rites (dàlǐ) case and those who submitted remonstrances,
he held firm and refused.
In the sixteenth year of Jiājìng (嘉靖) (1537),
the Associate Prefect (tóngzhī) Jiāng Lù (姜輅) brutally murdered a commoner.
The Grand Censor Wáng Tíngxiāng (王廷相) memorialized that he should be banished beyond the passes.
However, the emperor specifically ordered him to be pardoned and exempted as per the imperial edict,
and held Wáng Tíngxiāng and others responsible for violating the edict.
In the forty-first year (1562),
when the Three Great Halls (sāndiàn) were completed,
the officials requested a general amnesty.
The emperor said:
"Amnesty is a stroke of luck for the petty people."
And refused.
When Mùzōng (穆宗) ascended the throne, he extended his grace broadly.
Even those convicted of penal servitude (túlìu) who had already reached their assigned locations
were permitted to return home.
This was primarily for the sake of the exiled officials.
This broadly describes the criminal law during the Míng (明) dynasty.
At the beginning of Tàizǔ's (太祖) reign,
to punish the corruption prevalent during the late Yuán (元) dynasty,
he severely punished corrupt officials.
He posted the names of officials who violated the law in the Shēnmíng Tíng (申明亭) to serve as a warning.
He also ordered the Ministry of Justice (xíngbù) that,
whenever an official committed an offense but was pardoned and reinstated,
their transgression should be recorded and posted on their door,
so they might reflect on it.
If they did not reform,
they would be punished according to the law.
He repeatedly issued "Offender Edicts" (fànyù), "Warning Edicts" (jièyù), and "Proclamation Edicts" (bǎngyù),
all illustrated with punishments,
and proclaimed them to the whole world.
When the Great Edicts (dàgào) were completed in the eighteenth year (1385),
the preface stated:
"If any official dares to neglect public duty for private gain,
their origins will be thoroughly investigated and they will be punished."
The instances of death by a thousand cuts (língchí), public display of heads (xiāoshì), and extermination of families (zhǒngzhū) listed in the Three Great Edicts
were no less than a thousand,
and those executed in the marketplace (qìshì) or lesser numbers were in the tens of thousands.
Xià Bóqǐ (夏伯啟) and his nephew, scholars from Guìxī (貴溪), cut off their fingers to avoid serving in office.
Yáo Rùn (姚潤) and Wáng Mó (王謨), talented individuals from Sūzhōu (蘇州), were summoned but did not appear.
All were executed and their families' property confiscated.
This is the origin of the "Scholar-officials of the realm who do not serve the monarch" (huánzhōng shìfū bù wéi jūn yòng) law.
The third compilation (sānbīan) was slightly more lenient,
yet the names of scholars and imperial students (jìnshì jiānshēng) recorded as offenders,
from one offense to four offenses, still numbered 364.
Fortunately, they did not die and were reinstated in their positions,
often managing affairs while carrying the stigma of a death sentence.
The investigation into the origins of corruption within and outside the court
identified the Six Ministries (liùcáo) as the main culprits
and Guō Huán (郭桓) as the principal offender.
Guō Huán
was an Assistant Minister of the Ministry of Revenue (hùbù shìláng).
The emperor suspected that officials from the two bureaus in Běipíng (北平), Lǐ Yù (李彧) and Zhào Quándé (趙全dé), were conspiring with Guō Huán for illicit gains.
Consequently, everyone from the Assistant Ministers of the Six Ministries downwards was executed.
The embezzled sum was seven million,
and the confessions implicated officials from various provinces and prefectures,
leading to tens of thousands of deaths.
The examination of the embezzled funds, lent and borrowed, was widespread throughout the realm,
and most middle-class families among the common people were ruined.
At that time, everyone blamed the censors Yú Mǐn (余敏) and Dīng Tíngjǔ (丁廷舉).
When this was mentioned,
the emperor personally issued an edict listing Guō Huán's crimes
and sentenced the Assistant Justice Administrator Wú Yōng (吳庸) and others to extreme punishment
to appease public sentiment.
He said:
"I ordered my officials to eliminate corruption,
yet they have instead created trouble for my people.
Henceforth, if such things occur, they will not be pardoned even if an amnesty is granted."
Earlier, in the fifteenth year (1382), the "empty seal" (kōngyìn) incident occurred.

Each year, officials from the Provincial Administration Commissions (bùzhèngsī) and various prefectures and counties went to the Ministry of Revenue to verify taxes, provisions, and military supplies.
Because of the long distance,
they would bring blank documents with seals already affixed,
and if the ministry rejected anything, they would simply make corrections.
This was a common practice.
At this time,
the emperor suspected foul play
and was furious.
He sentenced all chief officials to death
and ordered their deputies to be flogged one hundred times and exiled to the frontier.
Zhèng Shìlì (鄭士利) from Nínghǎi (寧海) submitted a memorial pleading their innocence,
but he was also flogged and exiled.
The killings in these two cases were already excessive.
Moreover, the Hú Wéiyōng (胡惟庸) and Lán Yù (藍玉) cases
implicated and killed nearly forty thousand people.
However, at times, he considered the greater good
and showed leniency.
Zhāng Jié (張傑), the magistrate of Yuánlíng (沅陵), was due to perform labor service.
He pleaded that his mother, Hè (賀),
had remained chaste during the chaos of the late Yuán dynasty
and was now old and without support.
The emperor believed this could encourage morality,
granted him a special pardon,
conferred a rank upon Zhāng Jié,
and allowed him to care for his mother until her death.
The Supervising Secretary (gěishìzhōng) Péng Yǔmín (彭與民) was imprisoned.
His father submitted a memorial expressing his sorrow.
The emperor immediately released him
and also exempted seventeen others who were imprisoned with him.
The wife or concubine of a death row inmate appealed her husband's injustice.
The Ministry of Justice requested that she be tattooed (qíng).
The emperor said that a woman appealing for her husband
was her duty
and did not punish her.
The Censorate (dūcháyuàn) had twenty-four prisoners sentenced to death.
The emperor ordered his officials to investigate,
and for those who were wrongly accused,
several lives were spared.
Eighteen commoners from Zhēnzhōu (真州) conspired to rebel.
They were executed,
but their mothers and children, who were subject to collective punishment, were released.
The severe legal officials he employed, such as Kāijì (開濟), Zhān Huī (詹徽), Chén Níng (陳寧), and Táo Kǎi (陶凱)
were later largely executed for their crimes.
He also repeatedly issued benevolent pronouncements,
not wishing to rely solely on punishment.
Once, while traveling to the suburban altars,
the crown prince accompanied him.
He pointed to the thorns (jīngchǔ) by the roadside and said:
"The ancients used these for flogging punishments,
because they could dispel wind,
and thus did not cause injury even in the cold."
When the Minister (shàngshū) Kāijì proposed strict laws,
the emperor instructed him:
"If you drain the pond to catch fish,
it harms even the roe;
if you burn the forest to hunt,
it harms even the fawns and chicks.
If the laws are too cunning and strict,
how can the people protect themselves?"
Kāijì was ashamed and apologized.
When the Administrator (cānzhèng) Yáng Xiàn (楊憲) wished to make the laws harsher,
the emperor said:
"To seek life under severe laws
is like trying to find fish in a boiling pot;
it is difficult to survive."
The Assistant Censor-in-Chief (yùshǐ zhōngchéng) Chén Níng (陳寧) said:
"If laws are severe, people will not easily commit crimes.
If officials are vigilant, those below will have no way to hide their true intentions."
Tàizǔ said:
"Not so.
The ancients devised punishments to prevent evil and protect goodness.
Thus, during the Táng (唐) and Yú (虞) periods, they marked clothing and differentiated uniforms as a form of punishment,
and the people did not offend.
The Qín (秦) dynasty had punishments like drilling skulls and pulling out ribs,
and the extermination of families,
yet prisons became like markets,
and the empire resented and rebelled.
I have never heard that by using the laws of Shāng (商) and Hán (韓),
one can achieve the governance of Yáo (堯) and Shùn (舜)."
Chén Níng retreated in shame.
He also once said to the Minister Liú Wéiqiān (劉惟謙):
"Benevolence and righteousness
are the nourishing food for the people.
Punishments
are the medicine and stones for curing evil.
To abandon benevolence and righteousness and solely employ punishments
is like nourishing people with medicine and stones;
how can that be called good governance?"
Indeed, Tàizǔ used severe penalties to punish for a time,
but also formulated moderate laws for future generations.
Therefore, his fierce governance
and benevolent edicts
functioned in conjunction,
never abandoning one for the other.
Jiànwén Dì (建文帝), succeeding to the throne,
wished solely to transform the people with benevolence and righteousness.
In the first year of his reign, when the Ministry of Justice reported prisoners,
the number had decreased by thirteen compared to Tàizǔ's time.
Chéngzǔ launched the Jìngnán campaign.
He indiscriminately labeled loyal officials as a treacherous faction.
More severely, he inflicted clan extermination and tomb desecration.
Wives and daughters were sent to the Huànyī Jú and Jiàofāng Sī.
Relatives and partisans exiled to military garrisons, even as late as the Lóngqìng and Wànlì reigns, were still being assigned to various ranks without end.
After all who resisted or defied him were killed,
fearing that people might secretly criticize him,
he was particularly severe against slander.
Dīng Yù, a commoner from Shānyáng, reported his fellow villagers for slander,
incriminating dozens of people.
The judicial authorities, catering to the imperial will,
stated that Yù was talented and usable,
and immediately appointed him as a supervising secretary in the Ministry of Justice.
In the seventeenth year of Yǒnglè (1419), the prohibition was reiterated.
Moreover, Chén Yīng, Lǚ Zhèn, Jì Gāng, and their ilk successively held power,
specializing in harshness to secure imperial favor.
Consequently, Xiāo Yì, Zhōu Xīn, Xiè Jìn, and many others died innocently.
However, the emperor knew in his heart that severe laws were wrong,
and occasionally showed magnanimity.
A certain chiliarch used a leather whip soaked in tung oil to beat people,
and the Ministry of Justice intended to punish him with a bamboo staff;
the emperor ordered him to be dismissed from his post as well.
When the judicial authorities reported officials who had fraudulently drawn imperial grain,
the emperor ordered them to be immediately executed;
the Ministry of Justice submitted a re-memorial.
The emperor said:
"This was an outburst of my anger,
which was excessive.
Let it be according to the law.
From now on, all criminal cases must undergo five re-memorials."
Upon reaching Rénzōng, whose nature was very benevolent and forgiving,
immediately after his enthronement,
he said to Jīn Chún and Liú Guān:
"You are all great ministers of the state.
If I err in administering justice,
you must firmly remonstrate again.
I am not reluctant to follow good advice."
Thereupon, he summoned the Grand Secretaries Yáng Shìqí, Yáng Róng, and Jīn Yòuzī to his bedside,
and instructed them, saying:
"How could I not know
the abuses of the judicial authorities in recent years?
Their proposed charges of 'great rebellion and unfilial conduct'
often stem from forced interpretations;
the late emperor repeatedly warned against this.
Therefore, death penalties must undergo four or five re-memorials,
yet the judicial authorities pay little attention,
content to be cruel officials without shame.
From now on, when reviewing serious prisoners,
you three must go and deliberate together.
If there is any injustice, no matter how minor,
you must report it."
When Hóngxī was established as the reign title,
in the second month, he instructed the Censor-in-Chief Liú Guān and the Minister of the Grand Court of Revision Yú Qiān, saying:
"In the past,
the judicial authorities regarded false accusation as merit.
If someone spoke a single word regarding state affairs,
they would immediately be accused of slander,
leading to the ruin of their family,
with no opportunity to clear their name.
Now, in the past few months,
this tendency has resurfaced.
What is urgent in governing is to seek criticism,
what is troublesome is to avoid discussion with words;
how can one prohibit slander?"
Thereupon, he looked at Shìqí and the others and said:
"This matter must be promulgated by imperial edict."
Consequently, Shìqí received the imperial decree,
and recorded the emperor's words in the Jǐchǒu Edict, stating:
"If I, at any time, excessively resent evil,
and apply confiscation of property or slow slicing, which are outside the law,
the judicial authorities shall remonstrate two or three times.
If three remonstrances are not accepted, they shall continue to five.
If five remonstrances are not accepted, they shall remonstrate with the Three Dukes and other great ministers
until accepted, and then stop;
this shall be a permanent institution.
Civil and military bureaus shall also not use cruel methods such as flogging the back,
or arbitrarily apply castration to cut off heirs.
Those who castrate themselves shall be treated as unfilial.
Except for those plotting rebellion and grand treason,
other offenders shall only be punished in person,
and the law of collective punishment shall not be applied universally.
Those who report slander shall not be prosecuted."
While on the throne for less than a year,
his benevolence and grace were thoroughly comprehensive.
Xuānzōng inherited this,
and further implemented many benevolent policies.
In the first year of Xuāndé (1426),
the Grand Court of Revision overturned the wrongful conviction of Wáng Gǔdū, a commoner's wife from Yīshì, for murdering her husband.
The emperor severely reprimanded the judicial officials,
and Minister Jīn Chún and others apologized,
upon which the matter ceased.
Nine義yong soldiers, including Yán Qún'ér, were falsely accused of being bandits,
and were to be executed.
Their families struck the Dengwen drum to appeal their innocence.
Upon re-investigation, it was confirmed that they were not bandits.
The emperor ordered Qún'ér and the others to be released,
and severely reprimanded Censor-in-Chief Liú Guān.
Thereafter, whenever a memorial concerning prisoners was presented,
the emperor's expression would be grim,
and his imperial meals would be abandoned.
Sometimes he would push away the documents with his hand,
and say to his attendants:
"Tell the judicial officials to go easy on them."
One day,
in the Wénhuá Diàn, he discussed ancient corporal punishments with his officials.
An attendant replied:
"When the Han dynasty abolished corporal punishments,
people then became less hesitant to break the law."
The emperor said:
"This is due to moral education,
how can it be related to the presence or absence of corporal punishment?
Shùn's laws included banishment, leniency, and redemption by fine,
and the crimes of the Four Fiends were only punished with banishment and execution.
It can be seen that those who received corporal punishment at that time
must all have committed serious crimes,
and it was not indiscriminately applied.
Moreover, the Han dynasty succeeded the abuses of the Qín,
which had laws against possessing books.
If corporal punishment were generally applied,
many would surely be harmed."
The next year, he authored "Fifty-five Chapters of Imperial Instructions,"
one of which concerned showing compassion in judicial matters.
Zhū Miǎn, Earl of Wǔjìn, said:
"Previously, I dispatched Palace Attendants Lín Kuān and others to send one hundred and seventeen prisoners to military garrisons on the frontier.
Only fifty arrived;
the rest died on the way."
The emperor was enraged
and ordered the judicial authorities to thoroughly investigate the matter.
The emperor issued lenient edicts annually,
and reviewed prisoners, often releasing them;
sometimes as many as three thousand people.
He instructed the judicial officials:
"I fear that they will die of prolonged detention,
hence I show leniency;
this is not a permanent institution."
At that time,
officials who paid one hundred or fifty *shi* of grain
could redeem themselves from miscellaneous capital crimes;
soldiers and commoners received a two-tenths reduction.
For various frontier garrisons, twelve *shi*,
and for Liáodōng, twenty *shi*;
these amounts were considered too light by the regulations.
However, the punishment for corrupt officials was uniquely strict.
He ordered civil officials who committed bribery to be punished according to the law.
Consequently, the application of law was lenient,
and the trend of corruption was not excessively rampant.
However, the Míng system heavily punished factions.
When Censor-in-Chief Xià Dí was urging grain collection in Chángzhōu,
Censor Hé Chǔyīng falsely accused him of accepting gold.
The various bureaus, fearing punishment,
knew he was innocent but dared not speak up.
Dí ultimately died of indignation as an inn courier.
Despite the emperor's benevolence and compassion,
a high official died unjustly;
this was a flaw in the legal system.
After Emperor Yīngzōng,
the benevolent and sagacious governance of Rénzōng and Xuānzōng declined.
In the early Zhèngtǒng reign,
the Three Yángs were in power,
still strictly observing the ancestral laws,
and prohibiting internal and external agencies from fabricating criminal cases.
Wèi Yuán, Minister of Justice, reported on suspicious cases during droughts and calamities,
and requested that the various Grand Coordinators conduct reviews.
This was granted.
For areas without Grand Coordinators, the Investigating Censors were ordered to do so.
The Investigating Censors for Military Affairs and the Censorate at the Provisional Capital also reported on suspicious cases,
and they were all jointly reviewed.
Censor Chén Zuò stated:
"When judicial officials rule on cases,
many violate the established laws,
and exclusively pursue severity.
For example, Wú Xǐ, Vice Minister of Revenue, recommended Wú Yuè, a Principal of dissolute conduct.
He should have been charged with the crime of recommending an unsuitable person for appointment,
but instead, a charge of 'evading regulations in presenting memorials to the throne,' punishable by decapitation, was added.
And when Yuè committed suicide by hanging,
the crime of the prison officials and guards
clearly has a graduated scale of punishment,
yet they cited 'not undertaking a matter that should have been done, resulting in grave consequences,'
and indiscriminately subjected them to flogging.
The ancestral laws, which were formulated by considering circumstances,
were meticulously designed by our ancestors for prevention,
but the judicial officials have suppressed leniency and exaggerated severity to this extent.
This is not how to broaden the benevolence and generosity of the Sacred Dynasty.
Henceforth, if anyone presumes to cite severe laws inappropriately,
I request that they be punished for 'altering established laws.' "
The emperor agreed with his words
and issued a warning.
By the sixth year,
Wáng Zhèn began to disrupt the government,
frequently humiliating court officials,
and causing great disorder in the penal code.
Liú Qiú, a Lecturer-in-Waiting, memorialized ten matters,
among which he said:
"Heaven sends down calamities and condemnations,
often due to the injustice of punishments.
It is advisable to let the judicial agencies act on their own,
and punish those who act out of personal favoritism or impropriety.
Even if there is a perceived affront,
like the incident of the Han emperor's carriage being obstructed by a thief who stole a ring,
one should still listen to Zhāng Shìzhī's insistence and follow it."
The emperor could not use his advice.
And Liú Qiú immediately incurred Wáng Zhèn's wrath with this memorial
and died in prison.
However, most of the cruel and abusive acts
were committed by Wáng Zhèn;
the emperor's heart was generally broad and fair.
In the eleventh year,
Yú Shìyuè, Minister of the Dali Temple, reported on more than a hundred people involved in cases like assault and murder,
and requested clemency;
they were all spared death and exiled to the frontier.
During the Jǐngtài reign,
Mǎ Yànbīn, county registrar of Yánggǔ, was to be executed.
His son, Zhèn, requested to die in his place.
Yànbīn was specially pardoned,
and Zhèn was conscripted to serve in a frontier guard unit.
Xuē Xuān, Vice Minister of the Dali Temple, said:
"When judicial agencies propose sentences for prisoners,
they often add supplementary remarks and requests in their memorials,
altering the intent of the laws."
An imperial edict ordered judicial officials, when questioning cases,
to strictly adhere to the laws and ordinances,
and not to make unauthorized supplementary remarks.
In the sixth year,
due to natural disasters, criminal cases both inside and outside the capital were reviewed,
and many lives were saved.
During the Tiānshùn reign,
imperial prisons flourished,
and the Three Judicial Offices and the Jǐnyīwèi prisons held many unadjudicated prisoners.
Officials often leaked prison information for illicit gain.
Xiāo Wéizhēn, the Censor-in-Chief, sided with Xú Yǒuzhēn,
and unjustly killed Wáng Wén, Yú Qiān, and others.
However, Liú Guǎnghéng, Vice Minister of Justice, was immediately charged with fabricating an imperial decree,
and Xú Yǒuzhēn was sentenced to decapitation.
Afterwards, the imperial guards were dispatched everywhere,
causing unrest throughout the country.
However, the practice of reviewing severe prisoners after the frost fell
actually began during the Tiānshùn period.
By the early Chénghuà reign,
Lù Yú, Minister of Justice, and others requested it,
and it was ordered to be carried out.
For cases presented to the throne, those whose circumstances were pitiable or doubtful were flogged,
and exempted from death, being sent to frontier garrisons.
This was implemented in successive reigns,
and people received grace beyond the law.
When Emperor Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
he issued an edict to the Three Judicial Offices:
"All civil and military officials, both inside and outside the capital, except for those guilty of embezzlement,
whose crimes have been recorded in official documents,
shall have them completely expunged."
Thereafter, this became an annual practice.
In the tenth year,
when prisoners were to be executed,
as the Winter Solstice festival was approaching,
it was specifically ordered that executions be carried out after the festival.
Later, Supervising Secretaries stated
that executions after the Winter Solstice were not timely,
so an edict was issued to wait until the winter month of the following year.
Hé Qiáoxīn, Grand Coordinator of Shānxī, impeached Shàng Jìng and Liú Yuán, Assistant Judicial Commissioners, for delaying legal proceedings,
and consequently stated:
"All those in the two judicial offices who fail to decide lawsuits
for over half a year
should all be reported to the throne for interrogation."
The emperor said:
"Criminal cases are grave matters.
The 'Book of Zhōu' says,
'For important prisoners,
meditate for five or six days, up to ten days,'
but this refers specifically to those whose true circumstances have not yet been ascertained.
If their true circumstances are known,
then a decision should be made immediately.
Those imprisoned without guilt
often die in prison from hardship;
this is killing by the penal officials.
Therefore, the law specifically includes articles on 'delaying the imprisonment of prisoners.'
Therefore, what Hé Qiáoxīn has memorialized
shall be circulated throughout the empire."
He also established a new regulation:
"For all cases of robbery where the stolen goods and weapons are not verified, or cases of homicide or injury that have not been thoroughly investigated,
if severe punishment is arbitrarily applied, leading to death in prison,
after a clear investigation of whether there was deliberate fault,
regardless of whether they are military or civilian officials,
they shall all be demoted to commoner status, in accordance with the precedent for cruel officials."
The wife of Minister Yáng Xuān was fierce and jealous,
killing more than ten maids.
The Ministry proposed applying the law for official wives who should be complicit,
but the emperor specifically ordered fifty strokes of the rod.
At that time, the emperor made many improvements to governance,
and was especially cautious regarding criminal cases,
with only one or two errors.
He once wanted to execute a prisoner
and refused a second review.
Censor Fāng Yòu again requested it,
and the emperor, enraged,
flogged and demoted Fāng Yòu.
Xǔ Cōng, Prefect of Jí'ān, was guilty of a crime,
and the eunuch Huáng Gāo incited the judicial agencies to sentence him to decapitation.
Bái Áng, a Supervising Secretary, requested that he not be executed without review,
but was not listened to,
and Xǔ Cōng was summarily decapitated that very night.
Upon Emperor Xiàozōng's ascension,
forty-eight people condemned to death were pardoned.
In the first year,
Liú Gài, a Prefect, was sentenced to decapitation for the crime of seditious speech.
Due to Wáng Shù's protest,
he was granted indefinite imprisonment.
In his later years,
Mǐn Guī, Minister of Justice, deliberated on a severe case,
but his judgment displeased the emperor,
and the memorial was withheld for a long time.
The emperor spoke of it with Liú Dàxià.
Liú Dàxià replied:
"A minister upholds the law and demonstrates loyalty;
what Mǐn Guī did is not extraordinary."
The emperor said:
"Tell me, has there ever been such an incident between a ruler and minister throughout history?"
Liú Dàxià replied:
"As a child, I read Mencius and
saw the passage where Gǔsǒu killed someone,
and Gāoyáo apprehended him.
What Mǐn Guī insists upon
should not be harshly criticized."
The emperor nodded.
The next day, the memorial was released,
and the decision followed Mǐn Guī's proposal.
The successive Ministers of Justice appointed—Hé Qiáoxīn, Péng Sháo, Bái Áng, and Mǐn Guī—were all impartial upholders of the law,
and the whole country universally praised their benevolent virtue.
In the fifth year of Zhèngdé, during a joint review of severe prisoners,
two were spared death.
At that time, wrongful imprisonments filled the jails.
Lǐ Dōngyáng and others cited a dust storm as a reason,
and special clemency was granted.
However, judicial officials, fearing Wáng Jǐn's wrath,
only submitted this much.
Later, the bandit leader Zhào Suì and others were dismembered in the marketplace,
and the skins of six ringleaders were peeled off.
The judicial agencies memorialized that ancestral instructions prohibited this,
but they were not listened to.
Soon after, the skins were made into saddles and stirrups,
which the emperor rode upon frequently.
And the court flogging of outspoken ministers was also most severe under Emperor Wǔzōng.
Shìzōng assumed the throne in the seventh month.
Due to a disaster at the Rìjīngmén Gate,
he redressed grievances and injustices.
He ordered the re-interrogation of thirty-eight individuals who had received a reprieve from execution,
among whom were Liáo Péng, Wáng Huán, and Qí Zuǒ.
The Supervising Secretary, Lǐ Fùlǐ, and others stated:
“Péng and the others are all associates of Jiāng Bīn and Qián Níng,
whom the imperial law must execute.”
Thereupon, they were ordered to remain imprisoned as before.
Later, they all gradually met their demise by execution.
From the time he flogged those who disputed the Grand Rites,
he severely curbed court officials.
In the sixth year, he ordered Zhāng Cōng, Guì È, and Fāng Xiànfū to concurrently manage the three judicial offices,
to revise the case of Lǐ Fúdá,
intending to convict Mǎ Lù under the law for traitorous factions.
Yáng Yīqīng strongly contended against this,
so Mǎ Lù was merely exiled to the frontier,
but over forty people were convicted.
Cōng and others considered this their achievement,
and thus requested the emperor to compile the "Qīnmíng Dàyù Lù" (Record of the Great Case of Enlightenment) and distribute it throughout the empire.
The convictions in this case
were mostly against those whom Cōng and the other two had long harbored resentment towards.
Using the laws of the ancestors
to allow powerful officials to frame and eliminate others,
the emperor did not realize this.
In the eighth year,
a commoner in the capital, Zhāng Fú, killed his mother,
but claimed that Zhāng Zhù had killed her.
The Director of the Ministry of Justice, Wèi Yìngzhāo, re-investigated and found the truth.
However, the emperor, because Zhāng Zhù was a servant of Wǔzōng's empress's family,
intended to wrongfully execute him.
He ordered Vice Minister Xǔ Zàn to completely overturn the verdict,
and then imprisoned the Censor-in-Chief Xióng Jiá and Wèi Yìngzhāo.
Thereafter,
his suspicion and jealousy grew daily,
and there were many cases of wrongful imprisonment and abuse.
Although he occasionally ordered leniency and compassion,
his intention was severe and harsh.
He once instructed his grand secretaries:
“In recent successive years, due to disasters and anomalies, punishments have been commuted.
Now it is again time for the Criminal Division to submit cases for triple review and imperial decision.
I consider capital punishment a grave matter.
I wish to make decisions on those who have stolen from imperial tombs or temples, and those who have beaten and cursed their parents and severely harmed human relations.
The rest shall be re-investigated by the judicial offices.
I will discuss this with you,
be cautious, be cautious.”
At the time, this was considered a sound policy.
Several years later,
the Grand Court of Revision received an imperial edict to review and report on prisoners whose death sentences should be commuted.
The emperor believed that the crimes of these prisoners were all unforgivable,
and that granting clemency would be an act of indulgence that would undermine the law.
He demoted and dismissed officials from the Grand Court of Revision up to the rank of Secretary, in varying degrees.
From the ninth year, when a ritual of thanksgiving was held in autumn, prisoners awaiting execution were spared.
Thereafter, whether due to auspicious omens
or grand sacrifices to heaven and earth,
the practice of suspending executions was observed every year.
However, he frequently condemned and angered the law enforcement officials,
believing that they did not request imperial instructions in a timely manner,
waiting until the winter solstice was approaching,
thereby abandoning justice and seeking to curry favor.
Consequently, he stripped Wú Shān, Minister of Justice, of his post,
and demoted Liú Sānwèi, a Supervising Secretary in the Criminal Division, and others.
In his middle years, he indulged even more in executions;
even the Grand Secretary Xià Yán was not spared.
By the thirty-seventh year,
he issued an imperial handwritten instruction,
stating:
“Those who govern the people are not all capable;
they act arbitrarily and wield power.
Wú Yīkuí, a young commoner from Húguǎng, suffered two wrongful executions, and his mother was also apprehended.
Desperate and with no one to appeal to,
he traveled ten thousand *lǐ* to knock at the imperial gate.
From this, it can be inferred
that there are countless others who are unjustly treated.
You should all diligently understand My intentions
and show greater compassion.
Furthermore, issue this throughout the empire,
so all may understand.”
This edict
expressed a profound sense of sorrow and pain.
In his final years,
the Secretary Hǎi Ruì submitted a memorial that offended him.
The Ministry of Justice deemed it a capital offense.
The emperor, however, held back the memorial and did not issue a decision,
so Hǎi Ruì was kept in long-term imprisonment.
Upon Mùzōng's ascension,
Xú Jiē, acting on the emperor's wishes, drafted a dying testament,
reinstating all banished officials,
showing special compassion for the dead,
and releasing those in custody.
All who read the imperial edict sighed in admiration.
In the early years of Wànlì,
in the winter months,
executions were halted three times by imperial decree.
In the ninth month of the fifth year,
the Director of the Directorate of Ceremonial, Sūn Déshèng, again conveyed an imperial decree:
“By order of the Empress Dowager,
as the grand wedding date approaches,
the Grand Secretaries are commanded, upon the triple review of memorials,
to draft an edict to commute punishments.”
Zhāng Jūzhèng stated:
“According to the old system of the ancestors,
whenever a capital crime was clearly investigated,
the offender was executed in the marketplace according to the law.
In the late Jiājìng era,
Shìzōng Emperor, due to his Taoist rituals,
first issued orders for temporary reprieve from execution,
or occasionally made decisions based on his imperial annotations,
determining executions as appropriate.
This is merely a recent malpractice of leniency,
not an old system.
My colleagues and I have thoroughly reviewed the crimes of these prisoners;
they have all extinguished natural justice
and corrupted human relations.
The Empress Dowager only sees the pitiful aspect of the criminals facing execution,
but does not realize that those they have harmed
are filled with grievances and indignation in the underworld.
If their pain is not avenged,
the spirit of resentment
will ascend and disturb cosmic harmony,
causing much damage.
If executions are not carried out,
year after year,
prisons will be full.
This not only incurs costs for custody
but also goes against the national statutes,
which is a great error in terms of governance.”
The Supervising Secretary Yán Yònghé and others also echoed these sentiments.
The imperial decree granted their request.
In the twelfth year,
Censor Tú Shúmíng requested the release of relatives of loyal officials who had been purged.
The emperor ordered that, except for Qí and Huáng,
all those implicated with Fāng Xiàorú and others should be investigated and cleared.
The emperor's nature was benevolent and gentle,
but he especially disliked outspoken critics.
From the twelfth to the thirty-fourth year,
one hundred and forty officials, both inside and outside the court, were flogged, exiled, or reduced to commoner status.
Later, he no longer held court,
and capital punishment was rarely used.
Death row prisoners were frequently reprieved or pardoned.
During the Tiānqǐ reign,
there were many cruel punishments,
which are discussed elsewhere
and will not be detailed here.
As soon as Emperor Zhuāngliè ascended the throne,
he executed Wèi Zhōngxián.
In the second year of Chóngzhēn, the Case of Rebellious Officials was officially determined into six grades,
which was met with universal acclaim.
However, this was after the laxity of Emperor Shénzōng and the chaos of Emperor Xīzōng;
he was keen to set things right,
and his use of punishment was rather severe.
Many high-ranking officials were imprisoned.
In the winter of the sixth year, when prisoners were to be judged,
the Emperor, dressed in plain clothes, presided over the Jiànjí Diàn.
He summoned the Grand Secretaries for deliberation,
but Wēn Tǐrén made no attempts at exoneration.
Xú Zhàoqí, the Magistrate of Huátíng in Shǎnxī, arrived at his post for seven days,
when the city fell,
and he was sentenced to death.
The Emperor felt pity for him,
but Tǐrén did not intercede.
In the eleventh year,
Xú Shíqí, the Southern Vice Minister of the Office of Transmission, submitted a memorial to save Zhèng Sānjùn,
and in it he said:
“Since Your Majesty ascended the throne,
nearly a thousand officials have been condemned to the red register,
filling the prisons.
Even if all the facts and laws were fully consistent,
it would still be regrettable,
let alone those who are terrified under the awe of your authority.
There are those who go along with the flow without turning back,
those who speculate without offering remedies,
implicating and spreading like vines,
with nine chances of death and one of life.
How can this be the intention of the sage who only pities punishment?”
The Emperor could not accept it.
In the winter of that year,
due to the appearance of a comet,
executions were suspended.
For cases concerning border defenses, provisions, and bandit suppression,
the Ministry of Justice was ordered to present the verdicts within five days.
In the twelfth year,
Censor Wèi Jǐngqí was discussing prisoners at Xīshì,
when Censor Gāo Qīnshùn, Ministry of Works Senior Secretary Hú Lián, and fifteen others were about to be executed.
Suddenly, the eunuch Běnqīng arrived with an imperial order to commute their sentences,
and eleven people were released.
The next day,
Jǐngqí reported back,
and was blamed and sent to the Jǐnyī Prison.
This was because the Emperor, upon hearing that some prisoners had voiced grievances,
suspended the executions and sought imperial instruction,
but Jǐngqí, in his haste, did not differentiate,
and thus incurred blame.
In the fourteenth year,
Grand Secretary Fàn Fùcuì submitted a memorial requesting a clearing of the prisons,
saying:
“There are over one hundred and forty imprisoned civil and military officials in the prisons,
which is deeply regrettable.”
No reply was given.
At that time, national affairs deteriorated daily,
but only severe laws were used to discipline officials.
There was no time to remedy past mistakes,
and ultimately, it did not save the dynasty from chaos and demise.
Textual Notes
Volume Seventy-one, Penal Law Three
There were penal laws created in the Míng dynasty
that did not conform to ancient systems:
the court flogging, the Eastern and Western Depots, the Jǐnyīwèi, and the prisons of the Zhènfǔ Division.
These few methods
killed people most cruelly,
yet were not subject to the law.
They were continued and implemented,
reaching their peak in the late dynasty.
The lives of all in the court and throughout the land
were entirely at the mercy of military men and eunuchs,
which is truly lamentable.
Emperor Tàizǔ often discussed with his attendants the proper etiquette for treating high officials.
Grand Astrologer Liú Jī said:
“In ancient times, when dukes and ministers committed crimes,
a basin of water and a sword were offered,
and they would go to a private chamber to commit suicide.
They were never lightly disgraced or humiliated,
so as to preserve the dignity of high officials.”
Assistant Reader Zhān Tóng then presented the Dà Dài Lǐ Jì and Jiǎ Yí’s memorial,
and also said:
“In ancient times, punishment did not extend to high officials,
to encourage integrity and a sense of shame.
Only in this way
can the grace and etiquette between ruler and ministers be fully maintained.”
The Emperor deeply approved of this.
In the sixth year of Hóngwǔ,
Wáng Sù, Minister of Works, was legally subject to flogging,
but Emperor Tàizǔ said:
“The six ministers are of high status and importance,
and should not be humiliated for minor offenses.”
He ordered him to atone for his crime with his salary.
After this, when officials made mistakes,
they were permitted to redeem themselves with their salaries,
which started here.
However, Zhū Liàngzǔ, Marquis of Yǒngjiā, and his son were both flogged to death,
and Xuē Xiáng, Minister of Works, died under the杖 (flogging).
Therefore, those who submitted memorials stated that while high officials might deserve execution,
they should not be subjected to humiliation.
The punishment of court flogging
also began with Emperor Tàizǔ.
In the third year of Xuāndé, angered by Censors Yán Ái, Fāng Dǐng, Hé Jié, and others who indulged in wine and women,
and neglected their court attendance for a long time,
he ordered them to be paraded in cangues.
From then on, censors were subjected to wearing cangues.
By the Zhèngtǒng reign,
when Wáng Zhèn wielded power,
Minister Liú Zhōngfū,
Vice Ministers Wú Xǐ and Chén Cháng,
and Libationer Lǐ Shímǐan were all subjected to this humiliation,
and court flogging became a common practice in the palace.
In the fifteenth year of Chénghuà,
Wāng Zhí falsely accused Vice Minister Mǎ Wénshēng, Censor-in-chief Móu Fèng, and others.
An imperial decree blamed Li Jùn, Wáng Jùn, and fifty-four other Supervising Censors for connivance,
