and each was subjected to twenty strokes of court flogging.
In the fourteenth year of Zhèngdé,
for opposing the Southern Tour,
Shū Fēn, Huáng Gǒng, and one hundred and forty-six others were subjected to court flogging,
and eleven died.
In the third year of Jiājìng,
when officials disputed the Great Rites,
Fēng Xī and one hundred and thirty-four others were subjected to court flogging,
and sixteen died.
In his middle years, the penal laws became even more severe,
and even high officials could not escape flogging and humiliation.
Zhái Péng, Grand Coordinator of Xuāndà, and Zhū Fāng, Pacification Commissioner of Jìzhōu, for withdrawing defenses too early;
Guō Zōnggāo, Grand Coordinator of Xuāndà, and Chén Yào, Pacification Commissioner of Dàtóng, for allowing bandits to enter Dàtóng;
Péng Àn, Vice Minister of Justice, Tú Qiáo, Left Censor-in-chief, and Shěn Liángcái, Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, for delaying deliberation on the case of Dīng Rúkuí;
Jiǎng Yīngkuí, Vice Minister of War, and Táng Guóxiāng, Left Vice Minister of the Office of Transmission, for their children falsely claiming achievements;
all were arrested and flogged.
Fāng and Yào died under the flogging,
while Àn, Qiáo, Liángcái, and others, after being flogged,
were immediately ordered to attend to their duties.
Such humiliation for dukes and ministers
had never happened before.
Furthermore, during the New Year's Day court audience,
the Emperor, angered by Zhāng Sījìng and other Supervising Censors of the Six Offices,
ordered them all to be flogged while in their court robes,
which shocked everyone in the realm.
Within forty-odd years,
the number of court officials flogged to death
was five times more than in previous dynasties.
In the fifth year of Wànlì,
for disputing Zhāng Jūzhèng’s refusal to observe mourning,
Wú Zhōngxíng and four others were flogged.
Later, Lú Hóngchūn, Mèng Yǎnghào, Wáng Déwán, and others were all flogged,
some receiving as many as one hundred strokes.
Later, the Emperor grew more tired of those who spoke up,
and many memorials were kept in the palace without reply,
and court flogging was suspended.
During the Tiānqǐ era,
the eunuch Wáng Tǐgān, acting on an imperial decree for a major review,
severely flogged Lǐ Chéng'ēn, a relative of the imperial family,
to please Wèi Zhōngxián.
Thereupon, Wàn Zǔ and Wú Yùzhōng died under the flogging,
and the Censorate and ministries' strong protests were in vain.
Grand Secretary Yè Xiànggāo said:
“This abusive policy, which has not been implemented for several decades,
has appeared three times within ten days.
It must not be implemented again.”
Zhōngxián then abolished court flogging,
but sent all those he wished to kill to the Zhènfǔ Division,
and officials were left with even less chance of survival.
Court flogging in Nánjīng
began in the eighteenth year of Chénghuà.
Nánjīng Censors Lǐ Shān and others requested relief due to a bad harvest.
The Emperor picked out erroneous characters in their memorial,
and ordered the Jǐnyīwèi to go to Nánjīng’s Wǔmén before noon,
where each person was flogged twenty times,
supervised by the garrison eunuch.
During the Zhèngdé reign,
Nánjīng Censor Lǐ Xī impeached corrupt officials, which angered Liú Jǐn,
who fabricated an imperial decree for thirty strokes of flogging.
At that time, Nánjīng’s imperial guards had not performed executions for a long time,
so selected soldiers practiced for several days
before flogging him,
nearly to death.
The establishment of the Eastern Depot [Dōngchǎng],
began with Emperor Chéngzǔ.
The prisons of the Embroidered Uniform Guard [Jǐnyīwèi],
Emperor Tàizǔ had once used them,
but later they were prohibited.
Their re-use also dates from the Yǒnglè reign.
The Depot [chǎng] and the Guard [wèi] relied on each other,
hence those who spoke of them referred to them as "Depot and Guard" [chǎngwèi] together.
Initially,
when Emperor Chéngzǔ rose in Běipíng,
he often used the attendants of Emperor Jiànwén [Jiànwéndì]
as his eyes and ears to gather intelligence on palace affairs.
Therefore, after his ascension, he exclusively relied on eunuchs,
establishing the Eastern Depot [Dōngchǎng] north of Dōng'ānmén.
He ordered his favored eunuchs to supervise it,
to investigate sedition, treacherous speech, major villains, and other such matters.
It shared power and influence equally with the Embroidered Uniform Guard [Jǐnyīwèi].
This was after the capital was moved.
However, Guard [Wèi] commanders Jì Gāng [Jì Gāng], Mén Dá [Mén Dá], and others were greatly favored
and frequently held power,
so the Depot's [Chǎng] power could not match theirs.
By the time of Emperor Xiànzōng,
Shàng Míng [Shàng Míng] headed the Eastern Depot [Dōngchǎng].
A Western Depot [Xīchǎng] was also separately established to investigate matters,
with Wāng Zhí [Wāng Zhí] as its supervisor.
The number of embroidered-uniform cavalry [tíqí] under his command was double that of the Eastern Depot [Dōngchǎng].
From the capital to the entire realm,
they extensively investigated matters,
and even princely estates [wángfǔ] were not exempt.
Zhí [Zhí] was twice dismissed and reappointed,
serving for a total of six years.
The unjustly killed were countless,
and his power far exceeded that of the Guard [Wèi].
At a time when Zhí [Zhí] frequently went out to supervise armies on the border,
Grand Secretary Wàn Ān [Wàn Ān] then said:
"Emperor Tàizōng built Běijīng [Běijīng],
and ordered Embroidered Uniform officials and officers to investigate.
hence he established the Eastern Depot [Dōngchǎng],
ordering inner officials to supervise it.
It operated for fifty to sixty years,
and affairs had fixed regulations.
Recently, the 'fox demon' [yāohú] appeared at night,
causing people's hearts to be alarmed and frightened.
This caused Your Majesty's concern,
leading to the addition of the Western Depot [Xīchǎng],
and specifically appointing Zhí [Zhí] to supervise investigations,
to guard against the unforeseen.
This was a temporary expedient
to calm people's hearts.
As for the past disturbances,
I will not elaborate.
Now Zhí [Zhí] is garrisoned in Dàtóng [Dàtóng].
In the capital, everyone unanimously
considers it convenient to abolish the Western Depot [Xīchǎng].
I humbly hope for Your Majesty's grace to specifically issue an edict to abolish it,
and for all officials and officers to return to their original Guard [Wèi].
The imperial ancestral temples and altars of state would be most fortunate."
The emperor followed his advice.
Shàng Míng [Shàng Míng] then solely held power,
but was also dismissed not long after.
In the first year of Hóngzhì [Hóngzhì],
Assistant Minister Zhāng Lún [Zhāng Lún] requested the abolition of the Eastern Depot [Dōngchǎng].
It was not reported.
However, Emperor Xiàozōng [Xiàozōng] was benevolent and kind,
and the Depot and Guard [chǎngwèi] dared not act presumptuously.
The supervisors of the Depot, Luó Xiáng [Luó Xiáng] and Yáng Péng [Yáng Péng],
merely carried out their duties.
In the first year of Zhèngdé [Zhèngdé], the Eastern Depot [Dōngchǎng] eunuch Wáng Yuè [Wáng Yuè] was killed,
and Qiū Jù [Qiū Jù] was ordered to replace him.
A Western Depot [Xīchǎng] was again established and Gǔ Dàyòng [Gǔ Dàyòng] was appointed to head it.
Both were partisans of Liú Jǐn [Liú Jǐn].
The two Depots [chǎng] competed for power,
sending out secret agents to investigate affairs in all directions.
In Nánkāng [Nánkāng], Wú Dēngxiǎn [Wú Dēngxiǎn] and others playfully competed in dragon boat races,
and died while their families' properties were confiscated.
In distant prefectures and remote areas,
those who saw men in splendid clothes and furious horses speaking the capital's dialect [Jīngshīyǔ]
would avoid and hide from them.
Local officials, upon hearing rumors,
secretly offered bribes.
Thus, scoundrels seized the opportunity to commit villainy,
and everyone in the realm stood on tiptoe in fear.
And the Guard [Wèi] commander Shí Wényì [Shí Wényì] was also a private retainer of Jǐn [Jǐn],
so the power of the Depot and Guard [chǎngwèi] merged.
Jǐn [Jǐn] also changed the Xīxīn [Xīxīn] Bureau's Outer Fuel Depot [Wàixīnchǎng] to the Affairs-Handling Depot [Bànshìchǎng],
and the old warehouse grounds of the Róng [Róng] Princely Estate into the Inner Affairs-Handling Depot [Nèibànshìchǎng],
which he personally commanded.
In the capital, it was called the Inner Travelling Depot [Nèixíngchǎng].
Even the Eastern and Western Depots [Dōngxīchǎng] were under its surveillance,
and its cruelty was even more severe.
Moreover, it established the precedent
that all crimes, regardless of severity, were punished by flogging [juézhàng]
and eternal banishment to the frontier,
or by being sent away in a cangue.
Cangues weighed up to 150 catties,
and people often died within a few days.
Director of the Imperial Seal Gù Xuán [Gù Xuán],
Vice Envoy Yáo Xiáng [Yáo Xiáng], Minister of Works Láng Zhāng Wěi [Láng Zhāng Wěi], Censor Wáng Shízhōng [Wáng Shízhōng] and others were not exempt,
being banished to the frontier only after being near death.
Censors Chái Wénxiǎn [Chái Wénxiǎn] and Wāng Chéng [Wāng Chéng] were even subjected to slow slicing [língchí] for minor offenses.
Thousands of officials, soldiers, and common people died illegally.
When Jǐn [Jǐn] was executed,
the Western Depot [Xīchǎng] and Inner Travelling Depot [Nèixíngchǎng] were both abolished,
but only the Eastern Depot [Dōngchǎng] remained as before.
Zhāng Ruì [Zhāng Ruì] led it,
and together with Guard [Wèi] commander Qián Níng [Qián Níng], he wantonly framed people by investigating affairs.
The term "Depot and Guard" [chǎngwèi] thus became renowned.
In the second year of Jiājìng [Jiājìng],
Rén Jǐngxián [Rén Jǐngxián] of the Eastern Depot [Dōngchǎng] employed Battalion Commander Táo Chún [Táo Chún],
who made many false accusations.
Investigating Censor Liú Zuì [Liú Zuì] reported this,
and was demoted to Prefect of Guǎngdé [Guǎngdézhōu].
Censor Huáng Déyòng [Huáng Déyòng] used relays of post-horses to travel there.
At that time, Yán Rúhuán [Yán Rúhuán] traveled with him,
carrying luggage wrapped in a yellow cloth.
Jǐngxián [Jǐngxián] immediately reported this,
and they were arrested and imprisoned.
Zuì [Zuì] and others were banished to military garrisons with varying sentences.
Investigating Censor Liú Jì [Liú Jì] said:
"Zuì's [Zuì] crime does not warrant banishment.
Moreover, he was arrested at the gate of a eunuch,
framed by the hands of a military officer,
and judged by an imperial decree from within the palace.
How can this be shown to the world?"
It was not reported.
At this time,
all frontier-guarding eunuchs throughout the realm were dismissed,
yet the high officials adhered to past practices,
saying that the Eastern Depot [Dōngchǎng] was established by the imperial ancestors [Zǔzōng],
and could not be abolished.
They did not know that it was not instituted by Emperor Tàizǔ [Tàizǔ].
However, Emperor Shìzōng [Shìzōng] strictly controlled the inner officials,
who dared not act wantonly.
The Depot's [Chǎng] power was far inferior to that of Guard [Wèi] commander Lù Bǐng [Lù Bǐng].
In the early Wànlì [Wànlì] reign,
Féng Bǎo [Féng Bǎo], holding both the Directorate of Ceremonial [Sīlǐ] and Depot affairs,
established a Depot north of the Eastern Upper North Gate [Dōngshàngběimén].
It was called the Inner Depot [Nèichǎng],
while the original one was called the Outer Depot [Wàichǎng].
Bǎo [Bǎo] and Zhāng Jūzhèng [Zhāng Jūzhèng] instigated the "King and Ministers" [Wáng Dàchén] case,
wanting to exterminate the clan of Gāo Gǒng [Gāo Gǒng].
Guard [Wèi] commander Zhū Xīxiào [Zhū Xīxiào] strongly resisted it,
and Gǒng [Gǒng] escaped punishment.
The Guard [Wèi] was still not greatly subservient to the Depot [Chǎng].
In the middle years,
the mining tax envoys frequently caused harm,
but the Eastern Depot [Dōngchǎng] officials Zhāng Chéng [Zhāng Chéng], Sūn Xiān [Sūn Xiān], and Chén Jǔ [Chén Jǔ] were all tranquil.
Jǔ [Jǔ] handled the "Demon Book" [Yāoshū] case
without implicating the innocent,
which was quite praised at the time.
At that time, the emperor also had no intention of being harsh and strict,
and punishments were rarely used.
Green grass even grew in the prisons of the Depot and Guard [chǎngwèi].
By the Tiānqǐ [Tiānqǐ] reign,
Wèi Zhōngxián [Wèi Zhōngxián], as Director of Supervising Calligraphy [Bǐngbǐ] and head of Depot affairs,
used Guard [Wèi] commander Tián Ergēng [Tián Ergēng] and Centennial Commander Xǔ Xiǎnchún [Xǔ Xiǎnchún] and their ilk,
and exclusively used cruelty and tyranny to control both internal and external affairs.
The poison of the Depot and Guard [chǎngwèi] reached its extreme.
Those eunuchs who held the seal of the Sīlǐ Jiān,
their subordinates called them Zōngzhǔ,
while the overseer of the Dōngchǎng was called Dūzhǔ.
The Dōngchǎng's subordinates had no dedicated officials;
there was one Zhǎngxíng Qiānhù
and one Lǐxíng Bǎihù,
also called Tiēxíng,
all of whom were guard officials.
Their servants and runners were all supplied by the guards;
only the most agile, clever, and crafty were assigned to these roles.
The head of the runners was called Dàngtóu;
his cap was pointed at the top,
he wore a plain blue pleated robe,
a small sash,
and white leather boots,
specializing in surveillance.
Below him were several Fānzi who acted as executive agents.
Outlaws in the capital,
who cheated people out of money or bore grudges,
regarded these executive agents as their lairs.
If one discovered a secret affair,
they would relay it privately to the Dàngtóu.
The Dàngtóu, assessing the gravity of the matter,
would first give them gold.
The matter was called Qǐshù,
and the gold was called Mǎiqǐshù.
Once the matter was obtained,
the Dàngtóu would lead the Fānzi to the culprit's home,
where they would sit on either side, a practice called Dǎzhuāng.
The Fānzi would then burst in, seize the person, and interrogate them.
If there were no corroborating evidence or documents,
and the bribe was paid as requested,
they would leave immediately.
If there was the slightest dissatisfaction,
they would beat and torture them,
a method called Gānzhájiǔ,
or also Bānzēng'ér,
whose pain was ten times worse than official punishments.
Furthermore, they would hint that the accused should implicate influential people.
If the influential people gave a large sum of gold,
then there would be no trouble.
If they were stingy and refused,
or gave too little,
the matter would immediately be reported to the emperor,
and the accused would be sent to the Zhènfǔsī prison,
where they would die instantly.
On the first day of each month,
hundreds of factory agents
would draw lots in the courtyard,
to divide up the surveillance of officials.
Those who monitored the joint trials of major cases in the central yamen and other places, and the interrogations of serious offenders by the Běizhènfǔsī, were called Tīngjì.
Those who visited and investigated other government offices and city gates were called Zuòjì.
When an official performed a certain act,
or a certain city gate apprehended a certain villain,
the clerks would report these details to the factory through the Zuòjì, a process called Dǎshìjiàn.
Upon reaching the Dōnghuámén,
even in the dead of night,
they would find an opening to enter,
and immediately present the report to the emperor without others present.
Thus, matters, whether big or small,
all reached the emperor's ears.
Even trivial household affairs
were sometimes circulated as jokes in the palace,
and everyone, high and low, was anxious and fearful of Dǎshìjiàn.
The regulations of the guards were also like those of the factory.
However, they had to submit memorials
before they could reach the emperor,
which is why their influence was far less than that of the factory.
There were four men drinking in a secret room one night.
One, in a drunken state,
cursed Wèi Zhōngxián.
The other three dared not utter a sound.
Before the cursing finished,
Fānzi seized the four men and brought them to Zhōngxián's residence.
The curser was immediately dismembered,
while the other three were rewarded with gold.
The three men were terrified and dared not move.
When Emperor Zhuāngliè ascended the throne,
Zhōngxián was executed.
However, Wáng Tǐqián, Wáng Yǒngzuò, Zhèng Zhīhuì, Lǐ Chéngfāng, Cáo Huàchún, Wáng Déhuà, Wáng Zhīxīn, Wáng Huàmín, Qí Běnzhèng, and others successively took charge of factory affairs,
and the practice of secret informing never ceased.
Zhīxīn and Huàchún were rewarded for their success in apprehending villains,
and their younger brothers and nephews were granted positions as Jǐnyīwèi Bǎihù.
Meanwhile, Déhuà and Wú Dàozhèng, the Dōngchǎng's Lǐxíng official, and others investigated the secret affairs of the Grand Secretary Xuē Guóguān,
which led to Guóguān's death.
At that time, the Jǐnyīwèi officials had long been awed by the factory's power,
and mostly bowed their heads and allowed themselves to be used.
In the fifteenth year of Chóngzhēn (1642),
Censor Yáng Rényuàn said:
"Emperor Gāo Dì established officials,
but there was no such thing as a 'secret investigation yamen.'
If subordinates broke the law,
censors would directly impeach them,
without secret denunciations.
Later, to purge the imperial capital,
the Dōngchǎng was established.
I, as a humble official in Nánchéng,
have reviewed many lawsuits
where people falsely claimed to be Fānzi to appeal their grievances.
If even false claims of the Dōngchǎng
cause such harm,
how much more so the real thing?
This is due to the accumulated power that has grown too strong.
This 'accumulated power that has grown too strong' refers to
the official regulations comparing cases,
where Fānyì often offered prices to buy cases.
Those who sold cases would even lure people into committing illicit acts and robberies to sell them,
and the Fānyì would not question their origins,
while the persuaders would share the profits and leave.
Those harboring grudges would make accusations,
falsely charging people with serious crimes,
and their grudges would be fully satisfied.
I humbly pray that the Dōngchǎng's handling of cases be relaxed,
after which the Dōngchǎng's comparisons can be moderated.
When the Dōngchǎng's comparisons are moderated,
then the Fānyì's buying and selling of cases can both cease,
and the accumulated power that has grown too strong may perhaps be slightly alleviated."
Later, he again spoke critically of the inappropriate deployment of Tíqí.
The Emperor then issued an edict to the Dōngchǎng,
stating that their investigations should be limited to treason and incest.
As for committing illicit acts and violating laws,
these fell under the purview of the proper authorities
and should not be investigated by the factory.
He also warned the Jǐnyīwèi校尉 (jiàowèi) against extortion.
However, the Emperor relied on the factory and guards even more heavily
until the fall of the dynasty.
The Jǐnyīwèi prison
was what the world called Zhàoyù.
In ancient times, prisons and lawsuits were solely managed by the Sīkòu.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn first established twenty-six Zhàoyù,
and throughout successive dynasties, changes were inconsistent.
During the Five Dynasties, Emperor Míngzōng of Táng established the Shìwèi Qīnjūn Mǎbùjūn Dūzhīhuīshǐ,
which was the title for the emperor personally commanding the troops.
By the Hàn dynasty, there was the Shìwèisī prison,
where all major matters were decided.
The Míng Jǐnyīwèi prison was similar;
its confinement was cruel and brutal,
and there was no greater harm than this.
In the eighth month of the fifteenth year of Hóngwǔ, she fell ill.
The officials requested prayers and sacrifices,
and sought good physicians.
The Empress said to the Emperor:
“Life and death
are matters of fate;
what good are prayers and sacrifices?
Moreover, how can physicians bring people back to life?
If the medicine proves ineffective,
will you not punish the physicians on account of me?”
As her illness worsened,
the Emperor asked what she wished to say.
She replied:
“I wish that Your Majesty would seek out the worthy and accept remonstrances,
be as prudent at the end as at the beginning,
ensure that all your descendants are virtuous,
and that your ministers and people find their proper place – that is all.”
On the day bìngxū of that month, she passed away,
aged fifty-one.
The Emperor wept bitterly,
and never again appointed an Empress.
In the ninth month, on the day gēngwǔ of that year, she was buried at Xiàolíng,
and posthumously given the title Xiàocí Huánghòu.
The palace women remembered her
and composed a song, saying:
“Our Empress, holy and benevolent,
her influence spread through home and state.
She nurtured us, she raised us,
her virtue remembered, never forgotten.
Her virtue remembered, never forgotten,
for ten thousand years.
Like that deep spring,
and the vast, distant heavens.”
In the first year of Yǒnglè, she was granted the honorable posthumous title Xiàocí Zhāoxiàn Zhìrén Wéndé Chéngtiān Shùnshèng Gāo Huánghòu.
In the seventeenth year of Jiājìng, she was further granted the honorable posthumous title Xiàocí Zhēnhuà Zhéshùn Rénhuī Chéngtiān Yùshèng Zhìdé Gāo Huánghòu.
Consort Chéngmù, Lady Sūn,
was a native of Chénzhōu.
During the military upheavals at the end of the Yuán dynasty,
both of her parents died,
and she fled with her second elder brother Fān to Yángzhōu to escape the conflict.
When the Qīng army captured the city,
Marshal Mǎ Shìxióng took her in
and raised her as an adopted daughter.
At eighteen,
Tàizǔ took her into his household.
Upon his ascension to the throne,
she was enfeoffed as Guìfēi,
ranking above all other consorts.
In the ninth month of the seventh year of Hóngwǔ, she passed away,
aged thirty-two.
Since the Consort had no children,
the Emperor ordered Zhōu Wáng Shū to observe three years of mourning as for a compassionate mother,
and the Heir Apparent and all other princes to observe one year.
He commanded the Confucian scholars to compile the Xiàocí Lù.
The practice of secondary sons mourning their birth mothers for three years,
and all sons mourning their secondary mothers for one year,
began with this Consort.
She was buried at Chǔgāng.
Her elder brother Yīng was granted three hundred dàn of land rent,
to provide for sacrifices annually.
Later, she was re-interred at Xiàolíng.
Consort Shú, Lady Lǐ,
was a native of Shòuzhōu.
Her father, Jié,
at the beginning of Hóngwǔ,
participated in the northern expedition as a Commander of Guǎngwǔ Wèi,
and died in battle.
In the ninth month of the seventeenth year,
after the mourning period for Empress Xiàocí concluded,
she was enfeoffed as Shúfēi
and took charge of the six palaces.
Not long after,
she passed away.
Consort Níng, Lady Guō,
was the daughter of Guō Shānfǔ from Háo.
Shānfǔ was skilled in physiognomy.
When Tàizǔ was still obscure, he passed by Shānfǔ’s house,
and Shānfǔ examined his features,
exclaiming in great surprise:
“Your appearance indicates unspeakable nobility!”
He then said to his sons Xīng and Yīng:
“I see that you both can be enfeoffed as Marquis because of this.”
He promptly sent them to cross the river
and also sent his daughter, the Consort, to attend Tàizǔ.
Later, she was enfeoffed as Níngfēi.
After Consort Shú Lǐ passed away,
the Consort took charge of the six palaces.
Shānfǔ was repeatedly posthumously honored as Yíngguó Gōng,
and Xīng and Yīng were both enfeoffed as Marquises for their accomplishments;
their biographies are recorded elsewhere.
Empress Mǎ of Huìdì
was the daughter of Quán, the Junior Steward of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
In the twenty-eighth year of Hóngwǔ, she was enfeoffed as the Imperial Grandson's Consort.
In the second month of the first year of Jiànwén, she was enfeoffed as Empress.
In the sixth month of the fourth year,
when the city fell,
she perished in the fire.
Empress Rénxiào Xú of Chéngzǔ
was the eldest daughter of Zhōngshān Wáng Dá.
As a child, she was chaste and quiet,
fond of reading,
and was called a female scholar.
Tàizǔ heard of her virtuousness
and summoned Dá, saying:
“You and I
were commoner friends.
In ancient times, rulers and ministers who were close
often formed marriage alliances.
You have an excellent daughter;
let her be betrothed to my son Dì.”
Dá bowed his head in thanks.
In the ninth year of Hóngwǔ, she was enfeoffed as the Consort of Yān Wáng.
Empress Gāo loved her deeply.
She accompanied the Prince to his fief,
and observed three years of mourning for Empress Xiàocí Gāo,
eating vegetables as prescribed by ritual.
The Empress could recite every one of Empress Gāo’s parting words without omission.
When the Jingnàn campaign began,
the Prince attacked Dàníng,
and Lǐ Jǐnglóng took the opportunity to besiege Běipíng.
At that time, Rénzōng, as the Heir Apparent, was in charge of the defense,
and all preparations and defenses
were largely carried out according to the Empress's orders.
When Jǐnglóng attacked the city fiercely,
there were few soldiers in the city.
The Empress inspired and encouraged the wives of the generals, officers, soldiers, and common people;
they all put on armor and ascended the ramparts to resist and defend,
and thus the city was preserved.
When the Prince ascended the throne,
she was enfeoffed as Empress.
She said:
“The annual wars in the north and south
have exhausted the soldiers and people;
they should be given rest.”
She also said:
“The worthy talents of this era are all left by Gāo Huángdì;
Your Majesty should not discriminate between old and new.”
She also said:
“Emperor Yáo’s benevolence began with his own kin.”
The Emperor always welcomed and accepted her advice.
Originally,
the Empress’s younger brother Zēngshòu often relayed state secrets to Yān,
and was executed by Huìdì.
At this point, the Emperor wished to posthumously grant him a title,
but the Empress strongly argued against it.
The Emperor did not listen,
and ultimately enfeoffed him as Dìngguó Gōng.
He then ordered his son Jǐngchāng to inherit the title
and reported this to the Empress.
The Empress said:
“This is not my wish.”
And she never expressed gratitude.
She once said that the two Princes of Hàn and Zhào were disobedient,
and that officials should be selected from court ministers to concurrently manage their affairs.
One day,
she asked:
“Your Majesty, who do you consult for governance?”
The Emperor replied:
“The Six Ministers manage state affairs,
and the Hanlin Academy is responsible for deliberation and remonstrance.”
The Empress then requested to summon all their wives,
and bestowed upon them caps, robes, paper money, and silk.
She admonished them, saying:
“A wife’s service to her husband
is not merely providing food and clothing;
she must also be a helper.
The words of friends
may be followed or rejected,
but the words between husband and wife, when gentle and compliant, are easily accepted.
I attend His Majesty day and night,
concerned only with the welfare of the people;
you all should strive for this.”
She once compiled twenty chapters of "Nèixùn" from "Nǚxiàn" and "Nǚjiè,"
and also categorized and edited the admirable words and good deeds of ancient people,
creating the "Quànshàn Shū,"
which was distributed throughout the realm.
The Empress had no fault, but was deposed.
The world heard of it and pitied her.
Xuānzōng later regretted it too.
He once excused himself, saying:
"This was an act of mine when I was young."
In the sixth year of Tiānshùn,
Grand Empress Sūn passed away.
Empress Qián spoke to Yīngzōng:
"The Empress was virtuous and blameless,
but was deposed to become an immortal master.
When she died,
people feared the Grand Empress,
so her embalming and burial did not accord with ritual."
She then advised him to restore her title and rank.
Yīngzōng asked Grand Secretary Lǐ Xián.
Xián replied:
"Your Majesty's intention,
Heaven, Earth, ghosts, and spirits truly oversee it.
However, I believe that the imperial tomb, ancestral hall, and spirit tablet should all follow the style of the Fèngxiān Hall,
to be worthy of Your Majesty's filial piety."
In the intercalary seventh month of the seventh year,
she was respectfully granted the posthumous title Gōngràng Chéngshùn Kāngmù Jìngcí Zhāng Huánghòu,
her imperial tomb was repaired,
but she was not enshrined in the ancestral temple.
Empress Xiàogōng of Xuānzōng, née Sūn,
was a native of Zōupíng.
In her youth, she possessed great beauty.
Her father, Zhōng,
was the registrar of Yǒngchéng County.
The mother of Empress Chéngxiào, the Lady of Péngchéng Bó,
was also from Yǒngchéng.
She often entered the inner court
and spoke of Zhōng having a virtuous daughter.
Thus, she was able to enter the palace.
When she was just over ten years old,
Chéngzǔ ordered Empress Chéngxiào to raise her.
Later, when Xuānzōng married,
an imperial edict selected née Hú of Jìníng as his consort,
and née Sūn was made a concubine.
When Xuānzōng ascended the throne,
she was enfeoffed as Guìfēi.
According to custom,
Empresses received a golden seal and a golden investiture scroll;
Guìfēi and below
received a scroll but no seal.
The concubine was favored.
In the fifth month of the first year of Xuāndé,
the Emperor requested from the Grand Empress
that a golden seal be made and bestowed upon her.
Guìfēi having a seal began from this point.
The concubine also had no son.
Secretly, she took the son of a palace woman as her own son,
who was Yīngzōng.
Because of this, her favor and affection grew even deeper.
Empress Hú submitted a memorial yielding her position,
requesting an early settlement of the national foundation.
The concubine feigned modesty, saying:
"When the Empress recovers from her illness, she will naturally have a son.
How dare my son precede the Empress's son?"
In the third month of the third year,
Empress Hú was deposed,
and she was then instated as Empress.
When Yīngzōng ascended the throne,
she was honored as Huáng Tàihòu.
When Yīngzōng was captured in the North,
the Grand Empress ordered the Prince of Chéng to supervise the state.
When Jǐngdì ascended the throne,
she was honored as Shàngshèng Huáng Tàihòu.
At that time, Yīngzōng was in Yǐběi,
and she frequently sent him warm clothing and furs.
Upon his return,
he was confined in the Southern Palace.
The Grand Empress frequently visited and comforted him.
Shí Hēng and others plotted to seize the gate,
and first secretly informed the Grand Empress.
She permitted it.
When Yīngzōng was restored to the throne,
she was granted the honorable title Shènglìe Císhòu Huáng Tàihòu.
The granting of honorable titles to empresses in the inner palace
began from this point in the Ming dynasty.
In the ninth month of the sixth year of Tiānshùn, she passed away.
She was respectfully granted the posthumous title Xiàogōng Yìxiàn Círén Zhuāngliè Qítiān Pèishèng Zhāng Huánghòu,
interred together in Jǐnglín,
and enshrined in the Grand Ancestral Temple.
As for Yīngzōng's birth mother,
no one ultimately knew who she was.
Grand Empress Wú,
the mother of Jǐngdì,
was a native of Dāntú.
When Xuānzōng was the Crown Prince,
she was selected to enter the palace.
In the third year of Xuāndé, she was enfeoffed as Xiánfēi.
When Jǐngdì ascended the throne,
she was honored as Huáng Tàihòu.
When Yīngzōng was restored to the throne,
she was again referred to as Xiānmiào Xiánfēi.
She passed away during the Chénghuà reign.
Concubine Guō,
given name Ài,
courtesy name Shànlǐ,
was from Fèngyáng.
She was virtuous and literate,
and died two tens of days after entering the palace.
Knowing her death was imminent,
she wrote a Chu-style lament to express her sorrow.
The lyrics said:
"Length of life has its number,
not worth comparing.
Life is like a dream,
death is awakening.
Returning before my parents,
I am ashamed of my failure in filial piety.
My heart is sorrowful and cannot stop,
this then is to be lamented."
In the eighth month of the first year of Zhèngtǒng, imperial concubine Húi Hē Shì, the imperial common mother, was posthumously granted the title Guìfēi,
with the posthumous name Duānjìng;
née Zhào as Xiánfēi,
with the posthumous name Chúnjìng;
née Wú as Huìfēi,
with the posthumous name Zhēnshùn;
née Jiāo as Shúfēi,
with the posthumous name Zhuāngjìng;
née Cáo as Jìngfēi,
with the posthumous name Zhuāngshùn;
née Xú as Shùnfēi,
with the posthumous name Zhēnhuì;
née Yuán as Lìfēi,
with the posthumous name Gōngdìng;
née Zhū as Shúfēi,
with the posthumous name Zhēnjìng;
née Lǐ as Chōngfēi,
with the posthumous name Gōngshùn;
née Hé as Chéngfēi,
with the posthumous name Sùxī.
The investiture text read:
"She dedicated her body and trod the path of righteousness,
following the imperial carriage to become an honored guest above.
It is fitting to recommend a glorious title,
to manifest her virtuous conduct."
These were concubines who died by immolation for Xuānzōng.
Initially,
when Tàizǔ passed away,
many palace women followed him to death.
During the Jiànwén and Yǒnglè reigns,
they were successively given generous condolences.
For example, the families of Zhāng Fèng, Lǐ Héng, Zhào Fú, Zhāng Bì, Wāng Bīn, and others,
all advanced from probationary centurions of the Jǐnyī Wèi and scattered cavalry guards with swords to centurions and chiliarchs,
holding hereditary stipends.
People called them
"Tàizǔ's Heavenly Maiden Households."
Throughout Chéngzǔ's reign, and the reigns of Rénzōng and Xuānzōng, immolation was also practiced.
Jǐngdì, as the Prince of Chéng, still followed this system when he died,
as it was customary for all princely households at that time.
It was not until Yīngzōng's last will
that it was finally abolished.
Empress Xiàozhuāng of Yīngzōng, née Qián,
was from Hǎizhōu.
In the seventh year of Zhèngtǒng, she was enthroned as Empress.
The Emperor pitied her family for being small and weak,
and wished to enfeoff them as marquises,
but the Empress consistently declined.
Therefore, her family alone received no enfeoffment.
When Yīngzōng was captured in the North,
she exhausted the wealth of her central palace to assist in welcoming back the imperial carriage.
At night, she cried sadly to Heaven,
and when tired, would lie on the ground,
damaging one of her legs.
Due to her weeping, she also damaged one eye.
When Yīngzōng was in the Southern Palace,
he was not content,
but the Empress tried her best to comfort and appease him.
The Empress had no son,
but Noble Consort Zhōu had a son,
who was established as Crown Prince.
When Yīngzōng was gravely ill,
he left a dying wish:
"When Empress Qián passes away after a thousand autumns and ten thousand years,
she shall be buried with me."
Grand Secretary Lǐ Xián withdrew and recorded it in a scroll.
When Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
he conferred honorable titles upon the two empresses,
and sought deliberation from his court officials.
Grand Eunuch Xià Shí, catering to the Noble Consort's wishes,
conveyed an imperial decree to exclusively honor the Noble Consort as Huáng Tàihòu.
Grand Secretaries Lǐ Xián and Péng Shí strongly argued against it,
so both empresses were honored together,
and the Empress was called Cíyì Huáng Tàihòu.
When the Yùlíng mausoleum was being constructed,
Xián and Shí requested the construction of three burial chambers,
and it was put to court deliberation.
Xià Shí again argued against it,
and the matter was ultimately dropped.
In the third month of the seventeenth year of Hóngzhì, she passed away.
She was posthumously honored with the title Xiàosù Zhēnshùn Kāngyì Guāngliè Fǔtiān Chéngshèng Ruì Huánghòu (孝肅貞順康懿光烈輔天承聖睿皇后),
and was interred together with Yùlíng.
By the deliberation of Grand Secretaries Liú Jiàn (劉健), Xiè Qiān (謝遷), and Lǐ Dōngyáng (李東陽),
she was enshrined separately in Fèngcí Diàn (奉慈殿),
not together with the ancestral temple,
and was still referred to as Tài Huáng Tàihòu.
In the fifteenth year of Jiājìng,
she, along with the two Tài Hoù, Jǐ (紀) and Shào (邵), were moved to be enshrined in the imperial tomb hall.
Their spirit tablets were inscribed "Huánghòu,"
without linking to the emperor's posthumous title,
to distinguish between empresses by birthright and concubines.

Thereafter, this system was followed for Mùzōng’s (穆宗) mother, Xiàokè (孝恪); Shénzōng’s (神宗) mother, Xiàodìng (孝定); Guāngzōng’s (光ōng) mother, Xiàojìng (孝靖); Xīzōng’s (熹宗) mother, Xiàohé (孝和); and Zhuāngliè Dì’s (莊烈帝) mother, Xiàochún (孝純).
Empress Wāng (汪氏), the deposed empress of Jǐngdì (景帝),
was from Shùntiān.
In the tenth year of Zhèngtǒng, she was enfeoffed as the Princess Consort of Chéng Wáng (郕王).
In the winter of the fourteenth year,
the Prince ascended the imperial throne,
and she was enfeoffed as empress.
The empress possessed virtue and wisdom.
She often thought of those who died in service in the capital and the elderly and weak victims whose bones lay exposed in the wilderness,
and ordered imperial guards to bury them.
She gave birth to two daughters,
but no sons.
In the third year of Jǐngtài,
Consort Háng (杭氏) gave birth to her son, Jiànjì (見濟).
Jǐngdì wished to establish him as crown prince,
and depose Xiànzōng.
The empress firmly opposed this.
Because of this, she displeased the emperor,
who then deposed her
and established Consort Háng as empress.
In the seventh year,
Empress Háng passed away,
and was posthumously named Sùxiào.
When Yīngzōng was restored to the throne,
he stripped her of her empress title,
destroyed her tomb,
and she was again referred to as the Princess Consort of Chéng Wáng.
When Jǐngdì passed away,
Yīngzōng intended to have his palace women, such as Concubine Táng (唐氏), immolated,
and discussed including the former empress.
Lǐ Xián (李賢) said,
"The consort has already been deposed and confined.
Moreover, her two daughters are young,
making her particularly pitiable."
The emperor then desisted.
When Xiànzōng was re-established as crown prince,
he well knew that the empress had not wished for his deposition,
and served her with great respect.
He then spoke to the emperor on her behalf,
and she was moved to an external princely mansion,
allowed to take all her possessions from the palace.
She got along very well with Empress Dowager Zhōu (周),
visiting the palace annually
like a family member.
However, she was stubborn by nature.
One day,
Yīngzōng asked the eunuch Liú Huán (劉桓),
"I recall a jade linglong tied to my waist.
Where is it now?"
Huán replied that it was likely with the consort.
Yīngzōng ordered it to be retrieved.
The empress threw it into a well,
and told the envoy,
"There is none."
Later, she told someone,
"Seven years as emperor—
can't he even forgo these few pieces of jade!"
Afterward,
there were rumors that the empress had carried out an enormous amount of valuables.
Yīngzōng sent an envoy to search and seize them,
and all were confiscated.
She passed away in the twelfth month of the first year of Zhèngdé.
The funeral and sacrificial rites were debated.
Grand Secretary Wáng Ào (王鏊) said,
"Bury her as a consort,
but sacrifice to her as an empress."
Thus, she was interred together at Jīnshān.
The following year, she was honored with the posthumous title Zhēnhuì Ānhé Jǐng Huánghòu (貞惠安和景皇后).
Empress Wú (吳氏), the deposed empress of Xiànzōng,
was from Shùntiān.
In the seventh month of the eighth year of Tiānshùn, she was established as empress.
Previously,
when Xiànzōng resided in the Eastern Palace,
Consort Wàn (萬貴妃) already monopolized his favor.
After the empress was established,
she found fault with Consort Wàn
and had her flogged.
The emperor was enraged,
and issued an edict stating:
"The late emperor sought a virtuous and gentle lady for me,
and had already settled on Lady Wáng (王氏), who was being nurtured in another palace awaiting her time.
The eunuch Niú Yù (牛玉) arbitrarily brought the previously rejected Lady Wú to the Empress Dowager for re-selection.
After the enfeoffment ceremony was completed,
I observed her conduct to be frivolous
and her manners crude.
Her virtue did not match her position.
Upon investigating the truth,
I discovered she was not the one originally intended.
Therefore, I had no choice
but to request the Empress Dowager's permission
to depose Lady Wú to a separate palace."
Her enthronement had barely lasted a month.
Her father, Jùn (俊),
who had previously been appointed Dūdū Tóngzhī (都督同知),
was now imprisoned and exiled to the border.
Niú Yù was demoted to cultivating vegetables at Xiàolíng.
Yù's nephew, Tàicháng Shǎoqīng Lún (太常少卿綸), and his sister's son, Lìbù Yuánwàiláng Yáng Cóng (吏部員外郎楊琮), were both dismissed from office.
His in-law, the Marquis of Huáiníng Sūn Táng (懷寧侯孫鏜), was retired.
Thereupon, Nanjing Censor Wáng Huī (王徽), Wáng Yuān (王淵), Zhū Kuān (朱寬), Lǐ Ào (李翺), Lǐ Jūn (李鈞), and others jointly memorialized, stating that Yù's crime was severe but his punishment light,
and simultaneously impeached Grand Secretary Lǐ Xián.
The emperor was angered,
and Huī and the others were all demoted to assistant magistrates in border prefectures.
Later, when Xiàozōng was born in the western palace,
the empress carefully nurtured and protected him.
When Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
remembering her kindness,
he ordered her attire and meals to be treated with the same courtesies as an empress mother,
and appointed her nephew to Jǐnyī Bǎihù (錦衣百戶).
She passed away in the fourth year of Zhèngdé.
Liú Jǐn (劉瑾) wished to cremate her.
Grand Secretary Wáng Ào firmly opposed this,
so she was interred with the rites of a consort.
Empress Xiàozhēn (孝貞皇后), Lady Wáng (王氏),
was from Shàngyuán.
When Xiànzōng was in the Eastern Palace,
Yīngzōng selected a consort for him,
choosing twelve women.
The empress, along with Lady Wú (吳氏) and Lady Bǎi (柏氏), were kept in the palace.
After Lady Wú was enthroned and then deposed,
Lady Wáng was enfeoffed as empress.
This was in the tenth month of the eighth year of Tiānshùn.
Consort Wàn's favor surpassed all in the imperial harem,
but the empress treated it with indifference.
When Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
he honored her as Huáng Tàihòu.
When Wǔzōng ascended the throne,
he honored her as Tài Huáng Tàihòu.
In the twelfth month of the fifth year of Zhèngdé, she was granted the honorable title Císhèng Kāngshòu (慈聖康壽).
She passed away in the second month of the thirteenth year,
and was granted the honorable posthumous title Xiàozhēn Zhuāngyì Gōngjìng Réncí Qīntiān Fǔshèng Chún Huánghòu (孝貞莊懿恭靖仁慈欽天輔聖純皇后),
interred together at Màolíng,
and enshrined in the imperial ancestral temple.
Empress Xiàomù (孝穆), Lady Jǐ (紀氏),
was the birth mother of Xiàozōng,
and was from Hè Xiàn.
She was originally the daughter of a barbarian chieftain.
During a pacification campaign in Chénghuà,
she was captured and brought into the imperial harem,
where she was appointed a female scribe.
She was intelligent and literate,
and was ordered to guard the imperial treasury.
At that time, Consort Wàn monopolized imperial favor and was jealous,
causing all pregnant women in the harem to suffer abortions.
Even Consort Bǎi Xián (柏賢妃), who gave birth to Crown Prince Dàogōng (悼恭太子),
was harmed by her.
The emperor happened to visit the imperial treasury,
and her responses were pleasing to his will.
Delighted,
he favored her,
and she became pregnant.
Consort Wàn learned of this and was extremely enraged,
ordering a maid to abort the pregnancy.
The maid falsely reported that she was suffering from abdominal distension.
So, she was demoted and resided in Ānlè Táng.
After a long time,
she gave birth to Xiàozōng.
The palace gate supervisor, Zhāng Mǐn (張敏), was ordered to drown him.
Mǐn was alarmed and said,
"The emperor has no son yet;
how can we abandon this one?"
He secretly fed the child with powdered sweets and honey,
hiding him in another room.
Consort Wàn watched daily but found nothing.
By the age of five or six,
his birth hair had not yet been cut.
At this time, the deposed Empress Wú resided in the western palace,
near Ānlè Táng.
She secretly knew of the matter
and came and went to nourish him,
though the emperor was unaware.
Initially,
the empress dowager Xīngguó, having entered as a consort from a princely household,
was still treated by the empress dowager according to old customs.
The emperor was quite displeased.
When the emperor held court,
the empress dowager treated him with further arrogance.
It happened that the empress dowager's younger brother, Yánlíng, was accused by someone.
The emperor condemned Yánlíng to death for plotting rebellion.
The empress dowager was in a desperate situation with no way out.
When crown prince Āichōng was born,
she requested to come in and offer congratulations,
but the emperor declined to see her.
She sent people to plead,
but it was not granted.
Grand Secretary Zhāng Fúqìng also pleaded for Yánlíng,
to which the emperor hand-wrote a decree saying:
"The empire
is that of Gāo Huángdì.
Xiàozōng Huángdì upheld Gāo Huángdì's laws.
You worry about hurting your imperial aunt's feelings,
but do you not worry about hurting the feelings of the two imperial ancestors, Gāo and Xiào?"
Fúqìng again memorialized, saying:
"When Your Majesty ascended the throne,
following my words,
you referred to your imperial aunt as Huáng Tàihòu.
The court officials blamed Your Majesty for this,
and it has not ceased even now.
Now, all officials, great and small, are silent, not saying a single word,
truly hoping that the empress dowager will not die a natural death,
to heap more blame upon Your Majesty.
As for the crime of plotting rebellion,
when the verdict is rendered, it entails the extermination of the entire clan.
Is Zhāoshèng not also of the Zhāng clan?
How will Your Majesty handle this?"
In the winter month, when reviewing prisoners,
the emperor again wanted to kill Yánlíng,
but again stopped because of Fúqìng's words.
Not long after,
a treacherous person named Liú Dōngshān reported an incident,
and Hèlǐng was also arrested and imprisoned in the imperial dungeon.
The empress dowager even wore tattered clothes and sat on straw to plead,
but was also not heard.
After a long time,
Hèlǐng died of hardship in prison.
When the empress dowager died,
the emperor finally killed Yánlíng.
The details are found in the biographies of imperial relatives.
Empress Xià, Xiàojìng of Wǔzōng, was from
Shàngyuán.
In the first year of Zhèngdé, she was made empress.
In the first year of Jiājìng, she was honored with the title Zhuāngsù Huánghòu.
She died in the first month of the fourteenth year,
and was interred with Wǔzōng in Kānglíng,
and her spirit tablet was enshrined in the ancestral temple.
Initially,
the ritual officials presented the funeral ceremonies.
The emperor said:
"There is no mourning attire for a brother-in-law and sister-in-law,
and with two empress dowagers above,
I will wear plain blue,
and officials and common people shall wear mourning attire as for an empress mother."
Minister of Rites Xià Yán said:
"If Your Majesty observes no mourning for a sister-in-law,
then officials will not dare to appear before Your Majesty in plain attire.
I request a temporary suspension of court attendance."
This was permitted.
Later, when discussing the posthumous title,
Grand Secretary Zhāng Fúqìng said:
"The late empress,
being the emperor's sister-in-law,
is different from the principal empresses of previous dynasties.
It is appropriate to use two or four characters."
Lǐ Shí said:
"Eight characters should be used."
Censor-in-chief Wáng Tíngxiāng and Vice Minister of Personnel Huò Tāo, among others, said:
"They are all imperial empresses,
what is the difference?"
Yán gathered the opinions of the assembly,
and then memorialized, saying:
"Ancient people valued simplicity,
and the posthumous titling method was brief,
describing their conduct.
Later generations added characters;
this is the sentiment of subjects.
Born in this era,
it is appropriate to follow current regulations.
The late empress should receive a posthumous title like the principal empresses of previous sagely emperors.
Using two, four, or eight characters
has no basis in ritual."
The emperor did not comply and
ordered a re-discussion.
The officials requested to follow Fúqìng's words.
The emperor said:
"Use six,
in accordance with the yin number."
Thus, she was posthumously titled Xiàojìng Zhuānghuì Ānsù Yì Huánghòu.
In the fifteenth year,
the emperor felt Fúqìng's words were incorrect,
and decreed:
"The posthumous title of Empress Xiàojìng is incomplete
and does not befit her as Wǔzōng's consort."
So, it was changed to Xiàojìng Zhuānghuì Ānsù Wēnchéng Shùntiān Xiéshèng Yì Huánghòu.
Empress Chén, Xiàojié of Shìzōng, was from
Yuánchéng.
In the first year of Jiājìng, she was made empress.
The emperor was by nature strict and severe.
One day,
while sitting with the empress,
consorts Zhāng and Fāng presented tea.
The emperor looked closely at their hands.
The empress was resentful,
threw her cup, and rose.
The emperor became furious.
The empress was startled and frightened,
miscarried, and died.
This was in the tenth month of the seventh year.
The funeral rites were reduced.
The emperor wore plain attire and resided in the Xījiǎomén for ten days,
then immediately wore a black crown and black robes and resided in Fèngtiānmén.
She was posthumously titled Dàolíng,
and buried in the Áo'ér Yù.
On the day of the burial,
the coffin exited the Wángmén,
and all officials attended the mourning only for one day.
Censor Wáng Rǔméi remonstrated.
He was not heard.
In the fifteenth year,
Minister of Rites Xià Yán proposed and requested a change of posthumous title.
By this time, the emperor's anger had long subsided,
so she was renamed Xiàojié.
When Mùzōng ascended the throne,
the ritual officials deliberated:
"Empress Xiàojié,
being the principal consort of the late emperor,
should be interred with him and enshrined in the ancestral temple.
If the empress Xiàoliè is enshrined according to the late emperor's will,
then the principal consort would be abandoned.
If both are enshrined together,
then there would be two empresses.
When the late emperor is enshrined,
Empress Xiàojié should be offered as consort,
and her burial moved to Yǒnglíng.
Empress Xiàoliè's spirit tablet should be worshipped separately."
The report was approved.
In the second month of the first year of Lóngqìng, she was honored with the full posthumous title Xiàojié Gōngyì Círuì Ānzhuāng Xiàngtiān Yìshèng Sù Huánghòu.
The deposed empress Zhāng,
Shìzōng's second empress.
Initially, she was enfeoffed as Shùn Fēi.
In the seventh year,
after Empress Chén died,
she was then established as empress.
At this time,
the emperor was pursuing ancient
rites, ordering the empress to lead the consorts in personally tending silkworms in the northern suburbs,
and also to daily lead the six palaces in listening to lectures on the teachings for imperial women in the palace.
In the first month of the thirteenth year, she was deposed and resided in a separate palace.
In the fifteenth year, she died,
and her funeral rites were observed according to those of the deposed empress Hú of Xuānzōng.
In the 17th year of Jiājìng,
Mù● passed away.
His son Qínxī had died earlier,
so his grandson, Zhuāng Wáng Zhāo Gāng, succeeded him.
He passed away in the 30th year.
His son, Jìng Wáng Zài Tǐng, succeeded him.
He passed away in the 10th year of Wànlì.
His son, Duān Wáng Sù Zhēn, succeeded him.
He passed away.
His son, Gōng Xiāo, succeeded him.
In the winter of the 14th year of Chóngzhēn,
Lǐ Zìchéng attacked Kāifēng.
Gōng Xiāo disbursed 500,000 in treasury gold
to reward those defending the battlements.
He set up a bounty system,
offering 50 gold for each bandit killed.
When the bandits dug tunnels under the city,
the defenders threw fire at them.
The bandits were burned to death,
countless of them,
so they lifted the siege and left.
In the first month of the following year,
the emperor issued an edict of commendation,
and also added a message of comfort, saying:
“This is the divine spirit of Gāo Huángdì pitying his imperial clan descendants, whose fortified cities were not secure,
opening the king’s heart and bestowing blessings upon him.”
In the fourth month of that same year,
Zìchéng again besieged Biàn,
building a long surrounding wall,
cutting off the city’s access to firewood and foraging.
In the ninth month,
the bandits breached the river to flood the city,
and the city walls collapsed.
Gōng Xiāo ascended the city tower from the rear mountain,
leading his palace consorts and the princes of Níngxiāng, Ānxiāng, Yǒngshòu, and Rénhé to shelter in the rain for several days.
Reinforcement troops were stationed north of the river,
and they came by boat to receive them,
whereupon they finally escaped.
When the matter was reported,
an imperial letter was bestowed to express sympathy and comfort,
along with treasury gold and fine silks,
ordering them to reside temporarily in Zhāngdé.
When Biàn City fell,
hundreds of thousands died,
and all the imperial clan members perished.
The treasures and artifacts stored in the palace were all submerged in the great flood.
A year later,
the golden images of Gāo Dì and Gāo Hòu, which they revered, were recovered from the water,
and brought to Zhāngdé for worship.
After a long time,
the king passed away,
but the posthumous title and commendation had not yet been issued
when the dynasty fell.
His grandson fled south,
and died in Guǎngzhōu.
Zhènpíng Wáng Yǒu Kuàng
was the eighth son of Dìng Wáng.
He was fond of learning,
and skilled in poetry.
He wrote a tens of thousands of words on the “Dàotǒng Lùn” (Treatise on the Orthodox Transmission of the Way).
He also collected records of worthy members of imperial clans throughout history,
from the Five Sons of Xià to Yuán Tàizǐ Zhēnjīn, over a hundred individuals,
and compiled several volumes of “Xián Wáng Chuán” (Biographies of Worthy Princes).
Bópíng Wáng Ān●
was the thirteenth son of Huì Wáng.
Huì Wáng had twenty-five sons,
but Ān● alone was virtuous.
He once compiled books such as “Yí Hòu Lù” (Records for Posterity) and “Yǎng Zhèng Lù” (Records for Nurturing Rectitude).
He was diligent in managing his livelihood;
his fields, gardens, servants, chariots, and horses were all well-equipped.
When guests visited his gate,
he would generously host them.
At that time, anyone mentioned for his moral character
would certainly be referred to as Bópíng.
Nánlíng Wáng Mù Yǎng
was the ninth son of Dào Wáng.
He was intelligent, perceptive, and knowledgeable.
In the 41st year of Jiājìng,
Censor Lín Rùn stated:
“Of the empire’s revenue,
four million *shí* of rice are supplied to the capital annually,
while the annual stipends for various princely establishments amount to 8,530,000 *shí* of rice.
Shānxī and Hénán retain 2,363,000 *shí* of rice,
while the imperial clan’s stipends total 5,040,000 *shí* of rice.
Even without disasters or remissions,
the annual revenue is insufficient to provide even half of the stipends.
Year after year,
the number of imperial clan members increases,
leading to financial exhaustion and extreme hardship.
How will it be sustained?”
The matter was sent down to the various princes for discussion.
The following year,
Mù Yǎng submitted seven proposals: requesting the establishment of clan schools to promote morality and education;
setting up examinations for talent selection to encourage worthy individuals;
strict verification to prevent fraudulent claims;
abolishing superfluous positions to eliminate idlers;
prohibiting eager competition for office to curb greed;
regulating ancestral worship to expand filial piety;
and establishing mourning regulations to save on stipends.
An edict ordered the court officials to deliberate and adopt them.
Thereafter, various princely establishments gradually presented their views on advantages and disadvantages,
which Minister Lǐ Chūnfāng compiled and submitted.
When the “Zōng Fān Tiáolì” (Regulations for Imperial Clan and Princely Establishments) were promulgated,
many of Mù Yǎng’s proposals were adopted, it is said.
Zhènguó Zhōngwèi Mù●,
courtesy name Guànfǔ,
was a grandson of Zhènpíng Wáng.
His father, Fèngguó Jiāngjūn Ānhé, was known to the court for his filial piety,
and received imperial commendation and rewards.
After his death,
Zhōu Wáng and hundreds of other imperial clan members requested the construction of a shrine.
An edict bestowed the shrine name as
“Chóngxiào” (Exalting Filial Piety).
Mù● was intelligent and perceptive from a young age.
Lǐ Mèngyáng, a local of the commandery, considered him exceptional.
As he grew up,
he adopted a scholarly and simple lifestyle,
devoting his intellect to classical studies,
associating with erudite scholars from the Hénán and Luòyáng regions.
By twenty, he had mastered the Five Classics,
and was particularly profound in the “Yì” (Book of Changes) and “Chūnqiū” (Spring and Autumn Annals).
He believed that the classical studies of the current dynasty entirely followed the Sòng Confucian tradition,
and that ancient scholars’ commentaries on the Classics were incomplete and lost.
Thus, he sought out knowledgeable scholars throughout the realm,
and meticulously copied and collected their works.
Works like Lǐ Dǐngzuò’s “Yì Jiě” and Zhāng Qià’s “Chūnqiū Zhuàn”
were all transmitted by him.
Lǚ Nán once discussed the “Yì” with him,
and left in admiration.
He further sought to acquire ancient books and maps,
obtaining tens of thousands of volumes from the Gě family of Jiāngdū and the Lǐ family of Zhāngqiū.
His textual criticisms were clear and distinct,
and commentators compared him to Liú Xiàng of the Hàn dynasty.
He built a residence in Dōngpō,
invited scholars,
was broad-minded and fond of gentlemen,
and maintained a pure personal conduct.
He attended to his parents morning and evening, never leaving their side.
For three years of mourning, he resided in an outer dwelling.
He had five younger brothers,
whom he personally instructed and supervised,
and to whom he relinquished all his inheritance.
In the fifth year of Wànlì, he was nominated for his outstanding literary and moral conduct,
serving as the Zōngzhèng for the Zhōu princely establishment,
and head of the clan school.
He arranged for clan students to lecture on the “Yì,” “Shī” (Book of Poetry), and “Shū” (Book of Documents) before noon on the 3rd, 6th, and 9th days [of each lunar month],
and on “Chūnqiū” and “Lǐjì” (Book of Rites) in the afternoon,
never ceasing even in extreme cold or heat.
His compiled works include “Wǔjīng Jīyí” in six *juàn*,
“Shòujīng Túchuán” in four *juàn*,

“Yùnpǔ” in five *juàn*, and he also authored “Míng Dì Shìbiǎo” (Genealogical Table of Ming Emperors), “Zhōuguó Shìxìbiǎo” (Genealogical Table of the Zhōu Princedom), “Jiànwén Xùnguó Bāozhōnglù” (Record of Commendations for Loyalty in the Abdication of Jiànwén), “Hénán Tōngzhì” (Comprehensive Gazetteer of Hénán), “Kāifēng Jùnzhì” (Gazetteer of Kāifēng Commandery), and other books.
Circuit Censor Chǔ Fū proposed a slight reduction in the annual stipends of princes below the rank of *jùnwáng*,
to be distributed equally among poor clan members.
The emperor dispatched Supervising Secretary Wàn Xiàngchūn to discuss this with Zhōu Wáng.
Xīnhuì Wáng Mù Mì declared among the crowd:
“The plan to reduce stipends originated with Mù●.”
He gathered over a thousand imperial clan members to attack him,
tearing his robes and cap,
and submitted a memorial defying the edict.
The emperor was enraged,
and demoted Mù Mì to commoner status.
Mù● repeatedly submitted memorials citing illness and requesting retirement,
but the emperor’s edict encouraged him to continue his service.
He died three years later,
at the age of seventy.
Five hundred members of the imperial clan praised his virtues,
and an edict bestowed upon him the title of Fǔguó Jiāngjūn,
and granted him a ceremonial burial,
an exceptional honor.
Scholars referred to him as Xītíng Xiānshēng.
At that time, there was a general named Ān●,
who lost his mother within a year,
and was known for his filial piety towards his father.
When his father was critically ill,
he cut his arm to make broth for his father,
and his father recovered well.
At seventy,
recalling that he had not been able to care for his mother,
he wore mourning clothes and resided by her tomb for three years,
and an edict commended his household.
He was inherently skilled in the principles of names and logic,
and his reputation was widely known.
People referred to Mù● as
“Dàshān” (Great Mountain),
and Ān● as
“Xiǎoshān” (Small Mountain).
Another diligent official was
Zhèn Guó Zhōngwèi.
During the Jiājìng reign,
he submitted a memorial, saying:
“Your Majesty possesses the資 of a supreme sage,
yet you do not emulate the ancient emperors who diligently managed myriad affairs.
Instead of choosing policies and appointing capable people,
you indulge in the pursuit of immortality,
repeatedly holding fasts and rituals,
and frequently undertaking construction projects.
For several years, court rituals have been neglected,
and responsibilities have been entrusted to unsuitable individuals.
Consequently, bribery is openly practiced,
punishments are inverted,
and intense competition has become the norm.
Both public and private resources are exhausted.
Should an unexpected calamity occur,
your servant does not know what the outcome will be.”
The emperor was enraged upon reading the memorial.
He charged him with defamation,
demoted him to a commoner,
and imprisoned him in Fèngyáng.
His son, Cháo (●), had already been granted a name.
As the son of a criminal, no one dared to petition for his ennoblement.
He submitted a memorial pleading for his father's release
and also presented four suggestions for a mid-reign revival.
An imperial edict ordered that he too be imprisoned.
Upon Mùzōng's ascension,
he was released and allowed to return home.
The authorities were ordered to provide for him.
Zhū Zhēn, Prince Zhāo of Chǔ,
was Tàizǔ's sixth son.
When he was first born,
news of the pacification of Wǔchāng arrived.
Tàizǔ, delighted, said:
“When this son grows up,
I will enfeoff him as Prince of Chǔ.”
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, he was enfeoffed as Prince of Chǔ.
In the fourteenth year, he took up his fief in Wǔchāng.
He often kept the Imperial Commentary on the Great Plan and the Great Treasure Admonition by his side.
In the eighteenth year, fourth month,
the various Man tribes of Tónggǔ and Sīzhōu rebelled.
Zhēn was ordered to lead an army with Duke Xìnguó Tāng Hé and Marquis Jiāngxià Zhōu Déxīng to suppress them.
Hé and others divided their forces to garrison the various caves,
erecting fences and farming alongside the Man people.
After a long time,
their leaders were captured,
and the remaining rebels scattered.
In the thirtieth year,
the Man of Gǔzhōu rebelled.
The Emperor ordered Zhēn to lead an army,
with Prince Xiāng Bǎi as his deputy,
to conquer them.
Zhēn requested 300,000 in provisions
but did not personally oversee the army.
The Emperor interrogated and reprimanded him,
ordering him to build a fort at Tónggǔ Guard and return.
That year,
Yínghuò (Mars) entered Tàiwēi.
An edict instructed Zhēn to be cautious.
Zhēn wrote down ten points to admonish himself.
Not long after,
Zhēn's son, the Prince of Bālíng, died.
The Emperor again sent him an imperial letter, saying:
“Last year, Yínghuò entered Tàiwēi.
Tàiwēi is the Celestial Court,
located in Yì and Zhěn constellations,
which correspond to the region of Chǔ.
If the five planets enter without cause,
the disaster will be severe.
Your son's untimely death
makes me fear that the calamity will not stop here.
You should still be mindful and cautious to reverse Heaven's will.”
By winter,
the Prince's consort had died.
At that time, the Zōngrén Fǔ was newly established,
and Zhēn was appointed Right Zōngrén.
In the early Yǒnglè period,
he was promoted to Zōngzhèng.
He died in the twenty-second year.
His son, Prince Zhuāng Zhū Mèngwán, succeeded him.
He was respectful, cautious, and fond of learning.
During the Xuāndé reign,
Earl Píngjiāng Chén Xuān secretly memorialized:
“Húguǎng is a great frontier region in the southeast,
embracing Hú and Xiāng,
and controlling the Man and Yuè peoples.
The population is prosperous,
and merchants gather there.
Chǔ has three guards.
From the time of its initial enfeoffment until now,
the population has grown daily,
and the military is strong and the state is wealthy.
If petty individuals act recklessly,
they may harbor evil intentions.
I request that their elite troops be selected,
under the pretext of transporting grain,
and after they arrive in the capital,
they should be retained there.
This would prevent future troubles.”
The Emperor said:
“Chǔ has committed no wrongdoing;
this is unacceptable.”
Mèngwán was fearful upon hearing this.
In the fifth year, he submitted a memorial requesting to relinquish two guards,
keeping only one for himself.
The Emperor praised him and granted his request.
He died in the fourth year of Zhèngtǒng.
His son, Prince Xiàn Zhū Jì’nì, succeeded him.
He was extremely filial towards his mother, Consort Dèng.
Yīngzōng sent a letter commending and admonishing him.
He authored the Dōngpíng Héjiān Tú Zàn,
which was recited by the literati.
He died in the eighth year.
His younger brother, Prince Kāng Zhū Jìchū, succeeded him.
He died in the sixth year of Tiānshùn.
His second cousin, Prince Jìng Zhū Jūnyī, succeeded him.
He died in the fifth year of Zhèngdé.
His son, Prince Duān Zhū Róng (●), succeeded him.
He was renowned for his benevolence and filial piety.
Wǔzōng inscribed a tablet for him, saying,
“Memorial Archway of Illustrious Filial Piety.”
He died in the thirteenth year of Jiājìng.
His son, Prince Mǐn Zhū Xiǎnrǒng, succeeded him.
He was deeply grieved during the mourning period
and refused congratulations on festive occasions.
Prince Duān's son-in-law, the Yi Bīn Shěn Bǎo, had a grudge against Xiǎnrǒng.
He sent someone to falsely accuse Xiǎnrǒng's attendants of shouting "Long live Xiǎnrǒng!"
and also enticed Xiǎnrǒng to stage a water play to practice naval tactics.
Shìzōng sent down the memorial,
and the local officials fully reported that Xiǎnrǒng observed mourning rituals properly.
Bǎo was charged with false accusation
and stripped of his status as a commoner.
Xiǎnrǒng's consort, née Wú,
gave birth to the heir apparent Yīngyào.
He was lustful and wicked,
and once committed adultery with Xiǎnrǒng's palace woman.
Xiǎnrǒng, knowing this,
beat to death Táo Yuán’ér, the servant whom Yīngyào had used.
Yīngyào then ordered the soldier Liú Jīn to bring the courtesan Sòng Me’ér to a separate residence.
Xiǎnrǒng intended to punish Jīn,
who then enticed Yīngyào to plot rebellion.
On the eighteenth day of the first month of the twenty-fourth year of Jiājìng,
lanterns were lit and wine was served to entertain Xiǎnrǒng.
Xiǎnrǒng's younger brother, Prince Wǔgāng Zhū Xiǎnhuái, was separately entertained in the west chamber.
Midway through the feast,
Jīn and others emerged from behind the seats
and struck Xiǎnrǒng on the head with a bronze mace,
killing him instantly.
Xiǎnhuái was startled and tried to rescue him,
but was wounded and fled.
Yīngyào moved Xiǎnrǒng's corpse into the palace
and ordered the Chief Administrator Sūn Lì to report that he died of a stroke.
A royal attendant, Zhū Guì, forced his way out and reported the change,
which the patrolling and investigating officials reported to the throne.
Yīngyào, frightened,
submitted a detailed memorial to defend himself
and forced Prince Chóngyáng Zhū Xiǎnxīu to vouch for him.
Prince Tōngshān Zhū Yīngchuī did not comply,
but directly reported Yīngyào's regicide.
An imperial edict ordered eunuchs, the駙馬都尉 Wū Jǐnghé, and Vice Minister Yù Máojiān to investigate.
Yīngyào confessed.
An edict ordered his arrest and transfer to the capital.
In the ninth month of that year,
after informing the Tàimiào,
he was executed,
his corpse was burned, and his ashes scattered.
All his confederates were executed.
Xiǎnxīu's stipend was reduced by three-tenths.
Xiǎnhuái and Yīngchuī were both awarded gold and silk.
Xiǎnrǒng's second son, Prince Gōng Zhū Yīng (●), succeeded him.
He died in the fifth year of Lóngqìng.
His son, Zhū Huákuí, was young.
In the eighth year of Wànlì,
he finally succeeded to the peerage.
The guard official Wáng Shǒurén reported:
“The distant ancestor, Dìngyuǎn Hóu Bì,
was the father of Prince Chǔ Zhēn's consort.
He left hundreds of thousands in precious treasures in the Chǔ royal treasury,
which were embezzled by the succeeding prince.”
An imperial edict ordered eunuchs to investigate and verify.
Huákuí submitted a memorial in defense
and requested to vacate the palace for a search.
Neither request was answered.
After a long time,
the palace attendants and others were interrogated,
but nothing was found.
At that time, the eunuchs were eager to please the emperor by confiscating wealth,
so they did not want to expose Wáng Shǒurén's crime.
The emperor, realizing this somewhat,
dismissed the matter.
Huákuí then memorialized
to donate 20,000 gold pieces to aid in the construction of the Three Great Halls.
Sù Zhuāng Wáng Yǎng,
was Tàizǔ's fourteenth son.
In Hongwǔ eleven years (1378), he was enfeoffed as Hán Wáng.
In twenty-four years (1391), he was ordered to join the five princes, Wèi, Gǔ, Qìng, Níng, and Mín, in training troops at Línqīng.
The next year (1392), he was re-enfeoffed as Sù.
The year after that (1393),
an imperial edict commanded him to proceed to his domain.
As the troops from various garrisons in Shǎnxī had not yet assembled,
he was ordered to station at Píngliáng.
In twenty-eight years (1395), he finally took up his post in Gānzhōu.
An imperial edict commanded the prince to administer the military affairs of the five garrisons in Gānzhōu under the Shǎnxī Provincial Military Commission.
In thirty years (1397), he was ordered to supervise military cultivation for grain;
when a campaign was launched, he was to follow Chángxīng Hóu Gěng Bǐngwén.
In Jiànwén one year (1399), he requested to move inland,
and subsequently relocated to Lánzhōu.
In Yǒnglè six years (1408),
because he beat three palace guards to death and accepted horses offered by Hāmì,
his chief secretaries and officials were arrested.
Later,
he again listened to the words of the company commander Liú Chéng,
and punished the troops of the Píngliáng Guard.
An imperial edict ordered Chéng and others to be manacled and sent to the capital.
In seventeen years (1419), he passed away.
His son, Kāng Wáng Zhānyàn, succeeded him.
In Xuāndé seven years (1432), he submitted a palace guard.
His residence was robbed,
so he posted a reward to recruit informants to apprehend the culprits.
An censor reported that this was not in accordance with regulations,
and punished his chief secretary Yáng Wēi.
Zhānyàn also requested an increase in his annual stipend.
The imperial edict stated:
"During the Hóngwǔ and Yǒnglè reigns,
the annual stipend was no more than five hundred *shí*.
The reason Zhuāng Wáng did not mention it
was because the court considered the difficulty of transporting goods to distant regions.
When Rénkǎo ascended the throne,
an additional five hundred *shí* was granted.
I adhere to the ancestral system and dare not deviate."
In Zhèngtǒng one year (1436), he reported:
"The old residence in Gānzhōu has been converted into a Provincial Military Commission office,
but the former prince's tomb and garden still exist.
I request a ban on firewood collection and foraging near the residence."
This was granted.
In Tiānshùn three years (1459), he presented five hundred horses for border defense,
but refused payment.
The emperor insisted on paying him.
In eight years (1464), he passed away.
His son, Jiǎn Wáng Lùpí, succeeded him.
In Chénghuà fifteen years (1479), he passed away.
His son, Gōng Wáng Gòngcǐ, succeeded him.
In Jiājìng fifteen years (1536), he passed away.
His heir apparent Zhēnyū and eldest grandson Bìhuán both died young.
His second grandson, Dìng Wáng Bìkuàng, succeeded him.
In forty-one years (1562), he passed away.
His son Jìnjiǒng had died earlier.
His grandson, Huái Wáng Shēndǔ, succeeded him.
He passed away two years later.
Having no son,
Jìng Wáng's fourth son, Bìshìzi Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Jìndù (Gěng),
was deemed suitable to succeed because of his close relation.
The ceremonial officials argued that
Jìndù,
being the paternal cousin of Huái Wáng,
should not succeed.
An imperial edict ordered him to manage the affairs of the princely establishment in his current capacity,
while the imperial seal and patent were withheld,
and all official retainers were dismissed.
When Mùzōng ascended the throne,
Dìng Wángfēi Wú Shì and Yáncháng Wáng Zhēnqǐ and others successively memorialized:
"Shèngzǔ cut down the powerful chieftains
and brought peace to the realm.
The ordinances for rewarding meritorious service are to be exalted, not diminished.
My ancestor, Zhuāng Wáng, was enfeoffed in a border region,
trained and deployed troops,
and protected the imperial family.
Unfortunately, the main lineage was cut off,
yet the succession was restricted by the order of paternal seniority,
rather than by the principle of inheriting the achievements of meritorious military service.
This is not how to honor the imperial clan branches
and strengthen the imperial bulwarks."
This was sent to the ministries for deliberation.
They deliberated that a commander of a commandery should administer the princely government.
The emperor did not permit it.
In Lóngqìng five years (1571),
Jìndù was specially ordered to succeed as Sù Wáng,
and half the usual number of officials were appointed to his establishment.
In Wànlì sixteen years (1588), he passed away,
posthumously named Yì.
His son, Xiàn Wáng Shēnyáo, succeeded him.
In forty-six years (1618), he passed away.
His son Shíhóng succeeded him.
In the winter of Chóngzhēn sixteen years (1643),
Lǐ Zìchéng captured Lánzhōu,
and he was seized.
All his clan members perished.
Liáo Jiǎn Wáng Zhí,
was Tàizǔ's fifteenth son.
In Hóngwǔ eleven years (1378), he was enfeoffed as Wèi Wáng.
In twenty-five years (1392), he was re-enfeoffed as Liáo.
The next year (1393), he took up his post in Guǎngníng.
As his palace was not yet completed,
he temporarily stationed north of the Dàlíng River,
erecting fences to form a camp.
The emperor ordered Wǔdìng Hóu Guō Yīng to build the city walls and palace for him.
Yīng,
was the prince's father-in-law,
and supervised the construction with great urgency.
It happened that Gāolí had stockpiled grain from its country to the Yālù River.
The emperor, fearing they had a hidden agenda,
and also considering the hardships of the conscripted soldiers,
ordered the work to cease.
Not until thirty years (1397),
did he finally order Grand Coordinator Yáng Wén to supervise the repair and construction by the troops of the various garrisons in Liáodōng,
increasing their battlements
to strengthen the border defense.
He also had maps drawn of the strategic points along the northwestern border,
showing them to Zhí and Níng Wáng Quán,
instructing them:
"From Dōngshèng westward to Níngxià, Héxī, Cháhǎnnǎo'ér,
and from Dōngshèng eastward to Dàtóng, Xuānfǔ, Kāipíng,
and further southeast to Dàníng,
and further east to Liáodōng,
reaching the Yālù River,
and north to the Great Desert,
and also from outside Yànmén Pass,
westward to the Yellow River,
crossing the river to Cháhǎnnǎo'ér,
and further east to Zǐjīng Pass,
and further east to Jūyōng Pass and Gǔběi Pass,
and further east to Shānhǎi Guard,
in all areas where soldiers and civilians cultivate land,
do not allow livestock to graze freely.
As for the barren lands and mountain areas,
allow the princes and imperial sons-in-law to pasture their animals and collect firewood,
moving east and west to set up camps,
and thereby train troops and prevent banditry in a timely manner.
Violators will be punished."
Zhí was on the border,
accustomed to military life,
and repeatedly achieved military merits.
During the Jiànwén reign,
when the "Jìngnán"
campaign began,
Zhí and Níng Wáng Quán were summoned back to the capital.
Zhí crossed the sea to return to court,
and was re-enfeoffed in Jīngzhōu.
In Yǒnglè one year (1403), he came to court.
The emperor, considering that Zhí had initially been disloyal to him,
resented him.
In ten years (1412), his palace guards were abolished,
leaving three hundred military clerks and kitchen staff
for service.
In twenty-two years (1424), he passed away.
His son, Chángyáng Wáng Guìyǎn, succeeded him.
Initially,
Zhí's illegitimate sons, Yuǎn'ān Wáng Guìxiè and Bādōng Wáng Guìxuān, had once accused their father of having ulterior motives.
After their father's death,
they also did not attend the funeral.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
both were stripped of their princely titles and demoted to commoners.
In Zhèngtǒng one year (1436), the officials of the princely establishment requested an increase in the prince's stipend.
The imperial edict stated:
"Jiǎn Wáng offended the court,
yet Chéngzǔ treated him with special generosity.
During Rénzōng's reign, his stipend was increased,
allowing him to receive two thousand *shí*.
Xuānzōng also granted three hundred banner troops.
The care for kinsmen has already been considerable.
The prince has always been ill-mannered,
and the officials of the establishment do not correct him,
but instead ask for favors for the prince!"
It was not granted.
In three years (1438),
the巡撫 (Patrolling Grandee) and junior vice-minister Wú Zhèng memorialized that the prince was not friendly to his younger brothers,
treated his stepmother with little kindness,
beat his chief secretary Dù Shù to death,
and committed many transgressions in his domain.
He was summoned to the capital for interrogation,
where all his illicit, immoral,
violent, and unlawful deeds were uncovered.
In the fourth month of the next year (1439), he was stripped of his princely title and demoted to commoner,
to guard Jiǎn Wáng's garden.
His younger brother, Sù Wáng Guìqǔ, succeeded him.
In Chénghuà seven years (1471), he passed away.
His son, Jìng Wáng Háocchéng, succeeded him.
In fourteen years (1478), he passed away.
His son, Huì Wáng Ēnhuá, succeeded him.
In the fifth year of Hóngzhì
Zhū Zōngrén Ēn and others from the Prince of Sōngzī's mansion intruded into Jīngzhōu Prefecture to receive their annual stipends.
Ēnkuàng forbade this,
and they all resented him.
Later,
Yí bīn Yuán Yōng further incited Ēnkuàng and others to gather small-time thugs
and seize profits from soldiers, civilians, merchants, and peddlers.
Ēnkuàng exposed their deeds,
which increased Ēn and the others' resentment,
and they plotted to kill the Prince.
The imperial court dispatched officials to investigate the facts,
imprisoning Ēn and the others in Fèngyáng
and banishing their confederates with varying sentences.
Ēnkuàng secretly ordered the escorts to shackle them,
resulting in the deaths of over eighty people.
A few days later,
the heir apparent died suddenly.
In the eighth year
Ēnkuàng died of a carbuncle on his back.
His son, Prince Gōng Chǒnglún, succeeded him.
He was very fond of his younger brother, Prince Guāngzé Chǒngyǒu,
and they always ate, drank, and dressed together.
Chǒnglún possessed excellent virtues,
and Chǒngyǒu would always consult him before acting on any matter.
Chǒnglún died in the sixteenth year of Zhèngdé
His son, Prince Zhuāng Zhìgé, succeeded him,
but was ill and did not attend to affairs.
His consort, Lady Máo, was learned in history,
calm, resolute, and decisive.
Both inside and outside the court, she was held in awe,
and her reputation for wisdom was known throughout the land.
In the sixteenth year of Jiājìng
Zhìgé died.
His son, Prince Xiànchún, succeeded him.
Because of his devotion to Daoism, he was favored by Shìzōng,
who bestowed upon him the title "Qīngwēi Zhōngjiào Zhēnrén" [Pure Subtlety, Loyal Teacher, Perfected Person]
and gave him a golden seal.
In the first year of Lóngqìng
Censor Chén Shěng impeached Xiànchún for various unlawful acts.
An imperial edict stripped him of the title of Zhēnrén and the seal.
The following year,
Investigating Censor Gào Guāngxiān again impeached him for thirteen major crimes.
Hóng Cháoxuǎn, a Vice Minister of the Ministry of Justice, was ordered to investigate,
and fully uncovered his licentious, tyrannical, and usurping crimes.
The Emperor believed Xiànchún deserved execution,
