but out of consideration for him being a member of the imperial clan, spared his life.
He was deposed as a commoner
and confined behind a high wall.
Initially,
Assistant Surveillance Commissioner Shī Dǔchén harbored a deep grudge against Xiànchún.
When Cháoxuǎn arrived in Húguǎng,
Dǔchén forged a letter from Xiànchún and presented it to Cháoxuǎn,
then used it to coerce and control him.
Xiànchún erected a white banner,
saying
"This is the banner for redressing grievances."
Dǔchén, alarmed, said,
"The Prince has rebelled!"
He ordered five hundred soldiers to surround the Prince's palace.
When Cháoxuǎn returned to court,
he confirmed the Prince's crimes
but did not mention rebellion.
Grand Secretary Zhāng Jūzhèng, whose family was from Jīngzhōu,
had a previous enmity with Xiànchún.
He was displeased that Cháoxuǎn did not convict Xiànchún of rebellion.
After a long time,
he instructed the Grand Coordinator Láo Kān to fabricate charges against Cháoxuǎn,
who died in prison.
Later, after Jūzhèng's death,
Xiànchún appealed his case,
and Jūzhèng's family property was confiscated,
while Dǔchén also died.
After the state of Liáo was abolished,
all its imperial clan members were affiliated with the Chǔ princely establishment,
with Prince Guǎngyuán Shùshēn as their clan manager.
Prince Qìngjìng Xiàn,
the sixteenth son of Tàizǔ.
He was enfeoffed in the twenty-fourth year of Hóngwǔ
In the twenty-sixth year
As supplies were insufficient,
he was ordered to reside in the old city of Wéizhōu, north of Qìngyáng,
and draw taxes and grain from Yán'ān, Suí, and Níng.
In the twenty-eighth year
His residence was first built in the thirtieth year
The Prince was fond of learning and well-educated,
and his loyalty and filial piety were inherent.
Chéngzǔ approved of him
and ordered him to spend one summer each year in Wéizhōu.
In the early Xuāndé reign,
he stated that Níngxià was low-lying and damp,
with bad water,
and requested to reside in Wéi again.
This was not granted;
he was ordered to travel back and forth once a year,
as during Chéngzǔ's time.
In the early Zhèngtǒng reign,
Shǐ Zhāo, the Grand Commander of Níngxià, memorialized that the Prince was hindering border affairs,
occupying the pastureland of Língzhōu for livestock,
and sending envoys through the grasslands of Suídé,
inciting local people.
Before the memorial was acted upon,
someone reported that the Prince was reviewing troops,
manufacturing weapons,
and buying astronomical texts.
Xiàn suspected that Zhāo was behind all of this.
In the third year
requesting to move his princedom to avoid Zhāo.
Yīngzōng disagreed
and sent a letter of comfort and admonition.
That year he died.
His son, Prince Kāng Zhìkuí, succeeded him.
In the first year of Jǐngtài
he requested to move to the interior,
but was not permitted.
He died in the fifth year of Chénghuà
His son, Prince Huái Suìjī, succeeded him
and died in the fifteenth year
His younger brother, Prince Zhuāng Suìpíng, succeeded him
and died in the fourth year of Hóngzì
His son, Prince Gōng Zhìgù, succeeded him
and died in the eleventh year
His son, Prince Dìng Táihóng, succeeded him.
In the fifth year of Zhèngdé
when Prince Ānhuà Zhìfán rebelled,
Táihóng bowed in submission, performing the rites of a subject to his lord.
An edict ordered the abolition of his guard,
the reduction of his stipend by one-third,
and the banishment of his Chamberlain and Chief Secretary.
In the third year of Jiājìng
Táihóng bribed the Grand Defender Eunuch Lǐ Xīn and Grand Commander Zhǒng Xūn
to request the restoration of his stipend.
Xīn and Xūn did not accept,
and Táihóng resented them.
At this time, Yáng Qīn, Commander of the Níngxià Garrison, and others, having incurred the displeasure of Grand Coordinator Zhāng Xuán,
plotted to use the Prince to kill Xuán and Xūn.
When the plot was discovered,
it was submitted to the Provincial Military Commission and the Provincial Surveillance Commission for investigation.
Qīn and others falsely accused Táihóng of disloyalty,
and Xuán reported this.
The Emperor sent Eunuch Fú Ān, Vice Censor-in-Chief Wáng Shízhōng, and others to reinvestigate,
who reported:
"Táihóng has other crimes,
but no plotting of disloyalty."
An imperial edict ordered court officials to deliberate and conclude
that because of his previous submission to Zhìfán,
and failing to repent after receiving imperial grace,
and inciting small-minded individuals
to plot harm against supervising officials,
he was deposed as a commoner,
allowed to remain in his residence,
and given three hundred *shi* of rice annually.
His uncle, Prince Gǒngchāng Zhìkuí, was appointed to manage the affairs of the princely establishment.
Zhìkuí cut the salaries and rice of the Prince of Qìng's palace consorts
and took tens of thousands in gold and silk from the residence.
Táihóng's son, Zīzhì, who had lost his father's affection at a young age,
fled to Zhìkuí.
Zhìkuí fabricated rumors that Táihóng was plotting rebellion,
and had eunuchs induce Zīzhì to recite them,
scheming to implicate Táihóng and enthrone himself.
Princess Huái, Lady Wáng, memorialized that Zhìkuí had cut their clothing and food,
to the point where they could not sustain themselves.
Prince Fēnglín Táihàn also wished to implicate Zhìkuí
and consequently exposed his various crimes of profaning human relations.
Upon verification,
he was deposed as a commoner
and confined behind a high wall.
Court deliberations concluded that Táihóng and his son were estranged,
so Táihóng was moved to Xī'ān,
and Zīzhì was enfeoffed as the heir apparent
and appointed to manage the princely establishment's affairs.
This was in the tenth month of the eleventh year
In the fifteenth year
and he died.
Zīhuì先卒,
his younger brother, Prince Huì, Zīfāng, succeeded.
He loved learning and delighted in goodness.
He used ritual to regulate all the imperial relatives.
Shìzōng bestowed an imperial edict upon him,
and erected an archway to honor him.
When border walls were built in Níngxià,
Zīfāng contributed silver and grain to assist the work.
He passed away in the second year of Wànlì.
His son, Prince Duān, Nícuì, succeeded,
and passed away sixteen years later.
His son, Prince Xiàn, Shēnyù, succeeded,
and passed away nineteen years later.
The following year,
the Níngxià rebel Bō Bài revolted.
Princess Fāng hid her son, Shuàixīn, in a cellar,
and then hanged herself.
At that time, Sīwáng Níhuò of Shòuyáng,
was coerced into surrender by Bō Bài.
He refused to yield,
and was imprisoned by him.
Prince Shēnkuān of Zhènyuán managed the affairs of the princely mansion,
and plotted to attack the rebels but failed.
Everyone in the mansion was killed.
When the rebellion was quelled,
Censor Liú Fāngyù stated:
"All imperial relatives who died for their principles should be compensated and recorded,
and Princess Fāng should have a shrine built to honor her."
The emperor decreed to follow this,
and provided fifteen thousand taels of silver,
to be distributed among the imperial relatives.
Shuàixīn succeeded,
and then passed away.
His son, Zhuówò, succeeded.
In the sixteenth year of Chóngzhēn,
the roving bandits broke into Níngxià,
and he was captured.
Prince Zhìjiǒng of Ānsài,
was the youngest son of Prince Jìng.
He was orphaned at twelve,
and his mother, Wèi Shì, taught him.
He was intelligent and quick-witted,
remembering everything he read,
and was skilled in classical prose.
When he met gentry scholars,
he would question difficulties and discern confusions,
never tiring even after a whole day.
His writings include "Suíbǐ" in twenty volumes.
The commoner Zhìfán
was the grandson of Zhìjī,
the fourth son of Prince Jìng.
He was enfeoffed as Prince Ānhuà.
His father, Suìtán,
was a Zhènguó Jiāngjūn.
Zhìfán inherited the princely title.
He was wild and unrestrained.
A physiognomist said that he would achieve great nobility.
The shaman Wūwáng Jiǔ'ér taught parrots to speak recklessly about good and bad fortune,
and Zhìfán thus coveted what was not rightfully his.
Zhōu Áng, a commander in Níngxià,
He Jǐn and Dīng Guǎng, chiliarchs,
and students from the military academy such as Sūn Jǐngwén, Mèng Bīn, Shǐ Lián, and others,
all associated with Zhìfán.
In the fifth year of Zhèngdé,
the emperor sent Zhōu Dōng, a junior minister of the Grand Court of Revision, to Níngxià to establish military colonies.
Dōng tried to please Liú Jǐn's intentions,
by taking fifty *mǔ* as one *qǐng*,
and also collecting silver per *mǔ* as bribes for Jǐn.
The beatings and cruelty were severe,
and the garrison generals and soldiers were all resentful.
Meanwhile, the Governor-Censor Ān Wéixué repeatedly beat and humiliated the wives of the generals and soldiers,
who harbored deep resentment.
Zhìfán knew of the public anger,
and ordered Jǐngwén to offer wine to the military officials,
and incite them with words.
Many military officials were willing to follow Zhìfán.
He also sent people to connect with the garrison generals of Pínglǔ City and those he had always been close to, such as Zhāng Qīn.
There was a border alert,
and Assistant Commander Qiú Yuè and Vice Commander Yáng Yīng led troops out for defense.
Commander-in-Chief Jiāng Hàn selected sixty elite soldiers as imperial guards,
and ordered Zhōu Áng to lead them.
Thus, an agreement was made with He Jǐn.
On the fifth day of the fourth month,
Zhìfán hosted a banquet,
inviting the governor and commander officials to drink at his residence.
Wéixué and Dōng did not attend.
Jǐn and Áng led the imperial guards directly in,
killing Jiāng Hàn and eunuchs Lǐ Zēng and Dèng Guǎng at the banquet.
They dispatched soldiers to kill Wéixué, Dōng, and Commander Yáng Zhōng at the government office.
They then burned down the government buildings,
released the prisoners,
and moved the Yellow River ferry boats to the west bank to cut off crossings.
They sent people to summon Yáng Yīng and Qiú Yuè,
who both feigned agreement.
Yīng led his men to defend Wánghóng Fort,
but the troops dispersed,
and Yīng fled to Língzhōu.
Yuè returned.
Zhìfán seized his army,
and distributed gold and silk to reward the generals and soldiers.
He falsely appointed He Jǐn as Grand General,
Zhōu Áng and Dīng Guǎng as Vice Generals,
Zhāng Qīn as Vanguard,
and Wèi Zhèn, Yáng Tài, and others as Commander-in-Chief Protectors.
He ordered Sūn Jǐngwén to write a proclamation,
using the pretext of punishing Liú Jǐn.
When Commander-in-Chief Cáo Xióng of Shǎnxī heard of the change,
he dispatched Commander Huáng Zhèng to garrison Língzhōu,
and ordered Yáng Yīng to oversee the Língzhōu troops to defend the Yellow River.
Commander Hán Bīn, Commander-in-Chief Hóu Xūn, and Assistant Commander Shí Yuán each brought their troops to converge.
Yīng secretly sent a servant to inform Qiú Yuè to act as an inside agent,
and ordered Shǐ Yǒng to cross the river, seize the boats on the west bank,
and set up camp east of the river,
burning the grass at the two large and small dams.
Zhìfán was afraid,
and ordered Jǐn and others to go out to resist,
leaving only Áng to guard the city,
and sent envoys to summon Yuè.
Yuè claimed illness.
Áng came to inquire about his illness.
Yuè stabbed Áng to death.
He ordered his personal guards to rush to Zhìfán's residence,
killing Jǐngwén, Lián, and more than ten others,
then captured Zhìfán,
and welcomed Yīng's troops in.
Zhìfán was captured eighteen days after his rebellion.
Jǐn, Guǎng, Tài, Qīn, and others were all captured one after another,
chained and sent for execution.
Zhìfán was granted death.
All his sons and younger brothers were sentenced to death.
One grandson, Zīcái, escaped,
shaved his head and became a monk,
living in the mountains of Yǒngníng.
Not long after,
he was bullied by local monks,
and went to the officials to report the situation.
The report reached the capital.
Zuǒ Bǎopíng, a palace woman from the Ānhuà palace, was in the Laundry Bureau.
She was sent to verify it,
and exclaimed:
"This is His Highness Zīcái!"
The emperor, mindful of his voluntary surrender,
spared him from death.
He was resettled in Fèngyáng.
Níngxiàn Wáng Quán,
Tàizǔ's seventeenth son.
He was enfeoffed in the 24th year of Hóngwǔ.
Two years later,
he took up his post in Dàníng.
Dàníng was outside Xǐfēngkǒu,
the ancient territory of Huìzhōu,
bordered Liáozuǒ to the east,
and Xuānfǔ to the west,
serving as a major garrison town.
It had eighty thousand armored soldiers
and six thousand leather chariots.
The cavalry of the affiliated Sānyán Sān Wèi were all brave and skilled in battle.
Quán often joined other princes in expeditions beyond the Great Wall,
and was known for his good strategies.
When the Yān Wáng first raised his army,
he discussed with his generals, saying:
"Earlier, when I patrolled beyond the Great Wall,
I saw that the armies of Dàníng were fierce and valorous.
If I can acquire Dàníng,
cut off Liáodōng,
and gain the border cavalry's assistance,
the great enterprise will be accomplished."
In the first year of Jiànwén,
the court deliberated, fearing Quán would ally with Yān.
They sent someone to summon Quán,
but Quán did not come.
Consequently, three of his guard units were abolished.
In the ninth month of that year,
Jiāngyīn Hóu Wú Gāo attacked Yǒngpíng,
and the Yān Wáng went to relieve it.
When Gāo retreated,
the Yān Wáng then took a shortcut from Liújiākǒu to Dàníng,
falsely claiming to be in dire straits and seeking help.
Quán invited the Yān Wáng, riding alone, into the city.
He grasped his hands and wept bitterly,
explaining in detail the unavoidable reasons for raising his army,
and asked for help in drafting a memorial to apologize.
After several days,
Quán was completely unprepared.
Elite soldiers from Běipíng were ambushed outside the city.
Officials and soldiers gradually entered the city,
secretly forming alliances with the chiefs of the Sān Wèi and the garrison soldiers.
When the Yān Wáng bade farewell,
Quán saw him off in the suburbs.
The hidden troops arose
and escorted Quán away.
The elite cavalry of the Sān Wèi and the various garrison soldiers
responded to a single call and gathered.
The defending general Zhū Jiàn could not resist
and died in battle.
The prince's consorts, concubines, and heir apparent all followed into Sōngtíngguān
and returned to Běipíng.
Dàníng city became empty.
Quán joined the Yān army,
and from time to time drafted proclamations for the Yān Wáng.
The Yān Wáng told Quán that
if the enterprise succeeded,
they would divide the empire.
Upon his ascension,
the prince requested a move to the southern territories.
He asked for Sūzhōu,
but was told:
"It is within the imperial domain."
He asked for Qiántáng,
but was told:
"The August Emperor (my father) gave it to my fifth brother,
but it was never realized.
Jiànwén was without dao,
and though he enfeoffed his brother there,
he also could not enjoy it.
Jiànníng, Chóngqìng, Jīngzhōu, and Dōngchāng are all good places;
only my brother should choose."
In the second month of the first year of Yǒnglè, he was re-enfeoffed in Nánchāng.
The emperor personally composed a poem to see him off
and decreed that the Nánchāng administration office be used as his residence,
with no changes to its roof tiles or regulations.
Later, people accused Quán of witchcraft and slander.
Secret investigations yielded no evidence,
and he was cleared.
From then on, he increasingly kept a low profile.
He built a quiet study
and played the qín and read books there,
remaining free from trouble throughout the reign of Chéngzǔ.
During Rénzōng's time,
the legal restrictions were somewhat relaxed,
so he submitted a memorial stating that Nánchāng was not his rightful feoff.
The emperor replied:
"Nánchāng,
uncle, has been received by you from the August Emperor (my father) for over twenty years.
What else but a feoff could it be?"
In the third year of Xuāndé, he requested fields in the nearby Guànchéng Xiāng.
The next year, he further argued that imperial relatives should not be ranked.
The emperor was angered
and issued several reprimands.
Quán submitted a memorial apologizing for his offense.
By then, he was old,
and officials often picked on him to show their authority.
Quán daily associated with scholars of literature,
aspiring to transcend worldly affairs and become an immortal,
styling himself Qúxiān (Emaciated Immortal).
He was once ordered to compile two juan of Tōngjiàn Bólùn,
and also authored six chapters of Jiāxùn,
seventy-four chapters of Níngguó Yífàn,
two juan of Hàntáng Mìshǐ,
one juan of Shǐduàn,
eight juan of Wénpǔ,
one juan of Shīpǔ,
and dozens of other annotations and compilations.
He died in the 13th year of Zhèngtǒng.
His heir apparent Pánshí had died earlier,
and his grandson Jìng Wáng Diànpéi succeeded him.
Diànpéi was good at literature,
but his nature was quick-tempered
and prone to suspicion.
In the seventh year of Jǐngtài,
his younger brother Yìyáng Wáng Diànjiǎn accused him of rebellion,
which Surveillance Commissioner Hán Yōng reported.
The emperor sent officials to investigate,
but it was found to be untrue.
At that time, six or seven hundred soldiers and civilians were implicated and arrested.
Upon Yīngzōng's restoration to the throne,
all were pardoned and released,
except for his tutor Yóu Jiān, who was banished to the frontier.
Diànpéi consequently resented the local officials
and did not treat them with courtesy.
The Provincial Administration Commissioner Cuī Gōng, having accumulated grievances,
often obstructed the affairs of the princely establishment.
Diànpéi then impeached Gōng for unlawful conduct.
Gōng and the Provincial Surveillance Commissioner Yuán Jié also accused Diànpéi of privately offering the palace women of the Xiàn and Huì princes (to others),
and forcing the eunuch Xióng Bì to commit suicide.
Upon investigation, these accusations were found to be true,
and his guard units were consequently revoked.
More than three years later,
Diànjiǎn was given death for his crimes.
Initially,
Luò Gǎo, Commander of the Jǐnyī Wèi, upon hearing from his informants,
falsely accused Diànjiǎn of incest with his mother.
The emperor ordered Diànpéi to report the truth,
and then sent the Imperial Son-in-law Commandant Xuē Huán with Gǎo to investigate.
Diànpéi reported that there was no such thing,
and Gǎo's investigation also found no evidence.
The emperor was angry
and interrogated Gǎo.
Gǎo, fearing,
still insisted it was true,
and consequently, Diànjiǎn and his mother were granted death,
and their bodies were burned.
On that day, a great thunderstorm erupted,
and the flat ground was several feet deep in water.
Everyone felt they had been wronged.
In the fourth year of Hóngzhì
Diànpéi died.
His son, Prince Kāng Jìn-jūn, succeeded him.
He died ten years later.
His son, Prince Shànggāo Chén-háo, succeeded him.
His mother
was a former prostitute.
When he was first born,
Prince Jìng dreamed a snake devoured his chamber.
The next day, an owl hooted,
which was considered an ill omen.
When he grew up,
he was flighty and lacked dignity,
but he was good at disguising himself with cultured behavior.
Diviners Lǐ Zì-rán and Lǐ Rì-fāng falsely claimed he had an unusual appearance,
and also said there was an "emperor's aura" southeast of the city.
Chén-háo was pleased.
From time to time, he spied on court affairs,
and rejoiced whenever he heard slanderous remarks.
If someone said the Emperor was wise and sagacious
or that the court was well-governed,
he would become angry.
At the end of Wǔzōng's reign, he had no sons,
and the officials repeatedly requested that a prince from the imperial clan be summoned to adopt.
Chén-háo's lineage was distant,
but he secretly cultivated close ties with the Emperor's attendants,
who spoke of his virtues before the Emperor.
Initially,
Chén-háo bribed Liú Jǐn
to restore his revoked guards.
When Jǐn was executed,
the guards were again revoked by decree.
When Lù Wán became Minister of War,
Chén-háo colluded with the Emperor's favorites Qián Níng and Zāng Xián to act as his internal agents.
He intended to request their restoration again,
but Grand Secretary Fèi Hóng insisted it was not permissible.
The favorites then took advantage of Hóng's reading of the palace examination papers
to implement the imperial edict.
Chén-háo became even more unrestrained.
He arbitrarily killed Garrison Commander Dài Xuān,
expelled Provincial Administration Commissioner Zhèng Yuè and Censor Fàn Lù,
and imprisoned Prefects Zhèng Yǎn and Sòng Yǐ-fāng.
He seized all the private homes of the people attached to the princely estate,
demanded usurious loans from the populace,
forcibly took fields, residences, sons, and daughters,
sheltered bandits,
and robbed property between the Jiāng and Hú regions.
The local authorities dared not question him.
Daily, he conspired with retired Censor-in-Chief Lǐ Shì-shí, scholar Liú Yǎng-zhèng, and others regarding rebellious acts.
Vice Commissioner Hú Shì-níng requested the court to restrain him early.
Chén-háo repeatedly impeached Shì-níng,
and Shì-níng was exiled to a garrison.
Thereafter, no one dared to speak out.
In the twelfth year of Zhèngdé
Court Ceremony Official Yán Shùn
and palace eunuchs Chén Xuān and Liú Liáng secretly went to the capital to report his impending rebellion.
Níng, Xián, and others protected Chén-háo
and did not investigate.
Chén-háo suspected Chief Steward Zhōu Yí,
and killed Yí's family and several hundred others, including Guard Commander Zhā Wǔ.
Governor and Censor-in-Chief Sūn Suì listed his crimes,
but was intercepted en route
and could not deliver the report.
Chén-háo again bribed Qián Níng
to obtain an imperial edict
to summon his son to perform incense offerings at the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
Níng spoke to the Emperor,
who used special colored dragon paper
and added gold to the imperial gifts.
Special colored dragon paper
was traditionally used for imperial letters bestowed upon regents.
Chén-háo was greatly pleased
and arranged a ceremonial guard to receive congratulations.
He then compelled scholars and elders to submit memorials to the court,
praising his filial piety and diligence.
At this time, border general Jiāng Bīn had newly gained imperial favor.
Eunuch Zhāng Zhōng, who was attached to Bīn,
wished to undermine Níng and Xián.
Seizing an opportunity, he said to the Emperor:
"Níng and Xián highly praise Prince Níng.
What do Your Majesty think of this?"
The Emperor said:
"To recommend civil and military officials,
they are suitable for appointment.
But why recommend a prince?"
Zhōng said:
"When Xián praises Prince Níng's filial piety,
he is satirizing Your Majesty's lack of filial piety.
When he praises Prince Níng's diligence,
he is satirizing Your Majesty's lack of diligence."
The Emperor said:
"Indeed."
An edict was issued to expel the prince's household members,
forbidding them to remain at the capital.
At this time, Chén-háo, along with Shì-shí and Yǎng-zhèng, conspired day and night.
He further dispatched cunning men like Lú Kǒng-zhāng to distribute along water and land arteries
to transmit reports for a thousand *lǐ*.
Within ten days, messages went back and forth,
and his movements were greatly exposed.
Both court and commoners knew he would surely rebel.
Governor and Censor-in-Chief Sūn Suì submitted seven memorials speaking of this,
but all were intercepted and hindered.
Many corrupt officials had received money from Chén-háo
and concealed the matter, not reporting it.
In the fourteenth year
Censor Xiāo Huái memorialized Chén-háo's numerous crimes,
saying that if he were not restrained early,
the future troubles would be immeasurable.
The memorial was sent to the Grand Secretariat.
Grand Secretary Yáng Tíng-hé said it should be handled like Xuānzōng's treatment of the Zhào princely estate:
send high-ranking officials and imperial relatives to deliver an imperial edict
and instruct the prince to reform himself.
The Emperor ordered the Imperial Son-in-Law Cuī Yuán, Censor-in-Chief Yán Yí-shòu, and eunuch Lài Yì to carry the edict there,
to confiscate his guards,
and to order him to return the seized official and private lands.
When Chén-háo heard Yuán and others were approaching,
he finalized his plan.
He hosted a banquet for all the local officials on his birthday.
The next morning, all entered to express gratitude.
Chén-háo ordered armed guards to surround them,
claiming to have received a secret imperial edict from the Empress Dowager
to raise an army and march on the capital.
Sūn Suì and Vice Commissioner Xǔ Kuí refused to comply,
were bound, led out, and executed.
Censor Wáng Jīn,
Secretaries Mǎ Sī-cōng and Jīn Shān,
Consultants Huáng Hóng and Xǔ Xiào-lián,
Provincial Administration Commissioner Hú Lián,
Administration Vice Commissioners Chén Gǎo and Liú Fěi,
Surveillance Commissioner Lài Fèng,
Commanders Xǔ Jīn and Bái Áng, and others were imprisoned.
Administration Vice Commissioners Wáng Lún and Jì Xiào,
Surveillance Commissioners Pān Péng and Shī Kuí,
Provincial Administration Commissioner Liáng Chén,
Provincial Surveillance Commissioner Yáng Zhāng,
and Vice Commissioner Táng Jǐn all joined the rebellion.
Lǐ Shì-shí and Liú Yǎng-zhèng were appointed Left and Right Chancellors,
and Wáng Lún was appointed Minister of War.
They gathered an army, numbering 100,000.
He ordered his Chief Steward Tú Qīn, along with the bandits he had long harbored, such as Mǐn Niàn-sì,
to plunder Jiǔjiāng and Nánkāng,
and they captured them.
He then issued a flying manifesto denouncing the court.
On the first day of the seventh month, Rén-chén,
Chén-háo left Jiāngxī,
leaving his partisans, Prince Yíchūn Gǒng-gē and eunuch Wàn Ruì, to defend the city.
He personally led his naval forces down the Jiāng river,
attacking Ānqìng.
Upon hearing of the rebellion, Governor and Censor-in-Chief of Tíng-gàn, Wáng Shǒu-rén,
along with Ji'ān Prefect Wǔ Wén-dìng and others, issued orders for the armies of various prefectures to arrive one after another.
Then he sent Fèngxīn County Magistrate Liú Shǒu-xù to destroy the rebel's tomb factory ambush.
On Wù-shēn,
he directly attacked Nánchāng.
On Xīn-hài,
the city fell.
Gǒng-gē, Ruì, and others were all captured.
Palace women set themselves on fire and died.
Chén-háo was still besieging Ānqìng unsuccessfully.
When he heard Nánchāng had fallen,
he was greatly alarmed,
lifted the siege, and returned.
Wáng Shǒu-rén intercepted and attacked him.
On Yǐ-mǎo,
they met at Huángjiā-dù.
The rebel forces, using the wind to their advantage, pressed forward,
and were extremely arrogant.
Wú Wén-dìng and Commander Yú Ēn feigned retreat,
luring the rebels to pursue profits,
causing their front and rear to become separated.
Prefects Xíng Xún, Xú Lián,
and Dài Dé-rú attacked them fiercely from behind.
Wén-dìng led the returning troops to press the attack.
The rebels collapsed,
with tens of thousands killed or drowned.
He also separately dispatched Prefects Chén Huái, Lín Jiān,
Zēng Yú, and Zhōu Cháo-zuǒ to retake Jiǔjiāng and Nánkāng.
The next day,
they fought again.
The government troops slightly retreated,
but Wén-dìng's soldiers fought desperately.
Two thousand enemy heads were taken or captured.
Chén-háo then retreated to Cháo-shě for defense.
The next day,
the government army attacked with fire.
Chén-háo was utterly defeated.
All his concubines drowned themselves.
More than thirty thousand officers and soldiers were burned to death.
Chén-háo, his heir apparent, the commandery princes, his sons-in-law, along with Lǐ Shì-shí, Liú Yǎng-zhèng, Tú Qīn, Wáng Lún, and others, were all captured.
From the start of Chén-háo's uprising to his defeat,
it had been forty-three days.
At that time, the Emperor heard that Chén Háo
had rebelled. He issued an edict denouncing his crimes,
informed the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
and stripped him of his princely status, reducing him to a commoner.
He ordered the arrest and imprisonment of Minister Lù Wán,
the favorites Qián Níng and Zāng Xián, and others,
and confiscated their properties.
Jiāng Bīn and Zhāng Zhōng urged the Emperor to personally lead the punitive expedition.
Upon reaching Liángxiāng,
Wáng Shǒurén’s victorious report arrived,
and an urgent dispatch halted the Emperor’s advance.
Wáng Shǒurén had already captured and imprisoned Chén Háo and his cohorts,
taking the route through Zhèjiāng.
The Emperor remained in Nánjīng,
sending Xǔ Tài, Zhū Huī, and the eunuchs Zhāng Yǒng and Zhāng Zhōng to search for remaining rebels in Jiāngxī,
causing immense distress to the people.
An urgent dispatch ordered Wáng Shǒurén to return to Jiāngxī.
When Wáng Shǒurén arrived in Hángzhōu,
he met Zhāng Yǒng,
and handed the captives over to him,
instructing him to send them to the Emperor’s traveling court.
In the twelfth month of the fifteenth year,
the Emperor, having received the delivered captives, returned to the capital.
Upon reaching Tōngzhōu, he executed them,
and their fiefdoms were abolished.
Initially,
when Chén Háo was plotting rebellion,
his consort, Lady Lóu, had often advised against it.
When he was defeated,
he sighed, saying:
“In the past, King Zhòu perished by heeding a woman’s words;
I perish by not heeding a woman’s words.
What good is regret now?”
In the fourth year of Jiājìng,
Prince Gǒngkuǐ of Yìyáng and others stated:
“The descendants of the four branches of Prince Xiàn and Prince Huì
are all meant to jointly worship them, it is not Chén Háo alone who sprang from them.
If subjects like us can all be distinguished and exonerated,
and maintain our offices as before,
but the two princes do not receive temple sacrifices,
this causes me great sorrow.”
The memorial was submitted three times.
The Emperor ordered Prince Gǒngkuǐ of Yìyáng, as a commandery prince, to conduct the sacrifices,
and granted half the stipend for music, dances, and sacrificial attendants.
After the Níng Principality was abolished,
the various commandery princes rivaled each other in power,
unable to unify.
The Emperor ordered Gǒngkuǐ to oversee the affairs of the princely establishment.
When he died,
Prince Gǒngluó of Lè’ān took over.
Gǒngluó memorialized that the three princes of Jiàn’ān, Lè’ān, and Yìyáng should divide the administration of the eight branches,
and this was established as a regulation.
Prince Diàndǔ of Shíchéng,
was the fourth son of Prince Huì.
He was solemn and resolute by nature,
and his family governance was very strict.
Prince Diànpéi of Jìng and the other commandery princes were at odds,
and Línchuān and Yìyáng were both framed and fell into disfavor.
Diàndǔ alone was cautious and self-restrained,
so no fault could be attributed to him.
His son, Jìnháo,
was filial and friendly, with a good reputation,
but died young.
His grandson, Chénfú, inherited the title.
He, along with his full younger brother Chénpǔ, his illegitimate elder brother Chénmǐn, and his younger brother Chénhuà, were all lewd, unruly, and murderous.
In the twelfth year of Hóngzhì, they impeached each other in memorials.
Chénfú and Chénpǔ were both stripped of their princely status and reduced to commoners,
while Chénhuà and Chénmǐn had their stipends revoked.
Chénhuà then joined Chén Háo’s rebellion,
and was killed by a lightning strike.
In the twenty-fourth year of Jiājìng,
Chénfú and Chénpǔ had their princely robes and belts restored.
Chénmǐn’s son, Gǒngtǐng, submitted a letter to clear his father’s name,
and his title was also restored.
Chénhuà’s younger brother, Chénmó, was always upright.
Chén Háo tried to coerce him,
but failed.
He repeatedly sent people to set fire to his residence,
and subtly instructed other princely relatives to provide him with aid to show favor,
but Chénmó declined to accept.
When Chén Háo was defeated,
Chénmó was spared.
His son, Regent-General Gǒnggài,
his grandson, State-Defending General Duōkuò,
and his great-grandson, Palace Guardian Lieutenant Móuyí,
were all upright and self-respecting for three generations.
Móuyí, in particular, was thoroughly versed in numerous classics
and deeply understood court precedents and regulations.
Among the princely descendants who were fond of learning and virtuous in conduct,
apart from Palace Guardian Lieutenant Mùyù of the Zhōu Principality,
none could match Móuyí.
In the twenty-second year of Wànlì,
the court deliberated on establishing additional administrators for Shíchéng and Yíchūn,
and ordered Móuyí, as a lieutenant, to manage the affairs of the Shíchéng Princely Establishment,
empowering him to impeach and punish those who violated the law.
He administered the princely affairs for thirty years,
and all the imperial clansmen submitted to his discipline.
In his leisure, he would close his door and read,
producing *Yì Xiàng Tōng*, *Shī Gù*, *Chūnqiū Dài Jì Lǔ Lùn Jiān*, and other works,
a total of one hundred and twelve kinds,
all personally copied by him.
When Huáng Rǔhéng was the magistrate of Jìnxián,
he visited with a stiff courtesy.
After a long and intense discussion,
he hesitantly changed his seat.
The next day,
he faced north and called himself a disciple,
and people praised them both.
When he was critically ill,
he was still discussing the *Yìjīng* with his sons.
He had eight sons,
all worthy and fond of learning.
His cousin, Móujìn, built a house in Lóngshā,
tilled the land himself, and composed poetry until his death.
State-Defending General Gǒngyáo
was the fourth-generation descendant of Prince Diànchán of Ruìchāng.
His father, Chénqú, was implicated in Chén Háo’s affair
and arrested and imprisoned in Zhōngdū.
His elder brother, Gǒngruì, requested to take his place,
and Gǒngyáo assisted him,
eventually clearing his name.
In the ninth year of Jiājìng, he submitted a memorial requesting the establishment of clan schools,
ordering imperial clansmen to set up altars,
perform rituals for farming and sericulture,
carefully observe sacrificial rites,
and pay more attention to judicial leniency.
All these requests received imperial approval.
He donated land to Báilùdòng to support scholars.
Later, because his proposals on rites were in accordance with the imperial will,
Gǒngruì submitted a grand eulogy for the great rites,
and both were honored with imperial edicts of commendation.
Many of his sons and cousins were renowned.
Duōwēn and Duōkuò were known for their filial piety and fraternity.
Duōyóu and Duōkuò were praised for their adherence to rites and solemnity.
Duōmó, Duōkuí, and Duōxīn were famous for their skill in poetry and rhapsodies.
However, Duōwēn and his cousin Duōzhěn alone secluded themselves at home,
extensively acquiring rare books,
and found joy in collating and proofreading them.
During the Wànlì era,
the Grand Coordinator and Provincial Inspector recommended him to manage the affairs of the Ruìchāng Princely Establishment,
but he declined and did not take office.
Duōyóu’s father, Gǒngjiū, was arrested due to Chén Háo’s affair.
Duōyóu, barely ten-odd years old,
cried and ran to the military gate,
begging to take his father’s place.
Wáng Shǒurén saw him and was surprised.
In the second year of Jiājìng, he memorialized to plead his father’s innocence,
and his father was released and returned home,
and his princely title restored.
At that time, the various commandery princes were under the authority of Yìyáng,
and the first prince of Ruìchāng was not offered sacrifices.
Duōyóu felt that as a cadet branch, he should preside over the ancestral shrine.
He petitioned the court,
and a special imperial edict granted his request.
Thereupon, he increased the sacrificial land,
and meticulously managed family affairs,
making them as solemn as court rituals.
His four sons were all solemn, cautious, and fond of learning.
State-Defending General Duōhuáng
was the fifth-generation descendant of Prince Diàndiǎn of Yìyáng, the fifth son of Prince Huì.
He was filial, friendly, and fond of learning.
The Yìyáng line died out after five generations.
The clansmen recommended Duōhuáng as capable and virtuous,
and an imperial edict ordered him to oversee the princely establishment,
to which all the Ruìchāng princely relatives belonged.
By nature, he was honest, tranquil, and had few desires.
His wife, Lady Xióng, died early,
and he did not remarry,
living alone in his study for twenty-six years.
In the forty-first year of Wànlì,
the Grand Coordinator and Provincial Inspector reported his virtuous conduct.
An imperial edict commended him.
He happened to die of illness,
and an edict ordered the local officials to offer an additional sacrifice.
Another was Duōzhèng,
also a State-Defending General,
who was intelligent and skilled in poetry and song.
He once changed his name and traveled,
his footsteps covering Wú and Chǔ.
In his later years, though frail with illness,
he still did not cease his chanting and recitation.
When he died,
his disciples privately conferred on him the posthumous title of Master Qīngmǐn.
His son Móutuí also had his father’s style.
At that time, Regent-General Duōwēn of Lè’ān had a poetry addiction,
and he and Móutuí indulged themselves in literature and wine,
throughout their lives.
Collation Notes

Biographies, Volume 6, Imperial Princes, Part 3: Sons of Tàizǔ: Prince Biàn of Mín, Prince Huì of Gǔ, Prince Sōng of Hán, Prince Mó of Shěn (Prince Chéngjiē of Qìnshuǐ, Prince Yòubō of Qīngyuán), Prince Yíng of Ān, Prince Jìng of Táng (Prince Zhīguǐ of Sānchéng, Prince Míqián of Wénchéng, Mízhèn, Regent-General Yǔjiá), Prince Dòng of Yǐng, Prince Wǔ of Yī, Imperial Son Nán, Prince Shǒuqiān of Jìngjiāng. Sons of Xīngzōng: Prince Xióngyīng of Yú, Prince Yǔntēng of Wú, Prince Yǔnjī of Héng, Prince Yǔnhuì of Xú. Sons of Huìdì: Crown Prince Wénkuí, Youngest Son Wénguī. Sons of Chéngzǔ: Gāoxù, Prince Gāosuì of Zhào, Gāoxī.
Mín Zhuāng Wáng Biǎn,
was the eighteenth son of Tàizǔ.
In the twenty-fourth year of Hóngwǔ, he was enfeoffed in Mínzhōu.
In the twenty-eighth year, because Yúnnán had newly submitted,
it was deemed appropriate for a prince to guard and pacify it,
so he was transferred to Yúnnán.
The officials requested to build a palace,
but the emperor ordered him to temporarily reside in a thatched pavilion,
and to build it later when the people's resources were somewhat relieved.
In the first year of Jiànwén,
Xīpíng Hóu Mù Shèng impeached him for his transgressions,
and he was deposed as a commoner
and exiled to Zhāngzhōu.
In the early Yǒnglè reign, he was reinstated as prince,
but he became hostile with Shèng.
The emperor sent a letter to admonish Biǎn
and issued an edict to caution Shèng.
Biǎn indulged in heavy drinking and neglected rites,
unlawfully seized seals from various offices,
and killed officials and common people.
The emperor was enraged
and stripped him of his princely seal and insignia.
Soon after, recalling that the prince had been long imprisoned during the Jiànwén reign,
he restored them to him,
but Biǎn did not reform.
In the sixth year,
his guard was abolished,
and his retainers were dismissed.
Upon Rénzōng's ascension,
he was transferred to Wǔgāng,
residing temporarily in the prefecture's administrative office.
After a long time,
his princely residence was finally built.
He passed away in the first year of Jǐngtài.
His son, Gōng Wáng Huīróu, succeeded.
Initially,
the heir apparent, Huīyì,
in the early Xuāndé reign,
accused his younger brother, Zhènnán Wáng Huīróu, of slandering Rénmiào.
Xuānzōng suspected deceit,
and summoned both to the capital,
along with the eunuchs they implicated, for face-to-face questioning.
The matter indeed proved to be a false accusation;
the eunuchs were executed, and Huīróu and others were sent back.
Huīróu succeeded to the throne.
His younger brother, Guǎngtōng Wáng Huīyè, possessed courage and strength.
His household retainer, Duàn Yǒuhóng, gained favor through his skills.
After retirement, the Military Commandery Magistrate, Yú Lìbīn, said that Huīyè had an unusual appearance
and was destined to rule the empire,
whereupon they plotted rebellion.
They forged an imperial edict
and separately dispatched Yǒuhóng, as well as Méng Néng and Chén Tiānháng, into the Miao territories,
enticing various Miao tribes with silver seals and gold and silk,
to make them raise troops and attack Wǔgāng.
The Miao leaders, Yáng Wénbó and others, dared not accept.
The plot was discovered,
and Yǒuhóng was seized by Huīróu.
The Censor-in-Chief Lǐ Shí reported this,
and the Emperor dispatched the Imperial Son-in-Law, Duke Escort Jiāo Jìng, and the Palace Eunuch Lǐ Cóng to summon Huīyè to the capital.
The Governor-General of Húguǎng, Wáng Lái, and the Commander-in-Chief Liáng Bǎo further exposed the connivance of Yángzōng Wáng Huīguāng,
who was also summoned.
All were stripped of their titles
and confined to the high wall.
This was the tenth month of the second year of Jǐngtài.
In the seventh year of Tiānshùn,
Huīróu passed away.
His son, Shùn Wáng Yīnlà, succeeded,
but suffered from paralysis
and was bedridden for many years.
His second son, Ānchāng Wáng Yīngpū, attended to his medicine
and stayed by his side morning and night.
Xiànzōng heard of this
and bestowed an imperial edict of commendation.
In the sixteenth year of Chénghuà,
Yīnlà passed away.
The heir apparent, Yīngpū, during the mourning period,
gambled excessively.
The director of the Prince's Household, Liú Zhōng, tried to restrain him,
whereupon Yīngpū killed Zhōng.
The incident was reported,
verified,
and he was stripped of his insignia and stopped from being enfeoffed.
After four years,
he finally succeeded.
He passed away in the thirteenth year of Hóngzhì,
and was posthumously named Jiǎn.
His son, Jìng Wáng Yàntài, succeeded.
In the fourth year of Jiājìng,
he and his younger brother, Nán'ān Wáng Yànní, accused each other of secret misdeeds.
Yànní was deposed as a commoner,
and Yàntài was also stripped of his title for resisting control and usurping power.
In the eighth year, the heir apparent, Yùróng, was ordered to manage the princely affairs.
Yùróng submitted a memorial earnestly declining,
stating:
"Your subject enjoys honor and luxury,
while my father suffers in solitude;
how can my heart be at peace?
Moreover, my younger brother, Shànhuà Wáng Yùjié, was previously nominated,
but the court deliberated that a son has no right to control his father,
and the proposal was shelved.
Your subject is also a son;
how can I not feel ashamed before my younger brother!"
The emperor read the memorial and pitied him,
referring it to the ministries for deliberation.
In the twelfth year, Yàntài was granted his insignia
to manage the princely affairs.
In the fifteenth year,
by imperial grace for the titles of the two empress dowagers, he was reinstated as prince.
He passed away eight years later.
His son, Kāng Wáng Yùróng, succeeded,
and passed away in the thirty-first year.
His son, Xiàn Wáng Dìngyào, succeeded,
and passed away in the thirty-fourth year.
His great-grandson, Yīn Hóng,
succeeded in the second year of Tiānqǐ,
and passed away in the first year of Chóngzhēn.
Having no son,
his cousin Qǐfēng succeeded.
In the sixteenth year,
he was killed when the rebel army occupied Wǔgāng.
Gǔ Wáng Huì,
was the nineteenth son of Tàizǔ.
Enfeoffed in the twenty-fourth year of Hóngwǔ.
In the third month of the twenty-eighth year, he took up his fief in Xuānfǔ.
Xuānfǔ
was in the area of Shànggǔ,
hence he was called Gǔ Wáng.
When the Yàn army rose,
Huì fled back to the capital.
When the Yàn army crossed the Jiāng River,
Huì was ordered to guard the Jīnchuān Gate.
Seeing Chéngzǔ's banners and canopy from the city wall,
he opened the gate and surrendered.
Chéngzǔ valued this,
and upon ascending the throne,
granted Huì seven musical performances,
three hundred guards,
and bestowed many generous gifts.
He was re-enfeoffed in Chángshā,
and his annual stipend was increased by two thousand *shi* of grain.
Huì behaved extremely arrogantly in his domain.
When Zhōngchéng Bó Rú Cháng passed through Chángshā and did not pay his respects to Huì,
Huì reported it to the emperor,
and Cháng was found guilty and died.
Huì then became even more arrogant and unrestrained,
seizing people's land,
encroaching on public taxes,
and killing innocent people.
His Chief Secretary, Yú Tínggāng, repeatedly admonished him,
but Huì falsely accused Tínggāng of slander
and had him dismembered.
He harbored fugitives,
practiced military strategies and battle formations,
and built warships, bows, crossbows, and other weaponry.
He extensively built Buddhist temples,
ordained a thousand monks,
and had them perform curses.
Daily he conspired with the Commander-in-Chief Zhāng Chéng
and the eunuchs Wú Zhì and Liú Xìn,
calling Chéng
"Master and Father of the State,"
and Zhì and Xìn
"Elder Statesmen and Dukes."
He falsely cited an apocalyptic text,
saying:
"I am the eighteenth son of Gāo Huángdì,
which matches the prophecy."
Huì was the nineteenth in order of birth,
but because Zhào Wáng Shí died young,
he claimed this.
They planned to offer lamps during the Lantern Festival,
select strong men and teach them music,
and enter the forbidden palace together
to seize an opportunity to rebel.
He also sent a letter to the King of Shǔ using veiled language,
hoping to gain Shǔ as an ally.
The King of Shǔ sent a letter severely reprimanding him.
He did not listen.
Later, the King of Shǔ's son, Chóngníng Wáng Yuèzhuàn, committed a crime
and fled to Huì's residence.
Huì then deceived the populace, saying:
"Years ago, I opened the Jīnchuān Gate and let out the Jiànwén Emperor,
who is now in my residence.
I will restore great righteousness for him,
the time for this event is approaching."
When the King of Shǔ heard this,
he reported the treason.
When Wénzhèng was banished,
Shǒuqīan was barely four years old.
Tàizǔ stroked his head and said:
“Child, do not be afraid.
Your father was twice taught and trained,
causing me worry,
but I will ultimately not abandon you because of your father.”
He was raised in the palace.
Shǒuqīan's childhood name was Tiězhù.
In the first year of Wú, his naming as a prince was announced at the ancestral temple,
and his name was changed to Wěi.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, his name was changed to Shǒuqīan,
and he was enfeoffed as Jìngjiāng Wáng.
His stipend was that of a Jùnwáng,
and his officials were half the number of a Qīnwáng's.
The venerable scholar Zhào Xūn was appointed as his Chángshǐ (Chief Administrator) and tutor.
Once he grew up,
he went to his domain in Guìlín.
Guìlín had the former residence of Yuán Shùndì,
which was converted into a royal palace.
He submitted a memorial to express his gratitude.
Tàizǔ issued an imperial edict to his subordinate officials, saying:
“My grandson is young and will govern far away in the southwest;
you must guide him well.”
Shǒuqīan was learned,
but he enjoyed associating with petty people,
and the Yuè people resented and complained.
He was summoned back
and admonished.
Shǒuqīan wrote a poem expressing resentment.
The Emperor was enraged
and demoted him to commoner status.
After residing in Fèngyáng for seven years,
his title was restored.
He was transferred to govern Yúnnán,
and his consort’s younger brother, Xú Pǔ, was sent with him.
He was given a letter of admonition,
the words of which were extremely sincere and earnest.
Shǒuqīan remained as tyrannical as before.
He was summoned back
and made to reside in Fèngyáng again.
Later, for forcibly seizing grazing horses,
he was imprisoned in the capital.
He died in the twenty-fifth year.
His son Zànyí was young,
and was appointed as the heir apparent.
In the spring of the thirtieth year, he was sent to visit the thirteen princes, Jìn, Yān, Zhōu, Chǔ, Qí, Shǔ, Xīang, Dài, Sù, Líao, Qìng, Gǔ, and Qín.
He entered Shǔ from Xīang and Chǔ,
passed through Shǎnxī,
reached Hénán and Shānxī, and Běipíng,
then went east to Dàníng and Líaoyáng,
and returned from Shāndōng.
This was to make him understand the principle of kinship,
become familiar with the difficult and easy terrains of mountains and rivers,
and get accustomed to hardship.
Zànyí was respectful, cautious, and fond of learning.
In the first year of Yǒnglè, he returned to his domain in Guìlín,
and Xiāo Yòngdào was appointed as his Chángshǐ.
Yòngdào was good at guidance,
and Zànyí also treated him with respect.
He died in the sixth year
and was posthumously named Dàoxī.
His son, Zhuāngjiǎn Wáng Zuǒjìng, succeeded him.
Initially, he was given a silver seal.
During the Xuāndé reign,
it was changed to a gold-plated one.
In the early Zhèngtǒng reign,
he and his younger brother, Fèngguó Jiāngjūn Zuǒmǐn, mutually impeached each other,
and the matter implicated Grand Secretary Yáng Róng.
The Emperor was enraged
and sent their messenger into exile.
He died in the fifth year of Chénghuà.
His son, Xīang Chéngxiān, had died earlier,
so his grandson, Zhāohé Wáng Guīyù, succeeded him.
He died in the second year of Hóngzhì.
His son, Duānyì Wáng Yuēqí, succeeded him
and was known for his filial piety and prudence.
He died in the eleventh year of Zhèngdé.
His son, Ānsù Wáng Jīngfú, succeeded him.
He was fond of learning and had a frugal character,
and once wrote an admonition on respect and righteousness.
He died in the fourth year of Jīajìng.
His son, Gōnghuì Wáng Bāngníng, succeeded him
and mutually impeached the Circuit Censor Xú Nánjīn.
His stipends were reduced,
and his officials and guards were punished.
He died in the sixth year of Lóngqìng.
His son, Kāngxī Wáng Rènchāng, succeeded him.
He died in the tenth year of Wànlì.
His son, Wēnyù Wáng Lǚtáo, succeeded him.
He died in the twentieth year.
Having no sons,
his cousin, Xiàndìng Wáng Rènchéng, succeeded him.
He died in the thirty-eighth year.
His son, Róngmù Wáng Lǚhù, succeeded him
and died.
His son, Hēngjīa, succeeded him.
After Lǐ Zìchéng captured the capital,
he proclaimed himself regent in Guǎngxī
and was executed by Governor Qú Shìsì.
At that time, Táng Wáng Yùjiàn was in Fújiàn
and was notified of the victory.
Xīngzōng had five sons.
Empress Cháng gave birth to Yúhuái Wáng Xióngyīng and Wú Wáng Yǔntēng.
Empress Lǚ gave birth to Huìdì, Héng Wáng Yǔnjiān, and Xú Wáng Yǔnlián.
Yúhuái Wáng Xióngyīng,
Xīngzōng’s eldest son,
was Tàizǔ's eldest legitimate grandson.
He died in the fifth month of the fifteenth year of Hóngwǔ.
He was eight years old.
His enfeoffment and posthumous name were added.
Wú Wáng Yǔntēng,
Xīngzōng’s third son.
In the first year of Jiànwén, he was enfeoffed in Hángzhōu,
but did not go to his domain.
When Chéngzǔ ascended the throne,
he was demoted to Guǎngzé Wáng
and resided in Zhāngzhōu.
Soon after,
he was summoned back to the capital,
demoted to commoner status,
and imprisoned in Fèngyáng.
He died in the fifteenth year of Yǒnglè.
Héng Wáng Yǔnjiān,
Xīngzōng’s fourth son,
was enfeoffed in the first year of Jiànwén.
Chéngzǔ demoted him to Huái’ēn Wáng
and he resided in Jiànchāng.
Both he and Yǔntēng were summoned back,
imprisoned in Fèngyáng,
and died one after another.
Xú Wáng Yǔnlián,
Xīngzōng’s fifth son,
was enfeoffed in the first year of Jiànwén.
Chéngzǔ demoted him to Fūhuì Wáng
and he resided with his mother, Empress Dowager Lǚ, at Yìwén Líng.
In the second year of Yǒnglè, an imperial edict changed his title to Ōuníng Wáng
to offer sacrifices to the Crown Prince.
In the twelfth month of the fourth year,
there was a fire in his residence,
and he died suddenly.
He was posthumously named Āijiǎn.
Huìdì had two sons.
Both were born to Empress Mǎ.
Crown Prince Wénkuí.
In the first year of Jiànwén, he was established as the Crown Prince.
When the Yān army entered,
he was seven years old,
and his fate is unknown.
The younger son was Wénguī.
He was two years old when Chéngzǔ entered,
and was imprisoned in Guǎng’ān Gōng in Zhōngdū,
known as Jiànshùrén (Commoner Jiàn).
When Yīngzōng was restored to the throne,
he pitied the commoner, who had been unjustly imprisoned for a long time,
and wanted to release him.
Those around him sometimes thought it was not advisable.
The Emperor said:
“One who possesses the mandate of Heaven
should act on their own accord.”
Grand Secretary Lǐ Xían praised him, saying:
“This is the heart of Yáo and Shùn.”
He then petitioned the Empress Dowager,
who ordered the eunuch Niú Yù to release him.
He was allowed to reside in Fèngyáng,
and was free to marry and move about.
He was given twenty gatekeepers
and more than ten maids and concubines
to serve him.
Wénguī had been imprisoned since childhood;
by then he was fifty-seven years old.
He died soon after.
Chéngzǔ had four sons.
Rénzōng, Hàn Wáng Gāoxù, and Zhào Wáng Gāosuì were all born to Empress Wén.
Gāoxī's birth mother is not detailed.
Hàn Wáng Gāo Xù,
was the second son of Chéng Zǔ.
His nature was fierce and violent.
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
all the princes were summoned to study in the capital.
Gāo Xù refused to study,
and his words and actions were frivolous,
which was disliked by Tài Zǔ.
When Tài Zǔ passed away,
Chéng Zǔ sent Rén Zōng and Gāo Xù to the capital to mourn.
His maternal uncle Xú Huīzǔ, seeing his untrustworthiness,
secretly warned him.
He did not listen,
and stole Huīzǔ's fine horse,
then directly crossed the river and galloped back.
On the way, he often killed commoners and officials.
Upon reaching Zhuōzhōu,
he again attacked and killed the postmaster.
Thus, court officials raised this to blame Yān.
When Chéng Zǔ raised an army,
Rén Zōng remained to guard,
while Gāo Xù followed,
often serving as the vanguard.
During the Battle of Báigōuhé,
Chéng Zǔ was nearly overtaken by Qú Néng.
Gāo Xù led several thousand elite cavalry,
charged directly forward to decisive battle,
and slew Néng and his son on the battlefield.
When Chéng Zǔ was defeated at Dōngchāng,
Zhāng Yù died in battle,
and Chéng Zǔ fled alone.
Just then, Gāo Xù led his army to arrive,
and repelled the southern army.
Xú Huīzǔ defeated the Yān army at Pǔzikǒu,
and Gāo Xù led his tribal cavalry to come.
Chéng Zǔ was greatly pleased,
saying:
"My strength is exhausted.
Son, you should courageously fight again."
Gāo Xù commanded his tribal cavalry to fight fiercely,
and the southern army then retreated.
That Chéng Zǔ repeatedly approached danger and turned defeat into victory
was largely due to Gāo Xù's efforts.
Chéng Zǔ thought he resembled himself,
and Gāo Xù also took pride in this,
relying on his merits to become arrogant and indulgent,
committing many unlawful acts.
When Chéng Zǔ ascended the throne,
he ordered him to lead troops to Kāipíng to guard the border.
At that time, there was discussion about establishing an heir.
Qíguógōng Qiū Fú and Fùmǎ Wáng Níng were on good terms with Gāo Xù,
and often praised Gāo Xù's great achievements,
almost usurping the legitimate heir.
Chéng Zǔ ultimately decided that his eldest son, Rén Zōng, was benevolent and worthy,
and also had been established by Tài Zǔ,
and Gāo Xù had many faults,
so it did not come to pass.
In the second year of Yǒnglè (1404),
Rén Zōng was established as Crown Prince,
Gāo Xù was enfeoffed as Hàn Wáng,
and granted Yunnan as his domain.
Gāo Xù said:
"What crime have I committed
to be banished a myriad miles?"
He refused to go.
He followed Chéng Zǔ on his inspection tour to Běijīng,
and strongly requested to return to Nánjīng with his sons.
Chéng Zǔ had no choice but
to consent.
He requested to have the Tiāncè Wèi as his guard,
and often compared himself to Táng Tài Zōng.
Later,
he again took the opportunity to request two additional guards,
and his behavior became even more unrestrained.
Chéng Zǔ once ordered him to visit Xiàolíng with Rén Zōng.
Rén Zōng was corpulent
and had a foot ailment,
so two eunuchs supported him as he walked,
but he stumbled.
Gāo Xù, following behind, said:
"The stumble of the one in front
serves as a warning to those behind."
At that time, Xuān Zōng was the Imperial Grandson.
He responded from behind:
"There are even those further behind who should take warning."
Gāo Xù looked back, his face losing color.
Gāo Xù was over seven feet tall,
nimble and skilled in horsemanship and archery,
with several patches on his armpits resembling dragon scales.
Not only was he proud of his martial prowess,
but he also accompanied Chéng Zǔ on every northern campaign,
always by his side.
He often stirred up trouble regarding the Eastern Palace,
slandering Xiè Jìn to his death,
and Huáng Huái and others were all imprisoned.
In the fifth month of the thirteenth year (1415), he was re-enfeoffed as Qīngzhōu,
but again did not wish to go.
Chéng Zǔ began to suspect him,
and issued an imperial decree stating:
"Having received a princely enfeoffment,
how can you constantly reside in the capital?
Previously, you balked at the distance to Yúnnán.
Now, enfeoffed in Qīngzhōu,
you again make excuses to wish to remain to serve.
Your intentions, both past and present, are likely not sincere.
This order can no longer be refused."
However, Gāo Xù procrastinated as usual.
He privately selected strong soldiers from various guards,
and also recruited three thousand men
who were not registered with the Ministry of War,
allowing them to plunder.
The Cavalry Commander Xú Yělǘ captured and disciplined them.
Gāo Xù was enraged,
and personally used an iron mace to bludgeon Yělǘ to death.
No one dared to speak.
He then presumptuously used imperial carriages and artifacts.
Chéng Zǔ heard of this and was angry.
In the tenth month of the fourteenth year (1416), he returned to Nánjīng,
and discovered dozens of his unlawful acts.
He severely reprimanded him,
stripped him of his official robes and cap,
and imprisoned him within Xīhuámén,
intending to depose him as a commoner.
Rén Zōng tearfully pleaded earnestly,
so Chéng Zǔ only abolished two of his guards,
and executed his close associates and hangers-on.
In the third month of the following year (1417), he was transferred and enfeoffed in Luò'ānzhōu,
and immediately ordered to depart that very day.
When Gāo Xù arrived in Luò'ān,
he harbored resentment and discontent,
and his seditious plans became more urgent.
Rén Zōng repeatedly warned him by letter,
but he did not reform.
Chéng Zǔ passed away during a northern campaign.
Gāo Xù's son Zhān Qí, who was in Běijīng,
observed court affairs and reported them rapidly,
six or seven times a day and night.
Gāo Xù also daily sent people to secretly observe the capital,
hoping for a disturbance.
Rén Zōng knew of this,
but treated him even more generously.
He sent a letter summoning him,
increased his annual stipend,
bestowed countless gifts,
and still ordered him to return to his domain.
He enfeoffed his eldest son as the Heir Apparent,
and all the others as Commandery Princes.
Previously,
Zhān Qí resented his father for killing his mother
and repeatedly exposed his father's wrongdoings.
Chéng Zǔ said:
"How can you father and son be so cruel?"
When Gāo Xù came to court at this time,
he presented all of Zhān Qí's previous reports on court affairs.
Rén Zōng summoned Zhān Qí and showed them to him, saying:
"You, caught between father and son, brother and brother,
have slandered and instigated to this extent.
A young child is not worthy of execution."
He sent him to guard the imperial tombs in Fèngyáng.
Not long after,
Rén Zōng passed away.
Xuān Zōng rushed from Nánjīng for the mourning.
Gāo Xù planned to ambush him on the road,
but in his haste, he failed.
When the Emperor (Xuān Zōng) ascended the throne,
he granted Gāo Xù and Zhào Wáng especially generous treatment compared to other princely estates.
Gāo Xù made daily requests,
and also presented four proposals beneficial to the state and peaceful for the people.
The Emperor ordered the relevant authorities to implement them,
and also wrote back to thank him.
He then said to his officials:
"My imperial grandfather once warned my imperial father,
saying that my uncle had seditious intentions
and should be guarded against.
However, my imperial father treated him extremely generously.
Now, if what he says
is truly sincere,
then his old intentions have changed,
and we should not fail to comply."
Whenever he made a request,
the Emperor would accommodate his wishes.
Gāo Xù became even more unrestrained.
In the fifth month of the twenty-first year,
the Emperor became unwell.

The Imperial Bodyguard Commander Mèng Xián (孟賢) and others conspired with Wáng Shèchéng (王射成), an official of the Imperial Astronomical Bureau, and Yáng Qìng (楊慶)'s adopted son, an inner attendant, to forge an imperial edict.
They planned to administer poison to the Emperor,
and once he passed away,
the edict would be issued from within,
deposing the crown prince
and establishing Zhào Wáng (趙王) [Gāo Suì (高燧)].
Wáng Yú (王瑜), a battalion commander, had an in-law, Gāo Yǐzhèng (高以正),
who helped Mèng Xián (孟賢) and others plan the conspiracy.
Once the plot was set, Gāo Yǐzhèng (高以zhèng) informed Wáng Yú (王瑜).
Wáng Yú (王瑜) reported the conspiracy.
The Emperor said,
"How could such a thing happen!"
Mèng Xián (孟賢) was immediately arrested,
and the forged edict was found.
Mèng Xián (孟賢) and the others were all executed,
and Wáng Yú (王瑜) was promoted to Qianhu (千戶) of the Liáohǎi (遼海) Guard.
The Emperor looked at Gāo Suì (高燧) and asked,
"Was this done by you?"
Gāo Suì (高燧) was greatly frightened
and unable to speak.
The Crown Prince (Zhū Gāozhì 朱高熾) strongly interceded for him, saying,
"This was done by inferiors;
Gāo Suì (高燧) surely had no knowledge of it."
From then on, Gāo Suì (高燧) became more restrained.
When Rénzōng (仁宗) ascended the throne,
he increased the annual stipends of the two princes of Hàn (漢) and Zhào (趙) by twenty thousand shí (石) of grain each.
The following year,
he went to his domain in Zhāngdé (彰德) [city],
and bid farewell to the two guards of Chángshān (常山), the Left and Right.
When Xuānzōng (宣宗) ascended the throne,
he bestowed eighty qǐng (頃) of fields and gardens.
When the Emperor (Xuānzōng 宣zōng) captured Gāo Xù (高煦) and returned,
upon reaching Dānqiáo (單橋),
the Minister Chén Shān (陳山) welcomed the imperial carriage
and said,
"Zhào Wáng (趙王) [Gāo Suì (高燧)] and Gāo Xù (高煦) have been conspiring rebellion for a long time.
It would be advisable to move troops to Zhāngdé (彰德) [city]
and capture Zhào Wáng (趙王).
Otherwise, Zhào Wáng (趙王) will be restless and uneasy,
and will cause trouble again in the future, burdening your sacred thoughts."
The Emperor was undecided.
At that time, only Yáng Shìqí (楊士奇) believed it was not permissible.
Chén Shān (陳山) again invited Ministers Jiǎn Yì (蹇義) and Xià Yuánjí (夏原吉) to plead together.
The Emperor said,
"The late emperor greatly loved his two uncles.
Hàn Wáng (漢王) [Gāo Xù (高煦)] has cut himself off from Heaven,
and I dare not pardon him.
Zhào Wáng (趙王)'s rebellious intentions are not yet manifest,
and I cannot bear to betray the late emperor."
When Gāo Xù (高煦) arrived in the capital,
he also said that he had sent people to communicate with Zhào Wáng (趙王) to conspire.
Lǐ Yí (李儀), a supervising secretary in the Ministry of Revenue, requested to abolish his guards,
and Minister Zhāng Běn (張本) also spoke to that effect.
The Emperor did not listen.
Afterward, those who spoke out became more numerous.
The following year,
the Emperor, taking his words and the memorials of his officials, dispatched the Imperial Son-in-Law and Marquis of Guǎngpíng (廣平), Yuán Róng (袁容), to show them to Gāo Suì (高燧).
Gāo Suì (高燧) was greatly frightened,
and then requested to return the Chángshān (常山) Central Guard and the offices of the various pastures and ceremonial guards.
The Emperor ordered the collection of the returned guards
but granted him the ceremonial guards.
He died in the sixth year of Xuāndé (宣德).
His son, Huì Wáng (惠王) Zhān Què (瞻塙), succeeded him and
died in the fifth year of Jǐngtài (景泰).
His son, Dào Wáng (悼王) Qí Zī (祈鎡), succeeded him and
died in the fourth year of Tiānshùn (天順).
His son, Jìng Wáng (靖王) Jiàn Zhuó (見灂), succeeded him.
Both Huì Wáng (惠王) and Dào Wáng (悼王) had considerable faults,
but Jiàn Zhuó (見灂)'s wickedness was even greater.
He repeatedly robbed and killed people,
and also once, while drunk, tried to kill his uncle.
In the twelfth year of Chénghuà (成化),
the matter was reported.
An edict was issued to confiscate two-thirds of his stipend,
remove his official attire,
and wear a commoner's headscarf,
to study and practice rites.
Two years later,
Jiàn Zhuó (見灂)'s birth mother, Consort Lǐ (李氏), pleaded for him,
and he regained his official attire as before.
Jiàn Zhuó (見灂) was ultimately unable to change.
He doted on his youngest son, Yòu Zhǐ (祐枳),
and then falsely accused his eldest son, Yòu Cǎi (祐棌), of high treason,
and was again reprimanded by imperial edict.
He died in the fifteenth year of Hóngzhì (弘治).
His son, Zhuāng Wáng (莊王) Yòu Cǎi (祐棌), succeeded him and
died in the thirteenth year of Zhèngdé (正德).
His son, Kāng Wáng (康王) Hòu Yù (厚煜), succeeded him and
was known for his filial piety towards his grandmother, Consort Yáng (楊妃).
In the sixth month of the seventh year of Jiājìng (嘉靖),
an imperial rescript commended him.
In the winter of the following year,
there was a great famine within the borders.
Hòu Yù (厚煜) submitted a memorial,
requesting to relinquish one thousand shí (石) of his stipend to aid famine relief.
The Emperor praised the prince's concern for the country
and ordered the relevant officials to distribute grain,
not approving his resignation of the stipend.
When the Emperor made a southern tour,
Hòu Yù (厚煜) traveled far to welcome him,
and was ordered to increase his stipend by three hundred shí (石).
Hòu Yù (厚煜) was by nature generous and gentle.
He built a tower named
"Sī Xùn (思訓),"
where he often resided alone to read,
and his literary talent was abundant and beautiful.
His kinsman, the General of Aiding the State, Yòu Liáng (祐椋), and others frequently broke the law,
creating difficulties for the local authorities.
Hòu Yù (厚煜) shielded Yòu Liáng (祐椋).
Yòu Liáng (祐椋) was ultimately convicted
and both were censured.
Thereafter, the authorities became more determined to restrict the various imperial kinsmen by force.
A slave of Luòchuān Wáng (洛川王) Yì Lǜ (翊鏴) fought with a subordinate of Assistant Prefect Tián Shíyǔ (田時雨) over melons and beat him.
Tián Shíyǔ (田時雨) arrested the prince's slave.
Hòu Yù (厚煜) requested his release but did not get it;
the slave was eventually sentenced to military exile.
Soon after,
dozens of imperial kinsmen demanded their stipends.
Tián Shíyǔ (田時雨), seeing that the imperial kinsmen had beaten a prefectural official,
reported it to his superiors.
Prefect Fù Rǔlì (傅汝礪) arrested all the people from the various princely households.
Hòu Yù (厚煜) was consequently enraged and indignant,
and ultimately starved himself to death.
This was in the tenth month of the thirty-ninth year.
Hòu Yù (厚煜)'s son, Chénggāo Wáng (成皐王) Zài Yuán (載垸), memorialized the court,
and the case was handed to the judicial authorities for investigation.
Tián Shíyǔ (田時雨) was beheaded in the marketplace of Hénán (河南),
and Fù Rǔlì (傅汝礪) was exiled to the extreme frontier.
Hòu Yù (厚煜)'s son Zài Péi (載培) and Zài Péi (載培)'s son Yì Zī (翊錙) had both died earlier.
Yì Zī (翊錙)'s son, Mù Wáng (穆王) Cháng Qīng (常清), succeeded him and
was commended for his good conduct.
He died in the forty-second year of Wànlì (萬曆).
His heir apparent, Yóu Sōng (由松), had died earlier.
His younger brother, Shòuguāng Wáng (壽光王) Yóu Guì (由桂)'s son, Cí Xiāo (慈𤊟), succeeded him and
died.
Having no son,
Mù Wáng (穆王)'s younger brother, Cháng Huàn (常𡎦), succeeded him.
In the seventeenth year of Chóngzhēn (崇禎),
Zhāngdé (彰德) fell,
and he was captured.
Textual Notes

Biographies, Volume 7, Princes 4: Rénzōng's Sons: Zhèng Wáng (鄭王) Zhān Jùn (瞻埈) (Lújiāng Wáng (廬江王) Zài Yīn (載堙)), Yuè Wáng (越王) Zhān Yōng (瞻墉), Qí Wáng (蘄王) Zhān Yín (瞻垠), Xiāng Wáng (襄王) Zhān Shàng (瞻墡) (Zǎoyáng Wáng (棗陽王) Yòu Sī (祐楒)), Jīng Wáng (荊王) Zhān Gāng (瞻堈), Huái Wáng (淮王) Zhān Ào (瞻墺), Téng Wáng (滕王) Zhān Kǎi (瞻塏), Liáng Wáng (梁王) Zhān Máo (瞻𣚨), Wèi Wáng (衛王) Zhān Yán (瞻埏). Yīngzōng's Sons: Dé Wáng (德王) Jiàn Lín (見潾), Xǔ Wáng (許王) Jiàn Chún (見淳), Xiù Wáng (秀王) Jiàn Shù (見澍), Chóng Wáng (崇王) Jiàn Zé (見澤), Jí Wáng (吉王) Jiàn Jùn (見浚), Xīn Wáng (忻王) Jiàn Zhì (見治), Huī Wáng (徽王) Jiàn Pèi (見沛). Jǐngdì's Son: Huáixiàn Tàizǐ (懷獻太子) Jiàn Jì (見濟). Xiànzōng's Sons: Dàogōng Tàizǐ (悼恭太子) Yòu Jí (祐極), Qí Wáng (岐王) Yòu Lún (祐棆), Yì Wáng (益王) Yòu Bīn (祐檳), Héng Wáng (衡王) Yòu Huī (祐楎) (Xīnlè Wáng (新樂王) Zài Xǐ (載壐)), Yōng Wáng (雍王) Yòu Wén (祐橒), Shòu Wáng (壽王) Yòu Zhī (祐榰), Rǔ Wáng (汝王) Yòu Piāo (祐𣚨), Jīng Wáng (涇王) Yòu Shùn (祐橓), Róng Wáng (榮王) Yòu Shū (祐樞), Shēn Wáng (申王) Yòu Kǎi (祐楷). Xiàozōng's Son: Wèi Wáng (蔚王) Hòu Wěi (厚煒).
Rénzōng (仁宗) had ten sons.
Empress Zhāo (昭皇后) gave birth to Xuānzōng (宣宗), Yuè Wáng (越王) Zhān Yōng (瞻墉), and Xiāng Wáng (襄王) Zhān Shàng (瞻墡).
Consort Lǐ Xián (李賢妃) gave birth to Zhèng Wáng (鄭王) Zhān Jùn (瞻埈), Qí Wáng (蘄王) Zhān Yín (瞻垠), and Huái Wáng (淮王) Zhān Ào (瞻墺).
Consort Zhāng Shùn (張順妃) gave birth to Jīng Wáng (荊王) Zhān Gāng (瞻堈).
Consort Guō Guì (郭貴妃) gave birth to Téng Wáng (滕王) Zhān Kǎi (瞻塏), Liáng Wáng (梁王) Zhān Máo (瞻𣚨), and Wèi Wáng (衛王) Zhān Yán (瞻埏).
Zhèng Jìng Wáng (鄭靖王) Zhān Jùn (瞻埈)
was Rénzōng (仁宗)'s second son.
He was enfeoffed in the tenth month of the twenty-second year of Yǒnglè (永樂).
When Rénzōng (仁宗) died, the Empress ordered him and Xiāng Wáng (襄王) to oversee the state
to await Xuānzōng (宣宗).
In the first year of Xuāndé (宣德), when the Emperor campaigned in Luò'ān (樂安),
he again ordered him and Xiāng Wáng (襄王) to guard the capital.
In the fourth year, he took up his fief in Fèngxiáng (鳳翔).
In the eighth year of Zhèngtǒng (正統), an edict commanded him to move to Huáiqìng (懷慶),
to stay at the capital residence,
and the following year to go to his domain.
Zhān Jùn (瞻埈) was violent and cruel,
and repeatedly caused people to die under flogging.
Yīngzōng (英宗) appointed Censor Zhōu Yīng (周瑛) as his chief clerk,
and he became somewhat restrained.
He died in the second year of Chénghuà (成化).
His son, Jiǎn Wáng (簡王) Qí Yīng (祁鍈), succeeded him.
When Qí Yīng (祁鍈) was heir apparent,
Xiāng Wáng (襄王) came to the capital.
Passing through Xīnxiāng (新鄉), Qí Yīng (祁鍈) did not seek permission
but sent his chief clerk to welcome him.
Yīngzōng (英宗) heard of this and
was displeased,
sending a letter of rebuke.
Upon succeeding as prince, he committed many unlawful acts
and treated his heir apparent with little kindness.
Chief Clerk Jiāng Wànchéng (江萬程) admonished him
and was reprimanded and humiliated.
Jiāng Wànchéng (江萬chéng) reported this.
The Emperor sent the Duke of Yīngguó (英國公), Zhāng Mào (張懋), and the eunuch Wáng Yǔnzhōng (王允中) with an imperial edict to admonish him,
and he finally submitted a letter of apology.
He died in the eighth year of Hóngzhì (弘治).
His heir apparent, Jiàn Zī (見滋)'s mother, Consort Hán (韓妃), was not treated with respect by Qí Yīng (祁鍈).
Jiàn Zī (見滋) died prematurely, feeling dejected.
His son, Kāng Wáng (康王) Yòu Xīn (祐枔), succeeded him and
died in the second year of Zhèngdé (正德).
Having no son,
his cousin, Yì Wáng (懿王) Yòu Zé (祐檡), succeeded him and
died in the sixteenth year.
His son, Gōng Wáng (恭王) Hòu Wán (厚烷), succeeded him.
Shìzōng visited Chéngtiān.
Hòuwán welcomed and greeted him in Xīnxiāng,
and was granted an increase of three hundred dàn of salary.
He submitted a memorial detailing the virtuous and filial deeds of his mother, Yán Tàifēi.
An imperial edict ordered it to be handed to the Imperial Historiography Academy.
Afterward, when the Emperor held fasting rituals and Daoist offerings (zhāijiào),
the various princes competed to send envoys to offer incense,
but Hòuwán alone did not send any.
In the seventh month of Jiājìng twenty-seventh year (1548), he submitted a memorial,
asking the Emperor to cultivate virtue and study,
and presented four admonitions on "retaining reverence," "investigating principles," "restraining oneself," and "preserving sincerity,"
as well as ten chapters of linked pearls (liánzhū)
to remonstrate against the pursuit of immortality and elaborate construction (tǔmù).
His words were direct and cutting.
The Emperor was enraged
and imprisoned his envoy.
An imperial edict stated:
"Previously, there were members of the imperial clan who slandered, but they were not punished.
Now he imitates them again.
The Prince
is today's Xībó,
let him do as he pleases."
Two years later, the affair of Yòuzhān occurred,
and Hòuwán was consequently found guilty.
Originally,
Qíyīng had ten sons.
The heir apparent was Jiànzī,
the second was Jiànxīng, Prince of Méngjīn,
and the third was Jiànbó, Prince of Dōngyuán.
Jiànxīng's mother was favored by Qíyīng.
She tried to usurp the position of heir apparent,
but failed.
She secretly took the heir apparent's golden册 (cè, imperial seal/investiture) and left.
Qíyīng searched for it urgently,
and because of this resentment, he no longer attended court,
and his conduct became increasingly lawless.
Qíyīng reported this to Xiànzōng,
who reduced him to a commoner.
When Kāngwáng died
without a son,
Jiànxīng's son Yòuzhān would have been the one to succeed,
but he was disqualified due to his previous crime.
Instead, Yòuzé, son of the Prince of Dōngyuán, was established.
At this point, Yòuzhān sought to reclaim his title of Junwang (Prince of a Commandery).
Resentful that Hòuwán did not memorialize on his behalf,
he took advantage of the Emperor's anger,
listed forty crimes of Hòuwán,
and accused him of treason.
An imperial edict ordered the Fùmǎ and eunuchs to immediately interrogate him.
They returned with a report that there was no evidence of rebellion,
but that he had indeed built palaces and adopted titles resembling those of the imperial carriage.
The Emperor angrily said:
"Hòuwán slandered Our person,
and in his state, he was arrogant and disrespectful;
this is a great offense."
He was stripped of his title and imprisoned in Fèngyáng.
In Lóngqìng first year (1567), he was restored to his princely title
and his salary was increased by four hundred dàn.
From youth to old age, Hòuwán
wore plain clothes and ate vegetarian food.
His heir apparent, Zǎiyù, was diligent in his studies and possessed a profound nature.
Grieved that his father was unjustly imprisoned,
he built a hut outside the palace gate
and lived alone on straw for nineteen years.
When Hòuwán returned to his residence,
he finally entered the palace.
In Wànlì nineteenth year (1591),
Hòuwán died.
Zǎiyù said:
"According to the succession order of the Zhèng clan,
Méngjīn is the eldest.
The former Prince Jiànxīng,
having already been granted a posthumous title and restored to his rank,
the princely title should rightly go to Méngjīn."
Later, he repeatedly submitted memorials to earnestly decline.
The court officials of rites said:
"Although Zǎiyù deeply insists on humility and yielding,
the succession to the Prince of Zhèng has already passed through three generations.
There is no reason to change the established order in the middle.
It is appropriate for Zǎiyù's son, Yìxī, to succeed."
Zǎiyù persisted in his initial petition.
Therefore, Yòuzhān's grandson, Zǎixǐ, succeeded,
and Zǎiyù and Yìxī were allowed to live out their lives with the stipends of heir apparent and heir presumptive,
while their descendants would continue to be enfeoffed as Princes of Dōngyuán.
In the first month of twenty-second year (1594),
Zǎiyù submitted a memorial,
requesting that all members of the imperial clan be allowed to wear Confucian robes and take examinations,
regardless of whether they were domestic or foreign officials,
and that those who passed be appointed according to their talent and character.
An imperial edict granted his request.
The following year, he again presented his method for astronomical calculations of the precession of the equinoxes,
as well as his writings on musical theory.
His analyses were detailed and accurate,
and those who understood praised him.
He was posthumously granted the title Duānqīng.
During the Chóngzhēn reign,
Zǎixǐ's son Yìzhōng was granted death for his crimes,
and the state (princedom) was abolished.
Zǎiyīn, Prince of Lújiāng,
was the great-grandson of Prince Jiǎn.
In the second month of Chóngzhēn seventeenth year (1644),
when the rebels captured Huáiqìng,
Zǎiyīn straightened his official cap and robes,
and sat upright in the main hall.
When the rebels arrived,
he was seized,
and they tried to make him surrender.
He sternly cried:
"I am a feudal prince of the Celestial Dynasty,
how could I surrender to you rebel thieves!"
He cursed them without yielding and
was killed.
The rebels seized his eldest son Yìqín
and forced him north.
In the third month, passing through Dìngxīng,
he wrote a dying poem in an inn
and then starved himself to death.
Zhānyōng, Prince Yuèjìng,
was the third son of Rénzōng.
In Yǒnglè twenty-second year (1424), he was enfeoffed in Qúzhōu.
Before he went to his fief,
Xuānzōng granted him the farm estate in Chāngpíng.
He died in Zhèngtǒng fourth year (1439).
His consort Wú Shì committed suicide to accompany him,
and was posthumously named Zhēnhuì.
He had no descendants.
Zhānyín, Prince Qíxiàn,
was the fourth son of Rénzōng.
He was initially enfeoffed as Prince Jìnglè.
He died in Yǒnglè nineteenth year (1421),
and was posthumously named Zhuāngxiàn.
Upon Rénzōng's ascension,
he was additionally enfeoffed and given a posthumous title.
He had no descendants.
Zhānshàn, Prince Xiāngxiàn,
was the fifth son of Rénzōng.
He was enfeoffed in Yǒnglè twenty-second year (1424).
He was solemn and respectful, and had a good reputation.
In Xuāndé fourth year (1429), he went to his fief in Chángshā.
In Zhèngtǒng first year (1436), he was moved to Xiāngyáng.
When Yīngzōng was captured in the north,
among the princes,
Zhānshàn was the eldest and most virtuous,
and the hopes of many rested upon him.
The Empress Dowager ordered that the golden tally of Xiāngguó be brought into the palace,
but he was not summoned.
Zhānshàn submitted a memorial,
requesting the establishment of the eldest imperial son,
and that the Prince of Chéng supervise the state,
and that brave and wise men be recruited to welcome back the imperial carriage.
By the time the memorial arrived,
Jǐngdì had already been enthroned for several days.
When Yīngzōng returned to the capital
and resided in the Southern Palace,
Zhānshàn again submitted a memorial, suggesting that Jǐngdì should visit daily to inquire about his meals and well-being,
and lead his officials to pay respects on the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month,
without forgetting humility and obedience.
After Yīngzōng's restoration,
Shí Hēng and others falsely accused Yú Qiān and Wáng Wén of having plotted to enthrone an external prince.
The emperor somewhat suspected Zhānshàng.
After a long while,
two letters written by Zhānshàng were found in the palace,
and the golden tally of Xiāngguó was indeed in the empress dowager's chamber.
So, the emperor sent a letter to summon Zhānshàng,
comparing the two letters to the Jīnténg.
Upon entering the court,
he was banqueted in the private hall,
and rising from his mat, he requested:
"When your servant passed through Biàn,
the elders of Biàn blocked the road,
saying that the Regional Inspector Wáng Gài, a worthy man,
was unjustly arrested and sent to the imperial prison.
They wished for Your Majesty to investigate further."
The emperor immediately released Gài
and appointed him Minister of the Grand Court of Judicial Review.
An edict was issued to establish the Xiāngyáng Guard,
and officials were ordered to construct a tomb for the prince during his lifetime.
When he returned,
the emperor personally saw him off outside the Wǔmén,
shaking hands and weeping as they parted.
Zhānshàng bowed again hesitantly.
The emperor said,
"Uncle, what else do you wish to say?"
He bowed his head and said,
"The myriad lands await governance as a hungry man awaits food and a thirsty man awaits drink.
I wish for you to reduce punishments and lighten taxes."
The emperor bowed and replied,
"I respectfully accept your instruction."
He watched him leave through the Duānmén before returning.
Four years later, he again came to court.
The emperor ordered all officials to pay respects to the prince at his residence
and decreed that the prince should go to Chāngpíng to visit the Three Mausoleums.
When he took his leave to return,
the send-off ceremony was even more grand,
