and the emperor furthermore ordered that the prince and his sons could leave the city for hunting during the seasons,
which was an exceptional favor.
In the sixth year, he was summoned again,
but declined due to old age.
He received inquiries and gifts seasonally,
and the lavishness of his treatment
was unprecedented among the princes.
He passed away in the fourteenth year of Chénghuà.
His son, Prince Dìng Qíyōng, succeeded him and
passed away in the first year of Hóngzhì.
His son, Prince Jiǎn Jiànshū, succeeded him and
passed away in the third year.
His son, Prince Huái Yòucái, succeeded him.
He was fond of eagles and dogs,
and kept excellent horses.
He could travel eight hundred *lǐ* to Nányáng and back,
still before dusk.
His consort's father, Jǐng Hǎi, incited him to kill people.
Xiàozōng warned and admonished him
and exiled Hǎi and his associates.
Yòucái was fond of Taoist arts,
and his gifts were without restraint.
He also once contended with the Xīng residence over land,
leading to the arrest of over seventy families,
and the case remained unresolved for a long time.
The Minister of the Grand Court of Judicial Review, Wāng Lún, resolved it twice,
and then it was settled.
He passed away in the seventeenth year.
His younger brother, Prince Kāng Yòuzhì, succeeded him
and was also fond of Taoist arts.
He passed away in the twenty-ninth year of Jiājìng.
Having no sons,
his cousin, Prince Zhuāng Hòujíng, succeeded him from the Prince of Yángshān,
being a great-grandson of Prince Dìng.
At that time, the princely residence suffered a fire,
and the accumulated wealth of previous generations was all lost.
Hòujíng became humble and frugal,
saving his salary to supply the border,
and contributing gold to aid in the construction of the three halls.
He was twice granted letters and silks.
He served his adoptive mother, Grand Consort Wáng, and his birth mother, Grand Consort Pān,
and was known for his filial piety.
When Pān died,
she was temporarily placed in the eastern wing.
Grand Consort Wáng said,
"Your mother had a son,
and the state relies on him.
Do not, for my sake, avoid the main hall."
Hòujíng wept and said,
"Your servant dares not treat his mother with impropriety."
When she was buried,
he walked barefoot, supporting the coffin for fifty *lǐ*.
Scholars and officials who passed through Xiāng
all befriended him in humble attire.
He passed away in the forty-fifth year.
His son, Prince Jìng Zǎiyáo, succeeded him
and passed away in the twenty-third year of Wànlì.
His son, Yìmíng, succeeded him.
In the fourteenth year of Chóngzhēn,
Zhāng Xiànzhōng captured Xiāngyáng,
and Yìmíng was killed.
Previously,
when Grand Secretary Yáng Sìchāng was inspecting the army,
he designated Xiāngyáng as a military headquarters,
increasing the battlements, deepening the moats,
and storing military provisions, gold, bows, swords, and firearms from five provinces there.
In the second month of that year,
Xiànzhōng ambushed and killed Sìchāng's envoy on the road,
seized his credentials,
and entered Xiāngchéng by trickery with a few dozen cavalry.
A fire broke out at midnight,
and at dawn,
the bandits arrived in force.
They seized Yìmíng on the south city gate tower
and offered him a cup of wine, saying,
"The prince is innocent.
When the prince dies,
Sìchāng can repay the prince with his own death."
Then they killed the prince and Prince Guìyáng Chángfǎ,
set fire to the city gate tower,
and burned their bodies.
When the bandits left,
only a few inches of skull fragments were collected,
and forty-three consorts and concubines died.
Prince Fúqīng Chángchéng and Prince Jìnxián Chánggàn escaped.
When the news reached the emperor,
he was greatly shocked and saddened,
ordering the relevant authorities to prepare a funeral,
and conferred the posthumous title of Zhōngwáng.
Sìchāng paid respects to Prince Huì in Jīngzhōu.
The messenger thanked him, saying,
"Sir, your gracious visit to me,
I wish it had been to Xiāngyáng first."
This implied that the fall of Xiāngchéng
was Sìchāng's fault.
In the seventeenth year, Chángchéng succeeded as Prince Xiāng.
He resided temporarily in Jiǔjiāng,
later moved to Tīngzhōu,
and his final whereabouts are unknown.
Prince Zǎoyáng Yòusī
was a great-grandson of Prince Xiàn.
He was talented and skilled in writing,
and extensively read in books on astrology, calendrical calculations, medicine, and divination.
In the early Jiājìng period, he submitted a memorial,
requesting an investigation into Emperor Xīngxiàn.
Shìzōng, considering that this proposal came from a member of the imperial clan,
was sufficient to satisfy the general sentiment,
and praised him.
He further requested the abolition of the imperial clan's salaries,
to allow them to make a living through the four occupations,
and for the worthy among them to respond to the imperial examinations by shooting the target.
This was shelved and not implemented.
At that time, Prince Xiāng Yòuzhì was ill and incapacitated, neglecting affairs,
and the palace attendant Shào Hēng abused his power, acting wantonly,
even beating to death the maternal uncle of Prince Zhènníng.
Yòusī lured him there
and gouged out his eyes.
The emperor dispatched the Vice Minister of the Grand Court of Judicial Review, Yuán Zōngrú, along with eunuchs and Jǐnyī (guards) to investigate.
Hēng was sentenced to death,
and Yòusī was punished by being stripped of his princely title.
The emperor visited Chéngtiān,
and remembering Yòusī's earlier memorial,
restored his title.
Prince Jīng Xiàn Zhāngāng
was the sixth son of Rénzōng.
He was enfeoffed in the twenty-second year of Yǒnglè.
In the fourth year of Xuāndé, he took up his fief in Jiànchāng.
There was a giant snake in the palace,
coiling and hanging from the beam to the ground,
sometimes leaning on the prince's throne.
Zhāngāng was greatly frightened
and requested to move.
In the tenth year of Zhèngtǒng, he moved to Qízhōu.
In the second year of Jǐngtài, he submitted a memorial requesting an audience with the retired emperor.
This was not granted.
He passed away in the fourth year.
His son, Prince Jìng Qíhào, succeeded him
and passed away in the fifth year of Tiānshùn.
His son, Jiànxiāo, succeeded him.
Jìng Wáng's three sons.
The eldest was Jiàn Xiāo,
the second Dūliáng Wáng Jiàn Pǔ, and Fánshān Wáng Jiàn Jǐng.
Jiàn Xiāo and Jiàn Pǔ were born of the same mother.
Resenting his mother's favoritism towards Jiàn Pǔ,
Jiàn Xiāo imprisoned his mother,
deprived her of clothing and food,
and she eventually died.
Her coffin was left outside the gate.
He summoned Jiàn Pǔ to the rear garden
and flogged him to death.
He deceived Jiàn Pǔ's consort, Hē Shì, into the palace
and forced himself upon her.
His cousin, Dūchāng Wáng Jiàn Tán's wife, Máō Shì, was beautiful,
and he sought to have relations with her.
Jiàn Tán's mother, Mǎ Shì, guarded her strictly.
Jiàn Xiāo shaved Mǎ Shì's head and whipped her.
He piled earth on Jiàn Tán, crushing him to death,
and shackled Máō Fēi into the palace.
He often gathered hooligans,
lightly armed and in disguise,
crossed the Hàn Shuǐ,
and abducted people's wives and daughters.
Jiàn Jǐng, fearing that he too would be affected,
secretly informed Xiàozōng,
who summoned Jiàn Xiāo to the capital.
The emperor, presiding at Wénhuá Mén,
ordered court officials to convene a trial.
Jiàn Xiāo confessed,
was stripped of his princely status and made a commoner,
and imprisoned in the western palace.
After two years,
Jiàn Xiāo, from the western palace, made an accusation against Jiàn Jǐng,
falsely accusing him of plotting rebellion with the Chǔ Fǔ's Yǒng'ān Wáng.
The emperor sent an envoy to investigate,
but found no truth in it.
Jiàn Jǐng then reported that Jiàn Xiāo had privately manufactured bows and arrows
and had illicit designs with his son Yòu Bǐng.
This was verified as true,
and Jiàn Xiāo was granted death.
Yòu Bǐng was demoted,
and Jiàn Pǔ's son, Yòu Mǔ, inherited the title of Jīng Wáng.
This was the seventh year of Hóngzhì.
In the seventeenth year, he passed away,
and was posthumously named Hé.
His son, Duān Wáng Hòu Quán, succeeded.
He was humble and gentle by nature,
and keenly devoted to classical texts.
During the Jiājìng era, he fell ill
and resigned his emoluments.
This was not granted,
and Fùshùn Wáng Hòu Kūn was ordered to deputize in court audiences.
Hòu Kūn,
Hé Wáng's second son,
and his younger brother Yǒngxīn Wáng Hòu Huáng, were renowned for their poetry and painting.
When Hòu Quán's eldest son, Yǒngdìng Wáng Zài Sà, came of age,
Hòu Kūn immediately relinquished his temporary duties,
which people especially considered virtuous.
In the thirty-second year of Jiājìng,
Hòu Quán passed away.
Zài Sà had died earlier,
so his son, Gōng Wáng Yì Jù, succeeded.
From the time of Jìng Wáng's sons' mutual animosity, the Jīng [Princes]
lost their good reputation.
When Hòu Quán and his brothers felt the misfortune of their ancestors' family troubles,
they used ritual and deference to instruct and regulate their clan members.
Jiàn Jǐng's great-grandson, Zài Cěn, was especially humble and respectful,
and was praised for his literary accomplishments and conduct.
By custom, daughters of Jun Wáng requested emoluments from the court;
Zài Cěn's four daughters were all married to scholars
and did not request titles.
He once submitted two memorials, one "Yìng Zhào" and one "Zhèng Lǐ".
They received no reply.
He studied the Yì [Jīng] to exhaust its principles
and authored the Dà Yǐn Shān Rén Jí.
His sons, Yì Quán, Yì Yù, and Yì Jué, were all skilled in poetry.
The brothers often lived together in one building,
known as the Huā È Shè.
Yì Jù presented Zài Cěn as virtuous to instruct his sons.
His sons did not follow his teachings,
and the heir apparent Cháng Líng was especially cruel and self-indulgent.
Yì Jù reported this to the court,
and Cháng Líng was stripped of his status and made a commoner.
In the fourth year of Lóngqìng,
Yì Jù passed away.
His second son, Cháng Hōng, succeeded,
and died in the fourth year of Wànlì.
Having no sons,
his younger brother, Kāng Wáng Cháng Xiá, succeeded from the Ānchéng Wáng lineage,
and died in the twenty-fifth year of Wànlì.
His son, Dìng Wáng Yóu Fán, succeeded,
and died in the second year of Tiānqǐ.
His son, Cí Hóng, succeeded.
During the Chóngzhēn era,
the roving bandits Gē Lùyǎn and Zuǒ Jīn Wáng feigned surrender to the Chǔ commander.
Cí Hóng wished to befriend them,
so he invited them to a banquet
and lavishly displayed female musicians.
In the first month of the sixteenth year,
Zhāng Xiànzhōng captured Qízhōu.
Cí Hóng had died one month prior.
The bandits surrounded the princely palace
and plundered all the courtesans and musicians they found.
Huái Jìng Wáng Dǎn Ào,
Rénzōng's seventh son.
He was enfeoffed in the twenty-second year of Yǒnglè.
In the fourth year of Xuāndé, he took up his fief in Sháozhōu.
In the tenth month of Yīngzōng's ascension,
because Sháo had much malaria,
in the first year of Zhèngtǒng, he was moved to Ráozhōu.
He passed away in the eleventh year of Zhèngtǒng.
His son, Kāng Wáng Qí Quán, succeeded,
and passed away in the fifteenth year of Hóngzhì.
The heir apparent, Jiàn Lián, had died young,
without sons,
so his cousin, Dìng Wáng Yòu Qǐ, succeeded.
His amusements were without limit;
his attendants, relying on his power, were violent and tyrannical,
causing suffering in the territory.
His Chief Secretary, Zhuāng Diǎn, resigned, citing dereliction of duty in assistance and guidance.
An imperial edict did not permit it.
The investigating censor, Wāng Wénshèng, frequently challenged matters concerning the princely palace.
There was a madman named Gù Sōng,
who entered the princely gate with a knife and axe.
Palace guards apprehended and interrogated him,
and he falsely claimed Wāng had instructed him.
Diǎn reported this to the defending official.
The garrison eunuch, Lí Ān, once came to Ráo on official business,
and his retinue entered Duānlǐ Mén,
where they were flogged.
He bore a deep grudge against Yòu Qǐ.
Before this,
Yòu Qǐ possessed a famous qín named
"Tiān Fēng Huán Pèi".
Níng Wáng Chén Háo sought it,
but could not obtain it.
He also sought land by the lake,
but was not given it.
At this time, Chén Háo instigated Ān to memorialize Yòu Qǐ's transgressions and Wénshèng's false accusation.
An imperial edict was issued to the governor and inspector for interrogation.
Ān conspired with Chén Háo,
and without waiting for a report,
immediately arrested Diǎn and the palace guards for interrogation.
Diǎn's replies were arrogant,
so Chén Háo flogged him,
and he died in prison.
Many others were implicated.
Thereupon, Yòu Qǐ memorialized that Ān, harboring a grudge, had killed Diǎn and shielded Sōng.
The emperor sent the Chief Censor Jīn Xiànmín and the Grand Eunuch Zhāng Qīn to investigate.
Yòu Qǐ feared Chén Háo
and could not clear himself.
Qīn and others reported again that Yòu Qǐ trusted treacherous individuals and allowed them to be violent,
requesting he be severely warned.
Over twenty military guards were sentenced to frontier exile,
and Diǎn's injustice was never redressed.
In the third year of Jiājìng,
Yòu Qǐ passed away.
Having no sons,
his younger brother, Zhuāng Wáng Yòu Kuí, succeeded,
and died in the sixteenth year.
His son, Xiàn Wáng Hòu Táo, succeeded,
and died in the forty-second year.
His son, Gōng Wáng Zài Tái, succeeded,
and died in the fifth year of Wànlì.
His younger brother, Shùn Wáng Zài Jiān, succeeded,
and died in the twenty-third year.
His son, Yì Quán, succeeded.
Before Yì Quán became king,
he was intimate with the courtesan Wáng Ài,
who was secretly brought into the palace under the guise of a concubine.
Moreover, he ordered her to raise his concubine-born son Cháng Hóng as her own,
while Concubine Chén and the heir apparent Cháng Qīng both lost favor,
and secretly plotted to change the legitimate heir.
Censor Chén Wángdào reasoned with the king
and moved Wáng Ài to an outer residence.
Cháng Hóng then conspired with clan members Yì Quán and others,
entered the princely palace at night,
stole the seals, treasures, and goods, and left.
The defending official reported the matter.
Wáng Ài was sentenced to death,
Cháng Hóng was forced to commit suicide,
Yì Quán and others were stripped of their clan registration and permanently imprisoned,
and Yì Quán's four years of emoluments were revoked.
After a long time,
he passed away.
His son, Cháng Qīng, succeeded.
When the dynasty fell,
his whereabouts became unknown.
Téng Huái Wáng Zhān Kǎi,
Rénzōng's eighth son.
He was enfeoffed in Yúnnán in the twenty-second year of Yǒnglè,
but before he took up his fief,
he died in the first year of Hóngxī.
He had no heir.
Liáng Zhuāngwáng Zhānchán,
Rénzōng's ninth son.
Enfeoffed in the 22nd year of Yǒnglè.
In the early Xuāndé reign,
an edict granted Zhèng, Yuè, Xiāng, Jīng, and Huái, five princes, an annual stipend of 50,000 strings of paper money;
only Liáng received double that amount.
In the fourth year, he proceeded to his fief in Ānlù,
which was the former Yǐng princely residence.
Xiāngwáng Zhānshàn moved from Chángshā to Xiāngyáng.
Passing through Ānlù,
he lingered with Zhānchán, reluctant to leave.
Approaching their farewell,
Zhānchán sorrowfully said,
"Brothers will not see each other again,
what can be done!"
Those around him all wept.
In the first year of Zhèngtǒng, he stated that his residence was low and damp,
requesting a higher and drier location.
The emperor issued an edict saying that Yǐngzhong had suffered a poor harvest,
and that the matter would be handled after a good harvest.
It ultimately did not come to pass.
He died in the sixth year.
Having no son,
his enfeoffment was abolished.
The fields, residences, gardens, and lakes originally obtained by Liáng in Yǐng
were later all bestowed upon Xiāngwáng.
When Ruìzōng was enfeoffed in Ānlù,
he acquired all the fields of the Yǐng and Liáng princely residences,
to provide for the ancestral sacrifices of the two princes.
Wèi Gōngwáng Zhānshān,
Rénzōng's tenth son.
Enfeoffed in Huáiqìng in the 22nd year of Yǒnglè.
He was sickly in childhood,
and Xuānzōng loved him,
so he did not proceed to his fief.
When it was time to visit the imperial tombs annually,
he was always ordered to perform the sacrifices on behalf of others.
He was filial, cautious, and fond of learning,
known for his wisdom.
He died in the third year of Zhèngtǒng.
His consort, Lady Yáng, committed suicide,
and was granted the posthumous title Zhēnlìe.
Having no son,
his enfeoffment was abolished.
Yīngzōng had nine sons.
Empress Dowager Zhōu gave birth to Xiànzōng and Chóngwáng Jiànzé.
Consort Wàn Chénfēi gave birth to Déwáng Jiànlín, as well as imperial sons Jiànshí, Jíwáng Jiànjùn, and Xīnwáng Jiànzhì.
Consort Wáng Huìfēi gave birth to Xǔwáng Jiànchún.
Consort Gāo Shúfēi gave birth to Xiùwáng Jiànshù.
Consort Wéi Défēi gave birth to Huīwáng Jiànpèi.
Dé Zhuāngwáng Jiànlín,
Yīngzōng's second son.
Initially named Jiànqīng.
Enfeoffed as Róngwáng in the third year of Jǐngtài.
In the third month of the first year of Tiānshùn, the Crown Prince was reinstated,
and on the same day, Dé, Xiù, Chóng, and Jí, four princes, were enfeoffed,
each with an annual stipend of 10,000 *shí* of grain.
Initially established in Dézhōu,
he was later moved to Jǐnán.
He proceeded to his fief in the third year of Chénghuà.
He requested to obtain the fallow lands in Dōngchāng and Yǎnzhōu left by the two commoners of Qí and Hàn, and the lands of Báiwán, Jǐngyáng, and Guǎngpíng, three lakes.
Xiànzōng granted them all to him.
He further requested to cultivate Nánwàng Hú,
but this was disallowed due to the grain transport canal.
He then requested the former horse pastures of the commoner of Hàn.
Prefect Zhào Huáng stated that the land had reverted to private ownership,
and had been paying taxes for a long time,
so it should not be taken.
The emperor agreed.
In the early Zhèngdé reign,
an edict decreed that princely estates be taxed three *fēn* of silver per *mǔ*,
to be a permanent rate.
Jiànlín memorialized:
"In earlier years,
the princely estates in Yǎnzhōu were taxed twenty *shēng* per *mǔ* annually.
In Qīnghé county alone,
in the mid-Chénghuà reign, following the proposal of Vice Minister Sòng Mín,
it was five *shēng* per *mǔ* annually.
If the new edict is followed,
I will have no means to support myself."
The Ministry of Revenue insisted that Shāndōng had suffered continuous droughts and floods,
and the people were destitute,
so the edict should be followed.
The emperor said,
"Why should the prince worry about poverty?
Do not permit his request."
He died in the 12th year.
His son, Yìwáng Yòuróng, succeeded him.
In the Jiājìng reign,
the Ministry of Revenue discussed reviewing the mountain lands, lakes, and marshes requested by princely residences,
decreeing that all granted after the Xuāndé reign should be returned to the government.
The edict was approved for implementation.
Thereupon, the Governor-General of Shāndōng, Censor-in-Chief Shào Xī, memorialized that Défǔ's estates were all among those to be reclaimed.
He and Yòuróng impeached each other in memorials,
with Xī pressing the matter more urgently.
The Guard of Honor had an authorized strength of 1,700 soldiers.
Those who fled or died out were replaced by surplus able-bodied men.
Xī deemed this irregular,
and issued an order to Prefect Yáng Fǔ of Jǐnán to register all those who had been supplemented and not pay them.
The military officers rioted,
destroying the princely residence gate.
An edict ordered the arrest and interrogation of the Chief Secretaries Yáng Gǔ and
Yáng Mèngfǎ, the banishment of Vice Commander Xuē Níng of the Guard of Honor and military officer Táo Róng.
The prince was admonished to observe proper conduct
and not be influenced by common people to stir up more trouble.
Commentators said that Xī deliberately provoked the crime,
and that it was not entirely Yòuróng's fault.
This occurred in the eighth month of the 11th year.
By the 18th year,
Jīng and Huī, two princes, again requested to recover their reclaimed estates.
Yòuróng used this as a precedent for his own request.
An edict allowed him to retain the three lake lands,
and to levy taxes from them himself.
He died that year.
His grandson, Gōngwáng Zǎidēng, succeeded him,
and died in the second year of Wànlì.
His son, Dìngwáng Yìguǎn, succeeded him,
and died in the 16th year.
His son, Chángchí, succeeded him,
and died in the fifth year of Chóngzhēn.
His heir apparent, Yóushū, succeeded him.
In the first month of the 12th year,
the Dà Qīng army captured Jǐnán,
and he was taken captive.
Jiànshí,
Yīngzōng's third son.
Died young.
After the restoration,
no posthumous titles were conferred upon him.
Xǔ Dàowáng Jiànchún,
Yīngzōng's fourth son.
Enfeoffed in the third year of Jǐngtài.
Died the following year.
The ritual officials requested a princely funeral.
The emperor, considering the prince's youth,
reduced the scale of the ceremony.
Xiù Huáiwáng Jiànshù,
Yīngzōng's fifth son.
Born in Nángōng,
enfeoffed in the first year of Tiānshùn.
Proceeded to his fief in Rǔníng in the sixth year of Chénghuà.
Chief Secretary Liú Chéng presented a *Qiānqiū Rìjiàn Lù* (Record of Daily Observations through a Thousand Autumns),
which Jiànshù recited morning and night.
When proceeding to his fief,
fearing disturbance to the people along the way,
he ordered travel on alternate days.
His princely residence was cramped;
his attendants requested to move the Confucius Temple to expand it.
Jiànshù did not agree,
saying,
"Living near the academy,
and hearing the sounds of music and chanting from time to time,
is this not beautiful?"
When discussing the Classic of History concerning Xībó Kān Lí,
Chief Secretary Chéng supported Mr. Wú's theory,
saying,
"The one who *kān lí* was
Wǔwáng."
Right Chief Secretary Zhào Ruì supported Mr. Kǒng's theory,
saying,
"It was actually a matter of Wénwáng."
They debated until they lost color.
Jiànshù said,
"The meaning of the classics has no fixed conclusion;
it is not objectionable to go back and forth.
To be like this now
is not what the late emperor intended by selecting you two gentlemen."
He died in the eighth year of Chénghuà.
Having no son,
his enfeoffment was abolished.
Héng Gōng Wáng Yòuhuī
was Emperor Xiànzōng's seventh son.
In the twelfth year of Hóngzhì (1499), he was enfeoffed in Qīngzhōu.
He died in the seventeenth year of Jiājìng (1538).
His son, Zhuāng Wáng Hòuhuàn, succeeded him.
He once declined a stipend of five thousand *shí* to provide for the imperial clan,
and the clan members held him in high regard for it.
He died in the sixth year of Lóngqìng (1572).
His son, Kāng Wáng Zàiguī, succeeded him.
He died in the seventh year of Wànlì (1579).
He had no son.
His younger brother, Ān Wáng Zàifēng, succeeded him.
He died in the fourteenth year (1586).
His son, Dìng Wáng Yìhuò, succeeded him.
He died in the twentieth year (1592).
His son, Chángmóu, succeeded him.
Xīnlè Wáng Zàixǐ
was a grandson of Gōng Wáng.
He was learned and skilled in literary arts.
He sought out the compilations of various princes
and obtained dozens of them,
which he printed and circulated.
He also authored works such as "Hóngwǔ Shèngzhèng Sòng" and "Huángmíng Zhèngyào,"
many of which are worthy of transmission.
His paternal uncles, Gāotáng Wáng Hòuyīng and Qídōng Wáng Hòubǐng, were both renowned for their extensive learning and steadfast conduct.
During the Jiājìng era,
they twice received imperial edicts of commendation.
Yōngjìng Wáng Yòuyún
was Emperor Xiànzōng's eighth son.
Initially enfeoffed as Bǎoníng,
in the twelfth year of Hóngzhì (1499), he was enfeoffed in Héngzhōu.
The land was low and damp,
and the palace buildings were decaying and uninhabitable.
Strange occurrences repeatedly happened in his residence,
so he requested a relocation to Dōngpíngzhōu in Shāndōng.
Court officials argued that choosing another site and building anew
would be burdensome to the people and wasteful of resources.
They suggested that since Shēn Wáng's former residence was in Sìchuānzhōu,
it would be appropriate to move there.
The emperor approved the edict.
Soon after, it was deemed too far to move.
In the second year of Zhèngdé (1507),
the ground cracked,
the palace buildings were ruined,
and the prince died.
He had no son,
so the enfeoffment was abolished.
Shòudìng Wáng Yòuzhī
was Emperor Xiànzōng's ninth son.
In the fourth year of Hóngzhì (1491), he was enfeoffed on the same day as the four princes, Rǔ, Jīng, Róng, and Shēn.
In the eleventh year (1498), he took up residence in Bǎoníng.
In the first year of Zhèngdé (1506), because the line of Qí Wáng had died out,
he was reassigned to the Qí residence in Dé'ān.
His imperial guards wantonly harassed citizens.
Lǐ Chóng, the prefect, suppressed them
and was impeached and arrested.
Liú Péng, a commoner from Ānlù, accompanied Lǐ Chóng to the Grand Court of Revision for trial.
Lǐ Chóng had not known him
and was surprised.
Liú Péng said:
"The prefect is benevolent.
He suffered for the people,
and all the people are willing to die for him.
Why would he need to know me?"
Lǐ Chóng was eventually exonerated.
Yòuzhī heard this and regretted his actions,
later becoming known for his virtue.
He died in the twenty-fourth year of Jiājìng (1545).
He had no son,
so the enfeoffment was abolished.
Rǔ'ān Wáng Yòusì
was Emperor Xiànzōng's eleventh son.
In the fourteenth year of Hóngzhì (1501), he was enfeoffed in Wèihuī.
In the fifteenth year of Zhèngdé (1520), he requested an advance of ten years' worth of salt rations for wedding expenses.
An imperial edict granted an additional two thousand *yǐn* of Chánglú salt,
while his regular salt rations remained unchanged.
When Emperor Shìzōng toured the south,
he respectfully greeted him on the road.
He was greatly praised.
His stipend was increased by five hundred *shí*,
and he was bestowed with gold and silk.
He died in the twentieth year of Jiājìng (1541).
He had no son,
so the enfeoffment was abolished.
Jīngjiǎn Wáng Yòushùn
was Emperor Xiànzōng's twelfth son.
In the fifteenth year of Hóngzhì (1502), he was enfeoffed in Yízhōu.
He died in the sixteenth year of Jiājìng (1537).
His son, Hòují, died before being enfeoffed.
He had no son,
so the enfeoffment was abolished.
Róngzhuāng Wáng Yòushū
was Emperor Xiànzōng's thirteenth son.
In the early Zhèngdé era, he was still residing in the capital.
He requested land in Xìn'ānzhèn, Bàzhōu,
which was formerly pastureland.
A ministerial official stated:
"During the Yǒnglè era,
grass fields were established
to raise horses
for military preparedness.
It was not until the Chénghuà era that
favored courtiers began to request it as their estates.
Later, the two princely establishments of Qí and Shòu followed suit,
and this was never rectified.
When Emperor Xiàozōng focused on military affairs,
he cleared and returned the land to its original purpose,
not allowing private interests to override public good.
Now, Róng Wáng is scheduled to take up his domain soon,
so his request should not be granted."
In the third year (1508), he was enfeoffed in Chángdé.
Yòushū's appearance resembled that of Emperor Gāodì,
and he was somewhat arrogant and unrestrained in his domain.
Emperor Shìzōng decreed that the fishing and harbor taxes from Yuánjiāng Yǒugǎng, Tiānxīn, and Tuánpíng should be allocated to his princely residence.
He died in the eighteenth year of Jiājìng (1539).
His grandson, Gōng Wáng Zàijǐn, succeeded him.
He died in the twenty-third year of Wànlì (1595).
His son, Yìzhěn, succeeded him.
He died in the fortieth year (1612).
His son, Chángyuàn, succeeded him
and died.
His son, Xiàn Wáng Yóuxiāo, succeeded him
and died.
His son, Cízhào, succeeded him.
When Zhāng Xiànzhōng entered Húnán,
he fled to Chénxī with his consort mother, Lady Yáo,
and their ultimate fate is unknown.
Shēn Yì Wáng Yòukǎi
was Emperor Xiànzōng's fourteenth son.
He was enfeoffed in Zhōu,
but had not yet taken up his domain.
He died in the sixteenth year of Hóngzhì (1503).
He had no son,
so the enfeoffment was abolished.
Emperor Xiàozōng had two sons:
Emperor Wǔzōng and Wèi Wáng Hòuwěi,
both born to Empress Zhāng.
Wèi Dào Wáng Hòuwěi,
Emperor Xiàozōng's second son,
died at the age of three.
He was posthumously granted an additional title and谥号.
Collation Notes

Biographies, Chapter 8: Princes (Part 5) Emperor Shìzōng's Sons: Āichōng Tàizǐ Zàijī, Zhuāngjìng Tàizǐ Zàihòu, Jǐng Wáng Zàizhèn, Yǐng Wáng Zàikāng, Qī Wáng Zàiqì, Jì Wáng Zàiliè, Jūn Wáng Zàichóng. Emperor Mùzōng's Sons: Xiànhuái Tàizǐ Yìyì, Jìng Wáng Yìlíng, Lù Wáng Yìliú. Emperor Shénzōng's Sons: Bīn Wáng Chángbīn, Fú Wáng Chángxún, Yuán Wáng Chángzhì, Ruì Wáng Chánghào, Huì Wáng Chángrùn, Guì Wáng Chángyíng. Emperor Guāngzōng's Sons: Jiǎn Wáng Yóuhuì, Qí Wáng Yóují, Huái Wáng Yóumó, Xiāng Wáng Yóuxǔ, Huì Wáng Yóuzhēn. Emperor Xīzōng's Sons: Huáichōng Tàizǐ Círán, Dàohuái Tàizǐ Cíyù, Xiànhuái Tàizǐ Cíjiǒng. Emperor Zhuāngliè's Sons: Tàizǐ Cílàng, Huái Wáng Cíxuǎn, Dìng Wáng Cíjiǒng, Yǒng Wáng Cízhào.
Emperor Shìzōng had eight sons.
Consort Yán gave birth to Āichōng Tàizǐ Zàijī.
Consort Wáng gave birth to Zhuāngjìng Tàizǐ Zàihòu.
Empress Dowager Dù gave birth to Emperor Mùzōng.
Concubine Lú Jìngfēi gave birth to Jǐng Wáng Zàizhèn.
Concubine Jiāng Sùfēi gave birth to Yǐng Wáng Zàikāng.
Concubine Zhào Yìfēi gave birth to Qī Wáng Zàiqì.
Concubine Chén Yōngfēi gave birth to Jì Wáng Zàiliè.
Concubine Zhào Róngfēi gave birth to Jūn Wáng Zàichóng.
Āichōng Tàizǐ Zàijī,
Emperor Shìzōng's first son,
died young at the age of two months.
Zhuāngjìng Tàizǐ Zàihòu,
Emperor Shìzōng's second son.
In the eighteenth year of Jiājìng (1539),
when Emperor Shìzōng was about to embark on a southern tour,
he was appointed Crown Prince.
At just four years old,
he was ordered to oversee the state,
with Grand Secretary Xià Yán serving as his tutor.
Huo Tāo, Minister of War, and Zōu Shǒuyì, a director in the Ministry of Rites, presented a "Sacred Learning Charts for the Eastern Palace" to the prince.
It was suspected of being slanderous and critical,
and they nearly incurred punishment.
After the Emperor obtained the alchemist Duàn Cháoyòng,
he considered practicing cultivation and ritual arts.
He instructed the Ministry of Rites
to formulate the ceremonies for the Crown Prince's regency.
Yáng Zuì, the Minister of the Imperial Stud, remonstrated
and was beaten to death with a staff,
and the proposal for regency was also abandoned.
Luó Hóngxiān, Zhào Shíchūn, and Táng Shùnzhī, all officials in the Crown Prince's household, requested that the Crown Prince move out of his palace
to study in the Wénhuá Palace.
All were dismissed from office.
When the Imperial Ancestral Temple was completed,
the Crown Prince was ordered to preside over the sacrifice.
In the third month of the twenty-eighth year (1549), he underwent the capping ceremony.
He died two days later.
The Emperor ordered that a寝园 be built for him and Āichōng Tàizǐ together,
with annual sacrifices,
following the arrangement for other imperial mausoleums.
Jǐnggōngwáng Zài-zhèn
was the fourth son of Shìzōng.
In the eighteenth year of Jiājìng, he was made Crown Prince.
On the same day, Mùzōng Yùwáng was enfeoffed, and Zài-zhèn was enfeoffed as Jǐngwáng.
Later, the Crown Prince died.
Court officials stated that Yùwáng was next in line to be established.
The Emperor, considering that the former Crown Prince had not lived long,
delayed the decision.
He later believed the words of a Daoist alchemist,
and neither of the two princes was allowed to be seen.
Zài-zhèn, having been raised in the same residence as Yùwáng,
had no distinction in dwelling or clothing.
Zài-zhèn was young,
and those around him harbored ambitions to usurp the throne.
Their whispers gradually became known,
and there was considerable dissent both within and outside the court.
In the fortieth year, he went to his fiefdom in Dé'ān.
He died four years later.
The Emperor said to Grand Secretary Xú Jiē:
"This son always plotted to usurp the heir,
and now he is dead."
Initially,
when Zài-zhèn went to his fiefdom,
he requested many estates and fields.
The Board deliberated and granted them.
Shāshì in Jīngzhōu was not among the requests.
However, an imperial envoy demanded market taxes.
Prefect Xú Xuémó insisted on not giving them.
Another envoy collected firewood taxes from Liújiāgè in Hànyáng.
The judicial assistant, Wú Zōngzhōu, resisted.
Both were reprimanded.
Other lands, fields, lakes, and ponds that were encroached upon amounted to tens of thousands of qǐng.
The Prince had no sons.
He was buried in Xīshān.
His consorts and concubines all returned to reside in the capital residence,
and the enfeoffment was abolished.
Yǐngshāngwáng Zài-jùn
was the fifth son of Shìzōng.
He died before he was a month old.
Qīhuáiwáng Zài-fú
was the sixth son of Shìzōng.
Jì'āiwáng Zài-yíng
was the seventh son of Shìzōng.
Jūnsīwáng Zài-yú
was the eighth son of Shìzōng.
All three princes died before they were a year old.
They were posthumously granted additional titles and posthumous names.
Mùzōng had four sons.
Empress Lǐ gave birth to Xiànhuái Tàizǐ Yǐ-yì.
Empress Dowager Xiàodìng gave birth to Shénzōng and Lùwáng Yǐ-liú.
As for Jìngwáng Yǐ-líng,
his mother is unrecorded.
Xiànhuái Tàizǐ Yǐ-yì
was the eldest son of Mùzōng.
He died at the age of five,
and was posthumously granted the title Yùshìzǐ.
In the first year of Lóngqìng, he was posthumously honored.
Jìngdàowáng Yǐ-líng
was the second son of Mùzōng.
He died before he was a year old,
and was posthumously granted the title Lántiánwáng.
In the first year of Lóngqìng, he was posthumously granted additional titles and posthumous names.
Lùjiǎnwáng Yǐ-liú
was the fourth son of Mùzōng.
He was born in the second year of Lóngqìng,
and was enfeoffed at the age of four.
In the seventeenth year of Wànlì, he went to his fiefdom in Wèihuī.
Initially,
Yǐ-liú, as the Emperor's younger brother, resided in the capital residence.
Princely shops and princely estates were all over the imperial domain.
When he went to his fiefdom,
he returned them all to the government,
which were then managed by eunuchs.
Imperial shops and imperial estates became increasingly extravagant from this point on.
While Yǐ-liú resided in his fiefdom,
he frequently requested land for sustenance and salt,
and all his requests were granted.
Later, Fúfān thus made this a precedent.
In the early Míng dynasty,
in addition to the annual stipend for imperial princes,
pastureland and grazing grounds were allocated in appropriate amounts.
Occasionally, some would request abandoned land and river shoals,
most of which did not exceed a thousand qǐng.
Board officials could object in their memorials,
and not all requests were granted.
When Jǐngwáng went to his fiefdom,
gifts and grants were generally reduced.
As the Chǔ region was vast
and had much idle land,
an imperial decree granted it all to him.
When Jǐngfān was abolished,
Lù obtained Jǐng's former registered land,
amounting to as much as forty thousand qǐng,
and Board officials found no difficulty in it.
When Fúwáng Cháng-xún went to his fiefdom,
the land registers were revised again,
and the people's strength was further exhausted.
Every inch was seized from the common people,
causing unrest throughout the realm.
Commentators, tracing the origin of the matter,
often used Yǐ-liú as a pretext.
Yǐ-liú was fond of literature and
diligent and disciplined by nature.
He remitted his annual income to the court,
contributing to construction and border defense without reservation,
which pleased the Emperor even more.
In the forty-second year,
when the Empress Dowager's mournful inquiry arrived,
Yǐ-liú was so overcome with grief that he neglected sleep and food,
and died shortly thereafter.
His heir Cháng-fāng was young,
so his mother, Concubine Lǐ, managed the affairs of the fiefdom.
At that time, Fúwáng often submitted requests
and obtained imperial decrees directly.
The Emperor also issued decrees directly
in response to the princely consort's requests,
showing no difference.
Board officials stated:
"The princely consort's four proposals,
such as the due payment of monthly stipends to military officers
and the prevention of encroachment on Yìhé Diàn,
should certainly be allowed.
However, as for the desire for advance payment of the annual stipend
and the desire to establish more princely estates,
these should not be allowed.
Furthermore, they bring no benefit whatsoever to the Prince,
but merely allow those in the princely residence to daily exploit the common people
and fill their private purses.
In the future, with thousands of branches and millions of descendants,
requests will become more frequent daily,
and even all the land registers of the imperial treasury
will not be enough to satisfy the princely residences."
No reply was received.
In the forty-sixth year,
Cháng-fāng succeeded.
During the Chóngzhēn reign,
roving bandits disturbed Qín, Jìn, and Héběi.
Cháng-fāng submitted a memorial reporting the emergency,
stating:
"The city walls of Wèihuī are low and the soil is poor.
I request three thousand selected guards to assist in defense,
and I will donate ten thousand gold coins from my annual income to fund the provisions,
without bothering the Minister of Agriculture."
The court praised him.
When bandits desecrated the tomb of his princely consort,
Cháng-fāng reported:
"The bandits are spreading, gradually reaching north of the Yangtze.
The imperial tombs of Fèng and Sì are at risk,
and they should be suppressed and annihilated early."
At that time, among the princes, only Zhōu and Lù were able to respond promptly to the national crisis.
Later, when the bandits reached Zhōngzhōu,
Cháng-fāng became a refugee in Hángzhōu.
In the sixth month of the second year of Shùnzhì, he surrendered to our Great Qīng dynasty.
Shénzōng had eight sons.
Empress Wáng gave birth to Guāngzōng.
Consort Zhèng Guìfēi gave birth to Fúwáng Cháng-xún and Yuánwáng Cháng-zhì.
Consort Zhōu Duānfēi gave birth to Ruìwáng Cháng-hào.
Consort Lǐ Guìfēi gave birth to Huìwáng Cháng-rùn and Guìwáng Cháng-yíng.
As for Bīnwáng Cháng-yù
and Yǒngsīwáng Cháng-pǔ,
their mothers are unrecorded.
Bīn'āiwáng Cháng-yù
was the second son of Shénzōng.
He died at the age of one.
Fúgōngwáng Cháng-xún
was the third son of Shénzōng.
Initially,
Empress Wáng had no sons.
Princely Consort Wáng gave birth to the eldest son,
who later became Guāngzōng.
Cháng-xún was next,
and his mother, Consort Zhèng Guìfēi, was the most favored.
The Emperor delayed establishing a Crown Prince for a long time,
leading to suspicions both within and outside the court that Guìfēi intended to establish her own son.
Memorials on this matter were submitted in succession,
leading to banishments one after another,
but those who spoke out did not stop.
The Emperor was deeply annoyed by this.
Only in the twenty-ninth year was Guāngzōng established as Crown Prince.
Cháng-xún was enfeoffed as Fúwáng,
with wedding expenses reaching three hundred thousand,
and construction of his Luòyáng residence reaching two hundred eighty thousand,
ten times the usual standard.
Court officials submitted hundreds of memorials requesting that the Prince go to his fiefdom.
No reply was received.
It was not until the forty-second year that he was finally ordered to go to his fiefdom.
Previously,
within the Four Seas, there was great prosperity.
The emperor's dispatched tax envoys and mine envoys were all over the realm.
Monthly tributes arrived,
with bright pearls, rare treasures, fine furs, and brocades piled up like mountains.
Other extorted gains and profits amounted to hundreds of millions.
By this time, much of it was used to support Cháng Xún.
As he was about to depart, passing through the palace gate,
he was recalled several times,
with a stipulation to enter court once every three years.
An imperial edict granted him 40,000 qǐng of farmland.
The supervising officials strongly argued against it,
and Cháng Xún also submitted a memorial declining it,
so it was reduced by half.
As the fertile lands of the Central Plains were insufficient,
land was taken from Shāndōng and Húguǎng to supplement it.
He also memorialized requesting the confiscated properties of the late Grand Secretary Zhāng Jūzhèng,
as well as miscellaneous taxes from the reed-covered islets along the Jiāng river from Jiāngdū to Tàipíng,
and Sichuan salt wells and tea monopoly silver for his own benefit.
The accompanying readers and attendants,
under the pretext of surveying land,
traveled by post-horse between Hénánběi, Qí, and Chǔ,
causing disturbance wherever they went.
He also requested 1,300 yīn of Huái salt,
to set up shops in Luòyáng to trade with the people.
The imperial envoys arriving in Huái and Yáng to collect salt
often extorted several times the amount through embezzlement.
And while the Central Plains traditionally consumed Hédōng salt,
due to the switch to Huái salt,
it was forbidden to sell salt not originating from the princely shops.
The Hédōng salt permits were blocked and could not circulate,
which consequently depleted border provisions.
Court officials requested that the princely salt be reissued to Hédōng,
and moreover, that he should not trade with the common people.
This was not heeded.
The emperor had long remained secluded,
and generally did not review the memorials submitted by his officials.
Only the Fú Fān's envoys were allowed access through the Zhōngzuǒmén,
making several requests a day,
with approvals given in the evening for morning requests.
Villains and fugitives from all directions,
probing for imperial intentions,
rushed to profit like wild animals.
This continued throughout the reign of Wànlì.
By the time of Chóngzhēn,
Cháng Xún, being a close relative of exalted status,
was treated with respect by the court.
Cháng Xún spent his days secluded, drinking strong wine,
his only interests being women, entertainers, and music.
When roving bandits arose in Qínzhōng,
and Hénán suffered a great drought and locust plague,
people resorted to cannibalism.
There was widespread murmuring among the populace,
saying that the late emperor had depleted the realm to enrich the prince,
and that Luòyáng was wealthier than the imperial palace.
Reinforcements passing through Luòyáng
loudly declared:
"The princely mansion has millions in gold and silver,
yet we are left to starve and die at the hands of bandits!"
Lǚ Wéiqí, the Nánjīng Minister of War, who was then at home,
was frightened upon hearing this,
and informed Cháng Xún of the dangers,
but he paid no attention.
In the winter of the thirteenth year,
Lǐ Zìchéng successively captured Yǒngníng and Yíyáng.
In the first month of the following year,
Councillor Wáng Yìnchāng led his troops to prepare for defense.
Grand Commander Wáng Shàoyǔ,
and Deputy Generals Liú Jiànyì and Luó Tài each led their forces to arrive.
Cháng Xún summoned the three generals,
and hosted a banquet for them, treating them with special courtesy.
A few days later,
the bandits arrived in large numbers,
attacking the city.
Cháng Xún offered a thousand pieces of gold to recruit brave warriors,
who rappelled out and,
using spears, entered the bandit camp.
The bandits retreated slightly.
At midnight,
Shàoyǔ's personal guard called out to the bandits from atop the city wall, chatting and laughing,
then brandished their swords, killed the defenders on the parapet,
burned the city tower,
and opened the North Gate to let the bandits in.
Cháng Xún rappelled down the city wall
and hid in the Yíng'ēnsì temple.
The next day,
the bandits tracked him down and seized him,
whereupon he was killed.
Two attendants prostrated themselves over his body and wept.
The bandits dragged them away.
The attendants cried out:
"The prince is dead, we do not wish to live.
We beg for a coffin to collect the prince's bones,
and we will have no regrets even if we are ground to powder."
The bandits, moved by their righteousness, granted their wish.
A single inch-thick paulownia wood coffin,
loaded onto a broken cart,
and the two men immediately hanged themselves beside it.
Prince's Consort Zōu Shì and the heir apparent Yóu Sōng fled to Huáiqìng.
The bandits set fire to the princely palace,
which burned for three days without ceasing.
Upon hearing of the event,
the emperor was greatly shocked and saddened,
and suspended court for three days,
ordering the Hénán officials to re-inter the body.
In the seventh month of autumn in the sixteenth year,
Yóu Sōng inherited the title.
The emperor personally selected a precious jade belt from the palace and bestowed it upon him.
In the third month of the following year,
the capital fell,
and Yóu Sōng, along with Prince Lù Cháng Fāng, both fled from the bandits to Huái'ān.
In the fourth month,
Mǎ Shìyīng, the Governor-General of Fèngyáng, and others welcomed Yóu Sōng into Nánjīng.
On the day Gēng Yín in the fifth month,
he was proclaimed Regent.
Shǐ Kěfǎ, Minister of War, Gāo Hóngtú, Minister of Revenue, and Shìyīng were all appointed Grand Secretaries,
with Shìyīng retaining command of Fèngyáng military affairs.
On the day Rén Yín, he enthroned himself in Nánjīng,
adopting the spurious reign title Hóngguāng.
Shǐ Kěfǎ was appointed Commander-in-Chief north of the Jiāng river.
Shìyīng was summoned to court,
and Huái, Yáng, Fèng, and Lú were divided into four garrisons,
commanded by Grand Commanders Huáng Dégōng, Liú Liángzuǒ, Liú Zéqīng, and Gāo Jié.
Yóu Sōng was dim-witted by nature,
and indulged in wine, women, and entertainment,
delegating authority to Shìyīng and Shìyīng's partisan Ruǎn Dàchéng,
who was promoted to Minister of War,
and put in charge of inspecting river defenses.
The two spent their days selling official posts and titles, and settling personal grudges.
Details of these matters are found in the biographies of various ministers.
Not long after,
a man named Wáng Zhīmíng fraudulently claimed to be the Crown Prince of Emperor Zhuāngliè,
and was imprisoned.
There was also a woman, Tóng Shì,
who claimed to be Yóu Sōng's consort,
and was also imprisoned.
Thereupon, there was an uproar both within and outside the court.
In the third month of the following year,
Zuǒ Liángyù, Marquis of Níngnán, raised an army in Wǔchāng,
under the pretext of rescuing the Crown Prince and executing Shìyīng,
and sailed eastward down the river.
Ruǎn Dàchéng, Huáng Dégōng, and others led armies to resist him.
Meanwhile, our great Qīng army crossed the river on the day Jǐ Chǒu in the fifth month of that year.
On the night of Xīn Mǎo,
Yóu Sōng fled to Tàipíng,
presumably heading for Dégōng's army.
On Rén Chén,
Shìyīng, accompanied by Yóu Sōng's mother-consort, fled to Hángzhōu.
On Guǐ Sì,
Yóu Sōng arrived in Wúhú.
On Bǐng Shēn,
the great army arrived north of Nánjīng city,
and civil and military officials surrendered.
On Bǐng Wǔ,
Yóu Sōng was captured and brought to Nánjīng.
On the day Jiǎ Yín in the ninth month,
he was taken to the capital.
Yuán Huái Wáng Cháng Zhì,
the fourth son of Shénzōng.
Died in infancy at one year old.
Ruì Wáng Chánghào,
was the fifth son of Shénzōng.
Initially,
the Crown Prince had not yet been established.
There was an imperial decree to enfeoff three princes simultaneously,
namely Guāngzōng, Fú Wáng, and Chánghào.
Soon after, due to disputes among officials,
it was dropped.
In the twenty-ninth year [of Shénzōng's reign],
the Eastern Palace was established,
and he was enfeoffed on the same day as Fú, Huì, and Guì Wáng.
Chángxún, being the eldest,
was the first to go to his domain.
Chánghào was already twenty-five years old,
but his marriage had not yet been arranged.
Officials repeatedly submitted memorials,
but generally received no reply.
Instead, funds were daily extracted from the Ministry of Revenue for marriage expenses,
amounting to over one hundred and eighty thousand [taels],
which were stored in the palace.
Moreover, it was said that ceremonial robes and caps could not be prepared.
In the seventh year of Tiānqǐ, he went to his domain in Hànzhōng.
During the Chóngzhēn era,
the roving bandits became rampant,
and his domain was in the path of the bandits.
In the seventh year, he submitted a memorial stating:
“Your servant, a kinsman of the late emperor,
had the fortune to serve in the western domain.
Before a year had passed, the bandits arrived.
When the western bandits crossed the river again,
they infiltrated Hànxīng,
sacked Xúnyáng,
and pressed towards Xīng'ān.
Zǐyáng, Pínglì, and Báihé successively fell.
The supervising minister, Hóng Chéngchóu, rode alone with armor wrapped around him, entering and exiting the myriad mountains,
and only then did the bandits retreat in defeat.
Your servant donated over seven thousand taels of silver for rewarding the army and relieving the hungry.
At this time, Governor Liàn Guóshì moved his troops to Shāng and Luò,
and Investigating Censor Fàn Fùcuì rushed to Hànzhōng,
and the border area became somewhat peaceful.
Soon after, Fèngxiàn was again captured,
the Sichuan bandits entered Qínzhōu,
and the Chu bandits advanced on Xīng'ān.
In the sixth month, they then invaded the prefecture’s borders.
Fortunately, the generals staunchly resisted them relying on the river,
and the bandits' strength slightly receded.
Your servant is in a deep valley amidst the myriad mountains,
with bandits approaching from all four sides.
Annihilation is imminent.
Your servant, a close relative,
is in the most remote of domains,
yet the bandits are extremely pressing.
I only implore Your Majesty to take pity.”
Chánghào, while in the palace,
had his clothing and ceremonial rank downgraded.
He was fond of Buddhism and did not approach women.
When the bandits pressed into Qínzhōng,
the generals and officials could not rescue him,
and he begged for troops from Shǔ.
Commander-in-chief Hóu Liángzhù reinforced him,
and he then fled to Chóngqìng.
Many scholars and officials from Lǒngxī brought their families to follow him.
In the seventeenth year [of Chóngzhēn's reign],
Zhāng Xiànzhōng captured Chóngqìng,
and Chánghào was seized
and killed.
At that time, there was no cloud in the sky, yet it thundered three times,
and many followers died with him.
Huì Wáng Chángrùn
was the sixth son of Shénzōng.
When Fú Wáng went to his domain,
the imperial treasury was emptied.
Eunuchs, under the pretext of royal marriages and enthronements,
demanded funds from the Ministry of Revenue to fill the palace coffers.
The required amount often reached several hundred thousand,
with jewels of comparable value.
The Ministry of Revenue could not provide them.
Chángrùn and his younger brother Chángyīng were twenty years old,
but neither had their marriages arranged.
Later, military affairs became urgent,
and the ceremonies were finally reduced and completed.
In the seventh year of Tiānqǐ, he went to his domain in Jīngzhōu.
In the twelfth month of the fifteenth year of Chóngzhēn,
Lǐ Zìchéng again captured Yílíng and Jīngmén.
Chángrùn fled to Xiāngtán,
and Zìchéng entered and occupied Jīngzhōu.
When Chángrùn crossed the Xiāng River,
he encountered a storm at Língyángjī,
and many palace women were swept away and drowned.
He barely escaped with his life
and joined Jí Wáng in Chángshā.
In the eighth month of the sixteenth year,
Zhāng Xiànzhōng captured Chángshā.
Chángrùn fled to Héngzhōu,
joining Guì Wáng.
Héngzhōu subsequently fell,
and he fled with Jí Wáng and Guì Wáng to Yǒngzhōu.
Investigating Censor Liú Xīzuò dispatched people to escort the three princes into Guǎngxī,
while he himself confronted the bandits.
Yǒngzhōu fell,
and Xīzuò died.
Guì Duān Wáng Chángyīng
was the seventh son of Shénzōng.
In the seventh year of Tiānqǐ, he went to his domain in Héngzhōu.
In the sixteenth year of Chóngzhēn,
Héngzhōu fell.
He fled with Jí and Huì Wáng to Guǎngxī,
residing in Wúzhōu.
In the second year of Dà Qīng Shùnzhì,
the grand army pacified Jiāngnán,
and Fú Wáng was captured.
Former Minister Chén Zǐzhuàng and others intended to enthrone Chángyīng as regent.
However, Táng Wáng had already enthroned himself in Fújiàn,
so the plan was dropped.
That year,
he died in Cāngwú.
His eldest son had already died earlier,
and his second son, Ānrén Wáng Yóuláng, also died not long after.
His third son, Yóuláng,
was enfeoffed as Yǒngmíng Wáng during the Chóngzhēn era.
In the eighth month of the third year [of Shùnzhì],
the grand army took Tīngzhōu
and captured Táng Wáng Yùjiàn.

Thereupon, Governor-general of Guǎngdōng and Guǎngxī Dīng Kuíchǔ, Governor of Guǎngxī Qú Shìsì, Investigating Censor Wáng Huàchéng, and veteran minister Lǚ Dàqì and others jointly nominated Yóuláng as regent.
His mother, Consort Wáng, said:
“My son is not equal to this task;
I wish you would choose a more suitable person.”
But Kuíchǔ and the others became even more resolute
and conspired to welcome him in Wú.
On the fourteenth day of the tenth month, he was inaugurated as regent in Zhàoqìng,
with Kuíchǔ, Dàqì, and Shìsì appointed as Grand Secretaries,
and others receiving various official posts.
In the same month, the grand army took Gànzhōu.
Eunuch Wáng Kūn hurriedly escorted Yóuláng back to Wúzhōu.
Shìsì and others strongly argued against it,
so he returned to Zhàoqìng.
In the eleventh month,
Táng Wáng’s younger brother Yùyuè sailed from Mǐn to Yuè.
At that time, former Minister Sū Guānshēng withdrew his troops and fled to Guǎngzhōu.
He conspired with Administration Commissioner Gù Yuánjìng and Commander-in-chief Lín Chá and others to enthrone Yùyuè,
who took the false reign title Shàowǔ,
and confronted Yóuláng.
In the same month, Yóuláng also enthroned himself in Zhàoqìng,
taking the false reign title Yǒnglì,
and dispatched Vice Minister of War Lín Jiādǐng to suppress Yùyuè.
Meanwhile, the grand army advanced from Fújiàn to take Guǎngzhōu,
captured Yùyuè,
and Guānshēng hanged himself.
Libationer Liáng Cháozhōng, Minister of the Imperial Stud Hò Zihéng, and others all died.
Zhàoqìng was greatly shaken,
and Wáng Kūn again escorted Yóuláng to Wúzhōu.
In the second month of the following year,
he fled via Pínglè and Xúnzhōu to Guìlín.
Kuíchǔ abandoned Yóuláng
and fled to Cēnxī,
surrendering to the grand army.
Soon after, Pínglè could not be defended,
and Yóuláng was greatly terrified.
At that time, Commander-in-chief of Wǔgāng Liú Chéngyǐn arrived with troops in Quánzhōu.
Wáng Kūn requested to go to him.
Shìsì strongly advised against it.
He did not listen.
Then he left Shìsì and Commander-in-chief Jiāo Lián to defend Guìlín,
enfeoffed Chén Bāngchuán as the Marquis of Sī'ēn,
to guard Zhāopíng,
and then proceeded to Chéngyǐn's army.
In the third month, he enfeoffed Chéngyǐn as Duke of Ānguó,
and Imperial Guards Commander Mǎ Jíxiáng and others as Earls.
Chéngyǐn took Yóuláng back to Wǔgāng,
renamed it Fèngtiān Fǔ,
and all governmental affairs were decided there.
SuíPíng Gōngzhǔ,
in the seventh year of Tiānqǐ, married Qí ZànYuán.
At the end of ChóngZhēn,
ZànYuán fled to Nánjīng,
but the Princess had died earlier.
Lè'Ān Gōngzhǔ
married Gǒng YǒngGù.
YǒngGù,
courtesy name HóngTú,
was from WǎnPíng.
He loved to read
and was full of talent.
In the second month of the sixteenth year of ChóngZhēn,
the emperor summoned dukes, marquises, and earls to the DéZhèng Diàn,
saying:
"According to ancestral tradition,
meritorious officials and imperial sons-in-law are to enter the Directorate of Education to study
and practice military strategy, archery, and horsemanship.
Do any of you officials have sons or younger brothers?"
ChéngGuó Gōng Zhū ChúnChén, DìngGuó Gōng Xú YǔnZhēn, and others all replied that theirs were too young.
But YǒngGù alone submitted a memorial,
requesting to enroll in the Imperial Academy.
The emperor praised and rewarded him.
When Governor Zhào GuāngBiàn was imprisoned due to border affairs,
YǒngGù specially memorialized to plead for him.
He also requested the restoration of the temple name and posthumous title for Emperor JiànWén.
Although these matters were not carried out,
contemporary opinion approved of them.
In the spring of JiǎShēn,
when rebels broke through Xuān and Dà,
Lǐ BāngHuá requested that the Crown Prince move south,
but was blocked by dissenting opinions.
When the situation became critical,
the emperor secretly summoned YǒngGù and XīnLè Hóu Liú WénBǐng to escort the journey.
They kowtowed and said:
"As close subjects, we do not keep armor;
it is difficult for us to fight the rebels empty-handed."
They all wept facing each other.
On the nineteenth day,
the capital fell.
At that time, the princess had already died
and was not yet buried.
YǒngGù tied his five children with yellow ropes to the side of her coffin,
saying:
"These are the emperor's nephews and nieces;
they must not be defiled by rebel hands."
He then drew his sword and cut his own throat,
and his entire family immolated themselves.
Emperor XīZōng had two daughters.
Both died young.
Emperor ZhuāngLiè had six daughters.
KūnYí Gōngzhǔ
was born to Empress Zhōu.
She was posthumously enfeoffed.
ChángPíng Gōngzhǔ
was sixteen years old,
and the emperor had chosen Zhōu Xiǎn to marry the princess.
As the wedding approached,
it was postponed due to the rebel threat.
When the city fell,
the emperor entered the ShòuNíng Gōng.
The princess tugged at the emperor's clothes and wept.
The emperor said:
"Why were you born into my family!"
He swung his sword and struck her,
severing her left arm;
he also struck ZhāoRén Gōngzhǔ in the ZhāoRén Diàn.
Five days later,
Princess ChángPíng revived.
In the second year of DàQīng ShùnZhì, she submitted a memorial saying:
"This servant, who narrowly escaped death,
lives precariously under the vast heaven;
I wish to shave my head and become a nun dedicated to the Void King,
to slightly express my boundless sorrow."
An edict disallowed this,
ordering Xiǎn to remarry the former princess,
and granting her land, residences, money, carriages, and horses with generous additions.
The princess wept.
She died of illness the following year.
She was granted a burial outside GuǎngNíng Mén.
The remaining three daughters
all died young,
and there are no records.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter Ten: Guō ZǐXīng, Hán Lín'Ér
Guō ZǐXīng's
ancestors were from CáoZhōu.
His father, Duke Guō,
as a young man, traveled to DìngYuǎn practicing prognostication,
and his predictions of good and ill fortune were often accurate.
A wealthy man in the district had a blind daughter with nowhere to go,
so Duke Guō married her,
and his family became increasingly prosperous.
They had three sons,
ZǐXīng being the middle one.
When he was first born,
Duke Guō divined a good omen for him.
When he grew up,
he was chivalrous
and enjoyed entertaining guests.
At a time when the Yuán government was in turmoil,
ZǐXīng dispersed his family wealth,
slaughtered oxen, and poured wine,
forming alliances with brave men.
In the spring of the twelfth year of ZhìZhèng,
he gathered several thousand young men
and suddenly occupied HáoZhōu.
Tàizǔ went to join him.
The gatekeepers, suspecting him of being a spy,
seized him and reported him to ZǐXīng.
ZǐXīng was struck by Tàizǔ's appearance,
untied him, spoke with him,
took him into his command,
made him a squad leader of ten,
and he often distinguished himself in battles.
ZǐXīng was pleased,
and his second wife, the younger Lady Zhāng, also pointed at Tàizǔ and said:
"This is an extraordinary person."
So she married him to Miss Mǎ, whom she had raised,
who later became Empress XiàoCíGāo.
Initially,
ZǐXīng had four co-initiators, Sūn DéYá and others,
making five including ZǐXīng.
Each called himself a Marshal and refused to submit to the others.
The four were crude and foolish,
engaging in daily plunder,
which ZǐXīng disdained.
The four were displeased
and conspired to overthrow ZǐXīng.
Because of this, ZǐXīng often stayed at home and did not attend to affairs.
Tàizǔ took the opportunity to persuade him, saying:
"They unite more each day,
while we become more divided;
eventually, we will be controlled by them."
ZǐXīng could not heed him.
When the Yuán army broke through XúZhōu,
Marshal Péng Dà and Zhào JūnYòng led their remaining forces to Háo.
DéYá and the others, recognizing them as famous former bandit leaders,
jointly supported and honored them,
placing them above themselves.
Dà was intelligent and cunning;
ZǐXīng became close to him but slighted JūnYòng.
Thereupon, DéYá and the others slandered ZǐXīng to JūnYòng, saying:
"ZǐXīng only recognizes General Péng,
and does not recognize Your Excellency."
JūnYòng became enraged,
seized ZǐXīng when he had a chance,
and imprisoned him in DéYá's house.
Tàizǔ, returning from another division,
was greatly alarmed and urgently led ZǐXīng's two sons to appeal to Dà.
Dà said:
"While I am here,
who would dare to oppress your elder?"
He went with Tàizǔ to DéYá's house,
broke open ZǐXīng's shackles,
and escorted him home.
When the Yuán army besieged HáoZhōu,
they set aside their old grievances
and jointly defended the city for five months.
When the siege was lifted,
Dà and JūnYòng both proclaimed themselves kings,
while ZǐXīng and DéYá remained marshals as before.
Not long after,
Dà died,
and his son ZǎoZhù led his troops.
JūnYòng became even more arrogant and cruel.
He coerced ZǐXīng into attacking XūYí and SīZhōu,
intending to harm him.
Tàizǔ had already captured Chú,
so he sent someone to persuade JūnYòng, saying:
"When Your Majesty was in dire straits,
Duke Guō opened his gates and welcomed you,
showing immense kindness.
If Your Majesty cannot repay him,
but instead listens to petty men and plots against him,
you will be clipping your own wings
and losing the hearts of heroes.
I privately believe Your Majesty should not do this.
Moreover, his troops are still numerous;
would you not regret killing him?"
JūnYòng, hearing that Tàizǔ's army was very strong,
was wary of him.
Tàizǔ also sent men to bribe JūnYòng's close associates,
and ZǐXīng was thus able to escape.
He then led his division of over ten thousand men to Tàizǔ in Chú.
Guō Zǐxīng (郭子興) was a fierce and skilled fighter,
but also hot-tempered and intolerant.
When affairs were urgent,
he would consult Dàzǔ (太祖) for strategies and advice,
trusting him like his right and left hands.
When the matters were resolved,
he would believe slanders and distance Dàzǔ.
He summoned away all of Dàzǔ's trusted subordinates,
and gradually stripped Dàzǔ of his military authority.
Dàzǔ served Guō Zǐxīng even more diligently.
Whenever generals and soldiers presented offerings,
Empress Xiàocí (孝慈) would always give them to Guō Zǐxīng's wife.
When Guō Zǐxīng arrived at Chú (滁),
he wanted to occupy it and declare himself king.
Dàzǔ said:
"Chú is surrounded by mountains on all four sides,
and water transport and merchants cannot pass through.
It is not a place where one can be secure for long."
Guō Zǐxīng then desisted.
When Hézhōu (和州) was captured,
Guō Zǐxīng ordered Dàzǔ to lead the generals and defend that territory.
Déyá (德崖) was hungry and
sought food in the Hó (和) region.
He requested to station his army within the city,
and Dàzǔ accepted him.
Someone slandered Dàzǔ to Guō Zǐxīng.
Guō Zǐxīng arrived at Hó (和) at night.
When Dàzǔ came to pay respects,
Guō Zǐxīng was extremely angry
and refused to speak to him.
Dàzǔ said:
"Déyá once troubled you, my lord;
it is fitting to be prepared."
Guō Zǐxīng remained silent.
Déyá heard of Guō Zǐxīng's arrival
and planned to withdraw.
His vanguard had already departed.
Déyá was still supervising the rearguard,
when his army clashed with Guō Zǐxīng's army,
resulting in many deaths.
Guō Zǐxīng captured Déyá,
and Dàzǔ was also captured by Déyá's army.
Guō Zǐxīng heard of this
and was greatly alarmed.
He immediately dispatched Xú Dá (徐達) to replace Dàzǔ
and released Déyá.
Déyá's army released Dàzǔ,
and Xú Dá also escaped and returned.
Guō Zǐxīng deeply resented Déyá
and wished to take revenge,
but on account of Dàzǔ, he reluctantly released him,
remaining sullen and unhappy.
Not long after,
he fell ill and died,
and was buried in Chúzhōu (滁州).
Guō Zǐxīng had three sons.
His eldest son had died in battle earlier,
the next were Tiān (天) and Tiānjúe (天爵).
After Guō Zǐxīng's death,
Hán Lín'ér (韓林兒) issued a proclamation appointing Tiān (天) as Dūyuánshuài (都元帥),
and Zhāng Tiānyòu (張天祐) and Dàzǔ as his deputies.
Zhāng Tiānyòu was
Guō Zǐxīng's wife's younger brother.
When Dàzǔ crossed the Yangtze River,
Tiān (天) and Zhāng Tiānyòu led troops to attack Jíqìng (集慶).
Chén Yěxiān (陳埜先) rebelled first,
and they were all killed.
Hán Lín'ér then appointed Tiānjúe (天爵) as Zhōngshū Yòuchéng (中書右丞).
Later, Dàzǔ became Píngzhāng Zhèngshì (平章政事).
Tiānjúe lost his position and harbored resentment.
After a long time, he plotted against Dàzǔ
and was executed.
Thus, Guō Zǐxīng's lineage ended.
He had one daughter,
born of the younger Lady Zhāng (張),
who served Dàzǔ as Consort Huìfēi (惠妃),
and gave birth to the three princes of Shǔ (蜀), Gǔ (谷), and Dài (代).
In the third year of Hóngwǔ (洪武), Guō Zǐxīng was posthumously enfeoffed as Chúyáng Wáng (滁陽王),
and an imperial edict ordered the relevant authorities to build a temple,
offering a mid-level sacrifice.
His neighbors, the Yòu (宥) clan, were reinstated
to guard the king's tomb for generations.
In the sixteenth year,
Dàzǔ personally wrote down Guō Zǐxīng's deeds
and ordered Tàicháng Céng Zhāng Láiyí (太常丞張來儀) to compose the inscription for his stele.
Guō Lǎoshè (郭老舍) of Chú (滁),
during the Xuāndé (宣德) period, traveled to the capital
as a relative of Chúyáng Wáng (滁陽王).
During the Hóngzhì (弘治) period,
Guō Hǔ (郭琥) claimed that his fourth-generation ancestor was Guō Lǎoshè,
the fourth son of Chúyáng Wáng,
and he was granted official attire to perform ancestral worship.
Later,
he was impeached by the Yòu (宥) clan.
The ritual official stated:
"The sacrificial rites for Chúyáng Wáng
were established by Dàzǔ.
It was stated that he had no descendants,
as clearly recorded on the temple stele.
Guō Lǎoshè is not a son of Chúyáng Wáng."
His right to perform ancestral worship was revoked.
Hán Lín'ér (韓林兒) was from Luánchéng (欒城),
or some say he was a son of the Lǐ (李) clan.
His ancestors, by means of the White Lotus Society, used incense burning to deceive the masses,
and were banished to Yǒngnián (永年).
At the end of the Yuán (元) dynasty,
Hán Lín'ér's father, Hán Shāntóng (山童), spread heretical rumors,
saying
"the world would soon be in great chaos,
and Maitreya Buddha would descend to be reborn."
Many ignorant people in Hénán (河南), Jiāng (江), and Huái (淮) regions believed him.
Liú Fútōng (劉福通) from Yǐngzhōu (潁州) and his associates Dù Zūndào (杜遵道), Luó Wénsù (羅文素), Shèng Wényù (盛文郁) and others further claimed
"Hán Shāntóng is the eighth-generation descendant of Emperor Huīzōng (徽宗) of Sòng (宋),
and should rule China."
They then killed a white horse and a black ox,
swore an oath to heaven and earth,
and plotted to raise an army,
using red turbans as their emblem.
In the fifth month of the eleventh year of Zhìzhèng (至正)
the matter was discovered.
Liú Fútōng and others hastily entered Yǐngzhōu (潁州) and rebelled,
while Hán Shāntóng was captured and executed by officials.
Hán Lín'ér and his mother, Lady Yáng (楊), fled into the Wǔ'ān (武安) mountains.
Liú Fútōng occupied Zhū Gāo (朱皐),
conquered Luóshān (羅山), Shàngcài (上蔡), Zhēnyáng (真陽), Quèshān (確山),
attacked Yè (葉) and Wǔyáng (舞陽),
and captured Rǔníng (汝寧), Guāng (光), and Xī (息).
His forces reached over a hundred thousand,
and the Yuán (元) army could not resist them.
At that time, Xú Shòuhuī (徐壽輝) and others rose in Qí (蘄) and Huáng (黃),
Bù Wángsān (布王三) and Méng Hǎimǎ (孟海馬) and others rose in Xiāng (湘) and Hàn (漢),
Zhīmá Lǐ (芝蔴李) rose in Fēng (豐) and Pèi (沛),
and Guō Zǐxīng also occupied Háo (濠) in response.
At that time, they were all called
"Red Army" (紅軍),
also known as
"Incense Army" (香軍).
In the second month of the fifteenth year,
Liú Fútōng sought out Hán Lín'ér
and found him at Jiáhè (夾河) in Dàngshān (碭山).
He welcomed him to Bó (亳),
where he presumptuously claimed the title of Emperor,
also known as Xiǎo Míng Wáng (小明王),
established the state of Sòng (宋),
and adopted the era name Lóngfèng (龍鳳).
He dismantled the materials from Lùyì Tàiqīng Gōng (鹿邑太清宮)
to build palaces in Bó (亳).
He honored Lady Yáng (楊) as the Empress Dowager,
Dù Zūndào (遵道) and Shèng Wényù (文郁) as Chéngxiàng (丞相),
Liú Fútōng (福通) and Luó Wénsù (文素) as Píngzhāng Zhèngshì (平章政事),
and Liú Liù (劉六) as Zhīshūmìyuàn Shì (知樞密院事).
Liú Liù was
Liú Fútōng's younger brother.
Dù Zūndào was favored and held power.
Liú Fútōng envied him,
secretly ordered armored soldiers to beat Dù Zūndào to death,
and appointed himself Chéngxiàng (丞相),
with the added title of Tàibǎo (太保).
All power reverted to Liú Fútōng.
Soon after, the Yuán (元) army decisively defeated Liú Fútōng at Tàikāng (太康),
and advanced to besiege Bó (亳).
Liú Fútōng took Hán Lín'ér and fled to Ānfēng (安豐).
Not long after,
his army grew strong again,
and he sent his associates to seize territory in different directions.
In the seventeenth year,
Lǐ Wǔ (李武) and Cuī Dé (崔德) captured Shāngzhōu (商州),
then broke through Wǔguān (武關) to capture Guānzhōng (關中),
while Máo Guì (毛貴) captured Jiāo (膠), Lái (萊), Yìdū (益都), and Bīnzhōu (濱州).
Many prefectures and counties in Shāndōng (山東) fell.
In the sixth month of that year,
Liú Fútōng led his forces to attack Biànliáng (汴梁),
and also divided his army into three routes: Guān Xiānshēng (關先生), Pòtóu Pān (破頭潘), Féng Chángjiù (馮長舅), Shā Liú'èr (沙劉二), and Wáng Shìchéng (王士誠) advanced towards Jìn (晉) and Jì (冀);
Bái Bùxìn (白不信), Dàdāo Áo (大刀敖), and Lǐ Xǐxǐ (李喜喜) advanced towards Guānzhōng (關中);
and Máo Guì (毛貴) emerged from Shāndōng (山東) and attacked northward.
Their momentum was very strong.
Tián Fēng (田豐),
who was a Yuán (元) commander of ten thousand righteous soldiers guarding the Yellow River,
rebelled and joined Liú Fútōng,
capturing Jìníng (濟寧),
but soon fled after being defeated.
That autumn,
Liú Fútōng's forces captured Dàmíng (大名),
then from Cáo (曹) and Pú (濮) captured Wèihuī (衞輝).
Bái Bùxìn (白不信), Dàdāo Áo (大刀敖), and Lǐ Xǐxǐ (李喜xǐ) captured Xīngyuán (興元),
then entered Fèngxiáng (鳳翔),
were repeatedly defeated by Cháhǎn Tièmù'ér (察罕帖木兒) and Lǐ Sīqí (李思齊),
and fled into Shǔ (蜀).
Yuán Zhèn originally had the surname Tián.
He was famous for his skill in battle.
When Yù Chūn besieged Gàn,
Yuán Zhèn secretly went out to scout the enemy.
Yù Chūn also led a few horsemen out,
and suddenly encountered him.
Yuán Zhèn did not know it was Yù Chūn,
and passed him by.
When Yù Chūn returned,
Yuán Zhèn first realized,
and then rode alone to attack Yù Chūn.
Yù Chūn sent a cavalryman to strike him with a saber.
Yuán Zhèn fought and fled, wielding his iron mace.
Yù Chūn said:
"He is a brave man."
And let him go.
From then on, he admired his talent and bravery.
After submitting with Tiān Ruì,
he was recommended to be a Zhǐhuīshǐ.
When Tiān Ruì was executed,
he reverted to his former surname, it is said.
Zhāng Shìchéng,
whose courtesy name was Jiǔsì,
was a native of Báijūchǎng Tíng in Tàizhōu.
He had three younger brothers,
and all of them made a living by operating boats and transporting salt,
engaging in illicit profiteering.
He was rather generous with money and fond of giving,
winning the hearts of his associates.
He often sold salt to wealthy families,
and many of these wealthy families would bully him,
or refuse to pay his due.
The archer Qiū Yì especially humiliated Shìchéng severely.
Shìchéng, enraged,
immediately led his brothers and eighteen strong men, including Lǐ Bóshēng, to kill Yì,
and also destroyed the wealthy families,
setting fire to their residences.
He entered a nearby district's salt-field,
recruiting young men to raise an army.
The salt workers were suffering from heavy labor,
so they jointly acclaimed him as their leader,
and he captured Tàizhōu.
Lǐ Qí, the defender of Gāoyóu, admonished him to surrender,
but he rebelled again.
He killed Zhào Lián, the Cāngōng of the Xíngshěng,
and also captured Xīnghuà,
establishing a stronghold at Déshèng Hú,
with over ten thousand men.
The Yuán government tried to entice him with a Wànhù patent.
He did not accept.
He tricked and killed Lǐ Qí,
and then seized Gāoyóu,
proclaiming himself Chéng Wáng,
illicitly adopting the reign title Dà Zhōu,
and establishing the era name Tiānyòu.
This was the thirteenth year of Zhìzhèng.
The following year,
Tuōtuō, the Right Chancellor of the Yuán, led a large army to suppress him,
defeating Shìchéng several times,
besieging Gāoyóu,
and destroying its outer wall.
The city was about to fall when
Emperor Shùn, believing slander,
relieved Tuōtuō of his military command,
stripped him of his official titles and ranks,
and replaced him with another general.
Shìchéng seized the opportunity to attack fiercely,
and the Yuán army scattered and retreated,
thus he revived his forces.
A year later,
Huáidōng suffered a famine.
Shìchéng then sent his brother Shìdé across the Jiāng from Tōngzhōu to enter Chángshú.
In the second month of the sixteenth year, he captured Píngjiāng,
and also captured Húzhōu, Sōngjiāng, and various routes in Chángzhōu.
He renamed Píngjiāng to Lóngpíng Fǔ,
and Shìchéng came from Gāoyóu to make it his capital.
He made Chéngtiān Sì his official residence,
sitting in the main hall,
and shot three arrows into the ridgepole to mark it.
That same year,
Tàizǔ also captured Jíqìng,
and sent Yáng Xiàn to establish good relations with Shìchéng.
His letter read:
"In the past, Kuí Xiāo dominated Tiānshuǐ;
now Your Excellency also holds sway in Gūsū.
The circumstances are similar,
and I am deeply pleased for Your Excellency.
Maintaining friendly relations with neighbors and defending one's borders
is valued by the ancients,
and I deeply admire this.
From now on, when envoys travel back and forth,
do not be swayed by slander,
to avoid causing border disputes."
Shìchéng received the letter,
detained Xiàn, and did not reply.
Afterwards,
he sent a naval force to attack Zhènjiāng.
Xú Dá defeated it at Lóngtán.
Tàizǔ sent Dá and Tāng Hé to attack Chángzhōu.
Shìchéng's forces came to reinforce,
but were utterly defeated,
losing two generals, Zhāng and Tāng.
He then sent a letter to seek peace,
requesting to pay an annual tribute of two hundred thousand *shí* of grain,
five hundred *liǎng* of gold,
and three hundred *jīn* of silver.
Tàizǔ replied with a letter,
demanding the return of Yáng Xiàn
and an annual tribute of five hundred thousand *shí* of grain.
Shìchéng again did not reply.
Initially,
after Shìchéng obtained Píngjiāng,
he immediately used his army to attack Jiāxīng.
The Yuán commander, Miáo Shuài Yáng Wánzhě, defeated his troops several times.
So he sent Shìdé to break through Hángzhōu by a secret path.
Wánzhě returned to rescue,
but was again defeated and retreated.
The following year,
Gěng Bǐngwén took Chángxīng,
Xú Dá took Chángzhōu,
Wú Liáng and others took Jiāngyīn.
Shìchéng's forces could not sally forth,
and his situation gradually worsened.
Not long after,
Xú Dá's army advanced to Yíxīng,
and attacked Chángshú.
Shìdé engaged in battle but was defeated,
and was captured by the vanguard Zhào Déshèng.
Shìdé,
whose courtesy name was Jiǔliù,
was skilled in battle and resourceful,
able to win the hearts of his soldiers.
The lands west of Zhèjiāng were all subjugated by him.
After he was captured,
Shìchéng was greatly disheartened.
Tàizǔ wanted to keep Shìdé to entice Shìchéng.
Shìdé secretly sent a letter to Shìchéng,
urging him to surrender to the Yuán.
Shìchéng then decided to request surrender.
Dáshí Tiēmùěr, the Right Chancellor of Jiāngzhè, spoke on his behalf at court,
bestowing upon Shìchéng the title of Tàiwèi,
and granting official positions to his generals and officers accordingly.
Shìdé, in Jīnlíng, eventually died by refusing food.
Although Shìchéng abandoned his false title,
he still controlled his army and territory as before.
Dáshí Tiēmùěr in Hángzhōu had a grudge against Yáng Wánzhě,
and secretly summoned Shìchéng's forces.
Shìchéng sent Shǐ Wénbǐng to attack and kill Wánzhě,
thus taking possession of Hángzhōu.
Emperor Shùn sent envoys to demand grain,
bestowing upon him dragon robes and imperial wine.
Shìchéng transported one hundred and ten thousand *shí* of grain to Dàdū by sea,
making it an annual custom.
Subsequently, he became even more arrogant,
ordering his subordinates to praise his achievements and virtues,
and to demand a princely title.
This was not granted.
In the ninth month of the twenty-third year,
Shìchéng again proclaimed himself King of Wú,
honored his mother, Lady Cáo, as the Royal Grand Consort,
established his own officials,
and built a separate official residence in the city,
appointing Shìxìn as the Left Chancellor of the Zhèjiāng Xíngshěng,
and imprisoning Dáshí Tiēmùěr in Jiāxīng.
He no longer provided grain to the Yuán when they requested it.
Yú Sīqí, a Cānjūn
whose courtesy name was Zhōngfú,
a native of Tàizhōu,
remonstrated with Shìchéng, saying:
"Formerly, as a rebel,
you could not pay tribute;
now, as a subject,
how can you not pay tribute!"
Shìchéng was enraged,
slammed the table and fell to the ground.
Sīqí then feigned illness and left.
At that time,
the territory controlled by Shìchéng
extended south to Shàoxīng,
north beyond Xúzhōu,
reaching Jìníng's Jīngōu,
west to Rǔ, Yǐng, Háo, and Sì,
and east to the sea,
covering over two thousand *lǐ*,
with several hundred thousand armored soldiers.
He relied on Shìxìn and his son-in-law Pān Yuánshào as his close confidantes;
Left Chancellor Xú Yì, Lǐ Bóshēng, and Lǚ Zhēn as his strong arms;
Cānjūn Huáng Jìngfū, Cài Yànwén, and Yè Déxīn managed strategy and deliberation;
and Yuán Xuéshì Chén Jī and Right Chancellor Ráo Jiè were in charge of literary affairs.
He also enjoyed inviting and hosting guests,
providing them generously with carriages, horses, residences, and various utensils.
Many poor and unregistered sojourners competed to seek his patronage.
Zhāng Shìchéng為人 (Wéirén)
outwardly seemed reserved, grave, and spoke little,
as if he had great capacity and bearing,
but in reality, he lacked a long-term vision.
Once he had taken control of Wúzhōng,
Wú had been peaceful for a long time,
its population prosperous and numerous.
Shìchéng gradually became extravagant and self-indulgent,
neglecting political affairs.
Zhāng Shìxìn and Pān Yuánshào (also referred to as Yuánshào in the text) were especially fond of accumulating wealth;
gold, jade, precious treasures, ancient calligraphy, and famous paintings
were all abundantly filled.
They entertained themselves with song and dance day and night.
His generals also became arrogant and disobedient;
whenever there was a battle or campaign,
they would claim illness,
demanding official titles, ranks, fields, and residences before setting out.
Upon reaching the army,
their loaded maids, concubines, and musical instruments followed one after another without end.
Some would hold large gatherings with wandering talkers,
playing chūpú (a dice game) and cùjú (ancient football),
none of them caring about military affairs.
When they returned after losing troops and territory,
Shìchéng generally ignored and did not question it.
Later,
he reappointed them as generals.
Superiors and subordinates alike indulged in pleasure,
leading to their downfall.
Tàizǔ's territory bordered Shìchéng's.
Shìchéng repeatedly attacked Chángzhōu, Jiāngyīn, Jiàndé, Chángxīng, and Zhūquán with his army,
but always withdrew after suffering disadvantages.
Meanwhile, Tàizǔ sent Shào Róng to attack Húzhōu,
Hú Dàhǎi to attack Shàoxīng,
and Cháng Yùchūn to attack Hángzhōu,
but they were also unable to capture them.
Liáo Yǒng'ān was captured,
Xiè Zàixīng rebelled and surrendered to Shìchéng,
and Tàizǔ was at the time locked in a stalemate with Chén Yǒuliàng,
so he had no leisure to attend to this.
Yǒuliàng also sent an envoy to Shìchéng, proposing a joint attack on Tàizǔ,
but Shìchéng wanted to guard his borders and observe the changes;
he promised the envoy,
but ultimately did not act.
After Tàizǔ pacified Wǔchāng
and his army returned,
he immediately ordered Xú Dá and others to plan the capture of Huáidōng.
They captured Táizhōu and Tōngzhōu,
and besieged Gāoyóu.
