Shìchéng came to their aid with a fleet of boats, sailing upstream,
but Tàizǔ personally led an attack and drove them back.
Dá and the others then captured Gāoyóu,
took Huái'ān,
and completely pacified the lands north of the Huái River.
Thereupon, he dispatched a proclamation to Píngjiāng,
enumerating Shìchéng's eight crimes.
Xú Dá and Cháng Yùchūn led their troops from Tàihú towards Húzhōu.
The Wú people met them in battle at Píshān,
and again at Qīlǐqiáo;
they were both defeated,
and Húzhōu was then besieged.
Shìchéng sent Zhū Xiān and Wǔ Tàizǐ (Five Princes), among others, with 60,000 men to relieve the siege;
they encamped at Jiùguǎn,
and built five strongholds to secure themselves.
Dá and Yùchūn built ten forts to block them,
cutting off their supply route.
Shìchéng, realizing the urgency of the situation,
personally supervised his troops in battle,
but was defeated at Zàolín.
His general Xú Zhìjiān was defeated at Dōngqiān,
Pān Yuánshào was defeated at Wūzhèn,
and all the water and land camps at Shēngshān were broken.
Aid to Jiùguǎn was cut off,
and Wǔ Tàizǐ, Zhū Xiān, and Lǚ Zhēn all surrendered.
Wǔ Tàizǐ was
Shìchéng's adopted son,
short, sturdy, and fierce,
able to leap more than ten feet on flat ground,
and also skilled at diving into water.
Zhēn and Xiān were both veteran generals skilled in battle,
and they surrendered at this point.
Dá and others paraded them through Húzhōu.
The defending general Lǐ Bóshēng and others surrendered the city,
and Jiāxīng and Sōngjiāng surrendered one after another.
Pān Yuánmíng also surrendered Hángzhōu to Lǐ Wénzhōng.
In the eleventh month of the twenty-sixth year,
the main army advanced to attack Píngjiāng,
building a long siege line to encircle it.
Shìchéng held out for several months.
Tàizǔ sent a letter to persuade him, saying:
"The heroes of antiquity
were considered wise for revering Heaven and obeying the people,
and intelligent for preserving themselves and their families;
Dòu Róng of Hàn and Qián Chù of Sòng are examples of this.
You should think thrice,
lest you bring about your own annihilation
and become a laughingstock of the world."
Shìchéng did not reply,
and repeatedly attempted to break out and fight,
but without success.
Lǐ Bóshēng knew Shìchéng was in great distress,
and sent a trusted guest to scale the wall and persuade Shìchéng, saying:
"Initially, what you relied on
were Húzhōu, Jiāxīng, and Hángzhōu;
now they are all lost.
If you alone defend this city,
I fear rebellion will arise from within,
and even if you wish to die,
you may not be able to.
It would be better to submit to the will of Heaven,
send an envoy to Jīnlíng,
express your intention to surrender and save the people,
open the city gates,
wear a simple headscarf and await orders,
and you will surely not lose the title of Wànhù Hóu (Marquis of Ten Thousand Households).
Furthermore, your territory
is like that of a gambler
who gains someone's possessions and then loses them;
what harm is it to you?"
Shìchéng looked up for a long time and said:
"I will think about it."
He then dismissed the guest,
but ultimately did not surrender.
Shìchéng had a unit called the Yǒngshèng Jūn
"Shí Tiáo Lóng" (Ten Dragons),
who were all valiant and skilled fighters.
They often wore silver armor and brocade robes when entering and exiting battles,
but by this time, they were all defeated,
drowning under the Wànlǐ Qiáo (Myriad Li Bridge).
Finally, Prime Minister Shìxìn died from a cannon shot,
and the city was in turmoil with no firm will.
In the ninth month of the twenty-seventh year,
the city fell.
Shìchéng gathered his remaining troops and fought in Wànshòu Sì Dōng Jiē (East Street of the Longevity Temple),
but his forces dispersed and fled.
In a panic, he returned to his mansion,
locked the door, and hanged himself.
His former subordinate Zhào Shìxióng untied him.
Grand General Dá repeatedly sent Lǐ Bóshēng, Pān Yuánshào, and others to convey his intentions,
but Shìchéng closed his eyes and did not respond.
He was carried out through the Fēng Mén (Feng Gate),
put into a boat,
and refused to eat again.
Upon reaching Jīnlíng,
he finally hanged himself,
at the age of forty-seven.
An order was given to provide a coffin and bury him.
When Shìchéng was under siege,
he said to his wife Liú:
"I am defeated and about to die;
what will you do?"
Liú replied:
"My lord, do not worry;
I will surely not fail you."
She piled firewood beneath the Qíyún Lóu (Cloud-Reaching Tower).
When the city fell,
she drove her concubines up the tower,
ordered her adopted son Chén Bǎo to set it on fire,
and then hanged herself.
Two young sons were hidden among the common people,
their fates unknown.
Previously,
Huáng Jìngfū and two others were in power.
The Wú people knew Shìchéng would surely be defeated,
and there was
a folk rhyme
"Huáng Cài Yè" (Yellow Vegetable Leaf) of seventeen characters,
which was later confirmed to be true.
Mò Tiānyòu
gathered a crowd at the end of the Yuán dynasty to defend Wúxī Zhōu.
Shìchéng invited him to join,
but he refused.
Shìchéng attacked him with troops,
but also could not conquer him.
After Shìchéng accepted the Yuán official title,
Tiānyòu then surrendered.
Shìchéng repeatedly recommended him to be Tóngqiān Shūmìyuàn Shì (Assistant Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs).
When Píngjiāng was besieged
and other cities had all fallen,
only Tiānyòu held out steadfastly.
When Shìchéng was defeated,
Hú Tíngruì immediately attacked him,
and he surrendered.
Tàizǔ, because he had inflicted many casualties on his troops,
executed him.
In the first year of Wú, Hángzhōu was conquered.
Fāng Guózhēn remained in control of his territory as before,
sending spies under the guise of offering tribute to observe the outcome of battles.
He also repeatedly sought good relations with Kùokuò Tiēmù'ér and Chén Yǒudìng,
plotting to form a pincer movement.
When Tàizǔ heard of this, he was enraged.
He sent a letter enumerating Guózhēn's twelve crimes,
and further demanded two hundred thousand *shí* of military grain.
Guózhēn gathered his advisors to discuss the matter.
Lángzhōng Zhāng Běnrén and
Zuǒchéng Liú Yōng and others all said that his demands could not be followed.
There was one Qiū Nán,
who alone argued, saying:
"What he says is not beneficial to the Duke.
Only wisdom can decide affairs,
only trustworthiness can guard a state,
only straightforwardness can employ troops.
The Duke has been operating in eastern Zhèjiāng for over ten years now,
procrastinating and hesitating,
and failing to make a decision early.
This cannot be called wisdom.
Having already promised to surrender,
and then to renege on it,
cannot be called trustworthiness.
When he raises an army,
he will have a valid reason,
for we have indeed wronged him.
This cannot be called straightforwardness.
If we are fortunate, we might prostrate ourselves and beg for our lives,
perhaps like Qián Chǔ."
Guózhēn did not listen,
but only moved treasures day and night,
prepared boats,
and made plans for a sea voyage.
In the ninth month,
Tàizǔ had already conquered Píngjiāng,
and ordered Cānzhèng Zhū Liàngzǔ to attack Táizhōu.
Fāng Guóyīng met them in battle but was defeated and fled.
They advanced and conquered Wēnzhōu.
Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn Tāng Hé led a large army and marched straight to Qìngyuán.
Guózhēn, leading his subordinates, fled into the sea.
He was pursued and defeated at Pányǔ,
and his generals surrendered one after another.
Hé repeatedly sent people to explain the distinction between loyalty and rebellion to him,
whereupon Guózhēn sent his son, Fāng Guān, to present a memorial begging for surrender, saying:
"Your servant has heard that there is nothing heaven does not cover,
and nothing earth does not bear.
The King embodies heaven and emulates earth,
and can tolerate anyone.
Your servant has long been graced by the covering and bearing virtue of the Sovereign;
I dare not cut myself off from heaven and earth,
and thus I present my foolish thoughts.
Your servant is but a mediocre talent,
who encountered a time of many troubles,
and rose from an island.
I had no strength to rely on from father or elder brothers,
nor did I have the ambition to establish an empire for myself.
When the Sovereign struck like thunder and lightning,
reaching Wùzhōu,
your foolish servant immediately sent my son to attend,
for I already knew the Sovereign would have this day,
and intended to rely on the last ray of sunlight and moonlight,
and hope for the remaining moisture of rain and dew.
Yet the Sovereign showed sincerity and openness,
allowing me to guard my native commandery,
as in the former affairs of Wúyuè.
Your servant abided by the treaties,
and dared not cause any further trouble.
My sons and nephews were not warned,
and secretly stirred up discord,
unnecessarily bringing forth an army to punish me.
My private heart trembled,
and so I instructed my guards to go out and welcome them.
However, I could not avoid fleeing to the sea,
why is this?
A filial son, when facing his parents,
accepts a small stick,
but runs from a large stick.
My situation is exactly like this.
Though I wished to bind myself and await punishment at the court,
I feared the execution of the axe and battle-axe,
which would leave future generations unaware of the depth of my offense,
and they might say that the Sovereign could not tolerate his servant,
would this not diminish the great virtue of heaven and earth?"
This was in fact the composition of his staff member Zhān Dǐng.
Tàizǔ read it and pitied him,
and bestowed a letter saying:
"You disobeyed my edict,
did not immediately submit and surrender your life,
and lingered abroad.
Your ingratitude is truly great.
Now, being in dire straits and without recourse,
your words are mournful and earnest.
I shall take your present sincerity as sincerity,
and not consider your past faults as faults.
Do not doubt yourself."
He then urged Guózhēn to come to court,
and reprimanded him to his face, saying:
"Did you not come too late!"
Guózhēn kowtowed and expressed gratitude.
He was appointed Zuǒchéng of the Guǎngxī Xíngshěng,
receiving salary but not taking up office.
After several years,
he died in the capital.
His son Lǐ
served as Guǎngyángwèi Zhīhuī Qiānshì;
Guān
was a Zhènfǔ of the Hǔběnwèi Qiānhùsuǒ.
Guān's younger brother Xíng,
courtesy name Míngmǐn,
was skilled in poetry,
and Chéngzhǐ Sòng Lián once praised him.
Liú Rénběn,
courtesy name Déyuán,
was from the same county as Guózhēn.
He passed the imperial examination with the second class in the late Yuán dynasty,
and successively served as Lángzhōng of the Zhèjiāng Xíngshěng.
He and Zhāng Běnrén both joined Guózhēn's staff.
He often composed poems with famous scholars such as Zhào Chǔ, Xiè Lǐ, and Zhū Yòu,
and was praised at the time.
Guózhēn's sea transport of goods to the Yuán court
was actually managed by Rénběn.
When Zhū Liàngzǔ attacked Wēnzhōu,
he captured Rénběn.
Tàizǔ enumerated his crimes,
and he died from a severely flogged back.
Other officials who surrendered with Guózhēn were all exiled to Chúzhōu,
but Qiū Nán alone was pardoned
and made Zhīfǔ of Sháozhōu.
Zhān Dǐng,
a native of Nínghǎi,
possessed talent and learning.
He served as Dūshì in Guózhēn's administration
and was appointed Pàn of Shàngyú,
where he gained a reputation for good governance.
Upon arriving in the capital,
he was not yet employed.
He drafted a memorial of ten thousand words
and waited for the emperor to leave his carriage to present it.
The emperor stopped his horse to receive and read it,
and ordered the Prime Minister to appoint Dǐng to office.
Yáng Xiàn, jealous of his talent,
obstructed him.
After Xiàn's downfall,
Dǐng was appointed Liúshǒu Jīnglì,
and then promoted to Xíngbù Lángzhōng,
but died implicated in an incident.
Míng Yùzhēn,
a native of Suízhōu.
He was over eight *chǐ* tall and
had double pupils in his eyes.
When Xú Shòuhuī rose up,
Yùzhēn and the elders of his village gathered over a thousand men
and encamped at Qīngshān.
When Shòuhuī proclaimed himself emperor,
he sent someone to summon Yùzhēn, saying:
"If you come, we will share wealth and honor;
if you do not come, I will raise an army and slaughter you."
Yùzhēn led his followers to surrender,
and was made Yuánshuài defending Miǎnyáng.
He fought against the Yuán general Hāmātū in the lake,
and an arrow struck his right eye,
blinding him.
After a long time,
Yùzhēn led fifty *dòu* boats to plunder grain between Chuān and Xiá,
intending to return.
At that time, the Yuán Zuǒchéng Wánzhědū was recruiting soldiers in Chóngqìng.
Yìbīng Yuánshuài Yáng Hàn responded to the call and arrived,
intending to kill Wánzhědū and annex his army,
but failed.
Hàn fled through the gorges
and met Yùzhēn, telling him:
"Chóngqìng has no strong army,
and Wánzhědū and Zuǒchéng Hāmātū are at odds.
If you turn your boats back and attack them by surprise,
you can take it."
Yùzhēn was undecided.
His general Dài Shòu said:
"The opportunity must not be missed.
You can divide the boats into two,
half storing grain to return to Miǎnyáng,
the other half using Hàn's soldiers to attack Chóngqìng.
If it doesn't succeed, plunder property and return."
Yùzhēn followed his plan,
attacked Chóngqìng,
drove away Wánzhědū,
and captured Hāmātū to present to Shòuhuī.
Shòuhuī appointed Yùzhēn Zuǒchéng of the Lǒngshǔ Xíngshěng.
This was in the seventeenth year of Zhìzhèng.
Soon after, Wánzhědōu (完者都) came from Guǒzhōu (果州),
and met with Píngzhāng (平章) Lǎnggédǎi (朗革歹) and Cānzhèng (參政) Zhào Zī (趙資),
to plan the recapture of Chóngqìng (重慶).
They encamped at Dàfósì (大佛寺) in Jiāqìng (嘉定).
Yùzhēn (玉珍) dispatched Wànshèng (萬勝) to defend against them.
Shèng (勝)
was a native of Huángpí (黃陂).
He possessed both wisdom and bravery.
Yùzhēn (玉珍) doted on him,
allowing him to adopt his surname.
The masses called him Míng Èr (明二).
Later, he reverted to his original surname.
Shèng (勝) attacked Jiāqìng (嘉定)
for half a year without success.
Yùzhēn (玉珍) led his forces to besiege it,
and sent Shèng (勝) with light troops to raid and capture Chéngdū (成都),
seizing Lǎnggédǎi (朗革歹) and Zī's (資) wife and children.
Lǎnggédǎi's (朗革歹) wife drowned herself in the river.
Yùzhēn (玉珍) displayed Zī's (資) wife and children outside Jiāqìng (嘉定),
trying to persuade Zī (資) to surrender.
Zī (資) drew his bow and shot his wife dead.
Soon after, the city fell.
Zī (資), Wánzhědōu (完者都), and Lǎnggédǎi (朗革歹) were captured and brought back to Chóngqìng (重慶).
They were housed in Zhìpíngsì (治平寺),
as Yùzhēn (玉珍) intended to use them for his own purposes.
The three firmly refused,
so they were executed in the marketplace
and buried with full rites.
The people of Shǔ (蜀) called them
"The Three Loyalists" (三忠).
Thereupon, various prefectures and counties successively came to submit.
In the twentieth year,
Chén Yǒuliàng (陳友諒) murdered Xú Shòuhuī (徐壽輝) and established himself.
Yùzhēn (玉珍) said:
"Yǒuliàng (友諒) and I both served the Xú (徐) clan,
yet he is so rebellious."
He ordered troops to block Qútáng (瞿塘)
to completely sever communication with him.
He erected a temple for Shòuhuī (壽輝) in the southern corner of the city,
offering sacrifices seasonally.
He proclaimed himself King of Lǒngshǔ (隴蜀王),
and appointed Liú Zhēn (劉楨) as Cānmóu (參謀).
Zhēn (楨),
courtesy name Wéizhōu (維周),
was a native of Lúzhōu (瀘州).
He was a Yuán (元) *jìnshì* (進士).
He had served as a *jīnglì* (經歷) in Dàmíng Lù (大名路),
but abandoned his office and lived at home.
When Yùzhēn (玉珍) attacked Chóngqìng (重慶),
passing through Lú (瀘),
his subordinate general Liú Zémín (劉澤民) recommended him.
Yùzhēn (玉珍) went to see him,
and was greatly pleased after conversing with him.
That same day, he invited him to his boat,
treating him with utmost respect and courtesy.
The following year,
Zhēn (楨), dismissing others, said to him:
"Xīshǔ (西蜀) is a strategically important land.
If Your Majesty can pacify and possess it,
recuperate the wounded and disabled,
employ worthy individuals, and train the army,
you can establish an unprecedented dominion.
If you do not proclaim a grand title at this time to unite the hearts of the people,
should the officers and soldiers one day become homesick
and disperse like broken tiles,
with whom will Your Majesty establish a state?"
Yùzhēn (玉珍) approved of this,
and then consulted with his subordinates.
In the spring of the twenty-second year, he presumptuously ascended to the imperial throne in Chóngqìng (重慶),
naming his state Xià (夏),
and establishing the reign era Tiāntǒng (天統).
He appointed his wife, née Péng (彭), as Empress,
and his son Shēng (昇) as Crown Prince.
Following the Zhōu (周) system,
he established Six Ministers (六卿),
appointing Liú Zhēn (劉楨) as Zōngbó (宗伯).
He divided the Shǔ (蜀) territory into eight circuits,
and changed the names of the prefectural, sub-prefectural, and county officials.
The Shǔ (蜀) army was considered weak compared to other states,
with fighting troops numbering less than ten thousand.
Yùzhēn (玉珍) had always lacked far-reaching strategies,
but he was by nature frugal
and quite fond of learning,
humbling himself before scholars.
After his enthronement,
he established the Guózǐjiān (國子監)
to educate the children of dukes and ministers,
set up the Tíyǔ Sī Jiàoshòu (提舉司教授),
built altars for the Gods of Land and Grain (社稷) and ancestral temples,
sought out elegant music,
opened the *jìnshì* (進士) examination,
and fixed taxes,
taking one-tenth.
The people of Shǔ (蜀) were all content and at peace with this.
All of this was planned by Liú Zhēn (劉楨).
The following year,
he sent Wànshèng (萬勝) via Jièshǒu (界首),
Zōu Xīng (鄒興) via Jiànchāng (建昌),
and another commander, Lǐ (李), via Bāfān (八番),
to attack Yúnnán (雲南) by separate routes.
The two routes did not reach their destination;
only Shèng's (勝) troops penetrated deep,
causing the Yuán (元) Prince of Liáng (梁王) to encamp at Jīnmǎ Shān (金馬山).
More than a year later,
the Prince, with Dàlǐ (大理) forces, attacked Shèng (勝).
Shèng (勝), with an isolated army and no reinforcements, had to withdraw.
He again sent Xīng (興) to capture Bāzhōu (巴州).
After a long time,
he again changed the Six Ministers (六卿) to the Zhōngshū Shěng (中書省) and Shūmì Yuàn (樞密院).
He renamed Zhǒngzǎi (冢宰) Dài Shòu (戴壽) and Sīmǎ (司馬) Wànshèng (萬勝) as Left and Right Chéngxiàng (丞相),
Sīkòu (司寇) Xiàng Dàhēng (向大亨) and Sīkōng (司空) Zhāng Wénbǐng (張文炳) as Zhīshūmìyuàn Shì (知樞密院事).
Sītú (司徒) Zōu Xīng (鄒興) was garrisoned in Chéngdū (成都),
Wú Yǒurén (吳友仁) in Bǎoníng (保寧),
Sīkòu (司寇) Mò Rénshòu (莫仁壽) in Kuíguān (夔關),
all as Píngzhāng Shì (平章事).
In that year,
he sent Shèng (勝) to capture Xīngyuán (興元),
and Cānzhèng (參政) Jiāng Yǎn (江儼) to establish good relations with Tàizǔ (太祖).
Tàizǔ (太祖) sent Dūshì (都事) Sūn Yǎnghào (孫養浩) as a return envoy,
and sent a letter to Yùzhēn (玉珍) which read:
"You reside in Xīshǔ (西蜀),
and I in Jiāngzuǒ (江左),
which is akin to Sūn (孫) and Liú (劉) at the end of the Hàn (漢).
Recently, Wáng Bǎobǎo (王保保) with his iron cavalry and elite troops,
has occupied the Central Plains like a tiger.
His ambition is surely not inferior to Cáo Cāo (曹操).
If he has strategists like Yōu (攸) and Yù (彧),
and fierce generals like Liáo (遼) and Hé (郃),
can the two of us truly rest easy without worries?
You and I are truly like lips and teeth to each other's states.
I wish for us to take the mutual devouring of Sūn (孫) and Liú (劉) as a warning."
Thereafter, envoys traveled back and forth without interruption.
In the spring of the twenty-sixth year,
Yùzhēn (玉珍) was critically ill.
He summoned Shòu (壽) and others, and instructed them:
"Xīshǔ (西蜀) is fortified and secure.
If you work together with one heart
to assist the heir,
then you can hold your own.
Otherwise, the future is beyond my knowledge."
Then he passed away.
He reigned for five years in total,
and was thirty-six years old.
His son Shēng (昇) succeeded him,
changing the reign era to Kāixī (開熙).
Yùzhēn (玉珍) was buried north of the Jiāngshuǐ (江水),
named Yǒngchāng Líng (永昌陵),
and given the temple name Tàizǔ (太祖).
His mother, née Péng (彭), was honored as Empress Dowager (皇太后),
and she participated in governing.
Shēng (昇) was barely ten years old,
and all the high ministers were crude and violent,
unwilling to yield to each other.
Wànshèng (萬勝) and Zhāng Wénbǐng (張文炳) had a feud.
Shèng (勝) secretly sent someone to kill Wénbǐng (文炳).
Míng Zhāo (明昭), Yùzhēn's (玉珍) adopted son, who was close to Wénbǐng (文炳), then falsely issued an order from Empress Péng (彭) to hang and kill Shèng (勝).
Shèng (勝) had contributed the most to the Míng (明) clan,
and at his death,
many people in Shǔ (蜀) pitied him.
Wú Yǒurén (吳友仁), from Bǎoníng (保寧), issued a proclamation,
under the pretext of "purging the emperor's entourage."
Shēng (昇) ordered Dài Shòu (戴壽) to suppress him.
Yǒurén (友仁) sent a letter to Shòu (壽) saying:
"If Zhāo (昭) is not executed,
the state will surely not be peaceful,
and the people will surely not submit.
If Zhāo (昭) is executed in the morning,
I will arrive by evening."
Shòu (壽) then memorialized for Zhāo's (昭) execution,
and Yǒurén (友仁) entered the court to apologize for his offense.
Thereupon, the various high ministers took power,
and Yǒurén (友仁) became especially autocratic,
allowing the reins of government to fall into others' hands,
and the state further declined.
After Wànshèng (萬勝) died,
Liú Zhēn (劉楨) became Right Chéngxiàng (丞相).
Three years later, he died.
In that year,
Shēng (昇) sent an envoy to inform Tàizǔ (太祖) of the mourning.
Afterwards,
he again sent an envoy to pay respects.
Tàizǔ (太祖) also sent Shìyùshǐ (侍御史) Cài Zhé (蔡哲) as a return envoy.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ (洪武) (1368),
Tàizǔ (太祖) conquered the Yuán (元) capital.
Shēng (昇) sent a letter of congratulation.
The next year,
Tàizǔ (太祖) sent an envoy to request large timber.
Shēng (昇) then also presented local products.
The Emperor replied with an imperial letter sealed with his seal.
That winter,
Píngzhāng (平章) Yáng Jǐng (楊璟) was sent to advise Shēng (昇) to surrender.
Shēng (昇) did not comply.
Jǐng (璟) again sent a letter to Shēng (昇) saying: "Ancient rulers,
who united their strength and virtue,
and united their virtue with righteousness,
were therefore able to preserve both their persons and families,
and leave behind endless renown.
Those who acted contrary to this invariably failed.
Your Highness
When [you were] young and immature,
you inherited your ancestors' legacy,
and occupied Ba and Shǔ.
You did not consult great plans,
but listened to the counsel of your subordinates,
who relied on the dangers of Qūtáng and Jiàngé,
[saying that] one man with a spear
could repel ten thousand.
These are all words from those who do not understand the changes of the times and thus mislead your Excellency.
In the past, among those who held Shǔ most prosperously,
none was like Hàn Zhāoliè.
Moreover,
he was assisted by Zhūgě Wǔhóu,
who meticulously reviewed officials' duties,
trained soldiers,
and when resources were insufficient,
all were obtained from Nánzhāo.
Yet, he still could not plan from morning till evening,
barely able to
maintain himself.
Now, your Excellency's borders
do not extend south beyond Bōzhōu,
nor north beyond Hánzhōng.
Comparing this to that,
the difference is immense,
and yet you wish to rely on a corner of the land
to prolong
your life for a moment.
Can this be called wise?
My lord, the Emperor, is benevolent, sagacious, and awe-inspiring,
with divine providence responding [to him].
Those who submit receive nothing but grace;
only those who stubbornly resist are then punished.
Because of the friendly relations
with your Excellency's ancestors,
we could not bear to send troops,
and repeatedly sent envoys to convey our intentions.
Also, because your Excellency is young,
and has not experienced events,
we fear you might be deluded by mad and ignorant people,
losing sight of a long-term plan.
Therefore,
we again dispatched Jǐng to personally explain the fortunes and misfortunes.
The profound benevolence and great virtue
with which the Míng clan is treated are not shallow.
Ought your Excellency not to ponder this deeply?
Moreover, formerly, those like Chén and Zhāng,
who usurped Wú and Chǔ,
built ships that blocked rivers,
accumulated grain higher than mountains,
and had strong generals and valiant soldiers,
calling themselves invincible.
Yet, in one battle at Póyáng,
Yǒuliàng was beheaded;
then, turning east to attack,
Zhāng Shì submitted with his hands bound.
This was not by human effort,
but truly by Heaven's will.
What does your Excellency think of this?
Yǒuliàng's son fled to Jiāngxià;
the royal army launched an attack,
and in desperation, he surrendered with a jade disc in his mouth.
The Emperor pardoned his transgressions,
bestowing on him a tally and a peerage.
The grandeur of this grace and honor
is known
throughout the world.
Your Excellency has not committed their transgressions,
and if you can suddenly awaken to the truth,
seeking greater fortune for yourself,
you will certainly enjoy an enfeoffment of land,
preserve your ancestors' sacrifices,
and your lineage
will never be cut off.
Would this not be wise and sagacious?
If you are determined to stubbornly resist in a corner,
eking out a momentary existence,
like fish swimming in a boiling cauldron,
or swallows nesting on a precarious curtain,
with disaster imminent,
and yet you remain unaware.
Jǐng fears that once the Heavenly army arrives,
all those who now plan for your Excellency
might one day plan for themselves
to obtain wealth and honor.
At that
time,
where will your old mother and young children
find refuge?
Fortunes, misfortunes, benefits, and harms
are clearly discernible.
It is up to your Excellency to consider them carefully.
Shēng ultimately did not listen.
The following year,
the defending general of Xīngyuán surrendered the city.
Wú Yǒurén attacked it several times,
but failed.
That year,
Tàizǔ sent an envoy to request passage to conquer Yúnnán,
but Shēng did not obey the imperial decree.

In the first month of the fourth year, he ordered General Tāng Hé, the Commander of the Western Expedition, leading Deputy General Liáo Yǒngzhōng and others, to advance by naval forces from Qūtáng to Chóngqìng.
General Fù Yǒudé, leading Deputy General Gù Shí and others, advanced with infantry and cavalry from Qín and Lǒng to Chéngdū,
to attack Shǔ.
Initially,
Shòu said to Shēng:
"Even with the strength of Wáng Bǎobǎo and Lǐ Sīqí, they could not resist Míng,
how much less our Shǔ!
Once there is an alarm,
what plan is there?"
Yǒurén said:
"Not so.
Our Shǔ is bordered by mountains and girded by rivers, unlike the Central Plains.
It is better to maintain good external relations while strengthening internal defenses."
Shēng agreed,
and sent Mò Rénshòu to block the mouth of Qūtáng Xiá with iron chains.
By this time, he again sent Shòu, Yǒurén, Zōu Xīng, and others with additional troops for assistance.
They relied on Yángjiǎoshān to the north and Nánchéngzhài to the south,
carving out the rock walls on both banks
and installing iron chains for a flying bridge,
placing wooden planks and cannons to resist the enemy.
When Hé's army arrived,
they could not advance.
Fù Yǒudé reconnoitered Jiē and Wén, finding them unprepared,
advanced and broke through them,
then also broke through Miánzhōu.
Shòu then left Xīng and others to guard Qūtáng,
and he himself returned with Yǒurén,
meeting with Xiàng Dàhēng's army to reinforce Hánzhōu.
They suffered great defeats in several battles;
Shòu and Dàhēng fled to Chéngdū,
while Yǒurén fled to Bǎoníng.
At this time, Yǒngzhōng also broke through Qūtáng Guān.
The flying bridge and iron chains were all burned through;
Xīng died from an arrow,
and all the Xià soldiers scattered.
Consequently, Kúizhōu was taken,
and the army then reached Tóngluó Xiá.
Shēng was greatly alarmed.
Right Chancellor Liú Rén advised him to flee to Chéngdū.
Shēng's mother, Péng, wept and said:
"Even if we reach Chéngdū,
it will only prolong our lives for a few days.
The great army is passing through like a broken bamboo.
It is better to surrender early to save the lives of the people."
Thereupon, he sent an envoy with a memorial to beg for surrender.
Shēng, with hands bound and a jade disc in his mouth, carried a coffin,
and along with his mother Péng and officials, surrendered at the army gate.
Hé accepted the jade disc,
and Yǒngzhōng untied his bonds,
conveying the imperial command to comfort them,
and ordering all generals not to harass anyone.
And Shòu and Dàhēng also surrendered Chéngdū to Yǒudé.
Shēng and the others were all sent to the capital.
The ministers of rites memorialized:
"The Emperor is in Fèngtiān Diàn.
Míng Shēng and others prostrate themselves, awaiting punishment outside Wǔmén,
and the relevant official proclaims the imperial decree of pardon,
following the precedent of Mèng Chǎng's surrender to Sòng."
The Emperor said:
"Shēng is young and weak;
the matter was caused by his subordinates,
which differs from Mèng Chǎng.
He should be exempted from the ceremony of prostrating and presenting a memorial while awaiting punishment."
On that day, Shēng was granted the title of Guīyì Hóu
and bestowed a residence in the capital.
In the tenth month of winter,
Hé and others completely pacified all the commanderies and counties of Chuān and Shǔ,
captured Yǒurén in Bǎoníng,
and then returned with their army.
Shòu, Dàhēng, and Rénshòu all scuttled their boats and drowned themselves.
Dīng Shìzhēn,
the defending general of Wénzhōu,
resisted with all his might from a dangerous position when Yǒudé attacked Wénzhōu,
and Wāng Xīngzǔ died there.
When Wénzhōu was broken,
he fled.
He later regrouped his forces and again attacked Wénzhōu,
killing Zhū Xiǎnzhōng,
but Yǒudé struck and drove him away.
After Xià fell,
he again gathered remnants and besieged Qínzhōu for fifty days.
His army was defeated,
and he spent the night at Zǐtóng Miào,
where he was killed by his own subordinates.
When Yǒurén arrived at the capital,
the Emperor, because he had invaded Hánzhōng,
initiated the military conflict,
and caused the Míng clan to lose their state,
had him executed in the marketplace.
Other generals and officers were garrisoned in Xúzhōu.
The following year, Shēng was exiled to Gāolí.
A eulogy: Zhāng Yǒuliàng and Zhāng Shìchéng rose from humble beginnings, as scribes and peddlers,
and usurped power amidst the chaos.
They relied on their wealth and strength,
but ultimately, they were defeated by the very things they relied upon.
Tracing the reasons for their rise and fall, from beginning to end,
Tàizǔ's judgment was indeed keen.
Míng Guózhēn was the first to rebel,
being faithless and fickle,
yet he eventually died a natural death.
Míng Yùzhēn seized the opportunity,
carved out a corner for himself,
and claimed the imperial title for two generations.
None of this can be said to be anything but fortunate.
Guózhēn was also named Gǔzhēn,
presumably to avoid the Ming imperial taboo after his surrender.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 12: Kuòkuò Tiēmù'ér (Cài Zǐyīng), Chén Yǒudìng (Bǎi Yán Zǐzhōng et al.), Bǎzālà Wǎěrmì.
Kuòkuò Tiēmù'ér
was from Shěnqiū.
His original surname was Wáng,
and his given name was Bǎobǎo.
He was the nephew of Yuán Chancellor Cháhǎn Tiēmù'ér.
Cháhǎn adopted him as a son,
and Emperor Shùn conferred upon him the name Kuòkuò Tiēmù'ér.
When bandits rose in Rǔ and Yǐng,
and the Central Plains fell into great disorder,
the Yuán army was long without success.
In the twelfth year of Zhìzhèng (1352),
Cháhǎn raised an army of righteousness,
fought in Hénán and Héběi,
attacked the rebels in Guānzhōng and Hédōng,
recovered Biànliáng,
drove away Liú Fútōng,
pacified Shāndōng,
accepted the surrender of Tián Fēng,
and almost completely annihilated the rebels.
Soon after, he led a large army to besiege Yìdū.
Tián Fēng rebelled,
and Cháhǎn was assassinated by Wáng Shìchéng.
The details are found in the Yuán Shǐ.
After Cháhǎn's death,
Emperor Shùn immediately appointed Kuòkuò Grand Commandant, Chancellor of the Central Secretariat, and Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs in the army camp,
giving him the same official posts as Cháhǎn.
He led the army to besiege Yìdū,
tunneled underground to enter,
and captured it.
He seized Fēng and Shìchéng,
gouged out their hearts as an offering to Cháhǎn,
and bound Chén Náotóu and over twenty others, presenting them at the imperial court.
He then took Jǔzhōu to the east,
and all of Shāndōng was pacified.
This was in the twenty-second year of Zhìzhèng (1362).
Initially,
when Cháhǎn pacified Jìn and Jì,
Bólúo Tiēmù'ér was in Dàtóng,
and disputed the territory with his army,
attacking each other multiple times.
The imperial court issued edicts for reconciliation,
but they ultimately did not comply.
After Kuòkuò pacified Qí,
he led his army back,
stationing them in Tàiyuán,
and continued to feud with Bólúo as before.
At this time, court officials Lǎo Díshā and Tū Jiān incurred the displeasure of the Crown Prince,
and fled to Bólúo,
who harbored them.
An edict was issued to strip Bólúo of his offices
and relieve him of his military authority.
Bólúo then raised an army and rebelled,
invading the capital,
killing Chancellor Shuòsījiān,
and making himself Left Chancellor.
Lǎo Díshā became Chancellor,
and Tū Jiān Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs.
The Crown Prince sought aid from Kuòkuò.
Kuòkuò dispatched his general Bái Suǒzhù with ten thousand cavalry to defend the capital,
but the battle was unfavorable,
and he escorted the Crown Prince to Tàiyuán.
A year later,
Kuòkuò, acting on the Crown Prince's order, raised an army to suppress Bólúo,
entered Dàtóng,
and advanced to threaten Dàdū.
Emperor Shùn then had Bólúo assassinated at court.
Kuòkuò followed the Crown Prince to the imperial audience,
and was made Grand Tutor and Left Chancellor.
At that time,
without Kuòkuò,
the Crown Prince would have been in grave danger.
Although Kuòkuò's achievements were great,
having risen from the ranks
to quickly reach the chancellorship,
many old officials at court were jealous of him.
And Kuòkuò, having long commanded armies,
was also not happy staying at court.
After two months,
he requested to go out and manage the army,
to pacify Jiāng and Huái in the south.
An edict approved this,
and he was enfeoffed as King of Hénán,
commissioned to command all the armies of the realm,
to lead expeditions in place of the Crown Prince,
and was given half of the Central Secretariat's officials to accompany him.
His imperial retinue and armored guards stretched for tens of li,
his military might was very impressive.
At this time, Tàizǔ had already annihilated Chén Yǒuliàng,
and controlled all the lands of Jiāng and Chǔ.
Zhāng Shìchéng held Huáidōng and Zhèxī.
Kuòkuò knew the southern army was strong
and could not be lightly advanced upon.
So he stationed his army in Hénán,
and issued a summons to the four generals of Guānzhōng to assemble their forces for a major expedition.
The four generals were
Lǐ Sīqí, Zhāng Sīdào, Kǒng Xìng, and Tuōlièbó.
Sīqí,
a native of Luóshān,
had raised a righteous army together with Cháhǎn,
and their standing was roughly equal.
Upon receiving the summons, he was furious and said,
"I was friends with your father;
your hair isn't even dry yet,
how dare you summon me!"
He ordered his subordinates that not a single armor should leave Wǔguān.
Sīdào and the others also refused to obey the command.
Kuòkuò sighed and said,
"I have received an imperial edict to command all the armies of the realm,
yet the garrison generals do not submit to my control.
How can I suppress the rebels!"
So he dispatched his younger brother Tuōyīn Tiēmù'ér with an army to garrison Jǐnán,
to defend against the southern army,
while he himself led his troops west into the passes,
to attack Sīqí and the others.
Sīqí and the others assembled their forces in Cháng'ān,
made an alliance on the old foundation of Hányuán Palace,
and jointly resisted Kuòkuò.
They were locked in a stalemate for a year,
fighting hundreds of battles without a decisive outcome.
Emperor Shùn sent an envoy to order them to cease hostilities
and focus solely on Jiāng and Huái.
Kuòkuò wanted to first pacify Sīqí and the others,
and then lead his army east.
He therefore dispatched his brave general Mò Gāo to advance rapidly towards Hézhōng,
intending to strike Fèngxiáng unexpectedly
and destroy Sīqí's stronghold.
Many of Mò Gāo's troops were from Bólúo's former division.
When they reached Wèihuī,
the army mutinied,
coerced Mò Gāo to betray Kuòkuò,
attacked and occupied Wèihuī and Zhāngdé,
and formally accused Kuòkuò at court.
Initially,
when the Crown Prince fled to Tàiyuán,
he wished to establish himself as emperor, following the precedent of Emperor Sùzōng of Táng at Língwǔ.
Kuòkuò refused.
When he returned to the capital,
the Empress issued an edict ordering him to lead a large army into the city with the Crown Prince,
to coerce Emperor Shùn into abdicating.
Kuòkuò stopped his army thirty li from the capital,
and entered the court with only a few horsemen.
Because of this, the Crown Prince resented him,
and Emperor Shùn also became secretly wary of Kuòkuò.
Court officials clamored that Kuòkuò had been ordered to pacify Jiāng and Huái,
but instead attacked Guānzhōng to the west,
and now refused to cease hostilities as commanded,
showing signs of defiance.
When Mò Gāo's memorial arrived,
Emperor Shùn then stripped Kuòkuò of his titles of Grand Tutor and Left Chancellor of the Central Secretariat,
ordering him to reside in his fief of Rǔnán as King of Hénán,
and distributed his army among various generals.
Meanwhile, Mò Gāo was appointed Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs and Chancellor,
commanding all the Héběi forces,
and his army was bestowed the title
"Loyal and Righteous Meritorious Servants."
The Crown Prince established the Bureau for Pacifying the Army in the capital,
to command all the military forces of the realm,
specifically to prepare against Kuòkuò.
Kuòkuò 既受詔,
退軍澤州,
其部將關保亦歸於朝．
朝廷知 Kuòkuò 勢孤,
乃詔 Lǐ Sīqí 等東出關,
與 Mògāo 合攻 Kuòkuò,
而令 Guānbǎo 以兵戍太原．
Kuòkuò 憤甚,
引軍據太原,
盡殺朝廷所置官吏．
於是 Shùndì 下詔盡削 Kuòkuò 官爵,
令諸軍四面討之．
是時明兵已下山東,
收大梁．
梁王 Ālǔwēn,
Cháhàn 父也,
以河南降．
Tuōyīn Tiēmù'ér 敗走,
餘皆望風降遁,
無一人抗者．
既迫潼關,
Sīqí 等倉皇解兵西歸,
而 Mògāo、 Guānbǎo 皆為 Kuòkuò 所擒殺．
Shùndì 大恐,
下詔歸罪於太子,
罷撫軍院,
悉復 Kuòkuò 官,
令與 Sīqí 等分道南討．
詔下一月,
明兵已逼大都,
Shùndì 北走．
Kuòkuò 入援不及,
大都遂陷,
距 Cháhàn 死時僅六年云．
明兵已定元都,
將軍 Tāng Hé 等自澤州徇山西．
Kuòkuò 遣將禦之,
戰於韓店,
明師大敗．
會 Shùndì 自開平命 Kuòkuò 復大都,
Kuòkuò 乃北出雁門,
將由保安徑居庸以攻北平．
Xú Dá、 Cháng Yùchūn 乘虛擣太原,
Kuòkuò 還救．
部將 Huòbímǎ 潛約降於明．
明兵夜劫營,
營中驚潰．
Kuòkuò 倉卒以十八騎北走,
明兵遂西入關．
Sīqí 以臨洮降．
Sīdào 走寧夏,
其弟 Liángchén 以慶陽降,
既而復叛,
明兵破誅之．
於是元臣皆入於明,
唯 Kuòkuò 擁兵塞上,
西北邊苦之．
洪武三年,
Tàizǔ 命大將軍 Xú Dá 總大兵出西安,
擣定西．
Kuòkuò 方圍蘭州,
趨赴之．
戰於沈兒峪,
大敗,
盡亡其衆,
獨與妻子數人北走,
至黃河,
得流木以渡,
遂奔和林．
時 Shùndì 崩,
太子嗣立,
復任以國事．
踰年,
Tàizǔ 復遣大將軍 Xú Dá、 左副將軍 Lǐ Wénzhōng、 征西將軍 Féng Shèng 將十五萬衆,
分道出塞取 Kuòkuò．
大將軍至嶺北,
與 Kuòkuò 遇,
大敗,
死者數萬人．
Liú Jī 嘗言於 Tàizǔ 曰：
「 Kuòkuò 未可輕也． 」
至是帝思其言,
謂晉王曰：
「吾用兵未嘗敗北．
今諸將自請深入,
敗於和林,
輕信無謀,
致多殺士卒,
不可不戒． 」
明年,
Kuòkuò 復攻雁門,
命諸將嚴為之備,
自是明兵希出塞矣．
其後,
Kuòkuò 從其主徙金山,
卒於哈剌那海之衙庭,
其妻 Máo Shì 亦自經死,
蓋洪武八年也．
初,
Cháhàn 破山東,
江、淮震動．
Tàizǔ 遣使通好．
元遣戶部尚書 Zhāng Zhuó、 郎中 Mǎ Hémóu 浮海如江東,
授 Tàizǔ 榮祿大夫、 江西等處行中書省平章政事,
賜以龍衣御酒．
甫至而 Cháhàn 被刺,
Tàizǔ 遂不受,
殺 Mǎ Hémóu,
以 Zhāng Zhuó 才,
留官之．
及 Kuòkuò 視師河南,
Tàizǔ 乃復遣使通好,
Kuòkuò 輒留使者不遣．
凡七致書,
皆不答．
既出塞,
復遣人招諭,
亦不應．
最後使 Lǐ Sīqí 往．
始至,
則待以禮．
尋使騎士送歸,
至塞下,
辭曰：
「主帥有命,
請公留一物為別． 」
Sīqí 曰：
「吾遠來無所齎． 」
騎士曰：
「願得公一臂． 」
Sīqí 知不免,
遂斷與之．
還,
未幾死．
Tàizǔ 以是心敬 Kuòkuò．
一日,
大會諸將,
問曰：
「天下奇男子誰也？ 」
皆對曰：
「 Cháng Yùchūn 將不過萬人,
橫行無敵,
真奇男子． 」
Tàizǔ 笑曰：
「 Yùchūn 雖人傑,
吾得而臣之．
吾不能臣 Wáng Bǎobǎo,
其人奇男子也． 」
竟冊其妹為秦王妃．
Zhāng Zhuó 仕明,
累官中書省參知政事,
有才辨,
明習故事,
裁決如流,
甚見信任．
自以故元臣,
心嘗戀戀．
會 Tàizǔ 縱降人北還,
Zhuó 附私書訪其子存亡．
Yáng Xiàn 得書稿以聞,
下吏按問．
Zhuó 大書牘背曰：
「身在江南,
心思塞北． 」
Tàizǔ 乃殺之．
而 Kuòkuò 幕下士不屈節縱出塞者,
有 Cài Zǐyīng．
Huīzǔ died more than a month later.
Chéngzǔ issued an edict to his ministers, saying:
“Huīzǔ conspired with Qí and Huáng and their ilk to endanger the state.
I, remembering Zhōngshān Wáng’s great achievements,
pardoned him by stretching the law.
Now that Huīzǔ is dead,
Zhōngshān Wáng cannot be without an heir.”
So he ordered Huīzǔ’s eldest son, Qīn, to succeed him.
Nine years later,
Qīn, along with Chéngguó Gōng Yǒng, Dìngguó Gōng Jǐngchāng, Yǒngkāng Hóu Zhōng, and others,
were all impeached by censors for their unrestrained behavior.
The Emperor pardoned Yǒng and the others,
but ordered Qīn to return home to study.
In the nineteenth year, he came to court,
then abruptly resigned and returned home.
The Emperor was enraged
and stripped him of his status as a commoner.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
he restored his former title,
which was passed to his sons Xiǎnzōng and Chéngzōng.
Chéngzōng,
at the beginning of the Tiānshùn era,
served as the Garrison Commander of Nánjīng,
also leading the Zhōngjūn Fǔ.
He was public-spirited, honest, and cared for his soldiers, earning a reputation for wisdom.
He died,
and his son Fǔ succeeded him.
Fǔ, courtesy name Gōngfǔ,
was steady and discreet,
and had excellent deportment.
The position of Nánjīng Garrison Commander was of the highest rank.
Huáiróu Bó Shī Jiàn, who was also a joint garrison commander, was ranked above Fǔ.
Fǔ was displeased
and reported it to the court.
An edict was issued, stipulating that rank should be determined by peerage,
and this was established as a regulation.
In the twelfth year of Hóngzhì,
Gěishì Zhōng Hú Yì and Yùshǐ Hú Xiàn were imprisoned for submitting memorials concerning natural disasters.
Fǔ submitted a memorial to rescue them.
During the Zhèngdé era,
he submitted a memorial advising against hunting,
his words being sharp and direct.
He once disputed land with a commoner from Wúxī,
and bribed Liú Jǐn,
which earned him much criticism at the time.
Fǔ died after succeeding for fifty-two years,
and was posthumously granted the title of Tàifù
and the posthumous name Zhuāngjìng.
His grandson Péngjǔ succeeded him.
He favored his concubine,
falsely designating her as a夫人 (fūrén),
and wished to establish her son as the legitimate heir,
for which he was punished by having his emoluments withheld.
The title was passed to his son Bāngruì,
then to his grandson Wéizhì,
and his great-grandson Hóngjī.
From Chéngzōng to Hóngjī, six generations
all served as Garrison Commanders of Nánjīng,
and managed the affairs of the military headquarters.
Hóngjī was successively promoted to Tàifù.
He died
and was posthumously named Zhuāngwǔ.
His son Wénjué succeeded him.
With the fall of the Míng dynasty,
the title was abolished.
Zēngshòu, through his father’s official position, rose to the rank of Zuǒ Dūdū.
Jiànwén Dì, suspecting the King of Yān was planning a rebellion,
once asked Zēngshòu about it.
Zēngshòu prostrated and replied:
“The King of Yān is of the same blood as the late emperor,
and has reached the pinnacle of wealth and honor;
why would he rebel?”
However, when the Yān army rose,
he repeatedly conveyed information about the capital’s strengths and weaknesses to Yān.
The Emperor became aware of this
but had no time to question him.
When the Yān forces crossed the Jiāng River,
the Emperor summoned Zēngshòu to interrogate him.
He did not respond.
The Emperor personally used a sword to strike him down in the palace corridor.
When the King entered,
he wept over the body.
Upon ascending the throne,
he posthumously enfeoffed him as Wǔyáng Hóu
and gave him the posthumous name Zhōngmǐn.
Soon after, he was further enfeoffed as Dìngguó Gōng,
with an emolument of two thousand five hundred *dàn* of grain.
His son Jǐngchāng succeeded him.
He was arrogant and unrestrained,
and was impeached several times,
but Chéngzǔ always pardoned him.
When Chéngzǔ passed away,
Jǐngchāng was punished for not residing in his designated lodging during the mourning period,
and was stripped of his official attire, cap, and annual emolument,
but these were later restored.
The title passed through three generations to his great-grandson Guāngzuò.
He successively held military appointments,
was promoted to Tàishī,
and died after holding the title for forty-five years,
receiving the posthumous name Róngxī.
The title passed through his son to his grandson Wénbì.
During the Wànlì era,
he led the Hòujūn Fǔ.
He was favored by the Emperor for his carefulness and reverence,
and several times officiated at the imperial sacrifices to Heaven,
being promoted to Tàishī.
He repeatedly submitted memorials requesting the establishment of an heir,
the abolition of mining taxes,
and the release of those wrongfully imprisoned.
He died after holding the title for thirty-five years,
receiving the posthumous name Kānghuì.
It passed through two more generations to his great-grandson Yǔnzhēn,
who was killed by rebel bandits at the end of the Chóngzhēn era.
Among the meritorious officials of Hóngwǔ,
only Dà’s descendants had two dukes,
residing separately in the two capitals.
The descendants of Wèiguó Gōng were mostly worthy,
but across successive reigns, Dìngguó Gōng’s [family] often received double the imperial favor.
During the Jiājìng era, an edict was issued to cut down hereditary enfeoffments granted by imperial favor,
and there were those who argued that Dìngguó Gōng’s merits did not warrant it,
but in the end, it was not rescinded.
Tiānfú died early.
Yīngxù
was appointed Shàngbǎo Sī Qīng,
and successively promoted to Zhōngjūn Dūdū Qiānjì,
attending court as a respected official,
and holding the hereditary position of Zhǐhuī Shǐ.
Cháng Yùchūn,
courtesy name Bórén,
was a native of Huáiyuǎn.
He had a remarkable and imposing appearance,
was immensely brave and strong,
and, with his long arms, was skilled in archery.
Initially, he followed Liú Jù as a bandit,
but perceiving that Liú Jù would never succeed,
he returned to Tàizǔ at Héyáng.
Before arriving,
he lay exhausted in a field,
dreaming of a divine figure in armor and holding a shield, who called out:
“Rise, rise!
Your lord is coming!”
He woke with a start,
just as Tàizǔ arrived,
and immediately went to greet and bow to him.
This was in the fourth month of the fifteenth year of Zhìzhèng.
Shortly after,
he volunteered to be the vanguard.
Tàizǔ said:
“You merely came for food because you were hungry.
How can I keep you?”
Yùchūn insisted.
Tàizǔ said:
“Wait until we cross the river;
it won’t be too late to serve me then.”
When the army reached Niúzhǔ Jī,
the Yuán soldiers were arrayed on the cliff.
The boats were still more than three *zhàng* from the bank,
and no one could land.
Yùchūn’s swift boat arrived,
and Tàizǔ signaled him to advance.
Yùchūn responded instantly,
brandishing his *gē* and rushing forward.
The enemy engaged his *gē*.
He used the momentum to leap ashore,
shouting loudly and scattering the enemy.
The Yuán army was routed.
The various generals pressed the attack,
thus capturing Cǎishí,
and then advancing to take Tàipíng.
He was appointed Xiānfēng of the Zǒngguǎn Fǔ
and later promoted to Zǒngguǎn Dūdū.
At that time, the soldiers' wives, children, and baggage were all in Hézhōu.
Yuán Middle Chancellor Mánzǐ Hǎiyá (蛮子海牙) again used a naval force to raid and occupy Cǎishí,
blocking the road.
Tàizǔ personally led an attack against it,
sending Yùchūn to deploy many feints to divide the enemy's strength.
When the battle was joined,
Yùchūn steered a light boat,
ramming Hǎiyá's boats and splitting them in two.
His left and right wings launched an attack,
defeating them utterly,
and capturing all their boats.
The river route was reopened.
Soon after, he was ordered to guard Lìyáng,
and then followed in the attack on Jíqìng,
where his achievements were the most outstanding.
He followed Marshal Xú Dá (徐達) to take Zhènjiāng,
and then advanced to take Chángzhōu.
When Wú (吳) troops besieged Dá at Niútáng,
Yùchūn went to reinforce him,
breaking the siege,
capturing their general,
and was promoted to Commander-in-Chief Grand Marshal (Tǒngjūn Dàyuánshuài).
After conquering Chángzhōu,
he was promoted to Middle Wing Grand Marshal (Zhōngyì Dàyuánshuài).
He followed Dá to attack Níngguó,
was struck by a stray arrow,
but fought on with his wound bandaged,
and conquered it.
He separately took Mǎtuóshā (馬駝沙),
attacked Chízhōu with a naval force,
and took it,
then was promoted to Provincial Grand Marshal of Infantry, Cavalry, and Naval Forces (Xíngshěng Dūdū Mǎbù Shuǐjūn Dàyuánshuài).
He followed in taking Wùzhōu,
was transferred to Co-Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Tóngqiān Shūmìyuàn Shì),
and guarded Wùzhōu.
He moved his troops to besiege Qúzhōu,
and with a surprise attack, broke into the southern gate's barbican,
destroyed their war equipment,
and urgently attacked,
thereby taking the city.
He obtained ten thousand armored soldiers,
and was promoted to Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Qiān Shūmìyuàn Shì).
He attacked Hángzhōu,
but suffered a defeat,
and was recalled to Yìngtiān.
He followed Dá in capturing Zhào Pǔshèng's (趙普勝) naval camps,
then followed in guarding Chízhōu,
and thoroughly defeated the Hàn (漢) army at the foot of Jiǔhuáshān (九華山).
The details are in Dá's biography.
Yǒuliàng (友諒) approached Lóngwān;
Yùchūn set up an ambush with five wings of troops,
utterly defeating them,
and then recaptured Tàipíng.
His achievements were the most outstanding.
When Tàizǔ pursued Yǒuliàng to Jiāngzhōu,
he ordered Yùchūn to remain behind to guard it.
His enforcement of the law was strict,
and the military and civilians were solemn, none daring to transgress.
He was promoted to Vice Administrator of the Provincial Secretariat (Xíngshěng Cānzhī Zhèngshì).
He followed in taking Ānqìng.
When Hàn troops sallied out along the river to scout,
Yùchūn attacked them,
and they all fled back.
He seized the opportunity to take Jiāngzhōu.
Returning to guard Lóngwān,
he reinforced Chángxīng,
capturing and killing over five thousand Wú (吳) troops.
Their general Lǐ Bóshēng (李伯昇) lifted the siege and fled.
He was ordered to build brick walls for Ānqìng city.
Previously,
the most prominent generals appointed by Tàizǔ were
Administrator Shào Róng (邵榮), Right Chancellor Xú Dá, and Yùchūn, who formed a trio.
Róng, in particular, was a veteran general skilled in warfare,
but by this time, he had become arrogant, unruly, and harbored disloyal intentions.
He conspired with Vice Administrator Zhào Jìzǔ (趙繼祖) to set up an ambush and stage a revolt.
When the plot was discovered,
Tàizǔ wanted to pardon Róng from death,
but Yùchūn stepped forward and said:
"When a subject is branded a rebel,
how can he still be pardoned?
I will not live alongside him."
Tàizǔ then made Róng drink wine,
and with tears flowing, executed him.
Because of this, Tàizǔ loved and respected Yùchūn even more.
The commander of Chízhōu, Luó Yǒuxián (羅友賢), occupied Shénshān Zài (神山寨)
and communicated with Zhāng Shìchéng (張士誠).
Yùchūn defeated and beheaded him.
He followed in reinforcing Ānfēng.
By the time they arrived,
Lǚ Zhēn (呂珍) had already captured the city
and killed Liú Fútōng (劉福ōng).
Hearing of the arrival of the large army,
he deployed a strong force to resist and defend.
Tàizǔ's left and right armies were both defeated.
Yùchūn attacked their formation from the flank,
winning three battles and breaking their lines three times,
capturing countless soldiers and horses.
He then followed Dá in besieging Lúzhōu.
As the city was about to fall,
Chén Yǒuliàng besieged Hóngdū,
and they were recalled.
The armies joined to attack Hàn,
encountering them at Kānglángshān (康郎山) in Pénglǐ.
The Hàn army's boats were large,
and they held the advantage of the upper stream,
their vanguard was extremely sharp.
Yùchūn, along with the other generals, fought a great battle,
their shouts shaking heaven and earth,
each one fighting against a hundred.
Yǒuliàng's brave general Zhāng Dìngbiān (張定邊) directly attacked Tàizǔ's boat.
The boat became stuck in the shallows,
and was almost lost.
Yùchūn shot and wounded Dìngbiān,
allowing Tàizǔ's boat to escape,
but then Yùchūn's boat also became stuck in the shallows.
A damaged boat floated downstream,
colliding with Yùchūn's boat and freeing it.
They fought for three days,
setting fire to the Hàn boats.
The lake water turned red,
and Yǒuliàng dared not fight again.
The generals believed the Hàn army was still strong
and wanted to let them go,
but Yùchūn alone remained silent.
When they exited the lake mouth,
the generals wanted to let the boats go downstream to the east,
but Tàizǔ ordered them to block the upstream.
Yùchūn then sailed upstream along the river,
and the generals followed him.
Yǒuliàng, in dire straits,
attempted to break through the encirclement with a hundred boats.
The generals intercepted and attacked them,
and the Hàn army was utterly routed.
Yǒuliàng died.
When the army returned,
Yùchūn was ranked as having the most outstanding achievements,
and was greatly rewarded with gold, silk, and land.
He followed in besieging Wǔchāng.
Tàizǔ returned to Yìngtiān,
leaving Yùchūn to supervise the army and trap them.
The following year,
Tàizǔ ascended to the throne as the King of Wú,
and promoted Yùchūn to Administrator of the Central Secretariat (Píngzhāng Zhèngshì).
Tàizǔ again inspected the army at Wǔchāng.
Hàn Chancellor Zhāng Bìxiān (張必先) arrived from Yuè (岳) to reinforce.
Yùchūn attacked him swiftly before his forces could gather,
and captured him.
The morale within the city was thus broken,
and Chén Lǐ (陳理) subsequently surrendered,
allowing them to take all the territory of Jīng (荊) and Hú (湖).
He followed Left Chancellor Xú Dá to take Lúzhōu,
and separately led troops to pacify and capture the various forts of Shākēng (沙坑), Máling (麻嶺), and Niúpí (牛陂) in Línjiāng,
capturing the pseudo-Prefect Dèng Kèmíng (鄧克明),
and then took Jí'ān.
He besieged Gànzhōu,
but Xióng Tiānruì (熊天瑞) held out stubbornly and did not surrender.
Tàizǔ sent an envoy to instruct Yùchūn:
"When you conquer a city, do not kill too many.
If you gain territory,
what good is it without people?"
Thus, Yùchūn deepened the moats and erected palisades to trap them.
After six months of encampment,
Tiānruì's strength was exhausted and he surrendered.
Yùchūn indeed did not kill.
Tàizǔ was greatly pleased
and sent a letter praising and encouraging him.
Yùchūn then, using military might, persuaded Nánxióng (南雄) and Sháozhōu to surrender,
and returned to pacify Ānlù and Xiāngyáng.
He again followed Xú Dá to conquer Tàizhōu,
defeated Shìchéng's (士誠) reinforcing troops,
and supervised the naval forces to build a wall at Hǎi'ānbà (海安壩) to block them.
That autumn, he was appointed Vice-General.
He attacked Wú.
He defeated the Wú army at Tàihú,
at Píshān,
and at Sānlǐqiáo,
and then approached Húzhōu.
Shìchéng sent troops to reinforce,
stationing them at Jiùguǎn,
to emerge behind the main army.
Cháng Yùchūn led a detachment of elite troops from Dàquángǎng, through the eastern path of the encampment,
and came out behind them.
The enemy dispatched elite soldiers to engage in combat,
but Cháng Yùchūn's forces fought bravely and routed them.
He ambushed their Right Chancellor Xú Yì at Píngwàng,
completely burned their "Red Dragon" ships,
and again defeated them at Wūzhèn.
He pursued them to Shēngshān,
destroyed their land and water camps,
captured all the soldiers from Jiùguǎn,
and Húzhōu then fell.
He advanced to besiege Píngjiāng,
and encamped at Hǔqiū.
Shìchéng secretly led his army towards Cháng Yùchūn.
Cháng Yùchūn engaged him in battle at Běiháo,
defeated him,
and almost captured Shìchéng.
After a long time,
the various generals breached Fēngmén,
and Cháng Yùchūn also breached Chāngmén to enter,
and Wú was pacified.
He was promoted to Grand Chancellor with equal authority over military and state affairs,
and enfeoffed as the Duke of È.
He was again appointed Vice-General,
and, with Grand General Xú Dá, led troops on a northern expedition.
The Emperor personally instructed him, saying:
"Among a million troops,
to break through the front lines and assault fortified positions,
none is like the Vice-General.
I do not worry that you cannot fight,
but I worry about your readiness to fight lightly.
As a great general,
to delight in contending with junior officers
is far from what I expect."
Cháng Yùchūn bowed and expressed his gratitude.
After they departed,
Cháng Yùchūn was concurrently appointed Junior Guardian of the Crown Prince,
and followed in taking the various prefectures of Shāndōng,
capturing Biànliáng,
and advancing to attack Hénán.
Five myriad Yuán soldiers were arrayed north of the Luòshuǐ.
Cháng Yùchūn, on a lone horse, charged their formation.
Over twenty enemy cavalrymen clustered around him, piercing and stabbing.
Cháng Yùchūn killed their vanguard with a single arrow,
shouted loudly, and galloped in.
His brave warriors followed him.
The enemy was utterly routed.
He pursued the fleeing enemy for over fifty lì.
Liáng Wáng Ālǔwēn surrendered,
and the prefectures and counties of Hénán fell one after another.
He met the Emperor in Biànliáng,
and then, with the Grand General, took the various prefectures of Héběi.
He was the vanguard in taking Dézhōu,
led the naval forces along the river,
defeated the Yuán army at Héxīwù,
captured Tōngzhōu,
and then entered the Yuán capital.
Separately, he took Bǎodìng, Héjiān, and Zhēndìng.
He attacked Tàiyuán with the Grand General.
Kuòkuò Tièmù'ér came to reinforce.
Cháng Yùchūn said to Xú Dá:
"Although our cavalry is assembled,
our infantry has not yet arrived.
If we fight precipitously, we will suffer many casualties.
If we raid them at night, we can achieve our goal."
Xú Dá said:
"Good."
It happened that Kuòkuò's general, Huōbímǎ, came to negotiate surrender,
and offered to be an inside accomplice.
So, elite cavalry were selected to raid them silently at night.
Kuòkuò was still burning candles, examining military documents.
In his haste, he did not know where to go.
Barefoot on one foot,
he rode a weak horse,
and fled with eighteen cavalrymen to Dàtóng.
Huōbímǎ surrendered,
and four myriad armored soldiers were obtained.
Tàiyuán was then captured.
Cháng Yùchūn pursued Kuòkuò to Xīnzhōu and then returned.
An imperial edict renamed Cháng Yùchūn as Left Vice-General,
placing him above Right Vice-General Féng Shèng.
He took Dàtóng in the north,
then went to Hédōng,
took Fèngyuán Lù,
joined forces with Féng Shèng's army,
and captured Fèngxiáng in the west.
At that time, Yuán general Yěsù attacked Tōngzhōu.
An edict ordered Cháng Yùchūn to return to defend,
with Chancellor Lǐ Wénzhōng as his deputy,
leading nine myriad infantry and cavalry,
departing from Běipíng,
directly to Huìzhōu,
defeating enemy general Jiāng Wénqīng at Jǐnzhōu,
and defeating Yěsù at Quánníng.
He advanced to attack Dàxīng Zhōu,
dividing a thousand cavalry into eight ambushes.
The defending general fled during the night,
and all were captured.
Kāipíng was then captured.
The Yuán Emperor fled north.
He pursued the fleeing enemy for several hundred lì.
He captured the imperial prince Qìngshēng and generals such as Chancellor Dǐngzhù, totaling one myriad soldiers,
ten thousand carriages,
three thousand horses,
five myriad cattle,
and a corresponding amount of women, children, and treasures.
When the army returned,
and was stationed at Liǔhé Chuān,
he suddenly died of a violent illness,
at merely forty years old.
Tàizǔ, hearing of it,
was greatly shocked and mourned.
When the funeral arrived at Lóngjiāng,
he personally went out to offer sacrifices,
and ordered the ritual officials to deliberate on the rites for an Emperor mourning a great minister.
The deliberation was presented,
and the precedent of Sòng Tàizōng mourning King Hán Zhào Pǔ was used.
The imperial decree stated:
"Approved."
He was granted burial at Zhōngshān Yuán,
and ninety funerary objects were provided for interment in his tomb.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Yìyùn Tuīchéng Xuāndé Jìngyuǎn Gōngchén, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, Shàng Zhùguó, Tàibǎo, and Zhōngshū Yòuchéngxiàng,
and posthumously enfeoffed as King of Kāipíng,
with the posthumous name Zhōngwǔ.
He was enshrined in the Tàimiào,
his likeness placed in the temple of meritorious ministers,
both ranking second.
Cháng Yùchūn was firm, fierce, and resolute,
and skilled at comforting his soldiers.
Breaking through enemy lines and charging into formations,
he never suffered defeat.
Though not well-versed in literature and history,
his military strategies always aligned with ancient methods.
He was two years older than Grand General Xú Dá,
and often participated in campaigns with him,
obediently following commands with utmost care.
At the time, the famous generals were called Xú and Cháng.
Cháng Yùchūn once boasted that he could command one hundred thousand troops
and sweep across the world.
In the army, he was also known as
"Cháng Shíwàn"
(Cháng One Hundred Thousand).
Cháng Yùchūn's younger cousin, Cháng Róng,
accumulated merits to become an Assistant Commander,
and followed Lǐ Wénzhōng beyond the frontier,
dying in battle at Lúqú Hé.
Cháng Yùchūn had two sons:
Cháng Mào and Cháng Shēng.
Mào, for his merit in encountering spring,
was enfeoffed as Zhèngguó Gōng,
receiving a salary of two thousand dàn of grain.
He was granted a hereditary charter.
He was arrogant and inexperienced in affairs.
In the twentieth year of Hóngwǔ, he was ordered to follow the Grand General Féng Shèng on an expedition against Nàháchū at Jīnshān.
Shèng
was Mào's father-in-law.
Mào often disregarded Shèng's commands,
and Shèng repeatedly admonished and reprimanded him.
Mào responded slowly,
which made Shèng even more furious,
but he had no opportunity to vent his anger.
Coincidentally, Nàháchū requested to surrender
and went to the camp of the Right Deputy General Lán Yù.
During a drinking session,
Nàháchū quarreled with Yù.
Nàháchū poured wine on the ground,
and, looking at his subordinates, spoke in an angry tone.
Mào was present at the time.
His subordinate, Commander Zhào,
who understood Mongolian,
secretly told Mào:
"Nàháchū is about to flee."
Mào, caught by surprise,
went straight forward and wrestled with him.
Nàháchū was greatly startled
and stood up, wanting to get on his horse.
Mào drew his saber
and cut his arm, wounding him.
Nàháchū's subordinates, hearing of this,
some were startled and fled in disarray.
Shèng, already angry with Mào,
exaggerated the situation
and reported Mào for instigating a mutiny.
Consequently, Mào was shackled and brought to the capital.
Mào also spoke of Shèng's various unlawful acts.
The emperor confiscated Shèng's commander-in-chief seal,
and resettled Mào in Lóngzhōu.
He died in the twenty-fourth year.
Previously,
the indigenous official of Lóngzhōu, Zhào Tiējiān, died.
His cousin, Zōngshòu, was supposed to inherit.
Tiējiān's wife, Huáng, gave her beloved daughter to Mào as a concubine
and usurped control of the prefecture's affairs.
After Mào's death,
Huáng and Zōngshòu contended for the prefectural seal,
accusing each other.
Someone fabricated rumors,
claiming that Mào was not actually dead,
and Zōngshòu knew the truth.
The emperor was furious
and ordered Zōngshòu to present Mào to redeem himself,
and commanded Yáng Wén and Hán Guān to lead an army to attack Lóngzhōu.
Later, it was known that Mào had indeed died,
and Zōngshòu also paid a ransom,
so the troops were withdrawn.
Mào had no sons.
His younger brother, Shēng,
was re-enfeoffed as Kāiguó Gōng.
He frequently led armies for training
and was promoted to Tàizǐ Tàibǎo.
The records do not contain
the details of Shēng's death.
Other historical accounts and biographies state
that at the end of Jiànwén's reign,
Shēng and Wèiguó Gōng Huīzǔ fought bravely at Pǔzǐkǒu
and died in the early Yǒnglè period.
Others say that Shēng was implicated in Lán Yù's faction during the Hóngwǔ reign,
and someone reported him for gathering troops at Sānshān;
he was executed.
The Cháng clan was the maternal relatives of Xīngzōng.
During the Jiànwén period, their favor and courtesies should have been ample.
After the events of the revolution,
there is nothing to verify,
and thus conflicting accounts of his death were passed down.
Shēng's son, Jìzǔ,
was relocated to Lín'ān Wèi in Yúnnán in the first year of Yǒnglè,
being only seven years old at the time.
Jìzǔ's son was Níng,
and Níng's son was Fù.
In the fifth year of Hóngzhì, an imperial edict stated:
"Among the meritorious officials enshrined in the Tàimiào,
those who were posthumously granted princely titles
all assisted Our Imperial Ancestor in pacifying the empire
and had great achievements.
Yet their descendants sometimes do not receive any official emolument
and fall into the ranks of commoners.
We cannot bear this.
The relevant department should seek out their legitimate heirs
and grant them an appropriate official position
to maintain the ancestral sacrifices."
So Fù was summoned from Yúnnán
and appointed as the hereditary Commander of the Nánjīng Jǐnyī Wèi.
In the eleventh year of Jiājìng, after the re-enfeoffment of the four princes,
Fù's grandson, Xuánzhèn, was enfeoffed as Huáiyuǎn Hóu.
This title was passed down to his great-grandson, Yánlíng,
who had virtuous conduct.
In the sixteenth year of Chóngzhēn,
the entire province of Chǔ fell.
Yánlíng requested to command the capital's troops to Jiǔjiāng to assist in its defense.
He also said that there was a place in Jiāngdū called Chángjiāshā,
where several thousand clan members were distant descendants of his first ancestor.
He requested to inspire them with loyalty and righteousness
and train them as personal guards.
The emperor praised him,
but it was not carried out.
Many noble relatives and imperial in-laws in Nándū were arrogant and unrestrained,
but Yánlíng alone was known for upholding his duty.
When the state fell,
he personally tended his garden,
living a simple life as a commoner until his old age.
A eulogy states: Míng Tàizǔ rose from Chúyáng,
pacifying the four directions.
Although it is said to be heaven-sent,
the strength of the two princes contributed greatly.
Zhōngshān was prudent and strategic,
his achievements great yet he did not boast.
No assistant of historical renown can surpass him.
Kāipíng broke through enemy lines and charged into battle,
conquering wherever he went.
His wisdom and bravery were not inferior to Zhōngshān's.
Moreover, he was publicly loyal and modest,
skilled at preserving his fame and achievements,
truly the foremost of the founding ministers.
His body was likened to the sun and moon,
he was granted seals and lands;
such as these two princes,
it can be said to be the height of glory.
However, Zhōngshān's rewards extended to his descendants,
who continuously enjoyed honor and favor,
while Kāipíng was not granted longevity by heaven,
and his descendants also declined.
Their noble status and achievements were equal,
yet their rewards sometimes differed.
What was the reason for this?
Tàizǔ once said to his generals:
"If a general does not kill wantonly,
it is not only beneficial to the state,
but your descendants will truly receive its blessings."
Indeed,
this can serve as a lesson for those who are commanders and generals.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 14: Lǐ Wénzhōng, Dèng Yù, Tāng Hé, Mù Yīng
Lǐ Wénzhōng,
courtesy name Sīběn, small name Bǎo'ér,
a native of Xúyí,
was the nephew of Tàizǔ.
At the age of twelve, his mother died,
and his father, Zhēn, carried him through the midst of the rebellious armies,
coming close to death several times.
More than two years later, he met Tàizǔ in Chúyáng.
Tàizǔ, seeing Bǎo'ér,
was exceedingly pleased.
He adopted him as his son
and ordered him to take his surname.
He was exceptionally intelligent in his studies, as if he had always been accustomed to them.
At nineteen,
as a gentleman, he commanded the imperial guards.
He followed in reinforcing Chízhōu,
defeated the Tiānwán army,
and was outstanding in valor among all the generals.
He separately attacked Qīngyáng, Shídài, Tàipíng, and Jīngdé,
all of which he took.
He defeated Yuán judge Ālúhuī at Wànnián Jiē
and again defeated the Miáo army at Yúqián and Chānghuà.
Advancing to attack Chún'ān,
he launched a night raid on Grand Marshal Hóng,
causing over a thousand of his troops to surrender.
He was appointed Left Deputy Commander of the Tent Guard
and concurrently managed the affairs of the Grand Marshal's Residence.
Soon after, he joined the forces of Dèng Yù and Hú Dàhǎi
to capture Jiàndé,
making it Yánzhōu Fǔ,
and defended it.
The Miáo commander Yáng Wánzhě suddenly arrived with tens of thousands of Miáo and Liáo troops by land and water.
Wénzhōng led light troops to defeat their land army,
took the captured heads,
and floated them on a large raft.
The naval forces, seeing this, also fled.
Wánzhě attacked again,
and he and Dèng Yù repelled him.
He advanced and captured Pǔjiāng,
forbidding burning and plundering,
and demonstrating grace and trustworthiness.
The Zhèng clan of Yìmén, who had taken refuge in the mountains and valleys to avoid the war,
were summoned back,
and he protected them with troops.
The people were greatly pleased.
After Wánzhě died,
his subordinate generals requested to surrender,
and he pacified them,
gaining over thirty thousand men.
When Emperor Jiànwén ascended the throne,
Jǐnglóng was intimately trusted as a close relative,
and was once ordered to arrest Prince Zhōu, Zhū Sù.
When the Yān army rose,
Chángxīng Hóu Gěng Bǐngwén's campaign against Yān failed.
Qí Tài, Huáng Zǐchéng, and others jointly recommended Jǐnglóng.
So Jǐnglóng was appointed Grand General in place of Bǐngwén,
leading an army of five hundred thousand for the northern expedition.
He was bestowed with a 'Connecting Heaven Rhinoceros' belt;
the Emperor personally pushed his carriage wheel,
and saw him off by the river,
ordering him to act with full discretion.
Jǐnglóng was a pampered son of a noble family,
ignorant of warfare,
and only full of self-importance.
Many veteran generals were discontent and refused to serve him.
Jǐnglóng rushed to Dézhōu,
and assembled his troops to encamp at Héjiān.
The Prince of Yān heard of this with delight,
and said to his generals:
"Lǐ Jiǔjiāng [Lǐ Jǐnglóng]
is but a silken youth,
easy to deal with."
He then ordered his heir apparent to stay and defend,
cautioning him not to engage in battle,
while he personally led his troops to reinforce Yǒngpíng,
marching directly to Dàníng.
Jǐnglóng heard of this,
and advanced to besiege Běipíng.
Dūdū Qú Néng attacked the Zhāngyè Gate,
and was on the verge of breaking through.
Jǐnglóng, jealous of Néng's achievements,
stopped him.
When the Yān army defeated Dàníng
and returned to attack Jǐnglóng,
Jǐnglóng suffered repeated major defeats,
fled to Dézhōu,
and all his armies scattered.
In the first month of the following year,
the Prince of Yān attacked Dàtóng.
Jǐnglóng led his army out of Zǐjīng Pass to relieve it,
but returned without success.
The Emperor, fearing Jǐnglóng's authority was still too light,
sent an imperial eunuch bearing an imperial seal document and bestowing a yellow battle-axe and bow and arrows,
granting him full authority over campaigns.
While crossing the river,
a storm wrecked the boat,
and all the bestowed items were lost.
New ones were then made and bestowed.
In the fourth month,
Jǐnglóng held a grand oath-taking ceremony at Dézhōu,
and met with Wǔdìng Hóu Guō Yīng, Ānlù Hóu Wú Jié, and others at Zhēndìng.
Combining their armies to six hundred thousand,
they advanced and encamped at Báigōu River.
Engaging in continuous battle with the Yān army,
they were again utterly defeated.
The imperial seal document, axe, and battle-axe were all abandoned.
He fled to Dézhōu,
then fled to Jǐnán.
In this campaign,
hundreds of thousands of imperial troops died,
and the southern army could no longer resist.
The Emperor then ordered Jǐnglóng to return.
Huáng Zǐchéng, ashamed and indignant,
seized Jǐnglóng in the court ranks
and requested his execution to appease the world.
When the Yān army crossed the river,
the Emperor was greatly distressed.
Fāng Xiàorú again requested Jǐnglóng's execution.
The Emperor did not inquire into any of these matters.
He sent Jǐnglóng, along with Shàngshū Rú Cháng and Dūdū Wáng Zuǒ, to the Yān army
to cede territory and sue for peace.
When the Yān army was stationed at Jīnchuānmén,
Jǐnglóng and Prince Gǔ, Zhū Huì, opened the gates and welcomed their surrender.
When the Prince of Yān ascended the imperial throne,
he conferred upon Jǐnglóng the title of Fèngtiān Fǔyùn Tuīchéng Xuānlì Wǔchén, Tèjìn Guānglù Dàfū, Zuǒ Zhùguó,
and increased his annual stipend by a thousand *shi*.
When major court affairs arose,
Jǐnglóng still presided over discussions as the head of the ranks,
which displeased all the meritorious officials.
In the second year of Yǒnglè,
Prince Zhōu exposed Jǐnglóng's acceptance of bribes at his residence during the Jiànwén era.
Xíngbù Shàngshū Zhèng Cì and others also impeached Jǐnglóng for harboring malicious intentions,
sheltering fugitives,
and plotting rebellion.
An edict ordered no inquiry into the matter.
Later,
Chéngguó Gōng Zhū Néng, Lìbù Shàngshū Jiǎn Yì, and civil and military officials
publicly impeached Jǐnglóng and his younger brother Zēngzhī for clear signs of treasonous plotting.
The six divisions of the supervising secretaries, Zhāng Xìn and others, also impeached him.
An edict stripped him of his meritorious titles,
prohibited him from court attendance,
and sent him home as a duke
to conduct sacrifices for the Eldest Princess.
Not long after,
Lǐbù Shàngshū Lǐ Zhìgāng and others again stated:
"Jǐnglóng, at home,
sits and receives kowtows from his gatekeepers as if he were an emperor,
which is utterly rebellious;
Zēngzhī has established many estates,
and harbors thousands of servants and pages,
his intentions are unfathomable."
Thereupon, Jǐnglóng was stripped of his peerage,
and he, Zēngzhī, and dozens of family members were confined to their private residence,
and their property was confiscated.
Jǐnglóng once fasted for ten days but did not die,
and only passed away at the end of the Yǒnglè era.
It was not until the thirteenth year of Zhèngtǒng that an edict was issued allowing Zēngzhī and others to open their gates
and live as they pleased.
In the early Hóngzhì period,
when recording the descendants of Wénzhōng,
Jǐnglóng's great-grandson Xuán was appointed hereditary Commander of the Nánjīng Jǐnyīwèi.
He died,
and his son Lián succeeded.
He died,
and his son Xìng succeeded.
In the eleventh year of Jiājìng, an edict enfeoffed Xìng as Línhuái Hóu,
with a stipend of a thousand *shi*.
He died the following year,
without sons,
so Lián's younger brother Yí was made to succeed to the enfeoffment.
He died,
and his son Tíngzhú succeeded.
He frequently served as head of military bureaus,
supervised naval operations,
wore the seal of the Píngmán General,
and garrisoned Húguǎng.
He died,
and his son Yángōng succeeded.
He served as Guard Commander in Nánjīng,
then entered to supervise the imperial garrisons,
and was successively promoted to Shàobǎo.
Yángōng,
courtesy name Wéiyín,
was fond of learning and skilled in poetry,
and humble towards the poor.
His son Zōngchéng
was known for his literary talent from a young age.
During the Wànlì reign,
when Japanese pirates invaded Cháoxiǎn,
Bīngbù Shàngshū Shí Xīng advocated for enfeoffment and tribute,
and recommended Zōngchéng's talent,
appointing him Dūdū Qiānshì,
to serve as the chief envoy.
He carried the imperial insignia and departed,
with Commander Yáng Fānghēng as his deputy.
When Zōngchéng reached Bùshān, Cháoxiǎn,
the number of Japanese increased,
and rumors spread
that they would capture the two envoys.
Zōngchéng became frightened,
changed his clothes, and fled back.
Meanwhile, Fānghēng crossed the sea
and was humiliated by the Japanese.
Zōngchéng was imprisoned and sentenced to military exile,
but his son Bāngzhèn succeeded to the marquisate.
When the Míng dynasty fell,
the peerage was abolished.
Dèng Yù,
a native of Hóng.
His initial name was Yǒudé;
Tàizǔ bestowed his given name.
His father Shùnxīng occupied Línháo
and died fighting the Yuán army.
His elder brother Yǒulóng succeeded him,
but also died of illness.
The assembly pushed Yù to lead military affairs.
Yù was only sixteen,
and in every battle, he would be the first to charge into the enemy lines.
The army universally admired his bravery.
When Tàizǔ rose at Chúyáng,
Yù came from Xūyí to pledge allegiance,
and was appointed Guǎnjūn Zǒngguǎn.
He followed in crossing the Jiāng.
He captured Tàipíng,
defeated and captured Chén Yěxiān,
subdued Lìyáng and Lìshuǐ,
took Jíqìng,
and captured Zhènjiāng,
all with merit.
He was promoted to Guǎngxīng Yì Yuánshuài
and posted to guard Guǎngdé Zhōu,
where he defeated the Long Spear Marshal Xiè Guóxǐ beneath the city walls,
captured his Zǒngguǎn Wǔ Shìróng,
and seized a thousand armored soldiers.
He was transferred to garrison Xuānzhōu,
and with his troops, took Jìxī,
and along with Hú Dàhǎi, captured Huīzhōu,
and was then transferred to serve as Pànguān of the Xíng Shūmìyuàn to guard it.
The Miao commander, Yáng Wánzhě (楊完者), attacked with 100,000 men.
The defense was thin and weak,
but Yu (愈) further encouraged his officers and soldiers,
and, combining forces with Hú Dàhǎi (胡大海),
defeated and routed them.
He advanced and captured Xiūníng (休寧) and Wùyuán (婺源),
captured three thousand soldiers,
and then took the Gāohé (高河) stronghold.
With Lǐ Wénzhōng (李文忠) and Hú Dàhǎi (胡大海), he attacked Jiàndé (建德),
passing through Suí'ān (遂安).
He defeated Yú Zǐzhēn (余子貞), the commander of the long spears,
pursued him north to Chún'ān (淳安),
and again defeated his reinforcing troops,
thus capturing Jiàndé (建德).
Yáng Wánzhě (楊完者) came to attack,
but Yu (愈) defeated and captured his general, Lǐ Fùshū (李副樞),
and three thousand soldiers from the mountain caves surrendered.
A month later,
he again defeated Wánzhě (完者) at Wūlónglǐng (烏龍嶺).
He was twice promoted to Qiān Xíng Shūmìyuàn Shì (僉行樞密院事).
He advanced on Lín'ān (臨安),
and Lǐ Bóshēng (李伯昇) came to its aid,
but was defeated at Xiánlínzhài (閑林寨).
Yu (愈) sent an envoy to persuade Yú Guāng (于光), the defending general of Ráozhōu (饒州), to surrender,
and then moved his garrison to Ráo (饒).
Ráo (饒) bordered Lake Pénglǐ (彭蠡湖),
and was adjacent to (Chén) Yǒuliàng (友諒)'s territory,
who frequently invaded,
but Yu (愈) always repelled them.
He was promoted to Cāncè (參政) of the Jiāngnán Xíngshěng (江南行省),
overseeing all divisions of the army.
He took Fúliáng (浮梁),
and advanced on Lèpíng (樂平).
Yúgān (餘干) and Jiànchāng (建昌) all fell.
Dèng Kèmíng (鄧克明), Yǒuliàng (友諒)'s defending general of Fǔzhōu (撫州), was attacked by Wú Hóng (吳宏).
He sent an envoy to feign surrender to delay the army.
Yu (愈) knew his true intentions,
donned his armor and galloped two hundred *lǐ* (里) overnight,
entering the city by dawn.
Kèmíng (克明) was caught by surprise
and fled on a single horse.
Yu (愈)'s commands were strict,
not even harming a single hair (i.e., not disturbing the common people),
and thus Fǔzhōu (撫州) was pacified.
Kèmíng (克明) had no choice but to surrender.
At that time, Hú Tíngruì (胡廷瑞), Yǒuliàng (友諒)'s prime minister, offered Lóngxīng Lù (龍興路),
which was renamed Hóngdū Fǔ (洪都府).
Yu (愈) was appointed Cāncè (參政) of Jiāngxī Xíngshěng (江西行省) to defend it,
and the surrendered generals Zhù Zōng (祝宗) and Kāng Tài (康泰) were ordered to follow him with their troops.
The two initially did not wish to surrender,
and when they were ordered to follow Xú Dá (徐達) to attack Wǔchāng (武昌),
they revolted.
Their boats reached Nǚ'ér Gǎng (女兒港),
they hastened back,
and entered by breaking through the Xīnchéngmén (新城門) gate under cover of night.
Yu (愈) heard of the rebellion suddenly,
and fled with a few dozen cavalry,
frequently encountering the rebels.
His cavalry guards were almost all killed,
and he was in dire straits.
He changed horses three times in succession,
but each horse stumbled.
Finally, he obtained his adopted son's horse and rode it,
and was able to escape through the Fǔzhōumén (撫州門) gate,
returning to Yìngtiān (應天).
Tàizǔ (太祖) did not punish him.
Soon after, Xú Dá (徐達) returned with his army to retake Hóngdū (洪都),
and again ordered Yu (愈) to assist Grand Commandant Zhū Wénzhèng (朱文正) in guarding it.
The following year,
Yǒuliàng (友諒)'s army of 600,000 invaded.
