Their tower ships were as high as the city walls,
and they sailed straight to the city under high tide,
besieging it hundreds of layers deep.
Yu (愈) was responsible for defending the Fǔzhōumén (撫州門),
a vital point.
Yǒuliàng (友諒) personally commanded his troops to attack.
The city wall was damaged for over thirty *zhàng* (丈),
but Yu (愈) both built and fought.
The enemy's attack intensified,
and he did not remove his armor day or night for three months.
Tàizǔ (太祖) personally came to reinforce,
and the siege was finally lifted.
His merits were deemed equal to those who captured the enemy.
After Tàizǔ (太祖) had pacified Wǔchāng (武昌),
he sent Yu (愈) to lead troops to pacify the unattached prefectures and counties in Jiāngxī (江西).
Dèng Zhìqīng (鄧志清), Dèng Kèmíng (鄧克明)'s younger brother, occupied Yǒngfēng (永豐)
with two thousand soldiers.
Yu (愈) attacked and defeated them,
capturing over fifty of their main commanders.
He followed Cháng Yùchūn (常遇春) in pacifying the strongholds of Shākēng (沙坑) and Málǐng (麻嶺),
then advanced to take Jí'ān (吉安),
and besieged Gànzhōu (贛州),
which he captured in the fifth month.
He was promoted to Yòuchéng (右丞) of Jiāngxī Xíngshěng (江西行省).
At this time, he was twenty-eight years old.
When the rebellion began,
no other generals achieved such high positions at an early age as Yu (愈) and Lǐ Wénzhōng (李文忠).
Yu (愈) was known for his simplicity, seriousness, and meticulousness,
not fearing danger or hardship.
His command was strict,
and he was good at comforting those who surrendered and attached themselves to him.
When he took Ānfú (安福),
some of his soldiers engaged in looting.
The judicial officer Pān Shū (潘樞) came to see him,
and openly criticized him.
Yu (愈) rose in alarm and apologized,
immediately ordering that those who plundered the people should be executed,
and demanded that all captured women and children found among the troops be released.
Shū (樞) then confined them in an empty house,
and sat outside the house himself,
preparing gruel for them.
When some soldiers plotted to raid and take them again at night,
Yu (愈) flogged them publicly.
Shū (樞) personally escorted all of them back to their homes,
and the people were greatly pleased.
Afterward, Yùchūn (遇春) captured Xiāngyáng (襄陽),
and appointed Yu (愈) as Píngzhāng (平章) of Húguǎng Xíngshěng (湖廣行省) to guard the area,
granting him a letter saying:
"When you garrison Xiāngyáng (襄陽),
you should carefully observe laws and regulations.
For those from mountain strongholds who come to surrender,
both soldiers and civilians should retain their original registrations.
All junior officers and below should be ordered to settle and farm,
both tilling and fighting.
The area you are garrisoning borders Kuòkuò (擴廓).
If you show kindness to the people
and enforce the law among the army,
then all those under his command will admire your righteousness and come to surrender,
like escaping a tiger's mouth to a kind mother.
I rely on you as a great wall;
you must strive for this."
Yu (愈) cleared the wilderness,
established military headquarters and encampments,
and pacified and attracted the people,
his authority and benevolence becoming very prominent.
In the first year of Wú (吳), the Yùshǐ Tái (御史臺) was established,
and he was summoned to be Yòu Yùshǐ Dàfū (右御史大夫),
leading the affairs of the bureau.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ (洪武), he concurrently served as Tàizǐ Yùdé (太子諭德).
As the main army campaigned in the Central Plains,
Yu (愈) served as the Zhēngshù Jiāngjūn (征戍將軍),
leading the Xiāng (襄) and Hàn (漢) troops to take the unattached prefectures north of Nányáng (南陽).
He then captured Tángzhōu (唐州),
advanced to attack Nányáng (南陽),
defeated the Yuan (元) army at Wǎdiàn (瓦店),
pursued them to the city walls,
and then captured it,
taking captive Shǐ Guógōng (史國公) and twenty-six others.
Suí (隨), Yè (葉), Wǔyáng (舞陽), and Lǔshān (魯山) and other prefectures and counties surrendered one after another.
He captured the mountain strongholds of Niúxīn (牛心), Guāngshí (光石), and Hóngshān (洪山),
and the lands of Jūn (均), Fáng (房), Jīn (金), and Shāng (商) were all pacified.
In the third year,
as Zhēnglǔ Zuǒ Fù Fùjiāngjūn (征虜左副副將軍), he followed the Grand General on an expedition to Dìngxī (定西).
Kuòkuò (擴廓) was encamped at Chēdàoxiàn (車道峴).
Yu (愈) advanced directly to his camp,
erected palisades to press him,
and Kuòkuò (擴廓) was defeated and fled.
He divided his troops and advanced from Líntáo (臨洮) to capture Hézhōu (河州),
and summoned and placated the various Tibetan chiefs.
Xuānwèi Hésuǒnánpǔ (宣慰何鎖南普) and others all presented their seals and requested to surrender.
He pursued Yù Wáng (豫王) to the western Héhuáng Hé (西黃河),
reached Hēisōnglín (黑松林),
and defeated and beheaded his chief general.
All the tribes west of Hézhōu (河州), including Jīngān (京甘) and Wūsīzàng (烏斯藏), submitted.
He returned after an expedition of several thousand *lǐ* (里) northwest of Gānsù (甘肅).
For his merits, he was awarded the title Kāiguó Fǔyùn Tuīchéng Xuānlì Wǔchén (開國輔運推誠宣力武臣), Tèjìn Rónglù Dàfū (特進榮祿大夫), Yòu Zhùguó (右柱國),
enfeoffed as Wèiguó Gōng (衞國公),
and concurrently participated in military and national affairs,
with an annual salary of three thousand *shí* (石)
and an hereditary warrant.
In the fourth year, when Shǔ (蜀) was to be attacked,
Yu (愈) was ordered to go to Xiāngyáng (襄陽) to train cavalry
and transport provisions for the soldiers.
In the fifth year,
when the various tribes of Chén (辰) and Lǐ (澧) rebelled,
Yu (愈) was appointed Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn (征南將軍), with Jiāngxià Hóu Zhōu Déxīng (江夏侯周德興) and Jiāngyīn Hóu Wú Liáng (江陰侯吳良) as deputies,
to suppress them.
Yu (愈) led Yáng Jǐng (楊璟) and Huáng Bīn (黃彬) out from Lǐzhōu (澧州),
captured the Forty-Eight Caves,
and also captured and beheaded the rebels from Fángzhōu (房州).
In the sixth year,
as Yòu Fùjiāngjūn (右副將軍), he followed Xú Dá (徐達) on a tour of the northwestern border.
In the tenth year,
when the Tubo (吐番) of Chuānzàng (川藏) caused trouble
and plundered the tribute envoys,
Yu (愈), as Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn (征西將軍), together with Deputy General Mù Yīng (沐英), campaigned against them.
They divided their troops into three routes,
pursued them relentlessly to the Kūnlún Shān (崑崙山),
captured and beheaded tens of thousands,
and seized over one hundred thousand horses, cattle, and sheep.
He then garrisoned troops in strategic locations before returning.
He fell ill on the way
and died in Shòuchūn (壽春)
at the age of forty-one.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Nínghé Wáng (寧河王)
and given the posthumous title Wǔshùn (武順).
In the seventeenth year,
the chieftains of Qǔjìng also rebelled.
They were suppressed and pacified.
Thereupon, the various Mán tribes of Pǔdìng and Guǎngnán were settled,
and the grain transport route to Tiánzhōu was opened.
In the twentieth year, the Làngqióng Mán were pacified.
He was ordered to travel from Yǒngníng to Dàlǐ,
setting up a fort every sixty lǐ,
and leaving troops to cultivate fields.
The following year,
Sīlúnfā of the Báiyí rebelled,
inciting various Mán tribes to raid Móshālè Village.
Dūdū Níng Zhèng was dispatched to defeat them.
In the twenty-second year,
Sīlúnfā again invaded Dìngbiān,
with a host numbering three hundred thousand.
Yīng selected thirty thousand cavalry to rush to the rescue,
arranging fire cannons and powerful crossbows in three rows.
The Mán drove a hundred elephants,
clad in armor and bearing palisades,
with large bamboo tubes on their left and right sides.
The tubes contained pointed spears,
which were extremely sharp.
Yīng divided his army into three;
Dūdū Féng Chéng led the vanguard,
Níng Zhèng led the left,
and Dūzhīhuī Tóngzhī Tāng Zhāo led the right.
Before the battle,
he gave the order:
“Today’s matter
is to advance, not retreat!”
Then, riding the wind, he let out a great shout,
and the cannons and crossbows fired simultaneously.
All the elephants turned and fled.
Xīlà Yìzhě,
a chieftain of the raiding rebels,
fought desperately,
and the left flank retreated slightly.
Yīng ascended a height to observe,
took out his saber,
and ordered his attendants to bring him the head of the commander.
When the left flank commander saw a man grasping a saber galloping down,
he was afraid
and bravely shouted, breaking through the enemy formation.
The main army seized the opportunity,
beheading over forty thousand people,
capturing thirty-seven elephants alive,
and all other elephants were killed.
The rebel chieftains were each struck by over a hundred arrows,
and died on the backs of their elephants.
Sīlúnfā fled,
and the various Mán were terrified.
Lùchuān then no longer caused trouble.
Afterward,
Fù Yǒudé, the Duke of Yǐng Guó, campaigned and pacified the Dōngchuān Mán.
He also pacified Āzī, the chieftain of Yuèzhōu, and the Àchì tribe of Guǎngxī.
In the winter of that year,
he went to court,
was granted a banquet in the Fèngtiān Diàn,
and was awarded two hundred liǎng of gold, five thousand liǎng of silver, five hundred dìng of paper money, and a hundred pǐ of colored silk.
He was then sent back.
When he bid farewell at the palace,
the Emperor personally patted him and said:
“It is you, Yīng,
who allows me to sleep soundly without worry about the south.”
Upon returning to his post,
he again defeated the Báiyí at Jǐngdōng.
Sīlúnfā begged for surrender,
offering local tribute.
Āzī rebelled again,
and he attacked and pacified him.
All of Nánzhōng was then settled.
He sent envoys to persuade various Fan tribes to surrender with military might.
Some Fan tribes offered tribute through multiple interpreters.
In the sixth month of the twenty-fifth year,
upon hearing of the Crown Prince’s death,
he wept with extreme sorrow.
Earlier,
when Empress Gāo died,
Yīng wept until he vomited blood.
At this time, he fell ill
and died at his post,
aged forty-eight.
The soldiers and common people cried in the streets,
and even distant夷 shed tears.
He was buried in the capital,
posthumously enfeoffed as the Prince of Qiánníng,
given the posthumous title Zhāojìng,
and enshrined in the imperial ancestral temple.
Yīng was resolute and taciturn,
admired the virtuous, and treated scholars with courtesy.
He treated his soldiers with kindness,
and never killed recklessly.
In Diān,
all affairs were well managed.
He streamlined local officials,
promoted agriculture and sericulture,
and annually assessed the increase or decrease in military farm production for rewards and punishments.
Reclaimed land reached over a million mù.
The Diān Chí was narrow,
so he dredged and widened it,
eliminating the problem of flooding.
He opened up the salt well industry to attract merchants and travelers,
identified local products to determine tribute and taxes,
and counted the population to equalize corvée labor.
His administration was broad and tolerant,
making the people comfortable and at peace.
He often read books without letting go of the scroll.
In his leisure, he would invite scholars to lecture on classics and history.
When Tàizǔ first rose up,
he often adopted children of other surnames.
Upon conquering prefectures and counties,
he would often send them out to govern,
numbering over twenty people.
Only Yīng had the greatest achievements in the southwest.
His sons Chūn, Shèng, and Áng all governed Yúnnán.
Xīn was a Fùmǎ Dūwèi,
and married Princess Chángníng, a daughter of Chéngzǔ.
Chūn,
whose courtesy name was Jǐngchūn,
was brave and martial, inheriting his father’s style.
At seventeen,
he followed Yīng in campaigns against the Xīfān,
again in the campaign against Yúnnán,
and again in pacifying the Jiāngxī rebels,
always being the first to ascend.
For his accumulated merits, he was appointed Qiānshì of the Hòujūn Dūdūfǔ.
His officials requested that he be given a probationary position,
but the Emperor said:
“My son
is my family,
there is no need for probation.”
Thus, he was granted a full appointment.
He was once ordered to record prisoners in Lièshān,
and also to interrogate rebel partisans in Wèizhōu,
releasing several hundred people in each case.
When Yīng died,
he was ordered to inherit the peerage
and govern Yúnnán.
In the twenty-sixth year of Hóngwǔ,
the eleven stockades of Wéimó rebelled,
and Qú Néng was dispatched to pacify them.
The following year, the Yuèsuì Mán were pacified,
and Láncāng Wèi was established.
In the winter of that year,
Āzī rebelled again,
and he campaigned against him with Hé Fú.
Chūn said:
“This bandit has evaded punishment for years,
owing to his marriage alliances with various local chieftains, constantly fleeing and hiding.
Now, we will mobilize all these chieftains to join the army,
confine them,
and establish many camps and forts
to control their movements;
his capture is certain.”
So he hastened to Yuèzhōu,
approaching its city from different routes,
laying ambushes of elite troops along the road.
He used weak troops to lure the enemy,
then launched a sudden attack, thoroughly defeating them.
Āzī fled into the mountains and valleys.
Chūn secretly allied with nearby local officials,
who helped him ascertain Āzī’s location.
He built fortifications and cut off their food supply.
The rebels were severely distressed.
Soon after,
he launched a surprise attack on their stronghold,
capturing Āzī
and executing two hundred and forty of his partisans.
Yuèzhōu was thus pacified.
Nóng Zhēnyòu, the chieftain of Guǎngnán, gathered a band of Mán to resist the imperial army.
He defeated and captured them,
taking thousands of prisoners and decapitated heads.
Dāo Bàilàn, the chieftain of Níngyuǎn, resisted orders by relying on Jiāozhǐ.
Hé Fú was dispatched to suppress and pacify him.
In the 30th year,
Sìlúnfā (思倫發), the Pacification Commissioner of Lùchuān (麓川), was expelled by his subordinate Dāogānmèng (刀幹孟).
He came to seek refuge.
Mù Chūn (沐春) escorted him to court,
received strategies from the emperor,
and was thereupon appointed General who Conquers the Barbarians (征虜前將軍).
He commanded Hé Fú (何福) and Xú Kǎi (徐凱) to suppress them.
First, he sent troops to escort Sìlúnfā (思倫發) to Jīnchǐ (金齒),
then issued a proclamation for Gānmèng (幹孟) to come and welcome him.
He did not respond.
So, Mù Chūn (沐春) selected 5,000 soldiers
and ordered Hé Fú (何福) and Qú Néng (瞿能) to lead them,
crossing Mount Gāoliánggōng (高良公山),
and directly attacking Nándiàn (南甸),
where they decisively defeated them,
beheading their chief Dāomíngmèng (刀名孟).
The army then turned back to attack Jǐnghǎnzhài (景罕寨).
The rebels held firm from their high, fortified position,
and the imperial army's provisions were almost exhausted.
Hé Fú (何福) reported the emergency.
Mù Chūn (沐春) led 500 cavalry to relieve them,
crossing the Nù Jiāng (怒江) at night.
By dawn, they reached the fort,
and Mù Chūn (沐春) ordered the cavalry to charge,
raising dust that obscured the sky.
The rebels were greatly alarmed and dispersed.
They pressed their advantage to attack Kōngtóngzhài (崆峒寨),
which also dispersed.
In total, 70,000 surrendered.
The generals and soldiers wanted to massacre them,
but Mù Chūn (沐春) forbade it.
Gānmèng (幹孟) begged for surrender,
but the Emperor did not permit it.
He ordered Mù Chūn (沐春) to command the armies of Diān (滇), Qián (黔), and Shǔ (蜀) to attack him.
Before they could depart, Mù Chūn (沐春) died,
aged 36.
He was posthumously granted the title Huìxiāng (惠襄).
Mù Chūn (沐春) served in the garrison for seven years.
He extensively reformed the Túnzhèng (屯政) (military-agricultural colony system),
opening up over 300,000 *mǔ* (畝) of land.
He dug the Tiěchí Hé (鐵池河),
irrigating tens of thousands of *mǔ* (畝) of dry fields in Yíliáng (宜良).
Over 5,000 households returned to their occupations,
and a shrine was built to worship him.
He had no sons,
so his younger brother, Mù Shèng (沐晟), succeeded him.
Mù Shèng (沐晟),
courtesy name Jǐngmào (景茂),
was grave and steady in his youth,
spoke little and rarely smiled,
and loved to read.
Tàizǔ (太祖) (Emperor Hongwu) loved him.
He successively served as Left Chief Commissioner of the Rear Army (後軍左都督).
In the first year of Jiànwén (建文), he inherited the marquisate.
By the time he arrived at the garrison,
Hé Fú (何福) had already defeated and captured Dāogānmèng (刀幹孟),
returning Sìlúnfā (思倫發) to power.
Not long after,
Sìlúnfā (思倫發) died,
and the various barbarian tribes divided and occupied his territory.
Mù Shèng (沐晟) attacked and pacified them.
He reorganized the territory into three prefectures (府), two departments (州), and five chiefdoms (長官司).
He also established a military-agricultural guard (屯衞千戶所) west of the Nù Jiāng (怒江) to garrison it,
and Lùchuān (麓川) was thus pacified.
Originally,
King Mín (岷王) was enfeoffed in Yúnnán (雲南).
His lawlessness
led to his imprisonment by Emperor Jiànwén (建文帝).
When Chéngzǔ (成祖) ascended the throne,
he sent the king back to his fief,
which only made him more arrogant and dissolute.
Mù Shèng (沐晟) gradually kept him in check.
The king grew angry
and slandered Mù Shèng (沐晟).
On account of the king, the Emperor issued an edict to caution Mù Shèng (沐晟),
and sent a letter to King Mín (岷王),
praising Mù Shèng's (沐晟) father's merits,
and telling him not to dwell on past faults.
In the third year of Yǒnglè (永樂),
the Bābǎi Dàdiàn (八百大甸) barbarians raided the border,
obstructing tribute envoys.
Mù Shèng (沐晟) joined forces with Chēlǐ (車里) and Mùbāng (木邦) to attack and pacify them.
The next year, a large army was dispatched to attack Jiāozhǐ (交阯).
Mù Shèng (沐晟) was appointed Left Deputy General who Conquers the Yi (征夷左副將軍),
and entered from Yúnnán (雲南) by a different route than Grand General Zhāng Fǔ (張輔).
He then proceeded from Méngzì (蒙自) directly to Yěpú (野蒲), cutting timber to open a road,
and capturing the mountain passes of Měngliè (猛烈) and Pénghuá (掤華).
He ferried boats and emerged at night on the Táo Shuǐ (洮水),
crossed the Fùliáng Jiāng (富良江),
and joined forces with Zhāng Fǔ (張輔).
Together they captured Duōbāng Chéng (多邦城),
attacked its eastern and western capitals,
cleared out all the rebel strongholds,
and captured the self-proclaimed king, Lí Jìlí (黎季犛).
The details are in Zhāng Fǔ's (張輔) biography.
For his merits, he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Qián (黔國公),
with an annual stipend of 3,000 *shi* (石) of grain,
and was granted a hereditary patent.
When Jiāozhǐ (交阯) once again rebelled after being pacified,
Mù Shèng (沐晟) was ordered to carry the seal of the General who Conquers the Yi (征夷將軍) and attack them.
He fought at the Jué Jiāng (厥江),
but suffered a defeat.
Zhāng Fǔ (張輔) was again dispatched to lead an army and combine forces to attack,
capturing Dìng (定) and sending him to the capital.
When Zhāng Fǔ (張輔) returned,
Mù Shèng (沐晟) remained to capture Chén Jìkuò (陳季擴),
but after repeated battles, he could not subdue him.
Zhāng Fǔ (張輔) was again dispatched to lead an army and rendezvous with Mù Shèng (沐晟).
They pursued Chén Jìkuò (陳季擴) to Zhànchéng (占城),
where they captured him.
Then they returned with their troops,
and Mù Shèng (沐晟) also received high rewards.
In the 17th year,
the barbarians of Fù Zhōu (富州) rebelled.
Mù Shèng (沐晟) led his troops to their vicinity,
but did not attack.
He sent envoys to explain the situation,
and they eventually submitted.
When Rénzōng (仁宗) ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Grand Tutor (太傅),
and a seal for the General who Pacifies the South (征南將軍) was cast and given to him.
It became customary for successors of the Mù (沐) family in the garrison
to be given this seal.
In the first year of Xuāndé (宣德),
the power of Lí Lì (黎利) in Jiāozhǐ (交阯) grew strong.
Mù Shèng (沐晟) was ordered by edict to join Marquis Ānyuǎn (安遠侯) Liǔ Shēng (柳升) in a punitive expedition.
Liǔ Shēng (柳升) was defeated and died,
and Mù Shèng (沐晟) also withdrew his troops.
Numerous officials impeached Mù Shèng (沐晟),
but the Emperor sealed their memorials and showed them to him.
In the third year of Zhèngtǒng (正統),
Sī Rènfā (思任發) of Lùchuān (麓川) rebelled.
Mù Shèng (沐晟) arrived at Jīnchǐ (金齒),
and joined forces with his younger brother Mù Áng (沐昂) and Chief Commissioner Fāng Zhèng (方政).
Fāng Zhèng (方政) served as the vanguard,
breaking the rebel strongholds along the river.
The main army pursued them north to the foot of Gāolí Gòng Shān (高黎共山),
and again defeated them.
The next year, they again broke their old strongholds.
Fāng Zhèng (方政) fell into an ambush and died,
and the imperial army suffered a defeat.
Mù Shèng (沐晟) retreated,
and out of shame and fear, he fell ill
and died in Chǔxióng (楚雄).
He was posthumously granted the title King Dìngyuǎn (定遠王),
and his posthumous name was Zhōngjìng (忠敬).
Mù Shèng (沐晟), inheriting his father's and brother's legacy,
was not skilled in military tactics,
and often met with unfavorable outcomes in battles.
The court, considering his remote location
and his hereditary generalship,
treated him leniently.
And the people of Diān (滇) were in awe of Mù Shèng's (沐晟) and his father's prestige and authority,
serving them with the same reverence as they would the imperial court.
When a mere scrap of paper was sent down,
the local chiefs would ceremoniously emerge from the city walls to welcome it,
wash their hands before opening it,
and say:
"This is an imperial order."
Mù Shèng (沐晟) garrisoned for a long time,
establishing 360 estates and gardens.
His wealth was abundant,
and he was adept at serving the influential figures at court,
with gifts and bribes never ceasing,
thus gaining a reputation both within and outside the capital.
Mù Shèng (沐晟) had a son, Mù Bīn (沐斌),
courtesy name Wénhuī (文輝),
who inherited the ducal title in childhood
and resided in the capital,
while Mù Áng (沐昂) served as the acting garrison commander.
Áng,
courtesy name Jǐnggāo,
initially served as an Assistant Commander of the Left Guard of the Palace Army.
As Chéngzǔ was about to send Shèng to campaign in the south,
he promoted Áng to Assistant Regional Commander,
in charge of the Yúnnán Regional Military Commission.
He was successively promoted to Right Chief Military Commissioner.
In the fourth year of Zhèngtǒng, he was given a general's seal
to suppress Lùchuān,
reaching Jīnchǐ.
Fearing the strength of the rebels,
he procrastinated for a long time.
When Participating General Zhāng Róng, leading the vanguard, was defeated at Mángbù,
Áng did not rescue him
and led his troops back,
for which he was demoted two ranks.
Afterward,
Sī Rènfā invaded,
and he repelled him.
He also captured and executed the rebels of Shīzōng.
In the sixth year,
Minister of War Wáng Jì and Earl of Dìngxī Jiǎng Guì led a large army to suppress Sī Rènfā,
with Áng in charge of provisions and transport.
When the rebels were defeated,
Áng's position was restored,
and he was ordered to supervise the army in capturing Sī Rènfā,
but he failed.
In the tenth year,
Áng died.
He was posthumously granted the title of Earl of Dìngbiān
and the posthumous name Wǔxiāng.
When Bīn first took office,
it happened that Miǎndiàn captured Sī Rènfā and sent him to the capital.
His son Sī Jīfā then came to attack,
and Bīn repelled him.
Sī Jīfā then reoccupied Mèngyǎng.
In the thirteenth year, a large army was again dispatched,
with Jì and others to suppress him,
while Bīn served as the rear guard,
ensuring no shortage of provisions.
Upon his death,
he was posthumously granted the title of Grand Tutor
and the posthumous name Róngkāng.
As his son Cóng was young,
at the beginning of Jǐngtài,
Áng's grandson Lín was ordered to take over the post as Assistant Chief Military Commissioner.
Lín, courtesy name Tíngzhāng,
was always cultured and refined.
The people of Diān treated him lightly,
but soon his orders were strict and not to be violated.
He died at the beginning of Tiānshùn.
Cóng was still young,
so Lín's younger brother Zàn, a Vice Commander of a Thousand Households of the Brocade Guard, was promoted to Assistant Chief Military Commissioner
to replace him.
He served for seven years,
successively suppressing Zhānlù and other villages and the native officials who engaged in warfare.
He received the surrender of Sī Bófā
and forced the barbarians to return the encroached lands.
He achieved many merits,
though he was somewhat avaricious.
In the spring of the third year of Chénghuà,
Cóng first took office,
with Zàn as Vice Regional Commander,
relocating his garrison to Jīnchǐ.
Cóng, courtesy name Tíngfāng,
was well-versed in the classics
and skilled in literary composition.
He accepted no gifts from the tributary barbarians.
When the chieftain of Xúndiàn killed his nephew
and sought to be appointed as governor,
Cóng captured and executed him.
When the native official of Guǎngxī was tyrannical
and his subjects rebelled,
Cóng requested the establishment of regular officials,
which greatly benefited the people.
He then successively suppressed the rebellious barbarians of Mǎlóng, Lìjiāng, Jiànchuān, Shùnníng, and Luóxióng,
and captured the rebels of Qiáodiàn and Nánwō.
Upon his death,
he was posthumously granted the title of Grand Preceptor
and the posthumous name Wǔxī.
He had no son,
so Zàn's grandson Kūn succeeded him.
Kūn, courtesy name Yuánzhōng,
initially inherited the position of Assistant Commander of the Brocade Guard.
Cóng adopted him as his son.
The court deliberated that Kūn, being a descendant of the Marquis of Xīpíng, should inherit the marquisate.
However, the defending officials disputed this,
saying that the people of Diān knew the Duke of Qiánguó but not the Marquis of Xīpíng.
They feared that a marquis would be looked down upon.
Xiàozōng agreed,
ordering him to succeed as Duke
and to wear the seal as before.
In the twelfth year of Hóngzhì, he pacified the barbarians of Guīshān and Zhúqìng,
and then pacified the rebels of Pǔ'ān,
for which his annual stipend was increased twice.
In the second year of Zhèngdé,
when the people of Shīzōng, led by Āběn, rebelled,
he and Censor-in-chief Wú Wéndù commanded troops to advance in three routes.
One went out from Shīzōng,
one from Luóxióng,
and one from Mílè.
Another army was separately dispatched to ambush Pánjiāng
and cut off the rebel stronghold,
thus utterly defeating them.
In the seventh year,
when Nàdài of the Ānnán local official's office contested the succession
and killed the native official,
he and Censor-in-chief Gù Yuán again suppressed and captured him,
for which he was again promoted to Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent.
Kūn initially enjoyed literature
and was self-assured,
but later he bribed powerful courtiers,
and all his requests were granted.
He gradually became arrogant,
disrespecting the Three Judicial Offices,
making them enter through a side gate.
Officials who impeached him
were invariably punished and dismissed.
Upon his death,
he was posthumously granted the title of Grand Preceptor
and the posthumous name Zhuāngxiāng.
His son Shàoxūn succeeded him.
When the native chief Ān Quán of Xúndiàn rebelled,
Censor-in-chief Fù Xí suppressed him
but suffered a defeat.
The native chief Fèng Cháowén of Wǔdìng also rebelled,
and joining forces with Quán, attacked Yúnnán,
causing great disturbance.
Shìzōng sent Minister Wǔ Wéndìng to lead a large army to quell them.
Before his arrival,
Shàoxūn led his troops forward,
announcing to the sons of native officials who were to succeed
that they would first be granted official caps and sashes,
and after defeating the rebels, their succession would be petitioned for.
Many fought bravely,
and the rebels were utterly defeated.
Cháowén fled across the Pǔdù River,
and was pursued and beheaded in Dōngchuān.
Quán returned to Xúndiàn
and set up dozens of stockades.
The government forces attacked and broke them,
capturing Quán in Mángbù.
They successively captured over a thousand rebel partisans
and killed and captured countless others.
This was in the seventh year of Jiājìng.
When the victory was reported,
he was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent
and his annual stipend was increased.
At this time, Lǎowō, Mùbāng, Mèngyǎng, Miǎndiàn, and Mèngmì were fighting among themselves,
and Shīzōng, Nàlóu, Sītuó, and Bāzhài were all in turmoil,
which remained unresolved for a long time.
Shàoxūn sent envoys to visit all the barbarian tribes,
hinting at the affairs of Wǔzhèng and Xúndiàn.
All were awed and submitted,
willing to return the encroached lands,
and Mùbāng and Mèngyǎng both offered tribute and apologized.
The whole South was thus pacified.
Shàoxūn possessed courage and strategy,
and his military campaigns were always victorious.
Upon his death,
he was posthumously granted the title of Grand Preceptor
and the posthumous name Mǐnjìng.
His son Cháofǔ succeeded him.
When Censor-in-chief Liú Qú demanded bribes,
Cháofǔ gave them to him,
and then submitted a memorial stating:
"My family has guarded this land for generations,
succeeding one another.
Now, the local officials frequently alter regulations and systems
concerning my official duties,
often without consulting me,
and receiving me not according to old precedents.
I am isolated and vulnerable,
my actions constrained,
unable to control the barbarian regions.
I beg Your Majesty to issue a strict decree to all officials
to restore everything to its former state."
The emperor's edict granted this.
Investigating Censor Wàn Yúkǎi impeached Cháofǔ
and also implicated Qú.
An edict dismissed Qú but allowed Cháofǔ to manage affairs as before.
Upon his death,
he was posthumously granted the title of Grand Guardian
and the posthumous name Gōngxī.
The two sons, Róng 融 and Gǒng 鞏, were both young.
An imperial edict, having examined the precedents of Cóng 琮 and Lín 璘,
ordered Róng 融 to inherit the ducal title,
granting him half the salary.
Cháo Bǐ 昭弼, Cháo Fǔ’s 昭輔 younger brother, was appointed Dudū Qiānshì 都督僉事,
given an official seal, and sent to govern in their stead.
After three years,
Róng 融 died.
Gǒng 鞏 was to succeed him.
Cháo Bǐ 昭弼 harbored ill intentions.
Thereupon, Cháo Bǐ’s 昭弼嫡母 (principal mother), Lǐ 李, requested to protect Gǒng 鞏 by taking him to the capital,
to wait for him to grow up before returning to govern.
The request was granted.
Gǒng 鞏 died before reaching the capital,
and Cháo Bǐ 昭弼 thus obtained the succession.
In the 30th year of Jiājìng 嘉靖 (1551),
the local chieftain Nà Jiàn 那鑑 of Yuánjiāng 元江 rebelled.
An imperial edict ordered Cháo Bǐ 昭弼 and Dudū Yùshǐ 都御史 Shí Jiǎn 石簡 to suppress him.
They divided their forces into five armies and advanced upon his city.
The city was on the verge of being captured
when illness caused by the miasma forced them to withdraw.
An imperial edict dismissed Jiǎn 簡,
intending to dispatch another expedition.
Jiàn 那鑑, in fear, took poison and died,
and so the matter ended.
In the 44th year (1565), the rebellious barbarians Ā Fāng 阿方 and Lǐ Xiàngyáng 李向陽 were suppressed and captured.
In the early years of Lóngqìng 隆慶 (1567-1572),
the rebellious chieftain Fèng Jìzǔ 鳳繼祖 of Wǔdìng 武定 was pacified,
and over thirty bandit lairs were destroyed.
Cháo Bǐ 昭弼 was always arrogant,
treating his mother and sister-in-law disrespectfully,
seizing his brother’s fields and residences,
harboring criminals such as Jiǎng Xù 蔣旭,
and using military tallies to send people to spy on the capital.
Consequently, Cháo Bǐ 昭弼 was dismissed,
and his son Chāngzuò 昌祚 succeeded,
receiving half the salary.
Cháo Bǐ 昭弼 was resentful
and became even more unrestrained.
When he buried his mother in Nánjīng 南京,
the Dudū Yùshǐ 都御史 requested that he be detained there.
An imperial edict permitted his return to Diān 滇,
but forbade him from interfering in Diān 滇 affairs.
Cháo Bǐ 昭弼, enraged,
sought to kill Chāngzuò 昌祚.
The Fǔ 撫 (governor) and Àn 按 (investigating censor) jointly reported his actions,
also revealing his murders, collusion with foreign powers, and other unlawful acts.
He was arrested, imprisoned, and condemned to death.
In consideration of his past merits,
he was confined in Nánjīng 南京,
where he died.
Chāngzuò 昌祚 initially served as Dudū Qiānshì 都督僉事 and Zǒngbīngguān 總兵官, defending the region;
after a long time, he inherited the ducal title.
In the first year of Wànlì 萬曆 (1573),
the Yao'an 姚安 barbarians under Luó Sī 羅思 rebelled,
killing the prefect.
Chāngzuò 昌祚 and Dudū Yùshǐ 都御史 Zōu Yìnglóng 鄒應龍 mobilized local and Han troops to suppress them,
destroying over ten stockades, including Xiàngníng 向寧 and Zhàmó 鮓摩,
razed their lairs,
and captured all of Sī 羅思 and his followers.
In the eleventh year (1583),
the Lǒngchuān 隴川 bandit Yuè Fèng 岳鳳 rebelled and allied with Burma,
using their troops to invade neighboring Tǔsī 土司.
Chāngzuò 昌祚 encamped by Ěrhǎi 洱海,
overseeing auxiliary generals Dèng Zǐlóng 鄧子龍 and Liú Tíng 劉綎, who beheaded Hǎn Qián 罕虔, the rebellious chieftain of Mùbāng 木邦.
They then retreated due to the summer miasma.
The following year, they again attacked Hǎn Qián’s 罕虔 former lair,
advancing along three routes,
capturing his chieftain Hǎn Zhāo 罕招 and others.
They also defeated the Burmese army at Měngliǎn 猛臉.
Yuè Fèng 岳鳳 was successful.
For his merits, he was awarded the title of Tàizǐ Tàibǎo 太子太保
and received his full former salary.
Subsequently, he pacified the rebellious barbarians of Luóxióng 羅雄 and other regions,
and was again bestowed with silver and silk.
When the Burmese army attacked Měngguǎng 猛廣,
Chāngzuò 昌祚 assembled his forces and encamped at Yǒngchāng 永昌.
The Burmese fled.
He pursued them to Nàmò Jiāng 那莫江,
but returned when the miasma appeared.
In the twenty-first year (1593),
the Burmese again invaded.
Chāngzuò 昌祚 drove them out.
He won successive battles,
then advanced to Burma,
but returned when the various barbarians fell into internal strife.
The Mù 沐 family had been in Diān 滇 for a long time,
their power and influence growing daily,
respected to the point of rivaling a prince.
When Chāngzuò 昌祚 went out,
Qiānshì 僉事 Yáng Yínqiū 楊寅秋 did not yield the right of way.
Chāngzuò 昌祚 flogged his sedan chair bearers.
Yínqiū 寅秋 appealed to the court,
and an imperial edict severely reprimanded Chāngzuò 昌祚.
Later,
due to illness,
he ordered his son Ruì 叡 to govern in his stead.
The Wǔdìng 武定 chieftain Ā Kè 阿克 rebelled,
attacked the provincial capital,
and seized the prefectural seal.
Ruì 叡 was arrested and imprisoned,
and Chāngzuò 昌祚 resumed governing.
He died,
and his grandson Qǐyuán 啟元 succeeded him.
He died,
and his son Tiānbō 天波 succeeded him.
After more than ten years, the Tǔsī 土司 Shā Dìngzhōu 沙定洲 rebelled,
and Tiānbō 天波 fled to Yǒngchāng 永昌.
When the rebellion was quelled,
he returned to Diān 滇.
When Yǒngmíng Wáng 永明王 Yóuláng 由榔 entered Diān 滇,
Tiānbō 天波 retained his position as before.
Later,
he followed Yóuláng 由榔 to Burma.
The Burmese tried to capture him,
but he refused to surrender and died.
Originally,
during Shā Dìngzhōu’s 沙定洲 rebellion,
Tiānbō’s 天波 mother, Chén 陳氏, and wife, Jiāo 焦氏, committed suicide by self-immolation.
Later, when Tiānbō 天波 fled to Burma,
his concubine, Xià 夏氏, unable to follow,
hanged herself.
After several tens of days, her body was collected and buried;
her limbs had not decayed,
which people attributed to the power of her integrity and righteousness.
Praise: Among the generals who rose with the Ming dynasty,
the Six Princes were preeminent.
This was not only due to their outstanding achievements,
but also because their loyalty and sincerity resonated with the emperor’s trust.
None were closer than Qíyáng 岐陽, none were older associates than Dōng'ōu 東甌,
and both Nínghé 寧河 and Qiánníng 黔寧, at a young age, were entrusted with crucial responsibilities.
Their arduous efforts in service were
purely diligent and unwavering;
their banners and accolades shone brightly,
truly without blemish.
Qíyáng 岐陽 was respected for his cultured refinement and knowledge of rites,
while Dōng'ōu 東甌 requested to retire to his estate,
safeguarding himself through sagacity,
both were exceptional and beyond the reach of others.
Only Qiánníng 黔寧's might shook distant lands,
and his charter was passed down through generations,
his merits and fame enduring from the beginning to the end of the Ming dynasty.
Nínghé 寧河, however, exhausted himself in his endeavors,
his achievements great but his life short,
and his descendants showed little distinction.
Commentators say that the legacy of the various princes
saw varying degrees of prosperity and decline.
However, Zhōngshān 中山 had Zēngshòu 增壽,
and Qíyáng 岐陽 had Jǐnglóng 景隆.
Looking back at their ancestors' glorious deeds,
there are indeed some regrets.
The disparity in their fortunes
also makes it difficult to distinguish between lucky and unlucky fates.
Editorial Notes
Biographies, Volume 15: Lǐ Shàncháng 李善長, Wāng Guǎngyáng 汪廣洋
Lǐ Shàncháng,
courtesy name Bǎishì,
was a native of Dìngyuǎn.
In his youth, he read books and possessed wisdom and foresight.
He studied the teachings of the Legalists,
and his strategies often hit the mark.
When Tàizǔ seized territory in Chúyáng,
Shàncháng went to greet him.
Knowing him to be an elder of the village,
Tàizǔ treated him with respect
and kept him to manage documents.
He once calmly asked:
"The four directions are engaged in battle;
when will they be settled?"
He replied:
"When Qín was in chaos,
Gāo (zu) of Hàn arose from common cloth,
broad-minded and magnanimous,
knowing men and good at employing them,
not delighting in killing,
and in five years established an imperial enterprise.
Now the Yuán dynasty's order is already disturbed,
and the empire is crumbling like earth and tiles.
Your Excellency hails from Háo,
not far from Pèi.
The royal aura of mountains and rivers
should be received by Your Excellency.
Emulate his actions,
and the empire is not difficult to settle."
Tàizǔ praised his words.
Following him to conquer Chúzhōu,
he served as a staff advisor,
participating in strategic planning,
and overseeing provisions and supplies.
He was deeply trusted and relied upon.
As Tàizǔ's prestige and fame grew day by day,
Shàncháng observed the talents of the generals who came to defect
and reported them to Tàizǔ.
He also laid out Tàizǔ's sincerity,
allowing them all to feel secure.
For those who had conflicts over matters or power,
he skillfully mediated and protected them.
Guō Zǐxìng was swayed by rumors
and suspected Tàizǔ,
gradually seizing his military authority.
He also wanted to take Shàncháng to assist himself,
but Shàncháng firmly refused to go.
Tàizǔ relied on him deeply.
When Tàizǔ's army was in Héyáng,
he personally led an attack on Jīlóng Shānzhài,
leaving a small force to assist Shàncháng in guarding the base.
A Yuán general, knowing this through espionage, came to attack,
but Shàncháng set up an ambush and defeated them.
Tàizǔ considered him capable.
When Tàizǔ obtained the Cháohú navy,
Shàncháng strongly advocated crossing the river.
After capturing Cǎishí
and advancing to Tàipíng,
Shàncháng had already prepared proclamations to restrain the soldiers.
Upon entering the city,
he immediately posted them on the main thoroughfare,
and it was so orderly that no one dared to offend.
Tàizǔ appointed him Dàyuánshuài of Tàipíng Xīngguó Yì,
and he became a secretary in the Marshal's office.
He followed in conquering Jíqìng.
When about to take Zhènjiāng,
Tàizǔ feared that the generals would not restrain their subordinates,
so he feigned anger and wanted to punish them according to the law.
Shàncháng strongly interceded and resolved the matter.
When Zhènjiāng fell,
the people did not even realize there had been soldiers.
Tàizǔ established the Xíng Zhōngshūshěng of Jiāngnán as Píngzhāng,
and appointed Shàncháng as Cānyì.
At that time, Sòng Sīyán, Lǐ Mènggēng, Guō Jǐngxiáng, and others were all officials in the province,
but military strategies, advances and retreats,
and regulations for rewards and punishments
were mostly decided by Shàncháng.
The Mìmì Yuàn was changed to the Dàdūdū Fǔ,
and he was ordered to concurrently hold the position of Fǔ Sīmǎ,
and further promoted to Xíngshěng Cānzhī Zhèngshì.
When Tàizǔ became King of Wú,
he was appointed Yòu Xiàngguó.
Shàncháng was well-versed in historical precedents,
and made decisions smoothly;
he was also [⿱羔天] (versed) in writing official documents.
Whenever Tàizǔ wanted to recruit or appease someone,
he would order Shàncháng to write the letter.
Throughout the period, whenever Tàizǔ personally led expeditions,
he would order Shàncháng to remain behind to guard the base.
The generals and officials were obedient,
the residents lived in peace,
and the transfer of troops and provisions was never lacking.
He once requested to monopolize salt from the two Huái regions
and establish tea laws,
all of which were based on Yuán regulations
but removed their harmful practices.
He then restored the currency system,
opened iron smelters,
and fixed fishing taxes,
making the national treasury more abundant
without burdening the people.
In the ninth month of the first year of Wú, for his meritorious service in pacifying Wú,
Shàncháng was enfeoffed as Xuānguó Gōng.
When the official system was reformed
to honor the left,
he was made Zuǒ Xiàngguó.
When Tàizǔ first crossed the river,
he often employed harsh laws.
One day,
he said to Shàncháng:
"The law has three articles of collective punishment;
is this not excessive?"
Shàncháng then requested that all be abolished except for high treason.
Consequently, he was ordered, along with Zhōngchéng Liú Jī and others, to revise and finalize the legal code,
which was then promulgated both domestically and abroad.
When Tàizǔ ascended the imperial throne,
for posthumously honoring his ancestors and appointing empresses, consorts, crown princes, and various kings,
Shàncháng was always appointed Dàlǐshǐ.
When establishing officials for the Eastern Palace,
Shàncháng concurrently served as Tàizǐ Shàoshī,
and was granted Yínqīng Rónglù Dàfū, Shàng Zhùguó,
to record important military and state affairs,
with other duties remaining as before.
Subsequently,
he led the ritual officials to finalize the rites for the suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples.
When the Emperor visited Biànliáng,
Shàncháng remained to guard the capital,
and everything was to be handled expediently according to his discretion.
Soon after, he submitted a memorial to finalize the official system for the Six Boards,
and discussed the mourning attire for officials and commoners, as well as the ceremonies for court audiences and greetings in the Eastern Palace.
He was ordered to supervise the compilation of the Yuán Shǐ,
and to compile books such as Zǔxùn Lù and Dàmíng Jílǐ.
He finalized the titles of gods of mountains and rivers throughout the empire,
enfeoffed the various kings,
and bestowed noble titles and rewards upon meritorious officials.
No matter how great or small the matter,
everything was entrusted to Shàncháng to deliberate and act upon with the various scholar-officials.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, great enfeoffments were made to meritorious officials.
The Emperor said:
"Although Shàncháng did not have the toil of battle,
he has served me for a long time
and supplied military provisions;
his功 is very great,
and he should be advanced to a great state."
Thereupon, he was granted the title Kāiguó Fǔyùn Tuīchéng Shǒuzhèng Wénchén, Tèjìn Guānglù Dàfū, Zuǒ Zhùguó, Tàishī, Zhōngshū Zuǒ Chéngxiàng,
enfeoffed as Hánguó Gōng,
with an annual stipend of four thousand shí,
and his descendants to inherit the title.
He was granted an iron certificate,
exempting him from two deaths,
and his son from one death.
At that time, the six men enfeoffed as Gōng were
Xú Dá, Cháng Yùchūn's son Mào, Lǐ Wénzhōng, Féng Shèng, Dèng Yù, and Shàncháng.
And Shàncháng ranked first,
with the imperial decree comparing him to Xiāo Hé,
praising him exceptionally.
Shàn Cháng was outwardly gentle and benevolent,
but inwardly often resentful and cruel.
When Counselor Lǐ Yǐnbīng and Yáng Xīshèng
slightly encroached upon Shàn Cháng's authority,
he immediately impeached and dismissed them based on their offenses.
He quarreled with Vice Censor-in-Chief Liú Jī over the law and humiliated him.
Jī felt uneasy,
and requested leave to return home.
Zhāng Chǎng, Yáng Xiàn, Wāng Guǎngyáng, and Hú Wéiyōng, all appointed by Tàizǔ, were all found guilty,
but Shàn Cháng's position remained unchanged.
His wealth and honor reached their peak,
and his attitude became somewhat arrogant,
which the Emperor began to subtly dislike.
In the fourth year, due to illness, he retired,
and was granted several qǐng of land in Línháo,
with 150 families designated as tomb guardians,
1,500 tenant families,
and 20 families of honor guards.
The following year,
his illness improved,
and he was ordered to oversee the construction of palaces in Línháo.
140,000 wealthy families from Jiangnán were relocated to Háo Zhōu,
with Shàn Cháng managing them,
and they remained in Háo for several years.
In the seventh year, Shàn Cháng's younger brother Cúnyì was promoted to Vice Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud,
and Cúnyì's sons, Shēn and Yòu, both became officials in the Bureau of Imperial Pasturage.
In the ninth year, Princess Lín'ān was married to his son Qí,
who was appointed Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law.
When the marriage rites were first established,
the Princess observed wifely virtues with great solemnity.
Their glory and honor were resplendent,
and people of the time envied them.
A month after Qí married the Princess,
Censors-in-Chief Wāng Guǎngyáng and Chén Níng memorialized, saying:
"Shàn Cháng presumes upon imperial favor and acts unrestrainedly.
Your Majesty has been ill and has not held court for nearly ten days,
yet he has not inquired about your health.
Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law Qí has not attended court for six days,
and when summoned to the front of the palace,
he did not admit his fault,
which is a great disrespect."
Consequently, his annual salary of 1,800 dàn was reduced.
Soon after, he was ordered to, together with Cáo Guógōng Lǐ Wénzhōng, take charge of the Central Secretariat, the Chief Military Commission, and the Censorate,
to jointly discuss military and state affairs,
and to supervise the palace guards and public works.
Chancellor Hú Wéiyōng was initially the magistrate of Níngguó;
through Shàn Cháng's recommendation,
he was promoted to Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
and later became Chancellor,
leading to frequent interactions between them.
Moreover, Shàn Cháng's younger brother Cúnyì's son Yòu
was Wéiyōng's niece's husband.
In the thirteenth year,
Wéiyōng was executed for plotting rebellion,
and many who were implicated died,
yet Shàn Cháng remained unaffected.
The Censorate lacked a Censor-in-Chief,
so Shàn Cháng was put in charge of its affairs,
and often submitted proposals.
In the eighteenth year,
someone accused Cúnyì and his son of actually being Wéiyōng's partisans.
An imperial edict spared them from death
and exiled them to Chóngmíng.
Shàn Cháng did not express gratitude,
and the Emperor resented this.
Five more years passed,
and Shàn Cháng was already seventy-seven years old,
elderly and unable to control his subordinates.
He once wanted to build a mansion
and borrowed 300 palace guards from Xìnguógōng Tāng Hé.
Hé secretly reported this.
In the fourth month,
among the capital's commoners who were to be exiled to the frontier for their crimes, Shàn Cháng repeatedly requested the exemption of his private relative Dīng Bīn and others.
The Emperor angrily investigated Bīn.
Bīn had formerly served in Wéiyōng's household,
and consequently reported Cúnyì and others' past collusion with Wéiyōng.
An order was issued to arrest Cúnyì and his son for interrogation.
Their testimony implicated Shàn Cháng,
stating:
"Wéiyōng had rebellious intentions
and sent Cúnyì to secretly persuade Shàn Cháng.
Shàn Cháng was shocked and yelled:
'What are you saying?!
If that's true,
our nine generations of kin will be exterminated!'
Later,
he again sent Shàn Cháng's old friend Yáng Wényù to persuade him, saying:
'If the matter succeeds, you will be enfeoffed as a king with the land of Huáinán.'
Shàn Cháng was shocked and refused,
but was somewhat moved.
Wéiyōng then personally went to persuade Shàn Cháng,
who still refused.
After a long time,
Wéiyōng again sent Cúnyì to persuade him.
Shàn Cháng sighed and said:
'I am old.
After I die, you all can do as you please.'"
Someone also accused Shàn Cháng, saying:
"When General Lán Yù campaigned beyond the frontier,
reaching Lake Bǔyú'ér, he captured Fēng Jī, Wéiyōng's envoy to the desert tribes.
Shàn Cháng concealed this and did not report it."
Thereupon, censors repeatedly impeached Shàn Cháng in memorials.
And Shàn Cháng's slave Lú Zhòngqiān and others
also reported that Shàn Cháng and Wéiyōng exchanged bribes
and secret communications.
When the case was concluded, it was stated that Shàn Cháng, a meritorious minister and imperial relative,
knowing of the treasonous plot, did not report it,
hesitated, observed, and harbored dual intentions,
which was high treason and unfilial.
At that time, there were reports of astronomical anomalies,
the omen of which indicated the removal of high-ranking ministers.
Consequently, he and his wife, daughters, younger brothers, nephews, and over seventy members of his household
were all executed.
And Jí'ān Hóu Lù Zhònghēng, Yán'ān Hóu Táng Shèngzōng, Píngliáng Hóu Fèi Jù, Nánxióng Hóu Zhào Yōng, Xíngyáng Hóu Zhèng Yùchūn, Yíchūn Hóu Huáng Bīn, Hénán Hóu Lù Jù, etc.,
were all simultaneously implicated as Wéiyōng's partisans and died.
Additionally, several deceased individuals, such as Yíngyáng Hóu Yáng Jǐng and Jìníng Hóu Gù Shí, were posthumously implicated.
The Emperor personally wrote an edict listing their crimes,
attached it to the prison confessions,
and compiled it into three volumes titled 'Exposing the Treasonous Faction,'
which were distributed throughout the empire.
Shàn Cháng's son Qí and the Princess were exiled to Jiāngpǔ,
where Qí died after a long time.
Qí's sons, Fāng and Mào,
were spared due to the Princess's grace.
Fāng became a Commander of the Central Guard of the Garrison,
and Mào became a Pacification Commissioner of the Flag Guard,
but their hereditary titles were abolished.
The year after Shàn Cháng's death,
Wáng Guóyòng, a Director of the Bureau of Waters, memorialized, saying:
"Shàn Cháng was of one mind with Your Majesty,
faced myriad deaths to secure the empire,
and was the foremost meritorious minister.
Alive, he was enfeoffed as a Duke;
dead, he was enfeoffed as a King;
his son married a Princess;
and his relatives were appointed to office.
His status as a subject reached its peak.
Even if he wished to plot rebellion for himself,
it would still be uncertain.
But to now say that he wished to assist Hú Wéiyōng
is greatly mistaken.
Human nature dictates that one loves one's own son
more than one's brother's son.
One who enjoys perfect wealth and honor
will surely not gamble for a one-in-ten-thousand chance of wealth and honor.
Shàn Cháng and Wéiyōng
were merely related as nephew and uncle,
while to Your Majesty, he was related by blood through your son and daughter.
If Shàn Cháng had helped Wéiyōng succeed,
he would at most still be the foremost meritorious minister,
a Grand Tutor and Duke enfeoffed as King,
and have his son marry a princess and take concubines.
Could he possibly have achieved more than he had today?
Moreover, how could Shàn Cháng not know that the empire cannot be won by chance?
In the late Yuán period,
how many wished to do this,
yet without exception, their bodies were pulverized,
their clans wiped out, and their ancestral worship extinguished?
How many were able to preserve their lives?
Shàn Cháng had personally witnessed such events,
so how could he, in his declining years, personally involve himself in such a venture?
All who do such things
must have deep hatred driving them to rebellion,
or be utterly compelled,
even to the point of a father and son coercing each other to escape disaster.
Now, Shàn Cháng's son Qí is Your Majesty's blood relative,
without the slightest suspicion,
so why would he suddenly do this?
If it is said that heavenly phenomena portended change,
and high-ranking ministers were to suffer disaster,
and they were killed to conform to the heavenly phenomena,
then this is even more unacceptable.
I fear that when the empire hears of it,
they will say that even a meritorious figure like Shàn Cháng met such a fate,
and the four corners of the realm will consequently disintegrate.
Now Shàn Cháng is dead,
and speaking of it is of no benefit,
but I only wish Your Majesty to take heed for the future."
When Tàizǔ received the letter,
he ultimately did not punish him.
Wāng Guǎngyáng,
courtesy name Cháozōng,
was a native of Gāoyóu,
who resided in Tàipíng.
When Tàizǔ crossed the Yangtze River,
he was summoned to be a clerk in the Marshal's office,
and Controller of the Jiāngnán Provisional Secretariat.
When the Directorate of Military Admonishment was established,
he was promoted to Censor,
then transferred to the Provincial Secretary,
and successively advanced to Director of the Right Bureau of the Central Secretariat.
Soon after, he was put in charge of the Swift Cavalry Guard
and participated in Cháng Yùchūn's military affairs.
After Gànzhōu was taken,
he remained to guard it,
and was appointed Provisional Counselor of Jiāngxī.
In the first year of Hongwǔ,
Shāndōng was pacified.
As Guǎngyáng was known for his integrity, clarity, and steadfastness,
he was ordered to administer the Xíngshěng,
pacifying and bringing into submission those who had newly joined,
and the people were greatly at peace.
That year, he was summoned to serve as Cānzhèng of the Zhōngshūshěng.
The next year, he went out to serve as Cānzhèng in Shǎnxī.
In the third year,
Lǐ Shàncháng fell ill,
and there were no officials in the Zhōngshūshěng.
Guǎngyáng was summoned to be Zuǒ Chéng.
At that time, Yáng Xiàn, the Yòu Chéng, monopolized decision-making.
Guǎngyáng went along with him in a vague manner,
but was still resented by him.
Xiàn incited an imperial censor to impeach Guǎngyáng for neglect of his mother.
The Emperor severely reprimanded him
and sent him back to his hometown.
Xiàn then played a second memorial,
and he was exiled to Hǎinán.
When Xiàn was executed,
Guǎngyáng was recalled.
That winter,
he was enfeoffed as Zhōngqín Bó,
receiving a stipend of three hundred sixty shí of grain.
The imperial edict praised him for managing complex and difficult affairs,
and repeatedly offering loyal counsel,
comparing him to Zǐfáng and Kǒngmíng.
When Shàncháng left his post due to illness,
Guǎngyáng was made Yòu Chéngxiàng,
and Cānzhèng Hú Wéiyōng became Zuǒ Chéng.
Guǎngyáng made no proposals,
and after a long time,
he was demoted to Guǎngdōng Xíngshěng Cānzhèng.
However, the Emperor's heart remained favorably disposed towards Guǎngyáng,
and he was again summoned to be Zuǒ Yùshǐ Dàfū.
In the tenth year, he was again appointed Yòu Chéngxiàng.
Guǎngyáng was rather fond of wine.
Serving as prime minister with Wéiyōng,
he merely drifted along and held his position.
The Emperor repeatedly warned and instructed him.
In the twelfth month of the twelfth year,
Zhōng Chéng Tú Jié reported that Liú Jī had been poisoned to death by Wéiyōng,
and Guǎngyáng should know the circumstances.
The Emperor questioned him,
and he replied:
"There is nothing of the sort."
The Emperor was enraged,
accused Guǎngyáng of collusion and deception,
and demoted him to Guǎngnán.
As his boat reached Tàipíng,
the Emperor, still angry, recalled that he had unduly protected Wénzhèng in Jiāngxī,
and had failed to expose Yáng Xiàn's treachery in the Zhōngshūshěng,
and granted an edict for his execution.
Guǎngyáng had studied under Yú Què when young.
He was extensively versed in the classics and history,
skilled in zhuàn and lì scripts,
and adept at composing songs and poems.
He was by nature lenient, harmonious, and self-restrained.
He served in the same position as treacherous individuals but was unable to remove them,
hence he met with disaster.
Eulogy says: In the early Míng, the Zhōngshūshěng was established,
and Zuǒ and Yòu Chéngxiàng were appointed,
managing crucial affairs.
They were usually led by meritorious officials.
However, Xú Dá, Lǐ Wénzhōng, and others were repeatedly commanded to campaign,
and never exclusively managed provincial affairs.
Those who served comfortably as prime ministers
were only Lǐ Shàncháng, Wāng Guǎngyáng, and Hú Wéiyōng.
After Wéiyōng's downfall,
the office of Chéngxiàng was abolished and not re-established.
Therefore, throughout the Míng dynasty,
only Shàncháng and Guǎngyáng were referred to as Chéngxiàng.
It is regrettable that Shàncháng, as a commoner on foot,
was able to choose a lord at the beginning of chaos,
devoting himself and exerting his strength
to assist in establishing a grand enterprise.
He thus obtained the sealing of a charter and founding of the nation,
was ennobled as a supreme duke,
and even became exceedingly wealthy and powerful,
only to bring about his own destruction in his declining years.
Guǎngyáng, cautious and steadfast,
was also unable to expose treachery and avert disaster.
Both met with severe condemnation.
Was this not a great betrayal of their initial aspirations
and a source of shame for the duties placed upon them?
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 16: Liú Jī (Zǐlián, Jǐng), Sòng Lián, Yè Chēn, Zhāng Yì (Zǐcúndào)
Liú Jī,
courtesy name Bówēn,
was a native of Qīngtián.
His great-grandfather, Háo,
served the Sòng as Hàlín Zhǎngshū.
After the fall of Sòng,
a local man, Lín Róng, initiated a righteous army.
When the endeavor failed,
the Yuán dispatched an envoy to register their party,
and many were implicated.
The envoy lodged at Háo's house en route.
Háo intoxicated the envoy and burned his dwelling,
destroying all the records.
The envoy had no recourse
and therefore re-registered them,
and all those implicated were spared.
Jī was exceptionally brilliant in his youth.
His teacher, Zhèng Fùchū, told his father, Yuè:
"Your ancestor's virtue is profound.
This son will surely glorify your family."
During the Zhìshùn reign of the Yuán,
he passed the Jìnshì examination
and was appointed Gāo'ān Chéng,
earning a reputation for integrity and uprightness.
The Xíngshěng invited him,
but he declined and left.
He was appointed Jiāngzhè Rúxué Fù Tí Jǔ,
but he criticized the Yùshǐ for neglecting their duties,
was obstructed by the Táichén,
and twice resigned and returned home.
Jī was broadly versed in the classics and history,
prying into every book,
and particularly skilled in the study of celestial phenomena and divination.
Zhào Tiānzé of Xīshǔ, when discussing prominent figures south of the Yangtze,
first mentioned Jī,
considering him a peer of Zhūgě Kǒngmíng.
Fāng Guózēn rose up along the coast,
plundering prefectures and counties,
and the officials were unable to restrain him.
The Xíngshěng again invited Jī to be Yuánshuàifǔ Dūshì.
Jī proposed building various cities in Qìngyuán to pressure the bandit,
and Guózēn's morale was dampened.
When Zuǒ Chéng Tiēlí Tiēmù'ér sought to appease Guózēn,
Jī stated that the Fāng family brothers were the primary instigators of rebellion,
and if not executed, there would be no means to warn future generations.
Guózēn was afraid
and heavily bribed Jī.
Jī did not accept.
Guózēn then sent people by sea to the capital
to bribe those in power.
Consequently, an imperial edict was issued to pacify Guózēn,
granting him an official position,
while Jī was accused of unauthorized use of power
and placed under supervision in Shàoxīng.
The Fāng family subsequently became even more rampant.
Not long after,
mountain bandits rose up in swarms.
The Xíngshěng again invited Jī to suppress and capture them,
and he defended Chǔzhōu with Xíngyuànpàn Shímò Yísūn.
Jīnglüèshǐ Lǐ Guófèng reported his achievements,
but the ruling officials, due to the Fāng family, suppressed him,
appointing him Zǒngguǎnfǔ Pàn,
without military authority.
Jī then abandoned his office and returned to Qīngtián,
writing Yùlí Zǐ to express his resolve.
At that time, those fleeing the Fāng family vied to rely on Jī.
Jī made some deployments,
and the bandits dared not invade.

視近而明,

自少至老,

在朝,
郊社宗廟山川百神之典,

旁及元勳巨卿碑記刻石之辭,
