Xǔ Qiān 門人也,
教授鄉里,
講解經義,
聞者多感悟.
Zhāng Yì 從之遊,
同志聖賢學,
天性孝友.
嘗遊 Jīnhuá,
Yuán Xiànshǐ Tūjiān Bùhuā 禮之,
改官 Qínzhōng,
要與俱行.
至 Húlín,
心動,
辭歸.
歸八日而父歿,
未葬,
火焚其廬.
Zhāng Yì 搏顙籲天,
火至柩所而滅.
Qí, Huáng 寇犯 Lóngquán,
Zhāng Yì 從子 Cúnrén 被執,
Zhāng Yì 挺身告賊曰:
"吾兄止一子,
寧我代."
賊素聞其名,
欲降之,
縛於柱,
Zhāng Yì 不為屈.
至夜紿守者脫歸,
集里民為義兵,
擊破賊.
俄府官以兵來,
欲盡誅詿誤者.
Zhāng Yì 走說 Shímò Yísūn 曰:
"貧民迫凍餒,
誅之何為."
Shímò Yísūn 然其言,
檄止兵,
留 Zhāng Yì 幕下.
從平 Qìngyuán, Púchéng 盜.
授 Lóngquán Zhǔbù,
不受歸.
Shímò Yísūn 守 Táizhōu,
為賊所圍.
Zhāng Yì 以鄉兵赴援,
却賊.
已而賊陷 Lóngquán,
Jiānxiàn Bǎo Hūdīng 遁去,
Zhāng Yì 與其師 Wáng Yì 帥壯士擊走賊.
Bǎo Hūdīng 還,
內慚,
殺 Wáng Yì 以反.
Zhāng Yì 時在 Shímò Yísūn Mùfǔ,
聞之馳歸,
偕 Hú Shēn 執戮首惡,
因引兵平 Sōngyáng, Lìshuǐ 諸寇.
Chángqiāng Jūn 攻 Wù,
聞 Zhāng Yì 兵至,
解去.
論功累授 Zhèdōng Dū Yuánshuàifǔ Qiānshì.
Zhāng Yì 曰:
"吾所將皆鄉里子弟,
肝腦塗地,
而吾獨取功名,
弗忍也."
辭不受.
以義兵屬其子 Cúndào,
退隱 Kuāngshān.
Tàizǔ attacked Jiāngzhōu.
When he reached Xiǎogū Shān,
Yǒudé led his部部 [部部, which is likely a typo for 所部 (suǒ bù)] to surrender.
The emperor spoke with him
and, admiring him,
appointed him as a general.
He followed Cháng Yùchūn to reinforce Ānfēng
and seize Lúzhōu.
Upon returning,
he followed in the battle of Póyáng Hú,
where his light boats crushed Yǒuliàng's vanguard.
Though he sustained several injuries,
he fought with even greater vigor.
He then joined the other generals in intercepting and attacking at Jīngjiāngkǒu,
where Yǒuliàng was defeated and killed.
He followed the expedition to Wǔchāng.
Southeast of the city, Gāoguān Shān overlooked the city,
and the Hàn army occupied it.
The generals looked at each other, none daring to advance.
Yǒudé led several hundred men
and captured it in one charge.
A stray arrow pierced his cheek and his ribs,
but he was not deterred.
After Wǔchāng was pacified,
he was appointed Commander of the Xióngwǔ Guard.
He followed Xú Dá to capture Lúzhōu,
and with a detached force, he took Yílíng, Héngzhōu, and Xiāngyáng.
Attacking Ānlù,
he sustained nine wounds,
but broke through and captured its general, Rèn Liàng.
He followed the main army down Huáidōng,
defeated Zhāng Shìchéng's relief force at Mǎluó Gǎng,
capturing a thousand warships,
and then inflicted a major defeat on the Yuán general Zhú Zhēn at Ānfēng.
He and Lù Jù jointly defended Xúzhōu.
Kuòkuò sent his general Lǐ Èr to attack,
halting at Língzǐ Cūn.
Yǒudé, judging his forces to be too few to match the enemy,
held firm within the walls and did not engage in battle.
Spying that the enemy troops were scattered plundering,
he took two thousand men upriver to Lǚliáng,
landed and attacked them.
He charged alone, thrusting his spear and piercing their general, Hán Yǐ.
The enemy fled in defeat.
Expecting them to return soon,
he immediately went back,
opened the city gates, and arrayed his forces in the field,
laying down their spears to wait,
having agreed to rise upon hearing the drum.
Lǐ Èr indeed arrived.
When the drums sounded,
the soldiers leaped up and fought,
defeating and capturing Lǐ Èr.
He was recalled [to court],
and promoted to Cānzhī Zhèngshì of the Jiānghuái Acting Provincial Administration Commission,
and with the emperor's ceremonial parasol [and banner] removed,
he was escorted to his residence with ceremonial music.
The following year, he accompanied the grand general on the Northern Expedition,
defeating Yízhōu
and capturing Qīngzhōu.
When the Yuán Prime Minister Yěsù came to reinforce,
he used light cavalry to lure the enemy into an ambush,
then fiercely attacked and routed them.
He then took Láiyáng and Dōngchāng.
The next year, he participated in pacifying Biàn and Luò,
capturing various mountain strongholds.
He crossed the river to take Wèihuī and Zhāngdé,
and upon reaching Línqīng,
captured a Yuán general to serve as a guide,
taking Dézhōu and Cāngzhōu.
After conquering the Yuán capital,
he scouted the Gǔběi pass,
guarded Lúgōu Qiáo,
seized Dàtóng,
and then returned to capture Bǎodìng and Zhēndìng,
and garrisoned Dìngzhōu.
He followed the attack on Shānxī,
capturing Tàiyuán.
Kuòkuò came to reinforce from Bǎo'ān,
with ten thousand cavalry suddenly arriving.
Yǒudé, with fifty cavalry, charged and repelled them,
then launched a night raid on their camp.
Kuòkuò fled in haste,
pursued to Tǔmén Guān,
where tens of thousands of his soldiers and horses were captured.
He then defeated Hè Zōngzhé at Shízhōu
and Tuōlièbó at Xuānfǔ,
then proceeded west to meet the Grand General,
besieging Qìngyáng.
He stationed a detached force at Língzhōu
to block enemy reinforcements,
and thus Qìngyáng was captured.
Upon his return,
he was bestowed with white gold and fine silk.
In Hóngwǔ 3rd year, he followed the grand general to assault Dìngxī,
inflicting a major defeat on Kuòkuò.
He then shifted forces to campaign against Shǔ,
leading the vanguard out through the Yībǎi Bābā Dù,
capturing the Lüèyáng Pass,
and then entering Miǎn.
He divided his troops to jointly attack Hànzhōng from Liányún Zhàn,
and captured it.
Due to an inadequate supply of provisions,
the army returned to Xī'ān.
The Shǔ general Wú Yǒurén then encroached on Hànzhōng.
Yǒudé, with three thousand cavalry, went to relieve it,
attacking Dǒushān Zhài.
He ordered his troops to light ten torches and spread them across the mountain,
and the Shǔ troops fled in alarm.
That winter,
in recognition of his merits, he was granted the title of Kāiguó Fǔyùn Tuīchéng Xuānlì Wǔchén, Rónglù Dàfū, Zhùguó, and Tóngzhī Dàdūdū Fǔshì,
ennobled as Yǐngchuān Hóu,
receiving a stipend of 1,500 shi of grain,
and given an hereditary warrant.
The next year, he was appointed Conqueror-Barbarian Front General,
and with the Conqueror-West General Tāng Hé, they divided their routes to campaign against Shǔ.
Tāng Hé led Liáo Yǒngzhōng and others with a naval force to attack Qútáng,
while Yǒudé led Gù Shí and others with infantry and cavalry from Qín and Lǒng.
Tàizǔ instructed Yǒudé, saying:
"The people of Shǔ, hearing of our western expedition,
will surely concentrate their elite forces to defend Qútáng in the east
and block Jīnniú in the north,
to resist our army.
If you act unexpectedly,
directly attacking Jiē and Wén,
once their 'gates and doors' are destroyed,
their 'heart and belly' will collapse on their own.
Speed is paramount in warfare,
the only concern is a lack of courage."
Yǒudé swiftly marched to Shǎn,
gathered his armies, publicly declared he would exit via Jīnniú,
but secretly led his troops towards Chéncāng.
Scaling cliffs and ravines,
they traveled day and night.
Reaching Jiēzhōu,
he defeated the Shǔ general Dīng Shìzhēn,
and captured his city.
The Shǔ people cut off the Báilóng Jiāng bridge.
Yǒudé repaired the bridge to cross,
broke through Wǔlǐ Guān,
and then captured Wénzhōu.
He crossed the Báishuǐ Jiāng
and hurried towards Miánzhōu.
At that time, the Hàn Jiāng was swollen,
making it impassable,
so they felled trees to build warships.
Wishing to convey his army's presence to Qútáng,
he carved several thousand wooden plaques,
inscribed them with the dates of the capture of Jiē, Wén, and Mián,
and cast them into the Hàn Shuǐ,
letting them float downstream.
When the Shǔ defenders saw them,
they all disintegrated.
Earlier,
when the Shǔ people heard of the grand army's western expedition,
Prime Minister Dài Shòu and others indeed concentrated all their forces to defend Qútáng.
But upon hearing that Yǒudé had captured Jiē and Wén
and was assaulting Jiāngyóu,
they began to divide their troops to reinforce Hànzhōu
to protect Chéngdū.
Before they arrived,
Yǒudé had already defeated their defending general Xiàng Dàhēng beneath the city walls.
He told his officers and men:
"The relief army has come a long way.
Hearing that Dàhēng has been defeated,
they are already disheartened
and can do nothing."
He met and attacked them,
inflicting a major defeat.
He then captured Hànzhōu
and advanced to besiege Chéngdū.
Dài Shòu and others fought with elephants.
Yǒudé ordered strong crossbows and fire weapons to charge them.
Though struck by a stray arrow himself, he did not retreat,
and his officers and men fought to the death.
The elephants turned and fled,
trampling many to death.
Dài Shòu and others, hearing that their lord Míngshēng had already surrendered,
registered their treasuries and granaries, bound themselves, and went to the army gate.
Chéngdū was pacified.
He divided his troops to secure the unconquered prefectures and counties,
captured Bǎoníng,
arrested Wú Yǒurén and sent him to the capital,
and the entire Shǔ territory was pacified.
When Yǒudé attacked Hànzhōu,
Tāng Hé was still stalled at Dàxī Kǒu.
After he found the wooden plaques in the river,
he then advanced his army.
Dài Shòu and others had withdrawn their elite troops to the west to relieve Hànzhōu,
leaving the old and weak to defend Qútáng.
Therefore, Yǒngzhōng and others were able to press their advantage to assault Chóngqìng,
and Míngshēng surrendered.
Thereupon, Tàizǔ composed the "Text on the Pacification of Western Shǔ,"
greatly praising Yǒudé's achievements as first,
and Liáo Yǒngzhōng's as second.
Upon the army's return,
he received the highest reward.
He had twelve sons.
Guō Zhèn
married Princess Yǒngjiā.
Guō Míng
was a diǎnbǎo in the Liao Princely Establishment.
Guō Yōng
was the Right Dūdū of the Central Army.
He had nine daughters,
two of whom became consorts of the Prince of Yǐng in Liao.
His granddaughter became Noble Consort of Rénzōng,
she was Guō Míng's daughter.
Because of this, Guō Míng's son, Guō Xuán, was able to inherit the marquisate.
During the Xuāndé reign,
Guō Xuán served as the acting head of the Zōngrén Fǔ,
and seized fields and houses from the people of Héjiān.
He also seized a thousand acres of garrison land in Tiānjīn.
His servant was punished for his crimes, but Guō Xuán was pardoned.
At the beginning of Yīngzōng's reign,
Princess Yǒngjiā petitioned for her son, Guō Zhēn, to inherit the marquisate.
Guō Zhēn
was the principal grandson of Guō Yīng.
He was granted the position of Commander Aide of the Jǐnyīwèi.
When Guō Xuán died,
his son, Guō Cōng, competed with Guō Zhēn for the succession.
Consequently, both were suspended from inheriting,
and Guō Cōng was granted the same official position as Guō Zhēn.
In the first year of Tiānshùn,
Guō Zhēn's son, Guō Chāng, was granted the succession due to an imperial edict.
Guō Cōng contested this but did not succeed.
When Guō Chāng died,
his son, Guō Liáng, was supposed to succeed.
However, Guō Cōng again claimed that Guō Liáng was not Guō Chāng's son,
and the succession was again suspended.
Guō Liáng was appointed Commander Aide.
He was imprisoned for repeatedly petitioning for the succession,
but was soon released and reinstated.
Later, the kinsmen of the Guō clan jointly petitioned for one of Guō Yīng's grandsons to inherit Guō Yīng's title.
All the court officials stated that Guō Liáng was originally Guō Yīng's principal grandson
and should inherit the marquisate.
The emperor approved the edict.
He died at the beginning of the Zhèngdé reign.
His son, Guō Xūn, inherited.
Guō Xūn was shrewd and resourceful,
and quite knowledgeable in history books.
During the Zhèngdé reign,
he governed Liǎngguǎng
and later became the commander of the Sānqiān Yíng.
At the beginning of Shìzōng's reign,
he was in charge of the Tuányíng.
When the Great Rites Controversy arose,
Guō Xūn understood the emperor's intentions
and was the first to support Zhāng Cōng.
Shìzōng greatly favored him.
Guō Xūn, relying on imperial favor,
became quite arrogant and self-indulgent.
Grand Secretary Yáng Yīqīng disliked him.
When his bribery and petitions came to light,
he was dismissed from his camp duties
and stripped of his 保傅 (bǎofù) official rank.
After Yáng Yīqīng was dismissed,
Guō Xūn again took charge of the Wǔjūn Yíng
and oversaw construction projects in the four suburbs.
The following year, he supervised the Tuányíng.
In the eighteenth year, he concurrently led the Hòufǔ.
When he accompanied the emperor on a visit to Chéngtiān,
he requested that his fifth-generation ancestor, Guō Yīng, be enshrined in the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
The court officials resisted, deeming it unacceptable,
and Minister Táng Zhòu argued particularly strongly.
The emperor did not listen,
and Guō Yīng was eventually enshrined.
The following year,
Xiànhuáng was granted the ancestral temple name,
and enshrined in the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
Guō Xūn was promoted to Yìguó Gōng
and given the additional title of Tàishī.
Before this,
the sorcerer Lǐ Fúdá claimed he could transform medicines into gold and silver.
Guō Xūn became close to him.
When Lǐ Fúdá was defeated,
Guō Xūn strongly defended his case,
and many court officials incurred punishment.
At this time, he again introduced the Daoist practitioner Duàn Cháoyòng,
who claimed that by using the gold and silver he transformed as eating utensils,
one could achieve immortality.
The emperor increasingly regarded him as loyal.
Censor Qī Xián impeached Guō Xūn for abusing his power,
illegally profiting, and oppressing the people, among other things.
Lǐ Fènglāi and others also spoke against him.
When the relevant authorities investigated,
it was found that Guō Xūn owned more than a thousand shops and properties in the capital.
Vice Censor-in-Chief Hú Shǒuzhōng also impeached Guō Xūn for appointing his paternal cousin, Guō Xiàn, to handle legal cases in the Eastern Depot,
where he wantonly abused innocent people.
The emperor ignored these charges.
At that time, the emperor, acting on the words of supervising officials,
issued an imperial edict to Guō Xūn,
ordering him to clear military service matters together with Minister of War Wáng Tíngxiàng and Earl of Suí'ān Chén Huì.
When the edict was prepared,
Guō Xūn did not accept it.
The supervising officials impeached him for abusing his power and forming factions.
Guō Xūn submitted a memorial in defense,
which contained the phrase,
"Why bother to grant another imperial edict?"
The emperor was then greatly enraged,
reprimanding him for his arrogance, defiance, and lack of propriety expected of a subject.
Thereupon, Censor Gāo Shí fully exposed Guō Xūn's corrupt and illicit activities,
and also stated that he was colluding with Zhāng Yánlíng.
The emperor grew even angrier
and sent Guō Xūn to the Jǐnyīwèi prison.
This was in the ninth month of the twentieth year.
Soon after, an imperial decree instructed the zhènfǔsī not to torture him.
Upon receiving the memorial,
Guō Xūn was found guilty of a capital offense.
The emperor ordered the legal authorities to re-examine the case.
Censor Liú Dàzhí further investigated Guō Xūn for twelve crimes of misgovernance
and requested that they all be prosecuted.
The legal authorities then confirmed all the charges in the memorials
and found Guō Xūn guilty of hanging.
The emperor ordered a detailed discussion.
The legal authorities further found Guō Xūn guilty of treason and recommended execution by beheading,
and confiscation of his wife, children, fields, and residences.
The memorial was submitted,
but it was held by the emperor and not acted upon.
The emperor intended to spare Guō Xūn
and repeatedly hinted at this intention.
However, the court officials despised Guō Xūn greatly
and pretended not to understand,
instead re-sentencing Guō Xūn to severe punishment.
The following year, when supervising officials were evaluated,
a special imperial edict demoted Gāo Shí by two ranks to warn other court officials.
However, the court officials ultimately did not plead for Guō Xūn.
That winter,
Guō Xūn died in prison.
The emperor pitied him
and reprimanded the legal authorities for his prolonged detention.
Minister of Justice Wú Shān was stripped of his office,
and the Vice Ministers and Censors-in-Chief below were demoted by varying degrees.
However, Guō Xūn's property was not confiscated,
and only his imperial patents and certificates were revoked.
Since the rise of the Míng dynasty,
meritorious officials had not participated in government affairs.
Only Guō Xūn, by relying on imperial favor, usurped state power, and indulged in villainy, brought about his downfall.
Several years after Guō Xūn's death,
his son, Guō Shǒugān, inherited the marquisate.
It passed down to his great-grandson, Guō Péimín,
who, at the end of the Chóngzhēn reign,
died at the hands of rebels.
Huá Yúnlóng
was from Dìngyuǎn.
He gathered a crowd and resided in Jiǔshān.
When Tàizǔ raised his army,
Huá Yúnlóng came to pledge allegiance.
He followed in conquering Chú and Hé,
and became a qiānfūzhǎng.
He followed in crossing the river,
destroyed the naval camp at Cǎishí and the Fāngshān camp,
took Jíqìng Prefecture,
captured a Yuán general alive,
obtained ten thousand soldiers,
conquered Zhènjiāng,
and was promoted to Zǒngguǎn.
He attacked and captured Guǎngdé,
fought at Jiùguǎn,
captured Marshal Tāng,
and was promoted to Right Vice Marshal.
In the Battle of Lóngjiāng,
Huá Yúnlóng ambushed at Shīhuīshān.
In the ensuing battle,
the casualties were considerable.
Huá Yúnlóng leapt on his horse and shouted,
charging into the enemy's strongpoint,
and thus utterly defeated Chén Yǒuliàng's forces,
and, taking advantage of the victory, recaptured Tàipíng.
He followed in taking Jiǔjiāng and Nánchāng,
and then divided his forces to attack and capture Ruìzhōu, Línjiāng, and Jí'ān.
He followed in reinforcing Ānfēng,
fought at Pénglí,
and pacified Wǔchāng.
His accumulated merits led him to become Commander of the Bàotāo Guard.
He followed Xú Dá in commanding troops to capture Gāoyóu,
then advanced to conquer Huái'ān,
and was then ordered to defend it,
being reassigned as Commander of the Huái'ān Guard.
Soon after, he attacked Jiāxīng,
received the surrender of the Wú general Sòng Xīng,
besieged Píngjiāng,
and encamped at Xūmén.
He followed the main army on the Northern Expedition,
campaigning through Shāndōng prefectures and counties,
joined forces with Xú Dá at Tōngzhōu,
and then advanced to conquer the Yuán capital.
He was promoted to Aide of the Grand Dūdū Fǔ,
commanding the six guards remaining as garrison,
and concurrently as Cānzhī Zhèngshì of the Běipíng Province.
The following year,
he attacked and captured Yúnzhōu,
taking Grand Councillor Huǒ'érhútá and Right Chancellor Hāhǎi captive.
He was promoted to Dūdū Tóngzhī,
and concurrently as Left Chancellor to the Prince of Yān.
Zhāng Lóng,
a native of Háo.
He joined in crossing the Yangzi River,
and contributed to the pacification of Chángzhōu, Níngguó, and Wùzhōu,
achieving merits in all.
He joined the campaign against Jiāngzhōu,
serving as the vanguard commander.
After the pacification of Wǔchāng,
he was appointed Qianhù of the Huāqiāng Commandery.
He joined in the pacification of Huáidōng,
defending Hǎi'ān.
He fought against Zhāng Shìchéng's general at Hǎikǒu,
captured Marshal Péng,
and took several hundred of his soldiers prisoner.
He then attacked Tōngzhōu,
slaying a bandit general,
and was promoted to Zhīhuī Qiānshì of the Wēiwǔ Guard.
He joined in the pacification of Shāndōng and Hénán.
When the main army captured Tóngguān,
Lóng was appointed vice-acting defender.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, he was transferred to defend Fèngxiáng,
and became the Zhīhuī of the Fèngxiáng Guard.
Hè Zōngzhé besieged the city with all his forces,
but Lóng held firm.
Zōngzhé attacked the north gate;
Lóng led his troops out to engage in fierce combat.
An arrow wounded his right flank,
but he remained undeterred.
He then decisively defeated them,
and advanced to capture Fèngzhōu,
seizing more than twenty people, including Supervisor Lǐ.
Grand General Dá entered Miǎnzhōu,
and dispatched Lóng to lead a separate army.
They went from Fèngxiáng into Liányúnzhàn,
attacked Xīngyuán,
and secured the surrender of its defending general, Liú Sīzhōng.
When the Shǔ general Wú Yǒurén came to invade,
Lóng repelled him.
Yǒurén then returned with all his troops to press against the city,
and prepared numerous siege engines.
Lóng suddenly sallied out from the north gate,
circled behind Yǒurén's army;
the enemy abandoned their armor and weapons and fled.
From then on, they no longer dared to spy on Xīngyuán.
He was summoned to serve as Qiān Dàdūdùfǔshì.
In the eleventh year, he served as deputy to Lǐ Wénzhōng in the campaign against the Xīfān (Tibetans) in Táozhōu.
For his merits,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Fèngxiáng,
with a stipend of two thousand shí,
and hereditary command of the Zhīhuīshǐ.
He again joined Fù Yǒudé's campaign against Yúnnán,
garrisoned Qīxīngguān,
defeated Dàlǐ and Hèqìng,
and pacified the various Mán (barbarian) caves.
His stipend was increased by five hundred shí,
and he was granted an hereditary charter.
In the twentieth year, he accompanied Féng Shèng out to Jīnshān,
and secured the surrender of Nàhāchū.
The following year,
Shèng transferred the surrendered troops to campaign against Yúnnán.
When they reached Chángdé,
they rebelled and left.
Lóng pursued them to Chóngqìng,
and captured them.
In the spring of the twenty-third year, he, along with the Marquis of Yán'ān, Táng Shèngzōng, supervised military agricultural colonies in Píngyuè, Zhènyuǎn, and Guìzhōu,
and discussed establishing the Lónglǐ Guard.
When Dōuyún rebelled,
he assisted Lán Yù in suppressing them.
Due to old age and illness, he requested retirement,
and died in the thirtieth year.
His son, Lín, married Princess Fúqīng,
and was appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
His grandson, Jié, served the princess in the capital.
In the early years of Yǒnglè,
the marquisate was lost.
Jié's son succeeded,
and in the tenth year of Xuāndé,
requested to inherit the title based on an imperial edict of grace.
The Ministry of Personnel stated that the marquisate of Lóng had not been inherited for forty years,
and did not permit it.
Wú Fù,
courtesy name Bóqǐ,
a native of Héféi.
From a young age, he was courageous and strategic.
At the end of the Yuán dynasty,
he gathered a multitude to protect his hometown.
He joined Tài Zǔ in Háo,
and participated in the capture of Sì, Chú, Hé, Cǎishí, and Tàipíng,
accumulating promotions to Wànhù.
He participated in the defeat of Mánzǐ Hǎiyá's naval camp,
and the pacification of Jíqìng.
He joined Xú Dá in attacking Zhènjiāng,
beheaded the Yuán Píngzhāng Dìng Dìng,
took Dānyáng and Jīntán,
captured Chángzhōu,
and was promoted to Tǒngjūn Yuánshuài.
He then took Jiāngyīn and Wúxī,
and returned to defend Chángzhōu.
When Zhāng Shìchéng's army suddenly arrived,
he fought fiercely and defeated them,
pursuing the fleeing enemy to Chángxīng.
He repeatedly defeated them at Gāoqiáo, Tàihú, and Zhōngjiémén,
causing Shìchéng to lose morale.
He participated in the relief of Ānfēng,
and the pacification of Wǔchāng.
He joined Xú Dá in capturing Lúzhōu,
and taking various prefectures and counties in Hàn, Miǎn, and Jīng.
He was appointed Zhènwǔ Wèi Zhīhuī Tóngzhī,
and defended Miǎnyáng.
He joined Cháng Yùchūn in taking Xiāngyáng,
and led a separate force to defeat Ānlù,
capturing the Yuán Tóngqiān Rèn Liàng,
and then defended it.
He captured Rǔzhōu and Lǔshān.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, he was appointed Huáiyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Ānlù Wèi Zhīhuīshǐ,
and completely pacified the unaligned mountain strongholds in Yún, Jūn, Fáng, and Zhú.
In the third year, he joined the Grand General in the campaign against Shǎnxī,
defeated Kuòkuò,
and captured his generals.
He again defeated Kuòkuò in Qínzhōu.
He campaigned against Tǔbō (Tibetans),
captured Hézhōu,
relieved Hànzhōng,
and took Nánzhèng.
The following year, he joined Fù Yǒudé in pacifying Shǔ.
The year after that, he joined Dèng Yù in pacifying the various Mán in Jiǔxī and Chénzhōu,
captured forty-eight caves,
and returned to defend Ānlù.
In the seventh year, he was promoted to Dàdūdùfǔ Qiānshì.
After inspecting Běipíng and returning,
he was appointed hereditary Zhīhuīshǐ.
In the eleventh year, he joined Mù Yīng in a second campaign against the Xīfān,
captured three vice-envoys,
and gained the territory of Nàlín Hā's seven stations.
The following year,
the army returned,
and for his merits he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Ānlù,
with a stipend of two thousand shí.
In the fourteenth year,
he joined Fù Yǒudé in campaigning against Yúnnán,
captured Pǔdìng,
and built a city at Shuǐxī.
He was appointed commander-in-chief,
to suppress and capture the various Mán.
He then opened a path through the wilderness from Guānsǔolǐng,
and took Guǎngxī.
In the sixteenth year, he captured Mòdìng Miáo,
reached Jílào Fort,
built Ānzhuāng and Xīnchéng,
pacified the various strongholds of the Seven Hundred Houses,
killing and capturing tens of thousands,
and transported provisions across Pánjiāng.
In October of that year,
his old wounds recurred,
and he died in Pǔdìng.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Duke of Qiánguó,
given the posthumous name Wēiyì,
his stipend was increased by five hundred shí,
and he was granted an hereditary charter.
Fù always fought valiantly in battle,
charging into arrows and stones,
with no part of his body left unharmed.
In peacetime, he was humble and cautious,
and did not speak of military campaigns.
In Pǔdìng, he bought a concubine, Lady Yáng,
who was seventeen years old.
After Fù's death,
after she had attended to his burial,
she bathed, changed clothes, and hanged herself.
She was enfeoffed as Zhēnliè Shúrén.
His son, Jié, succeeded him.
He repeatedly went out to Shān, Shǎn, Hénán, and Běipíng,
training troops and participating in campaigns.
In the twenty-eighth year,
he committed a crime,
but joined the campaign against Lóngzhōu,
and redeemed himself through his achievements.
During the Jiànwén reign,
he led an army to relieve Zhēndìng,
and fought at Báigōuhé.
He suffered a defeat,
and was demoted to Nánníng Wèi Zhīhuīshǐ.
In the first year of Yǒnglè,
his son, Jǐng, requested to succeed him.
During the Zhèngtǒng reign,
he requested repeatedly,
but was never permitted.
In the sixth year of Hóngzhì,
Jǐng's grandson, Duó, requested to succeed him based on an imperial edict,
but was also not permitted.
In the eighteenth year, Fù's descendants were granted the hereditary post of Qianhù.
Zǐróng,
had merit during the campaign in Yúnnán,
and was appointed Suǐjūn Yòuwèi Zhǐhuīshǐ.
Sūn Jiàn,
was Fújiàn Dūzhǐhuīshǐ.
In the Yǒnglè reign,
he was stationed in Jiāozhǐ.
Huá Gāo
was a native of Hézhōu.
He, along with Yú Tōnghǎi and others, joined with the Cháohú naval forces.
He followed them to conquer Tàipíng,
and was granted the title Zǒngguǎn.
He followed them to defeat the forces at Cǎishí and Fāngshān,
and to take Jíqìng and Zhènjiāng,
and was promoted to Qínhuái Yì Yuánshuài.
He, with Dèng Yù, pacified Guǎngdé.
The defending general deployed troops below the city walls.
Gāo, with a few horsemen, challenged them to battle.
The Yuán forces held their defenses firm and did not move.
Gāo charged and utterly routed them,
and then took the city,
obtaining ten thousand soldiers
and several thousand hù of grain.
He followed them to pacify Chángzhōu,
and was promoted to Qiān Xíng Shūmìyuànshì.
He served as deputy to Yú Tōnghǎi in defeating Zhào Pǔshèng's stockaded camp on the river.
He again defeated Chén Yǒuliàng,
relieved Chángxīng,
and conquered Wǔchāng,
and was granted the title Húguǎng Xíngshěng Zuǒchéng.
He commanded the naval forces, following them to conquer Huáidōng,
and reclaim Zhéxī,
and was promoted to Xíngshěng Píngzhāng Zhèngshì.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, he was enfeoffed as Guǎngdé Hóu,
with an annual stipend of six hundred shí.
Gāo was timid by nature,
and also had no son,
so he requested to remain on guard duty.
Whenever there was a campaign,
he would claim illness and not go.
When ordered to train the navy,
he again declined, saying he was unfamiliar with it.
The emperor, because of their old acquaintance, treated him leniently.
At that time, many meritorious officials were dispatched to the frontiers,
but only Gāo was not sent.
Finally, when repairing the coastal fortifications of Guǎngdōng,
Gāo requested to go.
The emperor said:
"You are exerting yourself again,
which is very good."
In the fourth year, in the fourth month, the task was completed,
and he died upon reaching Qióngzhōu.
Initially,
there were those who said Gāo amassed wealth,
which is why his annual stipend was particularly meager.
By this time, he was so poor he could not afford a burial.
The emperor pitied him,
and ordered an additional stipend of three hundred shí.
As he had no son,
his imperial patent and deed were placed in his tomb.
He was posthumously granted the title Cháo Guógōng,
and given the posthumous name Wǔzhuāng.
His nephew, Yuè, was granted the title Zhǐhuī Qiānshì.
Zhāng Quán,
was a native of Dìngyuǎn.
He followed them to take Tàipíng,
and pacify Jíqìng, Zhènjiāng, Chángzhōu, and Wùzhōu.
He attacked Jiāngzhōu,
fought at Póyáng Hú,
and took Èzhǔ.
He reclaimed Huáidōng,
and pacified Wú.
For his accumulated merits, he became Zhǐhuī Qiānshì.
He followed them to take the Central Plains, Yān, Jìn, Qín, and Shǔ,
and was promoted to Dūdū Qiānshì.
He was sent to construct the Qí Wáng Fǔ.
Upon completion of the task,
he served as deputy to Jiāngxià Hóu Zhōu Déxīng in campaigning against the Wǔxī Mán.
Soon after, when the chieftains of the Suǐjìnyuán, Tōngtǎpíng, and Sǎnmáo caves revolted,
he again served as deputy to Déxīng to suppress them.
He followed them on the campaign to Yúnnán,
conquering Wūsà via Yǒngníng.
After some time,
he again followed Fù Yǒudé to pacify Wūsà and the various Man tribes of Qǔjìng, Pǔdìng, Lónghǎi, and Mèngdìng.
In the twenty-third year of Hóngwǔ, he was enfeoffed as Yǒngdìng Hóu,
with a stipend of one thousand five hundred shí,
and the hereditary title Zhǐhuīshǐ.
Hé Zhēn,
courtesy name Bāngzuǒ,
was a native of Dōngguǎn.
In his youth, he was heroic and distinguished,
and fond of books and swords.
At the beginning of the Zhìzhèng reign of Yuán,
he served as Héyuán Xiànwù Fùshǐ,
then transferred to Dànshuǐchǎng Guǎngōu,
before abandoning his office and returning home.
At the end of the Yuán dynasty, when bandits rose,
Zhēn gathered a multitude to protect his hometown.
In the fourteenth year,
when Wáng Chéng and Chén Zhòngyù of the county revolted,
Zhēn reported it to the Yuánshuàifǔ.
The Marshal accepted a bribe,
and instead arrested Zhēn.
He escaped and resided in Nígāng,
then raised an army to attack Chéng,
but did not succeed.
After some time,
Wáng Zhònggāng of Huìzhōu, with the rebel general Huáng Cháng, occupied Huì.
Zhēn attacked and drove away Cháng,
and killed Zhònggāng.
For his merits, he was granted the titles Huìyáng Lù Tóngzhī and Guǎngdōng Dū Yuánshuài,
and defended Huìzhōu.
The sea bandit Shào Zōngyú captured Guǎngzhōu.
Zhēn used his troops to defeat and drive him away,
recovering the city,
and was promoted to Guǎngdōng Fēnshěng Cānzhèng,
and soon after to Yòuchéng.
Xióng Tiānruì of Gànzhōu led tens of thousands of naval forces, intending to attack Zhēn.
Zhēn met them at Xūjiāng.
There was a great thunderstorm,
which broke Tiānruì's boat masts,
and drove him away.
The people of Guǎng relied on this to remain safe.
Earlier, Zhēn had attacked Chéng a second time,
executed Zhòngyù, while Chéng remained firmly entrenched.
In the twenty-sixth year, he again besieged Chéng,
offering a reward of ten thousand banknotes
to whoever captured Chéng.
Chéng's slave bound Chéng and brought him out.
Zhēn gave the slave the banknotes,
then ordered a boiling pot prepared,
and rushed to cook the slave,
announcing to the multitude:
"Let all slaves who betray their masters look at this!"
All rebels along the coast surrendered.
At that time, the Central Plains were in great chaos,
and the Lingnan region was cut off.
There were those who advised Zhēn to emulate the story of Wèi Tuó.
He did not listen.
He repeatedly sent envoys by sea to offer local products as tribute to the court,
and was successively promoted to Zīdé Dàfū and Xíngshěng Zuǒchéng.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ,
Tàizǔ ordered Liáo Yǒngzhōng to be Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn,
to command naval forces to take Guǎngdōng.
Yǒngzhōng reached Fúzhōu,
and sent a letter to Zhēn,
then sailed by sea towards Cháozhōu.
When the army arrived,
Zhēn sent Dūshì Liú Kèzuǒ to the military camp to surrender his official seal,
register the households, population, soldiers, and grain of his subordinate commanderies and counties,
and submit a memorial to surrender.
Yǒngzhōng reported this to the court,
and an imperial edict praised Zhēn, saying:
"We believe that ancient heroes,
who protected their borders and pacified their people,
awaiting the virtuous ruler,
such as Dòu Róng and Lǐ Jì,
who commanded troops and occupied strategic positions,
standing among competing heroes,
would not yield except to a true lord.
These were famous ministers of Hàn and Táng,
but none like them have been seen today.
You, Zhēn, with the forces of several commanderies,
without troubling a single soldier,
protected your territory and came to surrender.
Even Dòu and Lǐ would concede to this."
When Yǒngzhōng arrived at Dōngguǎn,
Zhēn, with his officials, welcomed and consoled him,
and then, following the imperial edict, went to court.
He was promoted to Jiāngxī Xíngshěng Cānzhī Zhèngshì,
and was further admonished, saying:
"When the world is divided and contested,
there are three types of so-called heroes.
Those who transform chaos into order are
the highest.
Those who protect the people, adapt to change, and know where to return are
the next.
Those who stubbornly hold on to their strongholds and indulge in temporary peace,
dying without regret,
are the lowest.
You, Minister, wholeheartedly offered your territory and
did not go against our will;
you may be called one who understands the times."
Zhēn bowed his head in thanks.
While in office, he gained considerable prestige,
especially enjoying Confucian scholarship,
reading and composing essays.
Later,
he was transferred to Shāndōng Cānzhèng.
In the fourth year, he was ordered to return to Guǎngdōng
to gather old soldiers.
Upon completion of the task,
he again presided over Shāndōng.
In the ninth year, he retired.
The Grand Army was campaigning in Yúnnán,
and Zhēn was ordered to go with his son, the cavalry and infantry commander Guì,
to plan military provisions
and establish post stations.
He was promoted to Vice Provincial Administration Commissioner of Shānxī.
He was again ordered with Guì to mobilize troops in Guǎngdōng,
and Guì was promoted to Assistant Commander of the Zhènnán Guard.
Soon after, Zhēn was appointed Provincial Administration Commissioner of Zhèjiāng,
then transferred to Húguǎng.
In the twentieth year, he retired again,
was enfeoffed as the Earl of Dōngguǎn,
with a stipend of one thousand five hundred shí,
and granted an hereditary certificate.
He died.
His son Róng succeeded him.
Róng, along with his younger brother Guì and Shàngbǎosī Chéng Hóng, all died for their involvement in the Lán Party.
Zhēn's younger brother Dí, suspecting that misfortune would befall him,
then rebelled,
killing over three hundred imperial troops from Nánhǎi,
and fled to an island in the sea.
The Guǎngdōng Dūsī dispatched troops to suppress and capture him,
and he was executed.
The encomium states: When Chén Yǒuliàng conquered Tàipíng,
his vanguard was extremely sharp;
had it not been for Mào Cái, the safety of Jīnlíng would have been uncertain.
Wú Liáng defended Jiāngyīn,
Gěng Bǐngwén defended Chángxīng,
preventing the Wú people from achieving their ambitions.
Their efforts were crucial
for the foundation of the dynasty.
As for Huá Yúnlóng, Zhāng Hè, Wú Fù, Hú Hǎi and others,
some made their prestige felt on the frontiers,
while others rendered service in maritime transport.
They raised banners and breached enemy formations,
crushing all in their path.
Compared to meritorious officials of previous generations,
how much do they yield?
Moreover, they were all able to preserve their stipends and positions,
and enjoy a peaceful end with grace and courtesy.
Is this not especially commendable!
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 19: Gù Shí, Wú Zhēn, Xuē Xiǎn, Guō Xīng, Chén Dé, Wáng Zhì, Méi Sīzǔ, Jīn Cháoxīng, Táng Shèngzōng, Lù Zhònghēng, Fèi Jù, Lù Jù, Zhèng Yùchūn, Huáng Bīn, Yè Shēng.
Gù Shí,
courtesy name Shíjǔ,
was a native of Háo.
He was unconventional and fond of unusual strategies.
He followed Tàizǔ across the Jiāng,
accumulating merits from a centurion to be appointed Yuánshuài.
He captured Ānqìng, Nánchāng, Lúzhōu, and Tàizhōu,
and was promoted to Assistant Commander of the Tiāncè Guard.
When Lǐ Jì occupied Háo Zhōu,
Shí followed Píngzhāng Hán Zhèng to attack and subdue him.
Attacking Zhāng Shìchéng’s Shēngshān Water Stockade,
he led small boats to circle the enemy vessels.
Many in the boats looked down and laughed.
Shí, taking advantage of their complacency,
led several brave men,
shouted loudly, and leapt into the boats.
The crowd fell into great disarray,
and the remaining boats rushed forward.
The Fifth Prince came to reinforce,
but Xuē Xiǎn defeated him again,
and the Fifth Prince and others surrendered.
He then followed the Grand General to pacify Wú,
and after returning, took Shāndōng.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, he was appointed Vice Administrator of the Grand Dūdū Office and concurrently Assistant Commander of the Shuàifǔ.
He followed the Grand General to pacify Hénán and the North,
dredging sluices to allow the passage of naval forces,
from Línqīng to Tōngzhōu.
He captured Yuán Dū
and, with other generals, patrolled the passes of Gǔběi.
He followed the Grand Army to take Píngyáng,
conquered Guōzhōu,
and captured forty-six fleeing generals, including Wáng Xìn.
He took Lánzhōu and
besieged Qìngyáng.
Zhāng Liángchén paraded his troops outside the city,
but Shí defeated him,
capturing nine of his elite generals.
Liángchén then dared not sally forth again.
Qìngyáng was pacified.
Xú Dá returned to the capital,
ordering Shí to lead cavalry to briefly attack Jìngníng Prefecture,
driving away Hè Zōngzhé.
The western border was completely pacified.
In the third year, he was promoted to Assistant Grand Dūdū,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Jìníng,
with a stipend of one thousand five hundred shí,
and granted an hereditary certificate.
In the fourth year, he was appointed Left Vice General,
assisting Fù Yǒudé in leading the infantry and cavalry of Hénán and Shǎnxī to attack Shǔ.
From Xīngyuán, they advanced to conquer Jiē and Wén,
defeated the Shǔ army in Hànzhōu,
and then conquered Chéngdū.
The following year, he assisted Lǐ Wénzhōng in the northern expedition,
entering the desert by different routes.
He lost his way,
provisions were almost exhausted,
and they encountered bandits;
the soldiers were too weary to fight.
Shí led several hundred men from his command,
charged on horseback,
causing the enemy multitude to withdraw.
He captured their baggage, provisions, and livestock and returned,
greatly boosting the army's morale.
In the sixth year, he followed Xú Dá to garrison Běipíng.
The following year,
he was recalled.
In the eighth year, he again went out to garrison.
In the twelfth year, he died,
at the age of forty-six.
He was buried on Zhōngshān.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Duke of Téng,
given the posthumous name Xiāngjìng,
and ritually honored in the Temple of Meritorious Officials.
Shí was able to use a few to strike many,
being resolute and not boastful.
The emperor greatly esteemed him.
His son Jìng,
Jinwú Guard Town Commandant,
succeeded to the marquisate in the fifteenth year.
He became Left Vice General
and performed meritorious service in pacifying the bandits of Lóngquán Mountain.
In the twenty-third year, when the Hú Wéiyōng Faction was investigated,
a list of implicated officials was posted,
with Shí named as the leader.
Jìng was executed for his involvement,
and his noble rank was abolished.
Wú Zhēn was
the younger brother of Wú Liáng, Duke Xiāngliè of Jiāng State.
His original name was Guóbǎo,
and he was granted the name Zhēn.
He and Liáng both participated in the conquest of Chú and Hé,
crossed the Jiāng to conquer Cǎishí,
followed in the pacification of Jíqìng,
and took Zhènjiāng, Guǎngdé, Chángzhōu, Xuānchéng, and Jiāngyīn.
All these yielded meritorious service.
He also followed Cháng Yùchūn from Tónglíng to take Chízhōu,
using naval forces to destroy its north gate
and enter the city.
When over a hundred enemy ships arrived,
he again greatly defeated them,
thus conquering Chízhōu.
Accumulating merits, he rose from Account Vanguard Commander
to successively become Vice Yuánshuài of the Tiānxīng Wing.
With one thousand men, he assisted Liáng in defending Jiāngyīn,
repeatedly defeating the Wú army,
destroying Shìchéng's water stockade,
and capturing his fierce general Zhū Dìng.
He was appointed Commander of the Yīngwǔ Guard Imperial Troops.
He also greatly defeated the Wú army at Fúzǐmén.
He followed Grand General Xú Dá, leading cavalry, infantry, and naval forces to take Húzhōu,
deploying surprise troops from Jiùguǎn,
achieving a great victory.
Húzhōu was pacified,
and he was then stationed there.
He followed in besieging Píngjiāng,
breaching the Fèng and Xū gates,
and was promoted to Assistant Dūdū of the Grand Dūdū Office,
pacifying Píngjiāng.
Soon after, he assisted the General who Pacifies the South, Tāng Hé, in attacking Fāng Guózhēn.
Riding the tide into the Cáoyú River,
he destroyed dams to clear a path,
unexpectedly reaching the enemy's barracks.
Guózhēn fled into the sea,
and Zhēn pursued him to Pányǔ,
where they engaged in battle
from shēn (3-5 PM) to xū (7-9 PM),
defeating him
and capturing all his warships, soldiers, and baggage.
Guózhēn surrendered.
He then advanced by sea to capture Fúzhōu,
besieging its west, south, and water gates,
conquering them in one assault.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, he advanced to defeat Yánpíng
and captured Chén Yǒudìng.
The entire Mǐn Sea region was pacified.
He returned to Chāngguó.
Coincidentally, sea pirates raided Lánxiù Mountain,
and he suppressed them.
He concurrently served as Vice Administrator of the Shuàifǔ,
and later became Left Chancellor of Wú King and concurrently Assistant Dūdū of the Grand Dūdū Office.
In the second year,
when the Grand General returned after pacifying Shǎnxī,
Zhēn and Vice General Féng Shèng were stationed in Qìngyáng.
In the third year, he suppressed the bandits of Yízhōu's Dáshān Mountain.
He was appointed General who Pacifies the Sea,
training troops on the sea.
In that winter,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Jìnghǎi,
enjoying a stipend of one thousand five hundred shí,
and granted an hereditary certificate.
He, along with the tutors of the two princes of Qín and Jìn, Jīn Cháoxīng and Wāng Xīngzǔ, exclusively tutored the princes,
and was relieved of his duties in the Dūdū Office.

bié jiàng yóujūn qǔ Déqīng,
gōng Shēngshān shuǐzhài.
Shìchéng yǎn qí Wǔ Tàizǐ shèng bīng lái yuán,
Yùchūn yǔ zhàn xiǎo què.
Xiǎn shuài zhōushī fènjī,
shāo qí chuán.
Zhòng dà kuì,
Wǔ Tàizǐ jí Zhū Xiān, Lǚ Zhēn děng yǐ Jiùguǎn jiàng,
dé bīng liù wàn rén.
Yùchūn wèi Xiǎn yuē:
"Jīnrì zhī zhàn,
jiāngjūn gōng,
Yùchūn fú rú yě."
Wǔ Tàizǐ děng jì jiàng,
Wú rén zhènkǒng,
Húzhōu suì xià.
Jìn wéi Píngjiāng,
yǔ zhū jiàng fēnmén ér jūn.
Wú píng,
jìn Xíngshěng Yòuchéng.
Mìng cóng Dàjiāngjūn Xú Dá qǔ Zhōngyuán.
Pín xíng,
Tàizǔ yù zhū jiàng,
wèi Xuē Xiǎn, Fù Yǒudé yǒnglüè guànjūn,
kě dāng yī miàn.
Jìn kè Yǎn, Yí, Qīng, Jì,
qǔ Dōngchāng, Dìzhōu, Lè'ān.
Huán shōu Hénán,
dǎo Guān, Shǎn.
Dù hé,
qǔ Wèihuī, Zhāngdé, Guǎngpíng, Línqīng.
Shuài mǎbù zhōushī qǔ Dézhōu, Chánglú,
bài Yuán bīng yú Héxīwù,
yòu bài zhī Tōngzhōu,
suì kè Yuándū.
Fēnbīng luó Gǔběi zhū àikǒu,
lüè Dàtóng,
huò Qiáo Yòuchéng děng sānshísì rén.
Jìn zhēng Shānxī,
cì Bǎodìng,
qǔ Qīduǒzhài,
zhuī bài Tuōyīntiěmù'ér.
Yǔ Yǒudé jiàng tiěqí sānqiān,
lüè Píngdìngxī,
qǔ Tàiyuán,
zǒu Kuòkuò,
jiàng Huòbímǎ.
Yāojī Hè Zōngzhé yú Shízhōu,
bá Báiyá, Táohuā zhū shānzhài.
Yǔ Dàjiāngjūn Dá huì Píngyáng,
yǐ jiàngjiàng Dù Wàng děng shíyī rén jiàn,
suì cóng rù Guānzhōng,
dǐ Líntáo.
Bié jiàng gōng Mǎ'ānshān Xīfānzhài,
dà huò qí xùchǎn,
xí zǒu Yuán Yùwáng,
bài Kuòkuò yú Níngxià,
fù yǔ Dá huìshī qǔ Píngliáng.
Zhāng Liángchén wěi yǐ Qìngyáng jiàng,
Xiǎn wǎng nà zhī.
Liángchén púfú dào yíng,
yè jié Xiǎn yíng,
tūwéi miǎn.
Liángchén jù chéng pàn,
Dá jìn wéi zhī.
Kuòkuò yǎn Hánzhā'ér gōng Yuánzhōu,
yǐ náo Míng shī.
Xiǎn zhù bīng Língzhōu è zhī.
Liángchén yuán jué,
suì bài.
Zhuī Hè Zōngzhé yú Liùpánshān,
zhú Kuòkuò chū Sàiwài,
Shǎnxī xī píng.
Hóngwǔ sān nián dōng dà fēng gōngchén,
yǐ Xiǎn shàn shā xūlì, shòuyī, huǒzhě, mǎjūn jí Qiānhù Wú Fù,
miàn shǔ qí zuì.
Fēng Yǒngchéng Hóu,
wù yǔ quàn,
zhé jū Hǎinán.
Fēn qí lù wèi sān,
yī yǐ shàn suǒ shā Wú Fù jí mǎjūn zhī jiā,
yī yǐ gěi qí mǔqī,
lìng gōngguò wú xiāngyǎn.
Xiǎn jū Hǎinán yú nián,
Dì niàn zhī,
zhào huán,
yǔ shì quàn,
shílù yīqiān wǔbǎi shí.
Fù cóng Dàjiāngjūn zhēng Mòběi.
Shù fèng mìng xúnshì Hénán,
túntián Běipíng,
liànjūn Shānxī,
cóng Wèiguógōng xún Běibiān,
cóng Sòngguógōng chū Jīnshān.
Èrshí nián dōng zhào huán,
cì Shānhǎiwèi,
zú.
Zèng Yǒngguógōng,
shì Huánxiāng.
Wú zǐ,
dì Gāng yòu.
Èrshísān nián zhuī zuò Xiǎn Hú Wéiyǒng dǎng,
yǐ sǐ bù wèn,
jué chú.
Guō Xīng,
yī míng Zǐxīng,
Háo rén.
Chúyángwáng Guō Zǐxīng jù Háo,
chēng Yuánshuài,
Xīng lì huīxià.
Tàizǔ zài shēngguǎn,
Xīng guīxīn yān.
Jūn xíng,
cháng bèi sùwèi,
lěi gōng shòu Guǎnjūn Zǒngguǎn,
jìn Tǒngjūn Yuánshuài.
Wéi Chángzhōu,
zhòuyè bù jiějiǎ zhě qī yuè.
Chéng xià,
shòu shàng shǎng.
Cóng gōng Níngguó, Jiāngyīn, Yíxīng, Wùzhōu, Ānqìng, Qúzhōu,
jiē xià zhī.
Zhàn yú Póyáng,
Chén Yǒuliàng lián jùjiàn yǐ jìn,
wǒ shī lǚ què,
Xīng xiàn jì yǐ huǒgōng zhī.
Yǒuliàng sǐ.
Cóng zhēng Wǔchāng,
zhǎnhuò duō,
jìn Yīngyángwèi Zhǐhuīshǐ.
Cóng Xú Dá qǔ Lúzhōu,
yuán Ānfēng,
dà bài Zhāng Shìchéng bīng.
Píng Xiāngyáng, Héng, Lǐ,
huán kè Gāoyóu, Huái'ān,
zhuǎnzàn Húzhōu,
wéi Píngjiāng,
jūn yú Lóumén.
Wú píng,
zhuó Zhènguó Jiāngjūn, Dàdūdūfǔ Qiānshì.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, he followed Dá to take the Central Plains.
They conquered Biànliáng
and defended Hénán.
Féng Shèng took Shǎnzōu
and requested more troops to guard Tóngguān.
Dá said:
“No one is as good as Xīng.”
So, he was transferred to guard it.
Tóngguān,
the gateway to the Three Qín,
was at that time occupied by Hāmātú in Fèngyuán.
Lǐ Sīqí, Zhāng Sīdào, and others formed a pincer movement with him,
spying daily and wishing to move eastward.
Xīng put all his effort into defending it.
When Wáng Zuǒchéng came to attack,
he was soundly defeated.
He followed Xú Dá, leading light cavalry directly to Fèngyuán.
The main army followed,
and they conquered it.
He was then moved to garrison Gǒngchāng,
and the border became peaceful.
In the third year, he became the Martial Tutor to Qínwáng,
and concurrently Assistant Commissioner of Shǎnxī Provincial Capital Command.
That winter,
when meritorious officials were enfeoffed,
Xīng, due to his failure to adhere to discipline,
was only enfeoffed as Gǒngchāng Hóu,
with a stipend of one thousand five hundred shí of grain,
and granted a hereditary charter.
In the fourth year, he campaigned against Shǔ,
conquering Hànzhōu and Chéngdū.
In the sixth year, he followed Xú Dá to garrison Běipíng,
and together with Chén Dé, defeated the Yuán troops at Dálàhǎikǒu.
In the eleventh year, he trained troops at Línqīng.
In the sixteenth year, he patrolled the northern border.
He was recalled,
and passed away the following year.
He was posthumously granted Shǎnguógōng
and given the posthumous title Xuānwǔ.
In the twenty-third year, he was posthumously implicated as a member of Hú Wéiyōng’s faction,
and his noble title was revoked.
Xīng’s younger sister was Níng Fēi,
and his younger brother Yīng was Wǔdìng Hóu.
His youngest brother Déchéng
was intelligent and quick-witted,
and fond of wine.
While his two elder brothers accumulated merits to become marquises,
Déchéng remained a Xiāoqí Shèrén.
Tàizǔ, for the sake of Níng Fēi,
wished to elevate his status.
Déchéng declined.
The Emperor was displeased.
He kowtowed and apologized, saying:
“Your servant is by nature fond of alcohol
and too ignorant to manage affairs.
If I held a high position and heavy emolument,
I would certainly be assigned official duties.
If the matters are not well managed,
Your Majesty might kill me.
In life, it is most important to be content.
As long as I get more money
and can drink fine wine, that is enough;
I do not desire anything else.”
The Emperor praised him,
granted him a hundred jars of wine
and an equivalent amount of gold and silk,
and his favor and treatment became even more generous.
Once, while attending a banquet in the imperial garden, he became drunk,
crawled forward, removed his cap, and apologized.
The Emperor looked at Déchéng and saw his disheveled hair,
and laughed, saying:
“Drunken madman,
your hair is like this,
is it not due to excessive drinking?”
Déchéng looked up and said:
“Your servant is even annoyed by it;
only by shaving it all off will I be truly pleased.”
The Emperor remained silent.
When he sobered up,
he was greatly afraid.
He feigned madness and abandoned himself,
shaved his head, wore monastic robes,
and continuously chanted Buddhist scriptures.
The Emperor said to Níng Fēi:
“At first, I made a jest about your brother,
but now he has truly become like this.
He is indeed a madman.”
Later, when the factional incident occurred,
those implicated and executed were numerous,
but Déchéng ultimately escaped.
Chén Dé,
courtesy name Zhìshàn,
was a native of Háo.
His family had been farmers for generations,
and he possessed great courage and strength.
He followed Tàizǔ at Dìngyuǎn,
and as a commander of ten thousand men, he rendered meritorious service in all battles,
becoming the vanguard general of the imperial tent.
Together with various generals, he took cities such as Níng, Huī, Qú, and Wù,
and was promoted to Marshal.
Lǐ Bóshēng attacked Chángxīng;
Dé went to reinforce and repelled him.
He followed to reinforce Nánchāng,
fought a great battle at Póyáng Hú,
and captured Yáo Píngzhāng of the water stockade.
When Tàizǔ’s boat ran aground,
Dé fought bravely,
was struck by nine arrows,
but did not retreat.
He followed in pacifying Wǔchāng.
He soundly defeated Zhāng Shìchéng’s troops at Jiùguǎn,
and was promoted to Commander of the Tiāncè Guard Imperial Army.
After Wú was pacified,
he was promoted to Assistant Administrator of the Grand Capital Command.
He followed the Grand General in the northern campaign to take the Central Plains,
and conquered Yuán Biànliáng.
The Hénán Provisional Capital Command was established,
with Dé appointed to manage its affairs,
and he pacified the various bandits.
He campaigned in Shānxī,
defeated the Mópánzhài stronghold in Zézhōu,
captured Cāncè Yù Rén,
and then joined the main army to conquer Píngyáng, Tàiyuán, and Dàtóng.
He crossed the river to take Fèngyuán and Fèngxiáng,
reaching Qínzhōu.
The Yuán defending general Lǚ Guógōng fled,
and he pursued and captured him.
Xú Dá besieged Zhāng Liángchén at Qìngyáng;
Liángchén relied on his elder brother Sīdào for external aid,
with spies frequently coming and going.
Dé captured them all,
and Qìngyáng was subsequently taken.
He also greatly defeated Kuòkuò at Gǔchéng,
and captured eighty thousand of his soldiers.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, he was enfeoffed as Línjiāng Hóu,
with a stipend of one thousand five hundred shí of grain,
and granted a hereditary charter.
The following year, he followed Yǐngchuānhóu Fù Yǒudé to campaign against Shǔ,
entering Miánzhōu by a separate route,
defeating Lóngdé,
and soundly routing Wú Yǒurén’s forces.
Capitalizing on the victory, he took Hànzhōu.
Xiàng Dàhēng, Dài Shòu, and others fled to Chéngdū;
he pursued and defeated them,
and then besieged Chéngdū with Yǒudé.
After Shǔ was pacified,
he was granted white gold and silk,
and returned to Biàn.
In the fifth year, he became Left Deputy General,
and campaigned with Féng Shèng in the northern desert,
defeating the enemy at Biédù Shān,
capturing and beheading tens of thousands.
He conquered Gānsù,
took Yìjínǎi Lù,
left troops to guard the pass, and returned.
The following year, he again led the main force out of Shuòfāng,
defeated the enemy at Sānchà Shān,
and captured their Deputy Commander Shīlàhǎn and over seventy others.
That autumn,
he again went out to battle at Dálàhǎikǒu,
beheading six hundred,
and capturing their co-commander Xīndū and fifty-four others.
In total, three battles and three victories.
In the seventh year, he trained troops at Běipíng.
In the tenth year, he returned to Fèngyáng.
In the eleventh year, he passed away.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Qǐguógōng,
and given the posthumous title Dìngxiāng.
His son Yōng inherited the title.
In the sixteenth year, he became Left Deputy General for the Southern Expedition,
pacifying the various mountain bandits in Lóngquán,
and training troops at Biànliáng.
In the nineteenth year, together with Jìnghǎi Hóu Wú Zhēn, he fortified Huìzhōu.
In the twentieth year, he followed Féng Shèng to campaign against Nàháchū.
When nearing Jīnshān,
he became separated from the main army due to a different route
and was defeated and lost.
In the twenty-third year, Dé was posthumously implicated as a member of Hú Wéiyōng’s faction.
The imperial edict stated that during his western campaign,
he had committed transgressions and been reprimanded,
and subsequently conspired with Wéiyōng.
His noble title was revoked.
Wáng Zhì,
a native of Lín Huái.
He followed Tàizǔ from Háo with local troops,
and took Chú and Hé.
He followed in crossing the Yangtze River,
repeatedly scaling palisades and being the first to ascend,
exposing himself to arrows and stones.
He was appointed Right Deputy Grand Marshal.
He followed in taking Cháng Zhōu, Níng Guó, and Jiāng Yīn,
recovered Yí Xīng,
attacked Gāo Yóu,
struck Jiǔ Jiāng,
took Huáng Méi,
and fought a fierce battle at Pó Yáng.
He followed in pacifying Wǔ Chāng,
returned and conquered Lú Zhōu,
defeated Zhāng Shìchéng's army,
and pursued them for forty lǐ.
He was transferred from Commander of the Imperial Guard to Lù Ān Guard,
and garrisoned Lù Ān.
He followed in visiting Biàn Liáng,
crossed the river,
took Huái Qìng, Zé, and Lù,
and remained to guard Píng Yáng.
When Grand General Xú Dá campaigned west,
Zhì joined forces and captured Xīng Yuán.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, he was promoted to Assistant Administrator of the Chief Military Commission,
enfeoffed as the Marquis of Lù Ān,
received an annual stipend of nine hundred shí of grain,
and was granted a hereditary patent.
He was moved to guard Hàn Zhōng,
led troops out of the Cháhǎn Nǎo'ér pass,
and returned to garrison Píng Yáng.
He again followed the Grand General on an expedition to the desert.
Later, when troops were deployed in the Southwest,
he always followed as a subordinate general;
though he achieved no primary功 (gōng),
he was prudent
and never suffered defeat.
His attack on Hé Féi, where he defeated Lóu'ér Zhāng,
and captured Deputy Envoy Wú,
was his foremost military achievement.
He oversaw the military affairs of the guards in the Shān Xī Regional Military Commission,
and the Emperor praised his proper management.
In the sixteenth year, he commanded troops to Pǐn Diàn in Yún Nán,
repaired city walls,
established garrisons,
set up relay stations,
and pacified its people.
He died in the nineteenth year.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Duke of Xǔ Guó,
and given the posthumous title Xiāng Jiǎn.
His son, Wēi,
succeeded him as Marquis in the twenty-second year.
The following year,
for an offense, he was demoted to Commander of Ān Nán Guard.
He died
without a son.
His younger brother, Mǒu, succeeded,
and was transferred to Qīng Píng Guard,
with hereditary succession.
Zhì was also posthumously implicated in the Hú Wéiyōng faction,
but due to his death, no inquiry was made.
Méi Sīzǔ,
a native of Xià Yì.
Initially, he was a Grand Marshal of the Yuán righteous army,
then rebelled and joined Liú Fútōng.
Kuòkuò minced his father.
Soon after, he abandoned Fútōng and submitted to Zhāng Shìchéng,
serving as Left Grand Councilor of the Central Secretariat,
and guarding Huái Ān.
When Xú Dá's army arrived,
he welcomed them and surrendered,
also presenting four prefectures.
Shìchéng killed several of his brothers.
Tàizǔ promoted Sīzǔ to Deputy Administrator of the Chief Military Commission.
He followed the grand army in attacking Wú,
captured Shēng Shān Water Stockade,
took Hú Zhōu,
and besieged Píng Jiāng,
achieving merit in all.
After Wú was pacified,
he was promoted to Right Councilor of the Zhè Jiāng Provincial Administration Commission.
He followed the Grand General in campaigning against the Central Plains,
captured Shān Dōng,
took Biàn and Luò,
broke through Shǎn Zhōu,
and seized Tóng Guān.
The army then turned back to pacify Hé Běi,
reaching Wèi Huī.
Yuán Administrator Lóng Èr abandoned the city and fled to Zhāng Dé,
and the army pursued him.
Lóng Èr fled again,
so they captured his city
and garrisoned it.
He briefly pacified the prefectures and counties in Běi Píng that had not yet fallen.
He followed the grand army in pacifying Jìn and Jì,
then again followed in pacifying Shǎn Xī,
and separately led troops to capture Bīn Zhōu,
capturing Yuán Vice Administrator Máo Guì and thirty others.
He followed the Grand General in defeating Kuòkuò at Dìng Xī.
Returning from Qín Zhōu,
he broke through Lüè Yáng,
entered Miǎn Zhōu,
and took Xīng Yuán.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, based on his merits, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Rǔ Nán,
received a stipend of nine hundred shí of grain,
and was granted a hereditary patent.
In the fourth year, he campaigned against Shǔ.
In the fifth year, he campaigned against Gān Sù.
Upon his return, he was ordered to inspect the city walls of Shān Xī, Shǎn Xī, and Liáo Dōng.
In the fourteenth year,
when the tribal chiefs of Shuǐ Jìnyuán, Tōng Tǎ Píng, and Sàn Máo caves in Sì Chuān rebelled,
Sīzǔ was appointed Deputy General Who Pacifies the South,
and with the Marquis of Jiāng Xià, Zhōu Déxīng, he led troops to suppress them.
In the fifteenth year, he again pacified Yún Nán with Fù Yǒudé,
established the Guì Zhōu Regional Military Commission,
and appointed Sīzǔ as acting Regional Military Commissioner.
Soon after, he was appointed acting Administrator of the Yún Nán Provincial Administration Commission,
and guarded Yún Nán with Administrator Pān Yuánmíng.
Sīzǔ was skilled at conciliation,
and distant people found peace under him.
He died that year,
and was granted burial on the shady side of Zhōng Shān.
His son, Yì,
was the Regional Military Commissioner of Liáo Dōng.
In the twenty-third year, Sīzǔ was posthumously implicated as a member of the Hú Wéiyōng faction,
and his family was annihilated.
Sīzǔ's nephew, Yīn,
was a Son-in-law Commandant,
and has a separate biography.
Jīn Cháoxīng,
a native of Cháo.
When Huái Xī was in turmoil,
he gathered a multitude and built stockades to protect themselves.
After Yú Tōnghǎi and others submitted to Tàizǔ,
Cháoxīng also led his multitude to join.
He followed in crossing the Yangtze River,
participating in all campaigns and expeditions,
and achieving merit.
He captured Cháng Zhōu,
serving as Chief Vanguard.
He recovered Yí Xīng,
serving as Deputy Grand Marshal of the Left Wing.
He pacified Wǔ Chāng,
and was promoted to Assistant Commander of Lóng Xiāng Guard.
He pacified Wú,
and was transferred to Commander of Zhèn Wǔ Guard.
He captured Dà Tóng,
and was transferred to Commander of Dà Tóng Guard.
He took Dōng Shèng Zhōu,
and captured Yuán Administrator Liú Lín and eighteen others.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, based on his merits, he was made Assistant Administrator of the Chief Military Commission concurrently Right Chancellor to the Prince of Qín.
Soon after,
he was relieved of his duties in the Chief Military Commission,
and solely tutored the Prince.
In the fourth year, he followed the grand army in campaigning against Shǔ.
In the seventh year, he led the army to Hēi Chéng,
capturing Yuán Grand Marshal Lú Bóyán, Administrator Tiē'ér Bùhuā, and twenty-five other officials from the province and court.
He then followed Lǐ Wénzhōng, taking separate command of the eastern route army,
and took Hélín;
the details are in Wénzhōng's biography.
Cháoxīng was brave, resolute, and strategically astute;
wherever he went, he achieved victory with a detached force.
Though not a Grand Marshal,
his achievements surpassed those of other generals.
In the eleventh year, he followed Mù Yīng on the western expedition,
and incorporated seven relay stations near Nà Lín.
The following year, based on his merits, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xuān Dé,
received a stipend of two thousand shí of grain,
and his commandership was hereditary.
In the fifteenth year, he followed Fù Yǒudé on the expedition to Yún Nán,
stationing troops at Lín Ān.
Yuán Right Councilor Wù Bǔtái, Grand Marshal Wán Zhědōu, and local chieftain Yáng Zhèng all surrendered.
Cháoxīng's conciliation methods were effective,
and the soldiers and civilians were all pleased.
He died while advancing to Huì Chuān,
and was posthumously enfeoffed as Duke of Yí Guó,
with the posthumous title Wǔ Yì.
In the seventeenth year, in recognition of his merit in pacifying Yún Nán,
his hereditary patent was changed,
and his stipend increased by five hundred shí.
His eldest son, Zhèn, succeeded to the marquisate.
In the twenty-third year, Cháoxīng was posthumously implicated in the Hú Wéiyōng faction,
and Zhèn was demoted to Commander of Píng Bà Guard.
He achieved merit in subsequent campaigns,
and was promoted to Regional Military Commissioner;
thereafter, his family inherited the commandership of the guard.
In the first year of Jiājìng,
an order was given to erect temples for Fù Yǒudé, Méi Sīzǔ, and Cháoxīng in Yún Nán,
with the inscribed plaque reading
"Bào Gōng" (Recognizing Merit).
Táng Shèngzōng,
a native of Háozhōu.
When Tàizǔ raised his army,
Shèngzōng, eighteen years old,
came to pledge allegiance.
He followed in crossing the Yangtze River,
and for his accumulated merits, became Zhongyì Yuánshuài.
He followed Xú Dá in capturing Chángzhōu,
then advanced to besiege Níngguó.
He guarded a strategic pass and fought fiercely,
defeating the enemy's reinforcements.
The city subsequently surrendered.
He followed in the campaign against Wùzhōu,
and captured it.
He followed in the campaign against Chízhōu,
fighting fiercely and defeating Chén Yǒuliàng's troops,
and was promoted to Lóngxiáng Wèi Zhīhuī Qiānshì.
He followed in the campaign against Yǒuliàng,
reaching Ānqìng,
where the enemy held firm.
Shèngzōng, making a feint with land forces,
unexpectedly,
stormed and captured their naval camp.
He followed in taking Nánchāng,
and pacifying various prefectures in Jiāngxī.
He relieved Ānfēng,
attacked Lúzhōu,
fought at Póyáng,
and ambushed at Jīngjiāngkǒu.
He was meritorious in all these,
and was promoted to Piāojì Wèi Zhīhuī Tóngzhī.
He followed in pacifying Wǔchāng,
then occupied Chángshā, Yuánlíng, and Lǐyáng.
He followed Xú Dá in taking Jiānglíng,
then returned to pacify Huáidōng.
He dug tunnels to capture Ānfēng,
and pursued and captured the Yuán general Xīndū.
He was appointed Ānfēng Wèi Zhīhuīshǐ to guard it.
He followed the Grand General in campaigning against the Central Plains,
capturing Biànliáng, Guīdé, and Xǔzhōu,
and was often left behind to guard them.
He followed the main army in capturing Yán'ān,
and was promoted to Dūdū Fǔ Tóngzhī.
In the winter of the third year of Hóngwǔ, he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yán'ān,
with a stipend of one thousand five hundred shí of grain,
and granted a hereditary charter.
He was implicated for unauthorized use of post horses,
stripped of his peerage,
and demoted to Zhīhuī.
He then apprehended rebels in Dàixiàn.
After a long time,
his peerage was restored.
In the fourteenth year,
when the Zhejiang Eastern mountain bandits Yè Dīngxiāng and others rebelled,
he was ordered to lead the army to suppress them,
capturing the bandit leader and over three thousand of his followers.
He divided his troops to pacify the bandits of Ānfú,
and upon reaching Lín'ān,
received the surrender of the Yuán Right Chancellor Wūbǔtái and others.
In the fifteenth year, he inspected Shǎnxī,
supervising agricultural garrisons,
and reviewing soldiers.
The next year, he was stationed in Liáodōng,
receiving an imperial edict not to communicate with Gāolì.
When a Gāolì envoy arrived,
he detected their deception,
and reported it to the throne.
He was awarded an imperial edict praising him,
comparing him to Wèi's Tián Yù who rejected the Wūhuán bribe,
and calling him a worthy minister.
He served at the garrison for seven years,
and his authority and trustworthiness became greatly renowned.
He was recalled,
and led an army to suppress the Mán rebels in Guìzhōu,
training troops in Huángpíng.
In the twenty-third year, he was executed for being involved in the Hú Wéiyōng faction,
and his peerage was abolished.
Lù Zhònghēng,
a native of Háozhōu.
He pledged allegiance to Tàizǔ,
and followed in the campaign against Chúzhōu,
and took the various stockades of Dàliǔshù.
He captured Héyáng,
defeated the Yuán army,
and pursued the bandits of Qīngshān.
He followed in crossing the Yangtze River,
took Tàipíng,
pacified Jíqìng,
followed Xú Dá in taking various prefectures and counties,
and was granted the title Zuǒyì Tǒngjūn Yuánshuài.
He followed in the campaign against Chén Yǒuliàng,
and for his many merits,
was promoted to Piāojì Wèi Zhīhuīshǐ.
He followed Cháng Yùchūn in campaigning against Gànzhōu,
received the surrender of Xióng Tiānruì,
and was appointed Gànzhōu Wèi Zhīhuīshǐ,
controlling the newly surrendered prefectures north and south of the Lingnan Mountains.
He mobilized troops to capture Méizhōu, Huìchāng, and Xiāngxiāng,
and completely pacified all the mountain stockades.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, he led the garrison army with Liáo Yǒngzhōng and others to campaign against Guǎngdōng,
subduing various prefectures and counties,
and rendezvoused with Yǒngzhōng in Guǎngzhōu,
receiving the surrender of the Yuán general Lú Zuǒchéng.
Guǎngdōng was pacified.
He was changed to Měidōng Wèi Zhīhuīshǐ,
and promoted to Jiāngxī Xíngshěng Píngzhāng.
He replaced Dèng Yù in garrisoning Xiāngyáng,
and was changed to Tóngzhī Dūdū Fǔ Shì.
In the winter of the third year, he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Jí'ān,
with a stipend of one thousand five hundred shí of grain,
and granted a hereditary charter.
He was demoted to Zhīhuīshǐ for the same offense as Táng Shèngzōng.
He captured bandits at Yànmén,
and was restored to his peerage at the same time.
In the twelfth year, he, along with Zhōu Déxīng, Huáng Bīn, and others, followed Tāng Hé to train troops in Línqīng.
Not long after,
the three men were arrested in the army and brought to the capital,
but later released.
He was transferred to garrison Chéngdū,
and pacified the rebellious Mán of Jùjīnzhōu.
When the Mán of Wūsà rebelled again,
he followed Fù Yǒudé to suppress them.
In the twenty-third year, during the investigation of Hú Wéiyōng's treacherous faction,
his house slave Fēng Tièmù accused Zhònghēng, along with Shèngzōng, Fèi Jù, and Zhào Yōng, of being involved in the conspiracy,
and they were handed over to officials for interrogation.
When the case was concluded,
the Emperor said:
"I always wondered why he looked troubled while holding a high position."
Consequently, Zhònghēng was executed,
and his property confiscated.
Originally,
when Zhònghēng was seventeen,
he was plundered by rebellious soldiers,
and his parents and siblings all died.
He hid in the grass with one shēng of wheat.
The Emperor saw him,
and called out
"Come!"
He then followed in campaigns,
eventually becoming a Marquis.
The Emperor once said:
"This man was my trusted confidant and right-hand man when I first rose."
Yet, he was ultimately executed.
Fèi Jù,
courtesy name Zǐyīng,
a native of Wǔhé.
His father, Déxīng,
was a patrol officer known for his talent and bravery.
Jù learned martial arts in his youth.
Tàizǔ met him in Háozhōu,
was impressed by his appearance,
and formed a deep bond with him.
At Zhāngjiābǎo in Dìngyuǎn, there were militia with no affiliation.
Guō Zǐxīng wanted to recruit them,
but thought there was no one suitable to send.
Tàizǔ, despite being ill, requested to go,
and rode there with Jù,
accompanied by nine foot soldiers.
Upon reaching Bǎogōng Hé,
they saw that the camp was very orderly,
with all bows and crossbows facing outwards.
The foot soldiers were afraid and
wanted to flee.
Tàizǔ said:
"If they attack us with cavalry,
where can we run?"
So he advanced to their camp.
After persuading them,
and agreeing on three days,
Tàizǔ returned first,
leaving Jù to wait.
Their leader wanted to join another faction,
and Jù returned to report.
Tàizǔ then went back with Jù and three hundred men,
devised a plan to capture their leader,
and acquired three thousand soldiers.
At Huòbí Shān, there were over eight hundred men under Qín Bǎtóu.
Jù again persuaded them to surrender.
He then followed in taking Língbì,
and capturing Sì, Chú, and Hézhōu.
He was granted the title Chéngxìn Xiàowèi.
Once Jiangdōng was settled,
he captured Chángxīng,
and established the Yǒngxīng Yì Yuánshuài Fǔ,
appointing Jù as Deputy Commander to Gěng Bǐngwén.
When Zhāng Shìchéng invaded,
he defeated him.
He was summoned to lead the imperial guards.
He was granted Ānfēng,
twice pacified Jiāngxī,
and captured Wǔchāng,
participating in all these campaigns.
The Yǒngxīng Yì Yuánshuài Fǔ was reorganized into the Yǒngxīng Qīnjūn Zhǐhuī Sī,
with Jù remaining as Deputy Commander (zhǐhuī tóngzhī) to Bǐngwén.
Shìchéng invaded again,
but his commander Sòng Xīngzǔ was captured,
and he was defeated once more.
Shìchéng lost morale
and dared not attempt to spy on Chángxīng again.
He subsequently participated in the campaigns to conquer Huái'ān, Húzhōu, and Píngjiāng,
and having distinguished himself in all,
was promoted to Zhǐhuī Shǐ.
When Tāng Hé campaigned against Fāng Guózhēn,
Jù, with his naval forces, sailed by sea to intercept the enemy.
After Zhèdōng was pacified,
he again traveled by sea to take Fúzhōu,
and captured Yánpíng.
Returning, he stopped at Chāngguó,
and annihilated the pirates of the Yè and Chén clans on Lánxiù Shān.
It was from this point that Jù began to command independently.
In the second year of Hóngwǔ, he joined the grand army to take Xī'ān,
was appointed Xī'ān Wèi Zhǐhuī Shǐ,
promoted to Dūdū Fǔ Qiānshì,
and garrisoned Píngliáng.
In the third year, he was enfeoffed as Píngliáng Hóu,
with an annual stipend of one thousand five hundred dàn of grain,
and granted a hereditary patent.
At that time, various generals on the border were engaged in military farming and recruiting soldiers,
with a fixed quota each year.
Jù, however, was quite indulgent in wine and women,
and did nothing.
Moreover, as he had no success in attracting surrenders,
he was recalled
and severely reprimanded.
The following year, he accompanied Fù Yǒudé on the campaign to Yúnnán,
fought a great battle at Báishí Jiāng,
and captured Dálǐmá.
After Yúnnán was pacified,
they advanced to take Dàlǐ.
Not long after,
the various barbarian tribes rebelled again,
so he was ordered to assist Ānlù Hóu Wú Fù as Commander-in-Chief,
was given strategy,
and jointly attacked Guānsǔo Lǐng and the various strongholds of Āzā,
all of which were taken.
The barbarian lands were then pacified.
The Guìzhōu Dū Zhǐhuī Shǐ Sī was established,
with Jù temporarily in charge of its affairs.
In the eighteenth year, he was appointed Commander-in-Chief
and led Commander Dīng Zhōng and others to campaign in Guǎngnán,
capturing Huǒlìdá
and taking ten thousand captives.
He returned to garrison Yúnnán.
In the twenty-third year, he was recalled.
When Lǐ Shàncháng fell,
Jù was implicated.
The emperor said:
“Jù, when he served in Gūsū, did not act according to my wishes,
and I once scolded him.
Is he now trying to rebel?!”
Ultimately, he was executed for his association
and his title was revoked.
His son Chāo,
who campaigned against Fāng Guózhēn,
died in battle.
Xuán,
due to his talent, was appointed Jiangxī Cāncè.
His grandson Hóng,
who accompanied the campaign to Yúnnán,
rose through merits to become Yòuwèi Zhǐhuī Shǐ.
For making an untruthful statement in a memorial,
he was exiled to Jīnchǐ.
Lù Jù,
whose origins are unknown,
was a Co-Administrator of the Yuán Privy Council (Shūmì Yuàn).
When Tuōtuō defeated Zhīmá Lǐ at Xúzhōu,
Péng Dà and others fled to Háo,
Jù pacified the refugees,
repaired the city walls to protect the border,
and the bandits dared not invade.
When Xú Dá was managing the affairs of Jiāng and Huái,
Jù surrendered Xú and Sù prefectures.
Tàizǔ once issued an edict stating:
“These two prefectures are my native land,
and I cannot bear to use force against them.”
When he submitted,
Tàizǔ was greatly pleased
and appointed Jù as Cāncè of Jiāngnán Xíngshěng,
remaining in charge of Xúzhōu.
He dispatched troops to conquer Pèi, Yútái, Pī, Xiāo, Sùqiān, and Suīníng.
Kuòkuò sent Assistant Chancellor Lǐ to invade Xú,
stationing him at Língzicūn.
Jù sent Commander Fù Yǒudé to attack him,
capturing his troops
and Assistant Chancellor Lǐ.
He also defeated Yuán forces at Sùzhōu,
capturing Director Xíng Duān and others.
He participated in the pacification of Shāndōng
and the capture of Biànliáng.
Returning to garrison,
he was appointed Cāncè of Shāndōng Xíngshěng.
He participated in the pacification of Yuán Dū,
campaigning in Dàtóng, Bǎodìng, and Zhēndìng,
captured Chēzi Shān and the various strongholds of Fèngshān, Chéngshān, and Tiěshān,
garrisoned the old pass of Jǐngxíng,
joined forces in Shǎnxī,
and captured Chéngtiān Zhài.
All the troops under Jù's command were crack soldiers from Huáiběi,
and even the elite cavalry of Yān and Zhào could not compare.
During the northern campaign,
the mountain people of Yí and Pī rebelled opportunistically.
Jù was recalled
and pacified them.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, he was enfeoffed as Hénán Hóu,
with an annual stipend of nine hundred dàn of grain,
and granted a hereditary patent.
In the eighth year, he joined Wèiguó Gōng Yú in military farming in Shǎnxī
and establishing garrisons.
In the twelfth year, he joined Xìnguó Gōng Hé in training troops at Línqīng.
Soon after, he managed military affairs in Fújiàn.
He was recalled
and granted a mansion in Fèngyáng.
In the twenty-third year, he was executed for being part of the Hú Wéiyōng faction
and his title was revoked.
Zhèng Yùchūn,
a native of Háo.
Both he and his elder brother Yùlín were known for their bravery and strength.
Yùlín had a grudge with a villager
and wanted to kill him.
Yùchūn vigorously protected the villager, allowing him to escape.
Everyone feared Yùlín,
but considered Yùchūn to be virtuous.
When Tàizǔ captured Chúzhōu,
Yùlín served as vanguard
and took Tiěfó Gāng, Sān [gé yì] Hé, Dàliǔ, and other strongholds.
Yùchūn also accumulated merits, rising to Zǒngguǎn.
When attacking Wúhú,
Yùlín died in battle,
and Yùchūn took command of his troops.
At that time, the troops under each general were no more than a thousand men,
but Yùchūn commanded two contingents,
and his troops were particularly fierce and brave,
accumulating many battle merits,
and he was appointed Zuǒyì Yuánshuài.
He followed in the campaign to pacify Chén Yǒuliàng,
leading his soldiers into battle,
never boasting of his achievements,
which Tàizǔ found remarkable.
He took Liù'ān
and became Liù'ān Wèi Zhǐhuī Qiānshì.
He followed the Grand General in pacifying Shāndōng and the north of Hénán,
captured Shuòzhōu,
and was appointed Shuòzhōu Wèi Zhǐhuī Fùshǐ.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, he was promoted to Tóngzhī Dà Dūdū Fǔ Shì,
enfeoffed as Xíngyáng Hóu,
with an annual stipend of nine hundred dàn of grain,
and granted a hereditary patent.
The following year, he was ordered to reside in Línháo,
where he established the Dà Dūdū Fǔ.
He was later stripped of his title due to involvement in an offense.
Soon after, it was restored,
and he resumed guarding Shuòzhōu.
He accompanied Fù Yǒudé in pacifying Yúnnán,
leading Yáng Wén and others in managing the cities and military settlements.
Returning to the capital,
he supervised the Jīnwú guards,
built one hundred and eighty seagoing vessels,
transported provisions to Liáodōng,
and registered the official horses of the various guards in Mínzhōu, Shǎnxī.
In the twenty-third year, he was executed for being part of the Hú Wéiyōng faction
and his title was revoked.
Huáng Bīn,
a native of Jiāngxià.
He followed Ōu Pǔxiáng in capturing the dependent counties of Yuán and Jí.
Xú Shòuhuī appointed Pǔxiáng to guard Yuánzhōu.
When Chén Yǒuliàng killed Shòuhuī
and usurped a false imperial title,
Bīn advised Pǔxiáng, saying:
"You and Yǒuliàng are equals;
why should you submit to him?
Yǒuliàng is arrogant and tyrannical;
he is no match for the forces of Jiāngdōng.
If you secure your territory and await the eastern army,
you will surely not lose your wealth and honor."
Pǔxiáng then sent an envoy to pledge allegiance.
Yǒuliàng dispatched his younger brother, Yǒurén, to attack them.
Bīn and Pǔxiáng defeated Yǒurén's troops
and captured Yǒurén.
Yǒuliàng, fearful,
agreed to divide their territories and not infringe upon each other,
and so Yǒurén was released.
At that time, all the commanderies of Jiāng and Chǔ were held by the Chén clan,
and Yuánzhōu blocked their vital passage,
preventing troops from Tán, Yuè, and Gàn from advancing.
Yǒuliàng's power was greatly diminished.
When Tàizǔ's army approached,
Yǒuliàng abandoned Jiāngzhōu,
which was due to Bīn's efforts.
When Tàizǔ arrived at Lóngxīng,
he ordered Pǔxiáng to continue guarding Yuánzhōu
and appointed Bīn as an Administrative Vice Commissioner (Cānzhèng) of the Jiāngxī Branch Secretariat (Xíngshěng).
Not long after,
Pǔxiáng died,
and Bīn took command of his troops.
Pǔxiáng had been cruel and tyrannical;
Bīn completely reversed his policies,
and the people were very much at peace.
He followed Cháng Yùchūn in campaigning against Gànzhōu.
Ráo Dǐngchén occupied Jí'ān
to support Xióng Tiānruì.
When Yùchūn's army arrived,
Dǐngchén fled to Ānfú,
and Bīn pursued him with his troops.
Dǐngchén then fled to Chálíng,
whereupon Tiānruì surrendered.
Zhōu Ān, the commander of Yǒngxīn, rebelled,
and Bīn, accompanying Tāng Hé, captured Ān;
Dǐngchén also perished.
He moved his garrison to Yuánzhōu
and gathered various mountain strongholds,
and Jiāngxī was entirely pacified.
He was promoted to Left Executive Assistant (Zuǒ Chéng) of the Jiānghuái Branch Secretariat.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ (1370), he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yíchūn,
with an annual stipend of 900 dàn of grain,
and granted a hereditary charter.
In the fourth year (1371),
mountain bandits in Shàngyóu, Gànzhōu, rebelled, and he suppressed them.
In the fifth year (1372),
the Man tribes of Gǔzhōu and other caves rebelled.
Dèng Yù was appointed General Pacifying the South (Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn),
and three routes were dispatched.
Bīn and the Marquis of Yíngyáng, Jǐng,
marched out from Lǐzhōu.
When the army returned,
he was granted a residence in Zhōngdū.
The following year (1373), he accompanied Xú Dá to garrison Běipíng
and was dispatched to train troops in Yízhōu and Línqīng.
In the twenty-third year (1390), he was executed for his involvement in the Hú Wéiyǒng faction,
and his peerage was abolished.
Yè Shēng,
a native of Héféi.
When Zuǒ Jūnbì occupied Lúzhōu,
Shēng extricated himself and came to pledge allegiance.
As Right Wing Marshal (Yòuyì Yuánshuài), he participated in the campaign against Jiāngzhōu;
as Aide to the Commander (Zhīhuī Qiānshì), he participated in the capture of Wú;
as Commander of the Palace Guard (Fǔjūn Wèi Zhīhuīshǐ), he participated in the pacification of Míngzhōu.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ (1370), for his merits,
he was appointed Assistant Commissioner of the Chief Military Commission (Qiān Dà Dūdū Fǔshì).
The following year (1371), he accompanied General Pacifying the West (Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn) Tāng Hé with a naval force to conquer Shǔ.
Two years later (1373),
he was appointed Regional Commander (Dū Zhīhuīshǐ)
and garrisoned Xī'ān,
where he suppressed rebellious bandits in Qìngyáng.
In the twelfth year (1379), he was again appointed Assistant Commissioner of the Chief Military Commission.
When the Western Fan tribes rebelled,
he campaigned with Commander Wáng Bì
