and obtained the surrender of Qǐshījiā,
pacifying his tribes.
He then suppressed Bóyán Tiēmù'ér of Yán'ān
and captured the Fan chieftain of Táozhōu.
For his merits,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Jìngníng,
with an annual stipend of 2,000 dàn of grain,
and made a hereditary Commander.
He garrisoned Liáodōng
and repaired the three cities of Hǎi, Gài, and Fù.
He served in the garrison for six years,
during which border defenses were well-maintained,
and foreign invaders dared not intrude.
He was known for distributing bribes from Gāolì;
the Emperor repeatedly issued edicts
commending him alongside Táng Shèngzōng.
In the twentieth year (1387), he was ordered, along with the Marquis of Pǔdìng, Chén Huán, to command all armies in Dìngbiān and Yáo'ān in Yúnnán,
establishing military colonies for cultivation
and managing the Bìjié Guard.
The following year (1388),
the Man tribes of Dōngchuān and Lónghǎi rebelled.
Shēng, as a participating general, followed Mù Yīng to suppress them.
Later, Xià Dézhōng, a chiliarch of Ānfú Commandery in Húguǎng, incited the Man tribes of Jiǔxī Cave to become bandits.
Shēng, along with Hú Hǎi and others, campaigned against them.
He secretly led troops to attack the bandits from the rear,
captured Dézhōng,
and established the two Guards of Yǒngdìng and Jiǔxī.
Subsequently, he remained to garrison Xiāngyáng.
Mountain bandits in Gànzhōu again colluded with the Man tribes of Húguǎng to become bandits.
Shēng served as Vice General (Fù Jiāngjūn)
and, along with Hú Hǎi and others, suppressed them,
capturing 17,000 people.
Shēng pacified rebellious Man tribes three times
and was twice dispatched to train troops in Gānsù and Hénán.
In the eighth month of the twenty-fifth year (1392), he was executed when his collusion with Hú Wéiyǒng was discovered.
The Duke of Liáng, Lán Yù,
was Shēng's relative by marriage.
When Yù was defeated,
it again implicated Shēng,
which is why his name is associated with both factions.
A eulogy states:
These generals, during the nascent period,
observed the mandate of Heaven
and committed themselves to an enlightened lord,
winning battles and taking territories,
thereby establishing extraordinary merits.
All were wise and brave men of their time.
Yet, when the empire became peaceful,
their names were inscribed in party registers,
or they were posthumously condemned,
or they were personally executed.
Few were able to preserve themselves.
Though the bestowal of jade tablets and ceremonial robes was sufficient to reward their achievements,
the oath of iron certificates could not be passed down to the next generation,
which is indeed cause for lament!
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 20: Zhū Liàngzǔ, Zhōu Déxīng, Wáng Bì, Lán Yù (Cáo Zhèn, Zhāng Yì, Zhāng Wēn, Chén Huán, Zhū Shòu, Cáo Xīng), Xiè Chéng, Lǐ Xīn.
Zhū Liàngzǔ,
a native of Liù'ān.
The Yuán court appointed him Marshal of the Righteous Army.
When Tàizǔ captured Níngguó,
he seized Liàngzǔ.
Pleased by his bravery and ferocity,
he bestowed upon him gold and silks,
and reinstated him in his former position.
After several months,
he rebelled and returned to the Yuán.
He repeatedly fought against our forces,
capturing over six thousand men.
He then entered Xuānchéng and occupied it.
Tàizǔ was then taking Jiànkāng,
and had no time to suppress him.
Later,
he dispatched Xú Dá and others to besiege him.
Liàngzǔ broke through the encirclement and fought.
Cháng Yùchūn was wounded and returned,
and none of the generals dared to advance.
Tàizǔ personally went to supervise the battle,
captured him,
and had him brought in bound.
He asked,
"What do you intend to do?"
He replied,
"If I live, I will serve with all my might;
if I die, I die."
Tàizǔ admired his spirit and released him.
For accumulated merits, he was appointed Assistant Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmìyuàn Pàn).
He followed in the conquest of Nánchāng and Jiǔjiāng,
fought at Lake Póyáng,
and captured Wǔchāng.
He was promoted to Commander of Guǎngxìn Guard (Guǎngxìn Wèi Zhǐhuīshǐ).
When Lǐ Wénzhōng defeated Lǐ Bóshēng at Xīnchéng,
Liàngzǔ, taking advantage of the victory, burned dozens of his camps,
capturing over six hundred people, including Assistant Marshals (Tóngqiān Yuánshuài), three thousand soldiers, and eight hundred horses.
The military supplies and armor were innumerable.
Bóshēng barely escaped with a few riders.
Tàizǔ commended his achievements,
and rewarded him generously.
Hú Shēn requested to join forces to attack Chén Yǒudìng.
Liàngzǔ advanced from Qiánshān to take Pǔchéng,
and captured Chóng'ān and Jiànyáng,
having the most merits.
He participated in the attack on Tónglú,
besieged Yúháng,
and was promoted to Administrator (Cānzhèng) of the Zhèjiāng Provincial Administration Commission (Zhèjiāng Xíngshěng).
He served as deputy to Lǐ Wénzhōng in guarding Hángzhōu.
He led tens of thousands of cavalry, infantry, and naval forces to suppress Fāng Guóyīng,
captured Tiāntái,
and then attacked Táizhōu.
Guóyīng fled,
and was pursued to Huángyán,
where the defending general Hā'érlǔ surrendered.
He then conquered Xiānjū and other counties.
He advanced his troops to Wēnzhōu.
Fāng Míngshàn resisted and fought,
but was defeated,
and its city was captured.
He then conquered Ruì'ān,
and again defeated Míngshàn at Pán Yǔ,
pursuing him to Chǔmén.
Guóyīng and Míngshàn came to the army to surrender.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ (1368), he served as deputy to General-in-chief for the Southern Campaign (Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn) Liáo Yǒngzhōng, taking Guǎngdōng by sea.
Hé Zhēn surrendered,
and the entire region was pacified.
He then advanced to take Guǎngxī,
and captured Wúzhōu.
The Yuán Grand Secretary Pǔxián Tiēmù'ér died in battle,
and then Yùlín, Xún, Guì, and other prefectures were pacified.
He joined forces with Pacification Commissioner (Píngzhāng) Yáng Jǐng to attack and capture Jìngjiāng,
and together with Liáo Yǒngzhōng, captured Nánníng and Xiàngzhōu.
Guǎngxī was pacified.
Upon returning with the army,
the Crown Prince led all officials to welcome and comfort them at Lóngwān.
In the third year, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yǒngjiā,
receiving an annual salary of one thousand five hundred *dan* of grain,
and was granted a hereditary land deed.
In the fourth year, he campaigned against Shǔ.
The Emperor, seeing that the generals had long achieved no merits,
appointed Liàngzǔ as Vice General-in-chief of the Right for the Punitive Expedition (Zhēnglǔ Yòu Fù Jiāngjūn).
The army arrived in Shǔ,
but Míngshēng had already surrendered.
He then conquered the unattached prefectures and counties.
When the army returned,
he was not included in the rewards for having arbitrarily executed a military officer.
In the eighth year, he was stationed at Běipíng with Fù Yǒudé.
Upon his return,
he again supervised military agricultural colonies (túntián) with Lǐ Shàncháng,
and patrolled the sea routes.
In the twelfth year, he was sent to guard Guǎngdōng.
Liàngzǔ was brave, fierce, and skilled in battle, but uneducated,
and his actions were often unlawful.
Dào Tóng, the Magistrate of Pānyú, reported this.
Liàngzǔ falsely impeached Tóng,
and Tóng died.
The incident is detailed in Tóng's biography.
The Emperor soon realized the truth.
In the ninth month of the following year, Liàngzǔ was summoned,
and he and his son, the Commander (Zhǐhuīshǐ) of the Capital Army Guard (Fǔjūn Wèi) Xiān, were both beaten to death.
An epitaph was personally composed by the Emperor,
and he was buried with the rites of a marquis.
In the twenty-third year, Liàngzǔ was posthumously implicated as a member of Hú Wéiyōng's faction,
and his second son Yù was also executed.
Zhōu Déxīng,
a native of Háo.
He was from the same village as Tàizǔ
and they were close in their youth.
He followed in pacifying Chú and Hé.
After crossing the river,
he had merits in every battle he fought,
and was promoted to Grand Marshal of the Left Wing (Zuǒyì Dà Yuánshuài).
He followed in taking Jīnhuá, Ānqìng, and Gāoyóu,
relieved Ānfēng,
and campaigned against Lúzhōu.
He was promoted to Commander (Zhǐhuīshǐ).
He followed in suppressing Gànzhōu, Ānfú, and Yǒngxīn,
captured Jí'ān,
and was further promoted to Assistant Administrator of the Left (Húguǎng Xíngshěng Zuǒ Chéng) of the Húguǎng Provincial Administration Commission.
He suppressed Guǎngxī with Yáng Jǐng,
and attacked Yǒngzhōu.
Yuán Pacification Commissioner (Píngzhāng) Āsīlán and Zhōu Wénguì came from Quánzhōu to reinforce.
Déxīng defeated them again,
beheaded Yuán Vice Administrator (Yuàn Pàn) Zhū,
pursued the fleeing forces to Quánzhōu,
and then captured it.
Dàozhōu, Níngzhōu, and Lánshān all fell.
He then captured Wǔgāng Prefecture (Wǔgāng Zhōu),
divided his troops to hold strategic points,
and cut off reinforcements to Jìngjiāng.
Guǎngxī was pacified,
and he had many merits.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ (1370), he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Jiāngxià,
with an annual salary of one thousand five hundred *dan* of grain,
and was granted a hereditary land deed.
In the same year,
the aboriginal chieftain Tán Hòu of Cílí, along with various stockades in Máogāng, rebelled.
The Miáo people in Chángshā Dòng all instigated unrest.
Tàizǔ appointed Déxīng as General-in-chief for the Southern Campaign (Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn),
and he led his army to suppress and pacify them.
In the following year, he campaigned against Shǔ.
He served as deputy to Tāng Hé as Vice General of the Left for the Western Campaign (Zhēngxī Zuǒ Jiāngjūn),
and captured Bǎoníng.
Before this,
Fù Yǒudé had already captured Jiē and Wén,
but the naval forces led by Hé had not advanced.
After Bǎoníng fell,
the armies from the two routes finally converged.
When Shǔ was pacified,
when discussing merits,
the Emperor attributed Hé's merits to Déxīng,
rewarding Déxīng and personally reprimanding Hé.
He also recounted the campaign against the barbarians,
stating that in the campaign against Tán Hòu,
Yáng Jǐng failed to overcome them,
and Zhào Yōng returned midway,
and no one's merits could compare to Déxīng's.
He again served as deputy to Dèng Yù as Vice General of the Left for the Southern Campaign (Zhēngnán Zuǒ Jiāngjūn),
leading Zhào Yōng and Zuǒ Jūnbì out of Nánníng,
pacifying the barbarians of Lánfèng and Āntián prefectures,
and capturing Sīchéng Prefecture (Sīchéng Zhōu).
His merits again surpassed those of other generals.
His rewards were double those of a major general,
and he was ordered to take charge of the Central Executive Office (Zhōnglì Fǔ),
acting as the Grand Military Commission (Dà Dūdū Fǔ).
Déxīng's merits were already great,
and he also relied on his status as an old acquaintance of the Emperor,
building residences exceeding regulations.
Officials listed his crimes,
but an imperial edict specifically pardoned him.
In the thirteenth year, he was ordered to manage military affairs in Fújiàn,
but was recalled shortly after.
The following year,
the Wǔxī barbarians rebelled.
Déxīng was already old,
but strongly requested to go.
The Emperor admired his spirit and sent him,
giving him a personal letter that said:
"Zhào Chōngguó planned to campaign against the Western Qiāng,
and Mǎ Yuán requested to suppress Jiāozhǐ.
I have always admired these deeds,
considering them difficult for people today.
You are loyal, diligent, and untiring,
how could you fall short of these former worthies?
Pacifying the rebellion and bringing peace to the people
rests on this mission."
Upon arriving at Wǔxī,
the barbarians all scattered and fled.
At that time, the Shuǐjìnyuán and Tōngtǎpíng caves in Sìchuān also rebelled.
Déxīng was again ordered to suppress and pacify them.
In the eighteenth year,
when Prince Zhēn of Chǔ campaigned against the Wǔkāi barbarians of Sīzhōu,
Déxīng was again appointed Vice General.
In the 20th year,
with the title of Assistant Commander-in-chief of the Pacifying-Barbarians Left Army (Zhēnglǔ Zuǒfùjiàngjūn), [Lán] Yù followed Grand General Féng Shèng to campaign against Nàhāchū.
They arrived at Tōngzhōu.
Hearing that Yuan troops were stationed at Qìngzhōu,
Yù, amidst heavy snow,
led light cavalry to surprise and defeat them.
He killed Píngzhāng Guǒlái
and captured his son Bùlánxī, returning with him.
Meanwhile, the main army advanced to Jīnshān.
Nàhāchū sent an envoy to Grand General Féng Shèng's camp to offer surrender.
Yù went to accept the surrender.
Nàhāchū arrived with several hundred cavalry.
Yù was overjoyed
and offered him wine.
Nàhāchū poured wine to toast Yù.
Yù took off his own clothes and gave them to Nàhāchū,
saying:
"Please wear these and drink."
Nàhāchū refused to wear them.
Yù also refused to drink.
They contended and yielded for a long time.
Nàhāchū poured the wine onto the ground,
looked at his subordinates, and spoke agitatedly,
about to flee.
Zhèngguógōng Cháng Mào was present.
He stepped forward and wounded Nàhāchū with a sword.
Dūdū Gěng Zhōng seized him and brought him to see Féng Shèng.
Nàhāchū's troops panicked and dispersed.
The surrendered general Guān Tóng was dispatched to persuade them to surrender.
Returning to Yì Míhé,
all the remaining troops surrendered.
At that time, Féng Shèng was found guilty,
and the Grand General's seal was confiscated.
Yù was ordered to act as the Supervisor-in-chief (Zǒngbīngguān).
Soon after, Yù was appointed Grand General (Dàjiàngjūn) in the army
and moved his camp to Jìzhōu.
At this time, Emperor Shùn's grandson, Tuōgǔsī Tiēmù'ér, had succeeded to the throne
and was harassing the frontier.
In the third month of the 21st year, Yù was ordered to lead an army of 150,000 to campaign against him.
They set out from Dàníng
and reached Qìngzhōu.
Spies reported that the Yuan lord was at Bǔyú'ér Hǎi.
They took a shortcut and marched day and night, arriving at Bǎiyǎnjǐng.
They were forty *lǐ* from the sea.
Seeing no enemy,
Yù intended to retreat.
Dìngyuǎnhóu Wáng Bì said:
"We, leading more than 100,000 troops,
have penetrated deep into the northern desert.
Having achieved nothing,
if we hastily return to base,
how will we report back?"
Yù said:
"Indeed."
He ordered his soldiers to dig holes in the ground for cooking,
to avoid showing smoke or fire,
and proceeded to the south of the sea by night.
The enemy camp was still more than eighty *lǐ* to the northeast of the sea.
Yù ordered Wáng Bì to be the vanguard,
to swiftly approach the enemy camp.
The enemy believed that our army lacked water and forage
and could not penetrate deep,
so they were unprepared.
Also, a strong wind raised sand,
darkening the day.
As the army advanced,
the enemy was unaware.
When they suddenly arrived,
the enemy was greatly alarmed
and engaged in battle,
but was defeated.
Tàiwèi Mánzǐ and others were killed,
and their troops surrendered.
The Yuan lord and Crown Prince Tiānbǎonú fled with a few dozen cavalry.
Yù pursued them with elite cavalry
but did not catch them.
He captured his second son Dìbǎonú, his consort, a princess, and over a hundred others.
He also pursued and captured Wúwáng Ér Zhǐ, Dàiwáng Dá Lǐmá, and three thousand officials of Píngzhāng rank and below, as well as over 77,000 men and women.
All the imperial seals, tallies, edicts, golden plaques, gold and silver seals, and other valuables, along with over 150,000 horses, camels, cattle, and sheep were captured.
Their armor, weapons, and countless accumulated stores were burned.
The victory was reported to the capital.
The Emperor was greatly pleased
and bestowed an imperial edict commending and rewarding him,
likening him to Wèi Qīng and Lǐ Jìng.
He also broke the Hālāzhāng camp
and captured 60,000 people and livestock.
When the army returned,
he was promoted to Liángguógōng.
The following year, he was ordered to supervise the repair of city walls in Sìchuān.
In the 23rd year,
the indigenous people of the two Xuanfusi of Shī Nán and Zhōng Jiàn rebelled.
Yù was ordered to suppress them.
He also pacified the Sǎnmáo caves of Dū Yún Anfusī,
was given an additional stipend of 500 *dàn* of grain,
and was ordered by imperial edict to return home.
In the 24th year, Yù was ordered to command the troops of Lánzhōu, Zhuānglàng, and five other garrisons
to pursue the fugitive bandit Qízhěsūn,
and then he briefly occupied the Hǎndōng region of Xīfān.
The local chieftain Hāzǎn and others fled.
At that time, Jiànchāng Commander Yuèlǔ Tiēmù'ér rebelled.
An imperial edict ordered Yù to move his troops to suppress him.
Upon his arrival, Dūzhīhuī Qú Néng and others had already greatly defeated the rebel forces.
Yuèlǔ fled to Bǎixīngzhōu.
Yù sent Bǎihù Máo Hǎi to lure and capture Yuèlǔ Tiēmù'ér and his son,
sent them to the capital for execution,
and received the full surrender of their followers.
He then requested to increase the number of屯衛 (Túnwèi, military agricultural garrisons).
The request was approved.
He further requested to register civilians as soldiers
to campaign against Ègān and Bǎiyí.
An imperial edict denied the request,
and so the army returned to base.
Yù was tall with a ruddy face,
brave and resourceful,
possessing the talent of a great general.
Even after Zhōngshān and Kāipíng (i.e., Xú Dá and Cháng Yùchūn) had passed away,
he frequently commanded large armies
and achieved many merits.
Tàizǔ treated him generously.
Gradually, he became arrogant, self-indulgent,
and accumulated many estate servants and adopted sons,
abusing his power and acting tyrannically.
He once seized common land in Dōngchāng.
A censor investigated the matter.
Yù became angry
and drove the censor away.
Upon returning from the northern campaign,
he knocked on Xǐfēngguān at night.
When the gatekeeper did not admit him promptly,
he unleashed his soldiers to destroy the gate and enter.
The Emperor was displeased upon hearing this.
It was also rumored that he had a private relationship with the Yuan lord's consort.
The consort, out of shame, hanged herself.
The Emperor severely reprimanded Yù.
Initially,
the Emperor wanted to enfeoff Yù as Liángguógōng,
but due to his transgressions, changed it to Liáng (涼) (a homophone for 'cool' or 'cold'),
and engraved his faults on the patent.
Yù still did not reform.
He was arrogant and disrespectful at banquets.
In the army, he arbitrarily dismissed and appointed generals and officers.
He acted independently in all movements.
The Emperor repeatedly admonished and reprimanded him.
Upon returning from the western campaign,
he was appointed Crown Prince Grand Tutor (Tàizǐ Tàifù).
Yù was unhappy being placed below the two dukes, Sòng Guógōng (Féng Shèng) and Yǐng Guógōng (Fù Yǒudé),
and said:
"Am I not capable of being Grand Preceptor (Tàishī)?"
Subsequently, many of his memorials were not heard,
making him even more resentful.
In the second month of the 26th year,
Jǐnyīwèi Commander Jiǎng Huán accused Yù of rebellion.
He was handed over to officials for interrogation.
The court confession stated:
"Yù, along with Jǐngchuānhóu Cáo Zhèn, Hèqìnghóu Zhāng Yì, Zhúlúhóu Zhū Shòu, Dōngguǎnbó Hé Róng, as well as Lìbù Shàngshū Zhān Huī, Hùbù Shìláng Fù Yǒuwén, and others, plotted treason,
intending to strike when the Emperor went to the ritual plowing field."
The case was concluded,
and his entire clan was executed.
The number of marquises and others who were implicated and exterminated was countless.
An imperial edict was issued throughout the realm,
listing the details of the court records as the 'Record of Rebellious Officials' (Nìchén Lù).
By September,
an imperial edict was finally issued, stating:
"The Lán 'bandits' caused disorder;
their plot was exposed,
and 15,000 people were executed along with their clans.
From now on, all members of the Hú faction and Lán faction shall be pardoned and not questioned."
Hú referred to Prime Minister Hú Wéiyǒng.
At this point, all the original meritorious generals and veteran commanders were gone.
In total, those listed in the 'Record of Rebellious Officials' included
one duke, thirteen marquises, and two earls.
Yè Shēng had been executed earlier for a different offense.
Hú Yù and other minor marquises are listed elsewhere.
As for the six marquises Cáo Zhèn, Zhāng Yì, Zhāng Wēn, Chén Huán, Zhū Shòu, and Cáo Xīng,
they are appended on the left side.
Cáo Zhèn,
a native of Háo.
He joined Tàizǔ when he raised an army,
and successively served as Zhǐhuīshǐ.
In the twelfth year of Hóngwǔ,
for his meritorious service in conquering Xīfān, he was enfeoffed as Jǐngchuān Hóu,
with a stipend of two thousand shí.
He accompanied Lán Yù on the expedition to Yúnnán,
taking Lín'ān and other routes by different paths.
Upon reaching Wēichǔ,
he secured the surrender of the Yuán Píngzhāng Yán Nǎimǎdǎi and others.
After Yúnnán was pacified,
he requested to subjugate the Mán of the Róngměi and Sǎnmáo caves, and the Xīfān Qūgān and SīnǎngRì tribes.
The edict disallowed it.
He then requested that the Xīfān horses traded by the two DūSī of Guìzhōu and Sìchuān
be distributed to the generals and soldiers of Shǎnxī and Hénán.
He also said:
"From Sìchuān to the Jiànchāng post station,
the road passes through the Dàdù Hé,
and many travelers die of malaria.
Upon inquiring of the elders,
there is an ancient post road from Méizhōu Éméi to Jiànchāng
that is flat, easy, and free from miasma.
I have already ordered the military and civilians to repair it.
I request that the post horses from Lúzhōu to Jiànchāng
be moved
to the new Éméi post station."
This was approved.
In the twenty-first year, he and Jìngníng Hóu Yè Shēng divided their forces to suppress the rebellious Mán of Dōngchuān,
capturing over five thousand people.
Soon after, he was again ordered to manage military affairs in Sìchuān,
and together with Lán Yù, he audited the soldiers of the southern expedition.
At that time, the Yǒngníng Xuānwèisī reported
that within its jurisdiction there were one hundred and ninety rapids,
of which more than eighty were obstructed and difficult.
An edict ordered Zhèn to dredge and clear them.
Zhèn went to Lúzhōu to inspect them.
There was a branch river that connected to Yǒngníng,
so he chiseled rocks and cut cliffs to make it deep and wide,
to facilitate water transport.
He also opened up land routes,
built post houses and courier stations,
erected bridges and set up plank roads,
from Màozhōu,
one route to Sōngpān,
and one route to Guìzhōu,
reaching Bǎoníng.
Previously, the traveler Xǔ Mù had said:
"The land of Sōngzhōu is barren and poor,
unsuitable for military farming.
With three thousand garrison soldiers,
grain transport is insufficient.
I request to move the garrison to Màozhōu,
to facilitate military farming nearby."
The Emperor deemed Sōngzhōu crucial for controlling Xīfān
and not to be moved.
By this time, the transport routes were open,
and Sōngpān consequently became an important town.
The Emperor praised his efforts.
The following year, he again presented four proposals.
First,
he requested to utilize well salt in the Dàníng territory of Yúnnán,
recruiting merchants to transport grain to supply the border.
Second,
he requested merchants to transport grain to Jiànchāng in Yúnnán,
and be given permits for trading horses in Chóngqìng and Qíjiāng.
Third,
he requested to remit the overdue taxes in Máhú.
Fourth,
the military provisions for the Shīzhōuwèi relied on Húguǎng,
which was dangerous and distant upstream.
He requested that grain from Chóngqìng be transported downstream to supply it.
All were approved.
Zhèn stayed in Shǔ for a long time,
and all his plans
were extremely meticulous.
The people of Shǔ admired him.
When Lán Yù was defeated,
it was alleged that Zhèn, Zhū Shòu, and others had conspired with Zhǐhuī Zhuāng Chéng to rebel.
He was accused of being a rebel leader,
with Zhèn as the ringleader,
and he and his son Bǐng were executed.
Zhāng Yì,
a native of Línhuái.
His father Jù,
as a former Yì Yuánshuài, accompanied the pacification of Jiāngnán and Huáidōng,
and through accumulated merit became Dàtóngwèi Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī,
then retired.
Yì followed his father in the army,
was brave and skilled in battle,
and succeeded his father's position as Fù Qiānhù.
He joined the expedition to Shǎnxī,
capturing rebellious bandits.
He was promoted to Dū Zhǐhuī Qiānshì,
and then advanced to QiāndūdùFǔ Shì.
He accompanied Lán Yù on the expedition to Yúnnán,
conquering Pǔdìng and Qǔjìng,
taking Hèqìng and Líjiāng,
annihilating the Qībǎibáng Shānzhài,
attacking Jiànchuān,
and striking Shímén.
In the seventeenth year, for his merits, he was enfeoffed as Hèqìng Hóu,
with a stipend of two thousand five hundred shí,
and given an hereditary patent.
In the twenty-sixth year, he was executed as a member of Lán Yù's faction.
Zhāng Wēn,
his origin is unknown.
He followed Tàizǔ across the Jiāng,
and was appointed Qiānhù.
Through accumulated merit, he reached Tiāncèwèi Zhǐhuī Qiānshì.
He followed the main army to recover the Central Plains,
conquering Shǎnxī,
attacking and taking Lánzhōu, and defending it.
The Yuán general Kuòkuò, upon learning that the Grand General had returned south,
led his infantry and cavalry from Gānsù and unexpectedly arrived.
The generals requested to hold fast and await reinforcements.
Wēn said:
"They have come a long way;
they do not know our strength or weakness.
If we attack them at dusk,
we can blunt their advance.
If they do not retreat,
it will not be too late to hold fast."
Thereupon, he arrayed his troops and went out to battle;
the Yuán army slightly recoiled.
Soon after, they surrounded the city in several layers.
Wēn gathered his troops and held fast.
The enemy attacked but could not take it,
so they withdrew.
Tàizǔ called it a remarkable achievement
and promoted him to Dà Dūdùfǔ Qiānshì.
Later,
he was also ordered to concurrently serve as Shǎnxī Xíng Dūdùfǔ Qiānshì.
When Lánzhōu was besieged,
the Yuán army scaled the city walls by night.
Qiānhù Guō Yòu was sleeping, drunk,
and other patrolling generals repelled them.
After the siege was lifted,
Wēn intended to execute Yòu.
Tiāncèwèi Zhīshì Zhū Yǒuwén argued, saying:
"When the bandits were assaulting the city,
the general executing Yòu to command the troops
would have been military law.
Now that the bandits have retreated,
only then to pursue and kill him
would be too late for the matter,
and moreover, would incur the name of arbitrary killing."
Wēn thanked him, saying:
"Without you, I would not have heard these words."
So he flogged Yòu and released him.
The Emperor heard of this and praised both actions,
and also rewarded Yǒuwén with fine silk.
The following year,
as Cāncāngjiàng, he accompanied Fù Yǒudé in campaigning against Shǔ,
achieving many merits.
In the eleventh year,
as Fùjiàng, he joined Wáng Bì and others in suppressing the Xīqiāng.
The next year, for his merits, he was enfeoffed as Huìníng Hóu,
with a stipend of two thousand shí.
The year after that, he was ordered to go and manage military affairs in Hénán.
In the fourteenth year, he accompanied Fù Yǒudé on the expedition to Yúnnán.
In the autumn of the twentieth year, he led an army to suppress the remaining followers of Nàhāchū.
He participated in the northern expedition,
all with merit.
Later, for his residence and utensils exceeding his status,
he incurred guilt,
and was consequently executed as a member of Lán Yù's faction.
Chén Huán,
an individual from Háozhōu.
He followed in the conquest of Chúzhōu and Hézhōu.
Crossing the Yangzi River,
he was the first to scale the walls in the capture of Jíqìng.
He followed in taking Níngguó and Jīnhuá,
fought at Lóngjiāng and Pénglí,
recovered Huáidōng and Zhèxī,
and pacified the Central Plains.
For his accumulated merits, he was appointed Dūdū Qiānshì.
In the fourth year of Hóngwǔ, he joined the expedition to Shǔ.
In the fourteenth year, he joined the campaign to Yúnnán,
leading five myriad troops with Hú Hǎi and Guō Yīng,
proceeding from Yǒngníng towards Wūsà.
The path was perilous and narrow;
advancing from Chìhé,
they engaged in a major battle with the various Man tribes of Wūsà,
defeating and routing them.
They then broke the local chieftain of Mángbù,
routing Yuán's Right Chancellor Shíbǔ,
subsequently taking the city of Wūsà,
and receiving the surrender of the various Man tribes of Dōngchuān and Wūméng.
They further captured Dàlǐ,
and generally pacified the various prefectures and districts of Rǔníng and Jìngníng.
In the seventeenth year, he was enfeoffed as Pǔdìng Hóu,
with an annual salary of two thousand five hundred dàn of grain,
and was granted a hereditary charter.
In the twentieth year, he campaigned against Dōngchuān with Jìngníng Hóu Yè Shēng,
capturing many prisoners.
He was then appointed overall commander of the various armies in Yúnnán.
He further pacified the Man tribes of Jiǔxī Dòng,
established military camps and fortresses,
and implemented屯tiúntúntiún.
Upon his return,
he was implicated in the Yù Dǎng case and died.
Zhū Shòu,
his origin is not detailed.
As a Myriad-household, he followed in crossing the Yangzi River,
capturing the prefectures and districts of Jiāngdōng,
and was promoted to Zǒngguǎn.
He recovered Chángzhōu and Wùzhōu,
captured Wǔchāng,
pacified Sūzhōu and Húzhōu,
fought battles across north and south,
and for his accumulated merits, became a Zhǐhuī of Hēnghǎi Wèi,
then promoted to Dūdū Qiānshì.
He oversaw grain transport with Zhāng Hè,
achieving success.
In the twentieth year of Hóngwǔ, he was enfeoffed as Zhúlú Hóu,
with an annual salary of two thousand dàn of grain,
and was granted a hereditary charter.
He was implicated in the Yù Dǎng case and died.
Cáo Xīng,
also known as Xīngcái,
his origin is not detailed.
He followed in pacifying Wǔchāng,
and was appointed Zhǐhuī Qiānshì.
In taking Píngjiāng,
he was promoted to Zhǐhuīshǐ.
He captured Sū Jiǔchóu's Tànshān Zhài.
He was promoted to Dūdū Qiānshì,
concurrently holding the position of Tàiyuán Wèi Zhǐhuī.
He was promoted to Cāncǐng of the Shānxī Xíngshěng,
overseeing military affairs,
and served as adviser to Jìn Wáng.
In the eleventh year of Hóngwǔ, he joined Mù Yīng in suppressing the Qiāng of Táozhōu,
receiving the surrender of the Dǐgān chieftain,
and capturing three deputy envoys, among others.
When the army returned,
he was enfeoffed as Huáiyuǎn Hóu,
with the hereditary title of Zhǐhuīshǐ.
He managed military affairs in Shānxī,
and performed meritorious service in the northern campaigns.
Several years later,
he was implicated in the Yù Dǎng case and died.
At the same time, those implicated in the party case

among the Dūdū included Huáng Lù, Tāng Quán, Mǎ Jùn, Wáng Chéng, Niè Wěi, Wáng Míng, Xǔ Liàng, Xiè Xióng, Wāng Xìn, Xiāo Yòng, Yáng Chūn, Zhāng Zhèng, Zhù Zhé, Táo Wén, Máo Dǐng, in all over ten individuals,
many of whom were junior officers under Yù.
Thus, strong and valiant warriors were almost entirely eliminated,
with few surviving.
Xiè Chéng,
an individual from Háozhōu.
He followed in the conquest of Chúzhōu and Hézhōu.
Crossing the Yangzi River,
he secured Jíqìng,
and was appointed Zǒngguǎn.
He captured Níngguó and Wùzhōu,
and was promoted to Guǎnjūn Qiānhù.
He fought at Póyáng,
pacified Wǔchāng,
and took Sūzhōu and Húzhōu,
and was promoted to Zhǐhuī Qiānshì.
He followed the grand army in campaigning against the Central Plains,
captured the Yuán capital,
attacked Qìngyáng,
and swept through Dìngxī,
becoming Dūdū Qiānshì and adviser to Jìn Wáng.
He followed Mù Yīng in campaigning against Dǐgān,
received the surrender of Qǐshījiā,
and pacified the eighteen tribes of Táozhōu.
In the twelfth year of Hóngwǔ, he was enfeoffed as Yǒngpíng Hóu,
with an annual salary of two thousand dàn of grain,
and the hereditary title of Zhǐhuīshǐ.
In the twentieth year, he joined Zhāng Wēn in pursuing the remnants of Nàhāchū,
and was then recalled.
In the twenty-seventh year, he was executed for a certain offense,
and his fields and residences were confiscated.
Lǐ Xīn,
an individual from Háozhōu.
He followed in crossing the Yangzi River,
repeatedly achieving meritorious service.
He fought at Lóngwān,
and was appointed Guǎnjūn Fùqiānhù.
In taking Jiānglíng,
he was promoted to Lóngxiáng Wèi Zhèngqiānhù.
In capturing Píngjiāng,
he was transferred to Shénwǔ Wèi Zhǐhuī Qiānshì,
then reassigned to garrison Chálíng Wèi,
and was repeatedly promoted until he reached Zhōngjūn Dūdū Fǔ Qiānshì.
In the fifteenth year,
for his role in constructing Xiàolíng,
he was enfeoffed as Chóngshān Hóu,
with an annual salary of one thousand five hundred dàn of grain.
In the twenty-second year, he was ordered to rebuild the Dìwáng Miào at Jīmíng Shān.
Lǐ Xīn had a strategic mind;
the construction officials merely followed his designs.
The next year, he was sent back to his hometown,
and granted gold, silk, fields, and residences.
At this time, the various noble families of merit became somewhat arrogant and unrestrained,
and the Emperor deeply resented this,
with many being implicated in party affairs.
Lǐ Xīn was the first to propose
that dukes' and marquises' household members and retainers should each have a fixed number,
and any excess should be returned to the authorities.
The Emperor approved this,
and all were sent to Fèngyáng to be registered as commoners.
He ordered the Ministry of Rites to compile and record regulations,
strictly prohibiting extravagance and transgressions by dukes and marquises.
Consequently, Wǔdìng Hóu Yīng returned tenant farmers for taxation,
Xìnguó Gōng Hé returned retainers,
Cáo Guó Gōng Jǐnglóng returned his estates,
all initiated by Lǐ Xīn.
In the twenty-sixth year, he supervised the authorities in digging the Yānzhī Hé at Lìshuǐ,
connecting west to the Great River and
east to the two Zhè regions,
to facilitate grain transport.
When the canal was completed,
the people greatly benefited from it.
In the twenty-eighth year, he was executed for an offense.
A eulogy states: To govern the realm without laws is impossible;
in times of chaos, laws are still loose,
but in times of peace, laws gradually become strict,
which is certainly dictated by circumstances.
Commentators often lament the saying "when the birds are gone, the bow is put away,"
attributing it to the suspicion and schemes of enlightened rulers,
which is far from an understanding of the principles of governance.
When the realm is largely settled,
as secure as a firm rock,
and commands can be issued across ten thousand miles,
with people rushing to obey for fear of being left behind,
what further doubts or jealousies could there be to cause such ruthless elimination?
Rather, it is because armored warriors are fierce and difficult to control;
while at the peak of their power,
all can establish themselves in the frontier regions,
but once they are in positions of wealth and nobility,
their ambitions fulfilled and spirits overflowing,
being close to them invites danger through arrogance and license,
while keeping them at a distance causes resentment and defiance against the law.
The sovereign cannot abolish laws to protect them,
which also stems from necessity,
and is not a private calculation for elimination.
As for Liàngzǔ and the others mentioned below, they both failed to grasp the wisdom of protecting themselves
and violated the principles of moderation and prudence,
thus meeting their demise together,
which was their own doing.
Collation Notes

Biographies, Chapter Twenty-one Liáo Yǒng'ān, Yú Tōnghǎi (younger brothers Tōngyuán, Yuān), Hú Dàhǎi (adopted sons Déjì, Luán Fèng), Gěng Zàichéng, Zhāng Déshèng (Wāng Xīngzǔ), Zhào Déshèng (with appended loyal ministers of the two temples of Nánchāng and Kāngláng Shān), Sāng Shìjié (Liú Chéng), Máo Chéng (Yáng Guóxīng), Hú Shēn, Sūn Xīngzǔ, Cáo Liángchén (Zhōu Xiǎn, Cháng Róng, Zhāng Yào), Pú Yīng (Yú Guāng and others).
Liáo Yǒng'ān,
courtesy name Yànjìng,
was the elder brother of Déqìng Hóu Yǒngzhōng.
When Tàizǔ first rose,
Yǒng'ān and his brothers, along with Yú Tōnghǎi and others, came to pledge allegiance with their naval forces from Cháohú.
Tàizǔ personally went to receive their army,
and then used the naval forces to attack Yuán Central Censor Mánzi Hǎiyá at Mǎchánghé.
The Yuán forces, maneuvering their tower ships,
were at a disadvantage in advancing and retreating,
while Yǒng'ān and his group steered their boats as if flying.
They fought twice and twice defeated the Yuán soldiers,
finally deciding on the strategy to cross the Jiāng.
A short while later,
they departed from Jiāngkǒu.
Yǒng'ān hoisted the sail
and asked for the direction,
and was ordered to head straight for Niúzhǔ.
A northwest wind was blowing fiercely,
and in an instant they reached the shore.
Tàizǔ urgently commanded the armored soldiers to bravely ascend,
and the defending troops at Cǎishí Zhèn all collapsed.
They then took advantage of the victory to capture Tàipíng.
He was granted the title of Guǎnjūn Zǒngguǎn.
With his naval forces, he broke Hǎiyá's water stockade,
captured Chén Zhàoxiān,
and entered Jíqìng.
He was promoted to Jiànkāng Yìtǒngjūn Yuánshuài.
He followed in a naval capacity to take Zhènjiāng,
conquered Chángzhōu,
and was promoted to Tóngqiān Jiāngnán Xíngshūmìyuàn Shì.
He also, with his naval forces, accompanied Cháng Yùchūn from Tónglíng to Qíchízhōu,
where they jointly attacked,
breaching its north gate,
capturing Xú Shòuhuī's defending general,
and thus conquered Qíchízhōu.
Together with Yú Tōnghǎi, he pulled out the Shípái garrison in Jiāngyīn,
and accepted the surrender of Zhāng Shìchéng's defending general Luán Ruì.
He was promoted to Tóngzhī Shūmìyuàn Shì.
With his naval forces, he again defeated Shìchéng's soldiers at Fúshāngǎng in Chángshú,
and again defeated them at Lángshān in Tōngzhōu,
capturing their warships and returning.
He then followed Xú Dá to recapture Yíxīng,
and pushed deep into Tàihú, taking advantage of the victory.
They encountered the Wú general Lǚ Zhēn,
and engaged in battle.
The rear army did not follow,
and the boats became stuck in shallow water,
leading to his capture.
Yǒng'ān excelled in naval warfare,
and achieved merit wherever he went.
Shìchéng admired his talent and bravery
and wished for him to surrender.
He refused,
and was imprisoned by them.
Tàizǔ admired Yǒng'ān's unyielding spirit
and remotely appointed him Xíngshěng Píngzhāng Zhèngshì,
and enfeoffed him as Chǔguó Gōng.
Yǒng'ān was imprisoned for eight years
and eventually died in Wú.
When Wú was pacified,
his remains were returned,
and Tàizǔ personally welcomed and offered sacrifices in the suburbs.
In the sixth year of Hóngwǔ,
the emperor, mindful that the empire was now completely settled,
and that various meritorious officials like Yǒng'ān, Yú Tōnghǎi, Zhāng Déshèng, Gěng Zàichéng, Hú Dàhǎi, Zhào Déshèng, and Sāng Shìjié had already passed away,
and yet had no posthumous titles,
issued an order to the Lǐbù to deliberate and decide.
The deliberation stated:
"When Yuán lost control,
the four seas boiled with chaos.
Heroes and valiant individuals
either raised righteous armies
or protected a region,
scattered and confused,
with no clear allegiance.
When the True Man arose with vigor,
they came unbidden;
the dragon's movement brought clouds,
the tiger's roar brought wind.
Such as Chǔguó Gōng Minister Yǒng'ān and others,
all were bear-like warriors,
talented in strength and valor.
If not breaking through defenses and dying in battle,
they suffered misfortune and sacrificed their lives.
Righteousness and loyalty were combined,
their names shining between heaven and earth.
Your Majesty has united the empire,
recalling their past efforts,
bestowed titles and emoluments upon their descendants,
and established their sacrificial rites in the ancestral temples.
Changing names and assigning posthumous titles
is appropriate according to ritual.
We respectfully refer to the Shìfǎ:
for 'facing the enemy and encountering hardship,'
Minister Yǒng'ān is posthumously titled Wǔmǐn;
for 'sacrificing oneself and overcoming the enemy,'
Minister Tōnghǎi is posthumously titled Zhōngliè;
for 'serving the sovereign and achieving resolute results,'
Minister Zhāng Déshèng is posthumously titled Zhōngyì;
for 'defeating the enemy and achieving strength,'
Minister Dàhǎi is posthumously titled Wǔzhuāng;
for 'expanding territory and pushing back borders, martial but not fully successful,'
Minister Zàichéng is posthumously titled Wǔzhuàng;
for 'repelling attacks and resisting insults,'
strong and capable,
Minister Zhào Déshèng is posthumously titled Wǔhuán.
As for Minister Shìjié,
he was already enfeoffed as Yǒngyì Hóu,
similar to how Hàn Shìzǔ enfeoffed Kòu Xún and Jǐng Dān,
this should immediately be taken as his posthumous title."
The imperial edict stated:
"Granted."
In the ninth year,
all were posthumously granted the titles of Kāiguó Fǔyùn Tuīchéng Xuānlì Wǔchén, Guānglù Dàfū, and Zhùguó.
Later,
Yǒng'ān was again enfeoffed as Yún Guó Gōng.
Having no sons,
his grandnephew Shēng was appointed Zhǐhuī Qiānshì.
Yú Tōnghǎi,
courtesy name Bìquán,
his ancestors were from Háoyáng.
His father, Tíngyù, moved to Cháo,
and had three sons:
Tōnghǎi, Tōngyuán, and Yuān.
At the end of the Yuán dynasty,
bandits rose in Rú and Yǐng.
Tíngyù and his sons, along with Zhào Pǔshèng and Liáo Yǒng'ān, established a stronghold in Cháohú,
possessing a naval force of a thousand ships.
They were frequently put in a difficult position by Zuǒ Jūnbì of Lúzhōu,
and dispatched Tōnghǎi to secretly return to Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ was then stationed in Héyáng,
planning to cross the Jiāng,
but had no boats or rafts.
When Tōnghǎi arrived,
he rejoiced greatly, saying:
"Heaven is aiding me!"
He personally went to pacify their army,
but Zhào Pǔshèng rebelled and left.
The Yuán soldiers blockaded Mǎchánghé and other river mouths with tower ships;
only one port along the lake could be accessed,
but it had long dried up.
Coincidentally, there was heavy rain,
and the water depth reached over a zhàng.
They then led their boats out to the Jiāng
and reached Héyáng.
Tōnghǎi was a resolute and steadfast person.
He governed his army strictly but with kindness,
and his soldiers were happy to serve him.
Of the generals from Cháohú, all were skilled in naval warfare,
but Tōnghǎi was the best.
He followed in destroying the various naval stockades at Hǎiyá,
and was awarded the rank of Myriad Households (Wànhù).
He followed in crossing the river,
conquering Cǎishí,
taking Tàipíng,
and sweeping through the subordinate counties.
Hǎiyá again intercepted Cǎishí with warships,
while Chén Zhàoxiān gathered 200,000 Huái soldiers and encamped at Fāngshān,
forming a pincer movement.
Tōnghǎi, along with Liáo Yǒng'ān and others, attacked them,
greatly defeating their forces,
and Hǎiyá fled.
They advanced and defeated Zhàoxiān,
taking Jíqìnglù.
He followed Tāng Hé in capturing Zhènjiāng,
and was promoted to Commander of the Qínhuái Wing (Qínhuái Yì Yuánshuài).
Together with other generals, he took Dānyáng, Jīntán, and Chángzhōu,
and was promoted to Judge of the Mobile Secretariat-Council (Xíng Shūmìyuàn Pànguān).
He followed in conquering Níngguó,
and taking Shuǐyáng.
Consequently, with his navy, he swept through Tàihú,
accepting the surrender of Zhāng Shìchéng's defending general at Mǎjīshān,
and mooring his boats at Xūkǒu.
Lǚ Zhēn's troops suddenly arrived,
and the other generals wished to retreat.
Tōnghǎi said:
"We cannot.
They are numerous, and we are few.
If we retreat, our fear will be evident.
It is better to attack them."
Then he personally led a fierce charge.
Arrows fell like rain,
and he was hit in the right eye,
rendering him unable to fight.
He ordered a soldier from his retinue to wear his armor and oversee the battle.
The enemy thought it was Tōnghǎi,
and dared not press forward,
so they gradually withdrew.
From this, he lost sight in one eye.
Later,
together with Yǒng'ān and others, he captured Shípái Garrison,
seized Mǎtuóshā, and returned.
Pǔshèng had rebelled and returned to Yǒuliàng,
capturing Chízhōu.
He dispatched a separate general to guard it,
while he himself occupied the Cōngyáng naval stockade.
Tàizǔ was then campaigning in Zhèdōng,
and was concerned about Cōngyáng.
Tōnghǎi went to attack it,
and greatly defeated him.
Pǔshèng fled by land,
and all his boats were captured.
Thus, Chízhōu was recovered.
He was promoted to Assistant Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Qiān Shūmìyuàn Shì).
When Chén Yǒuliàng attacked Lóngwān,
Tōnghǎi, with other generals, attacked and repelled him,
pursuing and burning his boats at Cíhú,
capturing seven commanders,
and chasing the defeated to Cǎishí.
His merit was the greatest,
and he was promoted to Associate Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmìyuàn Tóngzhī).
He followed in attacking Yǒuliàng,
taking Tónglíng,
conquering Jiǔjiāng,
and plundering Qí and Huáng.
He followed Xú Dá in attacking the rebellious generals Zhù Zōng and Kāng Tài,
and recovered Nánchāng.
He followed in relieving Ānfēng,
defeating Shìchéng's troops,
and then attacked Lúzhōu.
When Yǒuliàng heavily besieged Nánchāng,
he followed Tàizǔ in attacking him.
They met at Kānglángshān.
Their boats were small and could not attack uphill,
and they fought fiercely, almost unable to hold on.
Tōnghǎi, taking advantage of the wind, set fire to over twenty of their boats,
and the enemy suffered a slight setback.
Tàizǔ's boat became stuck,
and Yǒuliàng's brave general Zhāng Dìngbiān advanced directly to attack Tàizǔ's boat.
Cháng Yùchūn shot Dìngbiān,
and Tōnghǎi's fast boat arrived as reinforcement.
As his boat advanced rapidly, the water surged,
and Tàizǔ's boat managed to escape.
But Tōnghǎi's boat was again pressed by an enemy battleship,
and all the soldiers rammed their heads against the hull,
their helmets all shattered,
barely escaping.
The next day they fought again.
Tōnghǎi, along with Liáo Yǒngzhōng and others, used seven boats loaded with gunpowder
to burn hundreds of enemy boats.
Two days later,
they again penetrated deep with six boats.
The enemy resisted fiercely with interconnected large ships.
Tàizǔ climbed the stern tower and watched,
and for a long time saw nothing,
thinking they had been lost.
A moment later,
the six boats circled out from behind the enemy ships,
swaying like swimming dragons.
The soldiers cheered and shouted,
their courage multiplied a hundredfold,
and they fought with renewed vigor.
Yǒuliàng's army was greatly defeated.
When the army reached Zuǒlí,
Tōnghǎi advanced and said:
"The lake has shallow parts,
making it difficult for boats to maneuver.
It would be better to enter the river,
and occupy the upstream position relative to the enemy.
When their boats enter,
they will be captured immediately."
So, the army moved out of the lake,
setting up barricades by water and land.
Yǒuliàng dared not come out.
He stayed in the lake for a month.
When his food ran out,
he led his troops to break out and flee,
and was ultimately defeated and killed.
In this campaign,
Tōnghǎi's merit was the greatest.
When the army returned,
he was bestowed with good land, gold, and silk.
The following year, he followed in pacifying Wǔchāng.
He was appointed Grand Councillor of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshūshěng Píngzhāng Zhèngshì).
He commanded troops to strategize at Liújiāgǎng,
and advanced to pressure Tōngzhōu,
defeating Shìchéng's troops
and capturing his generals Zhū Qióng and Chén Shèng.
He was promoted to acting Administrator of the Jiānghuái Mobile Secretariat (Shè Jiānghuái Xíng Zhōngshūshěng Shì),
and garrisoned Lúzhōu.
He followed Xú Dá in pacifying Ānfēng.
He also followed in conquering Húzhōu,
and sweeping through Tàicāng,
not harming even a single autumn hair.
The people were greatly pleased.
While besieging Píngjiāng,
he fought at Mièdùqiáo,
and attacked Táohuāwù.
He was struck by a stray arrow,
and his wound was severe.
He returned to Jīnlíng.
Tàizǔ visited his residence,
and asked:
"Does Píngzhāng know I have come to inquire about your illness?"
Tōnghǎi could not speak.
Tàizǔ wiped away tears and left.
The next day, he died,
at the age of thirty-eight.
Tàizǔ wept over him with great sorrow,
and his attending officials and guards were all moved to tears.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Duke of Yù (Yù Guógōng),
enshrined in the Imperial Ancestral Temple (Tàimiào),
and his portrait placed in the Temple of Meritorious Officials (Gōngchén Miào).
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, he was re-enfeoffed as Duke of Guó (Guó Guógōng),
and given the posthumous name Zhōngliè.
Tōnghǎi's father, Tíngyù, who was an Assistant Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Qiān Shūmìyuàn Shì),
had died earlier,
and was posthumously enfeoffed as Duke of Héjiān Commandery (Héjiān Jùngōng).
Tōnghǎi had no sons,
so his younger brother Tōngyuán succeeded to his office.
Tōngyuán,
courtesy name Bǎichuān.
He followed the Grand General in his campaign against the Central Plains.
He joined Deputy General Féng Shèng and others to muster troops at Tàiyuán,
pacified Hézhōng,
crossed the river,
captured Lùtái,
took Fèngxiáng, Gǒngchāng, and Jīngzhōu,
and defended Kāichéng.
At this time, Zhāng Liángchén rebelled again, holding Qìngyáng.
The Grand General ordered his generals to divide their forces to press him.
Tōngyuán swiftly moved from Líntáo to Jīng,
attacking its west;
Gù Shí attacked its north;
Fù Yǒudé attacked its east;
Chén Dé attacked its south;
and the Grand General pressed the city walls.
Liángchén’s reinforcements were cut off and provisions exhausted.
He was defeated and died,
and Qìngyáng was then captured.
In the campaign against Dìngxī,
he captured Xīngyuán,
always being the first to ascend the walls.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Nán'ān,
with an annual stipend of one thousand five hundred *shi* of grain,
and a hereditary patent was granted.
In the fourth year, he followed Liáo Yǒngzhōng in attacking Shǔ,
and also followed Xú Dá beyond the frontier,
pacified Gānsù,
and rendered meritorious service.
He moved one hundred forty thousand wealthy households from Jiāngnán to cultivate land in Fèngyáng.
He also attacked Yúnnán,
campaigned against the Mán of Guǎngnán,
capturing and beheading tens of thousands.
In the twenty-second year, an imperial edict ordered him to return to his hometown,
bestowing fifty thousand in paper currency,
and building a mansion in Cháo.
He died before departing.
His son, Zǔ,
was ill and could not inherit.
The following year,
a posthumous investigation into the Hú party was launched.
Since Tōngyuán was already dead, he was not questioned,
but his peerage was abolished.
Yuān, due to his father and elder brother,
was appointed as a junior court attendant (*cān shì shèrén*).
He followed in campaigns,
and accumulated merits, being appointed Assistant Commissioner-in-Chief (*dūdū qiānshì*).
After Tōngyuán was implicated in the party,
Tàizǔ, mindful of Tíngyù and Tōng Hǎi’s merits,
in the twenty-fifth year, enfeoffed Yuān as Marquis of Yuèsuī,
with an annual stipend of two thousand five hundred *shi* of grain,
and a hereditary patent was granted.
He led an army to suppress the rebel bandits of Jiànchāng,
and fortified Yuèsuī city.
The following year, he lost his marquisate due to being implicated,
and was sent back to his hometown.
In the first year of Jiànwén, he was recalled and his peerage restored.
He followed the grand army in campaigning against Yān,
and was killed in battle at Báigōuhé.
His second son, Jìng, inherited his office.
Hú Dàhǎi,
courtesy name Tōngfǔ,
was a native of Hóng.
He was tall with an iron face,
and possessed extraordinary intelligence and strength.
When Tàizǔ first rose,
Dàhǎi went to meet him in Chúyáng,
and was appointed as a vanguard.
He followed in crossing the river,
and with other generals seized territory.
For his merits, he was appointed Grand Marshal of the Right Wing Army (*yòuyì tǒngjūn yuánshuài*),
and served as a guard beneath the tent.
He followed in capturing Níngguó.
Deputy Assistant Administrator Dèng Yù garrisoned it.
He then captured Huīzhōu,
and pacified its surrounding territory.
The Yuán general Yáng Wánzhě attacked with one hundred thousand troops.
Dàhǎi fought beneath the city walls,
heavily defeating and routing him.
He then, with Dèng Yù and Lǐ Wénzhōng, attacked Jiàndé from Yùlǐngguān.
They defeated the Yuán commander at Chún'ān,
and then captured Jiàndé.
They again defeated Yáng Wánzhě,
and received the surrender of thirty thousand Xī dòng soldiers.
He was promoted to Assistant Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs (*shūmìyuàn pàn guān*).
He captured Lánxī,
and followed in taking Wùzhōu,
being promoted to Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs (*qiān shūmìyuàn shì*).
He took Zhūjì.
The defending general fled by night,
and Commander Shěn Shèng, who had surrendered, rebelled again.
Dàhǎi defeated him,
capturing over four thousand people alive.
Zhūjì was renamed Zhūquánzhōu.
He moved his troops to attack Shàoxīng,
and again defeated Zhāng Shìchéng’s forces.
Tàizǔ considered Níng and Yuè important territories,
and summoned Dàhǎi to defend them.
Shìchéng’s general Lǚ Zhēn besieged Zhūquán.
Dàhǎi went to relieve it.
Zhēn dammed the water to flood the city.
Dàhǎi seized the dam and redirected the water to flood Zhēn’s camp.
Zhēn's situation became desperate.
He broke an arrow on horseback and swore an oath,
requesting that both sides withdraw their troops.
Dàhǎi agreed.
Minister Wáng Kǎi said:
“Zhēn is a cunning bandit, not to be trusted.
It would be better to strike him now.”
Dàhǎi said:
“To go back on one’s word is to be untrustworthy.
To release him and then strike him is unchivalrous.”
The army returned,
and everyone admired his authority and trustworthiness.
Soon after, he attacked Chǔzhōu,
driving away the Yuán general Shímò Yísūn,
and thus pacified the seven counties of Chǔzhōu.
When Chén Yǒuliàng invaded Lóngjiāng,
Dàhǎi was ordered to divide his army and attack Xìnzhōu,
to divert the enemy.
Dàhǎi followed Wáng Kǎi’s advice,
personally leading troops there,
and then captured Xìnzhōu,
making it Guǎngxìnfǔ.
Xìn was then running out of provisions.
Some advised him to return his army.
Dàhǎi said:
“This is the throat of Mǐn and Chǔ.
How can it be abandoned?”
He built walls and dug moats to defend it.
Previously,
army provisions were scarce.
In the captured prefectures and counties,
the generals and soldiers all levied grain from the people,
calling it "fortress grain" (*zhàiliáng*),
which greatly afflicted the people.
Dàhǎi spoke of this,
and an order was issued to abolish it.
He was promoted to Assistant Administrator of the Jiāngnán Branch Secretariat (*Jiāngnán xíngshěng cānzhī zhèngshì*),
and garrisoned Jīnhuá.
Earlier,
after Yánzhōu was taken,
the Miáo generals Jiǎng Yīng, Liú Zhèn, and Lǐ Fú all came from Tónglú to surrender.
Dàhǎi was pleased with their bravery and valor,
and kept them under his command.
At this point,
the three conspired to rebel.
In the morning, they entered the branch secretariat’s office,
and asked Dàhǎi to observe crossbows at Bāyǒnglóu.
When Dàhǎi came out,
Yīng sent his partisans to kneel before his horse,
falsely accusing Yīng of wrongdoing.
Before Dàhǎi could respond,
he looked back at Yīng.
Yīng pulled a hammer from his sleeve and struck Dàhǎi,
hitting his head and knocking him to the ground.
Both his son Guānzhù and Minister Wáng Kǎi were killed.
Yīng and others plundered the city greatly,
and fled to Wú.
Afterwards, Lǐ Wénzhōng attacked Hángzhōu.
The people of Hángzhōu seized Yīng and surrendered.
Tàizǔ ordered Yīng to be executed,
and his blood was used to sacrifice to Dàhǎi.
Dàhǎi was skilled in warfare.
He often recited:
“I am a military man and know no books.
I only know three things: I do not kill people,
I do not plunder women,
and I do not burn houses.”
Because of this, his army was welcomed everywhere they went.
When he died,
all who heard wept.
He also cherished scholars,
always seeking out outstanding talents wherever he went.
It was Dàhǎi who recommended Liú Jī, Sòng Lián, Yè Chēn, and Zhāng Yì when they were invited.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Duke of Yuè (*Yuèguógōng*),
with the posthumous title Wǔzhuāng.
His portrait was placed in the Temple of Meritorious Officials (*Gōngchén Miào*),
and he received sacrificial offerings in the Imperial Ancestral Temple (*Tàimiào*).
Earlier,
when Tàizǔ captured Wùzhōu,
he forbade brewing alcohol.
Dàhǎi’s son was the first to violate this.
Tàizǔ was enraged,
and intended to enforce the law.
At that time, Dàhǎi was campaigning in Yuè.
Secretary Wáng Kǎi pleaded not to execute him,
to ease Dàhǎi’s mind.
Tàizǔ said:
“I would rather Dàhǎi rebel against me
than have my laws go unenforced.”
He personally executed him with his own sword.
When Guānzhù was subsequently killed,
Dàhǎi was left without heirs.
Yǎngzǐ Dèjì,
courtesy name Shìměi,
his origins are unknown.
Hú Dàhǎi brought him to Tàizǔ.
He followed in the attack on Wùzhōu,
serving as a decoy,
and greatly defeated the Yuan forces outside Méihuāmén.
He captured their general, Jì Mízhāng,
thereby becoming renowned.
After Xìnzhōu was captured,
Tàizǔ appointed Dèjì as a tóngqiān of the Xíng Shūmìyuàn,
and tasked him with defending it.
Chén Yǒuliàng's general Lǐ Míngdào came to invade,
and Dèjì fought fiercely with him.
Hú Dàhǎi came to reinforce,
and they attacked him from both sides,
capturing Míngdào and his Xuānwèi Wáng Hàn'èr.
When Hú Dàhǎi was killed by Jiǎng Yīng,
Lǐ Yòuzhī, a surrendered general from Chǔzhōu, also killed Yuàn Pàn Gěng Zàichéng and rebelled.
Zhāng Shìchéng, hearing of the chaos in Zhèdōng,
sent his brother Shìxìn to attack Zhūquán.
Dèjì went from Xìnzhōu to relieve the siege,
and taking advantage of their slackness, he entered the city.
He, along with Zhīzhōu Luán Fèng and Yuàn Pàn Xiè Zàixìng, divided the gates for defense.
At midnight,
unexpectedly for the enemy,
he attacked Shìxìn's camp,
defeating and routing him.
He was promoted to Cānzhī Zhèngshì of the Zhèjiāng Xíngshěng,
and transferred to defend Xīnchéng.
Shìchéng's general Lǐ Bóshēng led a large force of infantry and cavalry to invade.
Dèjì held fast in defense,
and requested aid from Lǐ Wénzhōng.
Wénzhōng rushed to his rescue,
and Dèjì sallied forth to attack from both sides,
greatly defeating them.
Details are in Wénzhōng's biography.
At that time, some of Dèjì's subordinates secretly moved their families into Xīnchéng.
Wénzhōng suspected Dèjì of instigating this,
and executed his Dūshì Luó Yànjìng,
intending to subtly warn Dèjì.
All the officers and soldiers were enraged
and rushed to tell Dèjì.
Dèjì calmly said:
"The Yòuchéng killed Yànjìng
because he himself thought the battle uniforms for Guǎngxìn were worn out.
Anyone who speaks of it again will be executed."
Thereupon, Tàizǔ summoned Dèjì, praised and consoled him,
and reprimanded Wénzhōng for losing the hearts of his officers and soldiers,
saying further:
"Hú Dèjì's magnanimity
is beyond your reach."
He was promoted to Yòuchéng of the Zhèjiāng Xíngshěng
and bestowed a fine horse.
Not long after,
he was changed to Zuǒchéng
and transferred to garrison Hángzhōu.
He followed Dà Jiāngjūn Xú Dá on an expedition to Dìngxī.
Dèjì's army suffered a defeat,
and Dá executed several of his subordinate generals
and sent him in chains to the capital.
The Emperor, mindful of his past achievements,
released him.
He was reinstated as a Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ,
garrisoning Shǎnxī,
and died there.
Luán Fèng,
a native of Gāoyóu,
served as Zhī Zhūquán
and was known for his competence.
When Shìxìn attacked,
he and Xiè Zàixìng defended strenuously,
repeatedly sending out surprise troops to frustrate the enemy.
Zàixìng sent his subordinate officers to sell goods in Hángzhōu.
Tàizǔ, fearing that they might reveal the strengths and weaknesses of his army,
recalled Zàixìng
and appointed Cānjūn Lǐ Mènggēng to command all the troops in Zhūquán.
Later, remembering Zàixìng's contributions,
he arranged for his nephew Wénzhèng to marry Zàixìng's eldest daughter,
and ordered Xú Dá to marry his youngest daughter,
then sent him back to guard Zhūquán.
Zàixìng resented Mènggēng being placed above him,
and Fèng further disciplined him for minor offenses.
Consequently, he rebelled
and killed Fèng.
Fèng's wife, Wáng Shì, shielded Fèng with her body
and was killed along with him.
Mènggēng was captured
and surrendered to Shìchéng,
where Mènggēng also died.
Tàizǔ, considering Zàixìng's numerous past achievements
and that his rebellion was not his true intention,
stated that neither Fèng nor Mènggēng received posthumous honors.
Gěng Zàichéng,
courtesy name Dépǔ,
a native of Wǔhé.
He followed Tàizǔ in Háo,
capturing Sì and Chúzhōu.
Yuan forces besieged Liùhé.
Tàizǔ rescued it,
and with Zàichéng's army at Wǎliánglěi,
they fought fiercely.
Realizing they were outnumbered, they retreated.
The Yuan forces pursued them.
Tàizǔ set an ambush by a ravine,
ordering Zàichéng to lure the enemy,
and severely defeated them.
As a Zhènfǔ, he followed across the river
and took Jíqìng.
As Yuánshuài, he defended Zhènjiāng.
As a Pànguān of the Xíng Shūmìyuàn, he defended Chángxìng,
and later defended Yángzhōu.
He followed in capturing Jīnhuá,
serving as vanguard,
stationing at Huánglóng Shān in Jìnyún to block the enemy's advance.
He, with Hú Dàhǎi, defeated Shímò Yísūn in Chǔzhōu,
captured his city,
and defended it.
Yísūn attacked again,
and they defeated him at Qìngyuán.
Zàichéng managed his army strictly.
When soldiers entered and exited among the populace,
not even a single vegetable or fruit was taken.
The Miáo commander Jiǎng Yīng and others in Jīnhuá rebelled
and killed Hú Dàhǎi.
The Miáo commander Lǐ Yòuzhī and others in Chǔzhōu, hearing of this,
also rebelled.
Zàichéng was dining with guests
when he heard of the change, mounted his horse,
gathered fewer than twenty soldiers,
and confronted the rebels, cursing:
"You rebel slaves!
What has the state done to wrong you
that you rebel?"
The rebels thrust their spears at Zàichéng.
Zàichéng swung his sword, breaking several spears consecutively,
was wounded and fell from his horse,
cursing without ceasing until he died.
Hú Shēn and others collected his body
and buried it in straw.
Later, he was reburied in Jùbǎo Shān in Jīnlíng,
posthumously enfeoffed as Gāoyáng Jùngōng,
and his spirit tablet was placed in the Tàimiào,
his portrait in the Gōngchén Miào.
In the tenth year of Hóngwǔ, he was additionally granted the title of Sì Guógōng,
and given the posthumous name Wǔzhuàng.
His son, Tiānbì,
hearing of his father's demise,
gathered his troops and killed the rebels.
By the time he arrived,
Lǐ Wénzhōng had already defeated and executed the rebels.
Consequently, Tiānbì was appointed to guard Chǔzhōu,
and he distinguished himself in repelling both Fāng Guózhēn and Zhāng Shìchéng,
promoted to Zhǐhuī Fùshǐ.
He captured Pǔchéng,
attacked Jiànníng,
and routed Chén Yǒudìng.
He campaigned in Xiāngyáng,
advanced to Xī'ān,
and persuaded Hézhōu and Líntáo to surrender,
all of which were brought under control.
He was changed to Hángzhōu Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī.
In the seventh year, he went out to sea to capture pirates,
penetrated deep into the outer ocean,
and drowned.
Zhāng Déshèng,
courtesy name Rénfǔ,
was a native of Héféi.
His talent and strategy were outstanding.
With Yú Tōnghǎi and others, he brought his naval forces from Cháo to submit.
He followed in crossing the Jiāng,
capturing Cǎishí and Tàipíng.
When Chén Yěxiān attacked,
he, with Tāng Hé and others, defeated and captured him,
and was granted the title of Tàipíng Xīngguó Yì Zǒngguǎn.
He defeated Mánzi Hǎiyá’s naval stockade,
and captured Chén Zhàoxiān.
He took Jíqìng,
captured Zhènjiāng,
and was granted the title of Qínhuái Yì Yuánshuài.
He captured Chángzhōu,
and was promoted to Pàn of the Shūmìyuàn.
He captured Níngguó,
and recruited the long-spear soldiers.
He took Tàihú,
and raided Mǎjì Shān.
He attacked Yíxīng,
captured Mǎtuó Shā and Shípái Zhài.
He was promoted to Qiān Shūmìyuàn Shì.
When Zhào Pǔshèng captured Chízhōu,
Déshèng went to reinforce,
but did not arrive in time,
so he returned and followed Xú Dá to retake Yíxīng.
Pǔshèng again plundered Qīngyáng and Shídài.
Déshèng fought him at Zhàjiāngkǒu,
defeated and routed him.
Afterwards,
he again, with Tōnghǎi, defeated his forces,
and subsequently recovered Chízhōu.
He led his troops from Wúwéi towards Fúshān,
routing Pǔshèng’s general Hú Zǒngguǎn,
pursuing and defeating him at Qīngshān,
and chasing him north to Qiánshān.
Chén Yǒuliàng’s general Guō Tài counter-attacked at Shāhé,
but was defeated and beheaded by Déshèng,
who then captured Qiánshān.
When Yǒuliàng invaded Lóngjiāng,
Déshèng commanded the naval forces to meet him in battle,
with heavy casualties on both sides.
Déshèng shouted loudly,
urging his generals to fight fiercely.
Yǒuliàng’s army was scattered,
and was utterly defeated.
He and the generals pursued him to Cíhú,
and set fire to his boats.
Upon reaching Cǎishí,
a great battle ensued,
and he died in battle.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Càiguó Gōng,
given the posthumous name Zhōngyì,
his likeness was placed in the Gōngchén Miào,
and he was enshrined in the Tàimiào.
His son Xuān was young,
so his adopted son Xīngzǔ succeeded to his post.
Xīngzǔ was
a native of Cháo.
His original surname was Wāng.
After succeeding to the post,
he followed in defeating Ānqìng,
capturing Jiāngzhōu,
taking Qí and Huáng,
and capturing Nánchāng.
He followed in relieving Ānfēng,
and heavily defeated Zhāng Shìchéng’s forces.
In the Battle of Póyáng,
he, with Liáo Yǒngzhōng and others, penetrated deep with six boats,
and also intercepted Yǒuliàng at Jīngjiāngkǒu,
making the greatest contribution,
and was promoted to Cāncèng of the Húguǎng Xíngshěng.
He followed in pacifying Wǔchāng,
then captured Lúzhōu,
and raided territories up to Tōngzhōu before returning.
He was promoted to Qiānshì of the Dàdūdūfǔ.
He followed Xú Dá in taking Huáidōng,
and capturing Zhèxī.
He was promoted to Tóngzhī Dàdūdūfǔ Shì.
When the grand army launched the Northern Expedition,
he separately led the guard army from Xúzhōu to capture Yí, Qīng, and Dōngpíng,
riding on the victory to Dōng'ē,
where he accepted the surrender of Yuán Cāncè Chén Bì and his部 of over 50,000 men.
Kǒngzǐ's 56th generation descendant Yǎnshèng Gōng Xīxué, leading Qūfù Zhīxiàn Xījǔ, Zōuxiàn Zhǔbù Mèng Sīliàng and others, came to pay respects at the military gate,
and Xīngzǔ treated them with courtesy.
Counties in eastern Yǎn submitted upon hearing of his arrival,
and he then captured Jìníng and Jǐnán.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ,
as Dūdū concurrently Yòuluàifǔ Shǐ,
he followed in attacking Lè'ān,
captured Biànliáng, Hé, and Luò,
and returned to defend Jìníng.
He joined the Dàjiāngjūn’s forces at Dézhōu,
led the naval forces upstream along the river,
and then captured Yuándū.
He then attacked and captured Yǒngpíng,
took Dàtóng to the west,
and stationed three guard units there to defend it.
He twice defeated the Yuán army,
with countless casualties inflicted and prisoners taken.
At this time, Déshèng’s son Xuān had grown up,
and was appointed Xuānwǔ Wèi Zhīhuī Tóngzhī.
Xīngzǔ, however, reverted to his original surname Wāng.
In the third year, he further captured Wǔ and Shuò prefectures,
and captured Yuán Zhīyuàn Mǎ Guǎng and others.
He led his troops to the northern pass of Dàtóng,
heavily defeated the Yuán army,
and captured Kuòkuò’s younger brother Jīngāngnú and over 400 others.
Not long after,
he was appointed Jìn Wáng Wǔfù,
concurrently Qiānshì of the Shānxī Xíng Dūdūfǔ.
In the fourth year, he followed Qián Jiāngjūn Fù Yǒudé to combine forces and attack Shǔ,
capturing Jiē and Wén,
and riding on the victory to Wǔlǐ Guān,
where he was struck by a flying stone and died.
When Shǔ was pacified,
an imperial edict declared that Dūdū Xīngzǔ had died in the service of the state,
generously rewarded his son,
posthumously enfeoffed him as Dōngshèng Hóu,
and granted him an hereditary charter.
Xīngzǔ’s son was young,
and was ordered to live with Xuān.
He later died of illness,
and his noble title was revoked.
Zhào Déshèng,
was a native of Háo.
He was a leader of the Yuán militia,
skilled with a horse-lance,
and always led the charge in battle.
He was under the command of Wáng Mánggē,
but perceived that he would certainly be defeated.
When Tàizǔ captured Chúyáng,
Déshèng’s mother was in the army,
so he abandoned his wife and came to submit.
Tàizǔ was pleased,
bestowed a name upon him,
and made him the vanguard in front of the tent.
He followed in taking Tiěfógāng,
attacked Sānchàhé,
defeated Zhāngjiāzhài,
and captured Quánjiāo and the various stockades of Hòuhé.
While reinforcing Lìuhé,
he was struck by a stray arrow,
nearly dying.
He attacked Jīlóng Shān,
raided Wūjiāng,
and took Hézhōu and Hánshān.
He launched a night attack on Chén Yěxiān’s camp,
captured Bǎnmén and Tiěchángguān two stockades,
and then took Yízhēn.
He was appointed Xiānfēng of the Zǒngguǎnfǔ.
He followed in crossing the Jiāng,
took Tàipíng,
and captured Wúhú, Jùróng, Lìshuǐ, and Lìyáng,
all with meritorious service.
He followed Cháng Yùchūn in defeating Mánzi Hǎiyá at Cǎishí,
defeated Chén Zhàoxiān’s camp at Fāngshān,
and took Jíqìng,
with the greatest contribution.
He followed Xú Dá in taking Zhènjiāng,
and defeating the Miáo army’s naval stockade.
He took Dānyáng and Jīntán,
and pacified Níngguó.
He was transferred to become Lǐngjūn Xiānfēng.
He took Guǎngdé,
defeated Zhāng Shìchéng’s naval stockade,
and again followed Yùchūn in attacking Chángzhōu,
relieving the siege of Niútáng,
and recovering Guǎngdé and Níngguó.
He took Jiāngyīn,
attacked Chángshú,
and captured Zhāng Shìdé.
He followed in attacking Húzhōu.
When Yíxīng rebelled,
he returned with his troops to suppress it.
He was promoted to Zhōngyì Zuǒ Fùyuánshuài.
When Chén Yǒuliàng invaded Lóngjiāng,
the first pass of Lóngjiāng was called Hǔkǒuchéng,
which Tàizǔ entrusted to Déshèng.
When Yǒuliàng arrived,
he fought fiercely.
Ambush troops rose up,
Yǒuliàng was utterly defeated,
and Tàipíng was subsequently recovered.
He took Tónglíng Línshān Zhài,
raided Huángshān Qiáo and Mǎtuó Shā,
and performed meritoriously in the campaign against Gāoyóu.
He was promoted to Hòuyì Tǒngjūn Yuánshuài.
Following Tàizǔ on his western campaign,
he defeated Ānqìng’s naval camp,
and sailed with the wind upstream to Xiǎogū Shān.
When they were five lǐ from Jiǔjiāng,
Yǒuliàng first learned of it
and fled in a hurry.
They then captured Jiǔjiāng,
and campaigned through Huángméi and Guǎngjì,
capturing Ruìchāng, Línjiāng, and Jí’ān.
Returning, they took Ānqìng,
advanced and captured Fǔzhōu,
and took Xīngàn.
He attacked the rebel general in Nánchāng,
recaptured its city,
and was wounded in the shoulder by cannon fire.
He was appointed Qiān Jiāngnán Xíng Shūmìyuàn Shì.
He defended Nánchāng with Zhū Wénzhèng and Dèng Yù.
He pacified Luó Yǒuxián in Chízhōu,
defeated Yǒuliàng’s general in Xīshān,
and recaptured Línjiāng, Jí’ān, and Fǔzhōu.
Soon after,
Yǒuliàng raised a large army and besieged Nánchāng.
Déshèng led his several thousand troops to fight the enemy with their backs to the city,
shooting and killing their general,
which greatly disheartened the enemy.
The next day, they re-engaged,
encircling the city multiple times.
Yǒuliàng personally supervised the battle,
attacking day and night,
and the city walls were on the verge of collapsing.
Déshèng led all the generals to fight desperately,
fighting and building simultaneously,
so that the broken walls were repaired again.
In the evening, he sat in the city gate tower,
directing the soldiers.
An arrow struck his waist and back,
the arrowhead penetrating six cùn.
He pulled it out,
and sighed, saying:
“Since I joined the army in my prime,
I have been wounded by arrows and stones many times,
but none as severe as this.
A man dying is no regret;
my only regret is not being able to clear the Central Plains.”
Having said this, he died
at the age of thirty-nine.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Liángguó Gōng,
given the posthumous name Wǔhuán,
enshrined in the Shrine of Meritorious Officials,
and honored in the Tàimiào.
Déshèng was upright and resolute,
and disciplined his subordinates strictly.
He had never studied,
but he adapted to circumstances
and his actions always conformed to ancient methods.
In everyday life, he was devoutly filial and brotherly, like a scholar.
Yǒuliàng besieged Nánchāng for eighty-five days,
and a total of fourteen people died in battle, one after another.
Zhāng Zǐmíng
was a commander of a thousand households.
As the siege of Hóngdū dragged on,
communication between inside and outside was cut off.
Zhū Wénzhèng sent Zǐmíng to request urgent aid in Yìngtiān.
Using a small fishing boat from Dōnghú, he secretly slipped out through the water gate,
traveling at night and resting by day,
reaching his destination after half a month.
Tàizǔ asked about Yǒuliàng's military strength.
He replied,
“Although the troops are numerous,
not a few have died in battle.
Now the Jiāng River is drying up daily,
which will be disadvantageous for the enemy’s large ships.
With reinforcements, they can be defeated.”
Tàizǔ said to Zǐmíng,
“Go tell your commander
to hold firm for one month;
I will take care of it myself.”
On his return to Húkǒu,
he was captured by Yǒuliàng,
who ordered him to persuade the city to surrender.
Zǐmíng feigned agreement.
Upon reaching the city walls,
he shouted loudly,
“I am Zhāng Dàshè.
I have seen His Majesty,
who ordered you all to hold firm;
help is coming soon!”
The enemy was enraged
and speared him to death.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Zhōngjié Hóu.
When Yǒuliàng attacked Fǔzhōu,
Lǐ Jìxiān, a judge of the Shūmìyuàn, died fighting on the city walls;
Niú Hǎilóng, the Marshal of the Left Wing, died breaking through the encirclement;
Zhào Guówàng, the Deputy Marshal of the Left, led troops to burn warships.
When the enemy pursued him,
he jumped under a bridge and died;
Xú Míng, a commander of a hundred households, rode out to shoot the enemy.
The enemy, knowing Míng’s name,
concentrated their efforts to attack him
and he was captured and killed;
Zhāng Déshān, a soldier, secretly left the city at midnight
and set fire to enemy boats.
The enemy discovered him
and he died;
Xià Màochéng, defending the city tower,
was killed by a flying cannonball;
Zhū Qián, the Deputy Marshal of the Right Wing, and Xǔ Guī, the Marshal of the Armies, both died in battle.
When Jiǎng Bìshèng captured Jí’ān,
Liú Qí, the Cānzhèng, and Zhū Wénhuá, the Zhīfǔ, were captured
and died unyielding.
Zhào Tiānlín defended Línjiāng.
Yǒuliàng attacked it,
and he died unyielding when the city fell.
Zhù Zōng and Kāng Tài rebelled
and captured Hóngdū.
Yè Chēn, the Zhīfǔ, and Wàn Sīchéng, the Dūshì of the Xíngshěng, met them in battle
and both died.
After the situation was pacified,
all were posthumously granted titles of Marquis or Count and below, with various distinctions.
A Shrine of Loyal Officials was erected in Yùzhāng,
enshrining the fourteen individuals,
with Déshèng as the foremost.
And thirty-five people died in the battle of Kāngláng Shān,
led by Dīng Pǔláng.
Pǔláng was initially a general under Chén Yǒuliàng,
defending Xiǎogū Shān.
He came to surrender with Fù Yǒudé,
was appointed Tóngzhī of the Xíng Shūmìyuàn,
and had several achievements.
When he reinforced Nánchāng,
there was a great battle on Pōyáng Hú.
From chén to wǔ hours,
Pǔláng suffered more than ten wounds.
His head was severed but he still stood upright,
holding his weapon as if fighting,
which the enemy took for a deity.
This was on the jǐchǒu day of the seventh month.
He was posthumously granted the title of Jìyáng Jùn Gōng.
Zhāng Zhìxióng was also a general under Yǒuliàng,
always known for his bravery and skill,
nicknamed “Long Zhāng.”
He served under Zhào Pǔshèng, defending Ānqìng.
When Yǒuliàng killed Pǔshèng,
Zhìxióng, resentful, came to surrender
and became a judge of the Shūmìyuàn.
At this point, his boat’s mast broke,
and the enemy speared him.
Knowing he could not escape,
he committed suicide by slitting his throat.
Marshal Yú Chǎng, Right Marshal Chén Bì, and Xú Gōngfǔ all died in battle on that day.
The day before,
Hán Chéng, the Left Deputy Commander,
and Marshals Sòng Guì and Chén Zhàoxiān died in battle.
Zhàoxiān was
Yěxiān’s nephew.
After being captured,
Tàizǔ used his troops for the imperial guard.
Moved by the emperor’s magnanimity,
he dedicated his life to service
and died in battle at this time.
Hán Chéng’s son, Guān, rose to Dūdū;
he has a separate biography.
Four days later,
on the xīnmǎo day,
there was another great battle,
and Deputy Marshal Chāng Wénguì, Left Marshal Lǐ Xìn, Wáng Shèng, and Liú Yì died.
On the rénxū day of the eighth month, they blocked the enemy at Jīngjiāng Kǒu.
Lǐ Zhìgāo, the Tóngzhī Yuánshuài, and Wáng Yǎozhù, the Fùshǐ, also died in battle.
Other sub-commanders and lesser officials who died in service were:
Qīanhùs Jiāng Rùn, Wáng Fèngxiǎn, Shí Míng, Wáng Dé, Zhū Dǐng, Wáng Qīng, Cháng Déshèng, Yuán Huá, Chén Chōng, Wáng Xǐxiān, Wāng Zé, Dīng Yǔ, Shǐ Déshèng, Péi Zhěn, Wáng Lǐ, Wáng Rén;
Zhènfǔs Cháng Wéidé, Zhèng Xīng, Lù Déshān, Luó Shìróng, Cáo Xìn.
In total, one was granted the title of Gōng, twelve as Hóu, two as Bó, fifteen as Zǐ, and six as Nán.
Their portraits were displayed in the Shrine of Loyal Officials on Kāngláng Shān,
and officials performed sacrifices annually.
Chéng Guóshèng,
a native of Huī,
returned with a righteous army marshal.
He defeated Yáng Wánzhě,
accumulated merits to become a Wànhù,
and defended Nánchāng.
He raided Yǒuliàng’s camp at night with Niú Hǎilóng.
Hǎilóng was killed by a stray arrow,
but Guóshèng escaped by swimming
and reached Jīnlíng.
He followed Tàizǔ to battle at Pōyáng.
Zhāng Dìngbiān advanced directly and attacked Tàizǔ’s boat.
Guóshèng, Hán Chéng, and Chén Zhàoxiān piloted small boats and fought fiercely on both sides.
Tàizǔ’s boat escaped,
but Guóshèng and the others circled behind the enemy ships,
lost support, and died fighting desperately.
However, those in Nánchāng City believed Guóshèng had already died,
thus he was enshrined in both the Yùzhāng and Kāng Shān shrines.
Sāng Shìjié,
a native of Wúwéi,
also came to surrender from Cháohú.
Zhào Pǔshèng harbored ulterior motives,
and Shìjié exposed his plot.
Pǔshèng fled.
Following the crossing of the Yangzi River,
he used a naval force to defeat the Yuán navy.
He was appointed Field Marshal of Qínhuái Wing.
After taking Zhènjiāng,
he attacked Jīntán and Dānyáng,
assaulted the various long-spear armies at Níngguó,
captured Shuǐyáng,
and pacified Chángzhōu.
He was appointed Acting Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs.
He captured territories in Jiāngyīn and Yíxīng.
Initially,
a rogue salt merchant named Zhū Dìng from Shípái village,
who had a feud with the wealthy Zhào clan,
reported a rebellion,
which led to the extermination of the Zhào clan.
Zhū Dìng was appointed Magistrate of Jiāngyīn.
Soon after, he reverted to banditry,
and the Yuán sent troops to arrest him.
Dìng, hearing that Zhāng Shìchéng occupied Gāoyóu,
then led Shìchéng to cross the Yangzi River via Tōngzhōu.
They subsequently captured Píngjiāng,
appointed Dìng as a Counsellor,
and dispatched Field Marshal Luán Ruì to garrison Shípái.
When the main army had already taken Jiāngyīn,
Ruì still occupied Shípái,
guiding the naval forces back and forth.
Tàizǔ ordered Yǒng'ān and Shìjié to attack him.
Shìjié died fighting bravely,
Ruì also surrendered,
and Zhāng's attempt to spy on the river route was cut off.
Tàizǔ, remembering his achievements,
posthumously awarded him the titles of Grand General of Ānyuǎn, Commandant of Light Chariots, and Marquis of Yǒngyì,
and allowed his tablet to be placed in the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
His son, Jìng, because of his father's death in service,
rose through various official positions to become Assistant Administrator of the Chief Military Commission.
In the twenty-third year of Hóngwǔ (1390), he was enfeoffed as Earl of Huīxiān,
with an annual stipend of one thousand seven hundred *dan* of grain,
and was granted hereditary privileges.
The following year, he was sent with Xú Huīzǔ and others to guard the border,
and soon after was ordered to station troops in Píngyáng.
He died due to his involvement in the Lán Yù faction.
Another was Liú Chéng,
a native of Língbì.
As a Commander-in-Chief leading troops, he followed Gěng Bǐngwén in pacifying Chángxīng,
