and was appointed Left Vice Field Marshal of Yǒngxīng Wing.
He repeatedly assisted Bǐngwén in defeating Shìchéng's forces.
Lǐ Bóshēng came to attack with a hundred thousand men,
while the city had only seven thousand troops.
Tàizǔ dispatched troops to reinforce them,
but they had not yet arrived.
Bǐngwén fortified the city and defended.
Chéng led several tens of cavalry out the west gate,
defeated Bóshēng's forces,
captured their general, Marshal Sòng,
and then moved to the east gate.
The enemy surrounded him with all their troops,
and he died in battle.
He was posthumously awarded the title General of Huáiyuǎn,
and a temple was erected for him in Chángxīng.
Máo Chéng,
a native of Dìngyuǎn.
He joined the army from Hézhōu,
serving under Cháng Yùchūn,
and after capturing Tàipíng,
was first granted the title of Myriad-Householder.
Following the pacification of Chángzhōu and Níngguó,
he was promoted to Commander-in-Chief.
After capturing Qúzhōu,
he was appointed Vice Field Marshal.
While defending Jīnhuá,
he was reassigned as Field Marshal of Tàipíng Xīngguó Wing.
He participated in the capture of Ānqìng,
reinforced Ānfēng,
fought at Póyáng,
and captured Wǔchāng,
after which he was appointed Myriad-Household of Wǔdé Guard.
Soon after, he was promoted to Assistant Commissioner.
He rendered meritorious service in taking Gànzhōu, Ānlù, Xiāngyáng, and Tàizhōu.
He participated in Xú Dá's attack on Píngjiāng,
burned Zhāng Shìchéng's warships,
and built a long siege embankment to trap him.
When Dá attacked Lóumén,
Shìchéng sent out troops to fight,
Chéng defeated them,
advanced to the outer city wall,
and died there, struck by a fork.
He was posthumously awarded the title Duke of Dōnghǎi Commandery,
and was worshipped in the Temple of Meritorious Officials.
Among those who died at the same time
was Yáng Guóxīng,
also a native of Dìngyuǎn,
who defended Yíxīng as Right Wing Field Marshal.
Initially,
Chén Bǎo'èr, a native of Chángzhōu, gathered a crowd and called them
"Yellow-Bag Army."
After surrendering, they rebelled again,
lured and captured Generals Zhān and Lǐ.
Guóxīng captured and executed them.
He was appointed Commissioner of Shénwǔ Guard.
At this point, he died fighting while attacking Chāngmén.
His son, Yì, succeeded him as Commissioner.
Hú Shēn,
courtesy name Zhòngyuān,
was a native of Lóngquán, Chǔzhōu.
He was exceptionally intelligent and resourceful,
well-versed in the classics, history, and the various schools of thought.
At the end of the Yuán dynasty, amidst the chaos of war,
he sighed,
"The earth energy of eastern Zhèjiāng is completely white,
disaster will soon strike."
So he gathered the young men from his village to protect themselves.
Shímò Yísūn, as a Myriad-Household, garrisoned Chǔzhōu,
and invited Shēn to be his military advisor.
Shēn recruited several thousand soldiers
and captured various mountain bandits.
When Hán Hǔ and others in Wēnzhōu killed their commander and rebelled,
Shēn went to admonish them.
The soldiers and civilians were moved to tears,
killed Hú, and surrendered the city.
Afterwards,
he accompanied Zhāng Yì to quell the rebellion in Lóngquán,
searched for bandits in neighboring counties,
and pacified them one by one.
Yísūn had by then been promoted to Provincial Counsellor,
and by his authority appointed Shēn as Field Marshal.
In the twelfth month of the *wùxū* year (1358),
Tàizǔ personally led an expedition against Wùzhōu.
Shēn led several hundred carts of troops to reinforce,
but upon reaching Sōngxī, could not help,
and was defeated and withdrew.
Wùzhōu then fell.
The following year,
Gěng Zàichéng invaded Chǔzhōu.
Yísūn dispatched Field Marshal Yè Chēn, Advisor Lín Bīnzhǔ, Garrison Commander Chén Zhōngzhēn, and Shēn to lead troops to resist.
Just then, Hú Dàhǎi's army arrived,
and joined with Zàichéng,
thoroughly defeating them and advancing to the city walls.
Yísūn was defeated,
and fled to Jiànníng with Yè Chēn and Zhāng Yì.
Chǔzhōu then fell.
Shēn surrendered the four counties of Lóngquán, Qìngyuán, Sōngyáng, and Suíchāng.
Tàizǔ had long known Shēn's reputation,
summoned him for an audience,
appointed him Supernumerary Secretary of the Left Bureau,
and sent him back to Chǔzhōu
to recruit his former troops.
He participated in the campaign against Jiāngxī.
After its pacification,
he was ordered to guard Jí'ān with personal troops as a commander.
When the Miáo army in Chǔzhōu rebelled,
killing the garrison commander Gěng Zàichéng,
Shēn followed Pacification Commissioner Shào Róng in quelling and punishing them.
At that time, the Branch Secretariat was reorganized into the Zhèdōng Provisional Branch Secretariat,
and Shēn was appointed Secretary of the Left and Right Bureaus of the Provisional Secretariat,
in overall command of military and civilian affairs in Chǔzhōu.
At that time, mountain bandits frequently emerged,
and public sentiment was not yet firm.
Shēn recruited over ten thousand soldiers,
and captured and executed the bandit leaders.
The coastal army was originally fierce;
he executed several of the most unruly among them,
and the trouble then ceased.
In the ninth month of the *guǐmǎo* year (1363),
Xiè Zàixīng, a rebellious general from Zhūquán, attacked Dōngyáng with Zhāng Shìchéng's forces.
Left Grand Councillor Lǐ Wénzhōng ordered Shēn to lead troops as the vanguard,
and Zàixīng was defeated and fled.
Shēn suggested that Zhūquán be the outer screen for Zhèdōng,
so he surveyed the land fifty *li* from Zhūquán and near Wǔzhǐshān,
built a new city,
and stationed troops there.
When Tàizǔ first heard of Zàixīng's rebellion,
he urgently dispatched an envoy to Wénzhōng,
devising a separate plan for city defense,
but by the time the envoy arrived, the construction was already complete.
Later, Shìchéng's general Lǐ Bóshēng launched a major invasion,
encamped below the new city,
but could not breach it,
and was defeated and retreated.
Tàizǔ commended Shēn for his achievements,
and bestowed upon him a renowned horse.
Tài-zǔ called himself King of Wú,
and appointed Shēn as the Staff Officer of the Prince's Household,
still guarding Chǔzhōu.
The Wēnzhōu magnate Zhōu Zōngdào gathered a crowd and occupied Píngyáng.
He was repeatedly harassed by Fāng Guózhēn's nephew Míngshàn,
so he surrendered the city.
Míngshàn, enraged, attacked it.
Shēn dispatched troops to strike and drive away Míngshàn,
then took Ruì'ān,
and advanced his troops to Wēnzhōu.
The Fāng clan was fearful,
and requested to pay 30,000 taels of silver annually to fund the army.
Shēn was then ordered to withdraw his troops,
and return to his post.
Chén Yǒudìng's troops arrived,
Shēn defeated them,
pursued them to Pǔchéng,
and again defeated its defending troops,
so the city was taken.
He advanced to capture Sōngxī,
and captured its defending general Zhāng Zǐyù.
Therefore, he requested to dispatch troops from the three circuits of Guǎngxìn, Fǔzhōu, and Jiànchāng,
planning to capture the entire Mǐn region.
Tài-zǔ rejoiced, saying:
"Zǐyù is a fierce general;
capturing him will break Yǒudìng's spirit.
If we attack while taking advantage of the situation,
there is no reason we will not conquer them."
He then ordered Guǎngxìn Commander Zhū Liàngzǔ to proceed via Qiánshān and Jiànchāng,
Assistant Chancellor Wáng Pǔ via Shānguān,
to meet Shēn and advance together.
Soon after,
Liàngzǔ and others captured Chóng'ān,
and advanced to attack Jiànníng.
Yǒudìng's general Ruǎn Dézhōu held out stubbornly.
Shēn observed that the omens were unfavorable
and wished to delay.
Liàngzǔ said:
"The army has already reached this point;
how can we delay?
Moreover, the ways of Heaven are distant and profound,
and the atmospheric changes in mountains and marshes are inconstant;
what is there to rely on?"
At that time, Dézhōu's troops were stationed at Jǐnjiāng,
pressing against the rear of Shēn's camp,
and Liàngzǔ pressed the attack even more urgently.
Shēn led his troops back,
and broke through their two palisades.
Dézhōu's army fought fiercely,
and Yǒudìng personally led his elite troops to attack from both sides.
As evening fell,
Shēn broke through the encirclement and fled,
but his horse stumbled and he was captured,
and subsequently killed,
at the age of fifty-two.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Count of Jìnyún Commandery.
Tài-zǔ once asked Sòng Lián:
"What kind of man is Hú Shēn?"
He replied:
"A talent in both civil and military arts."
Tài-zǔ said:
"Indeed.
The barrier of Zhèdōng,
I truly relied on him for it."
And Shēn, having long served in his home region,
was determined to pacify Mǐn to repay the favor,
and ultimately died in loyal service.
Shēn governed his troops with generosity and kindness;
in over ten years of military campaigns,
he never arbitrarily killed a single person.
While guarding Chǔzhōu,
he established schools and cultivated scholars.
The land tax in Jìnyún was heavy,
so he used the rent from newly confiscated land to compensate for the amount.
The salt tax was one-tenth,
he requested to collect half of it,
to facilitate trade.
Both soldiers and civilians cherished his benevolence.
Sūn Xīngzǔ,
was a native of Háo.
He followed Tài-zǔ across the Yangtze River,
and accumulated merits to become Chief Vanguard.
In the battle of Lóngjiāng,
he was promoted to Commander-in-chief.
After breaking the Eight Arrays Camp at Ruìchāng,
he was promoted to Commander of the Tiāncè Guard.
Xīngzǔ was resolute and resourceful,
and Grand General Xú Dá greatly esteemed him.
After capturing Tàizhōu,
upon Dá's request,
he was ordered to guard Hǎilíng.
Hǎilíng was
a vital strategic point where Shìchéng's troops entered Huái.
Xīngzǔ rectified military regulations,
trained his soldiers,
and his defenses were very strict.
Wú troops came to invade from the sea,
he defeated them,
and captured Commander Péng.
After Píngjiāng was taken,
Xīngzǔ was ordered to take Tōngzhōu.
Shìchéng's defending general had already surrendered to Xú Dá.
He was promoted to Vice Commissioner of the Grand Capital Commandery,
and transferred to guard Péngchéng.
After Dá had pacified Guānshǎn,
he turned his army northward,
and issued an order for Xīngzǔ to meet him at Dōngchāng.
He followed in the capture of the Yuan capital,
established the six Guards of Yānshān,
left 30,000 soldiers,
and ordered Xīngzǔ to guard it,
leading the affairs of the branch office of the Grand Capital Commandery.
When the main army campaigned in the west,
Kuòkuò entered Běipíng via Jūyōng,
Dá told his generals:
"Běipíng has Commander Sūn,
so there's no need to worry,"
and then directly attacked Tàiyuán.
The details are in Dá's biography.
In Hóngwǔ's third year, he led the soldiers of the six Guards to follow Dá out of the Great Wall,
and at the Sānbùlà River,
he encountered the enemy and died fighting bravely,
at the age of thirty-five.
Tài-zǔ mourned and regretted his loss,
posthumously enfeoffed him as Marquis of Yānshān,
with the posthumous title Zhōngmǐn,
and enshrined him in Cháng Yùchūn's ancestral temple in Tōngzhōu.
Not long after,
the Central Secretariat memorialized the emperor about Commissioner Wāng Xīngzǔ being concurrently paid for his duties.
The Emperor, hearing the name Xīngzǔ,
sighed,
and ordered that the monthly salary be given to the family of the late Marquis of Yānshān, Xīngzǔ.
His eldest son Kè inherited the position of Commander of the Wǔdé Guard.
After a long time,
he successively became Assistant Commissioner.
In the twenty-first year,
as Right Assistant General, he accompanied Lán Yù on the northern expedition,
reaching Lake Pǔyú'ér.
For his merits, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Quánníng,
with an annual stipend of two thousand *shí* (grain),
and a hereditary patent.
Kè was prudent, agile, and possessed the demeanor of a scholarly general.
He accompanied campaigns in Chǔ and Shǔ,
and then was stationed at Miǎnyáng,
inspecting the soldiers of various garrisons to prepare for border defense.
In the twenty-fifth year, he was promoted to concurrently hold the title of Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
Not long after,
he registered soldiers in Shānxī,
and trained troops with Duke Sòng, Shèng.
He was soon recalled,
and granted a residence in the Middle Capital.
Later, he was implicated in Lán Yù's faction and died.
Cáo Liángchén,
was an Ānfēng native.
When the Yǐng bandits rose,
he gathered his villagers and built a stronghold to defend themselves.
He submitted to Tài-zǔ in Yìngtiān,
and became an Administrator of the Jiānghuái Provincial Branch Secretariat.
He followed in taking Huáidōng,
recovering Zhèxī,
and was promoted to Left Assistant Chancellor of the Branch Secretariat.
He followed the grand army to take the Yuan capital,
and expanded territory to Zé and Lù.
He was promoted to Chancellor of the Shānxī Provincial Branch Secretariat,
and returned to guard Tōngzhōu.
At that time, the grand army had marched out of Shānxī,
and the defense of Tōngzhōu was weak,
his command consisting of less than a thousand men.
Yuan Chancellor Yěsù led ten thousand cavalry to camp by the Báihé River.
Liángchén said:
"Our troops are few, we cannot fight them directly.
Although their numbers are many,
they are remnants of a fallen dynasty,
their morale is broken and spirit low.
We should use stratagem to make them flee."
So he secretly dispatched Commander Wǔ Yǒng and others to place many red banners on boats along the river,
extending over thirty *lǐ*,
with gongs and drums sounding within earshot.
Yěsù was greatly alarmed
and fled.
Liángchén led his elite cavalry to pursue them for over a hundred *lǐ*,
and from then on, the Yuan soldiers dared not encroach upon Běipíng.
He again followed Grand General Dá to strike Kuòkuò Tièmù'ér at Dìngxī,
and defeated him.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, he was enfeoffed as Xuānníng Hóu.
His annual stipend was nine hundred shí of grain,
and he was granted a hereditary charter.
The following year, he followed in the campaign against Shǔ,
capturing the mountain stronghold of Guīzhōu
and taking control of the various tǔsī of Róngměi.
Zhōu Déxīng at that time captured Tán Hòu's stronghold at Máogāng.
He cleared a path by felling trees from Báiyán Shān,
emerging at Zhǐfāng Xī to advance towards Kuízhōu,
then captured Chóngqìng.
The next year, he followed Deputy General Wénzhōng on the northern expedition,
reaching Lúqú Hé,
and capturing its tribes.
Wénzhōng led Liángchén, who carried twenty days' worth of rations,
to advance rapidly to Tǔlà Hé.
Hālāzhāng crossed the river to resist the battle,
but soon retreated.
They pursued him to Ālǔhún Hé,
where enemy cavalry gathered in large numbers.
The generals and soldiers all fought to the death.
The enemy was thoroughly defeated and fled,
but Liángchén, along with Commanders Zhōu Xiǎn, Cháng Róng, and Zhāng Yào, all died in battle.
When the matter was reported,
Liángchén was posthumously granted the title of Ānguó Gōng,
with the posthumous name Zhōngzhuàng,
and was enshrined in the Temple of Meritorious Officials.
His son, Tài, inherited the marquisate,
but died due to his involvement in the Lán Yù faction,
and his title was revoked.
Xiǎn
was from Héféi.
He joined the crossing of the river
and, through accumulated merits, rose to Commander Đồngzhī.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, for capturing the Hóngluó Shān stronghold in Yìngchāng,
he was promoted to Commander Shǐ.
Róng
was the great-grandnephew of Kàipíng Wáng Yùchūn,
and served successively as Commander Qiānshì.
When Yùchūn died in the army,
Róng escorted his coffin back.
He followed Zhū Liàngzǔ in pacifying Shǔ,
and successively rose to Zhènwǔ Wèi Commander Đồngzhī.
Yào
was from Shòuzhōu.
He initially served Chén Yěxiān.
After Jiànkāng fell,
he first defected.
Through accumulated merits, he became Shǒuyù Fújiàn Commander Shǐ,
and guarded Xìnghuà.
By this time, all of them had died in battle.
The emperor generously compensated the families of these officials
and ordered the relevant authorities to erect steles at their tombs.
Pú Yīng
was from Lúzhōu.
Initially, due to his bravery and strength, he became a Centurion.
Through accumulated merits, he rose to Xī'ān Wèi Commander.
Due to his failure to properly administer military affairs,
he was recalled and reprimanded.
Yè Shēng was sent to replace him.
Shēng, however, spoke highly of his virtues,
so he was ordered to return to the guard post.
In the nineteenth year of Hóngwǔ,
Tàizǔ ordered Gěng Bǐngwén to select soldiers from the Shǎnxī Dūsī guard posts to defend the border.
Only those trained by Yīng were considered elite troops,
and he was promoted to Dūdū Qiānshì.
The next year, he was ordered to lead his unit to follow Grand General Féng Shèng on the northern expedition.
Upon reaching Jīnshān,
Nàhāchū surrendered,
and the army then returned.
Yīng was assigned to command three thousand crack troops as the rear guard.
Hundreds of thousands of Nàhāchū's remaining followers were still in hiding.
Hearing of the army's return,
they set an ambush on the road,
planning to seize the main army after it passed.
They had not yet acted.
Yīng arrived later
and was suddenly attacked.
He could not break through the encirclement.
His horse stumbled, and he was captured.
Once the enemy had Yīng,
they thought of using him as a hostage.
Yīng refused food and remained silent.
Seizing an opportunity, he drew his waist-knife and disemboweled himself, dying.
When the matter was reported,
he was posthumously granted the title of Jīnshān Hóu,
with the posthumous name Zhōngxiāng.
The next year, he was further posthumously granted the title of Lèlàng Gōng.
His son, Yú, was enfeoffed as Xīliáng Hóu,
with a stipend of two thousand five hundred shí of grain,
and was granted a hereditary charter.
In the twenty-third year,
he was ordered to train troops in Dōngchāng,
and also to be stationed in Línqīng
to train soldiers.
In the twenty-fifth year,
he was recalled
to jointly inspect soldiers and horses in Shānxī with Sòngguó Gōng Shèng and others.
Yú was able to fulfill his father's duties,
and the emperor greatly praised him.
He was again ordered to register civilian militias in Shānxī.
The number of registered prefectures and counties was the highest,
and the task was completed without disturbance.
The next year, he was implicated in the Lán Yù faction
and died while in exile in Wǔkāi.
Among the Commander Shǐ who died in service during the Hóngwǔ reign,
there were also Yú Guāng, Yán Dé, and Sūn Hǔ.
Guāng
was from Dūchāng.
He initially served Xú Shòuhuī,
and was stationed in Fúliáng.
When Chén Yǒuliàng assassinated Shòuhuī,
Guāng surrendered Fúliáng,
was granted the title of Shūmìyuàn Pàn,
and through accumulated merits, became Yīngyáng Wèi Commander,
stationed in Gǒngchāng.
Kuòkuò besieged Lánzhōu,
and Guāng rushed to reinforce.
Upon reaching Mǎlán Tān,
he was defeated in battle and captured,
then paraded below the city walls.
Guāng shouted loudly:
"Gentlemen, just hold firm!
General Xú will arrive with a large army morning or night!"
The bandits were enraged,
slapped his cheek,
and then killed him.
He was enshrined in the Temple of Meritorious Officials.
Yán Dé
was from Tàipíng.
He joined the uprising
and, through accumulated merits, became Hǎiníng Wèi Commander.
He followed Zhū Liàngzǔ in suppressing Fāng Guózhēn,
and died in battle in Táizhōu.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Tiānshuǐ Jùn Gōng.
Sūn Hǔ,
his origin is unknown.
He joined the relief effort for Chízhōu,
conquered Yúqián and Chānghuà,
and pacified Jiàndé and Zhūquán.
He had merits in all these actions,
and was granted the title of Qiānhù.
He captured Xīnchéng, Tóng, and Lú,
and was promoted to Hǎiníng Wèi Commander Shǐ.
He suppressed bandits in Jiāxīng.
He followed Deputy General Lǐ Wénzhōng on the northern expedition,
entering Yìngchāng via the eastern route.
He died in battle against the Yuán army at Luòmǎ Hé.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Kāng'ān Jùn Bó.
There was also Commander Qiānshì Liú Guǎng,
who died fighting against invaders while guarding Yǒngpíng.
Liú Lín, a Centurion of Liángzhōu Wèi, was stationed in Liángzhōu.
When Yěxiān Tiěmù'ér rebelled,
he died in battle.
The border people admired him,
and named his residence, Dòu Róng Tái, as Liú Lín Tái.
Yuán Xīng, a Centurion of Qiántáng Wèi,
was from Quánjiāo.
He joined the expedition to Yúnnán,
volunteered to be the vanguard,
and died while charging into the enemy lines.
All were commended and posthumously granted titles of varying degrees.
A eulogy states:
When Míngzǔ rose,
from the decision to cross the river,
he first struggled mightily within thousands of lì in the southeast,
crushing Yǒuliàng
and eliminating Shìchéng.
Only then did he pacify the Central Plains in the north
and scheme to conquer Mǐn and Yuè in the south.
How could the merits of Liáo Yǒng'ān, Hú Dàhǎi, and others,
from them downwards, be considered small?
They wasted no time,
offering their lives on the frontiers.
Although their achievements and careers were not fully realized,
they were honored and enshrined in temples,
their names splendidly recorded in bamboo and silk.
Compared to those whose accomplishments led to titles, but who eventually suffered from factional purges,
they were surely fortunate!
Collation Notes

Biographies, Volume 22: Hé Wénhuī (Xú Sīmǎ), Yè Wàng (Mǎ Yún), Miáo Dàhēng (Wǔ Dé), Cài Qiān (Chén Wén), Wáng Míng, Níng Zhèng (Yuán Yì), Jīn Xīngwàng (Fèi Zǐxián), Huā Mào, Dīng Yù, Guō Yún (Wáng Pǔ).
Hé Wénhuī,
courtesy name Démíng,
was a native of Chú.
When Tàizǔ attacked Chúzhōu,
he captured Wénhuī,
who was fourteen years old.
Tàizǔ raised him as his own son
and bestowed upon him the surname Zhū.
In the early days of Tàizǔ’s rise,
he adopted many righteous sons.
When they grew up,
he ordered them to accompany various generals in garrisoning different routes.
Zhōu Shè guarded Zhènjiāng,
Dào Shè guarded Níngguó,
Mǎ'ér guarded Wùzhōu,
Chái Shè and Zhēntóng guarded Chǔzhōu,
Jīngāngnú guarded Qúzhōu.
All of them were adopted sons.
Jīngāngnú's later records are unknown.
Zhōu Shè was Mù Yīng,
also called Mù Shè by the army.
Chái Shè
was Zhū Wéngāng,
who died in the disaster at Chǔzhōu with Gěng Zàichéng.
There was also Zhū Wénxùn,
whose courtesy name is not recorded in history,
who also died at Tàipíng as an adopted son.
Apart from Mù Yīng,
the most prominent were Dào Shè and Mǎ'ér.
Mǎ'ér was Xú Sīmǎ,
and Dào Shè was Wénhuī.
Wénhuī, as the Heavenly Pacification Wing Marshal, guarded Níngguó
and was promoted to Provincial Administrator of the Jiāngxī Branch Secretariat.
He repeatedly attacked the unconquered prefectures and counties in Jiāngxī,
and campaigned against Dèng Zhònglián of Xīngàn,
beheading him.
He relieved Ānfú,
drove off Ráo Dǐngchén,
and pacified Shānjiānzhài.
He followed Xú Dá to take Huáidōng,
and again followed in subjugating Píngjiāng.
He was granted embroidered silks
and promoted to Assistant Administrator of the Branch Secretariat,
and his original surname was restored.
As Vice General-in-Chief of the Southern Expedition, he, along with Pingzhang Hú Měi, took Fújiàn from Jiāngxī.
They crossed Shānguān,
entered Guāngzé,
swept through Shàowǔ and Jiànyáng,
and advanced directly to Jiànníng.
The Yuán co-administrator Dá Lǐmá and provincial administrator Chén Zǐqí closed the gates and resisted.
Wénhuī and Měi jointly attacked them.
After more than ten days,
Dá Lǐmá could not hold out
and secretly went to Wénhuī's camp at night to beg for surrender.
The next morning,
commander Zhái Yěxiānbùhuā also surrendered with his troops to Wénhuī.
Měi was angry that the two did not come to him
and wanted to slaughter the city.
Wénhuī galloped to Měi and said:
"We both received orders to come here
to bring peace to the common people.
Now that they have surrendered,
how can we kill people out of personal resentment?"
Měi then stopped.
The army entered the city,
and did not harm a single hair.
Upon hearing this, the various prefectures and counties of Tīng and Quán
all successively submitted.
At that time, the imperial carriage traveled to Biànliáng,
and Wénhuī was summoned to accompany it.
He was then appointed Commissioner of the Hénán Guard
to pacify the remaining bandits in Rǔzhōu.
He followed the Grand General to take Shǎnxī
and was left to guard Tóngguān.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ (1370), he was appointed Commander-in-chief of the Grand Military Commission
and granted a hereditary position as Commissioner.
He again, as a participating general, followed Fù Yǒudé and others to pacify Shǔ,
was granted gold and silk,
and left to guard Chéngdū.
Wénhuī's orders were clear and strict,
and both soldiers and civilians esteemed his virtue.
The emperor once praised his strategy and prestige.
He was promoted to Co-administrator of the Grand Military Commission.
In the fifth year (1372), he was ordered to lead the Shandong troops with Lǐ Wénzhōng out to Yìngchāng.
The next year, he was transferred to garrison Běipíng.
When Lǐ Wénzhōng campaigned in the north,
Wénhuī commanded troops to patrol Jūyōngguān,
but was recalled due to illness.
He died in the sixth month of the ninth year (1376),
at the age of thirty-six.
An official was sent to oversee his burial on the Shāhé River east of Chúzhōu,
and the condolences and grants were very generous.
His son, Huán,
was Commissioner of the Chéngdū Protective Guard,
and died in battle during an expedition to Yǐběi.
Xú Sīmǎ,
courtesy name Cóngzhèng,
was a native of Yángzhōu.
During the chaos of war at the end of the Yuán dynasty,
at the age of nine,
he had no one to depend on.
Tàizǔ found him,
adopted him as a son,
and also bestowed a surname upon him.
When he grew up,
he attended the emperor's side.
When Wùzhōu was taken,
he was appointed General Administrator
and ordered to assist Marshal Cháng Yùchūn in guarding Wù.
In the first year of Wú (1367), he was appointed Co-administrator of the Jīnhuá Guard.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ (1368), he followed Vice General-in-Chief Lǐ Wénzhōng on the northern expedition,
capturing the Yuán princely lord Qìngshēng.
He was promoted to Commissioner of the Hángzhōu Guard
and soon advanced to Grand Commissioner.
An imperial decree restored his original surname.
In the ninth year (1376), he was transferred to garrison Hénán.
At that time, a new Northern Capital was established in Biànliáng,
called a vital strategic point.
The emperor had always highly regarded Sīmǎ
and specially entrusted him with this responsibility.
The Duke of Sòng, Féng Shèng, was then training troops in Hénán.
At one point, a celestial phenomenon appeared,
interpreted as pertaining to Dàliáng.
The emperor sent an envoy with a secret decree to Shèng,
and also said:
"Also inform Mǎ'ér of this matter."
Afterward, he issued another decree to both men, saying:
"Celestial phenomena have appeared repeatedly,
and with the mix of military and civilian populations in Dàliáng,
special caution is required.
Now the Prince of Qín and Prince of Jìn are returning to the capital,
and strict military guard should be maintained.
When the princes arrive in Biàn,
if the Duke of Sòng goes out to welcome them,
then the Grand Commissioner shall remain in charge of the garrison;
if the Grand Commissioner goes out to welcome them,
then the Duke of Sòng shall do likewise."
The imperial decree referred to them by their official titles and not by name,
showing that Sīmǎ was held in equal esteem with the Duke of Sòng.
In the nineteenth year (1386), he entered the court for an audience
and was subsequently promoted to Commander-in-chief of the Central Military Commission.
In the twenty-fifth year (1392),
as Left Vice General-in-Chief, he followed Lán Yù to campaign in Jiànchāng
and suppress Yuèsuī.
He died the first month of the following year (1393) upon returning to Chéngdū.
He was posthumously implicated in Lán Yù's faction,
and both his sons were punished.
Sīmǎ loved literature,
and his nature was modest and magnanimous.
Wherever he went, he consoled and cared for his soldiers,
winning the hearts of the people.
He was in Hénán for a long time
and implemented especially benevolent policies.
In his leisure time, he lived in retirement,
his room simple and austere as if he were a commoner.
Although his military achievements did not surpass Wénhuī's,
his magnanimity exceeded his,
and he was also praised as a worthy general.
Yè Wàng,
a native of Lù'ān.
He and Mǎ Yún, a native of Héféi, were both centurions (qiānhù) serving under Xiè Zàixīng in the Long Spear Army.
When Zàixīng rebelled,
the two extricated themselves and returned.
After numerous campaigns,
they accumulated merits and were both appointed Assistant Commanders (zhīhuī qiānshì).
In the fourth year of Hóngwǔ (1371), they were sent to garrison Liáodōng.
Initially,
after the Yuán emperor fled north,
Liú Yì, a councilor (cānzhèng) of the Liáoyáng Branch Secretariat (xíngshěng), garrisoned Gàizhōu,
and he and Administrator (píngzhāng) Gāo Jiānú supported each other,
holding Jīn and Fù prefectures.
The Emperor dispatched Adviser (duànshì) Huáng Chóu with an imperial edict to persuade Yì.
Yì submitted a register of his troops, horses, provisions, and territory, and surrendered.
Thus, the Liáoyáng Regional Military Commission (zhīhuīshǐ sī) was established,
with Yì appointed as Co-Administrator (zhīhuī tóngzhī).
Not long after,
Yuán Administrators Hóng Bǎobǎo and Mǎ Yànfēi conspired to kill Yì.
Right Chancellor (yòuchéng) Zhāng Liángzuǒ and Left Chancellor (zuǒchéng) Shāng Gǎo captured Yànfēi and killed him.
Bǎobǎo seized Chóu and fled to Nàháchū's camp.
Liángzuǒ then temporarily took charge of the guard affairs
and reported the situation.
He also said:
"Liáodōng is situated in a remote corner of the sea,
with enemy territories on all sides.
Administrator Gāo Jiānú holds the mountain stronghold of Liáoyáng;
Administrator (zhīyuàn) Hālázhāng garrisons the old city of Shěnyáng;
at Kāiyuán is Right Chancellor Yěxiānbùhuā;
at Jīnshān is Grand Commandant (tàiwèi) Nàháchū.
They rely on each other
and frequently plan invasions.
Now that Bǎobǎo has fled,
conflict is inevitable.
I request that Adviser Wú Lì be left to pacify the military and civilians,
and that the captured Administrator Bādān and Administrator Sēngrú, among others, be sent in shackles to the capital."
The Emperor ordered Lì, Liángzuǒ, and Gǎo to all be made Assistant Commanders of the Gàizhōu Guard (wèi).
Later, considering Liáoyáng a strategic location,
he re-established the Regional Military Commission (dū zhīhuīshǐ sī) to command the various guards,
appointing Wàng and Yún both as Regional Military Commissioners (dū zhīhuīshǐ) to garrison it.
Soon after,
learning that Chóu had been killed
and Nàháchū was planning an invasion,
he issued an edict for Wàng and others to make preparations.
Not long after,
Nàháchū indeed arrived with his forces.
Seeing the strict defenses,
he dared not attack,
and bypassed Gài to Jīnzhōu.
The Jīnzhōu city wall was incomplete,
so Commanders Wéi Fù, Wáng Shèng, and others directed the soldiers to defend the various gates.
Nǎláwúzhe,
a brave enemy general,
led several hundred elite cavalry to challenge at the city walls.
He was hit by a hidden crossbow bolt and fell,
captured by our soldiers.
The enemy was greatly discouraged.
Fù and others unleashed their troops to attack,
and the enemy retreated.
They dared not follow their original route
but fled along the Zuòhé river, ten li south of Gàichéng.
Wàng had already positioned troops to block the Zuòhé.
From Liányúndǎo to Kūtuózài, over ten li,
ice walls were built along the river,
doused with water,
and after a night, they froze solid like a city wall.
Spiked boards were placed in the sand,
pits were dug on the sides,
and ambush troops lay in wait.
Yún and Commanders Zhōu È, Wú Lì, and others erected large flags within the city,
kept their troops in strict formation without moving,
as if no one were there.
Soon,
the bandits reached the south of the city.
Ambush troops rose on all sides,
flags and banners covered the sky on both mountains,
and arrows and stones rained down.
Nàháchū frantically headed towards Liányúndǎo,
encountered the ice city,
tried to go around,
but all fell into the pits,
and consequently suffered a great rout.
Yún emerged from the city,
combined forces, and pursued the enemy to Jiāngjūnshān and Bìlìhé.
Countless enemies were slain, captured, or froze to death.
They pressed the pursuit to Zhū'éryù.
Nàháchū barely escaped with his life.
For their achievements,
Wàng and Yún were both promoted to Assistant Commander-in-Chief (dūdu qiānshì).
This was the eighth year of Hóngwǔ (1375).
In the twelfth year (1379), Yún was ordered to campaign against Dàníng.
Upon hearing of his victory,
he was rewarded
and recalled to the capital.
He died several years later.
Wàng remained garrisoned as before.
At this time, Góulí sent envoys with letters and gifts,
and Zhèng Bái and others from Lóngzhōu requested to surrender.
Wàng reported this.
The Emperor said that officials should not engage in foreign diplomacy,
that this was the beginning of espionage,
and should not be lightly trusted.
They were merely showing weakness to us
to scout for border conflicts.
He returned them,
so they would have no pretext.
The next year,
Wàng again sent the Góulí envoy Zhōu Yì to the capital.
The Emperor, considering their regicide in their country
and treacherous killing of imperial envoys,
found them untrustworthy and deceitful.
He severely reprimanded Wàng and others to break off relations with them,
and kept Yì without sending him back.
In the nineteenth year (1386), Wàng was summoned to be Assistant Commander-in-Chief of the Rear Army Regional Military Commission (hòujūn dūdufǔ qiānshì).
After three months,
there was an alert in Liáodōng,
and he was again ordered to return to garrison.
He died in the third month of the twenty-first year (1388).
During Wàng and Yún's garrisoning of Liáo,
they cleared thorny bushes,
established military prefectures,
pacified and gathered soldiers and civilians,
and reclaimed over ten thousand qǐng of farmland,
thus securing lasting benefits.
Wàng served particularly long,
a total of seventeen years.
The people of Liáo appreciated him.
In the early Jiājìng era,
because of their contributions to Liáo,
officials were ordered to establish shrines
and offer sacrifices in spring and autumn.
Miáo Dàhēng,
a native of Dìngyuǎn.
Initially, he rallied a volunteer army to attack Háo for the Yuán dynasty.
He failed.
When the Yuán army was routed,
Dàhēng alone, with a force of twenty thousand, and Administrator Zhāng, garrisoned Héngjiànshān,
holding it firmly for over a month.
Tàizǔ attacked their camp by stratagem at night,
defeating them.
Dàhēng and his son escaped.
By dawn,
he had reassembled his scattered troops
and arrayed them in wait.
Tàizǔ sent his uncle, Zhēn, to persuade him to surrender.
He was ordered to lead his division in campaigns,
and after several achievements,
was promoted to Marshal (yuánshuài).
He commanded troops to take Yángzhōu
and captured it.
He accepted the surrender of the Blue Army Marshal, Zhāng Míngjiàn.
Initially,
Míngjiàn gathered a force in Huáixī,
using blue cloth as a symbol,
calling themselves
"Blue Army" (Qīngjūn).
Also, being skilled with long spears,
they were called
"Long Spear Army" (Chángqiāngjūn).
From Hánshān, they moved to plunder Yángzhōu.
Yuán Prince of Zhènnán, Bólúopǔhuà, persuaded them to surrender,
appointing Míngjiàn as Marshal of the Háo and Sì Volunteer Army.
More than a year later,
their provisions ran out,
and they plotted to lead the Prince in rebellion.
The Prince fled and died in Huái'ān.
Míngjiàn then occupied the city
and slaughtered residents for food.
Dàhēng told Tàizǔ,
"The bandits are hungry and distressed.
If they scatter to plunder for food, they will be difficult to control.
Moreover, they are fierce and can be used,
so we should not let others gain them."
Tàizǔ ordered Dàhēng to attack immediately.
Míngjiàn surrendered,
yielding tens of thousands of troops and over two thousand horses.
All their officers' wives and children were sent to Yìngtiān.
The Huáihǎi Wing Marshal's Office (huáihǎi yì yuánshuàifǔ) was renamed the Jiāngnán Branch Bureau of Military Affairs (jiāngnán fēn shūmìyuàn),
with Dàhēng appointed as Associate Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs (tóngqiān shūmìyuàn shì),
in overall charge of Yángzhōu and Zhènjiāng.
Dàhēng had governing strategies;
he was lenient and did not disturb the people,
yet his military discipline was strict.
He suppressed violence and eliminated evildoers,
and the people greatly rejoiced in him.
He died not long after.
When Tàizǔ passed through Zhènjiāng,
he sighed, saying:
"General Miáo was upright throughout his life,
never having committed a fault.
It is a pity I no longer see him."
He dispatched an envoy to sacrifice at his tomb.
Wǔ Dé,
a native of Ānfēng.
During the Zhìzhèng reign of the Yuán dynasty, he served as a chiliarch (qiānhù) in the righteous army.
Knowing that the Yuán dynasty was about to fall,
he said to his commander Zhāng Jiàn:
"We are talented and brave, worth ten thousand men,
but now we are suffering defeats in the east and setbacks in the west.
The situation is clear;
it's better to choose a patron early."
Zhāng Jiàn agreed with his words,
and they led their men to pledge allegiance to Tàizǔ.
He was subordinate to Lǐ Wénzhōng,
and followed him to Chízhōu.
He fought bravely,
and a stray arrow struck his right thigh.
He pulled it out,
and continued fighting as if nothing had happened.
He participated in the capture of Yúqián and Chānghuà,
and the conquest of Yánzhōu,
all of which he was involved in,
and was promoted to myriad-householder (wànhù).
When the Miáo commander Yáng Wánzhě's army was stationed at Wūlónglǐng,
Wǔ Dé requested, saying:
"This can be taken by surprise attack."
Wénzhōng asked why.
He replied:
"Observing them from a height,
their troops move restlessly and are noisy."
Wénzhōng said:
"Excellent."
They immediately attacked Yáng Wánzhě by surprise,
overthrowing his camp.
He took Lánxī,
conquered Zhūjì,
and attacked Shàoxīng.
In all these, he was the first to scale the walls and penetrate the enemy lines,
disregarding an injury to his right arm.
Wénzhōng sighed, saying:
"If every officer and soldier were like this,
what battle would not be victorious?"
When Jiǎng Yīng and Hè Réndé rebelled,
eastern Zhèjiāng was greatly shaken.
He followed Wénzhōng to pacify Jīnhuá,
then followed him to attack Chǔzhōu.
He encountered Hè Réndé at Liúshān,
and a spear struck his right thigh.
Wǔ Dé drew his sword and cut off the spear,
then pursued and attacked him.
Hè Réndé fought again,
was defeated again and fled,
and was subsequently killed by his own subordinates.
Wǔ Dé returned to guard Yánzhōu.
Two years later,
when the official system was established,
he was reappointed as a hundred-householder (bǎihù) of the military administration.
He followed Wénzhōng to defeat Zhāng Shìchéng's forces at Zhūjì,
and joined other generals to reinforce Pǔchéng,
taking all mountain strongholds along the way.
He again followed Wénzhōng to conquer the three prefectures of Jiànzhōu, Yánpíng, and Dīngzhōu,
and pacified all the strongholds in Mǐnxī,
advancing to chiliarch (qiānhù) of the military administration.
He was transferred to guard Qúzhōu,
and granted hereditary succession.
Finally, he followed the Marquis of Jìnghǎi, Wú Zhēn, to patrol the sea.
Wú Zhēn considered Wǔ Dé capable,
and ordered him to guard Píngyáng.
He served for eight years,
then retired.
When Yúnnán was later conquered,
the Emperor, considering Wǔ Dé an experienced general,
ordered him to accompany the other great commanders.
Zhāng Jiàn,
also known as Míng Jiàn,
was from Huáixī.
After submitting to Tàizǔ,
he always accompanied Wǔ Dé in every campaign,
and died before Wǔ Dé.
His highest office was Vice Commissioner of the Jiānghuái Branch Secretariat Council (Xíng Shūmìyuàn Fùshǐ).
Cài Qiān,
whose native place is unknown,
followed Zhīmá Lǐ to occupy Xúzhōu at the end of the Yuán dynasty.
After Zhīmá Lǐ was defeated,
he submitted to Tàizǔ,
serving as vanguard.
He followed in crossing the river,
capturing Cǎishí,
conquering Tàipíng,
taking Lìshuǐ,
and defeating Mánzi Hǎiyá's naval camp and Chén Yěxiān;
he was meritorious in all these.
After pacifying Jíqìng,
he was granted the title of chiliarch (qiānhù).
He followed Xú Dá to take Guǎngdé and Níngguó,
and was promoted to myriad-householder (wànhù).
He advanced to attack Chángzhōu,
captured Commander Huáng,
and was then made Chief Vanguard (Dū Xiānfēng).
He followed in the campaign at Mǎtuóshā,
conquered Chízhōu,
attacked Cōngyáng,
and followed in the campaign against Qúzhōu and Wùzhōu.
He was granted the title of Commander of the Left Wing in front of the Tent (Zhàngqián Zuǒyì Yuánshuài).
He defeated Chén Yǒuliàng at Lóngjiāng,
advanced to retake Tàipíng,
captured the Ánqìng naval camp,
recovered Jiǔjiāng,
defeated Chén Yǒuliàng's Eight Array Commander at Ruìchāng,
and then conquered Nánchāng.
He followed in reinforcing Ānfēng,
attacking Héféi,
fighting at Póyáng,
and campaigning against Wǔchāng.
He was promoted to Assistant Commander (Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī).
He followed Cháng Yùchūn to pacify the remnants of Dèng Kèmíng's party,
advanced to attack Gànzhōu,
took Nán'ān and Nánxióng commanderies,
and returned with his army to pursue Ráo Dǐngchén at Chálíng.
He was transferred to Assistant Commander of the Lóngxiáng Guard (Lóngxiáng Wèi Tóngzhī).
He followed Xú Dá to conquer Gāoyóu,
defeated Mǎgǎng,
was granted the title of Commander of Wǔdé Guard (Wǔdé Wèi Zhǐhuīshǐ),
and guarded Huái'ān,
then was transferred to guard Huángzhōu.
He followed in taking Xiāngtán, Chénzhōu, Quánzhōu, Dàozhōu, and Yǒngzhōu,
and was transferred to Commander of Jīngzhōu Guard (Jīngzhōu Wèi Zhǐhuī).
He advanced to conquer Guǎngxī,
and was transferred to Administrator of the Guǎngxī Branch Secretariat (Guǎngxī Xíngshěng Cānzhèng),
also serving as Chancellor to the Prince of Jìngjiāng (Jìngjiāng Wáng Xiāng).
He pacified all the rebellious "barbarians".
He died in the ninth month of the third year of Hóngwǔ (1370).
An imperial edict ordered his burial in the capital,
and he was posthumously enfeoffed as Marquis of Ānyuǎn (Ānyuǎn Hóu)
and given the posthumous name Wǔxiāng.
Cài Qiān served as a general for fifteen years,
never acting alone,
but mostly accompanying other generals on campaigns.
He personally participated in dozens of battles,
always bravely charging forward,
wielding his sword left and right.
The enemies all scattered, daring not to approach.
Upon returning,
his body was covered in battle wounds.
People considered them unbearable,
but Cài Qiān paid little attention to them.
He was greatly beloved and respected by Tàizǔ.
When he died,
the Emperor especially grieved for him,
and personally composed a eulogy and sacrifice for him.
Chén Wén of Héféi,
who campaigned north and south,
accumulated many military achievements,
was also comparable to Cài Qiān.
Chén Wén was orphaned young,
and served his mother with extreme filial piety.
At the end of the Yuán dynasty, he brought his family to pledge allegiance to Tàizǔ,
and successively rose to the rank of Assistant Military Commissioner (Dūdū Qiānshì).
After his death,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as Marquis of Dōnghǎi (Dōnghǎi Hóu)
and given the posthumous name Xiàoyǒng.
Among the ministers of the Míng dynasty who received the posthumous name Xiào,
Chén Wén was the only one.
Wáng Míng,
courtesy name Zǐjìng,
was a native of Hézhōu.
He initially served under Grand Marshal Yú Tōnghǎi.
He followed him in attacking Mánzi Hǎiyá at Cǎishí.
Because Míng was brave and fierce,
he was selected to be a commando.
When the battle was joined,
the marshal led his death-defying warriors to shout and charge,
capturing their water stockade.
From then on, he had several successes.
During a battle with the Wú army at Tàihú,
a stray arrow struck his right arm.
He drew his belt-knife to remove the arrowhead,
and resumed fighting.
Tōnghǎi commended him.
He then captured the Huángqiáo and Éxiàng stockades in Tōngzhōu.
He was awarded white gold and patterned silk.
During the Battle of Lóngwān,
he pursued the routed enemy to Cǎishí.
Míng alone charged into the enemy formation.
Enemy soldiers thrust their spears at Míng,
wounding his cheek.
Míng charged in and out three times,
killing and wounding an extraordinary number.
He was awarded patterned silk and a silver bowl,
and selected to serve in the imperial guard.
He followed in taking Jiāngzhōu,
fought at Kānglángshān and Jīngjiāngkǒu,
and again captured the various stockades in Yīngshān,
being promoted to Commandant of a Hundred Households overseeing troops.
He followed Vice General Cháng Yùchūn in battle at Shēngshān in Húzhōu,
then fought again at Jiùguǎn.
After this,
he also fought at Wūzhèn.
After dozens of battles before and after,
he amassed many merits,
and was ordered to guard Sōngjiāng.
He was transferred to Tàicāng,
where he captured and beheaded over a thousand Japanese pirates,
and was again awarded gold and silk.
In the fourth year of Hóngwǔ, during the imperial examination for commanders of a hundred households who were skilled with spears,
none could contend with Míng.
He was successively promoted to Assistant Commander of Chánghuái Guard,
and then transferred to guard Wēnzhōu.
He submitted a memorial saying:
“The commandery under my jurisdiction
controls the island barbarians from outside.
The city walls and watchtowers are still crude and rudimentary,
which is not only insufficient to enhance national prestige,
but in the event of sudden winds and tides,
there would be nowhere to defend.
It is imperative that they be rebuilt.”
The emperor approved.
Thereupon, the city walls were repaired and the moats dredged,
all twofold larger than before.
An outer wall was additionally built,
extending from Hǎishénshān to Guōgōngshān,
with a total length of over two thousand zhàng.
It was grand, spacious, and magnificent,
standing majestically as a major stronghold in eastern Zhèjiāng.
The emperor greatly praised him,
and granted him hereditary succession.
Míng once requested leave to return temporarily to Hézhōu.
The gentry and women of Wēnzhōu lined the roads to see him off and welcome him.
The senior officials all looked at each other and sighed, saying:
“We serve as shepherds of the people for the Son of Heaven.
The people are indifferent to our comings and goings.
We are much ashamed before Commander Wáng.”
He successively held the post of Assistant Military Commissioner of the Right Army Command,
but in the twenty-sixth year, he was implicated in the Lán Yù faction and died.
Níng Zhèng,
courtesy name Zhèngqīng,
was a native of Shòuzhōu.
As a child, he was adopted by Wéi Décchéng,
and assumed the surname Wéi.
At the end of the Yuán dynasty, he followed Décchéng and came to pledge allegiance,
following him across the river.
When Décchéng died in battle at Xuānzhōu,
Zhèng was appointed to lead his troops,
and accumulated merits to become Assistant Commander of Fèngxiáng Guard.
He followed in pacifying the Central Plains,
entered the Yuán capital,
and persuaded over eight thousand Yuán officers and soldiers to surrender.
Fù Yǒudé pacified Dìngzhōu after a lightning campaign from Zhēndìng,
and Zhèng was ordered to guard Zhēndìng.
After this,
he followed the main army to capture Shǎnxī.
When Féng Shèng captured Líntáo,
Zhèng was left to guard it.
When the main army besieged Qìngyáng,
Zhèng was stationed in Bīnzhōu,
cutting off enemy reinforcements.
After Qìngyáng fell,
he returned to guard Líntáo.
He followed Dèng Yù in defeating Dìngxī
and capturing Hézhōu.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, he was appointed Commander of Hézhōu Guard.
He memorialized, saying:
“The people of the west are greatly exhausted by transporting grain to provision the army,
but tea and cloth can be exchanged for grain.
I request that tea and cloth be given to the soldiers,
allowing them to trade among themselves,
thus relieving the hardship of transportation.”
The emperor decreed to follow this.
When Zhèng first arrived at the guard,
the cities and towns were desolate,
so he diligently worked to comfort and encourage the people.
In a few years,
Hézhōu became a land of prosperity.
An imperial edict commended and rewarded him,
and he finally restored his surname Níng.
He concurrently oversaw the affairs of Níngxià Guard,
repaired and built the old Hàn and Táng canals,
diverted river water to irrigate fields,
opened up tens of thousands of qǐng of military farms,
and the soldiers had abundant food.
In the thirteenth year, he followed Mù Yīng in the northern campaign,
capturing Yuán Administrator Tuōhuǒchì and Chief Administrator Àizú,
and took the four departments of Quánníng.
In the fifteenth year, he was promoted to Military Commissioner of Sìchuān,
and pacified the various prefectures of Sōng and Mào.
When Yúnnán was first pacified,
Zhèng was ordered to guard it together with Féng Chéng.
When Sīlúnfā rebelled,
Zhèng defeated him at Mósālè stockade,
beheading one thousand five hundred.
After this,
the enemy forces gathered in great numbers,
besieging Dìngbiān.
Mù Yīng divided his troops into three teams,
and Zhèng commanded the left army.
After fierce fighting,
they inflicted a great defeat on the enemy.
The account is in Yīng's biography.
When the local chief Āzī rebelled,
he again followed Yīng and subjugated him.
When Yīng died,
an imperial edict appointed Zhèng as Left Grand Military Commissioner to take his place.
After this,
he was again appointed Pacifying Qiāng General,
commanding the Sìchuān and Shǎnxī troops to pacify the rebellious bandit Zhāng Zhě in Jiē and Wén.
In the twenty-eighth year, he followed the Prince of Qín in pacifying the Fān people of Táozhōu,
and returned to the capital.
He died the following year.
Also, Yuán Yì,
a native of Lújiāng,
originally surnamed Zhāng,
was a cousin of Déshèng.
He initially served as General Manager of Shuāngdāo Zhào,
guarding Ānqìng,
and defeated Assistant Commander Zhào and Dīng Pǔláng at Shāzǐgǎng.
Zuǒ Jūnbì invited him to join,
but he refused.
After Déshèng died in battle,
he first came to pledge allegiance,
serving as Grand Marshal of the Imperial Guard,
and was granted his surname and given name.
He repeatedly followed in campaigns,
accumulating merits to become Assistant Commander of Xīngwǔ Guard.
He followed the Grand General in the northern campaign,
defeating Yuán Administrator Ānpǔdá and others at Tōngzhōu,
and driving Hè Zōngzhé and Zhān Tóng from Zé and Lù.
His merits were outstanding.
He again followed in pacifying Shǎnxī,
defeating the troops of Yuán Prince Yù.
He joined other generals in attacking Qìngyáng.
When Zhāng Liángchén's troops suddenly pressed against Yì's camp,
Yì firmly held his defenses and did not move.
Waiting for them to become complacent,
he launched a powerful attack and routed them.
He drove Kuòkuò's army from Dìngxī,
took Xīngyuán to the south,
was promoted to Vice Commander of his original guard,
transferred to Yǔlín Guard,
and moved to guard Liáodōng.
After this,
he followed Mù Yīng in the campaign against Yúnnán,
capturing the various cities of Pǔdìng,
and was left to guard Chǔxióng.
The local barbarians rebelled repeatedly,
but Yì accumulated provisions and built high ramparts,
both defending and fighting,
and was promoted to Commander of Chǔxióng Guard for his merits.
He once came to court,
and the emperor greatly comforted and rewarded him.
Because of his old age,
he ordered a physician to dye his beard and hair,
so that he could return to his post to overawe distant people,
and specially bestowed upon him a silver seal as a mark of favor.
For twenty years,
he reclaimed land, built dams,
and managed city walls, bridges,
with very comprehensive plans.
The military and civilians were grateful to him.
In the first year of Jiànwén, he was summoned back,
serving as Assistant Commissioner of the Right Army Command,
promoted to Vice Commander,
and died in office.
Jīn Xīngwàng,
his origin is unknown.
He served as a Commander Assistant of the Wēiwǔ Guard,
then promoted to Vice Commander.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ,
Grand General Xú Dá traveled from Hénán to Shǎnxī.
He requested additional troops to guard Tóngguān,
and appointed Xīngwàng to assist Guō Xīng in defending it,
promoting him to Commander.
The following year, when Líntáo was attacked,
Xīngwàng was reassigned to guard Fèngxiáng
and transfer military provisions.
Soon after,
Hè Zōngzhé attacked Fèngxiáng.
Xīngwàng and Prefect Zhōu Huàn defended the city.
The enemy wove thorns into large baskets,
shaped like half-boats.
Each basket held five men,
who carried them to attack the city.
Arrows and stones could not penetrate them.
They threw straw to burn them,
but the wind always scattered the flames.
So, hooks were placed among the straw,
and thrown into the gaps.
The fire then became fierce,
and the enemy abandoned the baskets and fled.
They then dug tunnels beneath the city wall.
Inside the city, spears were used to stab them,
and many enemies died,
but the attack did not cease.
Xīngwàng discussed with Huàn, saying:
“They think our relief forces will not arrive,
and we will surely not dare to sally out.
If we attack them by surprise,
we can defeat them.”
They secretly sallied out from the northwest gate,
and fought fiercely.
The enemy retreated slightly.
Coincidentally, Company Commander Wáng Lù was returning eastward from Líntáo with surrendered soldiers from Lǐ Sīqí.
He immediately led his troops into the city to defend together.
The enemy broke camp and left.
The troops wanted to pursue them,
but Lù said:
“To retreat without being defeated
is to lure us.”
They sent cavalry to scout,
and upon reaching Wǔlǐpō,
the ambush was indeed sprung.
The enemy returned and re-besieged the city.
The troops discussed fleeing,
but Xīngwàng shouted:
“The Emperor entrusted this city to us;
how can we abandon it!”
Since Lù’s troops were all newly surrendered,
he worried about a mutiny.
So, he gathered all the city's wealth and livestock in the courtyard,
and announced:
“When the enemy eases their attack,
we will greatly reward the new soldiers.”
The new soldiers were delighted
and cooperated in steadfast defense.
After a standoff of fifteen days,
the enemy heard that Qìngyáng had fallen,
and then withdrew.
The Emperor sent an envoy with gold brocade to reward Xīngwàng and others.
The following year,
when Dá entered Miǎnzhōu,
he sent Xīngwàng and Zhāng Lóng to enter Liányúnzhàn from Fèngxiáng,
and jointly attack Xīngyuán.
The defending general surrendered,
and Xīngwàng was appointed to guard it,
promoted to Assistant of the Grand Military Commission.
Shǔ General Wú Yǒurén led an army of thirty thousand to raid Xīngyuán.
Xīngwàng led all three thousand soldiers in the city to resist the enemy.
He was struck by a stray arrow in the face,
but pulled out the arrow and continued fighting,
slaying several hundred men.
The enemy grew in numbers,
so he gathered his troops and re-entered the city.
Yǒurén drained the moats and filled the trenches,
planning for a sure victory.
When Dá heard of this,
he ordered Fù Yǒudé to launch a night raid on Mùcáo Pass,
and attack Dòushān Stockade.
Each man carried ten torches,
stretching across the mountain.
Yǒurén fled in alarm.
Xīngwàng led his troops out to pursue them;
countless enemies fell from cliffs and rocks to their deaths.
Yǒurén’s morale was broken thereafter.
At that time, Xīngwàng's prestige suppressed Lǒng and Shǔ.
Among the Grand Commanders in the early days of the dynasty,
for their achievements in city defense,
besides Xīngwàng, Fèi Zixián was especially lauded.
Zixián,
his origin is also unknown.
He followed across the river,
serving as the Marshal of Guǎngdé Wing,
and achieved many merits.
He captured Wǔkāng,
then captured Ānjí,
and built a city to defend it.
Zhāng Shìchéng's troops attacked several times,
but were always defeated and retreated.
Finally, Left Chancellor Zhāng attacked with eighty thousand soldiers,
while Zixián’s command had only three thousand men,
yet he defended very resolutely.
He set up carriage ballistas on the city walls,
shooting down two of their brave generals,
and the enemy then withdrew.
For his achievements, he was promoted to Commander Vice Commander.
He rendered meritorious service in capturing Fújiàn,
and in seizing Yuándū and Dìngxī,
and was appointed Assistant of the Grand Military Commission,
and his post as Commander was made hereditary.
Huā Mào,
a native of Cháoxiàn.
He initially followed Chén Yěxiān,
but later came over to pledge allegiance.
He participated in the pacification of Jiāngzuǒ,
the annihilation of Chén Yǒuliàng,
and the pacification of Zhōngyuán, Shānxī, and Shǎnxī.
Accumulating merits, he was appointed Vice Company Commander of Wǔchāng Guard.
He campaigned in Xīshǔ,
captured Qútáng Pass,
entered Chóngqìng,
subdued the left and right Jiāng rivers and Tiánzhōu,
and was promoted to Commander Assistant of Shéncè Guard,
then transferred to Guǎngzhōu Left Guard.
He pacified the rebellious Man barbarians in the mountain stockades of Yángchūn, Qīngyuǎn, Yīngdé, Wēngyuán, Bóluó, and the unruly commoners in Dōngguǎn, Lóngchuān counties,
and was promoted to Commander Vice Commander.
He pacified the bandits of Diànbái and Guīshàn,
and was again promoted to Vice Regional Commander,
with a hereditary post as Commander.
He frequently suppressed the Yáo bandits of Liánzhōu, Guǎngxī, and Húguǎng.
He reported:
“The southern border of Guǎngdōng faces the vast ocean,
where villains and outlaws frequently appear.
The runaway boat-dwellers in Dōngguǎn and Sǔngāng counties
reside on offshore islands.
When they encounter government troops, they falsely claim to be fishing,
but when they encounter foreign pirates, they join them in raiding.
They are erratic and unpredictable,
making it difficult to interrogate them.
It would be better to register them as soldiers,
which would facilitate control.”
He also requested the establishment of twenty-four guards and posts along the coast and mountains, such as Guǎnghǎi, Jiéshí, Shéndiàn, etc.,
to build cities and deepen moats,
and to gather the hidden, unregistered soldiers from the islands.
Furthermore, he proposed establishing fortresses and stationing troops in strategic mountain and coastal locations,
to guard against unforeseen events.
All his proposals were approved.
He was promoted to Regional Commander.
He died after a long time,
and was granted burial outside Āndémén.
His eldest son Róng inherited his position.
His second son Yīng,
resolute and brave with his father's style,
also became a Guǎngdōng Regional Commander through military merit,
and was renowned during the Yǒnglè reign.
Dīng Yù,
originally named Guózhēn,
a native of Hézhōng.
He served Hán Lín'ér as a Censor,
known for his talent and eloquence at the time.
When Lǚ Zhēn captured Ānfēng,
Yù came to pledge allegiance.
He followed in the campaign of Pénglǐ,
and became the Prefect of Jiǔjiāng.
When the main army returned to Jiànkāng,
the mountain people of Péngzé rebelled.
Yù gathered local militias and suppressed them.
Tàizǔ praised his military strategy,
appointed him concurrently as Commander,
and changed his name to Yù.
He followed Fù Yǒudé in capturing Héngzhōu,
and was appointed Commander Vice Commander to garrison that area,
then transferred to guard Yǒngzhōu.
Yù possessed both civil and military talents,
and his efforts in pacifying the newly surrendered earned him great prestige.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, he was promoted to Commander-in-chief,
then concurrently acting Provincial Administration Commissioner,
garrisoning Guǎngxī.
In the tenth year, he was summoned to serve as Right Censor-in-chief.
When Dǒng Tiēlǐ, a native chieftain in Wēimào, Sìchuān, rebelled,
Yù was appointed Pacifier of the Qiāng General to suppress him.
When he arrived at Wēizhōu,
Tiēlǐ surrendered.
By imperial authority, he established the Wēizhōu Thousand-Household Guard.
In the twelfth year, Sōngzhōu was pacified.
Yù sent Commander Gāo Xiǎn and others to build its city,
and requested the establishment of a military guard.
The emperor said that Sōngzhōu had many mountains and little arable land,
and farming could not sustain the army,
so holding it was not a good strategy.
Yù stated that Sōngzhōu was a crucial strategic point for the Western Qiāng,
and the military guard could not be abolished.
So, officials were appointed and fortifications were built according to Yù's suggestion.
At that time, the sorcerer Péng Pǔguì caused unrest in Sìchuān,
burning and plundering fourteen prefectures and counties.
Commander Pǔliàng and others could not defeat him,
so Yù was ordered to move his troops to suppress and exterminate them.
The emperor personally issued an edict praising him,
and he was transferred to Left Censor-in-chief.
When the army returned,
he was appointed Left Grand Commandant of the Grand Commandant's Office.
In the thirteenth year, he was executed for involvement with Hú Wéiyōng's relatives.
Guō Yún,
a native of Nányáng.
He was over eight *chǐ* tall,
with a burly and imposing physique.
At the end of the Yuán dynasty, he gathered a righteous army to defend Quánbái Zhài in Yùzhōu,
and was successively promoted to Provincial Administration Commissioner of Húguǎng.
When the Yuán emperor fled north,
all the prefectures and counties in Hénán submitted,
but Yún alone held firm.
Grand General Xú Dá sent Commander Cáo Liàng to besiege him.
Yún sallied out to fight,
and was captured.
The Grand General ordered him to kneel.
Yún stood upright,
and cursed, seeking death.
He was threatened with a blade,
but did not flinch.
The Grand General admired his bravery,
and sent him bound to the capital.
Tàizǔ was struck by his appearance,
and released him.
At that time, the emperor was reading the *Hàn Shū*,
and asked if he was literate.
He replied:
"I am."
The emperor then gave him a book.
Yún recited the book very skillfully.
The emperor was greatly pleased,
bestowed generous rewards,
and appointed him Magistrate of Lìshuǐ,
where he achieved a reputation for good governance.
The emperor thought him even more virtuous,
and specially promoted him to Assistant Commander of Nányáng Guard,
sending him back to his hometown to gather his old subordinates,
and garrison that area.
He died after several years.
His eldest son, Hóng,
was only thirteen years old.
The emperor issued an edict for him, saying:
"Yún emerged from the fields,
raised a banner of righteousness to protect his homeland,
endured hardships for many years,
and devoted his heart to his duties.
When Our imperial army campaigned in the north,
both men and gods responded,
yet Yún fought repeatedly without yielding,
though his forces were depleted and aid cut off,
he ultimately harbored no disloyal intentions.
We commend his integrity and spirit.
When We tested him in official posts,
the common people praised his virtue;
when We allowed him to guard his homeland,
the soldiers and civilians enjoyed their livelihoods.
Although he had no deeds of great military merit,
nor did he turn his weapons against the enemy,
his administrative achievements were outstanding,
and his loyalty and righteousness shone forth.
His son, Hóng, may be included in the ranks of the founding meritorious officials,
and is appointed Xuānwǔ General, Assistant Commander of the Fēixióng Guard Imperial Army Commander's Office,
a hereditary position."
Among the surrendered generals at that time who were granted hereditary posts was Wáng Pǔ.
Pǔ,
a native of Ānrén.
He served Chén Yǒuliàng as Provincial Administration Commissioner,
defending Jiànchāng.
Tàizǔ ordered his generals to attack it,
but they failed.
Zhū Liàngzǔ attacked him at Ānrén Gǎng in Ráo,
and also suffered a defeat.
When Yǒuliàng's general Lǐ Míngdào invaded Xìnzhōu,
Pǔ's younger brothers, Hàn'èr, were in the army,
and both were captured by Hú Dàhǎi,
and surrendered to Provincial Administration Commissioner Lǐ Wénzhōng.
Wénzhōng ordered the two brothers to persuade Pǔ.
That year, Tàizǔ captured Jiāngzhōu,
and Yǒuliàng fled to Wǔchāng.
Pǔ then sent an envoy to surrender,
and was ordered to continue defending Jiànchāng.
The following year,
Tàizǔ stopped at Lóngxīng,
and Pǔ led his troops to meet him,
and was frequently consoled and praised.
He followed to return to Jiànkāng,
and was granted a residence outside Jùbǎomén.
His street was named
"Prime Minister Street"
to honor and distinguish him.
Soon after, he was dispatched to take Fǔzhōu and the counties in Jiāngxī that had not yet submitted.
He followed in the capture of Wǔchāng,
and was promoted to Right Grand Councilor of the Central Secretariat.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, he was ordered to concurrently serve as Vice Commissioner of the Court of Imperial Accouterments.
He followed the Grand General on the northern campaign,
and repeatedly achieved merits.
He was bestowed with silks and currencies,
and promoted to Provincial Administration Commissioner of Hénán,
but did not manage affairs,
receiving an annual salary comparable to Lǐ Bóshēng and Pān Yuánmíng.
Initially,
when Pǔ had not yet entered officialdom,
he took his mother, Lady Yè, to避兵 Guìxī.
During the chaos, he became separated from his mother.
After eighteen years,
he dreamt his mother seemed to tell him her whereabouts.
At this point, he calmly spoke to the emperor,
requesting to return home to visit his ancestral graves.
This was granted,
and the emperor also ordered ritual officials to prepare sacrificial offerings.
Pǔ led soldiers to Guìxī,
but could not find her.
He wept day and night.
A local resident, Wú Hǎi, said that his mother had been coerced by bandits
and had thrown herself into a well to die.
Pǔ searched and found the well.
A rat emerged from the well,
jumped into Pǔ's arms,
and then returned to the well.
They drew water from the well and searched,
and his mother's body was there.
He cried out uncontrollably in grief.
He then prepared a coffin and shroud,
and buried her right there.
When Pǔ died,
his descendants inherited the position of Assistant Commander.
The encomium says: Wénxuī and Sīmǎ were entrusted with vital responsibilities,
Yè Wàng and Mǎ Yún distinguished themselves in border regions,
Dàhēng was remembered for his uprightness,
and Guō Yún received favor for his administrative achievements.
Others, such as Cài Qiān, Wáng Míng, Níng Zhèng, Jīn Xīngwàng and their like,
were either good at fighting,
or good at defending,
or good at pacifying;
they were all excellent generals of their time.
Indeed, when the Míng dynasty first arose,
talents emerged in abundance.
Beyond those granted iron certificates and cinnabar tallies,
there were still so many others worthy of praise.
Compared to the poet's ode in "Tù Jū,"
how much more they yielded!
Collation Notes

Biographies, Chapter 23: Chén Yù (Qín Cónglóng), Yè Duì, Fàn Cháng (Pān Tíngjiān), Sòng Sīyán (Xià Yù), Guō Jǐngxiáng (Lǐ Mènggēng, Wáng Lián, Máo Qí), Yáng Yuángǎo (Ruǎn Hóngdào, Wāng Hé), Kǒng Kèrén.
Chén Yù,
courtesy name Zhōngxíng,
his ancestors were from Cáo.
His great-grandfather, Yìfǔ, a Sòng Hanlin Academician,
moved to Jiànkāng,
and his descendants made it their home.
Yù was naturally profound and pure,
dedicated to extensive study,
and skilled in the study of numerology and astronomy.
At the end of the Yuán dynasty, he served as a professor in Wēnzhōu,
but later resigned from office and lived in seclusion.
Scholars referred to him as Master Jìngchéng.
When Tàizǔ crossed the Jiāng river,
upon recommendation by Qín Cónglóng,
he sent a letter inviting him,
using Yī, Lǚ, and Zhūgě as comparisons.
When Yù arrived,
the emperor was greatly pleased with their conversation,
and kept him to participate in confidential discussions,
seeing him daily with trust.
When Tàizǔ became King of Wú,
he offered Yù the position of Assistant Administrator of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
but Yù declined.
Upon ascending to the imperial throne,
he offered him the position of Hanlin Academician three times,
but Yù declined all of them.
Therefore, he bestowed upon him an imperial sedan chair,
and ten guards to escort him in and out,
to show his honor and favor.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, he was ordered to Zhèjiāng to inspect the hidden grievances of the people.
Upon his return, he was bestowed with gold and silk.
He was appointed Minister of the Left (Zhōngshū Zuǒchéng),
but he again declined.
The following year, he was summoned to an audience at the Huágài Diàn,
granted a seat,
and ordered to draft a proclamation for pacifying the West (Píngxī Zhào).
He was appointed Vice Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shìláng),
concurrently Grand Academician of the Hóngwén Guǎn,
but he again declined.
When fine horses were presented from the Western Regions,
Yù cited stories from the Hàn dynasty to remonstrate.
He was appointed Junior Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Shǎoqīng),
but firmly declined.
When pressed,
he refused.
Finally, he was appointed Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū),
and again firmly declined.
The Emperor pondered for a long time,
and then acquiesced.
From then on, he was no longer pressured to accept official positions.
The Emperor once casually mentioned wanting to give his son an official post,
to which Yù replied:
“Your servant’s three sons are all young,
and their studies are not yet complete.
Please allow them to wait for a later date.”
The Emperor also did not press him.
From the very beginning of the dynasty's founding, Yù
had served in the Imperial Tent.
The Emperor once asked for his comprehensive plan for preserving the state and pacifying the people.
Yù responded by prioritizing not indulging in killing,
light taxation, employing the worthy,
and restoring the rites and music of the former kings.
When court officials committed transgressions and were condemned,
Yù strenuously interceded for them,
and many were completely pardoned.
Many of his plans were kept secret and not transmitted,
but the profound honor and deference shown to him
was unmatched by any meritorious relative or high-ranking minister.
The Emperor frequently visited his residence,
always addressing him as "Xiānshēng" (Mister),
or sometimes as "Jūnzǐ" (Noble Man).
He invariably declined any offer of nobility,
thus preserving his lofty integrity to the end.
He passed away in the seventeenth year (of Hóngwǔ),
and was granted burial at Zhōngshān.
His son, Gōng,
was a jǔrén (provincial graduate)
and rose through the ranks to become Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shàngshū),
renowned for his capability.
Yù’s younger brother, Yuǎn,
courtesy name Zhōngfù,
often accompanied Yù in serving the Emperor.
In the early years of Yǒnglè,
he became a Hanlin Academy Attendant (Hànlín Dàizhào),
and was skilled in painting.
Yuǎn’s son, Mèngyóng,
was skilled in calligraphy.
Qín Cónglóng,
courtesy name Yuánzhī,
was from Luòyáng.
He served the Yuán dynasty,
holding the position of Imperial Censor of the Jiāngnán Branch Secretariat (Jiāngnán Xíngtái Shìyùshǐ).
During the chaos of war,
he sought refuge in Zhènjiāng.
When Xú Dá attacked Zhènjiāng,
Tàizǔ said to him:
“I hear there is a Qín Yuánzhī,
who is talented and mature.
You should inquire about him
and convey my wish to see him.”
After Dá captured Zhènjiāng,
he found him.
Tàizǔ ordered his nephew Wénzhèng and his maternal nephew Lǐ Wénzhōng to bring gold and fine silk to his dwelling to invite him.
Cónglóng came with his wife, Chén,
and Tàizǔ personally welcomed them at Lóngjiāng.
At that time, Tàizǔ was residing in a wealthy commoner’s house,
and he invited Cónglóng to stay with him,
consulting him morning and evening on current affairs.
Afterwards,
he established his headquarters in the former Yuán Censorate,
and Cónglóng resided outside the Xīhuá Mén,
consulting him on all matters, large and small.
He often used a brush to write on lacquered slips,
their discussions being so private
that none of his attendants could understand them.
On Cónglóng’s birthday,
Tàizǔ and the Crown Prince (Shìzǐ) would send generous gifts,
or even personally visit his home for a feast.
In the winter of the twenty-fifth year of Zhìzhèng,
Cónglóng’s son, Zé, died,
and he requested leave to return home.
Tàizǔ went out to the outskirts to clasp his hand and see him off.
Soon after, he fell ill and died,
aged seventy.
Tàizǔ was shocked and grieved.
At that time, he was directing his army to Zhènjiāng,
and personally went to mourn him,
generously providing for his family,
and ordering the officials to arrange his burial.
Yè Duì,
courtesy name Liángzhòng,
was from Nínghǎi.
He prided himself on his economic abilities,
and was particularly skilled in astronomy, geography, and divination.
At the end of the Yuán dynasty, knowing that the mandate of heaven had shifted,
he, as a commoner, presented a letter to Tàizǔ,
outlining one main principle and three detailed points,
addressing grand strategies for the empire.
At that time, Tàizǔ had already pacified Níngyuè,
and planned to seize Zhāng Shìchéng and Fāng Guózhēn.
However, Cháhàn’s military power was very strong,
and he had sent envoys to Jīnlíng to recruit Tàizǔ.
Therefore, Duì’s letter elaborated on strategies concerning these three parties.
Its summary states: “I have heard that those who would seize the empire
must have a definite plan.
This is like Hán Xìn’s initial meeting with Gāozǔ,
where he outlined the success and failure of Chǔ and Hàn,
and Kǒngmíng, while in his thatched cottage,
discussing
the tripartite division of power with the Former Lord (Xiānzhǔ).
The present plan
should be to cut off Lǐ Cháhàn in the north,
annex Zhāng Jiǔsì in the south,
pacify Wēn and Tái,
defeat Mǐn and Yuè,
establish the capital in Jiànkāng,
expand territory in Jiāng and Guǎng.
Advancing, we cross the two Huái rivers to campaign in the north;
retreating, we draw the Chángjiāng as a boundary for self-defense.
Jiānlíng has long been known as a coiled dragon and crouching tiger,
a capital for emperors.
Relying on its military strength and resources,
it ensures victory in attack
and solidity in defense.
What can a hundred Cháhàns do to us?
Among the defenses along the Jiāng,
none is more urgent
than the upper reaches.
Now, our righteous army has already captured Jiāngzhōu,
sufficient to cover all of Wú.
Moreover, from Chú and Hé to Guǎnglíng,
all are ours.
This not only defends the Jiāng,
but also can defend
the Huái.
The collapse of the Zhāng clan can be awaited with folded hands,
and the various commanderies of Huáidōng will also come to us.
Campaigning north to the Central Plains,
the Lǐ clan can be annexed.
Now I hear that Cháhàn presumptuously
exalts himself,
sending a letter to Your Excellency (Mínggōng),
like Cáo Cāo inviting Sūn Quán.
I privately believe that the Yuán dynasty’s fate is nearing its end,
and the hearts of the people are not with them.
Cháhàn wishing to imitate Cāo’s actions,
the circumstances are not comparable.
It is advisable to follow Lǔ Sù’s plan,
to establish a tripartite division in Jiāngdōng,
and observe the rifts in the empire.
This is the main principle.
As for the three points:
Zhāng Jiǔsì’s territory
encompasses Háng and Shào in the south,
and crosses Tōng and Tà in the north,
with Píngjiāng as his stronghold.
Now, if we wish to attack him,
it is best to declare our intention to capture Háng, Shào, Hú, and Xiù,
while our main army strikes directly at Píngjiāng.
If the city is too strong to be taken quickly,
then besiege it with the ‘locked city’ method.
Outside the city, in a place beyond arrow and stone range, build a long circumvallation,
assigning generals and soldiers to set up camps on all four sides,
cultivate fields, and hold firm,
cutting off his routes of ingress and egress.
Dispatch troops to capture
and pacify the dependent prefectures,
collecting their taxes and grain to supply the army.
If he sits idly guarding an empty city,
how can he not be in distress?
Once Píngjiāng falls,
his stronghold is shattered,
Háng and Yuè will certainly
submit,
and the remaining prefectures will disintegrate.
This is the superior plan.
The Zhāng clan’s major stronghold is in Shàoxīng.
Shàoxīng is separated by rivers and seas,
which is why repeated attacks have failed.
This is because their supply route is through the Sānjiāng Dòumén.
If one army attacks Píngjiāng,
cutting off its supply route,
and another army attacks Hángzhōu,
severing its reinforcements,
Shàoxīng will certainly be captured.
The target of attack is Sū and Háng,
but what is gained is Shào.”
Sòng Sīyán
was of unknown origin.
When Tàizǔ conquered Tàipíng,
he appointed Sīyán to his staff.
After Qìjìng was pacified,
the Jiāngnán Branch Secretariat (Xíng Zhōngshūshěng) was established.
Tàizǔ was in charge of the provincial affairs,
and appointed Lǐ Shàncháng and Sīyán as Counselors (Cānyì).

At the same time, dozens of other officials were appointed to the province, including Lǐ Mènggēng, Guō Jǐngxiáng, Hóu Yuánshàn, Yáng Yuángǎo, Táo Ān, Ruǎn Hóngdào, Kǒng Kèrén, Wáng Kǎi, Luán Fèng, and Xià Yù.
However, Sīyán alone was appointed Counselor alongside Shàncháng,
indicating his position was more significant than the others.
Later,
when the Grand Military Commission (Dà Dūdūfǔ) was established,
Sīyán was concurrently appointed Military Advisor (Cānjūnshì).
Tàizǔ once conducted affairs in the eastern pavilion.
The weather was hot,
and sweat drenched his clothes.
His attendants offered him fresh clothes,
all of which had been washed and rewashed many times.
Sīyán said:
"Your Highness practices frugality,
truly setting an example for your descendants.
I only wish that you would remain consistent from beginning to end."
Tàizǔ praised his honesty
and bestowed upon him silk.
Another day, Sīyán again advised:
"The tigers in Jùróng are causing harm.
Now that they have been captured,
they should be eliminated.
What good is it to keep them in captivity among the common people?"
Tàizǔ was pleased
and immediately ordered the tigers to be killed.
His loyal advice on various matters was generally like this.
Later, he was sent out as Surveillance Vice Commissioner (Ànchá Qiānshì) of Hénán Circuit (Dào),
and died in an incident.
Xià Yù,
courtesy name Yǔnzhōng,
was from Jiāngníng.
He possessed outstanding talent
and was skilled in poetry.
He was appointed Erudite (Bóshì) in the Secretariat (Zhōngshūshěng).
When Wùzhōu was pacified,
he was transferred to the Zhèdōng Branch Province (Fēnshěng).
He served as envoy to Fāng Guózhēn twice,
and both times his missions were satisfactory.
When Tàizǔ campaigned against Chén Yǒuliàng,
among the literati, only Liú Jī and Yù accompanied him.
After the victory at Póyáng,
Yù was one of those
with whom Tàizǔ drafted proclamations and composed poems.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, he was appointed to oversee the various prefectures of Zhèdōng.
He, along with Gāo Jiànxián, Yáng Xiàn, and Líng Shuō, were four individuals entrusted with surveillance and enforcement.
Later, all of them died due to misconduct.
Guō Jǐngxiáng
was from Háo.
He and Lǐ Mènggēng from Féngyáng both followed across the Yangtze River.
He managed documents
and assisted in deliberations,
serving concurrently as Director (Lángzhōng) of the Left and Right Bureaus of the Branch Secretariat.
After being transferred together to the Zhèdōng Branch Province,
they were soon recalled to serve together as Military Advisors in the Grand Military Commission.
Jǐngxiáng was honest and straightforward by nature,
well-read in history,
and dared to speak out on matters.
Tàizǔ trusted him deeply.
He once said:
"Jǐngxiáng is a civil official,
yet he possesses the talent to repel and resist invaders.
He can be utterly loyal to me
and can be entrusted with great responsibility."
Before this,
after Chúzhōu, Tàipíng, and Lìyáng were captured,
their city walls being incomplete,
Jǐngxiáng was repeatedly ordered to oversee their construction.
Later, when the defending official of Hézhōu reported that the city walls had long been in ruins,
Jǐngxiáng was ordered to survey the site.
He rebuilt the city on its old foundations,
and the work was completed in ninety days.
Tàizǔ considered him capable
and appointed him Hézhōu Administrator (Zǒngzhì).
Jǐngxiáng further improved the city walls, moats, towers, and ramparts,
