expanded military farms,
and trained soldiers,
establishing a formidable reputation.
Hézhōu thus became an important strategic town,
and he received imperial commendations.
He eventually served as Administration Commissioner (Cānzhèng) of Zhèjiāng Province.
When Xiè Zàixīng was garrisoning Zhūquán,
his subordinate general privately traded with the territory of Wú.
Tàizǔ angrily executed the subordinate general,
summoned and admonished Zàixīng,
and ordered Mènggēng to Zhūquán to oversee military affairs.
When Zàixīng returned to his post,
he resented Mènggēng for being placed above him
and consequently rebelled,
capturing Mènggēng and surrendering to Wú.
Mènggēng died as a result.
At that time,
among those assisting in the Branch Secretariat
were also Máo Qí and Wáng Lián.
Lián,
courtesy name Xígǔ,
was from Dìngyuǎn
and was Lǐ Shàncháng's wife's elder brother.
He was fond of learning in his youth
and was filial to his parents.
Initially, he followed the bandits from Rǔ and Yǐng.
When Tàizǔ captured Jíqìng,
he crossed the Yangtze and came to submit.
Shàncháng spoke on his behalf,
and he was granted an audience
and appointed as a law enforcement officer (Zhífǎguān),
handling cases fairly.
He was promoted to Assistant Director (Yuánwàiláng) of the Secretariat
and then sent out as Surveillance Vice Commissioner of Zhèjiāng,
where his governance was renowned.
During a great wind that darkened the sky at midday,
Lián responded to the imperial summons by speaking of the people's suffering
and requested a reduction in taxes.
Tàizǔ accepted his advice.
He died in the third year of Hóngwǔ.
The Emperor said to Shàncháng:
"Lián possessed the talent of a king's assistant.
Now that he is dead,
I have lost an arm."
Later, when Shàncháng was implicated in an incident,
the Emperor sighed:
"If Wáng Lián were alive,
this would surely not have happened."
Qí,
courtesy name Guóxiáng,
was from the same village as Lián.
When Tàizǔ led his troops from Háo towards Dìngyuǎn,
Qí assisted the county magistrate in surrendering.
Tàizǔ was pleased,
kept him for food and drink,
and discussed military affairs with him,
finding all his suggestions satisfactory.
After Chúzhōu was taken,
he was promoted to Experience Officer (Jīnglì) of the General Administration Bureau (Zǒngguǎnfǔ),
overseeing granaries,
and also managing the daily calendar,
and checking on commanders who deserted their ranks.
He followed across the Yangtze
and was promoted to Director of the Branch Secretariat.
At that time, among Tàizǔ's close advisors,
only Shàncháng and Qí
jointly assisted in handling confidential documents.
Soon after, he was appointed Counselor.
When Wùzhōu was being campaigned against,
he was ordered to temporarily manage the affairs of the Secretariat,
entrusted with great confidence.
He soon died of illness.
Tàizǔ personally composed a eulogy for him
and oversaw his funeral.
His son, Xiāng,
was a Military Household (Guǎnjūn Qiānhù).
Through accumulated merits, he was promoted to Commander Vice Commissioner (Zhīhuī Qiānshì) of the Imperial Guards.
He followed in the pacification of the Central Plains
and was promoted to Commander (Zhīhuīshǐ).
When Duàn Shìxióng rebelled in Téngzhōu,
Xiāng suppressed him.
He hunted Japanese pirates in Zhèdōng,
achieving many beheadings and captures,
and was promoted to Grand Military Commissioner Vice Commissioner (Dūdū Qiānshì).
He was highly trusted
and once managed the affairs of the Brocade-Clad Guard (Jǐnyīwèi)
and oversaw imperial prisons.
Later, he died for his involvement in Hú Wéiyōng's faction.
Yáng Yuángǎo and Ruǎn Hóngdào
were both from Chú,
and their families had been scholars for generations.
They followed across the Yangtze
and both served as Assistant Directors of the Left and Right Bureaus of the Branch Secretariat,
rotating with Táo Ān and others in managing the logistical documents.
Yuángǎo was promoted from Director to manage military provisions in Jīnhuá,
while Hóngdào, in the same year, also followed Grand Military Commissioner Wénzhèng to garrison Nánchāng as a Director,
both achieving merits.
Both men were among Tàizǔ's oldest acquaintances,
and both were refined scholars fond of literature,
experienced and astute in political administration.
Yuángǎo's foresight and meticulousness were particularly noteworthy.
The Emperor once said:
"Among the civil officials who crossed the Yangtze
and managed documents and writings,
working diligently for over ten years,
none compare to Yáng Yuángǎo, Ruǎn Hóngdào, Lǐ Mènggēng, Hóu Yuánshàn, and Fán Jǐngzhāo."
Subsequently,
Yuángǎo successively served as Prefecture Magistrate (Fǔyǐn) of Yìngtiān,
and Hóngdào successively served as Administration Commissioner of Fújiàn and Jiāngxī Branch Provinces,
both dying in office.
Yuángǎo's son, Bì,
was widely learned and had an excellent memory.
He was known for his literary talent.
Recommended for office, he was appointed County Magistrate (Zhīxiàn) of Dàmíng,
and rose to the position of Record Keeper (Jìshàn) for the Prince of Zhōu's establishment.
Yuán Shàn,
a native of Quánjiāo,
successively held the office of Cānzhī Zhèngshì,
but, like Fán Jǐngzhāo, showed no remarkable achievements.
There was also Wāng Hé,
a native of Shūchéng,
who once studied under Yú Quē
and was famous for his writing.
He followed the crossing of the river
and became a clerk in the Xíng Zhōngshū Shěng,
frequently presenting memorials on current affairs.
Tàizǔ esteemed his talent greatly,
and promoted him to Dà Dūdūfǔ Dūshì.
When dispatched to Cháhǎn,
his discussions pleased the emperor.
Later, he was ordered to accompany Qián Zhēn to Hénán
to reciprocate Kuòkuò's invitation,
but was detained by him.
Tàizǔ sent seven letters to Kuòkuò before and after,
but received no reply.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ,
the main army advanced on Hé and Luò;
Kuòkuò fled to Dìngxī,
and Wāng Hé was finally able to return,
having been held captive for six years.
The Emperor greatly praised him,
promoted him to Lìbù Shìláng,
and fully heard his strategies for the western campaign.
In the second year, he was transferred to Yùshǐtái Shìyùshǐ.
In the ninth year, he was appointed Zuǒ Xiàng to the Jìn Wáng,
and the emperor personally summoned him to the Biàndiàn to instruct and send him off.
After a few years,
he died in office.
Kǒng Kèrén
was a native of Jùróng.
He advanced from Xíngshěng Dūshì to Lángzhōng.
He once attended Tàizǔ with Sòng Lián,
and Tàizǔ frequently discussed with him the state of affairs in the realm and the rise and fall of previous dynasties.
After Chén Yǒuliàng was annihilated,
Tàizǔ resolved to conquer the Central Plains,
and said to Kèrén:
"The Yuán's destiny has crumbled,
and heroes contend with each other;
their weakness can be exploited.
I intend to command the people of the Liǎnghuái and Jiāngnán prefectures
to plow and sow in due season,
and additionally train them,
so that they serve as both soldiers and farmers,
capable of both advance and defense.
Furthermore, in places in the Liǎnghuái where transport is feasible,
provisions should be stored in anticipation.
Once the army and food are sufficient,
the Central Plains can be conquered.
What do you think of this?"
Kèrén replied:
"Accumulating provisions and training soldiers, observing weaknesses and awaiting the opportune moment,
this is a long-term strategy."
At that time,
the military power of Jiāngzuǒ grew daily,
and Tàizǔ likened himself to Hàn Gāo.
He once said to Kèrén:
"The Qín government was tyrannical;
Emperor Gāo of Hàn rose from commoner ranks,
and governed the various powerful figures with leniency and magnanimity,
thus becoming the ruler of the realm.
Now, various powerful figures are rising,
but none know how to cultivate laws and regulations to clarify military administration;
this is why they will achieve nothing."
He sighed for a long time.
He also said:
"In the realm, concerning military campaigns,
in Hébĕi there is Bóluó Tièmù'ér,
in Hénán there is Kuòkuò Tièmù'ér,
and in Guānzhōng there are Lǐ Sīqí and Zhāng Liángbì.
However, Hébĕi has soldiers but no discipline;
Hénán has some discipline but its soldiers are not strong;
Guānzhōng has impassable roads and insufficient supplies.
In Jiāngnán, there are only I and Zhāng Shìchéng.
Shìchéng is full of cunning schemes,
favors espionage,
and governs his troops without discipline.
I, with hundreds of thousands of troops,
cultivate military administration,
appoint commanders and generals,
and act according to the opportune moment;
how can their power not be subdued?"
Kèrén bowed his head and said:
"Your Majesty is divinely martial;
you will surely bring peace to the realm."
Once, when reading the Hànshū,
Lián and Kèrén were in attendance.
Tàizǔ asked:
"Why was the Hàn's way of governance impure?"
Kèrén replied:
"Because the ways of the king and the hegemon were mixed."
Tàizǔ asked:
"Who bears the blame for this?"
Kèrén said:
"The blame lies with Gāozǔ."
Tàizǔ said:
"Gāozǔ founded the empire,
after the Qín destroyed scholarship,
and the people, having just recovered from their suffering,
naturally had not yet focused on rites and music.
Xiàowén was a good ruler;
he should have established rites and created music
to restore the old ways of the Three Dynasties.
Instead, he hesitated and did not attend to it,
causing the Hàn's enterprise to end up as it did.
The way of an emperor
is to not go against the times.
The kings of the Three Dynasties had their time and were able to act;
Hàn Wén had his time but did not act;
Zhōu Shìzōng, however, acted without having his time."
He also once asked Kèrén:
"Emperor Gāo of Hàn rose from a commoner to become the ruler of myriad chariots;
what way did he employ?"
Kèrén replied:
"Knowing men and being good at employing them."
Tàizǔ said:
"Xiàng Yǔ faced south, claiming to be an orphan ruler,
but did not practice benevolence and righteousness,
instead boasting of his merits and conquests.
Gāozǔ, knowing this,
responded with gentleness and humility,
and supplemented it with magnanimity and benevolence,
ultimately defeating him.
Now there is more than one hero;
I guard Jiāngzuǒ,
employing the virtuous and pacifying the people,
observing the changes in the realm.
If I merely contend with them in strength,
it would be difficult to settle things quickly."
When Xú Dá and others subdued Huáidōng and Huáixī,
he further said to Kèrén:
"The chaos of Rénchén
plunged the people into misery.
Among the various generals in the Central Plains,
Bóluó, wielding troops, offended the imperial court,
violating倫 and discipline,
and has already been annihilated.
Kuòkuò, holding the Crown Prince captive, wielded his spear,
focused on private vendettas,
and had no ambition to repel the enemy.
Sīqí and his ilk are mediocre,
usurping control over one region,
and the people suffer their harm.
Shìchéng outwardly used the Yuán's name,
but was fickle and two-faced.
Míng Yùzhēn and his son occupied Shǔ and proclaimed themselves emperors,
delighting in self-indulgence without long-term vision.
Observing their actions,
none can achieve anything.
I assess the heavenly timing
and scrutinize human affairs,
and there is an opportunity to bring stability.
Now, our army advances west from Xiāng and Fán,
and east over the Huái and Sì,
with head and tail responding to each other;
striking them will surely bring victory,
the great endeavor can be accomplished,
and the realm will not be difficult to settle.
After it is settled,
restoration and recovery will still be difficult;
that is when true effort and thought will be needed."
Kèrén served longest in the imperial tent,
hence he heard most of Tàizǔ's plans and strategies.
In the fourth month of the second year of Hóngwǔ, Kèrén and others were ordered to teach the classics to the various princes,
and the sons of meritorious officials were also ordered to enter school.
Later,
he was dispatched to govern Jiāngzhōu,
then entered service as a Cānyì,
and died due to an incident.
Commendation says: Tàizǔ rose from commoner ranks,
managing the affairs of the realm.
Since crossing the river,
his vision has been grand and far-reaching,
and his influence spread like the wind.
Though it is said to be by heavenly mandate,
was it not also aided by many national talents among his left and right chief ministers?
Chén Yù was treated with no less courtesy than Liú Jī,
and was transcendent beyond fame and profit.
Yè Duì, regarding the grand plans for the realm,
deliberated them carefully,
and was also able to uphold his integrity and live in reclusion,
their noble aspirations being difficult for others to match.
Kǒng Kèrén has little to commend him,
but because Tàizǔ's heroic schemes and grand strategies are recorded in his account,
he is included in this chapter.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 24 Táo Ān (Qián Yòngrén) Zhān Tóng Zhū Shēng Cuī Liàng (Niú Liàng Dálù Yǔquán Zhāng Chóu Zhū Mèngyán Liú Zhòngzhì) Táo Kǎi Céng Lǔ Rèn Áng Lǐ Yuánmíng Yuè Sháofèng
Táo Ān,
courtesy name Zhǔjìng,
was a native of Dāngtú.
In his youth, he was quick-witted and astute,
and extensively studied the classics and histories,
especially excelling in the Yì.
At the beginning of the Zhìzhèng era of the Yuán dynasty,
he passed the Jiāngzhè provincial examination,
and was appointed Shānzhǎng of the Míngdào Academy.
He later stayed at home to avoid unrest.
When Tàizǔ captured Tàipíng,
Ān, along with the elder scholar Lǐ Xí, led the elders to welcome him.
Tàizǔ summoned him for a discussion.
Ān stepped forward and said:
"The realm is in turmoil,
and heroes are competing,
but their intentions are focused on women, children, jade, and silk,
they do not have the heart to quell chaos, save the people, and bring peace to the world.
Your Excellency's crossing of the Jiāng,
with divine might and without excessive killing,
has won the hearts of the people.
Responding to Heaven and complying with the people,
you carry out a punitive expedition,
and pacifying the world will be no challenge."
Tàizǔ asked:
"What do you think of my desire to take Jīnlíng?"
Ān replied:
"Jīnlíng is an ancient imperial capital;
if you take possession of it
and govern from this strategic location overlooking the four directions,
what direction would you not conquer?"
Tàizǔ said:
"Excellent."
He was retained to serve in the staff headquarters,
appointed Yuánwàiláng of the Zuǒ Sī,
and Xí was made Zhīfǔ of Tàipíng.
Xí, courtesy name Bóyǔ,
was over eighty years old,
and died in office.
Ān followed in the capture of Jíqìng,
and was promoted to Lángzhōng.
When Liú Jī, Sòng Lián, Zhāng Yì, and Yè Chēn were invited and arrived,
Tàizǔ asked Ān:
"What do you think of these four men?"
He replied:
"My strategies are not as good as Jī's,
my scholarship is not as good as Lián's,
and my talent for governing the people is not as good as Yì's or Chēn's."
Tàizǔ admired his humility.
When Huángzhōu was first taken,
he wanted to find a high-ranking official to govern it,
and none surpassed Ān,
so he was appointed Zhī Huángzhōu.
He reduced rents and alleviated forced labor,
and the people lived happily in their occupations.
Due to an incident, he was demoted to Zhī Tóngchéng,
then transferred to Zhī Ráozhōu.
Chén Yǒudìng's troops attacked the city.
Ān summoned officials and commoners, instructing them on the distinction between righteousness and rebellion,
and defended the city steadfastly.
When relief troops arrived,
the attackers were defeated and fled.
The generals wanted to kill all the commoners who had followed the invaders,
but Ān objected.
Tàizǔ bestowed a poem praising him.
The people of the prefecture built a shrine and worshipped him while he was still alive.
In the first year of Wú,
when the Hànlín Yuàn was first established,
Ān was the first to be summoned as its Xuéshì.
At that time, scholars were summoned to discuss rituals,
and Ān was appointed Zǒngcáiguān.
Soon after, with Lǐ Shàncháng, Liú Jī, Zhōu Zhēn, Téng Yì, Qián Yòngrén, and others, he edited and codified laws and ordinances.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, he was appointed Zhī Zhìgào and concurrently Xiū Guóshǐ.
The Emperor once held court in the Dōnggé,
and discussed the rise and fall of previous dynasties with Ān, Zhāng Yì, and others.
Ān stated that the root of chaos and destruction
lay in arrogance and extravagance.
The Emperor said:
"Those in high positions easily become arrogant,
and those living in ease and pleasure easily become extravagant.
Arrogance prevents good words from being heard,
and faults from being known.
Extravagance prevents good principles from being established,
and actions from being considered.
Such people
have never failed to perish.
Your words are very apt."
They also discussed scholarship.
Ān said:
"If the Way is unclear,
heterodox theories will harm it."
The Emperor said:
"Heterodox theories harming the Way are like delicious flavors pleasing the mouth,
or beautiful sights dazzling the eyes.
If heterodox theories are not eliminated,
the orthodox Way will not flourish,
and how can the world be governed?"
Ān bowed his head and said:
"Your Majesty's words
can be said to have profoundly explored the root of the matter."
Ān served the Emperor for over ten years,
and was the most senior among the scholars.
When he became a court attendant,
he received even greater favor.
The Emperor personally composed a couplet for his door, bestowing it upon him, which read:
"A peerless scholar in strategy for the present dynasty,
the foremost family in literary works in the Hànlín Academy."
People of the time considered this an honor.
An imperial censor once reported Ān for concealing a transgression.
The Emperor questioned:
"How could Ān have done this,
and how do you know?"
He replied:
"I heard it on the streets."
The Emperor was greatly angered
and immediately dismissed him.
In the fourth month of the first year of Hóngwǔ,
there was a vacancy for the Cānzhèng of the Jiāngxī Xíngshěng.
The Emperor appointed Ān to it,
instructing him:
"When I crossed the Jiāng,
you were the first to visit the military headquarters,
expounding the Kingly Way.
Then, serving in the staff headquarters,
you provided much benefit.
Subsequently, entering the Hànlín,
I heard more of your upright opinions.
Jiāngxī is an upstream region,
and no one is better than you to pacify it."
Ān declined.
The Emperor did not permit it.
Upon taking office,
his administrative achievements became even more notable.
In the ninth month of that year,
he died in office.
When his illness was critical,
he drafted twelve items concerning current affairs.
The Emperor personally wrote a eulogy for his sacrifice,
and posthumously enfeoffed him as Gūshú Jùngōng.
His son, Shèng,
served as the Zhèjiāng Ànchásǐ during the Hóngwǔ era,
and was executed for corruption and bribery.
His elder brother, Yù, also died by execution,
and over forty family members were conscripted into the army.
Later, almost all of them died,
and the authorities again came to Shèng's household to round up more.
Ān's second wife, Chén, appealed to the Emperor.
The Emperor, remembering Ān's merits,
removed their names from the conscription register.
Previously,
when Ān was determining various rituals,
Qián Yòngrén of Guǎngdé also proposed many ideas.
Yòngrén,
courtesy name Chéngfū,
was the first-place Jinshì in the Southern Examination of the Yuán dynasty,
and was appointed Hànlín Biānxiū.
He was sent as an envoy to Zhāng Shìchéng,
who detained him
and offered him an official post.
When the grand army captured Huái and Yáng,
he returned to allegiance.
He successively served as Yùshǐtái Jīnglì,
and participated in the codification of laws and ordinances.
Soon after, with Táo Ān and others, he extensively discussed the rituals for Jiāomiào, Shèjì, and other ceremonies.
His proposals for Shìdiàn and Jìtián
were based on classical texts and precedents from the Hàn and Wèi dynasties to establish their systems,
and the imperial edict approved them,
details of which are found in the Lǐ Zhì.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, when the six ministries were established,
Yòngrén was appointed Lǐbù Shàngshū.
All policies regarding rituals, sacrifices, banquets, and imperial examinations
were exclusively entrusted to the ritual officials.
An imperial edict also commanded him to discuss and determine the styles of caps and clothing, from the imperial carriage downward, with other Confucian scholars.
At that time, many Confucian scholars studied ancient meanings,
but Yòngrén's textual research was particularly detailed and accurate.
However, many of these ceremonies and rituals were later revised.
In the twelfth month of that year,
he requested leave and returned home.
Zhān Tóng,
courtesy name Tóngwén,
originally named Shū,
was a native of Wùyuán.
As a child, he was exceptionally intelligent.
Scholar Yú Jí saw him and said,
"He is a talented young man,"
and married his younger brother Pán's daughter to him.
In the Zhìzhèng period,
he was recommended as an exceptional talent
and appointed Education Officer of Chēnzhōu.
During the chaos,
his family settled in Huángzhōu,
and he served Chén Yǒuliàng as a Grand Academician-Compiler of the Hànlín Academy.
When Tàizǔ captured Wǔchāng,
he was summoned to be a Director of the Imperial Academy
and was bestowed the name Tóng.
At that time, the sons and younger brothers of meritorious officials were taught within the imperial palace.
The various directors each specialized in one classic,
not being thoroughly conversant with all.
Tóng's knowledge was vast and profound;
he was best at lecturing on the Yì and the Chūnqiū.
When commanded to compose essays,
his talent and thought flowed like a spring,
and no one at the time could rival him.
He was promoted to Supervising Secretary of the Bureau of Merits,
and concurrently served as a Diarist of the Imperial Court.
During a discussion on the rites of collective sacrifices (xiá dì),
Tóng's proposal was deemed appropriate
and was subsequently adopted.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, he, along with Censor Wén Yuánjí and Diarist Wèi Guān, toured the country
to seek out virtuous and talented individuals.
Upon his return, he was promoted to Straight Academician of the Hànlín Academy,
then to Academician Reader.
The emperor was strict with his subordinates.
Censor-in-Chief Liú Jī said,
"In ancient times, when high officials and ministers committed crimes,
they were provided with a basin of water and a sword,
and went to a private chamber to take their own lives.
This was to encourage integrity and shame,
and to preserve the dignity of the state."
Tóng was attending at the side at that time,
and so he brought forth the Dàijì and Jiǎ Yì's memorial to present,
and spoke persuasively again.
The emperor once told his attending ministers that the harm of indulgence in music and women was worse than poisoned wine.
Founding emperors, whose actions are precedents for their descendants,
must be especially careful.
Tóng then cited Chéng Tāng, who did not indulge in music and women,
and thus set a lasting example for future generations, in response.
Such was his way of offering loyal advice based on circumstances.
In the fourth year, he was promoted to Minister of Personnel.
In the sixth year, he concurrently served as Academician-Compiler,
and with Academician Lè Sháofèng, he settled the musical scores for the sacrifices to the Former Teachers.
Moreover, he noted that since the crossing of the river,
the achievements in military campaigns and pacification,
and the details of rites, music, and governance,
though recorded,
had not yet been compiled into a book.
He requested the compilation of a daily record (rìlì).
The emperor agreed,
and appointed Tóng and Sòng Lián as chief compilers,
and Wú Bózōng and others as compiling officials.
In the fifth month of the seventh year, the book was completed,
covering the period from the raising of troops in Línháo to the sixth year of Hóngwǔ,
totaling one hundred volumes.
Tóng and others further said,
"The daily records are kept in the imperial archives,
and people cannot see them.
We request that, following the model of the Zhēngguān Zhèngyào of the Táng dynasty,
the emperor's virtuous policies be separately compiled
and promulgated throughout the realm."
The emperor agreed.
Thus, it was divided into forty categories,
totaling five volumes,
named Huángmíng Bǎoxùn.
Thereafter, whenever there were governmental achievements,
the historians would record them daily
and add them to the relevant categories.
In this year, he was granted an imperial decree permitting him to retire,
with words of extreme praise.
Before he left,
the emperor again ordered him and Lián to discuss the rites of separate offerings for the Grand Sacrifices.
After a long time,
he was reinstated as Compiler-in-Chief
and then passed away.
Tóng gained the emperor's trust through his literary talent.
In responding to imperial commands and answering questions,
he was invariably quick and eloquent.
The emperor once said that writings should be clear and simple,
expounding on the principles of the Way,
and reaching practical matters,
without being superficial.
Most of Tóng's works accorded with the imperial will,
and his conduct was especially upright and unyielding,
hence, his favor remained undiminished even in old age.
His son, Huī,
courtesy name Zīshàn,
was recommended as a talented scholar in the fifteenth year of Hóngwǔ.
He rose to the office of Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent and concurrently Minister of Personnel.
He possessed talent and wisdom,
was firm and resolute, not to be offended,
and diligent in handling affairs,
for which he was praised and trusted by the emperor.
However, his nature was treacherous and cruel.
Huī played a significant role in Lǐ Shàncháng's death.
When Lán Yù was imprisoned,
the case implicated Huī and his son, Junior Minister of the Imperial Seal Fú,
and they were both executed.
Tóng's grand-nephew, Xīyuán,
was a Clerk of the Central Secretariat,
skilled in calligraphy.
The inscribed plaques of palace halls and city gates
were often written by Xīyuán.
Zhū Shēng,
courtesy name Yǔnshēng,
was a native of Xiūníng.
At the end of the Yuán dynasty, he was recommended from his prefecture
and became Education Officer of Chízhōu,
teaching with effective methods.
When bandits rose in Qí and Huáng,
he abandoned his office and lived in seclusion in Shímén.
He often fled from warfare and hid,
but never neglected his studies for a single day.
When Tàizǔ captured Huīzhōu,
he was recommended by Dèng Yù
and summoned to discuss current affairs.
He replied,
"Build high walls,
store abundant provisions,
and postpone proclaiming yourself king."
Tàizǔ greatly appreciated this.
In the first year of Wú, he was appointed Academician Lecturer,
concurrently drafting imperial edicts,
and assisting in compiling the national history.
Due to his old age,
he was specially exempted from court attendance.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, he was promoted to Academician of the Hànlín Academy,
and established the rites of fasting and purification for seasonal sacrifices in the ancestral temple.
Soon after, he was ordered with other scholars to compile the "Admonitions for Women,"
collecting exemplary deeds of ancient virtuous empresses and consorts to be presented.
When meritorious officials were greatly enfeoffed,
many of the edicts of investiture were drafted by Shēng,
which were praised at the time as elegant and precise.
After a year,
he requested to retire due to old age and returned home,
dying at seventy-two years old.
Shēng had been diligent in study since childhood,
and remained untiring even in old age.
He was particularly profound in classical studies.
His marginal notes on various classics
were concise in language and profound in meaning.
Scholars called him Mr. Fēnglín.
His son,
who served as Vice Minister of Rites,
died due to an incident.
Cuī Liàng,
courtesy name Zōngmíng,
was a native of Gǎochéng.
He was a clerk in the Zhèjiāng Provincial Administration at the end of the Yuán dynasty.
When the Míng army arrived at Jiùguǎn,
Liàng surrendered
and was appointed Principal of the Bureau of Rites in the Central Secretariat.
He was promoted to Prefect of Jǐnán.
He returned home due to his mother's mourning.
In the winter of the first year of Hóngwǔ,
Minister of Rites Qián Yòngrén requested leave and departed,
and Liàng was appointed to replace him.
Initially,
when Liàng served in the Bureau of Rites,
the rites for the emperor's enthronement and grand sacrifices were all drafted by him,
and Chancellor Shàncháng presented them to the court,
thus making him known.
When he became Minister,
for all the ceremonial systems that Yòngrén had previously proposed and implemented,
Liàng cited historical precedents
to finalize their arrangements.
His textual research was detailed and accurate,
surpassing Yòngrén's.
In the second year,
a proposal was submitted to name Rénzǔ's 陵 (líng) the Yīnglíng (英陵),
and to again request the performance of the sacrificial announcement rite.
Sūn Wúyǔ (孫吾與), a doctor of the Grand Court of Sacrificial Worship,
opposed it, citing that there was no precedent for such a practice in the Hàn and Táng dynasties.
Liàng (亮) argued:
"Hàn Guāngwǔ (漢光武) added the name Chāng (昌) to his ancestral tomb,
and Sòng Tàizǔ (宋太祖) likewise added the name Qīn (欽) to his great-grandfather's tomb,
Kāng (康) to his great-great-grandfather's tomb,
Dìng (定) to his grandfather's tomb,
and Ān (安) to his father's tomb.
Founding emperors honor their ancestors,
thus also honoring their tombs.
Since their tombs are honored,
it naturally follows that sacrifices and announcements should be made.
Rites inherently arise from human sentiment."
The court deliberation sided with Liàng.
Soon after,
Liàng stated:
"The Lǐyùn (禮運) says, 'When rites are performed in the suburbs,
all spirits receive their offices.'
Therefore, altars for all the deities of the realm should now be added to the east of the Circular Mound [altar]
and to the west of the Square Pool [altar]."
He also said:
"The Jiāotèsān (郊特牲) mentions 'utensils made of pottery and gourds,'
and the Zhōulǐshū (周禮疏) states 'earthenware is used for outer sacrifices.'
Currently, porcelain is used for sacrifices,
which is in line with the ancient meaning.
However, types of plates and bowls [used now]
are still different from ancient ones,
so they should all be replaced with porcelain,
with only the biàn (籩) [bamboo food containers] remaining as bamboo."
He also requested that seven days before major sacrifices,
the accompanying officials should go to the Chancellery to receive an oath and injunction,
with the injunction wording following the Táng (唐) rites.

Furthermore, based on the Zhōulǐ (周禮), he established the system for the Five Sacrifices, the seasonal offerings of new produce, the guàn (祼) libation rite, the guīzàn (圭瓚) [jade libation cup], and the yùchàng (鬱鬯) [aromatic wine].
He also stated that offering sacrifices to flags and banners on the first and fifteenth day of each month
was troublesome and disrespectful,
and should only be performed in the month of their designated sacrifice.
All were approved and implemented.
The Emperor once said to Liàng:
"Ancient sages have said, 'Seeing their life, one cannot bear to see their death;
hearing their sound, one cannot bear to eat their flesh.'
Now, the slaughtering of sacrificial animals for sacrifices is too close to the spirit altars,
and my heart is truly uneasy."
Liàng then submitted a memorial proposing to research the ancient ritual for slaughtering animals,
moving it two hundred paces away from the spirit altars.
The Emperor was greatly pleased.
The Emperor was concerned that at the suburban and communal sacrifices,
the altars lacked roofs,
and sudden rain might drench the garments.
Liàng cited the incident in the ninth year of Xiángfú (祥符) of the Sòng (宋) dynasty, when rain occurred during the southern suburban sacrifice,
and the ritual was performed by worshipping from a distance in the Grand Commandant's hall.
He also mentioned the Yuan (元) dynasty's Jīngshì Dàdiǎn (經世大典) where buildings were erected inside and outside the altar enclosure to avoid wind and rain.
He presented these precedents in a memorial.
Consequently, an imperial edict ordered the construction of a hall south of the altar,
so that if it rained, the worship could be performed from a distance.
Furthermore, various Língxīng (靈星) temples also had altar houses built based on Liàng's suggestions.
At that time, Rénzǔ (仁祖) had already been enshrined in the northern and southern suburban sacrifices,
and after the suburban sacrifice rites were completed, one would again proceed to the Grand Ancestral Temple to express gratitude.
Liàng proposed that this should be abolished,
and instead,
only three days before the main sacrifice,
one should go to the Grand Ancestral Temple to announce the joint sacrifice.
The edict approved this.
The Emperor, seeing sunspots,
suspected that it was due to improper sacrifices to Heaven,
and wished to increase the number of deities accompanying the sacrifice at the suburban altar.
Liàng firmly argued that the Hàn and Táng practices were excessive and disrespectful,
and should not be emulated,
so the Emperor stopped.
One day, the Emperor asked Liàng:
"When I perform the suburban sacrifice to Heaven and Earth,
I bow in the exact center.
However, when officials attend court, they are arrayed on the east and west sides.
Why is this?"
Liàng replied:
"The Son of Heaven sacrifices to Heaven,
ascending from the Wǔ (午) steps [south side],
facing north,
which symbolizes responding to the yang.
When sacrificing to the earth,
he ascends from the Zǐ (子) steps [north side],
facing south,
which symbolizes responding to the yin.
As for when officials attend court,
they must avoid the supreme dignity of the sovereign,
so they ascend and descend only by the Mǎo (卯) steps [east side],
and the court ranks are arranged on the east and west sides
to avoid the imperial road.
Their meanings are different."
Liàng's impromptu replies,
which invariably cited classical meanings,
were often of this kind.
Besides the suburban and ancestral temple sacrifices,
the court greetings and "mountain calls," memorials from various offices, upper and lower official attire, the use of cushions on the palace floor, and the grand archery and military rites,
were all deliberated and decided by Liàng.
However, when he stated that for major sacrifices, the Emperor should personally inspect the animals,
while for medium and minor sacrifices, officials should be dispatched to act on his behalf,
the Emperor decreed that for all sacrifices personally offered, the inspection should also be personal.
He also requested that, following the Táng (唐) system,
prefectures and states should report auspicious omens.
The Emperor considered disasters and anomalies to be of greater importance,
and ordered the relevant authorities to report them by post-relay,
which differed from Liàng's suggestion.
In the ninth month of the third year, he died in office.
After him, Niú Liàng (牛諒), Dá Lù Yǔquán (答祿與權), Zhāng Chóu (張籌), Zhū Mèngyán (朱夢炎), Liú Zhòngzhì (劉仲質) and others,
also each presented their discussions and proposals.
Niú Liàng,
courtesy name Shìliáng (士良),
was a native of Dōngpíng (東平).
In the first year of Hóngwǔ (洪武), he was recommended as a xiùcaí (秀才) [talented scholar],
and served as a diǎnbù (典簿) [registrar].
He returned with Zhāng Yǐníng (張以寧) from a mission to Ānnán (安南),
and was praised by the Emperor,
being promoted three times to Minister of Rites.
He revised and established the rites for the Shìdiàn (釋奠) [ceremony for Confucius] and the ritual for separate offerings at major sacrifices,
and discussed the inspection of sacrificial animals and official attire with Zhān Tóng (詹同) and others.
Censor Dá Lù Yǔquán (答祿與權) requested sacrifices to the Sānhuáng (三皇) [Three Sovereigns].
Tàizǔ (太祖) referred the discussion to the officials in charge of rites,
and also ordered them to investigate which emperors of past dynasties had merits and virtues to be honored with temple sacrifices.
In the first month of the seventh year,
Liàng memorialized that temples for the Sānhuáng (三皇) should be established in the capital,
with sacrifices offered in spring and autumn,
and for emperors from Hàn (漢) and Táng (唐) onwards,
temples should be erected at their tombs.
The Emperor revised and implemented this,
which is also detailed in the Lǐzhì (禮志).
That year, he neglected his duties,
and was demoted to zhǔshì (主事) [secretary].
Not long after,
he was reinstated,
but later dismissed again for incompetence.
Liàng produced many writings,
which were widely circulated and recited by his contemporaries.
Dá Lù Yǔquán,
courtesy name Dàofū (道夫),
was a Mongolian.
He served the Yuán (元) dynasty as a qiānshì (僉事) [assistant investigator] in the Henan and North Circuit Surveillance Commissioner's Office.
Upon entering the Míng (明) dynasty,
he resided in Yǒngníng (永寧), Henan.
In the sixth year of Hóngwǔ, he was recommended and appointed as Jìshàn (紀善) [Secretary of Good Counsel] in the Qín (秦) princedom,
and later transferred to Censor.
He requested the reprinting of the laws and decrees.
When the people of Xúyí (盱眙) presented auspicious wheat,
Yǔquán requested that it be offered to the ancestral temple.
The Emperor said:
"To attribute auspicious wheat to my virtue,
I dare not accept;
it must be attributed to the ancestors.
The Censor's words are correct."
The next year, he was appointed as Assistant Surveillance Commissioner for Guǎngxī (廣西).
Before he departed,
he was reinstated as Censor.
He submitted a memorial requesting sacrifices to the Sānhuáng (三皇).
This was referred to the officials of rites for deliberation,
and consequently, temples for emperors were also established.
Furthermore, envoys were dispatched to inspect the various imperial tombs and mausoleums of past dynasties,
two tomb-guarding households were assigned,
and sacrifices were offered every three years;
this system all began from this.
He also requested the performance of the Dì (禘) ritual,
but his proposal was rejected and not implemented.
He was reassigned as a Compiler of the Hànlín (翰林) Academy,
and for an offense, was demoted to Diǎnjí (典籍) [Archivist],
but soon promoted to Yìngfèng (應奉) [Attendant].
In the eleventh year, he retired due to old age.
The Dì (禘) ritual was only finally established during the Jiājìng (嘉靖) reign.
Zhāng Chóu,
courtesy name Wéizhōng,
was a native of Wúxí.
His father, Yì,
once persuaded Mò Tiānyòu, a general under Zhāng Shìchéng, to surrender,
and then requested of Píngzhāng Hú Měi not to slaughter the surrendered men,
so the people in the city were spared.
Recommended by Zhān Tóng,
he was appointed Hànlín Yìngfèng,
then transferred to Lǐbù Zhǔshì.
By imperial decree, he and Shàngshū Táo Kǎi compiled the deeds of vassal kings from the Hàn and Táng dynasties into the Zhāojiàn Lù.
In the ninth year of Hóngwǔ, he was promoted from Yuánwàiláng to Shàngshū,
and with Xuéshì Sòng Lián, he established the regulations for mourning attire for imperial princes' consorts.
Chóu had an extensive memory and deep knowledge,
having served long in the Ministry of Rites,
he was well-versed in the evolution of ritual texts through the dynasties.
However, he was rather good at making forced interpretations.
Initially,
Táo Ān and others had established the rituals for the Yuánqiū, Fāngzé, Zōngmiào, and Shèjì,
which had been practiced for several years.
In the ninth year of Hóngwǔ,
Chóu, as Shàngshū,
proposed revising them to combine the Shè and Jì into a single altar,
abolishing the Gōulóng and discarding supplementary offerings,
instead enshrining Rénzǔ for shared sacrifice,
to demonstrate Míngzǔ's principle of respecting and loving the Shè.
Thus, the Shèjì and the sacrifices to the suburbs and ancestral temples were elevated to the highest class of sacrifice.
Those with discernment secretly disapproved.
Later,
he was sent out as Húguǎng Cāncèng.
In the tenth year, he was punished with penal labor for an offense.
In the twelfth year, he was again appointed Lǐbù Yuánwàiláng.
Later, he was reinstated to office,
but was dismissed due to another matter.
Zhū Mèngyán,
courtesy name Zhòngyǎ,
was a native of Jìnxián.
He was a Yuán dynasty Jinshì,
and served as Jīnqī Céng.
Tàizǔ summoned him to reside in the royal guesthouse,
ordering him and Xióng Dǐng to compile ancient stories into plain language,
to teach the sons of dukes and high officials,
naming it Gōngzǐ Shū.
In the eleventh year of Hóngwǔ,
he was promoted from Lǐbù Shìláng to Shàngshū.
The emperor was then studying antiquity and favoring literary pursuits;
Mèngyán cited ancient examples to prove contemporary points,
analyzing origins and developments,
as if pointing to his palm.
His writings were detailed, elegant, and well-founded.
The emperor greatly esteemed him.
He died in office.
Liú Zhòngzhì,
courtesy name Wénzhì,
was a native of Fēnyí.
In the early Hóngwǔ era,
he was recommended from Yíchūn Xùndǎo to the capital,
promoted to Hànlín Diǎnjí,
and commissioned to proofread the Chūnqiū Běnmò.
In the fifteenth year, he was appointed Lǐbù Shàngshū,
and ordered to establish the Shìdiàn rituals with other Confucian scholars,
which were promulgated to schools throughout the realm,
to universally offer sacrifices to Kǒngzǐ every year in the middle months of spring and autumn, as prescribed.
At that time, the Guózǐxué was newly completed,
and the emperor was about to perform the Shìcài ceremony.
Attending officials suggested,
"Although Kǒngzǐ is a sage,
he is a subject,
so according to ritual, one libation and two bows are appropriate."
The emperor said:
"In the past, Zhōu Tàizǔ visited Kǒngzǐ's temple,
and his attendants said it was inappropriate to bow.
Zhōu Tàizǔ said: 'Kǒngzǐ is the teacher of emperors for a hundred generations,
how dare I not bow?'
Now that I possess the realm,
I respectfully observe rituals to all gods,
and for the Former Master, the rites should be further elevated."
He then ordered Zhòngzhì to deliberate in detail.
Zhòngzhì requested that the emperor wear a píbiàn cap and hold a guī tablet,
proceed to the Former Master's altar and bow twice,
offer wine,
then bow twice again,
withdraw to change clothes,
and then proceed to the Yílúntáng to command a lecture,
thus making the ceremony grand and solemn.
The imperial edict stated,
"Approved."
He also established twelve articles of school regulations,
which combined with the nine articles decreed by the emperor,
were promulgated to teachers and students.
Subsequently,
he was again commanded to distribute Liú Xiàng's Shuōyuàn and Xīnxù to schools,
instructing students to lecture and read them.
In the winter of that year, he was transferred to Huágài Diàn Dàxuéshì,
and the emperor personally composed his imperial edict of appointment.
He was demoted to Yùshǐ due to an incident,
and later retired due to old age.
Zhòngzhì was a person of gravitas and sincerity,
broadly knowledgeable in the Classics and histories,
and his prose was elegant and precise,
often aligning with the emperor's intentions.
Táo Kǎi,
courtesy name Zhōnglì,
was a native of Línhǎi.
He passed the Zhìzhèng rural examination,
and was appointed Yǒngfēng Jiàoyù,
but did not take office.
In the early Hóngwǔ era,
he was summoned by recommendation,
and participated in compiling the Yuán History.
After its completion,
he was appointed Hànlín Yìngfèng,
taught at Dàběntáng,
and instructed the Prince of Chǔ in the Classics.
In the seventh month of the third year, he and Cuī Liàng were both made Lǐbù Shàngshū,
and each presented memorials.
The military rites and the system for official tombs
were Kǎi's proposals.
In that year,
Liàng died,
and Kǎi took sole charge,
establishing the imperial examination format.
The next year, for the metropolitan examination,
Kǎi was appointed chief examiner.
He selected Wú Bózōng and one hundred twenty others whose essays were submitted to the emperor.
Kǎi arranged his own essay first,
thus setting a precedent.
The emperor once instructed Kǎi, saying:
"Serving the dead is like serving the living;
my care for my parents when they were alive was inadequate,
so I should fully observe the way of remembering the distant past."
Kǎi, noting that the Tàimiào already had regular sacrifices,
requested that a separate Fèngxiān Diàn be built to the left of the Qiánqīng Gōng to enshrine ancestral spirits.
The system of the Fèngxiān Diàn began with this.
In the fifth year,
Kǎi said:
"During the Hàn, Táng, and Sòng eras, there were all Huìyào,
which recorded contemporary governance.
Although the Qǐjūzhù is now established,
the imperial edicts and memorial records received by various ministries
should be compiled and categorized into books, following the Huìyào,
so that they can serve as precedents for future generations.
Those distributed to the táishěngfǔ [central government offices]
should each be stored in copper cabinets,
for future reference,
to prevent omissions."
This was adopted.
In the second month of the following year, he was sent out as Húguǎng Cāncèng.
He retired from office.
In the eighth year, he was reappointed Guózǐ Jìjiǔ.
The next year, he was transferred to Jìnwángfǔ Zuǒxiàng.
Kǎi was broadly learned
and skilled in poetry and prose.
The emperor often disliked the praises in former dynastic music, which were often sycophantic
or not elegant and refined,
so he ordered Kǎi and Zhān Tóng to rewrite them,
which greatly pleased him.
During the winter solstice, while observing purification in the sacrificial palace,
he suggested that there should be poems to commemorate the celebration.
So Kǎi was ordered to compose the first,
and all other officials harmonized,
with Sòng Lián writing the preface.
Afterwards, when accompanying the emperor on sacrifices,
he made various offerings,
which the emperor invariably praised.
It is said that many imperial edicts, enfeoffment documents, eulogies, and stele inscriptions from that period came from his hand.
Kǎi once styled himself Nàijiǔ Dàorén.
The emperor heard of it and disliked it.
For an incident during his time in the Ministry of Rites, where an imperial envoy mistakenly used a tally for Koryŏ,
he was condemned to death.
Zēng Lǔ,
courtesy name Dézhī,
was a native of Xīngàn.
At the age of seven,
he could recite the Five Classics from memory,
without missing a single character.
As he grew older,
he became broadly learned in ancient and modern times.
Regarding the national systems and talents of several millennia,
and the evolution of institutions,
there was nothing he could not speak of.
He was known for his literary talent at the time.
In the middle of the Yuán Zhìzhèng era,
Lǔ led the local gentry,
gathering young men to protect their homeland.
He frequently prepared cattle and wine,
and expounded upon the principles of order and chaos.
Everyone obeyed his rules,
and no one dared to act unjustly.
People called his village Jūnzǐxiāng.
Early in the Hóngwǔ reign,
the compilation of the Yuán History began.
Zēng Lǔ was summoned to serve as the chief editor.
When the history was completed,
he was bestowed with gold and silk,
with Zēng Lǔ ranked first.
He requested to return to his mountain home,
but was retained to assist in compiling and categorizing ritual texts.
At that time, many people were debating rites.
Zēng Lǔ publicly declared among the crowd:
"According to a certain theory, this rite is correct;
according to another theory, it is not."
When someone questioned or argued,
he would always cite historical records and biographies to explain.
Soon after, he was appointed Secretary of the Ministry of Rites.
When Kàipíng Wáng Cháng Yùchūn died,
Gāolí sent envoys to offer sacrifices.
Zēng Lǔ requested to see their memorial text.
It was covered with a golden dragon yellow silk cover,
and the text did not bear the Hóngwǔ reign title.
Zēng Lǔ reproached them, saying:
"The dragon silk cover is a mistake.
How can you pay tribute and claim vassalage without observing the imperial calendar?
What does this mean for propriety?"
The envoy apologized for the error
and was immediately ordered to change it.
When Ānnán's Chén Shúmíng usurped the throne,
fearing punishment,
he sent envoys to offer tribute to gauge the court's intentions.
The Office of Guest Relations had already accepted his memorial.
Zēng Lǔ took the sealed copy and examined it,
then reported to the Minister to question the envoy, saying:
"The former king was Rìyān;
why the sudden change of name now?"
The envoy dared not conceal the truth
and fully explained the situation.
The Emperor said:
"These island barbarians are truly cunning!"
He rejected their tribute.
From then on, the Emperor highly valued Zēng Lǔ.
In the second month of the fifth year,
the Emperor asked the Chancellor:
"What is Zēng Lǔ's official position?"
He replied:
"He is merely a Secretary."
On that very day, he was promoted six ranks,
and appointed Zhōngshùn Dàfū and Vice Minister of Rites.
Zēng Lǔ declined, citing that the character "shùn" offended his father's taboo name,
and requested to be demoted at court.
The Ministry of Personnel, adhering to regulations,
did not permit it.
A frontier general captured some Wōrén (Japanese).
The Emperor ordered them returned.
When the Confucian officials drafted the edict,
the Emperor read Zēng Lǔ's draft and was greatly pleased, saying:
"Before, Táo Kǎi's writing already inspired people,
and now Zēng Lǔ is like this again.
Perhaps literary fortune is flourishing!"
Not long after,
he was appointed to preside over the provincial examination in the capital region.
When sweet dew descended upon Zhōngshān,
the officials presented poems and odes.
The Emperor uniquely praised Zēng Lǔ.
In the twelfth month of that year, he resigned due to illness and returned home,
but died en route.
Xú Zūnshēng of Chún'ān once said:
"There are two learned scholars in Nánjīng:
Sòng Jǐnglián is one who uses a brush as a tongue,
and Zēng Dézhī is one who uses a tongue as a brush."
Zēng Lǔ did not keep drafts of his writings,
and although his disciples occasionally compiled some,
they never formed a complete book, it is said.
During the Hóngwǔ period,
there were over twenty Vice Ministers of Rites.
Among the well-known ones,
besides Zēng Lǔ,
were Liú Sōng, Qín Yuē, Chén Sīdào, and Zhāng Héng.
Liú Sōng has his own biography.
Qín Yuē,
a native of Chóngmíng,
courtesy name Wénzhòng.
He was widely learned
and skilled in prose and poetry.
Early in the Hóngwǔ reign,
he was recommended for his literary talent.
He was summoned to take an examination on the "Admonition on Solitary Reflection,"
and Qín Yuē's essay was first,
so he was immediately promoted to Vice Minister of Rites.
His mother was old, so he requested to return home.
Later,
he was summoned to court to present three matters,
all of which were direct and incisive.
He still requested to return home
and eventually died.
Chén Sīdào,
a native of Shānyīn,
courtesy name Zhízhōng.
He was appointed Secretary of the Ministry of Punishments upon passing the civil service examination.
The Emperor admired his adherence to the law,
and he was promoted to Vice Minister of War.
He further exerted himself in integrity and moral conduct,
and no one dared to approach him with private requests.
He was transferred to the Ministry of Rites,
then requested to return home.
He did not engage in production at home,
and local officials could not gain an audience with him when they visited.
After a long time,
he died.
Zhāng Héng's affairs are recorded separately.
Rén Áng,
courtesy name Bóyóng,
was from Héyīn.
He passed the civil service examination at the end of the Yuán dynasty
and was appointed Magistrate of Níngjìn County,
but did not take office.
Early in the Hóngwǔ reign,
he was recommended to serve as Instructor of Xiāngyuán,
then promoted to Censor.
In the fifteenth year, he was appointed Minister of Rites.
The Emperor paid special attention to the Imperial Academy,
dismissed the Libationers Lǐ Jìng and Wú Yóng,
and ordered Rén Áng to revise and expand eight regulations for the academy.
Then he appointed Cáo Guógōng Lǐ Wénzhōng and Grand Academician Sòng Nà to concurrently oversee the Guózǐjiàn.
At this time, Supervising Censor Guān Xián submitted a memorial, stating:
"Recently, officials in prefectures and counties have been unsuitable,
the teaching profession is not established,
and many selected scholars are lacking each year.
Even outstanding students
are assigned to menial tasks,
which contradicts the court's intention to nurture talent."
Rén Áng then memorialized to establish that all annual tribute scholars from across the empire should be examined by the Hànlín Academy,
to determine their merits.
The following year,
the Emperor ordered that both imperial examinations and recommendations be implemented concurrently.
Rén Áng presented established rules for the examination system,
which were more detailed than before,
and the system for selecting scholars was thus finalized.
Dī Chóng and Wáng Zhēn, Regional Military Commanders of Guǎngdōng, requested ennoblement for their concubines as principal wives.
The matter was sent to court for deliberation,
and Rén Áng firmly opposed it.
His view was adopted.
Consequently, Rén Áng and the Hànlín Academy were ordered to establish precedents for ennobling principal wives and concubines.
An edict was issued, also with the Ministry of Personnel, to establish eleven precedents for ennobling civil officials,
and five precedents for hereditary privilege,
which were promulgated throughout the empire.
Soon after, he requested to revise the system of ceremonial robes and crowns
and the seating arrangement for court audiences.
He also memorialized to destroy all lewd shrines in the empire
and to rectify the titles of official sacrifices.
"The people of Shǔ sacrifice to the Qin Governor Lǐ Bīng,
and include the Han Governor Wén Wēng and Song Governor Zhāng Yǒng.
Mì County sacrifices to Grand Tutor Zhuó Mào.
Jūn Prefecture sacrifices to Chancellor Huáng Bà.
Péngzé sacrifices to Chancellor Dí Rénjié.
All these left behind love for the people.
Lǐ Lóngqiān is sacrificed in Lóng Prefecture,
and Xiè Yífǔ is sacrificed in Fú Prefecture.
Both protected the people from calamity.
The Wu Chancellor Lù Xùn established the state through his efforts,
and should be sacrificed in Wú,
with his son Kàng and nephew Kǎi as secondary deities.
The Yuán General Administrator Lǐ Fǔ is enshrined in Jiāng Prefecture,
and Yuán Marshal Yú Quē has a temple in Ānqìng.
All of them diligently served until death.
Among those who followed Yú Quē in defending Wǎn
and whose entire families died for righteousness
was the Myriad-Household Commander Lǐ Zōngkě,
who should be co-sacrificed in Yú Quē's temple."
All these requests were approved.
The following year, the Emperor ordered the "Rural Archery Ritual" to be promulgated throughout the empire
and further commanded the creation of grand musical instruments for the Confucian temple,
to be distributed to various schools.
At this time,
eight criteria were used to evaluate external officials,
and the rewards for the Yunnan campaign were also prioritized.
Although these matters did not fall under the Ministry of Rites,
the Emperor ordered Rén Áng to preside over their discussion.
Soon after, he took leave and returned home.
Lǐ Yuánmíng,
courtesy name Zīshàn,
was from Ānzhōu.
In the fifteenth year of Hóngwǔ, he was recommended as a Censor because he was a Confucian scholar who was well-versed in the classics.
In the twentieth year, he returned from a mission to Píngmiǎn,
and reported:
"Sīlúnfā harbors deceit and is watching for an opportunity;
it is advisable to strengthen border defenses.
The Prince of Jìngjiāng uses the seal of Dàlǐ to issue decrees,
which is illegal
and makes him lightly regarded by distant people."
The emperor approved of his words,
and promoted him to Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū).
From then on, matters concerning distant regions were often referred to him for consultation.
Gāolí (Goryeo) reported that Wén, Gāo, Hé, and Dìng prefectures in Liáodōng were all old territories of their country,
and requested to set up garrisons at Tiělǐng.
Yuánmíng said:
"These several prefectures all entered the Yuán dynasty's territory
and belonged to Liáo,
with the Yālù Jiāng (Yalu River) as the border of Gāolí land.
Now a guard (wèi) has already been established at Tiělǐng,
so it is not appropriate to make further requests."
The emperor ordered that Gāolí be instructed to keep to its assigned territory
and not cause trouble.
Ānnán (Annam) made annual tributes of local products.
The emperor, mindful of the burden on their people,
had Yuánmíng convey his intention,
ordering them to make tribute once every three years.
From then on, this became the established rule.
He also, by imperial decree, implemented policies for elder care,
reiterated the regulations regarding the quantity of annual tributes from prefectures, subprefectures, and counties,
and established the styles of headwear and clothing for officials and commoners.
All these were enacted as laws.
Initially,
based on the words of Dálùyǔ Quán (Ta'er-yü Ch'üan),
a temple for emperors of past dynasties was built.
At this time, Yuánmíng requested that Fēnghòu, Lìmù, and thirty-six other individuals be included in the sacrifices.
The emperor removed Zhào Pǔ, Āntóng, and Āshù, and added Chén Píng, Féng Yì, Pān Měi, and Mùhuálí,
while the rest followed Yuánmíng's memorial.
When the Prince of Lǔ died,
the regulations for mourning attire were established.
The jinshi Wáng Xīzēng requested mourning for an estranged mother.
Yuánmíng deemed it inappropriate
and advised against it.
All regulations concerning suburban sacrifices, ancestral temples, altars of soil and grain, and sacred mountains and rivers,
were debated and finalized by Confucian scholars over time.
There were sometimes detailed and sometimes brief versions,
but the emperor ordered Yuánmíng to revise them all.
Among the officials of rites, only Yuánmíng held his post for a long time.
In the twenty-third year, he retired due to old age.
Yuè Sháofèng,
courtesy name Shùnyí,
was from Quánjiāo.
He was learned and skilled in writing.
He met Tàizǔ (Emperor Hongwu) at Héyáng,
followed him across the Yangtze River,
and served as a military advisor (cānjūnshì).
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, he was appointed Diarist of the Emperor's Activities (Qǐjūzhù),
and was promoted several times.
In the sixth year, he was appointed Minister of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū),
and, along with the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshūshěng), Censorate (Yùshǐtái), and Chief Military Commission (Dūdūfǔ), established regulations for training soldiers.
He was reassigned as Compiler of the Imperial Lectures (Shìjiǎng Xuéshì),
and with Chengshi Zhān Tóng, corrected the music for the sacrifice to Confucius and his disciples.
He also compiled the Dà Míng Rìlì (Daily Records of the Great Míng Dynasty).
In the seventh year,
the emperor, after returning from a sacrificial ceremony,
required musical and dance performances to lead the procession.
He ordered Sháofèng and others to compose lyrics.

Consequently, they composed songs such as "Divine Blessings Descend" (Shén Jiàng Xiáng), "Divine Favor Bestowed" (Shén Kuàng Huì), "Indulging in Wine" (Hān Jiǔ), "Excessive Desire" (Sè Huāng), and "Excessive Hunting" (Qín Huāng), and presented them,
totaling thirty-nine chapters,
named "Songs of Returning to the Palace" (Huílúan Yuègē),
all subtly conveying admonitions.
The Ministry of Rites presented diagrams of the music and dances,
and the Grand Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Sì) was ordered to practice them.
The following year,
the emperor, noting that the old rhymes from the Jiangzǔ (regions south of the Yangtze)
were often incorrect,
ordered him and other court officials to consult the elegant sounds of the Central Plains to correct them.
When the work was completed,
it was named Hóngwǔ Zhèngyùn (Standard Rhymes of Hóngwǔ).
He was also ordered to investigate the ceremonies for the new moon and full moon sacrifices at imperial tombs and the rituals for ascending the altar and removing shoes.
He thoroughly researched historical facts,
and all his suggestions were adopted.
Soon after, he was dismissed due to illness,
but not long after,
he was reinstated as Libationer (Jìjiǔ).
By imperial decree, he established the rituals for correspondence between the Crown Prince and various princes.
His research and documentation were precise and detailed,
and he was frequently praised and rewarded.
In the thirteenth year, he retired and returned home,
and died of old age.
His younger brothers Huī, Lǐ, and Yì
were all renowned.
A eulogy says: When rites were debated at the beginning of the Míng dynasty,
Sòng Lián was at home,
and most ceremonies were decided by Táo Ān.
The grand sacrificial rites exclusively followed Ān's proposals,
while others incorporated various suggestions,
adopting their strengths: the combined ancestral sacrifices (xiá dì) used Zhān Tóng,
seasonal sacrifices (shí xiǎng) used Zhū Shēng,
sacrifices to Confucius and plowing ceremonies (shì diàn, gēng jí) used Qián Yòngrén,
the five sacrifices (wǔ sì) used Cuī Liàng,
court assemblies (cháo huì) used Liú Jī,
prayers and sacrifices (zhù jì) used Wèi Guān,
and military rites (jūnlǐ) used Táo Kǎi.
All were able to cite classical meanings
and weigh ancient practices against current needs,
thus achieving a brilliant and prosperous reign for the era.
Although the final decisions and judgments
were made by the emperor himself,
the contributions of these officials should by no means be underestimated.
Collated Notes

Biographies (Lièzhuàn) Twenty-five: Liú Sānwú (Wāng Ruì, Zhū Shàn), Ānrán (Wáng Běn and others), Wú Bózōng (Bāo Xún, Rèn Hēngtài), Wú Chén, Guì Yànliáng (Lǐ Xīyán, Xú Zōngshí, Chén Nánbīn, Liú Chún, Dǒng Zǐzhuāng, Zhào Jìtōng, Yáng Fǔ, Jīn Shí and others), Sòng Nà (Xǔ Cúnrén, Zhāng Měihé, Niè Xuán, Bèi Qióng), Zhào Chù (Qián Zǎi, Xiāo Zhí), Lǐ Shúzhèng, Liú Sōng, Luó Fùrén (Sūn Rǔjìng).
Liú Sānwú,
was from Chálíng.
His original name was Rúxūn,
but he was known by his courtesy name.
His elder brothers Gēngsūn and Táosūn both served the Yuán dynasty.
Gēngsūn
was the Judicial Commissioner (tuīguān) of Níngguó Circuit,
and died during the rebellion of the Long Spear bandits.
Táosūn
was the Education Officer (xuézhèng) of Chángníng Prefecture,
and died at the hands of local bandits.
Sānwú avoided the warfare by going to Guǎngxī,
where the provincial administration (xíngshěng) provisionally appointed him Deputy Education Intendant (rúxué fùtíjǔ) of Jìngjiāng Circuit.
When the Míng forces entered Guǎngxī,
he returned to Chálíng.
In the eighteenth year of Hóngwǔ, he was summoned upon the recommendation of Rú Cháng,
already seventy-three years old.
His replies to the emperor's questions were pleasing to the imperial mind,
and he was appointed Left Mentor (Zuǒ Zànshàn),
and successively promoted to Hanlin Academician (Hànlín Xuéshì).
At that time, the empire had just been pacified,
and institutions and regulations were incomplete.
The emperor was eager to establish new systems,
but old scholars had passed away.
He was pleased to get Sānwú at a late stage.
He delighted in him.
Many ritual systems and the methods for selecting scholars in the three-stage examinations were revised and finalized by him.
Sānwú was learned and skilled in writing.
When the emperor completed the Dà Gào (Great Pronouncements) and the commentary on the Hóngfàn (Grand Norms),
he ordered Sānwú to write prefaces for both.

He was entrusted with the compilation of the Shěnggōng Lù (Record of Self-Reflection), Shūchuán Huìxuǎn (Anthology of Historical Records and Commentaries), Huányǔ Tōngzhì (Comprehensive Gazetteer of the Empire), and Lǐzhì Jíyào (Collection of Essential Rites),
and presided over all these matters,
receiving generous rewards.
The emperor once said:
"I observed black qi between the Kuí and Bì constellations,
which has now dissipated.
Could it be that literary fortune is on the rise?
You all should write and compose
to fulfill my wishes."
The emperor composed poetry,
and often ordered his officials to compose rhyming replies.
He once bestowed upon Sānwú a Korean tortoiseshell brush.
During court audiences,
he was ordered to stand in front of the imperial guards.
At banquets,
he was granted a seat in the main hall.
He, Wāng Ruì, and Zhū Shàn were called
"the Three Elders."
However, as Sānwú grew older,
his talent and vigor diminished,
and he often displeased the emperor.
His courteous treatment also gradually lessened.
In the twenty-third year, he was appointed tutor to the Crown Prince of Jìn.
Hóu Yōng, a Vice Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shìláng), impeached him for dereliction of duty.
He was demoted to Erudite of the National Academy (Guózǐ Bóshì),
but soon reinstated.
Sān Wú
was a magnanimous person
who harbored no schemes, and styled himself Tǎntǎnwēng.
When faced with crucial matters,
he stood firm and unyielding.
When Yìwén Tàizǐ died,
the Emperor held court at Dōnggé Mén,
summoning and confronting his ministers,
and wept bitterly.
Sān Wú stepped forward and said:
"It is according to ritual that the Imperial Grandson, as the direct descendant, should succeed to the throne."
The Grand Imperial Grandson's establishment was due to this.
Zhào Miǎn, the Hùbù Shàngshū,
was Sān Wú's son-in-law,
and died for corruption.
Sān Wú sought to retire.
The Emperor permitted it.
Not long after,
he was reinstated as Xuéshì.
Thirty years later, he, along with Jǐshàn Bái Xìndǎo and others, presided over the Huìshì examinations.
When the results were announced,
Sòng Cóng from Tàihé was first,
but no northern scholars were among the successful candidates.
Thereupon, the students claimed that Sān Wú and the others were southerners,
and had favored their own region.
The Emperor was furious,
and ordered Shìjiǎng Zhāng Xìn and others to re-examine the papers,
but their findings did not please him.
Someone suggested that Zhāng Xìn and his colleagues had deliberately presented poor papers,
and that Sān Wú and the others had indeed judged fairly.
The Emperor grew even angrier,
and Bái Xìndǎo and his colleagues were sentenced to death.
Sān Wú, due to his age, was exiled to the frontier,
and Sòng Cóng was also sent into exile.
The Emperor personally set the policy questions,
and promoted sixty-one more individuals,
all of whom were northern scholars.
At the time, this was called
"Nánběi Bǎng"
or
"Chūnxià Bǎng."
In the early Jiànwén reign,
Sān Wú was recalled
and died some time later.
Sòng Cóng rose to Hángbù Jiǎnjiào.
While his fellow townsmen, such as Yáng Shìqí, became prominent,
Sòng Cóng had no one to rely on.
During the Xuāndé era, he still held the position of Jiǎntǎo in charge of assistant instructors
and died in office.
Wāng Ruì,
courtesy name Zhònglǔ,
was a native of Wùyuán.
At the end of the Yuán dynasty, he and his younger brother gathered people to protect their hometown,
helped recapture Ráozhōu,
and were offered the position of Fúliáng Zhōutóngzhī,
but he declined.
When Hú Dàhǎi captured Xiūníng,
Wāng Ruì and his brother joined him.
A branch of the Xīngyuán Yìfēnyuàn was established in Wùyuán,
and his brother was made Yuànpàn.
Wāng Ruì returned to his fields.
In the autumn of the Gēngzǐ year (1360),
his brother led troops to contend for Póyáng,
but failed.
He abandoned his wife and children
and fled to Zhèxī.
The headquarters suspected Wāng Ruì
and issued an order for him to enter Yìngtiān as a hostage.
Later,
when it was heard that his brother had been killed by Zhāng Shìchéng,
Wāng Ruì was appointed Ānqìng Shuìlìng.
Not long after,
he was summoned to be Cānzàn Chuān Shǔ Jūnsì,
but he declined due to illness and left.
In the 17th year of Hóngwǔ (1384), he was again summoned for an audience,
ordered to lecture on the Xībó Kānlí chapter,
and appointed Zuǒ Chūnfāng Zuǒsīzhí.
He was often ordered to continue the "Xūnfēng Zì Nán Lái" poem and other imperial compositions,
all of which pleased the Emperor.
He requested that death sentences be suspended in spring and summer,
embodying the benevolence of Heaven and Earth in nurturing life.
This was granted.
The following year,
he fell ill
and requested leave to return home.
Wāng Ruì was earnest and quiet,
not prone to idle talk or laughter,
but when lecturing,
he would speak whenever an issue arose.
The Emperor often
called him "Shànrén" (good person).
Zhū Shàn,
courtesy name Bèiwàn,
was a native of Fēngchéng.
At the age of nine, he understood the main ideas of the classics and histories
and was able to compose essays.
During the military upheavals at the end of the Yuán dynasty,
he lived in seclusion in the mountains
and was known for his filial piety towards his stepmother.
In the early Hóngwǔ reign,
he served as Nánchāng Jiàoshòu.
In the 8th year (1375), he was ranked first in the court examination
and appointed Xiūzhuàn.
The following year,
his responses during an audience displeased the Emperor,
and he was reappointed Diǎnjí
and sent back to his hometown.
He was later recalled to be Hànlín Dàizhào.
He submitted a memorial discussing the marriage law, stating:
"Among the common people, marriages between children of paternal aunts and maternal uncles, or children of two maternal aunts,
are forbidden by law.
When rivals bring lawsuits,
some are annulled after engagement,
or divorced after marriage.
Even when children have been born,
officials compel their separation.
According to the old laws,
marriages between those of senior and junior generations were prohibited.
This meant that a mother's sisters
and one's own self
were considered paternal aunts and maternal uncles,
and it was improper for juniors to marry their seniors.
However, there is no generational impropriety
between the children of paternal aunts and maternal uncles.
During the Chéng Zhōu period,
the royal houses that intermarried
were limited to Qí, Sòng, Chén, and Lí,
hence a great state of a different surname was called 'Bójiù' (paternal uncle),
and a small state 'Shújiù' (maternal uncle).
The various states of Qí, Sòng, Lǔ, Qín, and Jìn also regarded each other as甥舅 (nephew-uncle) states.
In later generations,
the Wáng and Xiè clans of Jìn,
the Cuī and Lú clans of Táng,
the closeness of Pān and Yáng,
and the good relations of Zhū and Chén,
all married into each other for generations.
Wēn Jiǎo married his maternal aunt's daughter,
and Lü Xínggōng's wife, Madame Zhāng, was the daughter of his mother, Madame Shēnguó's, sister.
There are many such examples among ancient people.
I respectfully request that this matter be discussed among the ministers
and the prohibition be relaxed."
The Emperor granted his request.
In the 18th year (1385), he was promoted to Wényuāngé Dàxuéshì.
He once lectured on the Jiārén hexagram and Xīnzhēn,
and the Emperor was greatly pleased.
Not long after,
he requested leave to return home.
He died at the age of seventy-two.
His works, Shījīng Jiěyí and Shǐjí Zhuàn, were published.
During the Zhèngdé era,
he was posthumously given the title Wénkè.
Ān Rán,
a native of Xiángfú,
relocated to Yǐngzhōu.
At the end of the Yuán dynasty, he served as Zuǒchéng defending Láizhōu.
When the Míng forces entered Shāndōng,
he led his people to surrender.
He successively held the post of Shāndōng Cānzhèng.
He pacified and settled migrants,
and used all his surplus salary for public expenses.
The Emperor heard of this and praised him.
In the 2nd year of Hóngwǔ (1369), he was summoned to be Gōngbù Shàngshū,
then appointed Hénán Cānzhèng,
then Zhèjiāng Bùzhèngshǐ,
and finally became Yùshǐtái Yòudàfū.
In the 13th year (1380), he was reassigned as Zuǒzhōngchéng,
but was dismissed due to an incident.
Not long after,
he was recalled to be a Sīfúguān.
Previously,
Hú Wéiyōng 謀反 (conspired rebellion) and was executed.
The emperor, considering that chancellors throughout history often usurped power,
abolished the Zhōngshū Shěng (Central Secretariat)
and distributed its functions among the Lìubù (Six Ministries).
Later, realizing that there must be people to discuss and deliberate on confidential matters,
he established the Four Assistants (Sìfǔguān) positions,
naming them after the four seasons.
He issued an edict to the entire realm to recommend virtuous and talented individuals.
Hùbù Shàngshū Fàn Mǐn recommended esteemed scholars Wáng Běn, Dù Yòu, Gōng Xiào, Dù Xiào, Zhào Mínwàng, Wú Yuán, and others.
When they were summoned,
the emperor announced it at the Tàimiào (Imperial Ancestral Temple).
Běn, Yòu, and Gōng Xiào were appointed as Spring Officials (Chūnguān);
Dù Xiào, Mínwàng, and Yuán as Summer Officials (Xiàguān).
The Autumn and Winter positions were vacant,
so Běn and the others were ordered to temporarily fill them.
Their rank was below that of Dūdū (Commanders).
The emperor frequently bestowed imperial edicts,
honored them with the禮 (lǐ, rites) of "sitting and discussing,"
and commanded them to assist in governmental affairs
and regulate the four seasons.
When winter arrived,
the north wind brought cold.
The emperor considered this in accordance with the winter season,
attributing it to the efforts of Běn and the others,
and bestowed an imperial edict commending them.
They also divided each month into three ten-day periods (xún),
with each person in charge of one,
to verify their competence by whether the rain and sunshine were timely and favorable.
When the Xíngguān (Ministry of Justice officials) deliberated on cases,
the Sìfǔ (Four Assistants) and Jiànyuàn (Censorate) reviewed and reported their findings.
If there were doubtful judgments,
the Sìfǔguān (Four Assistants) could seal and reject them.
Before long,
Xiào and four others successively retired.
Rán was summoned to replace them.
Běn was later executed for an offense.
All these men were old scholars
who came from farming families,
honest and unpretentious without other special talents.
Only Rán had extensive experience both within and outside the capital,
was experienced and adept in various matters,
and received especially high favor.
He died in the eighth month of the fourteenth year (of Hóngwǔ).
The emperor, remembering Rán's sincerity in returning to serve,
personally composed an eulogy to sacrifice to him.
Those who succeeded Rán as Sìfǔ (Four Assistants) were
Lǐ Gàn and Hé Xiǎnzhōu.
Gàn was appointed Zhīfǔ (Prefect) elsewhere,
and Yòu and Xiǎnzhōu were both dismissed.
This office was subsequently abolished and never reinstated.
Běn’s native place is not detailed.
Yòu
was from Ānyì.
He had presided over the Bùzhèngsī (Provincial Administration Commission) provincial examinations three times
and was praised for selecting talented individuals.
Gōng Xiào
was from Qiānshān.
He was highly esteemed in his hometown for his conduct and integrity.
After his retirement,
he was recalled to serve as Guózǐ Sīyè (Assistant Director of the Imperial Academy)
and later as Jìjiǔ (Director of the Imperial Academy).
He was dismissed for granting leave to students without reporting it.
Dù Xiào,
courtesy name Zhìdào,
was from Húguān.
He placed first in the Yuán provincial examinations
and successively served as Táizhōu Xuézhèng (Magistrate of Education for Táizhōu).
He returned home to teach,
proficient in the three classics: Yì, Shī, and Shū.
Yuán
was from Pútián.
He was also twice summoned to serve as Guózǐ Sīyè (Assistant Director of the Imperial Academy)
and died in office.
Mínwàng
was from Gǎochéng.
Gàn
was from Jiàngzhōu.
Xiǎnzhōu
was from Nèihuáng.
Wú Bózōng,
personal name Yòu,
was known by his courtesy name,
and was from Jīnxī.
In the fourth year of Hóngwǔ,
he placed first in the imperial palace examination.
This was at the beginning of the civil service examination system,
and the emperor, who personally composed the policy questions, was very pleased to get Bózōng.
He was bestowed with a cap, belt, robe, and ceremonial tablet,
appointed Yuánwàiláng (Assistant Minister) of the Lǐbù (Ministry of Rites),
and participated in compiling the Dàmíng Rìlì (Great Ming Calendar).
When Hú Wéiyōng was in power,
he sought people to attach themselves to him, but
Bózōng refused to submit.
Wéiyōng resented him,
and he was exiled to Fèngyáng for an offense.
He submitted a memorial discussing contemporary governance,
and consequently stated that Wéiyōng was autocratic and lawless,
unsuitable for sole responsibility,
and would eventually become a national disaster.
His words were very sincere and pointed.
The emperor received the memorial, summoned him back,
and bestowed clothes and paper money.
He was dispatched as an envoy to Ānnán (Annam)
and fulfilled his mission satisfactorily.
He was appointed Guózǐ Zhùjiào (Assistant Instructor of the Imperial Academy)
and ordered to lecture in the Dōnggōng (Eastern Palace),
where he first expounded on the theories of "rectifying the mind and making intentions sincere."
He was transferred to Hànlín Diǎnjí (Record Keeper of the Hanlin Academy).
The emperor composed ten topics and commanded him to write poems.
He took up his brush and finished them instantly.
His words and meaning were elegant and pure,
and he was bestowed with an embroidered gold brocade robe.
He was appointed Tàicháng Sīchéng (Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices),
but he declined.
He was reassigned as Guózǐ Sīyè (Assistant Director of the Imperial Academy),
but he declined again.
Offending the emperor's will,
he was demoted to Jīnxiàn Jiàoyù (Instructor of Jīn County).
Before he reached his post,
he was recalled to be Hànlín Jiǎntǎo (Reviser of the Hanlin Academy).
In the fifteenth year, he was promoted to Wǔyīngdiàn Dàxuéshì (Grand Academician of the Wǔyīng Hall).
The following winter,
he was demoted to Jiǎntǎo (Reviser)
because his younger brother Zhòngshí, the Zhīxiàn (Magistrate) of Sānhé, made an untruthful recommendation,
and the accusation implicated Bózōng.
Bózōng was mild-mannered,
but inwardly resolute,
never condescending or flattering,
which is why he frequently suffered setbacks.
More than a year later,
he died in office.
Bózōng became a Jìnshì (Palace Graduate);
his examination officials were Sòng Lián and Bāo Xún.
Xún,
courtesy name Zhòngfú,
was from Chóngdé.
He studied the Yì (Book of Changes) under Wú Chéng of Línchuān,
loved antiquity, and acted diligently.
He authored Dàyì Chuányì (Commentary on the Great Book of Changes),
which scholars praised.
In the Zhìzhèng era of the Yuán dynasty,
he was recommended and appointed Wēnzhōulù Xuézhèng (Magistrate of Education for Wēnzhōu Circuit).
He was soon summoned to the Hànlín (Hanlin Academy)
but did not accept.
In the fourth year of Hóngwǔ,
when the civil service examinations were first established to select scholars,
he was summoned to be a Tóngkǎoguān (Associate Examiner).
After the examination,
he resigned and left.
In the fifteenth year, he, along with Yú Quán of Ānjí,
Zhāng Chángnián of Gāoyóu, and Zhāng Shēn of Dēngzhōu,
were all recommended by Lǐbù Zhǔshì (Secretary of the Ministry of Rites) Líu Yōng for their profound understanding of the classics and their venerable age.
They were summoned to the capital.
Xún was over eighty,
and Chángnián and Quán were both over seventy.
They were granted seats and consulted.
The next day, they were all appointed Wénhuádiàn Dàxuéshì (Grand Academicians of the Wénhuá Hall).
They all firmly declined due to old age and illness,
so they were released and sent back home.
Shēn arrived later
and was appointed Hùxiàn Jiàoyù (Instructor of Hù County).
Soon after, he was summoned to be Yòu Qiāndū Yùshǐ (Vice Censor-in-Chief on the Right)
and eventually Zèjiāng Zuǒ Bùzhèngshǐ (Left Provincial Administration Commissioner of Zèjiāng).
The following year, among those summoned as esteemed scholars was
Quán Sīchéng,
courtesy name Xīxián,
from Shànghǎi,
who was also appointed Wénhuádiàn Dàxuéshì (Grand Academician of the Wénhuá Hall).
The year after that, he requested retirement due to old age,
and was granted an imperial edict allowing him to retire.
When Bózōng was envoy to Ānnán,
his distinguished virtue was highly respected by the Jiaorén (people of Annam).
After him,
