Rèn Héngtài of Xiāngyáng also placed first in the Jìnshì examination in the twenty-first year of Hóngwǔ.
He went as an envoy to Ānnán as Lǐbù Shàngshū (Minister of Rites),
and the Jiaorén considered it an honor.
Those who served as envoys to Ānnán, both before and after, were equally praised as Wú and Rèn.
When Héng Tàih was Lǐbù Shàngshū,
a commoner from Rìzhào, Jiāng Bó’ér, due to his mother's illness, killed his three-year-old son to sacrifice to Dàiyuè.
The authorities reported it.
The Emperor was enraged by this destruction of human ethics,
ordered him flogged one hundred times,
and exiled him to Hǎinán.
He then commanded Héng Tàih to establish regulations for commending filial piety.
Héng Tàih deliberated, saying:
"A child serving their parents
should show reverence when dwelling with them,
bring them joy when providing for them,
and carefully manage their medicine when they are ill.
Lying on ice or cutting flesh
are not standard practices.
If cutting flesh is not enough,
then it comes to cutting liver;
if cutting liver is not enough,
then it comes to killing a child.
Violating the Dao and harming life,
nothing is worse than this.
To cause one's lineage to perish and sacrifices to cease
is the greatest unfilial act.
This should be strictly warned against.
If people are ignorant and unwitting,
then let them do as they will;
they are not to be included in the examples for commendation."
The imperial edict stated
"Approved."
The next year,
the funeral rites for Qín Wáng were discussed,
and the rituals for all princes succeeding to their titles were established.
When Longzhōu Zhào Zōngshòu was being suppressed,
Héng Tàih was ordered to go with Yùshǐ Yán Zhènzhí as envoys to Ānnán,
to instruct them to guard their borders carefully
and not harbor fugitives.
At that time, the Emperor, because Ānnán had usurped the throne and murdered,
had cut off their tribute missions.
Now, hearing that the imperial envoys had arrived,
they were greatly alarmed.
Héng Tàih wrote a letter,
explaining the court's reasons for deploying troops to appease them,
which greatly pleased the Jiāorén.
When the envoys returned,
for privately buying indigenous people as servants,
Yán Zhènzhí was demoted from his post as Yùshǐ.
Shortly after,
the indigenous official of Sīmíng and Ānnán disputed their border,
and the accusations again implicated Héng Tàih,
leading to his dismissal from office.
Wú Chén,
courtesy name Jùnzhòng,
was a native of Lánxī.
He was the son of Yuán Guózǐ Bóshì Shī Dào,
and was known for his learning and conduct.
When Tàizǔ captured Wùzhōu,

he summoned Chén and his fellow provincials Xǔ Yuán, Yè Zànyù, Hú Hàn, Wāng Zhòngshān, Lǐ Gōngcháng, Jīn Xìn, Xú Zī, Tóng Jì, Dài Liáng, Wú Lǚ, Sūn Lǚ, and Zhāng Qǐjìng to dine together in the provincial office,
and ordered two of them daily to lecture on the classics and history.
Afterward,
he appointed Chén as a Jùn Xué Xùndǎo.
In the early Hóngwǔ era,
the prefecture recommended him as a scholar,
but mistakenly listed his name as Xìnzhòng,
and he was appointed Hànlín Yuàn Dàizhì.
Chén said to Xiūzhuàn Wáng Lí:
"If the name error is not corrected,
it is deception."
He intended to report it to the court.
Lí said he feared it would provoke the Emperor's anger.
Chén did not listen,
and submitted a petition requesting correction.
The Emperor was pleased and said:
"He is truly a sincere person."
Subsequently, he treated Chén favorably,
summoning him to attend at his side.
Due to an incident, he was demoted to Biānxiū.
Gěishìzhōng Zhèng Xiāngtóng said:
"According to established practice for memorials to the Eastern Palace,
only officials subordinate to the Eastern Palace refer to themselves as 'your servant,'
while court officials do not.
Now everyone refers to themselves as 'your servant,'
which is not appropriate according to etiquette."
Chén refuted this, saying:
"The Eastern Palace is
the great foundation of the state.
Honoring the Eastern Palace
is how the sovereign is honored.
Xiāngtóng's statement is incorrect."
The Emperor agreed with him.
Soon after, due to an error in his response during an imperial audience,
he was demoted to Hànlín Yuàn Diǎnjí.
Afterward,
he was promoted to Dōnggé Dàxuéshì.
Previously,
the Emperor had said to Chén:
"The sages established three teachings: reverence for Heaven,
loyalty to the ruler,
and filial piety to parents.
These are scattered in the classics,
and it is not easy to grasp their essence.
You all should compile them based on these three matters."
By this time, the book was completed,
named Jīngchénglù,
and Chén was ordered to write the preface.
A year later,
he was demoted to Hànlín Shìshū,
then reassigned as Guózǐ Bóshì,
and retired due to old age.
Chén once wrote a辩 (biàn) [discourse],
stating that the enfeoffment of Confucius as a king was against etiquette.
Later, Bùzhèngshǐ Xià Yín and Jìjiǔ Qiū Jùn all followed his theory.
Until the ninth year of Jiājìng, when the sacrificial rites were revised,
and the title was changed to
"Zhìshèng Xiānshī,"
it was in fact initiated by Chén.
Guì Yànliáng,
given name Déchēng,
was known by his courtesy name,
and was a native of Cíxī.
He was a Yuán Xiānggòng Jìnshì,
and served as a Píngjiāng Lù Xué Jiàoshòu,
then was dismissed and returned home.
Zhāng Shìchéng and Fāng Guózhēn both invited him to serve,
but he declined.
In the sixth year of Hóngwǔ, he was summoned to the capital,
and appointed Tàizǐ Zhèngzì.
The Emperor once presented his imperial poems and essays,
and Yànliáng recited them aloud before the imperial seat,
his voice carrying outside the hall.
Those around were astonished,
and the Emperor praised his simple honesty.
At that time, Guózǐ students such as Jiǎng Xué were selected as Gěishìzhōng,
and Jǔrén such as Zhāng Wéi were selected as Biānxiū,
to study in Wénhuá Táng.
Yànliáng, Sòng Lián, and Kǒng Kèbiǎo were appointed as their teachers.
The Emperor often leisurely consulted him,
and Yànliáng's replies were always principled.
The Emperor often praised them,
and wrote his words to be displayed in the side hall.
On the winter solstice of the seventh year,
the court scholars composed a prayer for the Southern Suburbs using
the character "yú" (予)
and "wǒ" (我).
The Emperor considered this disrespectful.
Yànliáng said:
"Chéng Tāng, when sacrificing to the Lord on High, said 'Yú xiǎozǐ Lǚ' (予小子履),
and King Wǔ's poem sacrificing to King Wén says 'Wǒ jiāng wǒ xiǎng' (我將我享);
such words existed in antiquity."
The Emperor's expression softened, saying:
"Zhèngzì's words are correct."
At that time, the Yùshǐ Tái presented judicial cases,
and ordered court scholars to review them.
Yànliáng reviewed and released dozens of people.
He was promoted to Jìn Wáng Fǔ Yòu Fù.
The Emperor personally wrote an essay and bestowed it upon him.
Yànliáng entered to express his gratitude.
The Emperor said:
"Among the great Confucians of Jiāngnán,
only you are one."
He replied:
"I am not as good as Sòng Lián or Liú Jī."
The Emperor said:
"Lián
is merely a man of letters.
Jī is rigid and narrow-minded,
not as good as you."
When Yànliáng arrived in Jìn,
he created the Géxīn Tú (格心圖) and presented it to the Prince.
Later, the official system of the princely establishments was changed,
and he was reassigned as Zuǒ Chángshǐ.
When he came to the capital,
he presented twelve policies for achieving peace.
The Emperor said:
"What Yànliáng has presented
is thorough in its understanding of affairs
and beneficial to the art of governance.
The world says that Confucians are stuck in antiquity and do not understand the present;
if so, Yànliáng can be called a thorough scholar."
In the eighteenth year, he requested leave to return home,
and died two years later.
In the early Míng Dynasty,
great importance was placed on mentors.
Sòng Lián was ordered to teach the Crown Prince,
and the selection of tutors for the various princes was also careful.
Yànliáng and Chén Nánbīn were all veteran scholars,
while Lǐ Xīyán and Fùmǎ Dūwèi Hú Guān, who served as tutors to Xú Zōngshí,
were particularly feared for their strictness.
Lǐ Xīyán,
courtesy name Yú'ān,
was from Jiá.
He lived in reclusion and did not take office.
Tàizǔ personally wrote to summon him.
Upon arriving in the capital,
he became the tutor to the various princes.
His standards were strict and severe.
If any of the princes failed to follow his teachings,
he would sometimes strike them on the forehead.
The Emperor stroked them (the princes) and was angry.
Empress Gāo said:
"How can you be angry with someone who instructs our sons in the ways of the Sages?"
Tàizǔ's anger subsided,
and he appointed him Right Supervising Secretary (Yòu Zànshàn) of the Left Spring Palace (Zuǒ Chūnfāng).
When the princes departed for their fiefdoms,
Xīyán returned to his old hermitage.
When there were gatherings in the villages,
he often went wearing a scarlet robe and a bamboo hat.
When a guest asked the reason,
he smiled and said:
"The hat is my original simple nature,
the scarlet (robe) is a gift from the sovereign."
Xú Zōngshí,
given name Hòu,
was known by his courtesy name,
and was from Huángyán.
In his youth, he was intelligent and perceptive,
and earnest in his studies.
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
he was recommended
and appointed County Registrar (bù) of Tónglíng.
He requested leave to care for his parents,
which displeased the Emperor,
and he was banished to garrison the Huái'yīn Post Station.
It happened that Hú Hǎi, Marquis of Dōngchuān, sought a husband for his daughter the Princess,
and the Emperor was selecting a tutor for Gūan (the prospective son-in-law).
Finding it difficult to find the right person,
he entrusted the task to Zōngshí.
A eunuch, citing the example of other princely households,
placed the驸马's seat in the center of the main hall facing south,
while spreading the tutor's mat on the west steps facing east.
Zōngshí personally pulled the驸马's seat down,
and only then began to lecture.
Those around him were greatly astonished,
and exchanged glances.
The Emperor heard of this and praised him,
summoning Zōngshí and consoling him repeatedly.
At the end of the Hóngwǔ reign,
he was appointed Assistant Prefect (Tōngpàn) of Sūzhōu.
He petitioned to release two hundred thousand *shí* of official grain to save the famine victims.
When the spring waters violently eroded the dike,
he initiated the proposal to repair and build it.
The people of Wú all considered it convenient.
He requested to honor the virtuous widow Wáng,
but the Ministry of Rites argued that matters from the previous dynasty should not be granted.
Zōngshí said:
"King Wǔ ennobled Bǐgān's tomb;
was that not also a matter of a previous dynasty?"
Thus, she was honored.
In the second year of Jiànwén (1400),
he was exceptionally promoted to Right Vice Minister of War (Bīngbù Yòu Shìláng). He was demoted for an offense,
but soon restored to his post.
As the situation with Yān became urgent,
he was sent to Zhejiang to recruit volunteers.
When Chéngzǔ ascended the throne,
he submitted a memorial requesting to return home.
More than two years later,
he was arrested for an incident
and died on the way.
Chén Nánbīn,
given name Guāngyù,
was known by his courtesy name,
and was from Chálíng.
At the end of the Yuán dynasty, he was the Education Instructor (Xuézhèng) of Quánzhōu.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ (1370), he was invited to the capital
and appointed Assistant Magistrate (丞) of Wúdì.
He successively held the post of Assistant Prefect (Tóngzhī) of Jiāozhōu.
Wherever he served, he governed by classical learning.
He was summoned to be Assistant Instructor (Zhùjiào) of the Imperial Academy (Guózǐ).
He once had an audience
and lectured on the Nine Categories of the Grand Plan (Hóngfàn Jiǔchóu).
The Emperor was greatly pleased
and inscribed his name on a palace pillar.
Later, when the Emperor wrote commentaries on the Grand Plan,
he adopted many of Chén Nánbīn's ideas.
He was promoted to Chief Administrator (Zhǎngshǐ) of the Shǔ Princedom.
The Reverent Prince of Shǔ (Shǔ Xiànwáng) was fond of learning,
and treated him with extraordinary respect.
He had an an-chē (comfortable carriage) made and bestowed it upon him.
He also built him a residence,
naming it
"Hall of Peaceful Elderly" (Ānlǎotáng).
In the twenty-ninth year (1396),
he served as an examination official for Sìchuān together with Fāng Xiàorú.
His poetry and prose were clear, vigorous, and well-structured.
He died at the age of eighty.
Subsequently, Chief Administrators of other princely households such as Liú Chún, Dǒng Zǐzhuāng, Zhào Jìtōng, Yáng Fǔ, Jīn Shí, Xiāo Yòngdào, and Sòng Zǐhuán,
all were renowned.
Liú Chún
was from Nányáng.
At the end of the Hóngwǔ reign, he was an Instructor (Xùndǎo) of Yuánwǔ.
The Prince of Zhōu invited him to be the tutor to his heir apparent.
Soon after, he made a statement at court
and was appointed Right Chief Administrator (Yòu Zhǎngshǐ)
to assist the Prince in a proper manner.
A *huái* tree at the Duānlǐ Gate withered in midsummer.
Chún presented an admonition regarding this omen of fault.
The Prince acted on his words, rectifying and reflecting,
and the withered branches revived.
The Prince honored the *huái* tree, naming it
"Displaying Loyalty" (Chū Zhōng).
He retired from office for over ten years before he died,
at the age of ninety-seven.
Dǒng Zǐzhuāng,
given name Yǎn,
was known by his courtesy name,
and was from Lè'ān, Jiāngxī.
He possessed learning and integrity.
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
he was promoted from an educational official to Magistrate (zhī) of Màomíng County.
During the Yǒnglè era,
he was appointed Right Chief Administrator (Yòu Zhǎngshǐ) of the Prince of Zhào's household from Director of Studies (Sīyè) of the Imperial Academy (Guózǐ),
and corrected the Prince as circumstances required.
The Prince often erred,
and the Emperor would frequently reprimand the Chief Administrator for it.
Zǐzhuāng, being skilled in remonstrance,
managed to avoid blame.
In the spring of the eighteenth year (1420), he was to participate in the national sacrifice to the earth god (Guó Shè).
He rose early,
sat upright in his formal attire, and passed away.
Zhào Jìtōng,
courtesy name Shīdào,
was from Tiāntái.
He also rose from an educational official, successively serving as Magistrate (zhī) of Yǒngfēng and Lóngxī,
participated in the compilation of the Veritable Records of Tàizǔ (Tàizǔ Shílù),
and was successively promoted to Director of Studies (Sīyè).
He was appointed Left Chief Administrator (Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ) of the Prince of Zhào's household,
and worked together with Zǐzhuāng to assist and guide the Prince.
Among the worthy officials in princely households, Zhào and Dǒng were considered the foremost.
Yáng Fǔ
was from Jíshuǐ.
He served as a Censor (Yùshǐ).
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
he submitted a memorial proposing ten matters (for good governance).
He was promoted to Right Chief Administrator (Yòu Zhǎngshǐ) of the Prince of Wèi's household.
He devoted himself to offering suggestions and criticisms,
never taking even a single coin improperly.
In the early Xuāndé reign,
he died.
Jīn Shí
was from Kāihuà.
In the early Yǒnglè reign,
he submitted a letter discussing principles of governance.
The Emperor praised him.
He further presented policy suggestions that accorded with the imperial will,
and was appointed Imperial Academy Scrivener (Hànlín Diǎnjí).
He participated in the compilation of the Veritable Records of Tàizǔ (Tàizǔ Shílù) and the Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn,
was selected as a lecturer for the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng),
and successively served as Left Supervising Secretary (Zuǒ Sīzhí) of the Left Spring Palace (Zuǒ Chūnfāng).
When Rénzōng was established,
he was appointed Left Chief Administrator (Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ) of the Wèi household.
In the early Zhèngtǒng reign,
he died.
He was a filial and friendly person,
who earnestly practiced righteousness.
He read classics and histories,
with a fixed schedule each day,
never ceasing even in old age.
Xiāo Yòngdào,
a native of Tàihé.
During the Jiànwén reign,
he was recommended for his talent and virtue,
and went to the imperial court to take the literary examination.
He was promoted to Grand Secretary of the Prince of Jìngjiāng’s Household,
then summoned to the Hànlín Academy
to compile the Lèiyào.
When the Yān forces crossed the Huái River,
he, together with Zhōu Shìxiū, submitted a memorial
censuring those in power.
In the Yǒnglè period,
he participated in the compilation of the Tàizǔ Shílù (Veritable Records of Emperor Tàizǔ),
and was transferred to Right Grand Secretary,
accompanying the prince to Guìlín.
He once presented eight matters to the prince,
saying: "Be cautious in daily life,
reduce desires,
be diligent in study,
cultivate virtue,
simplify corporal punishments,
do not infringe upon the interests of inferiors,
regularly meet with palace officials to understand public sentiment,
and carefully select honest and discreet people for assignments."
He also wrote "Admonitions for the Four Gates: Duānlǐ, Tǐrén, Zūnyì, and Guǎngzhì" and presented them to the prince.
After a long time,
he requested to return home due to illness.
Emperor Chéngzǔ was angry
and demoted him to Patrol Inspector of Yāo'érlǐng in Xuānfǔ,
where he died.
His son, Xuǎn,
became Left Administration Commissioner of Húguǎng after passing the imperial examination.
In the fourth year of Tiānshùn, he was cited for his outstanding administration
and appointed Minister of Rítual.
Initially,
when the post of Minister was vacant in the two capitals,
Administration Commissioners were often appointed.
After Xuǎn,
however, there were no more appointments of Administration Commissioners as Ministers.
Xuǎn was steady, honest, and serene,
but not good at making official reports.
He was transferred to Nánjīng,
where he died.
Sòng Zǐhuán,
a native of Lúlíng.
From a Shùjíshì, he rose to Director of the Bureau of Merits.
He accompanied Shī Kuí to procure timber in Húguǎng,
and won the hearts of the people with his generosity and leniency.
When Emperor Rénzōng ascended the throne,
he was appointed Right Grand Secretary of the Prince of Liáng’s Household,
and then transferred to the Prince of Yuè’s Household.
He was amiable and indifferent to fame and fortune,
and wherever he went, he had a reputation for wisdom.
In the Xuāndé period,
he died in office.
From then on,
officials of princely households were no longer considered "qingliu" (pure stream),
and there was nothing further worth recording.
Sòng Nà,
courtesy name Zhòngmǐn,
a native of Huá.
His father, Shòuqīng,
was a Censor in the Yuán dynasty.
Nà was inherently steadfast
and had extensive learning.
In the Zhìzhèng period,
he passed the imperial examination
and served as Magistrate of Yánshān,
then resigned and returned home.
In the second year of Hóngwǔ, eighteen scholars were summoned to compile books on rituals, music, and other subjects,
and Nà was among them.
After the task was completed,
he did not seek office and returned home.
After a long time,
upon the recommendation of Dù Jiào, one of the Four Counsellors,
he was appointed Assistant Instructor of the Guózǐ (National Academy),
and scholars revered him for his interpretations of the classics.
In the fifteenth year, he was exceptionally promoted to Hànlín Academician,
and ordered to write an inscription for the temple of Xuānshèng (Confucius).
This pleased the emperor,
and he was richly rewarded.
He was transferred to Grand Academician of the Wényuān Pavilion.
Once, when cold, he warmed himself by a fire,
and his clothes under his ribs were singed,
which he only noticed when it reached his skin.
The emperor wrote a text to warn him.
Soon after,
he was promoted to Libationer.
At that time, sons of meritorious officials all studied there,
and there were sometimes several thousand annual tribute students.
Nà strictly established academic rules,
sat upright and lectured all day without wasting a moment,
and stayed in the student dormitories at night.
In the eighteenth year, the imperial examination for jinshi was reopened,
and four hundred seventy-odd scholars were selected,
two-thirds of whom were from the Guózǐ.
When the scholars were tested again,
it was the same.
The emperor was greatly pleased
and wrote an encomium.
Assistant Instructor Jīn Wénzhēng and others, jealous of Nà,
colluded with Minister of Personnel Yú Xī,
who issued a dispatch ordering Nà to retire.
Nà bade farewell to the emperor.
The emperor, surprised, asked why,
and was greatly enraged,
executing Xī, Wénzhēng, and others,
and retaining Nà in his post.
Nà once fell ill,
and the emperor said:
"Nà has the bones of longevity,
no need to worry."
He soon recovered.
The emperor sent a painter to secretly observe Nà and depict his image;
he was sitting stiffly with an angry expression.
The next day, when he entered for audience,
the emperor asked why he was angry yesterday.
Nà, surprised, replied:
"Some students stumbled,
breaking some teaware.
Your subject was ashamed of his failure in teaching,
and so was blaming himself.
But how did Your Majesty know this?"
The emperor showed him the painting.
Nà bowed his head in thanks.
His eldest son, Lín,
passed the imperial examination
and was promoted to Censor,
then sent out as Chief Clerk of Wàngjiāng.
The emperor, remembering Nà's old age,
recalled him to attend to his father.
In the spring of the twenty-third year,
Nà became seriously ill,
and stayed in the student dormitory.
Lín requested to return to their private residence,
but Nà rebuked him, saying:
"It is time for the Dīng festival sacrifice,
how dare you be disrespectful!"
After the sacrifice, he was carried home and died,
at the age of eighty.
The emperor mourned and regretted his passing,
and personally wrote a eulogy for him.
He also sent officials to offer sacrifices at his home,
and arranged for his burial site.
It was from Nà that civil officials of the fourth rank began to be granted sacrificial burial.
In the Zhèngdé period,
he was posthumously given the epithet Wénkè.
Nà once responded to an imperial edict to discuss frontier matters,
saying:
"Within the four seas, there is peace,
but the deserts still trouble Your Majesty’s thoughts.
If we pursue and attack them far away,
it will inevitably be arduous and costly.
For the sake of Your sacred sons and divine grandsons,
Your Majesty need only strengthen frontier defenses.
Frontier defense lies in solidifying the army,
and solidifying the army lies in military屯túntián farming colonies.
Hàn’s Zhào Chōngguó led forty thousand cavalry,
dividing them into garrisons along the nine border commanderies,
and the Chányú then retreated.
Your Majesty should select several brave and resourceful generals,
establish a system of five hundred *lǐ* east and west,
create laws for divided garrisons,
deploy them at strategic points,
respond to each other from near and far,
fight when encountering enemies,
and farm when the invaders leave.
This is a long-term strategy."
The emperor largely adopted his words.
After Nà died,
the emperor missed him
and appointed his second son, Fùzǔ, as Vice Libationer,
admonishing all students to adhere to Nà’s academic rules,
with transgressors facing the death penalty.
At the founding of the Míng dynasty,
the positions of master-scholar officials were already highly valued.
Xǔ Cúnrén and Wèi Guān served as Libationers,
both mature and dignified.
Nà joined a little later,
and received the most favor.
Those who established the academic rules with Nà were Vice Libationers Wáng Jiāhuì and Gōng Jiào.
All three were old,
with white hair and beards,
and sat upright all day,
making the hall solemn.
Moreover, Zhāng Měihé, Niè Xuán, Bèi Qióng, and others were all famous scholars
who, during the Hóngwǔ period,
successively served as Erudites, Assistant Instructors, and Academic Recorders,
which is why many students achieved great success.
The matter of Wèi Guān is recorded separately.
Jiā Huì,
courtesy name Yuánlǐ,
was a native of Jiāxīng.
He was summoned through recommendation,
and successively served as Sìyè of the Guózǐjiān.
In the sixteenth year,
he also requested to retire due to old age,
but an imperial edict graciously kept him.
He died at the age of eighty,
and was granted a very generous funerary allowance.
Xǔ Cúnrén,
given name Yuán,
was known by his courtesy name.
He was the son of Xǔ Qiān from Jīnhuá.
Tàizǔ had long heard of Qiān's reputation.
Upon conquering Jīnhuá,
he sought out and found Cúnrén.
He was greatly pleased after conversing with him,
and ordered him to tutor his sons.
He was promoted to Guózǐ Bóshì.
He was once ordered to lecture on the prognostication of good and ill omens in the Hóngfàn chapter of the Shàngshū.
He was also asked what saying of Mèngzǐ was most important.
Cúnrén replied with "practicing the kingly way, reducing punishments, and lightening taxes."
In the first year of Wú, he was promoted to Jìjiǔ.
Cúnrén was close to the emperor for nearly ten years,
and from matters of ancient rites and texts,
to the advancement and dismissal of talent,
nothing was not discussed with him.
When the emperor was about to assume the imperial throne,
Cúnrén announced his return home.
Sìyè Liú Chéngzhí said:
"The sovereign is currently responding to heaven and complying with the people;
you should wait a little."
Cúnrén did not listen,
and indeed displeased the emperor.
The Qiānshì Chéng Kǒngzhāo impeached him for concealing matters,
and he was subsequently arrested and died in prison.
Zhāng Měihé,
given name Jiǔsháo,
was known by his courtesy name,
and was a native of Qīngjiāng.
He was skilled in cí and fù.
In the late Yuán dynasty,
he repeatedly passed examinations but did not serve.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ,
he was recommended to be a Xiànxué Jiàoyù.
Later, he was transferred to Guózǐ Zhùjiào,
and then reassigned as a Biānxiū of the Hànlín Yuàn.
When he retired and returned home,
the emperor personally wrote an essay and bestowed it upon him.
He was again summoned, along with Qián Zǎi and others, to compile historical texts.
Once completed,
he was sent back.
Niè Xuán,
courtesy name Qìzhī,
was from the same district as Měihé.
He passed the Jìnshì examination in the fourth year of Hóngwǔ.
He served as Guǎngzōng Chéng,
and submitted a memorial to exempt taxes due to drought.
After his term expired, he entered the court for an audience,
and presented the Nándū Fù and Hóngwǔ Shèngdé Shī.
He was appointed Hànlín Yuàn Dàizhì,
then reassigned as Guózǐ Zhùjiào,
and promoted to Diǎnjí.
He was granted leave to return home along with Měihé.
In the eighteenth year, he was again summoned to preside over the Huìshì,
and the emperor wished to keep him in service.
He begged for a convenient place to live out his days.
He was ordered to receive the salary of the Lúlíng Jiàoyù
for the rest of his life.
Bèi Qióng,
courtesy name Tíngjū,
was a native of Chóngdé.
He was frank and straightforward by nature,
and diligently devoted to study.
At the age of forty-eight,
he first received the Xiāngjiàn.
Zhāng Shìchéng repeatedly invited him to serve, but he declined.
In the early Hóngwǔ period,
he was invited to compile the Yuán Shǐ.
Once completed,
he received a reward and returned home.
In the sixth year, he was recommended as a scholar,
and appointed Guózǐ Zhùjiào.
Qióng once lamented the absence of ancient music,
and wrote the Dàsháo Fù to express his aspirations.
When Sòng Lián served as Sìyè,
he proposed establishing four academies,
and also worshipping Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, and Wén as former sages.
Tàizǔ rejected his proposal,
and Qióng then wrote the Shìdiàn Jiěbó to refute it.
Many discerning individuals agreed with Qióng's view.
He was as famous as Měihé and Xuán,
and at the time they were called
"the Three Zhùjiào of Chéngjūn."
In the ninth year, he was transferred to the Zhōngdū Guózǐjiān,
to teach the sons of meritorious officials.
Qióng's scholarship and conduct had always been excellent,
and even generals and military officers all knew and respected his adherence to ritual.
In the eleventh year, he retired.
He died.
Zhào Chù,
courtesy name Běnchū,
was a native of Shānyīn.
He was a Yuán Jìnshì.
In the sixth year of Hóngwǔ, he was summoned and appointed Guózǐ Bóshì.
The emperor once presided over the Fèntiān Diàn,
and summoned Chù, along with Qián Zǎi, Bèi Qióng, and others, saying:
"You all should teach solely the classics established by Kǒngzǐ;
be careful not to mix in the 'vertical and horizontal alliance' speeches of Sū Qín and Zhāng Yí."
All the officials bowed their heads and accepted the order.
Chù then requested that the officially sanctioned Thirteen Classics be promulgated throughout the realm,
and that the Zhànguó Cè and all books on yin-yang divination and prognostication
not be placed in the academies.
The following year, thirty-five exceptionally talented students were selected,
and Chù was specifically tasked to lead them,
teaching them classical prose.
Soon, Lǐ Kuò, Huáng Yì, and others were promoted to be imperial lecturers in the Wénhuá and Wǔyīng halls,
and all were employed.
In the ninth year,
the Yùshǐ Tái stated that Bóshì Chù had taught the Shī Jīng at Chéngjūn for four years,
and many of his disciples had become important officials in various regions or held credentials in different ministries.
Now that he was past the age of retirement,
they requested that he be granted his retirement.
Thus, he retired as Hànlín Yuàn Dàizhì,
and was given money from the imperial treasury for travel expenses.
Sòng Lián, along with his colleagues and over a thousand students, saw him off.
He died at the age of eighty-one.
His son, Guīyù,
was a Bīngbù Shìláng,
and later served as Zhī Láizhōu,
achieving renown.
Qián Zǎi,
courtesy name Zǐyǔ,
was a native of Kuàijī.
He was the fourteenth-generation descendant of Wǔsù Wáng of Wúyuè.
During the Zhìzhèng era, he passed the Jiǎkē examination,
but did not serve due to his aged parents.
In the second year of Hóngwǔ, he was summoned to be Guózǐ Zhùjiào.
He wrote the Jīnlíng Xíngshèng Lùn and the Lìdài Dìwáng Miào Yuèzhāng,
all of which pleased the emperor.
In the tenth year, he requested retirement.
He was promoted to Bóshì,
granted an imperial edict, and sent home.
By the twenty-seventh year,
the emperor was reading Cài Shì's Shūchuán,
and found that its description of celestial movements
contradicted Zhū Zǐ's Shīchuán.
Other annotations also had problematic parts compared to what Zōu Jìyǒu of Póyáng had discussed.
He summoned eminent scholars from across the realm to correct them.
Bīngbù Shàngshū Táng Duó recommended Zǎi, along with the retired Biānxiū Zhāng Měihé, and Zhùjiào Jìn Quán, among others.
Messengers rode swift horses to summon them,
and Liú Sānwú was appointed to oversee the project.
When the wine towers outside the gates of Jiāngdōng were completed,
the emperor bestowed paper currency upon all officials,
and held a banquet there.
Zǎi and others composed poems to express their gratitude.
The emperor was greatly pleased.
He instructed that any of the old scholars who wished to return home
should be sent back first.
Zǎi was the oldest,
but he requested to stay.
The emperor was delighted.
When the book was completed,
it was named Shūchuán Huìxuǎn,
and promulgated throughout the realm.
He was generously rewarded
and sent home by courier.
He died at the age of ninety-six.
There was also Xiāo Zhí,
courtesy name Zǐsuǒ,
a native of Tàihé.
In the fourth year of Hóngwǔ, he passed the xiāngjǔ examination.
He served as Guózǐ Xuélù.
The following year, at the summer solstice,
the emperor performed rituals at the northern suburb,
and summoned Shàngshū Wú Lín and Zhǔshì Sòng Lián to lead the literary scholars to accompany him.
Zhí, along with Táo Kǎi and twelve others, entered to pay respects at the fasting hall.
They were ordered to compose poems,
and then again ordered to compose poems on the gardenia flower.
The emperor especially favored Zhí's composition,
showing it to all the officials,
and his imperial favor was extraordinary at the time.
At that time, the emperor paid close attention to literature,
often personally testing his court officials.
Zhí and Chén Guān received especially remarkable recognition.
Guān was guided and introduced into an audience,
and was tested with Wáng Měng's essay on crushing lice.
He was immediately promoted to Cānzhèng of Shǎnxī.
Soon after, he was recalled to attend by the Emperor's side.
He composed the Zhōngshān Fù upon request,
and was bestowed with gold and silk.
In Shǎn, he was renowned for his integrity and diligence.
Someone once asked what the gold produced in Shǎn looked like.
Guān was greatly astonished and said:
"I am merely serving as a local official;
why ask about gold?"
When he died,
his wife and children almost had no means to support themselves.
Zhí requested leave to return home to care for his elderly parents,
and after his parents passed away, he built a hut by their grave.
Shēnguógōng Dèng Zhèn was suppressing bandits at Lóngquán,
but his subordinates were not disciplined.
Zhí went and reproached him,
and Dèng Zhèn then enforced discipline,
bringing peace to the people of the district.
Both men were sincerely virtuous gentlemen.
Lǐ Shúzhèng,
courtesy name Kèzhèng,
originally named Zōngyí,
was a native of Jìng'ān.
At twelve, he could compose poetry,
and as he grew, he became more learned and erudite.
At that time, there were ten talented scholars in Jiāngxī,
and Shúzhèng was one of them.
He was recommended and appointed Guózǐ Xuézhèng.
In the early years of Hóngwǔ,
he requested to return home.
Not long after,
he was again recommended to be Xuézhèng,
and then promoted to Wèinán Chéng.
The people of Tóngzhōu and Púchéng were disputing a land boundary,
which remained unresolved for many years.
The Xíngshěng entrusted the matter to Shúzhèng.
He arrived alone on horseback
and resolved it with a few decisive words.
Wèinán annually remitted twenty thousand (shí) of grain,
but powerful gentry conspired with corrupt officials,
and the land tax had no fixed quota.
Shúzhèng personally measured the fields,
establishing precise laws,
and eliminated all abuses.
He was promoted to Xīnghuà Zhīxiàn.
Soon after, he was summoned to be Lǐbù Yuánwàiláng.
Due to his old age, he requested to return home,
but this was not permitted.
He was reassigned as Guózǐ Zhùjiào,
thus Shúzhèng arrived at the Tàixué for the third time.
The Emperor was then keen on promoting cultural governance,
and paid particular attention to the talents in the Guóxué.
However, many of the students were noble youths
and did not follow instructions.
Shúzhèng strictly established regulations,
sat upright morning and evening,
and supervised lessons without any sign of weariness.
The court considered him worthy.
He was promoted to Jiānchá Yùshǐ,
and was ordered to inspect the Lingbiǎo region.
A clerk in Qióngzhōufǔ impeached its prefect for occupying a public seat and signing documents.
Shúzhèng investigated him.
The prefect was cleared,
and the clerk was punished.
Tàizǔ praised him, saying:
"People say the old Censor is weak,
yet he is so discerning and decisive!"
He successively held the office of Lǐbù Shìláng.
In the fourteenth year, he was promoted to Shàngshū,
and died in office.
Shúzhèng's wife, Lady Xià,
threw herself into a well and died when Chén Yǒuliàng's forces captured Nánchāng.
Shúzhèng was moved by her righteousness,
and never remarried for the rest of his life.
Liú Sōng,
courtesy name Zǐgāo,
a native of Tàihé,
was formerly named Chǔ.
His family was poor, but he studied diligently.
In winter, he had no stove fire,
his hands cracked,
but he continued transcribing.
At the end of the Yuán dynasty, he was recommended in his鄉 [Xiāng] (prefecture).
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, he was recommended for his profound understanding of the classics and virtuous conduct,
and his name was changed to the current one.
He was summoned for an audience at Fèngtiān Diàn,
and appointed Bīngbù Zhífāngsī Lángzhōng.
He was ordered to levy grain in Zhènjiāng.
Zhènjiāng had many fields belonging to meritorious officials,
and the taxes and levies burdened the people.
Sōng earnestly requested a slight reduction, which was granted.
He was promoted to Běipíng Ànchásī Fùshǐ.
He lightened punishments and simplified affairs,
gathered scattered and displaced people,
and all the people resumed their livelihoods.
He established a Wén Tiānxiáng temple beside the school campus.
He had an inscription carved on a stone at the school gate,
instructing the prefectures and counties not to burden the students with corvée labor.
He once requested to reduce the number of post horses in remote areas to augment those in Wǎnpíng.
The Emperor approved his memorial,
and turning to his attending ministers, said:
"The uneven distribution of labor and ease in the postal service has existed for a long time.
Sōng can speak of it;
should not governing the people be like this?"
He was disliked by Hú Wéiyōng,
and was convicted of an offense and exiled to forced labor,
but was soon released and returned home.
In the thirteenth year,
Wéiyōng was executed,
and Sōng was summoned and appointed Lǐbù Shìláng.
Not long after,
he was promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū.
When lightning struck Jǐnshēn Diàn,
the Emperor held court and instructed his officials to present their views on gains and losses.
Sōng kowtowed,
and replied by emphasizing cultivation of virtue and benevolent governance.
Soon after, he retired.
In March of the following year, he was summoned along with the former Xíngbù Shàngshū Lǐ Jìng.
Jìng was appointed Guózǐ Jìjiǔ,
and Sōng was Sīyè.
They were bestowed with saddles and horses,
and ordered to attend court morning and evening.
Whenever they met, they would converse leisurely for some time.
He died within ten days.
When his illness struck,
he still forced himself to sit and instruct the students.
When he was on his deathbed,
Jìng asked what he wished to say.
He said:
"The Son of Heaven sent me to teach the students of the Guózǐ.
He will expect success from me,
but I am to die so suddenly!"
He did not mention family matters even once.
The Emperor ordered the relevant authorities to arrange his funeral and burial,
and personally composed an elegy and offered a sacrifice to him.
Sōng was learned from a young age,
and by nature was honest and cautious.
His three brothers shared a single thatched hut,
and had fifty mú of land.
When he became noble,
there was no increase in their possessions.
A single cotton quilt lasted him ten years;
when it was damaged by mice,
he only then replaced it,
still mending the old one to use for his son.
While in office, he never brought his family burdens with him.
When he took up his post in Běipíng,
he brought one boy servant,
but sent him back upon arrival.
In the evening, after the officials had left,
he would read by a solitary lamp,
often until dawn.
He was skilled in poetry,
and the people of Yùzhāng referred to his style as
"Xījiāng Pài."
Luó Fùrén,
a native of Jíshuǐ.
Young, he loved learning.
Chén Yǒuliàng appointed him Biānxiū.
Afterwards,
realizing Chén Yǒuliàng would achieve nothing,
he fled.
He paid homage to Tàizǔ in Jiǔjiāng,
and was kept by his side.
He followed in the battle of Póyáng,
carrying a secret letter to persuade the yet-unconquered prefectures of Jiāngxī to surrender.
He was appointed Zhōngshū Zīyì.
He followed in the siege of Wǔchāng.
Tàizǔ wished to persuade Chén Lǐ to surrender,
and as Fùrén was a former minister of Chén Yǒuliàng,
he sent him into the city to persuade him,
adding:
"If Lǐ comes,
he will not lose wealth and nobility."
Fùrén kowtowed and said:
"If the orphaned heir of the Chén family can preserve his life and position,
allowing me not to break my word in the future,
I will die without regret."
Tàizǔ said:
"Go,
I will not mislead you."
Fùrén arrived at the city gate
and wept bitterly all day.
Lǐ lowered him into the city with a rope.
He saw Lǐ and wept profusely,
conveying Tàizǔ's intentions,
and further said:
"Wherever our great army advances, it crushes all in its path.
If you do not surrender, there will be a massacre.
What crime have the people in the city committed?"
Lǐ listened to his words,
and consequently led his officials and subordinates out to surrender.
He was transferred to be an assistant instructor (Zhùjiào) in the National Academy (Guózǐ),
and due to his old age, he was specially permitted to enter and exit in a small carriage.
Whenever he had an audience at a banquet,
he was granted a seat and food and drink.
Afterwards,
he was again sent to Kuòkuò.
Previous envoys had often been detained,
but Fùrén, with his generous and impassioned arguments,
was the only one to return.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, he was promoted to compiler (Biānxiū),
and again went with the department director (Zhǔshì) Zhāng Fú to instruct Ānnán to return the territory it had encroached upon in Zhànchéng.
Ānnán obeyed the imperial decree
and sent Fùrén a considerable amount of gold, cowrie shells, and local products,
all of which he refused.
The emperor heard of this and esteemed him.
In the third year, the Hóngwénguǎn was established,
and Fùrén was made an academician (Xuèshì),
holding the same position as Liú Jī.
Before the emperor, he spoke freely, pointing out what was advantageous and disadvantageous,
often speaking in a Southern accent (Nányīn).
The emperor, on the other hand, liked his straightforwardness
and called him
"Old Honest Luó" (Lǎoshí Luó)
without using his given name.
Occasionally, the emperor visited his dwelling,
a poor alley against the city wall.
Fùrén was whitewashing a wall,
and quickly called his wife to bring a stool for the emperor to sit on.
The emperor said,
"How can a virtuous scholar live here?"
So, he bestowed upon him a residence within the city.
On the Tiānshòu Festival, Fùrén composed a *Shuǐlóngyín* (a *cí* tune) and presented it.
The emperor was pleased
and amply rewarded him.
Soon after, he requested to retire due to illness.
When he took leave at the palace,
he was given a coarse cloth robe,
and a poem praising him was inscribed on its collar.
Later,
he was again summoned to the capital
and memorialized to reduce the autumn grain tax in Jiāngxī.
This was approved.
After staying for three months,
he was given a jade belt, an iron walking stick, a sitting stool, furs and a horse, and eating utensils, and sent back,
where he died of old age.
His grandson, Rǔjìng,
whose given name was Jiǎn,
was known by his courtesy name (zì).
In the second year of Yǒnglè, he became a *Shùjíshì* (supernumerary scholar),
studying in the Wényuángé.
He recited books but failed to please the emperor,
and was immediately exiled to Jiāngnán.
After several days, he was recalled.
From then on, he rigorously applied himself to his studies,
and was successively promoted to lecturer (Shìjiǎng).
During Rénzōng's reign,
he presented a memorial on fifteen matters of current governance,
which displeased the emperor and led to his imprisonment.
Later, he was appointed censor (Yùshǐ) along with Lǐ Shímǐan,
and his reputation for integrity shook the times.
At the beginning of Xuānzōng's reign,
he wrote a letter to the Grand Secretary (Dàxuéshì) Yáng Shìqí, saying:
"Emperor Gāohuang (Tàizǔ) (Hóngwǔ) ruled over the four seas,
and Emperor Wén (Tàizōng) (Yǒnglè) restored the empire,
yet they were still cautious and watchful,
daring not to be negligent.
The former emperor (Rénzōng) had not yet reigned for a month
when he suddenly abandoned his ministers.
The reason for this, when examined,
was entirely due to treacherous and petty individuals
who offered 'elixirs of immortality' (jīnshí zhī fāng) that caused his illness.
Last winter,
Jiǎn, in his foolish bluntness, responded to the imperial summons with a memorial,
and his words touched upon disrespect,
a crime punishable by ten thousand deaths.
The former emperor (Rénzōng) pitied his solitary straightforwardness,
withheld the thunderous punishment,
and allowed him to remain in the censorate (yánlù).
Examining my conscience,
there is nothing commendable to report.
I humbly observe that in June of this year,
the imperial carriage went to Tiānshòushān,
personally visiting the two imperial tombs.
The people of the capital looked on and sighed with admiration,
considering it a great act of filial piety by the sagely emperor.
Soon after, rumors spread on the road
that immediately after the rituals, there was a hunting exercise (jiàoliè jiǎngwǔ).
The only attendants were Yěxiān Tǔgān (Esentai) and several hundred of his followers,
galloping like the wind and lightning,
chasing each other back and forth.
When I heard this,
my heart pounded and my courage failed.
Indeed, spring hunting (sōumiáo), summer hunting (xúnshòu), and autumn hunting (mǐnshòu)
are indeed customary practices of the state.
However, to go out for a tomb visit
and then engage in a hunting contest with a surrendered general in the mountain valleys —
the warning against 'sitting beneath a tottering wall' (chuítáng zhī jiè)
and the danger of 'reins and bits' (xiánjué zhī yú)
cannot but be deeply considered.
Your Excellency is an old minister of four reigns,
and the chief grand councilor (yuánfǔ) to two sagely emperors.
If you do not speak on this matter,
then who else can speak on it?
I humbly hope you will specifically consider and adopt this,
to greatly expand the thought of 'presenting peace' (jìngxiàn zhī sī)
and glorify the meaning of 'aiding straightness' (bìzhí zhī yì)."
Soon after, he was promoted to Right Vice Minister of Works (Gōngbù Yòushìláng),
and made two missions to Ānnán.
At that time, Lí Lì claimed that his ruler, Chén Gǎo, had died,
and held a banquet with female musicians.
Rǔjìng rebuked him,
and Lí Lì, in fear, apologized.
He returned to oversee grain transport in both Zhèjiāng provinces,
and managed military agricultural colonies (túntián) in Shǎnxī,
making many arrangements.
He was charged with accepting bribes
and demoted to a functionary (shìguān).
When Yīngzōng ascended the throne,
he received a general amnesty.
Rǔjìng mistakenly cited the imperial decree to resume his former post,
and was again arrested and imprisoned.
Due to his meritorious arrangements in Shǎnxī,
he was spared death and exiled to the border.
Soon after, he was reinstated
to his former post.
When there was an alert on the frontier,
Rǔjìng went to supervise provisions.
He encountered the enemy at Hóngchéngzi,
was struck by a stray arrow,
and fell from his horse but escaped.
He requested to return home due to illness
and died.
The encomium says: When the Míng dynasty was first established,
it prioritized talent,
recruiting from all four directions.
Seasoned scholars (sùrú) gathered at the palace,
and were employed according to their strengths.
Apart from deliberating on rites and establishing institutions,
some participated in legislative decisions,
others served in the imperial secretariat,
and the officials from the National Academy (Chéngjūn Zhòuzǐ) were particularly praised for their competence,
truly showing that the right people were found.
Indeed, these ministers, in the late Yuán period,
delved into classics and pursued learning,
confined to their humble dwellings in the countryside,
almost passing their lives without being known.
But when the peaceful era (tàiyùn) first arrived,
they emerged together like connected gourds,
each displaying their inner wisdom
to enrich the grand policies
and adorn the civil administration.
As the ancients said, the world does not lack talent;
it only depends on how the ruler gathers them.
Is this not true!
Collated Notes
Biographies (Lièzhuàn) Twenty-Six: Chén Xiū (Téng Yì, Zhào Hǎodé, Zhái Shàn, Lǐ Rén, Wú Lín), Yáng Sīyì (Téng Démào, Fàn Mǐn, Fèi Zhèn, Zhāng Wǎn), Zhōu Zhēn
(Liú Wéiqiān, Zhōu Zhēn, Duān Fùchū, Lǐ Zhì, Lí Guāng, Liú Mǐn), Yáng Jìng (Líng Hàn, Yán Demǐn), Shàn Ānrén (Zhū Shǒurén), Xuē Xiáng (Qín Kuí, Zhào Zhù, Zhào Jùn), Táng Duó (Shěn Jìn), Kāi Jì
Chén Xiū,
courtesy name Bóáng,
was from Shàngráo.
He followed Tàizǔ (Hóngwǔ) in pacifying Eastern Zhèjiāng,
and was appointed a judicial official (lǐguān).
In applying laws and decrees,
he always based them on leniency and generosity,
completely reforming the corrupt practices of the late Yuán.
He was promoted to department director (lángzhōng) in the Ministry of War (Bīngbù),
and then transferred to be the prefect (zhīfǔ) of Jǐnán.
At that time, after the chaos, households were withered and fragmented,
and there were also many military generals training troops and farming fields among them.
Chén Xiū had effective methods for governance,
so soldiers and commoners lived in peace,
and displaced people returned to their livelihoods.
The emperor praised him.
In the fourth year of Hóngwǔ, he was appointed Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū).
The establishment of the Six Boards
began in the first year of Hóngwǔ.
Téng Yì of Zhènjiāng was the first to head the Board of Civil Office (Lìbù).
He assisted the provincial administration in establishing the preliminary laws for appointments, removals, evaluations, and assessments.
By this time, Xiū and Vice Minister Lǐ Rén meticulously studied old regulations,
adapting them to contemporary needs.
According to the remoteness or importance of a locality,
they determined the complexity or simplicity of official appointments.
All laws concerning the promotion and demotion of civil officials, as well as the evaluation of their performance and verification of their achievements,
were carefully planned,
making the appointment system orderly.
Not long after,
he died in office.
Subsequently, the departmental system underwent several innovations.
The practice of having officials attending court recommend those they knew,
and establishing regulations for internal and external enfeoffment, commendation, and hereditary privilege,
began with Lǐ Xìn of Fúshān.
The system where all court officials nationwide submitted records of their deeds, documents, maps, land, and population,
and the method for allocating and employing clerks,
began with Yú Jì of Kūnshān.
Following the model of the Táng dynasty's Six Canons,
from the Five Commanderies (Wǔfǔ), Six Boards, and Censorate (Dūcháyuàn) down to all other offices, officials were appointed and duties divided,
compiled into a book called *Zhūsī Zhízhǎng* (Duties of Various Offices).
The method for evaluating clerks and servants at the end of their term and issuing their certifications for heads of offices (sī), guards (wèi), prefectures (fǔ), and counties (xiàn),
and the selection of Imperial Academy students (jiānshēng) skilled in writing to concurrently serve as officials in zhōu and xiàn, as well as academic instructors (xuézhèng) and pedagogues (jiàoyù),
began with Zhái Shàn of Tàixīng.
The practice of triennial court attendance
and performance reviews based on grades
began with Dù Zé of Yíshuǐ.
These are the general outlines of the personnel administration during the Hóngwǔ era.
Initially, the Six Boards were subordinate to the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshūshěng),
holding little power,
often deferring to the intentions of the chancellors.
Yì, Xiū, and people like Zhān Tóng, Wú Lín, and Zhào Hàodé,
were praised as virtuous while serving in the Board of Civil Office,
but they did not achieve major accomplishments.
By the thirteenth year,
the Central Secretariat was abolished,
and the Boards' authority became independent,
with personnel administration becoming particularly crucial.
However, the emperor's use of law was strict.
Jì was executed for denouncing Sòng Nà,
Shàn was demoted,
and Zé, after being appointed Minister (shàngshū),
was dismissed within a few months.
Only Xìn served as Vice Minister,
then was appointed Minister,
for nearly two years,
dying in office, it is said.
Téng Yì,
courtesy name Zhònghóng.
When Tàizǔ campaigned against Wú,
he was introduced as a scholar
and remained under Xú Dá's command.
Soon, he was appointed Diarist of the Court (qǐjūzhù),
ordered to compile with Yáng Xùn a collection of deeds of ancient unrighteous rulers such as Jié, Zhòu, Qín Shǐhuáng, and Suí Yángdì.
The emperor said:
"I wish to observe the causes of chaos and destruction,
to serve as a clear warning."
In the first year of Wú, he was assigned as Provincial Surveillance Commissioner (ànchásǐ) of Húguǎng.
Soon recalled,
he was promoted to the Board of Civil Office for one month,
then transferred to be an Administrative Assistant (cānzhèng) in Jiāngxī province,
where he died.
Zhào Hàodé,
courtesy name Bǐngyí,
from Rǔyáng.
He entered as Vice Minister of the Board of Revenue (Hùbù) from his post as Prefect of Ānqìng.
He was promoted to Minister,
then transferred to the Board of Civil Office.
The emperor praised him for his fair administration of appointments.
He was once summoned with the Four Assistant Officials (sìfǔguān) to the inner palace,
where they sat and discussed governance.
The emperor ordered court painters to create his portrait within the forbidden palace.
He ended his career as Administrative Assistant of Shǎnxī province.
His son, Yì,
during the Yǒnglè reign,
rose to the position of Vice Minister of the Board of Works (Gōngbù).
Zhái Shàn,
courtesy name Jìngfū,
through recommendation and examination, served successively as Principal of the Bureau of Selection in the Board of Civil Office.
In the twenty-sixth year,
after Minister Zhān Huī and Vice Minister Fù Yǒuwén were executed,
Shàn was ordered to manage the affairs of the Board,
and was twice promoted to Minister.
He was learned in classical studies and his memorials pleased the emperor.
The emperor said:
"Although Shàn is young,
his spirit is broad and magnanimous;
others cannot compare."
The emperor wished to build a residence for him in his hometown,
but Shàn declined.
He also wished to exempt his family from military service,
but Shàn said:
"The number of soldiers should be increased;
how can an exception be made for your servant?"
The emperor considered him even more virtuous.
In the twenty-eighth year, he was demoted to Magistrate of Xuānhuà for an offense,
and died in that position.
Lǐ Rén,
from Tángxiàn.
He initially served Chén Yǒuliàng.
When the royal army captured Wǔchāng,
he surrendered.
Upon recommendation by Cháng Yùchūn,
he replaced Táo Ān as Prefect of Huángzhōu.
He served successively as Vice Minister
and was promoted to Minister.
For an offense, he was demoted to Qīngzhōu,
where his administration was outstanding.
He was promoted to Vice Minister of the Board of Revenue
and then retired.
Wú Lín,
from Huánggǎng.
When Tàizǔ captured Wǔchāng,
through Zhān Tóng's recommendation,
he was summoned to be Assistant Instructor of the National Academy (guózǐ zhùjiào),
his classical learning surpassing Tóng's.
In the first year of Wú, he was appointed Assistant Surveillance Commissioner (ànchásī qiánshì) of Zhèjiāng,
then re-entered as Diarist of the Court,
ordered to carry silks and seek books throughout the land.
In the sixth year of Hóngwǔ,
he was transferred from Minister of the Board of War (Bīngbù) to the Board of Civil Office.
He often took turns with Tóng in managing the Board's affairs.
After more than a year,
he requested to retire.
The emperor once sent an envoy to observe him.
The envoy secretly went to a nearby house.
A farmer sat on a small stool,
then rose to plant rice seedlings in the field,
his demeanor very proper and respectful.
The envoy stepped forward and said:
"Is there a Minister Wú here?"
"Is he present?"
The farmer bowed and replied:
"Lín is he."
The envoy reported the situation.
The emperor greatly praised him.
Yáng Sīyì,
his origin and hometown are unknown.
When Tàizǔ was acclaimed King of Wú,
he was appointed Diarist of the Court.
Initially,
money and grain affairs belonged to the Central Secretariat.
In the first year of Wú, the position of Minister of Agriculture (sīnóngqīng) was first established,
with Sīyì appointed to it.
The next year, the Six Boards were established,
and he was renamed Minister of the Board of Revenue.
After the great chaos,
many people had abandoned their professions.
Sīyì requested that the common people all plant mulberries and hemp.
Taxes would only be collected after four years.
Those who did not plant mulberries would pay in silk,
and those who did not plant hemp would pay in cloth,
similar to the Zhou official system of village cloth.
The edict was approved.
The emperor worried about untimely floods and droughts,
and having nothing to rely on in emergencies.
He ordered Sīyì to establish emergency granaries (yùbèicāng) throughout the realm
to guard against floods and droughts.
Sīyì, as the head of national accounts,
prioritized agriculture, sericulture, and storage.
All the institutions he initiated,
although inspired by the emperor's will,
were meticulously planned,
and he was praised for his ability at the time.
He was transferred to be Administrative Assistant of Shǎnxī province
and died in office.
Throughout the Hóngwǔ reign,
over forty individuals served as Minister of the Board of Revenue,
none remaining in the position for long,
and few having notable achievements.
Only Rú Tàisù, Yáng Jìng, Téng Démào, Fàn Mǐn, and Fèi Zhèn
were somewhat renowned.
Tàisù and Jì have their own biographies.
Démào,
courtesy name Sīmiǎn,
was from Wú.
He served successively in the Central Secretariat and in external posts.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, he was summoned and appointed Minister of the Board of War,
soon after transferred to the Board of Revenue.
He was talented and articulate,
with a broad and magnanimous mind,
skilled in writing memorials.
Many edicts and proclamations for recruitment at the time came from his hand.
He was dismissed from office due to an incident
and died.
Fàn Mǐn,
a native of Ménxiāng.
In the eighth year of Hóngwǔ, he passed the xiùcái examination,
and was promoted to Lángzhōng of the Ministry of Revenue.
In the thirteenth year, he was appointed acting Shàngshū.
He recommended senior scholars such as Wáng Běn,
all of whom were appointed Sīfǔ Guān.
The emperor, finding the labor services unevenly distributed,
ordered the compilation of yellow registers.
Mǐn proposed that one hundred and ten households form a *lǐ*,
with ten men from households with many adult males serving as *lǐzhǎng*,
who would manage the affairs of the *lǐ* to provide for annual labor services.
This would rotate every ten years.
The remaining one hundred households would be divided into ten *jiǎ*.
Later, this system was maintained and not abolished.
The following year, he was dismissed for incompetence.
Fèi Zhèn,
a native of Póyáng.
In the early Hóngwǔ period, he was summoned as a worthy and able person,
and served as Zhīzhōu of Jǐshuǐ.
His kindness and benevolence won the hearts of the people.
He was promoted to Zhīhànzhōng.
During a famine, when bandits arose,
he disbursed over ten thousand *hú* of grain from the granaries to lend to the people,
so that they might return it to the granaries after the autumn harvest.
When the bandits heard this,
they all came and surrendered.
He ordered them to occupy residences and form their own defense units,
numbering several thousand households.
The emperor heard of this and praised him.
Later, he was arrested for a certain matter,
but because of his good governance,
he was specially released and appointed Bǎochāo Tíyǔ.
In the eleventh year,
the emperor said to the Ministry of Personnel:
"Qualifications are set for ordinary people;
those with talent should be employed without regard to rank."
Ninety-five people were promoted extraordinarily,
and Zhèn was appointed Hùbù Shìláng,
soon after advancing to Shàngshū.
He was commanded to determine the system of annual salaries for all officials from thechéngxiàng and Yùshǐ Dàfū downwards.
He was sent out as Húguǎng Bùzhèngshǐ,
and retired due to old age.
In the early Hóngwǔ period,
there was a Zhāng Wǎn,
a native of Póyáng.
As a Gòngshì, he achieved a high rank in the examination,
and was appointed Gěishìzhōng,
then transferred to Hùbù Zhǔshì.
One day,
the emperor asked about the empire's financial revenue and population figures.
He answered everything from memory without omission.
The emperor was pleased,
and immediately promoted him to Zuǒ Shìláng.
When the Jǐnshēndiàn suffered a fire,
he submitted a memorial on current government affairs.
During a famine,
he requested the remission of over a million *shí* of people's land tax.
All his suggestions were favorably received.
Wǎn was talented, intelligent, and had a keen mind.
At the age of twenty-seven,
he died in office.
People of the time regretted his passing.
Zhōu Zhēn,
courtesy name Wéndiǎn,
a native of Jiāngníng.
At the end of the Yuán dynasty, he became an expatriate in Húnán.
When Tàizǔ pacified Wǔchāng,
he was employed as Qiānshì of the Jiāngxī Xíngshěng,
and successively served as Dàlǐ Qīng.
Tàizǔ believed that while the Táng and Sòng dynasties both had established laws for judging cases,
the Yuán dynasty only used temporary administrative regulations,
which made it easy for clerks to commit abuses.
He issued an edict to Zhēn, Lǐ Shàncháng, Liú Jī, Táo Ān, Téng Yì, and others to compile laws and statutes.
Shà qīng Liú Wéiqiān and Chéng Zhōu Zhēn also participated.
When the book was completed,
Tàizǔ praised it as excellent.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, the Ministry of Justice was established,
with Zhēn as Shàngshū,
soon after changed to Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ.
The following year, he was sent out as Cāncè of Guǎngdōng Xíngshěng.
At that time, the provincial administration was newly established,
many principal official posts were vacant,
and there was little encouragement or deterrence in official governance.
Xiāngshān Chéng Chōng Jìng had good governance,
and died in office from overwork.
Zhēn composed a memorial to him.
Those who heard it were moved.

At that time, among the upright officials of prefectures and counties were Léizhōu Tóngzhī Yú Qí, Huìzhōu Zhīfǔ Wàn Dí, Rǔyuán Zhīxiàn Zhāng Ānrén, Qīngliú Zhīxiàn Lǐ Duó, Jiēyáng Xiànchéng Xǔ Dé, Liánzhōu Zhīfǔ Tuō Yīn, and Guīshàn Zhīxiàn Mù Yín.
Zhēn listed all their administrative achievements and reported them.
Mù Yín
was a Tǔsī.
Tuō Yīn
was a Mongolian.
Consequently, subordinate officials became more diligent.
In the ninth month of the third year, he was summoned to be Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
Soon after, he resigned due to illness.
When the emperor first ascended the throne,
he, punishing the Yuán dynasty's leniency and laxity,
applied the law too strictly,
causing those who carried it out to stand still, fearing to move.
Once the laws and statutes were complete,
officials and commoners began to know how to follow them.
Afterwards, there were several revisions,
all taking Zhēn's work as the foundation.
Liú Wéiqiān,
it is not known where he was from.
In the first year of Wú, he was recommended for his talent and learning.
In the early Hóngwǔ period,
he successively served as Húbù Shàngshū.
In the sixth year, he was ordered to meticulously revise the new laws,
deleting the superfluous and pruning the old,
achieving appropriate balance in severity.
The emperor personally made the final decisions and promulgated them.
Later, he was dismissed for a certain matter.
Zhōu Zhēn,
courtesy name Bóníng,
a native of Póyáng,
and one of the Ten Talents of Jiāngxī.
He also rose to the rank of Húbù Shàngshū.
Throughout the Hóngwǔ era,
there were nearly forty individuals who served as Húbù,
with Yáng Jìng being the most prominent,
while Duān Fùchū, Lǐ Zhì, Lí Guāng, and Liú Mǐn were also well-known.
Fùchū,
courtesy name Yǐshàn,
a native of Lìshuǐ.
He was a descendant of Zǐgòng,
and used the abbreviated surname,
referring to himself as Duān.
At the end of the Yuán dynasty, he was a petty official.
Cháng Yùchūn, when garrisoning Jīnhuá,
summoned him to his staff.
Not long after,
he resigned.
Tàizǔ knew his reputation,
and summoned him to be Jīnglì of Huīzhōu Prefecture.
He ordered the people to declare their land themselves,
compiling it into cadastral registers,
thus eradicating accumulated malpractices.
He was gradually promoted to Mó kàn Sīlìng.
At that time, the official yamen was newly established,
with documents piled high,
but Fùchū meticulously reviewed everything without omission.
The emperor once praised him in court.
His character was severe and upright,
and no one dared to approach him with private requests.
Many of his colleagues were corrupt and failed,
but Fùchū alone was spared due to his integrity.
In the fourth year of Hóngwǔ, he was exceptionally appointed Húbù Shàngshū,
and his application of the law was just.
When the incident of "flying grain" in Hángzhōu came to light,
over a hundred people were arrested.
An edict ordered Fùchū to investigate,
and he immediately distinguished between truth and falsehood,
whereupon the Zhīfǔ and all below him confessed their guilt.
The following year, he was sent out as Húguǎng Cāncè,
and ordered that those who returned should have their taxes remitted for one year.
All the displaced people gathered,
and he became known for his administrative competence.
He was recalled due to a certain matter,
and died.
His son Xiàowén
was a Hànlín Dàizhào;
and Xiàosī
was a Hànlín Shìshū.
They were sent to Cháoxiān successively,
and both were noted for their integrity,
so the Koreans built the Shuāngqīng Guǎn for them.
Lǐ Zhì,
courtesy name Wénbīn,
was a native of Déqìng.
He possessed talent and strategy.
At the end of the Yuán dynasty, he served under Hé Zhēn.
He once raised troops to pacify rebellious commoners in Déqìng,
and neighboring prefectures largely relied on his protection.
Renowned scholars who were sojourning in Lǐngnán,
such as Liú Sānwú from Chálíng, Báiyán Zǐzhōng from Jiāngyòu, Sūn Fén from Yángchéng, and Zhāng Zhì from Jiàn'ān,
all treated him with respect.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, he surrendered along with Zhēn
and was appointed Secretary of the Central Secretariat's Bureau of Judicial Review.
The following year, he was transferred to be Secretary of the Chief Military Commission's Bureau of Judicial Review,
where he enforced the law vigorously.
In the fifth year, he was promoted to Vice Minister of Justice,
and then to Minister,
administering justice with fairness and leniency.
He was sent to distribute relief in Shāndōng,
and the emperor composed a poem to bid him farewell.
Soon after, he was appointed Administration Commissioner of the Zhèjiāng Provincial Administration Commission.
He served for three years,
and his benevolent achievements became widely known.
The emperor, mindful of Zhì's age,
recalled him.
He once had an audience in a private palace,
where the emperor inquired about current political affairs.
Zhì spoke candidly without concealment.
He was appointed Right Grand Counselor to the Prince of Jìngjiāng.
When the prince was deposed for his crimes,
Zhì was consequently implicated and executed.
Lí Guāng,
was a native of Dōngguǎn.
He was appointed Censor by local recommendation,
and while inspecting Sūzhōu,
he requested relief for flood victims,
saving many lives.
While inspecting Fèngyáng,
he submitted a sealed memorial,
all of which addressed critical contemporary issues.
The emperor praised him.
In the ninth year of Hóngwǔ, he was promoted to Vice Minister of Justice,
enforcing the law impartially.
He was, however, envied by the Grand Censor Chén Níng,
and was implicated in an incident and died in exile.
Liú Mǐn,
was a native of Sùníng.
He passed the examination for filial and incorrupt officials
and became an official in the Central Secretariat.
He once bought reeds from the market by the Lúlóng River in the evening,
transported them home at dawn,
had his wife weave mats,
sold them to support his mother,
and only then attended to his official duties.
His character was honest and upright;
if someone gave him porcelain or earthenware,
he would not accept it.
When he was a record-keeper in the Chǔ Chancellor's Office,
the Central Secretariat assigned women confiscated by the government to the families of civil officials.
Many urged him to request one to serve his mother.
Mǐn firmly declined, saying:
"Serving one's mother
is the duty of one's wife and daughters;
what concern is it of others?"
When the provincial officials were later defeated,
many clerks were executed,
but Mǐn alone was not implicated.
The emperor admired him
and promoted him to Vice Minister of Works,
then transferred him to the Ministry of Justice.
He was sent out as an Assistant Prefect of Huīzhōu Prefecture,
where he had benevolent governance,
and died in office.
Yáng Jìng,
courtesy name Zhòngníng,
was a native of Shānyáng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the eighteenth year of Hóngwǔ
and was selected as a probationary official in the Ministry of Personnel.
The following year, he was promoted to Vice Minister of Revenue.
At that time, those serving in various departments
were mostly *jìnshì* or students of the Imperial College,
but sometimes there were those who acted unlawfully.
The emperor issued the Great Edict,
citing the Transmission Commissioner Cài Xuān, Left Transmission Commissioner Rú Cháng, Vice Minister of Works Qín Kuí, and Jìng to admonish and encourage them, saying:
"These are also *jìnshì* and Imperial College students;
they can perform their duties in a manner that pleases Our heart."
Such was the praise he received.
In the twenty-second year, he was promoted to Minister.
In May of the following year, an edict decreed that all capital officials who had served for three years should be transferred or promoted,
establishing it as a regulation.
Thus, Zhào Miǎn, the Minister of Justice, and Jìng exchanged offices.
The emperor instructed:
"Ignorant commoners who break the law
are like those who eat and drink.
If laws are established to prevent them,
the number of offenders only increases.
If we extend leniency and practice benevolence,
perhaps they can be transformed.
From now on, only those who commit the Ten Abominations or murder will be put to death;
for all other crimes, they shall be ordered to transport grain to the northern frontier."
He further said:
"For prisoners in the capital's jails,
you, our ministers, shall review and report to Us,
and We will personally examine and decide,
still fearing there might be errors.
How can the decisions made by various officials outside the capital
be entirely appropriate?
You, our ministers, should meticulously examine them,
and then send officials to review and decide."
Jìng followed the imperial decree, investigated and deliberated,
and corrected many miscarriages of justice.
The emperor praised and accepted his advice.
He once interrogated a military officer,
and a gate guard searched his person,
finding a large pearl.
Subordinate officials were astonished.
Jìng calmly said:
"It's fake.
How could there be a pearl so large?"
He then crushed it.
When the emperor heard this,
he sighed, saying:
"Jìng's action
has four virtues.
He did not present it to Us to curry favor;
that is the first virtue.
He did not relentlessly pursue the one who offered it;
that is the second virtue.
He did not reward the gate guard,
thus preventing opportunism by lesser men;
that is the third virtue.
A pearl worth a thousand gold pieces appeared suddenly,
yet he remained completely unmoved.
He possesses intelligence superior to ordinary men
and the ability to adapt to changing circumstances;
that is the fourth virtue."
In the twenty-sixth year, he concurrently held the post of Grand Mentor of the Heir Apparent,
and was granted two salaries.
Later,
he was dismissed due to an incident.
At the time of the expedition against Zhào Zōngshòu of Lóngzhōu,
an imperial edict commanded Jìng to instruct Ānnán to supply grain to the army.
He went as a commoner.
The Ānnán minister Lí Yīyuán, considering land transport difficult and perilous,
intended not to obey the edict.
Jìng repeatedly explained and persuaded him,
and also promised water transport.
Yīyuán then transported twenty thousand *dàn* of grain to Hǎijiāng,
and separately built a pontoon bridge to reach Lóngzhōu.
The emperor was greatly pleased
and appointed Jìng Censor-in-Chief of the Left.
Jìng was public-spirited, loyal, and possessed wisdom and strategy.
He was skilled at managing complex and arduous tasks,
and his administration of justice was clear and discerning without resorting to excessively harsh legalism.
He received the most profound favor and trust,
with none among his peers comparable.
In the seventh month of the thirtieth year, he was implicated for having drafted a petition for a fellow villager to redress a grievance,
and was impeached by a censor.
The emperor was enraged
and consequently granted him death.
He was thirty-eight years old at the time.
At that time there was Líng Hàn (凌漢),
courtesy name Dǒunán (斗南),
a native of Yuánwǔ (原武).
He was recommended as a Xiùcái (秀才),
and presented the "Essay on Magpies."
He was granted an official post,
and successively served as an Yùshǐ (御史).
When he inspected Shǎnxī (陝西),
he submitted memorials regarding several instances of severe hardship suffered by his subordinates.
The emperor approved of this,
and summoned his son, bestowing clothes and money upon him.
Hàn (漢) adjudicated cases fairly and impartially.
When he returned to the capital,
a person whom Hàn (漢) had treated kindly
invited him to a banquet,
intending to give him a generous gift of gold.
Hàn (漢) said:
"Wine can be drunk,
but gold cannot be accepted."
The emperor heard of this and praised him greatly,
promoting him to Yòu Dū Yùshǐ (右都御史).
At that time, Zhān Huī (詹徽) was the Zuǒ (左),
and their opinions did not align.
Each time Hàn (漢) directly rebuked Huī (徽) to his face,
Huī (徽) bore a grudge.
Hàn (漢) was demoted to Xíngbù Shìláng (刑部侍郎),
then transferred to Lǐbù (禮部).
Later, he was impeached by Huī (徽),
and demoted to Zuǒ Qiāndū Yùshǐ (左僉都御史).
The emperor pitied his decline,
and ordered him to return to his hometown.
Hàn (漢), knowing that Huī (徽) was still in power,
feared future trouble,
and dared not leave.
More than a year later, Huī (徽) was executed,
and Hàn (漢) was again promoted to Yòu Qiāndū Yùshǐ (右僉都御史),
and soon thereafter retired and returned home.
Hàn (漢) was not careful in his speech,
and repeatedly suffered setbacks in office.
However, his integrity and straightforwardness were known to the emperor,
and thus he was ultimately able to preserve his life and reputation.
Furthermore, Yán Demín (嚴德珉), a native of Wú (吳),
was promoted from Yùshǐ (御史) to Zuǒ Qiāndū Yùshǐ (左僉都御史),
and requested to return home due to illness.
The emperor was enraged,
tattooed his face,
and exiled him to garrison duty in Nándān (南丹),
but he was released and returned upon an amnesty.
Dressed in common clothes and traveling on foot,
he considered himself among the common people,
and was still alive during the Xuāndé (宣德) era.
Once, he was arrested by an Yùshǐ (御史) for some matter.
Demín (德珉) knelt beneath the hall,
and stated that he had once handled official business in the Censorate,
and understood the law.
The Yùshǐ (御史) asked what his official rank was.
He replied:
"During the Hóngwǔ (洪武) era, I was the head of the Censorate;
I am the one called Yán Demín (嚴德珉)."
The Yùshǐ (御史) was greatly astonished,
and bowed, helping him up.
The next day, when he went to visit,
Demín (德珉) had already packed his bags and moved on.
A professor, drinking with him,
saw his tattooed face
and worn-out cap,
and asked:
"Elder, what law did you violate?"
Demín (德珉) recounted his past experiences,
and then said,
"In earlier times, the national law was very strict;
officials could not even guarantee their own heads.
This worn-out cap is not easy to wear."
Then, facing north, he cupped his hands
and exclaimed,
"By the grace of the Sage!
By the grace of the Sage!"
Sì Ānrén (單安仁),
courtesy name Défū (德夫),
was a native of Háo (濠).
In his youth, he was a prefectural clerk.
At the end of the Yuán (元) dynasty, during the military unrest in Jiānghuái (江淮),
Ānrén (安仁) gathered righteous troops to protect his hometown,
and was appointed Pàn Guān (判官) of the Shūmì (樞密) Bureau.
He followed Zhènnán Wáng (鎮南王) Bólúopǔhuà (孛羅普化) in defending Yángzhōu (揚州).
At that time, warlords rose everywhere,
and Ānrén (安仁) sighed, saying:
"These people are merely being driven out by others.
When a true king rises,
it will be distinctly different."
When Zhènnán Wáng (鎮南王) was driven away by the Chángqiāng Jūn (長槍軍),
Ānrén (安仁) had no one to follow.
Hearing that Tàizǔ (太祖) had pacified Jíqìng (集慶),
he then said:
"This is truly it."
He led his troops to submit.
Tàizǔ (太祖) was pleased,
and immediately ordered him to lead his army to defend Zhènjiāng (鎮江).
He strictly disciplined his troops,
and the enemy dared not invade.
He was transferred to defend Chángzhōu (常州);
his son rebelled and surrendered to Zhāng Shìchéng (張士誠).
Tàizǔ (太祖), knowing Ānrén's (安仁) loyalty and caution,
did not doubt him.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Zhèjiāng Fùshǐ (浙江副使).
A fierce commander extorted the people,
calling it "stockade grain."
Ānrén (安仁) brought him to justice.
He was promoted to Ànchásǐ (按察使),
then summoned to serve as Zhōngshū Zuǒsī Lángzhōng (中書左司郎中),
assisting Lǐ Shàncháng (李善長) in his judgments.
He was transferred to be Shǒuyù Qiānhù (守禦千戶) of Ruìzhōu (瑞州),
then entered service as Jiāngzuò Qīng (將作卿).
In the first year of Hóngwǔ (洪武), he was promoted to Gōngbù Shàngshū (工部尚書),
still concurrently overseeing the affairs of the Jiāngzuò (將作) Bureau.
Ānrén (安仁) was shrewd and resourceful,
and all his constructions,
whether large or small, met the standards,
greatly pleasing the emperor.
The following year, he was transferred to Bīngbù Shàngshū (兵部尚書),
and requested to retire due to old age.
He was granted three thousand mù (畝) of land,
seventy head of cattle,
and was given half a Shàngshū (尚書) salary annually.
In the sixth year, he was appointed Shāndōng Cāncānjī (山東參政).
He earnestly declined,
and it was granted.
While at home,
he once memorialized requesting the dredging of the Yízhēn Nánbà (儀真南壩) to Púshù Wān (朴樹灣) to facilitate official and civilian transport,
and proposed diverting the Grand Canal to the deep port of Jiāngdū (江都) to prevent silting,
and relocating the Guāzhōu (瓜州) granaries to the west of Yángzǐ Qiáo (揚子橋)
to avoid the dangers of the great river's winds and tides.
The emperor approved of his words.
He was again appointed Bīngbù Shàngshū (兵部尚書),
and then retired.
Initially,
the rank of Shàngshū (尚書) was Zheng San Pin (正三品).
In the thirteenth year,
the Zhōngshū Shěng (中書省) was abolished,
and it was then advanced to Zheng Er Pin (正二品),
but Ānrén (安仁) had retired before that.
The emperor, remembering Ānrén's (安仁) meritorious service and seniority,
specifically bestowed upon him the title of Zīshàn Dàfū (資善大夫) in the twentieth year.
He died in the twelfth month of that year,
at the age of eighty-five.
Zhū Shǒurén (朱守仁) of Xúzhōu (徐州),
courtesy name Yuánfū (元夫),
also served as Shūmì Tóngzhī (樞密同知) at the end of the Yuán (元) dynasty due to his protective achievements,
defending Shūchéng (舒城).
When the Míng (明) army advanced on Lúzhōu (廬州),
he surrendered the city and defected,
and successively served as Gōngbù Shìláng (工部侍郎).
In the fourth year of Hóngwǔ (洪wu), he was promoted to Shàngshū (尚書),
and was ordered to inspect officials in Shāndōng (山東),
which pleased the emperor.
Soon after, he was transferred to Běipíng Xíngshěng Cānzhèng (北平行省參政).
Due to inadequate supplies and provisions,
he was demoted to Zhīxiàn (知縣) of Cāngwú (蒼梧).
Initially,
Shǒurén (守仁) governed Yuánzhōu (袁州),
where he pacified the devastated region,
and the people greatly admired him.
Subsequently, he successively governed Róngzhōu (容州) and Gāotángzhōu (高唐州),
and in both places implemented good governance.
In the tenth year, he was promoted to Sìchuān Bùzhèngshǐ (四川布政使),
and his governance was simple yet strict.
He retired due to old age.
He was implicated in a matter and sentenced to forced labor,
but was specially pardoned.
In the fifteenth year,
after Yúnnán (雲南) was pacified,
the Xuānfǔsī (宣撫司) of Wēichǔ (威楚), Kāinán (開南), and other circuits were reorganized into Chǔxióng Fǔ (楚雄府),
and Shǒurén (守仁) was appointed Zhīfǔshì (知府事).
He attracted displaced people,
equalized corvée labor,
and established schools,
