bringing great order to the region.
In the twenty-eighth year, he went to court to submit his annual report,
and the people of the prefecture saw him off with tears.
He was appointed Tàipú Qīng (太僕卿).
He first requested the establishment of horse pastures in Chúzhōu (滁州) and other places north of the river.
His jurisdiction included fourteen supervisorates and ninety-eight herds,
and the horses greatly multiplied.
The reform of horse administration
began with Shǒurén (守仁).
After a long time,
he retired.
In the early Yǒnglè (永樂) era,
he came to court,
contracted an illness, and died.
Xuē Xiáng,
courtesy name Yànxiáng,
was a native of Wúwèi.
He came to submit with Yú Tōnghǎi,
and after crossing the Yangtze River, he was appointed Commanding Army Administrator of the Water Stockade,
repeatedly achieving merit in campaigns.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, he was transferred to transport grain to Hénán.
Late at night, upon reaching the Càihé River,
bandits suddenly arrived.
Xiáng remained unperturbed,
and with kind words, persuaded them to disperse.
The Emperor heard of this and was greatly pleased.
As troops were then being deployed
and supplies were difficult to provide,
he was appointed Capital Circuit Superintendent of Grain Transport,
with his office in Huái'ān.
He dredged rivers and built dikes,
extending hundreds of *lǐ* from Yángzhōu to Jìyáng,
and the corvée labor was fair and equal,
so the people had no complaints.
Those who showed diligence were immediately reported,
and granted official positions.
When the Yuán capital fell,
officials and commoners migrated south,
passing through Huái'ān.
Xiáng provided them with care and assistance in many ways.
When the people of Shānyáng and Hǎizhōu rebelled,
Imperial Son-in-Law Commandant Huáng Chēn apprehended and prosecuted them,
implicating a great many innocent people.
Xiáng participated in the interrogation,
and released all those for whom there was no evidence.
He governed Huái'ān for eight years,
and the people encouraged each other to do good.
When his term of service was completed and he returned to the capital,
they all burned incense and prayed for his return,
or created portraits to worship him.
In the eighth year, he was appointed Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shàngshū).
At that time, the palaces in Fèngyáng were being constructed.
The Emperor was sitting in a hall,
when it seemed as if someone was holding weapons and fighting on the ridge of the hall.
Grand Mentor (Tàishī) Lǐ Shàncháng reported that the craftsmen were using sorcery (yānzhèn fǎ),
and the Emperor was about to kill them all.
Xiáng distinguished between those who were not involved in the work rotation,
and all iron- and stone-workers who were not involved,
saving thousands of lives.
When constructing the Jǐnshēn Hall,
the relevant department listed ordinary craftsmen as superior craftsmen.
The Emperor was enraged by their deception,
and ordered them to be executed in the marketplace.
Xiáng, who was at his side, contended, saying:
"If reports are not truthful,
and people are simply killed,
I fear it would be unlawful."
He received an imperial decree to apply castration (fǔxíng).
Xiáng again slowly reported, saying:
"Castration
renders a person useless;
it would be better to flog them and send them back to work."
The Emperor agreed.
The next year, all provincial administrations (Xíngshěng) in the empire were reformed into Administration Commissions (Chéngxuān Bùzhèng Sī).
As Běipíng was an important strategic location,
Xiáng was specifically appointed there,
and for three years his governance was praised as the best.
He was resented by Hú Wéiyōng,
and was impeached for disturbing the populace with construction projects,
and demoted to serve as Prefect of Jiāxīng Prefecture.
When Wéiyōng was executed,
he was again summoned to be Minister of Works.
The Emperor said:
"Slanderous officials harmed you,
why did you not speak?"
He replied:
"Your subject did not know."
The next year, he was implicated and died from flogging,
and the empire mourned him.
His four sons
were exiled to Qióngzhōu,
and thus became natives of Qióngshān.
His grandson, Yuǎn,
became a *jìnshì* in the seventh year of Zhèngtǒng,
and during the Jǐngtài era,
served as a Bureau Director (Lángzhōng) in the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù).
In the first year of Tiānshùn, he was promoted to Vice Minister (Yòu Shìláng) of this ministry,
then transferred to the Ministry of Works.
He was ordered to dam the breached river at Kāifēng.
Upon his return,
he was again transferred to the Ministry of Revenue.
In the early Chénghuà era,
he supervised military provisions for the two Guǎng provinces,
reaching the position of Minister of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū) in Nánjīng,
but was dismissed from office for offending Wāng Zhí.
Among those who succeeded Xiáng as famous Ministers of Works,
there was Qín Kuí and others.
Kuí,
courtesy name Wényòng,
was a native of Xuānchéng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the eighteenth year of Hóngwǔ.
He successively served in the Censorate (Dūchá Yuàn).
He was dispatched to clean up the prison population,
and handled severity and leniency appropriately.
The Emperor praised his ability,
and promoted him to Vice Minister of Works.
At that time, construction affairs were numerous,
and the ministry lacked a minister,
so Kuí oversaw all construction projects.
Initially,
there was a proposal to register craftsmen from all directions,
assess their strength and ability,
designate them into three-year shifts,
and have them take turns coming to the capital,
with a three-month rotation,
named
"Rotation Craftsmen" (Lúnbān Jiàng),
but it had not yet been implemented.
At this time, Kuí proposed to arrange shifts according to the distance of their localities,
register them,
and issue them identification documents (kānhé),
which they would bring to the ministry at the appointed time,
exempting their families from corvée labor,
and this was established as a regulation.
The Emperor, mindful of Kuí's diligence,
decreed that the relevant department restore his family's status.
In the twenty-second year, he was promoted to Minister.
The next year, he was transferred to the Ministry of War.
Not long after,
he was again transferred to the Ministry of Works.
The Emperor believed that schools were where the nation cultivated talent,
but the attire of scholars was indistinguishable from that of clerks,
and ought to be changed,
so he ordered Kuí to design new styles and present them.
After three revisions,
the designs were finalized.
Students of the Imperial Academy (guózi jiàn) were each granted a blue gown (lánhán) and a sash (tāo),
to serve as an example for the whole empire.
The attire of scholars in the Míng dynasty
is said to have been originated by Kuí.
There was Zhào Zhù,
a native of Yǒngníng.
He possessed ambition and integrity,
and was known for his learning and conduct.
From Instructor (Xùndǎo), he was recommended as a worthy and capable person,
promoted to Grandee of Advice (Zànshàn Dàfū),
and appointed Minister of Works.
He proposed fixing the annual number of military weapons to be manufactured throughout the empire,
and discussed and set the architectural standards for the palace cities of the imperial princes (fānwáng).
Zhào Jùn,
whose origin is unknown.
He was promoted from Vice Minister of Works to Minister.
The Emperor noted that the printing blocks stored in the Imperial Academy (Guózǐ Jiān)
had become old and damaged over the years,
so he ordered various scholars to review and amend them,
and the Ministry of Works to supervise craftsmen in their repair.
Jùn received the imperial decree to oversee this,
and thus ancient texts were completed.
In the twelfth year of Hóngwǔ,
Zhù was transferred to serve in the Ministry of Justice (Xíngbù),
and soon after retired,
while Jùn
was dismissed in the seventeenth year.
As for Kuí, in the ninth month of the twenty-fifth year, he committed suicide due to an incident.
Táng Duó,
courtesy name Zhènzhī,
was a native of Hóng.
When Tàizǔ first raised his army,
he was already by his side.
He defended Háo Zhōu,
followed in pacifying Jiāngzhōu,
was appointed Xi'ān County Magistrate,
and then summoned to be a Manager (Guǎngōu) in the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shěng).
In the first year of Hóngwǔ,
when Tāng Hé conquered Yánpíng,
Duó was appointed to govern the prefecture,
and he consoled and rallied the newly surrendered people,
so the gentry and commoners were at peace.
After three years there,
he entered the court as an Imperial Censor (Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ).
He then left to govern Shàoxīng Prefecture.
In the twelfth month of the sixth year, he was summoned and appointed Minister of Justice.
The next year, he was transferred to be Grand Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng).
When his mother passed away,
he was specially granted half his salary.
Zuǒ Kèxīn,
a native of Gǒngchāng.
He was the Instructor of Tàizhōu.
In the twenty-sixth year,
his term of office ended and he came to court.
He was summoned and questioned about the classics, histories, and the gains and losses of governance.
Kèxīn spoke frankly without reservation.
He was appointed as Zànshàn.
At that time, Wáng Jùnhuá of Shàoxīng, who was skilled in literary composition,
was also appointed to this position.
The Emperor issued an edict to the Ministry of Personnel, saying:
"Zuǒ Kèxīn on the left,
Wáng Jùnhuá on the right;
this is to emphasize frank speech."
Previously,
when instructional officials arrived in the capital after receiving their passes,
the Emperor inquired about the people's suffering.
Wú Cóngquán from Kělán and Zhāng Huán from Shānyīn both said, "My duty lies in educating scholars,
and I have nothing to do with the affairs of the people."
The Emperor was enraged and said:
"Hú Yuàn of the Sòng dynasty served as a professor in Sūzhōu and Húzhōu,
and his teaching encompassed both classical interpretations and practical governance.
Jiǎ Yì and Dǒng Zhòngshū of the Hàn dynasty both rose from the countryside
to expound on current affairs.
Mǎ Zhōu of the Táng dynasty, though unable to meet Emperor Tàizōng in person,
still instructed military officials to speak on matters.
Now that you are gathered in the imperial court,
and I personally inquire,
you all have nothing to say.
Is this how those who aspire to the Way of the sages and worthies truly are?"
He ordered them banished to the frontier,
and moreover, posted a proclamation to all schools in the realm,
to serve as a warning.
By this time, Kèxīn was highly regarded for his uprightness and forthrightness.
Not many years later,
he was promoted to Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū).
Soon after, he pleaded illness,
and the imperial physicians were ordered to provide medicine,
without stopping his salary.
When he died,
officials were ordered to escort his coffin back for burial.
Féng Jiān,
whose origin is unknown,
was the Dian Shi (Registrar) of Nánfēng.
In the twenty-fourth year of Hóngwǔ, he submitted a memorial on nine matters.
First, nurturing the sacred body:
He requested the Emperor to clear his mind and reduce his involvement in affairs,
not interfering with minor matters,
considering it a blessing for the people and the state.
Second, selecting the experienced:
As the princes were in their prime,
for their guidance and assistance,
he wished for experienced officials to be selected and appointed as princely officers,
so they could speak frankly and earnestly to offer corrections and assistance.
Third, defending the distant frontiers:
He requested to focus on agriculture and military training,
stationing troops at the borders,
to be prepared for unforeseen circumstances.
Fourth, encouraging officials:
He requested to find upright and steadfast individuals,
appointing them to significant positions,
distinguishing their subordinates,
reporting their true performance for promotion or demotion,
to encourage people to govern themselves diligently.
Fifth, commending sacrificial rites:
He requested to command officials to collect names of loyal and brave ministers from past dynasties,
adding posthumous titles and honors,
so that later generations would have something to be inspired by and encouraged.
Sixth, reducing eunuchs:
Being in close proximity day and night,
their words are easily accepted,
fostering calamities unknowingly.
He requested to cut redundant personnel,
to prevent future abuses of decline and usurpation.
Seventh, rotating frontier generals:
When granted military authority,
and remaining on the frontier for a long time,
they often become lax and undisciplined.
He requested periodic rotation and annual transfers,
not allowing them to stay in their posts for too long.
This would not only preserve meritorious officials,
but also effectively prevent the gradual problem of arrogant generals, lazy soldiers, and the weakening of the center while strengthening the periphery.
Eighth, investigating official administration:
Talented and honest officials
might be resented by their superiors
or envied by their colleagues;
if the emperor does not investigate,
it is not a way to motivate and encourage.
He requested to widely deploy observers,
to investigate honesty and corruption,
to clarify promotions and demotions.
Ninth, strengthening controls:
Various departments would issue warrants to junior clerks,
ordering them to supervise their subordinates,
who would then frequently inflict floggings,
harming the people.
He requested to increase the use of official tallies (kànhé) to be given to various departments,
allowing them to fill in and dispatch assignments,
and report back after the task was completed,
so that officials would not lightly issue orders to distress the people,
and general affairs would also not be neglected.
After the memorial was submitted,
the Emperor praised him,
saying he understood current affairs
and was perceptive about changes in circumstances.
He also said to his attending ministers:
"Féng Jiān's suggestion about rotating frontier generals is not entirely correct.
If frontier generals are frequently changed,
then the strength and weakness of the troops,
the movements of the enemy,
and the topography of the mountains and rivers
cannot be fully known.
If one could obtain people like Zhào Chōngguó or Bān Chāo,
why would there be a need for frequent rotations?"
Thus, he ordered the Ministry of Personnel to promote Féng Jiān to Zuǒ Qiāndū Yùshǐ,
and he generally maintained proper conduct in the Censorate.
The following year,
he died in office.
Rú Tàisù,
a native of Zézhōu.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, he passed the provincial examination,
and his memorial pleased the Emperor,
so he was appointed Censor (Jiānchá Yùshǐ).
In the sixth year, he was promoted to Sichuan Surveillance Commissioner (Sìchuān Ànchásǐ),
and was known for his fairness.
In the seventh year, fifth month, he was summoned to serve as Vice Minister of Justice (Xíngbù Shìláng).
He memorialized:
"From the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shěng) to all internal and external departments,
they are subject to review by Censors and Surveillance Commissioners,
but the Censorate (Yùshǐ Tái) does not have a fixed evaluation system.
It is appropriate to order the Censors in charge of the Censorate to uniformly investigate and verify.
The officials in the Audit Department (Mócān Sī) are few in number,
making it difficult to inspect the finances and provisions of the entire realm.
I request to increase the number of officials
and divide them into various sections.
In the outer provinces and garrisons,
when deliberating on military and civilian matters,
they often disagree,
causing delays.
I request to use one official from the Surveillance Commission to rectify this."
The Emperor accepted all his suggestions.
The following year,
due to being implicated, he was demoted to Principal of the Ministry of Justice (Xíngbù Zhǔshì).
He presented a memorial on current affairs, comprising tens of thousands of words.
Emperor Tàizǔ ordered Zhōngshū Láng Wáng Mǐn to read it aloud for him.
It stated that among talented individuals,
only one or two out of a hundred had survived in recent years,
and those currently in office were mostly pedantic scholars or vulgar clerks.
His words were often offensive.
The Emperor was angry,
summoned Tàisù for a direct interrogation,
and had him flogged in court.
The next evening,
he again had someone read it aloud in the palace,
and found four actionable points.
He sighed with emotion, saying:
"It is difficult to be a monarch,
and not easy to be a minister.
The reason I seek frank speech
is that I want it to be pertinent to the actual situation.
Too many words
can confuse the listener.
What Tàisù presented
could have been summarized in just over five hundred words."
Consequently, he ordered the Central Secretariat to standardize the format for memorials,
so that those who spoke on gains and losses would avoid verbose writing.
He extracted the actionable points from Tàisù's memorial and sent them to the relevant departments.
The Emperor personally wrote the preface,
and promulgated it to the entire realm.
In the tenth year,
he and his colleague Zēng Bǐngzhèng were both dispatched consecutively as Administrating Councilors (Cānzhèng),
and Tàisù went to Zhèjiāng.
Soon after, he was granted permission to return to his hometown to attend to his parents.
In the sixteenth year, he was summoned to serve as acting Director of the Ministry of Justice (Xíngbù Shìlángzhōng).
After a month,
he was promoted to Vice Censor-in-Chief (Dūcháyuàn Qiāndū Yùshǐ),
then demoted again to Compiler of the Hanlin Academy (Hànlín Yuàn Jiǎntǎo).
In the eighteenth year, ninth month, he was promoted to Minister of Revenue (Hùbù Shàngshū).
Tàisù was unyielding and straightforward,
repeatedly nearing conviction,
but the Emperor often pardoned him.
One day,
during a banquet in the private palace,
the Emperor offered him wine and said:
"With a golden cup, I drink with you,
but with a white blade, I will not spare you."
Tàisù kowtowed,
and immediately continued the rhyme in response, saying:
"With sincere heart, I plan to repay the nation,
not fearing the emperor's vexation."
The Emperor was moved by compassion.
Not long after,
he was demoted to Censor (Yùshǐ),
and again implicated for slandering and framing Zhān Huī.
He and twelve colleagues were all shackled and forced to carry out their duties.
Later, he eventually died by law.
Zēng Bǐngzhèng
was from Nánchāng.
In the early Hóngwǔ reign,
he was recommended to be appointed as the Xúezhèng of Hǎizhōu.
In the ninth year [of Hóngwǔ] (1376),
due to celestial anomalies, an edict was issued calling on all officials to speak their minds.
Bǐngzhèng submitted a memorial of several thousand words,
which generally stated:
“Ancient sagely rulers did not rejoice at the absence of calamities or anomalies from Heaven;
they only took the respectful fear of Heaven's condemnation to heart.
Your Majesty is sagely, cultured, and divinely martial,
having unified the entire realm.
Heaven's entrustment [to you]
can be said to be immense.
After more than twenty years of military campaigns,
peace has finally been achieved.
Heaven's intention for great peace
has also been long-standing,
and the people's longing for good governance is equally ardent.
The policies for founding an empire and for preserving it
are generally different.
In the initial period of founding,
one employs methods to enrich the state and strengthen its military,
and uses people who are eager to achieve tasks and merits.
Once the great unified rule is established,
and the state's power is secure,
then throughout the world,
everything produced by land and water,
and all that is accomplished by human effort,
are accumulations in the state's warehouses.
Children still being nursed,
and old men with white hair,
are all people whom the state should nurture and care for.
One need not worry about not being prosperous;
the only difficulty lies in preserving the established enterprise permanently.
At this time,
one should completely change previous practices.
What actions truly respond to Heaven's will?
What actions truly console the hopes of the people?
The principle of sympathetic resonance
shows its effects very quickly.”
He also said that since Heaven had issued a warning,
the change would not occur without reason.
He extensively discussed the essence of the *Dà Yì* (I Ching) and *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals).
The Emperor praised him
and summoned him to be Sīwén Jiāncéng.
Soon after,
he was transferred to be Xíngbù Zhǔshì.
In the tenth year, he was promoted to Shǎnxī Cāncè.
It happened that the Tōngzhèng Sī was newly established,
and Bǐngzhèng was immediately appointed as its Shǐ.
While in office, he spoke out on various matters several times,
and the Emperor was rather lenient towards him.
Eventually, however, he was dismissed for opposing the imperial decree.
He was too poor to return home
and sold his four-year-old daughter.
The Emperor, hearing of this, was furious,
sentenced him to castration,
and his ultimate fate is unknown.
Lǐ Shìlǔ,
courtesy name Zōngkǒng,
was from Pú.
In his youth, he was intelligent, diligent in study,
and for three years, he did not step out of his door.
Hearing that Zhū Gōngqiān of Póyáng had inherited the teachings of Sòng's Zhū Xī,
he went to study with him
and completely received his scholarship.
Tàizǔ already knew Shìlǔ by name.
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
an edict was issued seeking scholars who could expound Zhū Xī's teachings,
and the authorities recommended Shìlǔ.
Upon his audience,
Tàizǔ joyfully said:
“I have sought you for a long time;
why do we meet so late?”
He was appointed Tóngzhī of Huángzhōu.
The Emperor said:
“I shall first test you with civil affairs;
I will summon you [to the capital] soon.”
Within a year,
his administrative achievements were well known.
In the fourteenth year,
he was appointed Dàlǐ Sì Qīng.
Since ascending the throne, the Emperor
had been quite fond of Buddhist teachings.
He issued edicts to summon eminent monks from the southeast,
and frequently held Dharma assemblies at Jiǎngshān.
Those whose responses pleased him were immediately granted golden-embroidered kasaya robes,
summoned into the Forbidden City,
and given seats to lecture and debate.
Wú Yìn, Huá Kèqín, and their like
were all promoted to high offices,
and were often relied upon as imperial informants.
Consequently, their followers became extremely unruly,
slandering and defaming high officials.
The entire court dared not speak,
except for Shìlǔ and Gěishìzhōng Chén Wénhuī, who successively argued against them.
Wénhuī's memorial stated:
“Since ancient emperors,
it has never been heard that gentry and Buddhist monks
cohabited and worked together
in a way that could be mutually beneficial.
Now, veteran officials and esteemed elders all wish to resign their salaries and positions,
while monks and treacherous villains increasingly sow discord with slander.
Like Liú Jī and Xú Dá, who were suspected,
and Lǐ Shàncháng and Zhōu Déxīng, who were slandered—
compared to Xiāo Hé and Hán Xìn,
how great is the difference in their perilous and doubtful situations?
I humbly hope Your Majesty will appoint as your trusted advisors
all those who are talented in virtue and literary achievement,
and then great peace can be immediately achieved.”
The Emperor did not listen.
The monks, emboldened by imperial favor,
then requested the establishment of official positions for Buddhism.
Thus, the previously established Shànshì Yuàn was changed to Sēnglù Sī,
and offices such as Zuǒyòu Shànshì, Zuǒyòu Chǎnjiào, and Zuǒyòu Jiǎngjīng Juéyì were established,
all with high ranks.
Daoism also followed suit.
The number of ordained monks, nuns, and Daoist priests exceeded tens of thousands.
Shìlǔ memorialized, saying:
“Your Majesty is now founding an empire;
whatever your will points to
immediately sets a legal standard for your descendants for ten thousand generations.
How can you abandon sagely learning and uphold heterodox doctrines?”
Dozens of memorials were submitted,
but they were also not heeded.
Shìlǔ was naturally upright and unyielding.
He rose through Confucianism
and intended to promote Zhū Xī's teachings
by taking on the task of refuting Buddhism.
When his words were not adopted,
he abruptly requested before the Emperor:
“Your Majesty is deeply immersed in their teachings,
no wonder my words do not penetrate.
I return Your Majesty's tablet;
I beg to be granted my bones [i.e., permission to retire]
and return to my hometown.”
Thereupon, he placed his tablet on the ground.
The Emperor was enraged,
ordered his warriors to seize and beat him,
and he died immediately at the foot of the steps.
Chén Wénhuī,
courtesy name Gěngguāng,
was from Zhào'ān.
He was recommended to be appointed Lǐkē Gěishìzhōng,
and rose through various offices to Dàlǐ Sì Shǎoqīng.
He frequently spoke on success and failure,
all very pointed and direct.
Finally, he opposed an imperial decree,
feared punishment,
and threw himself into the Jīnshuǐ Qiáo, where he died.
Several years after Shìlǔ and Wénhuī died,
the Emperor gradually realized that many actions of the monks were unlawful,
and issued an edict to rectify the two religions of Buddhism and Daoism.
Yè Bójù,
courtesy name Jūshēng,
was from Nínghǎi.
He was well-versed in classical studies.
As a Guózǐshēng, he was appointed Píngyáo Xùndǎo.
In the ninth year of Hóngwǔ (1376), there was a celestial anomaly,
and an edict sought direct criticisms.
Bójù submitted a memorial,
which generally stated: “Your servant observes that the current affairs
have three excesses: the enfeoffment is too extravagant,
the use of punishment is too frequent,
and the pursuit of governance is too hasty.
The system of the former kings
generally did not exceed one-third of the state's territory.
There were fixed distinctions in rank between superiors and inferiors,
which served to strengthen the trunk and weaken the branches,
to curb the sources of disorder, and to
uphold
the foundation of governance.
Now, territories are split and enfeoffed,
allowing all the princes to have their own allocated lands.
This is probably to remedy the defects of the Sòng and Yuán dynasties, which were isolated [in their imperial power]
and had inactive imperial clans.
However, the states of Qín, Jìn,
Yān, Qí, Liáng, Chǔ, Wú, and Shǔ,
all comprise dozens of contiguous counties,
and their cities, palaces, and residences are inferior only to the Emperor's capital.
They are moreover generously provided with abundant
armor, weapons, and guards.
Your servant fears that after a few generations,
the tail will be too big to wag the dog.
If their territories are then curtailed and their powers seized,
it will inevitably lead to resentment,
and in serious cases, they will take advantage of opportunities to rise up,
against which no defense will be sufficient.
Some argue that
since all the princes are the Emperor's flesh and blood,
even if their allocated lands are vast and
the laws are extravagant,
how could there be any reason for them to contend with the imperial court?
Your servant humbly believes that
it is not so.
Why not observe the affairs of the Hàn and Jìn dynasties?
Xiàojǐng,
was the grandson of Gāodì.
The kings of the Seven States
were all brothers,
sons, and grandsons of Jǐngdì’s common paternal ancestors.
Once their territories were reduced,
they immediately raised armies and marched westward.
The kings of the Jìn dynasty
were all the direct sons and grandsons of Wǔdì.
After a change of generation,
they successively attacked each other,
leading to the troubles of Liú and Shí.
From this perspective,
if enfeoffment exceeds the prescribed limits,
calamities will immediately arise.
Drawing on antiquity to prove the present,
this is very clear.
This is what your minister considers
to be excessive.
In the past, Jiǎ Yì advised Hàn Wéndì
to completely divide the territories of the various states
and leave them vacant, awaiting the various princely descendants.
If Wéndì had followed Jiǎ
Yì’s advice earlier,
then there would surely have been no calamity of the Seven States.
I wish that before the various kings are sent to their states,
the scale of their capitals and cities be curtailed,
their guard troops reduced,
and their boundaries limited,
also
to await the enfeoffment of the sons and grandsons of the various kings.
Once this system is established,
then those kings who are virtuous and talented may enter to serve as辅相 (fǔxiàng, grand counselors).
The rest shall for generations serve as a protective screen,
and share
prosperity with the state.
To sacrifice temporary favor
to secure benefits for ten thousand generations,
to eliminate heavenly anomalies and stabilize the altars of soil and grain,
there is nothing more important than this.
Your minister also observes that the founding monarchs of successive dynasties
have never failed to win the people's hearts by entrusting virtue,
and lost the people's hearts by entrusting punishment.
The longevity of the dynasty
entirely depended
on this.
In ancient times, when death sentences were issued,
the Son of Heaven would stop music and reduce meals,
sincerely believing that Heaven gave birth to these people
and established shepherds for them,
surely desiring them to live together,
not desiring
their immediate death.
Unfortunately, if there were those who did not follow instruction among them,
then punishment had to be imposed out of necessity.
Some argue that
in the mid-periods of the Sòng and Yuán dynasties,
they exclusively
practiced leniency,
with disordered rewards and punishments,
leading to their downfall.
The emperor deeply regrets their shortcomings,
hence the establishment of unpardoning punishments
and the flexible laws of divine change,
to make people fearful
and unable to predict their outcome.
Your minister, however, believes this is not so.
The founder of a dynasty sets a standard for a hundred generations;
every action, every stillness,
must provide something for descendants to uphold.
Moreover, punishment
is the destiny of the people;
how can it not be treated with caution!
Flogging, caning, penal servitude, exile, and death
are the five punishments of today.
In applying these five punishments,
if there is no leniency
or pardon,
and it proceeds entirely from great impartiality and uprightness, that would be acceptable.
However, in the application of punishment,
many decisions are made directly by the emperor,
thus causing judicial officials to strive to anticipate imperial intentions,
where those who are severe
gain merit,
and those who correct miscarriages of justice are punished.
How can one hope for fairness in judicial cases,
how can it be easily achieved!
Recently, a special decree
allowed those guilty of various capital crimes to be spared death and sent to the military colonies,
and also revised
old legal statutes,
reducing and granting pardons with distinctions.
However, I have not heard of any injunctions commanding judicial officials to prioritize leniency and fairness,
which is why the judicial authorities still follow old precedents.
Although the name of leniency is heard,
the reality of leniency is not seen.
The so-called reality
truly lies with the emperor,
not with the ministers.
Therefore, there must be the intention to treat doubtful cases with lightness,
and only then will the virtue of cherishing life permeate the hearts of the people;
this cannot be achieved superficially.
How can this be made clear?
In ancient times, scholars
considered entering officialdom an honor,
and being dismissed from office a disgrace.
Today's scholars
consider obscurity and unrenown
a blessing,
and being implicated but not recorded an good fortune.
They consider penal servitude and forced labor a certain punishment,
and flogging and caning a common humiliation.
In the beginning,
the imperial court recruited scholars from all under Heaven,
extensively gathering them,
leaving no one out.
Officials pressed them to embark,
as if arresting dangerous criminals.
By the time they arrived in the capital,
official appointments
were often based on appearance,
what they studied might not be what they were used for,
and what they were used for might not be what they studied.
Once in office,
if they made a single mistake,
if they were lucky enough to escape execution,
they would certainly
fall under the category of penal servitude and forced labor.
This has become the norm,
with little regard or pity.
Is this what Your Majesty enjoys doing?
It is surely to make people fearful and not dare to transgress.
Your minister secretly observes that in recent years,
executions can also be said to be numerous,
yet transgressors follow one after another.
This is truly because encouragement and dissuasion are unclear,
good and evil are not distinguished,
and the laws for discussing
the worthy and the capable have been abolished,
people do not exert themselves,
and those who do good become lazy.
If there were someone here,
incorruptible as Yí and Qí,
wise as Liáng and Píng,
who slightly violated
the law,
would the emperor record their strengths and overlook their weaknesses and employ them?
Or would he abandon their strengths, be harsh on their weaknesses, and subject them to the law?
If their strengths were taken and their weaknesses
overlooked,
then those of average talent would strive to distinguish themselves in integrity and wisdom.
But if their weaknesses were harshly treated and their strengths abandoned,
then those who do good would all say: "So-and-so was this incorruptible,
so-and-so was this
wise,
yet the court showed them no leniency;
where can we find a place for ourselves!"
This leads to people living hand-to-mouth,
abandoning their integrity and shame,
or engaging in exploitation
to prepare
funds for penal servitude and forced labor.
This is generally the case.
Is this not due to the excessive use of punishment?
The Hàn dynasty once relocated prominent families to the imperial tombs,
but it has not been heard that
criminals were used to populate them.
Now, where Fèngyáng imperial mausoleums are located,
the land of the dragon's rise,
is generally populated by criminals,
and sounds of lamentation and sorrow fill the imperial grounds and surrounding towns.
This is surely
not in line with the intention of reverently honoring the ancestral temple.
Furthermore, if a formidable enemy is ahead,
then to exert strength and raise morale,
to attack them and surely conquer,
to capture them and surely apprehend,
is acceptable.
Now, the bandits have fled and scattered into mountain valleys,
and by strategy one seeks
them,
perhaps they can be caught.
However, by deploying heavy troops,
they are startled and dispersed,
entering inaccessible places.
After several years of pursuit,
there is still no clear method,
and yet blame is attributed
to the common people newly registered in the household records,
and they are relocated.
This causes turmoil over thousands of miles,
families cannot rest in their homes,
and even chickens and dogs cannot find peace.
Moreover, the newly submitted populace,
who previously had moved elsewhere,
the imperial court permitted them to resume their livelihoods.
Now that they are registered,
and yet again moved,
this means the law is not trusted by the people.
Indeed,
only when the population is prosperous can the fields be opened up,
and taxes increase.
Now, the expectation for governors to annually increase the population
is precisely for this reason.
Recently, families
who have already paid their taxes and grain,
although they have received an imperial edict to be released and return home,
their hearts are still uneasy.
Those whose households have already been registered,
though they have received compassion and care,
are still detained in Kāifēng for duty,
with rumors
stirring unrest,
and they do not know what will become of them.
Furthermore, in the various commanderies of Tàiyuán,
which are external border regions,
with the people's hearts in such a state,
this is very much not a plan for securing the frontier.
Your servant requests that from now on, the imperial
court should prioritize the greater good,
pardon minor transgressions,
issue a clear edict to the entire realm,
and implement
the "Bā Yì"
statutes,
strictly forbidding harsh and exploitative officials.
Those who judge cases fairly and justly should be promoted
swiftly,
while those who are cruel and avaricious should be dismissed.
Regarding the Fèngyáng military colonies system,
those currently residing in the colonies
should be allowed to farm and pay taxes.
Those whose households have been registered and are currently detained in
Kāifēng
should all be released to resume their livelihoods.
Doing so would be sufficient to enhance the virtue of cherishing life,
establish the blessing of a long-lasting national destiny,
and the common people would naturally be at peace,
and heavenly anomalies would naturally
disappear.
In ancient times, from King Wén and King Wǔ of Zhōu to King Chéng and King Kāng,
moral education flourished.
From Emperor Gāo to Emperor Wén and Emperor Jǐng of Hàn,
the realm first became known for its wealth and prosperity.
The peace or
disorder of the world,
the transformation of influences,
and the inclination of people's hearts
are not achieved in a single day.
Now, the nation's era
has been nine years thus far;
weapons are laid down,
the people are at rest,
the world is largely settled,
the principles are largely rectified,
and laws are perfected and clear;
it can be called well-governed.
Yet Your Majesty is constantly anxious that popular customs are decadent,
people know no fear,
laws are issued but cunning arises,
and edicts are promulgated but deceit springs up.
Thus, there are those who are trusted in the morning and suspected in the evening,
and those who were advanced yesterday
are executed today.
Even
edicts are issued and then quickly changed,
pardoned individuals are rearrested,
and the officials and people of the realm do not know whom to follow.
Your humble servant believes that the world's trend towards order
is like the melting
of solid ice.
The melting of ice
cannot be achieved abruptly by the sun alone;
solar energy develops,
the earth's脉 slightly moves,
and only then can it thaw.
The sagely ruler's governance of the world
is also like this.
Punishments awe them,
rites guide them,
people are gradually instilled with benevolence,
and people are influenced by righteousness,
and only then does their transformation become harmonious.
Confucius said:
"If there were
a true king,
it would take a generation for benevolence to prevail."
This is not empty talk.
The path to seeking good governance
is none other than first rectifying customs.
The path to rectifying customs
is none other than first making governors aware of their duties.
To make governors aware of their duties
is none
other than first making the Censors aware of what they should prioritize.
To make the Censors aware of what they should prioritize
is none other than first making the imperial court aware of what it should value.
Ancient commandery governors and county magistrates
led their subordinates with rectitude,
guided the
people with goodness,
making transformations complete and customs beautiful.
Collecting taxes, holding meetings, and handling lawsuits and documents
were certainly secondary concerns.
Today's governors regard population, money, grain, and lawsuits as urgent
duties,
while matters such as agriculture, sericulture, and schools,
which are the foundations of royal governance,
are considered mere formalities and neglected.
How then can these people be educated and nurtured?
Speaking of agriculture and sericulture,
in spring, the prefectures and counties issue a white notice,
and the village heads simply return a written report,
while governors never personally inspect the sequence of planting and cultivation or the methods of preparing for drought and flood.
Speaking of schools,
students who receive stipends are the means by which the state obtains talent.
Now, throughout the realm, the number of teachers and students
is severely lacking.
Even if the
number of personnel is complete,
governors rarely act with the substance of propriety and deference
to cultivate them into useful individuals.
The imperial court is deeply concerned with community schools,
repeatedly ordering investigations into the names of teachers and students
and their
studies and assignments.
Yet now, in communities, towns, and cities,
only a nameplate is sometimes put up,
and in remote villages and secluded places, only the name exists in vain.
Governors merely prepare official documents
for inspection
and review.
When high officials are assigned to inspect,
they also merely follow old routines,
reviewing based on paper records,
never actually inspecting in person.
The reality of their establishment or abolition
is regarded
as a mere formality by both superiors and subordinates.
The common people do not know what filial piety, brotherly love, loyalty, and trustworthiness are,
and propriety, righteousness, integrity, and shame are swept away.
The Censorate,
therefore, represents the imperial court
in promoting virtue and moral transformation,

Hearing lawsuits and judging cases

Now, it exclusively regards lawsuits as paramount.
Loyal ministers, filial sons, righteous men, and chaste women

Initially, they only knew to consider removing a corrupt official or settling a lawsuit as governance,
but they did not realize that encouraging people to form good customs
and leading them to move towards goodness and away from crime
is the greater form of governance.
This is the failing of governors and Censors who have not properly discerned the priorities.
The royal regulations state that outstanding local scholars ascending to the Minister of Education
are called "selected scholars";
the Minister of Education selects outstanding scholars to ascend to the Imperial University,
calling them "eminent scholars";
the Grand Music Master further selects outstanding scholars and promotes them to the Minister of War, calling them "advanced scholars";
the Minister of War identifies and discusses official talents,
and after they are decided upon, they are appointed to office,
and after being appointed to office, they are granted noble titles.
The thoroughness of their examination
was like this,
which is why the flourishing Zhōu dynasty had an abundance of talented people.
Now, let all scholars of the realm be examined by the Ministry of Rites,
ascend to the Imperial University,
undergo training in various positions,
and be entrusted with responsibilities.
This
can cleanse the shortcomings of past eras' selection systems
and emulate the flourishing Zhōu.
However, those who ascend to the Imperial University
are sometimes, in less than a few months,
suddenly selected for official posts,
and occasionally entrusted with administering the
people.
Your servant fears that such individuals are not yet conversant with current affairs,
nor proficient in the imperial court's rites and laws,
and thus unable to promote virtue and moral transformation,
which would go against national policies above
and distress the common people below.
Since the founding
of the dynasty,
the selection of outstanding talents has not been few,
and the positions appointed have not been unimportant.
Counting from now,
how many remain?
Your servant fears that future generations will view
Now,
it is just like our present view of the past.
Are not those whom were appointed in former years
deeply regrettable?
All of this is my fault for seeking to achieve governance too quickly.
In the past, the Sòng (宋) dynasty held the empire for over three hundred years.
In the beginning, it taught its people with ritual and righteousness (lǐyì, 禮義).
During its prosperous period,
in every village and alley, there was a spirit of
loyalty and generosity,
even to the point of being ashamed to speak of others' faults.
By its later years,
loyal officials and righteous scholars faced death as if returning home,
and women were ashamed to be defiled.
These were all the effects
of moral transformation.
The Yuán (元) dynasty, when it possessed the nation,
did not establish its foundation.
It violated the principles of ritual and righteousness,
and corrupted the defense of integrity and shame (liánchǐ, 廉恥).
Within not many decades,
those who abandoned cities and surrendered to enemies were
innumerable.
Even old Confucian scholars and great officials willingly endured humiliation.
This was the failing of ritual, righteousness, integrity, and shame not being upheld.
The remaining customs and prevailing practices have not changed to this day,
which is deeply strange.
Your servant suggests that it would be better to foster benevolence and righteousness,
to value integrity and shame.
Governors and magistrates should be charged with prioritizing agriculture, sericulture, and schools.
Censors should be charged with prioritizing moral transformation and reviewing laws
to make light judgments and lenient punishments their priority.
If this is done, then virtue and benevolence will flow downwards,
and the way to achieve governance will likely be attained.
Regarding the students from prefectures and districts who enroll in the Imperial College (Tàixuè, 太學),
they must be made to
study and complete their education there,
either for three years
or five years,
thoroughly mastering one classic
and additionally learning one art.
Only then should they be selected
to serve in the imperial guard
or handle affairs,
to observe the abilities of the grandees
and high officials,
and thereafter be entrusted with administration.
Then their learning and knowledge will both be excellent,
and there will likely be no failures.
Moreover, it will make them understand that positions and emoluments are all granted by Heaven,
and this can
stop covetous desires.
Once the path of governance is attained,
Your Majesty will simply sit peacefully,
waiting for months and years.
Then the yīnyáng (陰陽) will be in harmony, and the winds and rains will be timely.
All blessings and auspicious omens will
not fail to arrive.
What heavenly anomalies will not dissipate then?
The memorial was submitted.
The emperor was furious and said:
“This brat is sowing discord among my flesh and blood!
Quickly arrest him and bring him here;
I will shoot him with my own hands!”
When he arrived,
the Grand Councilor (Chéngxiàng, 丞相) took advantage of the emperor’s delight to present a memorial,
and he was sent to the Ministry of Justice (Xíngbù, 刑部) prison,
where he died.
Previously,
Bójù (伯巨) was about to submit a memorial.
He said to his friend:
“Today, there are only three things in the world that are cause for concern.
Two of them are easy to see but their trouble is slow to manifest.
One of them is hard to see but its trouble is quick to manifest.
Even without a clear edict,
I would still speak of it,
let alone when seeking advice.”
His intention was probably referring to the enfeoffment.
However, at that time, the princes merely held princely titles
and had not yet been granted territories,
so it was not entirely as Bójù (伯巨) had said.
By the end of the Hóngwǔ (洪武) era,
the Prince of Yān (Yānwáng, 燕王) had repeatedly been ordered to go beyond the Great Wall,
and his power began to strengthen.
Later, due to the reduction of his fief, he raised troops
and consequently took control of the empire.
People then considered Bójù (伯巨) to have been prescient.
Zhèng Shìlì (鄭士利),
courtesy name Hàoyì (好義),
was a native of Nínghǎi (寧海).
His elder brother, Shìyuán (士元),
was upright and talented, and possessed great learning.
Having passed the imperial examination (jìnshì, 進士), he successively served as Assistant Judicial Commissioner (Ànchásǐ qiānshì, 按察使僉事) in Húguǎng (湖廣).
When the soldiers from Jīng (荊) and Xiāng (襄) took advantage of the chaos to plunder women,
officials dared not question them.
Shìyuán (士元) immediately spoke to the generals and made them return what they had plundered.
There was a wrongful imprisonment case in Ānlù (安陸).
The Censorate (Yùshǐtái, 御史臺) had already reviewed it and submitted its findings,
but Shìyuán (士元) memorialized its injustice
and got it cleared.
At that time, when examining the account books for taxes and grain,
the "empty seal" (kōngyìn, 空印) affair came to light.
All those who presided over seals were sentenced to death,
and those below the deputies were flogged one hundred times
and exiled to distant regions.
Shìyuán (士元) was also implicated in this and imprisoned.
At that time, the emperor was still furious,
believing it to be deceit and deception.
No Grand Councilor (Chéngxiàng, 丞相) or censor dared to remonstrate.
Shìlì (士利) sighed and said:
“The emperor does not know,
and considers the empty seal a great crime.
If someone could sincerely speak to him,
the sagacious and enlightened emperor
would surely understand.”
Just then, there was an unusual celestial phenomenon, and the emperor sought advice.
Shìlì (士利) said,
“Now is the time.”
But then he read the edict,
which stated that those who made public statements for private gain would be punished.
Shìlì (士利) said:
“What I wish to say
is about the emperor killing innocent people.
My brother is not the one who presided over the seals;
he certainly should be released.
I will wait until my brother is released after his flogging to speak;
even if I die, I will have no regrets.”
When Shìyuán (士元) was released,
Shìlì (士利) then wrote a memorial of several thousand words,
speaking of several matters,
and elaborating especially on the empty seal affair.
He said:
“Your Majesty wishes to severely punish those involved in the empty seal matter,
fearing that corrupt officials might use blank sealed papers
to create documents and oppress the people.
However, official documents must have complete seals to be valid.
Now, when examining the account books,
the seal must span both halves of a seam,
which is not the same as a single seal on a single piece of paper.
Even if one were to obtain it,
it could not be used,
let alone that it is impossible to obtain.
The figures for taxes and grain
must be reconciled by the prefecture with the province,
and by the province with the ministry.
The figures are difficult to finalize in advance;
they are only determined at the ministry.
Prefectures and provinces distant from the ministry are six or seven thousand lǐ (里) away,
and even nearby ones are three or four thousand lǐ (里).
If seals were to be applied only after the books are completed,
the round trip would take more than a year.
Therefore, seals are applied first, and then the writing is done.
This is a pragmatic measure
that has been in practice for a long time.
How can it be considered a grave offense?
Moreover, when the state enacts laws,
it must first clearly inform the world before punishing those who violate the law,
because they committed the offense knowingly.
From the establishment of the state until now,
there has never been a law concerning empty seals.
Officials have succeeded each other,
unaware of its being a crime.
Now, to execute them all at once,
how can those being punished have no words of protest?
The imperial court seeks worthy scholars
and appoints them to various positions;
obtaining them is very difficult.
Those who attain the position of prefect
are all accomplished over decades.
Enlightened and incorruptible scholars
are not like weeds
that can be mown down and grow back again.
How can Your Majesty, for a crime not worthy of punishment,
destroy useful talents?
Your servant secretly laments this for Your Majesty.”
After the memorial was completed,
he closed the door of the inn and wept for several days.
His nephew asked:
“Uncle, what troubles you?”
Shìlì (士利) said:
“I have a memorial I wish to submit.
If I provoke the emperor’s wrath, I will surely suffer disaster.
However, if my death saves hundreds of lives,
what regret could I have?”
He then went in to present the memorial.
The emperor read the memorial,
was greatly enraged,
and sent it to the Grand Councilor (Chéngxiàng, 丞相) and censor for joint interrogation,
also investigating the messenger.
Shìlì (士利) smiled and said:
“I only care whether my memorial is useful or not.
I have already spoken for the state’s affairs,
and I consider myself certain to die.
Who will advise me?”
When the investigation was complete,
he and Shìyuán (士元) were both sent to labor in Jiāngpǔ (江浦),
but many of those involved in the empty seal case were ultimately not spared.
Fāng Zhēng,
courtesy name Kějiǔ,
was a native of Pútián.
By virtue of passing the provincial examination, he was appointed Investigating Censor (gěishìzhōng).
He once attended an imperial excursion to the rear garden,
and composed poems collaboratively with the emperor.
Tàizǔ, knowing he had a mother still living,
bestowed white silver upon him
and dispatched an express relay for him to return home and visit her.
Upon his return, he was re-appointed Supervising Censor (jiānchá yùshǐ),
and then sent out to be the Prefect of Huáiqìng.
Zhēng possessed great ambition and integrity,
and dared to speak frankly when issues arose.
While serving in the prefecture,
due to an anomalous celestial phenomenon, a call for advice was issued.
He submitted a memorial, stating:
"Censors are tasked with clarifying the turbid and elevating the pure.
But now, we do not hear of the virtuous being praised or the capable being promoted;
instead, they are solely devoted to fabricating charges against people,
and excessively levying fines and confiscations.
This is a great affliction.
Only when the court's rewards and punishments are clear and trustworthy
can they encourage and deter.
Last year, officials from various provinces who used 'empty seals' (kōngyìn) incurred heavy penalties.
However, the Provincial Administration Commissioner (cānzhèng) Ānrán of Hénán and the Provincial Administration Commissioner Zhū Fú of Shāndōng both had 'empty seals,'
yet were promoted to Provincial Administration Commissioner (bùzhèngshǐ).
How does this demonstrate encouragement and deterrence?"
The Emperor asked who was fabricating charges and excessively levying fines.
Zhēng pointed to the Assistant Surveillance Commissioner (qiānshì) Péng Jīng of Hénán in reply.
He was demoted to Relay Station Chief (yìchéng) of Cìnyáng.
In the thirteenth year [of the Hongwu reign],
he was arrested for an offense and brought to the capital,
where he died.
Zhōu Jìngxīn
was a native of Shāndōng
and a student of the Imperial Academy (tàixuěshēng).
In the twenty-fifth year of Hóngwǔ, an imperial edict sought those knowledgeable in calendrical calculations.
Jìngxīn submitted a memorial offering strong remonstrance,
also touching upon several current political matters.
It roughly stated: "Your subject has heard that the longevity of a dynasty
depends on the depth or shallowness of its virtue,
not on calendrical calculations.
The Three Dynasties are ancient;
among dynasties since the Three Dynasties,
the longest-lasting were Hán, Táng, and Sòng,
and the shortest were Qín, Suí, and the Five Dynasties.
Their longevity was due to righteous governance (yǒudào),
and their brevity was due to unrighteous governance (wúdào).
Your Majesty received Heaven's favor and mandate,
quelling rebellion and executing tyrants.
However, Your Majesty's divine
martial prowess and decisive authority are more than sufficient,
but magnanimity and sincerity are lacking.
If Your Majesty were to emulate the magnanimity of the Two Hán dynasties
and the sincerity of the Táng and Sòng dynasties,
and study the reasons why the Three Dynasties had
righteous governance that endured,
then the imperial lineage could be transmitted for ten thousand generations.
Why must you consult those who practice minor arts?
Your subject has also heard that Your Majesty has engaged in continuous distant campaigns for years,
advancing north into the desert,
due to the shame of not possessing the imperial seal (chuánguóxǐ).
In the time of King Píng of Chǔ,
Biàn Hé's jade was carved.
It was not until Qín Shǐhuáng that it was named 'xǐ' (seal).
It was passed down through successive dynasties until the Later Táng.
Order and chaos, rise and fall,
all do not depend on this.
When Shí Jìngtáng rebelled,
Prince Lù carried it and immolated himself,
so the Qín seal must have already been destroyed.
When Jìngtáng entered Luò,
he had a new one made of jade.
When Jìn fell, it entered Liáo;
when Liáo fell, it was abandoned by the Sānggān River.
During the reign of Yuán Shìzǔ,
Zhālál
ěr fished it out and obtained it.
The one now held by the Yuán people
is merely Shí's seal.
In ancient times, the Three Dynasties did not know of a 'xǐ.'
Benevolence served as its seal.
Therefore, it is said:
'The great
treasure of a sage is his position.
What keeps his position is benevolence.'
How can Your Majesty neglect the great seal of all under Heaven,
and seek the minor seals of Hán, Táng, and Sòng?
Currently, forced labor is overly burdensome,
and taxes are excessively heavy.
Education is widespread, yet the people are not pleased.
Laws are strict, yet the people do not comply.
Once, Jí Àn said to Emperor Wǔ:
'Your Majesty is full of desires internally, yet outwardly displays benevolence and righteousness.
How can you wish to emulate the governance of Táng and Yú?'
Currently, the state desires wealth,
the military desires strength,
city walls
desire height and depth,
palaces desire grandeur,
territory desires expansion,
and the populace desires multitude.
Consequently, many soldiers are recruited,
wealth is extensively registered,
campaigns
are incessant,
and constructions are limitless.
How can such a state be well-governed?
Your subject has also observed that in the fourth year of Hóngwǔ, officials nationwide were recorded.
In the thirteenth year, many were implicated in Hú's party.
In the nine
teenth year, officials who had for years harmed the people were arrested.
In the twenty-third year, those who spoke rashly were punished.
Great slaughter of officials and commoners occurred,
without distinguishing between good and bad.
Among them, how could there not have been loyal ministers,
heroic gentlemen, good people, and noble men?
From this, Your Majesty's meager virtue and reliance on punishment are evident.
Floods and droughts occur year after year;
how could this be without cause?"
All his words were incisive.
The report was heard.
Wáng Pǔ
was a native of Tóngzhōu.
He was a successful candidate in the imperial examination in the eighteenth year of Hóngwǔ.
His original name was Quán;
the Emperor changed it for him.
He was appointed Investigating Censor (gěishìzhōng) in the Department of Personnel (lìkē).
He was dismissed for his outspoken remonstrance, which displeased the Emperor.
Soon after, he was reinstated as Censor (yùshǐ),
and presented a memorial of over a thousand words on current affairs.
His nature was upright and frank.
He often debated right and wrong with the Emperor,
and would not yield.
One day,
he strongly contended over an issue.
The Emperor was enraged
and ordered his execution.
When he reached the marketplace,
he was recalled,
and the Emperor admonished him, saying:
"Will you change?"
Pǔ replied:
"Your Majesty, not considering your subject unworthy,
promoted him to Censor.
How can you humiliate him to this extent!
If your subject is innocent,
how can he be executed?
If he is guilty,
why keep him alive?
Your subject wishes to die quickly today!"
The Emperor was furious
and immediately ordered the execution to proceed.
As he passed the Imperial Historiography Academy (shǐguǎn),
he shouted loudly:
"Grand Academician Liú Sānwú, record this: on such and such a date,
the Emperor executed the innocent Censor Pǔ!"
He was ultimately executed.
The Emperor compiled the Great Edict (Dàgào),
stating that Pǔ had slandered him,
yet still listed his name.
There was a Zhāng Héng,
a native of Wàn'ān,
who passed the imperial examination in the same year as Pǔ.
He was appointed Investigating Censor (gěishìzhōng) in the Department of Rites (lǐkē).
His memorials were pertinent.
He was promoted to Vice Minister of Rites (lǐbù shìláng).
He was praised for his integrity and prudence,
and recorded in the Great Edict.
Later, he also died for speaking out on affairs.
A eulogy says: Tàizǔ was heroic, martial, and decisive,
and court officials often faltered in their replies.
However, Qián Táng, Hán Yíkě, Lǐ Shìlǔ, and others
held to their honest sincerity,
and strongly remonstrated in the imperial hall.
They can be called the surviving upright figures of antiquity.
Bójù and Jìngxīn, as scholars in simple robes, spoke of the ultimate plans for the realm.
Although this deviated from the principle of remonstrating only after gaining trust,
yet examining their original intention,
it stemmed from loyalty and love.
Compared to those in later ages who sought fame and sold their integrity,
they are not to be spoken of in the same breath.

Biographies, Chapter 28: Wèi Guān, Táo Hòuzhòng (Wáng Yòu), Liú Shìhuán (Wáng Pǔ, Xú Jūn), Wáng Zōngxiǎn (Wáng Xīngzōng, Lǚ Wénsuì, Wáng Xīngfú, Sū Gōngràng, Zhào Tínglán), Wáng Guān (Yáng Zhuó, Luó Xìng), Dàotóng (Ōuyáng Míng), Lú Xī (his brother Xióng, Wáng Shìhóng, Ní Mèngxián, Láng Mǐn), Qīng Wénshèng
Wèi Guān,
courtesy name Shíshān,
was a native of Púqí.
During the late Yuán dynasty, he lived as a recluse on Mount Pú.
When Tàizǔ captured Wǔchāng,
he was invited and appointed as Assistant Instructor of the Guózǐ (Imperial Academy),
then promoted to Investigating Censor for the Zhèjiāng Surveillance Commissioner's Office.
In the first year of Wú, he was promoted to Commissioner of Transport for Liǎnghuái,
and entered court as a Diarist.
He was ordered to accompany Wú Lín to seek forgotten talents throughout the land with gifts of silks and fabrics.
In the first year of Hóngwǔ, the Dàběntáng was established,
and he was ordered to serve as tutor to the Crown Prince,
and later to teach the classics to the various princes.
Not long after,
he was again ordered to accompany Wén Yuánjí, Zhān Tóng, Wú Fǔ, Zhào Shòu, and others to travel across the empire,
seeking forgotten talents,
and many of those he recommended were promoted.
In the third year, he was transferred to Grand Master of Ceremonies,
where he reviewed and corrected the various sacrificial rituals.
His work pleased the emperor,
so he was appointed Scholarly Remonstrator,
and soon after promoted to Libationer.
The following year, he was dismissed for failing to report the examination of the rites for sacrificing to Kǒngzǐ in a timely manner,
and demoted to Magistrate of Lóngnán County,
but was soon recalled to serve as Principal of the Ministry of Rites.
In the fifth year,
court officials recommended Guān's talent,
and he was dispatched to govern Sūzhōu Prefecture.
The previous prefect, Chén Níng, was harsh,
and people called him "Iron Brand Chén."
Guān completely reformed Níng's policies,
governing by enlightening the people and rectifying customs.
He established schools,
invited Zhōu Nánlǎo, Wáng Xíng, and Xú Yòngchéng,
and with Professor Gòng Yǐngzhī, established academic protocols.
Wáng Yí, Gāo Qǐ, and Zhāng Yǔ were appointed to edit the classics and histories,
and respected elders Zhōu Shòuyì, Yáng Mào, and Lín Wényǒu conducted the village drinking rituals.
His reforms were widely implemented,
and his administrative performance was the best in the empire.
The following year, he was promoted to Assistant Administrator of the Sìchuān Branch Secretariat.
Before he departed,
due to the pleas of the local populace for him to stay,
he was ordered to return to his post.
Originally,
Zhāng Shìchéng had used Sūzhōu's old administrative office as his palace,
moving the prefectural office to the Dūshuǐ Xíngsī.
Guān, finding that location narrow and cramped,
moved the office back to its old foundation.
He also dredged the Jǐnfān Jīng,
improving water conservancy.
Someone slandered Guān, accusing him of rebuilding the foundations of a vanquished regime.
The emperor sent Censor Zhāng Dù to investigate the matter,
and Guān was subsequently executed.
The emperor soon regretted it,
and ordered that he be buried properly.
Táo Hòuzhòng,
whose given name was Zhù,
used his courtesy name,
and was from Yín.
In the sixteenth year of Hóngwǔ,
as a student of the Guózǐ, he was promoted to Investigating Censor.
He impeached without fear of powerful officials,
accusing Minister of Justice Kāi Jì to his death,
and his integrity stirred the empire.
Not long after,
he was promoted to Fújiàn Surveillance Commissioner,
where he executed dozens of corrupt officials,
promoted education and encouraged scholars,
and provided relief to soldiers and civilians.
The emperor issued an edict commending him.
When the Provincial Administration Commissioner Xuē Dàfāng proved greedy and tyrannical,
Hòuzhòng impeached him.
Dàfāng's confession implicated others,
and he was arrested and brought to the capital.
After verification,
Dàfāng was convicted,
and Hòuzhòng was ordered by imperial edict to return to his post.
Hòuzhòng said:
"My father was formerly a subordinate of the Fāng clan,
and according to official regulations, was relocated to Fèngyáng.
As a child, I was weak
and raised by my elder brother,
until I achieved success.
Now my brother is also a military officer in Fèngyáng.
I have received the emperor's grace,
and hold a position in the Censorate.
I wish to use my salary to support my parents and repay the kindness of my birth and upbringing,
so that my parents and siblings can be reunited,
truly experiencing the ultimate intention of the sagely emperor's filial rule over the empire."
The emperor specially permitted him to bring his parents to live with him,
and removed their relocated household registration.
Hòuzhòng was pure and upright,
using all his salary to support guests.
Not long after,
he died in office.
At that time, Wáng Yòu, a Censor in Guǎngxī,
was from Tàihé.
The Surveillance Commissioner Xún Shì once consulted him on governance.
Yòu said:
"The people of these barbarian regions violate ethics and harm civilization.
If we do not clarify rites and laws now,
and show both encouragement and punishment,
it will be difficult to govern later."
Shì followed his advice,
and Guǎngxī was well-governed.
After Shǔ was pacified,
Yòu was transferred to govern Chóngqìng Prefecture,
where he attracted and settled people,
and greatly won their hearts.
He was dismissed from office due to an incident,
and died.
Liú Shìhuán,
courtesy name Bózhēn,
was from Ānfú.
His father, Hàn,
lived as a recluse and did not serve in office at the end of the Yuán dynasty.
Shìhuán received his father's teaching from a young age.
When the Red Turban rebels caused chaos,
they plundered his village,
and his mother, Lady Zhāng, led a group of women to drown themselves in Cítán.
The rebels captured Shìhuán,
but he was released after a long time.
In the early Hóngwǔ period,
he was humiliated by Zhāng Xǐ, the Ānfú County Assistant Magistrate, while performing forced labor.
Shìhuán was indignant,
and studied even harder.
In the fifteenth year, he responded to
the "Xiánliáng" (Worthy and Good)
examination,
and his policy recommendations pleased the emperor,
so he was appointed Investigating Censor for the Guǎngdōng Surveillance Commissioner's Office,
with jurisdiction over Qióngzhōu.
The local custom in Qióng was to practice witchcraft (gǔ).
When a high official arrived,
they would offer precious goods as tribute.
If accepted, they were pleased;
if rejected, they feared an investigation,
and would use gǔ to kill the official.
Many who served in Qióng were thus corrupted.
Shìhuán was honest and benevolent,
lightening corvée labor and rectifying injustices,
thereby greatly winning the people's hearts.
Although he refused their tribute,
the indigenous people did not harm him.
Zhāng Xǐ, who had humiliated Shìhuán,
happened to be transferred to Assistant Magistrate of Qióngshān,
and came to pay respects as a subordinate official,
feeling great shame and fear.
Shìhuán treated him the same as other officials.
Not long after,
the court deliberated on reducing the number of Censors,
and he was, by rule, demoted to Dōngguǎn River Fishery Commissioner.
While crossing the river, he encountered a storm
and drowned.
His colleague Zhāng Shìxiáng buried him at Yājī.
Later, there was Wáng Pǔ,
a native of Guìlín.
At the end of Hóngwǔ, he served as Assistant Administrator of Guǎngdōng,
also known for his integrity.
When his younger brother came from home to visit the province,
a subordinate official shared a boat with him
and gave him a cloth robe.
Pǔ ordered it returned,
saying:
"Though a single garment is trivial,
one must not be careless,
for this is the beginning of defiling one's conduct and disgracing oneself."
Grain transport by sea often resulted in losses.
Pǔ went to Yú Lǐng,
surveyed the terrain,
and ordered the officials to cut through rocks and fill trenches,
repair bridges,
and switch to cart transport.
The people found this very convenient.
After several years in office,
his chest contained no spare clothes,
and his kitchen had no extra food.
He was falsely accused and arrested, taken to the imperial prison,
and refused all gifts from his colleagues,
saying:
"How can I change my heart because of misfortune?"
The matter was clarified, he was released and returned home,
and died.
At that time, there was Xú Jūn
who was the Sub-prefect of Yángchūn.
The place was remote,
and local strongmen were able to entrench themselves and commit villainies.
When a magistrate arrived,
they would always bribe him with generous gifts,
and then control him.
When Jūn arrived,
the clerks reported that he should go and visit Mò Dàlǎo.
Mò Dàlǎo
was the Master of the Caverns (dòngzhǔ).
Jūn said,
"Is this man not a subject of the king?
If he doesn't come, he will be executed!"
He showed a pair of swords to them.
Dàlǎo, terrified,
came to pay his respects.
Jūn, being incorruptible, discovered his illegal activities
and imprisoned him.
The next morning,
two melons and several pomegranates were sent as gifts,
all made of gold and beautiful pearls.
Jūn did not look at them,
but sent him in shackles to the prefecture.
The prefectural official, having accepted bribes, released him,
and he again sent the previous gifts.
Jūn was enraged
and wanted to arrest and prosecute him,
but a prefectural dispatch ordered Jūn to temporarily assume office in Yángjiāng.
Yángjiāng was greatly reformed.
He left office due to distress.
Wáng Zōngxiǎn,
a native of Hézhōu,
resided in Yánzhōu as an immigrant.
When Hú Dàhǎi conquered Yánzhōu,
he respectfully invited Zōngxiǎn to his staff.
When Tàizǔ marched on Wùzhōu,
Dàhǎi presented Zōngxiǎn,
and Tàizǔ said,
"He is from my hometown."
He ordered him to go to Wùzhōu to scout the enemy.
Zōngxiǎn secretly learned the city's strengths and weaknesses and the merits and demerits of the various generals,
then returned to report to Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ joyfully said,
"When I take Wùzhōu,
I will make you its Prefect."
Soon after, Yuán Grand Councilor Níng Ānqìng and the defending general Tiēmùlièrèsī had a disagreement,
and Ānqìng sent a staff officer to rappel down the wall to request surrender,
opening the East Gate to admit the troops,
which matched the information Zōngxiǎn had gathered.
Wùzhōu was renamed Níngyuè Fǔ,
and Zōngxiǎn was appointed Prefect.
Zōngxiǎn was originally a scholar,
broadly versed in classics and history.
He opened the commandery school,
inviting Yè Yí and Sòng Lián as Five Classics masters,
Dài Liáng as academic director,
and Wú Chén, Xú Yuán, and others as instructors.
Since the wars began,
schools had long been neglected;
it was only then that the sound of stringed instruments and chanting was heard again.
Not long after,
he died in office.
When Tàizǔ took Wùzhōu,
he also appointed Wáng Xīngzōng as Magistrate of Jīnhuá.
Xīngzōng
was formerly a servant.
Lǐ Shàncháng and Lǐ Wénzhōng both thought this was inappropriate.
Tàizǔ said,
"Xīngzōng has followed me for a long time;
he is diligent, incorruptible, and decisive.
No scholar or legal official surpasses him."
After three years,
he was indeed renowned for his administrative conduct.
He was promoted to Assistant Prefect of Nánchāng,
then transferred to Prefect of Sōngzhōu.
At that time, the populace was being registered for military service.
Xīngzōng memorialized, saying,
"At the end of the Yuán dynasty, people were gathered as soldiers,
but dispersed, they returned to being civilians.
Now, the military and civilian populations are separate.
If they are registered as soldiers,
then there will be no civilians.
From where will taxes be collected?"
The Emperor said,
"Good."
He was promoted to Prefect of Huáiqìng.
When he presented his annual report in the capital,
the Emperor questioned various prefects about their affairs.
When it came to Xīngzōng,
he alone said,
"This prefect is public-spirited, diligent, and not greedy;
there is no need to question him."
He was again promoted to Sūzhōu,
then elevated to Provincial Administration Commissioner of Hénán.
When he took leave from the palace,
the Emperor said,
"I haven't seen you for a long time;
you've grown old,
and my beard has also turned white."
He hosted a banquet and sent him off,
and Xīngzōng became even more diligent in his duties.
Later, he was implicated in a matter but exonerated,
and died in office.
At the same time, there was Lǚ Wénsuì,
courtesy name Yòngmíng,
a native of Yǒngkāng.
When bandits rose at the end of the Yuán dynasty,
Wénsuì distributed his family wealth
and recruited three thousand brave men.
He fought continuously with the bandits
and defeated them.
He was offered office three times,
but he refused all.
When Tàizǔ pacified Wùzhōu,
he established the Yǒngkāng Commandery,
appointing Wénsuì as Left Deputy Marshal concurrently serving as Magistrate.
Soon after, he was summoned to be an Assistant Commissioner in the Office of Agrarian Affairs,
then promoted to Prefect of Lúzhōu.
When Western Zhèjiāng was pacified,
he was transferred to Prefect of Jiāxīng.
When the people of Sōngjiāng rebelled
and invaded Jiāxīng,
Wénsuì barricaded his office
and led brave men to defend it.
When Lǐ Wénzhōng's reinforcements arrived,
the rebels were captured.
The generals then wanted to massacre the city.
Wénsuì said,
"Those who rebelled are the bandits.
What crime have the people committed?"
He vehemently stopped them.
After three full years,
he returned to court.
By imperial decree, he carried the imperial staff to convey a message to the Kingdom of Shéyīpó,
but fell ill and died
at Xīnghuà.
The following year,
tens of officials from Jiāxīng, from the Assistant Prefect downwards, were executed for violations of the salt laws.
The authorities, noting that Wénsuì had signed official documents,
requested to confiscate his family's property.
The Emperor said,
"Wénsuì was honest and trustworthy;
he would certainly not engage in corrupt practices.
Moreover, he died while on an imperial mission;
this is lamentable.
Do not confiscate."
At that time, among the prefects renowned for their administrative conduct
were also Wáng Xīngfú and Sū Gōngràng.
Xīngfú,
a native of Suí,
first served as Prefect of Huīzhōu,
where he implemented good governance.
He was promoted to Hángzhōu.
Hángzhōu had just submitted,
and the people were not yet settled,
but Xīngfú was skilled at pacifying and organizing them.
The people deeply appreciated him.
When his term was completed and he was due for promotion,
the people of the commandery blocked the roads, pleading for him to stay.
Xīngfú explained as he sent them away, saying,
"It is not that I have bestowed favor upon you, elders,
but that you, elders, have skillfully upheld the law."
Tàizǔ praised him
and promoted him to Minister of Personnel.
He was later demoted to Prefect of Xī'ān due to an incident
and died in office.
Gōngràng,
a native of Yùtián,
was recommended
as "intelligent and upright."
He served as Prefect of Hànyáng,
where his administration was strict and fair but not harsh.
When there was a heavy labor service,
he would go to his superiors and repeatedly present his case,
often succeeding in obtaining reductions.
And the Magistrate of Hànyáng County, Zhào Tínglán,
a native of Xú,
was also capable of loving the people and taking responsibility for affairs.
The imperial court once sent envoys to recruit the dispersed soldiers of the Chén clan.
Many other counties responded with civilian men,
but Tínglán alone stated that the county had none.
The people of Hànyáng always spoke of Gōngràng when referring to the Prefect, and Tínglán when referring to the Magistrate.
Wáng Guān,
courtesy name Shàngbīn,
was from Xiángfú.
His nature was upright and outspoken,
his bearing was impressive and grand,
and he was skilled in discussion.
He entered the Imperial Academy through a provincial recommendation,
and was promoted to Prefect of Sūzhōu Fǔ.
He was honest and awe-inspiring.
The cunning official Qián Yīng had repeatedly implicated previous superiors,
but Guān flogged him to death.
When the matter was reported,
Tàizǔ sent an envoy with an imperial edict to commend him,
and rewarded him with imperial wine.
During a year of great famine,
many people defaulted on their taxes,
and the provincial commissioner pressed them very hard.
Guān prepared a banquet,
invited the wealthy people,
and persuaded them to lend money to the poor to pay their taxes.
His words were sincere and earnest,
and all the wealthy people were moved,
so the unpaid taxes were fully paid.
The imperial court praised his ability,
and posted a notice to encourage the whole empire.
Among those who governed Sūzhōu, before him were Jì Hēng and Wèi Guān,
and after him were Yáo Shàn and Kuàng Zhōng;
all were virtuous,
and were called
"Five Grand Prefects of Gūsū,"
and were all enshrined in the Temple of Literature.
Yáng Zhuó,
courtesy name Zìlì,
was from Tàihé.
He became a *jìnshì* in the fourth year of Hóngwǔ,
and was appointed as a principal of the Ministry of Personnel.
After a year,
he was promoted to Assistant Administrator of Guǎngdōng Xíngshěng.
A peasant woman, walking alone in the mountains,
encountered a woodcutter
who tried to assault her.
The woman resisted,
and was killed.
Officials interrogated twenty fellow woodcutters,
and all confessed.
Zhuó said:
"There are many woodcutters;
surely there are good and bad among them.
Can all be held guilty?"
He lined up the twenty men in the courtyard,
observed them carefully for a long time,
and then pointed to two woodcutters, saying:
"You two are the murderers."
The two woodcutters were greatly astonished
and confessed their crime.
He was demoted to Tián Fèngyáng due to an incident,
then reinstated as Vice-Prefect of Hángzhōu.
There were brothers who had been disputing land
for several years without resolution.
When Zhuó arrived, he tearfully exhorted and enlightened them,
and they ceased their dispute.
Zhuó was adept in official affairs,
and clerks could not deceive him.
His administration was peaceful and lenient,
and the people were pleased and submitted to him.
He resigned due to illness,
and died.
Zhuó's fellow townsman was Luó Xìng,
courtesy name Zǐlǐ.
In the early Hóngwǔ era, he was recommended from his hometown,
and appointed Co-Prefect of Dé'ān.
There was a great bandit who had not been apprehended for a long time,
and hundreds of people were implicated and imprisoned.
When Xìng arrived in the prefecture,
he released all the prisoners,
promising to fully pardon them if the bandit was caught within ten days.
Everyone prostrated themselves and vowed to do their best,
and indeed, the bandit was caught in seven days.
Once, while tending a vegetable garden,
he discovered over ten thousand catties of iron in a pit.
At that time, there was a levy of iron for making military weapons,
and people eagerly sought to sell it.
Xìng said:
"This is how Heaven helps the people;
what business is it of mine?"
He used all of it to fulfill the levy.
When his term expired, he went to the capital.
