He was demoted and exiled to Xī'ān for using jujube wood to dye military clothing.
Xìng was broadly learned.
At that time, there were dozens of venerable scholars and seasoned Confucians from all directions in Xī'ān.
Zōu Yì of Wú said:
"All the books we have read
might perhaps amount to half of what Master Luó knows."
He died at the age of seventy.
Dào Tóng,
was from Héjiān.
His ancestors were of the Mongol ethnicity.
He was known for his filial piety towards his mother.
In the early Hóngwǔ era,
he was recommended and appointed as a ceremonial official in the Imperial Sacrificial Court,
and then assigned out as Magistrate of Pānyú.
Pānyú was formerly known for being troublesome and difficult,
and the military garrisons were particularly arrogant,
often whipping and humiliating the subordinate officials in the county;
previous magistrates were generally unable to bear it.
Tóng enforced the law strictly,
resisting and not complying with anything unreasonable,
and the people relied on him for a measure of peace.
Not long after,
Marquis Yǒngjiā, Zhū Liàngzǔ, arrived.
He frequently tried to intimidate Tóng with his power,
but Tóng was not swayed.
Dozens of local magnates would forcibly buy precious goods in the market.
If they were slightly displeased,
they would cunningly frame others with charges.
Tóng shackled their leader in the main street,
and the powerful families competed to bribe Gāozǔ (likely a mistake for Liàngzǔ) to get him released.
Liàngzǔ hosted a banquet and summoned Tóng,
casually mentioning the matter.
Tóng sternly said:
"You are a high official,
how can you allow yourself to be used by petty individuals!"
Liàngzǔ could not make him yield.
Another day,
Liàngzǔ broke the shackles and freed the man,
then flogged Tóng on some other pretext.
There was a wealthy commoner, of the Luó clan,
who had given his daughter to Liàngzǔ.
His brothers then relied on their influence to commit misdeeds.
Tóng again investigated and prosecuted them,
but Liàngzǔ again took them away.
Tóng, having accumulated many grievances,
listed the incidents and reported them to the emperor.
Before his memorial arrived,
Liàngzǔ had already impeached Tóng for being scornful and disrespectful.
The emperor, unaware of the full situation,
sent an envoy to execute Tóng.
Coincidentally, Tóng's memorial also arrived.
The emperor understood,
and believed that Tóng, though very humble in position,
dared to frankly speak of a high official's unlawful acts.
Such a person was upright and useful,
so he sent another envoy to pardon him.
The two envoys arrived in Pānyú on the same day.
The second envoy had just arrived
when Tóng had already died.
The county people mourned and regretted him.
Some carved wooden effigies to worship him at home,
and divinations often proved effective,
so Tóng was then widely regarded as a deity.
When Tóng was not yet dead,
the Provincial Administration Commissioner, Xú Běn, deeply respected Tóng.
Tóng was in the midst of flogging a doctor and had not finished,
but Běn urgently needed the doctor,
and sent a soldier to tell Tóng to release him.
Tóng, with a stern demeanor, said:
"Is Lord Xú also imitating Marquis Yǒngjiā?"
He only released the doctor after the flogging was complete.
From then on, superior officials became even more strict and fearful of him,
but Tóng ultimately brought disaster upon himself because of this.
Earlier, there was a man named Ōuyáng Míng,
who had also once resisted General Cháng Yùchūn on an issue.
Míng,
courtesy name Rìxīn,
was from Tàihé.
He was appointed County Vice-Magistrate of Jiāngdū by recommendation.
After the ravages of war,
seventy or eighty percent of the people had died or migrated.
Míng attracted and comforted them,
and they gradually resumed their livelihoods.
There was a stepmother who accused her son of being unfilial.
He summoned them before his desk,
and patiently reasoned with them in detail.
Mother and son left weeping and grateful,
and eventually became known for their kindness and filial piety.
Once, while clearing a vacant plot behind the official residence,
he found one hundred taels of silver.
As it happened, a provincial order had requested lacquer,
so he immediately bought it with the silver and submitted it.
Míng knew Línzī.
When Chūn Shī passed through his territory,
soldiers entered people's homes to take wine,
fought each other,
and the entire city was in an uproar.
Míng had them flogged and sent away.
The soldiers accused him of cursing the general.
Yùchūn questioned him.
He said:
"The soldiers
are the King's army,
and the people are also the King's people.
If the people are beaten and almost killed,
should the soldiers not be flogged?
Although Míng is foolish,
how could he curse the general?
The general is a great worthy;
how can he, for the sake of one soldier, bend the national law?"
Yùchūn understood and
reprimanded his soldiers in apology.
Later, when Grand General Xú Dá arrived,
the soldiers warned each other:
"This is a capable official
who once stood up to General Cháng;
do not offend him."
Míng's administration was clean, quiet, fair, and compassionate.
In his leisure time, he often invited scholars to discuss literature and art.
Sometimes, he rode alone through the fields,
inspecting plowing and harvesting,
and the county was very well governed.
Upon completion of his term, he entered the court for an audience
and died.
Lú Xī,
courtesy name Gōngjì,
was from Kūnshān.
His elder brother, Xióng,
courtesy name Gōngwǔ,
was the Zhīfǔ of Yǎozhōu.
At that time, military conflicts had just settled.
It happened that the Prince of Lǔ's residence was being built,
and rivers were also being dredged;
great projects were undertaken simultaneously.
Xióng devoted himself to managing them,
and the people were not disturbed.
Later, he died due to implication in a case.
Xī was recommended and appointed Tóngzhī of Suīzhōu.
He was benevolent and loved,
and was ordered to act as Zhīfǔ.
At that time, an imperial censor was sent to search for former soldiers.
A thousand Suī people had been wrongly conscripted.
A summons was issued for Xī to send them back.
Xī ordered the people to report themselves,
and several who had previously served in the military were found and given over.
The imperial censor was angry,
imprisoned the clerks,
demanding all of them be found,
otherwise he would be charged with obstructing an imperial edict.
All his colleagues were fearful.
Xī said:
"I am the shepherd of my people.
If the people scatter,
what use is a shepherd?"
He then went to the imperial censor himself and said:
"The military register of the prefecture is all here.
If you press them,
the people will scatter,
and only the Tóngzhī will remain.
Please let me fill the service."
The imperial censor angrily dismissed him,
but he stood firm and did not move.
Eventually,
knowing he could not be swayed,
the censor desisted.
Later, he died in office,
too poor to afford a funeral.
The government provided for his interment.
When his coffin was returned home,
officials and commoners blocked the road, weeping to see him off.
Despite heavy rain,
not one person turned back.
There was also Wáng Shìhóng,
Zhīxiàn of Nínghǎi.
The Jìnghǎi Hóu, Wú Zhēn, was ordered to round up former soldiers of the Fāng clan.
Unscrupulous rascals falsely implicated innocent commoners,
causing turmoil in Táizhōu and Wēnzhōu.
Shìhóng submitted a memorial,
the words of which were extremely earnest.
An imperial edict ordered the cessation of the arrests,
and the people relied on this to find peace.
Ní Mèngxián,
from Nánchāng,
was Zhīxiàn of Líshuǐ.
There was a fortune-teller among the people who attempted to curry favor with a wealthy family without success.
So he went to the capital to accuse fifty-seven prominent families, including Chén Gōngwàng, of conspiring a rebellion.
An order was issued for Zhōu Yuán, a Qiānhù of the Jǐnyīwèi, to apprehend them.
Mèngxián investigated and found the truth.
He said to his subordinates:
"The imperial court appointed Mèngxián to govern this county.
How can I bear to stand by and watch good people be cruelly harmed?"
He immediately drew up a memorial to report it.
He also ordered forty elders to go to the palace to appeal.
The case was sent to the judicial authorities for investigation and confirmation,
and the accuser was punished according to law.
Again, treacherous people from Lèpíng also went to the palace to accuse over fifty prominent families of treason.
Láng Mǐn, the Zhīzhōu of Ráozhōu, strongly pleaded and argued on their behalf.
An imperial edict ordered the execution of the treacherous commoners,
and those who had been falsely accused were all released.
Qīng Wénshèng,
courtesy name Zhìfū,
was from Kuízhōu.
He served as Diǎnshǐ of Lóngyáng.
Lóngyáng bordered Dòngtíng Lake,
suffering from annual floods,
resulting in hundreds of thousands of unpaid taxes,
and those who died from beatings followed one after another.
Wénshèng lamented this and went to the palace to submit a memorial,
pleading for the people.
He submitted it twice,
but neither was reported back.
He sighed:
"How can I return to face the elders?"
He prepared another memorial,
struck the Dēngwéngǔ drum to present it,
and then hanged himself under the drum.
The emperor was greatly shocked upon hearing this,
pitied him for sacrificing his life for the people,
and issued an edict to reduce Lóngyáng's taxes by over 24,000 *shí* of grain,
setting it as the permanent quota.
The people of the county built a shrine to worship him.
His wife and children were too poor to return home,
so they were supported with one hundred *mǔ* of public land.
In the fourteenth year of Wànlì, an edict ordered officials to offer sacrifices in spring and autumn,
naming his shrine Huìliè.
The encomium says: Tàizǔ rose from the common people,
was familiar with corrupt officials who harmed the populace,
and often dealt with them with extreme punishment.
However, he frequently commended and promoted the worthy and capable
to encourage them,
not relying solely on law.
He once sent an envoy with an imperial edict and thirty *dìng* of paper currency,
along with a jug of wine,
to bestow upon Zhāng Chǔ, the Zhīxiàn of Píngyáng.
Also, Guō Bótài, the Zhīxiàn of Jiànyáng, and Lù Yì, the Chéng,
governed without fear of power or influence.
He sent an envoy to commend them with wine,
and promoted their offices.
Hú Mèngtōng, the Zhīxiàn of Dāntú, and Guō Bógāo, the Chéng;
Lǐ Sījìn, the Chéng of Jīntán;
were due to be arrested for an incident.
The people went to the palace
to speak of their many good policies.
The emperor bestowed internal wine vessels upon them all,
and issued an edict of commendation.
Yú Yánchéng, the Shǒu of Yǒngzhōu, Zhèng Mǐn, the Lìng of Qídōng, and ten others were imprisoned for various incidents.
The local people listed their achievements and petitioned for them,
and all were reinstated to their official positions.
Shěn Chāng, the Lìng of Yíchūn, and four others were even promoted to Gùnshǒu.
Among those promoted extraordinarily from lower ranks were:
Wáng Shàngxián, the Wèi of Níngyuǎn, as Cānzhèng of Guǎngxī;
Zōu Jùn, the Chéng of Xiángfú, as Dàlǐ Qīng;
Yuán Shàn, the Zhōupàn of Jìngníng, as Qiāndū Yùshǐ;
Lǐ Xíngsù, the Lìng of Zhīyáng, as Xíngbù Shìláng.
As for Chén Xīwén, the Chéng of Huáiníng, and Wáng Fùchūn, the Bù of Yíxīng,
they were first promoted for good governance,
but when their greed and recklessness became known,
they were soon subjected to severe punishment.
Thus, the encouragement and admonishment were profound,
which is why the administration of officials at that time was largely noteworthy.
Proofreading Notes:

Biographies, Volume 29: Qí Tài, Huáng Zǐchéng, Fāng Xiàorú (Lú Yuánzhì, Zhèng Gōngzhì, Lín Jiāyóu, Hú Zǐzhāo, Zhèng Jūzhēn, Liú Zhèng, Fāng Fǎ, Lóu Lián), Liàn Zǐníng (Sòng Zhēng, Yè Xīxián), Máo Dàfāng (Zhōu Xuán), Zhuó Jìng (Guō Rèn, Lú Jiǒng), Chén Dí (Huáng Kuí, Jù Jìng), Jǐng Qīng (Lián Yíng), Hú Rùn (Gāo Xiáng), Wáng Dù (Dài Déyí, Xiè Shēng, Dīng Zhìfāng, Gān Lín, Dǒng Yōng, Chén Jìzhī, Hán Yǒng, Yè Fú).
Qí Tài,
from Lìshuǐ.
His original name was Dé.
In the seventeenth year of Hóngwǔ, he placed first in the Yìngtiān provincial examination.
The following year, he passed the Jìnshì examination.
He successively served as Zhǔshì in the Boards of Rites and War.
When lightning struck the Jǐnshēndiàn,
Tàizǔ prayed at the suburban altars and ancestral temples.
He selected those who had served nine years in office without fault to assist in the sacrifice.
Dé was among them
and was bestowed the name Tài.
In the twenty-eighth year, he was promoted from Lángzhōng of the Board of War to Zuǒ Shìláng.
Tàizǔ once asked for the names of frontier generals;
Tài recited them all without omission.
He also asked about various maps and records.
Tài presented a concise and detailed handbook from his sleeve,
which greatly impressed the emperor.
The Grand Imperial Heir Apparent had always highly esteemed Qí Tài.
Upon his ascension to the throne,
he ordered Qí Tài to participate in national governance alongside Huáng Zǐchéng,
and soon promoted him to Shàngshū.
At that time, the imperial testament commanded that the various princes, when in their states,
were not to rush to the imperial funeral,
and that the officials and common people of the kingdoms were to be subject to the court's regulation.
The princes believed that Qí Tài had falsified the imperial testament of the deceased emperor,
sowing discord among kin,
and were all displeased.
Earlier,
when the Emperor was the Grand Heir Apparent,
many princes, being of senior lineage,
commanded large armies.
He was concerned about this,
and so at this time, he secretly deliberated on curtailing the power of the feudatories.
In the first year of Jiànwén (1399),
the five princes of Zhōu, Dài, Xiāng, Qí, and Mín were successively deposed for crimes.
In the seventh month,
the Prince of Yān raised an army and rebelled,
naming his forces
"Jìngnàn" (Pacification of Difficulties),
and identifying Qí Tài and Huáng Zǐchéng as treacherous ministers.
When this news was heard,
Qí Tài requested that the Prince of Yān be removed from the imperial clan registry,
to proclaim his crimes and launch an expedition against him.
Some found this difficult,
but Qí Tài said:
"By making it clear he is a rebel,
the enemy can then be overcome."
Thereupon, the decision was made to attack Yān,
and this was announced to the world.
At that time, very few of Tàizǔ's meritorious officials remained.
Thus, Gěng Bǐngwén, Marquis of Chángxīng, was appointed Grand General,
to lead the army in separate routes for the northern expedition.
Upon reaching Zhēndìng, they were defeated by Yān.
Zǐchéng recommended Lǐ Jǐnglóng, Duke of Cáoguó, to replace him as general.
Qí Tài strongly argued against it.
Zǐchéng did not listen,
and ultimately appointed Lǐ Jǐnglóng as general.
At this time,
the Emperor gave Lǐ Jǐnglóng an army of 500,000,
believing Yān could be destroyed overnight.
The Prince of Yān, looking on, greatly rejoiced, saying:
"In the past, Hàn Gāo could only command 100,000.
What talent does Lǐ Jǐnglóng possess,
that his troops are just enough to serve as resources for me?"
That winter,
Lǐ Jǐnglóng was indeed defeated,
and the Emperor showed signs of fear.
Coincidentally, the Prince of Yān submitted a letter severely denouncing Qí Tài and Zǐchéng.
The Emperor then relieved the two men of their posts to appease Yān,
but secretly kept them in the capital,
still involving them in confidential discussions.
Lǐ Jǐnglóng sent a letter to the Prince of Yān,
stating that the two men had been exiled,
and that hostilities could cease.
The Prince of Yān did not listen.
The following year,
Shèng Yōng achieved a victory at Dōngchāng.
The Emperor announced it to the ancestral temple,
and ordered the two men to resume their former positions.
After the defeat at Jiāhé,
he again dismissed the two men from office to seek an end to hostilities.
The Prince of Yān said:
"This is merely to delay me."
And pressed on even more urgently.
When the proposal to curtail the feudatories first arose,
the Emperor accepted the words of Qí Tài and Zǐchéng,
believing that controlling a corner of the realm with the full might of the empire was very easy.
After repeated defeats,
he felt regret in his heart,
and thus was at a loss, advancing and retreating.
When the Yān army drew nearer day by day,
he again summoned Qí Tài back.
Before he arrived,
the capital was already undefended.
Qí Tài fled to an outer commandery to plan a restoration.
At that time, the pursuit of Qí Tài was urgent.
Qí Tài dyed a white horse black and fled.
When he had traveled a little distance,
the sweat caused the dye to wash off.
Someone said:
"This is Shàngshū Qí's horse!"
He was then captured and taken to the capital,
where he, along with Zǐchéng and Fāng Xiàorú, died unyielding.
Qí Tài's cousins Jìngzōng and others were all executed.
His uncles Shíyǒng and Yángyàn and others were banished to the frontier.
His son Fǔ, only six years old,
was spared death and assigned to a commoner's household;
he was pardoned and returned during Rénzōng's reign.
Huáng Zǐchéng's
given name was Shí,
but he was known by his courtesy name.
He was from Fēnyí.
In the eighteenth year of Hóngwǔ (1385), he placed first in the metropolitan examination.
From editor, he advanced to compiler,
served as a tutor to the Heir Apparent in the Eastern Palace,
and was successively promoted to Grand Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
When Huìdì was the Grand Imperial Heir Apparent,
he once sat at the Eastern Corner Gate and said to Zǐchéng:
"The various princes, being of senior lineage, command large armies,
and many act unlawfully.
What should be done?"
He replied:
"The princes' guard troops
are barely sufficient for self-defense.
Should there be a disturbance,
if we confront them with the six armies,
who among them could withstand it?
The Seven States of Hàn were not weak,
yet they ultimately perished.
The power dynamic of large and small, strong and weak, is different,
but the principle of compliance and rebellion varies."
The Grand Heir Apparent approved of his words.
Upon his ascension,
he appointed Zǐchéng concurrently as Hanlin Academician,
to participate in national governance with Qí Tài,
saying:
"Sir, do you recall the words spoken at the Eastern Corner Gate that day?"
Zǐchéng bowed his head and said:
"I dare not forget."
Retreating, he deliberated with Qí Tài.
Qí Tài wanted to deal with Yān first.
Zǐchéng said:
"Not so.
The princes of Zhōu, Qí, Xiāng, Dài, and Mín,
during the late emperor's time,
still acted unlawfully many times.
There is a clear justification for curtailing them.
If we now wish to punish them,
we should start with Zhōu.
The Prince of Zhōu
is the younger brother of Yān by the same mother.
Curtailing Zhōu is like severing Yān's limbs."
Once the plan was settled,
they reported it to the Emperor the next day.
Coincidentally, there was a report that Zhōu Wáng Sū was acting unlawfully.
Thereupon, Lǐ Jǐnglóng was ordered to lead troops to surprise and capture him,
and the testimony implicated the households of Xiāng and Dài.
Thus, Sū and Mín Wáng Pián were demoted to commoners,
Dài Wáng Guì was imprisoned in Dàtóng,
and Qí Wáng Bó was confined in the capital.
Xiāng Wáng Bǎi immolated himself.
The matter of Zhōu Wáng's crimes was submitted to Yān for consideration.
The Prince of Yān submitted a memorial to plead for him.
The Emperor, reading the letter, felt sympathy,
and said the matter should cease for now.
Zǐchéng and Qí Tài argued against this.
While undecided,
they went out and spoke to each other, saying:
"Given the current situation,
how can we not decide?"
The next day, they again came in and said:
"Now, the only one we worry about is the Prince of Yān.
We should take advantage of his feigned illness to launch a surprise attack."
The Emperor hesitated, saying:
"I have not been on the throne long,
and have already successively deposed several princes.
If I also curtail Yān,
how can I justify myself to the world?"
Zǐchéng replied:
"One who acts first controls others;
do not be controlled by others."
The Emperor said:
"The Prince of Yān is wise and brave, skilled in warfare.
Even if he is ill,
I fear he will be difficult to deal with suddenly."
And so he stopped.
Thereupon, Dūdū Sòng Zhōng was ordered to deploy frontier troops to garrison Kāipíng,
select elite and strong guards from the Yān princely establishment to serve under Sòng Zhōng's command,
and summon guard cavalry commanders such as Guān Tóng to the capital,
to weaken Yān.
Furthermore, the left and right guard troops of Yǒngqīng in Běipíng were deployed to station in Zhāngdé and Shùndé,
Dūdū Xú Kǎi was to train troops at Línqīng,
and Gěng Huàn was to train troops at Shānhǎiguān,
to control Běipíng.
These were all Qí Tài and Zǐchéng's schemes.
At that time, the Prince of Yān was anxious and fearful.
As his three sons were all in the capital,
he feigned a serious illness,
and begged for his three sons to return.
Qí Tài wanted to seize them at once.
Zǐchéng said:
"It is better to send them back,
to show him no suspicion,
and then we can surprise and capture him."
They were eventually sent back.
Not long after,
the Yān army rose up.
The Prince wept and swore to his generals and officials, saying:
"The persecution of the princes
was not the intention of the Son of Heaven,
but the work of the treacherous ministers Qí Tài and Huáng Zǐchéng."
Initially, the Emperor trusted Zǐchēng and Qí Tài.
They suddenly began reducing the power of the feudal lords.
Both were originally scholars,
and military matters were not their forte.
When Gěng Bǐngwén suffered a defeat,
Zǐchēng said that victory and defeat were common occurrences,
and not worth worrying about.
He then recommended Cáo Guógōng Lǐ Jǐnglóng as capable of a great responsibility.
The Emperor then replaced Bǐngwén with Jǐnglóng.
But Jǐnglóng was even more incompetent,
suffering successive defeats at Zhèngcūnbà and Báigōuhé,
losing hundreds of thousands of military supplies, soldiers, and horses.
Afterward,
he was again defeated beneath the walls of Jǐnán.
The Emperor urgently recalled Jǐnglóng,
pardoning him from execution.
Zǐchēng wept bitterly,
requesting that Jǐnglóng be punished for his crime.
The Emperor did not listen.
Zǐchēng beat his chest and said:
"The great matter is lost!
Recommending Jǐnglóng has ruined the country;
ten thousand deaths are not enough to atone for this sin."
When the Yān army gradually advanced south,
he was exiled to an outer region along with Qí Tài,
with secret orders to recruit soldiers.
Zǐchēng traveled in disguise from Tài Hú to Sūzhōu,
and together with the prefect Yáo Shàn, he advocated for loyalty to the emperor and military service.
Shàn submitted a memorial saying:
"Zǐchēng's talent is sufficient to defend against calamity;
he should not be abandoned in a remote place to please the enemy."
The Emperor again summoned Zǐchēng,
but before he arrived, the capital fell.
He wanted to sail overseas with Shàn to beg for troops.
Shàn disagreed,
so he sought to plan an uprising with Yáng Rèn in Jiāxīng.
They were reported,
and both were arrested.
When Zǐchēng arrived,
Chéngzǔ personally interrogated him.
He argued defiantly and did not yield.
He was executed by dismemberment.
All members of his clan, young and old, were beheaded,
and his in-laws and party members were all exiled to the frontier.
One son changed his name to Tián Jīng,
and after an amnesty,
settled in Xiánníng, Húguǎng.
During the Zhèngdé era,
the *jìnshì* Huáng Biǎo was said to be his descendant.
Yáng Rèn,
during the Hóngwǔ era, rose to prominence through his talent,
serving successively as prefect of Yuánzhōu.
At that time, he had retired,
and harbored Zǐchēng in his home,
and was also executed by dismemberment.
His two sons, Lǐ and Yì, were both beheaded.
His relatives were exiled to the frontier.
Fāng Xiàorú,
courtesy name Xīzhí,
also Xīgǔ,
was from Nínghǎi.
His father, Kèqín,
was an upright official during the Hóngwǔ era;
he has his own biography.
Xiàorú was intelligent and quick-witted as a child,
his eyes shining brightly.
He read a *cùn* of text daily,
and local people called him
"Little Hán Zǐ."
As an adult, he studied under Sòng Lián;
all the famous scholars from Lián's school were inferior to him.
His seniors Hú Hàn and Sū Bóhéng also admitted their inferiority.
Xiàorú, however, regarded literary arts as trivial,
taking it as his duty to clarify the kingly way and achieve great peace.
He once fell ill
and ran out of food.
When his family informed him,
he smiled and said:
"The ancients ate nine meals in thirty days;
am I the only one who is poor?"
His father Kèqín was executed for the
"empty seal"
incident.
He carried his father's coffin home for burial,
and his grief moved passersby.
After the mourning period,
he resumed his studies and completed them under Lián.
In the fifteenth year of Hóngwǔ,
recommended by Wú Chén and Jiē Shū,
he was summoned for an audience.
Tàizǔ was pleased with his upright demeanor,
and said to the Crown Prince:
"This is a resolute scholar;
his talent should be fully utilized in his old age."
He was honorably sent back.
Later, implicated by an enemy,
he was arrested and taken to the capital.
Tàizǔ saw his name
and released him.
In the twenty-fifth year,
he was again summoned upon recommendation.
Tàizǔ said:
"Now is not the time to employ Xiàorú."
He was appointed Professor of Hànzhōng,
where he tirelessly lectured to students daily.
Shǔ Xiànwáng heard of his virtue
and invited him to be the Crown Prince's tutor.
Whenever they met,
he expounded on morality.
The King respected him with special rites,
naming his study retreat
"Zhèngxué."
When Huìdì ascended the throne,
he was summoned to be a Hànlín Attendant Lecturer.
The following year, he was promoted to Attendant Academician,
and the Emperor frequently consulted him on major state affairs.
The Emperor was fond of reading,
and whenever he had doubts, he would summon Xiàorú to explain them.
When conducting court matters,
officials would debate pros and cons in person,
or Xiàorú would be ordered to write replies before the imperial seat.
At that time, the *Tàizǔ Shílù* and other essential compendiums were being compiled,
and Xiàorú was the chief editor for all of them.
When the official system was reformed,
Xiàorú was appointed Literary Erudite.
When the Yān army rose,
the court deliberated on punitive measures,
and all edicts and proclamations came from his hand.
In the third year of Jiànwén,
the Yān army plundered Dàmíng.
The King heard that Qí and Huáng had already fled,
and submitted a memorial requesting the dismissal of Shèng Yōng, Wú Jié, and Píng Ān's troops.
Xiàorú suggested:
"The Yān army has been bogged down in Dàmíng for a long time.
With hot weather and rain,
they will tire themselves out without fighting.
Urgently order the generals from Liáodōng to enter Shānhǎiguān and attack Yǒngpíng,
and the generals from Zhēndìng to cross the Lúgōu River and strike Běipíng.
They will surely return to rescue it.
If we follow closely with a large army,
we can capture them.
Their memorial has just arrived now;
we should first reply to them.
The back-and-forth will take more than a month,
making their generals and soldiers complacent.
When our plans are set and our forces aligned,
advancing and crushing them
will not be difficult."
The Emperor agreed.
He ordered Xiàorú to draft an edict,
and sent Dàlǐ Sì Shǎoqīng Xuē Yán to rush it to Yān,
pardoning all of Yān's crimes,
and ordering them to cease military action and return to their fiefdom.
He also prepared several thousand words of a declaration for Yán,
to be carried to the Yān army,
and secretly distributed among the generals and soldiers.
When he arrived,
Yán hid the declaration and dared not release it,
and the Yān King also did not obey the edict.
In the fifth month,
Wú Jié, Píng Ān, and Shèng Yōng dispatched troops to harass the Yān supply routes.
The Yān King again sent Commander Wǔ Shèng to submit a memorial reiterating his previous request.
The Emperor was about to agree.
Xiàorú said:
"If the troops are disbanded,
they cannot be reassembled.
I beg you not to be misled."
The Emperor then executed Shèng to sever ties with Yān.
Shortly thereafter,
the Yān army plundered Pèixiàn
and burned grain ships.
At that time, the Héběi army was exhausted and ineffective,
and the supply route from Dézhōu was also cut off,
causing Xiàorú deep concern.
Knowing that the Yān Crown Prince was kind and benevolent,
while his younger brother Gāo Xù was cunning and treacherous,
and favored by the Yān King,
and had often wanted to usurp the heir apparent,
he planned to sow discord between them by stratagem,
to cause internal strife.
He then suggested to the Emperor
to send Jǐnyīwèi Qiānhù Zhāng Ān to carry an imperial letter to Běipíng to bestow upon the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince received the letter but did not open it,
and sent Ān together with it to the Yān army front,
so the discord could not be sown.
The following May,
the Yan (Yān) army reached the north bank of the Yangtze River.
The Emperor issued an edict to conscript soldiers from all four directions.
Fāng Xiàorú (Fāng Xiàorú) said,
"The situation is urgent!
Send someone to promise a cession of territory,
to delay for several days.
The newly recruited soldiers in the southeast will gradually gather.
The northern army is not skilled in naval warfare.
If we fight a decisive battle on the river,
the outcome is yet unknown."
The Emperor sent Princess Qìngchéng (Qìngchéng) to the Yan (Yān) army
to present this argument.
The King of Yan (Yān) did not listen.
The Emperor ordered his generals to gather their fleet on the river,
but Chén Xuān (Chén Xuān) surrendered his warships to Yan (Yān).
The Yan (Yān) army then crossed the river.
This was on the Yǐmǎo (Yǐmǎo) day of the sixth month.
The Emperor was anxious and fearful.
Some advised the Emperor to flee to another place
to plan a restoration.
Fāng Xiàorú (Fāng Xiàorú) strongly urged him to hold the capital city and await reinforcements,
stating that even if the effort failed,
he should die for the state.
On the Yǐchǒu (Yǐchǒu) day,
the Jīnchuānmén (Jīnchuānmén) gate was opened,
and the Yan (Yān) army entered.
The Emperor immolated himself.
On that day,
Fāng Xiàorú (Fāng Xiàorú) was arrested and imprisoned.
Earlier,
when Chéngzǔ (Chéngzǔ) departed Běipíng (Běipíng),
Yáo Guǎngxiào (Yáo Guǎngxiào) entrusted Fāng Xiàorú (Fāng Xiàorú) to him,
saying,
"When the city falls,
he will certainly not surrender.
Please do not kill him.
If Fāng Xiàorú (Fāng Xiàorú) is killed,
the lineage of scholars in the empire will be severed."
Chéngzǔ (Chéngzǔ) nodded in agreement.
By now, he wanted Fāng Xiàorú (Fāng Xiàorú) to draft an edict.
When summoned,
his sorrowful wails resounded through the palace.
Chéngzǔ (Chéngzǔ) descended from his couch to comfort him, saying,
"Sir, do not torment yourself.
I wish to emulate Duke of Zhōu (Zhōu Gōng) in assisting King Chéng (Chéng Wáng)."
Fāng Xiàorú (Fāng Xiàorú) said,
"Where is King Chéng (Chéng Wáng)?"
Chéngzǔ (Chéngzǔ) said,
"He immolated himself and died."
Fāng Xiàorú (Fāng Xiàorú) said,
"Why not enthrone King Chéng's (Chéng Wáng's) son?"
Chéngzǔ (Chéngzǔ) said,
"The country needs a mature ruler."
Fāng Xiàorú (Fāng Xiàorú) said,
"Why not enthrone King Chéng's (Chéng Wáng's) brother?"
Chéngzǔ (Chéngzǔ) said,
"This is my family affair."
He looked to his attendants, handed him a writing brush and tablets,
and said,
"An edict to the empire
cannot be drafted by anyone but you, Sir."
Fāng Xiàorú (Fāng Xiàorú) threw the brush to the ground,
and weeping and cursing, said,
"I would rather die;
the edict cannot be drafted."
Chéngzǔ (Chéngzǔ) was enraged
and ordered him to be dismembered in the marketplace.
Fāng Xiàorú (Fāng Xiàorú) went to his death with composure,
composing a farewell poem that read:
"Heaven sends chaos and separation, who knows its cause?
Treacherous ministers achieve their plans, conspiring against the state with cunning.
Loyal ministers burst with indignation, blood and tears intermingle.
To die for my lord in this way, what more can I seek?
Alas, how sorrowful! May none blame me."
He was forty-six years old at the time.

His disciple Yōng (Yōng), grandson of Dégìng Hóu (Dégìng Hóu) Liáo Yǒngzhōng (Liáo Yǒngzhōng), and his brother Míng (Míng) collected his remains and buried them on the mountain outside the Jùbǎomén (Jùbǎomén) gate.
Fāng Xiàorú (Fāng Xiàorú) had an elder brother, Fāng Xiàowén (Fāng Xiàowén),
who was diligent in study and steadfast in conduct,
and died before Fāng Xiàorú (Fāng Xiàorú).
His younger brother, Fāng Xiàoyǒu (Fāng Xiàoyǒu), was executed along with Fāng Xiàorú (Fāng Xiàorú),
and also composed a poem before his death.
His wife, Zhèng (Zhèng), and two sons, Zhōngxiàn (Zhōngxiàn) and Zhōngyù (Zhōngyù), had already hanged themselves.
His two daughters threw themselves into the Qínhuái (Qínhuái) River and died.
Fāng Xiàorú (Fāng Xiàorú) excelled in writing,
his style was pure, profound, heroic, and unrestrained.
Each time a piece of writing was published,
it was eagerly copied and recited throughout the country.
During the Yǒnglè (Yǒnglè) reign, those who possessed Fāng Xiàorú's (Fāng Xiàorú's) writings were punished with death.
His disciple Wáng Tú (Wáng Tú) secretly transcribed them as the Hóuchéng Jí (Hóuchéng Jí),
which is why they were later able to circulate in the world.
When Rénzōng (Rénzōng) ascended the throne,
he issued an edict to the Ministry of Rites:
"The officials of the Jiànwén (Jiànwén) era
have already suffered severe execution.
Their families, whose household registers were confiscated by the government,
are all pardoned as commoners
and their land returned.
Their extended relatives who were exiled to the borders
shall have one person remain at the border post,
and the rest released."
In the third month of the thirteenth year of Wànlì (Wànlì), the descendants of those implicated by Fāng Xiàorú (Fāng Xiàorú) and exiled were released,
numbering over 1,300 people from Zhèjiāng (Zhèjiāng), Jiāngxī (Jiāngxī), Fújiàn (Fújiàn), Sìchuān (Sìchuān), and Guǎngdōng (Guǎngdōng).
However, Fāng Xiàorú (Fāng Xiàorú) himself had no descendants.
Only Kèqín's (Kèqín's) brother, Kèjiā (Kèjiā), had a son named Fāng Xiàofù (Fāng Xiàofù).
In the twenty-fifth year of Hóngwǔ (Hóngwǔ), he had submitted a memorial to the court,
requesting a reduction in the tax of Nínghǎi (Nínghǎi) imposed by Xìnguógōng (Xìnguógōng) Tāng Hé (Tāng Hé).
He was exiled to Qìngyuǎn Wèi (Qìngyuǎn Wèi)
and was exempted due to his military registration.
Fāng Xiàofù's (Fāng Xiàofù's) son, Wǎn (Wǎn),
was later also released as a commoner.
During the Shìzōng (Shìzōng) era,
Yú Bīn (Yú Bīn) from Sōngjiāng (Sōngjiāng) claimed to be a descendant of Fāng Xiàorú (Fāng Xiàorú).
At one point, literati and officials believed him
and compiled the Guīzōng Lù (Guīzōng Lù) for him.
Subsequently, the Fāng (Fāng) clan discovered his deception
and reported it to the authorities,
and the matter ceased.
At the beginning of Shénzōng's (Shénzōng's) reign,
an edict was issued to praise and record the loyal officials of the Jiànwén (Jiànwén) era,
and a shrine, Biǎozhōng Cí (Biǎozhōng Cí), was built in Nánjīng (Nánjīng).
Xú Huīzǔ (Xú Huīzǔ) was listed first,
followed by Fāng Xiàorú (Fāng Xiàorú).
Following Fāng Xiàorú's (Fāng Xiàorú's) death,
hundreds of his clan members, relatives, and friends were implicated and executed.
Among his students, some died in loyalty to him:
Lú Yuánzhì (Lú Yuánzhì), Zhèng Gōngzhì (Zhèng Gōngzhì), and Lín Jiāyóu (Lín Jiāyóu),
all from Nínghǎi (Nínghǎi).
Lú Yuánzhì (Lú Yuánzhì), courtesy name Xīlǔ (Xīlǔ),
was Fāng Xiàorú's (Fāng Xiàorú's) cousin on his mother's side.
He became an editor after passing the imperial examination,
and successively served as Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
During the Jiànwén (Jiànwén) era,
he repeatedly submitted memorials and suggestions.
When the Yan (Yān) army arrived,
he refused to submit
and was killed along with his brother Lú Yuánpǔ (Lú Yuánpǔ) and others.
Zhèng Gōngzhì (Zhèng Gōngzhì), courtesy name Shúzhēn (Shúzhēn).
Lín Jiāyóu (Lín Jiāyóu), personal name Shēng (Shēng),
was known by his courtesy name.
Both were disciples of Fāng Xiàorú (Fāng Xiàorú).
Fāng Xiàorú (Fāng Xiàorú) once said,
"Those who will help me are
these two men."
Zhèng Gōngzhì (Zhèng Gōngzhì) was recommended as a worthy and capable person
and gained fame as a Censor.
Lín Jiāyóu (Lín Jiāyóu),
in the Bǐngzǐ (Bǐngzǐ) year of Hóngwǔ (Hóngwǔ), served as a literary examiner in Sìchuān (Sìchuān) as a scholar.
In the early Jiànwén (Jiànwén) era,
he joined the Imperial Academy as an editor
and was soon promoted to Assistant Surveillance Commissioner of Shǎnxī (Shǎnxī).
He once entered the Yan (Yān) princely residence on official business
and learned of Zhū Gāoxù's (Zhū Gāoxù's) plot to overthrow the heir apparent.
Fāng Xiàorú (Fāng Xiàorú)'s knowledge of the Yan (Yān) plot
was actually revealed by Lín Jiāyóu (Lín Jiāyóu).
Hú Zǐzhāo (Hú Zǐzhāo),
courtesy name Zhòngcháng (Zhòngcháng),
originally named Zhìgāo (Zhìgāo),
was from Róngxiàn (Róngxiàn).
When Fāng Xiàorú (Fāng Xiàorú) was a professor in Hànzhōng (Hànzhōng), he went to study under him.
The King Xiàn (Xiàn Wáng) of Shǔ (Shǔ) recommended him as a county instructor.
In the early Jiànwén (Jiànwén) era,
he participated in compiling the Veritable Records of Tàizǔ (Tàizǔ),
was appointed Reviewer,
and successively promoted to Vice Minister of the Ministry of Justice.
Zhèng Jūzhēn (Zhèng Jūzhēn),
a native of Mǐn (Mǐn).
He was a close friend of Fāng Xiàorú (Fāng Xiàorú). After serving as a registrar, he became Gongchang Tongpan (Gǒngchāng Tōngpàn) and then Henan Canzheng (Hénán Cāncī),
and achieved good results wherever he served.
When Fāng Xiàorú (Fāng Xiàorú) was a professor in Hànzhōng (Hànzhōng),
Zhèng Jūzhēn (Zhèng Jūzhēn) wrote "Ode to the Young Phoenix" to encourage him.
All these individuals were executed for their association.
Fāng Xiàorú (Fāng Xiàorú) presided over the provincial examination in Yìngtiān (Yìngtiān),
and among the successful candidates were Liú Zhèng (Liú Zhèng) from Chángzhōu (Chángzhōu) and Fāng Fǎ (Fāng Fǎ) from Tóngchéng (Tóngchéng).
Liú Zhèng (Liú Zhèng),
courtesy name Zhònglǐ (Zhònglǐ).
When the Yan (Yān) army rose, he drafted a strategy to pacify Yan (Yān)
and was about to present it,
but was dissuaded by his family due to illness.
When he heard of Fāng Xiàorú's (Fāng Xiàorú's) death,
he vomited blood and died.
Fāng Fǎ (Fāng Fǎ),
courtesy name Bótōng (Bótōng),
served as a judicial officer in the Sìchuān Dūsī (Sìchuān Dūsī).
When all departments submitted memorials congratulating Chéngzǔ (Chéngzǔ) on his ascension,
he was supposed to sign,
but refused,
threw down his brush, and left.
When he was arrested and
reached Wàngjiāng (Wàngjiāng),
he bowed towards his hometown, saying,
"It is enough to glimpse my ancestors' homes."
He then drowned himself in the river.
After Chéngzǔ had killed Fāng Xiàorú,
he ordered the attendant-reader Lóu Lián to draft the imperial edict.
Lián,
a native of Jīnhuá,
had once studied under Sòng Lián.
He received the command and dared not refuse.
Returning home, he told his wife and children:
"I am certainly willing to die,
but I fear only that you all will be implicated."
That evening,
he hanged himself.
Some say that the draft edict was by Wáng Jǐng of Kuòcāng,
while others say it was by Wáng Dá of Wúxī.
Liàn Zǐníng,
whose given name was Ān,
was known by his courtesy name,
and was a native of Xīngàn.
His father, Bóshàng,
was skilled in poetry.
In the early years of Hóngwǔ,
he served as an official of the Imperial Diary.
He was demoted to an outer post for his forthright words,
and ultimately ended his career as the Assistant Prefect of Zhèn'ān.
Zǐníng was eminent and exceptional,
and in the eighteenth year, as a Presented Scholar, he presented a policy essay at the imperial examination,
forcefully arguing:
"Heaven's production of talent is limited.
How can Your Majesty endure, for trivial reasons,
to unleash endless executions?
How can this be governance?"
Tàizǔ approved of his sentiment,
and promoted him to second place in the first rank,
appointing him as a Compiler of the Hanlin Academy.
When his mother passed away,
he diligently observed ancient rites.
After the mourning period,
he resumed his office,
and was successively promoted to Vice Minister of Works.
In the early years of Jiànwén,
he and Fāng Xiàorú were equally trusted.
He was reassigned as the Left Vice Minister of Personnel,
taking it upon himself to promote or demote officials based on their virtue or lack thereof,
and he made many proposals.
Not long after,
he was appointed Censor-in-Chief.
When the Yān army rose,
Lǐ Jǐnglóng suffered repeated defeats in the northern campaign
and was recalled.
Zǐníng, from the court, counted his crimes
and requested his execution,
but this was not granted.
He angrily and passionately kowtowed and shouted loudly:
"It is this villain
who has ruined Your Majesty's affairs!
As an official upholding the law,
I cannot eliminate the traitor who sells out the court;
death for me is a surplus of guilt.
Even if Your Majesty pardons Jǐnglóng,
there will certainly be no pardon for me."
He then wept bitterly, asking for death,
and the emperor adjourned the court.
Sòng Zhēng, an Administrator in the Imperial Clan Court, and Yè Xīxián, a Censor, both remonstrated in memorials, stating that Jǐnglóng had lost battles and armies,
harbored disloyalty,
and ought to be executed.
Neither was accepted.
After the Yān army crossed the Huái River,
Xiāo Yòngdào, the Chief Administrator of Jìngjiāng Prefecture, and Zhōu Shìxiū, a Benevolent Instructor of the Héng Commandery, submitted memorials discussing grand strategies,
and pointedly criticized those in power.
The memorials were sent down to the court officials for discussion,
and those in power angrily denounced the two men.
Zǐníng said:
"The state of the nation has come to this;
can we still not tolerate those who speak out?"
The accusers were ashamed and stopped.
When the King of Yān ascended the throne,
Zǐníng was arrested and brought before him.
His words were insolent,
and he was dismembered and killed,
his family exterminated,
and his relatives banished to the frontier.
Zǐníng's nephew, Dàhēng,
who was the Magistrate of Jiādìng,
hearing of the calamity,
drowned himself and his wife in the Liújiā River.
Xú Zǐquán, a local man who was a Presented Scholar and served as a Director in the Ministry of Justice,
hearing of Zǐníng's death,
wept bitterly, composed a poem, and hanged himself.
Zǐníng was skilled in literature,
and Fāng Xiàorú praised him for his extensive learning and literary talent.
During the Hóngzhì era,
Wáng Zuǒ carved his collected writings, naming them the Jīnchuān Yùxiè Jí.
Lǐ Mèngyáng, the Vice-Commissioner of Education, established the Jīnchuān Academy to worship Zǐníng,
naming its main hall
"Hàorán."
Zhēng,
it is not known where he was from.
He once submitted a memorial requesting the removal of criminal princes from the imperial registry.
When the Yān army entered,
he refused to yield,
and he and his wife and children all died.
Xīxián,
a native of Sōngyáng.
He was also implicated as a member of the treacherous faction and killed.
Some say he became a monk,
known as Monk Xuě'ān.
Máo Dàfāng,
whose given name was Pǔ,
was known by his courtesy name,
and was a native of Tàixīng.
He was learned and skilled in poetry and prose.
During the Hóngwǔ era,
he served as an education official in Huáinán,
and when summoned for an audience, his replies pleased the emperor.
He was promoted to Chief Administrator of the Qín Prince's establishment,
and his imperial mandate spoke of Dǒng Zhòngshū.
Dàfāng was even more inspired and enthusiastic,
dedicating himself to assisting and guiding,
and inscribed his hall
"Xī Dǒng" (Emulating Dǒng),
for which Fāng Xiàorú wrote a record.
In the first year of Jiànwén, he was promoted to Vice Censor-in-Chief.
When the Yān army rose,
he sent a poem to Méi Yīn, the commander of Huáinán,
with fierce words and meaning.
Those who heard it were inspired.
Zhōu Xuán,
at the end of Hóngwǔ, made proposals as a clerk of the Tiāncè Guard,
and was promoted to Left Assistant Censor-in-Chief.
When the King of Yān proclaimed himself emperor,
he and Dàfāng were both arrested,
and died refusing to yield.
And Dàfāng's sons Shùntóng and Dàoshòu were both condemned to execution,
and his two grandsons died in prison.
Zhuó Jìng,
courtesy name Wéigōng,
was a native of Ruì'ān.
He was exceptionally intelligent,
reading ten lines at a glance.
He passed the imperial examination in the twenty-first year of Hóngwǔ.
He was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Revenue,
and was upright and fearless.
At that time, institutions were not yet fully established,
and the princes' attire and carriages resembled those of the Son of Heaven.
Jìng seized an opportunity to say:
"The capital,
is where the whole empire looks for example.
If Your Majesty does not early distinguish ranks and prestige among the princes,
and allows their attire to be on par with the Crown Prince,
the legitimate and illegitimate will be confused,
and the superior and inferior without order,
how can you command the empire?"
The emperor said:
"Your words are correct,
I had not considered this."
He valued him even more.
Another day, when he met with his colleagues,
there were exactly eighty-one of them,
and he ordered their official titles changed to Yuánshì.
Soon, considering the Six Bureaus as the source of governmental affairs,
he again changed the title to Yuánshì.
Later,
it reverted to Supervising Secretary.
He successively served as Vice Minister of Revenue.
In the early years of Jiànwén,
Jìng secretly memorialized, saying that the King of Yān was extraordinarily intelligent and insightful,
with heroic talent and great strategy,
and bore a striking resemblance to Gāodì.
Běipíng was a strategically important location,
with strong soldiers and horses,
from where the Jīn and Yuán dynasties had risen.
Now, he ought to be moved to Nánchāng;
if a rebellion were to occur,
it would also be easier to control.
"That which is about to sprout but has not yet moved,
is opportunity;
that which is feasible by assessing the times,
is circumstance.
Circumstance cannot be decided unless one is extremely resolute,
and opportunity cannot be perceived unless one is extremely clear-sighted."
The memorial was submitted,
and he was summoned for questioning the next day.
Jìng kowtowed and said:
"What I have said is the ultimate strategy for the empire;
I hope Your Majesty will consider it."
The matter was ultimately shelved.
When the King of Yān became emperor,
Jìng was apprehended,
and accused of suggesting the relocation of Yān,
and alienating the imperial family.
Jìng said sternly:
“It is a pity that the late emperor did not use my words!”
The emperor was enraged,
but still pitied his talent,
and ordered him imprisoned,
sending someone to subtly prompt him with the stories of Guǎn Zhòng and Wèi Zhēng.
Jìng wept and said:
“A minister, having pledged his service,
would rather die than be disloyal.
The late emperor never made a single error,
yet you suddenly acted wantonly and usurped the throne.
I regret not having died immediately to meet my former lord in the netherworld.
Do you still wish for me to serve you?”
The emperor still could not bear to kill him.
Yáo Guǎngxiào, who had a long-standing grudge against Jìng,
came forward and said:
“If Jìng’s words had truly been used,
Your Majesty would not have this day.”
Thereupon, he was beheaded,
and his three kindreds were executed.
Jìng stood in court with integrity and eloquence,
had a beautiful appearance,
and was skilled in discussion.
He was extensively knowledgeable in all fields, including astronomy, geography, law, calendar studies, military strategy, and criminal justice.
Chéngzǔ once sighed:
“The state has nurtured scholars for thirty years,
and only obtained one Zhuó Jìng.”
In the early years of Wànlì,
following the words of Censor Tú Shúfāng,
his tomb was marked and a shrine was built.
Among the Vice Ministers of Revenue who died at the same time
were Guō Rèn and Lú Jiǒng.
Rèn,
a native of Dāntú,
or, by another account, Dìngyuǎn.
He was honest, prudent, and capable.
In the early Jiànwén reign,
he assisted the Ministry of Revenue,
and his eating, drinking, and daily life
were all conducted within the public office.
At that time, various feudal lords were being demoted and stripped of power.
Rèn said:
“In state affairs, if one attends to the fundamental before the trivial, success is easy.
Today, we accumulate wealth and grain,
and prepare military supplies;
what is it all for?
Yet we go north to attack Zhōu,
and south to attack Xiāng,
abandoning the fundamental and focusing on the trivial.
This is not a sound strategy.
Moreover, military action values speed.
If we drag on for a long time,
our sharp morale will be exhausted,
and appeasement will follow,
leading us to wear ourselves out.”
The King of Yān heard this and disliked him.
When the war broke out,
Rèn and his colleague Lú Jiǒng were in charge of deploying troops and supplies.
When the capital fell,
he was captured,
but he did not yield
and died.
His son Jīng was also sentenced to death,
and his younger son was exiled to Guǎngxī.
Jiǒng,
a native of Xiānjū.
He was cheerful and not constrained by trivial matters.
He enjoyed drinking,
and after drinking, he would often sing loudly,
people called Jiǒng "the madman".
When he became an official,
he disciplined himself to be respectful and cautious.
In the third year of Jiànwén, he was appointed Vice Minister of Revenue.
When the Yān army entered,
he did not yield,
and was bound for execution,
singing loudly until his death.
People in Tái offered sacrifices to him in the Shrine of Eight Loyalists.
Chén Dí,
courtesy name Jǐngdào,
a native of Xuānchéng.
His grandfather, Yòu Xián,
in the early Míng dynasty,
rendered meritorious service in expeditions,
and his family inherited the position of Centurion for the Fúzhōu garrison,
thus settling there.
Dí was outstanding and had lofty aspirations.
He was appointed instructor of the prefectural school,
and drafted a congratulatory memorial for the emperor's birthday on behalf of the prefecture.
Tàizǔ found him exceptional.
After a long time,
he was recommended for his knowledge of the classics,
and successively served as Attendant Lecturer.
He was sent out as Assistant Administrator of Shāndōng,
and implemented many benevolent policies.
When his mother died,
he was recalled to office
and appointed Right Administrator of Yúnnán.
The various barbarian tribes of Pǔdìng, Qǔjìng, Wūsā, and Wūméng incited rebellion.
Dí led local troops to defeat them,
and was bestowed with gold and silk.
In the early Jiànwén reign,
he was summoned to be Minister of Rites.
At that time, systems were being revised,
and Dí contributed many proposals regarding their evolution, reduction, and augmentation.
It happened that due to floods and droughts, officials were ordered to gather for deliberation.
Dí requested the clearing of prisons,
and the recruitment of displaced people,
among more than twenty other matters,
all of which were adopted.
Soon after, he was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent.
After Lǐ Jǐnglóng and others suffered several defeats,
Dí presented a grand strategy.
He was ordered to supervise the transportation of military provisions.
Later,
hearing of the change,
he rushed to the capital.
When the King of Yān ascended the throne,
he summoned Dí for questioning,
but Dí spoke defiantly and refused to yield.
He was ordered, along with his sons Fèngshān and Dānshān, and six others, to be dismembered in the marketplace.
After his death,
people found poems and "Five Sighs" songs in his sash,
the words and meaning were mournful and fierce.
His servant, Hóu Láibǎo, collected his remains and buried them.
His wife, Guǎn, hanged herself.
His infant son Zhū, five months old,
was secretly placed in a ditch by his wet nurse and thus escaped.
At eight years old,
he was accused by an enemy.
Chéngzǔ pardoned him from death,
and he was exiled to Fúníng,
then later moved to Dēngzhōu,
becoming a native of Pénglái.
In the early Hóngxī reign,
he was pardoned and returned to his hometown,
and given land and property.
During the Chénghuà era,
Tú Guān, the Prefect of Níngguó, built a shrine to sacrifice to Dí.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
his descendant Dǐng Jǔ passed the imperial examination,
and rose to serve as Prefect of Yìngtiān,
known for his integrity and uprightness.
Huáng Kuí,
his origin is unknown.
He served as Vice Minister of Rites,
possessed learning and good conduct,
and was skilled in ceremonies.
Dí and Vice Minister Huáng Guān both respected and admired him.
When the Yān army entered,
he did not yield and died.
There was also Jù Jìng,
a native of Píngliáng.
He served as a Censor,
then was transferred to Ministry of Revenue Principal,
and served as a historiographer,
known for his integrity and caution.
He died unyieldingly along with Dí,
and his clan was exterminated.
Jǐng Qīng,
originally surnamed Gěng,
mistakenly called Jǐng,
a native of Zhēnníng.
He was unconstrained and highly principled,
reading a book once and never forgetting it.
He passed the imperial examination during the Hóngwǔ reign,
was appointed Compiler,
and then Censor.
In the spring of the thirtieth year, he was summoned for an audience,
and appointed acting Left Vice Censor-in-Chief.
Due to an error in a character in a memorial,
he secretly changed the seal,
for which he was impeached by a Supervising Secretary
and imprisoned.
He was soon pardoned.
He was ordered to inspect private tea sales in Chuān and Shǎn,
and then appointed Prefect of Jīnhuá.
In the early Jiànwén reign,
he served as a Council Member for Běipíng.
The King of Yān conversed with him,
and his discourse was clear and precise,
earning great praise.
He was twice promoted to Censor-in-Chief.
When the Yān army entered,
a great number of ministers died.
Qīng Sù had secretly plotted beforehand,
and even agreed with Fāng Xiàorú and others to die for the country together.
When the time came, he alone went to the palace gate and surrendered himself.
Chéngzǔ ordered that his official position be retained,
and he served in the court for a long time, outwardly compliant.
One day during morning court,
Qīng donned a crimson robe and entered with a concealed blade.
Previously,
diviners had reported an unusual red star encroaching upon the emperor's seat,
a very urgent matter.
Chéngzǔ was already suspicious of Qīng.
When court convened,
Qīng was the only one wearing crimson.
An order was given to search him,
and the hidden blade was found.
When interrogated and rebuked,
Qīng rose defiantly and said:
"I merely wish to avenge my former lord!"
Chéngzǔ was enraged,
and had him executed by dismemberment,
and his clan exterminated.
His hometown was registered,
and through successive denunciations,
this was called the "melon vine implication,"
leaving villages desolate.
Initially,
when the Jīnchuān Gate was opened,
Censor Lián Yíng struck at Chéngzǔ's horse, attempting to assassinate him,
but was killed.
His body remained standing upright.
Yíng was
from Xiāngyuán.
Hú Rùn,
courtesy name Sōngyǒu,
was from Póyáng.
When Tàizǔ campaigned against Chén Yǒuliàng,
he passed the temple of Wú Ruì, the King of Chángshā,
saw a poem inscribed on the wall,
and admired it.
He immediately summoned Rùn to his tent.
In the fourth year of Hóngwǔ,
he was recommended as a talented scholar by the prefecture
and was granted an audience.
The Emperor said:
"Is this the scholar who inscribed that poem on the wall of the Póyáng temple?"
He was appointed Director in the Chief Military Commission,
and later promoted to Administrator.
At the beginning of Jiànwén's reign,
he was selected as Right Supervising Secretary,
and soon advanced to Junior Minister of the Grand Court of Revision.
When the Yān army rose,
he and Qí Tái, Huáng Zǐchéng, and others discussed military strategies day and night.
When the capital fell,
Rùn was summoned,
but he refused to yield,
and died with his son Chuándào.
His youngest son Chuánqìng was exiled to the frontier.
His four-year-old daughter, Jùnnú, was taken into a meritorious minister's household.
As she grew older and understood the great principle,
she daily smeared her face with stove ash.
At the beginning of Hóngxī's reign,
she was pardoned and returned home.
Being extremely poor,
she vowed never to marry.
Those who saw her vied to give her money and grain,
saying:
"This is the daughter of a loyal minister!"
Gāo Xiáng
was from Cháoyì.
During the Hóngwǔ era,
he became an Investigating Censor through his mastery of the classics.
During Jiànwén's reign,
he exerted himself in military affairs.
Chéngzǔ heard of his reputation
and summoned him along with Rùn,
intending to employ him.
Xiáng entered the audience wearing mourning clothes,
and spoke disrespectfully.
His clan was exterminated.
His ancestral tombs were exhumed,
and all his relatives and associates were exiled to the frontier.
All who had been granted property belonging to the Gāo family were subjected to increased taxes,
with the explanation:
"Let them curse Xiáng for generations."
Wáng Dù,
courtesy name Zǐzhōng,
was from Guīshàn.
In his youth, he diligently studied,
excelling in literary composition.
Through his mastery of the classics, he was recommended as an Investigating Censor for the Shāndōng circuit.
During Jiànwén's reign,
when the Yān army rose,
Dù wholeheartedly assisted in strategy.
When the royal army suffered repeated defeats,
Dù memorialized to request the recruitment of soldiers.
After the victory at Xiǎohé,
he was ordered to comfort the troops in Xúzhōu.
Upon his return,
Fāng Xiàorú wrote to Dù,
swearing to die for the country.
When the Prince of Yān proclaimed himself emperor,
he was implicated as a member of Fāng's faction and banished to Hèxiàn as a garrison soldier.
He was again implicated for disrespectful speech
and his clan was exterminated.
Dù possessed wisdom and stratagem.
When Shèng Yōng replaced Jǐng Lóng,
Dù secretly presented advantageous plans,
which led to the victory at Dōngchāng.
When Jǐng Lóng was recalled to the capital,
he was pardoned from execution
and even regained influence.
He was jealous of Yōng and others' achievements
and slandered them, creating discord,
whereupon Dù also became estranged.
Commentators lamented that his talents were not fully utilized,
which was a pity.
Dài Déyí
was from Fènghuà.
He earned his *jìnshì* degree in the twenty-seventh year of Hóngwǔ.
He successively held the position of Palace Reader.
Tàizǔ instructed him, saying:
"Although the Hanlin Academy's duty is literature,
since you are among those close to the Forbidden City,
you should speak without reservation about the gains and losses of state governance
and the advantages and disadvantages for the people's livelihood.
In the past, Táng dynasty's Lù Zhì, Cuī Qún, and Lǐ Jiàng, while in the Hanlin Academy,
were all able to speak frankly and offer sound advice,
benefiting their times.
You should take these ancients as your standard."
Later,
he was reassigned as an Investigating Censor.
During Jiànwén's reign,
he was reassigned as Left Remonstrance Official.
When the Prince of Yān entered,
he was summoned for an audience,
but refused to yield
and died.
At the time of Déyí's death,
his brothers were also in the capital.
His sister-in-law, Xiàng, was at home.
Upon hearing of the disaster,
she realized that the calamity would extend to the clan.
She ordered everyone in the household to flee,
hid Déyí's two sons in the mountains,
destroyed the Dài clan genealogy,
and remained alone at home.
When the captors arrived,
they found nothing.
Xiàng was shackled and taken to the capital,
where she was beaten and tortured but never uttered a single word,
thus preserving the Dài clan.
At that time, among the censors who refused to yield and died
were Xiè Shēng from Zhūchéng and Dīng Zhìfāng from Liáochéng.
Gān Lín from Huáiníng went to his execution with composure,
and his descendants warned each other never to serve as officials again.
Also, Dǒng Yōng,
whose origins are unknown.
Those censors with aspirations and integrity
would often gather at Yōng's place,
swearing to die for the country.
When generals and officers hesitated and did not fight vigorously,
Yōng would openly submit memorials impeaching them.
When the city fell, he was killed,
and his family was exiled to the farthest frontier.
Among the Supervising Secretaries who died,
there were Chén Jìzhī, Hán Yǒng, and Yè Fú, three individuals.
Jìzhī
was from Pútián,
and earned his *jìnshì* degree in the second year of Jiànwén.
At that time, monks and Daoists in Jiāngnán owned many fertile fields.
Jìzhī proposed limiting each person to five *mǔ*,
and distributing the rest to the common people.
This was followed.
As military affairs grew urgent,
he frequently submitted memorials on strategic matters.
When the Yān army entered,
he refused to yield
and was killed.
His parents and brothers were all exiled to the frontier.
Yǒng
was from Xī'ān,
or some say Fúshān.
He was large and imposing in appearance,
and his voice was loud and clear.
He often spoke passionately about military affairs.
When the Prince of Yān entered,
he wanted to appoint him to office,
but Yǒng defiantly refused and died.
Fú
was from Hòuguān,
and was Jìzhī's classmate from the same year.
When the Yān army arrived,
he defended the Jīnchuān Gate.
When the city fell,
he died.
A eulogy states: The achievements of emperors and kings
are truly bestowed by Heaven.
Yǒng-lè Dà-dì’s (Chéng-zǔ’s) acquisition of the empire
was not something human power could resist.
The likes of Qí Bēng (Qí), Huáng Zǐ-chéng (Huáng), Fāng Xiào-rú (Fāng), and Liàn Zǐ-níng (Liàn),
though holding loyal intentions to govern the country,
lacked strategies to achieve victory.
However, their fierce loyalty and indignation
made them regard execution by knife, saw, cauldron, or boiling as sweet as honey.
Hundreds of generations later,
their awe-inspiring spirit still lives on.
How could this be compared to those who carelessly neglected state affairs and offered their lives merely as an apology?
From this perspective,
it truly cannot be judged by the common standard of success or failure.

Biographies Chapter 30 Tiě Xuàn, Bào Zhāo (Hóu Tài), Chén Xìng-shàn (Chén Zhí, Wáng Bīn, Chóng Gāng), Zhāng Bǐng (Xiè Guì, Péng Èr, Gě Chéng, Yú Fēng-chén), Sòng Zhōng (Yú Tián), Mǎ Xuān (Zēng Jùn, Bǔ Wàn, Zhū Jiàn, Shí Zhuàn), Qú Néng (Zhuāng Dé, Chǔ Zhì, Zào-qí Zhāng, Wáng Zhǐ-huī, Yáng Běn), Zhāng Lún (Chén Zhì), Yán Bó-wěi (Táng Zǐ-qīng, Huáng Qiān, Xiàng Pǔ, Zhèng Shù, Zhèng Huá), Wáng Shěng, Yáo Shàn (Qián Qín), Chén Yàn-huí (Zhāng Yàn-fāng).
Tiě Xuàn
was a man from Dèng.
During the Hóng-wǔ reign,
he was appointed Investigative Censor of the Ministry of Rites from a National University student,
then transferred to Judicial Officer of the Chief Military Commission.
He once judged a difficult case
and immediately cleared it.
Tài-zǔ was pleased
and gave him the courtesy name Dǐng-shí.
At the beginning of the Jiàn-wén reign,
he served as Administration Vice-Commissioner of Shān-dōng.
When Lǐ Jǐng-lóng marched north,
Xuàn supervised the provisions without shortage.
When Jǐng-lóng's army was defeated at Bái-gōu-hé,
he fled on a single horse to Dé-zhōu;
all garrisons in the city collapsed at the mere sight of the enemy.
Xuàn and Staff Officer Gāo Wēi were deeply moved and wept,
then rushed from Lín-yì to Jǐ-nán,
swearing with Shèng Yōng and Staff Officer Sòng and others to defend to the death.
When the Yān army attacked Dé-zhōu,
Jǐng-lóng fled to seek refuge with Xuàn.
When Dé-zhōu fell,
the Yān army seized over a million in its stores,
its power grew,
and then attacked Jǐ-nán.
Jǐng-lóng was again soundly defeated
and fled south.
Xuàn and Yōng and others defended the city.
The Yān army dammed water to flood the city,
built a long siege line,
and attacked day and night.
Xuàn used a stratagem to burn their siege equipment
and occasionally sent out troops for fierce counterattacks.
He also sent a thousand men out of the city to feign surrender.
The Prince of Yān was overjoyed,
and the army cheered loudly.
Xuàn hid brave warriors on the city walls,
waiting for the Prince to enter,
to drop iron plates to strike him,
and set up another ambush to cut off the bridge.
However, the timing was off,
the Prince had not yet entered the city,
the plates suddenly dropped,
and the Prince, startled, fled.
The ambush was sprung,
but the bridge could not be cut off in time,
and the Prince spurred his horse and galloped away.
Filled with rage,
he tried every means to attack.
For three full months,
they firmly held out and could not be taken.
At this time,
Píng Ān commanded twenty thousand troops
and was about to retake Dé-zhōu
to cut off Yān's supply route.
The Prince of Yān was afraid
and lifted the siege, returning north.
Since the Prince of Yān raised his army,
he attacked Zhēn-dìng for two days without success
and then abandoned it.
Only by taking Jǐ-nán to cut off the north-south route
did he plan to establish a defensive line;
Nán-jīng would then not be difficult to capture.
Therefore, riding on the momentum of his great victory over Jǐng-lóng,
he attacked with all his might,
expecting to surely capture it,
but was ultimately frustrated by Xuàn and others.
The Emperor heard of this and was greatly pleased,
sending officials to console and commend him,
bestowing gold and silk,
and ennobling his three generations.
Xuàn entered to express gratitude
and was given a banquet.
All his proposals were adopted.
He was promoted to Provincial Administration Commissioner of Shān-dōng,
and soon advanced to Minister of War.
Shèng Yōng was appointed General to Pacify Yān to replace Jǐng-lóng,
and Xuàn was ordered to participate in his military affairs.
In the winter of this year,
Yōng severely defeated the Prince of Yān at Dōng-chāng,
executing his great general Zhāng Yù.
The Prince of Yān fled back to Běi-píng.
Since the Yān army rebelled,
the north and south daily engaged in warfare,
but the imperial army's victory
had never been as great as at Dōng-chāng.
From then on, the Yān army, when marching south, went via Xú and Pèi,
daring not to pass through Shān-dōng.
As the Yān army gradually pressed closer,
the Emperor ordered Yáng Wén, the Regional Commander of Liáo-dōng, to lead his ten thousand troops to join Xuàn
and cut off Yān's rear.
Wén's army reached Zhí-gū,
was defeated by Yān generals Sòng Guì and others,
and not a single man reached Jǐ-nán.
In the fourth year, fourth month,
the Yān army pursued the imperial army at Xiǎo-hé.
Xuàn and the generals occasionally made gains.
After continuous battles, they reached Líng-bì,
where Píng Ān's and other armies were routed and captured.
Soon after, Yōng also suffered a defeat.
When the Yān army crossed the river,
Xuàn was stationed on the Huái River,
and his army also collapsed.
When the Prince of Yān ascended the imperial throne,
Xuàn was brought to him,
and he sat with his back to the court, cursing insolently.
Ordered to turn his head once,
he never did.
He was then dismembered in the marketplace
at the age of thirty-seven.
His son, Fú-ān,
was exiled to Hé-chí.
His father, Zhòng-míng,
aged eighty-three,
and his mother, Xuē,
were both relocated to Hǎi-nán.
The name of Staff Officer Sòng
is lost.
When the Yān army attacked Jǐ-nán unsuccessfully,
they left and went south.
Staff Officer Sòng advised Xuàn to directly attack Běi-píng.
Xuàn, due to his exhausted troops,
did not carry it out.
His ultimate fate is unknown.
Bào Zhāo
was a man from Lù-zhōu.
During the Hóng-wǔ reign,
he was appointed Secretary of the Grand Court of Judicial Review from a National University student.
In the thirtieth year, he was promoted to Vice-Minister of Justice, Right.
The following year, he advanced to Minister.
He was upright and had strict moral integrity,
known for his purity and frugality, wearing coarse clothes and hemp shoes.
He was known for his probity and frugality.
At the beginning of the Jiàn-wén reign,
he served as Imperial Commissioner for Investigations in Běi-píng,
discovered the Prince of Yān's unlawful activities,
secretly reported them,
and requested advance preparations be made.
When the Yān army rose,
a Pacification Office of Yān for Administration was established in Zhēn-dìng.
Zhāo, as Minister, presided over its affairs,
and with Tiě Xuàn and others, meticulously planned.
After Píng Ān's armies were defeated,
he was recalled.
When the Jīn-chuān Gate fell,
he fled,
was captured.
He did not yield
and was dismembered to death.
The successor to Zhāo as Minister of Justice was Hóu Tài,
courtesy name Shùn-huái,
a man from Nán-hé.
He rose to prominence through recommendations.
At the beginning of the Jiàn-wén reign,
he served as Minister.
When the Prince of Yān raised his army,
he strongly advocated for a strategy of resistance.
He once supervised provisions at Jì-níng and Huái-ān.
When the capital could not be held,
he was traveling to Gāo-yóu
when he was captured and imprisoned,
and with his younger brother Jìng-zǔ
and son (name missing),

Chén Xìngshàn,
courtesy name Fùchū,
was known by his courtesy name,
and was a native of Shānyīn.
He became a *jìnshì* in the 30th year of Hóngwǔ.
During the imperial announcement of examination results, as he passed before the Emperor,

saying:
"He is a *jūnzǐ* (gentleman)."
He was appointed Assistant Vice-Commissioner of the Bureau of Diplomatic Messengers (*Xíngrén Sī Fù*),
and later promoted to Hanlin Compiler (*Hànlín Jiǎntǎo*).
Chén Xìngshàn was skilled in calligraphy.
He was once summoned to the inner court
to transcribe the posthumous writings of his father, Liú Jī, the Earl of Chéngyì, which his son Liú Lián had presented.
The Emperor was awe-inspiring;
many who saw him were terrified,
to the point of being so flustered and sweaty that they could not write a single character.
Chén Xìngshàn's movements were calm and collected,
and his handwriting was elegant and well-formed.
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
bestowed wine and food upon him,
and kept him for the entire day before he departed.
While the Huìdì Emperor was still the crown prince,
he had already known Chén Xìngshàn's reputation.
Upon his enthronement,
he promoted him to Vice Minister of Rites (*Lǐbù Shìláng*),
and recommended the reinstatement of several exiled individuals, such as Xuē Zhèngyán.
Hán Yíké, the Provincial Administration Commissioner of Yúnnán, was also on the list of exiled officials;
through Chén Xìngshàn's recommendation,
he was reinstated as Vice Censor-in-Chief (*Fù Dū Yùshǐ*).
One day,
after the Emperor left court,
he detained Chén Xìngshàn alone, offering him a seat.
He asked about the essential principles for governing the empire,
which Chén Xìngshàn then submitted in writing.
Chén Xìngshàn laid out all his proposals,
and the Emperor adopted them entirely.
Later,
these policies were obstructed by the relevant authorities.
Chén Xìngshàn advanced and said:
"Your Majesty, not deeming your humble servant unworthy,
condescended to consult me.
Since I have presumptuously sullied your sacred ears,
and you promised that my proposals would be implemented,
to change or discontinue them so soon
would be like reversing a sworn oath.
How then can you gain the trust of the empire?"
The Emperor was moved.
When the Yān forces rose,
he was reappointed Vice Censor-in-Chief
and overseen the various armies.
After the defeat at Língbì,
he, along with Péng Yǔmíng, Grand Judge of the Court of Judicial Review (*Dàlǐ Chéng*), and Liú Bówán, Assistant Commissioner of the Directorate of Astronomy (*Qīntiān Jiān Fù*), were all captured.
Afterward,
they were all released.
Chén Xìngshàn said:
"To disgrace one's commission
is a crime.
How can I face my sovereign?"
He donned his court robes, leaped on his horse, and plunged into the river, dying by suicide.
Huáng Chí and Chén Zǐfāng from Yúyáo,
who were friends with Chén Xìngshàn,
also died with him.
When the Prince of Yān entered the capital,
he issued an edict to posthumously punish Chén Xìngshàn
and exile his family to the frontier.
Péng Yǔmíng,
a native of Wàn'ān,
entered the Imperial Academy as a *gòngshì*,
and successively served as Supervising Secretary (*Gěishì Zhōng*).
In the early years of Jiànwén,
he became Right Grand Judge (*Dàlǐ Yòuchéng*),
known for his integrity, diligence, and perceptiveness.
He was captured while supervising the army.
Upon his release,
he felt shame and indignation,
tore his official robes and hat,
changed his name,
and fled with Liú Bówán,
their whereabouts unknown.
At that time, among those who served as *Shìláng* supervising the army,
was Chén Zhí from Lújiāng.
Chén Zhí,
at the end of Yuán dynasty, passed the provincial examination (*xiāngshì*),
but did not enter officialdom.
During the Hóngwǔ era,
he served as Secretary in the Ministry of Personnel (*Lìbù Zhǔshì*).
In the second year of Jiànwén, he became Right Vice Minister of War (*Bīngbù Yòushìláng*).
When the Yān forces approached the Yangtze River,
Chén Zhí supervised the battle from the riverside,
displaying great courage and determination.
When some of his generals proposed surrendering,
Chén Zhí sternly rebuked them with the principle of righteousness.
The generals then killed him to surrender,
and even sought rewards.
The Prince of Yān was enraged,
immediately executed the generals,
and provided a coffin and buried Chén Zhí on Báishí Mountain.
When the Yān forces reached the north bank of the Yangtze,
Censor Wáng Bīn, who was on an inspection tour of the Jiānghuái region,

He, along with Garrison Commander Chóng Gāng, defended the city resolutely.
At that time, Shèng Yōng's army had already been defeated,
and the people had lost their will to resist.
The defending general Wáng Lǐ plotted to surrender the city.
Wáng Bīn arrested him and his accomplices,
imprisoning them.
Chóng Gāng led training exercises,
while Wáng Bīn repaired defensive structures,
working tirelessly day and night.
There was a strongman who could lift a thousand *jīn*,
whom Wáng Bīn always kept by his side.
The Yān forces sent a letter into the city,
saying, "Whoever binds Censor Wáng

Those around him feared the strongman
and dared not act.
Wáng Lǐ's younger brother, Chóng Lù, bribed the strongman's mother,
enticing her son to leave.
Taking advantage of Wáng Bīn taking off his armor to bathe,
they suddenly bound him.
They released Wáng Lǐ from prison
and opened the gates to admit the Yān forces.
Wáng Bīn and Chóng Gāng both died unyielding.
Wáng Bīn,

was a native of Dōngpíng,
and a *jìnshì* during the Hóngwǔ era.
As for Chóng Gāng,

There was also Fán Shìxìn, Secretary in the Ministry of War (*Bīngbù Zhǔshì*),
a native of Yìngchéng.
He defended Huái,
fiercely resisting the Yān forces.
Overwhelmed,
he died.
Zhāng Bǐng,
a native of Zézhōu,
during the Hóngwǔ era,
rose through various official positions due to his talent, eventually becoming Right Vice Minister of Works (*Gōngbù Yòushìláng*).
Xiè Guì,

In the early years of Jiànwén,
the court officials discussed curtailing the power of Yān

Thus, Zhāng Bǐng was appointed Provincial Administration Commissioner of Běipíng,

At that time, the Prince of Yān had feigned illness and remained secluded for a long time.

Lǐ Yǒuzhí, Zhāng Bǐng's storeroom clerk, knew of their plan in advance

On the sixth day of the seventh month of the first year of Jiànwén,

The Prince feigned binding the officials and guards, placing them in the courtyard,

He deceived Zhāng Bǐng and Xiè Guì into entering.

The Yān generals Zhāng Yù, Zhū Néng, and others led brave soldiers to attack the nine gates,

Regional Military Commissioner Péng È leaped on his horse and shouted in the market:

He gathered over a thousand soldiers

Just then, Yān's elite warriors emerged from the residence,

His soldiers then dispersed,

Initially,
after Zhāng Bǐng was killed,
his body was recovered.
After the "Jìngnàn"
campaign,
Zhāng Bǐng's corpse was exhumed and burned,
and his family and close relatives all died.
Gě Chéng,
his origins are unknown.
At the end of Hóngwǔ's reign,
he served as the Chief Scribe of the Yān Fǔ.
He once received a royal command to report affairs to the capital.
The emperor summoned him for an audience
and inquired about matters in the prince's residence.
Chéng reported everything truthfully.
Upon his return,
the Prince of Yān feigned illness.
In the height of summer, he sat by a brazier,
complaining of being extremely cold.
Bǐng and Guì, among others, came in to inquire about his illness.
Chéng stated that the prince was not actually ill

He also secretly submitted a memorial to the emperor.
When Bǐng and Guì were about to plot against the prince,
Chéng allied with Lú Zhèn, the Commander of the Guards, to act as an inside accomplice.
When the plot failed,
Chéng and Zhèn were both killed,
and their clans were exterminated.
Another person was Yú Féngchén, the accompanying tutor,
whose courtesy name was Yànzhāng,
a native of Xuānchéng.
He was known for his learning and conduct.
The Prince of Yān trusted him,
and thus he learned of the prince's rebellious plans.
He took the opportunity to strongly remonstrate.
Knowing that the rebellion was imminent,
he wrote a letter to his son,
vowing to die for his cause.
When the troops rose,
he again tearfully remonstrated,
saying that one could not betray both one's sovereign and one's father.
He died for it.
There was a man from Běipíng named Dù Qí,
a talented and outstanding scholar.
When the Prince of Yān raised troops,
he was summoned to the prince's residence.
Qí then strongly remonstrated that one should uphold the loyalty of a minister.
The prince was enraged
and immediately executed him.
Sòng Zhōng,
his origin is unknown.
At the end of Hóngwǔ's reign,
he served as Commander of the Jǐnyī Wèi.
A centurion was sentenced to death for an unjust crime.
Zhōng submitted a memorial to intercede.
A censor impeached him,
but Tàizǔ said:
"Zhōng is straightforward and hides nothing.
He interceded for someone;
what crime has he committed?"
Thus, the centurion was pardoned.
Soon after, he was impeached by Liú Guān, the Vice Censor-in-Chief,
and was transferred to be Commander of the Fèngyáng Central Guard.
In the 30th year,
General Píngqiāng Qí Ràng failed in his campaign against the southwestern barbarians.
Zhōng was appointed as a參將 (cānjiàng, assistant general)
to accompany General Yáng Wén in attacking them.
After the army returned,
he was reinstated as an official in the Jǐnyī.
In the first year of Jiànwén, as a Dūdū (military governor), he was commanded to command 30,000 border troops stationed at Kāipíng,
selectively recruiting robust guards from the Yān Fǔ to accompany him.
Also, Dūdū Xú Kǎi was stationed at Línqīng,
and Gěng Huán at Shānhǎi Guān,
to support each other.
Běipíng originally had the Yǒngqīng Left and Right Guards.
Zhōng transferred the Left Guard to Zhāngdé and the Right Guard to Shùndé to prepare against Yān.
When Zhāng Bǐng and Xiè Guì plotted to seize the Prince of Yān,
Zhōng also led troops toward Běipíng.
Before he arrived, the Yān troops rebelled,
Jūyōng Pass fell,
and he could not advance.
He retreated to secure Huáilái.
The Prince of Yān calculated that Zhōng would certainly contest Jūyōng,
so he led 8,000 elite soldiers,
armored and marching at double speed, toward Huáilái.
At that time, among the Běipíng officers and soldiers under Zhōng's command,
Zhōng informed them that their families had all been slaughtered by Yān,
urging them to fight bravely to avenge them and repay the national grace.
The Prince of Yān, having detected this,
immediately ordered his family members to display old banners as the vanguard,
calling out to their fathers, brothers, sons, and younger brothers, greeting them.
The officers and soldiers were all delighted, saying:
