"Our families are indeed unharmed;
General Sòng has deceived us."
Thus, they lost their will to fight.
Zhōng hastily deployed his formation,
which was not yet complete.
The Prince of Yān waved his banner, crossed the river,
and advanced with battle cries.
Zhōng was defeated
and died.
When Zhōng defended Huáilái,
Dū Zhǐhuī Yú Tián, Péng Jù, and Sūn Tài were with him.
During the battle,
Tián was captured,
but refused to surrender and died.
Tài was struck by a stray arrow,
blood soaked his armor,
he bandaged his wound and fought fiercely,
perishing on the battlefield along with Jù.
At that time,
over a hundred officers and soldiers captured by Yān
all refused to surrender and died,
but unfortunately, many of their names were not passed down.
Mǎ Xuān,
his origin is also unknown.
He held the office of Dū Zhǐhuī Shǐ.
When Sòng Zhōng marched toward Jūyōng,
Xuān also led troops from Jìzhōu to Běipíng.
Hearing of the change, he fled back.
After the Prince of Yān conquered Huáilái,
he turned his army around, intending to go south.
Zhāng Yù advanced and said:
"Jìzhōu borders Dàníng,
which has many cavalrymen.
If we do not take it, it may become a future problem."
Coincidentally, Xuān dispatched troops to attack Běipíng,
fought the Yān army at Gōnglè Yì (Gongle Post Station),
was defeated and returned,
defending the city with Zhènfǔ Zēng Jùn.
Yù and others went to attack it.
Xuān came out to fight, was captured,
and cursed incessantly.
He and Jù both died.
When the Yān army attacked Dàníng,
the defending general Dū Zhǐhuī Bǔ Wàn, along with Dūdū Liú Zhēn and Chén Hēng, led troops to guard Sōngtíng Guān.
Hēng wanted to surrender to Yān,
but feared Wàn and dared not act.
Yān employed a counter-espionage tactic,
sending a letter to Wàn,
praising Wàn highly
and severely denigrating Hēng.
They generously rewarded the captured Dàníng soldiers,
sealing the letter inside their clothing,
instructing them to secretly deliver it to Wàn.
They deliberately allowed other captured soldiers to see this,
also releasing them but without reward.
Those who received no reward exposed the matter.
Zhēn and Hēng searched the soldiers' clothing,
found the letter,
and then seized Wàn, imprisoned him, and he died.
His family property was confiscated.
Wàn was loyal and brave, but died by stratagem;
commentators regret this.
When Dàníng fell,
Commander Zhū Jiàn fought bravely and died rather than surrender.
Shí Zhuàn, the Left Chief Scribe of the Níng Fǔ,
was a native of Píngdìng.
He was known for his learning and conduct.
When the Prince of Yān raised troops,
Zhuàn immediately devised defensive plans,
often admonishing the Prince of Níng with the loyalty of a minister,
and the prince also respected him in his heart.
When the city fell,
he cursed indignantly and refused to submit,
and was dismembered and died.
Qú Néng,
a native of Héféi.
His father, Tōng,
during the Hóngwǔ era,
was promoted through various offices to Dūdū Qiānshì.
Néng inherited the official position,
and as the Sìchuān Dū Zhǐhuī Shǐ, he accompanied Lán Yù across the Dàdù River to attack the Xīfān,
achieving merit.
He also, as a Fù Zǒngbīng (deputy commander-in-chief), attacked the rebellious chieftain Yuèlǔ Tièmù'er of Jiànchāng,
defeating him at Shuāngláng Zhài.
The Yān forces rose,
and he followed Lǐ Jǐnglóng on the northern expedition.
They attacked Běipíng.
He and his son led over a thousand elite cavalry to attack Zhāngyìmén,
almost capturing it.
Jǐnglóng, jealous of this,
ordered them to await the main army before advancing together.
At this, the Yān people drew water at night to pour on the city walls.
It was bitterly cold,
so the ice solidified and made scaling impossible.
Jǐnglóng consequently suffered a great defeat.
Afterwards,
he again followed Jǐnglóng and advanced to garrison Báigōu Hé,
where they fought the Yān forces.
Níng Fùzǐ fought bravely,
sweeping away all in their path.
At dusk,
each side withdrew its troops.
The next day they fought again,
and the Yān Wáng was almost caught.
The Wáng urgently feigned summoning the rear guard to confuse them,
allowing him to escape.
Towards evening,
Níng again led his troops to engage in fierce battle,
shouting "Exterminate Yān!"
and beheading several hundred.
Generals Yú Tōngyuān and Téng Jù then led their troops to join.
Just then, a whirlwind rose,
and the Wáng suddenly charged in to attack.
Níng Fùzǐ died in the battle,
Tōngyuān and Jù both died,
and over ten thousand elite soldiers were all lost.
The Southern army was disheartened thereafter.
Among those who died fighting the Northern army at this time
were Commander Zhūang Dé, Chǔ Zhì, and Zàoqí Zhāng.
Dé
was formerly subordinate to Sòng Zhōng.
In the defeat at Huáilái,
his unit alone remained intact.
Later, he fought under Shèng Yōng at Jiā Hé,
where he beheaded the Yān general Tán Yuān.
Subsequently, the Yān Wáng, with elite cavalry, launched a surprise attack at dusk,
and Dé died fighting fiercely.
Zhì
had previously served under Féng Shèng and Lán Yù on expeditions beyond the Great Wall and had meritorious service.
At the beginning of Jiànwén's reign,
he defended Běipíng,
but was soon recalled.
When the Yān were being suppressed,
he led troops under Jǐnglóng,
fighting bravely in every battle.
The Northerners trembled at the sight of his banner.
By this point,
his horse became trapped, he was captured, and died.
Zàoqí Zhāng's
given name is unknown;
some say Zhāng Níng could lift a thousand catties.
In every battle, he would wave a black banner and lead the vanguard,
so the army called
him "Zàoqí Zhāng".
When he died, he was still holding the banner, unfallen.
There was also Commander Wáng,
a native of Línhuái.
He always rode a small horse,
so the army called
him "Xiǎomǎ Wáng".
He was severely wounded at the battle of Báigōu Hé.
Taking off his helmet, he gave it to his servant, saying:
"I sacrifice myself for the country;
take this back to my family."
He stood his horse, planted his spear, and died.
These two deaths were especially extraordinary.
Also, Yáng Běn from Zhōngmóu,
originally a grand student,
was skilled in divination by birds,
and was recruited and appointed Jǐnyī Zhènfǔ.
He rendered meritorious service by following Jǐnglóng to suppress Yān.
Jǐnglóng, jealous of him,
did not report it.
He was soon impeached for losing troops and disgracing the nation,
so he ventured out alone with a single army,
was captured,
imprisoned in Běipíng,
and later killed.
Zhāng Lún,
whose origin is unknown,
was a commander of various garrisons in Hébĕi.
He was brave, fierce, and spirited,
and enjoyed reading about ancient loyal and righteous deeds.
Mǎ Xuān raised an army from Jìzhōu to attack Běipíng,
but failed
and died.
Lún, enraged,
gathered officials from two garrisons,
led his subordinates to flee south,
and formed an alliance to serve the nation.
He served under Lǐ Jǐnglóng and Shèng Yōng in battles,
all with merit.
When the Yān Wáng ascended the throne,
he summoned Lún to surrender.
Lún laughed and said:
"Will Zhāng Lún sell himself for Dīng Gōng?"
He then died.
When the capital fell,
all military officials surrendered.
Lún was the only one
who calmly died for righteousness.
There was also Chén Zhì,
who defended Dàtóng as a participant general
and was promoted to Dū Dūdūngzhī of the Central Army.
He assisted Sòng Zhōng in protecting Huáilái.
After Zhōng's defeat,
he retreated to defend Dàtóng.
The Dài Wáng wanted to raise an army to respond to Yān,
but Zhì restrained him from doing so.
When the Yān army attacked Dàtóng but could not take it,
Wèizhōu and Guǎngchāng defected to Yān.
Zhì then recaptured them.
When Chéngzǔ ascended
the throne, he had Zhì executed
for coercing the Dài Wáng
and plundering those who had already defected.
Yán Bówěi,
whose given name was Guī,
used his courtesy name,
and was from Lúlíng.
He was a descendant of Táng's Lǔguó Gōng Zhēnqīng.
In the first year of Jiànwén's reign, he was summoned as a worthy scholar
and appointed Magistrate of Pèixiàn.
Lǐ Jǐnglóng was garrisoned at Dézhōu,
and the people of Pèi spent the entire year transporting supplies.
Bówěi was good at planning,
so they were not distressed.
At the time, a Military-Civilian Commandery was established for Fēng and Pèi,
so he gathered five thousand militia
and built seven forts as a defense strategy.
Soon, his troops were transferred to reinforce Shāndōng,
leaving behind only the weary and weak, unfit for battle.
When the Yān army attacked Pèi,
Bówěi sent County Assistant Hú Xiān to secretly go to Xúzhōu to report the emergency.
No reinforcements arrived,
so he ordered his younger brother [Wáng] Yù and his son Yǒuwéi to return home to serve their father.
He inscribed a poem on the wall of the public office,
vowing to die.
The Yān army entered the east gate at night,
and Commander Wáng Xiǎn surrendered to welcome them.
Bówěi, dressed in his official attire, ascended the hall,
bowed facing south,
and hanged himself.
Yǒuwéi could not bear to leave,
so he returned,
saw his father's corpse,
and slit his own throat beside it.
Chief Clerk Táng Zǐqīng and Recorder Huáng Qiān were both captured.
The Yān general wanted to release Zǐqīng.
Zǐqīng said:
"I wish to follow Yán Gōng into the afterlife."
He then died.
Qiān was sent to Xúzhōu to persuade surrender.
Qiān refused,
and also died.
Also Xiàng Pú,
from Cíxī,
diligently studied and supported his parents.
At the end of Hóngwǔ's reign,
he was summoned for his talent
and became Magistrate of Xiànxiàn.
The county had no city walls.
When Yān general Tán Yuān arrived,
Pú gathered militia to fight,
was captured,
and died clutching his official seal.
Zhèng Shù,
from Xiānjū,
was Magistrate of Xiāoxiàn.
When Yān general Wáng Cōng captured Xiāo,
he died unyielding.
His two daughters, who were to be married,
also died.
Zhèng Huá,
from Línhǎi,
was demoted from a court emissary to an assistant clerk in Dōngpíng.
When the Yān army arrived,
the principal and deputy officials of the prefecture all abandoned the city and fled.
Huá said to his wife Xiāo:
"It is my duty to die,
but what about your youth?"
Xiāo wept and said:
"If you do not fail the nation,
how dare I fail you?"
Huá said:
"That is enough."
He led officials and commoners to defend the city stoutly.
When the city fell,
he fought fiercely and died unyielding.
Wáng Shěng,
courtesy name Zǐzhí,
was a native of Jíshuǐ.
In the fifth year of Hóngwǔ, he passed the xiāngjǔ examination.
Upon reaching the capital,
an imperial edict exempted him from the huìshì,
and he was ordered by the Lìbù to be appointed to office.
Shěng stated that his parents were old
and requested leave to care for them.
Soon after, he was summoned for his literary talent.
Tàizǔ personally tested him
and was pleased with the result,
indicating he deserved a special promotion.
He pleaded that his talent was meager and his parents were old,
requesting to remain at home to care for them.
He was appointed as a jiàoyù of Fúliáng.
He served as an education official three times,
finally obtaining Jìyáng.
When the Yān forces arrived,
he was captured by marauding soldiers.
Calmly, he drew analogies,
his words and meaning were fervent and impassioned.
The soldiers released him.
He returned and sat in the Mínglúntáng,
beat the drum to gather all the students,
and said to them:
"Do you know the name of this hall,
and what the loyalty between ruler and subject means today?"
He then wept loudly,
and the students also wept.
Shěng struck a pillar with his head and died.
His daughter, Jìng,
who was married to Zhōu Qífèng, the zhǔbù of Jìmò,
heard that the Yān forces had reached Jìyáng
and knew her father would surely die.
She sent people three times to search
and brought his remains back for burial.
Yáo Shàn,
courtesy name Kèyī,
was a native of Ānlù.
Initially, his surname was Lǐ.
In the Hóngwǔ reign, he passed the xiāngjǔ and successively served as a xiànchéng of Qímén,
and a tóngzhī for the two prefectures of Lúzhōu and Chóngqìng.
In the thirtieth year, he was promoted to zhīfǔ of Sūzhōu.
Initially,
Tàizǔ, seeing the extravagance and presumption of Wú customs,
wished to strictly enforce laws,
and the cunning even used trivial matters to attack and incriminate each other.
Shàn governed with a broad perspective,
not being overly harsh or petty,
so litigation gradually subsided,
and Wúzhong was greatly pacified.
He was good at humbling himself to treat scholars with respect,
honoring recluses like Wáng Bīn, Hán Yì, Yú Zhēnmù, and Qián Qín.
On the first day of the lunar month, he would gather at the xuégōng,
welcome Qín to the seat of honor,
and ask him to discuss classical meanings.
Qín said:
"This is not what is urgent now."
Shàn rose in alarm and asked.
Qín then gave him a scroll.
He looked at it
and found it contained strategies for defense.
At that time, the Yān forces had already moved south,
and he secretly allied with the governors of the four prefectures of Zhèn, Cháng, Jiā, and Sōng,
training militias for preparation.
He recommended Qín to the court,
who was appointed xíngjūn duàanshì.
Shàn soon went to the capital.
At that time, the court, based on the Yān King's memorial, had demoted Qí Tài and Huáng Zǐchéng to outside posts.
Shàn argued that they should not be demoted,
so the two were recalled.
In the fourth year of Jiànwén, an imperial edict ordered him to simultaneously oversee the military of the five prefectures of Sū, Sōng, Cháng, Zhèn, and Jiāxīng for the royal defense.
Before the troops could be assembled,
the Yān King had already entered the capital.
At that time, Zǐchéng was hiding at Shàn's place,
and they planned to sail together to raise an army.
Shàn declined, saying:
"You,
as a court official,
should go to gather troops and plan for restoration.
I, as a local guardian,
will live and die with the city."
Zǐchéng left,
and Shàn was bound by a qīanhù under his command named Xǔ and offered to the enemy.
He refused to submit and died.
He was forty-three years old.
His son Jié and three others were all exiled.
Qín,
courtesy name Jìzhōng,
was known for his extraordinary integrity in his youth.
At the end of the Yuán dynasty,
he tried to serve various generals
but was not successful.
In the early Hóngwǔ reign,
he was appointed a yuàn of the Dàdūdūfǔ
and accompanied Zhōngshānwáng on an expedition north of Běipíng,
reaching the Great Desert.
Upon his return, he resigned from his post.
He lived at home for twenty years,
content with poverty and enjoying the Dao.
He was re-appointed through Shàn's recommendation.
He accompanied Lǐ Jǐnglóng on his northern campaign
and was dispatched to the court to report on matters.
He fell ill on the way and was about to die,
but still presented a detailed report on military affairs.
He was seventy-three years old.
Chén Yánhuí,
courtesy name Shìyuān,
was a native of Pútián.
His father, Lìchéng,
who was the xiànchéng of Guī'ān,
was falsely accused and died.
Yánhuí was exiled to Yúnnán,
and many family members and attendants died on the way.
By the time they reached Shǔ,
only Yánhuí and his grandmother Guō remained.
There was an amnesty,
but he was not pardoned,
and the supervising escort took pity on him and released him.
Too poor to return home,
he relied on a fellow countryman, the zhīxiàn Huáng Jīliáng,
and adopted the surname Huáng.
After a long time,
he was recommended by Yán Dézhèng, the jiàoyù of Làngzhōng,
and appointed xùndǎo of Bǎoníng.
After completing his term, he went to the capital.
He was summoned for an audience and appointed zhīxiàn of Píngjiāng.
More than a year later,
Tàizǔ died,
and Yánhuí went to mourn.
Again, he was recommended by Yáng Wéikāng, the gěishìzhōng,
and promoted to zhīfǔ of Huīzhōu.
In the first year of Jiànwén, he received a high reward for his integrity.
When his grandmother Guō died,
he was supposed to leave,
but the common people went to the capital to beg for his retention.
Yánhuí, in mourning attire, rushed to the imperial palace to make a personal plea,
requesting to resume his original surname.
When Yánhuí was exiled to Yúnnán,
his younger brother Yàn ● was also exiled to Liáodōng.
By this time,
an imperial edict removed Yàn ● from the exile register.
He repeatedly requested to complete the mourning period.
This was not granted.
Guō was buried on the south side of Běishān, ten lǐ north of Huīchéng.
He often went to the tomb,
weeping with great sorrow,
and people called that place
"Tàishǒu Shān".
He once wept before the common people, saying:
"I am a criminal,
who once fled and adopted another surname.
Because my grandmother was alive,
I feared that confessing would lead to punishment,
so I endured for twenty years.
Now that my grandmother is gone,
I should ask for death myself.
The Emperor has specifically pardoned me,
and I will ultimately die to repay the country."
When the Yān forces approached the capital,
Yánhuí organized volunteers to go to the aid.
He was subsequently captured,
chained and brought to the capital,
where he died.
Zhāng Yànfāng,
was a native of Lóngquán.
Initially, he served as a gěishìzhōng,
but requested a change to zhīxiàn of Lèpíng for the care of his parents.
In response to the imperial edict, he joined the royal defense,
leading his troops to Húkǒu.
He was captured,
chained and brought to Lèpíng,
and executed.
His head was displayed on the watchtower,
and in the summer month,
not a single fly gathered,
and for ten days, his face looked as if he were alive.
The local people secretly buried him behind the Qīngbáitáng.
Among those who died for the royal defense at the same time,
was the tóngzhī of Sōngjiāng,
whose death was especially fierce, it is said.
The name of this tóngzhī cannot be ascertained;
some say it was Zhōu Jìyú.
When the edict for royal defense was issued,
he posted a notice recruiting volunteers to come to the aid,
eloquently expounding on the great righteousness,
moving people's hearts,
and also condemning
"Jìngnán"
forces for violating grace and betraying the Dao.
He was chained and brought to the capital
and dismembered in the marketplace.
Zàn yuē: Yān shī zhī nán xiàng yě,
lián bài èr dà jiàng,
qí fēng gài bùkě dāng.
Tiě Xuàn yǐ shūshēng jiélì kàngyù yú Qí, Lǔ zhī jiān,
lǚ cuò Yān zhòng.
Shè yǔ Gěng, Lǐ yìdì ér chǔ,
tiānxià shì gù wèikě zhī yǐ.
Zhāng Bǐng, Xiè Guì, Gě Chéng tú Yān yú zhǒuyè,
ér shì bù jiù.
Sòng Zhōng, Mǎ Xuān dōng xī jì bài,
Qú Néng zhū jiàng chuí shèng zhàn wáng,
Yān bīng zú dé chángqū nán xià.
Ér Yáo Shàn, Chén Yàn Huí zhī shǔ,
yù yǐ jùn yì zhī jiǎ fèn jù yú dàshì yǐ qù zhī hòu,
cǐ Huáng Yuè suǒwèi bīng zhì Jiāngnán,
yù zhī wú jí zhě yě.
Jiàokān jì

Lièzhuàn Dì sānshíyī Wáng Gěn (Gāo Xùnzhì) Liáo Shēng (Wèi Miǎn Zōu Jǐn Gōng Tài) Zhōu Shìxiū Chéng Běnlì Huáng Guān Wáng Shúyīng (Lín Yīng) Huáng Yuè (Zēng Fèngsháo) Wáng Liáng Chén Sīxián (Lóngxī Liùshēng Tái Wēn Èr Qiáo) Chéng Tōng (Huáng Xīfàn Yè Huìzhòng Huáng Yànqīng Cài Yùn Shí Yǔncháng) Gāo Wēi (Hán Yù) Gāo Xiánníng Wáng Jìn Zhōu Jìn Niú Jǐngxiān (Chéng Jì děng)
Wáng Gěn,
zì Jìngzhǐ,
Jíshuǐ rén.
Jiànwén èr nián jìnshì.
Duì cè dì yī.
Mào qǐn,
yì yǐ Hú Jìng,
jí Hú Guǎng yě,
Gěn cì zhī,
yòu cì Lǐ Guàn.
Sān rén jiē tóng lǐ,
bìng shòu xiūzhuàn,
rú Hóngwǔ zhōng gùshì,
shè wénshǐguǎn jū zhī.
Yù xiū Tàizǔ Shílù jí Lèi Yào, Shízhèng Jì zhū shū.
Yī shí dà zhùzuò jiē zōnglǐ zhī.
Shù shàngshū yán shíwù.
Yān bīng bó Jīngchéng,
Gěn yǔ qīzǐ jué yuē:
“Shí rén zhī lù zhě,
sǐ rén zhī shì,
wú bù kě fù shēng yǐ.”
Xiè Jìn, Wú Pǔ yǔ Gěn, Jìng bǐ shè jū.
Chéng xiàn qián yī xī,
jiē jí Pǔ shè.
Jìn chénshuō dà yì,
Jìng yì fèn jī kāngkǎi,
Gěn dú liútì bù yán.
Sān rén qù,
Pǔ zǐ Yǔ Bì shàng yòu,
tàn yuē:
“Hú shú néng sǐ,
shì dà jiā shì.”
Pǔ yuē:
“Bùrán,
dú Wáng shú sǐ ěr.”
Yǔ wèi bì,
gé qiáng wén Jìng hū:
“Wài xuān shèn,
jǐn shì tún.”
Pǔ gù Yǔ Bì yuē:
“Yī tún shàng bù néng shě,
kěn shě shēng hū?”
Xūyú Gěn shè kū,
yǐn zhèn sǐ yǐ.
Jìn chí yè,
Chéngzǔ shèn xǐ.
Míngrì jiàn Jìng,
zhào zhì,
kòutóu xiè.
Guàn yì yíng fù.
Hòu Chéngzǔ chū Jiànwén shí qúnchén fēngshì qiānyú tōng,
lìng Jìn děng biānyuè.
Shì shè bīng nóng qián gǔ zhě liú zhī,
zhū yányǔ gānfàn jí tā yīqiè jiē fénhuǐ.
Yīn cóngróng wèn Guàn, Jìn děng yuē:
“Ěr děng yí jiē yǒu zhī.”
Zhòng wèi duì,
Guàn dú dùnshǒu yuē:
“Chén shí wèi cháng yǒu yě.”
Chéngzǔ yuē:
“Ěr yǐ wú wéi měi yé?
Shí qí lù,
rèn qí shì,
dāng guójiā wēijí,
guān jìnshì dú wú yī yán kě hū?
Zhèn tè è fū yòu Jiànwén huài zǔ fǎ luàn zhèng zhě ěr.”
Hòu Guàn qiān zhōngyǔn,
zuò lèi,
sǐ yù zhōng.
Lín zú tàn yuē:
“Wú kuì Wáng Jìngzhǐ yǐ.”
Yǒu Gāo Xùnzhì zhě,
Gěn zuòzhǔ yě,
Xiāoxiàn rén,
yù Jiāxīng.
Yòu shì xué,
shī Gòng Shītài, Zhōu Bóqí děng,
wénzhāng diǎnyǎ,
chéng yī jiā yán.
Zhēng xiū Yuán Shǐ,
rù Hànlín,
lěi qiān shì Lìbù Shìláng,
yǐ shì zhé Qúshān.
Jiànwén chū,
zhào wèi Tàicháng Shàoqīng,
yǔ Dǒng Lún tóng zhǔ huìshì.
Dé shì zì Gěn wài,
Hú Jìng, Wú Pǔ, Yáng Róng, Jīn Yòuzī, Yáng Pǔ, Hú Yíng, Gù Zuǒ děng jiē wéi míng chén.
Yān shī rù,
cún mó wú kěkǎo.
Liáo Shēng,
Xiāngyáng rén.
Bù zhī qí suǒyǐ jìn,
xuéxíng zuì zhīmíng,
yǔ Fāng Xiàorú, Wáng Shēn xiāng yǒushàn.
Hóngwǔ mò,
yóu Zuǒ Fǔ Duànshì zhuó Tàicháng Shàoqīng.
Jiànwén chū,
xiū Tàizǔ Shílù,
Dǒng Lún, Wáng Jǐng wèi zǒngcái guān,
Shēng yǔ Gāo Xùnzhì wèi fù zǒngcái guān,
Lǐ Guàn, Wáng Shēn, Hú Zǐzhāo, Yáng Shìqí, Luó Huī, Chéng Běnlì wèi zuǎnxiū guān,
jiē yī shí xuǎn.
Yān shī dù Jiāng,
cháotíng yǎnshǐ qǐng gēdì.
Bù xǔ.
Shēng wén ér tòngkū,
yǔ jiārén jué,
zìyì sǐ.
Xùnnàn zhū chén,
Shēng sǐ zuì xiān.
Qí hòu Chén Yīng zòu zhū chén nì tiānmìng,
xiàosǐ Jiànwén jūn,
qǐng xíng zhuī lù,
yì shǒu jí Shēng yún.
Shí wèi Yīng zhuīlùn zhě,
yǒu Wèi Miǎn děng.
Miǎn guān Yùshǐ,
Yān bīng fàn Quē,
Dūdū Xú Zēngshòu páihuái diàntíng,
yǒu yì zhì.
Miǎn shuài tóngguān ǒu zhī,
yǔ Dàlǐ Chéng Zōu Jǐn dà hū,
qǐng sù jiā zhū.
Míngrì,
gōng zhōng huǒ qǐ,
yǒu quàn Miǎn jiàng zhě,
lì shēng chì zhī,
suì zìshā,
Jǐn yì sǐ.
Jǐn, Miǎn jiē Yǒngfēng rén.
Qí tóng lǐ Zōu Pǔ,
guān Qín fǔ Chángshǐ,
wén Jǐn sǐ,
fèn shèn,
bù shí zú.
Huò yuē jí Jǐn zǐ yě.
Yòu Dū Gěishìzhōng Gōng Tài,
Yìwū rén.
Yóu xiāng jiàn qǐjiā.
Yān Wáng rù Jīnchuānmén,
Tài bèi fù,
yǐ fēi jiāndǎng shì bù shā,
zì tóu chéng xià sǐ.
Tài cháng yóuxué gōng,
kuángrén jī zhī,
nì chí zhōng jǐ sǐ,
fú jiào,
rén fú qí liàng.
Zhōu Shìxiū,
míng Dé,
yǐ zì xíng,
Tàihé rén.
Hóngwǔ mò,
jǔ míngjīng,
wéi Huòqiū Xùndǎo.
Tàizǔ wèn jiājū hé wèi.
Duì yuē:
“Jiào rén zǐdì,
xiàodì lì tián.”
Tàizǔ xǐ,
zhuó Zhōu fǔ Fèngsìzhèng.
Yú nián,
cóng Wáng běizhēng zhì Hēishān,
huán qiān Jìshàn.
Jiànwén yuán nián,
yǒu gào Wáng bùfǎ zhě,
guān shǔ jiē xià lì.
Shìxiū yǐ cháng jiàn Wáng dé miǎn,
gǎi Héng fǔ Jìshàn.
Héng Wáng,
Huì Dì mǔ dì,
wèi zhī fān.
Shìxiū liú Jīngshī,
yù Hànlín zuǎnxiū,
hào jiàn shì,
chénshuō guójiā dàjì.
When the Yan兵 crossed the Huai River,
Shì Xiū and Xiāo Yòngdào submitted a memorial criticizing those in power.
The powerful officials were enraged,
and together they tried to suppress him,
but Shì Xiū remained unmoved.
When the capital fell,
he left letters to his friends Jiāng Zhònglóng, Xiè Jìn, Hú Jìng, Xiāo Yòngdào, and Yáng Shìqí,
entrusting them with his posthumous affairs.
He donned his formal attire,
and tied a eulogy to his belt.
He entered the Yìngtiān Fǔ School,
bowed to the Former Sages,
and then hanged himself in the Zūnjīng Gé.
He was forty-nine years old.
When the Prince of Yan ascended the throne,
Chén Yīng stated that Shì Xiū had defied the Mandate of Heaven,
and requested that he be posthumously punished.
The Emperor said:
“He ate their salaries,
and thus exerted his utmost loyalty.
Do not pursue this.”
Shì Xiū was outwardly gentle but inwardly firm,
his will and integrity were outstanding.
If something was not righteous,
he would not unjustly accept even a single thing.
He once said:
“A loyal minister does not consider gains or losses,
therefore his words are always straightforward;
a virtuous woman does not worry about life or death,
therefore her actions are always decisive.”
He once compiled stories of loyal and upright people throughout history into the Guāngǎn Lù.
His studies covered the Classics and Histories, the Hundred Schools of Thought,
Yin and Yang, medicine, and divination,
there was nothing he did not thoroughly master.
When writing, he would take up his brush and finish immediately,
and his prose was elegant, rich, and clear.
Initially, he, Yáng Shìqí, Xiè Jìn, Hú Jìng, along with Jīn Yòuzī, Huáng Huái, and Hú Yǎn, had pledged to die together.
When disaster struck,
only Shì Xiū ultimately carried out his resolve.
Chéng Běnlì,
courtesy name Yuándào,
was from Chóngdé.
He was a descendant of the former scholar Yí.
His father, Dé Gāng,
possessed talent and spirit but did not serve as an official.
When Yuán general Lù Chéng's troops passed through Zàolín,
they plundered violently.
Dé Gāng explained the advantages and disadvantages to him.
Lù Chéng was pleased,
restrained his troops,
and wished to recommend him for an official position,
but he declined and left.
Běnlì had great ambitions from a young age,
and studied without focusing on mere phrases and sentences.
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
when filial sons were commended,
Tàizǔ once said to him:
“Scholars compete for imperial examinations,
using the mastery of classics as a pretext,
but lack true learning.
Your character is naturally honest and sincere,
you should devote yourself to the learning of the sages and worthies.”
Běnlì redoubled his efforts.
He heard that Zhū Kèxiū of Jīnhuá had inherited Zhū Xī's teachings from Xǔ Qiān,
so he went to study with him.
He passed the Mingjīng and Xiùcai examinations,
and was appointed as a Master of Ceremonies for the Prince of Qín's household,
and was bestowed with paper currency and a saddled horse.
When his mother passed away, he resigned from office.
After the mourning period,
he was reassigned as a ritual official for the Prince of Zhōu's household,
and followed the Prince to Kāifēng.
In the spring of the twentieth year, he was promoted to Chief Administrator,
and followed the Prince to the capital for an audience.
Due to an accumulated offense, he was demoted to a clerk in the Mǎlóng Tālangdiàn Chiefdom of Yúnnán,
leaving his family in Dàliáng,
and taking one servant with him to his post.
The local chieftain Shī Kěfá incited the various barbarians to rebellion.
Běnlì rode alone into their stronghold,
explained the consequences of disaster and fortune,
and all the chieftains submitted.
Not long after,
they rebelled again.
The Marquis of Xīpíng, Mù Yīng, and the Provincial Administration Commissioner, Zhāng Dǎn, knowing Běnlì's wisdom,
assigned him to tour the counties and manage military affairs.
He both pacified and defended,
traveling from Chǔxióng and Yáo'ān to Dàlǐ, Yǒngchāng, Hèqìng, and Lìjiāng.
He traveled through mountains and slept in the wilderness,
pacifying and consolidating for nine years,
and the people, both Han and Yi, lived in peace.
In the thirty-first year, he reported his accounts to the capital.
Academicians Dǒng Lún and Fǔyǐn Xiàng Bǎo both recommended him.
He was summoned into the Hànlín Academy,
participated in the compilation of the Tàizǔ Shílù,
and was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief.
Aside from his official salary,
he accepted no gifts.
In the third year of Jiànwén, he was demoted for failing to attend an accompanying sacrifice,
but was still kept for compilation work.
After the Veritable Records were completed,
he was appointed as the Vice Commissioner of Jiāngxī.
Before he could depart,
the Yan兵 entered,
and he hanged himself.
Huáng Guān,
courtesy name Bólán,
also known as Shàngbīn,
was from Guìchí.
His father married into the Xǔ family [赘],
so he took the surname Xǔ.
He studied under the former Yuán Attendant-in-waiting Huáng Xǔ.
After Huáng Xǔ died as a martyr,
Huáng Guān became even more determined.
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
he was recommended to the Imperial Academy.
He drew a picture of his parents' graves,
and would weep whenever he looked at it and bowed.
In the twenty-fourth year,
he came first in both the metropolitan and palace examinations.
He was successively promoted to Right Vice Minister of Rites,
and then memorialized to restore his original surname.
In the beginning of the Jiànwén reign,
the official system was reformed,
with the Left and Right Grand Counselors ranking above the Ministers of the Six Boards.
Huáng Guān was changed to Right Grand Counselor,
and was personally employed alongside Fāng Xiàorú and others.
When the Prince of Yan raised an army,
Huáng Guān drafted an imperial edict satirizing him to disperse his troops and return to his fief,
and to submit himself and beg for forgiveness.
His words were extremely critical and condemning.
In the fourth year, he received an imperial edict to recruit troops in the upper reaches of the river,
and to supervise the various prefectural troops to come to the aid.
When he reached Ānqìng,
the Prince of Yan had already crossed the river and entered the capital.
An order was issued to expose the crimes of the treacherous ministers of the Left Bureau of Civil Officials,
and Huáng Guān's name was sixth on the list.
Later, when the imperial seal was sought,
its whereabouts were unknown.
Someone said it had been given to Huáng Guān when he went out to gather troops.
Officials were ordered to pursue and arrest him,
and his wife, Wēng Shì, and two daughters were taken and given to elephant slaves.
The slaves demanded hairpins and bracelets to buy wine and food.
Wēng Shì gave them all and they took them away.
She quickly took her two daughters and ten other family members,
and threw themselves into the Huáiqīng bridge to their deaths.
When Huáng Guān heard that Jīnchuān Mén had fallen,
he sighed and said:
“My wife has integrity and resolve,
she will surely die.”
He called her spirit and buried her by the river.
He ordered his boat to Luóchà Jī,
donned his court robes, bowed facing east,
and threw himself into the swift current to his death.
Huáng Guān's younger brother, Gòu,
had previously hidden his young son
and escaped to another place.
Some say that Gòu's wife, Bì Shì, lived as a widow in her maternal home,
and later gave birth to a posthumous son,
thus the Huáng clan had descendants in Guìchí.
Originally,
when Huáng Guān's wife threw herself into the water,
she vomited blood onto a stone,
forming a small image.
It would appear on cloudy or rainy days,
and was widely believed to be an image of Guānyīn.
Monks carried it to an nunnery,
and Wēng Shì appeared in a dream saying:
“I am the wife of Huáng Zhuàngyuán.”
By dawn,
when water was poured on it,
the image became even clearer,
showing a sorrowful expression.
Later, it was moved to Huáng Guān's ancestral temple,
and named the “Blood Image Stone of Lady Wēng.”
It still exists today.
Wáng Shūyīng,
courtesy name Yuáncǎi,
was from Huángyán.
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
he was summoned along with Yáng Dàzhōng, Yè Jiàntài, Fāng Xiàorú, and Lín Yòu.
Wáng Shūyīng firmly declined and returned home.
In the twentieth year, he was recommended to be an instructor in Xiānjū,
then changed to professor in Dé'ān.
He was promoted to magistrate of Hànyáng,
and implemented many benevolent policies.
In a year of drought,
he fasted to pray,
and rain immediately followed.
During the [Jiànwén] era,
he was summoned to be a [Hànlín Xiūzhuàn].
He submitted eight policies for governance,
which stated: diligently pursue learning,
be careful with likes and dislikes,
distinguish between good and evil,
accept remonstrance,
assess talent,
be prudent with punishments,
understand benefits and harms,
and establish laws.
All were supported with evidence from ancient and modern times,
and were practicable.
He also said:
“[Tàizǔ] eliminated traitors and purged impurities,
suppressed the powerful and uprooted the stubborn,
like a doctor removing disease,
or a farmer weeding.
In an urgent removal of disease, the body might be harmed;
in severe weeding, the crops might be damaged.
Once the disease is removed, the vital energy should be harmonized;
once the weeds are gone, the roots and seedlings should be nurtured.”
The Emperor greatly appreciated and accepted these.
When the [Yān] army reached [Huái],
he received an imperial decree to recruit soldiers.
When he arrived at [Guǎngdé],
the capital had fallen.
Meeting [Qí Tài] who had fled there,
[Shūyīng] suspected [Tài]'s duplicity [貳心] and wanted to arrest him.
[Tài] explained his reasons.
They then embraced and wept bitterly,
planning for future actions together.
Soon after,
knowing that nothing could be done,
he bathed, changed his clothes and cap,
wrote a farewell poem,
hid it in his robe,
and hanged himself beneath a ginkgo tree in the [Xuánmiào Guān].
The [Tiāntái] Daoist [Shèng Xīnián] buried him five [lǐ] west of the city.
His poem read:
“Born between heaven and earth,
loyalty and filial piety are most precious to fulfill.
Alas, in serving my sovereign and father,
I reflect on many faults and transgressions.
My ambitions unfulfilled,
a strange illness suddenly afflicts me.
Rich food lies untouched on the table,
I cannot swallow it when I face it.
Perhaps the divine creator
has destined me to return to the netherworld.
I recall [Yí] and [Qí],
who starved to death on [Shǒuyáng] Peak;
was [Zhōu]'s grain not good?
Their perspective was truly biased.
Their lofty conduct is hard to emulate,
mine is merely unworthy of transmission.
May the historian's brush through the ages
be careful not to call me a worthy sage.”
He also inscribed on his table:
“My life is already over,
having brought no benefit to my time.
My death is also in vain,
yet I hope to have no shame before later generations.”
When the Prince of [Yān] ascended the throne as emperor,
[Chén Yīng] confiscated his family's property.
His wife, Lady [Jīn], hanged herself and died.
His two daughters were imprisoned in the Brocade Guards' prison [Jǐnyī yù] [錦衣獄] and
drowned themselves in a well.
[Shūyīng] was a close friend of [Xiàorú],
and they discussed moral principles.
At the beginning of the [Jiànwén] era,
[Xiàorú] wanted to implement the well-field system [Jǐngtián].
[Shūyīng] wrote to him, saying:
“It is certainly difficult for a person to have talent,
but it is even harder to be able to utilize that talent.
[Zǐfáng] for [Hàn Gāo] was one who could utilize his talent;
[Jiǎ Yí] for [Hàn Wén] was one who could not utilize his talent.
[Zǐfáng] observed that Emperor [Gāo] could be advised and then spoke,
thus Emperor [Gāo] used him,
and benefited from him at that time.
Even close relatives like [Fán], [Lì],
trusted figures like [Píng], [Bó],
and responsible officials like [Xiāo], [Cáo],
could not interfere.
[Jiǎ Shēng] spoke easily without observing,
and moreover spoke excessively,
thus people like [Jiàng] and [Guàn] were able to disparage him.
Currently, wise ruler and able minister meet,
a rare opportunity in a thousand years.
However, some things were practiced in antiquity
and can also be practiced today,
like the [Xià] dynasty's cap and the [Zhōu] dynasty's crown.
Some things were practiced in antiquity
but cannot be practiced today,
like the well-field system and the feudal system.
If practicable things are implemented,
people will easily follow,
and the populace will enjoy its benefits.
If difficult things are implemented,
people will find it hard to follow,
and the populace will suffer its woes.”
Although the well-field system was not implemented at that time,
[Xiàorú] eventually used the Rites of [Zhōu] [Zhōu Guān] to change institutions,
which brought no practical benefit,
and became a pretext for the Prince of [Yān].
Commentators admired [Shūyīng]'s insight,
and regretted that [Xiàorú] could not use his words.
At that time, Censor [Gǔtián Lín Yīng] was also recruiting soldiers in [Guǎngdé].
Knowing that nothing could be saved,
he made a double bow and hanged himself.
His wife, Lady [Sòng], was imprisoned
and also hanged herself.
[Huáng Yuè],
courtesy name [Shúyáng],
was a native of [Chángshú].
He was fond of learning in his youth.
His family had land in [Gězé Pí],
and [Yuè]'s father ordered him to oversee the farming there.
[Yuè] borrowed books from a friend's house
and secretly read them without cessation.
The county recommended worthy scholars,
and he was appointed as [Yízhāng Diǎnshǐ].
In the first year of [Jiànwén], he passed the provincial examination in [Húguǎng].
The next year, he was granted the [Jìnshì] degree,
and appointed as a Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Punishments [Xíngkē Jǐshìzhōng].
In the third year, he observed mourning for his father.
[Fāng Xiàorú] visited him to offer condolences,
and dismissing others, asked:
“The [Yān] army is advancing south daily.
[Sū], [Cháng], [Zhènjiāng]
are the capital's left flank.
You are a native of [Wú],
and a close official of the court.
Although you are leaving now,
you should have something to teach me.”
[Yuè] replied:
“Among the three prefectures, [Zhènjiāng] is the most crucial.
If the guardian is not the right person,
it is like tearing down a wall to invite a thief.
The Commander [Tóng Jùn] is cunning and unreliable.
When he reports to the emperor,
he looks far but speaks superficially,
his heart is unfathomable.
The Prefect of [Sūzhōu], [Yáo Shàn],
is loyal and fervent,
with the bearing of a national hero,
but he is too benevolent and lenient with his subordinates,
which I fear is insufficient to quell the chaos.
Moreover, the general strategic situation for the state
requires holding the upper reaches of the river;
if the troops reach [Jiāngnán],
it will be too late to resist them.”
[Xiàorú] then had [Yuè] take a letter to [Shàn].
[Shàn] received the letter,
and wept with [Yuè],
swearing to die for the country.
[Yuè] returned home
and resided by his father's coffin during the mourning period.
When the [Yān] army reached the river,
[Shàn] received an imperial decree to lead troops to defend the emperor,
and sent a letter inviting [Yuè].
[Yuè] knew the situation was hopeless,
and declined, saying he would go after finishing the funeral arrangements.
Soon after, [Tóng Jùn] indeed surrendered [Zhènjiāng] to [Yān].
[Yuè] heard of the national change,
closed his door, and did not go out.
The next year, he was summoned as Left Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Revenue [Hùkē Zuǒ Jǐshìzhōng],
but halfway there, he threw himself into the water.
It was reported that he drowned,
thus his family was spared punishment.
[Zēng Fèngsháo],
a native of [Lúlíng].
He passed the [Jìnshì] examination in the last years of [Hóngwǔ].
At the beginning of [Jiànwén],
he served as a Supervising Censor [Jiānchá Yùshǐ].
When the Prince of [Yān] ascended the throne,
he was summoned to his original post,
but did not go.
He was then summoned as a Vice Minister [Shìláng].
Knowing it was unavoidable,
he pricked his finger and wrote in blood on his robe's lapel:
“I was born in [Lúlíng], a region of loyalty and integrity,
and have always possessed a resolute and upright heart.
I studied, attained the [Jìnshì] degree,
and served as a Censor [Xiùyī Láng].
I sigh that a fitting death
will allow me to smile in the afterlife,
and not shame my [Wén Tiānxiáng].”
He instructed his wife, Lady [Lǐ], and son, [Gōngwàng]:
“Do not change my clothes;
bury me in these.”
Then he committed suicide,
at the age of twenty-nine.
Lady [Lǐ] also maintained her integrity and died.
Wáng Liáng,
courtesy name Tiānxìng,
was a native of Xiángfú.
At the end of the Hóngwǔ reign,
he successively held the office of Qiān Dū Yùshǐ.
He was implicated in a case of delaying the trial of an associate,
and demoted to Xíngbù Lángzhōng.
During the Jiànwén reign,
he was successively promoted to Xíngbù Zuǒ Shìláng.
He proposed reducing the sentences of those implicated in the case of the Yān principality,
but his suggestion was not to the emperor's liking,
and he was sent out to be Zhèjiāng Ànchásǐ.
When the Prince of Yān ascended the throne,
he rather appreciated Wáng Liáng
and sent an envoy to summon him.
Wáng Liáng seized the envoy and was about to execute him,
but the crowd rescued the envoy and he left.
Wáng Liáng gathered the seals of all departments in his private residence,
intending to commit suicide,
but did not immediately decide.
His wife asked him why.
He said:
"It is my duty to die,
but I do not know how to arrange for you."
His wife said:
"You are a man;
how can you be concerned about a woman?"
She brought Wáng Liáng food.
After eating,
she took their child into the rear garden,
placed the child by the pond,
and drowned herself.
After Wáng Liáng had interred his wife,
he entrusted his child to a friend's family,
then piled up firewood and burned himself to death,
destroying all the seals.
Chéngzǔ said:
"It was indeed Wáng Liáng's duty to die,
but the court seals must not be destroyed.
By destroying the seals,
Wáng Liáng cannot be considered innocent."
His family was relocated to the frontier.
Chén Sīxián,
was a native of Màomíng.
At the end of the Hóngwǔ reign,
he served as Zhāngzhōu Jiàoshòu,
exhorting students with the great principles of loyalty and filial piety.
Whenever an imperial envoy visited Zhāngzhōu,
Chén Sīxián would always ask during his audience:
"Is His Sacred Majesty well?"
When the edict of the Prince of Yān's ascension to the throne arrived,
he wept bitterly and said:
"The principle of clarifying human relations
is precisely for today."
He resolutely lay down and did not receive the edict.
He led his disciples Wú Xìngyuán,
Chén Yìngzōng, Lín Yù, Zōu Jūnmò, Zēng Tíngruì, and Lǚ Xián—six people—
to the Mínglúntáng, where they set up a shrine for the former ruler,
and mourned according to ritual.
The officials arrested them and sent them to the capital,
where Sīxián and the six students all died.
The six students were all natives of Lóngxī.
During the Jiājìng reign,
the Tíxué Fùshǐ Shào Ruì erected a temple to sacrifice to Sīxián,
with the six students as secondary sacrificants.
Moreover, in Táizhōu, there was a woodcutter
who daily carried firewood to the market,
never asking a double price.
When he heard that the Prince of Yān had ascended the throne,
he wept bitterly and drowned himself in Dōnghú.
And in Wēnzhōu, Lèqīng, there was also a woodcutter
who, upon hearing that the capital had fallen
and his fellow townsman, Attendant Secretary Zhuó Jìng, had died,
wailed and threw himself into the water.
The names of both woodcutters are unknown.
Chéng Tōng,
was a native of Jīxī.
He once submitted a memorial to Tàizǔ,
requesting the removal of his grandfather's military household registration.
His words were very sorrowful,
and he eventually obtained the request.
Afterward,
he was appointed Jìshàn of the Liáo principality.
When the Yān army rose,
he accompanied the Prince across the sea back to the capital,
and submitted a memorial of several thousand words,
proposing strategies for defense,
and was promoted to Zuǒ Chángshǐ.
In the early Yǒnglè reign,
he accompanied the Prince in his relocation to Jīngzhōu.
There were those who claimed that his earlier memorial contained many criticisms.
He was brought in shackles
and died in prison.
His family was banished to the frontier.
His friend, Huīzhōu Zhīfǔ Huáng Xīfàn, was also arrested,
sentenced to death,
and his property confiscated.
Yè Huìzhòng,
was a native of Línghǎi.
He and his elder brother Yízhòng were both renowned for their literary talent.
As a Zhīxiàn, he was summoned to compile the Tàizǔ Shílù,
and later promoted to Zhī Nánchāng Fǔ.
In the first year of Yǒnglè, he was implicated for directly recording the
"Jìngnàn"
event,
and his entire clan was executed.
Huáng Yànqīng,
was a native of Shè.
He served as Guózǐ Bóshì,
and distinguished himself by his integrity.
He was implicated for privately posthumously honoring Emperor Jiànwén while in Méi Yīn's army,
and was executed.
Cài Yùn,
was a native of Nánkāng.
He successively served as Sìchuān Cāncèng,
was upright and did not conform to convention,
and was dismissed and returned home.
He was later reappointed as Zhī Bīnzhōu,
where he implemented benevolent policies.
In the early Yǒnglè reign,
he was also prosecuted as a member of the treacherous party and died.
Shí Yǔncháng,
was a native of Nínghǎi.
He passed the imperial examination in the 27th year of Hóngwǔ.
He served as Hénán Qiānshì,
and was known for his integrity.
He was demoted to Chángzhōu Tóngzhī due to an incident.
At the end of the Jiànwén reign,
he commanded troops to defend the river.
His army was routed,
and he abandoned his office and left.
Later, he was prosecuted for the case of the abolished Prince of Zhōu,
imprisoned for two years,
and exempted from death but banished to the frontier.
Gāo Wēi,
was a native of Liáozhōu,
valued integrity,
and was skilled in writing.
His mother, Lady Xiāo, suffered from a chronic illness,
and Gāo Wēi attended to her constantly,
showing no slack even in old age.
After his mother died,
he ate vegetarian food and lived by her tomb for three years.
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
his filial piety was commended.
As a Tàixuéshēng, he was tested and appointed Zuǒ Duànshì of the Qiánjūn Dūdū Fǔ.
He submitted a memorial on reclaiming wasteland in Hénán, Shāndōng, and Běipíng,
and also enumerated several matters concerning suppressing minor crafts, carefully selecting officials, and valuing titles.
Tàizǔ praised and accepted them.
Soon after, because a judgment he made was not to the emperor's liking,
he was to be punished.
His death sentence was commuted to banishment to Guìzhōu Guānsuǒlǐng,
and he was specially permitted to have his younger brother or nephew serve in his place,
with the emperor saying:
"This is to commend a filial son."
When Emperor Huì ascended the throne,
Gāo Wēi submitted a memorial requesting to return to his hometown.
Soon after,
the Liáozhōu Zhīzhōu Wáng Qīn, in response to an imperial edict, invited Gāo Wēi to serve.
Gāo Wēi then went to the Lìbù and submitted a memorial discussing current political affairs.
Those in power were then debating the reduction of the princes' power,
but Gāo Wēi alone, along with Censor Hán Yù, successively requested that favors be extended.
He briefly stated:
"Emperor Gāo Dì's enfeoffment of the princes,
compared to ancient systems,
was already excessive,
and the princes, moreover, were mostly arrogant, unruly, and unlawful,
violating court regulations.
If their power is not reduced,
the court's discipline will not be established;
if it is reduced,
the grace towards kin will be harmed.
Jiǎ Yì said: 'If you want peace and order in the world,
nothing is better than to establish many princes but reduce their power.'
Now, why not adopt his idea,
and not implement Cháo Cuò's plan of reduction and seizure,
but instead emulate Zhǔfù Yǎn's strategy of extending grace?
For the princes in the north,
their sons and younger brothers should be enfeoffed in the south;
for those in the south,
their sons and younger brothers should be enfeoffed in the north.
In this way, the power of the feudal princes
will be reduced without explicit reduction.
I also wish to further enhance the rites of kinship,
sending envoys to inquire and present gifts during seasonal festivals.
The worthy ones should be praised and rewarded by imperial edict.
For those who are arrogant, unruly, and unlawful,
their first offense should be tolerated,
their second offense pardoned;
if they do not change after the third offense,
then report it to the Imperial Ancestral Temple and have them deposed.
How could there be any who would not submit?"
The memorial was submitted,
and the emperor nodded in approval.
Soon after, the Yan army rose.
He was ordered to accompany Lǐ Jǐnglóng out on campaign to assist in military affairs.
Wēi again submitted a memorial,
saying:
"Your subject wishes to go as an envoy to Yan,
to reveal my loyal heart,
to present the principles of righteousness and propriety,
to explain the blessings and misfortunes,
and to move him with the affection due to kinsmen,
to make him cease hostilities and return to his fief."
The Emperor admired his words
and permitted it.
When Wēi arrived in Yan,
he introduced himself, saying: "Gāo Wēi, a recluse of the national dynasty, respectfully bows twice and submits a memorial to His Highness the Prince of Yan: Since Tàizǔ ascended to heaven,
the Son of Heaven has succeeded to the throne,
implementing policies of renewal.
The empire loves and supports him,
all saying
'Within, there is a sagely and enlightened ruler;
without, there are loyal princely guards.
The rule of Chéng and Kāng
is seen again today.'
Unexpectedly, Your Highness has clearly broken with the court,
mustering three armies
to resist the six divisions.
Your subject does not know what Your Highness intends.
The various officials currently at court,
the civil ones are wise and resourceful,
the military ones are brave and resolute.
They uphold justice and righteousness,
to punish the
rebellious with the obedient.
The chances of victory and defeat are clear as day.
All say
'Your Highness uses the pretext of executing the civil officials of the left ranks,
but in reality, this is the old stratagem of Wú Wáng Bì.
His true intentions are known
to every passerby.'
Wēi secretly fears that cunning and unscrupulous villains
will seize the opportunity to launch an attack.
Should there be any mishap,
Your Highness will have offended the late Emperor.
Now Your Highness occupies Běipíng,
has taken Mìyún,
subdued Yǒngpíng,
attacked Xióngxiàn,
and surprised Zhēndìng.
Although it was as easy as pouring water from a high place,
since the war began,
it has
already been several months,
yet you still cannot get out of a tiny corner of land.
Moreover, the generals and soldiers under Your Highness's command
number no more than 300,000.
To use a country's limited multitude to confront
the armies of the entire realm
will easily lead to exhaustion.
Between Your Highness and the Son of Heaven,
in terms of righteousness, you are sovereign and subject;
in terms of kinship, you are blood relatives.
Yet estrangement has arisen;
how much less can you guarantee that these 300,000 men of different surnames
will be united in heart and effort,
and devote their lives to Your Highness?
Whenever Wēi thinks of this,
he cannot help but shed tears for Your Highness.
May Your Highness believe Wēi's words,
submit a memorial to apologize,
and restore good relations.
The imperial court, discerning that Your Highness has no other intentions,
will surely grant clemency,
and the spirit of Tàizǔ in heaven
will also be at peace.
If you remain stubbornly unrepentant,
abandoning the尊 of a thousand chariots,
donating the wealth of a nation,
relying on small victories,
forgetting great righteousness,
and resisting the many with the few,
doing perverse deeds that cannot
succeed by chance,
Wēi does not know where Your Highness will take refuge.
Moreover, the great mourning period has not ended,
yet you cruelly raise armies.
How greatly does this not deviate from the righteousness of Tàibó, Bó Yí, and Shú Qí, who sought benevolence and yielded
their states?
Even if Your Highness has the intention of purifying the court,
the world will not be without discussions of usurping the legitimate succession.
Even if you are lucky enough not to fail,
what kind of person will Your Highness be called?
Wēi is a white-haired scholar,
a fleeting, insignificant life,
whose nature does not fear death.
In the seventeenth year of Hóngwǔ, I was commended by Tàizǔ Gāo Huángdì for my filial conduct.
Wēi secretly
considers it my duty:
since I am a filial son,
I should be a loyal subject.
To die in loyalty and to die in filial piety
is Wēi's greatest wish.
If I am granted death,
and may see the spirit of Tàizǔ in heaven,
Wēi will also be
without shame.
He submitted several memorials,
all without reply.
Soon after, Lǐ Jǐnglóng's army was defeated,
and Wēi escaped south.
When he reached Línyì,
he met the Assistant Administrator Tiě Xuàn,
and they wept bitterly together.
He rushed to Jǐnán,
swearing to defend it to the death,
and repeatedly defeated the Yan army.
When the capital fell,
Wēi hanged himself in a post station.
Yù Shū's brief memorial said: "The various princes are Tàizǔ's surviving flesh and blood,
in nobility they are Xiàokāng Huángdì's siblings,
in status they are Your Majesty's uncles.
If the spirits of the two emperors in heaven
were to see their descendants become
Sons of Heaven,
while their brothers and sons suffer mutilation and slaughter,
would their hearts be at peace?
Whenever your subject thinks of this,
he never fails to shed tears.
These are all the biased views of shallow scholars,
who are troubled by the
overly powerful feudal domains,
and harbor excessive suspicions,
leading to this situation.
Indeed, when the lips are gone, the teeth feel cold;
everyone feels endangered.
Zhōu Wáng has been deposed,
Xiāng Wáng has immolated himself,
the fief of Dài has been destroyed,
and now the officials of Qí have accused the prince of rebellion.
Those who plan must say,
'If we do not raise troops, disaster will surely befall us.'
Thus, it is the officials in charge of the court who incited this.
The Yan army has been raised for two months now.
Previously, over 500,000 troops were mobilized,
yet not a single arrow was gained.
Can it be said that the country has wise strategists?
After long
preparation,
the army immediately ran short of supplies.
Generals do not offer strategies,
soldiers do not exert effort.
This only causes the innocent common people of the Central Plains to be afflicted by transport duties,
the people have no means to live,
growing worse
day by day.
The Emperor's worries are deep,
yet those who move in and out of the imperial chambers and manage state affairs
are still self-satisfied and triumphant.
What exactly were the intentions of those who advised Your Majesty to reduce the feudal domains?
Indeed,
what were their intentions?
As the proverb says:
'What is close cannot be cut off,
what is distant cannot be firmly attached.'
This is profoundly true.
If Your Majesty does not observe this,
before ten years pass,
regret
will be too late.
Your subject is most foolish,
but his gratitude is profound,
and he dares not remain silent.
May you kindly show discernment,
restore what has been overthrown and continue what has been cut off,
release Dài Wáng from prison,
entomb Xiāng Wáng,
return Zhōu Wáng to the capital,
and welcome Chǔ and Shǔ as the dukes of Zhōu,
allowing each to send their designated heir with a letter to persuade Yan,
to cease hostilities and guard their fiefs,
to comfort the spirits of the ancestral temple.
Clearly
proclaim to the world
the restoration of order from chaos,
and sincerely strengthen kinship ties.
The imperial altars will be fortunate.
He was not listened to.
When the Yan army crossed the Jiāng,
Yù abandoned his post and fled,
his whereabouts unknown.
Gāo Xiánníng,
a student from Jǐyáng Prefecture,
once studied under the Education Director Wáng Shěng,
and they encouraged each other in integrity and righteousness.
During the Jiànwén reign,
he was recommended to the Imperial Academy.
When the Yān army broke through Dézhōu
and besieged Jǐnán,
Xiánníng happened to be within the siege,
unable to report for duty.
At this time, the Yān army's power was very strong.
Huáng Zǐchéng and others plotted to send envoys to negotiate peace to wear them down.
Lǐ Déchéng, a Vice Director of the Court of Imperial Accoutrements,
valiantly volunteered to go.
He met the Prince of Yān beneath the city walls.
The Prince did not listen,
and the siege intensified.
Deputy Administrator Tiě Xuàn and others used every means to defend against them.
The Prince shot a letter into the city announcing terms of surrender.
Xiánníng wrote "On Dàn, Duke of Zhōu, Assisting King Chéng"
and shot it outside the city.
The Prince was pleased with his words
and delayed the assault.
After a two-month standoff,
the Yān army finally broke off and left.
After the Prince of Yān ascended the throne,
Xiánníng was captured and brought to him.
Chéngzǔ said:
"Is this the talented scholar who wrote the essay?
He is a good man;
grant him an official post."
Xiánníng firmly declined.
Jǐnyīwèi Commander Jǐ Gāng,
who had been a student expelled for misconduct,
was an old friend of Xiánníng's
and urged him to accept the position.
Xiánníng said:
"You were abandoned by the academy,
so you should do as you wish.
I have received an official stipend for many years,
and it is against my righteousness to accept.
Moreover, I have received the teachings of Master Wáng."
Jǐ Gāng spoke to the Emperor on his behalf,
and he was eventually allowed to return home,
dying at the age of ninety-seven.
Wáng Jìn,
courtesy name Qìzhī,
was from Rìzhào.
He was widely versed in the classics and histories,
especially skilled in the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Initially, he served as a professor,
but was exiled to a distant land for an offense.
At the end of the Hóngwǔ reign,
he was recommended for his talent and ability
and appointed Prefect of Níngbō.
At the fourth drum (around 1 AM), he would light a candle and read,
his voice carrying outside the yamen.
Occasionally, he would go to the academy to instruct the students.
The students would usually rise at the fourth drum
and study diligently, not daring to slacken.
He destroyed illicit temples within his jurisdiction;
the Shrine of the Three Sovereigns was also among those destroyed.
Some found this questionable.
Jìn said:
"A shrine that should not be worshipped is called illicit;
a shrine where worship is not permitted is called sacrilegious.
Only the Son of Heaven may sacrifice to the Three Sovereigns;
it has nothing to do with scholars or commoners.
What is questionable about destroying it?"
He lived frugally.
One day, his meal included fish soup.
Jìn said to his wife:
"Do you not remember when I ate grass roots?"
He ordered it to be removed and buried.
People called him
"Prefect Who Buried the Soup."
When the Yān army approached the Yangtze River,
Jìn built boats and ships, planning to assist the emperor.
He was bound by a garrison soldier and sent to the capital.
Chéngzǔ asked why he built the boats.
He replied:
"I wanted to sail across the sea to Guāzhōu
and obstruct the army's southward crossing."
The Emperor did not punish him
and sent him back to his hometown,
where he died of old age.
Zhōu Jìn,
courtesy name Bóshēn,
was from Wǔchāng.
He entered the Imperial Academy as a recommended candidate,
and was appointed Magistrate of Yǒngqīng,
acting as the county magistrate.
When Chéngzǔ raised his army,
the local officials and magistrates all welcomed his surrender.
Yǒngqīng was particularly close,
but Jìn alone made plans for defense.
Later,
judging it impossible to succeed,
he fled south, taking his official seal with him.
On the way, he heard his mother had died,
so he returned to mourn her.
With the Yān army already pressing on,
he gathered a righteous militia to assist the emperor.
Hearing that the capital could not be held,
he then went into hiding.
The Ministry of Personnel stated:
"The two hundred ninety officials from the prefectures and counties formerly under Běipíng, such as Zhū Níng,
abandoned their posts and fled
when His Majesty carried out the 'Jìng Nàn' campaign.
They should be punished according to law."
An imperial edict ordered them to pay grain to redeem their crimes
and be exiled to Xīngzhōu.
The authorities then arrested Jìn
and sent him in chains to the place of exile.
After several years,
his son replaced him there,
and he died at eighty.
No records exist for Zhū Níng and others.
Niú Jǐngxiān,
his origin unknown.
He served as a Censor.
When the Jīnchuān Gate opened,
he changed clothes and fled by night,
dying in a Buddhist temple in Hángzhōu.
Later, the partisans of Qí and Huáng were thoroughly investigated,
and their properties confiscated.
When the Yān army entered,
over forty court officials lowered themselves from the city wall and fled in one night.
Their names, titles, and origins
cannot be ascertained.
However, it is traditionally said
that there were Chéng Jì and others like the Hexi porter and the pot mender.
Chéng Jì,
was from Cháoyì.
He possessed magical arts.
At the end of the Hóngwǔ reign, he was an education director in Yuèchí.
When Emperor Huì ascended the throne,
Jì submitted a memorial stating
that in a certain month and day, northern troops would rise.
The Emperor deemed it inappropriate to say
and had him arrested,
intending to execute him.
Jì cried out:
"Your Majesty, please imprison your servant.
If my words are not proven,
it will not be too late to die."
So he was put in prison.
Later, when the Yān army rose,
he was released
and appointed as a compiler.
He participated in the northern expedition army on the Huái River.
After a defeat,
he was recalled.
Some say
that after the victory at Xúzhōu,
the generals erected steles to commemorate their achievements.
Jì went to sacrifice there one night;
no one could fathom why.
Later, when the Prince of Yān passed Xúzhōu,
he saw the steles and was furious,
ordering his attendants to smash them.
After smashing twice,
he suddenly said:
"Stop,
record the inscription for me."
Afterward,
he punished people according to the steles,
and no one was spared,
but Jì's name happened to be on the part that was smashed off.
However, upon investigation,
there was no victory at Xúzhōu.
When the Jīnchuān Gate opened,
Jì fled.
Some say the Emperor also fled as a monk,
and Jì followed him.
His ultimate fate is unknown.
The hél-xī [Héxī] laborer
—no one knew where he was from.
In the winter of Jiànwén [Jiànwén] fourth year (1402),
he wore a kudzu-fiber robe and begged for food in the streets of Jīnchéng [Jīnchéng].
Later,
he went to hél-xī [Héxī] and became a laborer for the Lǔ [Lǔ] family in Zhuānglàng [Zhuānglàng].
He earned wages to buy a sheepskin cloak,
and covered it with his old kudzu-fiber robe.
Though tattered and torn, he refused to discard it.
When exhausted from hard labor,
he would hum to himself,
or sometimes be heard weeping at night.
After a long time,
a court official from the capital arrived,
recognized the laborer,
and wanted to speak with him.
The laborer fled to the Nánshān [Nánshān] to avoid him.
Someone asked the court official,
"Who is this laborer?"
The official also did not answer.
After several years in Zhuānglàng [Zhuānglàng],
he fell ill and was about to die.
He called his master and entrusted him, saying:
"When I die, do not shroud me.
When the northwest wind rises,
cremate me,
and do not bury my bones."
The Lǔ [Lǔ] family followed his instructions.
The pot-mender
often traveled between Kuízhōu [Kuízhōu] and Chóngqìng [Chóngqìng],
working as a pot-mender.
For several years,
many people in Sìchuān [Sìchuān] knew him.
One day,
in the market of Kuízhōu [Kuízhōu], he met a person,
and they looked at each other in astonishment.
After a moment,
they embraced and wept,
then went together into a mountain cave,
sitting and talking all day.
They embraced and wept again,
then parted ways.
That person was Fēng-wēng [Féng Wēng].
Wēng [Wēng] was in Kuízhōu [Kuízhōu], teaching texts to children,
providing them with food and clothing.
He was skilled at writing ancient poetry.
His poems were later signed Mǎ Èrzi [Mǎ Èrzi],
or Mǎ Gōng [Mǎ Gōng],
or Sàimǎ Xiānshēng [Sàimǎ Xiānshēng].
Later, both men's whereabouts were unknown.
Also, in Kuàijī [Kuàijī], there were two recluses: one a Yúnmén [Yúnmén] monk,
the other a woodcutter from Ruòyē Xī [Ruòyě Xī].
The monk would often boat and compose poems,
then burn them upon returning.
The woodcutter would often use reeds to draw characters on the creek sand,
then,
he would always disturb the sand.
Some people, suspicious of him,
embraced him from behind to observe,
and found that all [the characters] were laments of lonely officials exiled from their country.
At that time, there was also a Yùshān [Yùshān] woodcutter,
who lived on Dōngshān [Dōngshān] in Jīnhuá [Jīnhuá].
He wore hemp clothes and a bamboo hat,
which he never changed throughout his life.
He once inscribed a poem for someone named Wáng [Wáng],
titled "Zōngrén" [Zōngrén] (Clan Member),
hence it was suspected that his surname was Wáng [Wáng].
Xuě'ān Héshàng [Xuě'ān Héshàng] (Monk Xuě'ān)
was suspected by people to be Yè Xīxián [Yè Xīxián],
as seen in the biography of Liàn Zǐníng [Liàn Zǐníng].
Several decades later,
Wáng Zhào [Wáng Zhào] from Sōngyáng [Sōngyáng] traveled to Zhìpíng Sì [Zhìpíng Sì],
and found a scroll of writing on the revolving scripture cabinet.
It recorded the deeds of over twenty fugitive officials of Jiànwén [Jiànwén],
but the paper and ink were so decayed
that only nine persons could be identified:
Liáng Tiányù [Liáng Tiányù], Liáng Liángyù [Liáng Liángyù], Liáng Liángyòng [Liáng Liángyòng], and Liáng Zhōngjié [Liáng Zhōngjié],
all from Dìnghǎi [Dìnghǎi],
of the same clan,
and serving in the court together.
Tiányù [Tiányù]
was an Administrator (lángzhōng [lángzhōng]).
When the capital fell,
he left to become a monk.
Liángyù [Liáng Liángyù]
was a Middle Secretariat Drafter (zhōngshū shèrén [zhōngshū shèrén]).
He changed his name,
fled to Hǎinán [Hǎinán],
and lived out his old age by selling books.
Liángyòng [Liáng Liángyòng] was a naval officer
and died by drowning.
Zhōngjié [Zhōngjié] was fond of Lǎozi [Lǎozi] and the Tàixuán Jīng [Tàixuán Jīng],
and became a Daoist priest.
Hé Shēn [Hé Shēn], Sòng Hé [Sòng Hé], and Guō Jié [Guō Jié],
all of unknown origin,
served as Middle Secretariat officials together.
Shēn [Shēn] was an envoy to Shǔ [Shǔ].
Upon hearing of the upheaval at Xiágkǒu [Xiágkǒu],
he vomited blood,
developed a carbuncle on his back, and died.
Hé [Hé] and Jié [Jié] carried divination books and fled to foreign lands,
dying as sojourners.
Hé Zhōu [Hé Zhōu],
from Hǎizhōu [Hǎizhōu].
His official post is unknown,
he also left to become a diviner,
and died as a sojourner.
Guō Liáng [Guō Liáng],
whose office and records are untraceable,
agreed with Liáng Zhōngjié [Liáng Zhōngjié] to abandon their official posts and become Daoist priests.
The names of the other eleven persons are lost.
Zhèng Xī [Zhèng Xī] from Jìnnyún [Jìnnyún] recorded these events in his Zhōngxián Qímì Lù [Zhōngxián Qímì Lù] (Record of Loyal and Virtuous Secrets),
which was transmitted to the world.
During the Wànlì [Wànlì] era,
there was another Zhìshēn Lù [Zhìshēn Lù] (Record of Self-Realization) in Jiāngnán [Jiāngnán],
said to have been found in a Daoist text from Máoshān [Máoshān].
It was narrated by Shǐ Zhòngbīn [Shǐ Zhòngbīn] of Wújiāng [Wújiāng], who served as attendant scribe during the Jiànwén [Jiànwén] period,
and recorded the emperor's escape and subsequent events in great detail.
Zhòngbīn [Zhòngbīn], Chéng Jì [Chéng Jì], Yè Xīxián [Yè Xīxián], and Niú Jǐngxiān [Niú Jǐngxiān] were all officials who fled with the emperor.
There were also names like Liáo Píng [Liáo Píng] and Jīn Jiāo [Jīn Jiāo],
and Xuě'ān Héshàng [Xuě'ān Héshàng], the pot-mender, etc.,
all with their names and official titles clearly stated.
Officials and gentry of the time all believed it.
The Supervising Secretary Ōuyáng Diàolǜ [Ōuyáng Diàolǜ] presented this book to the court,
hoping to request posthumous titles and establish shrines for them.
However, upon investigation, Zhòngbīn [Zhòngbīn] had in fact never been an attendant scribe.
The record must have appeared late
and is unreliable as an embellishment.
An appreciation states:
In the "Jìngnàn" [Jìngnàn]
Campaign,
many court officials sacrificed themselves for the nation.
The calm dedication to principle by people like Wáng Gěn [Wáng Gěn] and others
could only be achieved by those with a profound understanding of great righteousness.
Gāo Wēi [Gāo Wēi], a commoner,
valiantly submitted a memorial,
requesting the return to the feudal domain;
his arguments were grand,
and he was also able to transcend and retreat far away,
concealing his tracks to preserve himself,
truly a remarkable scholar.
As for the various worthies who fled into seclusion,
although their names appear scattered in various family biographies and records,
they are not fully verifiable.
Yet, their loyalty, righteousness, and extraordinary integrity
are widely cherished and spoken of by people.
The tradition says:
"Rather than overlook and dismiss them,
it is better to overlook and preserve them."
This is also sufficient to uphold moral principles
and inspire the weak to set their aspirations.
Collations and Notes
Biographies Thirty-Two: Shèng Yōng [Shèng Yōng], Píng Ān [Píng Ān], Hé Fú [Hé Fú], Gù Chéng [Gù Chéng]
Shèng Yōng [Shèng Yōng],
no one knew where he was from.
During the Hóngwǔ [Hóngwǔ] reign,
he successively rose to the position of Commander-in-chief (dū zhīhuī [dū zhīhuī]).
At the beginning of Jiànwén [Jiànwén]'s reign,
as a參將 (cānjīang [cānjīang], assistant general), he accompanied Gěng Bǐngwén [Gěng Bǐngwén] in attacking Yàn [Yàn].
When Lǐ Jǐnglóng [Lǐ Jǐnglóng] replaced Bǐngwén [Bǐngwén],
he then served under Jǐnglóng [Jǐnglóng].
In the fourth month of the second year (1400),
Jǐnglóng [Jǐnglóng] was defeated at Báigōu Hé [Báigōu Hé],
and fled to Jǐnán [Jǐnán].
The Yàn [Yàn] army followed closely,
and Jǐnglóng [Jǐnglóng] fled south again.
Yōng [Yōng] and Cāncèng [Cāncèng] Tiě Xuán [Tiě Xuán] exerted their full strength to defend steadfastly.
The Yàn [Yàn] army attacked and besieged for three months but could not overcome them.
Yōng [Yōng] and Xuán [Xuán] led their troops out at night to ambush the enemy.
The Yàn [Yàn] forces suffered a great defeat,
lifted the siege and departed.
Taking advantage of the victory, they recaptured Dézhōu [Dézhōu].
In the ninth month, for his merits, he was enfeoffed as Lìchéng Hóu [Lìchéng Hóu],
with a stipend of a thousand dàn [dàn] of grain.
Soon after, he was appointed General Pacifying Yàn [Yàn] (píngyàn jiāngjūn [píngyàn jiāngjūn]),
serving as Commander-in-chief (zǒngbīng guān [zǒngbīng guān]).
Chén Huī [Chén Huī] and Píng Ān [Píng Ān] were made Assistant Commanders-in-chief of the left and right,
and Mǎ Pǔ [Mǎ Pǔ] and Xú Zhēn [Xú Zhēn] were made Assistant Generals of the left and right.
Xuán [Xuán] was promoted to Minister of War (bīngbù shàngshū [bīngbù shàngshū]) and Military Advisor (cāncàn jūnwù [cāncàn jūnwù]).
At that time, Wú Jié and Píng Ān were stationed in Dìngzhōu,
Shèng Yōng in Dézhōu,
and Xú Kǎi in Cāngzhōu,
forming a flanking position.
That winter,
the Yān army attacked Cāngzhōu,
defeated and captured Xú Kǎi,
plundered his baggage,
and advanced to attack Jìníng.
Shèng Yōng led his troops to station in Dōngchāng to intercept them,
arraying his forces with their backs to the city.
The Yān King led his troops straight forward to attack the left wing of Shèng Yōng's army,
but it did not move.
He then charged the center;
Shèng Yōng opened his formation, letting the King in,
and surrounded him with several layers.
Yān general Zhū Néng led barbarian cavalry to rescue him,
and the King seized the opportunity to break out of the encirclement.
However, the Yān army suffered heavy casualties from firearms,
and grand general Zhāng Yù died on the battlefield.
The King, with only a hundred horsemen, brought up the rear guard,
retreating to Guǎntáo.
Shèng Yōng sent a dispatch to Wú Jié and Píng Ān to intercept the Yān army's retreat route from Zhēndìng.
In the first month of the following year,
Wú Jié and Píng Ān fought unfavorably at Shēnzhōu,
and the Yān army was finally able to return.
In this battle,
the Yān elite forces were almost completely lost,
and Shèng Yōng's army's prestige greatly increased.
The Emperor offered sacrifices in the ancestral temple to announce the victory.
In the third month,
the Yān army again marched south to Bǎodìng.
Shèng Yōng camped along the river.
The King led light cavalry to reconnoiter,
passing by the formation.
Shèng Yōng sent a thousand cavalry to pursue them,
but they were shot back by the Yān army.
When the battle commenced,
Shèng Yōng's army advanced in a shield formation.
The King ordered his infantry to attack first,
and his cavalry to charge in when an opportunity arose.
Shèng Yōng commanded his army to fight fiercely,
slaying their general Tán Yuān.
However, Zhū Néng, Zhāng Wǔ, and others led their troops to fight desperately,
and the King, with his crack cavalry, broke through the formation to join Zhū Néng.
Shèng Yōng's brave generals Zhuāng Dé, Zàoqí Zhāng, and others all died in battle.
That day,
the Yān army was almost defeated.
The next day they fought again,
the Yān army in the northeast,
Shèng Yōng's army in the southwest,
from 7 AM to 3 PM,
each side having victories and defeats.
Both armies were exhausted,
and the generals and soldiers each sat down to rest.
They rose to fight again,
when suddenly a strong northeast wind arose,
and flying dust obscured the sky.
The Yān army, taking advantage of the wind, shouted loudly
and attacked horizontally from both sides.
Shèng Yōng was utterly defeated,
and fled back to Dézhōu,
his morale shattered thereafter.
Soon after, Yān general Lǐ Yuǎn burned the grain ships in Pèixiàn,
and Shèng Yōng's army consequently ran out of provisions.
The next year,
they were defeated in the battle of Língbì,
and Píng Ān and others were captured.
Shèng Yōng alone led his army south,
arraying his warships on the south bank of the Huái River.
Yān general Qiū Fú and others secretly crossed the river,
appearing behind Shèng Yōng.
Shèng Yōng could not hold out,
and retreated to formulate a plan to defend the Jiāng (Yangtze) River.
The Yān army crossed the Huái River,
capturing Yángzhōu via Xūyí.
Shèng Yōng engaged in battle at Liùhé and Pǔzikǒu,
but suffered losses in both.
Grand Coordinator Chén Xuān led his fleet to surrender to Yān,
and the Yān army then crossed the Jiāng.
Shèng Yōng hastily gathered sea vessels and went out from Gāozī Harbor to engage them,
but was again defeated,
and his army further disintegrated.
When Chéngzǔ entered the capital,
Shèng Yōng surrendered with his remaining troops,
and was immediately ordered to guard Huái'ān.
Soon after, an imperial edict was bestowed, saying:
"Previously, as Shāndōng was not yet pacified,
I ordered you,卿, to garrison Huái'ān.
Now that Tiě Xuàn has been captured,
and all the commanderies are pacified.
I observe that Shāndōng has long been troubled by warfare,
and is exhausted by transportation.
You should gather soldiers and nurture the people,
to accord with My wishes."
In the first year of Yǒnglè, he retired.
Not long after,
Commander Wáng Qīn impeached Shèng Yōng for his crimes,
and Wáng Qīn was immediately promoted to Assistant Commander.
Thereupon, Censor-in-Chief Chén Yīng impeached Shèng Yōng for harboring resentment and having ulterior motives.
Shèng Yōng committed suicide.
Píng Ān,
a native of Chú,
had the childhood name Bǎo'ér.
His father, Píng Dìng,
followed Tàizǔ in raising an army,
and served as Assistant Commander of Jìníng Guard.
He followed Cháng Yùchūn in taking Yuán Dū,
and died in battle.
Píng Ān was initially an adopted son of Tàizǔ,
fierce and skilled in battle,
capable of lifting several hundred *jin*.
He inherited his father's position,
was promoted to Commander of Mìyún,
and then to Assistant Grand Coordinator of the Right Army.
In the first year of Jiànwén, when the Yān was attacked,
Píng Ān served as a leading general in the expedition.
When Lǐ Jǐnglóng took over as commander,
he employed Píng Ān as vanguard.
When the Yān King was about to cross the Báigōu River,
Píng Ān ambushed him with ten thousand cavalry on the river bank.
The Yān King said:
"Píng Ān,
is but a young rascal;
in previous years, when he accompanied me beyond the frontier,
he learned my military tactics.
Today I must first defeat him."
When the battle commenced,
he could not defeat Píng Ān.
At that time, the southern army of six hundred thousand
was arrayed along the river.
The King led his generals and soldiers to charge into the formation,
fighting until dusk,
with mutual casualties.
As night deepened,
they each withdrew their armies.
The Yān King lost his way,
with only three attendants on horseback;
he dismounted and lay on the ground, observing the river to distinguish east from west,
and only then did he know the location of his camp.
The next day they fought again,
and Píng Ān defeated Yān generals Fáng Kuān and Chén Hēng.
Seeing the situation was critical,
the Yān King personally braved arrows and stones to fight fiercely.
His horse was wounded, his arrows exhausted,
and his sword broken and unusable.
He ran and climbed an embankment,
feigning to raise his whip to summon his rear cavalry to deceive the enemy.
Coincidentally, Gāo Xù arrived with reinforcements,
and he was thus spared.
At this time,
among all the generals, Píng Ān fought the most vigorously,
and the King was almost reached by Píng Ān's spear.
Afterwards, he was defeated,
the details are in the biography of Chéngzǔ.
The Yān army besieged Jǐnán.
Píng Ān camped at Dānjiāqiáo,
planning to emerge from the Yùhé River and seize the Yān supply boats.
He also selected five thousand skilled water soldiers to cross the river,
intending to attack Dézhōu.
The siege was then lifted.
Píng Ān and Wú Jié advanced and garrisoned Dìngzhōu.
The next year,
Yān defeated Shèng Yōng at Jiāhé,
and then turned its army to fight Píng Ān at Dānjiāqiáo.
Píng Ān fought fiercely and greatly defeated them,
capturing their general Xuē Lù,
but not long after,
he escaped.
They fought again at Hūtuó River,
and Píng Ān again defeated them.
Píng Ān constructed a wooden tower in the formation,
several *zhang* high.
When the battle was fierce,
he would climb the tower to observe,
firing powerful crossbows at the Yān army,
killing many.
Suddenly a great wind arose,
tearing off roofs and uprooting trees,
sounding like thunder.
Grand Coordinators Dèng Jiǎn, Chén Péng, and others were trapped among the enemy,
and Píng Ān then fled to Zhēndìng.
The Yān King fought several major battles with the southern army,
personally charging into the formations each time,
sweeping away all in his path,
but only Píng Ān's and Shèng Yōng's armies repeatedly frustrated him.
In the battle of Hūtuó,
arrows gathered on the King's banner like hedgehog quills.
The King sent someone to send the banner to Běipíng,
instructing the Heir Apparent to carefully preserve it to show to future generations.
Gù Chéng had already been captured and was in Yān;
upon seeing it, he wept and said:
"I have been in the army since youth.
Now I am old,
having experienced many battles,
but I have never seen anything like this."
After a month,
the Yān army sallied out from Dàmíng.
Ān, along with Yōng, and Wú Jié, etc., divided their troops to harass its supply routes.
The Yān king worried about this,
and sent Commander Wǔ Shèng to submit a letter to the court,
requesting the withdrawal of Ān and others to cease hostilities,
as a strategy to delay the army.
The emperor did not permit it.
The Yān king also decided to march south,
sending Lǐ Yuǎn and others to secretly go to Pèixiàn,
burn grain boats,
plunder Zhāngdé,
destroy Wěijiān Zhài,
and persuade Línxiàn to surrender.
At this time, Ān was in Zhēndìng,
and judging Běipíng to be undefended,
he led ten thousand cavalry directly to Běipíng.
He reached Píngcūn,
and camped fifty lǐ from the city.
The Yān king feared,
and sent Liú Jiāng and others to gallop back to relieve it.
Ān fought unsuccessfully,
and withdrew.
At this time, Fáng Zhāo, the garrison commander of Dàtóng, led troops into Zǐjīng Guān,
occupying Yìzhōu Xīshuǐ Zhài to scout Běipíng,
and Ān supplied them from Zhēndìng.
In the eighth month,
the Yān army returned north.
Ān and the Yān general Lǐ Bīn fought at Yángcūn,
and Ān defeated him.
In the fourth year,
the Yān army again marched south,
and destroyed Xiāoxiàn.
Ān led his army to follow closely behind it,
reaching Féihé.
The Yān generals Bái Yì, Wáng Zhēn, and Liú Jiāng met the enemy.
Ān fought,
and slew Zhēn.
Zhēn was
a valiant general,
of whom the Yān king once said:
"If all generals are as brave as Wáng Zhēn,
what cannot be accomplished?"
By this point, he was killed by Ān.
The Yān king then personally went to meet the battle.
Ān's subordinate Huǒ'ěrhūi (Huo'erhui) wielded his spear and shouted loudly,
advancing directly to stab the king.
His horse suddenly stumbled, and he was captured,
so Ān slightly retreated.
After a while,
he advanced again to Xiǎohé,
