spreading out his left and right wings to attack the Yān army,
and slaying its general Chén Wén.
After a while,
he again moved his army to Qíméishān,
and with his generals arrayed for a great battle,
from noon to dusk,
he again defeated them.
The Yān generals plotted to return north,
to plan for a later advance.
The king did not listen.
Soon, Hé Fú's army also arrived,
and joined with Ān.
The Yān army became even more frightened,
and the king wore his armor day and night for several days.
Fú wanted to prolong the battle and wear out the Yān army,
so he moved his camp to Língbì,
fortifying himself with deep trenches and high ramparts,
but his grain supply was blocked by the Yān army,
and could not reach him.
Ān divided his troops to go and meet it,
but the Yān king used elite cavalry to cut off Ān's army,
dividing it into two.
Fú opened his ramparts to come to the rescue,
but was defeated by Gāo Xù.
The generals planned to move the army to Huáihé for supplies,
and at night ordered the army to retreat upon hearing three cannon shots.
The next day,
the Yān army suddenly attacked the ramparts,
and fired three cannon shots.
The army mistakenly thought it was their own signal,
and rushed to the gate,
thus falling into great disarray.
The Yān army took advantage of this,
and people and horses filled the trenches and moats.
Fú escaped alone on horseback,
while Ān, along with Chén Huī, Mǎ Pǔ, Xú Zhēn, Sūn Chéng, and thirty-seven others were all captured.
One hundred fifty-odd civil officials and eunuchs in the army were also captured,
this was the xīn-sì day of the fourth month.
Ān had long been stationed in Zhēndìng,
repeatedly defeating the Yān army,
and slaying several valiant generals,
so no Yān general dared to meet his vanguard.
When he was captured at this time,
the army cheered so loudly that it shook the earth, saying:
"We are safe from now on!"
They all clamored to kill Ān.
The Yān king valued his talent and bravery,
and selected elite soldiers to escort him to Běipíng,
ordering the heir apparent and Guō Zī and others to treat him well.
When the king ascended the throne,
he appointed Ān as the Běipíng Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ,
and soon promoted him to Xíng Hòufǔ Dūdū Qiānshì.
In the third month of the seventh year of Yǒnglè,
the emperor toured Běijīng.
As he was about to arrive,
he reviewed a memorial and saw Ān's name,
and said to his attendants:
"Is Píng Bǎo'ér still alive?"
When Ān heard this,
he committed suicide.
An order was given to grant his son the salary of a Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ.
Hé Fú was
a native of Fèngyáng.
In the early Hóngwǔ era,
he accumulated merits and became Jīnwǔ Hòuwèi Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī.
He followed Fù Yǒudé to conquer Yúnnán,
and was promoted to Dūdū Qiānshì.
He also followed Lán Yù beyond the Great Wall,
reaching Pǔyú'ér Hǎi.
In the twenty-first year,
Wú Gāo, Marquis of Jiāngyīn, led the surrendered people from Yíběi south on a campaign.
Upon reaching Yuánjiāng,
the multitude rebelled,
exiting from Sīzhōu through Jīng and Fán,
and via Wèihé,
they wished to flee back to the desert.
In the first month of the following year,
Fú and Dūdū Niè Wěi pursued and attacked them,
reaching various Fū and Yán,
annihilating them completely,
and then moved their troops to suppress the Dūyún barbarians,
capturing and beheading tens of thousands.
In the twenty-fourth year,
he was appointed Píngqiāng Jiāngjūn,
to suppress the rebel barbarians Ā Zī of Yuèzhōu,
defeating and subjugating them.
He selected a place to build stockades and settle their people,
establishing Níngyuè Bǎo.
He then pacified the various barbarians of Jiǔmíng and Jiǔxìng.
Soon, he joined forces with Dūdū Máo Dǐng to lead troops to attack Wǔkāi.
Before they could set off,
the various barbarians of Bìjié rebelled again,
greatly plundering the garrisons,
and killing officials and soldiers.
Fú ordered the various guards of Bìjié to prepare strictly,
and dispatched Dūdū Táo Wén and others to join Dǐng in assaulting their lair.
They captured the rebel chiefs,
executed them,
divided their troops to capture all the barbarians,
built forts and established garrisons,
then proceeded to Wǔkāi.
He requested to use his military strength to suppress Shē Xiāng of Shuǐxī.
This was not allowed.
In the third month of the thirtieth year,
Jū Zōngbìdēng and other Shuǐxī barbarians rebelled,
and he joined Gù Chéng to suppress them.
In that winter, he was appointed Zhēnglǔ Zuǒ Jiāngjūn,
assisting Xīpíng Hóu Mù Chūn in suppressing Dāo Gànmèng, the rebel barbarian of Lùchuān.
The following year,
Fú and Dūdū Qú Néng crossed Gāoliáng Gōngshān,
assaulted Nándiàn,
and captured its chief Dāo Míngmèng.
They returned to attack Jǐnghǎn Zhài,
but failed to take it.
Chūn arrived with elite troops,
the rebels panicked and scattered,
Gànmèng feared,
and begged for surrender.
Soon after, Chūn died,
and the rebels again harbored disloyalty.
At this time, Tàizǔ had already passed away,
and Huìdì had just ascended the throne,
appointing Fú as Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn.
Fú then defeated and captured Dāo Gànmèng,
subjugating his seventy thousand followers,
divided his troops to attack and take various stockades,
and the Lùchuān territory was entirely pacified.
In the first year of Jiànwén, he returned to the capital,
and was promoted to Dūdū Tóngzhī based on his merits.
He trained troops in Dézhōu,
and was promoted to Zuǒ Dūdū.
He joined Shèng Yōng and Píng Ān with their armies to attack Yān,
fought unsuccessfully north of Huái River,
and fled back.
Chéngzǔ 成祖 ascended the throne,
and, recognizing Fú Sùjiāng's 福宿將 military knowledge,
he sincerely put him to use.
He arranged for Fú Sùjiāng's 福宿jiāng niece, Lady Xú 徐, to marry Zhào Wáng 趙王.
Soon after, he ordered Fú Sùjiāng 福宿將 to wear the seal of the Commander-in-chief for Conquering Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn Yìn 征虜將軍印),
appointed him Commander-in-chief (Zǒngbīng Guān 總兵官),
garrisoned him at Níngxià 寧夏,
and gave him control over the armies of Shānxi 山西, Shǎnxī 陝西, and Hénán 河南.
When Fú Sùjiāng 福宿將 arrived at the garrison,
he proclaimed the emperor's virtues and intentions,
attracting people from afar,
and various tribes from beyond the frontier surrendered one after another.
The border was peaceful.
He then requested to establish post stations, cultivate fields, store grain,
and fix rewards and punishments
as a long-term plan.
At this time, there were those who slandered him.
The emperor did not listen,
and issued an edict praising and comforting him.
In the eighth month of the fifth year of Yǒnglè 永樂 (1407), he was transferred to Gānsù 甘肅.
Fú Sùjiāng 福宿將 was strict in governing the army,
and many subordinates found this inconvenient.
The emperor secretly sent an envoy to warn Fú Sùjiāng 福宿將,
telling him to protect himself well
and not to be harmed by petty individuals.
In the sixth year (1408),
Fú Sùjiāng 福宿將 requested to send a frontier general from the capital (Jīngshī Fānjiāng 京師蕃將) to lead the surrendered people from beyond the north.
The emperor replied:
"You have long commanded both frontier and Han soldiers;
I fear that your large force might lead to slander.
You are an old general,
and I sincerely trust and rely on you;
do not worry."
Soon after, he requested to use cloth to purchase horses,
select the good ones, group them separately,
and appoint officials to specially manage them with seals.
As a result, the horses greatly multiplied.
The horse pastures of Yǒngchāng Yuàn 永昌苑 began from this time.
The following year (1409),
Běnyàshīlǐ 本雅失里 and Ālǔtái 阿魯台 intended to invade
but were defeated by the Wǎlà 瓦剌,
fleeing to the Lúqú Hé 臚朐河.
They wished to gather the scattered troops of various tribes and spy on Hexi 河西.
An edict ordered Fú Sùjiāng 福宿將 to prepare his troops rigorously.
Over ten people, including the princes, dukes, and Sītú 司徒 from beyond the north, led their subordinates to station at Yìjí nǎi 亦集乃
and requested to join the empire.
Fú Sùjiāng 福宿將 reported this.
The emperor ordered his imperial son Yáng Róng 楊榮 to assist Fú Sùjiāng 福宿將 in managing them,
and all their people surrendered.
Fú Sùjiāng 福宿將 personally went to Yìjí nǎi 亦集乃 to pacify them,
sending their chiefs to the capital (Jīngshī 京師).
The emperor praised Fú Sùjiāng's 福宿將 achievements,
ordering Yáng Róng 楊榮 to immediately confer the title of Níngyuǎn Hóu 寧遠侯 on Fú Sùjiāng 福宿將 in the army,
with a stipend of one thousand dàn 石,
and an edict that Fú Sùjiāng 福宿將 could act first and report later on military matters.
In the eighth year (1410),
the emperor led a northern expedition
and summoned Fú Sùjiāng 福宿將 to accompany him beyond the frontier.
Initially,
the emperor, recognizing Fú Sùjiāng's 福宿將 talent and strategy,
favored and trusted him above other generals.
Fú Sùjiāng 福宿將 also knew how to avoid suspicion;
he never made decisions alone in important matters.
While at the garrison, he once requested to take horses from the Xīpíng Hóu's 西平侯 family's stables in Gǒngchāng 鞏昌
to increase the stock.
The emperor replied:
"During the time of the late emperor (Huángkǎo 皇考), many noble and close families were allowed to keep horses
to show the intention of sharing wealth and honor.
Your proposal is indeed for the country,
but it is not the way to treat meritorious relatives."
He did not approve.
For other requests, he usually granted them,
entrusting him with heavy responsibilities.
However, during the expedition,
Fú Sùjiāng 福宿將 repeatedly disregarded commands.
When officials spoke of his offenses,
Fú Sùjiāng 福宿將 became increasingly resentful and complained.
When the army returned,
Metropolitan Censor (Dū Yùshǐ 都御史) Chén Yīng 陳瑛 again impeached him.
Fú Sùjiāng 福宿將, fearful,
hanged himself,
and his title was abolished.
Zhào Wángfēi 趙王妃 was also soon deposed.
Gù Chéng 顧成,
courtesy name Jǐngsháo 景韶,
was originally from Xiāngtán 湘潭.
His grandfather operated boats,
traveling between the Jiāng 江 and Huái 淮 rivers,
and thus settled in Jiāngdū 江都.
Gù Chéng 顧成 was tall and imposing in his youth,
with extraordinary physical strength.
He was skilled in horse-spear fighting
and tattooed his body to distinguish himself.
When Tàizǔ 太祖 crossed the Jiāng 江,
Gù Chéng 顧成 came to surrender.
Because of his bravery, he was selected as a personal guard (Zhàngqián Qīnbīng 帳前親兵),
carrying the canopy during the emperor's movements.
Once, when accompanying the emperor on an outing,
the boat became stuck in sand.
Gù Chéng 顧成 carried the boat and walked.
Following the attack on Zhènjiāng 鎮江,
he and ten warriors fought their way into the city.
He was captured,
and the ten warriors all died.
Gù Chéng 顧成 leaped up, broke his bonds,
struck down the one holding the knife,
and escaped.
He led the troops to attack the city,
captured it,
and was appointed Centurion (Bǎihù 百戶).
After dozens of battles, large and small,
he always achieved merit,
and was promoted to Assistant Commander of Jiānchéng Wèi 堅城衛.
Following the expedition to Shǔ 蜀,
he attacked Luójiāng 羅江,
capturing over twenty people including the Marshal (Yuánshuài 元帥),
then advanced to Hànzhōu 漢州 which surrendered.
Shǔ 蜀 was pacified,
and he was transferred to Chéngdū Hòuwèi 成都後衛.
In the sixth year of Hóngwǔ 洪wǔ (1373), he captured the rebel leader Wáng Yuánbǎo 王元保 in Chóngqìng 重慶.
In the eighth year (1375), he was transferred to guard Guìzhōu 貴州.
At that time, the various Man 蠻 tribes were rebellious and unpredictable.
Gù Chéng 顧成 campaigned for several years,
completely pacifying them.
Afterward,
he accompanied Yǐngchuān Hóu 潁川侯 Fù Yǒudé 傅友德 in the expedition to Yúnnán 雲南,
serving as vanguard.
He was the first to capture Pǔdìng 普定,
where Gù Chéng 顧成 was left to build palisades and defend.
Tens of thousands of Man 蠻 came to attack.
Gù Chéng 顧成 went out of the palisade,
personally killing hundreds of people,
and the bandits retreated.
The remaining bandits were still in the southern city.
Gù Chéng 顧成 beheaded a captive but released one, saying:
"I will come at the second watch tonight to kill you."
At the second watch that night,
horns were blown and cannons fired.
The bandits heard this and all fled,
leaving countless weapons and armor,
and Gù Chéng 顧成 was promoted to Commander (Zhǐhuīshǐ 指揮使).
All the Man 蠻 tribes subservient to Pǔdìng 普定 were pacified.
In the seventeenth year (1384), he pacified Āhēi 阿黑, Luóshī 螺螄, and over ten other stockades.
The following year, he memorialized to abolish Pǔdìng Fǔ 普定府,
dividing its territory into three prefectures and six chiefdoms,
and was promoted to Vice-commander of Guìzhōu 都指揮同知.
There were accusations that he accepted bribes and illicitly used jade articles and other items,
but due to his long service, he was not questioned.
In the twenty-ninth year (1396), he was promoted to Assistant Military Commissioner of the Right Army (Yòujūn Dūdū Qiānshì 右軍都督僉事),
wearing the seal of the Commander-in-chief for Conquering the South (Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn Yìn 征南將軍印),
and joined Hé Fú 何福 in suppressing the Shuǐxī Man 水西蠻,
beheading their chief Jū Zōngbìdēng 居宗必登.
The following year (1397), the Man 蠻 tribes of Xībǎo 西堡 and Cānglàng 滄浪 revolted.
Gù Chéng 顧成 sent Commander Lù Bǐng 陸秉 and his son Tǒng 統 to suppress them separately.
Gù Chéng 顧成 was in Guìzhōu 貴州 for over ten years,
suppressing hundreds of Miáo 苗 caves and stockades,
executing their leaders
and pacifying the remaining people.
His benevolence and trustworthiness were widely spread,
and the Man 蠻 people submitted.
In the second month of that year,
he was recalled to the capital.
In the first year of Jiànwén 建文 (1399), he became Military Commissioner of the Left Army (Zuǒjūn Dūdū 左軍都督),
and followed Gěng Bǐngwén 耿炳文 to resist the Yān 燕 army.
He fought at Zhēndìng 真定
and was captured.
Yān Wáng 燕王 untied him, saying:
"Heaven has delivered you to me."
He was sent to Běipíng 北平
to assist the crown prince (Shìzǐ 世子) in guarding it.
When the southern army besieged the city,
defense and deployment were entirely up to Gù Chéng 顧成.
When Yān Wáng 燕王 ascended the throne,
Gù Chéng 顧成 was enfeoffed as Zhènyuǎn Hóu 鎮遠侯 for his merits,
with a stipend of one thousand five hundred dàn 石,
given a hereditary warrant,
and ordered to continue guarding Guìzhōu 貴州.
In the first year of Yǒnglè 永樂 (1403), he submitted a memorial
requesting strict preparations for the northwestern borders
and the early establishment of the crown prince (Dōnggōng 東宮).
The emperor praised and responded to him.
In the third month of the sixth year (1408),
he was summoned to the capital (Jīng 京)
and given gold and silk before being sent back.
Tián Chēn 田琛, the Pacification Commissioner of Sīzhōu 思州, and Tián Zōngdǐng 田宗鼎, the Pacification Commissioner of Sīnán 思南, were at war.
An edict ordered Gù Chéng 顧成 to lead fifty thousand troops to press their borders,
and Tián Chēn 田琛 and others were captured.
Consequently, the territories of Sīzhōu 思州 and Sīnán 思南 were divided and re-established as prefectures and counties,
and then the Guìzhōu Administration Commission (Guìzhōu Bùzhèng Sī 貴州布政司) was established.
In the eighth month of that year (1408),
the Táiluó Miáo 臺羅苗 Pǔliàng 普亮 and others revolted.
An edict ordered Gù Chéng 顧成 to lead the troops of two regional military commissions and three guards to suppress them.
Chéng was naturally loyal and cautious,
having a wide knowledge of books and history.
He first resided in Běipíng,
offering many plans and strategies.
However, he ultimately refused to lead troops,
and even when granted weapons, he would not accept them.
He was again appointed to Guìzhōu,
and repeatedly pacified the rebellious Mán of Bōzhōu and Dūyún.
His might awed the southern region (Nánzhōng),
and the local people erected shrines to him while he was still alive.
When he was summoned to the capital (Jīng),
he was ordered to assist the crown prince (Tàizǐ) in supervising the state.
Chéng bowed his head and said:
"The crown prince is benevolent and enlightened,
and the court officials are all virtuous.
The task of assisting and guiding is beyond my humble abilities.
I request to return to prepare against the Mán."
At that time, a group of petty individuals plotted to usurp the heir,
and the crown prince felt uneasy.
Chéng entered to bid farewell in the Wénhuá Palace,
and then said:
"Your Highness should only wholeheartedly practice filial piety and respect,
diligently care for the people.
All matters are in heaven's hands,
and petty individuals are not worth your concern."
He died in the fifth month of the twelfth year,
at the age of eighty-five.
He was posthumously granted the title Duke of Xià (Xiàguógōng)
and the posthumous name Wǔyì.
He had eight sons.
The eldest, Tǒng,
was a Commander of Pǔdìng Guard.
He was executed because Chéng surrendered to Yān.
Tǒng's son, Xīngzǔ, inherited the marquisate.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
the Mán of Guǎngxī rebelled.
Xīngzǔ was ordered by imperial edict to be the Commander-in-Chief (Zǒngbīngguān) to suppress them.
He successively pacified the Miáo of Xúnzhōu, Pínglè, Sī'ēn, and Yíshān,
and a great number surrendered.
In the Xuāndé reign,
Límì of Jiāozhǐ rebelled again,
seizing the Àiliú Pass
and besieging Qiūwēn.
At that time, Xīngzǔ was in Nánníng,
and was accused of holding back troops and not providing aid.
He was summoned and imprisoned in the Jǐnyīwèi jail,
and was released after more than a year.
At the end of the Zhèngtǒng reign,
he joined the northern expedition,
and returned safely from Tǔmù,
but was sentenced to death.
When Yěxiān pressed upon the capital,
he was reinstated with his official attire,
served as Vice Commander-in-Chief (Fù Zǒngbīng),
and defended against the enemy outside the city.
He was appointed Assistant Military Governor (Dūdū Tóngzhī)
and garrisoned Zǐjīng Pass.
In the third year of Jǐngtài, he was imprisoned again
for accepting bribes,
but was soon released.
By the grace of establishing the Eastern Palace,
he was granted the title of Earl (Bójúe).
In the early Tiānshùn reign,
he was reinstated as Marquis,
guarded Nánjīng,
and died.
His grandson Chún inherited,
died,
and had no son.
His cousin Pǔ inherited,
and was in charge of the Right Wing of the Five Armies (Wǔjūn Yòuyì).
In the second year of Hóngzhì, he was appointed General for Pacifying the Mán (Píngmán Jiāngjūn)
and garrisoned Húguǎng.
Upon his arrival,
he captured and executed the chief culprits among the Miáo.
In the tenth month of the fifth year,
Mièfùjià of Dūyún Miáo in Guìzhōu rebelled,
proclaiming himself King Dūshùn (Dūshùnwáng),
obstructing the roads to Diān and Shǔ.
Pǔ was ordered by imperial edict to be the Commander-in-Chief (Zǒngbīngguān),
leading eighty thousand troops to suppress them,
dividing them into five routes to advance simultaneously according to schedule.
He executed Fùjià and his son,
beheading tens of thousands,
was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàibǎo),
and had his salary increased by two hundred dàn of grain.
He was summoned to be the Supervisor of the Training Camps (Tídū Tuányíng)
and was in charge of the affairs of the Front Army Military Governor's Office (Qiánjūn Dūdūfǔ).
He died in the sixteenth year.
His posthumous name was Xiāngkè.
Pǔ was clean, cautious, and law-abiding.
On the day of his death,
he had no remaining assets in his purse.
Zhāng Mào, the Duke of Yīngguó, provided cloth for his funeral.
His son Shìlóng inherited,
managed the Left Picket of the Divine Machine Camp (Shénjīyíng Zuǒshào),
and gained the trust of his soldiers.
In the early Zhèngdé reign,
he was appointed Commander-in-Chief of Grain Transport (Cáoyùn Zǒngbīng),
and repeatedly requested relief for the soldiers.
He garrisoned Huái'ān for over ten years,
known for his integrity.
When Wǔzōng made his southern tour,
Jiāng Bīn was extremely arrogant,
humiliating many high officials.
Only Shìlóng refused to yield.
In the early Jiājìng reign,
he was transferred to garrison Húguǎng.
Soon after, he was summoned back.
Based on his merits in escorting the emperor and defending the capital,
he was promoted to Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàifù)
and was in charge of the affairs of the Central Army Military Governor's Office (Zhōngjūn Dūdūfǔ).
Wáng Bāngqí, a Commander of the Imperial Guard (Jǐnyī Qiānhù),
resented Grand Secretary Yáng Tínghé and Minister of War Péng Zé,
and submitted a memorial stating:
"The errors in the Hāmì strategy
were caused by these two."
The emperor was furious,
and arrested Yáng Tínghé's sons and sons-in-law.
Investigating Censor Yáng Yán submitted a memorial to intercede,
which displeased the emperor.
The matter was referred to the Five Chief Military Commissions, Nine Ministers, and Censors for deliberation.
Shìlóng stated:
"Yáng Tínghé's merits lie with the state.
Wáng Bāngqí is a petty individual,
who uses frontier matters to mislead Your Majesty and
harm the national prestige."
An imperial edict severely reprimanded him,
and he feigned illness to resign from his camp duties
and died.
He was posthumously granted the title Grand Preceptor (Tàifù)
and the posthumous name Róngjìng.
His son Huán inherited,
guarded Nánjīng,
and by imperial edict, reviewed legal cases,
righting many wrongs.
In the seventeenth year, he became Commander-in-Chief of Grain Transport (Cáoyùn Zǒngbīngguān).
The following year,
when the Empress Dowager Xiàn's coffin was transported to Chéngtiān,
three thousand grain boats were delayed because they had to make way for the coffin.
Moreover, the regions north and south of the Yangtze River suffered many disasters.
Huán requested that the disaster-stricken areas be exempted from grain transport for one year,
allowing them to pay in silver.
This benefited both the military and the people.
He also submitted seven proposals on grain transport administration,
all of which were implemented.
Those who profited from corruption in grain transport were displeased,
and spread rumors,
leading to his impeachment by Investigating Censor Wáng Jiāo.
Later,
the investigation found the accusations to be false,
and he was again appointed to garrison Huái'ān.
When the Annam incident occurred,
he was transferred to garrison Liǎngguǎng.
Mò Hóngyì was
the son of Mò Fúhǎi, the Commander-in-Chief of Annam (Ānnán Dūtǒngshǐ).
When Fúhǎi died,
Hóngyì was young.
His powerful minister Ruǎn Jìng and kinsman Mò Zhèngzhōng engaged in conflict,
causing chaos in the country.
Mò Zhèngzhōng fled into Qīnzhōu.
At that time, there was a proposal to take advantage of the situation to seize Annam.
Huán and Supervising Minister Zhōu Yán made a decisive plan,
requesting the court
to allow Hóngyì to inherit the title of Commander-in-Chief (Dūtǒngshǐ),
and Annam was thus pacified.
This occurred in the thirtieth year.
Soon after, he led troops to pacify the rebellious Yáo of Guìlín and Pínglè.
He was again ordered to garrison Huái,
and had achievements in repelling Japanese pirates (wō).
He was transferred to oversee the capital garrisons (Jīngyíng),
and was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàibǎo).
He was again sent out to supervise grain transport.
He was summoned back.
He requested retirement due to old age.
In the fifth year of Lóngqìng, he was specially appointed as Commander-in-Chief of the Capital Garrisons (Jīngyíng Zǒngdū).
Soon after, he requested to retire.
When Shénzōng ascended the throne,
he was re-appointed to be in charge of the Left Military Governor's Office (Zuǒfǔ).
After a long time,
he retired from office.
He was promoted to Junior Guardian (Shàobǎo).
He died in the ninth year of Wànlì.
He was posthumously granted the title Grand Preceptor (Tàifù)
and the posthumous name Róngxī.
From Pǔ to Huán,
three generations were all lenient, harmonious, honest, and upright,
and their conduct within the family was disciplined and cautious,
and they were knowledgeable in literature and art.
Shìlóng and Huán, for two generations, supervised grain transport,
and were both diligent in their duties.
Three generations later, his grandson Zhàojì,
died at the hands of bandits
when the capital fell.
The encomium says: In the battles of Dōngchāng and Xiǎohé,
Shèng Yōng and Píng Ān repeatedly frustrated the Yān army,
slaying its valiant generals.
Their achievements were truly magnificent.
Yet, when they were defeated in battle and captured,
they failed to uphold righteousness by taking their own lives,
instead enduring and clinging to life.
Compared to Tǐe Xuàn, Bào Zhāo and their ilk,
how could they not feel ashamed?
Hé Fú and Gù Chéng were both veteran generals from Tàizǔ's time,
who achieved merits on the frontiers.
But once they encountered the Yān army,
some retreated south,
while others were captured or beheaded.
Chéngzǔ, overlooking their faults and acknowledging their past,
granted them all feudal domains;
this was indeed fortunate.
Hé Fú did not end his career with glory,
and Gù Chéng's descendants were affected,
their glory outweighed by disgrace.
What was there to take pride in?
Collations and notes

Biographies, Volume 33: Yáo Guǎngxīao, Zhāng Yù (son Ní, Yuè, nephew Xìn), Zhū Néng, Qiū Fú (Lǐ Yuǎn, Wáng Zhōng, Wáng Cōng, Huǒ Zhēn), Tán Yuān, Wáng Zhēn, Chén Hēng (son Mào, Xú Lǐ, Fáng Kuān, Líu Cái)
Yáo Guǎngxīao
was from Chángzhōu,
originally the son of a physician.
At fourteen,
he was ordained as a monk,
named Dàoyǎn,
with the courtesy name Sīdào.
He served the Taoist Xí Yìngzhēn,
and learned his arts of yin-yang and divination.
Once, he traveled to Sōngshān Temple,
where the physiognomist Yuán Gǒng saw him and said:
"What an unusual monk!
With triangular eyes and
a shape like a sick tiger,
his nature must be bloodthirsty,
a follower of Líu Bǐngzhōng."
Dàoyǎn was greatly pleased.
During the Hóngwǔ era,
an imperial edict summoned learned Buddhist monks to be tested by the Board of Rites.
He did not accept an official position,
and was given a monk's robe to return.
Passing by Běigù Mountain,
he composed a poem reminiscing about the past.
His peer Zōng Lè said:
"Are these the words of a Buddhist monk?"
Dàoyǎn smiled and did not answer.
When Empress Gāo died,
Tàizǔ selected eminent monks to attend the various princes,
to chant scriptures and pray for blessings.
Zōng Lè, then the Left Shànshì,
recommended Dàoyǎn.
The Prince of Yān found their conversation very congenial
and requested him to accompany him.
Upon arriving in Běipíng,
he became the abbot of Qìngshòu Temple.
He frequented the princely mansion,
his movements very secretive,
often speaking privately with the prince.
When Tàizǔ died
and Huìdì ascended the throne,
he gradually stripped the powers of the various princes.
The princes of Zhōu, Xiāng, Dài, Qí, and Mǐn successively incurred his displeasure.
Dàoyǎn then secretly urged Chéngzǔ to raise an army.
Chéngzǔ said:
"The people's hearts are with him,
what can be done?"
Dàoyǎn said:
"I know the ways of Heaven;
what do the hearts of the people matter?"
He then introduced Yuán Gǒng and the diviner Jīn Zhōng.
Thereupon, Chéngzǔ's resolve grew stronger,
and he secretly selected generals and officers,
enlisted soldiers,
and gathered brave and exceptionally capable men.
The Yān princely residence
was the former Yuán palace,
deep and secluded.
Dàoyǎn trained soldiers in the back garden.
He dug tunnels to create multiple rooms,
surrounded them with thick walls,
and densely paved them with tiles, bricks, jars, and pots,
forging weapons day and night,
and keeping geese and ducks to mask the sounds.
In the sixth month of the first year of Jiànwén,
Ní Liàng, a centurion of the Yān princely guard, reported a conspiracy.
An edict was issued to arrest officials and attendants in the mansion.
The Regional Commander Zhāng Xìn pledged loyalty to Chéngzǔ,
and Chéngzǔ then resolved to raise an army.
Just then, a great storm arrived,
and the eaves tiles fell to the ground.
Chéngzǔ's expression changed.
Dàoyǎn said:
"This is an auspicious sign.
A flying dragon is in the sky,
followed by wind and rain.
The falling tiles
mean they will soon be replaced with yellow ones."
When the army was raised,
it was in the name of punishing Qí Tài and Huáng Zǐchéng,
and their forces were called
"The Army of Jìngnàn."
Dàoyǎn assisted the heir apparent in defending the city.
In the tenth month of that year,
Chéngzǔ attacked Dàníng,
and Lǐ Jǐnglóng seized the opportunity to besiege Běipíng.
Dàoyǎn defended very resolutely,
repelling the attackers.
At night, he lowered brave men by ropes to wound the southern soldiers.
When the relieving army arrived,
they attacked from both inside and outside,
killing countless enemies.
Jǐnglóng, Píng Ān, and others were successively defeated and fled.
Chéngzǔ besieged Jǐnán for three months,
but could not take it.
Dàoyǎn sent an urgent letter saying:
"The army is weary;
please withdraw."
So he returned.
He then attacked Dōngchāng again,
was defeated in battle,
lost the great general Zhāng Yù,
and returned once more.
Chéngzǔ intended to rest for a while,
but Dàoyǎn strongly urged him on,
recruiting more brave men,
defeating Shèng Yōng,
and breaking Fáng Zhāo's Xīshuǐ stronghold.
Dàoyǎn said to Chéngzǔ:
"Do not bother with cities and towns;
hurry towards the capital.
The capital is weak and isolated;
it will surely fall."
He followed this advice.
Consequently, he repeatedly defeated the various generals at Féihé and Língbì,
crossed the Yangtze River, and entered the capital.
When Chéngzǔ ascended the imperial throne,
he appointed Dàoyǎn Left Shànshì of the Saṅghaloka (Sēnglù Sī Zuǒ Shànshì).
When the emperor was a prince,
he mostly associated with military men;
only Dàoyǎn strategized the uprising.
When the emperor fought his way through Shāndōng and Héběi,
spending three years in the military,
sometimes advancing, sometimes not,
all strategic decisions for battle and defense were made by Dàoyǎn.
Dàoyǎn never personally went to the battlefield,
yet the emperor's use of force to gain the empire
owed much to Dàoyǎn's efforts,
and he was ranked first in merit.
In the fourth month of Yǒnglè's second year, he was appointed Zīshàn Dàfū and Tàizǐ Shàoshī,
had his surname restored,
and was granted the name Guǎngxīao.
His ancestors were posthumously granted titles corresponding to his offices.
When the emperor spoke with him,
he addressed him as Shàoshī, not by his name.
He ordered him to grow his hair,
but he refused.
He was granted a mansion and two palace women,
but he accepted none of them.
He always lived in a Buddhist temple,
wearing official attire for court,
and returning to his monk's robes afterwards.
When he went out to provide relief in Sūzhōu and Húzhōu,
he arrived in Chángzhōu,
and distributed the gold and silk he had been granted to his relatives and fellow villagers.
He supervised the revision of the Tàizǔ Shílù.
Guǎngxīao was the chief editor.
He also collaborated with Xiè Jìn and others in compiling the Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn.
When the book was completed,
the emperor praised him highly.
When the emperor traveled between the two capitals,
and campaigned beyond the northern frontier,
Guǎngxīao always remained to assist the Crown Prince in Nánjīng.
In the fourth month of the fifth year,
the Imperial Grandson began his studies outside the inner palace,
and Guǎngxīao attended him as a tutor.
In the third month of the sixteenth year, he came for an audience.
He was eighty-four years old.
He was gravely ill
and unable to attend court,
remaining in Qìngshòu Temple.
The emperor visited him twice,
speaking very cheerfully.
He bestowed a golden spittoon upon him
and asked what he wished to say.
Yáo Guǎngxiào said:
"The monk Pǔqià has been imprisoned for a long time;
I request that he be pardoned."
Pǔqià
was Emperor Jiànwén's chief recorder monk.
Initially,
when the emperor entered Nánjīng,
there were rumors that Emperor Jiànwén had escaped as a monk,
and Pǔqià knew the situation.
Some also said he was hidden at Pǔqià's place.
The emperor then imprisoned Pǔqià on other charges
and ordered the Supervising Secretary Hú Yíng and others to search everywhere for Emperor Jiànwén.
After a long time, he could not be found.
Pǔqià remained imprisoned for over ten years.
At this time,
the emperor, moved by Yáo Guǎngxiào's words,
immediately ordered his release.
Yáo Guǎngxiào bowed in thanks.
Soon after, he died.
The emperor was deeply grieved
and suspended court for two days,
ordering the officials to manage the funeral
and bury him with monastic rites.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Tuīchéng Fǔguó Xiémóu Xuānlì Wénchén, Tèjìn Rónglù Dàfū, Shàngzhùguó, and Róngguó Gōng,
with the posthumous name Gōngjìng.
He was granted a burial place northeast of Fángshān County.
The emperor personally composed a spirit way inscription to record his achievements
and appointed his adopted son, Jì, as Shàngbǎo Shà qīng.
Yáo Guǎngxiào was fond of learning in his youth
and skilled in poetry.
He was good friends with Wáng Bīn, Gāo Qǐ, and Yáng Mèngzài.
Sòng Lián and Sū Bóhéng also highly praised him.
In his later years, he wrote Dàoyú Lù,
which rather disparaged earlier Confucians,
and discerning people disdained it.
When he arrived in Chángzhōu,
he visited his biological sister.
His sister did not receive him.
He then visited his friend Wáng Bīn.
Bīn also did not see him,
but only said from a distance:
"Monk, you are mistaken!
Monk, you are mistaken!"
He went back to see his sister.
His sister cursed him.
Yáo Guǎngxiào was bewildered.
In the first year of Hóngxī, he was additionally granted the title of Shàoshī
and honored with sacrifice in the temple court of Chéngzǔ.
In the ninth year of Jiājìng,
Emperor Shìzōng instructed his Grand Secretaries, saying:
"Yáo Guǎngxiào assisted in the founding and rise of the dynasty;
his achievements and merits are all present.
However, as he was a follower of the Buddhist order,
to rank him among the meritorious officials
and offer him sacrificial food in the Grand Ancestral Temple
might not be sufficient to show respect to the ancestors."
Thereupon, Minister Lǐ Shí, together with Grand Secretaries Zhāng Cōng and Guì È, etc., deliberated and requested to move his sacrifice to Dàxīnglóng Temple,
with the Grand Court of Sacrifices offering rites in spring and autumn.
The imperial edict said:
"Granted."
Zhāng Yù,
courtesy name Shìměi,
was a native of Xiángfú.
He served the Yuán dynasty as a Zhīyuàn of the Privy Council.
When the Yuán dynasty fell,
he followed them north to the desert.
In the eighteenth year of Hóngwǔ, he returned to allegiance.
He followed the grand army out of the frontier
to Pǔyú'ér Hǎi,
and for his achievements, he was appointed Assistant Commander of Jǐnán Guard,
then promoted to Commander Abridged of Ānqìng Guard.
He again followed in campaigns against the caves of Yuǎnshùn and Sǎnmáo,
and pursued the Yuán people who harassed the border northward
to Yāhán Shān before returning.
He was transferred to the Left Guard of Yānshān.
He followed the Prince of Yān out of the frontier
to Hēisōnglín.
He again followed in campaigns against various barbarian tribes.
Due to his bravery and skill in planning,
he was trusted and appointed by the prince.
In the first year of Jiànwén,
Chéngzǔ raised an army.
Zhāng Yù led his troops to capture the nine gates of Běipíng,
killing Mǎ Xuān,
subduing Zūnhuà,
and dispatching troops to capture Yǒngpíng and Mìyún,
all of which yielded elite armor to strengthen the army.
He was promoted to Commander Abridged.
At this time, the imperial court dispatched a large army to punish Yān.
Dū Dū Xú Kǎi's army was in Héjiān,
Pān Zhōng and Yáng Sōng's armies were in Màozhōu,
and Marquis of Chángxīng Gěng Bǐngwén commanded three hundred thousand men in Zhēndìng.
Zhāng Yù advanced a suggestion, saying:
"Pān and Yáng are brave but without strategy;
they can be ambushed and captured."
Chéngzǔ ordered Zhāng Yù to lead the imperial guards as the vanguard
to Lóusāng.
It was the Mid-Autumn Festival,
and the southern army was feasting.
At midnight,
they swiftly attacked and broke Xióngxiàn.
Pān Zhōng and Yáng Sōng came to their aid,
but were intercepted and attacked at Yuèyàng Qiáo,
where they were captured alive.
Màozhōu was then captured.
He personally led light cavalry to scout Gěng Bǐngwén's army.
Upon returning, he reported that the army was undisciplined
and showed signs of defeat;
it should be attacked quickly.
Chéngzǔ then led his troops westward
to Wújí,
and consulted his generals on where to proceed.
The generals, seeing the southern army's strength,
requested to encamp at Xīnlè.
Zhāng Yù said:
"Although they are numerous,
they are newly assembled.
Our army, riding on its victory, should advance directly to Zhēndìng;
its defeat is certain."
Chéngzǔ rejoiced, saying:
"I rely on Zhāng Yù to accomplish this great task!"
The next day, they reached Zhēndìng
and thoroughly defeated Gěng Bǐngwén's army,
capturing Vice Generals Lǐ Jiān and Níng Zhōng,
Dū Dū Gù Chéng, etc.
Thirty thousand heads were taken.
They then defeated the army of Marquis of Ānlù Wú Jié.
The Yān army was greatly invigorated by this.
Marquis of Jiāngyīn Wú Gāo, with Liáodōng troops, besieged Yǒngpíng.
Duke of Cáoguó Lǐ Jǐnglóng led hundreds of thousands of men to attack Běipíng.
Chéngzǔ consulted with Zhāng Yù
and decided to first relieve Yǒngpíng.
Upon arrival, Wú Gāo had fled,
and Zhāng Yù pursued and slew many.
They then took a shortcut to raid Dàníng,
capturing its troops before returning.
They halted at Huìzhōu.
Initially, five armies were established,
with Zhāng Yù leading the Central Army.
At this time, Lǐ Jǐnglóng had already besieged Běipíng.
Chéngzǔ's army returned,
and a great battle took place at Zhèngcūn Bà.
Lǐ Jǐnglóng was defeated,
and Chéngzǔ, riding on his victory, reached the city walls.
Soldiers from within the city rushed out with drums and shouts,
attacking from both inside and outside,
and the southern army was utterly routed.
The following year, he followed in attacks on Guǎngchāng, Wèizhōu, and Dàtóng.
Intelligence reported that Lǐ Jǐnglóng had gathered his scattered soldiers,
numbering a million,
and was coming again.
Zhāng Yù said:
"Speed is paramount in warfare;
please occupy Báigōuhé first,
and await the weary enemy in comfort."
They encamped by the river for three days.
Lǐ Jǐnglóng arrived,
and they attacked with elite cavalry,
defeating him again.
They advanced to capture Dézhōu,
pursuing the fleeing enemy to Jǐnán.
They besieged the city for three months
before lifting the siege and returning.
Soon after, they set out again,
defeated Cāngzhōu,
captured Xú Kǎi,
and advanced to attack Dōngchāng.
They encountered Shèng Yōng's army.
Chéngzǔ, with dozens of cavalry, circled around to their rear.
Shèng Yōng surrounded him with several layers,
but Chéngzǔ fought fiercely and broke out.
Zhāng Yù, unaware of Chéngzǔ's location,
charged into the formation and fought with all his might,
slaying dozens of people
before being wounded and dying.
He was fifty-eight years old.
When the Yān army rose,
they fought for three years,
their vanguard being extremely sharp.
At this point, a great general was lost,
and the whole army lost morale.
The army returned to Běipíng,
and the generals prostrated themselves, begging for punishment.
Chéngzǔ said:
“Victory and defeat are common occurrences;
they are not worth mentioning.
My regret is the loss of Zhāng Yù.
At this difficult juncture,
I lost my excellent assistant.”
He then wept uncontrollably,
and all the generals also wept.
Later, Tán Yuān died at Jiāhé,
and Wáng Zhēn died at Féihé.
Although he mourned and cherished them,
it was not like his grief for Zhāng Yù.
In the sixth month of the fourth year of Jiànwén,
Chéngzǔ declared himself emperor,
and posthumously granted Zhāng Yù the title of Dūzhīhuī Tóngzhī.
In the ninth month, on the day of Jiǎshēn, he was posthumously granted the title of Róngguó Gōng,
with the posthumous name Zhōngxiǎn.
In the third month of the first year of Hóngxī, he was further enfeoffed as Héjiān Wáng,
his posthumous name changed to Zhōngwǔ,
and he was accorded sacrificial honors alongside Dōngpíng Wáng Zhū Néng, Jīnxiāng Hóu Wáng Zhēn, and Róngguó Gōng Yáo Guǎngxiào in the ancestral temple of Chéngzǔ.
He had three sons:
the eldest Fǔ,
the second Ní,
and the third Yuè.
His cousin Xìn.
A separate biography exists for Fǔ.
Ní,
as the son of a meritorious minister, became Shéncè Wèi Zhīhuīshǐ.
In the fifth year of Zhèngtǒng,
Yīngguó Gōng Fǔ accused Ní of assaulting the tomb guardians,
and his words implicated the former minister,
with much insolence and disrespect.
The emperor ordered the Jǐnyī Wèi to investigate the facts,
and he was imprisoned,
but soon released.
He was thrice promoted to Zhōngfǔ Yòudūdū,
commanding the imperial guard.
In the third year of Jǐngtài, he was granted the title of Tàizǐ Tàibǎo.
When Yīngzōng was restored to the throne,
on account of Yuè's merit in welcoming and establishing the emperor,
Ní was simultaneously enfeoffed as Wén'ān Bó,
receiving a stipend of 1,200 dàn of grain.
He died in the sixth year of Tiānshùn.
He was posthumously granted the title of Hóu,
with the posthumous name Zhōngxī.
His son Bīn inherited,
but was stripped of his title
for engaging in curses.
Yuè,
during the Yǒnglè reign, joined the imperial guard,
serving as Jǐnyī Wèi Zhīhuī Qiānshì.
He followed Xuānzōng to campaign against Gāo Xù,
and also followed Chéngguó Gōng Zhū Yǒng out of the frontier to Zhānmào Shān.
In the thirteenth year of Zhèngtǒng, he served as Fùzǒngbīng in the campaign against Lùchuān.
Upon his return,
he suppressed the rebellious Miáo in Guìzhōu.
Accumulating merit, he became Qiánfǔ Yòudūdū,
commanding the capital garrisons.
In the second year of Jǐngtài, he was imprisoned for his arrogance, extravagance, and misconduct,
but soon released.
When Emperor Jǐng became unwell,
he, along with Shí Hēng and Cáo Jíxiáng, welcomed the abdicated emperor at the southern city,
and was enfeoffed as Tàipíng Hóu,
receiving a stipend of 2,000 dàn of grain.
In the deaths of Yú Qiān, Wáng Wén, and Fàn Guǎng,
Yuè played a significant role.
He accepted bribes and disrupted governance,
second only to Shí Hēng.
He died in the second year of Tiānshùn,
posthumously granted the title of Yùguó Gōng,
with the posthumous name Yǒngxiāng.
His son Jǐn inherited,
but in the first year of Chénghuà,
the merit of the
“Duómén”
incident was revoked,
and his marquisate was stripped,
and he was appointed Zhīhuīshǐ.
Xìn
ranked first in the Jiànwén second year provincial examination.
During the Yǒnglè reign,
he successively served as Xíngkē Dūgěishìzhōng,
frequently submitting memorials.
He was promoted to Gōngbù Yòushìláng.
He was ordered to inspect the breach of the Yellow River at Kāifēng,
and requested to dredge the old channel of the Yúwángkǒu to Zhōngluán, over twenty *lǐ* long.
An imperial edict approved his proposal,
details of which are in the biography of Sòng Lǐ.
He was dispatched to manage the sea wall in Zhèjiāng,
but was demoted and exiled to Jiāozhǐ due to an incident.
In the early Hóngxī reign,
he was summoned to be Bīngbù Zuǒshìláng.
The emperor once said to Yīngguó Gōng Fǔ:
“Are there any brothers who can be granted favors?”
Fǔ bowed his head and said:
“Ní and Yuè have received imperial grace
and served as close attendants,
but both are extravagant.
Only my cousin, the attendant minister Xìn Xián,
is capable.”
The emperor summoned Xìn and asked:
“Is this Yīngguó Gōng's cousin?”
He was quickly granted a military official's cap,
and his position was changed to Jǐnyī Wèi Zhīhuī Tóngzhī,
hereditary.
At that time, it was not long after the founding of the dynasty,
so military ranks were highly valued.
He was known for fairness and leniency in his office.
In the sixth year of Xuāndé, he was transferred to Sìchuān Dūzhīhuī Qiānshì.
He retired after fifteen years in Shǔ.
Zhū Néng,
courtesy name Shìhóng,
was a native of Huáiyuǎn.
His father Liàng
followed Tàizǔ across the Yangtze River,
accumulating merit to become Yānshān Hùwèi Fùqiānhù.
Néng inherited the position
and served Chéngzǔ in his princely residence.
He once accompanied him on a northern expedition,
subduing the Yuán Grand Commandant Nǎi'érbùhuā.
When the Yān army rose,
he and Zhāng Yù initiated the plan to kill Zhāng Bǐng and Xiè Guì,
capturing the nine gates.
He was appointed Zhīhuī Tóngzhī.
He led his troops to capture Jìzhōu,
killed Mǎ Xuān,
and took Zūnhuà.
He followed in the assault on Xióngxiàn,
fought at Yuèyàng Qiáo,
captured Yáng Sōng and Pān Zhōng,
and received the surrender of their forces at Màozhōu.
He pressed on to Zhēndìng,
decisively defeating Gěng Bǐngwén's army.
Alone, with thirty daredevil cavalry, he pursued the fleeing enemy to the Hūtuó River,
leaping on his horse and shouting loudly to charge the southern army.
Tens of thousands of soldiers scattered,
many died from being trampled,
and over three thousand surrendered.
Chéngzǔ sent a handwritten letter to commend him,
and promoted him to Dūzhīhuī Qiānshì.
He followed to relieve Yǒngpíng,
put Wú Gāo to flight,
and surprised and captured Dàníng.
Returning,
he commanded the left army.
He defeated Lǐ Jǐnglóng at Zhèngcūn Bà.
He followed in the attacks on Guǎngchāng, Wèizhōu, and Dàtóng,
fought at Báigōu Hé,
serving as the vanguard,
and twice defeated Píng'ān's army.
Advancing to attack Jìnán,
he encamped at Huáshān.
The southern army arrayed themselves on high ground,
but Néng, with a surprise attack, circled behind them
and routed them,
capturing over ten thousand men.
He followed in the attack on Cāngzhōu,
breaching the east gate and entering,
beheading over ten thousand.
In the Battle of Dōngchāng,
Shèng Yōng and Tiě Xuàn besieged Chéngzǔ several layers deep,
and Zhāng Yù died in battle.
The situation was critical,
Néng led Zhōu Cháng and others to fight desperately,
protecting Chéngzǔ as he broke through the encirclement.
He then followed to fight at Jiāhé,
where Tán Yuān died,
and the Yān army was repulsed.
Néng arrived,
fought again and won again,
and the army regained its vigor.
He fought Píng'ān at Gǎochéng,
defeated him,
pursued the fleeing enemy to Zhēndìng,
seized land in Zhāngdé and Dìngzhōu,
and destroyed the Xīshuǐ stronghold.
Leading a thousand light cavalry, he plundered Héngshuǐ,
captured Commander Jiǎ Róng,
and took Dōng'ē and Dōngpíng,
destroying all the strongholds in Wènshàng.
Soon after, Wáng Zhēn 王真 died in battle at Féihé 淝河.
The Yān 燕 army suffered repeated defeats,
and the generals discussed withdrawing.
Zhū Néng 朱能 alone gripped his sword and said:
"Gāo Hòu 高後 of Hàn 漢 was defeated nine times in ten battles,
but ultimately gained the empire.
Now, we have won successive victories since initiating this campaign.
If we retreat after a minor setback,
can we still face north and serve others?!"
Chéngzǔ 成祖 also reprimanded the generals, saying:
"Go wherever you please!"
The generals then dared not speak.
So, they led the army south,
and defeated Píng'ān's 平安 Yínpáijūn 銀牌軍.
Dūdū 都督 Chén Huī 陳暉 came to their aid,
and was again defeated.
They then captured Língbìjūn 靈璧軍,
captured Píng'ān 平安 and others,
and accepted the surrender of 100,000 men.
He was successively promoted to Yòujūn Dūdū Qiānshì 右軍都督僉事.
They advanced and captured Sìzhōu 泗州,
crossed the Huái 淮 River,
and defeated Shèng Yōng's 盛庸 troops.
They captured Xūyí 盱眙,
took Yángzhōu 揚州,
crossed the Jiāng 江 River,
and entered Jīnchuānmén 金川門.
In the ninth month, on the day of Jiǎshēn 甲申, when merits were discussed,
he was ranked second only to Qiū Fú 丘福.
He was granted the titles of Fèngtiān Jìngnàn Tuīchéng Xuānlì Wǔchén 奉天靖難推誠宣力武臣, Tèjìn Rónglù Dàfū 特進榮祿大夫, Yòu Zhùguó 右柱國, Zuǒjūn Dūdūfǔ Zuǒ Dūdū 左軍都督府左都督,
and enfeoffed as Chéngguó Gōng 成國公.
His stipend was 2,200 dàn 擔 of grain,
and he was given an hereditary warrant.
In the second year of Yǒnglè 永樂 (1404), he was also appointed Tàizǐ Tàifù 太子太傅,
and his stipend was increased by 1,000 dàn 擔.
In the seventh month of the fourth year (1406), an imperial edict ordered Zhū Néng 朱能 to wear the seal of Zhēngyí Jiāngjūn 征夷將軍.
Mù Shèng 沐晟, Marquis of Xīpíng 西平, was appointed Zuǒ Fùjiāngjūn 左副將軍.
They were to march from Guǎngxī 廣西 and Yúnnán 雲南 respectively to subjugate Ānnán 安南.
The Emperor personally saw them off at Lóngjiāng 龍江.
In the tenth month, while on their way, he died in the army at Lóngzhōu 龍州.
He was
thirty-seven years old.
Among the generals, Zhū Néng 朱能 was the youngest,
and excelled in battle.
Zhāng Yù 張玉 excelled in strategy.
The Emperor relied on them as his right and left hands.
After Zhāng Yù's 張玉 death,
all military movements were decided in consultation with Zhū Néng 朱能.
Zhū Néng 朱能 was eight chǐ 尺 tall.
He was imposing, resolute, and open-minded.
At home, he was filial and fraternal.
Though holding the highest public office,
he never became arrogant due to his wealth and status.
He was good at treating his officers and soldiers kindly.
On the day of his death,
all the generals and officers wept for him.
An imperial decree ordered his burial in Chāngpíng 昌平.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Dōngpíng Wáng 東平王,
and given the posthumous title Wǔliè 武烈.
During the Hóngxī 洪熙 reign,
he was granted a place in Chéngzǔ's 成祖 ancestral temple.
His son, Yǒng 勇, inherited his title.
As the son of a founding meritorious minister, he was particularly favored and appointed.
He successively held charge of the Dūdūfǔ 都督府 affairs,
and served as the garrison commander of Nánjīng 南京.
In the twenty-second year of Yǒnglè 永樂 (1424), he followed the Emperor on his northern expedition.
When Xuānzōng 宣宗 ascended the throne,
he followed in the pacification of Hàn Shùrén 漢庶人 (Zhū Gāoxù 朱高煦),
and in the expedition against Wūliánghā 兀良哈.
When Zhāng Fǔ 張輔 relinquished military command,
an imperial edict appointed Yǒng 勇 to replace him.
Yǒng 勇 stated that the military preparations and logistics of the various guard units in the north and south were
intertwined and inconvenient.
He requested that the southern army be solely responsible for logistics,
and the northern army for border defense.
He also said:
"Many capital troops are stationed far away,
which is not the way to maintain the vital forces and manage the light ones.
I request that 100,000 elite soldiers be selected to augment them."
He also requested that the sons and younger brothers of dukes, marquises, earls, and military governors undergo training.
All these requests were approved.
In the ninth year of Zhèngtǒng 正統 (1444), he marched out of Xǐfēngkǒu 喜峯口,
attacked the various tribes of Wànyán 瓦顏,
and returned after reaching Fùyùchuān 富峪川.
He was impeached by Xú Xī 徐晞, Minister of War.
The Emperor decreed not to pursue the matter.
Soon after, his merits were discussed,
and he was promoted to Tàibǎo 太保.
Yǒng 勇 had a red face and a curly beard,
and a very imposing appearance.
He lacked sufficient courage and strategy,
but he respected scholars and officials.
In the fourteenth year (1449), he followed the imperial procession to Tǔmù 土木.
He engaged in battle at Yàozérlǐng 鷂兒嶺,
fell into an ambush, and died.
The 50,000 cavalry he commanded were all annihilated.
Yú Qiān 于謙 and others posthumously criticized Yǒng's 勇 transgressions,
and his enfeoffment was revoked.
In the first year of Jǐngtài 景泰 (1450),
Yǒng's 勇 son, Yí 儀, requested a burial and sacrifices.
The Emperor stated that Yǒng 勇, as a great general,
had lost the army and disgraced the nation,
leading to the capture of the imperial carriage,
and refused the request.
Later,
he requested to inherit the title.
Hú Yíng 胡濙, Minister of Rites, supported him.
He was allowed to inherit the title due to the grace of establishing the Crown Prince,
but his annual stipend was reduced to 1,000 dàn 擔.
In the early Tiānshùn 天順 reign,
Yǒng 勇 was posthumously enfeoffed as Píngyīn Wáng 平陰王,
and given the posthumous title Wǔmǐn 武愍.
Yí 儀 and his son Fǔ 輔 both served as garrison commanders in Nánjīng 南京.
Three generations later, Xīzhōng 希忠,
followed Shìzōng 世宗 to Chéngtiān 承天,
and was in charge of the affairs of the Xíngzài Zuǒfǔ 行在左府.
Upon reaching Wèihuī 衞輝,
the temporary imperial palace caught fire at night.
Xīzhōng 希忠, along with Dūdū 都督 Lù Bǐng 陸炳, helped the Emperor escape.
Because of this, he received imperial favor
and was appointed to serve in Xīyuàn 西苑.
He successively took charge of the Hòu 後 and Yòu 右 military commands,
was overall commander of the Shénjīyíng 神機營,
and supervised the Shí'èr Tuányíng 十二團營 and Wǔjūnyíng 五軍營.
He was successively promoted to Tàishī 太師,
and his annual stipend was increased by 700 dàn 擔.
He performed the suburban sacrifices to Heaven on behalf of the Emperor thirty-nine times,
and the rewards he received were countless.
Upon his death,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as Dìngxiāng Wáng 定襄王,
and given the posthumous title Gōngjìng 恭靖.
In the eleventh year of Wànlì 萬曆 (1583), at the recommendation of Gěishìzhōng 給事中 Yú Màoxué 余懋學,
his princely title was posthumously revoked.
His younger brother, Xīxiào 希孝, also reached the position of Dūdū 都督,
and was promoted to Tàibǎo 太保.
Upon his death,
he was posthumously granted the title Tàifù 太傅,
and given the posthumous title Zhōngxī 忠僖.
Five generations after Xīzhōng 希忠, his great-grandson Chúnchén 純臣,
was relied upon during the Chóngzhēn 崇禎 reign.
When Lǐ Zìchéng 李自成 approached the capital,
the Emperor personally issued an edict appointing Chúnchén 純臣 as overall commander of all military forces, both inside and outside the capital,
to assist the Crown Prince.
Before the edict could be issued,
the city had already fallen,
and he was killed by the rebels.
Qiū Fú 丘福,
a native of Fèngyáng 鳳陽.
He rose from the ranks of a common soldier,
and served Chéngzǔ 成祖 in his princely residence.
After many years of service,
he was appointed Qiānhù 千戶 of Yānshān Zhōnghùwèi 燕山中護衞.
When the Yān 燕 army was raised,
he, along with Zhū Néng 朱能 and Zhāng Yù 張玉, was the first to capture the Jiǔmén 九門 gates.
In the great battle of Zhēndìng 真定,
he broke into the inner city.
In the battle of Báigōuhé 白溝河,
he used elite soldiers to pierce the enemy's center.
In the major battles of Jiāhé 夾河, Cāngzhōu 滄州, and Língbì 靈璧,
he was always at the forefront of the army.
When Shèng Yōng's 盛庸 troops blocked the Huái 淮 River,
thousands of warships covered the riverbanks.
Qiū Fú 丘福 and Zhū Néng 朱能 led several hundred men,
marched twenty lǐ 里 to the west,
secretly crossed upstream,
and suddenly approached the southern army.
Shèng Yōng 盛庸 fled in panic,
and all his warships were captured,
allowing the army to cross.
He was successively promoted to Zhōngjūn Dūdū Tóngzhī 中軍都督同知.
Qiū Fú 丘福 was simple, honest, and fiercely brave.
In planning and strategy, he was inferior to Zhāng Yù 張玉,
but in daring to fight and penetrate deep into enemy lines, he was equal to Zhū Néng 朱能.
After every victory,
the other generals would scramble to present their captured spoils first,
but Qiū Fú 丘福 alone would hold back.
Chéngzǔ 成祖 often sighed and said:
"I myself know the merits of General Qiū 丘."
Upon his ascension,
he greatly enfeoffed his meritorious ministers,
and ranked Qiū Fú 丘福 first.
He was granted the titles of Fèngtiān Jìngnàn Tuīchéng Xuānlì Wǔchén 奉天靖難推誠宣力武臣, Tèjìn Rónglù Dàfū 特進榮祿大夫, Yòu Zhùguó 右柱國, Zhōngjūn Dūdūfǔ Zuǒ Dūdū 中軍都督府左都督,
and enfeoffed as Qíguó Gōng 淇國公.
His stipend was 2,500 dàn 擔 of grain,
and he was given an hereditary warrant.
He was ordered to discuss the enfeoffment and rewards of the various meritorious ministers,
and whenever he was commanded to deliberate on governance,
Qiū Fú 丘福 was always the first.
Hànwáng Gāo Xù (高煦) often led troops and achieved merit.
Chéngzǔ (成祖) loved him.
Qiū Fú (丘福) was a military man,
and was close to him,
frequently urging that he be made crown prince.
The emperor hesitated for a long time,
but eventually established Rénzōng (仁宗) as crown prince,
and appointed Fú as Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince.
Six years later, his annual salary was increased by a thousand dàn (石) of grain.
Soon after, he was ordered to assist in tutoring the imperial eldest grandson with Jiǎn Yì (蹇義), Jīn Zhōng (金忠) and others.
In July of the following year, he led a large army out of the frontier,
reached the Lúqú Hé (臚朐河),
and was defeated and perished.
Prior to this,
Běnyǎshīlǐ (本雅失里) had killed the envoy Guō Jì (郭驥),
and the emperor was furious,
dispatching troops to punish him.
He ordered Fú to wear the seal of the Commander-in-Chief for Punishing Rebels,
and serve as the overall commander.
Wǔchéng Hóu (武城侯) Wáng Cōng (王聰) and Tóng'ān Hóu (同安侯) Huǒ Zhēn (火真)
were made Left and Right Deputy Commanders,
and Jìng'ān Hóu (靖安侯) Wáng Zhōng (王忠) and Ānpíng Hóu (安平侯) Lǐ Yuǎn (李遠)
were made Left and Right Assistant Commanders,
leading one hundred thousand cavalry.
The emperor feared that Fú would be complacent,
and instructed him:
“Military affairs must be approached with caution.
Even if no enemies are seen north of Kāipíng (開平),
you should still
always act as if facing an enemy,
advancing or halting according to circumstances,
and not adhering rigidly to one plan.
If one attempt is unsuccessful,
wait for another.”
After he had set out,
the emperor repeatedly issued edicts,
stating that if there were those in the army who said the enemy was easy to defeat,
they should on no account be believed.
Fú exited the frontier,
and with over a thousand men, first reached the south bank of the Lúqú Hé (臚朐河).
They encountered enemy scouts,
defeated them,
and then crossed the river.
They captured one of their ministers,
gave him wine to drink,
and asked about Běnyǎshīlǐ's (本雅失里) whereabouts.
The minister said:
“Hearing of the large army's arrival,
he panicked and fled north,
about thirty lǐ (里) from here.”
Fú was greatly pleased and said:
“We must hasten to capture him.”
The generals requested to wait for all the armies to gather,
and scout the enemy's strength before advancing.
Fú refused.
He used the minister as a guide,
and went straight to the enemy camp.
They fought for two days.
In each battle,
the enemy feigned defeat and withdrew,
and Fú eagerly pressed the attack.
Lǐ Yuǎn (李遠) remonstrated, saying:
“General, you lightly believe the enemy's deception,
and are advancing with an isolated army.
The enemy feigns weakness to lure us deep;
advancing will surely be disadvantageous,
and retreating risks being attacked.
The only option is to build a fortified camp.
By day, display flags and beat drums,
sending out elite troops to challenge them;
by night, light many torches and fire cannons,
to exaggerate our military strength,
making them unable to gauge us.
Once our armies have all arrived,
we can attack with combined force,
and victory will be certain.
Otherwise, we can at least return with our army intact.
What did the emperor tell you at the beginning,
and have you forgotten it so soon?”
Wáng Cōng (王聰) also strongly argued against it.
Fú listened to none of them,
and sternly said:
“Those who disobey orders will be beheaded!”
He then rode ahead,
waving his soldiers to follow.
Those holding the horses all wept.
The generals had no choice but to go with him.
Soon after, a large enemy force arrived,
surrounding them in several layers.
Cōng died in battle,
and Fú and all the generals were captured and killed,
at the age of sixty-seven,
the entire army was lost.
When the defeat was reported,
the emperor was furious,
and believing that no other generals were competent enough,
decided to personally lead an expedition.
He stripped Fú of his hereditary title,
and moved his family to Hǎinán (海南).
Lǐ Yuǎn (李遠)
was from Huáiyuǎn (懷遠).
He inherited his father's position as Assistant Commander of Wèizhōu Wèi (蔚州衞).
When the Yān (燕) army attacked Wèizhōu (蔚州),
he surrendered the city.
The Southern army was stationed in Dézhōu (德州),
and its supply route ran between Xú (徐) and Pèi (沛).
Yuǎn, with six thousand light troops,
falsely donned the robes and armor of the Southern army,
each man sticking a willow branch on his back,
and proceeded directly to Jìníng (濟寧), Shāhé (沙河) and then Pèi (沛),
undetected.
He burned tens of thousands of grain boats,
the river water became entirely hot,
and all the fish and turtles floated dead.
The Southern general Yuán Yǔ (袁宇) pursued with thirty thousand cavalry,
but Yuǎn's ambush defeated them.
In the first month of Jiànwén (建文) 4th year (1402),
the Yān (燕) army was stationed in Líxiàn (蠡縣).
Yuǎn's scouts reached Gǎochéng (藁城),
where they encountered Dézhōu (德州) general Gě Jìn (葛進) with over ten thousand infantry and cavalry,
crossing the Hūtuó Hé (滹沱河) on ice.
Yuǎn met them in battle.
Jìn tethered his horses in a forest,
and engaged with infantry.
Yuǎn feigned retreat,
secretly dividing his forces to come out behind them,
untethered the horses,
and engaged in battle again.
Jìn retreated, losing his horses,
and was utterly defeated.
Four thousand heads were severed,
and a thousand horses captured.
Chéngzǔ (成祖), pleased with the great victory at the start of the year,
sent a letter commending and praising him, saying:
“General, with eight hundred light cavalry,
you defeated tens of thousands of enemies,
employing unexpected tactics and adapting to changes,
even ancient famous generals could not surpass this.”
He was again sent to scout on the Huái (淮) River,
where he defeated the defending Huái (淮) generals and soldiers,
beheading over a thousand.
For his accumulated merits, he became a Commissioner of the Chief Military Commission (Dūdū Qiānshì, 都督僉事),
was enfeoffed as Ānpíng Hóu (安平侯),
with a salary of one thousand dàn (石) of grain,
and granted an hereditary伯 (bó) warrant.
In Yǒnglè (永樂) 1st year (1403), he accompanied Wǔ'ān Hóu (武安侯) Zhèng Hēng (鄭亨) in guarding Xuānfǔ (宣府).
Yuǎn was resolute and brave,
and his speeches were impassioned.
After accompanying Qiū Fú (丘福) beyond the frontier,
they reached the Lúqú Hé (臚朐河).
He remonstrated with Fú,
but was not heeded.
When the army was defeated,
Yuǎn led five hundred cavalry to break through the enemy lines,
killing several hundred men.
His horse stumbled and he was captured,
dying while cursing ceaselessly.
He was forty-six years old.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Jǔguó Gōng (莒國公),
and given the posthumous title Zhōngzhuàng (忠壯).
His son, Ān (安),
succeeded to the Earl (Bó, 伯) title.
In Hóngxī (洪熙) 1st year (1425), he became an Assistant Commander in Jiāozhǐ (交阯),
but failed to maintain discipline,
and was demoted to an ordinary officer.
Later,
he returned with Wáng Tōng (王通) after abandoning Jiāozhǐ (交阯),
was imprisoned, stripped of his warrant,
and demoted to serve at Chìchéng (赤城) to earn merit.
When Yīngzōng (英宗) ascended the throne,
he was reinstated as Commissioner of the Chief Military Commission.
He campaigned against Ātái (阿台) and Yǎ'érzhībó (𩽆兒只伯).
He was promoted to Vice Commissioner of the Chief Military Commission,
serving as overall commander,
and garrisoned Sōngpān (松潘).
In Zhèngtǒng (正統) 6th year (1441), he served as Deputy to Dìngxī Bó (定西伯) Jiǎng Guì (蔣貴) in the campaign against Lùchuān (麓川).
Guì ordered Ān to garrison troops at Lùjiāng (潞江) to protect supplies,
while he himself led the main army forward.
When the rebels were defeated,
Ān, ashamed of having achieved nothing,
heard there were remaining rebels encamped on Gāolí Gòngshān (高黎貢山),
and went directly to attack them.
He was defeated,
losing over a thousand soldiers,
and Commander Zhào Bīn (趙斌) and others all died.
He was arrested and imprisoned,
and demoted to serve in Dúshí (獨石).
Upon his death,
an imperial edict appointed his son Qīng (清) as Vice Commander of the Chief Military Commission.
Wáng Zhōng,
a native of Xiàogǎn.
He surrendered with Lǐ Yuǎn at Yùzhōu.
In every battle,
he led elite cavalry as a surprise force,
achieving many beheadings and captures.
He was successively promoted to Dūdū Qiānshì,
ennobled as Jìng'ān Hóu,
with a stipend of one thousand dàn of grain.
He died in battle beyond the frontier,
aged fifty-one,
and his peerage was abolished.
Wáng Cōng,
a native of Qíshuǐ.
He joined the uprising as a Bailù of the Yānshān Zhōnghùwèi.
He captured Jìzhōu,
attacked Zūnhuà,
and campaigned in Zhuōzhōu.
He fought battles at Chípíng
and Huákǒu,
defeating the Southern army,
and capturing one thousand five hundred horses.
He then returned to guard Bǎodìng.
While on campaign at the riverside,
he commandeered Southern army boats to ferry troops.
He was successively promoted to Dūzhīhuīshǐ,
ennobled as Wǔchéng Hóu,
with a stipend of one thousand five hundred dàn of grain.
He was stationed with Huǒzhēn, the Tóng'ān Hóu, to defend Xuānfǔ.
He frequently received imperial edicts to patrol the border.
He followed Qiū Fú beyond the frontier
and died in battle,
aged fifty-three.
He was posthumously ennobled as Zhāng Guó Gōng,
and granted the posthumous title Wǔyì.
His son Yǎn succeeded him.
Cōng and Yuǎn had once advised Fú,
thus they received commendation and posthumous benefits.
Huǒzhēn,
a Mongol.
His original name was Huǒlǐhuǒzhēn.
During the Hóngwǔ era, he pledged allegiance
and became a Qiānhù of the Yānshān Zhōnghùwèi.
He followed in the attack on Zhēndìng,
being the first to charge and break through Gěng Bǐngwén's formation.
The main army pressed on,
and victory was achieved.
He followed in the raid on Dàníng,
and fought at Zhèngcūnbà.
As evening fell,
the weather was very cold.
Zhēn gathered old saddles and burned them before Chéngzǔ.
Several armored soldiers rushed to warm themselves by the fire,
but the guards stopped them.
Chéngzǔ said:
"I wear heavy furs and still feel cold.
These are all brave men,
do not stop them."
Those who heard were moved to tears.
Zhēn often led cavalry.
In every battle, he achieved beheadings and captures.
He would return to camp with shouts and cheers,
and the troops admired his bravery.
He was successively promoted to Dūdū Qiānshì,
ennobled as Tóng'ān Hóu,
with a stipend of one thousand five hundred dàn of grain.
He died in battle beyond the frontier,
aged sixty-one,
and his peerage was abolished.
His descendants inherited the position of Qiānhù of the Guānhǎiwèi for generations.
His distant descendant, Bīn,
was a military *jǔrén* during the Jiājìng era.
When Japanese pirates invaded Eastern Zhèjiāng,
he led naval vessels to fight the bandits.
The bandits threw fireballs at Bīn's ship,
but Bīn caught them with his bare hands
and threw them back to burn the bandit ships.
The bandits encamped at Pǔtuóshān.
Bīn directly attacked their camp,
inflicting many casualties.
The rear army failed to follow up,
and he was captured.
He did not submit.
The bandits dismembered him.
The officials erected a shrine for him called
"Zhōngyǒng" (Loyal and Brave).
Tán Yuān,
a native of Qīngliú.
He succeeded his father's post as Fùqiānhù of the Yānshān Yòuhù.
When the Yan army rose,
he followed in seizing Jiǔmén.
He captured Xióngxiàn.
Pān Zhōng and Yáng Sōng came from Màozhōu to reinforce.
Yuān led over a thousand brave men
and ambushed them in the water beneath Yuèyàng Qiáo,
each man holding a bundle of straw
to cover their heads, allowing for breathing through the nose.
After the Southern army had passed,
they emerged and took control of the bridge.
Zhōng and others were defeated in battle
and rushed towards the bridge but could not cross,
thus they were captured.
He was successively promoted to Dūzhīhuī Tóngzhī.
Yuān was valiant and skilled in battle,
able to draw a two-dàn bow,
and never missed his target.
However, he was naturally bloodthirsty.
When Cāngzhōu was captured,
Chéngzǔ ordered that passes be issued to the surrendered soldiers for their dispersal.
Over three thousand men who had not yet been dispatched
were awaiting the clear issuance of passes.
Yuān killed them all in one night.
The King was furious.
Yuān said:
"These men are all brave warriors;
releasing them would be a future problem."
The King said:
"If as you say,
we should kill all enemies.
Can all enemies be killed?"
Yuān felt ashamed and withdrew.
In the Battle of Jiāhé,
the Southern army's formation stirred up dust.
Yuān abruptly charged forward to fight,
his horse stumbled and he was killed.
Chéngzǔ lamented and cherished him.
Upon his ascension to the throne,
he posthumously granted him the title of Dūzhīhuīshǐ,
posthumously ennobled him as Chóng'ān Hóu,
granted him the posthumous title Zhuàngjié,
and erected a shrine to worship him.
His son, Zhōng,
had meritorious service by following into the capital.
Also, because of Yuān, he was ennobled as Xīnníng Bó,
with a stipend of one thousand dàn of grain.
In the twenty-first year of Yǒnglè, he led the right vanguard on an expedition to the desert.
In the first year of Xuāndé, he followed in the campaign against Lè'ān.
In the third year, he was imprisoned and sentenced to death for violating military regulations during the campaign in Jiāozhǐ,
but was later released
and then died.
His son, Jǐng, petitioned to succeed him.
The Ministry of Personnel stated that since Zhōng died due to a crime,
he should not be succeeded.
The Emperor said:
"The patent contains a clause for exemption from death;
let him succeed."
After two more generations, his grandson, Yòu,
in the Chénghuà era,
assisted in guarding Nánjīng.
Upon his return,
he managed the Qiánfǔ Tídū Tuányíng,
was successively promoted to Tàifù,
succeeded as Bó,
and only died at the age of sixty-nine.
He was granted the posthumous title Zhuāngxī.
His son, Lún, succeeded him.
In the fourteenth year of Jiājìng, he garrisoned Húguǎng.
He had meritorious service in suppressing the Jiǔxī Mán,
and his stipend was increased.
He was deprived of his peerage for occupying and conscripting soldiers.
After several more generations, Hóngyè
died at the hands of bandits
when the dynasty fell.
Wáng Zhēn,
a native of Xiánníng.
During the Hóngwǔ era,
he rose from the ranks of common soldiers.
Through accumulated merit, he reached the position of Bailù of the Yānshān Yòuhùwèi.
When the Yan army rose,
he attacked Jiǔmén.
He fought at Yǒngpíng and Zhēndìng,
captured Guǎngchāng,
and campaigned in Yànmén.
He followed in the defeat of Cāngzhōu,
and pursued the Southern army to Huákǒu,
capturing over seven thousand people.
He was successively promoted to Dūzhīhuīshǐ.
In the Battle of Fèihé,
Zhēn, with Bái Yì and Liú Jiāng, each leading a hundred cavalrymen,
lured the Píng'ān army.
They tied straw into bundles resembling silk and placed them in bags.
As Ān pursued,
Zhēn and others feigned abandoning the bags and fled,
whereupon Ān's soldiers eagerly snatched them.
The ambush was sprung,
and the two armies fought fiercely.
Zhēn led brave men directly forward,
slaughtering countless enemies.
The rear army failed to follow up,
and Ān's army surrounded him several times.
Zhēn was severely wounded,
but he continued to fight and kill dozens of men.
He looked to his left and right and said:
"It is not my duty to die at the hands of the enemy."
Then he committed suicide by cutting his own throat.
Upon Chéngzǔ's ascension to the throne,
he was posthumously ennobled as Jīnxiāng Hóu,
and granted the posthumous title Zhōngzhuàng.
Zhēn Yǒngjiàn had wisdom and strategy.
Chéngzǔ often mourned him, saying:
"If a valiant warrior like Wáng Zhēn
had not died,
what achievement could not have been accomplished?
His merit would have surpassed all generals."
In Rénzōng's time,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as Níngguó Gōng
and given the additional title Xiàozhōng.
His son, Tōng, has his own biography.
Chén Hēng,
a native of Shòuzhōu.
He was a wànhù in Yángzhōu at the end of the Yuán dynasty.
He followed Tàizǔ at Háozhōu,
served as a leader of armored soldiers,
and was promoted to qiānhù.
He followed the Grand General on the northern campaign
and defended Dōngchāng.
When tens of thousands of enemies suddenly arrived,
Hēng held fast,
using surprise tactics to lure and defeat them.
He then followed in attacking and subduing other unconquered cities.
In the second year of Hóngwǔ, he defended Dàtóng.
Through his accumulated merits, he rose to Yānshān Zuǒwèi Zhǐhuī Qiānshì.
He frequently participated in expeditions beyond the Great Wall.
He was promoted to Běipíng Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ.
When Huìdì ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Dūdū Qiānshì.
When the Yān forces rose,
Hēng, Liú Zhēn, and Bǔ Wàn defended Dàníng.
They moved their troops out of Sōngtíng Guān,
encamped at Shāhé,
and planned to attack Zūnhuà.
When the Yān forces arrived,
they retreated to defend the pass.
At this time,
Lǐ Jǐnglóng commanded an army of five hundred thousand to attack Běipíng.
Běipíng was weak,
but the twenty-plus guards of Xīngzhōu and Yíngzhōu under the Dàníng Xíngdū Sī
were all elite forces from the northwest.
The three guards of Wūyán, Tàiníng, and Fúyú,
comprised of cavalry and elite soldiers led by surrendered Yuán generals,
were especially valiant.
Bǔ Wàn was about to join Jǐnglóng's army.
Chéngzǔ was fearful,
and by stratagem deceived Hēng into imprisoning Wàn.
He then swiftly attacked Dàníng via a secret path from Liújiākǒu.
Hēng and Liú Zhēn returned from Sōngtíng to provide relief,
but halfway heard that Dàníng had fallen.
So they, along with commanders Xú Lǐ and Chén Wén, planned to surrender to Yān.
At the second watch of the night,
they raided Liú Zhēn's camp.
Zhēn fled to Guǎngníng on a single horse,
while Hēng and others led their troops to surrender.
Chéngzǔ took all the armies and the cavalry of the three guards,
and returned with Níngwáng as his captive.
From then on, the three guards' soldiers were often at the forefront of charges and breaking enemy lines.
Chéngzǔ's conquest of the empire
began with the capture of Dàníng.
After Hēng and Lǐ surrendered,
they repeatedly participated in defeating the Southern army.
In the Battle of Báigōuhé,
Hēng was severely wounded and nearly died.
Later,
attacking Jǐnán,
he fought Píng Ān at Huáshān,
and suffered a great defeat.
He was severely wounded
and carried back to Běipíng.
He was promoted to Dūdū Tóngzhī.
When Chéngzǔ returned with his army,
he personally visited Hēng's residence to offer condolences and inquire about him.
He died in the tenth month of that year.
Chéngzǔ personally wrote an elegy to offer sacrifices.
Upon his enthronement,
he posthumously enfeoffed him as Jīngguó Gōng
and gave him the posthumous title Xiāngmǐn.
His eldest son, Gōng,
inherited the position of Dūdū Tóngzhī.
His youngest son, Mào,
initially joined the army as a shèrén,
distinguished himself, and became a Zhǐhuī Qiānshì.
Later, he led Hēng's troops,
and achieved many merits,
rising to Yòu Dūdū.
In the first year of Yǒnglè, he was enfeoffed as Níngyáng Bó,
with a stipend of a thousand dàn of grain.
In the third month of the sixth year, he was appointed General Zhēngxī
and garrisoned Níngxià,
where he was skilled at pacifying surrendered soldiers.
In the autumn of the following year,
the former Yuán Prime Minister Zànbǔ, along with more than ten officials including Píngzhāng, Sītú, Guó Gōng, and Zhīyuàn,
all led their people and surrendered successively.
Later, Píngzhāng Dōulián and others rebelled and fled.
Mào pursued and captured them at Hēishān,
seizing all the people and livestock of their subordinate tribes.
He was promoted to Hóu
and his stipend was increased by two hundred dàn of grain.
In the eighth year, he participated in the northern campaign
and supervised the Left Flank.
In the eleventh year, he patrolled the border of Níngxià.
Soon after, he was ordered to lead the troops of the two Dū Sī of Shānxī and Shǎnxī, and the guards of Gǒngchāng and Píngliáng,
and garrison Xuānfǔ.
In the following year, he participated in the northern campaign,
leading the Left Vanguard.
Fighting at Hūshīwēn,
he and Chéngshān Hóu Wáng Tōng were the first to ascend,
and Dūdū Zhū Chóng and others pressed the attack,
achieving a great victory.
In the following year, he again garrisoned Níngxià.
In the twentieth year, he participated in the northern campaign.
He led the imperial elite cavalry
and defeated the enemy at Qūliè Hé.
He separately led five thousand cavalry along the river to the northeast,
capturing the remaining rebels
and annihilating them in the mountains and marshes.
When the army returned,
Wǔ'ān Hóu Zhèng Hēng led the baggage train ahead,
and Mào lay in ambush at the pass.
When the enemy came to pursue,
the ambush sprang and attacked,
killing more than half of the enemy.
Upon returning to the capital,
he was bestowed with dragon robes and a jade belt,
and his daughter was made Lì Fēi.
In the following year, he led the troops of the three garrisons of Shǎnxī, Níngxià, and Gānsù,
participating in the campaign against Ālǔtái
as the vanguard.
The year after that, he again led the vanguard
in the northern campaign.
When Chéngzǔ died at Yúmù Chuān,
the six armies were away,
and the capital's defenses were weak.
Rénzōng summoned Mào and Yángwǔ Hóu Xuē Lù to lead three thousand elite cavalry to rush back and guard the capital.
He was ordered to take charge of the Qiánfǔ,
was given the additional title Tàibǎo,
and was granted hereditary noble status.
In the first year of Xuāndé,
he participated in the suppression of Lè'ān.
Upon returning,
he again garrisoned Níngxià.
In the third year, he proposed relocating the city of Língzhōu,
and presented two rabbits, one black and one white.
Xuānzōng was pleased
and personally drew a horse to bestow upon him.
Mào had been garrisoned for a long time,
and his prestige and name shook the Mòběi.
However, he presumed on imperial favor and indulged himself,
embezzling enormous sums.
He was repeatedly impeached,
but the emperor leniently forgave him,
ordering the relevant authorities to collect his ill-gotten gains.
Mào pleaded that he had already spent everything,
and an imperial edict pardoned him.
When Yīngzōng ascended the throne,
he was ordered to consult on court affairs with Zhāng Fǔ,
and then went out as Píngqiāng Jiāngjūn
to garrison Gānsù.
That winter,
raiders plundered Zhènfān.
Mào dispatched troops to relieve it,
and the raiders withdrew.
He reported the number of enemy killed and captured.
Cāncàn Shìláng Chái Chē impeached Mào for his lack of discipline that led to the raid,
and also for taking the remaining old and weak,
falsely claiming them as the merits of Dū Zhǐhuī Mǎ Liàng and others,
and receiving promotions and rewards.
The charge was execution.
An imperial edict pardoned him from death
and stripped him of his stipend.
After a long time, his stipend was restored,
and he attended court.
In the thirteenth year,
the Fujianese bandit Dèng Máoqī rebelled.
The Censor-in-Chief Zhāng Kǎi led an expedition against him but was unsuccessful.
Therefore, an imperial edict appointed Mào to bear the seal of the General who Conquers the South,
serving as the Grand Commander,
leading the Capital Guards and troops from Jiangnan and Zhejiang to suppress the rebellion.
Upon reaching Zhejiang,
some wanted to divide the troops to block the sea passage.
Mào said:
"This would only drive the bandits to fight to the death against us."
The next year, he arrived at Jiànníng.
Máoqī had already died,
and the remaining bandits gathered in Yóuxī and Shāxiàn.
The generals wanted to slaughter them.
Mào said:
"This would only harden the bandits' resolve."
He then issued an order for pacification and recruitment,
and many of the bandit factions surrendered.
He divided his forces to pursue and capture them,
and completely pacified the region.
Soon after, the bandits in Shāxiàn became active again,
and it remained unsettled for a long time.
At this time, Emperor Yīngzōng was captured by the Mongols,
and Emperor Jǐngdì ascended the throne.
He then issued an edict for the army to return.
Censors impeached Mào,
but as the bandits had been pacified, no questions were raised.
He was still promoted to Grand Protector (Tàibǎo),
given charge of the Central Prefecture,
and concurrently oversaw the affairs of the Imperial Clan Court.
When Emperor Yīngzōng was restored to the throne,
his stipend was increased by two hundred *dàn* of grain.
He died in the seventh year of Tiānshùn,
at the age of eighty-four.
He was posthumously granted the title of Duke of Jùn (Jùn Guógōng)
and given the posthumous name Wǔjìng.
Mào had a long beard and a magnificent appearance,
and his voice was like a great bell.
He was open-minded and magnanimous,
and treated scholars and officials with respect.
Of the meritorious officials of the 'Jìngnàn'
campaign, none were still alive by the Tiānshùn era.
Only Mào enjoyed wealth and position for a long time,
being dismissed and reinstated several times,
and ultimately died with honor and achievement.
