His eldest son, Shèng, committed a crime,
so his younger brother Rùn succeeded him.
When Rùn died,
his younger brother Yīng succeeded him,
with half the stipend,
as hereditary marquis.
Sixteen years later, Shèng's son Fǔ had grown up,
so Fǔ was ordered to succeed,
and Yīng was exempted from military service and became an imperial guard.
Fǔ later lost his marquisate due to an incident.
When he died,
he had no sons.
Yīng's grandson Jìzǔ was again enfeoffed as marquis,
and the title was passed down until the fall of the Míng dynasty.
Xú Lǐ,
a native of Xīpíng.
During the Hóngwǔ era,
he served as Assistant Commander of the Yongqing Central Guard,
then was transferred to the Yíngzhōu Guard.
After his surrender,
he became Deputy General of the Right Army.
He was always the first to charge in battle
and distinguished himself.
When Emperor Chéngzǔ planned to attack Cāngzhōu,
he ordered Lǐ and Chén Xù to secretly build a pontoon bridge at Zhígū to transport the troops.
He was successively promoted to Assistant Commander-in-chief
and enfeoffed as Earl of Wǔkāng (Wǔkāng Bó).
He returned to guard Běipíng.
Lǐ was lenient with his subordinates
and won the hearts of his officers and soldiers.
He died in the sixth year of Yǒnglè.
The title was passed down twice until his grandson Yǒng,
who had no sons, ending the enfeoffment.
Chén Wén,
after his surrender, served as Left Deputy General of the Front Army.
He died in battle
at Xiǎohé.
Fáng Kuān,
a native of Chénzhōu.
During the Hóngwǔ era,
as Commander of the Jìníng Left Guard, he followed Xú Dá to train troops in Běipíng,
and subsequently became Associate Commander-in-chief of Běipíng,
then moved to guard Dàníng.
Kuān had been on the border for a long time,
and knew everything about the mountains, rivers, and strategic passes,
as well as the true nature of foreign lands.
However, he was unable to manage his officers and soldiers.
When the Yān army suddenly arrived,
the people in the city captured Kuān and surrendered.
Emperor Chéngzǔ released him
and allowed him to lead his troops.
At the Battle of Báigōuhé,
he commanded the Right Army
and suffered a defeat.
He followed in conquering Guǎngchāng and Zhāngdé,
and was promoted to Assistant Grand Commissioner.
As an old minister,
his transgressions were overlooked,
and he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Sī'ēn (Sī'ēn Hóu),
with a stipend of eight hundred *dàn* of grain,
and his commandership was hereditary.
He died in the seventh year of Yǒnglè.
Liú Cái,
courtesy name Zǐcái,
a native of Huòqiū.
At the end of the Yuán dynasty, he was a marshal.
When the Míng dynasty rose, he pledged allegiance,
and successively served as Assistant Commander of the Yíngzhōu Central Guard.
When the Yān army attacked Dàníng,
Cái surrendered.
He fought with distinction.
He was enfeoffed as Earl of Guǎng'ēn (Guǎng'ēn Bó),
with a stipend of nine hundred *dàn* of grain,
and his associate commandership was hereditary.
In the eighth year of Yǒnglè, he joined the northern expedition,
supervising the Right Flank.
He was accused of a breach of discipline
but was later pardoned.
In the twenty-first year, he managed border affairs in Yǒngpíng and Shānhǎi with the Marquis of Lóngpíng, Zhāng Xìn.
The following year, he again joined the northern expedition,
but returned due to illness
upon reaching Huáilái.
Cái was sincere and unadorned,
never compromised his principles,
nor did he lightly slander others.
He was highly esteemed by Emperor Rénzōng.
He died in the fifth year of Xuāndé.
A eulogy states: Emperor Huìdì inherited the awe and glory left by Emperor Tàizǔ.
The national power was initially strong,
and his benevolent fame spread far and wide,
winning the hearts of the people.
Emperor Chéngzǔ rose from a corner of the realm,
daring to challenge the unrighteous to contend for the empire,
without ever having a foolproof plan.
It was Dàoyǎn who first supported the secret conspiracy,
initiating the plot and making the decisions.
Zhāng Yù, Zhū Néng, and others worked diligently in the ranks,
fighting victoriously everywhere,
not caring even if they died.
Thus, they gathered strong armies,
crushed powerful forces,
and completed the imperial enterprise in four years.
It seems that what Heaven raises,
with collective wisdom and effort,
succeeds in due course.
That these individuals could be ranked as the foremost meritorious officials,
can it not be called extremely fortunate?
Collation Notes

Biographies, Volume 34: Zhāng Wǔ, Chén Guī, Mèng Shàn, Zhèng Hēng, Xú Zhōng, Guō Liàng (Zhào Yí), Zhāng Xìn (Táng Yún), Xú Xiáng, Lǐ Jùn, Sūn Yán (Fáng Shèng), Chén Xù, Chén Xián, Zhāng Xīng, Chén Zhì, Wáng Yǒu.
Zhāng Wǔ,
a native of Liúyáng.
He was magnanimous and courageous,
and somewhat acquainted with history.
He served as a Centurion in the Yānshān Right Guard.
He followed Emperor Chéngzǔ in raising an army,
conquered Jìzhōu,
took Xióngxiàn,
fought at Yuèyàng Qiáo,
and advanced victoriously to Mòzhōu.
He and other generals defeated Gěng Bǐngwén at Zhēndìng.
In the Battle of Jiāhé,
he led brave warriors as the vanguard,
charged the enemy formation,
and feigned retreat.
The Southern army pursued him,
but Wǔ turned back to attack,
and the Southern army collapsed.
When attacking Xīshuǐ Zhài,
the vanguard lost its way at night,
and the Southern army came in pursuit.
Wǔ led his troops to ambush them at a strategic pass,
and repelled them.
At the Battle of Xiǎohé,
Chén Wén died in battle.
Wǔ led a contingent of "death-defying" soldiers to burst forth from the woods,
joined forces with the cavalry,
and utterly routed the Southern army,
beheading twenty thousand,
with countless drowned.
He was successively granted the title of Associate Grand Commissioner.
Chéngzǔ 成祖 ascended the throne,
and for his meritorious service, he was enfeoffed as Chéngyáng Hóu 成陽侯,
with a stipend of one thousand five hundred dàn 石,
ranked below Zhū Néng 朱能.
At this time, the thirteen marquises were
Chén Guī 陳珪, Zhèng Hēng 鄭亨, Mèng Shàn 孟善, Huǒ Zhēn 火真, Gù Chéng 顧成, Wáng Zhōng 王忠, Wáng Cōng 王聰, Xú Zhōng 徐忠, Zhāng Xìn 張信, Lǐ Yuǎn 李遠, Guō Liàng 郭亮, and Fáng Kuān 房寬.
He was the first among the martial (generals).
He returned to guard Běipíng 北平.
In the tenth month of the first year of Yǒnglè 永樂, he died.
Imperial horses were issued from the palace for his funeral expenses.
He was posthumously granted the title of Lù Guó Gōng 潞國公,
and given the posthumous name Zhōngyì 忠毅.
He had no sons,
so his peerage was abolished.
Chén Guī 陳珪 was
a native of Tàizhōu 泰州.
In the early Hóngwǔ 洪wǔ reign,
he followed Grand General Xú Dá 徐達 to pacify the Central Plains,
and was appointed Bailù Hùwèi Bǎihù 龍虎衞百戶.
He was later transferred to Yānshān Zhōng Hùwèi 燕山中護衞.
He followed Chéngzǔ 成祖 as the vanguard on an expedition beyond the Great Wall,
and was promoted to Fù Qiānhù 副千戶.
Later,
he joined the uprising,
and through accumulated merit, reached the rank of Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī 指揮同知.
He then assisted the Heir Apparent in guarding the capital.
He was successively promoted to Dūdū Qiānshì 都督僉事,
enfeoffed as Tàiníng Hóu 泰寧侯,
with a stipend of one thousand two hundred dàn 石,
and continued to assist the Heir Apparent in guarding the capital as before.
In the fourth year of Yǒnglè 永樂, he oversaw the construction of the palace buildings in Běijīng 北京,
and his planning and management were orderly,
for which he was greatly praised and valued.
In the eighth year,
the Emperor campaigned in the north,
and he, along with Fùmǎ Dūwèi Yuán Róng 駙馬都尉袁容, assisted Zhào Wáng 趙王 in garrisoning Běijìng 北倞.
In the fifteenth year, he was ordered to cast and issue the Shànggōng Yìn 繕工印 (Seal of the Office of Works) to Guī 珪,
and also established subordinate officials,
concurrently managing the Xíngzài Hòufǔ 行在後府 (Rear Office of the Traveling Palace).
In the fourth month of the seventeenth year, he died
at the age of eighty-five.
He was posthumously granted the title Jìng Guó Gōng 靖國公,
and given the posthumous name Zhōngxiāng 忠襄.
His son, Yú 瑜, succeeded him.
In the twentieth year, Yú 瑜 accompanied the northern expedition.
He committed a breach of discipline,
was imprisoned, and died.
His elder brother's son, Zhōng 鐘, succeeded him.
After two more successions, to Yíng 瀛,
he died at Tǔmù 土木,
and was posthumously granted the title Níng Guó Gōng 寧國公,
and given the posthumous name Gōngmǐn 恭愍.
His younger brother, Jīng 涇, succeeded him.
In the sixth year of Tiānshùn 天順, Jīng 涇 garrisoned Guǎngxī 廣西.
In the ninth month of the following year,
Yaó 瑤 rebels started a disturbance,
and Jīng 涇 led several thousand men to garrison Wúzhōu 梧州.
That winter,
several hundred Dàténg 大籐 bandits entered the city by night,
causing many deaths and much plunder.
Jīng 涇 held back his troops and did not rescue them.
He was recalled,
imprisoned, and sentenced to beheading,
but was later pardoned.
After his death,
his son, Huán 桓, succeeded him.
In the early Hóngzhì 弘治 reign,
Huán 桓 garrisoned Níngxià 寧夏.
Many influential eunuchs tried to claim rewards for their protégés through false merits.
Huán 桓 refused them,
was slandered by them,
recalled,
and died.
After several successions, to Yánzuò 延祚,
the Míng 明 dynasty fell,
and his peerage was abolished.
Mèng Shàn 孟善 was
a native of Hǎifēng 海豐.
He served the Yuán 元 dynasty as Tóngqiān 同僉 of the Shāndōng Shūmìyuàn 山東樞密院.
In the early Míng 明 dynasty, he pledged allegiance,
and followed the grand army on its northern expedition,
being appointed Dìngyuǎn Wèi Bǎihù 定遠衞百戶.
He followed in the pacification of Yúnnán 雲南, and was promoted to Yānshān Zhōng Hùwèi Qiānhù 燕山中護衞千戶.
When the Yān 燕 army rose,
he attacked Sōngtíng Guān 松亭關,
and fought at Báigōu Hé 白溝河,
achieving meritorious service in both.
Later,
he defended Bǎodìng 保定.
Tens of thousands of Southern army troops attacked the city,
but with only a few thousand soldiers inside,
Shàn 善 held fast,
and the city remained intact.
He was successively promoted to Yòujūn Dūdū Tóngzhī 右軍都督同知.
He was enfeoffed as Bǎodìng Hóu 保定侯,
with a stipend of one thousand two hundred dàn 石.
In the first year of Yǒnglè 永樂, he garrisoned Liáodōng 遼東.
In the seventh year, he was recalled to Běijīng 北京,
with his beard and eyebrows already white.
The Emperor pitied him
and ordered him to retire.
In the sixth month of the tenth year, he died.
He was posthumously granted the title Téng Guó Gōng 滕國公,
and given the posthumous name Zhōngyǒng 忠勇.
His son, Yīng 瑛, succeeded him.
He commanded the Left Army,
and again followed the northern expedition,
supervising the transport of provisions.
Upon Rénzōng's 仁宗 ascension to the throne,
he served as Zuǒ Cāncānjìang 左參將,
garrisoning Jiāozhǐ 交阯.
He was implicated in his illegitimate elder brother Xián's 賢 attempt to establish Zhào Wáng 趙王 as emperor during the Yǒnglè 永樂 reign,
and was stripped of his peerage,
his patent (quàn 券) destroyed,
and was banished to Yúnnán 雲南.
In the sixth year of Xuāndé 宣德, he was allowed to return,
and served as an officer for specific duties in Xuānfǔ 宣府.
Upon Yīngzōng's 英宗 ascension to the throne,
he was appointed Jīngwèi Zhǐhuīshǐ 京衞指揮使.
After his death,
his son, Jùn 俊, inherited the office.
In the early Tiānshùn 天順 reign,
he was granted the title of Earl (Bójúe 伯爵) by imperial grace.
After his death,
his son, Áng 昂, succeeded him.
Upon Áng's 昂 death,
the peerage was abolished.
Zhèng Hēng 鄭亨 was
a native of Héféi 合肥.
His father, Yòng 用,
during the Hóngwǔ 洪武 reign,
accumulated merits and became Dàxīng Zuǒwèi Fù Qiānhù 大興左衞副千戶.
Upon his request to retire due to old age,
Hēng 亨 succeeded to his position.
In the twenty-fifth year of Hóngwǔ 洪武, he volunteered to carry an imperial edict to the Dádá 韃靼 (Tatars),
reaching the Ōnnàn Hé 斡難河.
Upon his return,
he was promoted to Mìyún Wèi Zhǐhuī Qiānshì 密雲衞指揮僉事.
When the Yān 燕 army rose,
he surrendered with his unit.
In the battle of Zhēndìng 真定,
he was the first to scale the wall,
and was promoted to Zhǐhuīshǐ 指揮使.
When attacking Dàníng 大寧,
upon reaching Liújiā Kǒu 劉家口,
the generals were about to attack the pass.
Chéngzǔ 成祖 worried that the soldiers guarding the pass might flee and report to Dàníng 大寧, allowing them to prepare.
So he ordered Hēng 亨 to lead several hundred elite cavalry,
roll up their banners and ascend the mountain,
secretly emerge behind the pass,
cut off their retreat,
and attack them swiftly.
All the pass defenders were captured,
and they then unexpectedly reached Dàníng 大寧. He was promoted to Běipíng Dūdū Zhǐhuī Qiānshì 北平都指揮僉事.
At night, he led his troops to defeat the army at Zhèngcūn Bà 鄭村壩,
then broke through Zǐjīng Guān 紫荊關 to the west,
plundered Guǎngchāng 廣昌,
captured Wèizhōu 蔚州,
and advanced directly to Dàtóng 大同.
He returned to fight at Báigōu Hé 白溝河,
pursued the fleeing enemy to Jǐnán 濟南,
and was promoted to Dūdū Tóngzhī 都指揮同知.
He attacked Cāngzhōu 滄州,
stationed his army at the North Gate,
and blockaded the supply route at Dōngchāng 東昌.
After a defeat in battle,
he rallied the scattered soldiers
and returned to the army at Shēnzhōu 深州.
The following year, he fought at Jiáhéo 夾河 and Gǎochéng 藁城,
took territory as far as Zhāngdé 彰德,
and displayed military might along the river.
He then returned to garrison Wánxiàn 完縣.
The next year, he joined in defeating Dōngpíng 東平 and Wènshàng 汶上,
and stationed his army at Xiǎohé 小河.
In a battle there, he suffered a defeat,
Wáng Zhēn 王真 died,
and all the generals wanted to return north,
except for Hēng 亨 and Zhū Néng 朱能.
Upon entering the capital,
he was successively promoted to Zhōngfǔ Zuǒ Dūdū 中府左都督,
enfeoffed as Wǔ'ān Hóu 武安侯,
with a stipend of one thousand five hundred dàn 石,
and was granted an hereditary patent (shì quàn 世券).
He remained to guard Běijīng 北京.
At that time, his father, Yòng 用, was still alive,
and received a peerage and stipend equal to Hēng's 亨.
In the first year of Yǒnglè (1403), [Hēng] was appointed Commander-in-Chief.
He led Wǔchéng Hóu Wáng Cōng and Ānpíng Hóu Lǐ Yuǎn to defend Xuānfǔ.
When Hēng reached the border,
he assessed the strategic advantages of Xuānfǔ, Wànquán, and Huáilái.
For every few forts that were close together,
he selected one fort in the middle that could accommodate the soldiers and horses of several forts,
making it a high-walled and deep-moated stronghold.
He dug wells to store water
and maintained vigilant watch.
When invaders arrived,
he would light fires at night
and fire cannons during the day.
With combined strength, they would hold fast.
His planning was meticulous,
and later generations could not improve upon it.
In the second month of the third year (1405), he was recalled,
then soon dispatched back to his post.
In the autumn of the seventh year (1409),
he defended the border at Kāipíng.
The following year,
the Emperor campaigned north,
ordering Hēng to supervise logistical transport.
He went out beyond the passes,
commanding the right vanguard,
and pursued and defeated Běnyǎshīlǐ.
The main army then encountered Ālǔtái.
Hēng led his troops forward first
and utterly routed them.
For his merits, he was ranked first among all generals.
That winter, he again garrisoned Xuānfǔ.
In the twelfth year (1414), he again accompanied the northern expedition,
leading the central army.
During the battle of Hūshīwēn,
he was hit by an arrow while pursuing the enemy and had to retreat,
but then rejoined the main army and helped defeat them.
In the twentieth year (1422), he again went out beyond the passes,
commanding the left vanguard,
leading ten thousand soldiers.
He cleared the Lóngmén road for the army to pass
and defeated the Wùliánghā at Qūliè Hé.
When returning with the baggage train,
he repelled the pursuing invaders
and then continued to guard Kāipíng.
Chéngzǔ made five expeditions beyond the passes,
and Hēng was present for all of them.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
he garrisoned Dàtóng.
In the second month of the first year of Hóngxī (1425), imperial edicts and general's seals were issued to the various border commanders-in-chief.
Hēng bore the seal of the Commander of the Vanguard for Punishing the West.
While at his post, he reclaimed land and accumulated grain,
and the border defenses were made secure.
From then on, Dàtóng rarely suffered from bandit raids.
In the first year of Xuāndé (1426), he was summoned to manage the affairs of the Rear Military Bureau.
Soon after,
he was again stationed at Dàtóng,
transporting provisions to Xuānfǔ.
He induced forty-nine chieftains from north of the border to surrender.
He requested the court
to treat them generously,
and those who pledged allegiance came in continuous succession.
In the second month of the ninth year (1434), he died at his post.
Hēng was stern and dignified,
skilled at managing his soldiers,
and ashamed of exploitation.
While he was at Dàtóng,
the eunuch guarding the region interfered with military administration.
Hēng restrained him with reason,
which displeased the eunuch,
but upon Hēng's death,
the eunuch deeply mourned and regretted his passing.
He was posthumously granted the title Zhāng Guógōng
and the posthumous name Zhōngyì.
His concubine, Lady Zhāng,
hanged herself to follow him in death
and was posthumously granted the title Shūrén.
His son, Néng, succeeded him,
and the title was passed down until the fall of the Míng dynasty.
Xú Zhōng,
a native of Héféi,
inherited his father's title as Vice Commander of Qiānhù in Hénán Guard.
He repeatedly accompanied the main army on northern expeditions,
capturing many enemies,
and was promoted to Commissioner of the Jìyáng Guard.
At the end of Hóngwǔ's reign,
he was stationed at Kāipíng.
When the Yān army breached Jūyōng and Huáilái,
Zhōng surrendered with Kāipíng.
He then followed them to seize Luánhé
and captured its city with Chén Xù.
When Lǐ Jǐnglóng attacked Běipíng,
the Yān army returned from Dàníng to relieve it.
Upon reaching Huìzhōu,
they organized five armies.
Zhāng Yù commanded the central army,
Zhū Néng the left army,
Lǐ Bīn the right army,
Fáng Kuān the rear army.
Zhōng, known for his bravery and fierceness,
was ordered to command the vanguard.
They then defeated Chén Huī at Báihé
and Lǐ Jǐnglóng at Zhèngcūnbà.
In the battle of Báigōuhé,
Zhōng charged into the enemy lines alone on horseback.
An arrow struck one of his fingers;
he had no time to remove the arrowhead,
so he quickly drew his saber and cut it off.
He then tightened his grip on the reins and galloped fiercely,
fighting to the death.
The King of Yān, observing from a height,
said to his attendants,
"Truly a brave warrior!"
They then attacked Jǐnán,
captured Cāngzhōu,
and fought major battles at Dōngchāng and Jiāhé.
They attacked Zhāngdé,
broke through the Xīshuǐ stronghold,
captured Dōng'ē, Dōngpíng, and Wénshàng,
and fought a great battle at Língbì.
Finally, he followed them across the Yangtze River and entered the capital.
From Assistant Commander, he was successively promoted to Assistant Regional Military Commissioner,
ennobled as Yǒngkāng Hóu,
with a stipend of one thousand one hundred *shí* of grain,
and granted a hereditary patent.
In every battle, Zhōng
spearheaded the attack and charged forward,
leading all the generals.
Yet, he disciplined his army very strictly,
and they caused no disturbance wherever they went.
He was good at pacifying those who surrendered,
gaining their utmost loyalty.
He was known for his filial piety towards his stepmother.
Upon returning home at night, he would always bow to the family shrine before entering.
He was frugal, modest, and respectful,
never making a mistake.
When Chéngzǔ made his northern tours,
he considered Zhōng to be seasoned and reliable,
and entrusted him to assist the Crown Prince in overseeing state affairs.
He died in the eighth month of the eleventh year of Yǒnglè (1413).
He was posthumously granted the title Cài Guógōng
and the posthumous name Zhōngliè.
The title was passed down to his distant descendant Xīdéng.
At the end of Chóngzhēn's reign,
Xīdéng died at the hands of rebels.
His cousin, Xīyìn, once inherited the marquisate
but died
without a son.
His wife, Lady Zhū,
was the daughter of Chéngguó Gōng Chúnchén.
After her husband's death,
she lived in an upper story for over ten years,
never setting foot on the ground.
When the city fell,
she held the ancestral tablets and immolated herself.
Guō Liàng,
a native of Héféi,
was a Qiānhù of the Yǒngpíng Guard.
When the Yān army arrived at Yǒngpíng,
he surrendered the city with Commander Zhào Yí,
and was immediately appointed its defender.
At that time, the Yān army had just risen
and first swept through neighboring prefectures and counties.
After capturing Jūyōng and Huáilái,
all the prefectures north of the mountains fell.
Yǒngpíng, however, bordered Shānhǎiguān
and separated Liáodōng.
Once it surrendered,
Běipíng was safe from further threats,
so Chéngzǔ then moved south to defeat Gěng Bǐngwén at Zhēndìng.
Soon after, the Liáodōng garrison commanders Jiāngyīn Hóu Wú Gāo and Regional Military Commissioner Yáng Wén and others besieged Yǒngpíng.
Liàng defended it very staunchly.
When relief forces arrived,
they attacked from both inside and outside,
and Wú Gāo retreated.
Not long after,
Wú Gāo was dismissed due to slander,
and Yáng Wén took over as commander,
again leading his troops to attack.
Liàng and Liú Jiāng jointly attacked
and utterly routed them.
He was successively promoted to Assistant Regional Military Commissioner.
When Chéngzǔ ascended the throne,
for his merit in defending the city, he was ennobled as Chéng'ān Hóu,
with a stipend of one thousand two hundred *shí* of grain,
a hereditary earldom.
In the seventh year of Yǒnglè (1409), while guarding Kāipíng,
he was reported for lax discipline.
He died in the third month of the twenty-first year (1423).
He was posthumously granted the title Xìng Guógōng
and the posthumous name Zhōngzhuàng.
His concubine, Lady Hán, hanged herself to follow him in death
and was posthumously granted the title Shūrén.
His son, Shèng, was supposed to inherit the earldom,
but Rénzōng specially ordered him to inherit the marquisate.
In the fifth year of Xuāndé (1430), he was stripped of his title for returning early from an imperial escort,
but it was soon restored.
He had no sons,
so his younger brother, Áng, inherited the earldom,
and the title was passed down until the fall of the Míng dynasty.
Zhào Yí,
a native of Hóng.
During the Hóngwǔ era,
he served as a Baihù of the Yànshān Right Guard.
He followed Fù Yǒudé on the northern expedition,
fortifying Xuānfǔ, Wànquán, and Huáilái,
and was promoted to Zhīhuī Qiānshì of the Yǒngpíng Guard.
He surrendered to Yān [Wang]
and distinguished himself in all subsequent battles,
rising successively to Dū Zhīhuīshǐ.
When Chéngzǔ became emperor,
he was enfeoffed as Xīnchéng Bó
with a stipend of a thousand dàn of grain.
In the eighth year of Yǒnglè, he garrisoned Xuānfǔ.
He once followed on a northern expedition,
but was imprisoned for stealing provisions,
though he was later released.
Soon after, due to the dangerous rapids of Lǚliáng Hóng,
Yí was ordered to garrison Xúzhōu and manage its affairs.
He was again impeached by Dū Yùshǐ Lǐ Qìng
for unauthorized killing of transport workers
and stealing official grain.
He was ordered to be judged by the judicial authorities,
but was again released.
Upon Rénzōng's ascension,
he was recalled.
He died in the early Xuāndé era.
His son Róng inherited.
After several generations, the title passed to Zhīlóng.
At the end of Chóngzhēn,
he assisted in defending Nánjīng.
When the Dà Qīng army advanced into Jiāngnán,
Zhīlóng welcomed them and surrendered.
Zhāng Xìn,
a native of Línhuái.
His father, Xīng,
was a Zhīhuī Qiānshì of the Yǒngníng Guard.
Xìn inherited his official position,
and was transferred to guard Pǔdìng and Píngyuè.
Through accumulated merit, he advanced to Dū Zhīhuī Qiānshì.
When Huìdì first ascended the throne,
high officials recommended Xìn for his strategy and bravery,
and he was transferred to the Běipíng Dūsī.
He received a secret imperial edict
ordering him to conspire with Zhāng Bǐng and Xiè Guì against the Yān Wáng.
Xìn was worried and fearful, not knowing what to do.
His mother, noticing his distress, questioned him,
and Xìn told her.
His mother was greatly surprised and said:
"No!
Your father always said that the imperial aura resides with Yān.
Do not act rashly,
lest you bring destruction upon your family."
Chéngzǔ feigned illness,
and Xìn visited the Yān residence three times,
but was refused an audience.
Xìn insisted,
entered and bowed before the bed,
secretly conveying the situation to Chéngzǔ.
Chéngzǔ rose in alarm,
summoned his generals to plan a rebellion,
and seized the Nine Gates.
When Chéngzǔ entered Jīngshī,
he ranked Xìn's achievements comparable to those of other generals,
promoted him to Dūdu Dū Qiānshì,
enfeoffed him as Lóngpíng Hóu,
with a stipend of a thousand dàn of grain,
and granted him a hereditary patent of nobility.
Chéngzǔ greatly esteemed Xìn,
calling him
"En Zhāng" (Benevolent Zhāng).
He wished to take Xìn's daughter as a consort,
but Xìn firmly declined.
Because of this, he was held in even higher regard.
All secret matters concerning the movements of the imperial princes
were entrusted to Xìn.
Xìn, relying on imperial favor, became quite arrogant.
In the winter of the eighth year of Yǒnglè,
Dū Yùshǐ Chén Yīng stated that Xìn had no significant military achievements,
yet undeservedly held the title of Marquis,
and was greedy and corrupt,
forcibly occupying over eighty lǐ of Liànhú in Dānyáng
and over seventy qǐng of official land in Jiāngyīn.
He requested that Xìn be handed over to the authorities for investigation and punishment.
The Emperor said:
"Yīng's words are correct.
Formerly, the Zhōngshān Wáng had a sand island,
through which farmers' waterways passed,
but his household servants obstructed them to gain illicit profits.
When the Wáng heard of it,
he immediately returned the land to the government.
How dare Xìn act like this!"
He ordered the judicial authorities to conduct a joint investigation,
but he was soon unpunished due to his past merits.
In the twentieth year, he followed on a northern expedition,
supervising the transport of provisions.
During a grand review at Xíníng,
Xìn pleaded illness and did not attend,
and was demoted to a mere official.
He was later reinstated.
Upon Rénzōng's ascension,
he was given the additional title of Shàoshī,
and received two stipends,
and a hereditary patent of Marquis.
In the first year of Xuāndé, he followed on the expedition to Yuè'ān.
In the third year,
the Emperor inspected the border,
and campaigned against the Wùliánghā,
Xìn was ordered to remain and guard the capital.
The following year, he supervised fifteen thousand soldiers in dredging the Héxīwù river channel.
In the fifth month of the seventh year of Zhèngtǒng, he died in Nánjīng.
He was posthumously granted the title of Yún Guó Gōng,
and given the posthumous name Gōngxī.
His son, Yōng,
had already distinguished himself as a Zhīhuī Qiānshì,
but died earlier.
His son, Chún, inherited the title,
which was passed down until the fall of the Míng dynasty.
There was a Táng Yún,
a Zhīhuī of the Yànshān Central Guard,
whose origins are unknown.
After Chéngzǔ had killed Zhāng Bǐng, Xiè Guì, and others,
the generals and soldiers still occupied the Nine Gates,
closed the outer gate of the barbican,
and arrayed their spears and halberds facing inwards.
Zhāng Yù and others attacked them by night,
and had already captured eight,
but the Xīzhímén (West Straight Gate) remained untaken.
Chéngzǔ ordered Yún to remove his armor,
and ride a horse as an escort as usual,
and instruct the defenders, saying:
"The Son of Heaven has already allowed the King to rule one region independently.
You must retreat quickly,
those who lag behind will be executed."
Yún was the eldest among the various Zhīhuī,
and was known for his trustworthiness and prudence,
so the generals and soldiers believed he was not deceiving them,
and dispersed.
At that time, the hearts of the populace were not yet settled,
but Yún informed them of the will of Heaven,
and the populace was then pacified.
Yún had followed Chéngzǔ for a long time,
and was constantly by his side,
and was greatly trusted and relied upon.
Whenever the army was dispatched,
he was always left to assist the heir apparent.
The southern armies attacked the city several times,
but he defended it with great strength,
never suffering a defeat in battle,
and was successively promoted to Dū Zhīhuīshǐ.
When Chéngzǔ became emperor,
he was enfeoffed as Xīnchāng Bó,
with the hereditary position of Zhīhuīshǐ.
He died in the seventh month of the following year.
He was given very generous posthumous rewards.
Xú Xiáng,
a native of Dàyě.
He first served Chén Yǒuliàng,
but later returned to Tàizǔ in Jiāngzhōu,
and through accumulated merit reached the position of Fù Qiānhù of the Yànshān Right Guard.
Chéngzǔ, seeing his prudence and integrity,
ordered him to attend to him personally.
He followed in the rebellion,
fighting for four years,
distinguishing himself in all battles,
and was successively promoted to Dū Zhīhuīshǐ.
When Chéngzǔ ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as Xīng'ān Bó for his merits,
with a stipend of a thousand dàn of grain.
At that time, of those enfeoffed as Bó,
Xiáng, along with Xú Lǐ, Lǐ Jùn, Zhāng Fǔ, Táng Yún, Tán Zhōng, Sūn Yán, Fáng Shèng, Zhào Yí, Chén Xù, Liú Cái, Rú Cháng, Wáng Zuǒ, and Chén Xuān, were fourteen individuals,
and Xiáng was the first among them.
Xiáng was somewhat older among the generals.
Upon his enfeoffment,
he became even more diligent and cautious.
He died in the fifth month of the second year of Yǒnglè.
He was seventy-three years old.
His grandson, Hēng, inherited.
In the twelfth year, he followed on a northern expedition,
serving as a Fù Jiāng of the Central Army.
Upon reaching the Tǔlá Hé,
he captured three thousand horses.
He returned to guard Kāipíng,
leading light cavalry to patrol between Xīnghé and Dàtóng for border defense.
Later, he frequently followed on expeditions beyond the Great Wall.
In the first year of Xuāndé, he campaigned against Jiāozhǐ as a Right Fù Jiāng,
but achieved no merit,
and was stripped of his title.
Upon Yīngzōng's ascension,
he was reinstated.
In the ninth year of Zhèngtǒng, he campaigned against the Wùliánghā,
passing through Jièlíngkǒu and Héběi Chuān,
was promoted to Hóu,
then garrisoned Shǎnxī,
and was later recalled.
He died in the early Tiānshùn era,
and was given the posthumous name Wǔxiāng.
Zǐxián 嗣 Bó,
due to his limp, was excused from court audiences
and given half salary.
He died.
His son, Shèng, succeeded
but died
without issue.
His second cousin, Liáng, succeeded.
Liáng's paternal grandmother
was a former concubine.
His step-grandmother,
the daughter of Dìngxiāng Bó Guō Dēng,
had her grandson contend for the succession at this time.
The court deliberated that as Lady Guō had initially married someone else,
legally she could not be the principal wife,
so Liáng ultimately succeeded.
Liáng was fifty years old at the time,
and his family was poor.
He worked as a laborer drawing water at Dàzhōng Qiáo.
When the Dūdū Fǔ sought the heir of Xīng'ānbó,
Liáng then bid farewell to his neighbors and left,
serving as Qiānshū Nánjīng Zhōngfǔ.
He displeased Liú Jǐn
and had his salary of two hundred dàn of grain revoked.
The title was passed down until the fall of the Míng dynasty.
Lǐ Jùn
was a native of Hézhōu.
His father, Wàng,
was the Fùqiānhù of Yànshān Zuǒ Hùwèi during the Hóngwǔ reign.
Jùn succeeded to the office
and joined the uprising,
seizing the Nine Gates.
He recruited several thousand brave and strong men from Jìzhōu and Yǒngpíng
and defeated the Southern army at Zhēndìng.
He participated in the recapture of Dàníng.
In the Battle of Zhèngcūnbà,
he led elite cavalry to charge the enemy formation.
The troops shouted and pressed on,
achieving a great victory.
He fought across Shāndōng
as the vanguard.
Upon reaching Xiǎohé,
he suddenly encountered the Southern army.
He led dare-to-die soldiers to first cut off the river bridge,
and the Southern army could not contend.
When Chéngzǔ arrived,
they were then utterly defeated.
He was repeatedly promoted to Dūzhīhuīshǐ
and enfeoffed as Xiāngchéng Bó,
with a salary of a thousand dàn of grain.
In the first year of Yǒnglè, he was sent to guard Jiāngxī.
When bandits rose in Yǒngxīn,
he captured and executed their leaders.
Soon after, he was recalled.
He died in the eleventh month of the third year.
His son, Lóng,
courtesy name Yànpíng,
succeeded to the title at age fifteen.
He was imposing and had military strategy.
He frequently accompanied the northern campaigns,
employing surprising tactics and accurately assessing the enemy,
which Chéngzǔ highly valued.
After the capital was moved,
considering Nánjīng as the fundamental base,
Lóng was ordered to remain and guard it.
Upon Rénzōng's ascension,
he was ordered to garrison Shānhǎiguān.
Not long after,
he was again ordered to guard Nánjīng.
Lóng loved reading and literature,
spoke candidly on matters,
was upright, cautious, and law-abiding,
and especially respected literati and officials.
He served in Nánjīng for eighteen years,
receiving over two hundred imperial edicts throughout.
When recalled,
the people of Nándū wept as they saw him off at the river.
In the fifth year of Zhèngtǒng, he took overall command of the Imperial Army.
In the eleventh year, he inspected the border at Dàtóng,
and was bestowed with a precious saber,
with stern warnings to be prepared,
which instilled awe both inside and outside.
Upon his return,
he had not punished a single person.
He died the following year.
His son, Zhēn, succeeded.
He perished at Tǔmù,
and was posthumously granted Hóu
and the posthumous name Dàoxī.
He had no son.
His younger brother, Jǐn, succeeded.
In the third year of Chénghuà,
the Dūzhǎng Mán in Sìchuān rebelled.
He was ordered to bear the seal of Zhēngyí Jiāngjūn
and serve as the Zǒngbīngguān to suppress them,
with Bīngbù Shàngshū Chéng Xìn overseeing him.
The army reached Yǒngníng
and advanced in six routes.
Jǐn and Xìn centrally controlled the operations
and completely destroyed all the Mán stockades.
In total, over four thousand five hundred heads were taken,
and countless armor, weapons, and livestock were captured.
The Dūzhǎng territory was divided,
and officials were appointed and administrations established to control it.
Upon the army's return,
he was promoted to Hóu
and successively given the title Tàibǎo.
He died in the second year of Hóngzhì.
He was posthumously granted Ruìguó Gōng
and the posthumous name Zhuàngwǔ.
Jǐn was magnanimous
and capable of being humble towards scholars.
His elder brother, Lián, was unable to succeed due to his unappealing appearance.
Jǐn treated him with great respect.
After Lián died,
he treated his son ● as his own.
Jǐn's son, Fǔ, succeeded as Bó
but died after several years.
Having no son,
● was then able to succeed.
Four generations later, down to Shǒuqí,
he successively managed military encampment affairs
and was granted Tàizǐ Shàobǎo.
In the early Chóngzhēn reign,
he served as Zǒngdū Jīngyíng.
He was dismissed from office due to camp soldiers committing theft
and died of grief and indignation.
His son, Guózhēn, succeeded.
He was eloquent.
Once summoned for an audience,
he expounded on military affairs in great detail,
and the Emperor believed him to be talented.
In the sixteenth year, he was appointed Zǒngdū Jīngyíng,
and heavily relied upon,
but Guózhēn actually had no other abilities.
In the third month of the following year,
Lǐ Zìchéng attacked the capital,
and the troops of the three grand camps collapsed without a fight.
After two nights,
the city fell.
The rebels coerced Guózhēn into surrender,
and Guózhēn removed his armor and obeyed.
When the demanded bribe was insufficient,
he was tortured and had his ankle broken,
then hanged himself.
Sūn Yán
was from Fèngyáng.
He followed Tàizǔ across the Yangtze River
and was successively promoted to Yànshān Zhōng Hùwèi Qiānhù,
then retired.
When the Yàn army rose,
the Tōngzhōu garrison commander, Fáng Shèng, surrendered the city.
The Prince, considering Yán an experienced general,
appointed him to assist Shèng in defending it.
When the Southern army arrived,
they attacked the city with great urgency,
destroying all the watchtowers and battlements.
Yán and Shèng defended it in many ways.
Afterward,
they again sallied forth and fought fiercely,
pursuing the fleeing enemy to Zhāngjiāwān,
capturing three hundred supply boats.
He was successively promoted to Dūzhīhuī Qiānshì.
For his merits,
as an old minister with the merit of defending the city,
he was enfeoffed as Yìngchéng Bó,
with a salary of a thousand dàn of grain.
In the eleventh year of Yǒnglè, he was garrisoned at Kāipíng,
then moved to Tōngzhōu.
Due to a private grudge, he bludgeoned a Qiānhù to death,
was stripped of his title,
and exiled to Jiāozhǐ.
Later, he was reinstated,
and died in the sixteenth year.
He was posthumously granted Hóu
and the posthumous name Wēiwǔ.
His son, Hēng, succeeded
and the title was passed down until the fall of the Míng,
when the peerage was abolished.
Fáng Shèng
was from Jǐnglíng.
He initially followed Chén Yǒuliàng.
He later surrendered,
and through successive merits, reached Tōngzhōu Wèi Zhīhuī Qiānshì.
When the Yàn army rose from Běipíng,
Shèng was the first to surrender Tōngzhōu.
Upon Chéngzǔ's ascension,
for his merit in defending the city,
he was enfeoffed as Fùchāng Bó,
with a salary of a thousand dàn of grain,
and the hereditary position of Zhīhuīshǐ.
He died in the fourth year of Yǒnglè.
Chén Xù,
a native of Quánjiāo.
His father, Bīn,
followed Tàizǔ as a zhǐhuī qiānshì.
Xù inherited the office
and became Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī of Huìzhōu Wèi.
He surrendered the city to Yān.
He followed in the campaign at Luánhé,
and his achievements were numerous.
He fought bravely at Zhēndìng.
When he was defending Dézhōu,
Shèng Yōng's army arrived,
and he abandoned the city and fled.
This was not held against him.
He followed into the capital,
was enfeoffed as Yúnyáng Bó,
with a stipend of one thousand dàn of grain.
In the first year of Yǒnglè, he was ordered to inspect the military horses and city defenses of Zhōngdū and the Zhílì Wèisuǒ.
In the fourth year, he followed Yīngguó Gōng Zhāng Fǔ to conquer Jiāozhǐ,
serving as Yòu Cānjìang.
Together with Fēngchéng Hóu Lǐ Bīn, he broke through Xīdū.
When the army returned,
he and Bīn were each granted an additional five hundred dàn of grain.
Later, Chén Jìkuò rebelled,
and he again followed Fǔ to suppress the rebellion.
When Fǔ returned,
he was again ordered to assist Mù Shèng.
In the eighth year, he died of illness in the army.
He had no sons,
so the peerage was extinguished.
Chén Xián,
a native of Shòuzhōu.
He first distinguished himself by following Tàizǔ,
and was granted the position of Bǎihù of Xióngwǔ Wèi.
He followed in campaigns against Xīfān and Yúnnán,
and in the northern expedition to Bǔyú'ér Hǎi,
and in all cases achieved merit.
He successively rose to Yānshān Yòu Hùwèi Zhǐhuī Qiānshì.
When the Yān army rose,
he followed the generals in battle,
often breaking through enemy lines and capturing strongholds.
The army praised his bravery and might.
He was successively promoted to Dūdū Qiānshì.
In the fourth month of the first year of Yǒnglè,
Chéngzǔ, concerned that some meritorious officials might have been overlooked for enfeoffment,
ordered Qiū Fú and others to deliberate.
Fú and the others stated that Dūdū Qiānshì Lǐ Bīn's merits were not inferior to Fáng Kuān's,
and that Jīngguó Gōng Zǐ Mào and Jīnxiāng Hóu Zǐ Tōng had not yet inherited their titles,
while Chén Xián, Zhāng Xīng, Chén Zhì, and Wáng Yǒu's merits were comparable to Liú Cái and others.
Thereupon, Bīn was enfeoffed as Fēngchéng Hóu;
Mào, Tōng, and the four, including Xián, were all enfeoffed as Bó,
each with a stipend of one thousand dàn of grain.
Xián was enfeoffed as Róngchāng Bó.
In the eighth year, he served as Shénjī Jiāngjūn,
following in the northern expedition.
He died in the eleventh month of the thirteenth year.
His son, Zhì,
who had previously distinguished himself as Zhǐhuī of Chángshān Yòu Hùwèi,
inherited his father's peerage.
During the Xuāndé reign, he, as a Cānjīang, was entrusted with the seal of Zhēngyí Jiāngjūn,
and garrisoned Jiāozhǐ.
He was timid and unfit for battle.
He also had a falling out with Dūdū Fāng Zhèng.
Lí Lì's power grew,
and he could not resist,
suffering a defeat.
He was stripped of his peerage
and served as an official for specific duties.
He distinguished himself by following Wáng Tōng.
Soon after, for abandoning territory and returning,
he was imprisoned,
but released.
At the beginning of the Zhèngtǒng reign,
he was reinstated as Zhǐhuīshǐ.
Zhāng Xīng,
a native of Shòuzhōu.
He started as an ordinary soldier
and became Zhǐhuī Qiānshì of Yānshān Zuǒ Hùwèi.
He followed in the uprising,
achieved many merits,
and successively rose to Dū Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī.
His nephew Yǒng was brave, strong, and dared to fight;
he followed Xīng in battle, acting as his closest aide.
Xīng once pursued the enemy alone on horseback,
suffering dozens of wounds,
and was too severely injured to fight.
Yǒng inherited the position of Zhǐhuīshǐ
and took command of his troops.
When merits were again assessed,
Xīng was enfeoffed as Ānxiāng Bó.
He died in the first month of the fifth year of Yǒnglè.
He had no sons.
Yǒng succeeded him.
In the eighth year of Yǒnglè, he followed in the northern expedition,
but suffered a military reverse,
and was banished to Jiāozhǐ.
He was pardoned, restored to his peerage,
and then died.
His son Ān succeeded.
In the thirteenth year of Zhèngtǒng, he garrisoned Guǎngdōng.
When Huáng Xiāoyǎng raided Guǎngzhōu,
Ān led a naval force and encountered the bandits at Dòngchuán Ào.
Ān was lying drunk,
and the government forces could not hold,
retreating to Shājiǎo Wěi.
The bandits pressed in,
the army routed,
and Ān drowned.
The peerage was passed down to Guāngcàn,
who died at the hands of marauding bandits.
Chén Zhì,
a native of Bā.
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
he served as Zhǐhuī Qiānshì of Yānshān Zhōng Hùwèi.
He followed in the uprising,
successively rose to Dū Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī,
and was enfeoffed as Suí'ān Bó.
Zhì was always known for his reverence and caution,
devoting himself to military service,
without slackening from beginning to end.
He died in the fifth month of the eighth year of Yǒnglè.
His grandson Yīng succeeded.
He repeatedly followed on expeditions beyond the Great Wall,
garrisoning Yǒngpíng, Shānhǎi, and Jìzhōu,
and fortified Yúnzhōu and Dúshí.
Shuǎngkāi possessed military talent,
but was greedy and cruel,
and many resented him.
He died,
and his son Xūn succeeded.
He perished at Tǔmù,
and was given the posthumous name Rónghuái.
His younger brother Sháo succeeded.
After his death,
his grandson Huì succeeded.
He commanded the Jìzhōu army.
When Dùyán invaded,
he repelled them.
At the beginning of Jiājìng,
for his meritorious service in welcoming the emperor,
he was promoted to Tàizǐ Tàibǎo,
then to Shàobǎo,
and his responsibilities were second only to Wǔdìng Hóu Guō Xūn.
He held the peerage for over sixty years before he died.
After five more generations, the Míng dynasty fell.
Wáng Yǒu,
a native of Jīngzhōu.
He inherited his father's position as Bǎihù of Yānshān Hùwèi.
He followed in the uprising,
and settled the capital.
His merits warranted enfeoffment as Hóu,
but due to his arrogance and indulgence, he was only granted Dū Zhǐhuī Qiānshì.
When Qiū Fú and others submitted their recommendations,
he was then enfeoffed as Qīngyuǎn Bó.
The following year, he was appointed Zǒngbīng Guān,
leading a naval force along the coast to capture Japanese pirates.
The pirates frequently raided the sea,
and Yǒu achieved no success,
for which the emperor severely reprimanded him.
Later,
he dealt a great defeat to the Japanese pirates.
The emperor was pleased,
issued an imperial edict commending and rewarding him,
and soon recalled him.
In the fourth year, he followed in the conquest of Jiāozhǐ,
and together with Zhǐhuī Liǔ Cóng, combined forces to break through the Chóujiāng palisades,
besieging the various mountains of Méi and Pǔlài,
beheading over thirty-seven thousand enemies.
In the seventh month of the sixth year, he was promoted to Hóu,
with an additional stipend of five hundred dàn of grain,
and a hereditary certificate.
The following year, he again campaigned in Jiāozhǐ,
serving as Fù Zǒngbīng.
In the eighth year, he returned
and followed in the northern expedition,
supervising the central army.
Separately, he and Liú Cái built a city on the Yǐnmǎhé river.
At that time, Zhīyuàn Shī Nǎigān wished to surrender.
The emperor ordered Yǒu to lead his troops ahead,
instructing him to adapt to the situation and annihilate the enemy if encountered.
When Yǒu and his troops arrived,
they were a day's march from the enemy,
but they took a detour to avoid them and went to Yìngchāng.
The army lacked food,
and many died.
The emperor was furious,
repeatedly sending edicts of severe reprimand,
and transferred his troops to Zhāng Fǔ.
Upon his return, the emperor ordered his officials to deliberate his punishment,
but later pardoned him.
In the twelfth year, he was accused by his concubine of slander against his wife and himself.
The accusation was proven,
and he was stripped of his peerage.
He died not long after.
Upon Rénzōng's ascension,
his son Shùn was appointed Zhǐhuī Qiānshì.
An encomium states: Zhāng Wǔ, Chén Guī, and others
either followed in the establishment of fiefdoms,
or were among the first to submit.
All were merely subordinate officers and colonels,
not possessing the courage, strategy, or wisdom to be called great generals.
Yet, once they encountered a confluence of destiny,
they were granted authority and their merits were celebrated,
proclaimed as vital assistants
ranking alongside the founding ministers of Tài-zǔ.
Was not the recompense for their services exceedingly generous?
Collated Notes
Biographies Thirty-Five: Xiè Jìn, Huáng Huái, Hú Guǎng, Jīn Yòuzī, Hú Yǎn
Xiè Jìn,
courtesy name Dàshēn,
was a native of Jíshuǐ.
His grandfather, Zǐyuán,
served as the Judge of Ānfú Prefecture during the Yuán dynasty.
During times of war and chaos,
he died upholding righteousness.
His father, Kāi,
was once summoned by Tài-zǔ to discuss matters of the Yuán dynasty;
though offered an official post,
he declined and left.
Jìn was intelligent and perceptive from a young age.
In the twenty-first year of Hóngwǔ, he passed the imperial examination for jinshì.
He was appointed Shùjíshì of the Central Secretariat.
He was greatly favored and respected,
often attending the emperor.
One day,
the emperor was in the west room of the Grand Kitchen
and instructed Jìn:
"I and you are bound by the righteousness of sovereign and minister,
and by the grace of father and son.
You should speak without reservation."
That very day, Jìn presented a memorial of ten thousand words,
which roughly stated: "Your servant has heard that if decrees are frequently changed, the people become confused;
if punishments are too numerous, the people become indifferent.
From the founding of the dynasty until now,
nearly twenty years have passed,
with no period without changing laws,
and no
day without transgressors.
Your servant has heard that Your Majesty, in your great wrath,
has rooted out evil and cut down its branches,
punishing the treacherous and rebellious.
But your servant has not heard of one great good being praised,
its reward extending for generations,
and even reaching
their hometown,
consistent from beginning to end.
Your servant observes that Your Majesty enjoys reading miscellaneous books like Shuōyuàn and Yùnfǔ, as well as the so-called Dàodéjīng and Xīnjīng.
Your servant secretly believes this is highly inappropriate.
Shuōyuàn
originated with Liú Xiàng,
and contains many arguments from the Warring States period's strategists.
Yùnfǔ was produced by the Yīn clan of the Yuán dynasty,
a compilation of crude and muddled material,
with little of value to extract.
If Your Majesty prefers them for
their convenience in checking,
then your servant wishes to gather one or two determined scholars and outstanding Confucians.
Your servant requests to hold the brush and follow after them,
tracing upwards to Táng, Yú, Xià, Shāng, Zhōu, Kǒng,
and downwards to Guān,
Mǐn, Lián, Luò,
with a clear and solid foundation,
categorizing matters as appropriate,
to compile a classic.
Connecting upwards to the classics and histories,
would this not be one aspect of an age of peace's grand creation?
Moreover, the current
Six Classics are incomplete.
Lǐjì, originating from Hàn Confucians,
is particularly contradictory and confusing;
it should be revised promptly.
Seek out scholars who understand music,
to fully prepare the institutions of a hundred kings,
and compose
a classic of music to benefit ten thousand generations.
Venerate Fúxī, Shénnóng, Huángdì, Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, Wǔ, Gāoyáo, Yī Yǐn, Tàigōng, Zhōu
Gōng, Jì, Xiè, Yí, Yì, Fù Yuè, and Jī Zǐ in the Imperial Academy.
Kǒngzǐ should be universally worshipped as the Foremost Teacher, from the Son of Heaven down to the common people,
and
be accompanied by Yán, Zēng, Zǐsī, and Mèngzǐ.
From Mǐn Zǐ downwards,
each should be sacrificed to in their respective hometowns.
At Quèlǐ in Lǔ,
a temple for Shúliáng Hē should still be built,
and he be granted a royal
title,
accompanied by Yán Lù, Zēng, and Kǒng Lǐ.
To completely wash away the remnants of previous dynasties,
and inaugurate the culture and institutions of the Celestial Dynasty,
would this not be magnificent!
As for sacrifices to Heaven,
the custom of sweeping the ground should be restored; to honor ancestors, the system of seven ancestral temples should be fully prepared.
Fèngtiān殿
should not be a place for banquets;
Wényuān閣 is not yet fully equipped for
the grandeur of an academy and library.
The Grand Court of Sacrifices should not be a place to practice vulgar music;
official prostitutes are not humanely justifiable.
Prohibit actors and entertainers,
and replace the palace eunuchs.
Those holding halberds at the imperial
steps
should all be worthy gentlemen;
the imperial guards and stablemen
should all be excellent and upright individuals.
Abolish taxes on mountains and marshes,
and exempt merchants from duties at garrisons.
Live in simple wooden carriages and plain dwellings,
and do not
undertake civil engineering works.
Spread out and cultivate wasteland,
and do not covet the lands of the four barbarians.
Expel robust Buddhist and Daoist monks
to restore them to normal human life.
Burn the
deceptive scriptures and incantations
to eradicate their deceit.
Eliminate ghost-worshipping witches,
destroy illicit shrines,
reduce redundant officials,
and diminish small counties.
Severely punish extra-legal cruelties,
and permanently abolish imperial construction
labor in the capital.
Exile for ten years and then permit return;
administer eighty strokes of the杖 and nothing more.
Women whose households are not in disarray
should not be arrested and imprisoned.
If a high official has committed a capital offense,
he should be executed,
not humiliated.
Regulate the calendar to clarify the seasons,
and instruct the people in their work.
Only emphasize the appropriateness of sowing and planting;
what use are the errors of 'Jianchu' (daily omens)?
What should be clearly recorded
are the movements of the sun
and moon,
and the positions of the stars.
Observing above and examining below,
matters should align with natural order;
the alignment of the Seven Regulators
is precisely this kind of thing.
In recent years,
the imperial censorate's discipline has been lax.
They consider the severity of punishments as their skill,
and the number of prisoners interrogated as their merit.
This is certainly not how to encourage integrity
and enhance dignity.
When censors impeach,
they all act on secret imperial decrees.
Whenever they hear that an amnesty is granted,
they deliberately hold back,
thinking that by doing so,
the emperor's favor
will be greater.
These are all petty tactics of sycophantic small-minded men seeking favor.
Why does Your Majesty not see through them with a clear heart?
Your Majesty appoints people without regard for their worth,
and assigns offices without considering their importance.
Laws are established that are not used by the ruler,
where 'every penny is extracted' is the saying,
and rules are set up for colluding
and bending the law,
where 'they are treated like dirt.'
Imperial students and jinshì, well-versed in classics and upright in conduct,
are often relegated to lower positions.
Filially pious and talented individuals,
though stumbling blindly
and progressing without insight,
are sometimes
placed in the imperial court.
Violent and stubborn ruffians,
and foolish and incompetent fellows,
throw away their knives and combs in the morning,
and in the evening don caps and robes;
they cast aside their baskets and boxes on the left,
and on the right
tie on official cords and seals.
Consequently, the virtuous are ashamed to be ranked with them,
while mediocre people all emulate their ways.
They consider greed and dodging punishment as clever strategy,
and integrity punished as
a mere excuse.
Those who emerge from the Ministry of Personnel have no distinction between worthy and unworthy;
those who enter the Ministry of Justice have no judgment between right and wrong.
The whole empire says that Your Majesty executes
or spares according to your whims,
unaware that it is all due to the lack of loyal and good officials.
In ancient times, good and evil
were certainly recorded by neighbors.
Although there are now measures to proclaim and commend good deeds,
there are no regulations for local schools and village academies.
Although the system of mutual knowledge
sternly.
The methods of instruction and admonition are not yet complete.
Your minister wishes to seek the ancient people's rites for managing a household,
and methods for harmonizing with neighbors,
such as the village compact of the ancient Lán tián Lǚshì,
and the family rules of the contemporary Yìmén
Zhèngshì,
and promulgate them throughout the empire.
Hereditary officials and prominent clans
should take the lead in encouraging these practices,
honoring and exempting them [from certain obligations],
to serve as models for the people.
Then we shall see transformation and renewal,
until
it will not be difficult for every household to be worthy of enfeoffment.
Your Majesty's natural endowments are supremely high,
in harmony with the subtle Dao.
As for deities, monsters, and absurdities,
your minister knows Your Majesty sees through them completely.
Yet still, there is no escape from what is called "setting up
teachings by means of divine ways."
Your minister says this is not necessarily so.
The unified map of the empire is already settled;
the hearts of the people of the time are already subdued;
all treacherous heroes have been awed.
There are no calamities from Heaven,
no harms to the people,
the Sacred Person is healthy and peaceful,
and the Sacred Sons and Sacred Grandchildren continue in unbroken succession.
This is what is called "having truly obtained the [heavenly] mandate."
Why must one raise an army using the pretext of acquiring
treasures,
and inform the populace that immortals serve as omens and validations?
Your minister observes that lands have their times of prosperity and decline,
and things have their periods of abundance and scarcity,
yet the collection of commercial taxes
is uniformly at a fixed quota.
This causes that when there is abundance,
the cunning and wicked can encroach
and deceive;
when there is scarcity,
the good and honest are distressed by having to make up the deficit.
The summer tax is one thing,
but for tea and pepper there are grain taxes,
and for fruits and silk there are [additional] taxes.
They are already taxed at the place of production,
and
again taxed at the ferries they pass through.
How excessively they deprive the people of their profit!
Moreover, many poor households
cannot avoid the fault of abandoning their land.
The land
of today does not have the same productivity
as that of previous days, yet the collections
of today match the tax-grain
of previous days.
Some sell their property to pay taxes,
losing their property while the tax remains;
some pay compensation to serve in corvée,
finding the corvée burdensome and the people distressed.
The quality of the fields is uneven,
but the starting levy has no distinction between light and heavy.
Fertile lands are taxed lightly,
while barren lands
are taxed heavily.
To rescue the distressed and reform these abuses,
nothing is better than implementing the system of land allotment and equal fields,
and concurrently promoting the Ever-Normal Granaries and Righteous Granaries initiatives.
Accumulate gradually,
until having nine years' worth of food will not be difficult.
Your minister heard Kǒngzǐ say:
"Kings and dukes establish defenses to guard their states."
Recent generations, accustomed to peace and ease,
demolish famous cities,
melt down weapons,
and forbid military matters,
taking
this as great peace.
Should an unforeseen danger arise one day,
even connected cities would crumble at the sight of the enemy.
It is now fitting to order the responsible officials to repair them,
allowing them time in years,
and guarding them with
village elders,
setting a quota for archers,
and concurrently training citizen soldiers.
Open military examinations to attract heroes from all under Heaven,
and expand village schools to extend the reach to talented individuals from all under Heaven.
In ancient times,
there were many academies with educational lands,
scholars had estates,
and righteous fields were associated with clans.
All of these should be revived and expanded.
Moreover, criminals' wives and children should not be implicated,
and punishment should not extend to descendants.
Collective punishment originated from Qín law,
and the execution of wives and children stemmed from fabricated texts.
Today, those who do good deeds may not necessarily bring
honor to their wives and children,
but those who err are certainly implicated by village elders.
Furthermore, the law considers human relations paramount,
yet there are provisions for assigning women [as slaves],
permitting injustice.
Then what
is the purpose of cherishing integrity and righteousness?
This is where moral transformation lies.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"If names are not correct, then words will not be smooth."
Shàngshū and Shìláng
are internal attendants,
yet they are placed above the Six Ministers.
Lángzhōng and Yuánwài
are internal
officials,
yet they are named among the six departments.
Censors and literary officials
are meant to reside in favored positions in the imperial court;
prefects and county magistrates
should not avoid their native places.
Officials should cooperate
reverently,
promoting courtesy among themselves.
Yet now, internal and external officials of all departments beat their subordinates,
worse than slaves.
This causes those who are weak and cowardly
to lose all sense of shame,
advancing and retreating with servility,
their bodies not protected.
This is utterly not conducive to fostering filial conduct or encouraging integrity and righteousness.
Your minister believes that from now on, unless officials are dismissed for criminal offenses,
the punishments of flogging and caning should not
be used.
For pressing taxes and demanding urgency,
if there is a minor error or discrepancy,
a switch made of reeds for symbolic humiliation
is sufficient to deter.
Your minister only knows to pour out his foolish heart,
eager to present his suggestions,
without any particular order.
May Your Majesty kindly take heed.
After the memorial was presented,
the Emperor praised his talent.
Later,
he again offered "Ten Strategies for Great Peace,"
but the text is lengthy and not recorded here.
Jìn once entered the Ministry of War to demand servants [for his personal use],
and his words were arrogant.
Shū Chén Jìn reported this.
The Emperor said:
"Does Jìn presume upon his idleness and freedom?"
He ordered him to be reassigned as a Censor.
Hánguó Gōng Lǐ Shàncháng was convicted and died.
Jìn, on behalf of Lángzhōng Wáng Guóyòng, drafted a memorial to appeal his innocence.
He also drafted a memorial for his colleague Xià Chángwén,
impeaching Dū Yùshǐ Yuán Tài.
Yuán Tài deeply resented him.
At that time, fathers of close ministers were all allowed to be received in audience.
Jìn's father, Kǎi, arrived,
and the Emperor said to him:
"Great talent matures late.
If you take your son home,
and further encourage him to study,
coming back ten years later,
it will not be too late for great employment."
In the eighth year of Guī,
Tàizǔ passed away.
Jìn entered the capital to mourn.
The officials impeached Jìn for disobeying the imperial edict,
and furthermore, his mother's funeral was not yet held,
and his father was ninety years old.
It was improper to leave them to travel.
He was demoted to a guard official in Hézhōu.
At that time, Dǒng Lún, a Minister of the Board of Rites, was highly trusted by Huìdì.
Jìn therefore sent a letter to Lún, saying:
"Jìn is frank, wild, and foolish,
avoiding nothing and fearing nothing.
I have repeatedly submitted sealed memorials,
arguing that the enfeoffment of powerful princes
might, in the event of misfortune,
certainly lead to troubles like Lìzhǎng and Wúbì.
When Hāsù returned,
I respectfully received his inquiries,
and suggested that he should be treated with courtesy.
Slightly offending the influential figures
would surely cause their followers to become disloyal.
There are many such instances,
and most of them were guessed correctly.
I also once drafted a memorial of remonstrance for Wáng Guóyòng,
speaking of matters concerning Hánguó,
which incurred the hatred of Zhān Huī,
who wished to ensnare me with dangerous laws.
I humbly received the holy grace,
which issued a comforting decree,
and bestowed a generous reward in money,
ordering me to write for ten years
and then return to court with a cap and belt.
The Yuán Shǐ had errors,
and I was commanded to revise it.
I also continued to complete the Sòng Shū
and delete and revise the Lǐ Jīng;
all the prefaces and principles have already been submitted to the emperor.
In my leisure time from serving my parents,
I shut myself indoors to compile and write,
gradually making progress,
which has lasted for nearly eight years.
The news of the emperor's passing suddenly arrived,
and my grief was so intense I wished to die.
My mother's coffin is still awaiting burial,
and I have not had time to lay her to rest.
My family has a ninety-year-old parent,
leaning on the door, longing for me;
I could not even indulge in affection for them.
I hoped to pay my respects at the imperial mausoleum
and shed tears on the earth.
How could I have erred
and been sent far away by imperial grace?
The people of Yáng and Yuè
cannot endure the heat and cold,
and furthermore, many suffer from illness.
Having to bow and hurry about,
ranked among common clerks and soldiers,
is truly unbearable.
I weep day and night,
constantly fearing the unexpected,
betraying my lifelong aspirations
and bearing eternal sorrow.
Therefore, I frequently express my gratitude.
I hope to return to the capital,
to gaze upon the imperial countenance,
or perhaps to return south,
to see my father and son;
that would be like being reborn."
Lún then recommended Jìn,
who was summoned to be an Academician of the Hanlin Academy.
When Chéngzǔ entered the capital,
Jìn was promoted to侍讀 (Shìdú)
and ordered, along with Huáng Huái, Yáng Shìqí, Hú Guǎng, Jīn Yòuzī, Yáng Róng, and Hú Yǎn, to concurrently serve in the Wényuāngé
and participate in state affairs.
The Cabinet's participation in state affairs began from this point.
Soon after, he was promoted to侍讀學士 (Shìdú Xuéshì),
and was commanded to serve as the chief editor of the Tàizǔ Shílù and the Liè Nǚ Zhuàn.
When the books were completed,
he was bestowed with silver and silk.
In the second year of Yǒnglè,
the Crown Prince was established,
and Jìn was promoted to Hànlín Xuéshì concurrently with Yòu Chūnfāng Dàxuéshì.
The emperor once summoned Jìn and others, saying:
"You seven serve by my side day and night.
I commend your diligence and prudence,
and often speak of it within the palace.
● Human nature
is easy to maintain at the start,
but difficult to preserve to the end.
I wish us to encourage each other."
Thereupon, each was granted a fifth-rank official robe,
and the wives of the seven men were ordered to pay respects to the Empress at Rouruídiàn;
the Empress greatly bestowed favors upon them.
On Lìchūn (Beginning of Spring) day, Jìn and others were also given golden brocade robes,
on par with those of the Shangshū.
When Jìn and others entered to express their gratitude,
the emperor said:
"The office of speaking on my behalf
is related to state secrets,
and furthermore, you attend me day and night,
your beneficial contributions are no less than those of the Shangshū."
One day,
the emperor ascended Fèngtiānmén,
and instructed the officials of the Six Bureaus to speak frankly.
He then looked at Jìn and others, saying:
"The virtues of Wáng and Wèi
are rare in the world.
If those who offer advice have nothing to fear,
and those who listen have nothing to resent,
what trouble would there be in governing the world?
I and you shall strive together in this."
In the autumn of that year,
Hú Yǎn left to become the Jijiu,
and Jìn and the other six leisurely offered their advice.
The emperor often emptied his mind to listen.
Jìn ascended to court at a young age,
was highly talented,
and was direct in handling affairs,
expressing himself clearly and articulately.
He promoted scholars and gentlemen,
and whenever there was a good quality, he would praise it without restraint.
However, he liked to judge others
without reservation,
and many court officials resented his favor.
Also, due to his counsel on the establishment of the heir,
he was resented by the King of Hàn, Gāo Xù,
which eventually led to his downfall.
Prior to this,
the position of heir was not yet settled.
Qíguógōng Qiū Fú argued that the King of Hàn had rendered meritorious service,
and should be established.
The emperor secretly asked Jìn.
Jìn stated:
"The eldest imperial son is benevolent and filial,
and the hearts of the people turn to him."
The emperor did not respond.
Jìn then bowed his head again, saying:
"And there is the good holy grandson."
Referring to Xuānzōng.
The emperor nodded in agreement.
The Crown Prince was thus settled.
Gāo Xù therefore deeply resented Jìn.
Coincidentally, a large army was dispatched to suppress Ānnán,
and Jìn remonstrated against it.
His advice was not heeded.
It was eventually pacified,
and prefectures and counties were established.
After the Crown Prince was established,
he also frequently displeased the emperor.
Gāo Xù's favor grew,
and his ceremonial status exceeded that of the heir apparent.
Jìn again remonstrated, saying:
"This will stir up conflict,
it is impermissible."
The emperor was angered,
believing that he was sowing discord among family members,
and his grace and courtesy gradually declined.
In the fourth year, Huáng Huái and five others were granted second-rank gauze and silk robes,
but Jìn was not included.
After a long time,
the discussions of Fú and others gradually reached the outer court,
and Gāo Xù then slandered Jìn for divulging confidential palace matters.
The following year,
Jìn was punished for unfairness in marking examination papers in the imperial examination,
and was demoted to an assistant administrator in the Guǎngxī Provincial Administration Commission.
After he departed,
Lǐ Zhìgāng, a Director in the Board of Rites, stated that Jìn harbored resentment,
so he was reassigned to Jiāozhǐ,
and ordered to supervise provisions in Huàzhōu.
In the eighth year of the Yǒnglè reign,
Xiè Jìn went to the capital to report on affairs.
He arrived when the Emperor was on a northern expedition.
Xiè Jìn paid his respects to the Crown Prince and then returned.
The Prince of Hàn (Hàn Wáng) said that Xiè Jìn had waited until the Emperor was away,
privately visited the Crown Prince,
and then simply left,
without observing the etiquette of a subject.
The Emperor was furious.
At that time, Xiè Jìn was traveling through Guǎngdōng with the Reviser Wáng Chēng,
observing the mountains and rivers.
He submitted a memorial requesting the dredging of the Gàn Jiāng River to connect north and south.
When the memorial arrived,
Xiè Jìn was arrested and imprisoned in the imperial dungeons,
where he was subjected to extensive torture.
His testimony implicated Tāng Zōng, Assistant Minister of the Grand Court of Justice;
Gāo Déyáng, Registrar of the Zōngrén Fǔ;
Lǐ Guàn, Associate Editor;
Wáng Rǔyù, Assistant Tutor;
Zhū Hóng, Compiler;
Jiǎng Jì, Pān Jī, Xiāo Yǐngāo, all Revisers; and Lǐ Zhìgāng.
All were imprisoned.
Rǔyù, Guàn, Hóng, Yǐngāo, and Déyáng all died in prison.
In the thirteenth year,
Jǐn Yīwèi Commander Jǐ Gāng submitted a list of prisoners.
When the Emperor saw Xiè Jìn's name, he said:
“Is Xiè Jìn still alive?”
Jǐ Gāng then intoxicated Xiè Jìn with wine,
buried him in accumulated snow,
and he died immediately.
He was forty-seven years old.
His property was confiscated,
and his wife, children, and clan were exiled to Liáodōng.
When Xiè Jìn was serving in the Hànlín Academy,
the eunuch Zhāng Xīng, presuming on imperial favor, beat someone outside the Zuǒshùnmén gate.
Xiè Jìn reprimanded him,
and Zhāng Xīng withdrew, bowing.
The Emperor once wrote down the names of court officials
and ordered Xiè Jìn to list their strengths and weaknesses.
Xiè Jìn said:
“Jiǎn Yì has a naturally profound and steady character,
but lacks firm opinions within.
Xià Yuánjí has virtue and magnanimity,
but does not keep scoundrels at a distance.
Liú Jùn has talent and ability,
but is not mindful of righteousness.
Zhèng Cì can be called a gentleman,
but is rather lacking in talent.
Lǐ Zhìgāng is arrogant and power-hungry;
though talented, he is not upright.
Huáng Fú has an easy and straightforward heart,
and definite convictions.
Chén Yīng is harsh in enforcing the law,
but can still maintain integrity.
Sòng Lǐ is blunt, honest, and strict,
and disregards the grievances of others.
Chén Qià is open-minded and quick-witted,
and also does not deviate from righteousness.
Fāng Bīn has the talent of a clerk,
but the heart of a merchant.”
The Emperor gave this to the Crown Prince,
who then asked about Yǐn Chānglóng and Wáng Rǔyù.
Xiè Jìn replied:
“Yǐn Chānglóng is a gentleman, but not broad-minded.
Wáng Rǔyù's literary skill is hard to come by,
but regrettably, he has a mercenary heart.”
Later, when Rénzōng ascended the throne,
he showed Xiè Jìn's memorial to Yáng Shìqí and said:
“People say Xiè Jìn was mad;
but observing what he discussed and listed,
he had firm opinions on everything,
he was not mad.”
An edict was issued to return Xiè Jìn's wife, children, and clan.
Earlier, Xiè Jìn and Hú Guǎng attended a banquet given by Chéngzǔ together.
The Emperor said:
“You two were born in the same village,
studied together when you grew up,
and served as officials together.
Xiè Jìn has a son;
Hú Guǎng can give his daughter to him in marriage.”
Hú Guǎng kowtowed and said:
“My wife is currently pregnant,
and we do not yet know the sex.”
The Emperor laughed and said:
“It will definitely be a girl.”
Soon after, a daughter was indeed born,
and the marriage was arranged.
When Xiè Jìn was ruined,
his son Zhēnxī was exiled to Liáodōng.
Hú Guǎng wanted to annul the marriage.
The daughter cut off her ear and swore:
“This ill-fated marriage
was presided over by His Majesty,
and personally agreed to by my father.
I will die rather than be disloyal.”
When the amnesty came and they returned,
she ultimately married Zhēnxī.
In the eighth month of the first year of the Zhèngtǒng reign, an edict restored their confiscated family property.
In the first year of the Chénghuà reign, Xiè Jìn's official post was posthumously restored,
and he was granted the title of Cháoyì Dàfū.
Originally, Xiè Jìn suffered misfortune for speaking about the Prince of Hàn and affairs concerning Ānnán.
Later, Gāo Xù was executed for rebellion.
Ānnán rebelled several times,
and after officials were stationed there for a short time,
it was abandoned again.
Everything was as Xiè Jìn had predicted.
Xiè Jìn's elder brother, Xiè Lún,
also served as a Censor during the Hóngwǔ reign.
His nature was upright and firm.
Later, he was appointed Instructor of Yìngtiān.
His son, Xiè Zhēnqī,
was famous for his calligraphy.
Huáng Huái,
courtesy name Zōngyù,
was a native of Yǒngjiā.
His father, Huáng Xìng,
when Fāng Guózhēn occupied Wēnzhōu,
went into hiding to avoid false appointments.
Huáng Huái passed the imperial examination at the end of the Hóngwǔ reign,
and was appointed Scholar of the Grand Secretariat.
When Chéngzǔ ascended the throne,
he was summoned for an audience and his answers pleased the Emperor.
He was ordered to stand with Jiě Jìn
to the left of the imperial couch
to be available for consultation.
Sometimes, it was past midnight.
The Emperor would go to bed,
but still grant them seats before the couch to talk,
and all secret and important matters were heard by them.
Soon after, he and five others, including Xiè Jìn, were appointed to the Wènyuāngé,
and were re-appointed as Hànlín Compilers,
then promoted to Imperial Diarist.
When the establishment of the Crown Prince was discussed,
Huáng Huái requested the establishment of the legitimate eldest son.
When the Crown Prince was established,
he was promoted to Left Shùzǐ concurrently Imperial Diarist.
In the fifth year of Yǒnglè,
Jiě Jìn was demoted,
and Huáng Huái was promoted to Grand Secretary of the Right Spring Pavilion.
The following year, he, along with Hú Guǎng, Jīn Yòuzī, Yáng Róng, and Yáng Shìqí, jointly tutored the Imperial Grandson.
In the seventh year,
the Emperor made a northern tour,
and appointed Huáng Huái, Jiǎn Yì, Jīn Zhōng, and Yáng Shìqí to assist the Crown Prince in supervising the state.
In the eleventh year, he again went on a northern tour,
and Huáng Huái remained in charge.
The following year,
when the Emperor returned from campaigning against the Oirats,
the Crown Prince's envoy sent to greet him was somewhat delayed.
The Emperor, swayed by the slander of Gāo Xù,
summoned all officials of the Eastern Palace to the imperial dungeons.
Huáng Huái, Yáng Pǔ, and Jīn Wèn were all imprisoned for ten years.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
their official posts were restored.
Soon after, he was promoted to Commissioner of the Office of Transmission,
concurrently Grand Secretary of the Wǔyīngdiàn,
and jointly managed imperial edicts with Yáng Róng, Jīn Yòuzī, and Yáng Shìqí.
When his mother passed away,
he requested to observe the full mourning period.
This was not permitted.
The following year, he was promoted to Junior Guardian and Minister of Revenue,
concurrently Grand Secretary as before.
When Rénzōng died,
the Crown Prince was in Nánjīng.
The Prince of Hàn had long harbored rebellious ambitions,
and there was suspicion and fear both inside and outside the court.
Huáng Huái was so worried and anxious that he vomited blood.
In the first year of Xuāndé,
the Emperor personally led a campaign to Lè'ān,
and appointed Huáng Huái to remain in charge.
The following year, he requested retirement due to illness,
which was granted.
His father, Huáng Xìng, was ninety years old,
and Huáng Huái attended to him joyfully.
When Huáng Xìng died,
the Emperor granted a burial and sacrifice.
Huáng Huái went to the palace to express his gratitude.
During the Lantern Festival,
he was granted a visit to the Xīyuàn (Western Garden),
and an edict permitted him to ascend Wànsuì Shān in a palanquin.
He was appointed to preside over the metropolitan examination.
When he finally took leave to return home,
he was seen off at the Tàiyè Chí (Taiye Pool).
The Emperor composed a long song to bid him farewell,
and also said:
“On my birthday,
you must return.”
The following year, he came to offer congratulations.
When Yīngzōng ascended the throne,
he again came to court.
He died in the sixth month of the fourteenth year of Zhèngtǒng.
He was eighty-three years old,
and was posthumously named Wénjiǎn.
Huáng Huái was intelligent and resolute,
and understood the principles of governance.
During the Yonglè reign,
the sorcerer Lǐ Fǎliáng rebelled in Chángshā.
As Rénzōng was then supervising the state,
he ordered Lǐ Bīn, the Marquis of Fēngchéng, to suppress him.
The Prince of Hàn, jealous of the Crown Prince's achievements,
deceitfully claimed that Bīn was unsuitable.
Huái said:
"Bīn
is an old general;
he will surely crush the rebels.
I request that he be dispatched immediately."
Bīn subsequently captured Fǎliáng.
At another time, someone reported a party of traitors.
Huái said to the Emperor:
"An imperial edict was issued at the end of the Hóngwǔ reign prohibiting this;
it is not appropriate to reopen such cases."
The Ministry of Personnel retrospectively investigated
those from the south
who, when the "Jìngnán" campaign began,
were officials in the north and did not immediately submit,
proposing they be exiled to border garrisons.
Huái said:
"If this is done,
I fear it will not demonstrate broadmindedness to the people."
The Emperor followed all his advice.
Ālǔtái submitted to the court
and requested permission to control the various Túbō tribes.
He asked the court to engrave a gold oath,
grind the gold into wine,
and have the chieftains drink it to seal the alliance.
The general consensus was to grant this.
Huái said:
"If their power is divided, they are easy to control;
if unified, they will be difficult to handle."
The Emperor looked to his attendants and said:
"When Huáng Huái discusses matters,
it is like standing on a high ridge,
seeing everything, no matter how distant."
When the Western Regions monk, Dàbǎo Fǎwáng, came to court,
the Emperor intended to carve a jade seal to bestow upon him,
and showed the uncarved jade to Huái.
Huái said:
"When the court bestows imperial edicts upon various foreign states,
it uses the 'Chìmìng'
and 'Guǎngyùn'
two seals.
This jade is comparatively large,
which is not the way to show respect to distant people and dignify the court."
The Emperor praised and accepted his suggestion.
His proposals and critiques were generally like this.
However, his capacity was rather narrow.
If his colleagues made a minor mistake,
he would immediately report it.
Some say that Xiè Jìn's banishment
was partly due to Huái.
When he fell out of favor with Xuānzōng,
it was also said that Yáng Róng claimed Huái had consumption
and could infect others.
Hú Guǎng,
courtesy name Guāngdà,
was a native of Jíshuǐ.
His father, Zǐqí,
whose given name was Shòuchāng,
went by his courtesy name.
When Chén Yǒuliàng captured Jí'ān,
Tàizǔ sent troops to retake it,
intending to kill over a thousand people who had been coerced into compliance.
Zǐqí rushed to see the commander,
strongly argued against it,
and they were spared.
In the third year of Hóngwǔ, he was selected as an Imperial Censor for his literary skills,
and submitted a memorial requesting the capital be moved to Guānzhōng.
The Emperor praised it,
and sent the Crown Prince to inspect Shǎnxī,
but later, due to the Crown Prince's death,
it did not materialize.
Zǐqí was appointed Assistant Surveillance Commissioner of Guǎngxī,
then changed to Prefect of Péngzhōu.
Wherever he served, he rectified
unjust cases,
destroyed improper shrines,
and repaired dilapidated dikes,
for which the people greatly esteemed him.
He was promoted to Prefect of Yánpíng,
and died in office.
Guǎng was his second son.
In the second year of Jiànwén, at the palace examination,
when the campaign against Yān was underway,
Guǎng's policy essay contained the phrase:
"The imperial princes are behaving unruly,
and people's hearts are wavering."
The Emperor personally ranked Guǎng first,
bestowed upon him the name Jìng,
