and appointed him Compiler of the Hànlín Academy.
When Chéngzǔ ascended the throne,
Guǎng, along with Xiè Jìn, welcomed and submitted to him,
and was promoted to Lecturer,
then changed to Reader,
had his name restored to Guǎng,
and was promoted to Right Sub-expositor of the Right Spring Palace.
In the fifth year of Yonglè, he was advanced to Academician of the Hànlín Academy,
concurrently Grand Academician of the Left Spring Palace.
When the Emperor campaigned in the north,
he followed with Yáng Róng and Jīn Yòuzī.
He was frequently summoned for discussions in the tent-palace,
sometimes until midnight.
When passing mountains and difficult passes,
they would halt their horses to discuss,
and if he fell a little behind while traveling,
riders would be sent out to find him.
Once, he lost his way,
took off his clothes, and rode a battle horse across a river,
the water submerging the horse up to its waist and above.
The Emperor looked on and expressed concern for his hardship.
Guǎng was skilled in calligraphy;
whenever inscriptions were to be carved in stone,
he was always ordered to write them.
In the twelfth year, when the Emperor campaigned north again,
the imperial grandson accompanied them,
and Guǎng was ordered, along with Róng and Yòuzī, to lecture on classics and history in the army.
In the fourteenth year, he was promoted to Grand Academician of Wényuān Pavilion,
with his concurrent duties unchanged.
When the Emperor summoned monks from Wūsī Zàng to perform a ritual
to pray for blessings for Gāodì and Gāohòu,
and spoke of seeing various auspicious omens,
Guǎng then presented a "Song of Filial Piety and Auspicious Responses."
The Emperor adapted it into a Buddhist song
and had it sung and danced to in the palace.
Zhōu Nà, a Ministry of Rites official, requested the performance of the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices.
Guǎng argued against it,
so it was not permitted.
Guǎng submitted a "Song Rejecting the Fēng and Shàn Sacrifices,"
and the Emperor became even more fond of him.
Guǎng was meticulous.
What the Emperor had said or the duties he handled,
he never told others after leaving.
People at the time compared him to Hú Guǎng of the Hàn dynasty.
However, he was generally able to uphold the overall good.
When he returned to court after mourning his mother,
the Emperor asked about the well-being of the common people.
He replied:
"They are well,
but the prefectures and counties are rigorously pursuing 'traitorous parties' from the Jiànwén era,
implicating even distant relatives,
which is a scourge upon the people."
The Emperor accepted his words.
He died in the fifth month of the sixteenth year,
aged forty-nine.
He was posthumously granted the title of Minister of Rites
and given the posthumous name Wénmù.
It was from Guǎng that civil officials began to receive posthumous names.
When his coffin was returned,
passing through Nánjīng,
the Crown Prince performed a memorial sacrifice for him.
The following year, his son Tǒng was appointed Compiler of the Hànlín Academy.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
Guǎng was further posthumously granted the title of Junior Tutor.
Jīn Yòuzī,
given name Shàn,
went by his courtesy name,
and was a native of Xīngàn.
He became a *jìnshì* in the second year of Jiànwén.
He was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Revenue.
When Chéngzǔ ascended the throne,
he was reassigned as Compiler of the Hànlín Academy,
and along with Xiè Jìn and others,
served concurrently in Wényuān Pavilion,
and was promoted to Lecturer.
At that time, the officials of the Hànlín Academy and the various offices who lectured to the Eastern Palace
all first prepared the meaning of the classics,
which the Grand Academicians reviewed and corrected,
and presented to the Emperor for his perusal,
before delivering the lecture.
Xiè Jìn wrote,
Yáng Shìqí corrected,
Hú Guǎng versified,
and Yòuzī handled the Spring and Autumn Annals,
and thus presented three scrolls on the "Essential Meaning of the Spring and Autumn Annals."
In the fifth year of Yǒnglè, he was transferred to Right Yuùdé, concurrently Shìjiǎng.
He then instructed the Ministry of Personnel,
that those officials serving directly in the Grand Secretariat, such as Hú Guǎng, Jīn Yòuzī, and others, whose full terms had expired,
should not be reassigned to other posts.
In the seventh year, he accompanied the emperor on a visit to Běijīng.
The following year, during the northern campaign,
Yòuzī, along with Guǎng and Róng, attended the emperor.
When the imperial carriage halted at Qīngshuǐyuán,
a spring gushed forth.
Yòuzī presented an inscription,
and Róng presented a poem,
both of which were rewarded with the finest wine.
The emperor valued Yòuzī’s literary talent.
Wherever they passed mountains, rivers, and strategic locations,
he would order him to record them.
Yòuzī would draft these records immediately while on horseback.
When envoys came from Wǎlà,
the emperor summoned Yòuzī and others to walk beside his palanquin,
discussing the enemy’s dispatches,
showing great personal trust.
Once, he, along with Guǎng, Róng, and Vice Minister Jīn Chún, lost their way and fell into a valley.
Late at night,
Yòuzī fell from his horse,
and Guǎng and Chún rode off without looking back.
Róng helped him secure his saddle and continued,
but he kept falling again.
Róng then let him ride his own horse.
They finally reached the emperor's traveling palace the next day.
That night,
the emperor sent more than ten envoys to track Róng and Yòuzī,
but they were not found.
When they finally arrived,
the emperor's face lit up with joy.
Thereafter, he accompanied the emperor on all northern campaigns,
and authored two records: "Before the Northern Campaign" and "After the Northern Campaign."
In the twelfth year, he was ordered to compile the "Wǔjīng Sìshū Xìnglǐ Dàquán" with Guǎng, Róng, and others,
and was promoted to Hànlín Xuéshì.
In the eighteenth year, he and Róng were both advanced to Wényuān Gé Dàxuéshì.
In the twenty-second year, he accompanied the emperor on the northern campaign.
Midway, the troops were exhausted.
The emperor questioned his ministers about it.
No one dared to answer,
only Yòuzī said that they should not penetrate too deeply.
The emperor did not listen.
Upon reaching Kāipíng,
the emperor said to Róng and Yòuzī:
"I dreamt of a divine being saying 'The Supreme Emperor loves life' twice.
What auspicious sign is this?"
Róng and Yòuzī replied:
"Your Majesty's expedition,
is indeed to eliminate tyranny and bring peace to the people.
However, when fire burns Kūngāng,
both jade and stone are destroyed.
We only ask Your Majesty to be mindful."
The emperor agreed,
and immediately ordered the drafting of an edict
to summon and appease the various tribes.
When the army returned to Yúmùchuān,
the emperor passed away.
The death was kept secret.
Róng reported the news to Jīngshī,
while Yòuzī escorted the imperial coffin back.
Upon Rénzōng's ascension,
he was appointed Right Shìláng of the Ministry of Revenue, concurrently Wényuān Gé Dàxuéshì.
Soon after, he was granted the additional title of Tàizǐ Shàobǎo, concurrently Wǔyīng Diàn Dàxuéshì.
In the tenth month of that year, Yòuzī, Róng, and Shìqí were ordered to jointly review imprisoned criminals outside Chéngtiānmén.
The imperial edict to the judicial authorities stated
that the review of serious criminals must be done jointly with the three Grand Secretaries,
thus increasing their responsibility and trust.
The emperor reviewed the official proclamations of the court ministers at the West Corner Gate,
and looked at the three Grand Secretaries, saying:
"You three, along with Vice Ministers Jiǎn and Xià,
are all old officials of the late emperor.
I rely on you to assist me.
I have seen that past rulers disliked hearing frank words.
Even those they deeply trusted,
out of fear of imperial power and compliance with imperial will,
remained silent to gain favor.
Worthy and good officials,
whose words were not heard,
would withdraw and seal their lips.
You and I must take this as a deep warning."
He then took the proclamations of the five men,
and personally added two phrases:
"Do not deem the exalted too difficult to approach,
and do not be remiss due to agreement or disagreement."
Yòuzī and others bowed their heads in gratitude.
In the first year of Hóngxī, he was promoted to Lǐbù Shàngshū, concurrently Dàxuéshì; his title of Xuéshì remained as before,
and all three salaries were provided.
Soon after, he requested leave to visit his mother.
The following year,
his mother passed away.
Upon Xuānzōng’s enthronement,
he was ordered to resume his duties and
to compile the Veritable Records of the two previous reigns,
serving as Chief Editor.
In the third year, he was sent with an imperial staff to Níngxià
to enfeoff the consort of the Prince of Qìngfǔ.
Wherever he passed, he inquired about the hardships of the soldiers and common people,
and reported them upon his return,
which the emperor greatly praised and accepted.
He accompanied the emperor on a border inspection,
crossing Jīmíngshān.
The emperor said:
"Emperor Táng Tàizōng, relying on his bravery and martial prowess, campaigned against Liáo,
and once passed this mountain."
Yòuzī replied:
"Tàizōng later regretted that campaign,
which is why he built the Mǐnzhōng Gé."
The emperor said:
"This mountain collapsed during the reign of Yuán Shùndì,
which was a sign of the fall of the Yuán dynasty."
He replied:
"Shùndì was a ruler who lost his country.
Even if the mountain had not collapsed,
the country would still have fallen."
He died in the twelfth month of the sixth year of Xuāndé.
He was sixty-four years old.
He was posthumously granted the title of Shàobǎo,
and given the posthumous name Wénjìng.
Yòuzī was simple, quiet, and reserved,
generous and tolerant.
Although highly favored,
he became even more humble in his conduct.
He named his private residence
"Tuì'ān."
When he was critically ill,
his family urged him to request posthumous favors,
but he refused,
saying:
"This is a disgrace for a gentleman."
Hú Yǎn,
courtesy name Ruòsī,
was from Nánchāng.
In his youth, he loved learning,
and thoroughly studied astronomy, geography, musical temperament, calendrical science, medicine, and divination.
During the Hóngwǔ era, he was appointed Jiàoyù of Huátíng as a Jǔrén,
and was able to fulfill his duties as a teacher.
After mourning his mother,
and completing the mourning period,
he was transferred to Chángyuán.
He requested a more convenient location to care for his parent,
and was then transferred to Yúgān.
The practice of education officials requesting convenient locations started with Yǎn.
In the first year of Jiànwén, he was recommended and appointed Zhīxiàn of Tóngchéng.
He dug the Tóngpí canal,
irrigating fields for the benefit of the people.
There was a tiger in the county that injured people.
Yǎn purified himself and reported to the gods,
and the tiger fled.
The people of Tóngchéng enshrined him in the Zhū Yì Temple.
In the fourth year,
Vice Metropolitan Censor Liàn Zǐníng recommended him to the court, saying:
"Yǎn's learning is sufficient to understand the workings of heaven and man,
and his wisdom is enough to advise on strategy."
When he was summoned,
the Yān army had already crossed the river.
Upon Chéngzǔ's enthronement,
he said:
"Yǎn understands astronomy;
let him be tested by the Qīntiān Jiān."
After the test,
it was reported that Yǎn was indeed skilled in the studies of celestial phenomena, constellations, and climate.
Soon after, recommended by Xiè Jìn,
he was appointed Hànlín Jiǎntǎo,
and, along with Jìn and others, served directly in the Wényuān Gé.
He was promoted to Shìjiǎng,
then advanced to Zuǒ Shùzǐ.
After his father's death,
he was recalled to office.
While in the Grand Secretariat, Yǎn
offered advice,
often not wishing to take precedence over others,
though he was somewhat blunt in his youth.
In the ninth month of the second year of Yǒnglè, he was appointed Guózǐ Jiān Jìjiǔ,
and thereafter no longer participated in state affairs.
At that time, the law was strict and severe.
Students of the Guózǐ Jiān who cited excuses to return home were punished by being sent to the border for military service.
Upon Yǎn's arrival,
he immediately memorialized to abolish this.
In the seventh year,
the emperor visited Běijīng and
summoned Yǎn to the traveling palace.
The following year, during the northern campaign,
he was ordered to concurrently serve as Jìjiǔ and Shìjiǎng,
presiding over the Hànlín Yuàn,
and assisted the Imperial Grandson in guarding Běijīng.
In the nineteenth year, he was transferred to Guózǐ Jiān Jìjiǔ of Běijīng.
At that time,
the realm was unified,
for nearly fifty years.
The emperor was then promoting rites and music internally,
and extending his benevolent influence to distant and wild lands externally.
The Dukes, ministers, and Grand Masters were cultivated and numerous in literary talent.
Hú Yǎn, a venerable scholar of the imperial academies,
many great literary works from the court came from his hand.
He served as Chief Compiler for the revision of the Tàizǔ Shílù, the Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, and the Tiānxià Túzhì.
He resided in the Guóxué for over twenty years,
leading by example in his teaching,
his actions always serving as a model for teachers.
In the first year of Hóngxī,
he requested retirement due to illness.
Rénzōng bestowed an imperial edict commending and rewarding him,
promoting him to Tàizǐ Bīnkè,
while still retaining the post of Jìjiǔ.
After retiring,
his children and grandchildren were restored to their former status.
When Xuānzōng ascended the throne,
he was summoned to serve as Lǐbù Shìláng,
but he declined and returned home.
He lived at home for twenty years,
and regional high officials all treated him with the respect due to a teacher.
When Hú Yǎn spoke with others,
he never touched upon personal matters.
He lived a simple and detached life,
his annual clothing and food barely sufficient.
When he first served as examiner in Húguǎng,
he discovered Yáng Pǔ's writing,
and was greatly impressed by it,
writing on it:
"He will certainly be able to speak righteous words like Dǒng Zǐ,
and not be crooked like Gōngsūn."
The world regarded him as a judge of character.
He died in the eighth month of the eighth year of Zhèngtǒng,
at the age of eighty-three.
The eulogy states: In the early Míng, the Prime Minister was abolished,
and governmental powers were divided among the Six Ministries.
Chéngzǔ first ordered Confucian ministers to serve in the Wényuān Gé,
participating in state affairs.
This continued through Rénzōng and Xuānzōng,
and the power of the Grand Secretariat grew daily,
effectively performing the duties of the Prime Minister.
Jiě Jìn and the five others below him,
were the first of the literary elite to enter the Grand Secretariat.
Indeed, those in such a secluded and critical position
must maintain fairness and integrity,
and especially value discretion and secrecy.
Jiě Jìn, young and highly talented,
was confident in his grand strategies for national salvation.
Tàizǔ had allowed him ten years to study,
showing deep affection for him.
That he was slandered at every turn,
and could not achieve a good end,
was it entirely due to the persistent efforts of those who envied the virtuous and harmed the capable?
Huáng Huái's merit lay in his guidance and assistance;
Hú Guǎng and Jīn Yòuzī's labors were notable in their attendance;
Hú Yǎn spent a long time in the Guóxué.
Observing these ministers acting with composure and diligence,
offering loyal advice according to circumstances,
it is clear that their contributions were not merely in writing and calligraphy.
Biographies, Volume 36: Yáng Shìqí, Yáng Róng (great-grandson Dàn), Yáng Pǔ (Mǎ Yú)
Yáng Shìqí,
his given name was Yù,
but he was known by his courtesy name,
a native of Tàihé.
He was orphaned early,
and followed his mother when she married into the Luó clan.
Later, he reverted to his original clan.
He was extremely poor.
He studied diligently,
supporting himself by teaching students.
He often traveled between Hú Nán and Xiāng Yuán,
staying longest in Jiāngxià.
In the early Jiànwén reign,
when scholars were gathered to revise the Tàizǔ Shílù,
Yáng Shìqí was already appointed as a professor through recommendation.
Wáng Shúyīng again recommended him for his historical talent.
He was then summoned to the Hànlín Academy,
to serve as a compiler.
Soon, the Ministry of Personnel was ordered to evaluate the scholars of the Historiography Institute.
Shàngshū Zhāng Dǎn, upon reading Yáng Shìqí's policy recommendations,
said:
"These are not the words of a mere classical scholar."
He was ranked first.
He was appointed as Vice-Director of Judicial Review in the Wú King's Household,
while still retaining his position in the Historiography Institute.
When Chéngzǔ ascended the throne,
he was reassigned as Compiler.
Soon after,
he was chosen to enter the Grand Secretariat,
and managed state affairs.
Within a few months, he was promoted to Shìjiǎng.
In the second year of Yǒnglè, when selecting palace officials,
Yáng Shìqí was appointed Zuǒ Zhōngyǔn.
In the fifth year, he was promoted to Zuǒ Yùdé.
Yáng Shìqí performed his duties with extreme diligence,
and when in private, he would not discuss public affairs;
even his closest relatives were not allowed to hear.
Before the Emperor,
his demeanor was respectful and cautious,
he was skilled in answering questions,
and his advice on matters was always pertinent.
If someone made a small mistake,
he often tried to cover it up.
Xú Qí, the Provincial Administration Commissioner of Guǎngdōng, transported local products from Língnán to present to court officials.
Someone obtained the manifest and presented it.
The Emperor, seeing no mention of Yáng Shìqí's name,
summoned and questioned him.
He replied:
"When Xú Qí departed for Guǎngdōng,
all the ministers composed poems and essays to see him off.
I happened to be ill and did not participate,
which is why I was not included.
Whether he has received it or not is unknown,
and the items are minor,
so there should be no other intention."
The Emperor immediately ordered the manifest to be burned.
In the sixth year,
when the Emperor went on a northern tour,
he ordered Yáng Shìqí, along with Jiǎn Yì and Huáng Huái, to remain and assist the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince enjoyed literary composition,
and the Attendant-in-Waiting Wáng Rǔyù presented him with poetic techniques.
Yáng Shìqí said:
"Your Highness should pay attention to the Six Classics,
and in your leisure, read the imperial edicts of the Two Hàn dynasties.
These minor skills
are not worth pursuing."
The Crown Prince praised his words.
Initially,
when the Emperor raised his army,
the Prince of Hàn repeatedly fought bravely and achieved merit.
The Emperor had promised him that if he succeeded, he would be made Crown Prince.
However, he was not enthroned,
and harbored resentment.
The Emperor also pitied the young Prince of Zhào,
and showed him special favor.
Because of this, the two princes conspired to alienate the Crown Prince,
and the Emperor's heart was somewhat swayed.
In the ninth year, upon returning to Nánjīng,
the Emperor summoned Yáng Shìqí and asked about the state of the regency.
Yáng Shìqí replied with filial piety and reverence,
and further said:
"Your Highness has a high natural talent;
even if he has faults, he will surely know them,
and knowing them, he will certainly correct them.
He is mindful of loving others,
and will definitely not fail Your Majesty's trust."
The Emperor was pleased.
On New Year's Day of the eleventh year,
there was a solar eclipse.
Lǐbù Shàngshū Lǚ Zhèn requested that the court audience and congratulatory ceremonies not be canceled.
Shìláng Yí Zhì strongly disagreed.
Yáng Shìqí also cited the example of Sòng Rénzōng and argued strongly.
Thus, the congratulatory ceremonies were canceled.
The following year,
the Emperor went on a northern expedition.
Yáng Shìqí continued to assist the Crown Prince in guarding the capital.
The Prince of Hàn's slanders against the Crown Prince became more urgent.
When the Emperor returned,
he seized upon the slow reception of his carriage
and had all officials of the Eastern Palace, including Huáng Huái, imprisoned.
Yáng Shìqí arrived later,
and was pardoned.
The Emperor summoned him and questioned him about the Crown Prince.
Yáng Shìqí bowed his head and said:
"The Crown Prince is as filial and respectful as ever.
Any delays
are all our fault as ministers."
The Emperor's anger subsided.
The ministers at the imperial camp collectively submitted memorials impeaching Yáng Shìqí for not being pardoned alone,
so he was sent to the Jǐnyī Wèi prison,
but was released soon after.
In the fourteenth year,
the Emperor returned to the capital.
He vaguely heard rumors of Hàn Wáng's
plotting to usurp the succession and other rebellious acts. He questioned Jiǎn Yì about them.
Yì did not respond.
Then he asked Shìqí.
Shìqí replied:
"Your servant and Yì both served the Crown Prince.
Outsiders dared not speak to either of us about Hàn Wáng's affairs.
However, Hàn Wáng was sent to his fief twice,
but he refused to go both times.
Now, knowing that Your Majesty is about to move the capital,
he immediately requested to remain as the Defender of Nánjīng.
May Your Majesty thoroughly examine his intentions."
The Emperor was silent,
rose, and returned to his palace.
After a few days,
the Emperor learned all about Hàn Wáng's affairs.
He stripped him of two guard units
and exiled him to Lè'ān.
The next year, Shìqí was promoted to Hànlín Xuéshì,
also retaining his former office.
In the nineteenth year, he was appointed Zuǒ Chūnfāng Dàxuéshì,
still concurrently holding the title of Xuéshì.
The following year, he was again impeached for deficiencies in his輔導 (fǔdǎo - guidance/tutoring)
and imprisoned in the Jǐnyī Wèi prison.
He was released after ten days.
Upon Rénzōng's accession,
he was promoted to Lǐbù Shìláng and concurrently Huágài Diàn Dàxuéshì.
When the Emperor was in the side hall,
Jiǎn Yì and Xià Yuánjí had not yet retired after reporting on affairs.
The Emperor saw Shìqí in the distance
and said to the two men:
"The new Huágài Xuéshì is coming;
he must have some frank words.
Let's listen to him together."
Shìqí entered and said:
"The imperial edict to reduce annual tributes had only been issued two days ago,
when the Xīxīn Sī (Bureau of Firewood) conveyed an order to collect eight hundred thousand catties of dates,
which contradicts the previous edict."
The Emperor immediately ordered it to be cut by half.
When the twenty-seven-month mourning period was over,
Lǚ Zhèn requested an immediate return to normal life.
Shìqí disagreed.
Zhèn shouted at him sternly.
Jiǎn Yì presented both opinions.
The next day,
the Emperor held court wearing a plain cap, sackcloth, and mourning armbands.
Among the court officials, only Shìqí and the Duke of Yīngguó, Zhāng Fǔ, were similarly dressed.
After the morning court,
the Emperor said to his attendants:
"With the imperial coffin still in mourning,
how could changing clothes be something a minister or son would bear to suggest?
Shìqí's stance is correct."
He was promoted to Shàobǎo,
and along with his colleagues Yáng Róng and Jīn Yòuzī, was granted
a silver seal inscribed with "繩愆糾繆" (Shéng qiān jiū miù - to correct errors and rectify mistakes),
allowing him to present sealed memorials.
Soon after, he was promoted to Shàofù.
At that time, when provincial officials and magistrates came to court,
Shàngshū Lǐ Qìng suggested distributing surplus military horses to the officials,
and assessing them for foals annually.
Shìqí said:
"The court selects the virtuous and grants them office,
yet it makes them herd horses.
This values animals and demeans scholars.
How can this be shown to the world and future generations?"
The Emperor assented to an imperial decree to abolish it,
but then there was silence.
Shìqí again strongly argued.
Still, there was no response.
After a while,
the Emperor was at the Sīshàn Mén
and summoned Shìqí, saying:
"Did I truly forget it earlier?
I heard that Lǚ Zhèn, Lǐ Qìng and their ilk are all displeased with you.
I considered you to be isolated
and feared you would be harmed,
so I did not want to abolish it based on your words alone.
Now I have an excuse."
He personally presented a memorial from the Shǎnxī Ànchásǐ Chén Zhì
stating the inconvenience of horse-raising,
and told Shìqí to draft an edict to implement it.
Shìqí bowed his head in thanks.
When the officials practiced the New Year's Day ceremony,
Lǚ Zhèn requested the use of music.
Shìqí and Huáng Huái memorialized to stop it.
There was no response.
Shìqí again memorialized,
waiting in the courtyard until the tenth刻 (kè - quarter of an hour) of the night.
The response was favorable.
The next day,
the Emperor summoned him and said:
"Zhèn always misleads me in every matter.
If it weren't for your words,
I would regret it too late."
He ordered Shìqí to concurrently hold the office of Bīngbù Shàngshū,
receiving three salaries simultaneously.
Shìqí declined the Shàngshū salary.
When the Emperor was regent,
he harbored resentment against the Censor Shū Zhòngchéng,
and now wished to punish him.
Shìqí said:
"Upon Your Majesty's accession,
an edict was issued granting amnesty to all who had previously offended the imperial will.
If Zhòngchéng is punished,
then the imperial edict will lose its credibility,
and many will be fearful.
Is it not preferable to treat him as Hàn Jǐngdì treated Wèi Wǎn?"
The Emperor immediately dropped the case and did not prosecute him.
Someone reported that Dàlǐ Qīng Yú Qiān had spoken indiscreetly on matters of state.
The Emperor was angry
and demoted him by one rank.
Shìqí spoke on his behalf, stating he was wronged,
and Qiān was reinstated to his rank.
Furthermore, Dàlǐ Shàopù Yì Qiān
incurred displeasure for speaking on state affairs.
Shìqí said:
"Qiān responded to the imperial call to present his views.
If he is punished for it,
then all ministers will thenceforth hold their tongues."
The Emperor immediately promoted Qiān to Fù Dū Yùshǐ
and issued an edict acknowledging his own fault.
At that time, someone presented a memorial praising the era of great peace.
The Emperor showed it to his ministers,
and they all agreed.
Shìqí alone said:
"Although Your Majesty's benevolence covers all under Heaven,
those who have been displaced have not yet returned,
and the wounds have not yet healed.
The people still struggle for food.
If we rest and recover for a few more years,
then perhaps an era of great peace can be expected."
The Emperor said:
"Indeed."
He then looked at Jiǎn Yì and others and said:
"I treat you with utmost sincerity
and hope for your guidance and assistance.
Only Shìqí has submitted five memorials;
you all have not uttered a single word.
Is it truly that there are no deficiencies in court governance
and all under Heaven is at peace?"
The ministers were ashamed and apologized.
In April of that year,
the Emperor bestowed a sealed letter upon Shìqí, saying:
"In the past, when I received the mandate to be regent,
you attended to me,
with one heart and one virtue,
sacrificing yourself for the state,
enduring many hardships and dangers,
without ever changing your resolve.
Since my ascension to the throne,
your excellent counsel has been submitted to me,
guiding me towards good governance.
Your uprightness and unwavering loyalty
are etched in my heart.
I now create and bestow upon you the 'Yáng Zhēnyī Yìn'
seal.
May you continue to work together
to achieve the renown of a wise ruler and loyal minister."
Soon after, he was tasked with compiling the Tàizōng Shílù,
serving as Chief Editor along with Huáng Huái, Jīn Yòuzī, and Yáng Pǔ.
Not long after,
the Emperor fell ill.
He summoned Shìqí, Jiǎn Yì, Huáng Huái, and Yáng Róng to the Sīshàn Mén,
and ordered Shìqí to write an edict summoning the Crown Prince from Nánjīng.
Xuānzōng 繼位,
修 Rénzōng 實錄,
仍充總裁.
Xuāndé 元年,
漢王 Gāo Xù 反.
帝親征,
平之.
師還,
次 Xiànxiàn 之 Shānjiāqiáo,
侍郎 Chén Shān 迎謁,
言漢、趙二王實同心,
請乘勢襲 Zhāngdé 執 Zhào Wáng.
Róng 力贊決.
Shìqí 曰：
「事當有實,
天地鬼神可欺乎？ 」
Róng 厲聲曰：
「汝欲撓大計耶！
今逆黨言趙實與謀,
何謂無辭？ 」
Shìqí 曰：
「Tàizōng Huángdì 三子,
今上惟兩叔父.
有罪者不可赦,
其無罪者宜厚待之,
疑則防 之,
使無虞而已.
何遽加兵,
傷皇祖在天意乎？ 」
時惟 Yáng Pǔ 與 Shìqí 合.
將入諫,
Róng 先入,
Shìqí 繼之,
閽者不納.
尋召 Yì、Yuánjí 入.
二人以 Shìqí 言白帝.
帝初無罪趙意,
移兵事得寢.
比還京,
帝思 Shìqí 言,
謂曰：
「今議者多言 Zhào Wáng 事,
奈何？ 」
Shìqí 曰：
「趙最親,
陛下當保全之,
毋惑羣言. 」
帝曰：
「吾欲封羣臣章示王,
令自處何如？ 」
Shìqí 曰：
更得一璽書幸甚. 」
於是發使奉書至趙.
Zhào Wáng 得書大喜.
泣曰：
「吾生矣. 」
即上表謝,
且獻護衞,
言者始息.
帝待 Zhào Wáng 日益親而薄 Chén Shān.
謂 Shìqí 曰：
「Zhào Wáng 所以全,
卿力也. 」
賜金幣.
時 Jiāozhǐ 數叛.
屢發大軍征討,
皆敗沒.
Jiāozhǐ Lí Lì 遣人偽請立 Chén shì 後.
帝亦厭兵,
欲許之.
Yīngguógōng Zhāng Fǔ、尚書 Jiǎn Yì 以下,
皆言與之無名,
徒示弱天下.
帝召 Shìqí、Róng 謀.
二人力言：
「陛下卹民命以綏荒服,
不為無名.
漢棄 Zhūyá,
前史以為美談,
不為示弱,
許之便. 」
尋命擇使 Jiāozhǐ 者.
Jiǎn Yì 薦 Fú Bó'ān 口辯.
Shìqí 曰：
「言不忠信,
雖蠻貊之邦不可行.
Bó'ān 小人,
往且辱國. 」
帝是之,
別遣使.
於是棄 Jiāozhǐ,
罷兵,
歲省軍興鉅萬.
五年春,
帝奉 Huáng Tàihòu 謁陵,
召 Yīngguógōng Zhāng Fǔ、尚書 Jiǎn Yì 及 Shìqí、Róng、Yòuzī、Pǔ,
朝太后於行殿.
太后慰勞之.
帝又語 Shìqí 曰：
「太后為朕言,
先帝在 Qīnggōng,
惟卿不憚觸忤,
先帝能從,
以不敗事.
又誨朕當受直言. 」
Shìqí 對曰：
「此皇太后盛德之言,
願陛下念之. 」
尋敕 Hónglúsì,
Shìqí 老有疾,
趨朝或後,
毋論奏.
帝嘗微行,
夜幸 Shìqí 宅.
Shìqí 倉皇出迎,
頓首曰：
「陛下奈何 以社稷宗廟之身自輕？ 」
帝曰：
「朕欲與卿一言,
故來耳. 」
後數日,
獲二盜,
有異謀.
帝召 Shìqí,
告之故.
且曰：
「今而後知卿之愛朕也. 」
帝以四方屢水旱,
召 Shìqí 議下詔寬恤,
免災傷租稅及官馬虧額者.
Shìqí 因請並蠲逋賦薪芻錢,
減官田額,
理冤滯,
汰工役,
以廣德意.
民大悅.
踰二年,
帝謂 Shìqí 曰：
「恤民詔下已久,
今更有可恤者乎？ 」
Shìqí 曰：
「前詔減官田租,
戶部徵如故. 」
帝怫然曰：
「今首行之,
廢格者論如法. 」
Shìqí 復請撫逃民,
察墨吏,
舉文學武勇之士,
令極刑家子孫皆得仕進.
又請廷臣三品以上及二司官,
各舉所知,
備方面郡守選.
皆報可.
當是時,
帝勵精圖治,
Shìqí 等同心輔佐,
海內號為治平.
帝乃倣古君臣豫遊事,
每歲首,
賜百官旬休.
車駕亦時幸 Xīyuàn Wànsuìshān,
諸學士皆從,
賦詩賡和,
從容問民間疾苦.
有所論奏,
帝皆虛懷聽納.
When the emperor first ascended the throne,
there were seven ministers in the Grand Secretariat.
Chén Shān and Zhāng Yīng, who entered based on old favors from the Eastern Palace,
were deemed unsatisfactory
and dismissed to other official posts.
Huáng Huái retired due to illness.
Jīn Yòuzī died.
Only Shìqí, Róng, and Pǔ remained in the Grand Secretariat.
Róng was candid, bold, and decisive,
daring to act in matters he encountered.
He frequently accompanied Chéngzǔ on northern campaigns
and was able to discern the competence of border generals,
the difficulty and ease of passes and strategic points, and
the enemy's disposition.
However, he was quite amenable to gifts and offerings,
and border generals would send fine horses annually.
The emperor, being somewhat aware of this,
inquired about it with Shìqí.
Shìqí strongly asserted:
"Róng is thoroughly knowledgeable about border affairs,
and we are not his equal;
it would be inappropriate to be concerned about a minor flaw."
The emperor laughed and said:
"Róng once disparaged you and Yuánjí;
are you now defending him?"
Shìqí replied:
"I hope Your Majesty will tolerate Róng as you have tolerated your servant."
The emperor's displeasure then abated.
Later,
when these words gradually became known,
Róng was ashamed towards Shìqí because of this,
and they became very cordial.
The emperor also grew increasingly intimate and generous with him,
bestowing countless rare fruits, fine wine, gold, silk, garments, currency, books, and vessels over time.
When Xuānzōng passed away,
Yīngzōng ascended the throne,
being only nine years old.
Major military and state affairs were handled by the Grand Empress Dowager.
The Grand Empress Dowager fully trusted Shìqí, Róng, and Pǔ,
and when there was an issue, she would send eunuchs to the Grand Secretariat for consultation
before making a decision.
The three also had self-confidence
and spoke their minds frankly.
Shìqí first requested to train soldiers,
strengthen border defenses,
establish a minister for military affairs in Nánjīng,
dispatch civil and military officials to govern Jiāngxī, Húguǎng, Hénán, and Shāndōng,
and abolish surveillance officers.
He further requested to progressively reduce taxes,
be cautious in legal cases,
and rigorously examine all departments.
All were approved and implemented.
In the early days of Zhèngtǒng,
the court administration was clear and just,
which was due to the efforts of Shìqí and others.
In the third year,
the Veritable Records of Xuānzōng were completed,
and he was promoted to Junior Preceptor.
In the fourth year, he requested to retire.
This was not granted.
An imperial decree ordered him to return home to visit his ancestral tombs.
Not long after,
he returned.
At this time, the eunuch Wáng Zhèn enjoyed the emperor's favor
and gradually interfered in external court affairs,
guiding the emperor to govern subordinates strictly,
and high-ranking ministers were often imprisoned.
The Prince of Jìngjiāng, Zuǒjìng, privately presented Róng with gold.
Róng had visited his ancestral tombs earlier
and was unaware of it upon his return.
Zhèn wished to use this to incriminate Róng,
but Shìqí strongly intervened,
and the matter was dropped.
Róng soon died,
leaving Shìqí and Pǔ more isolated.
The following year, a large army was dispatched to conquer Lùchuān,
depleting the imperial treasury,
and tens of thousands of soldiers and horses perished.
The year after that,
the Grand Empress Dowager died,
and Zhèn's power grew even stronger.
He wielded immense authority and intimidated officials,
and any slight disagreement from an official
would result in their arrest and imprisonment.
All court officials lived in fear,
and Shìqí was also unable to restrain him.
As Shìqí grew old,
his son Jì became arrogant and violent,
and once assaulted and killed someone.
Censorate officials submitted numerous memorials impeaching Jì.
The court deliberated not to immediately apply the law
and sealed the indictment to show to Shìqí.
Later, someone else exposed dozens of Jì's tyrannical acts,
and he was then handed over for investigation.
Shìqí was on leave due to old age and illness.
The emperor, fearing to upset Shìqí,
issued an edict to comfort and encourage him.
Shìqí was moved to tears,
and worried so much that he could not recover.
In the third month of the ninth year, he died
at the age of eighty.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Preceptor
and given the posthumous name Wénzhēn.
The authorities then sentenced Jì to death.
Initially,
at the beginning of Zhèngtǒng,
Shìqí had stated that the Wǎlà were growing stronger
and would become a border threat,
but the border army lacked horses,
and feared they would be unable to resist.
He requested that horses be obtained from the nearby Grand Stables,
and that all horses contributed by Xīfān also be supplied.
Not long after Shìqí's death,
Yěxiān indeed invaded,
leading to the Tǔmù Disaster,
and those who understood remembered his words.
He was also exceptionally good at judging people
and liked to recommend obscure scholars,
some of whom he had never even met.
Yú Qiān, Zhōu Chén, Kuàng Zhōng, and others
were all appointed on Shìqí's recommendation,
serving in office for ten or twenty years,
renowned throughout the realm for their integrity and competence,
and considered famous ministers of their generation.
His second son, Máo,
was appointed Assistant Director of the Imperial Seal Office through hereditary privilege.
During the Chénghuà reign,
he was promoted to Junior Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
presiding over its affairs.
Yáng Róng,
courtesy name Miǎnrén,
was from Jiàn'ān.
His original name was Zǐróng.
He passed the imperial examination in the second year of Jiànwén.
He was appointed compiler.
When Chéngzǔ first entered the capital,
Róng greeted him at his horse's head and said:
"Does Your Highness first visit the imperial tombs,
or first ascend the throne?"
Chéngzǔ immediately urged his carriage to visit the tombs.
From then on, he gained his recognition.
After ascending the throne,
he was selected to enter the Wényuāngé
and had his name changed to Róng.
Among the seven officials on duty together,
Róng was the youngest and
most astute.
One evening,
a report arrived from Níngxià stating it was under siege.
The seven officials were summoned,
but all had already left,
only Róng remained.
The emperor showed him the memorial.
Róng said:
"Níngxià has strong fortifications.
Its people are all skilled in warfare,
and the memorial was submitted over ten days ago;
the siege must have been lifted."
At midnight,
a memorial indeed reported the siege was lifted.
The emperor said to Róng:
"How accurately you predicted!"
When bandits rose in Jiāngxī,
envoys were dispatched to pacify them,
while Commander Hán Guān was ordered to lead troops following behind.
When the memorial arrived stating the bandits had surrendered,
the emperor wished to bestow an imperial edict of commendation upon Guān.
Róng said:
"Considering the time the memorial was sent,
Guān had not yet arrived,
so his merit cannot be discussed."
The emperor held him in even higher regard,
and he was twice promoted to Lecturer.
When the Crown Prince was established,
he was promoted to Right Remonstrator,
still holding his former posts,
and was granted second-rank attire along with other officials on duty.
His discussions and judgments on various departmental matters
pleased the emperor,
and he was again bestowed with garments and currency.
The emperor was stern,
and when deliberating with other high officials, if matters were undecided,
he would sometimes become angry.
When Róng arrived,
his countenance would often soften,
and the matter would then be decided.
In the fifth year, he was ordered to Gānsù to plan military affairs.
Wherever he went, he surveyed the terrain and topography of the mountains and rivers,
investigated the military and the populace,
and inspected the fortresses.
Upon his return, he reported to the Wǔyīng Diàn.
The Emperor was greatly pleased.
It was the height of summer,
and the Emperor personally cut a melon and offered it to him.
Soon after, he was promoted to Yòu Shùzǐ,
with his concurrent duties remaining as before.
The following year, due to his father's mourning, he was granted a travel warrant to return home.
After the burial,
he was reinstated to his duties.
The year after that,
he requested leave for his mother's mourning.
The Emperor, citing the imminent northern expedition, did not permit it,
and ordered him to accompany Hú Guǎng and Jīn Yòuzī on the retinue.
Hé Fú, the Grand Commander of Gānsù, reported that Tuōtuō Bùhuā and others wished to surrender,
and awaited orders in Yìjí Nǎi.
Róng was ordered to Gānsù to receive the surrender with Fú,
and, bearing the imperial insignia, to enfeoff Fú as Níngyuǎn Hóu on the spot in the military camp.
He then went to Níngxià,
and consulted with Níngyáng Hóu Chén Fán on frontier defense planning.
Upon his return, he presented ten advantageous proposals.
The Emperor graciously accepted them.
In the eighth year, he followed the expedition out of the frontier,
and reached the Lúqú Hé.
Three hundred brave warriors were selected as guards,
not to be subordinated to other generals,
and Róng was put in command of them.
When the army returned,
supplies were insufficient.
Róng requested that all surplus imperial provisions be given to the army,
and that those in the army with surplus could lend to others,
and upon entering the frontier,
the officials would repay them twofold.
The army was saved by this.
The following year, he requested leave for urgent mourning,
and an imperial eunuch was ordered to escort him.
Upon his return, the Emperor inquired about the people's conditions in Mǐnzhōng and the abundance or scarcity of the harvest.
Róng answered fully.
Soon after, he was ordered to attend the imperial grandsons in their studies at the Wénhuá Diàn.
In the tenth year,
Sòng Hǔ, the guardian minister of Gānsù, reported
that the rebel leader Lǎodehǎn had fled to Chìjīn Ménggǔ,
and was causing frontier troubles.
Róng was again dispatched to Shǎnxī,
to meet with Fēngchéng Hóu Lǐ Bīn to discuss military strategies.
Róng returned and reported,
"Mid-winter is not the time for military operations,
and the culprits are but a few individuals;
troops should not be dispatched yet."
The Emperor followed his advice,
and the rebels also surrendered.
The following year, he again accompanied Guǎng and Yòuzī on a northern inspection tour.
The year after that, there was a campaign against the Wǎlà,
and the Crown Prince Regent accompanied the expedition.
The Emperor ordered Róng to explain the classics and history in his spare time,
and also to manage the affairs of the Shàngbǎo (Office of Imperial Seals).
All imperial edicts and orders issued,
as well as flags, emblems, and tallies for verification,
required Róng's report before being dispatched.
The Emperor once sat late in the imperial tent,
and summoned Róng to discuss military provisions.
Róng replied,
"If generals are chosen to establish military colonies,
training is conducted skillfully,
and farming is done at the right time,
then military provisions will be sufficient."
In the fourteenth year, he and Jīn Yòuzī were both promoted to Hànlín Xuéshì,
still concurrently serving as Shùzǐ,
and followed the Emperor back to the capital.
The following year, he again accompanied the northern expedition.
In the sixteenth year,
Hú Guǎng passed away,
and Róng was ordered to manage the affairs of the Hànlín Yuàn,
showing even greater trust and reliance.
Many high officials were jealous of Róng
and wished to distance him,
so they jointly recommended him for Jìjiǔ.
The Emperor said,
"I certainly know he is capable of that,
but find someone to replace Róng in his current post."
The ministers then dared not speak further.
In the eighteenth year, he was promoted to Wényuān Gé Dàxuéshì,
with his concurrent Hànlín Xuéshì post remaining as before.
The following year, the capital was established in Běijīng.
When the three palaces suffered a fire,
Róng directed the guards to remove maps, records, and imperial edicts,
carrying them outside the Dōnghuá Mén.
The Emperor praised him for this.
Róng and Yòuzī presented ten advantageous proposals.
They were approved.
In the twentieth year, he again followed the expedition out of the frontier,
and all military affairs were entrusted to him for consultation and decision,
receiving generous rewards.
When the army returned,
the generals and soldiers were honored,
and a banquet was given in four grades.
Róng and Yòuzī were both seated at the front,
receiving the highest awards.
Later,
another imperial edict was issued to campaign against Ālǔtái.
Someone requested to mobilize the militia gathered in Jiāngxī during the Jiànwén era.
The Emperor asked Róng.
Róng replied,
"Your Majesty promised the people to resume their livelihoods nearly twenty years ago;
to levy them again suddenly
would not demonstrate trustworthiness to the empire."
The Emperor followed his advice.
The following year, he followed the expedition out of the frontier,
and all military affairs were entrusted to Róng,
who met with the Emperor day and night without specific times.
The Emperor at that time referred to him as Scholar Yáng,
not by his given name.
The year after that, he again followed the northern expedition.
At this time,
the Emperor had made five expeditions out of the frontier,
and the soldiers suffered from hunger and cold,
with supply lines disrupted,
and twelve or thirteen out of every hundred died.
The main army reached the Dálán Nàmùr Hé,
but did not encounter the enemy.
The Emperor asked his ministers whether to advance further.
The ministers all assented,
only Róng and Yòuzī calmly suggested returning the army.
The Emperor permitted it.
Upon returning to Yúmù Chuān,
the Emperor passed away.
Eunuchs such as Mǎ Yún did not know what to do,
and secretly consulted with Róng and Yòuzī in the imperial tent.
The two deliberated that
with the great army outside,
still far from the capital,
the news of death should be kept secret.
The body was ritually prepared,
and a tin coffin was made,
carried in the imperial palanquin.
Wherever they went, meals were offered morning and evening as per usual custom,
and military discipline was further enforced,
so no one suspected anything.
Someone suggested issuing an edict under another pretext
to inform the Crown Prince by urgent dispatch.
The two said,
"Who dares do that!
An edict is issued when the late emperor is alive;
to issue an edict after he has ascended to heaven
is a deception,
and the crime is not small."
The multitude said,
"Indeed."
So they prepared a document detailing the date of the great passing and the intent of the imperial will for succession,
and sent it to the Crown Prince.
Róng and the Junior Supervisor Hǎi Shòu were the first to rush with the obituary.
Upon their arrival,
the Crown Prince ordered them to discuss with Jiǎn Yì and Yáng Shìqí what actions should be taken.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
Róng was promoted to Tàicháng Qīng,
with his other posts remaining as before.
Soon after, he was promoted to Tàizǐ Shàofù and Jǐnshēn Diàn Dàxuéshì.
Later, there were reports of Róng's actions regarding the funeral rites and military dispositions during the great passing.
The Emperor bestowed an edict of praise and commendation,
with very generous rewards,
and promoted him to Gōngbù Shàngshū,
receiving three salaries.
At that time, Shìqí and Huái both declined the Shàngshū salary,
and Róng and Yòuzī also firmly declined.
It was not permitted.
In Xuāndé first year (1426),
Hàn Wáng Gāo Xù rebelled.
The Emperor summoned Róng and others to devise a plan.
Róng was the first to request the Emperor to personally lead the expedition,
saying,
"He believes Your Majesty, having just ascended,
will surely not go in person.
Now, by acting unexpectedly,
and confronting him with imperial might,
nothing will fail."
The Emperor followed his plan.
Upon reaching Yuè'ān,
Gāo Xù surrendered.
When the army returned,
for his decisive strategic contribution,
he received the highest award,
was given five silver seals,
and was praised and rewarded exceedingly.
In the third year, he accompanied the Emperor on a border inspection tour,
reaching Zūnhuà.
Hearing that the Wūliánghā were about to invade the border,
the Emperor left the accompanying civilian officials in the main camp,
and only ordered Róng to follow.
He personally led light cavalry out of Xǐfēngkǒu,
defeated the enemy, and returned.
In the fifth year, he was promoted to Shàofù,
and declined the Dàxuéshì salary.
In the ninth year, he again accompanied a border tour,
reaching Xǐmǎ Lín and returning.
Yīngzōng ēnterred the throne,
and his trust remained as before.
In the third year of Zhèngtǒng,
he and Shìqí were both promoted to Shàoshī.
In the fifth year, he requested to return home to visit his ancestral tombs.
An imperial eunuch was ordered to accompany him.
Upon returning to Wǔlín station, he died
at the age of seventy.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tàishī,
given the posthumous name Wénmǐn,
and his descendants were granted the hereditary title of Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ.
Róng served four reigns,
and was able to make decisions after deliberation.
At the end of Yǒnglè,
mountain bandits arose in Zhè and Mǐn.
A discussion was held to dispatch troops.
The emperor was then beyond the Great Wall.
When the memorial arrived,
he showed it to Róng.
Róng said:
“The common people suffer under the officials
and are forced to gather together to protect themselves.
If troops are sent out,
they will only gather in greater numbers and become impossible to disperse.
If envoys are sent to offer amnesty and conciliation,
it will not be necessary to trouble the troops.”
This was followed,
and the bandits indeed ceased.
Regarding the abandonment of Ānnán,
many high officials believed it was not permissible.
Only Róng and Shìqí strongly argued that it was not advisable to exhaust the Central Kingdom for a wild territory.
His mature and steady conduct was always like this.
When discussing matters, he could be quite outspoken
and could not tolerate others' faults.
However, when someone angered the emperor and faced imminent danger,
he would often subtly guide the emperor's thoughts with veiled remarks,
and they would invariably be pardoned.
The survival of Xià Yuánjí and Lǐ Shímǐn,
and the exemption of Dū Yùshǐ Liú Guān from frontier exile,
were all due to his efforts.
He once said to others:
“Serving the sovereign has its proper conduct,
and presenting remonstrance has its methods.
I would not invite disaster through reckless straightforwardness.”
Therefore, his favor and treatment remained uninterrupted from beginning to end.
He was the chief editor
for the revision of the Veritable Records of Tàizǔ, as well as the Veritable Records of the three reigns of Tàizōng, Rénzōng, and Xuānzōng.
The honors and gifts bestowed upon him
before and after
were countless.
He enjoyed entertaining guests,
and despite his high status and power, he was never arrogant,
so many scholars devoted themselves to him.
Some said that Róng, in handling major state affairs,
was not inferior to Yáo Chóng of Tang,
and his disregard for minor details
was also quite similar.
His family was wealthy.
His great-grandson, Yè, was a Jiànníng Zhǐhuī,
and failed due to his wealth.
Detailed information can be found in the Biographies of Eunuchs.
Yè's cousin, Dàn,
courtesy name Jìnshū,
was a jinshi during the Hóngzhì reign.
He served successively as Tàicháng Qīng.
For opposing Liú Jǐn,
he was demoted to Zhī Wēnzhōu Fǔ.
His administration was excellent,
and he was gradually promoted to Zhèjiāng Tíxué Fùshǐ.
After Jǐn was executed,
he was successively promoted to Hùbù Shìláng,
overseeing the capital and Tōng warehouses,
and then sent to manage military provisions in Gānsù.
Upon his return,
he was promoted to Yòu Dū Yùshǐ,
and concurrently served as Commander-in-Chief of the military affairs of Liǎngguǎng,
suppressing the Yao people of Pānyú, Qīngyuǎn, and Héyuán.
In the early Jiājìng reign,
he was transferred to Nánjīng Lìbù Shàngshū.
When Zhāng Cōng and Guì È were rapidly promoted,
Dàn, leading the Nine Ministers, strongly argued against it.
At that time, Lìbù Shàngshū Qiáo Yǔ was dismissed,
and Dàn was summoned to replace him.
Before he arrived,
he was impeached by Gěishìzhōng Chén Guāng,
and ordered to retire.
He died at over seventy years of age.
Yáng Pǔ,
courtesy name Hóngjì,
was from Shíshǒu.
He passed the jinshi examination together with Yáng Róng.
He was appointed Biānxiū.
In the early Yǒnglè reign,
he served the Crown Prince as Xǐmǎ.
The Crown Prince once read the Book of Han,
and praised Zhāng Shìzhī as virtuous.
Pǔ said:
“Shìzhī was indeed virtuous,
but without Emperor Wén's magnanimity and benevolence,
he would not have been able to carry out his aspirations.”
He compiled and presented anecdotes about Emperor Wén.
The Crown Prince was greatly pleased.
After a long time,
he returned home due to mourning.
At that time, the Crown Prince was supervising the state,
and ordered him to resume his duties.
In the twelfth year,
the Eastern Palace sent an envoy to welcome the emperor late,
and the emperor was enraged.
Huáng Huái was arrested and imprisoned in Běijīng.
When Jīn Wèn arrived,
the emperor became even more furious and said:
“Who is Wèn,
to be able to serve the Crown Prince!”
He was handed over to the judicial authorities for interrogation,
which implicated Pǔ.
Pǔ was arrested and imprisoned in the Jǐnyīwèi prison.
His family's food supply was often cut off.
The emperor's intentions were unpredictable,
and he faced death at any moment.
Pǔ became even more determined,
and continued to read without interruption.
He was imprisoned for ten years,
during which he read the classics, histories, and various philosophers several times.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
he was released from prison
and promoted to Hànlín Xuéshì.
He once secretly submitted memorials on state affairs.
The emperor praised and responded to him,
bestowing paper money and silks.
Later,
remembering that Pǔ had suffered for a long time because of him,
he took special pity on him.
The following year, the Hóngwén Gé was established to the left of the Sīshàn Mén.
Scholars of excellent learning and conduct were selected to serve there.
Shìqí recommended Shìjiǎng Wáng Jìn and the scholar Chén Jì;
Jiǎn Yì recommended Xuélù Yáng Jìng and Xùndǎo Hé Chéng.
An imperial edict appointed Jì as Bóshì,
Jìng as Biānxiū,
and Chéng as Gěishìzhōng,
to serve daily in the阁 (Pavilion).
Pǔ was commanded to oversee the affairs of the Pavilion,
and the imperial seal for the Pavilion was personally handed to him,
with the words:
“I employ you by my side
not only for your scholarship.
I wish to extensively learn about the affairs of the people,
to aid in the way of governance.
If you have any proposals,
seal and present them.”
Soon after, he was promoted to Tàicháng Qīng,
retaining his concurrent duties as before.
When Xuānzōng ascended the throne,
the Hóngwén Gé was abolished.
Pǔ was summoned to the Nèigé
to jointly manage state affairs with Yáng Shìqí and others.
After four years,
he left due to his mother's mourning,
but was reinstated.
In the ninth year, he was transferred to Lǐbù Shàngshū,
and continued to serve in the Nèigé as a Xuéshì as before.
When Yīngzōng
first ascended the throne, along with Shìqí and Róng, he requested the opening of the imperial lecture series (jīngyán)
and the pre-selection of lecturing officials.

He insisted on securing several individuals who possessed profound knowledge and upright conduct, whose words and actions were principled and discreet, and who were mature and understood the greater good to serve in these positions.
He also requested the careful selection of trusted eunuchs to serve morning and evening within the palace.
The Empress Dowager was greatly pleased.
One day,
the Empress Dowager was seated in the private hall (biàndiàn),
and the Emperor stood facing west.
She summoned the Duke of Yīng, Zhāng Fǔ, as well as Shìqí, Róng, Pǔ, and Minister Hú Yíng to enter,
and instructed them, saying:
"You, my esteemed elder ministers,
the successor to the throne is young.
May you all be of one mind to secure the nation."
She then called Pǔ forward and said:
"Rénzōng Emperor often spoke of your loyalty
with sighs of admiration;
I never expected to still see you today."
Pǔ was moved to tears,
and the Empress Dowager also wept,
and all those around them were filled with sorrow.
Originally, when Rénzōng was the Crown Prince,
he was slandered,
and many officials died in imperial prisons.
Pǔ and Huáng Huái were imprisoned for ten years,
and were repeatedly on the verge of death.
Rénzōng often thought of these ministers in the palace,
and the Empress Dowager had long pitied them,
which is why she spoke to Pǔ in this manner.
The Empress Dowager then turned to the Emperor and said:
"These five ministers
were selected and appointed by three reigns
to assist future generations.
For the myriad affairs of the Emperor,
it is fitting to consult with these five ministers."
In the third year of Zhèngtǒng,
the Veritable Records of Xuānzōng (Xuānzōng Shílù) were completed,
and Pǔ was promoted to Junior Guardian (Shàobǎo) and Grand Academician of the Wǔyīng Hall.
Pǔ had joined the Grand Secretariat (nèi gé) more than twenty years after Shìqí and Róng,
but by this time, he was on par with Shìqí and Róng.
In the sixth year, he returned home to visit his ancestral graves,
and soon after, he returned to office.
At this time,
Wáng Zhèn had not yet become overbearing;
the realm was peaceful and orderly,
and there were no political failures at court.
Officials and commoners, both inside and outside the capital, unanimously hailed
"the Three Yángs."
Based on their residences, Shìqí was referred to as "Western Yáng,"
Róng as "Eastern Yáng,"
while Pǔ had once signed his regional origin as Nánjùn,
and was thus known as "Southern Yáng."
Pǔ was straightforward, honest, and quiet,
without hidden motives.
His nature was respectful and cautious;
whenever he entered court,
he walked along the wall.
When other grand ministers debated matters, arguing their pros and cons,
sometimes even leading to disagreements,
Pǔ handled them with an impartial mind,
and all the grand ministers admired and respected him.
At the time, it was said that Shìqí possessed learning and conduct,
Róng possessed talent and discernment,
and Pǔ possessed elegant principles,
all of which were unmatched by others.
When Róng and Shìqí successively died,
those remaining in the Grand Secretariat—Mǎ Yú, Gāo Gǔ, and Cáo Nài—were all junior and less influential.
Pǔ stood alone,
and Wáng Zhèn became even more powerful.
In the seventh month of the eleventh year,
Pǔ died at the age of seventy-five.
He was
posthumously granted the title of Grand Preceptor (Tàishī)
and the posthumous name Wéndìng.
His grandson, Shòu, was appointed Assistant Minister of the Imperial Seal Office (Shàngbǎosī Chéng).
Three years later,
Zhèn then led Yīngzōng on a northern campaign,
resulting in the disaster at Tǔmù,
which nearly plunged the realm into great chaos.
People at the time regretted that if these three men had been alive,
this would not have happened.
However, later generations vied to expose their shortcomings,
accusing them of ambiguity and compliance with imperial decrees,
thereby fostering the disaster of the treacherous eunuch.
This is also an instance of being overly harsh.
Mǎ Yú,
courtesy name Xìnghé,
was a native of Línqú.
In the second year of Xuāndé, he achieved the highest rank in the imperial examinations (jìnshì).
He was appointed Compiler of the Hànlín Academy (Hànlín Xiūzhuàn).
In the autumn of the ninth year, by special imperial decree, thirty-seven historiographers and probationary bachelors (shùjíshì) were admitted to the Wényuán Pavilion for further study,
with Yú at the head.
In the first year of Zhèngtǒng, he served as a lecturer for the imperial lecture series,
and was subsequently promoted to Academician-in-waiting (Shìdú Xuéshì).
At that time, Wáng Zhèn wielded great power.
One day,
he said to Yáng Shìqí and Róng:
"The affairs of the court have long burdened you, sirs.
You are all advanced in years
and must be weary."
Shìqí replied:
"As old ministers, we will exert ourselves to the utmost in service to the nation until death."
Róng said:
"We are old and infirm,
unable to render effective service.
We should select capable young men to repay the Emperor's grace."
Zhèn was pleased and withdrew.
Shìqí reproached Róng for his careless words.
Róng said:
"He is tired of us.
What if one day a slip of paper emerges from within the palace ordering someone to join the Grand Secretariat?
At this time, if we recommend one or two worthy individuals
to work together wholeheartedly,
there may still be something that can be done."
Shìqí agreed with this.
The next day,
he thus submitted the names of Academician-in-waiting Miáo Zhōng, Lecturer-in-waiting (Shìjiǎng) Cáo Nài, and Yú.
Thus, Yú was promoted and employed.
In the fifth year, an imperial edict ordered him to enter the Grand Secretariat with his current official title,
to participate in confidential affairs,
and soon after he was promoted to Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù Yòushìláng).
He died in the twelfth year.
He was posthumously granted the title of Minister (Shàngshū) and Academician (Xuéshì).
The posthumous grant of both official title and concurrent post
began with Yú.
Yú was dignified, solemn, and reserved,
and his household had no private visitors seeking favors.
In discussing affairs, he was lenient and generous.
He once memorialized that many prisoners awaiting judgment across the realm died of long confinement,
and that special envoys should be dispatched to various regions to resolve and release them.
The Emperor accepted this.
When there was a border alert,
and generals were being appointed,
an envoy from another department arrived.
The general consensus was to detain him.
Yú said:
"Rewarding good and punishing evil is
the foundation of governance.
To implicate the good
is unlawful.
To seize someone upon their arrival
is not chivalrous."
The Emperor agreed,
and generously sent the envoy away.
Eulogy says: During the reign of Chéngzǔ,
Shìqí, Róng, and Xiè Jìn, among others, served concurrently in the Grand Secretariat.
Pǔ also served as a palace official under Rénzōng.
These three men served through four reigns,
and were esteemed elders of their time.
Although Pǔ joined the Grand Secretariat later,
his virtue and prestige were comparable.
Thus, when the Ming dynasty lauded virtuous chancellors,
they invariably began with the Three Yángs.
All were able to uphold the origins of Confucianism,
understand the intricacies of affairs,
cooperate and assist each other,
and perform their duties diligently and without slackness.
History records that Fáng and Dù presented all their good qualities to their lord,
assisting, patching, and concealing them for practical use.
It also states that Yáo Chóng was skilled at adapting to change
to accomplish the affairs of the realm;
Sòng Jǐng was skilled at preserving established institutions
to maintain the rectitude of the realm.
The Three Yángs were perhaps quite similar to them.
Collation Notes
Biographies Chapter 37: Jiǎn Yì, Xià Yuánjí (Yú Shìjí, Lǐ Wénnì, Zōu Shīyán)
Jiǎn Yì,
courtesy name Yízhī,
a native of Bā,
originally named Róng.
He became a jìnshì in the eighteenth year of Hóngwǔ.
He was appointed Imperial Secretariat Drafter (Zhōngshū Shèrén),
and his memorials pleased the Emperor.
The Emperor asked:
"Are you a descendant of Jiǎn Shú?"
Róng kowtowed and dared not reply.
The Emperor praised his honesty and sincerity,
changed his name to Yì,
and personally wrote and bestowed it upon him.
He was due for promotion after three years of service,
but was specially ordered to serve for nine years,
with the Emperor saying:
"I intend to employ Yì."
Thus, he attended the Emperor morning and evening,
acting with utmost care and caution,
never showing any displeased expression.
When Huìdì ascended the throne,
following Tàizǔ's wishes,
he was exceptionally promoted to Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù Yòushìláng).
At this time, Qí Tài and Huáng Zǐchéng were in power,
launching large military campaigns externally
and reforming institutions internally.
Yì offered no proposals.
Wáng Shēn, a National University Academician (Guózǐ Bóshì), sent a letter reproaching him,
to which Yì could not reply.
When the Yàn [燕] army entered,
he welcomed and submitted to them,
and was appointed Assistant Minister (Zuǒ Shìláng [左侍郎]).
A few months later,
he was promoted to Minister (Shàngshū [尚書]).
At that time, the priority was to reverse the policies of the Jiànwén [建文] reign.
All the changes made during that period were abolished.
Jiǎn Yì [蹇義] calmly said:
"Benefit and harm (or addition and reduction) should be timely and appropriate.
The previous changes were indeed improper,
but to insist on restoring everything now
is also not entirely appropriate."
He then cited several matters and explained their full context.
The Emperor praised him,
and followed his advice.
In the second year of Yǒnglè [永樂] (1404), he concurrently served as Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhānshì [太子詹事]).
Whenever the Emperor had an edict to transmit to the Crown Prince,
he would send Jiǎn Yì [蹇義],
who was able to guide the meaning with meticulous care.
Both the Emperor and the Crown Prince loved and respected him.
In the seventh year (1409),
when the Emperor toured Běijīng [北京],
he ordered Jiǎn Yì [蹇義] to assist the Crown Prince in supervising the state.
Jiǎn Yì [蹇義] was well-versed in historical precedents
and understood the principles of governance,
so all military and state affairs relied on him.
At that time, among the old officials who were favored and employed,
Minister of Revenue (Hùbù Shàngshū [戶部尚書]) Xià Yuánjí [夏原吉] was as famous as Jiǎn Yì [蹇義],
and they were referred to by the public as
"Jiǎn [蹇] and Xià [夏]".
After three full terms (of nine years),
the Emperor personally hosted a banquet for the two in a side hall,
praising them excessively.
He was often commanded to concurrently manage affairs of other ministries;
though his duties piled up,
he handled them with ease.
In the seventeenth year (1419), he returned home due to his father's funeral.
Both the Emperor and the Crown Prince sent officials to offer sacrifices.
An imperial edict ordered his recall to office.
In the nineteenth year (1421),
the Three Great Halls (Sān Diàn [三殿]) caught fire.
An imperial decree commanded twenty-six court officials to tour the empire.
Jiǎn Yì [蹇義] and Supervising Secretary (Gěishìzhōng [給事中]) Mǎ Jùn [馬俊] were assigned to tour the prefectures of Yìngtiān [應天],
inquiring about the hardships of the military and common people.
They dismissed several civil and military chief officials who disturbed the populace
and presented dozens of proposals for reforms, which were then implemented.
Upon returning, he resumed his duties at the ministry.
The following year (1422),
when the Emperor returned from a northern campaign,

he held Jiǎn Yì [蹇義] accountable for not correcting the Crown Prince, who had leniently pardoned Lǚ Zhèn's [呂震] son-in-law, Principal Secretary (Zhǔshì [主事]) Zhāng Hè [張鶴], for impropriety during a court audience.
Jiǎn Yì [蹇義] was accused of failing to rectify the Crown Prince's actions
and was arrested and imprisoned in the Imperial Bodyguard (Jǐnyīwèi [錦衣衞]) prison.
He was released in the spring of the year after that.
Upon Rénzōng's [仁宗] accession,
Jiǎn Yì [蹇義] and Xià Yuánjí [夏原吉], as elder statesmen, were trusted by both the court and the populace.
The Emperor also remembered Jiǎn Yì's [蹇義] past efforts during his regency,
and particularly relied heavily on him.
First, he promoted Jiǎn Yì [蹇義] to Grand Guardian (Shàobǎo [少保]),
bestowing upon him court robes, an ivory tablet, and a jade belt,
along with a double salary.
He was successively promoted to Grand Tutor (Shàoshī [少師]),
and was given a silver seal,
inscribed with the words
"Rectifying Faults and Correcting Errors" (Shéngqiān Jiūmiáo [繩愆糾繆]).
Later,
he was again granted an imperial letter which stated:
"Previously, when I supervised the state,
you, as an old minister of the former reign,
attended to me daily.
With the establishment of the two capitals
and the pressing nature of governmental affairs,
you toiled and worried,
disregarding your own person and family.
For over twenty years,
you remained steadfast through both ease and difficulty.
Upon inheriting the great succession,
you assisted in governance,
remaining diligent and ever more respectful.
I cherish these memories and do not forget.
Thus, by my own intention,
I have specially created the 'Jiǎn Zhōngzhēn Yìn' (Jiǎn the Loyal and Upright Seal) [蹇忠貞印]
to bestow upon you,
to be kept in your home
and passed down through generations,
so that they may know that I, the sovereign, and my minister worked together through difficulties
and achieved success together."
At that time, only Yáng Shìqí [楊士奇] also received a
"Zhēnyī" (貞一, Upright and Constant)
seal and imperial letter.

Soon after, he was commanded, along with the Duke of Yīng (Yīngguógōng [英國公]) Zhāng Fǔ [張輔] and Xià Yuánjí [夏原吉], to jointly supervise the compilation of the Veritable Records of Tàizōng (Tàizōng Shílù [太宗實錄]).
Jiǎn Yì [蹇義] regarded Xià Yuánjí [夏原吉] as particularly substantial and reliable,
though he himself was overly cautious.
Yáng Shìqí [楊士奇] once said to Jiǎn Yì [蹇義] in front of the Emperor:
"Why such excessive worry?"
Jiǎn Yì [蹇義] replied:
"I fear that recklessness will lead to future troubles."
The Emperor approved of both.
Yáng Róng [楊榮] once slandered Jiǎn Yì [蹇義].
The Emperor did not approve of Yáng Róng [楊榮].
Jiǎn Yì [蹇義] bowed his head and said:
"Yáng Róng [楊榮] has no ill intentions.
Even if those around you slander him,
I hope Your Majesty will investigate carefully."
The Emperor smiled and said:
"I certainly do not believe them."
Upon Xuānzōng's [宣宗] accession,
his trust and reliance grew even heavier.
At that time, the Xiànlíng [獻陵] mausoleum was being constructed.
The Emperor wished to follow the previous Emperor's will for frugality,
and consulted Jiǎn Yì [蹇義] and Xià Yuánjí [夏原吉].
The two strongly advocated, saying:
"Your sagely vision is lofty and far-reaching,
stemming from profound filial piety,
a benefit for ten thousand generations."
The Emperor personally planned it,
and the mausoleum was completed in three months.
Its grandeur was not equal to that of Chánglíng [長陵],
and subsequent emperors followed this as a model.
It was not until Shìzōng [世宗] constructed Yǒnglíng [永陵]
that extravagance began to increase.
When the Emperor campaigned at Yuè'ān [樂安],
Jiǎn Yì [蹇義], Xià Yuánjí [夏原吉], and the various academicians all accompanied him,
participating in military strategic affairs,
and were bestowed with saddled horses, armor, helmets, bows, and swords.
Upon their return,
they received generous rewards.
In the third year (1428), he returned from a border tour.
The Emperor, considering Jiǎn Yì [蹇義], Xià Yuánjí [夏原吉], Yáng Shìqí [楊士奇], and Yáng Róng [楊榮] were all old,
bestowed an imperial letter which stated:
"You are all elder statesmen from the time of my ancestors,
entrusted to assist me.
Now with your yellow hair and precarious teeth,
it is no longer suitable for you to manage burdensome and complex affairs,
which would harm the court's etiquette of honoring the aged and treating the virtuous.
You may cease your current duties,
and morning and evening remain by my side to discuss profound principles,
and together bring peace to the nation and family.
Your official emoluments shall remain as before."
The following year (1429),
Guō Jǐn [郭璡] replaced him as Minister.
Soon after, following Hú Yíng's [胡濙] suggestion,
Jiǎn Yì [蹇義] and the other four were commanded to deliberate on memorials and petitions from officials, military personnel, and common people across the empire.
Jiǎn Yì [蹇義] was again granted a silver seal,
inscribed with the words
"Loyal, Magnanimous, and Broad-minded" (Zhōnghòu Kuānhóng [忠厚寬宏]).
In the seventh year (1432), an imperial edict commanded the relevant authorities to build a new residence for Jiǎn Yì [蹇義] inside the Wénmíngmén [文明門] gate.
Upon Yīngzōng's [英宗] accession,
he fell ill while fasting in his residence.
An imperial physician was sent to attend to him, and he was asked if he had any final words.
He replied:
"Your Majesty has just inherited the great throne.
I hope you will respectfully uphold the established laws of your ancestors
and remain steadfast in this from beginning to end."
He then died,
aged seventy-three.
He was posthumously granted Grand Preceptor (Tàishī [太師])
and given the posthumous name Zhōngdìng [忠定] (Loyal and Steadfast).
Jiǎn Yì [蹇義] was by nature simple, upright, filial, and friendly.
He was good at interacting with colleagues
and never said a word to harm anyone.
Yáng Shìqí [楊士奇] often said:
"Zhāng Yǒng's [張詠] disregard for worldly pleasures,
Fù Yáoyú's [傅堯俞] sincerity towards people,
and Fàn Jǐngrén's [范景仁] lack of hidden motives —
Jiǎn Yì [蹇義] possessed all of these."
His son, Jiǎn Yīng [蹇英],
was known for his poetry.
By virtue of his father's position, he became an Assistant Administrator (Chéng [丞]) in the Imperial Seal Bureau (Shàngbǎosī [尚寶司])
and successively served as Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Shǎoqīng [太常少卿]).
Xià Yuánjí,
courtesy name Wéizhē,
was originally from Déxīng.
His father, Shímǐn,
served as an instructor (jiàoyù) in Xiāngyīn,
and so they settled there.
Yuánjí became an orphan early,
studied diligently, and supported his mother.
He was recommended by the district to enter the Imperial Academy,
and was selected to write imperial edicts in the forbidden palace.
Some students would laugh loudly,
but Yuánjí sat upright and solemnly.
Tàizǔ observed this and found him remarkable.
He was promoted to Principal of the Ministry of Revenue (hùbù zhǔshì).
The official duties were numerous and complex,
but he handled them all with perfect order,
and Shàngshū Yù Xīn greatly respected him.
There was a Liú lángzhōng
who was jealous of his ability.
At that time, Yù Xīn impeached officials who were negligent in their duties.
The Emperor wanted to pardon them,
but Yù Xīn insisted it was unacceptable.
The Emperor was enraged,
and asked:
"Who taught you this?"
Yù Xīn bowed his head and said:
"The ledger keeper behind the hall."
The Emperor then sent the ledger keeper to prison.
Liú lángzhōng then said:
"The one who taught the Shàngshū
was Yuánjí."
The Emperor said:
"Yuánjí is capable of assisting the Shàngshū in managing the ministry's affairs,
do you wish to frame him!"
Both Liú lángzhōng and the ledger keeper were executed in the marketplace.
At the beginning of Jiànwén's reign,
he was promoted to Right Vice Minister of Revenue (hùbù yòu shìláng).
The next year, he was appointed Imperial Inspector (cǎifǎngshǐ).
He toured Fújiàn,
and in every prefecture and county he visited,
he investigated official administration
and inquired into the people's grievances.
Everyone was pleased and submitted to him.
After some time,
he was transferred to Qízhōu.
When Chéngzǔ ascended the throne,
someone seized Yuánjí and presented him.
The Emperor released him,
and transferred him to Left Vice Minister (zuǒ shìláng).
Someone said that Yuánjí was influential during Jiànwén's time,
and could not be trusted.
The Emperor did not listen,
and promoted him and Jiǎn Yì together to Shàngshū.
He and Jiǎn Yì deliberated and settled various systems of taxation and corvée.
They made over thirty proposals,
all of which were simple, convenient, and easy to follow.
He said:
"Measures that are difficult to sustain when implemented
will only further burden the people,
and I cannot bear it."
There was a great flood in Zhèxī,
and the local officials' efforts to control it were ineffective.
In the first year of Yǒnglè, Yuánjí was ordered to manage it.
Soon after, Vice Minister Lǐ Wényù was appointed as his deputy,
and then Censor-in-Chief Yú Shìjí was sent with a book on water conservancy to give to him.
Yuánjí requested to follow the ancient path of Yǔ's three rivers entering the sea,
to dredge the lower reaches of Wúsōng,
connecting it to Tàihú upstream,
and to build sluice gates based on the terrain,
to store and release water at appropriate times.
This was approved.
Over one hundred thousand people were employed.
Yuánjí, in plain clothes and on foot,
planned day and night,
and did not use an umbrella in the intense heat,
saying:
"The people are toiling,
how can I alone seek comfort?"
When the work was completed,
he returned to the capital,
and reported that although the water flowed into the sea through the old channels,
the branch streams had not been fully dredged,
which was not a long-term solution.
In the first month of the next year,
Yuánjí went again,
to dredge Báimáo Táng, Liújiā Hé, and Dàhuáng Pǔ.
Yuán Fù, a Grand Judge (Dàlǐ shàopíng), served as his deputy.
Later,
Sòng Xìng, a Provincial Administration Commissioner (Shǎnxī cāncānj), was again ordered to assist him.
In the ninth month, the work was completed,
the water was drained,
and the agricultural lands of Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng greatly benefited.
He returned in the third year.
That summer,
Zhèxī suffered a great famine,
and Yuánjí was ordered to lead Yú Shìjí, Yuán Fù, and Left Administration Commissioner (zuǒ tōngzhèng) Zhào Jūrèn to provide relief,
distributing three hundred thousand shi of grain
and providing cattle and seeds.
When someone requested to summon people to cultivate the re-emerged silty fields after the flood for increased taxes,
Yuánjí immediately submitted a memorial to stop it.
Yáo Guǎngxiào returned from Zhèxī,
and praised Yuánjí, saying:
"He is a remnant of ancient benevolence."
Not long after,
Yù Xīn passed away,
and Yuánjí was recalled
to manage the ministry's affairs.
He first requested to reduce superfluous expenditure,
equalize taxes and corvée,
strictly enforce salt laws and currency prohibitions,
clear granaries,
and expand cultivation
to supply the border and relieve the people,
and also facilitate commerce.
All were approved.
Regarding the numbers of households, treasuries, and land taxes, whether surplus or deficit, both within and outside the capital,
he would write them on small slips and keep them in his bosom,
reviewing them from time to time.
One day,
the Emperor asked about the amount of money and grain in the realm,
and he answered very thoroughly,
which led the Emperor to value him even more.
At that time,
military conflicts had just settled,
discussions were held
on "Jìngnán"
meritorious officials' enfeoffments and rewards,
various princes were granted fiefs,
and hundreds of military guard offices were established.
Later,
eight hundred thousand troops were sent to punish Ānnán,
eunuchs built giant ships to communicate with overseas nations,
and grand palace complexes were erected in the Northern Capital,
with supplies and transport amounting to tens of millions,
all drawn from the Ministry of Revenue.
Yuánjí meticulously calculated and managed these,
and the national expenditure did not fall short.
In the sixth year, he was ordered to oversee the transport of materials by soldiers and civilians to the Northern Capital,
with an imperial edict stating that Jǐnyīwèi officials and guards should accompany him
to punish those who neglected their duties.
Yuánjí, fearing many would offend,
warned and admonished them before proceeding,
and everyone felt grateful and pleased.
In the seventh year,
the Emperor went on a northern tour,
and Yuánjí was ordered to concurrently manage the Ministry of Rites, Ministry of War, and Censorate in the travelling court.
There were two commanders who falsely claimed monthly stipends,
and the Emperor wanted to execute them.
Yuánjí said:
"This is not according to the law;
if they were to commit actual theft,
what greater punishment could there be?"
The Emperor then stopped.
In the eighth year,
the Emperor went on a northern expedition,
and Yuánjí assisted the Grandson in guarding Beijing,
managing all affairs of the nine ministers in the travelling court.
At that time, various departments were newly established,
and every morning,
Yuánjí entered to assist the Grandson in deliberating on various matters.
After the court session,
officials from various departments and censors surrounded him, requesting guidance.
Yuánjí answered orally and wrote replies,
without changing his expression.
He sent reports to the travelling court in the north,
and instructed the regent in the south,
and the capital remained orderly.
When the Emperor returned,
he bestowed currency, silk, saddles, horses, and a sacrificial feast,
and offered abundant words of comfort and reward.
Soon after, he accompanied the Emperor back to Nánjīng,
and was ordered to attend the Grandson in touring villages,
to observe the hardships of the common people.
Yuánjí took some salted millet to present,
saying:
"May Your Highness eat this,
to know the difficulties of the people."
After nine years,
he and Jiǎn Yì were both entertained in a private hall,
and the Emperor pointed to the two men and said to his officials:
"Gāo Huángdì cultivated virtuous men to bequeath to me.
If you wish to see ancient famous officials,
these are they."
From then on, he repeatedly attended the Grandson,
traveling between the two capitals,
offering loyal advice as opportunities arose on the road,
which greatly benefited affairs.
In the eighteenth year,
the palaces in Běijīng were completed.
He sent Yuán Jí south to summon the Crown Prince and Imperial Grandson.
When he returned,
Yuán Jí said:
"Construction has been ongoing for years,
and is now complete.
It is fitting to pacify the displaced,
and remit overdue taxes to ease the people's burden."
The next year,
the Three Great Halls caught fire.
Yuán Jí again reiterated his previous request.
The emperor immediately ordered the relevant officials to implement it.
Initially, due to the hall fire, an edict was issued seeking frank advice.
Many ministers said that moving the capital to Běijīng was not advisable.
The emperor was angry
and killed Xiāo Yí, the official in charge,
saying:
"When the capital was being moved,
I secretly discussed it with the great ministers,
