and it was only settled after a long time;
it was not a rash decision."
The speakers then impeached the great ministers.
The emperor ordered them to kneel outside the Wǔmén and debate.
The great ministers fiercely reviled the speakers,
but Yuán Jí alone reported:
"They responded to the edict and are innocent.
We, as great ministers,
were unable to assist in the grand plan,
the fault lies with us."
The emperor's anger subsided,
and he pardoned both sides.
Some criticized Yuán Jí for betraying the initial discussion.
He said:
"We have served for a long time;
even if our words were mistaken,
the emperor might take pity on us.
If the censors were punished,
the loss would not be small."
Everyone then began to admire him.
Although Yuán Jí resided in the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù),
the emperor often ordered him to deliberate on major state affairs.
Whenever the emperor held court in the private hall (Biàndiàn) or by the Qùémén,
he would summon Yuán Jí and speak for a long time,
and those on the left and right could not hear them.
When he retired, he was as humble as if he had no part in it.
When Jiāozhǐ was pacified,
the emperor asked whether granting official positions or rewards was more beneficial.
He replied:
"Rewards are spent at once
and are limited;
granting official positions incurs future expenses
that are endless."
The emperor followed his advice.
A Dharma King from the Western Regions came to court.
The emperor wanted to welcome him in the suburbs,
but Yuán Jí disagreed.
When the Dharma King entered,
Yuán Jí saw him
but did not bow.
The emperor smiled and said:
"Are you trying to emulate Hán Yù?"
Táng Sài'ér revolted in Shāndōng.
After the rebellion was quelled,
over three thousand coerced followers were captured and brought back.
Yuán Jí pleaded with the emperor
to pardon them all.
When Gǔ Wáng Huì rebelled,
the emperor suspected there were collaborators in Chángshā.
Yuán Jí guaranteed them with his life,
and the matter was dropped.
In the winter of the nineteenth year,
the emperor planned a major campaign to conquer the desert.
He ordered Yuán Jí, together with Lǚ Zhèn, Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū), Fāng Bīn, Minister of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū), and Wú Zhōng, Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shàngshū), to deliberate.
They all said that the army should not be dispatched.
Before they could present their report,
the emperor summoned Fāng Bīn.
Fāng Bīn strongly argued that military expeditions were costly and depleted resources,
and the emperor was displeased.
He summoned Yuán Jí and asked about the abundance or scarcity of border provisions.
He replied:
"In recent years, expeditions have been fruitless,
and military horses and supplies have been depleted by eight or nine tenths.
Disasters have repeatedly occurred,
and both internal and external resources are exhausted.
Moreover, Your Sacred Majesty is only slightly recovered
and still requires care;
I beg you to send generals to campaign,
and not trouble the imperial carriage."
The emperor was enraged
and immediately ordered Yuán Jí to go and manage grain storage in Kāipíng.
When Wú Zhōng entered and spoke like Fāng Bīn,
the emperor grew even angrier.
He summoned Yuán Jí and imprisoned him in the Imperial Household Department (Nèiguānjàn),
and also imprisoned Dàlǐchéng Zōu Shīyán,
because he had once served in the Ministry of Revenue.
Fāng Bīn, in fear, committed suicide.
Then Yuán Jí's family property was confiscated.
Apart from the banknotes granted by the emperor,
there were only plain clothes and earthenware.
The next year, the northern expedition was launched,
but it returned due to lack of provisions.
Afterwards,
he repeatedly ventured beyond the Great Wall for several years,
but never encountered the enemy.
When he returned to Yúmùchuān,
the emperor fell ill
and looked at his attendants, saying:
"Xià Yuánjí loves me."
Three days after the news of his death reached him,
the Crown Prince rushed to the prison,
called out Yuán Jí,
and cried as he informed him.
Yuán Jí prostrated himself and wept,
unable to rise.
The Crown Prince ordered him released from prison
to discuss the funeral rites,
and then asked what should be included in the amnesty edict.
He replied by suggesting famine relief,
reducing taxes and labor services,
and abolishing the treasure ships sent to the Western Oceans and the gold and silver mining taxes in Yúnnán and Jiāozhǐ.
All were followed.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
he restored Yuán Jí's official position.
While Yuán Jí was in prison,
his mother had died,
so he now requested to return home to complete the mourning period.
The emperor said:
"You are an old minister;
you should help me overcome difficulties.
If you have mourning,
do I not also have mourning?"
He generously bestowed gifts upon him,
ordered his family to observe the mourning,
and provided rapid transport for him to return home for the burial,
with officials handling the funeral arrangements.
Yuán Jí dared not speak again.
Soon after, he was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shàofù).
Lǚ Zhèn, as Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shàoshī), ranked above Yuán Jí.
The emperor ordered the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Hónglú) to arrange Lǚ Zhèn below him.
He was promoted to Junior Guardian (Shàobǎo),
and concurrently remained Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince and Minister as before,
receiving three salaries.
Yuán Jí firmly declined,
and was then allowed to decline the salary of Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
He was bestowed a silver seal
inscribed "Rectify errors and correct mistakes"
(Shéngqiān Jiūmiù),
and mansions were built for him in both capitals.
Subsequently, Rénzōng died,
and the Crown Prince arrived from Nánjīng.
Yuán Jí, bearing the imperial will, welcomed him at Lúgōuqíáo.
When Xuānzōng ascended the throne,
he held the old grand councilor in even greater trust and respect.
The next year,
Hàn Wáng Gāoxù rebelled,
also using "Quelling the Difficulties" (Jìngnàn) as his pretext.
He issued a manifesto denouncing the great ministers,
with Yuán Jí named first.
The emperor summoned his ministers at night to discuss.
Yáng Róng was the first to advise the emperor to personally lead the campaign.
The emperor hesitated.
Yuán Jí said:
"Do you not recall the matter of Lǐ Jǐnglóng?
I saw the generals who were dispatched yesterday;
their faces changed as soon as the order was given,
so their conduct in action can be imagined.
Moreover, speed is paramount in war;
we should don armor and rush there.
This is what is called 'striking first to seize the enemy's will.'
Yáng Róng's plan is good."
The emperor's decision was thus made.
When the army returned,
rewards were increased,
and three gatekeepers were bestowed upon him.
Yuán Jí declined, saying he had no merit.
But his refusal was not accepted.
In the third year,
he accompanied the emperor on a northern tour.
The emperor took some dried rations and parched rice from Xià Yuánjí and tasted them.
He smiled and said,
"Why is this so bad?"
He replied,
"There are still starving men in the army."
The emperor then ordered a feast of high officials' cuisine to be given to him,
and also rewarded the generals and soldiers.
They proceeded to review the troops at Tù'ér Shān.
The emperor was angered by the generals' laxity
and stripped them of their clothes.
Xià Yuánjí said,
"Generals are
the country's claws and teeth.
How can we let them freeze to death?"
He repeatedly and forcefully remonstrated.
The emperor said,
"For your sake, I will release them."
Again, he and Jiǎn Yì were jointly bestowed with silver seals,
inscribed
"Hán Hóng Zhēn Jìng" (Embracing Magnanimity, Upholding Rectitude, and Being Tranquil).
The emperor was highly skilled in painting,
and once personally painted a picture of the God of Longevity to bestow upon him.
Other gifts of paintings, clothing, utensils, silver coins, and curios
were given daily.
In the first month of the fifth year,
the *Liǎngcháo Shílù* (Veritable Records of Two Reigns) was completed,
and he was again given gold coins, saddles, and horses.
He went in the morning to express his gratitude,
returned home, and died
at the age of sixty-five.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tàishī,
and given the posthumous name Zhōngjìng.
An imperial edict instructed the Ministry of Revenue to restore his family's status,
and they were exempt from all levies for generations.
Xià Yuánjí possessed a magnanimous spirit;
no one could fathom its depth.
If a colleague excelled,
he would immediately acknowledge it.
If there was a minor fault,
he would certainly conceal it.
An official stained the gold-embroidered robes he had been granted.
Xià Yuánjí said,
"Do not be afraid;
the stain can be washed out."
Another official mistyped a confidential document;
the official kowtowed and begged for death.
Xià Yuánjí did not question him;
he went to court himself and took the blame.
The emperor ordered it to be changed.
Lǚ Zhèn once tried to undermine Xià Yuánjí.
Zhèn begged for an official post for his son,
and Xià Yuánjí, considering Zhèn's
"Jìngnàn"
merit in defending a city at the time,
interceded on his behalf.
Chén Xuān, the Earl of Píngjiāng, initially disliked Xià Yuánjí,
but Xià Yuánjí often praised Xuān's talent.
Someone asked Xià Yuánjí,
"Can magnanimity be learned?"
He replied,
"When I was young,
I never failed to get angry when provoked.
At first, I restrained it on my face;
then I restrained it in my heart;
after a long time, there was nothing left to restrain."
He once reviewed legal documents at night,
patted the desk and sighed,
his brush about to fall, then stopped.
His wife asked him about it.
He said,
"This is a memorial for capital punishment at the end of the year."
He was drinking with colleagues elsewhere,
and returning home at night when it snowed,
they passed the forbidden gate.
Someone wished not to dismount.
Xià Yuánjí said,
"A gentleman does not let the darkness diminish his conduct."
Such was his circumspection.
Xià Yuánjí and Jiǎn Yì both began their careers during Tàizǔ's reign.
Jiǎn Yì managed official appointments,
while Xià Yuánjí oversaw the Ministry of Revenue,
both for twenty-seven years,
their status and position preceding the Sān Yáng.
During the reigns of Rénzōng and Xuānzōng,
they concurrently held positions in both the Tái and Shěng (Censorate and Ministries),
and participated in the Guǎngé (Grand Secretariat),
assisting the government with the Sān Yáng in one accord.
Jiǎn Yì was good at strategizing,
Yáng Róng was good at decisive action,
while Xià Yuánjí and Yáng Shìqí were particularly adept at upholding the broader principles,
possessing the demeanor and integrity of ancient grand ministers.
His son, Xuān,
became a Shàngbǎo Sì Chéng (Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Accoutrements) through hereditary privilege.
He enjoyed discussing military affairs;
during the Jǐngtài era,
he repeatedly submitted memorials concerning military matters,
but met with opposition
and was not employed.
He eventually became Nánjīng Tàicháng Shàoqīng (Assistant Minister of the Nanjing Court of Imperial Sacrifices).
Yú Shìjí,
courtesy name Yòngzhēn,
was a native of Xiàngshān.
During the Jiànwén reign,
he served as a Yǎnzhōu Xùndǎo (Instructor of Yanzhou Prefecture).
He submitted a memorial on current affairs
and was promoted to Yùshǐ (Censor).
He was dispatched to inspect Fèngyáng, Huīzhōu, and Húguǎng,
and was able to discern and redress unjust cases.
When Chéngzǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Qiāndū Yùshǐ (Assistant Censor-in-Chief).
By imperial decree, he presented a book on water conservancy to Xià Yuánjí,
and was consequently retained to oversee agricultural administration in Zhèxī.
The arrears in grain tax in Húzhōu amounted to 600,000 *shi*;
his colleagues wanted to reduce the number before reporting it.
Yú Shìjí said,
"Deceiving the emperor and harming the people,
I will not do it."
He presented the full truth in his memorial,
and all were exempted.
Soon after, he was impeached by the Dū Yùshǐ (Censor-in-Chief) Chén Yīng,
and was imprisoned with Dàlǐ Shàoqīng (Assistant Minister of the Court of Judicial Review) Yuán Fù.
Yuán Fù died in prison,
while Yú Shìjí was demoted to Shìguān (service official)
to manage waterworks in Sū and Sōng.
Later, he was reinstated
and submitted a memorial titled *Shèngxiào Ruìyìng Sòng* (Ode to Sagely Filial Piety and Auspicious Omens).
The emperor said,
"You are a high minister;
you do not speak of the people's sufferings and needs,
but instead offer flattery!"
He threw it back at him.
At the beginning of the Xuāndé reign,
he served as Nánjīng Xíngbù Shìláng (Assistant Minister of the Nanjing Ministry of Justice)
before retiring.
Lǐ Wénnyù,
was a native of Xiāngyáng.
At the beginning of the Yǒnglè reign,
as Hùbù Shìláng (Assistant Minister of the Ministry of Revenue), he assisted Xià Yuánjí in water conservancy and rendered meritorious service.
Later, he was demoted for an offense and exiled to Liáodōng for twenty years.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
he was recalled
and became Nánjīng Tōngzhèng Cānyì (Administrator of the Nanjing Office of Transmission),
then retired.
Zōu Shīyán,
was a native of Yídū.
At the beginning of the Yǒnglè reign,
he served as Jiāngxī Cānzhèng (Vice-Administrator of Jiangxi Province),
and was dismissed for an offense.
Soon after, he was recommended and promoted to Yùshǐ (Censor),
known for his outspokenness.
He was transferred to Dàlǐ Chéng (Secretary of the Court of Judicial Review),
and concurrently served in the Ministry of Revenue,
where he was imprisoned with Xià Yuánjí.
Upon Rénzōng's ascension,
he was released and became Lǐbù Shìláng (Assistant Minister of the Ministry of Rites).
Returning from visiting his ancestors' grave,
he reached Tōngzhōu
and died.
Being poor, he could not afford to be transported home for burial.
Shàngshū (Minister) Lǚ Zhèn reported this to the court,
and Xuānzōng ordered an official boat to transport him.
An edict was issued that all deceased capital officials
should be provided with official transport,
establishing it as a regulation.
The encomium states: The *Shū* (Book of Documents) says,
"Seek out wise men
to assist your successors."
Jiǎn Yì and Xià Yuánjí, from the very beginning of their official careers,
were recognized by Tàizǔ for their sincerity, trustworthiness, and competence,
and Chéngzǔ further entrusted them with complex and arduous tasks.
These two men were indeed able to comprehend the principles of governance
and were well-versed in regulations,
proving themselves worthy of assisting the ruler.
When Rénzōng and Xuānzōng succeeded to the throne,
they were given great trust and favor,
and with shared virtue and concerted effort,
they supported and aided their enlightened lord.
This led to reformed and clarified administration,
and a harmonious and joyful populace,
with outstanding achievements,
establishing them as eminent foundational ministers.
The efficacy of nurturing such talent
was profound indeed.
Collation Notes

Biographies, Volume 38: Yù Xīn, Zhào Hóng, Jīn Zhōng, Lǐ Qìng, Shī Kuí, Gǔ Pǔ (Xiàng Bǎo), Chén Shòu (Mǎ Jīng, Xǔ Sīwēn), Liú Jìchí, Liú Chén, Yáng Dǐ, Yú Qiān (Lǚ Shēng, Yǎng Zhān, Yán Běn), Tāng Zōng
Yù Xīn,
courtesy name Dūn-běn,
was from Lín-huái.
During the Hóng-wǔ reign,
he was summoned for his talent
and appointed Director of the Bureau of Finance (Dù-zhī zhǔ-shì) in the Ministry of Revenue (Hù-bù).
He was promoted to Chief Minister (Láng-zhōng).
After a year,
he was promoted to Vice Minister of the Right (Yòu shì-láng) of the same Ministry.
He was once asked about the population, land tax,
and geographical advantages and disadvantages of the empire,
and he answered without omission,
so the Emperor praised his talent.
Soon after, he was promoted to Minister (Shàng-shū).
At that time, the annual stipend of grain for imperial princes (qīn-wáng) was fifty thousand shí.
Yù Xīn deliberated and proposed a reduction by four-fifths,
and also stipulated varying stipends for princes of commanderies (jùn-wáng) and below.
Furthermore, due to insufficient provisions for the border armies,
he formulated the 'call for merchants to open up the market' (zhào-shāng kāi-zhōng fǎ) method,
ordering merchants to transport grain to the border regions
and receive salt vouchers accordingly.
Border provisions were thus made sufficient.
When Xià Yuán-jí was a Director of the Bureau (zhǔ-shì) in the Ministry of Revenue,
Yù Xīn held him in high regard
and entrusted all matters of the various bureaus to him.
In the second year of Jiàn-wén, he retired due to illness.
When Chéng-zǔ ascended the throne,
he was summoned to take charge of the Ministry of Revenue.
Gǔ Pǔ was appointed Vice Minister (shì-láng) to assist him.
In the first year of Yǒng-lè,
there was a locust plague in Hé-nán,
but the local officials did not report it.
Yù Xīn impeached and punished them.
Initially,
when grain was to be transported to Běi-jīng,
Yù Xīn said:
"From Huái-hé to Huáng-hé,
there are many shallow shoals and steep slopes,
making boat transport difficult.
I request that shallow boats carrying three hundred shí be used
to transport from the Huái-hé and Shā-hé rivers to the steep slope below the Yǐng-xī estuary in Chén-zhōu.
Then, shallow boats carrying two hundred shí should be used to transport above the steep slope,
and large boats should be used to transport into the Huáng-hé.
At Bā-liǔ-shù and other places,
Hé-nán carters should be ordered to transport by land to the Wèi-hé river,
then transfer to Běi-jīng."
This was adopted.
He also said:
"The produce from military farm (tún-tián) lands in Hú-guǎng varies,
so I request that all be allowed to be delivered to the government.
Two shí of millet, broomcorn millet, barley, or buckwheat
should be equivalent to one shí of rice.
Two shí five dòu of paddy rice or glutinous millet,
and three shí of barnyard grass
should each be equivalent to one shí of rice.
Beans, wheat, and sesame should be equivalent to rice."
This was enacted as a regulation.
In the second year, he proposed that for dukes (gōng), marquises (hóu), earls (bó), imperial sons-in-law (fù-mǎ), and consorts' relatives (yí-bīn)
whose stipends were two hundred shí or more,
they should, like civil and military officials,
be given a combination of rice and paper currency.
In the third year, due to the hardship of the soldiers,
he proposed reducing the annual military farm harvest by four or five tenths if it did not meet the quota.
He also proposed that those redeeming punishments by paying rice to Běi-jīng should do so at the Nán-jīng granaries.
All were approved.
In the eighth month of that year, he died in office.
The Emperor sighed, saying:
"Yù Xīn has managed the state's revenue for thirteen years,
measuring income and expenditure.
Now, who can replace him?"
The court was suspended for one day,
and burial sacrifices were bestowed.
Xià Yuán-jí was recalled to manage the Ministry's affairs.
Yù Xīn was skilled at comprehensive management,
meticulous yet not cumbersome.
His plans
could not be altered later.
Zhào Hóng,
courtesy name Yún-hàn,
was from Xià,
then moved to Xiáng-fú.
During the Hóng-wǔ reign,
he entered the Imperial Academy (Tài-xué) through a local recommendation
and was appointed Director (zhǔ-shì) of the Bureau of Military Provisions (Zhí-fāng Sī) in the Ministry of War (Bīng-bù).
He presented maps of the empire's strategic points and passes,
along with suitable locations for military farms and garrisons.
The Emperor considered him talented
and promoted him to Assistant Department Director (Yuán-wài-láng).
At the beginning of Jiàn-wén,
he was promoted to Administration Commissioner (Cān-zhèng) of Zhè-jiāng.
He proposed a plan to capture sea pirates
and achieved success.
In the second year of Yǒng-lè, he was sent on a mission to Jiāo-zhǐ,
and his return report pleased the Emperor.
He was promoted to Vice Minister (shì-láng) of the Ministry of Justice (Xíng-bù),
then transferred to the Ministry of Works (Gōng-bù),
and again transferred to the Ministry of Rites (Lǐ-bù).
In the fifth year, he was promoted to Minister (Shàng-shū),
and was granted a banquet at the Huá-gài Palace.
He had the food leftovers sent to his mother.
Initially,
Zhào Hóng was often impeached for various matters,
but the Emperor ignored it.
In the autumn of the ninth year,
Korean envoys were about to return,
and by custom, gifts were to be bestowed,
but Zhào Hóng did not report this.
The Emperor angrily said:
"This will cause me to lose the hearts of distant people!"
So he was imprisoned.
He was soon released
and ordered to supervise the construction of Lóng-qìng, Bǎo-ān, Yǒng-níng, and other prefectures and counties,
and to pacify the newly gathered people.
The people were secure in their livelihoods.
In the fifteenth year, he mourned his mother.
He was reinstated
and reassigned as Minister (Shàng-shū) of the Ministry of War (Bīng-bù),
specializing in military affairs beyond the frontier.
When the Emperor campaigned north,
he was skilled in grain transport.
When Rén-zōng succeeded to the throne,
he was transferred to the Nán-jīng Ministry of Justice.
In the fifth year of Xuān-dé,
Censor Zhāng Kǎi impeached Zhào Hóng and Vice Minister Yú Shì-jí for idleness and laxity.
He was summoned
and ordered to retire.
Zhào Hóng was shrewd and sharp,
served five reigns,
held high official positions,
yet lived simply.
He died in the first year of Zhèng-tǒng
at the age of seventy-three.
Jīn Zhōng
was from Yín.
In his youth, he studied
and was skilled in Yi divination.
His elder brother, serving in the garrison at Tōng-zhōu, died.
Jīn Zhōng was to fill his place,
but being poor, he could not travel.
The physiognomist Yuán Gǒng provided him with funds.
Upon arrival,
he was assigned to the ranks of soldiers.
He practiced divination in the Běi-píng market
and was often accurate.
Market people spread tales, thinking him divine.
The monk Dào-yǎn recommended him to Chéng-zǔ.
When Chéng-zǔ was about to raise an army,
he feigned illness and summoned Jīn Zhōng for a divination.
He received a hexagram signifying "casting seals and riding in a carriage."
Jīn Zhōng said:
"This sign indicates nobility beyond words."
From then on, he had free access to the燕Prince of Yān's mansion,
often using his divinations to encourage the undertaking of great affairs.
Chéng-zǔ deeply trusted him.
When the Yān forces rose,
Chéng-zǔ appointed his own officials
and made Jīn Zhōng a Recorder (Jì-shàn) of the Prince of Yān's mansion,
entrusting him to guard Tōng-zhōu.
The Southern army attacked the city several times but could not conquer it.
Afterwards,
he was summoned to be at the Prince's side,
and any doubts were immediately put to him.
His divinations became even more accurate,
and he constantly offered strategies.
He was then appointed Right Senior Administrator (Yòu Zhǎng-shǐ),
assisting in military affairs
as a strategist.
When Chéng-zǔ became Emperor,
and meritorious service to the new dynasty was recognized,
Jīn Zhōng was promoted to Vice Minister of the Right (Yòu shì-láng) of the Ministry of Works (Gōng-bù),
assisting the Crown Prince in guarding Běi-jīng.
Soon after, he was recalled
and promoted to Minister (Shàng-shū) of the Ministry of War (Bīng-bù).
When the Emperor raised his army,
his second son Gāo-xù, who fought with merit,
was promised the position of Crown Prince.
At this time, Qiú Fú, Duke of Qí, and others sided with Gāo-xù
and urged the Emperor to establish him.
Only Jīn Zhōng thought it was unacceptable,
and before the Emperor, he enumerated historical cases of legitimate and illegitimate heirs.
The Emperor could not sway him
and secretly informed Jiě Jìn, Huáng Huái, and Yǐn Chāng-lóng.
Jiě Jìn and others all agreed that Jīn Zhōng's words were correct.
Thus, the eldest son was established as the Imperial Crown Prince (Huáng Tài-zǐ),
and Jīn Zhōng became an instructor for the Eastern Palace (Dōng-gōng),
serving as Minister of War (Bīng-bù Shàng-shū) concurrently with Grand Tutor (Jiān-shì) of the Eastern Palace Administration (Zhān-shì-fǔ).
In the sixth year, he was ordered to concurrently assist the Imperial Grandson (Huáng Tài-sūn).
The emperor marched north.
He left Zhōng with Jiǎn Yì, Huáng Huái, and Yáng Shìqí to assist the crown prince in supervising the state.
At this time, Gāo Xù's ambition to usurp the succession grew more urgent,
spreading rumors to defame the crown prince.
In the twelfth year, when the emperor returned from the northern campaign,
he ordered all officials of the Eastern Palace to be imprisoned.
Due to Zhōng's past merits and seniority, he was not questioned,
but secretly ordered to investigate the crown prince's affairs.
Zhōng stated there was nothing amiss.
The emperor was furious.
Zhōng removed his cap, kowtowed, and wept,
wishing to be implicated along with the crown prince to protect him.
Because of this, the crown prince was spared from being deposed,
and his palace officials, such as Huáng Huái and Yáng Pǔ, also survived.
Zhōng rose from the ranks of a common soldier to a high position,
and was greatly trusted and relied upon.
Whenever he was consulted,
he spoke without reservation,
yet was discreet and did not leak secrets.
When dealing with colleagues, he did not play both sides,
and in retirement, he was humble and modest.
He died in April of the following year.
An imperial envoy was provided for his return burial,
and officials were ordered to build a shrine and tomb for him,
and his family was exempted from service.
In the first year of Hóngxī,
he was posthumously granted the title of Rónglù Dàfū Shàoshī,
and given the posthumous name Zhōngxiāng.
His son Dá was appointed a Hànlín Jiǎntǎo.
Dá was upright and outspoken,
and rose to the position of Zhǎnglú Dū Zhuǎnyùnshǐ.
Zhōng had an elder brother named Huá,
who possessed integrity and principles.
When Zhōng achieved merit in defending Tōngzhōu,
he wished to extend the imperial favor by offering Huá an official position,
but Huá declined.
He was once summoned and bestowed with gold and fine silk,
but also refused it.
Chéngzǔ called him "Yūsǒu" (an old-fashioned recluse)
and sent him back.
One day,
he was reading the Sòng History and came across the story of Wáng Lún's adherence to Qín Huì,
and he let out a long sigh and passed away.
The villagers called him Bái Yún Xiānshēng.
Lǐ Qìng,
courtesy name Défú,
was a native of Shùnyì.
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
as a Guózǐshēng, he was appointed acting Yòu Qiāndū Yùshǐ,
later made a Xíngbù Yuánwàiláng,
and then promoted to Shàoxīng Zhīfǔ.
In the first year of Yǒnglè, he was summoned to be Xíngbù Shìláng.
He was resolute and capable,
with a strong administrative ability,
and was very strict with his subordinates.
The emperor considered him talented,
and often ordered him to handle other affairs,
so he could not always be present in the ministry.
However, if junior officials or criminals engaged in private dealings or bribery,
Qìng would always find out,
and punish them severely according to the law.
In the fifth year, he was transferred to Zǎo Fùdū Yùshǐ.
He twice experienced the loss of a parent,
and was reinstated both times.
At that time, many noble and military officials allowed their sons, younger brothers, and household members to engage in salt trading,
which harmed both officials and common people.
Qìng said:
"According to old regulations,
officials of the fourth rank and above were not permitted to compete with the common people for profit.
Now that Dūdū Cài Fú and others have already been punished,
if dukes and marquises commit such offenses,
I also request an investigation."
The emperor ordered strict prohibitions in accordance with the regulations.
Xīnchéng Bó Zhào Yí unauthorizedly killed transport laborers
and illicitly sold military provisions.
Dūdū Tán Qīng and Zhū Chóng were corrupt and unrestrained.
Qìng impeached them,
and they were all handed over to the authorities.
Afterwards,
he impeached Dūdū Fèi Huán for deception,
Liáng Míng for greed and tyranny,
and Zhènshǒu Dézhōu Dūdū Cáo Dé for venality.
All were reprimanded.
Both inside and outside the court, people held his demeanor in awe.
In the eighteenth year, he was promoted to Gōngbù Shàngshū,
and soon after concurrently managed the affairs of the Bīngbù.
Upon Rénzōng's ascension,
he was transferred to Bīngbù,
and granted the additional title of Tàizǐ Shàobǎo.
Yì Qiān, for speaking out against an imperial decree, offended the emperor,
and Lǚ Zhèn and others unanimously disparaged him.
Only Qìng and Xià Yuánjí said nothing.
The emperor soon realized his mistake,
issued an edict reproaching himself,
and also reprimanded Zhèn and the others.
Zhèn and the others were greatly ashamed before these two men.
There were many matters concerning the imperial mausoleum;
when eunuchs pressed for quick completion and made demands,
he firmly refused to comply.
Many people greatly feared and respected him,
calling him
"Lǐ the Living."
He was ordered to attend the crown prince on a visit to Xiàolíng.
On the journey, he strictly disciplined the generals and soldiers,
ensuring not even a hair was disturbed.
When the crown prince wished to hunt,
Qìng remonstrated and stopped him.
When the crown prince returned to Běijīng,
Qìng was then left in the Nánjīng Bīngbù.
In the second year of Xuāndé,
when Ānyuǎn Hóu Liǔ Shēng was to suppress Lí Lì,
Qìng was appointed to participate in military affairs,
and allowed to select capable officials from the ministry to accompany him.
When the army reached Zhènyíguān,
Shēng underestimated the enemy
and made no preparations.
Lángzhōng Shǐ Ān and Zhǔshì Chén Yōng spoke to Qìng.
By then, Qìng was already severely ill,
but he forced himself to rise and warn Shēng.
Shēng did not listen,
advanced directly,
fell into an ambush, was defeated and died.
Qìng's illness then worsened,
and he also died the next day,
the entire army was wiped out.
Shī Kuí,
courtesy name Jiǔdá,
was a native of Dōng'ē.
Orphaned young,
he served his mother with extreme filial piety.
At thirteen,
his mother fell ill
and yearned for wisteria flowers.
Kuí went out of the city, more than twenty *lǐ* to the south, and found them.
When he returned,
it was the second watch of the night,
and he encountered a tiger.
Kuí cried out to heaven in alarm,
and the tiger left him and departed.
His mother's illness soon improved.
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
as a Guózǐshēng, he followed a Censor to investigate a case,
but was impeached by the Censor
and arrested.
The emperor admired his appearance,
released him,
and demoted him to copy documents at the Yùshǐtái.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Censor,
and then transferred to Shǎnxī Ànchásǐ.
There were a thousand prisoners held for a long time;
within ten days, all were dealt with and dispatched,
each receiving their due punishment.
He resigned his office due to his mother's mourning,
lived by her tomb,
and abstained from alcohol and meat for three years.
Chéngzǔ ascended the throne,
and summoned him to be Bīngbù Shìláng,
then transferred him to Lìbù.
In the fourth year of Yǒnglè, when the palaces in Běijīng were being built,
various ministers were dispatched to procure timber.
Kuí went to Hú and Xiāng,
led a hundred thousand people into the mountains to clear roads,
summoned merchants,
and allowed soldiers to trade,
thus completing the task.
However, he was quite strict and harsh,
and the people could not endure it,
many joined Lǐ Fǎliáng in rebellion.
Zuǒ Zhōngyǔn Zhōu Gàn impeached him.
At that time, Rénzōng was supervising the state,
and since Kuí was specifically dispatched by the emperor,
the matter was left unquestioned.
In the eighth year,
when the emperor marched north,
he was ordered to oversee the transport of provisions.
Kuí requested that relay stations be set up according to the distance,
to facilitate transfer and transport.
This was approved.
Kuí assisted Jiǎn Yì in the Lìbù for twenty years,
and no one dared to approach him with personal requests.
Upon Rénzōng's succession,
he, along with Zhào Gǒng and Gǔ Pǔ, were all transferred to official positions in Nánjīng,
but Kuí was promoted to Hùbù Shàngshū,
concurrently managing the Lìbù.
He died in office in the first month of the second year of Xuāndé,
at the age of sixty-two.
Kuí was incorruptible,
did not accumulate property,
and distributed all his salary and grants to his clan members.
He had eight sons,
to the point that he could not support himself.
Chéngzǔ once said to his attendants in Běijīng:
"Among the six ministers accompanying me,
only Kuí is not corrupt."
Gǔ Pǔ,
courtesy name Wénzhì,
was a native of Chénzhōu.
During the Hóngwǔ reign, as a grand student of the Imperial Academy, he was assigned to sort out the land tax registers of the prefectures and counties.
Upon his return, he was appointed to the Five Army Commands to manage judicial and penal affairs.
He stated that his family was poor
and wished to receive a salary to support his mother.
The Emperor praised him
and appointed him as a zhǔshì in the Ministry of Works.
When his mother died,
the government provided a boat for her burial.
After the mourning period,
he was transferred to the Ministry of War
and successively promoted to lángzhōng.
In the third year of Jiànwén, he was promoted to bīngbù shìláng.
When Chéngzǔ ascended the throne,
he was transferred to the Ministry of Revenue.
In the second year of Yǒnglè,
Pǔ memorialized:
"Previously, an imperial edict ordered Jiāngxī, Húguǎng, and the prefectures of Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng to transport grain to Běijīng.
Now it is heard that they are all suffering from floods,
making transport difficult,
while the various counties of Běijīng have fortunately had a good harvest this year.
It would be appropriate to issue paper money and order the officials to purchase grain at increased prices,
reducing the burden of transport from the south."
This was approved.
During the construction of Běijīng,
he was ordered to procure timber from Jiāngxī
and was commended for his compassion towards the people.
In the seventh year,
when the Emperor went on a northern tour,
the Crown Prince supervised the state.
He was recalled
to assist Xià Yuánjí in managing the Ministry of Revenue.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
he was transferred to Nánjīng to serve as tōngzhèngshǐ.
The following year, he was appointed Hùbù Shàngshū
and dispatched to supervise land taxes within the imperial domain.
When Shī Kuí fell ill,
Pǔ was ordered to replace him.
He died in office in the second month of the third year of Xuāndé.
Originally,
Liú Liáng, a zhǔshì in the Ministry of Revenue, was undisciplined
and sought a eunuch's help to get a superior evaluation.
Pǔ refused.
Liáng then falsely accused Pǔ of a crime,
and Pǔ was arrested.
Chéngzǔ investigated and found the accusation false,
and Pǔ was released.
Another day,
the Ministry of Personnel memorialized to grant Liáng a royal patent.
Rénzōng said:
"This person has always been ill-behaved
and once falsely accused a high official;
he should not be granted it."
Liáng later indeed fell due to corruption.
Pǔ served in the court for over thirty years,
from a lángshǔ to a shàngshū.
He was steadfast in his principles,
never accepting favors or intercessions,
and, like Xiàng Bǎo, the Right Grand Censor,
was known for his integrity and uprightness.
Bǎo,
courtesy name Kèzhōng,
was a native of Jìnxián.
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
he was appointed yuánwàiláng in the Ministry of War as a jìnshì.
After nine years without fault,
he was promoted to tōngzhèngshǐ,
but he strongly declined due to his inability to make proper reports to the throne,
and was reassigned as Yìngtiān Fǔyǐn.
During the Jiànwén era,
he was demoted to Guǎngxī for an offense.
When Chéngzǔ ascended the throne,
he was recalled and reinstated.
Later,
he was again imprisoned for an offense
and demoted to salt transport judge in Liǎngzhè.
Rénzōng, while still Crown Prince,
knew of his integrity.
Upon ascending the throne,
he summoned him to be Right Grand Censor concurrently with Minister of the Crown Prince's Household,
and granted him two salaries.
Soon after, in response to an edict, he presented eight proposals,
many of which were adopted.
In the early Xuāndé period,
he was transferred to Nánjīng.
In the third year, he came for an audience.
The Emperor pitied his old age
and ordered him to retire.
He died on his way home.
Bǎo was learned,
generous, and loved the people,
while maintaining a clean and upright character.
He endured numerous hardships without wavering,
and in his daily life, never spoke of personal gain.
He served for over forty years,
and on the day he died,
his household was utterly bare.
Chén Shòu,
was a native of Suízhōu.
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
he was appointed zhǔshì in the Ministry of Revenue as a student of the Imperial Academy.
In the first year of Yǒnglè, he was promoted to yuánwàiláng.
He was sent out as Cāncè in Shāndōng,
and wherever he went, he made loving the people his duty.
Based on Xià Yuánjí's recommendation,
he was recalled to serve as Left Shìláng in the Ministry of Works.
When the Crown Prince supervised the state in Nánjīng,
Shòu daily spoke of the hardships of the soldiers and the people,
and also took the opportunity to say that many around the Prince sought favor,
fearing it would tarnish the Prince's virtue.
The Prince deeply accepted his words.
He once watched him leave,
and turning to his attendants, said:
"He is the foremost among the shìláng."
In the ninth year, due to the slander of Hán Wáng Gāo Xù,
he was imprisoned,
and was so poor he could not afford daily necessities.
When officials offered him provisions,
he refused to accept them,
and eventually died in prison.
More than a year later,
when his coffin was opened, he looked as if he were still alive.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
he was posthumously granted the title of Gōngbù Shàngshū,
with the posthumous name Mǐnsù,
and his son Cháng was appointed zhōngshū shèrén,
later also rising to Gōngbù Shìláng.
Those who were imprisoned and died with Shòu
included Mǎ Jīng and Xǔ Sīwēn.
Jīng
was a native of Wǔgōng.
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
he was appointed hànlín biānxiū as a jìnshì,
and successively served as Left Tōngzhèng and Dàlǐ Qīng.
In the first year of Yǒnglè, he became Left Shìláng of the Provisional Ministry.
When the Crown Prince guarded Běijīng,
he was ordered to concurrently assist and guide him,
dedicating himself to supporting him,
and the Prince greatly esteemed him.
He was repeatedly slandered by Gāo Xù,
exiled to serve in Guǎngxī,
and later again arrested and imprisoned
for the previous matter.
Sīwēn,
courtesy name Shúyōng,
was a native of Wúzhōu.
As a student of the Imperial Academy, he was provisionally appointed zhǔshì in the Ministry of Punishments,
and successively rose to Běipíng Ànchá Fùshǐ.
When the燕Army arose,
Sīwēn rendered meritorious service in assisting the city's defense,
and was promoted to Xíngbù Shìláng,
then transferred to the Ministry of Personnel,
concurrently serving as Zànshàn.
He was also imprisoned due to slander.
All died in prison.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
Jīng was posthumously granted the title of Shàofù,
with the posthumous name Wénjiǎn;
Sīwēn was posthumously granted Hùbù Shàngshū,
and his son Jùn was appointed Zànlǐ Láng,
and later entered the Hànlín Academy.
Liú Jìchí,
personal name Sháo,
was commonly known by his courtesy name,
and was a native of Yúyáo.
He became a jìnshì during the Hóngwǔ reign.
He was appointed xíngrén.
When dispatched to Cháoxiǎn,
he refused their gifts.
The Emperor heard of this,
bestowed clothes and paper money upon him,
and promoted him to Shǎnxī Cāncè.
In Shǎnxī, there were outstanding taxes,
and officials harshly enforced collection,
which the people could not pay.
When Jìchí arrived,
he and his colleagues traveled to various prefectures and counties,
releasing all those who had been shackled,
and granting them an extended deadline.
The people were grateful for his virtue
and paid all their taxes in full.
Shǎnxī did not produce nítre (guīshā),
yet there was an annual quota for it.
Jìchí reported this to the court,
and the quota was abolished.
When the Hóng Canal overflowed,
he managed to build a weir to store and release water,
which then became a permanent benefit.
During the Jiànwén reign,
he was summoned to be an Assistant Minister of the Ministry of Justice (Xíngbù Shìláng).
There was a commoner implicated by a bandit.
When he was arrested and brought in,
the bandit had already died.
So he summoned the bandit's wife and children to identify him.
After hearing their testimony,
it was a false accusation,
and he released the commoner.
An official embezzled public funds
and falsely implicated over a thousand people.
He exonerated them all.
In Héyáng, two men, Zhū and Zhào, were staying in different rooms at an inn.
Zhào was murdered,
and the authorities suspected Zhū of the murder.
They tortured him until he falsely confessed.
Jì Chí alone said,
"This is not an old enmity,
and there was nothing valuable among his belongings."
He delayed the case,
and eventually the real killer of Zhào was found.
In a commoner's house in Yángzhōu,
a thief entered at night and committed murder,
leaving a knife by the corpse.
The knife had a distinctive mark,
and it belonged to a neighbor.
Officials arrested and interrogated the neighbor.
The neighbor said,
"I lost this knife a long time ago."
Unable to endure the torture,
he falsely confessed.
Jì Chí sent someone to carry the knife into the village and subtly observe.
A young boy recognized it and said,
"This is our family's item."
The thief was then apprehended.
In the early Yǒnglè reign,
when the Great Canon (Dàdiǎn) was being compiled,
Yáo Guăngxiào, Xiè Jìn, and Jì Chí were ordered to oversee the project.
In the eighth year, he was imprisoned for a dereliction of duty
and banished to an outside post.
He hesitated and did not go,
and was imprisoned again.
After a long time, he was finally released.
He was ordered to serve as a compiler in the Hànlín Yuàn in scholar's attire.
Soon after, he was appointed Principal of the Ministry of Works (Gōngbù Zhǔshì)
and died in office.
Liú Chén,
courtesy name Bójìng,
was from Jīnhuá.
In the early days of the dynasty,
he was provisionally appointed to serve Fāng Guózhēn as a document clerk (diănqiān).
Fāng Guózhēn adorned two courtesans to present to him,
but he shouted at them to leave.
Lǐ Wénzhōng stationed his army in Yánzhōu
and invited Liú Chén to join his staff.
Marshal Gě Jùn, defending Guăngxìn,
ordered commoners to dredge the city moat in the dead of winter.
Lǐ Wénzhōng tried to stop him.
Gě Jùn refused to listen.
Lǐ Wénzhōng was enraged
and intended to confront him with troops.
Liú Chén requested to go and persuade him.
Gě Jùn repented and apologized,
and the matter was settled.
Due to his aging parents, he resigned and returned home.
During the Jiànwén reign,
he was recommended and promoted to Censor (Jiānchá Yùshǐ),
and then sent out to govern Zhènjiāng Prefecture.
He was diligent in his duties.
Over eighty qīng (mou) of riverside land,
long submerged,
were still taxed as before.
Thanks to Liú Chén's words, the tax was abolished.
The gate at Jīngkǒu was dilapidated,
forcing grain transporters to use a new canal to reach the river,
and many boats were wrecked.
Liú Chén repaired the old gate,
benefiting both public and private interests.
The grain transport canal was prone to drying up,
relying on Lìanhú Lake for water,
but the Sāndòu Gate had long been in disuse.
Liú Chén repaired and rebuilt it.
Once transport boats could pass through,
the fields below the lake became more productive.
In the early Yǒnglè reign,
Lǐ Jǐnglóng stated that Liú Chén was knowledgeable about events from the early dynasty,
so he was summoned
to participate in compiling the Veritable Records of Tàizǔ (Tàizǔ Shílù).
He was promoted to Administration Commissioner of Jiāngxī (Jiāngxī Bùzhèngsī Cāncè),
and memorialized to exempt taxes on barren land in nine prefectures.
In a year of famine,
he encouraged wealthy commoners to lend to the hungry,
and exempted their corvée labor as interest.
Officials would issue promissory notes,
to be repaid within a year.
Liú Chén was upright, diligent, and spirited in office.
He was at odds with the Regional Military Commissioner (Dū Sī) and Surveillance Commissioner (Ànchásǐ),
often quarreling,
and was dismissed from office.
In the fourteenth year, he was reinstated as Assistant Minister of War (Xíngbù Zuǒ Shìláng),
but remained in Nánjīng for three more years.
The Emperor, considering his old age,
bestowed an imperial edict and currency,
ordering him to retire.
He died on the journey,
aged seventy-eight.
Yáng Dǐ,
courtesy name Dàyòng,
was from Zézhōu.
At the end of the Hóngwǔ reign,
he was appointed Assistant Director of the Bureau of Diplomatic Messengers (Xíngrén Sī Yòusīfù) after passing the civil service examination.
He submitted a memorial stating:
"Yáng Xióng served Wáng Măng as a Grandee (Dàfū),
leaving a stain for ten thousand generations.
Dǒng Zhòngshū's 'Three Strategies on Heaven and Man' (Tiānrén Sāncè) and his words on 'rectifying righteousness and clarifying the Way' (zhèngyì míngdào)
are sufficient to support and assist worldly teachings.
Now, among those enshrined in the Temple of Confucius (Kǒngmiào), there is Yáng Xióng but no Dǒng Zhòngshū;
this is not right."
The Emperor agreed.
He successively served as Consultative Official of the Húguăng Provincial Administration Commission (Húguăng Bùzhèngsī Cānyì).
During the Jiànwén reign,
he stated:
"The virtue of Emperor Yáo began with cherishing the nine clans.
Now, it is appropriate to strengthen harmony among the various princely states
and not to prune one's own branches and leaves."
This was not reported.
He returned home for his father's mourning.
When Chéngzǔ ascended the throne,
he was reinstated as Minister of the Court of State Ceremonials (Hónglú Sì Qīng),
but begged to complete his mourning period.
After the mourning period ended,
he was promoted to Assistant Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shìláng).
For failing to attend to his duties regarding canals,
he was demoted to Principal of the Ministry of Works (Gōngbù Zhǔshì),
and then reassigned to the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù).
In the tenth year of Yǒnglè, he was transferred to serve as Acting Minister of the Grand Court of the Imperial Stud in Běijīng (Běijīng Xíng Tàipú Sì Qīng).
At that time, there was a great flood from Wúqiáo to Tiānjīn, which breached dikes and damaged crops.
Yáng Dǐ requested to open the old course of the Yellow River (Huánghé) southeast of Dézhōu and the Tǔhé River to reduce the water's force.
The Emperor ordered Assistant Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shìláng) Lìn Fāng to manage this.
He established regulations for horse husbandry,
requesting that commoners with five adult males raise one breeding horse,
ten horses be assigned one group leader,
fifty horses be assigned one herd chief,
and families raising horses be exempted from half their annual rent and grain taxes.
And in the various garrisons from Jìzhōu eastward to Shānhǎi,
where the land was vast
and water and grass abundant,
military colonists raising one breeding horse
would also be exempted from half their taxes.
The Emperor ordered that all military taxes be exempted,
and the rest followed his proposal.
Consequently, horses multiplied greatly.
Yáng Dǐ was upright, resolute, and steadfast,
and especially devoted to filial piety.
In the sixteenth year,
he was grief-stricken by his mother's death,
and died before reaching home.
Yú Qiān,
courtesy name Bóyì,
was from Jīntán.
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
he was promoted from a student of the National Academy (Guózǐshēng) to Director of the Ministry of Justice (Xíngbù Lángzhōng),
and then sent out to govern Hángzhōu Prefecture.
During the Jiànwén reign, he requested to limit the land holdings of monks and Daoists,
no more than ten mù per person,
with the remainder to be equally distributed among the poor.
This was adopted.
In the early Yǒnglè reign, he was summoned to be Vice Minister of the Grand Court of Judicial Review (Dàlǐ Sì Shàonqīng).
At that time, an edict was issued,
stating that all who had memorialized to change old systems during the Jiànwén reign should present themselves in person.
Yú Qiān then spoke of his previous actions and requested punishment.
The Emperor saw Yú Qiān's fear
and smiled, saying,
"This scholar merely attacked the old and Buddha."
He was released without questioning.
However, the regulation limiting land for monks and Daoists was ultimately abolished.
The Censorate (Dūcháyùan) judged fraud and deception crimes,
according to the Hóngwǔ edict, to be punished by decapitation and public display.
Yú Qiān memorialized:
"Recently, an edict was received to judge crimes according to the law;
fraud and deception should be punished by caning and exile.
Decapitation is not the intent of the edict."
The Emperor agreed.
A fire broke out in the Tiānjīn Garrison granary,
burning hundreds of thousands of shí of grain.
The Censor (Yùshǐ) stated that the responsible officials had embezzled a large amount
and deliberately set the fire to cover it up.
Nearly eight hundred people were arrested,
and a hundred were to be executed.
Yú Qiān argued against the excessive punishment,
and the sentences were reduced.
In the seventh year,
the emperor traveled north.
The crown prince memorialized for Yú Qiān to be made Right Vice Censor-in-Chief.
The following year, along with Supervising Censor Dù Qīn, he toured Huái and Fèng, arriving at Chénzhōu, which was afflicted by disaster.
He remitted land taxes
and redeemed children sold by the people.
The following year,
Qiān requested relief funds.
The crown prince admonished him, saying:
"The army and the people are in extreme distress,
yet you all leisurely request [relief] at your convenience.
What kind of person was Jí Àn?"
Soon after, he was ordered to supervise the transport of grain from the prefectures of Liǎngzhè and Sū-Sōng,
to be shipped to Nánjīng, Běijīng, Xúzhōu, and Huái'ān.
Wealthy citizens bribed officials
and were generally assigned nearby destinations,
while poor citizens often had to transport over long distances.
Qiān suggested dividing them into four grades: those with many adult males (dīng) but the least grain would transport to Běijīng;
the next least would transport to Xúzhōu;
those with equal dīng and grain would transport to Nánjīng and Huái'ān;
and those with few dīng but much grain would keep it in their local area.
The people benefited greatly from this.
He also said: "At the two dikes of Xúzhōu and Lǚliáng,
boat travel is often obstructed.
I request that each dike be augmented with two hundred additional trackers,
who will be given monthly stipends,
and one hundred government oxen.
In their leisure time, the people may use them for plowing,
and when large boats arrive,
they can be used for tracking."
People considered this convenient.
He once supervised timber transportation,
and the laborers suffered a severe plague.
Qiān ordered them to be dispersed,
and the plague then ceased.
Before long,
he, along with Supervising Censor Xǔ Néng, was appointed Pacification Commissioner of Zhèjiāng.
Upon Rénzōng's accession, he was recalled
and made Grand Judge of the Grand Court of Judicial Review (Dàlǐ Sì Qīng).
At that time, Lǚ Shēng was Vice Grand Judge,
Yǎng Zhān was Assistant Grand Judge,
and Qiān further recommended Yán Běn as Principal Judge.
The emperor was particularly cautious about criminal justice,
and Qiān and others also meticulously handled memorials on the matter.
For all cases submitted by the judicial offices and from various regions,
Qiān and his colleagues repeatedly reviewed and reconsidered them,
always seeking fairness.
He once told people:
"If they have no regrets,
then I too will have no regrets."
He once responded to an imperial decree by submitting seven suggestions,
all of which were pertinent to current affairs.
Some claimed he was not discreet in reporting matters
and sought public favor.
The emperor was angered
and demoted him to Vice Grand Judge.
One day,
Yáng Shìqí, having finished his report,
did not withdraw.
The emperor asked:
"What do you wish to say?
Is it perhaps about Yú Qiān?"
Shìqí then fully explained the slander
and also stated that Qiān had served three reigns
and possessed the bearing of a high minister.
The emperor said:
"I also regret it."
He then ordered his reinstatement.
When Xuānzōng ascended the throne,
Qiān said:
"According to the old system,
those who committed capital offenses
were sentenced to lifelong penal servitude.
Now, the offenses are not all equal;
it is appropriate to divide the term lengths according to their severity."
This was approved.
In the third month of Xuāndé second year (1427), he died in office.
Qiān had a handsome appearance
and a dignified demeanor.
He was skilled in poetry and painting,
and proud of his talent and reputation.
When Sū Zàn, Vice Minister of Works, who was vulgar and crude, was ranked above Qiān,
Qiān was discontented,
and people considered this a sign of his narrow-mindedness.
Lǚ Shēng,
a native of Shānyīn,
was appointed Instructor of Lìyáng in the early Yǒnglè reign.
He successively served as Surveillance Commissioner of Jiāngxī and Fújiàn,
and earned a reputation for integrity and prudence wherever he went.
He entered court as Vice Grand Judge of the Grand Court of Judicial Review.
He retired and died in Xuāndé eighth year.
Yǎng Zhān,
a native of Chángzhōu.
During the Yǒnglè reign, he was promoted from Judicial Officer of the Hǔbēn Guard to Assistant Grand Judge of the Grand Court of Judicial Review.
During the Zhèngtǒng reign,
the eunuch Wáng Zhèn wielded power,
and most officials flocked to his gate;
only Zhān and Grand Judge Xuē Xuān did not.
It happened that he and Xuān argued over a wrongful case of a murdered husband,
which further offended Zhèn.
He was imprisoned
and banished to garrison duty in Dàtóng.
In the early Jǐngtài reign,
he was recalled as Right Assistant Grand Judge,
and became even firmer in upholding the law,
which displeased many in power.
He feigned illness and returned home,
and was promoted to Vice Grand Judge of the Grand Court of Judicial Review.
Yán Běn,
courtesy name Zhìdào,
a native of Jiāngyīn.
In his youth, he was proficient in many texts
and well-versed in law.
Because Fù Lín's "Xíngtǒng" (Compendium of Punishments) had concise rhetoric and broad meaning,
and more than one commentator,
he compiled the "Jíyì" (Collected Meanings) in four volumes.
In Yǒnglè eleventh year, he was summoned on recommendation
and tested with difficult legal cases,
which he analyzed with clarity and fluency.
He was appointed Principal Secretary in the Ministry of Justice.
Vice Minister Zhāng Běn, who was in charge of the ministry,
was rarely satisfied with officials,
but he alone held Běn in high regard,
and often entrusted him with questioning in difficult cases.
He was sent on a mission to Huīzhōu,
at a time when those who supervised work and fell behind schedule
were routinely fined.
Běn could not bear to pressure the people.
Someone mentioned this,
and Běn said:
"I have handled it."
He had already written to his son
to sell land to pay for the work.
Upon Rénzōng's accession,
on the recommendation of Minister of Justice Jīn Chún and Yú Qiān,
he was made Principal Judge of the Grand Court of Judicial Review.
Judges often sentenced cases
with "knowing the circumstances and deliberately releasing"
or
"great disrespect"
as the basis for conviction.
Běn argued:
"Aside from a few articles concerning rebellion,
the law has no text
of 'deliberately releasing.'
Even for 'disrespect,'
the circumstances vary in severity;
how can they all be categorized as serious?"
Qiān approved of this
and corrected all such rulings.
A citizen of Liángxiāng lost his horse,
suspected his neighbor,
reported it to the Assistant Judge,
who tortured the neighbor to death.
The Assistant Judge was charged with judging and punishing contrary to law,
and was to be sentenced to penal servitude,
while the accuser was charged with slander.
Běn said:
"The Assistant Judge's crime is established.
But the accuser sued out of suspicion.
If the law considers false accusation leading to death [as the crime],
then the Assistant Judge and the accuser each killed one person.
Is this proper?"
He overruled and corrected it.
A garrison soldier in Jǔxiàn seized a citizen's land.
The citizen sued the official,
and the soldier was flogged.
At night, the soldier stole the citizen's donkey.
The citizen found it,
and the soldier, in turn, accused the citizen of false accusation,
seizing and sending him to the Chiliarch,
and the citizen was detained until death.
The judicial office sentenced the Chiliarch to penal servitude.
Běn said:
"If the Chiliarch lives,
then the deceased's injustice remains."
He then correctly determined the original crime and guilt.
More than ten soldiers from Sūzhōu Guard robbed a passenger boat at Héxīwù at night,
and one soldier died.
Fearing discovery,
they falsely accused a neighboring boat of being robbers who released prisoners,
and when their companions went to rescue them, they were killed.
All confessed under false pretenses.
Běn suspected it, saying:
"Those who released people were on the same boat as the prisoners.
If they were robbers, the prisoners would surely know."
Upon investigation and verification,
the truth was indeed discovered,
and the soldiers were convicted.
Běn was upright and severe in his conduct,
never acting improperly.
When he was sent to Huīzhōu,
he even refused wine and food offered by the prefect.
He died at the age of seventy-eight.
Tāng Zōng,
courtesy name Zhèngchuán,
was from Píngyáng, Zhèjiāng.
At the end of the Hóngwǔ reign,
from a Grand Student, he was promoted to Assistant Surveillance Commissioner of Hénán,
then transferred to Běipíng.
During the Jiànwén reign, he reported a matter,
stating that Surveillance Commissioner Chén Yīng had received money from the Yān principality
and harbored rebellious intentions.
An imperial edict ordered Chén Yīng's arrest,
and he was placed in Guǎngxī,
while Tāng Zōng was transferred to be Surveillance Commissioner of Shāndōng.
For an offense,
he was demoted to Director in the Ministry of Justice,
and then sent out to govern Sūzhōu Prefecture.
Sūzhōu suffered floods for successive years,
the people were displaced,
and overdue rent amounted to over a million dàn of grain.
Tāng Zōng instructed wealthy citizens to provide rice to pay on behalf of others.
The wealthy citizens, knowing his love for the people,
paid all within three months.
In the first year of Yǒnglè, there were accusations that he had ignored the suffering caused by the floods.
He was arrested and imprisoned,
then demoted to Judicial Commissioner of Lùzhōu.
Through Huáng Huái's recommendation,
he was recalled to be Vice Minister of the Grand Court of Revision.
Someone mentioned that Tāng Zōng had previously exposed matters concerning the latent principality.
The emperor said:
"An emperor employs only the talented;
why discuss old grievances?"
At that time, a foreign envoy died of illness,
and his entourage accused a physician of murder.
When the case was prepared,
Tāng Zōng read the documents and sighed:
"What enmity did the physician have with the envoy,
that he would deliberately kill him?"
He eventually proved him innocent.
Soon after, he was ordered to relieve famine in Hénán,
and upon return, he was put in charge of the Ministry of Revenue.
Xiè Jìn was imprisoned,
and Tāng Zōng was implicated in the charges,
leading to his imprisonment for over ten years.
Upon Rénzōng's ascension,
he was reinstated to office,
and again promoted to Grand Minister of the Grand Court of Revision in Nánjīng.
At the beginning of Xuānzōng's reign,
he was tasked with inspecting the military in Shāndōng.
As there had been no rain for a long time,
he strongly presented the dire conditions of hunger among the people.
The emperor, for this, remitted taxes and exempted corvée labor,
and suspended non-urgent tasks.
He died in the second year of Xuāndé.
The eulogy says: During the Yǒnglè and Xuāndé reigns,
official administration was strictly disciplined and enforced,
and duties were well performed.
Figures like Yù Xīn in managing taxation,
Yáng Dǐ in horse administration,
and Liú Jìchí and Yú Qiān in judicial affairs
can be said to have excelled in their offices.
Lǐ Qìng, Shī Kuí and others
were upright and principled,
all excellent among the high ministers.
Chén Shòu and Mǎ Jīng were slandered and ruined early,
it is a pity their talents were not fully utilized.
Jīn Zhōng rose from the ranks of soldiers,
advancing from a background in minor arts,
yet possessed the conduct of a scholar-gentleman.
When he held firm arguments between Emperor Wén and his son,
loyal and unyielding,
he ultimately moved the sovereign with sincerity and trustworthiness—
how not great!
Collational Notes
Biographies Volume Thirty-Nine Rú Cháng, Yán Zhènzhí, Zhāng Dǎn (Máo Tàihēng), Wáng Dùn, Zhèng Cì, Guō Zī, Lǚ Zhèn, Lǐ Zhìgāng, Fāng Bīn, Wú Zhōng, Liú Guān
Rú Cháng,
was from Héngshān.
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
from a National University student, he was appointed Palace Usher,
and successively served as Commissioner of the Office of Transmission.
Diligent in his duties,
Tàizǔ esteemed him.
In the twenty-third year, he was appointed Right Vice Censor-in-Chief,
then provisionally served as Minister of War,
and soon after was formally appointed,
and granted the title of Junior Guardian of the Crown Prince.
When Emperor Huì ascended the throne,
he was transferred to the Ministry of Personnel,
and was at odds with Huáng Zǐchéng.
Minister of Justice Bào Zhāo exposed his corrupt practices,
and he was sent to manage the affairs of the Hénán Provincial Administration Commission.
Soon after, he was recalled to be Minister of War.
When the Yān forces reached Lóngtán,
the emperor dispatched Rú Cháng, along with Duke Cáo Lǐ Jǐnglóng and Grand Coordinator Wáng Zuǒ, to the Yān army to negotiate peace.
Rú Cháng and the others met Chéngzǔ,
prostrated themselves on the ground, sweating,
unable to utter a single word.
Chéngzǔ said:
"You gentlemen should simply speak if you have something to say,
why are you so afraid?"
After a long while, they said they had been commanded to cede territory and make peace.
Chéngzǔ laughed and said:
"I am innocent yet was reduced to a commoner;
now that I am saving my life,
what use is land to me!
Moreover, the Imperial Grandfather enfeoffed his sons,
and each already has their allotted territory.
Bring the treacherous ministers here,
and I will immediately disarm, visit Xiàolíng, and return to my fiefdom."
Rú Cháng and the others merely bowed and returned.
When Chéngzǔ entered the capital,
he summoned Rú Cháng.
Rú Cháng was the first to urge his ascension.
After Chéngzǔ ascended the throne,
he issued an edict stating that Lǐ Jǐnglóng, Rú Cháng, Wáng Zuǒ, and Chén Xuān had served Tàizǔ loyally,
and their merits were very great.
He enfeoffed Rú Cháng as the Earl of Zhōngchéng,
with a stipend of one thousand dàn of grain,
for life.
He retained the posts of Minister of War and Junior Guardian of the Crown Prince.
His son, Jiàn, was selected to be the ceremonial consort for the Princess of Cháng'ān in the Qín principality.
He immediately ordered Rú Cháng to oversee the construction of the princess's mansion.
Upon his return to court,
he was implicated for not seeing off the Prince of Zhào,
and was sent back to his hometown.
Soon after, he was sued by a family member,
arrested and brought to the capital,
then released and returned.
Passing through Chángshā, he did not visit the Prince of Gǔ,
and the prince complained about it.
At that time, the rites for princely vassals were highly regarded,
and the Prince of Gǔ had also contributed to opening the Jīnchuān Gate,
so the emperor favored him.
Chén Yīng then impeached Rú Cháng for violating ancestral regulations,
and he was arrested and imprisoned in the Imperial Guard's prison.
Knowing he could not escape,
Rú Cháng ordered his son, Quán, to buy poison,
which he took and died.
This was in the second month of the seventh year of Yǒnglè.
The judicial authorities impeached Quán for poisoning his father,
requesting he be sentenced as for patricide.
Later, as Quán had indeed followed his father's command,
his sentence was commuted from death,
and he, along with twenty-seven family members, including his brothers, were exiled to Héchí in Guǎngxī.
Upon Rénzōng's ascension,
they were released and returned.
Xuānzōng restored their confiscated fields and residences.
Rú Cháng was cautious in office,
modest, gentle, and tolerant.
At his death,
people deeply lamented him.
Yán Zhènzhí,
courtesy name Zǐmǐn,
was from Wūchéng.
During the Hóngwǔ reign, as a wealthy citizen chosen to be a grain overseer,
he transported ten thousand dàn of grain to the capital annually,
without delay,
and the emperor appreciated his talent.
In the twenty-third year, he was specially appointed Counselor of the Office of Transmission,
then promoted twice to Vice Minister of Works.
In the sixth month of the twenty-sixth year, he was promoted to Minister.
At that time, the court was undertaking construction projects,
gathering over two hundred thousand artisans from across the empire in the capital.
Yán Zhènzhí requested that for each household, one person be designated for corvée,
their name and profession recorded by the government,
and when service was needed, they would be summoned in rotation according to the registry,
which the laborers found convenient.
When villagers accused his younger brother and nephew of illegal acts,
the emperor handed the case to Yán Zhènzhí for investigation.
He submitted the complete case,
and the emperor, believing him to be truthful,
pardoned his younger brother and nephew.
Later,
he was demoted to Censor for an offense,
and repeatedly redressed wrongful convictions.
In the twenty-eighth year, when Lóngzhōu was being pacified,
Yán Zhènzhí was sent with Minister Rèn Hēngtài to issue a proclamation of peace to Ānnán.
Upon his return,
he presented a memorial on advantages and disadvantages,
which pleased the emperor.
Soon after, he was ordered to repair the Língqú Canal in Xīng'ān County, Guǎngxī.
He surveyed the terrain,
guided the Xiāng and Lí rivers,
dredged the canal for over five thousand zhàng,
built earthen dikes at Měitán and Lóngmǔ Cí for over one hundred and fifty zhàng,
and also heightened the central stone dike,
built thirty-six sluice gates,
and cleared away rocks obstructing boats,
making all transport by canal accessible.
Upon his return and report,
the emperor praised him.
In the second month of the thirtieth year, a memorial was submitted, stating:
"Guǎngdōng formerly transported over 850,000 *yǐn* of salt to Guǎngxī,
where merchants were invited to buy it.
Now, the amount transported throughout the year
is barely one-tenth of that.
I request that over 308,000 *yǐn* be stored in Guǎngdōng,
and that other merchants be recruited to transport grain to the grain-deficient garrisons in Guǎngxī,
distribute salt in Guǎngdōng,
and sell it conveniently in the four prefectures of Nán'ān, Gànzhōu, Jí'ān, and Línjiāng in Jiāngxī."
The emperor approved it.
The circulation of Guǎngdōng salt in Jiāngxī began from this time.
In the fourth month of that year, he was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief,
and soon after, he was reinstated as Minister of Works.
During the Jiànwén reign,
he once supervised grain transport in Shāndōng,
and then retired.
When Chéngzǔ ascended the throne,
he was summoned for an audience,
and ordered to inspect Shānxī with his former office.
When he reached Zézhōu,
he died of illness.
Zhāng Dǎn,
whose courtesy name was Zhāo Jì,
was a native of Fùpíng.
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
he was selected as a *míngjīng*.
He served as a copyist for the Crown Prince,
and was successively promoted to Provisional Left Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
In the fifteenth year,
Yúnnán was pacified,
and he was appointed Left Vice Administrator.
When he bade farewell at court,
the emperor composed two poems and bestowed them upon him.
He successively held the post of Left Provincial Administration Commissioner.
In the spring of the twentieth year, he came for an audience.
His administrative conduct was considered the best in the realm,
and the Ministry of Personnel was specifically ordered not to conduct an assessment.
The emperor bestowed an imperial letter, which read:
"Formerly, when the southwest was pacified,
officials were appointed to govern and guard it.
You, Dǎn, were indeed the first to go,
and it has been five years now.
The various barbarians are obedient,
and sincerity and trust are mutually maintained.
You have diligently performed your duties,
and without assessment, I know that your merits surpass those of the twelve regional administrators.
Therefore, I commend your achievements,
and order you to continue governing Diānnán.
Go forth,
and be reverent!"
Dǎn served in Yúnnán for seventeen years in total,
and all matters of land tribute, taxation, laws, and regulations were decided by him.
There were established customs for funerals, sacrifices, capping ceremonies, and weddings among the people,
as he strove to change their old ways.
The people of Yúnnán followed and adopted them.
Court officials Dǒng Lún and Wáng Jǐng and their like, who were banished to that region,
were all received by him with courtesy and respect.
When Huìdì ascended the throne,
he was summoned to be Minister of Personnel.
An edict called for reclusive scholars to gather at the capital.
Those Dǎn selected and employed
all proved to be suitable for their talents.
During the compilation of the *Tàizǔ Shílù*,
he was ordered to provisionally serve as a Hanlin compiler.
Dǎn recommended Yáng Shìqí as the top candidate.
Shìqí became known from this.
When Chéngzǔ entered Jīngshī,
he listed twenty-nine treacherous ministers of the central court,
and Dǎn was among them.
Based on Rú Cháng's recommendation,
he was pardoned and retained his former office.
Not long after,
the emperor sighed during a court session,
blaming those who had changed the official system during the Jiànwén era.
He then ordered Dǎn and Hùbù Shàngshū Wáng Dùn to resign their duties,
receive half their salary monthly,
and reside in Jīngshī.
Dǎn, in fear,
hanged himself in the rear hall of the Ministry of Personnel;
his wife and children followed suit by throwing themselves into a pond and dying.
While Dǎn was at the Ministry of Personnel,
he presided over the change in the official system.
A minor official, Zhāng Zǔ, said:
"Emperor Gāo established laws and initiated institutions,
with a very far-reaching vision.
Changing them now
may not necessarily be better,
but merely invite criticism.
I wish, my lord, that you would firmly uphold them."
Dǎn could not adopt this advice,
but he inwardly admired Zǔ,
and memorialized to have him appointed as a Steward of the Capital Guard.
After Dǎn's death,
none of his subordinates dared to attend to his affairs,
only Zǔ managed his funeral.
It is traditionally said that when the Yān army entered the capital,
Dǎn immediately hanged himself;
and that when Yán Zhènzhí was sent on a mission to Yúnnán,
he met the Jiànwén Emperor, became heartbroken, and swallowed gold to die.
Upon examination of the national histories,
these are not the facts.
At that time, there was a Máo Tàihēng,
who was Minister of Personnel Vice Minister during the Jiànwén era,
and worked with Dǎn.
When Dǎn died,
Tàihēng also died.
Wáng Dùn,
whose courtesy name was Shìlǔ,
was a native of Tàikāng.
At the end of the Yuán dynasty, he was the Magistrate of Yīshì County.
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
he was summoned and appointed Principal of the Ministry of Rites,
and successively served as Vice Administrator of Fújiàn,
known for his honesty and prudence.
When sent to convey an imperial decree to Lùchuān,
he refused their gifts.
Someone said:
"If you do not accept them,
the distant people might become suspicious and disloyal."
Dùn then accepted them,
and upon returning to Yúnnán,
he deposited them in the official treasury.
In the twenty-third year, he was promoted to Left Provincial Administration Commissioner of Zhèjiāng.
He served in Zhèjiāng for ten years,
and his reputation was equal to Zhāng Dǎn's.
The emperor once praised him at court,
to encourage other officials.
At the beginning of the Jiànwén reign,
he was appointed Minister of Revenue.
When Chéngzǔ entered,
he fled over the city wall,
and was captured by patrol soldiers.
An edict reinstated him to his former office.
Not long after,
he and Dǎn were both dismissed.
Soon after, he was ordered, along with Minister of Works Yán Zhènzhí and others, to separately inspect Shānxī, Hénán, Shǎnxī, and Shāndōng,
and also, with Xīnchāng Bó Táng Yún, to manage military agricultural settlements in Běipíng.
He again submitted memorials on affairs in response to imperial mandates,
all of which were approved and implemented.
In the fourth month of the second year of Yǒnglè, he was granted an imperial edict to retire as Provincial Administration Commissioner.
After returning,
he died of melancholy.
His son, Yuè,
became a *jìnshì* in the fourth year of Yǒnglè.
During Rénzōng's reign, he was promoted to Left Chief Clerk of the Prince of Zhèng's establishment,
and repeatedly admonished the prince with propriety.
He once emulated Xún Qīng's *Chéng Xiāng Piān*,
and composed twelve chapters as a presentation.
His words were direct,
which did not sit well with the prince.
He was summoned and reassigned as a Director in the Ministry of Revenue.
When Yīngzōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Right Vice Minister of Revenue,
and served as Grand Coordinator of Zhèjiāng,
where he implemented benevolent policies.
After his mother's mourning period, he was reinstated to office and
came for an audience,
and was kept to provisionally manage ministry affairs.
Soon after, he requested to retire due to old age,
and then died.
Zhèng Cì,
courtesy name Yànjiā,
was from Jiànníng.
In the 18th year of Hóngwǔ, he became a *jìnshì*.
He was appointed Censor.
At that time, many county and prefectural officials throughout the realm were convicted of crimes and banished to frontier garrisons.
Zhèng Cì was once ordered to organize these ranks at Lóngjiāng.
It was summer,
and the prisoners were extremely fatigued.
Zhèng Cì released their shackles,
allowed them to rent lodgings to rest,
provided them with food and drink,
and gave medicine to the sick.
Many lives were saved.
When his term expired, he was due for promotion.
There was a vacancy for Counsel to the Administration Commission of Húguǎng.
Zhèng Cì and Compiler Wú Wén were appointed to it.
The two worked together to eradicate abuses,
and the people lived in peace and order.
The Miáo and Liáo people revered them.
Upon his mother's death,
he resigned.
After the mourning period,
he was reassigned as Counsel of Běipíng,
serving Chéngzǔ with great diligence.
Later, he was again implicated and banished to garrison duty at Āndōng Tún.
When Emperor Huì ascended the throne,
Chéngzǔ and Prince Zhēn of Chǔ both recommended Zhèng Cì to be Chief Administrator.
The Emperor did not permit it,
but summoned him to be Minister of Works.
When the Yān army rose,
he was ordered to command the Hénán army to block Yān.
When Chéngzǔ entered the capital,
Lǐ Jǐnglóng impeached Zhèng Cì, accusing him of crimes as serious as those of Qí and Huáng.
When he was brought in,
the Emperor said:
"How have I treated you,
that you should turn your back on me?"
Zhèng Cì replied:
"I merely fulfilled my duty as a subject."
The Emperor smiled and released him,
appointing him Minister of Justice.
In the 1st year of Yǒnglè, he impeached Grand Commissioner Sūn Yuè for unauthorized demolition of a temple built by Tàizǔ.
An imperial edict ordered Sūn Yuè to be relocated to Hǎinán.
Sūn Yuè,
who guarded Fèngyáng during the Jiànwén reign,
had previously demolished temple materials
to repair warships to resist the Yān army.
The Yān army, knowing of his preparations,
took another route south.
Thus, Zhèng Cì impeached him.
In the 2nd year, he impeached Lǐ Jǐnglóng for secretly harboring fugitives
and plotting rebellion.
He also, with Chén Yīng, impeached Gěng Bǐngwén for extravagance and presumption.
Gěng Bǐngwén hanged himself.
In all these cases, he anticipated the Emperor's dislikes.
Kāng Kǒnggāo, a teaching official from Qíyáng, returned to the capital after an imperial audience.
He deviated from his route to visit his mother.
His mother happened to be ill,
so he stayed to attend to her for nine months without leaving.
Zhèng Cì requested Kāng Kǒnggāo's arrest and interrogation.
His crime was punishable by caning.
The Emperor said:
"Mother and son have been separated for several years.
It is difficult to leave immediately once they meet,
especially when she is ill.
He is to be pitied."
He ordered his official position restored.
In the autumn of the 3rd year,
he replaced Lǐ Zhìgāng as Minister of Rites.
In the 1st month of the 4th year,
the Western Regions presented Buddhist relics as tribute.
Zhèng Cì then requested the release of prisoners.
The Emperor said:
"Emperor Wǔ of Liáng and Emperor Shùn of Yuán indulged in Buddhism.
They did not punish offenders,
and the state's discipline greatly deteriorated.
How can this be emulated!"
On the 1st day of the 6th month of that year,
there was to be a solar eclipse.
Dark clouds obscured it from view.
Zhèng Cì requested to offer congratulations.
The Emperor did not permit it.
Zhèng Cì stated
that "the Sòng dynasty had done so during its prosperous period."
The Emperor said:
"The world is vast.
If it is not seen in the capital,
what if it is seen elsewhere in the world?"
Ultimately, he did not permit it.
Zhèng Cì was rather gentle and magnanimous,
but he lacked a sense of overall strategy.
The Emperor held him in low esteem.
He was slandered by his colleague Zhào Hóng,
and died in the 6th month of the 6th year from anxiety and fright.
The Emperor suspected he had committed suicide.
Yáng Shìqí said:
"Zhèng Cì had been ill for several days,
and was too terrified to request to step down.
Yesterday, standing at the Yòushùnmén,
he collapsed to the ground from weakness,
breathing out but not in."
Before he finished speaking,
the Emperor said:
"Without your words,
I would have wrongly suspected Zhèng Cì.
Zhèng Cì was indeed a good man,
just lacking in talent."
He ordered a funeral and sacrifice for him.
In the 1st year of Hóngxī, he was posthumously granted Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
and given the posthumous title Wén'ān.
Guō Zī,
was from Wǔ'ān.
In the 18th year of Hóngwǔ, he became a *jìnshì*.
He successively served as Left Administration Commissioner of Běipíng,
secretly aligning himself with Chéngzǔ.
When the army rose,
Zhāng Bǐng and others died.
Guō Zī, along with Left Policy Adviser Sūn Yú, Vice Commissioner of the Surveillance Bureau Mò Lín, and Reviewer Lǚ Zhèn, were among the first to surrender,
shouting "Long live!"
Chéngzǔ was pleased,
and ordered them to assist the Heir Apparent in guarding the capital.
Chéngzǔ fought battles for three years,
and Guō Zī was responsible for supplying military provisions.
When Chéngzǔ ascended the throne,
Guō Zī was made Minister of Revenue,
and was in charge of the Běipíng Administration Commission.
When Běijīng was established,
he was transferred to Minister of the Executive Department,
overseeing the six ministries.
When the capital was finalized,
he was again transferred back to the Ministry of Revenue.
At that time, building city walls and palaces,
appointing officials, and launching northern expeditions beyond the frontier,
meant a multitude of construction projects and tasks.
Guō Zī fulfilled his duties without neglecting any.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
due to his long service, he was additionally granted Tutor to the Heir Apparent.
Soon after, due to old age and illness,
he was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent,
