and granted an imperial edict to retire.
In the 4th year of Xuāndé, he was again appointed Minister of Revenue,
and served with even greater diligence.
He died in the 12th month of the 8th year,
at the age of seventy-three.
He was posthumously granted Earl of Tāngyīn,
and given the posthumous title Zhōngxiāng.
His son, Yòu, was appointed Department Director in the Ministry of Revenue.
Guō Zī was praised for his ability in managing money and grain.
Rénzōng once asked Yáng Shìqí about this.
He replied:
"Guō Zī is strong and resolute by nature,
and people cannot influence him with private interests.
However, imperial edicts to reduce taxes were issued multiple times but not implemented,
preventing Your Majesty's benevolence from flowing down.
That was Guō Zī's doing."
Lǚ Zhèn,
courtesy name Kèshēng,
was from Líntóng.
In the 19th year of Hóngwǔ, he entered the Imperial Academy through a local recommendation.
At that time, Imperial Academy students were ordered to inspect the lands of various prefectures and counties,
to equalize tribute and taxes.
Lǚ Zhèn, following the summons, went to Liǎngzhè.
Upon his return, his report pleased the Emperor,
and he was promoted to Provisional Reviewer in the Shandong Surveillance Bureau.
He entered the capital as Department Director in the Ministry of Revenue,
and was then transferred to Reviewer in the Běipíng Surveillance Bureau.
When the Yān army rose,
Lǚ Zhèn surrendered to Chéngzǔ,
and was ordered to attend to the Heir Apparent who was guarding the capital.
In the early Yǒnglè period,
he was promoted to Prefect of Zhēndìng,
and then entered the capital as Vice Minister of the Grand Court of Revision.
In the 3rd year, he was promoted to Minister of Justice.
In the 6th year, he was transferred to the Ministry of Rites.
When the Crown Prince was regent,
Lǚ Zhèn's son-in-law, Department Director Zhāng Hè, committed an impropriety during a court audience.
The Crown Prince pardoned him because of Lǚ Zhèn.
The Emperor heard of this and was enraged,
imprisoning Lǚ Zhèn and Jiǎn Yì in the Imperial Guard prison.
Later,
they were reinstated.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
he was appointed concurrently Junior Tutor of the Heir Apparent,
and soon after promoted to Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent concurrently Minister of Rites.
He died in the 4th month of the 1st year of Xuāndé.
Zhèn (震) once three times received orders to visit his parents.
Twice it happened during a famine in Guānzhōng (關中).
He commanded the officials in charge to release grain to relieve the people,
and only reported it upon his return.
However, he lacked scholarship,
and as a ritual official,
he did not understand the overall principles.
When Chéngzǔ (成祖) died,
the imperial edict stated that mourning attire should be cast off after twenty-seven days.
When the time came,
Zhèn (震) suggested that all officials should change into black gauze caps [wūshā mào (烏紗帽)]
and black jade belts [hēijiǎo dài (黑角帶)].
A close official said:
"When Rénxiào (仁孝) Empress died,
after casting off mourning attire,
Tàizōng (太宗) changed into a plain cap and a cloth waist-girdle [bù yāojié (布腰絰)]."
Zhèn (震) suddenly changed color,
and denounced him for being a dissenter.
Rénzōng (仁宗) rejected Zhèn's (震) proposal
and changed into a plain cap and a cloth waist-girdle.

In the first year of Hóngxī (洪熙), he dispatched officials to offer sacrifices to the sacred mountains [yuè (嶽)], important peaks [zhèn (鎮)], seas [hǎi (海)], and rivers [dú (瀆)], as well as the tombs of previous emperors.
Zhèn (震) requested to offer sacrifices to King Wén (文), King Wǔ (武), King Chéng (成), and King Kāng (康) of Zhōu (周).
On his way to visit his mother,
he privately transported his deceased wife's coffin together with incense and silk.
While observing ritual abstinence [zhìzhāi (致齋)] for the imperial ancestral temple [tàimiào (太廟)],
he drank alcohol in a Tibetan monk's dwelling,
got completely drunk, and returned home,
dying overnight.
Zhèn (震) was a fawning, flattering, and treacherous person.
During the Yǒnglè (永樂) era,
Cáoxiàn (曹縣) presented a zōuyú (騶虞) [a mythical beast],
and the kingdoms of Bǎnggélà (榜葛剌) and Máliń (麻林) offered qílín (麒麟) [mythical creatures].
Zhèn (震) requested to offer congratulations.
The Emperor said:
"If the world is peaceful and well-governed,
what harm is there in not having a qílín (麒麟)?"
Jiǎng Tíngzàn (蔣廷瓚), the Provincial Administration Commissioner of Guìzhōu (貴州), said:
"When Your Majesty returned from the northern expedition,
an edict reached Dàyánshān (大巖山) in Sīnán (思南),
and there were three shouts of 'Long live the Emperor!'"
Zhèn (震) said:
"This is the mountains and rivers showing their efficacy."
The Emperor said:
"The sounds of valleys,
corresponding to emptiness,
may reasonably occur.
Zhèn (震) is a great minister of the state,
yet he cannot discern its falsity,
and even wishes to use it to flatter me.
How can this be the way a gentleman serves his ruler?"
Lángzhōng (郎中) Zhōu Nà (周訥) requested a Fēngshàn (封禪) ceremony,
and Zhèn (震) strongly supported it.
The Emperor rebuked him for his absurdity.
Although Zhèn (震) was repeatedly rebuked to his face,
he ultimately could not change.
The ice on the Jīnshuǐhé (金水河) and Tàiyèchí (太液池)
formed shapes of pavilions, dragons, phoenixes, flowers, and plants.
The Emperor summoned his officials to view it.
Zhèn (震) then requested to offer congratulations.
This was not permitted.
However, Lóngpíng Hóu (隆平侯) Zhāng Xìn (張信) reported the sighting of five-colored clouds on Tàihéshān (太和山),
and Shìláng (侍郎) Hú Yíng (胡濙) submitted a drawing of auspicious light, lángméi (榔梅) flowers, and língzhī (靈芝) mushrooms.
Zhèn (震) led the officials in submitting congratulatory memorials one after another.
When Chéngzǔ (成祖) first toured Běijīng (北京),
he ordered the establishment of proper procedures for the Crown Prince's regency.
Zhèn (震) requested that ordinary matters be handled by the Crown Prince,
and memorials be separately stored in the Six Offices [liùkē (六科)] in Nánjīng (南京),
to be presented collectively on the day of the Emperor's return.
This was approved.
In the eleventh and fourteenth years,
Zhèn (震) again requested the same arrangement as before.
In the seventeenth year,
the Emperor was in Běijīng (北京),
and needed some memorials for a certain matter.
Attendant officials said they were in Nánjīng (南京).
The Emperor, having forgotten Zhèn's (震) earlier request,
said:
"Memorials should reach the imperial traveling palace [xíngzài (行在)].
Did the Ministry of Rites [lǐbù (禮部)] make a different proposal?"
He asked Zhèn (震).
Fearing punishment, Zhèn (震) said:
"No,
there was no such thing.
Memorials should reach the imperial traveling palace."
He was asked three times,
and replied as before.
Consequently, Right Supervising Secretary [yòu gěishìzhōng (右給事中)] Lǐ Néng (李能) was executed
for unauthorized retention of memorials.
Everyone knew Néng (能) was innocent,
but fearing Zhèn (震), no one dared to speak.
The calamity of Yǐn Chānglóng (尹昌隆)
was instigated by Zhèn (震).
The details are in Chānglóng's (昌隆) biography.
Xià Yuánjí (夏原吉) and Fāng Bīn (方賓) were punished for speaking about the shortage of provisions for the northern expedition,
and Zhèn (震) was concurrently put in charge of the Ministries of Revenue [hùbù (戶部)] and War [bīngbù (兵部)].
Zhèn (震) also felt his position was precarious.
The Emperor ordered ten imperial guards [guānxiào (官校)] to accompany him,
saying:
"If Zhèn (震) takes his own life,
all ten of you will die."
Zhèn (震) had energy and strength,
and a good memory,
talents sufficient to facilitate his conduct.
For all matters presented to the throne,
other Ministers [shàngshū (尚書)] would hold duplicates,
and also take turns presenting them with the Left and Right Vice Ministers [zuǒyòu shìláng (左右侍郎)].
Since Zhèn (震) concurrently held three ministries,
the number of memorials increased,
and he presented them all himself,
without the Vice Ministers' involvement.
The circumstances were intricate,
with thousands of threads and ten thousand ends,
yet he recited them flawlessly from memory,
never making a mistake.
He once accompanied the Emperor on a northern expedition.
The Emperor saw a stele standing in the sandy desert,
and led his attendants to read its inscription.
A year later,
discussing the stele with various literary officials,
the Emperor ordered the Ministry of Rites [lǐbù (禮部)] to dispatch an official to transcribe it.
Zhèn (震) said there was no need to send an envoy,
and requested to write it out before the Emperor.
The Emperor secretly sent someone to take a rubbing of the original and compare it,
and not a single character was missing or mistaken.
His son was Xióng (熊).
When Xuānzōng (宣宗) first ascended the throne,
Zhèn (震) repeatedly begged for an official position before the Emperor,
even weeping.
The Emperor had no choice
but to appoint him Supervising Secretary of the Bureau of Military Affairs [bīngkē gěishìzhōng (兵科給事中)].
Lǐ Zhìgāng (李至剛),
whose given name was Gāng (鋼),
used his courtesy name [zì (字)] for public affairs.
He was from Huátíng (華亭), Sōngjiāng (松江).
In the twenty-first year of Hóngwǔ (洪wu), he passed the exam for "Profound Studies" [míngjīng (明經)].
He was selected to serve the Heir Apparent Yìwén (懿文),
and appointed Minister [lángzhōng (郎中)] in the Ministry of Rites [lǐbù (禮部)].
Due to implication in a case, he was demoted and exiled to the frontier,
but was soon recalled to be Minister [lángzhōng (郎zhong)] in the Ministry of Works [gōngbù (工部)],
then promoted to Right Assistant Administrator [yòu cānyì (右參議)] of Hénán (河南).
When the Yellow River breached the Biàn (汴) embankment,
Zhìgāng (至剛) proposed borrowing timber accumulated in princely estates [wángfǔ (王府)]
to make rafts to help.
During the Jiànwén (建文) era,
he was transferred to Left Assistant Administrator [zuǒ cānyì (左參議)] of Húguǎng (湖廣),
and was imprisoned for an offense.
When Chéngzǔ (成祖) ascended the throne,
his attendants praised his talent,
so he was appointed Right Vice Commissioner of the Office of Transmission [yòu tōngzhèng (右通政)].
He participated in compiling the Veritable Records of Tàizǔ (太祖),
and was constantly by the Emperor's side,
recounting events from the Hóngwǔ (洪wu) reign,
gaining considerable trust,
and was soon promoted to Minister of Rites [lǐbù shàngshū (禮部尚書)].
In the second year of Yǒnglè (永樂), when the Crown Prince was established,
Zhìgāng (至剛) concurrently held the post of Grand Academician of the Left Quarter [zuǒ chūnfāng dàxuéshì (左春坊大學士)],
lectured at the Eastern Palace [dōnggōng (東宮)] lecture hall,
and lectured with Xiè Jìn (解縉) and others.
Afterward,
he was again imprisoned for an offense,
and after a long time, was released,
demoted to Minister [lángzhōng (郎中)] in the Ministry of Rites [lǐbù (禮部)].
He resented Xiè Jìn (解縉)
and harmed him.
When Jìn (縉) was imprisoned,
Zhìgāng (至剛) was implicated in the testimonies,
and was also imprisoned for over ten years.
When Rénzōng (仁宗) ascended the throne,
he was released,
and again appointed Left Vice Commissioner of the Office of Transmission [zuǒ tōngzhèng (左通政)].
Supervising Secretary [gěishìzhōng (給事中)] Liáng Shèng (梁盛) and others impeached Zhìgāng (至剛) and more than ten others,
stating that during the Emperor's great demise [dàxíng yànjià (大行晏駕)],
they did not stay in their public offices,
but drank alcohol and ate meat,
showing no sign of sorrow.
The Emperor, mindful that Zhìgāng (至剛) was an old official from the previous reign,
appointed him Prefect of Xīnghuà (興化).
At that time, he was already seventy years old.
Two years later,
he died in office.
Zhìgāng was quick-witted and astute,
able to handle complex and difficult tasks,
and skilled at making connections.
He was the first to propose building the capital in Běipíng,
and requested a ban on officials speaking with private motives,
which Chéngzǔ followed.
Once he gained the emperor's favor,
he devoted himself to flattery.
He once suggested that on Tàizǔ's death anniversary,
a practice similar to that of the Sòng dynasty should be adopted,
ordering monks and Daoist priests to chant sutras.
When wild silkworms in Shāndōng formed cocoons,
Zhìgāng requested to offer congratulations.
When auspicious wheat was presented from Shǎnxī,
Zhìgāng led all officials to offer congratulations.
The emperor did not heed any of these suggestions.
An eunuch envoy went to Zhēnlà (Cambodia),
and three of his attendants escaped.
The king replaced them with three people from his country.
The emperor ordered that the three be sent back.
Zhìgāng said:
"As for the three Chinese,
how do we know they weren't privately harbored by them?"
The emperor said:
"I treat both those within and without the court with utmost sincerity;
why employ deceitful stratagems?"
Many of his proposals were not adopted.
His father-in-law, Lì Zhòng, violated the law,
and Zhìgāng pleaded for his exemption.
The emperor said:
"As for the severity of the prison sentence,
how would an outsider know?"
Zhìgāng said:
"Dūyùshǐ Huáng Xìn told me."
The emperor was enraged
and executed Xìn.
Initially,
Zhìgāng and Xiè Jìn were very close.
The emperor wrote down the names of ten important officials,
ordered Jìn to describe their character,
and he said Zhìgāng was not upright.
Jìn was banished to Guǎngxī,
whereupon Zhìgāng reported that he was resentful and grumbling,
and he was re-banished to Jiāozhǐ.
Fāng Bīn,
a native of Qiántáng.
During the Hóngwǔ era, he was appointed Bīngbù Lángzhōng after testing from the Tàixué.
During Jiànwén's reign,
he was acting Yīngtiānfǔ affairs.
He was condemned and sent to guard the borders in Guǎngdōng.
Recommended by Rú Cháng,
he was recalled to office.
When Chéngzǔ entered Jīngshī,
Bīn, along with Shìláng Liú Jùn and others, welcomed and submitted to him,
and he was specially entrusted and employed,
promoted to Bīngbù Shìláng.
In the fourth year,
Jùn, as Shàngshū, went on an expedition against Lí Lì,
and Bīn managed the department's affairs.
He had executive talent and was efficient in handling tasks.
His nature was alert and perceptive,
able to discern the emperor's intentions,
and was favored by the emperor,
becoming somewhat presumptuous and greedy due to his imperial favor.
In the seventh year, he was promoted to Shàngshū,
accompanying the emperor to Běijīng,
and also overseeing the affairs of the Xíngzài Lìbù.
The next year, he joined the northern expedition,
and along with Xuéshì Hú Guǎng, Jīn Yòuzī, Yáng Róng,
and Shìláng Jīn Chún, he was involved in confidential matters.
Thereafter, whenever the emperor made a northern tour,
Bīn would accompany him.
In the nineteenth year, a personal expedition was discussed.
Shàngshū Xià Yuánjí, Wú Zhōng, Lǚ Zhèn, and Bīn jointly discussed
that it would be better to suspend military action and let the people recuperate.
Before it was presented,
the emperor summoned Bīn,
who spoke of insufficient provisions.
Yuánjí was then summoned
and also stated that supplies were inadequate.
The emperor was enraged,
sent Yuánjí to inspect provisions in Kāipíng,
then recalled him and imprisoned him.
Bīn was then overseeing the Língjìgōng palace.
An imperial envoy arrived to offer incense
and told Bīn of the emperor's anger.
Bīn was terrified
and hanged himself.
The emperor had no intention of killing Bīn,
and when he heard of Bīn's death,
he became even more enraged
and mutilated his corpse.
Wú Zhōng,
courtesy name Sīzhèng,
a native of Wǔchéng.
At the end of the Hóngwǔ era,
he was the Yíngzhōu Hòutúnwèi Jīnglì.
Chéngzǔ captured Dàníng,
and he welcomed and surrendered.
For his achievements in transporting provisions and defending,
he was progressively promoted to Yòudūyùshǐ.
In the fifth year of Yǒnglè, he was appointed Gōngbù Shàngshū.
He followed the northern expedition
and returned with difficulty.
Reinstated,
he was transferred to Xíngbù.
In the nineteenth year, he, along with Xià Yuánjí and Fāng Bīn,
was imprisoned for speaking of the scarcity of provisions for the northern expedition,
thus offending the imperial will.
Rénzōng ascended the throne,
released him,
restored his office,
concurrently served as Zhànshì,
and was given the title Tàizǐ Shàobǎo.
In the first year of Xuāndé, he accompanied the expedition to Yuè'ān.
In the third year, he was imprisoned for using government timber and stone to build a residence for the eunuch Yáng Qìng,
lost his Gōngbǎo title,
and had his salary confiscated for one year.
In the sixth year of Zhèngtǒng,
when the palace construction was completed,
he was promoted to Shàoshī.
He died the next year
at the age of seventy.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Cípíng Bó
and given the posthumous name Róngxiāng.
Zhōng was diligent,
meticulous, and calculating.
He served in the Gōngbù for over twenty years in total.
The palaces in Běijīng,
and the Cháng, Xiàn, Jǐng three imperial tombs
were all constructed under his supervision.
His duties were numerous and complex,
but his planning was orderly.
However, he showed no care for the artisans
and was also indulged in sensual pleasures,
for which he was scorned by contemporary opinion.
Liú Guān,
a native of Xióngxiàn.
He passed the imperial examination in the eighteenth year of Hóngwǔ.
He was appointed Tàigǔ Xiànchéng,
and by recommendation, he was promoted to Jiānchá Yùshǐ.
In the thirtieth year, he was transferred to acting Zuǒqiāndūyùshǐ.
He was imprisoned for an offense
and soon released.
He was then appointed Zhīfǔ of Jiāxīng
but left due to mourning his father.
In the first year of Yǒnglè, he was promoted to Yúnnán Ànchásǐ,
but before he could take office,
he was appointed Hùbù Yòushìláng.
In the second year, he was transferred to Zuǒfùdūyùshǐ.
At that time, Zuǒdūyùshǐ Chén Yīng was harsh and cruel,
while Yòudūyùshǐ Wú Zhōng was lenient and mild.
Guān maneuvered between the two,
striving to please both.
In the fourth year,
when palaces were being constructed in Běijīng,
Guān was ordered to procure timber from Zhèjiāng,
returning soon after.
In the winter of the next year,
the emperor, due to a drought in Shānxī,
ordered Guān to rush there by imperial messenger
and dismiss the military and civilian personnel involved in timber procurement.
In the sixth year,
Zhèng Cì died,
and Guān was promoted to Lǐbù Shàngshū.
In the twelfth month, he exchanged posts with Xíngbù Shàngshū Lǚ Zhèn.
He was reprimanded by the Crown Prince for an offense.
When the emperor in Běijīng heard of this,
he stated that a high official should not be abruptly humiliated
for a minor fault
and specially sent a letter to instruct the Crown Prince.
In the eighth year,
Dūdū Qiānshì Fèi Huán suppressed a rebellion by the Qiāng people in Liángzhōu,
and Guān was ordered to assist in military affairs.
Upon his return,
he was demoted to an official in his original department
for an offense.
In the thirteenth year, he was restored to his position
and transferred to Zuǒdūyùshǐ.
In the fifteenth year, he supervised the dredging of river transport.
In the nineteenth year, he was ordered to patrol Shǎnxī
and inspect officials.
Rénzōng ascended the throne,
and he was concurrently appointed Tàizǐ Bīnkè,
then later promoted to Tàizǐ Shàobǎo,
receiving two salaries.
At that time, Dàlǐ Shàoqīng Yì Qiān frequently offered advice,
and the emperor was annoyed by his tediousness.
Shàngshū Lǚ Zhèn and Dàlǐ Qīng Yú Qiān, seeking to please the emperor, impeached and reported him.
Guān further ordered the fourteen circuits of Censorate officials to denounce his accusations as false and absurd,
for which he was despised by public opinion.
At that time, there was no prohibition against official courtesans.
In the early Xuāndé reign,
ministers and officials feasted and entertained,
vying with each other in luxury,
with singing girls filling their presence.
Liú Guān privately accepted bribes,
and the various censors were also greedy and unrestrained.
In the sixth month of the third year, after the morning court,
the Emperor summoned Grand Academicians Yáng Shìqí and Yáng Róng to Wénhuá Mén,
and instructed them, saying:
"During the time of the Imperial Ancestors,
court officials were cautious and upright.
In recent years, greed and corruption have become rampant.
Why is this?"
Shìqí replied:
"It already existed at the end of the Yǒnglè reign,
but now it is much worse."
Róng said:
"During the Yǒnglè reign,
no one surpassed Fāng Bīn."
The Emperor asked:
"Who is the worst today?"
Róng replied:
"Liú Guān."
He asked again:
"Who can replace him?"
Shìqí and Róng recommended Gù Zuǒ, the Commissioner of the Office of Transmission.
The Emperor then sent Guān to inspect the waterways,
and appointed Zuǒ as Right Censor-in-Chief.
Thereupon, Censors Zhāng Xúnlǐ and others submitted memorials impeaching Guān,
detailing various acts of corruption and lawlessness by him and his son Fú.
The Emperor was enraged,
arrested Guān and his son,
and showed them the impeachment memorials.
Guān submitted a memorial defending himself.
The Emperor grew even more furious,
and brought out the secret memorials submitted by court officials, both past and present,
some of which mentioned perverting justice and accepting bribes up to a thousand gold taels.
Guān confessed,
and was then imprisoned in the Jǐnyīwèi prison.
The following year, he was to be severely punished.
Shìqí and Róng pleaded for his life.
So Fú was banished to guard the frontier in Liáodōng,
and Guān was ordered to accompany him;
Guān eventually died as a wanderer.
In the seventh year,
Shìqí requested that the censorate officials be ordered to investigate and dismiss corrupt local officials.
The Emperor said:
"Indeed.
Had Liú Guān not been dismissed in the past,
how could the censorate have become so upright?"
A eulogy says: Chéngzǔ enfeoffed Rú Cháng
for his meritorious service to Tàizǔ.
However, upon investigation,
no notable achievements are recorded;
perhaps history omitted them?
Yán Zhènzhí in Guǎngxī
and Zhāng Dǎn in Yúnnán
achieved outstanding administrative results.
Wáng Dùn and Zhèng Cì served as provincial governors and surveillance commissioners,
and their reputations and achievements were quite prominent,
yet in their later years,
they were all unable to uphold themselves.
What a pity!
Guō Zī, Lǚ Zhèn and their ilk
possessed talent for governing,
but their conduct was reprehensible.
Lǐ Zhìgāng's treachery,
and Wú Zhōng and Liú Guān's corruption,
are not even worth mentioning.
Biographies, Chapter 40: Dǒng Lún (Wáng Jǐng) Yí Zhì (Zǐ Míng) Zōu Jì (Xú Shànshù Wáng Rǔyù
Liáng Qián) Zhōu Shù (his brother Mèngjiǎn) Chén Jì (Chén Jì Yáng Zhù Yú Shān Yú Gāng Pān Chén) Wáng Yīng Qián Xílǐ Zhōu (Liú Yǎn) Kē Qián (Luó Jǐng) Kǒng Gōngxún (Sīmǎ Xún)
Dǒng Lún,
courtesy name Āncháng,
a native of ēn.
In the fifteenth year of Hóngwǔ, recommended by Zhāng Yǐníng,
he was appointed Zànshàn Dàfū,
and served the Crown Prince Yìwén,
offering earnest advice.
Tàizǔ praised him,
and promoted him to Left Grand Academician of the Spring Palace.
After the Crown Prince's death,
he was sent out as Left Councilor of Hénán.
When Lánxī Zhūgě Bóhéng, an administrative clerk of Zhàozhōu, was found to be honest,
Lún recommended him.
The Emperor immediately promoted him to Councilor of Shǎnxī.
He also suggested that Confucian instructors should be granted caps and sashes
to distinguish them from ordinary scholars.
Instructors then began to be selected for appointment.
In the thirtieth year, he was demoted to an educational official in Yúnnán for an offense.
When schools were first established in Yúnnán,
Lún taught by example,
and everyone was drawn to learning.
In the early Jiànwén reign,
he was summoned and appointed Vice Minister of Rites concurrently Grand Academician of the Hànlín Academy,
and attended imperial lectures with Fāng Xiàorú.
The Emperor inscribed a plaque with
"Yí Lǎo Táng" (Hall for Enjoying Old Age)
to honor him,
and also bestowed upon him a lacquered table and a jade pigeon staff.
Xiè Jìn, who had been banished to Hézhōu, was recalled through Lún's recommendation.
Lún was straightforward and honest,
and once advised the Emperor to maintain harmonious relations with the imperial relatives,
but was not listened to.
When Chéngzǔ ascended the throne,
Lún was already eighty years old,
and was allowed to retire.
He died shortly after.
Serving concurrently with Lún as Vice Minister of Rites
was Wáng Jǐng,
courtesy name Jǐngzhāng,
a native of Sōngyáng.
In the early Hóngwǔ reign,
he was an instructor in Huáiyuǎn.
He was summoned due to his extensive learning.
He was ordered to compose ceremonial music for imperial sacrifices
and to establish the protocol for princely court audiences.
He successively served as Provincial Administrator of Shānxī,
and was demoted to Yúnnán before and after Lún.
In the early Jiànwén reign,
he was summoned to the Hànlín Academy
to compile the Veritable Records of Tàizǔ.
Upon Zhāng Dǎn's recommendation,
he was appointed Vice Minister of Rites concurrently Lecturer in the Hànlín Academy.
When Chéngzǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Academician.
The Emperor asked about the rites for burying Emperor Jiànwén,
and Jǐng bowed his head and said:
"It should be done with the rites of an Emperor."
This was followed.
He died in office in the sixth year of Yǒnglè.
Yí Zhì,
courtesy name Jūzhēn,
a native of Gāomì.
At the end of the Hóngwǔ reign,
he was recommended as an elder scholar,
appointed instructor of Gāomì,
and later transferred to be an instructor in Shēnxǐan.
He was promoted to Prefect of Gāoyóu Prefecture,
where he encouraged agriculture and promoted education,
and officials and common people loved him.
In the first year of Yǒnglè, he was transferred to be Prefect of Bǎoqìng.
The local people were strong and fierce,
but only feared Zhì,
and warned each other not to offend him.
He was summoned to be Right Commissioner of Transmission concurrently Right Middle Remonstrator.
Not long after,
he was transferred to be Right Provincial Administration Commissioner of Húguǎng.
He was demoted to serve in Tōngzhōu for an offense.
In the winter of the sixth year,
Gōng Zhōng, the Regional Commander of Húguǎng, had an audience with the Emperor.
The Emperor asked about old scholars in the Hú-Xiāng region,
and Zhōng replied with Zhì.
He was immediately summoned that day.
Upon his arrival,
he was appointed Left Vice Minister of Rites.
On New Year's Day of the eleventh year,
there was to be a solar eclipse,
and Minister Lǚ Zhèn requested that the court celebration proceed as usual,
but Zhì firmly disagreed.
Coincidentally, Left Assistant Lecturer Yáng Shìqí also raised this concern,
so the celebration was cancelled as Zhì suggested.
In the fourteenth year, an imperial edict instructed the Ministry of Personnel and the Hànlín Academy to select elder scholars to attend the Imperial Grandson.
Shìqí and Jiǎn Yì first recommended Zhì.
The Crown Prince said:
"I once recommended Lǐ Jìdǐng,
which was a big mistake,
and I regret it immensely.
Zhì is indeed an upright gentleman,
but he is old."
Shìqí bowed his head and said:
"Zhì began his career as an academic official,
understanding principles and upholding righteousness.
Although old,
his spirit is not diminished.
Among court officials,
none are as mature and upright as Zhì."
That day at the midday court,
the Emperor looked at the Crown Prince and said:
"Have you found a suitable person to attend the Imperial Grandson for lectures and studies?"
The Crown Prince replied:
"Vice Minister of Rites Yí Zhì was recommended,
but the decision is not yet made."
The Emperor happily said:
"Although Zhì is old,
he can speak frankly,
and can be employed."
Thereupon, he was ordered to assist and guide the Imperial Grandson.
Whenever he lectured on books and history,
he would repeatedly enlighten and guide,
taking the rectification of the mind as the fundamental principle.
In the nineteenth year,
at the age of eighty,
he retired,
and died at home.
In the first year of Hóngxī, he was posthumously granted Junior Guardian of the Crown Prince,
and given the posthumous title Wénjiǎn.
Jì Zǐmíng,
courtesy name Zǐxīn.
When Xuānzōng ascended the throne,
recommended by Grand Secretary Dài Lún,
he was appointed Investigating Censor of the Ministry of Rites in the Traveling Imperial Court.
After nine years of service,
the Emperor, remembering his old and meritorious service,
reassigned Míng as a Compiler.
In the third year of Zhèngtǒng, he completed the compilation of the Veritable Records of Xuān Miào,
and was promoted to Palace Lecturer,
later reassigned as Senior Scribe of the Chéng Princely Establishment.
When the Prince of Chéng served as regent,
he presided over court at the Wǔmén.
Court officials impeached Wáng Zhèn,
their shouts and cries were indistinguishable.
Míng alone knelt before the Prince,
removed his cap, and presented his memorial.
An imperial decree was issued to punish Zhèn's entire clan,
and the clamor of the crowd finally subsided.
When Jǐngdì ascended the throne,
Míng strongly advocated for major matters of conquest and expedition.
Soon after, by virtue of his favor from the imperial residence,
he was appointed Junior Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites.
The following year, he also served as a Lecturer in the imperial lectures.
Whenever the Emperor attended the lecture tent,
he would order eunuchs to scatter gold coins on the ground,
allowing the lecturers to pick them up,
which was called a "benevolent gift."
Among the civil officials who participated,
apart from Gāo Gǔ and others from the Grand Secretariat,
only Míng, Yú Shān, Yú Gāng, Xiāo Zī, and Zhào Wǎn were among them.
Soon after, he was promoted to Minister of Rites in Nánjīng.
When Crown Prince Huáixiàn was established,
he was given the additional title of Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince,
and summoned to be Minister of War and concurrently Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
In Sūzhōu and Huái'ān and other prefectures, there was heavy snow,
and the people froze and starved to death, their bodies piled up.
At Shāwān, a river was being dredged,
mobilizing ninety thousand people from Shāndōng and Hénán,
and demanding tens of thousands of iron tools from the common folk.
Míng pleaded with the Emperor,
and much relief was provided.
Due to disasters and anomalies,
he stated that the way to eliminate them lay in respecting Heaven and following the ancestors,
reducing punishments and lightening taxes,
economizing and loving the people,
and he submitted a copy of the Imperial Ancestral Instructions,
which was greatly praised and accepted.
He died
and was posthumously given the epithet Zhōngxiāng.
Míng studied under Wú Nà in his youth.
He was naturally filial and fraternal,
straightforward and honest, possessing his father's character.
His eldest son, Hǎi,
was a Centurion of the Imperial Guard.
His youngest son, Tài,
passed the provincial examination,
and became an Investigating Censor of the Ministry of Rites.
Both received their appointments due to their father's favor.
Zōu Jì,
courtesy name Rǔzhōu,
was from Yúháng.
He was known for his filial piety towards his mother.
He was learned and had a strong memory,
especially skilled in the Spring and Autumn Annals.
As an instructor in Yúháng,
his teaching methods were strict.
He successively rose to Recorder and Assistant Instructor of the Imperial Academy,
and was appointed Prefect of Píngdù Zhōu by recommendation.
In the early years of Yǒnglè,
he participated in the compilation of the Veritable Records of Tàizǔ,
and was appointed Director of the Ministry of Rites.
During the campaign against Ānnán,
he served in the military secretariat, managing petitions and records.
Upon his return, he became Junior Vice Administrator of Guǎngdōng,
then was promoted to Left Palace Secretary of the Left Spring坊,
and taught the imperial grandson the classics.
Jì was gentle and honest,
and all, regardless of rank, enjoyed being close to him.
Upon completing his term,
he was promoted to Junior Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
At this time,
many palace officials fell into disfavor;
Xú Shànshù, Wáng Rǔyù, Mǎ Jīng, and Liáng Qián were slandered,
and successively imprisoned and died.
Jì accumulated worry and fell ill.
The Crown Prince consoled him with a letter, saying:
"My lord, take good care of yourself.
Should anything unfortunate happen,
I will take care of your sons,
not letting them fall into obscurity."
He died
at the age of sixty-eight.
In the first year of Hóngxī, he was posthumously granted the title of Junior Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince,
and given the epithet Wénmǐn.
An official was ordered to establish a shrine beside his tomb,
and sacrifices were offered in spring and autumn.
His son, Gàn,
courtesy name Zōngshèng,
was still young when Jì died.
Rénzōng, as regent,
appointed him a student of Yìngtiān Prefecture,
granting him monthly stipends of paper money and rice.
He passed the imperial examination in the fourth year of Zhèngtǒng.
In the early years of Jǐngdì,
he was exceptionally promoted from Director of the Ministry of War to Junior Vice Minister of the same ministry,
relied upon by Yú Qiān for his talent.
When Yěxiān invaded,
all nine gates were closed.
People fleeing the war
cried out outside the city for entry,
and Gàn opened the gates to admit them.
Soon after, he was reassigned to the Ministry of Rites,
concurrently serving as a Palace Secretary.
He inspected officials in Shānxī,
dismissing over fifty people, including Provincial Administrator Hóu Fù.
He inspected the floods in Hénán and Fèngyáng,
and requested relief with Wáng Hóng.
He also requested that students be allowed to donate grain to enter the Imperial Academy for study.
The practice of donating grain to enter the Imperial Academy began with this.
In the second year of Chénghuà, he relieved the famine in Jī Nèi,
was again promoted to Minister of Rites,
and given the additional title of Junior Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
He was impeached and requested retirement,
and died
with the posthumous epithet Kāngjìng.
Xú Shànshù,
courtesy name Hǎogǔ,
was from Tiāntái.
During the Hóngwǔ era,
the annual tribute system was implemented,
and Shànshù was the first to tribute and enter the Imperial Academy.
He was appointed Instructor of Guìyáng Prefecture.
In the early Yǒnglè years,
he was promoted from Imperial Academy Scholar to Palace Secretary of the Spring坊.
He was highly regarded by the Crown Prince,
who always referred to him as "Mister,"
and once sent him letters, wine, and poems.
He was promoted to Left Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
but was implicated and died.
On the same day as Zōu Jì, he was posthumously granted the title of Junior Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince,
and given the epithet Wénsù.
A shrine was built,
and sacrifices were offered in spring and autumn, also like Jì.
Wáng Rǔyù,
given name Suì,
went by his courtesy name,
and was from Chángzhōu.
He was exceptionally intelligent and had a strong memory.
In his youth, he studied under Yáng Wéizhēn.
At seventeen,
he passed the provincial examination.
In the early Yǒnglè years,
he was promoted from Instructor of Yìngtiān Prefecture Academy
to Erudite of the Five Classics in the Hanlin Academy.
He successively rose to Right Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent in the Right Spring坊,
and participated in the compilation of the Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn.
Rénzōng, while in the Eastern Palace,
showed him special favor.
When all officials were ordered to compose a "Divine Turtle Ode,"
Rǔyù's was first,
Xiè Jìn's second.
In the seventh year, he was accused of disordering regulations while compiling ritual texts,
and was to be exiled to the frontier.
The Crown Prince, acting as regent,
pardoned him,
making him an Archivist in the Hanlin Academy.
Soon after, he was promoted to Left Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
but was implicated in Xiè Jìn's case
and died in prison.
In the early Hóngxī years, he was posthumously granted the title of Guest of the Crown Prince,
and given the epithet Wénjìng,
and an official was sent to offer sacrifices at his home.
Liáng Qián,
courtesy name Yòngzhī,
was a native of Tàihé.
At the end of the Hóngwǔ reign,
he passed the provincial examination.
He was appointed Instructor of Cāngxī in Sìchuān.
By recommendation, he was made Magistrate of Sìhuì County,
then transferred to Yángjiāng and Yángchūn,
where he was acclaimed for his honesty and fairness.
In the first year of the Yǒnglè reign, he was summoned to compile the *Tàizǔ Shílù*.
After the book was completed,
he was promoted to Compiler.
Soon after, he concurrently served as Right Exhorter of the Right Spring Palace and
replaced Zhèng Cì as Chief Editor of the *Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn*.
When the emperor traveled to Běijīng,
he was repeatedly summoned by express courier to the imperial traveling palace.
In the fifteenth year, the emperor again traveled to Běijīng,
and the crown prince supervised the state.
The emperor personally selected his accompanying officials;
among the Hanlin Academicians, only Yáng Shìqí was chosen,
with Liáng Qián as his deputy.
There was a Commander Chén
who had unlawfully seized people's property,
and an imperial decree ordered him to be banished to Jiāozhǐ.
A few days later, remembering his military achievements,
he was pardoned and recalled.
Someone slandered him to the emperor, saying:
"The criminal whom Your Majesty banished
has been leniently pardoned by the crown prince."
The emperor was enraged,
and had Commander Chén executed.
The matter implicated Liáng Qián and Supervising Censor Zhōu Miǎn.
They were arrested and brought to the imperial traveling palace,
where the emperor personally interrogated them.
Liáng Qián and the others truthfully reported the facts.
The emperor said to Yáng Róng and Lǚ Zhèn:
"How could this matter have been caused by Liáng Qián!"
However, ultimately no one spoke up on their behalf,
and they were all imprisoned.
Someone slandered Zhōu Miǎn for being unbridled,
so Liáng Qián was also executed along with him.
Liáng Qián's wife, Lady Yáng, grieved his wrongful death
and starved herself to death.
His son, Mù,
became a Principal of the Ministry of Justice after passing the imperial examination,
and was skilled at redressing wrongful convictions.
By recommendation, he was promoted to Vice Surveillance Commissioner of Guǎngxī,
and then to Provincial Administration Commissioner.
Many military officers and soldiers would kill innocent civilians to claim merit.
Mù instructed their commander:
"For every distressed person brought alive,
one grade of merit will be awarded."
He saved countless lives.
The native official Cén Jiàn and his brothers in Tiánzhōu were at odds.
Mù resolved their conflict
and refused their generous gifts.
He pacified and subdued the rebellious female native official,
and both locals and non-locals respected his trustworthiness and integrity.
He ended his career as Provincial Administration Commissioner of Zhèjiāng.
Zhōu Shù,
courtesy name Chóngshù,
was a native of Jíshuǐ.
In the second year of the Yǒnglè reign, he and his cousin Mèngjiǎn both passed the imperial examination.
The emperor personally commented on their examination papers,
praised and rewarded them,
and appointed them both Hanlin Compilers.
Soon after, an imperial edict commanded Jiě Jìn to select Zēng Qǐ and twenty-eight others to study in the Wényuān Pavilion.
Zhōu Shù and Mèngjiǎn were among them.
The Directorate of Ceremonial provided paper and brushes,
the Court of Imperial Entertainments provided morning and evening meals,
the Ministry of Rites provided three ingots of paper currency per person monthly for lamp oil and candles,
and the Ministry of Works selected nearby residences for them.
At the time, this was considered a great honor.
Zhōu Shù once accompanied the emperor on a northern tour
and was successively promoted to Expositor-in-waiting of the Left Spring Palace.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
he was ordered to accompany the crown prince to visit the imperial tombs in Nánjīng.
Summoned to the emperor's bedside,
he was asked about how to advise and assist the heir apparent,
and his reply pleased the emperor.
During Xuānzōng's reign,
he was promoted to Grand Secretary of the Left.
At the beginning of the Zhèngtǒng reign,
he died in office.
Mèngjiǎn served in the Hanlin Academy for twenty years
before finally being transferred to Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Clan Affairs,
and then dispatched as Chief Administrator of the Prince of Xiāng's Household.
Someone suggested he should be retained for consultation,
but the emperor said:
"Assisting my brother
is even better than assisting me."
Zhōu Shù was gentle, modest, and quiet,
never speaking harshly or showing sudden anger,
and his writings were elegant and substantial.
Mèngjiǎn was humble and not boastful,
and never bore grudges against anyone throughout his life.
Both were highly esteemed by their contemporaries.
Chén Jì,
courtesy name Bózài,
was a native of Wǔjìn.
He could memorize what he read at a glance.
Once, on his father's orders, he went to Qiántáng,
and his family brought goods to sell along.
Upon his return,
he used half of the money to buy books,
reciting and copying them by hand.
After more than ten years,
he had mastered all the classics, histories, and writings of the various schools of thought.
When Chéngzǔ ordered the compilation of the *Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn*,
based on the recommendation of a high official,
he was summoned as a commoner to be Chief Editor,
with Compiler Zēng Qǐ and others as his deputies.
There were several thousand literary officials and scholars from the Imperial Academy participating in the compilation,
who consulted millions of volumes from the secret archives,
a vast and boundless task.
Chén Jì, along with Grand Mentor Yáo Guǎngxiào and several others,
established the general principles and rules,
categorized and verified the content,
and brought order to the work.
If those holding the brush had any doubts,
they would immediately consult Chén Jì,
who would answer and analyze without hesitation.
When the book was completed,
he was appointed Right Exhorter.
He was cautious and made no mistakes,
and the crown prince held him in high regard.
All matters of historical research and compilation
were entrusted to Chén Jì.
He offered reports and suggestions as events unfolded,
which were often very beneficial.
All five imperial grandsons received instruction in the classics from him.
He served in office for fifteen years before he died.
He was sixty-two years old.
When Chén Jì was young, he had a problem with drinking.
His mother warned him,
and for the rest of his life, he never became drunk.
His younger brother, Qià, who was Minister of War,
treated Chén Jì like a father.
Chén Jì greatly feared excessive success and honor,
and became even more humble and modest.
His dwelling had a thatched door and reed walls,
just enough to shelter from wind and rain.
He sat upright all day,
never letting go of a book.
His writings were based on the classics and histories,
and he did not pursue flowery language.
He once said:
"Writing should be like cloth, silk, beans, and grains—
beneficial to the world."
After him, there were Chén Jì and Yáng Zhù,
who also mastered the classics as commoners.
Through Yáng Shìqí's recommendation,
Chén Jì entered the Hanlin Academy from being an Academician.
Yáng Zhù, however, due to the favor received at Emperor Jǐngzōng's princely residence,
along with Yú Shān and Yú Gāng, all attained high official positions.
After the Tiānshùn reign,
the system gradually became more rigid regarding qualifications.
Compilers Mǎ Shēng and Revisers Fù Zōng, who did not enter through the examination system,
were all dismissed by Lǐ Xián to serve as Councilors.
Commoners were no longer allowed to participate in the Hanlin Academy,
but during the Hóngzhì reign, Pān Chén alone obtained such a position due to his talent and reputation,
which was considered a rare marvel at the time.
Chén Jì,
courtesy name Sìchū,
was a native of Wú.
He was orphaned young,
and his mother, Lady Wú,
personally wove to provide for his studies.
By the time he grew up,
he was thoroughly versed in the classics,
and people called him Chén Wǔjīng.
He served his mother with utmost filial piety,
and the prefecture and county jointly recommended him,
but he declined due to his mother's old age.
When his mother died,
his grief and emaciation surpassed others'.
During the Yǒnglè reign,
he was again recommended for his filial conduct,
and his mother was honored with the title Zhēnjié.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
he opened the Hóngwén Pavilion.
The emperor visited,
and asked:
"Are there any famous scholars in the mountains and forests now?"
Yáng Shìqí initially did not know Jì.
Xià Yuánjí, while managing water in Sū and Sōng,
obtained his writings,
and returned to show them to Shìqí,
who mentally noted him.
When the emperor asked,
he then replied with Jì.
Jì was summoned to be a Guózǐ Bóshì,
and soon after was changed to Hànlín Wǔjīng Bóshì,
and served in the Hóngwén Pavilion.
At the beginning of Xuānzōng's reign,
he was promoted to Jiǎntǎo.
He returned home citing illness,
and died.
Yáng Zhù,
courtesy name Zhòngjǔ,
was also a native of Wú.
Orphaned and poor in his youth,
he followed his brother to garrison Wǔchāng,
and supported himself by teaching.
When Yáng Shìqí was in humble circumstances,
exiled and in distress,
Zhù would immediately vacate his schoolhouse for him,
and teach elsewhere himself.
Shìqí admired him in his heart.
When he became distinguished,
he recommended Zhù for his profound understanding of the classics and upright conduct.
Xuānzōng decreed a test at the Lìbù,
and he met with approval,
was appointed Hànlín Yuàn Jiǎntǎo,
and subsequently Xiūzhuàn.
During the Zhèngtǒng reign,
a decree ordered the selection of officials for thechéng Wángfu.
All the Hànlín officials were unwilling to go,
so Vice-Supervisor Yí Míng and Zhù were sent out as Left and Right Chief Clerks.
After a long time,
he retired due to age.
When the Prince ascended the throne,
Zhù entered court,
and was appointed Lǐbù Yòu Shìláng.
In the third year of Jǐngtài, he was promoted to Shàngshū,
given a salary, and retired.
The next year he died,
at the age of eighty-five.
Zhù was earnest in his conduct and free from worldly ways;
among the gentry and high-minded individuals of his time,
Zhù was the foremost.
After his death,
Emperor Jǐng thought of him,
summoned his son Jǐn for an audience,
and appointed him as the principal clerk of his home county.
Yú Shān,
courtesy name Jīzhī,
was a native of Xiùshuǐ.
Through a local recommendation, he became a companion reader in the chéng Wángfu.
During Emperor Jǐng's reign,
he was appointed Lìbù Yòu Shìláng.
As for Yú Gāng of Jiāxīng, he transcribed historical records as a student,
passed the examination for Zhōngshū Shèrén,
and was appointed chief judge of the chéng Wángfu.
During Emperor Jǐng's reign,
he entered the cabinet as Bīngbù Yòu Shìláng to participate in military affairs.
After three days,
he firmly resigned,
retaining his original post.
When Emperor Jǐng was about to change the Crown Prince,
Shān secretly submitted a memorial to remonstrate.
It was not heeded.
When Prince Huáixiàn was established,
Shān was given the additional title of Tàizǐ Shǎofù,
but he felt uneasy,
and retired.
Gāng was given the additional title of Tàizǐ Shǎobǎo.
When Yīngzōng was restored to the throne,
Shān was spared due to his retirement.
As for Gāng, during the Jǐngtài era,
he was able to maneuver between the two emperors,
and thus was transferred to the Nánjīng Lǐbù.
He retired at the beginning of Chénghuà,
and died.
Pān Chén,
courtesy name Shíyòng,
was a native of Jǐngníng.
Orphaned young,
he followed his paternal relatives to the capital,
and was known for his literary talent.
In the sixth year of Hóngzhì, a decree ordered the recommendation of talented and virtuous scholars hidden in the mountains and forests throughout the empire.
The Prefect Táng Xún recommended Chén,
but the Lìbù set it aside because Chén had grown up in the capital.
Xún memorialized again,
and Vice-Ministers Wáng Lún and Xià Áng also jointly submitted memorials recommending him,
whereupon he was appointed Hànlín Dàizhào.
After a long time,
he was put in charge of典籍 (library affairs).
He participated in the compilation of the Huìdiǎn,
and upon its completion,
was promoted to Wǔjīng Bóshì.
During the Zhèngdé reign,
Liú Jǐn singled out minor flaws in the Huìdiǎn,
and Chén was demoted back to Diǎnjí,
but soon after returned to his former post.
The position of Nánjīng Jìjiǔ was vacant,
and the Lìbù recommended Shí Bǎo and Chén.
The emperor appointed Bǎo,
and promoted Chén to Biānxiū.
After nine years,
he was exceptionally promoted to Tàicháng Shàoqīng,
retired and returned home,
and died.
He was specially granted a state funeral.
Chén was diligent and cautious in office,
entering in the morning and returning at night.
When drafting decrees and edicts,
if someone offered payment,
he firmly refused it.
Scholars and officials respected his learning and conduct,
calling him Nánpíng Xiānshēng.
Wáng Yīng,
courtesy name Shíyàn,
was a native of Jīnxī.
He passed the imperial examination in the second year of Yǒnglè.
He was selected as a Shùjíshì,
and studied in the Wényuāngé.
The emperor observed his prudence and meticulousness,
and ordered him and Wáng Zhí to transcribe confidential documents.
He participated in the compilation of the Tàizǔ Shílù,
was appointed Hànlín Yuàn Xiūzhuàn,
and promoted to Shìdú.
In the twentieth year, he accompanied the emperor on a northern expedition.
When the army returned,
they passed Lǐ Líng Chéng.
The emperor heard there was a stone stele in the city,
and summoned Yīng to inspect it.
When he arrived,
he did not know where the stele was.
But at the north gate of the city, a stone protruded more than a foot from the ground.
When unearthed,
it was a stele of virtuous governance by a certain Xiè, the director of the Lǐ Líng Táiyì during the Yuán dynasty.
The back of the stele was engraved with the names of Dálǔhuāchì and others.
He reported this fully.
The emperor said:
"The stele has Mongol names,
which in the future will be taken as their land,
initiating disputes."
He ordered him to go again and smash it.
He sank it in the river,
and returned to report.
The emperor was pleased with his thoroughness,
and said:
"You are the scholar among the twenty-eight,
I shall employ you."
He then asked about the northern expedition.
Yīng said:
"With the Emperor's might personally leading,
they will surely flee far away,
I hope you will not pursue them relentlessly."
The emperor smiled and said:
"Do you, a scholar, think I am fond of war?"
Then he said:
"Report any movements in the army immediately upon hearing them."
And he instructed the eunuchs not to obstruct him.
When the officers and soldiers who had achieved merit committed faults,
he ordered their rations to be withheld,
and they gathered and wept.
Due to Yīng's memorial,
their rations were restored.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
Yīng was successively promoted to Yòu Chūnfāng Dàxuéshì,
and requested to return home to visit his parents.
Xuānzōng 宣宗 was enthroned,
and [he] returned to court.
At this time, the realm was at peace,
and the Son of Heaven had a refined appreciation for literature.
He often conversed with various academicians about literature and art,
admired flowers, and composed poems,
treating them with utmost courtesy.
He once said to Yīng 英:
“During the Hóngwǔ 洪武 reign,
the academicians included Sòng Lián 宋濂, Wú Chén 吳沉,
Zhū Shàn 朱善, and Liú Sānwú 劉三吾.
In the early Yǒnglè 永樂 reign,
there were Xiè Jìn 解縉 and Hú Guǎng 胡廣.
You should strive,
so that these predecessors do not exclusively claim this excellence.”
After the Veritable Records of Tàizōng 太宗 and Rénzōng 仁宗 were compiled,
he was promoted to Junior Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent,
and bestowed a qílín 麒麟 belt.
When his mother died,
he was specially granted permission for burial and sacrifices,
and an eunuch was dispatched to escort him home.
He was soon reinstated.
In the first year of Zhèngtǒng 正統, he was ordered to attend the imperial lectures,
preside over the compilation of the Veritable Records of Xuānzōng 宣宗,
and was promoted to Vice Minister of Rites.
In the eighth year, he was ordered to manage the affairs of the Ministry of Rites.
When a plague broke out among the people of Zhèjiāng 浙江,
he was dispatched to offer sacrifices at the Southern Marchmount.
At that time, there had been a long drought.
When Yīng 英 arrived,
there was heavy rain.
The people called it "Vice Minister's Rain."
At seventy years old,
he again requested retirement.
It was not granted.
In the twelfth year,
Yīng’s 英 son, Yù 裕, who was a Vice Commissioner of the Provincial Surveillance Office, was imprisoned for an offense.
Yīng 英 submitted a memorial, awaiting punishment.
He was pardoned and not questioned.
The following year, he was promoted to Minister of Rites of Nánjīng 南京,
to allow him to enjoy leisure.
He died two years later,
at the age of seventy-five.
He was granted sacrifices and a burial,
and posthumously named Wén'ān 文安.
Yīng 英 was upright, composed, and steady,
serving under four emperors.
He spent over forty years in the Hànlín 翰林 Academy,
and repeatedly served as an examiner for the metropolitan examinations.
Many imperial edicts and documents originated from his hand,
and requests for epitaphs and steles from all directions were unceasing.
He was straightforward and magnanimous by nature,
and fond of pointing out others' faults.
The Sān Yáng 三楊 (the three Yangs) all disliked him,
and therefore he was not given a position of real power.
Yù 裕 later rose through the ranks to become the Surveillance Commissioner of Sìchuān 四川.
Qián Xílǐ 錢習禮,
whose given name was Gàn 幹,
was known by his courtesy name,
and was a native of Jíshuǐ 吉水.
He became a *jìnshì* 進士 in the ninth year of Yǒnglè 永樂.
He was selected as a probationary compiler,
and soon appointed Compiler.
Xílǐ 習禮 was related by marriage to Liàn Zǐníng 練子寧.
After he became an official,
his fellow villagers treated him as a member of a treacherous faction,
and he was apprehensive.
Yáng Róng 楊榮 took the opportunity to speak to the Emperor,
who smiled and said:
“If Zǐníng 子寧 were still alive,
I would still employ him,
let alone Xílǐ 習禮.”
Upon Rénzōng’s 仁宗 accession,
he was promoted to Attendant Reader,
and concurrently appointed Drafter of Imperial Edicts,
returning home to visit his parents.
In the first year of Xuāndé 宣德, when the Veritable Records of the two reigns were being compiled,
he was recalled along with Attendant Lecturer Chén Jìngzōng 陳敬宗 and Chén Xún 陳循,
and promoted to Attendant Academician.
When Yīngzōng 英宗 inaugurated the imperial lectures,
he served as a lecturer.
Upon the completion of the Veritable Records of Xuānzōng 宣宗,
he was promoted to Academician,
and put in charge of the academy.
In the seventh year, the former Hónglú Sì 鴻臚寺 (Court of Imperial Entertainments) was converted into the Hànlín Yuàn 翰lín 翰林院 (Hànlín Academy).
When it was completed,
all the Grand Academicians of the various halls and pavilions arrived.
Xílǐ 習禮 did not set seats for Yáng Shìqí 楊士奇 and Yáng Pǔ 楊溥,
saying:
“This is not the office of the Three Dukes.”
Shìqí 士奇 and others reported this.
The Emperor ordered that seats be provided.
This subsequently became a precedent.
In the ninth year of Zhèngtǒng 正統, he requested to retire.
It was not granted.
The following year,
many positions of Vice Minister in the Six Ministries were vacant.
The Emperor ordered the Minister of Personnel, Wáng Zhí 王直, to consult with the high officials to make recommendations,
and specifically decreed Xílǐ’s 習禮 promotion to the Ministry of Rites.
Xílǐ 習禮 vigorously declined.
It was not approved.
When Wáng Zhèn 王振 was in power,
many high officials paid visits to his gate,
but Xílǐ 習禮 was ashamed to humble himself.
In the sixth month of the twelfth year, he again submitted a memorial requesting retirement,
and was then allowed to return home.
Xílǐ 習禮 was earnest in his conduct and principles,
cherished antiquity and adhered to ritual,
and his actions always conformed to rules.
He died at home fifteen years later,
at the age of eighty-nine.
He was posthumously named Wénsù 文肅.
Zhōu 周,
courtesy name Gōng 公,
was a native of Jíshuǐ 吉水.
At the age of eleven,
he could compose poetry.
He became a *jìnshì* 進士 in the sixteenth year of Yǒnglè 永樂.
He was selected as a probationary compiler.
He composed the "Ode to the Yellow Parrot,"
which pleased the Emperor,
and was appointed Compiler.
He successively served as Attendant Reader,
and lectured during the imperial lectures.
In the sixth year of Zhèngtǒng 正統, he submitted a memorial on current affairs,
and the Emperor praised and accepted it.
In the eighth year, he again memorialized in the summer, saying:
“Recently, there has been a drought.
Your Majesty has taken responsibility and prayed devoutly,
but your ministers have not been heard to offer loyal words to compensate for deficiencies,
only submitting petitions to ask for appointments.
Those in charge of selections disregard worthiness,
and merely follow qualifications.
Those in charge of national finances do not inquire about farming,
only diligently collecting taxes.
Soldiers are exhausted by labor,
punishments are meted out without proper consideration of severity,
the censors offer no spirited remonstrance,
and the remonstrating officials maintain silence.
Tens of thousands of monks and Daoist priests
daily consume household resources,
and there are numerous displaced people,
yet no one shows them compassion.”
The Emperor showed the memorial to his high officials.
Wáng Zhí 王直 and others all admitted their faults and requested to be dismissed.
In the eleventh year, he was promoted to Attendant Academician of Nánjīng 南京.
When Chéng Wáng 郕王 became regent,
he swiftly submitted a memorial, saying:
“The enemy of one’s sovereign and father is not to be shared the heavens with.
Your Highness should sleep on brushwood and taste gall,
like Yuè 越 avenging itself against Wú 吳.
Let the wise offer strategies,
and the brave exert their strength,
to diligently sweep clean the northern court,
and wipe away the national shame.
First dispatch eloquent envoys,
with humble words and rich gifts, to beg for the return of the imperial carriage,
temporarily humbling yourself for your sovereign and father.”

He then itemized eight proposals: to encourage resolve, to be close to the classics and histories, to reform military administration, to select virtuous talents, to pacify the hearts of the people, to broaden avenues for remonstrance, to be cautious of subtle beginnings, and to reform all government affairs.
The King gladly accepted them.
In the second year of Jǐngtài 景泰, he again requested the restoration of the midday court audience,
to meet with high officials daily,
to consult on methods of governance.
After the imperial lectures,
he suggested summoning literary officials to discuss political affairs,
and also issuing an edict to all officials and commoners throughout the realm to speak frankly about the shortcomings of current policies.
The Emperor then issued an edict seeking advice.
He possessed a spirited integrity,
and was earnest in his conduct and principles.
His great-grandfather, Yǐlì 以立,
during the Yuán 元 dynasty, felt that the structure of the histories of Sòng 宋, Liáo 遼, and Jīn 金 was inappropriate,
and wished to recompile them.
Zhōu 周 wished to continue his ancestor’s ambition.
At the end of Zhèngtǒng 正統,
he petitioned the court.
An imperial edict permitted him to compile it himself.
He organized and arranged it for several years,
but died before completion.
Liú Yǎn 劉儼,
courtesy name Xuānhuà 宣化,
from the same prefecture, became the first-ranked *jìnshì* 進士 in the seventh year of Zhèngtǒng 正統.
He successively served as Junior Imperial Sacrifices.
During the Jǐngtài 景泰 reign,
he presided over the Shùntiān 順天 provincial examination,
and dismissed the sons of Grand Academicians Chén Xún 陳循 and Wáng Wén 王文,
nearly bringing disaster upon himself.
Detailed information is in the biography of Gāo Gǔ 高穀.
In the early Tiānshùn 天順 reign,
he was appointed to manage the affairs of the Hànlín Yuàn 翰林院,
and died in office.
He was posthumously granted the title of Vice Minister of Rites,
and posthumously named Wénjiè 文介.
Yǎn 儼 was upright when serving at court,
and also had a reputation for virtuous conduct in his hometown.
Kē Qián,
courtesy name Mèngshí,
was a native of Pútián.
In the second year of Jǐngtài, he passed the imperial examination as the top scholar (Jìnshì Dìyī).
He successively served as Xǐmǎ.
In the early Tiānshùn reign,
he was promoted to Shàngbǎo Shǎoqīng
and concurrently Xiūzhuàn.
When Emperor Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Hànlín Xuéshì for being an old palace official.
After the compilation of the Yīngzōng Shílù (Veritable Records of Emperor Yīngzōng) was completed,
he was promoted to Shǎo Zhānshì.
During the mourning for Empress Cíyì Tàihòu,
Qián, along with Xiūzhuàn Luó Jǐng, submitted a memorial
requesting a joint burial in Yùlíng.
Court officials successively contended for this.
No reply was given.
Qián said,
"For major affairs of the court,
and the great principles of a minister,
what else should one focus their mind on but this?"
Both he and Jǐng submitted a second memorial to contend for it,
and eventually, it was granted according to ritual.
He successively encountered the deaths of his parents,
and an imperial edict summoned him to serve as Jìjiǔ,
but he firmly pleaded to observe the full mourning period.
This was granted.
Not long after, he died.
Qián was profound in literature,
and his character was lofty and principled.
While serving as Hànlín Xuéshì,
he built the Qīngfēng Tíng (Pure Wind Pavilion) in the rear garden of the academy,
dug a pond and planted lotuses,
and planted two cypresses behind the main hall.
People called his pavilion Kē Tíng,
and the cypresses Xuéshì Bǎi (Scholar's Cypresses).
There was a well in the academy,
which Hànlín Xuéshì Liú Dìngzhī had dug.
Kē Tíng and Liú Jǐng
were considered admirable anecdotes in the Hànlín Academy.
Luó Jǐng,
courtesy name Míngzhòng,
was a native of Tàihé.
At the end of the Tiānshùn reign,
he passed the imperial examination.
He was appointed Biānxiū,
and then promoted to Xiūzhuàn.
He participated in the compilation of the Sòng Yuán Tōngjiàn Gāngmù.
He successively held various positions, eventually reaching Xǐmǎ.
When Emperor Xiàozōng was still the Crown Prince,
he was selected to attend him as a lecturer.
He returned home due to his mother's death.
Jǐng, along with Shàngshū Yǐn Mínzǐ and Shìjiǎng Lóng, all married into the Kǒng clan.
When Mín incurred disfavor,
Lǐ Zīxǐng pointed to Jǐng as Mín's partisan,
and he was demoted to Yuánwàiláng of the Nanjing Ministry of Rites.
When Emperor Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
Wáng Shù and others spoke of Jǐng's talent,
so he was appointed Fújiàn Tíxué Fùshǐ.
In the fifth year of Hóngzhì, he was summoned to serve as Nanjing Jìjiǔ.
After a long time,
he died.
Kǒng Gōngxún,
courtesy name Zōngwén,
was the 58th-generation descendant of the First Sage.
In the fifth year of Jǐngtài, he passed the Huìshì (Metropolitan Examination),
but hearing of his mother's illness,
he did not attend the Diànduì (Palace Examination).
The emperor inquired about this with the Ministry of Rites,
which fully explained the reason,
so an envoy was sent to summon him.
It was already past noon,
and he had no time to prepare his examination paper,
so the Hànlín Academy was ordered to provide him with writing materials.
He passed the examination,
and immediately returned home to observe mourning for his mother.
When the Yǎnshèng Gōng Kǒng Yànjìn died,
his grandson Hóngxù was young and weak,
so an imperial edict dispatched an official from the Ministry of Rites to manage the funeral,
and Gōngxún managed his family affairs.
In the early Tiānshùn reign,
he was appointed Lǐ Kē Jǐshìzhōng.
Hóngxù had already inherited the title,
and the Grand Secretary Lǐ Xián married him to his daughter,
whereupon Gōngxún gained acquaintance with Xián.
Xián said,
"Gōngxún
is a descendant of the Great Sage,
and Zànshàn Sīmǎ Xún
is a descendant of the great Song worthy, Wēnguó Gōng Guāng.
They are suitable to assist and guide the Crown Prince."
The emperor was pleased.
On the same day, he was extraordinarily promoted to Shǎo Zhānshì
to attend the Eastern Palace for lectures and readings.
He went in and spoke to Empress Xiàosù, saying,
"Today I have found descendants of sages and worthies to be the tutors for your son."
Empress Xiàosù
was Emperor Xiànzōng's birth mother,
and at that time, she was favored as Imperial Noble Consort.
Thereupon, she prepared her ceremonial robes and bowed in thanks,
and it was circulated in the palace as a grand event.
When Emperor Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
he reassigned Gōngxún as Dàlǐ Zuǒ Shǎoqīng.
Gōngxún said he was not proficient in law,
so he was reinstated as Shǎo Zhānshì.
In the second year of Chénghuà, he submitted a memorial on military affairs,
which caused an uproar among the various military officials,
and Jǐshìzhōng and Yùshǐ submitted memorials in succession to refute him.
He was imprisoned
and demoted to Zhīfǔ of Hànyáng.
Before he arrived,
he observed mourning for his father.
After the mourning period ended,
Shāng Lù requested that officials who had been punished for offering remonstrance be reinstated,
so he was restored to his former rank,
and assumed office at the Nanjing Zhānshì Fǔ.
After a long time,
he died.
Sīmǎ Xún,
courtesy name Xúnrú,
was a native of Shānyīn, Zhèjiāng.
At the end of the Zhèngtǒng reign,
he was promoted from Jǔrén to Xíng Kē Jǐshìzhōng,
and successively promoted to Shǎo Zhānshì.
When Emperor Xiànzōng ascended,
he was ordered to concurrently serve as Guózǐ Jìjiǔ.
Upon his death,
he was posthumously granted Lǐbù Zuǒ Shìláng.
Xún had a strong memory and was honest and tolerant;
he never offended anyone.
While in office, he did not show any particular achievements.
Zàn says: In the early Jiànwén reign,
the principle of honoring the worthy and respecting the aged was practiced.
Dǒng Lún was highly regarded as an experienced scholar;
although he showed few particular achievements,
he certainly did not act perfunctorily.
Yí Zhì and his son successively advanced through generations with their Confucian scholarship,
assisting and guiding with grace;
they were indeed worthy.
Zōu Jì and others,
who were favored as palace officials but could not escape slanderous machinations,
and Chén Jì and his kind, who rose from commoners
and served in close proximity to the emperor and ended well,
indeed experienced both fortune and misfortune.
The two Zhōus, Wáng Yīng, Qián Xílǐ, Zhōu, and Kē Qián were humble, harmonious, upright, and sincere,
each demonstrating their excellence;
they were indeed different from those who pursued superficial showiness and extensive but shallow learning.
Collated Notes
Biographies, Chapter 41: Sòng Lǐ (Lín Fāng), Chén Xuān (Wáng Yú), Zhōu Chén
Sòng Lǐ,
courtesy name Dàběn,
was a native of Yǒngníng, Hénán.
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
he was promoted from Guózǐshēng to Qiánshì of the Shānxī Ànchásī,
then demoted to Zhǔshì of the Ministry of Revenue.
In the early Jiànwén reign,
he was recommended and appointed Qiánshì of the Shǎnxī Ànchásī,
but again, due to an incident, he was demoted to Yuánwàiláng of the Ministry of Justice.
When Emperor Chéngzǔ ascended the throne,
he was ordered to provisionally manage the affairs of the Ministry of Rites,
and due to his diligence and experience, he was promoted to Shìláng of the Ministry of Rites.
In the second year of Yǒnglè, he was appointed Shàngshū of the Ministry of Works.
He once requested that cattle and seeds be provided for military agricultural colonies in Shāndōng,
and also requested that criminals who lacked the ability to pay fines through labor be relocated to Běijīng to become commoners,
both of which were approved.
In the seventh year, he observed mourning for his mother,
but an imperial edict ordered him to remain in office and attend to duties.
In the ninth year, he was ordered to open the Huìtōng Hé.
The Huìtōng Hé was,
in the Zhìyuán reign of the Yuán dynasty,
based on the words of Hán Zhònghuī, the magistrate of Shòuzhāng,
a river dug from Ānmín Shān in Dōngpíng to Línqīng.
It diverted the Wèn River to cut off the Jǐ River,
and connected it to the Wèi River,
serving as a transport canal.
It was named Huìtōng.
However, the banks were narrow and the water shallow,
rendering it unsuitable for heavy loads.
Thus, throughout the Yuán dynasty, sea transport was more common.
In the early Míng dynasty, provisions shipped to Liáodōng and Běipíng
also exclusively used sea transport.
In the twenty-fourth year of Hóngwǔ,
the river burst its banks at Yuánwǔ,
cutting off Ānshān Hú,
and the Huìtōng then became silted up.
In the early Yǒnglè reign,
Běijīng was established,
and both river and sea transport were used.
Sea transport was perilous and distant, often resulting in losses,
while river transport went from the Jiāng and Huái rivers to Yángwǔ,
requiring corvée laborers from Shānxī and Hénán
to haul goods overland for 170 lǐ into the Wèi River,
passing through eight relay stations.
The people suffered greatly from this labor.
At this time, Pān Shúzhèng, the Assistant Prefect of Jìníng Zhōu, submitted a memorial, saying:
"Of the old Huìtōng Hé, over 450 lǐ,
one-third is silted.
It would be convenient to dredge it."
Thereupon, Sòng Lǐ and Jīn Chún, the Vice Ministers of Rites and Justice, and Dū Dū Zhōu Cháng were ordered to oversee the work.
Sòng Lǐ believed that the source of the Huìtōng
must draw upon the Wèn River.
He then adopted the strategy of Bái Yīng, an old man from Wènshàng,
to build the Gāngchéng and Dàicūn Bà dams,
stretching five lǐ across,
to block the flow of the Wèn River,
preventing it from entering the Guāng River to the south and flowing into the sea to the north.
All the waters from the various springs were collected
and channeled out from Wènshàng,
reaching Nánwàng,
where they were divided into two channels:
four-tenths flowed south to connect with Xú and Pèi,
and six-tenths flowed north to reach Línqīng.
Nánwàng had high terrain,
so when its waters were released,
they flowed both north and south.
This was known as the water divide (shuǐ jí).
Accordingly, gates were installed based on the terrain
to store and release water as needed.
From the water divide north to Línqīng,
the land dropped ninety chǐ,
and seventeen gates were installed,
reaching the Wèi River;
from the water divide south to Gūtóu,
the land dropped one hundred sixteen chǐ,
and twenty-one gates were installed,
reaching the Huái River.
In total, 300,000 people from Shāndōng, Xúzhōu, Yìngtiān, Zhènjiāng, and Yánzhōu were conscripted,
and over 1,100,000 shí of rent were exempted.
The work was completed in twenty xún (120 days).
He also memorialized to dredge the Shā Hé into the Mǎcháng Bó lake
to supplement the Wèn River.
Details are in the Héqú Zhì (Treatise on Rivers and Canals).
That year,
the Emperor again adopted the advice of Zhāng Xìn, the Vice Minister of Works,
and ordered Xīng'ān Bó Xú Hēng and Jiǎng Tíngzàn, the Vice Minister of Works, to meet with Jīn Chún
to dredge from Yúwángkǒu in Xiángfú down to Zhōngluán,
restoring the old course of the Huáng Hé
to reduce the force of the water,
preventing the river from impeding grain transport.
Sòng Lǐ was ordered to oversee this concurrently.
In the eighth month, he returned to the capital,
was ranked first for his achievements,
and received a superior reward.
Pān Shúzhèng was also granted clothing and paper currency.
The following year,
due to the Censor Xǔ Kān's report on flooding in the Wèi River,
Sòng Lǐ was ordered to go and plan countermeasures.
Sòng Lǐ requested to open two branch canals from Wèijiāwān
to discharge water into the Tǔ Hé,
and also to open one branch canal from northwest of Dézhōu
to discharge water into the old Huáng Hé,
allowing it to enter the sea via the Dàgū Hé at Hǎifēng.
The Emperor ordered this to be done after the autumn harvest.
Sòng Lǐ returned and reported:
"Sea transport passes through dangerous obstacles,
and ships are damaged every year,
some even drifting away and sinking.
Officials responsible for repairs,
pressured by deadlines,
often extort money, causing hardship for the people,
and the ships are also not sturdy.
It is estimated that one sea vessel
uses one hundred men to transport one thousand shí,
and its cost could buy twenty river vessels, each holding two hundred shí.
These ships would use ten men
and could transport four thousand shí.
Based on this,
the advantages and disadvantages are clear.
I request to allocate grain from Zhènjiāng, Fèngyáng, Huái'ān, Yángzhōu, and Yǎnzhōu,
totaling one million shí,
to be transported by river to Běijīng.
Sea transport would then be used every two out of three years."
Soon after, Chén Xuān, the Earl of Píngjiāng, also reported the completion of his work on the rivers between the Jiāng and Huái.
Consequently, river transport became greatly convenient,
and the amount of transported grain increased.
In the thirteenth year, sea transport was thus abolished.
Previously,
when the Emperor was about to construct Běijīng,
he ordered Sòng Lǐ to procure timber from Chuānshǔ.
Sòng Lǐ cut paths through mountains
and reported:
"Several large trees were obtained,
all several zhàng long.
One night,
they emerged from the valley and reached the riverbank by themselves,
with a sound like thunder,
without bending a single blade of grass."
The court considered this an auspicious sign.
After the river project was completed,
he was again sent to Shǔ to procure timber.
In the sixteenth year, he was ordered to administer justice in Jiāngxī.
The following year, he was summoned back from Shǔ
after constructing "foreign boats" (fānzhōu).
Due to old age and illness, he was exempted from court attendance,
and if he had matters to report, he would have a Vice Minister submit them on his behalf.
In the seventh month of the twentieth year, he died in office.
Sòng Lǐ had a firm character
and was strict with his subordinates,
hence he was efficient in accomplishing tasks,
but for this reason, he was not well-liked by people.
On the day he died,
his family had no leftover wealth.
In the first year of Hóngxī,
Lǚ Zhèn, the Minister of Rites, requested that he be given a funeral and sacrifices according to regulations.
In the Hóngzhì reign,
Wáng Chǒng, a Secretary, first requested the establishment of a memorial temple.
An imperial decree ordered him to be worshipped on the Nánwàng Hú,
with Jīn Chún and Zhōu Cháng as co-worshippers.
In the sixth year of Lóngqìng, Sòng Lǐ was posthumously granted the title of Tàizǐ Tàibǎo.
Lìn Fāng
was from Xià Xiàn.
In the Hóngwǔ reign, he passed the Xiàolián examination.
He successively rose to be a Director in the Ministry of Justice.
In the Yǒnglè reign,
he was appointed as the Prefect of Jí'ān.
He was lenient, honest, and incorruptible,
and the people greatly respected his virtue.
People from Jíshuǐ went to the imperial court, claiming there was a silver mine in the county,
and an envoy was sent to investigate.
The elders blocked Lìn Fāng and complained, saying:
"We heard that in the late Sòng dynasty, someone also made such a claim,
and eventually incurred punishment for making a false statement.
Now, this is all cultivated land,
how could there be a silver mine?"
Lìn Fāng questioned the accuser
and found the claim to be false.
When the case was ready,
his colleagues dared not sign their names,
but Lìn Fāng requested to take sole responsibility.
When the memorial was submitted,
the Emperor said:
"I indeed knew it was false."
The matter was dropped.
Later,
he was demoted to an executive official (bànshì guān) due to an incident
and followed Sòng Lǐ to manage the Huìtōng Hé.
He was later reinstated as a Department Director of Water Conservancy in the Ministry of Works.
In the tenth year,
the Yellow River burst its banks at Yángwǔ,
inundating Zhōngmóu, Xiángfú, and Wèishì.
Fāng was dispatched to inspect it.
Fāng said:
"The salt dykes in the center are directly in the path of the torrent;
I request they be reinforced and blocked."
He further said:
"Diverting the river's flow from Zhōngluán
to make it follow its old course north into the sea
would truly be a benefit for ten thousand generations."
He also said:
"The newly constructed bank revetments
use only grass ropes,
and cannot last long.
It would be better to weave wood into large circular enclosures,
drive piles through them,
fill them with瓦 stones,
and then horizontally cross piles with wood,
attaching them to the dyke.
This would be a long-term strategy to reduce the water's force and secure the dyke."
An imperial edict ordered that all his suggestions be followed.
Thereafter, those who built dykes observed and used his methods.
Upon Sòng Lǐ's recommendation,
he was promoted to Right Vice Minister of the Board of Works.
Not long after,
the acting Grand Minister of the Imperial Stud, Yáng Dǐ, said:
"The fields at Wúqiáo, Dōngguāng, Xīngjì, Jiāohé, and Tiānjīn were damaged by floods when dykes burst.
I request that the old course of the Yellow River southeast of Dézhōu's Liángdiàn be opened
to divert the water's force."
Fāng was again ordered to go and manage it.
In the prefectures and districts he passed through,
he would regularly report any inconveniences to the people.
After the task was completed, he returned,
and in the eleventh month of the fifteenth year, he died in office.
Fāng lived frugally,
wearing plain clothes and eating vegetarian food.
He was extremely filial to his mother.
His mother was very virtuous.
Whatever matters Fāng handled,
he would surely inform his mother in the evening.
If anything was inappropriate,
she would instruct and admonish him.
Fāng respectfully accepted his mother's advice,
and thus he became a good official.
Chén Xuān,
courtesy name Yànchún,
was a native of Héfèi.
His father, Wén,
joined Tàizǔ with a thousand militiamen,
and was successively promoted to Assistant Regional Military Commissioner.
Xuān inherited his father's position.
When his father was exiled to Liáoyáng for an offense,
Xuān prostrated himself at the palace gate, requesting to take his place,
and an imperial edict pardoned both father and son.
As a youth, Xuān served in the Grand General's staff,
and was praised for his goose hunting skills.
He frequently joined expeditions against the southern barbarians,
and also campaigned against Yuèxī,
suppressing the rebellious barbarian Yuèlǔ Tièmù'ér of Jiànchāng.
He crossed Liángshān,
pacified Tiānxīng Zhài,
and defeated the various barbarians of Níngfān.
He again campaigned against Yánjǐng,
and advanced to attack Bǔshuǐ Wǎzhài.
The rebels were very fierce.
Xuān commanded the central army,
and the rebels surrounded him several layers deep.
Xuān dismounted and shot,
injuring his foot,
but continued to fight with his wound bandaged.
From 巳 (9-11 am) to 酉 (5-7 pm),
he returned with his entire army.
He also joined the campaign against Jiǎhālā,
using elite troops to cross the Dǎchōng River,
finding a secret path,
and building a pontoon bridge to ferry the army.
After crossing,
he dismantled the bridge,
showing the soldiers there was no turning back,
and continuously fought and defeated the rebels.
He also joined forces with the Yúnnán army in the campaign against the Báiyí with distinction,
and was promoted to Assistant Regional Military Commissioner of the Sìchuān Provincial Military Command.
At the end of Jiànwén's reign,
he was promoted to Assistant Military Commissioner of the Right Army.
As the Yān army approached,
he was ordered to command the navy to defend the river.
When the Yān army reached Pǔkǒu,
Xuān surrendered with his navy,
and Chéngzǔ was thus able to cross the river.
After his enthronement,
Xuān was enfeoffed as the Earl of Píngjiāng,
receiving a salary of one thousand dàn of grain,
granted an imperial patent,
and his position as Military Commissioner was made hereditary.
