In the first year of Yǒnglè, Xuān was appointed Commander-in-Chief,
overall supervisor of maritime transport,
and transported over 490,000 dàn of grain
to supply Běijīng and Liáodōng.
He then built the Bǎiwàn Cāng (Million Granary) at Zhígū,
and fortified Tiānjīn Wèi.
Previously,
when grain boats sailed on the sea,
the islanders, fearing the grain soldiers,
often hid themselves.
Xuān invited them to engage in mutual trade,
standardizing prices,
which benefited everyone.
Upon the return of the transport fleet,
they encountered Japanese pirates at Shāmén Dǎo.
Xuān pursued them to Jīnzhōu Bái Shān Dǎo,
burning almost all their boats.
In the ninth year, he was ordered to command the Zhèjiāng and Mǐnán troops with the Marquis of Fēngchéng, Lǐ Bīn, to capture sea pirates.
The sea overflowed and the dykes collapsed,
from Hǎimén to Yánchéng, a distance of one hundred and thirty *lǐ*.
Xuān was ordered to build and repair them with 400,000 soldiers,
constructing over 18,000 *zhàng* of tide-resistant dykes.
The next year,
Xuān said:
"The coastal area of Jiādìng
is where river currents converge.
When sea vessels anchor here,
there are no high mountains or large hills to rely on.
I request that an earthen hill be built at Qīngpǔ,
one hundred *zhàng* square,
and over thirty *zhàng* high,
with a marker post erected."
After its completion,
it was named Bǎoshān (Precious Mountain),
and the emperor personally wrote an inscription for it.
After Sòng Lǐ had completed the governance of the Huìtōng River,
the court debated abolishing maritime transport,
and Xuān was still placed in charge of grain transport.
It was proposed to build over two thousand shallow-draft boats,
initially transporting two million *dàn*,
gradually increasing to five million *dàn*,
which enriched the national treasury.
At that time, grain boats from Jiāngnán reaching Huái'ān
often had to portage overland across the dam,
crossing the Huái River to reach Qīnghé,
which was extremely laborious and costly.
In the thirteenth year,
Xuān, following the advice of elders,
dug a canal twenty *lǐ* long from Guǎnjiā Hú west of Huái'ān city,
creating Qīngjiāng Pǔ,
to guide lake water into the Huái River,
and built four sluices for timely drainage.
He also built a dyke ten *lǐ* along the lake to guide boats,
whereby grain boats could directly reach the river,
saving immeasurable expenses.
Afterwards, he again dredged the river from Xúzhōu to Jìníng.
Also, because the Lǚliáng Hóng was dangerous,
he dug another canal to the west,
installed two sluices,
and impounded water to facilitate transport.
He also built long dykes at Pèixiàn Diāoyáng Hú and Jìníng Nánwàng Hú,
and opened the Táizhōu Bái Tǎ Hé to connect to the Great River.
He also built dykes at Gāoyóu Hú,
and dug a canal forty *lǐ* long within the dykes
to avoid the dangers of wind and waves.
Furthermore, from Huái'ān to Línqīng,
he strategically placed forty-seven sluices according to water conditions,
and built forty permanent granaries at Huái'ān,
as well as granaries at Xúzhōu, Línqīng, and Tōngzhōu,
to facilitate transshipment.
Fearing that grain boats might run aground,
he established five hundred and sixty-eight posts from Huái'ān to Tōngzhōu,
each staffed with soldiers
to guide boats to avoid shallow areas.
He also dug wells and planted trees along the river dykes
to provide convenience for travelers.
All his plans
were precise and far-reaching.
He personally managed the Grand Canal for thirty years,
leaving no strategy untried.
In the ninth month of Rénzōng's (仁宗) accession to the throne,
Xuān (瑄) submitted a memorial detailing seven matters.
First, Nánjīng (南京) is the fundamental capital of the nation;
he requested stringent defensive preparations.
Second, recommendations and promotions should be carefully verified,
without adhering to strict qualifications,
and upright court officials should be selected to tour the empire.
Third, the empire's annual transportation of grain and provisions:
Húguǎng (湖廣), Jiāngxī (江西), Zhèjiāng (浙江), and the prefectures of Sūzhōu (蘇) and Sōngjiāng (松) are all far from Běijīng (北京),
the round trip taking over a year,
resulting in outstanding public taxes
and interference with farming.
He requested that the grain be transported to Huái (淮) and Xúzhōu (徐) and other places,
and then other imperial military personnel be ordered to take over the transportation to the capital.
Furthermore, fast boats and horse boats carry no more than fifty or sixty shí (石) of grain;
each boat has sufficient imperial military personnel,
but the authorities add military and civilian personnel for relaying,
detaining and gathering them to wait,
leading to freezing and starvation.
He requested these practices be abolished.
Fourth, many educational officials are not suitable for their posts;
he requested that those found incompetent be dismissed,
talented and outstanding individuals be selected to supplement the students,
and military children also be allowed to enter schools.
Fifth, regarding military desertion:
he requested that the old and infirm be verified
and replaced by their sons,
deserters be pursued and apprehended,
and households with no heirs be verified and removed from the register.
Sixth, Kaīpíng (開平) and other places
are vital border defense locations,
but their troops and provisions are deficient;
he requested that elite soldiers be selected and trained,
to both garrison and attend to their duties.
Seventh, the military personnel for grain transport
travel north every year,
and upon returning immediately repair their boats,
toiling diligently throughout the year.
The respective guards and outposts also take advantage of this time
to impose miscellaneous corvée duties, further burdening them.
He requested that this be strictly prohibited.
The emperor read the memorial and said,
"Xuān's (瑄) words are all appropriate."
He ordered the relevant departments to act quickly.
Subsequently, an imperial edict was issued to commend him,
and soon a certificate was bestowed,
granting him hereditary Earl of Píngjiāng (平江伯).
Upon Xuānzōng's (宣宗) accession,
he was ordered to guard Huái'ān (淮安)
and supervise grain transport as before.
In Xuāndé (宣德) fourth year, he stated:
"North of Jìníng (濟寧),
from Chánggōu (長溝) to Zǎolín (棗林), the waterway is silted up.
An estimated 120,000 people are needed to dredge it,
and it can be completed in half a month."
The emperor, mindful of Xuān's (瑄) long service,
ordered Grand Secretary Huáng Fú (黃福) to go and manage it with him.
In the sixth year,
Xuān (瑄) stated:
"Annually, 120,000 military personnel are used for grain transport,
enduring frequent hardships.
I request that civilian able-bodied men be separately recruited from the prefectures of Sūzhōu (蘇) and Sōngjiāng (松), and from Jiāngxī (江西), Zhèjiāng (浙江), and Húguǎng (湖廣),
and also soldiers be recruited from military posts with abundant troops,
totaling 240,000 people,
to transport in rotation.
Furthermore, the people of Jiāngnán (江南)
transport grain to Línqīng (臨清), Huái'ān (淮安), and Xúzhōu (徐州),
a round trip taking one year,
which delays and interferes with agriculture.
And the soldiers from Húguǎng (湖廣), Jiāngxī (江西), Zhèjiāng (浙江), and Sūzhōu (蘇), Sōngjiāng (松), Ānqìng (安慶)
travel with empty boats to Huái'ān (淮安) to load grain every year.
If the people of Jiāngnán (江南) were to allocate grain to nearby military posts,
and imperial military personnel transport it to the capital,
with a calculated allowance for wastage and travel expenses,
then both the military and civilians would benefit."
The emperor ordered Huáng Fú (黃福) and Vice Minister Wáng Zuǒ (王佐) to discuss and implement it.
The change from civilian transport to exchange transport began from this time.
In the eighth year, tenth month, he died in office,
at the age of sixty-nine.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Marquis of Píngjiāng (平江侯),
granted Grand Tutor (Tàibǎo, 太保),
and given the posthumous name Gōngxiāng (恭襄).
Initially,
Xuān (瑄) was virtuous to the people by dredging rivers,
and the people erected a temple for him in Qīnghé (清河) county.
During the Zhèngtǒng (正統) era,
the authorities were ordered to offer sacrifices in spring and autumn.
His grandson, Yù (豫),
courtesy name Lìqīng (立卿),
was studious and meticulous.
At the end of the Zhèngtǒng (正統) era,
when bandits rose in Shāxiàn (沙縣), Fújiàn (福建),
he, as Deputy Commander-in-Chief (Fù Zǒngbīng, 副總兵), followed Marquis of Níngyáng (寧陽侯) Chén Mào (陳懋) in separate routes to suppress them,
and was promoted to Marquis.
When Yěxiān (也先) invaded,
he was dispatched to garrison Línqīng (臨清),
where he built fortifications,
trained soldiers, and pacified the people,
maintaining peace and order without disturbance.
The following year, he was recalled,
but the elders of the area went to the court to request his retention.
This was granted.
In Jǐngtài (景泰) fifth year,
when Shandōng (山東) suffered famine,
he was ordered to provide relief.
Soon after, he was appointed Garrison Commander of Nánjīng (南京).
In Tiānshùn (天順) first year, he was recalled,
and his annual stipend was increased by one hundred shí (石).
He died in the seventh year.
He was posthumously granted Duke of Yīguó (黟國公),
and given the posthumous name Zhuāngmǐn (莊敏).
His son Ruì (銳) inherited the earldom.
In the early Chénghuà (成化) era,
he was assigned to manage the Three Thousand Camp and the Tuan Camp.
Soon after, he was given the seal of the General Pacifying Barbarians (Píngmán Jiāngjūn, 平蠻將軍),
and was made Commander-in-Chief of Guǎngdōng (廣東) and Guǎngxī (廣西).
He was then transferred to garrison Huáiyáng (淮陽),
and supervise grain transport.
He constructed stone sluice gates at the mouth of the Huái (淮) River and the north and south diversion gates at Jìníng (濟寧).
He built dikes, dredged springs,
and repaired neglected works.
He served as Chief Supervisor of Grain Transport for fourteen years,
submitting dozens of memorials.
A Japanese tribute envoy bought several civilian men and women to take back with him,
passing through Huái'ān (淮安).
Ruì (銳) detained them and did not let them go,
redeeming them and returning them to their families.
During famine and plague in Huái (淮) and Yángzhōu (揚州),
he cooked porridge and distributed medicine,
saving many lives.
In Hóngzhì (弘治) sixth year,
when the river burst its banks at Zhāngqiū (張秋),
he was ordered to stop the breach and repair it.
Upon his return,
his stipend was increased by two hundred shí (石),
and he was successively promoted to Grand Tutor (Tàifù, 太傅) and concurrently Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàifù, 太子太傅).
In the thirteenth year,
Huǒshāi (火篩) raided Dàtóng (大同).
Ruì (銳), as Commander-in-Chief (Zǒngbīng Guān, 總兵官) bearing the general's seal, went to reinforce.
Upon arrival,
he merely held his troops and defended himself,
for which he was impeached by the Supervising Secretary (Gěishìzhōng, 給事中) and Censor (Yùshǐ, 御史),
deprived of his stipend, and dismissed to his residence.
He died that same year.
His son Xióng (熊) succeeded.
In Zhèngdé (正德) third year, he was dispatched to supervise grain transport.
Liú Jǐn (劉瑾) demanded money,
but Xióng (熊) refused,
which earned Liú Jǐn's (劉瑾) resentment.
Accused of an offense,
he was arrested and imprisoned in the imperial prison,
then exiled to garrison Hǎinán (海南)衛,
and stripped of his patent and certificate.
Xióng (熊) was naturally corrupt
and had greatly harmed the people in Huáinán (淮南).
Although he was entrapped by Liú Jǐn (劉瑾),
no one felt sorry for him.
After Liú Jǐn's (劉瑾) execution,
he was pardoned and his title restored.
He died
without a son.
Then, Zǐguī succeeded him.
He was recommended to be appointed as the Grand Defender of Liǎngguǎng.
When rebels rose in Fēngchuān,
Guī commanded his generals to go and suppress them.
He captured their leader,
and thousands were taken captive or slain.
He was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Tàibǎo).
He then pacified the bandits in Liǔqìng and Hèlián Shān,
and was promoted to Grand Tutor (Tàibǎo),
and one of his sons was given an inherited position.
Fàn Zǐyí of Ānnán and others raided Qīn and Lián,
while Límí, a bandit, raided Qióngyá,
forming a pincer movement.
Guī sent a dispatch to Ānnán,
explaining the advantages and disadvantages,
and had them bind Fàn Zǐyí.
He then rapidly dispatched troops to attack Límí,
defeating and routing them.
In recognition of his merits,
another son was given an inherited position,
and his annual salary was increased by forty shi of grain.
Guī was able to share hardships with his soldiers.
Whenever he heard where the rebels were,
he would don his armor and be the first to ascend.
Through deep thickets and precipitous ravines,
he braved noxious miasma,
avoiding nothing.
Thus, wherever he went, he achieved victory.
He remained in Yuè for nearly ten years,
exterminating countless minor bandits.
He was recalled
to take charge of the Rear Army Command (Hòujūnfǔ).
Guī's wife was Lady Qiú,
the younger sister of Marquis of Xiánníng, Luán.
Guī deeply resented Luán,
and Luán repeatedly spoke ill of Guī to Shìzōng,
nearly causing him to be punished.
When Luán was defeated,
the emperor esteemed Guī even more,
ordering him to command all the Beijing garrison troops.
When bandits entered Zǐjīngguān,
Guī requested to engage them,
and encamped at Lúgōu.
The bandits retreated, and he stopped.
The following year,
bandits again entered Gǔběikǒu.
Some suggested arraying camps at the Nine Gates as a defense,
but Guī argued that this would merely show weakness and be useless.
The bandits also soon retreated.
He supervised the construction of the outer wall of the capital,
and was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Tàifù).
When he died,
he was posthumously granted the title of Grand Tutor (Tàifù),
and given the posthumous name Wǔxiāng.
His son, Wáng Mó, succeeded him.
He served as a Staff Supervising Secretary (Qiānshū) in the Rear Army Command,
and was appointed as the Grand Defender of Liǎngguǎng.
When the bandit Zhāng Lián rebelled,
he plundered and massacred several prefectures.
Wáng Mó joined forces with Commander-in-Chief Zhāng Niè to suppress and pacify him,
capturing and beheading over thirty thousand.
In recognition of his merits, he was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Tàibǎo),
and one of his sons was given an inherited position.
During the Wànlì era, he was appointed as the Grand Defender of Huái'ān,
overseeing all grain transport.
He then entered the court to take charge of the Front Army Command (Qiánjūnfǔ).
When he died,
he was posthumously granted the title of Junior Guardian (Shàobǎo),
and given the posthumous name Wǔjìng.
The title was passed down until the fall of the Míng dynasty,
when the peerage ceased.
Wáng Yú,
courtesy name Tíngqì,
was a native of Shānyáng.
He joined the household of the Prince of Zhào as a company commander (zǒngqí).
Towards the end of the Yǒnglè era,
Mèng Xián, commander of the Chángshān Guard, and others conspired with the eunuch Huáng Yǎn,
planning to assassinate the emperor,
depose the crown prince, and enthrone the Prince of Zhào.
Their associate, Gāo Zhèng,
who was Yú's maternal uncle,
secretly informed Yú.
Yú was greatly alarmed and said:
"How can you devise such a plan that would exterminate the clan?"
He tearfully remonstrated.
But Gāo Zhèng did not listen.
Zhèng feared the plot would be exposed
and intended to kill Yú.
Yú thereupon went to the imperial palace to report the treachery.
An investigation confirmed it,
and Mèng Xián and the others were all executed.
Yú was appointed as a Chiliarch (Qiānhù) of the Liáohǎi Guard.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Assistant Commander (Zhīhuī Tóngzhī) of the Jǐnyī Guard,
and generously rewarded.
The emperor also instructed his colleagues
that all matters must be reported to Yú before being acted upon.
Yú upheld the greater principles
and was not nitpicky,
and the court praised his sagacity.
In the eighth year of Xuāndé, he was promoted to Assistant Regional Commander (Dūzhīhuī Qiānshì),
and appointed as Deputy Commander-in-Chief of the Left (Zuǒ Fù Zǒngbīng).
He replaced Chén Xuān as Grand Defender of Huái'ān,
overseeing the grain transport,
and was successively promoted to Assistant Regional Commander of the Left Army (Zuǒjūn Dūdu Qiānshì).
Huái'ān was Yú's hometown,
and people considered it an honor.
He was in Huái'ān for several years,
maintaining Chén Xuān's established practices without change,
and governed well.
There was a case where a man whose mother was still alive sued his brother over property.
Yú said:
"To sue one's brother is unfraternal,
and to disregard one's mother is unfilial."
He flogged them and sent them away.
There was also a case where people who could not repay money owed
led to a father-in-law and son-in-law, and brothers, suing each other.
Yú said:
"How can you harm relationships for the sake of money?"
He immediately repaid the debt for them
and urged them to be harmonious.
Two soldiers stole a single plank from a damaged boat.
Officials, considering it theft of government property,
sentenced the soldiers to death.
Yú said:
"Are the lives of two soldiers worth a single plank from a damaged boat?"
Ultimately, their sentence was reduced.
In years of famine,
he opened government granaries to provide relief.
However, he was fond of wealth,
which drew a sharp rebuke from Yīngzōng.
And some of the previous cases of sedition he reported were found to have been wrongly handled.
In the fourth year of Zhèngtǒng,
he went to the capital for a discussion.
He fell ill,
his two hands were constricted as if held high,
and he cried out for help and release before he died.
Zhōu Chén,
courtesy name Xúnrú,
was a native of Jíshuǐ.
He obtained his *jìnshì* degree in the second year of Yǒnglè.
He was selected as a probationary scholar (shùjíshì).
The following year,
Chéngzǔ selected twenty-eight among them
and ordered them to study in the Wényuángé.
Chén stated that he was young and begged to be included.
The emperor praised his ambition
and allowed it.
Soon after, he was promoted to Principal (Zhǔshì) in the Ministry of Punishments,
and then to Assistant Director (Yuánwàiláng).
Chén possessed talent for governing the world,
but he languished in minor official posts for twenty years,
unrecognized by others.
Only Xià Yuánjí considered him exceptional.
In the first year of Hóngxī,
he was slightly promoted to Chief Administrator (Zhǎngshǐ) of the Yuè Prefecture.
In the early years of Xuāndé,
there were recommendations for him to be a Prefect.
Yuánjí said:
"This is an ordinary appointment,
how can it fully utilize Mr. Zhōu's abilities?"
In the ninth month of the fifth year,
the emperor, noting that the empire's financial and tax affairs were largely mismanaged,
especially in Jiāngnán,
where Sūzhōu prefecture alone
had accumulated arrears of eight million *shí* of grain,
desired to find a capable and important minister to rectify the situation.
Therefore, acting on the recommendation of Grand Secretary Yáng Róng,
he promoted Chén to Vice Minister of Works (Gōngbù Yòushìláng)
to serve as Grand Coordinator (Xúnfǔ) of the Jiāngnán prefectures
and supervise all tax grain matters.
When he first arrived,
he summoned the elders and asked about the reasons for the tax arrears.
They all said that the powerful households were unwilling to bear the surcharges,
and instead levied them on the common people.
The people, being poor, fled,
and the tax quota became even more deficient.
Chén then devised the Píngmǐ Fǎ (method of equal grain distribution),
ordering that all surcharges must be equally distributed.
He also requested an imperial edict for the Gōngbù (Ministry of Works) to issue iron *hú* (bushels),
which were to be sent to all counties as a standard,
thus eliminating the *liángzhǎng* (grain chiefs) who practiced "large intake, small output."
According to the old system,
there were three *liángzhǎng*, one principal and two deputies,
who would go to the Hùbù (Ministry of Revenue) in Nánjīng in the seventh month to collect the official warrants (*kānhé*).
Once completed,
they would bring them back to the ministry.
The expenses for travel and return
were all levied from the people.
Chén limited the number to one principal and one deputy,
who would take turns going to collect.
After the task was finished,
the officials would typically collect and send them to the ministry.
The people greatly benefited.
Chén observed that the counties had no granaries for collecting grain,
and the *liángzhǎng* stored it at home,
saying:
"This is the reason for the arrears."
So, he ordered all counties to establish granaries (*dùn*) along waterways,
with one *liángtóu* (grain head) and one *dùnhù* (granary household) appointed for each granary,
who were in charge of collecting.
When the amount reached six or seven tens of thousands of *dàn* (shi) or more,
one *liángzhǎng* was appointed to oversee it all,
known as the *zǒngshōu* (general collector).
The people would bring their receipts to the granaries,
and officials would supervise the collection,
while the *liángzhǎng* merely attended scheduled meetings.
He established two ledgers: *bōyùn* (allocation and transport) and *gāngyùn* (fleet transport).
The *bōyùn* recorded the allocated amounts for transport,
and estimated the consumption of grain to be transported to the imperial capital and Tōngzhōu granaries,
determining allocations accordingly.
The *gāngyùn* allowed for the entry of expenses for shallow drafts and other costs,
which were reimbursed upon return.
Any surplus from allocations,
stored in the granaries,
was called *yúmǐ* (surplus grain).
If there was a large surplus the next year, it would be levied with a *liùzhēng* (six-fold levy),
and the year after that, a *wǔzhēng* (five-fold levy).
Initially,
when Tàizǔ pacified Wú,
he completely registered the estates and fields of his meritorious officials' descendants as government property.
Later, disliking wealthy and powerful families,
he confiscated their land and property for crimes,
all of which were called *guāntián* (official land).
Taxes were levied according to their household rental registers,
which is why the tax burden in Sūzhōu was exceptionally heavy compared to other prefectures.
The total rent from official and private lands was 2.77 million *dàn*,
with the rent from official land alone reaching 2.62 million *dàn*.
The people could not bear it.
At that time, Xuānzōng repeatedly issued edicts to reduce official land rent.
Chén, together with Prefect Kuàng Zhōng, meticulously calculated for several months,
reducing it by over 720,000 *dàn*.
Other prefectures followed suit with reductions,
and the people began to recover slightly.
In the seventh year,
Jiāngnán experienced a great harvest.
An imperial edict ordered all prefectures and counties to purchase grain at a fair price with government paper currency for disaster relief and loans.
Sūzhōu thus obtained 290,000 *dàn* of grain.
At that time, the stipends of dukes and marquises,
and the monthly salaries of military officials,
were all paid by the Nán Hùbù.
For the people of Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng who transported grain to Nánjīng,
each *dàn* incurred an additional six *dòu* (pecks) in expenses.
Chén memorialized that it should be paid from the respective prefectures,
with one *dòu* of grain given for boat fees.
The remaining five *dòu*,
totaling over 400,000 *dàn* of grain,
plus the grain purchased with government paper currency,
amounted to over 700,000 *dàn* of grain.
He then established granaries to store it,
naming them Jìnóng (Aid to Farmers).
Beyond disaster relief and loans,
there was a surplus each year.
All losses from fleet transport, wind damage, or theft
were borrowed from this fund.
At harvest time,
the amount was repaid to the government.
Rations provided for repairing dikes, building embankments, digging canals, and dredging lakes
were not required to be repaid.
Farmers requesting loans
were given according to their medium and lower economic capacity and the amount of their land.
They repaid it with their autumn grain, and in years of famine, they received further relief.
Those who were cunning and did not repay
would not be granted loans again.
He established these regulations and reported them.
The Emperor praised and commended him.
Throughout Chén's tenure,
the common people of several large prefectures in Jiāngnán
did not experience famine,
and the two taxes were never in arrears.
This was due to Chén's efforts.
At that time,
military and civilian transport were about half and half.
Military boats were provided by the government,
while civilians had to hire boats,
incurring various extra costs,
often spending three *dàn* to transport one *dàn*.
The round trip took a year, disrupting their farming.
Chén discussed with the Earl of Píngjiāng, Chén Xuān,
that civilian transport should be handed over at Huái'ān or Guāzhōu waterways,
and the grain transport army would then carry it to Tōngzhōu.
An additional five *dòu* per *dàn* was added at Huái'ān,
and another five *shēng* (pints) at Guāzhōu.
For those nearby and Nánjīng military personnel who had not crossed the river,
delivery was made directly at the granary,
with an additional two *dòu* of grain for crossing the river,
and five *hé* (gills) of grain in lieu of straw mats for padding.
If the exchange army was delayed or obstructed by wind,
the prefectures and counties were ordered to provide surplus grain.
A storage shed was established at the Guāzhōu waterway,
where grain was moved and stored,
and a measured amount of surplus grain was given to the guards.
As a result, grain transport expenses were greatly reduced.
The annual transport of horse fodder to the two capitals
was costly and enormous.
Chén requested that each bundle be commuted to three *fēn* (cents) of silver,
so Nánjīng could purchase it locally with light funds.
The monthly salaries of officials in Jīngshī (the capital)
were all collected at Nánjīng with salary warrants.
When grain was cheap,
a salary warrant for seven or eight *dàn*
could only be exchanged for one *liǎng* (ounce) of silver.
Chén requested that for heavily taxed official lands and extremely poor households' two taxes,
they be allowed to pay in *jīnhuāyín* (gold flower silver),
with each *liǎng* equivalent to four *dàn* of grain,
which would be sent to the capital to pay salaries.
The people paid very little,
and official salaries were always sufficient.
Jiādìng and Kūnshān counties annually paid cloth,
with each bolt weighing three *jīn* (catties) equivalent to one *dàn* of grain.
By the time it was submitted,
eight or nine out of ten were rejected for being too coarse.
Chén said:
"If the cloth threads are fine, it must be light,
but its price will be higher.
Since it is already valuable,
it is impossible for it to be fine.
I request that from now on, without regard to weight,
it must conform to the standard length and width."
This was followed.
The post horses and all provisions for various prefectures
were previously all managed by the *mǎtóu* (horse head).
If there were losses or damages,
the *mǎtóu* would arbitrarily levy funds to replenish them.
Chén ordered that land pay an additional nine *hé* (gills) per *shēng* of rice,
collected along with the autumn grain,
and grain was directly issued to the *mǎtóu* based on the quality (upper, middle, lower) of the horses.
At the beginning of Zhèngtǒng,
Huái'ān and Yángzhōu suffered disasters,
and salt taxes were deficient.
An imperial edict ordered Chén to inspect the situation.
He memorialized that Sūzhōu and other prefectures should allocate one or two tens of thousands of *dàn* of surplus grain to be transported to the Yángzhōu salt fields,
which could be used to offset next year's land rent.
Salt producers could then pay salt tax and receive grain.
At that time, grain was expensive and salt was cheap.
The government accumulated salt,
and the people obtained grain,
benefiting both public and private interests.
Soon after, he was also ordered to manage the salt tax of Sōngjiāng.
Huátíng and Shànghǎi counties had salt tax arrears amounting to over 630,000 *yǐn* (salt certificates),
and salt-producing households fled.
Chén believed that land tax should support farmers,
and salt tax should support salt producers.
He then presented four convenient measures,
which were ordered to be implemented quickly.
Chén, in order to reduce the transport costs for salt-producing households,
obtained over 32,000 *dàn* of grain.
He also emulated the Jìnóng Cāng (Aid to Farmers Granary) system,
establishing a Shàn Yán Cāng (Salt Support Granary),
which further made up for the deficit caused by fleeing households.
As a result, salt tax greatly increased.
Zhèjiāng was tasked with building fifty seagoing ships.
Chén was ordered to assess the cost.
Chén summoned the master craftsmen and asked them,
who said each ship required one thousand *dàn* of grain.
Chén, believing that major undertakings should not be frugal,
only reduced it by twenty *dàn*,
and reported it to the court,
which eventually approved it.
Upon completing nine years of service,
he was promoted to Zuǒ Shìláng (Left Vice Minister).
Six years later, he was ordered to concurrently manage the tax grain of Húzhōu and Jiāxīng prefectures,
and also to jointly investigate criminal cases in Nánjīng with Guō Jǐn, the Dū Gěishìzhōng (Grand Supervisor) of the Xíngkē (Office of Scrutiny for Justice).
Chén ēn was naturally easy-going and lenient.
Previously,
the Grand Minister of Justice, Hú Gài (胡㮣), had served as the Grand Coordinator (Xúnfǔ),
and his methods were strict.
Chén ēn managed everything with simplicity and ease,
often disregarding accusers.
Someone once confronted Chén ēn, saying:
"Your Excellency is not as good as Duke Hú."
Chén ēn smiled and said:
"Minister Hú's imperial edict
was to eliminate harm to the people.
The court's command to me
merely said to pacify the military and the people.
The entrusted duties are simply different."
After serving in Jiāngnán for a long time,
he became familiar with the officials and common people as if they were family.
Whenever he visited villages,
he dismissed his retinue,
and conversed with farmers and women carrying provisions,
calmly asking about their sufferings,
and discussing solutions with them.
In his governance of subordinates,
even low-ranking officials and minor clerks
were openly consulted and listened to.
When he encountered capable senior officials,
such as Kuàng Zhōng (況鍾), Zhào Yù (趙豫) the prefect of Sōngjiāng, Mò Yú (莫愚) the prefect of Chángzhōu, and the assistant prefect Zhào Tài (趙泰) and their like,
he would sincerely consult with them,
making sure to utilize their strengths to the fullest,
so nothing was left undone.
He often went to Sōngjiāng to inspect water conservancy.
He saw that between Jiādìng and Shànghǎi,
lush weeds grew along the river,
and there was much silt accumulation.
So, he dredged the upper reaches,
allowing the waters from Kūnshān, Gùpǔ, and other places
to flow swiftly downstream,
and the obstructions were completely cleared.
In his leisure time, he would ride a single horse along the river,
and those who saw him did not know he was the Grand Coordinator.
Over the twenty years of Xuāndé and Zhèngtǒng eras,
the court's trust and appointment in him grew even stronger.
He twice experienced the death of parents,
but was reinstated to his duties both times.
Chén ēn thus became even more assertive;
when he saw advantages or disadvantages, he would certainly speak,
and his words were always heeded.
Initially,
he wanted to reduce the official land quota in Sōngjiāng
and levy taxes according to commoner land.
Hùbù (戶部) officials Guō Zī (郭資) and Hú Yíng (胡濙) memorialized that this was altering established laws
and requested his punishment.
Xuānzōng (宣宗) severely reprimanded Zī and others.
Chén ēn once said:
"There are one hundred and fifty qīng of sandy land and firewood fields by the Wúsōng Jiāng,
where water plants grow lushly,
and many insects and locusts breed there.
I request to recruit people to reclaim it,
which can sufficiently fulfill national revenue
and eliminate insect disasters."
He also said:
"For the fields in Dāntú and Dānyáng counties that have been swallowed by the river,
the tax has not yet been abolished.
In the early days of the dynasty, families whose taxes were exempted
often had their fields merged with those of wealthy households.
It is appropriate to collect rent from them,
and abolish the tax on fields swallowed by the river.
This way, the quota will not be reduced, and the rich and poor will be equalized.
The tax on white rice from official land in Wúxī is too heavy;
I request to change it to collecting rent in kind."
All were approved.
His requests for tax exemptions and loans due to disasters,
and the countless other advantages and disadvantages he presented,
were handled with discretion for minor matters,
without any scruples.
Over time, seeing the overflowing revenue,
he became even more inclined to expand spending.
He repaired yamens, schools, ancestral temples, tombs of former sages, bridges, and roads,
as well as renovating temples and monasteries,
gifting officials in the central court,
and providing provisions to travelers,
without any hesitation.
He also did not scrutinize much the petty officials and clerks who enriched themselves through corruption.
Because of this, he repeatedly drew criticism.
In the ninth year [of Zhèngtǒng],
Investigating Censor Lǐ Sù (李素) and others impeached Chén ēn for arbitrarily changing regulations
and monopolizing levies.
Chén ēn submitted a memorial defending himself.
The emperor, considering that the surplus rice had been used for public benefit,
let the matter drop.
Previously,
the cunning commoner Yǐn Chónglǐ (尹崇禮) had sought to obstruct Chén ēn's policies
and memorialized that Chén ēn should not collect excessive wastage rice,
requesting an investigation of the warehouse keepers.
Chén ēn consequently abolished the former policy.
However,
the two taxes subsequently fell into arrears again,
and the people had nothing to rely on,
all claiming inconvenience.
Chén ēn then memorialized to punish Chónglǐ
and reinstated the former policy as before.
After serving for another nine years,
he was promoted to Minister of Revenue (Hùbù Shàngshū).
Soon after, as people from Jiāngxī (江西) were not allowed to hold office in the Ministry of Revenue,
he was reassigned to the Ministry of Works (Gōngbù),
but continued to serve as Grand Coordinator.
In the first year of Jǐngtài,
Péng Shǒuxué (彭守學), a commoner from Lìyáng, again impeached Chén ēn with similar accusations as Chónglǐ.
The Ministry of Revenue then requested that Censor Lǐ Jiàn (李鑑) and others be dispatched to various prefectures to audit.
The following year, based on the words of Investigating Censor Jīn Dá (金達),
Chén ēn was recalled to the court.
Chén ēn then personally stated:
"Before I took office,
the tax grain in various prefectures was in arrears every year.
Since I assumed office,
I devised methods to eliminate abuses
and save unnecessary expenses.
Consequently, there were no annual tax arrears,
and surpluses even accumulated.
All that was previously required for public use and levied from the people
was disbursed from the surplus rice as needed.
Sometimes loans for relief were not repaid and were pardoned,
or the market value was not estimated at the time,
resulting in varying amounts.
Because I was granted imperial edicts by Emperor Xuānzōng (宣宗) and the Emperor Emeritus,
allowing me to act expediently,
these expenditures were not reported in detail,
which led to Shǒuxué's impeachment.
The Ministry of Revenue sent officials to pursue collection,
which is truly due to my imprudent management of receipts and disbursements;
I deserve more than death for my crimes."
Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū) Yáng Níng (楊寧) said:
"The crime of extravagant spending rests with Chén ēn,
but now, estimating the remaining value, it is all being collected from the common people,
even causing some to abandon their homes and flee.
I beg that collections for the period before Zhèngtǒng be waived."
The emperor approved it,
and recalled Jiàn and others.
However,
the censors still impeached Chén ēn in multiple memorials,
requesting his punishment.
Emperor Jǐng (景帝) had always known Chén ēn's virtue,
and many high officials also protected him.
He was merely ordered to retire.
Nevertheless, among those who discussed financial management at the time,
none surpassed Chén ēn.
His governance was founded on loving the people.
When the Relief Granary (Jìnóng Cāng) was established,
although agreements were made with the people,
the loans were often not collected when due.
Every year after the collection was completed,
exceeding the middle of the first lunar month,
he would issue a proclamation to release grain,
saying:
"This is the surplus that the people paid to the court.
Now it is returned to the people for their use.
Work hard to cultivate the court's fields,
and in autumn, you will pay the court's taxes again."
His adjustments and reforms
could all serve as future models.
The surplus rice in various prefectures
was so abundant that it was immeasurable,
enriching both public and private coffers,
and even extending to external prefectures.
In the early Jǐngtài era,
there was a great famine north of the Jiāng.
Minister of Censors Wáng Hóng (王竑) borrowed thirty thousand dàn of rice from Chén ēn.
Chén ēn calculated until the wheat harvest of the following year
and gave him one hundred thousand dàn.
His nature was sharp and perceptive.
He managed immense sums of money and grain,
and could calculate everything without omission by simply counting on his fingers.
He often secretly kept records of sunny, overcast, windy, and rainy days.
When someone claimed that they had lost rice to a storm on the river on a certain day,
Zhōu Chén said that there was no wind on the river on that day,
and the person was astonished and convinced.
There was a cunning civilian who intentionally disturbed Zhōu Chén's old records to test him.
Zhōu Chén said:
"You came to me at such-and-such a time to settle a matter,
and I adjudicated it for you.
How dare you deceive me?"
When the three halls were rebuilt,
an imperial edict summoned ten thousand *jīn* of ox glue
for the painted decorations.
Zhōu Chén happened to be going to the capital,
and said that the ox hides stored in the treasury
had decayed over the years,
and requested that they be taken out to be boiled into glue,
and that new hides be purchased to replenish the treasury upon his return.
During the Tǔmù Incident,
those in power discussed burning the granaries in Tōngzhōu
to cut off resources for the bandits.
Zhōu Chén happened to arrive for a meeting,
and said that the granaries contained several million *shí* of rice,
enough to feed the capital's army for a year.
If they were allowed to retrieve it themselves,
it would be consumed immediately,
so why should it be turned to ashes?
A short while later,
an imperial edict urged the manufacture of several million sets of helmets and armor.
Zhōu Chén calculated that the bright helmets made of quenched iron would require too much labor,
and ordered that they be merely coated with tin for the time being,
and they were completed within a few days.
After Zhōu Chén was impeached,
the emperor ordered Lǐ Mǐn to replace him,
and instructed him not to easily alter Zhōu Chén's methods.
However, from then on, the Ministry of Revenue confiscated accumulated surplus rice for public taxation,
and the reserves became depleted.
Later, a great famine occurred in Wú,
with corpses lining the roads,
yet the taxes remained outstanding as before.
The people missed Zhōu Chén even more,
and built shrines everywhere to worship him.
He died in the tenth month of JingTài (景泰) 4th year (1453).
His posthumous title was Wénxiāng (文襄).
Biographies of Kuàng Zhōng (況鍾) and others are available elsewhere.
A eulogy says: Sòng Lǐ (宋禮) and Chén Xuān (陳瑄) managed the rivers and opened up transport routes,
making long-term plans for the state,
and the common people benefited endlessly.
Zhōu Chén managed financial administration,
and the people were not troubled, while the granaries had surplus.
This was due to no other reason
than their complete devotion to public service in consideration of the state,
and their talent and ability were sufficient to achieve it.
They were truly different from those who initiated projects
to gain temporary merit,
or used clever schemes and deception
for the purpose of extortion.
However, the benefits of the canals and waterways
were enjoyed by generations,
while Zhōu Chén's good laws and excellent intentions
perished without a trace within a short time,
and the people suffered greatly.
Was this not because achievements with tangible results are easy to follow,
while methods that depend on the person are difficult to sustain?
Nevertheless,
it is regrettable for those who sought small gains and delighted in frequent changes,
and one cannot help but feel pity for those who clamored at the time.
Collation Notes

Biographies, Chapter 42: Zhāng Fǔ (張輔) (Gāo Shìwén (高士文), Xú Zhèng (徐政)), Huáng Fú (黃福), Liú Jùn (劉儁) (Lǚ Yì (呂毅), Liú Yù (劉昱)), Chén Qià (陳洽) (Hóu Bǎo (侯保), Féng Guì (馮貴), Wǔ Yún (伍雲), Chén Zhōng (陳忠), Lǐ Rèn (李任) et al.), Lǐ Bīn (李彬), Liǔ Shēng (柳升) (Cuī Jù (崔聚), Shǐ Ān (史安), Chén Yōng (陳鏞), Lǐ Zōngfǎng (李宗昉), Pān Yīn (潘禋)), Liáng Míng (梁銘), Wáng Tōng (王通) (Táo Jìróng (陶季容), Chén Tīng (陳汀)).
Zhāng Fǔ,
courtesy name Wénbì (文弼),
was the eldest son of Wáng Yù (王玉), King of Héjiān (河間).
When the Yan army rose,
he fought vigorously alongside his father,
serving as a Co-Commander (指揮同知).
After Wáng Yù died in Dōngchāng (東昌),
Zhāng Fǔ succeeded him in his post.
He participated in battles at Jiāhé (夾河), Gǎochéng (藁城), Zhāngdé (彰德), and Língbì (靈璧),
all with merit.
He followed the army into the capital,
was enfeoffed as the Count of Xìn'ān (信安伯),
with a stipend of one thousand *shí* of grain,
and was granted a hereditary patent.
His younger sister became the imperial consort.
Qiū Fú (丘福) and Zhū Néng (朱能) stated that the merits of Zhāng Fǔ and his father were equally high,
and their rewards should not be diminished due to private connections.
In YongLè (永樂) 3rd year (1405), he was promoted to Marquis of Xīnchéng (新城侯),
and his stipend was increased by three hundred *shí*.
At this time, Lí Jìlí (黎季犛) of Ānnán (安南) assassinated his sovereign,
proclaimed himself Taishang Huang (太上皇, retired emperor),
and made his son Cāng (蒼) emperor.
Lí Jìlí feigned an invitation for him to return to his country.
The emperor dispatched Commander-in-chief Huáng Zhōng (黃中) with five thousand soldiers to escort him,
with former Minister of the Grand Court of Justice Xuē Yán (薛嵓) as an assistant.
Lí Jìlí ambushed them at Qínzhàn (芹站),
The grandson of the former king, Chén Tiānpíng (陳天平), fled from Lǎowō (老撾).
and Xuē Yán also died.
The emperor was furious,
and ordered the Duke of Chéng (成國公) Zhū Néng to be the General who Conquers Barbarians (征夷將軍),
with Zhāng Fǔ as the Right Deputy General (右副將軍),
leading eighteen generals, including the Marquis of Fēngchéng (豐城侯) Lǐ Bīn,
with eighty thousand troops,
to rendezvous with the Left Deputy General (左副將軍) the Marquis of Xīpíng (西平侯) Mù Shèng (沐晟),
and advance on separate routes to suppress the rebellion.
Minister of War Liú Jùn assisted in military affairs,
and Minister of the Interior Huáng Fú
and Minister of the Grand Court of Justice Chén Qià supplied provisions.
In the tenth month of YongLè 4th year (1406),
Zhū Néng died in the army,
and Zhāng Fǔ took over command of his forces.
He advanced from Píngxiáng (憑祥),
crossed the Pōlěi (坡壘) Pass,
offered sacrifices from a distance to the mountains and rivers within the borders of Ānnán,
and issued a proclamation enumerating twenty crimes of Lí Jìlí.
He then broke through the Àiliú (隘留) and Jīlíng (雞陵) Passes,
passed Qínzhàn,
dispersed their ambushing forces,
and reached Xīnfú (新福).
Mù Shèng's army also arrived from Yúnnán (雲南),
encamping at Báihè (白鶴).
Ānnán had two capitals, East and West,
relying on the Xuān (宣), Táo (洮), Nóng (儂), and Fùliáng (富良) Rivers as natural defenses.
The rebels erected stockades along the north and south banks of the rivers,
gathered boats within them,
and built a city at Duōbāng (多邦) Pass.
The city, stockades, bridges, and ships stretched for over nine hundred *lǐ*,
with seven million soldiers,
intending to rely on the natural defenses to wear down Zhāng Fǔ's army.
Zhāng Fǔ moved his army from Xīnfú to Sāndàizhōu (三帶州),
built ships, and planned an advance.
Meanwhile, the emperor heard of Zhū Néng's death,
and issued an edict appointing Zhāng Fǔ as general,
the imperial decree likening him to Lǐ Wénzhōng (李文忠) replacing Kāipíng Wáng (開平王) Cháng Yùchūn (常遇春),
and further stating that while the winter months were free from malaria,
it was timely to destroy the rebels.
In the twelfth month,
Zhāng Fǔ's army reached the north of the Fùliáng River.
He sent Cavalry General (驃騎將軍) Zhū Róng (朱榮) to defeat the rebels at Jiālín (嘉林) River,
then joined forces with Mù Shèng to attack Duōbāng City.
Feigning an attack elsewhere to relax the rebels,
he ordered Commander-in-chief Huáng Zhōng and others to lead death-defying warriors,
each carrying torches and bronze horns.
At the fourth drum of the night,
they crossed the multiple moats,
and scaling ladders were placed against the city walls.
Commander Cài Fú (蔡福) was the first to ascend,
followed by soldiers swarming up like ants.
Horns sounded,
and ten thousand torches were raised simultaneously.
The soldiers below the city cheered and advanced,
and thus entered the city.
The rebels drove elephants to meet the attack.
Zhāng Fǔ countered them by covering horses with painted lions,
flanked by divine fire-weapons.
All the elephants stampeded back,
and the rebels suffered a great defeat.
They cut down two of their commanders,
pursued them to Sǎnyuán (傘圓) Mountain,
burned all the wooden stockades along the river,
and captured and killed countless rebels.
They then captured the Eastern Capital,
reconciled officials and common people,
and appeased those who surrendered,
with tens of thousands returning daily.
He sent separate generals Lǐ Bīn and Chén Xù (陳旭) to take the Western Capital,
and also divided his army to defeat rebel reinforcements.
Lí Jìlí burned his palaces and granaries and fled into the sea,
and all the prefectures and counties of the three rivers surrendered at the mere sight of the wind.
In the spring of the following year,
Fǔ dispatched Qīngyuǎn Bó Wáng Yǒu and others to cross the Zhùjiāng River,
and utterly defeated all the stockades at Chóujiāng, Kùnméi, Wànjié, and Pǔlài,
beheading over thirty-seven thousand.
The rebel general Hú Dù gathered his boats on Pántānjiāng River.
Fǔ sent the surrendered general Chén Fēng to attack and rout them,
seizing all their boats.
Thus, Dōngcháo and Liàngjiāng Prefectures and Subprefectures were pacified.
Soon after, they crushed Jì Lí's navy on Mùwánjiāng River,
beheading ten thousand,
capturing over a hundred of their generals and officers,
and countless drowned.
They pursued to Mènhǎikǒu in Jiāoshuǐ Xiàn,
then returned their army.
They built a fortress at Xiánzǐguān Pass,
and ordered Dūdū Liǔ Shēng to guard it.
After this,
the rebels entered via Fùliángjiāng River.
Fǔ and Shèng engaged them from opposite banks.
Shēng and others attacked from the flank with their navy,
utterly defeating them,
beheading tens of thousands;
the river water turned red.
They pressed on with their victory in hot pursuit.
At this time, there was a drought and the water was shallow,
so the rebels abandoned their boats and fled overland.
When the government troops arrived,
a sudden heavy rain caused the water to rise,
and they were able to cross completely.
In the fifth month, they reached Qíluó Hǎikǒu,
and captured Jì Lí and his son Cāng,
along with the false crown prince, various kings, generals, chancellors, and ministers,
and sent them in cages to the capital.
Ānnán was pacified.
They acquired forty-eight prefectures and subprefectures,
one hundred eighty counties,
and three million one hundred twenty thousand households.
They searched for descendants of the Chén clan but found none,
so they established the Jiāozhǐ Bùzhèngsī,
annexing the territory.
Since the fall of the Táng dynasty,
Jiāozhǐ had been under barbarian rule for over four hundred years;
now it was reincorporated into the empire's territory.
The emperor issued an edict to announce this to the realm,
and the various kings and officials presented memorials to offer congratulations.
In the sixth year, in summer,
Fǔ returned to the capital with his army.
He was again granted a banquet in Fèngtiāndiàn Hall,
the emperor composed the "Píng Ānnán Gē" for him,
and he was promoted and enfeoffed as Yīngguógōng,
with an annual stipend of three thousand dàn of grain,
and a hereditary patent.
In the winter of that year,
Chén's former minister Jiǎndìng rebelled again.
Mù Shèng was ordered to suppress him,
but suffered a defeat on Shēngjuéjiāng River.
In the spring of the following year,
Fǔ was again ordered to wear the seal of Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn,
and lead an army to suppress the rebellion.
At this time, Jiǎndìng had already usurped the title of Yuèshànghuáng,
and had separately enthroned Chén Jìkuò as emperor,
making their power very formidable.
Fǔ felled trees on Chìlǎnshān Mountain to build boats,
and encouraged those who had fled the bandits in the northern parts of Liàngjiāng to return to their occupations.
He then advanced to Cílián Zhōu,
defeated them at Hèménjiāng River,
and captured the Kǒngmù Stockade in Guǎngwēi Zhōu.
They encountered the rebels at Xiánzǐguān Pass.
The rebels had over six hundred boats,
and were defending the southeastern bank of the river.
Fǔ led Chén Xù and others to fight with paddle boats,
using the wind to set fires,
capturing over two hundred rebel commanders,
and seizing all their boats.
They pursued to Tàipíng Hǎikǒu.
The rebel general Ruǎn Jǐngyì met them with three hundred vessels,
but was again utterly defeated.
Thereupon, Jìkuò claimed to be a descendant of the Chén clan,
and sent envoys to request reinstatement and enfeoffment.
Fǔ said:
"Previously, we searched everywhere for descendants of the Chén kings but received no response.
This is a deception now.
I am under orders to suppress rebels;
I know nothing else."
So, he dispatched Zhū Róng and Cài Fú with infantry and cavalry to advance first,
while Fǔ led the navy to follow.
From Huángjiāng River to Shéntóuhǎi Sea,
the armies rendezvoused at Qīnghuà,
and then proceeded separately into Léijiāng River,
capturing Jiǎndìng in the Měiliángshān Mountains,
along with his followers, and sent them to the capital.
In the first month of the eighth year, they attacked the remaining rebel factions,
beheading several thousand,
and erected a Jingguan (a mound of enemy heads),
but Jìkuò had not yet been captured.
The emperor left Mù Shèng to suppress him,
and summoned Fǔ's army back.
He met the emperor at Xīnghé,
and was ordered to train troops in Xuānfǔ and Wànquán,
and supervise the transport of supplies for the northern campaign.
Although Chén Jìkuò had offered to surrender at that time,
he had no real intention of repenting.
Taking advantage of Fǔ's return,
he plundered and attacked as before,
and Shèng was unable to control him.
The people of Jiāo suffered from the restrictions imposed by China,
and were frequently harassed by officials and soldiers,
often rising to join the rebels,
sometimes submitting, sometimes rebelling,
and the generals became increasingly complacent about the bandits.
In the first month of the ninth year, Fǔ and Mù Shèng were again ordered to cooperate in advancing to suppress them.
When Fǔ arrived,
he reissued military orders.
Dūdū Huáng Zhōng was habitually arrogant,
and disobeyed the regulations.
When questioned, he was insolent,
so Fǔ beheaded him as a warning to all.
The generals and soldiers were terrified and solemn,
and none dared to disobey orders.
In the seventh month of that year, they defeated the rebel commander Ruǎn Jǐngyì on Yuèchángjiāng River,
captured over a hundred boats,
and captured alive the false marshal Dèng Zōngjì and others,
and also apprehended and beheaded several rebel leaders from other units.
Due to malaria, military operations were suspended.
In the eighth month of the following year, they attacked the rebels at Shéntóuhǎi Sea.
The rebels had over four hundred boats,
divided into three squadrons,
and were very aggressive.
Fǔ charged into their center,
the rebels retreated,
and the left and right squadrons advanced alternately.
The government troops engaged them in a desperate battle.
From máo hour to sì hour,
they utterly defeated the rebels,
capturing seventy-five chieftains.
They advanced to Yì'ān Fǔ,
and rebel generals surrendered one after another.
In the winter of the eleventh year,
Fǔ and Shèng met at Shùnzhōu,
and fought at Àizǐjiāng River.
The rebels drove elephants forward.
Fǔ warned his soldiers,
"One arrow to the elephant mahout,
two arrows to the elephant's trunk."
The elephants stampeded back,
trampling their own troops.
Assistant generals Yáng Hóng, Hán Guǎng, Xuē Jù and others seized the opportunity to advance,
arrows fell like rain,
and the rebels were utterly defeated.
They captured fifty-six of their commanders.
They pursued to Àimǔjiāng River,
and all their troops surrendered.
In the first month of the following year, they advanced to Zhèngpíng Zhōu.
Hearing that the rebels were encamped in the stockades of Xiānmán and Kūnpú,
they led their troops there.
The path was narrow on a cliffside,
and cavalry could not advance.
Fǔ and his officers walked on foot through the mountains and jungles.
At the fourth drum of the night, they reached their lair,
and captured all of Ruǎn Jǐngyì
and Dèng Róng and others.
Jìkuò fled to Lǎowō.
Fǔ dispatched commander Shī Yòu with troops to search for him,
and broke through his three passes.
Then they bound Jìkuò and his family,
and sent them to the capital.
The rebels were pacified.
By imperial decree,
the Champa territories seized by the rebels
were established as the four prefectures of Shēng, Huá, Sī, and Yì.
Garrisons were added,
the surrendered people were granted official positions,
and the army was left to guard them before returning.
In the spring of the thirteenth year, he arrived in the capital.
Soon after, he was appointed Jiāozhǐ Zǒngbīngguān to garrison the area.
However, the remaining rebels, Chén Yuèhú and others, rebelled again,
and Fǔ completely suppressed them.
In the winter of the fourteenth year, he was recalled.
Fǔ went to Jiāozhǐ four times in total,
and before and after, he established prefectures and counties, and added post stations for transport,
with very thorough planning.
Only Fǔ was feared by the people of Jiāo.
A year after Fǔ returned, Lí Lì rebelled,
and generals were repeatedly dispatched to suppress him,
but without success.
By Xuāndé's time,
Liǔ Shēng was defeated and perished,
Wáng Tōng made an alliance with the rebels,
and hastily retreated.
The court deliberated on abandoning Jiāozhǐ,
and Fǔ argued against it,
but could not succeed.
When Rénzōng 仁宗 ascended the throne,
[Zhāng Fǔ 張輔] was made Director-General of the Central Army Command (Zhōngjūn Dūdūfǔ 中央都督府),
advanced to Grand Preceptor (Tàishī 太師),
and received two salaries concurrently.
Soon after, he was ordered to have the Grand Preceptor's salary he received disbursed from the Beijing Granary.
At that time, all officials' salaries and rice were disbursed from Nanjing,
so this was a special favor.
Twenty-seven days after Chéngzǔ 成祖's funeral period concluded,
the Emperor wore a plain cap and sackcloth to court.
All other officials had already returned to auspicious attire,
but only Fǔ 輔 and Grand Secretary Yáng Shìqí 楊士奇 dressed like the Emperor.
The Emperor sighed and said:
"Fǔ 輔
is a military official,
yet he understands ritual better than the Six Ministers."
He was increasingly held in high esteem.
Soon after, he was appointed to supervise the Imperial Lectures (Jīngyán 經筵)
and oversee the compilation of the Veritable Records (Shílù 實錄).
In Xuāndé 宣德元年 (1426),
Hán Wáng Gāo Xù 漢王高煦 plotted rebellion,
enticing various meritorious officials to be his internal collaborators.
He secretly sent someone to Fǔ 輔's residence at night.
Fǔ 輔 apprehended him and reported the matter,
thereby fully uncovering the details of the rebellion,
and then requested to lead troops to attack him.
The Emperor decided to personally lead the campaign,
ordering Fǔ 輔 to accompany him.
After the affair was settled,
his stipend was increased by three hundred *dàn* (石) of grain.
Fǔ 輔's prestige grew even greater,
and he had long held military power.
In the fourth year (1429),
Censor-in-Chief Gù Zuǒ 顧佐 requested the preservation of meritorious officials.
An imperial edict ordered Fǔ 輔 to relinquish his duties at the Commandery,
attend the Emperor morning and evening,
deliberate on important military and state affairs,
and be promoted to Grand Master of Guanglu with the rank of Left Pillar of the State (Guānglù Dàfū Zuǒ Zhùguó 光祿大夫左柱國),
attending court on the first and fifteenth of the month.
When Yīngzōng 英宗 ascended the throne,
he was given the additional title of "Assistor in Sustaining Fortune and Managing Governance" (Yìyùn Zuǒlǐ 翊運佐理),
and continued to supervise the Imperial Lectures and compile the Veritable Records as before.
Fǔ 輔 was resolute and upright,
disciplined his army rigorously,
standing firm like a mountain.
He pacified Jiāonán 交南 three times,
and his prestige was known overseas.
Having served four reigns,
and being intermarried with the imperial family,
he was nonetheless cautious and respectful,
and worked with Jiǎn 蹇, Xià 夏, and the Three Yángs 三楊,
united in supporting the government.
For over twenty years,
the realm was peaceful,
and Fǔ 輔 played a significant role.
When Wáng Zhèn 王振 usurped power,
civil and military officials kowtowed at the mere sight of him,
but only Fǔ 輔 treated him with equal courtesy.
When Yěxiān 也先 invaded,
Zhèn 振 persuaded Yīngzōng 英宗 to lead a personal campaign,
and Fǔ 輔 accompanied him,
but was not allowed to participate in military and political affairs.
Fǔ 輔 was old,
and silently dared not speak.
Upon reaching Túmù 土木,
he died in the disaster,
at the age of seventy-five.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Dìngxīng Wáng 定興王,
with the posthumous title Zhōngliè 忠烈.
His son Mào 懋,
at nine years old, inherited the ducal title.
Xiànzōng 憲宗 reviewed cavalry archery in the Western Garden (Xīyuàn 西苑).
Mào 懋 hit the target three times consecutively,
and was bestowed with a golden belt.
He successively held command of military garrisons,
and was repeatedly promoted to Grand Preceptor (Tàishī 太師).
He once submitted a memorial on matters concerning border defense,
and advised against using Beijing garrison troops to build the Yuántōng Temple (Yuántōng Sì 圓通寺).
During the Hóngzhì 弘治 reign (1488-1505),
Censors Lǐ Xīng 李興 and Péng Chéng 彭程 were imprisoned,
and Mào 懋 argued for their release.
He further requested to stop the construction of the Zhēnwǔ Temple (Zhēnwǔ Guān 真武觀),
to waive weaving duties,
and to recall the palace eunuchs supervising weaving.
When Wǔzōng 武宗 ascended the throne,
and fraternized with petty individuals,
Mào 懋 led civil and military officials in remonstrance,
his words all being earnest and direct.
However, he was naturally extravagant,
and also somewhat exploited his soldiers,
being repeatedly impeached by censors.
He held the ducal title for sixty-six years,
wielded military power for forty years,
and was honored as the foremost meritorious official.
He died in Zhèngdé 正德十年 (1515),
also at the age of seventy-five.
He was posthumously granted the title Níngyáng Wáng 寧陽王,
with the posthumous title Gōngjìng 恭靖.
In Wànlì 萬曆 eleven years (1583), his princely title was revoked, along with Zhū Xīzhōng 朱希忠.
His grandson Lún 崙 inherited.
The title was passed down to Shìzé 世澤,
who was killed when the rebel bandits captured the capital.
Previously,
when Fǔ 輔 pacified Jiāozhǐ 交阯,
there were over a hundred battles, one after another.
Among those who died most notably while accompanying the campaign were
Gāo Shìwén 高士文 and Xú Zhèng 徐政.
Shìwén 士文,
a native of Xiányáng 咸陽.
During the Hóngwǔ 洪武 reign (1368-1398), as a junior officer, he distinguished himself in campaigns against Yúnnán 雲南 and Jīnshān 金山,
becoming a Hundred-Household Commander (Bǎihù 百戶) of the Left Guard of Yānshān 燕山.
He was honest, upright, firm, and decisive,
skilled in horsemanship and archery.
He joined Chéngzǔ 成祖's uprising,
and was successively promoted to Assistant Regional Commander (Dūdū Qiānshì 都督僉事).
He accompanied Zhāng Fǔ 張輔 in the campaign against Jiāozhǐ 交阯.
After Lí Jìlí 黎季犛 was captured,
the remaining rebels hid in mountain valleys,
appearing and disappearing as bandits.
In the eighth month of the fifth year (1407),
Shìwén 士文 led his troops to defeat them at Guǎngyuán 廣源,
then besieged their stronghold.
After urgent day and night attacks,
it was on the verge of falling,
when the bandits suddenly fled.
Shìwén 士文 pursued and fought them,
was struck by a flying stone, and died.
His troops continued to pursue the bandits,
who lost their base and scattered,
and were subsequently wiped out by Commander Chéng Yáng 程瑒.
The court, mindful of Shìwén 士文's merits,
posthumously enfeoffed him as Jiànpíng Bó 建平伯,
ordered his son Fú 福 to inherit,
granted him a stipend of one thousand three hundred *dàn* (石) of grain,
and awarded him a hereditary patent.
Three generations later, his grandson Méng 霳 had no son,
and adopted an義子 as heir.
When this was discovered,
the peerage was revoked.
Xú Zhèng 徐政,
a native of Yízhēn 儀真.
During the Jiànwén 建文 reign (1399-1402),
he was an Assistant Thousand-Household Commander (Fù Qiānhù 副千戶) of Yángzhōu Guard (Yángzhōu Wèi 揚州衞),
and surrendered the city to Chéngzǔ 成祖.
He was successively promoted to Assistant Regional Commissioner (Dū Zhīhuī Tóngzhī 都指揮同知).
He accompanied the campaign against Jiāozhǐ 交阯,
capturing ships at Sāndài Jiāng 三帶江 to transport the main army across.
He captured Xīdū 西都,
and fought at Xiánzǐ Guān 鹹子關,
all with merit.
When Chén Jìkuò 陳季擴 rebelled,
Pántān 盤灘 was a critical strategic point,
so Zhāng Fǔ 張輔 sent Zhèng 政 to guard it.
In the eighth month of the seventh year (1409),
rebel leader Ruǎn Jǐngyì 阮景異 came to attack.
He fought,
and a flying spear pierced his side,
yet he still commanded his troops to fight vigorously,
and ultimately defeated the rebels.
After the rebels retreated,
his abdomen burst, and he died.
Huáng Fú 黃福,
courtesy name Rúxī 如錫,
a native of Chāngyì 昌邑.
During the Hóngwǔ 洪wu reign (1368-1398), he rose from Imperial Academy student to Registrar (Jīnglì 經歷) of the Former Guard of the Imperial Insignia (Jīnwú Qiánwèi 金吾前衞).
He submitted a memorial discussing major state policies.
Tàizǔ 太祖 thought highly of him,
and exceptionally appointed him Right Vice Minister of Works (Gōngbù Yòu Shìláng 工部右侍郎).
During the Jiànwén 建文 reign (1399-1402), he was deeply trusted and relied upon.
Chéngzǔ 成祖 listed twenty-nine "treacherous individuals,"
and Fú 福 was among them.
When Chéngzǔ 成祖 entered the capital,
Fú 福 welcomed and joined him.
Lǐ Jǐnglóng 李景隆 pointed to Fú 福 as a "treacherous individual,"
and Fú 福 said:
"Your servant certainly deserves death,
but to be labeled a 'treacherous individual'—
this, your servant's heart does not accept."
The Emperor disregarded it,
and restored his office.
Not long after,
he was appointed Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shàngshū 工部尚書).
In Yǒnglè 永樂 three years (1405),
Chén Yīng 陳瑛 impeached Fú 福 for not caring for artisans,
and he was transferred to Minister of the Provisional Ministry of Works in Beijing (Běijīng Xíngbù Shàngshū 北京行部尚書).
The next year, he was implicated in an incident,
arrested and imprisoned in the imperial gaol,
and demoted to a functionary.
Later,
he was restored to his post,
overseeing military provisions for Ānnán 安南.
After Annam had been pacified,
its territory was organized into prefectures and counties.
Fú was ordered to take charge of the two offices of the Bùzhèngsī and the Ànchásī as a Shàngshū.
At that time, the distant regions had just been pacified,
military campaigns had not yet ceased,
and various affairs were numerous and complex.
Fú adapted measures to circumstances,
and everything was well-ordered.
He submitted a memorial, saying:
"The land tax in Jiāozhǐ varies in its lightness and heaviness;
I request that it be appropriately fixed,
always leaning towards lightness and ease."
He also requested:
"Along the north bank of the Lú Jiāng to Qīnzhōu,
establish guard posts and garrisons (wèisuǒ),
and set up courier stations (yìzhàn),
to facilitate travel.
Open up the 'salt exchange' (kāizhōng) system,
allowing merchants to transport grain (shūsù),
to broaden military provisions.
As for the salaries and stipends of officials,
if granary grain is insufficient, provide them with public land."
He also said:
"For the people of Guǎngxī to transport provisions,
the land route is difficult and perilous.
It is advisable to order Guǎngdōng to transport 200,000 shí of grain by sea to supply them."
All these requests were approved.
Thereupon, he compiled population registers,
fixed taxes,
established schools,
and appointed officials and teachers.
He frequently summoned elders to declare the imperial virtues and intentions,
and admonished his subordinates not to be harsh or disturbing.
He quelled everything with tranquility,
and superiors and subordinates were at peace.
At that time, many officials were demoted to Jiāozhǐ for minor offenses.
Fú helped and sympathized with them all,
selecting the worthy among them to work with him,
so that those who arrived felt at home.
The镇守中官 (Zhènshǒu Zhōngguān) Mǎ Qí, relying on imperial favor, oppressed the people.
Fú repeatedly curbed and restrained him.
Mǎ Qí falsely accused Fú of having ulterior motives.
The emperor discerned his falsehood
and did not question it.
Upon Rénzōng's ascension to the throne,
Fú was recalled
and appointed concurrent Zhānshì,
to assist the Crown Prince.
Fú served in Jiāozhǐ for a total of nineteen years.
When he returned,
the people of Jiāo carried and accompanied him,
weeping and unable to part.
After Fú's return,
the bandits in Jiāozhǐ became increasingly severe,
and could not be pacified in the end.
When Rénzōng died,
Fú supervised the construction of the Xiànlíng mausoleum.
In the first year of Xuāndé (1426),
Mǎ Qí incited Jiāozhǐ to rebel again.
At that time, Chén Qià, as Bīngbù Shàngshū, replaced Fú,
and repeatedly memorialized requesting Fú's return to pacify Jiāozhǐ.
It happened that Fú was on an imperial mission to Nánjīng.
He was summoned to the imperial court.
The imperial decree stated:
"You have long shown benevolence and love to the people of Jiāo.
The people of Jiāo miss you.
Go again for Us."
He was still appointed Gōngbù Shàngshū concurrently Zhānshì,
and took charge of the two offices.
By the time he arrived,
Liǔ Shēng had been defeated and killed.
Fú fled back.
When he reached Jīlíng Guān,
he was captured by the rebels.
He wished to commit suicide.
The rebels prostrated themselves, weeping, and said:
"Sir,
you are the father and mother of the people of Jiāo.
If you had not left,
we would not have come to this point."
They forcefully held him back.
Lí Lì, hearing this, said:
"If China were to send officials to govern Jiāozhǐ,
making everyone like Shàngshū Huáng,
how could I rebel?!"
He sent people to rush there to guard him,
and provided white silver and dry provisions,
and sent him out of the border in a sedan chair.
When he reached Lóngzhōu,
he returned all that he had been given to the authorities.
He returned to serve as Xíngzài Gōngbù Shàngshū.
In the fourth year, he worked with Píngjiāng Bó Dǒng on grain transport matters,
proposing that the people of Jiāngxī, Húguǎng, Zhèjiāng, and the various prefectures north and south of the Jiāng,
depending on the distance,
transport grain to Huái, Xú, and Línqīng,
and then have soldiers transport it to Běijīng.
The people greatly appreciated this convenience.
In the fifth year, he presented important points for ensuring sufficient military provisions and reducing labor.
Regarding ensuring sufficient provisions,
he said:
"During the Yǒnglè era, although Běijīng was constructed,
Jiāozhǐ was campaigned against in the south,
and the desert was campaigned against in the north,
resources were never lacking.
Now the state has no major expenses,
yet annual expenditures are barely met.
If, unfortunately, there are floods or droughts,
how will levies and requisitions be managed?
I request that 100,000 soldiers from the operational and garrison construction camps (cāobèi yíngshàn jūnsì)
be assigned to屯種 (túnzhǒng) along the river
north of Jìníng,
and east of Wèihuī and Zhēndìng.
In the first year, they would feed themselves.
In the second year, each person would harvest five shí.
In the third year, the harvest would double.
This would not only save 600,000 shí of rations from the imperial granaries in the capital
but also save 1,200,000 shí of monthly rations from their own garrisons,
potentially yielding 2,800,000 shí annually."
The emperor approved of this
and submitted it to the Xíngzài Hùbù and Bīngbù for deliberation.
Guō Zī and Zhāng Běn said:
"Establishing military farms along the river is indeed convenient.
We request that 50,000 qǐng be initially set as the standard,
and 50,000 residents from nearby areas be dispatched to cultivate it.
However, Shāndōng has experienced drought and famine in recent years,
and those who had migrated are only now returning.
Many garrison soldiers are engaged in labor.
It is advisable to first send officials to inspect the land in preparation for cultivation."
The emperor followed this advice.
Lángzhōng Zhào Xīn and others from the Lìbù were ordered to manage the military farms,
with Fú overseeing the entire matter.
Soon after, some argued that military personnel and civilians each have their regular occupations,
and if land were to be redistributed again,
the labor would increase and cause further disruption.
The plan was ultimately not implemented.
He was reassigned as Hùbù Shàngshū.
In the seventh year,
the emperor, while in the palace, reviewed Fú's memorial on the expediency of grain transport
and showed it to Yáng Shìqí, saying:
"Fú's words are profoundly insightful.
Who among the six ministers (liùqīng) can compare?"
He replied:
"Fú was recognized by Tàizǔ,
he is upright, discerning, and resolute,
single-mindedly devoted to the state.
In the early Yǒnglè period,
he established the Xíngbù in Běijīng,
pacifying and restoring order to the devastated areas.
When he was sent to Jiāozhǐ,
he oversaw both the Fānsī and Xiànsī,
achieving remarkable results.
Indeed, he is unmatched by the other liùqīng.
Fú is already seventy years old,
while young juniors sit high in public offices managing state affairs,
Fú, an old retainer from four reigns,
is busy running around and toiling from morning till night.
This is truly not the state's way of honoring the old and respecting the worthy."
The emperor said:
"Only from you could I hear such words."
Yáng Shìqí further said:
"Nánjīng is a fundamentally important place,
where the former emperor had the Crown Prince oversee the state.
Fú is experienced, loyal, and upright,
and can be relied upon in emergencies."
The emperor said:
"Indeed."
The next day, Fú's official post was changed to Nánjīng.
The following year, he concurrently took charge of the Nánjīng Bīngbù.
Upon Yīngzōng's ascension,
he was promoted to Shàobǎo
and participated in military affairs with the Nánjīng守備 (Shǒubèi) Xiāngchéng Bó Lí Lóng.
This was the first time that a civilian official in the auxiliary capital participated in military affairs,
beginning with Fú.
Lí Lóng followed Fú's advice,
and governance was strict, and the people were at peace.
He died in the first month of the fifth year of Zhèngtǒng (1440),
at the age of seventy-eight.
Huáng Fú's demeanor was proper and his conduct upright;
he did not speak or laugh idly.
He served through six reigns,
and offered many proposals.
He was fair, honest, and magnanimous,
and always enjoyed the trust of the people.
When in office, he did not seek a dazzling reputation;
in even the most trivial matters, he was always careful.
He worried for the country and forgot his home,
growing only more devoted in old age.
His self-provision was very frugal;
his wife and children barely had enough food and clothing.
The emoluments he received
were solely used to host guests and relieve the needy.
Initially,
Chéngzǔ personally listed ten important ministers,
and ordered Xiè Jìn to evaluate them.
Regarding Huáng Fú, he said:
"His heart is upright and honest,
firmly adhering to principles."
There was no slight depreciation.
When Huáng Fú participated in the administration of Nánjīng,
he once sat beside Lǐ Lóng.
Shìqí sent a message saying:
"How can an孤卿 (gū qīng) sit at the side?"
Huáng Fú replied:
"How can a少保 (shàobǎo) assist a守備 (shǒubèi)?"
He ultimately did not change his position.
However, Lǐ Lóng treated Huáng Fú with great respect.
After court,
he would immediately invite Huáng Fú to the place of honor,
and Huáng Fú also did not decline.
When Shìqí went to visit his ancestral tomb,
he passed through Nánjīng.
Hearing that Huáng Fú was ill,
he went to visit him.
Huáng Fú exclaimed:
"You, the Grand Guardian, assist the young emperor;
you cannot leave his side even for a day.
Why have you traveled so far?"
Shìqí was deeply impressed by his words.
When Xú Qí, the Minister of War, returned from his mission to Ānnán,
Huáng Fú met him outside Shíchéngmén.
Someone pointed to Huáng Fú and asked the person from Ānnán:
"Do you know this important official?"
He replied:
"Even the plants and trees of Nánjiāo [i.e., Ānnán] know your name,
how could I not know you?"
When Huáng Fú died,
he was not granted a posthumous title,
which caused much discontent among scholars.
In the early years of Chénghuà,
he was posthumously granted the title of Tàibǎo
and given the谥 (shì) of Zhōngxuān.
Liú Jùn,
courtesy name Zǐshì,
was from Jiānglíng.
He became a *jìnshì*
in the 18th year of Hóngwǔ.
He was appointed Minister of the Bureau of Military Personnel,
and later rose to Director.
He was skilled at resolving matters
and was highly valued by the emperor.
In the 28th year, he was promoted to Vice Minister of the Ministry of War.
During the Jiànwén reign,
he served as Attendant Censor.
When Chéngzǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Minister.
In the 4th year of Yǒnglè, a large expedition was sent to Ānnán,
and Liú Jùn was appointed to advise on military affairs.
Liú Jùn was meticulous, diligent, and agile;
he contributed significantly to military planning and strategy,
and received generous rewards upon his return.
Soon after,
Jiǎn Dìng rebelled again,
and Liú Jùn was again dispatched to advise Mù Shèng's army.
In the winter of the 6th year,
Mù Shèng and Jiǎn Dìng fought a battle at Juéjiāng,
suffering a defeat.
Liú Jùn traveled to the mouth of Dà'ānhǎikǒu.
A hurricane arose,
blinding sand obscured the day.
Fighting and marching,
he was surrounded by rebels
and hanged himself.
In the 3rd month of the 1st year of Hóngxī,
the emperor, noting that Liú Jùn had fallen to the rebels without yielding,
and that the relevant officials had not reported it
or bestowed honors and relief,
issued an edict reprimanding the Ministry of Rites officials.
He then granted a memorial sacrifice,
posthumously appointed him Junior Tutor of the Heir Apparent,
and gave him the谥 (shì) of Jiémǐn.
His son, Kuí, was appointed Supervising Secretary.
Lǚ Yì and Liú Yù died with Liú Jùn.
Lǚ Yì,
from Xiàngchéng,
followed Chéngzǔ across the river as a Hundred-Commander of the Jìnán Guard.
He accumulated merits until he reached the position of Vice Regional Commander.
He and Huáng Zhōng were appointed Left and Right Vice Generals,
assisting Hàn Guān, the General Suppressing the South, in garrisoning Guǎngxī.
Later, he and Huáng Zhōng led troops to escort Chén Tiānpíng, the grandson of the former King of Ānnán, back to his country.
Upon reaching Qínzhàn,
Chén Tiānpíng was abducted,
and Lǚ Yì was dismissed from office.
The emperor, lenient towards Lǚ Yì's crime,
reinstated him as Yīngyáng Jiāngjūn.
He followed Zhāng Fǔ in suppressing Jì Lí and distinguished himself,
taking charge of the administration of Jiāozhǐ Dūsī.
At this time, fighting the rebels,
he penetrated deep into the enemy lines and died in battle.
Liú Yù,
from Wǔchéng,
was promoted from Supervising Secretary of the Bureau of Personnel to Left Commissioner of the Office of Transmission,
then served as Assistant Administration Commissioner of Hénán,
and was later transferred to Jiāozhǐ.
He was stern and had administrative talent;
officials and common people feared him.
When the army was defeated,
he also died.
Chén Qià,
courtesy name Shúyuǎn,
was from Wǔjìn.
He loved antiquity and was diligent in his studies.
He and his elder brother Jì and younger brother Jùn were all renowned.
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
he was recommended for his good handwriting and appointed Supervising Secretary of the Bureau of Military Personnel.
He was once ordered to inspect troops;
he would recognize them after a single pass.
If anyone came a second time,
he would immediately send them away.
The emperor praised his ability
and bestowed upon him a gold-embroidered robe.
His father died while garrisoning Wǔkāi.
Chén Qià rushed to the funeral.
It happened that barbarians rebelled and blocked the road;
he risked danger and traveled secretly,
carrying his father's bones back home.
During the Jiànwén reign, recommended by Rú Cháng,
he was appointed Director of the Bureau of Selection.
When Chéngzǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel,
and later transferred to Minister of the Grand Court of Revision.
When Ānnán's army rose,
Chén Qià was ordered to Guǎngxī
to select soldiers with Hàn Guān for the expedition.
When the main army set out,
he was ordered to advise on military affairs
and manage provisions.
After Ānnán was pacified,
he was transferred to Left Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel.
At this time, Huáng Fú was in charge of the two Bureaus of Administration and Surveillance;
he focused on leniency and generosity,
and pacified the people.
Chén Qià selected talented individuals,
enforced discipline,
assessed the merits and demerits of generals and soldiers,
established native officials,
managed military provisions,
and made swift decisions.
Upon returning to court,
he was ordered to concurrently administer the Ministry of Rites and the Ministry of Works.
In the 7th year, he again advised Zhāng Fǔ's army in suppressing Jiǎn Dìng
and pacified him.
Upon returning,
he followed the emperor on a northern expedition
and trained troops with Zhāng Fǔ beyond the frontier.
In the 9th year, he again went to Jiāozhǐ with Zhāng Fǔ
to suppress Chén Jìkuò.
After five years there,
he was promoted to Minister of War
and again stayed to advise Lǐ Bīn's military affairs.
Rénzōng recalled Huáng Fú,
and appointed Qià to manage the Bù and Àn two departments,
still participating in military affairs.
The eunuch Mǎ Qí was greedy and tyrannical,
and Qià could not control him.
Rebels rose everywhere,
and Lí Lì was particularly cunning and formidable.
Furthermore, Earl Róngchāng Chén Zhì and Grand Commissioner Fāng Zhèng were at odds,
and the bandit forces grew daily.
Qià submitted a memorial stating:
"Although the bandits have begged for surrender,
they harbor treacherous intentions,
and their followers are gradually increasing,
soon they will be uncontrollable.
I beg you to instruct the generals to quickly annihilate the bandits,
and not be lured by them."
Xuānzōng issued an edict severely reprimanding Zhì and others,
ordering them to advance.
They were again defeated at Chálóngzhōu,
