and the Emperor then stripped Zhì and Zhèng of their official titles and ranks.
He ordered Marquis Chéngshān Wáng Tōng to take command as Grand General for Pacifying the Barbarians and go on an expedition,
with Qià still assisting his army.
In the ninth month of Xuāndé first year (1426),
Tōng arrived in Jiāozhǐ.
In the eleventh month, the army advanced to Yìngpíng,
and then to Níngqiáo.
Qià told the generals that the terrain was perilous,
fearing an ambush,
and suggested that they should halt the army to observe the enemy.
Tōng did not listen,
and waved his troops to cross directly,
getting stuck in a quagmire.
The ambush was sprung,
and the government army was routed.
Qià spurred his horse into the enemy formation,
and fell from his horse, severely wounded.
His attendants wanted to help him back,
but Qià opened his eyes and shouted:
"I am a high minister of the state,
having enjoyed a salary for forty years.
Repaying the country is today,
it is not righteous to cling to life."
He brandished his sword, killing several bandits,
and then committed suicide by slitting his own throat.
When the matter was reported,
the Emperor sighed, saying:
"How many high ministers sacrifice themselves for the country in an era!"
He was posthumously granted the title of Junior Guardian,
and given the posthumous name Jiémǐn.
His son, Shū, was appointed Investigating Censor of the Ministry of Justice.
Since Lí Lì's rebellion,
for three or four years of warfare,
many generals and officials died successively.
Hóu Bǎo,
was a native of Zànhuáng.
From a student of the Imperial Academy, he successively served as magistrate of Xiāngchéng, Gànyú, and Bóxīng three counties,
and had good governance.
When Jiāozhǐ was first established as prefectures and counties,
people were selected to pacify and comfort the populace.
Bǎo was appointed as Prefect of Jiāozhōufǔ,
and later promoted to Right Assistant Administrator.
In Yǒnglè eighteenth year (1420),
Lí Lì rebelled.
Bǎo, seeing Huángjiāng as a strategic point,
built a fortress to defend it.
When the bandits arrived,
he resisted strenuously for several months,
then went out to battle,
but was defeated and died.
Féng Guì,
was a native of Wǔlíng.
He passed the imperial examination for jinshi,
and became an Investigating Censor of the Ministry of War.
He followed Zhāng Fǔ in the expedition to Jiāozhǐ,
supervising military supplies.
He was successively promoted to Left Assistant Administrator.
He managed affairs with clarity and quickness,
and was good at comforting displaced people.
There were two thousand local soldiers,
valiant and skilled in battle.
Guì treated them with kindness and consideration,
and repeatedly achieved success in attacking the bandits.
The eunuch Mǎ Qí seized all of them.
When Lí Lì rebelled,
Guì, with a few hundred weak soldiers,
defended against the bandits at Guīxiàn,
but his strength gave out and he died.
During Rénzōng's reign,
Minister Huáng Fú reported their deeds,
and Guì was posthumously granted the title of Left Provincial Administration Commissioner,
and Bǎo the Right Provincial Administration Commissioner.
However, Guì had once said that Jiāozhǐ produced gold,
so he was ordered to serve as Consulting Official supervising gold mines,
which was criticized by public opinion at the time.
Wǔ Yún,
was a native of Dìngyuǎn.
As a Commander of the Jīngzhōu Guard, he followed the expedition to Jiāozhǐ,
defeated Pōlěi, Àiliú, and Duōbāng City,
and captured Dōng and Xī two capitals,
all with merit.
After the pacification of the bandits, he was transferred to Chāngjiāng Guard.
In the early Rénzōng reign,
he followed Fāng Zhèng to suppress Lí Lì at Chálóng,
where he plunged deep into the enemy lines and died.
Chén Zhōng,
was a native of Línhuái.
Initially, he was a Vice Myriarch of Kuānhé.
For his
"Jìngnàn"
achievements,
he was successively promoted to Commander.
He was exiled to Guǎngxī for an offense.
He followed the expedition to Jiāozhǐ,
from Gèzhāoshì, he carried small boats into the river,
raided Lí Jìlí's water fortress,
and destroyed it.
When attacking Duōbāng City,
he was the first to ascend.
For his merits,
he was restored to his former official position,
and transferred to Jiāozhōu Left Guard.
He repeatedly fought the bandits with merit,
and was promoted to Assistant Commissioner-in-chief.
When Lí Lì attacked Qīnghuà,
Zhōng died in battle.
Rénzōng pitied him,
and both he and Yún received generous posthumous favors according to regulations.
Lǐ Rèn,
was a native of Yǒngkāng.
As a Battalion Commander of the Yānshān Guard, he joined Chéngzǔ's uprising,
and through accumulated merits became an Assistant Commissioner-in-chief.
In Xuāndé first year, he followed the expedition to Jiāozhǐ,
and guarded Chāngjiāng.
Lí Lì regarded Chāngjiāng as a crucial route for the government army's movement,
and attacked it with all his might.
At that time, Commander-in-chief Cài Fú was captured by the bandits,
and was coerced to persuade Rèn to surrender.
Rèn, from atop the city wall, cursed Fú, saying:
"You are a great general,
unable to kill the bandits,
but instead used by them.
Even dogs and pigs would not eat your leftovers."
He fired cannons at him.
The bandits escorted Fú away,
and gathered a large force of elephants and flying chariots with assault ladders,
closing in on the city and attacking it from all sides.
Rèn and Commander Gù Fú led elite cavalry out of the city to ambush them,
and burned their siege equipment.
The bandits then built earthen mounds,
from which they shot into the city,
and dug tunnels to secretly enter the city.
Rèn and Fú defended against them from all directions.
They held out for over nine months,
fighting thirty battles before and after.
When the bandits heard that General for Pacifying the Barbarians Liǔ Shēng's army was approaching,
they increased their forces to attack.
In the fourth month of the second year, the city fell.
Rèn and Fú still led their sworn followers in three battles, defeating the bandits three times.
The bandits then advanced with a large number of elephants,
and they could not resist,
so they all committed suicide by slitting their own throats.
The eunuch Féng Zhì and Commander Liú Shùn both hanged themselves.
Thousands of soldiers, civilians, and women in the city died rather than surrender.
Liú Zǐfǔ,
was a native of Lúlíng.
From a student of the Imperial Academy, he was promoted to Supervising Censor,
and toured Zhèjiāng as inspector.
He was known for his integrity and fairness,
and the people of Zhèjiāng admired him.
Judicial Commissioner Zhōu Xīn, who was not easily impressed,
alone praised Zǐfǔ as virtuous.
He was promoted to Guǎngdōng Judicial Commissioner.
Due to implication in an incident,
he was demoted to Prefect of Liàngjiāng,
where he was good at comforting and guiding his people.
When Lí Lì rebelled,
Zǐfǔ and the defending general gathered soldiers and civilians to hold out for nine months,
and the city fell around the same time as Chāngjiāng.
Zǐfǔ said:
"It is not righteous for me to die by a bandit's blade."
He then hanged himself.
His son and concubine also died.
Hé Zhōng,
courtesy name Tíngchén,
was from Jiānglíng.
He became a Censor Supervising the Imperial Household through the Jinshì examination.
He was honest and cautious,
and no one dared to approach him with private matters.
During the Yǒnglè reign,
when the three palaces suffered a fire,
his memorial opposing the emperor’s will led to his demotion
to Zhīzhōu of Zhèngpíng,
where the people were content with his administration.
After the defeat at Níngqiáo,
Wáng Tōng deceitfully made peace with the rebels
and requested reinforcements from the court,
but his message was intercepted by the rebels and could not reach its destination.
The rebels sent an envoy with a memorial to express their gratitude.
Tōng then dispatched Zhōng and the Deputy Qianhu Guì Shèng to accompany him,
using the pretext of returning the land,
but secretly ordered them to request troops.
When they reached Chāngjiāng,
the eunuch Xú Xùn leaked their plan.
The rebels immediately seized Zhōng and Shèng
and threatened them with drawn blades.
The two glared in anger and cursed, refusing to yield,
and Zhōng’s son was also killed.
Xú Qí,
Commander of the Guìlín Central Guard,
and Nánníng Qianhu Cài Yǒng defended Qiūwēn.
At that time, the rebel power was already formidable,
and many officers and officials abandoned their cities and fled.
Qiūwēn was besieged,
but Qí and Yǒng still led exhausted troops to hold fast,
and when the city fell, they all died,
with not a single one surrendering.
Yì Xiān
was from Xiāngyīn.
As a Gúozǐshēng, he was appointed Zhīfǔ of Liàngshān,
where he governed well.
When his term expired and he was to return to court,
the people of the prefecture pleaded for him to stay.
An imperial edict promoted him to a third-rank official and returned him to his post.
When the rebels conquered Liàngshān,
Xiān hanged himself.
Zhōu Ān, as Commander Adjutant, was in charge of defending Yì'ān.
Lí Lì’s power grew,
and Grand Censor Cài Fú, with fodder and provisions running out,
retreated to Dōngguān.
After he left,
Qianhu Bāo Xuān led his troops to surrender to the rebels.
Ān and others were pressed by the rebels at Fùliángjiāng
and were all captured.
The rebels forced Cài Fú to go to various cities to persuade them to surrender.
Ān was greatly incensed
and secretly plotted with his men
to act as an inside force when the imperial army arrived.
Bāo Xuān discovered this
and reported it to Lì.
Lì arrested Ān
and was about to kill him,
when Ān said:
“I am a subject of the Heavenly Dynasty;
how can I die at the hands of rebels!”
He and Commander Chén Lín leaped up to snatch the rebels’ swords,
killed several men,
and then all committed suicide by slitting their own throats.
His nine thousand remaining men
were all massacred.
Yì Qiān, Provisional Administration Commissioner of Jiāozhǐ, reported the deaths of Rèn and twelve others in battle.
Xuānzōng sighed,
posthumously appointed Rèn as Dūdu Tóngzhī,
Fú and Shùn and Qí as Dūzhīhuī Tóngzhī,
Ān as Zhīhuī Tóngzhī,
Yǒng as Zhīhuī Qiānshì,
and Shèng as Zhèng Qiānfù,
and ordered their sons and grandsons to inherit their positions.
Sons Fǔ and Xiān were appointed Bùzhèngsī Cāncè,
Zhōng Fǔ Tóngzhī,
and Zhì Tàijiān,
and all were given imperial edicts and sacrificial rites.
However, Lín had once opened the city gates with Zhū Guǎng to let the rebels in,
so he was not included in the posthumous honors and condolences.
Later, Lí Lì declared himself a vassal,
returned Cài Fú, Zhū Guǎng, and six others,
who were all executed in the marketplace
and their families’ properties confiscated.
Lǐ Bīn,
courtesy name Zhìwén,
was from Fèngyáng.
His father, Xìn,
followed Tàizǔ across the Yangtze River
and, by accumulating merits, became Zhīhuī Qiānshì of Jìchuān Guard.
Bīn inherited the position
and followed Yǐngguógōng Fù Yǒudé on an expedition beyond the Great Wall,
where he made many captures and killings.
Upon returning,
he participated in building various border fortresses.
When Chéngzǔ raised an army,
Bīn joined him
as a vanguard,
fought many battles with distinction,
and was successively promoted to Yòujūn Dūdu Qiānshì.
In the fourth month of the first year of Yǒnglè (1403),
based on Qiū Fú’s recommendation,
he was enfeoffed as Fēngchéng Hóu,
with a stipend of one thousand dàn of grain,
and granted a hereditary patent.
The following year,
when Xiāngchéng Bó Lǐ Jùn was suppressing the rebellious bandits in Yǒngxīn,
Bīn was ordered to lead troops in support.
Before he arrived,
the bandits were pacified,
and he was ordered to command his troops to garrison Guǎngdōng.
In the fourth year, he was recalled
to capture bandits in Zàojūn Shān, Nányáng.
In the seventh month of that year,
he was given the seal of the Vice-General for Conquering the Yi, with Zǔ Cānjiàng Rèn serving under Mù Shèng,
to further campaign against Ānnán.
In the twelfth month,
Bīn and Yúnyáng Bó Chén Xù conquered Ānnán’s Xīdū
and then decisively defeated the rebels at Mùwán Jiāng.
After Ānnán was pacified,
when merits were assessed,
Bīn and Xù were both deemed slow in facing the enemy,
so they were not given additional enfeoffments,
but their stipends were increased by five hundred dàn of grain.
Soon after, he was appointed Grand General,
to guard against Wōkòu pirates along the coast.
He moved his troops to suppress and capture the Chángshā bandit Lǐ Fǎliáng,
and then led Zhèjiāng and Mǐnán troops to capture sea pirates.
In the tenth year, he was ordered to Gānsù to work with Xīníng Hóu Sòng Hǔ to manage the surrendered chieftains.
Bīn and Liǔ Shēng strictly guarded the border,
and ordered the native official Lǐ Yīng to defend Yěmǎ Chuān.
When Lǎodehǎn, a chieftain from Liángzhōu, rebelled,
Dūzhīhuī Hé Míng died in battle.
Yīng pursued him
and captured all his followers.
Lǎodehǎn fled to Chìjīn Ménggǔ.
The emperor wanted to dispatch troops,
but Bīn said that the road was long and provisions would be difficult to sustain,
and it was advisable to plan slowly.
The next year, he replaced Hǔ to garrison Gānsù,
and Chìjīn Ménggǔ captured Lǎodehǎn and presented him.
The emperor praised Bīn’s achievements
and bestowed generous rewards upon him.
In the twelfth year, he joined the northern expedition,
commanding the right vanguard,
and defeated the enemy at Hūshīwēn,
pursuing them to the Tǔlà Hé.
Upon the army’s return,
he received top honors
and was transferred to garrison Shǎnxī.
In the second month of the fifteenth year, he was ordered to bear the seal of the General for Conquering the Yi
and garrison Jiāozhǐ.
Upon arrival, he defeated and captured the bandit Ruǎn Zhēn of Lùnà County,
and dispatched Dūdu Zhū Guǎng and others to pacify Shùnzhōu and the various strongholds in Běizhòu.
The following year,
Lí Lì, a native patrol inspector from Qīnghuà Prefecture, rebelled.
Bīn dispatched Guǎng to suppress and defeat him.
Lì escaped.
In the seventeenth year, Dūdu Tóngzhī Fāng Zhèng was sent to ambush Lì at Kělán Zhà,
capturing his general Ruǎn Gèlì and others.
Lì fled to Lǎowō.
When the army returned,
he emerged again as a bandit.
Dūzhīhuī Huáng Chéng attacked and drove him off,
and then the army returned due to the summer rains.
At this time,
rebels in Jiāozhǐ rose up everywhere.
Bīn dispatched various generals to suppress them along different routes: Fāng Zhèng attacked Chē Miánzǐ and others in Jiāxīng,
Zhèng Gōngzhèng in Náncè,
Dīng Zōnglǎo in Dàwān;
Zhū Guǎng attacked Tán Xīngbāng and others in another department;
Grand Coordinator Xú Yuán attacked Fàn Ruǎn in Élè;
Commander Chén Yuánguī attacked Chén Zhíchéng in Èjiāng;
Grand Coordinator Wáng Zhōng attacked Yáng Gōng in Xiáshān.
All reported victories one after another.
Whenever the rebel forces were particularly severe,
Bīn would personally lead an attack.
Pān Liáo,
the native prefect of Yì'ān,
was brutalized by the eunuch Mǎ Qí,
and rebelled in Yíyá.
Bīn defeated him,
pursued him to Yùmá Zhōu,
captured his chieftain,
and advanced to burn the rebel stockades.
Liáo fled to Lǎowō,
and Bīn sent Grand Coordinator Shī Yòu to lead an army there.
Liáo engaged them with Lǎowō troops,
but was defeated at Nóngbālín,
and all his followers surrendered.
Fàn Yù,
a monk from Túshān Temple,
rebelled in Dōngcháo Zhōu.
Bīn went to suppress him,
defeating him in the river.
Yù escaped,
but was pursued and captured in Dōngcháo.
Then, Límá, a partisan of Zhèng Gōngzhèng, rose again.
Grand Coordinator Chén Zhōng and others repeatedly defeated him at Xiǎohuáng Jiāng.
Bīn personally led the pursuit,
reaching Zhènmán,
and capturing all his followers.
Thus, the various rebels were largely pacified,
except for Lí Lì, who frequently appeared and disappeared,
gathering followers in Léijiāng.
He was repeatedly defeated by Xú Yuán and Fāng Zhèng,
but always fled again.
In the 19th year [of Yǒnglè],
Bīn, due to insufficient supplies,
requested that the regular army and local troops be mixed to cultivate fields,
and also reported a proposal for adjusting the numbers for garrisoning, defending, and campaigning.
The emperor approved.
He was about to dispatch troops into Lǎowō to search for Lí Lì.
Lǎowō, in fear,
offered to capture and present him themselves,
but Bīn fell ill and the plan was abandoned.
He died in the first month of the following year.
His successors, Mèng Yīng, Chén Zhì, Lǐ Ān, and Fāng Zhèng,
were all unable to suppress the rebels.
Wáng Tōng took over the garrison,
but the rebel forces grew stronger,
and Jiāozhǐ subsequently became indefensible.
After Bīn's death,
he was posthumously granted the title of Mào Guógōng,
with the posthumous name Gāngyì.
His son, Xián, inherited.
In the third year of Xuāndé, he accompanied an expedition beyond the frontier,
and upon returning, repaired the cities of Yǒngníng and Lóngqìng.
In the early Zhèngtǒng period,
he was garrisoned in Dàtóng,
and soon after served as defender of Nánjīng.
He died in the second year of Jǐngtài,
posthumously granted the title of Fēng Guógōng,
with the posthumous name Zhōngxiàn.
His son, Yǒng, inherited.
The lineage continued for two more generations to his grandson, Mín.
In the Zhèngdé era, he was garrisoned in Guìzhōu,
where he captured bandits from Sīnán and Shíqiān,
and pacified various Man tribes in Wǔdìng with meritorious service,
earning the additional title of Crown Prince Grand Tutor.
In the early Jiājìng period,
he was garrisoned in Húguǎng,
where he was respected for his power and benevolence,
and the people of Chǔ felt secure under him.
He was transferred to Liǎngguǎng.
Wǔdìng Hóu Guō Xūn, who commanded the Imperial Camps,
was dismissed due to a crime.
Shìzōng, considering Mín's remote posting and lack of internal partisanship,
summoned him to replace Guō Xūn,
but he was soon dismissed due to an incident.
He died with the posthumous name Wǔxiāng,
and had no sons.
His cousin, Xī, inherited,
and was posted as garrison commander in Húguǎng.
During the Chǔ Crown Prince's imprisonment case,
many people were implicated.
Xī spoke to the Censor,
resulting in the exoneration of over two hundred people.
He suppressed the rebellious Man tribes in Yuánzhōu and Máyáng.
He died,
without sons.
His cousin, Rú, inherited.
The lineage continued to his grandson Chéngzuò.
During the Tiānqǐ era, he attached himself to Wèi Zhōngxián,
requesting the establishment of internal eunuchs as overseers overseas,
and also requested the bestowal of nine honors upon Zhōngxián.
In the early Chóngzhēn period,
his title was stripped, and he was exiled to the frontier.
His son, Kāixiān, inherited the title of Earl.
When the capital fell,
he was killed.
Liǔ Shēng,
a native of Huáiníng.
He inherited his father's position as a Centurion in the Yānshān Guard.
After more than twenty battles, large and small,
he was successively promoted to Assistant Regional Commander of the Left Army.
In the early Yǒnglè period,
he followed Zhāng Fǔ to conquer Jiāozhǐ,
defeating the rebels at Lǔjiāng,
and beheading their commander Ruǎn Zǐrén and others.
He guarded Xiánzǐ Pass.
When the rebels entered Fùliáng Jiāng,
their boats stretched for over ten li,
blocking the river and setting up camps,
with land forces also numbering tens of thousands.
Fǔ commanded the infantry and cavalry,
while Shēng commanded the naval forces.
They attacked from both sides,
utterly defeating them,
and capturing the pseudo-Minister Ruǎn Xīzhōu and others.
They also defeated the rebels at Qíluó Hǎikǒu,
capturing three hundred boats.
His troops captured Jì Lí and his son Chéng.
Shēng swiftly reported the victory and presented the captives,
for which he was rewarded.
Upon the army's return,
he was enfeoffed as Ānyuǎn Bó,
with a stipend of a thousand shi,
and granted a hereditary patent.
In the seventh year [of Yǒnglè], he accompanied Chén Xuān to command a naval patrol,
and in the sea off Qīngzhōu,
he severely defeated the Wō pirates,
pursuing them to Jīnzhōu Báishān Dǎo before returning.
The following year, he followed the northern expedition,
and at Huíqū Jīn,
commanding the divine mechanism firearms as the vanguard,
he utterly defeated Ālǔtái.
He was promoted to Marquis,
with an additional stipend of five hundred shi,
while retaining his hereditary earldom.
He was posted as garrison commander in Níngxià,
where he suppressed and beheaded the rebellious generals Féng Dálán Tièmù'ér and others.
He was recalled [to the capital],
and commanded the Imperial Camps.
In the twelfth year, he again followed the northern expedition,
commanding the main army and fighting at Hūlán and Hūshīwēn,
using firearms to defeat the enemy.
In the eighteenth year,
the demoness Táng Sài'ér rebelled in Pútái.
Shēng was ordered to lead the imperial army with Grand Coordinator Liú Zhōng to suppress her,
besieging her stronghold.
Shēng, considering himself a great general,
underestimated the rebels.
When the rebels requested surrender,
he believed them.
At night, they were ambushed,
Liú Zhōng was hit by a stray arrow and died,
and Táng Sài'ér escaped.
By dawn, [Shēng] finally realized,
and pursued and captured over a hundred of her followers.
Grand Coordinator Wèi Qīng fought valiantly to relieve the siege of Ānqīu.
Shēng was jealous of his achievement
and humiliated him.
Wèi Qīng was summoned and imprisoned,
but later
released.
In the twentieth year, he again followed the northern expedition,
commanding the central army and defeating the Wùliánghā at Qūliè'ér Hé,
for which he was granted the title of Marquis.
The emperor personally led five expeditions beyond the frontier,
and Shēng accompanied him in all,
repeatedly achieving merit,
and was favored above other marquises.
Upon Rénzōng's accession,
he was appointed to manage the Right Office,
and granted the additional title of Crown Prince Grand Tutor.
In the winter of Xuāndé元年 (1426),
Chéngshān Hóu Wáng Tōng was sent to suppress Lí Lì in Jiāozhǐ,
and news of his defeat arrived.
Liǔ Shēng was appointed Vice-General of Suppressing Captives (Zhēnglǔ Fù Jiàngjūn),
serving as Commander-in-Chief (Zǒngbīngguān),
Bǎodìng Bó Liáng Míng as Left Vice Commander-in-Chief (Zuǒ Fù Zǒngbīng),
and Grand Censor (Dūdū) Cuī Jù as Brigade General (Cānjìang).
Minister Lǐ Qìng was to assist in military affairs,
leading seventy thousand infantry and cavalry
to rendezvous with Qiánguó Gōng Mù Shèng for the punitive expedition.
At that time, the rebels' power had already grown strong,
and the roads were blocked,
so the imperial court had not received reports from Jiāozhǐ for a long time.
In the sixth month of the second year (1427),
three military soldiers, including Lǐ Màoxiān,
secretly made their way to the capital (Jīngshī),
reporting that Chāngjiāng was under urgent siege.
The Emperor granted the three men the rank of Battalion Commander (Bǎihù),
and issued an edict for Liǔ Shēng to advance urgently to reinforce them,
but Chāngjiāng had already fallen in the fourth month.
In the ninth month,
Liǔ Shēng finally entered the dangerous pass of Liúguān.
Lí Lì feigned loyalty by having local people submit a petition
requesting the establishment of a descendant of the Chén family as ruler.
Liǔ Shēng did not open the sealed letter but reported it.
The rebels occupied strategic points along the way and set up barricades.
The government forces repeatedly broke through them
and reached Zhènyíguān.
Liǔ Shēng, seeing the rebels' repeated defeats,
underestimated them.
At that time, Lǐ Qìng and Liáng Míng were both seriously ill.
Lángzhōng Shǐ Ān and Zhǔshì Chén Yǒng said to Lǐ Qìng:
"General Liǔ's words and demeanor are all arrogant.
Arrogance
is a taboo in military strategy.
The rebels might be feigning weakness to lure us,
which is not impossible.
The imperial edict warning against rebel ambushes
was very urgent.
You should strongly advise him."
Lǐ Qìng forced himself to rise and advise Liǔ Shēng,
but Liǔ Shēng paid no attention.
Upon reaching Dàomǎpō,
he rode ahead with over a hundred cavalrymen to cross the bridge.
The bridge suddenly broke,
and the rear guard could not advance.
Rebel ambushes rose on all sides,
Liǔ Shēng became trapped in the mud
and died from a dart wound.
On that same day,
Liáng Míng died of illness.
The next day,
Lǐ Qìng also died.
The day after that,
Cuī Jù led his army to Chāngjiāng.
The rebels arrived in greater numbers,
and the government forces fought desperately.
The rebels used elephants in a great battle.
The formation was disrupted,
and the rebels shouted:
"Those who surrender will not die!"
Some government soldiers died, some fled,
but none surrendered;
the entire army was annihilated.
Shǐ Ān, Chén Yǒng, Lǐ Zōngfǎng, and Pān Yīn all died there.
Cuī Jù was
a native of Huáiyuǎn.
He joined Chéngzǔ's uprising.
In the eighth year (1410), he accompanied the northern expedition,
defeating the enemy at Guǎngmòshù.
In Hóngxī元年 (1425), he was successively promoted to Assistant Regional Military Commissioner of the Left Army (Zuǒ Jūn Dūdū Qiānshì).
At this point, he fought fiercely and was captured.
The rebels tried every means to make him surrender,
but he never yielded and died.
Liǔ Shēng was straightforward, lenient, and gentle,
good at comforting his soldiers.
He was brave but lacked strategy,
which led to his defeat.
After Liǔ Shēng's defeat,
Mù Shèng's army could not advance
and also retreated.
Wáng Tōng's isolated army was cut off from reinforcements,
so he abandoned Jiāozhǐ.
The imperial court, considering Liǔ Shēng to have lost the army,
did not allow his son Liǔ Pǔ to inherit the title,
but after a long time, it was permitted.
In Zhèngtǒng十二年 (1447), Liǔ Shēng was posthumously granted the title Róngguó Gōng
and given the posthumous name Xiāngmǐn.
Liǔ Pǔ
initially managed the Central Military Command (Zhōngfǔ)
and was later sent to garrison Guǎngxī.
He was honest and cautious,
but lacked military strategy.
Following his ancestors like Liǔ Yún,
he could not maintain the established order
and was overly lenient and lax.
The Yáo and Zhuàng peoples incited each other to rebellion.
Liǔ Pǔ successively suppressed and executed rebel leaders at Dàténgxiá,
and broke through numerous barbarian strongholds in Liǔzhōu and Sī'ēn.
However, the rebels continued to spread as before.
In the early Jǐngtài era (1450s),
military affairs were urgent,
so he was recalled to manage the Right Military Command (Yòufǔ)
and command the Divine Machine Camp (Shénjī Yíng).
After the situation stabilized,
he was again sent out to garrison.
In the early Tiānshùn era (1457), he was recalled,
stationed to defend Xuānfǔ and Dàtóng,
and successively promoted to Grand Preceptor (Tàifù).
When there was an alert in Shǎnxī,
he was ordered to bear the seal of General-in-Chief Pacifying Barbarians (Pínglǔ Dà Jiàngjūn) and go to resist.
When the enemy re-entered Liángzhōu,
Liǔ Pǔ kept his troops within the walls and did not sally forth.
The enemy, having plundered their fill, departed.
He then pursued and took dozens of heads, reporting it as a victory,
but was impeached
and demoted from Grand Preceptor to a retired official.
Soon after, he was reinstated to manage the Divine Machine Camp.
Upon his death,
he was given the posthumous name Wǔsù.
His grandson Liǔ Jǐngsì,
Jǐng's son Liǔ Wén,
and Wén's son Liǔ Xún,
a total of three generations, all served as regional commanders in Guǎngdōng and Guǎngxī (Liǎngguǎng),
and achieved merits in pacifying the barbarians.
In Jiājìng十九年 (1540), Liǔ Xún was ordered to bear the seal of Vice-General of Punishing Barbarians (Zhēngyí Fù Jiàngjūn)
to suppress Mò Dēngyǒng in Ānnán.
Mò Dēngyǒng begged for surrender,
and Liǔ Xún was promoted to Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàifù).
Later, for his achievements in suppressing the Límín rebels in Qióngzhōu,
he was promoted to Junior Guardian (Shàobǎo).
Upon his death, he was posthumously granted Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo)
and given the posthumous name Wǔxiāng.
The title was passed down until the fall of the Míng dynasty,
when it was discontinued.
Shǐ Ān,
courtesy name Zhìjìng,
was a native of Fēngchéng.
He was honest, respected, and fond of learning, serving as Lángzhōng of the Bureau of Rites and Ceremonies (Yízhì Sī Lángzhōng) after passing the imperial examination (Jìnshì).
Chén Yǒng,
courtesy name Shúzhèn,
was a native of Qiántáng.
He was appointed Zhǔshì of the Bureau of Sacrifices (Cíji Sì Zhǔshì) after serving as a Junior Compiler (Shùjíshì).
Yáng Shìqí praised him as pure, upright, and firm,
whose outward appearance and inner disposition were entirely proper.
Lǐ Zōngfǎng,
of unknown origin,
also followed as a Zhǔshì.
Pān Yīn was
a native of Yín.
He followed as a Staff Officer of the Rear Army (Hòujūn Dūshì).
He once advised Liǔ Shēng to be cautious
and to deploy extensive scouts,
citing the incidents at Qínzhàn and Níngqiáo as warnings,
but Liǔ Shēng did not listen.
When the army was defeated,
he fought to the death.
Liáng Míng was
a native of Rǔyáng.
As a Battalion Commander (Bǎihù) of the Yānshān Forward Guard (Yānshān Qiánwèi), he followed Rénzōng to defend Běipíng.
When Lǐ Jǐnglóng besieged the city,
he fought very bravely.
Through accumulated merit, he rose to Assistant Regional Military Commissioner of the Rear Army (Hòujūn Dūdū Qiānshì),
serving Rénzōng as supervisor of state affairs.
In Yǒnglè八年 (1410), he was imprisoned for an offense.
In the nineteenth year (1421), he was pardoned and reinstated,
serving as assistant to Dūdū Hú Yuán in suppressing Japanese pirates in Guǎngdōng.
Upon Rénzōng's accession,
he was promoted to Associate Regional Military Commissioner (Dūdū Tóngzhī).
As a Brigade General (Cānjìang), he bore the seal of General Pacifying the West (Zhēngxī Jiàngjūn)
and, along with Associate Regional Military Commissioner Chén Huái, garrisoned Níngxià.
In recognition of his past merits in defending the city,
he was enfeoffed as Bǎodìng Bó,
with a stipend of one thousand dàn of grain,
and granted a hereditary patent (Shìquàn).
In the early Xuāndé era (1426),
Censor Shí Pú impeached him for greed and corruption,
and he was imprisoned.
He was to be stripped of his title,
but was pardoned.
He served as vice-general to Liǔ Shēng in the expedition to Jiāozhǐ.
After Liǔ Shēng's defeat,
Liáng Míng died of illness.
Liáng Míng was brave and skilled in battle,
and able to win the hearts of his soldiers.
After his death,
Cuī Jù alone led his troops in,
and the entire army was then annihilated.
Chén Tīng,
the Qianhūzhǎng of Gǔléi County,
frequently followed Fāng Zhèng in attacking rebels with distinction.
Zhèng trusted and relied on him.
When Wáng Tōng abandoned the territory,
Tīng traveled north
and was captured by the rebels.
They offered him an official post
and ordered him to guard Jiāozhōu's Eastern Pass.
Tīng took his family of over ninety people and fled by a secret path.
The rebels pursued them,
and his family members were all captured,
but Tīng alone escaped into Qīnzhōu.
The Emperor commended his righteousness
and appointed him a Zhǐhuī,
generously rewarding him.
Other local officials, such as Ruǎn Shìníng and Ruǎn Gōngtíng,
all refused to follow self-interest
and led their subordinates to surrender,
requesting to reside in the lands of Lóngzhōu and Chénzhōu.
The Emperor ordered that they be treated with special care and compassion,
with provisions, supplies, and implements provided by the government.
A eulogy states: Chéngzǔ, due to Jì Lí's usurpation,
raised an army to punish the crime and manifest Heaven's wrath.
Failing to find a successor of the Chén family,
he proceeded to establish prefectures and counties in their land,
thus obtaining a way to cause chaos and insult the fallen.
The barbarian frontier was dangerous and remote,
easy to stir up and difficult to pacify.
Within a few years, numerous rebellions arose.
Liǔ Shēng, due to underestimating the enemy, lost his army;
Wáng Tōng, due to fear, abandoned the territory.
Although Huáng Fú's benevolence and love were effective in Jiāo,
the hearts of the rebels were subdued,
the general situation was already lost,
and further efforts were fruitless.
Xuānzōng adopted the advice of experienced strategists,
utterly dismissing the territory from consideration,
truly because its acquisition would not be beneficial,
and its loss would not be detrimental.
It was a situation that did not necessarily warrant contention,
not merely due to reluctance to burden the people or a shortage of military provisions.
It is recorded that Huáng Fú wrote to Zhāng Fǔ, saying:
"The root of evil has not yet been completely eradicated,
and the garrison troops are insufficient.
If governed properly,
it can gradually be pacified.
If governed improperly,
it will inevitably change again."
Reflecting on the beginning and end of the Jiāo affairs,
one laments that Zhāng Fǔ could not become like the Mù family of Diānnán.
Collation Notes
Biographies Volume 43: Sòng Shèng, Xuē Lù (Guō Yì, Jīn Yù), Liú Róng, Zhū Róng, Fèi Huán, Tán Guǎng, Chén Huái (Mǎ Liàng), Jiǎng Guì (Sūn Wǎn), Rèn Lǐ, Zhào Ān, Zhào Fǔ, Liú Jù.
Sòng Shèng,
courtesy name Jǐngyáng,
was a native of Dìngyuǎn.
His father Cháoyòng
and elder brother Guóxīng
both followed in crossing the river,
accumulating merits to reach the rank of Yuánshuài.
During the attack on Jíqìng,
Guóxīng died in battle,
and Shèng succeeded to his post.
Afterwards, Cháoyòng requested retirement due to old age,
and Shèng, who was then following Dèng Yù in conquering Huīzhōu,
was recalled
to inherit his father's office.
He was progressively promoted to Dū Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī,
serving successively in Jiāngxī, Dàtóng, and Shǎnxī.
In the twelfth year of Hóngwǔ, he was demoted to Liángzhōu Wèi Zhǐhuīshǐ due to a legal transgression.
In the fifth month of the seventeenth year, he led an expedition against rebellious Western barbarians,
reaching Yìjí Nǎi Road.
He captured Yuán Hǎidào Qiānhù Yěxiān Tiēmù'ér, Guógōng Wúbǎdōulàchì, and others,
taking eighteen thousand captives.
He sent the chieftains to the capital
and selected a thousand elite soldiers to supplement the ranks,
releasing all the rest.
Recalled,
he was again made a Dū Zhǐhuī,
then promoted to Yòujūn Dūdū Qiānshì,
still garrisoning Liángzhōu.
In the twenty-fourth year, he was appointed Zǒngbīngguān
and, with Dūdū Liú Zhēn, attacked Hāmélǐ.
The place was over a thousand *li* from Sùzhōu.
Shèng ordered his army to carry abundant provisions
and travel twice the normal speed,
arriving at the city walls by night.
At dawn,
the sound of gongs and drums shook the earth,
and the entire city trembled,
thus it was conquered.
He captured its prince Bié'érqiè Tiēmù'ér and over thirty others, including pseudo-Guógōngs,
and returned with their tribes and baggage.
From then on, the barbarian tribes were awed and submitted,
and military might extended to the Western Regions.
In the fifth month of the following year, he followed Lán Yù to conquer Hǎndōng,
passing through Āzhēn Chuān,
where local chieftain Hāzàn and others fled.
When the army returned,
he was transferred to Zhōngjūn Dūdū Qiānshì.
In the sixth month of the twenty-eighth year, he followed Zǒngbīngguān Zhōu Xīng out of Kāiyuán
to Hūlà Jiāng.
Chief Xīyánghā fled,
and Shèng pursued him to Fǔdámí City,
capturing people and livestock before returning.
The next year, he was appointed Zhēngnán Yòufù Jiāngjūn
to suppress the Miáo of Píngméng and other stockades in Guǎngxī,
capturing and beheading over seven thousand people.
The year after that,
he commanded the eight battalions of Yǔlín troops to suppress the Miáo of Wǔkāi and Lónglǐ.
In the thirty-first year, he was sent to garrison Kāipíng
and followed the Prince of Yān beyond the Great Wall,
returning to garrison Wànquán and other garrisons.
In the first year of Jiànwén,
he still garrisoned Gānsù.
Upon Chéngzǔ's accession,
he came to court
and was promoted to Hòujūn Zuǒ Dūdū,
appointed Píngqiāng Jiāngjūn,
and sent back to his garrison.
In the third year of Yǒnglè, he induced the surrender of Bǎdōu Tiēmù'ér, Lúndū'érhuī, and other tribes, five thousand people in total,
capturing sixteen thousand horses, camels, cattle, and sheep.
He was enfeoffed as Xīníng Hóu,
with a stipend of one thousand one hundred *dan*,
and the hereditary post of Zhǐhuīshǐ.
Shèng garrisoned Liángzhōu four times in total,
for over twenty years,
establishing his prestige and credibility in remote regions.
The Emperor regarded Shèng as an old official
with the talent of a great general,
entrusting him exclusively with border affairs,
and always approving his proposals.
An censor impeached Shèng for acting independently.
The Emperor said:
"If a person is not given full authority,
he cannot achieve success.
Moreover, how can a great general commanding a frontier
be entirely bound by regulations?"
He then immediately issued an edict to Shèng to act as he saw fit.
Shèng once requested to come to court.
The reply was:
"The affairs of the northwestern frontier
are entirely entrusted to you,
unless summoned,
do not come arbitrarily."
Soon after, he was ordered to establish pastures west of the river
and to devise strategies for expeditions beyond the Great Wall.
He fell ill and died,
in the seventh month of the fifth year.
Shèng had three sons.
The eldest, Xuān,
was Fǔjūn Yòuwèi Zhǐhuīshǐ during Jiànwén's reign.
Fighting at Língbì,
he was the first to scale the walls,
slaying several enemies,
and died fighting bravely.
Xuān's younger brother Hǔ
married Chéngzǔ's daughter, Princess Ānchéng,
was allowed to inherit the marquisate,
and was granted a hereditary patent.
In the eighth year, he wore the seal of Qián Jiāngjūn
and garrisoned Gānsù.
In the tenth year, with Lǐ Bīn, he captured the rebellious chieftain Lǎodìhǎn,
taking many captives and killing many.
He was recalled.
In the first year of Hóngxī, he was deprived of his title for disrespect
and also stripped of his Fùmǎ Dūwèi office.
During Xuāndé's reign, he was reinstated as Dūwèi.
After Hǔ was deposed,
his younger brother Yīng succeeded.
Yīng married Princess Xiánníng.
During Zhèngtǒng's reign,
he successively oversaw the affairs of the Zuǒjūn Qiánfǔ.
When the Wǎlà leader Yěxiān invaded,
Yīng served as Zǒngbīngguān,
commanding Dàtóng garrison generals Zhū Miǎn and Shí Hēng and others to fight at Yánghé.
The entire army was defeated and annihilated,
and Yīng and Miǎn both died in battle.
He was posthumously granted the title Yùguó Gōng
and the posthumous name Zhōngshùn.
His son Jié succeeded.
During Jǐngtài's reign, he commanded the imperial guard
and was known for his prudence.
Upon his death,
his son Chéng succeeded.
He was appointed to oversee the Yòufǔ
and again wore the seal of Píngqiāng Jiāngjūn,
garrisoning Gānsù.
Chéng possessed talent and martial prowess.
Once, while hunting near Liángzhōu,
he encountered bandits who had plundered cattle and horses and were fleeing north.
Chéng killed three men with three arrows,
the bandits scattered in fright,
and he drove back all the plundered animals.
Nine generations later, to his grandson Yùdé,
who died in the rebellion of wandering bandits.
Xuē Lù,
a native of Jiāo.
He was the sixth child,
and in the army, he was called Xuē Liù.
When he became noble, he changed his name to Lù.
Lù followed Yān in the uprising from the ranks of soldiers,
and first captured Jiǔmén.
In the Battle of Zhēndìng,
Left Deputy General Lǐ Jiān advanced to fight.
As soon as their vanguards clashed,
Lù held his spear and stabbed Lǐ Jiān, who fell from his horse,
and captured him.
He was promoted to Zhǐhuī Qiānshì.
He followed in reinforcing Yǒngpíng,
and took Dàníng, Fùyù, Huìzhōu, and Kuānhé.
Returning to relieve Běipíng,
he was the vanguard who defeated the Southern army's skirmishers,
and was promoted to Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī.
He attacked Dàtóng,
serving as the vanguard.
In the Battle of Báigōuhé,
he pursued the fleeing enemy to Jǐnán,
and was promoted to Zhǐhuīshǐ.
In the Battle of Dōngchāng,
he defeated several hundred Southern soldiers with fifty cavalry.
At that time, Chéngzǔ was defeated by Shèng Yōng,
and retreated to Běipíng.
Yōng issued a declaration to the generals in Zhēndìng to garrison Wēixiàn and Shēnzhōu,
to block Yān's return route.
Lù defeated and drove them all away.
In the Battle of Hūtúohé,
the right army retreated.
Lù galloped to the front,
fighting in and out dozens of times,
and broke through,
pursuing the fleeing enemy to Jiāhé,
slaughtering countless enemies.
In the Battle of Shànjiāqiáo,
he was captured by Píng'ān,
but struggled free from his bonds,
drew his sword and killed the guards,
then galloped back to resume fighting,
greatly defeating Píng'ān's army.
He plundered Shùndé, Dàmíng, and Zhāngdé.
He attacked the Xīshuǐ stronghold,
and captured Commander Huā Yīng alive.
Following up on his victory, he took Dōng'ē, Dōngpíng, and Wénshàng,
fighting continuously at Féihé, Xiǎohé, and Língbì,
where his achievements were the greatest.
Upon entering Jīngshī,
he was promoted to Dūdū Qiānshì.
In the sixth year of Yǒnglè, he was promoted to Tóngzhī.
In the eighth year, he was appointed Piàojì Jiāngjūn,
and followed in the northern campaign,
promoted to Yòu Dūdū.
In the tenth year, he submitted a memorial stating:
"Since ancient times, when employing people,
it is essential to rely on their prior education.
Currently, the sons of military officials are idle and uninstructed,
and I fear that in times of urgency, there will be no one to use."
The emperor praised his words.
Coincidentally, tens of thousands of young soldiers arrived from all directions,
all of whom were assigned to Lù for training.
In the fifteenth year, he supervised construction as the Hángzài Hòujūn Dūdū.
In the twelfth month of the eighteenth year, the capital was established in Běijīng,
and he was conferred the title of Fèngtiān Jìngnàn Tuīchéng Xuānlì Wǔchén,
enfeoffed as Yángwǔ Hóu,
with a stipend of one thousand one hundred dàn of grain.
In the twenty-first year, he led the right vanguard in the northern campaign.
Upon returning,
he suppressed the bandits of Chángxīng.
In the twenty-second year, he again led the right vanguard in the northern campaign.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
he was ordered to take charge of the Zuǒfǔ,
and was granted the additional title of Tàizǐ Tàibǎo,
and given a hereditary patent.
In the first year of Hóngxī, he was appointed Zǒngbīngguān,
to guard the frontier beyond the passes.
Soon after, due to his achievements in capturing enemies,
his stipend was increased by five hundred dàn of grain.
In that year, general seals were distributed to various frontier garrisons;
Lù bore the seal of Zhènshuò Dàjiāngjūn,
and inspected Kāipíng,
reaching the frontier of Dàtóng.
When Xuānzōng ascended the throne,
he was recalled,
and presented five proposals for frontier defense.
Soon after, he was again dispatched to inspect the frontier.
In the first year of Xuāndé, he followed in the campaign against Yuè'ān,
serving as the vanguard.
When Gāo Xù was captured,
Lù was left with Minister Zhāng Běn to pacify the area.
In the spring of the following year,
he received an imperial decree to inspect the city walls of the prefectures in Jīnán,
strictly warning soldiers not to disturb the populace,
and stating that violators would be punished according to military law.
That summer, he again bore the Dàjiāngjūn seal,
and journeyed north to Kāipíng,
then returned to garrison Xuānfǔ.
The enemy attacked Kāipíng,
gaining nothing, and retreated,
reaching over three hundred lǐ from the city.
Lù led elite troops, moving by night and hiding by day,
arriving in three nights.
He unleashed light cavalry to raid the enemy camp,
defeated them,
and captured a large number of people and livestock.
When the army returned,
the enemy pursued them,
but he fought back and defeated them again,
whereupon the enemy fled far away.
He was recalled.
In the third year, he followed in the northern campaign,
defeated the enemy at Kuānhé,
and was left to garrison Jìzhōu and Yǒngpíng.
He repeatedly bore the Zhènshuò seal,
inspecting the frontier and protecting grain supplies,
operating between Kāipíng and Xuānfǔ.
In the fifth year, he encountered the enemy at Fènghuánglǐng,
slaying and capturing many,
and was granted the additional title of Tàibǎo.
He proposed that fortresses should be built at Tuánshān of Yǒngníng Wèi, as well as Diāo'è, Chéngchéng, Yúnzhōu, and Dúshí,
to facilitate defense.
An imperial decree ordered thirty-six thousand soldiers and civilians to proceed with the construction,
with one thousand five hundred elite cavalry to protect them,
all under Lù's command.
Before his departure, he was granted a poem,
comparing him to Shānfǔ and Nánzhòng.
Lù, being a military man, was not learned,
so he asked Yáng Shìqí.
Yáng Shìqí said:
"The Emperor treats you as an ancient worthy."
Lù thumped his chest and said:
"How dare Lù aspire to be like the ancients,
but I dare not fail to strive to repay a tiny fraction of the Emperor's grace!"
In the sixth month of that year, he fell ill,
and was recalled.
He died a month later.
He was posthumously granted Yín Guógōng,
and given the posthumous name Zhōngwǔ.
Lù was courageous and fond of strategy;
he fought after his plans were settled,
and always won.
His discipline was strict and clear,
not violating even a single hair.
He was good at treating his soldiers well,
sharing their hardships and pleasures,
and people were happy to serve him.
Among the meritorious officials of the
"Jìngnàn"
campaign, Zhāng Yù, Zhū Néng, and Lù were the three foremost,
and Lù served three reigns,
standing tall as a veteran general of his time.
His grandson, Sūn Shēn, succeeded him.
When his great-grandson, Hàn, died,
he had no son,
and his kinsmen disputed the succession.
For a long time, no request was granted,
and his fields and residences were confiscated by the government,
the line having been broken for over thirty years.
In the fifth year of Wànlì, Hàn's kinsman Cháng was again enfeoffed as Marquis.
Two generations later came Lián.
At the end of Chóngzhēn,
when Jīngshī fell,
he was killed.
During the Yǒnglè era, those who followed in the uprising from Běipíng,
and later through accumulated merit rose to become great generals,
and were enfeoffed as Marquis or Earl without
"Jìngnàn"
merit,
were Xuē Lù, Guō Yì, Jīn Yù, Liú Róng, and Zhū Róng, a total of five people,
and Yì, Yù, and Lù were enfeoffed on the same day.
Guō Yì,
a native of Jìníng.
During the Hóngwǔ era,
through accumulated merit, he became Yānshān Qiānhù.
He followed Chéngzǔ into Jīngshī,
and was successively promoted to Zuǒ Dūdū.
In the ninth year of Yǒnglè, he was demoted for dereliction of duty and sent to Jiāozhǐ to earn merit,
but was later pardoned.
He frequently joined campaigns beyond the passes,
and due to his achievements,
was enfeoffed as Ānyáng Hóu,
with a stipend of one thousand one hundred dàn of grain,
and was also awarded the title of Fèngtiān Jìngnàn Wǔchén.
At that time, Yì was in Nánjīng,
gravely ill,
and died upon hearing the news of his appointment.
Jīn Yù,
a native of Jiāngpǔ.
He inherited his father's office as a Baǐhù (Centurion) of the Yǔlín Guard,
then was transferred to the Yànshān Guard.
He had merit from joining the uprising,
and was successively promoted to Hénán Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ.
In the third year of Yǒnglè (1405), he was promoted to Dūdū Qiānshì.
In the eighth year (1410), he was appointed Yīngyáng Jiāngjūn to join the northern expedition.
When the army returned,
he served as the rearguard.
Upon reaching Chángxiùchuān,
he collected the cattle, sheep, and other livestock abandoned by the enemy, spanning tens of li.
In the fourteenth year (1416), he suppressed the demon-rebel Liú Zǐjìn in Shānxī.
Considering his past and present merits,
he was enfeoffed as Huì'ān Bó,
with a stipend of nine hundred shí.
He died in the nineteenth year (1421).
His concubine, Lady Tián, hanged herself in殉葬 (xùnzàng, ritual suicide),
and was posthumously granted the title of Shūfùrén.
Liú Róng,
a native of Sùqiān.
Initially, he used his father's name, Jiāng.
He followed Wèiguó Gōng Xú Dá in battling at Huīshān and Hēisōnglín.
He served as a Zǒngqí,
and was in service at the Yàn Prince's residence.
He was imposing and possessed great strategic wisdom,
and Chéngzǔ greatly valued him,
appointing him Baǐhù of the Mìyún Guard.
He served as vanguard in the uprising,
repeatedly achieving military success.
When campaigning in Shāndōng,
he and Zhū Róng led three thousand elite cavalry,
and attacked the Southern army by night at Huákǒu,
beheading several thousand men,
capturing three thousand horses,
and taking Dū Zhǐhuī Táng Lǐ and others prisoner.
He was successively appointed Dū Zhǐhuī Qiānshì.
Fighting at the Hūtuóhé River,
he captured a pontoon bridge,
and plundered Guǎntáo and Cáozhōu,
achieving great gains.
Returning with the army to relieve Běipíng,
he defeated Píng'ān's army at Píngcūn.
Yáng Wén besieged Yǒngpíng with Liaodōng troops;
Jiāng went to reinforce,
and Wén retreated.
Jiāng publicly announced his return to Běipíng,
and after marching more than twenty li,
he turned back and entered Yǒngpíng by night, clad in armor.
When Wén heard Jiāng had left,
he came to attack again.
Jiāng suddenly sallied out to ambush and attack,
defeating him severely,
beheading several thousand,
and capturing Dū Zhǐhuī Wáng Xióng and seventy-one others.
He was promoted to Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ.
Following to Fèihé,
he, along with Bái Yì and Wáng Zhēn, used light cavalry to lure Píng'ān,
and defeated him.
At that time, the Southern army was stationed at Sùzhōu,
stockpiling grain for a prolonged campaign.
Chéngzǔ was concerned about this,
and discussed cutting off their supply route.
He ordered Jiāng to lead three thousand men to go,
but Jiāng hesitated and did not proceed.
Chéngzǔ was furious,
and intended to execute him.
All the generals kowtowed and pleaded,
and he was thus spared.
Upon crossing the Jiāng (Yangtze River) and assessing merits,
due to his previous fault, he was not enfeoffed,
and was only granted the title of Dūdū Qiānshì.
He was promoted to Zhōngfǔ Yòu Dūdū.
In the eighth year of Yǒnglè (1410), he joined the northern expedition,
serving as a Yóují Jiāngjūn to oversee the vanguard.
He occupied Qīngshuǐyuán by night,
defeated the enemy at Wònnánhé,
and again defeated Ālǔtái at Jìnglǔ Zhèn.
When the army returned, he served as the rearguard,
and was promoted to Zuǒ Dūdū in the army,
then dispatched to garrison Liáodōng.
The enemy infiltrated and killed imperial soldiers.
The Emperor was enraged,
ordering Jiāng's execution,
but later pardoned him.
In the ninth year (1411), he again garrisoned Liáodōng.
In the twelfth year (1414), he again joined the northern expedition,
still serving as the vanguard,
leading elite cavalry to scout for the enemy at Yǐnmǎhé.
Seeing the enemy cavalry flee east,
he pursued them to Kānghālǐhái,
and attacked and killed dozens of men.
He then joined the main army to attack Mǎhāmù at Hūshīwēn,
dismounting and wielding short weapons to charge the formation,
killing and capturing many,
and received the highest reward.
He was again appointed Zǒngbīng Guān,
and garrisoned Liáodōng.
Japanese pirates repeatedly raided the coast,
reaching Liáo in the north,
and Zhè and Mǐn in the south,
and many coastal prefectures and counties suffered.
Jiāng assessed the situation,
and requested the construction of a fortress at Wànghǎiguō, northwest of Jīnxiàndǎo,
setting up beacon towers,
and strictly guarding with soldiers.
In the sixth month of the seventeenth year (1419),
scouts reported fires raised on an island in the southeastern sea.
Jiāng immediately led his troops to the fortress.
More than thirty Japanese pirate boats arrived,
anchored at Mǎxióngdǎo,
landed, and rushed towards Wànghǎiguō.
Jiāng set up an ambush relying on the mountains,
and dispatched other generals to cut off their retreat,
engaging with infantry,
feigning retreat.
The pirates entered the ambush,
cannons fired, and the ambush arose.
From chén (7-9 AM) to yǒu (5-7 PM),
the pirates were utterly defeated.
The pirates fled into an empty fort in Yīngtáoyuán.
Jiāng opened the west wall to let them escape,
then divided his forces into two routes for a pincer attack,
completely annihilating them,
beheading over a thousand,
and capturing one hundred thirty alive.
From then on, the Japanese pirates suffered a severe blow,
and dared not re-enter Liáodōng.
An imperial edict enfeoffed him as Guǎngníng Bó,
with a stipend of one thousand two hundred shí,
and granted an hereditary patent.
It was then that he changed his name to Róng.
Soon after, he was dispatched back to his garrison.
He died in the fourth month of the following year.
As a general, Róng
always served as the army's spearhead,
and no formation could withstand his advance.
He managed his officers and soldiers with discipline,
showing both benevolence and strictness.
For all who were [garrisoned] on the frontier,
he provided meticulous care and comfort.
After his death,
everyone remembered him fondly.
He was posthumously granted the title of Hóu,
with the posthumous name Zhōngwǔ.
His son, Tuān, succeeded him.
Upon Tuān's death,
he had no son,
so his younger brother, Ān, succeeded him.
In the fourteenth year of Zhèngtǒng (1449), Ān, along with Guō Dēng, garrisoned Dàtóng.
Yěxiān brought Emperor Yīngzōng to the city walls,
inviting Dēng to come out to meet,
but Dēng refused.
Ān went out to meet,
and prostrated himself, weeping before the emperor.
Emperor Jǐngdì issued an edict severely reprimanding him.
Ān rushed to the capital,
claiming to have received the former Emperor's order to report on the enemy situation,
and also requested his own promotion to Hóu.
All the officials impeached him,
and he was imprisoned and sentenced to death.
Coincidentally, the capital was under martial law,
so Ān was released and appointed Zǒngbīng Guān,
arraying his troops at Dōngzhímén.
After the enemy retreated,
he was promoted to Dūdū Tóngzhī,
and guarded Báiyángkǒu,
reinstated as a Bó.
When Emperor Yīngzōng was restored to the throne,
he was granted an hereditary Hóu title,
and his stipend was again increased by three hundred shí.
When Cáo Qīn rebelled,
Ān was wounded,
and given the additional title of Tàizǐ Shàofù.
He died in the Chénghuà era.
He was posthumously granted the title of Yìguó Gōng,
with the posthumous name Zhōngxī.
His peerage was passed down until the fall of the Míng dynasty.
Zhū Róng,
courtesy name Zhònghuá,
a native of Yí.
In the fourteenth year of Hóngwǔ (1381), as a Zǒngqí, he followed Xīpíng Hóu Mù Yīng to conquer Yúnnán.
He was successively promoted to Fù Qiānhù.
While guarding Dàníng,
he surrendered to Chéngzǔ.
He attacked Sūn Lín at Huákǒu,
besieged Dìngzhōu,
cut off the Southern army's supply route,
and fought over twenty battles, large and small.
For his merits, he was appointed Dūdū Qiānshì.
In the fourth year of the Yǒnglè reign, he followed Xīnchéng Hóu Zhāng Fǔ to campaign in Jiāozhǐ.
They captured Jīlíng Guān,
and met Mù Shèng at Báihè.
Fǔ and others deliberated on crossing the army upstream of the Jiālín Jiāng.
They sent Róng downstream eighteen *lǐ*,
increasing their numbers daily to confuse the enemy.
They also built boats and rafts, feigning an attempt to cross,
to pin down the enemy.
The enemy indeed divided their troops, crossed the river, and landed.
Róng and his men bravely attacked,
and utterly defeated them.
The main army then advanced and captured Duōbāng Chéng,
with Róng's contributions being the greatest.
The Emperor, because Róng had previously been slack in his duties,
only promoted him to Right Dūdū
when merits were discussed after the army's return,
and bestowed upon him white gold and banknotes.
In the seventh year, he again followed Fǔ to suppress the remaining rebels,
and pacified them.
The following year, he supervised the Right Yì [Flank],
and followed in the campaign against Ālǔtái.
He was promoted to Left Dūdū along with Liú Róng.
In the twelfth year, he again participated in the Northern Campaign,
serving as vanguard with Róng.
That winter, he was appointed Grand Commander (Zǒngbīngguān),
stationed at Dàtóng.
He repaired the cities of Mángniú Lǐng, Tùmáohé, Chìshān, Yúyáng Kǒu, and Láishèng.
The invaders dared not approach.
After three years,
he was recalled.
In the eighteenth year, he replaced Liú Róng as garrison commander in Liáodōng.
In the twentieth year, he again joined the Northern Campaign,
serving as vanguard.
He was stationed at Diāo'è to scout for invaders,
using five thousand cavalry to observe the enemy's movements.
The main army was at Yùshā Quán.
Róng led three hundred elite soldiers,
with three horses per person,
carrying twenty days' provisions, and penetrated deep.
The enemy had already abandoned their cattle, sheep, horses, and camels and fled north.
All these were collected.
Their baggage train was burned,
and the army moved to defeat Wùliánghā.
Upon the army's return,
he was enfeoffed as Wǔjìn Bó,
with a stipend of one thousand two hundred *shí*,
and remained stationed in Liáodōng.
In the twenty-second year, he again participated in the Northern Campaign.
Afterwards,
he returned to his post.
In the first year of the Hóngxī reign, he bore the seal of the Conquering Barbarians Front General (Zhēnglǔ Qián Jiāngjūn),
and continued his garrison duty as before.
In the seventh month of that year, he died at his post.
He was posthumously granted the title of Hóu,
and posthumous name Zhōngjìng.
His son, Miǎn, inherited the title.
As Jìn Wáng Jìhuáng had recently been deposed,
Miǎn was ordered to garrison Shānxī,
but was soon recalled.
In the sixth year, he was ordered to transport grain to Dúshí,
and consequently patrolled that area.
In the fourth year of the Zhèngtǒng reign,
he bore the seal of the Conquering West General (Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn),
and was stationed at Dàtóng.
In the fourteenth year, he joined the Northern Campaign,
fought at Yánghé,
and died there.
His posthumous name was Zhōngyì.
His son, Yīng, inherited the title.
The peerage was passed down until the fall of the Míng dynasty.
Fèi Huán,
was a native of Dìngyuǎn.
His grandfather, Yú,
served as Left Chancellor (Zuǒ Xiàng) of the Yān Princely Establishment during the Hóngwǔ reign,
and was later appointed Commander (Zhīhuīshǐ) of the Yānshān Central Guard.
The title was passed to his son, Sù.
When it reached Huán, he rendered meritorious service by joining Chéngzǔ in raising an army,
and was successively promoted to Assistant Regional Commander of the Rear Army (Hòujūn Dūdū Qiānshì).
In the spring of the eighth year of Yǒnglè,
Hǔ Bǎo, a Thousand-Householder (Qiānhù) of Liángzhōu Guard, and Yìlìng Zhēnbā, a Thousand-Householder of Yǒngchāng Guard, rebelled.
Their forces numbered several thousand,
occupying the courier routes.
Báiyán Tiēmù'ér and others who had recently submitted joined them.
The western frontier was in turmoil.
Dū Zhīhuī Lǐ Zhì attacked them but was defeated.
The rebels declared their intention to attack Yǒngchāng and Liángzhōu cities.
The Crown Prince ordered Huán to go and suppress them.
Upon reaching Liángzhōu,
Zhì and Dū Zhīhuī Chén Huái joined forces with him,
and they then advanced to Zhènfān.
They encountered the rebels at Shuāngchéng.
Huán attacked their left,
while Huái and others attacked their right.
The rebels were utterly defeated and fled,
with over three hundred heads taken.
They pursued the fleeing enemy to Hēiyú Hǎi,
capturing over a thousand rebels,
and one hundred and twenty thousand horses, camels, cattle, and sheep.
Hǔ Bǎo and others fled far away.
Then they returned with the army.
In the twelfth year, he was appointed Grand Commander (Zǒngbīngguān),
stationed at Gānsù.
Huán noted that the troops in Sùzhōu were numerous but provisions were scarce,
making it difficult to provision them quickly
if they were ever deployed.
He requested that the grain tax from Línkǒng be transported by the border troops nearby.
He also observed that there was much idle land in Liángzhōu,
and requested it be allotted to military agricultural colonies for reclamation.
This was granted.
In the first year of Hóngxī, he was granted the seal of the Pacifying Qiang General (Píngqiāng Jiāngjūn).
During the Yǒnglè era,
eunuchs generally assisted in commanding at the borders,
wantonly interfering with military affairs.
Huán was also controlled by them.
Rénzōng, aware of this,
sent him an imperial letter of censure, saying:
"You, as a descendant of a renowned minister,
bear a heavy responsibility for the state,
yet you bow your head and let others control you.
Is this the conduct of a true man!
You must severely chastise yourself,
and strive for future accomplishments."
Upon receiving the letter, Huán submitted a memorial of apology.
When Xuānzōng ascended the throne,
Huán was promoted to Left Dūdū of the Right Military Commissioner's Office (Yòufǔ Zuǒ Dūdū).
In the seventh month of the first year, he entered the court,
and was enfeoffed as Chóngxìn Bó,
with a stipend of one thousand one hundred *shí*.
He accompanied the campaign against Gāo Xù,
halting at Liúhé Yì.
The Emperor, mindful that the vanguard Xuē Lù had few troops,
ordered Huán to lead troops to reinforce him.
Upon his return,
he was granted an hereditary patent (shìquàn),
and again stationed at Gānsù.
In the second year,
the rebels of Shāzhōu Guard repeatedly plundered the envoys from Sāmǎ'érhǎn and Yìlìbǎlǐ.
Huán suppressed and defeated them.
The following year, he died at his post.
Huán was known for his gentle and easygoing nature,
and was skilled at managing his soldiers.
He served at his post for fifteen years,
and the region was peaceful.
His son, Zhāo, inherited the title.
He accompanied the campaign against Dèng Màoqī,
and upon returning, took charge of the Military Commissioner's Office (Dūdū Fǔ).
During the Tiānshùn era,
he accepted a bribe from Guō Zhāo, the second grandson of Wǔdìng Hóu Guō Yīng,
to falsely accuse the legitimate grandson Guō Chāng of unfilial conduct,
in an attempt to seize his peerage.
The judicial authorities requested his arrest and trial.
An imperial edict dismissed him from his duties at the Office.
He died,
and his son Huái inherited the peerage.
The title was passed down until the fall of the Míng dynasty, when it ceased.
Tán Guǎng,
courtesy name Zhònghóng,
was a native of Dāntú.
In the early Hóngwǔ reign,
he rose from the ranks of common soldiers,
participated in the campaign against Jīnshān,
and became a Hundred-Householder (Bǎihù) in the Yānshān Guard.
He followed Chéngzǔ in raising an army,
and with a hundred cavalry, plundered Zhuōzhōu,
capturing thirty officers alive.
He performed meritoriously in battles at Báigōu, Zhēndìng, and Jiāhé,
and was successively promoted to Commander (Zhīhuīshǐ),
garrisoning Bǎodìng.
Dūdū Hán Guān led an army of one hundred and twenty thousand to attack,
but Guǎng, with his isolated force, resisted for over forty days,
then seized an opportunity to defeat and rout them.
In the ninth year of Yǒnglè, he was promoted to Assistant Regional Commander of Dàníng (Dàníng Dū Zhīhuī Qiānshì).
He oversaw the construction of Běijīng.
Afterwards, he commanded the Divine Machine Camp (Shénjī Yíng),
joined the Northern Campaign,
and served as Gallant Cavalry General (Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn).
In the eleventh year, he trained troops in Shānxī.
The following year, he joined the campaign at Jiǔlóng Kǒu,
serving as vanguard.
Tens of thousands of rebels were entrenched on the riverbank.
Guǎng ordered archers to shoot at them.
Ten thousand arrows flew simultaneously,
inflicting countless casualties.
Seizing the advantage, they attacked from both flanks,
and the rebels were utterly defeated.
For his merits,
he was promoted to Assistant Military Commissioner (Dūdū Qiānshì).
Rénzōng 嗣位 ascended the throne.
He was promoted to Left Grand Censor (Zuǒ Dūdū)
and was bestowed with the seal of the Commander-in-Chief Pacifying the North (Zhènshuò Jiāngjūn Yìn),
to garrison Xuānfǔ.
In the third year of Xuāndé, he requested that military garrisons be treated as counties
and that altars for wind, clouds, thunder, rain, mountains, rivers, and the gods of land and grain (Shèjì Tán) be erected.
In the sixth year, because of the scarcity of grain in Xuānfǔ,
he requested that, like Kāipíng and Dúshí, merchants be invited to trade salt for grain,
to suffice the military provisions.
All were granted.
The next year,
the emperor, following the suggestion of the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù),
ordered that all soldiers from other garrisons stationed in Xuānfǔ
be sent back to their original posts to cultivate land.
Guǎng 上言 submitted a memorial, stating:
"The border I guard stretches over one thousand four hundred *lǐ*,
and enemies constantly spy
and launch sudden attacks without warning.
Should an alarm be raised,
summoning troops from several hundred *lǐ* away,
the situation would surely not allow for it.
As for the proposal of cultivating land,
your humble servant does not yet see its feasibility."
The emperor, considering that there were surplus border soldiers guarding,
only ordered that those transferred for garrison duty during the Yǒnglè reign should not be dispatched.
In the early years of Zhèngtǒng,
the court deliberated that although Tuōhuān had sought peace at the border,
his cunning schemes were unpredictable.
Guǎng and the regional commanders (Zǒngbīng Guān) of other garrisons, Chén Huái, Lǐ Qiān, and Wáng Yù, were ordered to draft strategies.
Guǎng and others each submitted their proposals,
the general gist being:
"Border marauders appear and disappear unpredictably;
therefore, defense is the best strategy.
Troops should be divided to guard strategic points,
while elite forces are occasionally dispatched to patrol beyond the border.
When encountering the enemy, they should fight or defend according to their strength,
using spies to scout them,
and light cavalry to pursue them.
If the marauders gain nothing when they come
and fear something when they leave,
then border troubles can be somewhat mitigated."
The emperor accepted their words.
In the eleventh month of the sixth year, for his merit in resisting the enemy,
he was enfeoffed as Earl of Yǒngníng (Yǒngníng Bó),
with a stipend of one thousand two hundred *shí* of grain,
and remained garrisoned in Xuānfǔ.
In the eighth year, he requested retirement.
A gracious edict denied it.
In the tenth month of the following year, he was summoned back for an audience.
The emperor, pitying his old age,
exempted him from regular court attendance.
He died that month,
at the age of eighty-two.
He was posthumously named Xiāngyì.
Guǎng was tall and strong,
rising from the ranks to become a great general.
He fought over a hundred battles, large and small,
and never suffered a defeat.
For twenty years in Xuānfǔ,
he repaired military colonies and fortresses,
strictly enforced defenses,
increased postal stations,
and also requested the distribution of firearms to various borders.
If a commander or officer violated regulations,
he would immediately memorialize to have them punished,
yet he treated his soldiers with kindness.
The border regions were peaceful,
and he was acclaimed as a famous general.
He once, in a fit of rage, flogged to death an assistant official of the Provincial Military Commission (Dūsī Jīnglì),
and also flogged a centurion (Bǎihù) due to a personal grudge,
both of which were impeached by censors.
These matters were left uninvestigated.
After his death,
the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù) stated that it was not a hereditary certificate (Shìquàn)
and appointed his son, Xù, as a commander (Zhǐhuīshǐ).
Chén Huái was
a native of Héféi.
He inherited his father's position as a deputy chiliarch (Fù Qiānhù) of Zhēndìng.
In the early years of Yǒnglè,
he accumulated merits and rose to Assistant Commander (Dūzhīhuī Qiānshì).
He followed Píng Ān to conquer Jiāozhǐ,
was promoted to Commander (Dūzhīhuīshǐ),
and took charge of the affairs of the Shānxī Provincial Military Commission (Shānxī Dūsī).
He again followed Zhāng Fǔ to capture the Jiāozhǐ rebel Jiǎn Dìng,
and followed Grand Censor Fèi Huán to conquer the Liangzhōu rebels Hǔ Bǎo,
all with merit.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Grand Censor Adjutant (Dūdū Tóngzhī).
In the first year of Xuāndé, he replaced Liáng Míng as Regional Commander (Zǒngbīng Guān)
and garrisoned Níngxià.
At that time, the imperial army repeatedly failed in their campaigns in Jiāozhǐ,
and an edict was issued to send troops from Sōngpān as reinforcements,
but the officers and soldiers dreaded going.
Chiliarch Qián Hóng conspired with the masses,
falsely claiming that the "barbarians" (fān) had rebelled,
and led troops to plunder the Màizá and other tribes.
The tribesmen were terrified
and subsequently revolted.
They killed Commander Chén Jié and others,
captured Sōngpān and Diéxī,
and besieged Wēi and Mào prefectures.
Commanders Wú Yù, Hán Zhěng, and Gāo Lóng successively suffered defeats,
and the western border was in turmoil.
An edict was issued to dispatch Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Hónglú Céng) Hé Mǐn and Commander Wú Wěi to recruit them,
and Huái was ordered to lead Liú Zhāo, Zhào Ān, and Zhuāng Guì with tens of thousands of troops following behind.
When Wěi and others arrived,
the rebels did not obey.
Wěi and Zhīzhōu Xuē Jìxián of Lóngzhōu attacked the rebels,
recovering Sōngpān.
By the time Huái arrived,
Wěi was still used as the vanguard,
and they subsequently recovered Diéxī,
receiving the surrender of over twenty stockades,
and repatriating over twelve thousand two hundred households of resettled people,
and over two thousand two hundred civilians who had been plundered.
The situation was thus settled.
He was promoted to Left Grand Censor,
richly rewarded with gold and silk,
but Wěi's merits were dismissed and not recorded.
Huái remained garrisoned in Sìchuān.
While in garrison, he was arrogant and lawless,
meddling in civil affairs,
accepting bribes to shelter criminals,
encroaching upon military farmlands,
and flogging and humiliating Assistant Administrators (Qiānshì) Chái Zhèn and others,
and was repeatedly impeached by censors.
The emperor issued an edict reprimanding him,
and also showed him a memorial of impeachment by Censor Wáng Lǐ.
Huái admitted his guilt.
The matter was left uninvestigated.
In the sixth year,
the Lèdū and Běidìng tribes of Sōngpān, as well as the Kōngláng and Lóngxī stockades of "barbarians," rebelled again.
Huái dispatched troops who were defeated,
and Commander Ān Níng and over three hundred others died.
Huái then personally led troops deep into the territory,
destroying the Gérgǔ stockade,
and advancing to attack the Kōngláng Qǐ'ér cave.
The rebels were defeated,
and countless were beheaded or fell to their deaths from cliffs.
The Gérgǔ rebels regrouped with "wild Miao" (Shēng Miáo) to challenge them to battle.
They were defeated,
and almost entirely annihilated.
Consequently, the tribes of Rènchāng and Niúxīn stockades, hearing of his reputation, begged for surrender,
and all the bandits were pacified.
After a long time,
the circuit censor (Xún'àn Yùshǐ) and the surveillance commissioner (Ànchásǐ) again memorialized:
"Huái is presumptuous and exceeds his authority.
Every morning,
he orders the officials of the Three Commissions (Sānsī) to stand in shifts,
kneeling to report matters.
Huái sits in the middle,
issuing orders as if they were imperial decrees.
Moreover, he is daily debauched by wine,
neglecting border defenses,
leading to the fall of cities and stockades."
Xuānzōng was enraged,
summoned Huái back,
and ordered civil and military officials to interrogate him;
his crime warranted execution.
He was sent to the prison of the Censorate (Dūcháyuàn),
pardoned from death but stripped of his office.
In the second year of Zhèngtǒng, he was restored to his original post and garrisoned Dàtóng.
At that time, those from the north who came to pay tribute were given daily rations,
which burdened the military and civilians.
Huái reported to the court,
and a reduction was achieved.
After two years,
he was recalled due to old age
and ordered to manage the affairs of the Central Military Commission (Zhōngfǔ).
In the spring of the ninth year,
he went out of Gǔběikǒu with the eunuch Dàn Zhù
to campaign against the Wùliánghā.
Upon his return, he was enfeoffed along with Mǎ Liàng and others,
and Huái received the title of Earl of Píngxiāng (Píngxiāng Bó).
In the fourteenth year, he accompanied the emperor on the northern campaign
and died at Tǔmù.
He was posthumously granted the title of Marquis (Hóu)
and named Zhōngyì.
His son Fǔ requested to inherit the peerage,
but the Ministry of Personnel stated that it was not a hereditary certificate
and firmly refused.
Emperor Jǐng, considering Huái's death in service,
permitted it.
After Fǔ's death,
his son Zhèng requested to inherit,
the Ministry of Personnel again firmly refused as before,
but an imperial decree (Zhōngzhǐ) permitted him to succeed.
Zhèng garrisoned Guǎngdōng and Guǎngxī for a long time,
and personally reported his military merits,
requesting a hereditary certificate.
The Ministry of Personnel again firmly refused,
but an edict granted it.
After Zhèng's death,
his son Xìn succeeded.
He died during the Hóngzhì reign,
without a son,
and his younger brother Jùn succeeded as a commander.
In the eighth year of Chénghuà, he was recalled
to assist in guarding Nánjīng,
and concurrently supervised river operations.
In the tenth year, he was appointed supervisor of the Shí'èr Tuányíng (Twelve Regimental Camps),
and soon after, concurrently took charge of the Shénjīyíng (Divine Machine Camp) troops.
He submitted a memorial stating:
"Tàizǔ originally established Nánjīng,
and outside the capital city, an earthen wall was also built to protect the residents;
this was truly a project for ten thousand generations.
Now, Běijīng only has an inner city.
During the Jǐsì zhī Biàn (Jǐsì Incident),
enemy cavalry rode swiftly to the city walls,
which can serve as a warning.
The old sites of the northwest corner still exist;
an order should be promptly issued to encourage donations,
supplemented by labor conscription for penalties,
and success will not be difficult."
He further stated:
"Below the passes of Dàtóng and Xuānfǔ,
there are hundreds of thousands of fertile fields,
all occupied by powerful magnates.
In the eight prefectures within the capital region,
half of the good land belongs to influential families,
leaving the common people jobless.
If the border passes were to face an emergency,
what resources would the inner prefectures have?
If supply routes were obstructed,
how would Jīngshī (the capital) be provisioned?
I request that Supervising Secretaries and Censors be dispatched to investigate the fields below the passes,
and determine their tax quotas;
for the common people's fields within the capital region,
sternly prohibit powerful magnates from encroaching upon them.
This way, soldiers and commoners will have sufficient food, and preparedness will be secured both internally and externally."
The memorial was sent to the relevant authorities.
Although it was not fully implemented,
contemporary opinion approved of it.
In the thirteenth year, he commanded the capital army to defend Dàtóng and Xuānfǔ during the autumn,
and presented more than ten strategic proposals.
All were approved.
In the fifteenth year, he accompanied Wāng Zhí to inspect border affairs in Liáodōng.
In the twentieth year, he bore the general's seal
and went out to resist border raiders.
When the raiders retreated, he returned with his army,
and was successively promoted to Tàibǎo and concurrently Tàizǐ Tàifù.
He died,
and was posthumously granted the title of Liángguógōng,
with the posthumous name Mǐnyì.
His son, Jì, succeeded him
and took charge of the capital garrisons.
During the Hóngzhì reign, he served as Zǒngbīngguān (Commander-in-chief),
successively garrisoning Jìzhōu, Liáodōng, and Húguǎng.
He served in official positions both within and outside the capital for twenty years,
with no surplus wealth in his home.
The title was passed down again to his grandson, Fù.
During the Jiājìng reign,
Fù successively held various military posts.
He bore the Zhēngmán Jiāngjūn (General Quelling the Barbarians) seal,
and garrisoned Liǎngguǎng.
For quelling maritime pirates and for his achievements against the Yáo people of Qìngyuǎn,
he was promoted to Tàizǐ Tàibǎo.
When the Míng dynasty fell,
his peerage ended.
Rèn Lǐ,
courtesy name Shàngyì,
was from Línzhāng.
As a soldier of Yānshān Wèi, he followed Chéngzǔ when he raised his army,
accumulating merits until he reached the position of Shāndōng Dūzhīhuīshǐ (Regional Military Commissioner of Shāndōng).
In the twentieth year of Yǒnglè, he was promoted to Dūdu Qiānshì (Vice Commissioner-in-chief),
and participated in the northern campaign.
He led the vanguard to scout for the enemy,
and upon his return received generous rewards.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
he was ordered to take charge of the affairs of the Guǎngxī Dūsī (Regional Military Commission of Guǎngxī),
and soon after was transferred to Liáodōng.
When Xuānzōng was enthroned,
he was promoted to Dūzhīhuī Tóngzhī (Regional Military Vice-Commissioner).
He participated in the pacification of Lè'ān,
and also in the campaign against Wùliánghā,
serving as the rearguard upon his return.
When Yīngzōng was enthroned,
he was promoted to Zuǒ Dūdu (Left Commissioner-in-chief).
In the first year of Zhèngtǒng, he bore the Píngqiāng Jiāngjūn (General Pacifying the Qiang) seal,
and served as Zuǒ Fùzǒngbīng (Left Vice Commander-in-chief), garrisoning Gānsù.
Ātái and Wǎ'érzhībó repeatedly raided Sùzhōu,
and imperial edicts were issued to reprimand them.
In the second year, they again raided Zhuānglàng.
Dūzhīhuī (Regional Military Commissioner) Wèi Róng attacked and repelled them,
capturing Bǎtū Bóluó, Wǎ'érzhībó's nephew.
Lǐ reported this.
In the third year, he joined Wáng Jì and Jiǎng Guì in an expedition beyond the passes,
defeating Wǎ'érzhībó at Shíchéng.
They then split their forces and reached Wútónglín and Yìjí'nǎi,
advancing to Hēiquán before returning.
They achieved many decapitations and captures,
and Lǐ was enfeoffed as Níngyuǎnbó (Earl of Ningyuan),
with a stipend of 1,200 shi of grain.
The following year, he returned to the court.
The year after that, he again garrisoned Gānsù, replacing Guì.
In the eighth year,
Qiěwàngshījiākǔ Yěxiān, the Dūdu (Commissioner-in-chief) of Chìjīn Ménggǔ Wèi, became tyrannical
and wanted to relocate to Yěluòbǔlá.
Lǐ, considering the proximity of that place to Sùzhōu,
firmly refused.
Later,
a memorial was submitted requesting permission to build a temple in that location.
Lǐ again argued that if they were allowed to build a temple,
they would certainly relocate there,
leaving a future problem,
and the matter was ultimately dropped.
At that time, for border generals' family retainers who cultivated land beyond the passes,
each qing of land was taxed twelve shi of grain.
Lǐ repeatedly petitioned the court,
and managed to get it reduced by four shi.
At that time, the border passes were peaceful.
Lǐ, together with the Grand Coordinator Cáo Yì, had the troops cultivate land to accumulate grain,
repaired armor, and trained soldiers,
making border defenses very secure.
In the eleventh year,
Nán'gē, the Dūdu (Commissioner-in-chief) of Shāzhōu Wèi, and his brothers quarreled,
and their followers became disloyal.
Lǐ wanted to take advantage of their hunger and distress
to resettle them in the interior.
It happened that Nán'gē also requested to reside within the territory of Sùzhōu.
Lǐ then dispatched Dūzhīhuī (Regional Military Commissioner) Máo Hālā to placate his followers,
while personally leading troops to follow behind.
Upon arrival,
Nán'gē again wavered.
His subordinates wanted to defect to Wǎlà.
Lǐ advanced his troops to pressure them,
and consequently brought back their entire group of over 1,200 people.
When the matter was reported,
Lǐ received generous rewards.
At that time, Wǎlà Yěxiān was rising in power,
and enfeoffed Nán'gē's brother, Suǒnánbēn, as Qíwáng (Prince of Qi).
Lǐ believed that if the two enemies united, their power would be even harder to control,
so he sent people to entice Suǒnánbēn.
Suǒnánbēn was undecided about complying,
