so Lǐ secretly led his army directly to Hǎndōng
and seized him to bring him back.
The Dì (Emperor) was greatly pleased,
and bestowed upon Lǐ an iron certificate of immunity from punishment,
allowing his descendants to inherit his title.
In the fourteenth year,
Yěxiān invaded by various routes
and reached Sùzhōu.
Lǐ dispatched a deputy general to resist him,
but they were defeated twice in battle,
losing tens of thousands of soldiers and horses.
He was recalled
and retired to his residence as an Earl.
In the early Jǐngtài reign,
he served as Grand Director of the Sānqiānyíng (Three Thousand Camp),
but retired due to old age.
After a long time,
he was again appointed as Garrison Commander of Nánjīng,
and entered to take charge of the Zhōngfǔ (Central Military Commission).
Lǐ rose from the ranks of common soldiers
to become a great general,
and always diligently upheld the law.
He died in the early Chénghuà reign.
He was posthumously granted the title of Hóu (Marquis),
with the posthumous name Xīwǔ.
His son, Shòu, succeeded him
and served as Zǒngbīng (Commander-in-chief) garrisoning Shǎnxī.
He was punished for losing control of Mǎnsì's rebellion,
but was pardoned from death and exiled to the border.
His grandson, Hóng,
was granted the hereditary position of Zhīhuīshǐ (Regional Commander).
Zhào Ān
was from Dídào.
His elder brother, Qí,
was a Tǔzhīhuī Tóngzhī (Native Commander Vice-Commissioner),
who died for his crimes.
Ān was demoted and exiled to Gānzhōu.
In the first year of Yǒnglè, he presented horses,
and was appointed Líntáo Bǎihù (Centurion of Líntáo),
and sent on a mission to Xīyù (the Western Regions).
He distinguished himself in the northern campaign,
and was successively promoted to Dūzhīhuī Tóngzhī (Regional Military Vice-Commissioner).
In the second year of Xuāndé,
the Fān (Tibetans/Qiang) of Sōngpān rebelled.
He was appointed Zuǒ Cānjiàng (Left Assistant General)
and followed Zǒngbīng (Commander-in-chief) Chén Huái to suppress them,
earning promotion to Dūdu Qiānshì (Vice Commissioner-in-chief).
At that time, there was discussion about campaigning against the Wùliánghā,
and an imperial edict ordered Ān and Shǐ Zhāo to lead their respective forces to Jīngshī (the capital).
The Wùliánghā soon came to court,
and Ān was ordered to return to his original guard post.
He was sent on a mission to Wūsīzàng (Ü-Tsang),
returning in the fourth year.
The following year, he again served as Zuǒ Cānjiàng (Left Assistant General) with Shǐ Zhāo to campaign against Qǔxiān,
achieving many decapitations and captures.
In the ninth year,
the eunuch Sòng Chéng and others were sent on a mission to Wūsīzàng,
and Ān was ordered to lead 1,500 soldiers to escort them to Bìlìzhù Jiāng (Bìlìzhù River).
Soon after, he and Vice Minister Xú Xī went beyond the passes to campaign against Ātái and Wǎ'érzhībó,
defeating them.
In the first year of Zhèngtǒng, he was promoted to Dū Dū Tóng Zhī,
and served as Yòu Fù Zǒng Bīng Guān,
assisting Rèn Lǐ in garrisoning Gānsù.
The next year, he went beyond the Great Wall with Jiǎng Guì,
but failed to suppress the bandits.
In the third year,
he again advanced with Wáng Jì, Rèn Lǐ, and Jiǎng Guì, dividing their forces,
and at Diāolìgōu, they captured thirty people including a Yòu Chéng and a Dálǔhuāchì.
For his merits, he was enfeoffed as Huìchuān Bó,
with a stipend of a thousand dàn of grain.
The next year, he was transferred to garrison Liángzhōu.
He settled his family in Líntáo,
and many of his relatives, partisans, and servants became bandits.
Fù Shǐ Chén Bīn reported this.
In Liángzhōu, he also recruited many ruffians as servants and slaves,
disturbing the populace,
and was again impeached by Yù Shǐ Sūn Yù.
The imperial edict decreed that none of it be investigated.
Ān was brave and had military strategy;
he was acclaimed along with Guì and Lǐ as a good general on the western frontier.
He died in the twelfth month of the ninth year.
His son Yīng served as Zhǐhuī Shǐ,
distinguished himself,
and was promoted to Dū Dū Tóng Zhī.
Zhào Fǔ,
courtesy name Liángzuǒ,
was from Fèngyáng.
He inherited the position of Jìníng Wèi Zhǐhuī Shǐ.
When Jǐng Dì succeeded to the throne,
Shàng Shū Wáng Zhí and others recommended him for his military talent,
and he was promoted to acting Dū Zhǐhuī Qiānshì,
serving as Zuǒ Cānjiāng,
defending Huáilái.
In the early Tiānshùn era,
he was summoned to the Yòu Fǔ to manage affairs.
In the first year of Chénghuà, he was appointed Zhēng Yí Jiāngjūn as Dū Dū Tóng Zhī of the Zhōng Fǔ,
and with Hán Yōng, campaigned against the southern barbarians in Liǎngguǎng,
conquering Dàténgxiá.
Upon his return, he was enfeoffed as Wǔjìng Bó.
Soon after, the barbarians entered Xúnzhōu,
and censorate officials jointly impeached him.
Guǎngxī Xún’àn Yùshǐ Duān Hóng stated:
"The bandits are spreading their poison intensely,
yet Fǔ falsely claimed the bandits were all eradicated,
presumptuously receiving titles and ranks.
If Fǔ is not punished, there will be no warning."
Fǔ then recounted his battle achievements,
shifting the blame to the defending general Ōu Xìn.
The emperor ignored all of it.
In the third year, he commanded a campaign to the east of Yí,
and with Dū Yùshǐ Lǐ Bǐng, penetrated deep from Fǔshùn.
After successive victorious battles,
he was promoted to Hóu.
In the eighth year,
the court deliberated a major expedition to search Hétào.
Fǔ was appointed general,
and the troops of the three garrisons of Shǎnxī, Yánsuī, and Níngxià all obeyed his command.
When Fǔ arrived at Yúlín,
the bandits had already penetrated deep and plundered extensively.
Fǔ could not control them,
and along with Wáng Yuè, submitted a memorial requesting to withdraw the troops.
Censorate officials jointly discussed his guilt.
An edict ordered Gěishìzhōng Guō Táng to investigate,
who returned and reported:
"The bandits entered Píngliáng, Gǒngchāng, and Líntáo in the sixth month,
killing and plundering people and livestock.
By the seventh month, they were rampaging through the territory of Qìngyáng.
Fǔ and Yuè arrived at Yúlín but did not advance;
they should be punished for relaxing their troops and underestimating the bandits."
The emperor did not accept this.
Fǔ returned,
still commanding the Capital Garrison.
Those who spoke out attacked even more fiercely,
and an edict decreed to provisionally set it aside.
Fǔ resigned his Hóu title,
and begged for the hereditary Bó title.
The emperor granted him the hereditary Bó,
and his Hóu title remained as before,
only reducing his stipend by two hundred dàn of grain.
Censorate officials strongly argued against this.
He did not listen.
Fǔ again submitted a memorial detailing his achievements,
saying that with the reduced stipend, he could not support himself in old age.
He also said that the emperor had ordered the eunuchs Lú Yǒng to campaign against the southern barbarians,
and Huáng Shùn and Wāng Zhí to campaign to the northeast,
none of whom achieved great merit,
and it would be proper to refer this to the Bureau of History.
Yú Zǐjùn and others requested to punish Fǔ according to the law,
but he was ultimately not questioned.
In the twelfth year, he was relieved of his garrison duties.
He lived at home for ten years and then died.
He was posthumously granted Róngguó Gōng,
and given the posthumous name Gōngsù.
Fǔ was intelligent, eloquent, and talented in his youth.
He was skilled in writing,
associated with many literati,
and also liked to cultivate powerful favorites.
Therefore, he was repeatedly impeached,
but ultimately suffered no harm.
His son Chéngqìng inherited the Bó title,
and assisted in defending Nánjīng.
In the early Zhèngdé era,
he was implicated for transcribing a memorial from the admonishing official Liú Yū,
which earned him the displeasure of Liú Jǐn,
and he was deprived of half his stipend and idled.
Four generations later, his great-great-grandson Guāngyuǎn,
garrisoned Húguǎng during the Wànlì era.
This line ended with the fall of the Míng dynasty.
Liú Jù was
the foster son of the Grand Eunuch Yǒng Chéng.
He served as Jīnwú Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī.
For his
"Duómén"
merit,
he was promoted to Dū Zhǐhuī Qiānshì,
and then rapidly promoted to Dū Dū Tóng Zhī.
He participated in the campaign against Cáo Qīn,
and was promoted to Yòu Dū Dū.
In the sixth year of Chénghuà, as Yòu Fù Zǒng Bīng, he followed Zhū Yǒng to Yánsuī,
pursuing the bandits at Huángcǎoliáng.
They encountered an ambush,
fought fiercely and he was wounded in the jaw,
but his subordinates bravely defended him and he escaped.
Soon after, he again, with Dū Dū Fàn Jǐn and others, attacked the bandits at Qīngcǎogōu,
defeating them.
Yǒng and others pursued the bandits to Niújiāzhài,
and Jù also occupied Nánshān and attacked fiercely.
The bandits were utterly defeated
and fled beyond the border.
For his merits, he was promoted to Zuǒ Dū Dū,
and specifically enfeoffed as Níngjìn Bó for his internal support.
In the winter of the eighth year, he replaced Zhào Fǔ as general,
commanding the troops of the various garrisons in Shǎnxī.
When the bandits entered Huāmǎchí,
he led Fù Zǒng Bīng Sūn Yuè and Yóujī Jiāngjūn Wáng Xǐ and others to repulse them.
Returning to Gāojiābǎo,
the bandits reappeared,
and he defeated them.
Pursuing the fleeing enemy to Màntiānlǐng,
an ambush sprang up to attack from both sides,
and he defeated them again.
Yuè and Xǐ also separately defeated the bandits at Jǐngyóushān.
When the victory was reported,
a hereditary patent was granted.
That winter,
Bóluhu, Mǎndǔlǔ, and Biéjiāsīlán united their forces and penetrated deep,
reaching Qínzhōu, Āndìng, and Huìníng and other prefectures and counties,
ranging over thousands of lǐ.
When the bandits retreated,
Wáng Yuè happened to return from Hóngyánchí,
and falsely reported a great victory,
receiving an imperial letter of commendation.
Soon after,
Jì Gōng Bīngbù Yuánwàiláng Zhāng Jǐn impeached Jù and Zǒng Bīng Guān Fàn Jǐn and five other generals,
for killing captured people and falsely claiming merits.
The Bộ Kē and Yùshǐ submitted memorials jointly impeaching them.
An edict ordered Gěishìzhōng Hán Wén to investigate,
who returned and reported as Jǐn had said.
Of the reported 150 first-class merits,
only nineteen heads were found.
The emperor, considering that the bandits had already fled,
did not question it.
Jù died shortly after.
He was posthumously granted Hóu,
and given the posthumous name Wēiyǒng.
His sons Lù and Fú inherited.
Fú,
during the Hóngzhì era, commanded the Sānqiān Yíng,
and was promoted to Tàizǐ Tàibǎo.
When he died,
his son Yuè inherited.
When Yuè died,
his cousin Wén requested to inherit.
The Lìbù stated that Jù had no great merits,
and his descendants should not inherit again.
Shìzōng did not approve,
and ordered Wén to inherit.
This line also continued until the fall of the Míng dynasty.
A eulogy states: Sòng Shèng, during Tàizǔ’s reign,
already participated in military campaigns alongside the founding grand meritorious officials.
Thereafter, he garrisoned Liángzhōu in four regions,
his might extending throughout the western frontier.
His two sons married princesses,
and his family was granted the title of Chèhóu for generations;
his achievements and fame were indeed magnificent.
As for Xuē Lù and the others below him,
they all participated in
the “Jìngnán Campaign.”
Lù distinguished himself in the battles of Dōngchāng and Hūtuó,
Liú Róng in defending Yǒngpíng,
and Tán Guǎng in defending Bǎodìng;
their contributions were most prominent.
Although on the day of their meritorious commendation,
they were not immediately granted the full insignia of nobility,
each received enfeoffment based on accumulated merits.
Their skill in managing soldiers,
their careful strengthening of their garrisons,
and their diligent performance of duties
are all worthy of praise.
Zhào Fǔ and Liú Jù’s achievements fell far short of their predecessors,
yet the oath of “Dài Lì”
ensured their loyalty to the state from beginning to end,
which was truly great good fortune.
These individuals were all ordered to guard the frontiers with their meritorious titles and ranks,
hence they are collectively recorded in this chapter.
Collation Notes

Biographies, Chapter 44 Wú Yǔnchéng (son Kèzhōng, grandson Jǐn) Xuē Bīn (son Shòu, younger brother Guì, Lǐ Xián) Wú Chéng (Téng Dìng, Jīn Shùn) Jīn Zhōng (Jiǎng Xìn) Lǐ Yīng (nephew Wén) Máo Shèng Jiāo Lǐ Máo Zhōng (grandson Ruì) Hé Yǒng Luó Bǐngzhōng
Wú Yǔnchéng
was a Mongol.
His name was Batū Temür.
He lived outside the Gānsù frontier in Tāgōu land,
and held the official position of Píngzhāng.
In the third year of Yǒnglè (1405), he, along with his associate Lúndū’érhuī, led his wife, children, and a tribe of five thousand people, with sixteen thousand horses and camels,
and came to surrender through Sòng Shèng.
The emperor, noting that many Mongols shared the same name,
decided to bestow surnames to differentiate them.
Shàngshū Liú Jùn requested that, following the precedent of Hóngwǔ,
they be compiled into authenticated records (Kānhé).
Yǔnchéng was granted a surname and given name,
and appointed as Yòujūn Dūdū Qiānshì.
Lúndū’érhuī was also granted the surname and name Chái Bǐngchéng,
and appointed as Hòujūn Dūdū Qiānshì.
The others were granted official positions, bestowed with caps and belts,
and given livestock, paper currency, and silks in varying amounts,
and were made to lead their respective tribes to reside in Liángzhōu for farming and pasturage.
Shèng, for his achievement in attracting their surrender,
was enfeoffed as Xīníng Hóu.
From then on, the number of those who surrendered and joined increased,
and the border became peaceful day by day,
starting with Yǔnchéng.
In the seventh year (1409), he went to Yìjí’nǎi to scout for enemies,
capturing more than twenty people including Hālā,
and was promoted to Dūdū Tóngzhī.
The following year, he accompanied the expedition beyond the Great Wall,
defeated Benyashiri,
and was promoted to Yòudūdū.
Soon after, he was promoted to Zuǒdūdū.
He pursued Kuòtuōchì with the palace eunuch Wáng Ān,
and captured him at the Bālì River.
He was enfeoffed as Gōngshùn Bó,
received an annual salary of 1,200 shí of grain,
and was granted a hereditary warrant.
Yǔnchéng had three sons: Dálán, Guǎnzhe, and Kèqín.
Yǔnchéng and two of his sons served in the army,
while his wife and Guǎnzhe remained in Liángzhōu.
The tribesmen Hǔbǎo and others incited and coerced Yǔnchéng’s people,
intending to rebel and leave.
Yǔnchéng’s wife and Guǎnzhe plotted,
summoned their subordinate commanders Dū Zhǐhuī Bǎozhù and Bǔyánbùhuā, and others, to capture the ringleaders,
and executed them.
The emperor was pleased,
issued an imperial edict to commend them,
and bestowed upon them a generous amount of silk, paper currency, sheep, and rice.
Guǎnzhe was appointed Zhǐhuī Qiānshì.
Bǎozhù was granted the surname and name Yáng Xiàochéng,
and appointed Zhǐhuī Qiānshì.
When the Tatar Khān Guǐlìchì was assassinated,
many of his subordinates scattered.
Dálán and Biélìgē requested to go beyond the Great Wall to prove themselves,
and achieved merit.
Biélìgē was
Bǐngchéng’s son.
When the emperor campaigned against the Oirats,
Yǔnchéng and his sons all participated.
When the army returned,
they were ordered to remain in Liángzhōu to guard the frontier.
Upon Yǔnchéng’s death,
he was posthumously granted the title of Guógōng,
and given the posthumous name Zhōngzhuàng.
Dálán was ordered to change his name to Kèzhōng
and inherited his title.
He accompanied the army on the second campaign against Ālǔtái.
He also accompanied them
on the third campaign against Ālǔtái.
His brothers all achieved merit.
In the first year of Hóngxī (1425), Kèzhōng was promoted to Hóu
due to his status as an imperial in-law.
At that time, Guǎnzhe had already accumulated enough merits to reach Dū Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī
and was also enfeoffed as Guǎngyì Bó.
Kèzhōng once served as Fù Zǒngbīng to patrol the frontier.
In the ninth year of Zhèngtǒng (1444), he led troops out of Xǐfēngkǒu
to campaign against the Wūliánghā,
achieved merit,
and was given the added title of Tàizǐ Tàibǎo.
During the Tǔmù Incident,
Kèzhōng and his younger brother Dūdū Kèqín’s son Jǐn served as the rear guard.
When the invaders suddenly arrived,
they fought fiercely but were unsuccessful.
The enemy soldiers occupied the mountain,
and arrows and stones rained down like water.
Almost all the government soldiers were killed or wounded.
Kèzhōng dismounted and shot arrows;
when his arrows were exhausted,
he still killed several people,
and he and Kèqín both died in battle.
He was posthumously granted the title of Bīnguógōng
and given the posthumous name Zhōngyǒng.
Kèqín was posthumously granted the title of Zūnhuà Bó
and given the posthumous name Xīmǐn.
Jǐn was captured,
escaped and returned,
and succeeded to the title of Hóu.
Yīngzōng once wanted to appoint Jǐn to guard Gānsù,
but Jǐn declined, saying:
"I am
an outsider;
if you appoint me to guard the frontier,
I fear that foreign tribes will disrespect the Middle Kingdom."
The emperor approved of his words
and therefore stopped.
When Cáo Qīn rebelled,
Jǐn and his cousin Cóng heard of the rebellion
and struck the Cháng’ānmén gate to report it.
The gate was closed,
and Qīn could not enter through his attack,
so he set it on fire.
Jǐn, leading five or six horsemen, fought valiantly with Qīn and died.
He was posthumously granted the title of Liángguógōng,
given the posthumous name Zhōngzhuàng,
and granted a hereditary warrant.
Three generations later, his great-grandson inherited the title
and once served as the defender of Nánjīng.
His son Rǔyìn and grandson Wéiyīng
both served as supervisors of the imperial garrisons’ military affairs.
At the end of Chóngzhēn’s reign,
when the capital fell,
Rǔyìn’s younger brother, Hūnwèi Rǔzhēng,
hanged himself with his wife and daughters.
Guǎnzhe died,
and his son succeeded.
Guǎnzhe’s wife, Zǎonú, also possessed wisdom and strategy,
and once personally came to court to present fine horses.
The imperial court highly regarded her loyalty.
When she died,
Guǎnzhe’s younger brother Kèqín’s son Cóng succeeded,
and garrisoned Níngxià.
In the fourth year of Chénghuà (1468),
Mǎn Sì rebelled.
Cóng was implicated in instigating the rebellion
and for retreating first during battle;
he was imprisoned and sentenced to death.
He was banished to the frontier,
and his title was abolished.
Xuē Bīn
was a Mongol,
originally named Tuhuàn.
His father, Xuē Tái,
surrendered during the Hóngwǔ era,
was granted the surname Xuē,
and successively rose to Yànshān Yòuhùwèi Zhǐhuī Qiānshì.
Bīn inherited the position,
participated in the uprising,
and was successively promoted to Dūdū Qiānshì.
He achieved merit during the northern expedition,
and was promoted to Dūdū Tóngzhī.
In the eighteenth year of Yǒnglè (1420), he was enfeoffed as Yǒngshùn Bó,
with a salary of 900 shí of grain,
and the hereditary title of Zhǐhuīshǐ.
Bīn died.
His son Shòu was only five years old.
His uncle Guì introduced him to Rénzōng.
The emperor immediately ordered him to succeed to the earldom [Bó],
and bestowed upon him the name Shòu.
When he grew up,
he was brave and skilled in battle.
In the autumn of the 14th year of Zhèngtǒng, he and Chéngguó Gōng Zhū Yǒng and others encountered the enemy at Yāor'ér Líng.
The army was defeated.
With his bowstring broken and arrows exhausted,
he still held an empty bow and struck the enemy.
The enemy, enraged,
dismembered him.
Later, when they learned he was originally a Mongol,
they said:
“This is one of our own kind;
no wonder he was so brave and strong.”
They wept for him together.
He was posthumously given the epithet Wǔyì.
His son Fǔ,
and grandson Xūn,
both succeeded to the earldom.
Xūn's son Xǐ then succeeded as commander [Zhǐhuīshǐ],
as per the writ.
Guì,
originally named Tuōhuǒchì,
was Bīn's younger brother.
As a chamberlain [Shèrén], he joined the Prince of Yān in raising an army,
and repeatedly rescued the prince from danger,
accumulating ranks up to Chief Military Commander [Dūzhǐhuīshǐ].
He again joined the northern expeditions,
and was promoted to Vice Commander-in-chief [Dūdū Qiānshì].
In the 20th year of Yǒnglè, he was enfeoffed as Earl of Ānshùn [Ānshùn Bó],
with a stipend of 900 dàn of grain.
In the 1st year of Xuāndé, he was promoted to Marquis [Hóu],
with an additional stipend of 300 dàn of grain,
and granted a hereditary writ.
When he died,
he was posthumously granted the title Duke of Bīn [Bīnguó Gōng],
and posthumously given the epithet Zhōngyǒng.
He had no son.
His nephew Shān succeeded him as commander [Zhǐhuīshǐ].
In the 1st year of Tiānshùn,
due to the grace of the restoration,
Shān's son Zhōng was ordered to succeed to the earldom.
When he died,
his son Yáo succeeded.
He died in the Hóngzhì period.
His son Áng inherited the reduced title of commander [Zhǐhuīshǐ].
Lǐ Xián,
originally named Chǒulǘ,
was a Tátáer (Tatar).
He was a Minister of Works [Gōngbù Shàngshū] during the Yuán dynasty.
In the 21st year of Hóngwǔ, he came to submit,
and was skilled in translating documents.
Tàizǔ bestowed upon him a surname and given name,
and appointed him as Assistant Instructor of the Prince of Yān's establishment [Yān Fǔ Jìshàn].
He served the Prince of Yān's heir apparent with utmost deference and caution.
When the "Jìngnán"
campaign began,
he rendered meritorious service,
and was successively promoted to Assistant Chief Military Commander [Dūzhǐhuī Tóngzhī].
All memorials from beyond the frontier and imperial edicts issued by the court
were assigned to Xián for translation.
Xián also repeatedly presented his insights.
Chéngzǔ adopted all of them.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
remembering his past services,
he promoted him to Vice Commander-in-chief of the Rear Army [Hòujūn Dūdū Qiānshì],
then further to Right Chief Military Commander [Yòu Dūdū],
and bestowed upon him lavish gifts.
Soon after, he was summoned for an audience.
Pitying his illness,
the emperor enfeoffed him as Earl of Zhōngqín [Zhōngqín Bó].
He received a stipend of 1,100 dàn of grain.
He died shortly after.
Wú Chéng,
a native of Liáoyáng,
was originally named Mǎilǘ.
His father Tōngbó was
Right Chancellor of the Liáoyáng Branch Secretariat [Liáoyáng Xíngshěng Yòuchéng] during the Yuán dynasty.
During Tàizǔ's time,
Guāntóng came to surrender,
and Tōngbó and his son accompanied him.
Mǎilǘ changed to his current name,
and served as a Chief of a Thousand [Zǒngqí],
often accompanying the main army beyond the frontier.
In the 1st year of Jiànwén, he was appointed Centennial of the Yǒngpíng Guard [Yǒngpíng Wèi Bǎihù].
He defected to Yān,
and rendered meritorious service in all battles,
being promoted three times to Vice Commander-in-chief [Dūzhǐhuī Qiānshì],
which was when he first became known.
The southern army, upon hearing the name Wú Mǎilǘ,
often pointed him out on the battlefield.
He set an ambush at Féihé,
advanced troops to Xiǎohé,
engaged in battle at Qíméi Shān,
and attacked and defeated the Língbì army.
In all these, he fought to the death,
accumulating many merits.
When Chéngzǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Chief Military Commander [Dūzhǐhuīshǐ].
He joined the expedition against Benyashiri.
He fought fiercely,
and Benyashiri escaped with seven riders.
He joined the expedition against Alutai,
combining forces with Zhū Róng as the vanguard,
pursuing the enemy to Kuòwānhǎi.
He was recalled,
and promoted to Vice Commander-in-chief [Dūdū Qiānshì].
He again participated in three expeditions beyond the frontier.
In the 1st year of Hóngxī, he was promoted to Left Chief Military Commander [Zuǒ Dūdū].
He accompanied Yángwǔ Hóu Xuē Lù in the expedition to Dàsōng Líng,
serving as the vanguard,
and for his merits,
his stipend of grain was increased.
At the beginning of Xuānzōng's reign,
because Chéng had once guarded the Eastern Palace,
remembering his past services,
he was enfeoffed as Earl of Qīngpíng [Qīngpíng Bó],
with a stipend of 1,100 dàn of grain,
and granted a hereditary writ.
He joined the expedition to Luò'ān,
again serving as vanguard with Xuē Lù.
After the matter was settled,
he was dispatched to guard Xīnghé.
Chéng enjoyed hunting but neglected military preparations.
Bandits, watching for him to go hunting,
suddenly entered the city,
plundered his wife and children, and left.
The emperor, hearing of this,
did not punish him.
Later, when Alutai came to pay tribute,
he returned Chéng's family.
In the 3rd year,
the emperor went on a northern expedition.
Chéng accompanied him in defeating the bandits at Kuānhé,
and was promoted to Marquis [Hóu],
with his stipend unchanged.
He died in the 8th year.
He was posthumously granted the title Duke of Qú [Qúguó Gōng],
and posthumously given the epithet Zhuàngyǒng.
His son Zhōng had died earlier.
Zhōng's son Yīng succeeded to the earldom.
When he died,
his son Xǐ succeeded.
He was deprived of his title for greed and debauchery.
After a long time, it was restored.
When he died,
he had no son.
His cousin Cóng succeeded.
Four generations later, down to his great-great-grandson Zūnzhōu.
At the end of Chóngzhēn,
when the capital fell,
he was killed.
Téng Dìng,
whose father Zànzhù
was a Grand Councillor of the Bureau of Military Affairs [Shūmì Zhīyuàn] during the Yuán dynasty.
During the Hóngwǔ period,
he came to surrender.
He was appointed Vice Commander of Huìzhōu Guard [Huìzhōu Wèi Zhǐhuī Qiānshì],
and granted the surname Téng.
He joined Yān in raising an army,
and was promoted to Commander of the Right Yānshān Guard [Yānshān Yòuwèi Zhǐhuīshǐ].
When he died,
Dìng succeeded to the office,
repeatedly participating in expeditions beyond the frontier,
and for his merits,
was promoted to Vice Commander-in-chief [Dūdū Qiānshì].
In the 4th year of Xuāndé, he was enfeoffed as Earl of Fènghuà [Fènghuà Bó],
with a stipend of 800 dàn of grain.
He died at the beginning of the Zhèngtǒng period.
His son Fú succeeded,
serving as commander [Zhǐhuīshǐ].
Jīn Shùn,
originally named Alugeshili.
During the Yǒnglè period, he came to surrender,
and was appointed Vice Commander of Dàníng [Dàníng Dūzhǐhuī Qiānshì].
He accompanied in defeating Benyashiri,
and again defeated Alutai,
being successively promoted to Vice Commander-in-chief [Dūdū Qiānshì].
In the 3rd year of Xuāndé, he accompanied the patrol of the northern frontier,
and achieved merits in killing and capturing.
The following year, he was enfeoffed as Earl of Shùnyì [Shùnyì Bó],
with a stipend of 800 dàn of grain.
When he died,
his son Zhōng succeeded,
serving as Vice Commander [Zhǐhuī Qiānshì].
Jīn Zhōng
was the Mongol prince Yēxiāntǔgān.
He was always cunning and unruly,
and was feared by Ālǔtái.
In the twenty-first year of Yǒnglè (1423),
Chéngzǔ personally led an expedition to the northern desert.
When he reached Shàngzhuāngbǎo,
Yēxiāntǔgān brought his wife, children, and subordinates to surrender.
At that time, the imperial army had penetrated deep,
and the enemy had already fled far away.
The emperor was ashamed of having achieved nothing,
so when he saw Yēxiāntǔgān come to submit,
he was greatly pleased.
He bestowed upon him the surname Jīn and the personal name Zhōng,
enfeoffed him as Zhōngyǒng Wáng (Prince of Loyalty and Valor),
granted him a cap, belt, and robes embroidered with gold,
ordered him to sit below the marquises,
and presented him with rare delicacies from the imperial table,
as well as gold, silver, and precious artifacts.
Jīn Zhōng was overjoyed beyond expectation.
On the return journey,
Jīn Zhōng rode alongside the emperor,
frequently inquiring about matters concerning the enemy,
and his favor and trust grew daily.
The following year,
Jīn Zhōng requested to serve as vanguard
to attack Ālǔtái and prove his loyalty.
The emperor initially refused.
However, alarm reports arrived from Dàtóng and Kāipíng,
and the generals requested to follow Jīn Zhōng’s suggestion.
The emperor again went out beyond the frontier.
Jīn Zhōng and Chén Mào served as the vanguard.
When Ālǔtái heard that the imperial army had again set out,
he hastily crossed the Dálánnàmù'ér River and fled.
Jīn Zhōng and Chén Mào reached the river but found no enemy.
They advanced to Báimáng Shān,
but still encountered no one,
so they returned.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
he promoted Jīn Zhōng to Tàizǐ Tàibǎo (Grand Guardian of the Crown Prince)
and allowed him to draw two salaries.
In the third year of Xuāndé (1428), Xuānzōng personally led an expedition against the Wùliánghā,
defeating the enemy at Kuānhé.
Jīn Zhōng and Bǎtái requested to distinguish themselves,
and the emperor permitted them.
Someone suggested that they should not be sent,
but the emperor said:
"Let them go or stay as they wish.
I possess the empire;
am I truly short of just these two men?"
The two captured several tens of people and hundreds of horses and cattle, which they presented.
The emperor was pleased,
ordered a court eunuch to pour wine for them in a golden goblet,
and then bestowed it upon them.
The following year, he was promoted to Tàibǎo (Grand Protector).
He died in the autumn of the sixth year (1431).
The emperor ordered the relevant authorities to manage his funeral.
Bǎtái
was Jīn Zhōng's nephew.
He surrendered with Jīn Zhōng
and was appointed Dūdū Qiānshì (Assistant Regional Military Commissioner).
In the early Xuāndé period,
he was granted the surname Jiǎng and the personal name Xìn.
During the Zhèngtǒng reign,
he was enfeoffed as Zhōngyǒng Bó (Earl of Loyalty and Valor).
While accompanying the emperor, he was trapped at Tǔmù.
Yēxiān placed him under the command of Sàihàn Wáng.
Although Jiǎng Xìn resided in the northern desert,
his heart was always with the Central Plains.
He often went to the Tàishàng Huáng’s (Emperor Emeritus) residence and wept bitterly,
providing him with considerable protection.
Later,
he eventually returned with the emperor,
and an imperial edict restored his salary.
He died in the fifth year of Jǐngtài (1454).
He was posthumously granted the title of Hóu (Marquis)
and the posthumous name Xīshùn.
His son, Yě'érsuǒhū, inherited his peerage.
In the early Tiānshùn period,
his name was changed to Shàn.
He died during the Hóngzhì reign.
Having no son,
his peerage became extinct.
Lǐ Yīng
was a Xīfān (Tibetan) man.
His father, Nángē,
led his people to submit during the Hóngwǔ reign,
was appointed Tóngzhī (Assistant Prefect) of Xīníng Zhōu,
and through accumulated merits, advanced to Xīníng Wèi Zhǐhuī Qiānshì (Assistant Commandant of Xīníng Guard).
Lǐ Yīng inherited his official position.
In the tenth year of Yǒnglè (1412),
the Tibetan chieftain Lǎo Díhǎn rebelled.
Lǐ Yīng attacked him.
He campaigned in Láichuān,
capturing and beheading 360 people.
It snowed at night,
and the rebels fled.
He pursued and captured all of them,
advancing to Dūzhīhuī Qiānshì (Assistant Regional Military Commissioner).
The Tibetan monk Zhāng Dálǐmá
was skilled in interpreting documents.
Chéngzǔ appointed him Zuǒ Juéyì (Left Upholder of Justice).
While residing in Xīníng,
he was extremely unrestrained.
He used schemes to seize wealth from Xīfān tribute envoys,
harbored fugitives,
and communicated with foreign regions,
committing evil for over ten years.
Lǐ Yīng exposed his deeds,
and Zhāng Dálǐmá was executed by dismemberment,
and his property confiscated.
The western frontier rejoiced.
In his later years,
the court eunuchs Qiáo Láixǐ and Dèng Chéng, among others, were sent as envoys to the Western Regions.
On their way through Āndìng and Qǔxiān,
they encountered bandits and were killed,
and the gold and silk they carried were plundered.
Rénzōng issued an imperial letter to Chìjīn, Hǎndōng, as well as Āndìng and Qǔxiān,
demanding the names of the bandit leaders.
He also ordered Lǐ Yīng and the local official, Dūzhīhuī Kāng Shòu, among others, to launch a punitive expedition.
Lǐ Yīng secretly learned that Āndìng Dūzhīhuī Hāsānsūn Sàngē and Qǔxiān Dūzhīhuī Sǎnjísī had actually killed the envoys.
He then led his troops westward.
The bandits were alarmed and fled.
He pursued and attacked them,
crossing the Kūnlún Shān,
penetrating several hundred *li* deep.
Upon reaching Yǎlìngkuò,
he encountered the Āndìng bandits
and utterly defeated them,
capturing and beheading over 1,100 people
and seizing 140,000 horses, cattle, and other livestock.
The Qǔxiān bandits, hearing the news, fled far away.
The Āndìng King, Sāng'ěrjiāshījiā, and others, fearful,
went to the capital to apologize.
Xuānzōng commended Lǐ Yīng’s achievement,
sent an envoy to praise and instruct him,
held a banquet to reward him,
and ordered him to travel by post horse to the court.
Upon his arrival,
he was promoted to Yòufǔ Zuǒ Dūdū (Left Regional Military Commissioner of the Right Military Command),
and his rewards were increased.
In the second year of Xuāndé (1427), he was enfeoffed as Huìníng Bó (Earl of Huìníng),
with a salary of 1,100 *shi* of grain,
and Nángē was also enfeoffed with a peerage equivalent to a Viscount.
Lǐ Yīng became arrogant due to his merits,
and many of his actions were lawless.
Shǐ Zhāo, the Grand Commander of Níngxià, memorialized that Lǐ Yīng and his son had rebellious intentions.
Nángē submitted a memorial in defense.
An imperial edict was issued to comfort and instruct him.
Lǐ Yīng, residing in Xīníng,
harbored over 700 households of fugitives,
established estates, reclaimed land,
and forcibly seized people’s property.
He was again impeached by the Ministry of War and censors.
The emperor pardoned Lǐ Yīng,
but the fugitives were to be conscripted into official service.
In the seventh year (1432),
Qí Zhèn’s son, Chéng, a Dūzhīhuī of Xīníng, was to inherit his father's position.
His illegitimate elder brother, Jiānzàng,
who was also Lǐ Yīng’s nephew,
wished to usurp it.
Chéng’s granduncle, Tàipíng, brought Chéng to the capital to argue their case.
Lǐ Yīng sent someone to seize Tàipíng and his adopted son and beat them.
The adopted son eventually died.
Censors jointly impeached Lǐ Yīng,
including his previous crimes.
Consequently, Lǐ Yīng was imprisoned by imperial edict,
stripped of his peerage, and sentenced to death.
He was finally released in the second year of Zhèngtǒng (1437).
Later, a portion of his salary was gradually restored.
He died soon after.
When Yīngzōng was restored to the throne,
his son, Bīng, was appointed Jǐnyī Dūzhīhuī Tóngzhī (Associate Commissioner of the Embroidered Uniform Guard).
Soon after, he was promoted to Dūzhīhuī Shǐ (Regional Military Commissioner),
and by recommendation, was elevated to Zuǒjūn Dūdū Qiānshì (Assistant Regional Military Commissioner of the Left Army).
He frequently oversaw military camp affairs,
and was known for his strictness and prudence.
Lǐ Yīng’s nephew, Lǐ Wén,
served as Shǎnxī Xíngdōusī Dūzhīhuī Qiānshì (Assistant Regional Military Commissioner of the Shǎnxī Provincial Military Command) during the Xuāndé reign.
The Xīfān, Sī'é Kě, once stole fine horses from another tribe.
Dūzhīhuī Mù Sù sought them but could not find them.
It happened that Sī'é Kě was selling livestock at the border.
Mù Sù falsely accused him of theft,
apprehended and plundered him, leading to his death.
The Tibetans were terrified and contemplated rebellion.
Lǐ Wén impeached Mù Sù,
who was arrested and handed over to the authorities,
thus pacifying the western frontier.
He was successively promoted to Dūzhīhuī Shǐ.
In the first year of Tiānshùn (1457), he falsely claimed credit for welcoming the emperor,
and was promoted to Dūdū Qiānshì.
Not long after,
he was appointed Yòu Dūdū (Right Regional Military Commissioner) and sent to garrison Dàtóng.
When over 2,000 enemy cavalry raided Wēiyuǎn,
Lǐ Wén led his troops to defeat them,
and was enfeoffed as Gāoyáng Bó (Earl of Gāoyáng).
When Shí Hēng fell from power,
officials who falsely claimed credit for the "Door Seizing" coup were stripped of their positions.
Lǐ Wén confessed,
but the emperor, considering his border defense service, did not prosecute him.
In the autumn of the fourth year,
Bólái (孛來) invaded in force.
Wén (文) held back his troops and did not engage in battle,
whereupon Bólái (孛來) entered Yànmén (雁門),
and extensively plundered Xīn (忻) and Dài (代) prefectures.
The capital was shaken with fear.
After the invaders retreated,
Wén (文) was summoned and imprisoned,
and sentenced to execution.
The emperor pardoned Wén (文) from death,
demoting him to Dūdū Qiānshì (都督僉事),
and ordered him to perform meritorious service in Yánsuí (延綏).
Soon after, he was promoted to Dūdū Tóngzhī (都督同知).
During the Chénghuà (成化) era,
Hāmì (哈密) was annexed by Tǔlǔfān (土魯番)
and sought aid from the court.
An imperial edict ordered Wén (文) and You Tōngzhèng (右通政) Liú Wén (劉文) to go to Gānsù (甘肅) to manage the situation,
but they returned without success.
He died in the early Hóngzhì (弘治) reign.
In the early Zhèngdé (正德) reign, he was posthumously granted the title of Gāoyáng Bó (高陽伯).
Máo Shèng (毛勝),
courtesy name Yòngqīn (用欽),
originally named Fúshòu (福壽),
was the grandson of Yuán (元) You Chéngxiàng (右丞相) Bó Bǔhuā (伯卜花).
His paternal uncle, Nāhǎi (那海),
submitted during the Hóngwǔ (洪武) reign,
and through his
"Jìngnán" (靖難)
merits, reached the position of Dū Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī (都指揮同知),
but had no son.
Shèng's (勝) father, Āntài (安太), succeeded him as Yǔlín Zhǐhuīshǐ (羽林指揮使),
and the position was passed to his son, Jì (濟),
who had no son.
Shèng (勝) then succeeded.
Because of Jì's (濟) merits in the northern campaign,
Shèng (勝) was promoted to Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ (都指揮使).
He once fled to beyond the frontier,
but soon returned on his own.
In the seventh year of Zhèngtǒng (正統), for his merits in the campaign against Lùchuān (麓川),
he was promoted to Dūdū Qiānshì (都督僉事).
Jìngyuǎn Bó (靖遠伯) Wáng Jì (王驥) requested that selected barbarian generals and retainers in the capital
be dispatched to Yunnan to capture Miao (苗) rebels.
So, Shèng (勝) and Dūdū (都督) Rǎn Bǎo (冉保) were ordered to lead six hundred men there.
Later,
in the second campaign against Lùchuān (麓川),
the two were appointed Zuo Cānjìang (左參將) and You Cānjìang (右參將).
When the rebels were pacified,
he was promoted to Dūdū Tóngzhī (都督同知).
In the summer of the fourteenth year,
Yěxiān (也先) planned to invade.
Shèng (勝), along with Píngxiāng Bó (平鄉伯) Chén Huái (陳懷) and others, led thirty thousand imperial troops to garrison Dàtóng (大同).
Huái (懷) encountered the invaders and died in battle,
while Shèng (勝) escaped and returned.
Upon the recommendation of Wǔqīng Bó (武清伯) Shí Hēng (石亨),
Jǐngdì (景帝) promoted Shèng (勝) to Zuǒ Dūdū (左都督),
and ordered him to supervise the training of the Three Thousand Camps.
When the Miao (苗) people in Guìzhōu (貴州) caused a major disturbance,
an edict ordered Shèng (勝) to go and suppress them.
Before he could depart,
Yěxiān (也先) advanced on the capital.
Shèng (勝) defended against him north of Zhāngyìmén (彰義門),
and repelled him.
Two days later,
he led his troops outside Xīzhímén (西直門),
and lifted the siege on Dūdū (都督) Sūn Táng (孫鏜).
The next day,
Dūdū (都督) Wǔ Xīng (武興) died in battle at Zhāngyìmén (彰義門),
and the invaders pressed their advantage.
Shèng (勝) and Dū Yùshǐ (都御史) Wáng Hóng (王竑) quickly reinforced them,
and the invaders then withdrew.
Shèng (勝) pursued them to Zǐjīngguān (紫荊關),
and achieved considerable斩獲.
When the situation stabilized,
he was ordered, as Zuǒ Fù Zǒngbīng (左副總兵), to lead the surrendered barbarians from Héjiān (河間) and Dōngchāng (東昌) to Guìzhōu (貴州).
The rebel leader Wéi Tóngliè (韋同烈) rebelled from Xiānglúshān (香爐山).
Shèng (勝), along with Zǒngbīng (總兵) Liáng Bǎo (梁珤) and You Fù Zǒngbīng (右副總兵) Fāng Yīng (方瑛) and others, followed Zǒngdū (總督) Wáng Lái (王來) to attack from different routes.
Shèng (勝) advanced from Zhòng'ān Jiāng (重安江)
and utterly defeated them.
The forces met at the foot of the mountain
and attacked from all four sides.
The rebels were cornered,
and tied up Tóngliè (同烈) to surrender.
He returned to suppress the rebels in Húguǎng (湖廣), Bāmǎ (巴馬) and other places,
capturing over twenty stockades,
apprehending rebel leaders Wú Fèngxiān (吳奉先) and 140 others,
and beheading over a thousand.
He was enfeoffed as Nánníng Bó (南寧伯),
and granted a hereditary certificate.
He submitted a memorial requesting to change his name,
which was granted.
He was transferred to garrison Téngchōng (騰衝).
Dāo Fànggé (刀放革), the Chángguān (長官) of the Jīnchǐ Mángshì (金齒芒市), secretly conspired with Sī Bófā (思卜發), a remnant of Lùchuān (麓川), to rebel.
Shèng (勝) devised a strategy and captured them.
The巡按御史 (Xún'àn Yùshǐ) Móu Fèng (牟俸) impeached him for dozens of acts of greed, tyranny, and lawlessness,
and further stated that Shèng (勝) was originally a surrendered person,
cunning and difficult to control,
and now frequently communicated with foreign barbarians,
fearing that this would cause border troubles.
An imperial edict ordered the Xúnfǔ (巡撫) to verify the facts,
but ultimately nothing was done.
He died in the second year of Tiānshùn (天順).
He was posthumously granted the title of Hóu (侯),
and given the posthumous name Zhuāngyì (莊毅).
His son Róng (榮) succeeded.
Implicated in the Shí Hēng (石亨) faction,
he was sent to Guǎngxī (廣西) to perform meritorious service.
In the early Chénghuà (成化) reign,
he garrisoned Guìzhōu (貴州),
and soon moved to Liǎngguǎng (兩廣).
He died,
and his son Wén (文) succeeded.
In the early Hóngzhì (弘zhi) reign, he assisted in defending Nánjīng (南京),
and the爵 (jué) was passed down until the fall of the Míng (明) dynasty, when it ceased.
Jiāo Lǐ (焦禮),
courtesy name Shàngjié (尚節),
was a Mongolian.
His father, Bǎsī tái (把思台),
submitted during the Hóngwǔ (洪wu) reign,
and became Tōngzhōu Wèi Zhǐhuī Qiānshì (通州衞指揮僉事).
His son Shèng (勝) succeeded,
and the position was passed down to Yìróng (義榮),
who had no son.
So, Shèng's (勝) younger brother Qiān (謙) succeeded,
and through accumulated merits reached the rank of Dū Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī (都指揮同知).
When he died,
his son Guǎnshīnú (管失奴) was young.
Qiān's (謙) younger brother Lǐ (禮) temporarily inherited his position,
and was responsible for defense in Liáodōng (遼東).
In the early Xuāndé (宣德) reign,
Lǐ (禮) was supposed to return the position.
Xuānzōng (宣宗), recalling Lǐ's (禮) arduous service in defending the border,
ordered him to remain in his post as before,
and separately appointed Guǎnshīnú (管失奴) as Zhǐhuīshǐ (指揮使).
Lǐ (禮) soon, due to his age and service,
was successively promoted to Dū Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī (都指揮同知).
During the Zhèngtǒng (正統) era,
through accumulated merits, he reached the rank of You Dūdū (右都督).
When Yīngzōng (英宗) was captured in the north,
Jǐngdì (景帝) appointed him as Zuǒ Fù Zǒngbīng (左副總兵)
to guard Níngyuǎn (寧遠).
Not long after,
Yěxiān (也先) approached the capital,
and an edict ordered Lǐ (禮) to lead troops to defend it.
After the invaders retreated, he returned to his garrison.
In the fourth year of Jǐngtài (景泰),
over two thousand enemy cavalry attacked Xīngshuǐbǎo (興水堡).
Lǐ (禮) repelled them.
An imperial letter commended and encouraged him,
and promoted him to Zuǒ Dūdū (左都督).
When Yīngzōng (英宗) was restored to the throne,
he summoned Lǐ (禮) for an audience due to his meritorious service in guarding the frontier,
enfeoffed him as Dōngníng Bó (東寧伯),
which was hereditary,
and bestowed upon him generous rewards,
then sent him back to his garrison.
The Ministry of War,
considering Lǐ (禮) was nearing eighty and
could not manage alone,
memorialized to send Dū Zhǐhuī (都指揮) Dèng Duó (鄧鐸) to assist in defense.
Not long after,
Lǐ (禮) reported that Duó (鐸) was disrespectful and abusive,
and requested a transfer.
Dū Zhǐhuī (都指揮) Zhāng Jùn (張俊) was ordered to replace Duó (鐸).
He died at his garrison in the seventh year of Tiānshùn (天順).
He was posthumously granted the title of Hóu (侯),
and given the posthumous name Xiāngyì (襄毅).
Lǐ (禮) possessed courage and strategy,
was skilled in cavalry archery,
and adept at defeating large forces with a small number.
He guarded Níngyuǎn (寧遠) for over thirty years,
and his officers and soldiers were happy to serve him,
resulting in peace along the border.
Sūn Shòu inherited the title.
He died,
leaving no son.
His younger brother, Jùn, succeeded.
In the late Chénghuà reign,
Jùn successively garrisoned Gānsù and Níngxià.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
he took charge of the Nánjīng Front Command,
and concurrently supervised naval operations on the river.
He was then sent to garrison Guìzhōu and Húguǎng.
Jùn had been involved in commerce when young.
After gaining prominence,
he was able to befriend scholars,
but he was not skilled in strategic maneuvers.
He died,
and his son Qí succeeded.
Qí once held a separate command in the Imperial Army.
During the Zhèngdé reign,
he bribed Líu Jǐn
and was sent to garrison Liǎngguǎng.
He died the following year,
and his younger brother Xún succeeded.
Although Xún inherited the title,
his family's former property was entirely owned by Qí's wife.
When his birth mother died,
he had no means to bury her.
Overcome with grief and indignation, he fell ill and died.
Having no son,
his second cousin Dòng succeeded.
During the Jiājìng reign,
Dòng was appointed Grand Coordinator of the Five Army Commands,
and concurrently took charge of the Central Command.
After more than ten years,
he was reassigned as Grand General of Húguǎng.
He died
and was posthumously granted the title of Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince,
with the posthumous name Zhuāngxī.
The title was passed down until the fall of the Míng dynasty, when it ceased.
Máo Zhōng,
courtesy name Yǔnchéng,
originally named Hālā,
was from the western frontier.
His great-grandfather, Hālādaǐ,
submitted in the early Hóngwǔ reign,
rose through the ranks to become a battalion commander (qiānhù),
and died in battle.
His grandfather, Bàidū, followed in the campaign against Hāmì
and also died in battle.
His father, Bǎo, was appointed a chief standard-bearer (zǒngqí) for his bravery
and rose to be a centurion (bǎihù) in Yǒngchāng.
When Zhōng inherited the position,
he was twenty years old.
He possessed extraordinary physical strength
and was skilled in horsemanship and archery.
He often followed Tàizōng on northern campaigns.
In Xuāndé 5th year (1430), he distinguished himself in the campaign against the rebellious Qǔxiān bandits.
He achieved merit.
In the 8th year (1433), during the campaign against Yìbùlàshān,
he captured the pretender Junior Tutor (shàoshī) Zhīyùan.
In the 9th year (1434), he marched out to Tuōhuānshān.
In the 10th year (1435), he campaigned against the Hēishān bandits.
In all cases, he captured their chiefs.
He was promoted one rank for each achievement,
successively becoming Assistant Commander (zhǐhūitóngzhī).
In Zhèngtǒng 3rd year (1438), he followed Grand Governor Jiǎng Guì in the campaign against Jiǎn'érzhǐbó.
He was the first to scale the defenses and break the enemy lines,
achieving a great victory.
He was promoted to Assistant Regional Commander (dūzhǐhuīqiānshì).
In the 10th year (1445), for his meritorious service in guarding the frontier,
he was promoted to Commander (tóngzhī)
and was first granted a Chinese surname.
The following year, he followed Grand General Rèn Lǐ to capture the Nángē tribe, a Grand Governor (dūzhǐ) of Shāzhōuwèi.
He resettled them within the pass
and was promoted to Regional Commander (dūzhǐhuīshǐ).
In the 13th year (1448), he led his army to Hǎndōng
and personally captured Nángē's brother, the pretender Prince Qí Suǒnánbēn, along with his followers.
He was promoted to Assistant Military Commissioner (dūdūqiānshì)
and was first granted the name Zhōng.
Soon after, he was appointed Assistant Regional Commander (yòucāncānjīang)
to assist in guarding Gānsù.
In the early Jǐngtài reign,
Vice Minister Lǐ Shí, who was on a mission to the Mòběi,
returned and reported that Zhōng had repeatedly sent envoys to communicate with the Wǎlà.
An imperial edict ordered his arrest and transfer to the capital.
Upon his arrival,
the Ministry of War discussed his crime,
requesting the death penalty.
Emperor Jǐng did not permit it.
They requested his demotion
and dispatch to Fújiàn to perform meritorious service.
He was then sent to Fújiàn,
but his official rank remained unchanged.
The Gānsù garrison commander was ordered to move his family to the capital.
Initially, when Zhōng campaigned in the desert,
he captured the Tibetan monk Jiāshǐ Lǐngzhēn and presented him to the emperor.
Emperor Yīng pardoned him instead of executing him.
Later, the monk escaped to the Wǎlà
and was employed by Yěxiān.
He harbored resentment towards Zhōng
and sought to implicate him,
so he spread the rumor that Zhōng was colluding with Yěxiān,
and the imperial court did not investigate.
Emperor Yīng, when he was outside the pass, alone knew the truth.
Upon his restoration,
he immediately summoned Zhōng back.
Meanwhile, Zhōng had also achieved repeated victories in Fújiàn,
so he was promoted to Assistant Military Commissioner (dūdūtóngzhī),
appointed Vice Grand General of the Left (zuǒfùzǒngbīng),
and garrisoned Gānsù.
When he was granted an audience,
he received exceptionally warm consolation and encouragement
and was bestowed a jade belt and a woven-gold python robe.
In Tiānshùn 2nd year (1458),
invaders made a major incursion into Gānsù.
Circuit Inspector Rùǐ Zhāo impeached the generals for their failures.
The ministry deliberated that Zhōng's merits were sufficient to atone for his faults,
and the matter was dropped.
In the 3rd year (1459), for his merit in defeating bandits at Zhènfān,
he was promoted to Grand Commissioner of the Left (zuǒdūdū).
In the 5th year (1461),
Bólái, with tens of thousands of cavalry, plundered the various routes of Xīníng, Zhuānglàng, and Gānsù,
and entered Liángzhōu.
Zhōng fought fiercely day and night,
until his arrows were exhausted and his strength failed.
The enemy grew ever more numerous,
and fear spread throughout the army.
Zhōng's spirit intensified,
and he encouraged his officers and soldiers,
then resumed a desperate struggle.
The bandits saw that he could not ultimately be defeated,
and reinforcements also arrived,
so they withdrew.
Zhōng ultimately returned with his entire army intact.
In the 7th year (1463),
various foreign tribes outside the passes of Yǒngchāng, Liángzhōu, and Zhuānglàng repeatedly caused border disturbances.
Zhōng and Grand General Wèi Yǐng divided forces to subdue them.
Zhōng first defeated the great clans of Bāwā.
As for the Zǎnzá, Mǎjíśī, and other clans,
which other generals could not subjugate,
Zhōng again attacked and defeated them.
When merits were evaluated,
Zhōng only received an increase of a hundred shi of salary,
while Yǐng received a hereditary patent.
Zhōng complained about this,
and was consequently enfeoffed as the Earl of Fúqiāng.
In Chénghuà 4th year (1468),
the Gùyuán bandit Mǎn Sì occupied Shíchéng and rebelled.
An edict ordered Zhōng to move his troops to suppress him.
He, along with Grand Governor Xiàng Zhōng and others, launched a pincer attack on the bandit stronghold.
Zhōng advanced directly from Mùtóugōu to the foot of Pàojiàshān,
achieving many kills and captures.
As the bandits somewhat retreated,
he braved arrows and stones to successively seize the northern and western peaks of the mountain.
Xiàng Zhōng's army and others also captured the eastern peak of the mountain
and the eastern and western gates of Shíchéng.
The bandits were in great distress
and wept to each other.
Suddenly, a thick fog arose,
and other outposts raised smoke signals and withdrew their troops.
The bandits then concentrated their forces to attack Zhōng.
Zhōng fought relentlessly
but was struck by a stray arrow
and died,
aged seventy-five.
His cousin Hǎi and grandson Kǎi, who had gone to rescue Zhōng,
also died.
As a general, Zhōng maintained strict discipline
and was good at treating his soldiers kindly.
When he died,
people from the western frontier mourned and cried, visible along the roads.
When this was reported to the emperor,
he was posthumously granted the title of Marquis,
with the posthumous name Wǔyǒng,
and a hereditary patent was conferred.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
following the suggestion of officials,
a Zhōngyì Archway was erected in Lánzhōu
to commemorate his native place.
Also, following the suggestion of Circuit Inspector Xǔ Jìn,
a Wǔyǒng Ancestral Temple was built east of Gānzhōuchéng,
with sacrifices offered in spring and autumn.
He was in Qú for seven years.
At the beginning of the Yǒnglè reign,
he was summoned due to implication in a case.
Hundreds of elders prostrated themselves before the palace gate, begging for him to be kept,
but it was not granted.
Later, court officials spoke of Dūn's integrity and uprightness,
and he was summoned to be appointed Supervising Secretary (Jiānchá Yùshǐ).
He was promoted to Left Administration Commissioner (Zuǒ Cānzhèng) of Hénán,
then transferred to Shǎnxī.
In the spring of the sixteenth year,
Hú Yíng said that Dūn had the demeanor of a great minister,
and he was promoted to Right Vice Minister (Yòu Shìláng) of the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù) and concurrently Grand Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud (Tàipú Sì Qīng).
He was dispatched with Censor (Gěishìzhōng) Táo Kàn to tour and pacify Shùntiān.
In the twentieth year, he supervised the provisions for the northern expedition.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
because he did not observe the fasting and lodging for the mourning of the late emperor,
he was demoted to Grand Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud.
Soon after, he was promoted to Left Vice Minister (Zuǒ Shìláng) of the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù),
concurrently Junior Supervisor (Shǎojìanshì) of the Supervisorate of Imperial Instruction (Zhānshì Fǔ).
In the second year of Xuāndé, he was promoted to Minister (Shàngshū).
When Shǎnxī suffered a drought,
he was ordered to go with the Marquis of Lóngpíng, Zhāng Xìn, to rectify matters that needed to be carried out,
and to consult with the officials of the Three Bureaus (Sānsī) to deliberate and report for implementation.
Dūn then requested the remission of overdue taxes,
the relief of the poor,
the evaluation and dismissal of corrupt officials,
and the cessation of non-urgent tasks,
amounting to more than ten matters.
All were followed.
After more than a year,
he was recalled.
While in the ministry, he initiated many reforms,
abolishing the seizure of people's land for royal estates,
and allowing people to reclaim barren land without being taxed.
He proposed a new system for grain transport (Cáoyùn):
the people transported grain to Guāzhōu and Yízhēn,
and then the garrison soldiers transported it to the capital.
The people found this very convenient.
Dūn was filial to his parents
and held himself with integrity.
If a fellow official acted unrighteously,
he would sternly rebuke them
until they repented and apologized.
He was fond of learning by nature.
After public duties,
he never let a book leave his hand.
In the sixth year,
he died in office,
at the age of sixty-two.
Guō Jǐn,
courtesy name Shíyòng,
originally named Jìn,
was a native of Xīn'ān.
At the beginning of the Yǒnglè reign,
he was promoted from Imperial College student to Principal (Zhǔshì) of the Ministry of Revenue.
He successively served as Left and Right Vice Minister (Zuǒ, Yòu Shìláng) of the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù).
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
he was ordered to concurrently serve as Junior Supervisor (Shǎojìanshì) of the Supervisorate of Imperial Instruction,
and his name was changed to Jǐn.
At the beginning of Xuānzōng's reign,
he took charge of the Traveling Supervisorate of Imperial Instruction (Xíngzài Zhānshì Fǔ).
When the Minister of Personnel, Jiǎn Yì, grew old
and stopped handling departmental affairs,
the emperor wanted to replace him with Jǐn.
Jǐn was steady, diligent, and quick-witted,
but lacked scholarship.
Yáng Shìqí said that Jǐn might not be sufficient for the position,
and it would be better to carefully select a great minister who understood the classics and knew both ancient and modern times.
The emperor then stopped the appointment.
After more than a year,
he finally became Minister.
The emperor advised him to follow the examples of Lǚ Méngzhèng's "pouch for worthy men"
and Yú Yǔnwén's "record of talented individuals."
Jǐn thus paid attention to talented people.
He recognized the Prime Ministerial talent in the advanced scholar Lǐ Xián,
appointed him Principal (Zhǔshì) of the Ministry of Personnel,
who indeed later became a famous chancellor.
At that time, when an external official's nine-year term of examination was complete,
the local people would go to the palace gate to beg for him to remain,
and he would usually be promoted in rank and reappointed.
Jǐn worried that there might be fraudulent cases,
and requested a review to confirm the facts.
This was followed.
Although Jǐn was the chief of the Six Ministries (Liù Qīng),
his prestige was light.
Moreover, governance was returned to the Grand Secretariat (Nèigé),
and vacancies from Administration Commissioner (Bùzhèngshǐ) down to Prefect (Zhīfǔ) were filled by recommendations from Beijing officials of the third rank or higher.
Later, Censors (Yùshǐ) and Magistrates (Zhīxiàn)
were also appointed based on recommendations from Beijing officials of the fifth rank or higher.
Crucial positions were selected and promoted,
all without involving the Ministry of Personnel.
At the beginning of the Zhèngtǒng reign,
Left Vice-Censor-in-chief (Zuǒ Tōngzhèng) Chén Gōng said:
“In ancient times, the selection of various officials
was entirely handled by the Ministry of Selection (Xuǎnbù),
where responsibilities were specialized and affairs unified.
Now, allowing court officials to each recommend those they know
might open the door to private solicitations
and encourage a spirit of vying for advancement.
I request that this practice be stopped
and affairs be unified.”
The matter was sent to the Ministry of Personnel for deliberation.
Jǐn humbly declined, not daring to take responsibility,
and the matter was thus shelved.
In the sixth year of Zhèngtǒng,
Censor Cáo Gōng, citing natural disasters,
requested the dismissal of incompetent high-ranking officials.
The emperor ordered the officials of the Censorate (Kēdào Guān) to deliberate.
Jǐn, Minister Wú Zhōng, Vice Minister Lǐ Yōng, and twenty others were impeached.
Jǐn and the others defended themselves.
The emperor sternly rebuked them but pardoned them.
Jǐn's son, Liàng, accepted bribes to seek official positions for others.
When the matter came to light,
Censor Sūn Yù and others impeached Jǐn.
Jǐn was then ordered to retire,
and Wáng Zhí was appointed in his place.
Zhèng Chén,
courtesy name Wénshū,
was a native of Xī'ān, Zhèjiāng.
He became an advanced scholar (Jìnshì) in the fourth year of Yǒnglè.
He was appointed Supervising Secretary (Jiānchá Yùshǐ).
When the people of Ānfú, Jiāngxī, reported a conspiracy of rebellion,
Chén was ordered to investigate it,
and he fully exposed the false accusation.
When foreign visitors in Fújiàn committed murder,
Chén was again sent.
He only punished the principal culprits,
releasing the others.
When the Bào'ēnsì Temple was built by imperial decree in Nánjīng,
ten thousand prisoners were conscripted.
Rumors spread that the laborers were slandering and conspiring,
fearing a change,
Chén was ordered to verify.
There was no truth,
and not a single person was punished.
When Gǔ Shùrén conspired for rebellion,
Chén was again ordered to investigate,
and he uncovered all his traces.
The emperor said to Fāng Bīn:
“This is truly a minister who serves as the ears and eyes of the state.”
In the sixteenth year, he was exceptionally promoted to Surveillance Commissioner (Ànchásǐ) of Shānxī,
and he strictly punished corrupt officials without leniency.
When bandits rose in Lùzhōu,
the authorities reported it as rebellion,
and an imperial edict ordered troops to be dispatched for suppression.
Chén was in the capital for official business at the time,
and he memorialized:
“The people are merely suffering from corvée labor;
please do not dispatch troops.”
The emperor agreed.
Upon his return, he dismissed his retinue
and personally entered the mountains and valleys to comfort and appease the bandits.
All the bandits were moved to tears,
and returned to being good citizens.
When Vice Minister of Rites, Yù Shòu, transported grain to supply the troops at Shānhǎi,
Chén was in charge of the cartage by the people of Shānxī.
The people were exhausted and many were in arrears or had wasted supplies.
Shòu ordered them to borrow and repay immediately at Shānhǎi.
Chén said:
“The people of Shānxī are poor and stubborn;
pressing them too hard might cause unrest.
It is better to relax the demand
and allow them to manage their own resources.”
His words were adopted,
and in the end, there were no arrears.
When he returned home to observe mourning for his parent,
the military and civilian populace went to the Censor (Yùshǐ) to beg for him to remain.
The Censor reported it,
and after the mourning period, he returned to his former post.
In the third year of Xuāndé,
he was summoned to be Right Vice Minister (Yòu Shìláng) of the Ministry of Works (Gōngbù) in Nánjīng.
Initially, when there were vacancies for the heads of the Six Ministries (Liù Bù) in both capitals,
the emperor ordered court officials to recommend regional officials suitable for internal positions.
Jiǎn Yì and others recommended nine people.
Only Chén, Shào Qǐ, and Fù Qǐràng
were known by name to the emperor,
and he immediately appointed them officially;
the others were merely given probationary appointments.
When Yīngzōng 英宗 ascended the throne,
he dispatched high officials to inspect local administrators throughout the empire.
Chén 辰 went to Sìchuān 四川, Guìzhōu 貴州, and Yúnnán 雲南,
and impeached all those who were not performing their duties.
The Yúnnán 雲南 Provincial Administration Commissioner Zhōu Jǐng 周璟, while in mourning for his wife,
remarried.
Chén 辰 impeached him for harming moral customs,
and Jǐng 璟 was consequently dismissed.
In the second year of Zhèngtǒng 正統 (1437),
he was ordered to provide famine relief in Nánjī 南畿 and Hénán 河南.
At that time, the river dikes had burst,
so Chén 辰 was immediately ordered to seize the opportunity to repair and block them.
Some proposed digging a canal from Dàmíng 大名
to divert various waters into the Wèihé 河,
benefiting irrigation.
Chén 辰 argued that it would be too much labor for the people and inconvenient,
so the plan was abandoned.
He was promoted to Vice Minister of War (Bīngbù Zuǒ Shìláng 兵部左侍郎),
and, with the Marquis of Fēngchéng 豐城 Hóu Lǐ Bīn 李彬, transported provisions to Xuānfǔ 宣府 and Dàtóng 大同.
The Grand Commandant (Zhènshǒu Dūdū 鎮守都督) Tán Guǎng 譚廣 obstructed the order,
so Chén 辰 impeached him,
and the matter was resolved.
In the eighth year (1443), he suffered from a wind-stroke,
and requested to return home.
He died the following year.
Chén 辰 was a man who valued righteousness and lightly regarded wealth.
When he first passed the imperial examination (jìnshì 進士),
he yielded all his property to his brothers.
While in Shānxī 山西, he had a disagreement with his colleague, Commissioner (Qiānshì 僉事) Dù 杜.
When Dù 杜 died,
Chén 辰 managed his funeral,
and provided funds for his wife and children to return home.
Chái Chē 柴車,
courtesy name Shúyú 叔輿,
was from Qiántáng 錢塘.
In the second year of Yǒnglè 永樂 (1404), as a recommended scholar (jǔrén 舉人), he was appointed Principal of the Bureau of Military Appointments (Bīngbù Wǔxuǎnsī Zhǔshì 兵部武選司主事) in the Ministry of War,
then promoted to Supervising Secretary (Yuánwàiláng 員外郎).
In the eighth year (1410),
when the emperor went on a northern expedition,
he accompanied Minister (Shàngshū 尚書) Fāng Bīn 方賓 on the imperial retinue.
Upon his return, he was transferred to Right Vice Commissioner (Yòucānyì 右參議) of Jiāngxī 江西.
Due to an incident,
he was demoted to Director of the Bureau of Military Appointments (Bīngbù Lángzhōng 兵部郎中),
then sent out to govern Yuèzhōu Fǔ 岳州府,
and later reinstated as Director (Lángzhōng 郎中).
In the fifth year of Xuāndé 宣德 (1430), he was promoted to Vice Minister of War (Bīngbù Shìláng 兵部侍郎).
The following year,
the Shānxī 山西 Circuit Censor (Xún'àn Yùshǐ 巡按御史) Zhāng Xù 張勖 reported that much of the garrison land in Dàtóng 大同 was occupied by powerful gentry,
so Chē 車 was ordered to investigate.
He recovered nearly two thousand qǐng 頃 of land,
and returned it to the military.
At the beginning of Yīngzōng's 英宗 reign,
the western frontier was not peaceful.
As Chē 車 was upright and capable,
he was ordered to assist in military affairs in Gānsù 甘肅.
He managed troop deployment and provision allocation,
all with efficiency.
Previously,
Wá'ér Zhǐbó 瓦兒只伯 had raided Liángzhōu 涼州,
and Vice General (Fùzǒngbīng 副總兵) Liú Guǎng 劉廣 suffered a defeat,
but did not report the truth,
instead embellishing his achievements to seek rewards.
Chē 車 impeached him for his crime.
Guǎng 廣 was shackled and brought to the capital,
and Chē 車 was awarded gold and silk,
to commend his integrity.
Hòu Néng 后能, a native official (tǔguān 土官) in Mínzhōu 岷州, falsely claimed achievements and received promotions and rewards.
Chē 車 requested to punish him.
Néng 能 again requested mercy,
and the emperor ordered his pardon.
Chē 車 repeatedly argued against it,
saying:
"Those who falsely claim achievements like Néng 能 are indeed numerous,
and I am just beginning to investigate them one by one.
If Néng 能 is pardoned now,
how can we deter the others?
If one can gain office without merit,
then how should those who sacrifice their lives fighting the enemy be treated?"
Although the court granted Néng's 能 request,
it admired Chē's 車 wisdom,
and sent an envoy to comfort and reward him.
In the third year of Zhèngtǒng 正統 (1438),
for his merit in defeating Wá'ér Zhǐbó 瓦兒只伯,
his salary was increased by one grade.
While on the frontier,
he submitted dozens of memorials,
all addressing contemporary issues.
Many of his colleagues were displeased,
but Chē 車 held his ground even more firmly.
He once suggested:
"As for the surrendered people from beyond the desert (Mòběi 漠北),
the court keeps them in the capital;
even with generous titles and rewards,
their hearts remain disloyal.
For instance, Cháng Tuōtuō Mù'ér 長脫脫木兒,
who once followed his chief and surrendered,
rebelled and fled shortly after.
Now he has returned again;
how can we know he won't rebel again in the future?
It would be advisable to resettle them in Jiāngnán 江南,
to separate them from their factions."
The matter was sent to the Ministry of War,
who requested they be placed in Héjiān 河間 and Dézhōu 德州.
The emperor approved.
Thereafter, all subsequent surrenders were dealt with according to this decree.
He investigated and cleared out the powerful gentry who occupied garrison lands,
recovering over six hundred qǐng 頃.
In the fourth year (1439), he was promoted to Minister of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū 兵部尚書),
continuing to assist in military affairs as before.
Soon after, he was ordered to also manage garrison lands in Shǎnxī 陝西.
The following year, he was recalled,
and ordered to alternate with Assistant Censor-in-Chief (Qiāndū Yùshǐ 僉都御史) Cáo Yì 曹翼 in defending the frontier annually.
When the time came, he was seriously ill,
so an imperial edict dispatched Grand Court of Justice Vice Minister (Dàlǐsì Shà qīng 大理寺少卿) Chéng Fù 程富 to replace Yì 翼,
and ordered Chē 車 to return home to treat his illness.
Before he could depart,
he died in the sixth month of the sixth year (1441).
When Chē 車 was in Jiāngxī 江西,
he went to Fújiàn 福建 to collect timber,
passing through Guǎngxìn 廣信.
The Prefect of Guǎngxìn 廣信,
an old acquaintance,
presented him with a jar of honey.
When he opened it and looked,
it was white silver.
He laughed and said,
"You don't know your old friend,"
and refused to accept it.
Many of his colleagues on the frontier considered banquets and entertainment to be grand gestures.
Chē 車 disliked this,
and consequently abstained from alcohol and meat.
Such instances of his resolute character were numerous.
Liú Zhōngfū 劉中敷,
from Dàxīng 大興,
was originally named Zhōngfú 中孚.
When the Prince of Yān 燕 raised an army,
he was appointed Magistrate of Chénliú 陳留 due to his merit in defending the city as a scholar (zhūshēng 諸生).
He was promoted to Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Works (Gōngbù Yuánwàiláng 工部員外郎).
When Rénzōng 仁宗 supervised the state,
he was ordered to manage the ministry's affairs,
and was bestowed his current name.
He was transferred to Right Vice Commissioner of Jiāngxī 江西.
In the third year of Xuāndé 宣德 (1428), he was transferred to Right Administration Vice Commissioner (Yòucānzhèng 右參政) of Shāndōng 山東,
and promoted to Left Provincial Administration Commissioner (Zuǒ Bùzhèngshǐ 左布政使).
He was honest, straightforward, incorruptible, and calm,
respected and cherished by officials and common people.
In a year of great famine,
he spoke to the Provincial Governor (Xúnfǔ 巡撫),
reducing the tax by two-thirds.
When Zhèngtǒng 正統 began,
he was forced to prematurely end his mourning for his father to return to duty (duóqíng 奪情),
and soon was summoned and appointed Minister of Revenue (Hùbù Shàngshū 戶部尚書).
The emperor, being young when he ascended the throne,
feared that his subordinates would deceive him,
and his rule was rather strict.
The eunuch Wáng Zhèn 王振, however, exploited this to establish his authority,
repeatedly seizing upon minor faults of high officials,
and guiding the emperor to apply severe punishments,
so that not a year passed without high officials being imprisoned.
In the third year (1438), Wáng Zhèn 王振 instigated the investigating censors (gěishì yùshǐ 給事御史) to impeach Zhōngfū 中敷 and Vice Minister (Zuǒ Shìláng 左侍郎) Wú Xǐ 吳璽, among others.
They were imprisoned,
then released and returned to their posts.
In the sixth year (1441),
officials criticized Zhōngfū 中敷 for acting arbitrarily.
An imperial edict ordered the Ministry of Justice (Fǎsī 法司) to try them together in the inner court.
They were sentenced to exile,
but allowed to pay a fine for redemption.
The emperor specifically pardoned them.
That winter,
Zhōngfū 中敷, Xǐ 璽, and Right Vice Minister (Yòu Shìláng 右侍郎) Chén Cháng 陳瑺 requested to distribute imperial cattle and horses among the people for grazing.
Officials impeached them for altering established laws,
and they were all imprisoned and sentenced to death.
An imperial edict ordered them to be paraded in stocks outside Cháng'ānmén 長安門,
for sixteen days before their release.
When the Oirats (Wǎlà 瓦剌) brought tribute,
the emperor asked about the number of horses, camels, fodder, and beans,
but they could not answer.
They were again, with Xǐ 璽 and Cháng 瑺, sentenced to death and imprisoned.
Zhōngfū 中敷 was granted special permission to visit his sick mother.
The following winter,
when prisoners were to be executed,
the Ministry of Justice submitted a request.
Xǐ 璽 and Cháng 瑺 were ordered to be garrisoned on the frontier,
and Zhōngfū 中敷 was to await his mother's death before submitting a memorial.
Later,
he was released as a commoner.
When Emperor Jǐngdì ascended the throne,
he was appointed Assistant Minister of the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù Zuǒ Shìláng) and concurrently Guest of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Bīnkè).
At that time, military campaigns were ongoing,
and there was not a single day without awards for merit.
Zhōng Fū submitted that the national treasury was finite,
and it was advisable to economize for emergencies.
The emperor graciously accepted.
He died in the fourth year of Jǐngtài.
He was posthumously granted the title of Minister (Shàngshū).
Zhōng Fū was of a simple and detached nature;
his meals were never extravagant,
and after fifty years in officialdom,
his family had no surplus wealth.
His son Lián,
became a Jinshì in the tenth year of Zhèngtǒng.
He was appointed Supervising Secretary in the Bureau of Punishment (Xíngkē Jǐshìzhōng),
and rose through the ranks to Grand Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud (Tàipú Sì Qīng).
He was extravagant,
but resolute in office.
He was demoted to Minister of the Liaodōng Imperial Stud (Liáodōng Yuànmǎ Sì Qīng),
and died there.
His son Jī,
was filial from a young age.
He became a Jinshì in the fourteenth year of Chénghuà.
He was appointed Shùjíshì (compiler in the Hanlin Academy).
During the Zhèngdé reign,
he succeeded Zhāng Cǎi as Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū),
but requested to retire due to public criticism.
He was recalled to serve as Minister of War in Nanjing (Nánjīng Bīngbù Shàngshū),
participating in and advising on important state affairs.
When marauding bandits attacked the region along the river,
the assembly debated the selection of a general.
Just then, Commandant Lǐ Áng returned from Guìzhōu after being dismissed from office,
and Jī immediately summoned and appointed him.
Áng declined, citing the lack of an imperial decree.
Jī said:
"I have received an imperial edict that states,
'What is not specified in the edict,
may be handled at your discretion.'
This is therefore an imperial decree."
The assembly admired his courage and insight.
He retired and returned home,
where he died.
Zhāng Fèng,
courtesy name Zǐyí,
was from Ānpíng.
His father Yì,
served as Supervising Secretary (Jǐshìzhōng).
In the eighth year of Yǒnglè, he followed an expedition to the northern desert,
and died in battle.
Fèng passed the Jinshì examination in the second year of Xuāndé.
He was appointed Principal of the Ministry of Justice (Xíngbù Zhǔshì).
He presided over the rebellion case in Jiāngxī,
and exonerated hundreds of people.
In the twelfth month of the third year of Zhèngtǒng,
all judicial officials were imprisoned for various offenses,
so Fèng was promoted to Assistant Minister of the Right in his ministry (Běnbù Zuǒ Shìláng).
To be promoted from Principal to Assistant Minister
was unprecedented at that time.
The next year, he was ordered to supervise the imperial granaries in the capital.
In the sixth year, he was transferred to the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù),
and soon after, dispatched to Nanjing.
As the Minister's position had been vacant for a long time,
Fèng thus took charge of the ministry's affairs.
Guìzhōu reported a shortage of grain for the garrisons,
and requested to transport grain from the Lóngjiāng granary and salt from Liǎnghuái to Zhènyuǎnfǔ to exchange for rice.
Fèng, noting that the Lóngjiāng salt was mixed with mud and sand
and unsuitable for exchange for grain for the troops,
gave them all the Huái salt,
and only then reported it.
The emperor praised him.
He also said that the auxiliary capital was a critical location,
and it was advisable to store two million *shí* of grain annually,
as a fundamental measure.
This was followed,
and thus became a regulation.
The grain storage in Nanjing
was formerly supervised by the Censor-in-Chief (Dū Yùshǐ).
In the winter of the twelfth year, Fèng was ordered to concurrently manage it.
He was honest, prudent, and good at enforcing the law,
and was known
as "Board Zhāng" (Bǎn Zhāng).
In the second year of Jǐngtài, he was promoted to Minister (Shàngshū).
In the fourth year, he was transferred to the Ministry of War (Bīngbù),
participating in and advising on military affairs.
When Minister of Revenue Jīn Lián died,
Fèng was summoned to replace him.
At that time, wars in the four directions ceased,
but natural disasters were particularly severe,
and the emperor repeatedly issued edicts for relief.
Fèng, with other court officials, proposed ten measures.
The next year, they subsequently proposed eight more measures.
All were approved.
Fèng, observing that many taxes were remitted due to disasters,
and national expenditure was further strained,
then memorialized:
"In the early days of the dynasty, there were over 8.49 million *qǐng* of land in the empire.
Now the number has been halved,
and with suspensions of collection due to floods and droughts,
how can the national expenditures be met?
In the capital region and Hénán, Shāndōng, there is unregistered land;
as soon as one party reclaims land,
another immediately denounces them for tax evasion.
I request permission to levy light rent,
which will not only forever eliminate disputes,
but also provide some assistance to the military and the state."
This was approved.
Supervising Secretary Chéng Zhāng and others impeached Fèng for unauthorized alteration of ancestral systems,
and Yáng Suì and others again debated against it.
The emperor said:
"In the early days of the dynasty, the capital was in Jiāngnán,
and transportation was easy.
Now residing in the far north,
can we adhere to the old regulations?"
When reports of severe famine came from various regions,
Fèng requested that imperial censors verify them.
Critics disapproved.
Upon Emperor Yīngzōng's restoration,
Fèng was transferred to the Ministry of Revenue in Nanjing,
still concurrently supervising grain storage.
He died in the second month of the fifth year.
Fèng was filial.
He was simple and honest by nature.
When an old friend died,
he betrothed his daughter to his own son,
educated the friend's son, and supported his mother for life.
His fellow student Sū Hóng was fond of openly criticizing Fèng's faults,
and continued to do so even when he became Fèng's subordinate.
Fèng treated him as before.
Upon hearing of his poverty,
he immediately provided relief.
Zhōu Xuān,
courtesy name Tíngyù,
was from Yángqǔ.
He entered the National Academy (Guóxué) through the provincial examination.
During the Zhèngtǒng reign,
he was appointed Principal of the Ministry of Justice (Xíngbù Zhǔshì),
and was skilled in handling judicial cases.
In the thirteenth year, he was promoted to Supernumerary Secretary (Yuánwàiláng).
The next year,
the emperor went on a northern expedition.
Many of the Directors (Lángzhōng) who were supposed to accompany him feigned illness,
but Xuān requested to go.
When the imperial army was annihilated,
Xuān returned wounded,
and was promoted to acting Director (Shǔ Lángzhōng).
A military attendant accepted bribes and released a criminal,
substituting an enemy in his place.
Xuān investigated and cleared the innocent party,
and punished the attendant.
From external prefectures, prisoners were sent,
up to eight hundred in a single day.
Xuān, fearing they would suffer from the heat,
disposed of almost all their cases within three days.
In the first year of Jǐngtài,
at the recommendation of Minister Wáng Zhí,
he was exceptionally appointed Assistant Minister of the Right in the Ministry of Justice (Xíngbù Zuǒ Shìláng).
After some time,
he was sent out to relieve famine in Shùntiān and Héjiān.
Before he completed his mission,
Emperor Yīngzōng was restored to power.
Officials requested his recall.
This was not granted.
An imperial edict was again issued,
ordering him to deal with matters at his discretion.
Xuān traveled throughout his assigned area,
undertook major relief efforts,
and successively relieved 265,000 famine victims,
provided over 10,000 oxen and seeds each,
and memorialized eight measures benefiting the people.
Upon completing his mission, he returned,
and the next year he was transferred to Assistant Minister of the Left (Zuǒ Shìláng).
The emperor was then employing Mén Dá and Lù Gǎo,
who frequently initiated major prison cases.
Xuān tactfully explained and persuaded,
correcting many injustices,
and further admonished the Directors not to avoid trouble.
Thus, cases transferred to the ministry for sentencing
did not result in wrongful or excessive punishments.
He served in the Ministry of Justice for a long time,
and his subordinates dared not deceive him.
He favored leniency and forgiveness,
and did not pursue strict interpretations of the law.
His colleague assisting in the ministry was Kǒng Wényīng from Ānhuà,
who, as a Censor, had investigated the case of seditious talk in Huángyán,
where three thousand people were implicated,
and he cleared all of them of false charges,
only shackling and punishing one principal leader.
When he was in the ministry,
he and Xuān were both known as benevolent elders.
In the seventh year, Xuān was ordered to provisionally manage the affairs of the Ministry of Public Works (Gōngbù).
Xuān (瑄) was tranquil and indifferent to honor and profit.
In the first year of Chénghuà (成化),
he had served as a Shìláng (侍郎) for sixteen years,
when he was finally promoted to Yòu Dū Yùshǐ (右都御史).
