He supervised the grain storage in Nánjīng (南京),
arrested and punished several wrongdoers,
and cleared up long-standing malpractices.
When Fèngyáng (鳳陽), Huái (淮), and Xú (徐) suffered famine,
forty thousand units of grain were released from the granaries based on Xuān’s (瑄) recommendation to provide relief.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Nánjīng Xíngbù Shàngshū (南京刑部尚書).
He ordered that for matters not requiring investigation by various offices,
the processing time should not exceed five days,
ensuring no prisoners were held unnecessarily.
During a summer epidemic,
he released all those with minor charges,
saying:
“Return when summoned.”
The prisoners left cheering,
and none failed to return on time.
He served as Shàngshū (尚書) for nine years,
and repeatedly submitted memorials requesting retirement.
Only after a long time was his request granted.
He had no land or gardens,
so he settled in Nánjīng (南京).
When he died,
he was posthumously granted Tàizǐ Shàobǎo (太子少保),
and given the posthumous name Zhuāngyì (莊懿).
His eldest son, Jīng (經),
was a Shàngshū (尚書),
and has his own biography.
His second son, Hóng (紘),
was a Jìnshì (進士),
and served as Nánjīng Lìkē Gěishìzhōng (南京吏科給事中).
He twice spoke on state affairs concerning disasters and unusual phenomena.
The emperor praised and accepted both.
Not long after,
while inspecting troops with the Yùshǐ (御史) Zhāng Bǐng (張昺),
he was falsely accused by the eunuch Jiǎng Cóng (蔣琮),
and demoted to Nánjīng Guānglù Shǔchéng (南京光祿署丞).
He ended his career as Shāndōng Cānyì (山東參議).
Yáng Dǐng (楊鼎),
courtesy name Zōngqì (宗器),
was a native of Xiánníng (咸寧), Shǎnxī (陝西).
Poor but diligent in his studies,
he achieved first place in both the local and metropolitan examinations.
In the fourth year of Zhèngtǒng (正統),
he placed second in the palace examination.
He was appointed Biānxiū (編修).
After a long time,
he, along with Shìjiǎng (侍講) Dù Níng (杜寧) and nine others,
was selected to study in the Dōnggé (東閣).
Dǐng (鼎), while serving as a Shìcóng (侍從),
was very eager to distinguish himself through achievement.
He once proposed two matters: renovating military defenses and improving the canal transport to the three borders.
His peers ridiculed him as impractical,
but Dǐng (鼎) became even more self-confident.
When Yěxiān (也先) was about to invade the capital,
an imperial decree appointed him to act as Jìnsè Yùshǐ (監察御史)
and recruit soldiers in Yǎnzhōu (兗州).
In the third year of Jǐngtài (景泰), he was promoted to Shìjiǎng (侍講) concurrently serving as Zhōngyǔn (中允).
In the fifth year, he was exceptionally promoted to Hùbù Yòu Shìláng (戶部右侍郎).
At the beginning of Tiānshùn (天順), he was transferred to Zuo (左).
Chén Rǔyán (陳汝言) slandered him.
The emperor did not listen.
In the winter of the third year, he was imprisoned for being negligent during a sacrifice at the imperial tombs,
but was reinstated after paying a fine and receiving a caning.
The emperor once ordered the eunuch Niú Yù (牛玉) to convey an imperial decree,
intending to take the silver for grain taxes from Jiāngnán (江南) to fill the imperial treasury,
and use other tax revenues to pay military officers’ salaries.
Dǐng (鼎) disagreed.
When horses and cattle lacked fodder,
there was a proposal to levy a tax of one-fifth,
but he strongly opposed it due to the hardship of the people.
Both proposals were rejected.
In the seventh year,
when Shàngshū (尚書) Nián Fù (年富) fell ill,
an imperial decree ordered Dǐng (鼎) to manage the affairs of the Ministry.
In the fourth year of Chénghuà (成化), he replaced Mǎ Áng (馬昂) as Hùbù Shàngshū (戶部尚書),
and Wēng Shìzī (翁世資) was appointed Shìláng (侍郎).
In the sixth year,
Dǐng (鼎) submitted a memorial stating:
“Shǎnxī (陝西) suffers from four external scourges of bandits,
and internal scourges of displaced people.
However, banditry is limited to the border areas,
whereas displaced people are a sickness in the very heart of the state.
Hànzhōng (漢中) is remotely located amidst myriad mountains,
commanding the route to Chuānshǔ (川蜀);
tens of thousands of displaced people from all directions,
if pressed, will incite rebellion; if left alone, will cause future worries.
I request that a supervisory official be temporarily appointed,
specifically to manage this matter.
Those who wish to register as residents should be allowed to do so;
those who do not should be provided with resources to leave.
Furthermore, they should train soldiers and horses with the local commanders,
and repair city walls,
which may avert future calamities.”
The imperial decree complied.
Húguǎng (湖廣) suffered famine for several consecutive years,
and the granaries were depleted.
When a good harvest finally came,
following Dǐng’s (鼎) advice,
silver and cloth stored in the treasury were released,
to be exchanged for rice as a disaster reserve.
The four granaries of Huái (淮), Xú (徐), Lín (臨), and Dé (德)
previously stored over a million shí (石) of grain,
but later, when provisions were scarce and the people were starving,
requests were frequently made to reallocate and use it,
and the grain was almost exhausted.
Dǐng (鼎) proposed and implemented six measures: redemption of sins, salt certificates, silver for paper currency, and collection of arrears.
From then on, the granaries had reserves.
Soon after, he was granted Tàizǐ Shàobǎo (太子少保).
Dǐng (鼎), while serving in the Hùbù (戶部),
maintained integrity,
but his nature was somewhat rigid and stagnant.
In the autumn of the fifteenth year,
a Gěishì Yùshǐ (給事御史) impeached Dǐng (鼎) as not having the talent to govern the state,
and Dǐng (鼎) again submitted a memorial requesting to leave.
He was granted an imperial edict and dispatched by post-horse to return home,
with an order for the local officials to provide him two shí (石) of rice monthly,
and four servants annually,
for the rest of his life.
The provision of gifts and allowances to high officials upon retirement
began with Dǐng (鼎).
When he died,
he was posthumously granted Tàizǐ Tàibǎo (太子太保),
and given the posthumous name Zhuāngmǐn (莊敏).
His son, Shí (時),
was a Jìnshì (進士),
and rose through the ranks to Shìjiǎng Xuéshì (侍講學士).
He was knowledgeable in many classical allusions
and possessed talent for governing.
Shí Fū (時敷),
a Jǔrén (舉人),
was commended for residing by his parents' graves,
and served as Bīngbù Sīwù (兵部司務).
Wēng Shìzī (翁世資) was a native of Pútián (莆田).
He became a Jìnshì (進士) in the seventh year of Zhèngtǒng (正統).
He was appointed Hùbù Zhǔshì (戶部主事),
and successively served as Lángzhōng (郎中).
In the first year of Tiānshùn (天順), he was appointed Gōngbù Yòu Shìláng (工部右侍郎).
In the fourth year, an imperial order commanded a eunuch to go to Sū (蘇), Sōng (松), Háng (杭), Jiā (嘉), and Hú (湖) to increase the weaving of seven thousand bolts of patterned silk.
Shìzī (世資), noting the floods in the southeast
and the people's difficulty in obtaining food,
proposed reducing the order by half.
Shàngshū (尚書) Zhào Róng (趙榮) and Zuǒ Shìláng (左侍郎) Huò Xuān (霍瑄) found it difficult,
so Shìzī (世資) offered to bear the blame himself,
and then they jointly signed the remonstrance.
The emperor was indeed enraged
and questioned the chief proposer.
Róng (榮) and others blamed Shìzī (世資),
who was then imprisoned by imperial decree
and demoted to Zhīfǔ (知府) of Héngzhōu (衡州).
At the beginning of Chénghuà (成化),
he was promoted to Jiāngxī Zuǒ Bùzhèngshǐ (江西左布政使).
He was impeached for an incident and handed over to officials,
but was soon cleared.
When the large army campaigned in Liǎngguǎng (兩廣),
transferring provisions from Jiāngxī (江西),
it required one hundred thousand men.
Shìzī (世資) proposed taking cash to easily purchase rice in Lǐngnán (嶺南).
The people were thus not disturbed.
He was appointed Yòu Fù Dū Yùshǐ (右副都御史) to serve as Xúnfǔ (巡撫) of Shāndōng (山東).
Annually, he oversaw the granaries,
and was promoted to Shàngshū (尚書).
In the seventeenth year, he returned to manage the affairs of the Ministry.
After two years,
he retired.
Huáng Gǎo (黃鎬),
courtesy name Shúgāo (叔高),
was a native of Hóuguān (侯官).
In the twelfth year of Zhèngtǒng (正統), he took the Jìnshì (進士) examination in the Dūcháyuan (都察院).
Less than half a year later,
he was appointed Yùshǐ (御史) for his clear understanding of the law.
In the 14th year, while inspecting Guìzhōu,
all the Miáo tribes rebelled,
and the roads were blocked.
The Earl of Jìngyuǎn, Wáng Jì, and others, returning from Lùchuān,
had undisciplined troops.
The Miáo attacked their rear,
and the government army suffered a great defeat.
Háo went to Píngyuè,
and nearly died when he encountered the rebels.
At night, he leapt into the city,
which the rebels then surrounded.
Some advised abandoning the city and fleeing,
but Háo said:
"Píngyuè
is the throat of Guìzhōu;
without Píngyuè, there is no Guìzhōu."
So he, along with the other generals, held it fast.
He placed a secret memorial in a bamboo tube,
recruited local people to beg for aid from the court,
and also impeached Jì and others for the state of their defeated army.
Emperor Jǐngdì ordered the Earl of Bǎodìng, Liáng Bǎo, and others to combine the forces of Chuān and Hú to rescue them,
and the siege was finally lifted.
The city had been besieged for nine months;
they dug up grass roots and cooked crossbow armor to eat,
and the dead lay piled upon each other.
The city was ultimately saved,
with Háo's contribution being the greatest.
He remained as inspector for another year.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Surveillance Commissioner (qiānshì) of Guǎngdōng,
then transferred to Zhèjiāng.
At the beginning of the Chénghuà reign,
due to a joint recommendation by high officials,
he was promoted to Left Administration Vice Commissioner (zuǒ cānzhèng) of Guǎngdōng.
Gāo, Léi, and Lián, being coastal regions, were infested with pirates;
Háo suppressed them.
He was again promoted to Left Provincial Administration Commissioner (zuǒ bùzhèngshǐ) of Guǎngxī.
As Right Vice Censor-in-Chief (yòufù dūyùshǐ), he was overall supervisor of Nanjing's grain reserves,
and successively served as Left and Right Vice Minister of Personnel (lìbù zuǒ, yòu shìláng).
In the 16th year, he was appointed Minister of Revenue (hùbù shàngshū) of Nanjing.
Háo possessed talent and discernment,
was diligent in official duties,
and managed the salt administration,
making many reforms and clarifications.
Contemporary opinion praised him.
In the 19th year, he retired
and died on the way.
He was posthumously granted the title of Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent (tàizǐ shàobǎo)
and given the posthumous name Xiāngmǐn.
Hú Gǒngchén,
courtesy name Gòngzhī,
was a native of Chún'ān.
He passed the imperial examination in the 4th year of Zhèngtǒng.
He served as Magistrate (zhīxiàn) of Yīxiàn,
where he enacted benevolent policies,
and was promoted to Censor (yùshǐ).
He submitted a memorial detailing eight pressing issues of the time.
He returned home for his father's mourning.
When Emperor Jǐngdì ascended the throne,
an edict ordered all Censors and Supervising Secretaries (kēdào guān) in mourning to return to service.
Gǒngchén arrived
and repeatedly submitted memorials speaking of selecting generals, safeguarding the state, cultivating virtue, and averting disasters.
He was appointed Left Administration Vice Commissioner (zuǒ cānzhèng) of Guìzhōu.
Shěn Shíbǎo, the chieftain of the Gēlǎo in Báiishuǐpù, had always been resistant to assimilation.
Gǒngchén reported this to the Grand General (zǒngbīng) Fāng Yīng, who dispatched a commander to capture him.
One region was thus pacified.
Upon reaching Bìjié,
he pacified the rebellion of the Pacification Commissioner (xuānwèishǐ) Lǒng Fù,
and his authority extended to the border regions.
He left due to his mother's mourning.
A Censor later impeached him for accepting bribes,
and the case was handed to the Surveillance Commissioner (ànchén) of Zhèjiāng for interrogation.
The matter was clarified,
and he was transferred to Guǎngdōng.
He successively served as Left and Right Provincial Administration Commissioner (zuǒ, yòu bùzhèngshǐ) in Guǎngxī and Sìchuān,
achieving success in suppressing bandits in all posts.
In the 8th year of Chénghuà, he was appointed Right Vice Censor-in-Chief (yòufù dūyùshǐ) of Nanjing,
and supervised the river patrols (tídu dú cāojiāng).
In the 11th year, he was promoted to Right Vice Minister of War (bīngbù yòushìláng).
The position of Heir Apparent (chúwèi) had been vacant for a long time,
and he, along with Minister (shàngshū) Cuī Gōng and others, earnestly requested the establishment of an Heir Apparent.
Their words were very urgent.
In the same year, he was again transferred to Left Vice Censor-in-Chief (zuǒfù dūyùshǐ) and concurrently managed grain reserves,
and then promoted to Minister of Works (gōngbù shàngshū).
He economized on finances and streamlined affairs,
which was convenient for everyone.
Due to his age, he requested to retire.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
the Circuit Censor (xún'àn yùshǐ) Chén Quán stated:
"Gǒngchén has been retired for over ten years,
and his integrity throughout his life has been consistent.
I request that he be given special honors to encourage loyalty among officials."
An edict ordered local officials to provide him with two dàn of grain monthly
and four laborers annually.
In the 1st year of Zhèngdé,
at the age of ninety,
an envoy was sent to convey an imperial decree to inquire about his well-being,
present him with lamb and wine,
and grant him additional grain and laborers.
He died in the 1st month of the 3rd year.
He was posthumously granted the title of Junior Tutor of the Heir Apparent (tàizǐ shàofù)
and given the posthumous name Zhuāngyì.
Chén Jùn,
courtesy name Shíyīng,
was a native of Pútián.
He came first in the provincial examination (xiāngshì).
He passed the imperial examination in the 13th year of Zhèngtǒng.
He was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Revenue (hùbù zhǔshì).
He supervised the various garrisons (wèi) in Tiānjīn in gathering fodder
and memorialized to reduce the newly added quota by 350,000 bundles.
When powerful scoundrels embezzled over 700,000 liǎng of converted silver from Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng,
Jùn went to supervise,
and within a few months, all was paid.
Minister Jīn Lián considered him capable
and assigned him to manage memorials for all departments.
He successively served as Director (lángzhōng).
In the 5th year of Tiānshùn,
when military campaigns were underway in Liǎngguǎng,
Jùn supervised the provisioning.
At that time, prefectures and counties were ravaged,
and the treasuries were empty.
He relaxed the regulations allowing salt merchants to cross borders
and levied an additional two dòu of rice per permit,
ensuring that military supplies were not lacking.
He was not permitted to return for his mother's mourning
until the barbarians were pacified.
Initially,
when Jùn was a Supervising Secretary,
he rushed to his father's funeral
and refused all condolences.
Now, when civil and military officials pooled money for condolences,
he likewise did not accept it.
At the beginning of the Chénghuà reign,
he was promoted to Junior Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (nánjīng tàicháng shàoqīng).
In the 4th year, he was summoned and appointed Right Vice Minister of Revenue (hùbù yòushìláng).
Jùn was skilled in financial matters.
When various regions suffered disasters
and border garrisons urgently needed fodder and provisions,
his memorialized requests were always appropriate in their decisions,
and Minister Yáng Dǐng relied heavily on him.
When the capital suffered a great famine,
he successively released 800,000 dàn of grain from the Grand Granary for sale at fixed prices.
One dàn was valued at six qián,
and powerful scoundrels took advantage of the situation to profit.
Jùn requested that grain be sold in units of shēng and dòu,
and that no one be given more than one dàn,
which helped the starving people.
Soon after, discussions arose about military action in the Hétào region.
An imperial edict ordered Jùn to Hénán, Shānxi, and Shǎnxī
to meet with the巡撫 (xúnfǔ) and other officials to plan for fodder and provisions,
and released 200,000 liǎng of treasury gold to assist them.
Jùn, seeing that the border granaries were empty
and the harvest was poor that year,
and that the road to Yúlín was dangerous and distant,
making transport difficult,
released gold to be exchanged in the interior,
and repaired the roads in Xī'ān, Hánchéng, and Tóngguān
to facilitate swift transportation.
Upon his return to court,
he was promoted one rank in salary
and successively served as Left and Right Vice Minister of Personnel (lìbù zuǒ, yòu shìláng).
After serving nine years,
he was appointed Minister of Revenue (hùbù shàngshū) of Nanjing.
He was soon transferred to the Ministry of War (bīngbù)
to participate in advising on military affairs (cānzàn jīwù).
Previously,
the duty of advising on military affairs
was not exclusively assigned to the Ministry of War.
After Xuē Yuǎn,
Jùn succeeded him,
and this then became a fixed system.
After a long time,
he was transferred to the Ministry of Personnel (lìbù).
In the 21st year,
following a celestial phenomenon (xīngbiàn),
he led the Nine Ministers (jiǔqīng) to present twenty issues of current malpractices,
all of which were extremely critical.
The Emperor adopted many of them.
However, those that were inconvenient to powerful favorites
were ultimately blocked and not implemented.
The next year, he requested to retire.
An edict added the title of Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent (tàizǐ shàobǎo)
and granted him an imperial edict to return by imperial post.
He died
and was posthumously named Kāngyì.
Lín È,
courtesy name Yī’è,
was a native of Tàipíng, Zhèjiāng.
In the second year of Jǐngtài (1451), he became a *jìnshì*.
He was appointed Censor [Yùshǐ],
and supervised the provincial examination in the capital region.
Chén Xún and others impeached the examiners.
È's fellow townsman Lín Tǐng was among those he recommended,
and it was suspected È had acted partially.
Tǐng was arrested and interrogated.
Tǐng was truly innocent of any wrongdoing,
and was cleared.
When Emperor Yīngzōng was restored to the throne,
following the precedents of previous dynasties,
he dispatched court officials to serve as prefects.
È was assigned to Zhènjiāng.
He was summoned for an audience,
bestowed a meal and travel expenses,
and informed of the purpose of his promotion.
È was deeply moved.
He eliminated abuses and revived neglected matters,
and his governance was highly effective.
The grain transport had previously passed through the Mèngdú Canal,
which was extremely perilous.
The巡撫 (Xúnfǔ) Cuī Gōng proposed digging a canal,
diverting water from Qīlǐgǎng past Jīnshān to Dānyáng to bypass it.
È said:
"The route is long,
has many rocks,
and would destroy people's homes and graves.
I request that we dredge the old sites of the Jīngkǒu Sluice and Gānlù Dam,
making them navigable for boats.
Open the sluice in spring and summer,
and cross the dam in autumn and winter;
this would save effort and be convenient."
Gōng followed his suggestion,
and it became a permanent benefit.
After five years,
due to his talent in governing difficult areas,
he was transferred to Sūzhōu.
In the early Chénghuà era,
he was promoted exceptionally to Jiāngxī Ànchásǐ.
When someone who had committed a capital crime bribed high officials to save his life,
È remained unyielding in upholding the law.
Bandits from Guǎngdōng raided Gànzhōu urgently.
Troops were dispatched to resist them,
and they fled.
In Guǎngxìn, a demoniac rebel falsely claimed to be a heavenly deity to deceive the masses.
È captured and executed their leader,
and the group immediately dispersed.
He successively served as Zuǒ Bùzhèngshǐ and Yòu Bùzhèngshǐ.
During a famine,
he memorialized to reduce the people's land tax by 150,000 *shí*.
In the sixth year of Chénghuà (1470), he was promoted to Nánjīng Xíngbù Yòu Shìláng.
After his mourning period for his mother ended,
he was summoned to serve as Xíngbù Yòu Shìláng.
He upheld the law without wavering.
He died of illness in the twelfth year (1476).
È served his mother with filial piety and reverence,
and showed no laxity towards his wife and children.
He did not associate casually with others,
and during his free time, he would always sit upright and read.
Upon his death, he could not afford a coffin and shroud,
and his friends managed his funeral arrangements.
While È was in Sūzhōu,
the statues of the former sages were peeling.
È said:
"Clay statues are
not ancient practice.
Previously, Tàizǔ used spirit tablets at the imperial academy."
He ordered the change to be made accordingly.
During the Jiājìng era,
Censor Zhào Dàyòu memorialized about his integrity and conduct,
and he was posthumously granted the title of Xíngbù Shàngshū,
with the posthumous name Gōngsù.
Pān Róng,
courtesy name Zūnyòng,
was a native of Lóngxī.
In the thirteenth year of Zhèngtǒng (1448), he became a *jìnshì*.
He was sent to reward the troops in Guǎngdōng,
and upon his return,
he was appointed Lìkē Jǐshìzhōng.
In the early Jǐngtài era,
he memorialized to discuss several matters, including suspending reappointments and suppressing opportunistic competition.
The emperor accepted his advice.
Soon after, he was promoted to Yòu Jǐshìzhōng.
In the ninth month of the fourth year (1453), he memorialized, saying:
"The most crucial aspect of good governance
is nothing more than accepting remonstrance.
Recently, because some speakers displeased the imperial will,
an edict was issued to the Ministry of Rites,
stating that whenever a remonstrance is made,
it must be carefully examined,
and if it is falsely used for retaliation,
a memorial should be presented to punish them.
Once this order was issued,
court officials lost their spirit,
and speaking out became taboo.
If the state has advantages or disadvantages,
the people have gains or losses,
and high officials have treachery,
how can these be known?
Moreover, now that great bandits rampage
and there is much trouble on the frontier,
how can we instead block the path of those who speak out?
I hope for a clear imperial edict to the Censorate [Táijiàn],
to speak without reservation,
and to punish those who remain silent.
Also, instruct the Grand Secretaries and ministers [Gé Bù Dàchén]
not to seek out and criticize
and thereby harm the integrity of governance."
The memorial was submitted,
and the emperor was informed.
In the sixth year of Tiānshùn (1462), he was sent as an envoy to Liúqiú.
Upon his return,
he was transferred to Dū Jǐshìzhōng.
In the third month of the sixth year of Chénghuà (1470), he and his colleagues memorialized, saying:
"Recently, rain and snow have been untimely,
and disasters have occurred repeatedly.
Your Majesty has issued an edict reproaching yourself,
personally performing prayers,
and ordered ministers to speak freely.
Heaven should have been moved.
Yet now, wind and dust obscure the day,
and the baleful *qì* turns from red to black.
Is this not because the way of responding to Heaven has not been fully practiced?
Indeed, for a ruler to revere Heaven
is not merely about fasting and praying.
If government decrees are inappropriate,
the common people lose their livelihood,
precious objects are esteemed,
expenditures are extravagant,
the rear palace is disorderly,
favors are unevenly distributed,
titles are bestowed indiscriminately upon lowly artisans,
and rewards are given undeservedly—
all these are not the way of revering Heaven.
We wish Your Majesty would daily hold court in the private hall,
summon ministers to fully articulate shortcomings and rectify them,
so that disasters might be averted."
At that time, Consort Wàn held exclusive favor,
and small-minded individuals curried favor by presenting treasures and curiosities.
Official appointments and rewards were redundant and excessive,
hence Róng and others earnestly presented their advice.
The emperor could not make use of it.
In that year, he was transferred to Nánjīng Tàicháng Shǎoqīng.
Seven years later,
he was promoted to Hùbù Yòu Shìláng.
Soon after, he was reassigned as Yòu Fù Dū Yùshǐ, concurrently serving as Governor-General of grain reserves in Nánjīng.
He accumulated tens of thousands of *shí* of surplus grain in preparation for famine.
In the seventeenth year (1481), he was summoned to serve as Hùbù Zuǒ Shìláng,
and soon after, acted as minister of the board.
The Duke of Yīng, Zhāng Mào, and forty-three others self-reported that their ancestors had been granted noble titles for great achievements,
and their descendants inherited them,
but the responsible office often reduced their annual stipends,
which was contrary to the ancestors' intention of rewarding merit.
Róng and others stated:
"Zhāng Mào and others are asking for increased stipends without any achievements.
If there were achievements, how would rewards be encouraged?
Moreover, with frequent floods and droughts in recent years,
the national treasury is not abundant,
so their request cannot be granted."
The matter was then dropped.
The eunuchs Zhào Yáng and others requested 100,000 *yǐn* of salt from Liǎng Huái.
The emperor had already granted it.
Róng and others stated:
"Recently, the sale of salt by powerful families was prohibited,
and the imperial edict was just promulgated.
Yet Zhào Yáng and others are violating it.
Their crime should be punished."
The emperor severely reprimanded Zhào Yáng and others for this.
When Nánjīng Hùbù Shàngshū Huáng Gǎo was dismissed,
Róng was appointed to replace him.
After Emperor Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
he resigned from his post and returned home.
He was granted a monthly stipend and annual labor service as per regulations.
He died nine years later,
at the age of seventy-eight.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tàizǐ Tàibǎo.
Xià Shízhèng
had the courtesy name Jìjué,
and was a native of Réné.
He became a *Jìnshì* in the 10th year of Zhèngtǒng.
He was appointed Principal of the Ministry of Justice.
In the 6th year of Jǐngtài, as a *Lángzhōng*, he was sent to Fújiàn to review prisoners,
releasing over 60 people who had been sentenced to death.
Among them were some whose death sentences had been commuted, and who had been ordered to serve as soldiers in coastal garrisons.
Shízhèng, fearing they might escape to sea islands and cause trouble,
transferred them to Shāndōng,
and then reported it.
He then stated:
"All prisoners in Fújiàn whose death sentences are commuted
should be exiled to the frontier."
The Ministry of Justice agreed with his words,
but requested that he be punished for violating the imperial edict.
The Emperor specifically pardoned him.
Shízhèng further stated:
"Cases involving foreign trade and banditry
often wait for joint review,
which drags on for months,
and many prisoners die from illness in jail.
I request that the relevant authorities be ordered to decide them."
The edict adopted his suggestion,
and extended it throughout the empire.
In the early Tiānshùn era,
he was promoted to Assistant Minister of the Dali Court.
After a long time,
for the convenience of supporting his parents,
he was transferred to Vice Minister of the Nanjing Dali Court.
In the 5th year of Chénghuà, he was promoted to Minister of the Dali Court.
In the spring of the following year, he was ordered to inspect disaster relief in Jiāngxī.
He abolished over 100,000 *shí* of unnamed taxes,
dismissed tens of thousands of redundant officials in various departments,
impeached and dismissed over 200 incompetent officials,
and oversaw the reinforcement of the Nánchāng riverside embankment and the irrigation dikes in various counties like Fēngchéng.
The people benefited greatly from these actions.
He once submitted a memorial,
without including the name of the person who presented it,
for which the Ministry of Personnel criticized his arrogance.
The Emperor pardoned his offense,
showed him the impeachment memorial,
and he subsequently requested retirement.
He rented a civilian house.
The Provincial Administration Commissioner Zhāng Zàn built the Xīhú Academy for him to live in.
He lived on his family's income for thirty years,
and died at nearly ninety years old.
Shízhèng had a refined love for learning.
During his long retirement,
he produced many writings,
especially detailed in ancient rites and classical studies.
A eulogy states: Jīn Chún and others diligently served the public,
performing their duties competently.
Furthermore, they maintained personal integrity and purity,
their conduct unimpeachable,
truly excellent among high officials.
Zhèng Chén's incorruptibility,
and Zhōu Xuān's handling of justice,
both demonstrated the heart of a benevolent person,
truly exemplary gentlemen!
Collation Notes

Biographies, Chapter 46: Huáng Zōngzài, Gù Zuǒ, (Shào Chénmiǎn, Jiǎ Liàng, Yán Shēng), Duàn Mín, (Wú Shēn), Zhāng Chǎng (Xú Qí, Liú Jiǎn), Wú Nà (Zhū Yǔyán), Wèi Jì, Lǔ Mù, Gěng Jiǔchóu, Xuān Ní (Chén Fù), Huáng Kǒngzhāo.
Huáng Zōngzài,
also named Hòu,
with the courtesy name Hòufu,
was a native of Fēngchéng.
He became a *Jìnshì* in the 30th year of Hóngwǔ.
He was appointed *Xíngrén*.
He was sent on missions throughout the four directions,
never accepting gifts, and was successively promoted to Chief Minister.
In the early Yǒnglè era,
he was recommended to be Assistant Surveillance Commissioner of Húguǎng.
Many cunning and entrenched villains
were exiled to the area between Tónggǔ and Wǔkāi,
secretly controlling the merits and demerits of officials.
Zōngzài posted a list of their crimes,
saying:
"If they do not reform,
they will certainly be brought to justice."
None dared to offend again.
Wǔlíng had many people registered as barbarians,
and local families feared intermarriage with them,
believing that corvée and taxes would burden them,
so men and women remained unmarried even at forty years old.
Zōngzài persuaded them with reason,
and they all understood and enlightened.
In a short time, over three hundred families married.
Neighboring counties followed suit,
and their customs were thus changed.
He was summoned to the Wényuāngé to compile the Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn.
After the book was completed,
he received imperial rewards and returned to his post.
He supervised the construction of dozens of large ships for sea transport,
and the task was completed without troubling the people.
When the imperial carriage went on a northern expedition,
soldiers were conscripted from Húguǎng,
but the envoy was greedy and violent, missing the deadline.
Zōngzài was punished for failing to impeach him,
and was demoted to a postman at Yángqīng Post Station.
Soon after, he was reinstated as a Censor,
and dispatched to inspect Jiāozhǐ.
At that time, Jiāozhǐ had just been pacified,
and most prefectural and county officials were chosen from recommended candidates from Liǎngguǎng and Yúnnán, as well as tribute students willing to serve in distant regions;
none of them were good at governing and nurturing the people.
Zōngzài therefore said:
"Most officials are not competent.
If we wait for the nine-year evaluation and dismissal,
I fear things will become even more neglected.
I request that for those who have served for more than two years, the Grand Censor and the two chief provincial officials investigate and impeach or recommend them accordingly."
The Emperor approved this.
When he returned,
his baggage was sparse,
not bringing a single item from Jiāozhǐ.
Minister Huáng Fú said to others:
"I have been here for a long time,
and have interacted with many censors,
but only Zōngzài understood the greater good."
He observed mourning for his grandmother,
was recalled to office,
and appointed Assistant Minister of the Zhan Shi Fu.
In the 1st year of Hóngxī, he was promoted to Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel at the Traveling Court.
Grand Tutor Jiǎn Yì was in charge of the ministry,
and Zōngzài assisted him with integrity.
In the 1st year of Xuāndé, he was ordered to clear out the military in Zhèjiāng.
In the 3rd year, he supervised timber collection in Húguǎng and Húxiāng.
In the early Yīngzōng era,
Vice Minister Luó Rǔjìng was appointed Grand Coordinator of Shǎnxī,
and was working with his offense pardoned.
Rǔjìng falsely invoked an imperial edict to be reinstated,
and the Ministry of Personnel did not report it,
for which he was impeached by a Censor.
Zōngzài and Minister Guō Jìn were both imprisoned.
Not long after,
they were released,
and Zōngzài was transferred to Minister of the Nanjing Ministry of Personnel.
After nine years,
he requested retirement.
His memorial was submitted four times
before it was granted.
He died at home in the 7th month of the 9th year,
at the age of seventy-nine.
Zōngzài upheld integrity and rectitude,
neither exaggerating nor conforming,
and his scholarship and writings were highly regarded at the time.
Among the high officials and grandees known for their virtue and age,
Zōngzài was highly praised.
Gù Zuǒ,
with the courtesy name Lǐqīng,
was a native of Tàikāng.
He became a *Jìnshì* in the 2nd year of Jiànwén.
He was appointed Magistrate of Zhuānglàng.
On the Dūanyáng Festival,
the commanding general gathered officials to compete in archery.
He found it difficult to include Zuǒ, a scholar.
Zuǒ took a bow and arrow, shot once, and hit the target,
greatly impressing the commanding general.
In the early Yǒnglè era,
he entered the capital as a Censor.
In the 7th year,
Chéngzǔ was in Běijīng,
and ordered the Ministry of Personnel to select talented censors to go to the traveling court;
Zuǒ was among them.
He was ordered to pacify the barbarians of Qìngyuǎn,
supervise timber collection in Sìchuān,
accompany the northern expedition,
and inspect mountain passes.
He was promoted to Vice Surveillance Commissioner of Jiāngxī,
and then summoned to be Governor of Yìngtiān.
He was upright and unyielding,
and officials and common people feared and respected him;
people compared him to Bāo Xiàosù.
When Běijīng was established,
he was transferred to Governor of Shùntiān.
Many powerful and influential people found him inconvenient,
and he was sent out as Surveillance Commissioner of Guìzhōu.
In the 1st year of Hóngxī, he was summoned to be Commissioner of the Office of Transmission.
In the third year of Xuāndé,
Dū Yùshǐ Liú Guān was dismissed for corruption.
Dàxuéshì Yáng Shìqí and Yáng Róng recommended [Gu Guāng]zuǒ for being upright, incorruptible, and possessing authority.
In all his official posts, he had demonstrated remarkable integrity.
When he became Jīngyǐn (Magistrate of the Capital),
the administration was clean, and malpractices were reformed.
The Emperor was pleased,
and immediately promoted him to Yòu Dū Yùshǐ,
bestowing an imperial edict to commend and encourage him.
He was ordered to investigate any unsuitable censors and dismiss them.
When there was a vacancy for a censor,
he was to recommend candidates to the Lìbù for selection.
As soon as Gu Zuǒ took office,
he impeached and dismissed twenty people, including Yán Hǎi and Yáng Jūzhèng.
They were banished to various guards in Liáodōng to serve as clerks.
Eight people were demoted,
and three were dismissed.
He also recommended over forty people suitable for censor roles, including Jìnshì Dèng Qǐ, Guózǐshēng Chéng Fù, candidates for county magistrates Kǒng Wényīng, and educational officials Fāng Ruì.
The Emperor made them serve a three-month probation period before appointing them.
Jūzhèng and six others presented their arguments.
The Emperor was enraged,
and ordered all those serving as clerks to be exiled to garrisons.
Later, Yán Hǎi secretly returned to the capital from his place of exile,
extorting bribes.
Gu Zuǒ impeached him for this,
and also stated that Yán Hǎi had plotted to harm him.
An edict ordered Yán Hǎi to be executed in the marketplace.
When the Emperor went on a northern tour,
he ordered Gu Zuǒ to remain in the capital to guard it with Shàngshū Zhāng Běn and others.
Upon his return, another imperial edict was bestowed,
instructing him to regulate all censors.
Consequently, corrupt and unrestrained officials were impeached and dismissed,
and the court administration was solemnly rectified.
After a year or so,
a corrupt official impeached Gu Zuǒ for accepting money from his subordinates
and privately sending them home.
The Emperor secretly showed the document to Yáng Shìqí, saying:
"Did you not once recommend Gu Zuǒ as incorruptible?"
He replied:
"The court officials' salaries are meager.
Their horses and fodder are funded by their subordinates.
Sending subordinates home often involves them contributing money to avoid service.
The subordinates can return to their farms,
and the officials gain expenses.
All court officials do this,
and so do I.
The late Emperor knew this,
which is why he increased the salaries of court officials."
The Emperor sighed and said:
"Court ministers are this poor!"
He then angrily addressed the accuser:
"I am currently employing Gu Zuǒ.
How dare a petty person falsely accuse him?
You shall be handed over to the judicial authorities for punishment."
Shìqí replied:
"Such a minor matter is not worth the Emperor's anger."
The Emperor then gave the official's accusation to Gu Zuǒ, saying:
"You deal with this yourself."
Gu Zuǒ kowtowed in gratitude,
summoned the official, and said:
"The Emperor ordered me to deal with you.
If you change your ways,
I will pardon you."
The Emperor was even more pleased upon hearing this,
considering Gu Zuǒ to possess great integrity.
Someone accused Gu Zuǒ of not handling cases of wrongful appeals.
The Emperor said:
"This must be taught by severe criminals."
He ordered the judicial authorities to convene and investigate.
Indeed, Qianhù Zāng Qīng, who had killed three innocent people and deserved death,
had sent someone to falsely accuse Gu Zuǒ.
The Emperor said:
"If Zāng Qīng is not executed,
then Gu Zuǒ's law will not be enforced."
Zāng Qīng was dismembered in the marketplace.
In the autumn of the eighth year,
Gu Zuǒ fell ill and
requested to retire.
This was not granted.
Xiōng Gài, Nánjīng Yòu Dū Yùshǐ, was appointed to act in his stead.
Over a year later, Xiōng Gài died.
Gu Zuǒ's illness had truly recovered,
and he came to see the Emperor.
The Emperor consoled and encouraged him,
allowing him to be exempt from court greetings,
and to resume his duties as before.
In the early years of Zhèngtǒng, fifteen censors were found to be unsatisfactory during an evaluation
and were demoted or dismissed.
Shào Zōng, whose nine-year term was complete
and had already been rated as competent by the Lìbù,
was also included.
Shào Zōng submitted a memorial arguing his case,
and Shàngshū Guō Jìn also stated that Shào Zōng should not be evaluated together with those currently in office.
The Emperor then reprimanded Gu Zuǒ.
Furthermore, Censors Zhāng Péng and others again impeached Shào Zōng for minor faults.
The Emperor, considering Zhāng Péng and his associates to be deceitful,
severely rebuked Gu Zuǒ as well.
Gu Zuǒ submitted a memorial requesting to retire and left.
An imperial edict was bestowed, commending and comforting him,
granting him fifty strings of paper money,
and ordering the Hùbù to take care of his family.
He died in the ninth month of the eleventh year.
Gu Zuǒ was filial and friendly,
with a clean and upright conduct,
and a severe and resolute nature.
Every morning when he went to court,
he would rest briefly in the outer hall,
standing by the double bamboo screen outside the door.
All officials passing by
would turn and avoid him.
When he entered the inner duty room,
he would stay alone in a small side chamber.
Unless discussing state affairs, he would not sit with the other departments.
People referred to him as
"Gù Dúzuò" (Gu, the Solitary Sitter).
However,
his strict adherence to the law was considered excessive by critics.
At that time, Chén Miǎn of Yúdū and Jiǎ Liàng of Yìxiàn successively served as Fù Dū Yùshǐ,
and were appointed to censorate posts together with Gu Zuǒ.
Shào Guān of Lánxī served in Nánjīng,
and was as renowned as Gu Zuǒ.
Yán Shēng of Fánchāng was also only slightly less famous than Gu Zuǒ.
Gu Zuǒ,
courtesy name Yǐxiān,
became a Jìnshì during the Yǒnglè reign.
He was appointed Censor.
Rénzōng, while regent,
knew of his integrity and uprightness.
Whenever there was a vacancy in the judicial authorities,
he would be ordered to act in that capacity,
and important criminal cases were always entrusted to him.
Throughout his career, both inside and outside the capital,
no one dared to offend him wherever he served.
In the third year of Xuāndé, he entered the capital from his post as Fújiàn Ànchásǐ to become Nánjīng Zuǒ Fù Dū Yùshǐ.
He impeached and dismissed thirteen censors for dereliction of duty,
and identified and dismissed over eighty incompetent and unworthy officials from various departments,
thereby greatly reinvigorating discipline.
After two years,
he died in office due to illness.
He was strong-willed
and fond of slighting his colleagues.
His handling of judicial cases was quite severe.
Nevertheless, he maintained personal integrity.
His conduct at home was exemplary,
and he was known for his filial piety towards his mother.
Chén Miǎn,
was a Jìnshì in the same year.
In the early Rénzōng reign,
upon Yáng Shìqí's recommendation, he was promoted from Guǎngdōng Fùshǐ to Zuǒ Fù Dū Yùshǐ.
Bandits arose in Xìn and Fēng counties,
and Chén Miǎn was ordered to pacify them.
He recruited over three thousand six hundred people,
and the unrest was settled.
In the early Jǐngtài reign,
he rose to Nánjīng Yòu Dū Yùshǐ,
in charge of the censorate.
He retired
and died.
Chén Miǎn was outwardly gentle but inwardly firm,
proficient in law,
and officials dared not deceive him.
Jiǎ Liàng,
courtesy name Zǐxìn.
During the Yǒnglè reign, he entered the Tàixué through a provincial recommendation,
was selected to serve as a lecturer to the Imperial Grandson,
and was promoted to Xíngkē Jǐshìzhōng.
In the fourth year of Xuāndé, he impeached Qīngjūn Shìláng Jīn Xiáng for accepting bribes
and had him dismissed.
Lángzhōng Hú [Wángyù] and Xiāo Xiáng, among eleven others,
and three censors, Fāng Dǐng,
were impeached for dereliction of duty.
The Emperor was not convinced
and ordered Jiǎ Liàng and Zhāng Jūjié to investigate secretly.
The facts were confirmed, and all were demoted.
The following year, he again impeached Yángwǔ Hóu Xuē Lù for factionalism and disrespect,
and the court became solemn.
Soon after, he was appointed Yòu Fù Dū Yùshǐ.
He traveled with Jǐnyī Zhǐhuī Wáng Yù, Cānyì Huáng Hàn, and court eunuch Zhāng Yì to inspect Sìchuān, Jiāngxī, and Húguǎng,
strictly investigating powerful families without showing any leniency.
In the second year of Zhèngtǒng,
there were major floods in Jiāngběi and Hénán,
and Jiǎ Liàng and Gōngbù Shìláng Zhèng Chén were ordered to provide relief.
Bandits in Máng and Dàng mountains caused trouble,
and Jiǎ Liàng captured many of them.
In the fourth year, he returned to Dézhōu
and died.
Jiǎ Liàng's conduct at home was exemplary, and he displayed integrity in office.
Yán Shēng,
a *jìnshì* during the Jiànwén reign.
He successively held the office of Right Vice Minister of the Grand Court of Judicial Review (*Dàlǐ Sì Yòu Shà qīng*).
When the Qing armies cleared Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng,
he upheld the law without wavering.
He was transferred to Nánjīng as an Assistant Censor-in-Chief (*Qiān Dū Yùshǐ*),
and worked harmoniously with [name omitted in original text] in handling affairs.
He was resolute and self-confident.
He once composed the "Rhapsody on the Divine Ram" (*Shén Yáng Fù*) to express his aspirations.
Duàn Mín,
courtesy name Shíjǔ,
was a native of Wǔjìn.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the second year of Yǒnglè.
He was selected as a probationary compiler (*shùjíshì*).
He, along with Zhāng Chǎng and Wú Shēn and others, all studied in the Wényuān Pavilion,
and all were appointed as Principal of the Ministry of Justice (*Xíngbù Zhǔshì*).
Mín was soon promoted to Director (*lángzhōng*).
When the sorceress Táng Sàier stirred up rebellion in Shāndōng,
the officials of the Three Judicial Offices were executed for allowing the bandits to flourish,
and Mín was promoted to Left Administration Commissioner (*Zuǒ Cānzhèng*).
At that time, there was an urgent search for Sàier,
and all nuns in Shāndōng and Běijīng, and all women who had left home throughout the empire, were arrested,
totaling tens of thousands of people.
Mín exerted his efforts to pardon and show leniency,
and people's hearts finally found peace.
When the imperial carriage went on the northern expedition,
the grain boats traveled from Jìníng to Lùhé,
and land convoys proceeded out of Jūyōng to beyond the frontier.
Mín calculated deeply and meticulously,
and the people below were not disturbed, yet the task was accomplished.
After his return,

an imperial edict commanded him and the Circuit Censor (*Xún'àn Yùshǐ*) to investigate the honesty and corruption of officials in the prefectures and counties they had passed through, and report their findings.
In the third year of Xuāndé, he was summoned to the capital,
and appointed acting Right Vice Minister of Revenue for Nánjīng (*Nánjīng Hùbù Yòu Shìláng*),
and was formally appointed after a year.
The next year, he was transferred to the Ministry of Justice (*Xíngbù*).
Initially,
both ministries were known for their mismanagement.
Upon Mín's arrival,
the organizational structure was reformed and improved,
and long-standing malpractices were eliminated.
There was a man from Shàngyuán who was beaten by his nephew;
he was extremely indignant,
and went to the Office of Transmission (*Tōngzhèng Sì*) to report it.
At that time, people were allowed to redeem their crimes by paying grain,
but illegal appeals were strictly prohibited,
and offenders were exiled to Liáodōng.
Mín submitted a memorial saying:
"According to the established regulations,
the crimes of juniors can be redeemed,
but seniors are instead banished afar.
Judging by reason, this is inappropriate.
I request a reconsideration of the judgment."
The Emperor agreed with him.
The Emperor, considering Mín's integrity and uprightness,
specially bestowed an imperial edict,
ordering him to inspect all officials in Nánjīng.
In the eighth year,
an imperial edict decreed that all prisoners, except those guilty of the Ten Abominations, should have their sentences reduced by one degree.
There were over thirty serious offenders
who by rule could not be pardoned,
but Mín also reduced their sentences.
Later, an imperial decree ordered their execution,
so they were recalled,
but several had already escaped.
Mín stated his case,
but officials like Nián Fù impeached Mín.
The Emperor knew Mín was virtuous,
and did not pursue the matter.
In the second month of the ninth year, he died in office,
at the age of fifty-nine.
He was too poor to afford a burial,
so the Censor-in-Chief Wú Nà provided grave clothes.
The Emperor, upon hearing this,
ordered the relevant authorities to arrange the funeral.
During the Chénghuà reign,
Yè Shèng requested a posthumous commendation, but it was not carried out.
Over a hundred years later,
he was finally granted the posthumous title Xiāngjiè.
Wú Shēn,
courtesy name Shújìn,
was a native of Qúzhōu.
He served as a Principal of the Ministry of Justice (*Xíngbù Zhǔshì*),
and gained a reputation for his judicial work.
He successively became a Director (*lángzhōng*),
and was appointed Vice Minister of Rites (*Lǐbù Shìláng*).
Chéngzǔ said to Lǚ Zhèn:
"Shēn comes from the Hànlín Academy;
he can assist you in handling ritual matters."
Soon after, he was squeezed out by Zhèn,
and dispatched as Administration Commissioner of Guǎngdōng (*Guǎngdōng Cānzhèng*).
He was soon recalled to serve as Vice Minister of Justice for Nánjīng (*Nánjīng Xíngbù Shìláng*),
and was ordered by imperial edict to inspect local officials in Guǎngdōng, Guǎngxī, and Fújiàn.
There was an old acquaintance who served as Administration Commissioner (*cānzhèng*),
who was notoriously corrupt,
and many powerful figures interceded on his behalf.
When Shēn arrived,
he ultimately dismissed him,
and people at the time praised his impartiality.
He was again transferred to the Ministry of Rites (*Lǐbù*).
In the sixth year of Zhèngtǒng, he died in office.
Shēn was upright, strong, and resolute,
and indifferent to fame and gain.
When he was first appointed Vice Minister,
all well-wishers gathered,
but his room was utterly bare,
with absolutely no furnishings,
and the crowd laughed and left.
Zhāng Chǎng,
courtesy name Shàngwén,
was a native of Kuàijī.
He was appointed Principal of the Ministry of Justice (*Xíngbù Zhǔshì*) from a probationary compiler (*shùjíshì*).
When bandits emerged in Shānxī,
hundreds of people were arrested.
Chǎng perceived that they were wrongfully accused,
kept only one person whose demeanor and speech were unusual,
and released all the others.
The next day, upon interrogation,
the one he kept was indeed a bandit,
while the rest were not.
He was promoted to Director (*lángzhōng*),
and then transferred to the Ministry of Personnel (*Lìbù*).
In the sixth year of Xuāndé, he was promoted to Vice Minister of Rites (*Lǐbù Shìláng*).
He traveled with Xú Qí as envoy to Ānnán,
to command Lí Lì to provisionally govern the country's affairs.
Lì sent someone to clarify the protocol for their meeting,
but Chǎng said:
"Your respect for the envoys
is to honor the imperial court;
why clarify it?"
Lì obeyed,
hastening to bow and sit in a lower position.
He was tempted with pleasures of music and women,
but was not moved.
Upon their return, Lì presented them with a generous gift,
but they did not accept it.
Lì then entrusted it to the tribute envoy.
When they reached the pass,
Chǎng inspected all the tribute items,
sealed the gift,
and handed it to the pass official.
After Lì's death,
his son Lín succeeded him,
and Chǎng again went on imperial command,
refusing gifts as before.
In the early Zhèngtǒng reign,
he compiled the statutes and regulations since Hóngwǔ,
allowing all departments to consult them,
so that officials could not commit malpractices.
Minister Hú Yíng was magnanimous,
and Chǎng assisted him with strictness.
He died in the twelfth month of the second year.
His son Jǐn also successively rose to the rank of Vice Minister of Rites (*Lǐbù Shìláng*).
Xú Qí,
courtesy name Liángyù.
His ancestors were from Qiántáng,
but his grandfather was exiled to Níngxià as a military colonist,
and so his family settled there.
From a young age, he diligently studied,
and was proficient in the classics and histories.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the thirteenth year of Yǒnglè.
He was appointed Director of the Bureau of Scrutiny for Personnel (*Xíngrén*),
and successively served as Vice Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs (*Bīngbù Yuánwàiláng*).
He was intelligent, decisive,
and in office always focused on the overall picture.
In the sixth year of Xuāndé, he was promoted to Right Vice Commissioner of the Office of Transmission (*Yòu Tōngzhèng*).
He served as deputy to Chǎng as envoy to Ānnán,
and likewise did not accept gifts.
Upon his return, he was appointed Right Vice Minister of War for Nánjīng (*Nánjīng Bīngbù Yòu Shìláng*).
In the eighth year,
the Emperor, noting that Ānnán's tribute was not up to quota,
and that not all soldiers from the southern campaign had returned,
ordered Qí to go again.
At that time, Lí Lì had already died,
and his son Lín was hesitant and undecided.
Qí enlightened him about the consequences, both good and bad,
and Lín, struck with fear,
cast a golden statue to represent himself,
and offered local products as an apology.
The Emperor was pleased,
ordered Qí's name removed from the list of banished military colonists,
and lavishly entertained and rewarded him.
In the early Zhèngtǒng era,
Qí, along with Zhèng Chén, the Vice Minister of Works, was appointed to investigate officials in Nánjī.
They dismissed thirty individuals who were found to be corrupt.
At that time, disasters and anomalies frequently occurred,
so Qí presented ten measures to mitigate them.
All were graciously accepted.
In the fifth year, he was ordered to participate in the strategic affairs of Nánjīng.
In the fourteenth year, he was promoted to Minister (Shàngshū),
continuing his participation in strategic affairs as before.
There was a proposal that all military families who had been relocated to Nánjīng in previous years should be moved north.
The court deliberated on implementing this.
Qí memorialized,
“People are naturally attached to their native land and are reluctant to move.
This is human nature.
If tens of thousands of people are suddenly relocated,
the morale will be shaken,
and unforeseen troubles might arise.”
The matter was dropped.
As military garrisons lacked schools,
Qí requested that schools be established in all garrisons and guard posts nationwide, following the example of prefectures, departments, and counties.
This was approved.
In the first year of Jǐngtài,
Wáng Jì, Earl of Jìngyuǎn, participated in strategic affairs,
while Qí focused on managing the departmental matters.
When Jì left his post,
Qí continued to participate in strategic affairs.
He died in the third month of the fourth year,
aged sixty-eight.
He was posthumously given the epithet Zhēnxiāng.
Chǎng and Qí were both renowned for successfully completing their missions to Ānnán without disgrace.
Ānnán was rich in treasures;
later envoys often used waterways, bringing merchants along to profit,
which caused the Jiāo people to rather look down on them.
During the Hóngzhì era,
Liú Jiǎn, a Lecturer-in-Waiting, was dispatched to proclaim an imperial edict.
He traveled from Nánníng by post-horse to their country,
which greatly surprised the Jiāo people.
Jiǎn followed the old regulations,
received bows and greetings from the vassal officials,
exchanged not a single word,
and departed the morning after,
refusing all gifts.
Envoys tried to intercept him on the road
and insisted on giving him gifts,
but he ultimately waved them away.
He, along with Chǎng and Qí, was highly esteemed by the Jiāo people.
Jiǎn,
courtesy name Jǐngyuán,
was from Ānfú.
Wú Nè,
courtesy name Mǐndé,
was from Chángshú.
His father, Zūn,
served as a Registrar (Bù) in Yuánlíng,
but was imprisoned in the capital for an offense.
Nè memorialized, offering to take his father's place.
Before the matter was resolved, his father died,
and Nè, moved by this, diligently pursued his studies.
During the Yǒnglè era,
he was recommended as a physician to the capital.
When Rénzōng governed as regent,
he heard of Nè's reputation
and ordered him to teach the sons of meritorious officials.
Chéngzǔ summoned him for an audience and was pleased with his replies.
He was ordered to attend the inner court daily
to be available for consultation.
In the first year of Hóngxī,
Shěn Dù, a Lecturer-in-Waiting, recommended Nè for his profound knowledge of classics and upright conduct,
and he was appointed Censor (Jiānchá Yùshǐ).
He was respectful, cautious, incorruptible, and straightforward,
never engaging in affectation.
In the early Xuāndé era,
he was sent to inspect Zhèjiāng,
making it his duty to revitalize discipline and uphold moral principles.
At that time, deserting soldiers
often had their families file false accusations,
leading to the arrest and detention of up to a thousand people.
Nè requested strict prohibition, stating that even the wronged should not be allowed to make such reports beyond the local authorities.
This was approved.
Later, he inspected Guìzhōu,
where he wielded both benevolence and authority,
causing the indigenous people to respect and submit to him.
As he was about to be replaced and return,
the local people went to the imperial court to petition for his retention.
This was not granted.
In the seventh month of the fifth year,
he was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief (Yòu Qiāndū Yùshǐ) of Nánjīng,
and soon after, to Left Vice Censor-in-Chief (Zuǒ Fùdū Yùshǐ).
In the early Zhèngtǒng era,
Dǒng Zhèng, a Secretary of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, and others stole official property.
Nè exposed them,
and forty-four people were banished to military garrisons.
Lǐ Zhěn, a Right Surveillance Commissioner,
was dispatched to Sū and Sōng,
where his conduct was often improper.
Nè subtly admonished him.
Zhěn was displeased,
and falsely accused Nè of delaying imperial edicts and other matters.
Nè submitted a memorial in his defense.
Both were impeached by the Censorate and other provincial authorities,
and both were arrested and imprisoned,
but later released.
When Yīngzōng first presided over the imperial lectures,
Nè presented his compiled work, Xiǎoxué Jíjiě (Collected Explanations of the Minor Learning).
In the third month of the fourth year,
he retired due to old age,
and Zhū Yǔyán replaced him.
Nè was widely read,
and his arguments had solid foundations.
He made many discoveries regarding the profundities of human nature and reason,
and his writings are all worthy of being passed down to posterity.
Upon returning home,
he wore plain clothes and ate simple vegetarian meals,
and his house was utterly bare.
When Zhōu Chén governed Jiāngnán,
he wanted to renovate Nè's residence,
but Nè refused.
He lived at home for sixteen years before he died,
aged eighty-six.
He was posthumously given the epithet Wénkè,
and the local people worshipped him in the Yán Yǎn祠 temple.
Zhū Yǔyán,
courtesy name Yī’è,
was from Wàn’ān.
He became a successful candidate in the imperial examination in the ninth year of Yǒnglè,
and was appointed Surveillance Commissioner (Ànchá Qiānshì) of Húguǎng.
During the Xuāndé era, he was promoted to Vice Commissioner (Fùshǐ) of Sìchuān.
When bandits rose in Hézhōu,
he supervised the clerk Xióng Dǐng, who executed over sixty people,
and the bandit forces subsequently weakened.
When the matter was reported,
Dǐng was promoted to Assistant Prefect (Tóngzhī) of Hézhōu.
When sorcerers caused unrest in Yǎzhōu,
Yǔyán captured and sent them to the capital,
and the region became peaceful.
In the first year of Zhèngtǒng, he was summoned to be the Right Vice Censor-in-Chief (Yòu Fùdū Yùshǐ) of Nánjīng,
and took over Nè’s responsibilities at the Censorate.
He retired due to old age,
and then died.
Yǔyán was firm, upright, incorruptible, and cautious,
and in governing, he focused on the larger picture.
He frequently submitted proposals,
many of which addressed contemporary ills.
His home was pure and dignified.
If a villager behaved improperly,
they only feared that Yǔyán would know about it.
Wèi Jì,
courtesy name Zhòngfáng,
was from Xiāoshān.
During the Yǒnglè era,
he was appointed Instructor (Xùndǎo) of Sōngjiāng as a second-class jinshi.
He often worked late into the night, bringing tea and congee to comfort the students.
The students were moved and inspired,
many of whom achieved success.
He was summoned to compile the Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn.
After the book was completed,
he returned to his post.
Upon the recommendation of Shī Kuí,
he was promoted to Court Gentleman for Ceremonials (Tàicháng Bóshì).
The Emperor told him:
“Liú Lǚjié served as a Censor for nine years.
Emperor Gāo himself bestowed this office;
it is not lightly given to others.”
In the early Xuāndé era,
he was promoted to Supernumerary Director of the Bureau of Merits (Kǎogōng Yuánwàiláng) in the Ministry of Personnel,
and successively served as Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Sì Shàopǐng) in Nánjīng.
In the third year of Zhèngtǒng, he was summoned for examination and appointed Provisional Left Vice Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Zuǒ Shìláng) in the traveling court.
After a year, he was formally appointed.
He was repeatedly ordered to inspect the imperial domain for surviving locusts
and inquire about the people's hardships.
In the eighth year, he was transferred to the Ministry of Rites,
but soon after requested to retire due to old age.
Wáng Zhí, Minister of Personnel, stated that Jì was not yet frail,
and if his age was a concern,
he should be assigned to a less demanding role.
Thus, he was transferred to the Nánjīng Ministry of Personnel.
Again, he resigned due to old age.
This was not granted.
In the fourteenth year, he was promoted to Minister (Shàngshū).
When Yīngzōng was taken captive in the north,
Jì led various departments in submitting proposals on current affairs,
many of which were implemented.
In the first year of Jǐngtài,
at the age of seventy-seven,
he retired.
Wèi Jì 驥, while holding office, focused on the broader principles.
While serving as Tàicháng 太常,
when the mountain and river altars produced a pair of white rabbits,
and auspicious grain grew within the capital region,
he always declined to report them.
While serving in the Lìbù 吏部,
there was a *jìnshì* 進士 who had not yet completed his mourning period,
and sought an evaluation for promotion (*kǎogōng* 考功).
His colleagues were inclined to permit it.
Wèi Jì 驥 firmly opposed it.
When the judicial authorities granted clemency during a drought,
there was a certain Wáng Gāng 王綱,
whose crime of heinous rebellion merited execution.
Some, pitying his youth,
wished to delay his sentence.
Wèi Jì 驥 said:
"This is the benevolence of a woman,
and it is precisely for this reason that the ways of Heaven are out of season."
The judgment was rendered, and it rained.
During the Zhèngtǒng 正統 reign,
Wáng Zhèn 王振, relying on imperial favor,
abused high officials.
Yet he alone respected Wèi Jì 驥 deeply,
calling him
"Xiānshēng 先生."
In the early Jǐngtài 景泰 reign,
Wèi Jì 驥 came to the capital to request retirement due to old age.
Grand Secretary Chén Xún 陳循,
who was Wèi Jì's 驥 disciple,
privately asked him:
"Although you hold the position of a senior minister,
you have not yet served at court.
I hope you will wait a little longer;
the matter rests with people like us."
Wèi Jì 驥 replied sternly:
"As an imperial assistant, you should recommend worthy talents for the empire,
and not show partiality to a former examiner."
He retired and told others:
"He treats the affairs of the court as his own personal business;
how can he end well?"
Ultimately, he retired from office and left.
Wèi Jì 驥 was upright, honest, reverent, and cautious.
He was also resolute and straightforward,
and liked to distinguish between gentlemen and villains.
He said:
"One who lacks a sense of right and wrong
is not human."
At home,
he worried about the country and the people,
and this intensified with old age.
Xiāoshān 蕭山 had always suffered from floods,
and there were traces of dikes built by Yáng Shí 楊時, a county magistrate during the Sòng 宋 dynasty.
Wèi Jì 驥 initiated the repair of the Luóshān 螺山, Shíyán 石巖, and Bìgōng 畢公 ponds and weirs,
to defend against river tides and
promote the benefits of the lakes.
The villagers relied on him.
He lived in plain clothes and ate coarse food,
and did not accumulate property.
He served his elder brother, the instructor Qí 騏,
with increasing respect even in his old age.
He often wore a bamboo hat and walked through the fields.
Once, he encountered a *zhǔbù* 主簿 from Qiántáng 錢塘,
whose subordinate scolded him.
He replied:
"I am Wèi Jì 驥 of Xiāoshān 蕭山."
The *zhǔbù* 主簿 hurriedly apologized, comforted him, and left.
In the seventh year of Chénghuà 成化 (1471),
Censor Liáng Fǎng 梁昉 stated:
"Your subject previously served in Xiāoshān 蕭山
and saw the retired *shàngshū* 尚書, your subject Wèi Jì 驥, residing in his village,
mingling with the villagers,
teaching his sons and grandsons filial piety, fraternal duty, and diligence in farming,
and raising dikes and dredging lakes,
to ward off disasters.
His actions conformed to ritual and law,
he promoted Neo-Confucianism (*lǐxué* 理學),
and encouraged younger generations.
Even in retirement,
he contributed to good governance.
Wèi Jì's 驥 lifelong learning and conduct were pure and sincere,
his character was upright and magnanimous,
he was knowledgeable in worldly affairs,
and understood the national structure.
He has been retired for over twenty years,
and is ninety-eight years old.
People from all directions look up to his virtue,
like auspicious clouds.
A hundred years of cultivation
has nourished this human marvel.
Your subject has read the former histories,
wherein some who retired were granted stipends for life,
some were honorably cared for as 'three elders and five superiors' (*sānlǎowǔgēng* 三老五更),
some were summoned with comfortable carriages with padded wheels (*ānchēpúlún* 安車蒲輪),
and some were bestowed with a stool and a staff,
all honoring their age and virtue.
Wèi Jì's 驥 age and virtue are more than sufficient,
and his rank is that of a senior minister,
making him a truly respected figure.
I beg that the relevant authorities be instructed
to apply precedents from previous dynasties."
The emperor reviewed the memorial and praised it.
He dispatched an imperial envoy to inquire after him,
bestowed sheep and wine,
and ordered the relevant authorities to provide three *shí* 石 of rice monthly.
The imperial envoy had not yet arrived when Wèi Jì 驥 passed away.
He was granted a memorial ceremony and burial according to ritual,
and posthumously named Wénjìng 文靖.
His son, Wán 完, conveyed Wèi Jì's 驥 dying wish to the court, declining the elaborate burial,
and requesting that the funds be used to relieve the famine victims.
The emperor sighed with emotion, saying:
"Wèi Jì's 驥 dying wish
still feared burdening the people.
He can truly be called a loyal minister."
He granted the request.
The people of Xiāoshān 蕭山 were endlessly grateful to Wèi Jì 驥.
They went to the court to request that he be enshrined in the Déhuì Cí 德惠祠,
to be worshipped alongside Yáng Shí 楊時.
The imperial decree stated:
"Granted."
Lǔ Mù 魯穆,
courtesy name Xīwén 希文,
was a native of Tiāntái 天台.
He passed the *jìnshì* 進士 examination in the fourth year of Yǒnglè 永樂.
When he was at home,
he wore coarse clothes and ate vegetables,
and his footsteps never entered the administrative seats of prefectures or sub-prefectures.
When he was about to undergo selection for office,
the officials offered him parting gifts (*zhèn* 贐).
Lǔ Mù 穆 said:
"I am just about to enter officialdom;
I have not yet been able to benefit the people,
so how can I first harm my hometown?"
He refused them.
He was appointed as a Censor (*yùshǐ* 御史).
When Rénzōng 仁宗 was supervising the state,
Lǔ Mù 穆 repeatedly submitted memorials.
The retainers of the King of Hàn 漢王 often acted unlawfully,
and no one dared to speak.
Lǔ Mù 穆 submitted a memorial impeaching them,
but it received no reply.
Nevertheless, his reputation for integrity resounded throughout the court.
He was promoted to Surveillance Vice Commissioner (*qiānshì* 僉事) of Fújiàn 福建.
He redressed wrongful judgments and abuses,
and suppressed the powerful and tyrannical.
A certain Lǐ 李 from Quánzhōu 泉州 was transferred to an official post in Guǎngxī 廣西.
His relative, the wealthy merchant Lín 林, sent a servant to poison Lǐ 李 on the road,
and then took Lǐ's 李 wife as his own.
Lǐ's 李 clansmen reported it to the authorities,
but the officials accepted Lín's 林 bribe,
imprisoned the accusers,
who remained in jail for a long time.
Lǔ Mù 穆 diligently investigated and uncovered the truth,
and immediately punished Lín 林 for his crime.
Zhōu Yǔnwén 周允文 of Zhāngzhōu 漳州 had no son,
and adopted his nephew as his heir.
Later, his concubine gave birth to a son.
He then divided his property with his nephew,
entrusting him with the care of his concubine's son.
After Zhōu Yǔnwén's 周允文 death,
the nephew claimed that the child was not his uncle's son,
drove him away,
and seized all his property.
The concubine lodged a complaint.
Lǔ Mù 穆 summoned the county elders and Zhōu's 周 clan members,
and secretly placed the concubine's son among a group of children.
Everyone pointed to the child as resembling Zhōu Yǔnwén 周允文,
and thus his property was returned.
The people called him
"Lǔ Tiěmiàn 魯鐵面 (Iron Face Lu)."
At that time, Yáng Róng 楊榮 was in power.
When Yáng Róng's 楊榮 family members broke the law,
Lǔ Mù 穆 punished them without leniency.
Yáng Róng 榮 nonetheless considered Lǔ Mù 穆 worthy
and recommended him to the court.
Upon Yīngzōng's 英宗 accession to the throne,
Lǔ Mù 穆 was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief (*yòuqīandōuyùshǐ* 右僉都御史).
The following year, he was ordered to suppress locusts in Dàmíng 大名.
Upon his return,
he died of illness.
The emperor ordered a boat to transport his coffin home.
When Lǔ Mù 穆 first entered office as Surveillance Vice Commissioner,
he carried nothing more than a bag of clothes.
Minister Wú Zhōng 吳中 offered him household items,
which he refused.
Now, Wú Zhōng 吳中 arranged for his coffin and shroud,
and only then could he be entombed.
His son, Chóngzhì 崇志,
successively served as Administrator of Yìngtiān 應天,
and was known for his integrity and uprightness, embodying his father's character.
Gěng Jiǔchóu 耿九疇,
courtesy name Yǔfàn 禹範,
was a native of Lúshì 盧氏.
He passed the *jìnshì* 進士 examination at the end of Yǒnglè 永樂.
In the sixth year of Xuāndé 宣德, he was appointed as Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Rites (*Lǐkē Jǐshìzhōng* 禮科給事中).
His discussions upheld major principles
and he enjoyed a reputation for integrity.
In the early Zhèngtǒng era,
ministers stated that the salt administration in Liǎnghuái had long been corrupted,
and that someone of great renown and integrity should be appointed to govern it.
Thus, Zhōu Jiǔchóu 周九疇 was selected to be the Tóngzhī 同知 (Assistant Administrator) of the Yányùn Sī 鹽運司 (Salt Transport Commissioner's Office).
He vigorously reformed entrenched malpractices
and submitted five proposals for expedient measures,
which were enacted as regulations.
When his mother died, he resigned from office.
Thousands of salt field residents pleaded for him to remain.
In the first month of the tenth year (of Zhèngtǒng), he was appointed as the Dū Zhuǎnyùnshǐ 都轉運使 (Provincial Transport Commissioner).
He was frugal and had no other preferences;
after returning from public duties, he would burn incense and read books.
His reputation for integrity grew,
and women and children all knew his name.
He was falsely accused in a certain matter
and arrested by officials.
Later,
he was cleared,
and immediately retained as Yòushìláng 右侍郎 (Vice Minister) of the Xíngbù 刑部 (Ministry of Justice).
He repeatedly resolved difficult cases,
without being swayed or intimidated.
When Zhāng Jǐn 章瑾, the Shìláng 侍郎 (Minister) of the Lǐbù 禮部 (Ministry of Rites), was imprisoned,
Jiǔchóu and Jiāng Yuān 江淵 debated reducing his rank.
Jǐn's son-in-law, the Gěishìzhōng 給事中 (Investigating Censor) Wáng Rǔlín 王汝霖, resented this,
and along with his colleagues Yè Shèng 葉盛, Zhāng Gù 張固, Lín Cōng 林聰, and others, they argued that the Xíngbù was unjust.
Jiǔchóu and Yuān then impeached Shèng and the others,
and also stated that Rǔlín's father, Wáng Yǒnghé 王永和, had died at Tǔmùbǎo 土木堡,
yet Rǔlín behaved cheerfully as usual,
and was unfit for office.
At that time, Jǐngdì 景帝 had just ascended the throne
and was eager to appoint people,
so he left Rǔlín and others unquestioned,
and Jǐn's case proceeded as proposed.
When Fèngyáng 鳳陽 suffered a famine,
and bandits were about to rise,
an imperial edict ordered Jiǔchóu to inspect and pacify the region.
He proposed to keep the Yīngwǔ 英武 and Fēixióng 飛熊 Guards' troops to farm and defend,
and recruited 70,000 households of displaced people,
thereby bringing peace to the area.
In Liǎnghuái, after Jiǔchóu left,
the salt administration again became lax.
In the first year of Jǐngtài 景泰 (1450), he was again ordered to concurrently manage it.
Soon after, an imperial edict instructed him to review major prisoners in various prefectures,
and he corrected many injustices.
In the tenth month, he was ordered to concurrently govern the prefectures north of the Jiāng 江 (Yangtze River).
In the third month of the third year (of Jǐngtài), he replaced Chén Yì 陳鎰 to garrison Shǎnxī 陝西.
When Dū Zhǐhuī 都指揮 (Regional Military Commissioner) Yáng Déqīng 楊得青 and others privately conscripted soldiers for their own use,
Jiǔchóu impeached them.
An edict ordered an investigation,
and also commanded that all border generals like Déqīng
be impeached and reported.
When border generals requested to increase the garrison at Líntáo 臨洮 and other guards,
Jiǔchóu said:
"The border garrisons do not lack soldiers.
If generals can enforce strict discipline
and rewards and punishments are clear and trustworthy,
then everyone will exert themselves.
Otherwise,
they are merely redundant eaters."
Thus, the garrison was not increased.
Border residents would go out to farm in spring and summer,
but often moved back within the pass in autumn and winter.
Jiǔchóu said:
"Border generals are meant to repel invaders and protect the people.
If people have to flee invaders and lose their livelihoods,
what use are generals?"
Therefore, he prohibited people from moving inward.
If anyone was attacked by invaders,
the responsible defending general would be punished.
In the fourth year (of Jǐngtài),
Bùzhèngshǐ 布政使 (Provincial Administration Commissioner) Xǔ Zī 許資 said:
"A Shìláng serving as garrison commander
is not subordinate to the Xún'àn Yùshǐ 巡按御史 (Circuit Censor), leading to many delays in affairs.
I request that he be reassigned to a Censorate position, which would be more suitable."
Thus, he was transferred to Yòu Fù Dū Yùshǐ 右副都御史 (Vice Censor-in-Chief on the Right).
It was from Jiǔchóu onward
that ministers serving as garrison commanders and巡撫 (Grand Coordinators) were all granted the title of Dū Yùshǐ 都御史 (Censor-in-Chief).
There was an imperial decree to buy sheep horns for lamps.
Jiǔchóu cited Sòng's Sū Shì 蘇軾's remonstrance to Shénzōng 神宗 regarding the purchase of Zhèjiāng 浙江 lamps,
and the matter was then dropped.
When seeking criticism due to disasters and anomalies,
he requested the emperor to invite Confucian scholars,
make rewards and punishments public,
select good prefects and magistrates,
and choose capable generals.
The emperor responded with a gracious edict.
In the early Tiānshùn 天順 era,
he debated matters in the capital.
The emperor looked at his attending ministers and said:
"Jiǔchóu
is an upright and incorruptible person."
He was retained as Yòu Dū Yùshǐ 右都御史 (Censor-in-Chief on the Right).
Prisoners in the Dūcháyuan 都察院 (Censorate) prison were not given rice.
Jiǔchóu spoke on their behalf,
and thereafter one shēng 升 (liter) of rice was given daily,
which became a regulation.
Later,
he submitted a memorial on five matters: promoting integrity and shame,
clarifying judicial administration, encouraging agriculture and sericulture, moderating military rewards, and emphasizing the Censorate.
The emperor praised and accepted all of them.
In the sixth month of that year,
Yùshǐ 御史 (Censor) Zhāng Péng 張鵬 and others impeached Shí Hēng 石亨 and Cáo Jíxiáng 曹吉祥.
Hēng and others believed that Jiǔchóu had instigated them,
so he was also imprisoned,
and demoted to Jiāngxī Bùzhèngshǐ 江西布政使 (Jiangxi Provincial Administration Commissioner),
soon after transferred to Sìchuān 四川.
The next year,
the Lǐbù lacked a Shàngshū 尚書 (Minister).
The emperor asked Lǐ Xián 李賢.
Xián said:
"For an experienced, clear-minded, and upright person,
there is no one like Jiǔchóu."
Thus, he was recalled.
Upon his arrival,
pitying his old age,
he was reassigned to Nánjīng Xíngbù Shàngshū 南京刑部尚書 (Minister of Justice of Nanjing).
He died in the fourth year (of Tiānshùn).
He was posthumously granted the title Qīnghuì 清惠.
His son, Yù 裕,
has his own biography.
Xuan Ní 軒輗,
courtesy name Wéixíng 惟行,
was from Lùyì 鹿邑.
He obtained the Jìnshì 進士 degree in the late Yǒnglè 永樂 era.
He was appointed Fù 副 (Assistant) of the Xíngrén Sī 行人司 (Bureau of Receptions).
In the sixth year of Xuāndé 宣德, he was recommended and transferred to Yùshǐ.
He inspected Fújiàn 福建,
removed corrupt officials and eliminated villains,
and his conduct was very severe.
In the first year of Zhèngtǒng, he cleared the military administration in Zhèjiāng 浙江,
impeaching over forty incompetent officials.
In the fifth year, he said:
"Our ancestors established the office of Yùshǐ,
making its duties extremely important.
Now, many internal and external offices, when they have affairs,
presumptuously dispatch Yùshǐ,
which is not according to regulations.
I request that this be prohibited."
It was immediately approved.
That same year,
he was exceptionally promoted to Zhèjiāng Ànchásǐ 浙江按察使 (Provincial Surveillance Commissioner of Zhejiang).
The previous commissioner had been extravagant and wasteful,
and Ní vigorously rectified this.
In both cold and hot weather, he wore a single blue cloth robe,
almost completely covered with patches.
He usually ate vegetarian food,
and his wife and children personally managed household chores.
He made an agreement with his subordinates
that they could only use salary money to buy meat every three days,
and it must not exceed one jīn 斤 (catty).
Many of his subordinates found it unbearable.
When old friends visited,
they were served only one bean dish.
If chicken and millet were prepared,
people were astonished and considered it unusual.

At that time, the garrison eunuch Ruǎn Suí 阮隨, Bùzhèngshǐ Sūn Yuánzhēn 孫原貞, Hángzhōu Zhīfǔ 杭州知府 (Prefect of Hangzhou) Chén Fù 陳復, and Rénhé Zhīxiàn 仁和知縣 (Magistrate of Renhe) Xǔ Pú 許璞 were all incorruptible in office,
and the region was greatly well-governed.
Wēnzhōu 溫州 and Chǔzhōu 處州 had silver mines.
During the Hóngwǔ 洪武 era, the annual tax was only over 2,800 liǎng 兩 (taels),
but in the Yǒnglè era, it increased to 82,000 liǎng,
which the people could not bear.
When the emperor ascended the throne,
he abolished them based on ministerial discussions.
At this time, Cānzhèng 參政 (Policy Advisor) Yú Shìyuè 俞士悅 requested their reopening,
arguing that if the profits went to the state,
then mine bandits would naturally cease.
The matter was sent to the Sānsī 三司 (Three Judicial Offices) for deliberation,
and Ní strongly insisted against it,
so it was stopped.
Later, Gěishìzhōng Chén Fù 陳傅 again requested it,
and the court hastily agreed,
which then led to the uprising of Yè Zōngliú 葉宗留.
Zhào Bótài 趙伯泰 of Kuàijī 會稽,
a descendant of the Sòng 宋 dynasty,
reported that the tombs of Xiàozōng 孝宗, Lǐzōng 理宗, and the Prince of Fú 福王,
had all been encroached upon by powerful commoners.
Yùshǐ Wáng Lín 王琳 argued that the Prince of Fú had surrendered to the Yuán 元 dynasty
and gone north;
how could there be a tomb in Shānyīn 山陰?
Bótài was indignant
and appealed again.
The emperor ordered Ní and Xún'àn Yùshǐ Ōuyáng Chéng 歐陽澄 to re-investigate.
Ní stated that the Prince of Fú's tomb was likely a tomb for his clothes and cap,
and that Bótài's statement was not false.
An imperial edict exiled the powerful commoners to the border
and suspended Lín's and others' salaries.
He suffered the loss of his parents, but was reinstated to office.
In the thirteenth year (of Zhèngtǒng),
he presented four proposals,
all relevant to current malpractices,
and the emperor adopted all of them.
When Jǐngdì ascended the throne,
he was appointed Right Vice Minister of Censorate (Yòu Fù Dū Yùshǐ) to guard Zhèjiāng.
In the first year of Jǐngtài, he was ordered to concurrently manage the salt tax of the two Zhè regions.
Mín (Fújiàn) bandits Wú Jīnbā and others plundered Qīngtián and other counties.
Ní and Yuán Zhēn suppressed them.
Bandit leaders Luó Pī and Liáo Níngbā again came from Mín to Zhè.
Ní and others were effective in repelling them,
and their rank was advanced by one grade.
The next year, he was reassigned to supervise the grain storage in Nánjīng.
In the fifth year, he was again reassigned as Left Vice Minister of Censorate (Zuǒ Fù Dū Yùshǐ),
managing the affairs of the Southern Censorate (Nányuàn).
He impeached and dismissed several incompetent censors.
In the second month of the first year of Tiānshùn, he was summoned and appointed Minister of Justice (Xíngbù Shàngshū).
After several months,
he pleaded illness and requested to return home.
The emperor summoned him,
and asked:
"The former Zhèjiāng Inspector (Liánshǐ), when his term was up, returned
with only one basket for his luggage.
Was that you?"
Ní bowed his head and thanked him.
