He was granted white silver as a consolation and sent away.
The next year,
the post of supervisor of grain storage in Nánjīng was vacant.
The emperor asked Lǐ Xián
who among the high officials had held this position before.
Xián replied with Ní,
and also praised his integrity.
So, he was ordered to go as Left Censor-in-Chief (Zuǒ Dū Yùshǐ).
In the summer of the eighth year, he requested to retire due to old age,
and returned home without waiting for a reply.
Upon reaching home, he hurried to take a bath,
then yawned and died.
Ní was solitary and aloof.
He treated people, whether worthy or not,
by refusing to associate with them.
When he was Censor (Ànchásǐ),
he once drank at a colleague's house.
Upon returning, he patted his belly and said:
"There are ill-gotten gains in this."
While in Nándū (Nánjīng),
Censor-in-Chief Zhāng Chún hosted a banquet for guests.
Ní disliked his extravagance
and did not attend.
When the remaining dishes were sent to him,
he also did not accept them.
At the turn of the year, he would go to the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù) to pay respects with a memorial for congratulations.
He would isolate himself in one room,
extinguish the candle, and sit upright.
After the matter was concluded, he would return immediately,
never exchanging a word with his colleagues.
When his colleagues heard he was coming,
they would often avoid him,
not enjoying his presence.
His temperament was rather narrow-minded.
If a censor exposed someone's private secrets,
he would commend their ability.
He once ordered a censor to impeach Wú Jié, Libationer (Jìjiǔ) of Nánjīng.
Jié, in turn, exposed Ní's private affairs,
and many people considered Ní to be in the wrong.
However, his incorruptible conduct was renowned throughout the empire,
and he was as famous as Gěng Jiǔchóu.
When speaking of incorruptible officials, Hān (Xuān) and Gěng were always mentioned.
Chén Fù,
a native of Huái'ān, Fújiàn.
He was a Jinshì of the same year as Ní.
He served as a Bureau Director (Zhǔshì) in the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù) and then as Magistrate (Zhī) of Hángzhōu.
He was incorruptible and tranquil, without selfishness,
and lawsuits greatly decreased.
He would sit upright in the main hall every day,
only discussing and studying laws and regulations with his clerks (Cáoyuán).
When he experienced mourning,
the local people begged him to stay.
An imperial edict ordered him to resume his post,
but he died not long after.
Ní advocated for his colleagues to help him,
and thus he was able to be buried.
Officials and common people flocked to offer contributions,
but his son rejected all of them,
and returned after borrowing money.
Huáng Kǒngzhāo,
a native of Huángyán.
His initial name was Yào.
Later, he went by his courtesy name,
and his courtesy name was changed to Shìxiǎn.
At fourteen,
he suffered the loss of his parents,
and was so emaciated by grief that his bones protruded.
He passed the Jinshì examination in the fourth year of Tiānshùn,
and was appointed Bureau Director of Military Colonies (Túntián Zhǔshì).
He was sent on a mission to Jiāngnán,
and refused gifts.
He was promoted to Assistant Minister (Yuánwàiláng) of Canals (Dūshuǐ).
In the fifth year of Chénghuà,
Chén Yún, Director (Lángzhōng) of the Bureau of Civil Appointments (Wénxuǎn), and others were impeached by clerks,
and all were imprisoned and demoted.
Minister Yáo Kuí knew Kǒngzhāo was incorruptible,
and transferred him to Wénxuǎn.
In the ninth year, he was promoted to Director (Lángzhōng).
According to custom,
the Director of Appointments (Xuǎnláng) would usually close his door and refuse guests.
Kǒngzhāo said:
"The state's use of talent
is like a wealthy family accumulating grain.
If grain is not stored in advance,
how can it suffice for famine?
If talent is not reserved beforehand,
how can it be put to use?
If one considers staying secluded and rejecting guests as noble,
how can one know the talented people of the realm?"
After official duties,
when guests arrived,
he would always receive them,
inquiring about talented individuals,
and record them in a book.
When assigning officials,
he would match their talent to the complexity of the locale.
Thus, his appointments were fair and just.
He rejected
all those who sought private influence.
He once argued with Minister Yǐn Mín,
even pushing the desk in great anger.
Kǒngzhāo stood respectfully,
waited for his anger to subside,
and then spoke again.
Mín also trusted his sincerity and straightforwardness.
Mín was close to Tán Lún, Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review (Tōngzhèng),
and wanted to appoint him as Vice Minister (Shìláng).
Kǒngzhāo insisted it was unacceptable.
Mín eventually appointed him,
and Lún indeed failed.
Mín wanted to promote an old friend to be a Provincial Governor (Xúnfǔ),
but Kǒngzhāo did not agree.
That person came to the capital to visit Kǒngzhāo,
even bending his knees.
Kǒngzhāo despised him even more.
Mín ordered Kǒngzhāo to recommend him,
Kǒngzhāo said:
"What he lacks
is the proper demeanor of a high official."
Mín told that person:
"As long as Master Huáng remains in the Bureau of Civil Appointments,
you cannot be promoted."
After serving nine years as Director (Lángzhōng),
he was finally promoted to Right Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review (Yòu Tōngzhèng).
After a long time,
he was transferred to Right Vice Minister of Works (Gōngbù Yòu Shìláng) in Nánjīng.
There were more than ten plots of government land that had been encroached upon by influential families,
and he memorialized to have them recovered.
By imperial edict, he recommended officials for important regional posts (fāngmiàn),
proposing Prefect Fán Yíng and Reviewing Secretary (Qiānshì) Zhāng Mào.
Both later became famous officials.
The Director (Lángguān) in charge of the treasury offered several thousand taels of surplus silver,
but he rejected and dismissed him.
When an ancient tripod was unearthed,
he immediately ordered artisans to engrave "Wénmiào" (Confucian Temple) on it,
and sent it to the temple.
Soon after, a powerful eunuch (zhōngguì) wanted to present it to the court,
but seeing the engraved characters, he stopped.
Kǒngzhāo loved learning and was diligent in practice.
He was close friends with Chén Xuǎn, Lín È, and Xiè Duó,
and together they were respected by scholars.
He died in the fourth year of Hóngzhì.
During Jiājìng's reign,
he was posthumously granted Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū)
and given the posthumous title Wényì.
His son Fǔ
also passed the Jinshì examination
and became Director (Lángzhōng) of the Bureau of Civil Appointments.
Fǔ's son Wǎn,
through his discussion
of the "Great Rites" (Dàlǐ),
rose to Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū).
He has his own biography.
Praise says: In the prosperous times of the state,
many scholar-officials valued themselves for their integrity and moral rectitude.
Was it that they deliberately strove for virtuous conduct,
or liked to put on an appearance of fame?
It was also their indifference to desires,
their shame in seeking competition,
and their inherently upright and resolute nature.
During the reigns of Rénzōng and Xuānzōng,
to rectify the corruption of officialdom, they promoted upright, incorruptible, firm, and just scholars.
Zōng Zài assisted in the selection of officials (quánhéng),
and Gù Zuǒ managed the national discipline (bāngxiàn),
thus the moral standards (fēngjì) were greatly purified.
Duàn Mín, Wú Nà, Wèi Jì, and Lǔ Mù maintained the unblemished integrity of a lamb's white silk.
Xuān, Gěng, and Kǒngzhāo were exceptionally austere and transcended worldly customs,
unaffected by external influences.
Zhāng Chǎng, Xú Qí, and Liú Jiǎn were strict and upright in their self-discipline,
earning the admiration of distant lands.
The value of integrity is truly outstanding.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 47: Xióng Gài (Yè Chūn),

Chén Yì, Lǐ Yí (Dīng Xuán), Chén Tài, Lǐ Táng (Zēng Huī), Jiǎ Quán, Wáng Yǔ, Cuī Gōng, Liú Zī (Sòng Jié, Xíng Yòu), Lǐ Kǎn (Léi Fù, Lǐ Gāng), Yuán Jié, Péng Yì, Móu Fèng, Xià Xún (Zǐ Hóu), Gāo Míng, Yáng Jìzōng.
Xióng Gài,
styled Yuánjié,
was a native of Fēngchéng.
Orphaned in youth,
he followed his mother when she married into the Hú clan
and took their surname.
He became a *Jìnshì* in the ninth year of Yǒnglè (1411).
He was appointed Censor (*Yùshǐ*).
In the sixteenth year (1418), he was promoted to Guangxi Surveillance Commissioner (*Guǎngxī Ànchásǐ*).
When the Mán people of Dòngxī greatly plundered the area,
the Provincial Administration Commissioner (*Bùzhèngshǐ*) suggested requesting the troops of Prince Jìngjiāng to stop them.
Gài disagreed,
saying,
"We are in charge of this region;
if bandits arrive and we cannot defend against them,
should we trouble the Prince?
Moreover, the bandits will certainly not come;
a state of alert is enough."
Soon after, it turned out to be so.
After some time,
he was transferred to Guangdong.

In the first month of the first year of Hóngxī (1425), he was ordered, in his original office, along with Provincial Administration Commissioner Zhōu Gàn and Administration Vice Commissioner Yè Chūn, to inspect Nánjī and Zhejiang.
Previously,
when Xià Yuánjí returned from managing water conservancy in Jiāngnán,
he was replaced by Left Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review (*Zuǒtōngzhèng*) Zhào Jūrèn,
who also supervised agricultural affairs.
Jūrèn did not care for the people,
yet reported abundant harvests annually.
Emperor Chéngzǔ also knew his reports were false and deceptive.
After Jūrèn's death,
Left Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review Yuè Fú succeeded him;
he was mediocre and did not attend to matters.
When Rénzōng was regent,
he once ordered Gài, as a Censor, to act as Minister of Justice (*Xíngbù*),
knowing his virtue,
hence this appointment.
In the eighth month of that year,
Gàn returned,
reporting that many officials were unsuitable,
local bullies were rampant,
and Fú was not performing his duties.
Xuānzōng recalled Fú
and promoted Gài to Chief Minister of the Court of Judicial Review (*Dàlǐsìqīng*),
sending him with Chūn to act as Grand Coordinator (*Xúnfǔ*).
The establishment of Grand Coordinators for Nánjī and Zhejiang began from this time.
Local magnates in Western Zhejiang took advantage of the county and prefectural weaknesses to commit illegal acts.
In Hǎiyán, the commoner Píng Kāng was extremely tyrannical,
and when a Censor tried to arrest him,
he fled.
He returned during an amnesty,
and gathered more than eight hundred followers.
Gài arrested and executed them.
Afterward,
he arrested several dozen prominent evildoers,
shackled them, and sent them to the capital,
where they were judged according to the law;
consequently, crime subsided.
When grain transportation for various garrisons was disrupted,
the troops lacked food.
Gài, acting on his authority, issued over forty-two thousand *shí* of rice, collected as redemptions for crimes from various prefectures, to provision the troops,
and then reported it to the court.
The Emperor was pleased
and instructed the Ministry of Revenue (*Hùbù*) not to charge Gài with unauthorized action.
Gài was strict in enforcing the law,
and wicked commoners feared him,
sending slanderous letters to the court.
In the second year of Xuāndé (1427),
the acting Censor-in-chief (*Xíngzài Dūyùshǐ*) impeached Gài and Chūn, alleging they had abused their authority wherever they went
and allowed their soldiers to disturb the people.
The Emperor did not question it
but secretly sent a Censor to investigate;
nothing was found.
Because of this, the Emperor trusted Gài even more.
In the seventh month of the following year, he was granted an imperial letter of commendation.
Gài also had self-confidence,
and listed all matters needing reform or implementation for imperial consideration.
At that time, officials from various ministries were frequently sent to Jiāngnán to manufacture paper and procure copper and iron.
Gài reported that the people were starving due to floods
and requested that these activities be stopped.
In the fifth year (1430), he returned to court
and only then resumed his original surname.
Not long after,
he was promoted to Right Censor-in-chief (*Yòudūyùshǐ*),
managing affairs in the Southern Censorate (*Nányuàn*).
When the acting Censor-in-chief Gù Zuǒ fell ill,
Gài was urgently summoned by post to take over his duties
and concurrently act as Minister of Justice.
In the tenth month of the ninth year (1434), while reviewing prisoners,
he worked from morning until late in the day,
without time to eat.
Suddenly, he collapsed from dizziness and died.
He was granted a memorial sacrifice
and a boat to transport his coffin home.
Gài was resolute by nature;
during his inspection of Jiāngnán,
his prestige and reputation were very high.
However, when he took charge of the Censorate,
his reputation gradually diminished compared to his early career.
Yè Chūn
was a native of Hǎiyán.
He began his career as a clerk,
and successively served as a director in the Ministry of Rites (*Lǐbù Lángzhōng*) and Salt Commissioner of Liǎnghuái,
then was transferred to Right Administration Vice Commissioner of Sichuan (*Sìchuān Yòucāncōng*),
and with Gài, served as Grand Coordinator for the prefectures of Jiāngnán and Zhejiang.
Afterward, he was again ordered, along with Embroidered Uniform Guard Commander (*Jǐnyī Zhǐhuī*) Rèn Qǐ, Censor Lài Yīng, and Eunuch Liú Níng, to conduct an inspection.
He successively visited Western Zhejiang three times,
managing affairs in his hometown;
no one criticized him for private gain.
When Gài was promoted to Censor-in-chief,
Chūn was promoted to Right Vice Minister of Justice (*Xíngbù Yòushìláng*) on the same day.
He died in office.
Chén Yì,
styled Yǒujiè,
was a native of Wúxiàn.
He became a *Jìnshì* in the tenth year of Yǒnglè (1412).
He was appointed Censor.
He was promoted to Guangxi Vice Surveillance Commissioner (*Húguǎng Fùshǐ*),
and served successively in Shandong and Zhejiang,
where he was well-regarded in all posts.
In the third month of the year when Emperor Yīngzōng ascended the throne (1435),
he was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-chief (*Yòufùdūyùshǐ*),
and, with Grand Coordinator-in-chief (*Dūdū Tóngzhī*) Zhèng Míng, was assigned to garrison Shaanxi.
Many starving people from the north migrated there for food.
Yì saw them when he passed through Dàmíng,
memorialized about their condition,
and an imperial edict exempted them from taxes and corvée.
In the first year of Zhèngtǒng (1436),
Yì stated that military campaigns in Shaanxi
burdened the people with provisions,
and requested that all levies of materials
be completely suspended and remitted.
An imperial edict approved it.
In the fifth month of the following year,
he was given an imperial edict of commendation for his meritorious service,
and was subsequently ordered to inspect the borders of Yánsuī and Níngxià.
Wherever he went, he made recommendations for military and civilian convenience,
abolishing or establishing many things.
When the six prefectures under his jurisdiction suffered famine,
he requested to open granaries for relief.
The Emperor, following the advice of his ministers,
ordered the implementation of famine relief policies.
Yì requested that these be extended to all border regions,
and consequently, border garrisons all had reserves.
In the spring of the sixth year (1441),
because Yì had toiled long in the outer regions,
he was ordered to alternate annually with Wáng Áo.
In the seventh year (1442),
Áo was transferred to Liáodōng,
and Yì was again sent to garrison the area.
When his term was up, he was to be replaced,
but because the people of Shaanxi requested he be retained,
an edict ordered him to remain in his old post.
At that time, granaries were overflowing;
some military garrisons had enough to last ten years,
and others enough for a hundred years.
Yì considered the spoilage and waste regrettable,
and requested that every spring and summer,
the grain be distributed to imperial troops as monthly rations,
instead of being commuted to paper money.
This was granted.
In the spring of the ninth year (1444), he was promoted to Right Censor-in-chief,
remaining in his garrison post as before.
When Qínzhōng suffered famine,
he requested a four-tenths reduction in land rent,
and that the remaining portion be collected in both rice and cloth.
At that time, the Oirat leader Yèxiān was gradually growing stronger,
sending envoys to bestow titles like *Píngzhāng* on the *Dūdū* Nán'gē and others of various Hǎndōng garrisons,
and also establishing a "Gānsù Provincial Administration" title.
Yì reported this
and requested strict preparations be made.
Soon after,
he was ordered, with the Earl of Jìngyuǎn, Wáng Jì, to inspect border affairs in Gānsù, Níngxià, and Yánsuī,
with discretionary power to handle matters.
Due to frequent disasters,
he submitted twenty-four articles on pacifying and comforting the military and civilians,
many of which were adopted.
Yì often feared that displaced people between Xiāng and Hàn might gather to cause unrest,
and requested that officials from Hénán, Húguǎng, and Shǎnxī provinces personally go to those areas to comfort and support them.
An imperial decree granted this,
but the officials concerned did not take it seriously.
Wáng Wén also successively and forcefully stated that the officials were negligent
and feared that this would lead to disaster.
By the Chénghuà era,
there was indeed the campaign of Xiàng Zhōng,
and people increasingly recalled Yì's words.
When Emperor Yīngzōng was captured in the north,
Emperor Jǐngdi was regent,
and Yì joined with other ministers to impeach Wáng Zhèn in court.
Consequently, Wáng Zhèn's nephew, Wáng Shān, was executed.
When Yèxiān was about to invade,
Yì was recommended by Yú Qiān
and sent out to pacify the imperial domain.
After peace was restored,
he was recalled
and promoted to Left Censor-in-chief (*Zuǒdūyùshǐ*).
In the fourth year of Tiānshùn,
the Ministry of Personnel recommended officials from across the realm whose governance and conduct were exceptionally distinguished.
Among them, only Wéi Zī was selected as an Inspector,
and he was promoted to Left Administration Commissioner.
The following year in spring,
he was made Right Vice Censor-in-Chief and appointed Grand Coordinator of the ten prefectures of Jiāngnán.
After Zhōu Chén established laws for the revenue and tribute of Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng,
subsequent officials often changed them haphazardly.
Zī first sought out Zhōu Chén's legacy,
deliberated on it, and implemented it,
which the people found convenient.
In the first year of Chénghuà,
Yìngtiān suffered a famine.
While relief loans were being distributed,
a large number of famine victims from north of the river came seeking food.
Zī requested that all granaries in the various counties be opened,
saving countless lives.
At that time, the common people were often in deep distress.
Official lands near the river, long abandoned and flooded,
were still subject to tax collection.
The prefectures of Sūzhōu, Sōngjiāng, Hángzhōu, and Jiāxīng had wealthy households arbitrarily assigned to supplement taxes.
The verandas and rooms in Nánjīng, though dilapidated,
were still subject to paper currency levies.
Farmers in Shàngyuán and Jiāngníng were forced to catch shad for the river fishery office's netting households.
The various bureaus for the collection of commercial taxes and duties in Yìngtiān levied additional, unofficial taxes.
Households in Jiāngyīn and other counties had to pay taxes for barren land.
The official oxen in Liùhé and Jiāngpǔ were annually levied for calves.
Zī memorialized to abolish all these.
He was summoned and appointed Minister of Justice in Nánjīng,
and Sòng Jié replaced him.
In the fourth year, he retired due to illness
and died on the way.
Zī was honest and cautious,
and meticulously managed affairs.
However, he was overly strict in enforcing the law,
and at the time, people criticized him for his harshness.
Jié was a kind and respectable person.
He served for two years,
then was dismissed,
and Xíng Yòu replaced him.
Yòu,
a native of Wénchāng.
He passed the imperial examination in the thirteenth year of Zhèngtǒng.
He was appointed Censor
and dispatched to inspect Fújiàn.
Ten commoners were falsely accused of being bandits,
and cried out their innocence when about to be punished.
Yòu delayed their sentencing,
and indeed found the real bandits.
During the Tiānshùn era,
he was appointed Prefect of Táizhōu,
where he achieved administrative success,
but was implicated in a case and demoted to Assistant Magistrate of Jìnjiāng.
Emperor Xiànzōng restored him to his post
and reassigned him as Prefect of Sūzhōu.
When corrupt individuals monopolized the collection of autumn taxes,
he brought them to justice,
recovering 10,000 strings of stolen money,
which he used to build dikes on the Shāhé River
and pave official roads.
During a great flood,
the people suffered from famine.
Without waiting for a memorial, he immediately released 200,000 *hú* of rice for relief.
Yòu was always honest and upright;
when governing Sūzhōu,
he was strict but not harsh.
Jié recommended him to the court,
and an imperial edict added to his title Left Administration Vice Commissioner of Zhèjiāng, while he continued to manage prefectural affairs,
and he was bestowed with an imperial letter.
After serving for half a year,
he was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief and replaced Jié as Grand Coordinator.
He opened the Dānyáng River
and built the Bēnnníu sluice gate,
saving unnecessary expenses for canal transport,
which the people found convenient.
Soon after, he also managed the salt administration of the two Zhè regions,
investigating subordinate officials
and memorializing to dismiss over 170 incompetent individuals.
After several years,
he resigned due to illness.
Lǐ Kǎn,
courtesy name Xīzhèng,
was a native of Dōng'ān.
He passed the imperial examination in the seventh year of Zhèngtǒng.
He was appointed Investigating Censor of the Ministry of Revenue.
When Emperor Jǐngzōng served as regent,
he presented three proposals: selecting military talents, recruiting brave commoners, and using chariots in battle.
When Yěxiān approached the capital,
some deliberated burning the horse fodder outside the city.
Kǎn argued that the enemy was light and agile,
and would not persist for long,
pleading not to burn it,
to avoid repeated levies and burdens on the people.
All were granted.
At that time, his parents were in Róngchéng.
Kǎn wept day and night,
begged for leave,
and bravely went to welcome them.
In early Jǐngtài,
there was a discussion about posthumously honoring the descendants of officials who died attending the emperor.
Kǎn then stated that those who fled to save their lives
should be severely reprimanded to strengthen official integrity.
When the retired emperor was about to return,
he and fellow official Liú Fú and others argued that the rites should be generous.
This displeased the emperor,
and he was reprimanded.
Minister Hú Yìng interceded for him,
and the matter was dropped.
He was promoted again to Chief Investigating Censor.
When military campaigns began,
the salaries and stipends of teachers and scholars in schools across the realm were reduced.
Kǎn memorialized to restore them.
Minister of Revenue Jīn Lián collected taxes in violation of an imperial edict;
Kǎn impeached Lián,
and he was handed over to officials for punishment.
Shí Hēng's nephew Biāo encroached upon people's property;
Kǎn requested that he be severely punished,
and also strictly forbade imperial relatives, meritorious officials, and eunuchs from seizing property from commoners,
stating that officials who concealed such acts would be equally guilty.
The emperor pardoned Hēng and Biāo,
but accepted the rest of his request.
At that time, among the Investigating Censors who dared to speak out,
Lín Cōng was considered foremost,
and Kǎn also defied authority with a reputation for integrity.
When the court discussed replacing the heir apparent,
all the great ministers merely assented.
Kǎn wept, saying the Crown Prince had no moral failings.
Cōng and Censor Zhū Yīng also argued against it,
and public opinion at the time praised their bravery.
He was promoted to Assistant Administrator of the Hanlin Academy.
In the first year of Tiānshùn, he was transferred to Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices
and advanced to Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud.
The following year, the position of Grand Coordinator of Shānxī was re-established,
and Kǎn was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief to fill it.
He memorialized, saying:
“The lands north of the frontier
are no different from desolate wilderness.
Only those born and raised there
can live there peacefully and contend with the enemy.
Now, southerners stationed on the northwestern frontier
are afraid of the wind and cold,
and tremble at the mention of invaders.
Conversely, northerners stationed in the south
also cannot endure the heat
and often desert.
It would be appropriate to order soldiers drafted from the north and south
to return to their native lands to fill their ranks.
This would benefit everyone,
and border defenses could be improved.”
At the time, his proposal was not adopted.
He memorialized to expose the crimes of inspecting censor Lǐ Jié,
and Jié also denounced Kǎn.
Jié's crimes were verified by investigation,
and he was dismissed from office.
Kǎn had no charges of corruption
and was pardoned.
In the sixth year, he investigated subordinate officials
and memorialized to dismiss 160 individuals, including Administration Commissioners Wáng Yǔn and Lǐ Zhèngfāng.
He then said:
“Among these officials, if any are of my age and unfit for duty,
I have dismissed them all,
and I, too, should be dismissed.”
An imperial edict denied his request.
Kǎn was upright and firm by nature,
forcefully rectifying discipline and morals,
causing corrupt officials to disappear.
In the winter of that year, he returned home for his mother's mourning.
Soldiers and commoners wept and surrounded him,
preventing him from proceeding.
After the mourning period,
he never took office again,
staying at home for over ten years until his death.
Kǎn was filial to his parents,
loved learning, and was content in poverty;
upon his death, he could barely be interred.
In the early Hóngzhì era,
Guójìxué student Jiāng Jì and others stated that
the former Libationer Hú Yǎn,
and Censors-in-Chief Gāo Míng and Lǐ Kǎn, whose scholarship, conduct, and achievements
were widely known,
should all be granted posthumous titles.
The request was shelved and not implemented.
Kǎn had two sons: Déhuī,
Prefect of Yánzhōu;
and Dérén,
Salt Commissioner of Hédōng.
Léi Fù,
courtesy name Jǐngyáng,
was a native of Níngyuǎn, Húguǎng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the early Zhèngtǒng era.
He was appointed as a *xíngrén*,
and successively served as Vice Commissioner of Guǎngxī.
When the commoner Hú Zhàochéng of Téngxiàn, with the help of the Yao people, trapped the county magistrate,
Fù and Assistant General Fàn Xìn attacked and beheaded him.
In the early Chénghuà era, he was jointly recommended by high officials
and promoted to Right Administration Commissioner of Shāndōng.
In the seventh year, he was summoned to be appointed Right Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites.
Soon after, he was reappointed Right Vice Censor-in-Chief
and Grand Coordinator of Shānxī.
Following Lǐ Kǎn,
he was upright, diligent, and upheld the law,
winning the hearts of both soldiers and commoners.
He defeated the bandit Hóngshā Yān,
and defeated him again at Yān Sì Gōu and Shírén Cūn,
receiving an imperial edict of commendation and reward.
At that time, Shānxī suffered a great famine,
but the court deliberated that since Shǎnxī was at war,
it ordered the advance collection of fodder and provisions
to be transported to Yúlín.
Fù submitted a memorial saying:
"From Shānxī to Yúlín,
the roads are dangerous and impassable.
When people carry silver to exchange,
prices soar,
and they are forced to borrow,
many going bankrupt to repay their debts.
Now, with the untimely rain and snow,
starving people are falling ill and wandering,
suffering untold miseries.
Moreover, the silk, medicine, and fruit items to be delivered
also number no less than tens of thousands.
I beg that, following the example of Shāndōng, these be remitted,
and that funds from the treasury be issued for relief."
The emperor approved.
When the 30,000 gold pieces issued were insufficient,
he requested to sell 400,000 salt certificates,
and also allowed commoners to submit grain in exchange for minor official posts.
All were granted.
He died in office in the summer of the tenth year.
Lǐ Gāng,
courtesy name Tíngzhāng,
was a native of Chángqīng.
As a child, he accompanied his father to the capital.
He fell from a carriage,
and the carriage ran over his body,
yet he was unharmed.
People all regarded this as extraordinary.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the first year of Tiānshùn
and was appointed Censor.
He successively inspected the Southern Capital Region and Zhèjiāng,
impeaching and removing over 400 corrupt officials in Zhèjiāng,
and was at the time known as
"Iron Censor."
He was commissioned to compile a register of local troops in Shǎnxī and Yánsuí.
Upon his return,
he was promoted to Junior Supervisor of the Court of the Imperial Stud,
inspecting the horse administration in the capital region,
and refusing all gifts from officials.
While inspecting Jìzhōu,
he encountered bandits who asked his attendants:
"Is that His Excellency Lǐ of the Imperial Stud?
Where could he have gold?"
They left without opening his trunk.
In the thirteenth year of Chénghuà, he was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief.
He was transferred to Left Vice Censor-in-Chief,
and sent out to oversee grain transport,
working with the Earl of Píngjiāng, Chén Ruì.
He died the following year.
Ruì saw only worn clothes in his trunk
and, wiping away tears, said:
"He was a true gentleman."
He arranged for his coffin and burial,
and reported his integrity to the court.
The emperor specially ordered a memorial sacrifice and burial,
which was not the usual custom.
Gāng's integrity and firmness resembled Lǐ Kǎn,
and he was highly esteemed at the time.
Yuán Jié,
courtesy name Zǐyīng,
was a native of Yángchéng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the tenth year of Zhèngtǒng.
Two years later,
he was appointed Censor of Nánjīng,
soon after transferred to the northern capital.
He toured Jiāngxī as inspecting censor,
capturing and executing numerous notorious bandits,
and criminal activities ceased.
He then inspected the prefectures of Shùntiān.
After a great flood,
officials responsible for pasturing imperial horses lacked fodder,
and many horses died.
Officials were held accountable for compensation.
Jié requested their exemption,
and proposed selling salt certificates for rice to relieve the famine.
His memorial was submitted,
but blocked by the ministry.
Emperor Jǐngdì ultimately followed Jié's proposal.
He was exceptionally promoted to Surveillance Commissioner of Jiāngxī.
He exposed the debauchery of Prince Níng, Zhū Diànpéi,
and stripped his guard unit.
His effective governance was reported,
and he was granted an imperial edict of commendation,
then transferred to Left Administration Commissioner of Shāndōng.
In the second year of Chénghuà, he was appointed Right Vice Censor-in-Chief
and Grand Coordinator of that region.
In times of famine, he provided relief,
and no commoners were displaced.
He was summoned to serve as Left Vice Minister of the Ministry of Revenue.
At that time, the Yellow River frequently shifted and burst its banks,
what was submerged here became silted there.
Soldiers and commoners cultivated the silted land,
but unscrupulous individuals designated it as gardens, fields, or屯地,
and offered it to princely estates for rewards,
which the estates then appropriated.
Jié requested that those who offered such land be exiled,
and those who accepted it also be punished.
This was approved.
When bandits arose in Jiāngxī,
because Jié had governed the area twice and gained the trust of the people,
an imperial edict ordered him to go and pacify it.
He captured and executed over 600 people,
and the rest dispersed.
He was reappointed Left Vice Censor-in-Chief
and returned to assist in court affairs.
The hundreds of thousands of displaced people in Jīng and Xiāng were a source of concern for the court.
Chancellor of the Imperial Academy Zhōu Hóngmó had previously written a "Treatise on Displaced People,"
suggesting that new prefectures and counties be established,
allowing the displaced to register as commoners,
which would increase the population of Xiāng and Dèng,
and prevent problems for centuries.
Censor-in-Chief Lǐ Bīn reported this to the emperor.
The emperor approved.
In the twelfth year,
Jié was thus ordered to go and manage the region.
He traveled throughout the mountains and valleys,
proclaiming the benevolence of the imperial court,
and the displaced people eagerly wished to register.
Thereupon, he convened officials from Húguǎng, Hénán, and Shǎnxī—Grand Coordinators and Surveillance Commissioners—to register them,
obtaining over 113,000 households
and over 438,000 individuals.
Those who initially arrived without property or who were usually stubborn
were sent back to their hometowns,
while those who registered were granted light fixed land taxes.
The people were greatly pleased.
He then surveyed the terrain,
and considering that Yúnxiàn, under the jurisdiction of Xiāngyáng,
was situated among Zhú, Fáng, Shàngjīn, Shāng, and Luò counties,
with roads leading in all directions,
over 500 *lǐ* from Xiāngyáng,
and deep mountains and forests,
where generals and officials rarely reached,
and sudden banditry
was difficult for the prefecture to control from afar,
he expanded its city
and established Yúnyáng Prefecture,
with Yúnxiàn attached to it.
Furthermore, he established the Húguǎng Branch Regional Military Commission,
increased troops, and set up garrisons.
He then divided Zhúshān to create Zhúxī,
divided Yún to create Yúnxī,
and divided Xúnyáng from Hànzhōng to create Báihé,
with Zhúshān, Shàngjīn, and Fáng all subordinated to the new prefecture.
He also added Shānyáng to Xī'ān,
Nánzhào and Tóngbǎi to Nányáng,
and Yīyáng to Rǔzhōu,
each belonging to its old prefecture.
Once the system was established,
he recommended Wú Yuǎn, the Magistrate of Dèngzhōu, as the Prefect of Yúnyáng,
and for all other counties, excellent officials from neighboring areas were selected.
The displaced people found their homes,
and the four borders were pacified.
When he was about to return,
because the region bordered Húguǎng, Hénán, and Shǎnxī,
and affairs lacked overall coordination,
he recommended Censor Wú Dàohóng to take his place.
An imperial edict immediately promoted Dàohóng to Junior Minister of the Grand Court of Revision,
to oversee the governance of the six prefectures of Yúnyáng, Xiāngyáng, Jīngzhōu, Nányáng, Xī'ān, and Hànzhōng.
The establishment of a Grand Coordinator for Yúnyáng
began from this point.
Jié was promoted to Censor-in-Chief for his achievements.
Jié數敭歷於外，
Once he resided in the inner palace,
he did not wish to leave.
The appointments in Jīng and Xiāng
were not to his liking.
When the tasks were completed,
he urgently requested to return to court.
It happened that the position of Minister of War in Nánjīng was vacant,
and Jíé was appointed to it.
Jíé memorialized to decline.
It was not permitted.
He then died in Nányáng,
at the age of sixty-one.
The people of Yún and Xiāng built a shrine for him,
and an imperial edict posthumously granted him the title of Tàizǐ Tàibǎo,
and enrolled his son, Zōngmǐn, as a Guózǐshēng.
Péng Yì,
courtesy name Jǐngyí,
was from Dōngguǎn.
During the Zhèngtǒng reign,
he was appointed Sīwù of the Ministry of Works after passing the provincial examination.
He once debated matters with the minister,
without showing any favoritism.
When Emperor Jǐng ascended the throne,
he was recommended and promoted to Yùshǐ.
He followed Minister Shí Pú to block the breach in the Shāwān River,
and was promoted two ranks.
The river breached again,
and he went again to block it.
In the fifth year of Jǐngtài,
for accompanying Grand Secretary Wáng Wén on an inspection tour of Jiāng and Huái,
and capturing the Suzhou bandits,
he was promoted to Dàlǐ Sìchéng.
In the second month of the following year, he was promoted to Yòu Qiāndū Yùshǐ,
and appointed as the commander-in-chief of the Zǐjīng and Dàomǎ Passes.
He impeached commander Hú Xǐ for accepting bribes and condoning military misconduct.
At the beginning of the Tiānshùn reign,
the office of Xúnfǔ was abolished.
There were some at court who were displeased with Yì,
so he was demoted to Zhīfǔ of Shàoxīng.
When there was a famine,
he would immediately open granaries and provide relief loans.
Officials reported that they should wait for an imperial order,
but Yì said:
"The people are in urgent need;
how can we adhere to old precedents?"
He built the Báimǎ Gate to block the sea tides.
He served for nine years,
and his governance was greatly beneficial.
He was exceptionally promoted to Zuǒ Bùzhèngshǐ of Shāndōng,
and then entered court as Zuǒ Shìláng of the Ministry of Works.
In the fourth year of Chénghuà,
Zhāng Qí, the Xúnfǔ of Liáodōng, incurred offense,
and the Ministry of Personnel nominated a replacement.
The Emperor said:
"Since Wáng Áo,
Liáodōng has frequently changed Xúnfǔ,
and many have been unsatisfactory.
We should seek one from among the grand ministers."
Thus, Yì was appointed Yòu Fùdū Yùshǐ and sent there.
The eunuchs guarding the region extorted various subordinate garrisons.
Yì issued an order that
any official document not reviewed and approved by the Xúnfǔ
should not be acted upon by the relevant offices,
and their tyrannical influence was curbed.
In the winter of the tenth year,
the Ministry of Revenue ordered the local authorities to open the Hēishān gold mine.
Yì memorialized that in the Yǒnglè reign, eunuchs Wáng Yàn and others had opened this mountain,
supervising six thousand laborers,
but only obtained eight liǎng of gold in three months,
and requested its cessation.
It was consequently stopped.
Yì was fond of ancient studies and widely learned,
knowledgeable in law, calendrics, astrology, water conservancy, and military tactics.
In his daily life, he was humble, reserved, and silent,
but resolute and decisive when facing matters.
He guarded Liáo for eight years,
and military discipline was rigorous.
Before he was old,
he memorialized four times to resign,
and died at home after more than forty years.
Móu Fèng,
a Bā man.
He obtained his Jìnshì degree at the beginning of the Jǐngtài reign.
He was appointed Yùshǐ,
and patrolled Yúnnán.
When Nánníng Bó Máo Shèng was garrisoned at Jīnchǐ,
Fèng listed his transgressions and laxities,
which alarmed all the generals and officials.
In the first year of Tiānshùn, he was sent out as Qiānshì of Fújiàn.
At the beginning of the Chénghuà reign,
he was promoted to Fùshǐ.
After a long time,
he was transferred to Ànchásǐ of Jiāngxī,
where his governance was strict and severe,
and then entered court as Tàipú Qīng.
In the eighth year, he was appointed Zuǒ Qiāndū Yùshǐ and Xúnfǔ of Shāndōng.
That year, there was a bad harvest,
and he requested to open the Jǐnán granary and sell grain at reduced prices,
and ordered the Línqīng customs to collect rice and wheat for relief.
All these requests were granted.
At that time, the famine was severe;
although relief was provided,
the number of famine victims was large,
and more and more people were migrating.
Fèng requested an imperial edict for neighboring Xúnfǔ and Ànchá officials to pacify and settle the people wherever they were,
and to provide resources for them to resume their livelihoods after the autumn harvest.
He also requested to open a market for one million yǐn of salt from Huái and Zhè,
and to completely remit overdue taxes from prefectures and counties.
An imperial edict was issued in accordance with his requests,
and he was further ordered to transfer one hundred thousand shí of grain from the Línqīng granary for relief.
By July,
Fèng again reported that both public and private resources were exhausted,
and there was no strategy to relieve the famine.
He requested to open a system for accepting grain contributions,
allowing junior officials to be selected for positions,
and wealthy commoners to be granted honorary official titles,
and also to retain grain from the Grand Canal for relief.
In October, he again stated:
"Currently, those who relieve the famine only save the hungry,
but do not consider their cold.
Even if they get food,
they will still inevitably freeze to death.
I request to lend cloth and cotton to the poor."
The Emperor approved all these requests.
Fèng also issued an order to release over one hundred thousand shí of grain from the Dōngchāng and Jìníng granaries as monthly rations for soldiers,
and to use the silver stored in Dézhōu and Línqīng to exchange for rice for relief,
and then submitted a memorial admitting his unauthorized actions.
The Emperor specifically pardoned him.
Subsequently,
Fèng again memorialized to exempt the silver payment in lieu of firewood,
to transfer grain from Hénán to the border to relieve Shāndōng,
and to provide separate silver for border provisions,
and to use the two hundred thousand shí of grain from Shāndōng's imperial tribute
for local needs.
In the tenth year, there was another famine,
and he requested to open granaries for loans.
He served as Xúnfǔ of Shāndōng for five years,
devoting himself to famine relief policies,
saving countless famine victims.
He was transferred as Yòu Fùdū Yùshǐ to Xúnfǔ Sū and Sōng.
Fèng's nature was strict.
Because his jurisdiction had many powerful families,
he intentionally sought to suppress them.
Thus, he prohibited the collection of private rents,
and encouraged wealthy families to donate grain for relief, amounting to thousands of units,
leading to widespread resentment and slander.
When the eunuch Wāng Zhí had business in Nánjīng,
someone slandered Fèng.
Zhí returned,
but had not yet acted.
Initially, when Fèng was in Shāndōng,
he and Bùzhèng Chén Yuè were at odds and would not yield to each other.
Later, Yuè casually spoke ill of Fèng,
and Zhí believed him.
In the fourteenth year,
when Fèng came to the capital to discuss matters,
Zhí requested to arrest Fèng and imprison him in the imperial prison.
Earlier,
his close friend, scholar Jiāng Cháozōng, had returned to court after his mourning period.
Fèng went to Jiǔjiāng to greet him,
and they traveled downstream together by boat.
Wherever they went,
the local officials provided lavish entertainment.
Zhí therefore accused Cháozōng of lobbying,
and both were imprisoned.
The charges implicated more than ten people, including Qiānshì Wú Xī,
all of whom were arrested.
After half a year in prison,
they were banished to Húguǎng.
When Fèng was in Jiāngxī,
he participated in the conviction of Xǔ Cōng,
and many people criticized him for being overly strict in interpreting the law.
When he was subsequently afflicted with disaster,
everyone knew he was falsely accused by Zhí,
but no one cleared his name.
More than a year later,
he died at the place of exile.
Xià Xún,
courtesy name Zōngchéng,
was from Tiāntái.
He obtained his Jìnshì degree in the second year of Jǐngtài.
He was appointed Yùshǐ.
At the beginning of the Tiānshùn reign,
he was appointed Xúnfǔ of Fújiàn,
and then 清軍 of Jiāngxī,
where he exposed the tyrannical behavior of the garrison eunuch Yè Dá,
and Dá was forced to restrain his power.
By recommendation, he was exceptionally promoted to Ànchásǐ of Guǎngdōng.
At that time, the military campaigns had lasted for years,
and the people were conscripted to guard the cities.
When Xún arrived, he dismissed all of them.
In the early years of the Chénghuà reign,
he reported:
"The Yáo and Zhòng are not pacified,
and military campaigns are without success.
This is because officials in charge of pacification act improperly,
allowing bandits to lure good citizens into their ranks.
A few hundred hardened brigands
coerce tens of thousands of followers.
When advancing, they drive them to the front;
when retreating, they kill them to vent their anger.
Harm always befalls the people,
while benefit always accrues to the bandits.
Moreover, if military campaigns do not cease,
levies and collections will increase daily.
With easily swayed hearts,
to demand endless military expenses,
I fear that before external threats are removed,
internal strife will arise first.
I request that upright supervising censors, prefects, and magistrates be carefully selected
to pacify the remaining people.
Those who were coerced will naturally come to submit upon hearing this."
The Emperor deeply accepted his words.
Soon after, he was promoted to Provincial Administration Commissioner
and transferred to Jiāngxī.
In the eighth year, he was appointed Vice Censor-in-Chief on the Right to patrol and pacify Sìchuān.
The Miáo and Liáo frequently rebelled at that time.
Xún established a mutual notification and arrest method,
and the bandits were suppressed by it.
Over ten thousand Miáo in Gǔzhōu
had long resided in fallow land;
the contemporary opinion was to expel them,
but Xún argued that this was not a good plan.
Yáo Yù, the Assistant Regional Commander of Sōngpán, requested an increase of three thousand garrison troops,
but Xún again strongly argued against it.
Both proposals were shelved.
Afterward,
he reported that many of the commanders and officers under his jurisdiction had violated the law,
and that memorializing requests often took too long,
leading to their escape.
He requested to apprehend and detain them first,
and then report it to the throne.
The Emperor approved.
Xún was resolute and upright,
skilled in listening and judging,
so the people wherever he served were not wronged.
During his two years in Shǔ,
the local people and non-Han tribes feared and submitted to him.
However, he disliked complex affairs
and often clashed with his contemporaries.
His son, Huò, presented a poem advising him to retire,
and Xún gladly accepted it.
Before he was fifty,
he sought to retire.
After submitting four memorials,
his request was granted.
Upon returning,
he closed his door, cared for his parents,
and did not receive guests.
Five more years later, he passed away.
Huò became a Presented Scholar.
In the fourth year of Hóngzhì, he went to the capital for an appointment selection,
and submitted a memorial requesting the reinstatement of officials like Lǐ Wénxiáng and Zōu Zhì,
and the dismissal of Grand Secretary Liú Jí.
This displeased the Emperor,
and he was imprisoned,
but later released.
After a long time,
he was appointed Judge of the Court of Judicial Review in Nánjīng.
He memorialized on the pros and cons of taxation, corvée, horse administration, and salt taxes,
as well as the corruption of imperial relatives and powerful families.
There was no response.
Huò had always had little interest in officialdom.
He served as an official for barely over a year,
and, thinking of his aged mother,
requested to return home to care for her,
and thus he returned.
He lived at home for over thirty years,
and never again went out to serve.
Gāo Míng,
courtesy name Shàngdá,
was from Guìxī.
As a child, he was known for his filial piety to his mother.
He passed the Presented Scholar examination in the second year of Jǐngtài,
and was appointed Censor.
Upon hearing that dragon boats were being built in the Inner Park,
he strongly remonstrated.
When a commandant was framed by a high official
and sentenced to death,
he argued for his release.
The people of Xúzhōu sued an official at court.
At that time, the rule was
that those who bypassed proper channels to sue were exiled to the frontier.
Míng explicitly stated:
"Exile to the frontier
is to prevent malicious lawsuits.
Now, the lawsuit is not malicious,
so the law only mandates caning."
When there was a person who spread seditious rumors,
the eager official falsely accused him of rebellion.
Míng investigated and found no evidence of rebellion,
and only convicted him under the law for spreading seditious rumors.
All were approved.
While inspecting Hénán,
he dismissed sixty subordinate officials.
He then inspected Jīfǔ again
and was put in charge of all provincial memorials.
In the early Tiānshùn reign,
Minister Chén Rǔyán committed a crime,
and Míng, along with other censors, impeached him,
sending him to prison.
In the fourth year,
Censor Zhào Míng and others impeached all officials who came to court for audience,
angering the Emperor,
who demanded to know the principal author of the draft memorial.
Everyone was greatly terrified,
but Míng alone stepped forward to take responsibility.
Censor-in-Chief Kòu Shēn said:
"Memorials for many years
have all come from Míng's hand;
please do not punish him for a minor matter."
The Emperor's anger subsided,
and he even praised Míng's ability.
After Shí Hēng was executed,
all his servants and pages were arrested.
Míng argued against this,
and a hundred people were released.
He was promoted to Assistant Minister of the Grand Court of Judicial Review.
When Emperor Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
he was appointed Assistant Censor-in-Chief on the Right of Nánjīng.
Because of continuous heavy spring and summer rains in the auxiliary capital,
he requested to rectify human affairs to influence Heaven's will.
At that time, over ten thousand horses were accepted into the stables;
Míng requested to differentiate them.
He recommended Department Directors Sūn Qióng, Chén Hóngjiàn, Méi Lún, and Hé Yí,
and Secretary Sòng Yīng,
all of whom were upright, honest, and incorruptible,
content with their lot,
and worthy of prominent promotion to set an example for those in high positions.
The memorial was sent to the relevant departments.
In the third year of Chénghuà,
salt bandits rose in Yángzhōu,
and the garrison troops suffered a defeat.
An imperial edict ordered Míng to suppress them.
He built large ships,
named "Chóutíng,"
and traveled along the Jiāng River to supervise the battle,
and established patrol forts along the river for observation.
The bandits had nowhere to hide their traces,
and he subsequently pacified them.
When eunuchs were selling private salt,
he confiscated it according to the law,
and salt administration was greatly reformed.
Consequently, he submitted a memorial detailing over ten points of benefit and harm,
many of which were adopted.
He was then restored to his original post
but requested to return home to care for his aged parents until their death.
In the fourteenth year,
a bandit uprising occurred in Shàngháng.
An imperial edict recalled him to serve as Circuit Inspector of Fújiàn,
leading troops to suppress them.
He captured and executed the ringleaders,
while the rest were given reduced sentences and exiled to the frontier.
As Shàngháng bordered Jiāngxī and Guǎngdōng,
where bandits easily gathered,
he requested to establish Yǒngdìng County by splitting the existing territory.
He then, citing illness, returned home directly.
After a long time,
he passed away.
Yáng Jìzōng,
courtesy name Chéngfāng,
was from Yángchéng.
He passed the Presented Scholar examination in the early Tiānshùn reign.
He was appointed Secretary in the Ministry of Justice.
Many prisoners were dying of plague,
so he regulated their food and drink,
and ordered them to comb their hair and bathe every three days,
saving many lives.
He was also good at discerning difficult cases.
When a bandit was caught in Héjiān,
villagers Zhāng Wén and Guō Lǐ were dispatched to escort him to the capital,
but the bandit escaped.
Wén said to Lǐ:
"We two will both surely die.
Your mother is old,
and you have few siblings.
Let me substitute for the bandit,
so that your mother and child may be spared."
Lǐ wept and thanked him,
agreeing to this.
Wén went to the Ministry in shackles,
but Jìzōng discerned that he was not the bandit
and ultimately acquitted him.
Shǎnxī qiānshì Mǎ Yīng (馬英) incited the barbarians of Sùzhōu (肅州) to revolt,
killing an imperial censor and the Regional Military Commissioner.
Zhāng (彰) impeached Yīng (英),
who was condemned to the highest punishment.
He also impeached Imperial Censor Chén Mèngxù (陳孟旭) for accepting bribes and perverting the law,
Wénxiàn (文獻) for embezzling silver tax,
and Jīnwú (金吾) Commander Lǐ Yán (李嚴) for driving out his mother and failing to support her.
All were sentenced to death.
The others he impeached were numerous.
In the eleventh year, he accompanied the emperor on a northern tour.
Zhāng (彰) had a mother over eighty years old,
so he was ordered to return home and visit her,
and his mother was granted court robes, gold, and silk.
The emperor instructed him, saying:
"A gentleman holding office does not forget his parents;
at home, he does not forget his sovereign.
Wherever you pass,
whether the people are at peace or not,
whether officials are worthy or unworthy,
report all to me."
When Zhāng (彰) returned,
his reports pleased the emperor.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief.
In the nineteenth year,
the emperor dispatched twenty-six court officials to tour and pacify the empire,
and Zhāng (彰), along with Grand Secretary Wáng Lì (王勵), went to Hénán (河南).
Throughout the Míng (明) dynasty,
Zhāng (彰) and Yè Chūn (葉春) were the only high officials who were allowed to pacify their hometowns.
There was a flood disaster in Hénán (河南),
and many people were displaced;
the senior officials did not offer relief.
Zhāng (彰) memorialized to dismiss over a hundred greedy and harsh officials,
abolished more than ten non-urgent levies,
recalled the displaced people,
and distributed grain from granaries for relief and loans,
saving many lives.
Upon returning to court,
he was ordered to supervise grain transport for the northern expedition.
Upon Rénzōng's (仁宗) accession,
the river overflowed at Kāifēng (開封),
and Zhāng (彰), along with Regional Military Commissioner Lǐ Xìn (李信), was ordered to go and provide relief.
In the fifth month of Xuāndé (宣德) first year, Zhāng (彰) was ordered to travel from Liángxiāng (良鄉) to Nánjīng (南京) to pacify the military and civilian population.
Soon after, because his reports were mostly about ordinary matters,
an imperial edict severely rebuked him,
ordering him to report in detail the advantages and disadvantages.
The emperor again instructed his attending ministers, saying:
"The two capitals are thousands of *lǐ* apart,
and the coming and going of messengers causes disturbance.
Should there be floods or droughts,
and the common people lose their homes,
imperial envoys returning or imperial censors on tour all fail to report it.
Therefore, I sent Zhāng (彰) to investigate.
Now his memorials are mostly minor matters.
If a high official is like this,
what more can I expect?
You, my ministers, should understand my intentions.
Sovereign and minister are one body,
so do not have any doubts."
Soon after, he was recalled
and ordered, along with Grand Commissioner Shān Yún (山雲), to inspect the passes from Shānhǎi (山海) to Jūyōng (居庸).
He returned after more than two months,
and memorialized about soldiers who had left their posts without permission.
The emperor ordered them arrested and punished.
Subsequently, the Ministry of War was ordered to dispatch imperial censors and grand secretaries every three months to inspect.
In the fourth month of the following year, he died in office.
Zhāng (彰) was stern and self-controlled,
refusing all solicitations;
however, he was excessively harsh in applying the law.
His mother repeatedly spoke about it,
but he could not change.
At that time, Liú Guān (劉觀) was the Left Censor-in-Chief.
People said that Zhāng (彰) was public-spirited but unmerciful,
while Guān (觀) was private but not harsh.
Wèi Yuán (魏源),
courtesy name Wényuān (文淵),
was from Jiànchāng (建昌) County.
In the fourth year of Yǒnglè (永樂), he became a *jìnshì*.
He was appointed Investigating Censor.
He vindicated Huáng Zǐwēi (黃子威), the Prefect of Sōngjiāng (松江), who had been falsely accused,
and memorialized to reduce the fishing tax along the coast of Zhèdōng (浙東).
He served as Inspecting Censor for Shǎnxī (陝西).
There was a severe plague in Xī'ān (西安),
and he cured many people.
He memorialized, saying:
"The granaries in the various prefectures have accumulated over nineteen million *shí* of grain,
enough to last ten years.
Now the people are suffering from plague, hindering agriculture.
I request permission to pay half of the two taxes in paper currency."
This was granted.
Bandits in Liángzhōu (涼州) were about to rebel.
He urgently requested their suppression,
and the unrest was quelled.
He suffered two periods of mourning,
and was reinstated both times.
In the first year of Hóngxī (洪熙), he was appointed Vice Surveillance Commissioner of Zhèjiāng (浙江).
In the third year of Xuāndé (宣ā德), he was summoned to act as Right Vice Minister of Punishments.
In the fifth year,
Hénán (河南) suffered a drought and famine,
and many people became displaced.
The emperor, considering Yuán (源) incorruptible and capable,
appointed him Left Administration Commissioner,
ordering him to proceed to his post by post-horse.
At that time, Vice Minister Xǔ Kuò (許廓) had gone to pacify and assist,
and the court council also reinstated Administration Commissioner Lǐ Chāngqí (李昌祺), who was in mourning, to his original post.
Yuán (源), along with Kuò (廓) and Chāngqí (昌祺), opened the granaries,
remitted overdue taxes and miscellaneous levies,
and the displaced people gradually returned.
Rain also soon fell,
and there was a great harvest.
After three years,
he was recalled and
appointed Left Vice Minister of Punishments.
The following year,
Xià Jiǔxù (夏九旭) and others from Yǒngfēng (永豐) rebelled, occupying Dàpán (大盤) Mountain.
The emperor, knowing Yuán (源) was from Jiāngxī (江西),
ordered him to pacify them,
with Grand Commissioner Rèn Lǐ (任禮) leading troops following him.
Before they arrived,
government troops captured Jiǔxù (九旭),
so the two were ordered to procure timber in Sìchuān (四川),
and also to oversee border affairs.
Upon Yīngzōng's (英宗) accession,
he was promoted to Minister.
In the fifth month of Zhèngtǒng (正統) second year, he was ordered to reorganize the borders of Dàtóng (大同) and Xuānfǔ (宣府),
with permission to act at his discretion.
Yuán (源) sent Assistant Commissioner Lǐ Qiān (李謙) to guard Dúshí (獨石),
with Yáng Hóng (楊洪) assisting him,
and impeached Dù Héng (杜衡), Commander of Wànquán (萬全) Guard, for being stationed in Guǎngxī (廣西).
The following year, he memorialized that Tán Guǎng (譚廣), the Regional Commander of Dàtóng (大同), was old,
so the emperor appointed Huáng Zhēn (黃真) and Yáng Hóng (楊洪) as Left and Right Assistant Commanders to assist in guarding,
and all the generals became reverent.
He inspected the strategic points of Tiānchéng (天城) and Shuòzhōu (朔州),
ordering generals and officials to defend their respective areas.
He established the Wēiyuǎn (威遠) Guard,
reinforced and repaired the walls of Kāipíng (開平) and Lóngmén (龍門) cities,
and from Dúshí (獨石) to Xuānfǔ (宣府),
increased the number of beacon towers.
He remitted the rent for garrison troops for one year,
stored firearms for border defense,
and gathered all those who had evaded service by relying on powerful nobles back into military ranks.
Soon after, due to the long-standing laxity of military affairs in Xuān (宣) and Dà (大),
he requested the recall of Inspecting Censor-in-Chief Lú Ruì (盧睿),
and recommended Vice Minister of War Yú Qiān (于謙) as an assisting supervisor for defense.
The court did not agree, as Qiān (謙) was currently pacifying Shānxī (山西) and Hénán (河南).
Thereupon, censors accused Yuán (源) of the crime of arbitrarily replacing high officials when near the border,
and collectively impeached him.
They also stated that Yuán (源), when he was an imperial censor, had once committed corruption,
but had fraudulently claimed an imperial mandate.
The emperor, considering Yuán (源)'s merits,
ignored the matter.
When his mission was completed and he returned to court,
he cursed with Censor-in-Chief Chén Zhì (陳智) in the office.
Zhì (智) reported this,
and an imperial edict rebuked both of them.
In a year of drought,
he recorded suspicious cases
and requested that this practice be extended throughout the empire,
which was approved.
Shortly after, he was imprisoned, along with Vice Minister Hé Wényuān (何文淵), for improper judgment of cases.
He was pardoned,
but again, for stating the crimes of Liáo (遼) Prince Guìxiá (貴烚)
without mentioning his internal rebellion,
he and the officials of the Three Judicial Offices were all imprisoned in the imperial jail.
After several months,
he was released and reinstated.
Yuán (源) had served in the Ministry of Punishments for a long time,
and his judgments were mostly fair and merciful.
Shǎnxī (陝西) Assistant Commissioner Jì Zī (計資) suggested that
military officials who committed various crimes
should have half their salary confiscated and
be banished to the farthest borders.
Yuán (源), considering the suggestion too harsh,
memorialized to reject it.

Director Lín Hòu (林厚) proposed four measures: prohibiting malicious litigation and slander, selecting competent judicial officials, and ensuring that serious prisoners were convicted based on solid evidence.
All were implemented based on Yuán (源)'s recommendations.
In the sixth year, due to a foot ailment, he was ordered to attend court only on the first and fifteenth days of the month.
In the eighth year, he retired
and died.
Jīn Lián,
courtesy name Zōnghàn,
was a native of Shānyáng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the 16th year of Yǒnglè.
He was appointed Censor.
At the beginning of Xuāndé's reign,
he toured Guǎngdōng as an inspecting censor,
and was most highly praised for his integrity and ability.
He was transferred to inspect Jiāngxī and Zhèjiāng.
When he failed to capture a notorious bandit,
he was removed from office.
After the bandit was apprehended,
he was reinstated.
He once stated that prefectural and county officials were corrupt,
and that the Circuit Intendancy Office (*Ànchásī*) and inspecting censors (*Xún'àn Yùshǐ*) should be ordered to identify honest and capable individuals,
following the precedents of the Hóngwǔ era.
He suggested that envoys be sent to reward and commend them,
which would distinguish the corrupt from the pure,
and encourage the upright.
The emperor praised and accepted his suggestion.
On recommendation, he was promoted to Vice-Commissioner of Shǎnxī.
In the first year of Zhèngtǒng, he submitted a memorial requesting the replenishment of vacant posts in the guard units,
an increase in the garrison troops at Níngxià,
and the establishment of a Grand Commander for the Defense of Hànzhōng.
Many of his proposals were adopted.
In the third year, he was promoted to Assistant Censor-in-Chief (*Qiān Dū Yùshǐ*),
participating in the military affairs of Níngxià.
Lián was meticulous and resourceful,
skilled in planning,
and the western border remained peaceful.
Níngxià originally had five irrigation canals,
but the Míngshāzhōu Qīxīng, Hànbó, and Shíhuī canals were silted up.
Lián requested their dredging,
which irrigated over 1,300 *qǐng* of wasteland.
At that time, an imperial edict encouraged wealthy citizens to donate grain to aid the border,
and those who contributed 1,000 *shí* or more were praised with an imperial letter.
Lián noted that grain was expensive in the border regions,
and requested that those who did not meet the quota also be commended,
thus enriching the stores.
In the sixth year, an edict ordered Assistant Censor-in-Chief Lú Ruì and Lián to rotate duties.
The following year,
Ruì was recalled,
and Lián returned to his post.
Soon after, he was promoted to Right Vice-Censor-in-Chief,
and he rotated with Ruì twice more.
In the autumn of the eighth year, he was appointed Minister of Justice (*Xíngbù Shàngshū*),
and attended the Imperial Lectures (*Jīngyán*).
In the eleventh year,
the Earl of Ānxiāng, Zhāng Ān, disputed emoluments with his brother,
and an imperial edict ordered their arrest and trial.
The Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of Revenue shifted blame between themselves.
Censors impeached Lián, Minister of Revenue Wáng Zuǒ,
Right Censor-in-Chief Chén Yì,
Vice-Ministers Dīng Xuàn and Mǎ Áng,
and Vice-Censors-in-Chief Dīng Xuán and Chéng Fù, among others.
They were all imprisoned.
After several days,
they were released.
Rebels led by Dèng Máoqī and others in Fújiàn caused unrest.
Grand Commander Liú Jù and Censor-in-Chief Zhāng Kǎi were sent to suppress them,
but failed.
In the eleventh month of the thirteenth year, a large army was dispatched,
with the Marquis of Níngyáng, Chén Mào, and others appointed as generals to quell the rebellion,
and Lián was assigned to participate in military affairs.
Upon their arrival,
Censor Dīng Xuān had already inflicted a major defeat on the rebels,
and Máoqī was dead.
The remaining rebels rallied around his nephew Bó Sūn, who occupied Jiǔlóng Shān,
resisting the government forces.
Lián consulted with his subordinates,
and they used a feigned retreat to lure the rebels out,
ambushed them with elite troops,
entered their camp,
and captured Bó Sūn.
The emperor then transferred Kǎi to suppress the Zhèjiāng rebels,
while Lián was left to defeat the remaining unpacified rebels.
It happened that Emperor Yīngzōng was taken captive in the north,
and military matters became urgent,
so Lián was recalled.
Although speakers repeatedly impeached Lián for his lack of achievement,
Emperor Jǐng did not question it,
and promoted Lián to Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (*Tàizǐ Bīnkè*),
granting him double salary.
Soon after, he was transferred to Minister of Revenue (*Hùbù Shàngshū*),
and advanced to Grand Guardian of the Crown Prince (*Tàizǐ Tàibǎo*).
At that time, military campaigns were ongoing in all directions,
and financial provisions were urgently needed.
Lián meticulously reviewed everything without omission,
and proposed sixteen measures for austerity and expediency,
which prevented the national treasury from becoming depleted.
Not long after,
the retired emperor returned,
and Yĕxiān requested to resume envoy exchanges as before.
The emperor firmly intended to refuse him.
Lián submitted two memorials to remonstrate.
But he was not heeded.
Earlier,
when the emperor ascended the throne,
an edict exempted three-tenths of the land tax for the second year of Jǐngtài across the empire.
Lián dispatched a writ to the relevant officials,
stating that only rice and wheat were to be reduced,
while taxes collected in silver, cloth, and silk were to be levied as before.
In the second month of the third year,
Grand Academician Jiāng Yuān reported this,
and the ministry was ordered to investigate.
Lián felt inwardly ashamed,
and insisted there was no such thing.
Investigating Censor Lǐ Kǎn and others requested an inquiry into why officials nationwide had violated the imperial edict.
Fearing that the matter would be exposed,
Lián then said:
"Silver, cloth, and silk [as items for tax collection]
were not mentioned in the imperial edict;
if they were all reduced or exempted,
how would the national expenditure be funded?"
Thereupon, the Investigating Censors and Censors impeached Lián for losing the people's trust,
amassing popular resentment for the state,
and also exposed his secret dealings.
The emperor wished to pardon him,
but Kǎn and Censor Wáng Yǔn strongly argued against it,
so he was imprisoned in the Censorate's jail.
Three days later, he was released,
his palace title was revoked,
and he was transferred to the Ministry of Works (*Gōngbù*).
Minister of Personnel (*Lìbù Shàngshū*) Hé Wényuān argued that only Lián could manage finances,
so he was reinstated to the Ministry of Revenue.
Lián submitted a memorial defending himself,
and then requested to retire due to old age,
but the emperor comforted him and persuaded him to stay.
When the Crown Prince's palace was established,
his palace title was restored.
Soon after, he again listed ten items regarding the reduction of military artisans and idle monks and Daoists.
In the fifth year, he died in office.
For his military merits, he was posthumously enfeoffed as Earl of Shùyáng,
and given the posthumous name Róngxiāng.
Lián was resolute and talented.
Wherever he served, he was known for his strict efficiency,
though he was often prone to violent anger when dealing with subordinates.
In the Ministry of Justice, he applied the law somewhat strictly.
When he became Minister of Revenue,
as military campaigns arose and finances were strained,
he was rather heavy-handed in his levies to meet expenditures.
Shí Pú,
courtesy name Zhòngyù,
was a native of Línzhāng.
In the ninth year of Yǒnglè, he was recommended from his prefecture,
and entered the National Academy.
He was selected and appointed Censor.
At the beginning of Zhèngtǒng's reign,
he successively served as Surveillance Commissioner (*Ànchásǐ*) of Jiāngxī.
In the third year, he was demoted to Vice-Commissioner for allowing a prisoner to escape.
He was demoted to Vice-Commissioner.
Pú was skilled at resolving difficult cases.
A man married a wife,
who returned to her parents' home on the third day,
and disappeared.
The father-in-law sued his son-in-law for killing his daughter,
and he was falsely confessed and sentenced to death.
Pú prayed to the gods,
and dreamed that the god showed him the character *mài* (麦, wheat).
Pú said:
"*Mài*
is two people sandwiching one person."
By morning,
the prisoner was shackled and rushed to execution.
Before he was led out,
a young boy peered through the door screen.
He was apprehended,
and turned out to be a Daoist's disciple.
Pú sternly asked:
"Did your master order you to spy on this matter?"
The boy confessed the truth,
that indeed two Daoists had hidden the woman in a pile of dried wheat (*gǎomài*).
They were immediately arrested
and sentenced according to the law.
After several years in Jiāngxī,
discipline was strict,
and even women and children knew of Commissioner Shí.
In the seventh year, he was promoted to Provincial Administration Commissioner (*Bùzhèngshǐ*) of Shānxī.
The following year,
as the court's annual material expenses caused officials to impose levies that disturbed the populace,
he requested that 1,000 taels be annually reserved from the silver collected in lieu of grain tax,
to be used by officials for purchases,
so that official expenses could be covered,
and the people would also not be troubled.
This was granted.
Gōngbù Shàngshū Wáng Jǐn, because he could not bend to the will of Wáng Zhèn,
retired from office in the thirteenth year.
Pú was favored by Zhèn,
and so was summoned to be Shàngshū.
The following year,
the bandit Yè Zōngliú caused trouble in Chǔzhōu.
Zǒngbīngguān Xú Gōng and others went to suppress him,
and Pú was ordered to participate in their military affairs.
Before the army arrived,
Zōngliú had already been killed by Chén Jiànhú, one of his own party.
Xúnfǔ Zhāng Jì persuaded Jiànhú to surrender,
and the bandit threat somewhat subsided.
Pú and others dallied without achieving anything,
and were impeached by Yùshǐ Zhāng Hóng and others.
An imperial edict ordered that they await the army's return before reporting.
Later, Jǐngdì ascended the throne
and recalled them.
For their merits,
Pú was concurrently appointed Dàlǐ Sìqīng.
Soon after, he was dispatched to recruit volunteers throughout the realm,
and then returned to court.
At that time, the eunuch Jīn Yīng was imprisoned.
The judicial authorities impeached Pú for having once bribed Yīng,
and so Pú was also imprisoned.
He was sentenced to execution,
but was specially pardoned.
He was released to manage military provisions in Dàtóng.
When the enemy attacked Mǎyíng,
he was ordered to be Tídū of the military affairs of Xuānfǔ.
When he arrived, the invaders had already retreated.
He returned to manage the affairs of the Ministry.
He was granted the title of Tàizǐ Tàibǎo
and given two salaries.
When the river breached at Shāwān,
he was ordered to manage it.
Pú believed that the breach was not easy to block,
so he dug a separate canal
from Hēiyángshān to Xúzhōu
to facilitate the passage of grain barges,
while the breach remained as before.
Then the inner officials Lí Xián and others, along with Yùshǐ Péng Yì, were ordered to assist him.
A stone dike was built at Shāwān to defend against the breached river,
and two Yuèhé canals were opened
to divert water into the Grand Canal to reduce the water's force,
and only then was the breach blocked.
Pú returned and reported:
"Many thieves and robbers in the capital come from the military ranks.
Occasionally when they are caught,
they invariably say, 'Our rations and provisions have been reduced,
and our wives and children are starving and freezing.'
Moreover, I hear that in Liǎngjī, Shāndōng, and Hénán, many poor people affected by disasters are engaging in looting.
If they are not appeased now,
I fear that future worries will be worse than border troubles.
The garrison troops outside the passes
travel at night and hide during the day,
experiencing extreme hardship.
Now that the borders are not yet pacified,
rations should be increased to boost morale,
but instead their monthly provisions are reduced.
This is truly the beginning of inviting theft and harming the state;
it is not a method to conserve funds and make them sufficient."
The Emperor deeply accepted his words.
Shāwān breached again,
and Pú went to manage it a second time.
He returned home due to his mother's mourning,
but was recalled to office.
In the sixth year, he was transferred to Bīngbù Shàngshū,
working with Yú Qiān to manage the affairs of the Ministry.
The following year,
the Miáo people in Húguǎng rebelled,
and Pú was appointed Zǒngdū of military affairs
to suppress them with Nánhé Bó Fāng Yīng.
In Tiānshùn first year, news of victory arrived.
He was recalled,
and ordered to retire.
Later, his merits were discussed,
and he was bestowed with paper money and silks.
In the winter of the fourth year, based on Lǐ Xián's recommendation,
he was summoned to be Nánjīng Zuǒ Dūyùshǐ.
By this time, Pú was old and deaf,
and unable to perform his duties.
In the seventh year, he was impeached and dismissed by Jǐnyīwèi Zhǐhuī Qiānshì Mén Dá,
returned home, and died.
Wáng Jǐn,
a native of Méi.
He passed the provincial examination during the Yǒnglè reign,
and successively served as Shāndōng Zuǒ Bùzhèngshǐ,
bringing beneficial policies wherever he went.
In the sixth year of Zhèngtǒng, he entered the court as Gōngbù Shìláng,
and replaced Wú Zhōng as Shàngshū.
He returned home and died fifteen years later.
Luó Tōng,
courtesy name Xuégǔ,
a native of Jíshuǐ.
He became a Jìnshì in the tenth year of Yǒnglè.
He was appointed Yùshǐ,
and toured as inspector in Sìchuān.
Dūzhīhuī Guō Yūn and Qīngjūn Yùshǐ Wāng Lín colluded for illicit gain.
Tōng impeached and reported them,
and they were arrested and tried.
When the three palaces caught fire,
he, along with his colleague Hé Zhōng and others, earnestly pointed out the shortcomings of contemporary governance.
This displeased the Emperor,
and he was sent out to serve as Zhīzhōu of Jiāozhǐ Qīnghuà.
In the first year of Xuāndé,
Lí Lì rebelled,
and Wáng Tōng was defeated in battle,
unilaterally issuing a proclamation to cede Qīnghuà and the areas south of it to the rebels.
At that time, the rebels were besieging Qīnghuà,
and Tōng, with Zhǐhuī Dǎ Zhōng, held fast,
breaking out to defeat the rebels at an opportune moment,
killing and wounding many.
The rebels were about to flee when the proclamation arrived.
Tōng said:
"We have killed many rebels;
if we leave the city, there will certainly be no way to survive.
Rather than be captured,
why not die loyal to our duty?"
So he and Zhōng strengthened their defense.
The rebels attacked for a long time without success,
and ordered the surrendered general Cài Fú to persuade them to surrender.
Tōng ascended the rampart and loudly cursed him.
The rebels knew the city could not be taken,
and withdrew.
Upon his return to the capital,
Xuānzōng greatly praised and rewarded him.
He was transferred to Hùbù Yuánwàiláng,
and dispatched to manage military provisions in Xuānfǔ.
He reported:
"The court discusses storing provisions at Kāipíng,
ordering each soldier to transport one dàn,
and also requiring cavalry to escort them.
It is estimated that it costs two dàn and seven dǒu to deliver one dàn.
Now many soldiers and civilians are willing to transport grain in exchange for salt.
I request that the old regulation be reduced by two-fifths,
then people will gladly transport,
provisions will be sufficient, and soldiers will not be exhausted."
The Emperor approved.
In the early Zhèngtǒng reign,
he was promoted to Bīngbù Lángzhōng,
and followed Shàngshū Wáng Jì to rectify border affairs in Gānsù.
After returning from defeating the enemy at Wūlǔnǎi,
his greed and licentiousness were discovered by Jì.
Jì sent Tōng to report on the border situation,
and immediately memorialized Tōng's crimes.
He was imprisoned,
and demoted to Gǎnzāoguān of Róngshān in Guǎngxī.
Later,
he was transferred to Hébósuǒguān of Dōngguǎn.
In the ninth year,
Dū Tǒng Qiānshì Cáo Jiǎn recommended him for his civil and military talents,
requesting his employment.
The Ministry of Personnel insisted it was not permissible.
When Jǐngdì governed as regent,
on the recommendation of Yú Qiān and Chén Xún,
he was reinstated as Bīngbù Yuánwàiláng
and tasked with guarding Jūyōngguān.
Soon after, he was promoted to Lángzhōng.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Yòu Fù Dūyùshǐ.
When Yěxiān attacked the capital,
a separate detachment attacked Jūyōng very fiercely.
It was extremely cold,
so Tōng drew water to drench the city walls,
making the ice so solid that the attackers could not approach.
After seven days, they fled,
and he pursued and defeated them.
In the first year of Jǐngtài
At that time, Yáng Hóng (楊洪) was supervising the Beijing garrison,
and he was ordered to participate in military affairs and concurrently manage the affairs of the Censorate.
He said:
"When alarms are reported from various borders,
it is usually because the defending generals fear conscription [into the field]
and embellish falsehoods to deceive the imperial court.
When encountering a few dozen bandits, they always claim to have killed thousands.
Previously, outside Déshèng Gate (德勝門) countless heads were supposedly taken,
and yet those who received official promotions numbered as many as sixty-six thousand.
If this is the case near the capital,
how much more so beyond the frontier?
Moreover, Hán Xìn (韓信) rose from the ranks of common soldiers,
and Ráng Jū (穰苴) was elevated from obscurity.
It is appropriate to widely search among the generals and soldiers for those like Xìn (信) and Jū (苴),
and discuss military matters with them.
As for those who now wear jade belts and sable tails,
they are all people who prioritize saving their lives and preserving their titles and salaries,
hating the worthy and envying talent,
able to speak but not to act.
They are not worthy of discussing matters with."
His intention was likely to criticize Yú Qiān (于謙) and Shí Hēng (石亨) and their ilk.
Yú Qiān (于謙) submitted a memorial in defense,
saying:
"To generally blame border reports for being untrue –
if there is indeed an alarm,
not reporting it will certainly lead to miscalculations.
Regarding the promotions of officers and soldiers outside Déshèng Gate (德勝門),
only the Marquis of Wǔqīng (武清侯), Shí Hēng (石亨), had nineteen thousand eight hundred people whose merits were officially listed first,
along with over three thousand who died in battle.
How could there be as many as sixty thousand?
If Tōng (通) believes this to be excessive,
then the titles of your servant and Hēng (亨) and others should be revoked.
If there are individuals like Hán Xìn (韓信) and Ráng Jū (穰苴),
I humbly request that they be immediately designated and recommended,
