and that your servant's military duties be dismissed,
allowing me to solely manage the affairs of my department."
The memorial was sent down for court deliberation.
The court officials unanimously stated that Yú Qiān (于謙), Shí Hēng (石亨), and Yáng Hóng (楊洪) were indeed competent for their roles,
and also said that Tōng (通) was dedicated to defeating bandits,
with no other intentions.
The emperor reconciled the two parties.
Soon, an imperial decree ordered Yú Qiān (于謙) to record merits,
but not to allow false or excessive claims as before,
this was indeed prompted by Tōng's (通) words.
Qín Hào (覃浩) and other supervising secretaries said that Tōng (通) was originally employed for his military knowledge,
and it was inappropriate for him to manage Censorate affairs,
so his concurrent post was relieved.
Many soldiers and civilians on the frontier were plundered by the bandits.
Tōng (通) requested that proclamations be made to all border regions, stating that those who voluntarily returned,
if soldiers, would be exempted from garrison duty for three years,
and if civilians, would have their corvée labor restored for life.
He also requested the offer of high titles and generous rewards
to recruit those who could capture or kill Yěxiān (也先), Bóyántiēmù'ér (伯顏帖木兒), and Xǐníng (喜寧).
Later,
he further said:
"Ancient generals and commanders made it their business to seek out and elevate various talents.
For example, those who understood mountain and river terrains could be made guides for the army;
those who could scale heights and traverse dangers could be made scouts;
those who could interpret winds and bird omens could be made to prepare for changes.
Currently, such people are not seen in the army.
I humbly request an imperial decree for court officials to each recommend those they know,
and that Grand Commander Yáng Hóng (楊洪) and Vice Commander Sūn Táng (孫鏜) be ordered to test them with your servant."
The emperor ordered that all these proposals be implemented.
When there was an alarm in Xuānfǔ (宣府),
Grand Commander Zhū Qiān (朱謙) sent an urgent report.
The court recommended Governor-General Fàn Guǎng (范廣) to lead troops there,
with Tōng (通) serving as director of military affairs.
When the bandits retreated,
he stationed his forces at Huáilái (懷來) and Xuānfǔ (宣府).
Due to insufficient border provisions,
he was recalled.
In June,
Yú Qiān (于謙), as Shānxī (山西) was close to the bandits,
requested that a high official be dispatched to pacify it.
Yáng Hóng (楊洪) also requested that a senior minister be sent to escort provisions to Dàtóng (大同) from Yànmén Pass (雁門關).
The emperor assigned this task to Tōng (通).
Tōng (通) did not wish to go,
and requested to go with Yú Qiān (于謙) and Yáng Hóng (楊洪).
Yú Qiān (于謙) said that the nation faced many difficulties,
and it was not a day for a subject to shirk labor,
so he memorialized to humbly request to go himself.
The emperor did not agree,
and ultimately ordered Tōng (通).
Tōng (通) was originally recommended by Yú Qiān (于謙),
yet they frequently clashed on matters,
which led people to view Tōng (通) as unrighteous.
In the second year, he was recalled
and continued to assist in military affairs.
When the Eastern Palace was renovated,
he was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
He memorialized, saying:
"The tribute envoys brought over forty thousand horses.
It is advisable to appropriately increase the price paid for them.
If the price is increased, more will come later.
This is also a strategy to strengthen China and weaken the foreign tribes."
The emperor believed that the horses offered as tribute were generally unusable,
and that increasing the price would only fall into the bandits' trap,
so he shelved Tōng's (通) memorial.
In the fourth year, he was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief
and continued to assist in military affairs as before.
Tōng (通) was fond of grandiloquence,
and whenever he met people, he would talk about military strategy.
He presented his achievements in killing bandits
and sought hereditary military office,
which led to him being impeached by Supervising Secretary Wáng Hóng (王竑).
The emperor released him without punishment.
In the early Tiānshùn (天順) era,
he claimed that he had participated in planning to welcome the emperor back,
fearing that Shí Hēng (石亨) and others would conceal his contribution,
so his two sons were granted the post of Commandant.
In the third year, he retired.
He died in the sixth year of Chénghuà (成化)
He was granted sacrifices and burial according to regulations.
Luó Qǐ (羅綺),
a native of Cízhōu (磁州).
He became a *jìnshì* in the fifth year of Xuāndé (宣德)
When Yīngzōng (英宗) ascended the throne,
he was appointed Censor,
and gained a reputation for competence while inspecting Zhílì (直隸) and Fújiàn (福建).
In the ninth year of Zhèngtǒng (正統)
The following year, when his term was due to expire,
the military and civilians went to the Grand Censor who guarded the region, Chén Yì (陳鎰), to beg for him to stay.
When this was reported,
he was ordered to resume his post.
Soon after, he was promoted to Right Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review,
continuing his participation in military affairs as before.
He often impeached Commanders Rèn Xìn (任信) and Chén Bīn (陳斌) for various matters.
Both of them were members of Wáng Zhèn's (王振) faction.
In the fourth month of the eleventh year
Rèn Xìn (任信) and Chén Bīn (陳斌) accused Luó Qǐ (羅綺) of illegal activities.
The case was sent to Grand Commander Huáng Zhēn (黃真) for review.
Huáng Zhēn (黃真) claimed that Luó Qǐ (羅綺) often cursed eunuchs as "old slaves,"
thereby provoking Wáng Zhèn's (王振) anger.
He was recalled to the capital.
The judicial authorities proposed redemption,
but Wáng Zhèn (王振) changed the order, sending him to the Embroidered Uniform Guard for further interrogation.
Commander-in-Chief Mǎ Shùn (馬順) fabricated a case against him,
and he was banished to Liáodōng (遼東).
When Jǐngdì (景帝) ascended the throne,
Luó Qǐ (羅綺) appealed his injustice,
but was not heard.
Soon after, recommended by Ministers Yú Qiān (于謙) and Jīn Lián (金濂),
he was recalled to his former office
and promoted to Right Vice Minister,
serving as deputy to Lǐ Shí (李實) on a mission to Oirats (瓦剌).
When the Retired Emperor returned,
he was promoted to Left Vice Minister of the Ministry of Justice for his efforts.
In the second month of the following year
he was dispatched to supervise military provisions in Yúnnán (雲南) and Sìchuān (四川).
Later,
he replaced Kòu Shēn (寇深) as the garrison commander of Sōngpān (松潘).
The bandit leader Zhuóláo (卓勞), in league with Ā'ěrjié (阿兒結) from other stockades, frequently committed depredations,
and Luó Qǐ (羅綺) captured and executed them.
Local officials Wáng Yǒng (王永), Gāo Màolín (高茂lín), and Dǒng Mǐn (董敏) engaged in mutual vendettas and killings,
and the defending generals could not control them.
Luó Qǐ (羅綺) raided Wáng Yǒng's (王永) stronghold and executed him.
He also defeated the Fān (番) tribes of Hēihǔ (黑虎) and other stockades,
beheading three hundred and fifty.
He was stationed there for seven years,
and his prestige was greatly feared.
In the early Tiānshùn (天順) era
he was recalled to serve as Left Vice Censor-in-Chief,
and for his achievements, he was granted a stipend of the second rank.
Censors Zhāng Péng (張鵬) and Yáng Xuān (楊瑄) impeached Shí Hēng (石亨).
Shí Hēng (石亨) claimed that Luó Qǐ (羅綺) and Right Censor-in-Chief Gěng Jiǔchóu (耿九疇) had instigated them,
and they were all imprisoned
and demoted to Policy Advisor in Guǎngdōng (廣東).
Luó Qǐ (羅綺) was dejected and did not immediately proceed to his post.
In the intercalary second month of the following year
Luó Qǐ's (羅綺) fellow townsman reported that Lóng Yuē (龍約), an assistant prefect of Cízhōu (磁州), had returned from the capital,
and told Luó Qǐ (羅綺) that the emperor still favored eunuchs,
and had carved a fragrant wooden figure of Wáng Zhèn (王振) for burial.
Luó Qǐ (羅綺) smiled slightly and said:
"The court's misgovernance
led to our demotion and banishment."
This was reported to the throne,
and Luó Qǐ (羅綺) was arrested and handed over to the authorities.
He was condemned to death,
his property was confiscated,
and the confiscated wealth was displayed at Wénhuá Gate (文華門) for all officials to see.
His family members were exiled to the frontier,
and the women were enslaved in the Wǎnyī Bureau (浣衣局).
When Xiànzōng (憲宗) ascended the throne,
he was pardoned and made a commoner,
and his assets were returned.
Those who served as Regional Commanders in Sìchuān, one after another, alongside Qǐ, were
Zhāng Gù,
whose courtesy name was Gōngzhèng,
a native of Xīnyù.
He obtained his *jìnshì* degree in the eighth year of Xuāndé.
In the early Zhèngtǒng reign,
he was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Justice.
He was transferred to the Ministry of Personnel
and was ordered to pacify the displaced people of Yùzhōu.
In the first year of Jǐngtài,
Supervising Secretary Lǐ Shí requested the establishment of a Grand Protector in the Sìchuān Provincial Military Command,
so Gù was promoted to Right Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review
and garrisoned Jiànchāng.
He had administrative achievements.
In the third year, he returned to handle matters at the Court of Judicial Review.
When bandits arose in Shāndōng,
he was ordered to oversee their suppression.
As it happened, there were continuous rains and floods,
and refugees filled the roads.
Gù devoted himself to their relief and assistance,
and the bandits dispersed.
Upon his return,
he died in office.
While in the remonstrance office, Gù dared to speak out;
many high officials were impeached by him.
He also impeached Grand Censor Chén Yì and others for recommending subordinates who had started as clerical aides to become prefects.
From then on, clerical aides were not allowed to be promoted to prefect,
and this was established as a rule.
When Yīngzōng was about to embark on a northern expedition,
he, along with his colleagues, submitted a memorial advising against it.
Upon Yīngzōng’s restoration,
he remembered Gù,
who had already passed away.
An envoy was sent to offer sacrifices to him,
and one of his sons was given an official post.
His son, Fǔ,
rose to the position of Provincial Surveillance Commissioner of Guǎngxī.
Zhāng Xuān,
whose courtesy name was Tíngxǐ,
was a native of Jiāngpǔ.
He obtained his *jìnshì* degree in the seventh year of Zhèngtǒng.
He was appointed Director of the Ministry of Justice
and successively served as Department Director,
gaining a reputation for ability.
During the Jǐngtài reign,
he was given an imperial edict to serve as Prefect of Jí'ān.
The local customs highly favored shamanism,
with no day off for welcoming gods.
Xuān encountered them on the road
and threw the idols into the water.
Soon after, he fell gravely ill,
and the elders all said it was the gods causing trouble,
asking him to restore them.
Xuān was angry
and refused,
and his illness also recovered.
During a severe famine,
he submitted a memorial to his superiors,
but without waiting for a reply,
he immediately opened the granaries to provide relief loans.
After serving for eight years,
he was recommended and promoted to Right Provincial Administration Commissioner of Guǎngdōng.
Bandits like Mò Wénzhāng from Guǎngxī crossed the border and captured Liánshān.
Xuān attacked and beheaded them.
He also defeated Zhōu Gōngzhuǎn, a bandit from Yángshān,
and Dèng Lǐbǎo, a bandit from Xīnxīng, among others.
Later, bandits from the Dàténg Xiá frequently attacked surrounding counties,
and Xuān was penalized by having his salary suspended.
In the early Chénghuà reign,
when Hán Yōng pacified the bandits,
he recorded Xuān's efforts in transporting grain and supplies,
granted him silver and silk,
and restored his salary as before.
Xuān inspected his jurisdiction,
supervised the construction of sixty-two granaries for emergencies,
repaired four thousand six hundred dikes, ponds, and embankments,
and reinforced and built twelve city walls in Guǎngzhōu and Xīnhuì.
The people were grateful to Xuān
and feared only his departure.
When he was transferred to Left Provincial Administration Commissioner,
it happened that his nine-year term was full,
and he was due to report to the capital.
The military and civilians together
petitioned for him to stay. Governor Chén Lián and others pleaded for him,
so he remained in his former post.
In the eighth year, he was appointed Right Vice Censor-in-Chief to serve as Governor of Fújiàn.
He pacified bandits like Lín Shòulù and Wèi Huáisān.
In counties like Fú'ān and Shòuníng, bordering Jiāng and Zhè,
bandit leaders Yè Wàng and Yè Chūn held strong positions in treacherous terrain.
Xuān captured and executed them,
and the rest completely dispersed.
The emperor issued an edict to commend him,
and he was transferred to govern Hénán.
He went to the capital to discuss matters,
presenting eighteen proposals on pacifying displaced people and assisting neglected talents,
many of which were adopted by the relevant departments.
When the Yellow River overflowed,
Xuān requested relief,
and also to move the stipends of the imperial princes to other locations,
to retain the grain intended for Yúlín for famine relief,
and for stone to be bought at eight *qián* per *shí* and sent to Yúlín,
which the people found convenient.
He returned to manage affairs at the Censorate.
Soon after, he was promoted to Vice Minister of Justice of Nánjīng.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Minister.
In the twentieth year,
when a celestial phenomenon occurred,
he was impeached,
but the emperor did not question it.
Three years later,
the Supervising Secretaries and Censors impeached him again,
and he was dismissed from office.
When Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
he was reinstated
and retired.
Zhāng Péng,
whose courtesy name was Téngxiāo,
was a native of Láishuǐ.
He obtained his *jìnshì* degree in the second year of Jǐngtài.
He was appointed Censor.
He submitted a memorial stating:
"Seeking personal gain while serving the ruler
is what ministers should guard against.
Recently, whenever there is an Imperial Birthday,
some present sheep, horses, brocades, and silks,
intermingling in the palace courtyard.
If not for avarice,
how could they have surplus wealth to offer as tribute?
Moreover, Your Majesty possesses wealth from all four seas,
how could the nation rely on these to be sufficient?
It is fitting to abolish all such practices,
to block the path of flattery and contention."
The memorial contained four points,
which the emperor largely adopted.
He was sent out to inspect Dàtóng and Xuānfǔ,
and he memorialized:
"The soldiers of these two garrisons wear worn-out clothes and eat meager food.
The sick have no medicine,
and the dead have no coffins.
I request that the government provide medicine and coffins,
establish public burial grounds,
and allow for sacrificial rites to the spirits of the dead.
If the deceased receive grace,
then the living will be encouraged."
The emperor immediately approved this,
and ordered it to be generally implemented in all border regions.
He memorialized to halt the collection of taxes in Huái and Yáng
and to provide oxen and seeds.
In the first year of Tiānshùn,
his colleague Yáng Xuān impeached Shí Hēng and Cáo Jíxiáng.
Péng also joined Liú Tài, Wèi Hàn, and Kāng Jì in the impeachment.
All incurred punishment
and were imprisoned.
Many censors were demoted,
while Péng and Xuān were exiled to Liáodōng.
After a short while, they were pardoned,
but then exiled again to Nándān.
When Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
court officials collectively recommended them,
and Péng was recalled to his original post,
and soon exceptionally promoted to Provincial Surveillance Commissioner of Fújiàn.
In the fourth year of Chénghuà,
he was appointed Right Vice Censor-in-Chief to serve as Governor of Guǎngxī,
achieving merit in suppressing barbarian bandits.
That winter, the office of Governor was abolished,
and he was ordered to return to manage affairs at the Nánjīng Censorate.
He was transferred to oversee grain transport,
also concurrently governing the four prefectures of Huái and Yáng.
Soon after, he was relieved of his grain transport duties,
and solely managed gubernatorial affairs.
He returned to the Nánjīng Censorate again,
was promoted to Vice Censor-in-Chief,
and served as Governor of Níngxià.
He was recalled,
and successively served as Left and Right Vice Minister of War.
In the eighteenth year, Chén Yuè was Minister of War.
Wéi Zhù, the eunuch guarding the Pearl Pool, requested permission to travel to Gāo, Zhào, Qióng, and Lián,
to meet with the patrolling officials to apprehend bandits.
Péng insisted it was not permissible,
but the Emperor ultimately granted it.
When sending imperial edicts and horses to the north and south,
eunuchs and meritorious officials were customarily dispatched.
Later, due to natural disasters, only Censor was sent.
That year,
the Emperor again wished to send eunuchs,
but Péng and others insisted it was not permissible.
The Emperor reluctantly complied,
ordering that they await a later time and then revert to the old practice.
Wāng Zhí, the eunuch garrisoning Dàtóng, stated that Xiǎo Wángzǐ was planning a major offensive,
and requested the dispatch of capital troops for reinforcement.
Péng and others said:
"Dàtóng's four myriad soldiers and horses are already sufficient for use,
so the request should not be granted.
Moreover, the capital troops are exhausted by construction work,
their energy depleted,
so if an emergency suddenly arises,
how can they display their might and fierce spirit?
We request that all their duties be suspended."
The imperial edict approved.
Soon after, he was promoted to Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
When Péng first became a Censor,
he was upright and valued integrity,
enjoying a great reputation.
Later, as he served in various posts both inside and outside the capital,
he merely sought peace and quiet.
When petty individuals usurped power,
and cabinet ministers Wàn Ān and Liú Jí and their ilk were solely preoccupied with their private interests,
Péng merely performed his duties,
unable to rectify or save the situation.
In the twenty-first year,
when a celestial phenomenon occurred,
Péng, along with his colleagues, said:
"The number of commissioned military officials has reached over eight hundred;
we request that they all be ordered to retire,
and that military merit be the only criterion for appointment.
All eunuchs serving as garrison commanders, spear inspectors, and defense commissioners in the four directions,
who were not originally established during the Zhèngtǒng reign,
should all be recalled."
Court officials also submitted numerous requests to this effect,
which were forwarded to the Ministry of War for review.
Péng feared the eunuchs,
and dared not firmly adhere to his proposal,
so the Emperor retained them all.
Public opinion at the time all blamed Péng.
The treacherous commoner Zhāng Jǐn presented precious treasures,
and obtained the position of Commander of the Imperial Bodyguard.
When a judicial post became vacant,
Péng's recommendation was not approved.
Knowing the Emperor's intention favored Jǐn,
he immediately nominated him.
Censors and supervising censors impeaching incompetent high officials often implicated Péng,
who strenuously sought to retire.
He was then granted an imperial edict and post-horses to return home.
He died in the fourth year of Hóngzhì.
His posthumous title was Yìjiǎn.
Lǐ Yù,
courtesy name Zīdé.
A native of Fēngchéng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the fifth year of Jǐngtài.
He was appointed Censor.
During the Tiānshùn reign,
he served as inspecting censor of Shǎnxī,
and submitted eight proposals for border pacification.
When Shí Biāo falsely reported a large number of enemy heads as merit,
an imperial edict ordered Yù to verify the facts.
Biāo's uncle, Hēng, sent a letter to Yù,
but Yù burned it,
and reported the truth.
Hēng also soon after suffered defeat.
From then on, Yù gained a reputation for integrity and righteousness.
Kòu Shēn, the Censor-in-Chief, was strict with his subordinates,
but only Yù did not bend to him.
For his talent, he was promoted to Surveillance Commissioner of Shāndōng.
There were over two hundred serious prisoners,
some of whom had not been judged for over ten years;
Yù settled and dispatched almost all of them within a month.
There were over seventy bandit strongholds in Dàxiànshān;
Yù captured and executed their leaders,
released those who were coerced,
and cleared their outstanding debts,
whereupon the rebellion was pacified.
In the early Chénghuà reign,
he was promoted to Left Administration Commissioner of Shǎnxī,
and then entered the capital as Prefect of Shùntiān Prefecture.
His administrative reputation was greatly distinguished.
He was promoted to Vice Censor-in-Chief,
and concurrently supervised grain transport and acted as巡抚 (Patrolling Inspector) for the various prefectures north of the Huái River.
He dredged the Báitǎ and Mèngdú rivers to facilitate grain transport.
At Zhāngqiū Nánwàng and Xīhú in Huái'ān, logs were traditionally used to reinforce and resist erosion,
which was endlessly laborious and costly.
Yù, with Department Director Yáng Gōng and others, planned
to replace them with stone,
which resulted in permanent benefit.
Huái and Fèng were then suffering from famine,
yet the Grand Court of Imperial Sacrifices levied 20,000 horses for reserve.
Yù argued for its abolition.
During his six years in Huái, each year he reported on affairs,
presenting advantages and disadvantages,
and many of his proposals were implemented.
He returned home for his father's mourning,
and after the mourning period,
he was retained to assist with affairs in the Censorate.
In the nineteenth year, Dài Jìn became Right Censor-in-Chief.
Jìn was attached to Wāng Zhí,
and had once requested the re-establishment of the Western Depot;
while in the Censorate, discipline was not maintained.
Yù wished to restore it.
If a Censor made a mistake,
they might be flogged,
which led to him being slandered.
After Wāng Zhí's downfall,
Yù, along with Vice Censor-in-Chief Tú Yǒng, requested the exoneration of those who had offended Zhí and been punished.
The Emperor was displeased,
and withheld their salaries.
He was also implicated and transferred to the Southern Capital Censorate.
He was transferred to the Southern Capital Censorate due to being implicated.
After his performance review, he went to the capital
and was retained as Minister of Works.
Initially,
when Yǐn Mín, Minister of Personnel, was dismissed,
Gěng Yù replaced him.
Due to his uprightness, he was not liked by Wàn Ān.
However, Lǐ Zīshěng was then powerful and favored,
and wishing to promote people from his hometown,
he conspired to remove Gěng Yù,
and replaced him with Yù.
Yù was originally upright and esteemed at the time,
but because of Zīshěng,
his reputation was somewhat damaged.
His appointments were also fair.
By custom,
there were four categories for evaluation: old age and illness,
incompetence and weakness,
greed and cruelty,
and indiscretion.
Yù said:
"People's talents and dispositions differ.
Being opinionated is akin to cruelty,
and being slow-witted is akin to weakness.
I request the establishment of a category 'lack of talent and ability'
to embody the idea of cherishing talent."
The Emperor approved of this,
and it was made into law.
The Emperor approved of it,
and it was then made into a regulation.
When Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
officials repeatedly impeached Yù, stating his advancement was through Zīshěng.
Yù felt indignant,
wrote a record to clear his name, and repeatedly submitted memorials requesting to retire.
He died during the Zhèngdé reign,
at the age of eighty-eight.
A eulogy states: Wáng Zhāng and others were sometimes criticized for their imperfect conduct.
Reviewing their entire lives,
flaws and merits were both evident.
However, having served in various posts both inside and outside the capital,
many of their achievements and contributions are worthy of record.
The *Shū* says,
"In dealing with people, do not demand perfection."
The principle of *Chūnqiū* is to praise good deeds.
Then these individuals certainly do not fail to be capable and resourceful talents for the state.
Then these individuals certainly do not fail to be capable and resourceful talents for the state.
Collation Notes

Biographies Volume 49 Zhōu Xīn Lǐ Chāngqí (Xiāo Shěnshēn) Chén Shìqǐ Yìng Lǚpíng Lín Shuò Kuàng Zhōng (Zhū Shèng) Chén Běnshēn (Luó Yǐlǐ Mò Yú Zhào Tài) Péng Xù (Sūn Dǐng) Xià Shí Huáng Rùnyù Yáng Zàn (Wáng Mào Yè Xī Zhào Liàng) Liú Shí Chén Xuǎn Xià Yín Chén Zhuàng Zhāng Bǐng Sòng Duānyí
Zhōu Xīn,
a native of Nánhǎi.
His original name was Zhìxīn,
courtesy name Rìxīn.
Chéngzǔ often called him simply
"Xīn,"
which then became his given name,
and he consequently used Zhìxīn as his courtesy name.
During the Hóngwǔ reign, as a *zhūshēng*, he was recommended to enter the Imperial Academy.
He was appointed Grand Judge of the Grand Court of Judicial Review,
and was known for his skillful judgment of cases.
Chéngzǔ 成祖 ascended the throne,
and [Zhōu Xīn 周新] was appointed Censor.
He dared to speak out,
and impeached many.
The imperial relatives and powerful officials were terrified,
calling him
“Cold-faced Iron.”
In the capital, his name was even used to frighten small children,
who would all run and hide.
When he toured Fújiàn 福建,
he memorialized requesting that the Dūsī 都司 and Wèisuǒ 衛所 not be allowed to oppress the fǔ 府, zhōu 州, and xiàn 縣,
and that fǔ 府 and wèisuǒ 衛所 officials should treat each other with equal courtesy.
Martial men were thus restrained.
He was then transferred to tour Běijīng 北京.
At that time, officials ordered that commoners sentenced to exile for crimes should cultivate idle land in Běijīng 北京.
Those imprisoned awaiting detailed review and approval
often died of neglect due to delays in communication.
Zhōu Xīn 周新 requested that henceforth, detailed review and approval for such cases be conducted by the itinerant officials or censors in Běijīng 北京, allowing for immediate dispatch
to avoid prolonged stagnation.
This was adopted.
Moreover, it was ordered that criminals in the imperial domain facing execution might be allowed to ransom themselves.
The Emperor knew Zhōu Xīn 周 Xīn,
and there was nothing he memorialized that was not approved.
Upon his return to court,
he was immediately promoted to Judicial Commissioner of Yúnnán 雲南.
Before he could depart,
he was transferred to Zhèjiāng 浙江.
Wronged commoners, long imprisoned,
hearing of Zhōu Xīn's 周新 arrival,
rejoiced, saying:
“We shall live!”
Upon his arrival, he indeed cleared their names.
Earlier,
when Zhōu Xīn 周新 entered the region,
a swarm of gnats met his horse's head.
He tracked them to a dead body in a thicket,
on which was tied a small wooden seal.
Zhōu Xīn 周新 examined the seal,
knowing the deceased was a former cloth merchant.
He secretly ordered the wide purchase of cloth,
and those whose cloth bore a matching seal were arrested and interrogated,
leading to the capture of all the thieves.
One day,
while attending to official duties,
a whirlwind blew a leaf onto his desk.
The leaf was unlike those of other trees.
He inquired of his attendants,
and only one Buddhist temple possessed such trees.
The temple was far from the city,
but Zhōu Xīn 周新 suspected the monk had committed murder.
He ordered the tree cut down,
and indeed, a woman's corpse was found.
After interrogation, the facts were confirmed,
and the monk was executed by dismemberment.
A merchant, returning home at dusk,
fearing robbery,
hid his gold under a stone in a roadside shrine.
Upon returning home, he told his wife.
The next morning, he went to retrieve the gold but could not find it,
so he reported it to Zhōu Xīn 周新.
Zhōu Xīn 周新 summoned the merchant's wife and questioned her,
and it turned out she had a lover.
When the merchant suddenly returned,
her lover was still hidden in her quarters.
Hearing the merchant's words,
he took the gold that night.
Both the wife and her lover were sentenced to death.
Other cases of uncovering treachery and exposing hidden crimes
were all of this nature.
Zhōu Xīn 周新, traveling incognito to inspect the region,
offended a county magistrate.
The magistrate intended to flog and torture him,
but hearing that the Judicial Commissioner was about to arrive,
he imprisoned Zhōu Xīn 周新 instead.
From prison, Zhōu Xīn 周新 questioned the other inmates,
and learned of the magistrate's corruption.
He then told the prison guard:
“I am the Judicial Commissioner.”
The magistrate, shocked, apologized and confessed,
and was impeached and dismissed.
In the tenth year of Yǒnglè 永樂 (1412),
Zhèxī 浙西 suffered a great flood.
The Grand Secretariat, Zhào Jūrèn 趙居任, concealed it and did not report it.
Zhōu Xīn 周新 memorialized it.
Xià Yuánjí 夏原吉 defended Zhào Jūrèn 趙居任.
The Emperor ordered a review,
and relief and aid were granted as Zhōu Xīn 周新 had stated.
The bandit Ní Hóngsān 倪弘三 of Jiāxīng 嘉興 plundered neighboring prefectures,
with several thousand followers,
repeatedly defeating government troops.
Zhōu Xīn 周신 led troops to capture him,
erecting wooden barricades in various harbors and inlets.
The bandits fled overland,
and he pursued them to Táoyuán 桃源,
capturing them and presenting them [to the court].
At that time,
Commissioner Zhōu's 周名 Xīn's fame was known throughout the land.
Jǐnyīwèi 錦衣衛 Commander Jì Gāng 紀綱 sent a chiliarch to conduct investigations in Zhèjiāng 浙江,
who extorted bribes and wielded power.
Zhōu Xīn 周新 intended to investigate and punish him,
but he fled.
Shortly thereafter,
Zhōu Xīn 周新 traveled to the capital with documents.
He encountered the chiliarch in Zhuōzhōu 涿州,
arrested and imprisoned him in the prefectural jail.
The chiliarch escaped and reported to Jì Gāng 紀綱,
who falsely impeached Zhōu Xīn 周新 for a crime.
The Emperor was enraged,
and ordered Zhōu Xīn's 周新 arrest.
The flag-bearers and校 guards were all Jǐnyīwèi 錦衣衛 private retainers,
and they flogged and beat him on the way until no part of his skin was intact.
Upon arrival,
he prostrated before the imperial steps and defiantly declared:
“Your Majesty's decree mandates the Judicial Commissioner to act,
with powers equivalent to the Censorate.
I, your subject, received an imperial decree to capture wicked villains;
how can I be punished?”
The Emperor grew even angrier,
and ordered his execution.
Before the execution, he cried out loudly:
“Alive, I was an upright official;
dead, I shall be an upright ghost!”
He was then killed.
Another day,
the Emperor repented,
and asked his attendants:
“Who was Zhōu Xīn 周新?”
They replied:
“From Nánhǎi 南海.”
The Emperor sighed, saying:
“To think there was such a man beyond the岭 mountains,
I wrongly killed him.”
Later, if the Emperor saw a person in crimson robes standing in the sun,
he would say:
“My subject, Zhōu Xīn 周新, has become a spirit,
punishing corrupt officials for Your Majesty.”
So it was said.
Later, Jì Gāng 紀綱 was executed for his crimes,
and the matter became even clearer.
His wife had integrity.
Before Zhōu Xīn 周新 achieved success,
she supported herself through sewing.
When he became noble,
she once attended a ladies' banquet hosted by an official's wife,
dressed in coarse clothes like a peasant woman.
The other ladies were ashamed,
and all changed their attire and ornaments.
Zhōu Xīn 周新 died without sons.
His wife returned home,
extremely poor.
Yáng Xìnmín 楊信民, the Provincial Governor of Guǎngdōng 廣東, said:
“Zhōu Xīn 周新 was the foremost man of his generation;
how can his wife starve all day?”
He regularly provided her with relief.
When his wife died,
all Zhèjiāng 浙江 natives serving in Guǎngdōng 廣東 attended her funeral.
Lǐ Chāngqí 李昌祺,
whose given name was Zhēn 禎,
was known by his courtesy name.
He was from Lúlíng 廬陵.
He became a Jìnshì 進士 in the second year of Yǒnglè 永樂 (1404).
He was selected as a Shùjíshì 庶吉士.
He participated in the compilation of the Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn 永樂大典,
and for obscure books and doubtful matters,
many sought his counsel.
He was promoted to Bureau Director in the Ministry of Rites,
then transferred to Left Administration Commissioner of Guǎngxī 廣西.
He was demoted for an offense and assigned labor,
but was soon pardoned and reinstated.
In the first year of Hóngxī 洪熙 (1425), he was appointed to his former post in Hénán 河南.
Together with the Right Administration Commissioner Xiāo Xǐngshēn 蕭省身, he curbed powerful bullies,
removed corrupt and cruel officials,
cleared backlogs, rehabilitated the dismissed,
and relieved disaster victims and aided the poor.
Within a few months, his governance greatly succeeded.
He retired due to mourning,
and Xuānzōng 宣宗 had already appointed Vice Minister Wèi Yuán 魏源 as his replacement.
But at that time, Hénán 河南 suffered a severe drought,
and court officials, noting Lǐ Chāngqí's 李昌祺 integrity and magnanimity,
and that the people of Hénán 河南 cherished him,
requested that he be reinstated.
He was ordered to forgo mourning and proceed to his post,
where he showed great compassion and solicitude.
Upon the change of era to Zhèngtǒng 正統,
he submitted a memorial with three proposals,
all of which were approved.
In the fourth year (1439), he retired.
He lived at home for over twenty years,
keeping himself aloof from public affairs.
His old dwelling barely sheltered him from wind and rain,
and his food for sacrifices and festivals was insufficient.
He died in the second year of Jǐngtài 景泰 (1451).
Xiāo Shěngshēn
was from Táihé.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the same year as Chāngqí.
In the first year of Hóngxī (1425),
when the term of his Provincial Administration Commission service expired,
he was due to receive a patent of nobility.
He memorialized, stating that his father was over eighty
and he wished to bestow it upon his father.
The emperor praised and permitted it,
which subsequently became a precedent.
He resided in Hénán for twelve years,
and his administrative performance was on par with Chāngqí's.
Chén Shìqǐ,
whose given name was Léi,
was known by his courtesy name.
He was from Táihé.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the second year of Yǒnglè (1404).
He was selected as a *shùjíshì* (supernumerary Hanlin bachelor)
and promoted to Director of the Ministry of Rites.
The Minister, Lǚ Zhèn, was treacherous and vicious;
all his subordinates feared him
and served him with extreme caution,
but Shìqǐ alone did not yield in the slightest.
In the third month of the twelfth year (1414),
the Ministry of Personnel reported that there were many vacancies in the two provincial commissions (*bù* and *àn*).
The emperor said:
"The Provincial Administration Commissioners (*bùzhèng*) and Provincial Surveillance Commissioners (*ànchá*)
are Our regional officials,
and several thousand *lǐ* of land are entrusted to the hands of but a few people.
Select the virtuous and capable among the court officials
and appoint them accordingly."
Thereupon, over twenty Directors of various bureaus and Censors were dispatched to serve as Provincial Censors (*jiānsī*),
and Shìqǐ was appointed Assistant Provincial Administration Commissioner for Shāndōng.
He dedicated himself wholeheartedly to official duties,
not seeking a reputation for being overly meticulous.
When supervising corvée and taxes,
he did not set strict deadlines.
When Qīngzhōu suffered a famine,
he submitted a memorial requesting grain for relief.
When the envoy arrived,
the number of famine victims had doubled.
Shìqǐ again submitted a memorial,
first distributing grain to the people,
and told the envoy:
"I alone will bear the blame if there is any."
The court discussion ultimately followed his proposal.
He was imprisoned due to the rebellion of Táng Sài'ér.
After several months,
he was released and reinstated to his position.
When Gāo Xù plotted rebellion,
Shìqǐ rode from Qīngzhōu at dusk to inform the three provincial commissions,
and secretly reported it to the court.
After Gāo Xù was captured,
he, together with Xuē Lù and Zhāng Běn, recorded the remaining accomplices
and pacified the people.
When the task was complete,
he was ordered to clear and organize the military registers of Shāndōng.
He died in office in the sixth year of Xuāndé (1431).
Yìng Lǚpíng
was from Fènghuà.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the second year of Jiànwén (1400).
He was appointed Magistrate of Déhuà.
He successively served as Director of the Ministry of Personnel
before being dispatched to serve as Prefect of Chángdé.
At the beginning of Xuānzōng's reign,
he was promoted to Provincial Surveillance Commissioner of Guìzhōu.
Wherever he went, he rooted out corruption
and frequently commented on current governmental affairs.
According to the old system,
when the Chief Military Commissions dispatched envoys to other regions,
they had to obtain internal authentication documents,
which were then submitted to the Provincial Military Commands,
and they dared not directly issue orders to the guards.
However, by this time, the military commands had gradually become arrogant;
envoys, carrying official documents, traveled everywhere,
visiting various guards,
and extorting from the soldiers.
In the seventh year of Xuāndé (1432),
Lǚpíng protested in a memorial, saying:
"The establishment of authentication documents
is to prevent fraud and deception.
Now, those dispatched by the Right Chief Military Commission to Qián (Guìzhōu)
do not follow the old rules;
petty individuals, relying on their power, make unreasonable demands,
making it impossible to check for fraud."
Xuānzōng approved of his words,
and Chief Military Commissioner Chén Zhèng admitted his fault.
The emperor ordered all commissions to adhere to this permanently,
and the military commissions were curbed.
Shān Yún was stationed in Guǎngxī to guard against the barbarians,
and each year ten thousand troops from Guìzhōu were deployed there.
They were replaced in spring and autumn,
but many fled upon their return.
Then, troops from the original guards were taken to replenish,
and the fugitives were not pursued.
Lǚpíng memorialized:
"Guìzhōu's four borders are all inhabited by Miáo and Mán peoples;
if the military ranks are hollow,
who will fight and defend in an emergency?
Now, the guard troops flee to Guǎngxī,
and those remaining in the guards are used to replenish.
In a few years, Guìzhōu's military ranks will be entirely empty,
and border conflicts will arise."
The emperor then ordered Yún to strictly admonish the various guards in Guǎngxī,
retrieve the escaped soldiers,
and once sufficient numbers were met,
send them back,
thus ending the deployment of Guìzhōu garrison troops.
Yún,
a famous general,
had rendered meritorious service in guarding Yuè (Guǎngxī),
and looked down upon Lǚpíng as a mere scholar.
In the first year of Zhèngtǒng (1436),
Lǚpíng impeached Yún for abusing his power
and arbitrarily wielding authority.
The emperor ordered Yún to explain himself.
Yún was greatly alarmed
and admitted his fault.
The emperor pardoned him.
The following year,
he submitted a memorial detailing four matters.
Firstly,
the six prefectures of Zhènyuǎn,
having been transferred from Húguǎng to Guìzhōu,
should consume Sichuan salt.
However, as the route to Shǔ (Sichuan) was distant,
it would be more convenient to continue consuming Huái salt.
Secondly,
military guard provisions were supplied from Chóngqìng,
but river transport was difficult,
and it was easy for light transport to incur much waste.
He requested that the autumn grain from Zhènyuǎn, which was remitted to Húguǎng, be used for nearby distribution.
Thirdly,
discontinue the annual provision of yellow and white wax by the prefectures of Lípíng.
Fourthly,
when Guìzhōu was first established,
the monthly salary of the three commissions was only one *shí* of grain.
Now that grain was gradually abundant,
he requested an increase in their salary.
All
were adopted.
At that time, officials on circuit for public business were
not provided with post-station services by regulation.
Lǚpíng said that hiring carts and boats would disturb the populace,
and requested post-station services for convenience.
Also, due to the shortage of military personnel,
he requested that officials, standard-bearers, criminals, and those sentenced to exile or death in the guard garrisons
all be sent to the garrison commanders to earn merit,
and return to their ranks upon completion of their term;
border troops who committed theft, and local officials and commoners, as well as officials and standard-bearers whose crimes were minor,
could redeem their sins by contributing grain to fill shortages in storage.
All were adopted.
In the third year (1438), he was promoted to Left Provincial Administration Commissioner of Yúnnán.
At that time, there was warfare in Lùchuān,
and he repeatedly memorialized his achievements.
He retired and returned home in the eighth year (1443).
Lín Shuò,
courtesy name Màohóng,
was from Mǐnxiàn.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the tenth year of Yǒnglè (1412).
He was appointed Censor
and dispatched to supervise Shāndōng.
At the beginning of Xuāndé's reign (1426),
he supervised Zhèjiāng.
His administration was strict and solemn,
and he was soon promoted to Provincial Surveillance Commissioner.
A chiliarch, Tāng Mǒu, colluded with the eunuch Péi Kěliè for illicit gain,
and Shuò intended to punish him according to the law.
The eunuch falsely accused Shuò of destroying an imperial edict,
and he was arrested.
Shuò kowtowed and said:
"I was formerly a Censor,
an official of the seventh rank.
Now I am promoted to Provincial Surveillance Commissioner,
an official of the third rank.
Day and night I strive,
thinking of repaying the emperor's grace.
A petty person, for his inconvenience,
wishes to remove me;
may Your Majesty discern and decide."
The emperor, moved, said:
"We indeed did not believe it,
We summoned you to question you in person, that is all."
Shuò was immediately released,
reinstated to his office,
and Péi Kěliè was reprimanded by imperial decree.
Shuò had been in Zhèjiāng for a long time,
and the people remembered his kindness.
In the third year of Zhèngtǒng (1438), he mistakenly applied a pardon precedent, causing a death penalty case.
The Assistant Surveillance Commissioner Gěng Dìng impeached him.
He was arrested and interrogated,
and returned to his post after paying a fine.
That winter, he was transferred to Provincial Administration Commissioner of Guǎngdōng,
but died before taking up the appointment.
Later, Zhèng Luò, the Prefect of Níngbō, impeached Kěliè for unlawful conduct,
and Kěliè was ultimately dismissed.
Kuàng Zhōng,
courtesy name Bólǜ,
was from Jìng'ān.
He initially served as a clerk under Shàngshū Lǚ Zhèn.
Lǚ Zhèn, impressed by his talent,
recommended him for appointment as a Zhǔshì of the Yízhì Division.
He was promoted to Lángzhōng.
In the fifth year of Xuāndé (1430),
the emperor, finding that many prefects were not performing their duties competently,
and with nine prefectures including Sūzhōu vacant,
all of which were important and difficult territories,
ordered ministers from the boards and Censorate to recommend honest and capable subordinates to fill the positions.
Kuàng Zhōng was recommended by Shàngshū Jiǎn Yì, Hú Yíng, and others,
and was promoted to Zhī Sūzhōu (Prefect of Sūzhōu).
An imperial edict was issued to dispatch him.
Sūzhōu suffered from heavy taxes and labor service,
and powerful rascals manipulated laws for their own corrupt gain,
making it notoriously difficult to govern.
Kuàng Zhōng traveled by post-horse to the prefecture.
When he first took office,
the clerks stood around him, asking for judgments on documents.
Kuàng Zhōng pretended not to understand,
consulting those around him,
simply following whatever the clerks wished to approve or reject.
The clerks were greatly pleased,
believing the Grand Prefect was ignorant and easy to deceive.
Three days later,
he summoned and questioned them, saying:
"Previously, a certain matter should have been approved,
but you stopped me;
a certain matter should have been stopped,
but you forced me to approve it;
you scoundrels have been manipulating the law for a long time,
and your crime deserves death."
He immediately flogged several people to death,
and dismissed all greedy, tyrannical, and incompetent subordinate officials.
The entire prefecture was greatly shaken,
and everyone obeyed the law.
Kuàng Zhōng then abolished vexatious and harsh regulations,
established new rules and teachings,
and for anything inconvenient to the people,
he immediately submitted a memorial to speak about it.
The Qingjūn Yùshǐ (Censor for Military Review) Lǐ Lì abused military personnel,
and the Tóngzhī (Assistant Prefect) Zhāng Huī, following his lead,
frequently used cruel punishments to force common people into military service.
Kuàng Zhōng memorialized to exempt 160 people,
and for 1240 people, their service was limited to their own lifetime.
The subordinate counties had arrears in taxes for four years,
totaling over 7.6 million dàn of grain.
Kuàng Zhōng requested to commute a portion into paper currency,
but this was blocked by the board's deliberation;
however, from then on, some reductions and exemptions were made.
He also said:
"Recently, an imperial edict was received to recruit people to cultivate official and private wasteland.
Official land was to be taxed at the same rate as private land,
and for land that no one cultivated, the tax quota was to be abolished.
In Kūnshān and other counties, there were over 33,400 households
whose members had died, moved, or joined the military and had their registrations cancelled.
The official land they left behind amounted to over 2,980 qǐng,
which should reduce taxes by over 149,000 dàn.
Other official land that has been submerged by the sea
still has its tax quota,
and all of these should be handled according to the imperial edict.
The seven counties under my administration
have an autumn grain tax of over 2.779 million dàn.
Among this, the tax on private land is only over 153,000 dàn,
while the tax on official land amounts to over 2.625 million dàn,
with some fields taxed as much as three dàn per acre,
showing such an uneven distribution of burden.
During the Hóngwǔ and Yǒnglè reigns,
orders were issued to provide horses for various postal stations in the north,
totaling over 400 horses.
They were supposed to be returned after three years,
but now it has been over thirty years.
When a horse dies, it is replaced,
with no end in sight.
The Gōngbù (Ministry of Works) demands 800 bolts of san suo kuò bù (three-shuttle wide cloth),
while the eleven prefectures of Zhèjiāng only provide 100 bolts,
but Sūzhōu alone provides 700.
I beg that the relevant authorities be ordered to address this."
The emperor granted all his requests.
At that time,
repeated imperial edicts reduced the heavy taxes in Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng.
Kuàng Zhōng and the Xúnfǔ (Grand Coordinator) Zhōu Chén meticulously planned together
and memorialized to exempt over 700,000 dàn of grain.
Whatever good policies Zhōu Chén implemented,
Kuàng Zhōng always cooperated to achieve them.
The accumulated grain in the Jìnóng Cāng (Granary for Aiding Agriculture) amounted to hundreds of thousands of dàn annually.
Besides famine relief,
it was used to substitute for various popular levies and outstanding rents.
His governance
was meticulous and thorough.
He once kept two registers to record the good and bad deeds of the people,
to facilitate encouragement and punishment.
He also established a Tōngguān Kānhé Bù (Ledger for Pass Permits)
to prevent fraud in receipts and disbursements.
He established a Gāngyùn Bù (Ledger for Transportation Crews)
to prevent embezzlement by transport laborers.
He established a Guǎnfū Bù (Ledger for Guesthouse Servants)
to prevent unreasonable demands.
He spared no effort
in promoting what was beneficial and eradicating what was harmful.
He curbed the powerful
and nurtured the virtuous,
and the people revered him like a god.
Before this,
eunuchs dispatched for weaving, purchasing, and acquiring flowers, trees, birds, and animals arrived one after another.
Officials below the prefectural assistant
were often subjected to flogging and binding.
And the soldiers and officers of the guard stations
often oppressed the common people.
While Kuàng Zhōng was in office,
they restrained their behavior and dared not act wantonly.
Even superior officials and clerks from other provinces who passed through his territory
were all intimidated by him.
Although Kuàng Zhōng started as a clerk,
he valued schools,
respected scholars,
and often supported poor scholars from humble backgrounds.
There was a Zōu Liàng
who presented a poem to Kuàng Zhōng.
Kuàng Zhōng wanted to recommend him,
but someone wrote an anonymous letter slandering Zōu Liàng.
Kuàng Zhōng said,
"This person wishes me to quickly establish Zōu Liàng's reputation,"
and immediately memorialized to the court.
Zōu Liàng was summoned and appointed Sīwù (Chief Clerk) in both the Ministry of Personnel and the Ministry of Justice.
He was later promoted to Yùshǐ (Censor).
Earlier,
when Kuàng Zhōng was a clerk,
Píng Sīzhōng from Wújiāng also rose from a clerk position
to become Sīwù of the Lìbù (Ministry of Personnel),
and had shown kindness to Kuàng Zhōng.
At this time, Kuàng Zhōng frequently invited him for visits,
treated him with extreme deference,
and even had his two sons attend to him,
saying:
"It is not that I lack servants,
but I wish to repay your kindness through this."
Píng Sīzhōng's family was always poor,
but he never sought any advantage based on their past acquaintance.
People praised both for their virtue.
Kuàng Zhōng once had to observe mourning for his mother,
but the people of the prefecture went to the capital to beg for him to be retained.
An imperial edict ordered his reinstatement.
In the sixth year of Zhèngtǒng (1441),
his term ended, and he was due for promotion,
but over 20,000 people from his jurisdiction
went to protest to the Xún'àn Yùshǐ (Circuit Censor) Zhāng Wénchāng,
begging for him to be reappointed.
An edict promoted him to the third official rank (zhèng sān pǐn) in salary,
while still allowing him to oversee prefectural affairs.
He died in office in the twelfth month of the following year.
Officials and commoners gathered and wept,
and erected a shrine for him.
Kuàng Zhōng was upright and incorruptible,
and diligently loved the people;
none of the subsequent prefects of Sūzhōu could match him.
After Kuàng Zhōng, Lǐ Cóngzhì and Zhū Shèng successively served as Zhī Sūzhōu (Prefect of Sūzhōu).
They all acted according to imperial edicts,
but the trust and authority granted by the edicts were not as great as for Kuàng Zhōng.
Lǐ Cóngzhì
was from Yíbīn.
Zhū Shèng
was from Jīnhuá.
Zhū Shèng was honest, tranquil, sharp, and meticulous,
and his subordinates could not deceive him.
He once said:
"If clerks are corrupt,
I will not accept many documents.
If subordinates are corrupt,
I will not use the rod.
If jailers are corrupt,
I will not imprison people."
Consequently, the public court was clear and solemn,
and the people lived in peace and were influenced by him.
After seven years in office,
he was exceptionally promoted to Jiāngnán Zuǒ Bùzhèngshǐ (Left Administration Commissioner of Jiāngnán).
Initially,
those recommended along with Kuàng Zhōng were:
Hùbù Lángzhōng (Bureau Director of the Ministry of Revenue) Luó Yǐlǐ, who became Zhī Xī'ān (Prefect of Xī'ān);
Bīngbù Lángzhōng (Bureau Director of the Ministry of War) Zhào Yù, who became Zhī Sōngjiāng (Prefect of Sōngjiāng);
Gōngbù Lángzhōng (Bureau Director of the Ministry of Works) Mò Yú, who became Zhī Chángzhōu (Prefect of Chángzhōu);
Hùbù Yuánwàiláng (Assistant Bureau Director of the Ministry of Revenue) Shào Mín, who became Zhī Wǔchāng (Prefect of Wǔchāng);
Xíngbù Yuánwàiláng (Assistant Bureau Director of the Ministry of Justice) Mǎ Yí, who became Zhī Hángzhōu (Prefect of Hángzhōu);
Chén Běnshēn, who became Zhī Jí'ān (Prefect of Jí'ān);
Yùshǐ (Censor) Chén Dǐng, who became Zhī Jiànchāng (Prefect of Jiànchāng);
Hé Wényuān, who became Zhī Wēnzhōu (Prefect of Wēnzhōu).
All were granted imperial edicts and traveled by post-horse.
Chén Běnshēn,
courtesy name Yǒuyuán,
was a native of Yín.
In the early Yǒnglè reign,
he entered the Guózǐjiān through the xiāngjǔ examination.
He was appointed Investigating Censor of the Ministry of Justice.
He was skilled at uncovering treachery.
A robber in the capital region murdered someone,
then fled and hid.
The officials imprisoned eighteen innocent people.
Běnshēn captured the robber through a stratagem,
and all eighteen people were released.
He was promoted to Yuánwàiláng.
He and Kuàng Zhōng and others were simultaneously appointed prefects by imperial decree;
Běnshēn governed Jí'ān.
Jí'ān had many powerful families
who loved to engage in lawsuits and expose others.
Nineteen great villains, including Péng Tuán, terrorized the neighborhoods.
Běnshēn sent people to associate with them.
He prepared a banquet and invited them to drink.
Strongmen were ambushed in the rear hall,
and they were seized and killed.
Their corpses were all dragged out,
astonishing the entire prefecture.
Zēng Zǐliáng, a great bandit of Lè'ān, occupied Mount Dàpán,
with a host of over ten thousand men.
Běnshēn set up an ambush and decisively defeated them,
beheading Zǐliáng.
Běnshēn's governance focused on the main principles,
disdaining trivial details.
Once the great villains were eliminated,
there were no major issues in the prefecture.
He would rise early,
beat the drum and ascend the hall.
As the clerks had nothing to report,
he would simply beat the drum and dismiss the court.
Occasionally, when there was a lawsuit,
he would summon the parties to his couch,
analyze the right and wrong, and send them away,
without even accepting formal complaints.
If someone felt wronged and unredressed,
even a three-foot-tall child
could go and report it.
Over time,
the people became ashamed of litigation.
He especially humbled himself before scholars,
renovated and beautified the academic temples,
and memorialized for the shrines of the recently deceased Confucian masters Ōuyáng Xiū, Zhōu Bìdà, Yáng Bāngyì, Hú Quán, Yáng Wànlǐ, and Wén Tiānxiáng.
In the sixth year of Zhèngtǒng,
after completing nine years, he was due for promotion.
The people of the prefecture begged him to stay,
and an imperial decree granted him a salary of the third principal rank.
When a civilian in front of his yamen married off a daughter,
Běnshēn heard the drums and music,
and laughed, saying:
"When I arrived,
she was still a suckling infant.
Now she is getting married;
should I still remain here?"
He then requested to retire.
He governed Jí'ān for eighteen years in total.
After he left,
the people of the prefecture made his image and worshipped him.
Luó Yǐlǐ
was a native of Guìyáng.
He became a Jìnshì in the thirteenth year of Yǒnglè.
He became Prefect of Xī'ān Prefecture after serving as Lángzhōng.
He mourned his parents,
and was then appointed to Shàoxīng.
He left again for mourning.
His replacement was not competent,
and the people of the prefecture missed him,
begging the court for Yǐlǐ.
An imperial decree ordered him to be reinstated to his duties.
When his term was complete,
he was promoted in rank and reappointed.
Afterwards,
he was transferred to govern Jiànchāng.
Wherever he went, he brought benefits and was loved.
He served in three prefectures,
for a total of twenty-seven years,
before retiring.
Mò Yú
was a native of Línkuì.
He entered officialdom through the xiāngjǔ examination,
and was appointed Prefect of Chángzhōu from Lángzhōng.
He memorialized to reduce the annual tribute of tea from Yíxīng,
to prohibit official envoys from oppressing local officials,
and to strictly verify the truth of recommendations and impeachments made by superior officials.
All were approved.
Chén Sībǎo, a twelve-year-old commoner from the prefecture,
whose family had been fishermen for generations.
His father and elder brothers committed robbery,
and Sībǎo was in the boat.
The officials considered him an accomplice,
and he was to be executed.
Yú submitted a memorial, stating:
"A young child follows his father and elder brothers;
this does not count as being an accomplice.
If a whole family lives on a boat,
should the whole family be punished?"
Xuānzōng ordered his release,
and said to his court officials:
"For a prefect to be able to say this,
he can be said to have a benevolent heart."
In the sixth year of Zhèngtǒng, when his term was complete,
the people of the prefecture begged him to stay.
The governor, Zhōu Chén, reported this.
An imperial decree promoted him two ranks and reinstated him.
At the same time as Yú, Zhào Tài of Lùchéng,
whose
courtesy name was Xīhé,
entered the Guózǐjiān through the xiāngjǔ examination.
He successively served in the Dūcháyuan
and was appointed Tóngzhī of Chángzhōu.
He dredged the Mèngdú and Déshèng rivers
and built the Wèicūn Lock.
When Zhōu Chén and Kuàng Zhōng discussed reducing the heavy grain taxes in Sūzhōu,
Tài also inspected the official land rents in Chángzhōu
and requested their concurrent reduction.
He was promoted to Lángzhōng of the Ministry of Works
and ordered to close the breached river at Dōngchāng.
Chén recommended him to be Xié tóng dōuyùn,
and he worked even harder at his post.
Not long after,
he died of illness.
Péng Xù,
courtesy name Zǔqī,
was a native of Yǒngfēng.
At the age of seven,
he entered a Buddhist temple and did not bow.
When the monk forced him,
he shouted:
"He wears no cap or gown, but is shirtless and barefoot.
Why should I bow?"
He became a Jìnshì in the thirteenth year of Yǒnglè.
His parents were old,
so he requested a nearby position to support them.
He was appointed Professor of Nánxióng Prefecture.
There was a shrine behind the school building
where strange lights often appeared.
The school officials and students often prayed and sacrificed there.
Xù demolished and burned it.
After his term,
he was appointed Professor of Jiànníng.
Vice Envoy Wáng Zēng fell ill,
and the physician Xǔ Zōngdào falsely accused the student Yóu Hēng of sorcery,
citing the shrine of the child Wǔláng next to his house as evidence.
Zēng was enraged
and inflicted severe punishment on seven members of Hēng's family,
imprisoning four hundred households of residents near the shrine.
Xù argued vehemently that the Yóu family were not sorcerers,
and Wǔláng was not an evil deity,
but a person who had originally donated land to build the city,
a fact recorded in the prefectural gazetteer.
Zēng was startled
and requested a map and local records to verify it,
feeling greatly ashamed and regretful,
and the matter was resolved.
In the former residence of Zhū Zǐ in Jiànníng,
there was a shrine but no sacrifices.
Xù memorialized to request spring and autumn sacrifices
and exemption of corvée for Zhū Zǐ's descendants.
He also founded the Zūnxiántáng (Hall for Honoring Worthies),
where Hú Ānguó, Cài Shěn, and Zhēn Déxiù were worshipped.
The students were all eager to study.
In the first year of Zhèngtǒng,
based on Yáng Shìqí's recommendation,
he was summoned and appointed Censor.
At that time, the position of Tíxuéguān (Education Commissioner) was newly established,
and he was ordered to supervise schools in the Southern Capital region.
He meticulously established teaching regulations,
greatly revitalizing scholarly conduct.
He memorialized, saying:
"The ancestral sacrifices of the current dynasty
are recorded by the ritual officials.
The practice of setting up fasts began with Emperor Wǔ of Liáng,
and establishing jiao rituals began with Emperor Huīzōng of Sòng.
All of these should be abolished.
Prohibit the establishment of Buddhist and Daoist temples
and cease issuing ordination certificates to monks and nuns."
He further stated:
"Tens of thousands of people from Zhēndìng, Bǎodìng, and Shāndōng have fled to Fèngyáng and Yǐngzhōu.
This is all due to prefects and magistrates concealing disasters and levying excessive taxes.
I request that they be deeply cared for.
For the performance evaluation of prefects and magistrates,
the increase or decrease in household population should be used as the criterion for the best or worst."
He also requested the establishment of military academies in the various guards of Nánjīng.
All were approved.
Wherever he went, he repaired the graves and shrines of former worthies.
When his mother died, he returned home for mourning,
and Sūn Dǐng replaced him.
Xù was reinstated
and transferred to Lángzhōng of the Personnel Evaluation Bureau in the Ministry of Personnel,
then sent out as Vice Envoy of Shāndōng.
During the Tǔmù Incident,
he repeatedly spoke on military matters.
Because of his straightforwardness, he was not tolerated by the times,
so he retired and returned home.
Sūn Dǐng,
courtesy name Yíxuàn,
was a native of Lúlíng.
He was a jǔrén during the Yǒnglè reign.
He successively served as a Professor in Sōngjiāng.
In the eighth year of Zhèngtǒng (1443),
Yáng Pǔ recommended him as a Yùshǐ,
and he oversaw the education administration of Nánjī.
He established the Běnyuán Lù (Record of Origins),
which recorded the good deeds of scholars.
When on inspection tours, he would not let people know in advance,
arriving suddenly in a simple carriage.
When students came to visit,
he would immediately close the gates and test them,
determining their grades on the same day.
When the students returned after the test,
the results were already posted on the main thoroughfare,
leaving no room for those seeking favors.
When Tōngzhōu suffered from drought and famine,
he memorialized to remit over 3,400 dàn of grain taxes.
When Yīngzōng was captured in the north,
Dǐng, having finished testing,
told the students:
"It is customary to hold a 'pin flower banquet' [for successful candidates],
but now is a time for officials and subjects to sleep on their weapons.
I dare not lead you into injustice."
He offered tea [instead],
and personally escorted them to the gates.
Soon after, he went to the imperial court and submitted a memorial,
requesting to offer his life in whatever capacity was needed.
It was not approved.
Not long after,
he retired due to his parents' old age.
The Prefect Zhāng Xuān submitted a memorial stating:
"Dǐng's filial piety rivals Zēng [Shēn] and Mǐn [Zǐqián],
and his scholarship follows Zhū [Xī] and Chéng [Hào/Yí].
He should be appointed to a position of advising the emperor."
The emperor did not agree.
In the first year of Tiānshùn (1457), he died at home.
Xià Shí,
courtesy name Yǐzhèng,
was a native of Qiántáng.
He became a jìshì in the sixteenth year of Yǒnglè (1418).
He was appointed Investigating Censor of the Ministry of Revenue.
In the first year of Hóngxī (1425), there was a discussion about reforming the paper currency system.
Shí strongly argued at the time that it would disrupt the markets
and not benefit national expenditure.
His memorial was held back.
The paper currency indeed suffered a great setback,
and many commoners violated the prohibitions,
so the discussion was eventually shelved.
The emperor remembered Shí's words,
and ordered him to accompany the Crown Prince in sacrificing at Xiàolíng.
Wherever they passed and there were disasters or injuries,
he would report to the Crown Prince,
who would then distribute grain to relieve the suffering.
He was retained to serve in the Ministry of Revenue of Nánjīng.
In the early years of Xuāndé (1426-1435),
he submitted three memorials in one day.
These pleased the emperor,
who ordered him to serve in the Shàngbǎo Division,
concurrently managing the four sections of Personnel, Rites, Military, and Justice,
and overseeing seven seals,
leaving no unfinished business.
He was ordered to audit the Yellow Registers of Hòuhú
and presented fourteen proposals for public benefit.
When Pī, Xú, Jìníng, Línqīng, and Wǔqīng suffered from drought,
upon Shí's request,
officials were dispatched to provide relief.
Soon after, he was promoted to Jiānshì of Jiāngxī.
In the third year of Zhèngtǒng (1438), he memorialized:
"Currently, many local officials impose harsh punishments on the innocent,
harming harmony and violating regulations.
I request that the Yùshǐ and Investigating Censors thoroughly examine all prisoners,
release those wrongly detained,
and arrest and investigate officials who have perverted the law."
This was approved.
He was promoted to Cānyì.
In the seventh year (1442), he memorialized six measures to care for the people,
many of which were adopted.
In the twelfth year (1447), based on recommendations from high officials,
he was exceptionally promoted to Assistant Administrator of Guǎngxī.
He submitted over ten more memorials before and after,
and although not all were adopted,
the people admired his courage in speaking out.
Before reaching the age of seventy,
he retired and returned home,
where he died.
When he was a Jiānshì,
he presented the "Articles for Instructing the People" and the "Equalization of Corvée Labor Register Form" written by the Zhīzhōu Kē Xiān,
and had them published as regulations,
which everyone found convenient.
Shí was a person of integrity and righteousness.
After his parents' deaths,
there were unusual signs when he resided by their tombs.
After his death, his fellow villagers enshrined him,
naming his shrine
"Xiàolián" (Filial and Incorruptible).
Huáng Rùnyù,
courtesy name Mèngqīng,
was a native of Yín.
At five years old,
attending to his sick mother,
he did not sleep at night.
At ten years old,
he saw lost gold on the road but did not pick it up.
In the early years of Yǒnglè (1403-1424),
wealthy families from the south were relocated to settle Běijīng.
Rùnyù requested to go in place of his father,
but the official looked down on him for his youth.
He replied:
"If my father goes,
he will grow older day by day.
If I go,
I will grow older day by day."
The official was surprised by his words
and allowed it.
In the eighteenth year (1420), he passed the Shùntiān provincial examination.
He was appointed Instructor of the Jiànchāng Prefecture School.
After the mourning period for his father,
he was reassigned to Nánchāng.
During the Xuāndé reign,
he was promoted by recommendation to Yùshǐ of Jiāozhǐ Circuit.
He was sent out to inspect Húguǎng,
and impeached one hundred and twenty incompetent officials from the two highest provincial administrations downwards.
In the early years of Zhèngtǒng (1436-1449),
an imperial edict called for the recommendation of education officials.
Based on the recommendation of Yáng Shìqí,
he was promoted to Jiānshì of Guǎngxī,
and appointed Superintendent of Education.
At that time, bandits arose and military campaigns were launched.
A Commander-in-chief wantonly plundered over ten thousand men, women, and children.
Rùnyù impeached him and returned the captives.
The Vice Commissioner Lǐ Lì had sentenced hundreds of commoners to death.
Rùnyù also exonerated them.
The Nándān Guard was located deep in the mountains,
and many garrisons died from malaria.
He memorialized to relocate the ethnic people to a spacious area.
He returned home for his mother's mourning,
then was reinstated as an official in Húguǎng.
He argued for the dismissal of two relatives of the Grand Coordinator Lǐ Shí.
Shí was infuriated,
and memorialized that Rùnyù was unfamiliar with criminal law,
leading to his demotion to Magistrate of Hánshān County.
He returned home due to old age.
He lived at home for twenty years,
and died at the age of eighty-nine.
Scholars referred to him as Nánshān Xiānshēng.
Yáng Zàn,
was a native of Lǐxiàn.
He became a jìshì at the end of the Yǒnglè reign.
As Magistrate of Zhàochéng County,
his administrative achievements were rated the best in Shānxī,
and he was exceptionally promoted to Prefect of Fèngyáng.
In the tenth year of Zhèngtǒng (1445), during the Grand Review of officials throughout the empire,
it was ordered for the first time to recommend those with outstanding governance;
Zàn, Wáng Mào, Yè Xī, Zhào Liàng, and others were among them.
Fèngyáng was the emperor's hometown,
and many descendants of meritorious officials and generals often violated regulations.
Zàn requested to establish households to monitor their comings and goings,
and from then on, they began to obey restrictions.
Zàn stated that there were many capable youths among the common people,
and requested to increase the number of students without a fixed quota.
The Ministry of Rites adopted Zàn's suggestion
to examine and admit students to schools.
The system of "attached students" in schools throughout the empire
began with Zàn's proposal.
He was promoted to Right Assistant Administrator of Zhèjiāng.
He collaborated with the Garrison Vice Minister Sūn Yuánzhēn to suppress the rebellion of Táo Dé'èr.
In the second year of Jǐngtài (1451),
Zàn, noting that the official land taxes in Húzhōu and other prefectures were heavy,
requested to equalize them with the lighter taxes on private land,
and strictly prohibit the malpractice of fraudulent transfers.
An imperial edict ordered him and Yuánzhēn to oversee this,
and land taxes became fair.
After a long tenure,
he died in office.
Wáng Mào,
was a native of Xiūwǔ.
He became a jìshì at the end of the Yǒnglè reign,
and served as Magistrate of Hǎifēng.
Later, he was exceptionally promoted to Prefect of Xī'ān,
and also gained a good reputation.
Yè Xī,
a native of Yǒngjiā.
He became a Jìnshì in the fifth year of Xuāndé.
He served as the Zhīxiàn of Wúxiàn,
and was promoted for his outstanding administration.
When treacherous people impeached him at court,
and he was about to be arrested and imprisoned,
the people of Wú rushed to the palace to praise Yè Xī.
The emperor then ordered him to resume his duties as before,
and punished those who had made false accusations.
Soon after, he was promoted to Zhīfǔ of Níngguó.
Zhào Liàng, who was the Diǎnshǐ of Qìngyún,
was also among those selected [for outstanding service],
and both were honored with a banquet and gifts.
People at the time considered this an honor.
When his term expired,
he was promoted to Zhīxiàn of his home county.
Liú Shí,
courtesy name Jiāxiù,
a native of Ānfú.
He became a Jìnshì in the fifth year of Xuāndé.
After three years,
he was chosen as a Shùjíshì.
In the early Zhèngtǒng era,
he was appointed Tōngpàn of Jīnhuá Fǔ.
During a continuous year of famine and drought,
he requested a remission of taxes,
and also redeemed the children of starving people.
The Zhèng clan of Yìmén, being very large,
could not support themselves.
They had also bought horses and provided laborers
for postal transport in Shānxī,
and were in great distress.
They also obtained exemption due to Liú Shí’s honest report.
He returned home for his mother's mourning,
and dwelled by her tomb for three years.
He then became Zhìzhōng of Shùntiān Fǔ.
During the Jǐngtài era,
attendant ministers recommended him for his literary talent.
He was summoned to revise the Sòng Yuán Tōngjiàn Gāngmù.
Liú Shí was a person of integrity and forthrightness.
If he deemed something unacceptable,
he would not yield even to high officials or nobles.
However, he was quite conceited.
When he saw that the compilation by his colleagues [in the same office] was inappropriate,
he would laugh loudly,
his voice reaching the imperial court steps.
People also resented him for this.
In the early Tiānshùn era,
he was restored to his original post.
Four years later, he was promoted to Zhīfǔ of Nánxióng Fǔ.
The commercial taxes amounted to millions,
which traditionally all went into the prefect's private purse,
but Liú Shí took nothing for himself.
When an imperial eunuch arrived in Nánxióng,
and made slanderous remarks,
the prefectural officials paid their respects.
The eunuch detained Liú Shí and insulted him,
but the people rushed forward to escort him out.
The eunuch felt ashamed,
and intended to summon Liú Shí to apologize,
but Liú Shí did not go.
When the eunuch left,
he reached Sháozhōu.
Hearing people in Sháozhōu say that the Prefect of Nánxióng was about to lodge a complaint at court,
he was frightened.
He immediately submitted a memorial,
falsely accusing Liú Shí of destroying an imperial edict,
an act of great disrespect.
Liú Shí was arrested and imprisoned in the imperial dungeon.
From prison, Liú Shí submitted a letter, stating:
"Your servant has been an official for thirty years.
I have never brought my wife and children with me.
I eat coarse food and wear worn-out clothes.
I have cherished and nurtured the common people for the state,
and could not bear to distress them,
and it is for this reason that I have offended the imperial envoy."
The emperor read the letter,
and his anger somewhat subsided.
He was about to release him,
but Liú Shí unfortunately died in prison.
Liú Shí maintained strict self-discipline.
Despite the myriad of administrative duties,
he never neglected his studies.
Scholars and officials esteemed his learning and conduct.
When he died,
the people of Nánxióng mourned him and built a shrine in his honor.
Sūn Bǐng,
has his own biography.
Chén Xuǎn,
courtesy name Shìxián,
a native of Línghǎi.
His father, Yuántāo,
became a Jìnshì in the fifth year of Xuāndé.
As a Yùshǐ,
he was dispatched to inspect Sìchuān.
He dismissed corrupt officials and praised honest ones,
and cleared the names of over forty death row prisoners.
Towards the end of the Zhèngtǒng era,
when a large army was campaigning against Dèng Màoqī,
he went to appease the local people,
releasing over a thousand families who had been falsely accused of being rebels.
He impeached and dismissed Dū Zhǐhuī Jiǎng Guì who extorted bribes from his subordinates,
and Dūdū Fàn Xióng who was ill and unable to command his troops.
Both were dismissed.
He successively served as Guǎngdōng Yòu Cānzhèng,
and Fújiàn Yòu Bùzhèngshǐ.
Guǎngdōng was still recovering after the rebellion of Huáng Xiāoyǎng,
and in Fújiàn, pirate activities had only recently ceased.
Wherever Yuántāo went,
he comforted, guided, and nurtured the people,
winning the hearts of scholars and common folk.
Chén Xuǎn was upright and taciturn from childhood,
aspiring to be a sage.
In the fourth year of Tiānshùn, he ranked first in the Huìshì,
and became a Jìnshì.
He was appointed Yùshǐ,
and toured Jiāngxī as an inspector,
dismissing all corrupt and cruel officials.
People at the time said:
"First there was Hán Yōng,
then there is Chén Xuǎn."
When bandits from Guǎngdōng flowed into Gànzhōu,
he reported it to the court,
but without waiting for a reply,
he dispatched troops to pacify them.
Upon Emperor Xiànzōng's ascension,
he once impeached Shàngshū Mǎ Áng, Shìláng Wú Fù, and Hónglú Qīng Qí Zhèng.
He also saved Xiūzhuàn Luó Lún,
and Xuéshì Ní Qiān and Qián Pǔ.
Although his words were not fully implemented,
people at the time were intimidated by his integrity.
Later,
he supervised education in Nánjī,
distributing the rites of capping, marriage, sacrifice, and archery in the academies,
ordering students to practice them regularly.
He compiled the Xiǎo Xué Jízhù to instruct the students.
During his inspections, he often stayed overnight in the academies,
patrolling the two wings of the buildings at night,
observing students' recitation and reading.
He abolished the malpractice of covering names on examination papers,
saying:
"If one does not trust oneself,
how can one trust others?"
In the sixth year of Chénghuà, he was promoted to Hénán Fùshǐ.
Soon after, he was reassigned to supervise education,
establishing teaching methods as in Nánjī.
When Wāng Zhí went on an inspection tour,
all officials from the Dū Yùshǐ downwards bowed to him,
but Chén Xuǎn alone greeted him with a long bow.
Wāng Zhí asked what his official rank was,
Chén Xuǎn replied:
"Tíxué Fùshǐ."
Wāng Zhí said:
"Is that greater than a Dū Yùshǐ?"
Chén Xuǎn replied:
"How can Tíxué be compared to Dū Yùshǐ?
But I am a humble teacher,
and dare not humble myself or be disgraced."
Chén Xuǎn's words and demeanor were stern and righteous,
and students also gathered in front of the office.
Wāng Zhí was overawed,
and politely dismissed him.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Ànchásǐ.
He released hundreds of minor offenders,
and many serious cases were re-examined and redressed,
emptying the prisons.
His governance was simple and easy,
but he showed no leniency towards corrupt officials.
However, for those who accepted bribes of a hundred gold or more,
he would stop at a sentence of six or seven shackles.
Someone asked him about this,
and he said:
"Treacherous people value both wealth and life.
If they were to use all their bribes to buy off important people,
then the law would be compromised."
He successively served as Guǎngdōng Zuǒ and Yòu Bùzhèngshǐ.
When Zhàoqìng suffered a great flood,
he issued grain for relief without waiting for approval.
In the twenty-first year, an imperial edict ordered a reduction in tributes,
but Wéi Juàn, the maritime trade eunuch, memorialized requesting sixty corvée households to be added for procuring local products.
Chén Xuǎn argued against this, holding the imperial edict,
The emperor ordered that half be granted,
and Wéi Juàn consequently harbored resentment against Chén Xuǎn.
A foreigner, Mǎlìmá, falsely claimed to be an envoy from Sūméndálà wishing to pay tribute,
but was privately engaged in trade.
Wéi Juàn, coveting his generous bribes,
was about to permit it,
but Chén Xuǎn immediately drove him away.
An envoy from Sāmǎ'érhǎn, who had offered a lion as tribute from Gānsù,
was planning to return by sea via Guǎngdōng,
claiming he wished to go to Mǎnlàjiā to purchase more items for tribute.
Chén Xuǎn memorialized saying this should not be permitted,
fearing it would make China a laughingstock to foreign countries,
and belittle China.
The emperor accepted his words,
but Wéi Juàn greatly resented Chén Xuǎn.
Previously,
Gāo Yáo, the Zhīxiàn of Pānyú, whose family had illicitly traded with foreign powers and amassed vast wealth,
was commended with a transfer and a commendation by Xuǎn,
and this was reported to the imperial court.
By this time, Gāo Yáo's family made a false accusation to the throne, alleging that Xuǎn and Yáo conspired in corruption.
An imperial edict dispatched Lǐ Xíng, a Yuánwàiláng of the Ministry of Punishments, to investigate the matter jointly with Xú Tóng'ài, the Circuit Censor.
Xuǎn had previously dismissed an official named Zhāng Jiǒng.
Gāo Yáo's family, believing that Jiǒng resented Xuǎn,
induced him to provide false testimony against Xuǎn.
Jiǒng firmly refused to comply.
Despite being seized and tortured, Jiǒng did not change his statement.
Xíng and Tóng'ài, intimidated by Gāo Yáo's family,
eventually convicted Xuǎn as per the family's accusation,
and both he and Yáo were summoned to the capital.
Tens of thousands of gentry and commoners wept and blocked their path, pleading for them to stay.
The imperial envoys had to forcefully clear the way before they could proceed.
Upon reaching Nánchāng,
Xuǎn fell ill.
Xíng obstructed his access to medicine and treatment,
and he eventually died.
He was fifty-eight years old.
Biānxiū Zhāng Yuánzhēn arranged Xuǎn's funeral
and interment.
When Jiǒng heard of Xuǎn's death,
he grieved deeply,
and then submitted a memorial stating: "Your subject has heard that mouths can melt gold,
and slander can dissolve bones.
I humbly observe that the late criminal Xuǎn
upheld solitary loyalty,
standing alone amidst a group of villains,
isolated in a
place of widespread hatred.
When the eunuch Gāo Yáo's illicit trade with foreign powers was exposed,
Zhīxiàn Yáo dealt with him according to the law.
Xuǎn issued a document to commend and encourage him,
to stimulate the greedy and the weak,
which was indeed the duty of a virtuous supervisor.
The Censor-in-chief Sòng Mín and Tóng'ài, out of fear of power, harbored evil,
allowing Gāo Yáo's family to act arrogantly and unrestrained,
defiling the pure stream of officialdom.
Investigating official Xíng, following their directions, fabricated evidence,
yet found no corroborating proof.
Your subject
was originally a petty official,
