who inadvertently violated the law,
and was dismissed by Xuǎn;
this was truly self-inflicted.
Gāo Yáo's family believed that your subject harbored resentment against Xuǎn,
and offered lavish bribes to entice me.
Though your subject is but a clerk,
I dared not betray my innate
conscience.
When Gāo Yáo's family realized that your subject could not be swayed,
they incited Xíng and others to arrest your subject and subject him to trial,
torturing him for over a month.
Your subject endured the suffering, appealing to Heaven,
and never changed his testimony.
Xíng and others then
sided with Gāo Yáo's family's words,
crafting their charges,
impeaching Xuǎn for inaccurately investigating disasters,
unauthorized opening of granaries,
improperly protecting subordinate officials,
and intending to seek repayment.
If this were true,
it would be like slandering Jìang as Xià Jī,
or disparaging Bó Yí as Zhuāng Qiāo.
A while ago, an earthquake and flood occurred beyond the Líng mountains,
sweeping away people's homes.
Subordinate prefectures reported the disaster,
and the old and young eagerly awaited sustenance,
yet the Fǔ, Àn, Fān, and Niè officials seemed to have no
knowledge of it.
Only Xuǎn harbored a hidden worry,
unable to eat.
He believed that if he went through the lengthy process of investigation,
the lives of the people would be at stake.
Therefore, he expediently proposed relief,
his intention being to save the people,
nothing else.
Xuǎn was inherently upright and firm,
unable to bear humiliation.
Filled with indignation for ten days,
he fell ill and died.
Xíng, delighting in his demise,
obstructed his medical treatment.
On the day of his
death,
he secretly reported it to Gāo Yáo's family.
The sycophantic malice of petty men
has reached such an extent!
Your subject, a banished criminal,
holds a plow in the fields,
with no other schemes,
sincerely grieving that a loyal and good man suffers
injustice,
thereby bringing discredit upon the sagely dynasty."
The memorial received no response.
Yuán Tāo and his son Xuǎn both maintained extremely pure conduct.
However, Yuán Tāo had a broad mind that could tolerate others,
while Xuǎn was committed to self-restraint,
thus styling himself Kè'ān,
and his approach to things was somewhat stricter.
People said that Yuán Tāo's moral character
encompassed all four seasons,
while Xuǎn embodied its autumn.
He once allocated one hundred forty *mǔ* of land to support his clansmen.
When he died,
his clansmen, seeing that Xuǎn's son, Dài, was poor, returned the land to him.
Dài refused, and so they stopped.
In the early Hóngzhì reign,
Zhǔshì Lín Yí memorialized to clear Xuǎn's injustice,
and an imperial edict restored his official title and granted him a state funeral.
During the Zhèngdé reign,
he was posthumously granted the title of Guānglù Qīng
and given the posthumous name Zhōngmǐn.
Xià Yín,
courtesy name Zhèngfū,
was from Huátíng, Sōngjiāng.
He passed the Jinshi examination in the thirteenth year of Zhèngtǒng.
He was appointed Zhǔshì of the Ministry of Personnel in Nánjīng.
He was diligent in study
and known for his profound and comprehensive writings.
He was promoted to Lángzhōng.
In the first year of Chénghuà, after completing his term, he came to the capital
and presented a memorial saying:
"Xúzhōu is suffering from drought and flood,
the people are unable to make a living,
and severe hunger will certainly
turn them into bandits.
I beg Your Majesty to specially dispatch a high minister to pacify them,
and to remit taxes and issue grain from granaries.
Along the route, the tribute boats
lack sufficient laborers,
and even the old and young are conscripted.
Yet the official goods carried amount to only one box,
the rest being private belongings.
I beg Your Majesty to strictly prohibit and stop this.
The soldiers in Huái, Xú, and Jìníng
are dispatched to the capital for training.
However, these areas are crucial strategic points between the north and south.
It is fitting to establish civil and military officials in each to garrison them,
train soldiers, and cultivate fields,
constantly maintaining communication between the two capitals' forces,
so that in an emergency, they can respond to changes."
The memorial was sent to the relevant departments for implementation,
but the establishment of civil and military officials was not adopted.
He was transferred to be a Fùshǐ of Jiāngxī,
overseeing schools.
His educational priority was moral conduct.
He was promoted to Yòucānzhèng of Zhèjiāng.
The people of Chǔzhōu suffered under oppressive governance
and fled to the mountains and valleys.
Yín issued an order to summon them,
and they all dispersed and returned.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Yòubùzhèngshǐ of Shāndōng.
In the early Hóngzhì reign,
he retired and returned home.
Yín was upright and honest, without partisan affiliations.
He once said to people:
"A junzi has three regrets.
Not studying in this life
is one regret.
Passing this day idly
is the second regret.
Failing in this life
is the third regret."
These are widely regarded as famous words.
Chén Zhuàng,
courtesy name Zhífū,
his ancestors were originally from Shānyīn, Zhèjiāng.
His grandfather was exiled to Jiāozhǐ for an offense.
Later, he was transferred to a capital guard unit,
and thus settled there.
Zhuàng passed the Jinshi examination in the eighth year of Tiānshùn
and was appointed Nánjīng Yùshǐ.
When Biānxiū Zhāng Mào and others were punished for their remonstrances,
he submitted a memorial to save them.
When the emperor dispatched eunuchs to gather flowers and trees,
he again memorialized to admonish.
When Shàngshū Chén Yì proposed substituting horse beans for the salaries of all officials,
Zhuàng argued that feed for horses
should not be used to support scholars and officials.
The matter was then dropped.
Zhuàng Jiā's family was always poor,
apart from his regular salary, he never took anything else.
When his parents died,
he built a hut by their grave,
and observed the mourning rites strictly according to ancient customs.
He served as jiānshì in Jiāngxī,
then retired to return home.
He lived at home for over ten years,
during the Hóngzhì reign,
he was recommended by Shàngshū Zhāng Yuè,
and was appointed to office in Fújiàn.
After two years,
he again requested to retire.
At that time, Ní Yuè was Lìbù,
and always esteemed him,
so he was promoted to Hénán Fùshǐ.
During a famine, he distributed grain to relieve the starving,
and the people cherished his kindness.
Qiāndūyùshǐ Lín Jùn pleaded illness and retired,
and recommended Zhuàng to succeed him.
Before he could be transferred,
Zhuàng again requested to retire.
Xúnfǔ Sūn Xū memorialized to keep him.
After another two years,
he finally retired and left.
Zhāng Bǐng,
courtesy name Zhòngmíng,
was a native of Cíxī,
and the grandson of Dūyùshǐ Kǎi.
He passed the imperial examination as a Jìnshì in the eighth year of Chénghuà,
and was appointed Zhīxiàn of Qiánshān.
He was firm and clear-minded by nature,
and good at judging cases.
There was a man who married off his daughter,
but when they reached the groom's door, the daughter was lost,
and they sued each other at the yámen,
which could not be resolved.
Bǐng was inspecting the county borders,
and saw a large tree obstructing the crops,
and wanted to cut it down.
The people said there was a spirit's nest at its peak.
Bǐng did not listen,
and led a crowd to cut it down.
Three robed figures bowed on the left side of the road.
Bǐng shouted at them,
and they suddenly disappeared.
When the tree was cut,
blood flowed out from between the branches.
Bǐng angrily chopped it with an axe,
and finally felled the tree.
Two women fell out of the nest,
saying a strong wind had blown them to the top of the tower.
One of them was the daughter who had previously been married.
There was a sorcerer who could make himself invisible,
and commit adultery with people's wives and daughters.
Bǐng seized the sorcerer and severely flogged him,
but he felt no pain.
Then,
both the sorcerer and the whips disappeared.
Bǐng quickly tied him up and brought him back,
and branded the sorcerer's back with a whip,
and he died instantly.
Then he destroyed all the idolatrous shrines.
A widow had only one son,
who was devoured by a tiger,
and she reported it to Bǐng.
Bǐng made an appointment with the woman for five days,
then fasted and offered sacrifices to the chénghuáng god.
When the time came,
two tigers crouched in the courtyard,
Bǐng shouted:
"Which of you harmed my people,
and by law deserves to die?
The innocent one may leave."
One tiger stood up,
tucked its tail, and left.
One tiger remained crouched and unmoving,
Bǐng shot and killed it,
and gave it to the chaste woman.
The whole county called him divine.
In the custom of Qiánshān,
when a woman's husband died, she would immediately remarry;
some would even accept betrothal gifts and prepare medicine while their husband was ill but not yet dead.
Bǐng wanted to change this custom,
and ordered all widows to submit a petition for judgment.
He erected two wooden posts.
One was labeled
"Shame,"
and those who remarried knelt before it.
The other was labeled
"Chastity,"
and those who did not remarry knelt before it.
A commoner, Fù Sì Qī, swore to remain chaste until death,
but her parents-in-law tricked her into kneeling under the
"Shame"
post.
Bǐng ruled in their favor,
and Fù Sì Qī threw herself into the pond in the backyard and died.
The county suffered a great drought,
and Bǐng dreamt of a weeping woman bowing.
Upon waking, he recognized her village, address, and name,
and went to inquire about her situation.
When her grave was opened,
her appearance was as if alive.
Bǐng cried mournfully, saying:
"The one who killed this woman
is I."
He wrote a eulogy and offered sacrifices,
and reburied her.
Heaven then sent a great rain.
Many other extraordinary administrative acts were similar to this.
He was promoted to Nánjīng Yùshǐ.
In the seventh month of the first year of Hóngzhì, he joined fellow officials in memorializing:
"Recently, the censors have submitted numerous memorials on current affairs,
but those who attended the imperial procession to correct ceremonies have not escaped the humiliation of being beaten by the Jǐnyīwèi.
This is a gradual obstruction of the path of remonstrance.
The Jīngyán lectures have been held,
yet numerous memorials have been submitted,
but ultimately could not reverse the talk of suspending lectures due to heat or cold.
This is a gradual slackening of imperial learning.
Although the inner favorite Liáng Fāng has been dismissed,
sacrificial offerings are still granted to sycophants.
This is a gradual re-opening of the door to favored flatterers.
Although the imperial relative Wàn Xǐ has been punished,
imperial farms are again granted to imperial relatives.
This is a gradual encouragement of arrogance and indulgence among in-laws.
Although heterodox practices have been banished,
talismans are still displayed within the imperial palace,
and Tibetan monks soon return to the capital.
This is a gradual resurgence of heterodoxy.
Although the practice of 'chuánfèng' (appointment by imperial message) has been abolished,
Zhāng Zhì is again appointed Qiānhù,
and Zhāng Miáo is not removed from Tōngzhèng.
This is a gradual re-opening of chuánfèng.
Textile manufacturing has been halted,
yet we still hear of the weaving of dragon robes and 'ox-dipper' patterns.
Will extravagant crafts gradually reappear?
Precious stones have been banned,
yet we again hear of ill-timed gifts to imperial relatives.
Will valuable curios gradually be prized again?
The Shī Jīng says, 'There is none who does not have a beginning,
but few can bring it to a good end.'
We wish Your Majesty to take this as a warning."
The Emperor graciously accepted it.
Before this,
Bǐng, on account of lightning striking the cypress trees at Xiàolíng,
together with fellow officials impeached Grand Secretary Liú Jí and over ten others.
Jǐshìzhōng Zhōu Hóng also joined fellow officials in impeaching Jí,
and Jí resented him.
That winter,
Bǐng and Hóng were ordered to inspect the army.
Many military units had absent soldiers,
and the two wanted to impeach the eunuch guardian, Jiǎng Cóng.
However, Cóng impeached the two first.
The memorial was sent to the Nèigé,
and Jí, seizing the opportunity,
proposed to dismiss them.
Shàngshū Wáng Shù strongly argued in a memorial:
"If the crime of absent soldiers is not punished,
but the officials who enforce the law are punished,
how can the empire be appeased!"
He submitted another memorial to dispute,
and the censors also spoke in their defense.
Consequently, Bǐng was transferred to Nánjīng Tōngzhèng Sī Jīnglì,
and Hóng to Nánjīng Guānglù Sì Shǔchéng.
After a long time,
Bǐng was promoted to Sìchuān Qiānmìshǐ on recommendation.
A wealthy man committed murder,
and repeatedly escaped punishment by bribery.
The Yùshǐ ordered Bǐng to investigate,
and he indeed uncovered the truth.
Soon after, he was promoted to Fùshǐ.
A eunuch guardian,
whose name is not mentioned, was about to present the occultist Zhōu Huì to the court.
and sentenced him to exile to the remote border.
After more than a year,
he cited illness and returned home.
His home was desolate, with only bare walls,
and he found joy in embracing classics and histories.
Dūyùshǐ Wáng Jǐng arrived to relieve the famine,
and presented Bǐng with a hundred gold pieces.
He firmly refused, but Wang Jǐng insisted, so Bǐng gave the grain to poor starving commoners to express his gratitude.
Zhīxiàn Dīng Hóng,
who was a scholar Bǐng had selected in Qiánshān,
attended to his daily needs,
and prepared vegetarian food for him.
Bǐng said:
"I am indeed unable to support myself,
but why should I trouble Your Honor with this?"
He ultimately refused.
His cooking fire often went out,
but he remained calm and unconcerned.
When he died,
he lacked even proper burial clothes,
and Dīng Hóng managed his funeral arrangements.
Sòng Duānyí,
courtesy name Kǒngshí,
was from Pútián.
He passed the imperial examination in the 17th year of Chénghuà.
He served as a Principal of the Ministry of Rites.
When the position of Education Commissioner for Yúnnán became vacant,
the Ministry proposed Duānyí,
but a clerk leaked the news prematurely.
Duānyí said,
"The memorial hasn't even been submitted,
yet it's already the talk of the town.
People will surely say I solicited the position!"
He vehemently declined it.
Later,
he was promoted to Assistant Director of the Bureau of Receptions.
When tribute envoys offered gifts upon their audience,
he rejected all of them.
Earlier, while at the National Academy,
he was recognized by Sacrificial Libationer Qiū Jùn.
When Jùn held power,
Duānyí never once visited his gate.
When the position of Education Commissioner for Guǎngdōng became vacant,
the Ministry submitted Duānyí's name,
but Jùn ultimately obstructed it.
After Jùn died,
Duānyí was finally appointed Surveillance Vice Commissioner to oversee the schools in Guǎngdōng.
He died in office.
Duānyí lamented that the loyal officials of the Jiànwén reign were forgotten,
so he collected their forgotten deeds
and compiled the *Géchú Lù* (Record of Expulsion).
The existence of a record for Jiànwén's loyal officials
began with Duānyí.
A eulogy states: In the early Míng dynasty, the duties of Surveillance Commissioners, Prefects, and Magistrates were highly valued.
There were instances of Ministers becoming Provincial Administration Commissioners,
and Vice Ministers becoming Administration Vice Commissioners;
and it was common
for Surveillance Commissioners to be promoted to Ministers or Vice Ministers.
Prefects and Magistrates who performed their duties well
might have their ranks increased, even to the second rank.
After Tiānshùn,
the responsibility of the Grand Coordinators (Xúnfǔ) became specialized,
and Surveillance Commissioners, Prefects, and Magistrates could not fully exercise their authority,
thus establishing the tendency to value the internal over the external.
Governing outside the capital
is what is closest to the people.
Lǐ Chāngqí and Chén Běnshēn, among others,
loved the people with tranquility;
Kuàng Zhōng and Zhāng Bǐng were capable in their positions.
Were these not what are called "transmitting the virtues of the emperor
and sharing the emperor's concerns"?
Zhōu Xīn and Chén Xuǎn
died unjustly, which is lamentable.
Reading Zhāng Jiǒng's book,
one also sees the ultimate triumph
of fairness in winning over people
and the enduring nature of righteousness.
Collation Notes

Biographies, Volume 50 Yǐn Chānglóng Gěng Tōng (Chén È) Dài Lún (Lín Chángmào) Chén Zuò (Guō Xún) Liú Qiú (Zǐ Yuè Jū) Chén Jiàn (Hé Guān) Zhōng Tóng (Mèng Yángjí) Zhāng Lún (Zǐ Xuányìng) Liáo Zhuāng Ní Jìng (Shèng Yǒng, etc.) Yáng Xuān (Zǐ Yuán, Shèng Yǒng, etc.)
Yǐn Chānglóng,
courtesy name Yànqiān,
was from Tàihé.
He passed the imperial examination with highest honors during the Hóngwǔ reign.
He was appointed Compiler,
then transferred to Censor.
When Emperor Huì first ascended the throne,
he held court late.
Chānglóng submitted a memorial, advising:
"Emperor Gāo would rise at the crow of the cock,
hold court at dawn,
and oversee all officials before sunrise.
Thus, all affairs prospered,
and the realm enjoyed peace.
Your Majesty, inheriting this great enterprise,
should emulate your ancestor's footsteps,
be diligent and cautious,
and diligently attend to myriad affairs.
Now, however, you indulge in ease,
and even several *kè* (quarter-hours) after sunrise,
you have not yet appeared in court.
Your assembled ministers, guarding the palace,
are wearied by waiting,
neglecting their duties and abandoning their work,
leading to slackness from top to bottom.
If this spreads throughout the realm
and reaches the four borders,
it will not be a blessing for the state."
The Emperor said,
"Chānglóng's words are direct and sincere.
Let the Ministry of Rites announce this throughout the realm,
so that my failings are known."
Not long after,
because of a memorial concerning an earthquake,
he was demoted to Magistrate of Fúníng.
When the Yàn army pressed close,
Chānglóng, in his memorials from the north, repeatedly cited the Duke of Zhōu assisting King Chéng
as a precedent, urging the Emperor to cease hostilities
and permit the Prince (of Yàn) to enter the court.
"Should there be any mishap,
immediately relinquish your position to him.
If you hesitate and remain indecisive, losing your footing in advance or retreat,
you will not even be able to attain the status of a commoner in Dāntú."
When Chéngzǔ entered the capital,
Chānglóng's name was among the "treacherous officials."
Due to his earlier memorial, he was spared death,
and ordered to tutor the Heir Apparent in Běipíng.
In the second year of Yǒnglè,
when the Heir Apparent was officially appointed Crown Prince,
Chānglóng was promoted to Left Expositor of the Left Spring Palace.
He offered timely advice and remonstrance,
and the Crown Prince greatly valued him.
When Xiè Jìn was dismissed,
Chānglóng was transferred to Principal of the Ministry of Rites on the same day.
Minister Lǚ Zhèn was then in power,
and was by nature harsh and malicious.
When he was alone in deep thought,
and would scratch the end of his eyebrow with his finger,
there would surely be a secret and profound scheme afoot.
Officials warned each other
not to report matters to him.
Chānglóng went forward to report a matter,
but Zhèn angrily did not respond.
After some time, he reported it again;
Zhèn became even angrier
and rose, brushing his robes.
Chānglóng retreated and reported it to the Crown Prince,
who then issued an imperial decree to carry it out.
Zhèn was furious
and impeached Chānglóng, accusing him of falsely claiming to represent palace officials,
secretly seeking to establish connections,
and harboring disloyal intentions.
He was arrested and imprisoned.
Soon after, he was pardoned and reinstated.
After mourning his father, he was recalled to office and
visited Zhèn,
who received him with warm words.
But when Zhèn later reviewed Chānglóng's earlier memorials,
he was again imprisoned by the Jǐnyī Wèi,
and his family property was confiscated.
Whenever the Emperor went on tours,
those imprisoned in the imperial prison were often carried along in palanquins,
known as "heavy prisoners accompanying the imperial carriage";
Chānglóng was among them.
Several years later,
the plot of Prince Gǔ to rebel was uncovered.
Because the Prince had previously recommended Chānglóng as his Chief Clerk,
he was implicated as a co-conspirator.
The Emperor ordered the grandees to jointly interrogate him.
Chānglóng debated incessantly,
but Zhèn refuted him.
The case was closed,
and he was sentenced to death by extreme punishment,
and his clan was exterminated.
Later, when Zhèn was gravely ill and near death,
he cried out
"Prime Minister Yǐn!"
saying he saw Chānglóng guarding and trying to kill him.
Gěng Tōng
was from Qídōng.
He was recommended by his locality during the Hóngwǔ reign.
He was appointed Professor of Xiāngyáng.
In the early Yǒnglè reign,
he was promoted to Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Justice,
serving successively as Left and Right Supervising Secretary.
He was upright and outspoken.
He once impeached the Censor-in-Chief Chén Yīng,
and Censors Yuán Gāng and Tán Héng for conspiring to conceal facts
and framing the innocent.
Gāng and Héng had already been imprisoned;
Yīng, as their superior,
should not be pardoned alone.
He also reported that the granaries of the various Metropolitan Cavalry Guards were in disrepair,
and Assistant Minister of Works Chén Shòu had not arranged for their timely repair,
causing much grain to be lost and damaged due to lack of storage, afflicting the people;
and Minister of Works Sòng Lǐ was uncaring towards his subordinates,
for when the quota of artisans and laborers was filled,
he did not immediately send them home,
causing many to lose their livelihoods.
Yīng and others
were all demoted or reprimanded.
At that time,
the Supervising Secretaries brave enough to speak out
were Tōng and Chén È,
and the entire court feared their moral authority.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Right Vice Minister of the Grand Court of Revision.
The emperor went on a northern tour.
The crown prince supervised the state.
Zhū Gāo Xù (朱高煦), Prince of Hàn, plotted to seize the succession.
He secretly colluded with the emperor's attendants to spread slander and create dissension,
and many palace officials were implicated.
Many of the actions taken by the supervising crown prince
were subsequently reversed.
Tán Tōng (譚通) calmly remonstrated with the emperor:
“The crown prince has not committed any major faults or errors;
there is no need to reverse them.”
He repeated this several times.
The emperor was displeased.
In the autumn of the tenth year,
there were accusations that Tán Tōng (譚通) had accepted bribes to release criminals.
The emperor was furious.
He ordered the Dū Chá Yuàn (都察院) to convene civil and military officials to interrogate him at Wǔ Mén (午門),
saying:
“Tán Tōng (譚通) must be killed without pardon.”
The assembled officials, in accordance with the decree,
sentenced Tán Tōng (譚通) to execution by beheading.
The emperor said:
“This 'release of criminals'
is a minor matter.
Tán Tōng (譚通) interceded for the Eastern Palace,
thereby violating ancestral law,
and sowing discord between father and son.
He is unforgivable.
Impose the most severe punishment.”
The court officials dared not argue.
He was ultimately condemned as a traitor
and dismembered.
Chén È (陳諤),
courtesy name Kè Zhōng (克忠),
was from Pān Yú (番禺).
During the Yǒnglè (永樂) reign,
he entered the Tàixué (太學) through a provincial recommendation
and was appointed Xíng Kē Gěi Shì Zhōng (刑科給事中).
He was firm and resolute in his actions,
and feared nothing in his impeachments.
Whenever he presented a memorial,
his voice was as loud as a bell.
The emperor ordered him to be starved for several days,
but his responses remained as before.
The emperor said:
“This is his innate nature.”
Whenever he met him,
the emperor called him
“The Loud Xiùcái (秀才).”
Once, when his words displeased the emperor,
he was ordered to be buried up to his neck at Fèng Tiān Mén (奉天門),
with his head exposed.
He did not die after seven days,
and was pardoned and restored to his post.
Later,
he again displeased the emperor,
and was punished by being assigned to repair the elephant stables.
Being poor, he could not afford to hire laborers,
so he performed the work himself.
When the imperial carriage happened to pass by,
the emperor asked who it was.
Chén È (陳諤) prostrated himself and crawled forward,
explaining the whole situation.
The emperor pitied him
and ordered him reinstated.
He successively served as Shùntiān Fǔ Yǐn (順天府尹).
His governance was strict and severe.
Those in power resented him,
and he was sent out to serve as Húguǎng Àncháshǐ (湖廣按察使).
He was transferred to Shānxī (山西),
but was dismissed from office due to an incident.
When Rénzōng (仁宗) ascended the throne,
he was eligible for reinstatement to his former office under a general amnesty.
However, because the emperor knew that Chén È (陳諤) had previously in Húguǎng (湖廣) extensively scrutinized minor affairs involving the Prince of Chǔ,
he was demoted to Zhīxiàn (知縣) of Hǎiyán (海鹽).
He was promoted to Chángshǐ (長史) for the Prince of Jīng,
but was disliked and troubled by the princely household.
In Xuāndé (宣德) third year, he was promoted to Tóngzhī (同知) of Zhènjiāng (鎮江).
He retired from office and returned home,
where he died.
Dài Lún (戴綸)
was from Gāomì (高密).
During the Yǒnglè (永樂) reign,
he was promoted from Xùndǎo (訓導) of Chāngyì (昌邑) to Lǐ Kē Gěi Shì Zhōng (禮科給事中).
He and Biānxiū (編修) Lín Chángmào (林長懋) both served as tutors to the imperial grandson.
He successively held the positions of Zhōngyǔn (中允) and Yùdé (諭德).
When Rénzōng (仁宗) ascended the throne,
and the imperial grandson became the crown prince,
Dài Lún (戴綸) was promoted to Xǐmǎ (洗馬),
and continued to serve as a lecturer.
Initially, Chéngzǔ (成祖) ordered the imperial grandson to practice military affairs,
and the imperial grandson himself also greatly enjoyed it,
often going out for riding and archery.
Dài Lún (戴綸) and Lín Chángmào (林長懋), considering that the imperial grandson was still young and in his prime,
thought it inappropriate for him to neglect his studies for hunting expeditions,
and frequently offered remonstrances.
Dài Lún (戴綸) also submitted a detailed memorial to the emperor about this.
Another day,
when the imperial grandson was in attendance,
the emperor asked:
“Who among your palace officials do you get along with best?”
The imperial grandson replied with Dài Lún (戴綸).
The emperor then took out Dài Lún’s (戴綸) memorial and gave it to him.
From this, the imperial grandson resented Dài Lún (戴綸).
Lín Chángmào (林長懋)
was from Pútián (莆田).
Through a provincial recommendation, he successively served as Jiàoshòu (教授) of Qīngzhōu (青州),
and was promoted to Biānxiū (編修).
At the beginning of Rénzōng’s (仁宗) reign,
he was promoted to Zhōngyǔn (中允).
He was firm and strict in character,
repeatedly offered candid advice,
and was on good terms with Dài Lún (戴綸).
When Xuānzōng (宣宗) ascended the throne,
he extended favor to palace officials,
and promoted Dài Lún (戴綸) to Bīngbù Shìláng (兵部侍郎).
Soon after,
again for remonstrating against hunting and displeasing the emperor,
he was ordered to serve as Cānzàn Jiāozhǐ Jūn Wù (參贊交阯軍務).
Lín Chángmào (林長懋), who came later from Nánjīng (南京),
also came to be sent out as Zhīzhōu (知州) of Yùlín (鬱林).
Not long after,
they were both arrested and brought to the capital on charges of resentment and discontent,
and imprisoned in the Jǐnyī Wèi (錦衣衞) jail.
The emperor personally presided over their interrogation.
Dài Lún (戴綸) argued vehemently,
provoking the emperor’s wrath.
He was immediately beaten to death with a rod,
and his property confiscated.
His elder brothers Dài Xián (戴賢), the Zhīfǔ (知府) of Hénán (河南),
and Dài Xīwén (戴希文), the Tàipú Sì Qīng (太僕寺卿), were both imprisoned.
Lín Chángmào (林長懋), however, remained in prison for ten years.
When Yīngzōng (英宗) ascended the throne,
he was finally released.
His office was restored to him,
and he returned to govern Yùlín (鬱林),
where he implemented benevolent policies.
When he died,
the people of the prefecture erected a temple to worship him.
Chén Zuò (陳祚),
courtesy name Yǒngxī (永錫),
was from Wú (吳).
He became a Jìnshì (進士) during the Yǒnglè (永樂) reign.
He was promoted to Hénán Cānyì (河南參議).
In the fifteenth year, he, along with Bùzhèngshǐ (布政使) Zhōu Wénbāo (周文褒) and Wáng Wénzhèn (王文振), jointly submitted a memorial arguing that establishing the capital in Běijīng (北京) was inconvenient,
and all were demoted to tenant farmers on Tàihé Shān (太和山) in Jūnzhōu (均州).
He personally tilled the land and worked hard,
and lived contentedly.
When Rénzōng (仁宗) ascended the throne,
an imperial edict was issued to select and employ those officials who had been demoted.
Chén Zuò (陳祚) was among those selected.
However, the emperor died,
and he was not ultimately employed.
In Xuāndé (宣德) second year, the Xìanchén (憲臣) were ordered to test all the officials in Jūnzhōu (均州),
and Chén Zuò’s (陳祚) policy essay was ranked first.
He was tested by the Lìbù (吏部),
and again ranked first.
He was then promoted to Yùshǐ (御史),
and appointed Circuit Inspector of Fújiàn (福建).
Many high-ranking local officials were impeached by him.
He prohibited forced purchases,
and the people of Mǐn (閩) were grateful to him.
Upon his return, he reported that Bái Tǎ Hé (白塔河) connected to Shàobó Hú (邵伯湖) upstream,
and flowed into the Dà Jiāng (大江) downstream.
Many boats from Sūzhōu (蘇州) and Sōngjiāng (松江) passed through it.
It was shallow, narrow, and obstructed,
so he requested that it be dredged.
This was approved,
and grain transport indeed became much easier.
Soon after,
he was sent out to inspect Jiāngxī (江西).
At that time, the empire was at peace,
and the Emperor indulged somewhat in hunting and amusements.
Zuò (祚) submitted a memorial urging the Emperor to diligently pursue sacred studies.
Its summary read:
"The study of emperors and kings begins with clarifying principles,
and clarifying principles lies in reading books.
Although Your Majesty possesses sagely virtue,
the imperial lectures have not been greatly promoted,
and the standard for scholarship has not been established.
How then can the profound subtleties of the sages,
and the governance and disorder of past and present,
be fully known and clearly understood?
Zhēn Déxiù's (真德秀) work, *Dàxué Yǎnyì* (大學衍義),
contains all the maxims of the sages.
I wish that during the leisure from attending to government affairs,
Your Majesty would command scholarly officials to lecture on it,
and unless there is a major reason,
there should be no interruption.
This will enable you to know how the past was governed,
and how political affairs were achieved.
It will surely broaden your intelligence,
enhance your virtuous achievements,
and those sycophants who use cunning and cleverness to sway the imperial heart will naturally be estranged,
and the people of the empire will receive boundless blessings."
The Emperor saw the memorial and was furious, saying:
"Does this petty scholar mean to say that I have not read *Dàxué* (大學)?!
To slight me to this extent,
I must not fail to execute him."
The Grand Academician Chén Xún (陳循) kowtowed and said:
"This common fellow lives far away
and does not know that there is no book His Majesty has not read."
The Emperor's anger somewhat subsided.
Zuò (祚) was cast into prison,
and over ten members of his family were arrested,
separated and confined for five years,
and his father eventually died of illness in prison.
At that time,
Guō Xún (郭循), a Ministry of Justice junior secretary, advised against expanding the Western Imperial City to repair a detached palace.
He was arrested and interrogated face-to-face.
Xún (循) argued defiantly and unyieldingly,
and was also imprisoned.
When Yīngzōng (英宗) ascended the throne,
Zuò (祚) and Xún (循) were both released and restored to office.
Zuò (祚) was again appointed to inspect Húguǎng (湖廣).
Because he reported that Liáo Wáng (遼王) Guìjiǎ (貴烚) had concealed some of his crimes,
he and the巡撫 Xúnfǔ (巡撫) Vice Minister Wú Zhèng (吳政) were arrested and brought to the capital,
and imprisoned.
They were soon pardoned and released.
At that time, Wáng Zhèn (王振) was in power,
and the laws were enforced with great severity.
Zuò (祚) submitted a memorial saying:
"Recently, the judicial authorities, in deciding cases,
have often violated established laws.
For example, Vice Minister Wú Xǐ (吳璽) mistakenly nominated junior secretary Wú Yuè (吳軏);
he should have been charged under the law concerning 'nominating unsuitable persons for official selection,'
but instead, he was sentenced to decapitation under the law concerning 'evasion in reporting matters.'
And when Yuè (軏) hanged himself,
the prison officials and wardens should have had their sentences successively reduced,
but instead, they were all flogged, citing the rule for 'not committing a serious crime.'
If one matter is like this,
the rest can be inferred.
The heavens are out of accord,
and calamities are frequently seen;
this may not be unrelated."
The Emperor approved of this,
and showed his memorial to the judicial authorities.
Soon after, he was transferred to Nánjīng (南京),
and promoted to Assistant Investigating Censor of Fújiàn (福建).
He wielded both authority and benevolence;
all shrines not recorded in the sacrificial canon were demolished.
After a long time,
he returned home due to illness,
and died.
Zuò (祚) was by nature stern and resolute;
even his children rarely heard his laughter,
but he uniquely esteemed his townsman Xíng Liáng (邢量).
Liáng (量) was a widely learned scholar,
who lived in seclusion as a diviner,
with a few dilapidated rafters for a house,
sometimes not lighting a fire for an entire day.
Zuò (祚) often brought books to him to ask questions,
often staying until evening.
Guō Xún (郭循),
courtesy name Xúnchū (循初),
was a native of Lúlíng (廬陵).
He had a reputation for talent in officialdom.
After being reinstated,
he was promoted to Lángzhōng (郎中),
and through the recommendation of Minister Wèi Yuán (魏源),
he was promoted to Administrative Vice Commissioner of Guǎngdōng (廣東),
where he had achievements in suppressing bandits.
He died early in the Jǐngtài (景泰) reign.
Liú Qiú (劉球),
courtesy name Tíngzhèn (廷振),
was a native of Ānfú (安福).
He became a *jìnshì* (進士) in the nineteenth year of Yǒnglè (永樂).
He studied at home for ten years,
and many came to learn from him.
He was appointed Junior Secretary of the Ministry of Rites.
Hú Yíng (胡濙) recommended him to serve in the imperial lectures,
and he participated in compiling the Veritable Records of Xuānzōng (宣宗),
after which he was transferred to Hanlin Compiler.
His cousin, Bīn (玭), who was Magistrate of Pútián (莆田),
sent him a piece of ramie cloth.
Qiú (球) returned it sealed,
and sent a letter warning him.
In the sixth year of Zhèngtǒng (正統),
the Emperor, swayed by Wáng Zhèn's (王振) words,
launched a major expedition against Lùchuān (麓川).
Qiú (球) submitted a memorial saying: "When emperors and kings govern the four barbarian tribes,
they must pardon their minor offenses and guard against their major threats,
so as to adapt to the exigencies of the situation,
and plan for the long-term peace of the empire.
Zhōu (周) attacked Chóng (崇)
without success,
and retreated to cultivate virtue and teachings to await its submission.
As for the Xiǎnyǔn (玁狁),
Nán Zhòng (南仲) was ordered to build a city at Shuòfāng (朔方) to prepare for them.
Hàn (漢) was unsuccessful in conquering Nányuè (南越),
and immediately withdrew
troops, bestowed letters, and established friendly relations.
As for the Xiōngnú (匈奴),
even after having established a 'harmonious kinship' policy,
the people were still recruited to relocate to the border,
and grain was brought in to provision the border,
and Wèi Shàng (魏尚) was again ordered to guard Yúnzhōng (雲中) and resist them.
Now, Sī Rènfā (思任發), the remnant leader of Lùchuān (麓川), was originally a subject,
but due to the border general's mismanagement,
he caused the deployment of a large army.
Although the chief villain has not been annihilated,
many of his followers have been killed.
Whether to execute or to spare,
it is not a matter of minor or major importance.
The imperial edict pardoned his crimes,
allowing him to reform,
which is a great virtue.
The border general, failing to grasp the sacred intention,
again proposed a major expedition,
intending to station 120,000 troops in Yúnnán (雲南),
to compel his surrender;
if he does not surrender, then to attack him.
They do not consider that the imperial army should not be easily deployed,
that barbarian nature cannot be quickly tamed,
that the terrain
is treacherous and unsuitable for large armies,
and that guest troops cannot be stationed for long.
Moreover, the southern regions are plagued by successive droughts and floods,
leaving both soldiers and civilians in distress.
If troops are mobilized again,
it will lead to widespread worry and chaos.
Your servant humbly
suggests that the heavenly punishment should be delayed,
just as Zhōu (周) and Hàn (漢) treated Chóng (崇) and Yuè (越).
As for Wǎlà (瓦剌),
they will eventually become a border threat.
Before they begin to cause immediate trouble,
it is precisely the right time to defend against them.
Yet, they want to transfer the Gānsù (甘肅) garrison commander to engage in the southern campaign.
If a sudden alert arises,
how will it be defended?
Your servant humbly believes that cautious defense and resistance are appropriate,
just as Zhōu (周) and Hàn (漢) treated the Xiǎnyǔn (玁狁) and Xiōngnú (匈奴).
I earnestly hope that Your Majesty will dismiss the proposal for a major expedition,
select wise and strategic generals,
assist them with capable and discerning high officials,
mobilize imperial troops proportionally,
and station them at the strategic points of Jīnchǐ (金齒)
and other crucial locations,
and forge alliances with the various tribes of Mùbāng (木邦) for support,
attacking when opportune,
and pacifying when convenient.
The rebels will then naturally submit.
As for the northwestern barriers and fortresses,
border officials should be ordered to patrol
and inspect,
dredge and build moats and walls,
reinforce and repair castles,
diligently train,
and strictly guard and watch,
to prevent unforeseen events,
which is the way of being prepared and having no worries."
The memorial was sent to the Ministry of War.
They stated that the southern campaign had already been decreed,
and Qiú's (球) words were not adopted.
In the fifth month of the eighth year, lightning struck the Fèngtiān Diàn (奉天殿).
Qiú (球) responded to the imperial summons by submitting a memorial outlining ten priorities.
Its summary read: "Ancient sage kings did nothing useless,
thus their hearts were upright and Heaven did not oppose them.
Your servant wishes that His Majesty would diligently attend the imperial lectures,
frequently summon scholarly officials,
and earnestly seek the ultimate Way,
It is essential that scholarship reaches its ultimate
depth, and that reason and desire are clearly distinguished;
then the sagely mind will be upright, and the heavenly mind will naturally be compliant.
When government originates from oneself,
power will not be transferred downwards.
Tàizǔ and Tài
zōng observed three audiences daily,
and often summoned high ministers to the private palace to decide on all matters of government,
centralizing power with the emperor.
Your Majesty has been on the throne for nine years,
and governmental affairs are becoming increasingly familiar.
It is hoped
that Your Majesty will adhere to the established rules of the two sagely emperors,
and personally resume deciding on routine matters,
so that power is unified.
In ancient times, when choosing high ministers,
one would invariably consult those on the left and right, grand masters, and the people of the state.
When they committed an offense,
even if it warranted the death penalty, no torture would be inflicted;
they would merely be granted
death.
Nowadays, the appointment of high ministers is not always based on public opinion,
and when they make a small mistake,
they are immediately bound and flogged.
However, not long after,
they are reinstated to their positions,
which is certainly not the
way to treat high ministers.
From now on, when selecting high ministers,
public opinion should be fully satisfied.
Minor offenses should be overlooked.
If they are truly intolerable,
they should be handed over to the judicial authorities to determine the penalty,
allowing them
to plan for themselves.
Do not readily imprison them,
so as not to violate the spirit of sharing heavenly duties.
The contemporary Tàicháng
is the Zìzōng of ancient times.
One must appoint officials who are incorruptible, cautious, and well-versed in rituals,
only then can they communicate with the gods and spirits.
Currently, both the chief and deputy positions are vacant;
it is advisable to select
Confucian scholars
to take on these roles.
In ancient times, rulers inspected the four quarters and made imperial tours
to observe the successes and failures of officials,
and to inquire about the people's hardships.
During the flourishing periods of the Two Hàn, Táng, and Sòng dynasties,
envoys were frequently dispatched to tour the commanderies and counties.
During the Hóngwǔ and Yǒnglè reigns, this practice was also carried out.
It has not been performed for a long time now,
which is why many officials are corrupt and cruel,
and the people are struggling to survive;
the military garrisons are particularly affected.
It is advisable to select upright, fair, incorruptible, and capable
ministers
to travel throughout the realm.
Ancient rulers did not personally handle criminal cases;
they invariably entrusted them to judicial officials,
fearing that they might be swayed by their likes and dislikes, leading to arbitrary decisions of leniency or severity.
Recently, among the cases submitted by the judicial authorities,
many have been subject to imperial edicts
to increase or decrease the severity.
The judicial authorities are unable to remonstrate,
and when questioning other prisoners,
they also observe and imitate these changes in severity,
leading to many injustices among the people.
It is advisable to let each perform their duties.
As for
regulations such as transporting bricks and supplying rice,
they are all not ancient practices,
and should especially be abolished.
The Spring and Autumn Annals recorded all construction projects,
as a warning against burdening the people.
Construction in the capital has been ongoing for five or six years;
it is said not to trouble the people but to employ the army.
Are the soldiers not also the nation's own
children?
Moreover, much of the construction is complete;
it is advisable to halt the work to allow them to recover their strength.
In various places suffering from floods and droughts,
since the officials do not provide relief,
the request to reduce taxes
might also be a mere formality.
It is advisable to order the Hùbù to provide timely relief,
and to appropriately reduce
and exempt taxes,
so that people do not lose their livelihoods.
Lùchuān has been at war for consecutive years;
seventy or eighty percent have died,
and military expenses and rewards are countless.
Now, Jiǎng Guì has again been dispatched to campaign against Miàndiàn,
to demand the capture of Sī
jīfā.
If he is captured and brought back,
he will merely be executed in the public thoroughfare.
The Miàndiàn general, taking this as his achievement,
will surely demand to share the territory with Mùbāng.
If not granted, it
will lead to anger;
if granted, both barbarian tribes will grow powerful,
which means reducing one Lùchuān to create two Lùchuān.
Should there be any setback,
the military conflict will be endless.
Your servant has observed that Your Majesty, when
recording serious criminals,
often pardons them and orders them to join the army;
such is Your compassionate heart.
Now, to capture alive an exiled bandit who has lost his territory,
and yet drive tens of thousands of innocent people to their
deaths,
would this not be contrary to the benevolence of cherishing life?
Moreover, Sī Jīfā has already sent people to offer tribute,
not without the intention of repenting and begging for pardon.
If an edict were issued to Miàndiàn to behead
Rènfā and bring his head as tribute,
and another edict were issued to Sī Jīfā to cede all territory within his four borders,
distributing it among the newly surrendered barbarian tribes in various stockades,
then the region could be pacified.
The number of tribute envoys from Yǐběi increases daily;
they harbor malicious intentions,
which are truly unpredictable.
It is advisable to dispatch Gěishì and Yùshǐ officials to inspect the imperial and border garrisons,
and train them in a timely manner,
not allowing them to borrow labor for various workshops
or serve in private households.
Make public the selection of military scholars to seek good generals,
establish a method for recruitment to attract brave warriors,
expand military farms,
and make the salt
laws public
to accumulate reserves,
so that military preparedness is complete,
and external threats are guarded against.
The memorial was submitted
and sent to the court for deliberation.
Regarding the matters raised by Yán Qiú,
only the selection of Tàicháng officials was approved,
ordering the Lìbù to make recommendations.
Xiūzhuàn Dǒng Lín then requested to change his official post to Tàicháng
to preside over sacrificial rites.
Initially,
when Qiú spoke about the Lùchuān affair,
Zhèn Gù already resented him.
Péng Déqīng, the Director of the Qīntiānjiān,
was a fellow townsman of Qiú
and had always been a close confidant of Zhèn.
Whenever there were astronomical anomalies,
he would conceal them and not report them,
relying on Zhèn's influence to commit wicked deeds.
Many high officials and nobles would visit him,
but Qiú absolutely refused to associate with him.
Déqīng hated him,
and thus picked out the phrase about usurping power from Qiú's memorial,
saying to Zhèn:
"This refers to you, sir."
Zhèn became even more furious.
At that time, Lín's memorial was submitted,
and Zhèn then accused Qiú of being a co-conspirator,
arresting both and sending them to the imperial prison,
and ordering Commander Mǎ Shùn to kill Qiú.
Late at night, Shùn took a junior officer with a knife to Qiú's cell.
Qiú, who was lying down,
stood up
and loudly called out "Tàizǔ! Tàizōng!"
His neck was severed,
but his body remained upright.
They then dismembered him
and buried him beneath the prison door.
Lín secretly took a blood-stained skirt from the side and sent it to Qiú's family.
Later, his son Yuè found an arm,
wrapped it in the skirt, and interred it.
Shùn's son, who had been ill for a long time,
suddenly rose, grabbed Shùn's hair,
punched and kicked him, saying:
"Old villain!
May your future calamity exceed mine!
I am
Liú Qiú!"
Shùn was terrified.
Soon after, his son died,
and the junior officer also died.
Lín,
courtesy name Déwén,
was from Gāoyóu.
He was known for his filial piety.
After being released from prison,
he returned home
and never served again.
Liú Qiú died several years later,
and the Wǎlà indeed invaded.
Yīngzōng was taken captive to the north,
and Zhèn was killed.
The court officials together struck Shùn,
killing him.
Meanwhile, Déqīng, having escaped from Tǔmù, returned,
was imprisoned and sentenced to execution.
Soon after, he died in jail from illness.
An imperial edict ordered his corpse to be dismembered.
Jǐngdì, pitying Liú Qiú's loyalty,
posthumously bestowed upon him the title of Hàlín Xuéshì,
and the posthumous name Zhōngmǐn.
A shrine was erected for him in his hometown.
Liú Qiú had two sons,
the elder Yuè and the younger Jū.
Both were diligent in their studies,
and personally tilled the land to support their mother.
Once Liú Qiú's posthumous honors were granted,
the brothers then came out to take the imperial examinations,
and successively became Jìnshì.
Yuè served as
Guǎngdōng Cāncèng;
Jū served as
Yúnnán Ànchásǐ.
Chén Jiàn,
courtesy name Zhēnmíng,
was a native of Gāo'ān.
He became a Jìnshì in Xuāndé 2nd year.
He was appointed Xíngrén.
During the Zhèngtǒng reign,
he was promoted to Yùshǐ.
He was dispatched to inspect Shùntiān.
He reported that the customs in the capital were corrupt and degenerate,
the reasons for which were five: Firstly,
excessive devotion to Buddhism;
secondly,
impoverishing families through elaborate funerals;
thirdly,
extravagant clothing and food;
fourthly,
actors and singers causing harm;
fifthly,
gambling becoming widespread.
The memorial was sent to the Lǐbù,
but was not implemented.
He was reassigned to inspect Guìzhōu.
At that time, the chieftain of Lùchuān, Sī Rènfā's son Sī Jīfā, had fled to Mèngyǎng,
and repeatedly submitted petitions requesting pardon for his crimes and permission to offer tribute.
This was not granted,
and instead a large-scale distant expedition was launched again.
The war dragged on without resolution,
and the military and civilians of Yúnnán and Guìzhōu were exhausted.
The Miáo seized the opportunity to incite unrest,
and bandits arose in great numbers between Mǐn and Zhè.
The entire court knew that this was unsustainable,
but, remembering the disaster that befell Liú Qiú,
none dared to remonstrate.
In the first month of Zhèngtǒng 14th year,
Jiàn boldly submitted a memorial stating that the bandit chieftain had fled far away,
and no longer posed a border threat.
He suggested that the Yúnnán defense officials should be solely responsible for evaluating the situation and剿滅 them,
without exhausting the imperial armies with distant campaigns.
Wáng Zhèn was furious,
and wanted to make things difficult for him.
He reassigned Jiàn as Yúnnán Cānyì,
sending him to Téngchōng to recruit the bandits.
Afterward,
he further accused Jiàn of having once requested, when he was a circuit inspector, that the Sìchuān Bōzhōu Xuānwèisī be transferred to Guìzhōu,
making this a crime of Jiàn's.
He ordered the Bīngbù to impeach him,
and he was sentenced to death and imprisoned.
When Jǐngdì ascended the throne,
he was pardoned.
Soon after, he was appointed Hénán Cānyì.
He retired and returned home,
where he died.
From the middle of the Zhèngtǒng reign,
Liú Qiú died unjustly for offending Wáng Zhèn,
and Jiàn was subsequently imprisoned.
For several years, no one, neither inside nor outside the court, dared to speak up.
It was not until Jǐngdì's time
that the path for remonstrance finally opened,
and people vied to express their indignation through memorials.
There was Hè Guān,
who again incurred displeasure by his words and was dismissed.
Guān was a Zhōngshū Shèrén because of his good calligraphy.
In Jǐngtài 2nd year, he impeached ministers like Wáng Zhí, saying that during the Zhèngtǒng reign, they had flattered powerful corrupt officials,
and thus should not be by the emperor's side.
The eunuchs saw "powerful corrupt officials" in his words,
and took it as an attack on themselves.
They incited the emperor's anger,
who then sent it to the Kēdào for deliberation.
Máo Yù of the Lìkē drafted the memorial,
strongly criticizing Guān.
Lín Cōng and Yè Shèng insisted on it,
so they revised and submitted the memorial.
At the same time, an imperial censor's memorial was also submitted,
which contained
the words: "Guān, not promoted after his term,
secretly resented the Lìbù."
The emperor was furious,
imprisoned Guān in the imperial prison,
caned him,
and demoted him to Jiǔxī Wèi Jīnglì.
Zhōng Tóng,
courtesy name Shìjīng,
was a native of Yǒngfēng, Jí'ān.
His father, Fù,
obtained the Jìnshì degree in the Xuāndé reign.
He successively served as Xiūzhuàn,
and was good friends with Liú Qiú.
When Liú Qiú submitted his sealed memorial,
he invited Fù to go with him.
Fù's wife persuaded him to desist.
Liú Qiú went to Fù's residence
to invite him to go together.
Fù had already gone elsewhere,
and his wife, from behind a screen, scolded, saying:
"You submit your own memorial,
why involve others!"
Liú Qiú left, sighing:
"He even consults his wife."
He then submitted the memorial alone,
and ultimately died.
Not long after,
Fù also died of illness.
His wife deeply regretted it,
and whenever she cried, she would say:
"Had I known this,
why not have died together with Master Liú!"
Tóng, as a child, heard his mother's words,
and was immediately inspired,
thinking of fulfilling his father's ambition.
He once entered the Jí'ān Zhōngjié Shrine,
and seeing the enshrined figures of Ōuyáng Xiū, Yáng Bāngyì, and others,
he sighed:
"To die without entering this place
is not to be a true man."
In Jǐngtài 2nd year, he obtained the Jìnshì degree,
and the following year was appointed Yùshǐ.
After Huáixiàn Tàizǐ had died,
everyone, both inside and outside the court, hoped for the restoration of Yí Wáng to the Eastern Palace.
Tóng and Lángzhōng Zhāng Lún met at court early in the morning,
and when they spoke of Yí Wáng,
both shed tears,
and thus agreed to memorialize requesting the restoration of the heir apparent.
In the fifth month of Jǐngtài 5th year,
Tóng submitted a memorial discussing current affairs,
and then also brought up the matter of restoring the heir apparent.
Its gist was: "Recently, I received intelligence from a bandit spy,
who said that Yěxiān had sent scouts to reconnoiter the capital and Línqīng for their vulnerabilities,
planning a large-scale deep invasion in early autumn,
directly advancing to Hénán.
Upon hearing this, I cannot help but
feel a chill in my heart,
yet the high ministers in the imperial court are all nonchalant.
In ancient times, when Qín attacked Zhào,
the other feudal lords remained indifferent,
but Kǒngzǐ Shùn alone worried about it,
and people all thought him mad.
My
words today,
how are they different from this?
When I was a commoner,
I heard that the eunuchs conspired wickedness,
murdering the upright official Liú Qiú,
which led to the court officials being silenced.
Supposing that at that time,
Had there been someone at that time who dared to speak frankly,
they would surely have been able to admonish and stop the actions of the Former Emperor,
and thus avoid the disaster of being captured and humiliated.
Your Majesty has gloriously achieved a middle restoration,
uprooting traitorous factions,
commending the loyal and upright,
and ordering the six armies to guard against the enemy in the suburbs.
Without even fighting, the morale of the three armies has spontaneously doubled.
Your servant believes that Your Majesty is about to whip and chastise the four barbarian tribes,
and thus bring about great peace.
How then, when the border turmoil has barely subsided,
and the wounds have not yet healed,
can a desire for extravagance suddenly arise,
disappointing the hopes of the empire?
I humbly implore you to take warning from past mistakes,
and exert yourself with renewed vigor.
Do not succumb to wealth and women,
do not indulge in pleasure and games.
Personally attend to state affairs to centralize authority,
strengthen ethical principles to improve social customs,
distinguish between good and evil to ensure proper appointments,
enforce strict rewards and punishments to clarify right and wrong,
and uphold the supervisory system to rectify discipline.
Eliminate wasteful expenditures,
dismiss redundant officials,
prohibit Buddhist and Daoist priests from preying on the people,
and select worthy generals to train the soldiers.
Then, personally lead all your ministers
to offer apologies at the ancestral temples and altars,
emulating Chéng Tāng's (成湯) self-reproach with six matters,
and Táng Tàizōng's (唐太宗) swift correction of ten transgressions.
Perhaps then the will of Heaven can be turned,
and the national power can be revived.
He further said: A father who possesses the empire
is naturally expected to pass it on to his son.
However, the Crown Prince has passed away,
which clearly indicates that Heaven's mandate lies elsewhere.
Your servant humbly believes that the son of the Former Emperor
is also Your Majesty's son.
Yí Wáng (沂王) is endowed with profound natural gravity,
and is fully capable of safeguarding the ancestral altars.
I humbly hope that you will expand your boundless magnanimity,
and embrace the benevolence of brotherly affection,
abolish the mourning
rites,
and reinstate the Crown Prince's position.
This would truly be an immeasurable blessing for the ancestors.
He also said: Your Majesty ordered the generals and commanders to each present their strategies,
but for days and weeks,
they merely shifted blame among themselves.
And when Shí Hēng (石亨) and Liǔ Pǔ (柳溥) spoke,
their plans were nothing more than those of common folk or mere children.
If it is like this in peacetime,
what strategy will be used to control the situation
should an emergency suddenly arise?
Indeed, in methods of resisting the enemy,
nothing is more important than employing the worthy.
Your Majesty seeks worthy individuals as if parched,
yet
the obstruction and suppression by senior ministers are even more severe.
Those recommended are mostly relatives, old acquaintances, and wealthy families.
If truly talented individuals are suppressed,
who would be willing to speak?
The court officials are deceitful to this extent;
this is why your servant clutches his chest and weeps,
for this day's obstruction of the worthy and harm to the state is shameful.
When the memorial was submitted,
the Emperor was displeased,
and sent it down to the court officials for deliberation.
Níngyáng Hóu (寧陽侯) Chén Mào (陳懋) and Minister of Personnel Wáng Zhí (王直) and others requested the Emperor to accept his words,
and then pleaded guilty and sought retirement.
The Emperor consoled and retained them.
A few days later,
Zhāng Lún (章綸) also submitted a memorial concerning the reinstatement of the Crown Prince,
and was consequently imprisoned along with him.
In August of the following year,
Dàlǐ Shàopíng (大理少卿) Liáo Zhuāng (廖莊) was also flogged for speaking about Yí Wáng (沂王).
Those around the Emperor said that the matters stemmed from the same instigator,
so the Emperor sealed a large club and sent it to the prison to flog him,
and he died there.
He was thirty-two years old at the time.
When he submitted his memorial,
he rode out on his horse,
but the horse lay down on the ground and refused to get up.
He reprimanded it, saying:
"I am not afraid of death,
what are you doing?"
The horse still hesitated and balked repeatedly,
before finally proceeding.
When he died,
the horse also let out several long cries and died.
When Yīngzōng (英宗) was restored to the throne,
he posthumously appointed him Dàlǐ Zuǒ Sìchéng (大理左寺丞),
and enrolled his son Qǐ (啟) as a Guózǐshēng (國子生),
later appointing him Zhīxiàn (知縣) of Xiánníng (咸寧).
Qǐ (啟) requested to take his father's remains home for burial,
and an imperial edict provided boats, carriages, and travel expenses.
During the Chénghuà (成化) reign,
his second son Yuè (越) was appointed Tōngzhèng Zhīshì (通政知事),
and his wife, Madame Luó (羅), was given a monthly stipend.
Later, he was granted the posthumous title Gōngmǐn (恭愍),
and was honored with sacrifices in the Zhōngjié Cí (忠節祠),
his position aligned with that of Qiú (球),
thus finally fulfilling his initial aspirations.
At the time he was imprisoned,
there was a Lǐbù Láng (禮部郎) named Mèng (孟),
who also submitted a memorial concerning the reinstatement of the Crown Prince.
The Emperor did not punish him.
Meanwhile, the Jinshì (進士) Yáng Jí (楊集) wrote a letter to Yú Qiān (于謙), saying:
"The treacherous person Huáng Xiàn (黃獻) proposed changing the heir apparent,
which was nothing more than a plan to escape death,
yet you and others swiftly agreed to it.
You are pillars of the state,
do you not consider how to handle the aftermath well?
Now he and others are again imprisoned.
If these individuals die under the cudgel,
and you and others enjoy high positions,
what will public opinion say?!"
Yú Qiān (于謙) showed the letter to Wáng Wén (王文).
Wáng Wén (王文) said:
"This scholar does not know taboos,
but he has courage.
He should be promoted one rank."
So, Yáng Jí (楊集) was appointed Zhīzhōu (知州) of Ānzhōu (安州).
He was from Mǐn (閩);
Yáng Jí (楊集) was from Chángshú (常熟).
Zhāng Lún (章綸),
courtesy name Dàjīng (大經),
was from Lèqīng (樂清).
He passed the Jinshì (進士) examination in the fourth year of Zhèngtǒng (正統).
He was appointed Nánjīng Lǐbù Zhǔshì (南京禮部主事).
At the beginning of the Jǐngtài (景泰) reign,
he was summoned to be Yízhì Lángzhōng (儀制郎中).
Zhāng Lún (章綸) saw that the nation was in great trouble,
and often spoke out passionately on affairs of state.
He once submitted sixteen policies for great peace,
comprising over ten thousand words.
After Yěxiān (也先) had agreed to peace, Zhāng Lún (章綸) urged vigorous efforts to repair and prepare for changes.
The palace eunuch Xīng'ān (興安) asked the Emperor to build the Dàlóngfú Sì (大隆福寺),
and was about to visit it,
but Zhāng Lún (章綸) submitted a detailed memorial of admonition.
Yáng Hào (楊浩) of Jǐnán (濟南), the Salt Transport Sub-Prefect of Hédōng (河東), who had been appointed but not yet taken office,
also submitted a memorial of admonition.
The Emperor immediately canceled the visit.
Yáng Hào (楊浩) later rose through the ranks to Fù Dū Yùshǐ (副都御史),
and served as Xúnfǔ (巡撫) of Yánsuī (延綏).
Zhāng Lún (章綸) also inquired into the reasons for transformations due to natural disasters,
his words being quite urgent and direct.
In the fifth year, in the fifth month,
Zhōng Tóng submitted a memorial requesting the restoration of the heir apparent.
Two days later,
Lún also strenuously memorialized on fourteen matters concerning cultivating virtue and averting disaster.
The major points were:
“Inner officials must not interfere with external governance;
sycophantic ministers must not be given authority over affairs;
the inner palace must not be filled with music and beautiful women.
All matters pertaining to the flourishing of yin [power],
I request be entirely prohibited and abolished.”
He further stated:
“Filial piety and brotherly submission
are the foundation of all conduct.
I wish that after the morning court, Your Majesty would visit the two Grand Empresses Dowager,
to observe the rites of inquiring about their well-being and supervising their meals.
The former Emperor reigned over the world for fourteen years;
he is the father of the world.
Your Majesty personally received the enfeoffment;
you are the former Emperor’s subject.
Your Majesty and the former Emperor,
though different in form,
are in reality one person.
I respectfully read the edict welcoming him back to the palace, which stated: ‘Ritual is only to be augmented, not abolished;
righteousness dictates serving the exalted with humility.’
I hope Your Majesty will truly follow these words.
Whether on the first and fifteenth day of the lunar month,
or on festival days,
lead your assembled officials to pay respects at Yánhé Mén,
to display the affection between brothers,
which is truly the deepest wish of the world.
Furthermore, I request the restoration of Empress Wāng to the central palace,
to set the motherly example for the world;
and the restoration of the Prince of Yí to the position of heir apparent,
to establish the great foundation of the world.
If this is done, harmony will overflow,
and calamities will naturally be averted.”
When the memorial was submitted,
the Emperor was greatly enraged.
At that time, it was already dark,
and the palace gates were closed.
He then issued an imperial decree through a crack in the gate,
and immediately ordered Lún and Zhōng Tóng to be arrested and imprisoned in the imperial prison.
They were subjected to brutal torture,
forced to implicate masterminds and confess to communicating with Nángōng.
Nearing death,
they uttered not a single word.
It happened that a great wind blew up sand,
making it dark during the day,
so the imprisonment was slightly eased,
and they were ordered to be confined.
The following year, Liáo Zhuāng was flogged below the palace gate;
then the same flogging staff was taken to the prison to flog Lún and [Zhōng] Tóng one hundred times each.
Zhōng Tóng died,
while Lún remained imprisoned as before.
When Yīngzōng was restored to the throne,
Guō Dēng stated that Lún, along with Liáo Zhuāng, Lín Cōng, Zuǒ Dǐng, Ní Jìng, and others, had all spoken frankly and offended the times,
and ought to be honored and promoted.
The Emperor then immediately released Lún.
He ordered an inner official to retrieve the former memorial,
but it could not be found.
An inner official recited a few sentences from memory,
and the Emperor sighed and praised him repeatedly,
promoting him to Vice Minister of Rites (Yòushìláng).
Although Lún was esteemed by the Emperor for his great integrity,
his nature was proud and unyielding,
and he could not get along with common customs.
Shí Hēng, a favored noble, invited high officials to drink;
Lún declined to go.
He also frequently disagreed on matters with Minister Yáng Shàn.
Shí Hēng and Yáng Shàn together slandered Lún,
who was then transferred to the Ministry of Rites in Nánjīng,
and subsequently reassigned to the Ministry of Personnel.
When Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
the relevant authorities, citing the posthumous edict, requested a grand wedding.
Lún said:
“The imperial tomb is still new,
the new year has not yet been changed [to reflect the new reign],
and one hundred days of mourning for good fortune should be observed.
It will certainly settle itself.
At the beginning of Your Majesty’s reign,
you should govern the world with filial piety,
as the three cardinal guides and five constant virtues truly originate from this.
I beg that it be held next spring.”
Although the proposal was not adopted,
the world respected his words.
In the first year of Chénghuà,
there was a famine in the two Huái regions;
he memorialized four measures for famine relief.
All were approved.
In the autumn of the fourth year,
his son Xuányìng fraudulently registered to sit for the imperial examination in the capital.
Censor Zhū Qīng and Imperial Censor Yáng Zhì, among others, impeached Lún on this account,
and Minister Yè Shèng was ordered to investigate.
The following year,
Lún and Vice Censor-in-Chief Gāo Míng conducted an evaluation of minor officials,
After the memorial was submitted,
and the two did not agree.
and further stated that Gāo Míng was stubborn and self-willed,
and that many of his own words were not heeded,
requesting that both he and Gāo Míng be dismissed.
Both memorials were sent down to Yè Shèng and others.
Consequently, Wáng Ràng and the officials who received low evaluations jointly impeached Lún.
Lún also repeatedly memorialized to request his dismissal.
The Emperor did not allow it.
Soon after, Yè Shèng and others confirmed that Xuányìng had indeed fraudulently registered.
The Emperor pardoned Lún,
and his other memorials [regarding the evaluation]
were also entirely disregarded.
Not long after,
he was again transferred to the Ministry of Rites.
Fàn Kuí, the Prefect of Wēnzhōu, was criticized and reassigned.
Lún said:
“Wēnzhōu is my hometown,
and Kuí has greatly won the hearts of the people.
On the day he left office,
thirty thousand scholars and commoners wept and clung to his carriage,
detaining him for eighteen days before he could depart.
I request that he be reinstated to satisfy the people’s hopes.”
The memorial was sent to the relevant department,
but was ultimately shelved.
Lún was foolishly blunt,
fond of frank speech,
and not liked by those in power.
He served as Vice Minister for twenty years,
and was not promoted,
so he requested to retire.
He died after a long time.
Several years later,
his wife, née Zhāng, presented his memorial drafts,
and requested imperial favor.
The Emperor praised him,
posthumously appointed him Minister of Rites of Nánjīng,
gave him the posthumous name Gōngyì,
and gave one of his sons a position as a Honglu Temple official (Hónglú Diǎnbù).
Xuányìng later passed the imperial examination,
and became a Censor of Nánjīng.
Together with fellow officials, he criticized Chén Yuè,
which displeased the Emperor, and his salary was suspended.
When Xiàozōng succeeded to the throne,
he submitted five proposals on fundamental governance.
He ultimately served as Provincial Administration Commissioner of Guǎngdōng.
Liáo Zhuāng,
courtesy name Ānzhǐ,
was from Jíshuǐ.
He became a *Jìnshì* in the fifth year of Xuāndé.
In the eighth year, he was reassigned as a *Shùjíshì*,
and along with Magistrate Kǒng Yǒuliàng and seven others, served in the six offices.
At the beginning of Yīngzōng’s reign,
he was appointed Censor of the Ministry of Punishments (Xíngkē Gěishìzhōng).
In the second year of Zhèngtǒng,
Imperial Censor Yuán Liàng requested, in accordance with the imperial edict, to remit the misappropriated grain rations for border troops,
but this was not granted.
Surveillance Commissioner Gōng Suì also requested, in accordance with the imperial edict, to pardon unapprehended thieves,
but the Ministry of Justice also shelved the matter.
Liáo Zhuāng believed that imperial edicts should be trustworthy,
and memorialized to argue for it.
In the fifth year, an edict ordered capital officials to go out to manage famine relief,
and simultaneously collect outstanding taxes from the people.
Liáo Zhuāng, fearing that envoys would press the distressed people,
requested leniency for disaster-stricken prefectures and counties,
to wait until the autumn harvest,
which was granted.
He provided famine relief in Shǎnxī,
saving many lives.
Upon returning, he memorialized nine matters for leniency and relief,
many of which were enacted.
When Yáng Shìqí’s family committed crimes,
he, along with fellow officials, reported them.
Someone said:
“Do you not make allowances for Master Yáng?”
He replied:
“Precisely because it is for Master Yáng.”
In the eighth year, he was ordered to jointly manage affairs of the Dali Temple with Imperial Censor Zhāng Jì.
After more than a month,
he was appointed Assistant Minister of Dali Temple (Zuǒ Sìchéng).
In the eleventh year, he was promoted to Vice Minister of Dali Temple of Nánjīng (Nánjīng Dàlǐ Shǎoqīng).
More than two years later,
a villain named Chén Fū,
and his relative Jiǎ Fú, disputed the hereditary commandery office.
Qí Sháo, the Vice Minister of Punishments of Nánjīng, accepted a bribe from Chén Fū,
intending to seize Jiǎ Fú’s office and give it to him,
but this was rejected by Liáo Zhuāng.
Qí Sháo beat Jiǎ Fú to death,
and was arrested.
Chén Fū also falsely accused Liáo Zhuāng,
and both were summoned to the imperial prison.
It happened that Qí Sháo’s other crimes were also discovered,
and he was executed in the marketplace,
whereupon Liáo Zhuāng was released.
In the seventh month of the fifth year of the Jǐngtài reign, he submitted a memorial which stated:
"When I was formerly in court,
I saw the Former Emperor send envoys to enfeoff Your Majesty.
Whenever there was a felicitous occasion,
he would certainly order all officials to pay respects at the eastern wing (Dōngwǔ),
showing abundant grace and courtesy.
All officials were moved and exclaimed,
'The Former Emperor's brotherly affection is truly remarkable.'
Now Your Majesty holds the empire to serve the Former Emperor.
I wish that Your Majesty would frequently pay respects at the Southern Palace (Nángōng),
perhaps to explain the family rules,
or to discuss the methods of governance.
On seasonal festivals,
allow officials to pay their respects,
to comfort the heart of the Former Emperor.
Then the spirits of the ancestors in heaven will be at peace,
and the heart of Heaven and Earth will also be at peace.
The Crown Prince
is the foundation of the empire.
The Former Emperor's son
is Your Majesty's nephew.
It is fitting to appoint scholars as his companions,
to study books and records,
in anticipation of the birth of the imperial heir.
This will make it clear to the officials and common people of the empire that Your Majesty possesses a heart of public spirit for the empire.
Would this not be excellent?
For the empire
belongs to Tàizǔ and Tàizōng.
Rénzōng and Xuānzōng, who inherited and preserved it,
ruled this empire.
The Former Emperor's northern expedition
was also for this empire.
Now Your Majesty governs and possesses it;
it is fitting to remember the ancestors' hardship in founding the enterprise,
and to ponder how to secure the hearts of all under Heaven.
There is no better way to avert disaster and invite auspiciousness than this."
The memorial was submitted,
but there was no reply.
The following year,
Zhuāng went to the capital for his mother's mourning,
to apply for a verification document (kānhé),
and went to the Eastern Corner Gate (Dōngjiǎomén) to pay respects.
The Emperor remembered Zhuāng's previous memorial,
and ordered him to be flogged eighty times with the court staff,
and demoted him to stationmaster of Dìngqiāng (Dìngqiāng Yìchéng).
At the beginning of the Tiānshùn reign,
he was recalled.
At that time, his mother's mourning was not yet over,
and he again suffered his father's passing.
He was specially granted rites and burial,
ordered to be restored to office,
and continued his post in Nánjīng.
In the fifth year of Tiānshùn, he was promoted to Right Vice Minister of the Board of Rites (Lǐbù Yòu Shìláng),
then transferred to the Board of Punishments (Xíngbù).
At the beginning of the Chénghuà reign,
he was summoned to be Left Vice Minister of the Board of Punishments (Xíngbù Zuǒ Shìláng).
He died the following year.
He was posthumously granted the title of Minister (Shàngshū)
and the posthumous name Gōngmǐn.
Zhuāng was of a resolute nature,
and liked to openly point out people's faults,
but he was truly open-minded and bore no grudges.
He disdained meticulous propriety,
and enjoyed entertaining guests with familiarity and fondness.
After he became an official in the judicial administration (fǎsī),
some advised him to somewhat reduce his social interactions
to avoid suspicion.
Zhuāng laughed and said,
"An ancient said, 'An official's gate is like a market,
but an official's heart is like water.'
I have no shame in my heart, that is all."
On the day of his death,
there was nothing for his burial,
so people pooled money to assist with his funeral.
Initially,
during the Jǐngdì Emperor's reign,
Yīngzōng was in Nángōng,
and his attendants caused estrangement.
When Crown Prince Huáixiàn died,
the petty officials feared that Prince Yí would be re-established,
and their slanders and schemes became even more intense.
Therefore, Zhōng Tóng, Zhāng Lún, and Zhuāng successively spoke forcefully,
and all incurred punishment,
yet the Emperor was somewhat moved and enlightened.
On the Xīnsì day of the seventh month of the sixth year,
Xú Zhèng, a supervising secretary of the Ministry of Punishments (Xíngkē Gěishìzhōng), requested a private audience to speak.
He was urgently summoned,
and then he said:
"The Former Emperor governed for many years,
and Prince Yí once held the position of heir apparent;
the officials and common people of the empire looked up to him.
It is fitting to move him to his enfeoffed territory
to cut off people's hopes.
And select another son of a princely relative to raise in the palace."
The Emperor was startled,
became greatly enraged,
and immediately ordered him to be expelled,
wanting to punish him.
Fearing to alarm the populace,
he ordered him demoted to a distant post,
but the Emperor's anger had not yet subsided.
Soon after,
further immoral acts were discovered,
and he was demoted to garrison at Tiělǐng Guard (Tiělǐng Wèi).
Although the Emperor was angry at the excessive words of Tóng and others,
he did not immediately listen to the words of petty individuals either.
When Yīngzōng was restored to the throne,
Yú Qiān and Wáng Wén were executed for planning to establish an external prince,
and the matter was thus never clarified.
That is all.
Ní Jìng,
courtesy name Rǔjìng,
was a native of Wúxī.
He became a *jìnshì* in the thirteenth year of Zhèngtǒng.
He was promoted to Censor (Yùshǐ).
At the beginning of the Jǐngtài reign,
the capital region (jīfǔ) suffered from famine,
and he was ordered to inspect it.
He requested the exemption of land taxes,
but the Board of Revenue (Hùbù) maintained that it was impossible.
He memorialized twice in protest,
and eventually received approval.
He then served as Circuit Censor (Xún'àn) in Shānxī.
At that time, there was an order allowing people to donate grain for official appointments;
Jìng memorialized to have it abolished.
He investigated and punished all garrison generals who embezzled provisions,
and the powerful and cunning ceased their activities.
He then served a second term as Circuit Censor in Fújiàn.
At that time, there was a discussion about reopening the silver mines;
Jìng, before he had departed,
submitted a strong memorial arguing against it,
and it was shelved.
After arriving,
he memorialized to abolish the excessive requisitioning of articles from the people by various government offices.
The garrison eunuch Dài Xìbǎo was corrupt and tyrannical,
and Jìng listed his crimes for the Emperor to hear.
The Emperor recalled Dài Xìbǎo
and ordered Jìng to arrest and prosecute his associates;
officials and common people rejoiced.
Upon his return from the assignment,
he stayed at home for four months,
was arrested and prosecuted,
but soon reinstated.
In the seventh month of the sixth year,
due to numerous calamities and unusual phenomena at the time,
he, along with his colleagues Wú Jiāng Shèng Yuán (吳江盛●), Jiāngyīn Dù Yòu, Wúhú Huáng Ràng, Ānfú Luó Jùn, and Gùshǐ Wāng Qīng, submitted a memorial stating:
"The wealth in the imperial treasury
should not be given away without reason;
matters of sightseeing
should not be carried out at inappropriate times.
Formerly, to provide meals for monks,
imperial funds were repeatedly used to purchase rice.
How then can the border soldiers, who endure wind and rain,
and the poor people, who diligently attend to public duties,
be assisted?
Recently, we heard of the construction of dragon boats,
the building of banquet halls,
daily increasing construction,
and no small amount of leisurely enjoyment.
This is not the way to nourish the imperial person.
Zhāng Lún and Zhōng Tóng spoke frankly and met with displeasure,
imprisoned for over a year.
This is not the way to manifest sagely virtue.
We humbly request that the offerings to Buddhist monks be stopped,
the pleasures of banquets and leisure be ceased,
the construction projects be halted,
and the imprisonment of upright officials be leniently handled."
The Emperor received the memorial with displeasure,
and sent it to the Board of Rites (Lǐbù).
The Board officials praised their loyalty and love.
The Emperor heard their report,
but his resentment ultimately did not dissipate.
Soon after,
an imperial edict ordered Grand Censor Xiāo Wéizhēn to evaluate his subordinates,
instructing him to dismiss them.
Sixteen censors were dismissed and demoted,
and Jìng and others were among them;
all were demoted to records keepers (diǎnshǐ),
and Jìng was assigned to Yíshān in Guǎngxī.
When Yīngzōng was restored to the throne,
an edict ordered all of them to be appointed county magistrates (zhīxiàn),
so Jìng was made magistrate of Xiángfú.
The Marquis of Ānyuǎn, Liǔ Pǔ, appreciated Jìng,
and when he went on a western expedition,
requested that Jìng accompany him,
so Jìng was changed to Secretary of the Chief Military Commission (Dūdūfǔ Dūshì).
He died the following year after the army returned.
Scholars lamented his passing.
Shèng ● and four others,
all were *jìnshì*.
● Jùn was forthright and strong-willed.
He once inspected Guǎngdōng,
and impeached Vice Minister Jiē Qí, the Provincial Governor, for dereliction of duty.
Qí was demoted.
● Later, he became the Magistrate of Luójiāng,
and was promoted to Prefect of Zhōu.
