He also had achievements in repelling bandits.
Dù Yòu was the Magistrate of Yīngdé.
The neighboring areas were plagued by bandits,
so he established a county wall.
He was once besieged, and provisions ran out,
but Yòu held out steadfastly.
At night, he lowered a suicide squad to burn the bandit camp,
and only then did the bandits scatter in panic.
He was transferred to be the Assistant Prefect of Sháozhōu,
but resigned due to illness.
Huáng Ràng was the Magistrate of Ānyuè,
and was transferred to be the Senior Clerk of the Central Prefecture.
Because he flogged a subordinate of the Imperial Bodyguard,
he was slandered by Mén Dá
and exiled to Guǎngxī.
After an amnesty, he returned
and regained his official rank.
He was very poor,
and supported himself by farming.
Luó Jùn once inspected Sìchuān,
and had a reputation for integrity.
His career ended as the Prefect of Nánxióng.
Yáng Xuān,
courtesy name Tíngxiàn,
was from Fēngchéng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the fifth year of Jǐngtài
He was appointed Censor.
He was upright and valued integrity.
When Emperor Jǐng was unwell,
court officials requested the establishment of an heir apparent.
The emperor did not consent.
Xuān and his colleagues Qián Jǐn, Fán Yīng, and others planned to submit a memorial to argue for it,
but
the "seizure of the gate"
incident occurred,
so they stopped.
In the early Tiānshùn era,
horses were being registered within the capital region.
When they reached Héjiān,
the people complained that Cáo Jíxiáng and Shí Hēng had seized their land.
Xuān reported this,
and also listed the two men's abuses of power due to imperial favor.
The emperor said to Grand Secretaries Lǐ Xián and Xú Yǒuzhēn:
"He is a true Censor!"
He then dispatched officials to investigate,
and ordered the Ministry of Personnel to note Xuān's name,
intending to promote him.
Jíxiáng heard of this and was afraid.
He complained to the emperor,
requesting that Xuān be punished.
The emperor did not allow it.
Not long after,
Hēng returned from his western campaign.
Just as a comet appeared,

the thirteen supervising censors of circuits Zhāng Péng, Shèng Yóng, Zhōu Bīn, Fèi Guǎng, Zhāng Kuān, Wáng Jiàn, Zhào Wénbó, Péng Liè, Zhāng Kuí, Lǐ Rén Yí, Shào Tóng, Zhèng Miǎn, Táo Fù, and Censors Liú Tài, Wèi Hàn, Kāng Jì were about to impeach Hēng and Jíxiáng for various illegal acts.
One day earlier,
Assistant Minister Wáng Xuàn leaked the information to Hēng.
Hēng and Jíxiáng tearfully complained to the emperor,
falsely accusing Péng and the others of being the nephews of the already executed eunuch Zhāng Yǒng,
who had formed a faction to frame them,
seeking revenge for Yǒng.
The next day, when the memorial was submitted,
the emperor was furious
and arrested Péng and Xuān.
He held court in the Wénhuá Hall,
summoned all the censors,
threw their impeachment memorial,
and made them read it themselves.
Bīn read and answered,
his expression calm.
When he reached the part about "falsely claiming credit and abusing positions,"
the emperor questioned him, saying:
"He led generals and soldiers to welcome the imperial carriage.
The court discussed their merits and awarded them.
How can you say it was false claim and abuse?"
Bīn replied:
"At that time, only a few hundred people welcomed the imperial carriage.
The Imperial Banqueting Court provided food and drink,
and the attendance records are all there.
Now, the number of those promoted has reached several thousand.
What is this if not false claim and abuse?"
The emperor remained silent,
and eventually sent Xuān, Péng, and the other censors to prison.
They were severely tortured
to extract the mastermind,
but Xuān and the others implicated no one.
Thus, Metropolitan Censors Gěng Jiǔchóu and Luó Qǐ were deemed the masterminds
and also imprisoned.
Xuān and Péng were sentenced to death,
and the rest were exiled to garrisons.
Hēng and others again slandered other remonstrating officials.
The emperor instructed the Ministry of Personnel
to retain assistant ministers and censors over thirty,
and transfer all others to external posts.
Minister Wáng Áo listed thirteen assistant ministers including Hé,
and twenty-three censors including Wú Zhēn.
An imperial edict ordered Hé and the others to be prefectural judges,
and Zhēn and the others to be county magistrates.
At that time, there was a great wind and thunder,
uprooting trees and unroofing houses,
followed by a sudden downpour of hail.
The large trees at Hēng's and Jíxiáng's homes were all broken,
and the two also became fearful.
Tāng Xù, Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites and head of the Imperial Astronomical Bureau, who was originally Hēng's partisan,
also stated that Heaven was showing a warning,
and that the prisons should be treated mercifully.
At this, the emperor was enlightened,
exiled Xuān and Péng to Tiělǐng Guard,
demoted the others to county magistrates,
reinstated Tài, Hàn, and Jì,
and Hé, Zhēn, and the others also escaped transfer.
When Xuān and Péng were halfway on their journey,
the Chéngtiān Gate suffered a disaster,
and a general amnesty was issued, releasing them.
Some suggested they should go to Hēng and Jíxiáng to express gratitude,
but the two ultimately refused,
and were again demoted and exiled to Nándān.
Upon Emperor Xiànzōng's ascension,
they were all restored to their former offices.
Xuān soon moved up to be Zhejiang Surveillance Vice Commissioner.
He inspected the sea routes
and forbade officers from privately releasing garrison soldiers.
He repaired sea defenses,
and built two thousand three hundred *zhàng* of seawalls in Hǎiyán,
allowing the people to settle peacefully.
He served as Vice Commissioner for over ten years,
with outstanding administrative achievements,
and was promoted to Surveillance Commissioner.
The waters of the West Lake traditionally irrigated forty-six thousand *qǐng* of fields in various counties,
but by then, more than half was silted up.
Xuān requested to dredge it.
He set up defenses and installed sluice gates
to facilitate irrigation,
but before the project was completed,
he died.
The people of Hǎiyán worshipped him in a shrine.
His son, Yuán,
courtesy name Běnqīng,
studied astronomy from a young age,
and was appointed to the Five Offices of the Astronomical Bureau.
In the first year of Zhèngdé
when Liú Jǐn and others were corrupting the government,
Yuán submitted a memorial:
"Since the beginning of the eighth month,
the stars in Dàjiǎo and Xīnsù have been constantly restless.
Dàjiǎo is
the seat of the Heavenly King,
and the central star of Xīnsù is
the true position of the Heavenly King.
Both should be calm,
but now they are restless.
The prognostication states: 'The ruler is uneasy,
and the nation has worries.'
Perhaps Your Majesty's impulsive pleasure trips,
and excessive hunting,
have led to this.
Moreover, the second, third, and fourth stars of the Northern Dipper
are not as bright as usual.
The second, called Tiānxuán,
is the symbol of the empress and imperial concubines.
If empresses and concubines do not receive favor, it will not be bright;
if grand palaces are built or mountains and tombs are senselessly excavated, it will not be bright.
The third, called Tiānjī,
if the people are not loved,
or if sudden levies and conscriptions are imposed, it will not be bright.
The fourth, called Tiānquán,
if decrees are inappropriate, it will not be bright.
I humbly wish that Your Majesty would revere Heaven's warnings,
reside peacefully in the deep palace,
forsake frivolous amusements,
forbid hunting expeditions,
cease riding and archery,
halt construction projects,
reinforce strict decrees,
do not lightly go in and out,
suppress and distance favored sycophants,
curtail and economize grants,
befriend elder ministers,
devote days to study and practice,
and truly cultivate your virtue,
to avert disasters."
The memorial was sent to the Ministry of Rites.
Minister Zhāng Shēng and others praised Yuán's loyalty and love.
The report was acknowledged.
By the tenth month,
haze and fog often appeared.
Yuán said:
“This is the emanation of all evil influences,
Yīn overriding Yáng,
ministers deceiving their ruler,
petty men usurping power,
and inferiors about to rebel against superiors.”
His analogies were very apt.
Jǐn was enraged,
and falsely ordered him to be flogged thirty times,
then released him.
He also submitted a memorial saying:
“Since the second year of Zhèngdé,
astrological observations show Huǒxīng entering before the Dìzuò in the Tàiwēi Yuán,
sometimes east, sometimes west,
moving irregularly.
I beg Your Majesty to reclaim the reins of government
and think of troubles to prevent them beforehand.”
This was clearly aimed at Jǐn.
Jǐn was furious,
summoned him, and scolded him, saying:
“What official are you,
to also try to act as a loyal minister?”
Yuán retorted sternly:
“The rank of official differs in size,
but loyalty is one.”
Again, a false imperial order was given for him to be flogged sixty times
and exiled to Sùzhōu.
When he reached Hèyáng Station,
he died from his injuries.
His wife cut reeds to cover him,
and buried him behind the station.
The Yáng family father and son were renowned throughout the empire for their loyal remonstrance,
and were highly regarded by scholars.
However, Yuán, as a minor official, upheld his integrity,
which was especially difficult for others.
At the beginning of Tiānqǐ,
he was posthumously granted the title Zhōnghuái.
Shèng Yǒng,
courtesy name Shíwàng,
was from Wúxī.
Zhōu Bīn,
courtesy name Guóyòng,
was from Chānglí.
Wáng Jiàn
was from Tàiyuán.
Zhào Wénbó
was from Dàizhōu.
Péng Liè
was from Xiájiāng.
Lǐ Rényí
was from Lóngchāng.
Shào Tóng
was from Mǐnxiàn.
Zhèng Miǎn
was from Lèpíng.
All were successful candidates in the imperial examinations,
and were appointed Censor.
Yǒng was demoted to Magistrate of Shùlù;
Bīn
to Jiāngyīn;
Jiàn
to Fūshī;
Wénbó
to Chúnhuà;
Liè
to Jiāngpǔ;
Rényí
to Xiāngyáng;
Tóng
to Bóluó;
Miǎn
to Héngshān.
All had excellent administrations.
In Shùlù, the corvée labor was unfairly distributed,
so Yǒng established the "Nine Regulations Law,"
which his successors could not change.
He left due to mourning his mother.
After the mourning period,
the people collectively went to the imperial court to petition for his return.
Yǒng served a second term,
and increasingly avoided using whips and floggings.
When litigants appeared,
he would instruct them,
and they would invariably kowtow and no longer dispute.
Unresolved disputes from neighboring prefectures
also came to him for judgment,
and he would settle them with a single word,
each person leaving satisfied.
There was vacant land outside the city,
and people flocked to build houses and live there,
which then became a market,
known as
“Qīngguān Diàn” (Shop of the Honest Official).
Bīn had benevolent policies in Jiāngyīn.
The people sang:
“When drought brought disaster,
Zhōu Gōng prayed and sweet dew came;
when flood brought calamity,
Zhōu Gōng prayed and the overcast rain dispersed.”
In the seventh year of Tiānshùn,
he was first promoted to Prefect of Kāifēng by recommendation.
As for Yǒng and the others, when Xiànzōng succeeded to the throne,
the appropriate offices reported on their administrative achievements.
The emperor said:
“These officials remonstrated directly and were suppressed by powerful favorites,
yet they could still perform their duties competently.
Let them all be granted prefectures.”
Thereupon, Yǒng was promoted to Prefect of Shàowǔ;
Jiàn
to Yán'ān;
Wénbó
to Wèihuī;
Liè
to Hénán;
Rényí
to Jīngzhōu;
Tóng
to Wēnzhōu;
Miǎn
to Héngzhōu.
Yǒng was again transferred to Yánpíng
due to his ability to govern difficult areas.
The Supervising Censor submitted a report on Yǒng’s administrative achievements,
and the governors of Shǎnxī and Húguǎng also reported on Jiàn and Rényí’s administrative conduct while serving as magistrates,
all of whom were specially granted imperial edicts of commendation.
Yǒng was successively promoted to Left Administration Commissioner of Shǎnxī.
At that time, the three borders frequently faced alarms,
and the year was again plagued by continuous famine.
Yǒng managed the provisioning and supplies without shortage,
and both soldiers and civilians were peaceful.
In the seventeenth year of Chénghuà, he was summoned to be Right Vice Minister of the Ministry of Justice.
After two years,
Shāndōng suffered from drought and famine,
and bandits rose up.
Yǒng was transferred to Left Vice Censor-in-Chief to go and act as Grand Coordinator.
When Yǒng arrived, he prayed in the open,
and a great rain moistened and irrigated the land,
reviving the withered crops.
He implemented policies for famine relief,
and after recovery,
there were still over a million piculs of surplus grain.
He also extended the Nine Regulations Law to various prefectures,
dismissing tyrants and abolishing harsh policies,
for which the people greatly admired him.
After three years,
he retired due to old age.
He died during the Hóngzhì reign.
Bīn
successively served as Right Administration Commissioner of Guǎngdōng.
When he first left Jiāngyīn,
the people erected a shrine for him while he was still alive.
And when he was transferred from Kāifēng,
the people also sent him off with tears.
Jiàn,
when first a Censor,
once openly rebuked a palace eunuch for impropriety at the Zuǒshùnmén.
The eunuch was extremely angry,
and during an evaluation, instructed Censor-in-Chief Xiāo Wéizhēn to dismiss him,
but Wéizhēn refused and stopped.
Wénbó
eventually served as Right Vice Censor-in-Chief overseeing Hénán.
Liè
was Left Administration Commissioner of Guǎngdōng.
Fèi Guǎng and others are not recorded.
The encomium says:
Scholars who spoke frankly and dared to remonstrate,
stirred by events,
and heedless of their own safety,
were certainly content to incur punishment.
However, observing Yǐn Chānglóng’s death at the hands of Lǚ Zhèn;
Gěng Tōng’s entrapment by Gāo Xù;
Liú Qiú’s demise
and Chén Jiàn’s imprisonment
due to Wáng Zhèn;
Yáng Xuān’s exile
suffered at the hands of Shí Hēng and Cáo Jíxiáng;
and even Dài Lún’s remonstrance against hunting,
Chén Zuò’s request for diligent study,
Zhōng Tóng, Zhāng Lún, and Liáo Zhuāng’s advocacy for the restoration of the heir apparent,
and Ní Jìng and others’ frank comments on current affairs,
all led to disaster.
That the aspirations of loyal ministers were suppressed and could not be fulfilled
is also lamentable!
Biographies, Chapter 51: Lǐ Shímiǎn, Chén Jìngzōng, Liú Xuàn (Sà Qí), Xíng Ràng (Lǐ Sháo), Lín Hàn (Zǐtíng •) (Tíngjī, Sūn •, Jīng), Xiè Duó, Lǔ Duó (Zhào Yǒng)
Lǐ Shímiǎn,
whose given name was Mào,
was known by his courtesy name,
and was from Ānfú.
When he reached adulthood,
in the cold winter, he would wrap his feet in a quilt and place them in a bucket,
reciting and studying without ceasing.
He passed the imperial examination in the second year of Yǒnglè.
He was selected as a Shùjíshì,
and advanced his studies in the Wényuān Gé,
participating in the compilation of the records of Tàizǔ.
He was appointed as a principal of the Ministry of Justice,
and again participated in the re-compilation of the records.
When the book was completed,
he was transferred to the Hanlin Academy as a侍讀 (shìdú).
His nature was stern and upright,
and he earnestly took the responsibility for the empire upon himself.
In the nineteenth year,
the three halls caught fire,
and an imperial edict sought forthright remonstrance.
He submitted a memorial detailing fifteen matters concerning current affairs.
Chéngzǔ had decided to make Běijīng the capital,
and at that time was inviting people from distant lands.
But Shímiǎn spoke against the construction projects,
and also that people from distant tribute-paying countries should not be allowed to reside in groups near the imperial palace,
which displeased the Emperor.
Subsequently,
upon examining his other proposals,
many of which hit upon the maladies of the time,
the Emperor threw them to the ground,
but then picked them up again to review them twice more,
and ultimately many were implemented.
Soon after, he was slandered and imprisoned.
After more than a year, he was released,
and Yáng Róng recommended his reinstatement.
In the first year of Hóngxī, he again submitted a memorial regarding current affairs.
Rénzōng was extremely angry,
and summoned him to the side hall,
where he remained unyielding in his replies.
The Emperor ordered warriors to beat him with golden maces,
threatening to break his bones three times,
and he was dragged out nearly dead.
The next day,
he was transferred to be a Censor of the Jiāozhǐ Circuit,
ordered to deliberate on one prisoner a day,
and to speak on one matter.
After his memorials were submitted three times,
he was finally sent to the prison of the Jǐnyīwèi.
Shímiǎn had shown kindness to a certain Jǐnyī Qīanhù,
and this Qīanhù happened to be overseeing the prison;
he secretly summoned a doctor,
who treated him with "overseas dragon's blood,"
and thus he did not die.
When Rénzōng was gravely ill,
he said to Xià Yuánjí:
"Shímiǎn insulted me in court."
After speaking,
he flared up in anger,
but Yuánjí comforted and pacified him.
That evening,
the Emperor passed away.
More than a year after Xuānzōng ascended the throne,
someone recounted how Shímiǎn had offended the late emperor.
The Emperor was furious,
and ordered his envoys:
"Bind him and bring him here;
I will personally interrogate him,
and he shall surely die."
Immediately after,
he further ordered Commander Wáng to immediately bind and execute him in the western market,
without allowing him to enter for an audience.
Commander Wáng exited through the western side gate of the Duān Mén,
but the previous envoy had already bound Shímiǎn and entered through the eastern side gate of the Duān Mén,
so they did not meet.
The Emperor saw him from a distance and cursed, saying:
"You, a minor official, dared to provoke the late emperor!
What did your memorial say?
Quickly tell me."
Shímiǎn kowtowed and said:
"Your servant said that during the mourning period, one should not be close to concubines,
and the Crown Prince should not be far from his attendants."
When the Emperor heard this,
his expression somewhat softened.
He slowly counted to six matters and stopped.
The Emperor ordered him to present all of them.
He replied:
"Your servant is too terrified to remember them all."
The Emperor's anger further subsided,
and he said:
"These are just difficult to speak of, where is the draft?"
He replied:
"It has been burned."
The Emperor then sighed deeply,
praised Shímiǎn's loyalty,
and immediately pardoned him,
reinstating him as a侍讀 (shìdú).
By the time Commander Wáng returned from the prison,
Shímiǎn was already adorned with his official hat and belt, standing before the steps.
In the fifth year of Xuāndé, the compilation of Chéngzǔ's Veritable Records was completed,
and he was promoted to侍讀學士 (shìdú xuéshì).
The Emperor visited the Imperial Historiography Academy,
and scattered golden coins to bestow upon the academicians.
Everyone else bent down to pick them up,
but Shímiǎn alone stood upright.
The Emperor then took out the remaining money and gave it to him.
In the third year of Zhèngtǒng, with the completion of Xuānzōng's Veritable Records,
he was promoted to學士 (xuéshì),
managing the affairs of the academy and also serving as an official of the imperial lectures.
In the sixth year, he replaced Bèi Tài as Libationer.
In the eighth year, he requested retirement,
but it was not granted.
Previously,
Shímiǎn had requested the renovation of the Imperial Academy.
The Emperor ordered Wáng Zhèn to go and inspect it,
but Shímiǎn did not show special deference to Zhèn.
Zhèn held a grudge against him,
and sought out his flaws,
but found none.
Shímiǎn had once trimmed the side branches of trees near the Yílún Táng,
and Zhèn then reported that Shímiǎn had unauthorizedly cut down official trees for his own home.
He obtained an imperial decree,
and Shímiǎn, along with the Director of Studies Zhào Wǎn and the Chief Steward Jīn Jiàn, were all put in cangues in front of the Guózǐjiàn.
When the imperial guards arrived,
Shímiǎn was sitting in the east hall reviewing examination papers,
and calmly called the students to rank their performance,
consulting his colleagues to decide on their grades,
and only left after the results were posted.
It was the height of summer,
and the cangue was not removed for three days.
Over a thousand students, including Lǐ Guì, went to the imperial court to beg for his release.
There was one Shí Dàyòng,
who submitted a memorial offering himself as a substitute.
The students gathered in a circle at the court gate,
their shouts reaching the palace hall.
Zhèn heard of the students' discontent,
and feared it might incite a rebellion.
When the Tōngzhèng Sī presented Dàyòng's memorial,
Zhèn felt inwardly ashamed.
Assistant Instructor Lǐ Jì requested intervention from the Marquis of Huìchāng, Sūn Zhōng.
Zhōng
was the father of the Empress Dowager.
On Zhōng's birthday,
the Empress Dowager sent someone to bestow gifts upon Zhōng's family.
Zhōng appended a report to the Empress Dowager,
and the Empress Dowager spoke to the Emperor on his behalf.
The Emperor had initially been unaware,
and immediately released him.
Jì was unrestrained in his conduct,
and Shímiǎn had often admonished him.
Jì did not fully heed his advice,
but his heart was moved by Shímiǎn's words,
and so now he indeed received his help.
Dàyòng
was from Fēngrùn.
He was simple and unrefined,
and initially unknown to the Six Academies,
but at this point, his name became famous in the capital.
The next year, he passed the provincial examination,
and rose to the post of principal of the Ministry of Revenue.
In the ninth year,
the Emperor visited the academy.
Shímiǎn lectured on the Shàngshū,
his words clear and articulate.
The Emperor was pleased,
and bestowed additional gifts upon him.
He repeatedly submitted memorials requesting retirement,
but it was not granted.
In the spring of the twelfth year, his request was finally granted.
Nearly three thousand court officials and students from the Guózǐjiàn saw him off outside the city gate,
some even escorting him to board his boat,
waiting until the boat departed before leaving.
When Yīngzōng was captured in the north,
Shímiǎn grieved day and night.
He sent his grandson Jì to the imperial court to submit a memorial,
requesting the selection of generals and training of troops,
to draw close to upright gentlemen,
to distance oneself from petty individuals,
to commend loyal and virtuous individuals,
to welcome back the imperial carriage,
and to avenge the humiliation.
In the first year of Jǐngtài, an imperial decree praised and responded to him,
but Shímiǎn had already passed away,
at the age of seventy-seven.
He was posthumously given the epithet Wényì.
In the fifth year of Chénghuà,
at the request of his grandson Yōng,
his posthumous epithet was changed to Zhōngwén,
and he was posthumously appointed Vice Minister of Rites.
Shí Miǎn served as Jìjiǔ for six years.
He established four designations: gé (格), zhì (致), chéng (誠), zhèng (正),
and his instructions and encouragements were very earnest.
He esteemed integrity and honor,
suppressed corrupt competition,
distinguished between the worthy and the unworthy,
and offered both encouragement and punishment.
For students who were poor and unable to afford weddings or funerals,
he saved meal money to provide for them.
He urged them to study diligently,
their lamps burned until dawn,
and the sound of their recitation was ceaseless.
Talented individuals flourished more than in past times.
Initially,
Tàizǔ appointed Sòng Nà as Jìjiǔ,
who was most famous.
Later, Zhāng Xiǎnzōng from Nínghuà clarified the academic regulations,
and people compared him to Nà.
And Hú Yǎn, during the reign of Chéngzǔ,
was especially praised as a master teacher.
However, for his uprightness and high reputation that scholars relied upon,
none could compare to Shí Miǎn.
The Duke of Yīngguó, Zhāng Fǔ, along with other marquises and earls, submitted a memorial,
requesting to collectively attend lectures at the Guózǐjiān.
The emperor commanded them to go on the third day of the third month.
Shí Miǎn ascended the teacher's seat,
the students stood in their proper places,
and he lectured on one chapter from each of the Five Classics.
After the event concluded,
wine and food were served.
The marquises and earls demurred, saying:
"In this place of receiving instruction,
we ought to sit among the students."
Only Fǔ maintained a formal distance.
The students sang the poem Lù Míng,
and host and guests were harmonious and respectful.
They dispersed at dusk,
and people called it a grand event of peaceful times.
Chén Jìngzōng,
courtesy name Guāngshì,
was a native of Cíxī.
He became a Jìnshì in the second year of Yǒnglè.
He was selected as a Shùjíshì,
and entered the Wényuángé for advanced study,
participating in the compilation of the Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn.
After the book was completed,
he was appointed Zhǔshì of the Xíngbù.
He also participated in compiling the Wǔjīng Sìshū Dàquán,
and again in compiling the Tàizǔ Shílù,
after which he was appointed Hànlín Shìjiǎng.
He returned home for mourning.
In the first year of Xuāndé, he was recalled to compile the Liǎngcháo Shílù.
The following year, he was transferred to become Sīyè of the Nánjīng Guózǐjiān.
The emperor instructed him, saying:
"Shìjiǎng
is a selection for pure brilliance;
Sīyè
is the seat of a master scholar.
Though the position is not exalted,
the responsibility is heavy."
In the ninth year,
his term of office was completed,
and he was promoted to Jìjiǔ.
In the third year of Zhèngtǒng, he submitted a memorial stating:
"According to old regulations,
students were sent to various departments for practical experience
based on the length of their stay in the academy.
Recently,
some who were given leave due to affairs
delayed for several years,
only showing up at the time of allocation.
This truly encourages cunning and idleness.
I request that the order be determined by the amount of their studies.
Also, recently there has been a trend of wishing to take miscellaneous posts,
which debases the spirit of scholarship
and is truly no small matter.
I request that this be strictly prohibited."
This was approved.
Jìngzōng had a handsome beard,
a dignified and proper bearing,
and a measured gait.
He vigorously took upon himself the duty of a teacher.
He established regulations
and reformed bad practices.
Of the more than a thousand scholars in the six halls,
whenever they attended lectures or
shared meals,
they were as orderly as at court.
If anyone showed the slightest impropriety,
they were immediately made to await punishment below the hall.
His subordinates, fearing his strictness,
falsely accused him of other matters
and sued him before the judicial authorities.
Zhōu Chén, who was friendly with Jìngzōng,
said:
"Why not prepare a memorial to defend yourself?"
He drafted a text for him,
with slightly compromising language.
Jìngzōng was startled and said:
"Are you deceiving me?"
He did not submit it,
and the matter was eventually cleared.
Upon completing his term,
he went to Jīngshī.
Wáng Zhèn wished to see him,
and ordered Chén to convey his intention.
Jìngzōng said:
"I am a model for the students;
how can I privately visit a powerful eunuch
and still face the students?"
Zhèn knew he could not be swayed,
so he sent him brocade and fine silk, lamb, and wine,
requesting a copy of Chéngzǐ's Four Admonitions,
hoping he would come to express his thanks.
Jìngzōng wrote it,
signed his name, and that was all.
He returned the gifts
and never went to see him.
Wáng Zhí, as Lìbù Shàngshū,
casually remarked to him:
"Sir, you have been Sīchéng for a long time;
I will recommend you for Sīkòu."
Jìngzōng said:
"You understand me.
Today, I discuss matters all day long with the nation's elite talents;
am I not content?"
He was fond of drinking,
able to consume several dou without losing composure.
Xiāngchéng Bó Lǐ Lóng, who was garrison commander in Nánjīng,
often invited him for drinks,
with singers and musicians all around.
He would raise his cup all day,
without ever glancing at them.
Such was his gravity.
In the winter of the twelfth year, he requested retirement,
but it was not granted.
In the ninth month of the first year of Jǐngtài, he retired due to age, along with Shàngshū Wèi Jì.
At home, he rarely went out.
Those who were received by him
were all inspired to action.
He passed away in the fifth month of the third year of Tiānshùn,
at the age of eighty-three.
Later, he was posthumously granted Lǐbù Shìláng
and given the posthumous name Wéndìng.
Initially,
Jìngzōng and Lǐ Shímiǎn were both in the Hànlín Academy.
Yuán Zhōngchè once read their faces,
pulling the two of them to stand side-by-side, saying:
"These two gentlemen will achieve equal fame and success in the future."
Jìngzōng had a towering and impressive appearance,
while Shímiǎn's looks were somewhat less striking.
Later, the two simultaneously became Jìjiǔ of the two capitals.
Shí Miǎn was lenient and won over scholars,
while Jìngzōng was upright and strict.
Throughout the Míng dynasty, the worthy Jìjiǔ were known as
"Chén of the South and Lǐ of the North."
Liú Xuán,
courtesy name Zōngqì,
was a native of Chángzhōu.
He was orphaned a month after his birth.
When he grew up,
he cut flesh from his thigh to treat his mother's illness.
When his mother died,
he mourned so grievously that his health declined,
and he was known for his filial piety.
During the Yǒnglè reign,
he was recruited into the Hànlín Academy for his skill in calligraphy.
He passed the Shùntiān provincial examination
and was appointed Zhōngshū Shèrén.
During the Xuāndé reign,
he participated in compiling the Shílù of Chéngzǔ and Rénzōng,
was promoted to Bīngbù Zhǔshì,
and continued to serve in the inner court.
During the Zhèngtǒng reign,
he again compiled the Xuānzōng Shílù,
and was promoted to Shìjiǎng.
Upon the recommendation of scholar Cáo Nài and others,
he and Xiūzhuàn Wáng Zhèn instructed the Shùjíshì.
When Jǐngdì ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Shìjiǎng Xuéshì
and served as Zhí Jīngyán.
After three years,
on the recommendation of Gāo Gǔ,
he was transferred to Guózǐ Jìjiǔ.
At that time, due to insufficient national funds,
students were dismissed,
and those who did not wish to return home had their monthly stipends suspended.
Xuàn said:
"Nurturing talent
is an urgent matter for the state.
Currently, the granaries are still full;
why be so stingy with this?"
Consequently, the stipends were reinstated.
He also ordered a selection of students from the six colleges;
those who were old, uncomely, or shallow in scholarship and art
were to be dismissed as commoners.
Xuàn said:
"These students have long benefited from imperial instruction;
how could they be entirely without any merits?
Moreover, having left their relatives,
abandoned their ancestral graves,
and endured extreme hardships,
to be dismissed overnight
is not in line with the court's intention of nurturing talent.
I request that those who are advanced in age but scholarly
be granted suitable official positions."
The emperor approved his memorial.
Soon after, he returned home for his mother's mourning.
When the mourning period ended,
he went to the capital,
where Chén Xún had already become Jìjiǔ.
The emperor highly regarded Xuàn,
ordering him to serve alongside Xún.
In the early Tiānshùn era,
he was appointed Shào Zhànshì
and served the Crown Prince in lecturing and reading.
He died in the tenth month of the following year.
Both the emperor and the Crown Prince granted sacrifices,
and his funeral gifts were increased.
When Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
he was posthumously granted Lǐbù Shìláng
and given the posthumous title Wéngōng.
Xuàn was forthright and distinctive in character,
and his words and deeds were never careless.
When instructing probationary scholars and examining Guózǐ students,
his regulations were strict and orderly,
and his devotion to study deepened with age.
His second son, Hàn, became a Jìnshì and was sent on a mission to the south.
Before his departure,
Xuàn inspected his clothes and luggage.
When Hàn returned,
his luggage was as it had been,
and Xuàn happily said:
"You have not disgraced my family!"
Hàn's official career ended as a Fùshǐ,
and he was able to uphold his father's teachings.
Sà Qí,
courtesy name Tíngguī,
was originally from the Western Regions,
later registered in Mǐnxian.
He passed the Jìnshì examination in Xuāndé's fifth year.
He successively served as Lǐbù Shìláng兼 Shào Zhànshì.
He died in Tiānshùn's first year.
Qí possessed literary virtue,
was upright and uncompromised.
His reputation and conduct were comparable to Xuàn's.
Xíng Ràng,
courtesy name Xùnzhī,
was a native of Xiānglíng.
At eighteen,
he passed the provincial examination
and entered the Guózǐjiān.
He was highly regarded by Lǐ Shímǐan and was as famous as Liú Xǔ.
He passed the Jìnshì examination in Zhèngtǒng's thirteenth year.
He was appointed Shùjíshì
and then granted the position of Jiǎntǎo.
In Jǐngtài's first year,
Lǐ Shí returned from Wǎlà
and requested to send another envoy to welcome the Former Emperor.
Jǐngdì did not permit it.
Ràng memorialized:
"The Former Emperor has the duty of a lord towards Your Majesty,
and the grace of an elder brother;
how can he not be welcomed?
Moreover, if the barbarians use this great principle to question us,
what words shall we use to respond?
If you follow the request of your officials,
and still order Shí to carry an imperial edict to them,
and state the intention of welcoming him back,
even if it is uncertain whether the Former Emperor will return,
Your Majesty's profound benevolence and righteousness
will be clearly manifest to the world.
If by any chance he is welcomed but does not permit it,
then we can justly blame them,
and raise an army to punish them.
Would this not be excellent?"
When the memorial was submitted,
the emperor subtly explained and mollified him.
Towards the end of Tiānshùn,
he returned due to his father's mourning.
Before the mourning period was over,
he was recalled to compile the 'Yīngzōng Shílù' (Veritable Records of Emperor Yīngzōng),
and was promoted to Xiūzhuàn.
In Chénghuà's second year, he was exceptionally promoted to Guózǐ Jìjiǔ.
When Empress Dowager Cíyì passed away,
the ritual of entombment in the ancestral temple was debated,
and Ràng led his subordinates in a memorial of remonstrance.
It was customary that educational officials in the national academies of the two capitals
could not be promoted,
but Ràng and others argued against this,
stating that those who entered through examinations,
after a full term, should be eligible for selection.
While at the Grand Academy, Ràng
also strongly took on the responsibility of a teacher,
compiling the 'Bìyōng Tōngzhì' (Comprehensive Gazetteer of the Imperial College),
and supervising students to recite the 'Xiǎoxué' and various Classics.
He severely punished the malpractice of requesting leave;
at the time, he was praised for this,
but detractors were also numerous.
He was a man of talent but narrow-minded.
His preferences and dislikes
were often revealed in his words and expressions,
and many who competed with him for fame and position resented him.
In the fifth year, he was promoted to Lǐbù Yòu Shìláng.
Two years later,
regarding the matter of using funds for banquets at the Guózǐjiān,
he, along with the later Jìjiǔ Chén Jiàn, Sìyè Zhāng Yè, Diǎnjí Wáng Yǔn, and others,
were all found guilty and sentenced to death.
The students petitioned outside the palace gate,
requesting to take their place.
An imperial edict was again issued for court officials to conduct a joint investigation,
and they were ultimately sentenced to death,
but ransomed to become commoners.
After Jiàn was found guilty,
Lìbù Shàngshū Yáo Kuí requested to recall the retired Lǐbù Shìláng Lǐ Shào as Jìjiǔ.
An urgent summons was sent,
but Shào had already died.
Shào, courtesy name Kèshù,
was a native of Ānfú.
He passed the Jìnshì examination in Xuāndé's eighth year.
He was appointed Shùjíshì
and then granted the position of Jiǎntǎo.
When Grand Secretary Yáng Shìqí was ill in bed,
Yīngzōng sent an envoy to inquire about talented individuals,
and Shìqí named Shào and four others in response.
During the defeat at Tǔmù,
the capital was under martial law,
and many court officials sent their families south.
Shào said:
"When the lord is humiliated, the minister dies;
what use is a family?"
He ultimately did not send them away.
He was successively promoted to Hànlín Xuéshì.
On the recommendation of Lǐ Xián and Wáng Ào,
he was promoted to Lǐbù Shìláng.
In Chénghuà's second year, he requested to resign due to illness.
Shào was fond of learning,
upright and resolute in office, with great capacity,
and able to encourage younger talents.
When he died,
the emperor deeply mourned him.
Lín Hàn,
courtesy name Hēngdà,
was a native of Mǐn.
His father, Yuánměi,
passed the Jìnshì examination at the end of Yǒnglè's reign,
and served as the Zhīfǔ of Fǔzhōu.
Hàn passed the Jìnshì examination in Chénghuà's second year.
He was appointed Shùjíshì
and then granted the position of Biānxiū.
He was again promoted to Yùdé,
then requested urgent leave to return home.
In the early Hóngzhì era,
he was recalled to compile the 'Xiànzōng Shílù' (Veritable Records of Emperor Xiànzōng),
and served as Jīngyán Jiǎngguān.
He was gradually promoted to Guózǐjiān Jìjiǔ,
and then advanced to Lǐbù Yòu Shìláng,
continuing to oversee the Guózǐjiān as before.
He managed the national academy for nearly ten years,
and the banquet funds, which amounted to hundreds annually,
were all stored in the official treasury
and used sequentially to construct official residences.
The exemption for teachers and scholars from renting accommodation
began with Hàn.
He successively served as Lìbù Zuǒ and Yòu Shìláng.
In his thirteenth year, he was appointed Minister of Personnel for Nánjīng.
Due to natural disasters,
he led his subordinates in presenting twelve matters.
When Censor Wáng Xiànchén was arrested in Liáodōng and imprisoned by imperial decree,
and scholars Sūn Bójiān and others were illicitly promoted to Secretaries of the Grand Secretariat,
Hàn submitted a memorial disputing this,
which displeased the emperor.
He requested to be dismissed,
but this was not granted.
Later,
he submitted a memorial urging the reinforcement of fundamental principles: namely, to secure Nánjīng,
to protect and enlighten the imperial heir,
to comfort and pacify the common people,
and to promote virtuous and talented individuals.
In the fourth month of the first year of the Zhèngdé reign (1506),
Minister of Personnel Mǎ Wénshēng vacated his position.
Censors Qiū Jùn, Shí Jiè, and others recommended Hàn.
The emperor appointed Vice Minister Jiāo Fāng,
and thus Hàn was transferred to the Ministry of War in Nánjīng,
to participate in advising on state affairs.
Before the imperial order arrived,
Hàn pleaded illness and requested to retire,
and then presented four matters: cultivating a righteous heart, upholding the righteous Way, pursuing righteous learning, and befriending righteous people.
A gracious imperial edict was issued to comfort him and urge him to stay.
At that time, natural disasters appeared frequently,
and Hàn and the other Nánjīng officials drafted twelve articles on current governance.
Their words touched upon the emperor's favorites,
and many were rejected and not implemented.
Hàn was inherently rigid and upright,
and disagreed with the eunuch guarding Nánjīng.
Whenever other inner court eunuchs passed through his territory on tribute missions,
Hàn would often restrict and suppress them,
which led to them jointly slandering him to Liú Jǐn.
When Liú Jiàn and Xiè Qiān were dismissed from government,
Hàn sighed deeply upon hearing the news.
Censors Dài Xiǎn and others were impeached for advocating to retain Jiàn and Qiān.
Hàn alone saw them off with gifts,
which made Jǐn hate him even more upon hearing of it.
In the second month of the following year, using the interrogation records of Xiǎn and others as pretext,
Hàn was demoted to Provincial Administration Commissioner of Zhèjiāng.
He retired from office.
Soon after, he was accused of being a member of the "treacherous faction."
When Jǐn was executed,
he was reinstated to office,
and then retired again.
He was granted a monthly stipend and annual servants as per customary regulations.
Soon after, officials were ordered to visit him periodically.
Hàn was humble and benevolent,
yet meticulously upright in self-conduct.
He died at the age of eighty-six.
He was posthumously granted the title Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
and given the posthumous name Wén'ān.
He had nine sons,
among whom Tíngmó and Tíngjī were the most prominent.
Tíngmó,
courtesy name Lìzhān,
was Hàn's second son.
He became a *jìnshì* in the twelfth year of the Hóngzhì reign (1499).
He was appointed Section Chief in the Ministry of War.
He successively served as Director of the Bureau of Military Provisions.
Minister of Personnel Zhāng Cǎi wanted to transfer him to Censor,
but he firmly declined,
so he was made Prefect of Sūzhōu.
For several consecutive years, there were severe floods,
and he submitted memorials requesting to halt textile manufacturing,
abolish excessive taxes,
and allocate customs duties for disaster relief.
After submitting these twice,
they were finally approved.
He was promoted to Provincial Administration Commissioner of Yúnnán.
In the ninth year of the Zhèngdé reign (1514),
he requested to resign to attend to his elderly father.
At that time, his son Xuàn had already become a *jìnshì*,
serving as Section Chief in the Ministry of Rites,
and also requested leave to return home.
Three generations lived under one roof,
and the local people praised it as a grand event.
In the early Jiājìng reign,
after his father's mourning period,
upon its completion,
he was reappointed as an official in Jiāngxī,
and successively served as Senior and Junior Administration Commissioner of Húguǎng.
He was recommended for his outstanding governance,
and promoted to Vice Censor-in-Chief on the Right,
inspecting the prefectures of Bǎodìng.
He successively served as Vice Minister of Works on the Right.
In response to an imperial edict, he spoke about the major construction projects of the Altar of Heaven and Earth,
and the successive constructions of the southern city and the Western Garden,
pleading for frugality to set an example for the empire.
Also, due to disasters and damages,
he requested the recall of all envoys for timber collection and kiln burning.
He was promoted to Vice Minister on the Left,
then appointed Minister,
and additionally granted the title Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
At that time, the emperor was vigorously undertaking civil engineering projects,
and Tíngmó's plans largely met his expectations.
When an imperial edict was issued to build an imperial temporary palace at Shāhé,
Tíngmó proposed increasing land taxes across the empire,
which led to his impeachment by Censor Sāng Qiáo and Supervising Secretary Guǎn Jiàn.
He requested to be dismissed,
returned home, and died.
He was posthumously granted the title Junior Guardian,
and given the posthumous name Kāngyì.
Xuàn ended his career as a Councilor of the Office of Transmission.
Tíngjī,
courtesy name Lìrén,
was Hàn's youngest son.
He became a *jìnshì* in the fourteenth year of the Jiājìng reign (1535).
He was transferred to a *shùjíshì* (supernumerary bachelor),
appointed Compiler,
promoted to Vice Director of the Imperial Academy,
then promoted to Libationer of the Imperial Academy in Nánjīng,
and successively rose to Minister of Works.
When Mùzōng ascended the throne,
he was transferred to the Ministry of Rites,
both offices being in the secondary capital.
At that time, his son Zé had already become Libationer,
so he retired and returned home.
He died in the ninth year of the Wànlì reign (1581),
at the age of seventy-six.
He was posthumously granted the title Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
and given the posthumous name Wénxī.
He had sons Zé and Jīng.
Zé,
courtesy name Zhēn,
was Tíngjī's eldest son.
He became a *jìnshì* in the twenty-sixth year of the Jiājìng reign (1547).
He was transferred to a *shùjíshì*,
and appointed Compiler.
When Prince Jǐnggōng went to his principality,
Zé was ordered to serve as a lecturer.
He was thrice promoted to Libationer of the Imperial Academy.
From Zé's grandfather Hàn,
father Tíngjī,
three generations served as Libationers,
a feat unprecedented before this.
In the first year of the Lóngqìng reign (1567),
he was promoted to Vice Minister of Rites on the Right,
and served as a Daily Lecturer.
When barbarians invaded the border,
he presented seven articles on border defense.
He was transferred to the Ministry of Personnel,
then transferred to the Ministry of Personnel in Nánjīng,
and concurrently managed the affairs of the Ministry of Rites.
When Duke Wèi, Xú Péngjǔ, wanted to depose his eldest son and establish his younger son,
Zé firmly opposed it.
In the first year of the Wànlì reign (1573), he was promoted to Minister of Works,
then transferred to the Ministry of Rites,
still residing in Nánjīng.
His rank and position were entirely equal to his father Tíngjī.
He resigned from office due to his mother's death.
Upon the completion of the mourning period,
because Tíngjī was seriously ill and he had to attend to him,
he lived at home for seven years,
and died before his father Tíngjī.
He was posthumously granted the title Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
and given the posthumous name Wénkè.
In the Ming dynasty, three generations serving as Ministers,
all receiving the posthumous name Wén,
was only achieved by the Lín family.
His son Shìqín
was profoundly filial.
Lingzhi grew three times,
and withered bamboo turned green again.
A censor reported this event,
and he was honored.
Jīng, courtesy name Zhēnyào,
was Tíngjī's second son.
He became a *jìnshì* in the forty-first year of the Jiājìng reign (1562).
He was appointed Section Chief in the Ministry of Revenue,
and successively served as Vice Commissioner of Guǎngxī.
When his elder brother Zé died,
he requested urgent leave to care for his parents.
After a long time,
he successively served as Junior Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud.
Due to natural disasters, he strenuously denounced the harm of mining taxes,
and requested the release of imprisoned officials.
This was not reported.
He ended his career as Minister of Works in Nánjīng and retired.
The Lín family had five Ministers in three generations,
all of whom were upright and pure in their private conduct,
and were praised by their contemporaries.
Xiè Duó,
courtesy name Míngzhì,
was a native of Tàipíng, Zhèjiāng.
He became a *jìnshì* at the end of the Tiānshùn reign.
He was transferred to a *shùjíshì*,
appointed Compiler,
and participated in compiling the Veritable Records of Emperor Yīngzōng.
He was distinctive and upright,
diligent in study, admired the ancients,
and focused on statecraft.
In the ninth year of Chénghuà, he proofread the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn Gāngmù.
He memorialized:
“The book Gāngmù
is a mirror for emperors.
Your Majesty commanded its re-examination and correction,
which will surely be presented and expounded in the Jīngyán,
to serve as a resource for good governance.
Today, the world has the appearance of peace,
but not the reality of peace.
Old habits persist,
sacrificing reality for name.
Though it is said that the governmental discipline is restored,
petty individuals have no fear or apprehension.
Though it is said that customs are encouraged,
officials abandon integrity and shame.
Officials are admonished,
yet corruption and tyranny only worsen.
The military and populace are cared for,
yet their destitution and exhaustion only intensify.
There are regulations for reduction and frugality,
yet projects often exhaust people with constant demands.
There are edicts for tax exemptions,
yet levies often distress people with urgent calls.
Investigations are indeed carried out,
yet avenues for favoritism open daily.
Selections and training are indeed conducted,
yet private interference increases daily.
Rewards deplete the imperial treasury,
yet those who have accomplished merit are not encouraged.
Punishments exhaust judicial reviews,
yet those who are guilty are not disciplined.
To such an extent that commands for self-reflection and prayer are repeatedly issued,
yet floods, droughts, and disasters arrive without cease.
The Forbidden City was shaken by an earthquake,
city gates showed signs of calamity.
If one does not contemplate a profound change and reversal,
to greatly respond to the expectations of Heaven and man,
this is truly cause for concern.
I wish Your Majesty would use antiquity to verify the present,
and be diligent and cautious.
Only then can there be long-lasting peace and stability,
and historical records will not be useless.”
The emperor could not follow.
At that time, there were alarms on the frontier,
so he memorialized on matters of border defense,
requesting to maintain troops and accumulate grain,
and to recover the old territories of Dōngshèng and Hétào.
He also said:
“Today’s frontier generals
are no different from the ‘debt-commanders’ of the late Táng dynasty.
When defeated, the soldiers suffer the calamity;
when victorious, powerful and influential individuals reap the rewards.
Moreover, they embezzle military pay
and demand monthly contributions.
If the entire army is filled with resentment,
who would be willing to serve the country with their lives?”
His words all addressed contemporary弊.
Upon completing his term,
he was promoted to Shìjiǎng
and served in the Jīngyán.
After experiencing two mourning periods,
and his mourning period being over,
because he could not care for his parents,
he subsequently did not resume office.
In the early Hóngzhì reign,
many officials recommended him,
and he was summoned with his original post to compile the Xiànzōng Shílù.
In the third year, he was promoted to Nánjīng Guózǐ Jìjiǔ.
He memorialized six matters:
selecting teachers and scholars,
being cautious with civil service examinations,
rectifying sacrificial rituals,
expanding historical records,
restoring communal meals,
and fairly allocating student rotations.
Regarding rectifying sacrificial rituals,
he requested to admit the Sòng scholar Yáng Shí and remove Wú Chéng.
Fù Hàn, the Minister of Rítuál, insisted on it,
so Yáng Shí was admitted, but Wú Chéng’s worship remained as before.
The next year, he resigned due to illness.
He stayed at home for nearly ten years,
and recommendations for him increased.
When the position of Guózǐ Jìjiǔ became vacant,
the Ministry deliberated recalling him.
The emperor had always highly regarded Duó,
and promoted him to Rítuál Yòu Shìláng,
managing the affairs of Jìjiǔ.
He repeatedly declined,
but was not permitted.
At that time, Zhāng Mào was the Nánjīng Jìjiǔ;
both men were regarded as masters,
and the students rejoiced greatly.
After five years,
he resigned due to illness and returned home.
Duó’s knowledge of classics was profound,
and his essays had substance and clarity.
He twice served as Guózǐ master,
setting strict curricula,
preventing undue requests,
increasing student dormitories,
repairing halls and rooms,
expanding the temple gate,
and establishing over thirty public offices for his subordinates.
He provided relief to impoverished students,
and for those who died, he requested official arrangements for their funerals according to regulations.
At home, he was fond of helping his clan and relatives;
his personal life was simple, wearing plain clothes and eating vegetables.
He died in the fifth year of Zhèngdé.
He was posthumously granted Rítuál Shàngshū
and given the posthumous title Wénsù.
Lǔ Duó,
courtesy name Zhènzhī,
was from Jǐnglíng.
In the fifteenth year of Hóngzhì, he placed first in the metropolitan examination.
He successively served as Biānxiū.
He kept to himself,
not engaging in frivolous social interactions.
When Wǔzōng ascended the throne,
he was sent as an envoy to Ānnán,
and refused their gifts.
In the second year of Zhèngdé, he was promoted to Guózǐjiān Sīyè.
He was successively promoted to Nánjīng Jìjiǔ,
and soon after, transferred to Běijīng.
Duó repeatedly presided over the Guózǐjiān,
teaching scholars to focus on practical learning,
not just rote memorization.
If a scholar took leave and neglected his studies,
he would admonish him,
and only stop when the scholar repented.
After a long time,
he resigned due to illness and returned home.
In the early Jiājìng reign,
based on the recommendation of Xíngbù Shàngshū Lín Jùn,
following the precedent of Xiè Duó from the Xiàozōng era,
he was reinstated as Nánjīng Jìjiǔ.
After more than a year,
he again requested retirement.
He was repeatedly summoned but did not resume office,
and then died.
He was posthumously titled Wénkè.
Duó was highly esteemed for his virtue and reputation at the time.
When he was in his hometown,
bandits stole cattle and horses.
Someone tricked them by saying,
“These are the belongings of Jìjiǔ Lǔ,”
and they abandoned them and left.
On the birthday of Grand Secretary Lǐ Dōngyáng,
Duó was Sīyè,
and he and Jìjiǔ Zhào Yǒng were both Lǐ Dōngyáng’s students.
They agreed to present two handkerchiefs as a birthday gift.
When Duó checked his box,
there were none.
He slowly said:
“Someone in the village sent me some dried fish,
why not take that?”
He asked in the kitchen,
and more than half had already been eaten.
He took the remainder to Dōngyáng.
Dōngyáng was pleased,
cooked the fish and set out wine,
and kept the two for drinks,
parting in great joy.
Yǒng,
courtesy name Ěrxī,
was from Línhuái.
He was a Jinshì in the same year as Duó,
and also served as Biānxiū.
He then successively served as Jìjiǔ after Duó.
Soon after, he was promoted to Nánjīng Lǐbù Shìláng.
Grand Secretary Yáng Yīqīng valued his talent,
and wanted to draw him in to assist himself.
So he tried to provoke him with other words.
Yǒng replied sternly:
“Can I stain my principles with officialdom?”
He then requested to retire and leave.
People admired his integrity and uprightness.
A eulogy states: In the time of Míng Tàizǔ,
teachers and scholars of the imperial academy
were highly esteemed and respected.
Wèi Guān and Sòng Nà served as Jìjiǔ,
cultivating talent
and fulfilling their duties.
Students who were commissioned as envoys
were often promoted to high official positions,
not solely advancing through civil service examinations.
From the mid-period onwards,
the quality of personnel gradually became mixed,
and the student rotation system also became a mere formality.
The position of master at the Guózǐjiān
was nothing more than a stepping stone for scholarly officials’ promotions.
Lǐ Shímiǎn, Chén Jìngzōng, and others,
who were incorruptible, honest, and upright,
set an outstanding example.
By categorizing and transmitting their stories,
may observers have something to emulate.

Biographies, Volume 52: Zōu Jī (Zhèng Wéihuán, Kē Xiān) Yì Qiān (Huáng Jì) Huáng Zé (Kǒng Yǒuliàng) Fàn Jì Liáo Ràng (Guō Yòu, Hú Zhònglún, Huá Mǐn, Jiǎ Bīn) Zuǒ Dǐng (Liàn Gāng) Cáo Kǎi (Xǔ Shìdá) Liú Wěi (Shàng Chǐ) Shàn Yǔ (Yáo Xiǎn, Yáng Hào) Zhāng Zhāo (Hè Yáng) Gāo Yáo (Hǔ Chén)
Zōu Jī,
courtesy name Zhòngxī,
was a native of Jíshuǐ.
During the Hóngwǔ reign, he passed the Míngjīng examination
and was appointed Instructor of Xīngzǐ.
During the Jiànwén reign, he entered court as an Assistant Instructor of the Guózǐjiān.
When Chéngzǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Hanlin Imperial Lecturer.
When the Crown Prince was established,
he concurrently served as Left Middle Attendant and
repeatedly oversaw affairs of the Guózǐjiān.
In the nineteenth year of Yǒnglè,
when the three great halls suffered a disaster,
an edict sought frank words.
Zōu Jī submitted a memorial, saying: Your Majesty began constructing Běijīng,
laboring with a worried sagely mind
for nearly twenty years.
The work is vast, the expenses numerous,
and the allocations very extensive.
Superfluous officials devour resources,
depleting the national reserves.
The laborers for the work,
numbering in the millions,
are employed year-round,
unable to personally attend to their fields for cultivation.
Yet, requisitions are endless,
even to the extent of felling mulberry and jujube trees to
supply firewood,
and stripping mulberry bark to make paper.
Furthermore, corrupt officials impose levies,
worsening day by day.
For example, last year, when purchasing pigments,
which were not local products,
they arbitrarily levied thousands
of hundreds.
The people collectively raised money
to purchase them elsewhere.
One catty of indigo
cost as much as sixteen thousand strings of cash.
When submitting them,
there were often many obstructions,
requiring repeated back and
forth,
whereby twenty thousand strings of cash were needed,
but it was not enough for the use of a single pillar.
Later, although officials were dispatched to procure them from the source,
the purchasing still did not cease.
This is because
many artisans exploit for profit,
disregarding the people's hardships to this extent.
Indeed, the capital is the foundation of the empire.
If the people are at peace, the capital is at peace;
if the capital is at peace, the national foundation is secure, and the empire is at peace.
Since the construction began,
petty artisans
and commoners have exploited their authority,
driving and relocating people.
As soon as an order was issued,
houses were already destroyed.
Orphans and widows cried and wailed,
panic-stricken and exposed,
not
knowing where to go.
No sooner had they settled after being relocated
than they were driven to move elsewhere again,
some having to move three or four times without rest.
After they had left,
the empty land
remained
for months and more,
but construction had not yet begun.
This is what Your Majesty does not know,
but what the people resent and hate.
Corrupt officials are
ubiquitous both inside and outside the court,
exploiting people to the bone.
Every time the court dispatches someone,
it becomes a means for that person to make a living.
Cruel extractions
and harsh demands
initially knew no bounds.
Officials complied,
fearing they would not be quick enough.
Occasionally, if someone was honest and firm, upholding integrity and not engaging in flattery,
they would be slandered and ruined,
and often incur
punishment and condemnation,
unable to clear their name.
Thus, wherever envoys arrived,
officials openly engaged in bribery,
exploiting those below to flatter those above,
like a common transaction.
Indeed, how much do the common people accumulate
that such demands are made both inside and out, from top to bottom?
Now, Shāndōng, Hénán, Shānxī, and Shǎnxī have suffered successive floods and droughts,
and the people have resorted to stripping tree bark and digging grass roots to eat.
Old and young wander,
collapsing on the
roads,
selling wives and children to barely survive.
Yet, in the capital, over ten thousand monks and Daoists are gathered,
daily consuming over a hundred shí of grain,
this is taking food from the people to support the
useless.
As for the soldiers who volunteer their service,
the court provides ample provisions and rewards.
But when they are sent to work,
they become arrogant and unrestrained,
wandering idly.
These are all deceitful individuals
who fear returning to their original units,
using this as an excuse to evade duty,
not truly having a heart to serve.
The court annually orders the empire to weave brocade and mint coins,
and dispatches eunuchs to buy horses from foreign tribes,
expending tens of millions regularly,
but obtaining barely one or two in return.
Though many horses arrive,
most are inferior,
and the people are tasked with pasturing them,
causing severe harassment.
If they die or are injured,
compensation is ordered.
Horse-keeping households become impoverished,
even selling their wives
and children.
This is an even greater harm.
As for the surrendered people from Mòběi,
they are granted residences
and lavish provisions,
with the intention of attracting their kin.
Yet, those who come are all harboring intentions to spy,
not truly admiring the royal
transformative influence from afar,
nor gladly abandoning their homeland.
It would be proper, after they come to court,
to send them back to their own countries,
without necessarily keeping them to become a future problem for descendants.
As for matters of temples, monasteries, prayers, and sacrifices,
rulers of a state should be deeply wary.
The ancients had a saying,
licentious sacrifices bring no blessings.
How much more so when doing something useless harms what is useful,
wasting wealth pointlessly!
All these matters
cause the people below to lose heart
and displease Heaven above.
The rise of resentment and complaints
is indeed due to this.
The Fèngtiāndiàn
is where ministers are received and
edicts are issued,
what the ancients called the Míngtáng,
and yet disaster first struck it,
an extraordinary change.
Unless
Your Majesty reflects upon yourself and takes responsibility,
lavishly bestows benevolence,
reforms governance,
and relieves the impoverished people of the empire,
you cannot avert Heaven's wrath.
Previously, there were Imperial College students and
scholars
who, as only sons, requested to attend to their parents,
and consequently incurred guilt and were banished to the frontier,
this truly harms the principles of governance.
Recently, there was a great amnesty,
but judicial officials adhered to old regulations,
and those who should have been
pardoned were still detained.
I also beg that they be thoroughly cleansed again,
that rents and taxes be remitted,
and that all levies cease.
All officials of the various departments should receive their full salaries,
talented individuals should be selected,
recommendations should be widely implemented,
and corrupt officials who harm governance should have their crimes investigated and be dismissed.
Then the people's hearts will rejoice,
and harmony can be achieved,
thus securing the imperial ancestral altars,
establishing an endless foundation for the state for ten thousand years.
There is nothing greater than this.
Furthermore, what the state relies on for its longevity
is only Heaven's mandate and the people's hearts,
and Heaven's mandate constantly depends on the people's hearts for its presence or absence.
Now, Heaven's will is thus,
and it is not appropriate
to burden the people.
Your Majesty should return to Nánjīng,
visit the imperial tombs and temples,
and report the reasons for the disaster.
Nurture your sagely body and rest in non-action,
do not listen to the words of petty individuals,
and undertake new constructions,
lest you lead Your Majesty astray later.
The memorial was presented,
but not acted upon.
At that time, the Three Palaces had just been completed,
and the Emperor was about to issue an edict to the empire announcing the establishment of the capital,
when suddenly a fire disaster struck.
Greatly alarmed,
he issued an edict seeking frank advice.
However, when many of those who spoke out criticized the current administration,
the Emperor was displeased,
and his grand ministers, anticipating his wishes, in turn slandered the speakers.
The Emperor then became enraged,
stating that those who offered advice were slandering and reviling him,
and issued an edict strictly forbidding such actions,
with no pardon for offenders.
Grand Academician Lǐ Shímǐan and Lecturer Luó Rǔjìng were both imprisoned.
Censors Zhèng Wéihuán, Hé Zhōng, Luó Tōng, Xú Róng,
and Supervising Secretary Kē Xiān were all demoted to officials in Jiāozhǐ.
Only Jī, together with Principal Gau Gōngwàng and Junior Compiler Yáng Fù, were found innocent.
In the winter of that year,
Jī was promoted to Right Shùzǐ concurrently serving as Lecturer.
He died in office in the ninth month of the following year.
Jī had extensively studied numerous books,
was diligent and cautious in office,
and maintained a pure integrity like that of an impoverished scholar.
His son, Xún,
served as a Hanlin Academician during the Xuāndé reign,
and requested posthumous honors for his parents.
The Emperor instructed the Ministry of Personnel, saying:
"When the Imperial Grandfather campaigned in the desert,
and I guarded Běijīng,
Jī was by my side,
and his explanations were all of the righteous path.
He was a good minister,
so grant him the honors."
Zhèng Wéihuán was
from Cíxī.
He became a Jinshì in the thirteenth year of Yǒnglè.
He was dispatched to govern Nánqīng Zhōu in Jiāozhǐ,
where he died.
Kē Xiān was
from Jiàndé, Chí Zhōu.
Through the provincial examination, he was dispatched to govern Huān Zhōu in Jiāozhǐ.
He successively held positions as Surveillance Commissioner of Zhèjiāng and Yúnnán.
Yì Qiān was
from Dàizhōu.
He became a Jinshì in the ninth year of Yǒnglè.
He was appointed Investigating Censor.
He was dispatched to inspect Jiāngxī,
where his statements displeased the Emperor,
and he was demoted to Magistrate of Xiáshān.
He was later removed from office again due to another incident and returned home.
When Rénzōng was still Crown Prince,
he knew of Qiān's upright and unyielding character.
Upon ascending the throne,
he summoned him to be Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review.
Qiān directly criticized the current administration,
spoke of the greed and cruelty of officials,
stating that many government affairs were no longer like those of the Hóngwǔ era,
and that local officials excessively demanded levies without restraint.
The Emperor adopted much of his advice.
Later, he spoke on five more matters,
and his words were too vehement,
which displeased the Emperor.
Ministers Lǚ Zhèn and Wú Zhōng,
Vice Minister Wú Tíngyòng, Grand Minister of the Court of Judicial Review Yú Qiān, and others then impeached Qiān for slander and deception.
Metropolitan Censor Liú Guān ordered all the censors to collectively censure Qiān.
The Emperor summoned Yáng Shìqí and others to discuss it.
Shìqí replied:
"Qiān does not understand the broader principles,
but his heart is moved by the grace of his extraordinary promotion,
and he wishes to repay it.
When the ruler is sagacious, the minister is forthright.
May Your Majesty be lenient with him."
The Emperor then did not punish Qiān.
However, whenever he saw Qiān,
his words and demeanor were very stern.
Shìqí calmly said:
"Your Majesty issued an edict seeking frank advice.
Qiān's words were inappropriate,
incurring your wrath.
The outer court is apprehensive,
taking this as a warning regarding speech.
Now, ministers from all directions who come for audience are gathered at the palace gates.
Seeing Qiān in this state,
they will believe that Your Majesty cannot tolerate frank advice."
The Emperor said with alarm:
"This is indeed my intolerance,
but also Lǚ Zhèn and his ilk pandering to me and increasing my faults.
From now on, I shall set it aside."
He then excused Qiān from court attendance,
ordering him to focus solely on his departmental duties.
Not long after,
the Emperor, seeing that those who offered advice had become fewer,
again summoned Shìqí and said:
"I was angry with Qiān for being overly dramatic and exaggerating facts,
but now the court ministers have been silent for over a month.
You tell the various ministers
what is in my heart."
Shìqí said:
"My empty words are not enough to be believed.
I beg Your Majesty to personally issue a sealed decree."
The Emperor then ordered him to write an imperial edict by his couch, admitting his fault, saying:
"Since I ascended the throne,
the memorials submitted by ministers and common people have numbered in the hundreds,
and I have never failed to listen and accept them with joy.
If there was anything inappropriate,
I did not blame or rebuke them;
this is known by all ministers.
Recently,
what Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review Yì Qiān said
was mostly not factual.
The various ministers, pandering to my wishes,
collectively memorialized that he was feigning forthrightness
and requested he be punished according to the law.
I rejected all of them and did not listen,
merely excusing Qiān from court attendance.
But since then,
those who offer advice have become fewer.
Now, since last winter there has been no snow,
and in spring also little rain.
The yin and yang are out of harmony,
and there must be a fault for this.
How can there be nothing to say?
But as for those who are ministers,
they harbor thoughts of self-preservation,
withdrawing and remaining silent.
How can this be loyalty?
I, for a time, could not tolerate Qiān,
and I have never ceased to feel shame and blame myself.
All you ministers, do not take the past incident as a warning.
Regarding the nation's advantages and disadvantages, and inappropriate government decrees,
speak frankly without concealment.
Qiān shall resume court attendance as before."
At that time, court eunuchs were procuring timber in Sìchuān,
acting greedily and tyrannically.
The Emperor, seeing Qiān's integrity and uprightness,
ordered him to go and rectify the situation.
Qiān was promoted to Vice Censor-in-Chief,
and given paper money for his journey,
thus abolishing the timber procurement task.
In the early Xuāndé reign,
Right Administration Commissioner Qī Xùn of Jiāozhǐ was dismissed for corruption and lewdness.
Qiān was ordered to replace him.
When Wáng Tōng abandoned Jiāozhǐ,
Qiān was also condemned to death.
In the early Zhèngtǒng reign,
he was released as a commoner.
During the Tǔmù Incident,
Qiān, in commoner clothes, rushed to the palace gates,
recommending Tōng, along with Níng Mào, Ruǎn Qiān, and thirteen others,
all of whom were extraordinary talents and could be put to use.
Public opinion suggested Tōng assist Shí Hēng,
but Qiān requested Tōng be given sole command,
and the matter was thus dropped.
Court officials, knowing Qiān held a great reputation,
memorialized for him to be retained,
but this was also not granted.
In the second year of Jǐngtài, he again came to the capital,
memorializing to recommend Tōng and others,
but it was not accepted.
He retired and returned home,
and died not long after.
Rénzōng was broad-minded by nature
and tolerated frank advice.
Thus Qiān was spared punishment,
and instead Lǚ Zhèn and others were blamed.
And when Huáng Jì spoke of matters in the Western Regions,
the Emperor also admonished Zhèn and acted upon Jì's words.
Jì,
a native of Quánzhōu.
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
he passed the provincial examination.
He served as an instructor in Shāxiàn.
During the Yǒnglè era, he was promoted to Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Rites.
He frequently made three missions to the Western Regions.
At the beginning of Rénzōng's reign,
he submitted a memorial, stating:
“Many of the envoys presenting tribute from the Western Regions are merchants masquerading as such,
and unscrupulous minor individuals join them as attendants,
traveling by post-horse, causing trouble for people,
and transporting tribute items to the capital,
where they receive generous rewards.
The foreigners, coveting profit,
send tribute almost every month,
causing the common people to lose their livelihoods and neglect agriculture.
When their envoys return,
they carry many goods,
with cartloads numbering over a hundred.
With insufficient adult male laborers,
women are also pressed into service.
Wherever they go, they insult post officials,
and flog attendants and servants;
none dare to contend with them.
I beg Your Majesty to instruct the Shǎnxī Provincial Military Commission
that only kings from Hāmì and other states who send envoys to present tribute
be permitted to come to the capital,
and that only the chief and deputy envoys be allowed to use post-horses.
Thus, the people of Shǎnxī may find some relief.
As for the products of the Western Regions,
only horses are urgently needed for the frontier;
these should be supplied to the soldiers in Gānsù.
Other items like niter and wútóng wood,
are all useless for state expenditures;
I request that they all be refused.
Then, those who come will naturally become few,
and unnecessary expenses will be further saved.”
The emperor showed it to Grand Secretary Lǚ Zhèn,
and chided him, saying:
“Jì often served as an envoy,
and understands Western affairs thoroughly.
You are a Westerner;
do you not understand them?”
Jì’s words are correct;
let them be deliberated upon and implemented immediately.”
Later, he was promoted to Right Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
and together with Lǐ Qí and Luó Rǔjìng, he pacified and instructed Jiāozhǐ,
without failing his mission.
After returning from his mission,
he soon died.
Huáng Zé,
a native of Mǐnxiàn.
He passed the imperial examination in the tenth year of Yǒnglè.
He was promoted to Left Vice Administrator of Henán.
Nányáng had many displaced people;
he comforted and guided them to resume their livelihoods.
He once led conscripted laborers to Běijīng,
providing thorough relief and assistance.
After a long time,
he was transferred to Húguǎng.
Upon Rénzōng's ascension,
he entered for an audience,
and spoke on current affairs,
much of which was adopted.
When Xuānzōng ascended the throne,
he issued an edict seeking advice.

Zé submitted a memorial detailing ten matters: rectifying the mind, showing compassion to the people, revering Heaven, accepting remonstrance, training soldiers, valuing agriculture, stopping tribute, clarifying rewards and punishments, distancing favorites, and eliminating superfluous officials.
Regarding "distancing favorites," he said:
“Eunuchs,
their emotions are dark and hidden,
their thoughts are treacherous and cunning;
great wickedness appears as loyalty,
great deceit appears as trustworthiness,
and great cunning appears as foolishness.
Once intimacy is established with them,
it is like drinking fine wine,
one does not know one is drunk;
like eating sweet jerky,
one does not know its poison.
To favor them is very easy,
to distance them is very difficult.
Therefore, in ancient times, eunuchs were not allowed to manage military affairs or meddle in government,
which was to prevent trouble before it arose.
If a trickle is not stopped,
it will become a river.
These individuals should be completely alienated
and not allowed to handle affairs.
The past events of the Hàn and Táng dynasties
are clear examples to learn from.”
During Chéngzǔ's reign,
eunuchs gradually began to exercise power;
Xuānzōng increasingly favored them.
Of the ten matters Zé presented, this was particularly urgent.
Though the emperor praised and admired it,
he could not act upon it.
Later, the Inner Study Hall was established,
and many eunuchs became literate and understood literary meaning.
The ascendancy of eunuchs
began with Xuānzōng.
In the third year of Xuāndé, he was promoted to Provincial Administrator of Zhèjiāng.
He again memorialized, stating that the silver mines in Píngyáng, Líshuǐ, and other seven counties should be abolished,
and further requested the complete abolition of all mines and smelters.
His words were very earnest.
The emperor sighed and said:
“If the people are suffering like this,
how would I know?
Send officials to inspect and investigate,
and deliberate on a proposal to report.”
Zé had administrative achievements in office,
but often had violent fits of anger.
When Salt Commissioner Dīng Zī did not avoid his path,
he lashed him,
which led to a complaint being lodged against him.
Investigating Censor Mǎ Jǐn also impeached Zé. After completing nine years in office,
he traveled to the counties himself,
collected three thousand taels of silver to compensate official property,
and moreover, crossed the border to visit his home.
Consequently, he was arrested and imprisoned.
In the sixth year of Zhèngtǒng, he was dismissed and reverted to commoner status.
Initially,
Zé had memorialized that the population of Jīnhuá and Táizhōu had decreased compared to the Hóngwǔ era,
yet the annual production of bows and arrows remained the same;
he requested a reduction or exemption.
The matter was referred to the ministry for deliberation and was approved,
but Zé had already been dismissed from office for over a month.
Kǒng Yǒuliàng,
a native of Chángzhōu.
He became a *jìnshì* in the sixteenth year of Yǒnglè.
He was appointed as a *shùjíshì* (supernumerary Hanlin bachelor),
and later became the magistrate of Shuāngliú county.
At the beginning of Xuānzōng's reign,
he memorialized on six matters: Firstly,
regarding magistrates and county heads, who are officials close to the people,
in ancient times, there were no strict qualifications,
but suitable individuals had to be found,
without limits on years,
to enable them to exert their full effort.
Currently, those in office
often do not know the methods of comforting and nurturing the people,
and those who are honest and capable and have gained the people's trust
are frequently transferred or reassigned,
and their duties are inconsistent.
Or, due to implication in minor matters,
they labor day and night
in administration,
traveling back and forth on roads,
without a moment's rest.
I request that the Ministry of Personnel be instructed
to select those of established talent and reputation, or those who have long served as capital officials, to appoint them.
Superior officials should be warned
not to arbitrarily
transfer or reassign,
but to grant them sufficient time
and hold them responsible for administrative effectiveness.
As for distant posts lacking assistant officials,
many have been cut,
leaving a single official in charge.
Or, when an official must travel to the capital for business,
they often entrust miscellaneous officials
to act on their behalf,
resulting in delay and negligence,
inconsistent governance,
and the people not knowing fear.
Henceforth, for remote vacancies,
one principal official should always remain in charge of affairs,
and not be allowed to leave arbitrarily,
so that
the law may have constant observance.
Secondly,
the imperial examinations are for seeking virtuous individuals,
and merit must match the reality,
not merely be an exaggeration of numbers.
Currently, the autumn examinations select one or two hundred people at a time.
Abuses
are numerous,
and more than half succeed by luck.
At the metropolitan examination, eight or nine out of ten fail.
Those who pass the examination,
their actual conduct may be divergent.
I request that in the year the examinations are held,
the conduct
of all students be thoroughly verified.
Only those who are filial, fraternal, loyal, trustworthy, and possess excellent scholarship
should be permitted to take the examination.
This way, frivolous individuals will not be indiscriminately admitted,
and the state will obtain truly talented individuals for its use.
Thirdly,
salaries are for fostering integrity;
if income from salaries is too meager,
then daily life will not be sustained.
The regulations for official salaries in our dynasty
are considered meager compared to previous dynasties.
Currently, capital officials and
Officials in the provinces have their salaries slightly increased,
while other officials, high and low, besides having their paper money discounted,
receive no more than two *shí* of rice per month,
insufficient to feed several people.
To support parents and raise children,
and to host
travelers on the road,
where are the expenses to be sourced?
The corrupt exploit their positions for profit and personal gain,
while the incorruptible ultimately suffer poverty with no one to complain to.
I request an imperial edict for the Hùbù to verify the actual grain reserves throughout the empire,
and from the annual
surplus of expenditure,
to moderately increase official salaries.
Furthermore, let internal and external censorial officials
seek out and interview incorruptible officers,
and greatly commend and reward them.
Then the incorruptible will know encouragement,
and the corrupt
will know warning.
Fourth,
