in ancient times, taxes and corvée were assessed based on land suitability
and household population,
not demanding what was not there,
nor taking everything that was.
Now, besides the regular taxes,
there are also matters like "harmonious purchases" (*hé mǎi*) and "procurements" (*cǎi
bàn*) .
From the court's perspective,
it is merely ordering officials to use public funds for fair purchases.
However, unscrupulous individuals,
colluding with clerks and scribes,
monopolize goods,
and cleverly
invent pretexts like "verification" and "wastage"
to extort several times the amount,
leading to myriad corrupt practices.
I humbly request a complete cessation of procurements (*cǎi mǎi*)
and a reduction of non-urgent tasks,
so that state taxes may be regular,
and the people spared
from arbitrary levies and disturbances.
As for the two matters concerning the elimination of redundant officials
and the appointment of censorial officials,
many speakers have already addressed them,
so they are not fully recorded here.
In Xuāndé eight years (1433), the Lìbù was ordered to select sixty-eight literati from among the provincial officials for examination,
from whom Yǒuliàng and the *jìnshì* Hú Duānzhēn, among seven others, were chosen.
They were all assigned to handle affairs in the Six Offices of Scrutiny (*Liù Kē*).
After two years,
they were all appointed as Supervising Secretaries (*Gěishìzhōng*),
except for Yǒuliàng, who died before being appointed.
Fàn Jì was a
Yuán *jìnshì*.
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
he was appointed Prefect of Guǎngxìn due to his literary talent.
He was later implicated in an offense and exiled to Xīngzhōu.
When Xuānzōng ascended the throne,
Jì was over eighty years old.
He went to the imperial court and presented eight matters.
The first was:
The law of paper currency originated in
Hàn and Táng.
The Yuán dynasty created the Yuántǒng Silver Certificate (*Jiāochāo*),
and later also created the Zhōngtǒng Note (*Chāo*).
Over time, goods became valuable and notes
became cheap,
harming both public and private interests.
So the Zhìyuán Note was created to circulate alongside the Zhōngtǒng Note,
with old and new mutually balancing and universally accepted.
The people were also ordered to bring worn-out notes to the
Pingzhǔn Treasury,
where five strings of Zhōngtǒng Notes could be exchanged for one string of Zhìyuán Notes.
Furthermore, their method was to print ten thousand ingots daily,
totaling a certain amount for officials' salaries and internal palace expenses,
and a certain amount for regular taxes and miscellaneous levies throughout the empire.
Collection and distribution were orderly,
circulating smoothly without stagnation,
which allowed them to remain in circulation for a long time.
Emperor Tàizǔ created the Dàmíng Precious Note (*Bǎochāo*),
where one string of notes
was equivalent to one *liǎng* of silver.
The people happily embraced it.
Now, after more than fifty years,
the system has become somewhat flawed,
also due to goods being valuable and notes being cheap.
I wish Your Majesty
would adapt to the times and make changes,
re-issuing Precious Notes,
fully adhering to the initial Hóngwǔ system,
allowing new and old to circulate concurrently.
Take the number created during the Yuán dynasty and adjust it,
and carefully balance it with the state's
expenditure figures,
so that notes are few and goods are many,
notes are valuable and goods are cheap.
Strictly enforce regulations against counterfeiting,
and establish a method for exchange,
promoting the old and introducing
the new,
without depletion or obstruction.
Then the note system will circulate smoothly,
forever free from defects.
The second was:
The way to defend the borders
is to guard the strategic passes.
Places like Shuòzhōu, Dàtóng, Kāipíng, Xuānfǔ, and Dàníng
are the outer walls of the capital,
and the gateways
to the frontier.
The land is arable,
and the cities are defensible.
It is advisable to station abundant troops for defense,
extensively open up military farms (*túntián*),
repair and maintain castles and fortifications,
be diligent with beacon fires,
and clarify scout posts.
Do not
covet small gains,
do not lightly seek far,
fortify walls and clear the fields (*jiān bì qīng yě*),
leaving nothing for the enemy to gain.
Wait until they are exhausted and then attack them;
if you gain an advantage, stop,
do not pursue deeply.
This
is the great essential of border defense.
The third was:
Troops are not about quantity,
but about being able to fight.
Lately, many officials, clerks, and common people involved in incidents are sent to the frontier as military exiles,
either mere bookworms
or
the old, weak, sick, and disabled.
When there is a military expedition,
the powerful can avoid it,
while the poor and weak are counted to make up the numbers.
Their weapons are incomplete,
and their provisions are insufficient.
They tremble at the mere sight of the enemy,
how
can they fight to the death?
Now, it is advisable to select the strong and brave,
diligently train them,
and merely have the rest guard the city walls and beat night watches,
or run errands at the headquarters,
so that each may largely fulfill their purpose.
The fourth was:
Of the people's sufferings, none is worse than the conscription of soldiers (*gōu jūn*).
Garrison officials dispatch six or seven members,
and *bǎihù* dispatch two or three military standards,
all of whom are either powerful individuals who form connections
or those who fear and avoid conscription,
dispatched after heavy bribery.
Upon reaching the prefectures and counties,
they arbitrarily wield power and influence,
coercing the *lǐjiǎ*,
and indulging in corruption.
Households without male adults are relentlessly extorted;
households with male adults
are fraudulently claimed to be dead.
They create pretexts to stay,
delaying their return for a long time.
When they return,
they use the acquired property
to bribe
officials
and clerks everywhere,
and vaguely submit their reports.
Investigating the male adults they claim to have recruited,
not even one in ten is found,
making it difficult for the army not to have depleted ranks.
From now on, if a soldier has an incident,
let each garrison report
to the Dūdūfǔ and Bīngbù.
The Dūdūfǔ and Bīngbù will inform the Bùzhèngsī and Ànchásī,
ordering the prefectures, sub-prefectures, and counties to, according to their registered native place and name,
conscript and send them to the garrison.
Then the abuses of dispatched personnel causing disturbance
will naturally cease.
The fifth was:
During the Hóngwǔ reign, seven-tenths of the soldiers were ordered to cultivate military farms (*túntián*),
and three-tenths to guard the cities,
which was an excellent strategy.
Lately, deployments have become increasingly frequent,
and constructions increasingly
widespread.
The name of military farming exists in vain,
with many fields lying fallow.
Moreover, horse breeding, grass gathering, wood cutting, and charcoal burning,
and various other corvée duties are numerous,
how can military strength not be exhausted,
and agriculture not be abandoned?
I wish Your Majesty would order border generals to instruct their soldiers to reclaim wasteland,
with limits set on acreage,
the government providing cattle and seeds,
and assessing their diligence and idleness,
clearly enforcing rewards and punishments to show encouragement.
Chéng.
Then the fields beyond the frontier can be fully reclaimed,
the transport of provisions will be further eased,
and all border regions will become wealthy and substantial.
No plan is more convenient than this.
The sixth point states,
schools
are the source of moral transformation
and the origin of talent.
It is essential to cultivate character and practical application,
not merely to compare literary and artistic skills.
During the Hóngwǔ
reign, excellent teachers and scholars were selected;
their education and nurture were very comprehensive,
and talent flourished remarkably.
Recently, scholarly habits have become listless,
ambitions are not grand,
and principles are not firm.
In ordinary life, lacking
a spirit of integrity, rectitude, and magnanimity,
how can one expect them to become famous high officials when they enter court?
It is advisable to select virtuous scholars to serve as educational officials in prefectures and counties,
and to choose sons from the populace who are upright and diligent in character
to be students.
Instruct them in the classics and histories,
encourage them in their integrity and conduct.
When they have achieved success,
recommend them to the national academy.
Through constant refinement and rigorous training,
let their spirit be full and their aspirations firm,
so they can outstandingly
become talented individuals.
Then, employ them,
and there will be no difficulty in entrusting them with the affairs of the realm and the state.
The seventh point states,
weapons are instruments of ill omen;
sages use them only when left with no other choice.
When Hàn Gāozǔ lifted the siege of Píngchéng,
we never heard Xiāo and Cáo advise him to seek
revenge;
when Táng Tàizōng repelled the Tūjué at Biànqiáo,
we never heard Fáng and Dù advise him to retaliate.
Ancient wise rulers and good ministers did not wish to exhaust the people's strength to boast of military achievements;
their
foresight was profound.
In the early Hóngwǔ years, the emperor once grandly ordered generals
to clear the desert.
However, due to interrupted provisions,
he soon recalled the army.
Consequently, the Dōngshèng Guard was withdrawn to
Dàtóng,
the valley pass of Xīshānyángwǔ was blocked,
generals were selected, troops were trained,
and strategic points were held in readiness.
Internally, governance and education were cultivated;
externally, border defenses were strict.
Military agricultural colonies were expanded,
schools were established,
greedy officials were punished,
and stubborn people were relocated.
Within a few years,
Duǒ'érzhībā offered his daughter,
Bóyán Tiēmù'ér, Nǎi'érbùhuā, and others were successively captured,
Nàhā
chū also surrendered.
This is a clear demonstration of focusing solely on internal governance
and not engaging in distant military strategies.
We humbly hope that Your Majesty will look back to the Hàn and Táng dynasties,
and closely emulate Tàizǔ,
not finding joy in exhausting the army and engaging in excessive warfare,
nor taking pride in
razing enemy homes and sweeping out their lairs.
Abandon barren lands,
and allow the people within the civilized realm to recuperate,
so they may exert their utmost in farming and sericulture,
and dedicate themselves to the village
schools.
The border regions will be free from the suffering of wounds,
and the villages will be free from the sounds of groaning.
Generals will not seek unmerited achievements,
scholars will not suffer premature suppression,
people from afar will naturally submit,
and those from beyond the wilderness will naturally return.
The state's
lifespan will be spiritually extended for ten thousand years.
The eighth point states,
officials are not about numbers,
but about finding the right people.
After the great chaos, the state
adapted and made adjustments,
changing prefectures into zhoū,
and zhōus into counties.
Subsequently, small counties whose grain revenue was insufficient for salaries were merged,
and officials were appointed according to the population size.
Counties with large populations had a chéng and a bù;
those with small populations had only a zhīxiàn and a diǎnshǐ.
At that time, no official neglected duties,
and the people did not worry about hardship.
Now, the officials of the two Pān and Niè circuits and the prefecture, zhōu, and county officials
are more than double those in the Hóngwǔ period,
yet governance is less effective,
the people are more
uneasy,
malpractices proliferate,
and deception and fraud arise.
There are even officials who cannot hear and judge cases,
and scribes who are unfamiliar with official documents.
They allow ghostwriters to stay,
who secretly influence matters in the government,
take bribes openly,
and cause lawsuits to be delayed.
All this is due to
redundant officials and corrupt clerks.
We hope Your Majesty will decide from your imperial heart,
that all internal and external officials,
according to the quotas of the Hóngwǔ period,
will have all
redundant and corrupt individuals dismissed.
Then no heavenly work will be left undone,
all achievements will flourish,
and the world will be greatly ordered.
After the memorial was submitted,
the emperor ordered court officials to discuss it.
Minister Lǚ Zhèn considered the prose verbose,
and moreover, many of the proposed actions had already been implemented,
so it was not worth adopting.
The Emperor said:
"What he said shows great learning and knowledge,
and much accords with My heart.
Investigate his past conduct and report back."
Zhèn then said:
"Jì was a jinshì of the former Yuán dynasty,
once served as a prefect,
and was exiled to the frontier for an offense."
The Emperor said:
"What a pity this man
has long been stuck in the ranks;
he is still useful now."
Zhèn said:
"He is old."
The Emperor said:
"For the state to employ people,
it precisely needs seasoned individuals,
but they should not be assigned to overly complex or demanding tasks."
So, Jì was appointed as a Confucian instructor.
Liáo Ràng,
a native of Lánzhōu,
was a supernumerary attendant of the Sù Prefectural Guard Command.
He loved learning, had lofty aspirations,
and was well-versed in current affairs.
When Jǐngdì ascended the throne,
to punish Wáng Zhèn's deception,
he widely opened channels for remonstrance,
allowing officials and common people alike to submit memorials on state affairs.
In the sixth month of Jǐngtài first year (1450),
Ràng went to the palace gate and presented several matters,
the gist of which was: In recent years, construction projects have been numerous,
heterodox doctrines have flourished,
Tibetan monks have arrived in continuous streams,
and corrupt officials have run rampant.
Ministers have not rectified these wrongs,
and censors have not impeached their crimes.
High
and low are deluded,
and the people's lives are suffering.
Cunning bandits have invaded the frontier,
and the Former Emperor was exiled.
At this critical juncture when Your Majesty lies on a weapon and tastes gall,
how can you not promote the virtuous and employ the capable,
to completely renew
governance?
In the past, when Zōng and Yuè were generals,
enemy nations dared not call their names;
when Hán and Fàn guarded the frontier,
the Western bandits heard of it and lost their courage.
When Sīmǎ Guāng was prime minister,
powerful neighbors
were warned not to invade the border.
Now, those civil and military ministers with prestige and virtue
should be put in charge of key positions,
and talented individuals with wisdom and skill should be widely consulted
and deployed throughout the court.
Then Yěxiān will surely be overawed and submit,
and the Former Emperor can be brought back
in a matter of days.
Ministers are
yang;
eunuchs are
yin.
Gentlemen are
yang;
petty men are
yin.
Recently, there was a solar eclipse and an earthquake,
indicating that yin is ascendant and yang is weak. These are divine omens
Di.
I implore Your Majesty to take full control of the state's affairs,
restrain the palace eunuchs and prevent them from interfering in government,
and block petty individuals from holding office.
Then the yin and yang will be harmonious, and celestial anomalies will be averted.
The order or disorder of the empire
depends on the rectitude or perversity of the ruler's heart.
Hunting is entertainment,
palaces are extravagance,
eunuchs are intimates –
if any one of these three exists,
it is enough to corrupt the ruler's heart.
I wish Your Majesty would cultivate and overcome these temptations,
associate more with worthy scholars and officials,
and less with eunuchs and palace women.
Then you will naturally be able to reform extravagance,
abstain from idle pleasures,
and your heart will be free from perversity.
Yáo (堯) set up a slander-post,
fearing that people would not speak out,
which is why he was a sage.
Qín (秦) abolished posthumous titles,
fearing that people would criticize him,
which is why he perished.
If Your Majesty broadens the capacity to accept remonstrance,
and commends
officials who speak frankly,
then regarding the advantages and disadvantages of the state,
and the joys and sorrows of the common people,
your subordinates will have no misgivings,
and will speak their minds completely.
Sū Zǐ (蘇子) said:
"If in times of peace there are no officials who dare to
offend the ruler's dignity and offer remonstrance,
then in times of difficulty there will surely be no men who uphold integrity and die for righteousness."
I wish Your Majesty would remember these words and examine them carefully.
After the memorial was presented,
the emperor largely approved and accepted it.
Four years later,
Ràng (讓) passed the *jìnshì* examination.
He served as a county magistrate until his death.
In the second year of Jǐngtài (景泰) (1451),
the imperial student Guō Yòu (郭佑) also submitted a memorial concerning military affairs,
which roughly stated:
"The rebellious bandits have transgressed,
and the Retired Emperor is sullied;
this is an extraordinary change unseen in a thousand years,
and a grievance that must be avenged for a hundred generations.
Now, the envoys come
in numbers of several thousands,
always arrogantly demanding and expecting things from us,
while we merely tolerate and appease them,
leading to the daily expansion of the bandits' power
and the daily exhaustion of our spirit.
They seek peace, and we grant peace; they seek war, and we grant war.
Thus, the power of peace or war
does not rest with us, but with the bandits.
I wish Your Majesty would unite the hearts of the people
and draw close to the virtuous and good,
to solidify the foundation of the nation;
expand reserves
and train generals and soldiers,
to strengthen the national spirit.
Rectify the divisions and establish proper titles,
and decide matters with righteousness.
If they are obstinate and invade,
then mobilize troops to punish them.
If the lands south of the Great Desert
do not dare to let a single horse pass,
then we can ensure a hundred years of peace.
Otherwise, the strength of the northwest will be exhausted,
and the resources of the southeast will be depleted,
making it impossible to rest in peace for a single day.
Recently, due to the exhaustion of state funds,
the ministers formulating national policy, wishing to alleviate an immediate crisis,
ordered the people who offered grain to be granted official caps and sashes.
Now that the military situation is somewhat calmer,
this practice continues as before.
Farmers, artisans, merchants, and peddlers,
regardless of their wisdom or foolishness,
are given these only for their wealth.
They boast to their relatives,
and show off in their hometowns,
fostering improper and perverse ambitions.
Corrupt and incompetent officials who have been dismissed and returned to commoner status,
wishing to cover up the shame in their villages,
offer grain or fodder,
and return with caps and sashes.
Previously, they lost their positions due to accepting bribes;
now, they obtain office by offering goods.
How can we forbid corruption
and uphold the dignity of titles and ranks?
Moreover, when the empire is unified,
wealth is hidden among the people.
Before reaching an extreme necessity,
to take such measures
is to empty the treasury and invite the enemy's greed."
The memorial was sent down for deliberation by the court,
but it was not implemented.
There was also Hú Zhònglún (胡仲倫),
a clerk in the Yunnan Salt Tax Commissioner's Office.
He came to the capital for official business
and happened to be there when the Retired Emperor was taken north.
Yĕxiān (也先) wished to marry his sister to the Retired Emperor.
The Retired Emperor then sent Guǎngníng Bó (廣寧伯) Liú Ān (劉安) to relay this to the emperor.
Zhònglún (仲倫) submitted a memorial to argue against it.
He said:
"There are seven points today where we cannot yield.
To lower the dignity of the Son of Heaven
and engage in marital alliance is the first.
The enemy feigning peace talks
to make us unprepared is the second.
Their insistence on marriage,
acting arrogantly and self-important, is the third.
Demanding gold and silks
to exhaust us is the fourth.
Using the excuse of escorting the emperor
to seize the opportunity to invade is the fifth.
Coercing the Retired Emperor into issuing an imperial handwritten decree
to trick us into surrendering border cities is the sixth.
Wanting to acquire the land beyond the mountains is the seventh.
If we concede on even one of these,
the great cause will be lost.
In the past, when the Retired Emperor was on the throne,
Wáng Zhèn (王振) held exclusive power.
Loyal remonstrators died,
and outspoken individuals were banished.
Gentlemen were rejected,
while petty individuals were rapidly promoted.
Many memorials were decided by internal imperial decrees,
mixing black and white,
and inverting right and wrong.
The bandits in Fújiàn (福建) and Zhèjiāng (浙江) were rampant,
and the conflict with Wǎlà (瓦剌) greatly escalated.
Your Majesty should draw near to the virtuous and distance yourself from the wicked,
dispense rewards fairly and punishments strictly,
understand the sentiments of those above,
and convey the aspirations of those below.
Then, the treacherous individuals who sell out the country will find no loopholes,
and sudden crises will have no opportunity to erupt.
The imperial court will thenceforth be respected,
and the empire will thenceforth be at peace."
The emperor approved and accepted it.
There was also Huá Mǐn,
a supernumerary soldier of the imperial guard at Nánjīng.
He was spirited and generous,
read books and understood the great principles,
and was indignant that Wáng Zhèn had thrown the country into chaos.
Whenever he spoke with his peers, he would grit his teeth and curse angrily.
In the ninth month of the third year of Jǐngtài, he submitted a memorial, saying:
"In recent years,
the palace eunuchs Yuán Qí, Táng Shòu, Xǐ Níng, and Wáng Zhèn have monopolized power and harmed governance,
leading to the nation's affairs being in peril.
I hope Your Majesty will prevent problems from escalating,
take overall control of the reins of power,
and set an example for ten thousand generations of descendants.
Otherwise, I fear that calamity will brew within the palace,
and the evils of Cáo Jié and Hóu Lǎn
will reappear today.
Although your servant is humble and lowly,
I cannot help but weep bitterly.
I respectfully present ten harms inflicted upon the army and the people,
and speak of them earnestly to Your Majesty.
The palace eunuchs' homes are piled high with gold, silver, pearls, and jade,
filling rooms and coffers.
How did they come by these?
If not by secretly stealing from the imperial treasury,
then by externally exploiting the people's wealth.
This is the first harm.
They rely on their power and dote on their favorites,
occupying residences of dukes and marquises,
undertaking construction projects,
and causing trouble and hardship for the military and civilians.
This is the second harm.
Their family members and external relatives
are all unregistered individuals from the marketplaces,
acting wildly and arrogantly,
committing crimes as they please,
and buying official positions with grain,
thus mixing the noble and the lowly.
This is the third harm.
They construct Buddhist temples,
spending immeasurable sums,
to satisfy their personal desires,
thereby depleting the wealth of tens of thousands of families.
This is the fourth harm.
They extensively acquire farmlands,
which are not subject to taxes,
and register households with prefectures and counties,
who are then exempt from levies and corvée,
their fields stretching endlessly,
while the people have no place to stand a single awl.
This is the fifth harm.
Their family members monopolize salt,
falsely occupying salt certificates,
then reselling them to others,
doubling the price by enormous amounts,
thereby violating state law
and seizing merchant profits.
This is the sixth harm.
They request the establishment of rest houses,
to entertain merchants and travelers,
and relying on their power, they buy on credit,
and trusting in their strength, they do not repay,
causing merchants to suffer losses,
and no one dares to question them.
This is the seventh harm.
They illegally release military artisans,
calling them retainers,
making them pay monthly fees,
leading to a shortage of personnel for production in the imperial workshops and bureaus,
and the labor is heavy and the workforce insufficient.
This is the eighth harm.
When their family members trade and purchase materials,
the responsible officials, out of fear,
inflate the price ten-fold for one item,
thereby harming the state and exploiting the people.
This is the ninth harm.
Wherever they supervise work,
they impose illegal cruel punishments,
causing military artisans to suffer terribly,
and their bitter resentment is unbearable.
This is the tenth harm."
The memorial was sent to the Board of Rites,
which suppressed it and took no action.
There was also Jiǎ Bīn,
a native of Shānghé,
and a clerk in the Provincial Administration Commission of Shānxī.
He also memorialized about the harms caused by eunuchs,
citing Emperor Huán of Hàn, Emperor Wénzōng of Táng, and Emperors Huī and Qīn of Sòng as warnings.
He also presented his compiled work, *Zhōngyì Jí* (Collection of Loyalty and Righteousness), in four volumes,
which gathered records from historical biographies of upright admonishers, loyal and steadfast individuals,
and included examples of eunuchs who, relying on favor, corrupted governance,
serving as cautionary tales,
and he requested that it be printed and published.
The Board of Rites considered his words pertinent
and requested that the emperor examine and accept them,
but that it was unnecessary to print and circulate them.
The emperor acknowledged receipt.
Zuǒ Dǐng,
courtesy name Zhōu-qì,
was from Yǒngxīn.
He obtained his *jìnshì* degree in the seventh year of Zhèngtǒng.
The following year,
the Censor-in-Chief Wáng Wén, noting many vacancies among censors,
requested that the Board of Personnel meet to select and appoint from among the *jìnshì*.
The emperor agreed.
Minister Wáng Zhí examined Dǐng and Bái Guī and over ten others,
who were proficient in legal matters,
and all were appointed censors.
Dǐng received the appointment to Nánjīng.
Soon after, he was transferred to the North
and served as an investigating censor in Shānxī.
At that time, Emperor Yīngzōng had been captured by the Northern tribes,
and war and famine struck repeatedly.
He requested the remission of tax grain for the prefectures of Tàiyuán and others,
and the suspension of corvée for transporting provisions to Dàtóng,
to relieve their distress.
When the Oirats requested peace,
he adamantly argued against it.
Soon after, due to famine in Shāndōng and Hénán,
Dǐng was sent to inspect,
and the people relied on him for peace.
According to the law,
officials who intentionally caused the death of innocent people were to be punished.
At that time, on the recommendation of the Grand Secretariat Yu Tàimín,
all such offenders were leniently pardoned.
Dǐng said:
"Ignorant common people
may be pardoned if they confess.
But how is it any different from intentional killing when officials cunningly fabricate charges and twist the law?
Law is
the public standard of the world,
and its severity cannot be determined by personal whim."
From then on, judgments were made according to the law.
In the fourth year of Jǐngtài, he memorialized:
"The Wǎlā (Oirats) rebellion erupted,
and the generals and soldiers were useless,
because military governance was not established.
It was said that past弊 must be severely punished,
but now five years have passed.
Diaochan (official hats) fill the seats,
all belonging to dukes and marquises;
saddles and horses block the roads,
all belonging to generals and commanders.
The people's wealth is depleted annually,
and the national treasury is daily emptied.
With the vastness of the empire,
and the multitude of land and armed forces,
it is still unable to display power and might,
which means military governance is still not established.
In the early days of the dynasty, Emperor Tàizǔ established laws and regulations.
By Emperor Tàizōng's time,
it was temporarily allowed for offenders to redeem their crimes,
which was an expedient measure.
However, legal officials, adhering rigidly,
made it into a standing precedent,
where officials who accepted bribes to pervert justice
were all able to reduce their punishments through redemption.
With such crookedness,
what more scruples are there?
In the early days of the dynasty, official appointments were regular.
Recently, new positions have been added due to various matters.
Each department used to have two section chiefs (*zhǔshì*),
but now some have increased to ten.
There were sixty censors,
but now there are over a hundred.
Even one Board has two Ministers (*shàngshū*),
and Vice Ministers (*shìláng*) are also double the usual quota,
while Censors-in-Chief (*dūyùshǐ*) are counted in dozens.
These are the redundant capital officials.
Externally, officials for pacifying the people and managing military colonies have been added.
For example, the counselors (*cānyì*) in Hénán
increased by two to become four,
and the assistant officials (*qiānshì*) increased by three to become seven.
These are the redundant external officials.
Throughout the empire, each of the two commissions (Provincial Administration and Provincial Surveillance) had over ten officials,
yet censors are sent annually to inspect,
and high officials are again sent to patrol and guard.
Now, these patrol and guard officials
are the same as the regional censors of the past.
To be a regional censor meant that the combined strengths of many were insufficient,
but to be a patrol and guard official means that the wisdom of one person is more than enough.
Is there such a principle?
Furthermore, the rotation of censors is too rapid;
they should be appointed for a period of six years.
This would allow them to become thoroughly familiar with political affairs,
after which they can govern the people.
The duties of an investigating censor are especially important;
newly appointed officials should not be allowed
to try their hand carelessly.
The remaining hundred officials
should all be carefully selected and given long tenure."
The emperor largely approved and accepted these points.
Not long after,
he spoke again:
“The state has enjoyed peace for several decades,
yet public and private stores are not yet sufficient.
Once military campaigns arise,
requisitions and arbitrary levies,
and the sale of offices and titles,
are all policies of a declining age, expedient and makeshift.
This is the fault of those who manage the national accounts.
Your servant requests that we severely curb trivial crafts,
strictly prohibit idleness,
expel heterodox sects to return to agriculture,
reduce redundant officials to save on wasteful spending,
open up屯 tián (military agricultural colonies) to strengthen the borders,
and inspect military ranks to relieve provisions.
The construction of monasteries and temples,
the offering of food to Buddhas and monks,
as well as non-urgent projects,
and useless expenditures,
should all be stopped.
We must exclusively prioritize farming and value grain as fundamental,
and personally practice frugality to set an example.
Only then can the people be enriched and the nation made prosperous.
If, however, this is neglected,
and officials who exploit and extort are allowed to practice 'morning three, evening four' tactics,
the people's strength will be exhausted while levies continue endlessly,
and the people's wealth depleted while taxes increase daily.
If we merely relieve the immediate crisis,
without considering unforeseen dangers,
Your servant secretly fears it.”
The memorial was sent to the Hùbù (Ministry of Revenue).
The Shàngshū (Minister) Jīn Lián (金濂) requested to resign,
but the emperor did not permit it.
Dǐng's (鼎) proposals were also not fully implemented.
More than a month later,
due to natural disasters,
he, along with fellow officials, submitted seven proposals to remedy abuses and care for the people.
At the end, he said:
“Among the high officials, there is no lack of treacherous individuals.
It is fitting to dismiss the worst among them,
to purify the foundation of government.”
The emperor approved of his words
and issued an edict to investigate and distinguish,
but the high officials who offered to resign were persuaded to stay.
The Jǐshìzhōng (Supervising Secretary) Lín Cōng (林聰) requested a clear directive for Dǐng (鼎) and others to specifically impeach them.

Dǐng (鼎), Cōng (聰) and others then jointly censured Hébù Shàngshū (Minister of Personnel) Hé Wényuān (何文淵), Xíngbù Shàngshū (Minister of Justice) Yú Shìyuè (俞士悅), Gōngbù Shìláng (Vice Minister of Works) Zhāng Mǐn (張敏), and Tōngzhèngshǐ (Chief Censor of the Office of Transmission) Lǐ Xī (李錫) for dereliction of duty.
Xī (錫) was dismissed,
and Wényuān (文淵) retired.
Dǐng (鼎) was honest and diligent in office,
and enjoyed an excellent reputation.
The Yùshǐ (Censor) Liàn Gāng (練綱) was known for his forthright speech,
but Dǐng (鼎) was particularly skilled at drafting memorials.
A saying in the capital went:
“Zuǒ Dǐng's (左鼎) hand,
Liàn Gāng's (練綱) mouth.”
From the highest officials down, all feared him.
Dǐng (鼎) was posted out as Guǎngdōng Yòu Cānzhèng (Right Administration Commissioner of Guangdong).
When Yīngzōng (英宗) was restored to the throne,
based on Guō Dēng's (郭登) recommendation,
he was summoned back as Zuǒ Qiān Dū Yùshǐ (Assistant Censor-in-Chief of the Left).
He died a year later.
Liàn Gāng (練綱),
courtesy name Zōngyuán (從道),
was from Chángzhōu (長洲).
His grandfather, Zéchéng (則成), was a Yùshǐ (Censor) during the Hóngwǔ (洪武) reign.
Liàn Gāng (練綱) passed the provincial examination
and entered the Guózǐ Jiān (Imperial Academy).
He successively served in the Dūcháyuàn (Censorate).
When Chéng Wáng (郕王) served as regent,
he presented eight strategies for rejuvenation.
When Yěxiān (也先) was about to invade,
he again said:
“Peace talks must not be entered into;
moving the capital south must not be followed.
Anyone who advocates such proposals
should be immediately executed.
The security of the state depends
solely on Yú Qiān (于謙) and Shí Hēng (石亨) to command the central army,
while high officials are dispatched to guard the nine gates.
Loyal and filial imperial princes of renown should be selected
to join the defending officials in serving the emperor.
A dispatch should be sent to the commander in Shǎnxī (陝西) to mobilize frontier troops to defend the capital.”
The emperor followed all his advice.
Gāng (綱) possessed talent and eloquence,
and was eager for fame.
Dū Yùshǐ (Censor-in-Chief) Chén Yì (陳鎰) and Shàngshū (Minister) Yú Shìyuè (俞士悅) were both from Gāng's (綱) hometown.
Mindful of Gāng's (綱) repeated and acclaimed remonstrances regarding current politics,
and also fearing his words,
they recommended him,
and he was appointed Yùshǐ (Censor).
In the first year of Jǐngtài (景泰),
he submitted five proposals on current affairs.
He then inspected the salt administration in Liǎnghuái (兩淮).
When the Fùmǎ Dūwèi (Imperial Son-in-Law) Zhào Huī (趙輝) embezzled profits,
he impeached him.
In the winter of the third year,
he, along with fellow officials,
submitted eight proposals in response to an imperial request,
all of which were approved for implementation.
Not long after,
he again, with fellow officials, submitted a memorial stating:
“The Lìbù (Ministry of Personnel) is unjust in its selections,
arbitrarily promoting and demoting individuals.
We request that Shàngshū (Minister) Hé Wényuān (何文淵) and Yòu Shìláng (Vice Minister of the Right) Xiàng Wényào (項文曜) be brought to justice.
Shàngshū (Minister) Wáng Zhí (王直) and Zuǒ Shìláng (Vice Minister of the Left) Yú Shān (俞山), whose conduct has always been upright,
were misled by Wényào (文曜) and others.
All should be interrogated.”
Although the emperor did not punish them,
he ultimately sided with Gāng (綱) and others, considering them righteous.
The following year, he was ordered to assist in military affairs in Yánsūi (延綏),
but he stated that his rank was too low for such a heavy responsibility
and begged to be appointed Qiān Dū Yùshǐ (Assistant Censor-in-Chief).
The emperor said:
“Can one request a promotion oneself?”
Thus, the order was withdrawn.
Initially,
when the capital was in a state of emergency,
able-bodied men from all quarters were recruited and organized into camps for training.
After many years, many deserted,
or failed to report for drills on time.
The court debated registering them permanently in military rolls.
Gāng (綱) and others argued:
“At the beginning of recruitment,
they were inspired by loyalty and righteousness,
and promised dismissal once the situation was settled.
Now, continuous rotating drills
have already dashed their hopes.
Furthermore, their desertion
was indeed forced by cold and hunger.
How can they be suddenly registered in military rolls?
The border regions face many troubles;
if more are to be recruited,
who would respond again?”
An edict was issued to immediately revoke the previous order.
In the fifth year, he was appointed Circuital Inspector of Fújiàn (福建),
where he and the Ànchásǐ (Provincial Surveillance Commissioner) Yáng Yù (楊玉) mutually impeached each other,
and both were sent to the authorities.
Yù (玉) was demoted to Zhīfǔ (Prefect) of Huángzhōu (黃州),
and Gāng (綱) to Pàn guān (Magistrate) of Bīnzhōu (邠州).
He died after a long time.
Cáo Kǎi (曹凱),
courtesy name Zōngyuán (宗元),
was from Yìdū (益都).
He became a Jìnshì (Palace Graduate) in the tenth year of Zhèngtǒng (正統).
He was appointed Xíngkē Jǐshìzhōng (Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Justice).
He was upright and had many courageous acts.
When Yīngzōng (英宗) led the northern expedition,
he remonstrated very strongly,
and further said:
“Today's situation
is vastly different from Chányuān (澶淵).
Back then, both civil and military officials were loyal and brave, and the soldiers and horses were strong and fierce.
Now, eunuchs usurp power,
and people's hearts are apathetic.
These people not only regard Your Majesty as a single gamble,
but they also have no time to care for Huái (懷), Mǐn (愍), Huī (徽), or Qīn (欽)!”
The emperor did not listen,
and indeed the imperial carriage was captured.
Kǎi (凱) wept bitterly all day,
his voice reaching the forbidden palace.
Together with Wáng Hóng (王竑), he attacked Mǎ Shùn (馬順) until he died.
During the Jǐngtài (景泰) reign,
he was promoted to Zuǒ Jǐshìzhōng (Supervising Secretary of the Left).
Jǐshìzhōng (Supervising Secretary) Lín Cōng (林聰) impeached Hé Wényuān (何文淵) and Zhōu Xuán (周旋),
but an edict pardoned them.
Kǎi (凱) ascended to the imperial presence and strongly argued,
whereupon the two were sent to the authorities.
At that time, officials could be appointed by donating beans.
Kǎi (凱) argued:
“A recent regulation states
that those who donate over four thousand shí (石) of beans
are appointed Zhǐhuī (Commanders).
They have received emoluments for over ten years,
and their expenses have already been repaid,
yet they are now allowed hereditary succession.
This is to use the blood and sweat of the people to support unproductive descendants,
and they will continuously reap profits without end.
Those with merit will surely say among themselves,
'I obtained this by sacrificing my life,
while he obtained this by donating beans.
This means the court equates my life to beans.
Who would not be disheartened!'
I beg that from now on, they only receive stipends,
and not be allowed to hold office or pass it on by inheritance.
Civil officials should only receive stipends in their original places of residence.”
The emperor agreed,
decreeing that those already appointed would remain as they were,
but those not yet appointed would all follow Kǎi's (凱) proposal.
and Vice Minister Xuē Xīlián impeached each other,
and Kǎi was ordered to investigate.
Upon recommendation,
he was promoted to Right Administration Vice Commissioner of Zhèjiāng.
At that time, military officers of various garrisons collected monthly payments from soldiers,
numbering over 4,500 people.
Based on Kǎi's words, this was prohibited.
Grand Commandant Lǐ Xìn, who guarded the border, arbitrarily recruited commoners as soldiers,
wasting over ten thousand *shí* of provisions.
Kǎi impeached him in a memorial.
Although Xìn was pardoned,
all those who assisted Xìn in recruiting soldiers were found guilty.
He served in Zhèjiāng for several years,
and his reputation became widely known.
Initially,
when Kǎi was a Supervising Secretary,
he often impeached the Marquis of Wǔqīng, Shí Hēng.
When Hēng achieved his ambitions,
he nursed his old grudge,
and demoted Kǎi to Garrison Registrar,
where Kǎi eventually died.
Xǔ Shìdá was a native of Shè.
He became a *jìnshì* in the tenth year of the Zhèngtǒng era.
He was promoted to Censor.
In the fourth month of the first year of the Jǐngtài era,
he submitted a memorial stating that various calamities and misfortunes had repeatedly appeared,
and requested the emperor to reflect deeply and rectify himself.
The emperor accepted his advice profoundly.
Soon after,
he again requested that after the imperial lectures (jīngyán),
Confucian ministers be invited daily to lecture and discuss the classics and history.
The emperor also responded with an excellent edict of commendation.
While patrolling Fújiàn,
he impeached the eunuch Lìao Xiù, who was the guarding central official,
and had him imprisoned.
Xiù in turn impeached Shìdá,
who was then placed under the investigation of Vice Minister Xuē Xīlián and others who guarded the border.
Coincidentally, Shìdá also impeached Xīlián for greed and tyranny,
so Kǎi and Censor Wáng Háo were ordered to investigate.
Upon their return, they reported
that both parties had elements of truth and falsehood in their accusations,
but several thousand elders pleaded for Shìdá to be retained.
Supervising Secretary Lín Cōng,
a native of Mǐn,
also spoke on behalf of Shìdá.
Thus, he was ordered to remain in office,
and Xīlián was commanded not to stir up trouble.
Shìdá strictly enforced discipline,
and apprehended Mǎ Sìzōng, the Prefect of Zhāngzhōu, sending him to the capital.
The Grand Court of Judicial Review impeached him for unauthorized arrest,
but the emperor, deeming it an arrest of a corrupt official, did not pursue the matter.
When his term was due to expire,
elders went to the palace gate to request his retention,
but this was not granted.
Soon after,
he was appointed Left Administration Vice Commissioner of Fújiàn.
During the Tiānshùn era,
he successively served as Left and Right Administration Commissioner of Shāndōng and Guìzhōu.
Líu Wěi,
courtesy name Yǒuróng,
was a native of Cíxī.
He became a *jìnshì* in the fourth year of the Zhèngtǒng era.
He was appointed Supervising Secretary in the Ministry of Punishments, Nánjīng.
Assistant Censor-in-Chief Zhōu Quán beat a censor out of personal resentment.
Censors Fàn Lín, Yáng Yǒng, along with Shàng Chǐ and ten others, jointly impeached Quán,
and Wěi, along with his colleague Lú Xiáng and others, again impeached him.
Quán was sent to the imperial prison,
and he in turn impeached Lín, Yǒng, Wěi, Xiáng, and others.
Wáng Zhèn had always disliked officials who spoke out,
so he arrested them all and sent them to the imperial prison.
Lín and Yǒng were sentenced to strangulation,
but later their sentences were commuted to death.
Other censors were either exiled to garrisons or demoted.
Wěi and Xiáng were exonerated and retained in their positions,
but Quán had already died of illness earlier.
Wěi was successively promoted to Grand Supervising Secretary.
In the fourth year of the Jǐngtài era,
the Ministry of Revenue, finding border provisions insufficient,
memorialized to allow retired officials who were not guilty of corruption
to pay twenty *shí* of grain
in exchange for a patent of appointment.
Wěi and others argued:
"Among the officials who have retired,
many were dismissed for weakness, cruelty, debauchery, or lack of integrity,
not just for corruption.
On what grounds would we bestow patents of appointment upon them?
If we merely commend them for donating grain,
it would mean that the court's patents of appointment are worth only twenty *shí* of grain,
how would this be shown to the world and future generations?
This is due to Minister Jīn Lián's lack of understanding of the bigger picture,
leading to this erroneous proposal."
The emperor immediately adopted their suggestion.
When Shāndōng experienced a famine,
the Ministry of Revenue, knowing that Minister Shěn Yì was familiar with the people's suffering there,
requested that he be sent to provide relief.
However, when he went,
he had no strategy whatsoever.
Wěi then impeached Yì,
and also stated:
"That region already has Minister Xuē Xīlián and Assistant Minister Zhāng Gù to pacify it,
and also Vice Minister Zōu Gàn and Censor-in-Chief Wáng Hóng to provide relief,
and now Yì is added to them;
this is what is called 'ten sheep with nine shepherds.'
I request that Yì be returned to the Ministry of Revenue in Nánjīng,
and that Xīlián and others be solely entrusted with the task."
This was followed.
Marquis of Píngjiāng Chén Yù was stationed in Línqīng,
and his actions often violated regulations.
Wěi impeached him,
and Yù was reprimanded.
The following year,
Grand Commandant Huáng Xuán,
who had gained the emperor's favor through his proposal for a change in the heir apparent,
memorialized requesting land in Bázhōu and Wǔqīng County.
Wěi and others submitted a defiant memorial stating:
"Xuán is originally a barbarian official,
yet he has suddenly received such an important appointment.
Presuming upon imperial favor, he presumptuously interferes,
requesting sixty or seventy *lǐ* of land.
Is it truly without owners?
We request that he be punished for his crime."
The emperor pardoned Xuán,
and sent Ministry of Revenue Principal Secretary Huáng Gāng and Xiè Xuán to investigate.
Upon their return, they reported
that it was indeed private property.
The Ministry of Revenue again requested to punish Xuán,
but the emperor ultimately pardoned him.
Xuán rose to the position of Fújiàn Provincial Inspector,
and was praised for his integrity and prudence.
Wěi,
at the beginning of the Tiānshùn era, was appointed Administration Vice Commissioner of Yúnnán,
then transferred to Guǎngdōng,
where he was responsible for guarding the two prefectures of Huìzhōu and Cháozhōu.
There was a formidable bandit in Cháozhōu;
he refused to surrender when summoned,
so troops were assembled to suppress him,
and his leader was executed.
He was then transferred to administer Nánsháo.
When a large army was sent to conquer the Two Guǎngs,
he died in office from overwork.
Shàng Chǐ,
courtesy name Jǐngfú,
was a native of Luóshān.
He became a *jìnshì* in the fourth year of the Zhèngtǒng era.
He was appointed Director of the Bureau of Receptions.
He submitted a memorial requesting that high officials not be imprisoned.
He was promoted to Nánjīng Censor.
For impeaching Zhōu Quán, he was imprisoned,
and along with other censors, was demoted to Postmaster,
receiving the Xūrén Post in Yúnnán.
In the winter of the fifth year of the Jǐngtài era, due to unusual celestial phenomena, he submitted a memorial detailing several matters,
among which he said:
"Loyal and upright scholars risk death to present their views.
Those in power obstruct them with regulations;
if the offense is light, they are dismissed,
if heavy, they are slandered.
Thus, though the path for remonstrance is open, it is as good as closed.
Buddhism is flourishing,
misleading the ignorant populace,
because those in charge of state rituals feared Wáng Zhèn's power,
and allowed so many to become monks.
They should all be compelled to return to farming."
The memorial was sent to the Ministry of Rites,
but Minister Hú Yíng, disliking that it criticized him,
obstructed it entirely from being implemented.
He was leniently transferred to become the Magistrate of Fēngchéng County,
where he was falsely accused and imprisoned by local magnates,
but was soon released.
In the early Chénghuà era,
high officials jointly recommended him,
and he was promoted to Assistant Surveillance Commissioner of Húguǎng.
Initially, there was an imperial edict
allowing displaced people from Jīng and Xiāng
to register in any locality they resided in.
However, Censor-in-Chief Xiàng Zhōng again ordered them to return to their hometowns,
enforcing it very strictly,
causing many to die on the way.
Chǐ pitied them,
and presented a petition to Provincial Inspector Wú Chēn, requesting a halt to the order.
Chēn reported this to Zhōng,
who angrily impeached Chǐ.
The central court, knowing his intention was to show compassion for the people,
eventually reiterated the order that displaced people were allowed to register locally,
and if they did not wish to,
only then should they be sent back to their hometowns.
Chǐ served as Assistant Surveillance Commissioner for ten years,
and his administration was reported by his superiors,
earning him a patent of appointment and commendation.
He retired and died.
Shàn Yǔ,
courtesy name Shítài,
was a native of Línchuān.
He became a *jìnshì* in the fourth year of the Zhèngtǒng reign.
He was appointed as the magistrate of Shèngxiàn.
He managed his subordinates strictly.
The clerks wanted to falsely accuse Shàn Yǔ,
and Shàn Yǔ heard about it.
He was impeached for not simultaneously submitting the clerks' accusations,
and was arrested and imprisoned.
After the matter was clarified,
he was transferred to Zhūjì.
After the period of mourning for his parents ended,
he waited for an appointment in the capital.
It happened that Yīngzōng had been captured by the northern barbarians,
and Shàn Yǔ was indignant that the eunuchs acted as military supervisors,
preventing the generals from independently commanding advances and retreats,
leading to the defeat of the army.
He submitted a memorial requesting that they all be dismissed,
to strengthen the generals' authority.
Jǐngdì did not accept it.
Initially,
Wáng Zhèn was a devoted Buddhist,
and asked the emperor to ordain monks once a year.
The Dàxīnglóng Temple he had built
employed ten thousand laborers daily,
costing hundreds of thousands of taels,
and its grandeur surpassed all others in the capital.
Yīngzōng bestowed upon it the title
"First Monastery" ,
ordered monks to perform grand Buddhist ceremonies,
and personally visited it,
thereby causing Buddhism to flourish even more.
At this time, Shàn Yǔ submitted a memorial stating:
"In previous dynasties, rulers honored and revered Buddhism,
ultimately leading to disaster and chaos.
Recently, the number of men and women who have left home to become monastics has reached hundreds of thousands,
neither plowing nor weaving,
parasitically consuming the resources of the people.
Temples and monasteries are being constructed,
filling the capital city,
and the expenses are immeasurable.
I request that the timber and stones be dismantled to build military camps,
the copper and iron be melted to cast weapons,
and the monks and nuns be dismissed,
to return to civilian life,
so that the imperial customs may be pure and serene,
and foreign religions will not prevail."
The memorial was submitted,
but was rejected by the court's deliberations.
He was again appointed magistrate of Hóuguān.
Meanwhile, Yáo Xiǎn from Xiányáng, who had entered the National Academy through a provincial recommendation,
also submitted a memorial stating:
"Previously, the Dàxīnglóng Temple was renovated,
reaching the epitome of magnificence and splendor.
Furthermore, a monk surnamed Yáng was appointed as the Imperial Preceptor,
whose retinue rivaled that of a king.
He ate rich food,
wore embroidered robes,
and looked down upon the emperor as if he were a disciple.
Now, the former Emperor (Yīngzōng) is held captive by the barbarian court.
I beg that he be ordered to go to Wǎlà,
to enlighten Yěxiān.
If he can sincerely escort the Emperor back south,
then the power of protecting the nation will be seen.
Otherwise,
it will be clear that Buddhism is not to be trusted."
During the Jǐngtài reign,
many court officials remonstrated against worshipping Buddha,
but the emperor ultimately could not follow their advice.
Moreover, the eunuch Xīng'ān was the most influential,
and his devotion to Buddhism surpassed Wáng Zhèn's.
He requested the emperor to build Dàlóngfú Temple,
which was as grand and imposing as Xīnglóng Temple.
In the third month of the fourth year,
the temple was completed,
and the emperor set a date for a personal visit.
Yáng Hào of Jìníng, a salt transportation judge in Hédōng, strongly remonstrated,
and the visit was canceled.
Shàn Yǔ loved learning and had a reputation for literary talent.
He served as a county magistrate three times,
and was known for his benevolence and kindness in all his postings.
He resided in Hóuguān,
and passed away after a long time.
Yáo Xiǎn later became the magistrate of Qídōng,
and then was transferred to Wǔchéng,
where he was known for his impartiality, integrity, and uprightness.
Based on the recommendation of the巡撫 Xúnfǔ Wēng Shìzī,
he was promoted to Táipúchéng.
Yáng Hào initially entered the National Academy through a provincial recommendation,
and before he could assume his official post,
he submitted a direct memorial,
and gained a great reputation.
He successively held positions up to Yòu Fùdū Yùshǐ,
and served as Xúnfǔ of Yánsuī.
Zhāng Zhāo,
it is unknown where he was from.
At the beginning of the Tiānshùn reign,
he was a clerk in the Zhōngyì Qiánwèi.
Just a few months after Yīngzōng's restoration,
he wanted to send the Dūzhǐhuī Mǎ Yún and others as envoys to the Western Ocean,
but no court official dared to remonstrate.
Zhāng Zhāo heard about it,
and submitted a memorial saying:
"Maintaining internal stability and saving the people
are the urgent affairs of the state;
admiring foreign lands and seeking distant contacts
are the last resort policies of the court.
Hàn Guāngwǔ closed the passes and declined relations with the Western Regions,
and Táng Tàizōng did not accept the submission of the state of Kāng,
all profoundly understood fundamental strategies.
Now, the capital region and Shāndōng have suffered successive years of famine,
the common people are starving and fleeing,
their wives and children are scantily clad,
wrapped in straw mats,
selling their sons and daughters but finding no buyers.
Families cannot protect each other,
they die in ditches,
and before they can be buried,
they have already become like meat in a market,
this is truly heartbreaking.
I hope Your Majesty will use the funds for appeasing foreign tribes,
supplemented by the treasury's wealth,
and urgently send envoys to provide relief,
so that the starving people can be saved."
The memorial was sent down for broad discussion by the high officials,
who stated that Mǎ Yún and others had already been dismissed from their mission,
and it was appropriate to register the purchased goods and await further orders.
The emperor ordered the matter to be dropped for now.
In the autumn of the third year of Tiānshùn,
the elder Hè Yáng from Jiàn'ān also submitted a letter discussing current affairs,
saying:
"Currently, county magistrates are often appointed from
aged *jiànshēng*.
By the time they complete nine years in office,
they are nearly seventy years old,
and tend to be perfunctory and corrupt.
It is advisable to select those who are younger and talented,
and those of lower rank or reclusive scholars of virtue
should also be recommended.
During the Jǐngtài reign,
descendants of the former sages Yán, Mèng, Chéng, and Zhū were recorded,
and granted the title of Hàlín Bóshì,
to allow them to perform sacrifices.
However, they have official positions but no emoluments,
so they should be given salaries to demonstrate the intention of honoring Confucianism.
Huáng Gàn, Liú Yuè, Cài Shěn, and Zhēn Déxiù were enshrined alongside Zhū Zǐ,
which was also done during the Jǐngtài period at the request of the Qiānshì Lǚ Chāng,
but their names have not yet been included in the sacrificial prayers,
and should be added.
The establishment of community granaries (*yìcāng*)
was originally to relieve the poor,
but powerful and cunning individuals often fraudulently draw from them without repayment,
leading to empty granaries.
I request that upright citizens be ordered to contribute grain,
and each should identify the starving people in their community,
and distribute it together with the officials."
Soon after,
he again stated:
"The imperial court establishes schools and appoints teachers
to cultivate scholars.
However, teachers and scholars often lack profound learning,
while obscure commoners cleverly seek important positions,
having just begun to read basic texts,
they are already among the ranks of those recommended for high office.
When they assume their duties in the academy,
they are petty and greedy,
demanding all sorts of things,
but when it comes to teaching and resolving doubts,
they cannot utter a single word.
Students also often waste their time,
and frivolously wander through the capital,
waiting for their turn and relying on seniority,
improperly advancing to the Imperial Academy.
Gradually they become old and infirm,
fortunately gaining an official post.
They are only concerned with their personal livelihood,
with no thought of achievement or reputation.
If strict selection is not implemented now,
talent will decline daily,
and scholarly conduct will become increasingly improper."
The emperor approved his words,
and ordered the relevant departments to implement them.
Gāo Yáo,
courtesy name Tíngjiān,
was a native of Mǐn Xiàn.
Through a local recommendation, he became an instructor at the Jīngmén Zhōu academy.
In the fifth month of the third year of Chénghuà (1467), he submitted a memorial detailing ten matters.
In one, he said:
"During the change of the Jǐsì year of Zhèngtǒng (1449),
the Former Emperor was captured in the north,
and Your Majesty was still the Crown Prince.
The imperial ancestral temples and altars of state were in extreme peril.
If it hadn't been for Chéng Wáng (Jǐngtài Emperor) succeeding to the throne,
establishing a mature ruler for the state,
how could the calamities have been quelled,
and how could the imperial carriage have returned?
For six or seven years,
the realm enjoyed peace and tranquility,
and the common people lived happily in their occupations.
His achievements were not small.
However, upon the Former Emperor's restoration,
those who coveted his merits subjected him to grave slander,
preventing him from meeting a proper end.
The sacrifices for Jiéhuì (the Chéng Wáng's posthumous title) were
not in accordance with ritual.
I hope Your Majesty will specifically order the ritual officials to convene a discussion
to posthumously bestow a temple name,
thereby fulfilling the grace due to a close relative."
When the memorial was submitted,
the court deliberations remained unresolved for a long time.
It was not until the twelfth month that a report was finally presented:
"The posthumous bestowal of a temple name
is not something officials dare to deliberate upon without authorization;
only Your Majesty can decide."
However, Zuǒ Shùzǐ Lí Chún strongly argued
that it should not be restored,
and further stated:
"Yáo's statement incurs two capital offenses: one slanders the Former Emperor as being unenlightened,
and the other implicates Your Majesty in unfilial conduct.
I believe Yáo's action
is not intended to honor Chéng Wáng,
but merely serves as a ladder for a group of villains to advance.
There must be small-minded individuals instigating it."
The Emperor said:
"As for Jǐngtài's past transgressions,
I have never taken them to heart.
How can they be matters for officials and subjects to discuss?
Is Chún making this memorial
to offer flattery and seek favor?"
The discussion then ceased.
However, the Emperor was ultimately moved by Yáo's words.
After a long time,
he indeed restored Chéng Wáng's imperial title.
Yáo later served as the magistrate of Pānyú Xiàn,
where he implemented many unusual policies.
He exposed the affair of the eunuch Wéi Juàn's illicit trade with foreign countries,
confiscating his vast fortune to the government.
Juàn resented this deeply
and falsely accused him to the court.
Yáo and the Provincial Administration Commissioner Chén Xuǎn were both arrested,
and the grieving gentry and common people blocked the roads as they saw them off.
Yáo was eventually banished to Yǒngzhōu.
After being released and returning,
he died.
Lí Chún
was a native of Huáróng.
He placed first in the imperial examination in the first year of Tiānshùn (1457).
He rose to the position of Minister of Rites of Nánjīng
and enjoyed considerable renown.
When he argued with Yáo about the temple name for Chéng Wáng,
he was solely intent on flattering Xiànzōng,
even comparing Jǐngdì (Chéng Wáng) to Chāngyì and Gēngshǐ,
which was scorned by scholarly opinion.
During the Chénghuà era,
the avenues for remonstrance were largely blocked,
and many investigating censors and supervising secretaries were condemned.
Only Yáo, despite his humble official rank, offered perilous advice
and ultimately remained blameless.
Everyone at the time praised the Emperor's great virtue for this.
There was also Hǔ Chén,
a native of Línyóu.
During the Chénghuà era, he entered the Grand Academy as a tribute student.
He submitted a memorial stating that when gentlemen and officials of the realm passed by the temple of the Former Sage (Confucius),
they should dismount from their carriages and horses.
This was adopted.
Upon returning from visiting his parents,
there happened to be a great famine in Shǎnxī.
The provincial governor Zhèng Shí was about to request relief,
and Chén carried the memorial to deliver it,
detailing the famine conditions
in urgent and impassioned language.
Great relief and loans were granted.
Later,
he submitted a memorial saying:
"My hometown has suffered from disasters for consecutive years,
with people resorting to cannibalism,
due to the corrupt and cruel local officials
and unequal distribution of taxes and corvée labor.
I request an imperial edict for the relevant authorities to review household registrations
and categorize them into three grades to determine levies and corvée."
This was adopted.
When Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
he intended to build a palm-thatched pavilion on Wànsuì Shān
for viewing the scenery.
Chén submitted a strong remonstrance against it.
The Libationer Fèi Yín, fearing that calamity would strike him,
chained Chén beneath a tree in the hall.
Soon, court guards summoned Chén to the Zuǒ Shùnmén,
where an imperial edict was conveyed, comforting and instructing him:
"What you said is correct;
the palm-thatched pavilion has already been demolished."
Yín was greatly ashamed,
and Chén's name became known throughout the capital.
Shortly thereafter,
he was appointed to a seventh-rank official position,
made the magistrate of Yúnnán's ●jiā Xiàn,
and died in office.
The eulogy states: From the founding of the Míng dynasty by Tàizǔ,
the avenues for remonstrance were greatly expanded.
Officials and staff, both inside and outside the court,
were not restricted by their positions when offering advice.
Even the humble and lowly people of the countryside
could have their memorials reach the emperor.
This trend continued through Xuānzōng and Yīngzōng,
with the prevailing custom not diminishing.
Although it was a long period of peace and prosperity,
with the palace chambers deep and solemn,
scholars in simple attire,
clerical scribes,
supernumerary gate-keepers,
and soldiers bearing halberds
could present confidential memorials in the morning
and have them reach the imperial presence by evening.
Those whose suggestions were adopted were honored and elevated,
and those whose suggestions were rejected were not punished.
Like Rénzōng's restoration of Yì Qiān to court attendance
and his self-reproach for his own faults,
what more could be added to such an open policy
than hanging bells and setting up clappers?
With this as an invitation,
it is fitting that those who were passionate and indignant would clench their fists and discuss state affairs.
The events during the Yīngzōng and Jǐngtài periods,
as recorded in the veritable records,
are too numerous to enumerate.
Now, we have excerpted the most prominent ones and listed them in this chapter.
By the last years of Xiànzōng,
eunuchs dominated the court,
and circumstances frequently changed,
which will be compiled into a separate volume
for future reference.
Collation Notes
Biographies 53: Táo Chéng (Zǐlǔ), Chén Mǐn, Dīng Xuān, Wáng Déjiā (Zǐ Yīkuí), Yè Zhēn, Wǔ Jì, Máo Jí, Lín Jǐn, Guō Xù, Jiāng Áng (Zǐlóng)
Táo Chéng,
courtesy name Kǒngsī,
was a native of Yùlín.
During the Yǒnglè era,
he was recommended from his locality
and appointed as the Judicial Registrar of Fèngshān, Jiāozhǐ.
Minister Huáng Fú, recognizing his talent,
ordered him to temporarily serve as a professor in Liàngjiāng Prefecture,
and the local people were transformed by his influence.
After his term expired,
he was promoted to Inspector of the Shandong Surveillance Commission
and, upon recommendation, elevated to Grand Court Reviewer.
During the Zhèngtǒng era,
based on the recommendation of Liú Zhōngfū,
he was exceptionally promoted to Surveillance Commissioner of Zhèjiāng.
Chéng possessed wisdom and strategy,
and was decisive in handling affairs.
When Japanese pirates attacked Táozhǔ,
Chéng secretly laid iron spike boards in the sea sand.
When the pirates arrived,
they moored their boats and leaped ashore,
and the spikes pierced the soles of their feet.
The pirates, fearing this,
retreated far away.
After his term expired,
he was promoted to Vice Surveillance Commissioner.
The bandits from Chǔzhōu, Yè Zōngliú, Chén Jiànhú, Táo Dé'èr, and others, raided Lánxī.
Chéng attacked and beheaded several hundred people.
They advanced and encamped at Wǔyì,
building a wooden fort for defense.
Chéng enticed some of the bandit party to act as internal agents,
beheading several hundred before and after,
and capturing over a hundred alive.
He also personally went to the bandit lairs,
persuading over three thousand to surrender.
The bandit's power gradually waned,
with only Dé'èr still remaining.
After a long time,
their power became rampant again,
gathering a host to attack.
They first dispatched over ten of their party to pretend to be villagers fleeing the bandits,
wrapping firewood in worn out wadding,
and illicitly entering the city.
When Chéng went out to battle,
the bandits held the firewood and started a fire,
burning the wooden fort.
The government troops were shocked and scattered,
and Chéng and Commander Cui Yuán died in battle.
This was in the fifth month of Jǐngtài first year.
When the matter was reported,
Chéng was posthumously granted the title of Zǔo Cāncèng,
and his son Lǔ was appointed an eighth-rank official.
Lǔ,
whose courtesy name was Zìqiáng,
was appointed Assistant Magistrate of Xīnhuì through his father's privilege.
At this time,
the Yáo bandits in Guǎngxī were plundering the prefectures of Gāo, Lián, Huì, and Zhào,
breaking cities and killing officials every month without fail.
Between Xiāngshān and Shùndé,
local bandits rose in swarms,
and unruly youths from Xīnhuì gathered to join them.
Lǔ summoned the elders and said:
"The bandits are poised to swallow our city;
if we do not prepare early, it will fall. Can you lead your sons and brothers to defend against them?"
All replied,
"Yes."
So,
he built fortresses and strongholds,
repaired armor and weapons,
and trained skilled warriors,
defending the isolated city against the bandit's charge.
He built an outer wall, dug a moat,
and scattered iron caltrops and thorny bamboo outside.
The city's defenses became extremely solid.
When bandits came to attack,
they were always defeated.
In Tiānshùn seventh year,
his term ended.
Governor Yè Shèng reported his achievements,
and he was promoted to Magistrate.
Soon after, for his merits in defeating bandits,
he was promoted to Prefectural Judge of Guǎngzhōu,
while still concurrently serving as Magistrate.
In Chénghuà second year, he followed Grand Governor Hán Yōng to campaign at Dàténgxiá.
Yōng was very strict in the army,
but only with Lǔ did he always humble himself.
Whenever he used Lǔ's strategies,
they were always successful.
Yōng requested that Lǔ be promoted to Military Counselor,
to specifically manage the troops of Xīnhuì, Yángjiāng, Yángchūn, Lóngshuǐ, and Xīnxīng counties.
That winter, he joined Assistant Commander Wáng Yīng in defeating notorious bandit Liáo Póobǎo and others in Qīn and Huà prefectures,
achieving a great victory.
An imperial letter of commendation was sent.
The following year,
bandit leader Huáng Gōnghàn and others ran rampant.
He and Assistant Commander Xià Jiàn and others repeatedly defeated them in Sī'ēn and Xúnzhōu.
Not long after,
the bandits captured Shíkāng,
seizing Magistrate Luó Shēn.
He again joined Jiàn in pursuing them to Liùjúshān,
defeating them.
After Hán Yōng left the Liǎngguǎng region,
the position of Grand Governor was abolished,
and the military commanders hesitated and shirked responsibility,
causing banditry to spread.
Lǔ memorialized requesting that a high official be reinstated as Grand Governor in Wúzhōu,
which then became a permanent system.
When his term ended,
his performance was rated excellent,
and he was promoted to Surveillance Vice Commissioner.
Minister of War Yú Zǐjùn memorialized regarding his efforts in pacification and management,
and he was rewarded with silver and silk.
Lǔ had been in military service for a long time.
When bandits plundered the Liǎngyuè region,
the larger ones were jointly suppressed,
and the smaller ones were independently campaigned against,
achieving victories wherever he went.
The bandits hated him to the core,
plundering his former residence in Yùlín,
burning his imperial patents,
desecrating his ancestral graves,
and harming his clan members.
Lǔ was greatly saddened when he heard this.
An imperial edict ordered his household registration to be moved to Guǎngdōng,
his imperial patents to be reissued,
and extra comfort and rewards given,
which further strengthened his resolve to suppress the bandits.
In the twentieth year,
for his merits in campaigning against the Lìpǔ Yáo,
his salary was increased by one rank.
Nine years later,
his performance was rated excellent,
and he was promoted to Provincial Surveillance Commissioner of Húguǎng,
still managing the troops in Liǎngguǎng as before.
When the bandits Huáng Gōngdìng and Hú Gōngmíng and others from Yùlín and Lùchuān caused disturbances,
he and Assistant Commander Ōu Pán divided their forces into five routes for a punitive expedition,
greatly defeating them,
and destroying one hundred and thirty bandit lairs.
In Hóngzhì fourth year,
Grand Governor Qín Hóng dispatched him to pacify the Déqìng Yáo,
and he was promoted to Right Administration Commissioner of Húguǎng.
Lǔ stated that he resided in Liǎngguǎng,
but his official title was named after Húguǎng,
which was inconvenient for the actual work.
Therefore, his title was changed to Left Administration Commissioner of Húguǎng, concurrently serving as Surveillance Vice Commissioner of Guǎngdōng,
and overseeing affairs of the Lǐngxī Circuit.
People called him
"the Duke of Three Guǎngs."
In the eleventh year,
Grand Governor Dèng Tíngzàn requested that his son be given an official post,
so that he could command the strong soldiers Lǔ had recruited for campaigns.
So, his son Jīngmín was granted the position of Hundred-Household Officer of the Jǐnyī Guard.
That year,
Lǔ died.
Jīngmín again reported his father's merits,
and was subsequently promoted to Vice Thousand-Household Officer,
a hereditary position.
Lǔ was good at treating his soldiers well,
had many strategies and schemes,
and would only fight after his plans were settled.
He dug a pond behind his official residence,
and built a pavilion in it,
without a bridge.
At night, he would summon his subordinates to discuss matters.
He would measure one person with a plank,
and when the discussion was finished,
he would order them to retreat.
He did this with several people,
then he would choose the best of them and combine their ideas,
thus he always achieved victory and his strategies were not leaked.
Even when urgent military dispatches arrived frequently,
and he was dressed in military attire and on night alert,
his expression remained unchanged.
When he judged that the enemy could be exploited,
he would secretly lead troops out of the city,
encircle them in the middle of the night,
and report victory by dawn.
The bandits were skilled at reconnaissance,
but ultimately could not grasp his main points.
He served as an official for forty-five years,
remaining involved in military affairs from beginning to end.
In dozens of large and small battles,
he beheaded a total of over twenty-one thousand four hundred enemies,
recovered over one hundred thirty-seven thousand people who had been plundered, and pacified and resettled them,
and the people of Liǎngguǎng relied on him like a Great Wall.
However, Lǔ, when leading troops, did not solely advocate military force,
and often said:
"To deal with bandits,
transformation is primary;
killing is only done as a last resort."
Every time he pacified bandits,
he would often establish counties and build schools to promote education.
When Lǔ first served as Assistant Magistrate,
he was only twenty years old.
Magistrate Wáng Chóng miàn was known for his scholarship.
Chóng was an old Confucian scholar,
so Lǔ requested to serve him as a disciple.
Every morning, he would be taught classics and history before attending to his duties.
Later, Chóng died in office,
and Lǔ observed mourning as if for a father,
and also provided for his two sons.
He also respectfully served the renowned Confucian scholar Chén Xiànzhāng,
and Xiànzhāng also held him in high regard.
Sòng Lù Xiùfū and Zhāng Shìjié died for their country at Yáshān,
but had no ancestral temple.
He specially built a shrine for them,
requested a name plaque for the shrine,
and it was granted the name Dàzhōng (Great Loyalty).
In the early Jiājìng period,
Lǔ had been dead for thirty years.
The people of Xīnhuì remembered his virtue,
and memorialized the court,
which granted a shrine for his worship.
Chén Mǐn,
a native of Huátíng, Shǎnxī.
During the Xuāndé reign,
he served as the Zhīzhōu of Màozhōu, Sìchuān.
After suffering a bereavement, he left office.
One hundred and eighty people from the various chiefs' offices under his jurisdiction and the indigenous people went to the imperial court and reported,
"The zhōu is situated in a remote border region amidst ten thousand mountains,
neighboring the various tribes of Sōngpān and Diéxī.
Annually, we suffer from their depredations.
Since Mǐn arrived in the zhōu,
he has governed and managed us with skill,
and the people have been able to live in peace.
Now, he has left office due to mourning,
and the military and common people have lost their support.
We beg Your Majesty to show compassion for this distant region
and return this good shepherd to us."
The Emperor immediately granted approval.
During the Zhèngtǒng reign,
after nine years,
the military and common people again requested his retention.
He was promoted to Tóngzhī of Chéngdū Fǔ,
overseeing the affairs of Màozhōu.
Dū Sī Xú Fǔ reported that
Mǐn and Zhǐhuī Sūn Jìng were diligent in their duties,
and all the various tribes respected and obeyed them.
The memorial was sent down to Dū Yùshǐ Wáng Ào and others to verify the facts.
Mǐn was promoted to Yòu Cānyì,
still overseeing the affairs of the zhōu.
To govern a zhōu with the rank of a Jiānsī
was unprecedented before this.
The tribes from Hēihǔ Zhài raided the nearby borders
and were captured by the government army.
Mǐn followed their customs,
made an oath with them, and released them.
Later, they again plundered,
and Mǐn was impeached by Xún'àn Yùshǐ Chén Yuántāo.
An imperial edict pardoned them.
Tídu Dū Yùshǐ Kòu Shēn valued his talent
and stated that Mǐn frequently visited and comforted the indigenous people
and assisted in military and political affairs.
He requested to appoint a separate Zhīzhōu
to allow Mǐn to specialize in military matters.
The Lìbù considered that Mǐn had been in Màozhōu for a long time,
and if another person were appointed, they might not be familiar with the indigenous situation,
making it difficult to subdue them suddenly.
It was appropriate to add one Tóngzhī to assist him.
Approval was granted.
Mǐn, already governing the zhōu as a Cānyì,
his status was comparable to a Jiānsī.
He then impeached Ànchásǐ Chén Tài for causelessly beating an indigenous person to death.
Tài also exposed Mǐn's wrongdoings,
but the Emperor did not question Mǐn,
and Tài was imprisoned and sentenced.
In the first year of Jǐngtài,
after serving nine years as Cānyì,
he was promoted to Yòu Cānzhèng,
overseeing zhōu affairs as before.
He governed the zhōu for over twenty years;
his authority and trustworthiness were widely established,
and the indigenous people were all pleased.
His rank gradually rose,
and the various Jiānsī and Jùnshǒu were instead subordinate to him,
causing many colleagues to resent him.
He was impeached by Ànchásǐ Zhāng Shú
and dismissed from office.
Dīng Xuān,
his origin is unknown.
During the Zhèngtǒng reign, he served as a Yùshǐ.
Initially,
Fújiàn suffered greatly from mining bandits.
Yùshǐ Liǔ Huá was ordered to suppress them.
Huá commanded that watchtowers be erected in all villages and settlements,
and the populace be organized into jiǎ,
with the most influential chosen as leaders.
They were allowed to procure weapons themselves
and supervise the villagers in patrols.
Dèng Màoqī, a tenant farmer from Shāxiàn, was habitually lawless.
After becoming a jiǎ leader,
he increasingly exploited the villagers with his influence.
According to their custom, besides paying rent, tenant farmers
customarily presented gifts to the landlords.
Màoqī instigated his followers to refuse these gifts,
forcing the landlords to personally come and collect grain.
The landlords reported this to the county,
and the county arrested Màoqī.
He did not comply.
The Xúnjiǎn was ordered to pursue and arrest him,
but Màoqī killed several archers.
When the superior officials heard this,
they dispatched three hundred soldiers to apprehend him.
Nearly all were killed or wounded,
and the Xúnjiǎn and Zhīxiàn were both slain.
Màoqī then engaged in extensive pillaging,
falsely proclaiming himself "Chǎnpíng Wáng,"
and establishing officials.
His followers numbered several tens of thousands,
and they captured over twenty counties.
Dū Zhǐhuī Fàn Zhēn, Zhǐhuī Péng Xǐ, and others were successively killed.
At that time, Sòng Xīn, a Cānzhèng from Fújiàn and a native of Jiāozhǐ,
bribed Wáng Zhèn to be promoted to Zuǒ Bùzhèngshǐ.
His corruption and greed were unbearable for the people,
who increasingly joined the rebellion,
causing unrest in the southeast.
In the fourth month of the thirteenth year,
Màoqī besieged Yánpíng.
Shuājuǎn Yùshǐ Zhāng Hǎi ascended the city wall to pacify and persuade them.
The rebels pleaded for pardon from death
and exemption from three years of corvée labor,
promising to disperse and become good citizens.
Hǎi reported this.
Xuān was ordered to go and suppress them,
with the large army of Dū Dū Liú Jù and Qiān Dū Yùshǐ Zhāng Kǎi following him.
Upon Xuān's arrival,
he first sent someone with an imperial edict to pacify them.
Màoqī refused to surrender,
