so Xuān hurried to Shāxiàn to plan his strategy.
Rebel leaders Lín Zōngzhèng and others, numbering over ten thousand, attacked Hòupíng,
intending to establish a stronghold.
Xuān ordered Tōngpàn Ní Miǎn and others to lead the troops to first occupy strategic points,
while he, with Dū Zhǐhuī Yōng Yě and others, intercepted their retreat route,
beheading over two hundred rebels
and capturing their leader Chén Āyán.
In the second month of the following year,
Xuān lured the rebels to attack Yánpíng again,
and commanded the various armies to charge from different routes.
The rebels were utterly defeated
and fled.
Zhǐhuī Liú Fú pursued them,
then beheaded Màoqī,
and encouraged those who were coerced to return to their former occupations.
Soon after,
he again captured their associates Lín Zǐdé and others.
The Yóuxī rebel leader Zhèng Yǒngzǔ led four thousand men to attack Yánpíng.
Xuān, along with Yě and others, intercepted and attacked them,
capturing Zhèng Yǒngzǔ,
beheading over five hundred,
and the remaining rebels dispersed.
When Kǎi oversaw the large army to suppress the rebels,
he stopped at Jiànníng and did not advance,
spending his days feasting and composing poetry for pleasure.
Hearing that Xuān had defeated the rebels,
he rushed to Yánpíng to claim his功.
Xuān, under duress, reluctantly reported this to the emperor.
Fú, unable to tolerate this,
complained.
An imperial edict ordered Xuān to submit a detailed account.
Kǎi and others were all punished,
but Xuān, despite his merit, was not questioned,
nor was his achievement recorded.
Although Màoqī was dead,
his nephew Bósūn and others again flourished.
The imperial court then dispatched Chén Mào and others with a large army to suppress them,
and Xuān then returned to court.
In the early Jǐngtài reign,
he was sent out as Guǎngdōng Fùshǐ
and died there.
At this time,
bandits in Zhèjiāng and Fújiàn plundered everywhere, causing suffering to the people.
Generals and commanders often underestimated the bandits,
while civil officials encouraged civilian militias to resist the rebels,
frequently achieving many captures and beheadings.
In Fújiàn, there were Zhāng Yīng and Wáng Dérén and their like.
In Zhèjiāng, Shí Mào, Zhīfǔ of Jīnhuá, captured Sū Cái, a bandit from Suìchāng, in Lánxī,
and Zhāng Yòu, Zhīfǔ of Chǔzhōu, defeated the bandit forces
and captured and beheaded over a thousand people.
Thereupon, the Emperor issued an edict
repeatedly reprimanding the various generals and commanders.
Dū Zhǐhuī Dèng Ān and others then blamed the former Yùshǐ Liǔ Huá.
At that time, Wáng Zhèn intended to kill court officials to intimidate the populace,
and ordered Huá's arrest.
Huá had already been appointed Shāndōng Fùshǐ,
and upon hearing the order,
took poison and died.
An imperial edict confiscated his family's property,
sent the males to the frontier,
and enslaved the females in the Huànyī Jú.
Yùshǐ Wāng Chéng and Chái Wénxiǎn also incurred punishment for this reason.
Initially,
Chéng, while serving as Circuit Supervisor of Fújiàn,
due to the rebellion of Mào Qī,
issued a summons to Zhèjiāng and Jiāngxī to jointly suppress it.
Soon after, as the rebels were negotiating surrender,
he ordered the troops to halt their advance.
After realizing the rebels had no intention of surrendering,
he again urged the troops to advance,
but by then the rebels were already beyond control.
Huáng Yīng, the Censor-in-chief for Zhèjiāng, fearing implication,
fully reported Chéng's order to halt the troops.
The Ministry of War then impeached Chéng for missing a crucial opportunity.
The Three Judicial Offices of Fújiàn also stated that
when the rebels first arose,
Circuit Supervisor Chái Wénxiǎn concealed the matter and did not report it,
allowing the current disaster to develop.
Consequently, both were handed over to the authorities.
When the case was concluded,
an imperial edict ordered Wénxiǎn to be dismembered,
his property confiscated,
and Chéng to be executed in the marketplace.
Sòng Xīn and Ànchásǐ Fāng Cè, along with ten others, were all sentenced to beheading.
Upon a general pardon,
they were demoted to Yìchéng.
In the early Tiānshùn era,
they were reinstated to office.
Commentators argue that Huá's arrangements were not excessive,
and that Chéng and Wénxiǎn's crimes did not warrant death.
They believed that the military commanders' inability to suppress the rebels,
instead blaming civil officials,
leading to Huá and Wénxiǎn facing the same severe punishment as rebels,
was a miscarriage of justice due to Wáng Zhèn.
Huá was a native of
Wúxiàn.
Wénxiǎn was a native of
Jiàndé, Zhèjiāng.
Chéng was from Rénhé.
Wáng Dérén,
whose given name was Rén,
used his courtesy name,
and was a native of Xīnjiàn.
Originally surnamed Xiè,
his father, to avoid enemies, sought refuge with his maternal relatives,
and thus adopted the surname Wáng.
Dérén lost his mother at the age of five,
and his sorrowful cries were like those of an adult.
Initially a guard clerk,
he was recommended for his talent and appointed Jinglì of Tīngzhōu Prefecture.
He was honest, capable, diligent, and agile,
and loved by all, high and low.
When his term was complete and he was due for transfer,
thousands of soldiers and civilians pleaded for him to remain,
and an imperial edict granted him an increased rank and a second term.
After three years,
when the position of Tuīguān became vacant,
Yīngzōng, at the request of the soldiers and civilians,
promoted him to that post.
He repeatedly redressed wrongful convictions,
refused bribes,
and suppressed the exorbitant demands of the Zhenshǒu eunuchs,
his administrative achievements becoming even more notable.
Chén Zhèngjǐng, a bandit from Shāxiàn,
originally a follower of Dèng Màoqī,
rallied the bandits from Qīngliú, such as Lán Délóng, to attack the city.
Dérén, along with the defending general and Zhīfǔ Liú Néng, defeated them,
capturing Zhèngjǐng and eighty-four others,
while the remaining bandits scattered in fright.
The generals proposed a thorough search,
but Dérén, fearing that innocent common people might be implicated,
issued an order for pacification and recruitment,
and identified and released three hundred displaced people.
Dūzhǐhuī Mǎ Xióng obtained the names of those who had colluded with the bandits
and intended to execute them according to the register,
but Dérén strongly urged him to burn the register.
When the bandits again raided Nínghuà,
he led troops to reinforce it,
beheading a great many.
Many commoners spontaneously returned home,
and the bandit forces further weakened.
The bandits retreated to encamp at Jiānglè,
and Dérén was about to pursue and destroy them
when he suddenly fell ill.
The multitude wished to carry him back for medical treatment,
but Dérén refused,
saying,
"If I make a move,
the bandits will surely advance unopposed."
He then sat up in his tent,
instructed his generals and officials to work together to pacify the rebels,
and then died.
This was in the summer of the fourteenth year of Zhèngtǒng.
The soldiers and civilians mourned deeply.
When his coffin returned,
mourners lined the roads for lamentations and offerings,
many painting his portrait and sacrificing to him.
At the end of the Tiānshùn era,
officials and commoners pleaded for a temple to be built for him.
The authorities submitted the request,
and an imperial edict ordered it to be done according to the precedent of Yáng Xìnmín in Guǎngdōng,
with sacrifices offered in spring and autumn.
His son, Yīkuí,
achieved the highest rank in the imperial examinations in the fourth year of Tiānshùn.
He was appointed Xiūzhuàn and
promoted to Zuǒyùdé.
In the seventh year of Chénghuà,
when a comet appeared,
he responded to the imperial summons by presenting five proposals:
to rectify the imperial inner court,
to cultivate close relationships with senior ministers,
to open avenues for remonstrance,
to be cautious in criminal justice,
and to curb reckless spending.
His words were extremely earnest and sincere,
but he was severely reprimanded by imperial decree.
He was successively promoted to Gōngbù Shàngshū.
Upon his death,
he was posthumously granted the title Tàizǐ Shàobǎo.
During the Zhèngdé era,
he was posthumously honored with the epithet Wénzhuāng.
Yè Zhēn,
courtesy name Mèngjí,
was a native of Gāoyào.
He passed the provincial examination
and was appointed Tóngzhī of Xúnzhōu Prefecture.
He was reassigned to Fèngxiáng,
and then transferred to Qìngyuǎn.
When the Yáo bandits rose up fiercely in Liǎngguǎng,
all the prefectures suffered,
and generals and officials mostly cowered and watched.
Zhēn swore not to live alongside the bandits,
and recruited strong men for daily training.
The cave chieftain Wéi Fùqiáng had repeatedly defeated government troops,
but Zhēn captured him alive.
His party, enraged,
mobilized all their forces to attack the city,
while the defending general of Qíshān withheld troops and did not come to aid.
Zhēn led his strong men out to battle,
and the bandits retreated.
They soon tracked Zhēn,
and a fierce battle ensued,
in which Zhēn's son, Gōngróng, was killed.
A short while later,
the bandits besieged Jīcì and other villages.
Zhēn led three hundred men to rush to their aid.
On the way, they encountered the bandits at Rén Tóu Shān,
and a desperate battle took place.
Zhēn was struck by several spears,
personally slew one bandit,
and died along with his nephew Guānqìng and the three hundred men.
This was on the last day of the first month of the third year of Tiānshùn.
Lǐngnán traditionally had no snow,
but that night there was a great thunderstorm,
and snow fell to about a foot deep.
The bandits lifted the siege and departed,
and the villages were saved.
When the matter was reported,
he was posthumously granted the title Cháoliè Dàfū,
and Cānyì of Guǎngxī.
The defending officials built a temple to sacrifice to him.
Wǔ Jì,
courtesy name Délíng,
was a native of Ānfú.
He became a Jìnshì in the fifth year of Jǐngtài.
He was appointed Yùshǐ.
He was solemn, spoke little, and seldom smiled,
but dared to act when he saw justice.
In the seventh year of Tiānshùn, he served as Circuit Supervisor of Fújiàn.
Before this,
bandits had risen in Shàngháng.
Dūzhǐhuī Qiānshì Dīng Quán,
a native of Wénshàng,
was good at defense.
The bandits repeatedly attacked the city,
but were always repelled by him.
After some time, the bandits grew more rampant.
When Jì heard of this,
he immediately rushed into Tīngzhōu,
and reinforcements gathered from all four directions.
Jì rode alone to the bandit encampment.
The bandits did not expect a Yùshǐ to arrive suddenly,
and all were wearing armor and brandishing weapons.
Jì calmly stood his horse,
and explained to them the consequences of their actions.
The bandits, seeing his utmost sincerity,
were moved to tears and enlightened,
and over seventeen hundred households surrendered.
They were given oxen and seeds,
and allowed to return to their former occupations.
However, the chief bandit Lǐ Zōngzhèng 負固 (lit. relied on his strongholds) refused to submit.
Then, together with Quán, they advanced deep into the territory and crushed him.
Quán fought valiantly,
but was harmed by the bandits.
Jì mourned the dead and consoled the injured,
inciting them with loyalty and righteousness,
and again fought the bandits.
He successively broke eighteen stockades,
capturing and beheading over eight hundred people,
and the four borders were completely pacified.
However, Jì contracted an illness from the miasma,
and died at Shàngháng upon the return of the army.
The soldiers and civilians mourned him as if he were their parent;
thousands of people visited day and night,
competing to donate money to build a shrine.
During the Chénghuà reign, at the request of the Zhīxiàn Xiāo Hóng,
an imperial edict ordered him to be worshipped alongside Quán,
and the shrine was bestowed the name Bāozhōng.
Máo Jí,
courtesy name Zōngjí,
was from Yúyáo.
He became a Jìnshì in the fifth year of Jǐngtài.
He was appointed Zhǔshì of the Guǎngdōng Division of the Ministry of Justice.
This division had jurisdiction over the Jǐnyīwèi.
The Jǐnyīwèi soldiers would spy on the private affairs of all officials,
and a mere slip of paper presented to the emperor could lead to conviction,
so none of the high-ranking officials were not anxious and fearful.
The Duke of Gōng Xíng would ask for favors,
and insult officials;
even those who were charged and sent to the Ministry of Justice
dared not be flogged.
Jí alone upheld the law unyieldingly;
any offender would be severely punished.
His superior, Mén Dá, relied on imperial favor to act cruelly.
When officials encountered him on the road, they would usually avoid his horse,
but Jí alone would raise his whip and pass by with a salute.
Dá was extremely angry.
When Jí was absent from court due to illness,
he was imprisoned in the Jǐnyīwèi jail.
Dá was overjoyed,
selected strong soldiers,
and beat him with large cudgels.
His flesh was torn to the bone,
but he did not die.
In the fifth year of Tiānshùn, he was promoted to Qiānshì of Guǎngdōng,
and assigned to patrol the two prefectures of Huì and Cháo.
He severely suppressed the powerful gentry,
and the people were greatly pleased.
When his term was due for replacement,
they collectively pleaded for him to stay.
Yáng Huī, a bandit from Chéngxiāng,
was formerly a follower of the notorious bandit Luó Liúníng.
After being pacified, he rebelled again,
and together with his followers Zēng Yù and Xiè Yíng, they separately occupied the caves of Bǎolóng, Shíkēng, and others,
attacking and seizing Ānyuǎn in Jiāngxī,
and plundering between Mǐn and Guǎng.
Later,
they intended to attack Chéngxiāng.
Jí, before their arrival,
recruited brave men and combined them with government troops, numbering seven hundred,
and reached the bandit lair.
First, he broke Shíkēng,
beheading Yù,
then attacked Yíng,
capturing his head,
and further captured Huī alive.
All the caves were broken,
and a total of one thousand four hundred people were captured or beheaded.
Upon hearing the news of the victory,
Emperor Xiànzōng promoted Jí to Fùshǐ,
and sent an imperial letter of commendation.
He was transferred to patrol the three prefectures of Gāo, Léi, and Lián.
At that time, the people were ravaged by bandits,
and for hundreds of miles, there was no sign of human habitation.
All the generals closed their cities and defended themselves,
or if someone reported bandits,
they would be beaten instead.
Those who escaped from the bandit ranks and returned
were often falsely accused of collaborating with the bandits
and beaten to death.
Jí was filled with indignation,
and took the pacification of bandits as his own responsibility.
He inspected the department of Léizhōu.
Wáng Qí, the Zhīxiàn of Hǎikāng,
was from Tàihé, Yúnnán;
he daily inspired his people with righteousness,
and whenever bandits arrived, he would bravely counterattack.
Jí admired his courage and integrity,
and praised him.
Just then, news arrived that bandits were plundering villages,
and Jí and Qí each led their respective divisions to defeat them.
Jí recommended Qí,
who was promoted to Tōngpàn of Léizhōu.
Before the order was received,
he died in battle.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tóngzhī,
and his son was given a hereditary position as a Guózǐshēng.
In the second month of the first year of Chénghuà,
Xīnhuì sent an urgent plea for help.
Jí led Commander Yán Huá and the Tóngzhī Táo Lǔ, who was in charge of county affairs,
and assembled an army of ten thousand men.
They reached Dàdèng and defeated the bandits,
then pursued them victoriously to Yúnxiù Mountain,
about ten *lǐ* from the bandit camp.
It was already the second watch of the night;
he summoned the generals to divide into three detachments
to advance at dawn.
However, it was cloudy and dim,
and the troops missed the appointed time.
When they did advance to battle,
the bandits abandoned their camp and fled up the mountain.
Jí ordered a certain Centurion Pān to occupy their camp,
and the troops competed to seize treasures and goods.
The bandits galloped down,
killed the Centurion,
and Huá's horse also stumbled,
and he was killed by the bandits.
The various armies then collapsed.
Jí reined in his horse and shouted loudly to halt the army.
His subordinates advised Jí to retreat,
but Jí said:
"If many are killed or wounded,
can I alone survive?"
Before he finished speaking,
bandits with spears rushed towards Jí.
Jí cursed and fought at the same time,
slaying one man with his sword,
severing his arm.
His strength exhausted,
he was then killed.
On that day,
a great thunderstorm erupted,
shaking all the mountains and valleys.
Eight days later,
his body was finally recovered,
looking as if alive.
When the matter was reported,
he was posthumously granted the title of Ànchásǐ,
and his son Kē was enrolled in the Guózǐjiān.
He later became a Jìnshì
and ended his career as a Fùshǐ in Yúnnán.
When Jí was departing for the campaign,
he brought a thousand gold pieces as犒 (reward money),
and entrusted Yú Wén, the Yìchéng, to manage its receipts and expenditures.
Already three-tenths had been used.
After Jí died,
Wén, pitying his family's poverty,
gave the remaining gold to Jí's servant,
telling him to take it home to arrange the funeral.
That night,
the servant's wife suddenly sat in the central hall and spoke as Jí,
looking around and saying:
"Please invite Chief Xià Xiàn here."
The whole family was greatly alarmed,
and rushed to inform the Ànchásǐ Xià Xūn.
When Xūn arrived,
the wife stood up and bowed, saying:
"Jí received national grace and
unfortunately died at the hands of bandits.
Now Yú Wén has given the remaining official silver to Jí's family.
Although there are no account books to verify it,
Jí is defiled underground.
I wish for it to be returned to the officials immediately;
do not defile me."
After speaking,
she collapsed to the ground,
and only revived after a while.
Thereupon, the gold was returned to the officials.
Jí was forty years old when he died;
later he was granted the posthumous title Zhōngxiāng.
Lín Jǐn,
courtesy name Yànzhāng,
was from Liánjiāng.
In the early Jǐngtài era,
he was appointed Xùndǎo of Hépǔ through the Xiānggòng examination.
Yáo bandits were rampant,
and there were no preparations, internal or external.
Jǐn itemized strategies,
all of which hit upon the opportune measures.
The巡撫 Yè Shèng was surprised by this
and ordered him by dispatch to take charge of the county affairs of Língshān.
The city had been destroyed by bandits,
so Jǐn, taking advantage of the terrain,
built palisades for defense
and widely set up combat tools;
the bandits dared not approach.
When his full term was up and he left office,
the people said:
"If Your Excellency leaves,
the bandits will return.
Who will defend us?"
All of them fled into the mountains.
Shèng reported the situation,
and an imperial edict immediately appointed Jǐn as Zhīxiàn.
He hurried back to office by post-horse,
and the people returned.
That year there was a famine,
and the various Yáo became even more rampant in their plundering, with no day passing without incident.
Jǐn rode alone to their camps,
explaining to them the consequences of their actions.
The Yáo were moved and enlightened,
and twenty-five attached departments of the county all obeyed his commands.
Those who did not submit were suppressed.
In Tiānshùn sixth year (1462), he defeated the rebels at Luóhé Shuǐ,
then again at Huángjiāng Líng,
and a major defeat at Xīnzhuāng.
He captured and beheaded over a thousand enemies in total,
returned the plundered people,
and completely pacified the rebels.
He then removed the stockades
and built an earthen city.
Shèng Jí and the supervising officials repeatedly recommended his talent.
In Chénghuà first year (1465),
when Liánzhōu was captured by rebels,
Jǐn was appointed acting prefect.
Another great famine occurred that year,
and rebels emerged everywhere to loot.
Jǐn persuaded more than a thousand people to disperse,
executed those who resisted assimilation,
and pacified and settled the displaced.
The entire region was pacified.
In the fourth year (1468),
the senior officials successively recommended him,
requesting that he be reassigned to a Censorate post,
to specifically deal with the bandits of Qīn and Lián.
He was then made an Assistant Surveillance Commissioner (Ànchásǐ Qiānshì),
and became even more diligent in his administration.
In the tenth year (1474), he was granted an imperial edict commending his exceptional service.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Vice Commissioner (Fùshǐ).
As Jǐn's jurisdiction frequently experienced bandit alarms,
he contemplated long-term solutions.
He established the Tuánhé Camp in the west,
the Xīnliáo Camp in the south,
and an additional Hóngyá Camp to block the routes where the various bandits emerged and disappeared.
He renovated the earthen city of Língshān,
rebuilding its walls higher,
stretching five hundred zhàng,
eventually making it a strong fortress.
In the fourteenth year (1478),
the Ministry of War reported his achievements in pacifying and settling the region,
and he was rewarded.
During his time in military service,
Jǐn prioritized education and moral transformation.
As Língshān still worshipped spirits,
he banned unauthorized shrines,
repaired schools,
and encouraged agriculture and sericulture.
In his governance of Lián and Qīn,
he always rectified the academies
and revitalized cultural education.
He was honest and sincere,
seeing directly into people's hearts;
the Yáo and other indigenous peoples all loved and trusted him.
During his campaigns,
he shared hardships with his soldiers.
Whenever there was merit, he would attribute it to others.
Because of this, many soldiers were willing to fight to the death,
and he was worshipped in local shrines wherever he served.
Guō Xù,
courtesy name Jìyè,
was a native of Tàikāng.
He became a *jìnshì* in Chénghuà seventeenth year (1481).
Sent to the Chǔ Prefecture,
he refused their gifts.
He was appointed Minister (Zhǔshì) of the Ministry of Revenue,
supervising the transport of 200,000 *liǎng* of provisions to the army in Shǎnxī.
The officials in charge reported a surplus,
which he entirely returned.
He was successively promoted to Councilor (Cānyì) of Yúnnán.
Initially,
when the Mèngmì Pacification Commission (Mèngmì Xuānfǔsī) was established,
it was carved out of the territory of the Mùbāng Pacification Commission (Mùbāng Xuānwèisī).
Later, Sī Shè of Mèngmì again encroached on twenty-seven areas of Mùbāng territory beyond the border.
He was repeatedly ordered to return them,
but he refused.
Then, Sī Lù, the Pacification Commissioner of Mèngyǎng, was ordered to send troops to threaten him.
Sī Shè then returned the invaded territory,
but he killed many Mèngyǎng soldiers.
Sī Lù sought revenge,
dispatched troops across the Jīnshā Jiāng and seized thirteen areas of Mèngmì territory that had originally been taken from Mùbāng.
The two chieftains' enmity became ceaseless.
Governor Chén Jīn, acting on imperial decree,
sent Xù and Vice Commissioner Cáo Yù to go and admonish them.
After more than ten days, they arrived at Jīnchǐ.
Assistant Commander Lú Hé had previously led troops two stages away from the occupied territory and camped,
sending officials by post-horse to admonish them,
but all were detained and not reported back.
Hé was afraid
and returned with his army to Qiányá, where he met Xù,
explained the situation,
and warned him not to proceed.
Xù disagreed.
Yù resigned citing illness.
Xù then rode alone with several attendants,
and after ten days reached Nándiàn.
The terrain was so steep and dangerous that riding was impossible,
so they cut through thorns and walked, using ropes to ascend.
After another ten days, they reached a large marsh.
A local official arrived with an elephant palanquin,
and Xù rode it onward.
They traveled through poisonous mists,
with mud and sand making progress difficult.
After another ten days, they reached Mènglài,
only two stages from Jīnshā Jiāng.
He personally drafted a proclamation,
had it carried across the river,
admonishing them with the court's intention to invite submission.
The barbarians looked at each other in astonishment, saying:
"Has the envoy from the Middle Kingdom actually reached here?"
Sī Lù dispatched troops, numbering tens of thousands of elephants and horses, to cross the river by night,
carrying long pikes and powerful crossbows,
surrounding them in several layers.
Those accompanying Xù were afraid
and asked him not to proceed.
Xù drew his sword and shouted:
"Tomorrow we must cross the river;
whoever dares to obstruct will be beheaded!"
After Sī Lù received the proclamation,
he saw that the explanation of consequences was very thorough,
and also heard that only a few people had arrived,
so he sent chieftains to receive orders,
and also sent gifts.
Xù refused them,
and displayed the imperial edict.
Sī Lù also arrived shortly thereafter.
Xù first acknowledged his hardships,
then stated his grievances,
and only then reprimanded him for his rebellion.
When the chieftains heard this,
they all prostrated themselves, shouting "Long live the Emperor!"
and requested to return the invaded territory.
Xù questioned them about the envoys previously detained,
and they were all released and returned.
Hé and Yù heard the report and rushed there,
only to find that the territory had already been returned and peace submissions made.
This was in the fifth month of Hóngzhì fourteenth year (1501).
Three years later,
Xù was promoted to Surveillance Vice Commissioner (Cānzhèng) for supervising grain transport in Sìchuān.
When Wǔzōng ascended the throne,
for his achievements in Yúnnán,
his salary was increased by one rank.
He retired the following year and returned home.
Jiāng Áng,
courtesy name Fū,
was a native of Tàicāng.
He became a *jìnshì* in Chénghuà eighth year (1472).
He was appointed Magistrate (Zhīxiàn) of Zǎoyáng.
He was then appointed Censor (Yùshǐ).
Together with a colleague, he impeached the Daoist practitioner Lǐ Zīxǐng,
who was beaten outside the Wǔmén gate.
Because his mother was old, he requested to be transferred south,
and soon after was appointed Prefect (Zhīfǔ) of Hénán.
After his clerks finished reporting on affairs,
he would retire and close his door to read,
keeping his whip and rod unused.
If a person from the princely establishment committed a crime,
he would immediately decide and send them away.
He was reassigned to be Prefect of Níngbō,
and promoted to Surveillance Vice Commissioner (Cānzhèng) of Fújiàn.
He requested to retire to care for his parents,
and died after the mourning period ended.
While in office, Áng
bought a small amount of meat daily for his mother,
but ate only vegetables himself.
When his sons and younger brothers studied,
he did not allow them to use official paper and brushes.
His family home did not even provide shelter from wind and rain.
Zǐlóng,
courtesy name Mèngbīn,
was a *jìnshì* in the third year of Zhèngdé (1508).
He successively served as a *lángzhōng* in the Ministry of Rites.
When Emperor Wǔzōng made his southern tour,
he led his colleagues in remonstrating.
He was punished by kneeling for five days,
and was nearly beaten to death.
He was sent out as the *tóngzhī* of Jiànníng,
and soon after was promoted to Vice Commissioner of Yúnnán,
stationed with troops in Láncāng and Yáo'ān.
Diān (Yúnnán) was a traditional lair of bandits.
Lóng admonished a local chieftain, saying:
“You hold hereditary office.
If you indulge bandits, is it not bribery?”
The chieftain was afraid,
and pacified and appeased the various bandits,
who all obeyed his commands.
A great bandit named Fāng Dìng,
having surrendered, became poor,
and was reproached by his wives and concubines.
He ultimately could not bear to betray Lóng,
and so took poison and died.
There were a thousand great bandits in Nán'ān.
The Censor wanted to levy troops,
but Lóng issued a proclamation, and they all dispersed within three days.
Mǎ Rén, the salt well bandit in Sìchuān, and Hé Gēzhòng, the Shàijiāng bandit in Yúnnán, had been feuding and killing each other for several decades.
Lóng pacified and appeased them,
and they resolved their conflict.
Měng Guó, the local official of Dàhòuzhōu, relied on the dangerous terrain to commit atrocities,
but Lóng captured him.
He served in Diān for four years,
and the Fān (indigenous peoples) and Hàn (Chinese) were greatly well-governed.
Dèngchuānzhōu erected the Shrine of the Three Upright Men,
sacrificing to Guō Shēn of Yuánzhōu, Lín Jùn of Pútián, and Lóng.
The encomium says: Táo Chéng, Chén Mǐn, and others,
as Surveillance Commissioners and local administrators, achieved merit in suppression and extermination campaigns.
And Chéng, along with Máo Jí and Yè Zhēn, died for the royal cause.
Their arduous and brilliant achievements were evident,
and could even shame those military commanders who were timid and cowardly.
Lín Jǐn had the power to control and administer,
and enough talent to pacify and conciliate.
If all border regions could have such men,
what worry would there be of not achieving good governance?
Guō Xù entered dangerous territory alone,
and persuaded two chieftains to submit.
If he had lived between the Hóngwǔ and Yǒnglè reigns, how could he have remained in an ordinary position?
Those who govern the country in peaceful times
often suppress border achievements,
saying they fear creating trouble.
However, great commanders rely on internal assistance,
and their promotions are often excessively high,
which is precisely enough to foster complacency in military men towards bandits,
and fails to reward the loyalty of meritorious officials who are willing to die.
The state governs the world through rewards and punishments;
how can it not be impartial!
Collation Notes
Biography Fifty-four Hán Guān Shān Yún Xiāo Shòu (Wú Liàng) Fāng Yīng (Chén Yǒu) Lǐ Zhèn Wáng Xìn (Dū Shèng Guō Hóng) Péng Lún Ōu Pán Zhāng Yòu
Hán Guān,
courtesy name Yànbīn,
a native of Hóng (Hóngxiàn),
was the son of Hóu Chéng, the Loyal and Valiant Marquis of Gāoyáng.
He served in the imperial guard as a *shèrén*,
and his loyalty and diligence were known to Emperor Tàizǔ.
He was appointed *Zhǐhuī Qiānshì* of Guìlín Right Guard.
In the nineteenth year of Hóngwǔ (1386), he pacified the various aboriginals of Liǔzhōu and Róngxiàn.
He was successively promoted to Grand Commissioner of Guǎngxī.
In the twenty-second year (1389), he pacified the Fùchuān aboriginals,
and established the Língtíng Myriarchy.
In the twenty-fifth year (1392), he pacified the Shànglín aboriginals of Bīnzhōu.
In the twenty-seventh year (1394), he joined forces with Húguǎng troops to campaign against the various Yáo people of Quánzhōu and Guànyáng,
beheading over 1,400.
The following year, he captured the aboriginals of Yíshān and other counties,
beheading their false king and over 2,800 people from Myriarchs downwards.
As Vice General of the Left in the Southern Expedition, he followed Military Governor Yáng Wén to campaign against Zhào Zōngshòu, the local official of Lóngzhōu.
Zōngshòu admitted his guilt.
He then moved his troops to campaign against the various aboriginals of Nándān, Fèngyì, Dūkāng, Xiàngwǔ, Fùláo,
Shànglín, Sī'ēn, and Dúliàng,
successively beheading and capturing over 10,000.
Guān grew up amidst military affairs,
and possessed courage and strategy.
He was fierce and resolute by nature,
and showed no leniency in execution or punishment.
His orders were as firm as a mountain,
and no one dared to defy them.
Initially,
the various aboriginals rose up everywhere like swarms of bees,
plundering prefectures and counties,
killing local officials,
their power immensely fierce.
Officers and soldiers feared Guān's law,
and fought to the death.
When Guān captured bandits, he would always impose the severest punishment.
Occasionally, he would release one or two,
sending them back to report to the other aboriginals,
which struck terror into the hearts of the various aboriginals.
Thus, the region became peaceful.
In the twenty-ninth year (1396), he was recalled,
and promoted to Grand Commissioner Assistant.
The following year, he again followed Yáng Wén to pacify the rebellious Miáo of Jízhōu and Wǔkāi,
and with Gù Chéng, pacified the various aboriginal strongholds of Shuǐxī.
He then returned to manage the affairs of the Left Guard.
In the first year of Jiànwén (1399), he drilled troops in Dézhōu,
but was unsuccessful in resisting the Yān army.
When Emperor Chéngzǔ ascended the throne,
he entrusted him with duties as before.
He was ordered to Jiāngxī to drill troops for city defense,
and also to command the three Provincial Military Commissions of Guǎngdōng, Fújiàn, and Húguǎng.
When the people of Lúlíng gathered in mountains and marshes,
the emperor did not wish to use military force,
and sent the Messenger Xǔ Zǐmó with an imperial edict to summon and pacify them,
ordering Guān to oversee the appeasement.
When Guān arrived,
the populace all returned to their livelihoods,
and he was bestowed with an imperial letter of commendation.
He was ordered to bear the seal of the General of the Southern Expedition,
garrison Guǎngxī,
and command the government troops of the Two Guǎngs.
The emperor knew Guān was fond of killing,
and bestowed an imperial letter cautioning him, saying:
“The aboriginal people are easily rebellious but difficult to subdue.
The more you kill, the worse the governance will be.
When you go to garrison,
you must endeavor to pacify and conciliate them,
and not engage in wanton slaughter.”
At that time, the various aboriginals rebelled again.
The emperor sent the Assistant Minister Lǐ Zōngfǔ with an imperial edict to summon them.
Guān made a grand display of troops, indicating imminent departure,
but sent an envoy along with Zōngfǔ.
Six thousand families of Guìlín aboriginals returned to their livelihoods,
but only the Sī'ēn aboriginals had not yet submitted.
However, the aboriginals of Qìngyuǎn, Liǔ, and Xún were still plundering and killing officials and commoners.
So, he submitted a memorial requesting to campaign against them.
In the first year of Yǒnglè (1403), he and Commander Gě Sēn attacked and beheaded over 1,180 mountain bandits in Lǐdìng and other counties,
capturing over 50 of their chieftains,
and beheading them as a public warning.
He returned the plundered men and women to the people,
and pacified and gathered those who had fled and dispersed.
The following year, he sent Grand Commissioner Zhū Huī to persuade the mountain strongholds of Yíshān and Xīnchéng to surrender.
The Yáo of Lìbō were terrified,
and begged to be registered as households.
The emperor instructed Guān to pacify them,
and over eighty caves (settlements) all submitted.
The following year,
the aboriginals of the three prefectures of Xún, Guì, and Liǔ rebelled;
having been pacified, they rebelled again.
Zhū Huī was sent with a detachment to defeat them.
The aboriginals were greatly afraid.
At that time, the imperial court sent Minister Xú Zǐliáng,
whereupon they came to surrender,
returning the people, livestock, and tools they had plundered.
In the fourth year (1406), a large army was dispatched to campaign against Ānnán.
An imperial edict ordered Guān to draw up strategy,
and transport 200,000 *shí* of grain to provision the army.
Afterwards,
he was again ordered to join Grand Judge Chén Qià in selecting 30,000 aboriginal troops to assemble at Tàipíng,
and Guān was still ordered to scout the movements within the Ānnán enemy.
Soon after, he followed the main army from Píngxiáng,
arriving at Pōlěi Pass.
With his subordinate troops, he encamped below the pass,
felling trees to build bridges,
and supplying provisions to the army.
After Ānnán was pacified,
he was ordered to manage the various strongholds along the route to Jiāozhǐ.
But the aboriginals of Liǔ and Xún rebelled again
while Guān was away.
In the fifth year (1407), Guān returned his army to Liǔzhōu.
The bandits fled and hid at the sight of his arrival.
Guān requested to penetrate deeper when the autumn cooled,
and also requested reinforcements.
The emperor sent envoys to mobilize troops from the three Provincial Military Commissions of Húguǎng, Guǎngdōng, and Guìzhōu,
and also ordered Marquis Xīnchéng Zhāng Fǔ to send Grand Commissioners Zhū Guǎng and Fāng Zhèng with troops from the Jiāozhǐ campaign to assist.
In the tenth month,
all the armies assembled,
and advanced in separate routes to suppress the rebellion.
Guān personally led the Guìzhōu and Liangguang troops from Liǔzhōu to attack Mǎpíng, Láibīn, Qiānjiāng, Bīnzhōu, Shànglín, Luóchéng, and Róngxiàn,
all of which he captured.
He then joined forces at Xiàngzhōu,
and advanced further to Wǔxuān, Dōngxiāng, Guìlín, Guìpíng, and Yǒngfú.
He beheaded over 10,000,
and captured over 13,000.
The various aboriginals were again pacified.
When the victory was reported,
the emperor praised and rewarded him.
In the ninth year (1411), he was appointed Vice General of the Barbarian Expedition,
still bearing his former seal,
and was made Commander-in-Chief garrisoning Jiāozhǐ.
The following year, he was again ordered to transport grain to Zhāng Fǔ's army.
When Fǔ again led an expedition to pacify Jiāozhǐ,
Guān was in charge of provisions and transport,
and did not serve as a general,
thus his achievements were not prominent.
Hán Guān had been in Guǎngxī for a long time,
his might shook the southern regions,
and the indigenous people fearfully obeyed his orders.
Those who succeeded him,
from Shān Yún onwards,
none could match him.
He died in the ninth month of the twelfth year,
leaving no sons.
In the second year of Xuāndé,
Bǎodìng Bó Liáng Míng memorialized requesting Hán Guān’s former residence in Nánjīng,
and the emperor granted it.
When he heard that Hán Guān’s wife was living there,
he said:
"Guān
was a meritorious official.
Although he has passed away,
how can his home be taken from his family?"
So he did not permit it.
He ordered the relevant officials to bestow another residence upon Liáng Míng.
Shān Yún
was from Xú.
His father, Qīng,
as a centurion, followed Chéngzǔ in raising an army,
accumulating merits until he reached the position of Dūdū Qiānshì.
Yún was robust in appearance
and rich in strategies.
Initially, he inherited the position of Zhǐhuīshǐ of the Jīnwú Zuǒwèi.
He frequently participated in expeditions beyond the Great Wall
and achieved merit.
At that time, there were twenty-five young battalions,
subordinate to the Fǔjūn Qiánwèi,
and the commanders of the guard were incompetent.
So, Yún and five others, including Lǐ Yù, were reassigned to pacify them.
Upon Rénzōng’s ascension,
he was promoted to Xíngzài Zhōngjūn Dūdū Qiānshì.
In the first year of Xuāndé, the Běijīng Xíng Dūdū Fǔ was reformed,
and he was ordered to go with Dū Yùshǐ Wáng Zhāng from Shānhǎi to Jūyōng
to inspect the passes
and act according to exigency.
When the emperor campaigned against Yuè'ān,
he summoned Fǔ Zhèng Wáng and Xiāng Wáng to guard the capital.
The following year,
the indigenous peoples of Liǔ and Qìng, such as Wéi Cháoliè, plundered various counties of Línguì.
At that time, Zhènyuǎn Hóu Gù Xīngzǔ was arrested for failing to rescue Qiū Wēn,
and the dukes, marquises, and high officials recommended Yún.
The emperor also knew him personally.
In the first month of the third year, he was ordered to bear the seal of Zhēngmán Jiāngjūn
and serve as the Zǒngbīng Guān to suppress the unrest.
Upon Yún’s arrival,
he attacked Wéi Cháoliè
and defeated him.
The rebels held a mountain peak.
The mountain was steep and perilous,
with logs hung by vines
and stones piled on top.
When the government troops arrived,
they would cut the vines, dropping logs and stones,
and none dared approach.
At midnight, Yún tied burning torches to the horns of oxen and sheep,
followed by gongs and drums,
and drove them towards the rebels.
The rebels, thinking the government army had arrived,
hurriedly cut the vines.
By dawn,
most of the logs and stones were gone.
The troops shouted and ascended,
and thus completely defeated them.
The indigenous peoples of Nán'ān and Guǎngyuán all submitted.
That summer,
the indigenous people of Xīnchéng, Tán Tuán, rebelled,
and Yún attacked and captured them.
In the spring of the fourth year,
he attacked and pacified the indigenous peoples of Liǔ and Xún.
That autumn,
the indigenous people of Luòróng plundered,
and he dispatched Zhǐhuī Wáng Lún to defeat them.
Yún reported Lún’s merits,
but also impeached him for killing innocent civilians.
The emperor pardoned Lún but thought highly of Yún.
After Hán Guān’s death,
the various indigenous groups in Guǎngxī gradually became unruly.
Yún, considering Guǎngxī had few troops,
kept the Guìzhōu troops for use.
He successively attacked and pacified the indigenous peoples of Xún, Liǔ, Pínglè, Guìlín, Yíshān, and Sī'ēn.
In the ninth year, he again stated that the Miáo and Yáo of Qìngyuǎn and Yùlín were not subdued without a major blow,
and requested reinforcements.
An imperial edict ordered 1,500 Guǎngdōng troops to assist Yún.
Yún divided his forces and launched a suppression campaign,
capturing and beheading a great number of people.
He further dispatched Zhǐhuī Tián Zhēn to attack the rebels in Dàténg Xiá,
and defeated them.
While Yún was stationed there,
he fought more than ten major battles,
beheading 12,260 people,
receiving the surrender of 370 rebel chiefs,
recovering 2,580 men and women,
building thirteen castles,
and five hundred barracks.
He built with fired bricks and carved stone,
increasing their height and thickness.
From then on, the Yáo and Zhuàng disappeared,
and residents lived in peace.
For his merits,
he was promoted to Dūdū Tóngzhī,
and received an imperial letter of commendation.
Yún was profound in strategy and courage,
yet upright and incorruptible,
fair in rewards and punishments,
and strict in his commands.
He shared hardships with his soldiers.
He adapted to changing situations
and was victorious in every battle.
When a new commander first arrived in Guǎngxī,
the local officials customarily offered tribute.
If the commander accepted it,
he would be controlled by them.
When Yún first arrived,
he heard that the government clerk Zhèng Láo was upright,
so he summoned him and asked:
"Should I accept the tribute?"
Láo replied:
"Clean clothes cover the body;
once stained, they cannot be washed clean.
The general is like new, clean clothes."
Yún said:
"If I don't accept,
they might become suspicious.
What then?"
Láo replied:
"Corrupting oneself with wealth
is punishable by death according to the law.
Does the general not fear the emperor’s law,
but instead fears the local barbarians?"
Yún said:
"Good."
He completely rejected the tribute
and governed them strictly.
From then on, the local officials feared and obeyed him,
and none dared to delay their levies.
Wherever Yún went,
he consulted the village elders,
pacified the good and virtuous,
and investigated false accusations.
The local people all loved him.
Upon Yīngzōng’s accession,
Yún fell from his horse and injured his thigh.
The emperor dispatched a doctor to quickly attend to him.
He requested a replacement due to illness,
but an imperial edict graciously refused.
He was promoted to Yòu Dūdū.
In the second year of Zhèngtǒng, he memorialized:
"Xúnzhōu is interspersed with the mountains of Dàténg Xiá,
where Yáo bandits appear and disappear,
occupying fields nearby.
The local officials of the two rivers to the left and right
have many people but little land under their jurisdiction.
Their Lángbīng are always brave
and feared by the bandits.
If a certain number of Tiánzhōu indigenous soldiers are allotted to the nearby mountains for garrisoning and farming,
to divide boundaries for cultivation and defense,
cutting off the bandits’ movements,
within a few years,
the bandits will surely be trapped and weakened."
The report was approved.
Thereafter, when emergencies arose in the southeast,
the Lángbīng were often deployed;
this practice began from here.
In the winter of the following year,
he died while stationed there.
He was posthumously granted Huáiyuǎn Bó
and given the posthumous title Zhōngyì.
His eldest son, Jùn,
inherited the position of Zhǐhuīshǐ of the Fǔjūn Qiánwèi.
The people of Guǎngxī remembered Yún ceaselessly,
and erected a temple with his statue to worship him.
Previously,
when Hán Guān was stationed in Guǎngxī,
he was prone to killing.
Students from Qìngyuǎn came to greet him.
Hán Guān said:
"These are all spies watching me."
He beheaded them all.
Yún was fair and lenient.
If his subordinates committed offenses,
he would always report them to the emperor,
not killing wantonly,
so people did not dare to offend him.
Zhèng Láo once served Hán Guān.
When Hán Guān was drunk,
he would often kill people.
Láo would always restrain him,
and only report it to him when he sobered up.
Láo was highly respected by scholars and officials,
but he ultimately remained a subordinate official.
Xiāo Shòu,
a native of Huáróng.
Beginning as a Qiānhù, he followed Chéngzǔ in raising an army
and rose to Dūzhǐhuī Tóngzhī.
In the 16th year of Yǒnglè (1418), he was promoted to Yòujūn Dūdū Qiānshì,
appointed as a Zǒngbīngguān,
and stationed in Húguǎng and Guìzhōu.
In the 1st year of Xuāndé (1426),
the Silver (Yín) Mán, from Zhènyuǎn's Qióngshuǐ, rebelled.
Commander Zhù Guì went to pacify them
and was killed.
Shòu dispatched Dūzhǐhuī Zhāng Míng to defeat and execute them.
The various stockades of Guāixī and Bāxiāng, under the jurisdiction of the Guìzhōu Xuānwèi,
were in deep, perilous mountains and gorges.
Various Mán tribes lived there interspersed,
attacking and plundering other tribes,
injuring government troops,
and desecrating people's graves.
Moreover, the Kūn Zǔbǐ and other stockades also relied on their perilous terrain and refused to pay taxes.
In the 2nd year (1427),
Shòu dispatched Dūzhǐhuī Sū Bǎo to join Xuānwèi Sòng Bīn in attacking and capturing the Kūn Zǔbǐ stockade.
They pursued relentlessly,
executing several hundred people, including the self-proclaimed king.
All the Mán of Guāixī were awe-struck and submitted.
The Shuǐxī Mán, Ā Bìfángyí, rebelled.
Shòu allied with chiefs of neighboring stockades
and executed him by stratagem.
However, the Xībǎo Mán, Āgǔ, and others, along with the various Miáo of Zhàidǐ, Fēngníng, Qīngpíng, Píngyuè, and Pǔ'ān, gathered again to become bandits.
The various Mán of Sìchuān's Jūnlián responded to them.
Shòu alternately captured and pacified them.
The various Mán submitted one after another,
and he pardoned them by imperial decree.
As the chief of Fēngníng was notoriously wicked,
he was shackled and sent to the capital,
where he was executed.
In the 7th year (1432), he issued a decree to secure the surrender of Ānlóng chief Cén Jùn.
Soon after,
he campaigned against the Chénzhōu Mán,
capturing eighty of their chiefs
and killing countless others.
He moved his troops to attack the Jiānghuá Miáo
and campaigned against the Fùchuān mountain bandits,
defeating and capturing them one after another.
Previously,
the Miáo of the Gǔ and Dáiyì Zhǎngguānsī, under Guìzhōu's administration, frequently plundered.
Shòu built twenty-four forts,
encircling their territory,
and garrisoned them with troops,
preventing the bandits from succeeding.
After a long time,
their chief, Wú Bù'ěr, observing the government troops were few,
again plundered Qīnglàng
and killed officials.
Shòu dispatched Zhāng Míng to defeat them.
The bandits fled into Húguǎng territory,
allied with savage Miáo,
and their power grew again.
Shòu then mobilized troops from Qián (Guìzhōu), Chǔ (Húguǎng), and Shǔ (Sìchuān) to pursue and suppress them in different columns.
He advanced to Gānzipíng,
executed Bù'ěr,
and beheaded over 590 people.
The bandits were all pacified.
In the 9th year (1434),
the Dūyún Mán rebelled,
leading Guangxi bandits to plunder.
Shòu dispatched Commanders Chén Yuán and Gù Yǒng to intercept and attack them in different columns,
capturing bandit chief Wéi Wànliáng and others,
and securing the surrender of over fifty stockades, including Héjiāng's Cài Láng.
When Yīngzōng ascended the throne,
he ordered Shòu to carry the seal of the Zhēngmán Fùjiāngjūn
and remain in his post as before.
Considering Shòu's old age,
he appointed Dūdū Qiānshì Wú Liàng as his deputy.
In the 1st year of Zhèngtǒng (1436),
the Pǔdìng Mán, Āchí and others, rebelled,
usurped the title of king,
and plundered in all directions.
Shòu dispatched Gù Yǒng and others to attack their lair
and defeated them.
Meanwhile, the sixteen caves of Měnggù in Guǎngxī and runaway commoners from Húguǎng gathered and rose up in swarms.
Shòu led troops to besiege them.
After two battles,
all their chiefs were captured and executed,
and the remaining rebels were put to death.
Upon hearing of the victory,
he was promoted to Yòu Dūdū.
He reported:
"Jìngzhōu borders Guǎngxī,
and has often suffered from Miáo troubles.
Between the Yǒnglè and Xuāndé eras,
tens of thousands of shí of grain were stored
in preparation for military campaigns.
In recent years, grain storage has been low.
When there is an alert,
people are dispatched to transport provisions,
and the bandits always find out in advance,
which is why they cannot be caught.
I request that at the Qīnglàng and Jìngzhōu Two Guards,
an additional 50,000 shí of grain each be stored,
so that it can be relied upon in emergencies."
The request was approved.
In the 4th year (1439),
the Jìshā Miáo bandits, Jīnchóng,
and the Miáo general, Páijiū Hóngjiāng, instigated savage Miáo to rebel,
illegally assuming the titles of Tǒngqiānhóu and Tǒngwànhóu.
Shòu led troops to Jìshā,
and dispatched Dūzhǐhuī Zhèng Tōng to attack the Sānyáng Cave
and Mǎ Yè to attack Mount Huángbǎi,
achieving a great victory.
Wú Liàng pursued them to Pútóu and Hóngjiāng,
executed Páijiū,
and Qiānhù Yǐn Shèng enticed and executed Jīnchóng,
whereupon all the savage Miáo surrendered.
Shòu was resolute and resourceful,
and his subordinate officers all exerted their full talents,
while his army was strictly disciplined.
Since the death of Zhènyuǎnhóu Gù Chéng,
the various Mán had gathered and settled everywhere.
When government troops campaigned against them,
they all failed.
Shòu, stationed there for over twenty years,
had many plans based on those of Chéng,
and with time, became more skilled and experienced.
His authority and trustworthiness were widely established,
and whenever bandits arose, he would suppress them.
None of the previous commanders could match him.
For his merits,
he was promoted to Zuǒ Dūdū.
In the sixth month of that year, he was recalled
and retired due to old age.
Soon after, he was reappointed to oversee the Yòufǔ.
He died in the 10th year (1445).
He was posthumously granted the title of Línwǔbó
and given the posthumous name Jìngxiāng.
Wú Liàng,
a native of Láiyán.
In the early Yǒnglè era,
he was a Qíshǒuwèi Dūzhǐhuī Qiānshì.
In the middle of the Xuāndé era,
he served as acting Húguǎng Dūzhǐhuī Qiānshì.
Soon after, as Yòufù Zǒngbīng, he oversaw grain transport with Wáng Yú.
In the early Yīngzōng era,
he gained merit by campaigning against the Xīngàn bandits,
and was successively promoted to Dūdū Qiānshì,
deputizing for Shòu in Húguǎng and Guìzhōu.
After defeating the Pǔdìng Mán,
he was promoted to Dūdū Tóngzhī.
After pacifying the Jìshā Miáo,
he was promoted to Yòu Dūdū.
When Fāng Zhèng died in Lùchuān,
Liàng was recalled to the capital
and appointed Fù Zǒngbīng,
leading fifty thousand troops to campaign there.
When he arrived in Yúnnán,
the bandits grew stronger.
He was implicated for the defeat of the Jīnchǐ Cāncāng Zhāng Róng by not rescuing him,
and was arrested and imprisoned.
He was demoted to Dūdū Qiānshì,
but still carried the seal of the Zhēngnán Fùjiāngjūn,
stationed in Húguǎng and Guìzhōu,
and campaigned to pacify the Dūzhǎng Mán of Sìchuān.
Soon after, he was recalled
to oversee the Yòufǔ.
He died in the 11th year of Zhèngtǒng (1446).
Liàng had a majestic and robust appearance,
a broad and simple nature,
and disliked killing.
Wherever he went, the Mán people were loyal and submissive.
He loved reading,
and even in old age,
never let a book out of his hand.
Fāng Yīng
was the son of Dūdū Zhèng.
In the early Zhèngtǒng era,
as a Shèrén, he followed his father on the campaign to Lùchuān.
When his father died in battle,
Yīng was enraged
and vowed to avenge his father.
Initially, he inherited the title of Zhǐhuīshǐ.
Later,
based on Zhèng's merits in dying for the cause,
he was promoted to Dūzhǐhuī Tóngzhī.
In the 6th year (1441), he followed Wáng Jì on the campaign to Lùchuān.
He led six thousand troops to assault the bandit stronghold.
The bandit leader was wearing a yellow robe in his tent.
Yīng charged forward,
striking and killing several hundred people around him,
and countless more were trampled to death,
thus pacifying the area.
He was promoted to Dūzhǐhuīshǐ.
Soon after, he again followed Jì to defeat the various Mán of Gòngzhāng, Shābà, and Ālíng.
He was promoted to Dūdū Qiānshì,
oversaw the Hòufǔ,
and was appointed Yòu Cānjiāng,
assisting in guarding Yúnnán.
In the 13th year (1448), he again followed Jì on the campaign to Lùchuān.
He captured the Guǐshān Great Stockade
and remained to garrison Yúnnán.
In the first year of the Jǐngtài reign,
the court deliberated and, deeming Yīng to possess strategic military talent,
ordered Grand Commandant MáoSfúshòu to replace him.
Upon his return,
he was promoted to Assistant Grand Commandant.
No sooner had he arrived in the capital
than the various Miao tribes in Guìzhōu rebelled.
The roads were blocked,
and Jì requested Yīng be sent back to suppress them.
In the fourth month of that year, he was appointed Right Vice Regional Commander,
and together with the Count of Bǎodìng, Liángbǎo, and Vice Minister Hóujìn, he successively defeated and routed them.
He was promoted to Right Grand Commandant.
He again broke through the Zhǎnggǎi and other stockades,
capturing the false Miao King Wáng'ātóng and others.
After Jìn died,
Censor-in-Chief Wánglái was sent to take charge of military affairs.
They divided their forces to attack the rebels at Xiānglúshān.
Yīng entered from Lóngchǎng,
inflicting a great defeat and pacifying the area.
In the autumn of the third year,
Lái impeached Yīng for violating the law,
but the matter was dropped.
Lái was recalled,
and Yīng was ordered to guard Guìzhōu.
That winter,
he attacked the rebels at Báishíyá,
capturing and beheading 2,500 people,
and receiving the surrender of 460 stockades.
He was promoted to Left Grand Commandant.
In the fifth year,
the Cáotáng Miao in Sìchuān, Huánglóng and Wéibǎo, rebelled,
proclaiming themselves "Great King Who Pacifies Heaven,"
and plundering Xīpíng and Huángtān in Bōzhōu.
Yīng and Governor Jiǎnglín joined forces with Sìchuān troops to suppress them,
and all the rebel leaders were captured.
Thereupon, he divided his forces and captured Zhōngcháoshān and the three hundred beaches, Guāixī, Gǔzhǒng, and Guāilì stockades,
seizing the false king Gǔyǐdīng and others,
and beheading over seven thousand.
An imperial edict enfeoffed him as Count of Nánhé.
As a general, Yīng
maintained strict discipline,
was fair in rewards and punishments,
courageous in battle,
and skilled at consoling his soldiers.
All his soldiers were happy to serve him,
and thus he often achieved success.
Court officials stated that he should be entrusted with the imperial guards,
so he was recalled
to oversee the Beijing garrison military affairs with Shíhēng.
The next year,
Lín reported that when Yīng previously guarded Guìzhōu,
the border region was peaceful,
and the Miao and Man tribes feared and submitted to him,
requesting he be sent back.
The emperor refused.
Not long after,
the Húguǎng Miao rebelled,
and Yīng was appointed General Who Pacifies the Man,
leading the Beijing army to suppress them,
while ordering Censor Zhāngpéng to scout behind him.
Upon his return, Péng reported
that Yīng's army committed no transgression wherever they went,
and the emperor was greatly pleased.
In the seventh year,
the rebel leader Méngnéng attacked Píngxī Commandery.
Grand Commander Zhèngtài and others repelled him,
and Néng died from a firearm wound.
Yīng then advanced to Yuánzhōu,
successively breaking over 160 stockades, including Guǐbǎn.
With Minister Shípú, he moved his troops to Tiānzhù,
leading Chényǒu and others to attack the Tiāntáng stockades separately,
and again greatly defeating them.
They captured 270 stockades,
seizing 102 people, including false marquises and counts.
At this time, Emperor Yīngzōng had already been restored to the throne.
When the victory was reported,
Pú was recalled,
and Yīng remained to guard Guìzhōu and Húguǎng.
Yīng suppressed the remnants of Méngnéng's faction,
capturing Tónggǔ, Ǒudòng, and 195 other stockades.
The various Miao tribes of Qíntòng and Shànglóng each beheaded their leaders and offered their submission.
The emperor praised Yīng's achievements
and promoted him to Marquis.
In the second year of Tiānshùn,
the Eastern Miao under Gānbǎzhū and others usurped false titles
and attacked the various commanderies of Dōuyún.
Yīng was ordered to join forces with Governor Báiguī and troops from Sìchuān, Húguǎng, Yúnnán, and Guìzhōu to suppress them,
capturing over 600 stockades.
The entire border region was pacified.
Yīng successively captured nearly 2,000 stockades
and took over 40,000 prisoners and beheaded enemies.
His achievements in pacifying the Miao were unprecedented.
Soon after, he died in his post
at the age of forty-five.
The emperor was greatly grieved
and bestowed upon him the posthumous title Zhōngxiāng.
Yīng possessed a brilliant natural talent
and understood ancient military strategies.
He once presented methods for training troops and battle diagrams,
which many veteran generals praised.
He was incorruptible,
humble, and not boastful.
Wherever he served, he brought peace and tranquility,
and the people remembered him
for a long time without forgetting.
His son, Yì,
inherited the countship,
but he incited his grandmother to falsely accuse his paternal uncle Ruì of unfilial conduct,
and was consequently stripped of his title and relegated to retirement.
After he died,
his son Shòuxiáng inherited.
During the Zhèngdé reign,
he successively served as garrison commander in Guìzhōu and Húguǎng.
The title was passed down until the fall of the Ming dynasty, when it ceased.
Chényǒu,
whose ancestors were from the Western Regions,
resided in Quánjiāo.
In the early Zhèngtǒng reign,
he served as a chiliarch,
and was successively promoted to Assistant Regional Commander.
For many years, he rendered meritorious service on missions to the Oirat,
and was soon promoted to Regional Commander.
In the ninth year, he served as Guerrilla General in Níngxià,
and, with Commander-in-Chief Huángzhēn, attacked the Uriankhai.
They captured many,
and he was promoted to Assistant Grand Commandant.
Not long after,
he ventured beyond the frontier to recruit 400 people, including Dáhābǔ, who came to surrender.
When Emperor Jǐng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Assistant Grand Commandant,
and campaigned against the Húguǎng and Guìzhōu Miao.
Soon after, he was appointed Left Assistant General
and garrisoned Jìngzhōu.
In the second year of Jǐngtài, he joined Wánglái and others to attack the rebels at Xiānglúshān.
He entered from Wàncháoshān,
inflicting a great defeat.
He remained to guard Húguǎng.
For his merits,
he was promoted to Right Grand Commandant.
In the spring of the fourth year, he reported having beheaded over 500 Miao.
In the fifth year, he again reported having beheaded over 300 Miao,
but eight people, including Grand Commander Qī'ān, died in battle.
The Ministry of War doubted the veracity of the claims of achievement,
and Commander Càishēng also reported Yǒu's deception and recklessness.
Grand Supervisor Shípú was ordered to investigate,
and it was found that only thirty to forty people were captured or killed,
while 1,400 officers and soldiers were lost,
deserving punishment.
An imperial edict ordered him to prove himself by killing rebels.
In the first year of Tiānshùn, he accompanied Yīng in campaigning against the various Tiāntáng Miao,
achieving great success.
He was appointed Left Vice Regional Commander,
still guarding Húguǎng.
Afterwards,
he again joined Yīng in defeating the remnants of Méngnéng's faction.
He was summoned and enfeoffed as Count of Wǔpíng,
and granted a hereditary patent.
When Bólái invaded the border,
he was appointed Guerrilla General
and followed Marquis Ānyuǎn Liǔpǔ and others to resist.
He led Grand Commander Zhào'yīng and others to engage in battle,
and the enemy was defeated and fled.
They again attacked Zhènfān,
and he again repelled them,
capturing 160 people.
Soon after, he was given the general's seal
and appointed Commander-in-Chief
to suppress the Níngxià rebels.
Previously,
the rebels had greatly invaded Gān and Liáng,
and Pǔ and Commander-in-Chief Wèiyǐng and others could not resist,
but Yǒu achieved some success.
At this time, Governor Ruìzhāo listed the misdeeds of the various generals,
and the Ministry of War requested that Yǒu's punishment be waived.
An imperial edict pardoned Pǔ and the others as well,
and Yǒu was recalled,
promoted to Marquis,
and died.
The title passed down through his son to his grandson Gāng.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
Gāng requested a posthumous title for Yǒu.
An imperial edict bestowed the title Duke of Miǎnnation
and the posthumous name Wǔxī.
Gāng passed the title to his sons Xūn and Xī.
During the Jiājìng reign,
the Ministry of Personnel, noting that Yǒu's achievements in suppressing the Miao were largely exaggerated and fraudulent,
requested that the inheritance be stopped.
The emperor did not comply.
Xī's son Dàcè again inherited,
until the fall of the Ming dynasty, when the title ceased.
Lǐ Zhèn,
a native of Nányáng.
His father, Qiān,
was a Dūdū Qiānshì.
Zhèn inherited the position of Zhǐhuīshǐ.
In the ninth year of Zhèngtǒng, he gained merit in the campaign against Wùliánghā,
and was promoted to Dūdū Qiānshì.
Later,
he followed Wáng Jì to pacify Lùchuān,
and was promoted to Tóngzhī.
When Jǐngdì ascended the throne,
he was appointed Guìzhōu Yòu Cāncānjiāng.
He attacked the Miáo at Piānqiáo,
and defeated them.
In the second year of Jǐngtài, he followed Wáng Lái to campaign against Wéi Tóngliè,
and captured Suǒ'ér, Liúyuán, and other strongholds,
taking 1,600 captives and beheaded enemies.
Together, they conquered Xiānglúshān,
and captured Tóngliè.
He was promoted to Dūdūshǐ,
and garrisoned Jìngzhōu.
Soon after, he was recalled due to an offense.
When Fāng Yīng was campaigning against the Miáo,
he requested Zhèn to accompany the army.
An imperial edict permitted this, allowing him to atone for his crime by meritorious service.
Later,
he followed Yīng to crush the Tiāntáng Miáo,
and was reinstated as Zuǒ Cānjiāng.
When Yīng pacified the Tónggǔ rebels,
Zhèn also advanced to Wǔgāng,
capturing Niúlán and fifty-four other strongholds.
Many were captured and beheaded,
and he was promoted to Dūdū Qiānshì.
During the Tiānshùn era,
he again followed Yīng to pacify the Guìdōng Miáo chieftain, Gànbǎzhū.
When Yīng died,
Zhèn was immediately appointed Zǒngbīngguān,
and succeeded him in garrisoning Guìzhōu and Húguǎng.
Initially,
Lǐ Tiānbǎo, a man from Máchéng, had fled into Miáo territory due to unpaid taxes,
falsely claiming to be a descendant of Táng Tàizōng.
His followers numbered over ten thousand,
he usurped the title of king,
established the era name Wǔliè,
and plundered far and wide.
Zhèn advanced and attacked,
utterly defeating him.
Tiānbǎo fled into the Miáo territory of Guǐchí in Guìzhōu,
and again incited various Miáo groups to plunder.
Zhèn captured him,
and sent him to the capital.
Soon after, he crushed the Xībāo Miáo.
In the spring of the fifth year, he suppressed the Yáo and Tóng people of Chéngbù,
attacking the strongholds of Héngshuǐ, Chéngxī, Mòyí, and Zhōngpíng,
all of which he captured.
He advanced deep into Xīyán, Guǎngxī,
where he met Zǒngbīngguān Guò Xīng’s army,
and conquered the Yáo of Shíbātuán,
capturing and beheading several thousand people in total.
That winter, Zhèn was ordered to solely garrison Húguǎng,
with Lǐ Ān appointed Zǒngbīng
to defend Guìzhōu.
The following summer, he led his army from Jǐntián and Jiānghuá to the strongholds of Yúnchuān, Guìlǐng,
and Héngjiāng,
defeated the Yáo,
and captured and beheaded over 2,800 people.
In the winter of the seventh year,
the Miáo occupied Chìxī Nàndòng Zhǎngguānsī.
Zhèn and Ān advanced by separate routes,
beheaded the rebel leader Fēitiānhóu and others,
destroyed 200 strongholds,
and thus recovered the Zhǎngguānsī.
He was promoted to Dūdū Tóngzhī.
In the winter of the following year,
Guǎngxī Yáo invaded Húnán,
entering Guìyángzhōu by night and plundering extensively.
Zhèn dispatched troops to pursue and attack them by separate routes,
repeatedly defeating them,
and capturing and beheading over a thousand people.
In the first year of Chénghuà,
he was garrisoning Jìngzhōu.
Dūdū Tóngzhī Zhuāng Róng reported that the prefectures of Lípíng in Guìzhōu were close to the Wǔkāi Guards of Húguǎng,
and could not be overseen without a grand general.
Thus, Zhèn was again ordered to concurrently garrison Guìzhōu.
Not long after,
he captured the rebel leader Miáochóngxiā.
When the Jīng-Xiāng rebels Liú Qiānjīn and Shí Héshàng caused unrest,
Zhèn advanced to suppress them.
The rebels were repeatedly defeated,
and he pursued them in victory to the rebel stronghold at Méixī.
The government forces suffered a setback;
thirty-eight men, from Dūdū Zhǐhuī downwards, died.
An imperial edict severely reprimanded him.
When the large army of Bái Guī and others arrived,
Zhèn advanced from Nánzhāng to join the attack,
and utterly defeated them,
thus pacifying the rebels.
For his merits,
he was promoted to Yòu Dūdū.
At this time, the Miáo of Wǔgāng, Yuánjìng, Tónggǔ, and Wǔkāi rose up again,
and Guìzhōu also reported alarms.
Zhèn stated that Guìzhōu was ultimately difficult to control from afar,
and requested to solely garrison Húguǎng.
This was granted,
and he then returned his troops.
From Tónggǔ and Tiānzhù, he advanced in four routes,
repeatedly defeating the rebels,
reaching directly to the Qīngshuǐ Jiāng.
With the Miáo acting as guides,
he penetrated deep into rebel territory.
Within two months, he destroyed 800 strongholds,
burned 13,000 houses,
and captured and beheaded 3,300.
As for the Guǎngxī Yáo who raided Guìyáng,
he also attacked and beheaded over 3,800.
At that time,
Zhèn’s formidable reputation was established in the southwest.
The Miáo and Liáo heard of him and were terrified,
calling him
"Jīnpái Lǐ" (Golden Plaque Lǐ).
In the seventh year,
he collaborated with Xiàng Zhōng to pacify the roaming bandit Lǐ Yuán,
and resettled 900,000 displaced people.
Jīng-Xiāng was thus pacified.
The details are found in Zhōng's biography.
In the eleventh year,
the Miáo again raided Wǔgāng and Jìngzhōu,
causing great disturbance in Húxiāng.
Zhèn, along with Grand Coordinator Liú Fū and others, advanced in five routes,
destroying over 620 strongholds,
capturing and beheading over 8,500 people,
and taking tens of thousands of rebel families as captives.
For his merits, he was ennobled as Xīngníng Bó.
At that time, Wǔjìng Hóu Zhào Fǔ and Níngjìn Bó Liú Jù were also ennobled for their achievements,
and many critics found fault with them,
but Zhèn’s achievements were the greatest,
and no one disagreed.
The Cāncānjiāng Wú Jīng
had a grudge against Zhèn.
His younger brother, Qiānhù Shòu, was a confidant of Wāng Zhí.
Jīng instructed Shòu to defame him.
Coincidentally, Zhí was then undermining Xiàng Zhōng,
and Zhèn was implicated in the accusations.
Consequently, he was arrested and imprisoned,
stripped of his peerage,
demoted to Zuǒ Dūdū,
and relegated to idle residence in Nánjīng.
Not long after,
Zhí dispatched a military aide to investigate,
who reported that Zhèn had secretly colluded with the garrison eunuch Tán Bāo,
and engaged in private bribery.
The emperor was enraged,
and sent Zhí to Nánjīng to enumerate Bāo and others' crimes.
Bāo was reprimanded and demoted to serve as incense officer at Xiàolíng,
and Zhèn was ordered to return to the capital.
When Zhí fell,
Zhèn appealed and had his peerage restored,
and died shortly thereafter.
Zhèn had been in Húxiāng for a long time,
was familiar with Miáo affairs,
and was skilled in military tactics.
Among those who campaigned against the Miáo at that time,
Zhèn was second only to Fāng Yīng.
However, he was greedy for merit and eager for advancement,
and engaged in connections,
which ultimately led to his downfall.
Wáng Xìn,
courtesy name Jūnshí,
a native of Nánzhèng.
When he was six months old,
his father Zhōng died in battle during a northern campaign.
His mother, Lady Yuè, painstakingly raised him with strict virtue,
and both were later officially commended.
During the Zhèngtǒng era,
Xìn inherited the position of Qiānhù of Kuānhé Guard.
In the early years of the Chénghuà reign,
he accumulated merits until he became a Dū Zhǐhuī Qiānshì,
garrisoning Jīng and Xiāng.
When Liú Qiānjīn rebelled,
Xìn considered Fángxiàn strategically important,
and advanced to occupy it.
The militia numbered less than a thousand men.
The rebels, numbering four thousand, suddenly arrived
and besieged the city.
He resisted for over forty days,
then selected a group of suicidally brave soldiers,
who went out of the city five or six lǐ and fired cannons.
The rebels suspected reinforcements had arrived,
and fled in panic.
He pursued and defeated them.
Later,
when Bái Guī arrived with a large army,
he appointed Xìn as Yòu Cānjìang,
to take a separate route to the Hòuyán Shān.
The rebels were then eradicated.
For his merits,
he was promoted to Dū Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī.
When the rebel faction under Shí Lóng again captured Wūshān,
Xìn and the other generals jointly pacified them.
However, the displaced people continued to cause unrest between Jīng, Xiāng, and Nányáng.
Xìn was concerned about this,
and reported it to the court.
The court immediately ordered Xìn to concurrently supervise military affairs in Nányáng.
The rebel leaders Lǐ Yuán and others indeed caused trouble,
and Xìn again collaborated with Xiàng Zhōng to suppress them.
He was promoted to acting Dūdū Qiānshì,
and garrisoned Línqīng.
In the thirteenth year [of Chénghuà], he was given the seal of Píngmán Jiāngjūn in his current post,
and transferred to garrison Húguǎng.
The two Xūanwèi of Yǒngshùn and Bǎojìng had been feuding for generations.
Xìn explained to them the consequences of their actions, both good and bad,
and the conflict immediately ceased.
The Mán of Jìngzhōu and Wǔgāng had long been unruly,
and the defending officials debated whether to suppress them.
Xìn personally visited them,
rewarded them with cattle and wine,
and reprimanded them for their misconduct.
The multitude bowed their heads in submission and confessed their guilt.
In the seventeenth year, he memorialized, saying:
"Although the various Mán of Húguǎng are a festering wound in our midst,
they are actually powerless to achieve anything significant.
The reason they have been unruly for so long
is that our generals and soldiers profit from their sporadic uprisings to claim merit.
If we select elite troops
and strictly enforce defenses,
their troubles will naturally cease.
The displaced people of Jīng and Xiāng
originally fled due to corvée labor;
indiscriminate killings may harm the harmony of heaven.
The common people of the fields have no savings at all.
Before the harvest is complete,
their provisions are already empty;
when the loom has just stopped,
where are the cloths and threads?
I request that upright, benevolent, and generous officials be selected to govern,
and that more effort be put into pacifying and comforting the people.
Superfluous officials have been indiscriminately appointed,
numbering perhaps a thousand,
not one of whom has exerted any effort,
yet they presume to enjoy rewards of high rank.
I request that they be investigated, dismissed, and stripped of their ranks."
His subordinates Liú Bīn and Zhāng Quán were courageous and wise.
He strongly recommended them to the court.
He also said:
"Heroic individuals,
with upright and resolute hearts,
how could they be willing to bow their heads and seek favor?
If no effort is made to seek them out,
then men of ambition will remain obscure,
and how can the imperial court employ them?"
In the twenty-first year,
Circuit Inspector Mǎ Xùn and others reported
that Vice Grand Commander Zhōu Xián and Assistant General Péng Lún both held the rank of Dūdū Qiānshì,
while Xìn was merely an acting official.
It was appropriate to promote him one rank to strengthen his authority.
The Ministry of War stated that Xìn had no new military merits.
The Emperor specially promoted him to Dūdū Tóngzhī.
Soon after,
he was appointed Grand Supervisor of Grain Transport.
The governor's yámen formerly had a lake,
which was used for private gain.
Xìn opened it up to moor grain boats.
When powerful individuals obstructed the water,
he dealt with them strictly according to the law,
and the grain transport affairs were well managed.
He died the following year.
Xìn was resolute, straightforward, and serious,
and fond of reading.
He dressed like a scholar.
Having served in major garrisons,
he never amassed private property,
and often said:
"Frugality is sufficient for long-term endurance;
after death, not burdening one's descendants
is already a great legacy."
Thus, for the weddings and funerals of his acquaintances,
he would spend all his money to help them.
His sons, Jìshàn and Cóngshàn, both passed the Jìnshì examination.
Those who succeeded Xìn as Grand Supervisor of Grain Transport were
Níngjīn's Dū Shèng and Héféi's Guō Hóng.
Shèng inherited the post of Nánjīng Yǔlín Zuǒ Wèi Zhǐhuī Qiānshì,
while Hóng inherited the post of Péngchéng Wèi Zhǐhuī Shǐ.
In the early years of Chénghuà,
Shèng was promoted to acting Dū Zhǐhuī Qiānshì;
and Hóng also, for his merits in the campaign against Lìpǔ,
was promoted to Dū Zhǐhuī Qiānshì,
passed the military imperial examination,
and was transferred to Tóngzhī.
Shèng defended Yángzhōu against pirates,
defeating salt smugglers who caused unrest.
Yǐn Mín and others recommended Shèng as a military talent,
and Hóng was also recommended by Zhāng Mào.
Thus, Shèng was appointed as Cānjìang
to assist in grain transport,
while Hóng replaced him in defending against pirates.
When Shǎnxī suffered a great famine,
Shèng was ordered to transport a million shí of rice for relief.
When Xìn died,
he was then promoted to acting Dū Zhǐhuī Shǐ,
and appointed Grand Commander to replace him,
while Hóng replaced Shèng as Cānjìang.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
Shèng served as Dūdū Qiānshì with stipend in the Nánjīng Qiánfǔ.
At that time, Hóng had already garrisoned Guǎngxī as Vice Grand Commander,
and had defeated the Zhuàng rebels of Fǔjiāng.
Thus, he was promoted to Grand Supervisor of Grain Transport due to his reputation.
Hóng was resolute and had military strategies.
However, Shèng had no outstanding military achievements,
but merely due to his honesty and quietness in office,
he was frequently entrusted with duties.
He served for fifty-seven years,
and all the places he governed were rich lands,
yet he lived simply and frugally,
eating only tofu daily.
At times, this was used as his nickname.
Hóng was successively promoted to Dūdū Tóngzhī,
and often presented memorials to the court regarding the benefits and harms to the military and common people.
He once dredged the Tōngzhōu river for twenty lǐ,
and built dams,
allowing shallow boats to transport goods,
saving tens of thousands of silver taels annually.
During the reign of Xiàozōng,
court administration was well-ordered,
and many capable civil and military officials were appointed.
Hóng managed grain transport for thirteen years without change.
In the early years of Zhèngdé,
he was finally recalled to assist in the Hòufǔ,
and soon after died.
Péng Lún
initially served as Húguǎng Yǒngdìng Wèi Zhǐhuī Shǐ,
and accumulated merits until he became Dū Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī.
In the early years of Chénghuà,
he followed Zhào Fǔ to pacify the Dàténgxiá rebels.
He was promoted to Dū Zhǐhuī Shǐ,
and garrisoned Qīnglàng and other places in Guìzhōu,
and attacked and defeated the rebellious Miáo of Máopíng and Tónggǔ.
When rebels plundered Gānqī,
Lún attacked them.
The rebels returned what they had plundered,
made a covenant, and retreated.
Lún, seeing that when the rebels entered,
they passed through the various stockades of Qióngshuǐ
without being immediately intercepted,
issued an order:
whoever could capture rebels alive entering the border would receive a heavy reward;
those who let them go would be punished by law.
As a result, the various departments each ordered their subordinates
that whenever "raw Miáo" trespassed,
they should be immediately captured,
and many were sent to his tent.
Lún gathered the leaders, headmen, and captured prisoners from his command,
placed them on tall poles,
and assembled strong soldiers to shoot them indiscriminately, killing them.
He then cut and dismembered their bodies,
and cooked and fed them to his brave warriors.
Those whose crimes were lighter had their ears and noses cut off and were allowed to leave,
saying:
"This is to mark you;
if you offend again, you will not be pardoned."
He then ordered the various stockades to erect boundary markers, and the Miáo groups trembled in fear and dared not trespass.
The next year, he was promoted to right assistant commander [Yòu Cāncáng],
and remained stationed at Qīnglàng.
He devoted himself even more to frontier strategies,
and all military affairs were managed.
The rebellious bandit Shí Quánzhōu [石全州] secretly infiltrated Jiǎodòng [絞洞],
stirring up the Miáo [苗] of Gǔzhōu [古州].
The various Miáo of Hóngjiāng [洪江] and Gānzhuàn [甘篆] all responded to him.
Lún [倫] dispatched troops to intercept and capture them,
and also searched for and apprehended their wives and children.
When the various Miáo were about to attack Zhènyuǎn [鎮遠],
Lún [倫] utterly defeated them,
beheading countless individuals and causing many to fall to their deaths from cliffs.
Not long after,
the Miáo of the fourteen stockades of Qióngshuǐ [邛水] conspired with the raw Miáo of Hóngjiāng [洪江] to rebel.
Lún [倫] divided his forces into five patrols and set out.
As soon as they began to march,
the rain poured down like a torrent.
Lún [倫] said:
"The enemy does not expect us.
If we advance quickly,
we can achieve our goal."
They pressed forward, attacking from both sides,
seizing their leader [Kuí],
and capturing and beheading the remaining rebels.
The bandits were completely pacified.
When the Miáo of Jìngzhōu [靖州] rebelled,
the Grand Commander [Zǒngbīngguān] of Húguǎng [湖廣], Lǐ Zhèn [李震], issued a summons for Lún [倫] to join in the suppression.
When the army reached Qióngshuǐ Jiāng [邛水江],
the various 'cooked' Miáo [shúmiáo 熟苗] were alarmed
and wished to flee.
Lún [倫] and the Assistant Administrator [Qiānshì] Lǐ Huǎng [李晃] discussed this, saying:
"If the Miáo flee, they will surely aid the bandits."
So, they immediately pacified them.
Along the way, they also brought the Miáo of Tiāntáng [天堂] and Xiǎopíng [小坪] under submission.
Upon reaching Jìngzhōu [靖州],
Lún [倫] led the right patrol [Yòushào],
and set up camp behind the enemy.
The bandits fled to occupy a high mountain.
Lún's [倫] army attacked them uphill,
and the bandits were defeated and fled.
They then crossed the river,
raided their stronghold,
and gained a great victory.
Capitalizing on their victory, they attacked Báiyátáng [白崖塘].
The cliff was ten thousand ren [rèn 仞] high,
overlooking a deep abyss,
and was known for its extreme danger.
Lún [倫] joined the left patrol [Zuǒshào] in advancing together
and found a path.
They ascended at night,
and the bandits scattered in panic.
They pursued and beheaded over two thousand,
and captured a similar number,
completely razing their stockades.
Previously,
