the Miáo of the six caves of Zhēn Pǒu [臻剖] encroached upon the fields of the 'cooked' Miáo,
did not pay taxes,
and did not supply post horses.
The officials dared not question them.
Lún [倫] sent someone to instruct them,
and they bowed their heads, requesting to comply with the regulations.
For his merits,
he was promoted to Assistant Administrator [Qiānshì] of the Chief Military Commission [Dūdū Qiānshì].
After a long time,
Censors [Yùshǐ] Dèng Xiáng [鄧庠] and Director of a Bureau [Yuánwàiláng] Fèi Xuān [費瑄] investigated affairs in Guìzhōu [貴州].
The Grand Commander [Zǒngbīngguān] Wú Jīng [吳經] and others were all impeached,
but only Lún [倫] was recommended for his wisdom and mature counsel.
In the early Hongzhì [Hóngzhì 弘治] period,
when Wú Jīng [吳經] was dismissed from his post after deliberation,
Lún [倫] was immediately appointed to replace him.
Lún [倫], when deploying his forces,
planned first and then fought,
thus achieving many successes.
In the fourth year, due to old age, he retired.
When he died,
he was granted a pension as prescribed.
Ōu Pán [歐磐],
was from Chú [滁].
He inherited the hereditary post of Commander [Zhīhuīshǐ].
During the Chenghua [Chénghuà 成化] period,
he was promoted to Assistant Commander [Qiānshì] of Guangdong [Guǎngdōng] Chief Military Commission [Dūzhīhuī Qiānshì].
He repeatedly suppressed barbarian pirates with merit.
Based on the recommendation of Grand Supervisor [Zǒngdū] Zhū Yīng [朱英],
he was appointed Right Assistant Commander [Yòu Cāncáng] of Guangxi [Guǎngxī],
responsible for defending Liǔzhōu [柳州] and Qìngyuǎn [慶遠].
He, along with Left Assistant Commander [Zuǒ Cāncáng] Mǎ Yì [馬義], attacked the Yao [Yáo 瑤] of the eight stockades in Róngxiàn [融縣],
and captured them.
After the army returned,
the remaining bandits reappeared and plundered,
for which he was impeached.
The Emperor [Dì 帝] reduced Pán's [磐] and others' merits,
only granting pensions to the families of those who died in service.
When the Yao [Yáo 瑤] bandit Fāng Gōngqiáng [方公強] caused rebellion,
the Ministry of War [Bīngbù] impeached the Chief Commander [Zǒngzhèn] eunuch Gù [顧],
which also involved Pán [磐],
who was to be banished to a frontier garrison.
The Grand Coordinators [Dūfǔ 督撫] reported:
"The area Pán [磐] defends is a place where Yao [Yáo 瑤] and Zhuang [Zhuàng 僮] often appear.
Pán [磐] recruited brave soldiers,
entered the bandit's lair at night,
killed their leader Hú Gōngfǎn [胡公返],
and his prestige shook all the barbarians.
Considering his merits,
he can atone for his crime."
The Emperor [Dì 帝] then pardoned him,
and he returned to his former post.
In the twenty-third year,
the bandits Huáng Gōngdìng [黃公定] and Hú Gōngmíng [胡公明] from Yùlín [鬱林] and Lùchuān [陸川] rebelled.
Pán [磐], along with Surveillance Commissioner [Ànchásǐ] Táo Lǔ [陶魯] and others, attacked and defeated them in five routes.
He was promoted to Vice Commissioner [Tóngzhī] of the Chief Military Commission [Dūzhīhuī Tóngzhī].
In the early Hongzhì [Hóngzhì 弘治] period,
he resigned due to illness.
Grand Supervisor [Zǒngdū] Qín Hóng [秦紘] stated that Pán [磐] had much experience in battles,
possessed talent and integrity,
and requested his reinstatement.
An imperial edict ordered him to return to his post.
In the eighth year,
the Zhuang [Zhuàng 僮] of Fǔjiāng [府江] and Yǒng'ān [永安] rebelled.
Grand Supervisor [Zǒngdū] Mǐn Guī [閔珪] mobilized sixty thousand troops,
dividing them into four patrols to suppress them.
Pán [磐], starting from Xiàngzhōu [象州] and Xiūrén [修仁], directly attacked Lùdòng [陸峒],
smashing everything in his path.
Afterwards,
along with the other armies, he successively destroyed one hundred and eighty mountain stockades,
beheading over six thousand.
He was promoted to Commander [Zhīhuīshǐ] of the Chief Military Commission [Dūzhīhuīshǐ],
and transferred to Vice Grand Commander [Fù Zǒngbīng] of Guangxi [Guǎngxī].
The aboriginal official [tǔguān 土官] Cén Jùn [岑濬] of Sī'ēn [思恩] built a stone city at Dānliángzhuāng [丹良莊],
obstructing the river and appropriating commercial profits.
The Marshal's office ordered its destruction,
but he refused.
Pán [磐], returning from Tiánzhōu [田州],
led troops to demolish the city.
Cén Jùn [岑濬] led his people to resist,
but Pán [磐] defeated them,
and ultimately razed the city.
The Censor-in-Chief [Dū Yùshǐ] Dèng Tíngzàn [鄧廷瓚] and others, noting Pán's [磐] many achievements,
reported to the court,
and he was promoted to Assistant Administrator [Qiānshì] of the Chief Military Commission [Dūdū Qiānshì].
In the fifteenth year, he was ordered to wear the seal of the General [Jiāngjūn] for Pacifying Barbarians [Píngmán Jiāngjūn],
and to be stationed in Húguǎng [湖廣].
Pán [磐] was an honest general
and able to win over his soldiers.
Having been stationed in the southern region for a long time,
the barbarians feared and submitted to him.
In the eighteenth year, he requested retirement due to old age.
Two years later, he died.
His sacrifices and burial were carried out as prescribed.
Zhāng Yòu [張祐],
courtesy name Tiānyòu [天祐],
was from Guǎngzhōu [廣州].
From childhood, he loved learning and was skilled in writing.
During the Hongzhì [Hóngzhì 弘治] period, he inherited the hereditary post of Commander [Zhīhuīshǐ] of the Guǎngzhōu [廣州] Right Guard [Yòuwèi].
At nineteen,
he followed Grand Supervisor [Zǒngdū] Pān Fān [潘蕃] to suppress the Nánhǎi [南海] pirate Xūn Yuánzǔ [禤元祖],
being the first to climb the ramparts, thus achieving merit.
In the second year of Zhengde [Zhèngdé 正德], he was promoted to acting Assistant Commander [Qiānshì] of the Chief Military Commission [Dūzhīhuī Qiānshì],
and was stationed at Déqìng [德慶] and Lóngshuǐ [瀧水].
The Yao [Yáo 瑤] and Zhuang [Zhuàng 僮] who relied on the terrain heard of his prestige and trustworthiness,
and gradually fled.
Grand Supervisor [Zǒngdū] Lín Tíngxuǎn [林廷xuǎn] appointed him as the central army commander [Zhōngjūn],
consulting him on all matters, big or small.
He was stationed at Huì [惠] and Cháo [潮],
raided the lairs of bandit leaders Liú Wén'ān [劉文安] and Lǐ Tōngbǎo [李通寶],
and pacified them.
He was transferred to Right Assistant Commander [Yòu Cāncáng] of Guangxi [Guǎngxī],
stationed at Liǔ [柳] and Qìng [慶].
Grand Supervisor [Zǒngdū] Chén Jīn [陳金] attacked the Fǔjiāng [府江] bandits,
ordering Yòu [祐] to advance to Shénshākǒu [沈沙口],
where he decisively defeated them.
His salary was increased by one grade,
and he was promoted to Vice Grand Commander [Fù Zǒngbīng],
stationed in Guangxi [Guǎngxī].
Soon after, he was promoted to acting Assistant Administrator [Qiānshì] of the Chief Military Commission [Dūdū Qiānshì].
The various Yao [Yáo 瑤] and Zhuang [Zhuàng 僮] of Gǔtián [古田] rebelled.
Yòu [祐] said:
"In previous campaigns,
we mostly relied on the aboriginal soldiers [tǔbīng 土兵] of the two rivers,
but the rewards did not match their efforts.
Now, many fail to arrive on time when summoned.
I request that a resolution be made to generously reward them."
This was agreed to.
He supervised Commander [Zhīhuīshǐ] Shěn Xīyí [沈希儀] and others in suppressing the various Yao [Yáo 瑤] of Línguì [臨桂] and Guànyáng [灌陽],
beheading over five hundred.
An imperial letter praised and rewarded him.
He then successively defeated the Gǔtián [古田] bandits,
capturing and beheading four thousand seven hundred,
and was promoted to acting Vice Commissioner [Tóngzhī] of the Chief Military Commission [Dūdū Tóngzhī].
Afterwards,
he again suppressed and pacified the various barbarians of Luòróng [洛容], Zhàoqìng [肇慶], and Pínglè [平樂].
His salary was increased by one grade,
and his son was granted a hereditary
hundred-household position [Bǎihù 百戶].
In the first year of Jiajing [Jiājìng 嘉靖],
his mother passed away,
and he grieved so much that he became emaciated.
Soon after, he requested retirement due to illness,
and returned to his guard post.
Gōng Quán'ān,
a native of Lánxī.
He was a *jìnshì* [presented scholar],
and was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Works.
He was successively promoted to Left Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Diplomacy (*Zuǒ Tōngzhèng*).
After his death, he was posthumously granted the title of Minister of the Court of Imperial Diplomacy (*Tōngzhèng Shǐ*).
Huáng Yǎngzhèng,
whose given name was Méng,
was known by his courtesy name (*zì*).
He was a native of Ruì'ān.
Due to his skill in calligraphy, he was appointed Junior Compiler (*Zhōngshū Shèrén*).
He successively rose to the rank of Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*Tàicháng Shàoqīng*).
After his death, he was posthumously granted the title of Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*Tàicháng Qīng*).
Dài Qìngzǔ,
a native of Lìyáng,
and Wáng Yījū,
a native of Shàngyuán.
Both were imperial musicians and dancers (*yuèwǔ shēng*),
and successively rose to the rank of Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*Tàicháng Shàoqīng*).
After their deaths,
both were posthumously granted the title of Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*Tàicháng Qīng*).
Bāo Liángzuǒ,
courtesy name Kèzhōng,
a native of Cíxī.
He was a *jìnshì*,
and was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Personnel.
Bào Huī,
courtesy name Shúdà,
a native of Píngyáng, Zhèjiāng.
He was a *jìnshì*,
and was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Works.
He frequently offered proposals to the throne.
Zhāng Hóng,
a native of Ānfú,
and Huáng Shāng,
courtesy name Yuánjí,
a native of Qǔjiāng.
Both were *jìnshì*,
and were appointed Censors (*Yùshǐ*).
Shāng once reported that three *fǔ*—Níng, Shào, and Tái—suffered 30,000 deaths from plague.
He suggested that the dead should be exempted from taxes,
and the survivors should receive relief.
While inspecting the salt administration in the two Zhèjiang circuits,
he requested relief for flood victims.
His request was approved.
Wèi Zhēn,
a native of Huáiyuǎn.
He was a *jìnshì*,
and served as a Censor.
Shēn Yòu,
courtesy name Tiānxī,
a native of Wùchuān, Guìzhōu.
When his father was attacked by a tiger,
Yòu seized a club and fiercely struck it,
thus saving his father.
He was recommended in his home province,
entered the National Academy,
and led the students to rescue Minister of the Imperial Academy (*Jìjiǔ*) Lǐ Shímǐan.
Soon after, he passed the *jìnshì* examination,
and was appointed Censor of Sìchuān Circuit (*Sìchuān Dào Yùshǐ*).
He was known for his candid and straightforward speech.
Yǐn Hóng,
courtesy name Tàihé,
a native of Bá.
Tóng Cúndé,
courtesy name Jūjìng,
a native of Lánxī.
Both were *jìnshì*,
and served as Censors.
Lín Xiángfèng,
courtesy name Mínggāo,
a native of Pútián.
He was appointed Instructor (*Xùndǎo*) through a provincial recommendation,
and then promoted to Censor.
Qí Wāng,
courtesy name Yuánchéng,
a native of Tiāntái.
Having passed the *jìnshì* examination, he successively served as Director (*Lángzhōng*) of the Transport Bureau (*Chējià Sī*) in the Ministry of War.
Chéng Sīwēn,
a native of Wùyuán.
Chéng Shì,
a native of Chángshú.
Lù Duān,
a native of Rénhé.
All were *jìnshì*,
and served as Assistant Directors (*Yuánwàiláng*).
Yú Jiàn,
courtesy name Yuánjí,
a native of Tónglú.
Having passed the *jìnshì* examination, he was appointed Secretary (*Zhǔshì*) of the Bureau of Military Affairs (*Zhífāng Sī*) in the Ministry of War.
When the emperor went on a northern expedition,
Director Hú Níng was supposed to accompany him,
but requested a substitute due to illness.
Jiàn magnanimously agreed.
Someone asked:
"Your family is far away and your children are young, what will you do?"
Jiàn replied:
"For the country,
how can a minister and son consider his own family?"
Minister of War (*Shàngshū*) Kuàng Yě knew of his talent
and frequently consulted him on matters.
Jiàn said:
"I can only strongly advise the army to return."
At that time, his advice could not be adopted.
Zhāng Táng,
courtesy name Tíngyù,
a native of Cíxī.
He was a *jìnshì*,
and was appointed Secretary of the Ministry of Justice.
Yǐn Chāng,
a native of Jíshuǐ.
He was a *jìnshì*,
and served as Chief Commissioner (*Zhèng*) of the Bureau of Envoys (*Xíngrén Sī*).
Luó Rúyǒng,
courtesy name Běnchóng,
a native of Lúlín.
He was a *jìnshì*,
and was appointed Envoy (*Xíngrén*).
He accompanied the northern expedition.
On the verge of departure,
he bid farewell to his wife and children,
vowing to repay the country with his life,
and entrusted Hanlin scholar Liú Yǎn to compose his tomb inscription.
Yǎn was shocked and refused,
but Rúyǒng smiled and said:
"You will see if it proves true when I go."
A few days later, he indeed died.
Liú Róng,
Vice Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud (*Tàipú Shàoqīng*).
Líng Shòu,
Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Seals (*Shàngbǎo Shàoqīng*).
Xià Chéng and Sūn Qìng were both Censors.
Féng Xuémíng,
Director.
Wáng Jiàn,
Assistant Director.
Yú Gǒng, Pān Chéng, Qián Bǐng,
were all Junior Compilers.
Mǎ Yù,
Vice Minister of the Grand Court of Judicial Review (*Dàlǐ Sì Fù*).
Liú Xìn,
Chief of the Bureau of the Summer Palace (*Xiàguān Zhèng*).
Lǐ Gōng, Shí Yù,
Attendants (*Xùbān*).
Their native places are all unrecorded.
Sūn Xiáng,
a native of Dàtóng.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the 10th year of the Zhèngtǒng reign.
He was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of War.
He was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief (*Yòufù Dū Yùshǐ*),
and was stationed at Zǐjīng Pass.
When Yěxiān besieged the pass,
Regional Commander Hán Qīng died in battle.
Xiáng held out for four days.
Yěxiān entered through a secret path,
launched a pincer attack,
and the pass was broken.
Xiáng led his troops in street fighting,
but his army was routed and he was killed.
Imperial censors mistakenly impeached Xiáng for abandoning the city and fleeing.
After the invaders retreated,
officials repaired the pass,
found his body on the battlefield,
cremated and buried it,
but did not report it.
Xiáng's younger brother Qí went to the imperial court to protest the injustice,
and an edict was issued to provide relief to his family.
In the first year of the Chénghuà reign,
his son Shēn was appointed Right Reviewing Judge of the Grand Court of Judicial Review (*Dàlǐ Sì Yòupíngshì*).
Another was Xiè Zé,
a native of Shàngyú.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the 16th year of the Yǒnglè reign.
From Secretary of the Ministry of Justice in Nánjīng, he was dispatched as Administration Vice Commissioner of Guǎngxī (*Guǎngxī Cānzhèng*).
At the end of the Zhèngtǒng reign,
he was promoted to Minister of the Court of Imperial Diplomacy (*Tōngzhèng Shǐ*),
and was stationed at Báiyáng Pass.
When the imperial army was defeated at Tǔmù,
those guarding the borders had no firm resolve.
Zé bid farewell to his son Yǎn and set off.
Only a few days after taking up his post,
Yěxiān's army launched a major invasion,
and the defending general Lǚ Duó fled.
Zé led his troops to block the mountain pass.
A strong wind blew sand,
making it impossible to distinguish men from horses.
Someone suggested moving to another pass to avoid the enemy,
but Zé refused.
When the invaders arrived,
the troops collapsed.
Zé pressed his sword and loudly cursed the bandits,
and was then killed.
When the matter was reported,
an official was dispatched to conduct his funeral and sacrifices,
and Yǎn was appointed Reviewing Judge of the Grand Court of Judicial Review (*Dàlǐ Píngshì*).
Yuán Bīn,
courtesy name Wénzhì,
was a native of Xīnchāng, Jiāngxī.
At the end of the Zhèngtǒng reign,
he accompanied the emperor on the northern expedition as a Jǐnyī wèi (Brocade-clad Guard) battalion commander.
During the Tumù Incident,
Yěxiān detained the emperor and took him north.
All the accompanying officials fled and scattered,
but only Bīn remained with him,
never leaving his side.
When Yěxiān attacked Dàtóng and Xuānfǔ,
and then pressed towards the capital,
Bīn always accompanied the emperor.
Going up and down mountains and slopes,
crossing streams and ravines,
enduring dangers,
Bīn protected him without slackening.
When the emperor stopped at Tǔchéng,
he wished to write a letter to the Empress Dowager, send it to Emperor Jǐng, and instruct his officials.
Knowing Bīn was literate, he ordered him to draft it.
After the emperor entered the desert,
his dwelling was merely a felt tent and a worn curtain,
with a single cart and a single horse placed beside it,
ready only for relocation.
Bīn navigated through the hardships,
never disobeying or offending.
At night, he slept with the emperor,
and when it was very cold,
he used his side to warm the emperor's feet.
There was a man named Hāmíng,
a Mongol.
As a child, he followed his father as an interpreter,
and now he also served the emperor.
When the emperor conveyed messages to Yěxiān and his subordinates,
he often used Míng.
When Yěxiān had requests or petitions,
Míng also conveyed them.
The emperor often sat alone in his tent,
looking south with a heavy heart.
The two men sometimes offered humorous words to comfort the emperor,
and the emperor would also smile.
The eunuch Xǐ Níng was Yěxiān's confidant.
Yěxiān once said to the emperor:
"If the central court sends an envoy,
the emperor can return."
The emperor said:
"If you yourself send me back, that would be acceptable,
but if you want the central court to send an envoy,
it would merely be a waste of back-and-forth travel."
Níng heard this,
and angrily said:
"It is Bīn who wants to return quickly,
he must be killed."
Níng advised Yěxiān to invade Níngxià to the west,
plunder its horses,
and head directly to the south of the Yangtze,
settling the emperor in Nánjīng.
Bīn and Míng said to the emperor:
"The weather is cold and the road is long,
Your Majesty cannot ride,
you will only suffer from cold and hunger.
Moreover, if you reach there and the generals do not accept you,
what then?"
The emperor stopped Níng's plan.
Níng again wanted to kill the two,
but the emperor strongly intervened to prevent it.
Yěxiān intended to offer his sister to the emperor.
Bīn requested that the emperor return to the capital before formal betrothal,
and the emperor ultimately declined.
Yěxiān disliked Bīn and Míng,
and tried to kill them many times.
One day, Bīn was bound and taken to a wilderness,
to be dismembered.
When the emperor heard of it,
he felt as if he had lost his right and left hands,
and rushed to rescue him,
so he was spared.
Bīn once suffered from a severe cold.
The emperor was very worried,
and pressed his own body against Bīn's back.
Bīn sweated profusely and recovered.
During the year the emperor spent in the northern desert,
he regarded Bīn as his own flesh and blood.
When the emperor returned to the capital,
Emperor Jǐng merely appointed Bīn as an acting Baǐhù (Centurion) of the Jǐnyī wèi.
After the Tiānshùn Restoration,
he was promoted to Zhǐhuī qiānshì (Assistant Commander).
Soon after, he was advanced to Tóngzhī (Associate Administrator).
The emperor favored Bīn greatly,
and there was nothing he requested that was not granted.
After Grand Secretary Shāng Lù was dismissed,
Bīn begged for his residence.
Later, deeming it cramped and narrow,
he requested that the government build him a new one,
which the emperor also granted.
When Bīn married,
the emperor ordered his maternal relative Sūn Xiǎnzōng to preside over it,
and bestowed generous gifts.
He was often summoned for private banquets,
where they reminisced about their time of hardship,
as jovial and intimate as in former days.
In the twelfth month of that year, he was promoted to Zhǐhuī shǐ (Commander),
and jointly managed the affairs of the guard with Dū zhǐhuī qiānshì (Assistant Commander-in-chief) Wáng Xǐ.
The two once received instructions from the eunuch Xià Shí,
and privately dispatched Baǐhù Jì Fú to investigate matters in Jiāngxī.
Fú was
the husband of the emperor's wet nurse.
An imperial edict asked who had dispatched him,
and the two pleaded guilty.
The emperor said:
"There must be someone behind this."
So Fú was handed over to the authorities,
and the two's acceptance of instructions was uncovered.
The department concerned requested punishment for Shí and the two.
The emperor pardoned Shí,
and the two were allowed to redeem their sentences of penal servitude and return to their posts.
However, an edict was issued stating that from then on, anyone who dispatched officials based on private instructions
would be executed without mercy.
Later, due to the escape of a prisoner,
Xǐ was dismissed,
and Bīn consequently took sole charge of the guard's affairs.
In the autumn of the fifth year,
for his merit in suppressing Cáo Qīn,
he was promoted to Dū zhǐhuī qiānshì.
At that time, Mén Dá, relying on the emperor's favor,
wielded immense power, influencing both court and commoners.
Many court officials bowed to him,
but Bīn alone refused to yield.
Dá falsely accused him of a crime,
and requested his arrest and trial.
The emperor, wishing for the law to take its course,
told Dá:
"You may go and manage the trial,
but return Yuán Bīn to me alive."
Dá then fabricated the case.
Thanks to the lacquer artisan Yáng Xūn who appealed on his behalf,
the case was resolved.
However, he was still transferred to the Nánjīng Jǐnyī wèi,
and placed on inactive duty with salary.
The details are in Dá's biography.
Two months later,
Emperor Yīngzōng died,
Dá fell into disgrace,
and was demoted to Dūyún.
Bīn was recalled to his original post,
and again took charge of the guard's affairs.
Not long after,
Dá was summoned, imprisoned,
and exiled to Nándān.
Bīn saw him off in the suburbs,
and gave him travel money.
In the early Chénghuà reign,
he was promoted to Dū zhǐhuī tóngzhī (Associate Commander-in-chief).
After a long time,
he was promoted to Dū zhǐhuī shǐ (Commander-in-chief).
Previously,
those who managed the Jǐnyī wèi
often flaunted their power
and sought bribes.
Bīn, having served for a long time,
conducted himself with quiet integrity.
In the thirteenth year, he was promoted to Dūdū qiānshì (Assistant Grand Commandant),
overseeing the Qiánjūn Dūdū fǔ (Chief Military Commission of the Vanguard).
He died in office.
His descendants inherited the position of Jǐnyī qiānshì (Brocade-clad Guard Assistant Commander).
Hāmíng returned with the emperor,
and was granted the Chinese name Yáng Míng.
He successively held the post of Jǐnyī zhǐhuī shǐ (Brocade-clad Guard Commander),
and was frequently dispatched to foreign lands as an interpreter.
When Emperor Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
he purged officials appointed by imperial decree without formal recommendation;
Míng, due to his merit as a bodyguard beyond the Great Wall,
alone remained in his original position.
He died of old age while in office.
Yuán Mǐn (袁敏) was
the Zhīshì (知事) of Jīnchǐ Wèi (金齒衞).
When Yīngzōng (英宗) launched the northern expedition,
he volunteered to follow him to Dàtóng (大同).
When the imperial carriage returned,
it stopped at Wànquán Zuǒwèi (萬全左衞).
Mǐn (敏) saw that enemy cavalry was pressing in
and requested to leave thirty to forty thousand elite troops to guard the pass,
while the imperial carriage sped into the pass.
Wáng Zhèn (王振) did not accept this,
and the grand army was subsequently annihilated.
Mǐn (敏) escaped and returned,
presenting a memorial to Jǐngdì (景帝) saying:
"The former Emperor (Shànghuáng, 上皇) previously resided in the nine-layered palace (Jiǔchóng, 九重),
wore imperial robes,
ate rare delicacies,
and lived in magnificent palaces and jade chambers.
Now that the imperial carriage is trapped in the desert,
does he wear imperial robes?
Does he eat rare delicacies?
Does he live in palaces?
I have heard
that when the sovereign is disgraced, his ministers should die.
The former Emperor is disgraced to this extent;
how can his ministers and sons bear it in their hearts?
I do not begrudge shattering my head or gouging out my heart.
I beg that an official be dispatched,
or that I be ordered to carry a letter and imperial garments and objects to inquire after his well-being beyond the Great Wall,
to fulfill the duty of a minister and son.
Even if I die ten thousand deaths,
my heart would truly be content."
The Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù, 禮部) was ordered to deliberate,
but eventually reported it shelved.
A eulogy says: How strange
was the defeat at Tǔmù (土木)!
The invaders were not a deeply penetrating army,
nor was the country in a state of prolonged weakness.
It was merely because eunuchs usurped power,
treated the enemy lightly and trifled with military affairs,
went against the will of the multitude, and drove them to their deaths,
thus leading to the defeat of the grand army,
the displacement of the imperial carriage,
and the bodies of high ministers and officials being left on the wilderness.
Indeed, at the beginning, they could not prevent the expedition,
and after setting out, they could not make it return early,
resulting in a pile of bodies on the frontier,
which did not help avert the defeat.
However, at a time of desperate rout,
where "when the sovereign is disgraced, his ministers die,"
their resolve differed from clinging to life,
and thus they cannot be criticized for their impaired courage.
Collated Notes

Biographies (Lièzhuàn, 列傳) Fifty-six: Chén Xún (陳循) (Xiāo Zī, 蕭鎡), Wáng Wén (王文), Jiāng Yuān (江淵), Xǔ Bīn (許彬), Chén Wén (陳文), Wàn Ān (萬安) (Péng Huá, 彭華), Liú Xǔ (劉珝) (Zǐ Yǔn, 子鈗), Liú Jí (劉吉), Yǐn Zhí (尹直).
Chén Xún (陳循),
courtesy name Dézūn (德遵),
was from Táihé (泰和).
In the thirteenth year of Yǒnglè (永樂) (1415), he achieved first place in the imperial examinations for jinshi.
He was appointed Hanlin Xiūzhuàn (翰林修撰).
He was well-versed in court rituals and precedents.
When the emperor went to Běijīng (北京),
he was ordered to take books from the Mìgé (秘閣) to the temporary imperial residence,
and subsequently remained in attendance there.
In the first year of Hóngxī (洪熙) (1425), he was promoted to Shìjiǎng (侍講).
In the early Xuāndé (宣德) (1426) reign,
he was ordered to serve at Nángōng (南宮),
offering counsel daily.
He was granted a residence west of Yùhé Qiáo (玉河橋),
and never failed to accompany the emperor on his tours.
He was promoted to Shìjiǎng Xuéshì (侍講學士).
In the first year of Zhèngtǒng (正統) (1436), he concurrently served as Jīngyán Guān (經筵官).
After a long time,
he was promoted to Hànlín Yuàn Xuéshì (翰林院學士).
In the ninth year (1444), he entered the Wényuān Gé (文淵閣)
and presided over state affairs.
Initially,
the court deliberated on memorials and proposals from officials and common people across the empire,
all presided over by the three Yángs (三楊).
By this time, Róng (榮) and Shìqí (士奇) had already passed away.
Xún (循), Cáonài (曹鼐), and Mǎ Yú (馬愉) were in the Grand Secretariat (Nèigé, 內閣).
The Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù, 禮部) requested to follow old precedents.
The emperor, considering Yáng Pǔ (楊溥) old and
deserving of leisure,
ordered Xún (循) and others to participate in deliberations.
The following year, he was promoted to Hùbù Yòushìláng (戶部右侍郎),
concurrently serving as Xuéshì (學士).
During the Tǔmù (土木) incident,
people's hearts were filled with fear.
Xún (循), being in the central government,
had many of his suggestions adopted.
He was promoted to Hùbù Shàngshū (戶部尚書),
with his concurrent posts remaining as before.
When Yěxiān (也先) attacked the capital,
he requested an imperial decree for elite cavalry from various borders to enter the capital for defense,
and to send urgent dispatches to the Western Regions (Huífān, 回番) to confuse the enemy.
The emperor followed all his plans.
In the second year of Jǐngtài (景泰) (1451),
he was involved in a dispute with fellow villagers over a burial ground for his wife,
and was deemed in the wrong by successive Circuit Censors (Xún'àn Yùshǐ, 巡按御史).
Xún (循) repeatedly impeached them.
Gěishìzhōng (給事中) Lín Cōng (林聰) and others vehemently argued for Xún's (循) guilt.
The emperor agreed with Cōng (聰)
but let Xún (循) go unpunished.
Xún (循) had originally risen to prominence due to his talent and prestige,
but by this time, his long-standing reputation was ruined.
In the twelfth month of the second year (1451), he was promoted to Shàobǎo (少保) and concurrently Wényuān Gé Dàxuéshì (文淵閣大學士).
The emperor wanted to replace the crown prince,
but inwardly feared the Grand Secretaries.
In advance, he bestowed one hundred taels of silver upon Xún (循) and Gāo Gǔ (高穀),
and half that amount upon Jiāng Yuān (江淵), Wáng Yīníng (王一寧), and Xiāo Zī (蕭鎡).
When the imperial edict for deliberation was issued,
Xún (循) and the others dared not argue,
and he was further granted the concurrent title of Tàizǐ Tàifù (太子太傅).
Soon after, an imperial order from the crown prince granted silver and silk to all officials.
A month later,
the emperor again bestowed fifty taels of gold upon Xún (循) and the other five,
and promoted him to Huágài Diàn Dàxuéshì (華蓋殿大學士),
with his concurrent post at Wényuān Gé (文淵閣) remaining unchanged.
Xún's (循) son Yīng (英) and Wáng Wén's (王文) son Lún (倫) were rejected in the Shùntiān (順天) provincial examination,
and together they framed the examiners Liú Yǎn (劉儼) and Huáng Jiàn (黃諫),
for which they were impeached by Gěishìzhōng (給事中) Zhāng Níng (張寧) and others.
The emperor did not punish them either.
When Yīngzōng (英宗) was restored,
Yú Qiān (于謙) and Wáng Wén (王文) were executed,
Xún (循) was flogged one hundred times
and exiled to Tiělǐng Wèi (鐵嶺衞).
During the Xuāndé (宣德) reign,
Censor Zhāng Kǎi (張楷) presented a poem that displeased the emperor.
Xún (循) said,
"He too is loyal and loving,"
and thus Kǎi (楷) was released.
Censor Chén Zuò (陳祚) submitted a memorial that angered the emperor,
but Xún (循) subtly interceded for him,
saving him from death.
In Jǐngdì's (景帝) reign,
he once compiled the deeds of ancient emperors,
titled Qínzhèng Shuǎdiǎn (勤政耍典),
and presented it to the throne.
When there was heavy snow in Hénán (河南) and north of the Jiāng (江),
causing wheat seedlings to die,
he requested to release funds from the treasury to buy wheat seeds for the poor.
He often offered timely advice
that was worth adopting.
However, having held high office for a long time,
his harsh and impetuous nature was scorned by scholars.
His severe condemnation
was due to people like Shí Hēng (石亨),
not the emperor's intention.
After Hēng (亨) and his associates fell,
Xún (循) sent a memorial from his place of exile to plead his case,
stating:
"The imperial throne
is inherently Your Majesty's.
At the time when Heaven and the people were returning to you,
all officials prepared the imperial carriage and grand music,
respectfully proceeded to the Southern Palace (Nánnèi, 南內),
and requested Your Majesty to preside over court.
Not only would this have avoided alarming the imperial palace,
but it would also have served as an example for all under Heaven for ten thousand generations.
However, Hēng (亨) and his associates, through temporary opportunism,
did not conceive of this plan,
and ultimately brought disaster upon themselves.
I have served for successive reigns,
and have made minor contributions,
but was truly victimized by them.
I only ask Your Majesty to show compassion and understanding."
An edict released him as a commoner,
and he died a year later.
In the Chénghuà (成化) reign,
when Yú Qiān's (于謙) case was cleared,
Xún's (循) son cited this precedent to request a posthumous honor,
and thus his official title was restored and a sacrifice was granted.
Xiāo Zī
(courtesy name Mèngqín), from the same county.
He became a *Jìnshì* in the second year of Xuāndé.
He was waiting for an appointment at home.
In the eighth year,
the Emperor ordered Yáng Pǔ to jointly select *Jìnshì* from three examinations,
and twenty-eight men were chosen as *Shùjíshì*,
with Zī as the leader.
When Emperor Yīngzōng ascended the throne,
he was appointed *Biānxiū*.
In the third year of Zhèngtǒng, he was promoted to *Shìdú*.
After a long time,
he succeeded Lǐ Shímiǎn as *Guózǐjiān Jìjiǔ*.
In the first year of Jǐngtài, he resigned due to old age and illness.
After his resignation was approved,
Bāo Xiàng, the Supervisor of the Imperial Academy, led the students of the six colleges to repeatedly petition for him to stay.
The Emperor approved their memorial.
The next year, he concurrently held his original office and that of *Hànlín Xuéshì*,
and entered the Wényuāngé with Vice Minister Wáng Yīníng.
The year after that, he was promoted to Right Vice Minister of Revenue,
with his concurrent office remaining as before.
When the discussion about changing the heir arose,
Zī said:
"Not changing the appointed heir
is forbidden for a hegemon,
how much more so for the celestial court!"
He was not listened to.
He was promoted to Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
When the *Huányǔ Tōngzhì* was completed,
he was promoted to Minister of Revenue.
When the Emperor was unwell,
the ministers discussed restoring Emperor Xiànzōng to the Eastern Palace.
Lǐ Xián privately asked Zī,
and Zī said:
"Once retired,
it cannot be done again."
When Emperor Yīngzōng was restored,
he was stripped of his official status.
He died in the eighth year of Tiānshùn.
In the Chénghuà era,
his office was restored and a memorial sacrifice was granted.
Zī was profoundly learned
and his writings were elegant.
However, his nature was suspicious and jealous,
and he often retreated when faced with matters.
Wáng Wén
(courtesy name Qiānzhī),
originally named Qiáng,
was from Shùlù.
He became a *Jìnshì* in the nineteenth year of Yǒnglè.
He was appointed Censor.
He maintained integrity and upheld the law,
and was praised by the Censor-in-Chief Gù Zuǒ.
Towards the end of Xuāndé,
he was ordered to handle the case of the demon rebel Zhāng Pǔxiáng in Zhāngdé.
His return report pleased the Emperor,
and he was granted his current name.
When Emperor Yīngzōng ascended the throne,
he was transferred to Shǎnxī Provincial Surveillance Commissioner.
He suffered the death of his father,
was ordered to attend the funeral,
and then recalled to duty.
In the first month of the third year of Zhèngtǒng, he was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief
and pacified Níngxià.
In the fifth year, he was summoned to be Minister of the Grand Court of Revision.
The next year, he and Vice Minister of Justice Hé Wényuān reviewed criminal cases in the capital,
and soon after he was transferred to Right Censor-in-Chief.
In the ninth year, he was sent out to inspect border affairs in Yánsuí and Níngxià,
and impeached and punished the crimes of Dūdu Xīanshì Wáng Zhēn and Dūdu Tóngzhī Huáng Zhēn of the Dìngbiān camp for losing discipline,
whereupon the border regions were pacified.
The next year, he replaced Chén Yì as Grand Defender of Shǎnxī.
When Píngliáng, Líntáo, and Gǒngchāng suffered famine,
he memorialized to exempt their taxes.
Soon after, he was promoted to Left Censor-in-Chief.
He served in Shǎnxī for five years,
maintaining peace and order without disturbance.
In the first year of Jǐngtài,
he was summoned to preside over the Censorate.
Wén was a shrewd and calculating person,
with a stern and cold demeanor.
When he served with Chén Yì,
they never spoke beyond a single bow.
All the censors feared him like a god,
and no court official dared to approach him with private matters,
yet he was actually soft and ingratiating inside.
Initially,
when investigating the case of Grand Court of Revision Junior Minister Xuē Xuān,
he sought to cater to Wáng Zhèn's wishes
and wanted to sentence Xuān to death.
By this time, when dealing with the illegal actions of the eunuch Jīn Yīng's household servants,
he only punished the servants.
Censors Lín Cōng and others impeached Wén and Yì for fearing power and fostering evil,
and they were imprisoned.
Both confessed,
and were then pardoned.
In the sixth month of the second year,
Scholar Jiāng Yuān memorialized that judicial officials often made unjust rulings.
Wén and Minister of Justice Yú Shìyuè requested to be dismissed,
and also stated that Yuān had privately approached them with a matter,
which they refused,
hence they were slandered.
The Emperor disregarded both.
In the spring of the third year,
he was promoted to Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
At this time, Chén Yì was pacifying Shǎnxī,
and was about to return,
and Wén was to replace him.
All the censors jointly memorialized to keep Yì,
so Vice Minister Gěng Jiǔchóu was appointed instead.
When there was an earthquake in Nánjīng,
and severe flooding in the north of Jiāng and Huái,
he was ordered to inspect.
He and the nine ministers of Nánjīng discussed and submitted nine beneficial measures for the military and civilians.
He also said that the famine between Xú and Huái was severe,
while Nánjīng had surplus reserves,
so he requested to release all the grain from the granaries in Xú and Huái for relief and loans,
and to divert the grain that should have been sent to Nánjīng to Xú and Huái
to make up for the deficit.
All were approved.
At this time,
Chén Xún was most trusted,
and was stubborn and self-willed.
Gāo Gǔ and Xún were incompatible,
and Gǔ, seeing Wén's strong and resolute nature,
thought of bringing him into government to counter Xún,
so he memorialized to increase the number of Grand Secretariat members.
Xún nominated his fellow townsman Xiāo Wéizhēn,
and Gǔ then nominated Wén.
Wén also received assistance from the eunuch Wáng Chéng,
so an imperial edict was issued to employ Wén.
Soon after returning to court from Jiāng and Huái,
he was appointed Minister of Personnel,
concurrently *Hànlín Yuàn Xuéshì*,
and served in the Wényuāngé.
This was the first time a second-rank minister entered the Grand Secretariat, beginning with Wén.
Soon after, he suffered the death of his mother,
but was ordered to forgo mourning as before.
Although Wén was introduced by Gǔ,
Gǔ was slow and deliberate,
while Xún was decisive,
so Wén allied with Xún instead of Gǔ.
Later, because of his son Lún,
he wanted to undermine the examination officials,
and then acted on Gǔ's advice and stopped.
From then on, the two never got along.
In the third month of the fifth year,
when Jiāng and Huái suffered severe flooding,
he was again ordered to inspect.
Previously, the grain from the four prefectures of Sū, Sōng, Cháng, and Zhèn
was commuted at four *shí* for one *liǎng* of silver,
which the people found convenient.
Later, the Ministry of Revenue resumed collecting rice,
ordering it to be transported to Xú and Huái,
totaling over 1.1 million *shí*.
It generally took three *shí* to deliver one *shí*,
causing some families to go bankrupt.
Wén used his discretionary power to suspend this,
and also opened granaries to relieve over 3.6 million famine victims.
At this time, there was much banditry due to famine,
and Wén arrested 200 bandits from Chángzhōu, including Xǔ Dàoshī.
Wishing to exaggerate his achievement,
he charged them with treason.
Grand Court of Revision Minister Xuē Xuān exposed the falsity of the charge.
Censor Wáng Zhèn requested a joint investigation by court officials,
which resulted in sixteen bandits being executed according to law,
while the rest were released.
Upon his return, he was promoted to Junior Guardian,
and concurrently Grand Academician of the Dōnggé.
He was further promoted to Grand Academician of the Jǐnshēndiàn,
still concurrently holding the Dōnggé position.
Originally,
when Emperor Yīngzōng was to return,
court officials discussed the ceremony for receiving him.
Wén, then Censor-in-Chief,
sternly said:
"Do you gentlemen believe that the Former Emperor will truly return?
Will Yěxiān not demand land and gold and silks, but suddenly send the Emperor back?"
The crowd, who had always feared Wén,
were all startled and unable to decide, and dispersed.
When the discussion of changing the heir arose,
Wén was the first to obey the command.
When Emperor Jǐng was unwell,
the ministers wanted to request the return of Prince Yí to the Eastern Palace.
Wén said:
"How do we know who the Emperor intends?"
Then he memorialized to request an early selection of a worthy successor.
Because of this, it was widely rumored both inside and outside the court that Wén, along with the eunuch Wáng Chéng and others, plotted to summon the heir of Xiāng.
When Yīngzōng 復位 (was restored to the throne),
he immediately had Yú Qiān and Wén Yú apprehended within the court.
Censors impeached Wén Yú and others for plotting to install an external prince.
He was ordered to be interrogated in court.
Wén Yú strongly argued, saying:
"Summoning a princely vassal requires a gold tablet and tally;
sending someone requires a horse plaque.
The Imperial Household Department and Ministry of War can verify this."
His words were forceful and spirited.
When Shěn Jìng, an administrator of the imperial carriage, questioned him,
no evidence was found.
Court officials then implicated Qiān and Wén Yú, asserting that their plot to summon Jìng was not yet settled,
and had Wén Yú executed in the marketplace along with Yú Qiān.
All his sons were exiled to the frontier.
Jìng was also charged with knowing about the rebellion and deliberately letting it go,
his death sentence was commuted,
and he was exiled to Tiělǐng.
Everyone knew Wén Yú's death was a wrongful accusation.
Because of his usual harsh and envious nature,
and because his proposal to welcome the emperor back and restore the heir apparent did not please public opinion,
he died unjustly
without the people mourning him.
In the early Chénghuà reign,
his son was pardoned and returned.
Soon after, he was reinstated in office,
granted the title of Tàibǎo,
and given the posthumous name Yìmǐn.
Lún
changed his name to Zōngyí.
He became a *jìnshì* in the early Chénghuà reign.
He successively served as a *lángzhōng* in the Ministry of Revenue,
and was dispatched to manage provisions in Liáodōng.
When the eunuch Wāng Zhí went on an eastern expedition,
he praised Zōngyí for his diligence in supervising provisions,
and he was promoted to Tàipú Shàoqīng.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
he successively rose to the position of Nánjīng Lǐbù Shàngshū.
He died
and was given the posthumous name Ānjiǎn.
Jiāng Yuān,
courtesy name Shìyòng,
was from Jiāngjīn.
In Xuāndé fifth year, he became a *shùjíshì*
and was appointed *biānxiū*.
In Zhèngtǒng twelfth year, an imperial decree appointed him along with Dù Níng, Péi Lún, Liú Yǎn, Shāng Lù, Chén Wén, Yáng Dǐng, Lǚ Yuán, Liú Jùn, and Wáng Yù, a total of ten people,
to study in the Dōnggé,
with Cáo Nài and others as their teachers.
When the Prince of Chéng acted as regent,
Xú Yǒuzhēn advocated moving the capital south.
The eunuch Jīn Yīng reprimanded him and drove him out,
whereupon he stumbled past the Zuǒyèmén.
Yuān happened to enter
and asked him.
Yǒuzhēn said:
"It is because my proposal to move south was not accepted."
Thereupon Yuān entered
and strongly put forward a strategy of resolute defense.
He was thus recognized by the Prince,
and was exceptionally promoted from Shìjiǎng to Xíngbù Yòushìláng.
When Yěxiān approached the capital,
Yuān was ordered to participate in military affairs with Commander Sūn Táng.
In Jǐngtài first year, he was dispatched to inspect the passes of Zǐjīng, Dàomǎ, and Báiyáng,
and oversaw the repair of the Yànmén Pass with Commander-in-chief Tóngzhī Wēng Xìn.
That autumn, he was appointed to his original post concurrently as Hànlín Xuéshì,
entering the Grand Secretariat to participate in important state affairs.
Soon after, he was transferred to Hùbù Shìláng,
retaining his concurrent duties as before.
In the sixth month of the following year, due to celestial phenomena, he submitted three proposals: one,
to solidify relations with the various guards of Duǒyán and Chìjīn,
to form eastern and western bulwarks;
one,
to exempt the remaining conscripts of the capital army
to support their livelihoods;
one,
to prohibit accusations against the remaining partisans of Wáng Zhèn,
to avoid injustice and abuse.
An imperial edict ordered that all be followed.
In the second month of the next year, he was transferred to the Lìbù,
still concurrently serving as a scholar.
That spring,
the capital experienced prolonged rain and snow.
Yuān submitted a memorial saying:
"Liú Xiàng of Han said,
'All rain is yin,
and snow is the yin of rain.'
In mid-spring, *shàoyáng* is dominant,
yet cold air threatens it.
Divination methods consider this a sign of excessive and cruel punishments by the ruler.
Your Majesty's benevolence and might are widespread,
and you have always pardoned errors and excused crimes.
I fear that officials are not executing duties properly,
and injustices may not have been redressed.
Moreover, a clear edict was issued earlier
to exempt one-third of the land tax for Jǐngtài second year.
Now, however, orders are being reissued to collect it,
which means the court itself loses great trust among the people,
and their grievances are suppressed,
truly stemming from this."
The Emperor then ordered the judicial authorities to redress grievances and injustices,
questioned the Ministry of Revenue for violating the edict,
imprisoned Minister Jīn Lián,
and eventually exempted the tax as per the edict.
After the Eastern Palace was changed,
he was given the additional title of Tàizǐ Shàoshī.
The ineffective Governor of Sìchuān and Censor-in-chief Lǐ Kuāng
was dismissed based on Yuān's words.
He was recalled to office after mourning his mother.
Earlier, when the Attendant-Lecturer Ní Qiān suffered a loss,
Yuān recommended Qiān as a lecturer,
and Qiān thus ended his mourning.
At this point, Censor Zhōu Wén stated that Yuān's recommendation of Qiān
was precisely to lay the groundwork for his own future.
As the matter had already been dealt with, the Emperor
did not pursue it,
but decreed that from then on, officials suffering a loss should not be indiscriminately protected.
In the spring of the fifth year,
Shāndōng, Hénán, and Jiāngběi suffered famine.
He was ordered to go and comfort the people with the Earl of Píngjiāng, Chén Yù.
Yuān submitted over a dozen proposals concerning military and civilian expediency both before and after this.
He also requested the construction of a moon-shaped wall in Huái'ān to protect the Chángyíng Granary,
and the expansion of Xúzhōu's eastern wall to protect the Guǎngyùn Granary.
All were discussed and implemented.
At that time, Jiāngběi was repeatedly struck by famine,
and grain shipments for Huái'ān that were en route
were all recalled by Yuān for relief.
However, the transport soldiers took advantage of the situation to embezzle and consume the grain.
When this was reported,
a censor was dispatched to investigate the facts.
Yuān was impeached
and was to be stripped of his office.
Court officials argued that Yuān had acted expediently
and should not be punished.
The Emperor pardoned him.
As the Grand Secretaries were not harmonious,
Chén Xún and Wáng Wén were particularly harsh and selfish.
Yuān was fond of discussion,
and was often suppressed by his colleagues,
which made him feel unhappy and agitated.
Coincidentally, when Minister of War Yú Qiān was on sick leave,
an edict ordered one person to be recommended to assist in the ministry's affairs.
Yuān secretly wished to get the position.
Xún and others feigned recommending Yuān but secretly ordered Shāng Lù to draft a memorial,
showing him
the four characters "Shí Bīng Jiāng Gōng" (石兵江工).
Yuān, being nearby, did not know.
When the edict was issued,
Minister of Works Shí Pú was transferred to the Ministry of War,
and Yuān was appointed to replace Pú,
which greatly disappointed Yuān.
When Yīngzōng was restored to the throne,
he was banished to Liáodōng along with Chén Xún and others,
and died not long after.
Initially,
when Huáng Yǔ memorialized to change the heir apparent,
some suspected Yuān was behind it.
Qiū Jùn said:
"This is easy to distinguish;
Guǎngxī paper is different from capital paper."
They requested to see the memorial,
and indeed it was Guǎngxī paper,
thus his wrongful accusation was cleared.
In the early Chénghuà reign,
his office was restored.
Xǔ Bīn,
courtesy name Dàozhōng,
was from Níngyáng.
He became a *jìnshì* in Yǒnglè thirteenth year.
He was appointed *shùjíshì*
and then *jiǎntǎo*.
At the end of the Zhèngtǒng reign,
he successively rose to Tàicháng Shàoqīng,
concurrently serving as Hànlín Dàizhào,
and supervisor of the Sìyí Guǎn.
When the Retired Emperor was about to return,
Bīn was dispatched to Xuānfǔ to welcome him.
The Retired Emperor ordered him to write an edict confessing his faults and a decree instructing his officials,
and to offer sacrifices to the officials and soldiers who died at Tǔmù.
Through this, he gained the Retired Emperor's trust,
and upon his return, was promoted to his original post as Tàicháng Qīng.
When Shí Hēng and others plotted to restore the Retired Emperor,
they informed Bīn of their plan.
Bīn introduced Xú Yǒuzhēn to them.
The details are in Xú Yǒuzhēn's biography.
When Yīngzōng was restored to the throne,
he was promoted to Lǐbù Zuǒshìláng,
concurrently serving as Hànlín Yuàn Xuéshì,
and entered to serve in the Wényuāngé.
Not long after,
he was resented by Shí Hēng
and dispatched as Nánjīng Lǐbù Yòushìláng.
Immediately after his departure,
he was demoted to Shǎnxī Cānzhèng.
Upon arrival, he requested retirement and left.
When Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
he was ordered to retire as a Shìláng,
and died soon after.
Bīn's xìng was frank,
fond of making friends,
but unable to choose them well.
For a time, many dissolute scholars frequented his gate.
In his later years, he participated in grand governance,
and was about to shut his doors and decline guests.
However, his guests resented his change in demeanor,
and competed to spread slanders,
so that he ultimately could not maintain his position.
Chén Wén,
courtesy name Ānjiǎn,
was a native of Lúlíng.
He placed first in the provincial examination,
and passed the imperial examination in the first year of Zhèngtǒng (1436),
receiving the appointment of compiler.
In the twelfth year (1447), he was ordered to study in the Dōnggé.
After his term expired,
he was promoted to lecturing academician.
In the second year of Jǐngtài (1451),
Grand Secretary Gāo Gǔ recommended Wén for his talent,
and he was promoted to Right Administration Commissioner of Yúnnán.
Guìzhōu had been at war for successive years,
and Yúnnán supplied its provisions,
causing the people to suffer from transport duties.
Wén ordered merchants to transport on behalf of the people,
and the people paid twice the cost,
which everyone found convenient.
The annual tax quota was over 700,000 *shāo*,
from which official salaries were drawn.
However, those in charge embezzled funds,
and officials sometimes did not receive their salaries for several years.
Wén investigated all these matters,
and the tax revenue daily increased.
Yúnnán produced silver,
and people used silver for trade.
The value of silver was three times that in the interior.
Those registered as government laborers were exempt from service;
they paid three times the amount in silver,
and those who paid did not find it burdensome.
Wén said:
"Although it is so,
does it not harm integrity?"
He reduced it,
and again ordered a reduction by one-third of the registered laborers.
His reputation grew daily,
and he was promoted to Left Administration Commissioner of Guǎngdōng,
but did not take office due to mourning for his mother.
After Yīngzōng was restored to the throne,
he one day said to his attendants:
"Where is the senior compiler who attended me previously?"
His attendants replied that it was Wén,
and he was immediately summoned to be a Grand Secretary.
He requested to complete his mourning period,
but was not granted permission.
He entered to attend the Crown Prince in lectures.
When Academician Lǚ Yuán died,
the emperor asked Lǐ Xián who could replace him.
Xián replied:
"Kē Qián can."
He went out and told Wáng Áo.
Áo said:
"Chén Wén is next in line by seniority,
how can he be suppressed?"
The next day,
Xián entered to see the emperor,
and spoke as Áo had suggested.
In the second month of the seventh year (1461), Wén was promoted to Right Vice Minister of Rites concurrently with Academician,
and entered the Grand Secretariat.
Once Wén entered,
he often obstructed Xián to distinguish himself,
saying:
"I am not one of those you recommended."
Lecturing Academician Qián Pǔ lived in a neighboring house to Wén,
and their friendship was very joyful.
Pǔ had often tutored imperial eunuchs,
and many of his students were powerful and favored.
When they came to visit,
they would surely invite Wén to drink with them.
When Yīngzōng was gravely ill,
Crown Prince's eunuch Wáng Lún privately went to Pǔ to discuss matters,
but did not summon Wén.
Wén secretly observed them.
Lún said:
"The emperor is unwell.
How about the Crown Prince taking a consort?"
Pǔ said:
"One should act according to the emperor's last will."
Soon after, Yīngzōng died,
and Xián was to draft the imperial edict.
Wén rose and snatched his brush, saying:
"No need,
someone has already drafted it."
He then spoke of Lún and Pǔ's plan,
who wanted to dismiss Xián and replace him with Pǔ,
and to replace Minister of War Mǎ Áng with Vice Minister of War Hán Yōng.
Xián was enraged,
and exposed their plot.
At this time, Xiànzōng had just ascended the throne.
Lún, believing he should become the Director of the Directorate of Ceremonial,
was extremely arrogant.
During Yīngzōng's grand burial,
Lún wore mourning clothes over sable,
which the emperor saw and disliked.
Grand Eunuch Niú Yù feared that Lún would overshadow him,
and so listed Lún's crimes,
and had him expelled.
Pǔ was demoted to Magistrate of Shùndé County,
and Yōng to Surveillance Commissioner of Zhèjiāng.
Those implicated in the matter,
including Shùntiān Prefect Wáng Fú,
Vice Commissioner of the Office of Transmission Zhào Áng,
Earl of Nánníng Máo Róng,
Commanders Mǎ Liáng, Fèng Zōng, Liú Jù,
and Deputy Commander of the Imperial Bodyguard Mén Dá,
were all demoted.
Yōng was also someone Wén had long disliked.
Wén was transferred to Left Vice Minister of Personnel,
concurrently managing imperial lectures.
In the first year of Chénghuà (1465),
he was promoted to Minister of Rites.
Luó Lún criticized Xián for resuming office during mourning.
Wén felt inwardly ashamed,
and secretly helped Xián to expel Lún,
which further earned him the contempt of contemporary public opinion.
In the spring of the third year (1467),
the emperor ordered Minister of Revenue Mǎ Áng, Censor-in-chief Lín Cōng, and Supervising Secretaries Pān Lǐ and Chén Yuè to reorganize the capital garrisons.
Wén memorialized that imperial eunuchs must cooperate,
before old abuses could be eradicated,
and thus recommended Grand Eunuch Huái Ēn.
The emperor agreed.
Upon the completion of the *Veritable Records of Yīngzōng*,
Wén was granted the title of Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
concurrently Grand Academician of the Wén Yuān Gé.
He died in the fourth year (1468).
He was posthumously granted the title of Junior Tutor,
and given the posthumous name Zhuāngjìng.
Wén had always prided himself on his talent,
and had achieved considerable success outside the capital.
Many scholars and officials hoped for his advancement.
However, once he held a prominent position in the court,
his actions became vulgar and base.
After participating in grand governance,
he made no significant proposals.
After court was dismissed, he would invite guests and old friends, arrange banquets,
and exclusively focus on seeking favors.
He was by nature quick-tempered,
and would always retaliate for even the slightest grievance.
After Xián died,
Wén acted even more wantonly,
greatly losing his integrity and reputation.
After his death,
Minister of Rites Scribe Lù Yuānzhī and Censor Xiè Wénxiáng both memorialized that Wén should not have received such a fine posthumous name.
The emperor, however, because the matter had already been carried out,
did not permit it.
Wàn Ān,
courtesy name Xúnjí,
was a native of Méizhōu.
He was tall with a prominent face,
his eyebrows and eyes as if carved.
He appeared broad-minded but was deeply scheming.
He passed the imperial examination in the thirteenth year of Zhèngtǒng (1448).
He was appointed a probationary compiler,
then compiler.
In the early Chénghuà period,
he was repeatedly promoted to Left Vice Minister of Rites.
In the fifth year (1469), he was appointed concurrently Academician of the Hànlín Academy,
and entered the Grand Secretariat to participate in state affairs.
His contemporary, Grand Secretary Lǐ Tài,
was the adopted son of the imperial eunuch Yǒngchāng,
and younger than Ān.
Ān treated him as an elder brother,
and gained his favor.
Since they were colleagues,
whenever there was a promotion,
Tài would always recommend Ān above himself.
When it was time to select Grand Secretaries,
Tài again recommended Ān, saying:
"You go first,
I am not worried about not getting there eventually."
Thus, Ān was able to enter the Grand Secretariat, but Tài suddenly died of a sudden illness.
Ān had no academic learning.
Once he was in power,
he focused daily on making requests and recommendations,
and befriended various eunuchs as his internal support.
At that time, Consort Wàn Guìfēi enjoyed the emperor’s favor above all others in the inner palace.
Ān, through the palace attendants, sent her diligent regards,
calling himself a nephew.
The consort had often been ashamed of her lack of distinguished family background,
and when she heard this, she was overjoyed.
Her brother, Wàn Tōng, a commander of the Imperial Guards,
then visited Ān’s home several times, treating him as a family member.
Ān’s wife, née Wáng, had her mother come from Bóxīng.
Wáng asked her mother,
“When our family was poor in the past,
my younger sister was given to someone as a concubine.
Where is she now?”
Her mother replied,
“I only remember she was given to the Wàn compiler from Sìchuān.”
Tōng suspected it was Ān,
and when he inquired, it turned out to be Ān’s concubine.
From then on, the two families’ women frequently visited each other.
Tōng’s wife, being registered within the Forbidden City,
could enter and exit freely,
allowing Ān to know all the activities in the palace,
thus strengthening his position.
Assistant Minister Xíng Ràng and Libationer Chén Jiàn were of the same graduating class as Ān but did not get along with him.
Ān fabricated a case,
and had both their names removed.
In the winter of the seventh year,
a comet appeared in Tiān Tián,
violating Tài Wēi.
Many court officials said that the relationship between the emperor and his ministers was estranged,
and it was appropriate to summon senior ministers to discuss governance.
Grand Secretaries Péng Shí and Shāng Lù strongly urged this.
The director of the Directorate of Ceremonial then agreed to summon them for an audience on the day the emperor held court,
adding,
“When you first meet,
the rapport will not yet be established,
so do not speak too much;
wait for another day.”
As they were about to enter,
they were again reminded of the initial instructions.
During this audience,
Shí spoke of the fearsome heavenly anomaly,
and the emperor said,
“I already know;
you gentlemen should do your best.”
Shí then said,
“Yesterday, a censor submitted a memorial
requesting a reduction in the salaries of metropolitan officials,
which would inevitably cause dissatisfaction among military officials.
I beg that it be restored to the old system.”
The emperor approved.
Ān then prostrated himself, shouted “Long live the Emperor!”
and wished to leave.
Shí and Lù, having no choice,
all kowtowed and withdrew.
The eunuch joked to the court officials,
“You lot often complain about not being summoned for an audience.
But when you are seen,
all you know is to shout ‘Long live the Emperor!’”
This was laughed about at the time,
and they were called
“Long Live Grand Secretaries.”
From then on, the emperor no longer summoned senior ministers for audiences.
Later, Yǐn Zhí entered the Grand Secretariat
and wanted to request an audience with the emperor to discuss matters.
Ān stopped him, saying,
“In the past, Lord Péng requested an audience,
and when one word was not agreeable,
he immediately kowtowed and shouted ‘Long live the Emperor,’
thus becoming a laughingstock.
Now, we speak fully on every matter,
and the grand eunuchs select and report it.
The emperor never disapproves,
which is far better than a face-to-face audience.”
His sycophancy and lack of understanding of the greater good,
as well as his skill in shifting blame to others, were like this.
In the ninth year, he was promoted to Minister of Rites.
After a long time,
he was transferred to the Ministry of Revenue.
In the thirteenth year, he was granted the title of Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
and shortly after, he was made Grand Secretary of the Wényuān Pavilion.
When Emperor Xiàozōng left the imperial residence [to ascend the throne],
he was promoted to Minister of Personnel and Grand Secretary of the Jǐnshēn Hall,
and soon after, was additionally granted the title of Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
At this time, Péng Shí had already died,
and Shāng Lù had left due to opposing Wāng Zhí.
Those in the Grand Secretariat were Líu Xǔ and Líu Jí.
Ān was the Senior Grand Secretary,
and he formed a faction with southerners.
Xǔ, along with Ministers Yǐn Mín and Wáng Yuè, formed a faction of northerners,
and they competed with each other.
However, Xǔ was shallow and Ān was cunning and ruthless,
so Xǔ ultimately could not overcome Ān.
In the eighteenth year,
Wāng Zhí’s favor waned,
and officials requested the abolition of the Western Depot.
The emperor did not permit it.
Ān submitted a memorial again,
and it was approved.
Both inside and outside the court praised Ān for this.
After the compilation of the Wénhuá Dàxùn was completed,
he was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent and Grand Secretary of the Huágài Hall.
He was further promoted to Junior Tutor, Grand Preceptor of the Heir Apparent,
and then again to Junior Preceptor.
At this time,
there were many corrupt policies at court,
and reports of disasters and suffering from all directions came daily.
The emperor greatly believed in Taoism,
conferring the titles of Exalted Emperor upon the Golden Palace and Jade Palace True Lords,
and dispatched Ān to sacrifice at Língjì Palace.
As Lí Zīxǐng and Dèng Cháng'ēn were then being promoted,
Ān, through Péng Huá, secretly allied with them,
using them to eliminate opponents.
Consequently, Xǔ and other senior ministers such as Wáng Shù, Mǎ Wénshēng, Qín Hóng, and Gěng Yù were successively dismissed,
while Huá was promoted from Imperial Household Grandee to Assistant Minister of Personnel,
and entered the Grand Secretariat.
No court official dared to openly oppose Ān.
Huá,
a native of Ānfú,
was a younger cousin of Grand Secretary Péng Shí,
and ranked first in the metropolitan examination of Jǐngtài’s fifth year.
He was profound and had many schemes,
skilled at secretly finding people’s weaknesses,
and was compared to Ān and Zīxǐng.
He once instigated Xiāo Yànzhuāng to attack Lí Bǐng,
and also expelled Yǐn Mín and Luó Jǐng.
Everyone disliked and feared him.
The following year,
he became ill with a stroke and retired.
When Emperor Xiàozōng succeeded to the throne,
Ān drafted the imperial edict for his ascension,
forbidding censors from using rumors to pursue personal agendas,
which caused an uproar both inside and outside the court.
Censor Tāng Nài went to the Grand Secretariat.
Ān calmly said,
“This is the emperor’s intention.”
Nài immediately reported this statement to the throne,
saying that Ān suppressed criticism,
shifted blame to the emperor,
and lacked the manners of a loyal subject.
Thereupon, probationary secretary Zōu Zhì,
and censors Wén Guì and Jiāng Hóng, among others, submitted memorials one after another listing his crimes.
Before this,
there was a man from Shèxī named Ní Jìnxián,
who was roughly educated but without integrity.
He flattered Ān,
and discussed
“bedroom arts” with him daily.
Ān was fond of him,
and thus had him take the examination,
where he passed as a *jìnshì*.
He was appointed probationary secretary,
and later made a censor.
One day, the emperor found a small box of memorials in the palace,
all of which discussed “bedroom arts,”
and at the end was signed
“Your servant Ān Jìn.”
The emperor ordered eunuch Huái Ēn to carry it to the Grand Secretariat and said,
“Is this what a high minister does?”
Ān, ashamed and sweating, prostrated himself on the ground,
unable to utter a sound.
When the memorials of impeachment from the various ministers came in,
the emperor again ordered Ēn to read them to Ān.
Ān repeatedly knelt and rose, begging for mercy,
with no intention of leaving.
Ēn went directly forward and snatched his ivory tablet, saying,
“You may leave now.”
Only then did Ān, in a panic, search for a horse to return home,
requesting retirement.
He was already over seventy years old at the time,
and still looked at the Sāntái stars on the road,
hoping to be reinstated.
He died a year later,
was posthumously granted the title of Grand Preceptor,
and given the posthumous name Wénkāng.
Initially,
when Empress Xiàomù Huángtàihòu passed away,
rumors circulated within the inner court, pointing fingers at Consort Wàn Guìfēi.
When Emperor Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
Xú Xù, the county magistrate of Yútái, submitted a memorial revealing the matter.
Court officials discussed arresting and interrogating relatives of the Wàn clan who had entered and exited the palace.
Ān was terrified and did not know what to do,
saying,
“I have not been in contact with the Wàn clan for a long time.”
Líu Jí, who had an earlier marriage connection with the Wàn clan,
also felt himself in danger.
His associate Yǐn Zhí was still in the Grand Secretariat,
and together they drafted an edict to suppress the matter.
Emperor Xiàozōng was benevolent and kind,
and also chose not to pursue it,
so Ān and Jí were unharmed.
Ān was in the government for twenty years.
Every time there was an examination,
he would surely appoint his students as examiners,
and many of his sons, grandsons, nephews, and sons-in-law passed the examinations.
His son, Yì,
was the Nánjīng Minister of Rites.
His grandson, Hóngbì,
was a Hanlin Compiler.
Not long after Ān died,
Yì and Hóngbì died one after another,
and Ān ultimately had no descendants.
Liú Xǔ,
courtesy name Shūwēn,
was a native of Shòuguāng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the thirteenth year of Zhèngtǒng.
He was reassigned as a *shùjíshì*
and appointed as a Compiler.
During the Tiānshùn reign,
he successively held the position of Right Mid-Counsellor,
serving as a lecturer to the Crown Prince.
When Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
due to his former service as a palace official, he was repeatedly promoted to Grand Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
concurrently serving as a Scholarly Attendant-Lecturer,
and directly participating in daily lectures at the imperial study.
In the tenth year of Chénghuà, he was promoted to Left Vice Minister of Personnel,
continuing his role as a lecturer as before.
Whenever Xǔ delivered a lecture,
he would explain and guide repeatedly,
his words and demeanor being forthright and earnest,
making listeners feel awed.
The academician Liú Dìngzhī called him the foremost lecturer,
and Xiànzōng also held him in high regard.
The following year, an edict appointed him to concurrently hold the position of Hanlin Academician,
entering the Grand Secretariat to participate in state affairs.
The Emperor often called him
"Elder Mr. Liú from the East,"
and bestowed upon him a seal,
on which was inscribed
"Excellent counsel assists and supports."
Soon after, he was promoted to Minister of Personnel,
and further elevated to Junior Guardian of the Crown Prince and Grand Academician of the Wènyuān Pavilion.
After *Wénhuá Dàxùn* was completed,
he was promoted to Grand Guardian of the Crown Prince
and advanced to Grand Academician of the Jǐnshēn Hall.
Xǔ was frank and upright by nature.
Considering himself an old official from the imperial palace,
he would not show partiality in any matter.
When Staff Director Lín Jùn was imprisoned for impeaching Liáng Fāng and Jì Xiǎo,
Xǔ defended him before the Emperor.
When Lǐ Zīshěng and his ilk used heterodox methods to disrupt governance,
intending to destabilize the Crown Prince,
Xǔ secretly submitted a memorial to remonstrate,
which somewhat hindered their plans.
He had always held Wàn Ān in low esteem,
once denouncing Ān as unprincipled and betraying the country.
Ān accumulated resentment,
and plotted day and night to harm Xǔ.
Initially,
when Shāng Lù impeached Wāng Zhí,
Xǔ, along with Wàn Ān and Liú Jí, helped him in the dispute,
leading to the disbandment of the Western Depot.
Later,
Xǔ again defeated Wáng Yuè in court,
and Yuè retreated in shame.
Afterward, the Western Depot was re-established,
and Xǔ was unable to make any remonstrance.
By the eighteenth year,
Ān saw Zhí's favor decline,
and surmised that the Western Depot would be abolished,
so he invited Xǔ to jointly memorialize.
Xǔ declined to participate,
so Ān memorialized alone.
When the memorial was presented,
the Emperor was quite surprised that Xǔ's name was absent.
Ān secretly sent someone to accuse Xǔ of being connected with Zhí.
At that time, Xǔ's son, Zī, invited prostitutes for a private drinking party.
A local resident, Zhào Bīn, playfully composed a tune for "Master Liú,"
and someone embellished it with obscene words,
mixing it with tunes from the courtesan quarter and presenting it to the Emperor.
The Emperor was greatly angered,
and determined to remove Xǔ.
He sent the eunuch Qín Chāng to summon Ān and Jí to the West Corner Gate,
and showed them a sealed letter from the Emperor's hand.
Ān and others feigned surprise and tried to intercede.
The next day,
Xǔ submitted a memorial requesting retirement.
He was ordered to travel by post-horse,
and was generously bestowed with monthly stipends, annual servants, silver, and paper money.
In reality, it was the plot of Ān and Jí
to oust Xǔ.
At that time, there were three members in the Grand Secretariat.
Ān was greedy and cunning,
Jí was subtly malicious.
Xǔ was slightly superior,
but he liked to talk and debate,
and people regarded him as impetuous and irritable.
After Xǔ's sudden retirement,
Péng Huá and Yǐn Zhí successively entered the Grand Secretariat,
and the faction of Ān and Jí became even more entrenched.
Xǔ had initially suffered the loss of his mother,
and lived by her grave for three years.
Upon his return,
he served his father with utmost filial piety.
When his father died,
he again lived by the grave.
He died in the third year of Hóngzhì,
and was posthumously given the epithet Wénhé.
In the early Jiājìng reign,
at the request of remonstrating officials,
a shrine inscription was bestowed, reading Zhāoxián,
and an official was sent to offer sacrifices.
His son, Yǔn,
courtesy name Rǔzhōng.
When he was eight years old,
Xiànzōng summoned him for an audience,
admiring his intelligence,
and moreover, he bowed and rose according to etiquette,
so the Emperor immediately appointed him as a Drafter in the Central Secretariat.
The thresholds of the palace doors were high,
and his colleague Yáng Yīqīng often lifted him when entering and exiting.
The Emperor, fearing that his ivory tablet would be easily damaged,
ordered it to be replaced with silver.
He served in office for over fifty years,
reaching the position of Grand Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices during the Jiājìng reign,
concurrently serving as a Doctor of the Five Classics,
and still serving in the Grand Secretariat's Edict and Patent Office.
He was learned and virtuous in conduct,
and along with Liú Qǐ from Chángzhōu, he was equally well-versed in ancient history and precedents,
at the time being called
"The Two Liús."
Liú Jí,
courtesy name Yòuzhī,
was a native of Bóyě.
He became a *jìnshì* in the thirteenth year of Zhèngtǒng.
He was reassigned as a *shùjíshì*,
appointed as a Compiler,
and served as a lecturer in the imperial study.
After *Huányǔ Tōngzhì* was completed,
he was promoted to Reviser.
In the fourth year of Tiānshùn, he served as an attendant lecturer to the Crown Prince,
and returned home due to mourning.
When Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
he was summoned to compile the Veritable Records of Yīngzōng.
Upon arriving in the capital,
he submitted a memorial requesting to complete his mourning period.
This was not granted,
and he was promoted to Attendant Lecturer.
After the Veritable Records were completed,
he was transferred to Scholarly Attendant-Lecturer,
and directly participated in the imperial study lectures.
He was successively promoted to Left Vice Minister of Rites.
In the eleventh year of Chénghuà, he and Liú Xǔ were jointly appointed as Hanlin Academicians,
entering the Grand Secretariat to participate in state affairs,
and soon after, he was promoted to Minister of Rites.
When Xiàozōng left the imperial nursery,
he was promoted to Junior Guardian of the Crown Prince and concurrently Grand Academician of the Wènyuān Pavilion.
In the eighteenth year, he suffered the loss of his father,
and an imperial edict ordered his recall to office.
Jí submitted three memorials earnestly declining,
but secretly persuaded the imperial relative Wàn Xǐ to plead on his behalf,
and thus his request was not granted.
After *Wénhuá Dàxùn* was completed,
he was promoted to Grand Guardian of the Crown Prince,
and advanced to Grand Academician of the Wǔyīng Hall.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Minister of Revenue and Grand Academician of the Jǐnshēn Hall,
and soon after, he was additionally given the title of Junior Guardian and concurrently Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
When Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
the *shùjíshì* Zōu Zhì and Censor Jiāng Hóng strongly denounced Wàn Ān, Yǐn Zhí, and Jí as all being vile individuals,
who ought to be dismissed.
Jí held a deep grudge against them.
Ān and Zhí were both dismissed,
but Jí alone remained,
and his authority became even more concentrated.
Fearing that the remonstrating officials would not cease their attacks,
he then suggested super-promoting Censorate and Investigating Censor officials,
placing them in extraordinary positions.
An edict ordered the recall of those who were stagnant or retired,
and ten people, including Supervising Secretary Hè Qīn and Censor Qiáng Zhēn, had already been successively nominated for promotion.
Jí again submitted a memorial recommending them.
Among the departmental officials, only Lín Jùn was recommended.
He hoped to control the channels of remonstrance with this,
but the remonstrating officials still did not cease.
Vice Minister Zhāng Shēng,
Censors Cáo Lín and Ōuyáng Dàn,
Nánjīng Supervising Secretary Fāng Xiàng,
and Censor Chén Sōng, among others, successively impeached Jí.
Jí was greatly angered,
and had Shēng exiled.
He initiated several major prison cases,
Zhì and Xiàng were imprisoned and banished to distant places,
and Hóng was also demoted.
He further colluded with the eunuch Jiǎng Cóng,
expelling Nánjīng Censor Jiāng Wǎn and others,
leaving the Censorate vacant.
Both inside and outside the court, people looked on nervously,
and the remonstrating officials also somewhat subsided.
Initially,
Jí, Wàn'ān, and Liú Xǔ were in office during the Chénghuà reign,
when the emperor was morally lax [shī dé],
and they offered no rectification.
At that time, there was
a popular rhyme about
“three Grand Secretaries made of paper,
and six Ministers made of clay.”
By this time, seeing that Xiàozōng was benevolent and discerning,
and his colleagues Xú Pǔ and Liú Jiàn were all upright individuals,
and Jí was the senior Grand Secretary,
the two others would propose policies,
and Jí would also sign his name,
and often make upright statements,
secretly appropriating a good reputation to cover himself.
In the second month of the Hóngzhì second year (1489), there was a drought,
and the emperor ordered scholarly officials to draft a prayer for rain.
Jí and others said:
“Recently, treacherous individuals, following the old tricks of Lǐ Zīxǐng and Dèng Cháng'ēn,
seeing that the moon was in the constellation Bì,
and that the weather would soon turn cloudy and rainy,
then presented a request for prayers,
hoping for a single verification to gain advancement.
Once a path for undue influence is opened,
people will vie to talk of prayers,
seeking favor and inviting calamity.
This is truly the origin of it,
and we dare not accept the imperial decree to draft the prayer text.”
The emperor understood their intention [yì wù],
and so he stopped it.
In the fifth month, due to ominous natural phenomena, they asked the emperor to cultivate virtue and prevent minor transgressions,
being as careful at the end as at the beginning.
In the eighth month, again due to ominous natural phenomena, they presented seven proposals.
The Prince of Dài offered a sea eagle,
and Jí and others stated that the edict upon the emperor's ascension had already rejected tributes from all directions,
and begged him not to accept it.
The next year, in the third month, together with his colleagues, he memorialized:
“Your Majesty's constitution is pure and delicate,
different from the late emperor.
All banquets, entertainment, and sightseeing,
and all matters of indulgence,
should be greatly reduced.
Should any close attendants or officials request things according to the precedents of the late emperor,
they should be dismissed using the precedents of Tàizǔ and Tàizōng.
Your Majesty following the ancestral emperors would be fitting.”
When the envoy from Tǔlǔfān returned after presenting a lion,
the emperor ordered the Grand Secretariat to draft an edict [chì],
and dispatched a eunuch to escort him.
Jí and others said it was inappropriate to show excessive favor,
as it would cause the foreign barbarians to slight China.
The matter was then dropped.
Afterward, they further stated:
“The lion and other beasts [shòu],
fed two sheep daily,
would consume seven hundred and twenty annually.
Also, fifty guards and lieutenants [xiàowèi] are assigned daily,
all of which are costly and burdensome.
It would be better to cut off all food for these beasts,
and let them die naturally.”
The emperor could not adopt this.
In the twelfth month,
there was a celestial anomaly,
and they again stated:
“Recently, an inauspicious star appeared in Tiānjīn,
passed through Chǔjiù,
and approached Yíngshì.
Its omen signifies war,
famine,
and floods or droughts.
Currently, the two capital regions [liǎng jī], Hénán, Shānxī, and Shǎnxī are suffering from drought and locusts,
while Sìchuān and Húguǎng have had poor harvests.
If next year it is the same again,
we fear that bandits will rise up,
and chaos will ensue.
We humbly request Your Majesty to economize on expenditures,
cease banquets and entertainments,
repudiate slanders,
reject heterodox teachings,
devote yourself to the classics and histories,
and diligently seek the path to good governance.
Repairing the bridge at Shāhé,
producing porcelain in Jiāngxī,
and renovating the walls at Nánhǎi Zǐ
are all not urgent matters,
and should all be stopped.”
The emperor graciously accepted their advice.
The emperor, misled by his close attendants,
was quite devoted to prayers and offerings.
He issued Buddhist scriptures [jīng pái] and ordered the Grand Secretaries to compose praises,
and also to propose titles for divine generals.
Jí and others strenuously argued that heterodox beliefs should be rejected.
Jí was promoted to Junior Guardian [shǎo fù] upon the emperor's initial ascension,
concurrently serving as Grand Tutor to the Heir Apparent [tàizǐ tàishī] and Minister of Personnel [Lìbù Shàngshū].
When the Veritable Records of Xiànzōng [Xiànzōng Shílù] were completed,
he was further promoted to Junior Preceptor [shǎo shī] and Grand Academician of Huágài Hall [Huágài Diàn Dàxuéshì].
Jí had controlled the government for a long time,
and his power and influence were immense.
Initially, the emperor wholeheartedly listened and trusted him,
but later his favor somewhat declined,
yet Jí never showed any intention of leaving office.
In the fifth year (1492),
the emperor wished to enfeoff the empress's brother as a count [bójué],
and ordered Jí to draft the enfeoffment edict [gào quàn].
