Jí stated that it would only be proper if all the empress dowagers' [èrtàihòu] family members were enfeoffed.
The emperor was displeased,
and sent a eunuch to Jí's home,
hinting that he should retire,
whereupon he finally submitted a memorial to resign.
An edict bestowed upon him an imperial decree [chì],
and a post-horse carriage, as was customary.
Jí was very resourceful and cunning,
skilled at ingratiating himself,
and self-serving.
He was eager to pursue personal gain,
and was often attacked by the censors [yán lù].
He served in the Grand Secretariat for eighteen years,
and people referred to him as
“Liú Miánhuā” (Cotton Liú),
because of his resilience to criticism.
Jí suspected that this remark came from those who failed the provincial examination [xià dì jǔ zǐ],
and therefore requested that those who failed the metropolitan examination [huì shì] three times should not be allowed to participate again.
At that time, it was exactly the period for the metropolitan examination,
and candidates had already gathered in the capital.
The Ministry of Rites [Lǐbù] pleaded on their behalf.
An imperial edict temporarily permitted them to take the examination,
with the rule to be applied later.
However, after Jí was dismissed,
the rule was also not implemented.
Jí returned home,
and died a year later.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Preceptor [tàishī],
and given the posthumous name Wénmù.
Yǐn Zhí,
courtesy name Zhèngyán,
was from Tàihé.
He became a *jìnshì* in the fifth year of Jǐngtài (1454).
He was appointed a *shùjíshì* [shùjíshì],
and then granted the position of compiler [biānxiū].
In the early Chénghuà reign,
he served as a lecturer in the Imperial Lecture Hall [Jīngyán Jiǎngguān],
and participated in compiling the Veritable Records of Yīngzōng [Yīngzōng Shílù].
The chief editor [zǒngcái] wanted to abolish the imperial title of Emperor Jǐngtài,
citing Chāngyì and Gēngshǐ of the Han Dynasty as comparisons.
Zhí argued:
“In the Veritable Records, there are individuals who were initially ministers [dàchén]
and later became commoners.
When they were officials,
they were referred to as 'so-and-so official,'
and only after being dismissed were their titles changed.
For example, if a Han prince [Hàn fǔ] was demoted to commoner due to plotting rebellion,
before his rebellion,
he would still be referred to as 'Prince' or 'Uncle.'
How could one foresee his rebellion [nìjì qí fǎn]
and immediately demote him to the title of commoner?
Furthermore, Chāngyì was enthroned and deposed quickly,
whereas Emperor Jǐngtài was the lord of the ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain [zōngmiào shèjì zhǔ] for seven years.
Gēngshǐ received no mandate [wú suǒ shòumìng],
whereas Emperor Jǐngtài was formally appointed by the empress dowager [mǔhòu].
At that time, in the midst of extreme danger and crisis,
had it not been for the emperor, the capital would not have belonged to the state.
Although he committed the transgression of changing the heir [yì chǔ shī dé],
he was able to avoid being swayed by the words of Lú Zhōng and Xú Zhèn,
ultimately preserving the two empresses [liǎng gōng],
leading to the present day.
His merits and demerits are sufficient to balance each other;
it is not appropriate to remove his imperial title.”
At the time, no one could refute him.
Upon its completion,
he was promoted to Court Lecturer [shìdú],
and successively served as Academician-in-waiting [shìdú xuéshì].
In the sixth year (1470), he submitted a memorial requesting the compilation of the *Dàmíng Tōngdiǎn*,
and the continuation of *Sòng Yuán Gāngmù*.
The memorial was sent to the relevant department.
In the eleventh year (1475), he was transferred to Vice Minister of Rites [Lǐbù Yòushìláng],
which he declined,
but was not permitted to.
He mourned his father,
and after the mourning period,
he was appointed Nanjing Vice Minister of Personnel [Nánjīng Lìbù Yòushìláng],
and immediately transferred to Vice Minister of Rites [Lǐbù Zuǒshìláng].
In the spring of the 22nd year,
Wáng Zhí was summoned to assist in the Ministry of War.
The king of Zhànchéng, Gǔlái, was pressured by Ānnán,
abandoned his country, and came to seek aid.
The deliberators wanted to send him back,
but Wáng Zhí said:
"He is in distress and has come to us;
if we were to drive him back to his country,
that would be killing him.
It is proper to send a high minister to immediately inquire,
and then handle the matter as appropriate."
The emperor's edict followed this advice,
and he ordered the Censor-in-Chief Tú Yōng to go.
The鎮巡 officials of Guìzhōu reported that the Miáo had rebelled
and requested to dispatch troops.
The court deliberation was about to approve this.
Wáng Zhí said that they were stirring up trouble to gain merit
and should not be trusted.
Officials were ordered to investigate,
and indeed there was no alert.
In the ninth month of that year, he was transferred to the Ministry of Revenue and concurrently served as a Hanlin Academician,
entering the Grand Secretariat.
A month later,
he was promoted to Minister of War
and given the additional title of Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince.
Wáng Zhí was intelligent, knowledgeable,
and skilled in court procedures,
but he was eager for advancement.
He was arrogant and jealous by nature,
and did not restrain himself,
thus he was at odds with Minister of Personnel Yǐn Mín.
Wáng Zhí initially coveted the position of Vice Minister of Rites,
but Yǐn Mín recommended someone else.
Wáng Zhí obtained it through a secret imperial decree.
The next day, he met Yǐn Mín at court
and raised his tablet in thanks.
Yǐn Mín said:
"You are what is called 'chosen by the emperor's heart'."
From then on, their resentment deepened.
Later, he was in the south for eight years,
unhappy and unfulfilled.
He instructed his associates Wàn Ān and Péng Huá to conspire for his recall to the capital,
but Yǐn Mín always opposed it.
All the other court officials also feared Wáng Zhí
and were glad he was in the south.
When the Vice Ministers of War (Left and Right) were to be recommended,
the Ministry of Personnel listed Hécóng and eight others.
The imperial edict appointed Hécóng,
but Wáng Zhí, with the efforts of Wàn Ān, Péng Huá, and Lǐ Zīxǐng,
was recalled by a secret imperial decree.
At this point, he sought revenge,
colluding with Lǐ Zīxǐng and others,
implicating Yǐn Mín and his son in an offense.
He also fabricated charges to remove Mǐn Guī, the巡撫 of Jiāngxī,
causing a clamor of injustice in public opinion.
Yuán Qīng, a director in the Ministry of Punishments,
was Wàn Ān's private associate
and also favored by the eunuch Guō Rùn.
When investigating a case in Zhèjiāng,
he rode roughshod over the high officials,
and Minister of Personnel Lǐ Yù detested him.
Upon his return,
he was immediately appointed Prefect of Shàoxīng.
Yuán Qīng, fearing this,
submitted several memorials seeking a different appointment.
Lǐ Yù severely criticized his crimes
and had him imprisoned.
Wàn Ān and Guō Rùn appealed to Wáng Zhí
who spoke to Lǐ Zīxǐng for him,
obtaining a secret imperial decree to pardon him
and appoint him Prefect of Yúnyáng.
When Emperor Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
the *jìnshì* Lǐ Wénxiáng,
Censors Tāng Nài, Jiāng Hóng, Miào Chú,
and *shùjíshì* Zōu Zhì, among others, submitted numerous memorials impeaching Wáng Zhí.
The Supervising Secretary Sòng Cóng and Censor Xǔ Bīn stated that Wáng Zhí, from his initial appointment as Vice Minister to his entry into the Grand Secretariat,
had relied on connections and climbed through "secret imperial decrees."
The emperor then despised his character
and ordered him to retire.
In the 9th year of Hóngzhì, he submitted a memorial congratulating the emperor on his birthday
and also, as the Crown Prince was of age to leave his quarters,
presented the *Chénghuá Zhēn* (Admonitions on Receiving Glory),
citing the precedent of Grand Guardian Huáng Huái from the previous dynasty,
hoping for an imperial audience.
The emperor rejected it.
He died during the Zhèngdé reign
and was posthumously named Wénhé.
The encomium says: The *Yì* [Jīng] states that when the gentleman is within and the petty man without,
it is *Tài* (Peace);
when the gentleman is without and the petty man within,
it is *Pǐ* (Obstruction).
How much more so for the responsibility of the Grand Secretariat,
upon which all officials gaze!
Chén Xún and the others below him,
though not great villains,
had cruel and envious hearts,
and were bent on indulging their private interests.
They associated with those who agreed with them,
and were jealous of those who disagreed.
When allied, they supported each other;
when jealous, they ostracized each other.
As for Wàn Ān and Liú Jí, who colluded with favored intimates
and clung to their positions disgracefully,
it was fortunate that many of their colleagues were worthy
and worked together to mend and rectify things.
But their sordid deeds were glaringly evident,
the mark of petty men,
how could they be concealed!
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 57: Gāo Gǔ, Hú Yíng, Wáng Zhí
Gāo Gǔ,
courtesy name Shìyòng, was from Xīnghuà, Yángzhōu.
He became a *jìnshì* in the 13th year of Yǒnglè.
Selected as a *shùjíshì*,
he was appointed Secretary of the Grand Secretariat.
When Emperor Rénzōng ascended the throne,
he was reassigned as Sīzhíláng of Chūnfāng,
and soon promoted to Hanlin Lecturer.
When Emperor Yīngzōng ascended the throne,
the imperial lectures were opened,
and Yáng Shìqí recommended Gāo Gǔ, along with Miáo Zhōng, Mǎ Yú, and Cáo Nài, as lecturers.
In the 10th year of Zhèngtǒng, he was promoted from Hanlin Academician Lecturer to Right Vice Minister of Works,
entering the Grand Secretariat to manage state affairs.
In the early days of Jǐngtài,
he was promoted to Minister
and concurrently Hanlin Academician,
managing the affairs of the Grand Secretariat as before.
When Emperor Yīngzōng was about to return,
the welcoming ceremony was meager.
Gōng Suìróng, a Chiliarch, sent a letter to Gāo Gǔ,
detailing that the ceremony should be grand,
citing the precedent of Emperor Sùzōng of Táng welcoming the Retired Emperor.
Gāo Gǔ brought it to court in his sleeve,
showing it to all the court officials and saying:
"Even a military man knows propriety,
how much more so a scholar-official!"
Everyone praised his words.
Hú Yíng and Wáng Zhí wanted to report it.
Gāo Gǔ said:
"The deliberation on welcoming the emperor back has been ongoing,
and the emperor's will has long been undecided.
If this letter is presented,
making the emperor aware that the court and populace are of one mind,
it would also be a help."
The Censor-in-Chief Wáng Wén disagreed.
Soon after, a censor reported it.
When questioned where it came from,
Gāo Gǔ replied:
"From my possession."
He then presented a memorial earnestly pleading according to Gōng Suìróng's words.
Although the emperor did not follow it,
he also did not punish him.
In the second year, he was promoted to Grand Guardian and Grand Academician of the Dōnggé.
When the Crown Prince was changed,
he was given the additional title of Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince
and two salaries.
When Yìngtiān and Fèngyáng suffered disasters,
he was ordered to offer sacrifices to the three imperial tombs
and relieve the impoverished people.
In the seventh year, he was promoted to Grand Academician of Jǐnshēndiàn,
still concurrently holding the Dōnggé position.
There were seven people in the Grand Secretariat,
and their opinions often clashed.
Gāo Gǔ was upright and honest,
and his opinions were just.
Wáng Wén, recommended by Gāo Gǔ,
often undermined him.
Gāo Gǔ repeatedly requested to be relieved of state affairs,
but it was not permitted.
When the Supervising Secretary Lín Cōng offended powerful figures and was sentenced to death,
Gāo Gǔ strongly interceded,
and he received a light reprimand.
Chén Xún and Wén Gòu implicated examiners Liú Yǎn and Huáng Jiàn.
The emperor ordered the Ministry of Rites to review the examination papers with Gāo Gǔ.
Gāo Gǔ strongly argued that Liú Yǎn and others were impartial,
and furthermore said:
"It is already improper for noble offspring to compete for advancement with common scholars,
how much more so to be dissatisfied with fate
and wish to use this to frame the examiners?"
The emperor then granted Chén Xún and Wén Gòu's sons successful placement,
only dismissing Lín Tǐng.
The matter was concluded.
When Emperor Yīngzōng was restored,
Chén Xún and Wén Gòu were all executed or exiled.
Gāo Gǔ pleaded illness.
Emperor Yīngzōng considered Gāo Gǔ a virtuous elder
and told his court officials:
"Gāo Gǔ, in the Grand Secretariat, regarding the discussion of welcoming the imperial carriage and the affairs of the Southern Palace,
often supported me.
Let him be granted gold, silk, and court robes,
and provided with a relay boat to return home."
Soon after, he was again bestowed with an imperial edict of commendation.
Gǔ
had already left his post, he shut his gate and
refused guests. If anyone asked about affairs during the Jǐngtài and Tiānshùn reigns,
he would never respond.
He died in the first month of the fourth year of Tiānshùn,
at the age of seventy.
Gǔ had a beautiful appearance and bearing,
and enjoyed simplicity.
Though he reached the position of a high official,
he only had a dilapidated cottage and meager fields.
In the early Chénghuà reign,
he was posthumously granted the title of Tàibǎo
and given the posthumous name Wényì.
Hú Yíng,
courtesy name Yuánjié,
was from Wǔjìn.
He was born with white hair,
which turned black after a full month.
In the second year of Jiànwén, he passed the imperial examination to become a Jìnshì
and was appointed Bīngkē Jǐshìzhōng.
In the first year of Yǒnglè, he was promoted to Hùkē Dūjǐshìzhōng.
When Emperor Huì died in the fire,
some said he had escaped,
and many old officials had followed him,
which made the Emperor suspicious.
In the fifth year, Yíng was dispatched to distribute the Emperor's own writings,
and also to seek the immortal Zhāng Lātā.
He traveled throughout all the prefectures, counties, and townships in the realm,
secretly investigating the whereabouts of Emperor Jiànwén.
Yíng thus remained outside for the longest time,
not returning until the fourteenth year.
Wherever he went,
he also occasionally reported on the hardships of the people.
When his mother died, he requested to return home,
but was not permitted.
He was promoted to Lǐbù Zuǒshìláng.
In the seventeenth year, he was again sent out to inspect the prefectures of Jiāng, Zhè, Hú, and Xiāng.
In the twenty-first year, he returned to court
and rushed to pay respects to the Emperor in Xuānfǔ.
The Emperor had already retired to bed,
but hearing of Yíng's arrival,
he quickly rose and summoned him.
Yíng reported everything he had heard,
and did not leave until the fourth watch of the night.
Before Yíng arrived,
there were rumors that Emperor Jiànwén had fled to sea.
The Emperor had dispatched several eunuchs, including Zhèng Hé, to sail overseas to the Western Ocean.
It was only then that his suspicions were finally dispelled.
The Crown Prince was regent in Nánjīng,
and the Prince of Hàn spread rumors slandering the Crown Prince.
The Emperor reassigned Yíng to Nánjīng,
and ordered him to investigate the matter.
Upon arrival, Yíng
secretly submitted a memorial in seven points concerning the regent,
stating that he was sincere, respectful, filial, and diligent, with no ulterior motives.
The Emperor was pleased.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
he summoned Yíng to serve as Xíngzài Lǐbù Shìláng.
Yíng presented ten matters,
emphatically arguing that establishing the capital in Běijīng was inconvenient
and requesting a return to the Southern Capital,
to avoid the troubles of north-south transportation and supply.
The Emperor praised and accepted all his suggestions.
Later, hearing that Yíng had once submitted a secret memorial,
he became suspicious
and did not ultimately summon him.
He was transferred to Taìzǐ Bīnkè,
concurrently serving as Nánjīng Guózǐ Jìjiǔ.
When Xuānzōng ascended the throne,
he was again promoted to Lǐbù Zuǒshìláng.
The following year, he came to court
and was retained at the Xíngzài Lǐbù,
soon after being promoted to Shàngshū.
When the Prince of Hàn rebelled,
Yíng, along with Yáng Róng and others, advocated for a personal expedition.
When the rebellion was suppressed,
he was handsomely rewarded.
The following year, he was granted a residence outside Cháng'ān Yòumén,
given two gatekeepers,
and four silver seals.
On his birthday,
a banquet was held at his residence.
In the fourth year, he was ordered to concurrently manage affairs of the Zhānshìfǔ.
In the sixth year,
when Zhāng Běn died,
he also concurrently led the Xíngzài Hùbù.
At that time, national expenditures gradually increased,
and Yíng worried that the treasury would be insufficient.
When an edict to remit taxes was issued,
he often obstructed it.
The Emperor once sternly admonished him,
but his favor and treatment did not diminish.
The Emperor once hosted an informal banquet for Yíng, Yáng Shìqí, Xià Yuánjí, and Jiǎn Yì,
saying:
“The realm is at peace,
and you four gentlemen are responsible for it.”
When Yīngzōng ascended the throne,
he issued an edict to reduce extravagant spending.
Yíng consequently memorialized to reduce tribute goods
and to dismiss four to five hundred non-Buddhist monks below the rank of Fǎwáng,
greatly saving on unnecessary expenses.
In the fifth year of Zhèngtǒng,
there was a disaster in Shānxī.
An edict was issued to implement lenient relief measures,
but then an order came to purchase materials.
Yíng submitted a memorial arguing that imperial edicts should be trustworthy.
He also stated that military banners and camps sought
appointments, thereby disturbing the people,
and suggested they should be abolished.
All were approved.
The seal of the Xíngzài Lǐbù was lost,
and an edict was issued not to question it,
but to recast it.
After some time,
it was lost again,
and he was impeached and imprisoned.
Soon after,
the seal was recovered,
and he was reinstated.
In the ninth year,
at the age of seventy,
he requested to retire,
but was not permitted.
When Yīngzōng was captured in the north,
officials gathered and wept at court,
and some proposed moving the capital south.
Yíng said:
“Emperor Wén established the imperial tombs here,
showing his descendants a plan that could not be uprooted.”
He agreed with Vice Minister Yú Qiān,
and only then did officials inside and outside the court resolve to stand firm.
When Jǐngdì ascended the throne,
Yíng was promoted to Tàizǐ Tàifù.
When Yáng Shàn was sent as an envoy to Yěxiān,
Yíng said that the former Emperor had been in captivity for a long time
and should be sent food and clothing as an attachment,
but this was not reported.
When the former Emperor was about to return,
the Lǐbù was ordered to prepare the welcoming ceremony.
Yíng and others deliberated, suggesting that the Lǐbù should welcome him at Lónghǔtái,
the Jǐnyī Wèi should prepare the imperial carriage to welcome him at Jūyōngguān,
all officials should welcome him outside Tǔchéng,
all generals should welcome him at Jiàochǎngmén,
the former Emperor should enter through Āndìngmén,
proceed to Dōng'ānmén,
and sit facing south at Dōngshàng Běimén.
After the Emperor paid his respects,
and all officials paid their respects,
the former Emperor would enter the great palace in the southern city.
When the deliberation was presented,
an imperial decree ordered that a sedan chair and two horses should welcome him at Jūyōngguān,
and upon reaching Āndìngmén, he should switch to the imperial carriage,
with the rest as proposed.
Jǐshìzhōng Liú Fú and others said the ceremony was too meager.
The Emperor replied:
“I honor my elder brother as Tàishàng Huángdì;
there can be no greater honor.
If Fú and others still say it is too meager,
what is their intention?
The Lǐbù should convene officials to investigate thoroughly.”
Yíng and others said:
“The intention of the various officials is not ulterior;
they merely wish for Your Majesty to show deep affection for your kin.”
The Emperor said:
“Yesterday, I received a letter from the Tàishàng Huáng,
explicitly stating that the welcoming ceremony should be simplified and reduced.
How can I go against it?”
The officials then dared not speak further.
At that time, Commander Gōng Suìróng wrote a letter to Grand Secretary Gāo Gǔ,
suggesting that the welcome should be more substantial,
and detailing the precedent of Emperor Sùzōng of Táng welcoming the former Emperor.
Gǔ kept it in his sleeve and brought it to court,
sharing it with Wáng Zhí and others.
Zhí and Yíng wished to present it to the Emperor,
but were obstructed by Censor-in-Chief Wáng Wén.
However, Jǐshìzhōng Yè Shèng ultimately presented it.
Shèng's colleague Lín Cōng then impeached Zhí, Yíng, Gǔ, and others,
stating that as crucial ministers,
they should report everything they heard,
and should not secretly discuss matters in private.
An edict was issued to demand the letter.
Yíng and others then submitted the letter,
also stating:
“The ceremony of Emperor Sùzōng welcoming the former Emperor
can certainly be emulated today.
Your Majesty should personally welcome him outside Āndìngmén,
and dispatch ministers to welcome him at Lónghǔtái.”
The Emperor was displeased and said:
“Just follow my orders;
there is no need for contentious changes.”
Shànghuáng arrived,
residing in the Nánchénggōng Palace.
Hú Yíng requested the emperor to lead his officials to attend court at Yán'ānmén on the New Year's Day of the following year,
but this was not granted.
On Shànghuáng's Wànshòujié festival,
Hú Yíng requested to let all officials offer congratulations at Yán'ānmén,
which was also not granted.
In the first month of the third year, he and Wáng Zhí were both promoted to Shǎofù.
When the Crown Prince was changed,
he was additionally granted the concurrent title of Tàizǐ Tàishī.
Wáng Wén detested Lín Cōng.
Wáng Wén brought charges against him,
wishing to kill him.
Hú Yíng refused to sign the document
and then claimed illness,
not attending court for several days.
The emperor sent Xīng'ān to inquire about his illness.
Hú Yíng replied:
"This old minister has no illness,
but hearing that Lín Cōng was to be killed,
I was greatly startled and alarmed."
Because of this, Lín Cōng was released.
When Yīngzōng was restored to the throne,
Hú Yíng, despite his illness, attended court
and then requested to retire.
He was granted an imperial letter, white silver, paper currency, and a set of robes.
Post stations were provided,
and one of his sons was given an official position in the Jǐnyīwèi
as a hereditary Zhènfǔ.
Hú Yíng served six dynasties
for nearly sixty years,
and was renowned both inside and outside the court as a venerable elder of virtue.
When he returned home,
he had three younger brothers,
all over seventy years old.
Their beards and eyebrows were white.
They gathered together in a hall,
which was then named Shòukǎi.
He passed away seven years later,
at the age of eighty-nine.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tàibǎo
and given the posthumous name Zhōng'ān.
Hú Yíng was frugal and generous,
not showing joy or anger on his face,
and was able to humble himself before others.
He served in the Lǐbù for a long time.
When presenting memorials congratulating on auspicious omens,
his official position placed his name first,
so people said he was good at flattering and accommodating.
Gōng Qiān from Nánchéng practiced many magical arts.
Hú Yíng recommended him as an astronomical student.
He also recommended the Daoist Yǎng Mígāo, who was skilled in Yin-Yang and military strategy,
to guard the border.
This was quite ridiculed at the time.
Wáng Zhí,
courtesy name Xíngjiǎn,
was from Tàihé.
His father, Bózhēn,
was invited to the capital in the fifteenth year of Hóngwǔ based on his knowledge of the classics.
At that time, over five hundred people responded to the imperial summons,
and Bózhēn's reply was ranked first.
He was appointed Probationary Qiānshì,
touring Guǎngdōng's Léizhōu.
He restored the abandoned canal at Lǚtáng
and reformed the salt administration.
When the touring officials were dismissed,
he was recalled to serve as Hùbù Zhǔshì.
After the period of mourning for his father had ended,
he did not return to official duties in time,
and was banished to reside in Ānqìng.
In the early Jiànwén period,
he was again recommended to govern Qióngzhōu.
The Lí people of Yázhōu engaged in mutual slaughter,
reported as rebellion,
and troops were about to be deployed.
Bózhēn captured the chief culprits,
and the military action was halted.
The fields of Qióng always yielded three harvests a year.
This was taxed for the military,
but the military did not collect it in a timely manner.
They waited until the people were in need,
then hastily collected it to seek profit.
Bózhēn established a schedule for them,
collecting it in three installments,
and this malpractice ceased.
After several years,
great order was achieved,
with over ten thousand migrants registered as residents.
He became anxious to return home
and died there.
Wáng Zhí was dignified and serious in his youth,
and, despite his family's poverty, studied diligently.
He passed the imperial examination in the second year of Yǒnglè as a Jìnshì,
and was then appointed Shùjíshì.
He, along with Zēng Qǐ, Wáng Yīng, and twenty-five others, studied in the Wényuángé.
The emperor admired his writing
and summoned him to the Nèigé,
tasking him with drafting documents.
Soon after, he was appointed Xiūzhuàn.
He served Rénzōng and Xuānzōng,
and was successively promoted to Shǎozhànshì concurrently serving as Shìdú Xuéshì.
In the third year of Zhèngtǒng,
after the Xuānzōng Shílù was completed,
he was promoted to Lǐbù Shìláng,
retaining his title of Xuéshì.
In the fifth year, he was assigned to oversee the ministry's affairs.
Shàngshū Hú Yíng entrusted all ministerial matters to him,
and Wáng Zhí handled them as if he were already accustomed to them.
In the first month of the eighth year, he replaced Guō Jìn as Lìbù Shàngshū.
In the eleventh year,
Hùbù Shìláng Nài Héng, who was aligned with Wáng Zhèn,
fabricated charges against Lángzhōng Zhào Mǐn,
and the accusation implicated Wáng Zhí, as well as Shìláng Cáo Yì and Zhào Xīn,
all of whom were imprisoned.
The Three Judicial Offices conducted a public trial,
sentencing Nài Héng to be beheaded,
and Wáng Zhí and others to redemption from penal servitude.
The emperor pardoned Wáng Zhí and Cáo Yì,
and stripped Nài Héng and Zhào Xīn of their salaries.
When the emperor was about to personally lead an expedition against Yěxiān,
Wáng Zhí, leading the court officials, strongly advised against it, saying:
"The state maintains the most stringent border defenses.
Counsellors and fierce generals,
sturdy armor and sharp weapons,
are abundant everywhere,
both farming and guarding,
which is why there has been long-lasting peace.
Now the enemy is running rampant,
going against Heaven and reason.
Your Majesty should only secure the frontiers,
reinforce decrees,
fortify defenses and clear the fields,
and accumulate strength to await them.
This way, certain victory can be achieved,
there is no need for Your Majesty to personally lead the army
and venture far to the frontier.
Moreover, the autumn heat has not yet subsided,
the drought has not yet ended,
green grass is not abundant,
and water springs are still blocked.
Supplies for soldiers and horses are insufficient,
and warfare is dangerous.
Your ministers believe this is not advisable."
The emperor did not follow the advice
and ordered Wáng Zhí to stay and guard the capital.
When the imperial army was defeated at Tǔmù,
the great ministers collectively requested the Empress Dowager to establish the imperial son as Crown Prince
and appoint the Prince of Chéng to act as regent.
Afterward,
they urged the Prince to ascend the throne
to pacify the agitated populace.
At that time, changes arose suddenly,
and court officials repeatedly submitted proposals,
all led by Wáng Zhí.
However, Wáng Zhí considered himself inferior to Yú Qiān,
and deferred to him in every matter,
merely maintaining a composed and steady demeanor.
He was promoted to Tàizǐ Tàibǎo.
In the first year of Jǐngtài,
Yěxiān sent an envoy to discuss peace
and also requested the return of Shànghuáng.
The Lǐbù debated it without resolution.
Wáng Zhí, leading the officials, submitted a memorial stating:
"The Taishang Emperor was misled by the words of petty individuals,
rashly went forth,
and thus suffered disgrace.
Your Majesty has risen early and gone to bed late,
summoning troops from all under Heaven,
and united with your officials and the common people,
resolved to annihilate the enemy by breakfast,
to avenge the humiliation that cannot be shared under the same sky.
Now, Heaven has inspired his heart,
Yěxiān shows signs of remorse,
and has come to seek peace with us,
requesting the return of the emperor.
This is an opportunity to turn misfortune into fortune.
We hope Your Majesty will accede to his request,
send an envoy to reply,
and thereby ascertain his sincerity and loyalty, pacify and receive him,
and escort the Taishang Emperor home,
to slightly comfort the hearts of our ancestors.
Your Majesty's heavenly position is already established.
When the Taishang Emperor returns,
he will no longer oversee affairs of state.
Your Majesty only needs to honor him greatly.
Then familial bonds will be deepened and Heaven's favor will increase.
This is truly a great event of ancient and modern times."
The emperor said:
"What you and others say is indeed true.
However, five envoys have gone back and forth,
but in the end, no progress was made.
If we send an envoy again now,
and they falsely claim to be escorting the emperor back,
and come to attack the capital,
would this not be a disaster for the common people?
The treachery of the enemy is hard to trust;
let us deliberate on this further."
Soon after, an envoy from Ālā, another branch of the Wǎlà, arrived again.
Hú Yíng and others spoke on the matter again.
Thereupon, the Emperor ascended the gate of Wénhuá Diàn,
summoned all the grand ministers and censors, and instructed them on the necessity of severance.
[Zhí] directly replied:
"An envoy must be dispatched,
to avoid future regrets."
The Emperor was displeased.
Yú Qiān stepped forward to explain,
and the Emperor's anger subsided.
After the ministers withdrew,
the eunuch Xīng'ān crawled out and cried:
"If you insist on sending an envoy,
do you have people like Wén Tiānxiáng and Fù Bì?"
[Zhí] boldly declared:
"Court ministers only serve the Son of Heaven.
Having received their emolument,
how dare they shirk difficulty!"
He said it again,
his voice and expression becoming even more stern.
Xīng'ān was speechless.
It was then decided to send an envoy,
appointing Lǐ Shí and Luó Qǐ to go.
After they departed,
envoys from the Wǎlà Khagan Tuōtuō Bùhuā and Yěxiān arrived one after another,
and were about to be sent back.
The envoys told their hosts:
"The fourteen cities outside the passes of China are all ours.
When Ālā Zhīyuàn's envoy came previously,
people were still sent to accompany him.
Now, it is also essential that a grand minister accompanies us,
to ensure success."
Hú Yíng reported this,
and it was referred to a court deliberation.
[Zhí] and others strongly requested it,
so Yáng Shàn and others were sent to respond.
By the time Lǐ Shí returned,
an envoy from Yěxiān had also arrived,
fully stating Yěxiān's desire for peace.
[Zhí] and Níngyáng Hóu Chén Mào and others submitted a memorial,
requesting to send another envoy with gifts and silk to welcome back the Former Emperor,
but it was not permitted.
They submitted another memorial, saying:
"Your subjects have spoken with Lǐ Shí,
and fully understand the situation there.
The request for clothing, materials, and axes
came from the Former Emperor,
while the welcome of the imperial carriage
was Yěxiān's intention.
Previously, when envoys from Tuōtuō Bùhuā and Ālā Zhīyuàn came,
they all received a return envoy.
Now Yěxiān's envoy comes with the excuse of requesting a welcome,
yet no envoy is sent with him.
This is to distrust the enemy and invite war."
This was also not permitted.
Soon after, Lǐ Shí personally spoke to the Emperor.
The Emperor merely replied to Yěxiān's letter,
and simply ordered Yáng Shàn to welcome him back.
[Zhí] and others again submitted a memorial, saying:
"Now that the northern envoy has departed,
we wish to follow the Former Emperor's heart,
and fulfill the wishes of your subjects,
taking advantage of their regret,
to send an envoy to respond,
to plan for his return.
This is a matter to be decided without further deliberation.
Otherwise,
the will of the multitude is hard to violate,
and defying Heaven brings misfortune.
They will seize this as a pretext for war,
border affairs will become more difficult,
and the capital will not be able to rest easy."
The Emperor then ordered the ministers to choose an envoy.
[Zhí] and Chén Mào and others requested to send Lǐ Shí again.
The reply was:
"Wait until Yáng Shàn returns to discuss it."
Censors Bì Luán and others again submitted a memorial,
arguing strongly:
"Even if they come with deceit,
we go with sincerity.
Should the unexpected happen,
our military strength remains."
The Emperor ultimately did not listen.
Soon after, Yáng Shàn indeed brought the Former Emperor back.
In the second year,
Yěxiān sent envoys to pay tribute,
and also requested a return envoy.
[Zhí] repeatedly memorialized, saying:
"Border defenses are not yet repaired,
fodder and provisions are not yet accumulated,
and wounds are not yet healed.
It is advisable to comply with their request.
Send an envoy to observe their true intentions
and guide them towards good."
This was not permitted.
Before long,
Yěxiān sent cavalry to invade the passes,
using the lack of a return envoy as a pretext.
[Zhí] and the ministers again requested it,
but it was ultimately not permitted.
[Zhí] and others then submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your Majesty is keen on military training
and plans for war and defense,
truly a greatly enterprising ruler.
However, if communication is cut off,
it is hard to guarantee that they will not become bandits.
It is advisable to order the border defense officials
to send out troops for patrols.
If there is an alarm, they should take shelter;
if there is no incident, they should diligently farm.
When Your Majesty is free from official duties,
occasionally summon the supervisors and commanders of the imperial camps,
inquire about their strategies,
treat them sincerely and courteously,
and maintain their loyalty with clear rewards and punishments.
Then war and defense can be spoken of."
The Emperor said,
"Good."
The following year, in the first month, he was promoted to Shàofù.
The Emperor wished to change the Crown Prince,
but had not yet acted.
At that time, Huáng [Mǎo], the native prefect of Sīmíng, made a request for it.
The Emperor was pleased,
and referred it to the Ministry of Rites for deliberation.
Hú Yíng merely assented.
Ninety-one civil and military officials were to sign the deliberation.
[Zhí] showed reluctance.
Chén Xún dipped his brush and compelled him,
so he signed,
and the Crown Prince was indeed changed.
[Zhí] was promoted to concurrently Tàizǐ Tàishī,
and was given increased gold and silk.
He stamped his foot and sighed:
"What a major affair this is,
yet it has been ruined by a barbarian chieftain.
We are ashamed to death!"
When Emperor Jǐng became critically ill,
[Zhí], Hú Yíng, and others met with the grand ministers and remonstrating officials,
requesting to reinstate King Yí as Crown Prince,
and pushed Grand Academician Shāng Lù to draft the memorial.
Before it was submitted,
Shí Hēng, Xú Yǒuzhēn, and others staged the "Gate Seizure" (Duómén) to welcome the Former Emperor back to the throne,
and killed Wáng Wén and others.
The draft memorial remained with Yáo Kuí,
who once took it out to show Lángzhōng Lù Chǎng,
and sighed:
"This memorial could not be submitted;
it was fate."
[Zhí] then requested retirement.
He was granted an imperial letter, gold brocade, and paper money,
and provided with postal relays to return home.
[Zhí] was a man with a square face and a long beard,
of very imposing appearance.
His nature was serious,
and he rarely smiled.
However, when he interacted with people,
he was modest and humble.
He spent over twenty years in the Hànlín Academy,
and many matters concerning the compilation of ancient texts and historical records
came from his hand.
He was as famous as Wáng Yīng of Jīnqī,
and people called them
"the Two Wángs."
Based on their dwelling places, [Zhí] was called
"the Eastern Wáng,"
and Wáng Yīng was called
"the Western Wáng."
[Zhí] was next in line to enter the Grand Secretariat,
but Yáng Shìqí did not wish it.
When he later became head of the Ministry of Personnel,
he became even more incorruptible and cautious.
At that time, the practice of court officials recommending provincial grand officials had just been abolished,
and it became solely the responsibility of the Ministry of Personnel.
[Zhí] delegated responsibility to the department directors,
and strictly suppressed competition for promotion.
Whenever censors returned from provincial inspections,
he would always order them to report on the competence of their subordinates to prepare for selection and promotion,
and he was praised for selecting capable people.
His son [Mǎo] served as a Doctor in the Southern National University.
When his performance evaluation reached the ministry,
the director of personnel wanted to keep him to serve [Zhí],
but [Zhí] refused,
saying:
"Starting to violate the law from myself."
The court, considering [Zhí]'s age,
appointed Hé Wényuān as a Minister to assist him.
After Hé Wényuān left,
Wáng Áo was appointed,
so the ministry then had two ministers.
[Zhí] served as Minister for fourteen years;
his age increased,
and his reputation and virtue grew daily.
The Emperor treated him with great respect,
excusing him from daily court attendance.
When [Gāo Gǔ] was at home,
he used to join the tenants and servants in ploughing and sowing,
beating drums and singing.
His sons and grandsons took turns raising cups to offer longevity wishes,
and he would simply sigh,
“In the past, Xīyáng suppressed me,
not allowing me to work together [with others].
However, had I remained in the cabinet,
when the Emperor was restored to power,
I would certainly not have avoided the journey to Liáoyáng.
How then could I enjoy myself with you all now!”
He died in the sixth year of Tiānshùn
aged eighty-four.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tàibǎo [Grand Guardian]
and given the posthumous name Wénduān.
His son, [Gāo] Mǐn 敏, served as a Hanlin Compiler [Hànlín Jiǎntǎo 翰林檢討]
and was also renowned for his scholarship and conduct.
His great-grandson, [Gāo] Sī 思,
has his own biography.
The eulogy states: Gāo Gǔ’s purity and uprightness,
Hú Yíng’s 胡濙 generosity and magnanimity,
and Wáng Zhí’s 王直 solemnity and steadfastness
all exemplified the demeanor of great ministers.
During the period between [Emperor] Yīngzōng and [Emperor] Jǐngzōng,
when the national situation was in flux,
and people were watching for developments,
many high-ranking officials in charge of affairs would assent to prevailing opinions to curry favor.
However, Gāo Gǔ and Hú Yíng were diligently focused on the ceremony of welcoming back the Emperor,
while Wáng Zhí candidly pressed for the dispatch of envoys.
All of them firmly upheld righteous principles
and did not follow the crowd in obsequiousness.
Therefore, they were able to earn immense prestige
and maintain their integrity from beginning to end,
truly deserving to be called venerable elders.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 58: Yú Qiān 于謙 (Zǐmiǎn 子冕, Wú Níng 吳寧, Wáng Wěi 王偉)
Yú Qiān,
courtesy name Tíngyì 廷益,
was a native of Qiántáng 錢塘.
When he was seven years old,
a monk was struck by his exceptional nature and said:
“He will one day be a prime minister who saves the age.”
He passed the imperial examination as a *jìnshì* in the nineteenth year of Yǒnglè
In the early years of Xuāndé [1426-1435],
he was appointed Censor [Yùshǐ 御史].
When he presented memorials and responded to questions,
his speech was grand and fluent,
and the Emperor listened intently.
Gù Zuǒ 顧佐, as Censor-in-Chief [Dū Yùshǐ 都御史],
was very strict with his subordinates,
but he alone showed respect for Yú Qiān,
believing his talent surpassed his own.
When the Emperor’s retinue was at Lè’ān,
Gāo Xù 高煦 surrendered,
and the Emperor ordered Yú Qiān to publicly enumerate his crimes.
Yú Qiān’s words were sharp and precise,
and his voice and demeanor were stern and powerful.
Gāo Xù prostrated himself on the ground, trembling,
and pleaded for death a myriad times.
The Emperor was greatly pleased.
When the army returned,
he was rewarded on par with other high-ranking ministers.
He was dispatched to inspect Jiāngxī,
where he cleared hundreds of wrongful convictions.
He memorialized about the harm caused to the populace by imperial guards and officials in various places in Shǎnxī,
and an imperial edict was issued to dispatch censors to apprehend them.
The Emperor recognized Yú Qiān’s capacity for great responsibility.
Coincidentally, new Right Vice Ministers [Yòu Shìláng 右侍郎] were appointed for various ministries to serve as Provincial Governors [Xúnfǔ 巡撫].
The Emperor personally wrote Yú Qiān’s name and handed it to the Ministry of Personnel [Lìbù 吏部],
promoting him exceptionally to Right Vice Minister of War [Bīngbù Yòu Shìláng 兵部右侍郎]
and Governor of Hénán and Shānxī.
Upon arriving at his post, Yú Qiān
travelled lightly on horseback throughout his jurisdiction,
interviewing elders
to investigate what reforms and improvements were needed at the time,
and immediately submitted memorials detailing them.
He made several submissions each year;
even minor floods or droughts
were reported immediately.
In the sixth year of Zhèngtǒng
“Currently, Hénán and Shānxī each have several million *shí* 石 of accumulated grain.
I request that each year in the third month,
the prefectures, sub-prefectures, and counties report households experiencing food shortages,
and then distribute supplies accordingly.
Firstly, beans and sorghum;
secondly, millet and wheat;
thirdly, rice.
Upon the autumn harvest, they shall repay the government,
with exemptions for the elderly, sick, and those too poor to repay.
When county officials’ terms are complete and they are due for transfer,
if their emergency grain reserves are insufficient,
they shall not be allowed to leave their posts.
Furthermore, supervisory officials should inspect this regularly.”
An edict was issued to implement this.
Areas near the Yellow River in Hénán
were sometimes breached.
Yú Qiān ordered the construction of thick dikes and barriers,
setting up pavilions at intervals,
each with a head
responsible for supervising repairs.
He also ordered the planting of trees and digging of wells,
so that elms and willows lined the roads,
and no one on the path would suffer from thirst.
Dàtóng, isolated beyond the frontier,
was not reached by the inspectors of Shānxī, so he memorialized for a separate censor to govern it.
He confiscated all private lands cultivated by frontier generals
to convert them into official military farms [guāntún 官屯],
to provide for border defense.
His authority and benevolence spread,
and all bandits hiding in the Tàiháng Mountains fled.
After nine years in office,
he was promoted to Left Vice Minister [Zuǒ Shìláng 左侍郎],
receiving a second-rank stipend.
Initially,
the Three Yángs (Yáng Shìqí 楊士奇, Yáng Róng 楊榮, Yáng Pǔ 楊溥) were in the government
and greatly esteemed Yú Qiān.
Yú Qiān’s memorials
would be submitted in the morning and approved in the evening,
all through the sponsorship of the Three Yángs.
However, whenever Yú Qiān came to the capital for discussions,
he arrived with an empty purse,
which inevitably disappointed the powerful and influential.
By this time,
the Three Yángs had already died,
and the eunuch Wáng Zhèn 王振 was in power.
Coincidentally, there was a censor whose name was similar to Yú Qiān’s
who had once offended Wáng Zhèn.
When Yú Qiān came to court,
he recommended Assistant Administrators [Cānzhèng 參政] Wáng Lái 王來 and Sūn Yuánzhēn 孫原貞 to succeed him.
Lǐ Xī 李錫, Commissioner of the Office of Transmission [Tōngzhèng Shǐ 通政使], following Wáng Zhèn’s instructions,
impeached Yú Qiān, alleging that he resented not being promoted for a long time
and presumptuously recommended others to succeed him.
He was sent to the judicial authorities for sentencing to death
and imprisoned for three months.
Later, Wáng Zhèn realized his mistake,
and he was released,
demoted to Assistant Minister of the Court of Judicial Review [Dàlǐ Sì Shàonqīng 大理寺少卿].
Officials and common people from Shānxī and Hénán submitted petitions before the palace gate,
numbering in the thousands, requesting Yú Qiān be retained,
and the Princes of Zhōu and Jìn also spoke on his behalf,
so Yú Qiān was reinstated as Governor.
At that time, over two hundred thousand displaced people from Shāndōng and Shǎnxī had settled in Hénán seeking food.
Yú Qiān requested that accumulated grain from Hénán and Huáiqìng prefectures be distributed to relieve them.
He also memorialized to order the Provincial Administration Commissioner [Bùzhèng Shǐ 布政使] Nián Fù 年富 to settle the populace,
grant them land, and provide them with oxen and seeds,
and have village elders oversee them.
He served for nineteen years in total,
both within and outside the capital;
when he suffered the loss of parents, he was allowed to return home for mourning
and then reinstated.
In the thirteenth year
The following autumn,
Yěxiān 也先 launched a major invasion,
and Wáng Zhèn compelled the Emperor to personally lead the expedition.
Yú Qiān and Minister Kuàng Yě 鄺埜 strongly remonstrated,
but were not heeded.
Kuàng Yě followed to manage military affairs,
while Yú Qiān was left to handle matters of the ministry.
When the Emperor’s carriage was captured at Tǔmù,
the capital was greatly shaken,
and no one knew what to do.
Prince of Chéng [Chéng Wáng 郕王] was appointed regent,
and ordered his ministers to deliberate on war or defense.
Xu Chéng 徐珵, Lecturing Historian [Shìjiǎng 侍講], claimed that the celestial phenomena indicated change
and advocated moving the capital south.
Yú Qiān sternly declared:
“Those who speak of moving south
deserve to be beheaded!
The capital is the foundation of the empire;
once it moves, the great affair will be lost.
Do you not recall the Southern Song’s crossing of the river?”
The Prince agreed with his words,
and the decision to defend was settled.
At that time, the capital’s elite armor and cavalry were all lost,
and the remaining exhausted troops numbered less than a hundred thousand.
People were terrified,
and no one, from top to bottom, had a firm resolve.
Yú Qiān requested the Prince to issue an edict recalling the training armies from the two capitals (Nanjing and Beijing) and Hénán,
the coastal defense forces from Shāndōng and Nánjīng,
and the grain transport armies from north of the Jiāng River and various prefectures in Běijīng,
to immediately proceed to the capital.
He then planned and deployed them sequentially,
and people’s hearts gradually settled.
He was then promoted to Minister of War [Bīngbù Shàngshū 兵部尚書].
As Chéngwáng was temporarily presiding over the court,
the court officials petitioned for the extermination of Wáng Zhèn's clan.
However, Mǎ Shùn, one of Zhèn's partisans,
always shouted at the censors.
Thereupon, Grand Secretary Wáng Hóng struck Shùn in court,
and the crowd followed suit.
The court ranks fell into great disorder,
and the imperial guards' shouts were tumultuous.
The King, fearful, wanted to rise,
but Qiān pushed through the crowd, went straight to him, and supported him, telling him to stop.
He then advised the King to declare:
"Shùn and his accomplices deserve death;
no further discussion is needed."
The crowd then quieted down.
Qiān's robes and sleeves were completely torn in the process.
Upon exiting the Zuo Yèmén,
the Minister of Personnel, Wáng Zhí, held Qiān's hand and sighed, saying:
"The nation truly relies on you, my lord.
Even a hundred Wáng Zhí today could do nothing!"
At that time,
everyone, high and low, greatly relied on Qiān,
and Qiān, with determination, took the security of the state upon himself.
Initially,
the grand ministers, worried that the country had no ruler,
with the Crown Prince still young,
and the invaders approaching,
requested the Empress Dowager to enthrone Chéngwáng.
The King, startled, declined repeatedly.
Qiān spoke aloud, saying:
"We, your ministers, are truly concerned for the state,
not for private gain."
The King then accepted the mandate.
In the ninth month,
Jǐngdì was enthroned.
Qiān was summoned for an audience,
and he passionately wept as he memorialized, saying:
"If the enemy succeeds [in keeping the Emperor hostage],
they will certainly hold the Imperial Carriage [the former Emperor] hostage,
and this will inevitably make them look down upon China,
and they will advance southward.
I request that all border garrison commanders be ordered to work together to defend and repel them.
The capital's military equipment is almost depleted;
it is advisable to quickly raise civilian militias from different routes,
and order the Ministry of Works to repair weapons and armor.
Dispatch Grand Commanders Sūn Táng, Wèi Yǐng, Zhāng Jué, Zhāng Yí, and Léi Tōng to lead divisions to guard the nine gates' strategic locations,
and set up camps outside the city walls.
Censor-in-Chief Yáng Shàn and Grand Secretary Wáng Hóng should oversee this,
and move residents living near the city walls into the city.
As for the accumulated grain in Tōngzhōu,
order the imperial army to personally go to the passes to collect it,
and use the surplus rice as payment for them,
so as not to abandon it and supply the enemy.
Civil officials like Xuān Ní
should be appointed as巡撫 Xúnfǔ (Grand Coordinators).
Military officials like Shí Hēng, Yáng Hóng, and Liǔ Pǔ
should be appointed as generals.
As for military matters,
I will personally take charge;
if I fail, punish me for my crime."
The Emperor deeply accepted his advice.
In the tenth month, Qiān was ordered to supervise all the military camps.
But Yěxiān, holding the former Emperor captive, broke through the Zǐjīng Pass and marched straight in,
threatening the capital.
Shí Hēng proposed consolidating forces, fortifying walls, and wearing out the enemy.
Qiān disagreed,
saying:
"How can we show weakness
and make the enemy despise us even more?"
He quickly dispatched various generals,
leading an army of 220,000,
to array their forces outside the nine gates: Grand Commander Táo Jǐn at Āndìngmén,
Earl of Guǎngníng Liú Ān at Dōngzhímén,
Earl of Wǔjìn Zhū Yīng at Cháoyángmén,
Grand Commander Liú Jù at Xīzhímén,
Marquis of Zhènyuǎn Gù Xīngzǔ at Fùchéngmén,
Commander Lǐ Duān at Zhèngyángmén,
Grand Commander Liú Déxīn at Chóngwénmén,
Commander Tāng Jié at Xuānwǔmén,
while Qiān himself, with Shí Hēng, led Vice General Fàn Guǎng and Wǔ Xīng to array outside Dèshèngmén,
to confront Yěxiān.
He entrusted matters of the Ministry to Vice Minister Wú Níng,
and had all city gates closed,
personally supervising the battle.
He issued an order:
if a general at the front abandoned his troops and retreated first,
that general would be beheaded.
If troops abandoned their general and retreated first,
the rear ranks would behead the front ranks.
Thus, the generals and soldiers knew they must fight to the death,
and all obeyed orders.
Vice Generals Gāo Lǐ and Máo Fúshòu repelled the enemy north of Zhāngyìmén,
capturing one of their commanders.
The Emperor was pleased,
and ordered Qiān to select elite troops to garrison the drill grounds for deployment as needed,
and further commanded eunuchs Xīng Ān and Lǐ Yǒngchāng to manage military affairs together with Qiān.
Initially,
Yěxiān, having penetrated deep,
considered the capital could be taken overnight;
but upon seeing the imperial army in strict formation,
his morale slightly faltered.
The traitor eunuch Xǐ Níng incited him to invite ministers to welcome the Imperial Carriage [the former Emperor],
demanding gold and silk in the millions.
He further invited Qiān, Wáng Zhí, Hú Yíng, and others to discuss.
The Emperor did not permit it,
and Yěxiān's morale further dropped.
On Gēngshēn day,
the invaders scouted Dèshèngmén.
Qiān ordered Hēng to set an ambush in an empty house,
and dispatched a few cavalry to lure the enemy.
The enemy came in ten thousand cavalry to press upon them;
Vice General Fàn Guǎng fired gunpowder weapons,
and the ambush rose and attacked them in unison.
Yěxiān's brother, Bólúo, and Píngzhāng Mǎo Nàhái were killed by cannon fire.
The invaders turned to Xīzhímén;
Grand Commander Sūn Táng defended against them,
and Hēng also sent reinforcements,
whereupon the invaders retreated.
Vice General Wǔ Xīng attacked the invaders at Zhāngyìmén,
and together with Grand Commander Wáng Jìng, they checked their vanguard.
The invaders were about to retreat,
but several hundred cavalry of inner officials, eager for glory,
raced forward on horseback.
The formation broke,
and Xīng was killed by a stray arrow.
The invaders pursued to the earthen wall;
residents climbed onto roofs,
shouting and throwing bricks and stones at the invaders,
their clamor shaking the heavens.
Wáng Hóng and Fúshòu arrived as reinforcements,
and the invaders then retreated.
After a standoff of five days,
Yěxiān's invitations had not been answered,
and the battle was unfavorable;
he knew he could ultimately not achieve his goal,
and furthermore heard that the armies coming to the Emperor's aid were approaching,
fearing his retreat route would be cut off.
So he took the former Emperor and went west via Liángxiāng.
Qiān ordered his generals to pursue them,
returning upon reaching the pass.
For his merits,
Qiān was promoted to Shàobǎo [Grand Protector],
and concurrently supervised all military affairs.
Qiān said:
"Many fortifications around the capital [a sign of trouble]
is a shame for high officials;
how dare I seek meritorious rewards!"
He firmly declined,
but it was not granted.
He then increased troops to guard the prefectures and subprefectures of Zhēn, Bǎo, Zhuó, and Yì,
and requested that a grand minister be stationed in Shānxī
to prevent the invaders from invading southward.
In the third month of Jǐngtài's first year (1450),
General-in-Chief Zhū Qiān reported that twenty thousand enemies were besieging Wànquán,
and an imperial edict appointed Fàn Guǎng as General-in-Chief to defend against them.
Later, the invaders retreated.
Qiān requested that troops be stationed at Jūyōng,
to sally forth from the pass and annihilate the invaders if they came,
and retreat to the capital for provisions when they left.
Xǔ Guì, a Participator in Administration at Dàtóng, reported
that three people from Yǐběi had arrived at the garrison,
wishing the court to send envoys to make peace.
Qiān said:
"Previously, Commander Jì Duó and Yuè Qiān were sent,
but Yěxiān subsequently invaded.
Later, Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review Wáng Fù and Vice Minister Zhào Róng were sent,
but returned without seeing the former Emperor.
It is clear that peace cannot be relied upon.
Moreover,
we and they cannot coexist under the same heaven;
by principle, peace is not possible.
If by some chance we make peace and they make insatiable demands,
acceding will exhaust us,
and refusing will cause trouble;
thus, peace is not feasible.
As a armored official,
to be so timid,
how can you confront the enemy?
The law dictates punishment."
He issued a strongly worded rebuke.
From then on, all border generals advocated fighting and defending,
and none dared to speak of making peace.
Yú Qiān's nature was upright and unyielding.
When he encountered things that were not to his liking,
he would often beat his chest and sigh, saying:
“This ardent blood,
where on earth shall it be spilled!”
He somewhat looked down upon the soft and weak ministers, and the veteran noble relatives,
which made him quite contemptuous of them,
and increased the number of those who resented him.
Moreover, he never supported the peace negotiations,
and although the Retired Emperor (Tàishàng Huáng) was indeed able to return because of this,
he was not pleased.
Xú Chéng was rebuked by Yú Qiān
for advocating moving the capital south.
By this time, Xú Chéng had changed his name to Yǒu Zhēn,
and gradually gained prominence.
He often gnashed his teeth at Yú Qiān.
Shí Hēng had originally been dismissed from his post for losing a battle,
but Yú Qiān petitioned for his pardon and re-employment.
Shí Hēng commanded ten camps,
and fearing Yú Qiān, he could not act as he pleased,
so he also disliked Yú Qiān.
After the victory at Déshèng,
Shí Hēng’s merit was not inferior to Yú Qiān's, and he obtained the title of hereditary marquis.
Feeling inwardly ashamed,
he then submitted a memorial recommending Yú Qiān's son, Miǎn.
An imperial decree summoned him to the capital,
but he declined,
which was not permitted.
Yú Qiān said:
“The state has many affairs,
and a loyal subject should not consider personal favors.
Moreover, Hēng holds the position of a great general,
yet I have not heard of him recommending a single obscure talent,
or promoting a lowly soldier from the ranks,
to assist the military and the state.
To recommend only my son,
is this in accordance with public righteousness?
Regarding military achievements,
I firmly prevent opportunism
and would never dare to exploit my son for unmerited rewards.”
Shí Hēng was again greatly enraged.
Commander Zhāng Yuè, who lost a battle during the campaign against the Miao people,
was impeached by Yú Qiān.
He, along with the eunuch Cáo Jíxiáng and others, had long resented Yú Qiān.
On the Rénwǔ day of the first month of the eighth year of Jǐngtài (1457),
after Shí Hēng, Cáo Jíxiáng, Yǒu Zhēn, and others had welcomed the Retired Emperor back to the throne,
and finished proclaiming the imperial edict to the court officials,
they immediately arrested Yú Qiān and Grand Secretary Wáng Wén and imprisoned them.
They falsely accused Yú Qiān and others of conspiring with Huáng ● to form an evil plot
to establish a new heir apparent,
and also conspiring with the eunuchs Wáng Chéng, Shū Liáng, Zhāng Yǒng, Wáng Qín, and others to welcome and enthrone the Prince of Xiāng.
Shí Hēng and others led this conspiracy,
instigating the censors to submit the accusations.
The Censor-in-chief Xiāo Wéizhēn finalized the verdict,
convicting them of treason
and sentencing them to capital punishment.
Wáng Wén, unable to bear the false accusation,
argued vehemently.
Yú Qiān smiled and said:
“It is merely Shí Hēng and his ilk's intention;
what good will arguing do?”
When the memorial was submitted,
Emperor Yīngzōng was still hesitant, saying:
“Yú Qiān indeed has merits.”
Yǒu Zhēn stepped forward and said:
“If Yú Qiān is not killed,
this entire endeavor will be baseless.”
The emperor's decision was thus made.
On the Bǐngxū day, the reign name was changed to Tiānshùn.
On the Dīnghài day, Yú Qiān was executed in the marketplace,
his property confiscated,
and his family exiled to the frontier.
Wú Yù, the director of studies in Suìxī, argued that Yú Qiān's crime warranted the extermination of his clan,
and that all civil and military officials recommended by Yú Qiān should also be executed.
The Board considered it and then stopped the proposal.
Battalion Commander Bái Qí also requested that Yú Qiān's crimes be publicly posted,
carved on wooden boards and displayed to the world.
At that time, those who sought imperial favor
often used Yú Qiān as an excuse.
Ever since the change brought by Yěxiān,
Yú Qiān had sworn not to live with the rebels.
He often stayed overnight in the guardhouse
and did not return to his private residence.
He had long suffered from phlegm illness,
and when the illness flared up,
Emperor Jǐng sent Xīng Ān and Shū Liáng to take turns visiting him.
Hearing that his clothing was too thin,
an imperial decree ordered that special garments be made and bestowed from the palace,
along with everything from vinegar to vegetables.
He also personally visited Wànsuì Shān,
cut bamboos, and extracted sap to bestow upon him.
Some said that he favored Yú Qiān too much,
to which Xīng Ān and others replied:
“He shares the nation's worries day and night,
without regard for his personal property.
If he were to depart,
where could the court find another such person?”
When his property was confiscated,
there was nothing left in his house,
except for the main chamber which was locked very securely.
When it was opened,
it contained only the python robe and sword bestowed by the emperor.
On the day of his death,
dark clouds gathered,
and the world mourned his injustice.
Commander Duǒ’ér,
originally from Cáo Jíxiáng's command,
poured wine at the place where Yú Qiān died,
and wept bitterly.
Cáo Jíxiáng was enraged and
flogged him.
The next day, he again made offerings as before.
Dū Dū Tóng Zhī Chén Kuí, moved by Yú Qiān's loyalty and righteousness,
collected his remains and gave him a temporary burial.
A year later,
he was reburied in Hángzhōu.
Chén Kuí
was from Lùhé.
He was originally recommended as a military talent,
and was a student of Lǐ Shímǐan.
The Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu) initially did not know of Yú Qiān's death;
when she heard,
she lamented for several days.
Emperor Yīngzōng also regretted it.
After Yú Qiān's death,
Shí Hēng's partisan Chén Rǔyán replaced him as Minister of War.
Less than a year later, he was disgraced,
with accumulated bribes amounting to millions.
The emperor summoned his ministers to observe it,
and sadly said:
“Yú Qiān was favored during the Jǐngtài reign,
and after his death, he had no remaining property.
Why does Rǔyán have so much?”
Shí Hēng bowed his head, unable to reply.
Soon there was a border alarm,
and the emperor's worry showed on his face.
The Marquis of Gōngshùn, Wú Jǐn, was attending,
and stepped forward saying:
“If Yú Qiān were here,
he would not have allowed the invaders to reach this far.”
The emperor fell silent.
That year,
Yǒu Zhēn was framed by Shí Hēng
and exiled to Jīnchǐ.
A few years later,
Shí Hēng was also imprisoned and died,
and Cáo Jíxiáng’s rebellion led to the extermination of his clan.
Yú Qiān's case was cleared.
In the early years of Chénghuà,
Miǎn was pardoned and returned,
submitting a memorial to plead for his father's injustice,
and was reinstated in office and granted imperial sacrifices.
The imperial edict stated:
“When the state faced great difficulties,
he preserved the altars of grain and soil from danger.
He alone upheld public justice,
and thus was hated by the treacherous officials.
The late emperor already knew of his wrongful death,
and My heart truly pities his loyalty.”
This was widely circulated throughout the realm.
In the second year of Hóngzhì (1489), based on the recommendation of the Supervising Secretary Sūn Xū,
he was posthumously granted the titles of Tèjìn Guānglù Dàfū, Zhùguó, and Tàifù,
and given the posthumous epithet Sùmǐn.
A shrine was bestowed at his tomb, named Jīnggōng,
where officials offered sacrifices seasonally.
During the Wànlì reign,
his posthumous epithet was changed to Zhōngsù.
Hángzhōu, Hénán, and Shānxī all perpetually honored him with sacrifices.
Miǎn,
whose courtesy name was Jǐngzhān,
was appointed Vice Battalion Commander by imperial privilege
and was exiled to Lóngmén.
After Yú Qiān's injustice was redressed,
Miǎn's official position was also restored.
He stated that he did not wish for a military post,
and was instead appointed Yuánwàiláng of the Ministry of War.
He served with administrative capability
and was successively promoted to Prefect of Yìngtiān.
He retired from office and died.
He had no sons,
so he adopted his clansman Yǔnzhōng as his heir,
who inherited the position of Vice Battalion Commander of the Hángzhōu Guard
and oversaw the sacrifices.
When [Shàn] arrived,
his host drank with him in the tent.
The host said in surprise,
"During the Battle of Tǔmù,
why were the imperial armies so timid?"
Shàn replied,
"At that time, all the strong imperial troops had been sent on a southern campaign.
Wáng Sīlǐ had invited the Emperor to visit his village,
without making any preparations for battle.
That is why you were able to achieve your objective.
Now the generals and soldiers from the southern campaign have returned;
there are about two hundred thousand of them.
Furthermore, we have recruited skilled officers and combatants from within and outside the capital,
about three hundred thousand more.
All of them have been taught to use divine spears, firearms, and medicinal crossbows.
At over a hundred paces, they can pierce the belly of a man or horse, killing them instantly.
Moreover, following the advice of strategists,
at critical points along the border,
we have secretly buried three-foot iron spikes.
When a horse's hooves step on them, they will be pierced.
Additionally, there are assassins everywhere,
who can traverse camps at night like apes and monkeys."
The host's expression changed.
Shàn then said,
"What a pity!
Now all these have been rendered useless."
The host asked,
"Why is that?"
Shàn replied,
"The peace negotiations have been concluded,
and we are now as friendly as brothers.
Why would we need these things?"
He then gave the host the gifts he had brought.
The man was delighted
and told everything to Yěxiān.
The next day, when Shàn paid his respects to Yěxiān,
he also gave him substantial gifts.
Yěxiān was also pleased.
Shàn then questioned him, saying,
"During the time of the Tàishàng Huángdì,
the Tàishī sent tribute envoys of certainly three thousand people,
and tribute was bestowed twice a year.
Gold and silk filled the roads.
Why then did you break the alliance and attack us?"
Yěxiān replied,
"Why did you reduce the price of my horses,
and the silk given was often torn?
Many of the envoys sent before did not return,
and the annual賜 (gifts) were also reduced?"
Shàn responded,
"It was not a reduction.
The Tàishī's horses increased yearly,
and the price was difficult to maintain, but we were reluctant to refuse,
so it was slightly decreased.
Tàishī, judge for yourself,
which price was more generous compared to before?
As for the torn silk,
the 'tongshi' (interpreter) was responsible for that.
When the matter was exposed,
he was executed.
Even if the Tàishī's tribute horses were inferior or weak,
or the貂 (sables) were worn,
could that truly be the Tàishī's intention?
Furthermore, the envoys often numbered three or four thousand people.
Some engaged in theft or violated other laws,
and fearing punishment upon their return,
they simply disappeared themselves.
Why would we detain them?
When tribute envoys received banquets and gifts,
the names listed sometimes exceeded their actual number.
The imperial court verified the actual number and provided accordingly.
The reduction was only of fictitious numbers;
those who were actually present were certainly not reduced."
Yěxiān repeatedly praised Shàn.
Shàn further said,
"Tàishī attacked us again,
slaughtering hundreds of thousands.
The Tàishī's own troops also suffered no small number of casualties.
Heaven loves life,
but Tàishī loves killing.
Hence, there have been frequent thunder warnings.
Now, if the Tàishàng Huáng is returned,
and relations are restored as before,
Chinese gold and silk will arrive daily,
and both countries will rejoice.
Wouldn't that be wonderful?"
Yěxiān asked,
"Why does the imperial edict contain no words about welcoming him?"
Shàn replied,
"This is to establish the Tàishī's good name,
allowing him to do it on his own initiative.
If it were written in the imperial edict,
it would appear that the Tàishī was compelled by imperial command,
not acting out of sincerity."
Yěxiān was greatly pleased
and asked,
"When the Tàishàng Huáng returns, will he be able to become the Emperor again?"
Shàn replied,
"The position of Emperor has already been settled,
it is difficult to change it again."
Yěxiān asked,
"What about Yáo and Shùn?"
Shàn replied,
"Yáo abdicated in favor of Shùn;
now the elder brother is yielding to the younger,
which is exactly the same."
His Pingzhang, Ángkè, asked Shàn,
"Why did you not bring valuable treasures to ransom him?"
Shàn replied,
"If I had brought goods,
people would say the Tàishī was seeking profit.
But now, without them,
it shows the Tàishī's benevolence and righteousness,
making him a good man,
whose deeds will be recorded in historical annals
and praised for ten thousand generations."
Yěxiān laughed and praised Shàn.
The Zhiyüan, Bóyán Tiēmù'ěr, advised Yěxiān to keep the envoy
and send his own envoy to demand the Tàishàng Huáng's restoration to the throne.
Yěxiān feared losing trust
and refused.
He eventually agreed to allow Shàn to escort the Tàishàng Huáng back.
At that time, the entire court competed to praise Shàn's achievements,
but Jǐngdì, deeming it not in line with his initial envoy's instructions,
minimized his rewards.
He was promoted to Zuǒ Dū Yùshǐ
and continued to oversee the Hónglú affairs.
In the second year,
after the court officials finished their New Year's Day congratulations,
they repaired to the congratulatory hall.
Shàn again said,
"The Tàishàng Huáng is not receiving congratulations,
so why should we congratulate each other?"
In the first month of the third year, he was granted the title Tàizǐ Tàibǎo.
In the sixth year, citing old age, he requested to retire,
but an imperial edict graciously denied his request.
Shàn was imposing in appearance
and quick-witted in his responses.
However, he lacked scholarly learning,
was fond of humor,
and rarely spoke solemnly to guests.
His family was in the capital,
where he built a mansion outside the city walls.
His garden had many fine fruits,
which he periodically presented to high officials, imperial relatives, and influential eunuchs,
never failing to win their favor.
When Wáng Zhèn was in power,
Shàn flattered and served him.
Later, he allied himself with Shí Hēng and Cáo Jíxiáng.
In the first month of the first year of Tiānshùn,
Shí Hēng and Cáo Jíxiáng restored the Tàishàng Huáng to the throne.
As Shàn was involved in the conspiracy,
he was enfeoffed as Fèngtiān Yìwèi Tuīchéng Xuānlì Wǔchén, Tèjìn Guānglù Dàfū, Zhùguó, Xīngjì Bó,
with an annual salary of 1,200 dàn of grain,
granted an hereditary patent,
and put in charge of the Zuǒ Jūn Dūdū Fǔ affairs.
Shàngshū Hú Yíng praised Shàn's accomplishment in welcoming the Emperor,
and he was appointed concurrently Lǐbù Shàngshū,
later changed to Shǒuzhèng Wénchén.
When Shàn went to Wǎlà,
he took his four sons with him,
and by this time, they all obtained official positions.
He also sought favors for his nephews and adopted sons,
and more than ten of them obtained official positions.
His influence and power were immense,
and he engaged in soliciting power and accepting bribes.
Shí Hēng and his associates became jealous and sowed discord,
leading to his gradual estrangement.
He died in the fifth month of the second year.
He was posthumously granted the title Xīngjì Hóu
and given the posthumous name Zhōngmǐn.
Shàn was talented in debate
and skillfully gained fame and position,
but his treacherous and cunning nature was condemned by scholars.
When he was a xùbān (secretary),
he was imprisoned for an offense along with Shùjíshì Zhāng Pǔ.
After a long time,
they became familiar with each other.
At that time, the persecution of Fāng Xiàorú's partisans was severe.
Zhāng Pǔ mentioned that his family possessed a collection of Fāng Xiàorú's writings
which he had not yet had time to destroy.
Shàn borrowed it to read
and secretly reported it to the throne.
Zhāng Pǔ was consequently executed,
while Shàn regained his official position.
In the executions of Yú Qiān and Wáng Wén, and the exile of Chén Xún,
Shàn also played a significant role.
His son, Zōng, inherited the爵 (nobility),
but later his
"Duómén"
merit was revoked,
and he was demoted to Jīnwú Zhǐhuīshǐ.
His grandson, Zēng, married a princess.
Lǐ Shí,
courtesy name Mèngchéng,
was from Hézhōu.
He became a *jìnshì* in the seventh year of Zhèngtǒng.
He was unrestrained and uninhibited in his conduct,
and had a sharp tongue.
In the early years of Jǐngtài,
he served as a Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Rites.
When Yěxiān sent Wánzhě Tuōhuān to negotiate peace,
Shí requested to go.
He was promoted to Right Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites and sent as envoy,
with Assistant Minister Luó Qǐ as his deputy.
Upon arrival, he met with the Retired Emperor (Shànghuáng),
and somewhat grasped Yěxiān's intentions,
returning to report that Yěxiān's request for peace had no ulterior motives.
When Yáng Shàn subsequently went,
the Retired Emperor indeed returned.
In October of that year, he was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief
and served as Governor of Húguǎng.
In the fifth year, he was recalled
to manage the Censorate.
Initially,
when Shí was sent to visit the Retired Emperor,
he requested the Retired Emperor to return to the capital and accept blame,
which displeased the Retired Emperor.
Later, due to his tyrannical behavior in his hometown,
he was dismissed as a commoner.
Zhào Róng,
courtesy name Mèngchén,
was of Western Regions descent.
During the Yuán dynasty, his ancestors entered China
and settled in Mǐnxiàn.
His maternal uncle, Sà Qí,
served in the Hanlin Academy.
Róng followed him to the capital,
and was appointed Scholar of the Central Secretariat for his calligraphy skills.
In October of the fourteenth year of Zhèngtǒng,
when Yěxiān escorted the Retired Emperor to Dàtóng,
Prefect Huò Xuān went to pay his respects,
wept bitterly, and returned.
Yěxiān then invaded the capital,
escorted the Retired Emperor to ascend the earthen wall,
and invited high officials to come out and greet him.
Róng bravely volunteered to go.
Grand Secretary Gāo Gǔ patted his back and said:
"You,
are a loyal and righteous man."
He untied his rhinoceros belt and presented it to Róng,
who was then promoted to Right Assistant Minister of the Court of Judicial Review
and concurrently served as Minister of the Court of State Ceremonials.
He went out of the city with Right Vice Minister of Communications Wáng Fù to pay respects at the court,
presenting sheep, wine, and other items.
Yěxiān, deeming them not high officials,
sent them back,
and instead invited Yú Qiān, Shí Hēng, Wáng Zhí, and Hú Yíng to come out.
Emperor Jǐng did not send them.
Róng was reassigned as Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices
and continued to serve in the Grand Secretariat.
In July of the first year of Jǐngtài, he was promoted to Right Vice Minister of the Ministry of Works,
and went with Yáng Shàn and others.
The imperial edict did not contain words of welcoming the emperor back,
but Shàn was eloquent,
and Róng supported him,
and they eventually brought the Retired Emperor back.
He was promoted to Left Vice Minister.
When Envoy Wáng Yàn requested to open the Qìn River for grain transport,
the matter was debated again in court.
It was deemed inconvenient,
so Róng was sent to investigate.
Upon his return,
he also reported it to be inconvenient.
Soon after, he was ordered to consult with the three judicial offices of Shāndōng and Hénán to survey the river course.
Others slighted Róng because he had not entered officialdom through the imperial examinations.
Róng became angry,
and beat and humiliated many people,
even personally hitching up his clothes to test the water depth.
The three offices each submitted a memorial reporting that Róng galloped alone on horseback,
startling soldiers and civilians,
injured county officials with a staff,
and overcharged for grain from the granaries.
Governors Xuē Xīlián and Zhāng Chēn also reported this.
The memorial was sent to Vice Censor-in-Chief in charge of river conservancy, Xú Yǒuzhēn, for verification and report.
The judicial authorities stated that
although Róng had committed gross impropriety,
he was ultimately acting out of urgency for national affairs,
and the overcharging for grain was done by his subordinates;
the officials who insulted a high minister
and defied the imperial edict
should be arrested and punished,
and Xīlián and Chēn should also be punished.
The emperor ordered the inspecting officials to obtain statements from the various officials
and pardoned Róng.
In the first year of Tiānshùn, he was promoted to Minister.
When Cáo Qīn rebelled,
Róng galloped on horseback, shouting in the marketplace:
"The rebel Cáo has committed treason!
Brave men, join me in punishing him!"
Indeed, some came,
and he immediately led them to the battle.
After the rebellion was quelled,
Emperor Yīngzōng spoke with Lǐ Xián,
praising Róng's loyalty,
and ordered him to concurrently serve as Minister of the Court of Judicial Review,
receiving his salary.
In the seventh year, he was dismissed due to illness.
He died in the eleventh year of Chénghuà.
He was granted posthumous honors according to regulations.
Huò Xuān,
courtesy name Tíngbì,
was from Fèngxiáng.
He entered the Imperial Academy through a local recommendation
and was appointed Dàtóng Sub-prefect.
In the twelfth year of Zhèngtǒng,
he was recommended by the Earl of Wǔjìn, Zhū Miǎn,
and was promoted to Prefect.
When Yěxiān escorted Emperor Yīngzōng to the city walls,
Xuān, along with Minister for Provisions Shěn Gù and others, went out to pay their respects,
bowing before the horse and weeping loudly.
The crowd of enemies brandished their blades and shouted at them,
but they were unmoved.
The Retired Emperor ordered to collect gold and silk from within the city,
and Xuān offered all he had.
The Retired Emperor praised and marveled.
The invaders frequently appeared and disappeared around Dàtóng and Húnyuán,
lying in wait for soldiers and civilians gathering firewood,
and often drove them away and plundered them.
Those who fortunately escaped and returned
were often maimed.
The surviving people flocked into the city,
without shelter
and lacking food.
Xuān memorialized on all these matters.
The old and weak were allowed to temporarily relocate,
grain was distributed for relief,
and the able-bodied men remaining to defend the city were exempted from taxes and corvée labor.
When his term was complete and he was due for transfer,
the garrison commanders and inspecting officials requested him to stay.
An imperial edict promoted him to Right Administration Commissioner of Shānxī,
while he continued to manage prefectural affairs.
When Emperor Yīngzōng was restored to the throne,
Xuān was summoned and appointed Right Vice Minister of the Ministry of Works,
while Gù was also recommended by Shí Hēng
and appointed Minister of the Ministry of Revenue.
Later, the Governor reported on Xuān's administrative achievements,
and he was bestowed with an imperial edict commending his exceptional service.
Initially,
when Xuān was in Dàtóng,
Governor Nián Fù was arrested,
and Xuān provided financial assistance for his family to return home.
This was resented by the Grand Eunuch of the Garrison, Wéi Lìzhuǎn,
who lashed him over ten times.
At this point, Xuān reported this,
and also stated that Lìzhuǎn always used female entertainers at banquets,
his clothing and equipage were extravagant like a king's,
and he forcibly took local women as concubines.
Lìzhuǎn also impeached Xuān for illegal acts.
The Emperor pardoned both of them.
That year, he was transferred to Left Vice Minister,
and bestowed with second-rank attire.
In the early years of Chénghuà,
he was repeatedly impeached by censorate officials.
He was ordered to retire.
He died in the capital.
Xuān initially had a good reputation in governing his prefecture,
but his later years were unprincipled.
It was particularly because he was recognized by the emperor during difficult times
that he remained in prominent positions for a long time.
Shěn Gù,
was from Dānyáng.
In the Yǒnglè era,
