he began his career through a local recommendation
and gradually rose to the position of Minister.
After Shí Hēng's downfall,
he requested to retire.
Wáng Yuè,
courtesy name Shìchāng,
was from Jùn.
He was tall,
strong, and skilled in archery,
well-versed in history,
and had great strategic talent.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the second year of Jǐngtài.
On the day of the palace examination,
a whirlwind arose,
carrying away his paper.
He was given another paper,
and only then completed the examination.
He was appointed Censor,
and sent to inspect Shǎnxī.
Upon hearing of his father's death,
he returned without waiting for a replacement,
and was impeached by the Censor-in-Chief.
The Emperor specially pardoned him.
In the early Tiānshùn reign,
he was appointed to manage all provincial memorials and petitions.
He was exceptionally promoted to Surveillance Commissioner of Shāndōng.
In the seventh year,
Hán Yōng, Grand Coordinator and Censor-in-Chief of Dàtóng, was recalled.
The emperor found it difficult to find a replacement for him,
and sighed, saying:
"How can I find someone like Yōng to appoint?"
Lǐ Xián recommended Yuè,
who was summoned for an audience.
Yuè wore a grand robe with short sleeves,
and moved with ease and agility.
The emperor was pleased,
and promoted him to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief to proceed.
Upon his arrival,
he encountered the mourning period for his mother,
but was compelled to retain his post and attend to affairs.
Yuè then repaired armaments,
simplified military ranks,
repaired fortresses,
reduced taxes, and encouraged commerce,
making plans for the long term.
In the third year of Chénghuà,
Zhū Yǒng, Marquis of Fǔníng, campaigned against Máolǐhái,
with Yuè assisting in military affairs.
That autumn,
he also served as Grand Coordinator of Xuānfǔ.
In the winter of the fifth year,
the barbarians invaded the Hétáo region.
Wáng Ruì, Grand Coordinator of Yánsuí, requested reinforcements.
An imperial edict ordered Yuè to lead troops to respond.
The Hétáo region
was the Shuòfāng of Zhōu and the Hénán land of Qín,
with fertile soil
and abundant water and grass.
It stretched two thousand *lǐ*
from Piāntóuguān in Shānxī to the east,
to Níngxià in the west.
It was bordered by the river on three sides,
and pressed against the back of Yúlín to the north.
The three fortresses of Sān Shòuxiángchéng of Táng were outside the river,
hence it was inland territory.
In the early Míng dynasty,
the river served as a defense,
and Yánsuí was also peaceful.
Since the Tiānshùn reign,
the three tribes led by Máolǐhái began to invade.
However, they only appeared and disappeared periodically,
not daring to stay for long.
It was only then that they began to settle and pasture there,
repeatedly causing border troubles.
When Yuè arrived at Yúlín,
he dispatched guerrilla general Xǔ Níng to exit via the western route of Lóngzhōu and Zhènjìng forts,
and Fàn Jǐn to exit via the eastern route of Shénmù and Zhènqiāng forts,
while he himself, with the palace eunuch Qín Gāng, held Yúlín city as a strategic support.
Níng fought at Líjiājiàn,
and Jǐn fought at Yáyáochuān;
both were victorious.
Right Assistant Regional Commander Shén Yīng again defeated the enemy at Zhènqiāng,
and the barbarians then retreated.
In the first month of the following year, the victory was reported,
and Yuè led his troops back.
Upon reaching Piāntóuguān,
Yánsuí reported an emergency.
The Ministry of War impeached Yuè for unauthorized return.
An imperial edict cleared him of fault,
but ordered Yuè to station in the vicinity of Yánsuí for reinforcement.
More than ten thousand barbarian cavalry entered and plundered via five routes.
Yuè ordered Níng and others to repel them.
He was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief.
In the third month of that year,
the imperial court, seeing that Āluó Chū and others continued to harass the borders,
appointed Zhū Yǒng, Marquis of Fǔníng, as general,
to devise a plan with Yuè.
They defeated the enemy at Kāihuāngchuān.
The various generals pursued the fleeing enemy to Niújiāzhài.
Āluó Chū was hit by a stray arrow and fled.
For his merits,
he was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief.
The next year,
Yuè, being on a western campaign,
declined the post of Grand Coordinator of Dàtóng.
An imperial edict permitted this,
and he was additionally appointed Supreme Commander of Military Affairs,
specifically to manage the western affairs.
However, at that time, the barbarians numbered tens of thousands,
while the official army capable of fighting was only ten thousand,
and moreover, they were dispersed for defense,
making them no match in strength.
Yǒng and Yuè then proposed two strategies: battle and defense.
Minister Bái Guī also found it difficult,
and requested an imperial order for the generals to defend.
That year,
the barbarians again repeatedly entered Huáiyuǎn forts.
Yǒng and Yuè repelled them.
Guī again requested a major campaign to search the Hétáo.
The next year, Vice Minister Yè Shèng was sent to the army for deliberation.
At this time, Yǒng had already been recalled,
and Yuè, seeing that the soldiers' clothing and equipment were completely ruined,
and more than half the horses had died,
requested a temporary cessation of hostilities,
and returned with Shèng.
However, the court debated that if Hétáo was not extinguished,
the three borders would never know peace.
The previously mobilized armies had already exceeded eighty thousand,
but command was not unified,
and no success was achieved.
It was deemed appropriate to specifically dispatch a great general to oversee.
Therefore, Zhào Fǔ, Marquis of Wǔjìng, was appointed General Pacifier of Barbarians,
and an imperial edict ordered the troops of the three garrisons of Shǎnxī, Níngxià, and Yánsuí to all submit to his command,
with Yuè as Supreme Commander of Military Affairs.
When they arrived,
the barbarians were already deep in Huánqìng and Gùyuán, plundering extensively,
and the army achieved no success.
Yuè and Fǔ, seeing that Mǎndūlǔ, Bólúohū, and Biājiāsīlán were then powerful,
and their forces could not be broken,
then submitted a memorial stating:
"To thoroughly search Hétáo,
it would require no less than 150,000 elite troops.
Now, provisions are burdensome,
public and private resources are exhausted,
and further levies could lead to internal strife.
It would be advisable to temporarily adopt a defensive retreat,
disperse the soldiers and horses,
retain a measured elite force,
subsist on grain from Fū and Yán,
and relocate all border military and civilians inland.
In the areas where the barbarians appear and disappear,
many beacon fires should be set,
trenches dug and walls built,
to serve as protection."
When the memorial was submitted,
the court's deliberation was undecided.
Yuè and others again memorialized:
"The barbarians, knowing our army has gathered in force,
have moved their camp near the river,
secretly planning to cross north,
likely to retreat without a fight.
However, Shān and Shǎn provinces are suffering from drought,
fodder and provisions are scarce,
and the border regions are cold early,
with successive deaths from freezing and starvation.
Considering the season,
attack and capture are truly difficult.
We request to follow the defensive strategy,
and your subjects can also temporarily return to court."
At this, the various officials from the ministries and censorial offices impeached Yuè and Fǔ for deception.
Coincidentally, Fǔ fell ill,
was recalled,
and Liú Jù, Earl of Níngjìn, was appointed in his place.
The following year,
Yuè and Jù defeated the marauding bandits at Màntiānlǐng,
and he was promoted to Assistant Censor-in-Chief of the Left.
At this time, three major generals were dispatched,
all with Yuè as the Superintendent of Military Affairs.
Whenever the bandits encroached,
a small attack would cause them to retreat,
but as soon as the army withdrew, they would return,
often invading several times a year.
The officers and soldiers grew lax with the bandits,
while the bandit's strength became increasingly formidable.
In the ninth month of that year,
Mǎndūlǔ, along with Bólúohū and Gějiāsīlán, left their wives, children, old, and weak at Hóngyánchí,
and launched a major incursion,
advancing directly to Qínzhōu, Āndìng, and other prefectures and counties.
Yuè surmised that the bandits had committed their full strength to the west,
leaving the eastern flank unprepared.
He then led Xǔ Níng, the Grand General of Yánsuí, and Zhōu Yù, the Mobile Corps General, each with five thousand cavalry as left and right scouts,
departing from Yúlín,
crossing Hóng'érshān,
and traversing Báiyántān,
covering eight hundred *lǐ* in two days and nights.
As they approached,
a violent storm arose,
with dust obscuring their vision.
An old soldier stepped forward and said:
"Heaven helps us!
As we advance, the wind
will prevent the enemy from noticing us.
When we return with our army,
if we encounter the returning bandits,
we will be downwind.
Striking them with the wind,
there will be no defeat."
Yuè immediately dismounted and bowed to him,
promoting him to Commander of a Thousand Households.
He divided his thousand soldiers into ten platoons,
while he personally led Níng and Yù to spread out both wings,
approaching the enemy camp,
and utterly defeating them.
They captured and beheaded three hundred fifty,
seized countless camels, horses, and weapons,
and burned their tents before returning.
When Mǎndūlǔ and others, after having thoroughly plundered, returned,
they found their wives, children, and livestock all gone,
and they looked at each other and wept bitterly.
From then on, they migrated far north,
not daring to reside in Hétào again,
and the western frontier enjoyed several years of peace.
Initially,
civil officials supervising military campaigns
usually followed behind the main army,
only issuing orders and administering rewards and punishments.
Yuè was the first to select many agile and courageous warriors to be his trusted generals,
personally engaging in combat with the bandits,
and also using spies to repeatedly ambush and intercept the enemy,
or cutting off their scattered cavalry,
thereby achieving many successes.
In the spring of the tenth year,
the court deliberated on establishing a Grand Commandancy (*Zǒngzhìfǔ*) in Gùyuán,
appointing Jiǎng Wǎn, Marquis of Dìngxī, as Grand General (*Zǒngbīngguān*),
and Yuè as Commissioner of Military Affairs (*Tídū Jūnwù*),
controlling the three frontiers of Yánsuí, Níngxià, and Gānsù.
The Grand General, the Provincial Governor (*Xúnfǔ*), and all subordinates
were to be subject to his command.
An imperial edict dismissed Wǎn,
and immediately appointed Yuè to the post,
and the establishment of a Grand Commandancy for the three frontiers began from this point.
For his merits,
he was promoted to Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
and his stipend was increased by one grade.

Zhāng Jǐn, a secretary for meritorious service, and Guō Táng, a supervising secretary of the Ministry of War, among others, criticized Liú Jù and others for wantonly killing and falsely claiming merits,
and also impeached Yuè for making false reports.
Yuè, for his part, felt that his great merits had been poorly rewarded,
and thus became resentful,
claiming illness and returning to the capital.
The following year, he jointly managed the affairs of the Censorate with Lǐ Bīn, Assistant Censor-in-Chief of the Left,
and concurrently supervised the twelve Divisional Camps.
Yuè had always been proud of his talent
and disregarded minor details,
which earned him criticism from court deliberations.
At this point, he abandoned his reputation for integrity,
and associated with petty individuals.
A cunning man named Wéi Yīng,
an official slave, participated in the Yánsuí campaign
and falsely claimed merit to become a Commander of a Hundred Households.
Wāng Zhí was in charge of the Western Depot and held great power;
Yīng served as his henchman,
and Yuè used Yīng to establish a connection with Zhí.
When the Grand Secretariat debated the abolition of the Western Depot,
Yuè met Grand Secretaries Liú Jí and Liú Xǔ at court
and openly said to them:
"Wāng Zhí's actions are quite impartial.
For example, without Zhí, Huáng Cì, who monopolized power and accepted bribes, could not have been removed.
Shāng and Wàn have been in office for a long time,
and they are often apprehensive about right and wrong.
How many days have you two gentlemen been in the Grand Secretariat,
that you also do this?"
Xǔ replied:
"What we speak
is not for our own gain.
If Zhí's actions were all impartial,
why would the court have established high officials and ministers?"
Yuè was unable to respond.
When Xiàng Zhōng, Minister of War, was dismissed,
Yuè was due for promotion,
but the imperial decree assigned the post to Yú Zǐjùn, Governor of Shǎnxī.
Yuè became even more displeased,
requesting to resign from his camp duties,
but a gracious edict did not permit it.
He then submitted a petition describing his achievement of destroying the bandit stronghold,
which had been suppressed by the late Minister Bái Guī,
and how many of the officers and soldiers who participated in the campaign had not been recorded,
requesting that his additional official rank be used to reward them.
Zǐjùn also stated that Yuè's rewards did not match his merits,
so he was promoted to Minister of War,
still managing the affairs of the Censorate.
Soon after, he was granted the title of Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
Yuè was eager for fame and glory.
When Wāng Zhí first launched his eastern expedition,
Yuè hoped to supervise the army,
but was thwarted by Chén Yuè.
Yuè suddenly gained favor,
and his heart became even more envious of him.
In the spring of the sixteenth year,
the defending officials of Yánsuí reported that bandits had secretly crossed the river and entered Jìnglǔ.
Yuè then persuaded Zhí to dispatch an army.
An imperial edict appointed Zhū Yǒng, Duke of Bǎoguó, as General Pacifying Barbarians (*Pínglǔ Jiāngjūn*),
Zhí as Supervisor of the Army,
and Yuè as Commissioner of Military Affairs.
Yuè persuaded Zhí to instruct Yǒng to lead the main army via the southern route,
while he and Zhí would lead light cavalry along the frontier wall to the west,
all to rendezvous at Yúlín.
When Yuè reached Dàtóng,
he heard that the enemy's camp was at Wēiníng Háizǐ.
He then selected twenty thousand soldiers from the Xuān and Dà garrisons,
departed from Gūdian,
marched stealthily to Māo'érzhuāng,
and divided his forces into several routes.
Amidst a great storm of wind, rain, and snow, obscuring visibility,
they advanced to Wēiníng.
The bandits were still unaware,
and they were ambushed and utterly defeated.
They beheaded over four hundred thirty,
captured six thousand horses, cattle, and sheep,
and the army returned without reaching Yúlín.
Yǒng's route was circuitous,
and he did not encounter the enemy,
achieving no merit.
Because of this, Yuè was enfeoffed as Count of Wēiníng,
a hereditary title,
with an annual stipend of twelve hundred *dàn* of grain.
Upon receiving the enfeoffment,
Yuè should no longer have held the Censorate position,
but Yuè did not wish to join the military ranks.
Censors Xǔ Jìn and others praised his achievements,
citing the precedents of Wáng Jì and Yáng Shàn,
and requested that he continue to lead the Censorate
and supervise the divisional camps.
This was granted.
The following year, he again led the army with Zhí and Yǒng to Dàtóng.
Just as the bandits invaded and plundered,
they pursued them to Hēishíyá,
capturing and beheading over one hundred twenty people,
and seizing seven hundred horses.
He was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent,
and his annual stipend was increased by four hundred *dàn* of grain.
According to the Ming system,
civil officials could not be enfeoffed as dukes or marquises.
Yuè, following the precedent of meritorious officials,
was transferred to manage the Chief Military Commission of the Front,
commanding the troops of the Five Army Camps,
and supervising the divisional camps as before.
From then on, he truly became a military man,
and even hoped for the title of Marquis.
In the fifth month of that year,
Xuānfǔ reported an alarm.
He was ordered to bear the seal of General Pacifying Hu (*Pínghú Jiāngjūn*)
and serve as Grand General.
Zhí was again appointed to supervise military affairs,
and they led ten thousand metropolitan troops to confront the situation.
By the time they arrived,
the bandits had already departed,
so they remained stationed in that area.
By winter,
Zhí was alienated by his peers,
and his favor declined.
Yuè and others repeatedly requested to return the troops to the capital,
but it was not permitted.
Chén Yuè, residing in the Ministry of War,
also requested it on Zhí's behalf.
The emperor severely reprimanded them,
and the two men then became frightened.
Subsequently,
Sūn Yuè, Grand General of Dàtóng, died,
and Yuè was immediately ordered to replace him,
while Zhí was made Supreme Commander of Dàtóng and Xuānfǔ,
and all the metropolitan camp officers and soldiers were recalled.
The following year,
bandits attacked Yánsuí.
Yuè and others mobilized troops to relieve it,
achieving considerable kills and captures,
and an increase of fifty *shí* of emolument.
The emperor by this time increasingly understood the relationship between Yuè and Zhí.
Grand Secretary Wàn Ān and others, considering Yuè's intelligence and strategy,
feared he might induce Zhí to return to power,
and so requested to transfer Yuè to Yánsuí to separate them,
thus diminishing the influence of both men.
The following year,
Zhí incurred an offense,
and censorial officials jointly impeached Yuè.
An imperial edict stripped him of his title and removed him from office,
banishing him to reside in Ānlù.
His three sons, who had obtained official positions through his merit-based patronage,
were all struck from the rolls.
Furthermore, an envoy was dispatched with an imperial decree to instruct him.
When Yuè heard of the envoy's arrival,
he wanted to take his own life.
But seeing that the decree contained words of leniency,
he gradually felt more at ease.
Although Yuè was disliked by the scholars who upheld ritual and law,
he considered himself a hero,
and remained arrogantly self-possessed.
His food and attendance were likened to those of a king,
and he indulged in hunting, music, and pleasure as he pleased;
even in banishment, his behavior showed no decline.
Thus, when he incurred offense,
contemporary opinion largely considered it excessive,
yet ultimately no one came forward to exonerate him.
When Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
he was pardoned and recalled.
In the seventh year of Hóngzhì (1494),
Yuè repeatedly submitted memorials pleading his innocence.
An edict reinstated him as Left Censor-in-Chief,
and he retired.
Yuè was seventy years old
and senile.
He again conspired with the eunuch Lǐ Guǎng,
and by imperial decree was summoned to manage the affairs of the Censorate.
Investigating Censor Jì Yuán, Supervising Secretary Wáng Yīyán, and others submitted memorials arguing against this,
and the matter was dropped.
In the winter of the tenth year (1497),
bandits attacked Gānsù.
The court debated re-establishing the office of Grand Coordinator.
Seven individuals were successively nominated,
but none satisfied the imperial will.
Minister of Personnel Tú Yōng submitted Yuè’s name,
and an edict was issued to restore him to his original office,
confer upon him the title of Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent,
and make him Grand Coordinator of Gān and Liáng border affairs, concurrently serving as Provincial Governor.
Yuè stated that the troops in Gān Commandery were weak,
and without the assistance of troops from Yán and Níng Commandery, it would be difficult to defeat the enemy.
He requested to concurrently command both commanderies,
and be relieved of his duties as Provincial Governor.
This was granted.
The following year,
Yuè, noting that the bandit lair was behind Hèlán Shān
and frequently disturbed the border,
divided his troops into three routes to advance and suppress them.
Forty-three heads were taken,
and over a hundred horses and camels were captured.
He was promoted to Junior Guardian,
and concurrently Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent.
He then itemized proposals for administering Hāmì affairs.
Coincidentally, Lǐ Guǎng was found guilty and died.
Censors repeatedly impeached Lǐ Guǎng’s faction,
and Yuè was also implicated.
Yuè heard of this, worried, and resented it,
and died that winter in Gānzhōu.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Tutor
and given the posthumous name Xiāngmǐn.
Yuè's appearance was extraordinary and imposing,
and his discussions were spirited.
He had spent a long time on the frontier,
personally experienced more than ten battles,
understood the true nature of the enemy and the courage or cowardice of his officers and soldiers.
He employed ingenious strategies to achieve victory,
always acting with a well-formed plan.
He promoted and nurtured scholars,
captivated heroes and talented individuals,
and spent money like flowing water,
which is why people were happy to serve him.
He also once recommended people like Yáng Shǒusuí, ● Zhōng, and Tú Yōng,
all of whom gained fame in the world.
He was cordial with his relatives and kind to old acquaintances,
helping the poor and relieving the distressed,
as if fearing he would not be timely enough.
His courage and wisdom far surpassed that of others.
Once, when he and Zhū Yǒng led a thousand men on a border patrol,
the bandits suddenly arrived.
Zhū Yǒng wanted to flee,
but Yuè stopped him,
formed a battle array to secure their position,
making the bandits hesitate and not dare to advance.
At dusk,
he ordered all cavalry to dismount,
march in single file with gags in their mouths,
while he himself led the elite brave troops as the rearguard.
They marched fifty *lǐ* from behind the mountain until they reached the city.
He said to Zhū Yǒng:
"If I had made a move,
the bandits would have pursued and attacked,
and not a soul would have survived.
I feigned composure to mislead them.
Marching dismounted produced no military sounds,
so the bandits would not notice."
His nature was inherently audacious and uninhibited.
Once, when he traveled west to visit the Prince of Qín,
the prince held a banquet and presented female musicians.
Yuè said to the prince:
"Your humble servant has been a barking dog for Your Highness for a long time;
surely there is something to repay me with?"
He then asked for all the female musicians to take home.
One snowy night,
as he was drinking by the stove,
the female musicians surrounded him, holding *pípá*.
A junior officer returned from reconnaissance,
reporting on the enemy's situation.
Before he finished,
Yuè was greatly pleased,
poured a golden *zhī* of wine and offered it to him,
ordering the *pípá* to be played to accompany the wine,
and then bestowed the golden *zhī* upon him.
When the report was finished, he was even more delighted,
pointed to the most beautiful of the female musicians,
and said to the officer:
"What do you think of having this one?"
The officer, alarmed, expressed his thanks.
Yuè laughed heartily,
and immediately gave her to him.
The officer then exerted his utmost loyalty and effort wherever he went.
While Yuè was alive,
many blamed him for his greed for achievement.
But after his death,
generals became disheartened and soldiers grew lazy,
falsely claiming merit and squandering military provisions even more severely.
No border official ultimately matched Yuè.
The encomium states: It is not difficult for a person to possess talent,
but it is difficult to use one's talent well.
Wáng Jì and Wáng Yuè leading troops,
Yáng Shàn serving as an envoy,
Xú Yǒuzhēn managing river works—
their talents all surpassed others.
If they had merely followed the current and advanced steadily,
striving with their strategies and abilities,
they would still have been renowned officials and grandees.
Yet, due to their eagerness for advancement,
clinging to and relying on others,
although they received seals and were enfeoffed,
which for a civil official was a rare opportunity in their generation,
their reputation and prestige were thereby damaged,
and some even faced removal and confiscation.
The integrity of one's reputation is at stake;
how can one not take it seriously!
Collated Notes

Biographies, Chapter 60: Luó Héngxìn, Hóu Jìn, Yáng Níng, Wáng Lái, Sūn Yuánzhēn (Sūn Xū, Zhāng Xiàn), Zhū Jiàn, Yáng Xìnmín, Zhāng Jì (Zhú Yuān, Gěng Dìng, Wáng Shèng, Dèng Yóng), Mǎ Jǐn, Chéng Xìn, Bái Guī (son Yuè), Zhāng Zàn (Xiè Shìyuán), Kǒng Yōng (Lǐ Shímǐn), Dèng Tíngzàn, Wáng Shì, Liú Bǐng.
Luó Héngxìn,
courtesy name Yòngshí,
was from Dōngguǎn.
In the second year of Yǒnglè (1404), he passed the imperial examination.
He was reappointed as a *shùjíshì* (supernumerary Hanlin bachelor),
and then made Investigating Censor of the Ministry of Works.
He was dispatched to inspect flood damage in Zhèjiāng,
and memorialized to remit taxes for three counties.
He was promoted to Right Investigating Censor of the Ministry of Personnel,
but was implicated in an incident and demoted to an official in Jiāozhǐ.
After nine years,
Rénzōng ascended the throne,
and he was finally summoned back as a Censor.
He audited grain storage in Tōngzhōu,
inspected the capital region,
and cleared military accounts in Shānxī,
all with renown.
During the Xuāndé reign,
there were recommendations for him as suitable for a regional post.
He was ordered to receive the salary of an Assistant Surveillance Commissioner,
awaiting promotion.
In the third month after Yīngzōng Ēngzōng's Ēngzōng's enthronement,
he was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief [yòu qiān dū yù shǐ],
drilling troops in Píngliáng and Xīníng.
In the second year of Zhèngtǒng,
Jiǎng Guì attacked Ātái and Duǒ'érzhǐbó.
Hēngxìn participated in his military affairs.
Upon reaching Yú'érhǎi,
Guì and others, due to a lack of fodder and provisions,
stayed for ten days and then retreated.
Hēngxìn rebuked them, saying:
"You have received great favors from the state,
how dare you shrink back from the enemy?
Is it better to die by law or die by the enemy?"
Guì did not comply.
Hēngxìn submitted a memorial detailing Guì's procrastination.
The emperor showed his memorial to Supervising Minister Wáng Jì and others.
The following year, they advanced their troops
and thoroughly defeated them.
For his meritorious participation, Hēngxìn
was promoted one rank.
He returned home for his father's funeral and burial.
Upon returning to court,
he was reassigned to巡撫 Xúnfǔ Xuānfǔ and Dàtóng.
Assistant General Shí Hēng requested that one-third of Dàtóng's populace be conscripted into the army.
Hēngxìn memorialized to stop it.
In the tenth year, he was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief [yòu fù dū yù shǐ],
continuing as Circuit Inspector.
At that time, officials were dispatched to survey the military fields of the two garrisons.
Beyond eighty *mǔ* per soldier,
a tax of five *shēng* was levied on everything else.
Hēngxìn argued:
"During Emperor Wén's reign,
an edict was issued for border troops to exert their full strength in cultivating fields,
without levying taxes.
Your Majesty reiterated this command,
so why is such a measure suddenly being implemented now?
The various troops at the frontier,
toiling in defense of the border,
have no other means of livelihood;
they only engage in farming.
Every year, from winter to spring,
they welcome and send off Wǎlà envoys.
Only in March can they begin farming.
In July, they are again cutting grass.
After August,
they repair the passes and fortifications.
Counting the entire year, there is no respite.
Moreover, the borderlands are barren,
with meager harvests due to frost and drought.
If taxes are further levied,
the people will no longer cultivate,
which will inevitably lead to their flight.
The financial officials merely strive to accumulate grain,
unaware that the hearts of the people are not firm.
Even if there is grain,
who will guard it?"
The emperor accepted his words and stopped the measure.
Previously,
Hēngxìn had once memorialized:
"Yěxiān is specifically waiting for an opportune moment
to invade.
It is advisable to establish additional cities and garrisons at strategic locations directly to the north
as a precaution.
Otherwise,
I fear it will cause great trouble."
The Ministry of War discussed it,
but ultimately dismissed it.
When the Tǔmù Incident occurred,
people were terrified and panicked.
There was a proposal to abandon the city of Xuānfǔ.
Officials, soldiers, and civilians rushed out in disarray.
Hēngxìn, wielding a sword, sat below the city wall
and issued an order:
"Those who leave the city will be beheaded."
He also made the generals swear to defend the city to the death for the imperial court,
and only then did people's resolve settle.
Yěxiān brought the abdicated emperor to the south of the city
and sent a message demanding the gate be opened.
Hēngxìn ascended the city wall and responded:
"I am commanded to guard the city and
dare not open it without authorization."
Yěxiān hesitated and then withdrew.
The defenders of Chìchéng, Diāo'è, Huáilái, Yǒngníng, and Bǎo'ān abandoned their cities and fled;
they were all held accountable for their crimes.
At that time,
the imperial carriage had already gone north,
and enemy cavalry pressed on the city daily.
The areas around the pass gates were all battlefields.
Hēngxìn and Grand General Yáng Hóng, with an isolated city, faced the brunt of the attack,
defending against strong enemies externally
and shielding the capital internally.
After Hóng entered to defend,
he also guarded with Zhū Qiān,
and their meritorious services were very prominent.
Where his helmet rested,
his hair had all fallen out.
Upon Jǐngdì's enthronement,
he was promoted to Left Vice Censor-in-Chief [zuǒ fù dū yù shǐ].
The following year,
being seventy-four years old,
he requested retirement.
It was granted.
He returned home for eight years
and died at his residence.
Hóu Jǐn,
courtesy name Tíngyù,
was from Zézhōu.
He was courageous and principled from a young age.
He passed the imperial examination in the second year of Xuāndé
and was appointed Herald [xíngrén].
The indigenous officials of Wūsà and Wūméng, due to disputes over land, engaged in mutual killings.
An imperial edict was issued, sending Jǐn and his colleague Zhāng Cōng to mediate,
rectify their borders, and return.
When Vice Minister Zhāng Chǎng was sent as an envoy to Jiāozhǐ,
the pass gate was low.
The vanguard stooped to enter.
Jǐn reprimanded them, saying:
"This is but a dog's den!
How can you disgrace an imperial envoy!"
The Jiāo people then demolished the gate,
and he entered.
Upon his return,
he accepted no gifts.
He was promoted to Bureau Secretary [zhǔshì] in the Ministry of War.
In the early Zhèngtǒng period,
he followed Minister Chái Chē and others out of Tiěménguān to defend against Ātái, achieving merit,
and was promoted to Director [lángzhōng].
He followed Wáng Jì on the campaign to Lùchuān,
reaching Jīnchǐ.
Wáng Jì personally led the main army to attack Sī Rènfā,
while sending Jǐn to reinforce Dàhóuzhōu.
When the three-thousand-strong enemy arrived,
he supervised Commander-in-chief Mǎ Ràng and Lú Yuè to defeat and repel them.
He then traveled day and night over Gāolí Gòngshān
to rendezvous with the main army,
and pressed upon their stronghold.
After Lùchuān was pacified,
he was appointed Right Vice Minister of Rites [lǐbù yòu shìláng],
participating in the military affairs of Yúnnán.
An edict commanded him and Yáng Níng to alternate every two years.
When Wáng Jì campaigned against Lùchuān again,
Jǐn was promoted to Left Vice Minister [zuǒ] for his merits.
In the ninth year, he was replaced and returned.
During his mother's mourning,
he was recalled to service,
and soon after transferred to the Ministry of War.
In the eleventh year, he again replaced Níng to garrison Yúnnán.
When Sī Jīfā fled to Mèngyǎng,
Wáng Jì again marched south.
Jǐn and Commander-in-chief Zhāng Yuè divided their troops and advanced to the Jīnshājiāng,
defeating them at Guǐkūshān.
An imperial letter praised and rewarded him.
In the early Jǐngtài period,
the Miáo leader Wéi Tóngliè of Guìzhōu rebelled,
besieging Xīntiān, Píngyuè, Qīngpíng, and Xīnglóng garrisons.
Jǐn was ordered to oversee the Guìzhōu military affairs and suppress them.
At that time, Assistant General Tián Lǐ had already lifted the sieges of Xīntiān and Píngyuè.
Jǐn then dispatched troops to attack and defeat the various bandits of Dūlú and Shuǐxī,
and the Guìzhōu road was finally opened.
He also transferred Yúnnán troops
to converge via Wūsà,
opened various roads in Bìjié,
summoned Pǔ'ān local soldiers to reinforce Ānnán garrison,
and personally led his army to attack Zǐtáng, Mílè, and more than ten other strongholds.
When the bandits again besieged Píngyuè,
he returned his army and repelled them.
He then divided his scouts at Qīpánpō, Yángchánghé, and Yánglǎobǎo,
lifted the siege of Qīngpíng,
and advanced east to Chóng'ānjiāng,
where he met with Wáng Jì's forces.
The roads from Xīnglóng to Zhènyuǎn were all opened.
When the victory was reported,
he was promoted to Minister of War [bīngbù shàngshū].
He then advanced to conquer the Shǎnggǎi Miáo,
capturing their leader Wáng Ātóng and thirty-four others.
Another bandit, Ā Zhào, falsely proclaimed himself King Zhào,
and led his followers to raid Qīngpíng.
Jǐn again attacked and captured him.
The six tribes of Shuǐxī Miáo, including Ā Hū, all voluntarily requested to submit,
and Jǐn was commanded to handle them as appropriate.
In the eighth month of the first year of Jǐngtài, he died of exhaustion at Pǔdìng,
aged fifty-three.
He was granted a memorial sacrifice and burial,
and his son was inherited as a hereditary chiliarch of the Jǐnyīwèi.
Yáng Níng,
courtesy name Yānmì,
was from Shè.
He passed the imperial examination in the fifth year of Xuāndé.
He was appointed Bureau Secretary [zhǔshì] in the Ministry of Justice.
He was intelligent, versatile, and highly esteemed at the time.
In the early years of the Zhèngtǒng reign,
he followed Shàngshū Wèi Yuán to inspect Xuān and Dà.
In the fourth year, he joined Dūdū Wú Liàng in conquering Lùchuān.
The rebels offered to surrender at the army gate,
but Níng said:
“They surrender before a blow has been struck,
they are luring us.
We should maintain strict military readiness.”
This was not heeded,
and Níng was ordered to supervise the transport of supplies to Jīnchǐ.
Soon after, the rebels indeed launched a large attack,
and the government forces suffered a defeat.
The various generals were found guilty,
while Níng was promoted to Lángzhōng.
He again followed Wáng Jì to Téngchōng to defeat the rebels,
and Níng, along with Tàipú Shǎoqīng Lǐ Fén, supervised the battle,
both rendering meritorious service.
When the army returned,
Níng was exceptionally promoted to Xíngbù Yòushìláng.
He suffered a mother's mourning,
but was compelled to resume his duties.
In the ninth year, he replaced Hóu Jìn in assisting with military affairs in Yúnnán.
At that time, Lùchuān had just been pacified.
Níng, considering Téngchōng to be a strategic location,
together with Dūdū Mù Áng, built a city and established a guard unit,
stationing soldiers to control the various barbarian tribes.
The border region was thus stabilized.
After two years,
he was recalled.
When bandits arose in Mǐn and Zhè,
Níng was ordered to suppress them in Jiāngxī.
Whenever the bandits arrived,
he would defeat them.
During his leisure, he inquired about the people's hardships,
and the region became submissive.
In the early years of Jǐngtài,
he was recalled and appointed Lǐbù Shàngshū,
handling departmental affairs alongside Hú Yíng.
The Khān from Yībĕi sent envoys to offer tribute,
and Níng said:
“The envoys should be detained for several days,
entertained, rewarded, and given gifts,
twice as generously as Yěxiān's envoys.
He is by nature very suspicious,
and the two groups will surely stir up internal discord,
thus the border troubles can be alleviated.”
The Emperor, however, valued sincerity and trust,
and did not permit this.
That winter,
due to a foot ailment, he was transferred to the Nánxíngbù.
In the seventh year, he was impeached by Yùshǐ Zhuāng Shēng,
and an investigation was dispatched but not yet reported.
Níng strongly denounced the censor,
and the Dūcháyuàn again impeached Níng for suppressing official speech.
An imperial edict exempted him from punishment,
and a record of the case was shown to him.
Upon Yīngzōng's restoration,
he was ordered to retire.
He died the following year.
Níng was talented and good at cultivating relations with powerful nobles.
He once requested hereditary荫 from his past military achievements.
His son, Yū, was then one year old,
and consequently obtained the position of Fùqiānhù of Xīn'ānwèi.
Wáng Lái,
courtesy name Yuánzhī,
was from Cíxī.
In the second year of Xuāndé, he was appointed Jiàoyù of Xīnjiàn due to his performance on the civil service examination's乙榜.
The Níngwángfǔ ordered students to serve as musicians and dancers,
but Lái requested that Daoist priests be used instead.
The establishment of musician-dancers in the various princely estates began with this.
In the sixth year, he was promoted to Yùshǐ upon recommendation,
and was sent to inspect the four prefectures of Sū, Sōng, Cháng, and Zhèn.
He was ordered to work with Xúnfǔ Zhōu Chén to investigate subordinate officials,
with an imperial decree stating,
“Please seek imperial decision from above.”
Lái said:
“When dealing with corrupt officials,
we should remove them as quickly as possible.
If we must seek permission before acting,
the common people will suffer greatly.”
The Emperor therefore revised the decree and granted it to him.
The palace eunuch Chén Wǔ, acting on the Empress Dowager's orders,
was extremely abusive on his mission to Jiāngnán.
Lái repeatedly restrained him.
Upon Wǔ's return,
he complained to the Emperor.
The Emperor asked Dūyùshǐ Gù Zuǒ:
“Who is the巡按?”
Zuǒ replied with Lái's name.
The Emperor sighed and praised his virtue,
saying,
“I recognize him.”
When Lái reported on his mission,
the Emperor’s commendation and encouragement were exceptionally strong.
Upon Yīngzōng's enthronement,
recommended by Yáng Shìqí,
he was promoted to Shānxī Zuǒcāncè.
He said:
“Displaced people settle down wherever they are.
When they are recalled to their ancestral lands,
they often flee again due to loss of property.
I request that they be allowed to register wherever they reside.”
He further said:
“Local officials do not prioritize agriculture,
leading to many idle people.
When taxes are collected, it often leads to deaths.
The imperial court pities their unemployment
and issues decrees to waive taxes,
but fields become increasingly fallow,
and there is no tax revenue,
burdening good citizens.
Therefore, virtuous magistrates should be selected
and assigned the duty of promoting agriculture.
For fallow land,
nearby households should be allowed to cooperate,
and after providing rent,
they may divide the rest.
When the original owner resumes cultivation,
it should be returned to them.
Anything that can supplement the main occupation, like sericulture,
should be allowed to be planned.
Furthermore, the Tíxué Fēngxiàn officials should supervise this,
so that people will know to focus on fundamental matters.”
This was adopted.
Lái was incorrupt in office
and experienced in governance.
Shìláng Yú Qiān, while pacifying Shānxī,
highly praised his talent,
saying he could be placed in the emperor's close service.
However, Lái was strict in enforcing the law
and particularly abhorred evil,
beating ten incompetent county magistrates to death for official matters.
He was subsequently imprisoned
and sentenced to penal servitude.
He was pardoned,
and reassigned to Guǎngdōng with his original rank.
From this point, Lái began to change his ways and became more lenient,
and his administration also improved.
In the thirteenth year of Zhèngtǒng, he was promoted to Hénán Zuǒbùzhèngshǐ.
The following year, he was transferred to Zuǒfùdūyùshǐ,
and appointed Xúnfǔ of Hénán and Húguǎng Xiāngyáng and other prefectures.
When Yěxiān threatened the capital,
Lái was ordered to lead troops to defend the Emperor.
After crossing the river,
he heard that the invaders had retreated,
and then led his forces back.
In the first year of Jǐngtài,
the Miáo in Guìzhōu rebelled.
Zǒngdū Húguǎng, Guìzhōu Jūnwù Hóu Jìn died in battle,
and Lái was promoted to Yòudūyùshǐ to replace him.
He joined Bǎodìngbó Liáng Bǎo,
and Dūdū Máo Shèng and Fāng Yīng,
to combine forces and suppress the rebellion.
Upon reaching Jìngzhōu,
the rebels plundered Chángshā, Bǎoqìng, and Wǔgāng.
Lái and others divided their forces to intercept and attack,
capturing and beheading over three thousand people,
and the rebels fled.
Soon after,
they raided again,
but the government forces won successive battles.
The rebel leader Wéi Tóngliè occupied Xīnglóng,
and raided Píngyuè, Qīngpíng, and other garrisons.
Lái and Fāng Yīng defeated him.
The rebels retreated to defend Xiānglúshān,
a steep and precipitous mountain.
Shèng, Yīng, and Dūdū Chén Yǒu advanced along three routes,
with Lái and Bǎo's main army following.
They successively captured over three hundred stockades,
and their forces converged at the foot of Xiānglúshān.
They fired cannons, blasting the cliffs and rocks,
the sound shaking the earth.
The rebels, terrified,
tied up Tóngliè and fifty-eight other rebel generals and surrendered.
The rest all dispersed.
They then moved their army to Qīngpíng,
and also dispatched an order to Sìchuān troops to jointly suppress the rebels in Dūyún, Cǎotáng, and other areas.
The rebels, seeing the approaching army, prepared cattle and wine to surrender.
With the rebellion pacified,
the army returned.
An imperial edict ordered Lái and Bǎo to remain to govern.
Soon after, Lái was ordered to also serve as Xúnfǔ of Guìzhōu.
He submitted a memorial stating:
“Recently, due to military operations in Qián and Chǔ,
the practice of selling official ranks was temporarily implemented.
Now that the rebels are somewhat pacified,
only Píngyuè, Dūyún, and four other garrisons lack provisions.
Merchants should be summoned to trade for salt,
and the practice of accepting grain for payment should be abolished.”
This was approved.
In the tenth month of the third year, he was recalled,
and additionally made concurrent Grand Judge of the Court of Judicial Review (Dàlǐ Sì Qīng).
Bǎo stated that Lái had rendered great service,
and requested a special commendation for him.
The Censor-in-Chief (Dū Gěishì Zhōng) Sū Lín rebutted this,
and so it was stopped.
When Lái was returning and on the road,
because the Miáo people in Guìzhōu rebelled again,
an imperial edict ordered him to turn back his army and go to suppress them.
The next year,
the matter was settled.
He was recalled to serve as Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shàngshū) in Nánjīng.
When Emperor Yīngzōng was restored to the throne,
all six ministers were dismissed.
Lái returned home.
In the sixth year of Chénghuà, he died at home.
His grandson, Yuánzhēn,
whose given name was Yǔ,
was known by his courtesy name (zì),
and was from Déxīng.
In the thirteenth year of Yǒnglè, he passed the imperial examination for jinshi.
He was appointed Principal of the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù Zhǔshì),
and successively served as Director (Lángzhōng).
At the beginning of Emperor Yīngzōng's reign,
he was promoted to Right Administration Commissioner (Yòu Cānzhèng) of Hénán based on recommendations.
He was honest and prudent in office,
and had administrative talent.
In the eighth year of Zhèngtǒng,
the grand ministers jointly recommended him,
and he was promoted to Left Administration Commissioner (Zuǒ Bùzhèngshǐ) of Zhèjiāng.
After a long time,
bandits rose up in great numbers between Fújiàn and Zhèjiāng,
and rebelled again after being pardoned.
When Emperor Jǐngdì ascended the throne,
troops were dispatched to suppress them.
Yuánzhēn had predicted that the bandits would definitely rebel,
and submitted a strategy,
requesting preparations to be made.
At this point, he was immediately ordered to participate in discussing military affairs,
and to penetrate deep to capture their leaders.
However, the remaining bandits in Wēnzhōu had not yet been eliminated,
so the Grand Coordinator (Dū Zhǐhuī) Lǐ Xìn was appointed Assistant Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū Qiānshì),
and troops were mobilized to suppress them.
Consequently, Yuánzhēn was appointed Vice Minister of War (Bīngbù Zuǒ Shìláng),
to participate in Xìn's military affairs,
and to guard Zhèjiāng.
When his mother passed away,
he was supposed to leave,
but the Vice Censor-in-Chief (Fù Dū Yùshǐ) Xuān Ní requested that he be retained.
The request was granted.
In the first year of Jǐngtài,
Yuánzhēn advanced his troops to assault the bandit lairs.
He captured and beheaded bandit leaders such as Táo Dé'èr,
pacified and resettled over 3,600 people,
and recovered kidnapped men and women.
When the victory was reported,
an imperial rescript (xǐshū) praised and encouraged him.
He requested leave to mourn his mother.
After a month,
he returned to his post.
He then divided his troops to exterminate the remaining bandits.
He proposed to divide the land of Ruì'ān to establish Tàishùn,
and to divide the lands of Lìshuǐ and Qīngtián counties to establish the four districts of Yúnhé, Xuānpíng, and Jǐngníng.
Officials were appointed and garrisons established,
and the bandit problem thereupon ceased.
For his achievements,
he was promoted one rank.
The official land tax in Zhèjiāng was heavy.
The Right Administration Commissioner (Yòu Bùzhèngshǐ) Yáng Zàn requested to equalize it with the lighter rates on private land.
An edict ordered Yuánzhēn to oversee this,
and the land tax became equitable.
In the third year, he requested posthumous honors for military officers who died resisting bandits.
The Assistant Commander (Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī) Tuō Gāng and Wáng Yīng,
and the Assistant Grand Coordinator (Dū Zhǐhuī Qiānshì) Shěn Lín and Cuī Yuán,
all received posthumous gifts and aid.
In the sixth month, he was promoted to Minister of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū),
retaining his garrison duties as before.
Not long after,
he was ordered to inspect the various officials in Fújiàn,
and consequently remained to guard that region.
Fúzhōu and Jiànníng prefectures
formerly had silver mines,
which were suspended due to bandit disturbances.
The court deliberated reopening them,
but Yuánzhēn insisted that it was not permissible,
and so it was shelved.
In the winter of the fifth year,
he submitted a memorial saying: "Troops stationed in various regions
are often hindered in their farming by duties such as construction and transport.
It is advisable to select the elite and fill the ranks,
and return the rest entirely to agriculture.
If 10,000 more people
are settled for farming,
then 120,000 piculs of grain can be saved from the annual expenditure from the granaries,
and an additional 60,000 piculs of surplus grain can be accumulated.
How could there be a shortage of provisions for the troops?
This year, millions of piculs of grain are being transported by canal,
and the road expenses are immeasurable.
For example, for grain transported by military farmers in Zhèjiāng,
each picul has an additional loss of seven dou of rice;
for rice transported by the people themselves,
each
piculs has an additional loss of eight dou.
The rest is added based on the distance of the water route.
This means that the land is not increased,
but the levies are effectively doubled.
To wish for the people not to be distressed
is impossible.
Moreover, currently
the Grand Granary (Tàicāng) does not have a reserve for ten years,
and if floods or droughts occur,
how will it cope?
It is advisable to regulate expenditure according to revenue,
and eliminate redundant personnel and excessive expenses.
Once the granary reserves are abundant,
gradually
reduce the annual canal transport quota,
and the people's distress can be alleviated.
When I was an official in Hénán,
I investigated the registers of escaped commoners and found over 200,000 households,
all of whom had relocated to the areas between Nányáng, Táng, Dèng, Xiāng, and Fán.
They gather together to make a living;
how can we guarantee that they will not become bandits?
It is advisable, while this year is bountiful,
to send close ministers to tour the region,
to supervise officials to register them as permanent residents,
provide them with land and property,
encourage farming and sericulture,
establish community schools (shèxué),
village compacts (xiāngyuē), and charitable granaries (yìcāng),
to encourage them to focus on fundamental occupations.
Once their livelihoods are settled,
then gradually discuss taxes and corvée,
so that there will be no future troubles."
At that time, his advice was not fully adopted.
Later, during the rebellion of Liú Qiānjīn,
it turned out exactly as Yuánzhēn had predicted.
Afterwards,
he returned to guard Zhèjiāng.
When Emperor Yīngzōng was restored to power,
he was dismissed and returned home.
In the tenth year of Chénghuà, he died,
at the age of eighty-seven.
Wherever Yuánzhēn went, he rendered meritorious service,
and he was especially renowned in Zhèjiāng.
His grandson, Xū,
whose courtesy name was Fújí,
passed the imperial examination for jinshi in the eighth year of Chénghuà.
He served as Judicial Commissioner (Tuīguān) of Chángzhōu Prefecture,
and swiftly resolved difficult cases.
He was promoted to Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ) in Nánjīng.
He impeached the monk Jìxiǎo,
which displeased the emperor,
and he was flogged
and sent out to serve as Vice Commissioner (Fùshǐ) of Sìchuān.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
he successively served as Right Vice Censor-in-Chief (Yòu Fù Dū Yùshǐ),
and Grand Coordinator (Xúnfǔ) of Hénán.
The year was disastrous,
so he recruited people to build the embankment of the Biàn River;
when the embankment was completed, the hungry were also relieved.
The eunuch who served as Garrison Commander (Zhènshǒu Zhōngguān), Liú Láng, was greedy and tyrannical.
When cunning commoners reported cases to Láng,
Xū judged them according to law and sent them to exile.
Láng knelt and pleaded for them,
but Xū insisted and would not listen,
and Láng hated him to the bone.
When a minister's son behaved tyrannically in the countryside,
Xū restrained him.
Láng conspired with others
and had Xū transferred to serve as Grand Coordinator of Shǎnxī.
Soon after, he was transferred to serve as Grand Coordinator of Yún Yáng,
where he pacified and settled displaced people,
with over 90,000 households being registered.
In the first year of Zhèngdé, he was recalled to serve as Right Vice Minister of War (Bīngbù Yòu Shìláng) in Nánjīng.
In the fourth year, he was appointed Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū).
Before two months had passed,
Liú Jǐn disliked him,
and retroactively investigated his actions while Grand Coordinator of Hénán,
punishing him with grain payments to the frontier.
The court recommended Xū for Minister of Justice (Xíngbù Shàngshū),
but an imperial directive ordered him to retire.
After Jǐn was executed,
he was reinstated as Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shàngshū) in Nánjīng,
then transferred to the Ministry of Justice,
and again transferred to the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù).
In the thirteenth year, he requested retirement and left office.
At the beginning of the Jiājìng reign, he died,
and was posthumously named Qīngjiǎn.
Zhāng Xiàn,
courtesy name Tíngshì,
was from the same village as Xū,
and they both passed the *jìnshì* examination.
They successively served as Shàngshū.
He once served as the Right Administration Commissioner of Zhèjiāng,
and later, as the Right Vice Minister of Works, he supervised the mountain factories in Yìzhōu.
He took not a single hair's breadth from the public treasury for himself.
He successively held the post of Shàngshū of the Ministry of Rites in Nánjīng.
Liú Jǐn forced him to retire.
After Jǐn was executed,
he was reinstated to the Ministry of Works
and died.
Zhū Jiàn,
courtesy name Yòngmíng,
was from Jìnjiāng.
As a child, he cut flesh from his thigh to cure his father's illness.
Having passed the provincial examination,
he was appointed instructor of Púqí.
In the second year of Xuāndé, along with Kǒng Wényīng, the Prefect of Lúlíng, and forty-three others,
recommended by Gù Zuǒ,
he was summoned to observe government affairs in various circuits for three months,
and then promoted to Censor.
He toured Húguǎng as an Investigating Censor,
persuading the bandits Xiāo Qǐníng and others in Méihuā Tóng to surrender.
He requested the restoration of the old system,
whereby he, along with the Vice Commissioner and the Assistant Commissioner, would inspect their jurisdiction
and inquire into the hardships of the people.
It was the custom in Húxiāng
for men and women to marry mostly after the age of thirty.
Jiàn clarified the ritual system,
and the custom subsequently changed.
After three years, he was replaced and returned home.
In the fifth year of Zhèngtǒng, he again served as Investigating Censor in Guǎngdōng.
He memorialized for the establishment of a Garrison Commander-in-Chief in Qīnzhōu.
He was commanded to review prisoners,
and he redressed many injustices and
pacified a great many fugitives and rebels.
Upon his return to court,
he requested that one Assistant Commissioner be added to each Surveillance Commissioner's office throughout the empire,
specifically to manage military farms,
which subsequently became a permanent regulation.
In the seventh year, he was promoted, based on a recommendation, to Left Policy Advisor of Shānxī.
He memorialized for the reduction of the labor service for gathering firewood for border defenses in Píngyáng.
When Jǐngdì became regent,
he was promoted to Administration Commissioner.
Soon after, he was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief
and appointed Grand Coordinator of that region.
He memorialized, saying:
"Yěxiān is treacherous in a hundred ways,
and his killings and plunder are endless.
Again, under the pretext of 'harmonious relations,'
he sent envoys to spy.
Using 'escorting the Emperor' as a pretext,
he schemes to open the passes and be received.
Should we show even slight resistance,
he would then have an excuse.
Since his schemes are deep,
our foresight should be distant.
It is advisable to temporarily suspend the system of eunuchs supervising armies,
and grant powers of life and death to the Regional Commander,
so that his will is not obstructed
and his plans can be implemented.
Organize scattered soldiers,
recruit brave warriors,
offer generous rewards,
encourage loyal volunteers,
and levy 'rescue the Emperor' troops;
advancing on several fronts simultaneously,
let us exert ourselves to take revenge.
Then perhaps the Emperor can return,
and the enemy troops will retreat on their own.
Formerly, when bandits arose in Jiāngnán,
they all used 'punish Wáng Zhèn' as their slogan.
Indeed, affairs managed by the imperial court prosper,
but when managed by eunuchs, they fall into chaos.
In the past, when Gāo Huángdì discussed matters with his officials,
he would certainly send away his attendants,
fearing that secrets would be leaked.
I beg that the doors of powerful favorites be shut,
and that all important military and national affairs
be entrusted to great ministers;
they will certainly succeed."
Jǐngdì praised and adopted his advice.
At that time, the Wǎlà were menacing the border,
and Jiàn tirelessly made plans for defense day and night.
In the first year of Jǐngtài,
tens of thousands of enemy cavalry attacked Yànmén.
The Commander-in-Chief Lǐ Duān repelled them.
Soon after, they raided Héqu and Yìjǐng Bǎo,
killed two commanders,
and besieged the prefectures of Xīn and Dài.
Shí Hēng and others could not defend against them,
and they drove directly to the north of Tàiyuán city,
causing a great shock in Shānxī.
Jiàn was ordered to move his garrison to Yànmén,
while another Grand Commandant Assistant, Wáng Liáng, was dispatched to garrison Tàiyuán.
Reinforcements gradually gathered,
and the enemy, also satiated,
then withdrew.
At that time, Shānxī was still plagued by war and famine.
Jiàn externally enforced military preparations,
and internally comforted the disaster-stricken people,
working exhaustively to the utmost.
In the tenth month of the second year,
Luó Tōng, the Grand Censor in charge of Shānxī, was recalled,
and Jiàn was ordered to concurrently lead his affairs.
The following year, an imperial edict dispatched great ministers throughout the empire
to evaluate and dismiss officials.
Zōu Gàn, the Vice Minister of Rites, arrived in Shānxī
and impeached many officials.
Jiàn requested that Gàn be recalled,
whereupon Gàn severely criticized Jiàn for protecting [officials],
and the Emperor approved Gàn's words.
In the tenth month of that year, Jiàn was summoned to assist in court affairs.
Upon reaching the capital,
he retired from office.
Initially,
when Jǐngdì changed the heir apparent,
Jiàn wrote a letter to the Grand Secretary Chén Xún,
saying it was unacceptable.
Moreover, he said:
"Your Majesty, regarding the Retired Emperor,
you ought to abdicate your position to preserve the greater righteousness."
Xún was greatly alarmed.
When Yīngzōng was restored to the throne,
Jiàn went to the palace gate and presented a memorial of congratulation.
The Emperor said:
"Jiàn is old and ill,
why has he come rashly?
Let him be quickly ordered to return."
He lived at home for over twenty years and then died.
Yáng Xìnmín,
given name Chéng,
was known by his courtesy name,
and was from Xīnchāng, Zhèjiāng.
He passed the provincial examination and entered the Imperial Academy.
During the Xuāndé era,
he was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Works.
He returned home for his mother's mourning.
When preparing the burial, he personally carried earth and stones for several hundred paces,
saying:
"I am burying my mother,
and if I solely employ others,
I will not feel at peace."
After the mourning period ended,
he was reassigned to the Ministry of Justice.
During the Zhèngtǒng era,
he investigated military affairs in Jiāngxī.
Upon his return, he presented five memorials on the hardships of the people,
many of which were adopted.
Soon after, recommended by Wáng Zhí,
he was promoted to Left Policy Advisor of Guǎngdōng.
His integrity was beyond the ordinary.
He often traveled through the countryside,
investigating advantages and disadvantages to implement reforms.
His nature was strong and proud.
When Surveillance Commissioner Guō Zhì acted unlawfully,
Xìnmín impeached him and he was imprisoned.
Huáng Hàn replaced Zhì,
but Xìnmín again exposed his treachery.
Later,
he also impeached Assistant Commissioner Wéi Guǎng.
Guǎng then denounced Xìnmín,
and consequently, he and Hàn were both arrested.
The military and civilians clamored,
going to the palace gate to beg for Xìnmín to be retained.
An imperial edict reinstated Xìnmín's office,
while Hàn and Guǎng were found guilty after interrogation
and dismissed from office.
When Jǐngdì was regent,
Yú Qiān recommended him.
He was ordered to guard Báiyángkǒu.
At the time, Huáng Xiāoyǎng, a bandit from Guǎngdōng, was urgently besieging Guǎngzhōu.
The people of Lǐngnán pleaded for Yáng Xìnmín,
so he was appointed Right Assistant Censor-in-Chief to patrol and pacify the area.
The gentry and commoners heard of this and rejoiced among themselves, saying,
"Lord Yáng has come!"
At that time, Guǎngzhōu had been under siege for a long time.
The generals and soldiers were repeatedly defeated in battle,
and the people were prohibited from going in and out.
Firewood and foraging supplies were cut off,
and villagers who fled the bandits were refused entry,
many being harmed by the bandits.
The people grew more anxious and distressed and turned to the bandits.
When Xìnmín arrived,
he opened the city gates
and issued grain from the granaries.
He carved wooden tallies and gave them to the people,
allowing them to go in and out.
When the bandits saw the wooden tallies, they said,
"These were given by Lord Yáng,"
and dared not harm them.
All those who had fled the bandits were taken in and protected.
The people felt as if they had been reborn.
Xìnmín intensified his military preparations
and used various methods to recruit and pacify.
Those who surrendered arrived daily.
He then sent an envoy with a proclamation into the bandit camp,
explaining his benevolence and trustworthiness.
Xiāoyǎng said,
"To hear a single word from Lord Yáng,
I would die without regret."
He set a date to request a meeting.
Xìnmín went alone in a cart,
and spoke with him across the moat.
The bandit party looked on from afar,
shouting with joy,
"It truly is Lord Yáng!"
They vied to prostrate themselves in obeisance,
some even shedding tears.
The bandits offered a large fish,
and Xìnmín accepted it without suspicion.
Xiāoyǎng was about to surrender,
but when Dūdu Dǒng Xīng's large army arrived,
the bandits suddenly changed their minds.
That night, a large star fell outside the city.
Seven days later, Xìnmín died of a sudden illness.
This was on the Yǐmǎo day of the third month of Jǐngtài's first year.
The soldiers and commoners gathered and wept,
and the whole city wore white mourning clothes.
When the bandits heard of it,
they too wept, saying,
"With Lord Yáng dead,
we have no path to return."
Not long after,
Xīng pacified the bandits,
but many villages and settlements in his path were plundered and massacred.
The people looked up to heaven and cried,
"If Lord Yáng were alive,
how could we have come to this!"
Upon hearing the news,
an imperial burial and sacrifice were granted,
and his son, Yáng Jiǔ, was registered as a student of the Imperial Academy.
The people of Guǎngdōng went to the capital to request the erection of a shrine,
which was granted.
During the Chénghuà reign,
he was posthumously granted the谥 Gōnghuì.
Long after,
following the request of the selected official Lú Cóngyuàn,
the relevant authorities were ordered to offer sacrifices on his death anniversary each year.
Zhāng Jì,
courtesy name Zhòngdé,
was from Ānhuà.
During the Yǒnglè reign, he passed the provincial examination
and entered the Imperial Academy.
In the early Xuāndé reign, he was appointed Censor.
He went out to inspect Jiāngxī
and reviewed prisoners in Fújiàn,
earning a reputation for benevolence and integrity.
In the eighth year of Zhèngtǒng,
Wáng Zhí, the Minister of Personnel, and others responded to an imperial edict
to widely recommend court officials who were public-spirited, honest, and learned in their conduct.
Jì was among them.
He was promoted to Right Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review
and became巡抚 Shāndōng.
Previously,
Jǐnán had established an official for pacifying the people,
specifically for pacifying vagrants.
Later, this instead caused disturbance to the people,
so Jì memorialized to abolish it.
It was customary during droughts
to often cut open newly buried graves,
mutilating the bodies,
believing this to be the cause of the drought.
This was called
"striking the drought bones."
At Jì's suggestion, this was completely prohibited.
Upon returning to court,
he was promoted to Right Junior Minister.
After some time,
he was ordered to inspect the famine victims from Jìníng to Huái and Yáng.
Jì established laws for catching locusts,
suspended non-urgent matters,
remitted arrears, and distributed grain from granaries.
The people relied on him for relief.
In the winter of the thirteenth year,
he was appointed巡抚 Zhèjiāng.
Initially,
Yè Zōngliú from Qìngyuán and Chén Jiànhú from Líshuǐ
gathered crowds to steal from the Bǎofēng silver mines in Fújiàn.
Later, the bandits killed each other,
and chaos ensued.
In the seventh month of the ninth year,
Zhú Yuān, a Counselor in Fújiàn, went to capture them,
but was seized and killed.
Zōngliú usurped the title of King.
At that time, Dèng Máoqī in Fújiàn also gathered a crowd to revolt,
and his power grew immensely.
Zōngliú and Jiànhú joined him,
plundering across the borders of Zhèjiāng, Jiāngxī, and Fújiàn.
Counselor Gěng Dìng,
Assistant Magistrate Wáng Shèng, and Assistant Dūdu Chén Róng,
Commander Liú Zhēn,
Commander Wú Gāng, Gōng Lǐ,
and Yǒngfēng County Magistrate Dèng Yǒng
were defeated and perished one after another.
Bandits Sū Yá and Yú Bótōng from Suìchāng plundered Lánxī
and also joined them,
shaking the distant and nearby regions.
When Jì arrived,
he sent Shí Mào, the Prefect of Jīnhuá, to attack and kill Yá and others,
and pacify the remaining factions.
Meanwhile, Jiànhú, due to a dispute, killed Zōngliú,
monopolizing his followers.
He declared himself Great King,
named his state Tàipíng,
established the era name Tàidìng,
and appointed false generals and commanders.
He besieged Chǔzhōu
and divided his forces to plunder Wǔyì, Sōngyáng, Lóngquán, Yǒngkāng, Yìwū, Dōngyáng, and Pǔjiāng counties.
Not long after,
Máoqī died,
and Jiànhú's power became isolated.
Jì ordered Dīng Níng, the Assistant Magistrate of Líshuǐ, to lead the elder Wáng Shìchāng and others with a proclamation into the bandit lair to persuade them.
Jiànhú then surrendered with his followers.
Only Táo Dé'èr refused to be pacified,
killed the envoy,
and retreated into the mountains to cause trouble as before.
This was in the fourth month of the fourteenth year.
After Jì had persuaded Jiànhú to surrender,
other bandits like Sū Jìyǎng plundered Jīnhuá
and were also captured by the official army.
The bandit forces then further declined.
That autumn,
Jǐngdì ascended the throne,
recalled Jì,
who died on the way.
Wherever Jì went,
he always had accomplishments.
The people of Shāndōng and the two Zhè regions remembered him for a long time.
When Jiànhú arrived in the capital,
the Emperor pardoned him from execution.
Later, he benefited from another amnesty
and was released to serve in the garrison.
When Yěxiān invaded,
Jiànhú escaped during the chaos,
but was captured
and executed.
Zhú Yuān
was from Fènghuà.
Gěng Dìng
was from Hézhōu.
Wáng Shèng
was from Yùnchéng.
Dèng Yǒng
was from Lèchāng.
All were successful candidates in the imperial examination.
Yǒng's army was routed, and he was captured,
but he died unyielding.
An imperial edict ordered his burial.
Yuān and others were posthumously granted official titles
and one son was recorded for privilege.
Mǎ Jǐn,
courtesy name Shǒulǐ,
was from Xīnlè.
He passed the imperial examination in the second year of Xuāndé.
He was filial to his parents.
When they passed away,
he personally carried earth to bury them.
During the Zhèngtǒng reign,
he was dispatched as a Censor to inspect Zhèjiāng.
At that time, ships were being built to prepare against Japanese pirates,
and timber was requisitioned from the various prefectures of Yán and Qú.
Jǐn feared that soldiers would abuse their power and cut down trees indiscriminately,
so he requested a prohibition and rectification of this,
which was approved.
Wherever he went,
the corrupt and cunning disappeared.
He memorialized to relieve the famine in the four prefectures of Zhèn, Tái, Chǔ, and Níngshào.
The position of Lángzhōng of the Yànfēng Bureau in the Ministry of Personnel had been vacant for a long time,
and the Emperor ordered a selection.
It happened that Jǐn's nine-year term was complete,
and Shàngshū Guō Jǐn recommended Jǐn as honest and upright,
so he was appointed.
Ten years later, he was recommended and promoted to Right Administration Commissioner of Húguǎng.
At the end of the Zhèngtǒng reign,
rebellious Miáo from Húnán plundered Jìngzhōu.
Jǐn was ordered to pacify and persuade them together with Censor Hóu Jué,
while Assistant General Zhāng Shàn led troops to follow.
When Jǐn and the others arrived,
they recruited several thousand people to return to their occupations,
and those who had gone out to plunder were defeated.
Soon after, he and Shàn broke several strongholds in Qīxī.
At the beginning of the Jǐngtài reign,
he and Shàn again severely defeated several caves in Làpó.
Afterward,
together with Assistant General Lǐ Zhèn, they defeated the bandits at Qīnglóngdù and Mǎyángshān,
pursuing the fleeing enemy to Jīxīlǐng,
beheading more than 1,400 in total.
When the army returned,
the bandits from Jìngzhōu again came out to plunder,
so their stronghold was raided,
and the number of beheadings and captures was as before.
Bandits from Wǔgāng and Chéngxī allied with the Mán of Guǎngxī,
occupying Qīngfèishān,
and he again attacked and defeated them with Zhèn.
They captured 560 bandits, including Yáng Guāngquán,
and beheaded twice that number.
The various strongholds of Fúchéng,
hearing the news, [⿰⺨發] submitted.
facing arrows and spears,
Jǐn was in and out of the ranks for three years,
but his strategic planning and transportation of provisions contributed even more.
He was transferred to Left Administration Commissioner.
In recognition of his merit,
he was promoted one rank.
In the fifth month of the sixth year,
he was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief,
still receiving the salary of a second-rank official.
He became Grand Coordinator of Hénán,
and pacified over 31,000 households of displaced people.
At the beginning of the Tiānshùn reign,
the Grand Coordinator official position was abolished,
and Jǐn was also dismissed and returned home,
dying long after.
Jǐn was by nature honest and resolute.
Yáng Shìqí once called him
"ice, frost, iron, and stone."
Chéng Xìn,
courtesy name Yànshí,
his ancestors were from Xiūníng,
and during the Hóngwǔ reign, they garrisoned Héjiān,
and thus settled there.
Xìn passed the imperial examination in the seventh year of Zhèngtǒng,
and was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Personnel.
When Emperor Jǐng ascended the throne,
he recommended Xuē Xuān and two others for promotion.
When Yěxiān attacked the capital,
Xìn supervised the troops defending the West Gate,
and submitted a memorial with five proposals.
When Grand Commissioner Sūn Táng was defeated by Yěxiān,
and wanted to enter the city,
Xìn refused to admit him,
and ordered the troops to fire arrows and cannons from the city walls to assist him.
Táng fought with renewed vigor,
and Yěxiān then retreated.
In the first year of Jǐngtài, he requested relief for the famine victims in Jīfǔ,
and the reinstatement of Héjiān's school officials and students who had been dismissed due to the military campaign,
all of which were approved.
He was promoted to Left Supervising Secretary.
Due to heavenly portents, he submitted ten proposals for national revival and consolidation.
Regarding respecting Heaven,
he requested the Emperor to practice filial piety and brotherly love in reality to respond to Heaven's will.
The Emperor praised and accepted this.
In the second month of the following year, he was appointed Right Administration Vice Commissioner of Shāndōng,
and supervised the provisioning of Liáodōng.
Grand Coordinator Kòu Shēn memorialized that anyone stealing more than one dàn of grain should be executed,
and also introduced new measuring vessels that were larger than the old ones,
and instructed Xìn to verify them.
Xìn immediately smashed them,
saying:
"How can we lead people to death!"
From then on, Shēn was displeased with Xìn.
Soon after, he left due to mourning.
After the mourning period,
he was appointed Administration Vice Commissioner of Sìchuān.
He managed the provisions for Sōngpān,
and together with Attendant Censor Luó Qǐ, they broke several strongholds of Hēihǔ.
In the first year of Tiānshùn,
Xìn came to offer congratulations.
At that time, those who had offered advice during the Jǐngtài period were being recorded,
and Xìn was specially promoted to Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud.
The number of horses in the capital guards had often been depleted,
so Xìn set a regular schedule for their requisition.
The three camp generals, Shí Hēng, Sūn Táng, and Cáo Qīn, were all favored for their
"Seizing the Gate"
merit,
and shielded various military officials,
claiming that the Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud was harsh and urgent,
and requested that the department be transferred to the Ministry of War.
Xìn said:
"Emperor Gāo ordered that the number of horses in the Imperial Stud
should not be known to others.
If it is transferred to the Ministry of War,
and the horses are depleted,
the Imperial Stud will not know.
If there is an emergency,
and horses are insufficient,
who will bear the blame?"
The Emperor agreed with this,
and so it remained under the Imperial Stud as before.
The following year,
he was appointed Left Assistant Censor-in-Chief,
and Grand Coordinator of Liáodōng.
Commander Xià Lín acted lawlessly,
and Supervising Secretary Hú Dǐng exposed his forty crimes.
Xìn reported this,
and Lín was sent to the Jǐnyī Wèi prison.
Mén Dá said that Xìn should not have submitted the memorial on his behalf,
and the Emperor ordered him to state his case.
At that time, Kòu Shēn was in charge of the Censorate,
and resuming their previous disagreement,
impeached Xìn.
He was summoned to the imperial prison,
and demoted to Junior Minister of the Nanjing Court of the Imperial Stud.
In the fifth year, he was summoned to be Right Vice Minister of Justice.
He returned home for his mother's mourning.
In the first year of Chénghuà, he was appointed to the Ministry of War,
and soon after transferred to Left Vice Minister.
The Shāndūzhǎng Mán of Róngxiàn, Sìchuān, rebelled repeatedly,
capturing Hécí and nine other counties.
The court discussed dispatching a large army to suppress them.
Lǐ Jǐn, Earl of Xiāngchéng, was appointed Commander-in-Chief,
Eunuch Liú was appointed Superintendent,
and Xìn was promoted to Minister of War,
overseeing military affairs.
Upon reaching Yǒngníng,
the forces advanced along separate routes.
Grand Commissioner Ruì Chéng went via Róngxiàn,
Grand Coordinator of Guìzhōu and Censor-in-Chief Chén Yí and Assistant General Wú Jīng went via Mángbù,
Grand Commissioner Cuī Mín went via Pǔshì Bīngnǎo,
Earl of Nánníng Máo Róng went via Lǐzǐguān,
Grand Coordinator of Sìchuān and Censor-in-Chief Wāng Hào and Assistant General Zǎi Yòng went via Dùchuánpù,
and Left and Right Mobile Corps Generals Luó Bǐngzhōng and Mù Yì went via Jīnéchí,
while Xìn and Jǐn remained in the center to coordinate.
Fighting for six days,
they broke over 750 strongholds at Lóngbèi and Bàowěi.
The following year, they reached Dàbà,
and burned 1,450 strongholds.
In total, they beheaded over 4,500,
and captured countless others.
Those of the nine clans who refused to submit to civilization were moved to Lúzhōu Guard,
and a pass and fort were added at Dùchuánpù.
Dàbà was renamed Tàipíngchuān Chiefdom,
and the territory of Shāndūzhǎng was divided,
with officials appointed and administrations established to control it.
The Emperor issued an imperial letter praising and commending them.
In recognition of his merit,
he was promoted concurrently to Minister of the Grand Court of Revision,
and served in the Ministry of War with Bái Guī.
Censors impeached Xìn for exaggerating the number of enemy heads.
Xìn memorialized four times to request retirement,
but was not granted.
Xìn wanted to achieve something,
but was hindered by Guī,
and felt discontent,
often feigning illness.
In the spring of the sixth year, there was a drought,
and in response to an imperial edict, he spoke of four military affairs that should be reformed,
and five military abuses that should be rectified.
In summary, he said: Yánsuī and the two Guǎng regions suffered annual raids,
and a grand minister should be chosen to take overall command;
many displaced people from all directions gathered in Jīng and Xiāng,
and should be planned for early;
the training of the capital army was without method,
and promotions and rewards for merit were improper.
His words often implicitly criticized Guī.
Guī memorialized to suppress it.
He was transferred to the Nanjing Ministry of War,
participating in strategic affairs.
The following year, he retired,
and died a year later.
He was posthumously granted Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
and given the posthumous title Xiāngyì.
Xìn had talent and ability,
and understood the larger picture.
When he was campaigning against the southern Man,
he was granted the authority to act as he saw fit.
Until he returned with his troops,
he never arbitrarily awarded or punished a single person.
He said:
"Punishment and reward
are the great powers of a ruler.
It is only when there is no other choice that they are delegated to others.
If the task happens to succeed,
to then act on one's own authority
is not what a minister should do."
While he was in Nánjīng,
the defending minister wanted to interfere with financial, grain, and judicial matters.
Xìn said:
"The defending minister is a high-ranking official,
appointed to guard against emergencies.
To do this
is merely the duty of officials in charge of specific departments."
Those who discussed the matter praised him.
His son, Mǐnzhèng,
can be found in the Biographies of Literati.
Bái Guī,
courtesy name Zōngyù,
was a native of Nángōng.
He became a Jinshi in the seventh year of Zhèngtǒng.
He was appointed Censor,
supervised Zhū Yǒng's army,
and had merits in campaigning against the Wùliánghā.
While inspecting Shanxi,
he resolved over a hundred doubtful cases.
He accompanied the imperial carriage on the Northern Expedition
and was trapped at Tǔmù.
After escaping and returning,
Emperor Jǐng ordered him to Zézhōu to recruit soldiers.
Soon after, he was promoted to Shaanxi Surveillance Vice Commissioner,
then elevated to Zhejiang Right Administration Commissioner.
The Fújiàn bandit Zhèng Huái pretended to be a refugee and plundered Chǔzhōu.
He assisted the generals in pacifying them.
In the second year of Tiānshùn,
the Eastern Miao leaders Gānbǎzhū and others usurped titles
and attacked and plundered Dōuyún and other places.
An imperial edict promoted him to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief
to assist the army of Marquis Nánhé Fāng Yīng in the campaign.
Guī considered the Gǔzhǒng various barbarians as the wings of the Eastern Miao,
and first attacked and destroyed 147 stockades.
Then he joined forces at Qīngyá,
again breaking more than 470 stockades,
and pressed on to attack Liùměi Mountain.
Gānbǎzhū was captured,
and all the Miao tribes were terrified.
There was a disaster in Húguǎng,
so Guī was appointed to pacify it.
In the fourth year, he was summoned to become Right Vice Minister of War.
The following year,
Bólái raided Zhuānglàng.
Guī, along with Censor-in-Chief Wáng Hóng, assisted Grand Commissioner Féng Zōng with military affairs,
dividing troops to patrol the borders.
Guī defeated them at Gùyuán Prefecture.
In the seventh year, he was promoted to Minister of Works.
In the first year of Chénghuà,
the Jīng and Xiāng bandits Liú Qiānjīn and others rebelled.
Fúníng Bó Zhū Yǒng was ordered to be the commander-in-chief,
Grand Commissioners Xǐ Xìn and Bāo Zhèng were the left and right assistant generals,
eunuchs Táng Shèn and Lín Guì were ordered to supervise them,
and Guī was appointed to oversee military affairs,
deploying capital troops and troops from various circuits to jointly suppress them.
Qiānjīn,
whose given name was Tōng,
was a native of Xīhuá, Hénán.
The stone suanni at the county gate weighed a thousand jin,
and Tōng lifted it with one hand,
thus he was given the moniker.
In the Zhèngtǒng era,
refugees gathered between Jīng and Xiāng.
Tōng infiltrated them, spreading false prophecies,
secretly plotting to instigate rebellion.
Shí Lóng,
known as Shí Héshàng,
gathered followers and plundered.
Tōng joined him in raising an army,
falsely claiming to be the King of Hàn,
and establishing the era name Déshèng.
Forty thousand refugees followed them.
When Guī and others reached Nánzhāng,
the bandits met them in battle,
were defeated,
and pressed on to their stronghold with the momentum of victory.
Tōng fled to Shòuyáng,
intending to escape to Shaanxi.
Guī dispatched troops to block his path,
