so Tōng retreated to defend Dàshì,
and joined with Miáo Lóng.
The government army again defeated them at Yànpíng,
beheading Tōng's son Cōng and his followers Miáo Hǔ and others.
The bandits retreated to defend Hòuyán Mountain,
holding the treacherous terrain and raining down wood and stones.
The various armies attacked from four sides,
and Guī went back and forth supervising the battle.
All the soldiers climbed like ants.
The bandits were utterly defeated,
and Tōng and over 3,500 of his followers were captured.
More than 11,000 bandit women and children were captured,
their shelters were burned,
and the treacherous terrain was leveled before returning.
Shí Lóng and his follower Liú Chángzǐ and others escaped,
turning to plunder Sìchuān,
continuously capturing Wūshān and Dàchāng.
Guī and others divided their troops to press them.
Chángzǐ bound Lóng and surrendered,
and the remaining bandits were all pacified.
For his merits,
Guī was awarded太子少保 (Tàizǐ Shǎobǎo)
and his salary was increased by one grade.
He suffered the loss of his father.
After the burial,
he resumed his duties.
In the third year, he was transferred to Minister of War,
and concurrently supervised the Twelve Regimental Camps.
In the sixth year,
Āluōchū and others pastured in the Hétào region,
and Shaanxi was frequently raided.
Guī stated that the negligence of the Zhenxun officials should be punished.
The Yánsuí Pacification Commissioner Wáng Ruì, garrison eunuch Qín Gāng, and commander-in-chief Fáng Néng were all found guilty and dismissed.
Guī then proposed a major expedition to search Hétào,
deploying 100,000 capital troops and troops from other garrisons to Yánsuí.
However, the responsibility for supplying provisions was placed on the people of Hénán, Shānxī, and Shaanxi.
If they could not provide,
then the next year's taxes would be levied in advance,
which caused unrest in the interior.
And the three great generals sent before and after—Zhū Yǒng, Zhào Fǔ, and Liú Jù—
were all timid and unable to fight,
ultimately achieving nothing.
In the tenth year, he died in office
at the age of fifty-six.
He was posthumously granted 少傅 (Shǎofù)
and given the posthumous name Gōngmǐn.
Guī was naturally simple and dignified.
After returning from public duty, he would close his door and rest,
and no requests or visits were allowed.
When he was in Guìzhōu,
there was a person who, indignant at the abuses of a eunuch, wanted to assassinate him,
but mistakenly entered Guī's residence.
Guī, wrapped in his quilt, asked him.
The man was startled and said:
"Is it my Lord?"
Then he immediately cut his own throat,
but did not die,
and fell to the ground.
Guī called for a candle to examine him,
applied good medicine,
and sent him away.
People admired his magnanimity.
His second son, Yuè,
courtesy name Bǐngdé.
He passed the Jinshi examination with distinction,
and was appointed Compiler.
He successively held the posts of太子少保 (Tàizǐ Shǎobǎo)
and Minister of Rites.
He was skilled in historical precedents
and renowned for his literary talent.
Upon his death,
he was posthumously granted太子太保 (Tàizǐ Tàibǎo)
and given the posthumous name Wényù.
Zhāng Zàn,
courtesy name Zōngqì,
was a native of Xiàogǎn.
He became a Jinshi in the thirteenth year of Zhèngtǒng.
He was appointed Ministry of Works Principal,
then promoted to Section Chief,
and successively served as Prefect of Tàiyuán and Níngbō prefectures,
where he governed well.
In the early Chénghuà period,
Fú Zhù, the eunuch in charge of maritime trade, was greedy and tyrannical.
Zàn restrained his subordinates.
Zhù slandered Zàn at court,
so Zàn listed Zhù's crimes.
Zhù was reprimanded,
and many of his associates were punished by law.
High officials jointly recommended him,
and he was promoted to Guangdong Policy Advisor,
then transferred to Zhejiang Left Administration Commissioner.
In the winter of the tenth year,
he was appointed Right Vice Censor-in-Chief to pacify Sìchuān.
Yáng Huī, the retired Pacification Commissioner of Bōzhōu, reported
that the Yāobàgān and Wānxī stockades and the Zhòng'ān County Office under his jurisdiction were secretly occupied by "raw" Miao,
and requested imperial troops to advance and suppress them.
An imperial edict ordered Zàn to persuade them to return the encroached land,
and if they refused, to conquer them.
Zàn led troops to suppress and pacify them,
and requested the establishment of the Ānníng Pacification Commission.
Yáng Huī's son Yǒu was immediately appointed Pacification Commissioner to govern the area.
The edict approved it,
and he was awarded a commendation.
He requested to return due to his mother's old age,
but his mother had already passed away.
At that time, the rebels from Sōngmáo and Mào Fān encroached upon the border,
and an imperial edict reinstated him to his post.
Prior to this,
Secretary Lín Bì had stated:
“Sōngmáo was formerly a major stronghold.
Censor-in-chief Kòu Shēn and Vice Minister Luó Qǐ once, by invoking discretionary power,
exercised absolute control over that territory,
and thus achieved success.
Now, only two Assistant Regional Commanders are stationed there,
with a Vice Commissioner placed in the center to coordinate.
Their authority is slight;
when facing an enemy, they must report to the Governor-General for orders.
To request combat from a thousand miles away
leads to leaked plans and delayed action,
and no one has ever been able to gain an advantage.
It is advisable to appoint a high-ranking official to suppress them,
or perhaps even command Zàn to concurrently lead,
making him solely responsible for achieving results.”
In the seventh month of the twelfth year, Zàn was ordered to concurrently oversee military affairs in Sōngmáo, Ānmián, and Jiànchāng.
Upon Zàn’s arrival at the army,
he assessed the situation,
moved the former Assistant Commissioner’s station from Dàbà to Ānmián,
and ordered Vice Commander-in-chief Yáo Yù to be stationed in Sōngpān,
and Assistant Regional Commander Sūn Hào in Wēi and Dié,
as a pincer attack strategy.
Seizing the opportunity, he repaired the old road west of the river,
constructed a pontoon bridge,
and fortified Yuèchéng.
In Màozhōu and Diéxī,
wherever he passed, people surrendered and submitted.
He reached the three strongholds of Qǔshān
and attacked and broke them.
He then again suppressed the remaining rebels at Báicǎobà.
He successively destroyed fifty-two strongholds,
and all the rebel leaders, including Sāhā, were annihilated.
The other one hundred and five strongholds all offered horses and submitted,
and all the various barbarian tribes were pacified.
He left troops to guard strategic points
and increased the number of watchtowers and forts,
then returned with his army.
The Emperor commended his achievements,
summoned him to be appointed Left Vice Minister of Revenue,
but he declined and returned home to observe mourning until its completion.
In the fifteenth year, he was reinstated as Left Vice Censor-in-chief,
Director-General of Grain Transport,
and concurrently Governor of the prefectures north of the Huái River.
In the eighteenth year,
there was a great famine,
and he submitted a memorial requesting relief.
Fifty thousand taels of silver were issued,
and an imperial edict again ordered Zàn to move grain from Huái'ān granaries for distribution,
but Zàn had already died.
Zàn’s fame and achievements were well-known in Xīshǔ.
Later governors of Shǔ, such as Xiè Shìyuán and others,
though renowned,
did not equal Zàn.
However, regarding the campaign at Yāobàgān,
some said that Yáng Huī doted on his eldest illegitimate son, Yǒu,
and wished to make him an official.
He falsely claimed that the uncivilized Míáo were causing trouble,
and Zàn, believing him, launched the army.
Thus, his achievements were not without fabrication.
Xiè Shìyuán,
courtesy name Zhòngrén,
was a native of Chánglè.
He passed the imperial examination in the fifth year of Jǐngtài (1454).
He was appointed as a Section Chief in the Ministry of Revenue.
While supervising the granary at Tōngzhōu,
he detailed four abuses,
and repeatedly clashed with the eunuchs overseeing the granaries.
In the seventh year of Tiānshùn (1463), he was promoted to Magistrate of Jiànchāng Prefecture.
The area was infested with bandits,
who were protected by military generals.
Shìyuán used other matters to hold the generals accountable,
and their illicit acts were always discovered.
The people held old deeds and disputed land and houses.
Shìyuán shouted,
“These are fakes!
The deeds are in the current style,
but the disputes are about events from twenty years ago.”
The people were astonished and convinced,
and the disputes gradually ceased.
Upon completion of his term,
he was promoted to a salary of the third rank,
and continued to manage prefectural affairs as before,
until he left due to mourning.
After the mourning period,
he was reinstated as Magistrate of Guǎngxìn.
There was a silver mine in Yǒngfēng,
which people from Chǔzhōu illegally exploited,
gathering several thousand individuals.
The generals and soldiers feared their ferocity
and dared not suppress them.
Shìyuán led his troops to them,
and the rebels blocked and stabbed Shìyuán,
wounding his left thigh.
He fought fiercely with his wound bandaged,
captured their leader,
blocked the mine shafts, and returned.
Upon entering the capital for an audience,
he was transferred to Yǒngpíng.
He did not take up the post due to mourning.
After the mourning period,
he was promoted to Right Administration Commissioner of Sìchuān,
and then to Right Provincial Administration Commissioner.
In the first year of Hóngzhì (1488), he was directly promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-chief,
and served as Governor of that region.
When the local barbarians, Dàwá and Xiǎowá,
were about to instigate rebellion,
Shìyuán feigned an inspection tour of the border
and rode swiftly to their territory.
The rebels were afraid,
prostrated themselves by the roadside,
and he slowly comforted and dispatched them.
In a year of great famine,
migrant workers flocked to find food.
Shìyuán provided effective relief,
saving tens of thousands of lives.
The following year,
he was imprisoned for an incident.
After the matter was clarified,
he retired.
Kǒng Yōng,
courtesy name Sháowén,
was a native of Chángzhōu.
He passed the imperial examination in the fifth year of Jǐngtài (1454).
He served as Magistrate of Dūchāng County.
He divided households into nine classes to determine corvée labor,
and set up granaries along waterways,
facilitating collection,
which the people greatly relied upon.
Because his brother, Míng, was married to a Princess of the Níng Prefecture,
he was transferred to be Magistrate of Liánshān.
The Yáo and Zhòng tribes appeared and disappeared in neighboring areas,
and all the county residents fled.
Yōng went to invite them back,
but the people scattered in fear.
Yōng cooked rice in a civilian house,
left money to pay for it, and departed.
The people then gradually came to trust Yōng,
and returned en masse.
Yōng comforted and provided relief,
enabled them to resume their former livelihoods,
taught them how to fight and defend,
the roads gradually reopened,
and the county administration was thus restored.
Censor-in-chief Yè Shèng campaigned in Guǎngxī,
and took Yōng with him.
When generals recklessly killed,
Yōng always argued strongly,
saving many lives.
In the first year of Chénghuà (1465),
based on the recommendation of Yè Shèng and others,
he was promoted to acting Magistrate of Gāozhōu Prefecture.
The previous magistrate, Liú Hǎi, due to a Yáo alarm,
closed the city gates to protect himself.
Villagers fleeing the Yáo who arrived were never admitted,
and were instead killed by the Yáo.
He also suspected the people of secretly aiding the rebels
and often executed them.
Because of this, the rebels incited public anger,
gained internal support,
and the city was thus captured.
Upon Yōng’s arrival,
he opened the gates to admit those who came,
and the displaced people returned daily.
The city could not accommodate them,
so he built another city to the northeast for them to live in.
Many corpses lay exposed near the city walls;
people died of plague,
and he again established charitable graves to bury them.
At that time, there were more than ten bandit groups encamped within the borders.
Their leaders, Féng Xiǎo, were encamped in Huàzhōu,
and Dèng Gōngcháng in Máodòng.
They were repeatedly invited but would not submit.
Yōng one day rode alone with two men straight to Máodòng.
The stockade was about ten *lǐ* from the city.
On the way, they met bandits,
and he ordered them to return and announce:
"I am the new Grand Protector."
Gōngcháng suddenly heard that the new Grand Protector had arrived,
and urgently called his followers to don armor and welcome him.
When he saw Yōng, easygoing and without an escort,
his morale was greatly disheartened.
Yōng slowly dismounted,
entered and sat in the courtyard.
Gōngcháng led his followers to shed their armor and prostrate themselves.
Yōng instructed them, saying:
"You were originally good commoners,
forced by hunger and cold.
The former Grand Protector wanted to make war on you.
I am now ordered to be your father and mother.
You
are my children.
If you trust me,
then send me back,
and I will bestow upon you grain and silk.
If you do not trust me,
then kill me,
and when the great army arrives,
there will be no descendants left."
Gōngcháng hesitated,
but his followers were all enlightened and cried.
Yōng said:
"I am hungry;
you should feed me."
Gōngcháng knelt and offered him wine and dishes.
After eating,
he said:
"It's getting dark;
I should stay the night."
That night, he undressed and slept soundly.
The bandits looked at each other in awe and submission.
After two nights, he returned.
He saw many people hanging naked from trees by the roadside,
and when he inquired,
they were all scholars.
He ordered them all to be released.
Gōngcháng sent several tens of cavalry to escort him back.
The people in the city, seeing them from afar,
were all greatly alarmed,
thinking that the Prefect had been captured
and was coming to trick them into surrender.
They all ascended the battlements.
Yōng stopped the cavalry outside the city
and entered alone with an emaciated soldier,
took grain and silk,
and had it loaded and sent back.
Gōngcháng was even more grateful,
so he burned his camp
and led several thousand followers to surrender.
After Gōngcháng surrendered,
the other bandits gradually offered their submission.
Only Xiǎo, relying on his dangerous terrain, would not submit.
Yōng selected two hundred strong warriors
and arrived at Huàzhōu during the night.
Xiǎo fled in a panic and hid.
Yōng captured his wife and children and returned,
treating them very generously.
Xiǎo also surrendered with five hundred men.
Afterwards,
he and Commissioner Táo Lǔ defeated the bandit Liáo Pó Bǎo.
Other bandits came to invade successively,
many of whom were defeated and driven away.
The border region was greatly pacified.
Superior officials jointly recommended him,
and he was promoted to Vice Surveillance Commissioner,
inspecting the two prefectures of Gāo and Léi.
He further recruited serious bandits such as Liáng Dìng, Hóu Dàliù, and Dèng Xīnyǒu,
gave them land and property,
settled them in the interior as officials,
and prepared them against other bandits.
When Guangxī bandits invaded Xìnyí and Cénxī,
he defeated them all.
His administrative achievements became known,
and he was granted a decree and distinguished.
He suffered a bereavement,
and after the mourning period,
he was transferred to Guǎngxī.
When the Yáo and Zhòng heard of Yōng's arrival,
they all fled far away.
In the fourteenth year,
the Ministry of War reported his merits,
and he was awarded silver and silk.
Soon after, he was promoted to Surveillance Commissioner.
When the Lìpǔ bandits came to raid,
Grand Coordinator Zhū Yīng placed his troops under Yōng,
who defeated them,
and was promoted to a second-grade emolument.
Afterwards,
he was transferred to Left Administration Commissioner.
Soon after, he became Right Vice Censor-in-Chief and Grand Coordinator of Guìzhōu.
Á Xī, a Miáo leader from Qīngpíng,
was arrogant and cunning.
His adopted son, Á Lài, was especially powerful
and rampaged among the various tribes.
All the local officials accepted bribes from Á Xī,
and he became unmanageable in his arrogance.
When Yōng traveled to Qīngpíng,
he inquired and found two people close to Á Xī.
He then used a stratagem to capture Á Xī,
quartered him,
and also pacified the Jī Bèi Miáo.
The various tribes were awestruck.
Yōng was incorruptible in office.
Having served for over thirty years,
always on the frontier,
he contracted an illness due to the miasma.
He requested to retire due to old age,
but it was not granted.
In the second year of Hóngzhì, he was summoned to be Right Vice Minister of Works.
He died on the way,
at the age of sixty-three.
Lǐ Shímǐn from Pínglè
was the Magistrate of Xìnyí.
He had once collaborated with Yōng to pacify the Yáo rebellion and was meritorious,
being promoted to Prefect of Huàzhōu.
The people of Yuè often spoke of Kǒng and Lǐ together.
Dèng Tíngzàn,
courtesy name Zōngqì,
was from Bālǐng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the fifth year of Jǐngtài.
He served as Magistrate of Chún'ān County
and implemented benevolent policies.
He went into mourning for his mother,
and after the mourning period,
he was promoted to Assistant Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud.
The new prefecture of Chéngfān in Guìzhōu
was located amidst ten thousand mountains,
where Miáo and indigenous peoples lived mixed together.
The Ministry of Personnel found it difficult to find a suitable person,
so they specially promoted Tíngzàn to Prefect.
Upon arrival, he diligently planned
the construction of city walls, streets, schools, altars, temples, and offices
in succession.
He posted notices instructing the various local leaders to obey regulations.
His administration was peaceful and harmonious.
Grand Coordinator Chén Yǎn reported his administrative achievements.
The Emperor ordered him to remain in office for a long time.
After nine years, his term ended,
and he was then transferred to Left Policy Critic of Shāndōng,
and soon after promoted to Right Administration Commissioner.
In the second year of Hóngzhì, he became Right Vice Censor-in-Chief and Grand Coordinator of Guìzhōu.
Tíngzàn, from magistrate to prefect,
had been stuck in regular promotions for over thirty years.
Now, it had only been three years since he left the position of Prefect
when he finally became a Grand Coordinator.
He returned home due to mourning for his birth mother.
After the mourning period,
he returned to his original post.
When the Miáo leaders Miè Fùjià and Chángjiǎo of Dūyún revolted,
Tíngzàn was ordered to supervise military affairs
and jointly suppress them with Gù Pǔ, Grand Commander of Húguǎng, and Wáng Tōng, Grand Commander of Guìzhōu.
Vice Commissioner Wú Zhuó sent trusted Miáo to feign surrender to Fùjià,
lured them into invading,
and ambushed and captured his father and son.
The government army, taking advantage of the victory, consecutively broke more than a hundred stockades,
captured Chángjiǎo alive and returned.
The various tribes were terrified.
Tíngzàn said:
"Dūyún and Qīngpíng formerly had two guards and nine chieftaincies.
Their people all held hereditary stipends,
used their own laws,
and acted tyrannically,
inciting the Miáo people to rebellion,
causing chaos for over forty years.
Now that the chief culprits have been eliminated,
major reforms are necessary.
I request that they be reorganized into prefectures and counties,
establishing both regular and indigenous officials to govern jointly,
so that long-term peace can be achieved."
He then presented eleven proposals for post-war measures,
which the Emperor all approved.
Consequently, one prefecture was established,
named Dūyún;
two departments,
named Dúshān and Máhā;
and one county,
named Qīngpíng.
The Miáo troubles gradually ceased from then on.
For his merits,
he was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief.
In the eighth year, he was summoned to oversee the affairs of the Dūcháyuàn in Nánjīng.
After just a few months,
he was ordered to be Tídū of military affairs in Liǎngguǎng and concurrent Xúnfǔ.
Two years later,
he was promoted to Zuǒ (Assistant).
Tíngzàn's administration was generally simple and straightforward.
In official matters, he only grasped the main principles.
He bound the various indigenous tribes (mán) with kindness and trust,
and did not lightly resort to military action.
However, when his troops were deployed, they invariably achieved success.
When the various indigenous tribes of Yùlín, Yúnlú, and Dàguì, as well as the starving populace of Sìhuì, rose in rebellion,
he suppressed them one by one.
Liǎngguǎng then became peaceful.
In the thirteenth year, he was again summoned to oversee the Nányuàn.
Before he could depart,
he died.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tàizǐ Shàobǎo
and given the posthumous name Xiāngmǐn.
Tíngzàn had a magnanimous spirit,
and treated people without suspicion.
At the time, many praised him as a venerable elder.
Regarding his policies and arrangements,
they always hit upon the appropriate timing and circumstances.
His achievement in pacifying the Miáo in Guìzhōu was particularly great.
Wáng Shì,
courtesy name Yòngjìng,
was a native of Gōng'ān.
He became a Jìnshì in the eighth year of Tiānshùn.
He was appointed Yòupíngshì of the Dàlǐ Temple,
then promoted to Yòusìzhèng.
He investigated prisoners in Sìchuān,
reversing over a hundred unjust verdicts.
He was promoted to Sìchuān Fùshǐ.
When there was a famine,
he requested 100,000 liǎng of official silver for grain purchase.
Due to his investigation of the corruption of Jiādìng Tóngzhī Shèng Chóngrén,
he was impeached and imprisoned.
When the matter was cleared,
he was reinstated to his post,
and transferred to Shǎnxī.
In the early years of Hóngzhì,
he was promoted to Sìchuān Ànchásǐ.
In the third year, he was transferred to Nánjīng Yòuqiāndūyùshǐ,
Tídū of Cāojiāng.
In the eighth year, he was promoted to Yòufùdūyùshǐ,
responsible for the overall management of grain storage in Nánjīng,
and soon after was ordered to serve as Xúnfǔ of Guìzhōu.
The following year, he entered the capital as Dàlǐ Qīng.
An imperial edict ordered him and the Xíngbù to revise and finalize regulations to be promulgated throughout the empire.
In the thirteenth year, he was appointed Nánjīng Hùbù Shàngshū.
Soon after, he was ordered to concurrently serve as Zuǒfùdūyùshǐ,
to supervise military affairs in Guìzhōu,
and suppress the bandit woman Mǐ Lǔ of Pǔ'ān.
At that time, Zhènshǒu Zhōngguān Yáng Yǒu, Zǒngbīngguān Cáo Kǎi, and Xúnfǔ Qián Yuè jointly dispatched troops to suppress Lǔ,
but suffered a great defeat at Āmǎpō.
Dūzhīhuī Wú Yuǎn was captured,
and Pǔ'ān was nearly lost.
Yǒu and others requested reinforcements,
so the command was given to Shì.
Before Shì arrived,
Yǒu and others sent men to recruit the bandits.
The bandits publicly announced their intention to surrender,
but instead gathered more troops to besiege Pǔ'ān and Ānnán Wèichéng,
blocking the Pánjiāng road,
and their power grew even stronger.
They also seized the opportunity to abduct Yǒu.
Yòubùzhèngshǐ Lǘ Zhēng,
Ànchásǐ Liú Fú,
Dūzhīhuī Lǐ Zōngwǔ, Guō Rén, Shǐ Tāo, Lǐ Xióng, Wú Dá and others died there.
When Shì arrived,
he expediently mobilized 80,000 regular troops and indigenous soldiers from Guǎngxī, Húguǎng, Yúnnán, and Sìchuān.
Combining them with the Guìzhōu forces,
he advanced in eight columns,
and appointed the retired Dūdū Wáng Tōng to lead one army.
In the first month of the fifteenth year,
Cānjìang Zhào Shèng broke the Liùzhuìzhài.
The bandits fled,
crossing the Pánjiāng.
Dūzhīhuī Zhāng Tài and others crossed the river in pursuit,
and Zhīhuī Liú Huái and others then advanced to relieve the siege of Ānnán Wèi.
Meanwhile, Kǎi, Tōng, and Dūzhīhuī Lǐ Zhèng also each broke bandit strongholds.
The bandits counterattacked Píngyí Wèi and the fortresses of Dàhé and Èlè.
Dūyùshǐ Chén Jīn repelled them with Yúnnán troops.
The bandits fled back to Mǎwěilóngzhài.
The government forces intensified their attack,
and the indigenous official Fèng Yīng and others killed Mǐ Lǔ in battle.
The remaining rebels were then pacified.
The campaign lasted five months,
destroying over a thousand bandit strongholds,
beheading more than 4,800 enemies,
and capturing 1,200.
When the victory was reported,
the Emperor was overjoyed
and granted commendations.
Shì was recalled to the capital,
given additional rewards,
and in recognition of his merits,
was promoted to Tàizǐ Shàobǎo.
Later,
he was transferred to the Nánjīng Bīngbù,
participating in deliberating military affairs.
He repeatedly requested to retire,
but was not granted permission.
When Wǔzōng ascended the throne,
he again requested retirement due to illness.
An imperial edict promoted him to Tàizǐ Tàibǎo
and granted him an imperial decree and a relay post-horse to return home.
Upon his death,
he was posthumously granted the title of Tàibǎo
and given the posthumous name Xiāngjiǎn.
Liú Bǐng,
courtesy name Wénhuàn,
was the grandson of Nánxióng Zhīfǔ Shí.
At the end of Chénghuà,
he passed the Jìnshì examination.
He was selected as a Shùjíshì,
then changed to Yùshǐ,
and toured Yúnnán.
The clerks of the various departments in Yúnnán
were formerly not allowed to be issued official travel permits;
the son would replace the father upon his full term.
Bǐng requested that they be examined and appointed to office according to regulations.
When exiles and banished criminals were dispatched,
they had to pass through the Bīngbù,
often causing lengthy delays leading to death.
Bǐng requested that this be entrusted to the Xúnfǔ and Ànchásǐ.
For indigenous officials without heirs,
he requested that their younger brothers or nephews be recorded,
and not allow their wives or concubines to falsely assume official attire.
All these were established as precedents.
Later, he supervised the salt taxes of Liǎnghuái.
The Zhōngguān requested a grant of 20,000 (salt certificates) for weaving expenses.
The ministry deliberated and allowed it,
but Bǐng insisted it was unacceptable,
and succeeded in reducing it by three-quarters.
He successively served as Fùjiàn Fùshǐ and Sìchuān Fùshǐ,
both supervising schools.
He was thrice promoted to Sìchuān Zuǒbùzhèngshǐ.
In the sixth year of Zhèngdé, he became Yòufùdūyùshǐ and Xúnfǔ of Húguǎng.
Within his jurisdiction, Zhènxī Qiānhùsuǒ and Gānzǐpíng Chángguānsī, along with Tóngrén in Guìzhōu
and the various indigenous chiefdoms of Yǒuyáng and Méitóng in Sìchuān,
were interlocked like dog's teeth.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
the Miáo of Cuòxī, Lóng Má Yáng, and the Miáo of Tóngrén, Lóng Tóng Bǎo, gathered crowds to attack and plunder.
The indigenous official Lǐ Chūn and others actually condoned them,
and the Gānzǐ Bǎifūzhǎng Lóng Zhēn conspired with them.
Later, they plundered everywhere,
causing turmoil far and near.
Previous local officials were unable to control them.
Bǐng was about to suppress them.
The bandits entered the deep mountains of Liánshān,
planning to resist.
Bǐng led his army and broke several of their stockades.
The bandits fled and occupied Tiānshēngyá and Liùlóngshān.
Guìzhōu Xúnfǔ Shěn Lín's troops arrived afterward,
and jointly attacked and broke them.
They captured 200 people, including Tóng Bǎo,
and beheaded over 890.
Dūzhīhuī Pān Xūn also broke the stockades of Zhèn and Gān,
capturing 160 people, including Má Yáng,
and beheading a similar number as before.
The remaining bandits fled far away.
An imperial rescript commended him.
Bǐng had a pure and upright character,
and dared to take responsibility.
Wherever he went, he was strict and clear-headed,
and laws and regulations were properly enforced.
He was promoted to Gōngbù Yòushìláng,
responsible for timber procurement in the mountains.
Two years later,
he contracted a disease (fengbi, "wind-paralysis"),
and died.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him the title of Shàngshū
and the posthumous name Gōngxiāng.
A赞曰 (Zàn yuē, "Eulogy says"): During the Yīng and Jǐng reigns,
the Wǎlà pressed upon the western frontier,
making the border defenses extremely critical.
Meanwhile, followers of Huáng Xiāoyǎng and Yè Zōngliú plundered the regions of Lǐngnán, Zhè, and Mǐn.
Later, the displaced people of Jīng and Xiāng gathered and rebelled,
with Liú Tōng and Shí Lóng as their leaders.
Other such cases included the Miáo and Yáo of Dūyún, Sōng, Mào, Qián, and Chǔ,
who rebelled numerous times.
Luó Héngxìn, Hóu Jìn, and others
secured the frontiers,
punished the fierce and suppressed the chaos.
When suppressing, they achieved merits;
when pacifying, their trustworthiness was evident.
They exerted their efforts for the borders,
not disgracing their duties.
Kǒng Yōng, as Zhīfǔ, subdued the rebellious Yáo,
his talent and ability surpassed others.
Hán Yù said that Vice-Censor Liǔ's actions were appropriate for the circumstances,
and his demeanor was both awe-inspiring and admirable.
If one is not like this,
how can one achieve anything?
校勘記 (Jiàokānjì, "Collation Notes")
Biographies Volume 61: Yáng Hóng (son Jùn; grandnephew Néng; Xìn) Shí Hēng (nephew Biāo; grandnephew Hòu) Guō Dēng Zhū Qiān (son Yǒng; grandson Huī and others) Sūn Táng (Zhào Shèng) Fàn Guǎng
Yáng Hóng,
courtesy name Zōngdào,
was a native of Liùhé.
His grandfather, Zhèng,
was made a Hundred-Household Commander of Hànzhōng for his merits in the early Míng dynasty.
His father, Jǐng,
died in battle at Língbì.
Hóng inherited his post
and was transferred to Kāipíng.
He was skilled in horsemanship and archery.
Whenever he encountered the enemy, he would always be the first to charge into their lines.
Initially,
he followed Emperor Chéngzǔ on a northern expedition.
When they reached the Wònnán River,
he captured men and horses and returned.
The Emperor said,
"He is a talented general."
He ordered his name to be recorded
and promoted him to Thousand-Household Commander.
In Xuāndé fourth year, he was ordered to lead two hundred elite cavalrymen
to specifically patrol the border forts.
Later, he was ordered to build a fort at Māo'éryù west of the city
and station troops there.
He defeated bandits at Hóngshān.
When Emperor Yīngzōng ascended the throne,
Minister Wáng Jì remarked that the border troops were timid and weak,
due to a lack of training.
He then mentioned Hóng's capabilities.
An imperial edict promoted Hóng to Guerrilla General.
Hóng's command only consisted of five hundred men.
An edict ordered selection of cavalry from Kāipíng and Dúshí to reinforce him.
He was again promoted to Assistant Commander-in-chief.
At that time, all the veteran generals from the previous reign had passed away.
Hóng rose later
and became famous for his bravery in battle.
He was quick-witted and agile in strategy,
skilled at making unexpected moves and striking at weaknesses,
and never suffered a minor setback.
Although he was a lower-ranking officer,
the ministers in the central court all knew of his ability.
When anyone slandered him,
they would always protect him.
Because of this, Hóng was able to fully display his talents.
Minister Wèi Yuán supervised border affairs.
Commander Dù Héng and soldier Lǐ Quán both impeached Hóng for his crimes.
The Emperor followed Yuán's suggestion,
demoted Héng to Guǎngxī,
and handed Quán over to Hóng for self-discipline.
Soon after, Hóng was ordered to assist Assistant Regional Commander Lǐ Qiān in guarding Chìchéng and Dúshí.
Qiān was old and timid,
thus he was at odds with Hóng.
Whenever Hóng mobilized troops,
Qiān would secretly obstruct him.
Hóng once encouraged his officers and soldiers to kill the enemy.
Qiān laughed and said,
"Can all enemies be eliminated?
You'll only kill our own men."
Censor Zhāng Péng impeached and dismissed Qiān.
Consequently, Hóng was ordered to take his place,
and Hóng became even more determined.
The imperial court also treated him generously.
Whenever he reported a victory,
even if the merit was minor, it was always recognized.
Hóng first defeated the Wùliánghā troops
and captured their leader Duǒluán Tiēmù'ér.
After replacing Qiān in his post,
he again defeated their troops at Xīliángtíng.
The Emperor bestowed an imperial edict of commendation.
He also issued an edict to the commander-in-chief of Xuāndà, Tán Guǎng, and others, saying:
"These are the same bandits who previously invaded Yánsuí
and were defeated by Commander Wáng Zhēn.
They are very close to your army,
yet you cannot suppress them.
Do you feel ashamed when you look at Hóng and others?"
In the spring of the third year,
he attacked bandits at Bóyán Mountain.
Hóng's horse stumbled, injuring his foot,
but he fought with even greater strength,
capturing their leader Yělíngtái and four others.
He pursued them to Bǎochāng Prefecture
and captured five more, including Ātái Dálàhuā.
The bandits were utterly defeated
and fled.
An imperial rescript offered comfort and praise,
a physician was dispatched to attend to him,
he was promoted to Senior Commander-in-chief,
and bestowed with silver and silk.
Soon after, as Tán Guǎng was old,
Hóng was appointed as a Right Assistant General to assist him.
Hóng proposed reinforcing the Kāipíng city wall,
expanding the Lóngmén Garrison,
and from Dúshí to Cháohéchuan,
adding sixty signal towers.
Soon after, he was promoted to Commander-in-chief.
He fought against the Wùliánghā troops at Sānchàkǒu,
and also pursued bandits to Yìbǎtú River.
He was again promoted to Assistant Grand Commander.
In the ninth year,
when the Wùliánghā raided Yánsuí,
Hóng and the palace eunuch Hán Zhèng and others marched out from Dàtóng.
North of Hēishān,
they intercepted and defeated them at Kèlièsū.
He was promoted to Left Grand Commander,
and over nine thousand nine hundred soldiers received rewards.
Hóng once requested the issuance of flags and tallies,
which was not permitted.
So he made his own small feathered arrows and wooden tallies
for use by his army.
The authorities argued that he was acting on his own authority,
but the Emperor did not question it.
In the twelfth year, he was appointed Commander-in-chief
and replaced Guō Xuán as garrison commander of Xuānfǔ.
Since Xuāndé's reign,
there had been no major incursions from the north.
Only the three Dǒuyán Guard units would occasionally harass the border,
mostly not exceeding a hundred cavalry,
or sometimes a few dozen.
Other generals were timid and fearful,
but Hóng alone rose to be a great general through his bravery in battle.
The various tribes also feared him,
calling him
"King Yáng."
The Wǎlà Khagan Tuōtuōbùhuā and Grand Tutor Yěxiān had both written letters to Hóng
and sent him horses.
Hóng reported this to the court,
and an imperial edict ordered him to accept them and reciprocate with courtesy.
Thereafter, there were several gifts.
The Emperor relied heavily on Hóng
and did not blame him.
When the Emperor was captured in the north
and passed through Xuānfǔ,
Yěxiān relayed the Emperor's command to quickly open the city gates.
The people on the city wall replied,
"What we guard is His Majesty's city.
It is already dusk,
so we dare not open the gates.
Moreover, Hóng has already gone elsewhere."
Yěxiān then took the Emperor away.
When Emperor Jǐng became Regent,
he evaluated Hóng's past and present merits
and enfeoffed him as Earl of Chāngpíng.
Yěxiān again ordered the Emperor to write a letter to Hóng,
which Hóng sealed and presented to the court.
By this time, Emperor Jǐng had already ascended the throne.
He dispatched an envoy to inform Hóng:
"The letter from the former Emperor
is fake.
From now on, even if it is a genuine letter,
do not accept it."
Therefore, Hóng steadfastly held his position.
When Yěxiān pressed upon the capital,
an urgent edict summoned Hóng to lead twenty thousand troops to defend it.
By the time he arrived,
the invaders had already retreated.
An edict commanded Hóng, Sūn Tāng, Fàn Guǎng, and others to pursue the remaining invaders.
They defeated them at Bàzhōu,
capturing Āguī and forty-seven others,
and recovering tens of thousands of people and livestock that had been plundered.
When they reached the pass,
the invaders returned to fight,
killing hundreds of government troops.
Hóng's son, Jùn, was almost caught.
After the invaders left,
Hóng was promoted to Marquis for his merits,
and ordered to lead his troops to remain in the capital,
supervise the training of the capital garrisons,
and concurrently manage the affairs of the Left Military Bureau.
The court regarded Hóng as an experienced general,
and his suggestions were largely adopted.
He once proposed three strategies to counter the invaders,
and also memorialized to select and eliminate three thousand officers from various garrisons,
prohibiting the inclusion of the poor and weak in the ranks.
All his suggestions were followed.
In Jǐngtài first year,
Yú Qiān, noting that the border alarms had not ceased,
suggested that Hóng and others should formulate strategies.
Hóng proposed four items,
and the Ministry of War was ordered to deliberate and implement them.
Grand Commanders Gōng Jù, Wáng Xǐ, and Zhāng Bīn had previously been imprisoned for crimes.
Hóng and Shí Hēng recommended these three as skilled in warfare,
and requested their release to perform meritorious service.
The edict had already granted permission,
but censors impeached them for forming factions and disrupting government.
The Emperor, considering the state had many urgent matters
and needed talented people,
did not pursue the matter.
When the former Emperor returned,
Hóng and Shí Hēng were both granted the title of Fèngtiān Yìwèi Xuānlì Wǔchén,
and hereditary patents were issued.
The following summer,
he was invested with the seal of Grand General of Pacification of the North,
and returned to garrison Xuānfǔ.
His nephews Néng and Xìn served as Assistant Commanders of the Left and Right,
while his son Jùn became Right Grand Inspector-General,
commanding the Three Thousand Camp.
Hóng considered that within his family, father and son held the highest ranks,
commanding heavy troops;
such eminence was difficult to sustain.
He requested retirement,
and asked for Jùn and others to be transferred to other garrisons.
The Emperor did not permit it.
In the eighth month,
he was recalled to the capital due to illness,
and died a month later.
He was posthumously granted the title Duke of Yǐng,
and his posthumous name was Wǔxiāng.
His concubine, Lady Gé, hanged herself in殉;
an imperial edict posthumously granted her the title Shūrén.
Hóng had long resided in Xuānfǔ,
where he commanded his troops with strict discipline.
His soldiers and cavalry were elite and strong,
making him the foremost border general of his time,
yet he never wantonly executed anyone.
He was also quite fond of literature,
and once requested the establishment of a school in Xuānfǔ
to educate the sons of the generals.
His son Jié succeeded him.
He presented a memorial stating:
“My family has one Marquis and three Grand Inspector-Generals,
and sixteen of our household servants have received official positions.
I greatly fear that this is more than we can repay.
I request that the positions of the household servants Yáng Zhāo and others be suspended.”
An imperial edict granted this,
but still ordered their salaries to be paid.
After Jié died
without a son,
his elder half-brother Jùn succeeded him.
Jùn
initially joined the army as a retainer.
During the Zhèngtǒng reign, he successively held the provisional office of Assistant Commander-in-chief,
and supervised border affairs in places like Dúshí and Yǒngníng.
When Emperor Jǐng ascended the throne,
Jin Dá, an official of the Supervising Secretary’s office, was dispatched to Dúshí,
and impeached Jùn for greed and extravagance.
He was then recalled.
When Yěxiān attacked the capital,
Jùn defeated a separate contingent of his forces at Jūyōng,
and was promoted to Assistant Inspector-General.
Soon after, he was appointed Assistant Commander of the Right,
assisting Zhū Qiān in garrisoning Xuānfǔ.
The eunuch Xǐ Níng repeatedly lured enemies to invade,
which troubled the central court.
A reward of a thousand taels of gold,
twenty thousand taels of silver,
and ennoblement as a Marquis was offered for his capture or execution.
Níng was captured by Commander Jiāng Fú,
but Jùn falsely claimed the credit.
The court officials requested that the imperial decree be followed.
The Emperor, considering Jùn a border general
whose duty it was to act,
did not approve.
He was promoted to Right Grand Inspector-General
and awarded gold and silk.
Jùn, relying on his father's influence, was arrogant and unrestrained.
He once flogged Commander Táo Zhōng to death out of personal spite.
Hóng, fearing the consequences,
memorialized that Jùn was impulsive
and might jeopardize border affairs,
requesting that he be ordered to come to the capital
to train under him.
This was granted.
Upon his arrival,
censorate officials impeached him collectively,
and he was imprisoned and sentenced to execution.
An imperial edict ordered him to achieve merit under Hóng.
Not long after,
his false claim of capturing Xǐ Níng was exposed.
An imperial edict stripped him of his undeserved promotions,
rewarded Fú and others separately,
demoted Jùn,
and ordered him to suppress bandits to prove his worth.
Soon after, he was appointed Mobile Corps General,
patrolling the cities of Zhēn, Bǎo, Zhuó, and Yì,
and then returned to supervise the training of the Three Thousand Camp.
In the third year of Jǐngtài,
Jùn presented a memorial saying:
“Yěxiān has already assassinated his lord
and integrated his forces.
He harbors malicious intentions
and spies on our borders,
awaiting the right moment to act.
I hear his wives, children, and baggage
are only a few hundred *lǐ* from Xuānfǔ.
We have no less than several hundred thousand veteran troops along the border.
They should be divided into regular and surprise forces to await him,
luring him to attack.
The regular forces should encamp in Dàtóng and Xuānfǔ,
fortifying their defenses and observing the situation,
while the surprise forces march at double speed to raid his lair.
He will certainly return to defend himself,
and our forces, attacking from both sides,
can achieve our goal.”
The memorial was sent down for court deliberation,
but Yú Qiān and others deemed the plan not entirely sound,
and so it was shelved.
When the Tuan Camp was first established,
Jùn was ordered to jointly supervise four camps.
The following year, he was again appointed Mobile Corps General
to escort a Wǎlà envoy back.
Upon reaching Yǒngníng,
he was intoxicated
and flogged Commander Yáo Guì eighty times,
even intending to execute him.
The generals strongly intervened and stopped him.
Guì reported it to the court,
and Yè Shèng, the Administrator of Xuānfǔ, also argued for Jùn's punishment.
Because Jùn had once been defeated at Dúshí,
he was denounced as a defeated general.
Jùn submitted a memorial in his own defense,
returning the imperial edict he had been granted
to demonstrate his merit.
Censorate officials impeached him for being arrogant,
sentenced him to execution,
and imprisoned him.
Coincidentally, Jié died,
and Jié’s mother, Lady Wèi, requested Jùn’s temporary release to arrange Jié’s funeral.
His death sentence was pardoned,
and he was demoted to Assistant Inspector-General.
Soon after, he inherited Hóng’s position.
His household servants accused Jùn of embezzling military provisions.
He was again sentenced to death,
but paid a ransom to regain his title.
After a long time,
he was again accused of illicit affairs.
His death sentence was pardoned and his title stripped,
and his son Zhēn was ordered to inherit.
When Jùn first guarded Yǒngníng and Huáilái,
hearing that Yěxiān intended to escort the former Emperor back,
he secretly warned his officers not to admit him lightly.
Upon his return,
he also said that this would be the source of calamity.
When the former Emperor was restored to power,
Zhāng Yuè, who was at odds with Jùn,
reported him to the court.
He was then summoned and imprisoned,
and condemned to execution.
Zhēn’s title was stripped,
and he was exiled to Guǎngxī.
When Emperor Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
he was appointed Commander of the Dragon and Tiger Guard.
Néng,
whose courtesy name was Wénjìng,
was resolute and skilled in horsemanship and archery.
He repeatedly achieved merit following Hóng,
became Commander of Kàipíng Guard,
and was promoted to Assistant Commander-in-chief.
In the first year of Jǐngtài, he was promoted to Vice Commander-in-chief,
appointed Mobile Corps General,
and patrolled along the border.
When bandits attacked Wèizhōu,
he hesitated to advance.
Later, he and Jì Guǎng repelled bandits at Yěhú Lǐng,
where his right knee was injured.
He was impeached by Censor Zhāng Hào.
He was pardoned.
Soon after, he and Shí Biāo were each ordered to command three thousand elite troops
for training and deployment.
He was again promoted to Assistant Inspector-General,
and successively advanced to Left Vice Commander-in-chief,
assisting in guarding Xuānfǔ.
Governor Lǐ Bǐng impeached him for greed and indolence,
but it was ignored.
In the fifth year, he was recalled
to command the Divine Engine Camp.
In the early Tiānshùn reign,
as Left Grand Inspector-General, he became the Commander-in-chief of Xuānfǔ,
and with Shí Biāo, he defeated bandits at Mó'ér Shān,
and was enfeoffed as Earl of Wǔqiáng.
After Yěxiān died,
Bólái rose to power.
Néng wanted to ally with Wūliánghā to attack and plunder him,
and gave them signal cannons.
The Ministry of War impeached him for poor strategy.
The Emperor, seeing Néng’s intent to eradicate the bandits,
did not punish him.
When bandits attacked Xuānfǔ,
Néng suffered a defeat
and was again impeached by the Ministry of War,
but the Emperor again pardoned him.
He died that year.
He had no sons,
and his younger brother Lún inherited the position of Commander of the Imperial Guard.
Yáng Xìn,
courtesy name Wénshí.
As a youth, he followed Yáng Hóng to attack the enemy at Xīngzhōu.
When the enemy general 方跃 (Fāng Yuè) galloped out to the front of the array,
Yáng Xìn went straight ahead and captured him.
Because of this, he became famous.
Through accumulated merits, he rose to be Assistant Commander (Zhǐhuī Qiānshì).
At the end of the Zhèngtǒng reign,
he was promoted to Assistant Regional Commander (Dū Zhǐhuī Qiānshì)
and guarded Cháigōu Bǎo.
When Esen (Yěxiān) invaded the capital,
he entered to defend it
and was promoted to Vice Regional Commander (Dū Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī).
When the Jǐngtài reign began,
he guarded Huáilái,
but when the invaders entered, he was unable to repel them.
He escorted provisions to Yǒngníng,
and hearing cannon fire, he rushed back.
He was impeached for all these incidents.
The court deliberated that since troops were currently being deployed,
no investigation would be conducted.
He was successively promoted to Assistant Military Commissioner (Dūdū Qiānshì)
and replaced Néng as Left Vice Commander-in-Chief (Zuǒ Fù Zǒngbīng),
assisting in the defense of Xuānfǔ.
He memorialized, saying:
"The system of 'deer-horns' (lùjiǎo),
when facing the enemy, can defend against enemy cavalry,
and when setting up camp, can protect soldiers.
Each squad should be equipped with ten sets.
When encountering the enemy, the round shields (tuánpái) block in front,
the 'deer-horns' are arrayed behind,
and divine firearms (shénchòng) and bows and arrows are successively fired.
Then, defense will be impregnable,
and every battle will be victorious."
This was adopted.
In the early Tiānshùn reign,
he was transferred to guard Yánsuí
and was promoted to Vice Military Commissioner (Dūdū Tóngzhī).
The next year, he defeated the invaders at Qīngyáng Gōu
and made great gains.
He was enfeoffed as the Earl of Zhāngwǔ (Zhāngwǔ Bó),
bore the seal of Vice General (Fù Jiāngjūn),
and served as Commander-in-Chief (Zǒngbīng Guān),
guarding as before.
The establishment of a Commander-in-Chief bearing a seal in Yánsuí
began with Yáng Xìn.
A short while later,
he defeated invaders at Gāojiā Bǎo.
In the third year, he and Shí Biāo greatly defeated the invaders at Yěmǎ Jiàn.
The next year,
two thousand enemy cavalry entered Yúlín.
Yáng Xìn attacked and repelled them,
pursuing them to Jīnjī Yù,
where he beheaded the Grand Councilor (Píngzhāng) Āsūn Tièmù'ér
and recovered tens of thousands of people and livestock that had been plundered.
That winter,
he replaced Lǐ Wén in guarding Dàtóng.
When Emperor Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
Yáng Xìn personally recounted his past military achievements,
and was granted hereditary privileges.
In the winter of the first year of the Chénghuà reign, he failed to repel invaders in Yánsuí.
He was recalled
to supervise the Three Thousand Camps (Sānqiān Yíng).
When Máolǐhái occupied Hétào,
he was ordered to bear the seal of General (Jiāngjūn)
and lead the troops from all garrisons to defend against him.
The invaders had already crossed the Yellow River and gone north,
but later,
returned to occupy the Hétào region,
and plundered Shuǐquán Yíng and Shuòzhōu.
Yáng Xìn and others repeatedly repelled them.
The invaders then entered Dàtóng from the east,
and an imperial edict commanded Yáng Xìn to return to guard Dàtóng.
In the sixth year,
Yáng Xìn, with Vice General (Fù Jiāng) Xú Shù and Assistant General (Cānjiāng) Zhāng Yīng, sallied out beyond the frontier in separate columns,
defeated the invaders at Húchái Gōu,
and captured over five hundred horses.
An imperial letter of commendation was issued.
Yáng Xìn was on the frontier for thirty years,
guarding it with peace and quiet,
and people were happy to serve under him.
However, he was fond of making profits.
The Prince of Dài once memorialized his unlawful actions,
and an edict ordered his stipend to be suspended for one year.
In the thirteenth year, he died at his post.
He was posthumously granted the title of Marquis (Hóu)
and the posthumous name Wǔyì.
Yáng Hóng's father and sons, and brothers, all bore general's seals,
and three in his family became marquises or earls.
At that time, among those praised as famous generals,
the Yáng clan was preeminent.
After the Marquis of Chāngpíng was disgraced,
Néng's title became non-hereditary.
But Yáng Xìn's title alone was passed down to his son, Yáng Jǐn,
who in the early Hóngzhì reign served as a general in the imperial guard.
It was passed down three generations to his great-grandson, Yáng Bǐng.
In the Lóngqìng reign,
he assisted in guarding Nánjīng.
He was summoned to take charge of military and governmental affairs in the capital garrisons
and was repeatedly promoted to Junior Tutor (Shǎoshī).
After he died,
he was given the posthumous name Gōngxiāng.
It was passed down through his son to his grandson, Yáng Chóngyóu.
When Lǐ Zìchéng captured the capital,
he was killed.
Shí Hēng
was a native of Wèinán.
He was born with unusual features:
a square face and a mighty physique,
with a beautiful beard reaching his knees.
His nephew, Shí Biāo, was similarly robust
and also had a beard that went past his belly.
When they were drinking at a tavern,
a physiognomist said:
"In this time of peace,
how is it that these two possess the physiognomy of being enfeoffed as marquises?"
Shí Hēng inherited his adoptive father's position
and became Assistant Commander (Zhǐhuī Qiānshì) of the Kuānhé Guard.
He was skilled in horsemanship and archery
and was able to use a great saber.
In every battle, he invariably broke through.
In the early Zhèngtǒng reign,
for achieving initial merits, he was successively promoted to Assistant Regional Commander (Dū Zhǐhuī Qiānshì).
He defeated the enemy at Huángniú Pō
and captured many horses.
In January of the third year,
over three hundred enemy cavalry were watering their horses in the Yellow River.
Shí Hēng pursued and attacked them to the foot of Guānshān,
where he killed and captured many.
He was promoted to Vice Regional Commander (Dū Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī).
Soon after, he was appointed Left Assistant General (Zuǒ Cānjiāng),
assisting Earl of Wǔjìn (Wǔjìn Bó) Zhū Miǎn in guarding Dàtóng.
In the sixth year, he memorialized:
"The frontier provisions are difficult to sustain.
I request that the armies of the four guards of Dàtóng's left and right, Yùlín, and Yúnchuān be divided
to reclaim the desolate land west of Jìngshuǐ Píng.
If the government provides cattle and seeds,
an additional eighteen thousand shí of grain can be increased annually."
The next year, he further stated:
"The military colonies and forts on Dàtóng's western route
are all located on the extreme frontier.
The old city of Yùlín is fifty lǐ from the Right Guard
and connects with the city of Dōngshèng Chányú,
with convenient access to water and grass.
I request that troops be assigned to build fortifications
to protect the military colonies and farming."
An edict granted permission for both proposals to be implemented.
Soon after, for his merit in defeating the enemy at Hóngchéng,
he was promoted to Regional Commander (Dū Zhǐhuī Shǐ).
When the enemy invaded Yán'ān,
he pursued them to Jīnshān and defeated them.
He was again promoted to Assistant Military Commissioner (Dūdū Qiānshì).
Shí Hēng felt that the national system for discovering military talent was not broad enough,
and requested to imitate the systems of the Hàn and Táng dynasties,
establishing categories such as "profound military strategists" and "those with unparalleled wisdom and insight,"
allowing people to self-recommend,
testing them and promoting them,
rather than relying solely on recommendations.
This was approved.
In the fourteenth year,
he and Assistant Military Commissioner (Dūdū Qiānshì) Mǎ Lín patrolled beyond the frontier.
Reaching Jiànkuò Shān,
he defeated the Wùliánghā multitude
and was promoted to Vice Military Commissioner (Dūdū Tóngzhī).
At this time,
among the frontier generals, Yáng Hóng was considered the most intelligent and brave,
followed by Shí Hēng.
Although Shí Hēng was only a partial general,
the central court relied on him as if he were a great commander,
so Shí Hēng also exerted his full effort.
That autumn,
Esen (Yěxiān) launched a large-scale invasion of Dàtóng.
Shí Hēng, along with Marquis of Xīníng (Xīníng Hóu) Sòng Yīng and Earl of Wǔjìn (Wǔjìn Bó) Zhū Miǎn, fought at Yánghé Kǒu.
Sòng Yīng and Zhū Miǎn were killed in battle,
and Shí Hēng fled back on a single horse.
He was demoted,
and recruited soldiers to prove his worth.
When Chéng Wáng supervised the state,
Shàngshū Yú Qiān recommended him.
He was summoned to command the Five Armies Grand Camp,
and was promoted to Yòudūdū.
Before long,
he was enfeoffed as Wǔqīng Bó.
When Yěxiān pressed upon the capital,
he was ordered to join nine generals, including Dūdū Táo Jǐn,
to divide their troops and encamp outside the nine gates.
The Déshèngmén was in the path of the enemy's assault,
and was specially entrusted to Hēng.
Yú Qiān, as Shàngshū, oversaw the army.
When the invaders approached the Zhāngyìmén,
Dūdū Gāo Lǐ and others repelled them.
They then turned to outside the Déshèngmén,
where Hēng, following Qiān's orders,
ambushed and lured them into an attack,
resulting in many deaths.
Afterwards, they besieged Sūn Táng outside the Xīzhímén,
and Hēng's rescue effort caused them to withdraw.
After a five-day standoff,
the invaders gathered their forces and fled.
In the discussion of merits,
Hēng's were the most significant,
and he was promoted to Hóu.
In the second month of the first year of Jǐngtài, he was ordered to wear the seal of Zhènshuò Dàjiāngjūn,
and lead thirty thousand capital troops
to patrol Dàtóng.
He encountered invaders
and defeated them.
That autumn,
he was granted an inherited imperial edict.
When the heir apparent was changed,
Hēng was additionally granted the title of Tàizǐ Tàishī.
Yú Qiān established the Tuányíng,
and ordered Hēng to be its Tídū,
serving as Zǒngbīngguān as before.
In the eighth year,
the emperor was about to perform the suburban sacrifice,
and stayed in the fasting palace.
He became ill and could not perform the ceremony,
so he summoned Hēng to take his place.
Hēng received the order by the emperor's couch,
and seeing the emperor's grave illness,
he conspired with Zhāng Yuè, Cáo Jíxiáng, and others to welcome back and enthrone the former emperor (Shànghuáng).
After the former emperor was restored,
Hēng's primary contribution was recognized,
and his rank was advanced to Zhōngguó Gōng.
The emperor favored him exceptionally,
and his words were always heeded.
Over fifty of his younger brothers, nephews, and family members falsely claimed credit to become Jǐnyī (guards),
and over four thousand of his subordinates, relatives, and old friends, by falsely listing their names in the
"Duómén"
register, obtained official positions.
Ministers in both capitals
were almost all dismissed.
He accepted heavy bribes from private individuals,
and promoted Tàipúchéng Sūn Hóng,
Lángzhōng Chén Rǔyán, Xiāo Cōng, Zhāng Yònghàn, Hǎo Huáng, Lóng Wén, Zhū Quán,
and Yuánwàiláng Liú Běndào to be Shìláng.
At that time, there was a saying:
"Zhū is three thousand,
Lóng is eight hundred."
His influence was overwhelming,
and those eager for advancement flocked to his gate.
He then, out of personal grudge, killed Yú Qiān, Fàn Guǎng, and others.
He also demoted and dismissed Chéng Zhāng, a Gěishìzhōng, and Gān Zé, a Yùshǐ, along with seven others who had criticized his faults.
He frequently instigated major arrests,
and framed Gěng Jiǔchóu and Yuè Zhèng,
exiled Yáng Xuān and Zhāng Péng,
and demoted Zhōu Bīn, Shèng Yóng, and others.
He also disliked civil officials serving as Xúnfǔ,
and prevented military officials from acting freely,
recalling them all.
As a result, all major power went to Hēng.
Hēng met the emperor daily,
and frequently participated in political affairs.
If his requests were not granted,
he would show his displeasure in his words and expressions.
Even if not summoned,
he would certainly find a pretext to enter,
and upon leaving, he would exaggerate his influence,
and trade on his power.
After a long time,
the emperor could no longer tolerate it,
and once spoke about it with cabinet minister Lǐ Xián.
Xián said:
"Only by acting decisively can it be resolved."
The emperor agreed.
One day, he said to Xián:
"When cabinet ministers have matters,
they must have an audience.
frequently seek audiences?"
He then issued an edict to the Zuǒshùnmén,
stating that Zǒngbīngguān were not to be admitted unless summoned.
From then on, Hēng rarely had audiences.
Why does that military official
Hēng once petitioned the emperor to erect a stele at his ancestors' tomb.
The Ministry of Works, to please Hēng,
requested an imperial edict for the responsible officials to construct it,
and for the Hànlín Yuàn to compose the text.
The emperor stated that since the Yǒnglè era,
there had been no precedent for erecting steles for meritorious officials' ancestors,
and reprimanded the ministry officials,
ordering Hēng to erect it himself.
Initially,
the emperor ordered the relevant authorities to build a residence for Hēng.
When completed,
its grandeur exceeded the prescribed limits.
The emperor ascended the Xiángfèng Lóu and saw it,
asking who lived there.
Gōngshùn Hóu Wú Jǐn falsely replied:
"This must be a princely mansion."
The emperor said:
"No."
Jǐn said:
"If not a princely mansion,
who would dare to usurp such grandeur?"
The emperor nodded in agreement.
Not only did Hēng's power rival that of the sovereign,
but his adopted nephew Biāo was also enfeoffed as Dìngyuǎn Hóu,
and was as arrogant and overbearing as Hēng.
The two families kept tens of thousands of skilled officials and fierce warriors,
and half of the generals and commanders, both inside and outside the court, came from their patronage.
The people of the capital viewed them askance.
In the autumn of the third year,
Biāo planned to be stationed in Dàtóng,
and ordered Qiānhù Yáng Bīn and others to submit a memorial recommending him.
The emperor detected their deception,
arrested Bīn and others, and interrogated them until the truth was revealed.
Infuriated,
he sent Biāo to the imperial prison.
Hēng, fearful,
pleaded guilty,
but the emperor comforted and appeased him.
Hēng requested that all his younger brothers and nephews be stripped of their offices
and sent back to their hometowns,
but the emperor also refused.
When Biāo was interrogated,
embroidered python-dragon robes and irregular beds, among other unlawful items, were found,
making his crime punishable by death.
Consequently, Biāo's family property was confiscated,
and Hēng was ordered to recuperate from illness.
Hēng had once dispatched Jīngwèi Zhǐhuī Péi Xuān to go beyond the pass to purchase timber,
and Dàtóng Zhǐhuī Lú Zhāo to pursue fugitives.
When these matters came to light,
the judicial authorities requested Hēng's punishment,
but the emperor still ignored it.
The judicial authorities interrogated Biāo again,
and said that when Biāo was first a Dàtóng Yóují,
he claimed the increase in salary for the prince of Dài as his own achievement,
and the prince even knelt in thanks.
From then on, he frequently paid homage to Biāo,
bringing singers and prostitutes to serve wine.
Biāo's insolent treatment of a prince
was also punishable by death.
Thus, Hēng was impeached for abusing his power to accept bribes,
acting recklessly without restraint,
and secretly discussing astronomy with the diviner Zōu Shúyí and others,
making false predictions of good and ill fortune,
and therefore deserved severe punishment.
The emperor ordered Biāo to be imprisoned,
and Hēng to stay at home,
suspending his court attendance.
At that time, there was a discussion to revoke the merits of the
"Duómén"
incident,
and thoroughly investigate Hēng's faction.
Those who had obtained official positions through Hēng were all dismissed,
and the court became clean.
In the first month of the following year,
Jǐnyī Zhǐhuī Lù Gǎo memorialized that Hēng harbored resentment,
and together with his adopted grandson Hòu and others, spread seditious rumors,
harbored ruffians,
and specifically monitored the movements of the imperial court,
and his rebellious intentions were already evident.
All the court officials said he should not be lightly pardoned,
so Hēng was sent to the imperial prison,
convicted of plotting rebellion, and sentenced to be beheaded,
and his family's property was confiscated.
A month later,
Hēng died in prison from hardship.
Biāo and Hòu were also executed.
Biāo was fierce and courageous in battle,
and skilled in using an axe.
He began as a retainer serving in the army.
At the end of Zhèngtǒng,
he accumulated merits to reach Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī.
When Yěxiān pressed upon the capital,
after his retreat,
Biāo pursued the remaining invaders,
and gained considerable kills and captures,
advancing to Acting Dū Zhǐhuī Qiānshì.
In the first year of the Jǐngtài reign,
an imperial edict appointed me to a substantive post,
serving as a mobile corps general (yóují jiàngjūn),
garrisoning Wēiyuǎn Guard.
When the enemy besieged Tǔchéng,
Biāo used cannons to kill over a hundred people,
and they fled.
On the frontier, there was daily warfare;
Biāo’s bravery surpassed his peers.
Every battle he fought was victorious.
Because of this, he was promoted multiple times within a single year,
reaching the position of Assistant Military Commissioner-in-Chief (Dūdū Qiānshì).
Relying on Hēng’s influence,
he often indulged his family members in occupying people's property.
He also recruited over fifty households of displaced people,
illegally crossing the pass to establish manors and reclaim land.
This was impeached by Investigating Censor (Gěishìzhōng) Lǐ Kǎn and Censor (Yùshǐ) Zhāng Kuí,
who requested that Hēng also be punished.
Emperor Jǐng pardoned them all without question,
only ordering that the property be returned to the people
and the displaced households be sent back to their original occupations.
In the winter of the third year,
he was appointed Right Assistant General (Yòu Cāncānjòng),
assisting in the defense of Dàtóng.
He often resented that the Grand Coordinator (Xúnfǔ) Nián Fù suppressed him and prevented him from achieving his ambitions.
When Emperor Yīngzōng was restored,
Biāo was summoned back.
Hēng was just getting his way,
so Biāo falsely accused Fù,
leading to his imprisonment.
Soon after,
he was promoted to Vice Military Commissioner-in-Chief (Dūdū Tóngzhī).
He was again sent to Dàtóng as a mobile corps general to guard against the enemy.
He scouted Mó’ěrshān with Assistant General Zhāng Péng and others.
Over a thousand enemy cavalry came to attack.
Biāo led brave warriors to charge and strike,
beheading Bǎtúwáng,
capturing his banner,
and taking 120 captives and slain enemies.
He pursued them to Sānshāndūn,
where he killed another seventy-two people.
For this, he was enfeoffed as Earl Dìngyuǎn,
and continued as a mobile corps general.
In the second year of Tiānshùn, he was ordered to go to Yánsuí with Earl Gāoyáng Lǐ Wén to resist the invaders.
Due to illness, he was summoned back,
and soon after was appointed Grand General-in-Chief (Zǒngbīngguān).
The following year,
twenty thousand enemy cavalry entered and plundered Ānbiānyíng.
Biāo and Earl Zhāngwǔ Yáng Xìn and others resisted them.
They fought successive battles, all victorious,
beheading Guǐlìchì,
pursuing them out of the pass,
fighting and advancing for over sixty *lǐ*,
capturing alive over forty people,
beheading over five hundred,
and seizing over twenty thousand horses, camels, cattle, and sheep.
This was the greatest military achievement in the northwest.
When the victory was reported,
he was promoted to Marquis.
Biāo originally established himself through military merit,
without relying on the influence of his father or elder brothers.
However, with two marquises and earls in one family,
their power grew immense, and they became arrogant,
committing many unjust acts.
He plotted to guard Dàtóng,
and together with Hēng, they held military power,
which made the emperor suspicious,
leading to disaster.
Later,
a *jìnshì* in the first year of Tiānshùn,
assisted Hēng in his schemes.
Military Commissioner-in-Chief Dù Qīng was a subordinate of Hēng.
Later, he spread seditious rumors,
saying,
"Tǔmù holds military power,"
referring to Dù.
It refers to Dù.
When the matter was discovered,
he was executed,
and Qīng was also exiled to Jīnchǐ.
Guō Dēng,
courtesy name Yuándēng,
was the grandson of Marquis Wǔdìng Yīng.
As a child, he was bright and quick-witted.
When he grew up,
he was knowledgeable and had a strong memory,
skilled in debate,
and fond of discussing military affairs.
During the Hóngxī era,
he was awarded the rank of Xunwei (勳衞).
During the Zhèngtǒng reign,
he followed Wáng Jì in the expedition against Lùchuān and gained merit,
being promoted to Assistant Commander of the Imperial Bodyguard (Jǐnyīwèi Zhǐhuī Qiānshì).
He then followed Mù Bīn in the expedition against Téngchōng,
and was promoted to acting Assistant Commander (Shǔ Dū Zhǐhuī Qiānshì).
In the fourteenth year,
the imperial carriage went on a northern expedition.
He accompanied the emperor to Dàtóng,
was exceptionally promoted to Assistant Military Commissioner-in-Chief (Dūdū Qiānshì),
served as Assistant General (Cāncānjòng),
and assisted the Grand General-in-Chief (Zǒngbīngguān) Earl Guǎngníng Liú Ān in garrisoning the area.
When Zhū Yǒng’s army was annihilated,
a hasty retreat was discussed.
Dēng informed Academicians Cáo Nài and Zhāng Yì, saying,
"The imperial carriage should enter Zǐjīng Pass."
Wáng Zhèn did not follow,
and thus disaster struck.
At that time,
many soldiers in Dàtóng had died in battle,
the city gates were closed during the day,
and people's hearts were uneasy.
Dēng was filled with emotion and zeal,
repairing city walls,
maintaining weapons,
comforting soldiers,
mourning the dead and asking about the wounded.
He personally bandaged wounds and applied medicine,
saying,
"I swear to live and die with this city;
I will not let you all die alone."
In August,
Yěxiān, holding the emperor captive, went north.
Passing Dàtóng,
he sent Yuán Bīn into the city to demand gold and silk.
Dēng closed the city gates
and used a flying bridge to bring Bīn in.
Dēng, Ān, together with Attendant Minister (Shìláng) Shěn Gù, Investigating Censor (Gěishìzhōng) Sūn Xiáng, Prefect (Zhīfǔ) Huò Xuān, and others, went out to pay their respects,
prostrating themselves and weeping loudly.
They presented over twenty thousand pieces of gold and the family assets of Sòng Yīng, Zhū Miǎn, and the eunuch Guō Jìng to the emperor,
which were then bestowed upon Yěxiān and others.
That evening,
the enemy camped west of the city.
Dēng planned to send brave warriors to raid the camp and rescue the emperor,
but it did not materialize.
The next day,
Yěxiān took the emperor away.
When Emperor Jǐng became regent,
Dēng was promoted to Vice Military Commissioner-in-Chief (Dūdū Tóngzhī),
and served as Vice General-in-Chief (Fù Zǒngbīng).
Soon after, he was ordered to replace Ān as Grand General-in-Chief (Zǒngbīngguān).
In October,
Yěxiān attacked the capital.
Dēng was about to lead his troops to reinforce,
first sending a sealed letter reporting the situation.
When the report arrived,
the enemy had already retreated.
Emperor Jǐng issued a generous edict of praise and reward,
promoting him to Right Military Commissioner-in-Chief (Yòu Dūdū).
Dēng calculated that the capital's troops were newly assembled
and should not be used lightly,
and submitted over ten military strategies.
In the spring of the first year of Jǐngtài,
he detected several thousand enemy cavalry
entering Shāwō from Shùnshèngchuān.
Dēng led his troops to pursue them,
greatly defeating their forces.
He pursued them to Kǎoláoshān,
beheading over two hundred,
and recovering over eight hundred captured people and livestock.
After the defeat at Tǔmù, border generals
were timid and dared not fight the invaders.
Dēng, with eight hundred men, defeated several thousand enemy cavalry,
and the morale of the army was reinvigorated.
When the victory was reported,
he was enfeoffed as Earl Dìngxiāng,
and granted a hereditary patent.
In April,
several thousand enemy cavalry suddenly arrived.
Dēng went out the east gate to fight.
He feigned defeat,
luring them into Tǔchéng.
Ambush troops rose,
and the enemy fled in defeat.
Dēng estimated that the enemy would return,
so he ordered soldiers to carry poisoned wine, sheep, pigs, and paper money,
pretending to be offering sacrifices at graves,
and to abandon them and flee upon seeing the invaders.
When the invaders arrived,
they eagerly ate and drank,
and many died.
In June,
Yěxiān again invaded with two thousand cavalry.
Dēng attacked and repelled them again.
A few days later,
Yěxiān brought the Retired Emperor to the city outskirts,
claiming to be returning him.
Dēng and the other defenders devised a plan:
they prepared court attire and waited for the emperor inside the moon-shaped barbican,
with ambush troops on the city walls.
When the Retired Emperor entered,
they would immediately lower the barbican gate.
Yěxiān realized this just as he reached the gate,
and so he took the Retired Emperor away.
At that time, the eunuch garrison commander, Chén Gōng, was jealous of Dèng [Dèng Hóng 鄧洪].
It happened that someone reported Gōng for corruption and embezzlement.
Gōng suspected Dèng Hóng of instigating it,
and thus a conflict arose between them.
The Emperor said to Yú Qiān:
"Dàtóng [大同]
is Our fence.
If Gōng and Dèng Hóng act like this,
how can it be defended?"
He dispatched Assistant Censor Mǎ Qìng to replace Gōng and return him to the capital,
which made Dèng Hóng even more grateful and inspired.
Initially,
Yěxiān [也先] wanted to seize Dàtóng as his stronghold,
and therefore attacked it repeatedly.
But each time he arrived, he was defeated.
Once, an entire camp of dozens of men did not return,
which intimidated the enemy,
and only then did Yěxiān consider returning the Former Emperor.
After the Former Emperor had returned,
the Prince of Dài [Dài Wáng 代王] wrote a memorial praising Dèng Hóng's achievements,
begging for an imperial edict to commend and reward him.
The Ministry of War stated that Dèng Hóng had already been enfeoffed as an Earl,
and so it was stopped.
In the second year,
Dèng Hóng requested retirement due to old age and illness,
and recommended Shí Biāo to replace him,
and also requested that his son, Sōng, be allowed to serve as an imperial guard.
The Emperor appointed Sōng as a Sanqí Shèrén [散騎舍人],
but did not accept Dèng Hóng's resignation.
At this time, border troubles had just subsided,
and Dèng Hóng dedicated himself to planning,
hoping to find upright and capable individuals to work with him.
He then impeached Shěn Gù for dereliction of duty,
and recommended Minister Yáng Níng and Provincial Administration Commissioner Nián Fù.
He also stated that since Dàtóng already had a Censor,
and also a Circuit Censor,
Associate Censor-in-Chief Rèn Níng should only serve as Grand Coordinator of Xuānfǔ.
The Emperor followed all his suggestions,
appointing Nián Fù to replace Gù,
and recalling Gù and Níng.
That autumn,
he was recalled due to illness.
When Dèng Hóng first arrived in Dàtóng,
there were barely a few hundred soldiers fit for battle,
and just over a hundred horses.
By this time, the horses numbered fifteen thousand,
and elite troops numbered tens of thousands,
standing firm as a formidable garrison.
When Dèng Hóng left,
the people of Dàtóng missed him.
Initially,
Emperor Yīngzōng passed through Dàtóng
and sent someone to tell Dèng Hóng:
"We and Dèng Hóng are related by marriage,
why do you refuse Us like this?"
Dèng Hóng reported:
"Your subject has been ordered to defend the city;
I know nothing else."
Emperor Yīngzōng resented this.
When he was restored to power,
Dèng Hóng feared he would not escape punishment,
and first presented eight proposals,
many of which were to curry favor.
Soon after, he was ordered to take charge of the Nánjīng Central Guard Commander's Office.
The following year, he was recalled.
Officials impeached Dèng Hóng for colluding with Chén Rǔyán to secure his recall,
and after investigation, he was sentenced to execution by beheading.
He was pardoned from death,
demoted to Assistant Commander of the Chief Military Commission,
and sent to Gānsù to earn merit.
Upon Emperor Xiànzōng's accession,
an edict restored his earldom,
and appointed him Commander-in-Chief of Gānsù.
He reported that border troops had extreme difficulty replacing horses,
even to the point of selling their wives and children,
and requested to borrow a thousand horses each from the princely estates of Chǔ, Qìng, and Sù,
with the government compensating their value.
This was approved.
Based on the recommendation of Zhū Yǒng and others,
he was recalled to take charge of the Central Guard Commander's Office,
and command the Shenjiyíng [神機營] troops.
In Chenghuà [成化] four years, the twelve-regiment camp system was re-established,
and Dèng Hóng was ordered to supervise it jointly with Zhū Yǒng.
He died in the eighth year.
He was posthumously granted the title of Marquis [Hóu 侯]
and the posthumous name Zhōngwǔ [忠武].
Dèng Hóng had a magnificent appearance,
with a beard that hung past his belly.
As a general, he possessed both wisdom and courage,
his discipline was strict and clear,
he accurately assessed the enemy and secured victory,
always acting appropriately.
He once ingeniously created
"Ground-Churning Dragons" [jiǎodìlóng 攪地龍]
and
"Sky-Flying Nets" [fēitiānwǎng 飛天網].
He dug deep trenches
and covered them with earth and wood to appear like flat ground.
When the enemy entered the trap,
he activated the mechanisms,
causing them to collide with each other,
and they were all trapped in an instant.
He also imitated ancient designs to build "biased-box carriages" [piānxīangchē 偏箱車] and "four-wheeled carriages" [sìlúnchē 四輪車],
which concealed firearms inside,
and had flags erected on top.
Linked by hooks and rings,
they were arranged in formations,
useful for both offense and defense.
His army was organized into squads of five men.
He made them swear an oath in a temple.
If one person earned merit,
all five were rewarded together;
punishment was likewise applied.
Ten squads formed a team,
and the team's vanguard consisted of those capable of drawing a sixty-jin bow.
Ten teams were led by one Regional Commander.
He ensured that merits did not interfere with each other,
and responsibilities for crimes were specific,
which was praised as excellent at the time.
Dèng Hóng was filial to his mother
and observed propriety during mourning.
He was skilled in poetry,
and among military officials of the Míng dynasty, none surpassed him.
He had no sons,
so he adopted his elder brother's son, Sōng.
When Dèng Hóng was banished to Gānsù,
his family remained in the capital,
and Sōng stinted their food and clothing.
Dèng Hóng's concubine sewed to support herself,
almost to the point of destitution,
but Sōng paid no heed.
When Dèng Hóng returned,
he wanted to dismiss Sōng,
but because Sōng was married into the family of the Marquis of Huìchāng,
and the Marquis had once saved his life,
he suppressed his anger and did not act.
Upon his death,
Sōng succeeded to the title.
Later, because he was not Dèng Hóng's legitimate heir,
the title ended with Sōng,
and his son Cān was demoted to Commander of the Jǐnyīwèi [錦衣衞].
Zhū Qiān was
a native of Xiàyì.
At the beginning of Yǒnglè,
he inherited his father's post,
serving as Assistant Commander of the Left Guard of the Central Capital Garrison.
During Hóngxī's reign,
he was subordinate to Marquis Yángwǔ Xuē Lù,
and earned merit in the northern campaign,
advancing to Commander.
In Xuāndé first year, he advanced to Assistant Commander of Wànquán.
In Zhèngtǒng six years, while patrolling with Participant Commander Wáng Zhēn, they reached Bǎiyánshān [伯顏山]
where they encountered bandits and drove them away.
Next, at Mǐnānshān [閔安山],
they encountered three hundred cavalry of Wùliánghā,
and again defeated them.
They pursued them to Mǎngláiquán [莽來泉],
where the bandits fled over mountain ravines,
and then returned.
At this time, Qiān had already been promoted to Associate Regional Commander,
and was then made Regional Commander.
In the eighth year, he served as Right Participant Commander,
garrisoning the Left Guard of Wànquán.
The following year, he and Yáng Hóng defeated Wùliánghā troops at Kèlièsū [克列蘇],
and advanced to Assistant Commander of the Chief Military Commission.
His subordinates reported his illegal activities.
The Emperor, considering it was a time for autumn defense,
pardoned him.
Again, for his merits in the northern campaign,
he advanced to Associate Commander of the Chief Military Commission.
When the Emperor was captured in the north,
Yěxiān brought him to the city walls of Xuānfǔ [宣府]
and ordered the gates to be opened.
Qiān, along with Participant Commander Jì Guǎng and Censor-in-Chief Luó Héngxìn, refused,
and so Yěxiān left.
He was promoted to Right Commander of the Chief Military Commission.
He and Yáng Hóng entered the capital to defend it.
By then, the bandits had already retreated,
and they pursued them near the capital.
The battle was lost,
and Hóng impeached him.
The Ministry of War also impeached Hóng for not assisting.
Emperor Jǐng did not question either of them.
Hóng then took command of the Beijing Garrisons.
The court deliberated wanting someone like Hóng to replace him,
and all recommended Qiān.
Thus, he was promoted to Left Commander of the Chief Military Commission,
appointed Commander-in-Chief,
and garrisoned Xuānfǔ.
In the fourth month of the first year of Jǐngtài (1450),
three hundred cavalry of the invaders entered Shífēngkǒu,
then departed by the old route.
An imperial edict was issued, severely reprimanding them.
More than a month later,
they attacked again.
Qiān led troops to resist them,
stationing at Guānzǐkǒu.
Several thousand enemy cavalry suddenly arrived.
Qiān repelled them with deer-horn obstacles
and fired incendiary weapons,
