causing the invaders to retreat slightly.
This happened four times.
When Qiān’s army was about to withdraw,
the invaders pursued them again.
Dūdū Jiāng Fú reinforced them,
but also suffered a setback.
Qiān’s soldiers fought with all their might,
and the invaders could not break through.
In the sixth month, another two thousand cavalry invaded from the south.
Qiān dispatched Dū Zhǐhuī Niú Xǐ and others to resist them,
fighting at Nánpō.
Seeing dust rising,
Qiān led Cāncáng Jì Guǎng and others to gallop in support.
From sì (9-11 am) to wǔ (11 am-1 pm),
the invaders were defeated and fled.
For his merits,
he was enfeoffed as Fǔníng Bó.
At this time,
the invaders were extremely arrogant,
frequently harassing Xuānfǔ and Dàtóng,
intending to capture these two cities at any moment.
But Qiān defended Xuānfǔ,
and Guō Dēng defended Dàtóng,
repeatedly frustrating their forces.
Yěxiān, realizing that these two were difficult to overcome,
then solely focused on returning the former emperor.
In the eighth month,
the former emperor returned.
Passing through Xuānfǔ,
Qiān, with his son Yǒng, went out to meet him
and generously rewarded his envoys.
Soon after, Qiān falsely reported that five thousand enemy cavalry had breached the wall and entered.
Upon investigation,
it turned out to be Yěxiān’s tribute envoys.
An imperial edict severely reprimanded him,
and Qiān, in fear, apologized.
In the second month of the following year,
he died at his post.
He was posthumously granted the title of Hóu.
His son Yǒng succeeded him.
Qiān had been on the frontier for a long time
and was skilled in battle.
However, he was brave but lacked strategy,
so his fame was not as prominent as Yáng Hóng, Shí Hēng, or Guō Dēng.
During the Chénghuà reign,
he was posthumously given the epithet Wǔxiāng.
Yǒng,
whose courtesy name was Jǐngchāng.
He had a magnificent physique
and an imposing gaze.
When he first met the former emperor in Xuānfǔ,
the emperor frequently fixed his gaze on him.
During the Jǐngtài reign,
he inherited his noble title and participated in court functions.
When Yīngzōng was restored to the throne,
he saw Yǒng and recognized him, saying:
"Is this the one who saw Ourself in Xuānfǔ?"
Yǒng prostrated himself in thanks.
On that very day, he was summoned to attend by the emperor's side
and was given command of the Xuānwēi Battalion of the Imperial Guards.
In the fourth year of Tiānshùn (1460),
Xuānfǔ and Dàtóng declared an emergency,
and he was ordered to lead the imperial army to patrol the border.
In the seventh year, he commanded the Sānqiān Battalion,
and soon concurrently the Shénjī Battalion.
When Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
he was reassigned to supervise the Tuányíng
while retaining command of the Sānqiān Battalion.
In the first year of Chénghuà (1465),
the bandits Liú Tōng and others revolted in Jīng and Xiāng.
Yǒng was ordered to go with Shàngshū Bái Guī to suppress them.
Advancing his army to Nánzhāng,
he attacked and killed over nine hundred.
He then fell ill and stayed in Nánzhāng,
while Guī led the main army to defeat the bandits.
Yǒng went to rendezvous,
and on the way encountered remnants of the bandits,
capturing and killing several hundred people.
That autumn, he again advanced to suppress Shílóng and Féngxǐ,
achieving victories in both.
For his merits,
he was promoted to Hóu.
When Máolǐhái invaded the frontier,
he was ordered to wear the General's Seal
and rendezvous with Zhāngwǔ Bó Yáng Xìn to resist him.
When an envoy was sent to present tribute,
the army returned.
In the sixth year (1470),
Āluōchū raided Yánsuī.
He was again appointed General,
and together with Dū Yùshǐ Wáng Yuè
and Dūdū Liú Yù and Liú Jù, went to suppress them,
defeating them at Sūjiāzhài.
Ten thousand enemy cavalry arrived from Shuāngshānbǎo in five columns,
and a battle ensued at Kāihuāngchuān.
The invaders retreated slightly,
and capitalizing on the momentum, they were pursued,
abandoning all their baggage and fleeing.
At Niújiāzhài,
they encountered Dū Zhǐhuī Wú Zàn's smaller force,
which the invaders surrounded.
Zhǐhuī Lǐ Hào and Téng Zhōng arrived,
and fought fiercely again.
Jù, along with Dū Zhǐhuī Fàn Jǐn and Shén Yīng, took positions on the southern mountain and attacked from two sides,
whereupon the invaders were utterly defeated.
They beheaded one hundred and six,
captured several thousand horses and cattle,
and Āluōchū fled after being hit by a stray arrow.
At the time, the number of beheaded and captured was not large,
but all the generals fought bravely and pursued the enemy,
which border residents considered unprecedented in several decades.
For his merits,
he was granted the hereditary title of Shìhóu.
Although Āluōchū suffered a minor setback,
he still occupied the Hétào region.
In the first month of the following year (1471),
the invaders frequently attacked,
and Yǒng's units repeatedly made head-count achievements.
In the third month, they again raided Huáiyuǎn and other strongholds with over ten thousand cavalry.
Yǒng and Yuè and others divided their forces into five,
set up ambushes and defeated them,
pursuing them to the mountain pass and Huànghūdū River,
where the invaders were routed.
Meanwhile, Yóujī Sūn Yuè and Cài Xuān separately defeated other units at Lùjiàoshān.
When the victory was reported,
an imperial letter of commendation was sent.
Yǒng and others repeatedly requested to return to the capital,
but were all denied.
The invaders again attacked and plundered with over twenty thousand cavalry,
but were repelled.
As the year was drawing to a close,
Yǒng was finally recalled,
while Yuè was left to oversee the three frontiers.
In the fourteenth year (1478), Yǒng was promoted to Tàizǐ Tàibǎo.
In the winter of the following year,
he was appointed Jìnglǔ Jiāngjūn
and campaigned eastward,
with the eunuch Wāng Zhí supervising military affairs.
Upon his return,
he was promoted to the title of Bǎoguó Gōng.
In the first month of the year after that (1480),
Yánsuī reported an emergency.
Yǒng was ordered to be the General,
Yuè to supervise military affairs,
and Zhí to continue supervising,
departing beyond the frontier in separate routes.
Yuè and Zhí selected light cavalry and exited Gūdian Pass,
capturing invaders at Wēiníng Háizi.
However, Yǒng led the main army out from the southern route via Yúlín,
did not encounter the invaders,
and returned via Huíyuǎn,
expending an enormous amount of military provisions,
and over five thousand horses died.
Consequently, Yuè was granted the title of Bó,
Zhí received greater hereditary privileges,
but Yǒng had no achievements,
and no rewards were given.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Tàizǐ Tàifù.
In the second month of the seventeenth year (1481),
he again set out with Zhí and Yuè to Dàtóng
to resist Yìsīmǎ,
achieving one hundred and twenty head-count merits,
and was then granted the hereditary title of Shìgōng.
In the autumn of the nineteenth year (1483),
Xiǎowángzǐ entered the frontier,
and Xuānfǔ and Dàtóng reported emergencies.
Yuè and Zhí had already fallen from favor,
so Yǒng was appointed Zhènshuò Dàjiāngjūn,
with the eunuch Cài Xīn supervising his army,
and he commanded various generals such as Zhōu Yù and Lǐ Yú to defeat them.
Upon his return,
he continued to supervise the Tuányíng.
Someone submitted an anonymous letter accusing Yǒng of plotting rebellion,
and Yǒng requested to be relieved of military command,
but this was not permitted.
That winter,
an imperial letter personally added the titles of Tàifù and Tàizǐ Tàishī.
In the fourth year of Hóngzhì (1491), he supervised the completion of the renovation of the Tàimiào, and was promoted to Tàishī.
Yǒngzhì's army was strict and solemn,
and wherever he went, he often achieved merits.
He successively held the General's Seal eight times,
internally commanded the Twelve Regiment Camps and also managed the Chief Military Commission,
and among the marquis and meritorious officials, none could compare to him.
In the ninth year, he died.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Xuānpíng Wáng,
with the posthumous name Wǔyì.
His son, Huī, succeeded him.
Wang Tíngyán, a Grand Academician, argued that Yǒng's achievements should not merit a hereditary dukedom.
The court debated and decided to only allow the succession for one generation,
with subsequent generations being marquis.
The emperor decreed approval.
Huī,
courtesy name Dōngyáng.
He was tall with a beautiful beard;
people said his imposing presence resembled his father's.
He also frequently followed his father to the frontier,
gaining experience in military formations,
and was at the time considered capable.
In the fifth year of Hóngzhì, he was appointed Xūnwèi.
When he was nearly fifty,
he first succeeded to the peerage
and was put in charge of the Divine Machine Camp.
In the thirteenth year, when the capital's grand masters were reappointed,
Huī was ordered to supervise the Three Thousand Camp and concurrently lead the Right Commandery affairs.
When Huǒshāi invaded Dàtóng,
and Píngjiāng Bó Chén Ruì and others could not repel him,
Huī was ordered to take the Grand General's Seal and replace them.
By the time he arrived,
the invaders had already retreated,
so he returned.
The next spring,
Huǒshāi allied with Xiǎowángzǐ
and made a major invasion into Yánsuī and Níngxià.
Shǐ Lín, the Right Censor-in-Chief, requested reinforcement.
Huī was again ordered to carry the Grand General's Seal
and lead five generals: Dūdu Lǐ Jùn, Lǐ Chéng, Yáng Yù, Mǎ Yí, and Liú Níng,
while the eunuch Miáo Kuí supervised his army.
When they reached Níngxià,
the invaders had already plundered extensively and left.
So Huī, along with Lín and Kuí, led the five-route army to strike their lair in Hétáo.
The invaders had already moved their tents,
and they only managed to decapitate three enemies
and capture 1,500 horses, camels, cattle, and sheep before returning.
Not long after,
the invaders entered Gùyuán,
then plundered Píngliáng and Qìngyáng,
causing great alarm in Guānzhōng.
The generals of the two garrisons entrenched themselves and dared not fight,
while Huī and others were timid and did not rush to the rescue.
By the time they arrived,
they had decapitated twelve people
and recovered 4,000 captured persons,
and then reported it as a victory.
In this campaign,
the grand marshal was not skilled in winning battles,
the army's movements were circuitous and lacked discipline,
the border people died everywhere,
and all the prefectures were exhausted by transporting provisions for the army,
costing over 800,000 [cash],
with other levies being comparable,
yet they only achieved a total of fifteen enemy heads.
Court officials repeatedly impeached the three for their crimes.
The emperor did not question them.
Soon after, a report was made of over ten thousand officers and soldiers who had achieved merit in striking the lair.
Mǎ Wénshēng, Minister of War, and Liú Jiàn, Grand Secretary, opposed it.
The emperor sided with Kuí and others' statements,
and eventually recorded 210 people,
promoting them one rank,
while the rest were rewarded.
When the army returned to the capital,
the emperor still sent eunuchs with sheep and wine to greet and reward them.
Censorate officials vehemently criticized Huī's crimes,
but the emperor ultimately did not listen,
allowing Huī to remain as Governor-General of the Regiment Camps
and concurrently lead the Three Thousand Camp and the Right Commandery as before.
When Wǔzōng ascended the throne,
the invaders made a major incursion into Xuānfǔ.
Huī was again ordered to go with Kuí and Lín to lead the army.
The invaders then plundered Dàtóng.
Cānjiàng Chén Xióng attacked and decapitated over eighty enemies
and recovered over 2,700 captured people.
Huī and others reported a victory,
listing over twenty thousand meritorious officers and soldiers.
Yán Zhòngyǔ, Vice Minister of War, and Dèng Zhāng, Assistant Minister of the Dali Temple, went to investigate,
and found that many of the reports were untrue.
However, due to Kuí,
everyone received rewards.
When Liú Jǐn gained power,
Huī and others further reported that the merits recorded were too small,
requesting to follow the precedent of Báihúzhuāng during the Chénghuà era.
The Ministry of War strongly opposed it,
but it was not accepted.
Ultimately, Huī's words were followed,
and 1,563 people were promoted.
Huī was granted the title of Tàibǎo.
He died in the sixth year of Zhèngdé.
His son, Qí,
succeeded to the marquisate.
He once served as Commander-in-Chief,
garrisoning Liǎngguǎng.
He pacified Tiánzhōu with Yáo Mò
and executed Cén Měng,
and was promoted to Tàizǐ Tàibǎo.
In the early Jiājìng era,
he was recalled.
After a long time,
he served as Defender of Nánjīng
and died there.
His son, Yuè, succeeded him,
and also served as Defender of Nánjīng.
He died during the Lóngqìng era.
After four generations, his grandson was Guóbì.
During the Tiānqǐ era,
when Yáng Lián impeached Wèi Zhōngxián,
Guóbì also requested a swift resolution.
Zhōngxián was enraged
and suspended his annual stipend.
During the Chóngzhēn era,
he served as Governor-General of the Capital Camps.
When Wēn Tǐrén controlled the government,
Guóbì submitted a memorial impeaching him.
An imperial edict ordered the arrest of his retainers and the drafters of the memorial, throwing them into prison,
and suspended his stipend as before.
When he reached Nánjīng,
he was promoted to Bǎoguó Gōng.
He then allied himself with Mǎ Shìyīng and Ruǎn Dàchéng,
until the fall of the Míng dynasty.
Sūn Táng,
courtesy name Zhènyuǎn,
was a native of Dōngshèng Zhōu.
He inherited the position of Assistant Commander of Jìyáng Wèi.
Based on Zhū Yǒng's recommendation,
he was promoted to acting Commander.
At the end of the Zhèngtǒng era,
he was promoted to Assistant Commander
and served as Left Assistant General,
following Commander-in-Chief Xú Gōng to suppress Yè Zōngliú.
He defeated the rebels at Jīnhuá
and again broke them at Wūlóng Lǐng.
When Yīngzōng was captured in the north,
Jǐngdì recalled Táng,
and he was exceptionally promoted to Assistant Commander-in-Chief
and put in charge of the Three Thousand Camp.
When Yěxiān was about to invade,
he was promoted to Right Commander-in-Chief
and served as Commander-in-Chief,
leading ten thousand capital troops to defend Zǐjīng Guān.
As they were about to depart,
the invaders had already entered,
so they camped outside the capital city.
The invaders approached Déshèng Mén
but were repelled by Yú Qiān and others.
They then moved to Xīzhí Mén.
Táng fought a great battle with them,
killing several of their vanguards.
The invaders moved slightly north,
and Táng pursued them.
The invaders reinforced and surrounded Táng.
Táng fought vigorously and did not disengage.
Gāo Lǐ and Máofúshòu came to his aid,
and Lǐ was struck by an arrow.
When Shí Hēng's troops arrived,
the invaders retreated.
An imperial edict ordered Táng to assist Yáng Hóng in pursuit.
They fought at Zhúzhōu Shēnggōu,
achieving considerable kills and captures.
When the army returned,
he still managed the camp affairs.
In the early Jǐngtài era,
Yáng Hóng impeached Táng, who was then imprisoned.
Shí Hēng requested Táng's pardon,
and Jiāng Yuān also stated that in the battle outside the city,
only Táng fought with the most vigor,
so he was released.
In the winter of the third year, he served as Assistant Commander-in-Chief,
assisting Guō Dēng in garrisoning Dàtóng.
Dēng's command was strict,
and Táng could not act as he wished.
He wanted to divide the army with Dēng,
and even had his son, Centurion Hóng, insult Dēng.
The emperor arrested Hóng,
but pardoned him because of Táng.
Táng was recalled
and managed the Three Thousand Camp as before.
When Yīngzōng was restored to the throne,
for his
"Duómén"
merit, he was enfeoffed as Huáiníng Bó,
and soon after was granted hereditary certification.
Early in the Tiānshùn reign,
Gānsù reported an emergency.
An imperial edict appointed Sūn Táng as Commander-in-Chief,
to lead the capital's troops to suppress it.
As he was about to take leave of the emperor,
he fell ill and stayed overnight in the imperial antechamber.
At the second watch of the night,
eunuch Cáo Jíxiáng and the Earl of Zhāowǔ, Cáo Qīn, rebelled.
Their subordinate, Regional Commander Mǎ Liàng, reported the rebellion to the Marquis of Gōngshùn, Wú Jǐn.
Wú Jǐn hurried to inform Sūn Táng.
Sūn Táng hastily drafted a memorial,
knocked on the Dōngcháng'ān Gate,
and slipped through a crack in the gate into the inner court.
Only then was he able to gather troops to apprehend Cáo Jíxiáng
and guard the gates of the Imperial City.
Sūn Táng went to the home of the Marquis of Tàipíng, Zhāng Jǐn,
to request troops to attack the rebels,
but Zhāng Jǐn dared not come out.
Sūn Táng hastily returned to Xuānwǔ Street,
and urgently dispatched his two sons, Sūn Fǔ and Sūn Ruò, to summon the expeditionary generals and soldiers,
deceiving them by saying:
“Prisoners from the Ministry of Justice have revolted in prison;
those who capture them will be heavily rewarded.”
When about two thousand people had gathered,
he finally told them the truth.
By then it was already dawn,
and so they attacked Cáo Qīn.
Cáo Qīn was attacking the Dōngcháng'ān Gate,
but could not enter,
so he turned to attack the Dōng'ān Gate.
Sūn Táng's troops caught up,
and the rebels gradually dispersed.
Sūn Ruò chopped Cáo Qīn on the shoulder,
but Sūn Ruò was also killed.
Cáo Qīn knew that the plan had failed,
and fled back to his home,
still commanding his followers to resist Sūn Táng fiercely.
The situation was only settled by dusk.
Sūn Táng was ranked first for his meritorious service,
promoted to hereditary marquis,
and continued to command the Sānqiānyíng (Three Thousand Camp).
Sūn Ruò was posthumously granted the title of Bǎihù (Company Commander),
to be hereditary.
Sūn Táng was rough and fierce, and skilled in battle,
but frequently violated the law.
Initially, he bribed the eunuch Jīn Yīng,
and obtained a promotion to Dūdū (Chief Military Commissioner).
When the matter was discovered,
he was sentenced to decapitation,
but Emperor Jǐngdì specially pardoned him.
Towards the end of the Tiānshùn reign,
he was repeatedly impeached for accepting bribes from generals and soldiers.
Feeling uneasy,
he requested to retire.
An imperial edict relieved him of his duties in the military camps and the imperial guard,
but he still oversaw the Zuǒfǔ (Left Chief Military Commission).
When Emperor Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
the eunuch Niú Yù fell into disfavor.
Sūn Táng was implicated due to his marriage connection with Niú Yù,
and his salary was suspended, and he was placed on inactive status.
Soon after, he submitted a plea,
and was granted half his salary.
Later,
he again presented his meritorious achievements,
and his full salary was restored.
He died in the seventh year of Chénghuà (1471).
He was posthumously granted the title of Lái Guógōng (Duke of Lái),
and given the posthumous name Wǔmǐn.
His son, Sūn Fǔ, requested to inherit the title.
The Ministry of Personnel stated
that those with merit from the
"Duómén" (Seizing the Gate)
event
were not, by precedent, allowed to pass on their titles hereditarily.
However, the emperor, citing Sūn Táng's capture of the rebels,
granted it to him.
The title was passed down through his son to his grandson, Sūn Yìngjué,
who was Commander-in-Chief of the Tuányíng (Training Camps) during the Zhèngdé reign.
It was passed down four generations to his great-grandson, Sūn Shìzhōng.
During the Wànlì reign, he served as garrison commander of Húguǎng
and commander-in-chief of grain transport for twenty years.
It was passed down three more generations to his grandson, Sūn Wéifān.
When the roving bandits captured the capital,
he was killed.
As for Sūn Táng's falsely claiming
merit from the
"Duómén" (Seizing the Gate) event to be enfeoffed as an Earl,
Dūdū Dǒng Xīng, as well as Cáo Yì, Shī Jù, Zhào Shèng, and others all took advantage of this time to falsely claim enfeoffment,
and were granted hereditary certificates.
Dǒng Xīng, Cáo Yì, and Shī Jù have their own biographies.
Zhào Shèng,
courtesy name Kègōng,
was from Qiān'ān.
He inherited his hereditary post as Commander of the Yǒngpíng Guard.
Towards the end of the Zhèngtǒng reign,
he defended against invaders at Xīzhímén,
and was promoted to Vice Regional Commander.
Early in the Tiānshùn reign,
he, along with Sūn Táng and others, participated in
the
"Duómén" (Seizing the Gate)
event and was exceptionally promoted to Vice Chief Military Commissioner.
He also joined Sūn Táng in attacking the rebel Cáo Qīn,
and was promoted to Assistant Chief Military Commissioner.
When Bólái attacked Gānsù,
Zhào Shèng and Lǐ Gǎo served as left and right assistant commanders,
following Bái Guī on the western expedition to Gùyuán,
where they attacked the invaders
and repelled them.
When Emperor Xiànzōng ascended,
Zhào Shèng commanded the Gǔyǒngyíng (Drumming Valor Camp) for training.
In the first year of Chénghuà (1465),
Shānxī reported an emergency,
and he was appointed general.
When he reached Yànmén,
the invaders had already retreated,
so he returned.
The following year, he again went out to Yánsuí to defend against invaders.
As a peace agreement was then made,
he withdrew his troops.
Soon after, he commanded the Yàowǔyíng (Awe-Inspiring Martial Camp).
In the fourth year (1468), he served as Commander-in-Chief,
garrisoned in Liáodōng.
In the seventh year (1471), he was summoned to command the Wǔjūnyíng (Five Army Camp),
and later
it was changed to the Sānqiānyíng (Three Thousand Camp).
When Biéjiāsīlán attacked Xuānfǔ,
Zhào Shèng was appointed general by imperial edict,
to lead ten thousand capital troops to defend against them,
but was also recalled when the invaders fled.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Left Chief Military Commissioner,
and given the additional title of Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent.
In the nineteenth year (1483), he was enfeoffed as Earl of Chāngníng.
Zhào Shèng was initially as famous as Lǐ Gǎo.
Later, he repeatedly led large armies,
but never encountered the enemy
and achieved no merit.
He obtained his enfeoffment through illicit connections,
which greatly damaged his reputation.
Later, he was promoted to Grand Tutor,
and while constructing the tomb of Consort Wàn Guìfēi,
he fell into a rocky cliff and died.
He was posthumously granted the title of Marquis,
and given the posthumous name Zhuàngmǐn.
Early in the Hóngzhì reign,
his grandson, Zhào Jiàn, requested to inherit the title.
The Ministry of Personnel stated that Zhào Shèng had no merit
and thus his title should not be hereditary,
so Zhào Jiàn was appointed Commander of the Jǐnyī Guard.
Fàn Guǎng,
a native of Liáodōng.
During the Zhèngtǒng reign, he inherited his hereditary post
as Vice Commander of the Níngyuǎn Guard,
and was promoted to Commander.
In the fourteenth year (1449), his accumulated merits led to his promotion to Vice Regional Commander of Liáodōng.
Fàn Guǎng was skilled in cavalry archery,
exceptionally brave and fierce.
When Emperor Yīngzōng was taken captive in the north,
the court deliberated on selecting military talents,
and Minister Yú Qiān recommended Fàn Guǎng.
He was promoted to Vice Chief Military Commissioner,
serving as Left Deputy Commander-in-Chief,
and deputy to Shí Hēng.
When Yěxiān attacked the capital,
Fàn Guǎng charged into battle on horseback,
his subordinates following him,
their courage redoubled.
When the invaders retreated,
he pursued and defeated them again at Zǐjīngguān.
His merits were recorded,
and he was ordered to be given the substantive appointment.
Soon after, he was promoted to Assistant Chief Military Commissioner,
and sent to guard Huáilái.
Later he was recalled.
In the second month of the first year of Jǐngtài (1450),
Shí Hēng went on a border inspection tour.
At that time, Dūdū Wèi Yǐng commanded the Grand Camp,
and Fàn Guǎng was ordered to assist.
In the third month,
invaders attacked Xuānfǔ.
The Ministry of War was ordered to convene generals from various camps to select military talents,
and Fàn Guǎng was unanimously recommended.
He was appointed Commander-in-Chief to supervise troops with Censor-in-Chief Luó Tōng for patrols,
stationed outside Jūyōng Pass.
After several months, he returned to the capital,
and became Shí Hēng's deputy in charge of the Tuányíng (Training Camps) cavalry.
Shí Hēng's
actions were unlawful, and his subordinates were often
greedy and unrestrained. Fàn Guǎng repeatedly spoke about this.
Shí Hēng resented him,
slandered him to have him dismissed,
leaving him only in charge of one camp of the Yìyǒng.
Fàn Guǎng also could not get along with Dūdū Zhāng Yuè.
When Yīngzōng was restored to power,
Shí Hēng and Zhāng Yuè, relying on their
"seizing the gate"
merit,
falsely accused Fàn Guǎng of colluding with Yú Qiān
to plot the enthronement of an external prince.
Consequently, he was imprisoned and sentenced to death.
His son, Shēng, was exiled to Guǎngxī,
his family property was confiscated,
and his wife, children, and residence were bestowed upon the surrendered soldiers.
In the spring of the following year,
Zhāng Yuè returned from an early court session,
making bowing gestures along the way.
His attendants, surprised, asked him about it.
He said,
"Fàn Guǎng has passed by."
Thereupon, he fell ill, unable to sleep,
suffering in pain for over a month before he died.
In the early Chénghuà reign,
court officials pleaded Fàn Guǎng's case.
The emperor ordered his son, Shēng, to inherit his hereditary office.
Fàn Guǎng's nature was resolute and decisive.
Whenever he faced battle,
he would lead his soldiers from the front.
He never suffered a defeat,
and all the generals of his time were inferior to him.
He was most trusted by Yú Qiān,
which is why he was resented by his peers.
The eulogy says: Yáng Hóng, Shí Hēng and their ilk,
encountered a time of many affairs,
exerted the strength of their claws and teeth,
were enfeoffed as marquises with hereditary patents,
bringing glory to their families.
Their rewards were indeed excessively generous.
Yáng Hóng knew that excessive prosperity was to be feared,
while Shí Hēng was wicked, cruel, and arrogant,
presuming on imperial favor and becoming proud.
His family's extermination was fitting.
Zhū Qiān's bravery and strategy were not equal to Guō Dēng's,
yet Guō Dēng had no descendants,
while Zhū Qiān's son Yǒng
was promoted to the rank of Shànggōng,
and his descendants held hereditary marquisates without interruption.
Sūn Táng and Fàn Guǎng were equally skilled in warfare,
yet Fàn Guǎng died unjustly.
The fates they encountered were both fortunate and unfortunate.
How great was the difference between them!
Collations and Notes

Biographies Chapter 62: Shǐ Zhāo (Liú Zhāo, Lǐ Dá), Wū Kǎi (Cáo Yì, Shī Jù), Xǔ Guì (Zǐ Níng), Zhōu Xián (Zǐ Yù), Ōu Xìn, Wáng Xǐ, Lǔ Jiàn (Zǐ Lín, Sūn Jīng), Liú Níng (Zhōu Xǐ, Zhuāng Jiàn), Péng Qīng, Jiāng Hàn (Zǐ Shì, Sūn Yìngxióng), Ān Guó, Háng Xióng.
Shǐ Zhāo,
a native of Héféi.
In the early Yǒnglè reign,
through accumulated merits, he rose to Dū Zhǐhuī Qiānshì.
In the 8th year, he was appointed Zǒngbīngguān
and garrisoned Liángzhōu.
The local commander Lǎodíhǎn had previously rebelled with Qiānhù Hǔ Bǎo.
Hǔ Bǎo was defeated, and
Lǎodíhǎn submitted.
Shǐ Zhāo submitted a memorial stating that he would certainly rebel.
Before the memorial arrived,
Lǎodíhǎn indeed rebelled.
Shǐ Zhāo, with Dū Zhǐhuī Mǎndū and others, suppressed him.
He was then moved to garrison Xīníng.
When Rénzōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Dūdū Qiānshì.
He reported that the customs of Xīníng were rough and fierce,
and requested the establishment of schools similar to those in the central plains.
His request was granted.
In the early Xuāndé reign,
Shǐ Zhāo used garrison troops for defense,
leaving no time for farming and cultivation.
Over 770 family members expressed willingness to cultivate land.
He requested that they be allowed to farm,
and their taxes be collected to supplement military provisions.
This was approved.
In the 5th year,
Sànjí Sī, the Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ of Qǔxiān Wèi, ambushed and robbed envoys from the Western Regions.
Shǐ Zhāo led Cāncójiàng Zhào Ān, accompanied by eunuchs Wáng Ān and Wáng Jǐn, to suppress him.
They marched directly to Qǔxiān,
where Sànjí Sī fled upon seeing their approach.
They captured his associates, including Dádábùhuā,
and seized 340 men and women,
over 300,000 horses, camels, cattle, and sheep,
their might shaking the region beyond the Great Wall.
Upon hearing of the victory,
an imperial edict was sent to commend and reward them,
with additional prizes.
In the spring of the 7th year,
he was appointed Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn and garrisoned Níngxià.
When Bódídálǐmá invaded the border,
he dispatched troops to attack him.
Upon reaching Kuòtáicháhǎn,
they captured many.
He was promoted to Dūdū Tóngzhī.
In the early Zhèngtǒng reign,
Shǐ Zhāo noted that Níngxià was isolated beyond the Yellow River,
extending two thousand li east to Suídé,
vast and difficult to defend.
He requested the construction of a scout cavalry camp at Huāmǎchí,
and the addition of beacon towers,
directly connecting to the border of Hālāwūsù.
Border defenses were greatly strengthened.
Soon after, he was promoted to Yòu Dūdū.
At that time, Ātái and Wānrzhǐbó repeatedly raided the border.
An imperial edict ordered Shǐ Zhāo, along with the Gānsù commander Jiǎng Guì and Zhào Ān, to suppress them.
They achieved no success
and were severely reprimanded by imperial edict,
demoted to Dūdū Qiānshì.
Three years later, he was reinstated as Yòu Dūdū.
In the 8th year, he was recalled due to old age.
He died the following year.
Shǐ Zhāo resided in Níngxià for twelve years,
mature and steadfast, managing military and civil affairs effectively.
It also happened that enemy forces were weak,
and the border remained peaceful.
Bīngbù Shàngshū Wáng Jì and
Níngxià Cānjiàng Wáng Róng once pointed out his faults.
The court deliberated that Shǐ Zhāo had guarded the border for a long time
and was skilled in military affairs,
making him difficult to replace.
Among those who served as border generals for the longest time alongside Shǐ Zhāo
and had commendable achievements,
Dūdū Tóngzhī Liú Zhāo garrisoned Xīníng for twenty years,
and Dū Zhǐhuī Lǐ Dá garrisoned Táozhōu for up to forty years,
both feared and respected by both Tibetans and Han people.
Liú Zhāo,
a native of Quánjiāo.
In the 5th year of Yǒnglè, as Dū Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī, he was sent as an envoy to Wānr Gānsù and Wūsī Zàng,
establishing post stations.
Returning to Língzàng,
Tibetan bandits ambushed and robbed him,
but Liú Zhāo defeated them.
He was promoted to Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ
and garrisoned Hézhōu.
In the 2nd year of Xuāndé,
he assisted Chén Huái in suppressing the Sōngpān rebels.
He was successively promoted to Dūdū Tóngzhī,
moved to Xīníng,
then returned to garrison Hézhōu,
concurrently overseeing Xīníng.
Zházǐjiā, a chieftain of Hǎndōng, ambushed and killed an imperial eunuch envoy to the Western Regions,
seizing the imperial edict and gold and silk.
Shǐ Zhāo was ordered to assist Gānsù Zǒngbīngguān Liú Guǎng in suppressing him.
Zházǐjiā requested to return the stolen edict and silk,
and offered horses as tribute to atone for his crime.
The emperor, believing that a desperate enemy should not be pursued too deeply,
ordered Shǐ Zhāo and others to return.
Lǐ Dá,
a native of Dìngyuǎn.
He successively held the office of Dūdū Qiānshì.
During the Zhèngtǒng reign,
he retired from office.
Wū Kǎi,
a native of Jùróng.
From Bǎihù of Lúzhōu Wèi, he rose through accumulated merits to Dū Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī.
In the 6th year of Yǒnglè, for his merit in pacifying Jiāozhǐ with Yīngguógōng Zhāng Fǔ,
he was promoted to Liáodōng Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ.
In the 11th year, he was summoned to lead his unit to the capital.
The following year, he participated in the expedition to the desert,
and was ordered to return first.
Wū Kǎi stated that two-thirds of the troops from various commanderies should be for defense,
while one-third should farm for provisions,
and all horses purchased in Kāiyuán should be given to their respective commanderies for riding and training.
This was approved.
When Xuānzōng ascended the throne,
he was appointed Dūdū Qiānshì, bearing the seal of Zhēnglǔ Qián Jiāngjūn,
replacing Zhū Róng to garrison Liáodōng.
At that time, Chinese people who escaped from beyond the Great Wall
were ordered to be sent to the capital,
awaiting their relatives to claim them.
Wū Kǎi said that traveling long distances
might cause them to lose their homes,
and discourage distant people from wishing to return.
Thus, it was changed so that those with horses and who were young and strong were sent to the capital,
while the rest could decide for themselves.
When the enemy plundered Xīshān,
Wū Kǎi defeated them,
recovering all that was plundered,
receiving an imperial edict of praise and encouragement.
The emperor once sent envoys to build boats on the Sōnghuā Jiāng to recruit various tribes.
The place was distant,
and military and civilian transport faced great difficulties,
with many deserting.
Later, there was an alert,
and Wū Kǎi strongly requested to stop the project,
but over five hundred deserting soldiers had already entered the various tribes of the Hǎixī.
Afterwards, the boat-building project resumed,
with eunuch Ruǎn Yáomín and Dū Zhǐhuī Liú Qīng and others overseeing it.
They committed many illegal acts,
leading to an uprising.
Wū Kǎi impeached Ruǎn Yáomín and others,
handing them over to the authorities.
When Yīngzōng 登極 ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Dūdū Tóngzhī 都督同知,
and submitted a memorial on eight border issues.
He requested generous relief for the families of those who died in service,
an increase in the salaries of officials who took a pay cut,
the annual provision of winter clothing fabric and cotton for soldiers,
and that military rations of grain and fodder remain as per the old system,
and also to summon merchants to strengthen the border.
All were approved for implementation.
Not long after,
he was impeached by the Minister of War, Wáng Jì 王驥.
The imperial court, knowing Kǎi 凱 was virtuous,
ordered Kǎi 凱 to present his own case.
It also instructed the court officials
that civil and military officials with crimes should only be impeached after the facts were established,
and those who made false accusations would not be pardoned.
Kǎi 凱 was thus able to pursue his ambitions.
In the twelfth month of the third year of Zhèngtǒng 正統, he fell ill,
and an imperial physician was ordered to rush to him,
but he died before the physician arrived.
Kǎi 凱 was naturally firm and resolute,
rich in wisdom and strategy,
and strict yet benevolent in managing the masses.
He was in Liaodōng 遼東 for over thirty years,
exercising both authority and benevolence,
and border affairs were well-managed.
Among those who guarded the eastern frontier before and after him,
no one, except Cáo Yì 曹義, could compare.
Yì 義,
courtesy name Jìngfāng 敬方,
was a native of Yízhēn 儀真.
He rose from Yānshān Zuǒwèi Zhǐhuī Qiānshì 燕山左衞指揮僉事 through repeated merits to Dūdū Qiānshì 都督僉事,
and served as Kǎi's 凱副副 deputy in guarding Liaodōng 遼東.
When Kǎi 凱 died,
he succeeded him as Zǒngbīngguān 總兵官.
Kǎi 凱 was a famous general,
and Yì 義, who succeeded him,
was honest, upright, and steadfast,
and the people of Liáo 遼 found peace under him.
When the Wùliánghā 兀良哈 attacked Guǎngníng Qiántún 廣寧前屯,
an imperial edict sternly reprimanded him,
ordering Wáng Āo 王翺 to rectify military affairs
and impeach Yì 義 for a capital crime.
Shortly after,
Yì 義 captured the border-violating Bótái 孛台 and others,
and an edict ordered them to be executed in Bù 布.
From then on, Yì 義 frequently fought with the Wùliánghā 兀良哈.
In the ninth year of Zhèngtǒng 正統,
he joined Zhū Yǒng's 朱勇 army in a pincer attack,
achieving many beheadings and captures,
and was promoted to Dūdū Tóngzhī 都督同知,
eventually rising to Zuǒ Dūdū 左都督.
Yì 義 was at the border for twenty years,
without dazzling achievements,
but he was able to diligently guard the frontier.
His subordinates, such as Shī Jù 施聚 and Jiāo Lǐ 焦禮, all rose to become great generals.
When Yīngzōng 英宗 was restored,
Yì 義 was specially ennobled as Fēngrùn Bó 豐潤伯,
and Jù 聚 was also ennobled as Huáiróu Bó 懷柔伯.
Four years later,
Yì 義 died,
and was posthumously granted the title of Hóu 侯
and the posthumous name Zhuāngwǔ 莊武.
His second wife, Lady Lǐ 李氏, committed suicide to follow him in death,
and an imperial edict commended her.
Shī Jù 施聚,
whose ancestors were from the desert,
resided in Shùntiān Tōngzhōu 順天通州.
His father, Zhōng 忠, served as Jīnwú Yòuwèi Zhǐhuīshǐ 金吾右衞指揮使,
followed in the northern campaign,
and died in battle.
Jù 聚 inherited the position.
During the Xuāndé 宣德 reign,
he garrisoned Liaodōng 遼東,
and was repeatedly promoted to Dū Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī 都指揮同知.
Through Yì's 義 recommendation,
he was promoted to Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ 都指揮使.
When Yì 義 fought the Wùliánghā 兀良哈,
Jù 聚 always accompanied him.
When Yěxiān 也先 approached the capital,
Jǐngdì 景帝 ordered Jù 聚 and Jiāo Lǐ 焦禮 to enter and defend.
Jù 聚 wept bitterly
and immediately led his troops west.
His subordinates offered beef and wine,
but Jù 聚 waved them away, saying:
"Where is the Son of Heaven?
How can we enjoy this?"
By the time they arrived,
the invaders had already retreated,
so they returned.
Jù 聚 was known for his bravery,
and rose to the official position of Zuǒ Dūdū 左都督.
When Yīngzōng 英宗 extended his benevolence,
he was granted the title of Bó 伯.
He died two years after Yì 義,
was posthumously granted the title of Hóu 侯,
and the posthumous name Wēijìng 威靖.
The title of Yì 義 was passed down for three generations to Dòng 棟,
and that of Jù 聚 for four generations to Jǐn 瑾.
The Ministry of Personnel all said they should not be allowed to inherit again,
but Shìzōng 世宗 specifically allowed it.
The爵爵 title was passed down until the fall of the Míng 明 dynasty.
Xǔ Guì 許貴,
courtesy name Yònghé 用和,
was a native of Jiāngdū 江都,
and the son of Yǒngxīn Bó 永新伯 Chéng 成.
He inherited the position as Yǔlín Zuǒwèi Zhǐhuīshǐ 羽林左衞指揮使.
Ānxiāng Bó 安鄉伯 Zhāng Ān 張安 recommended Guì 貴 as a military talent.
His tests in equestrian archery and strategy were all excellent,
and he was promoted to acting Dū Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī 都指揮同知.
Soon after, recommended by Wǔjìn Bó 武進伯 Zhū Miǎn 朱冕, he was promoted to Shānxī Xíng Dūsī 山西行都司,
supervising the training of soldiers and horses of various guards in Dàtóng 大同.
At the end of the Zhèngtǒng 正統 reign,
he defended the western route of Dàtóng 大同.
When Yěxiān 也先 invaded,
he followed Shí Hēng 石亨 in battle at Yánghé Hòukǒu 陽和後口,
suffering a defeat,
but Guì 貴 fought valiantly and returned.
When Yīngzōng 英宗 was captured in the north,
the border cities were all ruined,
and Dàtóng 大同 bore the brunt of the enemy,
causing people's hearts to be especially fearful.
Guì 貴 inspired the soldiers with loyalty and righteousness.
When the enemy came,
he defeated them.
He was promoted to Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ 都指揮使.
In the spring of the first year of Jǐngtài 景泰,
he served as Yòu Cāncānjìng 右參將.
When the enemy attacked Wēiyuǎn 威遠,
he pursued and defeated them at Púzhōu Yíng 蒲州營,
recovering the people and livestock they had plundered.
When ten thousand enemy cavalry approached the city,
he repelled them.
He was again promoted to Dūdū Tóngzhī 都督同知.
Dàtóng 大同 lacked horses,
so he was ordered to seek them among the people,
obtaining over eight hundred.
The department in charge did not pay for them,
so Guì 貴 pleaded on behalf of the people,
and they were then compensated.
He once recruited a suicide squad to infiltrate the enemy camp,
and raided over a hundred horses,
all of which he gave to the soldiers,
who were all happy to serve him.
The eunuch Wéi Lìzhuǎn 韋力轉, who was guarding a sector, was abusive and tyrannical,
and no one dared to speak out,
but Guì 貴 impeached him.
In the third year,
he returned to the capital due to illness.
When Yīngzōng 英宗 was restored,
he was ordered to manage the affairs of the Zuǒ Fǔ 左府,
and soon after was transferred to Nánjīng 南京.
The region of Sōngpān 松潘 was inhabited by a mix of Fān 番 (Tibetans) and Miáo 苗 (Miao people),
and was close to Dǒngbǔ Hánhú 董卜韓胡.
Previously, one Cāncānjìng 參將 was stationed there.
In the fifth year of Tiānshùn 天順,
the defending officials reported an alarm,
and the court deliberated setting up a Fù Zǒngbīng 副總兵,
with Guì 貴 to guard the area.
Before he reached his post, the Shāndū Zhǎngmán 山都掌蠻 rebelled,
and an edict ordered him to suppress them first on his way.
Guì 貴 divided his forces into two detachments and advanced directly to their stronghold,
consecutively breaking over forty stockades,
beheading one thousand one hundred,
capturing over eight hundred alive,
while the remaining rebels fled far away.
Guì 貴 also suffered from mountain sickness,
and died before reaching Sōngpān 松潘.
The emperor suspended court for one day on his account,
and bestowed funeral gifts and sacrifices according to regulations.
His son, Níng 寧,
courtesy name Zhìdào 志道.
At the end of the Zhèngtǒng 正統 reign,
he, as a gentleman-in-waiting, served in the army and gained merit,
becoming a Jǐnyī Qiānhù 錦衣千戶.
After Guì's 貴 death,
he inherited the position of Zhǐhuīshǐ 指揮使.
Through recommendation, he was promoted to acting Dū Zhǐhuī Qiānshì 都指揮僉事,
and guarded Cháigōubǎo 柴溝堡.
At the beginning of the Chénghuà 成化 reign,
he served as a Yóují Jiāngjūn 遊擊將軍 in Dàtóng 大同.
When invaders attacked,
he, along with fellow official Qín Jié 秦傑 and others, repelled them at Xiǎolóngzhōujiàn 小龍州澗,
capturing their Right Chancellor Bǎtū 把禿 and ten others.
He was reassigned to supervise training in Xuānfǔ 宣府,
and then transferred to Yánsuí 延綏.
The area was close to Hétào 河套,
and invaders frequently plundered Gūshānbǎo 孤山堡.
Níng 寧 led an isolated force to vigorously attack them,
winning all three battles,
and the invaders crossed the river and fled.
The next year, they again entered Shāhédūn 沙河墩 with three thousand cavalry,
and he, with Zǒngbīngguān 總兵官 Fáng Néng 房能, repelled them.
The invaders retreated,
and then plundered Kāngjiāchà 康家岔.
Níng 寧 went out of the pass for one hundred and fifty lǐ,
pursued and fought them,
and returned with over a thousand horses, cattle, and sheep.
Shí Néng (時能) then defended Yánsuī (延綏),
lacking great strategic talent.
The Grand Coordinator, Wáng Ruì (王銳), requested reinforcements.
An imperial edict ordered the Grand Coordinator of Dàtóng (大同), Wáng Yuè (王越), to lead troops there.
Yuè (越) dispatched Níng (寧) to the western route,
where he defeated the enemy at Líjiājiàn (黎家澗).
He was promoted to Assistant Commander-in-chief.
Later, Yuè (越) again sent Níng (寧) with Commander Chén Huī (陳輝) to pursue the bandits,
capturing six hundred horses and mules.
The imperial court, seeing that Āluó Chū (阿羅出) had re-entered the Hétáo (河套) region
and was frequently harassing the border,
ordered Yuè (越) and Zhū Yǒng (朱永) to defend it.
Recognizing Níng's (寧) talent,
he was promoted to Assistant Chief Military Commissioner,
given the seal of the Deputy General who Pacifies the Captives,
and replaced Néng (能) as the Commander-in-chief.
Níng (寧) came from a prominent hereditary family,
and within less than ten years, reached the rank of a great general.
His peers deferred to him, acknowledging his superiority,
and many of his father's friends served under his command,
yet they did not consider this advancement too rapid.
A month later,
the bandits launched a large incursion.
Yǒng (永) sent Níng (寧) and Mobile Corps Commander Sūn Yuè (孫鉞) to repel them.
Arriving at Bōluóbǎo (波羅堡),
they were locked in a standoff for three days and nights,
whereupon the bandits finally withdrew.
There were many losses,
but Níng (寧) emerged through fierce fighting,
and was eventually rewarded.
In winter,
bandits entered Ānbiān (安邊),
and Níng (寧) pursued and attacked them with merit.
In the seventh year, he and generals Sūn Yuè (孫鉞), Zhù Xióng (祝雄), and others defeated the bandits at Huànghūdū Hé (滉忽都河),
receiving an imperial letter of commendation.
Bǎhā Bólúo (把哈孛羅), the King of Kāiyuán (開元) from the north, repeatedly wished to surrender,
but inwardly feared punishment from the imperial court
and outwardly feared Āluó Chū's (阿羅出) vengeance,
thus he wavered, unable to decide.
Níng (寧) requested that he be appeased to secure his loyalty,
and ultimately he surrendered.
The following year,
Participating General Qián Liàng (錢亮) suffered a defeat at Shīpójìàn (師婆澗),
with thirteen or fourteen tenths of his soldiers dying.
Níng (寧) and Yuè (越) were both impeached.
The Emperor did not fault them.
At that time, Mǎndūlǔ (滿都魯) and others frequently invaded Yánsuī (延綏),
and Níng (寧) led the garrison troops in fierce battles.
The bandits, failing to achieve their objective,
then went out via the western route,
directly invading Huánqìng (環慶) and Gùyuán (固原).
Níng (寧) led light cavalry in a night raid at Yāzǐ Hú (鴨子湖),
seizing horses and livestock before returning.
The year after that,
the bandits entered Yúlínjiàn (榆林澗),
and he and Grand Coordinator Yú Zǐjùn (余子俊) defeated them.
Mǎndūlǔ (滿都魯) and others made a large incursion into the western route,
leaving their families at Hóngyánchí (紅鹽池).
Yuè (越) seized the opportunity with Níng (寧) and Xuānfǔ (宣府) general Zhōu Yù (周玉) to attack and destroy their lair.
He was promoted to Acting Assistant Chief Military Commissioner.
He and Zǐjùn (子俊) built border walls
and increased the number of camps and fortresses,
causing the bandit menace to somewhat decline.
In the eighteenth year,
the bandits entered through several routes.
Níng (寧) pushed them back to the border wall,
capturing one hundred twenty heads.
He was given a substantive appointment.
At that time, Yuè (越) was garrisoned in Dàtóng (大同),
and Níng (寧) was ordered to replace him.
Upon his arrival, he did not get along with the garrison Eunuch Wāng Zhí (汪直).
Grand Coordinator Guō Táng (郭鏜) reported this,
and Zhí (直) was transferred to Nánjīng (南京).
The Little Prince launched a major invasion.
Níng (寧), knowing the enemy's strength,
wished to act cautiously and await an opportunity.
So, he gathered his troops and defended,
while separately dispatching generals Liú Níng (劉寧) and Dǒng Shēng (董升) to act in coordination with Zhōu Xǐ (周璽).
The bandits plundered heavily
and burned the Prince of Dài's (代王) separate fortress.
The prince urged battle,
making his followers cry outside the camp gate.
Níng (寧) was indignant
and, with Táng (鏜) and others, set up camp outside the city.
The bandits used over ten men as a decoy,
and the cavalry under Eunuch Cài Xīn (蔡新) charged to attack.
Níng's (寧) officers and soldiers eagerly rushed forward,
but encountered an ambush and were utterly defeated,
with over a thousand dead.
Níng (寧) fled to Xiàmǐzhuāng (夏米莊),
while Táng (鏜) and Xīn (新) galloped into the city.
Just then, Xǐ (璽) and others arrived as reinforcements,
and the bandits then retreated.
When Níng (寧) returned,
the wives and children of the fallen soldiers cried out and cursed him,
throwing tiles and bricks at him.
Níng (寧) was greatly disheartened.
Soon after, the bandits invaded again,
and Liú Níng (劉寧), Sòng Chéng (宋澄), Zhuāng Jiàn (莊鑑), and others repelled them.
After ten battles,
they gained a slight advantage,
and the bandits retreated.
Níng (寧) and others concealed their previous defeat
and instead reported a victory.
The Imperial Censor Chéng Chūnzhèn (程春震) exposed this,
and he, Táng (鏜), and Xīn (新) were all imprisoned.
Táng (鏜) was demoted by six ranks,
Xīn (新) was demoted by three ranks for his initial appointment,
and Níng (寧) was demoted to Assistant Commander and placed in retirement.
During the Hóngzhì (弘治) reign,
he was recommended to serve as Acting Commander-in-chief,
responsible for training.
He died in the twelfth month of the eleventh year.
He was posthumously granted the title of Assistant Chief Military Commissioner.
Níng (寧), from the time he tied his hair for military service,
fought in over a hundred major and minor battles,
and sustained twenty-seven wounds.
He was resolute and steadfast by nature,
held his office with integrity,
treated his soldiers with kindness,
and disdained seeking advancement through improper means.
Liú Níng (劉寧), Shén Yīng (神英), and Lǐ Gǎo (李杲) all served under his command.
His son, Tài (泰),
has his own biography.
Zhōu Xián (周賢),
a native of Chú (滁),
inherited the post of Thousand-household Commander of the Former Guard of Xuānfǔ (宣府).
In the early Jǐngtài (景泰) reign,
through accumulated merits, he rose to Assistant Commander-in-chief,
defending Xīmāo'éryù (西猫兒峪),
and assisting Deputy Commander-in-chief Sūn Ān (孫安) in defending Shíbā Chéng (石八城).
Soon after, he was appointed Right Participating General,
replacing Ān (安) as garrison commander.
When Wūliánghā (兀良哈) invaded,
Commander-in-chief Guò Xīng (過興) ordered Xuānfǔ (宣府) Deputy General Yáng Xìn (楊信) and Xián (賢) to launch a joint attack.
Xián (賢) did not wait for Xìn (信),
but directly attacked and defeated them.
Xìn (信) was impeached,
and Censor-in-chief Lǐ Bǐng (李秉) stated that Xìn (信) had delayed his forces,
while Xián (賢) had also abandoned the agreement.
The Emperor pardoned both of them.
In the early Tiānshùn (天順) reign,
Commander-in-chief Yáng Néng (楊能) memorialized for Xián's (賢) promotion to Assistant Chief Military Commissioner.
When the bandits were stationed below the frontier,
Néng (能) ordered Xián (賢) to rendezvous with the main army,
but he missed the deadline and
was summoned and imprisoned.
With his former official rank, he proceeded to Níngxià (寧夏),
subordinate to the Earl of Dìngyuǎn (定遠), Shí Biāo (石彪).
Two thousand bandit cavalry entered Ānbiānyíng (安邊營).
Biāo (彪) led Xián (賢) and others to attack them,
winning consecutive battles.
They pursued them to Yěmǎjiàn (野馬澗) and Bànpōdūn (半坡墩),
where the bandits were utterly routed.
However, Xián (賢) continued the pursuit relentlessly
and was struck by a stray arrow, dying.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him the title of Assistant Chief Military Commissioner.
When Xián (賢) was first imprisoned,
he thought he would never be reinstated.
After his release,
he was so grateful that he vowed to repay with his life,
and indeed fulfilled his aspiration.
His son, Yù (玉),
courtesy name Tíngbì (廷璧),
was to inherit the post of Commander.
Because his father died in service,
he was promoted two ranks to Assistant Commander-in-chief of the Wànquán (萬全) Regional Military Commission,
supervising agricultural garrisons.
He was promoted to Commander-in-chief
and served as the Mobile Corps General of Xuānfǔ (宣fǔ).
In the ninth year of Chénghuà (成化),
the Marquis of Huìchāng (會昌), Sūn Jìzōng (孫繼宗), and others were ordered to recommend talented generals,
and Yù (玉) was at the top of the list.
An imperial edict ordered him to lead his troops to reinforce Yánsuī (延綏),
following Wáng Yuè (王越) in raiding Hóngyánchí (紅鹽池).
He was promoted to Acting Assistant Chief Military Commissioner
and returned to defend Xuānfǔ (宣fǔ).
When the bandits entered Mǎyíng (馬營) and Chìchéng (赤城),
he defeated them.
The Ministry of War stated that the major commanders of Xuānfǔ (宣fǔ) had achieved no merit,
but Yù's (玉) three thousand men were able to pursue the enemy out of the territory,
and requested an additional rank to reward his efforts,
so he was given a substantive appointment.
Soon after, he was appointed Deputy Commander-in-chief of Xuānfǔ (宣fǔ).
West of the Huánghé,
from Zhuānglàng to the southern mountains of Sùzhōu,
was inhabited by the twenty-nine tribes of barbarians, such as Ājí, on its outer reaches.
During the Hóngwǔ reign,
a stone marker was erected and a boundary drawn,
agreeing that woodcutters and herdsmen should not cross the border.
After many years, it fell into disuse,
and various barbarians frequently encroached,
while lawless people from China secretly communicated with them, causing border trouble.
Xǐ requested
"to redraw the boundaries,
summon the various barbarian tribes,
and inform them that the boundary stones had fallen into disuse,
and fearing that imperial troops might bully the various tribes,
they are now re-erected.
They may pasture outside the boundary,
and enter the passes for mutual trade.
If this is done,
the barbarians will surely obey,
and future worries can be quietly eliminated."
The Emperor praised this,
and followed it.
In the seventeenth year, he was promoted to acting Dūdū Tóngzhī.
At that time, Xǐ was serving as Zǒngbīngguān with the title of Dūdū Qiānshì,
while Lǔ Jiàn was serving as Cānjìang with the title of acting Dūdū Tóngzhī.
Xǐ feared it would be difficult to control him,
and begged to be relieved of military command,
hence this appointment was made.
Initially,
Hāmì was harassed by Tǔlúfān,
who made their general Yálán defend it.
Dūdū Hǎnshèn resided temporarily at Kǔyùkǒu,
near Chìjīn and Hǎndōng,
and they frequently attacked each other.
Hǎnshèn's forces were exhausted and without aid.
The court deliberated and ordered Xǐ to build a city at Kǔyù,
and establish a separate Hāmì Wèi to house them.
Xǐ sent spies to alienate Yálán.
Yálán did not listen,
but the spies brought back over ninety people whom he had held captive and plundered,
and fully understood the situation.
In the seventeenth year, he gathered the officers and soldiers of Chìjīn and Hǎndōng,
rewarded them with cattle and wine,
and ordered them to assist Hǎnshèn.
Hǎnshèn combined the troops of the two guards,
and launched a night attack on Hāmì and eight other cities, including Lāmù,
thus recovering the territory,
and still ordered Hǎnshèn to reside there.
When the matter was reported,
he was praised and rewarded,
and bestowed with gold and silk.
Later,
Hǎndōng raided,
Xǐ repelled them,
and requested to raise an army to attack them.
The Emperor, remembering their frequent assistance to Hǎnshèn,
merely sent an envoy to admonish them.
The following year,
northern invaders killed scouting soldiers,
and Xǐ led Cānjìang Lǐ Jùn and the Chìjīn troops to attack them at Lángxīn Shān and the west of Hēihé,
killing and capturing many.
In the twentieth year, he was transferred to garrison Dàtóng.
Xǐ had rendered meritorious service in recovering Hāmì,
but his official rank was not advanced.
He presented this to the court,
and was then formally appointed Dūdū Tóngzhī.
Xǐ was skilled in military strategy,
and knowledgeable in civil affairs,
brave and resourceful.
Many court officials praised him.
He served on the border for over twenty years,
and was feared by the barbarians.
He died in the first year of Hóngzhì.
He was granted sacrificial rites and burial,
and posthumously honored with extra benefits.
Lǔ Jiàn's
ancestors were originally from Xīdàtōng.
His grandfather, Āshīdūgǒngbǔshījiā,
led his tribe to submit in the early Míng dynasty,
and Tàizǔ appointed him as Báifūzhǎng,
ordering him to command his部 and reside in Zhuānglàng.
His son Shījiā inherited,
and rose through ranks to Zhuānglàng Wèi Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī.
Towards the end of the Zhèngtǒng reign,
Jiàn inherited his father's position.
After a long time,
he was promoted to acting Dū Zhǐhuī Qiānshì.
In the fourth year of Chénghuà,
Mǎn Sì of Gùyuán rebelled.
Jiàn led a thousand native soldiers to participate in the campaign.
When the various armies besieged Shí chéng,
and challenged the enemy daily,
Jiàn would lead the vanguard when going out,
and cover the rear when retreating,
being most feared by the rebels.
After the rebellion was quelled,
he was promoted to acting Dūdū Tóngzhī.
Soon after, he was appointed Zuǒ Cānjìang,
and assigned to guard Zhuānglàng.
His son Lín was appointed Báihù,
to command the native troops.
In the seventeenth year, he was indicted for invaders entering the border,
but was allowed to redeem himself with meritorious service.
Soon after, he was appointed Zuǒ Fùzǒngbīng,
assisting in guarding Gānsù.
When invaders attacked Yǒngchāng,
he was impeached.
Jiàn submitted a memorial in defense,
and was merely suspended from his salary for two months.
Immediately after, he was appointed Zǒngbīngguān,
to garrison Yánsuí.
He presented his past merits,
and was given a formal appointment.
When Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
he fell ill,
and retired.
In the early Hóngzhì reign,
Lín was ordered to inherit the rank of Zhǐhuīshǐ,
and was promoted to Dū Zhǐhuī Qiānshì.
Later,
he was promoted to Tóngzhī,
and appointed Gānsù Yóujī Jiāngjūn.
The Lǔ family guarded the western frontier for generations,
achieving merits in defense.
By Jiàn's time, his official rank became even more prominent,
his hereditary estate grew larger,
and the population of the native troops under his command also increased daily.
Since Lín had moved to Gānsù,
the Emperor, believing that only Jiàn could manage the native troops,
specially recalled him to manage them,
and also ordered the relevant officials to erect an archway to honor his family's achievements.
Jiàn then submitted four proposals on border affairs,
most of which were adopted.
Jiàn possessed talent and courage;
when encountering the enemy, he would always brave arrows and stones,
and was injured multiple times but not deterred,
thus he was able to accumulate merits and rise to the rank of a great general.
In the fifteenth year, he died from a relapse of an old wound.
He was posthumously granted Yòu Dūdū,
and given benefits as per regulations.
At this time, Lín had already been promoted from Gānsù Cānjìang to Zuǒ Fùzǒngbīng;
he was brave and robust like his father,
but not as respectful and compliant.
Earlier, when he was Yóujī,
invaders entered Yǒngchāng,
and he lost control.
He blamed Fùjiāng Táo Zhēn,
and an Imperial Censor was sent to investigate,
whereupon he was supposed to be exiled to the border.
However, he was only demoted one rank,
and remained Yóujī as before.
As Fùjiāng,
he was transferred to Wéizhōu to defend against invaders.
When a large number of invaders entered, he was unable to attack,
and sent Dū Zhǐhuī Yáng Lín to intercept them at Kǒngbàgōu.
Lín was utterly defeated,
and Lín failed to provide assistance,
leading to repeated impeachments.
Lín pleaded his case,
and was merely suspended from his salary for two months.
At this time, Lín's son, Jīng, had already been granted an official position,
and was ordered to discipline the native troops.
However, Lín reported that Jīng was young,
and the native people would not be disciplined,
and begged to return to manage them.
Without waiting for a reply,
he returned directly.
The Emperor, following Liú Dàxià's suggestion,
granted his request.
When Wǔzōng ascended the throne,
Gānsù Xúnfǔ Bì Hēng recommended Jīng and Lín for their resourcefulness and bravery,
and ordered them to lead their respective troops to assist in battle and defense.
In the second year of Zhèngdé,
Jīng had already inherited the position of Zhǐhuīshǐ,
and stated that he had previously achieved merits with his father,
and was thus made Dū Zhǐhuī Qiānshì.
Not long after,
Lín died,
and was posthumously granted Dūdū Qiānshì,
and given sacrificial rites and burial.
According to custom,
a Dū Zhǐhuī was not entitled to such benefits.
However, at Jīng's request,
an exception was made to grant them.
After accumulating battle merits,
he was again promoted to Dūzhīhuǐshǐ, serving as Zuǒcānjiàng,
garrisoning Zhuānglàng.
He again reported his merits,
but the Bīngbù insisted it was not permissible.
The Emperor specially ordered him to be acting Dūdū Qiānshì.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he requested to retire.
The Xúnfǔ, Xǔ Fèngxiáng, stated that Jīng had been wounded in fierce battles,
and though he recovered from illness,
he was a hereditary general who dared to fight,
known in foreign lands.
Now that the border troubles were incessant,
it was not advisable to let him leave.
The Emperor then ordered him to stay,
and rewarded him with silver and silk.
Soon after, he was appointed Fùzǒngbīng to garrison as before.
In the winter of the sixth year of Jiājìng (1527),
he was appointed Dūdū Tóngzhī, serving as Zǒngbīngguān,
and stationed in Yánsuí.
Grand Secretary Yáng Yīqīng said:
“Jīng has garrisoned Zhuānglàng for over twenty years,
repeatedly achieving battle merits.
His subordinate local troops are unmatched by others.
Although his son, Zhān, is already a Zhīhuǐ Qiānshì,
and has been commanded to take charge,
he is still young.
Now the Zǒngbīngguān of Shǎnxī, Zhāng Fèng, is a hereditary general of Yánsuí.
If Fèng is transferred to Yánsuí,
and Jīng is transferred to Shǎnxī,
he can suppress Zhuānglàng,
and there will be no worries from the west.”
The Emperor immediately followed his advice.
After two years,
he eventually retired due to illness.
After a long time,
Zhān was ordered to serve as Shǒubèi of Shāndān with his original rank.
Jīng memorialized, saying:
“Since my great-grandfather,
we have hereditarily guarded this land.
Now I am at home,
and Zhān has moved to another garrison.
The local troops are anxious,
unwilling to attach themselves to others.
If other troubles arise from this,
it would be to abandon our ancestral achievements and betray the imperial favor bestowed on generations.
I beg that he be allowed to guard the ancestral territory.”
This was approved.
In the twenty-second year (1543),
there was an alert in Xuān and Dà.
An edict ordered Jīng to select five thousand brave men to go to their aid.
By the time he arrived, the border troubles had ceased,
so they were sent back.
Because Jīng had rushed to the call despite his illness,
he was handsomely rewarded.
The following year, Zhān died.
As Jīng’s second son and grandson were both young,
he requested to personally command the local troops.
An edict granted this.
Jīng was brave and fierce,
and performed his duties with few faults.
Following his ancestors, he became a great commander,
preserving his fame and merits,
and was known as a good general.
He died in the thirty-fifth year (1556).
He was granted posthumous honors according to regulations.
Liú Níng,
courtesy name Shì'ān,
his ancestors were from Shānyáng.
He inherited his hereditary position,
serving as Yǒngníng Wèi Zhīhuǐshǐ.
He was brave and skilled in battle.
Considering himself idle and unnoticed,
when there was a military campaign in Yánsuí,
he submitted a memorial requesting to fight to the death.
Shàngshū Bái Guī approved it.
He was repeatedly promoted for his merits to Dūzhīhuǐshǐ,
serving as Xuānfǔ Yóují Jiāngjūn.
Zhōu Xǐ,
courtesy name Tíngyù,
was from Qiān'ān.
He inherited the position as Kāipíng Wèi Zhīhuǐshǐ.
He was spirited and studied military treatises,
skilled in horsemanship and archery.
For his merit in the northern expedition,
he was promoted to acting Dūzhīhuǐ Qiānshì, serving as Yòucānjiàng,
garrisoning Yánghé,
and was ordered to train three thousand troops from his department for deployment.
In the sixteenth year of Chénghuà (1480), he followed Wáng Yuè in the campaign against Wēiníng Hǎizǐ,
and was successively promoted to Dūzhīhuǐshǐ.
At that time, border invaders were constant.
In the eighteenth year (1482), they invaded in separate routes.
Xǐ and Yóují Dǒng Shēng fought at Hēishíyá,
and Níng fought at Tǎ'érshān.
Both achieved merits.
Xǐ was promoted to acting Dūdū Qiānshì,
and transferred to Dàtóng Fùzǒngbīng.
Níng was promoted to Dūdū Qiānshì,
reassigned as Zuǒcānjiàng,
garrisoning Yánghé.
In the autumn of the nineteenth year (1483),
Yìsīmǎyīn made a large-scale invasion.
Dàtóng Zǒngbīngguān Xǔ Níng dispatched Xǐ to guard Huáirén,
and Níng and Dǒng Shēng to encamp at Xīshān.
He personally led the central army,
attacking them at Xiàmǐzhuāng,
but suffered a defeat.
Níng and Shēng were surrounded multiple times,
nearly trapped.
They urgently fired large cannons,
killing many enemies,
and the encirclement was broken.
When Xǐ heard of the central army's defeat,
he urgently brought his troops back to reinforce.
He encountered the enemy at night,
and, building on his momentum, advanced,
with great fierceness.
Xǐ encouraged his officers and soldiers, saying:
“Today, there is only advance, no retreat!”
He shouted and charged into the enemy lines,
and the enemy briefly fell back.
After a long time,
they engaged in close combat.
An arrow struck his arm.
He pulled out the arrowhead and fought even more fiercely,
killing dozens of people with his son Péng and brave warriors under his command.
Coincidentally, Níng’s troops arrived,
and the scattered soldiers of the central army also gradually regrouped.
The enemy then retreated,
and Xǔ Níng and others also returned.
Soon after, they invaded again.
Níng led three thousand troops,
encountered them west of Jùluòzhàn,
and defeated them in successive battles.
He again defeated them at Báidēng and Liǔlín,
and then pursued and defeated them at Xiǎo Bó gē Gǔ.
Meanwhile, Zhuāng Jiàn, the Dàtóng Xīlù Cānjiàng, also intercepted their retreat,
fighting at Niúxīnshān.
The enemy then fled.
At this time, many generals suffered defeats,
and Xǔ Níng and others were punished.
However, Xǐ was given substantive appointment for his merits,
Níng was exceptionally promoted to Dūdū Tóngzhī,
and Zhuāng Jiàn, because his unit suffered no losses,
was also rewarded with silver and silk.
Jiàn,
was from Liáodōng.
In the Tiānshùn era,
he inherited the position of Dìngliáo Yòuwèi Zhīhuǐshǐ.
He was brave, fierce, and decisive.
He always fought vigorously when encountering bandits,
and repeatedly achieved merits,
being successively promoted to Dūdū Qiānshì,
and was in charge of the Zuǒfǔ.
In the eleventh year of Hóngzhì (1498), he was granted the seal of Zhènshuò Jiāngjūn,
and stationed in Xuānfǔ.
Due to his talent, he exchanged garrisons with Dàtóng Zǒngbīngguān Zhāng Jùn.
Bīngbù Shìláng Xióng Xiù memorialized his planning merits,
and he was promoted to Dūdū Tóngzhī.
Xǐ was soon assigned as Yòufùzǒngbīng to garrison Dàizhōu,
also supervising Piāntóu and other passes,
while Níng was reassigned as Zuǒfùzǒngbīng,
assisting in guarding Dàtóng.
Both men achieved prominent merits on the northern frontier,
and were hailed as famous generals.
Xǐ, considering Piāntóu to be far from Tàiyuán,
requested to change its designation from "garrisoning" to "stationing" (镇守),
and also, since a "stationing" commander should not be subject to external control,
begged to change his title to Zǒngbīng.
Xiànzōng humored him in all these requests.
In the early Hóngzhì era,
he was transferred to Shǎnxī,
and pacified the Huíhuí who were registered in various counties of Fúfēng.
In the third year (1490), he was granted the seal of Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn,
and stationed in Níngxià.
He died barely a year later.
Before his death,
he summoned his sons and said:
“I have been granted an imperial seal and governed a region,
which is sufficient,
but I have never greatly defeated the enemy,
and I will carry this regret into the grave.”
He repeatedly cried out
“Kill the bandits!”
before closing his eyes.
His son, Péng,
was successively promoted to Jǐnyīwèi Zhīhuǐ Qiānshì.
Three years after Níng Xǐ's death,
Níng Pèi assumed the seal of Pacifying Qiāng General,
garrisoning Gānsù.
That winter,
raiders attacked Liángzhōu.
Níng fought them at Mòshāndūn,
capturing and beheading over fifty.
The battle lasted until dusk,
when he gathered his baggage and marched south.
The raiders attacked again,
and he captured one of their chiefs.
The next day,
Participating General Yán Yù arrived with reinforcements,
and Assistant General Táo Zhēn's troops also arrived.
The raiders then fled.
He captured their young and weak,
and obtained two thousand horses, camels, cattle, and sheep.
He was promoted to Right Supervising Censor (Yòu Dūdū).
The following year,
he and巡撫 Xǔ Jìn raided and defeated the Turpan at Hāmì.
He was promoted to Left Supervising Censor (Zuǒ Dūdū),
his salary was increased by one hundred dàn,
and he returned to the capital due to illness.
In the thirteenth year [of Hóngzhì],
Dàtóng reported an emergency.
Níng was appointed Assistant Commander-in-Chief (Fù Zǒngbīng),
and followed the Earl of Píngjiāng, Chén Ruì, to repel them.
Ruì lacked military strategy,
and disagreed with Níng,
ordering him not to fight.
The raiders thus had their way and departed.
Níng was punished by having half his salary suspended and being placed in idle residence.
Soon after, he assisted Participating General Zhū Huī in military affairs,
but also achieved no success.
Níng himself recounted his merits at Hāmì
and requested to be enfeoffed as an earl.
An imperial edict restored his full salary.
Níng possessed courage and wisdom.
When he was Assistant General (Fùjiāng) at Dàtóng,
tens of thousands of tribute bearers harbored ill intentions.
Níng led twenty horsemen directly to their camp,
and the multitude was startled and shocked.
A tribal chief reined in his horse and drew his bow, coming forth.
Níng dismounted ahead of him,
sat with the chiefs,
pointed and drew on a tablet,
and proclaimed the emperor's power and virtue.
One man spoke disrespectfully.
Níng slapped his face
and stood up with a raised arm.
Their chief shouted at him to retreat.
Níng sat back down and spoke with them,
calling for wine and drinking joyfully.
They were all enlightened,
and ultimately kept their promises.
He once imitated the ancient Fānshàng formation method,
organizing fifty-eight men into a squad.
Squads were layered to form a battle array,
with five-colored banners raised.
Additionally, five large banners of different colors were erected in the central army.
When the central banner was raised,
the five arrays would each respond according to its color,
circulating endlessly.
He used this to achieve victory in every battle.
Later, he was again dispatched to Dàtóng.
He was already old and sick,
and the commander was also timid and weak,
so he achieved no success.
Nevertheless, during Emperor Xiàozōng's reign, Níng was praised as a good general.
He died in the seventeenth year [of Hóngzhì],
and was posthumously granted the title of Earl of Guǎngchāng.
Péng Qīng,
courtesy name Yuánjié,
was from Yúlín.
Initially, he inherited the hereditary position of Commander (Zhīhuīshǐ) of Suídé Guard.
For his merits, he was promoted to Assistant Regional Commander (Dū Zhīhuī Qiānshì).
In the early Hóngzhì era,
he was appointed Right Participating General (Yòu Cānjiàng),
responsible for defending Sùzhōu.
When raiders invaded,
he led troops to pursue them,
capturing horses, camels, weapons, and the people and livestock they had plundered, and returned.
Soon after, he and巡撫 Wáng Jì rendered meritorious service in recovering Hāmì.
Although Qīng held a relatively low military rank,
he was fond of strategy and possessed courage and wisdom.
His name was known throughout the central court,
and he was especially esteemed by Minister (Shàngshū) Mǎ Wénshēng.
He once claimed illness and requested retirement,
but Wénshēng strongly argued for him at court,
and he was persuaded to stay.
In the eighth year [of Hóngzhì],
there was an alert in Gānsù.
Upon Wénshēng's recommendation,
he was promoted to Left Assistant Commander-in-Chief (Zuǒ Fù Zǒngbīng),
and continued to guard Gānsù.
Not long after,
巡撫 Xǔ Jìn requested to transfer Qīng to Liángzhōu.
But at that time, Hāmì had been re-occupied by the Turpan.
Wénshēng was secretly planning its recovery,
relying on Qīng for success.
He said,
"Sùzhōu has many troubles,
and Qīng's fame is renowned in the Western Regions,
so he cannot be easily replaced."
Thus, the transfer was dropped.
After Wénshēng obtained Yáng Zhù's strategy,
he was eager to attack Hāmì and surprise Yálán.
He dispatched troops from Hǎndōng, Chìjīn, and Hāmì,
ordering Qīng to command them as the vanguard,
following Xǔ Jìn stealthily.
After half a month's march,
they reached the city walls and
captured it.
Yálán had already fled.
They then pacified the remaining people of Hāmì
and returned with a complete army.
In this campaign,
Wénshēng provided the strategy,
proposing to take a secret route.
However, Xǔ Jìn still followed the old route,
allowing Yálán to escape.
The number of those killed or captured was few.
Nevertheless, the barbarian people had always looked down on China,
believing they could not traverse their territory,
but from this point on, they began to show fear.
Qīng's contribution was the greatest,
and he was slightly promoted to Commander (Dū Zhīhuīshǐ).
In the tenth year [of Hóngzhì],
Commander-in-Chief (Zǒngbīngguān) Liú Níng was dismissed,
and Qīng was promoted to Assistant Supervising Censor (Dūdū Qiānshì) to replace him.
That winter,
the Turpan returned Hāmì to the loyal and obedient Prince Shǎnbā,
and also requested to resume tribute.
The Western Regions were pacified again.
He repeatedly resigned due to illness,
requesting to relinquish military command,
but it was not granted.
He died in the fifteenth year [of Hóngzhì].
Qīng treated his soldiers with kindness.
He long garrisoned the western frontier,
and his prestige was very prominent;
the foreign tribes feared him.
He was by nature incorruptible.
While stationed there, he suffered the loss of his mother, wife, and two sisters,
and was too poor to return home for their burials.
On the day of his death,
soldiers, common people, women, and children all wept.
He left a dying wish that his sons should not accept any funeral contributions,
so his own funeral also could not be returned home.
When the Emperor heard of it,
he ordered the provincial governor to allocate treasury funds
to assist in sending him back to his hometown,
and granted imperial sacrifices and burial according to regulations.
Jiāng Hàn,
was from Yúlín Guard.
In the Hóngzhì era,
he inherited his hereditary post
as Commander (Zhīhuīshǐ) of his guard.
Censor Hú Xīyán recommended his talent and bravery,
and he was promoted to Assistant Regional Commander (Dū Zhīhuī Qiānshì),
serving as Mobile General (Yóujī Jiāngjūn) for Yánsui.
In the spring of the eighteenth year [of Hóngzhì],
raiders attacked Níngxià's Xīngwǔ Camp.
Hàn led his troops to race to their aid,
and encountered them at Zhōngshādūn,
defeating them.
He was awarded an imperial edict of commendation.
Upon Emperor Wǔzōng's ascension,
raiders launched a large-scale invasion of Xuān and Dàtóng.
Hàn, along with Assistant Commander-in-Chief (Fù Zǒngbīng) Cái Xióng and Participating General Wáng Jǐ, reinforced them from different routes,
achieving merit.
Soon after, he replaced Xióng as Assistant Commander-in-Chief (Fù Zǒngbīng),
co-defending Yánsui.
In the third year of Zhèngdé, he was transferred to guard Liángzhōu.
The following winter,
he was promoted to acting Assistant Supervising Censor (Dūdū Qiānshì),
serving as Commander-in-Chief (Zǒngbīngguān),
garrisoning Níngxià.
Hàn disciplined his army strictly and orderly,
winning the hearts of his generals and soldiers.
Only a few months later, Prince Ānhuà Zhì Pàn plotted rebellion.
He set a banquet, inviting Hàn and巡撫 Ān Wéixué, among others.
Midway through the feast,
his confederate Hé Jǐn and others led troops in,
seizing Hàn at the table.
Hàn leapt up,
cursing angrily and refusing to submit,
whereupon he was killed.
His son Shì escaped.
After the rebellion was quelled,
the matter was reported to the court.
An imperial edict ordered a posthumous sacrifice and burial.
Officials established a shrine for him,
offering sacrifices in spring and autumn.
During the Jiājìng era,
following another request from巡撫 Zhāng Héng,
an imperial plaque with the inscription
"Mǐn Zhōng" (Compassionate Loyalty) was bestowed.
Shì was to inherit the position.
The emperor, because Hān had died in service,
specially promoted him one rank,
making him a Dū Zhǐhuī Qiānshì.
In the eleventh year,
the Huí bandit Wèi Jǐngyáng rebelled,
and Huáyīn and other counties were all 피해.
The Xúnfǔ Xiāo Chōng ordered Shì to suppress them,
and Jǐngyáng was captured.
He was promoted to acting Dū Zhǐhuī Tóngzhī,
and appointed Yòu Cānjìang to guard Sùzhōu.
In the second year of Jiājìng,
he was promoted to Yòu Fù Zǒngbīng,
stationed in Liángzhōu,
then promoted to acting Dūdū Qiānshì,
and appointed Zǒngbīngguān,
to garrison Gānsù.
When Huí bandits attacked Gānzhōu,
Shì fought them at Zhāngqīnbǎo,
and routed them.
Not long after,
eight thousand Xīhǎi cavalry bandits attacked Liángzhōu.
Shì led the Yóujī Zhōu Lún and others to ambush
and decisively defeat them at Kǔshuǐdūn,
beheading over a hundred,
and killing their chief.
He recovered one thousand two hundred people and two thousand livestock they had plundered.
Dū Zhǐhuī Zhāng Jǐn also died in battle.
For his merits,
he was promoted to acting Dūdū Tóngzhī.
When Jínáng's other tribes raided Zhuānglàng,
Shì encountered them at Fēnshuǐlǐng,
winning again,
and then proceeded to Pínglǐng.
The enemy cavalry gathered in large numbers.
Shì hid troops to lure them,
and again beheaded one of their chiefs,
gaining seventy heads.
He was given the substantive appointment.
In the spring of the sixteenth year,
bandits greatly invaded Gānzhōu,
and he could not defend it.
He was demoted two ranks and held responsible.
Soon after, for his merit in defeating the enemy at Yǒngchāng,
he was again appointed acting Dūdū Qiānshì.
That winter,
he was dismissed for his previous offense.
After a long time,
he was recommended and promoted to Fù Zǒngbīng,
to assist in guarding Dàtóng,
but was impeached and dismissed by Zǒngdū Wēng Wàndá.
He died.
His son Yìngxíong
inherited the position of Zhǐhuīshǐ,
and was promoted to Xuānfǔ Xīlù Cānjìang.
In the spring of the twenty-seventh year,
Āndá attacked Dàtóng.
Zǒngbīngguān Zhōu Shàngwén fought at Cáojiāzhuāng.
Yìngxíong followed Wàndá from Huáilái, making noise and raising dust as they went west.
The bandits, unsure of the numbers,
then fled.
He was successively promoted to Dūdū Qiānshì,
appointed Zǒngbīngguān,
and garrisoned Níngxià.
In the thirty-second year,
tens of thousands of Tào bandits encamped at Hèlánshān,
sending elite cavalry to raid Hóngjǐng.
Yìngxíong instructed his officers and soldiers to hold fast and tie up the enemy,
while secretly attacking the enemy camp,
beheading one hundred forty.
He was promoted to Dūdū Tóngzhī.
Two years later,
tens of thousands of Tào bandits crossed the ice to the west,
and went directly from behind Níngxià Mountain to Zhuāngliáng.
Yìngxíong and others ambushed them,
gaining over a hundred heads.
He was promoted to Yòu Dūdū.
The Yùshǐ Cuī Jiǎn impeached him for letting bandits run loose,
and he was stripped of his office and arrested for questioning,
then appointed as an official for special service,
to earn merit at the frontier.
In the autumn of the fortieth year,
over sixty thousand bandits attacked Jūyōng Chàdàokǒu.
Yìngxíong was surrounded in Nángōu,
hit by five spears and fell from his horse.
Cānjìang Hú Zhèn killed several people and brought him back.
That winter,
he was reinstated as Yòu Dūdū,
appointed Zǒngbīngguān,
and garrisoned Dàtóng.
For attracting people from outside the frontier,
his salary was increased by one rank.
In the forty-second year,
bandits launched a major attack on Jīfǔ.
An imperial edict ordered Yìngxíong and others to come to the rescue.
All the garrison troops assembled,
but seeing the enemy's strength,
they dared not attack.
Gěishìzhōng Lǐ Yú then impeached Yìngxíong, as well as Xuāndà Zǒngdū Jiāng Dōng and Bǎodìng Zǒngbīngguān Zhù Fú, for sitting idly by while Hú Zhèn was besieged,
and not sending a single soldier.
The emperor was enraged
and issued a severe reprimand.
At that time, the bandits were about to flee,
and Yìngxíong intercepted them at Mìyún,
making quite a number of kills and captures.
After the bandits retreated,
the emperor ordered Jiāng Dōng to rank the merits of the generals,
with Yìngxíong first.
An edict ordered his ancestor's rank to be increased by two levels.
Later,
for his efforts in defending against the autumn raids,
he was promoted to Zuǒ Dūdū.
Zǒngdū Zhào Bǐngrán impeached him for letting bandits roam loose and engage in border trade,
and for devastating Shuòzhōu.
He was banished to the frontier.
Upon Mùzōng's ascension,
he was pardoned and returned.
His son Xiǎnzòu inherited the position,
and successively held the acting rank of Dūdū Qiānshì,
and Zǒngbīngguān,
garrisoning Shānxī and Xuānfǔ.
His son Bì
also reached Dūdū Qiānshì,
and was the Zǒngbīngguān for the relief of Liáodōng.
The Jiāng clan produced great generals,
