achieving border merits,
for five generations in all.
Ānguó,
courtesy name Liángchén,
was from Suídé Wèi.
Initially a student,
he was well-versed in the Spring and Autumn Annals, philosophical works, and histories,
and was well-known in his locality.
Later, he inherited a hereditary position,
becoming a Zhǐhuī Qiānshì.
In the third year of Zhèngdé, he came first in the military examination,
and was promoted to acting Zhǐhuīshǐ,
sent to the Three Frontiers of Shǎnxī to earn merit.
Liú Jǐn demanded bribes.
Ānguó and sixty others who took the examination had no money.
Jǐn then assigned them to the ranks,
to be deployed when there was an alarm,
and forbade them from returning without permission.
The sixty people were all in great distress,
treated like frontier soldiers,
and lived miserably.
And the frontier officials feared Jǐn,
so none took care of them.
When Zhì Pán rebelled,
a general amnesty was proclaimed,
and they were finally released and returned.
Tōngzhèng Cóng Lán requested that they be employed,
but Jǐn was angry,
and covertly encouraged Gěishìzhōng Zhāng Zàn and others to impeach them all as mediocre talents,
and all their promotions were revoked.
After Jǐn was executed,
Ānguó was finally appointed to his former post, defending the western route of Níngxià.
Soon after, he was promoted to acting Dū Zhǐhuī Qiānshì,
appointed Yòu Cānjìang,
promoted to Yòu Fù Zǒngbīng,
to assist in guarding Dàtóng,
then transferred to Yánsuí.
In the winter of the eleventh year,
twenty thousand bandits divided to raid Piāntóuguān and other places.
Ānguó, along with Yóujī Háng Xióng, rode to defeat them at Kělánzhōu,
beheading over eighty,
and capturing over a thousand horses.
The bandits then fled.
Earlier,
when bandits greatly invaded Báiyángkǒu,
the emperor sent the eunuch Zhāng Zhōng, Dūdū Liú Huī, and Shìláng Dīng Fèng to lead the capital army to suppress them.
By the time they arrived,
the bandits had already plundered extensively and left.
Zhōng and Huī were ashamed of having no merit.
Jìgōng Yùshǐ Liú Chéngfǔ appropriated the merits of Ānguó and others for them,
and great promotions and rewards were given.
Zhōng and others all had their salaries increased
and were given hereditary privileges.
Shàngshū Wáng Qióng also received the additional title of Shàobǎo,
and his son was given a position in Jǐnyīwèi.
Ānguó, at that time acting Dūdū Qiānshì and Níngxià Zǒngbīngguān,
was only given the substantive appointment.
Feeling unfairly treated,
he dared not report it himself,
so he submitted a memorial vehemently declining the honor,
and pleaded for the recognition of severely wounded soldiers.
Qióng requested to re-evaluate Ānguó's merits,
and he was then promoted to Dūdū Tóngzhī.
At that time,
sycophants controlled the court,
and the trend of buying military commissions was rampant.
Only Ānguó, by his talent and martial prowess, rose to be a great general.
He was upright and meticulous in military affairs,
and wherever he went, he sought to fulfill his duties.
Those who evaluated generals' talents always pointed to him.
He died after serving four years at the garrison.
He was posthumously given the title Wǔmǐn.
Háng Xióng,
courtesy name Shìwēi,
was from a family of hereditary suǒqí in Suídé Wèi.
Xióng inherited the position,
and was repeatedly the first to charge,
accumulating merit through his initial contributions.
He was promoted six times to Zhǐhuīshǐ.
In the seventh year of Zhèngdé, he was promoted to acting Dūzhīhuī Qiānshì,
and suppressed bandits in Sìchuān.
Soon after, he was appointed Guard Commander of Xīníng.
Recommended by Shàngshū Yáng Yīqīng,
he was promoted to Yánsuí Yóujī Jiāngjūn.
He followed Dūyùshǐ Péng Zé in managing the affairs of Hāmì,
and, along with Fùjiàng Ān Guó, defeated the enemy at Kělán.
He was promoted to Dūdu Qiānshì,
then transferred to Cānjàng,
and further promoted to Dūdu Tóngzhī,
commanding border troops for drills in the western interior.
When Wǔzōng visited Xuānfǔ and Dàtóng,
Xióng escorted him,
and was immediately appointed Dàtóng Zǒngbīngguān.
At the beginning of Jiājìng,
when officials appointed by imperial decree were purged,
Xióng was due for demotion.
However, as he was then defending the border,
he was ordered to act as Dūdu Qiānshì,
and continue his defense duties as before.
When Xiǎowángzǐ entered Shāhé Bǎo with over ten thousand cavalry,
Xióng fought and repelled them.
Soon after,
they invaded again in large numbers,
and he could not repel them.
He requested to be dismissed, but this was not allowed.
He was transferred to Yánsuí,
and summoned to serve as Qiānshū in the Hòujūn Dūdufǔ.
In the autumn of the third year,
when Tǔlǔfān invaded Gānsù,
an imperial edict ordered Shàngshū Jīn Xiànmín to oversee the troops.
Xióng was given the seal of Pínglǔ Dàjiāngjūn,
appointed Zǒngbīngguān,
and made Tídū of the military affairs of the four garrisons: Shǎnxī, Yánsuí, Níngxià, and Gānsù.
Originally, only titled marquises on campaign
were granted the Dàjiāngjūn seal,
never a Dūdu.
But now, it was specially bestowed upon Xióng.
Scarcely had he arrived
when the invaders were already routed and fleeing,
and Xióng also received an inherited position as Jǐnyī Qiānhù.
After returning with the army,
he was again sent to garrison Níngxià.
When Jínáng launched a major invasion,
Zǒngdū Wáng Xiàn ordered Xióng and others to defeat him,
and Xióng was promoted to Dūdu Tóngzhī.
Eight thousand cavalry invaded Níngxià across the ice.
Xióng and Fùzǒngbīng Zhào Zhèn defended against them.
Their vanguard fell into an ambush,
and Xióng and his men were all defeated.
Zǒngdū Wáng Qióng impeached him,
and he was stripped of his office and put into retirement.
He died the following year.
Xióng was daring in battle.
Once, while patrolling the border with a few cavalrymen,
the enemy swarmed upon them.
He dismounted, piled saddles to form a makeshift rampart,
and knelt to shoot at them.
When the enemy retreated,
he removed his clothes
and found a clot of blood in his armpit,
realizing he had been hit by a flying arrow.
When Wǔzōng was in Dàtóng,
he saw Xióng's horse canopy was very dilapidated
and said,
"Old Háng is truly impoverished."
When invaders approached,
the Emperor intended to personally attack.
Xióng knelt by his horse and admonished,
"A master keeps a dog
not to prevent it from barking at thieves,
what use is a dog then?
I beg Your Majesty to let your servants exert their efforts."
The Emperor smiled and desisted.
As a youth, he had served as an attendant at the Yánsuí Xúnfǔ Xíngtái.
After he became prominent,
whenever he came to the office to discuss matters,
he dared not sit properly,
saying,
"This is the place where I served as an attendant in those years."
During the Zhèngdé and Jiājìng eras,
among the famous generals in the northwest,
Mǎ Yǒng and those below him were praised as courageous.
A eulogy states: In times of peace,
military strategies have no opportunity to be displayed.
Or, holding office and defending the border, resisting invaders,
showing meritorious service,
and ending with fame and achievement,
is also something to be esteemed.
Xǔ Guì, Zhōu Xián, Lǔ Jiàn, and Jiāng Hàn came from families of hereditary generals,
their military exploits passed down through generations.
Among them, Xián and Hàn died even more heroically in service.
The integrity of Péng Qīng and Háng Xióng,
surely that is the most excellent of them.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 63 Wèi Qīng (Zǐyǐng) Dǒng Xīng Hé Hóng (Liú Xióng) Liú Yù Chóu Yuè Shén Yīng (Zǐzhōu) Cáo Xióng (Zǐqiān) Féng Zhēn Zhāng Jùn (Lǐ Hóng) Yáng Ruì (Cuī Wén)
Wèi Qīng,
courtesy name Míngdé,
was a native of Huátíng, Sōngjiāng.
As a Bǎihù of Jìzhōu, he surrendered to Chéngzǔ,
accumulated merits to become Dūzhīhuī Qiānshì,
served as the acting Commander of the Zhōngdū Liúshǒusī,
and was then transferred to be the Coast Guard Commander in Shāndōng.
In the second month of the eighteenth year of Yǒnglè,
the sorceress Lín Sān Qī Táng Sàier from Pútái caused unrest.
She claimed to have obtained divine books and swords from a stone casket,
commanded ghosts and spirits,
and cut paper to make human figures and horses fight.
Her followers, numbering several thousands,
occupied Xièshízhà Zhài in Yìdū.
When Zhīhuī Gāo Fèng was defeated and died,
her momentum became fierce.
Her partisans, Dǒng Yànshēng and others, captured Jǔ and Jìmò,
and besieged Ānqīu.
Zǒngbīngguān Ānyuǎn Hóu Liǔ Shēng led Dūzhīhuī Liú Zhōng to besiege Sàier's stockade.
Sàier raided the government troops at night.
The army fell into disarray,
Zhōng was killed in battle,
and Sàier escaped.
By dawn,
Shēng finally realized it,
but was too late to pursue.
He captured bandit leaders Liú Jùn and others, as well as over a hundred men and women.
Meanwhile, the bandits attacked Ānqīu even more fiercely.
Zhīxiàn Zhāng Yú and Chéng Mǎ Huī fought desperately,
and the bandits could not take it.
They gathered over ten thousand people from Jǔ and Jìmò to attack.
Qīng was then stationed on the coast.
Hearing of this,
he led a thousand cavalry
and galloped day and night to the city walls.
After two battles,
he utterly defeated them.
The people inside the city also shouted and sallied forth,
killing two thousand bandits,
and capturing over four thousand alive,
all of whom were executed.
At that time, the city could not have held for much longer;
if Qīng's rescue had been slightly delayed,
the city would surely have fallen.
When the bandits were defeated,
Shēng finally arrived.
Qīng went to greet him.
Shēng was angry that Qīng had not waited for him,
and dragged him out.
On that same day,
Wáng Zhēn, Zhīhuī of Áoshān Wèi, also annihilated bandits in Zhūchéng with 150 soldiers.
The bandit rebellion was thus suppressed.
However, Sàier was never captured.
The Emperor sent a letter to commend Qīng,
and severely reprimanded Shēng.
Shàngshū Wú Zhōng and others impeached Shēng,
and also stated that Shēng was jealous of Qīng's achievements.
Consequently, Shēng was imprisoned,
while Qīng was promoted to Shāndōng Dūzhīhuīshǐ,
Zhēn to Dūzhīhuī Tóngzhī,
and Yú and Huī to Zuǒyòu Cānyì,
with varying rewards.
Qīng returned to guarding the coast.
Soon after, he was imprisoned for a certain matter.
In the first year of Xuāndé,
the Emperor, mindful of his merits,
released him
and allowed him to resume his post.
At that time, construction work in the capital was extensive,
and included soldiers from the coastal defense.
Qīng spoke up about this,
and obtained a rotation system.
When Yīngzōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Dūdu Qiānshì,
and died soon after.
Qīng was known for his filial piety
and his ability to treat his soldiers well.
He lived on the coast for over ten years,
and the coastal people missed him.
They petitioned the court
to establish a shrine to worship him.
His second son, Yǐng,
in the early Zhèngtǒng reign,
inherited the post of Commander of the Jǐnán Guard.
When Emperor Jǐngdì ascended the throne,
he was ordered to enter the capital for defense,
and was successively promoted to Assistant Regional Commander-in-chief.
Upon recommendation by Shí Hēng,
he was promoted to acting Commissioner-in-chief,
managing the right flank of the Five Army Divisions.
For his achievements in repelling the invaders at Huánghuāzhèn, Báiyángkǒu, and Xīzhímén,
he was progressively advanced to Assistant Regional Commander-in-chief.
In the third year of Jǐngtài, he assisted in garrisoning Xuānfǔ.
A year later,
he was recalled.
In the first year of Tiānshùn,
for his
"Door Seizing"
achievement,
he was enfeoffed as the Earl of Xuānchéng,
granted an hereditary certificate,
and dispatched to garrison Gānsù.
When Bólái invaded,
he was unable to repel them,
and was impeached by the judicial authorities,
but an imperial edict ordered no inquiry.
When Hēng fell,
Yǐng was spared from being stripped of his title due to his frontier defense duties.
When Emperor Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
the court deliberated that Yǐng was not competent,
and so he was recalled.
At that time, all
"Door Seizing"
hereditary titles were abolished,
but Yǐng pleaded his case based on his achievements in subduing the Mǎjísī and Dōngshā tribes of the Western Fān during the Tiānshùn era,
and an edict restored his former status.
In the second year of Chénghuà, he served as the Commander-in-chief of Liáodōng,
but was soon dismissed due to illness.
Censor Chén Yuè and others impeached him,
and he was imprisoned,
but was soon pardoned.
He died during the Hóngzhì reign.
He was posthumously granted the title of Marquis
and given the posthumous name Zhuàngyǒng.
His lineage passed down to his grandson Chún.
During the Jiājìng reign,
he superintended the Divine Machine Division,
and was repeatedly promoted to Grand Preceptor and Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
Four generations later came Shítài.
During the Chóngzhēn reign,
he was in charge of the Rear Bureau.
When the capital fell,
he clutched his iron certificate,
and all seventeen members of his household jumped into a well and died.
Dǒng Xīng was
a native of Chángyuán.
Initially, he served as Commander of the Right Yānshān Guard,
and was successively promoted to acting Assistant Regional Commander-in-chief.
During the Zhèngtǒng reign,
Lǐ Yù, Earl of Xīnjiàn, and others recommended Xīng as a military talent,
promoting him to acting Regional Commander-in-chief,
managing drills in the Capital Garrisons.
He was again recommended,
promoted to acting Commissioner-in-chief,
and appointed Right Assistant General.
He followed Chén Mào, Marquis of Níngyáng, to suppress Dèng Màoqī,
defeating the remaining rebels at Jiànníng,
and was promoted to Assistant Regional Commander-in-chief.
When Huáng Xiāoyǎng, a bandit from Nánhǎi, besieged Guǎngzhōu,
Zhāng Ān, Earl of Ānxiāng, and Commander Wáng Qīng died in battle,
and the rebels attacked the city with increasing ferocity.
An edict appointed Xīng as Left Vice Commander-in-chief,
transferring troops from Jiāngxī and the two Guǎng provinces to suppress them,
with Attendant Minister Mèng Jiàn assisting in military affairs.
Xīng brought the astrologer Mǎ Shì with him.
Xīng was indeed fierce,
but could not restrain his subordinates,
and Shì cautioned him.
In the second month of the first year of Jǐngtài,
the army reached Guǎngzhōu.
The rebels had over a thousand boats,
and their power was immense,
but the conscripted troops had not yet arrived,
and the generals requested reinforcements.
Shì said:
"The people of Guǎngzhōu have been longing for relief for a long time.
Even if we attack with the Láng soldiers,
it will be like breaking decayed wood."
Xīng followed his advice.
Soon after, a large army gathered,
advancing to Dàzhōu to attack the rebels,
killing or drowning over ten thousand people,
and many others surrendered.
Xiāoyǎng was killed by a stray arrow,
his head was presented,
and his father and son were captured,
while the remaining rebels were all executed.
For his merits,
he was promoted to Right Regional Commander-in-chief
and remained to garrison Guǎngdōng.
Censor Huáng Shìjùn impeached Xīng for leniency,
and his official rank was demoted.
He was reinstated the following year.
After a long time,
he was recalled
to oversee the Capital Garrisons.
He married into the family of Cáo Jíxiáng,
and claimed
"Door Seizing"
merit,
being enfeoffed as the Earl of Hǎiníng.
Not long after,
he was appointed Commander-in-chief
to garrison Liáodōng,
and was granted an hereditary certificate.
When the abolition of
"Door Seizing"
titles was debated,
Xīng was exempted due to his frontier defense duties.
When Jíxiáng was executed,
Xīng's title was stripped,
but he remained Right Regional Commander-in-chief,
and was dispatched to Guǎngxī to perform meritorious service.
Upon recommendation by Lǐ Guì of the Imperial Guards,
his title was restored,
and he was made Commander-in-chief of Xuānfǔ,
again granted an hereditary certificate.
When Emperor Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
he was dismissed and returned home.
Later,
the hereditary succession was halted.
He died after living at home for over ten years.
Hé Hóng was
a native of Quánjiāo.
He inherited his hereditary position,
serving as Commander of the Front Chéngdū Guard.
During the Zhèngtǒng reign,
he participated in the campaign against Lùchuān,
and at the end of the Jǐngtài reign,
he participated in the campaigns against Tiānzhù and Tónggǔ,
all with distinction.
He was repeatedly promoted to Regional Commander-in-chief,
managing the affairs of the Sìchuān Regional Military Commission,
and pacified the eastern Miáo.
When Emperor Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
for his merits,
he was promoted to Commissioner-in-chief.
Governor Wāng Hào requested Hóng to remain in Sìchuān,
which was granted.
When Zhào Duó, a native of Déyáng, rebelled,
proclaiming himself King Zhào,
all the bandits in Hànzhōu joined him.
He allied with various tribes,
repeatedly capturing cities
and killing generals and officials.
He dispatched his followers Hé Wénràng and the monk Wùshēng to plunder Ānyuè and other counties.
Hóng beheaded Wùshēng
and captured Wénràng alive.
When Duó was about to press on Chéngdū,
the government army attacked in three routes.
Hóng, along with Commander Níng Yòng, hurried to Zhāngmíng,
and the rebels withdrew.
Pursuing them to Zhūjiāhé in Zǐtóng,
they fought fiercely,
and the rebels momentarily retreated.
Hóng seized the advantage and charged into the formation,
but the rear army did not follow,
and he was surrounded by the rebels.
He fought desperately left and right,
killing many rebels,
but died of exhaustion.
Hóng was brave
and good at treating his soldiers;
his commands were strict,
and no general in Shǔ could compare to him.
After his death,
the government army lost morale.
Meanwhile, Liú Xióng of Línhuái, Commissioner-in-chief of Sìchuān, also died in battle.
Xióng was strong and resolute,
always charging forward against the enemy.
He once captured bandits in Hànzhōu,
taking over seventy people alive.
When Duó rebelled,
he pursued him to Dàshuǐhé in Luójiāng,
personally beheading several people,
and the rebels suffered successive defeats.
When Centurion Zhōu Dǐng was wounded,
Xióng went forward to rescue him,
charging directly into the rebel formation,
and was stabbed to death.
An imperial edict posthumously granted Hóng the title of Assistant Regional Commander-in-chief,
and provided for his memorial rites and burial.
His son Jié inherited the post of Commissioner-in-chief.
Xióng was posthumously granted the title of Assistant Regional Commander-in-chief,
given a memorial sacrifice,
and his son was ordered to inherit his post,
a promotion of two ranks.
Though Hóng was dead,
Xiāo Ràng (蕭讓), the county magistrate of Miánzhú (綿竹), led the local militia to attack Duó (鐸),
and defeated him.
As the government troops pressed on with attacks,
Duó’s (鐸) followers gradually dispersed.
Duó (鐸) found himself isolated,
and led the remaining rebels to rush to Zhāngmíng (彰明).
Assistant Company Commander Tián Yí (田儀) and others set an ambush in Zǐtóng (梓潼),
while Assistant General Zhōu Guì (周貴) directly attacked their lair.
The rebels suffered a great defeat
and fled by night to Shízǐ Lǐng (石子嶺).
Yí (儀) advanced quickly,
beheaded Duó (鐸),
and completely pacified the rebels.
This was in the fifth month of the first year of the Chénghuà (成化) reign (1465).
Liú Yù (劉玉),
courtesy name Zhòngxǐ (仲璽),
was a native of Cízhōu (磁州).
He was born with great physical strength
and served in the household of Cáo Jíxiáng (曹吉祥).
He followed in the campaign against Lùchuān (麓川),
was appointed Assistant Company Commander,
and, through accumulated merit, rose to Assistant Regional Military Commissioner.
In the first year of the Tiānshùn (天順) reign (1457), for his role in the
"Door Seizure" (奪門)
event, he was promoted to Assistant Grand Commissioner-in-Chief.
Soon after, he was made Assistant Right General
and garrisoned Xúnzhōu (潯州).
When the barbarians from Qìngyuǎn (慶遠) raided Bó Bái (博白) and Níngchuān (寧川) in Guǎngdōng (廣東),
Yù (玉) joined Assistant Left General Fàn Xìn (范信) to intercept and attack them,
defeating them.
Soon he was ordered to take charge of the defense of Guìzhōu (貴州).
He followed Fāng Yīng (方瑛) in campaigning against the Eastern Miáo (苗),
annihilating Gānbǎzhū (干把猪).
He then campaigned against the Western Bǎo Miáo (堡苗)
and captured their leader, Chǔdé (楚得).
In total, he beheaded a thousand enemies
and returned after destroying their strongholds.
He was then re-designated Right Vice General-in-Chief
and garrisoned Guìzhōu (貴州).
When Jíxiáng (吉祥) was executed,
Yù (玉) was imprisoned and sentenced to death.
Because he was far away and not involved in the conspiracy,
he was spared execution
and demoted to Assistant Company Commander in Hǎinán (海南).
Six years later,
the emperor was about to appoint Gǔ Dēng (谷登) as Vice General-in-Chief of Gānsù (甘肅).
Lǐ Xián (李賢) stated that Dēng (登) was not competent,
but Yù (玉) was experienced.
Therefore, Yù (玉) was reinstated as Assistant Grand Commissioner-in-Chief and Right Vice General-in-Chief,
garrisoning Liángzhōu (涼州).
When the Jiùzā (咎咂) tribe rebelled,
he assembled troops and pacified them,
and was promoted to Grand Commissioner-in-Chief.
In the fourth year of Chénghuà (成化) (1468),
when Mǎn Jùn (滿俊) rebelled in Gùyuán (固原),
Bái Guī (白圭) recommended Yù (玉) as General-in-Chief
to lead Assistant Left and Right Generals Xià Zhèng (夏正) and Liú Qīng (劉清) in attacking them,
dividing their forces into seven.
Yù (玉) and Grand Supervisor Xiàng Zhōng (項忠) reached Shíchéng (石城),
where the rebels had already been defeated several times.
At that time, Máo Zhōng (毛忠) died,
and Yù (玉) was also surrounded,
struck by a stray arrow,
but fought bravely and escaped.
After a standoff of two months,
and over a hundred battles large and small,
they finally pacified the rebellion.
He was promoted to Left Grand Commissioner,
managing the affairs of the Right Military Bureau.
He then recounted his past meritorious service in Xībǎo (西堡),
and was granted an additional hundred *shí* (石) of salary
and placed in charge of the Yàowǔ (耀武) camp.
In the sixth year (1470), he served as Left Vice General-in-Chief
and followed Zhū Yǒng (朱永) out to Yánsuí (延綏).
In the fifth month,
the Hétào (河套) tribes invaded.
Yù (玉) led his troops to repel them.
He died the following year.
He was posthumously granted the title Earl of Gùyuán (固原伯)
and the posthumous name Yìmǐn (毅敏).
Although Yù (玉) rose from servitude,
he was exceptionally brave and decisive,
and skilled at managing his soldiers.
He never suffered a defeat wherever he went.
During Mǎn Jùn’s (滿俊) rebellion,
he occupied the strategic Shíchéng (石城) and
repeatedly defeated government troops,
but Yù (玉) fought with the most vigor.
When merits were discussed,
he was only granted one rank,
which was considered too meager at the time.
His son, Wén (文),
inherited the position of Company Commander.
Qí Yù (仇鉞),
courtesy name Tíngwēi (廷威),
was a native of Zhènyuán (鎮原).
Initially, he served as a mercenary in the General-in-Chief's office in Níngxià (寧夏),
where he was greatly trusted and favored.
When Assistant Regional Military Commissioner Qí Lǐ (仇理) died
without an heir,
Yù (鉞) was allowed to inherit his hereditary position
as Deputy Company Commander of the Níngxià (寧夏) Front Guard.
Lǐ (理) was
from Jiāngdū (江都),
hence Yù (鉞) referred to himself as Qí (仇) of Jiāngdū (江都).
He was again promoted for his merit in defeating rebels,
to Assistant Regional Military Commissioner.
In the second year of Zhèngdé (正德) (1507), upon the recommendation of the Grand Coordinator Yáng Yīqīng (楊一清),
he was promoted to Mobile Division Commander of Níngxià (寧夏).
In the fifth year (1510),
Prince Ānhuà (安化王) Zhìfān (寘鐇), Assistant Regional Military Commissioner Hé Jǐn (何錦), Zhōu Áng (周昂),
and Company Commander Dīng Guǎng (丁廣) rebelled.
Yù (鉞) was then stationed outside the city at Yùquán Yíng (玉泉營).
Upon hearing of the rebellion, he wanted to flee.
But he considered that his wife and children were in the city,
fearing they would be massacred,
so he led his troops into the city.
He doffed his armor and presented himself to Zhìfān (寘鐇),
then returned home, pretending to be ill,
and had his troops assigned to the rebel camps.
Jǐn (錦) and others trusted him
and often consulted him for advice.
Yù (鉞) also feigned loyalty.
But secretly, he gathered brave men
and sent someone to sneak out of the city
to report back that government troops would arrive imminently.
Yù (鉞) then tricked Jǐn (錦) and Guǎng (廣), saying
they should urgently send troops to guard the ford,
to block the eastern bank troops
from crossing the river.
Jǐn (錦) and Guǎng (廣) indeed left their camps with all their forces,
while Áng (昂) alone guarded the city.
Zhìfān (寘鐇) summoned Yù (鉞) for a pre-battle ritual,
but Yù (鉞) claimed his illness was severe.
When Áng (昂) came to visit,
Yù (鉞) was lying firmly in bed, groaning.
Hidden soldiers suddenly rose
and clubbed Áng (昂) to death.
Yù (鉞) then donned his armor, drew his sword,
held Áng’s (昂) head,
and on horseback, shouted loudly.
The brave men all gathered
and rode directly to Zhìfān’s (寘鐇) residence,
where they bound him.
He issued Zhìfān’s (寘鐇) order
to recall Jǐn (錦) and others,
while secretly informing his own subordinates about Zhìfān’s (寘鐇) capture.
The rebels then scattered in disarray.
Jǐn (錦) and Guǎng (廣) fled on single horses to Hèlán Shān (賀蘭山),
where they were captured by patrols.
The rebellion lasted only eighteen days before it was crushed.
Before this,
when the central court heard of the rebellion,
it was proposed that Shényīng (神英) be appointed General-in-Chief,
and Yù (鉞) his deputy.
Soon, a report spread that Yù (鉞) had surrendered to the rebels,
and there was a desire to revoke the imperial order.
Grand Secretary Yáng Tínghé (楊廷和) said:
“Yù (鉞) will certainly not follow the rebels.
Letting him know that the imperial court is promoting him
will only strengthen his resolve.
Otherwise,
we would be abandoning a good general and empowering the enemy.”
So the order was not revoked.
The situation was indeed resolved.
However, Liú Jǐn (劉瑾) favored the Shǎnxī (陝西) General-in-Chief Cáo Xióng (曹雄),
and attributed all of Yù’s (鉞) achievements to him,
so Yù (鉞) received no special promotion.
Investigating Censor Yán Ruì (閻睿) argued for his merits,
and an imperial edict docked his salary for three months.
When Jǐn (瑾) was executed,
Yù (鉞) was finally promoted to acting Assistant Grand Commissioner-in-Chief,
serving as General-in-Chief of Níngxià (寧夏).
Soon after, for his merits,
he was ennobled as Earl of Xiánníng (咸寧伯),
with an annual stipend of a thousand *shí* (石) of grain,
and granted a hereditary patent.
In the winter of the following year,
he was summoned to command the Three Thousand Camp.
The following spring,
Liú Huì and Zhào Suì caused unrest in Hénán.
They successively captured Lùyì, Shàngcài, Xīpíng, Suípíng, Wǔyáng, and Yè.
They plundered Nándùn, Xīncài, Shāngshuǐ, and Xiāngchéng,
then returned to garrison Xīpíng.
Zhēn, along with Deputy Commander-in-Chief Shí Yuán
and Battalion Commanders Shén Zhōu and Jīn Fǔ, defeated them.
The bandits fled into the city,
and the government troops blocked their gates.
They set fire to the city at night, killing over a thousand people,
and an equal number were decapitated.
The remaining bandits dispersed and fled west.
Governor Dèng Zhāng and others paid respects to Prince Chóng in Rǔníng,
feasting for several days.
The bandits recruited their scattered remnants,
and their power was restored.
They captured Yānlíng, Xíngyáng, Sìshuǐ, and Gǒng.
They besieged Hénán Fǔ for three days
before the various armies finally gathered.
The bandits encamped south of Luò,
observing that the government troops were hungry and weary,
and engaged them in battle.
The right vanguard, Jīn Fǔ, dared not cross the Luò River,
while Zhēn, Yuán, and Zhōu were forming their lines.
However, the troops of the rear vanguard, Battalion Commander Yáo Xìn, charged first,
suffered a defeat, and immediately fled.
The formation was broken,
and the bandits pressed their advantage.
Zhēn dismounted and fought desperately to the death,
his reinforcements cut off.
He was posthumously granted the title Earl of Luò Nán,
and was given a state funeral.
His son, Dàjīn, was appointed Assistant Commander-in-Chief.
Later, when the bandits were pacified,
his merits were recognized,
and another son was granted the hereditary position of Centennial Household.
On the same day the following year,
a great wind and dust storm arose where Zhēn died.
The year after that,
it happened again.
Prince Yī reported this,
and an imperial edict commanded the authorities to build a shrine
and offer sacrifices annually on the day of his death.
Soon after, at the suggestion of Supervising Secretary Lǐ Duó,
two shí of rice
and two pǐ of silk were granted annually
to support his family.
Zhāng Jùn was
a native of the former guard of Xuānfǔ.
He inherited a hereditary position
and became the commander of his guard.
He was successively promoted to Guerrilla General of Dàtóng.
In the twelfth year of Hóngzhì, he was promoted to Assistant Regional Commander-in-Chief for his merits.
Huǒshāi entered the Left Guard of Dàtóng,
plundering extensively for eight days.
Jùn dispatched three hundred soldiers to intercept him from the front,
and another three hundred as support,
while personally engaging him at Jīngdōng Zhuāng.
He set up camp along the river
and repulsed over thirty thousand cavalry.
The Emperor was greatly pleased
and immediately promoted him to Assistant Commander-in-Chief.
Not long after,
Commander-in-Chief Wáng Xǐ was impeached for an incident,
and Jùn was immediately ordered to replace him.
That winter,
he was charged for bandit incursions and served under penalty.
Soon after, he was transferred to garrison Xuānfǔ.
The eunuch Miáo Kuí, commanding the army in Yánsuí,
ordered troops from Dàtóng and Xuānfǔ to serve as scouts.
Jùn refused to dispatch them,
and Kuí impeached Jùn.
The Emperor pardoned Jùn,
but ordered the troops to be sent as Kuí had requested.
When Emperor Wǔzōng first ascended the throne,
bandits took advantage of the mourning period to make a major incursion,
their camps stretching over twenty lǐ.
Jùn dispatched his generals Lǐ Jī, Bái Yù, Zhāng Xióng, Wáng Zhèn, and Mù Róng, each leading three thousand men,
to guard strategic points.
Suddenly,
the bandits entered by destroying the wall at Xīnkāikǒu.
Jī immediately advanced to meet the enemy,
while Yù, Xióng, Zhèn, and Róng each led their units to resist at Yútái Lǐng.
Jùn urgently led three thousand men to provide assistance,
injuring his foot along the way,
and entrusted his troops to Regional Commander Cáo Tài.
Tài reached Lùjiǎoshān
and was surrounded.
Jùn, despite his illness,
additionally mobilized five thousand men,
carrying three days' rations,
and galloped to relieve Tài's siege,
then again rescued Zhèn.
He also detached troops to save Jī and Yù,
and Jī and Yù also broke out of the encirclement.
Only Xióng and Róng were blocked by mountain ravines,
their reinforcements cut off, and they died.
The various armies were already in dire straits;
they withdrew and returned.
The bandits pursued them,
fighting as they retreated,
barely managing to enter Wànquán Right Guard city,
where countless soldiers and horses perished.
Jùn, along with the eunuch Liú Qīng and Governor Lǐ Jìn, were all summoned back.
Censor Guō Dōngshān argued
that Jùn, despite his illness, had rushed to assist,
and that rewards and punishments should not be unfairly applied.
Thus, he was allowed to atone for his crime.
In the fifth year of Zhèngdé,
he was appointed acting Assistant Commander-in-Chief,
overseeing the training of the Shénwēi battalion.
In June of the following year,
bandits such as Yáng Hǔ returned from Shānxī's Shíbāpán,
destroyed Wǔ'ān,
and plundered Wēi, Qǔzhōu, Wǔchéng, Qīnghé, Gùchéng, and Jǐngzhōu,
then entered Wén'ān
and joined forces with Liú Liù and others.
Regional Commander Sāng Yù suffered repeated defeats,
and Assistant Commander Xǔ Chéngfāng requested reinforcements.
Jùn was then appointed Deputy Commander-in-Chief
and, with Battalion Commander Wáng Cóng, commanded a thousand imperial troops to suppress them.
They moved back and forth near the capital for several months
but could not harm the bandits.
Afterward,
the court deliberated and decided to dispatch border troops for assistance,
and the bandits were then repeatedly defeated.
In March of the following year,
Liú Liù, Liú Qī, Qí Yánmíng, Páng Wénxuān, and others were defeated and fled to the Hǎitào of Dēng and Lái.
Lù Wán ordered Jùn's army to Láizhōu
to join with generals like Lǐ Hóng to intercept them.
The bandits then fled north,
plundering Bǎodí, Xiānghé, and Yùtián.
Jùn urgently joined Xǔ Tài and Què Yǒng to block them.
The Emperor was pleased
and rewarded them with silver.
The bandits moved west through Wǔqīng.
Not long after,
Jùn fell ill and was recalled.
After the bandits were pacified,
he was formally appointed Assistant Commander-in-Chief.
After a long time,
he died.
As a border general, Jùn
was incorruptible,
resourceful and brave.
When he died,
his family had no surplus assets.
Lǐ Hóng was
a native of the Right Guard of Dàtóng.
He inherited the position of Assistant Commander,
and was successively promoted to Assistant Commander-in-Chief for his merits,
serving as Battalion Commander
and assisting in guarding Dàtóng.
When bandits rose in Shāndōng,
an imperial edict appointed him Guerrilla General.
Soon after, he was appointed Deputy Commander-in-Chief
and, with Jùn and others, intercepted the bandits.
He also repeatedly achieved merits with Fù Kǎi and Zhāng Chūn, generals under Liú Huī.
After the bandits were pacified,
he was promoted to Assistant Regional Commander-in-Chief,
serving as Commander-in-Chief,
garrisoning the various prefectures of Fèngyáng.
Soon after, due to rampant banditry in Jiāngxī,
he was promoted to acting Assistant Commander-in-Chief
and, with Censor-in-Chief Yú Jiàn, jointly supervised military affairs.
Bandit Wáng Hàobā occupied Péiyuán Shān,
firing arrows and stones from its height,
and the government troops nearly could not hold.
Hóng dismounted and, holding his saber,
urged his officers and soldiers to fight desperately to the death,
and the bandits then fled.
He pursued them for several dozen lǐ
and captured them.
He then successively suppressed Liú Chāngsān, Hú Hàosān, and others.
He moved his garrison to Yúgān,
intending to attack the remaining unsubdued bandits,
but a carbuncle developed on his back,
and he died in the army.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him the title of Right Commander-in-Chief
and granted his son the hereditary position of Assistant Commander-in-Chief.
Yáng Ruì,
courtesy name Jìnzhī,
was a native of Xiāoxiàn.
He inherited a hereditary position
and became the commander of the Imperial Guards (Yǔlín) Front Guard of Nánjīng.
In the early years of Zhèngdé,
he was promoted for his talent to oversee the Right Guard of Lóngjiāng
and supervise the construction of grain transport boats in Huái'ān.
In the second month of the second year of Jǐngtài
They were: to diligently pursue sacred learning,
to heed warnings and admonishments,
to restrain desires,
to abandon frivolous pleasures,
to be cautious in actions,
to promote frugality,
to fear heavenly anomalies,
to encourage high-ranking officials and close attendants,
to revitalize the morale of scholars,
and to win the hearts of the people.
The emperor approved of them,
and ordered the Hanlin Academy to transcribe them for display at his side,
for constant review.
Soon after, [Xián] also presented the advantages of chariot warfare and firearms,
and the emperor largely adopted them.
That winter,
he was promoted to Right Vice Minister of War,
then transferred to the Ministry of Revenue.
Yěxiān frequently offered horses as tribute.
Xián argued that using gold and silk to strengthen the enemy was self-defeating
and not a good policy.
He then presented the state of disrepair of border defenses.
Yú Qiān requested that his memorial be circulated to encourage the various generals.
Xián was then transferred to the Ministry of Personnel.
He compiled the commendable actions of twenty-two ancient rulers,
titled "Jiàngǔ Lù" (Record for Reflecting on Antiquity),
and submitted it.
When Yīngzōng was restored to the throne,
he was appointed concurrently as a Hanlin Academician,
and entered the Wényuān Pavilion to take up his duties,
participating in crucial state affairs together with Xú Yǒuzhēn.
Before long,
he was promoted to Minister.
Xián had a dignified and composed demeanor;
his replies to imperial questions were always pertinent to the situation,
and the emperor held him in deep regard.
When Shandong suffered a famine,
the allocation of treasury funds was insufficient for relief.
Yǒuzhēn and Xián were summoned for discussion.
Yǒuzhēn argued that much of the relief distribution was embezzled.
Xián said:
"To fear embezzlement and thus not provide aid,
and merely watch the people die,
is like giving up eating for fear of choking."
Consequently, additional silver was ordered to be distributed.
Shí Hēng and Cáo Jíxiáng contended for power with Yǒuzhēn,
and both resented Xián.
When various censors impeached Hēng and Jíxiáng,
Hēng and Jíxiáng suspected it was Yǒuzhēn's and Xián's idea,
and reported it to the emperor.
The two were imprisoned.
There was a sudden wind and thunder anomaly,
and they were released,
but Xián was demoted to Fujian Provincial Administration Commissioner.
Before he could depart,
Wáng Áo memorialized that Xián was capable of great use,
so he was retained as Left Vice Minister of Personnel.
A month later,
he was reinstated as Minister,
and resumed his duties in the Grand Secretariat as before.
Hēng knew the emperor favored Xián,
and was angry,
but could do nothing about it,
so he feigned friendliness.
Xián also deeply concealed himself,
not entering unless summoned,
but the emperor grew even closer to Xián,
consulting him daily.
Bólái hunted near the border.
Hēng said that the Imperial Seal was with him and
could be seized by surprise.
The emperor's expression changed.
Xián argued that a conflict should not be provoked,
and the seal was not worth treasuring.
The matter was dropped.
Hēng hated Xián even more.
At that time, the emperor was also weary of Hēng's and Jíxiáng's arrogance and tyranny.
He dismissed his attendants and said to Xián:
"These men interfere with governance;
those who submit memorials from the four directions first go to their gates.
What should be done about it?"
Xián replied:
"Your Majesty need only make independent decisions,
and their sycophancy will naturally cease."
The emperor said:
"I once tried not to follow their words,
and they showed their displeasure and resentment."
Xián said:
"I wish to restrain them gradually."
When Hēng and Jíxiáng were in power,
Xián was cautious and dared not speak fully,
yet he often calmly debated,
and his efforts to curb them were very effective.
When Hēng fell from favor,
the emperor again asked Xián about the
"seizing the gate"
incident.
Xián said:
"It was acceptable to welcome the emperor,
but 'seizing the gate'
should not be shown to posterity.
The imperial throne was inherently Your Majesty's;
to seize it implies it was not legitimate.
Moreover, it happened to succeed at that time,
but if the plot had been exposed prematurely,
Hēng and his ilk would not be worth regretting,
but I do not know where Your Majesty would have been placed."
The emperor realized and said:
"Indeed."
Xián continued:
"If the Prince of Chéng had truly not recovered,
and the officials had memorialized to request Your Majesty's restoration,
why would there have been such chaos?
And how would these men have been able to seek promotions and rewards,
and attract power and accept bribes?
The experienced elder statesmen would have remained in office,
and there would have been no need for killings, demotions, or dismissals,
which caused heavenly anomalies.
The Yìjīng says, 'To found a state and govern a family,
do not employ petty men,'
which speaks precisely of this."
The emperor said:
"Indeed."
An imperial edict forbade the use of the term
"seizing the gate"
in memorials from then on,
and further discussed stripping over four thousand people of their undeserved merits.
In the early years of Chénghuà,
those who had been stripped of their merits pleaded their case.
Based on Xián's words again,
the titles of Marquis Tàipíng Zhāng Jǐn and Earl Xīngjì Yáng Zōng were also revoked.
Public opinion at the time was greatly pleased.
After the emperor trusted Xián,
everything he said was heeded.
Yú Qiān had once dispatched surrendered soldiers to campaign in the south.
Chén Rǔyán, influenced by eunuchs,
recalled all of them.
Xián strongly argued against it.
The emperor said:
"I also regret it.
They have already set out,
hereafter, those who wish to leave should be allowed to."
The emperor worried that too many military officers were drawing salaries,
and annual revenue was insufficient.
Xián requested that the old and weak be discharged outside the capital,
which would save expenses without people noticing.
The emperor deeply accepted this.
At that time, there were border alarms annually,
and great floods throughout the realm,
especially severe south and north of the Yangtze.
Xián planned border strategies externally,
and internally requested leniency for the common people,
abolishing all levies and exactions.
The emperor adopted his advice,
and the four directions found respite.
In the second month of the seventh year [of Tiānshùn, 1463],
there was a sound in the sky.
The emperor wanted to avert the calamity [through ritual],
and ordered Xián to draft a blue memorial.
Xián stated that if the ruler did not care for the people,
and the world resented and rebelled,
then there would be demonic omens.
He then requested the implementation of lenient and compassionate policies,
and also requested the cessation of Jiangnan textile production,
the clearing of the Jǐnyī Wèi prison,
the stopping of border officials' tributes,
and the suspension of internal and external procurements.
The emperor found this difficult.
Xián adamantly argued several times,
and his colleagues were all fearful.
Xián retired and said:
"A great minister should speak all that he knows;
how can one hold one's tongue and steal a position?"
Throughout the reign of Tiānshùn,
Xián served as the Senior Grand Secretary,
assisted by Lǚ Yuán and Péng Shí,
but Xián held the most complete authority.
Initially,
Censor Liú Jùn (劉濬) impeached Liǔ Pǔ (柳溥) for battlefield defeat,
which incurred the Emperor's wrath.
Xián (賢) said that censors are the eyes and ears of the state,
and should not be reprimanded.
Shí Hēng (石亨) slandered Xián (賢) for unduly protecting him.
The Emperor gradually alienated Xián (賢),
but soon realized his mistake,
and treated him as before.
Whenever they met alone,
it was a long time before Xián (賢) emerged.
Whenever an issue arose, Xián (賢) was always summoned to be asked for his opinion,
or an eunuch would be sent to inquire.
Xián (賢) strove to uphold the greater good,
and particularly emphasized cherishing talent and opening channels for remonstrance.
Those he recommended and promoted, such as Nián Fù (年富), Xuān Ní (軒輗), Gěng Jiǔchóu (耿九疇), Wáng Hóng (王竑), Lǐ Bǐng (李秉), Chéng Xìn (程信), Yáo Kuí (姚夔), Cuī Gōng (崔恭), Lǐ Shào (李紹) and others,
all became famous officials.
At that time, he often advised the Emperor to grant audiences to high-ranking officials.
When he recommended someone,
he would first discuss and finalize it with the Ministry of Personnel and the Ministry of War.
When he had an audience,
and the Emperor asked about civil officials,
he would specifically ask about Wáng Áo (王翺);
for military officials,
he would specifically ask about Mǎ Áng (馬昂).
These two supported him,
so his words were always heeded,
and no one criticized him for monopolizing power,
except for a few petty individuals who opposed him.
When Cáo Qīn (曹欽) rebelled,
he attacked Xián (賢) in the Eastern Study,
seized him, intending to kill him,
and forced him to draft a memorial to absolve himself of guilt.
Thanks to Wáng Áo’s (王翺) rescue,
he was spared.
Xián (賢) secretly submitted a memorial requesting the capture of the rebels.
At that chaotic time,
no one knew where Xián (賢) was.
When the memorial was received,
the Emperor was overjoyed.
Xián (賢) entered the court with his wounds bandaged,
and was comforted and rewarded.
He was specially promoted to Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
Xián (賢) then said,
“Now that the rebels have been executed,
it is urgent to issue an imperial decree to the entire realm to suspend non-urgent matters,
and seek frank advice to address blockages.”
The Emperor followed his advice.
Mén Dá (門達) was then in power,
and the officers of the Brocade-Clad Guard were tyrannical and a serious menace.
Xián (賢) repeatedly requested their prohibition,
so the Emperor summoned Dá (達) and admonished him.
Dá (達), emboldened by imperial favor, grew even more arrogant.
Xián (賢) seized an opportunity to reiterate Dá’s (達) crimes,
and the Emperor again summoned and warned Dá (達).
Dá (達) harbored deep resentment,
and used Yuán Bīn’s (袁彬) case to incriminate Xián (賢),
who barely escaped.
This incident is recorded in Dá’s (達) biography.
When the Emperor fell ill,
he lay in the Wénhuá Hall.
At that time, there were those who alienated the Heir Apparent from the Emperor.
The Emperor was somewhat swayed,
and secretly informed Xián (賢).
Xián (賢) prostrated himself, bowing his head, saying:
“This is a grave matter,
may Your Majesty consider it carefully.”
The Emperor said:
“Then must I indeed pass the throne to the Heir Apparent?”
Xián (賢) again prostrated himself, saying:
“This would be a great fortune for the imperial ancestral temple and the state.”
The Emperor rose,
and immediately summoned the Heir Apparent.
Xián (賢) helped the Heir Apparent to thank the Emperor.
The Heir Apparent thanked him,
embraced the Emperor’s feet and wept,
and the Emperor also wept.
The slander ultimately failed.
Upon Emperor Xiànzōng’s (憲宗) ascension,
Xián (賢) was promoted to Junior Guardian and Grand Academician of the Huágài Hall,
and oversaw the Imperial Lectures.
In the spring of that year,
the sun was dim and lacked luster.
Xián (賢), together with his colleagues, submitted a memorial stating:
“The sun
symbolizes the monarch.
When the monarch’s virtue is clear,
the sunlight is abundant.
May Your Majesty cultivate your character with reverence,
govern your subordinates with integrity,
decide affairs with firmness,
and discern subtle matters with clarity.
If you persist without slackening,
then celestial anomalies will naturally cease,
and harmony will naturally prevail.”
The next day, they further stated:
“The weather is not harmonious,
due to an excess of yin energy.
From the Xuāndé (宣德) to the Tiānshùn (天順) eras,
too many palace women were selected.
The women of the Huànyī Bureau (澣衣局) who were confiscated into service are particularly sorrowful and resentful.
They should be allowed to return home.”
The Emperor followed this,
and those within and outside the court rejoiced.
In the fifth month, there was a great hailstorm,
a strong wind blew off tiles,
and uprooted trees at the suburban altars.
Xián (賢) said:
“Heaven’s majesty is fearsome.
Your Majesty should be solemnly reflective,
and not be too familiar with favored attendants.
Trust and rely on experienced elders,
and jointly plan the affairs of state.”
The officials concerned requested the manufacture of imperial ceremonial carriages.
Xián (賢) said:
“The imperial treasury still has some that have not yet been used.
Now that an imperial pardon has just been issued,
we are supposed to be saving expenses.
How can we do this again?”
The Emperor immediately halted it.
Whenever there was a disaster or anomaly,
he would always speak plainly with his colleagues without concealment,
and during the early reign of the Emperor,
his admonitions were particularly urgent.
After Mén Dá (門達) was banished,
many of his partisans sent anonymous letters to frame Xián (賢).
Xián (賢) requested to resign,
but an imperial edict comforted him and retained him.
When Empress Wú (吳后) was deposed,
remonstrating officials requested the execution of Niú Yù (牛玉),
which implicated Xián (賢).
There were also those who spread rumors to frame Xián (賢).
The Emperor ordered imperial guards to stay at Xián’s (賢) house,
and protect his comings and goings.
In the third month of the second year of Chénghuà (成化), he suffered the loss of his father.
An imperial edict ordered him to resume his post.
He declined three times but was not permitted,
and an eunuch was dispatched to escort him to his father’s burial.
Upon his return to the capital,
he again declined.
An envoy was sent to convey the imperial will,
and he then resumed his duties.
He died in the winter of that year,
aged fifty-nine.
The Emperor was greatly saddened,
posthumously granted him the title of Grand Preceptor,
and conferred the posthumous name Wéndá (文達).
Xián (賢) believed that since he had gained the confidence of the ruler,
he should speak his mind completely.
When Emperor Jǐngdì (景帝) died, there was a plan to have Empress Wāng (汪后) buried with him,
but it was stopped due to Xián’s (賢) words.
The youngest son of Emperor Huìdì (惠帝) had been imprisoned for sixty years.
Emperor Yīngzōng (英宗) pitied him and wanted to pardon him,
and consulted Xián (賢).
Xián (賢) bowed his head, saying:
“This is the intention of Yáo (堯) and Shùn (舜),
heaven and earth, and the ancestors will truly rely upon it.”
The Emperor’s resolve was then firm.
The Emperor once performed sacrifices at the altars of mountains and rivers,
but felt that going out at night was inconvenient,
and wished to send an official to perform the sacrifice in his place.
Xián (賢) cited ancestral instructions to argue against it,
and the Emperor ultimately completed the ritual and returned.
He often said that if the surplus funds in the imperial treasury
were not used to relieve famine and support the army,
then the ruler would surely develop an extravagant mindset,
and shift them to expenditures on construction, prayers, ceremonies, music, and women.
He frequently requested the release of funds to relieve famine, provide loans, and aid the border regions,
countless times.
According to precedent,
provincial officials were recommended by third-rank metropolitan officials.
Xián (賢) was concerned about their self-serving competition,
and ordered the Ministry of Personnel to nominate two candidates for each vacancy,
requesting the Emperor to make the selection.
The practice of parallel nominations began with him.
Since the era of the Three Yángs,
no one had gained the Emperor’s favor as much as Xián (賢).
However, having formed a friendship with Emperor Jǐngdì (景帝) when he was a minor official,
and being extraordinarily promoted to Vice Minister,
his writings contradictorily called Emperor Jǐngdì (景帝) "licentious and depraved."
His suppression of Yè Shèng (葉盛),
ousting of Yuè Zhèng (岳正),
and failure to save Luó Lún (羅倫)
are particularly regretted by the world.
Lǚ Yuán,
courtesy name Féngyuán,
was from Xiùshuǐ.
His father, Sìfāng,
was an instructor in Wànquán.
His elder brother, Běn,
was a teaching assistant in Jǐngzhōu.
When Sìfāng grew old,
he went to Jǐngzhōu to be cared for
and he and Běn died one after another.
Being poor, Yuán could not bring their coffins home for burial,
so he interred them in Jǐngzhōu.
Yuán would often go to their graves and weep bitterly.
After a long time,
he brought his mother back south,
but his family became even poorer.
The prefect Huáng Mǎoqi appreciated Yuán’s writings,
so he made him a *zhūshēng*
and sent him to school.
He was ranked first in the provincial examination.
In the seventh year of Zhèngtǒng (1442),
he passed the imperial examination
and was appointed compiler.
In the twelfth year (1447),
he was selected, along with the attendant lecturer Péi Lún and nine others, to study in the Eastern Pavilion
and serve in the imperial lectures.
At the beginning of Jǐngtài (1450),
he was promoted to attendant lecturer
and, with his colleague Ní Qiān, taught the young eunuchs in the east corridor of the Wénhuá Hall.
When the emperor arrived,
he ordered Qiān to lecture on the *Guófēng*
and Yuán on the *Yáodiǎn*.
Both pleased the emperor.
He asked what their offices were,
and they replied that they were both *zhōngyǔn* concurrently serving as attendant lecturers.
The emperor said,
“Their ranks are the same,
why hold concurrent posts?”
He promoted both of them to attendant academician,
concurrently *zhōngyǔn*.
Soon after, he was promoted to Grand Academician of the Left Spring Palace.
At the beginning of Tiānshùn (1457),
he was transferred to Right Policy Advisor of the Office of Transmission,
concurrently attendant lecturer.
The day after Xú Yǒuzhēn and Lǐ Xián were imprisoned,
he was ordered to enter the Grand Secretariat to participate in state affairs.
Shí Hēng and Cáo Jíxiáng were in power
and were arrogant,
but they alone respected Yuán.
When Yuán attended court meetings in a blue robe,
Hēng laughed and said,
“Sir, please change your attire.”
Yuán did not respond.
Soon after, he and Yuè Zhèng listed the crimes of Hēng and Jíxiáng in a memorial,
but the memorial was held back by the emperor.
The two became angry
and extracted phrases from imperial edicts,
accusing the Grand Secretaries of slander.
The emperor was furious.
He sat in the Biàndiàn,
summoned them for an audience,
and sternly said,
“Zhèng is daring enough to do this,
but Yuán has always been respectful and cautious.
Why are you siding with Zhèng?”
Zhèng was dismissed,
but Yuán was allowed to remain.
After Lǐ Xián was reinstated and returned to the Grand Secretariat to govern,
Yuán assisted him.
Soon after,
Péng Shí also joined,
and the three got along very happily.
Xián was open-minded
and made quick decisions in matters.
Yuán complemented him with his prudence,
and all state affairs were handled properly.
In the winter of that year,
he was promoted to Academician of the Hànlín Academy.
In the sixth year (1462), he suffered the loss of his mother,
and for three days, he did not touch food or drink.
An imperial edict ordered him to resume duty immediately after the burial.
Yuán requested to observe the full mourning period.
This was not granted.
So he went to Jǐngzhōu,
exhumed his father and brother for reburial,
and slept on straw and grieved in the boat.
He was usually robust,
but by then he was emaciated.
Upon arriving home, he had just completed the reburial when he died,
at the age of forty-five.
He was posthumously granted Left Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites
and given the posthumous name Wényì.
Yuán was firm internally but gentle externally,
and he did not compete with others.
He was frugal by nature,
wearing no fine silks.
His belongings on his return trip consisted only of a few sets of bestowed clothing,
and he distributed his salary to help his clan and relatives.
His son, Máo,
courtesy name Bǐngzhī.
By hereditary privilege, he was appointed a student of the Guózǐ (Imperial Academy),
served in the Hànlín,
and was promoted to Secretariat Drafter.
He memorialized requesting to take the imperial examinations,
but the office concerned refused, citing precedent.
Emperor Xiànzōng specially permitted it,
and he then passed the Shùntiān provincial examination.
Secretariat Drafters being allowed to take examinations began with Máo.
He was successively promoted to Director of the Ministry of Rites.
He was fond of learning and good at writing,
and knowledgeable about historical precedents.
When Liúqiú requested to send tribute once a year,
and when Huihui tribute envoys asked to return to their country via Guǎngdōng,
he rejected both requests as being against regulations.
He was recommended for promotion to Junior Supervisor of the Nánjīng Court of the Imperial Stud.
According to custom,
the number of horses in the Imperial Stud
was not to be known by other officials.
Because of this, records were destroyed,
and increases or decreases were unverifiable.
Máo said,
“It is right that other officials do not hear about it;
but should those in charge
be so careless?”
He proposed that an inventory be taken every three years,
and this was established as a rule.
He was successively promoted to Nánjīng Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
and compiled several volumes on precedents and reforms.
At the beginning of Zhèngdé (1506),
he retired and returned home.
Yuè Zhèng,
courtesy name Jìfāng,
was from Huòxiàn.
In the thirteenth year of Zhèngtǒng (1448), he ranked first in the metropolitan examination,
was granted the *jìnshì* degree,
appointed compiler,
and promoted to Left Grand Mentor.
At the beginning of Tiānshùn (1457),
he was transferred to Compiler
and taught the young eunuchs.
When the Grand Secretaries Xú Yǒuzhēn and Lǐ Xián were imprisoned,
the emperor had already appointed Lǚ Yuán to participate in government.
Shortly after,
Xuē Xuān also retired,
and the emperor sought a replacement.
Wáng Áo recommended Zhèng,
so he was summoned for an audience at Wénhuá Hall.
Zhèng was tall and had a handsome beard.
The emperor saw him from afar
and his expression brightened.
After ascending the steps,
he repeatedly praised him.
He asked his age,
where his home was,
and in what year he passed the *jìnshì* examination.
Zhèng answered truthfully.
The emperor was again greatly pleased and said,
“You are in your prime.
You are a northerner like Us,
and also one of the scholars We personally selected.
Now We appoint you to the Grand Secretariat.
Do your best to assist Us.”
Zhèng kowtowed and accepted the appointment.
As he hurried out,
Shí Hēng and Zhāng Yuè met him at the Zuǒshùn Gate
and were startled, saying,
“How did you get here?”
When they entered,
the emperor said,
“Today We personally selected a Grand Secretary.”
They asked who it was,
and the emperor said,
“Yuè Zhèng.”
The two feigned congratulations.
The emperor said,
“He is only a low-ranking official,
he should be given Left Vice Minister of Personnel concurrently Academician.”
The two said,
“Your Majesty has found the right person.
Once he proves himself competent,
it will not be too late to increase his rank.”
The emperor remained silent,
and then ordered him to enter the Grand Secretariat with his original rank.
Yuè Zhèng 岳正 was naturally magnanimous,
bold and outspoken.
When he was promoted by the Emperor,
he became even more grateful and wished to dedicate himself.
Tāng Xù 湯序, who was the vice director of the Qīn Tiān Jiān 欽天監 (Imperial Astronomical Bureau),
was a partisan of Shí Hēng 石亨.
He once reported a disaster and strange phenomena,
and requested that all corrupt officials be removed.
The Emperor asked Yuè Zhèng 岳正.
Yuè Zhèng 岳正 said:
"Corrupt officials are not specifically named.
If one were to seek them out,
everyone would feel insecure.
Moreover, Tāng Xù's 湯序's techniques are superficial;
why should he be trusted?"
The Emperor then stopped.
A monk was spreading seditious rumors.
The Jǐnyī Wèi 錦衣衛 (Brocade-Clad Guard) patrols apprehended him,
and he was charged with conspiracy to rebel.
The eunuch Niú Yù 牛玉 requested an official position for the patrols.
Yuè Zhèng 岳正 said:
"Even if the matter is proven,
it would only fall under the law for seditious rumors,
and the patrols should only be rewarded,
it is not appropriate to give them official positions."
Dozens of the monk's followers were thus spared.
Someone wrote an anonymous letter listing the crimes of Cáo Jíxiáng 曹吉祥.
Cáo Jíxiáng 曹吉祥 was enraged,
and requested that a public notice be issued to apprehend the author.
The Emperor instructed Yuè Zhèng 岳正 to draft the notice.
Yuè Zhèng 岳正 and Lǚ Yuán 呂原 came to an audience and said:
"There is a proper way to govern.
Thieves are the responsibility of the Bīng Bù 兵部 (Ministry of War),
and wicked people are the responsibility of the Fǎ Sī 法司 (Judicial Department).
How can the Son of Heaven issue a notice to recruit for their capture?
Furthermore, if the matter is delayed, it will expose itself;
if it is rushed, it will be hidden all the more.
This is human nature."
The Emperor agreed with his words,
and did not pursue the matter.
Shí Hēng's 石亨's nephew, Biāo 彪, was garrisoned in Dàtóng 大同.
When he presented a victory report,
it was sent to the Nèi Gé 內閣 (Grand Secretariat) for inquiry.
The envoy claimed countless captures and beheadings,
which could not all be brought back,
and that they were all displayed on trees in the forest.
Yuè Zhèng 岳正, consulting a map, questioned him,
saying:
"From such a place to such a place,
it is all desert.
Where did you display them?"
The man was speechless.
At that time, Shí Hēng 石亨 and Cáo Jíxiáng 曹吉祥 were extremely presumptuous,
and the Emperor was quite displeased with them.
Yuè Zhèng 岳正 calmly said:
"The two men's power is too great.
I request to sow discord between them by stratagem."
The Emperor consented.
Yuè Zhèng 岳正 went out and saw Cáo Jíxiáng 曹吉祥, saying:
"What is Du Qīng 杜清, who is often sent by Zhōngguó Gōng 忠國公 (Duke of Loyalty) [Shí Hēng 石亨], doing here?"
Cáo Jíxiáng 曹吉祥 replied:
"He is showing his sincere respect and affection for me, Shí Gōng 石公."
Yuè Zhèng 岳正 said:
"No,
he is
sent to spy on your actions."
He then persuaded Cáo Jíxiáng 曹吉祥 to resign his military authority.
He then went to Shí Hēng 石亨,
advising him to restrain himself.
Shí Hēng 石亨 and Cáo Jíxiáng 曹吉祥 perceived Yuè Zhèng's 岳正's intention and were enraged.
Cáo Jíxiáng 曹吉祥 saw the Emperor,
removed his hat,
and tearfully requested to die.
The Emperor felt inwardly ashamed,
comforted and admonished him,
and summoned Yuè Zhèng 岳正 to reprimand him for leaking information.
Coincidentally, the Chéngtiān Mén 承天門 (Gate of Heavenly Succession) suffered a disaster.
Yuè Zhèng 岳正 strongly asserted that Shí Hēng 石亨 was planning rebellion,
and also said:
"Chén Rǔyán 陳汝言 is
a petty man.
Now that he is a Shàngshū 尚書 (Minister),
Lú Bīn 盧彬 can be appointed as a Shìláng 侍郎 (Vice Minister).
Both of these men are cunning and fierce.
If they work together, they will certainly devour each other,
and taking advantage of their discord, both can be removed."
Xú Yǒuzhēn 徐有貞 was again imprisoned,
and he further said:
"If Xú Yǒuzhēn 徐有貞 is employed,
the celestial changes can be averted."
The Emperor did not accept any of these suggestions.
When an imperial edict was to be issued to the court officials,
Yuè Zhèng 岳正 was ordered to review the draft.
Yuè Zhèng 岳正 drafted the edict as follows:
"Recently, the Chéngtiān Mén 承天門 suffered a disaster.
My heart is shaken with fear,
not knowing what to do.
Is it that my reverence for Heaven and service to the spirits
have not been fully observed?
Are the established laws of the ancestors not being followed?
Are good and evil not distinguished,
and appointments and dismissals improper?
Are right and wrong not differentiated,
and are there injustices in prisons?
Are there too many levies and requisitions,
and are the military campaigns arduous?
Are rewards and gifts excessive,
and are the treasuries empty?
Are requests and solicitations incessant,
and are official titles granted indiscriminately?
Is bribery rampant,
and are state affairs neglected?
Are factions colluding in fraud,
and attaching themselves to power?
Are officials manipulating the law,
and arbitrarily exercising authority and favoritism?
Are taxes and corvée labor too heavy,
making the common people restless?
Are sycophants and ambitious flatterers being promoted,
while loyal advice and upright officials are not utilized?
Or are the responsible officials incompetent, cruel, and tyrannical,
greedy and insatiable,
causing the military and populace to be unsettled?
All these are causes that harm harmony and lead to disasters,
yet I am still unclear about them.
Now I reflect on my faults and contemplate my shortcomings,
filled with fear and apprehension.
You, my numerous officials, share equally in prosperity and adversity.
Therefore, cleanse your hearts and correct your mistakes,
do not repeat past errors,
and speak frankly without concealment about what should be done."
When the edict was issued,
the entire court widely circulated and recited it.
However, Shí Hēng 石亨 and Cáo Jíxiáng 曹吉祥 fabricated rumors,
accusing Yuè Zhèng 岳正 of "selling his uprightness and slandering."
The Emperor was angry,
and ordered him to be assigned again as an attendant scribe for the palace eunuchs.
The next day,
he was demoted to Assistant Prefect of Qīnzhōu 欽州.
On his way to Huò 漷,
he stayed for ten days due to his elderly mother.
Chén Rǔyán 陳汝言 ordered the patrol officer to report the situation,
and also said that Yuè Zhèng 岳正 had once seized a princess's land.
Consequently, he was arrested and imprisoned in the imperial prison,
received one hundred strokes with the rod,
and was exiled to Sùzhōu 肅州.
When he reached Zhuó 涿,
he lodged overnight at a relay station.
His handcuffs were too tight,
and he was short of breath and almost died.
Yáng Sì 楊四, a local of Zhuó 涿, who was a drunken soldier,
removed Yuè Zhèng's 岳正's handcuffs,
cut them open,
and generously bribed the soldiers,
allowing him to reach his place of exile.
After Shí Hēng 石亨 and Cáo Jíxiáng 曹吉祥 were executed,
the Emperor said to Lǐ Xián 李賢:
"Yuè Zhèng 岳正 indeed mentioned it before."
Lǐ Xián 李賢 said:
"Yuè Zhèng 岳正 has an elderly mother;
it would be fortunate
if he could be released to return to his hometown."
So he was released and became a commoner.
When Xiànzōng 憲宗 ascended the throne,
Censor Lǚ Hóng 呂洪 and others requested to reinstate Yuè Zhèng 岳正 and Yáng Xuān 楊瑄 to their official positions.
An edict ordered Yuè Zhèng 岳正 to serve as director of the Jīngyán 經筵 (Imperial Lectures) with his original rank,
and to compile the Yīngzōng Shílù 英宗實錄 (Veritable Records of Emperor Yīngzōng).
Previously,
when Yuè Zhèng 岳正 was disgraced,
Assistant Commander Jì Duó 季鐸 requested and obtained his residence.
Now, an edict returned it to Yuè Zhèng 岳正.
When Yuè Zhèng 岳正 returned to court,
he believed he would be greatly employed,
but Lǐ Xián 李賢 wanted to appoint him as Libationer of Nánjīng 南京,
which displeased Yuè Zhèng 岳正.
Those who were jealous fabricated a draft memorial by Yuè Zhèng 岳正 impeaching Lǐ Xián 李賢,
which Lǐ Xián 李賢 resented.
In the fourth month of the first year of Chénghuà 成化 (1465),
a court deliberation nominated candidates for Vice Minister of War to clear up "stick-on yellow" documents.
Yuè Zhèng 岳正's name and that of Supervising Secretary Zhāng Níng 張寧 were both submitted.
The Emperor decreed it a private matter,
appointed Yuè Zhèng 岳正 as Prefect of Xīnghuà 興化,
and Zhāng Níng 張寧 was also assigned to an outer post.
When Yuè Zhèng 岳正 arrived at his post,
he built dikes to irrigate several thousand qǐng 頃 of fields,
reduced extravagant expenses,
and managed the emergency granaries,
wishing to implement reforms.
The local gentry and officials disliked his actions,
spreading slanders.
Yuè Zhèng 岳正 also grew tired of official duties.
In the fifth year, he went to court for an audience,
and subsequently retired.
Five more years later, he died
at the age of fifty-five.
He had no sons.
Grand Secretary Lǐ Dōngyáng 李東陽 and Censor Lǐ Jīng 李經
were his sons-in-law.
Yuè Zhèng 岳正 was widely learned and skilled in writing.
He held high expectations for himself,
and his spirit was so unyielding that he would not humble himself before others.
He was in the Grand Secretariat for only twenty-eight days.
He was courageous in action and dared to speak,
debating and presenting memorials in the imperial private audience,
even to the point of his spittle splashing on the emperor's robes.
When someone advised him to first gain trust and then remonstrate,
he passionately declared,
“His Majesty treats me with such厚kindness,
and I fear I have no way to repay him.
Are you treating me as a mere remonstrating official?”
Yīngzōng 英宗 also understood his loyalty.
When Yuè Zhèng 岳正 was in exile,
the emperor once thought of him and said,
“Yuè Zhèng 岳正 is quite good,
just too bold.”
Yuè Zhèng 岳正, upon hearing this, composed an encomium for his own portrait,
relating the emperor's words,
and concluding with:
“Your subject once heard the words of the ancients,
that they would face death without regret.”
Such was his unyielding self-confidence.
However, his ambition was grand but his talent was shallow.
He attempted to use stratagems to break up the powerful factions,
but was instead devoured by them.
Everyone considered him naive yet pitied him.
During the Jiājìng 嘉靖 reign,
he was posthumously granted the title of Tàicháng Sìqīng 太常寺卿 [Grand Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices],
and given the posthumous name Wénsù 文肅.
Péng Shí 彭時,
courtesy name Chúndào 純道,
was from Ānfú 安福.
In the thirteenth year of Zhèngtǒng 正統 (1448), he achieved the highest rank in the imperial examination [Jinshì di-yī 進士第一],
and was appointed Xiūzhuàn 修撰 [compiler].
The following year,
Prince Chéng 郕 became regent.
Péng Shí 彭時 was ordered, along with Shāng Lù 商輅, to enter the Grand Secretariat and participate in state affairs.
Upon hearing of his stepmother's mourning,
he strenuously declined,
but was not permitted,
so he accepted the appointment.
To participate in grand state affairs barely a year after his first appointment was
unprecedented before this.
Soon after, he was promoted to Shìdú 侍讀 [reader-in-waiting].
In the first year of Jǐngtài 景泰 (1450), as military affairs somewhat subsided,
he obtained permission to complete his mourning period.
However, this displeased the emperor.
After his mourning period ended,
he was ordered to serve in the Hànlín Yuàn 翰林院 [Hanlin Academy],
and was no longer involved in Grand Secretariat affairs.
After the succession was changed,
he was promoted to Zuǒ Chūnfāng Dàxuéshì 左春坊大學士 [Grand Academician of the Left Spring Palace].
Upon the completion of the Huányǔ Tōngzhì 寰宇通志 [Comprehensive Gazetteer of the Empire],
he was promoted to Tàicháng Sì Shàocīng 太常寺少卿 [Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices].
Both positions included concurrent service as Shìdú 侍讀.
In the first year of Tiānshùn 天順 (1457),
after Xú Yǒuzhēn 徐有貞 was disgraced,
Yuè Zhèng 岳正 and Xǔ Bīn 許彬 were successively dismissed.
When the emperor summoned Péng Shí 彭時 to the Wénhuá Diàn 文華殿 [Hall of Literary Glory],
he said,
“Are you not the Zhuàngyuán 狀元 whom I personally selected?”
Péng Shí 彭時 bowed his head.
The next day, he was again ordered to enter the Grand Secretariat,
concurrently serving as Hànlín Yuàn Xuéshì 翰lín Yuàn Xuéshì 翰林院學士 [Academician of the Hanlin Academy].
After the Sān Yáng 三楊,
the protocol for the advancement and demotion of Grand Secretariat officials had become quite lax.
Only Péng Shí 彭時 and Yuè Zhèng 岳正 were
personally promoted by the emperor.
The emperor was then inclined to employ Lǐ Xián 李賢,
frequently summoning Lǐ Xián 李賢 for private audiences.
Lǐ Xián 李賢 greatly respected Péng Shí 彭時,
and would always consult him upon returning.
Péng Shí 彭 Shí 彭時 would argue forcefully for what was right or wrong,
sometimes to the point of Lǐ Xián 李 Xián 李賢 losing countenance.
Initially, Lǐ Xián 李 Xián 李賢 was slightly displeased,
but in time, he also respected Péng Shí 彭 Shí 彭時's fairness and uprightness,
saying,
“Péng Gōng 彭公 is
truly a gentleman.”
When the Císhòu Huángtàihòu 慈壽皇太后 was honored with a new title,
an edict was proclaimed to the empire.
Péng Shí 彭 Shí 彭時 wished to extend imperial benevolence,
but Lǐ Xián 李 Xián 李賢 thought it inappropriate to issue another amnesty within a year.
Péng Shí 彭 Shí 彭時 said,
“It is not an amnesty;
rather, it should be an act of special courtesy to the elderly.
Officials whose parents are seventy or older should be granted imperial decrees and patents of nobility;
commoners eighty or older should be given caps and sashes.
This is 'to respect our own elders and extend that respect to the elders of others.'
Lǐ Xián 李 Xián 李賢 praised this idea as excellent
and immediately memorialized for its implementation.
The emperor admired Péng Shí 彭 Shí 彭時's demeanor when selecting Shùjíshì 庶吉士 [bachelors of the Hanlin Academy].
He ordered Lǐ Xián 李 Xián 李賢 to select only northerners,
and for southerners, only those like Péng Shí 彭 Shí 彭時 would be acceptable.
Lǐ Xián 李 Xián 李賢 conveyed this to Péng Shí 彭 Shí 彭時.
Soon after, the eunuch Niú Yù 牛玉 delivered an imperial decree.
Péng Shí 彭 Shí 彭時 said to Niú Yù 牛玉,
“There are not a few southern scholars superior to me;
how can they be suppressed?”
Subsequently,
fifteen people were selected,
six of whom were southerners.
Mén Dá 門達 framed Lǐ Xián 李 Xián 李賢,
and the emperor was swayed,
saying,
“If Lǐ Xián 李 Xián 李賢 is removed,
I will rely solely on Péng Shí 彭 Shí 彭時.”
Someone transmitted these words,
and Péng Shí 彭 Shí 彭時 was startled, saying,
“Lǐ Gōng 李公 possesses talent for statecraft;
how can he be removed?”
Therefore, he strenuously defended Lǐ Xián 李 Xián 李賢.
Moreover, he said,
“If Lǐ Xián 李 Xián 李賢 leaves,
I cannot remain alone.”
When these words were heard,
the emperor's intent was resolved.
When the emperor was critically ill,
he orally dictated his last will,
establishing the ranks of empresses and consorts,
and forbidding the burial of imperial concubines with the deceased,
four matters in total,
entrusting them to the Grand Secretariat officials for embellishment.
Péng Shí 彭 Shí 彭時 finished reading,
and tears flowed,
overwhelmed by sorrow.
When the eunuch reported back,
the emperor also shed tears.
When Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
there was a discussion about conferring honorific titles on the two empresses dowager.
The eunuch Xià Shí, following Guìfēi Zhōu's instructions,
said that Empresses Qián had been ill for a long time
and should not be addressed as Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu).
Instead, Guìfēi Zhōu,
the Emperor's birth mother,
should be the only one to receive the honorific title.
Xián said:
"The imperial will has already been settled,
why so many words?"
Shí replied:
"Lǐ Gōng's words are correct.
The reason the imperial court commands the respect of all under heaven
lies in rectifying the cardinal principles.
If not,
the damage to the sacred virtue of His Majesty would be not small."
A moment later,
the eunuch again conveyed Guìfēi Zhōu's instructions:
"A son becoming Emperor
means his mother should be Grand Empress Dowager.
How can there be a Grand Empress Dowager who has no son?
There was a precedent during the Xuāndé reign."
Xián's expression changed,
and he looked at Shí.
Shí said:
"Today's matter is different from that during the Xuāndé reign.
Empress Hú formally abdicated
and retired to a separate palace,
which is why she was not honored at the beginning of the Zhèngtǒng reign.
Now, the proper status is clearly established,
how can it be compared?"
The eunuch said:
"If so, why not draft a letter of abdication?"
Shí replied:
"It was never done when the late Emperor was alive.
Who dares to draft it now?
If a subject caters to and complies with such wishes,
they will be a sinner for ten thousand generations."
The eunuch spoke in a stern voice, threatening with grave words.
Shí cupped his hands and looked up to heaven, saying:
"The spirits of Tàizǔ and Tàizōng are above.
Who would dare to harbor disloyal thoughts?
Empress Qián had no son,
what benefit is she seeking to contend for this?
It is my duty not to remain silent,
for I wish to preserve the sacred virtue of His Majesty.
If we consider the heart of great filial piety,
then honoring both empresses dowager equally is appropriate."
Xián also spoke strongly,
and the decision was thus made.
When the imperial seals were about to be conferred,
Shí said:
"If both empresses dowager are called the same, there will be no distinction.
Empress Dowager Qián should have two extra characters
to facilitate proper address."
So she was honored as Cíyì Huáng Tàihòu,
and Guìfēi Zhōu as Huáng Tàihòu.
A few days later,
the eunuch Tán Bāo came to the Grand Secretariat and said:
"His Majesty's true intention was indeed this.
But he was pressured by the Grand Empress Dowager
and dared not act on his own.
If not for the strong contention of the two sirs,
a great matter would have almost been ruined."
At that time, the Grand Secretary Chén Wén was silent,
but hearing Bāo's words,
he felt very ashamed.
After the ceremony,
Shí was promoted to Right Vice Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Yòu Shìláng),
concurrently a Grand Academician (Xuélìshì),
and concurrently in charge of the imperial lectures (Jīngyán).
In the first year of Chénghuà,
he was promoted to Minister of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū),
with his concurrent posts remaining unchanged.
In the autumn of the following year,
he requested leave to visit his parents.
In the second month of the third year, an imperial edict ordered his swift return to court.
When the Yīngzōng Shílù was completed,
he was promoted to Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shàobǎo),
and concurrently Grand Academician of the Wényuángé.
In the fourth year,
Cíyì Tàihòu passed away,
and an edict was issued to discuss the imperial tomb.
Shí, along with Shāng Lù and Liú Dìngzhī, said:
"The Grand Empress Dowager was the consort of the late Emperor,
and held the proper position of the central palace.
Your Majesty honored her as Grand Empress Dowager,
and an edict was shown to all under heaven.
The late Emperor maintained the relationship between husband and wife,
and Your Majesty fully expressed the love between mother and son.
Both are entirely fitting according to ritual.
Now, her coffin should be interred together with Yùlíng,
and her spirit tablet should be enshrined in the ancestral temple.
This is an unchangeable ritual.
We have recently heard that there is a desire to select a separate burial site,
which truly fills us with doubt and apprehension.
We humbly believe that the reason His Majesty hesitates
is surely because the current Grand Empress Dowager, after her passing,
will also be equally honored with the late Emperor,
and you are concerned that two empresses being jointly honored
is not in accordance with the system of the ancestors.
Examining history,
Emperor Wén of Hàn honored his birth mother, Grand Empress Dowager Bó,
yet Empress Lǚ's spirit tablet remained enshrined in Chánglíng.
Emperor Rénzōng of Sòng posthumously honored his birth mother, Consort Lǐ Chén,
yet Empress Liú's spirit tablet remained enshrined in the ancestral temple.
If the arrangements for the imperial tomb and ancestral temple are slightly unfitting now,
it will mar previous good deeds
and invite ridicule from future generations."
Thereupon, the various ministers spoke consecutively.
The Emperor still found it difficult to go against the Grand Empress Dowager's wishes,
so Shí, along with the court officials, prostrated themselves at Wénhuá Mén, weeping and pleading.
Both the Emperor and the Grand Empress Dowager were moved,
and only then did they follow Shí's proposal.
When a comet appeared in Sāntái,
Shí and others said:
"While major affairs of the outer court are certainly to be prioritized,
the fundamental matters within the palace are even more urgent.
The proverb says, 'Many sons come from many mothers.'
Currently, there are many concubines,
but no signs of sons.
This must be because Your Majesty's affections are exclusively devoted to one,
and the favored one has passed the age of childbearing.
We hope you will evenly distribute your affections,
for the great plan of the imperial family and the state."
At that time, the Emperor exclusively favored Wàn Guìfēi,
and she was already nearly forty years old,
which is why Shí said this.
They also said:
"The promotion and demotion of high officials
should be decided by Your Majesty's own heart,
or by gathering the ministers for deliberation.
It should not be entirely entrusted to subordinates,
allowing great power to fall by the wayside."
Although the Emperor could not follow this,
he admired their loyalty in his heart.
When the Censor-in-Chief (Dū Yùshǐ) Xiàng Zhōng failed in his campaign against Mǎn Sì,
