the court deliberated sending the Marquis of Fǔníng, Zhū Yǒng, to lead the capital's troops to assist.
Yǒng, however, found his deployment difficult
and made many demands.
Shí disliked his grandstanding,
and also believed that the troops might not need to be dispatched;
he merely ordered them to prepare and wait.
Soon, Zhōng sent an urgent report,
stating that he had already surrounded the bandits at Shíchéng.
The Emperor dispatched the eunuchs Huái Ēn and Huáng Cì, along with the Minister of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū) Bái Guī and Chéng Xìn, to the Grand Secretariat for discussion.
Shí said:
"The bandits have been raiding everywhere,
and their vanguard is indeed irresistible.
Now they have entered Shíchéng to protect themselves;
our army has them firmly besieged.
This is like a trapped beast, easy to capture."
Xìn said:
"How do you know Zhōng won't retreat?"
Shí replied:
"His deployment is already set,
why would he retreat?
Moreover, if we dispatch troops now,
when do you estimate they would arrive?"
Xìn said:
"Next spring."
Shí said:
"In that case,
it would be even slower and too late.
The success or failure of this matter
will be decided in winter."
Xìn was indignant
and made a dangerous remark:
"If Zhōng fails,
we must execute one or two people,
and then send out the army."
Everyone was apprehensive,
and asked Shí for his opinion.
He said:
"Observing the twists and turns in Zhōng's memorial,
I know he is capable.
If he hears that separate imperial guards are being dispatched,
he will likely withdraw and dare not take responsibility,
and the situation with the bandits will become unpredictable."
Only Shāng Lù agreed with Shí's words.
By winter,
the bandits were indeed pacified,
and everyone was greatly impressed.
He was reassigned as Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū).
In his fifth year, he fell ill and was on leave.
After more than three months,
the Emperor urged him to return to the Cabinet to attend to affairs,
and excused him from morning audiences.
That winter,
there was no snow.
He submitted a memorial saying:
"The purchasing by the Guānglùsì (Court of Imperial Entertainments),
and the levies collected at each city gate,
are excessively oppressive.
Furthermore, those who offer pearls and gems
overestimate their value and inflate their prices,
draining the national treasury.
I beg for these abuses to be reformed
to benefit the common people."
The Emperor issued an excellent edict praising and adopting it.
The Jīfǔ (Capital Region), Shāndōng, and Hénán suffered from drought.
He requested exemption from summer taxes and salt certificates,
and from the賠課馬 (fine for unreturned horses) of the Tàipúsì (Court of the Imperial Stud).
Rice prices were high in the capital,
and he requested the release of 500,000 shí (bushels) from granary reserves for sale at stable prices.
All were granted.
At the time, he was highly esteemed as an old minister,
and in dealing with matters, he argued and contended without evasion.
However, at this time, the Emperor was negligent in governance,
and high ministers rarely gained audience.
Wàn Ān (萬安), who was also in the Cabinet,
colluded with powerful eunuchs and imperial relatives,
obstructing communication between superiors and subordinates,
which often caused him great concern.
In his seventh year,
his illness recurred,
and he requested to retire.
The Emperor comforted him and asked him to stay,
so he could not leave.
In winter,
a comet reappeared.
At that time, he spoke of seven essential matters of governance: 1,
Do not be misled by Buddhist affairs,
wasting money;
The issuance of imperial edicts should be exclusively entrusted to the Sīlǐjiān (Directorate of Ceremonial),
and not to others,
to prevent fraud;
Regularly meet with high ministers to discuss state affairs;
Too many favors and rewards are bestowed upon favored courtiers,
and artisans are illicitly granted official ranks without discipline,
while severe criminals facing death or exile
are not adequately punished by law;
excessive punishments and unwarranted rewards should be restrained;
Be open-minded in accepting remonstrance,
and do not dislike blunt and direct criticism;
Exhort court officials not to be equivocal,
and whenever government decrees are inappropriate,
to speak directly in remonstrance;
Rectify the management of pasture lands
and reduce the estates of powerful figures.
All these points precisely addressed the pressing issues of the time.
Níngjìn Bó Liú Jù (寧晉伯劉聚) requested posthumous honors for his paternal uncle, the eunuch Yǒngchéng (永誠),
and also sought a temple plaque.
The Lǐbù (Ministry of Rites) rejected this based on precedent.
The Emperor specially granted a plaque inscribed "Bāogōng" (褒功),
and ordered the Nèigé (Grand Secretariat) to propose posthumous titles.
He and others stated:
"If Yǒngchéng is granted this,
future court officials guarding the borders will all cite this to make similar requests,
and the ancestral laws will begin to change from this day forward."
Someone mentioned that Sòng Tóng Guàn (宋童貫) was enfeoffed as a prince.
He replied:
"Guàn was enfeoffed as a prince in the late years of Huīzōng's (徽宗) reign.
How could that be an event of a prosperous era?"
So the matter was dropped.
He often submitted memorials due to natural disasters,
which were sometimes kept by the Emperor,
or sometimes forwarded to the relevant offices,
but often met with obstruction,
leaving him despondent and unfulfilled.
After his fifth year,
he was on leave seven times.
The Emperor always ordered physicians to visit him
and frequently sent eunuchs with gifts.
In the first month of his eleventh year,
he was promoted to Shàobǎo (Junior Guardian) upon completing his tenure.
A month later, he died
at the age of sixty.
He was posthumously granted Tàishī (Grand Preceptor)
and the posthumous title Wénxiàn (文憲).
He served in court for thirty years,
diligently serving the nation,
upholding righteousness and maintaining integrity.
After retiring from public duty, he never discussed state affairs with his children.
When he recommended someone,
he did not let that person know.
He showed no signs of idleness in his private life,
dressed and used objects with frugality,
had no musical entertainment,
and took nothing that was not rightfully his.
He possessed the demeanor of an ancient great minister.
Shāng Lù (商輅),
courtesy name Hóngzài (弘載),
was from Chún'ān (淳安).
He placed first in the provincial examination.
In the tenth year of Zhèngtǒng (正統),
he placed first in both the metropolitan examination and the palace examination.
Throughout the entire Míng (明) dynasty,
he was the only one who achieved first place in all three examinations.
He was appointed Xiūzhuàn (Compiler),
and soon, along with Liú Yǎn (劉儼) and ten others, entered the Dōnggé (Eastern Cabinet) for study.
Shāng Lù had a dignified and imposing appearance,
and the Emperor personally selected him as Zhǎnshūguān (Officer for Presenting Books).
When Chéngwáng (郕王) served as regent,
he was recommended by Chén Xún (陳循) and Gāo Gǔ (高穀) to join the Nèigé (Grand Secretariat),
participating in crucial state affairs.
When Xú Chéng (徐珵) advocated moving the capital south,
Shāng Lù strongly opposed it.
That winter,
he was promoted to Shìdú (Reader).
In the first year of Jǐngtài (景泰), he was sent to welcome the former Emperor (上皇) at Jūyōng (居庸),
and was promoted to Xuéshì (Academician).
In his third year,
Jǐnyī Zhǐhuī Lú Zhōng (錦衣指揮盧忠) ordered a guard to report a conspiracy,
accusing the former Emperor and Junior Eunuch Ruǎn Làng (阮浪) and Eunuch Wáng Yáo (王瑤) of planning to restore the throne.
The Emperor was furious
and had the two (Ruǎn Làng and Wáng Yáo) arrested and imprisoned in the imperial dungeons,
thoroughly investigating the matter.
Lú Zhōng consulted a diviner named Tóng Yín (同寅).
Tóng Yín admonished him with principles of righteousness
and said:
"This is a great ominous sign,
death will not atone for it."
Lú Zhōng was frightened
and feigned madness in hopes of avoiding punishment.
Shāng Lù and the eunuch Wáng Chéng (王誠) said to the Emperor:
"Lú Zhōng is mentally ill,
not to be trusted.
It is improper to heed his wild talk
and harm great human relations."
The Emperor's anger somewhat subsided.
Thereupon, Lú Zhōng was also imprisoned,
charged with other crimes,
and demoted to a service official to atone for his actions.
Wáng Yáo was executed,
and Ruǎn Làng was imprisoned,
and the matter was not pursued to its full extent.
After the太子 (Crown Prince) was replaced,
he was promoted to Bīngbù Zuǒ Shìláng (Vice Minister of War on the Left),
concurrently Zuǒ Chūnfāng Dàxuéshì (Grand Academician of the Left Spring Palace) as before,
and was granted a residence in Nánxūnlǐ (南薰里).
Fertile lands along the frontier were largely encroached upon by powerful magnates.
Shāng Lù requested that these lands be investigated and returned to the military.
Famine victims from Kāifēng (開封) and Fèngyáng (鳳陽) prefectures migrated between Jìníng (濟寧) and Línqīng (臨清),
only to be driven away by officials.
Shāng Lù feared this would lead to unrest
and requested that idle lands in the eight prefectures of the Jī (capital region) be opened for cultivation,
and that grain seeds be provided,
so that all the people would have a place to return to.
When Zhōng Tóng (鍾同) and Zhāng Lún (章綸) were imprisoned,
Shāng Lù exerted great effort to save them from death.
After the compilation of the Huányǔ Tōngzhì (寰宇通志),
he was additionally made concurrent Tàicháng Qīng (Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices).
Jǐngdì was unwell,
and his officials requested the establishment of an heir apparent.
He refused.
As they were about to present their plea again,
Luó Lù snatched up a brush and said:
"Your Majesty is the son of Xuānzōng Zhāng Huángdì,
so the descendants of Zhāng Huángdì should be enthroned."
Those who heard him were deeply moved.
As night fell,
the memorial had not yet been submitted,
but that very night, Shí Hēng and his associates had already welcomed the Grand Emperor back to the throne.
The next day,
Wáng Wén, Yú Qiān, and others were arrested.
Luó Lù was summoned with Gāo Gǔ into the private hall,
where the emperor gently explained the situation to them,
ordering them to draft the imperial edict for the emperor's restoration.
Shí Hēng secretly told Luó Lù
not to include separate clauses for the amnesty.
Luó Lù replied:
"This is the old system;
I dare not change it."
Shí Hēng and his group were displeased
and subtly instigated the censors to impeach Luó Lù for colluding with traitors,
sending him to prison.
Luó Lù submitted a memorial pleading his case, stating that his memorial for the restoration of the heir apparent was in the Ministry of Rites
and could be verified,
but it was ignored.
The eunuch Xīng'ān tried to mitigate the situation slightly,
but the emperor became even angrier.
Xīng'ān said:
"Previously, these people initiated the proposal to move the capital south;
they did not consider where that would leave Your Majesty."
The emperor's anger gradually subsided,
and he then dismissed Luó Lù to commoner status.
However, the emperor often reflected to himself,
"Luó Lù,
he is a scholar I personally selected,
and he once served in the Eastern Palace with Yáo Kuí,"
and could not bear to abandon him.
Due to envious parties,
he was ultimately not reinstated.
In the second month of the third year of Chénghuà, he was summoned to the capital
and ordered to enter the Grand Secretariat with his former rank.
Luó Lù submitted a memorial declining,
but the emperor said:
"The late emperor already knew of your injustice;
do not decline."

He first presented eight matters: diligent study, acceptance of remonstrance, appointment of generals, border defense, reduction of redundant officials, establishment of community granaries, honoring the titles of ancient sages, and expansion of the method for cultivating scholars.
In total, eight matters.
The emperor praised and accepted them.
Regarding his counsel on accepting remonstrance,
he requested that those who had been dismissed for their proposals since the first year of the reign be recalled and reinstated.
Thereupon, Luó Lún, Kǒng Gōngxún, and others were all restored to office.
The following year,
a comet appeared,
and the supervising secretary Dǒng Mín, censor Hú Shēn, and others impeached incompetent high officials,
including Luó Lù.
Censor Lín Chéng criticized Luó Lù for having been involved in the change of the heir apparent,
stating that he should not be employed.
The emperor did not listen.
Luó Lù then requested to be dismissed.
The emperor was angry
and ordered a court investigation of the censors,
intending to impose severe penalties.
Luó Lù said:
"I once requested that censors be treated leniently;
now, if they criticize me and are punished,
what becomes of public opinion?"
The emperor was pleased,
and Dǒng Mín and the others were each given a caning and reinstated.
Soon after, he was promoted to Minister of War.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Minister of Revenue.
After the compilation of the *Sòng Yuán Tōngjiàn Gāngmù* was completed,
he was additionally appointed Grand Secretary of Wényuāngé.
When the Crown Prince was established,
he was given the title of Junior Guardian of the Crown Prince
and promoted to Minister of Personnel.
In the thirteenth year, he was promoted to Grand Secretary of Jǐnshēndiàn.
Luó Lù's character was
upright, simple, and dignified,
broad-minded and tolerant;
but when facing major affairs
and making crucial decisions,
he was resolute and unyielding.
The tenants of Rénshòu Tàihòu's estates disputed land with commoners,
and the emperor wanted to relocate the commoners beyond the frontier.
Luó Lù said:
"The Son of Heaven takes the entire world as his home;
what use are imperial estates?"
The matter was then dropped.
When the Qiánqīnggōng gate caught fire,
the Ministry of Works requested to fell timber from Sìchuān and Húguǎng.
Luó Lù said it would be better to delay slightly
to maintain a sense of warning and awe,
and this was followed.
When the Dàogōng Tàizǐ died,
the emperor was worried about a successor.
Consort Jì had given birth to an imperial son,
who was six years old,
but those around the emperor feared Consort Wàn Guìfēi
and dared not speak.
After a long time,
it finally reached the emperor's ears.
The emperor was overjoyed
and wished to announce it to the outer court,
sending a eunuch to the Grand Secretariat to convey his intention.
Luó Lù requested that the Ministry of Rites be ordered to propose a name for the imperial son,
whereupon the court officials collectively offered congratulations.
The emperor immediately ordered the imperial son to be presented to the court officials.
A few days later,
the emperor again held court in Wénhuádiàn,
with the imperial son in attendance,
and summoned Luó Lù and the other Grand Secretaries.
Luó Lù bowed deeply and said:
"Your Majesty has reigned for ten years,
but no heir apparent has been established;
the world has long awaited this with eager anticipation.
He should immediately be established as Crown Prince
to secure the hearts of those within and outside the court."
The emperor nodded in agreement.
That winter,
the imperial son was thus established as the Crown Prince.
At first,
the emperor summoned the imperial son to remain in the palace,
but Consort Jì still resided in the Western Palace.
Luó Lù feared other troubles,
finding it difficult to speak plainly,
so he and his colleagues submitted a memorial stating:
"The imperial son is intelligent and brilliant,
and the foundation of the nation rests upon him.
Furthermore, with the protection of the Guìfēi,
her grace surpasses that for her own child.
However, external rumors say that the imperial son's mother lives separately due to illness
and has not been able to see him for a long time.
It is advisable to move her to a nearby residence,
so that mother and son can meet morning and night,
while the imperial son continues to be fostered by the Guìfēi,
which would be a great fortune for the imperial ancestral temple and the nation."
Consequently, Consort Jì was moved to Yǒngshǒugōng.
A month later,
the consort fell gravely ill,
and Luó Lù requested:
"Should there be an unfortunate passing,
the rites should be observed with generosity."
He also requested that the Directorate of Ceremonial be ordered to escort the imperial son
to the consort's palace to inquire about her condition and visit,
and to prepare mourning clothes and perform the rites.
The emperor agreed to all of this.
The emperor intended to restore the princely title of Chéng Wáng,
and submitted it for court deliberation.
Luó Lù strongly argued that the king had rendered service to the state,
and his title should be restored,
whereupon the emperor's decision was made.
The emperor constructed the Yùhuánggé north of the palace,
ordering eunuchs to manage its affairs,
with rites equivalent to suburban sacrifices.
Luó Lù and others argued for its cessation.
When a black anomaly appeared,
he submitted eight proposals to avert disaster,
saying: "Regarding the Tibetan Buddhist national preceptors and Dharma kings,
do not indiscriminately bestow seals;
beyond the regular tributes from the four directions,
do not accept playthings;
allow all officials to speak candidly;
dispatch officials from the ministries to review prisoners
to reduce unjust imprisonments;
halt non-urgent constructions;
strengthen military provisions on the three frontiers;
guard the border passes;
and establish a巡撫 (Xúnfǔ) for Yúnnán."
The emperor issued a gracious edict of praise and acceptance.
When the eunuch Wāng Zhí
supervised the Western Depot, he repeatedly launched great persecutions.
Lù, together with his colleagues, enumerated eleven crimes of Wāng Zhí,
saying:
“Your Majesty has entrusted judgment to Wāng Zhí,
and Wāng Zhí, in turn, has delegated his eyes and ears to petty individuals like Wéi Yīng and his ilk.
They all claim to act on secret imperial decrees,
claiming the authority to execute and punish,
arbitrarily wielding power and influence,
and cruelly oppressing good people.
If Your Majesty believes that exposing evildoers and curbing chaos
is an unavoidable necessity,
then why was it so peaceful and uneventful
for several years before this?
Moreover, Cáo Qīn’s rebellion
was provoked by Lù Gǎo’s investigative actions,
which should serve as a warning.
Since Wāng Zhí came into power,
scholars and officials are not secure in their positions,
merchants are not safe on their journeys,
and common people are not secure in their homes.
If he is not removed promptly,
the safety of the empire is uncertain.”
The Emperor grew angry and said:
“How can employing a single eunuch
immediately endanger the empire?
Who sponsored this memorial?”
He ordered Grand Eunuch Huái Ēn to convey his decree,
reprimanding them with great severity.
Lù, with a stern expression, said:
“Regardless of rank, all court officials,
when accused of a crime, require an imperial decree for arrest and interrogation.
Wāng Zhí arbitrarily confiscated the property of京官 (Jīngguān, Beijing officials) of the third rank and above.
Dàtóng and Xuānfǔ
are crucial border strongholds;
their garrisons cannot be absent even for a moment,
yet Wāng Zhí shackled several people in a single day.
Nánjīng,
the fundamental capital of our ancestors,
has its resident high officials,
whom Wāng Zhí arbitrarily arrested.
The close attendants by the Emperor’s side
are frequently replaced by Wāng Zhí.
If Wāng Zhí is not removed,
how can the empire be safe?”
Wàn Ān, Liú Xǔ, and Liú Jí also spoke up,
arguing passionately and eloquently,
and Huái Ēn and others yielded.
Lù looked at his colleagues and thanked them, saying:
“All you sirs have acted for the country in this way;
what more do I have to worry about?”
Coincidentally, the Nine Ministers, including Xiàng Zhōng, also impeached Wāng Zhí,
and that day, the Western Depot was abolished.
Although Wāng Zhí no longer managed the Depot’s affairs,
his imperial favor remained as before.
He slandered Lù, claiming he had accepted a bribe from Commander Yáng Yè,
intending to secure his release.
Lù felt uneasy,
and Censor Dài Jìn, moreover, praised Wāng Zhí’s achievements
and requested the reestablishment of the Western Depot.
Lù then strongly sought to resign.
An imperial edict conferred upon him the title of Shàobǎo
and granted him an imperial escort to return home.
After Lù departed,
scholars and officials bowed their heads even more to serve Wāng Zhí,
none daring to oppose him.
Qián Pǔ, once complaining about not being promoted,
wrote “The Biography of a Bald Woman” to satirize Lù.
Gāo Yáo requested the restoration of Jǐngdì’s imperial title,
and Lí Chún submitted a memorial refuting it,
severely denouncing Lù.
Lù did not contend with any of them,
treating them as usual.
Consort Wàn Guìfēi esteemed Lù’s reputation;
she brought out an image of her father
and asked him to compose a eulogy for it,
sending very generous gifts of gold and silk.
Lù politely declined,
but the envoy informed him of the Consort’s wishes.
Lù said:
“Unless it is an imperial command,
I dare not accept.”
The Consort was displeased,
but Lù remained unyielding.
His gentle yet firm character was like this.
When he retired from politics,
Liú Jí visited him
and, seeing his numerous descendants,
sighed, saying:
“I served alongside you for many years,
and I never saw you unjustly take a single life with your pen.
It is fitting that Heaven rewards you so generously.”
Lù replied:
“Precisely, I dared not allow the court to unjustly take a single life.”
He died ten years later,
at the age of seventy-three.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tàifù
and the posthumous name Wényì.
His son, Liángchén,
was a *jìnshì* in the early Chénghuà reign
and served as a Hanlin侍講 (shìjiǎng, Imperial Lecturer).
Liú Dìngzhī,
courtesy name Zhǔjìng,
was a native of Yǒngxīn.
From a young age, he displayed extraordinary talent.
His father taught him to read,
and he could recite several thousand characters daily.
He was not allowed to compose essays,
but one day, his father happened to see a sacrificial text he had written for the kitchen god,
and was greatly astonished by it.
He placed first in the metropolitan examination of the first year of Zhèngtǒng,
and passed the palace examination,
being appointed as an 編修 (biānxiū, compiler).
When the capital suffered a great flood,
he responded to the imperial summons by presenting ten proposals,
stating:
“Imperial decrees should emanate from great impartiality
and be based on utmost rectitude;
they should not be superficial or frequently changed.
The high officials and attendants
should be summoned frequently
to discern their talents and intentions before promotion or demotion.
The surrendered people scattered throughout the capital region
should be gradually relocated to the south.
County and prefectural posts should be filled by capital officials,
allowing them to rotate in and out,
preventing any imbalance of power between internal and external positions.
The method of recommendation
should not be restricted to officials of the fifth rank and above.
It could emulate the Táng system,
where, when a court official is promoted,
he recommends someone to replace himself,
and the Ministry of Personnel registers their names and selects from them.
The descendants of military officers
should be taught military strategy.
Governors and magistrates should prioritize nurturing the people,
not merely focus on efficiency.
Regarding officials who suffer a bereavement,
I request the permanent abolition of forced recall to office to encourage filial piety.
Buddhist and Daoist monks and nuns who are detrimental to the country must be strictly eliminated.
Wealthy commoners who donate grain and receive official positions,
if they commit an offense, should have their titles revoked.”
The memorial was submitted but withheld.
In the thirteenth year,
his younger brother, Yínzhī, and a fellow villager accused each other,
and the accusation implicated Dìngzhī,
who was imprisoned but later acquitted.
Upon completing his term,
he was promoted to Imperial Lecturer.
When Jǐngdì ascended the throne,
he again submitted ten proposals,
saying: “In ancient times, rulers like Jìn Huái and Mǐn,
Sòng Huī and Qīn,
all suffered from external border breaches
and internal collapse of regional strongholds,
with inadequate rescue efforts,
leading gradually to their displacement.
Never before
has it been like today, where, with the empire so vast,
a hundreds-of-thousands-strong army
attended the former Emperor in the northern desert,
entrusting him to the enemy.
Jìn and Sòng, when they suffered disasters and chaos,
abandoned their homeland,
and, though settling in a corner,
were still able to rally from their decline
to resist an aggressive foe.
Never before has it been like today,
where the enemy, Yěxiān, having achieved victory, advanced directly to the capital,
and our martial
officers and numerous troops
could neither fight valiantly to defeat the bandits
nor negotiate peace to welcome back the imperial carriage,
but allowed them to come and go as they pleased.
The weakness of the nation’s power,
though not reversible overnight,
should surely inspire us to contemplate and vigorously implement methods for self-strengthening.
I, your humble servant, dare to briefly state what I have observed.
In recent battles involving the capital army,
they only knew how to fortify their positions and play safe,
but could not employ ingenious tactics to win.
When the vanguard was defeated, the rear did not come to their aid;
when the left advanced, the right did not
follow.
It would be advisable to emulate the three-tier formation of Wú Jiè and Wú Lín of Sòng,
mutually supporting each other
and providing successive relief.
When confronted by charging cavalry,
axes and swords are essential for controlling
them.
Guō Zǐyí defeated Ān Lùshān’s eighty thousand cavalry
by using a thousand men wielding long sabers, advancing like a wall.
Hán Shìzhōng defeated Wùzhú’s ‘hooked-arm’ cavalry
by using five hundred
People wielding long axes
strike at people's chests
and hack at horses' legs.
Such axes and blades are swift and nimble,
superior to firearms.
The passes of Zǐjīng and Jūyōng,
though called fortifications,
are in reality level roads.
Now, soldiers should be increased,
watchtowers and barriers repaired,
and minor paths and tunnels blocked.
On land,
trenches should be dug crisscross,
named "earth nets."
In water, springs should be dammed to make them deep,
named "water chests."
Alternatively, many elms and willows should be planted
to impede sudden charges,
or many local militia recruited
to
assist the imperial army.
These are all methods practiced in antiquity
that have proven effective.
In the past, emissaries sent
were filled with postmen and porters,
provoking conflict and starting wars;
this was the reason.
Now, officials should be chosen who are
loyal and sincere within,
and skilled at diplomatic
negotiations without, such as Lù Jiǎ or Fù Bì.
They should be selected for their integrity and uprightness,
so as not to disgrace the nation with their words.
During the previous imperial reign, I
requested the relocation of surrendered people from the northern desert.
My counsel was short-sighted
and was not adopted.
Subsequently, taking advantage of national turmoil,
they fled back to their homeland,
and reports of their plundering the imperial
domain have been frequent.
It is advisable, while the great army is gathered,
to relocate them to the south.
This would mix them with Chinese soldiers and civilians,
allowing for their containment and transformation.
Furthermore, it would save on salaries
and reduce transportation costs;
this measure is highly
convenient.
The people of the realm produce grain from agriculture
and cloth from women
to support the army.
Soldiers receive grain from granaries
and cloth from storerooms
to defend the nation.
In the past, soldiers received
grain and cloth from public offices,
but paid monthly fees to private chambers.
Consequently, their hands did not practice methods of attack and thrust,
and their feet did not practice appropriate advances and retreats.
Instead, they transformed goods into merchandise
and turned their skills into crafts,
using the profits from commerce and industry
to cover their monthly fees.
The people's blood and sweat,
and the soldiers' vigor,
were all converted into gold and silver to benefit the corrupt.
If
they were led into battle one day,
it would be like driving sheep to resist wolves;
how could they not be defeated?
Now, this abuse should be thoroughly reformed,
and a new policy of selection and training implemented.
Commanders and generals who cling to old habits
should be executed without mercy.
If this is done, there has never been a case
where military might did not revive.
Governors and magistrates exploiting the people
is like commanders and generals exploiting soldiers.
Strict investigations and examinations should be enforced,
and promotions and demotions carefully handled.
If those who commit corruption share their punishment with their sponsors,
then corrupt officials
will be few,
recommenders will be cautious,
the people will be at peace, and the foundation of the state will be solid.
In ancient times, silk merchants and dog butchers
were all capable of helping achieve imperial undertakings.
Today, Yú Qiān and Yáng Shàn also did not come from military families.
However, generals are able to recognize generals;
it is advisable
to let each recommend those they know,
without restriction by family background.
Dukes, ministers, and attendants
should also be ordered to recommend brave and resourceful men
to serve as military talents.
Thus, recruitment will be broad,
and there will be people to
resist invaders.
In the past, when the Hàn sought restoration,
they relied on Zhūgě Liàng.
When the Southern Sòng resisted the Jīn,
they relied on Zhāng Jùn.
They were all renowned for their loyalty and righteousness,
and their achievements were long
established.
Yet, after one defeat at Jiētíng,
Liàng resigned as Chancellor.
Before victory at Fúlǐ,
Jùn relinquished his position as Grand Marshal.
Why?
When rewards and punishments are clear, generals and soldiers strive.
Yesterday's battle
outside Déshèng Mén
did not report routing strong enemies,
but merely alternating victories and defeats,
and mutual killing and wounding.
Though not enough for punishment,
it was also not enough for reward.
Yet, Shí Hēng
was promoted from Earl to Marquis,
and Yú Qiān from second rank to first rank.
The realm has not heard of their merits,
but only seen their rewards.
How can this not discourage the hearts of loyal and righteous officials?
They should be ordered to return to their old ranks,
not to prematurely advance to new positions.
In the future, when their meritorious fame is established and their ranks and rewards are increased,
it will certainly not be too late.
Indeed, to give and then be unwilling to take back
is a
policy of leniency;
to be promoted and then unwilling to retire
is the fear of loss.
If the emperor
does not practice a policy of leniency,
and the subordinates do not harbor the fear of loss,
then good governance can be
expected daily.
Previously, an Censor's memorial
proposing that high officials enter the palace for policy discussions
was rejected and not implemented.
However, the ruler should hold all authority
and personally decide on important matters.
Matters of
state that were not decided in the morning court
should be brought before the emperor daily in the private palace,
allowing high officials to present their views.
Censors should examine their rectitude and impeach them,
and historians should record them directly in the chronicles
to serve as
a warning and encouragement.
This is an old practice from previous dynasties,
and an established rule of the ancestors.
I wish Your Majesty would follow and implement it.
If only sealed memorials are submitted,
and imperial decrees are transmitted externally,
I fear that partial listening
and sole reliance
will lead to treachery and chaos,
making successful governance difficult.
The virtue of the ruler
should be as clear as the sun and moon to discern right from wrong,
as benevolent as heaven and earth to cover all living beings,
and as courageous as thunder and lightning to wield authority.
Thus,
Sīmǎ Guāng, when advising the sovereign,
spoke of benevolence, clarity, and martial spirit,
which is what the Doctrine of the Mean calls wisdom, benevolence, and courage.
Can wisdom, benevolence, and courage be attained without learning?
Among the Classics,
none is more important than the Shàngshū and the Chūnqiū;
among the histories, none is more accurate than the Tōngjiàn Gāngmù.
If Your Majesty pays attention and reads them,
then regarding rulers,
you will know why Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ
rose,
and why Jié, Zhòu, Yōu, and Lì declined,
and your choices for action will be clear.
Regarding managing internal officials,
you will know of the loyalty of Lǚ Qiáng and Zhāng Chéngyè,
and
also of the wickedness of Chóu Shìliáng and Chén Hóngzhì;
regarding managing court officials,
you will know of the excellence of Xiāo, Cáo, Fáng, and Dù,
and also of the treachery of Lǐ Línfǔ
and Yáng Guózhōng,
and your choices for employment and dismissal will be appropriate.
If this is so, then regarding the virtues of wisdom, benevolence, and courage,
how could it not be a great help?
If, on the other hand, it is merely as before, when Confucian
officials lectured,
reciting their virtues
and avoiding their vices,
it is like fearing pitfalls on the road
and passing them with eyes closed;
how can one avoid stumbling blindly?
how few.
Today, though the empire has suffered a great calamity,
it is still like a golden cup, as yet unbroken.
If one can truly base governance on sagely learning,
your minister believes that the national power can be strengthened,
the enemy's
shame can be avenged,
fraternal bonds can be fully preserved,
and the institutions of the ancestors can be restored.
Why then should one hesitate to do this?
The memorial was presented,
and the Emperor responded with a gracious edict.
Three years later, he was promoted to Xǐmǎ.
The Yěxiān envoys requested the dispatch of a return envoy,
but the Emperor firmly refused.
Liú Dìngzhī's memorial cited precedents to make the request,
the Emperor submitted it to court deliberation,
but ultimately, the envoy was not sent.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Yòu Shùzǐ.
In the year Tiānshùn, he was
transferred to Zuǒ Cānyì of the Tōngzhèng Sī,
still concurrently serving as Shìjiǎng,
and soon after, advanced to Hànlín Xuéshì.
Upon Xiànzōng's ascension,
he was promoted to Tàicháng Shàoqīng,
concurrently Shìdú Xuéshì,
and straight to the Jīngyán.
In the twelfth month of Chénghuà second year, he entered the Wényuān Gé with his current office,
and was promoted to Gōngbù Yòu Shìláng,
concurrently Hànlín Xuéshì.
Jiāngxī and Húguǎng suffered disasters,
and the officials were still collecting taxes from the people.
Liú Dìngzhī said that national granaries were full,
to the point where they could not hold any more,
yet these starving people,
were being forced to pay their rent and taxes.
This was not in keeping with the sagely ruler's concern for the people.
The Emperor was moved by his words,
and immediately ordered the collection to cease.
In the fourth year, he was promoted to Lǐbù Zuǒ Shìláng.
Guì-fēi Wàn had exclusive favor,
the Empress rarely saw the Emperor,
and no heir had yet been born.
The daughter of Chéng Wáng, though of age for marriage, had not yet been wed.
Liú Dìngzhī, due to a prolonged drought,
also brought up these matters.
He further requested that the Jīngyán lectures also include the various writings personally composed by Tàizǔ,
and that heterodox and evil cults be denounced,
so as not to harm governance and squander wealth.
The Emperor kept his memorial and did not issue it.
In the fifth year, he died in office.
He was posthumously granted Lǐbù Shàngshū,
and given the posthumous name Wén'ān.
Liú Dìngzhī was humble, respectful, honest, and straightforward,
and famous in his time for his literary talent.
Once, by imperial decree, he was ordered to compose Yuánxiāo poems,
and a eunuch stood waiting.
He sat at the desk, spread the paper,
and instantly completed a hundred seven-character quatrains.
Another time, in a single day, he drafted nine edicts,
writing without pause.
When someone inquired about the names of Sòng dynasty figures,
he would immediately list their generational order,
as if it were a genealogy,
and people admired his quick wit and extensive knowledge.
The encomium says: When Yīngzōng was restored to the throne,
it was after years of warfare and famine,
the people's spirit had not yet recovered,
treacherous officials were engaged in internal strife,
pillars of the state were tottering,
and affairs both at court and in the provinces were tumultuous.
The situation was indeed extremely critical.
Lǐ Xián, by himself, propped up the situation,
with an abundance of energy.
He encouraged talented individuals
and rectified the legal system.
By the reigns of Xiànzōng and Xiàozōng,
many famous ministers appeared consecutively,
many of whom were recognized and promoted by Lǐ Xián.
What a truly great prime ministerial talent!
Péng Shí and Shāng Lù spoke boldly and upheld righteousness,
dedicating themselves to loyal counsel,
and their actions were purely upright.
In matters of compassion and ritual,
were they not those who truly perfected the ruler's virtue?
Shāng Lù's examination achievements were on par with those of Sòng Wáng Zēng and Sòng Xiáng,
and his moral prestige was also worthy.
Although Lǚ Yuán, Yuè Zhèng, and Liú Dìngzhī did not achieve the highest ministerial rank,
Lǚ Yuán's conduct,
Yuè Zhèng's integrity,
and Liú Dìngzhī's remonstrances,
all have commendable aspects.
Therefore, arranged by their time,
they are also listed in this chapter.

Biographies, Chapter 65: Wáng Áo, Nián Fù, Wáng Hóng, Lǐ Bǐng, Yáo Kuí, Wáng Fù, Lín Cōng, Yè Shèng
Wáng Áo,
courtesy name Jiǔgāo,
was from Yánshān.
In the thirteenth year of Yǒnglè,
the first metropolitan examination for tribute scholars was held at the temporary capital.
The Emperor at that time wished to establish the capital in Běijīng,
and sought to employ scholars from the north.
Wáng Áo achieved top ranks in both examinations,
which greatly pleased the Emperor.
He was specially summoned and granted a meal,
made a Shùjíshì,
and appointed Zuǒ Sìzhèng of the Dàlǐ Sì,
then demoted to Xíngrén.
In the first year of Xuāndé, recommended by Yáng Shìqí,
he was promoted to Yùshǐ.
At that time, when officials committed crimes,
regardless of severity,
they were allowed to transport bricks to resume their duties.
Wáng Áo requested that corrupt officials only be allowed to redeem their guilt,
but not to recover their official positions,
as a deterrent against greed and corruption.
The Emperor followed his advice.
In the fifth year, he served as Circuit Inspector for Sìchuān.
The Mán people of Sōngpān rebelled,
but Dudū Chén Huái, stationed in Chéngdū,
over eight hundred *lǐ* away,
could not control them.
Wáng Áo submitted five advantageous proposals: he requested moving Chén Huái to Sōngpān;
that military provisions for Sōngmào be transported by the combined efforts of farmers during the agricultural off-season,
guarded by government troops,
so as not to unduly burden the common people
and lead to plunder;
that corrupt officials who extorted the people by not issuing permits be made to confess and not conceal their crimes;
that community schools be widely established in prefectures, counties, and native official districts;
that the Huìchuān silver mine, which transported over eight thousand *shí* of rice annually for the military,
causing significant labor and expense in transit,
allow those who committed crimes to redeem themselves by contributing grain.
An edict ordered the relevant offices to deliberate on the details of transporting provisions,
and transferred corrupt officials to Běijīng,
while all other proposals were approved.
Upon Yīngzōng's ascension,
the court deliberated on dispatching civil and military ministers to garrison various regions.
Wáng Áo was promoted to Yòu Qiāndū Yùshǐ,
and, along with Dudū Wǔ Xīng, was sent to garrison Jiāngxī.
He punished corruption and suppressed villainy,
and was both feared and loved by officials and commoners.
In the second year of Zhèngtǒng, he was recalled to the Censorate.
In the fourth year,
bandits from Chǔzhōu plundered Guǎngxìn,
and Wáng Áo was ordered to capture them,
bringing them all back as captives.
In the winter of that year,
Sōngpān Dū Zhīhuī Zhào Liàng deceitfully seized the National Preceptor Shāngbā,
plundered his wealth,
and, with fellow official Zhào Dé, falsely accused him of rebellion.
Shāngbā's younger brother, Xiǎo Shāngbā, was enraged
and gathered a mob to plunder.
Wáng Áo and Dudū Lǐ Ān were ordered to lead an army of twenty thousand to conquer them.
However, the Circuit Censor reported Shāngbā's wrongful treatment,
and an edict instructed them to act according to the situation.
Upon arrival, Wáng Áo released Shāngbā from prison,
sent someone to summon his brother,
pacified the remaining rebels,
and then impeached and executed Zhào Liàng,
exiled Zhào Dé,
and reinstated Shāngbā as National Preceptor.
Sōngpān was thus pacified.
In the sixth year, he replaced Chén Yì in garrisoning Shǎnxī.
For soldiers and commoners who borrowed grain and could not repay it,
he investigated and remitted their debts.
In the winter of the seventh year,
he was appointed Supervising Commander of Military Affairs in Liáodōng.
Wáng Áo noted that military discipline had long been lax,
and when invaders arrived,
the generals and soldiers did not fight vigorously.
Therefore, during a court audience with the generals,
he reprimanded them for dereliction of duty,
and ordered his attendants to drag them out and behead them.
All were terrified and prostrated themselves,
begging to atone for their crimes by fighting to the death.
Wáng Áo then personally traveled the border,
from Shānhǎiguān to Kāiyuán,
repairing city walls
and dredging moats.
He established garrisons every five *lǐ*
and military farms every ten *lǐ*,
ensuring that beacon fires were connected.
He trained generals and soldiers,
increasing their numbers where they were few.
The soldiers and commoners were greatly pleased.
Furthermore, because the border forts were isolated and distant,
and military provisions were scarce,
he enacted local laws
allowing those who committed crimes to redeem themselves with contributions.
Over more than ten years,
this yielded hundreds of thousands of *shí* of grain and cattle and sheep,
making the border prosperous.
In the third year of Xuāndé, he was rated highest in the performance review,
and was promoted to Inspector General of the Ministry of Personnel (Lìkē Jǐshìzhōng).
He corrected errors and omissions,
and was committed to upholding the greater good.
The emperor, considering the heavy responsibilities of the Six Inspectorates (Liùkē),
ordered two officials from each inspectorate to manage its affairs.
Thus, Fù and Jiǎ Quán were jointly placed in charge of the Inspectorate of Punishments (Xíngkē).
When the Censor-in-Chief Gù Zuǒ and others mistakenly condemned seventeen people to death,
Fù impeached them.
The emperor interrogated and reprimanded Gù Zuǒ and his associates.
When Yīngzōng ascended the throne,
Fù memorialized, saying:
"During the Yǒnglè reign,
surrendered people were recruited and accepted,
bound by official titles and ranks,
which exhausted the national treasury,
fostered chaos, and invited danger.
They should be sent back to their native lands.
The young soldiers of the Guards of the Prefectural Army (Fǔjūn Qiánwèi Yòujūn)
were originally selected from commoner families
to attend the Crown Prince.
Now, with deaths and disabilities,
random replacements cause disturbance.
I request that from the twenty-five garrisons (èrshíwǔsuǒ),
one be designated for recruitment and transfer,
to avoid further burdening the people.
Families of soldiers and commoners,
to evade taxes and corvée labor,
have falsely claimed to be Buddhist monks or Daoist priests, numbering tens of thousands.
All those not yet ordained should be sent back to their former professions."
Many of his proposals were implemented.
He was transferred to Assistant Administrator of Shǎnxī (Shǎnxī Zuǒ Cāncèng),
and soon after was ordered to oversee grain storage.
Each year, Shǎnxī wove over nine hundred rolls of silk, gauze, and coarse silk (língjuàn hé).
During the Yǒnglè reign,
an additional fifty rolls of coarse silk were ordered;
Fù requested its abolition.
The stipends and allowances for officials, scholars, and garrison soldiers,
were often reduced due to frontier expenses.
Fù requested their restoration to the former levels.
Some frontier commanders and officers had encroached upon and cultivated fertile land, up to thirty or forty qǐng.
Fù memorialized that they should pay twelve shí of tax per qǐng.
Grand Commandant Wáng Zhēn considered this excessively heavy
and submitted a memorial to dispute it.
The court deliberated and reduced it by two-thirds,
thus making it the fixed amount.
He also calculated annual expenditures
to raise military provisions,
saying:
"My department's annual revenue from the two taxes is 1.89 million shí,
and from garrison grain, over 700,000 shí.
Amidst floods, droughts, and displacement,
and the cancellation of arrears,
roughly one-third is reduced.
Yet annual expenditures amount to over 1.8 million,
with less income than outlay.
Now, the defending officials in the garrisons do not consider the national finances,
and compete to request more troops.
How can provisions be supplied?
I request the reduction of surplus soldiers,
the elimination of worn-out horses,
and the prevention of abuses from encroachment and consumption."
The emperor approved his memorial.
The provision of troops and horses in the three frontier regions
was excessively burdensome.
Soldiers and commoners were exhausted by distant transport,
while powerful rogues exploited the situation for illicit gains.
Fù assessed distances,
set tax levies,
and meticulously audited inflows and outflows.
Long-standing abuses were reformed,
and the people's hardship was greatly alleviated.
When Fù handled affairs,
he was resolute and proactive;
no power or influence could sway him.
His reputation resounded throughout Guānzhōng.
However, his enforcement of the law was overly strict,
and many who sought illicit gains were displeased,
which led to repeated false accusations.
The civil and military officials and commanders in Shǎnxī feared losing Fù
and all submitted memorials detailing his contributions,
thus allowing him to retain his post with a temporary suspension of salary.
After nine years in office,
he was promoted to Right Administration Commissioner of Hénán (Hénán Yòu Bùzhèngshǐ).
Again, there were those who reported Fù's harshness.
The emperor ordered an investigation into the accusers,
intending to punish them.
When it was discovered that the one who supported Fù
was the Junior Mentor Yáng Pǔ,
the emperor's suspicion was dispelled.
When Fù arrived in Hénán,
there was a famine,
and over 200,000 displaced people
openly plundered.
The Grand Coordinator Yú Qiān entrusted Fù with pacifying them,
and all were settled.
After the defeat at Tǔmù,
the frontier roads were obstructed.
The department ordered Fù to transport provisions,
and there were no delays.
He was promoted to Left Administration Commissioner.
In the spring of the second year of Jǐngtài,
he was appointed Right Vice Censor-in-Chief (Yòu Fù Dū Yùshǐ) to patrol Dàtóng,
and oversee military affairs.
At that time, after suffering losses,
the laws were relaxed,
and abuses were particularly severe.
Fù focused on appeasement and stabilization,
memorialized to exempt autumn taxes,
abolished tax collection bureaus in various prefectures and counties,
and suspended the people of Tàiyuán from transporting provisions to Dàtóng.
The Marquis of Wǔqīng Shí Hēng, the Marquis of Wǔ'ān Zhèng Hóng, and the Earl of Wǔjìn Zhū Yīng,
ordered their household members to collect silver and silk from government treasuries

Fù was the first to request an investigation.
An imperial edict pardoned Shí Hēng and others,
but punished their household members.
When soldiers sent by Shí Hēng crossed the pass and reached Dàtóng,
Fù again impeached Shí Hēng for acting arbitrarily.
Shí Hēng admitted his guilt.
Subsequently,
Fù abolished the vegetable households of the Prince of Xiāngyuán's (Xiāngyuán Wángfǔ) estate,
and flogged the kitchen staff who had usurped the position of instructor (jiàoshòu).
He also impeached the supervising eunuch Wéi Lìzhuǎn, Assistant Commander Shí Biāo, and Hénán Administration Commissioner Lín Hòu.
At this time,
Fù's prestige and reputation were renowned throughout the empire,
but powerful families grew increasingly resentful,
and conspired to fabricate charges against Fù.
Yú Qiān, who was then in power,
strenuously protected him.
The emperor also understood Fù deeply,
thus allowing him to pursue his ambitions.
When Lín Hòu vehemently slandered Fù,
the emperor said:
"Lín Hòu resents Fù,
and falsely accuses him.
I am entrusting Fù with frontier affairs;
how could I lightly listen to others' words and humiliate him?"
Lín Hòu was dismissed from office.
In the sixth year,
he went into mourning for his mother,
but was reinstated.
In the seventh year,
Fù memorialized, saying:
"The number of frontier garrison supervising eunuchs (jiānqiāng nèiguān) has increased compared to before.
For example, in Yánghé and Tiānchéng,
there are two eunuchs in one city,
causing extreme disturbance to the people.
I request their reduction and elimination."
The matter was blocked and not implemented.
He also said:
"Emperor Gāo had established a system where
military officers' private crimes could be redeemed,
but only for flogging (chī).
Caning (zhàng) resulted in demotion,
and penal servitude or exile (túliú) always meant banishment to the military.
The law is very clear.
Recently, those who committed embezzlement,
if the offense was light, were reinstated,
and if heavy, only needed to perform meritorious service.
Punishment is insufficient to deter,
and there is no longer any hesitation.
This is all the fault of judicial officials."
The matter was submitted to court deliberation,
and penal servitude and exile could still be redeemed as before,
but only by performing duties in their original guard,
and they could not lead troops.
The Duke of Yīngguó Zhāng Mào and Zhèng Hóng each established estates on the frontier,
and annually conscripted soldiers for cultivation.
Fù impeached them,
and returned the soldiers to their ranks.
In the first year of Tiānshùn, the office of Grand Coordinator was abolished,
and Fù was also dismissed and returned home.
Soon after,
Shí Biāo, bearing old grievances, impeached Fù,
who was arrested and sent to the Imperial Prison.
The emperor questioned Lǐ Xián,
who praised Fù's ability to eliminate abuses.
The emperor said:
"This must be because Shí Biāo was suppressed by Fù
and couldn't act on his private interests."
Lǐ Xián replied:
"Indeed, as Your Majesty says,
he should be exonerated soon."
The emperor instructed Mén Dá to investigate the matter impartially.
There was indeed no evidence,
so Fù was allowed to retire.
The following year,
recommended by court officials,
he was appointed Vice Minister of War of Nánjīng,
but before taking office,
he was reassigned to the Ministry of Revenue
as Grand Coordinator of Shāndōng.
On the way, he heard that a subordinate prefecture was suffering from locusts,
and immediately submitted a memorial to report it.
He was then reassigned as Vice Censor-in-Chief on the left,
but remained Grand Coordinator.
Officials became accustomed to Fù Wēi's prestige,
and were awed and submissive at the sight of him,
while powerful ruffians disappeared.
In the spring of the fourth year,
when the position of Minister of Revenue became vacant,
Lǐ Xián recommended Fù Wēi,
but those around him cleverly obstructed it.
The Emperor said to Lǐ Xián:
"The Ministry of Revenue cannot do without Fù Wēi.
Many people dislike Fù Wēi,
which is precisely why Fù Wēi is worthy."
He was specially summoned and appointed.
Fù Wēi assessed surpluses and deficits,
meticulously managed income and expenditure,
personally oversaw accounts,
so clerks could not deceive him.
For matters involving profit or harm,
his subordinates sometimes dared not take responsibility.
Fù Wēi would say:
"Just carry it out;
I will bear the responsibility.
You gentlemen need not sign your names."
Consequently, the affairs of the ministry were greatly rectified.
When his father passed away, he was ordered to cut short his mourning and resume his duties.
Upon Xiànzōng's ascension,
Fù Wēi, seeing that Shǎnxī was frequently engaged in warfare,
and that those managing provisions were not suitable,
requested the dismissal of the Left Administration Commissioner Sūn Yù,
and the appointment of the Right Administration Commissioner Yáng Xuán, Surveillance Commissioner Lóu Liáng, and Xi'ān Prefect Yú Zǐjùn.
The Minister of Personnel Wáng Āo accused Fù Wēi of overstepping his authority
and requested that he be brought to justice.
Fù Wēi forcefully argued:
"Recommending worthy men is for the country,
not for any private interest."
He then requested to retire.
The Emperor consoled and kept him,
and dismissed Sūn Yù instead.
Shortly after,
he died of a carbuncle.
He was posthumously granted the name Gōngdìng.
Fù Wēi was incorruptible, upright, and firm,
remaining consistent from beginning to end.
He and Wáng Āo were both called famous officials.
In the past,
Yīngzōng once advised Lǐ Xián:
"It is rare to find someone like Nián Fù for the Ministry of Revenue."
Lǐ Xián replied:
"If someday you need to appoint someone to succeed Āo as Minister of Personnel,
it cannot be anyone but Fù Wēi."
However, Fù Wēi was prone to suspicion,
and particularly disliked unsolicited requests.
Cunning subordinate officials
would deliberately do the opposite to test him.
If they wanted something to be carried out,
they would say it was impossible;
if they wanted it not to be carried out,
they would say it was possible.
Fù Wēi was often deceived by them.
Wáng Hóng,
courtesy name Gōngdù,
hailed from Jiāngxià.
His grandfather, Jùnqīng,
was exiled to Hézhōu for an offense
and thus settled there.
Wáng Hóng passed the imperial examination in the fourth year of Zhèngtǒng.
In the eleventh year, he was appointed Investigating Censor of the Ministry of Revenue.
He was magnanimous and possessed integrity,
speaking boldly with a righteous demeanor.
When Yīngzōng was captured in the north,
Prince Chéng presided over court at Wǔmén.
The officials impeached Wáng Zhèn for misleading the country.
Before the impeachment document was fully read,
the Prince ordered them to wait outside for instructions.
All the officials prostrated themselves and wept,
asking for Wáng Zhèn's clan to be exterminated.
Mǎ Shùn, a commander of the Imperial Bodyguard
and a partisan of Wáng Zhèn,
sternly shouted for those speaking to leave.
Wáng Hóng, enraged,
raised his arm, stood up,
grabbed Mǎ Shùn by the hair and shouted:
"You treacherous faction,
your crimes deserve execution,
how dare you still behave like this!"
He cursed and bit Mǎ Shùn's face,
and the crowd joined in, striking him,
killing him on the spot.
The court ranks fell into great disorder.
The Prince, frightened,
quickly rose and entered.
Wáng Hóng led the officials in following the Prince.
The Prince sent the eunuch Jīn Yīng to ask what they wished to say.
They replied:
"The eunuchs Máo Guì and Wáng Chángsuí are also Wáng Zhèn's partisans;
we request that they be brought to justice."
The Prince ordered the two men to be brought out.
The crowd again beat them to death,
their blood staining the palace steps.
At this time,
Wáng Hóng's name shook the realm,
and the Prince deeply respected Wáng Hóng for this.
He also summoned all the remonstrating officials
and offered them extremely strong words of comfort and reassurance.
When the Prince ascended the throne,
and Yěxiān attacked the capital,
Wáng Hóng was ordered, along with Wáng Tōng and Yáng Shàn, to defend the capital city.
He was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief
and oversaw the armies of Máo Fúshòu and Gāo Lǐ.
After the invaders retreated,
an imperial edict ordered him, along with Commander Xià Zhōng and others, to garrison Jūyōng.
Upon arrival, Wáng Hóng
inspected the soldiers and horses,
repaired the strategic passes,
and impeached incompetent generals,
completely renovating the defenses.
In the fourth month of the first year of Jǐngtài,
Lǐ Dé, the eunuch supervising Zhèjiāng, memorialized, saying:
"Mǎ Shùn and others had committed crimes,
but permission should have been sought for their execution;
instead, the officials dared to kill them without authorization.
Had there not been eunuchs supporting His Majesty,
it would have been perilous.
These are all rebellious officials who assaulted the palace
and should not be employed."
The memorial was sent down for court deliberation.
Yú Qiān and others memorialized, saying:
"The former Emperor was captured,
the disaster caused by the traitor Wáng Zhèn;
Mǎ Shùn and others were indeed Wáng Zhèn's confidants.
When Your Majesty supervised the state,
all the officials jointly requested their execution,
yet Mǎ Shùn still dared to reprimand them.
Therefore, the civil and military officials present in court, as well as the palace guards, were aroused by their loyal indignation,
heedless of consequences,
and beat the three men to death.
This is precisely the great principle of the Spring and Autumn Annals for executing rebellious traitors.
Had the imperial carriage been forced to flee
and the treacherous faction still remained,
the nation's safety and peril would perhaps be unknown.
We, your subjects, believe there is no need to question this."
The Emperor said:
"Executing rebellious officials
is to secure the resolve of the multitude.
I already know the loyalty and righteousness of the court officials,
and you, ministers, should not take Lǐ Dé's words to heart."
In the eighth month,
Wáng Hóng returned to court due to illness.
Soon after, he was ordered, along with Assistant Commander Xú Gōng, to oversee grain transport
and manage the Grand Canal from Tōngzhōu to Xúzhōu.
The following year,
the Bureau of Imperial Seals could not find Mǎ Shùn's official plaque,
and Mǎ Shùn's son requested that Wáng Hóng be held accountable.
The Emperor assented.
All the remonstrating officials stated:
"Mǎ Shùn's faction committed grave treacherous crimes,
and the court officials collectively eliminated them;
why concern ourselves with an official plaque?
Moreover, this was not Wáng Hóng's individual act;
if he is held accountable,
loyal officials will be apprehensive."
The previous imperial order was then rescinded.
In the winter of that year,
Gěng Jiǔchóu was recalled,
and Wáng Hóng was commanded to concurrently serve as Grand Coordinator of the three prefectures of Huái, Yáng, and Lú,
and the two subprefectures of Xú and Hé.
He was also ordered to concurrently manage the salt revenue of both Huái areas.
In the first month of the fourth year, due to successive natural disasters
and severe cold in early spring,
he memorialized, saying:
"I request an imperial edict to admonish all officials to earnestly reflect and reform themselves,
lighten punishments and reduce taxes,
cease useless public works,
strictly control rewards for those without merit,
distribute wealth to win the people's hearts,
and cherish the people to strengthen the foundation of the state.
May Your Majesty draw closer to virtuous scholars,
discuss the Way and virtue,
promote gentlemen,
and dismiss petty men,
to appease Heaven's will."
He also admitted his own faults and requested to retire.
The Emperor accepted his words,
and consequently issued an edict for self-reflection
and to seek forthright advice.
Previously,
Fèngyáng, Huái'ān, and Xúzhōu experienced great floods.
Famine victims lay along the roads as far as the eye could see.
Hóng submitted a memorial,
and without waiting for a reply,
opened granaries to provide relief.
At this time, famine victims from Shāndōng and Hénán arrived in droves to seek food,
and the granaries could not supply enough.
Only the Guǎngyùn Granary in Xúzhōu had surplus stores.
Hóng wanted to distribute all of it,
but the palace eunuch in charge of its custody refused.
Hóng went and told him:
"The people will become bandits any day now.
If you do not obey me,
should a change occur,
I will first behead you,
and then ask for my own death."
The palace eunuch, fearing Hóng's prestige and reputation,
reluctantly complied.
Hóng then impeached himself for the crime of acting without authorization,
and consequently stated,
"The stores in Guǎngyùn can only last for three months.
I request that those guilty of crimes punishable by death or lesser penalties
be allowed to redeem themselves by contributing grain in the disaster-stricken areas."
The emperor again ordered Vice Minister Zōu Gàn to swiftly proceed with imperial funds,
allowing him discretion.
Hóng then personally inspected and distributed relief.
When it was insufficient,
he ordered merchant boats along the Huái River, both upstream and downstream,
to contribute rice according to their size,
saving over 1.85 million people.
He encouraged wealthy families to contribute over 250,000 shí of rice,
which was given to 557,000 famine-stricken households.
He distributed over 74,000 oxen and seeds,
allowing 5,500 households to resume their livelihoods.
Over 10,600 households who had migrated from other regions were resettled.
The sick were given medicine,
the dead were provided with coffins,
children who had been sold were bought back,
and those returning home were given travel expenses.
People forgot their hunger,
and praises arose in great measure.
Initially, when the emperor heard of the famine in Huái and Fèng,
he was deeply worried.
Upon receiving Hóng's memorial about opening the Guǎngyùn Granary and impeaching himself,
he joyfully exclaimed:
"What a worthy Metropolitan Censor-in-Chief!
He has saved my people!"
Minister Jīn Lián, Grand Secretary Chén Xún, and others all praised Hóng's achievements.
In October of that year,
he was promoted to Left Vice Metropolitan Censor-in-Chief.
At that time, Jìníng was also suffering from famine.
The emperor sent Minister Shěn Yì with 30,000 liǎng of imperial funds to provide relief.
Yì distributed only 5,000 liǎng,
returning the rest to the imperial treasury.
Hóng impeached Yì for his inadequacy in carrying out his mission,
requesting that the funds be converted into rice for further relief,
which was granted.
In February of the following year, he submitted a memorial stating:
"In recent years, famines have occurred repeatedly,
and the people are in dire straits.
In the late winter and early spring,
snow piled several chǐ deep,
and the Huái River was frozen for over 40 lǐ from the sea,
causing over 10,000 people and animals to freeze to death.
The weak sold their wives and children,
the strong resorted to robbery and plunder,
their paths to food and clothing were cut off,
and they wandered along the roads.
Your Majesty resides high in the palace,
and your ministers are comfortably situated in the court,
unable to witness this.
If they were to see their condition with their own eyes,
there would be none who would not shed tears for them.
Since Your Majesty ascended the throne,
it is not that you have not revered Heaven and loved the people,
yet heavenly calamities and the people's destitution are particularly severe.
I humbly fear that although Your Sacred Virtue has been cultivated, it has not yet reached its peak;
although the Great Principles have been rectified, they have not yet been fully established;
although worthy talents have been employed, their effects have not yet been realized;
although wicked flatterers have been dismissed, their kind has not been entirely eliminated;
benevolence and love have been dispensed, but concrete benefits have not been universally spread;
expenditures have been reduced, but imperial provisions have not been curtailed;
punishments have been lenient, but unjust cases have not been redressed;
public works have been suspended, but the labor of artisans has not ceased;
laws and regulations have been promulgated, but their implementation may have been altered;
taxes have been remitted, but local officials may still be imposing them.
If there is any one of these,
it is sufficient to disrupt harmony and invite calamities.
I humbly hope Your Majesty will cultivate your virtue to renew your governance.
Reverence for Heaven's mandate,
emulation of the ancestors,
rectification of ethical principles,
strengthening of benevolence and righteousness,
abstention from indulgence and pleasure,
and eradication of heterodox doctrines—
these would truly constitute the cultivation of virtue.
Advancement of loyal and upright individuals,
distancing from wicked flatterers,
impartiality in rewards and punishments,
leniency in taxes and corvée,
economy in expenditures,
caution against excessive accumulation,
rejection of tribute,
and cessation of public works—
these would truly constitute practical governance.
If such measures are taken, yet calamities and changes do not cease,
that has never happened."
The emperor praised and accepted it,
issuing an edict for officials, both inside and outside the court, to jointly cultivate virtue and reflect on themselves.
In the sixth year,
Zhào Yùshān, a commoner from Huòshān, claiming to be a descendant of the Sòng dynasty,
misled the populace with sorcery and caused rebellion.
Hóng captured him.
Before and after, he impeached and punished corrupt officials,
and eliminated grain administrators who preyed on the people.
The people greatly praised his convenience.
Upon Yīngzōng's restoration,
the office of巡撫 (Patrolling Grand Coordinator) was abolished,
and Hóng was reassigned as Zhèjiāng Cānzhèng (Provincial Administration Vice Commissioner of Zhèjiāng).
A few days later,
Shí Hēng and Zhāng Jué raised the issue of Hóng's attack on Mǎ Shùn,
leading to his dismissal from office
and banishment to Jiāngxià.
Half a year later,
the emperor found Hóng's memorial in the palace,
and upon seeing the phrases
"rectify ethical principles" and
"strengthen benevolence and righteousness,"
he felt enlightened.
He ordered an official to escort him back to his hometown,
and issued an edict to local authorities to treat him well.
In the fifth year of Tiānshùn,
Bólái raided Zhuānglàng.
Grand Commander Féng Zōng and others went out to suppress him.
Following Lǐ Xián's recommendation,
Hóng was reinstated to his former office,
and, along with Vice Minister of War Bái Guī,
participated in military affairs.
In January of the following year,
Hóng and Zōng repelled Bólái at Hóngyázǐ Chuān.
Guī and the others returned,
while Hóng remained in command.
By winter,
he was recalled.
In the spring of the following year,
he was again ordered to oversee grain transport and govern Huái and Yáng.
When the people of Huái heard of Hóng's return,
they cheered and welcomed him,
continuously for hundreds of lǐ.
Upon Xiànzōng's ascension,
Supervising Secretary Xiāo Bīn and Censor Lǚ Hóng, among others,
jointly recommended Hóng and Lǐ Bǐng, the Patrolling Grand Coordinator of Xuānfǔ, for important positions.
This was sent down for court deliberation.
Minister Wáng Áo and Grand Secretary Lǐ Xián requested to follow their suggestion.
The emperor said:
"Ancient rulers dreamed and divined to seek worthy men;
why can I not follow public opinion today?"
He immediately summoned Hóng to be Minister of War
and Bǐng to be Left Metropolitan Censor-in-Chief.
Upon the issuance of the order,
the court and the populace rejoiced.
At that time, military operations were planned for Liǎngguǎng.
Hóng recommended Hán Yōng as Grand Commander.
Yōng had recently incurred punishment,
and many found it difficult to accept.
Hóng said:
"The Son of Heaven is currently overlooking flaws and employing talent.
If Yōng, being guilty, should not be employed,
was Hóng not also dismissed for a fault?"
Ultimately, Yōng was employed.
Hóng submitted detailed plans for attacking the bandits,
and also stated that generals and commanders on campaigns
should not be allowed to bring private attendants
or falsely claim the initial merits.
He also requested to restore the old quotas for the capital armies
and prohibit powerful families and prominent commanders from arbitrarily deploying imperial troops.
Thereupon, the emperor ordered Hóng, along with six Supervising Secretaries and Censors, to inspect the soldiers of the twelve camps.
Hóng believed that choosing generals was more important than choosing soldiers,
and jointly memorialized to dismiss over eighty officers from the camps,
carefully selecting capable and brave men to replace them.
The Ministry of War was clearing out vacant official positions by pasting yellow slips.
Hóng, along with other high-ranking officials, recommended Reviser Yuè Zhèng and Metropolitan Supervising Secretary Zhāng Níng.
However, Lǐ Xián obstructed them,
ultimately sending the two men out to the provinces
and abolishing the practice of collective recommendation.
Hóng indignantly said:
"Can I still remain here?"
He immediately claimed illness and sought retirement.
The Emperor was then eager to employ Hóng,
issuing a gracious edict to console and retain him,
and daily dispatching doctors to examine his illness.
Hóng's request became even more urgent.
In the ninth month, he was ordered to retire.
Hóng served as Minister for one year,
but spent four months claiming illness.
People regretted that his talents had not been fully utilized.
After he left,
over a hundred recommendations for him came from within and outside the capital,
but all were shelved.
Initially,
Hóng named his residence
"Hàn'ān" (Stalwart Hermitage).
After returning,
he changed it to
"Xiū'ān" (Retired Hermitage).
He shut his door to guests,
and his fellow villagers rarely saw him.
At that time, Lǐ Bǐng was also dismissed and returned home.
He daily went in and out of the neighborhood,
conversing, laughing, and feasting with old friends.
Hóng heard of this and said:
"How can a high-ranking official not maintain his dignity and cherish himself?"
Bǐng heard of this,
and also laughed, saying:
"The so-called high-ranking official,
would he make himself distinct in the countryside,
still acting in an exaggerated and extreme manner to be considered worthy?"
At the time, both were praised.
Hóng lived at home for twenty years,
and passed away in the twelfth month of the first year of Hóngzhì,
at the age of seventy-five.
During the Zhèngdé era,
he was posthumously granted the title of Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
and given the posthumous name Zhuāngyì.
People of Huái erected a temple to sacrifice to him.
Lǐ Bǐng,
courtesy name Zhízhōng,
was from Cáoxiàn.
He was orphaned young and studied diligently.
He passed the imperial examination in the first year of Zhèngtǒng,
and was appointed Judge of Yánpíng.
A powerful local in Shāxiàn falsely accused an honest citizen of being a thief and violated his wife.
Bǐng arrested and prosecuted the powerful local.
The powerful local falsely accused Bǐng,
leading to Bǐng's imprisonment.
Assistant Surveillance Commissioner Hóu Yuè cleared his name,
and the powerful local was sentenced according to law.
From this, Bǐng became well-known.
He was summoned to the Censorate to handle legal cases,
and was about to be appointed Censor. However, Metropolitan Censor Wáng Wén recommended him as an Administrator in his own office,
and he was soon transferred to be a Principal Secretary in the Ministry of Revenue.
The military colonies in Xuānfǔ were occupied by powerful families.
Bǐng went to inspect them,
returned the land to the people,
and requested the abolition of forced levies.
The border people relied on him.
Abuses in the salt tax of the two Huái prefectures were discovered,
and hundreds of people were arrested.
Bǐng went to investigate,
found counterfeit seals,
and those arrested were cleared.
When Emperor Jǐng ascended the throne,
Bǐng was promoted to Director.
In the second year of Jǐngtài, he was ordered to assist Vice Minister Liú Liǎn in supervising military provisions in Xuānfǔ.
He exposed Liǎn's corruption and exploitation.
He was immediately promoted to Right Assistant Censor-in-Chief to replace Liǎn,
and concurrently participated in military affairs.
The military and civilians of Xuānfǔ had suffered numerous bandit raids,
and all their cattle and farming tools had been plundered.
The imperial court dispatched officials to purchase fifteen thousand cattle to give to the garrison soldiers.
People were given money
to buy grain seeds.
Liǎn had given all of them to the imperial troops deployed for defense,
not a single one to the garrison soldiers,
and further suspended their monthly stipends,
while urgently collecting military colony grain.
Bǐng reversed all of Liǎn's policies
and provided generous relief.
All soldiers, except those on city defense,
were allowed to engage in farming.
All levies and requisitions by envoys, eunuchs, and garrison commanders
were reported and abolished,
with official funds used to cover expenses.
He soon submitted six proposals for border defense,
stating:
"Soldiers with wives are considered to have a family,
receiving one dàn of monthly stipend,
while those without have their stipend reduced by four-tenths.
Even if they have parents and siblings but no wife,
they are generally considered to have no family,
which is unjust.
They should all be given an increased stipend."
This was adopted.
At that time, the Yìwàn Treasury in Xuānfǔ was quite well-stocked.
Bǐng further invited merchants to trade salt for grain,
procured and organized military equipment,
and purchased plow oxen for the army.
The army became even more grateful and pleased.
In the winter of the third year, he was ordered to concurrently manage the duties of a Grand Coordinator.
Shortly thereafter,
he was again ordered to be the Supreme Commander of Military Affairs.
Bǐng dedicated himself to border strategy,
disregarding criticism and resentment.
He impeached Regional Commanders Yáng Wén and Yáng Jiàn,
and Grand Commissioner Jiāng Fú for corruption and tyranny,
punishing them.
He reported the eunuch Gōng Shèng, who guarded Dúshí, for disturbing the people with hunting,
and requested his recall.
He also impeached General-in-Chief Jì Guǎng and others for their crimes.
Guǎng slandered Bǐng to defend himself.
The Emperor summoned Bǐng back,
but due to repeated requests from censors,
he ordered Censor Liàn Gāng and Supervising Secretary Yán Chéng to investigate,
and Bǐng was ultimately retained.
At that time, many border people were displaced.
Bǐng extensively encouraged their return,
and those who resumed their livelihoods were granted monthly stipends.
He buried the exposed corpses at Tǔmù and Yāor'érlǐng,
and requested this practice be extended to all garrisons.
For military families whose members were killed or plundered by bandits and had no one to rely on,
the government provided sustenance,
or provided funds to send them back to their hometowns.
He rectified various malpractices.
Among the hundreds of chapters of proposals he submitted,
many were approved and implemented.
Spy reports indicated that bandits were pasturing near the border.
The court deliberated sending Yáng Jùn to join the Xuānfǔ forces to suppress them.
Bǐng said:
"The area beyond the passes is originally the pasturing ground of various tribes;
they are not violating the border.
To ambush and kill them for unearned merit is not something I dare to hear."
So, it was stopped.
The various tribes offered the men and women they had plundered in exchange for rice.
The court deliberated giving one dàn for adults,
and half a dàn for minors.
The tribes generally requested one dàn for all,
but the garrison generals disagreed.
Bǐng said:
"This is to value grain lightly and people heavily."
They were given according to his words.
He asked to be punished for acting on his own authority,
but the Emperor considered him to understand proper conduct.
In the early Tiānshùn era,
the Grand Coordinator position was abolished,
and he was reassigned to supervise grain storage in Jiāngnán.
Initially,
the tax quotas in Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng in Jiāngnán were uneven.
Chén Tài, as Grand Coordinator,
ordered that fields yielding five shēng should be taxed double,
while heavily taxed official lands would not have increased wastage,
thus equalizing the tax burden without decreasing the overall quota.
When Bǐng arrived,
he consistently followed this method.
He was soon arrested for recommending a prefect in violation of regulations,
but the Emperor considered Bǐng's fault minor
and pardoned him.
Reinstated,
he requested that all taxes from the Hǔshù Pass be collected in rice for famine relief.
He also exposed the eunuch Jīn Bǎo for demanding unauthorized levies while supervising the Huái'ān granary.
The imperial censors Lǐ Zhōu and others were demoted,
and [Lǐ] Bǐng submitted a memorial to rescue them.
The Emperor was enraged,
and was about to punish him.
It happened that a court discussion was held to re-establish the Circuit Inspector (Xúnfǔ) position.
The grand ministers recommended Bǐng for his talent,
so he was appointed as Circuit Inspector of Dàtóng.
The Regional Commander (Dū Zhǐhuī) Sūn Yīng had previously been demoted for a crime and returned to his guard post.
The Grand Coordinator (Zǒngbīng) Lǐ Wén falsely cited an imperial edict
to reinstate him.
When Bǐng arrived,
he immediately dismissed him.
When the deputy general Xú Wàng was leading cavalry troops in drill,
Bǐng, considering Wàng incompetent,
relieved him of his office.
Not long after,
the commander of the Tiānchéng garrison, the eunuch Chén Lì, had been ill for a long time.
Bǐng requested to replace him with Luó Fù.
The Emperor accused Bǐng of acting presumptuously,
and had him summoned to the imperial prison.
The Commander Mén Dá thereupon made Bǐng's previous recommendation of a prefect, rescue of the imperial censors, and dismissal of Sūn Yīng, among other things, into charges against him.
The judicial authorities, seeking to comply with the Emperor's wishes,
dismissed him to commoner status.
He lived as a commoner for three years,
then, through the recommendation of a Grand Secretary,
he was reinstated to his former office,
and assumed leadership of the Nánjīng Metropolitan Surveillance Office (Dū Cháyuan).
When Emperor Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief (Yòu Fù Dū Yùshǐ),
and again made Circuit Inspector of Xuānfǔ.
After several months,
he was summoned to be appointed Left Censor-in-Chief (Zuǒ Dū Yùshǐ).
In the first year of the Chénghuà era,
he was in charge of the Grand Assessment (Dàjì),
dismissing and removing corrupt and cruel officials,
more than double the previous number.
In the autumn of the following year,
he was ordered to inspect and reorganize the border defenses from Liáodōng to Dàtóng.
Upon arrival, he immediately impeached the Garrison Eunuch Lǐ Liáng and the Grand Coordinator Wǔ'ān Hóu Zhèng Hóng for military misconduct,
released the Regional Commander Péi Xiǎn from prison,
promoted Commanders Cuī Shèng and Fù Hǎi,
and attacked the enemy at Fènghuáng Shān.
When news of the victory was heard,
an imperial letter of commendation was issued.
Bǐng then went to inspect Xuānfǔ and Dàtóng,
replaced generals,
enforced military discipline, and then returned.
Not long after,
he was appointed Grand Supervisor (Zǒngdū),
and, with Wǔqīng Bó Zhào Fǔ, led five routes out of the frontier,
achieving a great victory.
