The Emperor rewarded him with sheep and wine,
bestowed upon him a qílín robe,
and added the title of Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shàobǎo).
In the winter of the third year,
the Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū) Wáng Ào retired.
When the court recommended his replacement,
the Emperor specially promoted Bǐng to the position.
Bǐng was determined to purify the officialdom.
There were over eight thousand imperial students (jiànshēng) awaiting appointment.
He requested that they be assessed individually,
and several hundred incompetent ones were dismissed,
which caused a flurry of resentment and slander.
The Left Vice Minister (Zuǒ Shìláng) Cuī Gōng, who by long service was due to become Minister,
but Bǐng received it,
was quite displeased.
The Right Vice Minister (Yòu Shìláng) Yǐn Mín had once studied under Bǐng.
Bǐng initially followed his advice,
but later distanced himself from him.
The Expositor (Shìdú) Péng Huá, who was close to the powerful eunuchs,
frequently approached Bǐng with private requests,
but Bǐng did not listen.
All of them harbored resentment against Bǐng.
The imperial censor Dài Yòng requested that officials from the two capitals above the fourth rank, as well as principal and assistant officials in the provinces,
follow the precedent of the Zhèngtǒng era,
and be recommended by a meeting of court officials;
and also that officials of the Ministry of Personnel and other ministries be rotated and transferred regularly,
and not be allowed to monopolize key positions for long,
nor be rapidly promoted.
His words implicated the Ministry of Personnel,
which resisted them.
The Emperor ordered that for officials of the two capitals of the fourth rank and above,
the Ministry of Personnel should list the vacancies
and submit them for imperial decision.
However, the imperial censors Liú Bì, Wú Yuǎn, and Féng Huī argued to return the authority to the Ministry of Personnel.
The Emperor was angry,
and reprimanded those who spoke.
It happened that during the imperial audience and evaluation,
Bǐng dismissed many officials,
many of whom were relatives or old acquaintances of grand ministers,
so a chorus of resentment arose.
And the Grand Judge (Dàlǐ Qīng) Wáng Yì also wanted to remove Bǐng and take his place,
so he conspired with Huá,
instigating the Supervising Secretary (Jìshìzhōng) Xiāo Yànzhuāng, who was from the same locality, to impeach Bǐng on twelve charges,
and also to say that he secretly allied with long-serving imperial censors to gather power.
The Emperor was enraged,
and sent the matter to a court deliberation.
Gōng and Mín immediately said,
"The two of us advised him, but he did not listen."
The Minister of Justice (Xíngbù Shàngshū) Lù Yú and others concurred with their opinion in a memorial.
The Emperor, believing Bǐng had indulged in favoritism and changed the laws,
and failed in his trust,
removed Bǐng's title of Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent and dismissed him to retirement.
Those implicated, Bào Kèkuān and Lǐ Chōng, were transferred to external posts;
Qiū Líng, Zhāng Mù, Chén Mínbì, Sūn Yù, Lǐ Líng, and Liǔ Chūn were all dismissed.
The Emperor ordered Yànzhuāng to name the imperial censors Bǐng had allied with,
but he could not answer.
After a long time,
the names of Bì and the other two were submitted,
and they were all sent to the imperial prison,
then exiled.
Líng and the others were actually well-known good officials,
who were dismissed due to slander,
which caused widespread dissatisfaction.
Líng was particularly indignant,
and repeatedly impeached Yànzhuāng in memorials.
During the court interrogation,
Líng's words were straightforward.
The Emperor was displeased with Yànzhuāng's fabrication and deception,
and demoted him to stationmaster of the Dàníng post-house.
When Bǐng was impeached,
the situation was tumultuous,
and there was even talk of arresting Bǐng.
Bǐng told someone,
"Please thank Mr. Péng for me.
My guilt is solely by imperial decree.
However, do not let me be imprisoned.
If I enter prison, I will certainly not come out,
which I fear would harm the dignity of the state."
Thereupon, he submitted a memorial confessing his faults,
without making any self-defense.
At that time, candidates from all over the country were gathering in the capital for the metropolitan examination.
They indignantly cursed, saying,
"Lord Lǐ is a righteous man of the realm,
falsely accused by corrupt evildoers.
If Lord Lǐ is punished,
we wish to abandon our examination as atonement."
It was only when the Emperor mildly reprimanded Bǐng
that the matter subsided.
When Bǐng departed,
his subordinate officials saw him off,
all sighing sadly,
some even shedding tears.
Bǐng gallantly saluted everyone,
got into his carriage, and left.
After Bǐng left,
Gōng became Minister.
Bǐng was sincere and upright,
maintaining his integrity whether in adversity or prosperity,
and, like Wáng Hóng, bore great prestige.
He remained at home for twenty years,
and though over ten memorials recommending him were submitted from inside and outside the court,
he ultimately did not return to office.
He died in the second year of Hóngzhì.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent.
Later, he was given the posthumous name Xiāngmǐn.
His sons Cōng, Míng, Zhì,
and grandson Bāngzhí,
all passed the provincial examination.
Cōng was
Magistrate of Nángōng.
He was dismissed and returned home due to Yànzhuāng's impeachment.
Míng was
Assistant Prefect (Tóngzhī) of Jiànníng Prefecture.
Zhì was
Prefect (Zhīfǔ) of Nányáng Prefecture.
Bāngzhí was
Assistant Prefect of Níngbō Prefecture.
After Yànzhuāng was demoted,
he was appointed to Dàníng County,
and was killed by bandits for extorting taxes.
Yáo Kuí,
courtesy name Dàzhāng,
was a native of Tónglú.
He was the grandson of the filial son Bóhuá.
He passed the imperial examination in the seventh year of Zhèngtǒng,
coming first in both the provincial and metropolitan examinations.
The following year, he was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Personnel (Lì Kē Jìshìzhōng),
and presented eight proposals on current governance.
He also said:
"The purpose of the relief granaries (yùbèi cāng) is to support impoverished people.
However, the lǐjiǎ, fearing that the poor could not repay,
often concealed the facts and did not report them.
This led to the poor borrowing from wealthy households,
repaying them double the amount.
As soon as the harvest was over,
they quickly ran out of supplies.
Thus, the poor suffered hunger in bad harvest years,
and also suffered hunger in good harvest years.
I request that all local officials be ordered
to distribute grain twice a year,
and personally investigate,
giving priority to the poorest."
The Emperor immediately ordered it to be implemented.
When Jǐngdì was overseeing the state,
all the high officials discussed and urged him to ascend the throne,
but it was not yet decided.
They asked the censors about it,
and Kuí said:
“The court appoints high officials
precisely for the sake of the state;
why all this discussion?”
The decision was then made.
When Yěxiān approached the capital,
Kuí urgently requested the dispatch of troops from Xuānfǔ and Liáodōng to defend it.
In the first year of Jǐngtài, he was exceptionally promoted to Right Vice Minister of the Ministry of Justice in Nánjīng.
In the fourth year, he was transferred to the Ministry of Rites,
and received an imperial edict to inspect officials in Yúnnán.
Upon his return to court,
he remained in the Ministry of Rites.
When Jǐngdì became unwell,
Minister Hú Yíng was on leave,
but Kuí strongly urged him to rise,
and together with other officials, they jointly petitioned for the restoration of the Crown Prince.
This was not granted.
The next day,
Kuí wanted to lead the hundred officials to kneel at the palace gate to plead,
but Shí Hēng and his ilk had already enthroned the Emperor Emeritus,
and dismissed Kuí to the Ministry of Rites in Nánjīng.
Yīngzōng greatly admired Kuí,
and upon hearing of the discussion to restore the Crown Prince,
he recalled him by post-horse,
and promoted him to Left Vice Minister.
In the second year of Tiānshùn, he was transferred to the Ministry of Personnel.
A certain prefect was ruined by corruption,
and bribed Shí Hēng to seek reinstatement,
but Kuí firmly opposed it,
and so it was stopped.
In the seventh year, he replaced Shí Mào as Minister of the Ministry of Rites.
In the second year of Chénghuà,
the Emperor followed the suggestion of Minister Lǐ Bīn Yán,
ordering scholars from the Southern Metropolitan Region, Zhèjiāng, Jiāngxī, and Fújiàn
to pay grain for disaster relief to be admitted to the Imperial Academy.
Kuí memorialized to stop this.
In the fourth year, due to repeated occurrences of disasters and unusual phenomena,
he memorialized requesting
“to treat the six palaces with equal love,
to expand the succession.
I beg to cease the newly built pagoda compound in Xīshān,
and to banish the followers of Āchìlǐ.
Diligently attend the imperial lectures,
and decide all government affairs.
Associate with gentlemen,
distance oneself from petty individuals,
economize expenses,
cherish honorable appointments,
and in all matters of dress, food, speech, and conduct,
strictly follow the established precedents of the ancestors,
to avert the will of Heaven.”
He further said
“It is sufficient to maintain the initial policies of Chénghuà today.”
The Emperor responded with a gracious edict.
His other ten requests
were all immediately approved.
When Empress Dowager Cíyì passed away,
there was an imperial instruction to discuss a separate burial,
but the Grand Secretaries opposed it,
and it was sent down for court deliberation.
Kuí said:
“The Empress Dowager was matched with the late Emperor for over twenty years;
joint burial and enshrined worship,
the rites are all established.
Any carelessness
would go against the late Emperor’s wishes,
and harm the virtue of the Empress Mother.
If in the future there are those who argue for alteration based on the rites,
what then of Your Majesty’s filial virtue?”
His memorial was submitted three times,
and he further led all officials to kneel at Wénhuá Mén crying out in remonstrance.
The Emperor then firmly requested it from Empress Dowager Zhōu,
and it was finally done according to the rites.
Later, when Xiàozōng saw Kuí’s and Péng Shí’s memorials,
he said to Liú Jiàn:
“The loyal and honest high officials of the previous reign were truly like this for the state.”
When a comet appeared,
the censors repeatedly impeached Kuí,
and Kuí sought to resign,
but it was not granted.
The Emperor trusted the Tibetan monks,
and there were those who were enfeoffed as Fǎwáng and Fózǐ,
whose clothing and possessions were excessively ostentatious.
Vicious individuals admired them,
and competed to become their followers.
Kuí strongly remonstrated,
and their influence somewhat diminished.
In the fifth year, he replaced Cuī Gōng as Minister of the Ministry of Personnel.
When snow fell out of season,
he presented twenty criticisms of current affairs.
In the seventh year, he was granted the title of Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
When a comet appeared again,
he once more joined with other officials to present twenty-eight matters,
the main points being to stop solicitations,
prohibit imperial procurements,
show compassion to soldiers and artisans,
reduce corvée labor,
pacify displaced people,
and prioritize frugality in superfluous expenditures.
The Emperor adopted many of these.
In September of the following year,
the Southern Metropolitan Region and Zhèjiāng suffered severe floods.
Kuí requested that court officials jointly seek methods to bring peace to the people and mitigate calamities.
Whenever disasters or anomalies occurred,
he would request the Emperor to provide relief,
with worry evident on his face.
He died the following year,
and was posthumously granted the title of Junior Guardian,
and the posthumous name Wénmǐn.
Kuí’s talent and capacity were vast and far-reaching,
his outward appearance and understanding were clear.
Matters in court discussions that remained undecided,
Kuí would resolve with a single word.
When he was in the Ministry of Personnel,
he paid close attention to talent,
and did not avoid relatives or old friends.
Initially,
when Wáng Áo was in the Ministry of Personnel,
he deliberately suppressed southerners,
which northerners appreciated.
When Kuí took office,
he favored southerners,
and their recommendations were often competent.
His son, Bì,
from a *jìnshì* degree, successively served as a director in the Ministry of War.
Xiàng Zhōng impeached Wāng Zhí,
and Bì was involved in his plan.
Wāng Zhí framed Xiàng Zhōng,
and Bì was also imprisoned,
then demoted to co-prefect of Sīmíng in Guǎngxī,
but returned home pleading illness.
Kuí’s younger cousin, Lóng,
passed the *jìnshì* examination with Kuí,
and was appointed principal in the Ministry of Justice,
then successively served as Left Administration Commissioner of Fújiàn.
Liú Ràng, the Right Administration Commissioner, passed the examination in the same year but they could not get along.
Liú Ràng was coarse and violent,
and Lóng also lacked integrity.
At the beginning of Chénghuà, they came for an audience,
and Wáng Áo dismissed both of them.
Wáng Fù,
courtesy name Chūyáng,
was from Gù'ān.
He became a *jìnshì* in the seventh year of Zhèngtǒng.
He was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Justice.
His voice and appearance were grand and impressive,
and he was skilled at making presentations.
He was promoted to Grand Secretariat Councillor.
When Yěxiān invaded the capital,
he invited high officials to go out and welcome the Emperor Emeritus.
Everyone was afraid to go,
but Fù requested to go.
He was then moved to Right Grand Secretariat,
acting as Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites,
and accompanied by Zhào Róng, a drafter in the Grand Secretariat.
The enemy openly held their swords and flanked them,
but Fù and others were not intimidated.
Upon returning, he resumed his duties in the Grand Secretariat,
and was again promoted to Grand Secretariat Administrator.
During the Tiānshùn period,
he successively served as Left and Right Vice Ministers of the Ministry of War.
In the first year of Chénghuà,
Fáng Néng, the regional commander of Yánsuí, memorialized about pursuing and attacking the tribes in Hétào,
and an imperial edict praised and rewarded him.
Fù, however, argued that pursuing battle over seven hundred *lǐ* was not advisable,
and feared that it might incite conflict through a fluke victory,
and requested an imperial edict to caution and admonish,
which the Emperor approved.
He was promoted to Minister.
Chén Yù, a chiliarch of the Imperial Bodyguard,
was originally a painter.
Upon his death,
his nephew Xī requested to inherit the position of centurion.
Fù said:
“Although the inheritance was ordered by the late Emperor,
it was not due to military merit,
and should not be permitted.”
So it was stopped.
When Máorǐhái (毛里孩) harassed the borders,
[Fù (復)] was again ordered to inspect the border defenses of Shǎnxī (陝西).
From Yánsuī (延綏) to Gānsù (甘肅),
he surveyed the terrain
and submitted a memorial, stating:
“Yánsuī (延綏) begins on the east bank of the Yellow River
and extends west to Dìngbiān (定邊) Camp,
connecting with Huāmǎchí (花馬池) in Níngxià (寧夏),
a winding stretch of over two thousand *lǐ* (里).
The strategic passes are all in the interior,
while outside the border there is no protective screen,
relying only on signal towers and forts for defense.
The army is stationed in the interior,
while the populace, conversely, resides outside.
Once the enemy enters the territory,
before the government troops can deploy,
the people will have already been completely plundered.
Furthermore, to the southwest, extending to Qìngyáng (慶陽),
a distance of over five hundred *lǐ* (里),
the beacon fires do not connect.
When invaders arrive,
the people remain unaware.
The signal towers to the north
are mostly spread far apart,
which is not a long-term strategy for border defense.
I request that nineteen forts, such as Fǔgǔ (府谷) and Xiǎngshuǐ (響水),
be relocated to critical border areas.
And from Ānbiān (安邊) Camp to Qìngyáng (慶陽),
and from Dìngbiān (定邊) Camp to Huánzhōu (環州),
a signal tower be built every twenty *lǐ* (里),
totaling thirty-four.
Trenches and walls should be constructed according to the terrain,
so that signals can be heard one after another,
making defense easier.”
Regarding his strategy for Níngxià (寧夏),
he said:
“South of Língzhōu (靈州) in the central route,
there were originally no signal posts.
On the eastern and western routes,
the camps and forts are far apart and isolated,
with no communication between them,
allowing the enemy to frequently penetrate deep.
I also request that signal towers be established as in Yánsuī (延綏),
totaling fifty-eight towers.”
Regarding his strategy for Gānsù (甘肅),
he said:
“Yǒngchāng (永昌), Xīníng (西寧), Zhènfān (鎮番), and Zhuānglàng (莊浪) all have defensible terrain.
However, Liángzhōu (涼州) is flat and open on all sides,
making it easiest for the enemy to enter.
Moreover, with convenient water and grass,
they often lightly stay there for a year.
Dispatching distant reinforcements
leads to exhausted and demoralized troops,
rendering them incapable of providing timely aid.
I request that within the five guards of Gānzhōu (甘州),
each contribute one thousand households,
to establish a central guard in Liángzhōu (涼州),
and issue them seals of authority.
The military personnel for these five units
should be selected from the remaining men within the five guards.
By both farming and training,
they will have resources for war and defense,
and military might will naturally be boosted.”
He also said:
“During the Hóngwǔ (洪武) reign, Dōngshèng (東勝) Guard was established,
and its western route, directly leading to Níngxià (寧夏),
was fully equipped with beacon towers.
Since the early Yǒnglè (永樂) era,
when the northern invaders retreated far away,
the army was moved to Yánsuī (延綏),
and the Yellow River defense was abandoned.
If the troops were strong and provisions ample,
adhering to the ancestral system,
holding the Yellow River,
would be a perfectly safe strategy.
Now, with the Hétào (河套) region not yet pacified,
how can we hastily revert to that?
However, improvements should still be made in accordance with the times.
The generals and officers in Yánsuī (延綏) are fewer than in other garrisons,
making deployment insufficient.
I request an increase of two assistant generals (*cānjìang*)
to command nine thousand troops,
stationing them in strategic locations
to mutually assist and connect,
which is today's urgent task.”
The memorial was submitted,
and all proposals were adopted.
His subsequent border constructions
were mostly appropriate to the circumstances.
Upon his return to court,
some critics argued that military administration was no longer his strong suit.
He was specifically ordered to be replaced by Bái Guī (白圭)
and reassigned to the Ministry of Works.
He meticulously adhered to laws and regulations,
and his reputation surpassed that of his time in the Ministry of War.
At that time, an imperial eunuch requested to repair the northwest corridor of the imperial city.
Fù (復) argued for delaying the project.
The Supervising Secretary (*gěishìzhōng*) Gāo Fēi (高斐) also stated that with frequent disasters and calamities,
it was inappropriate to employ ten thousand people in a useless project.
The emperor disallowed both requests.
The eunuch who commanded the Tengxiang (騰驤) Four Guards
requested the issuance of padded jackets (*pàng'ǎo*) and trousers (*xiékù*).
Fù (復) firmly refused,
saying:
“The court established this system
originally for soldiers on campaign,
so they could set off on an appointed day
without the trouble of sewing.
For the capital army, winter clothes and cotton cloth are provided annually;
this is an established precedent.
How can it be changed?”
When the Great Dhamma King (*Dà Yìng Fǎ Wáng*) Zhásí Bā (劄實巴) died,
a eunuch requested to build a temple and a pagoda.
Fù (復) responded:
“The Great Ci Dhamma King (*Dà Cí Fǎ Wáng*) only built pagodas,
never temples.
It is inappropriate to create this precedent now.”
Thus, only the construction of a pagoda was ordered,
though four thousand soldiers were still dispatched for the labor.
In the fourteenth year, he was promoted to Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince (*tàizǐ shàobǎo*).
Fù (復) was fond of antiquity and devoted to learning.
He maintained integrity and frugality,
was straightforward with people,
and grasped the bigger picture in official duties.
He served in the Ministry of Works for twelve years.
When disasters occurred,
censorial officials stated he was old and infirm,
and requested his retirement.
This was not granted.
Two months later,
Wāng Zhí (汪直) instigated censorial officials to impeach Fù (復), as well as Zōu Gàn (鄒幹) and Xuē Yuǎn (薛遠).
An imperial decree was then issued,
ordering all of them to retire and return home.
After a long time,
he died.
He was posthumously granted Grand Guardian of the Crown Prince (*tàizǐ tàibǎo*)
and given the posthumous name Zhuāngjiǎn (莊簡).
Lín Cōng (林聰),
courtesy name Jìcōng (季聰),
was from Níngdé (寧德).
He passed the imperial examination in the fourth year of Zhèngtǒng (正統).
He was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Personnel (*Lìkē Gěishìzhōng*).
In the first year of Jǐngtài (景泰), he was promoted to Chief Supervising Secretary (*Dū Gěishìzhōng*).
At that time, there were many difficulties,
and Cōng (聰) spoke out boldly on matters,
concealing nothing.
When the household of the eunuch Jīn Yīng (金英) committed a crime,
the Censor-in-Chiefs (*Dū Yùshǐ*) Chén Yì (陳鎰) and Wáng Wén (王文) handled it,
but did not punish Jīn Yīng (金英).
Cōng (聰), along with his colleagues, impeached Chén Yì (陳鎰) and Wáng Wén (王文) for fearing power and condoning evil,
and also implicated Censors (*Yùshǐ*) Sòng Lì (宋瑮) and Xiè Jū (謝琚),
all of whom were imprisoned.
Later, they were reinstated.
Cōng (聰) again stated that Sòng Lì (宋瑮) and Xiè Jū (謝琚) were unfit for disciplinary duties,
and the two were eventually transferred to external posts.
The eunuch Shàn Zēng (單增), who supervised the capital garrisons, was favored,
and officials who slightly offended him were often humiliated.
His household slaves committed murder in broad daylight,
seized people's property,
and encroached upon merchant taxes.
Cōng (聰) exposed his wrongdoings,
and he was sent to the imperial prison,
but later pardoned.
After this, Shàn Zēng (單增) dared not act recklessly.
In the spring of the third year,
he memorialized, stating:
“My duty is to investigate judicial matters.
The distant relatives, a hundred strong, of the demonic monk Zhào Cái (趙才)
should not have been implicated by law,
yet they were rounded up and brought to the capital.
As for the rebel Wáng Yīng (王英),
his brother was unaware of his actions,
and his family members should not have been arrested by law,
yet they were all exiled.
Although they were eventually pardoned,
their initial suffering was already unbearable.
The Governor (*xúnfǔ*) of Húguǎng (湖廣), Cài Xī (蔡錫), for impeaching Vice Commissioner (*fùshǐ*) Xíng Duān (邢端),
was in turn slandered,
and imprisoned for a year,
while Xíng Duān (邢端) remained in his post as before.
Assistant Minister (*Shìláng*) Liú Lián (劉璉) embezzled provisions while supervising their transport;
this is not without guilt,
but compared to Shěn Gù (沈固) and Zhōu Chén (周忱) who embezzled tens of thousands,
which is more serious?
Liú Lián (劉璉) was imprisoned and ordered to repay,
while Shěn Gù (沈固) and Zhōu Chén (周忱) were not questioned.
The offender Xú Nán (徐南) and his son, the Secretariat Drafter (*zhōngshū shèrén*) Yí (頤),
were both implicated as Wáng Zhèn's (王振) partisans and deserved execution,
yet Xú Nán (徐南) was sentenced to capital punishment,
while Xú Yí (頤) was only dismissed from office.
All of these are instances of unfair punishments.”
The emperor agreed with him.
Xíng Duān (邢端) was imprisoned,
Liú Lián (劉璉) was released,
and Xú Nán (徐南) also had his death sentence commuted
and was dismissed from office.
When the Eastern Palace was renovated,
Cōng had a dissenting opinion,
and was demoted to Assistant Director of the Spring Palace.
In the spring of the fourth year,
Scholar Shāng Lù stated that Cōng was courageous in speaking out
and should not be relegated to an idle position.
So, he was reinstated as Grand Supervising Secretary of the Personnel Department.
He memorialized that "being compelled to end mourning early" was not a normal practice
and requested that this practice be permanently abolished.
The Emperor accepted it.
Initially,
during the Zhèngtǒng reign,
the silver mines in Fújiàn had excessive quotas,
which the people could not bear.
Cōng feared that this would lead to unrest
and requested that the quotas be reduced.
At the time, his advice was not adopted,
and indeed, a great rebellion soon broke out.
By this time, he again strongly spoke about its harm,
and finally, a reduction and exemption were granted.
In the third month of the fifth year, due to calamities and unusual phenomena, he, along with his colleagues, submitted a memorial outlining eight matters,
citing various texts on the Five Phases,
totaling several thousand words.
The main points were that abstaining from excessive pleasures
and being careful with desires
were the foundation of cultivating virtue,
and that in governing human affairs,
it was crucial to promote the worthy and dismiss the wicked.
The Marquis of Wǔqīng, Shí Hēng, and Commander Zhèng Lún, though enjoying generous salaries,
frequently petitioned for land,
with Centurion Táng Xìng acquiring over 1,200 qǐng;
such requests should be restricted.
Other recommendations included abolishing Daoist rituals and offerings,
reducing the number of monks and Daoist priests,
being cautious with judicial punishments,
prohibiting the private employment of soldiers,
and reducing the number of rotating artisans.
All these deeply addressed the abuses of the time.
The Emperor adopted many of them.
Earlier,
Minister of Personnel Hé Wényuān had been imprisoned due to Cōng's words
and subsequently retired from office.
At this time,
the Ministry of Personnel appointed Vice Commissioner Luó Chí as Surveillance Commissioner,
and Administration Commissioner Lǐ Lù and Assistant Commissioner Chén Yǒng as Provincial Administration Commissioners.
Cōng submitted a memorial disputing these appointments,
and also stated that Wáng Yīng, the Provincial Administration Commissioner of Shānxī, was old
and should be dismissed.
Chí and the others were then returned to their former posts,
and Yīng retired.
Censor Bái Zhòngxián, due to his long service,
was promoted to Surveillance Commissioner of Guǎngdōng.
Cōng stated that Zhòngxián was seeking promotion improperly
and should not be promoted extraordinarily,
so he was transferred to Prefect of Zhènjiāng.
Officer Wú Chéng of the Ministry of War gained a position in the Ministry of Personnel through irregular means.
Cōng impeached him,
and he was consequently transferred to the Ministry of Works.
All bureaus feared Cōng's integrity and strictness;
none dared to disobey
what Cōng said,
especially the Ministry of Personnel.
The Grand Secretariat and all the censors also disliked Cōng's frequent discussions and proposals,
finding them undesirable.
In the winter of that year,
Cōng's nephew Chén Hé became an instructional official.
He wished for a nearby post to conveniently care for his parents,
and Cōng spoke on his behalf to the Ministry of Personnel.
Censor Huáng Pǔ and others then impeached Cōng for coercing the Ministry of Personnel;
they also alleged that his earlier impeachment of Zhòngxián was to benefit his fellow townsman, Administration Commissioner Fāng Yuán,
as he wished to take Zhòngxián's office and give it to him;
and that he had a grudge against Wú Chéng
and arbitrarily impeached him;
and that Fújiàn Administration Commissioner Xǔ Shìdá had asked Cōng for promotion,
and Cōng had recommended Shìdá as fit for a巡撫 (xúnfǔ) (grand coordinator).
They also impeached Minister Wáng Zhí for flattering Cōng.
The memorial was sent down for court investigation,
and he was convicted of arbitrarily controlling personnel selection,
sentenced to execution.
Gāo Gǔ and Hú Yíng strongly interceded for him.
The Emperor also knew Cōng's character,
and only demoted him to Instructor of the National Academy.
When Emperor Yīngzōng was restored to the throne,
he was extraordinarily appointed Left Vice Censor-in-Chief
and sent out to relieve famine in Shāndōng,
saving 1.45 million famine victims.
Upon his return, he was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief
and tasked with apprehending salt smugglers in the Jiāng and Huái regions.
Using his discretionary powers,
he captured and executed several ringleaders,
and dispersed all the others,
then memorialized to expose the commanders who had accepted bribes from the smugglers.
He was recalled to office during his mourning for his mother,
and declined twice.
It was not permitted.
In Tiānshùn 4 (1460),
Cáo Qīn rebelled.
Soldiers wantonly killed,
even cutting off the heads of beggars to report merits,
and townspeople dared not leave their homes.
Cōng took charge of the Censorate,
and urgently ordered that captured rebels must be brought in alive,
and that indiscriminate killing must cease.
The Jǐnyī Wèi officers resented Qīn for killing Commander Lù Gǎo,
and arrested all of Qīn's relatives and acquaintances.
Centurion Gōng Suíróng and his maternal uncle Hé Sān were also among those imprisoned.
People knew they were innocent
but dared not speak up.
Cōng distinguished their cases and released them.
Many others were also cleared of wrongdoing.
In the winter of the seventh year,
due to a prisoner's suicide in the Ministry of Justice,
the Supervising Secretaries impeached the lax discipline,
and he and Censor-in-Chief Lǐ Bīn were both imprisoned.
They were soon released.
In Chénghuà 2 (1466),
there was famine in Huáinán and Huáiběi,
and Cōng went to inspect.
He memorialized to loan grain from the tribute grain and surplus grain from Jiāngnán to relieve the famine,
and the people revered him as they did in Shāndōng.
The following year, he, along with Minister of Revenue Mǎ Áng, reorganized the capital garrisons
and was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief.
In the seventh year, he replaced Wáng Yuè as Grand Coordinator of Dàtóng.
After more than a year,
he fell ill and retired.
Two years later,
he was recalled to his former office to preside over the Southern Censorate.
Previous presidents of the Censorate mostly disliked censors speaking out,
but Cōng alone encouraged them.
Some blamed Cōng,
who said:
"If I myself do not speak,
and also forbid others from speaking,
is that acceptable?"
In the autumn of the thirteenth year,
he was summoned and appointed Minister of Justice,
and soon after, given the additional title of Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
Cōng was recalled due to his old virtues,
maintained the overall principle,
upheld public opinion,
and was revered without being severe,
and his prestige at the time grew even greater.
In the fifteenth year, he, along with Eunuch Wāng Zhí and Marquis of Dìngxī Jiǎng Wǎn, investigated the failures in Liáodōng.
Zhí protected Grand Coordinator Chén Yuè,
and Cōng could not contend with him,
which commentators regretted.
In the eighteenth year, he requested to retire but was not permitted,
and died in office
at the age of sixty-eight.
He was posthumously granted the title of Junior Guardian
and given the posthumous name Zhuāngmǐn.
When Cōng served as a remonstrating official,
he was solemn and unapproachable.
In reality, he was sincere, gentle, and amiable,
and did not engage in unconventional behavior.
Therefore, the unworthy feared him,
while the worthy were often pleased to approach him.
During the Jǐngtài era,
scholars and officials eagerly debated matters,
and there were many upright officials in the court,
with Cōng and Yè Shèng leading the way.
Yè Shèng,
courtesy name Yǔzhōng,
was from Kūnshān.
He became a *jìnshì* in Zhèngtǒng 10 (1445).
He was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of War.
After the army was defeated at Tǔmù,
many generals fled back.
Shèng, leading his colleagues, requested that those who had failed in accompanying the Emperor be punished first,
and also that generals be selected and troops trained
to avenge the defeat.
When Prince of Chéng ascended the throne,
there was a customary reward.
Shèng declined, citing that the sovereign and father were humiliated.
It was not permitted.
Yěxiān 迫都城,
asked to disband the Imperial Household Department's artisans who were preparing for military campaigns.
He also requested that officials store grain and provisions for soldiers,
and send out disbanded troops to collect weapons from Tiānjīn,
to bolster external support.
Within three days,
seven or eight memorials were submitted,
many of which hit upon opportune strategies.
When the invaders retreated,
he was promoted to Dū Gěishìzhōng.
He said:
"The way to encourage and punish
lies in clear rewards and penalties.
Those who dared to fight, like Sūn Táng,
and those who died in service, like Xiè Zé and Hán Qīng,
should be rewarded.
Others who were lax in defense
or ineffective in responding to difficulties
should all be punished."
Grand secretaries Chén Xún and others discussed recalling Luó Tōng, the Dū Yùshǐ guarding Jūyōng,
and also keeping Dūdū Yáng Hóng of Xuānfǔ to manage the capital garrisons.
Shèng vehemently argued:
"Regarding today's affairs,
border passes are the most urgent concern.
In the past, if Duóshí and Mǎyíng had not been abandoned,
how would the emperor have been captured at Tǔmù?
If Zǐjīng and Báiyáng had not been broken,
how would the invaders have reached the capital city?
Now, for passes like Zǐjīng and Dàomǎ,
almost a month after the invaders retreated,
defenses have still not been established.
Xuānfǔ serves as a reinforcement for Dàtóng,
and Jūyōng is close to the capital.
Its defense, in particular, cannot be entrusted to the wrong person.
Since Hóng and others are retained,
we must find someone like Hóng to replace them,
only then can we fulfill the heavy trust and achieve great success."
The emperor approved.
Soon after, he was ordered to go and settle the displaced people of Chénzhōu.
In Jǐngtài first year (1450), he returned to court and
said:
"The displaced people come from various regions,
and their situations are not uniform.
Although they have fortunately been registered as households,
fighting and vendettas occur from time to time,
so a dedicated official should be appointed to pacify them."
He also said:
"The Jīfǔ region has suffered continuous drought and locust plagues;
I request that relief be increased."
The emperor adopted most of his suggestions.
The military officials of the capital garrisons and their sons were often arrogant, lazy, and not skilled in warfare.
Shèng requested the selection of strong and capable men
to prepare for the defense of the capital city.
Market stalls set up by imperial relatives and nobles
were subject to monthly taxes.
Shèng, citing insufficient national expenditure,
requested that their taxes be registered to supplement military provisions.
All were followed.
The next year,
he presented eight measures to mitigate disasters and prevent calamities.
The emperor, with military activities having somewhat subsided,
indulged considerably in feasts and excursions.
Shèng requested the reinstatement of the morning court sessions,
and it was immediately approved.
At that time,
the emperor was open-minded in accepting advice,
and among the joint proposals submitted by the Six Bureaus,
many were led by Shèng and Lín Cōng.
When court officials discussed matters,
Shèng often spoke first,
engaging in back-and-forth arguments.
Some of the grand secretaries discussing with him were displeased and said,
"Is he not a Shàobǎo?"
Thus, he was called
"Yè Shàobǎo."
However, public opinion universally acclaimed Shèng's talent.
He was promoted to Yòu Cānzhèng,
overseeing provisions in Xuānfǔ.
Soon after, upon the recommendation of Lǐ Bǐng,
he assisted Dūdū Qiānshì Sūn Ān in military affairs.
Originally,
Ān had once commanded the defenses of the four cities of Duóshí,
Mǎyíng,
and Lóngmén Wèi and Suǒ.
After Yīngzōng was captured and taken north,
Ān, considering the four cities to be far beyond the Great Wall
and isolated,
memorialized to abandon them and relocate inland.
By this time, the court discussed and ordered Ān to repair them.
Shèng assisted in clearing overgrown land,
repairing dwellings,
preparing military equipment,
recruiting displaced people,
setting up warm shelters for travelers,
requesting treasury gold to buy a thousand oxen to distribute to屯卒 (túnzú),
establishing community schools,
setting up public burial grounds,
and treating illnesses and injuries.
Within two years,
the four cities and various forts like Chìchéng and Diāo'è were all successively restored.
Ān was consequently promoted to Fù Zǒngbīng.
However, the defending eunuch Gōng Shèng resented Ān
and memorialized that Ān was ill and should be replaced.
The emperor asked Shèng,
who said:
"Ān is tormented by Shèng,
hence his illness.
Currently, no general surpasses Ān."
So Ān was retained,
and a doctor was sent to examine his illness.
Soon after, Shèng impeached Shèng,
who was eventually transferred to another garrison.
When Yīngzōng was restored to power,
Shèng suffered the death of his father
and rushed home for mourning.
In Tiānshùn second year (1458), he was summoned to be Yòu Qiān Dū Yùshǐ,
巡撫 (xúnfǔ) of Liǎngguǎng.
He requested to complete his mourning period,
but it was not granted.
The Yao bandit Fèng Dìjī of Lóngshuǐ committed widespread looting,
and he directed the generals to capture him alive.
At that time, bandits proliferated in Liǎngguǎng,
everywhere breaking cities and killing generals.
The generals were timid and dared not fight,
instead killing innocent civilians to claim credit,
which led the people to join the bandits en masse.
Shèng, noting that the barbarians' movements were unpredictable,
requested that from then on, only attacks and raids on cities be reported,
and other incidents merely be summarized in memorials.
The memorial reached the Ministry of War,
but was rejected and not implemented.
Shèng and the Zǒngbīngguān Yán Biāo broke over seven hundred bandit strongholds.
Biāo was somewhat indiscriminate in his killings,
and slanderers consequently blamed Shèng.
In the sixth year, Wú Zhēn was appointed to patrol Guǎngxī,
while Shèng focused on patrolling Guǎngdōng.
When Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
he came to the capital to discuss matters.
Gěishìzhōng Zhāng Níng and others wanted to recommend him for promotion to the Grand Secretariat.
However, due to the words of Yùshǐ Lǚ Hóng, it was stopped,
and Hán Yōng was appointed to patrol Guǎngdōng in his place.
Previously,
Biānxiū Qiū Jùn and Shèng did not get along.
Dàxuéshì Lǐ Xián, having heard Jùn's words,
drafted Yōng's imperial edict, saying:
"Do not be like Yè Shèng, who killed those who surrendered."
Shèng did not dispute this.
He was slightly promoted to Zuǒ Qiān Dū Yùshǐ,
replacing Lǐ Bǐng as Xúnfǔ of Xuānfǔ.
He requested a moderate reduction in the price of salt and rice for internal trade
to encourage merchants and enrich the border region.
He reinstated the methods of official oxen and official fields,
reclaiming over four thousand qǐng of land.
With the accumulated surplus, he purchased one thousand eight hundred warhorses,
repaired over seven hundred forts,
and the border region became even more peaceful.
In the autumn of Chénghuà third year (1467),
he entered the capital as Lǐbù Yòu Shìláng,
and, along with Gěishì Máo Hóng, investigated affairs in Nánjīng.
Upon his return, he was transferred to the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù).
He was sent out to relieve famine in Zhēndìng and Bǎodìng,
proposed clearing imperial estates,
distributing breeding horses among the populace,
establishing granaries in Zhuōzhōu and Tiānjīn,
and accumulating grain to prepare for famine.
All these measures were timely and effective.
Mǎndūlǔ 諸部 (various tribes) had long been stationed in Hétào.
Bīngbù Shàngshū Bái Guī proposed a major expedition of 100,000 men to drive them out,
building cities along the river to Dōngshèng,
and moving civilians to farm and guard.
The emperor praised his proposal.
In the spring of the eighth year,
an imperial edict instructed Shèng to meet with Zǒngdū Wáng Yuè,
Xúnfǔ Mǎ Wénshēng, Yú Zǐjùn, and Xú Tíngzhāng to discuss in detail.
Initially,
Shèng, as a jiànguān (remonstrating official),
enjoyed discussing military matters,
and made many proposals.
After traveling to the three frontiers,
he realized that there were no good generals at the time,
border defenses had long been neglected,
and transportation was difficult and costly.
He concluded that clearing Hétào and recovering Dōngshèng should not be lightly undertaken.
So he met with the officials and submitted a memorial,
stating that defense was the best long-term strategy.
“If a decisive battle is unavoidable,
it is still advisable to strengthen fortifications and clear the fields (scorched earth policy),
and strike when they become complacent and retreat,
inflicting a major defeat
to prevent their return.
Alternatively, if they enter to plunder,
dispatch elite troops to raid their base,
forcing them to turn back,
and attack them from both inside and out.
This would be sufficient to achieve success.
However, fortifications must be secured
before battle can be considered.”
The emperor approved his words,
but Guī insisted on recovering Hétào.
The army was dispatched,
but achieved no success.
People admired Shèng’s foresight because of this.
In the eighth year, he was promoted to Zuǒ Shìláng.
He died in the tenth year,
at the age of fifty-five.
He was given the posthumous name Wénzhuāng.
Shèng was upright, studious,
valued integrity,
and had few personal indulgences.
At home, he often walked everywhere.
Throughout his life, he admired Fàn Zhòngyān,
and had his statue in his hall and bedchamber.
His ambition was for the sovereign and the people,
not for personal gain,
possessing the demeanor of an ancient minister.
A eulogy states: During the Tiānshùn and Chénghuà eras,
the Six Ministries were particularly well-staffed.
Wáng Áo and others were upright and principled,
all worthy of being called renowned and seasoned elders.
Observe Áo, Lǐ Bǐng, and Nián Fù in their frontier assignments,
Wáng Hóng in striking down corrupt factions and saving famine victims,
Wáng Fù in planning border defenses,
Yáo Kuí in overseeing rites,
Lín Cōng and Yè Shèng in their roles as censors—
their actions and achievements
were all outstanding.
Their reputation and accomplishments were widely known,
bearing the heavy expectations of both court and public.
Indeed, there was good reason for this.
校勘記 (Collation Notes)
Biographies, Chapter 66: Xiàng Zhōng, Hán Yōng, Yú Zǐjùn (Ruǎn Qín), Zhū Yīng, Qín Hóng
Xiàng Zhōng,
courtesy name Jìnchén,
was from Jiāxīng.
He became a Jìnshì in the seventh year of Zhèngtǒng.
He was appointed Xíngbù Zhǔshì,
and promoted to Yuánwàiláng.
He accompanied Yīngzōng and was captured by the Wǎlà,
ordered to feed horses.
He seized an opportunity to escape south with two horses.
When the horses tired,
he abandoned them,
and walked barefoot for seven days and nights,
finally reaching Xuānfǔ.
During the Jǐngtài era,
he was promoted from Lángzhōng to Guǎngdōng Fùshǐ.
While inspecting Gāozhōu,
spies reported that bandits were plundering villages, carrying hundreds of men and women.
Zhōng said:
“Bandits do not carry families;
these must be good people who have been robbed.”
He warned his generals not to kill indiscriminately.
Afterward,
he interrogated the captives,
and it was indeed as he suspected.
He released them all.
He distinguished himself in the campaign against the Yáo of Lóngshuǐ,
and his salary was increased by one rank.
In the early Tiānshùn era,
he served successively as Shǎnxī Ànchásǐ.
When his mother passed away, he returned home for mourning.
The local people went to the capital to plead for his retention,
and an imperial edict ordered him to resume his duties.
At that time, Shǎnxī suffered from continuous years of disaster.
Zhōng distributed grain from the granaries to relieve the distress,
and also requested that minor offenders be allowed to pay millet in lieu of punishment.
The people relied on him for salvation.
In the seventh year, he was summoned to serve as Dàlǐ Qīng,
but the people again pleaded for his retention, as before.
Consequently, he was reassigned as Yòu Fù Dū Yùshǐ,
and became Xúnfǔ of that region.
When the Qiāng of Táo and Mín rebelled,
Zhōng memorialized, saying:
“The Qiāng’s intent is plunder.
To exterminate them all would be inhumane,
but to immediately pacify them would show weakness.
I request permission to act according to my discretion.”
The request was approved.
He then dispatched troops to occupy strategic points,
and loudly proclaimed an impending punitive expedition,
and all the rebels surrendered.
The water springs in Xī’ān were brackish and undrinkable,
so he opened the Lóngshǒu Canal and the Zàohé River,
diverting water into the city.
He also dredged the Zhèng and Bái canals,
irrigating over 70,000 qǐng of farmland in the five counties of Jīngyáng, Sānyuán, Lǐquán, Gāolíng, and Líntóng.
The people built shrines to worship him.
Shǎnxī frequently suffered from military troubles.
In the first year of Chénghuà, he reported:
“When the great generals of the three frontiers encounter the enemy, they hesitate.
Although it is said to be due to their timidity,
it is also because their authority is too light.
Soldiers fear the enemy but not their generals,
which is why battles are unsuccessful.
It should be permitted to apply military law.
The imperial court has been searching for talented generals,
but for over a year, not a single person has responded to the summons.
Shǎnxī’s customs are robust,
and historically it has produced many famous generals.
It cannot be that there are no such people,
but rather that they are hindered by their inability to answer policy questions.
Today, among the students in schools nationwide, only one or two out of a hundred are good at answering policy questions.
How can we demand this of military men?”
The emperor approved his words,
but the responsible authorities stuck to old precedents and could not implement them.
When Máolǐhái raided Yánsūi,
an edict ordered Zhōng to accompany Zhāngwǔ Bó Yáng Xìn to resist him,
but they achieved no success.
The next year,
Xìn proposed a large-scale expedition to clear Hétào,
and an edict instructed Zhōng to supervise military affairs.
Zhōng was on his way to Yánsūi,
when the bandits again captured Kāichéng,
penetrated deep into the six prefectures and counties of Jìngníng and Lóngdé,
plundered extensively, and then departed.
The Bīngbù impeached Zhōng,
but the emperor specifically pardoned him,
and the expedition to clear Hétào was also not launched.
The year after that, he was summoned to manage affairs at the Dàlǐ Sì.
In the fourth year,
Mǎn Jùn rebelled.
Mǎn Jùn
was also named Mǎn Sì.
His ancestor was Bā Dān.
Since the early Míng dynasty, he led his部部 to pledge allegiance,
and for generations, they were considered powerful leaders of herdsmen, holding the position of *qiānhù*.
They retained their old customs,
and were exempt from taxes and corvée labor.
Their territory was in Gùyuán Lǐ of Kāichéng County,
adjoining the border.
Jùn was fierce and unruly;
he habitually harbored criminals and thieves,
and raided beyond the border.
It happened that a case implicated Jùn,
and officials tracked a fugitive to his home,
making many demands.
Jùn was enraged,
and thus incited the populace to rebellion.
The Grand Coordinator dispatched Jùn's nephew, Commander Shú, to apprehend him.
Jùn killed his followers,
kidnapped Shú, rebelled,
and occupied Shíchéng.
Shíchéng
was the Shíbǎo of the Tǔfān during the Táng dynasty.
The city was renowned for its strategic strength,
and could not be conquered without tens of thousands of men.
There were fortifications on the mountain,
with cliffs on all four sides.
Five stone wells were dug within to store water,
and there was only one path to ascend.
Jùn proclaimed himself Zhāoxián Wáng (Recruiting Worthies King),
and had a force of four thousand.
Regional Commander Xíng Duān and others resisted him,
but were defeated.
In less than two months,
his forces grew to twenty thousand,
and Guānzhōng was shaken.
Then Máo Zhōng was ordered to oversee military affairs,

and, with Superintendent of Military Affairs Grand Eunuch Liú Xiáng and Commander-in-Chief Grand Commissioner Liú Yù, lead the capital garrisons and the troops from the four garrisons of Shǎnxī to suppress them.
Before the army marched,
Governor Chén Jià and others first advanced with thirty thousand troops,
and were again greatly defeated.
The rebels, using the official army's weapons and armor,
grew even stronger.
The court debated sending more troops.
Zhōng worried that the capital troops were weak and unreliable,
and that sending another general would interfere with his authority.
Therefore, he memorialized:
"Your servants have mobilized more than thirty-three thousand troops,
which is sufficient to annihilate the rebels.
Now, as autumn deepens and the grass turns cold,
if other armies are mobilized,
it may take too long to travel back and forth,
allowing the rebels to flee far away.
Moreover, border troops cannot remain for long,
so adding more troops is not convenient."
Grand Academicians Péng Shí and Shāng Lù supported his proposal,
and the capital troops were spared from deployment.
Zhōng then, with Grand Coordinator and Censor-in-Chief Mǎ Wénshēng, divided the army into seven routes,
reaching the foot of Shíchéng.
They engaged in battle,
and achieved many kills and captures.
Earl of Fúqiáng Máo Zhōng, pressing the advantage, seized the northwest mountain.
They were on the verge of victory
when he was suddenly struck and killed by a stray arrow.
Yù was also surrounded.
The various armies wished to retreat,
but Zhōng beheaded a *qiānhù* as a warning.
The troops fought fiercely,
and Yù managed to escape.
They then formed a siege.
At that time, a comet appeared in Táidǒu,
and many in the central court said it portended ill for the Qín region,
indicating an unfavorable military campaign.
Zhōng said:
"Lǐ Shèng suppressed Zhū Cǐ when Yínghuò (Mars) stayed in Suì (Jupiter's year-star position);
what harm is there in this?"
Every day, he sent troops to press upon the city,
burning fodder and grass,
and cutting off the water supply routes.
The rebels, in distress, wanted to surrender
and invited Zhōng and Wénshēng to meet.
Zhōng, accompanied by Liú Yù, rode alone to the meeting.
Wénshēng also arrived with several dozen cavalrymen,
calling out to Jùn and Shú to urge their speedy surrender.
The rebels, seeing them from afar, prostrated themselves.
Zhōng rode straight forward and seized Shú, returning with him.
Jùn's morale was deflated,
and he hesitated to come out.
Zhōng ordered bridges to be built with wood,
and men to carry sacks of earth to fill the moats.
They attacked with bronze cannons,
and the casualties grew numerous.
The rebels relied on their beloved general Yáng Hǔlí as their strategist,
but he was captured when he went out at night to fetch water.
Zhōng pardoned him from death,
informed him of the reward scale for capturing rebels,
showed him gold,
and also bestowed upon him a gold belt buckle.
He was released
to lure Jùn out to battle,
where ambush troops captured him.
They immediately attacked and took Shíchéng,
capturing all the remaining rebels.
They destroyed the city
and carved a stone to commemorate their achievements.
One *wèi* (guard unit) was added to the abandoned city of Xī'ān northwest of Gùyuán,
and troops were left to garrison it before returning.
Initially,
before Shíchéng fell,
the weather was extremely cold,
and the soldiers were greatly distressed.
Zhōng worried that the rebels might break out
and cross the frozen river to join the bandits from Tào.
Day and night, he prepared siege equipment,
personally enduring arrows and stones without flinching,
fighting over three hundred large and small battles.
Péng Shí and Shāng Lù knew that Zhōng was capable of handling the rebels
and did not interfere with him,
thus the rebels were ultimately annihilated.
For his meritorious service,
he was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief,
and jointly managed the Censorate with Lín Cōng.
After Bái Guī had pacified Liú Tōng,
the displaced people in Jīng and Xiāng regions remained organized into camps as before.
A follower of Tōng, Lǐ Húzi, whose given name was Yuán,
falsely called himself Píng Wáng (Pacification King).
He, along with Xiǎo Wáng Hóng (Little King Hóng) and Wáng Biāo, raided Nánzhāng, Fáng, Nèixiāng, and Wèinán counties.
The displaced people who joined the rebels reached a million.
In the winter of the sixth year,
an imperial edict ordered Zhōng to oversee military affairs,
and, with the Huguǎng Commander-in-Chief Lǐ Zhèn, suppress them.
Zhōng then requested the deployment of indigenous troops from Yǒngshùn and Bǎojìng.
First, he divided his army to strategic locations,
setting up many flags, gongs, and drums,
and sending people into the mountains to recruit and persuade.
Over four hundred thousand displaced people surrendered,
and Biāo was also captured.
At that time, Bái Guī was in the Ministry of War.
He sent Jǐnyī Hundred-Household Officer Wú Shòu to assist Participatory Officer Wáng Xìn's army.
Shòu wanted to claim credit,
and did not want the rebels to disintegrate easily.
He spread rumors,
which Guī believed,
and stopped the deployment of indigenous troops.
Zhōng memorialized to dispute this,
and also impeached Shòu for his crimes.
The emperor recalled Shòu
and allowed the indigenous troops to be deployed as before.
Twenty-five thousand were assembled
and divided into eight routes to pressure them.
Tens of thousands more displaced people surrendered.
The rebels lay hidden in mountain strongholds,
waiting for opportunities to raid.
Zhōng ordered Vice Commissioner Yú Xún and Grand Commander Lǐ Zhèn to attack them.
They encountered them at Zhúshān.
Taking advantage of the swollen stream, they attacked them mid-crossing,
capturing Lǐ Yuán, Xiǎo Wáng Hóng, and others.
Many rebels drowned.
Zhōng moved his army to Zhúshān
to hunt down the remaining remnants.
He again recruited five hundred thousand displaced people,
beheaded six hundred forty,
captured over eight hundred,
and secured over thirty thousand family members.
From each household, one male was selected
to garrison the Huguǎng border *wèi*,
while the rest were ordered to return to their original registrations and be given land.
He memorialized ten post-campaign measures,
all of which were approved.
When Zhōng ordered the expulsion of the displaced people,
officials forcibly drove them all out.
If they did not advance,
they were killed.
Some people who had been registered since the Hóngwǔ era
were also among those expelled.
Many of those assigned to garrison duties died of disease during the boat journey.
Investigating Censor Liáng Jǐng, prompted by a celestial phenomenon, requested advice
and impeached Zhōng for arbitrary killings.
Bái Guī also stated that those displaced people who had already settled
should be registered where they were,
and he also refuted the discrepancies in the meritorious deeds submitted by Zhōng.
The emperor ignored all of these.
Zhōng was promoted to Left Censor-in-Chief,
his son Shòu was given the hereditary title of Jǐnyī *qiānhù*,
and the various generals were rewarded according to their merits.
Zhōng submitted a memorial stating:
"Your subject has successively recruited and pacified over 930,000 displaced people to return to their occupations.
The bandit factions fled into the deep mountains,
and another 500,000 were persuaded to disband and surrender voluntarily.
Only a hundred were captured,
all being ringleaders.
Now it is said that all are sons of respectable families.
Then who were those whom earlier memorials repeatedly described as rampant and irresistible?
Who were they?
The bandit leaders' crimes certainly warrant death,
but precisely because I could not bear to execute indiscriminately,
I ordered the able-bodied men to be exiled and sent to garrisons.
As for those long registered,
some occupied over forty *lǐ* of mountains,
gathered a thousand scoundrels,
and engaged in fighting, robbery, and murder.
If such people exist,
can they be allowed to remain permanently and not be expelled?
Your subject posted notices to inform the bandits,
claiming thousands had been killed.
This was to create a false deterrent and intimidate them,
not a factual statement.
Moreover, Guī did personally take charge of this matter,
and today's issues are also legacies from Guī.
Previously,
commentators both within and outside the court wondered when the trouble in Jīng and Xiāng would ever be pacified.
Now, fortunately, it is settled,
yet rumors are rife,
using your subject as a pretext.
In the past, Mǎ Yuán was slandered over coix seeds,
and Dèng Ài was summoned in a cage cart.
Their merits were not recorded,
and their lives were not even safe.
Your subject is fortunate to live in an enlightened reign,
and wishes to be granted his old bones,
lest your subject become a successor to Mǎ and Dèng."
The Emperor replied with a gentle edict.
In the eighth year, he was recalled
and, with Lǐ Bīn, managed the affairs of the court.
Two years later, he was appointed Minister of Justice (Xíng Shàngshū),
and soon after replaced Guī as Minister of War (Bīngbù).
Wāng Zhí opened the Western Depot (Xī Chǎng)
and acted with tyranny.
Zhōng was repeatedly insulted and could not bear it.
Coincidentally, Grand Secretary (Dàxuéshì) Shāng Lù and others impeached Zhí,
and Zhōng also led the Nine Ministers (Jiǔ Qīng) in impeaching him.
The memorial was kept in the palace,
and the Western Depot was subsequently abolished.
Zhí deeply resented this.
Before long,
the Western Depot was re-established.
Zhí took Wú Shòu as his confidant,
and Shòu, holding past grudges,
watched Zhōng even more closely.
Zhōng felt uneasy
and requested to return home to treat an illness.
Before he could leave,
Shòu instigated investigators to falsely accuse Zhōng.
Investigating Censor (Gěishìzhōng) Guō Táng and Supervising Censor (Yùshǐ) Féng Guàn and others again jointly impeached Zhōng,
implicating his son Jīng, eunuch Huáng Cì, Earl of Xīngníng Lǐ Zhèn, and Earl of Zhāngwǔ Yáng Xìn, among others.
An imperial edict ordered the Judicial Offices (Fǎ Sī) to jointly interrogate them with the Embroidered Uniform Guard (Jǐnyīwèi) at court.
Zhōng vehemently defended himself without yielding.
However, everyone knew it was Zhí's intention,
and no one dared to speak up for him.
He was ultimately dismissed as a commoner,
and Cì and Zhèn also received punishment.
When Zhí fell,
Zhōng was reinstated to office
and retired.
He lived at home for twenty-six years
and died in the fifteenth year of Hóngzhì
at the age of eighty-two.
He was posthumously granted Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Tàibǎo)
and given the posthumous title Xiāngyì.
Zhōng was magnanimous and had grand strategies,
was skilled in military affairs,
upright and unyielding,
and quick in governance.
Therefore, he was renowned wherever he served.
His son Jīng,
Jīng's son Xī,
and Xī's son Zhìyuán
all passed the imperial examinations.
Jīng was
an Administration Vice Commissioner (Cānzhèng) of Jiāngxī.
Xī was
a Minister of the Imperial Household (Guānglùsì Qīng) of Nánjīng.
Zhìyuán was
a Vice Director (Yuánwàiláng).
Hán Yōng,
courtesy name Yǒngxī,
was a native of Chángzhōu.
He passed the imperial examination in the seventh year of Zhèngtǒng.
He was appointed Supervising Censor (Yùshǐ).
He was spirited and decisive,
and known for his talent and strategy.
He recorded prisoners in the Southern Metropolitan Region (Nán Jī).
A certain *jiàoyù* (educational official) of Dàngshān flogged a chef;
the chef fled and hid.
His father accused the *jiàoyù* of killing his son
and dismembered another corpse to provide evidence.
After a forced confession was obtained,
Yōng traced and found the chef,
clearing the *jiàoyù*'s name.
He went out on patrol of the riverways.
Afterwards,
he was appointed Investigating Censor (Xún'àn Yùshǐ) of Jiāngxī,
dismissing fifty-seven corrupt officials.
When bandits rose in Lúlíng and Tàihé,
he captured and executed them.
In the winter of the thirteenth year,
the rebel Yè Zōngliú from Chǔzhōu moved from Fújiàn to invade Jiāngxī.
The imperial army suffered a defeat,
and Assistant Military Commissioner (Dūdū Qiānshì) Chén Róng and Commander (Zhǐhuī) Liú Zhēn died in an ambush.
An imperial edict ordered Yōng and Defense Vice Minister (Zhènshǒu Shìláng) Yáng Níng to supervise the military and civilians in a joint defense.
It happened that Fújiàn Investigating Censor (Xún'àn Yùshǐ) Wāng Chéng had sent a dispatch to neighboring areas to jointly attack the bandit Dèng Máoqī.
Soon after, due to negotiations for the bandits' surrender,
the troops were halted.
Yōng said:
"If the bandits truly surrender,
it is not too late to withdraw."
He pressed forward,
but the bandits had already rebelled,
and Chéng was punished and died for it.
People admired Yōng's discernment for this.
In the second year of Jǐngtài, he was promoted to Vice Commissioner (Fùshǐ) of Guǎngdōng.
Grand Secretary (Dàxuéshì) Chén Xún recommended him for Vice Censor-in-Chief (Yòu Qiān Dū Yùshǐ),
replacing Yáng Níng as Grand Coordinator (Xúnfǔ) of Jiāngxī.
During a famine,
he memorialized to exempt the autumn grain tax.
He impeached the Prince of Níng for unlawful conduct,
and all officials of the princely establishment were punished.
At that time, Yōng was only thirty years old,
yet he was conspicuously talented and esteemed.
All his plans and arrangements
could serve as future precedents.
At the beginning of Tiānshùn,
all Grand Coordinators (Xúnfǔ Guān) in the empire were dismissed.
He was reassigned as Vice Commissioner (Fùshǐ) of Shānxī.
The Prince of Níng, holding previous grudges, impeached him for unauthorized use of a sedan chair and other matters.
He was imprisoned
and stripped of office.
He was later appointed Junior Minister of the Grand Court of Judicial Review (Dàlǐ Shàopī).
Soon after, he was reinstated as Vice Censor-in-Chief (Yòu Qiān Dū Yùshǐ),
assisting Kòu Shēn in managing the affairs of the Censorate.
After Shí Hēng was executed,
Embroidered Uniform Guard Commander (Jǐnyī Zhǐhuī) Liú Jìng was found guilty of eating with Hēng in his private room
and sentenced to death under the law against factionalism.
Yōng argued:
"The law emphasizes factionalism
in the sense of colluding to disrupt court politics.
To apply it to a single meal,
how can that be the intent of the law?
Furthermore, when Hēng was powerful,
high officials visited his door morning and evening.
Why was it that no one else was punished,
but Jìng alone was?"
Shēn greatly admired and agreed with him,
and released Jìng.
When his mother died, he mourned,
but was recalled to service.
In the fourth year,
he became Grand Coordinator (Xúnfǔ) of Xuānfǔ and Dàtóng.
In the seventh year, he entered court for an audience to discuss matters.
The Emperor was impressed by his appearance
and kept him as Vice Minister of War (Bīngbù Yòu Shìláng).
When Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
he was implicated by Grand Academician (Xuélì) Qián Pǔ
and demoted to Administration Vice Commissioner (Zuǒ Cānzhèng) of Zhèjiāng.
The Yáo and Zhòng tribes of Guǎngxī plundered Guǎngdōng,
devastating almost all prefectures and counties.
In the first month of the first year of Chénghuà, a large army was dispatched.
Military Commissioner (Dūdū) Zhào Fǔ was appointed Commander-in-Chief (Zǒngbīng Guān),
with eunuchs Lú Yǒng and Chén Xuān supervising the army.
Minister of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū) Wáng Hóng said:
"Hán Yōng's talent and spirit are unmatched;
no one but Yōng can pacify the bandits."
Thereupon, Yōng was reassigned as Vice Censor-in-Chief (Zuǒ Qiān Dū Yùshǐ)
to assist in military affairs.
Yǒng sped to Nánjīng,
gathering the generals to discuss strategy.
Previously,
compiler Qiū Jùn had submitted a memorial to Grand Secretary Lǐ Xián,
stating that the bandits in Guǎngdōng should be driven out,
and those in Guǎngxī should be besieged.
He proposed stationing troops in Dàténgxiá,
blocking their movements,
and trampling their crops,
expecting to eliminate all bandits within one or two years.
Xián approved of this,
presented it to the court,
and an imperial edict ordered it to be recorded and shown to the generals.
The generals advocated this plan,
requesting that Mobile Corps General Hé Yǒng lead cavalry to Guǎngdōng,
while the main army would proceed directly to Guǎngxī,
dividing forces to suppress and eliminate them.
Yǒng said:
"The bandits have already spread over several thousand *lǐ*,
and if we engage them in every place they reach,
we will exhaust ourselves.
We should lead our entire army directly to Dàténgxiá.
To the south, we can support Gāo, Zhào, Léi, and Lián;
to the east, we can respond to Nán and Sháo;
to the west, we can take Liǔ and Qìng;
to the north, we can cut off all routes to Yángdòng.
With head and tail responding to each other,
attacking their heartland,
once their lair is overturned,
the rest will fall apart easily.
If we disregard this plan
and divide our forces in all directions,
the bandits will only scatter further,
and the prefectures and counties will be further devastated,
which is like fanning a fire while trying to put it out."
The multitude said,
"Excellent."
Fǔ also knew Yǒng was capable enough to handle the bandits,
and all military plans were left to Yǒng.
Yǒng and others then marched day and night towards Quánzhōu.
The Yángdòng Miáo plundered Xīng'ān,
and were defeated.
Upon arriving at Guìlín,
he executed Commander Lǐ Yīng and three others who had failed in their duties, to make an example.
He consulted the map and discussed with the generals, saying:
"The bandits consider Xiūrén and Lìpǔ as their wings;
we should first reclaim these two counties to isolate the bandit forces."
He then commanded 160,000 troops,
divided into five routes,
first defeating the bandits in Xiūrén,
pursuing them relentlessly to Lìshān.
Over 1,200 were captured,
and 7,300 heads were cut off.
Lìpǔ was also pacified.
In the tenth month, he arrived at Xúnzhōu,
and asked the elders,
who all said:
"The Gorge
is a natural stronghold,
impregnable by direct assault;
it should be besieged by stratagem."
Yǒng said:
"The Gorge stretches over 600 *lǐ*;
how can it be besieged?
If forces are divided, strength will be weakened;
if the army is exhausted, resources will be depleted;
when will the bandits ever be pacified?
My plan is decided."
So he marched directly to the mouth of the Gorge.
Several tens of scholars and village elders knelt on the left side of the road,
offering to serve as guides.
Yǒng saw them and immediately cursed, saying:
"How dare these bandits try to deceive me!"
He ordered his attendants to bind and execute them,
which astonished everyone.
Once bound,
sharp blades fell from their sleeves.
Upon interrogation,
they were indeed bandits.
All were dismembered and their internal organs removed,
then hung in segments in the forest and bamboo groves,
one after another.
The bandits were greatly alarmed, saying:
"Duke Hán is a god!"
Yǒng ordered Commander-in-Chief Ōu Xìn and others to form five detachments,
attacking their north from Xiàngzhōu and Wǔxuān;
he himself, with Fǔ, supervised Commander Bái Quán and others in eight detachments,
attacking their south from Guìpíng and Píngnán;
Assistant General Sūn Zhèn and others formed two detachments,
entering by water;
and additional troops were dispatched to guard various passes.
Bandit leaders Hóu Dàgǒu and others were greatly afraid,
first moving their heavy possessions to Héngshítáng in Guìzhōu,
and erecting stockades on Nánshān,
placing many rolling logs, tumbling stones, javelins, and crossbows to resist the government forces.
On the first day of the twelfth month,
Yǒng and others led the armies, advancing by land and water,
carrying shields to ascend the mountains,
fighting to the death.
They successively captured Shímén, Líndòng, Shātián, and Gǔyíng, destroying all their lairs,
burning their dwellings and accumulated goods,
and all the bandits fled in disarray.
They cut down trees to clear a path,
reaching Héngshítáng and the Jiǔcénglóu mountains directly.
The bandits again erected several layers of stockades,
relying on the high ground to resist.
The government forces lured the bandits to expend their arrows and stones,
estimating they were almost exhausted,
then Yǒng personally commanded all the troops to climb up by clinging to trees and vines.
He separately dispatched brave warriors to ascend first via secret paths,
occupying the mountaintop and firing cannons.
The bandits could not withstand,
and were then utterly defeated.
Before and after, 324 bandit strongholds were broken,
Dàgǒu and 780 of his followers were captured alive,
over 3,200 heads were cut off,
and countless perished by falling or drowning.
There was a great rattan in the Gorge, like a rainbow,
spanning between the two cliffs.
Yǒng had it cut down,
renamed the Gorge Duànténgxiá,
and carved a stone to commemorate the achievement before returning.
He divided his forces to attack the remaining factions,
and Yùlín, Yángjiāng, Luòróng, and Bóbái were successively pacified.
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
bestowed an imperial edict commending and rewarding him,
recalled Fǔ and others,
promoted Yǒng to Vice Censor-in-Chief of the Left,
and made him Governor-General of military affairs in the Two Guǎng regions.
Yǒng then dispersed the various armies
to save on provisions,
and the remaining rebels Hóu Zhèng'áng and others seized the opportunity to capture Xúnzhōu and the two counties of Luòróng and Běiliú.
Yǒng was impeached and admitted his fault,
but the Emperor pardoned him.
Yǒng further dispatched troops to suppress them.
At that time, various bandits arose everywhere;
Sī'ēn, Xún, Bīn, and Liǔchéng were all disturbed and plundered.
The wandering bandits reached Guǎngdōng,
and the two prefectures of Qīn and Huà were immediately broken and annihilated.
In the spring of the fourth year,
Yǒng, considering the vast territory and heavy affairs of the Two Guǎng regions,
requested that a Grand Coordinator be appointed for both the eastern and western parts,
which the Emperor approved.
Chén Lián was appointed Grand Coordinator of Guǎngdōng,
Zhāng Péng of Guǎngxī,
while Yǒng exclusively managed military affairs.
Soon after, he returned home due to mourning.
The following year,
banditry in the Two Guǎng regions arose again.
Section Chief Táo Lǔ stated:
"The terrain of the Two Guǎng regions is intricate and interwoven;
they should be like arms and fingers, used together,
not separated.
Recently, when bandits attacked Guǎngxī,
I discussed dispatching troops with the three Chief Offices of Guǎngdōng,
but it remained undecided for a month,
and the bandits feared nothing.
I beg that a high official be again appointed to be the Governor-General, which would be convenient."
At the same time, Section Chief Lín Jǐn and Investigating Censor Gōng Shèng also requested this.
So the two Grand Coordinators were abolished,
and Yǒng was reinstated as Right Censor-in-Chief,
serving as Governor-General as before.
In the first month of the year after that,
Yǒng submitted a memorial declining the new appointment,
requesting to remain in mourning until its completion,
but it was not permitted.
Upon arriving at his post,
Yǒng dispatched Assistant General Zhāng Shòu, Mobile Corps General Féng Shēng, and others to suppress the bandits in separate routes,
and the eight-stronghold barbarians of Xīnzhōu, as well as the various mountain Yáo and Zhòng who plundered prefectures and counties,
were all crushed and defeated.
The barbarians had always been awed by Yǒng's might,
and banditry gradually subsided.
In the ninth year,
the various barbarians in Liǔ and Xún rebelled again.
Assistant General Yáng Guǎng and others captured and killed 900 people.
Just as they were about to advance further,
the bandits captured Huáijí County.
The Ministry of War impeached Yǒng for false reporting.
The eunuch guarding Guǎngxī, Huáng Qìn, who resented Yǒng for suppressing him,
therefore accused Yǒng,
and further stated that he was greedy, indulged in alcohol,
and gave out excessive and wasteful rewards.
The Emperor dispatched Supervising Secretary Zhāng Qiān and others to investigate,
while the Provincial Administration Commissioner of Guǎngxī, Hé Yí, and Surveillance Vice Commissioner Zhāng Xiào, who resented Yǒng for always slighting them,
conspired to frame him.
Qiān returned and reported that
the accusations were half true and half false,
and Yǒng was ultimately ordered to retire from office.
Yōng Dòngdá 闓shuǎng,
重 xìn yì.
Fǔ Jiāngxī shí,
qǐng zhuī shì Wén Tiānxiáng, Xiè Fāngdé.
Zhào shì Tiānxiáng Zhōngliè, Fāngdé Wénjié.
Yǒu xióng lüè,
shàn duàn,
dòng zhōng shìjī.
Lín zhàn,
shuài gōngqīn shǐshí,
bù mùshùn.
Zìfèng zūn yán,
sānsī jiē cháng guì báishì.
Jūnmén shè tónggǔ shùshí,
yíjié xiángmì.
Bì jiàng yǐxià,
shéng xiá wú suǒ jiǎ.
Liǎng dì zhènshǒu huànguān sù jiāozì,
yì tìxī wú gǎn sì.
Jí è yán,
tǎn zhōng bù wéi yá'àn,
huīchì cáibó bù shǎo xī.
Gù suī lìng xíng jìnzhǐ,
mín dé āndǔ,
ér bàngyì yì yì qǐ.
Wéi zhōngguān suǒ yǐyě,
gōnglùn jiē bùpíng.
Liǎngguǎng rén niàn Yōng gōng,
yóu xī qí qù,
wèi lì cí sì yān.
Jiājū wǔ nián zú,
nián wǔshíqī.
Zhèngdé jiān,
shì Xiāngyì.
Chū yǐ jūngōng yǔ yī zǐ Jǐnyī Bǎihù,
Yōng yǐ shòu qí dì Mù.
Zhì shì,
lù yī zǐ Guózǐshēng.
Yú Jùnjùn,
zì Shìyīng,
Qīngshén rén.
Fù Xiáng,
Hùbù Lángzhōng.
Zǐjùn jǔ Jǐngtài èr nián Jìnshì,
shòu Hùbù Zhǔshì,
jìn Yuánwàiláng.
Zài bù shí nián,
yǐ liángàn chēng.
Chū wèi Xī'ān Zhīfǔ.
Suì jī,
fā lǐn shí wàn shí zhèndài.
Qūhuà yǐ cháng,
guān bù sǔn ér mín jì.
Chénghuà chū,
suǒ sī shàng zhìxíng dāng jīng zhě,
Zhīfǔ shí rén,
ér Zǐjùn wéi shǒu.
Yǐ Lín Cōng jiàn,
wèi Shǎnxī Yòu Cānzhèng,
suì yú zhuó Yòu Bùzhèngshǐ.
Liù nián zhuǎn Zuǒ,
diào Zhèjiāng.
Fǔ bàn zǎi,
bài Yòu Fù Dū Yùshǐ,
xúnfǔ Yánsuí.
Xiān shì,
xúnfǔ Wáng Ruì qǐng yán biān zhú qiáng jiàn bǎo,
wèi jiǔyuǎn jì,
gōng wèi xīng ér bà.
Zǐjùn shàngshū yán:
“Sān biān wéi Yánqìng dì píngyì,
lì chítū.
Kòu lǚ rù fàn,
huò biānrén wèi dǎo,
jìng rù Hétào tún mù.
Zì shì kòu gù jū nèi,
wǒ fǎn tún wài,
jí yí yú yán biān zhú qiáng zhì bǎo.
Kuàng jīn jiù jiè shí suǒzài,
duō gāoshān dǒu yá.
Yī shānxíng,
suí dìshì,
huò chǎn xuē,
huò lěi zhú,
huò tiāo qiàn,
mián yǐn xiāng jiē,
yǐ chéng biān qiáng,
yú jì wéi biàn.”
Shàngshū Bái Guī yǐ Shǎnmín fāng kùn,
zòu huǎnyì.
Jì ér kòu rù Gūshānbǎo,
fù fàn Yúlín,
Zǐjùn xiān hòu yǔ Zhū Yǒng, Xǔ Níng jībài zhī.
Shì shí,
kòu jù Hétào,
suì fā dàjūn zhēngtǎo,
zú wú gōng.
Bā nián qiū,
Zǐjùn fù yán:
“Jīn zhēng tào shìmǎ tún Yánsuí zhě bā wàn,
chú jiāo fán nèidì.
Ruò jīn dōng kòu bù běi qù,
yòu xū bèi láinián jūnzī.
Gū yǐ jīnnián zhī shù yuē zhī,
mǐ dòu xū yín jiǔshísì wàn,
cǎo liùshí wàn.
Měi rén yùn mǐ dòu liù dòu, cǎo sì shù,
yìngyòng sìbǎi líng qī wàn rén,
yuē fèi xíngzī bābǎi èrshíwǔ wàn.
Gōngsī fánrǎo zhì cǐ,
ān dé bù biànjì.
Chén qián qǐng zhú qiáng jiàn bǎo,
zhào shì níng jǔxíng.
Qǐng yú míngnián chūn xià kòu mǎ pífá shí,
yì Shǎnxī yùn liáng mín wǔ wàn,
gěi shí xīnggōng,
qī liǎng yuè bì shì.”
Guī yóu chí qián yì zǔ zhī.
Dì shì Zǐjùn yán,
mìng sù jǔ.
Zǐjùn xiān yòng jūngōng jìn Zuǒ Fù Dū Yùshǐ.
Míngnián,
yòu yòng Hóngyánchí dǎo cháo gōng,
jìn Yòu Dū Yùshǐ.
Kòu yǐ dǎo cháo gù yuǎnsǐ,
bù gǎn fù jū tào.
Nèidì huàn shāo xī,
Zǐjùn dé yīyì xīngyì.
Dōng qǐ Qīngshuǐyíng,
xī dǐ Huāmǎchí,
yánmào qiān qībǎi qīshí lǐ,
záo yá zhú qiáng,
jué qiàn qí xià,
lián bǐ bù jué.
Měi èr sān lǐ zhì dí tái yá zhài bèi xúnjǐng.
Yòu yú yá zhài kòngchù zhú duǎnqiáng,
héng yī xié èr rú jī zhuàng,
yǐ liáo dí bì shè.
Fán zhú chéngbǎo shíyī,
biān dūn shíwǔ,
xiǎo dūn qīshíbā,
yá zhài bābǎi yīshíjiǔ,
yì jūn sì wàn rén,
bù sān yuè ér chéng.
Qiáng nèi zhī dì xī fēn tún kěn,
suì dé liáng liù wàn shí yǒu qí.
Shí nián rùn liù yuè,
Zǐjùn jù shàng qí shì,
yīn yǐ mǔ lǎo qǐ guī,
wèiliú bù xǔ.
Chū,
Yánsuí Zhèn zhì Suídé Zhōu,
shǔ xiàn Mǐzhī, Wúbǎo xī zài qí wài.
Kòu yǐ qīngjì rù lüè,
zhènbīng jué ér zhuī zhī,
zhé bù jí,
wǎngwǎng dé lì qù.
Zì Zǐjùn xǐ zhèn Yúlín,
zēng wèi yì bīng,
tuò chéng zhì shù,
gōngshǒu qì bì jù,
suì wéi zhòng zhèn,
kòu chāo jiàn xī,
jūnmín dé ān gēngmù yān.
Shí'èr nián shí'èr yuè yí fǔ Shǎnxī.
Zǐjùn zhī Xī'ān shí,
yǐ jūmín huàn shuǐquán xián kǔ,
záo qú yǐn chéng xī Jué Hé rù guàn,
mín lì zhī.
Jiǔ ér shuǐ yì wú suǒ xiè.
Zhì shì,
nǎi yú chéng xīběi kāiqú xièshuǐ,
shǐ jīng Hàn gù chéng dá Wèi.
Gōngsī yì biàn,
hào Yú Gōng Qú.
Yòu yú Jīngyáng záo shān yǐnshuǐ,
gài tián qiān yú qǐng.
Tōng Nánshān dào,
zhí dǐ Hànzhōng,
yǐ biàn xínglǚ.
Xuéxiào, gōngshǔ pǐ zhě xī xīn zhī.
Zòu miǎn Mín, Hé, Táo sān wèi zhī shù nánfāng zhě wàn yǒu qí.
Yì zhì nán běi zhī gēng shù zhě liùqiān yǒu qí,
jiù shù běntǔ.
Mínzhōu Lìlín Qiāng wèi kòu,
Zǐjùn qián shī shè fú jī zǒu zhī.
In the thirteenth year, [Wáng] Zǐjùn was summoned to serve as Bīngbù Shàngshū.
He submitted a memorial proposing ten measures to clarify regulations,
and also presented a scale of rewards for military achievements.
From then on, both the court and the provinces had rules to follow.
The chieftain of Miǎndiàn, Buólàlàng, wished to seize the tribute land of Sīhóngfā,
and fabricated a request to the court.
Zǐjùn argued that it should not be granted,
so an edict was issued to stop him.
Guìzhōu Grand Coordinator Chén Yǎn and others, citing the frequent uprisings of the Miáo people in Bōzhōu,
requested to mobilize fifty thousand soldiers from Húguǎng, Guǎngxī, and Sìchuān,
to join with Guìzhōu troops in a combined suppression campaign.
Zǐjùn stated that the bandits were in Sìchuān,
yet Guìzhōu requested to attack them,
implying that they sought to claim credit.
He memorialized to shelve the matter.
Previously,
Zǐjùn had impeached Chén Yuè for slaughtering tribute envoys,
but the Emperor, for the sake of Wāng Zhí, pardoned him.
Yuè, in many ways, tried to implicate Zǐjùn through Zhí.
Coincidentally, Zǐjùn returned home for mourning his mother,
and thus escaped.
When Zǐjùn built the frontier wall,
some doubted that sandy soil would easily collapse,
and that it could not be relied upon when invaders arrived.
By the eighteenth year,
invaders encroached,
and Xǔ Níng and others pursued them.
The invaders, blocked by the wall and trenches,
dispersed and could not escape,
suffering a great defeat.
The border residents increasingly appreciated Zǐjùn's achievements.
After the period of mourning ended,
he was appointed Hùbù Shàngshū,
and soon after, given the additional title of Tàizǐ Tàibǎo.
In the twentieth year, he was ordered to concurrently hold the position of Zuǒ Fù Dū Yùshǐ,
and to serve as supreme commander of military affairs for Dàtóng and Xuānfǔ.
That winter, he returned to court.
The next year, in the first month,
there was a celestial anomaly.
He presented eight criticisms of contemporary弊,
many of which the Emperor adopted.
Not long after,
he again went to inspect the frontier.
Initially,
when Zǐjùn inspected Xuānfǔ and Dàtóng,
he proposed applying the Yánsuí frontier wall method to the two garrisons,
but stopped due to a famine that year.
When he went out again,
he eagerly sought to implement it.
He stated that from Sìhǎiyě in the east,
to the Yellow River in the west,
spanning over one thousand three hundred *lǐ*,
there were previously one hundred seventy beacon towers,
and four hundred forty should be added.
The height and width of the towers should all be three *zhàng*,
estimating eighty-six thousand laborers,
which could be completed in several months.
