An imperial edict ordered the work to begin in the fourth month of the following year.
However, at that time,
the harvests were poor for several years,
public and private resources were depleted,
and suddenly undertaking such a large project
caused difficulty for all.
Zǐjùn also wanted to entrust the responsibility to border officials,
without personally overseeing the matter,
which led to criticism and censure.
By winter,
he submitted a memorial requesting to return to the capital.
The Emperor, believing slanderous rumors,
ordered him to be reassigned as Zuǒ Dū Yùshǐ,
and to serve as Grand Coordinator of Dàtóng.
The eunuch Wéi Jìng slandered Zǐjùn, alleging that he embezzled funds during the border wall repairs,
and further impeached Zǐjùn for private favoritism and resentment,
and for arbitrarily replacing generals.
Bīngbù Shìláng Ruǎn Qín and others defended him.
The Emperor was angry,
and reprimanded Qín and the others.
Furthermore, metropolitan officials and censors repeatedly submitted memorials impeaching him,
and many at court sought to bring down Zǐjùn.
Gōngbù Shìláng Dù Qiān and others went to investigate,
and assessed the situation impartially.
They returned and reported that the replacement of generals was as Qín and the others had stated,
and that there was no private embezzlement of funds.
However, the project cost one million five hundred thousand *liǎng* of silver,
and two million three hundred thousand *shí* of grain and beans,
which exhausted resources and troubled the people, for which he could not be considered blameless.
Consequently, he was stripped of the title of Tàizǐ Tàibǎo,
and retired from office,
which was in the second month of the twenty-second year.
The following year, in the first month,
the position of Bīngbù Shàngshū became vacant.
The Emperor realized that Zǐjùn was not guilty,
and recalled him to serve again,
reinstating his title of Tàizǐ Tàibǎo.
After Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
he treated Zǐjùn, as an elder statesman from the previous reign,
with even greater respect.
In the first year of Hóngzhì, he submitted a memorial detailing ten matters.
Afterwards,
he also presented seven proposals concerning frontier defense,
many of which the Emperor approved.
The following year,
when his illness was critical,
he still personally edited memorial drafts,
proposing strategies to relieve famine and suppress banditry.
He died shortly after his requests were granted,
at the age of sixty-one.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tàibǎo,
and given the posthumous name Sùmǐn.
Zǐjùn was resolute and reticent,
possessing great strategic talent.
All memorials and official documents
he drafted himself,
often not sleeping until midnight.
He once said:
"A high official planning for the state
must bear the advantages and disadvantages personally,
how can one avoid resentment and seek favor as a strategy for self-preservation?"
Therefore, when the Yúlín project began,
a multitude of grievances and criticisms arose,
but Zǐjùn held firm,
ultimately achieving success,
which benefited several generations.
He was by nature filial and fraternal.
During his mother's mourning,
he instructed his son Zhì not to participate in the metropolitan examination,
saying:
"Though there is no law against it,
my heart cannot bear it."
When he was eligible to secure a hereditary position for his son,
he transferred it to his younger brother.
His son Huán,
passed the *jìnshì* examination,
and ultimately served as Hùbù Yuánwàiláng.
Zhì,
obtained a military hereditary position as Jǐnyī Qiānhù,
and ultimately served as Zhīhuī Tóngzhī.
His great-grandsons Chéngxūn and Chéngyè
were both *jìnshì*.
Chéngxūn
was a Hànlín Xiūzhuàn.
Chéngyè
was a Yúnnán Qiānshì.
Ruǎn Qín
was originally from Jiāozhǐ;
his father was internally exiled,
and registered as a resident of Chángzǐ.
Qín passed the *jìnshì* examination in the fifth year of Jǐngtài.
He successively served as Zhīfǔ of Táizhōu.
He was upright, cautious, and implemented beneficial policies,
for which he was granted an imperial edict of commendation.
He served as Yòu Fù Dū Yùshǐ, Grand Coordinator of Shǎnxī.
He built fourteen beacon towers
and repaired walls and trenches for over thirty *lǐ*.
During a famine,
he memorialized to exempt taxes of over four hundred thousand *shí* of grain from seven prefectures.
He was appointed as Shìláng,
and transferred to Nánjīng Xíngbù.
Among foreigners who gained renown in China,
Qín was the most prominent.
Zhū Yīng,
courtesy name Shíjié,
was from Guìyáng.
He was orphaned at five years old.
He studied diligently,
passed the *jìnshì* examination in the tenth year of Zhèngtǒng,
and was appointed Yùshǐ.
When bandits arose in Zhèjiāng and Fújiàn,
thirteen censors were chosen to jointly guard various prefectures with eunuchs.
Yīng guarded Chǔzhōu.
When Yè Zōngliú's faction spread out and plundered,
the roads to Chǔzhōu were blocked.
Yīng rushed there via a hidden path,
and pacified many who surrendered,
executing bandit leaders like Zhōu Míngsōng.
After the bandits dispersed, he returned.
In the early years of the Jǐngtài reign,
Censor Wáng Háo once, in investigating a land dispute involving Chén Xún,
offended Xún
and was impeached by him.
By this time,
Xún drafted an imperial edict
stating that censorial officials who had been impeached,
even if pardoned,
should all be dismissed from their external posts.
Thus, Háo was to be demoted to a county magistrate.
Yīng said,
"If it is as the imperial edict says,
then all those who have been censured by censors
will harbor grudges and falsely impeach them,
and censors will become even more silent."
The memorial was sent to the judicial authorities,
who requested that Yīng's words be followed,
and so Háo's position was restored.
Not long after,
he was sent out as Right Councilor of Guǎngdōng.
Passing through his home to visit his mother,
he had only ten taels of gold bestowed upon him in his purse.
Upon arriving at his post,
he comforted the sick and the displaced.
He established the equal corvée law,
to be changed every ten years,
which the people found convenient.
In the early Tiānshùn reign,
the bandits in the two Guǎng provinces grew more rampant,
and many generals wantonly killed and claimed false achievements.
Grand Coordinator Yè Shèng assigned Yīng to supervise and inspect.
Assistant General Fàn Xìn falsely accused the people of Sòngtài and Yǒngpíng villages of being bandits,
slaughtering almost all of them,
and then intended to slaughter the people of Jìnchéng village.
Yīng hastened to investigate,
and released all of them.
Xìn was furious
and held back his troops, not returning.
Yīng secretly reported to Shèng,
who issued an order for Xìn to withdraw his troops,
and only then did that region become peaceful.
The bandits of Cháozhōu, Luó Liúníng and others, raided far and wide,
repeatedly defeating government troops.
Yīng gathered his troops and crushed them.
He returned thousands of people who had been plundered,
and separately established a camp to house the women,
whom no one dared to violate.
He served as a Councilor for ten years,
and was promoted to Right Administration Commissioner.
He then mourned for his mother.
After the mourning period ended in the early Chénghuà reign,
he was appointed to Shǎnxī.
When the large army campaigned against Mǎn Sì,
Yīng was meritorious in managing provisions and supplies.
He successively served as Right and Left Administration Commissioner of Fújiàn and Shǎnxī,
in all of which he promoted the equal corvée law.
In the tenth year, he was appointed Right Vice Censor-in-Chief to patrol and govern Gānsù,
and successively presented twenty-eight proposals for securing the border.
His requests to relocate soldiers, settle displaced persons, and simplify tribute envoys
were particularly pertinent to the current affairs.
In the winter of the following year,
Wú Chēn, Governor-General of the two Guǎng provinces, died.
The court deliberated that Yīng had credibility and prestige in Guǎngdōng previously,
and so he was appointed to replace Chēn.
Since Hán Yōng's great campaign,
generals and commanders loved to claim achievements
and profited from capturing and plundering,
which was called
"forcible suppression."
When Yīng arrived,
he pacified the region with tranquility,
and disciplined the generals and soldiers,
preventing them from exaggerating the bandits' power
and arbitrarily requesting troops.
He recruited and pacified the Yáo and Zhuàng people who pledged allegiance,
registered them as households,
and granted them tax exemption for three years.
Consequently, the aboriginal people in Mápíng, Yángshuò, Cāngwú, and other counties all submitted at the mere mention of his reputation.
And the Lìbō bandit Lǐ Gōngzhǔ, who commanded tens of thousands of followers
and had long been entrenched,
also sent his son to offer submission.
He established Yǒng'ān Prefecture to settle them,
allowing their descendants to serve as police chiefs for generations.
From then on, the number of those who submitted increased daily,
totaling over forty-three thousand households
and over one hundred and fifty thousand people.
The emperor greatly praised him.
Regarding the seating arrangement for the eunuch in charge of guarding the region, the governor-general, and the commander-in-chief,
the eunuch sat in the middle,
and the governor-general sat to the left of the commander-in-chief.
At that time, Commander-in-Chief Chén Zhèng, as an Earl, wanted to force Yīng to sit to his right,
but Yīng refused,
memorializing to request a ruling.
An imperial decree ordered Yīng to be relieved of his governorship,
serving only as Grand Coordinator,
sitting below Zhèng.
Minister Yú Zǐjùn said that Yīng had achieved much in attracting people,
and should be promoted and rewarded,
but instead his authority was curtailed,
which might make it impossible to pacify the various aboriginal groups.
So Yīng was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief and still served as Governor-General,
with his seating position remaining as before.
Huáng Míng, chieftain of Tiánzhōu, defiled Cén Pǔ's grandmother, the prefect,
and intended to kill Pǔ.
Pǔ fled to Sī'ēn,
and Míng then indulged in slaughter.
Yīng was about to launch a punitive expedition,
but instead ordered Cén Qīn, the Prefect of Ēnchéng and a kinsman of Pǔ, to kill Míng to avenge the shame.
Qīn then executed Míng and his kinsmen,
sending their heads to the military gate.
Yīng was honest and gentle,
yet he enforced the law without leniency.
He clashed with Wéi Juàn, the eunuch in charge of maritime trade,
and Juàn collected evidence and memorialized that Yīng was autocratic and negligent towards bandits.
Shǐ Fāng, Prefect of Xúnzhōu, who had been reprimanded for an incident,
also impeached Yīng for corruption and deception.
Investigations found no evidence for any of these accusations,
so Fāng was demoted by two ranks,
and Juàn was criticized for failing to cooperate.
In the sixteenth year,
Jiāozhǐ attacked Lǎowō,
and some worried that it might invade internally,
so an imperial edict inquired about Yīng's appropriate handling.
Yīng replied that they were merely contending for a border outpost,
and that they should be admonished to regret and fear themselves.
The emperor followed his advice,
and they indeed submitted a memorial expressing apologies.
Bandits arose in Xúnzhōu, Wúzhōu, Gāozhōu, and Liánzhōu,
and Yīng, along with Zhèng and others, attacked them in separate routes.
After two battles,
many were captured and slain.
In the nineteenth year,
the aboriginal people of Guìlín and Pínglè attacked the city and killed a general.
Yīng and Zhèng again divided their troops into twelve routes and crushed them.
The following year, he took charge of the Censorate,
and soon after was made Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
In the first month of the year after that,
there was an astral anomaly,
and he presented a memorial with eight proposals: requesting a ban on border generals offering horses on festive occasions;
forbidding resident eunuchs and military generals from privately establishing manors
and encroaching upon official land;
severe punishment for those who concocted elixirs, used charms, or practiced heterodox arts;
prohibiting supervising eunuchs stationed in various regions from presenting tribute items;
abolishing and withdrawing additional eunuchs in granaries, stables, and the Upper Forest Park;
recalling officials who had been punished for offering remonstrance;
rectifying the accumulated abuses of the imperial household collecting white grain;
and punishing cunning commoners who presented manors, as well as aristocratic relatives who accepted such presentations.
Those in power and their favorites all found these inconvenient,
and many high-ranking officials held them back, preventing their implementation.
Yīng went to the Grand Secretariat and argued strenuously,
but ultimately could not get all of them adopted.
At that time, many displaced people gathered in the capital.
Yīng requested that each person be given three dou of rice monthly,
and half for children,
which was approved.
He died in the autumn of that year.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
As Governor-General, Yīng succeeded Hán Yōng and Wú Chēn.
Although Yōng had great achievements,
he was extravagant in his self-indulgence
and excessively lavish in his gifts,
which burdened officials with provisions,
depleting both public and private resources.
Chēn, however, was careful and incorruptible,
and Yīng was even more steadfast in his integrity,
bringing only one servant with him to his post.
He was repeatedly bestowed with imperial edicts and gold and silk over time,
and Yīng kept the imperial edicts
and stored the gold and silk in the treasury.
His prestige was not equal to Yōng's,
but his benevolence surpassed it.
In Gānsù, he accumulated 300,000 taels in military provisions,
and over 400,000 in Guǎngdōng,
none of which he reported.
Someone asked him about it,
and he replied,
"This is merely the usual duty of a border official,
why speak of it?"
People admired his understanding of the greater good.
During the Zhèngdé reign,
he was posthumously granted the谥号 Shìhào of Gōngjiǎn.
His son, Shǒu Fú,
was a *jìnshì*
and a director in the Ministry of Justice.
Qín Hóng,
courtesy name Shìyīng,
was a native of Dān County.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the second year of Jǐngtài (1451).
He was appointed Nanjing Censor.
He impeached and convicted the eunuch Fù Suǒ'ér
and advised against sending envoys to collect kingfisher feathers and fish roe in Jiāngnán.
The powerful and influential resented him,
and rumors spread about him.
During a performance review,
he was demoted to an驛丞 *yìchéng* (posthouse chief) in Húguǎng.
In the early Tiānshùn reign,
recommended by Censor Liàn Gāng,
he was promoted to Prefect of Xióng Xiàn.
When Palace Steward Dù Jiān was capturing swans and behaving arrogantly,
Hóng beat his followers with a stick,
and was consequently imprisoned by imperial decree.
Five thousand common people went to the imperial court to plead his case,
and he was then transferred to Prefect of Gǔ Zhōu.
Upon Xiànzōng's accession,
he was promoted to Prefect of Jiā Zhōu,
then transferred to Qín Zhōu.
He resigned from office due to his mother's mourning,
but the people of the prefecture requested Hóng to be retained.
After the mourning period ended, he returned to his former post.
Soon after, he was elevated to Prefect of Gǒngchāng,
then transferred to Xī'ān,
and promoted to Right Vice Administrator of Shǎnxī.
When the Fān people of Mín Zhōu rebelled,
he led three thousand troops to defeat them,
and was advanced one rank in salary.
In the thirteenth year of Chénghuà, he was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief,
and made巡抚(Xúnfǔ) of Shānxī.
He impeached Zhuó Zhèngguó Jiāngjūn Qí Jiàn and others for their crimes.
Qí Jiàn's father, Qìngchéng Wáng Zhōng Yì, pleaded on his behalf,
and also slandered Hóng.
The Emperor, reluctant to displease the Prince,
arrested Hóng and sent him to the Ministry of Justice for trial.
All accusations proved groundless.
However, the palace eunuch Shàng Hēng confiscated Hóng's home,
and presented a few worn clothes as evidence of his findings.
The Emperor sighed, saying:
"Is Hóng truly this poor?"
He was bestowed ten thousand strings of paper money in commendation.
Consequently, Qí Jiàn and two others were stripped of their titles,
the Prince's salary was also reduced by one-third,
and Hóng was reassigned as巡抚(Xúnfǔ) of Hénán.
Soon after, he was again transferred to Xuānfǔ.
When the Xiǎo Wángzǐ led tens of thousands of cavalry to raid Dàtóng,
they advanced deep into Shùnshèng Chuān,
plundering the Xuānfǔ territory.
Hóng, with Grand Coordinator Zhōu Yù and others, intercepted and attacked them,
and they fled.
Soon after, they raided Xīngníng Kǒu,
and after continuous battles, they were repelled.
The stolen goods were recovered,
and an imperial edict commended him.
He was promoted to Left Vice Censor-in-Chief,
and continued his duties as巡抚(Xúnfǔ).
Not long after,
he was recalled to manage affairs in the Censorate,
and promoted to Right Vice Minister of the Ministry of Revenue.
When Wàn Ān expelled Yǐn Mín,
he falsely accused Hóng of being Mín's partisan,
and Hóng was demoted to Right Vice Administrator of Guǎngxī.
He was then promoted to Left Administration Commissioner of Fújiàn.
In the first year of Hóngzhì, upon Wáng Shù's recommendation,
he was elevated to Left Deputy Censor-in-Chief,
and supervised the grain transport.
In the third month of the following year, he was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief,
and appointed Grand Coordinator of Military Affairs for Guǎngdōng and Guǎngxī.
He memorialized, stating:
"The palace eunuchs and military commanders who serve as Grand Coordinators in Guǎngdōng and Guǎngxī,
often allow their private retainers to harass merchants,
live in lavish private residences,
arbitrarily handle public affairs,
murder the innocent,
and collude with local officials for illicit gain.
Furthermore, all garrison commanders throughout the empire are permitted to arbitrarily assume military authority
and accept civilian lawsuits,
which is contrary to regulations.
I request that this be strictly prohibited.
The Grand Coordinator's residence formerly had a 'Merit Award Office,'
which stored tens of thousands in gold and silver annually.
Expenditures were unrecorded;
it should be audited by the Censor-in-Chief.
Guǎngzhōu, Cháozhōu, Nánxióng, and Sháozhōu have many bandits;
therefore, community schools should be established,
and the *bǎojiǎ* system implemented,
to eliminate the source of banditry."
The Emperor granted all his requests.
Cén Qīn, the Prefect of Ēnchéng, attacked and expelled Cén Pǔ, the Prefect of Tiánzhōu,
and along with Cén Yìng, the Prefect of Sìchéng, they divided the territory amongst themselves.
Hóng entered Tiánzhōu, expelled Qīn,
restored Pǔ to his prefecture,
and left imperial troops to garrison it,
whereupon the rebellion was settled.
He then dispatched generals to suppress the Lí bandits in Língshuǐ
and the Yáo bandits in Déqìng.
When Hóng first took up his post as Grand Coordinator,
he impeached the Grand Coordinator, Ānyuǎn Hóu Liǔ Jǐng, for corruption and tyranny,
who was then arrested and imprisoned.
Jǐng also accused Hóng,
but the investigation found no corroborating evidence,
and the Ministry of Justice determined Jǐng deserved death.
Jǐng was related by marriage to Empress Dowager Zhōu's family,
and had powerful connections.
He continued to accuse Hóng.
An imperial edict ordered Hóng's arrest as well.
The court trial ultimately found him innocent.
An imperial edict pardoned Jǐng's death sentence,
stripping him of his title and ordering him to reside at home,
while Hóng was also dismissed and returned home.
Ministers like Wáng Shù requested Hóng be retained,
but this was not accepted.
Court officials then repeatedly memorialized that Hóng was fit for greater use.
After several months,
he was appointed Minister of Revenue for Nánjīng.
In the eleventh year, he resigned due to illness.
In the autumn of the fourteenth year,
raiders made a major incursion into Huāmǎ Chí,
defeating government troops at Kǒngbà Gōu,
and directly reaching Píngliáng.
Those who spoke said that Hóng had a reputation for prestige and,
though old, could still be employed.
An imperial edict appointed him Minister of Revenue concurrently with Right Deputy Censor-in-Chief,
and Grand Coordinator of Military Affairs for the Three Borders.
Hóng quickly arrived at Gùyuán,
and inspected the scene of the defeat.
He personally sacrificed to the fallen generals and soldiers,
and buried their remains.
He memorialized for the commendation of the five deceased commanders, including Zhū Dǐng,
and offered condolences to the families of soldiers killed in battle.
He impeached and punished four defeated generals, including Yáng Lín,
and replaced the garrison commanders.
He trained valiant soldiers,
promoted military agricultural colonies,
and reissued clear orders,
greatly boosting military morale.
Initially,
before the raiders entered the Hétào region,
Píngliáng and Gùyuán were internal regions with no threat.
Since Bèi Lái settled there,
Gùyuán became a military crossroads,
serving as the gateway for Píngliáng, Qìngyáng, Líntáo, and Gǒngchāng.
However, the city was narrow, the people poor,
and military strength weak,
so merchants did not come.
Hóng then expanded and renovated the city walls,
attracted merchants,
and proposed its redesignation as a zhōu (prefecture),
while he himself remained to oversee it.
He memorialized, stating:
"Gùyuán's main and auxiliary forces number only eighteen thousand men,
scattered to guard twenty-four fortresses.
Their strength is divided and weak;
more troops are needed.
The former armies of Líntáo, Gǒngchāng, and Qínzhōu annually went to Gānzhōu and Liángzhōu for defense.
When there were alarms elsewhere,
troops were again transferred to Gānzhōu and Liángzhōu,
or imperial troops were dispatched for campaigns.
Now, the capital is the foundation of the empire,
and border generals hold significant military power.
Yet, whenever an incident occurs, they request imperial troops.
This is not the way to strengthen the trunk and weaken the branches.
I request that from now on, imperial troops not be lightly dispatched,
and the armies of Líntáo, Gǒngchāng, Gānzhōu, and Liángzhōu should each return to their respective garrisons.
Only select one or two experienced and knowledgeable generals to each guard their territory.
Let the people consider the garrison their home,
and the army consider the general their life.
They will then willingly perform their duties,
and have the will to fight.
This is the optimal strategy."
Qín Hóng saw that the area north of Gùyuán stretched for a thousand *lǐ*,
with hundreds of thousands of *qǐng* of idle land,
and the wilderness near the border
had no fortresses to rely on.
He proposed that from Huāmǎchí west to Xiǎoyánchí, a distance of two hundred *lǐ*,
a fortress be built every twenty *lǐ*.
Each fortress was to have a circumference of forty-eight *zhàng*,
and be manned by five hundred soldiers.
At various locations north of Gùyuán, garrison strongholds were also to be built.
People were to be recruited to settle and cultivate the land,
with an annual tax of five *shí* of rice per *qǐng*,
which could yield five hundred thousand *shí*.
The plan was finalized,
but Liú Xiàn, the巡fǔ of Níngxià, obstructed it.
Qín Hóng then memorialized, saying:
"I humbly observe the situation of the Three Borders:
Yánsuī, Gān, and Liáng, though extensive in territory,
have strong and elite cavalry.
Níngxià is timid and weak,
yet its rivers and mountains are perilous.
Only from Huāmǎchí to Gùyuán,
the troops are already weak,
and the watchtowers are sparse,
allowing enemy cavalry to drive deep into our territory.
Therefore, we must increase the construction of watchtowers and fortresses.
The same applies to Wéizhōu, Yùwàngchéng, and other places.
Now, the construction south of Gùyuán is almost complete.
Only the two hundred *lǐ* north of Huāmǎchí
requires the building of ten fortresses.
However, Xiàn's alarmist words are deterring the public
and abandoning a功 that is nearly finished.
I beg that Xiàn be put in charge of the Three Borders,
and I be reassigned as the巡fǔ of Níngxià,
so that I may complete the border defenses.
This would be more convenient for the matter."
The Emperor issued an edict reproaching Xiàn.
Xiàn admitted his fault
and ultimately carried out Qín Hóng's plan.
Over fourteen thousand border fortresses and strongholds were built,
and over six thousand four hundred *lǐ* of walls and moats.
Gùyuán stood firm as a major strategic town.
Qín Hóng also ingeniously designed a battle chariot,
named
"Quánshèng Chē" (All-Victorious Chariot).
An imperial edict ordered its design to be distributed to all border regions.
After three years in office,
the four border towns were peaceful.
No previous strategists in the western frontier could compare.
In the seventeenth year, he was granted the title of Tàizǐ Shàobǎo
and recalled to oversee ministerial affairs.
Due to his advanced age, he repeatedly memorialized to resign,
requesting retirement.
An edict granted him an imperial rescript and an official carriage to return home,
with monthly grain rations and annual stipends as prescribed.
He died in the ninth month of the following year,
aged eighty.
He was posthumously granted Shàobǎo
and given the posthumous title Xiāngyì.
Qín Hóng was upright and detached from worldly pursuits;
his wife and children often went hungry with only vegetable soup and wheat gruel.
He was resolute by nature,
courageous in eliminating harm,
and disregarded his own interests.
Scholars and officials, whether acquainted or not, called him a great man.
When he was arrested in Liǎngguǎng,
he was still discussing the suppression of mountain bandits.
After finishing his military duties,
he calmly set off,
his retinue and attendants undiminished.
Only after crossing the mountain range
did he put on prison clothes and submit to detention.
He said to the guards:
"In Liǎngguǎng, where barbarians and Chinese intermingle,
the Governor-General's status is honored.
To be immediately seized would damage the nation's prestige.
Now that we have crossed the range,
I am truly a prisoner."
Such was his solemnity and decorum.
In the fifth year of Zhèngdé,
Liú Jǐn caused political turmoil.
Qín Hóng's household servant resented Qín Hóng's wife's brother, Yáng Jǐn.
The servant handed a fire cannon left by Qín Hóng to an investigating officer,
falsely accusing Yáng Jǐn of possessing prohibited military equipment.
Liú Jǐn was enraged
and blamed Qín Hóng.
His house was searched,
but nothing was found.
Censors Zhāng Jiǔ and Tú Jìng, seeking to please Liú Jǐn, impeached Qín Hóng again.
The literati scorned them.
A eulogy says: Xiàng Zhōng and Hán Yōng both entered officialdom through literary excellence,
yet personally took command on the battlefield
and achieved military distinction.
Their ability to adapt to circumstances and secure victory,
and their well-conceived long-term strategies,
surpassed even seasoned generals.
How grand!
Yet rewards often fell short of their efforts,
and slanders arose afterwards.
Legalistic officials then sought to punish them,
a source of frustration and deep sighs for those seeking fame and achievement.
Yú Zǐjùn devoted himself to border strategies,
which benefited several generations.
Zhū Yīng was revered in Guǎngdōng,
and Qín Hóng's strategies distinguished him in the western frontier.
They possessed both civil and military talents,
truly great ministers of their generation!
Collated Notes
Biographies, Volume Sixty-Seven: Luó Lún (Tú Fěi),
Zhāng Mào (his nephew Zhěng), Huáng Zhòngzhāo, Zhuāng (character missing) Zōu Zhì, Shū Fēn (Cuī Tóng, Mǎ Rújí).
Luó Lún,
courtesy name Yízhèng,
from Yǒngfēng, Jí'ān.
At the age of five, he once followed his mother into a garden.
When fruit fell,
everyone scrambled for it,
but Luó Lún only accepted it after being offered.
His family was poor, so he gathered firewood and tended livestock,
always carrying a book and reciting continuously.
When he became a scholar,
he devoted himself to the learning of the sages.
He once said:
"Examinations do not corrupt people;
people corrupt themselves."
Zhāng Xuān, the Prefect, pitied his poverty
and offered him grain,
which he politely refused.
During his parents' mourning,
he abstained from salt and dairy
until after the Grand Sacrifice.
In the second year of Chénghuà,
he took the palace examination,
submitting a policy essay of over ten thousand words.
He directly criticized the ills of the time,
his fame shaking the capital.
He was ranked first in the *jìnshì* examination
and appointed Hanlin Xiūzhuàn.
Two months later,
Grand Secretary Lǐ Xián returned to court by imperial edict
after completing his mourning.
Luó Lún went to Lǐ Xián to discourage him,
but he did not listen.
So, Luó Lún submitted a memorial, saying: "I hear that the court, citing the precedent of Yáng Pǔ,
has recalled Grand Secretary Lǐ Xián to office.
I humbly submit that Lǐ Xián is a great minister,
and his recall to office is a major matter,
affecting moral principles and public customs.
Therefore, it must not be taken lightly.
Formerly, Your Majesty's policy essay stated:
'I, day and night, earnestly desire to rectify the main principles
and manage all affairs,
so that human relations are enlightened above
and customs are enriched below.'
I humbly submit that to enlighten human relations
and enrich customs,
nothing comes before filial piety.
According to ritual,
if a son is in mourning for his parents,
the ruler does not call at his gate for three years.
Zǐxià asked:
'During the three-year mourning period,
is it ritual to not avoid military service?'
Confucius said:
'Lǔ Gōng Bóqín did so for a specific reason.
But now, to take advantage of the three-year mourning
for one's own benefit,
I do not understand it.'
Your Majesty, regarding Lǐ Xián,
do you recall him to office
as if it were a matter of military emergency?
Then no such emergency exists.
Do you recall him to office
as a great minister?
Then it is not seen in ritual.
As a ruler,
one should use the rites of the former kings to teach one's ministers;
as a minister,
one should observe the rites of the former kings to serve one's ruler.
In the past, Sòng Rénzōng once recalled
Fù Bì to office.
Fù Bì declined, saying:
'I dare not follow precedents to continue the wrongs of previous eras;
I should only act according to the *Lǐjīng* to do what is right today.'
Rénzōng ultimately acceded
to his request.
Xiàozōng once recalled Liú Gǒng to office.
Liú Gǒng declined, saying:
'While I am in the wilderness,
the country has no external enemies at its gates.
It would be difficult to assume the name of military necessity
and privately
usurp the reality of gain and emolument.'
Xiàozōng did not suppress his feelings.
These two rulers
never compelled their ministers with precedents.
These two ministers
never yielded to precedents.
His lord.
Therefore, historical records write of it as a grand affair,
and scholar-officials傳 it as a beautiful tale.
There is no other reason:
the lord was able to teach his minister filial piety,
and the minister had filial piety that could be transferred to
his lord.
From then on,
there was no longer ritual propriety and righteousness.
Wáng Fǔ, Shǐ Sōngzhī, Chén Yízhōng, Jiǎ Sī Dào, and their like,
all invoked old precedents to be recalled to office (qǐfù).
However,
the world fell into chaos,
the state was in peril,
causing disaster at the time,
and leaving ridicule for later generations.
There is no other reason:
the lord did not teach his minister filial piety,
and the minister had no filial piety that could be transferred to his lord.
If Your Majesty must appoint Xián to take charge of the affairs of the world,
then Xián cannot be retained,
but a tangible justification can be given.
An encouraging imperial edict should be issued,
allowing him to speak on affairs, just as Liú Gǒng did.
Make it so that when Xián knows of something regarding the affairs of the world, he must speak,
and when he speaks, he must speak fully.
When Your Majesty hears Xián's words, you must act upon them,
and when you act, you must do so with vigor.
Even if Xián is not recalled to office,
it is as if he is
recalled.
If he knows but cannot speak fully,
or speaks but cannot act vigorously,
then even if Xián is recalled to office, it will be useless.
Furthermore, Your Majesty should not say that there are no worthy ministers in the imperial court,
or no worthy scholars among the various officials.
The lord
is the vessel;
the minister
is the water.
The shape of the water—whether square or round—
is truly determined by the vessel.
The uprightness or crookedness of ministers
is truly summoned by the lord.
If Your Majesty genuinely, during leisure after court,
associates with ministers who are upright, honest, and extensively knowledgeable,
discusses the essentials of sagely learning and imperial virtue,
inquires about the successes and
failures of government,
investigates the welfare and hardships of the people,
seeks out the worthiness or unworthiness of talent,
examines the rise and fall of ancient and modern times,
abandons the partiality of solitary trust,
and accepts unpalatable but truthful advice,
then all worthy individuals and their
strategies will converge at court.
Why then would one need to violate the ritual classics of the former kings,
and damage the reputation and integrity of great ministers,
before the world can be governed?
Your servant humbly observes that in recent years,
the court has made "dispensing with mourning" (duóqíng) a regular practice,
and scholar-officials consider "recall to office" (qǐfù) a good name.
Those who eat rice and wear brocade
crowd the court
halls,
but I do not know what connection these people have to the important affairs of the world.
Moreover, a wife observes three years of mourning for her parents-in-law,
and a grandchild observes mourning of the "qícuī" (齊衰) rank for grandparents.
To dispense with mourning
for one's husband
originally had nothing to do with his wife.
To dispense with mourning for one's father
originally had nothing to do with his son.
Now, some retain their residences as before,
and their wives and children do not return,
yet they proclaim to the world
saying,
"I
originally intended to complete the mourning period,
but the imperial command did not permit it."
Even a three-foot child,
your servant knows, would not believe it.
The hope of a father for his son's repayment,
how could
it ever reach this point?
The heart of a son in repaying his parent,
how could he bear to reach this point?
One who wrongs himself cannot correct others;
one who forgets his parents cannot
be loyal to his lord.
What does Your Majesty gain from such people,
that you recall them to office?
Now, when great ministers are recalled to office,
other ministers do not consider it wrong,
but rather assent to it.
When other ministers are recalled to office,
great ministers do not consider it wrong,
but rather assist in their
success.
Upper and lower levels form a custom,
mingling in the same current,
leading the people of the world to become without fathers.
Your servant cannot bear for this sagely and enlightened court
to reach such a point where the cardinal principles are ruined,
and customs
are corrupted,
to this extreme.
I wish Your Majesty would make a decisive decree from your sagely heart,
allowing Xián to return home and observe mourning.
For others already recalled to office,
order them to go for the funeral;
for those not
yet recalled,
allow them all to complete the mourning period.
Should there be a crisis of war,
they may exercise the expedient of "mòcuī" (墨衰),
allowing them to handle military affairs outside,
while fulfilling their filial mourning internally.
Then the court
will be upright, and the world will be unified;
great ministers will set the example, and other ministers will follow;
human relations will thereby be clarified,
and customs will thereby be made profound.
The memorial was submitted,
and he was demoted to Vice Supervising Secretary of the Fújiàn Maritime Trade Commissioner.
Censor Chén Xuǎn submitted a memorial to save him,
but it was not answered.
Censor Yáng Láng again pleaded for him,
and the Emperor severely reprimanded him.
Minister Wáng Áo, citing Wén Yànbó's rescue of Táng Jiè, implicitly advised Xián,
and Xián said:
"The Duke of Lù was showing favor and shifting blame to the court;
I cannot emulate him."
Not long after,
Xián died.
The following year, based on the words of Grand Academician Shāng Lù, he was recalled to his original post,
and transferred to Nánjīng.
After two years,
he resigned due to illness and returned home,
never again to emerge.
Lún was upright and steadfast,
strict with himself.
Where righteousness lay,
he would resolutely act,
and was indifferent to wealth, status, and fame.
In his hometown, he advocated and implemented the village compact (xiāngyuē),
and people followed it without daring to transgress.
His food and clothing were coarse;
if someone gifted him clothes,
he would see someone fallen by the roadside,
and remove them to cover the person.
One morning he kept a guest for a drink,
and his wife and children borrowed grain from a neighbor;
it was noon before they cooked,
but he was unconcerned.
Because Jīnniú Shān was inaccessible to human footsteps,
he built a house and wrote books there,
and many scholars from all directions came to study with him.
He died in the fourteenth year,
at the age of forty-eight.
At the beginning of Jiājìng's reign,
following the request of Censor Táng Lóng,
he was posthumously granted the title of Assistant Tutor of the Left Spring Palace,
and given the posthumous name Wényì.
Scholars referred to him as Master Yīfēng.
When Lún was the Supervising Secretary,
Censor Tú Fěi of Fēngchéng was inspecting Fújiàn.
The Palace Eunuch of the Directorate of Ceremonial, Huáng Cì,
was from Yánpíng.
He requested an audience,
but Fěi refused.
Lǐ Zōngxué, the Prefect of Quánzhōu, was impeached by Fěi for accepting bribes,
and impeached Fěi in self-defense.
Cì secretly assisted in submitting his memorial.
Fěi and Zōngxué were both summoned for inquiry,
and the testimony implicated Lún,
who was also to be arrested.
A certain official from the Garrison Command said:
"Can Master Luó come to this?"
The case was concluded and reported that day.
Lún was spared,
and Fěi was also reinstated to office.
Fěi,
a *jìnshì* in the fourth year of Tiānshùn.
During the Chenghuà era, he once said:
“In the imperial courts of the ancestors,
political affairs were always discussed face-to-face with the high ministers.
Ever since the former emperor was young,
and unable to make decisions,
those who held the reins of government, fearing omissions,
used the pretext of 'simplicity'
to facilitate pronouncements.
Whenever there was a court audience for presenting memorials,
the imperial edicts often said, 'The relevant office knows this.'
This was a temporary expedient,
not something that should be followed as a permanent system.
Moreover, many imperial rescripts were influenced by eunuchs,
and the Grand Secretariat sometimes had no say,
which was even more contrary to the ancestral system.
I beg for the resumption of face-to-face discussions,
to prevent the evils of obstruction and concealment.”
Xiànzōng could not adopt this.
He ended his career as a Vice Commissioner of Guǎngdōng.
Zhāng Mào,
courtesy name Démào,
was a native of Lánxī.
In the second year of Chenghuà, he placed first in the metropolitan examination,
became a *jìnshì*,
and was appointed as a *shùjíshì*.
In the winter of the following year,
he was appointed Compiler.
Xiànzōng was planning to display lanterns for the Yuánxī festival,
and ordered court poets to compose poems and lyrics for presentation.
Mào and his colleague Huáng Zhòngzhāo, and Reviser Zhuāng Móu, jointly memorialized, saying:
“Recently, Your Majesty instructed your ministers to compose poems and lyrics for the 'Áoshan' firework display.
Your ministers humbly believe
that this cannot be Your Majesty’s true intention,
but perhaps, with the two empress dowagers above,
you wish to fully demonstrate filial piety and please them.
However, true filial piety lies in nurturing their will,
not merely presenting trivial amusements for their eyes and ears as nourishment.
Currently, eastern Chuān is not yet pacified,
Liáozuǒ faces many anxieties,
Jiāngxī and Húguǎng are barren for thousands of *lǐ*,
the myriad people are wailing,
gaping for sustenance.
This is precisely the time when Your Majesty should be toiling day and night with anxiety,
and the two empress dowagers should share the world's worries.
As for Hanlin officials, whose duty it is to deliberate and advise,
how can vulgar words be presented to the emperor?
We humbly read Emperor Xuānzōng's imperial admonition for the Hanlin Academy, which states: 'Words of counsel,
only righteousness and benevolence.
The Way of Yáo and Shùn,
presented by Zōu and Lǔ.'
How can displaying lanterns be the Way of Yáo and Shùn? How can poems and lyrics be words of benevolence and righteousness?
If it is said that fireworks are trivial matters that do not tarnish sacred virtue,
then why did Shùn not make lacquerware?
Why did Yǔ not enjoy fine wine?
Why did Hàn Wén not build a 'dew-collecting terrace'?
Ancient emperors, who were cautious even in small matters and scrupulous in minor conduct,
did so precisely because desires must not be indulged,
and evil tendencies must not be allowed to grow.
We humbly beg that the fireworks be stopped,
that this attention be redirected to seeing clearly and hearing acutely,
and that these funds be used to relieve the hungry and assist the distressed.
Then disasters can be averted,
and great peace can be achieved.”
The emperor considered displaying lanterns for Yuánxī an ancestral custom,
detested Mào and others’ presumptuous words,
and had them all beaten at the palace gate,
demoting their official ranks.
Reviser Luó Lún had previously been dismissed for speaking out;
at the time, they were called
“The Four Hanlin Remonstrants.”
Mào was demoted to Magistrate of Línwǔ,
but before he could depart,
due to the intercession of Grand Supervisor of the Six Offices Máo Hóng and others,
he was reassigned as a Left Judicial Reviewer of the Grand Court of Judicial Review in Nánjīng.
After more than three years,
he was promoted to Assistant Surveillance Commissioner of Fújiàn.
He pacified the rebels in Tàiníng, Shā, and Yóu;
allowed the people of Fú’ān to mine to cut off sources of banditry;
and proposed mutual trade with foreign goods to enrich merchants and commoners.
His administrative achievements were very notable.
After completing his term and returning to the capital,
though only forty-one years old,
he strongly sought to retire.
Minister of Personnel Yǐn Mín insisted on retaining him,
but he refused.
After returning home,
he lived in seclusion and did not enter official circles.
In his leisure time from serving his parents,
he devoted himself entirely to reading and lecturing,
and the number of disciples who came with classics to study increased daily.
Poor and without means,
he lived only on coarse rice and vegetable soup.
Scholars and grandees from all directions highly esteemed his character,
calling him Mr. Fēngshān.
He lived at home for over twenty years;
officials both inside and outside the court repeatedly recommended him,
and ministerial summonses frequently called him to office,
but he steadfastly refused, citing his elderly parents.
During the Hóngzhì era,
Xiàozōng appointed many virtuous men.
It was widely agreed that eminent scholars should head the national academies in both capitals.
Xiè Duó was called to the Northern Directorate of Education.
When the position of Libationer for the Southern Directorate became vacant,
Mào was appointed to fill it.
Mào was then mourning his father and did not take the post.
At that time, the position of Director of Studies in the Southern Directorate had been vacant for nearly twenty years.
An imperial edict specifically appointed Luó Qīnshùn to that position,
leaving the Libationer post vacant to await Mào.
In the sixteenth year,
after the mourning period,
Mào again firmly declined.
This was not permitted,
so he finally assumed the office,
and the students in the six academies each felt they had gained a true teacher.
Yóu Yuè, a *guózǐshēng*, had a sick mother,
and by regulation was not allowed to return home to visit her;
he wept day and night.
Mào sent him home,
saying:
“I would rather incur guilt for violating regulations.”
When Wǔzōng ascended the throne,
he presented five matters: diligence in sacred studies, honoring continuation of legacy, prudence in grand marriage, reverence for imperial edicts, and respect for heavenly warnings.
In the first year of Zhèngdé, he sought retirement,
but his five memorials were not granted.
He again pleaded illness and earnestly resigned,
and in the third month of the following year, his request was finally granted.
In the fifth year, he was appointed Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices in Nánjīng;
the following year, he was again appointed Right Vice Minister of Rites in Nánjīng,
but he firmly declined both.
Remonstrators repeatedly spoke of Mào’s virtue and reputation,
requesting special courtesies for him.
An edict ordered local officials to visit him annually.
When Shìzōng succeeded to the throne,
he was immediately appointed Minister of Rites in Nánjīng from his home,
and then retired.
That winter,
an envoy was dispatched to inquire after him,
but Mào had already passed away,
at the age of eighty-six.
He was posthumously granted the title of Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent
and given the posthumous name Wén Yì.
In his scholarship, Mào
scrupulously adhered to the teachings of earlier Confucian scholars.
Someone once suggested he write essays;
he said:
“That is a minor skill;
I have no time for it.”
When someone advised him to write books,
he said:
“The words of earlier Confucian scholars are complete;
it is enough to prune their complexities.”
He was an official for over fifty years,
but his total salary terms barely exceeded three full assessments.
He was difficult to promote and easy to retire,
and all generations esteemed him for this.
He had three sons,
and made them all engage in farming.
When the county magistrate visited him,
his sons put down their plows and knelt to welcome him,
and no one knew they were sons of a high official.
His son visited Mào in the Southern Directorate,
traveling on foot.
On the way, he was flogged by a patrol inspector.
When Mào found out, he asked for the inspector to be punished,
but Mào consoled and dismissed him.
In his later years,
all three of his sons and one grandson died.
At eighty-two, he had a young son, Jiē,
who later became a *guózǐshēng* through imperial favor.
Cóng Zǐzhěng
had the courtesy name Yǐdào.
As a child, he studied under Mào.
He passed the imperial examination as a *jìnshì* in the 15th year of Hóngzhì (1502),
and served as a Principal of the Ministry of Justice.
In the early years of Zhèngdé,
he offended Liú Jǐn,
and was imprisoned in the imperial dungeons.
He was demoted to Assistant Prefect of Wúzhōu Prefecture.
When Jǐn was executed,
he was promoted to Director of the Nanjing Ministry of War.
During the Jiājìng era,
he successively rose to the position of Minister of Works.
Guì È wished to revive sea transport,
and invited high officials to discuss its pros and cons.
Zhěng said:
"Although sea transport has historical precedents,
the winds and waves are a hundred times worse than those on the river.
Moreover, the Tianjin estuary is heavily silted,
and since ancient times, no one has been known to dredge the sea."
The proposal was thus dropped.
When the debate over the Southern and Northern Suburbs arose,
Zhěng argued against it,
displeasing the emperor.
Soon after, he was dismissed from office and sent home
for a shortage in the supply of sacrificial vessels at the suburban altars.
After a long time, he was reinstated.
He retired
and died.
Huáng Zhòngzhāo,
whose given name was Qián,
was known by his courtesy name.
He was from Pútián.
His grandfather, Shòu shēng,
was an Academician Reviser of the Hànlín Academy,
renowned for his scholarship and conduct.
His father, Jiā,
was the Magistrate of Shùlù,
known for his good governance.
Zhòngzhāo was upright and diligent by nature.
At the age of fifteen or sixteen, he already aspired to orthodox learning.
He passed the imperial examination as a *jìnshì* in the 2nd year of Chénghuà (1466),
and was appointed a *shùjíshì*,
then awarded the post of Compiler.
Along with Zhāng Mào and Zhuāng Huì, he was caned for his direct remonstrance
and demoted to Magistrate of Xiāngtán.
While en route,
following the recommendation of a remonstrating official,
he was reassigned as a Judicial Reviewer in the Nanjing Grand Court of Revision.
It was customary for the various departments in both capitals to dismiss their subordinate clerks and attendants but still collect their monthly stipends.
Only Zhòngzhāo and Luó Lún
did not take them.
When a Censor's sons and younger brothers accepted bribes,
the Ministry of Justice bent the law to accommodate them,
but Zhòngzhāo corrected and rectified it.
When a group of people abducted and resold civilian women,
the Ministry only sentenced one ringleader.
Zhòngzhāo requested that all of them be punished.
He successively suffered the loss of both his parents,
and did not leave his mourning hut for four years.
After the mourning period ended,
feeling that he had been unable to care for his parents,
he did not return to officialdom.
When Hóngzhì was established as a new reign era,
Censor Jiāng Hóng submitted a memorial recommending him,
and Minister of Personnel Wáng Shù dispatched officials to urge him to take up office.
When he arrived,
Shù went to the main gate to greet him,
and after mutual bows, they ascended the hall,
bowing to each other again.
The world considered both highly.
He was appointed Surveillance Commissioner of Education for Jiāngxī,
teaching scholars orthodox learning.
After a long time, he submitted another memorial requesting retirement,
and devoted himself to writing.
Scholars called him Mr. Wèixuān.
He died at the age of seventy-four.
Zhòngzhāo's elder brother, Shēn,
was a Censor.
Shēn's son, Qiánhēng,
was an Official of the Bureau of Messengers.
He was sent as an envoy to Mǎlájiā (Malacca),
and died at sea.
Qiánhēng's son, Rújīn,
was a Vice Surveillance Commissioner of Education for Guǎngxī;
Xīyōng
was an Assistant Prefect of Sūzhōu.
Zhòngzhāo's grandson, Mào,
was an Assistant Minister of the Nanjing Ministry of Revenue.
Zhuāng Huì,
courtesy name Kǒngyáng,
was from Jiāngpǔ.
From a young age, he was grand and unconventional,
fond of ancient texts and widely learned.
He passed the imperial examination as a *jìnshì* in the 2nd year of Chénghuà (1466),
and was appointed a *shùjíshì*,
then awarded the post of Compiler in the Hànlín Academy.
Along with Compiler Zhāng Mào and Huáng Zhòngzhāo, he memorialized against the lighting of lanterns in the inner court,
which displeased the emperor, and he was caned twenty times in court.
He was demoted to Assistant Magistrate of Guìyáng Department.
Soon after, due to intercession by remonstrating officials,
he was reassigned as a Vice Commissioner of the Nanjing Bureau of Messengers.
After three years,
he left due to his mother's death.
Subsequently, he suffered his father's death,
grieved and became emaciated.
After the mourning period, he did not return to office.
He settled in Dìngshān for over twenty years,
and scholars called him Mr. Dìngshān.
Grand Coordinator Wáng Shù once wished to repair his dwelling,
but he declined.
Huì did not particularly value writing during his lifetime.
Whatever insights he gained
were often expressed in poetry.
More than ten recommendations were submitted,
and official dispatches repeatedly urged him,
but he never responded.
Grand Secretary Qiū Jùn always disliked Huì,
and told others:
"It is Huì
who leads the scholars of the empire to turn their backs on the court."
In the 7th year of Hóngzhì (1494), someone recommended Huì,
and an imperial edict summoned him to take up office.
Huì, considering that Jùn was in power,
feared that not going would lead to punishment,
so he reluctantly went to the capital.
Grand Secretary Xú Pǔ told Director Shào Bǎo:
"Mr. Dìngshān was formerly in the Hànlín Academy;
reinstate him."
Jùn heard this and said:
"I do not know anyone called Dìngshān."
So, he was only reinstated as a Vice Commissioner of the Bureau of Messengers.
Soon after, he was promoted to Director of the Nanjing Ministry of Personnel,
and suffered from a stroke.
The following year, he requested retirement,
but the ministerial officials did not memorialize for him.
The year after that, during the metropolitan evaluation,
Minister Ní Yuè dismissed him due to old age and illness.
He died two years later
at the age of sixty-three.
In the early years of Tiānqǐ,
he was posthumously granted the title Wénjié.
Zōu Zhì,
courtesy name Rǔyú,
was from Hézhōu.
At the age of twelve, he could write essays.
His family was poor,
and he studied by burning tree leaves to extend the daylight for three years.
He ranked first in the provincial examination of the 22nd year of Chénghuà (1486).
At that time, the emperor was increasingly weary of governance,
while Wàn Ān, Liú Jí, and Yǐn Zhí held positions in the government.
Zhì was indignant.
Passing through Sānyuán,
he visited the retired Minister Wáng Shù,
and passionately said:
"To govern the empire,
one must promote gentlemen and dismiss petty individuals.
Currently, petty individuals are in power,
poisoning the four seas,
yet you, Sir, choose to remain in retirement in the countryside.
My journey this time is not for official rank;
I wish to submit a memorial to the Son of Heaven,
to distinguish between the worthy and the villainous,
and to save these people from dire straits."
Shù was surprised by his words,
and smiled without replying.
The following year, he passed the *jìnshì* examination.
He was appointed a *shùjíshì*.
He then submitted a memorial stating: "Your Majesty, regarding your Grand Secretaries,
you always consult them on matters,
and extend extraordinary favors and special treatment to them;
this can be said to be entrusting them.
However, when it comes to appointing or dismissing an individual,
or handling a specific matter,
you
often issue imperial edicts from within the palace,
allowing one or two petty individuals to secretly hold sway.
This is entrusting them and then doubting them.
Does Your Majesty not wish to treat others with sincerity?
It
is because many of them gained their positions through private channels at the outset,
and have already incurred Your Majesty's displeasure.
When they participate in discussions,
they are overly deferential and cautious,
timid and hesitant,
as
if they dare not do anything.
They are, in fact, inferior to one or two common officials in their ability to handle affairs.
This is why Your Majesty doubts them,
but I humbly believe this to be a mistake.
In the past, Sòng Rénzōng, knowing
Xià Sǒng to be deceitful, dismissed him;
knowing Lǚ Yíjiǎn could correct his faults, he tolerated him;
and knowing Dù Yǎn, Hán Qí, Fàn Zhòngyān, and Fù Bí could be entrusted, he promoted them without regard to rank.
Zhī,
hence they could repel the Qìdān in the north,
and make Yuánhào their vassal in the west.
Never have I heard of a policy that involved alternating trust and suspicion
being able to accomplish great things in the world.
I pray Your Majesty discern who is Sǒng,
and who
is Yíjiǎn,
then dismiss or tolerate them accordingly; and who is Yǎn, Qí, Zhòngyān, Bì, and promote them.
Discuss the way of governance with them daily,
and do not allow petty individuals to participate therein,
then heaven's will shall surely be manifest.
Your servant also hears that only the grand counselors can deliberate on affairs of the realm,
and only the remonstrating officials can speak.
Though remonstrating officials are humble,
they are equal to grand counselors.
But today's remonstrating officials value
a large and imposing physique as beauty,
quick and agile responses as wisdom,
and clerical and judicial duties as their profession.
They do not fear heavenly portents,
nor do they pity the suffering of the people.
If one urges
them with loyalty and righteousness,
they say:
"It's not that I don't want to speak,
but if I speak, disaster will follow.
Who will listen to me?"
Alas,
since they cannot fully speak and fulfill their duties,
they instead attribute the fault
to the emperor.
Do people with human hearts truly act like this?
Your servant requests that the redundant and ineffective be dismissed,
and that officials of integrity and principle be widely sought.
Let them criticize and impeach from within the court,
and participate in deliberations in the Grand Secretariat.
Whether summoned for an audience,
or for rotational audiences,
or summoned at irregular times,
receive them with a calm countenance,
and guide them with gentle words,
allowing them to express their full sincerity and thoughts,
then the emperor's hearing will be open.
Your servant also hears that when Jí'àn was at court,
Huáinán ceased its plots.
The benefit that gentlemen bring to a nation is indeed great.
With Your Majesty's intelligence,
how could you not know that
gentlemen can be entrusted,
and yet deliberately suppress them?
It is merely the cunning slanders of petty individuals that sow discord and injure them.
Now, eminent virtues like Wáng Shù,
loyal and upright like Qiáng Zhēn,
and bright,
straightforward, rigid, and principled like Zhāng Mào, Lín Jùn, and Zhāng Jí,
are all highly esteemed by the people of their time.
They should not be demoted and banished,
thereby frustrating heaven's intention in producing such talents.
If Your Majesty truly summons these several
individuals,
places them in important positions,
and allows each to fully realize their lifelong aspirations,
then heaven's heart will be in accord.
Your servant also hears that Emperor Gāo instituted eunuchs
merely for sweeping and cleaning,
not to interfere with government.
Recently, the old regulations have daily deteriorated,
and crooked paths have daily opened,
so that the great power of the ruler
has entirely fallen into their hands.
Internally, they are relied upon as chancellors;
externally, they are relied upon as generals;
the border regions rely on them as military commissioners;
actors and artisans rely on them to create bizarre and excessive crafts;
Dharma kings and Buddhist disciples rely on them to freely enter and exit the palace.
How could Emperor Gāo have permitted this!
I pray Your Majesty considers the grand counselors as your arms and legs,
the remonstrating officials as your ears
and eyes,
and righteous gentlemen as your heart and mind.
Ponder deeply and deliberate thoroughly,
and establish long-term plans for the imperial ancestral temple and the state,
then the great principles will be rectified.
However, the root of it lies in how clearly Your Majesty comprehends principles.
I secretly hear that when侍臣 (shìchén) give lectures, there is no benefit of repeated discussion and debate,
and when Your Majesty listens to lectures, there is also no
benefit of leisurely assimilation.
To wish to comprehend principles in this way to respond to affairs,
your servant does not believe it.
I pray Your Majesty remembers the difficulty of fully comprehending righteousness and principles,
cherishes the swift passage of
days and months,
examines them in the classics and histories,
verifies them in your own mind and body,
ensuring no interruption throughout the year,
then your sacred learning will become clear and all matters will be well-governed.
How could it be limited to merely the appropriate handling of the four matters
mentioned?
The memorial was submitted,
but not answered.
Zhì, being generous and possessing extraordinary talent,
was at that time also on good terms with Censor Tāng Nài, Grand Secretariat Drafter Jí Rén, and Jinshi Lǐ Wénxiáng, all of whom shared his spirit.
They then together evaluated high officials and nobles,
and assessed figures.
Not long after,
Emperor Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
and many detrimental policies were reformed.
Zhì rejoiced,
believing his aspirations would soon be realized,
and so, due to an astrological anomaly, he again submitted a memorial, saying: "I humbly read the clear edict stating,
'Regarding the benefits and harms in the world that should be promoted or reformed,
officials and others in their respective posts are to itemize and report them.'
This is probably because Your Majesty knew that the previous enthronement
edict was misled by treacherous ministers,
forbidding remonstrating officials from making reports based on hearsay or personal bias,
leading to widespread public clamor,
hence this article was reissued to clear yourself.
Yet, it doesn't say,
'I
myself have erred,
or there are deficiencies in court governance,'
but says,
'benefits and harms should be promoted or reformed';
it doesn't say,
'all are permitted to speak frankly without concealment,'
but says,
'officials and others are to itemize
and report.'
The scope of Your Majesty's request for opinions is already not broad enough.
Now, to promote the world's benefits
and reform the world's harms,
one should seek the fundamental origins of benefits and harms
and then promote or reform them,
not meticulously list minor issues
as if the benefits and harms lie there.
Where are the fundamental origins?
They are the Grand Secretaries.
Grand Tutor Ān clings to his salary and abuses imperial favor,
Grand Guardian Jí condescends to his subordinates and deceives his superiors,
Crown Prince Grand Guardian Zhí harbors deceit and conceals
villainy—
these are the petty individuals of the age.
If Your Majesty retains them,
then your imperial virtue will surely not be perfected,
and court governance will surely not be reformed.
These are the harms that must be reformed.
Minister Wáng Shù, retired,
is loyal and upright and can be entrusted with important affairs;
Minister Wáng Hóng is firm and resolute and can suppress great villains;
Censor-in-Chief Péng Sháo is upright and principled and can resolve great doubts.
These are the gentlemen of the age.
If Your Majesty employs them,
then your imperial virtue will be enlightened and clear,
and court governance will be pure and solemn.
These are the benefits that must be promoted.
However, the reason why gentlemen are not promoted,
and petty individuals are not dismissed,
is largely due to the excessive power of the eunuchs.
Emperor Yuán of Hàn once employed Xiāo Wàngzhī and Zhōu
Kān,
yet ultimately was controlled by Hóng Gōng and Shí Xiǎn.
Emperor Xiàozōng of Sòng once employed Liú Jùnqīng and Liú Gǒng,
yet ultimately was alienated by Chén Yuán and Gān Shēng.
Lǐ Línfǔ and Niú
Xiānkè colluded with Gāo Lìshì,
and the Táng government became disorderly.
Jiǎ Sìdào and Dīng Dàquán collaborated with Dǒng Sòngchén,
and the Sòng dynasty did not revive.
The mechanism of promotion and demotion of
gentlemen and petty individuals
has never not been tied to the rise and fall of these groups.
I pray Your Majesty learns from the past,
is cautious about the future,
grasps the heavenly principles,
and makes firm decisions.
As for
how to treat eunuchs,
model it entirely after Emperor Gāo,
then gentlemen can be promoted,
petty individuals can be dismissed,
and the governance of the world will be unified.
With Your Majesty's intelligence surpassing the world,
how could you not know that treacherous officials cannot be fully trusted,
yet still inevitably misuse them?
This is probably because the study of rectifying the mind has not yet been thoroughly practiced.
If the mind
originates from heavenly principle,
then ears and eyes will be intelligent,
and words and actions will be in accord with moderation;
how can eunuchs possibly mislead?
If it originates from human desires,
then one's own self has no master,
and all affairs lose their guiding principle."
Exploiting opportunities and
deceiving, they gained influence.
Even with the capacity for divine martial prowess,
it will gradually change and diminish, losing its original essence.
How then could one advance gentlemen and dismiss petty individuals,
promote the welfare of the realm,
and reform its弊 evils?
It could not be achieved!
The Emperor received the memorial
and nodded in agreement.
Not long after,
Ān and Zhí were successively dismissed and banished.
Jí's trust remained as before,
and he harbored a bone-deep hatred for Zhì.
Nài often attended court and was to serve in the ranks.
Zhì told him:
"During the prosperous times of our ancestors,
Censors serving in the ranks
could directly present the successes and failures of state affairs
and immediately receive decisions.
Later, they only retired and submitted memorials,
which caused this estrangement between ruler and minister.
Since you are fortunate to live in a time of renewal,
why not follow the precedents of previous dynasties and act upon this?"
When Shù was summoned to the capital,
Zhì went to visit him and said:
"Later generations of officials did not get to see the Son of Heaven frequently,
so affairs often became perfunctory.
I wish you would not accept the official position for now,
but first request an audience,
and then list and denounce the unsatisfactory current policies,
strongly urging their abolition,
and only then accept the appointment.
Perhaps this might succeed.
If you accept the position first,
you will never again have the chance to see the Son of Heaven."
Nài and Shù were unable to act on his words.
Just then, Liú Gài's獄 prison case arose.
Jí had his partisan Wèi Zhāng implicate Zhì,
who was then imprisoned by imperial decree.
Zhì was personally bound in a cangue,
barely able to breathe,
yet he spoke defiantly during the interrogation:
"Zhì has seen the Classics Mat lectures suspended due to weather,
and the noon court fulfilling its duties perfunctorily with minor matters.
The fundamental principles are废弛 slackened,
customs are浮薄 frivolous,
the populace is憔悴 suffering,
and border defenses are空虛 empty.
I secretly worried about these.
That I exchanged discussions with Nài and others is true,
but I know nothing else."
The judges, following Jí's wishes,
eventually demoted him to Clerk of Shíchéngsuǒ in Guǎngdōng.
The details of the matter are in the biography of Tāng Nài.
When Zhì arrived in Guǎngdōng,
Governor-General Qín Hóng sent an official summons for him to edit books,
so he resided in the provincial capital.
Hearing that Chén Xiànzhāng was lecturing on Dao in Xīnhuì,
he went to become his student,
and from then on, his scholarship became purer.
In the tenth month of the fourth year of Hóngzhì, he suddenly fell ill and died,
at the age of twenty-six.
His classmate Wú Tíngjǔ, then Magistrate of Shùndé,
arranged his burial and sent his coffin home.
In the early Tiānqǐ era,
he was posthumously granted the title Zhōngjiè.
Shū Fēn,
courtesy name Guósháng,
was a native of Jìnxián.
At the age of twelve,
he presented his "Ode to the Tamed Geese" to Prefect Zhù Hàn,
and thus became famous.
In the twelfth year of Zhèngdé, he passed the Imperial Examination with the highest score,
and was appointed Compiler.
At that time, Wǔzōng frequently made incognito trips,
indulging in hunting and excursions without restraint.
The following year,
just over a month after Empress Xiàozhēn passed away,
he wished to visit Xuānfǔ.
He claimed he was going to inspect the imperial mausoleum,
and dismissed the guards along the route.
Fēn memorialized, saying:
"Your Majesty should remain deeply secluded for three years.
Even after shedding mourning attire,
you should still appear respectfully mournful.
Furthermore, since ancient times, the dignity of the Son of Heaven,
unless fleeing or hiding,
has always been accompanied by strict guards.
Moreover, there is no greater distinction of status than in carriages and attire.
For the Son of Heaven to lower himself to the level of commoners,
abandoning the grand carriage and ceremonial robes to use a dilapidated vehicle and casual clothes,
is not how to distinguish ranks and establish rites.
His words were not listened to.
Not listened to.
After the burial of Empress Xiàozhēn,
the spirit tablet was brought to be enshrined in the ancestral temple,
entering through Cháng'ān Mén.
Fēn again memorialized:
"Empress Xiàozhēn was wedded to Mào Líng,
and no loss of virtue has ever been heard of.
According to ancestral regulations,
after a burial, when the spirit tablet is brought,
it must enter through the main gate.
Yesterday, Empress Xiàozhēn's spirit tablet,
instead followed Your Majesty's carriage and entered through a side gate.
If future historians write, 'On the Jǐchǒu day of the sixth month,
the imperial carriage returned from the imperial mausoleum,
and Empress Xiàozhēnchún's spirit tablet entered Cháng'ān Mén,'
it will make Xiàozhēn appear to have not had a proper end.
How can this be explained to the world and future generations?
Last night, on the eve of the enshrinement,
there was a strong wind, swift thunder, and heavy rain.
Perhaps it was the spirits of the Sacred Ancestors, the arrayed forefathers, and Empress Xiàozhēn
warning and admonishing Your Majesty.
Your Majesty should immediately issue a clear edict to the inner and outer courts,
to demonstrate repentance."
There was no reply.
He then requested leave to care for his parents,
but it was not granted.
The following year, in the third month,
the Emperor debated making a southern tour.
At that time, Prince Níng, Chén Háo, had long harbored rebellious intentions,
and was connected with favored courtiers,
causing widespread fear among the populace.
Censors knelt before the palace gate to remonstrate,
but offended the imperial will and were reprimanded.
Fēn worried about this,

and with Xià Liángshèng, a Supernumerary Official of the Ministry of Personnel, Wàn Cháo, a Secretary of the Ministry of Rites, and Wāng Yìngzhěn, a Shùjíshì, he gathered officials from various departments to jointly submit a memorial,
to which the multitude assented.
Fēn then, accompanied by Compiler Cuī Tóng,
and Shùjíshì Jiāng Huī, Wáng Tíngchén, Mǎ Rǔjì, Cáo Jiā, and Yìngzhěn, submitted a memorial, saying:
"The reason ancient emperors conducted tours of inspection
was to harmonize musical scales,
unify weights and measures,
visit elderly wise men,
inquire about suffering,
promote the worthy and demote the unworthy,
and set in order those in office.
Thus, the feudal lords feared them,
and the common people were at peace.
If Your Majesty's outings
are merely like those of Qín Huáng and Hàn Wǔ,
indulging in extravagance for pleasure,
then you are not performing the rites of imperial inspection.
Bólàng and Báigǔ,
their disasters can also serve as a warning.
Recently, during the two northern and western tours,
the six armies were not managed,
and the four classes of people complained of hardship.
The cries of sorrow
reached the heavens
and spread throughout the four directions,
shaking people's hearts.
Therefore, upon hearing the edict for a southern tour,
everyone scattered like startled birds and frightened beasts.
Officials, under the pretext of welcoming and serving,
are imposing severe levies and demands,
leaving the region between the Jiāng and Huái rivers desolate and burdened with expenses.
Should desperate individuals
seize the opportunity to incite rebellion,
the disaster would be no small matter.
Moreover, Your Majesty refers to yourself as Zhènguó Gōng.
If you were to arrive in the territory of a princely state,
and the prince were to treat Your Majesty with the rites due to a meritorious minister,
would you face north to pay respects to him,
or would you face south to receive his homage?
If we were to strictly examine the names and responsibilities,
and deeply investigate the roots of this perversity,
then your favored confidants would have nowhere to die.
There is still something so painful that one cannot bear to speak of it with tears:
The imperial relatives harbor the discord of Liú Bì,
and the great ministers harbor the mind of Féng Dào.
They treat official salaries and positions as old trifles,
the court offices as a marketplace,
Your Majesty as a chess piece,
and the period of abolition and reform as a mere historical anecdote.
It is only that your favored confidants are short-sighted in their stratagems
and are incapable of conveying these words to Your Majesty.
If Your Majesty were to hear these words,
even outside the forbidden gates,
you would be alarmed and emerge, how then would you dare to travel carelessly on light steeds?"
When the memorial came in,
Lù Wán (陸完) met them and said,
"The emperor, hearing there are remonstrators, is often enraged,
and wishes to take his own life.
Gentlemen, please desist for now.
Do not attribute fault to the emperor,
and seek a reputation for uprightness."
Shū Fēn (舒芬) and the others did not respond and left.
A moment later,
Liáng Shèng (良勝) and Cháo Guòfēn (潮過芬) visited Shū Fēn (舒芬),
wringing their wrists, regretting Wán's words.
Shū Fēn (舒芬) then invited Dr. Chén Jiǔchuān (陳九川) to come,
and pouring him wine, said,
"A common man's will cannot be taken from him.
Can you gentlemen simply acquiesce?"
The next day, they indeed jointly submitted a memorial with the various Cáo (曹) officials.
The emperor was furious,
and ordered them to kneel beneath the palace gate for five days.
When the period was over, they were again beaten thirty strokes with a staff.
Shū Fēn (舒芬) was severely injured,
nearly dying,
and was carried to the Hànlín Yuàn (翰林院).
The head of the academy, fearing punishment,
ordered him to be expelled.
Shū Fēn (舒芬) said,
"I am an official here.
I will die here."
He was eventually demoted to Vice-Superintendent of the Maritime Trade in Fújiàn (福建),
and departed with his wounds bandaged.
When Shìzōng (世宗) ascended the throne,
he was recalled to his former office.
In the spring of Jiājìng (嘉靖) three years (1524),
on the birthday of Empress Dowager Zhāoshèng (昭聖),
an edict exempted the various court ladies from offering congratulations.
Shū Fēn (舒芬) stated,
"Previously, on the birthday of Empress Dowager Xìngguó (興國),
the court ladies offered congratulations as per custom.
Now, on the birthday of Her Imperial Majesty the Empress Dowager,
to suddenly issue an exemption
might disrupt the proper balance of importance.
I beg that the decree be rescinded,
to display holy filial piety."
The emperor was angered,
and docked his salary for three months.
At this time, the emperor wished to elevate his birth parents,
and Shū Fēn (舒芬), along with his colleagues, submitted repeated memorials vehemently remonstrating.
When Zhāng Cōng (張璁), Guì È (桂萼), and Fāng Xiànfū (方獻夫) were rapidly promoted to Grand Secretary,
Shū Fēn (舒芬) and his colleagues Yáng Wéicōng (楊維聰) and Compiler Wáng Sīxiū (王思羞) felt ashamed to be in the same rank,
and submitted a memorial requesting to resign.
Soon after,
he again, with colleagues Yáng Shèn (楊慎) and others, knelt at Zuǒshùnmén (左順門) and cried out in protest.
The emperor was angered,
imprisoned them, subjected them to a court beating,
and docked their salaries as before.
He soon suffered the loss of his mother and returned home,
dying in his residence
at the age of forty-four.
The world called him
"the loyal and filial Zhuàngyuán (狀元)."
Shū Fēn (舒芬) had a graceful bearing, standing like jade,
and possessed a lofty and severe disposition.
He could sit upright all day without showing fatigue,
and at night, he would review his mistakes and criticize himself.
He took it as his duty to advocate for profound and neglected studies.
His scholarship penetrated all the classics,
and he was also conversant in astronomy, musicology, and calendrical science,
but he was particularly skilled in the Zhōulǐ (周禮).
He once said,
"The Zhōulǐ (周禮) compared to the Yílǐ (儀禮) and Lǐjì (禮記),
is like Shǔ (蜀) compared to Wú (吳) and Wèi (魏).
Jiǎ Shì (賈氏) claimed the Yílǐ (儀禮) was fundamental and the Zhōulǐ (周禮) secondary;
this is wrong.
Why did Zhū Zǐ (朱子) not correct this?"
When his illness became critical,
his son asked for his last words,
and he only regretted not having had the chance to expound on the Zhōulǐ (周禮).
Scholars called him Zǐxī Xiānshēng (梓溪先生).
During the Wànlì (萬曆) era,
he was posthumously given the epithet Wénjié (文節).
Previously,
Compiler Luó Lún (羅倫) was demoted to Fújiàn Tíjǔ (福建提舉) for remonstrating.
Over sixty years later, Shū Fēn (舒芬) succeeded him.
He was from the same hometown as Luó Lún (羅倫) and held the same office,
and the place and office of his demotion were also the same.
Thus, the gentry of Fújiàn (福建) enshrined Shū Fēn (舒芬) alongside Luó Lún (羅倫).
Cuī Tóng (崔桐),
courtesy name Láifèng (來鳳),
was a native of Hǎimén (海門).
He placed first in the provincial examination,
and passed the imperial examination with Shū Fēn (舒芬).
He was appointed Compiler.
After remonstrating against the Southern Tour,
he also knelt beneath the palace gate,
and received a beating and had his salary docked.
During the Jiājìng (嘉靖) era,
as a Reader-in-waiting, he was dispatched as a Right Vice-Censor-in-chief for Húguǎng (湖廣),
and progressively promoted to Libationer of the Guózǐ Jiǔ (國子祭酒)
and Right Vice-Minister of the Ministry of Rites.
Mǎ Rǔjì (馬汝驥),
courtesy name Zhòngfáng (仲房),
was a native of Suídé (綏德).
He became a Jinshì (進士) in Zhèngdé (正德) twelve years (1517).
He was reappointed as a Shùjíshì (庶吉士).
He, along with Shū Fēn (舒芬) and others, remonstrated against the Southern Tour,
and was punished with kneeling and receiving a beating.
Upon completing his instruction period,
he was supposed to be appointed Compiler,
but was specially transferred to be Prefect of Zézhōu (澤州).
He punished the people of the princely mansion who abused commoners.
When the prince sent something to him,
he would throw the document into a cabinet without looking at it.
The Magistrate of Língchuān (陵川) was corrupt,
and Mǎ Rǔjì (馬汝驥) wished to dismiss him.
The Imperial Censor on circuit tried to make excuses for him,
but Mǎ Rǔjì (馬汝驥) did not listen
and ultimately stripped him of his office.
When Shìzōng (世宗) ascended,
he was recalled to his position as Compiler.
Soon after, his merit in direct remonstrance was recognized,
and his rank was increased by one grade.
He participated in compiling the Wǔzōng Shílù (武宗實錄),
and was promoted to Compiler.
He successively served as Director of Studies at both Capital National Universities,
was promoted to Right Vice-Minister of the Grand Court of Revision in Nánjīng (南京),
and then changed to Libationer of the Guózǐ Jiǔ (國子祭酒).
He was recalled and appointed Right Vice-Minister of the Ministry of Rites.
Minister Yán Sōng (嚴嵩) greatly esteemed Mǎ Rǔjì (馬汝驥),
and spoke highly of him in the Grand Secretariat.
The emperor specially added the title of Grand Academician of the Imperial Academy.
Mǎ Rǔjì (馬汝驥) conducted himself with strict integrity,
yet his nature was inherently gentle and easygoing,
and people looked up to him.
Upon his death, he was posthumously granted the title of Minister
and given the epithet Wénjiǎn (文簡).
The biographies of Yīng Zhěn (應軫) and others are recorded separately.
The Eulogy says: It is the duty of literary officials to attend with their literary talents,
not to bear the responsibility of remonstrance.
Yet, stirred by principles of righteousness,
they remonstrated fearlessly in court,
suffering punishment and demotion without regret.
Are these not truly men of pure resolve and integrity?
The custom of "forgoing mourning" did not begin with Lǐ Xián (李賢),
