but since Luó Lún's (羅倫) memorial was widely circulated,
court officials dared not consider "restoration to office before the mourning period" as an established practice.
How profound and significant was the benefit to ethical principles!
Zhāng Mào (章懋) and others cited Xuānzōng's (宣宗) admonition,
clarifying the state's intention in establishing officials,
not to highlight the ruler's faults.
Zōu Zhì (鄒智) pointed out the worthy and the treacherous,
correcting deceit and triviality.
Shū Fēn (舒芬)'s stern words were sharp and stirring,
possessing the spirit of Yuán Àng (爰盎)'s pulling the reins.
Moreover, with their pure cultivation and strict integrity,
their conduct was without blemish or fault.
Such gentlemen
were indeed sufficient to rectify the frivolous and boastful habits of literary scholars.
Biographies, Chapter 68:

Zhāng Níng (張寧), Wáng Huī (王徽) (Wáng Yuān (王淵) et al.), Máo Hóng (毛弘), Qiū Hóng (丘弘), Lǐ Sēn (李森), Wèi Yuán (魏元) (Kāng Yǒngsháo (康永韶) et al.), Qiáng Zhēn (強珍), Wáng Ruì (王瑞) (Zhāng Jì (張稷)), Lǐ Jùn (李俊), Wāng Kuí (汪奎) (his nephew Shùnmín (舜民), Cuī Shēng (崔陞) et al.), Tāng Nài (湯鼐) (Jí Rén (吉人), Liú Gài (劉㮣), Dǒng Jié (董傑)), Jiāng Wǎn (姜綰) (Yú Jùn (余濬) et al.), Jiāng Hóng (姜洪) (Ōuyáng Dàn (歐陽旦), Chàng Hēng (暢亨)), Cáo Lín (曹璘), Péng Chéng (彭程), Páng Pàn (龐泮) (Lǚ Xiàn (呂獻)), Yè Shēn (葉紳), Hú Xiàn (胡獻) (Wǔ Qú (武衢) et al.), Zhāng Hóngzhì (張弘至), Qū Shēn (屈伸), Wáng Xiànchén (王獻臣) (Wú Yīguàn (吳一貫), Yú Lián (余濂)).
Zhāng Níng (張寧),
courtesy name Jìngzhī (靖之),
was a native of Hǎiyán (海鹽).
He became a Jinshì (進士) in Jǐngtài (景泰) five years (1454).
He was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Rites.
In the summer of Jǐngtài (景泰) seven years (1456),
the emperor followed the memorial of Táng Yú (唐瑜) and others,
and conducted an audit of all officials, great and small, in Nánjīng (南京).
Zhāng Níng (張寧) said,
"The capital is especially the foundation;
it should not be exempted alone."
He further stated,
"The military officers in the capital garrisons who receive salaries,
with one garrison having up to two thousand people,
totaling over thirty thousand officers.
Annually, this requires 480,000 liǎng (兩) of silver,
360,000 dàn (石) of rice,
and other converted allowances,
often exceeding one million.
No other expenditure depletes the national reserves
as much as this.
And among them, many are old, weak, and unskilled in riding and archery.
It would be better to select those who are capable,
to fill vacant posts in the military commands and garrisons throughout the empire,
and completely eliminate the rest."
The proposal was blocked and not implemented.
The emperor fell ill.
It happened that there was a celestial anomaly,
so an imperial edict cancelled the New Year's grand assembly for the following year,
and officials were to attend court as on the first and fifteenth of the lunar month.
Níng said:
“People from the four directions come to pay respects.
If they cannot see the emperor’s face,
at a time of doubt and suspicion,
it will certainly lead to alarming rumors.
I pray that the old custom be followed with effort,
to comfort the people's hearts.”
The emperor, being ill, could not comply,
and
the “Duó Mén” (Seizing the Gate)
incident occurred.
During the Tiānshùn reign,
Cáo and Shí usurped power.
When matters concerned the Bureau of Rites,
Níng always pruned and curtailed them,
and Yīngzōng thereby recognized Níng.
Cháoxiǎn and the neighboring Máo Lín Wèi were locked in a blood feud,
so an imperial edict ordered Níng to go with Dudū Zhǐhuī Wǔ Zhōng to mediate.
Níng's words were spirited and righteous,
while Zhōng was brave and strong.
He bent two bows until they broke,
and shot down a wild goose with one arrow,
greatly astonishing and convincing the Cháoxiǎn people.
The two successfully resolved the feud and returned.
The eunuch Tán Bāo invited him to meet,
but he did not go.
Soon after, he was promoted to Dū Jìshìzhōng.
When Xiànzōng first attended the imperial lectures (jīngyán),
Níng requested that the Dàxué Yǎnyì be lectured daily.
In October of that year,
it was the empress dowager's birthday.
The Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū) Yáo Kuí followed the old custom
of setting up a vegetarian feast and performing a ritual (jiànjiào),
and gathered all officials to go to the altar to offer incense.
Níng said it was useless
and merely harmed the overall integrity,
and begged for it to be forbidden.
The emperor graciously accepted this.
Not long after,
Jìshìzhōng Wáng Huī impeached Grand Secretary (Dàxuéshì) Lǐ Xián over the matter of Niú Yù,
and incurred punishment.
Níng led the Six Bureaus (liù kē) in arguing for Lǐ Xián's rescue,
and from then on gradually became antagonistic toward the Grand Secretariat (Nèigé).
At that time, Wáng Hóng and others recommended Níng as qualified to be Qiān Dū Yùshǐ for cleaning up military posts and affixing yellow slips (qīng jūnzhí tiēhuáng),
and he was mentioned alongside Yuè Zhèng.
An imperial decree was issued,
stating that many recommendations were made out of favoritism,
and all were given external assignments.
Níng was sent out as Zhīfǔ of Tīngzhōu,
and governed with simplicity and tranquility.
Within a year, all his good policies were in place.
Níng was highly talented and ambitious,
adept at memorials,
and his reputation was well-known.
Yīngzōng once wanted to give him an important post,
but it did not happen.
He stayed in the remonstrance office (jiàn yuán) for a long time,
and was not liked by the high officials.
After being sent out as a prefect,
he became even more despondent and unfulfilled,
and retired due to illness.
He lived at home for thirty years;
though speakers repeatedly recommended him,
he was never recalled.
He had no sons.
He had two concubines;
after Níng's death,
they cut their hair and swore to die,
living upstairs for forty years without coming down.
An imperial edict commended them as
“Shuāng Jié” (Two Loyal Women).
Wáng Huī,
courtesy name Shàngwén,
was from Yìngtiān.
He became a Jìnshì in the fourth year of Tiānshùn.
He was appointed Nánjīng Xíngkē Jìshìzhōng.
A few months after Xiànzōng's ascension,
he, along with fellow officials Wáng Yuān, Zhū Kuān, Lǐ Xiáng, and Lǐ Jūn, submitted a memorial listing four matters.
The last point stated:
“Since ancient times, few eunuchs have been virtuous,
and many have been treacherous.
If they are given great power,
leading to ruin,
and then punished,
this is to love them at first and kill them in the end,
which is not the way to preserve them completely.
We wish you would follow Gāo Huángdì’s old system,
and not allow them to interfere in politics, command troops,
or acquire property and establish businesses.
Their family members and adopted sons
should all be registered as commoners in their original places of residence.
Strictly forbid officials from associating with them.
Only abundantly reward them,
so they may be prosperous and content,
without further ambitions.
This is a blessing for the country,
and also a blessing for the eunuchs.”
That winter,
the emperor, influenced by Wàn Fēi's slander,
deposed Empress Wú,
and punished the eunuch Niú Yù for presumptuously changing the empress (zhōnggōng),
banishing him to Nánjīng.
Huī, along with Yuān and others, again impeached him, saying: “Your Majesty's enthronement of the empress,
what kind of matter is this,
yet the treacherous minister Niú Yù brazenly committed fraud.
Now that the empress has been removed,
everyone believes Niú Yù deserves ten thousand
deaths.
Yet he is merely exiled to the secondary capital,
still retaining his head and body.
Then what will those who serve by Your Majesty’s side fear or dread?
The Grand Secretaries (Nèigé Dàchén),
serving as chief ministers,
viewed the major matter of enthroning an empress with indifference, not giving it serious thought.
At the beginning of Niú Yù's brazen deception,
before the marriage rites were completed,
the ritual officials, fearing power,
immediately flattered him.
And after Niú Yù’s affair
was exposed,
the national laws were difficult to pardon,
but the judicial officials, remembering old ties,
ended up being lenient.
And Lǐ Xián and others merely sat by and watched the success or failure,
not uttering a single word,
partying with evil and deceiving the emperor.”
Qiū Hóng
, courtesy name Kuānshū,
was a native of Shàngháng.
He became a *jìnshì* at the end of the Tiānshùn reign.
He was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Revenue.
He frequently presented memorials on current policies.
In the spring of the fourth year of Chénghuà (1468),
he and his colleagues jointly submitted a memorial stating:
"During the Hóngwǔ and Yǒnglè reigns,
because the capital region and Shāndōng had vast, sparsely populated lands,
an edict permitted people to reclaim and cultivate them,
and they would never be taxed.
Recently, powerful and influential individuals, relying on their authority,
often designate these as idle lands
and deceitfully request them through memorials.
For example, the eldest princess Jiāshàn requested land in various counties of Wén'ān,
and the Buddhist disciple Zhāshíbā from Xītiān requested land in Jìnghǎi County,
amounting to dozens or hundreds of *qǐng*.
A *qǐng* of land exceeding a hundred *qǐng*
was, in ancient times, the property of a hundred families.
How can one indulge the private desires of one person
and seize the property of a hundred families?"
The emperor accepted his words
and decreed that from now on, all such requests
would be disallowed,
and this was established as a regulation.
The land requested by Zhāshíbā
was eventually returned to the people.
Hóng was promoted twice,
reaching the position of Metropolitan Supervising Secretary.
In the summer of the sixth year (1470),
Shāndōng and Hénán suffered a severe drought.
Hóng requested relief.
He then said:
"When various regions report disasters,
the ministerial officials adhere to existing precedents,
requiring verification before exemption is granted.
Although the emperor remits taxes,
little actual benefit reaches the people below.
I request that from now on, when a disaster occurs,
the provincial censors and inspecting officials verify it,
and immediately grant exemption and relief."
This was adopted.
Consort Wàn had the emperor's favor,
and eunuchs Liáng Fāng and Chén Xǐ competed to present extravagant novelties.
Wicked individuals like Tú Zōngshùn daily offered strange and rare gemstones,
for which they were always generously rewarded,
wasting millions from the treasury.
Some even gained official positions through this.
People in the capital imitated them,
competing in extravagance,
and making excessive presumptuous imitations.
Hóng, with his colleagues, memorialized to denounce the crimes of Zōngshùn and others,
requesting the return of the treasury funds
and a strict prohibition of extravagant customs.
The matter was referred to the Ministry of Justice,
and Minister Lù Yú then requested that Zōngshùn and others be brought to justice
and their assets confiscated to relieve the famine victims.
The emperor did not agree,
but only ordered that those who practiced extravagance should be punished without mercy,
though he ultimately could not stop it.
The capital suffered a poor harvest and high rice prices,
while tens of thousands of itinerant monks from various regions were present.
Hóng requested their expulsion
to save on unnecessary food consumption.
He also requested that rice from Tàicāng granary be released
and sold at a reduced price,
to be given to the poorest among the common people.
The emperor agreed to all these requests.
He further stated:
"The various places in the capital, such as the Hundred Beasts' House and Qīnghé Temple,
which raise precious birds and wild animals,
are fed fish, meat, rice, and beans daily.
I request that they all be released
to save on unnecessary expenses."
This was reported and noted.
The following year, he was sent as an envoy to Liúqiú,
and died en route.
Hóng and Máo Hóng both served in the censorate,
and both dared to speak out;
people called them
"the two Hóngs."
Lǐ Sēn,
courtesy name Shímào,
was a native of Lìchéng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the first year of Tiānshùn (1457).
He was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Revenue.
He was high-spirited and dared to speak out.
When Emperor Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
he submitted a memorial requesting the prohibition of tributary officials' extortions and demands that harmed the people.
Minister of Personnel Wáng 'Áo requested that his words be followed,
and the emperor issued an edict prohibiting such practices.
Soon after,
he stated:
"Recently, there have been those who, without merit, have been promoted to marquis, earl, or regional commander;
those who, without talent or virtue, have held high official positions;
and those who have obtained official posts through skills in painting, chess, playing the zither, medicine, or divination.
Titles and ranks are becoming cheapened daily,
and official salaries are being wasted daily.
This is to trifle with the public instruments of the empire
and abandon the great authority of the state.
From now on, suitable individuals should be selected for appointments,
and those without talent should not be allowed to contend for advancement."
He also requested strict evaluation and dismissal/promotion for military officers,
and investigation into desertions and false food rations.
All these requests were approved.
When Censor Xiè Wénxiáng was imprisoned for impeaching Yáo Kuí,
Sēn and his colleagues tried to save him,
but their plea was not accepted.
The following summer,
there was a solar eclipse,
and Qióngshān County experienced an earthquake.
Sēn submitted a memorial listing ten matters.
Not long after,
regarding the encroachment on people's property by favored nobles,
he led the Supervising Secretaries to state:
"In the past, by imperial edict of the previous emperor,
imperial relatives who forcibly occupied military or civilian land
were to be punished without mercy,
and those who offered land were to be sent to the border for military service.
At that time, no powerful relatives dared to transgress.
Recently, Supervising Secretary Qiū Hóng memorialized to put an end to powerful nobles requesting land,
and Your Majesty also graciously complied.
Yet, Zhōu Yù, a commander of the Imperial Bodyguard and an imperial relative by marriage, requested over six hundred *qǐng* of land in Wǔqiáng and Wǔyì;
Lady Yìshèng Liú requested over three hundred *qǐng* of land in Tōngzhōu and Wǔqīng;
and imperial edicts granted all these requests.
How is this not contrary to the previous edict!
Their greed is insatiable,
but the fertile land within the capital region is limited.
The common people's clothing and food all come from this land.
If it is suddenly seized from them,
how will they live?
Furthermore, over the past hundred years of this dynasty, the population has grown daily.
How can there still be idle land that is not cultivated or sown?
What is called 'requesting land through memorial'
is in reality nothing but forcible seizure."
The emperor approved his words,
but the land already granted was not questioned.
Shanxī suffered a disaster,
and Shāndōng, Hángzhōu, Shàoxīng, Jiāxīng, and Húzhōu experienced severe floods.
Sēn and others requested tax exemption and relief,
and the emperor agreed to all.
At that time, the emperor had no heir,
and Consort Wàn monopolized his favor,
preventing other concubines from gaining access.
Those who spoke out often advised the emperor to extend his benevolence,
but no one dared to openly speak of the consort's jealousy.
Only Sēn submitted a bold memorial on this matter,
which displeased the emperor.
Sēn had already been promoted twice to Left Supervising Secretary.
When the position of Metropolitan Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Revenue became vacant,
the Ministry of Personnel listed Sēn's name,
but an edict appointed him to an outside post.
The Ministry proposed him as Prefect of Xīnghuà,
but this was not approved,
and he was eventually sent out as a Sub-prefect of Huáiqìng.
Not long after,
he resigned and returned home,
never to serve again.
Wèi Yuán,
courtesy name Jǐngshàn,
was a native of Cháochéng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the first year of Tiānshùn.
He was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Rites.
In the early Chénghuà reign,
when Consort Wàn's brothers were arrogant and domineering,
Yuán memorialized to impeach them.
In the fourth year (1468),
when Empress Dowager Cíyì passed away,
and was to be buried separately,
Yuán, along with thirty-nine colleagues, submitted a strong memorial in extreme remonstrance.
Censor Kāng Yǒngsháo, along with forty-one colleagues,
also argued against it,
prostrating and weeping at the Wénhuá Gate,
and eventually the burial was carried out according to proper rites.
In the ninth month of that year,
a comet appeared.
Yuán led the Supervising Secretaries to submit a memorial stating: "Since the beginning of spring,
disasters and unusual phenomena have occurred repeatedly.
Recently, a comet appeared in the east,
its light brushing the imperial constellation (Tái Yuán),
all of which are signs of strong *yīn* and weak *yáng*.
We have heard that the relationship between the sovereign
and the empress
is like that between heaven and earth;
they cannot be divided or have rivals.
Rumor has it that there is a highly favored concubine in the palace
who rivals the empress.
Minister Yáo Kuí and others previously
spoke of this,
and Your Majesty stated,
'I will personally decide on internal matters.'
We held our breath and listened intently
for nearly half a year,
but the provisions for Zhāodé Palace have not reportedly been reduced at all,
while the empress
not yet heard of any increase.
Although the imperial harem is distant,
the Emperor's sight and hearing are still as close as a cubit.
Even the subtleties of the sleeping mat
are revealed in the cosmic phenomena;
one cannot but be fearful.
Moreover, Your Majesty is in the prime of
life,
but the position of heir apparent is still vacant.
How can the great plan for the imperial ancestral temple and the state be entirely entrusted to one beloved and favored person,
without seeking means to solidify the foundation of the state and stabilize the people's hearts?
I wish
that the principles of a proper marital relationship be clarified,
and strict precautions be taken regarding wives and concubines,
so that the distinctions between noble and humble are clear,
and each person rests content in their proper place.
The foundation for a hundred generations of the main and collateral lines
truly lies in this.
In all directions, droughts and floods recur,
and the people's distress grows daily more severe.
Refugees from Jīng and Xiāng are reporting unrest.
Your Majesty, as the parent of the people,
has shown no initial alarm,
merely following established practices,
handing matters over to the ministries for implementation.
However, Hùbù Shàngshū Mǎ Áng,
whenever a report is made,
if it pleases the Emperor,
he says,
"Refer it to the relevant department for handling";
if it angers the Emperor,
he
says,
"The matter is obstructed and difficult to implement";
if there is even a slight matter of interest or harm,
he immediately requests an imperial decision.
Vacillating and indecisive,
what more can the people hope for?
Only by urgently halting taxes,
opening the imperial treasury,
and dispatching
officials to provide relief and sustenance
can the people's hearts perhaps be slightly consoled.
Your Majesty deeply believes in heterodox religions.
Whenever the birthday of a deity occurs,
large sums of money are frequently spent,
and many Daoist rituals are performed.
Moreover, Western monks such as Zhāshíbā,
are even given titles such as Fǎwáng,
and showered with numerous gifts.
They travel in palanquins made of palm fiber,
and are escorted by golden imperial guards,
gentry avoid their path,
their upkeep exceeding that of imperial princes.
Violating principles and disrupting discipline,
what
could be more extreme than this?
I beg that their titles be revoked,
they be sent back to their countries,
their excessive gifts be recovered,
to be used to relieve the starving people.
Furthermore, an edict should be issued to temples and monasteries,
permanently prohibiting them from again requesting Daoist rituals,
to prevent squandering state resources.
The wealth of the empire,
if not with the officials, then it is with the people.
Now, both public and private sectors are in distress,
due to too many frivolous amusements
and uncontrolled rewards.
Some build pagodas and temples,
others
purchase rare and precious items.
Even a small item
can cost millions,
how can the national treasury not be depleted?
I wish
that extravagant crafts be completely abolished,
banquets and outings be suspended,
all silver mines and non-
urgent affairs be completely prohibited.
As for the civil and military ministers in the two capitals,
there is no shortage of corrupt and greedy ones
who vie to deceive and obstruct.
Your Majesty, do not say that their positions are high and you cannot bear to remove them immediately,
nor say that they are old
officials and tolerate them for the time being.
They should be ordered to resign on their own accord,
to preserve the overall integrity.
Those who cling to their positions and refuse to leave
should be impeached by censors.
And we, your ministers, who improperly occupy
positions in the censorate,
are of no use to the times,
and also hope to be dismissed and return home,
as a warning against incompetence.
The Emperor issued a gracious edict praising and responding to him,
but ultimately did not implement his suggestions.
Yuán was repeatedly promoted to Dū Gěishìzhōng,
then went out as Fújiàn Yòucāncè.
He inspected the sea routes,
strictly prohibiting illegal private trading across the sea.
Large merchants offered him heavy bribes,
but Yuán angrily rebuked and dismissed them.
He returned home due to his mother's mourning,
living by her tomb for three years.
After the mourning period,
he was appointed Jiāngxī Cāncè,
and died.
Kāng Yǒngsháo,
courtesy name Yònghé,
a native of Qímén.
He passed the provincial examination,
entered the National Academy,
and was selected and appointed Yùshǐ.
In the early Chénghuà reign,
he toured and inspected Jīfǔ,
impeaching Shàngshū Mǎ Áng for suppressing market prices of land.
In the fourth year, along with fellow officials Hú Shēn and Zhèng Jǐ, etc., he disputed the matter of Empress Cíyì Tàihòu's mausoleum.
When a comet appeared,
he again, with fellow officials, presented a memorial listing eight matters,
the main points of which were similar to Yuán's previous memorial.
When the ministers of the two capitals investigated various minor officials,
many appointments and dismissals were inappropriate.
Yǒngsháo and others again impeached the ministers for acting selfishly,
and also pointed out the crimes of twelve people, including Xíngbù Zhǔshì Yú Zhì.
They were implicated by Yú Zhì,
and all were sent to imperial prison.
Yǒngsháo was demoted to Zhīxiàn of Shùnchāng,
then transferred to Fúqīng and Huì'ān.
After a long time,
someone recommended him as knowledgeable in astronomy,
and an imperial decree recalled him,
appointing him Qīntiān Jiānzhèng,
then promoted to Tàicháng Shàocīng,
in charge of the Qīntiān Jiān affairs.
As a Yùshǐ, Yǒngsháo had a reputation for uprightness,
but now he changed to catering to the Emperor for favor,
often concealing and distorting his astrological predictions,
even interpreting calamities as auspicious signs.
When Shǎnxī suffered a great famine,
Yǒngsháo said:
"This spring's celestial anomaly should bring a great disaster,
but thanks to the famine deaths of the people of Qín,
it will suffice to avert it,
truly a boundless blessing for the state."
The Emperor was very pleased,
and an imperial decree promoted him to Lǐbù Yòushìláng,
still in charge of Qīntiān Jiān affairs.
He was dismissed from office and returned home
due to many errors in the calendar.
Hú Shēn,
a native of Dìngyuǎn Wèi.
He was a *jìnshì* at the end of the Tiānshùn reign.
After disputing the matter of Empress Cíyì Tàihòu's mausoleum,
he again, with fellow officials Chén Hóng, Zhèng Jǐ, Hé Chún, Fāng Shēng, and Zhāng Jìnlù, presented a memorial requesting the expulsion of corrupt and evil individuals,
vehemently criticizing Xuéshì Shāng Lù,
and Shàngshū Chéng Xìn, Yáo Kuí, and Mǎ Áng.
The Emperor did not accept it.
The next day,
Gěishìzhōng Dǒng Mín, Chén Hè, and Hú Zhì also impeached Shāng Lù and others,
and presented their memorial directly to the Emperor.
According to custom,
impeachment memorials from censors were either publicly read in the grand court or sealed and submitted;
there had never been a case of presenting them directly without reading.
The Emperor was displeased,
saying:
"The advancement and dismissal of ministers have their proper forms.
How dare Dǒng Mín and others disregard old regulations and disrupt court decorum?"
Shāng Lù and others requested retirement,
but the Emperor only allowed Mǎ Áng to leave.
Yáo Kuí was greatly indignant,
and repeatedly submitted memorials seeking to retire.
Hú Shēn, Dǒng Mín and others again jointly attacked,
criticizing Yáo Kuí with great force.
The Emperor was angry,
and imprisoned Hú Shēn and eight others.
Previously,
Yùshǐ Lín Chéng had also impeached Shāng Lù,
which was not accepted,
and he left citing illness.
The Emperor also ordered Lín Chéng to be investigated by officials.
Máo Hóng and others all argued for their clemency,
and Shāng Lù also requested leniency,
so they were each caned twenty times,
and their official positions were restored.
Not long after,
Hú Shēn was implicated for having flogged to death a person who sought redress for injustice while he was inspecting Shǎnxī,
and was demoted to Qiányáng Chéng,
then gradually promoted to Zhīzhōu of Yùlín,
and died.
Zhèng Jǐ,
a native of Shānhǎi Wèi.
He became a *jìnshì* in the second year of Chénghuà (1466).
As Circuit Censor for Shǎnxī,
he requested the remission of overdue taxes in the border areas
and the classification of border troops,
ordering the strong to fight and guard,
and the old and weak to farm and herd.
His memorial was submitted to the appropriate departments.
When Dìngxī Hóu Jiǎng Wǎn garrisoned Gānsù,
Zhèng Jǐ intended to impeach him for his crimes.
The information leaked,
and he was instead impeached
and exiled to guard Xuānfǔ.
Zhèng Jǐ was arrogant by nature,
and contemporary opinion did not much regret his fate.
Dǒng Mín,
a native of Lèpíng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the second year of Chénghuà (1466).
He successively served as Dū Gěishìzhōng of the Ministry of Personnel.
He was impeached by an official,
imprisoned in the Imperial Prison,
and demoted to Magistrate of Shíjiù.
During Xiàozōng’s reign,
he died in office as a Cānyì in Sìchuān.
Qiáng Zhēn,
courtesy name Tíngguì,
a native of Cāngzhōu.
He became a *jìnshì* in the second year of Chénghuà (1466).
He was appointed Magistrate of Jīngxiàn.
He requested a reduction in the assessed taxes,
and the people were grateful to him.
He was promoted to Censor.
Initially,
Chén Yuè, the Grand Coordinator of Liáodōng, provoked conflict and invited enemies.
When the enemies arrived,
he deliberately concealed the truth and deceived.
The Circuit Censor Wáng Chóngzhī impeached Chén Yuè,
who became greatly alarmed.
He conspired with Wāng Zhí,
falsely accused and arrested Wáng Chóngzhī, who was imprisoned in the Imperial Prison.
He paid a redemption fine
and was transferred to be a Tuīguān in Yán’ān.
When Wāng Zhí and Chén Yuè engaged in military campaigns,
they were about to discuss their merits when a large enemy invasion occurred.
The eunuch Wéi Lǎng and Commander-in-Chief Gōu Qiān, among others, concealed this and did not report it.
Qiáng Zhēn went to investigate as Circuit Censor
and requested that Chén Yuè be punished for his crimes.
Yú Zǐjùn, the Minister of War, and others memorialized that Chén Yuè had repeatedly committed serious offenses
and should not be pardoned.
The Emperor did not follow their advice.
Soon after,
Commander Wáng Quán and others lured and killed people from Húyán Wèi.
Qiáng Zhēn exposed their actions,
and Wáng Quán and the others were all convicted.
Wāng Zhí was at that time boasting of his great achievements.
Hearing Qiáng Zhēn’s memorial, he was enraged.
Just then, Chén Yuè returned from a border inspection,
and Chén Yuè welcomed him fifty *lǐ* outside the city,
complaining that Qiáng Zhēn had falsely accused him.
Wāng Zhí became even more furious,
and memorialized that all of Qiáng Zhēn’s impeachments were false.
An imperial edict ordered Xiāo Jù, a Qianhù of the Jǐnyī Wèi, to investigate,
and Qiáng Zhēn was shackled and sent to the capital.
Upon his arrival,
Wāng Zhí first flogged and tortured him,
then reported it to the throne.
He was convicted of reporting false information
and ordered to pay a redemption fine.
An imperial edict specifically demoted him to guard Liáodōng,
and reprimanded the Ministry of War and the censors who had previously impeached Chén Yuè.
After three years,
Wāng Zhí fell from power,
and Qiáng Zhēn was reinstated in his office
and retired.
At the beginning of Hóngzhì,
he was appointed Vice Commissioner of Shāndōng,
and promoted to Junior Minister of the Grand Court of Revision.
The following year,
he was appointed Right Vice Censor-in-Chief and Grand Coordinator of Xuānfǔ.
At that time, Gōu Qiān had already been dismissed.
Qiáng Zhēn memorialized to retain Gōu Qiān, stating that his talent and ability were still useful.
A Supervising Secretary stated that Gōu Qiān had repeatedly missed opportunities,
and Qiáng Zhēn should not have memorialized to protect him.
Consequently, Qiáng Zhēn was reassigned to Nanjing Right Assistant Administration Commissioner.
Soon after, he requested retirement due to his mother’s old age,
and after a long time, he died.
Wáng Ruì,
courtesy name Liángbì,
a native of Wàngjiāng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the fifth year of Chénghuà (1469).
He was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Personnel.
He once vehemently argued in Wénhuá Diàn that the internal favorites were becoming excessive,
speaking with forthrightness and integrity.
The Emperor was furious,
and his colleagues trembled in fear,
but Wáng Ruì showed no sign of fear.
In the fifteenth year (1479), he memorialized to request that all officials coming to present memorials from across the realm should state the advantages and disadvantages of their localities.
The Emperor disliked the disruption
and had him flogged.
The Grand Coordinators and Circuit Censors of Húguǎng and Jiāngxī requested exemption from court audiences for officials in their jurisdictions
due to natural disasters, damage, and rising banditry in their areas.
Wáng Ruì and others said:
“When the year is poor and the people are in distress,
it is due to the incompetence of the officials.
They should be punished,
yet they are requested to be retained.
If the chief officials are retained,
then how can the advancement and demotion of talent
be properly assessed?
Thus, the two great ceremonies of court audience and performance review
would both be abolished and ruined.”
The Emperor agreed with his words
and immediately ordered the Ministry of Personnel to prohibit it.
He was promoted to Dū Gěishìzhōng,
and said:
“The three-year review of promotions and demotions
is a great imperial ceremony.
Currently, the evaluation of the good and bad among the two Provincial Administration and Surveillance Offices
is based on reports from the Grand Coordinators and Circuit Censors,
while others are evaluated by the Provincial Administration and Surveillance Offices themselves.
Arbitrary praise and criticism
often lead to inaccuracies.
I request that those who make erroneous nominations and impeachments
be held jointly accountable.”
In the winter of the nineteenth year (1483),
Wáng Ruì, concerned that the casually appointed supernumerary officials were disrupting the official career path,
led his colleagues in a memorial, saying:
“Our ancestors established fixed official positions,
and initially there was no path for opportunistic advancement.
Recently, the system of 'donating grain to wear official insignia' began,
but this only honored the individual
without assigning them official duties.
Now, the gate for opportunism is wide open,
and offices are sold and bought like in a marketplace.
Imperial favors are bestowed internally,
extending to clerks and scribes.
Military ranks and hereditary positions
reach down to commoners.
Some, whose selection period has not yet arrived,
leapfrog in official rank;
others, from miscellaneous external posts,
are suddenly promoted to metropolitan positions.
Even lowly servants and despicable commoners, children from the marketplace,
can all climb their way up,
usurping titles and honors inappropriately.
The excess has reached this point,
causing all discerning people to feel chilled to the bone.
We humbly observe that when Emperor Yīngzōng was restored to power,
all those who had opportunistically benefited during the Jǐngtài period were ultimately dismissed.
When Your Majesty ascended the throne,
all those who falsely claimed merits during the Tiānshùn period were eradicated.
We beg Your Majesty to make a resolute decision from your imperial heart
and dismiss all these individuals,
to uphold the dignity of the state.”
Censor Zhāng Jì of Bǎo’yīng and others also said:
“Recently, low-ranking individuals and base performers have presumptuously inserted themselves among the high officials,
and dog butchers and silk vendors have abusively occupied important positions.
Among civil officials, some do not even recognize a single character,
and among military ranks, some cannot even wield a single arrow.
Commoners are suddenly elevated,
frequently promoted within a few years,
or fathers and sons sit together in one hall,
or brothers separately occupy different offices.
There are even military craftsmen who have fled and concealed themselves,
changed their surnames, and advanced in their careers;
officials who have committed embezzlement
have hidden their crimes and sought favor.
Dozens of people obtain office in a single day,
and hundreds of people draw salaries from a single office.
Since ancient times,
has there ever been such a policy?”
When the Emperor received the memorial,
his intention was somewhat moved.
After three days,
he demoted Lǐ Zīxǐng, Líng Zhōng, and four others by one rank,
and stripped Huáng Qiān, Qián Tōng, and nine others of their offices.
People rejoiced.
In the first month of the following year,
Eunuch Shàng Míng was dismissed,
but his partisans Lǐ Róng, Xiāo Jìng, and others still held power.
Wáng Ruì and others again memorialized to impeach them,
but the Emperor did not comply.
Wáng Ruì served in the remonstrance office for more than ten years,
then was promoted to Right Cānyì of Húguǎng.
He resigned due to illness and returned home,
where he died.
Lǐ Jùn,
courtesy name Zǐyīng,
was a native of Qíshān.
He became a *jìnshì* in the fifth year of Chénghuà.
He was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Personnel (*Lìkē Gěishìzhōng*),
and was repeatedly promoted to Senior Supervising Secretary (*Dū Gěishìzhōng*).
In the fifteenth year,
the emperor appointed Lǐ Zīshěng as Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*Tàicháng Sìchéng*).
Lǐ Jùn, together with his colleagues, stated:
“Zīshěng is inherently a corrupt official,
and it is inappropriate for him to stain the pure ranks
of those who oversee the sacrifices to the altars and myriad deities.”
At the same time, an imperial censor also spoke out,
so Lǐ Zīshěng was reassigned as Vice Director of the Imperial Parks Administration (*Shànglín Jiānfù*).
At that time, Wāng Zhí held usurped power,
and implicated Mǎ Wénshēng and Móu Fèng, who were exiled.
The emperor blamed the remonstrating officials for not impeaching [Wāng Zhí],
and flogged Lǐ Jùn and twenty-seven of his colleagues,
as well as twenty-nine imperial censors including Wáng Jùn.
At that time,
the emperor indulged in pleasure,
and a multitude of petty individuals caused chaos in government,
repeatedly leading to disasters and divine reprimands.
On the first day of the first month of the twenty-first year, in the *shēn* hour (3-5 PM),
a star flowed westward,
transforming into a white vapor,
with a sound like thunder.
The emperor was somewhat fearful,
and issued an edict seeking straightforward advice.
Lǐ Jùn led the officials of the Six Bureaus (*Liùkē*) in submitting a memorial, saying: The greatest and most urgent of current malpractices
are: the interference of favored courtiers with regulations,
the dereliction of duty by high officials,
the excessive granting of titles and rewards,
the undue burden of labor services,
the
insatiable demands for tributes,
and the unrecovered state of displaced people.
The celestial changes that have occurred
are largely due to these.
As for the establishment of eunuchs,
there were fixed regulations at the beginning of the dynasty.
Now, in one directorate, there might be twenty or more people,
or in one affair, five, six, or seven individuals might be involved;
some
are distributed to the various provinces,
enjoying the emoluments of princes;
some take overall command of the border regions,
monopolizing the authority of great generals;
some rely on those close to the emperor,
and introduce treacherous and evil individuals;
some connect
with both the capital and the provinces,
offering strange and ingenious items.
When managing finances, they obtain wealth outside the law;
when collecting local tributes, they demand bribes through various means.
Soldiers and commoners are trapped in hardship,
while officials suffer misfortune.
Those who commit murder
are pardoned,
and those who ruin affairs escape punishment.
Individuals like Liáng Fāng, Wéi Xīng, Chén Xǐ, and their ilk
are too numerous to list.
We humbly implore Your Majesty to exercise great resolve,
to prevent interference with regulations,
to
recall all those sent out as envoys to the provinces,
and to strictly inspect and reduce those who hold power within the palace.
Then, favored courtiers will be curbed, and Heaven's will can be turned around.
As for the high officials of today,
when they are not yet promoted,
they cannot advance without bribing inner court officials;
when they are already promoted,
they cannot maintain their positions without relying on inner court officials.
These
buy offices with wealth,
while those sell wealth with offices,
so it is no wonder that they exploit all corners of the empire
and funnel resources to the powerful.
For example, Grand Secretaries Yīn Qiān, Zhāng Péng, and Lǐ Běn,
Vice
Ministers Ài Fú, Dù Míng, and Liú Jùn,
are all old and timid.
Grand Secretaries Zhāng Yǐng and Zhāng Xuān,
Vice Minister Yǐn Zhí,
and Minister of the Court of Judicial Review Tián Jǐngyáng,
all fail to satisfy
public opinion.
We humbly implore Your Majesty to severely dismiss and punish them,
and not to show leniency.
Then, high officials will know to be vigilant, and Heaven's will can be turned around.
Indeed, titles are for those with virtue,
and rewards are for those with merit.
Now, without cause, an ordinary person is granted a title,
or without merit, a favored noble is rewarded.
Those who pray for rain
and snow receive high offices;
those who present gold and jewels gain great profits.
Daoist priests offer books on elixir refinement,
and performers stage plays of prolonged life.
Clerks and petty officials all receive official
salaries,
and actors, monks, and Daoists also tarnish official ranks.
In one year, those appointed by imperial transmission may reach a thousand people,
and in a few years, several thousand.
The salaries of these several thousand people
amount to
hundreds of thousands annually.
These are all the lifeblood of the nation
and the fat of the people,
which could be used to support worthy scholars,
and to save the starving commoners.
It is truly regrettable.
Daoist priests
such as Assistant Commissioner of the Office of Transmission Lǐ Zīshěng and Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices Dèng Cháng'ēn,
are particularly absurd and deceitful.
This is what most invites celestial changes.
We request that all officials appointed by imperial transmission be dismissed,
and not be allowed to defile the court ranks.
Then, titles and rewards will not be abused, and Heaven's will can be turned around.
Currently, construction on Buddhist temples in the capital continues without rest,
and the soldiers of the capital garrisons are exhausted.
For example, the National Preceptor Jìxiǎo uses his artifice to serve his private interests,
wasting an extraordinary amount,
which causes
indignation both inside and outside the court.
We wish Your Majesty would cherish financial resources internally,
and cherish manpower externally,
and halt all non-urgent projects.
Then, labor services will not be burdensome, and Heaven's will
can be turned around.
Recently, those who seek profit
often use the pretext of presenting tributes to deplete state funds.
They might copy a local book,
purchase an curio,
acquire a painting,
or craft a hairpin
and earring.
The cost is not much,
but they gain ten times the profit.
We wish Your Majesty would clearly see through this malpractice,
and preserve the wealth in the imperial treasury for military and state preparations.
Then, tributes will cease, and Heaven's will
can be turned around.
Shaanxi, Henan, and Shanxi have thousands of miles of barren land.
Corpses lie everywhere,
the number of displaced people increases daily,
and banditry is a concern.
We wish Your Majesty would embody the compassionate love of Heaven,
pity the destitution of the common people,
reclaim the salt tax from favored nobles,
and temporarily reallocate funds meant for temple construction
to relieve the starving people,
allowing them to barely survive.
Then, the displaced will return, and Heaven's will
can be turned around.
Indeed, the empire can be likened to a human body.
The ruler
is the head;
high officials
are the limbs;
remonstrating officials
are the eyes and ears;
the capital
is the heart and belly;
the various
provinces
are the trunk.
If high officials are derelict, the limbs will be paralyzed;
if remonstrating officials are silent, the eyes and ears will be blocked;
if the capital is not disciplined, the heart and belly will suffer illness;
if the provinces
suffer disaster and famine, the trunk will be weakened.
How then can the head remain peacefully at ease?
We humbly implore Your Majesty to act on what is said,
to serve Heaven with sincerity,
to dismiss and keep at a distance the multitude of petty individuals,
and to draw
near worthy ministers.
Consult on the successes and failures of governance,
and investigate the rise and fall of previous dynasties.
Use the classic texts of sages and worthies as remedies for governance,
and use literary officials to replace Daoist priests.
Then, there will
certainly be upright principles sufficient to expand your sagely learning,
and forthright discussions sufficient to understand celestial changes.
Then, your hands and feet will be agile,
your eyes and ears sharp,
your heart and belly at peace,
your trunk strong and healthy,
and your
This head then became greatly enlightened.
The Emperor issued a lenient edict in response.
Lǐ Zīshěng was demoted to Assistant Manager of the Imperial Gardens,
Cháng Ēn to Assistant Manager of his original temple,
and Jìxiǎo was stripped of his Imperial Preceptor title and reduced to commoner status.
The Imperial Censor on circuit was ordered to reclaim their imperial patents.
When the edict was issued,
the entire court rejoiced greatly.
In the fifth month,
Jùn was appointed Councillor of the Húguǎng Provincial Administration Commission.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
he repeatedly held office as Provincial Administrator of Shānxī
and died.
Wāng Kuí,
courtesy name Wéncàn,
was a native of Wùyuán.
He passed the imperial examination in the second year of Chénghuà.
He served as Magistrate of Xiùshuǐ,
then was promoted to Imperial Censor.
In the twenty-first year,
a celestial phenomenon occurred,
and he, along with his colleagues, submitted a memorial detailing ten matters,
stating:
"Those ministers who offered remonstrance and were demoted or banished,
having shown loyalty to the state,
should have their posts restored.
The demon monk Jìxiǎo colluded with the eunuch Liáng Fāng,
depleting the imperial treasury.
I request that Fāng be punished,
and Jìxiǎo be beheaded in the marketplace.
Officials appointed by imperial edict, such as Gù Xián, are all nephews of eunuchs who falsely claimed to be Embroidered-Uniform Guards,
and Lǐ Zīshěng, a petty official, was granted the title of Minister of the Court of Grand Herald.
They should all be dismissed to clear the path for officials.
Ministers Yīn Qiān and Lǐ Běn,
and Vice Ministers Dù Míng and Yǐn Zhí,
all lack a reputation for integrity.
Ministers Zhāng Péng, Zhāng Yíng, and Zhāng Xuān,
Vice Ministers Dù Qiān, Ài Fú, Mǎ Xiǎn, and Liú Jùn,
Grand Judge Sòng Qīn,
and Provincial Grand Censors Lǔ Néng and Mǎ Xùn,
are all old and inept.
Vice Minister Tán Lún is shameless in his ambition,
Provincial Censor Zhào Wénbó is crude and reckless,
and Grand Judge Tián Jǐngyáng has always been careless in his conduct.
They should be ordered to retire.
The number of eunuchs serving as garrison commanders and defense commanders has increased severalfold since the Tiānshùn era,
abusing their power,
and oppressing local officials.
Zhāng Qìng in Zhèjiāng and Cài Yòng in Sìchuān have even been able to arrest and try officials of the fourth rank and below,
which severely harms the dignity of the state.
They should all be withdrawn.
The excessive number of eunuchs overseeing military camps and supervising firearms, both inside and outside the capital,
all privately employ soldiers
and collect monthly payments,
with some having as many as two or three hundred people.
Military generals also privately employ strong men,
leaving only the old and weak in the ranks.
Imperial relatives and eunuchs petition for salt profits,
traveling south fully laden.
Wherever they go, they display imperial yellow banners,
causing merchants to stop operating,
and border provisions to be depleted.
All of these should be strictly prohibited.
Shǎnxī, Shānxī, and Hénán have suffered floods and droughts for years,
with the majority of the population dying or migrating.
There are barely any people left in the Shānxī and Shǎnxī regions.
The affected prefectures and counties should be investigated
and granted general tax exemptions.
Attendant Zhāng Shànjí was previously demoted for a crime.
Upon reaching the capital for performance review,
he begged for mercy in the dim night
and was granted this position,
greatly disgracing the pure ranks.
He should be dismissed.
Many starving people from Shānxī, Shǎnxī, Hénán, and Luòyáng have flowed into Yúnxiáng,
to the point of cannibalism.
I request that a large amount of treasury grain be distributed for relief
to prevent further calamities."
At that time,
the Emperor sought advice due to the calamities.
Although Kuí's memorial touched upon imperial taboos,
he was not punished.
Soon after,
an Imperial Censor committed an impropriety.
Kuí corrected him face-to-face
and then reported it after court.
The Emperor, considering him slow and tardy,
had him beaten in court.
After several months,
he was again appointed Assistant Prefect of Kuízhōu,
where he suppressed the notorious bandits of Yúnyáng.
When Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
he was transferred to Assistant Prefect of a prefecture.
Upon recommendation,
he was promoted to Prefect of Chéngdū.
During a famine, there were many bandits.
His relief efforts helped many resume their livelihoods.
He was thrice promoted to Left Provincial Administration Commissioner of Guǎngxī.
In the fourteenth year of Hóngzhì, he served as Right Vice Grand Censor,巡抚貴州 Provincial Censor of Guìzhōu.
Before a full year had passed,
the bandit woman Mǐ Lǔ of Pǔ'ān rebelled,
and he was impeached and forced to retire.
He died in the sixth year of Zhèngdé.
His nephew Shùnmín,
courtesy name Cóngrén.
He passed the imperial examination in the fourteenth year of Chénghuà.
He was appointed Director of the Bureau of Receptions,
then promoted to Imperial Censor,
and dispatched to inspect Gānsù.
He impeached eunuchs and generals for their failures,
and submitted dozens of memorials on border strategies.
Previously,
when Kuí was beaten outside the palace,
Shùnmín supported him,
and the Emperor heard of it and was angered.
By this time,
he was demoted to Archivist of Ménghuà Guard
for an inappropriate legal judgment.
At the beginning of Hóngzhì,
he was promoted to Magistrate of Dōngguǎn,
but before he could take office,
he was promoted to Surveillance Commissioner of Jiāngxī.
He was skilled at judicial review,
analyzing cases with flowing clarity.
His methods for clarifying military law
were followed by later generations.
He was transferred to Vice Surveillance Commissioner for Military Colonies in Yúnnán.
He rectified lands seized by influential figures
and returned them to the government.
The remnant of Lùchuān, Sī Lù, crossed the Jīnshā River
and occupied Mèngmì.
Shùnmín was commissioned to pacify him.
He returned home for his mother's mourning.
After the mourning period,
Huái and Yáng suffered a great famine.
He was ordered to provide relief in his former post.
He expediently distributed grain,
and requested the suspension of non-urgent tasks,
saving 1.2 million starving people,
and helping over 8,000 displaced households return to their livelihoods.
He was promoted to Provincial Surveillance Commissioner of Fújiàn.
The treasury of Fúqīng County was robbed.
Someone falsely accused a rival
and the case was concluded.
Shùnmín, through investigation, found the true thief,
saving thirty people from death
and punishing the accuser.
During a drought,
prayers for rain were unanswered.
He personally visited the Fúzhōu prison,
releasing those wrongfully imprisoned or with minor offenses.
All officials in his jurisdiction cleared their prisons,
and then heavy rain fell.
He successively served as Left and Right Provincial Administration Commissioner of Hénán.
In the second year of Zhèngdé, he was appointed Right Vice Grand Censor to govern Yúnxiáng.
Barely a month later,
all Provincial Censors nationwide were dismissed,
and he was reassigned to the Nanjing Censorate,
dying on the way.
Kuí was simple and quiet by nature,
not carelessly taking or giving,
and was praised for his honesty and integrity.
Shùnmín, on the other hand, was fond of learning and disciplined in his conduct,
valiantly upholding moral integrity,
and was particularly held in high regard by his contemporaries.
When a celestial anomaly occurred and the emperor sought criticisms,
the Nine Ministers each submitted several memorials,
but they generally avoided sensitive topics,
none being particularly bold or severe.
Only Kuí and Lǐ Jùn’s statements were the most direct.
Furthermore, Wǔxuǎn Yuánwàiláng Cuī Shēng and Péng Gāng,
Zhǔshì Sū Zhāng,
Hùbù Zhǔshì Zhōu Zhěn,
and Xíngbù Zhǔshì Lǐ Dàn all spoke up.
Shēng and Zhāng criticized the crimes of eunuchs and demonic monks,
requesting their immediate execution and banishment.
They also stated that Shàngshū Wáng Shù was now like Yī and Fù,
and should not be kept in Nánjīng.
Gāng denounced Lǐ Zīshěng and Jìxiǎo,
requesting their execution to appease the populace.
Zhěn also requested the execution of Liáng Fāng and Lǐ Zīshěng,
along with the purging of inner palace attendants
and the abolition of Daoist rituals.
Dàn presented ten proposals,
and further stated:
“Immortals, Buddhist and Daoist masters, imperial relatives by marriage, female courtiers,
sensory pleasures and material gain,
and bizarre and elaborate crafts
are all things Your Majesty has long been enchanted by and indulged in,
while those close to you on your left and right mutually entice you into them.”
His words were very incisive.
The Emperor, being in a period of self-reflection,
did not punish any of them.
Later, due to the case of an official illegally selling old imperial edicts bestowed upon foreign vassals,
Gāng and Zhāng were handed over to the authorities
and demoted to provincial posts.
Secretly, the Emperor instructed Lìbù Shàngshū Yǐn Mín to dismiss Dàn and others,
and even wrote sixty names on a screen,
intending to demote them to remote and harsh lands once their promotions were announced.
Dàn, along with Gěishìzhōng Lú Yǔ, Qín Shēng, and Tóng Zhù, were all banished on the same day.
Seeing that many officials were being banished to distant places,
department ministers deliberately delayed the promotions of those due for one,
whereby Shēng and Zhěn thus escaped punishment.
Cuī Shēng,
courtesy name Tíngjìn,
was originally from Lè’ān.
His father was the storehouse supervisor of Zhāngdé,
and consequently settled there.
He became a *jìnshì* in the fifth year of Chénghuà.
He was appointed Zhǔshì of the Gōngbù, then transferred to the Bīngbù.
He gradually rose to become Zhīfǔ of Yán’ān
and Cāncè of Sìchuān.
He was an honest official,
and habitually wore plain cloth robes at home;
his household servant collected horse manure for fuel.
He lived at home for thirty years,
and died at the age of eighty-eight.
His son Xiǎn
has his own biography.
Péng Gāng was from Qīngjiāng.
He, Sū Zhāng, Zhōu Zhěn, Qín Shēng, and Tóng Zhù all became *jìnshì* in the eleventh year of Chénghuà.
He was demoted to Zhīzhōu of Yǒngníng,
then transferred to Rǔzhōu.
He dug canals to irrigate several thousand *mǔ* of fields.
He was again promoted to Tíxué Fùshǐ of Yúnnán.
Sū Zhāng was from Yúgàn.
He was demoted to Tōngpàn of Yáo’ān,
then again promoted to Zhīfǔ of Yánpíng.
He had a good administrative record.
He ended his career as Cāncè of Zhèjiāng.
Zhōu Zhěn was from Pútián,
the son of Fùshǐ Yīng’s cousin.
Later he advanced to Lángzhōng,
and ended his career as Yùnshǐ of Shāndōng.
Lǐ Dàn,
courtesy name Qǐdōng,
was from Xiànxiàn.
He became a *jìnshì* in the seventeenth year of Chénghuà.
He was demoted to Tōngpàn of Zhènyuǎn,
and died not long after.
Lú Yǔ was from Yínxiàn.
He became a *jìnshì* in the fifth year of Chénghuà.
As Xíngkē Gěishìzhōng,
he memorialized to exempt Huái and Yáng from over a hundred thousand
in arrears taxes,
and cleared up long-standing abuses of forced market purchases of warhorses in the northwest.
He once incurred the Emperor’s wrath
and was beaten with a staff.
He was promoted to Gōngkē Dū Gěishìzhōng.
He, Shēng, and Zhù all submitted memorials concerning the celestial anomaly,
and were condemned.
Yǔ was demoted to Tōngpàn of Chángshā,
and ended his career as Zhīfǔ of Guǎngpíng.
Qín Shēng was from Nánchāng,
and was demoted to Tóngzhī of Guǎng’ān Zhōu.
Tóng Zhù was from Lánxī,
and was demoted to Tóngzhī of Xīngguó Zhōu,
ending his career as Zhīfǔ of Yuánzhōu.
At this time,
Cuī Shēng had offended the Emperor by requesting the recall of Wáng Shù,
and Gōngbù Zhǔshì Wáng Chún was also beaten with a staff and demoted for admonishing against the dismissal of Wáng Shù.
Chún was from Xiānjū.
He became a *jìnshì* in the seventeenth year of Chénghuà.
He was demoted to Tuīguān of Sīnán.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
he was repeatedly promoted to Húguǎng Tíxué Qiānshì.
Tāng Nài,
courtesy name Yòngzhī,
was from Shòuzhōu.
He became a *jìnshì* in the eleventh year of Chénghuà.
He was appointed Xíngrén,
then promoted to Yùshǐ.
When Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
he first impeached Dàxuéshì Wàn Ān for deceiving the emperor and harming the country.
The next day,
he was summoned to Zuǒshùnmén.
Palace eunuchs stood in dense rows,
ordering him to kneel.
Nài said:
“Is it an imperial decree
that orders Nài to kneel,
or is it the grand eunuch’s intention?”
They replied:
“It is an imperial decree.”
Nài then knelt.
When the decree was proclaimed,
it stated that his memorial had already been withheld.
Nài loudly declared:
“What I have spoken of are matters of national importance;
how can they be withheld?”
Soon after, Ān was dismissed,
and Nài was also sent out to inspect horses in Jīfǔ.
He quickly submitted a memorial stating:
“After Your Majesty’s morning audience,
you should proceed to the private chambers,
select upright, prudent, and honest attendant ministers such as Liú Jiàn, Xiè Qiān, Chéng Mínzhèng, and Wú Kuān,
and discuss scholarship and principles with them daily,
taking this as the foundation for good governance.
As for cabinet ministers Yǐn Zhí, Shàngshū Lǐ Yù, Dū Yùshǐ Liú Fū, and Shìláng Huáng Jǐng,
they are treacherous and shameless,
either rising through connections with palace eunuchs,
or relying on sycophants to act selfishly.
If they are not quickly expelled,
they will surely harm Your Sagely Majesty.
The Sīlǐ palace eunuchs Lǐ Róng and Xiāo Jìng were previously impeached and dismissed by censorial officials,
but soon managed to return through connections.
They then picked faults with censorial officials,
demoting and banishing almost all of them,
which caused the morale of scholars to plummet.
It is fitting to quickly enforce just punishments,
and not be lenient.
As for all those who obtained office through imperial decrees delivered by eunuchs,
please send them all to malarial regions,
to serve as a warning to the entire realm.
Furthermore, summon the retired Shàngshū Wáng Shù and Wáng Hóng,
Dū Yùshǐ Péng Sháo,
Qiānshì Zhāng Mào, and others,
and reinstate all officials who were punished for their remonstrances,
to encourage upright conduct.”
This was reported to the emperor.
In the first month of the first year of Hóngzhì,
Nài again impeached Lǐbù Shàngshū Zhōu Hóngmó,
Shìláng Ní Yuè and Zhāng Yuè,
and Nánjīng Bīngbù Shàngshū Mǎ Wénshēng,
and then said:
“Shàofù Liú Jí,
along with Wàn Ān and Yǐn Zhí, are equally corrupt and greedy.
Ān and Zhí were dismissed,
but Jí alone was promoted,
without feeling ashamed.
I request a major enforcement of demotions and promotions,
to clearly show encouragement and punishment.”
He also impeached Lǐ Róng and Xiāo Jìng,
and recommended the banished *jìnshì* Lǐ Wénxiáng for a censorial post.
When Shàngshū Wáng Shù requested to suspend the imperial lectures due to the intense heat,
Nài strongly argued against it,
and his words even implicated Shù.
At this time,
the Emperor was reforming various administrative matters,
and the channels for remonstrance were wide open.
Newcomers vied to distinguish themselves with achievements.
Memorials arrived in rapid succession,
often being overly aggressive and critical,
and Nài’s fervor was particularly sharp.
His criticisms
sometimes reached figures of national renown,
which made many high officials fear him,
and Jí was especially unable to tolerate it.
He sent someone to bribe Yùshǐ Wèi Zhāng, saying:
“If you can get rid of Nài,
you will act as Qiānyuànshì.”
Zhāng was delighted,
and day and night sought Nài’s shortcomings.
Not long after,
the case involving Jí Rén arose.
Jí Rén (吉人)
was a Cháng'ān (長安) native.
He became a *jìnshì* in the late Chénghuà (成化) era
and served as a *Zhōngshū Shèrén* (中書舍人).
When Sìchuān (四川) suffered a famine,
the Emperor dispatched *Lángzhōng* (郎中) Jiāng Hàn (江漢) to provide relief.
Jí Rén said that Jiāng Hàn (江漢) was not up to the task,
and that four envoys should be sent to provide relief in different routes,
and a capable *Yùshǐ* (御史) should be selected as a *Xún'àn* (巡按)
to effectively aid the disaster relief.
He then recommended *Jǐshìzhōng* (給事中) Sòng Cóng (宋琮), Chén Qióng (陳璚), Hán Dǐng (韓鼎),
*Yùshǐ* (御史) Cáo Lín (曹璘),
*Lángzhōng* (郎中) Wáng Yí (王沂), Hóng Zhōng (洪鍾),
*Yuánwàiláng* (員外郎) Dōng Sīchéng (東思誠),
*Píngshì* (評事) Wáng Yín (王寅),
*Lǐxíng Zhīxiàn* (理刑知縣) Hán Fú (韓福), and *Shòuzhōu Zhīzhōu* (壽州知州) Liú Gài (劉㮣) as suitable candidates,
and that Nài (鼐) was fully capable of serving as the *Xún'àn* (巡按).
Zhāng (璋) then drafted a memorial,
falsely signing the names of *Yùshǐ* (御史) Chén Jǐnglóng (陳景隆) and others,
accusing Jí Rén (吉人) of resisting imperial decrees
and secretly forming cliques.
The Emperor, enraged,
sent Jí Rén (吉人) to the imperial prison
and ordered him to identify his faction.
Jí Rén (吉人) named Nài (鼐), Lín (璘), Sīchéng (思誠), Gài (㮣), and Fú (福).
Zhāng (璋) then incited *Yùshǐ* (御史) Chén Bì (陳璧) and others to say:
"Lín (璘), Fú (福), and Sīchéng (思誠) are not part of his faction.
His faction consists of Nài (鼐), Gài (㮣), and *Zhǔshì* (主事) Lǐ Wénxiáng (李文祥), *Shùjíshì* (庶吉士) Zōu Zhì (鄒智), and *Zhīzhōu* (知州) Dǒng Jié (董傑).
Gài (㮣) once gifted Nài (鼐) white silver
and sent him a letter,
saying he dreamt that a person riding an ox was about to fall,
and Nài (鼐) pulled him by the hand, preventing him from falling.
He also saw Nài (鼐) holding a five-colored stone, leading the ox on its way.
He then interpreted it, saying: 'A person riding an ox refers to Zhū (朱),
which is the imperial surname.
It means the state is on the verge of collapse,
relying on Nài (鼐) to support it,
and leading the ruler to the right path.'
Nài (鼐) and Gài (㮣) are self-promoting
and slandering current politics.
We request that Wénxiáng (文祥), Zhì (智), and Jié (傑) also be arrested and prosecuted."
When the memorial was submitted,
Jí (吉) orchestrated it from within,
and all were sent to the imperial prison,
intending to execute them all.
*Xíngbù Shàngshū* (刑部尚書) Hé Qiáoxīn (何喬新) and *Shìláng* (侍郎) Péng Sháo (彭韶) and others resisted,
and public opinion outside was also tumultuous and unfair.
Consequently, Gài (㮣) was condemned to be beheaded under the law against 'seditious speech';
Nài (鼐), for accepting bribes,
was exiled to Sùzhōu (肅州);
Jí Rén (吉人), for deception,
was stripped of his official status;
Zhì (智), Wénxiáng (文祥), and Jié (傑) were all demoted.
*Lìbù Shàngshū* (吏部尚書) Wáng Shù (王恕) memorialized, saying:
"The law imposes heavy penalties for 'seditious speech,'
which refers to fabricating prophecies and omens.
Although Gài's (㮣) letter was presumptuous,
it was truly because Nài (鼐) frequently spoke out on matters without avoiding personal risk,
and thus he was exaggerating his praise.
If this is to be considered 'seditious speech,'
then if someone were to create an omen predicting the fall of Qín (秦),
how would one punish them more severely?"
The Emperor was moved by the intent of the memorial
and ordered Gài (㮣) to be temporarily held in prison.
Later, during a review of cases in hot weather,
Qiáoxīn (喬新) and others said:
"Gài (㮣) originally should not be subject to the law against 'seditious speech.'
Moreover, Gài (㮣) was orphaned at five,
had no brothers,
and his mother, Lady Sūn (孫), remained a chaste widow for thirty years,
and had even been commended.
She is old, sick, and poor.
If Gài (㮣) dies,
his mother will surely not survive.
We implore Your Sacred Grace to show compassion."
Consequently, Gài's (㮣) death sentence was commuted,
and he was exiled to Hǎizhōu (海州).
Gài (㮣)
was from Jìníng (濟寧).
He became a *jìnshì* in the twentieth year of Chénghuà (成化).
He was appointed *Shòuzhōu Zhīzhōu* (壽州知州),
and nearly all idolatrous shrines in his jurisdiction were destroyed.
After three years, moral transformation was widely implemented.
In the early Hóngzhì (弘治) era, he submitted a memorial stating:
"Punishments, rewards, grants, and seizures are
the great prerogative of the ruler.
In later generations, these have been usurped by women, small-minded individuals, powerful ministers, and imperial relatives.
This is because such people have devious minds and cunning methods.
If the ruler shows them even a little trust,
they immediately fall into their schemes.
Those whom the ruler favors
take advantage of his joy to spread rumors and elevate themselves;
those whom the ruler dislikes
take advantage of his anger to make subtle remarks and strike them down,
causing worthy gentlemen to ultimately suffer obscurity and depart.
When there is a shortage of ministers,
they procrastinate and entice,
waiting for someone who is communicative, supplicating, soft-spoken, and easy to control,
then recommend and appoint them.
Those who are upright and unyielding
are then slandered and abandoned,
waiting until their spirit declines and their concerns shift,
no longer causing significant dissent,
before they are again taken into consideration.
Once the cunning schemes are implemented,
even though punishments, rewards, grants, and seizures are nominally controlled solely by the ruler,
they are actually entirely at their whim.
Once factions are established and power is consolidated,
they then fear sudden exposure,
so they go to great lengths to ostracize remonstrating officials,
making sure their ruler is isolated above,
hearing nothing,
seeing nothing,
to further their private interests,
and they do not stop until both they themselves and the state are ruined.
Therefore, punishments, rewards, grants, and seizures
must be proposed by high ministers
and deliberated by the censorate
before they can be implemented.
If there is any false accusation,
it must be thoroughly investigated without leniency,
then slanderers and sycophants will be unable to intervene,
and power will not be transferred downwards."
When he went to the capital for performance review,
he encountered this misfortune
and ultimately died in his place of exile.
After Nài (鼐) was exiled,
there was no one to intercede for him,
and he was only released and returned home after a long time.
Dǒng Jié (董傑)
was from Jīngxiàn (涇縣).
He became a *jìnshì* in the late Chénghuà (成化) era.
When Nài (鼐) memorialized about suspending lectures during the hot months,
Jié (傑), who was then awaiting selection for an official post,
also submitted a strong memorial arguing for it,
thus becoming well-known.
He was appointed *Miǎnyáng Zhīzhōu* (沔陽知州),
but only a few months later,
he was arrested and imprisoned in the imperial prison,
then demoted to *Sìchuān Xíngdū Sī Zhīshì* (四川行都司知事),
and successively promoted to *Hénán Zuǒ Bùzhèngshǐ* (河南左布政使).
Wherever he served, he fulfilled his duties,
and was cherished by the people.
In the sixth year of Zhèngdé (正德),
when bandits rose in Jiāngxī (江西),
*Xúnfǔ* (巡撫) Wáng Zhé (王哲)'s army was defeated and he was recalled.
Jié (傑) was promoted to *Yòufù Dūyùshǐ* (右副都御史) to replace him.
He died not long after.
Zhāng (璋), having become Jí (吉)'s confidant,
was indeed promoted to *Dàlǐ Sìchéng* (大理寺丞).
He was imprisoned for an offense,
demoted to *Jiǔjiāng Tóngzhī* (九江同知),
and died of melancholy.
Jiāng Wǎn (姜綰),
courtesy name Yùqīng (玉卿),
was from Yìyáng (弋陽).
He became a *jìnshì* in the fourteenth year of Chénghuà (成化).
From *Jǐnglíng Zhīxiàn* (景陵知縣), he was promoted to *Nánjīng Yùshǐ* (南京御史).
In the early Hóngzhì (弘治) era,
he presented ten proposals on governance.
He also stated that major policies should be discussed during the noon court,
and trivial matters should not be vaguely presented,
all of which were reported to the emperor.
In the second month of the second year,
Jiǎng Cóng (蔣琮), a eunuch serving as the Nanjing Garrison Commander (Nánjīng Shǒubèi Zhōngguān), referred the matter of the reed fields to Wǎn (綰) for review and investigation.
Cóng (琮) instructed Wǎn (綰) to rule in his favor.
Wǎn (綰) submitted a memorial stating:
"Cóng (琮), a high official of the garrison, contended with commoners for profit,
abusing public office for private gain,
using public notices to defy imperial decrees,
and publicly threatening secret retaliation,
coercing compliance.
Furthermore, he altered established laws;
his crimes number ten.
A palace eunuch encroaching upon the duties of an censor,
this is crime one.
Enviously harming a high official and slandering the Grand Censor (Dūyùshǐ) Qín Hóng (秦紘),
this is crime two.
Angered by the lack of proper welcome from the river gate official,
and desiring to have him dismissed by memorial,
this is crime three.
Accepting a civilian's petition without going through the Department of General Administration (Tōngzhèng),
this is crime four.
Dispatching trusted confidants
to embezzle national revenue,
this is crime five.
Collecting silver from artisans and craftsmen on a quarterly basis,
this is crime six.
Unauthorized employment of dismissed idle secretaries (dūshì),
this is crime seven.
Injuring officials who displeased him,
this is crime eight.
Falsely accusing Secretariat Drafter (Zhǔshì) Zhōu Qí (周琦) of crimes
and deceiving the imperial court,
this is crime nine.
Recommending dismissed inner palace officials
and usurping the Emperor's authority,
this is crime ten."
The matter was referred to the Three Judicial Offices (Sānfǎsī) of Nanjing.
Subsequently,
an official was specially dispatched to reinvestigate the case and report to the throne.
Previously,
Censor (Yùshǐ) Yú Jùn (余濬) had impeached the eunuch Chén Zǔshēng (陳祖生) for illegally reclaiming land in Hòuhú,
which caused the lake to become silted.
The memorial was sent down to Nanjing Secretariat Drafter (Zhǔshì) Lú Jǐn (盧錦) for investigation and report.
Jǐn (錦) had an old grudge with Zǔshēng (祖生).
Meanwhile, Supervising Secretary (Gěishìzhōng) Fāng Xiàng (方向) had led his colleague Miào Chú (繆樗) and others to impeach Zǔshēng (祖生) and other civil and military officials for dereliction of duty.
Also, due to lightning striking a cypress tree at Xiàolíng,
he impeached Grand Secretary (Dàxuéshì) Liú Jí (劉吉) and eleven others,
and criticized Zǔshēng (祖shēng) even more vigorously.
Zǔshēng (祖shēng) bore a deep grudge against Xiàng (向).
At that time, Xiàng (向) was supervising the Hòuhú Yellow Register,
so Zǔshēng (祖shēng) exposed Xiàng (向) and Jǐn (錦) for actually encroaching upon lake land.
An imperial edict ordered the Judicial Offices (Fǎsī) to investigate.
Before the investigation report was submitted,
Cóng (琮) was impeached by Wǎn (綰).
Thereupon, Cóng (琮), Zǔshēng (祖生), and Jí (吉) conspired to strip Jǐn (錦) of his official status,
demote Xiàng (向),
and arrest Wǎn (綰) and his colleagues Sūn Hóng (孫紘), Liú Xùn (劉遜), Jīn Zhāng (金章), Jì Jié (紀傑), Cáo Yù (曹玉), Tán Sù (譚肅), Xú Lǐ (徐禮), Yú Jùn (余濬),
and Supervising Secretary (Gěishìzhōng) Miào Chú (繆樗),
who were all taken to the capital for trial
and demoted to judicial prefect (zhōupànguān).
Wǎn (綰) was demoted to judicial prefect of Guìyáng (桂陽),
then transferred to Assistant Prefect (Tóngzhī) of Níngguó (寧國),
and later promoted to Prefect (Zhīfǔ) of Qìngyuǎn (慶遠).
He executed the notorious bandits Wéi Qīxuán (韋七旋) and Wéi Wànmiào (韋萬miào).
Their confederates gathered tens of thousands of bandits and attacked the city.
Wǎn (綰) held the city firmly,
summoned militia to attack from both sides,
defeated and routed them.
All the indigenous people (mán) of Dōnglán (東蘭) and other prefectures returned the encroached lands.
Grand Coordinator (Zǒngdū) Liú Dàxià (劉大夏) admired his talent
and recommended him as Vice Surveillance Commissioner (Bīngbèi Fùshǐ) of Yòujiāng (右江).
Cén Jùn (岑濬), Prefect of Sī'ēn (思恩), expelled Cén Měng (岑猛), Prefect of Tiánzhōu (田州).
Wǎn (綰) offered a strategy to Grand Coordinator (Zǒngdū) Pān Fān (潘蕃).
Fān (蕃) ordered him and Regional Commander (Dūzhǐhuī) Jīn Táng (金堂) to combine forces from various routes and severely defeat the bandits,
thus pacifying Sī'ēn (思恩).
Wǎn (綰) detailed the situation of the two prefectures
and requested the establishment of permanent officials (liúguān),
like in the central plains.
The imperial court debated and adopted this.
Wǎn (綰) retired due to illness.
Soon after, he was appointed Surveillance Commissioner (Ànchásǐ) of Hénán (河南),
but soon returned home due to illness
and died at home.
Yú Jùn (余濬) was from Cíxī (慈谿).
He obtained his Jinshi degree in the 17th year of Chénghuà.
At the beginning of Xiàozōng's (孝宗) reign,
he memorialized to permanently abolish the order allowing grain payment for prison release.
He also impeached the eunuch Zhāng Qìng (張慶), garrison commander of Zhèjiāng (浙江), and the eunuch Wéi Juàn (韋眷), garrison commander of Guǎngdōng (廣東).
Subsequently, he recommended Wáng Shù (王恕) as suitable for the Grand Secretariat (Nèigé),
and Mǎ Wénshēng (馬文shēng), Péng Sháo (彭韶), Zhāng Yuè (張悅), Ruǎn Qín (阮勤), Huáng Kǒngzhāo (黃孔昭) as suitable for the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù).
The investigation of Hòuhú (後湖) was initiated by Jùn (濬).
He was demoted to judicial prefect of Píngdù (平度)
and ended his career as a prefect (zhīfǔ).
Fāng Xiàng (方向),
courtesy name Yǔyì (與義),
was from Tóngchéng (桐城).
He obtained his Jinshi degree in the 17th year of Chénghuà.
He was demoted to courier station master (yìchéng) of Duōluó (多羅) in Yúnnán (雲南),
and later served as Prefect (Zhīfǔ) of Qióngzhōu (瓊州).
When he went to the capital for an audience,
his servant privately purchased a pearl,
which he confiscated and threw into the sea.
Miào Chú (繆樗),
courtesy name Quánzhī (全之),
was from Lìyáng (溧陽).
He obtained his Jinshi degree in the 11th year of Chénghuà.
At the beginning of Xiàozōng's (孝zōng) reign,
he presented eight matters concerning current administration.
He then impeached Grand Secretary (Dàxuéshì) Yǐn Zhí (尹直) and others,
and was known for his forthrightness at the time.
He ended his career as judicial prefect of Yíngzhōu (營州).
Sūn Hóng (孫紘),
courtesy name Wénmiǎn (文冕),
was from Yín (鄞).
He obtained his Jinshi degree in the 14th year of Chénghuà.
He was demoted to judicial prefect of Jiāozhōu (膠州),
promoted to Prefect (Zhīzhōu) of Guǎngdé (廣德),
and died in office.
Hóng (紘) was poor in his youth,
working as a scribe and selling meat to support his mother.
After entering officialdom,
he abstained from meat his entire life.
Liú Xùn (劉遜) was from Ānfú (安福).
He obtained his Jinshi degree in the 14th year of Chénghuà.
He was demoted to judicial prefect of Lǐzhōu (澧州),
and promoted to Prefect (Zhīzhōu) of Wǔgāng (武岡).
When Prince Mín (Mínwáng) was undisciplined,
Xùn (遜) restrained him
and also sought to reduce his annual stipend.
The Prince was enraged,
memorialized to the court,
and had Xùn (遜) summoned to the imperial prison.
He was demoted to Judicial Officer (Duànshì) of the Síchuān (Sìchuān) Acting Provincial Military Command (Xíng Dū Sī),
and later served as Vice Surveillance Commissioner (Fùshǐ) of Húguǎng (Húguǎng).
Liú Jǐn (劉瑾) demanded bribes and failed to get them,
so Xùn (遜) was accused of lacking military provisions and arrested.
He was later released.
He was again accused of delaying judicial cases
and fined a hundred dan (石) of rice.
Previously,
Prince Róng (Róngwáng) requested two thousand qǐng (頃) of land in Chénzhōu (辰州) and Chángdé (常德), eight hundred lǐ (里) of mountain land, and over a thousand civilian houses and shops.
Xùn (遜) and Provincial Governor (Xúnfǔ) Hán Zhòng (韓重) insisted on not granting them.
By this time,
Jǐn (瑾) granted all of them.
The Ministry proposed to appoint Xùn (遜) as Vice Surveillance Commissioner (Fùshǐ) of Qióngzhōu (瓊州),
but Jǐn (瑾) forced him to retire.
After Jǐn (瑾) was executed,
Xùn (遜) was reinstated
and later served as Surveillance Commissioner (Ànchásǐ) of Fújiàn (Fújiàn).
Jīn Zhāng (金章) and others had no other notable achievements.
Jiāng Hóng (姜洪),
courtesy name Xīfàn (希範),
was from Guǎngdé (廣德).
He obtained his Jinshi degree in the 14th year of Chénghuà.
He was appointed Magistrate (Zhīxiàn) of Lúshì (盧氏).
He rode alone to encourage agriculture and sericulture.
When the commoner Jiāng Zhònglǐ (姜仲禮) offered to die in place of his father who was sentenced to death,
Hóng (洪) memorialized to pardon him.
He was summoned to the capital and appointed Censor (Yùshǐ).
Upon Emperor Xiàozōng's (孝zōng) ascension,
he presented eight matters concerning current administration.
He successively criticized Eunuch Xiāo Jìng (蕭敬),
Grand Secretaries (Nèigé) Wàn Ān (萬安) and Liú Jí (劉吉),
Academician (Xuéshì) Yǐn Zhí (尹直),
Vice Ministers (Shìláng) Huáng Jǐng (黃景) and Liú Xuān (劉宣),
Grand Censor (Dūyùshǐ) Liú Fū (劉敷),
Ministers (Shàngshū) Lǐ Yù (李裕), Lǐ Mǐn (李敏), and Dù Míng (杜 Míng),
Grand Court Assessor (Dàlǐchéng) Sòng Jīng (宋經).
He also recommended retired Ministers (Zhìshì Shàngshū) Wáng Shù (王恕), Wáng Hóng (王竑), Lǐ Bǐng (李秉),
former Vice Minister (Qùrèn Shìláng) Xiè Duó (謝鐸),
Compilers (Biānyù) Zhāng Yuánzhēn (張元禎),
Reviewer (Jiǎntǎo) Chén Xiànzhāng (陳獻章),
Assistant Reviewer (Qiānshì) Zhāng Mào (章懋),
Judicial Reviewer (Píngshì) Huáng Zhòngzhāo (黃仲昭),
Censors (Yùshǐ) Qiáng Zhēn (強珍), Xú Yōng (徐鏞), Yú Dàjié (于大節),
Supervising Secretaries (Gěishìzhōng) Wáng Huī (王徽), Xiāo Xiǎn (蕭顯), Hè Qīn (賀欽),
Secretary (Yuánwài) Lín Jùn (林俊),
Secretariat Drafter (Zhǔshì) Wáng Chún (王純), and incumbent Ministers (Xiànrèn Shàngshū) Yú Zǐjùn (余子俊) and Mǎ Wénshēng (馬文shēng),
Provincial Governor (Xúnfǔ) Péng Sháo (彭韶),
Vice Minister (Shìláng) Zhāng Yuè (張悅),
and Grand Secretary (Zhānshì) Yáng Shǒuchén (楊守陳).
Moreover, he stated that Commander (Zhǐhuī) Xǔ Níng (許寧) and Eunuch Huái ēn (懷恩) were both outstanding among their peers
and fully capable of their appointments.
Many of his other memorials
criticized the Emperor's favored courtiers,
and his memorials of resignation amounted to tens of thousands of words.
The Emperor praised and accepted them.
Those he criticized held a lasting grudge against him.
In the first year of the Hóngzhì reign (1488), [Hóng] was dispatched to Húguǎng as an investigating censor.
He quarreled with the Superintendent of Grain Transport, Grand Censor Qín Hóng, over official documents.
He was impeached,
but the relevant authorities declared Hóng innocent.
Liú Jí wanted to entrap him,
so he was referred to the Ministry of Rites for a second deliberation.
Consequently, he was demoted to Magistrate of Xiàxiàn.
Censor Ōuyáng Dàn requested that Hóng and Chàng Hēng be recalled,
but this was not accepted.
He was promoted to Prefect of Guìlín.
When the Yáo and Zhuàng peoples invaded and harassed Gǔtián,
he requested troops to suppress them, which he successfully accomplished.
He was promoted to Surveillance Vice Commissioner of Yúnnán.
When the local chieftain Táo Hóng conspired with Bābǎixífù to rebel,
Hóng seized the opportunity to eliminate them.
He successively served as Left Surveillance Vice Commissioner of Shāndōng.
In the second year of the Zhèngdé reign (1507), he was promoted to Provincial Administration Commissioner of Shānxī.
Liú Jǐn demanded money for his congratulations on the appointment,
but Hóng refused.
In the second month of the fourth year (1509),
an imperial edict ordered him to retire due to illness.
After Jǐn was executed,
Hóng was reappointed as Left Provincial Administration Commissioner of Shāndōng.
In the seventh year (1512), he served as Right Vice Grand Censor and Grand Coordinator of Shānxī.
He died before completing a full year in office.
Hóng was honest and upright by nature;
after his death, his family could not afford a funeral.
In the early Tiānqǐ reign (early 17th century),
he was posthumously granted the honorific title Zhuāngjiè.
Ōuyáng Dàn
was from Ānfú.
He obtained his *jìnshì* degree in the seventeenth year of the Chénghuà reign (1481).
From Magistrate of Xiūníng, he was promoted to Censor.
He once requested the expulsion of Liú Jí
and the abolition of imperial estates.
He successively served as Assistant Surveillance Commissioner of Húguǎng and Vice Surveillance Commissioner of Zhèjiāng,
and ultimately as Right Vice Grand Censor of Nánjīng.
Chàng Hēng,
courtesy name Wéntōng,
was from Héjīn.
He obtained his *jìnshì* degree in the fourteenth year of the Chénghuà reign (1478).
From Magistrate of Chángyuán, he was promoted to Censor,
and then circuit inspector of Zhèjiāng.
During a famine,
he memorialized to abolish the tribute of silk and gauze, among other items.
In the second month of the first year of the Hóngzhì reign (1488),
in Jǐngníngxiàn, on Píngfēngshān, over ten thousand strange beasts,
as large as sheep,
white in color,
flew away in the air, tail to mouth.
Hēng requested the abolition of the silver tax from Wēn and Chǔ prefectures
and the punishment of the eunuch garrison commander Zhāng Qìng.
The memorial was sent to the relevant authorities,
