the silver tax was reduced,
and Qìng was ordered to submit a statement.
Qìng then exposed Hēng for unfair evaluation during an inspection,
and Hēng's salary was suspended for three months.
Hēng then impeached Assistant Surveillance Commissioner Zōu Pāng,
and Pāng also exposed Hēng.
Qìng and others conspired against him,
Hēng was arrested,
and demoted to Magistrate of Jīngyáng.
Censor Páang Pàn submitted a memorial arguing for him,
but it was not heeded.
Cáo Lín,
courtesy name Tínghuī,
was from Xiāngyáng.
He obtained his *jìnshì* degree in the fourteenth year of the Chénghuà reign (1478).
He was appointed *Xíngrén* (Herald).
After a long time,
he was selected and appointed Censor.
When Emperor Xiàozōng succeeded to the throne,
he submitted a memorial stating:
"When the imperial coffin is moved,
Your Majesty should, wearing mourning clothes and using a mourning staff, accompany it outside the Dàmíng Gate,
bowing and weeping to bid farewell,
and lead the palace in three years of mourning.
Consort Wàn Shì committed wrongdoing,
and it is proper to inform the late emperor,
revoke her posthumous title,
and rebury her elsewhere."
The Emperor accepted his memorial
but warned him not to speak of the Consort again.
Soon after,
he requested the promotion of ministers like Wáng Shù,
the restoration of offices to officials like Yú Dàjié who had spoken out in the previous reign,
the release of discontented palace women,
and the dismissal and removal of eunuchs supervising the capital garrisons and guarding the four frontiers.
He also said:
"Liáng Fāng, through commander Yuán Lù, offered land for building a temple,
and requested that Yuán Lù be granted hereditary peerage as Marquis of Guǎngpíng.
To obtain a marquisate for a few *mǔ* of land,
what meritorious officials would not be disheartened?
This should be swiftly reformed and abolished."
When this memorial was presented,
the Emperor largely adopted it.
In the seventh month of the first year of the Hóngzhì reign (1488), he memorialized:
"Recently there have been falling stars and earthquakes,
the planets Jīn (Venus) and Mù (Jupiter) appeared in daylight,
lightning struck the Forbidden Gate,
hail fell on the imperial tombs,
there was a fire in the Nánjīng Inner Park,
a madman shouted at the palace gate,
and in Jǐngníng, white vapor ascended.
Yet Your Majesty does not deeply seek the causes of these calamities
to thoroughly avert disaster.
Although the Imperial Lecture is attended,
it is merely a formality.
No sooner is it begun than it is suspended;
no sooner is it temporarily started than it is abruptly halted.
This is what is meant by 'to expose it to the sun for one day
and then freeze it for ten days.'
I wish Your Majesty would daily attend the lecture hall and discuss with Confucian ministers,
dismiss Grand Secretary Liú Jí and others,
to dispel these celestial anomalies.
Last winter, your servant requested Your Majesty to wear dark mourning attire while attending to governance.
Now, whenever a festival or season comes,
Your Majesty gradually dons yellow robes,
and attending officials wear red.
In three years,
how many days are there for mourning?
It is proper to only wear plain attire.
Moreover, Your Majesty is still in the period of silent mourning,
yet Junior Eunuch Guō Yōng requested the selection of imperial concubines.
Though you refused to accept,
Yōng is still employed.
How can this dispel the doubts of your officials and people?
The ancestors strictly forbade eunuchs from interfering in politics.
Now these individuals interfere and scheme confusingly;
they should be punished.
The court specially established a writing academy,
ordering Hanlin officials to teach inner palace servants.
This was not a system established by Gāo Huángdì.
Many literati officials exploit this to gain promotion,
and eunuchs also假儒術以文奸 (pretend to be scholars to cover up their wickedness).
This should be swiftly abolished.
Whenever there is an alert on the frontiers,
capital troops are ordered to campaign in the north.
These individuals have been arrogant and lazy for a long time;
they are useless.
I beg that from now on they not be dispatched,
and that the expenses for dispatching troops be used to reward frontier soldiers."
Upon receiving the memorial,
the Emperor was displeased
and issued an edict reprimanding him.
Later,
he was dispatched as investigating censor to Guǎngdōng.
He visited Chén Xiànzhāng in Xīnhuì,
was impressed by his teachings,
and then, feigning illness, returned home.
He lived in the mountains studying for thirty years, never entering the city.
Péng Chéng,
courtesy name Wànlǐ,
was from Póyáng.
He obtained his *jìnshì* degree at the end of the Chénghuà reign.
In the early Hóngzhì reign,
he was appointed Censor,
and circuit inspector of the capital city.
Many surrendered individuals, living mixed with the population in the capital region, became bandits.
When a crime was committed, they would take refuge with imperial relatives or eunuchs.
Chéng always acted decisively against them,
and whenever a case occurred, he caught them.
He then inspected the salt administration in the two Zhè regions.
After returning from his tour,
he inspected the Court of Imperial Entertainments.
In the fifth year, [Chéng] shàng submitted a memorial saying:
"Your subject has just seen the Court of Imperial Accoutrements (Guānglù Sì) constructing objects for the Imperial Altar (Huángtán).
The Imperial Altar
was where the late emperor performed fasting rituals and practiced methods.
When Your Majesty ascended the throne,
all such practices were abolished and discarded.
Why then is there again an Imperial Altar needing cumbersome construction of objects?
The money of the Court of Imperial Accoutrements
is entirely the people's blood and sweat.
Even if it is spent appropriately,
we still fear it might burden the people,
let alone pouring it into useless endeavors.
Previously, Lǐ Zīshěng, Jì Xiǎo, and their ilk promoted heretical theories,
and the late emperor sincerely believed them,
with the intention of distantly seeking good fortune and longevity.
Now these two have already been executed for grave crimes.
If calamity struck,
these two could not even save themselves,
how could they bring good fortune and longevity to others?
If Your Majesty indeed has such an undertaking,
it should be stopped before it even begins to sprout.
If not,
please punish those officials who have indulged in flattery."
The emperor had initially given no command for the construction of objects for the Imperial Altar;
it was merely that the Court of Imperial Accoutrements provisionally prepared for it.
Upon receiving Chéng's memorial, the emperor was furious,
believing it to be a blatant exposure of the late emperor's faults,
and immediately had him imprisoned in the Jǐnyī Wèi prison.
The Supervising Secretary (Gěishìzhōng) Cóng Lán also inspected the Court of Imperial Accoutrements
and subsequently submitted a memorial discussing it.
The emperor pardoned Lán,
confiscated the salaries of Hu Gōng, the Minister of the Court of Imperial Accoutrements (Guānglù Qīng), and others,
and handed Chéng over to the Ministry of Justice (Xíngbù) for sentencing.
Minister (Shàngshū) Péng Sháo and others proposed commuting his sentence to a beating with the heavy stick and reinstatement to office.
The emperor wanted to put him to death
and ordered him kept in custody.
Sháo and others again memorialized to intercede for him.
Chéng Zǐshàng, Chéng's son, submitted three petitions begging to die in place of his father,
but he was ultimately not listened to.
At this time, Lǐ Xīng from Sōng Xiàn, a Censor (Yùshǐ) on circuit inspection in Shǎnxī, was also imprisoned for severe torture.
During the autumn assize,
the crimes of Xīng and Chéng were presented.
An imperial edict ordered Xīng to be beheaded,
and Chéng and his family to be exiled to Lóngqìng.
High civil and military officials, including Zhāng Mào, the Duke of Yīngguó, jointly submitted a memorial stating:
"Most of those killed by Xīng were criminals,
so it is not appropriate to punish him with death.
Chéng's duty was to remonstrate.
If he is exiled to the border for this,
how then should those who commit malfeasance and pervert the law be dealt with?"
Minister Wáng Shù also submitted a special memorial to intercede.
Thereupon, Xīng's death sentence was commuted;
he was beaten with one hundred strokes,
and along with his wife and children, exiled to Bīnzhōu.
Chéng, however, received no reduction in his sentence.
Chéng's mother, Lǐ Shì, was old and had no other sons.
She knelt before the palace gate, begging to keep her son to care for her.
Máo Chéng, a Supervising Secretary (Gěishìzhōng) of Nánjīng, and others also memorialized, saying:
"In the past, Liú Yǔxī, for aligning with Wáng Shúwén, was to be banished to a distant place.
Péi Dù pleaded on account of his aged mother,
and he was allowed to be transferred to Liánzhōu.
Your Majesty's sagely virtue
cannot be compared to the middle Tang emperors,
and Chéng's crime is also different from Yǔxī's.
We pray for a little compassion
to keep the mother and son together."
This was not granted.
Zǐshàng accompanied his father to the place of exile
and subsequently passed the provincial examination in Guǎngxī.
The following year,
the emperor, remembering Chéng's aged mother,
released him to return.
Later,
when Liú Jǐn was disturbing the government,
Chéng was posthumously accused of having slightly underspent the prescribed quota during his time as Salt Inspector,
and his family was ordered to compensate.
Chéng had long been dead,
leaving only a granddaughter.
When their entire property was insufficient,
his granddaughter was also sold.
Passersby all shed tears.
Páng Pàn,
courtesy name Yuánhuà,
was a native of Tiāntái.
He obtained his *jìnshì* degree in the twentieth year of Chénghuà.
He was appointed Supervising Secretary (Gěishìzhōng) of the Ministry of Works (Gōngkē).
During the Hóngzhì reign,
an imperial decree ordered the selection of skilled bronze drum players.
Pàn submitted a memorial to remonstrate.
When Vice Commissioner (Fùshǐ) Yáng Màoyuán was arrested,
Pàn led his colleagues to intercede for him,
and Màoyuán received a light reprimand.
In the fourth month of the ninth year,
the emperor, because Prince Mín impeached Liú Xùn, the Prefect of Wǔgāng,
ordered his arrest.
Pàn, along with his colleagues Lǚ Xiàn and others, said:
"The Jǐnyī Wèi are the emperor's personal troops.
He was repeatedly promoted to Supervising Secretary (Dūgěishìzhōng) of the Ministry of Justice (Xíngkē).
Xùn's alleged crime is minor,
but the prince's memorial implicates a hundred witnesses,
making it difficult to arrest them all.
It is appropriate to order the Grand Coordinators (Fǔ) and Censors (Àn) to investigate."
The memorial was submitted,
going against the imperial will.
Pàn and forty-two others, along with twenty Censors (Yùshǐ) including Liú Shēn, were sent to the imperial prison (zhàoyù).
With the Six Offices of Scrutiny (Liùkē) empty,
the Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū) Tú Xiōng requested that the Grand Secretariat (Zhōngshū) collect the sealed memorials from the ministries and other offices on their behalf.
Censor Zhāng Chún returned from his mission,
ashamed that he alone was not involved,
and submitted a strong memorial discussing the situation.
Director of the Bureau of Merits (Kǎogōng Lángzhōng) Chǔ Qún also remonstrated,
and Xiōng and others again led the Nine Ministers (Jiǔqīng) to intercede.
The emperor then released Pàn and the others,
all of whom had their salaries suspended for three months.
Court eunuch Hé Dǐng was imprisoned for straightforward criticism.
Yáng Péng and Dài Lǐ, through connections, entered the Directorate of Ceremonial (Sīlǐ Jiān).
Pàn and others said:
"Dǐng's bluntness should be tolerated.
Péng and others, having committed crimes in the previous reign,
if allowed to participate in confidential matters,
the harm would not be small."
At the same time, Censors Huáng Shān, Zhāng Tài, and others also spoke on this matter.
The emperor was angry,
demanding to know how the outer court knew about affairs of the inner court,
and ordered them to provide an explanation,
suspending Pàn's and others' salaries for six months.
When Wēi Níngbó Wáng Yuè planned to be reinstated,
and court eunuchs Jiǎng Cóng and Lǐ Guǎng committed crimes,
and imperial relatives Zhōu Yù and Zhāng Hèlǐng allowed their household servants to commit murder,
Pàn thoroughly denounced them all,
and his reputation for uprightness became widely known.
In the eleventh year, he was promoted to Right Administration Commissioner (Yòucāncèng) of Fújiàn.
When a court eunuch seized the residence of the Song Dynasty Confucianist Huáng Gàn to convert it into a Buddhist nunnery,
Pàn changed it into an academy to commemorate Gàn.
He was transferred to Right Provincial Administration Commissioner (Yòubùzhèngshǐ) of Hénán.
An imperial decree ordered the collection of Luòyáng peonies;
he submitted a memorial requesting to abolish it.
He was transferred to Left Provincial Administration Commissioner (Zuǒbùzhèngshǐ) of Guǎngxī,
then retired from office.
Lǚ Xiàn,
a native of Xīnchāng, Zhèjiāng.
He obtained his *jìnshì* degree in the twentieth year of Chénghuà.
He was appointed Supervising Secretary (Gěishìzhōng) of the Ministry of Justice (Xíngkē).
For an offense,
he was beaten with the heavy stick in front of the imperial court.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
an imperial edict ordered the selection of an imperial son-in-law (Fùmǎ).
Lǐ Guǎng accepted gold from a wealthy man,
secretly making arrangements for him.
This was exposed by Xiàn,
earning him a reputation for uprightness.
During the Zhèngdé reign,
he ended his career as Right Vice Minister of War (Bīngbù Yòushìláng) in Nánjīng.
Yè Shēn,
courtesy name Tíngjìn,
was a native of Wújiāng.
He obtained his *jìnshì* degree at the end of the Chénghuà reign.
He was appointed Supervising Secretary (Gěishìzhōng) of the Ministry of Revenue (Hùkē),
then transferred to the Ministry of Personnel (Lìkē),
and successively held the post of Left Supervising Secretary (Zuǒgěishìzhōng) of the Ministry of Rites (Lǐkē).
In the tenth year of Hóngzhì
the crown prince was seven years old,
and had not yet left the inner court.
Shēn requested that讲官 (jiǎngguān) be chosen to teach him.
Soon after, on the occasion of an imperial self-reflection,
he presented eight matters.
He denounced the eunuch Lǐ Guǎng,
and also impeached Minister Xú Qióng, Tóng Xuān, and Hóu Zàn;
Vice-Minister Zhèng Jì and Wáng Zōngyí;
and Regional Inspector-General Liú Huán, Zhāng Gào, Zhāng Xiù, and twenty other individuals,
requesting their dismissal.
At the end, he stated,
"eliminate the great traitor,"
and then exclusively impeached Lǐ Guǎng for eight major crimes:
"He deceived Your Majesty with alchemy
and presented unauthorized medicines –
this is the first crime.
He established a 'substitute altar' for the crown prince
and propagated the theory of 'warming and clearing' –
this is the second crime.
He interfered with imperial relatives
to curry favor and seek patronage –
this is the third crime.
He illicitly diverted the Jade Spring (Yù Quán)
to flow through his private residence –
this is the fourth crime.
He was the first to open a corrupt gate
and indulge in extensive treachery and greed –
this is the fifth crime.
When Tàicháng Cuī Zhìduān and the Daoist master Wáng Yīng● and others called Guǎng 'Master and True Man (Jiàozhǔ Zhēnrén)',
Guǎng immediately sought good official posts for them
and requested jade belts –
this is the sixth crime.
Under the guise of 'fruit households' (guǒhù),
he seized land from the people of the imperial domain,
almost leading to rebellion –
this is the seventh crime.
For tribute from all four directions,
he used coercion and intimidation,
causing people to lose their property –
this is the eighth crime.
Within the court, imperial relatives and imperial sons-in-law serve him like a father;
outside, commanders-in-chief and garrison commanders call him 'Sir.'
How can Your Majesty tolerate such a great traitor at your elbow
and not think to drive him out!"
Censor Zhāng Jìn and others also echoed these sentiments.
The Emperor said,
"Let's set it aside for now."
After several months,
Guǎng was indeed found guilty
and died by drinking poison.
Shēn further vehemently criticized the widespread abuse of imperial favor, hereditary privileges, and funeral and sacrificial expenses among high officials.
The matter was referred to the relevant departments for deliberation,
and there were considerable reductions.
He was promoted to Junior Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Shàngbǎo Shǎoqīng),
and then passed away.
Hú Xiàn,
courtesy name Shíchén,
was from Xīnghuà, Yángzhōu.
He passed the imperial examination in the ninth year of Hóngzhì
He was appointed a probationary Hanlin bachelor (shùjíbì),
then became a censor.
Within a month,
he fiercely criticized several current political issues,
stating:
"Tú Pēi became Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū),
and Wáng Yuè and Lǐ Huì became Censor-Generals (Dū Yùshǐ),
all through collusion with the eunuch Lǐ Guǎng.
Guǎng was able to carry out his treachery
because Your Majesty did not rely on high officials for policy discussions,
but on Guǎng and his ilk.
In the time of our ancestors,
the Emperor would consult with the Grand Secretariat (Nèigé) to decide on memorials and policies,
and during daily lectures (Jīngyán Rìjiǎng), all current political successes and failures were discussed.
Also, scholars were regularly received.
I hope Your Majesty will restore the old system.
The eunuchs supervising and managing the two granaries in the capital (Jīng) and Tōngzhōu (Tōng)
extort ten taels of silver for every ten thousand stones of grain collected.
Calculating by the four million stones transported annually,
this amounts to four thousand taels per person.
Furthermore, each occupies two or three hundred 'grain measurers' (dòují)
and forces them to pay monthly fees.
Managing granary storage
is inherently the responsibility of the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù);
why use eunuchs?
I request that they be dismissed.
When soldiers for the capital garrison (Jīngcāo) arrive from thousands of li away,
commanders-in-chief (Zǒngbīng) and camp commanders (Zuòyíng) force them to pay monthly fees.
I beg for a strict reform to relieve their hardship.
When Your Majesty faces calamities and undertakes self-reflection,
last spring, you sought advice.
Censors, and officials like director Wáng Yúnfèng and secretary Hú Guāng, all submitted memorials,
but they were kept in the palace and not acted upon,
and Yúnfèng was soon found guilty.
If this is the case,
how is it different from not undertaking self-reflection at all?
I hope Your Majesty will make decisive judgments from your sacred heart,
and all beneficial or harmful matters that require reform
should be immediately implemented.
The guards of the Eastern Depot (Dōngchǎng Jiàowèi)
were originally meant to apprehend traitors,
but recently they only vent the anger and seek revenge for imperial relatives and eunuchs.
For example, Censor Wǔ Qú offended Marquis Shòuníng Zhāng Hèlín and Grand Eunuch Yáng Péng;
Secretary Máo Guǎng offended Grand Eunuch Wéi Tài.
All were exposed by the guards,
who fabricated minor incidents
and falsely accused them,
the entire court knew of their wrongful treatment,
but no one dared to speak.
I also know that by speaking today,
I will certainly be framed in the future,
but I am not afraid."
After the memorial was submitted,
Hèlín and Wéi Tài each submitted memorials in rebuttal.
At the same time, Supervising Secretary Hú Yì impeached the eunuch Hè Bīn, supervisor of granaries, for eight crimes of corruption,
and Bīn also denounced Yì.
The Emperor then sent Hú Xiàn and Hú Yì to the imperial prison (zhàoyù),
and demoted Hú Xiàn to Assistant Magistrate (chéng) of Lánshān.
After a long time,
Hú Yì was released.
Before Hú Xiàn took up his new post,
he was transferred to be Magistrate of Yíyáng.
Mǎ Wénshēng repeatedly recommended him to the court,
and he was promoted to Experiencer (Jīnglì) in the Nanjing Censorate (Nándū Cháyùan).
When Wǔzōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Assistant Surveillance Commissioner (Tíxué Qiānshì) of Guǎngxī,
then transferred to Vice Surveillance Commissioner (Tíxué Fùshǐ) of Fújiàn,
but died before taking office.
Wǔ Qú,
was from Yíshuǐ.
He passed the imperial examination in the twentieth year of Chénghuà
As a censor, he was demoted to Chief Registrar (zhǔbù) of Tōnghǎi, Yúnnán,
and ended his career as Magistrate of Fénzhōu.
Máo Guǎng,
was from Pínghú.
He passed the imperial examination in the twentieth year of Chénghuà
His deeds are not recorded.
Hú Yì,
was from Níngdū.
He passed the imperial examination in the third year of Hóngzhì
He served as Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Personnel (Lìkē Gěishìzhōng).
When Huá Chǎng impeached Chéng Mǐnzhèng,
the judicial ministers Bái Áng and Mǐn Guī, based on old regulations, ordered the six supervising offices (liùkē) to jointly interrogate.
The Eastern Depot (Dōngchǎng) impeached Hú Yì and others, arguing that they were Huá Chǎng's colleagues
and should not participate in the interrogation.
An imperial decree then sent them to the imperial prison (zhàoyù).
Bái Áng and Mǐn Guī requested punishment,
and both had their salaries suspended.
When Huá Chǎng's case was concluded,
Hú Yì and others were still imprisoned.
High officials spoke on their behalf,
and they were then allowed to resume their posts.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
other censors who were punished for offending eunuchs
included Rèn Yí and Chē Liáng.
Rèn Yí,
was from Lángzhōng.
He passed the imperial examination in the twenty-third year of Chénghuà
and became a censor.
In the autumn of the third year of Hóngzhì
an imperial edict ordered the construction of a fasting hall at Dàxīnglóng Temple (Dàxīnglóng Sì).
Wáng Yuè, the Magistrate of Líxíng, rode past it,
and a eunuch (zhōngshǐ) seized and humiliated Wáng Yuè,
forcing him to kneel in front of the temple.
Rèn Yí, feeling indignant,
impeached the eunuch.
His name was accidentally erroneous,
so Rèn Yí was also sent to prison.
He was released and became Magistrate of Zhōngbù,
and ended his career as a Surveillance Vice Commissioner (Cānzhèng) in Shānxī.
Chē Liáng,
was from Yǒngníng, Shānxī.
He passed the imperial examination in the third year of Hóngzhì
and became a censor.
In the fifteenth year
in which he stated that thieves apprehended by the Eastern Depot (Dōngchǎng) and the Imperial Bodyguard (Jǐnyīwèi)
were first severely tortured to produce a confession,
and only then sent to the judicial authorities (fǎsī),
who dared not overturn the conviction.
He requested that from then on, they be sent directly to the judicial authorities,
without prior torture.
The memorial was submitted,
but not responded to.
The head of the Eastern Depot stated that Chē Liáng's father's brother, Director Líng Tíng, had previously been implicated in a crime by the Eastern Depot,
and that Chē Liáng was speaking out of personal vendetta.
Thus, Chē Liáng was sent to the imperial prison (zhàoyù).
Supervising secretaries and censors jointly submitted memorials to rescue him,
and he was then released,
ending his career as Prefect of Hànyáng.
Zhāng Hóngzhì,
courtesy name Shíxíng,
was from Huátíng,
the son of Prefect Bì of Nán'ān.
He passed the imperial examination in the ninth year of Hóngzhì
was appointed a probationary Hanlin bachelor (shùjíbì), and then became Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of War (Bīngkē Gěishìzhōng).
In the twelfth year, in winter,
Chén’s initial administration gradually failed to complete eight matters:
“Initially, nearly all supernumerary officials of the Transmission Bureau were eliminated.
Recently, from artisan official Zhāng Guǎngníng and others, one transmission reached over 120 people,
and from Junior Minister Lǐ Lún and Commandant Zhāng and others, a second transmission reached over 180 people.
This is the first deviation from the initial administration.
Initially, Jì Xiǎo was pursued and executed,
and foreign monks and Buddhist disciples were expelled.
Recently, fasts and rituals have not ceased.
This is the second deviation from the initial administration.
Initially, Wàn Ān, Lǐ Yù, and their ilk were removed,
impeached in the morning and dismissed in the evening.
Recently, there have been dozens of impeachment memorials,
yet officials like Minister Xú Qióng still hold their positions.
This is the third deviation from the initial administration.
Initially, imperial edicts stated that major policies required summoning ministers for face-to-face discussion.
Recently, communication between superior and subordinate has been blocked.
This is the fourth deviation from the initial administration.
Initially, newly appointed eunuchs were removed.
Recently, those who had returned have gone again,
and those who had been dismissed have been reinstated.
This is the fifth deviation from the initial administration.
Initially, imperial decrees were handled with caution,
and those around the emperor dared not interfere arbitrarily.
Recently, requests for favors and pardons are frequently granted.
This is the sixth deviation from the initial administration.
Initially, the Ministry of War was ordered to enforce old regulations,
and those who presumptuously requested promotion to military ranks were to be prosecuted.
Recently, requests for promotion meet no refusal.
This is the seventh deviation from the initial administration.
Initially, the Grand Provisioning Court’s expenditures were curtailed.
Recently, superfluous eaters have increased daily,
and silver from the Grand Granary is used to purchase goods from markets on credit.
This is the eighth deviation from the initial administration.”
The Emperor sent the matter to the relevant authorities.
Border generals Wáng Gǎo, Mǎ Shēng, Qín Gōng, and Chén Yīng were condemned to death for losing opportunities,
and had been imprisoned for a long time.
Hóng Zhì requested their swift execution according to law.
When imperial princes went to their fiefdoms,
their temporary residences often involved constructing temporary palaces with mats,
and the accompanying officials’ quarters were also temporary tents,
all decorated with wool carpets and brocades.
Following Hóng Zhì’s advice, many such expenses were reduced.
In the later years of Xiàozōng’s reign,
following requests from court officials,
officials were dispatched to investigate the abuses of false claims and excessive spending in the four Tengxiáng Guards,
but this was halted due to the words of eunuch Níng Jǐn.
Hóng Zhì submitted a strong memorial arguing against it,
and the Ministry of War also spoke out about it,
so the investigation was finally carried out.
When Wǔzōng ascended the throne,
he was sent as an envoy to Ānnán as a Right Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Revenue.
Upon his return, he was promoted to Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Works,
but died at home during a period of mourning for his mother.
Qū Shēn,
courtesy name Yǐnzhī,
was a native of Rènqiū.
He obtained his *jìnshì* degree at the end of the Chénghuà reign.
He was selected as a *shùjíshì*,
and appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Rites.
In the ninth year of Hóngzhì, an edict ordered the ordination of monks,
which the Ministry of Rites argued against in vain.
Shēn vehemently put forward three reasons why it was impermissible,
but his arguments were not accepted.
When a rumor spread among the capital's populace that bandits were near the border,
the Ministry of War requested that a proclamation be posted.
Shēn said:
“If a proclamation is posted,
people’s hearts will be even more alarmed.
Formerly, during the Jiànshǐ reign of the Hàn dynasty,
the city dwellers spread rumors that a great flood was coming,
and there was a discussion to order officials and commoners to ascend the city walls to avoid it.
Wáng Shāng disagreed,
and soon it indeed subsided.
We should now take this as a precedent.”
The matter was then dropped.
When bandits attacked Dàtóng,
guerrilla commander Wáng Gǎo concealed the report of his defeat.
Shēn, along with his colleagues, exposed it,
and also impeached the commander-in-chief Wáng Xǐ and others for their crimes.
He was repeatedly promoted to Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of War.
The chief of the Tàiníng Guard carried out a major plunder in Liáoyáng.
The ministry discussed instructing the border commanders to send a letter,
stating that the court, being magnanimous, would not investigate past incidents,
and if the stolen goods were returned,
they would be heavily rewarded.
Shēn and others said:
“This shows our weakness,
and gives them no thought of remorse.
This is not the way for a king to display his authority and deter.
If we do not consider past border violations as crimes,
and instead consider returning captives today as merit,
it teaches them the profit of banditry
and encourages lawlessness.
This is also not the way for a king to pacify and conciliate.”
The Emperor understood,
and the letter was not sent.
Later,
he impeached the frontier eunuch Sūn Zhèn, commander-in-chief Jiǎng Jì, and巡抚Chén Yáo for botching affairs,
but the Emperor did not question them.
Guǎngníng again suffered a defeat,
but Yáo and others reported it as a victory.
Shēn and Censor Gěng Míng and others jointly memorialized, impeaching their deceit and trickery,
and an investigation was then carried out.
Eunuch Miáo Kuí, Duke Chéngguó Zhū Huī, and others raided a bandit lair and captured three heads.
When the bandits made a major incursion into Gùyuán,
they dared not rescue it.
Afterwards, they killed and captured twelve heads,
and reported these as victories both before and after.
Shēn and others impeached them repeatedly.
Upon their return to the capital,
he again argued vehemently, saying:
“Zhū Huī and others accomplished nothing in their western campaign.
The order for their return to the capital had barely been issued,
yet the generals and soldiers had already entered the city gates.
I do not know what imperial edict they followed.
Moreover, this campaign consumed over 1.6 million taels from the capital’s treasury and border provisions combined,
but only three heads were claimed as primary merit.
This means fifty thousand gold pieces were exchanged for one nameless head.
Yet, the number of meritorious generals and soldiers reported was over ten thousand.
If we were to capture one major chieftain like Huǒ Shāi,
or kill thousands of heads,
the entire wealth of the realm would not suffice to cover the expenses,
and the reports of merit would be in the hundreds of millions.
Zhū Huī, Miáo Kuí, Grand Censor Shǐ Lín, and supervising censor Wáng Yòngyí should all be subject to severe punishment.”
The Emperor did not listen.
Yúnnán had a frontier eunuch,
and again a supervising secretary Sūn Zhèn jīn téng was dispatched.
Shēn and others vehemently argued against it.
Jǐnyī Guard Commander Sūn Luán was convicted and put on inactive status.
An imperial directive reinstated him,
ordering him to manage the Southern Garrison affairs.
Shēn and others strongly protested,
so an edict ordered him to merely receive his salary.
An imperial directive ordered Commander Hú Zhèn to guard Tiānjīn.
Shēn strongly protested,
but was not listened to.
Frontier eunuch Liú Láng in Hénán requested personal servants.
The Emperor ordered fifty people be given to him.
According to precedent,
a minister only had twelve people.
Shēn and others strongly protested,
and an edict only reduced the number by twenty people.
Thereafter, all eunuchs invoked this precedent to request things,
and the ancestral system was thus destroyed.
Shēn served in the Censorate for a long time,
holding his opinions with candor and unyielding.
He died before being promoted.
Wáng Xiànchén,
courtesy name Jìngzhǐ,
was originally from Wú,
registered with the Jǐnyī Guard.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the sixth year of Hóngzhì.
He was appointed Director of the Bureau of Diplomatic Receptions,
and promoted to Censor.
During his inspection of the Dàtóng border,
he requested the swift punishment of generals Yáo Xìn and Chén Guǎng for closing their camps and avoiding bandits, and Mǎ Shēng, Wáng Gǎo, and Qín Gōng for losing battles.
He also requested the exemption of all overdue taxes in Dàtóng and Yánsuí due to drought damage,
to relieve the military and civilian population.
The Emperor largely agreed to his requests.
He once ordered soldiers to escort him on a mountain excursion,
which was discovered by an agent of the Eastern Depot.
The agent also reported that Wáng Xiànchén had unauthorizedly appointed military officials.
He was summoned to the imperial prison,
and his crime warranted a fine.
However, a special decree ordered thirty strokes of the cane,
and he was demoted to Assistant Magistrate of Shàngháng.
In the seventeenth year, he was again arrested due to the matter of Zhāng Tiānxiáng.
Zhāng Tiānxiáng was
the grandson of Zhāng Bīn, a Deputy Commander of Liáodōng.
Bīn was dismissed for a crime,
and Tiānxiáng obtained his ancestral official position by supplying grain.
When more than ten horsemen from the Tàiníng Guard shot and wounded a Hǎixī tribute envoy,
Tiānxiáng went out from the Máolǎ Pass and ambushed and killed thirty-eight men from other guards,
claiming them to be the ones who shot the tribute envoy.
Governor Zhāng Nài and others reported it as a victory,
but Xiànchén was suspicious.
He was in the process of issuing a dispatch to refute and investigate,
when Zhāng Mào, a commander and the wife's younger brother of Bīn, and his son Qīn, who had a grudge against Tiānxiáng,
forged a document from the Qiántún Guard and presented it to Xiànchén,
detailing the incident of raiding the camp.
Xiànchén immediately reported it.
Before a reply was received,
Xiànchén was summoned.
The Emperor ordered Grand Judge Wú Yīguàn, Jǐnyī Guard Commander Yáng Yù, and the new investigating censor Yú Lián to jointly investigate it,
and they uncovered the full truth.
Bīn and others were all condemned to death,
and Tiānxiáng died in prison.
Tiānxiáng's uncle, Hóng, repeatedly appealed his grievances.
The Emperor secretly ordered the Dōngchǎng to investigate the matter.
They returned with a report that all the accusations investigated were false.
The Emperor believed it
and wanted to overturn all previous judgments.
He summoned Liú Jiàn and others from the Grand Secretariat,
showed them the Dōngchǎng's memorial,
and ordered the arrest of all members of the Yīguàn sect for interrogation at the palace gate.
Jiàn and others said that the Dōngchǎng's memorial should not be circulated outside.
After they retired,
they argued again.
The Emperor summoned them again
and rebuked Jiàn and others.
Jiàn replied,
"The case was adjudicated by the judicial authorities,
all of whom are dukes, ministers, scholars, and officials.
Their words are credible."
The Emperor said,
"If the judicial authorities judge a case improperly,
they might not even save themselves.
Are their words credible?"
Xiè Qiān said,
"Matters should follow the majority.
If it's the word of one or two people,
how can it be trusted?"
Jiàn and others also said that the witnesses were far away
and could not all be arrested.
The Emperor said,
"This is a major case.
What does it matter to arrest a thousand people?
If merits and crimes are not clear,
which border official would be willing to exert their efforts?"
Jiàn and others argued repeatedly,
seeing the Emperor's stern demeanor,
but ultimately dared not speak deeply against the Dōngchǎng.
When the Yīguàn sect members arrived,
the Emperor personally presided over their interrogation at the Wǔmén,
intending to condemn Yīguàn to death.
Mǐn Guī and Dài Shān strenuously pleaded for him.
So, Sōng was demoted to Assistant Prefect of Míngzhōu,
Xiànchén to Courier Station Master in Guǎngdōng,
Lián to Registrar in the Yúnnán Provincial Administration Commission.
Mào and his son were sentenced to death,
while Bīn was spared,
and Hóng conversely received recognition for his merits.
Upon the ascension of Wǔzōng,
Xiànchén was promoted to Magistrate of Yǒngjiā.
Wú Yīguàn,
courtesy name Dàofū,
was a native of Hǎiyáng.
He passed the imperial examination in the 17th year of Chénghuà (1481).
He was promoted from Magistrate of Shànggāo to Censor.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
he successively inspected Zhèjiāng, Fújiàn, and Nánjī,
and was known for his strong competence.
He was promoted to Assistant Minister of the Court of Judicial Review.
When the Jīfǔ and Hénán suffered from famine,
he requested the release of 200,000 *shí* of grain for relief,
and also separately requested 20,000 *shí* for the people of the capital and Chāngpíng.
After being demoted from office,
in the early Zhèngdé reign,
he was transferred to Vice Commissioner of Jiāngxī.
He achieved merit in suppressing the Huálín bandits
and was promoted to Surveillance Commissioner.
He died while on a military campaign to Fèngxīn.
The soldiers and common people erected a shrine to him, the Zhōngjié Cí.
Yú Lián,
courtesy name Zōngzhōu,
was a native of Dūchāng.
He passed the imperial examination in the 6th year of Hóngzhì (1493).
During Wǔzōng's time,
he ended his career as Vice Commissioner of Yúnnán.
Xiàozōng exerted himself in governance,
entrusting important ministers,
and the eunuchs' power was somewhat diminished.
However, the affairs of Zhāng Tiānxiáng and Mǎn Cāng'ér both originated from the Dōngchǎng,
and court discussions were still obstructed by them.
The affair of Mǎn Cāng'ér
is detailed in Sūn Pán's biography.
The encomium states: Censors are the eyes and ears of the court,
and Supervising Secretaries manage memorials,
capable of arguing right and wrong before the emperor.
Both are known as the "avenue of speech."
Those who held these positions after Tiānshùn
invigorated their critical spirit and disdained silence.
From the Son of Heaven, ministers, to inner palace attendants, none were immune to their pointed and extreme remonstrances.
Memorials from the North and South came in succession,
with multiple names signed.
If one suffered demotion or banishment,
ministers would strenuously memorialize to rescue them,
which was considered a fine anecdote.
However, at that time, factions had not yet formed,
and personal integrity was self-imposed.
There was no instance of complying with the will of the government
or preying on powerful eunuchs,
as was done in later periods.
Therefore, while their words were sometimes apt and sometimes not,
their hearts were public-minded.
The superior ones loved the country,
the next loved their reputation.
Yet, when discussing state affairs to the point of loving one's reputation,
one would then only pursue what enhanced their name,
disregarding the success or failure of the matter itself.
Perhaps this is not the best way for advising and assisting the ruler.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 69: Xú Pǔ, Qiū Jùn, Liú Jiàn, Xiè Qiān, Lǐ Dōngyáng, Wáng Ào, Liú Zhōng.
Xú Pǔ,
courtesy name Shíyòng,
was a native of Yíxīng.
His grandfather, Jiàn,
was the Prefect of Qióngzhōu
and had benevolent policies.
Pǔ
passed the imperial examination in the 5th year of Jǐngtài (1454).
He was appointed Compiler.
At the beginning of Xiànzōng's reign,
he was promoted to Left Shùzǐ,
and then to Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices concurrently Grand Academician.
In the 15th year of Chénghuà (1479), he was appointed Right Vice Minister of Rites,
soon after transferred to Left Vice Minister,
and after a long time, moved to the Ministry of Personnel.
Upon Xiàozōng's ascension,
he concurrently served as Grand Academician of the Wènyuāngé,
participating in state affairs.
Soon after, he was promoted to Minister of Rites.
In the 5th year of Hóngzhì (1492),
Liú Jí was dismissed,
and Pǔ became the Senior Grand Secretary,
repeatedly promoted to Junior Guardian and Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
Pǔ, following the arbitrary rule of Liú Jí,
governed with tranquility,
diligently adhering to established laws,
and cooperated with his colleagues Liú Jiàn, Lǐ Dōngyáng, Xiè Qiān, and others to assist in governance.
Whenever something was inappropriate,
they would collectively argue against it.
Lǐ Huá, the Director of the Imperial Astronomical Bureau who had been dismissed, selected a burial site for Chāngguó Gōng Zhāng Luán,
and an imperial decree reinstated him to office.
Pǔ and others said,
"Since Your Majesty ascended the throne,
there has been no internal imperial decree.
If this door to favoritism is opened,
where will the consequences end?
We, your ministers, dare not obey the edict."
In the 8th year (1495),
the Grand Empress Dowager summoned the Prince of Chóng to the court.
Pǔ and others, along with Minister Ní Yuè, remonstrated,
and the Emperor's request was then dropped.
Champa reported invasions and harassment by Annam.
The Emperor intended to send a high minister to mediate.
Pǔ and others said,
"When foreign countries invade each other,
it is sufficient for the relevant authorities to issue a stern directive.
There is no need to send an envoy.
Should they defy the order,
it would undermine our national prestige,
and initiating a punitive expedition
would lead to greater future troubles."
Thus, the plan to send an envoy was abandoned.
In the twelfth month of that year,
an edict was issued to compose music for the Sānqīng.
Pǔ and others said:
"Heaven is supremely exalted and without peer.
The Hàn dynasty sacrificed to the Five Thearchs,
and scholars still deemed it improper.
How much more so the Sānqīng, which are merely the deluded fabrications of Daoists!
Above the one Heaven,
how could there be three great Thearchs?
Moreover, to include Lǐ Ěr, the Keeper of the Archives under the Zhōu, as one of them,
and to rank a human ghost among the celestial deities,
is an extreme deception and falsification.
The music for the suburban sacrifices was all personally composed by Grand Ancestor Tài Zǔ.
Now to have temporal, popular songs and tunes composed to offer to the deities
is an even greater blasphemy.
We, your ministers, recite and study Confucian classics,
and are unfamiliar with heterodox doctrines and vulgar songs.
We dare not use unrighteous matters to serve Your Majesty.
The state established the Wényuān Pavilion,
and ordered scholars to reside in it,
sincerely wishing them to strategize on governance,
discuss classics and histories,
cultivate fundamental principles,
and rectify shortcomings,
not to flatter and comply with imperial will,
and only say what is agreeable.
Now, the imperial lectures are suspended early,
and daily lectures have long been neglected.
Heterodox doctrines have seized the opportunity to enter.
This is all due to our unworthiness,
being insufficient to enlighten the Sacred Heart
or preserve the initial governance.
We are filled with sorrow and shame,
with nowhere to hide our faces.
For several months,
we have returned those imperial decrees that we deemed improperly handled,
and submitted remonstrances two or three times.
We beg Your Majesty to graciously listen and comply,
so that we, your dull and untalented ministers, may exert ourselves,
and provide some benefit,
and not merely in the matter of the music."
Upon the submission of the memorial,
the Emperor praised and accepted it.
After the eighth year of his reign,
the Emperor gradually began to hold court later,
and Pǔ and others repeatedly brought this up.
The palace eunuch Lǐ Guǎng gained favor through alchemy, fasting, and Daoist rituals.
In the second month of the tenth year,
Pǔ and others submitted a memorial strongly arguing:
"According to the old system,
memorials were submitted twice daily in the inner palace;
important matters were reported without delay,
and Confucian ministers were often summoned for an audience
to consult on state affairs.
Now, memorials are submitted only once a day,
and outside of court audiences,
we cannot even catch a glimpse of the imperial countenance.
The endorsements and replies to memorials are not decided promptly,
some are delayed for months,
or are not implemented at all.
Many matters are obstructed,
hindering the body politic.
Imperial lectures are given only a few days each year;
upright officials are estranged,
and heterodox doctrines are allowed to spread.
Recently, we heard that some have presented theories of fasting, Daoist rituals, and alchemical cultivation.
Sòng Huīzōng revered Daoism;
ceremonies, talismans, and registers were most prevalent,
culminating in the emperor's carriage being forced to relocate.
Alchemical medicines,
composed of minerals,
are often extremely potent and harsh.
Táng Xiànzōng trusted Liǔ Bì and died because of it;
their misfortune serves as a warning.
Now, the Shàngqīng Palace on Mount Lónghǔ, the Shénlè Monastery, the Zǔshī Hall, and the Fānjīng Factory in the Imperial Household are all completely burnt down.
If they had any divine power,
why could they not protect themselves?
Heaven's aversion to their impurity
is already abundantly clear.
If Your Majesty would draw close to Confucian ministers,
clarify the righteous path,
and practice benevolent governance,
blessings, auspiciousness, and good fortune
would arrive unbidden.
Why rely on delusive and false doctrines!
Throughout history, treacherous individuals who delude the ruler's heart
invariably speak of peace and tranquility.
The Táng minister Lǐ Jiàng once said: 'If one worries before matters arise,
one can avoid worry.
If one worries when matters have already arisen,
it is of no benefit.'
Now, with prolonged peace,
people are indulging in ease and comfort.
Though it may seem as if there are no problems at present,
however, construction projects are numerous,
taxes and levies are constantly imposed,
soldiers and horses are exhausted,
and the populace is impoverished.
The sounds of lamentation
reach the harmonious atmosphere,
causing Mercury to deviate from its path,
the sun to lose its brilliance,
heaven to roar and the earth to quake,
and plants and trees to exhibit anomalies.
Reports from all four directions are almost continuous month after month.
The future calamities are clearly cause for concern.
Your Majesty resides high in the nine-layered palace,
and remonstrating officials, fearing punishment, remain silent.
If we, your ministers, also remain silent,
who will speak for Your Majesty?"
The Emperor was moved by their words.
On the Jiǎzǐ day of the third month,
he presided at the Wénhuá Hall,
summoned Pǔ, Líu Jiàn, Lǐ Dōngyáng, and Xiè Qiān,
and handed them various memorials from government offices, saying:
"Discuss these with you gentlemen."
Pǔ and the others drafted a decree and submitted it;
the Emperor revised and settled it immediately.
When there were many matters,
Jiàn requested to go outside to review them in detail.
The Emperor said:
"Why not discuss them here face-to-face?"
After it was concluded,
they were given tea and withdrew.
Since the Chénghuà era,
when Xiànzōng summoned Péng Shí and Shāng Lù for an audience,
this was the first such reoccurrence,
and the entire court acclaimed it as a grand event.
However, throughout Pǔ's tenure,
this was the only summons he received.
Soon after, due to natural disasters, an appeal for frank advice was made,
but the sealed memorials submitted by court officials
went unanswered for months.
Moreover, officials who had remonstrated to save Hé Dǐng, thus incurring imperial displeasure, were still awaiting punishment for a long time.
Pǔ and others all spoke about these matters.
Consequently, all memorials were put down,
and the remonstrating officials were dismissed without further inquiry.
Pǔ was seventy years old at the time
and requested retirement due to age.
This was not granted,
and an edict excused him from court attendance during windy, rainy, cold, or hot weather.
In the eleventh year,
the Crown Prince left the inner palace,
and Pǔ was promoted to Junior Preceptor and Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince,
and advanced to Grand Academician of the Huágài Hall.
He then requested to return home due to an eye ailment.
The Emperor was reluctant to let him go,
but after a long time, granted permission,
bestowing extra favors.
He passed away the following year,
was posthumously granted the title of Grand Preceptor,
and given the posthumous name Wénjìng.
Pǔ was composed and dignified,
and served in the Grand Secretariat for twelve years,
assisting the emperor with ease.
If someone made a mistake,
he would often cover it up,
saying:
"Heaven gives birth to talent with great difficulty;
I cannot bear to discard it for a minor flaw."
He often intervened in major legal cases and arrests of remonstrating officials,
skillfully mediating.
Xiàozōng was benevolent and generous,
often accepting Pǔ's and others' advice,
and the empire secretly benefited.
He once said:
"The ancestral laws and systems that benefit the common people are complete;
the problem is the inability to uphold them."
He ultimately made no changes or replacements.
He was extremely filial,
and once again resided by his parents' tomb.
He lived very frugally
and was fond of charity.
He established 800 *mǔ* of communal land to support his clan,
requesting that it be officially registered
to endure permanently.
The Emperor exempted his family from corvée labor for this.
Qīu Jùn,
courtesy name Zhòngshēn,
was from Qióngshān.
He was orphaned young,
and his mother, Lǐ Shì, taught him to read.
He could memorize anything after one reading.
His family was poor and had no books,
so he often traveled hundreds of *lǐ* to borrow books,
not stopping until he obtained them.
He came first in the provincial examination,
and became a *jìnshì* in the fifth year of Jǐngtài.
He was appointed a *shùjíshì* [probationary Hanlin scholar],
and later a compiler.
Once Jùn became an official in the Hánlín Academy,
his knowledge expanded further,
and he became especially familiar with state institutions and precedents,
priding himself on his statesmanship.
In the fourth month of the thirteenth year,
Dàtóng reported an emergency,
and the capital was put under martial law.
The Ministry of War requested a review and selection of generals in the capital's garrisons.
The emperor summoned Jiàn, and Dōngyáng, and Qiān to Píngtái to discuss their retention or dismissal in person.
Suí'ān Bó Chén Sháo and two others were dismissed,
and Zhènyuǎn Hóu Gù Pǔ was summoned to supervise the regiment camps.
At that time, the emperor often began his morning court quite late.
Jiàn and the others spoke about this,
and he merely nodded.
In the autumn of the fourteenth year,
the emperor, due to military expenditures causing a shortage of funds,
repeatedly convened court discussions.
Jiàn and the others stated:
"The wealth of the empire
is finite in its generation.
Now, the annual offerings of the Guānglù Department have increased tens of times,
various weaving workshops strive for new and ingenious designs,
and sacrificial rituals daily cost vast sums.
The reserves in the Tàicāng granary are insufficient to provision the soldiers,
yet the privy treasury takes in four or five hundred thousand.
The demands for land and seizure of salt profits by imperial relatives and noble families
also amount to tens of millions.
Construction projects arise daily,
and taxes and levies are ceaseless.
The salaries of supernumerary officials granted by imperial decrees,
and the provisions for artisans in the privy treasury,
increase annually and accumulate monthly,
with no end in sight.
How can wealth not be depleted?
Now, border troubles in Shǎnxī and Liáodōng are pressing,
and military movements in Húguǎng and Guìzhōu follow one after another.
We do not know how to respond to them.
We hope Your Majesty will cut unnecessary expenses,
personally practice frugality,
and set an example for both within and outside the court,
and allow your ministers to fully express their sincerity,
to discuss strategies for reforming弊,
which would be a great fortune for the empire."
In the fourth month of the following year,
due to natural disasters, several matters were presented: diligent morning lectures, economizing on resources, abolishing sacrificial rituals, and fair rewards and punishments.
By winter,
Nánjīng and Fèngyáng suffered severe floods.
Many court officials submitted memorials on current affairs,
but for a long time, no action was taken.
Jiàn and the others then forcefully pointed out the shortcomings of negligent governance,
requesting diligent attention to judgment and decisions to restore order,
and the emperor graciously accepted all.
When the Dàmíng Huìdiǎn was completed,
he was promoted to Shǎoshī concurrently Tàizǐ Tàishī, Lìbù Shàngshū, and Huágài Diàn Dàxuéshì.
He, Dōngyáng, and Qiān were jointly bestowed with蟒袍.
The practice of granting蟒袍 to Grand Secretaries began with Jiàn and his colleagues.
The emperor showed extreme filial piety to the two empress dowagers,
and both empress dowagers were fond of Buddhism and Taoism.
Previously,
when Qīngníng Gōng was completed,
the emperor commanded the Guàndǐng Guóshī to set up an altar for celebration and blessing.
He also dispatched eunuchs carrying images of Zhēnwǔ
to build an altar and perform a ritual on Wǔdāng Shān,
and sent envoys to Tàishān to present divine robes,
or scatter lanterns in the market during the day.
The emperor was reluctant to go against the empress dowagers' wishes
and reluctantly complied,
but Jiàn and the others remonstrated very strongly.
In the sixth month of the fifteenth year, an imperial edict was drafted to compose praises for the Shìjiāyǎtǎ statue.
In the second month of the seventeenth year, an edict was issued to construct the Yánshòu Tǎ outside Cháoyáng Mén,
and to appoint five Taoist priests, including Dù Yǒngqí, as Zhēnrén.
All these were suppressed due to the strong remonstrances of Jiàn and others.
In the summer of that year,
Xiǎowángzǐ planned to invade Dàtóng.
The emperor summoned the Grand Secretaries.
Jiàn requested the selection of a great commander for the capital's garrisons,
and then stated that the capital's troops were timid and unfit for battle,
requesting that from now on, their construction duties be abolished to preserve their vigor.
The emperor agreed.
Upon returning, he again itemized and submitted proposals for border defense matters,
all of which were approved.
Soon after,
border alarms arrived frequently.
The emperor was swayed by the eunuch Miáo Kuí's words and eagerly wished to dispatch an army.
Jiàn, Dōngyáng, and Qiān tactfully tried to dissuade him,
but the emperor's resolve was still unmoved.
The Minister of War, Liú Dàxià, also said that the capital's army should not be moved,
and so it was stopped.
Since the emperor summoned and conversed with Jiàn and the others in the thirteenth year,
Grand Secretaries rarely had the opportunity to be received.
By this time, having been on the throne for a long time,
he became increasingly familiar with state affairs,
frequently summoning ministers,
wishing to gradually reform cumbersome matters
and eliminate old abuses.
Once, when discussing financial management,
Dōngyáng emphatically spoke of the severe corruption in the salt administration,
caused by numerous petitioners,
which led to private trafficking multiplying several times.
Jiàn submitted:
"During Tàizǔ's time, when the tea law was first implemented,
Fùmǎ Ōuyáng Lún was executed for private trafficking,
and Empress Gāo could not save him.
In a matter like Lún's,
who would dare to speak to Your Majesty?"
The emperor said:
"It's not that they dare not speak, but that they are unwilling to speak."
He then issued an edict to the Ministry of Revenue to investigate the pros and cons,
and report back with a detailed discussion.
At this time,
Jiàn and the other two were united in assisting in governance,
exerting their utmost sincerity and consideration,
speaking out on everything they knew.
Initially, some proposals were followed and some not,
but then they gained increasing trust,
and all their memorials and requests were accepted.
They were addressed as "Xiānshēng" and not by their personal names.
Whenever they were received in audience,
the emperor would always dismiss his attendants.
The attendants occasionally eavesdropped from behind screens,
only hearing the emperor repeatedly praising them.
Jiàn provided much assistance in promoting and demoting civil and military officials,
and in rectifying policies concerning garrison farms, salt, and horses.
Soon after,
the emperor's illness worsened greatly.
He summoned Jiàn and the others to Qiánqīng Gōng.
The emperor, despite his illness, sat up with effort,
and very detailedly recounted his reign from beginning to end,
ordering a close attendant to write it down.
Afterward,
he held Jiàn's hand and said:
"You Xiānshēng have endured much hardship in your guidance.
The Crown Prince is intelligent,
but he is still young,
and fond of ease and pleasure.
You Xiānshēng must constantly urge him to study,
and assist him in becoming a worthy ruler."
Jiàn and the others choked back tears, bowed their heads, received the command, and departed.
The next day, the emperor passed away.
Wǔzōng ascended the throne,
and Jiàn and the others rectified various malpractices.
All that Xiàozōng had wished to promote or abolish was carried out according to the imperial will.
Liú Jǐn,
an old servant of the Crown Prince,
along with Mǎ Yǒngchéng, Gǔ Dàyòng, Wèi Bīn, Zhāng Yǒng, Qiū Jù, Gāo Fèng, Luó Xiáng, and others, eight people in total, gained power.
They were then called
"the Eight Faction."
They daily led the emperor into pleasure,
and imperial edicts and articles were often obstructed and not implemented.
The capital experienced continuous rain from June to August.
Jiàn and the others then submitted a memorial:
"When Your Majesty's ascension edict was issued,
the court and the populace cheered,
anticipating great peace.
Now two months have passed,
yet we have not heard how many supernumerary officials have been eliminated,
or how many unnecessary expenses have been saved.
What is stated in the imperial edicts
is merely empty words.
This is why the yin and yang are out of balance,
and why the rain and sun are not as they should be.
For example, the inner eunuchs in charge of bureaus,
warehouses, city gates, and garrisons in various regions have increased several times over.
The court spends vast sums on maintaining soldiers and artisans,
barely enough to sustain their services.
How can they not be eliminated?
Civil and military officials who neglect their duties,
ruin affairs, and waste their salaries—how can they not be dismissed?
Painters and artisans who have been improperly granted official positions number several hundred.
How can they not be dismissed?
The Nèi Chéngyùn Kù has spent several million taels of silver over the years,
initially without any ledger.
The Sìyuè Kù stores several million coins,
but it is unknown if they exist.
How can they not be checked and audited?
As for releasing rare birds and exotic beasts from the imperial gardens,
and dispatching former court ladies—
these are all priorities for new governance,
yet Your Majesty is constrained from implementing them.
How can you comfort the hopes of the four seas?"
Although the emperor replied with a gentle edict,
the eunuchs around him grew increasingly unrestrained,
and their numbers increased daily.
During sacrifices at the imperial altars and ancestral temples,
they carried swords and wore armor, surrounding the emperor.
The numerous clerks in the various bureaus and offices of the privy treasury numbered as many as one hundred and thirty.
The daily provisions of the Guānglù Department suddenly increased several times over.
Jiàn and the others strongly pointed out these abuses,
requesting diligent governance and the study of classics,
but only received acknowledgments.
In the second month of the first year of Zhèngdé,
the emperor, following the suggestion of Shàngshū Hán Wén,
ordered the officials to collect taxes from the imperial estates in the capital region,
but still left one eunuch and ten military escorts in each estate.
Jiàn and the others stated,
"Since the imperial estates are for providing tribute to the two empress dowagers,
they should naturally be entirely entrusted to the officials.
They should not still be managed by private individuals,
which goes against the court's intention of honoring its elders."
They then fully elaborated on how inner eunuchs managing estates harassed the populace.
It was not heeded.
The Ministries of Lìbù, Hùbù, and Bīngbù, as well as the Dūcháyuan, each submitted memorials contending over their respective jurisdictions, which were being encroached upon by the close attendants.
Jiàn and others drafted an imperial decree,
but the Emperor did not comply,
ordering them to draft it again.
Jiàn and others strongly remonstrated,
saying:
"The corrupt merchant Tán Jǐngqīng's undermining of the salt administration,
the unwarranted official appointments of generals and soldiers from the northern campaign,
the military official Shén Yīng's defying the law while guilty,
and the Yùyòngjiān's indiscriminate recruitment and examination of calligraphers and seal carvers,
all stem from the private favors of one or two individuals,
ruining centuries-old established systems.
Moreover, while government decrees are now being renewed,
there have been earthquakes and heavenly thunder,
white rainbows piercing the sun,
stars seen in daylight,
and the sun without light.
Internal rebels run rampant,
external enemies are audacious,
wealth is depleted, the people are impoverished,
and grievances and slanders arise in unison.
Yet, officials and servants both inside and outside the court are taking the opportunity to commit villainy,
treating loyal and upright individuals as enemies,
and protecting corrupt individuals as if they were family.
Day after day,
it grows worse than before,
and the coming of disaster and calamity is probably not far off.
We, your servants, received the trust of the late Emperor,
and were appointed to positions of trust.
Recently, decrees have been issued from within the palace,
with which we were barely consulted.
When we propose something,
it is immediately altered.
Instances of this kind
cannot all be enumerated.
If we were to further cling to our personal safety and families,
and collectively yield in compliance,
then we would be deceiving the Emperor and misleading the state,
deserving death many times over.
The four memorials we drafted,
we dare not alter;
we respectfully submit them as originally drafted."
There was no reply.
A few days later,
they again said:
"We, your servants, had the good fortune to serve the late Emperor,
who, at his deathbed, entrusted to us [your Majesty] with earnest concern,
a pain etched in our bones,
swearing to repay him with our lives.
Upon your Majesty's enthronement, the imperial edict
made all under heaven crane their necks in anticipation,
yet morning decrees are changed by evening,
and there is never a day of peace.
All officials and government departments
emulate this trend,
not only rendering things ineffective and unimplemented,
but also changing almost everything.
Those who offer suggestions are considered verbose;
those who manage affairs are seen as creating trouble;
repeated memorials and remonstrances are called bothersome meddling;
and rectifying corrupt policies is called disruptive innovation.
Concerns for the people's livelihood and state finances
are treated as if unheard,
but matters involving favored attendants and powerful relatives
become impregnable.
We, your servants, know this is wrong,
and it is our duty to speak fully.
Recently, regarding the salt laws and rewards for merit,
we extensively presented the pros and cons,
and have waited respectfully for several days,
yet have not received a reply.
If your servants' words are correct,
they should be put into effect;
if our words are wrong,
we should be reprimanded.
Instead, they are kept in the palace without reply,
as if they do not exist.
With governance coming from many sources,
the blame falls on us, your servants.
The Sòng dynasty scholar Zhū Zǐ once said, 'If one stands in their position for a day,
then one must perform their duties for a day;
if one is not granted their duties,
then one dares not stand in their position for a day.'
If we were to merely bear the name of having received the deathbed commission without fully fulfilling the duty of assistance,
we would betray the late Emperor and also betray your Majesty.
What would all under heaven and future generations say of us?
We humbly beg your sagely wisdom to observe and investigate,
and grant us special permission to retire."
The Emperor issued a gracious decree to console and retain them,
but the memorial was still not acted upon.
Five days later,
Jiàn and others again submitted a memorial,
enumerating ten failings in government decrees,
and pointedly criticizing powerful relatives and favored attendants.
They then reiterated their previous request.
The Emperor, having no other choice,
finally issued the previous memorial,
ordering the relevant departments to deliberate in detail.
Jiàn knew that his aspirations would ultimately not be realized,
and was the first to submit a memorial requesting to retire,
followed by Lǐ Dōngyáng and Xiè Qiān;
the Emperor did not grant any of their requests.
Soon after, the relevant departments submitted their deliberation,
which was entirely in line with Jiàn and others' points.
The Emperor reluctantly complied,
which caused all those who had suffered losses to gnash their teeth.
On the *gēngwǔ* day of the sixth month, they again submitted a memorial, saying:
"Recently,
too many court audiences have been excused,
reporting on affairs has become progressively later,
leisure activities have become more widespread,
and daily lectures at the Jīngyán have been directly ordered to cease.
We, your foolish servants,
do not know what other matters in your Majesty's palace could be more urgent than these.
Indeed, extravagant rewards and reckless spending are not how one honors the virtue of frugality;
shooting and hunting are not how one cultivates a benevolent heart;
eagles, hounds, foxes, and rabbits, creatures of the wilderness, should not be kept in the court;
bows, arrows, armor, and the implements of battle should not be employed within the palace forbidden grounds.
Now, imperial studies have long been neglected,
upright individuals are not befriended,
honest words are not heard,
and sentiments are not conveyed or understood,
while these several activities are mixed and presented before you.
Your servants cannot but feel fear and worry."
The Emperor said:
"I have heard that emperors cannot be without fault,
but it is precious to correct one's faults.
Your words are correct,
and I shall act upon them."
Jiàn and others then compiled the crucial points of current governance articulated by court officials,
requesting that they be placed beside the Emperor's seat for daily review: namely, no solo galloping,
lightly leaving the palace forbidden grounds;
no frequent visits to palace offices,
or boating on the lake;
no engaging in falconry, dog-hunting, or shooting;
and no accepting food and drink offerings from palace eunuchs.
The memorial was submitted,
and its receipt was acknowledged.
Previously,
after Xiàozōng's mausoleum was completed,
Jiàn and others immediately requested the opening of the Jīngyán lectures.
The Emperor initially reluctantly agreed,
but later frequently suspended lectures due to audiences with the two Empress Dowagers,
or saying he was choosing an auspicious day to ride a horse.
Jiàn and others' remonstrances were very earnest and heartfelt.
In the eighth month,
after the Emperor's grand wedding,
Jiàn and others again requested the lectures to resume.
He ordered them to wait until the ninth month,
but when the time came, he again ordered the afternoon lectures to be suspended.
Jiàn and others, citing the precedent of the late Emperor, who had two lectures a day,
strongly contended but did not succeed.
At this time,
Jiàn and others had repeatedly offered earnest remonstrances through memorials,
but the Emperor, being close to petty individuals,
ultimately could not change.
Soon after, he dispatched the palace eunuch Cuī Gǎo and others to supervise textile production,
and requested 12,000 salt *yǐn* (vouchers).
The relevant departments firmly remonstrated;
supervising secretaries Táo Xié and Xú Áng,
censors Dù Mín, Shào Qīng, Yáng Yí, and others successively remonstrated,
and Jiàn and others also said it was unacceptable.
The Emperor summoned Jiàn and others to the Nuǎngé to discuss face-to-face,
questioning them somewhat,
but Jiàn and others all responded appropriately.
The Emperor could not refute them,
and finally said with a stern expression:
"Is it possible that all affairs of the realm are ruined by palace eunuchs?
Court officials ruin six or seven out of ten matters,
and you sirs yourselves know this."
He then ordered that all salt *yǐn* be granted as requested by Gǎo.
Jiàn and others withdrew,
and again submitted a memorial saying it was unacceptable.
The Emperor felt ashamed of his slip of the tongue,
and thus approved Jiàn and others' memorial.
Thereupon, both inside and outside the court were pleased,
believing that the Emperor might well correct his errors.
Jiàn and others then conspired to remove
the "Eight Factions" (bā dǎng),
submitting repeated memorials requesting their execution.
Censors also frequently debated the eunuchs' crimes.
Jiàn, Qiān, and Dōngyáng strongly supported these memorials.
The Emperor sent a Directorate of Ceremonial (sī lǐ) official to the Grand Secretariat (gé) saying:
"I am about to change;
for my sake, grant a special pardon to these fellows."
Jiàn and others said:
"These individuals have offended the ancestors,
and cannot be pardoned by Your Majesty."
They again memorialized, saying:
"If a ruler unknowingly misuses petty individuals,
the world still hopes that he will recognize and remove them.
If he knows and does not remove them, then the petty individuals will become even more unrestrained,
the upright gentlemen will be in greater danger,
and it will not stop short of chaos and ruin.
Moreover,
evil and righteousness cannot coexist.
Now the entire court wishes to decisively remove these few individuals,
yet Your Majesty, knowing their crimes, deliberately keeps them by your side.
This will not only cause suspicion and fear among the court officials,
but these few individuals will also not feel secure themselves.
With suspicion between high and low,
and disunity within and without,
the seeds of disaster and chaos begin here."
The Emperor did not listen.
Jiàn and others argued over their continued service or resignation.
Jǐn and the other eight were in dire straits,
weeping together.
Then memorials from Minister Hán Wén and others again arrived.
Thereupon, the Emperor ordered Wang Yuè and other Directorate of Ceremonial officials to go to the Grand Secretariat to deliberate.
They came three times in one day,
wanting to relocate Jǐn and the others to Nánjīng.
Qiān wanted to execute them directly.
Jiàn pushed the desk and wept, saying:
"The late emperor, on the verge of death,
held this old minister's hand,
entrusting me with important affairs.
Now, the soil on his mausoleum is not yet dry,
and these fellows have caused such ruin.
If I die, how can I face the late emperor!"
His voice and demeanor were stern.
Yuè, who was usually upright and hated evil,
said with indignation:
"The Grand Secretariat's proposal is correct."
His peers Fàn Hēng, Xú Zhì, and others also agreed.
That night,
the eight individuals became even more desperate,
weeping around the Emperor.
The Emperor was enraged,
immediately arrested Yuè and others, imprisoning them in the Imperial Prison (zhào yù).
But Jiàn and others did not know this,
still relying on Yuè's internal support.
The next day,
Hán Wén led the Nine Ministers (jiǔ qīng) to prostrate themselves before the palace gate, strongly arguing.
Jiàn had preemptively told them:
"The matter will succeed;
you all just hold firm."
Soon after,
the situation drastically changed:
the eight individuals were all pardoned without inquiry,
and Jǐn was put in charge of the Directorate of Ceremonial.
Jiàn and Qiān then requested to retire,
and were granted edicts and post-station services to return home,
with monthly stipends and yearly labor exemption as per old custom.
After Jiàn left,
Jǐn's resentment did not cease.
In the third month, xīn wèi day, of the following year, an edict listed fifty-three people as treacherous party members (jiān dǎng),
posted on the imperial court hall,
with Jiàn as the head.
Two years later, his official status was revoked and he became a commoner,
and his imperial patent (gào mìng) was posthumously stripped.
When Jǐn was executed,
Jiàn's official status was reinstated,
and he retired.
Later, when he heard the Emperor frequently went on tours,
he would sigh and refuse to eat, saying:
"I have failed the late emperor."
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he ordered an imperial envoy (xíng rén) to carry an edict to inquire after him,
comparing him to Sīmǎ Guāng and Wén Yànbó,
and granted him generous gifts.
When he reached ninety years of age,
an edict instructed the provincial governor (fǔ chén) to personally visit his residence to present silk, a fed sheep, and fine wine.
His grandson Chéngxué was appointed Scribe of the Central Secretariat (zhōng shū shè rén).
He died in the fifth year of Jiājìng,
at the age of ninety-four.
His posthumous memorial contained several thousand words,
advising the Emperor to rectify himself and study diligently,
to be close to the worthy and distant from the treacherous.
The Emperor was deeply grieved,
granted very generous funeral provisions,
posthumously appointed him Grand Preceptor (tài shī),
and bestowed the posthumous title Wénjìng.
Jiàn's demeanor was stern and upright,
rectifying himself and leading his subordinates.
After court was dismissed,
when his colleagues sought private audiences,
he would not exchange a single word.
Xǔ Jìn and seven others wanted to promote Jiāo Fāng to the Ministry of Personnel (lì bù).
Jiàn said:
"This old man will soon return to the fields.
Even if Jiāo gets this position,
I fear all of you will suffer harm from him."
Later, the seven indeed were displaced by Fāng.
Dōngyáng used poetry and prose to promote junior scholars,
and scholars across the land eagerly discussed literature,
but Jiàn seemed not to hear it,
instead teaching people to study classics and delve into principles.
His accomplishments were bright, outstanding, and grand;
few assisting ministers of the Míng dynasty could compare.
His grandson, Wàngzhī,
was a successful candidate in the imperial examination (jìnshì).
Xiè Qiān,
courtesy name Yúqiáo,
was from Yúyáo.
In the tenth year of Chénghuà, he placed first in the provincial examination (xiāng shì).
The following year, he passed the imperial examination,
again placing first.
He was appointed Compiler (xiū zhuàn),
and successively promoted to Left Supervising Secretary (zuǒ shù zǐ).
In the spring of the first year of Hóngzhì,
the eunuch Guō Yǒng requested to pre-select concubines to fill the six palaces.
Qiān memorialized:
"The imperial mausoleum is not yet complete,
so it is proper to wait.
The period of mourning (xiáng tán zhī qí) is also not far off.
Your Majesty is in the prime of life;
please wait until the mourning period (liàng yīn) is over;
it will not be too late to deliberate then."
Minister Zhōu Hóngmó and others agreed with Qiān's suggestion,
and it was followed.
When the Emperor was in the Eastern Palace (dōng gōng),
Qiān was already a lecture official (jiǎng guān).
By this time,
he participated in daily lectures (rì jiǎng),
striving to sincerely enlighten the Emperor.
The night before, he would always straighten his clothes and cap, and practice recitation.
When he delivered his lecture,
his words were detailed and precise,
and the Emperor often praised him.
He was promoted to Junior Grand Mentor (shǎo zhān shì) concurrent with Academician Expositor-in-Waiting (shì jiǎng xué shì).
In the eighth year, an edict commanded him to enter the Grand Secretariat (nèi gé) with Lǐ Dōngyáng to participate in crucial state affairs.
Qiān was then observing mourning (jū yōu),
and strongly declined.
He accepted the appointment only after the mourning period ended.
He was promoted to Grand Mentor (zhān shì) with his concurrent official positions remaining unchanged.
When the Crown Prince moved out of the palace (chū gé),

he was given the additional titles of Junior Guardian of the Crown Prince (tài zǐ shǎo bǎo) and Minister of War (bīng bù shàng shū) concurrent with Grand Academician of the Eastern Pavilion (dōng gé dà xué shì).
He memorialized, urging the Crown Prince to be close to the worthy and distant from the treacherous,
to study diligently,
and to guard against idleness and pleasure.
The Emperor commended him.
Minister Mǎ Wénshēng, citing border alerts in Dàtóng
and insufficient provisions,
requested an additional silver conversion for the two taxes (liǎng shuì zhé yín) in the south.
Qiān said:
"The former dynasty, recognizing the heavy taxation in the south,
allowed silver conversion to alleviate the burden.
If we again discuss adding to it,
I fear the people cannot bear the imposition.
Moreover, enriching the state lies in frugality.
If expenditures are not controlled,
what benefit is there in increasing taxes?"
Minister Ní Yuè also argued against it,
and the proposal was consequently shelved.
In the later years of Xiàozōng's reign, he was deeply moved to rectify corrupt practices.
However, eunuchs in the various storages of the Imperial Household (nèi fǔ), as well as in granaries (cāng chǎng) and horse stables (mǎ fāng), engaged in illicit acts and twisted laws,
making thorough investigation impossible.
The brave warriors of the Imperial Horse Bureau (yù mǎ jiān) and the Four Tengxiáng Guards (téng xiáng sì wèi), considering themselves imperial guards not subordinate to the Ministry of War,
often drew salaries for non-existent personnel (kōng míng zhī xiǎng),
and this abuse was particularly severe.
Qiān seized the opportunity to speak about this,
and the Emperor ordered drafting an edict to prohibit and restrict it.
Qiān said:
"Empty prohibitions are useless;
it is better to order the relevant departments (cáo sī) to thoroughly investigate the abuses
and clearly report them to the throne.
Then, strict regulations should be established,
and offenders must be punished,
so that accumulated malpractices can be removed."
The Emperor agreed.
Qiān had a magnificent appearance and bearing,
and was upright and honest in his principles.
He assisted in governing with Liú Jiàn and Lǐ Dōngyáng,
and Qiān was clear-sighted and astute in matters,
skilled in presenting arguments.
People at the time had a saying:
"Master Lǐ strategizes,
Master Liú decides,
and Master Xiè is especially eloquent."
The world acclaimed him as a worthy prime minister.
When Wǔzōng 嗣位 succeeded to the throne,
he repeatedly promoted him to Junior Tutor兼太子太傅.
He offered remonstrances many times,
but the emperor did not heed them.
Due to celestial phenomena, he earnestly sought to resign,
but the emperor always comforted him and kept him.
When he failed in his request to execute Liú Jǐn,
he then retired along with Jiàn and returned home,
receiving the same honors and treatment as Jiàn.
However, Liú Jǐn's resentment and vengefulness were not yet appeased.
After Jiāo Fāng had allied himself with Liú Jǐn and entered the Grand Secretariat,
he also resented Xiè Qiān for having once recommended Wáng Áo and Wú Kuān to replace him,
and not himself.
So, he obtained an imperial edict to force his younger brother, Dī, a Secretary in the Ministry of War, to resign,
and dismissed his son, Pī, a Compiler, as a commoner.
