In the second month of the fourth year,
because Zhōu Lǐ, Xú Zǐyuán, and Xǔ Lóng of Yúyáo,
and Xú Wénbiāo of Shàngyú—all gentlemen of talent and virtue recommended by Zhèjiāng in response to an imperial edict—
were all Xiè Qiān's compatriots,
and the imperial edict was drafted by Jiàn,
he wished to use this to incriminate the two men.
He fabricated an edict, stating that there were too many recluses in Yúyáo,
and that this must be a case of favoritism and biased recommendation,
and sent Lǐ and others to the imperial prison.
Their testimony implicated Jiàn and Xiè Qiān.
Liú Jǐn wanted to arrest Jiàn and Xiè Qiān
and confiscate their property,
but Dōngyáng strongly interceded for them.
Jiāo Fāng, from the side, said sternly:
"Even if we pardon them lightly,
they should still be stripped of their names."
An imperial edict was issued,
as Jiāo Fāng had suggested,
and Lǐ and others were all banished to the frontier.
Minister Liú Yǔ again impeached officials above the two superintendencies for inaccurate recommendations,
and they were punished with fines of rice;
some were stripped of their official status.
Furthermore, an edict was issued stating that from then on, people from Yúyáo should not be selected for metropolitan offices,
and this was made a permanent regulation.
In the twelfth month of that year,
remonstrating officials, seeking to curry favor with Liú Jǐn,
requested the revocation of the imperial patents of Jiàn and Xiè Qiān, as well as Ministers Mǎ Wénshēng, Liú Dàxià, Hán Wén, Xǔ Jìn, and others.
An edict was issued, also ordering the return of the jade belts and clothing that had been bestowed,
and at the same time, six hundred seventy-five people had their imperial patents revoked.
At this time,
everyone feared for Xiè Qiān,
but he remained calm, playing chess and composing poetry with guests.
After Liú Jǐn was executed,
he was reinstated,
and then retired again.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he sent an envoy to inquire after him,
and appointed Dī as a Consultative Official,
and Pī was reinstated to his Hanlin post.
Xiè Qiān then sent his son Zhèng to express gratitude,
and advised the emperor to diligently study, emulate his ancestors, and accept remonstrances.
The emperor replied with a gracious edict.
In the second year of Jiājìng, an edict again instructed officials to inquire after him.
In the sixth year,
Grand Secretary Fèi Hóng recommended Xiè Qiān as his own replacement,
and Yáng Yīqīng, wishing to obstruct Zhāng Cōng,
also strongly recommended Xiè Qiān.
The emperor then sent a messenger with a handwritten imperial letter to his home, summoning him,
and ordered the Surveillance and Provincial Administration officials to urge him to set out.
Xiè Qiān was seventy-nine years old by then,
and had no choice but to accept the command.
By the time he arrived,
Zhāng Cōng had already entered the Grand Secretariat,
and Yáng Yīqīng, whose rank was higher than Xiè Qiān's, had no intention of deferring to him.
Xiè Qiān held his position for several months,
and then earnestly sought to resign.
The emperor treated Xiè Qiān with increasing kindness,
exempting him from morning audiences due to the cold weather,
bestowing imperial poems on New Year's Eve,
and when he reported illness, sending doctors and bestowing medicines,
while the Court of Imperial Entertainments delivered wine and provisions;
envoys followed one another on the road.
Xiè Qiān finally resigned and returned home in the third month of the following year.
He died at home in the tenth year,
at the age of eighty-three.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Tutor,
and his posthumous name was Wénzhèng.
Dī rose to the position of Provincial Administration Commissioner of Guǎngdōng.
Pī came first in the provincial examination,
and became a successful candidate in the imperial examination at the end of Hóngzhì.
He successively served as Left Vice Minister of Personnel,
and was posthumously granted the title of Minister of Rites.
Lǐ Dōngyáng,
courtesy name Bīnzhī,
was from Chálíng,
but resided in the capital due to his military household registration.
At the age of four, he could write characters a foot in size.
Jǐngdì summoned him for a test,
was very pleased,
held him on his lap,
and bestowed fruit and paper currency.
Later, he was twice summoned to lecture on the major principles of the Book of Documents,
which pleased the emperor,
who ordered him to study in the capital.
In the eighth year of Tiānshùn,
at the age of eighteen,
he passed the imperial examination,
was selected as a probationer in the Hanlin Academy,
and appointed as a Compiler.
He was successively promoted to Academician-in-waiting,
and served as an instructor to the Crown Prince.
In the fourth year of Hóngzhì,
when the Veritable Records of Xiànzōng were completed,
he was promoted from Left Vice Supervisor兼侍講學士
to Minor Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
retaining his concurrent positions.
In the fifth year,
due to drought, the emperor sought advice.
Lǐ Dōngyáng itemized the major principles of the seven chapters of Mèngzǐ,
supplemented with discussions on the successes and failures of contemporary politics,
totaling several thousand words,
and presented them.
The emperor praised them.
Grand Secretaries Xú Pǔ and others, noting the proliferation of imperial edicts,
requested that, following the precedent of Wáng Zhí in earlier dynasties,
a specialized official be appointed to manage them.
Consequently, Lǐ Dōngyáng was promoted to Right Vice Minister of Rites兼侍讀學士,
and entered the Grand Secretariat to specifically manage imperial edicts.
In the eighth year, in his original capacity, he served in the Wènyuāngé and participated in state affairs,
being appointed on the same day as Xiè Qiān.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent, Minister of Rites, and Grand Secretary of the Wènyuāngé.
In the seventeenth year,
when the reconstructed Quèlǐ Temple was completed,
he was commissioned to offer sacrifices.
Upon his return, he submitted a memorial stating: "Your subject, having swiftly carried out his mission,
encountered a severe drought.
Along the entire Tiānjīn road,
summer wheat has withered,
and autumn grains have not yet been sown.
Boat pullers are in rags,
and those wielding hoes
have faces showing signs of starvation.
Bandits are rampant,
especially severe in Qīngzhōu.
People coming from the south say
that in Jiāngnán and eastern Zhèjiāng, refugees line the roads,
households are depleted,
military ranks are empty,
treasuries lack even ten days' worth of reserves,
and officials have not received their salaries for several years.
In the southeast, the source of revenue,
a single year of famine has led to this state.
The northern regions are barren and poor,
and have never
accumulated stores.
If this autumn brings another poor harvest,
how can they endure it?
The emergence of unforeseen events
may be beyond prediction.
If your subject had not personally passed through these areas,
then even if he had long served in official capacities,
daily handling memorials,
he would still not have grasped the details,
how much less Your Majesty, residing high above in the nine-layered palace?
Your subject has inquired on the roads,
and everyone says that superfluous officials are too numerous,
national expenditures are without proper management,
corvée duties are too frequent,
and levies are overlapping.
In the capital, construction projects are flourishing,
and the financial resources and labor of the soldiers supplying
these services are utterly exhausted.
Whenever a drill is commanded,
they would rather die than attend.
Powerful families and great clans,
whose fields connect across prefectures,
still ceaselessly beg for more.
When imperial princes
are enfeoffed,
provisions reach two to three hundred thousand.
Idlers,
claiming to be imperial relatives or servants,
often set up large markets at border passes and major cities,
ensnaring commercial taxes.
The nation's capital is established in the north,
reliant on the southeast for support.
Merchants are frightened away and dispersed,
which is by no means a trivial matter.
Furthermore, there are internal officials overseeing weaving,
who let their petty followers plunder,
and officials and clerks at the sluices
are all terrified and flee,
while impoverished people selling goods everywhere are greatly disturbed;
this is also what your subject has witnessed with his own eyes.
Indeed, the sentiments of the common people
cannot be known by the prefectures and counties.
The sentiments of the prefectures and counties
cannot be known by the imperial court.
The sentiments of the imperial court,
the nine-layered palace also
could not be known.
It began with connivance,
and was completed through deception.
The origin of connivance was very small,
but the calamity of deception was very profound.
Your minister, while in Shāndōng,
humbly heard
that Your Majesty, seeing the frequent appearance of natural disasters,
commanded all officials to speak without reservation.
However, imperial edicts were repeatedly issued,
and memorials were all submitted,
but matters concerning the inner court or noble relatives
were often
obstructed,
and after years and months,
they were all suppressed and dismissed.
I truly fear that what is said today
will again be mere empty words.
I beg that previous memorials, both internal and external, be gathered,
carefully
selected,
and decisively implemented.
The Emperor praised and sighed in admiration,
and submitted them all to the relevant offices.
At this time,
the Emperor frequently summoned Grand Secretaries to discuss government affairs face-to-face.
Dōngyáng, along with the Chief Grand Secretary Liú Jiàn and others, devoted their hearts to offering advice,
and whenever there were shortcomings or errors in current policies, they would speak fully and remonstrate strongly.
Dōngyáng was skilled in classical prose,
and many drafts of memorials in the Grand Secretariat were attributed to him.
When a memorial was released,
it was widely circulated and recited throughout the realm.
The following year,
he received the dying imperial charge along with Liú Jiàn and Xiè Qiān.
When Wǔzōng ascended the throne,
he was repeatedly promoted to Junior Tutor and concurrently Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
When Liú Jǐn entered the Directorate of Ceremonial,
Dōngyáng, along with Jiàn and Qiān, resigned their positions immediately.
An inner edict dismissed Jiàn and Qiān,
but Dōngyáng alone was retained.
Ashamed of this,
he repeatedly submitted memorials earnestly requesting to resign,
but was not permitted.
Initially,
Jiàn and Qiān had advocated for the execution of Jǐn,
using very stern language,
but only Dōngyáng was slightly more moderate,
which is why he alone was retained.
As Jiàn and Qiān were about to depart,
Dōngyáng hosted a farewell banquet for them and shed tears.
Jiàn sternly said:
"Why do you weep?
If you had strongly contended that day,
you would have left with us."
Dōngyáng remained silent.
Once Jǐn achieved his ambitions,
he was determined to suppress the gentry.
And Jiāo Fāng entered the Grand Secretariat to assist in his tyranny,
and old officials and upright loyalists were almost all banished.
Dōngyáng was disheartened and unfulfilled,
and also temporized to avoid disaster.
But Jiāo Fāng envied his position above him,
and plotted against him with Jǐn day and night.
Previously,
Dōngyáng had been commanded to compile the *Tōngjiàn Zuǎnyào*.
Upon its completion,
Jǐn ordered someone to pick out minor flaws in the brushstrokes,
and remove the names of several transcribers,
intending to implicate Dōngyáng through this.
Dōngyáng was greatly distressed,
and entrusted Fāng and Zhāng Cǎi to resolve it,
whereupon it ceased.
Jǐn's brutality intensified daily,
he slandered and insulted everything,
yet still outwardly showed respect to Dōngyáng.
For all the tyrannical acts Jǐn committed,
Dōngyáng often smoothed things over,
and provided many remedies.
Shàngbǎoqīng Cuī Xuán, Vice Envoy Yáo Xiáng, and Minister Zhāng Wěi for violating regulations by riding in sedan chairs,
and their attendants wantonly demanding post horses;
and Supervising Secretary Ān Kuí,
and Censor Zhāng Yù for failing to please Jǐn when auditing border provisions;
all were subjected to heavy torture and almost died.
Dōngyáng strenuously intervened,
and Xuán and others were banished as soldiers,
while Kuí and Yù were released as commoners.
In the sixth month, *rénchén* day, of the third year [of Zhèngdé (1508)],
after court was dismissed,
an anonymous letter enumerating Jǐn's crimes was left on the imperial pathway,
and an edict ordered all officials to kneel outside the Fèngtiānmén.
A moment later,
more than three hundred junior officials were arrested and imprisoned.
The next day,
Dōngyáng and others strongly intervened,
and as Jǐn also secretly learned that it was the work of his own faction,
the crowd was pardoned.
A few days later,
Dōngyáng submitted a memorial listing several measures for leniency,
and the memorial was sent to the relevant offices.
Afterward, the Ministry of Revenue submitted a counter-memorial,
stating that the deficit in grain and fodder
had its own dedicated officials,
and the provincial governors were in overall charge,
so it should be handled leniently.
Jǐn was furious,
and fabricated an edict of several hundred words of reprimand and blame,
which shocked and appalled officials inside and outside the court.
Jǐn was troubled by the daily increase in bandits,
and wanted to banish their families, neighbors, and those who provided them with resources.
Someone reported capturing seventy bandits,
and the relevant office wanted to deal with them according to the new regulations.
Dōngyáng said,
if this were so, then cases from a hundred years ago could all be reopened,
and thus they were spared.
Liú Jiàn, Xiè Qiān, Liú Dàxià, Yáng Yīqīng, and the Earl of Píngjiāng, Chén Xióng and his ilk, were all on the brink of grave danger,
but all were saved thanks to Dōngyáng.
His subtle and silent interventions,
and preservation of good people,
secretly benefited the whole realm,
yet many principled scholars criticized him.
Vice Minister Luó Guì submitted a letter urging him to retire early,
even requesting to remove his name from the list of disciples.
When Dōngyáng received the letter,
he merely bowed his head and sighed deeply.
Jiāo Fāng had allied himself with the eunuchs,
and although Wáng Ào maintained righteousness,
he could not resist Jǐn,
so Dōngyáng sought out Yáng Tínghé to work together,
somewhat relying on him to strengthen his position.
Soon after, Ào resigned,
and his successors Liú Yǔ and Cáo Yuán were both Jǐn's partisans,
making Dōngyáng's position even more isolated.
Dōngyáng had previously been promoted to Junior Tutor and concurrently Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince,
and later when Jǐn wanted to promote Fāng,
an edict granted Dōngyáng the stipend of a First Rank official.
In the fifth month of the fourth year [of Zhèngdé (1509)],
the *Xiàozōng Shílù* was completed,
and the officials who compiled it were due for promotion.
The relevant offices cited precedents from the *Huìdiǎn*.
An edict stated that Liú Jiàn and others had previously incurred great expenses while compiling the *Huìdiǎn*,
and thus all their promotions were revoked,
and Dōngyáng also suffered a reduction in salary.
A few days later,
he was reinstated for his meritorious work on the *Shílù*.
In the spring of the fifth year [of Zhèngdé (1510)],
there was a prolonged drought,
and an edict was issued to pardon prisoners.
Dōngyáng and others then submitted several additional proposals not covered by the imperial edict,
and the Emperor adopted all of them.
However, the judicial officials feared Jǐn,
and only two people had their death sentences commuted.
That autumn,
Jǐn was executed,
whereupon Dōngyáng submitted a memorial listing his own faults, saying:
"Your minister, serving in the Forbidden Precinct,
had duties related to Jǐn's.
Whenever imperial edicts were drafted or decrees were written,
they were either rejected repeatedly,
or directly altered,
or taken back to his private chambers,
using others' hands,
or passed out for transcription,
forcing them to be signed [with a dot to indicate approval],
mixing true and false,
making it impossible to distinguish.
Although your minister twisted and turned to maintain control,
hoping to achieve some relief,
by procrastinating and enduring,
much harm was also done.
It is fitting that I be dismissed."
The Emperor consoled and retained him.
Zhì Píng
was appointed Grand Master of Remonstrance, Left Pillar of the State.
His son was granted an蔭 (yìn, inherited privilege) to serve as Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
This was impeached by Censor Zhāng Qín.
The Emperor was enraged,
and stripped Qín of his salary.
Dōngyáng also requested retirement and declined the荫 (yìn),
but it was not permitted.
At this time, Jiāo Fāng and Cáo Yuán had already been dismissed,
and Liú Zhōng and Liáng Chǔ entered the government,
refreshing all political affairs.
However, Zhāng Yǒng, Wèi Bīn, Mǎ Yǒngchéng, Gǔ Dàyòng, and others were still in power,
and the Emperor indulged in revelry as before.
No imperial son had yet been born,
and the Emperor often stayed outside the palace overnight.
There was also discussion of undertaking a major construction project for the bàofáng (leopard chambers),
and building temples and monasteries within the forbidden city.
Dōngyáng and others worried about this,
and successively submitted memorials earnestly remonstrating,
but received no reply.
In the seventh year,
Dōngyáng and others noted that the capital, Shānxī, Shǎnxī, Yúnnán, and Fújiàn had successively experienced earthquakes,
yet the Emperor's lecture sessions were not held,
imperial audiences were long neglected,
the sacrifices to the imperial ancestors were not personally attended,
and there was unlimited access through the forbidden gates.
Gǔ Dàyòng had also reopened the Western Depot.
They repeatedly submitted urgent remonstrances,
but the Emperor ultimately did not listen.
After nine years, his term of office was completed,
and he concurrently received the salary of a Grand Secretary.
When the Henan rebels were pacified,
his son Shì Jǐnyī Qiānhù was granted an 蔭 (yìn).
He submitted memorials twice strongly declining,
and the 蔭 (yìn) was changed to a civil official of the sixth rank.
That winter,
the Emperor wished to transfer three thousand troops from Xuānfǔ to the capital for guard duty,
and have the capital's troops rotate to garrison the border.
Dōngyáng and others firmly opposed this,
and all high officials and censors spoke against it.
Eunuchs swarmed to request the draft edict,
and the Emperor sat at the gate of the Qiánqīng Gōng urging them,
but Dōngyáng and others ultimately did not obey the imperial decree.
The next day, an imperial decree was issued from within the palace to implement it,
and Jiāng Bīn and others then brought border troops into the bàofáng.
Dōngyáng, citing old age and illness, requested retirement.
His memorials were submitted numerous times,
and it was only now that it was permitted.
He was granted an imperial edict and provided with stipends and servants as was customary.
He died four years later,
at the age of seventy.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Preceptor,
and given the posthumous name Wénzhèng.
Dōngyáng served his father Chún with filial piety.
When he first served as a Hanlin official,
he often drank until late at night.
His father would not go to bed,
enduring the cold to wait for his return.
From then on, he never drank outside at night for the rest of his life.
His writings were elegant and fluid,
and many major imperial compositions came from his hand.
He excelled at seal and clerical script,
and his stele inscriptions, essays, and literary works were spread to the four corners of the world.
He encouraged and supported promising youngsters,
and recommended talented individuals.
Scholars and high officials who emerged from his tutelage
all achieved brilliant accomplishments.
Since the beginning of the Míng dynasty,
among prime ministers who led the literati in literary excellence,
after Yáng Shìqí,
there was only Dōngyáng.
He served in court for fifty years,
with unwavering integrity.
After his dismissal and return home,
those who requested poems, essays, and seal carvings filled his doorway,
and he largely relied on this to support his daily life.
One day,
as his wife was bringing in paper and ink,
Dōngyáng showed a weary expression.
His wife smiled and said:
"Today we are hosting guests,
can we have a table without fish and vegetables?"
So he cheerfully took up his brush,
and finished in a short while.
Such was his character.
Wáng Ào,
courtesy name Jìzhī,
was a native of Wú.
His father, Wǎn,
was the Magistrate of Guānghuà.
Ào was sixteen years old,
when he studied with his father.
The students of the Guózǐjiān (Imperial Academy) vied to recite his writings.
Vice Minister Yè Shèng and Investigating Censor for Education Chén Xuǎn were surprised by his talent,
and called him a man of global talent.
In the tenth year of Chénghuà, he passed the provincial examination,
and the following year, the metropolitan examination,
both with the first place.
In the palace examination, he placed third,
and was appointed Compiler.
He kept to his home to study,
avoiding power and influence.
At the beginning of Hóngzhì's reign,
he was promoted to Academician-in-waiting,
and served as a lecturer.
The influential eunuch Lǐ Guǎng escorted the Emperor on a tour of the Western Garden.
Ào lectured on King Wén not daring to indulge in hunting trips,
repeatedly and pointedly remonstrating,
which moved the Emperor.
After the lecture,
the Emperor told Guǎng:
"The lecturer is referring to you people."
Shòuníng Hóu Zhāng Luán had old ties with Ào,
but when Luán became influential,
Ào completely cut off communication with him.
When the crown prince left the inner court to set up his own establishment,
the high officials requested upright individuals to serve as his staff.
Ào, holding his original office, concurrently served as Tutor.
Soon after, he was transferred to Junior Supervisor of the Imperial Academy,
and promoted to Right Vice Minister of Personnel.
He once presented a memorial on border strategy,
briefly stating:
"Yesterday, Huǒshāi invaded Dàtóng,
and Your Majesty was anxious from dawn to dusk,
yet all the border generals merely defended their walled cities,
with no one daring to face their vanguard.
This is what I do not understand.
I humbly believe that today, Huǒshāi and the Little Prince are not to be feared,
but rather it is the favored flatterers corrupting government,
unclear rewards and punishments,
lack of dedicated appointments,
unenforced laws,
and empty border defenses that are deeply to be feared.
In recent years, border generals who lost battles
were often ordered to redeem themselves by killing rebels.
Vice General-in-chief Yáo Xìn held back his troops and did not advance,
yet also escaped punishment.
This is why people's morale slackens daily,
and the spirit of the soldiers is not invigorated.
I hope Your Majesty will exert your vigorous authority,
regularly summon high officials,
consult them on the courage and timidity of border generals,
punish those with faults,
reward those with merits,
and centralize the authority of the chief commanders.
Recall the retired Minister Qín Hóng to serve as Chief Coordinator,
to oversee all borders.
Let Inspector-General Shǐ Lín sit in command of the capital's garrisons,
providing distant support.
Greatly compassionate the families of those who died in service on the border,
recruit brave and skilled soldiers from border regions,
and use spies to alienate their subordinates.
Divide forces for surprise attacks,
and win through unexpected tactics,
and the invaders will surely not dare to penetrate deeply."
This was adopted.
He also said:
"It is appropriate to emulate the special examinations of previous dynasties,
such as the Erudite and Extensive Learning examinations,
to gather exceptional talents.
Held once every six years,
those who are particularly outstanding should be granted clean and important positions,
and those who already hold office should be promoted.
After several years,
the scholarly class will be refined,
and will surely consider mastery of classics and ancient learning as superior,
shedding the vulgarity of superficial knowledge."
This was not adopted at the time.
Soon after, he returned home due to his father's mourning period.
In the fourth month of the first year of Zhèngdé,
he was recalled as Left Vice Minister,
and together with Hán Wén and other high officials,
he requested the execution of Liú Jǐn and the other "Eight Tigers."
Shortly after, Jǐn entered the Directorate of Ceremonial,
and Grand Secretaries Liú Jiàn and Xiè Qiān successively departed,
leaving only Lǐ Dōngyáng in the Grand Secretariat.
Jǐn wanted to bring in Jiāo Fāng,
but public opinion in court overwhelmingly recommended Ào.
Jǐn, pressed by public sentiment,
ordered Ào to enter the Grand Secretariat concurrently as an Academician, along with Fāng.
Over a month later,
he was promoted to Minister of Revenue and Grand Secretary of the Wényuān Pavilion.
The next year, he was granted the additional title of Junior Guardian and Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince.
When Emperor Jǐng's Empress Wāng died,
the propriety of her funeral was questioned.
Áo said:
"Since the consort was deposed not for a crime,
it is proper to restore her former title.
She should be buried as a consort,
but sacrificed to as an empress."
So, an order was given to suspend court,
and the sacrifices were performed according to the regulations.
When Empress Wú, the deposed empress of Emperor Xiànzōng, died,
Jǐn suggested burning her to destroy any trace,
saying,
"It is improper to wear mourning for her."
Áo said:
"Mourning may not be worn,
but the burial must not be meager."
This was followed.
Shàngbǎo Qīng Cuī Xuán and three others, shackled, were on the verge of death.
Áo said to Jǐn:
"A scholar may be killed,
but not disgraced.
If they are now disgraced and killed,
what face do I have to remain here?"
Lǐ Dōngyáng also strenuously intervened,
and Xuán and the others were spared, sent into exile.
Jǐn bore a grudge against Shàngshū Hán Wén,
determined to kill him.
He also wanted to frame Jiàn and Qiān with other charges.
Áo repeatedly intervened to save them, and they escaped.
Someone spoke ill of Yáng Yīqīng to Jǐn,
saying that the construction of the border wall was a waste of money.
Áo argued:
"Yīqīng built the border for the country,
how can his achievement be counted as a crime?"
Jǐn was enraged at Liú Dàxià,
had him arrested and brought to the capital,
intending to sentence him to death for inciting rebellion.
Áo argued:
"Cén Měng merely delayed his departure;
he had not rebelled, so how can it be called 'inciting rebellion'?"
At that time, all major power, both inside and outside the court, belonged to Jǐn.
Áo initially spoke with him frankly,
and Jǐn sometimes listened and accepted.
However, Fāng was exclusively obsequious,
and Jǐn's tyranny grew even worse,
causing disaster to flow to the gentry.
Áo was unable to save them,
and strenuously sought to resign.
After four years,
he submitted three memorials,
and his request was granted.
He was granted an imperial letter, provided with a post carriage, and officials supplied him with stipends and servants,
all according to previous custom.
He lived at home for fourteen years,
and though court officials repeatedly recommended him, he did not return.
When Emperor Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he dispatched a xíngrén to inquire after him.
Áo submitted a memorial of thanks,
and consequently presented two essays: "On Study and Instruction" and "On Governing Personally."
The emperor replied with a gracious edict, acknowledging them,
and appointed one of his sons as Zhōngshū Shèrén.
In the third year of Jiājìng, another edict instructed officials to inquire after him.
Not long after, he died
at the age of seventy-five.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tàifù,
and his posthumous name was Wénkè.
Áo was widely learned and had keen discernment.
His writings were elegant,
and his discussions were clear and fluent.
In his later years, he wrote an essay titled "On the Goodness of Human Nature."
Wáng Shǒurén saw it and said:
"Lord Wáng has profound insights,
which the world has yet to fully appreciate."
In his youth, he was skilled at writing examination essays.
Later, he frequently oversaw provincial examinations,
setting the standard for essays for a generation.
He valued scholars who emphasized classical learning,
dismissing all those who were treacherous or strange.
During the Hóngzhì and Zhèngdé eras,
the literary style underwent a transformation.
Liú Zhōng,
courtesy name Sīzhí,
was from Chénliú.
He became a *jìnshì* in the fourteenth year of Chénghuà.
He was appointed a shùjíshì,
and then made a biānxiū.
In the fourth year of Hóngzhì,
after the Veritable Records of Emperor Xiànzōng were completed,
he was promoted to Shìjiǎng,
and served directly at the Jīngyán lectures.
Soon after, he also served as a lecturer for the crown prince (Shì Dōnggōng Jiǎngdú).
Nine more years later, he was promoted to Shìdú Xuéshì.
When Emperor Wǔzōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted from a palace official to Xuéshì,
presiding over the Hànlín Yuàn,
and still served directly at the Jīngyán lectures.
In the second year of Zhèngdé,
Liú Jǐn gained power,
daily leading the emperor into games,
disrupting the old regulations of the ancestors.
Zhōng memorialized on several matters, warning against excessive leisure and advocating for the promotion of orthodox learning.
Later,
during a Jīngyán lecture with Yáng Tínghé, he expounded on the classics,
admonishing the emperor for his shortcomings,
and particularly sharply criticized the recent favorites.
The emperor said to Jǐn:
"The Jīngyán
is for lecturing on books;
what are these empty words for?"
Jǐn had long resented the two men,
and consequently insinuated to Lìbù Shàngshū Xǔ Jìn to transfer them to Nánjīng.
In the various ministries in Nánjīng, there was only one Yòushìláng.
Jìn specifically requested to appoint Zhōng as Lǐbù Zuǒshìláng.
When the order was issued,
there was much public discussion.
Jìn was troubled by this,
and after barely two months,
he promoted Zhōng to Shàngshū of his own ministry.
That winter,
he was transferred to the Lìbù.
At that time, one imperial censor in the secondary capital
was notoriously arrogant and unruly,
and one Lángzhōng,
a favorite of Zhāng Cǎi,
upon completing his term,
both were assigned "inferior" evaluations.
He detested clerks who fraudulently registered names
and ordered all departments to verify and dismiss a thousand people.
In the Grand Review of capital officials,
more were dismissed than before.
He also memorialized, requesting untimely impeachments
to serve as encouragement and punishment,
without waiting for the six-year evaluation and dismissal.
An edict approved this.
Zhōng was upright and had a dignified demeanor in Nánjīng.
However, at that time,
Jǐn was severely humiliating literati and officials,
and Zhōng, in treating his subordinates, was strict according to rules,
and his impeachments were too severe.
Public opinion at the time therefore considered Zhōng to be colluding with Jǐn's intentions,
and much blame fell upon him.
In the second month of the fifth year, he was transferred to Lìbù Shàngshū, concurrent with Hànlín Xuéshì,
specifically in charge of drafting imperial edicts.
He submitted two memorials requesting retirement,
but they were not approved.
When Jǐn was executed,
Zhōng, in his original position, was made concurrent Wényuāngé Dàxuéshì,
entering the Grand Secretariat to participate in state affairs.
After only a few days, for his merit in pacifying Níngxià,
he was promoted to Shàofù, concurrent with Tàizǐ Tàifù.
According to custom,
it was unheard of for a Grand Secretary to be promoted so quickly to one of the Sāngū.
Zhōng, having gained this without merit,
felt uneasy,
and repeatedly submitted memorials to firmly decline,
but he was not permitted.
Although Jǐn had been executed,
Zhāng Yǒng, Wèi Bīn, and others usurped power,
and high officials again vied to curry favor with them.
Zhōng alone showed no such concern.
Yǒng once sent Liáo Péng to visit Zhōng,
but Zhōng's servants treated him poorly,
and he also rejected the gifts.
From then on, he was at odds with Yǒng and his group.
He submitted seven or eight memorials requesting retirement,
all of which were met with comforting retention.
The next year, he was appointed to oversee the metropolitan examination.
Immediately after it was finished,
the emperor, finding many errors in the literary style of the examination records,
summoned Lǐ Dōngyáng to show them to him.
Zhōng knew he was being impeached by palace eunuchs,
and requested to visit his ancestors' graves.
An edict allowed him to return by post carriage.
Upon arriving home,
he again memorialized to request retirement,
and the request was granted.
He was given a monthly stipend and annual servants for the rest of his life.
When Emperor Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was repeatedly recommended but did not return to office.
A xíngrén was dispatched to inquire after him,
and Zhōng submitted a memorial of thanks,
then offered advice.
The emperor praised his loyalty and love for the country.
In the second year of Jiājìng, he died
at the age of seventy-two.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tàibǎo,
and his posthumous name was Wénsù.
A eulogy says: Xú Pǔ [徐溥] was known for his broad-mindedness and magnanimity;
Qiū Jùn [丘濬] was renowned for his extensive learning.
Observing their pointed remarks and direct statements,
earnestly advocating measures to avert prosperity's peril and enlightened rule's decline,
they can be called diligent.
Liú Jiàn [劉健] and Xiè Qiān [謝遷] maintained proper conduct and spoke with integrity,
resolutely upholding their principles without selfish motives.
When eunuchs disrupted governance,
they steadfastly defended righteousness with remonstrance.
Though their aspirations were not fully realized,
their resolute and strict integrity remained unwavering from beginning to end.
Among the wise and capable chief ministers of the Míng dynasty,
apart from the Sān Yáng [三楊] (Three Yangs),
Péng [彭] and Shāng [商] were recognized earlier,
and Liú [劉] and Xiè [謝] were praised later.
They were perhaps those who served their sovereign with the Way.
Lǐ Dōngyáng [李東陽] incurred criticism for his equivocal stance,
yet the virtuous relied on him for support,
and what he preserved was not insignificant.
Ministers share the nation's fortunes;
it is not superior to simply resign,
nor purer to withdraw far away.
It depends on their true intentions.
Wáng Ào [王鏊] and Liú Zhōng [劉忠] upheld rectitude without bias,
and retired early to preserve themselves.
This indeed shows an understanding of when to serve and when to leave;
how could they possibly bend and bow to gain favor?
Collation Notes
Biographies Seventy: Wáng Shù [王恕] (son Chéngyù [承裕]), Mǎ Wénshēng [馬文升], Liú Dàxià [劉大夏]
Wáng Shù [王恕],
courtesy name Zōngguàn [宗貫],
a native of Sānyuán [三原].
He passed the imperial examination in the 13th year of Zhèngtǒng [正統] (1448).
From a Shùjíshì [庶吉士] (bachelor of the Hanlin Academy), he was appointed Left Judge of the Grand Court of Judicial Review (Dàlǐ Zuǒ Píngshì [大理左評事]),
then promoted to Left Vice-Minister (Zuǒ Sìfù [左寺副]).
He once presented six instances where punishments were inappropriate,
and all were deliberated and implemented.
He was transferred to be Prefect of Yángzhōu [揚州],
where he distributed grain to relieve famine without waiting for approval,
and established the Zīzhèng Shūyuàn [資政書院] (Zizheng Academy) to educate scholars.
In the 4th year of Tiānshùn [天順] (1460), for his excellent governance,
he was exceptionally promoted to Right Administration Commissioner of Jiāngxī [江西] (Jiāngxī Yòu Bùzhèngshǐ [江西右布政使]),
and pacified the bandits in Gànzhōu [贛州].
When Xiànzōng [憲宗] ascended the throne,
an imperial edict commanded high ministers to strictly scrutinize regional officials nationwide.
Consequently, thirteen people, including the Left Administration Commissioner of Hénán [河南], Hóu Chén [侯臣], were dismissed,
and Shù was appointed to replace Chén.
In the 1st year of Chénghuà [成化] (1465),
refugees in Nányáng [南陽], Jīng [荊], and Xiāng [襄] gathered and rebelled.
Shù was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief (Yòu Fù Dū Yùshǐ [右副都御史]) to pacify and govern them.
At that time, he was observing mourning for his mother,
but an imperial edict ordered him to return to duty after two months of mourning.
Shù declined,
but it was not permitted.
He collaborated with Minister of War Bái Guī [白圭] to suppress the great bandit Liú Tōng [劉通],
and subsequently attacked and defeated his confederate Shí Lóng [石龍].
He strictly restrained his subordinates from indiscriminate killing,
and the refugees returned to their occupations.
He was transferred to govern Hénán [河南].
For his merits,
he was promoted to Left Vice Censor-in-Chief (Zuǒ Fù Dū Yùshǐ [左副都御史]),
and later moved to be Right Vice Minister of Justice of Nánjīng [南京] (Nánjīng Xíngbù Yòu Shìláng [南京刑部右侍郎]).
After observing mourning for his father,
and completing the mourning period,
he was appointed concurrently as the original official to supervise river conservancy.
He dredged the Gāoyóu [高郵] and Shàobó [邵伯] lakes,
and repaired the four dams and sluices of Léigōng [雷公], Shàngxià Jùchéng [上下句城], and Chénggōng [陳公].
Due to natural disasters,
he requested discussions on disaster mitigation strategies.
The emperor then granted a one-year rent exemption for Shāndōng [山東],
and also greatly reduced and exempted taxes in Jīfǔ [畿輔] (the capital region).
He was soon transferred to be Left Vice Minister of Revenue of Nánjīng [南京] (Nánjīng Hùbù Zuǒ Shìláng [南京戶部左侍郎]).
In the 12th year (1476),
Grand Secretary Shāng Lù [商輅] and others argued that Yúnnán [雲南] was ten thousand li away,
controlling the various barbarians in the west,
and bordering Jiāozhǐ [交阯] (Annam) in the south,
and the garrison eunuch Qián Néng [錢能] was excessively greedy and arbitrary.
They proposed sending a high-ranking minister with prestige to serve as Grand Coordinator (Xúnfǔ [巡撫]) to suppress him.
Thus, Shù was reassigned as Left Vice Censor-in-Chief (Zuǒ Fù Dū Yùshǐ [左副都御史]) for this mission,
and immediately promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief (Yòu Dū Yùshǐ [右都御史]).
Initially,
Néng had dispatched Commander Guō Jǐng [郭景] to report to the capital,
claiming that Annamese soldiers pursuing bandits had crossed into Yúnnán [雲南] territory.
The emperor immediately ordered Jǐng to carry an imperial edict to warn and restrain them.
According to old regulations,
envoys to Annam had to pass through Guǎngxī [廣西],
but Jǐng went directly from Yúnnán [雲南].
Néng used Jǐng to send jade belts, precious girdles, python robes, and various rare treasures to King Lí Hào [黎灝] of Annam.
Hào dispatched generals and troops to escort Jǐng back,
intending to open the Yúnnán [雲南] route.
Jǐng, fearing future repercussions,
deceptively sent a message ahead to the border guards.
He then escaped and returned,
spreading rumors that Annamese invaders were coming,
causing the border officials to declare a state of emergency.
Mù Cóng [沐琮], Duke of Qiánguó [黔國公], sent someone to instruct their commander,
and only then did they retreat.
But the various officials feared Néng,
and concealed this incident without reporting it.
Néng also frequently dispatched Jǐng, Commander Lú Ān [盧安], Sū Běn [蘇本], and others to communicate with the indigenous officials of Gānyá [干崖] and Mèngmì [孟密],
receiving countless gold and treasures from them.
Shù thoroughly investigated and uncovered all of this.
He sent cavalry to arrest Jǐng,
who, fearing punishment, committed suicide.
Shù then impeached Néng for secretly communicating with a foreign country,
a crime punishable by death.
An imperial edict ordered Pān Fán [潘蕃], a director from the Ministry of Justice, to investigate.
Meanwhile, Néng
sent yellow parrots via courier.
Shù requested that this be forbidden,
and also fully exposed Néng's corrupt and tyrannical acts,
stating:
"In the past, Jiāozhǐ [交阯] was lost because the garrison commander was incompetent,
and the current situation is almost worse.
Why does Your Majesty spare one Néng,
and not secure the border region?"
Néng was greatly alarmed,
and urgently instructed powerful and close officials to request Shù's recall.
At that time, Shāng Lù [商輅], Xiàng Zhōng [項忠], and other righteous individuals had just been dismissed for opposing Wāng Zhí [汪直].
So Shù was reassigned to take charge of the Nánjīng Censorate (Nánjīng Dū Cháyuan [南京都察院]),
participating in and advising on defense matters.
Néng's case was immediately dropped,
and although Fán's investigation confirmed the facts,
it was left unaddressed.
Shù resided in Yúnnán [雲南] for nine months,
and his authority extended beyond the borders;
even the Duke of Qiánguó [黔國公] and others respectfully obeyed his orders.
He submitted a total of twenty memorials,
and his righteous reputation moved the entire country.
At that time,
Annam harbored a rebel from Jiāngxī [江西] named Wáng [王] as an advisor.
They secretly sent spies into Lín'ān [臨安],
and also cast weapons from copper bought in Méngzì [蒙自],
planning to seize an opportunity to attack Yúnnán [雲南].
Shù requested the addition of two Vice Commissioners (Fùshǐ [副使])
to strengthen border defenses,
and the plot was consequently thwarted.
After returning to Nánjīng [南京] for several months,
he was promoted to Minister of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū [兵部尚書]),
with his advisory role unchanged.
When selecting officials,
he strictly rejected all requests for favoritism,
which displeased his colleagues.
Meanwhile, Qián Néng [錢能] returned [to the capital]
and repeatedly slandered Shù to the emperor.
The emperor also held a grudge against Shù for his frequent direct remonstrances,
and thus ordered him to concurrently serve as Right Vice Censor-in-Chief (Yòu Fù Dū Yùshǐ [右副都御史]) and Grand Coordinator of Nánjī [南畿] (the Southern Metropolitan Region).
According to old regulations,
official lands in Yìngtiān [應天], Zhènjiāng [鎮江], Tàipíng [太平], Níngguó [寧國], and Guǎngdé [廣德] paid half rent,
while private lands were completely exempt.
Later,
private lands largely fell into the hands of powerful families, while official lands burdened the poor.
Shù then moderately reduced the wastage on official lands,
and slightly increased the tax on private lands.
Chángzhōu [常州] sometimes had surplus rice,
so he memorialized to use sixty thousand shí [石] (dan) to supplement the summer tax,
and also to supplement six million guàn [貫] of household salt certificates for other prefectures,
which benefited both public and private sectors.
When his jurisdiction suffered from floods,
he requested an exemption of over six hundred thousand shí [石] (dan) of autumn grain.
He extensively provided relief loans,
saving over two million lives.
Jiāngnán [江南] annually supplied white rice,
often causing people to go bankrupt,
but the Guānglù [光祿] (Court of Imperial Entertainments) generally distributed it to cooks and common laborers.
Furthermore, eunuchs were tyrannical and arrogant;
when tribute goods were sent from various regions,
the inspecting officials often demanded extra for themselves.
Those who wove silk and embroidered colors, or collected flowers, plants, and birds,
were constantly on the roads.
Shù repeatedly memorialized about these matters,
but none of his suggestions were accepted.
The eunuch Wáng Jìng (王敬), collaborating with the sorcerer-commander Wáng Chén (王臣), traveled south to collect medicinal herbs and rare treasures.
Wherever they went, there was great disturbance,
and many chief officials were humiliated.
When they reached Sūzhōu (蘇州),
they summoned scholars to write an evil book,
which caused a great uproar among the scholars.
Wáng Jìng (王敬) reported the scholars for defying orders.
Shù (恕) immediately submitted a memorial, stating:
“In these dire times,
it would be appropriate to send envoys to provide relief,
yet instead, prized possessions are being wantonly extorted.
In the past, Emperor Tài (太) of Táng (唐) hinted for Liángzhōu (梁州) to present a famous eagle,
and Emperor Míng (明) ordered Yìzhōu (益州) to weave half-sleeved jackets
and present objects like Pípá (琵琶) plectrums and carved ivory boxes.
Lǐ Dàliàng (李大亮) and Sū Tǐng (蘇頲) did not obey the imperial edicts.
Although I am unworthy,
I admire these men.”
He then fully listed Wáng Jìng’s (王敬) and others’ crimes.
Wáng Jìng (王敬) also falsely accused Shù (恕) and implicating Sūn Rén (孫仁), the Prefect of Chángzhōu (常州).
Sūn Rén (孫仁) was arrested.
Sūn Rén (孫仁),
a native of Xīngàn (新淦),
had risen through the ranks from *jìnshì* (進士) to Prefect.
He was a man of stern integrity,
and when Wáng Jìng (王敬) arrived, Sūn Rén (孫仁) did not treat him with courtesy,
which caused offense.
Shù (恕) submitted a strong memorial to save him,
and three memorials impeaching Wáng Jìng (王敬).
It happened that the eunuch Shàng Míng (尚銘) also exposed Wáng Jìng’s (王敬) misdeeds,
so Wáng Jìng (王敬) and his accomplices were imprisoned,
nineteen of his followers were exiled to the frontier,
and Wáng Chén (王臣) was executed in the marketplace,
his head sent to Nánjīng (南京).
Sūn Rén (孫仁) was also released and returned home.
Later, he accumulated official posts, eventually becoming the Right Vice Censor-in-Chief for the Grand Coordinator of Níngxià (寧夏).
Twenty years later, Shù (恕) was again appointed Minister of War for Nánjīng (南京).
At that time, Qián Néng (錢能) was also the Garrison Commander of Nánjīng (南京).
He told people:
“Lord Wáng (王),
is a heavenly man;
I simply serve him with reverence.”
Shù (恕) treated him with an open mind,
and Qián Néng (錢能) eventually restrained himself.
When Lín Jùn (林俊) was imprisoned,
Shù (恕) said:
“There is only one altar for Heaven and Earth,
only one ancestral temple for the ancestors,
yet there are over a thousand Buddhist temples.
For every temple established,
hundreds of families are displaced,
and hundreds of thousands from the imperial treasury are spent.
This is wrong.
Lín Jùn’s (林俊) words are appropriate;
he should not be punished.”
The Emperor was displeased upon reading the memorial.
Shù (恕) spoke frankly and without the slightest hesitation.
He responded to imperial requests for advice twenty-one times,
and submitted thirty-nine memorials,
all of which forcefully opposed powerful favorites.
The world admired him wholeheartedly.
Whenever there was an improper matter at court,
people would surely say,
“Why does Lord Wáng (王) not speak?”
Then they would also say,
“His memorial will arrive soon.”
Indeed,
Shù’s (恕) memorial would soon arrive.
At that time, a popular rhyme went:
“In the Twelve Ministries of the Two Capitals,
there is only one Wáng Shù (王恕).”
Because of this, all the high-ranking and close officials regarded him askance,
and the Emperor was also quite annoyed by him.
In the twenty-second year, *chuánfèng* (傳奉) officials were appointed,
and Shù (恕)’s remonstrance was particularly strong,
which further displeased the Emperor.
Shù (恕) had previously been granted the title of Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
When the Vice Minister of War for Nánjīng (南京), Mǎ Xiǎn (馬顯), requested to retire,
an imperial rescript was suddenly appended, removing Shù’s (恕) *gōngbǎo* (宮保) title and ordering his retirement.
The court and the populace were greatly alarmed.
Shù (恕) had frequently served as a Grand Coordinator,
and risen from Vice Minister to Minister,
all in the auxiliary capital.
Because he was fond of speaking frankly,
he never managed to serve in the central court.
After he returned home,
his reputation grew even higher,
and there was no month without recommendations from the Censorate and ministries.
Wáng Chún (王純) of Xiānjū (仙居), a principal secretary in the Ministry of Works, compared Shù (恕) to Jí Àn (汲黯),
for which he was beaten with a staff
and demoted to judicial assistant in Sīnán (思南).
When Emperor Xiàozōng (孝宗) ascended the throne,
he began to act on the recommendations of court officials,
summoning Shù (恕) to serve as Minister of Personnel,
and soon after adding the title of Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
Before this,
those inside and outside the court who impeached Grand Secretary Liú Jí (劉吉),
would invariably recommend Shù (恕).
Liú Jí (劉吉) was greatly resentful because of this.
Whatever Shù (恕) recommended,
Liú Jí (劉吉) would secretly obstruct it.
In the intercalary first month of the first year of Hóngzhì (弘治),
remonstrating officials impeached thirty-seven individuals, including Sòng Mín (宋旻), the Grand Governor of Liǎngguǎng (兩廣), and Qiū Nài (丘鼐), the Grand Governor of Grain Transport,
suggesting their demotion or dismissal.
Many among them were well-regarded at the time.
Liú Jí (劉吉) actually obtained an imperial edict to approve their dismissal,
and the document did not go through the Ministry of Personnel.
Shù (恕), feeling that his duties were being circumvented,
submitted a memorial requesting to resign,
but it was not granted.
When there was a vacancy for the Grand Coordinator of Shǎnxī (陝西),
Shù (恕) recommended Xiāo Zhēn (蕭禎), the Provincial Administration Commissioner of Hénán (河南).
An edict ordered other recommendations,
but Shù (恕) insisted in his memorial, saying:
“Your Majesty, not deeming me unworthy,
has entrusted me with the Ministry of Personnel.
If those I recommend are ineffective,
that is my crime.
Now, how can Your Majesty know that Xiāo Zhēn (蕭禎) is untalented and reject him?
This must be due to the preference of close attendants on your left and right.
I cannot anticipate your inclinations
to secure my salary and position.
Furthermore, if Your Majesty deems Xiāo Zhēn (蕭禎) unusable,
it means I am unusable.
I beg to retire.”
The Emperor then finally appointed Xiāo Zhēn (蕭禎).
At that time, many remonstrating officials praised Shù (恕) as wise and old,
suggesting he should not hold a demanding position,
but rather be placed in the Grand Secretariat to participate in major policy decisions.
Finally,
the Nanjing Censor Wú Tài (吳泰) and others reiterated this.
The Emperor said:
“I followed the precedents of Jiǎn Yì (蹇義) and Wáng Zhí (王直),
and appointed Shù (恕) to the Ministry of Personnel.
I have always listened to his advice and deliberations.
Why must he be in the Grand Secretariat?”
Shù (恕) once attended the imperial lectures (*jīngyán*),
and seeing the Emperor distressed by the summer heat,
requested that according to precedent, lectures be temporarily suspended during extreme heat and cold,
and that the lecture notes still be delivered to the palace.
The *jìnshì* (進士) Dǒng Jié (董傑), Censor Tāng Nài (湯鼐), and Supervising Secretary Hán Chóng (韓重) and others then jointly submitted memorials to dispute and refute him.
Shù (恕) requested punishment and to be relieved of his duties,
but the Emperor graciously refused.
Shù (恕) submitted another memorial, stating:
“Having received the profound grace of the nation,
I constantly think of how to repay it.
People see Your Majesty entrusting me with too heavy a responsibility,
and thus expect too much from me,
wishing me to completely reform court administration,
following the precedent of Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光) of Sòng (宋).
Not to mention that my talent is far inferior to Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光)’s,
even now, it is not the Yuányòu (元祐) period.
Moreover, the six ministers have divided responsibilities,
each with their own duties;
how dare I overstep and deliberate on them?
However, Dǒng Jié (董傑) and others’ criticism of me is correct;
I cannot escape the blame.
I only beg to be allowed to return home.”
The Emperor again graciously urged him to stay.
Shù (恕), moved by the Emperor’s favor,
further dedicated himself to state affairs.
While on sick leave,
he heard that the Emperor was promoting eunuchs,
some even being granted python robes and estates,
and he submitted a strong remonstrance.
The eunuch Huáng Shùn (黃順) requested that the artisan official Pān Jùn (潘俊) be reinstated for service.
Shù (恕) argued that a minor official should not be allowed to undermine important laws.
He insisted again,
but the request was eventually granted.
As Liú Jí (劉吉) resented Shù (恕),

and Shù (恕) again strongly defended Liú Gài (劉㮣), the Prefect of Shòuzhōu (壽州), who had been framed by Liú Jí (劉吉), as well as remonstrating officials Zhōu Hóng (周紘), Zhāng Bǐng (張昺), Tāng Nài (湯鼐), Jiāng Wǎn (姜綰), and others,
Liú Jí (劉吉) grew even more hateful,
and conspired with his cronies like Wèi Zhāng (魏璋) to collectively ostracize him.
Shù (恕) had previously recommended and appointed Luó Míng (羅明), Xióng Huái (熊懷), Qiáng Zhēn (強珍), Chén Shòu (陳壽), Qiū Nài (丘鼐), Bái Sīmíng (白思明), and others.
Liú Jí (劉吉) and Wèi Zhāng (魏璋) then instigated others to impeach them.
Shù (恕), knowing his will could not be carried out,
repeatedly submitted memorials requesting to resign.
The Emperor always consoled him and urged him to stay,
and due to his old age, specifically exempted him from the afternoon audience.
During heavy winds, rain, or snow, he was also exempted from the morning audience.
Huīwáng saw Péi ask for the return of his Dēzhōu fields,
and an imperial edict had been issued.
Shù said that princes are close relatives of the imperial family,
and should not contend for an inch of land,
causing common people to lose their livelihoods.
The Emperor politely declined and reported this.
When the Lúgōuqiáo Bridge was completed,
the eunuch Lǐ Xìng requested promotions for Pān Jùn and other officials, such as Vice-Commissioner of Wénsīyuàn.
Shù said:
"Construction is a regular duty;
how can it merit rewards?
This only started in the late Chénghuà period.
Your Majesty, during your initial reign, you fortunately abolished and eliminated this practice.
Why should it be revived?
Furthermore, no promotions have been heard of for the great work on the imperial mausoleum.
If they were to cite this as a precedent and request promotions,
how would we refuse them?"
The Emperor accepted his words.
Later,
when the capital's river bridges were repaired,
the Emperor again granted Xìng's request to confer offices on four people,
and permitted five people to wear official caps and belts.
Shù strongly remonstrated,
but was not heeded.
He again submitted a memorial, arguing:
"Your minister is in charge of official selections and appointments;
it is his duty to speak fully.
But a second memorial has failed to move the imperial ear,
believing that what has been promised cannot be changed.
However, matters should be handled appropriately.
If something is inappropriate,
what harm is there in changing it ten times?
Otherwise,
the resulting abuses will become irremediable."
This was reported to the Emperor.
Before and after this, he enumerated seven matters concerning calamities and anomalies,
and presented twenty matters regarding celestial changes,
all sharply addressing current abuses.
Shòuníng Bó Zhāng Luán requested a title of merit and a deed of enfeoffment.
Shù said:
"Empress Dowagers Qián and Wáng reigned in the inner palace for several decades,
and it was only then that Qián Céngzōng and Wáng Yuán received noble titles.
Now the Empress has only been enthroned for three years,
and Luán is already a Count.
Such a hasty request
would compromise the imperial virtue,
and should not be granted."
Gāo Lù, a Registrar of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
was Luán's brother-in-law.
He was unduly promoted to Consultative Official of his department.
Shù said:
"The offices of the empire are for the scholars of the empire.
Do not privatize them for powerful relatives and
hinder public fairness."
An imperial decree directly appointed Xu Shēng, a third-class imperial physician, as a supernumerary Court Administrator,
but Shù requested that only those with top evaluations be selected.
His request was not accepted.
Dù Chāng and others, Palace Secretaries of Wénhuádiàn, were promoted through personal connections.
Imperial physician Wáng Yù petitioned for a promotion himself.
Shù vigorously argued against all these, causing them to be rejected.
At this time, Liú Jí had already been dismissed,
and Qiū Jùn entered the Grand Secretariat.
He also could not get along with Shù.
Initially,
Jùn, as Minister of Rites, concurrently served as Grand Tutor to the Heir Apparent,
and he and Shù both held the title of Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince.
Shù, as the senior of the Six Ministries,
outranked Jùn.
When Jùn entered the Grand Secretariat,
Shù did not yield to him as Minister of Personnel,
which displeased Jùn.
Shù conducted evaluations of all civil officials in the empire,
and Jùn intervened to retain over ninety people whom Shù had already dismissed.
Shù repeatedly argued but could not succeed,
and thus strongly requested to be dismissed,
but was not permitted.
Liú Wéntài, an administrator of the Imperial Academy of Medicine,
had frequently visited Jùn's home to seek promotion,
but was thwarted by Shù.
He harbored great resentment against Shù.
While Shù was living in his hometown,
he once asked someone to write his biography,
which was engraved and circulated.
Jùn said that this was an attempt to gain fame by slandering the emperor,
and that if the emperor heard of it, the crime would be considerable.
Wéntài's heart was moved,
so he drafted a memorial himself,
and showed it to Wú Zhēn, a dismissed Censor-in-Chief, to polish it.
It accused Shù of distorting the selection laws,
and claimed that in his biography, he compared himself to Yī Yǐn and Zhōu Gōng,
and regarding memorials that were withheld,
he generally said they were not responded to,
to highlight the former emperor's refusal of remonstrance,
showing no proper deference as a subject,
intending to embroil him in a grave misfortune.
Shù, believing the memorial came from Jùn's instigation,
argued strongly:
"My biography was written in the 20th year of Chénghuà,
and I retired from office in the 22nd year.
It was not to seek favor from the former emperor.
Furthermore, what is recorded in the biography
all serves to manifest the former emperor's virtue in accepting remonstrance;
how can it be called highlighting his faults?
Wéntài is a scoundrel;
this must be orchestrated by an old hand in literature with many dark schemes."
The Emperor sent Wéntài to the Jǐnyīyù prison,
and an investigation confirmed the facts.
He then requested to summon Jùn, Shù, and Zhēn for a confrontation.
The Emperor was displeased with Shù,
so he demoted Wéntài to imperial physician,
reprimanded Shù for seeking fame,
ordered the burning of his engraved blocks,
and left Jùn unquestioned.
Shù submitted another memorial requesting clarification and resolution,
but it was not accepted,
so he vigorously sought to resign.
He was allowed to return home by imperial post-horse,
but was not granted an imperial edict,
and his monthly stipend and annual servants were also significantly reduced.
Court opinion at the time held that Jùn was in the wrong.
When Jùn died,
Wéntài went to offer condolences,
but Jùn's wife yelled at him to leave, saying:
"Because of you,
my husband maligned Lord Wáng,
and bore the name of injustice.
What are you doing here to offer condolences!"
Shù served in various posts both inside and outside the capital for over forty years,
being upright, strict, and
consistent from beginning to end.
Those he recommended, such as Gěng Yù, Péng Sháo, Hé Qiáoxīn, Zhōu Jīng, Lǐ Mǐn, Zhāng Yuè, Ní Yuè, Liú Dàxià, Dài Shān, and Zhāng Mào,
were all renowned officials of their time.
For other worthy talents long neglected in obscurity,
he feared being late in promoting them.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
many upright officials filled the court,
and official duties were well managed.
The period was known for its great prosperity,
which was due to Shù's efforts.
When Wǔzōng ascended the throne,
he sent an imperial envoy with an edict to inquire about his well-being,
bringing sheep and wine,
and increasing his stipend and servants.
He also instructed him to speak candidly without reservation.
Shù presented several major national policies,
and the Emperor replied with a gracious edict.
He died in the fourth month of the third year of Zhèngdé,
at the age of ninety-three.
Normally, he ate enough for two people,
but on the day of his death, he ate slightly less.
He sat alone with his door closed,
when suddenly there was a sound like thunder,
and white mist diffused around him.
When they looked, he had passed away.
Upon hearing the news of his death,
the court suspended its sessions.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Grand Master of the Imperial Household, Grand Pillar of State, Grand Preceptor,
and given the posthumous name Duānyì.
He had five sons and thirteen grandsons,
many of whom were virtuous and prominent.
His youngest son, Chéngyù,
styled Tiānyǔ.
At seven, he could compose poetry,
and at twenty, he authored an explanation of the Diagrams of Tài Jí Movement and Stillness.
When Shù was Minister of Personnel,
he ordered Chéngyù to receive guests daily.
Through this, he came to know all the worthy talents in the empire,
and his selections and appointments were always appropriate.
He passed the imperial examination as a *jìnshì* in the sixth year of Hóngzhì.
When Shù retired from office,
Chéngyù immediately resigned to attend to his father.
He was appointed as Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of War,
and later dispatched to manage the military agricultural colonies in Shāndōng and Hénán.
He reduced the grain quotas for Dēngzhōu and Láizhōu,
collecting one *dòu* per three *mǔ*,
and returned over 360 *qǐng* of military land in Qīngzhōu and Zhāngdé that had been previously granted to princely estates.
When Wǔzōng ascended the throne,
he was repeatedly promoted to Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Personnel.
He offended Liú Jǐn with his remonstrances,
and was penalized by being forced to transport grain to the frontier.
He was again promoted to Minister of the Imperial Stud.
In the sixth year of Jiājìng, he eventually rose to the rank of Minister of Revenue in Nánjīng.
He cleared 1.7 million *shí* of outstanding taxes
and accumulated 48,000 *liǎng* of surplus silver.
The Emperor personally wrote
"Clear, fair, and upright"
to commend him.
After three years in the ministry,
he retired from office
and died.
He was posthumously granted the title of Junior Guardian of the Crown Prince
and given the posthumous name Kāngxī.
Mǎ Wénshēng,
courtesy name Fùtú,
was a native of Jūnzhōu.
He had a striking appearance and great strength.
He passed the imperial examination in Jǐngtài second year (1451) to become a *Jìnshì*,
and was appointed Censor.
He successively served as inspecting censor in Shānxī and Húguǎng,
and his integrity and principles were widely known.
He returned to lead the compilation of memorials from various circuits.
After the mourning period for his mother,
he was exceptionally promoted to Fujian Provincial Surveillance Commissioner.
In the early Chénghuà reign,
he was summoned to serve as Nánjīng Grand Judge,
but returned home due to his father's death.
During the rebellion of Mǎnsì,
Chén Jiè, the Grand Coordinator of Shǎnxī, was imprisoned.
Mǎ Wénshēng was immediately called from home and appointed Right Vice Censor-in-Chief to replace Chén Jiè.
He rode swiftly to the army
and collaborated with Commander-in-Chief Xiàng Zhōng to suppress the rebellion.
The details are found in Xiàng Zhōng's biography.
For his meritorious service, he was promoted to Left Vice Censor-in-Chief,
and continued as Grand Coordinator.
Mǎ Wénshēng frequently submitted memorials on opportune measures,
focusing on selecting generals and training troops,
repairing the border defense camps up to the Tiěbiānchéng beacon towers,
and eliminating notorious bandits.
He completely annihilated the Xīgù barbarian tribes who refused to submit immediately.
He reformed the tea policy,
exchanging over eight thousand barbarian horses
to supply the soldiers.
He relieved the famine victims in Gǒngchāng and Líntáo
and pacified the displaced people.
His achievements were very notable.
At that time,
Bólúohū, Mǎndūlǔ, and Biéjiāsīlán raided the border year after year.
Mǎ Wénshēng requested to station troops in Wéizhōu,
and set up ambushes in various forts to await them.
Consequently, he defeated the invaders at Hēishuǐkǒu,
capturing their *Píngzhāng* Diélièsūn,
and then defeated them again at Tāngyánglǐng,
beheading two hundred.
He named the ridge
"Déshèngpō" (Victory Slope),
and had a stone tablet inscribed to commemorate it before returning.
Mǎ Wénshēng's military achievements were very significant,
but his reports of victory were not exaggerated,
nor was there anyone within the court to advocate for him,
hence his rewards were meager.
In the winter of the ninth year (1473),
Grand Commander Wáng Yuè reported a great victory,
and Mǎ Wénshēng also sent his son Xiù to report his merits.
However, court officials investigated and reported that it was not true,
and he was punished with a three-month suspension of salary.
In the spring of the eleventh year (1475),
he replaced Wáng Yuè as Grand Commander of the three border military affairs,
and soon after, he was appointed Right Vice Minister of War.
In August of the following year, he was appointed to rectify military affairs in Liáodōng.
The Grand Coordinator Chén Yuè was greedy and cunning;
whenever soldiers had a minor transgression, he would fine them horses,
causing horse prices to soar.
Mǎ Wénshēng presented fifteen border strategies,
and thereupon requested to prohibit this practice,
which caused Chén Yuè to resent Mǎ Wénshēng.
Mǎ Wénshēng returned to the ministry and was transferred to Left Vice Minister.
In the spring of the fourteenth year (1478),
Chén Yuè provoked a mutiny by falsely claiming credit for a massacre.
The eunuch Wāng Zhí wanted to go in person to pacify it.
The Emperor ordered the Director of Ceremonial Húai Ēn and seven others to meet with the Ministry of War in the Grand Secretariat to discuss.
Húai Ēn wanted to send a high minister to pacify,
to thwart Wāng Zhí's plan.
Mǎ Wénshēng quickly responded,
"Excellent."
Húai Ēn reported this to the Emperor,
and the Emperor immediately ordered Mǎ Wénshēng to go.
Wāng Zhí was displeased
and wanted his confidant Wáng Yīng to accompany him,
but Mǎ Wénshēng politely refused.
He rode swiftly to the garrison,
proclaimed the imperial edict to pacify and comfort,
and all submitted to his pacification.
He also requested that over ten people who had lost their official seals and edicts due to Yěxiān's rebellion
be allowed to resume their official positions.
When the matter was settled,
Wāng Zhí wanted to claim the credit,
so he requested the Emperor
and, taking Wáng Yīng with him, rode to Kāiyuán,
and issued another order for recruitment and pacification.
Mǎ Wénshēng then attributed the credit to Wāng Zhí,
but Wāng Zhí was inwardly ashamed.
Mǎ Wénshēng also treated Wāng Zhí with equal courtesy,
and treated his retinue as servants,
which made Wāng Zhí even more displeased.
Meanwhile, Chén Yuè increasingly flattered Wāng Zhí,
gaining Wāng Zhí's favor,
and slandered Mǎ Wénshēng day and night,
seeking an opportunity to incriminate him.
Upon Mǎ Wénshēng's return,
he was awarded wine and meat.
In the spring of the following year,
due to repeated failures in Liáodōng,
Wāng Zhí was sent with Marquis Dìngxī Jiǎng Wǎn, Minister Lín Cōng, and others to investigate.
At this time, Yú Zǐjùn impeached Chén Yuè,
who suspected it was Mǎ Wénshēng's idea,
and intensified his efforts to ruin him.
Wāng Zhí then reported that Mǎ Wénshēng's actions were misguided,
prohibiting border people from trading agricultural tools,
which led to resentment and rebellion.
Thereupon, Mǎ Wénshēng was put into the imperial prison
and demoted to garrison duty in Chóngqìng Guard.
After Wāng Zhí had ruined Mǎ Wénshēng,
he and Chén Yuè massively mobilized troops to seek merit,
and Chén Yuè was thus rapidly promoted to Minister.
In the nineteenth year (1483),
Wāng Zhí fell from power,
and Mǎ Wénshēng was reinstated to office.
The following year, he was appointed Left Vice Censor-in-Chief and Grand Coordinator of Liáodōng.
Mǎ Wénshēng served in Liáo three times in total,
and the soldiers and civilians rejoiced whenever they heard of his arrival.
He further suppressed eunuchs and regional commanders,
preventing them from exploiting the people,
which made the populace even happier.
In the twenty-first year (1485), he was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief,
and Grand Coordinator of Grain Transport.
When Huái, Xú, and Hé suffered from famine,
he transferred one hundred thousand *shí* of grain from Jiāngnán and fifty thousand *liǎng* of salt tax silver to relieve them.
In the winter of that year,
he was summoned to serve as Minister of War.
The following year,
due to Lǐ Zīxǐng's slander,
he was transferred to Nánjīng.
When Emperor Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
he summoned and appointed him Left Censor-in-Chief.
In the first year of Hóngzhì (1488), he memorialized:
"During Emperor Xiànzōng's reign,
in the temples of the Five Sacred Mountains and Four Seas,
following the words of Daoist practitioners, stone caskets were placed,
surrounded by talismans,
containing Daoist scriptures written in gold, gold and silver coins, precious stones, and five grains as apotropaic objects.
They should be destroyed."
This was approved.
He also memorialized on fifteen other matters,
all of which were deliberated and implemented.
When the Emperor plowed the sacred field,
the Imperial Music Bureau presented variety shows.
Mǎ Wénshēng sternly said:
"The new Son of Heaven should be made aware of the hardships of farming;
what is this for?"
He immediately dismissed them.
Censors Xú Mào and Hè Lín were imprisoned for failing to comply with an imperial decree.
Mǎ Wénshēng argued that in the early days of a new reign, speaking officials should not be lightly punished,
and they were subsequently released.
Soon after, he was ordered to oversee the Twelve Training Divisions.
The following year,
he replaced Yú Zǐjùn as Minister of War,
and continued to oversee the training divisions as before.
After a long period of peace,
military administration became neglected,
and northwestern tribes occasionally threatened the border.
Mǎ Wénshēng strictly investigated the various generals and officers,
dismissing over thirty who were greedy or cowardly.
Corrupt individuals greatly resented him,
waiting outside his gate at night with bows and arrows,
or making slanderous writings and shooting them inside the Dōngcháng'ānmén.
When the Emperor heard,
he issued an edict for the Imperial Bodyguard to arrest them,
and assigned twelve riders
to escort Mǎ Wénshēng on his comings and goings.
Mǎ Wénshēng requested retirement,
but an imperial decree graciously denied it.
Xiǎowángzǐ (Little Prince) with tens of thousands of cavalry grazed below the Dàtóng border,
a formidable force.
Mǎ Wénshēng was on leave due to illness,
so the Emperor sent a eunuch with a physician to visit him,
and inquire about his strategy.
Mǎ Wénshēng said that the enemy had recently been defeated by another tribe
and was incapable of much.
He suggested secretly preparing defenses,
and then making a show of force to pressure them,
and they would surely retreat.
It turned out to be so.
He then suffered the mourning for his stepmother,
but an imperial edict ordered his recall to office.
He memorialized twice to decline,
but it was not permitted.
A separate northwestern tribe, Yěmièkèlì,
whose chiefs were named Yìlàsī Wáng,
Mǎnggē Wáng,
and Yìlàyīn Wáng,
each sent envoys to approach the Sùzhōu border,
requesting tribute and mutual trade.
Grand Coordinator Xǔ Jìn and Commander-in-Chief Liú Níng pleaded on their behalf,
but Mǎ Wénshēng said that mutual trade could be allowed,
but tribute could not,
and thus rejected it.
Tǔlǔfān, having already taken and captured Shǎnbā,
ordered Yálán to hold Hāmì,
usurping the title of Kèhán.
He then invaded Shāzhōu
and forced the various tribes of Hǎndōng to submit to him.
Wénshēng deliberated,
"This bandit is arrogant and unruly.
If we don't deal him a great blow, he will never know fear.
It is fitting to use the story of Hàn's Chén Tāng to launch a surprise attack and behead him."
He observed that Commander Yáng Zhù was familiar with the local customs [fānqíng],
and summoned him to inquire about a strategy.
Zhù fully detailed the route from Hǎndōng to Hāmì,
requesting that 3,000 Hǎndōng soldiers be dispatched as the vanguard,
followed by 3,000 Hàn soldiers.
Carrying several days' provisions,
they would advance quickly by secret paths,
and success could be achieved.
Wénshēng was delighted
and subsequently requested it from the Emperor.
An imperial edict ordered the dispatch of troops from Hǎndōng, Chìjīn, and Hāmì,
with Vice General Páng Qīng leading them,
subordinate to Governor Xǔ Jìn, to suppress them.
They indeed succeeded,
the details of which are in Xǔ Jìn's biography.
The troops of the military camps were insufficient,
so he requested that selections be made from the Jǐnyī Guard and the Four Guards of Téngxiáng to replenish them.
The request had already been granted,
but Eunuch Níng Jǐn obstructed it.
Wénshēng and Bīngkē's Wèi Chūn and others stated that imperial decrees should be honored,
but their advice was not accepted.
Shǎnxī experienced a great earthquake.
Wénshēng said:
"This is an omen of foreign invaders.
Now, Huǒshāi is acting aggressively,
while within the country the people are distressed and resources exhausted,
and generals are weak and soldiers are feeble.
It is advisable to implement benevolent governance to nurture the people,
and practice military preparedness to solidify our defenses.
Economize on expenditures,
halt Daoist rituals,
stop the proliferation of redundant officials appointed by imperial decree,
forbid requests for unoccupied land,
and hold two court sessions daily
to diligently attend to state affairs.
Furthermore, recall the eunuchs in charge of textile production in Shǎnxī,
and provide relief to the families affected by disaster."
The Emperor accepted his words,
and the eunuchs were immediately recalled.
Wénshēng served in the Ministry of War for thirteen years,
devoting himself to military affairs.
He repeatedly submitted proposals on land reclamation for military colonies, horse administration, border defense, and fortifications.
Regarding matters of state that ought to be discussed,
even if they were not his direct responsibility,
he always spoke without reservation.
He once noted that the Crown Prince was already four years old
and should be educated early.
He requested that a virtuous, cautious, experienced, and knowledgeable scholar of history, like Wèi Shèng's Madame Yáng,
be chosen to nurse and assist him,
guiding him in all his words and actions towards correctness.
He also suggested that the Crown Prince should not witness
private banquets in the inner court,
performances by the Ministry of Bells and Drums,
the Lantern Festival's turtle mountains,
or Dragon Boat Festival races and other such entertainment.
As for Buddhist and Daoist teachings,
they should be especially prohibited,
lest they confuse his mind.
Shāndōng had suffered a long drought,
and Zhèjiāng and Nánjī were afflicted by floods.
Wénshēng requested that the relevant authorities provide relief
and train soldiers for unforeseen circumstances.
The Emperor deeply accepted all of his proposals.
The people were suffering from heavy taxes and corvée labor.
Wénshēng thoroughly explained their harms,
saying:
"Now, the people's land is taxed four or five tenths.
For those who transport grain to the frontier, one *shí* of grain costs more than one *liǎng* of silver,
and in a good year, eight or nine *shí* of grain are exchanged for only one *liǎng*.
As for silk, cotton, and cloth transported to the capital,
the cost of delivery exceeds the value of the goods.
In the south, transportation to Tōngzhōu sometimes means that three or four *shí* of goods result in only one *shí* reaching its destination.
In the central plains, fifty or sixty thousand people are conscripted annually for river management.
In Shāndōng and Hénán, the repair of breached dikes requires no fewer than two hundred thousand laborers.
Water management in Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng is similar.
In Húguǎng, the construction of the four princely mansions for Jí, Xīng, Qí, and Yōng,
and in Jiāngxī, the two mansions for Yì and Shòu,
and in Shāndōng, the Hénɡ Mansion,
altogether involve no less than a million laborers.
The conscripted laborers and provisions for the princely states also amount to four hundred thousand.
Furthermore, in Húguǎng, there are campaigns against indigenous tribes,
and in Shānxi and Shǎnxī, border defenses,
and those who supply provisions and logistics for the army are innumerable.
Never have taxes been so heavy and corvée duties so numerous as at this time.
It is advisable to strictly order all internal and external offices
to reduce unnecessary expenses,
alleviate corvée labor,
and not arbitrarily impose levies.
The construction of princely mansions should be completed quickly,
so that the exhausted people may find some relief.
I further implore Your Majesty to uphold orthodox learning
and suppress heterodox practices
to purify the sacred heart;
to economize on expenditures
and reduce construction projects
to strengthen the foundation of the nation."
An imperial edict was issued for the relevant authorities to deliberate.
His other memorials and arguments were numerous.
Among the court officials, he was the most respected elder,
and the Emperor also trusted him wholeheartedly.
From Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince, he was repeatedly promoted to Junior Guardian and concurrent Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince.
His annual gifts and rewards
were beyond the aspirations of other high officials.
When Minister of Personnel Tú Yǒng was dismissed,
Wénshēng was nominated by court recommendation.
Censor Wèi Yīng and others stated that the Ministry of War could not do without Wénshēng,
and the Emperor agreed.
Thus, Ní Yuè was appointed to replace Tú Yǒng,
and Wénshēng was given the title of Junior Tutor to appease him.
When Ní Yuè died,
Wénshēng was appointed to replace him.
Nánjīng and Fèngyáng experienced strong winds and rain that destroyed houses and uprooted trees.
Wénshēng requested the Emperor to reduce meals and halt music,
cultivate virtue and reflect on transgressions,
attend the imperial lectures,
cease pleasure outings,
suspend non-urgent matters,
stop extra textile production,
provide relief to the famine victims,
and apprehend bandits.
Later,
he also submitted ten proposals concerning the duties of the Ministry of Personnel.
The Emperor praised and accepted all of them.
After nine years in a first-rank position,
he was promoted to Junior Mentor and concurrent Grand Mentor of the Crown Prince.
The Emperor, intending to conduct an evaluation,
specifically summoned Wénshēng, Grand Censor Dài Shān, and Shǐ Lín to the Nuǎn Pavilion,
instructing them to uphold impartiality in promotions and demotions.
Also, because Wénshēng was old and hard of hearing,
he called out to him twice,
ordering his attendants to help him down the steps.
Initially, when Wénshēng was Grand Censor,
Wáng Shù was in the Ministry of Personnel.
Both were known for their integrity in handling national affairs.
Their memorials were published
and widely read throughout the realm.
After Wáng Shù departed,
all expectations fell upon Wénshēng.
By the time he became Minister of Personnel,
he was already eighty years old.
With a long beard and eyebrows,
he spoke with unwavering confidence and showed no signs of decline when dealing with affairs.
After Emperor Xiàozōng passed away,
