Wénshēng, acting on the imperial will, requested the dismissal of 763 officials appointed by imperial decree.
The Emperor ordered that seventeen people, including Grand Minister of the Court of Imperial Stud Lǐ Lún, be retained,
and the rest be dismissed.
In the first year of Zhèngdé,
Eunuch Wáng Ruì of the Directorate of Imperial Accoutrements again requested the re-appointment of seven of the newly dismissed individuals.
Wénshēng did not comply with the edict.
Investigating Censor Ān Kuí found evidence of Wáng Ruì taking bribes
and impeached him.
Wáng Ruì, resentful,
falsely accused Wénshēng of defying an imperial decree.
The matter was further debated in court,
where everyone supported Wénshēng,
but the Emperor ultimately did not listen.
Wénshēng then requested to retire,
but this was not permitted.
At this time,
court administration had already shifted to the eunuchs.
Wénshēng was old
and daily harbored the intention to leave.
It so happened that the Governor-General position for Liǎngguǎng was vacant,
and Wénshēng recommended Vice Minister of War Xióng Xiù.
Xióng Xiù was displeased and unwilling to take the post.
His fellow townsman, Censor Hé Tiānqú, then impeached Wénshēng for favoritism and deception.
Wénshēng repeatedly memorialized to request his departure,
which was finally granted.
He was bestowed an imperial letter, provided with imperial transportation,
and his monthly stipend and annual allowances were increased.
While at home,
he never entered the prefectural city unless for official matters.
When current affairs were mentioned,
he would often frown and not reply.
Three years later,
when Liú Jǐn was disrupting the government,
Wénshēng was implicated for having previously appointed Yōng Tài as a partisan,
and his official titles were revoked.
In the sixth month of the fifth year [of Zhèngdé], he died,
aged eighty-five.
After Liú Jǐn was executed,
Wénshēng's titles were restored,
and he was posthumously granted the titles of Grand Master of Glorious Happiness, Grand Tutor,
and given the posthumous name Duān Sù.
Wénshēng had both literary and martial talents,
excelling at adapting to change.
At the court, major decisions often awaited his resolution.
His achievements were in the frontier garrisons,
and foreign countries all knew his name.
He especially valued integrity,
was strict in his principles,
and acted with rectitude.
Although he suffered slander and abuse,
rising and falling repeatedly,
he was never diminished in the slightest.
His son, Cōng,
was a *xiānggòngshì* awaiting selection by the Ministry of Personnel.
Wénshēng told him to request an outside post,
saying:
"If the sons of all high officials receive metropolitan appointments,
who will serve in the provinces?"
More than a year after his death,
the great bandit Zhào Suì and others plundered Hénán.
When they reached Jūnzhōu,
seeing Wénshēng's family resided there,
they spared it and left.
They attacked Bìyáng
and burned Jiāo Fāng's house,
binding straw into a likeness of Fāng and tearing it apart.
In the early Jiājìng era,
Wénshēng was posthumously granted the titles of Zuǒ Zhùguó and Tàishī.
Liú Dàxià,
courtesy name Shíyōng,
was from Huáróng.
His father, Rénzhái,
became the magistrate of Ruìchāng County through a provincial recommendation.
Over a thousand refugee families hid in the mountains.
When the patrols failed to extort bribes,
they falsely accused the people of rebellion,
and the general consensus was to send troops.
Rénzhái went alone on horseback to persuade them,
and the people rushed out to plead their case.
Thus the troops were dismissed,
and he was promoted to Guangxī Assistant Surveillance Commissioner.
Dàxià placed first in the provincial examination at the age of twenty.
He passed the imperial examination in the eighth year of Tiānshùn,
and was appointed a *shùjíshì*.
In the early Chénghuà era,
he was slated to remain in the Hànlín Academy after the palace examination,
but he requested to be tested for an official post.
So he was appointed a Director in the Bureau of Military Provisions,
and was twice promoted to Department Director.
He was well-versed in military affairs,
and thoroughly reformed the long-standing abuses in the bureau.
Many of his memorials and reports pleased the emperor,
and the Minister relied on him as if he were his right and left hand.
Wāng Zhí was fond of military achievements on the frontier.
When Lí Hào of Ānnán was defeated by Lǎowō,
Wāng Zhí wanted to seize the opportunity to conquer it.
He spoke to the emperor
and sought old documents concerning the Yongle expedition against Ānnán.
Dàxià concealed them and did not hand them over,
secretly telling Minister Yú Zǐjùn:
"Once hostilities begin,
the southwest will immediately be ravaged."
Zǐjùn understood,
and the matter was dropped.
The Korean tribute route had traditionally passed through Yāgǔguān,
but at this time, they requested to change it to the Yālù Jiāng.
The Minister was about to agree,
but Dàxià said:
"The route along the Yālù Jiāng —
did our ancestors not know of it?
Yet they deliberately chose to meander through several major garrisons.
This must have had a subtle meaning.
It should not be granted."
So it was stopped.
A eunuch named Ājiǔ
had a brother who served as an Experience Officer in the Metropolitan Guard.
For a crime, he was flogged by Dàxià.
Emperor Xiànzōng believed Ājiǔ's slander
and had Dàxià arrested and imprisoned in the Imperial Prison,
ordering the Eastern Depot to investigate, but they found nothing.
Huái Ēn happened to intercede strongly,
so Dàxià was given twenty strokes and released.
In the nineteenth year [of Chénghuà],
he was promoted to Fujian Right Administration Vice Commissioner,
and was known for his administrative achievements.
Upon hearing of his father's death,
he departed after a single night.
After the mourning period ended in the second year of Hóngzhì,
he was promoted to Guangdong Right Administration Commissioner.
Tiánzhōu and Sìchéng were restless,
but Dàxià went to persuade them,
and they subsequently obeyed.
Later, mountain bandits rose,
and he was ordered to suppress them.
He commanded that any captured bandits must be brought in alive,
and only punished after verification,
thus more than half of them were saved.
He was transferred to the Left [Administration Commissioner],
and then moved to Zhèjiāng.
In the spring of the sixth year [of Hóngzhì],
the river breached at Zhāngqiū.
An imperial edict ordered a broad selection of talented officials to manage the repairs.
Minister of Personnel Wáng Shù and others recommended Dàxià,
who was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief and dispatched.
He then dredged the Jiǎlǔ Hé from Huánglínggāng,
and also dredged the upper reaches of Sūnjiā Dù and Sìfǔ Yíng
to divert the water flow.
He also built a long dyke,
starting from Zuòchéng, passing through Dōngmíng and Chángyuán, reaching Xúzhōu,
spanning three hundred sixty *lǐ*.
The river was greatly controlled,
and Zhāngqiū Zhèn was renamed
"Ānpíng Zhèn."
Emperor Xiàozōng praised him,
bestowing an imperial letter of commendation,
the details of which are in the *Héqú Zhì*.
He was recalled to serve as Left Vice Censor-in-Chief,
and subsequently as Left Vice Minister of Revenue.
In the tenth year [of Hóngzhì], he was ordered to concurrently hold the post of Left Assistant Censor-in-Chief
to manage military provisions in Xuānfǔ.
Minister Zhōu Jīng said to him:
"The powerful families on the frontier use grain purchases for private gain.
Do not invite trouble with your rigidity."
Dàxià replied:
"In handling affairs of the world,
one acts according to principle, not power.
I shall plan once I arrive there."
Initially,
to report grain and fodder purchases on the frontier, one had to declare at least a thousand *shí* of grain and ten thousand bundles of fodder.
Because of this,
eunuchs and military officials monopolized the profit.
Dàxià ordered that anyone with fodder and grain,
from a hundred bundles and ten *shí* upwards, was allowed to report.
The powerful families could no longer make a profit.
Within two months, reserves were abundant,
and the frontier people benefited.
In the autumn of the following year,
he submitted three memorials requesting leave due to illness and returned home,
building a thatched cottage at the foot of Dōngshān
to study there.
Two years later,
court officials jointly recommended him,
and he was reinstated as Right Censor-in-Chief,
overseeing military affairs in both Guǎngdōng and Guǎngxī.
When the imperial envoy arrived at his gate,
he departed with only two servants.
The people of Guǎngdōng had long missed Dàxià,
and cheered and celebrated.
Dàxià cleaned up official administration,
cut back on tribute demands,
and prohibited internal and external garrison officials from privately employing soldiers.
Banditry consequently declined and ceased.
In his fifteenth year, he was appointed Minister of War,
and only accepted the appointment after repeated refusals.
When he was summoned for an audience,
the Emperor said:
"I have appointed you many times,
why do you repeatedly plead illness?"
Dàxià bowed his head and said:
"Your servant is old and sick.
I secretly observe that the people of the empire are impoverished and their resources exhausted.
Should there be any unforeseen calamity,
the responsibility will fall on the Ministry of War.
I estimate that my strength is not equal to the task,
hence my resignation."
The Emperor was silent.
In Nánjīng and Fèngyáng, a great wind uprooted trees;
Hénán and Húguǎng suffered great floods;
the capital experienced bitter rain and persistent gloom.
Dàxià requested that all matters that were not ancestral customs but harmed the military and the people
be itemized and submitted for reform.
In the second month of the seventeenth year, he spoke of this again.
The Emperor ordered that for matters requiring reform,
the responsible offices should provide the facts and report them.
Thereupon, he convened court officials to itemize sixteen matters,
all of which were inconvenient for the powerful and favored,
who collectively resisted them forcefully.
The Emperor could not decide
and sent them back for reconsideration.
Dàxià and others said:
"Matters pertaining to the outer court
have all been approved.
But those that slightly touch upon the powerful and noble
are again ordered for re-examination.
We, your servants, are most foolish
and do not know why this is so."
After a long time,
an imperial decree was issued:
"Imperial edict officials are to be named and requested;
young artisans and kitchen staff shall have their monthly rice ration reduced by three dòu;
the establishment of eunuchs shall be increased,
and the Directorate of Ceremonial shall review memorials;
for the brave warriors of the Four Guards,
the Directorate of Imperial Stables shall provide the numbers and report them.
All other matters are as proposed."
Textile production and Taoist rituals were all suspended.
The wasteful expenditure of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, which amounted to millions,
and the abuse of false claims by brave warriors were also greatly reduced.
When the decree was issued,
the entire court rejoiced.
Previously,
imperial relatives and close favorites often sought imperial favors,
and the Emperor, deeply aware of their detrimental effect on governance,
was determined to rectify it.
As there were many disasters and anomalies at the time,
he again issued an edict to his ministers,
ordering each to state their shortcomings.
Dàxià then submitted several more proposals.
In the sixth month of that year, he again presented ten harms concerning military administration,
and requested to retire.
The Emperor refused,
ordering him to elaborate further on the abuses that should be reformed.
Thereupon,
Dàxià spoke at length about the hardships of the northern and southern armies' grain transport and rotational duty,
as well as the exhausted state of border troops and the corruption of border generals.
He spoke with utmost frankness.
The Emperor then summoned Dàxià to a private audience
and asked:
"You said earlier that the people of the empire are impoverished and their resources exhausted.
Since the time of the ancestors, levies and taxes have been constant,
why has it come to this today?"
He replied:
"Precisely because they have not been entirely constant.
For example, Guǎngxī annually extracts valuable timber,
Guǎngdōng extracts incense and medicines,
the costs of which certainly amount to tens of thousands;
from this, others can be known."
He then asked about the army,
to which Dàxià replied:
"They are as poor as the common people."
The Emperor said:
"They have monthly rations while stationed and travel rations when dispatched,
why are they poor?"
He replied:
"Their commanders embezzle more than half,
how can they not be poor?"
The Emperor sighed deeply and said:
"I have reigned for a long time,
yet I do not know the suffering of the military and the people.
What kind of ruler am I!"
Then he issued a decree to strictly forbid such practices.
At this time,
the Emperor was earnestly striving for peace and prosperity,
and Liú Jiàn was the chief grand secretary,
Mǎ Wénshēng, as an esteemed minister, headed the six ministries.
At this time, upright individuals filled many official positions.
The Emperor perceived Dàxià to be upright and resolute,
and also skilled in handling affairs,
and trusted him especially.
He frequently summoned him to make decisions,
and Dàxià also offered loyal advice on every matter.
There was a minor alert in Dàtóng,
and the Emperor, acting on the advice of the eunuch Miáo Kuí,
was about to dispatch an army.
Liú Jiàn and other members of the Grand Secretariat strongly remonstrated,
but the Emperor still hesitated.
He summoned and asked Dàxià:
"When you were in Guǎng,
did you know of Miáo Kuí's achievement in raiding the nest in Yánsuí?"
He replied:
"I have heard of it.
The captured women and children numbered only a dozen or so.
It was due to the court's prestige and virtue
that the entire army returned safely.
Otherwise,
it would be difficult to say."
The Emperor was silent for a long time,
then asked:
"Tàizōng frequently went out beyond the frontier,
why is it not possible now?"
He replied:
"Your Majesty's divine martial prowess certainly does not lag behind Tàizōng's,
but the generals, officers, and horses are far inferior.
Moreover, Qíguó Gōng slightly violated regulations
and committed hundreds of thousands of troops to the desert;
how can one speak of it lightly?
I estimate that the best policy now is merely to defend."
The Censor-in-chief Dài Shān also supported this decision from the side,
and the Emperor abruptly said:
"Without you, gentlemen,
I would have nearly erred."
Because of this,
the army was not dispatched.
Lǔ Lín, a local chieftain of Zhuānglàng, was appointed Assistant General of Gānsù.
When he failed to obtain the position of Grand General,
relying on the strength of his followers,
he directly returned to Zhuānglàng.
Court officials feared a rebellion,
some wanted to grant him the seal of a Grand General,
others wanted to summon him back to the capital
and assign him to an idle post.
Dàxià requested that his ancestors' loyalty and obedience be praised,
and that Lín be allowed to retire.
Lín was notoriously greedy and cruel, losing the hearts of his followers;
with military authority gone, he was powerless,
and eventually died discontented of illness.
The Emperor wanted to station troops in nearby areas to serve as left and right wings.
Dàxià said:
"Bǎodìng established a Regional Military Commission to command five guards;
the intention of the ancestors must have been similar.
I request that ten thousand training troops be sent back to form the Western Guard,
and that the troops from Mìyún and Jìzhōu in the eastern capital region be incorporated as the Eastern Guard."
The Emperor approved.
The eunuchs supervising the capital garrisons, enraged by the loss of troops,
posted slanderous rumors at the palace gate.
The Emperor showed them to Dàxià and said:
"How could outsiders reach the palace gate?
It must be these eunuchs who are displeased at losing their troops."
Because of this,
their machinations did not succeed.
The emperor once instructed Liú Dàxià, saying:
“When matters arise, I always think of summoning you,
but I stop myself, fearing to overstep my bounds.
Henceforth, if there are things that should be done or stopped,
prepare a memorial and submit it.”
Liú Dàxià bowed and said:
“Whether a matter is permissible or not,
it can be referred to the Six Ministries externally,
and consulted with the Grand Secretaries internally.
Memorials only breed corruption,
and should not be made a precedent for future generations.”
The emperor praised this as good.
He also once asked:
“When will there be peace under Heaven?”
Liú Dàxià replied:
“Seeking good governance should not be too hasty.
However, if all appointments and administrations are discussed face-to-face with the Grand Ministers,
and only acted upon after agreement,
then in time, the realm will govern itself.”
He once took the opportunity to speak of the harm caused by eunuch garrison commanders in the four directions.
The emperor asked for details,
and Liú Dàxià replied:
“While I was in Liǎngguǎng, I saw that the provisions supplied by the various civil and military high officials could not match a single garrison commander;
the trouble and expense can be imagined.”
The emperor said:
“Nevertheless, our ancestors established this system long ago,
how can it be suddenly abolished?
Only from now on, we must employ those who are as incorruptible as Dèng Yuán and Mài Xiù,
otherwise, let it be.”
Liú Dàxià bowed and assented.
Whenever Liú Dàxià was summoned,
he would kneel before the imperial couch.
The emperor would glance left and right,
and the attendants would withdraw.
He once conversed for so long
that he was too exhausted to rise,
and had to call the Director of Ceremonial, Grand Eunuch Lǐ Róng, to support him out.
One morning during an early court audience,
Liú Dàxià was indeed in his rank,
but the emperor happened not to see him.
The next day, he issued an edict saying:
“Did you miss court yesterday?
I feared the censors would impeach you,
so I did not summon you after all.”
Such was the depth of his imperial favor.
He was specially granted a jade belt and a qílín robe,
and the gold, silk, and imperial wine bestowed upon him
never ceased throughout the year.
Not long after,
Emperor Xiàozōng passed away,
and Emperor Wǔzōng ascended the throne.
Liú Dàxià received an edict requesting the withdrawal of eunuch garrison commanders in the four directions who were not regularly appointed.
The emperor only withdrew Qí Yuán from Jūnzhōu.
Liú Dàxià further proposed the withdrawal of twenty-four other individuals,
and also memorialized to reduce the eunuchs guarding the Imperial City and the capital city,
but none were accepted.
A short while later,
he listed and proposed the removal of 683 "transferred-appointment" military officials,
which was approved.
The 48 Grand Hàn Generals, including Xuē Fújìng, were also due to be stripped of their offices.
Xuē Fújìng and the others deliberately did not attend court to provoke the emperor's anger.
The emperor hastily ordered their reinstatement,
and held the Ministry of War responsible for explaining the situation,
intending to punish them.
The eunuch Níng Jǐn bowed and said:
“This was the late emperor's dying wish,
Your Majesty listed it in the edict upon your ascension;
it is not appropriate to punish them.”
The emperor then relented.
The eunuch Wéi Xīng, who had been disgraced and idled since the end of the Chénghuà reign,
managed through connections to become the commander of Jūnzhōu.
Censors repeatedly remonstrated,
and Liú Dàxià and others argued again and again,
but none were heeded.
In the spring of the first year of Zhèngdé (1506),
he again stated:
“Eunuch garrison commanders,
such as Dǒng Ràng in Jiāngxī, Liú Láng in Jìzhōu, Liú Yún in Shǎnxī, and Zhū Yún in Shāndōng, are particularly corrupt and cruel;
I beg that they be investigated and dealt with.”
The emperor was displeased.
Liú Dàxià knew that his words were not being used,
and repeatedly memorialized to request retirement.
In the fifth month of that year,
an imperial edict added the title of Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent,
granted a decree to return by post-horse,
and provided stipends and attendants according to regulations.
The Investigating Censors Wáng Yì and Zhāng Huì requested he be retained,
and the Ministry of Personnel also requested that Wáng Yì and Zhāng Huì's suggestion be followed,
but there was no reply.
Liú Dàxià was loyal and sincere,
recognized by Emperor Xiàozōng,
and sacrificed himself for the country,
suppressing many powerful favorites.
He once requested a strict review of brave warriors,
which incurred the hatred of Liú Jǐn.
Liú Yǔ also resented Liú Dàxià,
and so he and Jiāo Fāng slandered him to Liú Jǐn, saying:
“Confiscating Liú Dàxià's property
could cover twelve parts of the border expenses.”
In the ninth month of the third year (1508),
using the pretext of Cén Měng of Tiánzhōu's affair,
he was arrested and imprisoned in the imperial prison.
Liú Jǐn wanted to condemn him to death under the law for inciting rebellion,
but the Censor-in-Chief Tú Yōng resisted, saying it was not permissible.
Liú Jǐn cursed at him, saying:
“Even if he doesn't die,
can he avoid banishment?”
Lǐ Dōngyáng skillfully mediated,
and since Liú Jǐn's spies found Liú Dàxià's family was actually poor,
he was instead sentenced to banishment to a remote frontier.
Initially, Guǎngxī was suggested,
but Jiāo Fāng said,
“That would be like sending him home,”
so it was changed to Sùzhōu.
Liú Dàxià was already seventy-three years old.
In common clothes, he walked past Dàmíngmén,
bowed his head, and departed.
Onlookers sighed and wept,
and elders carried baskets of food to send him off.
Wherever he went, markets closed, and incense was burned to pray for Minister Liú's return alive.
When he arrived at the place of banishment,
all officials, fearing Liú Jǐn,
ceased to send him provisions or inquiries.
Scholars and students passed food to him.
When there was group drill,
he would always carry a spear and join the ranks.
The officials in charge repeatedly declined,
but Liú Dàxià said:
“As a soldier,
one is naturally bound to perform service.”
He brought only one servant.
Someone asked why he did not bring his children or relatives,
and he replied:
“When I was in office,
I did not beg for favors for my children and grandchildren.
Now that I am old and disgraced,
how can I bear to let them die with me in exile?”
After Liú Dàxià was exiled,
Liú Jǐn still found other pretexts to punish him, twice making him pay tribute grain to the border.
In the summer of the fifth year (1510),
he was pardoned and returned home.
When Liú Jǐn was executed,
Liú Dàxià's official rank was restored,
and he retired.
The Investigating Censor for Army Review, Wáng Xiāng, requested the restoration of his stipend and attendants,
and that his descendants be recorded.
However, the powerful eunuchs still bore grudges against him,
and did not allow it.
Upon returning home, Liú Dàxià
taught his children and grandchildren to farm for a living.
When he had a little surplus,
he distributed it to old friends and clansmen.
He prepared his own epitaph in advance,
saying:
“Let no one adorn it with flattery,
lest I feel ashamed in the underworld.”
He died in the fifth month of the eleventh year (1516),
aged eighty-one.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Tutor
and the谥 posthumous name Zhōngxuān.
Liú Dàxià once said:
“When holding office, rectifying oneself is paramount.
Not only should one guard against greed,
but also distance oneself from fame.”
He also said:
“In life, one's reputation is settled when the coffin lid is closed.
As long as one has not died,
the anxieties and responsibilities have not ceased.”
When he was arrested,
he was weeding in his vegetable garden.
He entered his house, took a few hundred coins,
mounted a small donkey, and set off.
After his pardon and return,
a former student of his who was a provincial governor
traveled a hundred li out of his way to visit him.
On the road, he encountered a man pushing a plow and asked,
“Who is from Minister Liú's family?”
The man led him into the hall,
and it was Liú Dàxià himself.
A Korean envoy staying at the Hónglú Temple encountered Zhāng Shēng, a fellow townsman of Liú Dàxià,
and inquired about Liú Dàxià's well-being, saying:
“Our country has long heard the name of Liú Dōngshān.”
An Annamese envoy paying tribute said:
“We heard that Minister Liú was banished to the border;
how is he now?”
Such was the respect he commanded from foreign countries.
The eulogy states: Wáng Shù 砥礪 (honed) his moral integrity and principles,
Mǎ Wénshēng was experienced and shrewd in government affairs,
Liú Dàxià was loyal and self-reliant in command,
all possessing far-reaching strategies for governance,
and harboring the upright ambition of a monarch.
They managed myriad affairs,
repeatedly offering frank advice.
Tracing their inner intentions and conduct,
they were magnanimous and brilliant,
firm, straightforward, and upright,
possessing the character and integrity of ancient high officials.
Having served several courts,
they enjoyed a long life,
were looked up to by both court and commoners,
and their fame was far-reaching.
Poetry praises the aged and accomplished,
history refers to "yellowed hair" elders;
these three officials were close to such descriptions.
Wáng Shù disregarded the warning against seeking distant fame,
and thus was alienated by the writing of his biography.
However, Mǎ Wénshēng and Liú Dàxià were favored in the court of Xiàozōng,
where sagacious ruler and upright minister were in accord,
and the sovereign and his chief minister were of one mind.
But when eunuchs gained power,
the old and venerable were expelled;
how weighty were the issues involved in their promotion and demotion!
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 71: Hé Qiáoxīn, Péng Sháo, Zhōu Jīng, Gěng Yù, Ní Yuè, Mǐn Guī, Dài Shān.
Hé Qiáoxīn,
courtesy name Tíngxiù,
was a native of Guǎngchāng, Jiāngxī.
His father, Wénchūn,
passed the imperial examination in the 16th year of Yǒnglè (1418).
He was appointed Censor,
and successively inspected Shāndōng and Sìchuān.
In Wūméng, a treacherous commoner named Shígē secretly took the wife of the prefect, Lù Zhāo.
Fearing punishment,
he falsely accused Zhāo of rebellion,
and an imperial edict ordered troops to be dispatched for suppression.
Wénchūn issued a dispatch to halt the mobilized troops,
and reported the falsity of the accusation.
In the 5th year of Xuāndé (1430), based on Gù Zuǒ's recommendation,
he was granted an imperial rescript to govern Wēnzhōu Prefecture.
He served for six years,
achieved the best administration,
and was given an increased salary and imperial seals.
Upon Hú Yíng's recommendation,
he was promoted to Right Vice Minister of the Ministry of Justice,
and supervised the salt taxes of the two Huái regions.
In the 3rd year of Zhèngtǒng (1438),
two of his judgments in criminal cases were deemed inappropriate,
and he was imprisoned with Minister Wèi Yuán,
but both were released.
When the court deliberated a campaign against Lùchuān,
Wénchūn memorialized, advising:
"Lùchuān is a small, remote territory beyond the frontier,
not worth troubling a large army.
If the Yúnnán garrison general were to station troops at Jīnchǐ,
and the officials of the three departments were ordered to pacify them with persuasion,
the people from afar would gain a new lease on life,
and the court would be spared from mobilizing troops and transporting provisions.
This is the best strategy."
The Emperor referred his suggestion for deliberation,
but many court officials advocated military action.
Consequently, the southwest was disturbed,
and it was only with great difficulty that it was conquered,
with many losses.
That winter,
he requested to retire due to illness.
When Jǐngdì ascended the throne,
he was recalled as Left Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel,
soon after promoted to Minister,
assisting Wáng Zhí in managing the ministry's affairs.
When the Eastern Palace was established,
he was given the additional title of Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
When anomalies appeared,
Censor Lín Cōng and others impeached Wénchūn for being treacherous and wicked.
The Left Chief Supervisor Zhōu Xuán memorialized, stating he was wronged,
and Cōng then also impeached Xuán.
Censor Cáo Kǎi again argued at court,
and subsequently both he and Xuán were imprisoned.
Cōng's memorial contained
the phrase "entrusted a eunuch,"
and the Grand Eunuch Xīng'ān requested the name of the principal.
Cōng dared not firmly respond,
so Wénchūn was released and ordered to retire.
When Yīngzōng was restored,
his additional official titles were stripped.
However, the edict for changing the heir apparent during the Jǐngtài era
stated "the father possesses the realm and passes it to his son,"
words attributed to Wénchūn.
It was rumored that an imperial order was issued for his arrest,
and in fear, he hanged himself.
At that time, Qiáoxīn had already passed the imperial examination in the 5th year of Jǐngtài (1454),
serving as a Section Chief in the Ministry of Rites in Nánjīng.
He rushed home for his father's funeral.
A local, former Vice Minister Jiē Jī, had studied under Wénchūn,
but was not on good terms with Qiáoxīn and his brothers.
He memorialized that Wénchūn's death was actually caused by his sons forcing him to hang himself,
and also compelling him to marry off the father's favorite concubine.
Qiáoxīn, in turn, exposed Jiē Jī that when he was a circuit inspector,
he had once recommended Huáng Mǒu (a specific person whose name is missing from the original text and represented by a square, I will transcribe this as Huáng Mǒu),
and also drafted the memorial for changing the heir apparent.
Both were summoned for confrontation in court.
The father's concubine cut off a finger [as an oath of innocence]
and pleaded for the sons' innocence;
the case was slightly alleviated.
The Emperor also, considering the matter had passed an amnesty,
released them without further inquiry.
Later,
he again mourned his mother.
After the mourning period,
he was reappointed as a Section Chief in the Ministry of Justice,
and successively served as a Director in the Guǎngdōng Department.
When a soldier of the Imperial Guard violated the law,
he was arrested and punished without the slightest leniency.
The Grand Commissioner Yuán Bīn made a request,
but he firmly refused.
Bīn was angry and
sent people to collect evidence against him but found nothing.
From then on, his reputation greatly increased.
In the 4th year of Chénghuà (1468), he was promoted to Vice Surveillance Commissioner of Fújiàn.
In the Shòuníng silver mine under his jurisdiction,
over a thousand illicit miners gathered,
pillaging wherever they went.
He recruited soldiers to attack and capture their leader, the strongman Yóu of Fúníng, who had committed murder,
and moved about with armed soldiers,
resisting arrest for twenty years.
The Xuē clan of Fúqīng often traded with various foreign tribes,
and when this was discovered,
they plotted rebellion.
All were captured and killed.
The silver mines of Fú'ān and Níngdé had long been abandoned,
but officials still demanded taxes,
causing many people to become bankrupt.
Qiáoxīn spoke out about this,
and the taxes were reduced by two-thirds.
The people of Xīnghuà, from the beginning of Hóngwǔ's reign, had received oxen from the government,
and by this time were still paying annual rent for them.
He memorialized to have it abolished.
The people of Guīhuà Township in Qīngliú, located between Shāxiàn and Jiānglè,
relied on the treacherous terrain to avoid paying taxes.
He reported to the Grand Censor, and Guīhuà County was established,
whereupon its people began to comply with regulations.
He was promoted to Surveillance Commissioner of Hénán.
There was a great famine that year.
According to custom,
relief loans ceased in autumn,
but Qiáoxīn said:
"Stopping in autumn implies that the autumn harvest can be relied upon.
Can autumn crops be sufficient now?"
Relief continued until the wheat harvest of the following year.
Grand Censor Yuán Jié, in an effort to pacify displaced people, arrived in Nányáng,
and invited Qiáoxīn to assist him.
Initially,
Xiàng Zhōng had driven the displaced people too harshly,
and when the people heard of Jié's arrival,
they fled even further into the mountains and valleys.
Qiáoxīn personally went to recruit them,
and over 60,000 households were registered.
He was promoted to Right Administration Commissioner of Húguǎng.
The people of Jīngzhōu suffered from corvée labor,
so he assessed the households by population and wealth,
categorizing them into nine grades,
which benefited the people.
In the sixteenth year [of Chenghuà], he was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-chief,
and served as Grand Coordinator of Shānxī.
When soldiers and civilians from the border areas often went outside the Great Wall to cut wood and hunt beasts,
Qiáo Xīn said:
"If these people were to encounter enemies,
they would surely betray information to save themselves;
they are all guides for the bandits.
They should not be allowed to go out without permission,
and those who violate this should be punished as garrison commanders."
An imperial edict approved this.
When the enemy attacked the border,
he, along with Assistant General Zhī Yù, ambushed them at Huīgōu Yíng,
killing and beheading many.
He was promoted to Left Vice Censor-in-chief.
During a famine,
he memorialized to exempt four-tenths of miscellaneous levies and household salt taxes.
He impeached Assistant Censors Shàng Jìng and Liú Yuán for delaying legal cases,
and requested an imperial decree to instruct all judicial officials in the empire
that those who delayed cases for more than half a year should all be punished.
The Emperor praised this,
and promptly followed it.
He was summoned to be appointed Right Vice Minister of Justice.
A great famine struck Shānxī,
where people resorted to cannibalism.
He was ordered to go and provide relief,
saving over 300,000 people
and resettling 40,000 households of displaced people.
Upon his return to court,
it happened that Yáng Yǒu, the Pacification Commissioner of Ānníng, wanted to seize the title of his younger brother, Yáng Ài, the Pacification Commissioner of Bōzhōu,
and falsely accused Ài of having rebellious intentions.
Qiáo Xīn went to investigate,
and together with Grand Coordinator Liú Zhāng, cleared Ài of the false accusation.
Yǒu was stripped of his office and relocated to another prefecture,
and the people of Bōzhōu were consequently pacified.
When Xiàozōng succeeded to the throne,
Wàn Ān, Liú Jí, and others, jealous of Qiáo Xīn's uprightness,
sent him out as Minister of Justice of Nánjīng.
The reed marshes along the river were mostly occupied by eunuchs,
who claimed they were for expenses related to imperial tribute.
Qiáo Xīn memorialized to return them to the people.
Initially,
when Qiáo Xīn was sent out,
the eunuch Huái Ēn felt it was unfair.
One day, he went to the Grand Secretariat on a matter and said:
"When the new ruler ascends,
he should employ upright people.
Why send out Master Hé?"
Ān and others remained silent.
Soon after, Dù Míng, Minister of Justice, was dismissed,
and everyone looked to Qiáo Xīn,
but Jí replaced Ān as chief grand secretary,
and remained jealous of him,
so the position was not filled for a long time.
When Hóngzhì ascended the throne,
Qiáo Xīn was recommended by Wáng Shù,
and was finally recalled to replace Míng.
He memorialized, saying:
"According to the old system, when officials were dispatched to investigate matters or make arrests,
they had to carry detailed written instructions,
which had to be verified by the local officials before proceeding.
Recently, only imperial warrants were used without matching tallies,
which is inappropriate. The old system should be restored
to prevent fraud."
The Emperor immediately granted his request.
At that time, Jí was hostile to upright people,
and frequently initiated major judicial cases.
Qiáo Xīn consistently upheld the law and justice.
Jí resented him even more,
and repeatedly found other pretexts to withhold his salary.
In the summer of the second year [of Hóngzhì],
there was a great flood in the capital.
Qiáo Xīn requested relief for the families of those affected,
and also, fearing injustice in legal cases,
listed several articles of law that should be reconsidered.
Jí blocked all of them.
When the position of Assistant Minister of the Court of Judicial Review was vacant,
Censor Zōu Lǔ coveted the promotion,
but Qiáo Xīn recommended Department Director Wèi Shēn.
It happened that Qiáo Xīn's maternal relatives were involved in a lawsuit with local villagers,
and Lǔ immediately falsely accused Qiáo Xīn of accepting bribes and unduly protecting them.
Jí obtained a secret imperial edict to send his maternal relatives to the imperial prison,
whereupon Qiáo Xīn submitted a memorial requesting retirement.
Shortly thereafter,
the thorough investigation yielded no evidence,
Lǔ was suspended from his salary,
and Qiáo Xīn was also allowed to retire.
Qiáo Xīn was known for his integrity and uprightness.
While observing government affairs in the Ministry of Works,
he once went on an assignment to Huáixī.
Yán Huī, the magistrate of Cháo, had studied under Wén Yuān when he was young,
and offered him gold and silk.
Qiáo Xīn refused it,
and Yán said:
"It is to honor my teacher."
Qiáo Xīn replied:
"If you wish to honor my parent, you may do so through others,
but not through me."
He ultimately did not accept it.
When a eunuch from the Fujian Maritime Trade Office died,
the garrison commander distributed his assets among the three judicial agencies,
but Qiáo Xīn alone firmly declined.
Unable to refuse,
he deposited it in the treasury.
After returning home,
Yáng Ài sent an envoy with generous gifts,
and also offered fine timber suitable for a coffin.
Qiáo Xīn firmly refused it.
When Qiáo Xīn was eleven years old,
he attended his father in the capital residence.
Zhōu Xuán, an editor, visited him.
Qiáo Xīn was then reading the *Tōngjiàn Xùbiān*.
Xuán asked:
"How does its historiography compare to the *Gāngmù*?"
He replied:
"Lǚ Wénhuàn's surrender to the Yuán is not recorded as rebellion,
Zhāng Shìjié's drowning in the sea is not recorded as dying a martyr,
the deaths of Cáo Bīn and Bāo Zhěng do not record their official titles,
and it frequently cites strange and absurd accounts of Xī and Xuān.
It seems inappropriate."
Xuán was greatly astonished.
When he grew older,
he extensively studied all kinds of books.
Whenever he heard of a rare book, he would borrow and copy it,
accumulating over 30,000 volumes,
all personally collated and proofread.
His writings were very abundant.
He had few close associates,
with Péng Sháo as his friend in character and integrity,
and Qiū Jùn as his friend in scholarship,
and that was all.
After his retirement,
Chén Quán, the circuit inspecting censor of Jiāngxī, memorialized:
"Qiáo Xīn maintained his integrity from beginning to end,
but was compelled to retire merely on suspicion of accepting gifts from relatives and old friends.
His advancement and retirement were obscured,
which is truly regrettable.
I request an investigation.
If the official has no illness, he should be recalled and appointed;
if he is ill, he should be comforted and praised,
to preserve the kindness shown to old acquaintances
and complete the integrity of his career path."
This was not granted.
Later, many within and outside the court recommended him,
but he was never reinstated.
He died in the fifteenth year [of Hóngzhì],
at the age of seventy-six.
Lín Jùn, the Grand Coordinator of Jiāngxī, requested posthumous titles for Péng Sháo and Qiáo Xīn.
The Ministry of Personnel reported favorably on this.
There was an imperial decree to state the reasons for Qiáo Xīn's retirement.
Investigating Censor Wú Shìzhōng said:
"Qiáo Xīn was outstanding in scholarship, conduct, and administration;
he was loyal, diligent, principled, and grew even more so in old age.
When Censor Zōu Lǔ falsely impeached him out of personal spite,
he did not utter a single word in defense,
but calmly retired,
closed his door to write books,
and had few interactions with others.
Scholars and officials universally esteemed his conduct.
If one must examine the reasons for his retirement
and doubt the canon of commending worthies,
then Jiǎng Zhīqí of the Sòng dynasty once falsely impeached Ōuyáng Xiū,
and Hú Hóng and others once falsely impeached Zhū Xī;
yet we have never heard of one person's private feelings overriding the public opinion of ten thousand generations."
The matter was ultimately dropped.
In the eleventh year of Zhèngdé,
Zhāng Jié, the Magistrate of Guǎngchāng, reiterated the matter,
and he was then posthumously granted the title of Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent,
and his descendants were granted hereditary privilege.
The following year, he was granted the posthumous title Wénsù.
Qiáo Yuán, Qiáo Xīn's fifth-generation grandson,
served as Right Vice Minister of Justice in the early Wànlì era.
He also possessed integrity.
Péng Sháo,
courtesy name Fèngyí,
was a native of Pútián.
He became a *Jìnshì* in the first year of Tiānshùn.
He was appointed Principal of the Ministry of Justice,
and advanced to Assistant Director.
In the second year of Chénghuà, he memorialized to denounce Assistant Censor-in-chief Zhāng Qí as treacherous and evil,
suggesting that Wáng Hóng, Lǐ Bǐng, and Yè Shèng should be recalled.
This displeased the emperor,
and he was sent to the imperial prison.
Investigating Censor Máo Hóng and others pleaded for him,
but it was not heard,
and he ultimately had to pay a ransom.
Soon after, he was promoted to Department Director.
Zhōu Yù, Commander of the Brocade Guards,
the Empress Dowager's younger brother,
memorialized to request that the private land of the people of Wǔqiáng and Wǔyì, which did not meet the tax quota,
be registered as idle land.
Sháo was ordered to accompany Censor Jì Cóng to review and investigate.
Sháo and others inspected the area briefly and returned,
then submitted a memorial impeaching himself, saying:
"The fields of Zhēndìng,
since the time of our ancestors, were permitted for the people to reclaim and cultivate,
and thus became their property.
Taxes and levies were remitted to encourage diligent farming.
meritorious officials and imperial relatives, whose families prosper with the nation,
should not compete with the people for an inch of land.
Your minister truly cannot bear to seize the livelihood of the common people
to enrich the imperial relatives.
I request to accept the charge of being an incompetent envoy."
When the memorial was submitted,
an imperial edict ordered the land returned to the people,
but blamed Sháo and others for seeking fame and disobeying orders,
and again sent them to the imperial prison.
Censors debated and interceded,
and they were released.
At this time,
Sháo held office with Hé Qiáoxīn,
both having great reputations,
and were known at the time as Hé and Péng.
He was promoted to Vice Commissioner of Sìchuān.
In Ānyuè, the Hù clan burned and destroyed the family of a certain Liú, twenty-one people in total.
In Dìngyuǎn, the Cáo clan killed twelve people from their elder brother's family.
The authorities considered these difficult cases,
and they remained unresolved for a long time.
Sháo, after one interrogation, uncovered the truth,
and all were punished.
He was promoted to Surveillance Commissioner,
and completely abolished all illicit temples within his jurisdiction.
For royal funerals and sacrifices, eunuchs were previously dispatched,
causing public and private inconvenience and expense.
He memorialized to abolish this practice.
Qián Néng, the Grand Eunuch guarding Yúnnán, presented golden lamps,
disrupting the roads.
Sháo impeached him,
but received no response.
In the spring of the fourteenth year,
he was transferred to serve as the Left Administration Commissioner of Guǎngdōng.
Imperial envoys, all eunuchs, came in droves.
Commander Gù, Maritime Trade Commissioner Wéi Juàn, and Pearl Pool Supervisor Huáng Fú,
all used the pretext of presenting tributes,
demanding goods wherever they went,
which the people could not bear.
Sháo memorialized on these matters repeatedly.
Finally,
Liáng Fāng's younger brother, Dé, a commandant of the Brocade Guards, claimed Guǎngdōng as his hometown,
and returned to collect birds, animals, flowers, and trees,
causing particularly severe harm.
Sháo vigorously memorialized,
with words that offended Fāng.
Fāng was enraged,
and slandered him to the emperor,
who transferred him to Guìzhōu.
In the twentieth year, he was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief,
and appointed Grand Coordinator of Yìngtiān.
In the first month of the following year,
a celestial anomaly occurred,
and he memorialized, saying:
"The comet, a sign of disaster,
appeared at the end of the year,
and then at New Year's Day.
The end of the year
is the conclusion of the heavenly cycle.
New Year's Day
is the beginning of the year's affairs.
This shows the benevolent heart of Heaven,
desiring Your Majesty to have a good beginning and a good end.
At the beginning of Your Majesty's reign,
household rituals were correct,
precautions against minor transgressions were thorough,
the virtue of frugality was manifest,
and personnel appointments were cautious.
Yet in recent years,
tributes for the imperial concubines
have surpassed those for the Empress,
and their families have been praised and favored,
almost on par with the families of the former emperor's empresses.
This is where the principle of regulating the household has not been fully maintained.
The number of eunuchs in offices and bureaus is in the tens of thousands;
sources of profit and military authority are entirely entrusted to them.
Violations of law and indulgence of villainy
are all tolerated and pardoned.
This is where the principle of preventing minor transgressions has not been fully maintained.
The eunuchs guarding the four directions
compete to present rare and exotic items,
always claiming imperial decrees,
thereby extorting and disturbing the common people.
This is where the principle of upholding frugality has not been fully maintained.
The six chief ministers are all given titles of grand tutors,
and eunuch directors concurrently hold high ranks.
When they retire and return home,
their stipends for food and sedan chair bearers are excessively bestowed upon the unworthy.
If titles and rewards are taken lightly,
who will be encouraged?
This is where the principle of employing people has not been fully maintained.
May Your Majesty only be as cautious at the end as you were at the beginning;
the empire would be exceedingly fortunate."
At the time, he was about to be summoned as Minister of the Grand Court of Revision.
The emperor was displeased upon receiving the memorial,
and ordered him to remain in his original post as Grand Coordinator of Shùntiān and Yǒngpíng prefectures.
He equalized corvée labor in the counties of Dàxīng, Wǎnpíng, and Chāngpíng,
and impeached the crimes of the guarding eunuch Táo Hóng.
After Emperor Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
he was summoned to be Right Vice Minister of Personnel.
Chén Fǔ, a centurion from Jiāxīng, engaged in banditry and illicit trade, causing chaos,
capturing the prefectural city and plundering it extensively,
then fleeing into Lake Tàihú.
Sháo was dispatched to inspect the situation.
When Sháo arrived,
the bandits had already been suppressed.
He was then ordered to concurrently serve as Vice Censor-in-Chief,
to reform the salt administration.
Soon after, he was promoted to Left Vice Minister.
Sháo, seeing that merchants suffered from forced requisitioning,
set a fixed discounted price,
and remitted old debts.
Pitying the salt households' difficulties with boiling, processing, collecting taxes, compensating losses, and suffering discounts,
he presented eight illustrations,
and listed six matters of benefit and harm,
which were all approved and implemented.
In the autumn of the second year of Hóngzhì,
he returned to court.
The following year,
he was transferred to the Ministry of Personnel.
With Minister Wáng Shù, he selected talented individuals
and verified their merits,
bringing clarity to officialdom.
When a comet appeared,
he memorialized that the eunuchs were too numerous
and must be drastically reduced.
He then requested to discuss major policies face-to-face during the noon audience,
instead of merely going through formalities.
Subsequently,
he again stated that too many officials were improperly appointed,
and begged that the gates to favoritism be strictly closed,
and that corrections be vigorously made.
The emperor agreed with his words,
but ultimately could not implement them.
In the autumn of the fourth year,
he replaced Hé Qiáoxīn as Minister of Justice.
The former Marquis of Ānyuǎn, Liǔ Jǐng, was implicated in corruption amounting to several thousand taels,
but only one-eleventh was collected,
as his mother pleaded for his exemption.
Sháo argued in a memorial, saying:
"In the past, Zhèng Guāng, the maternal uncle of Emperor Xuānzōng of Táng, did not pay rent on his official land,
and Wéi Ào, the Magistrate of Jīngzhào, shackled his estate manager.
Emperor Xuānzōng wished to pardon him,
but Ào did not obey the imperial edict.
Jǐng has no such maternal uncle kinship,
and his corruption is not comparable to unpaid rent.
If he alone receives a pardon,
then your ministers' adherence to the law would be shameful compared to Ào."
This was not accepted.
Censor Péng Chéng was imprisoned for criticizing the imperial altar vessels.
Sháo memorialized to save him,
and then extensively detailed the excessive waste of the Court of Imperial Entertainments,
which led to an order to report the annual expenditure.
Jīng Wáng, Xiànxiāo, had committed a crime;
a memorial was submitted,
but it was delayed for ten days without a decision.
Eunuchs Wáng Míng, Miáo Tōng, and Gāo Yǒng committed murder,
but their death sentences were commuted to exile.
Chāngguó Gōng Zhāng Luán built a tomb exceeding regulations,
employing tens of thousands of soldiers.
People in the capital region falsely claimed to be households serving imperial tombs and temples, or brave warriors and flag-bearers,
thereby escaping corvée labor,
causing existing households to become overburdened,
and the number of displaced people to increase daily.
Sháo vigorously memorialized on all these matters,
but they were merely sent down to the relevant authorities.
Sháo governed his ministry for three years,
speaking out boldly and with integrity,
upholding principles selflessly.
He, Wáng Shù, and Hé Qiáoxīn were called the "Three Elders,"
but he was resented by imperial relatives and close attendants,
and Grand Secretary Liú Jí also did not approve of him.
Sháo's ambitions could not be fully realized,
and he repeatedly memorialized to request retirement,
whereupon he was ordered to return by imperial post-horse.
His monthly stipend and annual servants were maintained as per regulations.
The following year,
an earthquake occurred in Nánjīng,
and Censor Zōng Yí and others stated that Sháo, Hé Qiáoxīn, Qiáng Zhēn, Xiè Duó, Chén Xiànzhāng, Zhāng Mào, and Péng Chéng should all be recalled to service,
but this was not accepted.
The year after that,
he died,
at the age of sixty-six.
He was posthumously granted the title Huì'ān,
and posthumously appointed Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
Sháo was fond of learning;
during his leisure, he always had a book in hand.
In the early years of Zhèngdé,
Lín Jùn stated that Sháo's posthumous title did not match his conduct,
and requested that, like Wèi Jì, Wú Nà, and Yè Shèng,
his posthumous title be changed to Wén.
It was not carried out.
Zhōu Jīng,
courtesy name Bó-cháng,
was the son of Xúān, Minister of Justice.
He became a *jìnshì* in the fourth year of Tiānshùn.
He was appointed a *shùjíshì* (supernumerary Hanlin bachelor)
and then a compiler (*jiǎntǎo*).
During the Chénghuà reign,
he successively served as a lecturer (*shìdú*) and a remonstrance official (*zhōngyǔn*),
attending Xiàozōng in the Eastern Palace.
When he lectured on the "Great Admonitions of Wénhuá,"
the Crown Prince stood up.
The Grand Secretaries considered this burdensome
and proposed that he be allowed to listen seated.
Jīng and all the other lecturers disagreed,
so the matter was dropped.
When Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
Jīng was promoted to Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*tàicháng shàoqīng*) concurrently with his post as lecturer (*shìdú*).
In the second year of Hóngzhì, he was elevated to Right Vice Minister of Rites (*lǐbù yòu shìláng*).
A eunuch requested the repair of the nunnery in Huángcūn,
for the worship of Empress Xiàomù.
Tǔlǔfān offered a lion as tribute, not through Gānsù,
but by borrowing a route through Mǎlájiā,
sailing across the sea to Guǎngdōng.
Jīng advocated destroying the nunnery
and refusing the tribute, cutting off communication.
He was transferred to the Ministry of Personnel,
and promoted to Left Vice Minister (*zuǒ shìláng*).
Shěn Lù, a *tōngzhèng jīnglì* (communications clerk),
was the empress's cousin-in-law.
While Minister Wáng Shù was on leave,
a eunuch conveyed an imperial decree promoting Lù to *cānyì* (senior clerk) in his own department.
Jīng stated that since he had not received the decree face-to-face
and there was no imperial edict,
he dared not comply.
He further submitted a memorial to argue against it with Shù.
Although the matter could not be stopped,
the court praised him.
Cunning people from Língshòu offered land to the eunuch Lǐ Guǎng,
but the Ministry of Revenue held it up.
and ultimately the land-offerers were punished.
He once memorialized:
"Families of imperial relatives without merit seek promotion,
without labor beg rewards,
and combine Taoist rituals, banquets, and excursions,
spending lavishly without restraint,
causing the imperial treasury to be depleted.
It is proper to greatly economize.
According to recent precedents,
those local officials whose reserve granaries (*yùbèicāng*) accumulated much grain
were granted imperial decrees
and promoted without regard to normal order,
leading to exploitation of the populace for personal advancement.
I request that, as in the Hóngwǔ era,
all grain be purchased at market prices with state funds,
without seizing the people's property,
and that performance evaluations not solely judge ability by accumulated grain.
Regarding the abuses in 'cleansing the army' (*qīngjūn*),
before Hóngxī they lay with banner officers,
and after Xuāndé they lay with village headmen.
When the abuses were with banner officers,
the household registers were still intact.
But with village headmen, they confused even the registers.
It is advisable to consult old records to eliminate these malpractices.
As for people suffering from disasters,
I beg for compassion.
The firewood and charcoal of the Xīxīn Directorate are sufficient for several years;
in disaster-stricken prefectures and counties,
these should be completely halted and exempted,
and the various paints and miscellaneous levies from the four directions likewise.
This is an urgent task to save the people."
The emperor largely adopted his suggestions.
In the eighth year,
civil and military officials presented a memorial on current governance due to portents and disasters.
Jīng drafted the memorial,
and notably criticized the matter of music and drama,
his words being especially pointed and direct.
The emperor secretly ordered a eunuch to investigate the drafter.
Minister Gěng Yù said:
"The Ministry of Personnel is at the head of the memorial;
Yù indeed drafted it."
Jīng said:
"The draft came from Jīng's hand.
If there is guilt,
blame Jīng."
The age praised both as virtuous.
The next year,
he succeeded Yè Qí as Minister of Revenue (*hùbù shàngshū*).
At that time, Xiàozōng was benevolent and lenient,
but the Ministry of Revenue was particularly a hotbed of corrupt officials and scoundrels;
those who abused their power for private gain were countless.
The slightest displeasure
would be followed by slander.
Jīng strictly adhered to the established regulations of the ancestors,
without any hesitation.
He extended deadlines for arrears, eased collection,
and curtailed excessive waste.
Whenever disasters were reported from various regions,
he would review them and propose exemptions.
He often dispatched officials to supervise tax collection;
those who collected too much were given a low evaluation,
which somewhat curbed the harsh and strict practices.
The Imperial Attendant Zhào Xúān offered land in Xióngxiàn as an estate for the Eastern Palace.
Jīng and others impeached Xúān for violating regulations,
and he was sent to imperial prison.
However, the emperor subsequently ordered an official to investigate the truth based on a report from the Censorate.
Jīng and others argued again, saying:
"Tàizǔ and Tàizōng established a system
where idle land was open for the people to cultivate.
If, due to the words of wicked people, it is registered as state land,
then the granting and seizure of land
will entirely depend on the words of wicked people,
and the common people will have no means of livelihood."
Soon after, the investigators and Circuit Censor Gāo Quán reported that there were only seventy *qǐng* of idle land,
all mixed with private land.
Therefore, the emperor followed Jīng's advice, returning the land to the people
and punishing Xúān.
The eunuch Hé Dǐng impeached the imperial relative Zhāng Hèlǐng, who was imprisoned.
Jīng memorialized to rescue him,
offending the emperor, who sharply reproved him.
Yōng Wáng Yòu-hùn requested the tax collection office of Héngzhōu and the fishing administration of Héngyáng County.
Jīng argued that this should not be allowed.
The emperor accepted his advice,
ordering that from now on, for tax collections in all regions,
imperial princes' establishments were not to make such requests.
Eunuchs in charge of textile production
requested an additional 20,000 salt warrants from Liǎngzhè.
Jīng and others stated:
"Salt revenue supports the border defenses,
and should not be lavishly disbursed.
Moreover, in the reigns of the ancestors, the various weaving and dyeing bureaus had a fixed number for imperial use.
If it is said that consumption has increased,
then Jiāngnán and Liǎngzhè have already produced extra beyond the usual.
If it is said that there are not enough artisans,
then more than a thousand people are fed by the public treasury;
what are they doing?
It is clear that supplies may not be lacking,
but this merely leads Your Majesty to exhaust the people and waste resources."
The emperor did not agree.
Jīng feared this would become an annual custom,
and memorialized again, requesting to stop it for the future.
The emperor then ordered 5,000 warrants to be granted annually.
Previously,
the eunuch supervisors of granaries and transport were reduced according to the regulations at the end of the Chénghuà reign.
In the autumn of the eleventh year,
the emperor again increased the number, employing three more junior supervisors, such as Mò Yīng.
Jīng strongly remonstrated in a memorial,
but the emperor did not listen, saying they had already been dispatched.
The Inner Spirit Observatory (*nèi língtái*) requested one hundred superfluous soldiers from the Imperial Guard for sweeping and cleaning.
Jīng and others admonished against it,
but it was not accepted.
Jīng said:
"The ancestors established the Inner Observatory;
its location is extremely secret.
Now, suddenly adding a hundred people,
there will inevitably be those who leak secrets or speak carelessly."
The emperor understood
and immediately stopped the plan.
Chóng Wáng (崇王) petitioned to be granted over twenty *lǐ* (里) of reclaimed land in Hénán (河南).
Jīng (經) stated that it was inappropriate to grant it.
Xīng Wáng (興王) Yòu Yuán (祐杬) repeatedly petitioned for over 1,300 *qǐng* (頃) of land in various *chìmǎ* (赤馬) river estuaries and near-lake areas.
Jīng (經) contended against this in three memorials,
and it was ultimately not granted.
The Emperor bestowed over 400 *qǐng* (頃) of land in Sùníng (肅寧) and other counties upon Shòuníng Hóu (壽寧侯) Zhāng Hèlǐng (張鶴齡).
His household then encroached upon three times that amount of commoners' land,
and even beat a commoner to death.
The case was sent down to Governor Gāo Quán (高銓) for investigation and report.
Quán (銓) reported that little of it was arable,
and requested that it remain assigned to the commoners for taxation,
but this was not allowed.
At that time, the estates of princely establishments and noble relatives were typically taxed at three *fēn* (分) of silver per *mǔ* (畝).
However, Hèlǐng (鶴齡) alone memorialized to increase the tax by two *fēn* (分),
and applied it universally even to sandy land.
Jīng (經) strongly protested and submitted a memorial,
whereupon the Emperor ordered Vice Minister Xǔ Jìn (許進) to accompany eunuch Zhū Xiù (朱秀) to re-examine it.
Jīng (經) said:
"The land has already been re-investigated twice.
Now, to send envoys again
only adds to the trouble and annoyance.
In the past, Tàizǔ (太祖) reduced the tax in Qīngtián (青田) because of Liú Jī (劉基),
collecting five *hé* (合) of rice,
desiring that Jī's (基) fellow villagers and descendants would praise Jī (基) for generations.
Now, Xīngjì (興濟) has given birth to the Empress.
It is precisely appropriate to show compassion to the people and reduce their taxes,
so that they may bear gratitude for generations.
Why then should the common people harbor endless resentment?"
Shortly thereafter,
Jìn (進) and others returned and reported that this land belonged to Bó Quán (柏權), a member of Xiàn Miào's (憲廟) imperial relatives, and to commoners;
it could not be seized.
The Emperor ultimately granted it to Hèlǐng (鶴齡),
and, as he requested, increased the tax,
but ordered that Quán (權) be compensated for its value,
and the commoners' rent quotas be abolished.
Jīng (經) and others again remonstrated, saying:
"The taxation of the Eastern Palace and princely estates has its own precedents.
It is inappropriate for Hèlǐng (鶴齡) to be uniquely favored.
Quán (權) is the family of the Late Emperor's consort;
he is also a relative of the imperial family.
Although it is nominally compensation,
it is in fact seizure.
The world will say that Your Majesty only favors the Empress's relatives,
and disregards the imperial relatives of the previous reign."
The Emperor ultimately did not accept it.
Dàtóng (大同) was short of warhorses,
and Mǎ Wénshēng (馬文升) requested silver from the Tàicāng (太倉) to purchase them.
Jīng (經) said:
"Grain and horses each have their own respective offices.
The ancestral instruction is that the Six Ministries should not encroach upon one another.
The Ministry of War encroaching upon the authority of the Ministry of Revenue is not in accordance with the ancestral instruction."
The Emperor therefore changed the allocation to silver from the Tàipú (太僕) to provide for it.
Supervising Secretary Lǔ Áng (魯昂) requested that all tax and corvée funds be collected and submitted to the Tàicāng (太倉).
Jīng (經) said:
"If the expenses for weaving, imperial grants, Daoist rituals, and construction are not curtailed,
yet one desires to collect all the wealth under heaven,
this is contradictory."
An internal official conveyed an imperial decree demanding 30,000 *liǎng* (兩) of silver from the Tàicāng (太倉) for lamp expenses.
Jīng (經) withheld it and did not give it.
Jīng (經) was upright and principled,
and fond of giving strong remonstrances.
Even if he seriously displeased the Emperor's will, he did not care.
Eunuchs and noble relatives all feared and resented him.
When Grand Eunuch Lǐ Guǎng (李廣) died,
the Emperor obtained a ledger of gifts from court officials,
and was greatly enraged.
The Censorate and Supervising Offices then impeached various officials for illicit connections,
and Jīng's (經) name was among them.
Jīng (經) submitted a memorial, saying:
"Yesterday, the Censorate and Supervising Offices impeached court officials for vying for Lǐ Guǎng's (李廣) favor,
and my name was improperly included.
Although I have received imperial grace by not being questioned,
I harbor hurt and pain,
with no way to clear myself.
People vying for Lǐ Guǎng's (李廣) favor
hoped that he would speak on their behalf to Your Majesty,
seeking imperial favor and patronage.
Your Majesty, please consider if Guǎng (廣) ever mentioned your servant's name when he was alive.
Furthermore, the ledger of illicit connections and gifts is complete and available;
I beg you to check if my name is on it.
Moreover, strictly interrogate Guǎng's (廣) family members.
If your servant possessed even an inch of gold or a foot of silk,
then punish your servant for the crime of illicit connections,
execute me in the public marketplace,
to serve as a warning against shameless vying for favor.
If I am not involved,
I also beg Your Majesty to clear my name,
so that I may fully exert myself
and continue to serve Your Sacred Intelligence.
If I am made to endure this stain and humiliation,
even if I die and fill a ditch,
my eyes will not close."
The Emperor responded with words of comfort.
In the thirteenth year,
there was a celestial anomaly.
He himself requested retirement.
The request was granted,
and he was bestowed with an imperial edict and a relay post,
promoted to Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent,
and ● Zhōng (鍾) succeeded him.
Court officials vied to submit memorials requesting him to stay,
and over eighty memorials recommending him came from within and outside the capital,
all were shelved.
Upon Wǔzōng's (武宗) ascension,
officials of the Censorate again recommended him.
He was summoned to be Minister of Revenue of Nánjīng (南京),
but did not assume the post due to mourning his stepmother.
In the third year of Zhèngdé (正德),
his mourning period ended.
Jīng's (經) son-in-law, Minister of War Cáo Yuánfāng (曹元方), who was close to Liú Jǐn (劉瑾),
said that Jīng (經), though old, could still be used.
So he was summoned to be Minister of Rites.
He firmly declined but was not permitted,
and was forced to accept the summons.
After serving for several months, he pleaded illness and departed.
In the third month of the fifth year, he died,
at the age of seventy-one.
He was posthumously granted Grand Tutor,
and given the posthumous title Wénduān (文端).
His son, Zēng (曾),
was a *jìnshì* (進士).
He served as Right Administration Vice Commissioner of Zhèjiāng (浙江).
Gěng Yù (耿裕),
courtesy name Hàowèn (好問),
was the son of Gěng Jiǔchóu (耿九疇), Minister of Justice.
He became a *jìnshì* (進士) in the fifth year of Jǐngtài (景泰).
He was appointed *shùjíshì* (庶吉士),
then conferred as Supervising Secretary of the Bureau of Revenue,
and later transferred to the Bureau of Works.
In the early Tiānshùn (天順) era,
because Jiǔchóu (九疇) was Right Censor-in-Chief,
Yù (裕) was reappointed as Compiler.
Jiǔchóu (九疇) was demoted for impeaching Shí Hēng (石亨),
and Yù (裕) was also banished as Prefectural Judge of Sìzhōu (泗州).
After completing his father's mourning,
he was reappointed to Dìngzhōu (定州).
In the early Chénghuà (成化) era,
he was summoned back to resume his post as Compiler,
and successively served as Director of Studies and Chancellor of the Guózǐjiàn (國子監).
Young marquises and earls all studied at the Directorate.
Yù (裕) compiled exemplary sayings and deeds of ancient feudal lords and noble relatives into a book and taught it to them.
The Emperor heard of this and praised it as good.
He successively served as Right and Left Vice Minister of Personnel.
Due to implication by Minister Yǐn Mín (尹旻),
his salary was suspended twice.
Later,
he succeeded Mín (旻) as Minister.
Grand Secretary Wàn Ān (萬安) was not in harmony with Yù (裕),
and Lǐ Zīshěng (李孜省) privately favored his fellow townsman Lǐ Yù (李裕),
wishing to have him replace Yù (裕),
so they conspired against him.
Implicated in an affair,
Yù (裕) was transferred to Nánjīng (南京) as Vice Minister Lǐ Chún (黎淳),
and his salary was confiscated.
Officials of the Censorate again jointly impeached,
but he was pardoned.
Yù (裕) entered to give thanks,
but after he left,
the Emperor angrily said:
"I have pardoned Yù's (裕) offense twice,
he should thank me twice.
Now he thanks me only once,
is it because of the salary confiscation
that he is discontented?"
Zīshěng (孜省) and others then conspired to ruin him,
so he was transferred to the Ministry of Rites in Nánjīng (南京),
and Lǐ Yù (李裕) took his place.
A year later,
Xiàozōng (孝宗) ascended the throne, and he was transferred to Nánjīng (南京) as Assistant to Military Affairs in the Ministry of War.
In the first year of Hongzhi's reign,
he was summoned and appointed as the Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū).
At that time, both public and private expenditures were extravagant,
with expenses increasing daily.
Yù corrected these issues as they arose.
In response to natural disasters and anomalies, he submitted memorials detailing current affairs and advocating for the rectification of abuses by censorial officials.
He made many representations both before and after,
the main thrust of which was to advocate for frugality.
When Investigating Censor (Jǐshìzhōng) Zhèng Zōngrén memorialized to cut down on the supplies of the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Guānglù Sì),
Yù and others requested that his memorial be accepted.

Censor (Yùshǐ) Tián Yūn, who was inspecting the Court of Imperial Entertainments, requested to borrow silver from the Grand Granary (Tàicāng) to repay the debt, because the insufficient supply funds had caused burdens on the common households.
He requested to borrow silver from the Grand Granary to repay it.
Yù and others stated
that they suspected corruption and embezzlement.
They requested an imperial edict instructing the relevant authorities to prohibit and prevent such abuses,
and the emperor followed all their suggestions.
The eunuchs guarding Nánjīng requested an increase in daily offerings for the Fèngxiān Temple (Fèngxiān Diàn).
Yù and others disagreed.
When the emperor first ascended the throne,
he expelled the Tibetan monks (fān sēng) back to their native lands,
only keeping fifteen individuals, such as the wet nurse's servant Bāndān.
Later, many of them secretly hid in the capital,
recruiting others,
and Daoist rituals (zhāi jiào) revived.
When censorial officials raised objections,
Yù and others then strongly requested their expulsion.
The emperor then allowed 182 people to stay,
expelling all the rest.
The office of the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù Gōngxiè) caught fire,
and Yù, along with Vice Ministers (Shìláng) Ní Yuè and Zhōu Jīng, requested punishment.
They were impeached and imprisoned.
Later,
they were released,
but their salaries were suspended.
Initially,
both Sāmǎ'érhǎn and Tǔlúfān offered lions as tribute.
The Grand Eunuch (Tàijiàn) Fù Dé, who was guarding Gānsù, first presented their likenesses.
Investigating Censor (Xún'àn Yùshǐ) Chén Yáo requested that they be rejected.
Yù and others begged to follow Yáo's request,
and to punish Dé for violating the imperial edict,
but the emperor did not agree.
Later, the foreign envoys came again,
stayed in the capital,
and were frequently summoned.
Yù and others stated:
"These foreigners are uncivilized.
We allowed them to come for tribute missions, giving them a chance to reform.
However, they secretly call themselves Khans (Kèhán) again,
and raise armies to violate our borders.
Your Majesty grants special favors to their envoys
at a time when they are being obstinate and defiant.
They will think that the Heavenly Court fears them,
which will only encourage their arrogance.
Moreover, lions are wild beasts;
they are not worth treasuring."
The emperor then sent their envoys back.
Soon after, he replaced Wáng Shù as Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū)
and was given the additional title of Grand Tutor to the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Tàibǎo).
When artisans such as Lǐ Lún from the Directorate for Imperial Manufactories (Yùyòng Jiān) obtained official posts through internal decrees,
Yù stated:
"There was an earlier edict that stated,
'Civil officials who are not recommended by Our Ministry and receive appointments without request
shall be referred to the Ministry of Justice (Fǎsī) for investigation and punishment.'
Now, appointing Lún and others
discredits the previous edict,
which is unacceptable."
Investigating Censors (Jǐshìzhōng) Lǚ Xiàn and others all memorialized on this issue.
Yù also submitted another memorial in protest,
but was ultimately not heeded.
Yù was frank, straightforward, and upright,
and well-versed in court regulations.
During his several years in charge of personnel,
he showed no partiality,
nor was he swayed by praise or criticism,
and his administration of personnel was deemed fair.
He lived simply.
Though his family enjoyed two generations of wealth and prominence,
his household remained unadorned,
and both father and son were renowned for their virtue.
He died in the first month of the ninth year,
at the age of sixty-seven.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Tutor (Tàibǎo)
and given the posthumous name Wénkè.
Ní Yuè,
courtesy name Shùnzī,
was from Shàngyuán.
His father, Qiān,
was commanded to offer sacrifices at the Northern Peak.
His mother dreamt of a crimson-robed deity entering the room,
and subsequently gave birth to Yuè,
hence he was named after the dream.
Qiān eventually served as Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū) in Nánjīng
and was given the posthumous name Wénxī.
Yuè became a Jinshi (Jìnshì)
in the eighth year of Tiānshùn.
He was appointed as a Bachelor in the Hanlin Academy (Shùjíshì)
and then as a Compiler (Biānxiū).
During the Chénghuà reign,
he successively served as a Reader-Academician (Shìdú Xuéshì)
and lectured the Heir Apparent in the Eastern Palace.
In the twenty-second year, he was promoted to Right Vice Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Yòu Shìláng)
and continued to attend the Imperial Lectures (Jīngyán).
In the early Hóngzhì reign,
he was appointed Left Vice Minister (Zuǒ Shìláng).
Yuè was fond of learning,
had a quick wit in writing,
and was broadly knowledgeable in matters of governance.
Minister Gěng Yù was upright and held firmly to principles,
but matters concerning ritual texts and regulations were often left to Yuè to decide.
In the sixth year,
Yù was transferred to the Ministry of Personnel,
and Yuè then replaced him as Minister (Shàngshū).
An imperial edict summoned the Imperial Preceptor (Guóshī) Língzhànzhú to Sìchuān.
Yuè strongly remonstrated,
but the emperor did not agree.
Investigating Censor (Jǐshìzhōng) Xià Áng, Censor (Yùshǐ) Zhāng Zhēn, and others successively argued against it,
and the matter was eventually dropped.
At that time, the construction of various princely mansions
was grand and magnificent,
exceeding the precedents of Yǒnglè and Xuāndé.
Yuè requested that standard regulations be promulgated.
Furthermore, concerning the natural disasters reported from all directions,
the Ministry of Rites would compile and memorialize them at the end of the year,
which often became a mere formality.
He then meticulously arranged them by month and day,
extensively citing classical texts and historical records for verification.
He urged the emperor to diligently study,
open avenues for expression,
lighten taxes and corvée,
be cautious with punishments,
dismiss corrupt officials,
promote loyal and upright individuals,
reduce redundant staff,
stop Daoist rituals,
curtail construction,
and cease indiscriminate rewards.
The emperor largely adopted his suggestions.
Left Vice Minister (Zuǒ Shìláng) Xú Qióng was related to the empress's family
and plotted to replace Yuè.
In the ninth year,
the position of Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū) in Nánjīng became vacant,
and Qióng was recommended by the court.
An edict granted Yuè the additional title of Grand Tutor to the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Tàibǎo) and sent him to assume that post,
and Qióng indeed replaced Yuè.
Soon after, Yuè was appointed Participant in Military Affairs of the Ministry of War (Bīngbù Cānzàn Jīwù) in Nánjīng.
Upon his return,
he replaced Tú Tōng as Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū).
He strictly rejected all requests for favoritism,
and was not swayed by reputation,
and his administration of personnel was deemed fair.
Yuè had a towering physique,
a stern and solemn demeanor,
and was good at making important decisions.
Whenever the entire court gathered for discussions,
he would make a decision with a single remark,
and those who heard him were pleased and convinced.
Among his colleagues,
he most admired Mǎ Wénshēng,
yet he never simply agreed with him on matters of discussion.
He presented over a hundred memorials before and after,
thoroughly exposing all corrupt practices in military and state affairs.
When his memorials were issued,
many people copied and circulated them.
His discourse on the harms of military campaigns in the northwest was particularly incisive.
Its outline stated: In recent years, Máolǐhái, Āluōhū, Bólúochū, and Jiājīasīlán have caused great border troubles.
This is because in the Hétào region,
the water and grass are lush and fertile,
making
it easy for encampment and grazing.
Thus, the bandits frequently occupy that land,
gathering their forces to raid.
The generals are cowardly,
often defending themselves within city walls.
If they ever encountered the enemy,
they were often defeated.
Since
they dared not break the enemy's vanguard,
they also could not intercept their retreat.
The enemy gained great profits when advancing,
and had no worries when retreating,
leading to persistent unrest by the military forces,
and endless border troubles.
Imperial
orders to launch expeditions resulted in three campaigns over four years,
without any achievement whatsoever.
Some returned having slept comfortably,
while others returned at their leisure.
They divided territories and received noble titles,
enjoying their time at court,
transporting silk
and carrying gold,
filling their private residences.
Moreover, every time a military campaign was launched,
reports of victories were immediately submitted,
rewards were indiscriminately bestowed,
and official ranks were lightly granted.
Some even wantonly killed innocent civilians,
falsely claiming
heads.
When the enemy had not yet been defeated,
they would always use fleeing as an excuse.
Those on whom rewards and honors were bestowed
were either children of private families or servants of powerful clans.
Meanwhile, the rank-and-file soldiers
and the people transporting provisions
would abandon their bones in desolate cities,
their flesh and blood nourishing wild grasses.
Heaven's wrath and human resentment,
misfortune deepens day by day,
this is no small matter.
The Jīngyíng (京營) has always been known for being superfluous and timid.
Keeping them stationed in the capital
was already feared to not strengthen the foundation,
yet they were lightly sent out to resist,
thereby profaning imperial majesty.
They would flee upon encountering battle,
nullifying the achievements of the border armies,
and becoming ridiculed by the enemy.
Moreover, Yánsuí (延綏) is a border region,
far from the capital.
Xuānfǔ (宣府) and Dàtóng (大同) are also border regions,
closer to the capital.
There is a saying about the outer gate,
but here there is no strictness of the imperial shield.
Is this acceptable?
Recently, the Ministry of War suggested: ordering Xuānfǔ to dispatch five thousand troops,
and Dàtóng to dispatch ten thousand troops,
combining their forces to aid Yánsuí.
But they did not consider that the distance between them is great,
making round trips impractical,
causing people to suffer from constant transfers,
and horses to be exhausted by continuous travel.
