To make a feint to the east
and attack in the west is
the cunning tactic of bandits.
To strike where the enemy is weak and hit where they are strong is
a supreme strategy for military strategists.
If the elite forces are all sent to the west,
and the old and weak are left in the north,
what if there is an alarm in the north,
and the west cannot be left?
Both ends will be cut off,
and both far and near will be trapped.
Can this be considered a good plan?
As for the massing of soldiers and horses in Yánsuí,
and the immeasurable cost of provisions,
the people of Shānxī (山西) and Hénán (河南) are tasked with the duty of rapid transport of grain.
Traveling a thousand lí on foot,
husbands transport while wives provide,
fathers pull carts while sons carry loads.
Roads are filled with sorrow and resentment,
villages are empty.
If they are fortunate enough to arrive,
a bundle of hay costs a hundred coins,
a dòu of grain is double the price.
If they are unfortunate
enough to encounter bandits,
their lives will be lost,
what else is there to say?
If regular contributions are insufficient, there are "light levies."
If light levies are insufficient, there are "pre-collections."
Droughts and floods cannot be known in advance,
abundance and scarcity cannot be predicted.
How can collections be pre-arranged?
Furthermore, people are ordered to contribute hay and grain to compensate officials,
and those who curry favor with powerful nobles, private relatives, or old acquaintances
are sometimes given empty receipts,
resulting in no grain entering the granaries.
As for contributing grain for salt,
powerful families would use their influence and connections,
often claiming empty titles and selling them,
while merchants' expenses would double
or quintuple.
Official ranks become less esteemed day by day,
and the salt law becomes increasingly ineffective,
yet the border provisions remain unfulfilled as before.
The imperial court also disburses funds from the treasury to the borders,
amounting to hundreds of thousands of silver taels annually.
Those from Shānxī and Hénán who transport light levies to the border
contribute no less than hundreds of thousands annually.
As silver accumulates daily and increases, silver becomes cheaper;
as grain is dispersed daily and decreases, grain becomes more expensive.
And those who are ignorant
thus practice the art of "feeding monkeys"
within the system of maintaining troops.
Whether with tea and salt,
or with silver and cloth,
ostensibly to offset grain prices,
in reality, it is to embezzle military provisions.
Therefore, the imperial court has worries about wasted provisions,
while soldiers have no joy
in satisfying their hunger.
As for wherever soldiers and horses pass,
they must by rule be provisioned.
In peacetime,
a person needs one dòu of rice daily,
a horse one bundle of hay daily.
In pursuit,
within a single day they might pass one
or two forts,
or three or four cities.
How can all be supplied?
And those in charge of custody skillfully devise schemes of embezzlement,
making expenses for everything encountered,
deceiving superiors and acting
selfishly,
nothing could be worse.
When inquiring about strategies to resist the enemy,
opinions are again divided.
Some suggest restoring the old strategic passes of Shòujiàng (受降),
and defending the old city of Dōngshèng (東勝),
so that mutual support can be established,
and coordinated actions can be easily controlled.
But to restore the cities north of the Hé (河),
troops must be stationed beyond the passes.
Sending an isolated and distant army,
traversing barren and desolate lands,
heavy baggage becomes a burden,
and providing provisions
is exceedingly difficult.
The enemy might raid in front,
and attack from behind.
Prolonging the campaign for a long time,
military provisions will run out.
Unable to advance and take the city,
unable to retreat and return,
one defeat will
greatly damage morale.
Others suggest leading an army of one hundred thousand,
carrying half a month's provisions,
brandishing military might,
sweeping clean the enemy's lairs,
leaving the Hétào (河套) empty.
This
is not a bad idea.
However, the armies of emperors
achieve victory by preserving their forces;
the methods of Sūn (孫) and Wú (吳)
involve waiting at ease for the weary enemy.
Now, to advance bravely,
searching far and attacking deep,
facing dangers and treading risks,
hoping for a one-in-ten-thousand chance of luck.
If supplies are carried far, heavy loads will be ineffective.
If troops penetrate deep, isolated forces cannot be reinforced.
Furthermore, the area in between is a thousand
lí,
with no cities or towns,
no accumulated stores to guard.
The enemy might move about and migrate,
exhausting our pursuit.
We would then be exposed and in a disadvantageous position,
trapped by the enemy.
Having
lost the opportunity for easy victory,
we will surely follow the path of utter defeat.
The most unresourceful suggestion
is to abandon Yánsuí and not defend it,
allowing soldiers and civilians to rest.
They do not know that every inch
of land and every commoner is received from our ancestors,
and cannot be neglected.
We previously lost Dōngshèng,
which is why today's harm is concentrated in Yánsuí,
and Guān (關) and Shǎnxī (陝西) are shaken.
If we abandon Yánsuí
now,
then future harm will fall upon Guān and Shǎnxī,
and the capital will be shaken.
The closer the bandits are, the greater the disaster.

Therefore, he proposed several matters: reinstating powerful generals, increasing fortifications, expanding watchtowers, recruiting militiamen, removing guest troops, clarifying rewards and punishments, tightening espionage, implementing military agricultural colonies, and restoring border transport.
At that time, the Ministry of War was advocating for military campaigns,
so not all of his proposals could be adopted.
He died in the tenth month of the fourteenth year,
at the age of fifty-eight.
He was posthumously granted the title of Shàobǎo (少保)
and given the posthumous name Wényì (文毅).
It was from Yuè (岳) that father and son in the Míng (明) dynasty served as officials in the Hánlín (翰林) Academy
and both received the posthumous name Wén (文).
Mǐn Guī,
courtesy name Cháoyīng,
was a native of Wūchéng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the eighth year of Tiānshùn (1464).
He was appointed an Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ).
He was sent out to inspect Hénán,
and became known for his forceful character.
In the sixth year of Chénghuà (1470), he was promoted to Vice Commissioner of Jiāngxī (Jiāngxī Fùshǐ),
and later to Surveillance Commissioner of Guǎngdōng (Guǎngdōng Ànchásǐ).
After a long time,
he was appointed Right Assistant Censor-in-Chief (Yòu Qiāndū Yùshǐ) to patrol and govern Jiāngxī (Xúnfǔ Jiāngxī).
The prefectures of Nán and Gàn were plagued by many bandits,
who were mostly household retainers of powerful clans.
Guī requested that if a bandit was caught, their master should be implicated (liánsít).
The judicial authorities deliberated and agreed to follow this.
Yǐn Zhí and his associates conspired with Lǐ Zīxǐng,
and obtained an imperial decree to reprimand Guī for failing to suppress the bandits,
demoting him to Surveillance Commissioner of Guǎngxī (Guǎngxī Ànchásǐ).
When Emperor Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief (Yòu Fùdū Yùshǐ),
and given charge of patrolling and governing Shùntiān (Xúnfǔ Shùntiān).
He entered the central government as Right Vice Minister of Justice (Xíngbù Yòu Shìláng),
and was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief (Yòu Dūdū Yùshǐ),
serving as Supreme Commander of Military Affairs in Liǎngguǎng (Zǒngdū Liǎngguǎng Jūnwù).
He collaborated with the Commander-in-Chief (Zǒngbīng Guān), Má Rùi, to suppress the Guǔtián tóng.
Associate Commander-in-Chief (Fùzǒngbīng) Mǎ Jùn and Consultative Official (Cānyì) Mǎ Xuàn penetrated deeply from Línguì,
were defeated and died,
and the army subsequently retreated.
An imperial edict ordered a suspension of his salary until the rebels were suppressed.
Guī again advanced his troops,
and successively captured seven stockades,
whereupon all other rebels submitted.
In the seventh year of Hóngzhì (1494), he was transferred to Minister of Justice in Nánjīng (Nánjīng Xíngbù Shàngshū),
and soon after was summoned to become Left Censor-in-Chief (Zuǒ Dūdū Yùshǐ).
In the eleventh year (1498),
when the Crown Prince came of age,
he was given the additional title of Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shǎobǎo).
In the thirteenth year (1500), he succeeded Bái Áng as Minister of Justice (Xíngbù Shàngshū),
and was again given the additional title of Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Tàibǎo).
Due to anomalies and disasters, he and Censor-in-Chief (Dūdū Yùshǐ) Dài Shān jointly presented eight matters concerning current administration,
and also presented four matters concerning penal justice,
most of which were approved.
Guī had long been a judicial official,
and in deliberating on cases, he always reconciled the circumstances with the law,
leaning towards benevolence and leniency.
In Xuānfǔ, the deviant person Lǐ Dàomíng gathered a crowd to burn incense.
The巡抚 Xúnfǔ Liú Cōng believed the words of the chiliarch (qiānhù) Huáng Zhēn,
and implicated dozens of families,
claiming that Dàomíng intended to lead northern invaders to attack Xuānfǔ.
When Dàomíng was arrested and interrogated, there was no evidence.
Guī then decided to convict Dàomíng alone,
and all others were released,
while Zhēn was punished for his crime,
and Cōng was also imprisoned and demoted.
When the Emperor personally interrogated Wú Yīguàn,
he intended to impose capital punishment.
Guī stepped forward and said:
"Yīguàn's confession was not true to the facts;
his crime warrants exile (tú)."
The Emperor did not agree,
but Guī insisted on his original opinion.
The Emperor was angry,
and Dài Shān intervened to mediate.
The Emperor then softened his wrath,
and ordered a new proposal.
Guī eventually submitted his original proposal,
and the Emperor was displeased.
He summoned Liú Dàxià to discuss it.
Liú Dàxià replied:
"It is the duty of a judicial official to uphold the law;
he should not be severely punished."
The Emperor remained silent for a long time,
then said:
"I also know that Guī is an old and experienced official, not easily found,
but he is too stubborn in this matter."
Ultimately, Guī's opinion was followed.
In the sixth month of the first year of Zhèngdé (1506),
being over seventy years old, he twice petitioned to retire,
but was not granted.
When Liú Jǐn rose to power,
the nine ministers (jiǔ qīng) knelt before the palace to earnestly remonstrate,
and Hán Wén was dismissed.
Guī again repeatedly submitted memorials requesting retirement.
In the second month of the following year, an imperial edict added the title of Grand Guardian (Shǎobǎo),
and he was granted a decree to return home by courier.
He died in the tenth month of the sixth year (1511)
at the age of eighty-two.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Tutor (Tàibǎo),
and given the posthumous name Zhuāngyì.
His great-grandson Rúlín
was Minister of Rites in Nánjīng (Nánjīng Lǐbù Shàngshū).
Rúlín's great-great-grandson Hóngxué
was Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū).
Hóngxué's cousin Mèngdé
was Minister of War (Bīngbù) with responsibility for military administration (Róngzhèng).
Several others also served as ordinary officials.
Dài Shān,
courtesy name Tíngzhēn,
was a native of Fúliáng.
His father, Hāng,
served as Professor of Jiāxīng (Jiāxīng Jiàoshòu) through a local recommendation (xiāngjǔ),
and was learned and upright in conduct.
Several wealthy families sent their servant boys to enroll in school,
but Hāng refused.
They bribed a superior official to pressure him,
but he remained even more steadfast in his refusal,
thus offending them,
and was dismissed on other charges.
Shān was fond of learning as a child.
Towards the end of the Tiānshùn era,
he and Liú Dàxià both passed the *jìnshì* examination.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ),
and was put in charge of educational administration in Nánjī (Dū Nánjī Xuézhèng).
In the fourteenth year of Chénghuà (1478), he was transferred to Vice Commissioner of Shǎnxī (Shǎnxī Fùshǐ),
still supervising educational administration.
He rectified himself and led by example in his teaching,
and scholars all loved and admired him.
He successively served as Surveillance Commissioner of Zhèjiāng (Zhèjiāng Ànchásǐ),
and Left and Right Administration Commissioner of Fújiàn (Fújiàn Zuǒ, Yòu Bùzhèngshǐ),
never taking any local products during his entire tenure.
In the second year of Hóngzhì (1489), on the recommendation of Wáng Shù, he was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief (Yòu Fùdū Yùshǐ),
and governed Yún​yáng (Fúzhì Yúnyáng).
The Shǔ bandits, led by Yěwánggāng, marauded and plundered Zhúshān and Pínglì.
Shān combined troops from Chuān and Shǎn,
and dispatched Associate Commissioner (Fùshǐ) Zhū Hàn and others to suppress and capture their leader.
The rest were treated as having been coerced (xiécóng),
and many lives were saved.
He successively served as Left and Right Vice Minister of Justice (Xíngbù Zuǒ, Yòu Shìláng),
working with Ministers (Shàngshū) Hé Qiáoxīn and Péng Sháo.
Zhōngbǐng, Prince Nínghuà of the Jìn Prefecture, was lecherous, cruel, and unfilial.
An investigation failed to confirm this,
so Shān and others were sent again to investigate,
and consequently, Zhōngbǐng was stripped of his title and imprisoned.
Shān was promoted to Minister of Justice in Nánjīng (Nánjīng Xíngbù Shàngshū).
After a long time,
he was summoned to become Left Censor-in-Chief (Zuǒ Dūdū Yùshǐ).
In the seventeenth year (1504),
when inspecting capital officials,
Shān was upright and not given to compromise.
Censors (Gěishìzhōng) Wú Shùn and Wáng Gài, suspecting they would be dismissed,
repeatedly submitted memorials slandering Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū) Mǎ Wénshēng,
and also accused Shān of allowing his wife and children to accept bribes.
Shān and others petitioned to be dismissed,
but the Emperor comforted them and asked them to stay.
Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ) Féng Yǔnzhōng and others stated:
"Wénshēng and Shān have served for successive reigns,
and their integrity and virtue are well-known;
we should not abandon the established regulations due to unfounded accusations."
Consequently, Shùn and Gài were sent to the imperial prison,
and Wénshēng and Shān were ordered to immediately proceed with the evaluation.
Shān and others said:
"The two men, anticipating their dismissal,
first impeached us.
If we dismiss them now, they will surely say that we are acting out of personal vendetta.
If we avoid dismissing them,
we will betray our commission and allow deceivers to prevail."
The Emperor ordered their records of service to be submitted,
and both were dismissed.
Subsequently,
Liú Jiàn and others, during an imperial audience,
strongly argued that Gài's crime was minor and
that he should be reassigned.
The Emperor, however, currently favored Wénshēng and Shān,
and ultimately did not accept this.
In his later years, the Emperor summoned high officials for audiences.
Shān and Dàxià had particularly frequent face-to-face meetings with him during banquets.
One day,
they were attending the Emperor.
The Emperor said:
“It is time for performance reviews,
and all the high officials are staying at home.
As for you two ministers,
what harm is there in seeing guests daily?”
He took out white gold from his sleeve and bestowed it upon them,
saying:
“You are young officials and incorruptible.”
He also instructed them not to thank him in court,
saying:
“I fear others might become jealous.”
Shān repeatedly requested retirement due to old age and illness,
but the Emperor always issued gracious edicts urging him to stay,
sending doctors and bestowing food,
with increasing comfort and reassurance.
Shān was deeply moved to tears,
and privately said to Dàxià:
“Shān is old and sick, and my son is young.
I fear I may pass away like the morning dew one day.
You are my friend of the same age,
why begrudge a word for me?”
Dàxià replied:
“Yes, yes.”
Later, after Dàxià finished his audience and banquet,
the Emperor asked about Shān’s illness.
Dàxià reported that Shān was truly ill,
and begged for compassion to allow him to return home.
The Emperor said:
“Did he ask you to speak for him?
When a host is firm in wanting to keep a guest,
the guest is strongly persuaded to stay.
Cannot Shān stay for Us?
Moreover, We entrust the affairs of the realm to you all,
treating you like family, like father and sons.
Now that peace has not yet manifested,
how can you bear to speak of returning?”
Dàxià went out and informed Shān,
who wept and said:
“This official will die in this office.”
After the Emperor passed away,
Shān, unwilling to leave due to the new emperor's succession,
forcefully attended to his duties despite his illness.
When his illness recurred,
he then died.
He was posthumously granted Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince,
and given the posthumous title Gōngjiǎn.
A eulogy says: Xiàozōng was indeed a sagacious ruler,
for good reason.
He was modest and self-disciplined,
and discerning in employing people.
Liú, Xiè, and other worthies held positions in the government,
while Wáng Shù, Hé Qiáoxīn, Péng Sháo, and others served as heads of the Seven Departments,
together maintaining and assisting him.
The court had many noble men,
almost comparable to the flourishing times of Kāiyuán and Qìnglì.
Although Qiáoxīn and Sháo did not fully realize their potential,
their reputation was prominent throughout the court and country.
History states that during the reign of Sòng Rénzōng,
the country was never without favorites,
yet they were insufficient to harm the essence of a well-governed era.
The court was never without petty individuals,
yet they were insufficient to overcome the spirit of the virtuous.
Xiàozōng’s early reign
was also somewhat similar.
Otherwise,
inheriting the later years of Xiànzōng’s reign,
and wishing to prevent government from being unduly interfered with,
prevent excessive waste of resources,
nurture the nation’s vitality,
and ensure peace both within and without,
how could it be easily achieved?
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 72: Zhōu Hóngmó, Yáng Shǒuchén (younger brother Shǒuzhǐ, son Màoyuán, Màorén), Zhāng Yuánzhēn (Chén Yīn), Fù Hàn, Zhāng Shēng, Wú Kuān, Fù Guī, Liú Chūn, Wú Yǎn, Gù Qīng, Liú Ruì
Zhōu Hóngmó,
courtesy name Yáobì,
a native of Chángníng.
In the tenth year of Zhèngtǒng,
he passed the imperial examination as a *jìnshì*.
He was appointed editor.
He was widely learned and had an excellent memory,
was skilled in literary composition,
familiar with the precedents and institutions of the current dynasty,
and enjoyed discussing statecraft.
In the first year of Jǐngtài, he submitted a memorial urging the Emperor to personally attend the imperial lectures
and diligently handle state affairs,
and then presented twelve current affairs matters.
He was promoted again to侍讀 (Attendant Reader).
In the second year of Tiānshùn, he took charge of the Southern Academy.
Upon Xiànzōng’s succession,
he again presented current affairs matters,
stating that there were three ways for a monarch to protect the country: to vigorously pursue sagely learning,
to cultivate internal governance,
and to repel foreign invasions.
The first item under vigorously pursuing sagely learning was: to rectify the mind.
The five items under cultivating internal governance were: to seek out true talents,
remove the unworthy,
commend the loyal and good,
abolish redundant positions,
and care for the grain transport system.
The six items under repelling foreign invasions were: to select generals,
train soldiers,
study battle formations,
maintain weapons,
ensure sufficient provisions,
and pacify the borders.
The Emperor praised and accepted his suggestions.
In the first year of Chénghuà,
the court discussed suppressing the Dūzhǎng Mán in Sìchuān.
Hóngmó submitted six strategies,
and an imperial edict ordered the military commanders to implement them.
He was promoted to Grand Secretary.
Soon after, he became Libationer of Nánjīng.
He reported that there were twenty red-board granaries in the Southern Directorate,
where Empress Gāo had stored grain to support the wives and children of the students;
he suggested they be repaired,
and the Emperor agreed to it.
After observing the mourning period for his mother,
he was transferred to the Northern Directorate.
In the eleventh year,
he stated that scholarly customs were becoming superficial,
and requested the restoration of the school regulations from the Hóngwǔ era.
The Emperor praised and accepted his suggestion,
ordering the Ministry of Rites to post the regulations.
The Earl of Chóngxìn, Fèi Huái, was ordered to study rites at the Directorate but
was long absent.
Hóngmó impeached him,
resulting in the stripping of his official cap and belt,
requiring him to attend the Directorate in a scholar’s kerchief,
and suspending half of his annual salary,
thus bringing solemnity to academic governance.
The image of Confucius was depicted with a twelve-streamer imperial crown,
but the number of dancers and ritual vessels did not match.
Hóngmó requested that the emperor’s ceremonial attire be fully prepared.
He also said:
“In ancient times, ringing jade chimes and zithers were the music for the hall,
while *shēng*, bells, *zhù*, and *yǔ* were the music for below the hall,
and the shield and feather dances were performed on the two staircases.
Now, the feather dance is performed above,
and musical instruments are below,
which is not the ancient system,
and should be changed.”
Minister Zōu Gàn countered and stopped him,
but Hóngmó submitted another memorial to dispute.
The Emperor ultimately approved his proposal.
He was promoted to Vice Minister of Rites, Right.
After a long time,
he was transferred to Vice Minister of Rites, Left.
As the *xuánjī yùhéng* (armillary sphere) interpreted by Cài Chuán,
which later generations had followed in its construction,
often did not match observations,
it should be remade.
The Emperor immediately entrusted this to Hóngmó.
Hóngmó replaced it with wood,
completing it in ten days.
In the seventeenth year, he was promoted to Minister.
In the twentieth year, he was granted Junior Guardian of the Crown Prince.
In the twenty-first year,
there were celestial phenomena,
and he presented various recommendations,
many of which the Emperor adopted.
In the fourth month of the first year of Hóngzhì,
thunder, wind, and hail struck Tiānshòushān,
destroying many tiles and animal figures on the roofs of the halls.
Hóngmó again strongly urged self-reflection and reform,
and the Emperor deeply accepted his advice.
Hóngmó was dignified and somewhat reserved,
and being from the same hometown as Wàn Ān,
he was quite friendly with him when Ān was in the government.
At this point,
censors successively memorialized against him,
and he retired from office and returned home.
He died three years later,
at the age of seventy-two.
He was given the posthumous title Wén'ān.
Hóngmó once said:
“When scholars enter official service,
they sometimes go thousands of *lǐ* from their hometowns,
becoming unfamiliar with local customs and
also offending local sentiments.
It is better to select and appoint them closer to home.
Officials of princely establishments remain un-promoted their entire lives,
which deviates from ancestral regulations,
and should be slightly altered.
The Dūzhǎng Mán and Báilúoluó Yìzǐ have rebelled repeatedly.
A special *zhǎngguānsī* (chief official’s office) should be established,
and suitable individuals selected to take charge,
to avoid future troubles.”
Before his death,
he still submitted ten proposals for “Pacifying China and Securing the Four Borders.”
Such was his fondness for making suggestions.
Yáng Shǒuchén,
courtesy name Wéixīn,
was a man from Yín.
His grandfather, Fàn,
possessed learning and integrity.
He once instructed Shǒuchén in the scholarship of profound thought and practical application.
Yáng Shǒuchén passed the imperial examination in the second year of Jǐngtài as a *Jìnshì*,
and was appointed as a *Shùjíshì*,
then granted the position of Compilator.
At the beginning of Chénghuà,
he served as a lecturer for the imperial lectures (*Jīngyán Jiǎngguān*),
and was promoted to Attendant Lecturer.
After the completion of the *Yīngzōng Shílù* (Veritable Records of Emperor Yīngzōng),
he was transferred to Assistant Grand Secretary.
Soon after, he was promoted to Attendant Academician,
and participated in the compilation of the *Sòng Yuán Tōngjiàn Gāngmù* (Outline and Digest of the Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance for the Sòng and Yuán Dynasties).
After the period of mourning for his mother ended,
he was reinstated to his former office.
When Emperor Xiàozōng left the imperial residence to establish his own household,
Yáng Shǒuchén became a lecturer for the Crown Prince (*Dōnggōng Jiǎngguān*).
At that time, the *Wénhuá Dàxùn* (Great Instructions of the Wénhuá Hall) was being compiled,
and all matters concerning eunuchs were omitted.
Shǒuchén considered this incorrect,
and fully enumerated their good and bad points, their successes and failures.
When the book was completed,
he was promoted to Junior Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent.
When Emperor Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
all palace officials were promoted.
The administrators proposed Yáng Shǒuchén as Vice Minister of Personnel for the Right in Nánjīng.
The emperor lifted his brush and removed
the character
"Nánjīng".
His attendants said that Liú Xuān had already been made Vice Minister of the Right.
The emperor then changed Xuān to the Left,
and appointed Shǒuchén to replace him.
He participated in the compilation of the *Xiànzōng Shílù* (Veritable Records of Emperor Xiànzōng),
serving as Deputy Chief Editor.
In the first month of the first year of Hóngzhì,
he submitted a memorial saying: Mèngzǐ said,
"I dare not present the Way of Yáo and Shùn before the King."
What then is the Way of Yáo and Shùn?
The *Shū* (Classic of History) states,
"The human mind is precarious,
the mind of the
Dào is subtle.
Be refined, be unified,
sincerely hold fast to the Mean."
This is how Yáo and Shùn deeply obtained from within,
and it became the root of their governance.
Consulting the Four Peaks,
opening
the Four Gates,
clarifying the Four Eyes,
and extending to the Four Ears –
this is how Yáo and Shùn broadly utilized external resources,
and it became the纲 (guiding principle) for achieving good governance.
I, your humble servant, once had the honor of being a palace official.
I humbly observed Your
Majesty's clear reading of the classics,
but you never diligently inquired with your sagacious questions to thoroughly investigate the profound principles of the sages.
The Confucian officials merely presented textual interpretations,
but never offered detailed explanations to fully expound the essential ways of emperors and kings.
This means that what Your Majesty obtains from within is not yet deep.
Now, when holding court,
those whom you meet
are merely the grand demeanor of the high ministers.
How can you discern the true situations of worthy and unworthy individuals,
or the talents and conduct of minor
officials and distant officials?
How can you know?
When you retire from court, those you peruse
are merely the memorials of the hundred officials.
How can you see the regulations of the various departments
and the malpractices of the many clerks?
How can you perceive them?
What is heard and believed in the palace
is merely the words of the inner officials.
How can you hear the upright discussions of the hundred officials
and the multitudinous words of the myriad people?
How can you listen?
I fear that Your
Majesty's external resources are not yet broad.
I wish that you would follow the old system of your ancestors,
open both large and small imperial lectures,
and hold court twice a day.
The large imperial lectures and the morning court
should remain as before.
As for the small imperial lectures,
you must
select upright and learned officials
to take turns lecturing.
Whatever is unclear,
you should graciously bestow clear inquiries.
All the profound principles of the sages,
the grand ways of emperors and kings,
as well as the
worthiness or unworthiness of your subjects,
the successes and failures of governance,
and the joys and sorrows of the common people,
must be explained clearly and without doubt,
only then can they be practiced earnestly and without defect.
As for the classics of previous dynasties,
the ancestral
ordinances and instructions,
and the memorials of the hundred officials,
they should all be stored behind the Wénhuá Hall,
for Your Majesty to peruse after retiring from court.
Daily, one Grand Secretary and two lecturers should reside in the front hall's
right wing.
If there are doubts, they should be inquired about,
and only cease after they are thoroughly understood.
In a single day,
if the time spent in the Wénhuá Hall is ample
and the time spent in the Qiánqīng Palace is less,
then desires
will be few and the mind clear,
and when facing governance, there will be no confusion.
The deep inward attainment and the root of good governance will be established.
For the noon court, you should preside at the Wénhuá Gate,
with high ministers and censors taking turns
on duty.
For matters already detailed in memorials, use a memorandum,
briefly summarizing the oral report.
Your Majesty should inquire in detail and make decisions.
When civil and military officials from outside come for an audience,
let them itemize local
affairs,
orally present the main points,
and submit them to the various departments for discussion and evaluation.
Those who are taking leave to assume their posts
should be admonished according to their duties.
For major policy decisions, you should preside at the Wénhuá
Hall,
allowing high ministers to fully express their views,
without mutual evasion.
If inappropriate, allow the remonstrating officials to refute and correct.
For other matters submitted via memorials,
summon the Grand Secretaries to discuss face-to-face whether it is
appropriate or not,
and then issue replies.
And for those officials who report on affairs or take leave from court,
you must lower your tone and soften your expression,
inquire in detail and widely seek information,
striving to understand the sentiments of your subjects,
so that worthy talents are always before your
eyes,
and your sight and hearing are not biased by those around you.
By combining the ears and eyes of the entire realm to achieve clarity and wisdom,
then external resources will be broadly utilized and the guiding principles of good governance will be implemented.
If the imperial lectures and regular courts merely follow old customs,
and all memorials are submitted to inner officials for drafting imperial decrees and replies,
I fear that accumulated弊 (malpractices) will not be reformed,
and future troubles will
deepen.
Moreover, the current accumulated malpractices are countless.
Officials lack a sense of shame,
and scholars harbor many habits of superficial competition.
Education and moral influence are declining,
and laws and prohibitions are lax.
Customs are extravagant,
and resources are increasingly scarce;
the people are distressed, and banditry proliferates daily.
The city walls of the garrisons are not repaired,
and the granaries of the various prefectures are meagerly stocked.
Weapons are decaying and blunt,
and military ranks are empty.
Generals are arrogant and lazy, ignorant of warfare;
soldiers are weary and weak, unpracticed in battle.
If there should be an alarm,
how can it be resisted?
This is why your servant worries day and night,
even to the point of
neglecting sleep and forgetting food.
The Emperor greatly praised and accepted his suggestions.
Later, the noon court was indeed revived,
and high ministers were summoned for face-to-face discussions on governance,
all initiated by Yáng Shǒuchén.
Soon, due to the busy historical compilation work,
he requested to be relieved of his departmental duties.
His memorial was submitted three times,
and then he was appointed concurrently as a member of the Household of the Heir Apparent,
devoting himself exclusively to the imperial history office.
He died two years later.
He was posthumously given the epithet Wényì,
and posthumously granted the title of Minister of Rites.
His younger brother Shǒuzhǐ.
Sons Mào Yuán, Mào Rén.
Shǒuzhǐ,
courtesy name Wéilì.
In the early Chénghuà reign,
he placed first in the provincial examination,
and entered the Guóxué (National Academy).
When the Libationer Xíng Ràng was imprisoned,
he led the students of the Six Institutes to kneel before the imperial palace gate and plead for his冤 (redress for wrong).
In the fourteenth year,
he passed the metropolitan examination.
He was appointed Compiler.
When his term was completed,
it was customary for those in the capital not to be transferred to the secondary capital.
It so happened that his cousin Shǒusuí had been expelled by Lǐ Zīshěng,
who also wanted to expel Shǒuzhǐ,
so he was appointed Nánjīng Shìdú (Reader-in-waiting of Nanjing).
In the early Hóngzhì reign,
he was summoned to compile the Xiànzōng Shílù (Veritable Records of Emperor Xianzong),
and served in the Jīngyán (Imperial Lectures),
then was promoted twice to Shìjiǎng Xuéshì (Expositor-in-waiting of the Hanlin Academy).
When the Supervising Secretary Páng Pàn and others were all imprisoned for rescuing the Prefect Liú Xùn,
the Minister of Personnel Tú Yōng proposed to send other officials to temporarily fill their posts.
Shǒuzhǐ wrote a letter,
severely criticizing Tú Yōng's mistakes.
In the tenth year, the grand review of capital officials took place.
Shǒuzhǐ was then in charge of the academy,
and said:
"Your servant and Wáng Ào, Academian in charge of the Zhānshì Fǔ (Court of Imperial Stud),
are both subject to the Ministry's examination.
However, your servants each have subordinate officials.
If we join the Ministry of Personnel to examine our subordinates,
we would sit in the main hall;
but if we withdraw to be examined ourselves,
we would have to wait below the steps.
Our dynasty gives special favor to Academians;
at celebratory banquets,
they rank above officials of the fourth grade;
when the imperial carriage visits the Yōng (Imperial Academy),
they sit inside the Yílún Táng (Hall of Moral Principles),
ranked as third-grade officials.
This is the established custom.
Now, officials of the fourth grade are not included in the examination,
so Academians should not be either.
Your servants' duty is to lecture, read, and compose;
our performance is judged by Your Sacred Majesty,
and does not require examination."
The emperor approved the edict.
Academians not being subject to examination
began with Shǒuzhǐ.
He served as Deputy Compiler-in-chief when the Huìdiǎn (Collected Statutes) were being compiled.
Soon after, he was transferred to Nánjīng Lìbù Yòushìláng (Right Vice Minister of Personnel in Nanjing).
He once temporarily served in the Ministry of War,
and submitted five proposals concerning contemporary abuses.
He was then transferred to temporarily serve in the Guózǐjiān (Imperial Academy).
When he came to the capital for his performance review,
the Huìdiǎn was still unfinished,
so he was retained as Compiler-in-chief.
When the work was completed,
he was promoted to Zuǒ Shìláng (Left Vice Minister) and returned to his post,
advancing two ranks.
Upon the accession of Wǔzōng,
he requested retirement due to age,
and returned home without waiting for approval.
An imperial edict conferred upon him the title of Shàngshū (Minister) upon retirement.
When Liú Jǐn caused chaos in government,
his added title was revoked.
After Liú Jǐn's defeat, it was restored,
and he passed away after a long time.
Shǒuzhǐ was extensively learned in numerous books,
and served his elder brother Shǒuchén as a teacher;
their learning and conduct were comparable.
His being a Jièyuán (first-place graduate of the provincial examination), Xuéshì (Academician), and Shìláng (Vice Minister)
were all the same as his brother.
Furthermore, they both held positions in charge of the Hànlín Yuàn (Hanlin Academy) in both capitals,
which people particularly praised.
When Shǒuchén died,
Shǒuzhǐ mourned and performed rites at his tablet for three years.
Mào Yuán,
courtesy name Zhìrén.
He passed the metropolitan examination in the eleventh year of Chénghuà.
He was appointed Xíngbù Zhǔshì (Secretary in the Ministry of Justice).
He successively became Lángzhōng (Director),
then went out to serve as Húguǎng Fùshǐ (Vice Surveillance Commissioner of Huguang),
and later transferred to Shāndōng.
In the seventh year of Hóngzhì,
the river burst its banks at Zhāngqiū.
An edict commanded the Censor-in-chief Liú Dàxià to manage it,
and subsequently sent the eunuch Lǐ Xīng and Earl of Píngjiāng Chén Ruì to follow.
Lǐ Xīng was tyrannical and cruel,
imprisoning and humiliating the Provincial Surveillance Commissioner.
Mào Yuán, temporarily in charge of the department,
memorialized, saying:
"In the river management project,
there are too many officials and responsibility is not concentrated.
The local authorities spend
a hundred gold pieces daily for provisions.
When the officials first offered sacrifices to the river,
the sky was dark and gloomy,
and the silk offerings could not burn.
The remnants of what was burned
clearly resembled a human face,
complete with ears, eyes, mouth, and nose;
onlookers were startled and amazed.
The gods and spirits showed this strangeness;
how could it be accidental?
I beg that Lǐ Xīng and Chén Ruì be recalled,
and responsibility be solely entrusted to Liú Dàxià;
success will surely be achieved.
Moreover, water is an yin phenomenon;
now the empress's relatives wield excessive power,
and those who exploit their names to commit greed and violence
are countless.
I request that stricter prohibitions be put in place
to eliminate these anomalies.
Painters and artisans
should all be dismissed.
Since Shāndōng already has eunuchs garrisoned,
and Lǐ Quán is again ordered to garrison Línqīng,
he should be recalled."
The memorial was submitted,
and sent to the Shāndōng Provincial Administration Commissioner and Surveillance Commissioner for investigation.
They memorialized, saying:
"The strangeness of the burning silk indeed occurred,
but the reported expenditures
were greatly exaggerated."
Thereupon, Lǐ Xīng and Chén Ruì jointly impeached Mào Yuán for making false statements,
and an edict commanded the Jin Yī Bǎihù (Centurion of the Embroidered Uniform Guard) Hú Jié to arrest him.
The elders blocked Hú Jié's path and pleaded,
begging for the return of Vice Commissioner Yáng.
When he had an audience,
Mào Yuán knelt for a long time but did not prostrate,
which angered the emperor,
who had him imprisoned in the imperial dungeon.
Hú Jié visited all the eunuchs,
fully recounting the elders' pleas for redress,
which moved many eunuchs.
At that time, various officials argued for his rescue,
and the Ministry proposed a penalty of a redemption fine and flogging, and restoration to his post,
but he was specially demoted to Chángshā Tóngzhī (Assistant Prefect of Changsha).
He resigned due to illness and returned home.
After a long time,
he was appointed Ānqìng Zhīfǔ (Prefect of Anqing),
and then promoted to Guǎngxī Zuǒcānzhèng (Left Administration Vice Commissioner of Guangxi).
In the fourth year of Zhèngdé,
Liú Jǐn sent the Censor Sūn Dí to audit finances and grain,
and Mào Yuán refused his demand for bribes.
Liú Jǐn also disliked Mào Yuán's cousin Shǒusuí,
so he forced Mào Yuán into retirement.
After Liú Jǐn's execution,
he was reinstated to an official position in Jiāngxī,
and soon after promoted to Yúnnán Zuǒbùzhèngshǐ (Left Administration Commissioner of Yunnan).
As Yòufù Dūyùshǐ (Right Assistant Censor-in-chief), he was巡撫 (Grand Coordinator) of Guìzhōu,
then transferred to preside over the Nánjīng Dūcháyuan (Nanjing Censorate),
and finally served as Xíngbù Yòushìláng (Right Vice Minister of Justice).
Mào Rén,
courtesy name Zhìdào,
passed the metropolitan examination at the end of Chénghuà.
He successively served as Xíngbù Lángzhōng (Director in the Ministry of Justice).
When the garrison eunuch of Liáodōng, Liáng Jǐ, was impeached,
he went with a Supervising Secretary to investigate,
and uncovered all his crimes.
He ended his career as Sìchuān Ànchásǐ (Provincial Surveillance Commissioner of Sichuan).
Zhāng Yuánzhēn,
courtesy name Tíngxiáng,
was a native of Nánchāng.
At five years old he could compose poetry.
The Prince of Níngjìng summoned him for an audience,
and named him Yuánzhēng.
The Grand Coordinator Hán Yōng appreciated him and said,
"He is a human auspicious omen."
Thus, his name was changed to Yuánzhēn.
He passed the metropolitan examination in the fourth year of Tiānshùn,
was appointed Shùjíshì (Bacheolor of the Hanlin Academy),
and then granted the post of Biānxiū (Compiler).
When Xiànzōng succeeded to the throne,
he submitted a memorial requesting the implementation of a three-year mourning period,
but it was not accepted.
In the fifth month of that year,
he submitted a memorial detailing three matters:
"First,
diligence in lecturing and studying.
May Your Majesty not abandon it due to hot or cold weather.
What is lectured upon must be pertinent to the practical aspects of cultivating virtue and governing,
and not necessarily be avoided for fear of touching upon matters of chaos, ruin, or offense.
After the lecture,
may Your Majesty further concentrate your mind and quietly reflect,
testing it against your own person, mind, and the transformation of governance.
For the lecture officials,
order high ministers to publicly recommend individuals who are upright, discerning, righteous, and magnanimous,
regardless of their official rank.
Second,
publicly listen to governance.
Please daily proceed to the Wénhuá Diàn.
Before noon, attend lectures;
afternoon, listen to governance.
For memorials from throughout the empire,
order the various ministers to thoroughly discuss and personally present their approval or disapproval,
and Your Majesty shall personally preside over and decide their right or wrong.
When free, summon officials from the fifth rank down,
and casually inquire about the gains, losses, advantages, and disadvantages of current affairs,
allowing the sentiments of the lower ranks to be fully expressed.
Third,
extensively employ the worthy.
Please order the Grand Secretaries (Gěishìzhōng) and Censors (Yùshǐ)
to each present the worthiness or unworthiness of the senior officials in both capitals.
If there is anything incomplete,
officials of the fifth rank in the capital are also permitted to point it out,
using this as a basis for promotion or demotion.
Also, order them to jointly recommend those with virtue and prestige,
to fill the vacated positions,
thus ensuring that all high ministers are rightly chosen.
Then, order them to each speak about the worthiness or unworthiness of officials in their respective jurisdictions, and in the regional prefectures and counties,
and hand this over to the Grand Secretariat (Nèigé) and Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù) for promotion or demotion.
Among officials both inside and outside the court,
those who are upright and dare to speak
should be recommended as Censors (Táijiàn),
regardless of their speech, appearance, official rank, or background.
However, they should not be entrusted to senior officials,
lest they fear their uprightness
and recommend pliable and obsequious individuals to fill the ranks.
Those recommended would feel indebted to their patrons
and dare not directly expose their faults.
This is why in ancient times, high ministers did not recommend Censors."
When the memorial was submitted,
because many of its words were deemed obstructive and difficult to implement,
it was shelved.
He was then involved in the compilation of the Veritable Records of Yīngzōng.
His views differed from those in power,
so he pleaded illness and stayed at home,
studying the doctrines of nature and destiny (xìngmìng zhī xué).
After twenty years,
he was recommended by officials both inside and outside the court,
but he did not accept any appointments.
At the beginning of Hóngzhì's reign,
he was summoned to compile the Veritable Records of Xiànzōng
and was promoted to Zǔozànshàn.
He submitted a memorial saying:
"A ruler who does not set his heart on practicing the kingly way
is not a sovereign of great accomplishment.
Your Majesty, having cultivated virtue in the Eastern Palace (Qīnggōng),
already bears the hope of great accomplishment.
Recently, however, you have somewhat favored heterodox doctrines
and indulged in close retainers,
thereby corrupting this mind;
accumulated wealth and profit
and indulged in amusements,
thereby wasting this mind;
opened doors to favoritism
and blocked avenues for speech,
thereby obscuring this mind.
Then you will not be able to achieve great things.
May Your Majesty stabilize your sacred resolve,
unify your sacred learning,
and broaden your sacred wisdom."
The memorial, repeatedly expressed, totaled tens of thousands of words,
and the Emperor largely accepted it.
When the Veritable Records were completed,
he was transferred to Nánjīng Shìjiǎng Xuéshì,
and then returned home to care for his mother.
After a long time,
he was summoned to be the Deputy Editor-in-Chief (Fùzǒngcái) of the Huìdiǎn.
Upon arrival, he was promoted to Xuéshì
and served as the daily lecturer in the imperial lectures (Jīngyán Rìjiǎng Guān).
The Emperor greatly leaned towards him.
Yuánzhēn was of slender build,
and his height did not exceed that of an average person.
The Emperor specially provided a low table for him to lecture.
A few months later,
he left due to his mother's mourning.
When the mourning period ended,
he was transferred to Nánjīng Tàicháng Qīng.
Later,
when the Tōngjiàn Zuǎnyào was compiled,
he was again summoned to be the Deputy Editor-in-Chief.
He held his former office concurrently with Xuéshì
and was appointed to preside over the Zhānshì Fǔ.
In his later years, the Emperor's virtue further improved.
Yuánzhēn then requested to include the Tàijítú, Tōngshū, and Xīmíng in the imperial lectures.
The Emperor eagerly took them to read,
and happily said:
"Heaven produced this man
to enlighten me."
He intended to appoint him to a high position,
but soon after, the Emperor passed away.
When Wǔzōng ascended,
he was promoted to Lìbù Zǔoshìláng concurrently with Xuéshì, entered the Dōnggé,
and was solely in charge of imperial edicts.
Yuánzhēn had always enjoyed a high reputation.
He lived in seclusion for a long time
and only reappeared in his later years.
All the officials in the Hanlin Academy (Guǎngé) were his juniors.
Seeing Yuánzhēn's words and demeanor,
they considered him impractical and broad-minded (yūkuò),
and many mocked him.
Moreover, their names and positions clashed,
leading to widespread slander.
Censors (Yánguān) repeatedly impeached Yuánzhēn in memorials.
Yuánzhēn submitted seven memorials requesting retirement,
and Liú Jiàn strenuously protected him.
When Liú Jiàn left,
Yuánzhēn also died.
At the beginning of Tiānqǐ's reign,
he was posthumously given the epithet Wényù.
Chén Yīn,
courtesy name Shīzhào,
was from Pútián.
He became a Jìnshì at the end of Tiānshùn's reign.
He was appointed Shùjíshì
and then conferred the title of Biānxiū.
In the third month of the sixth year of Chénghuà's reign,
due to natural disasters, he presented his views on current governance,
stating:
"The most important thing in learning is inquiry.
Although Your Majesty occasionally attends imperial lectures (Jīngyán),
the strict division of ranks prevents
Your Majesty from asking when in doubt,
and subordinates from daring to express their views.
I wish Your Majesty would invite Confucian scholars and grant them seats in the side palace (Biàndiàn),
to calmly consult and discuss,
thus inspiring Your Majesty's sagely wisdom.
As for heterodox doctrines,
which are the opposite of the righteous path,
those styled Dharma Kings (Fǎwáng), Buddha's Sons (Fózǐ), and True Men (Zhēnrén)
should all be dismissed and sent away."
The memorial was handed down to the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù).
A few days later,
he again memorialized:
"The state has nurtured scholars for a hundred years,
but those who can be employed
are not many.
For example, the retired Minister (Shàngshū) Lǐ Bǐng,
and the enrolled compiler (Xiūzhuàn) Luó Lún, compiler (Biānxiū) Zhāng Yuánzhēn, and Jǔrén from Xīnhuì Chén Xiànzhāng are all prominent figures of their time.
It is appropriate to recall Lǐ Bǐng and others,
and place Chén Xiànzhāng in the Censorate (Táijiàn).
Many Censors (Yánguān) remain silent.
I wish Your Majesty would recall Judge (Pànguān) Wáng Huī and Reviewer (Píngshì) Zhāng Mào and others,
to open up avenues for speech."
This displeased the Emperor, who severely reprimanded him.
When the mother of the Directorate of Ceremonial Grand Eunuch, Huáng Cì, died,
all court officials went to offer condolences,
but the Hanlin did not go.
Xu Qióng, a Supervising Remonstrator, consulted the group.
Chén Yīn indignantly said:
"The Son of Heaven's attendants
are leading each other to bow at the residence of an inner eunuch.
What about the pure public opinion?!"
Qióng was ashamed and disheartened.
When his term of office was complete,
he was promoted to Supervising Remonstrator.
Wāng Zhí's partisan Wéi Yīng, leading patrolling soldiers, entered the house of Yáng Shìwěi, a Bureau Director in the Ministry of War, at night.
He bound Shìwěi
and interrogated and tortured him and his wife and children.
Yīn, being a neighbor,
climbed onto the wall and shouted loudly:
"You presume to insult a court official!
Are you not afraid of the national law?!"
That person said:
"Who are you,
not to fear the Western Depot?!"
Yīn sternly said:
"I am Chén Yīn of the Hanlin Academy!"
After a long time,
he was transferred to be Nanjing Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
When Liú Jí's mourning period for his father was over and he was recalled to office,
Yīn wrote him a letter advising him to firmly decline,
but Jí was displeased.
Later, when the Ministry of Personnel proposed to appoint Yīn,
Jí always obstructed it, saying
"a rotten scholar,"
and because of this, he was not transferred for ten years.
He once argued with a commanding eunuch over a matter,
and was impeached by him,
but in the end, the matter was settled justly.
In the fifth year of Hóngzhì (1492),
when Jí was dismissed,
he was finally promoted to Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
He died two years later.
Yīn was learned in classical studies,
and many scholars visited his door.
However, he was prone to forgetfulness,
and understood nothing of worldly matters or trivial affairs.
People often attributed foolish acts to him to make fun,
but not all of it was true.
Fù Hàn,
courtesy name Yuēchuān,
was a native of Xīnyù.
He became a *jìnshì* in the eighth year of Tiānshùn (1464).
He was selected as a *shùjíshì*
and appointed as a compiler.
He was fond of learning and had a strong memory,
and was skilled in poetry and prose.
He was successively promoted to Left Expositor,
and lectured in the Eastern Palace.
When Emperor Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices concurrently Supervising Reader,
and successively held the posts of Left and Right Vice Ministers of the Ministry of Rites.
Soon, he was ordered to concurrently serve as an academician and enter the Eastern Cabinet,
specifically in charge of imperial edicts,
and also managed the affairs of the Supervisorate of the Heir Apparent.
In the thirteenth year of Hóngzhì (1500), he succeeded Xú Qióng as Minister of Rites.
When Bǎodìng presented a white magpie,
he memorialized to reject it.
Xióng Chōng, the Provincial Governor of Shǎnxī, presented a jade seal obtained by a commoner in Hùxiàn,
believing it to be the reappearance of the Qín seal.
Hàn, with his colleagues, stated:
"The completeness or damage of the Qín seal
is fully recorded in historical documents.
The seal now presented,
in its shape, color, and knob carving, is not similar;
it is likely a later imitation.
Moreover, the emperor's mandate comes from virtue, not from a seal.
Tàizǔ created six seals,
and successive emperors have inherited them.
For over 130 years,
heavenly blessings have continuously arrived.
It is clear that the symbol of the mandate does not lie in the Qín seal.
We request that it be temporarily stored in the imperial treasury."
The emperor agreed with his words
and gave a small reward to the person who found the seal.
In the capital, there were celestial anomalies, earthquakes, and hail,
and various strange phenomena in the four directions.
Hàn itemized the inconveniences to the military and common people,
and requested the emperor to personally practice frugality to set an example for the empire.
The arrears of the Court of Imperial Entertainments to households and in commodity prices reached over forty thousand taels.
Hàn stated that this was due to excessive supplies,
and wished to emphasize frugality,
to prevent unnecessary expenses.
His memorials
generally presented righteous opinions.
He died in the fifteenth year (1502),
and was posthumously granted Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
and given the posthumous name Wénmù.
Zhāng Shēng,
courtesy name Qǐzhāo,
was a native of Nánchéng.
He came first in the imperial examination in the fifth year of Chénghuà (1469).
He was appointed Compiler,
and successively Expositor.
When Hóngzhì became the era name,
he was promoted to Junior Supervisor.
When Grand Secretary Liú Jí was in power,
Shēng, taking advantage of celestial anomalies,
memorialized, saying:
"Upon Your Majesty's ascension,
remonstrators generally spoke against Wàn Ān, Liú Jí, and Yǐn Zhí.
Ān and Zhí were dismissed,
but Jí alone remained.
Jí then debased himself by flattering and fawning,
seeking to please the censors.
He would knock on their doors late at night,
pleading to be spared impeachment,
promising them rapid promotion.
Thus, the remonstrating officials remained silent,
and his treacherous schemes succeeded.
The imperial relative Wàn Xǐ, relying on his influence in the inner palace,
had his wicked power spread widely.
Jí formed a marriage alliance with him.
Even after Xǐ was imprisoned,
Jí still tried to save him.
While his father was alive, he lived separately and cooked his own meals;
after his father died, he resumed office despite mourning.
He laughed and chatted with guests,
without any sign of sorrow.
He lavishly took in beautiful concubines,
indulging in promiscuity."
He also enumerated ten of Jí's crimes, such as accepting bribes and indulging his sons.
Jí was extremely indignant
and prompted the censorial officials to impeach Shēng for slander and defamation,
transferring him to be a Vice Director in the Ministry of Works in Nanjing.
When Jí was dismissed,
he was reinstated to his former post,
and successively served as Left and Right Vice Ministers of the Ministry of Rites.
In the fifteenth year (1502), he succeeded Fù Hàn as Minister.
When Emperor Xiàozōng died,
the Daoist Master Chén Yìngxiū, the Tibetan Imperial Grand Preceptor Nàbǔjiānshēn, and others, under the pretext of exorcism,
led their followers into the Qiánqīng Palace.
Shēng requested they be punished by law.
An imperial edict stripped more than thirty people, including the Daoist Master, Imperial Grand Preceptor, and High Scholars, of their titles,
and expelled them.
Shēng served in the Ministry for five years,
and whenever there were disasters or anomalies,
he would offer straightforward remonstrances.
He was also frequently attacked by remonstrators,
but he maintained strict self-discipline.
When Emperor Wǔzōng indulged in amusement and neglected government affairs,
Grand Secretaries Hú Yù, Yáng Yīyīng, and Zhāng Guì all spoke against it,
and the memorials were sent down to the Ministry of Rites.
Shēng then submitted a memorial,
requesting the emperor to be close to the virtuous and far from the wicked,
and to diligently heed heavenly warnings.
The emperor approved but could not implement his advice.
Shēng then repeatedly submitted memorials requesting retirement,
but they were not granted.
In the second year of Zhèngdé (1507),
Zhèn-guó Jiāngjūn Chéngfú of the Qín Princedom requested to inherit the title of Prince of Bǎo'ān.
Shēng insisted on refusing.
He offended Liú Jǐn
and pleaded illness.
An imperial edict added the title Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
and he returned home by post-carriage,
with monthly rice and annual corvée laborers as per regulations.
He died at home.
Wú Kuān,
courtesy name Yuánbó,
was a native of Chángzhōu.
He was renowned among scholars for his literary talent and conduct.
In the eighth year of Chénghuà (1472),
he came first in both the metropolitan and palace examinations,
and was appointed Compiler.
He served Emperor Xiàozōng in the Eastern Palace,
and upon completion of his term, was promoted to Right Expositor.
When Emperor Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
due to his previous scholarship, he was promoted to Left Junior Supervisor,
participated in the compilation of the Veritable Records of Emperor Xiànzōng,
and was promoted to Vice Supervisor of the Heir Apparent concurrently Supervising Academician.
Liú Chūn,
courtesy name Rénzhòng,
was a Bārén.
He passed the imperial examination as a *jìnshì* in the twenty-third year of Chénghuà (1487).
He was appointed editor,
and repeatedly promoted to Hanlin Academician.
In the sixth year of Zhèngdé (1511), he was promoted to Vice Minister of the Right of the Ministry of Personnel,
then advanced to Vice Minister of the Left.
In the eighth year, he replaced Fù Guī as Minister of the Ministry of Rites.
Both Prince Huái Yòuqǐ and Prince Zhèng Yòuhé inherited their titles from collateral branches,
but Yòuqǐ claimed his biological father as his father,
and Yòuhé even wanted to posthumously ennoble his biological father and have him enshrined in the ancestral temple.
Prince Jiāochéng Bǐngfán inherited his princely title from the rank of General of the Pacified State,
and promoted his sister to Princess of a County.
Liú Chūn rebutted all these actions based on ritual principles,
and thus established them as precedents.
The emperor deeply trusted Western monks,
often wore their clothes,
and performed rituals within the Inner Factory.
There was one Chuòjíwǒxiē'ér,
who frequented the Leopard Chamber,
was enfeoffed as Great Virtuous Dharma King,
and sent two of his disciples back to Wūsīzàng
to request imperial patents for National Preceptor, like the Great Vehicle Dharma King,
to bring tribute annually,
and also to be allowed to carry tea for trade.
Liú Chūn held that this was unacceptable.
The emperor ordered a re-discussion,
and Liú Chūn insisted, memorializing:
"Wūsīzàng is far to the west,
its people are extremely stubborn and fierce.
Although four kings have been established to govern and civilize them,
their tribute must be subject to restrictions,
to prevent them from becoming a border menace.
If we permit them to carry tea
and grant them imperial patents,
what if they falsely use the imperial edict to entice the Qiāng people,
and make unreasonable requests?
If we don't comply, we will lose the hearts of foreign peoples;
if we do, it will cause further harm."
Upon receiving the memorial,
the carrying of tea was stopped,
but the imperial patents were ultimately granted.
Liú Chūn also memorialized:
"The Xīfān people customarily believe in Buddhism,
so our ancestors, following previous dynasties,
established various offices in Wūsīzàng,
as well as monasteries in Táo and Mín in Shǎnxī,
and Sōngpān in Sìchuān,
to guide and convert the Fān people,
and allowed them to pay tribute.
The tribute schedule and number of people were all fixed.
Recently, due to the remoteness of various Fān regions,
it's difficult to distinguish genuine from fake.
Fugitive criminals from China,
having learned their language,
hide among them,
and many also establish new monasteries to request plaques.
The Fān tribute has increased daily,
and banquets and rewards are a heavy expense.
I request strict limits on the timeframe,
a measured determination of the number of people,
and that each monastery be given ten passes (*kānhé*).
The border garrisons should keep a register of these passes,
and only if they match
should the tribute mission be allowed to proceed.
Furthermore, prohibit the indiscriminate construction of monasteries from now on."
This was approved.
Luó Róng and other Provincial Administration Commissioners of Guǎngdōng came for an audience,
each speaking of the harm caused by palace eunuchs garrisoned there who demanded tribute.
Liú Chūn listed the imperial edicts from previous reigns that had suspended or abolished tribute,
and also spoke of the droughts, floods, and banditry in the four directions,
and the suffering of the soldiers and common people,
requesting the dismissal of all garrisoning eunuchs.
This was not accepted.
Liú Chūn was in charge of Rites for three years,
and carefully upheld the established rituals.
He made many rectifications regarding requests for enfeoffment and marriage from imperial relatives, and sacrificial rites, burials, and posthumous titles for civil and military officials.
After experiencing a period of mourning,
he was appointed Minister of the Ministry of Personnel in Nánjīng upon the completion of his mourning period.
Soon after, he was made Minister of the Ministry of Rites, specifically in charge of imperial patents and edicts,
and oversaw the Zhan Affairs Office.
He died in the sixteenth year of Zhèngdé (1521).
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
and given the posthumous name Wénjiǎn.
The Liú clan was prominent for generations through success in the imperial examinations.
Liú Chūn's father, Guī,
was a Censor.
His younger brother, Tái,
was an Administration Vice Commissioner of Yúnnán.
His son, Péngnián,
was a Right Vice Censor-in-Chief supervising Guìzhōu.
Péngnián's son, Qǐzōng,
was a Minister of the Imperial Stud in Liáodōng.
Qǐzōng's son, Shìshǎng,
was a Left Provincial Administration Commissioner of Guǎngdōng.
Tái's son, Hènián,
was an Administration Commissioner of Yúnnán,
known for his clear reputation.
Hènián's grandson, Shìzēng,
was a Right Vice Censor-in-Chief supervising Yúnnán,
and had achievements in campaigns against Myanmar.
All of them achieved their positions through the *jìnshì* examination.
Wú Yǎn,
courtesy name Kèwēn,
was from Yíxīng.
He passed the imperial examination as a *jìnshì* in the twenty-third year of Chénghuà (1487).
He was appointed a *shùjíshì*,
then an editor,
and successively served as Reader-Academician,
and took charge of the Hanlin Academy in Nánjīng.
In the early Zhèngdé reign,
he was summoned to compile the *Veritable Records of Emperor Xiàozōng*,
and lectured at the imperial讲席.
When Liú Jǐn seized power,
he heard that Wú Yǎn's family was wealthy,
and sent someone to entice him with a high official position.
Wú Yǎn sternly refused him.
Liú Jǐn was furious.
During a grand assessment of all officials,
an imperial edict dismissed Wú Yǎn from office.
After Liú Jǐn was executed,
he was reinstated and successively served as Vice Minister of the Left and Right of the Ministry of Rites,
and was appointed Minister of the Ministry of Rites in Nánjīng.
In the twelfth year of Zhèngdé (1517),
when Emperor Wǔzōng made a northern tour,
Wú Yǎn strongly memorialized to remonstrate.
The following year, he again submitted a memorial with other ministers, saying:
"We, your subjects, first heard that Your Majesty was visiting Chāngpíng,
and had already submitted a memorial arguing strongly against it,
but it was not accepted.
Then we heard that you had left Jūyōng,
and visited Xuān and Dà.
The Grand Secretaries were not informed,
the officials could not follow,
the soldiers of the three armies could not guard you,
and the hearts of the people inside and outside the capital are in turmoil.
South of Xú and Huái,
there are a thousand *lǐ* of famine.
Last winter, snow and ice caused disaster,
and the people have no clothes or food.
How can we guarantee that they will not turn to banditry?
The invaders to be repelled are still far beyond Yīnshān,
but unforeseen disaster may suddenly arise at your very elbow.
This is what we greatly fear."
There was no reply.
He died in office in the fourteenth year of Zhèngdé (1519).
He was posthumously granted the title of Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
and given the posthumous name Wénsù.
Gù Qīng,
courtesy name Shìlián,
was from Huátíng, Sōngjiāng.
In the fifth year of Hóngzhì (1492), he placed first in the provincial examination.
The following year,
he passed the imperial examination as a *jìnshì*,
was appointed a *shùjíshì*,
and then an editor.
Together with his contemporaries Máo Chéng, Luó Qīnshùn, and Wāng Jùn,
he mutually encouraged a reputation for integrity.
He was promoted to Reader.
In the early Zhèngdé reign,
when Liú Jǐn seized power,
Gù Qīng's fellow townsman Zhāng Wénmiǎn became Liú Jǐn's chief strategist,
and those who attached themselves to Liú Jǐn were immediately elevated and honored.
Gù Qīng completely refused to associate with them,
and Liú Jǐn bore a grudge.
In the fourth year, Liú Jǐn found minor errors in the *Comprehensive Institutes*,
and demoted the Hanlin academicians.
Gù Qīng was demoted to editor.
Also, because the Hanlin academicians were not versed in government affairs,
he transferred them to provincial appointments and departmental positions in both capitals.
Gù Qīng received the post of Supernumerary Director in the Ministry of War in Nánjīng.
However, he then suffered a period of mourning for his father,
and did not take up the post.
After Liú Jǐn's execution,
he was reinstated as Reader,
and promoted to Reader-Academician, overseeing the Hanlin Academy.
Soon after, he was transferred to Junior Supervisor of the Imperial Household,
served as daily lecturer in the imperial讲席,
and was promoted to Vice Minister of the Right of the Ministry of Rites.
At this time, Máo Chéng was already Minister.
Gù Qīng dutifully assisted him,
and repeatedly requested the establishment of an Heir Apparent and the cessation of imperial tours,
submitting more than ten memorials.
When Emperor Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was impeached by Censor Lǐ Xiàn,
and dismissed from office to return home.
Qīng Xué was upright in conduct and cautious,
disinterested in advancement.
At home,
recommendations for him came continuously,
but he reported them all as declined.
In the 6th year of Jiājìng, an imperial edict called for the recommendation of experienced and capable officials for the Grand Secretariat.
The court deliberation included Qīng,
who was then appointed Nanjing Lǐbù Yòushìláng.
He presented a memorial, saying:
"The duty of the Jǐnyīwèi is to serve as imperial guards;
in the ancestral reigns, they were not dispatched unless it was for a secret matter.
During the Zhèngdé reign,
their patrols were sent out in all directions,
causing widespread unrest throughout the realm,
which Your Majesty personally witnessed.
Recently, a Qianhù was dispatched to investigate the private property dispute of Gāo Yuè in Yángzhōu,
imprisoning his daughter and wife,
subjecting them to extreme cruelty.
I request that from now on, all such matters be handed over to the relevant departments,
and that the dispatch of Qíxiào be halted."
This was approved.
He repeatedly requested to resign due to illness,
and an imperial edict promoted him to Shàngshū and allowed him to retire.
At that time, he was preparing to present a memorial and travel to the capital,
but he died on the way.
He was posthumously given the title Wénxī.
Liú Ruì,
courtesy name Défu,
was from Neijiāng.
His father, Shíxiào,
served as Shandōng Qiānshì,
known for his integrity and benevolence.
Ruì passed the Jìnshì examination in the 9th year of Hóngzhì,
was selected as a Shùjíshì,
and appointed Jiǎntǎo.
He was diligent in study and upright in conduct,
often offering opinions and proposals on matters.
When Qīngnínggōng was damaged by fire,
he requested the abolition of Daoist sacrificial altars.
When the Grand Secretariat lecturers were summoned to discuss governance,
he also said:
"The eunuchs who were retainers of the late eunuch Lǐ Guǎng
should all be punished.
Former Grand Eunuch Wāng Zhí,
an offender against the late emperor,
is now seeking employment,
and should be banished.
Vice Commissioner Yáng Màoyuán and Director Wáng Yúnfèng, who were punished for their forthright words,
should be recalled and reinstated.
In the capital, Wànchūngōng,
Xīngjì Zhēnwǔ Miào, and the mansion of Shòuníng Hóu,
and outside the capital, the prefectures of Xīng, Qí, Héng, Yōng, Rǔ, and Jīng,
where construction is extensive,
should all have non-urgent projects halted.
In the victory at Dōuyún,
Dèng Tíngzàn falsely claimed credit,
and in the campaign of Hèlán,
Wáng Yuè instigated the conflict;
I request that the crimes of deceit and fraud be investigated and rectified."
This was reported to the emperor.
When Quèlǐ Miào was completed,
Grand Secretary Lǐ Dōngyáng was dispatched to offer sacrifices.
Ruì requested a revision of the posthumous titles of the Former Sage,
but it was not carried out.
Upon the enthronement of Wǔzōng,
he memorialized nine matters on fundamental governance.
He requested the recall of Chancellor Zhāng Mào,
Vice Minister Wáng Ào,
and Censor-in-Chief Lín Jùn and Yōng Tài,
and the extraordinary promotion of Administration Commissioner Wáng Lún, Vice Commissioner Wáng Yúnfèng, Surveillance Commissioner Hú Xiàn, Prefect Yáng Màoyuán, and Record Keeper Yú Lián.
Because of this,
many officials were promoted and employed.
When Liú Jǐn came into power,
Ruì immediately feigned illness and resigned.
Impoverished and unable to return to his hometown,
he relied on Lǐ Chōngsì, his maternal cousin, in Lǐzhōu.
Jǐn listed Ruì as a member of his "treacherous party,"
and also, because of his earlier recommendation of Yōng Tài, removed his name from office,
and fined him rice to be transported to the border.
Because of this, he became even more destitute,
and taught students to support himself.
After Jǐn was executed,
he was appointed Vice Commissioner to oversee the Zhejiang provincial schools,
and was then recalled to serve as Nanjing Tàipú Shàoqīng.
In the 2nd year of Jiājìng,
he was promoted from Nanjing Tàicháng Qīng to Lǐbù Yòushìláng.
Due to natural disasters, he and his colleagues jointly presented six recommendations,
and also stated that Daoist rituals were useless and hindered governance,
and textile production was costly and burdened the people.
The emperor adopted many of his suggestions.
When the Great Rites Controversy arose,
Ruì, along with the nine ministers, submitted a joint memorial.
He extensively argued the principles of the major and minor lines of succession,
totaling several thousand words.
He died in office in the 4th year.
He was posthumously granted the title of Shàngshū.
In the early Lóngqìng reign,
he was posthumously given the title Wénsù.
The encomium states: Zhōu Hóngmó and others, as literary officials, served as ministers and vice-ministers.
Some were diligent in their duties,
others spoke out boldly with proposals,
lecturing with the intention of enlightening,
and serving in office by offering advice and criticisms.
In their selection as literary attendants,
none were found wanting.
Collation Notes

Biographies, Volume 73: Lǐ Fēng (Yè Qí), Jiǎ Jùn (Liú Zhāng), Huáng Fú, Zhāng Yuè (Zhāng Yíng), Wū Zhōng, Zēng Jiàn, Liáng Jǐng (Wáng Zhào), Xú Kè, Lǐ Jiè (Zǐ Kūn), Huáng Kē, Wáng Hóngrú, Cóng Lán, Wú Shìzhōng.
Lǐ Mǐn,
courtesy name Gōngmiǎn,
was from Xiāngchéng.
He became a Jìnshì in the 5th year of Jǐngtài.
He was appointed Yùshǐ.
In the early Tiānshùn reign,
he was commanded to pacify the barbarians in Guìzhōu.
Upon his return,
he was appointed巡按 Jī Nèi.
As the transport route for provisions to Jìzhōu passed through the Haikou,
many boats capsized,
so he proposed opening a new route via Sānhé to Jìzhōu
to avoid the dangers,
which benefited both the military and the populace.
In the early Chénghuà reign,
he was promoted extraordinarily by recommendation to Zhèjiāng Ànchásǐ.
He then served in Húguǎng.
He successively held the positions of Shānxī and Sìchuān Zuǒ and Yòubùzhèngshǐ.
In the 13th year, he was promoted to Yòufù Dūyùshǐ,
and served as Xúnfǔ of Dàtóng.
Enemy cavalry frequently appeared outside the frontier,
ambushing and killing the garrison troops.
Mǐn ambushed them with brave soldiers and captured them.
He repaired the city walls and moats,
and the enemy dared not invade.
In the 15th year, he was recalled to serve as Bīngbù Yòushìláng.
After four years,
he resigned due to illness and returned home.
During a severe famine in Hénán,
he proposed several measures for disaster relief.
An imperial edict appointed him Zuǒfù Dūyùshǐ and Xúnfǔ of Bǎodìng and other prefectures.
In the 21st year, he was reassigned to oversee grain transport,
and soon after was recalled to be appointed Hùbù Shàngshū.
Previously,
when Mǐn was in Dàtóng,
he observed that provisions transported from Shāndōng and Hénán
incurred high costs due to the long distance.
Therefore, after calculating the annual expenditure,
he ordered all payments to be made in silver.
The people found it easier to carry lighter goods and reach their destinations,
while the generals and soldiers could use the surplus to purchase military equipment,
benefiting both sides.
At this time,
he further requested that the prefectures and counties in the imperial capital region, Shānxī, and Shǎnxī, which annually transported grain to various borders,
should pay one liǎng of silver for every shí of grain,
with nineteen parts going to the border,
to be converted into military pay according to current market value,
and any surplus used to purchase grain for military contingencies.
The emperor approved.
From then on, the two taxes in the north were all converted to silver,
which began with Mǐn.
The taxes collected by the Chóngwénmén Xuānkèsī
were often embezzled by powerful individuals.
Mǐn, following Mǎ Wénshēng's advice, requested the addition of Yùshǐ and Zhǔshì to supervise.
Yùshǐ Chén Yáo accused Mǐn of extortion,
and Mǐn again memorialized to resign.
The emperor consoled him and urged him to stay.
When imperial relatives requested vacant land and thousands of qǐng of hawk kennels and horse pastures,
Mǐn insisted on rejecting the request,
and the matter was dropped.
When Xiànzōng's reign was ending,
eunuchs and sycophants were frequently bestowed with manor lands.
Once they fell from favor,
they would generally offer to return the lands to the government.
Those with heavier offenses had their lands confiscated,
but these lands were not distributed to the common people for taxation.
Lǐ Mǐn requested that tenants be summoned,
and that each *mǔ* be taxed three *fēn* of silver.
The emperor assented,
but other manor lands remained as they were.
At that time, the capital experienced a great flood,
and Lǐ Mǐn then fully detailed its harms,
saying:
"Currently, there are five imperial manors in the capital region,
totaling over 12,800 *qǐng* of land;
there are 332 manors belonging to noble relatives and eunuchs,
totaling over 33,100 *qǐng* of land.
Government agents recruit scoundrels to be manor heads,
who seize livestock,
murder people,
and violate women.
The common people's hearts are filled with pain and injury,
which is the origin of disasters and anomalies.
Imperial manors began during the Zhèngtǒng period,
when various princes, not yet enfeoffed,
were granted idle land to establish manors.
When the princes departed for their fiefs,
the land was supposed to revert to the government,
but later this practice was continued.
Under the whole heaven,
nothing is not the king's land,
so why is there a need for imperial manors?
I request that all manor households be abolished,
and the land be allotted to the people for cultivation,
with each *mǔ* uniformly taxed three *fēn* of silver,
to be used for the expenses of the various palaces.
Without the name of 'imperial manor,'
there will still be the effect of sufficient funds.
As for the manor lands of powerful officials,
I also request that tenants be selected to manage them,
and that the authorities collect the taxes,
allowing the various families to claim them.
To please the hearts of the people,
and to invoke harmonious *qì*,
nothing is more crucial than this."
At that time, his proposals could not be implemented.
An investigating censor in Nánjīng and the Grand Eunuch of the Garrison, Jiǎng Cóng, slandered each other.
All the investigating censors were arrested and banished,
while Jiǎng Cóng remained in his post as before.
Lǐ Mǐn submitted another memorial vigorously arguing,
but none were heeded.
In the fourth year of Hóngzhì (1491), he fell ill and requested retirement,
and the emperor dispatched a physician to treat him.
Later,
he again strongly requested,
and Yè Qí was appointed to replace him.
An imperial edict allowed Lǐ Mǐn to return by post-carriage.
He died before reaching home.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shàobǎo)
and given the posthumous name Gōngjìng.
Throughout his life, Lǐ Mǐn was earnest in his conduct and righteousness.
He distributed all his emoluments and rewards to his brothers and old acquaintances.
When he was residing in his hometown,
he built a house at the foot of Zǐyún Shān (Purple Cloud Mountain),
collected thousands of volumes of books,
and lectured to scholars.
When he became Pacification Commissioner of Dàtóng,
he memorialized to register it with the government,
and an edict granted it the name Zǐyún Shūyuàn (Purple Cloud Academy).
The Confucius Temple in Dàtóng lacked elegant music,
and it is said that through Lǐ Mǐn's memorial, it was granted according to the regulations.
Yè Qí,
courtesy name Běnqīng,
was a native of Shānyáng.
In the fifth year of Jǐngtài (1454), he passed the *jìnshì* examination.
He was appointed Investigating Censor.
In the early Tiānshùn period,
Shí Hēng slandered him, leading to his arrest and imprisonment.
The investigation found no evidence,
so he was released and appointed Magistrate of Wǔzhì.
During the Chénghuà period, he successively served as Pacification Commissioner of Dàtóng.
When Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
he was summoned to serve as Vice Minister of Revenue.
In the fourth year of Hóngzhì, he replaced Lǐ Mǐn as Minister,
and soon after was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shàobǎo).
When Hāmì (Hami) was captured by Tǔlǔfān (Turpan),
the defending officials requested that the remaining populace be given rations
and settled in the interior.
Yè Qí said:
"This is inviting disaster upon ourselves."
He rejected their memorial.
Treacherous commoners offered land in Dàmíng as imperial manors,
but Yè Qí proposed returning it to the authorities.
The eunuch Lóng Shòu requested the opening of silver mines,
but Yè Qí opposed it.
The emperor assented to Yè Qí's view.
Later,
Lóng Shòu requested 20,000 *yǐn* of salt from Chánglú,
to be sold in Liǎnghuái to fund weaving expenses.
Yè Qí strenuously argued against it,
but ultimately his advice was not taken.
Yè Qí served in the Ministry of Revenue for six years,
being upright, resolute,
and capable of conserving national resources.
Whenever military campaigns were debated in court,
he invariably opposed them.
However, he reformed the *kāizhōng* system,
ordering Huái merchants to pay silver instead of grain,
which suddenly increased salt taxes to a million,
all of which was delivered to the Transport Office.
The border provisions consequently became scarce.
In the fourth month of the ninth year (1496), he requested retirement
and died after returning home.
