He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Preceptor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Tàibǎo).
His nephew, Yè Zhì,
a *jìnshì*,
successively served as Vice Minister of Justice (Xíngbù Yòushìláng),
and was known for his integrity.
Jiǎ Jùn,
courtesy name Tíngjié,
was a native of Shùlù.
He entered the Imperial Academy (Guóxué) through a provincial recommendation.
During the Tiānshùn period,
he was selected and appointed Investigating Censor.
He successively toured Zhèjiāng, Shānxī, Shǎnxī, Hénán, and Nánjī,
and gained a reputation wherever he went.
In the thirteenth year of Chénghuà (1477), he was promoted from Assistant Surveillance Commissioner of Shāndōng to Vice Censor-in-Chief (Yòuqiān Dūyùshǐ),
and Pacification Commissioner of Níngxià.
He served in the garrison for seven years,
and the military and civilians lived in peace.
He was summoned to serve as Vice Minister of Works (Gōngbù Yòushìláng).
In the twenty-first year, he was ordered to relieve famine in Hénán.
Soon after, he was transferred to Vice Minister of Works (Gōngbù Zuǒshìláng),
and a few months later was appointed Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shàngshū).
At that time, *jìnshì* degree holders were highly valued,
and *jǔrén* (provincial graduates) rarely reached the rank of Six Ministers;
Jiǎ Jùn alone attained it due to his great reputation.
When Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
Ministers Wáng Shù, Lǐ Mǐn, Zhōu Hóngmó, Yú Zǐjùn, Hé Qiáoxīn,
and Censor-in-Chief Mǎ Wénshēng
were all praised by the people at that time,
and Jiǎ Jùn, participating among them,
also performed his duties competently.
For princely residences and tombs, the government fully provided the costs,
and ceremonial guards were regularly maintained and repaired.
The Directorate of Imperial Accoutrements (Nèiguān Jiān) wanted to frequently initiate large-scale projects,
but Jiǎ Jùn stated that since princely households already had stipends of grain and manor lands,
he requested only half the costs be provided;
if ceremonial guards were not severely dilapidated,
the authorities should not be bothered;
the only public works that should be undertaken
were granaries and city walls,
and all others should be suspended.
The emperor reported his approval.
In the fourth year of Hóngzhì,
eunuchs memorialized to repair the Shāhé Bridge,
requesting 25,000 capital troops and troops from the Five Guards of Chánglíng to assist in the work.
The Bureau of Imperial Banknotes (Nèifǔ Bǎochāo Sī) requested an increase in artisans.
Zhèjiāng and the prefectures of Sūzhōu and Sòngjiāng were suffering from floods, yet tens of thousands of pieces of brocade were being woven.
Jiǎ Jùn argued against all these,
and they were all shelved.
The administrative affairs of the Ministry of Works and the imperial directorates and bureaus were closely intertwined,
and the Directorate of Imperial Accoutrements specifically managed construction projects,
so their duties were particularly related.
Jiǎ Jùn was not swayed by them,
and construction projects were greatly reduced.
When the rear hall of the Imperial Ancestral Temple was completed,
he was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shàobǎo).
Due to a foot ailment,
he retired from office.
An edict permitted him to return by post-carriage,
and provided porters and rations according to regulations.
He died the following year.
Jiǎ Jùn was honest and cautious.
He served in the Ministry of Works for eight years,
and his reputation was respected by both court and commoners.
His successor was Liú Zhāng,
courtesy name Tíngxìn,
a native of Yánpíng.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the early Tiānshùn period.
He successively served in various influential posts, both inside and outside the capital, and was well-regarded.
While serving in the Ministry of Works,
he also frequently had disputes,
and his reputation was second only to Jiǎ Jùn's.
Huáng Fú,
courtesy name Yòngzhāng,
was originally from Fēngqiū.
His great-grandfather moved to Píngyuè,
and so his family settled there.
Fú passed the *jìnshì* examination in the 13th year of Zhèngtǒng,
and was appointed as a *xíngrén*.
He successively served as a *lángzhōng* in the Nánjīng Ministry of Justice.
He was upright and honest;
people called him
“Hard Huáng.”
A powerful scoundrel, Commander Tán,
occupied commoners' reed fields.
No one dared to question him,
but Fú confiscated the land and returned it to the people.
In the 9th year of Chénghuà, he was promoted to Left Counseling Official of Sìchuān.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Left Administration Commissioner.
When inspecting Chóngqìng,
a whirlwind rose before his sedan chair,
preventing it from moving.
Fú said:
“There must be an injustice here,
I must address it.”
The wind then dispersed.
Upon reaching the prefecture,
he prayed to the City God,
and dreamt of someone speaking of a temple west of the prefecture.
The temple was forty *lǐ* from the prefecture,
nestled against a mountain,
and overlooked a large pond.
Monks murdered people at night and sank them in the pond,
dividing their wealth.
Moreover, they hid many women in caves.
Fú dispatched officials and soldiers to surround it,
and after thorough interrogation,
uncovered the truth.
He executed the monks and destroyed their temple.
A granary official, relying on his connection to the imperial family, embezzled millions in official grain.
Fú pursued and prosecuted him according to the law,
and his authority was felt throughout the region.
He successively served as Left and Right Administration Commissioner in Sìchuān and Húguǎng.
He memorialized to close the Jiànchāng silver mine.
When construction began in the two capitals,
Húguǎng was required to supply twenty thousand *liǎng* of silver.
It was customary to levy this from the people,
but Fú used surplus funds from the treasury to cover it.
King Jīng memorialized to move his ancestral tombs.
Fú feared it would disturb the people,
and firmly refused.
In the 22nd year, he was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief,
and served as Grand Coordinator of Yánsuí.
He impeached and brought to justice Assistant Commander Guō Yōng,
Regional Commanders Zhèng Yìn, Lǐ Duó, Wáng Cóng, and others.
He devised a plan to capture the cunning and powerful Zhang Gāng.
He reasserted military discipline,
increased the number of watchtowers and fortresses,
and border administration was completely renewed.
When he saw soldiers' wives whose clothing did not cover their bodies,
he sighed,
“These brave men's families are so poor,
how can I face them as their superior?”
He immediately advanced three months' rations,
and personally comforted them.
At that time, there was an imperial edict to destroy Buddhist temples.
Fú took the opportunity to dismiss all the nuns,
and assigned them to the unmarried strongmen.
When Fú left,
many people, bringing their children, bowed and saw him off along the road.
In the 3rd year of Hóngzhì, he was appointed Minister of Revenue in Nánjīng.
Censorate officials considered Fú's promotion quite rapid,
and frequently spoke out.
The emperor did not listen,
and instead made him Left Censor-in-Chief.
He burned the roster of appointments in the courtyard, saying,
“What matters in affairs is finding the right person.
Whether one's experience and service are long or short,
how can that be the intent behind establishing official positions?”
Fú served in official positions for over forty years.
His nature was stern and quick-tempered,
and he could not tolerate others easily.
However, his conduct was pure and unblemished,
and wherever he went, he made achievements.
In the 6th year, he requested retirement,
but died before it could be carried out.
Zhāng Yuè,
courtesy name Shímǐn,
was from Huátíng, Sōngjiāng.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the 4th year of Tiānshùn,
and was appointed as a Principal of the Ministry of Justice,
then promoted to an Assistant Director.
During the Chénghuà era, he was appointed as a Surveillance Commissioner of Jiāngxī,
then transferred to supervise schools in Zhèjiāng.
He firmly resisted requests for favors,
and did not conceal the names of the students he examined,
saying:
“I only seek to trust myself.”
He was promoted to Vice Surveillance Commissioner of Sìchuān,
then advanced to Surveillance Commissioner.
He suffered a bereavement,
and after the mourning period, was appointed to Húguǎng.
Zhāng Tōng, a palace attendant from a princely mansion, acted wildly and recklessly,
but Yuè disciplined him according to the law.
When he entered the capital for an audience,
the eunuch Shàng Míng supervised the Eastern Depot.
Many vied to rush to his gate,
but Yuè alone did not go.
Míng resented him deeply,
but his investigations yielded nothing.
When Míng fell from power,
Yuè was summoned and appointed Left Vice Censor-in-Chief.
When Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Right Vice Minister of Works,
then transferred to Left Vice Minister of Personnel.
Wáng Shù was the Minister,
and Yuè assisted him;
he twice temporarily managed selection affairs.
In the summer of the 6th year of Hóngzhì,
there was a great drought,
and requests for opinions were made.
He submitted several proposals: to adhere to old regulations, to show compassion to the common people, to uphold frugality, to cut redundant officials, and to prohibit excessive punishments.
He also presented two memorials, "Cultivating Virtue" and "Governing Well,"
all of which were graciously accepted.
Soon after, he was transferred to Right Censor-in-Chief in Nánjīng,
and then appointed Minister of Personnel.
In the 9th year, he was again transferred to the Ministry of War,
to participate in crucial military affairs.
Due to his advanced age,
he repeatedly memorialized to request retirement.
An imperial edict conferred upon him the title of Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
and he returned home by imperial post-horse.
Upon his death, he was posthumously granted the title of Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
and given the posthumous name Zhuāngjiǎn.
At that time, Zhāng Yǐng,
courtesy name Tíngqì, who was from the same district as Yuè and had earlier served as Minister of War in Nánjīng,
passed the *jìnshì* examination in the 13th year of Zhèngtǒng.
At the beginning of the Jǐngtài reign,
he was promoted to Censor.
He successively served as Vice Surveillance Commissioner and Surveillance Commissioner of Jiāngxī, and Left Administration Commissioner of Shǎnxī.
In the 3rd year of Chénghuà, he was appointed Right Vice Censor-in-Chief and served as Grand Coordinator of Níngxià.
The city of Níngxià,
originally built of earth,
was first paved with bricks by Yǐng.
He diverted the Yellow River,
irrigating over seven hundred *qǐng* of military farms in Língzhōu.
He left due to his father's death.
After the mourning period,
he was appointed Grand Coordinator of the various prefectures in Héjiān,
then transferred to Dàtóng,
and successively served as Left and Right Vice Minister of Justice.
In the 18th year, he was promoted to Minister of this ministry.
The following year, he was granted the title of Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
And the year after that,
he again returned home due to bereavement.
In the 1st year of Hóngzhì, he was appointed Minister of War in Nánjīng,
and died in office.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
and given the posthumous name Zhuāngyì.
Qí Zhōng,
courtesy name Dàqì,
was from Yùnchéng.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the 2nd year of Chénghuà.
He was appointed Censor,
and inspected salt administration in Liǎnghuái.
Upon returning from inspecting Zhèjiāng,
he took charge of memorials from various circuits.
Wāng Zhí prompted Zhōng to impeach Mǎ Wénshēng,
but Zhōng refused,
and was slandered and beaten with a staff before the palace.
Due to the recommendation of Censor-in-Chief Wáng Yuè,
he was promoted to Assistant Minister of the Court of Judicial Review,
and again promoted to Right Vice Minister.
When invaders entered Dàtóng,
the court deliberated sending a high official to inspect the various prefectures of Bǎodìng,
and this task was assigned to Zhōng.
After several months,
he was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief to serve as Grand Coordinator of that area.
The coastal lands of Héjiān were occupied by powerful families,
and Zhōng took them back.
He was summoned to serve as Right Vice Minister of Justice.
During his mourning for his mother,
he hired a transport boat to carry his mother's coffin south.
The overall commander for grain transport, Wáng Xìn, memorialized about this,
and he was arrested and handed over to officials.
At the time, powerful figures were persecuting the faction of Yǐn Mín,
and since Zhōng was from the same hometown as Mín,
he was demoted two ranks to Prefect of Qǔjìng.
He was then transferred to Huīzhōu,
and later reinstated as Left Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review.
In the 3rd year of Hóngzhì,
he served as Right Vice Censor-in-Chief and Grand Coordinator of Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng prefectures,
devoting himself entirely to famine relief.
He was summoned to serve as Vice Minister of Revenue and concurrently Supervisor-General of Granaries,
and soon after was transferred to the Ministry of Personnel.
In the 11th year, he was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief.
After two years,
he was promoted to Minister of Revenue.
In the fifteenth year, the Emperor summoned the officials of the Ministry of Revenue to discuss financial matters.
He said:
"The regular incoming revenue,
due to exemptions, is gradually decreasing.
The regular outgoing expenses,
due to petitions and requests, are gradually increasing.
Income is insufficient to cover expenditure.
Before the Zhèngtǒng reign, military and state expenditures were frugal,
and the common people only paid their regular taxes.
From Jǐngtài to the present,
expenditures have grown daily,
leading to extraordinary levies.
The border provisions for Hénán and Shāndōng,
and the miscellaneous expenses for Zhèjiāng, Yúnnán, and Guǎngdōng,
were all unheard of in the past.
The people are already heavily burdened,
and nothing more can be added.
In former times, the four quarters enjoyed abundant harvests,
there were no troop mobilizations on the borders,
and no displaced persons in the prefectures and counties.
Now, the Grand Granary has no reserves,
the Imperial Household's funds are depleted,
and redundant officials and extravagant expenses daily exceed those of the past.
We wish Your Majesty would be vigilant and concerned,
strive to curb expenses,
and moreover, command your court officials to jointly seek methods to make ends meet."
The Emperor then referred the matter to his court officials for deliberation.
They submitted twelve proposals,
including the dismissal of supernumerary officials appointed by imperial decree,
the reduction of excessive recruitment of military artisans by the Imperial Household,
the purification of the 'Valiant Warriors' of the Tèngxíang Four Guards,
the suspension of vegetarian feasts and Daoist rituals in monasteries and temples,
the reduction of provisions for eunuchs, painters, and foreign monks,
the prohibition of excessive requests for salt licenses by princely estates and weaving factories,
and ordering officials to collect rents from imperial estates.
All these were inconvenient to the powerful favorites.
The memorial remained pending for several months.
Zhōng then spoke again about it.
Other matters were approved,
but those concerning the powerful favorites were ultimately obstructed and not implemented.
A wicked merchant, taking advantage of the Emperor's maternal uncle Zhāng Hèlín,
requested exemption from collecting salt taxes for 170,000 old Chánglú salt licenses,
offering to pay five fen of silver per license,
and separately purchase surplus salt from various fields in the same quantity at market price,
allowing him to sell it.
The Emperor granted permission.
Later, wicked commoners cited this precedent to request up to 1,600,000 old Liǎnghuái salt licenses.
Zhōng and others strongly resisted,
and all were rejected.
From this point, the salt administration greatly deteriorated,
and wicked people ran rampant throughout the Jiānghú region,
with officials powerless to stop them.
An investigator from the Eastern Depot discovered Zhōng Zǐruì's acceptance of bribes.
Zhōng repeatedly memorialized, requesting retirement,
and was ordered to return by express post.
During the Zhèngdé era,
Liú Jǐn accused Zhōng of various misdeeds during his time in the ministry,
resulting in three fines of rice.
He died a few years later.
Zēng Jiàn,
courtesy name Kèmíng,
his ancestors were from Guìyáng,
and resided in the capital due to their military registration.
He passed the imperial examination in the eighth year of Tiānshùn.
He was appointed Minister of the Ministry of Justice.
More than ten commoners from Tōngzhōu were accused of banditry,
and their cases were complete.
Jiàn discerned their innocence.
Later,
the true bandits were indeed caught.
At the end of the Chénghuà reign,
he successively served as Right Vice Minister of Communications,
and was repeatedly promoted to Left Vice Minister of the Ministry of Works.
In the thirteenth year of Hóngzhì, he was promoted to Minister.
Emperor Xiàozōng had reigned for a long time,
and the people within the seas were content with their work.
Provisions for the Imperial Household gradually increased,
and the Directorate of Palace Furniture requested the remanufacture of over one hundred dragon carpets and plain carpets.
Jiàn and others argued:
"Although carpets are a single item,
they require collecting wool from Shānxi and Shǎnxī,
sourcing cotton yarn and other materials from Hénán,
and summoning artisans from Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng.
This takes several years,
and involves a hundred kinds of labor and expense.
We implore Your Majesty to halt this."
The request was not granted.
The Imperial Household's Embroidery Bureau requested to recruit one thousand child artisans.
Jiàn and others argued:
"In previous years, the Directorate of Imperial Robes recruited one thousand artisans,
and the Directorate of Armaments imitated this,
recruiting up to two thousand people.
The Directorate of Ordnance and the Directorate of Palace Furniture also imitated this,
each recruiting one thousand people.
Once the source of corruption is opened,
its flow is endless."
Therefore, an order was issued to reduce the number by half.
Eunuch Lǐ Xīng requested to organize fireworks for the Lantern Festival.
An imperial edict ordered frugality,
and due to Jiàn's memorial, it was entirely canceled.
In the sixteenth year,
the Emperor, following the advice of his ministers, recalled the eunuchs managing weaving factories.
Eunuch Dèng Róng petitioned for this,
and the Emperor again granted permission.
Jiàn and others strongly argued,
and it was then ordered to reduce them by one-third.
That winter,
he reported that various provinces were engaged in military campaigns,
and moreover, there were floods, droughts, and many bandits.
He requested the cessation of all construction projects, and the following year's fireworks and the construction of the Shàngqīng Palace on Mount Lónghǔ.
The Emperor agreed to all.
In the first year of Zhèngdé,
lightning struck the pagoda of Nánjīng Bàonfú Temple.
The Defense Eunuch Fù Róng requested its repair.
Jiàn argued that this was a warning from Heaven,
and it was inappropriate to undertake major construction again, burdening the people's labor.
So, it was stopped.
The Supervisor of Imperial Stables Eunuch Chén Guì proposed relocating the stables.
Qīn̄tiānjiān (Imperial Astronomical Bureau) official Ní Qiān reviewed it,
and requested to follow the proposal.
Censor Táo Xié and others impeached Guì for using public office for personal gain,
and also impeached Qiān for flattering him,
but this was not accepted.
Jiàn insisted in his memorial,
stating that all stables were built under the supervision of the Qīn̄tiānjiān.
Any arbitrarily added structures afterwards
should be ordered demolished and rectified,
and rebuilt with his (Guì's) own funds,
so that horse rearing would not be hindered and the people would not be burdened.
The report was approved.
The Imperial Weaving and Dyeing Bureau requested to open weaving operations in Sūzhōu and Hángzhōu prefectures,
supplying over 24,000 pieces of brocade and silk for imperial use.
Jiàn strongly requested its suspension,
and managed to get half of it reduced by two-thirds.
Eunuchs Xǔ Yōng and others, each carrying imperial edicts, were transporting timber from various places in Zhèjiāng,
which was also halted due to Jiàn's remonstrance.
At the end of Xiàozōng's reign,
the Grand Secretariat and ministers of the Six Ministries were all chosen from the best of their time,
and Jiàn also upheld righteousness.
When he and Hán Wén and others requested the execution of eunuchs and were unsuccessful,
the remaining ministers generally became submissive to avoid disaster,
but Jiàn alone maintained his former principles.
There was an imperial edict granting a residence to the imperial relative Xià Rú.
The Emperor deemed it too small,
and wished to expand it.
Jiàn strongly remonstrated,
but was not heeded.
In the spring of the next year,
Eunuch Huáng Zhǔn, serving as Defense Commissioner of Fèngyáng,
following his request,
was granted a flag and tablet.
Jiàn and others stated that only generals on campaign and border commanders
were granted flags and tablets,
and there was no precedent for defense commissioners in the interior.
So, it was stopped.
That year, in the intercalary first month, he retired due to illness,
and soon died.
He was posthumously granted the title Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
Liáng Jǐng,
courtesy name Tíngměi,
a native of Guōxiàn.
He passed the imperial examination in the eighth year of Tiānshùn.
He was appointed Investigating Censor of the Ministry of War.
During the Chénghuà reign,
he was repeatedly promoted to Supervising Censor.
Xiàng Zhōng campaigned in Jīng and Xiāng,
forcing displaced people to return to their occupations.
Jǐng impeached him for allowing his soldiers to coerce and oppress,
which was more brutal than the bandits themselves,
the details of which are in Zhōng's biography.
When troops were deployed in Yánsuí,
Shānxī was ordered to pre-collect fodder and grain,
causing the people to flee en masse.
Jǐng memorialized about their distress,
and a reduction was granted.
The eight prefectures of Jīfǔ (the capital region) formerly had only one Grand Coordinator (Xúnfǔ),
stationed in Jìzhōu to defend the border,
unable to attend to both.
Jǐng requested that one Grand Coordinator be appointed separately for the two prefectures of Shùntiān and Yǒngpíng,
with the border affairs of Jìzhōu assigned to him,
and Grand Coordinator Chén Lián be dedicated to governing the six prefectures of Bǎodìng and overseeing the various passes of Zǐjīng.
The court deliberated and agreed,
thus setting a permanent regulation.
Later,
he and fellow officials Hán Wén and Wáng Zhào and others memorialized, requesting the recall of retired Ministers Wáng Hóng and Lǐ Bǐng,
and the dismissal of Censor-in-Chief Wáng Yuè,
also touching upon private matters of the imperial palace.
They were flogged in Wénhuá Hall.
Wǔjìng Bó Zhào Fǔ, during his western campaign, dared not fight,
claimed illness to request return,
and then plotted to take charge of the military administration.
Jǐng and others strongly denounced his crimes,
and he was ordered to recuperate at home.
After nine years in office,
he was promoted to Zǔo Cānzhèng of Shǎnxī,
assigned to guard Táo and Mín.
When the Western Barbarians invaded,
he commanded troops to slay their leader.
After the mourning period for his mother had ended,
he returned to his original post,
successively serving as Zǔo Bùzhèngshǐ and Yòubùzhèngshǐ.
He spent fifteen years in Shǎnxi both before and after,
achieving many political successes.
Upon Xiàozōng's ascension to the throne,
he was transferred to Yòu Fù Dū Yùshǐ,
and became Grand Coordinator of Húguǎng.
In Hóngzhì second year,
there was a famine among the people,
and he requested the exemption of over 890,000 shí of tribute grain from the two capitals,
which was granted.
The emperor's accession edict had already abolished additional contributions from all four directions,
yet the eunuch in charge of Wǔdāngshān continued to demand tribute of huángjīng, méisǔn, and cháyá.
Wǔdāng Daoist priests initially numbered only four hundred,
but by then they had doubled,
and the number of ordained Daoist novices doubled again,
all fed and clothed by the government,
receiving monthly allowances of oil, wax, incense, and paper offerings,
with thousands of laborers for sweeping and cleaning.
The eunuch Chén Xǐ also brought over thirty Daoist priests,
each holding an imperial decree for protection,
spreading their tyranny wherever they went.
Jǐng requested that all these be stopped and abolished,
and many of his proposals were adopted.
After the mourning period for his father had ended,
he again served as Grand Coordinator of Sìchuān.
In the seventh year, he was summoned to be appointed Nánjīng Lìbù Yòu Shìláng.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Hùbù Shàngshū.
He retired and returned home,
where he died.
Wáng Zhào,
courtesy name Wénzhèn,
was a native of Zhào.
He was born with an extraordinary appearance,
and the academician Cái Nài was impressed by him,
giving him his daughter in marriage.
At the end of Tiānshùn,
he passed the imperial examination,
and was appointed Gōngkē Jǐshìzhōng.
When Empress Ruì died,
it coincided with the autumn sacrifice at the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
The prevailing opinion at the time was that one should not abandon the venerated for the humble.
Zhào argued that according to ritual, one does not perform sacrifices during mourning;
if it was unavoidable,
then the date should be moved and awaited until the mourning period was over.
Although his proposal was not implemented,
those with discernment considered it right.
While investigating horse pastures,
he impeached Huìchāng Hóu Sūn Jìzōng and Fúníng Hóu Zhū Yǒng for embezzlement.
At that time, there was a shortage of high-ranking regional officials,
and officials of the third rank in the capital were ordered to recommend candidates.
Zhào stated that he feared this would encourage a spirit of unhealthy competition,
and it was not heeded.
He was successively promoted to Dū Jǐshìzhōng.
In the eighth year, seventh month, the construction of Lóngshàn Sì was completed by imperial decree,
and thirty artisans were granted official positions as Shàngbǎo Shà qīng,
while Rèn Dàoxùn and others were promoted for their calligraphy on steles.
Zhào submitted a memorial strongly remonstrating,
but it was not heeded.
Later,
together with Liáng Jǐng and others, he discussed matters concerning the inner court.
The emperor was greatly angered,
and summoned them to Wénhuá Diàn for a direct interrogation.
Zhào cried out,
"Although our words may not be appropriate,
our humble and sincere loyalty, like a dog or horse, is only for the sake of the country!"
Then they were flogged and released.
He was sent out as Húguǎng Yòu Cānzhèng.
Yuán Jié led the campaign in Jīng and Xiāng,
and Zhào's assistance contributed greatly to the success.
He left due to his father's mourning.
After the mourning period, he was reappointed,
and promoted to Yòu Bùzhèngshǐ.
In Hóngzhì first year, he was transferred to Guìzhōu Zǔo Bùzhèngshǐ.
That winter,
he was appointed Yòu Fù Dū Yùshǐ and Grand Coordinator of Yúnnán.
Local chieftains were fond of contending for succession,
and the relevant officials accepted their bribes,
distorting right and wrong,
causing border troubles.
Zhào did not accept bribes,
deciding all cases strictly according to law,
and also abolished inconvenient corrupt practices.
The various barbarians submitted,
and the border regions became peaceful.
There were former officials who could not return home,
many of whose wives and children were sold into slavery.
Zhào provided funds for their return,
and a great many were able to go home.
During Hóngwǔ,
Shàngshū Wú Yún died in service following Wáng Yī,
but later Yī was posthumously honored with the title Zhōngwén and annually sacrificed to,
while Yún was not.
Zhào requested this,
so Yún was posthumously honored with Zhōngjié,
and sacrificed to alongside Yī.
In the fourth year, he was summoned to be appointed Nánjīng Bīngbù Yòu Shìláng,
but he died
before taking office.
Xú Kè,
courtesy name Gōngsù,
was a native of Chángshú.
He passed the imperial examination in Chénghuà second year.
He was appointed Gōngkē Jǐshìzhōng.
When eunuchs wished to take charge of the "drawing-fee" factories,
Kè and others memorialized to dispute it.
The eunuchs were angered,
and requested Kè and others be immediately dispatched,
intending to find fault with them,
but found nothing and then stopped.
He was sent out as Húguǎng Zǔo Cānyì,
and promoted to Hénán Yòu Cānzhèng.
Shǎnxī suffered a famine,
and tens of thousands of shí of grain needed to be transported.
Kè, considering the long distance, requested payment in cash instead,
which was praised as convenient by all.
In early Hóngzhì,
he was successively promoted to Zǔo Bùzhèngshǐ and Yòu Bùzhèngshǐ.
Huī Wáng Fǔ Chéngfèng Sī illegally appointed officials,
and Kè abolished this.
The prince memorialized that Kè had encroached upon and insulted him,
but the emperor sent a letter admonishing the prince.
When the Yellow River shifted and threatened Kāifēng,
some suggested relocating the princely establishment and the Three Judicial Offices to Xǔzhōu,
but Kè stated it was not convenient,
and the idea was dropped.
In the fourth year, he was appointed Yòu Fù Dū Yùshǐ,
and Grand Coordinator of that region.
He memorialized:
"Figures like Qín Xiàng Liáng, Táng Páng Xùn, and Yuán Fāng Gǔzhēn often arose in the southeast.
Now the people's strength in the southeast is exhausted,
further exacerbated by successive floods and droughts.
Last winter, a comet swept Tiānjīn,
directly over the Wú-Yuè region.
I beg for the recall of the eunuchs in charge of weaving and manufacturing,
and an imperial edict for all grand coordinators and censors to pay extra attention to comforting and soothing the people,
to prevent extraordinary changes."
The emperor did not comply.
According to old customs,
when a princely establishment suffered a great loss,
eunuchs were sent to offer sacrifices, disturbing the populace along their way.
At the end of Chénghuà,
it began to be the practice to only send officials from the princely establishment.
When the emperor ascended the throne,
this practice was reinstated.
Kè requested adherence to the former emperor's system,
and also listed several matters to be carried out: reducing superfluous officials, clarifying land taxes, prohibiting undue exactions, standardizing redemption rates, and abolishing "drawing-fees,"
many of which were adopted.
When the Hùbù urgently pressed for arrears,
Kè, due to the disasters, requested a delay.
Censor Lǐ Xīng requested the establishment of separate Three Judicial Offices in Yún yáng,
attaching Nányáng, Jīngzhōu, Xiāngyáng, Hànzhōng, Bǎoníng, and Kuízhōu to it.
Kè presented five reasons why this was not feasible,
and it was then stopped.
Kè 恪 was by nature upright and firm.
Wherever he went,
he suppressed powerful gentry
and eradicated corrupt practices.
When he became a巡撫 (Xúnfǔ, Provincial Governor),
because his jurisdiction contained many princely establishments,
he enforced the law with even greater strictness.
Many members of the imperial clan were displeased.
The princes of Pínglè 平樂 and Yìníng 義寧 then impeached Kè 恪 for reducing their stipends and altering the status of their校尉 (jiàowèi, captains of guards) and other matters.
The investigation found no evidence.
Kè 恪 was instead punished for mistakenly entering the Duānlǐmén 端禮門 (Gate of Proper Rites) of a princely residence,
an attempt to appease the two princes.
The Emperor knew Kè 恪 was innocent,
but considering the two princes were young,
he issued an edict severely reprimanding them,
and ordered Húguǎng 湖廣 Xúnfǔ 巡撫 Hán Wén 韓文 to swap posts with Kè 恪.
The officials and common people closed their markets
and wept as they saw him off for dozens of *lǐ* 里 without ceasing.
Subordinate officials offered him surplus gold as a farewell gift,
but he waved them away.
Upon arrival, he happened upon the Prince of Qí 岐 returning to his fief.
Imperial eunuchs, carrying several hundred salt boats,
were forcing the sale of salt upon the people.
Kè 恪 blocked their progress.
Their faction secretly slandered him to the Emperor.
After a year,
an imperial decree transferred him to Nánjīng Nánjīng 南京 Gōngbù Yòu Shìláng 工部右侍郎 (Vice Minister of Works, Junior Second Rank) .
Kè 恪 submitted a memorial, saying:
"The promotion of high officials
should come from a court recommendation,
and I have never heard of anyone attaining it through an informal imperial decree.
Throughout my life, I have not dared to advance through other means;
I request that I be dismissed."
The Emperor consoled him and urged him to stay,
so he accepted the appointment.
He firmly refused requests from powerful families who arbitrarily demanded craftsmen.
In the eleventh year, he went to the capital for performance review,
fell ill,
then retired,
and
passed away.
Lǐ Jiè 李介,
courtesy name Shǒuzhēn 守貞,
was a native of Gāomì 高密.
He obtained his *jìnshì* 進士 degree in the fifth year of Chénghuà 成化.
He was selected as a Shùjíshì 庶吉士 (bachelor of the Hanlin Academy)
and later changed to a Yùshǐ 御史 (Censor).
He inspected salt administration in Liǎngzhè 兩浙,
and then was in charge of Hénán Dào 河南道 (Henan Circuit).
Due to widespread natural disasters,
he presented several proposals on current political affairs,
most of which the Emperor adopted.
Jiè 介 was outspoken;
whenever he encountered something he disapproved of,
he would often lead his colleagues in remonstrating.
He displeased the Emperor,
and was twice flogged in court.
After nine years,
he was promoted to Dàlǐchéng 大理丞 (Assistant Minister of the Court of Judicial Review),
then advanced to Shàoqīng 少卿 (Vice Minister).
In the first year of Hóngzhì 弘治,
he was transferred to Yòu Qiāndū Yùshǐ 右僉都御史 (Assistant Censor-in-Chief),
巡撫 (Xúnfǔ, Provincial Governor) of Xuānfǔ 宣府.
Soon after, he was summoned to assist in court affairs.
He successively served as Bīngbù Zuǒ Shìláng 兵部左侍郎 (Vice Minister of War, Senior Second Rank) and Bīngbù Yòu Shìláng 兵部右侍郎 (Vice Minister of War, Junior Second Rank).
In the summer of the tenth year,
northern invaders planned to attack Dàtóng 大同.
Jiè 介 was ordered to concurrently hold the post of Zuǒ Qiāndū Yùshǐ 左僉都御史 (Assistant Censor-in-Chief),
to supervise military provisions,
and to plan the defense.
By the time he arrived,
the invaders had already retreated,
so he extensively repaired military defenses.
He investigated and returned the official lands, cattle, and money to the army,
using these funds to pay off the outstanding horse prices owed by the military.
The border residents were grateful and pleased.
He successively submitted twenty proposals for expedient measures.
He passed away
and was posthumously granted the title of Shàngshū 尚書 (Minister).
His son, Kūn 昆,
courtesy name Chéngyù 承裕,
obtained his *jìnshì* 進士 degree in the early Hóngzhì 弘治 era.
He successively served as Lǐbù Zhǔshì 禮部主事 (Secretary of the Ministry of Rites).
When the eunuch Hé Dǐng 何鼎 was imprisoned for his remarks,
the Censorate officials pleaded for him,
and were all reprimanded.
Kūn 昆 again argued for his release,
but was not heard.
He returned home for his father's mourning period,
and then was appointed as Bīngbù Zhǔshì 兵部主事 (Secretary of the Ministry of War).
The Emperor was planning to build the Yánshòu Tǎ 延壽塔 (Pagoda of Longevity) outside the city,
and Kūn 昆 again submitted a memorial of remonstrance.
In the early Zhèngdé 正德 era,
petty individuals held sway.
He requested the dismissal of corrupt officials,
the promotion of loyal and upright ones,
the prevention of requests from eunuchs and imperial relatives,
and the reduction of extravagant spending both inside and outside the court.
All his proposals were rejected.
He was promoted to Yuánwàiláng 員外郎 (Assistant Director),
but displeased Shàngshū 尚書 Liú Yǔ 劉宇,
and was demoted to Zhī Jiězhōu 知解州 (Prefect of Jiězhōu).
He was repeatedly promoted to Shǎnxī Zuǒ Bùzhèngshǐ 陝西左布政使 (Chief Administrator of Shǎnxī, Senior Third Rank).
In the tenth year, he became Yòu Fùdū Yùshǐ 右副都御史 (Vice Censor-in-Chief, Junior Second Rank) and Xúnfǔ 巡撫 (Provincial Governor) of Gānsù 甘肅.
Together with Zǒngdū 總督 (Supreme Commander) Péng Zé 彭澤, he planned the affairs of Hāmì 哈密.
Bīngbù Shàngshū 兵部尚書 (Minister of War) Wáng Qióng 王瓊 impeached Zé 澤 for improper handling of matters,
and Kūn 昆 was implicated,
and arrested.
The judicial authorities stated that Kūn 昆's strategy to block the strong invaders
could not be ignored.
Qióng 王瓊 disagreed,
and Kūn 昆 was demoted to Zhèjiāng Fùshǐ 浙江副使 (Vice Commissioner of Zhèjiāng).
When Shìzōng 世宗 ascended the throne,
Qióng 王瓊 fell out of favor.
Kūn 昆 was reinstated,
and served as Xúnfǔ 巡撫 (Provincial Governor) of Shùntiān 順天.
Soon after, he was summoned to be Bīngbù Yòu Shìláng 兵部右侍郎 (Vice Minister of War, Junior Second Rank),
and in the early Jiājìng 嘉靖 era,
he was made Zuǒ 左 (Senior Second Rank).
There was a military revolt in Dàtóng 大同,
and Xúnfǔ 巡撫 Zhāng Wénjǐn 張文錦 was killed.
Kūn 昆 was ordered to go and pacify the situation.
He exercised his authority to grant a partial amnesty,
and upon his return, requested that Zhāng Wénjǐn 張文錦 be given posthumous honors and a pension.
The Emperor, at that time, was angry about the revolt,
and refused.
He fell ill and returned home,
and after a long time, passed away.
Huáng Kē 黃珂,
courtesy name Míngyù 鳴玉,
was a native of Suíníng 遂寧.
He obtained his *jìnshì* 進士 degree in the twentieth year of Chénghuà 成化.
He was appointed Zhīxiàn 知縣 (Magistrate) of Lóngyáng 龍陽.
His administrative achievements became known,
and he was promoted to Yùshǐ 御史 (Censor),
and sent to inspect Guìzhōu 貴州.
The Gold-reach chieftain Hé Lún 何碖 conspired to rebel,
and Kē 珂 captured him by stratagem,
and appointed regular officials.
When the bandit woman Mǐ Lù 米魯 rebelled,
he impeached Xúnfǔ 巡撫 Qián Yuè 錢鉞 and Zǒngbīngguān 總兵官 Jiāo Jùn 焦俊 and others,
who were all punished.
He was transferred to inspect Jīfǔ 畿輔 (the Capital Region),
and successively served as Shānxī Ànchásǐ 山西按察使 (Provincial Surveillance Commissioner of Shānxī).
In the fourth year of Zhèngdé 正德, he was promoted to Yòu Qiāndū Yùshǐ 右僉都御史 (Assistant Censor-in-Chief) and Xúnfǔ 巡撫 (Provincial Governor) of Yánsuí 延綏.
When the Prince of Ānhuà 安化, Zhìpàn 寘鐇, rebelled,
he issued a proclamation to the four directions,
using the pretext of punishing Liú Jǐn 劉瑾.
Other garrisons feared Jǐn 瑾 and
dared not report it.
Kē 珂 sealed and submitted his proclamation,
and then presented eight expedient measures,
and immediately ordered Fù Zǒngbīng Hóu Xūn 副總兵侯勛 (Vice General-in-Chief) and Cāncāng Shí Yuán 參將時源 (Assistant General) to divide their troops and guard the east of the river.
The rebels then dared not advance.
Yì Bùlà 亦不剌 (Ismail) invaded the border,
and Kē 珂, along with Zǒngbīngguān Mǎ Áng 總兵官馬昂 (General-in-Chief), led the army to battle,
defeating them at Mùguā Shān 木瓜山 (Papaya Mountain).
In the sixth year, they again invaded the border.
Kē 珂 dispatched Fù Zǒngbīng Wáng Xūn 副總兵王勛 and six other generals to occupy strategic points and launch a pincer attack,
defeating them again.
He was repeatedly awarded imperial letters and silver and silk.
In the autumn of that year,
he entered the capital as Hùbù Yòu Shìláng 戶部右侍郎 (Vice Minister of Revenue, Junior Second Rank),
and was made Zǒngdū Cāngchǎng 總督倉場 (Supreme Commander of Granaries).
When military operations began in Hénán 河南,
he was sent to manage military provisions.
The local and guest troops numbered over 100,000,
pursuing and fighting,
constantly changing their positions.
Kē 珂 continuously transported supplies as needed,
and there was no shortage during the military campaign.
For his merits, his salary was increased by one rank.
He was transferred to the Xíngbù 刑部 (Ministry of Justice),
promoted to Zuǒ Shìláng 左侍郎 (Vice Minister, Senior Second Rank),
and then transferred to assist the Bīngbù 兵部 (Ministry of War).
When the Prince of Níng 寧, Chénháo 宸濠, planned to restore his guards,
Kē 珂's opposition was uniquely firm.
In the ninth year, he was promoted to Nánjīng Yòu Dū Yùshǐ 南京右都御史 (Vice Censor-in-Chief of Nánjīng, Junior Second Rank),
and soon after, was appointed Gōngbù Shàngshū 工部尚書 (Minister of Works).
He requested retirement due to his age and returned home,
and passed away.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tàizǐ Shàobǎo 太子少保 (Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent),
and given the posthumous name Jiǎnsù 簡肅.
Wáng Hóngrú,
courtesy name Màoxué,
was a Nányáng native.
In his youth, he excelled at calligraphy,
and being from a poor family, he became a clerical assistant in the prefecture.
The Prefect Duàn Jiān admired his calligraphy
and kept him in his office,
personally teaching him.
He was sent to school as a student,
and subsequently came first in the provincial examination.
At the end of the Chénghuà reign,
he passed the imperial examination,
and was appointed as a director in the Nánjīng Ministry of Revenue.
He was successively promoted to bureau director,
then promoted to Circuit Censor of Shānxī,
and further promoted to Vice Commissioner,
all serving as Inspector of Education.
He served for nine years,
and scholarly customs flourished greatly.
Xiàozōng once said to Liú Dàxià:
“Among the provincial officials, if there is a Wáng Hóngrú,
he can be of great use in the future.”
In the first year of Zhèngdé,
he resigned due to illness.
When Liú Jǐn monopolized power,
he recalled famous scholars.
In the summer of the fourth year,
Wáng Hóngrú was appointed as Rector of the Guózǐ (Imperial Academy),
but left due to his father's mourning.
He was re-appointed as Nánjīng Vice Minister of Revenue,
then served as Right Vice Minister of Personnel,
and soon after was transferred to Left Vice Minister.
In the fourteenth year, he was promoted to Nánjīng Minister of Revenue.
Soon after he took office,
Chén Háo rebelled,
and he was ordered to supervise military provisions.
A carbuncle erupted on his back,
and he consequently died,
posthumously named Wénzhuāng.
Hóngrú’s scholarship
was dedicated to thoroughly understanding principles and applying them,
which was highly regarded by his contemporaries.
While in the Ministry of Personnel,
he maintained his integrity and self-discipline,
and his gate was free of private visitors.
His younger brother, Hóngjiàn,
also came first in the provincial examination.
As a *jìnshì*, he successively held the office of Right Provincial Administration Commissioner of Shāndōng,
and was known for his honesty and serenity.
Cóng Lán,
courtesy name Tíngxiù,
was a Wéndēng native.
He passed the imperial examination in the third year of Hóngzhì.
He served as Investigating Censor for the Ministry of Revenue.
The eunuchs Liáng Fāng, Chén Xǐ, Wāng Zhí, and Wéi Xìng,
having previously been dismissed due to their crimes,
had managed to return to the capital.
Taking advantage of a fire in the Qīngníng Palace,
Lán submitted a memorial detailing six matters,
strongly denouncing Fāng and the others’ crimes,
and these individuals were consequently purged.
Soon after, he stated:
“The Ministry of Personnel, in accordance with the imperial edict,
requested the promotion and appointment of officials who were mistakenly implicated for their remonstrances,
but the clear imperial decree was not fully followed,
which does not show trustworthiness.
For those disciplined for improper conduct,
I request they be exempted from being sent to the imperial prison.
Conscriptions and levies in the capital region are heavy;
wealthy households scheme to avoid them,
and other households bear the burden in their stead.
This should be rectified.”
The memorial was sent down to the relevant departments.
He was promoted to Right Investigating Censor for the Ministry of War.
The Grand Coordinator-cum-Censor-in-Chief Wú Ān had obtained his official post through imperial favor,
and Lán requested his dismissal.
At that time, an order was issued to dispatch eight thousand men from the training camps to repair the moat around the nine gates.
Lán stated:
“Your servant recently inspected the camp troops,
and an imperial edict permitted them to focus solely on training and instruction,
without further dispatch or assignment.
Not long after this order was issued,
they were again pressed into service.
What then of the previous edict?”
Consequently, the dispatch was cancelled.
He was promoted to Communication Assistant.
When the Little Prince invaded Dàtóng,
he was ordered to manage the defense of over a hundred accessible mountain passes and paths in Zǐjīng and Dàomǎ that could be used by enemy cavalry.
In the third year of Zhèngdé, he was promoted to Left Chief Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments.
In the winter of the following year, he was sent to manage the military colonies in Yánsuí.
When Prince Ānhuà Zhìpán rebelled,
Lán submitted a memorial detailing ten matters,
which included:
“Civil and military officials penalized with grain fines
cannot pay even by selling their property.
Court officials exiled to the garrisons are falsely accused by judicial officials who invoke new precedents to fabricate charges,
confiscating their household assets.
Patrol officers are widespread in the border regions,
their influence and power are overwhelming,
and people cannot protect themselves.”
Liú Jǐn was greatly displeased,
and issued a forged edict sternly reproving him.
Investigating Censor Zhāng Zàn and Censor Wāng Cì and others then, in an attempt to curry favor with the emperor, impeached Lán.
Jǐn was at that time preoccupied with border affairs,
and left the matter unaddressed.
Several months later,
Jǐn was executed,
and Lán was promoted to Chief Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments.
Soon after, he was promoted to Right Vice Minister of Revenue,
supervising military provisions for the three borders.
In the sixth year,
the Governor-General of Shǎnxī, Lán Zhāng, moved his headquarters to Hànzhōng due to banditry in April.
At that time, there was an alarm in the Hétào region,
so Lán was ordered to concurrently manage military affairs in Gù, Jìng, and other areas.
Lán memorialized:
“The grain and fodder transported from Shǎnxī
are frequently encroached upon by wealthy households.
I request that officials be assigned to escort them.
For each garrison, I request that tens of thousands of taels of silver be issued from the imperial treasury
to purchase grain and fodder in advance.
Censor Zhāng Yù has cleared out fields;
I request that grain taxes be exempted,
according to the rates before the eighteenth year of Hóngzhì.
For the salt duties in Língzhōu,
I request that they be opened for exchange as per precedent,
to invite merchants to purchase grain.
For the commutation of military pay,
those in charge often make deductions.
I humbly request that nearby local officials be selected and appointed to distribute it.”
This was approved.
In the winter of that year,
the Southern Zhílì and Hénán suffered from famine,
and Lán was ordered to go and provide relief.
Before he departed, bandits from Héběi crossed the river from Sùqiān,
threatening Fèngyáng.
Lán was then ordered, in his current capacity, to inspect Lú, Fèng, Chú, and Hé,
and concurrently manage relief efforts.
The White Lotus bandit Zhào Jǐnglóng from Hénán declared himself King of Sòng,
and plundered Guīdé.
Lán dispatched Commander Shí Jiān and Prefect Zhāng Sīqí and others to attack and execute him.
In September,
the banditry was quelled.
For his meritorious service, he was awarded gold and silk,
his salary was increased by one grade,
and he was recalled to manage affairs in the Ministry.
As there was no vacancy for a Vice Minister in the Ministry,
an additional position was created for him.
The following year,
there was an alarm in Dàtóng,
and he was ordered to inspect the Jūyōng, Lóngquán, and other passes.
Soon after, he concurrently supervised military provisions for Xuān and Dà,
and was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief,
controlling military affairs for Xuān, Dà, and Shāndōng.
He ordered that all inland areas build forts,
so that when invaders arrived, people could gather for protection as in the frontier.
When fifty thousand cavalry from Wànquán Right Guard marched to Wèizhōu and plundered extensively,
and another thirty thousand cavalry entered Pínglǔ South City,
he was suspended from half his salary for six months for failing in his duties.
In the summer of the tenth year,
he was transferred to supervise grain transport by canal,
and soon concurrently served as Governor of Jiāngběi.
The eunuch Liú Yǔn, en route to obtain a Buddhist treasure from Wū Sī Zàng,
passed through Lán’s jurisdiction.
Liú Yǔn came to pay his respects,
but Lán refused to see him.
Yǔn demanded over five hundred boats and over ten thousand laborers.
Lán swiftly submitted a memorial strongly denouncing the harm caused.
There was no reply.
After four years,
he offended the Minister of War Wáng Qióng over an incident,
was relieved of his duties regarding canal transport,
and solely appointed as Governor.
When Prince Níng Chén Háo rebelled,
Lán moved his headquarters to Guāzhōu.
In the fifteenth year, he was promoted to Nánjīng Minister of Works.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
Censor Chén Kèzhái impeached Lán for collaborating with Jiāng Bīn.
The Emperor, considering Lán to be consistently upright and cautious,
exonerated him without further inquiry.
Lán then requested retirement and left.
He died
and was posthumously granted the title of Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
Wú Shìzhōng,
courtesy name Màozhēn,
was a native of Jīnxī.
He obtained his *jìnshì* degree in the third year of Hóngzhì (1490).
He was appointed Investigating Censor of the Ministry of War (Bīngkē Jǐshìzhōng).
When the people of the Liǎng Jī and Shāndōng, Hénán, and Zhèjiāng provinces suffered from famine,
an imperial edict was issued for relief,
but the responsible officials awaited verification.
Shìzhōng strongly spoke of the abuses,
and thus proposed two matters: developing water conservancy and restoring the Ever-Normal Granary (Chángpíngcāng) system.
Many of his suggestions were implemented.
Later,
he requested compassion for the ministers who died as martyrs during the Jiànwén reign,
asking for them to be granted noble ranks and posthumous titles,
for them to be honored with temple sacrifices,
and moreover, for their descendants to be recorded,
and their clans reinstated,
to encourage loyalty and righteousness.
His memorial was sent to the Ministry of Rites,
but it was shelved and not acted upon.
When Minister (Shàngshū) Wáng Shù was slandered and sought to resign,
Shìzhōng submitted a memorial requesting his retention.
The Marquis of Shòuníng, Zhāng Hèlíng, sought an investigation into bestowed land in Héjiān,
and his mother, Lady Jīn (Jīn Fūrén), repeatedly pressed the issue.
The Emperor ordered an envoy to be dispatched.
Shìzhōng said:
“The Marquis’s family relies on their close imperial ties.
How can they contend with commoners over mere inches of land?
The Ministry was ordered to investigate, but before it was finished,
imperial eunuchs continued it.
Before the imperial eunuchs were finished,
senior ministers continued it again.
Stripping the people and accumulating resentment
is not a blessing for the state,
and especially not a blessing for the imperial relatives by marriage.”
The Emperor did not heed him.
The Grand Coordinator (Zǒngbīngguān) of Dàtóng, Shén Yīng, and the Vice Grand Coordinator (Fùzǒngbīng), Zhào Chǎng, and others,
used their family members at the horse market to illegally exchange horses for prohibited silk fabrics.
As a result, non-Han people trespassed to illegally trade for iron tools.
After leaving the frontier,
they secretly sent troops to plunder Yùzhōu,
captured the military stables (mǎyíng),
and then raided the Zhōng Dōng Èr Lù.
Yīng and others held back their troops and did not offer aid,
and the Grand Coordinator (Xúnfǔ) Liú Huán and the Garrison Eunuch (Zhènshǒu Zhōngguān) Sūn Zhèn also failed to report the truth.
In the eleventh year (1498),
the matter came to light,
and Shìzhōng went to investigate.
He submitted a memorial detailing the dilapidated state of Dàtóng’s frontier defenses,
and the suffering of the soldiers.
He then strongly stated that Yīng, Huán, and others were greedy for profit and fearful of the enemy,
utterly lacking in discipline.
Yīng was dismissed from office,
Huán and Zhèn were recalled,
and Chǎng, along with Mobile Corps Commander (Yóují) Liú Huái and Assistant Commander (Cānjìang) Lǐ Yǔ, were all arrested and interrogated.
Afterwards, Huán was reassigned as a Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review (Dàlǐ Shàoqīng),
and Chǎng, upon review by Minister (Dàlǐ Chéng) Wú Yīguàn, was merely demoted in rank.
Shìzhōng again vehemently argued Huán’s guilt,
and furthermore criticized Yīguàn,
but the Emperor ignored it all.
When the Confucian Temple (Wénmiào) in Quēlǐ suffered a fire,
he presented eight proposals,
but not all were adopted.
When bandits attacked Yánsuí and Dàtóng,
Shìzhōng said:
“At the beginning of the dynasty (Guóchū), seventy-two guards were established,
with no less than a million soldiers.
Recently, military administration has daily deteriorated,
and we cannot even get ten to twenty thousand elite soldiers.
This military is cause for concern.
The reserves of the Grand Granary (Tàicāng)
were originally for military provisions.
Recently, expenditures have daily expanded,
and diversions of funds have daily increased.
If an army of 100,000 were raised,
there would be no source for their provisions and rewards.
This food supply is cause for concern.
During the Tumu Crisis of Jǐsì in the Zhèngtǒng era (Zhèngtǒng Jǐsì zhī Biàn), there were still Shí Hēng and Yáng Hóng.
Recently, those employed, such as Lǐ Gǎo, Ruǎn Xīng, Zhào Chǎng, and Liú Huái,
have all successively failed.
Now Wáng Xǐ and Mǎ Shēng have also reported failures.
These generals are cause for concern.
When the nation has many troubles,
senior ministers should be there to stabilize it.
Recently, loyal and upright officials are mostly dismissed,
while greedy and mediocre ones survive.
With few talents for rectification and salvation,
and ignorant of the principles of resignation and appointment,
how can they deter powerful enemies and strengthen the nation’s prestige?
This appointment of personnel is cause for concern.
Governance is often flawed and erratic,
and the people daily sigh with resentment.
The capital army (Jīngjūn) is exhausted by corvée labor,
the capital commoners (Jīngmín) suffer from coercive tax collection,
and those in the capital region (Jīdiàn) yearn for imperial favor with particular urgency.
Seeing that they are so unhappy with their lives,
who will fight to the death in times of trouble?
This popular sentiment is cause for concern.
Heavenly portents frequently appear,
and fires repeatedly break out.
An earthquake in Yúnnán crushed over ten thousand homes,
and a horse plague in Dàtóng killed two thousand horses.
This will of Heaven is cause for concern.
I wish that Your Majesty would follow what is good and abhor what is evil to win the hearts of the people,
and seriously reflect to change the will of Heaven.
Dispatch important civil and military officials to manage Xuān and Dàtóng,
to strengthen border defenses.
Dismiss incompetent officials,
and appoint those who are naturally talented and reputable,
such as Qiáo Xīn, Liú Dàxià, Ní Yuè, Dài Shān, Zhāng Fūhuá, and Lín Jùn,
to take charge of state affairs.
Then the bandits will flee at the mere sight of them,
and the border regions can be free from worry.”
The Emperor, finding his words full of defamation,
severely reprimanded him.
Soon after, he requested the addition of more forts and towers in Dàtóng,
and that idle land be given to soldiers for cultivation,
with no taxes levied on them.
When Jiāngxī suffered famine and banditry in a certain year,
he requested the selection of a new Grand Coordinator (Xúnfǔ),
and the dismissal of corrupt and cruel officials.
He also requested the construction of the outer wall of the capital.
The responsible ministries mostly followed his proposals.
He was again promoted to Left Investigating Censor of the Ministry of Personnel (Lìkē Zuǒ Jǐshìzhōng),
then to Consultative Official (Cānyì) of Húguǎng,
but was demoted to Surveillance Commissioner (Qiānshì) of Shāndōng due to an incident.
In the intercalary ninth month of the fourth year of Zhèngdé (1509), he was summoned to serve as Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Guānglù Shàoqīng),
and soon after was transferred to Chief Minister of the Imperial Seal Office (Shàngbǎosī Qīng).
In the winter of that year,
he went with Cóng Lán, a Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Messengers (Tōngzhèng), and others to manage border settlements.
Shìzhōng went to Jìzhōu.
The next year, he memorialized:
“The abuses of occupying land for cultivation and illegally selling it
have accumulated for a long time.
If we investigate each case one by one,
it might cause public unrest.
I request that a moderate approach be taken for their disposition.”
This was accepted.
When Liú Jǐn was defeated,
censors impeached Shìzhōng, accusing him of having previously requested a clear audit of garrison lands,
thus assisting Jǐn in his tyrannical acts.
Shìzhōng was by nature upright and outspoken,
so the court deliberated leniently,
and he was pardoned.
He was again promoted to Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review (Dàlǐ Shàoqīng).
In the eighth year (1513), he was promoted to Vice Censor-in-Chief on the Right (Yòù Qiāndū Yùshǐ) and concurrently Grand Coordinator (Xúnfǔ) of Yánsuí.
When bandits were in the Hétào region,
he pursued them but suffered a defeat,
and then, citing illness, retired.
The encomium says: From the Yīngzōng Emperor onward in the Míng dynasty,
the gates of favoritism opened daily.
Imperial decrees were issued for favors and requests,
resulting in superfluous officials and excessive corvée,
and extravagant spending.
At the height of prosperity came decline,
and the national finances were thereby reduced.
Lǐ Mǐn and others painstakingly cherished the nation’s wealth,
resisted powerful favorites,
to seek relief for the people.
However, such meager help
could not mend a leaking jug.
When the nation is in an era of peace and prosperity,
a heart for extravagance easily arises.
Imperial favorites take advantage of this,
and wasteful expenditures daily increase.
The *Yì* says,
“Regulate with institutions,
so as not to injure wealth
or harm the people.”
It also says,
“If one does not regulate,
then one will sigh.”
These are the actions for a reverent and frugal ruler.●●
Collation Notes

Biographies Seventy-Four: Hán Wén (Gù Zuǒ, Chén Rén), Zhāng Fūhuá, Yáng Shǒusuí (brother Shǒuyú), Xǔ Jìn (sons Gào, Zàn, Lùn), Yōng Tài (Zhāng Jīn), Chén Shòu, Fán Yíng, Xióng Xiù, Pān Fān, Hú Fù, Zhāng Tài (Wú Wéndù), Zhāng Nài (Mào Zhèng), Wáng Jǐng, Zhū Qīn.
Hán Wén,
courtesy name Guàn Dào,
a native of Hóngdòng.
He was a descendant of Sòng Chancellor Qí.
When he was born,
his father dreamed of a man in purple clothes carrying Wén Yànbó and bringing him to their house,
hence he was named Wén.
In the second year of Chénghuà (1466), he passed the imperial examination as a *jìnshì*,
and was appointed as a supervising secretary of the Ministry of Works.
He audited military merits in Wéizhōu,
impeached the Earl of Níngjìn, Liú Jù,
and the Censors-in-chief Wáng Yuè and Mǎ Wénshēng for excessive killing and false reporting.
Soon after, he impeached Wáng Yuè for recommending Lǐ Bǐng and Wáng Hóng,
and his language somewhat touched upon the two palaces,
enraging the Emperor.
He was flogged in the courtyard of Wénhuá Diàn.
Afterward,
he was promoted to supervising secretary of the right,
then sent out as a right assistant administration commissioner of Húguǎng.
The eunuchs supervising Tài Hé Shān
embezzled public funds.
Hán Wén strongly suppressed them,
and used the surplus to buy ten thousand *shí* of grain,
to be prepared for relief and loans.
The local chieftains of Jiǔxī fought over land with neighboring territories.
Hán Wén went to admonish them,
and they all submitted.
After seven years,
he was transferred to the left.
When Hóngzhì began,
Wáng Shù, considering Hán Wén had been long overlooked,
appointed him as a left administration commissioner of Shāndōng.
After two years,
upon the recommendation of Ní Yuè,
he was promoted to left administration commissioner of Yúnnán.
He was appointed right vice censor-in-chief to serve as grand coordinator of Húguǎng,
then transferred to grand coordinator of Hénán,
and summoned to be a right vice minister of the Ministry of Revenue.
After the period of mourning for his mother,
he was reinstated and transferred to the Ministry of Personnel,
then promoted to left vice minister.
In the sixteenth year (1503), he was appointed Minister of War of Nánjīng.
That year, a famine occurred,
and rice prices soared.
Hán Wén requested to pre-distribute three months of military provisions,
but the Ministry of Revenue found it difficult.
Hán Wén said:
"Relieving famine is like fighting a fire.
If there is any fault,
I will bear it myself."
Then he distributed 160,000 *shí* from the granaries,
and the rice price stabilized.
The following year, he was summoned and appointed Minister of Revenue.
Hán Wén was dignified, composed, and refined,
usually reserved.
But when facing major affairs,
he was resolute and unyielding.
When Wǔzōng ascended the throne,
the expenses for awards, imperial tombs, and the grand wedding,
amounted to over 1.8 million *liǎng* of silver,
which the ministry's treasury could not supply.
Hán Wén requested to first draw from the Chéngyùn Treasury,
but the imperial edict did not permit it.
Hán Wén said:
"The treasury is empty.
Apart from the awards for the capital and border soldiers,
please distribute silver and paper currency separately,
supplemented slightly by funds from the inner treasury and imperial household,
and temporarily borrow the taxes from the bestowed estates of meritorious relatives;
furthermore, order the eunuchs of the Chéngyùn Treasury to audit the accumulated gold and silver,
and record it.
And completely abolish all non-urgent expenditures."
The Emperor did not want to draw from the inner treasury,
and ordered Hán Wén to gradually plan it.
Hán Wén upheld the general principles,
and was committed to saving money for the country.
When the Daoist master Chén Yìngxī and the Imperial Grand Preceptor Nàpǔjiāncān and others were dismissed from their posts,
Hán Wén requested to confiscate their property for the national treasury.
According to old regulations,
there were no more than two or three eunuchs in charge of bureaus and warehouses.
Later, more were gradually added,
sometimes over ten people per warehouse, and up to thirty-two people in the Shànglín Yuàn and Línhéng Shǔ.
Hán Wén strongly requested to reduce their numbers.
Princess Chún'ān was granted three hundred *qǐng* of land,
and then wanted to seize common people's property in Rènqiū.
Hán Wén strongly argued against it, and it was stopped.
During Xiàozōng's reign,
the emperor's relatives, the families of the Marquis of Qìngyún and Shòuníng, and merchants like Tán Jǐngqīng,
petitioned to buy residual salt amounting to 1.8 million *yǐn*.
Hán Wén listed seven long-standing abuses of salt administration,
and particularly sharply criticized the residual salt issue.
Xiàozōng approved it,
but died before it could be implemented.
It was immediately included in Wǔzōng's edict upon his ascension,
and abolished.
The Marquis's family again petitioned,
which was submitted to the ministry for further discussion.
Hán Wén and others repeatedly insisted on their objections,
but were not followed,
and the Marquis's request was ultimately granted.
In the first year of Zhèngdé (1506),
the Grand Secretariat and censors again debated it,
and an imperial edict ordered a court discussion.
Hán Wén said:
"The salt laws were established
specifically to provision the borders.
Now Shānxi and Shǎnxī are suffering from famine,
and bandits are invading on a large scale.
The treasury is depleted,
and transporting provisions is very difficult.
How can we undermine the ancestral laws
and disregard the importance of border defense?"
Tán Jǐngqīng again petitioned as before.
Hán Wén and others impeached him for his arrogance and defiance,
and requested he be handed over to legal officials.
The Emperor, having no choice,
finally rescinded his previous order.
Prince Róng requested estates in Bàzhōu,
and Prince Chóng requested to collect his estate rents directly,
without allowing officials to intervene.
Hán Wén rejected both.
Wáng Jǐng, the grand coordinator of Bǎodìng, requested to abolish imperial estates.
The court deliberated and agreed,
but the Emperor ordered further discussion.
Hán Wén requested that the grand coordinator officials summon commoners to lease the land,
collecting three *fēn* of silver per *mǔ* to be remitted to the inner treasury,
and entirely withdraw the eunuchs managing the estates.
Grand Secretaries Liú Jiàn and others also strongly argued that eunuchs managing estates disturbed the people.
Then an order was issued to keep one eunuch and ten guards for each estate,
with the rest following Hán Wén's proposal.
An imperial directive sought precious stones and Western pearls.
Hán Wén requested to completely reject rare treasures,
to cultivate frugality.
The request was approved.
The Emperor was to have a grand wedding,
and wanted to take 400,000 *liǎng* of silver from the Ministry of Revenue.
Hán Wén repeatedly submitted memorials,
and managed to exempt one-quarter of it.
for two years.
He vigorously suppressed powerful and favored individuals,
who deeply resented him.
At this time, eight former eunuchs of the Eastern Palace, including Liú Jǐn and others, were known as
"The Eight Tigers."
Daily, they led the Emperor to engage in dog racing, horse racing, hawk hunting, rabbit hunting, singing, dancing, and wrestling,
neglecting all state affairs.
Each time Wén retired from court,
he spoke of this with his colleagues,
often shedding tears.
Lángzhōng Lǐ Mèngyáng stepped forward and said:
"You are a great minister,
by duty sharing the country's weal and woe.
What good is merely weeping?
Censorate officials have already impeached these eunuchs,
and the executive officials are firmly supporting it.
If you, in good faith, seize this opportunity to lead the great ministers in a firm remonstrance,
removing 'The Eight Tigers'
will be easy."
Wén stroked his beard, raised his shoulders,
and resolutely changed his expression, saying:
"Excellent.
Even if the matter fails to succeed,
my age is enough to die,
and not dying would be insufficient to repay the country."
Immediately, he and the other great ministers knelt before the palace to present a memorial,
which roughly stated:
"A ruler who distinguishes the wicked is enlightened;
a minister who dares to challenge the ruler's face is loyal.
Moreover, a cabal of petty individuals
press close to the ruler's side,
and the country's safety and danger, order and chaos, all depend on this.
We, your subjects, humbly observe that in recent years, court governance has worsened daily,
and edicts are ill-suited.
Since autumn began,
court sessions have started progressively later.
Gazing up at Your Majesty's countenance,
it daily appears more drawn and haggard.
All say that Grand Eunuchs Mǎ Yǒngchéng, Gǔ Dàyòng, Zhāng Yǒng, Luó Xiáng, Wèi Bīn, Qiū Jù, Liú Jǐn, Gāo Fèng, and others invent cunning deceptions,
corrupting the imperial mind.
Polo, horse racing,
hawking, dog chasing,
actors and miscellaneous plays
are improperly arranged before Your Majesty.
They even lead the Son of Heaven to transact with commoners,
engaging in intimate and disrespectful behavior,
entirely devoid of proper etiquette.
Day's amusements are insufficient;
night is used to continue them,
exhausting Your Majesty's spirit
and impairing Your will and virtue.
This has caused the heavenly order to be disturbed,
the earthly qi to be restless,
with unusual thunder and stellar anomalies.
Peach and plum trees bloom in autumn.
Examining these omens,
none are auspicious.
These petty individuals
only know how to bewitch the ruler for their private gain,
without considering the majestic mandate of Heaven.
The grand imperial enterprise
rests upon Your Majesty alone.
Although the grand wedding is now complete,
an heir has not yet been established.
Should Your Majesty, by any chance, damage your spirit through pleasure-seeking
or lose moderation in daily life,
even if these individuals were ground to powder,
what good would it do the situation?
Emperor Gāo went through a hundred battles with great difficulty
to secure the realm.
Succeeding emperors have continued the lineage
down to Your Majesty.
The words of the late Emperor's deathbed charge
were heard by Your Majesty.
How can you tolerate these petty individuals,
keeping them by your side,
thereby harming your sacred virtue?
We humbly observe that in ancient times, eunuchs misleading the country
caused especially severe calamities,
as demonstrated by the Ten Regular Attendants of Hàn and the Gānlù Incident of Táng.
These are clear proofs.
Now that the crimes of Yǒngchéng and others are evident,
if they are allowed to go unpunished,
they will become even more reckless in the future,
surely becoming a danger to the state.
We humbly hope that Your Majesty will exert your resolute vigor,
cut off private affections,
report to the Two Empresses,
issue an edict to all officials,
clearly apply the law,
to reverse the changes in heaven and earth,
assuage the indignation of gods and men,
secretly eliminate the seeds of chaos,
and forever preserve the enduring imperial enterprise."
When the memorial was submitted,
the Emperor was startled and wept, refusing to eat.
Jǐn and the others were greatly alarmed.
At that time, Grand Secretaries Liú Jiàn and Xiè Qiān were firmly holding onto the censors' memorials and would not pass them on,
then Wén's memorial was submitted again.
The Emperor sent Directorate of Ceremonial Grand Eunuchs Lǐ Róng, Wáng Yuè, and others to the Grand Secretariat to discuss.
They came three times in one day,
but Jiàn and others held even more firmly to their stance.
Yuè, who was usually upright,
alone said:
"The Grand Secretariat's opinion is correct."
That night,
the eight individuals wept surrounding the Emperor.
The Emperor, in anger,
immediately arrested Yuè and sent him to imperial prison,
though the outer court was unaware of this.
The next day,
Wén initiated the Nine Ministers, Censors, and Remonstrance Officials to again proceed to the palace and firmly remonstrate.
Soon there was an imperial decree
pardoning the eight individuals and not questioning them.
Jiàn and Qiān hastily resigned and left.
The eight individuals each took control of important positions,
with Jǐn taking charge of the Directorate of Ceremonial,
and state affairs then underwent a great change.
Jǐn deeply hated Wén,
daily sending people to watch for Wén's mistakes.
Over a month later,
someone submitted counterfeit silver to the imperial treasury,
and this was used as Wén's crime.
An edict demoted him one rank and ordered his retirement,
and Lángzhōng Chén Rén was demoted to Assistant Prefect of Jūnzhōu.
Supervising Secretary Xú Áng petitioned to keep Wén in his original post,
but an imperial decree stated that there was clear evidence of his intervention,
stripping Wén of his position,
replacing him with Gù Zuǒ,
and also dismissing Áng.
In the third month of the second year, a list of treacherous officials' names was posted.
Apart from Liú Jiàn and Xiè Qiān,
among the Ministers, Wén was listed first.
The rest, such as Zhāng Fūhuá, Yáng Shǒusuí, Lín Hàn, and others, totaled fifty-three individuals,
and were displayed in the court hall.
Wén's son, Shìcōng, Prefect of Gāotáng,
and Shìqí, Principal in the Ministry of Punishments,
were both dismissed from office.
Wén left the capital gate
in a blue sedan chair,
with only one cart of luggage.
Jǐn's hatred was not appeased.
He was then accused of losing ministry records,
and Wén and Vice Minister Zhāng Jìn were arrested and sent to imperial prison.
They were released several months later,
and fined a thousand piculs of rice to be transported to Dàtóng.
Soon after, the rice fine was imposed again,
and his family property was completely depleted.
When Jǐn was executed,
Wén was reinstated to office,
and then retired.
Upon Emperor Shìzōng's ascension,
he sent an emissary with an imperial letter to inquire after Wén,
bringing mutton and wine.
He ordered the officials to provide four piculs of grain monthly,
and six laborers annually for the remainder of his life.
He was further promoted to Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince,
and one grandson was given the inherited position of Acting Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments.
He died in the fifth year of Jiājìng,
at the age of eighty-six.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Preceptor
and given the posthumous name Zhōngdìng.
Shìcōng
was a Jǔrén.
After being dismissed from office,
he did not serve again.
Shìqí was a Jìnshì,
and ended his career as a Provincial Administration Commissioner of Húguǎng.
His youngest son, Shìxián,
also became an Assistant Prefect of Kāifēng through the Jǔrén examination.
His grandson, Tíngwěi,
was a Jìnshì
and served as Acting Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud.
Gù Zuǒ,
courtesy name Liángbì,
was a native of Lín Huái.
He became a *jìnshì* in the fifth year of Chénghuà (1469).
He was appointed Director of the Bureau of Punishments,
and successively rose to become a Supervising Secretary.
When investigating the crimes of the Embroidered Uniform Guard Commander Niú Xún and the eunuchs Gù Xióng and Zhōng Qīn,
he showed no leniency.
He was sent out to be the Prefect of Héjiān.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
he was twice promoted to become a Junior Supervisor of the Court of Judicial Review,
then advanced to Right Censor-in-Chief and Grand Coordinator of Shānxī.
When members of the imperial clan had their residences
repaired by government officials,
the cost was exorbitant.
Zuǒ requested that they be made to handle their own repairs.
At the end of the Zhèngtǒng reign,
the people of Tàiyuán and Píngyáng were temporarily drafted to guard the border,
and for a long time afterward, they were not relieved.
Zuǒ memorialized for them to be replaced.
He entered the court as Left Vice Censor-in-Chief,
and was tasked with dismissing the Grand General of Liáodōng, Lǐ Gǎo, the eunuch Rèn Liáng, and the Grand Coordinator Zhāng Yù.
He successively served as Left and Right Vice Ministers of Revenue,
and was sent out to manage military provisions in Shǎnxī.
He was good at planning,
and accumulated enough reserves for more than three years.
When the Zhèngdé reign began,
he replaced Hán Wén as Minister.
Liú Jǐn bore a grudge against Wén,
and sought to find every conceivable fault.
There was an old register in the ministry that had gone missing.
He wanted to use this to incriminate Wén
and forced Zuǒ to report the matter.
Zuǒ refused,
and was consequently deprived of his salary for three months.
Zuǒ then submitted another memorial requesting retirement,
which was granted.
Jǐn's resentment did not cease;
he imposed three fines of rice to be transported to the frontier,
totaling over a thousand *shi*.
His family was poor,
so he had to borrow money to pay.
After his death,
he was posthumously granted the title of Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent.
Chén Rén,
courtesy name Zǐjū,
was a native of Pútián.
He became a *jìnshì* at the end of the Chénghuà reign.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
he served as a Supervising Secretary in the Ministry of Revenue.
When the temple of the Former Sage in Quē Lǐ suffered a fire,
he memorialized requesting its repair.
When Shǎnxī presented an ancient seal,
Rén boldly memorialized to expose its falsity.
When an imperial edict summoned the Tibetan monk Lǐng Zhànzhú to Sìchuān,
Rén memorialized to remonstrate.
He also requested the restoration of official titles for the loyal officials of the Jiànwén reign, such as Fāng Xiàorú.
Many of his proposals were blocked and not implemented.
In the early Zhèngdé reign,
Jǐn used the matter of silver to incriminate Minister Wén,
and Rén was also demoted.
After Jǐn was executed,
Rén was successively promoted to Right Administration Commissioner of Zhèjiāng.
Zhāng Fūhuá,
courtesy name Gōngshí,
was a native of Ānfú.
His father, Hóng,
an Imperial Censor,
died in the Tǔmù Disaster.
Fūhuá was resolute and principled from a young age.
At the age of seven,
when a village shrine tree was believed to be haunted,
he led a group of children to cut it all down.
In the early Jǐngtài reign,
as a descendant of someone who died for the state,
he entered the Imperial Academy.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the eighth year of Tiānshùn (1464)
and was selected as a *shùjíshì*.
In the first year of Chénghuà (1465),
he and Liú Dàxià wished to be assigned to a ministry.
He was appointed Director in the Ministry of War
and successively rose to become a Supervising Secretary.
He was honest, steadfast, and unyielding,
and his reputation equaled that of Dàxià.
In the eleventh year, he was sent out as a Surveillance Commissioner of Zhèjiāng.
When miners in Jǐngníng rebelled,
reaching several thousand people,
Fūhuá persuaded them to disperse
and captured twelve of their leaders.
He served in Zhèjiāng for over ten years,
successively as Administration Commissioner.
In the early Hóngzhì reign,
he was transferred to Húguǎng.
During a famine,
he ordered prefectures and counties to extensively repair school palaces,
using the wages to provide for the hungry.
He was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief
and Grand Coordinator of Shānxī.
He hurried home for his father's funeral midway,
and after the mourning period, returned to his former office.
The tributary grain and taxes in the department for Dàtóng
were plagued by discounted payments.
Fūhuá requested that for areas north of Tàiyuán accessible by cart, grain should still be submitted,
which benefited the people.
He was reassigned as Grand Coordinator of Shǎnxī,
where he established regulations for marriages and funerals,
guiding the people towards propriety.
When a demonic monk occupied Mount Zhōngnán and rebelled,
the court deliberated on military action.
Minister Mǎ Wénshēng said:
“Censor-in-Chief Zhāng can handle this.”
Fūhuá indeed captured the monk through stratagem.
He was promoted to Right Vice Minister of War in Nánjīng.
In the twelfth year, he was appointed Right Censor-in-Chief,
serving as General Supervisor of Canal Transport and concurrently Grand Coordinator of Huái and Yáng prefectures.
When the embankment of Gāoyóu Lake collapsed,
he dredged a deep channel to reduce the water's force.
He also built the Bǎoyìng embankment.
The people greatly benefited from this.
He was then reassigned to oversee the Nánjīng Censorate.
He, along with Minister of Personnel Lín Hàn, Surveillance Censor Lín Jùn, and Libationer Zhāng Mào,
were known as
“The Four Gentlemen of the Southern Capital.”
He was then promoted to Minister of Punishments.
In the first year of Zhèngdé (1506), he was summoned to serve as Left Censor-in-Chief.
In that winter,
ministers and remonstrating officials requested the removal of Liú Jǐn and others,
and the Grand Secretariat strongly supported this.
The emperor hesitated,
so Fūhuá then memorialized:
“Your Majesty indulges in banquets, entertainment, and leisurely travel,
