daily associating with wicked and treacherous individuals.
Government decrees contradict imperial edicts,
and actions diverge from established precedents.
This has led to celestial phenomena causing disturbance above
and public sentiment being agitated below.
Now, Censor Liú ●,
and Imperial Censors Zhū Tíngshēng and Xú Yù, among others, have repeatedly memorialized to report these matters,
but they are merely handed over to the relevant department.
The Duke of Yīng, Mào, and I have jointly submitted a request,
but only received the reply, ‘I will handle it myself.’
I secretly sigh in bewilderment,
and beg to briefly state the current political弊端 ills.
For instance, the four hundred thousand [taels] in the treasury are already depleted,
yet expenditures continue unabated.
What do six or seven-year-old boys know,
yet they are recruited as valiant soldiers?
Textile production had been halted,
and *chuánfèng* (imperial messages) had been abolished,
but soon reverted to their former state.
Officials were just dispatched to investigate the salt administration and imperial estates,
when memorials requesting them were heard.
Eunuchs supervising the capital garrisons and guarding the four quarters
were frequently replaced at one time.
Government decrees are confused,
and abuses proliferate.
Indeed, in matters of state,
one hundred people striving are not enough,
but a few people can ruin it with ease.
I wish Your Majesty would carefully examine this.”
The memorial was submitted,
but there was no response.
Shortly thereafter, a great change occurred in court affairs,
and the power of the eunuchs grew even stronger.
On New Year's Eve, after the morning audience,
an imperial decree suddenly ordered him and Yáng Shǒusuí to retire.
Fūhuá departed immediately.
When he reached Xúzhōu Hóng,
he was in a small boat which struck a rock and almost drowned him.
Jǐn’s hatred had not subsided;
he wanted to use the spoiled grain in Húguǎng’s granaries
to incriminate Fūhuá for corruption.
Compiler Kāng Hǎi passed by Jǐn and said:
“We Qin people love Duke Zhāng as our parents;
how can you treat him so lightly?”
Jǐn's intention somewhat softened,
but he still accused Fūhuá of being part of a treacherous clique,
and his name, along with Shǒusuí's, was posted in the imperial court.
The following year in June, he was gravely ill;
he donned his robes and cap, bowed to his family shrine,
then lay down on his bed and died.
Two years after Jǐn was executed,
he was posthumously granted the title of Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent
and given the posthumous name Jiǎnsù.
Fūhuá’s nature was rigid and upright.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
Liú Dàxià often recommended him,
and the emperor said:
“Fūhuá is indeed excellent,
but he is too severe.”
When he served as a Supervising Secretary and was dispatched on an imperial mission,
thieves searched his bag
and found only seven pieces of gold.
His grandson, Sūn Áoshan,
served as an Imperial Censor.
Yáng Shǒusuí,
courtesy name Wéizhēn,
was a native of Yín,
and a younger cousin of Vice Minister Yáng Shǒuchén.
He passed the imperial examination in the second year of Chénghuà (1466) as a Jìnshì,
and was appointed Censor.
He inspected the grain transport,
audited military provisions in Dàtóng,
and served as an investigating censor in Jiāngxī.
Wherever he went, his upright conduct inspired awe.
In the sixth year (1470), he submitted a memorial detailing six matters,
stating:
"When Prince Chéng received his mandate during a time of crisis,
he suppressed the rebellions and chaos,
rendering immense service.
Yet after his death, he was posthumously given the epithet 'Lì' (licentious/violent).
Public opinion considers this unjust.
This was not the intention of the late emperor,
but was done by treacherous villains indulging their private resentments.
It should be promptly changed,
to manifest Your Majesty's benevolence towards your kin.
Minister Lǐ Bǐng loyally upheld the law and
was an excellent official of his time,
but was falsely impeached by Xiāo Yànzhuāng and forced to retire.
I beg that he be immediately recalled.
According to the laws, those who commit public offenses are not to be dismissed.
Recently, Censors Zhū Xián and Lóu Fāng, among others, were all dismissed.
I beg that their offices be restored,
and that the relevant authorities be warned not to impose punishments beyond the law,
but to act strictly according to the statutes.
In the western campaigns,
tens of thousands of soldiers were dispatched to suppress constantly shifting bandits.
Supplies were transported over a thousand lì,
and the campaigns dragged on for a long time.
I fear that before the external threat is pacified,
the interior will already be exhausted.
I beg that the troops be recalled quickly,
and that border officials be admonished to guard their posts diligently.
According to recent precedents,
military officers whose cases of criminal offense have not been finalized
are pardoned if an amnesty occurs,
leading these individuals to procrastinate
in hopes of escaping punishment.
From now on, for those whose guilt is clearly established by numerous witnesses,
cases should be decided immediately according to the law,
without allowing them to escape punishment.
Even if they receive an amnesty,
they should not be allowed to command troops.
As for the salaries of officials stationed outside and military provisions,
some have gone unpaid for over a year,
due to the small reserves held by prefectures and counties.
I request that, in addition to the amounts transported,
a measured amount be allowed for retention,
to alleviate shortages."
When the memorial was submitted,
it was not followed at the time.
When Sūn Guǎng'ān, the Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, was recalled to office during his mother's mourning period,
Shǒusuí, together with Supervising Secretary Lǐ Hé and others, repeatedly memorialized on the matter,
whereupon Sūn was ordered to observe mourning.
In the winter of the eighth year (1472), due to natural disasters and unusual phenomena, he presented nine matters concerning current governance.
The court deliberated on the disasters and damages across the four directions,
and decided to suspend the dispatch of censors to audit archives.
The Marquis of Huìchāng, Sūn Jìzōng, requested that those already in the capital also be suspended.
Shǒusuí argued:
"Jìzōng and others act willfully and commit misdeeds;
fearing punishment,
they use this as a pretext to seek exemption."
The emperor disregarded Jìzōng's request,
and the auditing of archives proceeded as before.
When Shāndōng suffered famine,
the court deliberated on allowing officials to pay silver to be exempt from evaluations
and receive official attire.
Shǒusuí strongly argued against it,
and the emperor immediately abolished the measure.
He was promoted to Vice Prefect of Yìngtiān Prefecture,
but before he could take office,
he returned home for his mother's mourning.
After the mourning period, there was no vacancy,
so he was additionally appointed to supervise affairs.
Initially,
Lǐ Zīxǐng was appointed Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
Because of Shǒusuí's objection, this was changed to Vice Director of the Imperial Stud,
and Lǐ resented him for it.
At this time, Lǐ slandered him to the emperor,
and an imperial edict from within the palace criticized Shǒusuí for being improperly appointed to an additional post,
and transferred him to be Prefect of Nánníng.
At the beginning of Hóngzhì (1488),
he was recalled to serve as Prefect of Yìngtiān Prefecture,
and was tasked with investigating the crimes of the eunuch Jiǎng Cóng, who was Garrison Commander of Nánjīng.
Cóng instigated his associate Guō Yōng to impeach Shǒusuí, alleging injustice in his handling of the case involving Supervising Secretary Fāng Xiàng.
He was demoted to Assistant Surveillance Commissioner of Guǎngxī.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Surveillance Commissioner.
In the eighth year (1495), he was recalled to serve as Junior Censor-in-Chief of Nánjīng,
and concurrently Commander of River Patrols.
He successively served as Minister of the Grand Court of Revision in both capitals.
After completing his nine-year term,
he was promoted to Minister of Works,
and still concurrently presided over the Grand Court of Revision.
When cases from the Ministry of Justice were sent to the Grand Court of Revision for review, many had their sentences increased.
Secretary Zhū Liú argued against this.
Shǒusuí stated:
"Since the Yǒnglè period,
the court has already set up torture instruments.
Many prisoners from the Ministry of Justice have not had the facts of their cases fully ascertained;
how can they not be re-interrogated?"
The emperor then dismissed Zhū's memorial.
After Emperor Xiàozōng's death,
the eunuch Zhāng Yú and others were imprisoned for misusing imperial medicine.
Shǒusuí participated in their interrogation and had them flogged.
In the fourth month of the first year of Zhèngdé (1506),
Shǒusuí memorialized:
"The annual summer review of judicial cases
is conducted in the capital but not in Nánjīng.
A review and record of cases is done every five years,
detailed for those in the capital but brief for those outside.
None of this is correct.
I request that these regulations be revised."
His request was granted.
When the eunuch Lǐ Xīng illegally cut down timber from an imperial mausoleum and was sentenced to death,
his family offered 400,000 liǎng of silver to commute his sentence.
Shǒusuí stood firm,
and the case could not be dismissed.
When court officials debated the matter of excess salt,
an imperial edict from within the palace questioned why this was such a major issue.
Shǒusuí said to Hán Wén:
"There are indeed matters more important than this."
Hán Wén then, along with the Nine Ministers, knelt before the palace gates to remonstrate against
the "Eight Factions."
After Hán Wén and the others were dismissed,
Shǒusuí, in anger, alone submitted a memorial strongly arguing: "Since Your Majesty ascended the throne,
the close officials around you
have failed to respectfully uphold the virtuous intentions
of the former court, instead changing all its good laws,
and slandering and purging
all the great ministers of the former court.
The common people are crying out in distress,
unable to find a way out,
leading to disasters rarely seen in history,
accumulating within a few months.
Does Your Majesty not consider the
reasons for this?
The eunuch Liú Jǐn and seven others
are treacherous, cunning, and devious,
indulging in false accusations and arbitrary acts.
People call them
the 'Eight Tigers,'
with Jǐn being the worst,
daily leading Your Majesty
astray with extravagance and indulgence.
Sometimes you are in Xīhǎi holding hawks and chasing rabbits,
other times ascending steep heights in Nánchéng.
Drums and gongs within the forbidden palace shake far and wide,
while the sound of cannons in the palace echoes day and night.
They mix up the high and low,
degrading the noble and humble.
They lead out carriages and cavalry for their own menial services,
and set up markets to engage directly in commerce.
This causes Your Majesty to fail to hold court even after the sun is high,
and not to sleep until dawn.
These few individuals
are currently usurping power and authority,
falsely transmitting imperial edicts,
banishing high officials,
executing censors,
obstructing memorials,
and widely accepting
bribes.
The number of useless officials appointed by imperial decree
reaches thousands,
and they recruit brave warriors,
even children.
Purple sashes and golden mink sables are given indiscriminately to their henchmen,
while python robes and jade
belts are lavishly bestowed upon their confidants.
Those who attach themselves to them are promoted,
while those who displease them are dismissed from office.
Both internal and external officials
only know to fear Jǐn,
and do not know to fear Your Majesty.
Previously,
two or three great ministers were left to assist Your Majesty,
but now there are those who secretly collude and attach themselves,
leaking state secrets.
Previously, officials throughout the north and south
were united in their indignation,
but now there are those who devise strategies and draft documents,
attaching themselves to the powerful.
Furthermore, they have frequently changed border generals
and largely altered the positions of garrison commanders across the four directions.
What are their intentions
in doing this?
The hilt of the great sword must not be entrusted to others.
Now Your Majesty has entrusted them with all matters concerning military affairs, justice, finance,
and the fundamental mechanisms of government.
Some hold
Gathering at the military camp,
some presided over the Two Factories (dōngchǎng and xīchǎng),
some held sway over rites,
some supervised granaries and storehouses.
With great power in their hands,
what further dared they fear?
Thus, great massacres were carried out,
and extensive purges and
extortions were rampant.
The imperial treasury was depleted above,
the people's resources were exhausted below,
and the brave warriors were fatigued at the borders.
All, high and low, complained,
and both gods and men were indignant.
Yet, Your Majesty still fails to comprehend,
and
even says that the right people have been entrusted with authority.
How erroneous this is!
I humbly hope Your Majesty will greatly exert your imperial authority (gāng),
and immediately subject these individuals to severe punishment,
taking to heart the errors of the Yánxī (period),
lest your humble servant tread
the same path of destruction as Fān (Qú) and Wǔ (Liáng).
The memorial was submitted,
but the Emperor paid no heed.
Jǐn and his associates deeply resented this,
and an imperial decree ordered Sǒu Suí to retire.
Sǒu Suí departed,
and Lǐ Xīng was subsequently spared death by imperial decree.
Jǐn's resentment was not appeased.
In the fourth month of the third year, Sǒu Suí was implicated for erroneous findings in a review of a criminal case,
arrested, taken to the capital, and imprisoned.
He was fined one thousand dàn of rice to be transported to the frontier.
A year later,
he was again implicated for sheltering a fellow villager in a serious case,
stripped of his name,
and his imperial patents were revoked.
He was fined another two hundred dàn of rice.
Sǒu Suí's family was immediately ruined.
After Jǐn was executed,
he was reinstated in office.
He died ten years later,
at the age of eighty-five.
He was posthumously granted the title Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shàobǎo),
and given the posthumous name Kāngjiǎn.
His cousin, Sǒu Yú,
became a Jinshì and served successively as Jiangxi Provincial Administration Commissioner (Jiāngxī Cānzhèng).
He had administrative achievements.
For the Níng (Wáng) princely establishment's grain stipends,
one tael of silver was levied per dàn of rice,
which later gradually increased by fifty percent.
Sǒu Yú entered and requested the Prince (Wáng)
to reduce it back to the original rate.
Jǐn disliked Sǒu Suí,
and also dismissed Sǒu Yú from office.
After Jǐn's death,
Sǒu Yú was reappointed to office in Sìchuān,
and eventually became Guangxi Provincial Administration Commissioner (Guǎngxī Bùzhèngshǐ).
Xǔ Jìn,
courtesy name Jìshēng,
was a native of Língbǎo.
He became a Jinshì in the second year of Chénghuà.
He was appointed Censor (Yùshǐ).
He successively inspected Gānsù and Shāndōng,
and was well-regarded in both.
Chén Yuè caused a mutiny in Liáodōng,
and was impeached by Censor Qiáng Zhēn.
Xǔ Jìn also led his colleagues to remonstrate against him.
Wāng Zhí was enraged,
fabricated charges against Zhēn and had him imprisoned,
and picked out a wrong character in another of Jìn's memorials,
inflicting a court杖ing (tíngzhàng) that nearly killed him.
After completing three terms,
he was promoted to Shandong Vice Commissioner of Education (Shāndōng Fùshǐ).
He resolved difficult legal cases,
and people called him "divinely intelligent."
While patrolling Liáodōng,
he was implicated in a case,
and summoned to the imperial prison (zhàoyù).
When Emperor Xiàozōng ascended the throne,
he was released and returned.
In the first year of Hóngzhì, he was promoted to Vice Censor-in-Chief on the Right (Yòu Qiāndū Yùshǐ) and concurrently Grand Coordinator (Xúnfǔ) of Dàtóng.
The Little Prince (Xiǎo Wángzǐ) had long ceased to send tribute.
When he sent envoys, over fifteen hundred people, to approach the pass,
Xǔ Jìn, acting on his own discretion, accepted them.
He petitioned the court,
and an imperial edict allowed five hundred people to come to the capital.
Later, the border was repeatedly raided,
and Jìn was impeached,
but not questioned.
In the third year, they again probed the border,
and Jìn and others arrayed their troops to await them.
Tán Yòu, Earl of Xīnníng (Xīnníng Bó), arrived with reinforcements from the capital army,
whereupon they fled.
They again requested to send tribute,
and Jìn again petitioned on their behalf,
which the Emperor permitted.
At that time,
Dàtóng's cavalry and horses were strong,
and its border defenses were well-maintained.
Whenever tribute envoys arrived at the pass,
they would dismount and remove their bows and arrows before entering the guest quarters,
bowing their heads and obeying orders,
none daring to make a fuss.
Coincidentally, Jìn and the eunuch in charge of defending the region, Shí Yán, slandered each other.
Yán was recalled,
and Jìn was demoted to Prefect of Yǎnzhōu (Yǎnzhōu Zhīfǔ).
In the seventh year, he was promoted to Shaanxi Surveillance Commissioner (Shǎnxī Ànchásǐ).
Aheima of Túlǔfān attacked and captured Hāmì,
seizing Zhōngshùn Wáng Shǎnbā and taking him away,
and left his general Yálán to guard it.
Minister of Revenue (Hùbù Shàngshū) Mǎ Wénshēng said that no one but Xǔ Jìn could recover Hāmì,
and thus recommended him as Vice Censor-in-Chief on the Right (Yòu Qiāndū Yùshǐ),
concurrently Grand Coordinator of Gānsù.
The following year, upon arriving at the garrison,
he announced to his generals:
"These petty bandits are running rampant,
thinking that we dare not penetrate deep into their territory.
If our great Celestial Dynasty cannot even launch an arrow beyond the Great Wall,
how can we appease distant peoples?"
The generals found it difficult.
So, he secretly plotted with Commander-in-Chief (Zǒngbīng Guān) Liú Níng,
and heavily bribed Xiǎo Liètū,
sending him with four thousand cavalry.
They killed several hundred people,
and Xiǎo Liètū was killed by a stray arrow.
Xiǎo Liètū had always been an enemy of Túlǔfān,
and after his death,
his son Bǔliù Ādǎi was even more enraged.
Xǔ Jìn again heavily bribed him,
ordering him to cut off the enemy's supply routes,
preventing reinforcements from reaching Yálán from the east.
He also heavily rewarded the Jìjīn, Hǎndōng, and the remnants of Hāmì who lived in Kǔyù,
ordering them to send troops to assist in the attack.
In the eleventh month,
Vice General (Fùjiàng) Péng Qīng led fifteen hundred elite cavalry out of Jiāyù Guān to advance,
while Níng and the eunuch Lù Yín commanded two thousand five hundred cavalry to follow.
Eight days later,
all the armies met,
gathering like feathers in the Miē Chuān.
At dusk, a strong wind raised sand,
and the soldiers shivered and lay stiff with cold.
Xǔ Jìn came out of his tent to comfort the troops.
There was an unusual bird crying mournfully,
and many soldiers wept.
Xǔ Jìn said with emotion:
"It is a man's good fortune to die on the battlefield in service of his country,
why weep?"
The generals and soldiers were all moved and inspired.
At midnight, the wind ceased,
and heavy snow fell.
At this time, the Fān troops had all assembled,
but the Hǎndōng troops had not yet arrived,
and the assembly wanted to wait for them.
Xǔ Jìn said:
"For a surprise attack far into enemy territory,
speed is essential.
We have enough troops,
there is no need to wait."
At dawn,
braving the snow, they advanced at double speed.
Six days later, they suddenly arrived beneath the walls of Hāmì.
Yálán had already fled,
and the remaining bandits resisted.
The imperial army advanced from all four sides,
captured the city,
and seized Shǎnbā's wife and daughters.
The bandits retreated to defend Tǔlà.
Tǔlà,
in Chinese, means "Grand Platform."
Eight hundred defenders held it,
and the armies failed to take it after two battles.
Upon questioning the captives,
they were all Hāmì people who had been kidnapped by Yálán.
Xǔ Jìn then ordered not to attack.
Some wanted to exterminate them all,
but Jìn refused,
sending envoys to appease and persuade them to surrender.
Immediately, they surrendered.
Thus, they investigated Yálán's direction,
divided forces to guard key passes,
and memorialized to appease and gather the Hǎndōng garrisons as aid,
disbanding Túlǔfān's allies to isolate their power.
Then, they returned with the army.
For his achievements,
he was promoted to Vice Censor-in-Chief on the Right (Yòu Fùdū Yùshǐ).
The following year, he was transferred to Grand Coordinator of Shǎnxī,
and successively served as Vice Minister of Revenue on the Right (Hùbù Yòu Shìláng),
then on the Left.
In the thirteenth year,
Huǒshāi launched a major invasion of Dàtóng,
and the border generals were repeatedly defeated.
An imperial decree ordered Jìn, together with Eunuch Jīn Fǔ and Earl of Píngjiāng Chén Ruì, to lead the capital army to resist them,
but they achieved no success.
Censors impeached Fǔ and others for neglecting the enemy,
and also criticized Jìn,
who then retired from office.
When Wǔzōng ascended the throne,
he was appointed Left Vice Minister of War
and Supervisor of the regimented camps (Tuányíng).
In the first year of Zhèngdé (1506), he replaced Liú Dàxià as Minister.
In the seventh month, in response to an imperial summons, he presented eight matters concerning current governance,
forcefully pointing out the abuses of eunuchs employing capital troops
and the inner attendants guarding the imperial city extorting monthly fees.
Most of these proposals were rejected.
He also observed that the emperor was fond of associating with petty individuals,
and requested that the emperor promote sagely learning
and take warning from ancient emperors who indulged in profligacy and debauchery.
This was also not accepted.
The Palace Eunuch Wáng Yuè reported the merits of officers and clerks, such as Wáng Jìn, in apprehending criminals and suppressing banditry,
and each was promoted one rank.
Jìn submitted a memorial, stating:
"Border generals risk countless deaths to capture a single enemy,
only then do they earn promotion.
These individuals, however, obtain it by deception and abuse.
Who would not be disheartened?"
He also said:
"The troops in the regimented camps were not established for construction projects;
they should all be ordered to return to their military units."
He served in the Ministry of War for half a year,
then was transferred to the Ministry of Personnel.
The following year, he was granted the title of Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
Jìn was employed for his talent,
was capable of appointing suitable people,
and was intelligent and perceptive by nature.
When Liú Jǐn wielded power,
Jìn often yielded and conformed to his wishes,
yet Jǐn ultimately remained displeased.
When Jìn was supervising the regimented camps,
he worked with Jǐn.
Each time they reviewed drills,
he would direct with laughter and conversation,
his manner relaxed and elegant,
and Jǐn and the other generals were all impressed.
One day, after a drill,
he suddenly called three captains forward
and had each flogged dozens of times.
Jǐn asked the reason,
and Jìn showed him letters of solicitation from powerful and influential figures.
Jǐn outwardly praised him,
but inwardly was displeased.
By this time,
he wanted to remove Jìn and replace him with Liú Yǔ.
Jiāo Fāng, having failed in his own solicitations,
also took the opportunity to ostracize Jìn.
In the eighth month of the third year (1508),
there was a vacancy for a Director in the Nanjing Ministry of Justice.
There happened to be no incumbent Supernumerary Director,
so Jìn, following precedent, submitted the names of two Principal Secretaries serving as acting officials.
Jǐn deemed this contrary to regulations
and ordered Jìn to submit a defense.
Jìn refused to admit fault,
and three stern imperial edicts were issued, reprimanding him severely.
Having no choice, he requested punishment,
and was then ordered to retire.
Soon after,
he was stripped of his official status for employing Yǒng Tài.
His two sons, Gào and Zàn, who were in the Hanlin Academy,
were both made to pay a ransom and were reassigned to outer posts.
Subsequently, along with Liú Jiàn and six hundred and seventy-five others,
all their imperial patents (gàomìng) were posthumously revoked.
Jǐn also seized upon Jìn's action in Dàtóng of conscripting troops for hire and misappropriating their wages,
and his failure to audit them,
intending to confiscate his family's property.
By the time Jǐn was executed, Jìn was acquitted
and reinstated to his official position as a retiree.
He died before hearing the command,
at the age of seventy-four.
In the fifth year of Jiājìng (1526), he was granted the posthumous title Xiāngyì.
His sons were Gào, Zàn, Shī, Cí, and Lùn.
Shī was
a Director in the Ministry of Works.
Cí was
a Prefect.
Gào,
courtesy name Tínglún,
was Jìn's second son.
He became a *jìnshì* in the twelfth year of Hóngzhì (1499).
He was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Revenue.
He was sent to inspect military provisions in Yánsuí,
and discussed the harms of the *dīngliáng* (labor tax) and *dīngcǎo* (grass tax) systems.
The emperor praised and accepted his views.
He subsequently impeached the supervising eunuch Miáo Kuí for corruption and extravagance,
and was promoted to Right Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Justice.
In the first year of Zhèngdé (1506),
his father Jìn became Minister of War.
By custom,
the sons of high ministers could not hold censorate positions,
so he was transferred to Compiler of the Hanlin Academy.
When his father Jìn angered Liú Jǐn and was stripped of his status,
Gào was also demoted to Magistrate of Quánzhōu.
He returned home for his father's mourning.
After a long time,
he was recommended and appointed Palace Seal Keeper,
but again pleaded illness and returned home,
teaching students there.
At the beginning of Jiājìng,
he was appointed Nanjing Communication Supervisor,
then transferred to Academician Expositor,
and served in the imperial lectures.
He was promoted to Grand Master of Ceremonies and concurrently managed the Imperial Academy (Guózǐjiān).
He requested the construction of a Jìngyī Pavilion within the Imperial Academy,
and to engrave the Imperial Commentary on the Jìngyī Admonition, Master Chéng's Four Admonitions, and Fàn Jùn's Heart Admonition on stone.
The emperor was pleased and granted this.
When the emperor was about to rectify the sacrificial rites for the Temple of Culture (Wénmiào),
Gào requested the use of wooden spirit tablets.
In the east chamber of the Wénhuá Hall, there were formerly Buddhist statues,
which the emperor ordered removed.
In Gào's compiled *Dàotǒng Shū* (Book of the Way's Transmission), he suggested that the Five Emperors and Three Kings should be highly revered in sacrifices,
with Duke Zhōu and Confucius as co-worshipers.
The emperor immediately adopted his suggestion.
In the eleventh year (1532), he was promoted to Right Vice Minister of Personnel.
That winter,
he was appointed Nanjing Minister of Revenue,
and his younger brother Zàn also headed the Ministry of Revenue.
The brothers concurrently managed the finances of the two capitals,
which the gentry regarded as an honor.
He died in office,
and was posthumously granted the title Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
and given the posthumous title Zhuāngmǐn.
When Gào was Libationer,
more than thirty students whose coffins could not be returned home
were all buried by him,
and those who lacked food and clothing were all relieved.
However, he was quite good at ingratiating himself.
At that time, there was an auspicious omen of white magpies.
Gào presented a memorial,
and Sacrificial Superintendent Chén Huán presented an encomium,
both of which were sent to the Imperial Archives.
Supervising Secretaries Zhāng Yù and Xiè Cúnrú,
and Censor Féng Ēn all impeached Gào.
Yù even compared him to Zhù Qīnmíng.
The emperor was enraged
and imprisoned Yù,
demoting him to Registrar of the Fújiàn Provincial Administration Commission.
Cúnrú was also transferred to a border region.
Ēn denounced Gào's scholarship as circuitous and heterodox.
Gào requested to be dismissed.
The emperor said:
"Ēn's denunciation refers to the previous matter of removing clay idols and using wooden spirit tablets.
Are you bothered by this?"
Such was the emperor's favor towards him.
Zàn,
courtesy name Tíngměi,
was Jìn's third son.
He became a *jìnshì* in the ninth year of Hóngzhì (1496).
He was appointed Judicial Commissioner of Dàmíng.
He also became known for his ability to resolve difficult cases,
and was summoned and appointed Censor.
In the first year of Zhèngdé (1506), he was transferred to Compiler.
When Liú Jǐn dismissed Jìn,
Zàn was also sent out as Magistrate of Línzī.
He was successively promoted to Left Administration Commissioner of Zhèjiāng.
In the sixth year of Jiājìng (1527), he entered service as Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Guānglù Qīng),
and successively served as Left and Right Vice Minister of Justice.
The Prefect Jīn Lù was demoted to garrison duty
and bribed Marquis Wǔdìng Guō Xūn.
Xūn sent someone to seize him,
but Commander Wáng Chén refused to comply.
Chén was bound and brought back,
and his bribe was extorted.
When the matter came to light,
Zàn and others requested that they be judged according to the law.
The emperor pitied Xūn
and instructed the Ministry of Justice not to torture Lù and the others,
whereupon Lù and the others refused to confess.
Minister Gāo Yǒujī, who was on leave,
was impeached and dismissed for timidity and shrinking back.
Zàn requested a normal interrogation,
fully exposing Xūn's acceptance of bribes,
and then Xūn's stipend was again revoked.
In the eighth year,
Jìn was promoted to Minister of Personnel.
An imperial edict allowed supervising students who had served in the Six Ministries to report on the malpractices of court officials.
There was a man named Zhān Mì,
who impeached Xu Jìn, the Vice Minister of Personnel.
The case was handed over to Wāng Hóng, the Censor-in-Chief, for interrogation.
Mì was speechless,
and had already been sentenced,
but Mì again impeached Jìn and Chén Jīng, the Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, among others.
The case was again handed to Hóng for interrogation,
and Hóng strongly denounced its baselessness.
At this time, Péng Zé, the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, wanted to overthrow Jìn and replace him.
He falsely forged a letter from Jìn and sent it to Zhāng Fúqìng, seeking to resolve the matter,
and further instigated Fúqìng to impeach Jìn for bribing him.
Jìn submitted a memorial in his defense,
and an imperial edict commanded the Ministry of Justice to interrogate the matter jointly with the Embroidered Uniform Guard.
Zàn and others ultimately ruled Mì guilty of false accusation and deception,
but Jìn’s bribery could not be cleared,
and he was dismissed from office.
The Emperor, who initially praised Mì for daring to speak out in accordance with the edict,
eventually pardoned Mì's crime.
Consequently, unscrupulous individuals began to gather private information about court officials,
extort money,
and fabricated incidents to report to the throne,
causing all ministries to be anxious.
The soldier Tóng Yuán impeached the eunuch Zhāng Yǒng for building a tomb,
which encroached upon the 'dragon脉' (auspicious geomantic line) of Mount Tiānshòu.
He further instigated Yǒng's brother Róng and his servant Wáng Qiān, among others, to expose Róng's illegal activities.
The villain Zhāng Xióng also drafted a memorial for Qiān,
denouncing Zàn and his brother Gào, as well as Wāng Hóng, Liáo Dàonán, Shǐ Dào,
and dozens of internal officials like Huáng Jǐn, for accepting heavy bribes from Róng.
Yuán also submitted a memorial to assist them.
Upon investigation, the facts were uncovered,
and Yuán and others were all exiled to the farthest frontier.
Accusations and denunciations then began to wane.
In the tenth year, Zàn was transferred to Minister of Revenue.
He rushed home by post-station to visit his mother,
but his mother had already passed away.
Before the mourning period was over,
an imperial edict appointed him Minister of Personnel.
He only entered court after the mourning period ended.
The Emperor considered Zàn pure and cautious,
and kept the position open for him.
Upon his arrival,
his discussions and proposals did not meet the Emperor's expectations.
An edict was issued to select palace officials,
but many Grand Secretaries introduced their private factions.
Censors impeached and dismissed over ten people,
and the Emperor entrusted the matter to the Ministry of Personnel.
Zàn then recommended Huò Tāo, Máo Bówēn, Gù Lín, Lǚ Nán, Zōu Shǒuyì, Xú Jiē, Rèn Hàn, Xuē Huì, Zhōu Fū, Zhào Shíchūn, and others.
An edict ordered that Lín, Nán, and Huì retain their former offices,
while the rest were all employed.
He was repeatedly promoted to Junior Guardian and concurrently Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
When the Nine Ancestral Temples suffered a fire,
he reported himself and was excused.
After half a year,
the Emperor found it difficult to find a replacement,
and reinstated Zàn to his post.
He requested to use the imperial treasury,
borrow officials' salaries,
confiscate wealth from rich commoners,
and initiate the sale of official titles,
to meet the border's needs.
At that time, there was a proposal to build earth mounds and fortresses in the interior.
Zàn deemed it not a good plan.
The Emperor considered borrowing salaries and confiscating wealth not fitting for a prosperous era,
and stopped it.
The proposal for mounds and fortresses also ceased.
When Zhái Luán and Yán Sōng held power,
they made many requests and entreaties.
The director Wáng Yǔlíng advised Zàn to expose them.
Sōng's defense was strong,
and the Emperor favored Sōng,
instead severely reprimanding Zàn,
and removing Yǔlíng from office.
From then on, Zàn was intimidated by Sōng and dared not resist,
and also became somewhat known for accepting bribes.
When Luán was dismissed,
the Emperor pondered a replacement.
Sōng, seeing Zàn as gentle and easy to control,
recommended him.
An edict appointed him concurrently Grand Secretary of the Wényuān Pavilion, participating in government affairs, while retaining his original office.
All government affairs were decided by Sōng,
and Zàn had no say.
After a long time, he was promoted to Junior Tutor.
As he was over seventy,
he repeatedly begged to retire.
The Emperor reprimanded him for forgetting his sovereign and loving himself,
and stripped him of his office, allowing him to reside at home as an idle official.
He died three years after returning home.
Later, his office was posthumously restored,
he was granted the title of Junior Mentor,
and given the posthumous name Wénjiǎn.
Lùn,
whose courtesy name was Tíngyì,
was the youngest son of Jìn.
He passed the imperial examination in the fifth year of Jiājìng.
He was appointed Judicial Commissioner of Shùndé,
and later entered service as a Secretary in the Ministry of War,
then transferred to the Ministry of Rites.
He enjoyed discussing military affairs.
As a child, he traveled with his father through border regions,
gaining full knowledge of the strategic passes and their difficulties and ease.
Consequently, he wrote the "Nine Borders Map and Treatise" and submitted it.
The Emperor was pleased,
and distributed it to border officials for discussion and implementation.
From then on, he became known for his military knowledge.
He was successively promoted to Assistant Minister of the Grand Court of Judicial Review in Nánjīng.
When a court recommendation for the Governor of Shùntiān occurred,
Lùn's name was listed second.
The Emperor said,
"This is the one who submitted the 'Nine Borders Map and Treatise',"
and immediately appointed him Vice Censor-in-Chief,
assigning him to the post.
When the Báitōngshì attacked Huángyákǒu with over a thousand cavalry,
Lùn commanded his officers and soldiers to defeat them.
When they attacked Dàmùgǔ again,
they were once more repelled by the government forces.
For his merits,
he was promoted to Junior Vice Censor-in-Chief.
After more than a year,
he was dismissed due to illness.
When Āndá threatened the capital,
he was reinstated to his former office as Governor of Shānxī.
For his merits in autumn defense,
he was promoted to Junior Vice Minister of War,
and summoned to manage the military affairs of the Capital Garrisons.
He was transferred to Vice Minister on account of constructing the outer city wall of Jīngshī.
In the thirty-third year, he was sent out to supervise military affairs in Xuān, Dà, and Shānxī.
The villains Lǚ Hèchū and Qiū Fù initially misled the masses with unorthodox methods.
Fù rebelled and surrendered to Āndá,
becoming his chief strategist.
Hè sent his associates to cross the frontier,
leading the invaders to attack,
but they were captured by scouts.
Lùn dispatched troops to arrest Hè,
and executed his associates as well.
For his merits, he was promoted to Censor-in-Chief,
and again for his merits, promoted to Minister of War,
with his son being granted the hereditary title of Chiliarch of the Embroidered Uniform Guard.
Wēng Wàndá served as Grand Coordinator,
building a border wall of six hundred li in Dàtóng,
with a beacon tower erected inside the wall every li.
Later, due to insufficient troops, the wall could not be defended,
and all walls were removed, with defenses concentrated on the towers.
Lùn said:
"If the soldiers defend the towers,
the invaders will not be able to effectively attack the wall.
When the invaders enter the wall,
they are often shocked and scatter.
I request that the construction be moved outside the wall,
with a tower built every three hundred steps,
so that arrows and stones can reach each other.
It should be no more than thirty steps away from the wall,
four zhang and five chi in height and width,
with one-third of its top sloped,
and parapet walls and barracks placed on top,
guarded by ten brave soldiers.
A crescent wall should be built below,
with a hidden gate for entry and exit.
The estimated cost will not exceed ninety thousand gold,
and it can be completed in a few months."
An imperial edict immediately adopted his proposal.
When ten thousand cavalry attacked Shānxī,
Lùn led the troops to intercept and defeat them in Shuòzhōuchuān.
Those who attacked Xuānfǔ and Lóngmén
were also defeated by the officers and soldiers,
with over five hundred and thirty captives and decapitations in total.
He was promoted to Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
and his son was granted the hereditary title as before.
In the thirty-fifth year,
Yáng Bó (楊博), Minister of War, left due to his father's mourning.
Lùn (論) was summoned to replace him.
At that time,
Yán Sōng (嚴嵩) and his son were in power,
and generals were often promoted through bribery.
With wars raging in both the north and south,
the emperor severely blamed the central administration.
Dīng Rúkuí (丁汝夔), Wáng Bāngruì (王邦瑞), Zhào Jǐn (趙錦), and Niè Bào (聶豹)
all met unfortunate ends.
Lùn (論) was already old at the time
and greatly concerned for himself.
All promotions and demotions of generals,
and decisions regarding military strategy,
were entirely left to Shìfān (世蕃)’s command,
hoping to mitigate harm through this.
Xīn'ài (辛愛), a son of Āndá (俺答), angered that Governor-General Yáng Shùn (楊順) had taken his runaway concubine,
led his forces to besiege Dàtóng (大同) Right Guard city multiple times,
forcing those inside the city to dismantle houses for firewood.
When the emperor heard this,
he was deeply worried
and secretly asked Sōng (嵩).
Sōng (嵩) wanted to abandon the city but found it difficult to speak,
so he requested an imperial decree to question the Minister of War.
Lùn (論) requested to restore the army of the Right Guard,
providing five hundred thousand gold annually.
This was intentionally a difficult condition,
hoping to move the emperor.
The emperor quickly arranged for provisions and dispatched troops,
and replaced civil and military officials.
The siege of the Right Guard was also soon lifted.
Investigating Censor Wú Shílái (吳時來) impeached Yáng Shùn (楊順),
and then criticized Lùn (論) for echoing and agreeing with others,
being in a constant state of intoxication,
and disregarding border alarms.
The emperor then stripped Lùn (論) of his official status.
Sōng (嵩) subtly tried to defend him,
but could not save him either.
In the thirty-eighth year, he was reinstated to his former office,
supervising military affairs in Jì (薊), Liáo (遼), and Bǎodìng (保定).
Bǎdū'ér (把都兒) invaded west of Jì (薊),
and Lùn (論) amassed elite troops to await him.
When Bǎdū'ér (把都兒) arrived, he was defeated by Commander Hú Zhèn (胡鎮).
After looting Shā'érlǐng (沙兒嶺) and Yànziwō (燕子窩),
he was repelled again,
and then fled.
When the matter was reported,
he was richly rewarded with silver and silk.
Soon after, he also memorialized that Mìyún (密雲) and Chāngpíng (昌平) garrisons required over three hundred thousand silver taels for autumn defense.
Investigating Censor Zhèng Mào (鄭茂) stated that Lùn (論)'s requests were excessive,
and asked for an investigation into his possible embezzlement.
An imperial edict ordered Lùn (論) to return home for investigation.
Investigating Censor Dèng Dòng (鄧棟) went to verify,
and fully uncovered instances of false claims and embezzlement.
He was stripped of his office and retired.
Not long after, he died at the age of seventy-two.
At the beginning of the Lóngqìng (隆慶) era,
he was reinstated to office
and given the posthumous title Gōngxiāng (恭襄).
His great-grandson, Hàorán (浩然),
rose through inherited privilege to the office of Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince
and Left Chief Military Commissioner.
Hàorán (浩然)’s son, Dáiyìn (達胤),
was a commander in the Imperial Bodyguard.
When Lǐ Zìchéng (李自成) captured the capital,
he died rather than surrender.
His cousin, Jiāyìn (佳胤),
was a commander of the Hóngnóng (弘農) Guard.
In the fourteenth year of Chóngzhēn (崇禎), when the bandits broke through Língbǎo (靈寶),
he drew his sword and rushed into battle,
where he died.
Yōng Tài (雍泰),
courtesy name Shìlóng (世隆),
was from Xiánníng (咸寧).
He obtained his *jìnshì* degree in the fifth year of Chénghuà (成化).
He was appointed Magistrate of Wúxiàn (吳縣).
When Lake Tàihú (太湖) overflowed, submerging a thousand *qǐng* of fields,
Tài (泰) built a dike for the benefit of the people,
which was called Yōng Gōng Dī (雍公堤, Dike of Lord Yōng).
A woman's concubine ran away,
and the concubine's father accused her husband of secretly murdering his daughter and hiding the body under a rock in the lake.
Tài (泰) questioned him, saying:
"If he secretly killed your daughter,
how would you know where the body was hidden?
Moreover, this is not a corpse of two months;
you must have killed someone else's daughter,
hoping to gain a bribe."
After one interrogation, he confessed.
He was summoned to be a Censor,
inspecting salt in Liǎnghuái (兩淮).
For salt workers who had no wives,
Tài (泰) arranged marriages.
He was appointed Prefect of Fèngyáng (鳳陽) Prefecture.
He left due to his father's mourning.
After the mourning period, he was appointed Prefect of Nányáng (南陽).
Yú Zǐjùn (余子俊) recommended him, as he was leading the army,
to be Vice Commissioner of Military Preparedness for Dàtóng (大同),
and he was promoted to Provincial Surveillance Commissioner of Shānxī (山西).
Tài (泰) was upright and incorruptible,
and wherever he went, he liked to contend with powerful local families.
Yǐn Zhēn (尹珍), the Prefect of Tàiyuán (太原), encountered him on the road and failed to avoid him.
Tài (泰) summoned him
and denounced him while he knelt.
Zhēn (珍) refused to submit,
so Tài (泰) flogged him.
Zhēn (珍) appealed to the court,
and also accused Tài (泰) of unjustly flogging someone to death.
Tài (泰) was arrested and imprisoned.
Wáng Shù (王恕) pleaded for leniency for Tài (泰),
and as there was an amnesty at the time,
he was demoted to Provincial Administrator of Húguǎng (湖廣).
In the fourth year of Hóngzhì (弘治), he was transferred to Right Provincial Administration Commissioner of Zhèjiāng (浙江),
and again left due to his mother's mourning.
In the twelfth year, he was appointed Right Vice Censor-in-Chief,
and Pacification Commissioner of Xuānfǔ (宣府).
When official horses died,
soldiers could not afford to compensate,
so Tài (泰) spoke to the court,
and the court treasury bought them.
Border soldiers were poor,
and those with wives often sold them.
Tài (泰) requested official funds for their support.
Minister Zhōu Jīng (周經) then ordered that the poor be given betrothal gifts,
and those sold be redeemed,
to the great joy of the army.
When Assistant General Wáng Jié (王傑) committed a crime,
Tài (泰) impeached him,
and Tài (泰) was ordered to arrest and interrogate him.
Tài (泰) then requested to investigate eight commanders.
The emperor, seeing that Tài (泰) had repeatedly suppressed military officials,
then issued an edict to the Censorate to conduct an investigation.
Assistant General Lǐ Jī (李稽), who was involved in a case and feared Tài (泰)’s severe impeachment,
begged to receive a flogging.
Tài (泰) took a large staff and flogged him.
Jī (稽) then memorialized that Tài (泰) was abusive.
The emperor dispatched Investigating Censor Xú Rén (徐仁) along with an Imperial Bodyguard commander to investigate.
Jié (傑) again sent someone to beat the drum of remonstrance,
accusing Tài (泰) of arbitrarily arresting eighty-six generals and officers,
and also involving his son-in-law in bribery.
The judicial authorities verified and reported the findings,
and he was stripped of his official status and reduced to a commoner.
When Emperor Wǔzōng (武宗) ascended the throne,
Investigating Censor Pān Duó (潘鐸) and others recommended Tài (泰) for his courage to die for justice
and his talent to quell chaos.
Minister of Personnel Mǎ Wénshēng (馬文升) then reinstated Tài (泰) as Right Vice Censor-in-Chief of Nánjīng (南京),
and Supreme Commander of Naval Patrols.
He firmly declined the appointment.
In the spring of the third year of Zhèngdé (正德),
Xǔ Jìn (許進) became Minister of Personnel,
and again reinstated Tài (泰) to his former office.
In the seventh month, he was promoted to Minister of Revenue of Nánjīng (南京).
Liú Jǐn (劉瑾)
was Tài (泰)’s fellow townsman,
and angered that Tài (泰) did not communicate with him,
ordered him to retire after only four days.
He accused Jìn (進) of being partial to Tài (泰),
and then stripped both of them of their official status,
and posthumously denounced Mǎ Wénshēng (馬文升) and previous recommenders of Tài (泰), namely Minister Liú Dàxià (劉大夏), Investigating Censor Zhào Shìxián (趙士xián), and Censor Zhāng Jīn (張津) as commoners.
Over fifty others were also punished with fines of rice for the border.
Tài (泰) returned
and lived in his villa at Wéiqū (韋曲),
not entering the city.
After Jǐn (瑾) was executed,
he was reinstated to office
and then retired.
He died at the age of eighty.
When he died, there was a sound like thunder under his couch.
Tài (泰) lived a frugal and simple life.
When distinguished guests arrived,
there would be no more than two meat dishes.
As a Minister,
he did not wear crimson robes.
When he died,
his family only then made one for his burial.
During the Tiānqǐ (天啟) era,
he was posthumously given the title Duānhuì (端惠).
Zhāng Jīn,
courtesy name Guǎnghàn,
was a native of Bóluó.
He obtained the *jìnshì* degree at the end of the Chénghuà reign,
and was appointed Magistrate of Jiànyáng.
He built city walls,
suppressed mining bandits,
erected temples for Zhū Xī, Cài Yuándìng, and other worthies,
and provided sacrificial land for their descendants.
After returning home for a period of mourning,
he was appointed to Dàyě,
and was later summoned and appointed Censor (Yùshǐ).
In the winter of the fourteenth year of Hóngzhì (1501),
when the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù) lacked a Minister (Shàngshū),
court officials recommended Mǎ Wénshēng and Mǐn Guī.
However, Zhāng Jīn, along with his colleagues Wén Sēn and Zēng Dàyǒu, requested the appointment of the retired Minister Zhōu Jīng and the Grand Coordinator (Zǒngdū) of Liǎngguǎng, Liú Dàxià.
This displeased the emperor, and he was imprisoned in the imperial dungeons.
Censors (Gěishì Yùshǐ) argued for his release,
and he was freed.
Afterwards,
he said:
"Your Majesty consults with grand ministers,
but ordinary officials are not involved,
which is not how one achieves clear sight and sharp hearing.
I beg that you command high-ranking officials (qīngzuǒ), attendants (shìcóng), and outer officials (wàiliáo) who have completed their terms and come for imperial audiences,
to all be allowed to present themselves at the appropriate time,
to convey the sentiments of those below."
At the beginning of the Wǔzōng reign,
he served as an Imperial Inspector (Xún'àn) in Guǎngxī,
and impeached the Grand Garrison Commander (Zǒngzhèn) eunuch Wéi Jīng for unauthorized transfer of official funds.
He participated in the suppression of the Fùhè bandits,
and was rewarded.
He was then appointed Prefect of Quánzhōu.
He was dismissed from office for having previously recommended Tàichāng,
and forced to return to commoner status.
When Liú Jǐn was defeated,
he was reinstated as Prefect of Níngbō,
promoted to Left Administration Vice Commissioner (Zuǒ Cānzhèng) of Shāndōng,
then elevated to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief (Yòu Qiāndū Yùshǐ),
in charge of military river patrols (Tídū Cāojiāng).
He was further promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief (Yòu Fùdū Yùshǐ),
serving as Grand Coordinator (Xúnfǔ) of Yìngtiān and other prefectures.
When his jurisdiction suffered floods and droughts,
he requested a halt to textile production.
When the imperial carriage traveled north,
he submitted a memorial of remonstrance,
but received no reply.
Treacherous people in Xiàofēng, Zhèjiāng, occupied deep mountains and resisted arrest,
a situation that had persisted for twenty years and no one had been able to control.
Zhāng Jīn went to Zhèjiāng under the pretext of other business,
and apprehended them all.
He was promoted to Right Vice Minister of Revenue (Hùbù Yòu Shìláng),
but continued as Grand Coordinator.
When the emperor returned from Xuānfǔ,
he again wished to travel north.
Zhāng Jīn submitted a stern remonstrance,
but it went unheeded.
After his death,
he was posthumously granted the title of Minister of Revenue (Hùbù Shàngshū) of Nánjīng.
Chén Shòu,
courtesy name Běnrén,
hailed from Xīngàn.
His grandfather, Zhìhóng,
served in Liáodōng on behalf of his elder brother during the Hóngwǔ reign,
and thus his family was registered in Níngyuǎn Guard (Níngyuǎn Wèi).
When Chén Shòu was young, he was very poor.
Once, he found a sum of gold
and guarded it until midnight
before returning it to its owner.
He studied under Hè Qīn, a fellow townsman.
He obtained the *jìnshì* degree in the eighth year of Chénghuà (1472),
and was appointed Investigating Censor (Gěishì Zhōng) in the Ministry of Revenue (Hù Kē).
He inspected the border defenses of Xuānfǔ and Dàtóng,
and impeached and removed garrison eunuchs who were not disciplined.
He also impeached the brothers of Imperial Consort Wàn and the eunuchs Liáng Fāng and the monk Jìxiǎo,
and was imprisoned in the imperial dungeons.
After his release,
he was repeatedly promoted to Supervising Secretary (Dū Gěishì Zhōng).
In the first year of Hóngzhì (1488),
when Wáng Shù became Minister of Personnel,
Chén Shòu was promoted to Assistant Minister of the Court of Judicial Review (Dàlǐ Chéng).
Liú Jí resented Wáng Shù,
and instigated censors to impeach Chén Shòu for not being proficient in legal matters,
hoping to implicate Wáng Shù.
Chén Shòu was eventually transferred to serve as Junior Supervisor of the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Guānglù Shàogīng) in Nánjīng,
and then rotated to Minister of the Court of State Ceremonials (Hónglú Qīng).
In the winter of the thirteenth year (1500),
he was appointed Right Vice Censor-in-Chief (Yòu Qiāndū Yùshǐ) and served as Grand Coordinator (Xúnfǔ) of Yánsuí.
Huǒshāi repeatedly raided the border,
and previous garrison and patrol officials had all been dismissed.
When Chén Shòu arrived,
he collected military supplies,
broadened his network of spies,
and distributed soldiers and horses into ten routes,
so they could support each other.
The military's morale then revived.
The following year,
various tribes launched a large invasion.
They first sent over a hundred cavalry to lure them out.
The generals requested to attack them,
but Chén Shòu refused.
He personally stepped out of his tent,
with dozens of cavalry,
sat on a folding stool, and gestured for food and drink.
The bandits saw him,
suspected a trap,
and withdrew.
Various routes then launched surprise attacks,
inflicting many casualties and captures.
The court was just about to dispatch powerful forces under Miáo Kuí and others,
but Chén Shòu had already reported victory.
Emperor Xiàozōng commended him,
and increased his salary by one grade.
Miáo Kuí wanted to take advantage of the victory to raid the enemy's lair.
As his forces had been stationed in Yánsuí for a long time,
the three tens of thousands of warhorses daily consumed an immeasurable amount of fodder.
Chén Shòu suggested moving them to graze near the frontier,
where there was water and grass,
which made the crowd hesitant.
Chén Shòu rode ahead on horseback,
and everyone followed him,
saving several hundred thousand (units of currency).
At the time of the victory,
some advised him to list his sons and nephews in the official records,
but Chén Shòu said:
"My sons and nephews do not know how to use bows and spears.
How could they receive rewards alongside soldiers who fought with their lives?"
He ultimately refused.
In the sixteenth year, he was appointed Right Vice Censor-in-Chief (Yòu Fùdū Yùshǐ) and presided over the Nán Yuàn.
At the beginning of the Zhèngdé reign,
Liú Jǐn forged an imperial decree to arrest Imperial Censors (Kēdào) Dài Xiǎn, Bó Yànhuī, and others in Nánjīng.
Chén Shòu submitted a memorial arguing for their release.
Liú Jǐn was enraged
and ordered him to retire.
Soon after, he was implicated in the deficit of grain stores in Yánsuí,
and fined 2,300 *shi* of rice and 1,500 bolts of cloth.
Being poor, he could not pay,
so he submitted a memorial pleading his case.
Liú Jǐn, upon learning of Chén Shòu's poverty,
specially exempted him.
The eunuch Liáo Táng, who garrisoned Shǎnxī, was corrupt and tyrannical.
Yáng Yīqīng, knowing Chén Shòu's resoluteness,
appointed him Grand Coordinator of that region in the first month of the ninth year (1514).
Liáo Táng had initially been commanded by imperial decree to produce 160 felt tents,
earning tens of thousands in profit,
which he intended to give to powerful favorites.
Chén Shòu ordered the relevant authorities to retain them for famine relief,
and further warned Liáo Táng not to extort anything under the guise of tribute.
Liáo Táng was furious
and planned to ruin him.
Chén Shòu submitted four memorials requesting retirement,
but was refused.
Dozens of Liáo Táng's cronies scattered throughout the prefectures and counties, preying on the people for profit.
Chén Shòu ordered their arrest,
but they all fled back,
further disheartening him.
That autumn,
he was appointed Vice Minister of War (Bīngbù Shìláng) of Nánjīng.
The people of Shǎnxi cried out, surrounding his sedan chair,
preventing him from leaving for an entire day.
After a year,
he requested to return due to old age,
and was promoted to Minister of Justice (Xíngbù Shàngshū),
then retired.
When Chén Shòu was an Investigating Censor,
he spoke openly about current affairs,
but he particularly disliked impeaching others,
saying:
"My father warned me not to be a judicial official,
as it is easy to wrong people.
Censors (Yánguān) wrong people even more severely;
I dare not speak carelessly."
In the first year of Jiājìng (1522),
an imperial decree promoted him to the first rank,
and officials were dispatched to inquire after him.
At that time, he was eighty-three years old.
Chén Shòu was incorruptible.
After forty years in officialdom,
he had no home to return to.
He lived in Nánjīng,
in a dwelling that offered no shelter from wind and rain.
When he died,
Minister Lǐ Chōngsì and Prefect Kòu Tiān prepared his burial.
Several years later,
with financial assistance from relatives and old friends,
he was finally able to be buried in Xīngàn.
Fán Yíng,
courtesy name Tíngbì,
was a native of Chángshān.
At the end of the Tiānshùn reign,
he obtained the *jìnshì* degree,
but returned home due to illness to care for his parents.
After a long time,
he was appointed Messenger (Xíngrén).
When he was sent to Shǔ, he refused bribes,
and local officials erected a "Rejecting Gold Pavilion" to commemorate him.
In the eighth year of Chénghuà (1472), he was promoted to Censor.
When bandits rose in Shāndōng,
he was ordered to capture their leader.
He cleared the army north of the Jiāng River,
and many of his proposals were established as precedents.
He was reassigned to inspect Yúnnán.
When Jiāozhǐ enticed border residents to become bandits,
he dispatched a manifesto that foiled their plot.
He was posted as Prefect of Sōngjiāng Fǔ.
Transport laborers suffered greatly from losses and depreciation,
so Yíng reformed the system for civil laborers,
ordering the grain captains to manage transport exclusively,
while relaxing their quotas,
to provide them with better conditions.
He followed Zhōu Chén's old methods for taxes and corvée,
but made slight adjustments,
and the people's distress greatly eased.
He returned home due to a period of mourning,
then was reinstated as Prefect of Píngyáng.
In the early years of Hóngzhì (1488-1505),
the emperor issued an edict for ministers to recommend regional officials.
Vice Minister Huáng Kǒngzhāo recommended Yíng,
and Minister Wáng Shù also valued him,
so he was promoted to Provincial Surveillance Commissioner of Hénán.
The Huánghé River caused havoc,
and many people were displaced.
Yíng toured and provided relief,
saving a great many lives.
The land tax system in Hénán had many accumulated abuses,
and the Grand Coordinator and Censor-in-Chief Xú Kè wanted to investigate their origins,
but many found it difficult.
Yíng said:
"Treat ten thousand as a thousand,
and a thousand as a hundred;
what is so difficult?"
Kè assigned it to Yíng, whose subordinate officials investigated,
and within ten days,
the long-standing corruption was completely cleared.
In the fourth year (1491), he was promoted to Administrator of Yìngtiān Fǔ.
The garrison eunuch Jiǎng Cóng accused officials in memorials,
implicating many, leading to their dismissal.
Yíng was ordered to investigate the cases;
at first, he appeared to act no differently,
which greatly pleased Cóng.
Later, Yíng memorialized about Cóng damaging the Dragon Vein of Xiàolíng Mausoleum,
and Cóng was consequently imprisoned
and sentenced to serve as a pure army laborer.
In the seventh year (1494), he was promoted to Right Vice Minister of Works in Nánjīng,
and soon after, reassigned as Right Vice Censor-in-Chief, Grand Coordinator of Húguǎng.
When the bandits of Jǐntián allied with the Yáo and Zhuàng people of Liǎngguǎng to raid,
Yíng persuaded the remaining factions to disperse
and executed eighteen ringleaders.
After more than a year,
he requested retirement due to illness.
After seven years at home,
he was recommended by officials both inside and outside the court,
and was reinstated to his former position as Grand Coordinator of Yúnyáng,
then soon after, reassigned as Right Vice Minister of Justice in Nánjīng.
In the sixteenth year (1503),
Jǐngdōng Wèi in Yúnnán experienced seven days of darkness during the day,
Yíliáng had earthquakes like thunder,
Qǔjìng suffered several large fires,
and Guìzhōu also experienced many natural disasters.
Yíng was ordered to inspect.
Upon arrival, he impeached the crimes of the garrison and inspection officials
and dismissed 1,700 civil and military officials who were derelict in their duties.
He shrewdly discovered that the change in Jǐngdōng
was due to Commander Wú Yǒng embezzling public funds
and, to escape punishment,
falsely inflated the incident, claiming it was caused by clouds and dense fog.
Yíng impeached and convicted him.
Upon his return, he was promoted to Minister of the same Board.
When Wǔzōng ascended the throne,
he retired to his hometown.
Liú Jǐn, due to a joint investigation into the dispute over the succession of the Marquis of Lóngpíng,
implicated Yíng,
and he was stripped of his official status.
The following year, he was again penalized for reducing the official cloth quota in Sōngjiāng,
and fined five hundred shí of rice to be transported to the border.
Yíng had always been poor,
and by this time, his situation worsened.
He died in the eleventh month of the third year (1508),
aged seventy-five.
When Jǐn fell,
he was reinstated to office,
posthumously granted the title of Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
and given the posthumous name Qīngjiǎn.
Yíng was by nature sincere.
During farming season, he would sit in a basket palanquin, wearing a bamboo hat,
carried by his sons and grandsons through the fields,
saying:
"It's not just to observe the crops,
but to accustom my descendants to labor."
His descendants generally followed his teachings,
many being earnest, simple, and diligent scholars.
Xióng Xiù,
courtesy name Rǔmíng,
was from Dàozhōu.
His ancestors moved there from Fēngchéng due to military conscription.
Xiù passed the imperial examination in the second year of Chénghuà (1466),
and was appointed Executive Secretary of the Office of the Seal of the Imperial Court.
He was sent on an imperial mission to the state of Chǔ,
and inspected the tea trade in Sìchuān,
forcefully rejecting all gifts.
He was promoted to Censor
and toured Shǎnxī.
When Left Administration Commissioner Yú Fán gave imperial treasury silver as a gift to Shào Jìn, the Court Steward of the Imperial Stables,
Xiù exposed their crime.
Fán fled to the capital to accuse Xiù,
and the emperor imprisoned Xiù's officials as well,
and demoted him to Prefect of Qīngfēng.
Fán and Jìn were also dismissed.
After a long time,
when there was a vacancy for the Prefect of Fèngxiáng,
Xiù was promoted to fill the position.
In the early years of Hóngzhì (1488-1505),
he was promoted to Left Administration Vice Commissioner of Shāndōng,
then to Right Administration Commissioner.
In the seventh year (1494), he served as Right Vice Censor-in-Chief and Grand Coordinator of Yánsuí.
Yúlín was initially just a small fort,
where troops were stationed for winter defense.
In the Jǐngtài era (1450-1457),
the Grand Coordinator and Commander-in-Chief were first moved to reside there,
making it a major strategic town in the northwest.
The city walls were too narrow to accommodate everyone,
so Xiù requested to extend them by over 1,200 zhàng.
He governed the garrison for several years,
training soldiers and accumulating grain,
and border administration flourished.
He successively served as Left and Right Vice Minister of War,
and Minister Liú Dàxià greatly relied on and trusted him.
The registered number of brave warriors in the Téngxiáng Four Guards was thirty to forty thousand,
but mostly fictitious.
Hundreds of thousands of cash and grain were spent annually,
much of it ending up in the hands of eunuchs.
Court officials repeatedly requested an audit,
but were always obstructed.
In the eighteenth year (1505), Xiù was ordered to clarify the situation,
but before he could finish, Emperor Xiàozōng passed away.
Court politics gradually changed,
but Xiù firmly maintained his position without regard for consequences,
and uncovered 14,000 cases of fraudulent registrations.
The Grand Eunuch of the Imperial Stables, Níng Jǐn, and others memorialized to request a return to the old system,
but the Supervising Censors jointly impeached Jǐn in numerous memorials,
and Dàxià also strongly argued against it.
Wǔzōng reluctantly agreed,
but pardoned Jǐn and others without further inquiry.
In the first year of Zhèngdé (1506), he was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief,
concurrently overseeing military affairs of Liǎngguǎng and serving as Grand Coordinator.
Upon arriving at the garrison,
he completely abolished the expenditures of the military secretariat,
taking not even a tiny thing.
In the second year (1507), he and Commander-in-Chief Fúqiāng Bó Máo Ruì suppressed the Zhuàng people of Hèxiàn.
Liú Jǐn deeply resented Xiù for the previous reduction of brave warriors,
and sought to find fault but found none.
Xiù was summoned to take charge of the Nánjīng Censorate,
but soon after was dismissed by imperial decree.
Later,
Liú Jǐn again fabricated charges against Xiù concerning the spoiled grain in the Yánsuí granaries,
fining him five hundred shí of rice
and ordering Xiù to personally transport it to the border.
Xiù's family was consequently ruined.
He died in the intercalary fourth month of the tenth year (1515),
without a son.
Grand Coordinator Qín Jīn praised his integrity to the court,
and he was posthumously granted the title of Minister of Justice.
Grand Master of the Imperial Stud Hè Mèngchūn noted that Xiù's adopted grandson was young and poor,
with no means of support,
and requested that he be granted a monthly stipend, similar to the precedents of Director Zhāng Fèngxiáng and Kǒng Qí,
and also requested a posthumous name.
Consequently, he was posthumously named Zhuāngjiǎn,
and his grandson was given one shí of rice per month.
Pān Fān,
courtesy name Tíngfāng,
was from Chóngdé.
Initially, he falsely used the surname Zhōng,
but restored his original surname after becoming prominent.
He passed the imperial examination in the second year of Chénghuà (1466),
and was appointed Director in the Ministry of Justice.
He successively served as Bureau Director.
When the eunuch Qían Néng, who guarded Yúnnán, was impeached by Grand Coordinator Wáng Shù,
Fān was ordered to investigate,
and he uncovered the full truth.
He was posted as Prefect of Ānqìng,
and then reassigned to Yúnyáng.
At that time, the prefecture administration was newly established,
and migrants from Shǎn and Luò congregated there.
Fān carefully soothed and settled them,
and they all became permanent residents.
He was successively promoted to Left and Right Administration Commissioners of Shāndōng and Húguǎng.
In the ninth year of Hóngzhì (1496), he served as Right Vice Censor-in-Chief and Grand Coordinator of Sìchuān,
concurrently supervising military affairs of Sōngpān.
He proclaimed his authority and trustworthiness,
and the local indigenous people obeyed him.
He traveled through Sōng and Mào alone in a carriage without being dared to be molested.
He was promoted to Right Vice Minister of War in Nánjīng,
and soon after reassigned to the Ministry of Justice.
In the fourteenth year, he was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief,
and made Grand Coordinator of Guǎngdōng and Guǎngxī.
The number of soldiers under his command previously numbered not less than ten thousand,
but Fān reduced them,
leaving only enough for daily use.
Lí bandits led by Fú Nánshé caused chaos in Hǎinán,
gathering tens of thousands of followers.
Fān ordered Vice Envoy Hú Fù to dispatch Láng and Tǔ native soldiers to suppress and execute them,
and they pacified over 1,200 bandit strongholds.
Based on this achievement,
he was promoted to Left Censor-in-Chief.
Afterwards,
he also pacified the notorious bandits Gǔ Sānzǎi and Táng Dàbìn and others in Guīshàn.
Cén Jùn, the Prefect of Sī'ēn, and Cén Měng, the Prefect of Tiánzhōu, were feuding and killing each other.
Jùn attacked and captured Tiánzhōu,
and Měng, in dire straits, begged for aid.
Fān admonished Jùn to cease hostilities,
but he refused.
Thereupon, Fān, together with the Garrison Eunuch Wéi Jīng and the Grand General Fúqiāng Bó Máo Ruì, assembled over one hundred thousand troops,
and divided them into six detachments to suppress him.
Jùn died,
his head was presented at the military gate,
4,700 heads were taken,
and his territory was completely pacified.
The army then returned to suppress and pacify the bandit Tā Yuánzǔ in Fēnghú, Nánhǎi County.
When news of the victory arrived,
an imperial letter praised and rewarded him.
Fān reported in a memorial,
that Sī'ēn should establish regular officials,
and Měng, having provoked conflict and lost territory,
should be demoted to Assistant Prefect,
and allowed to return to guard his old land.
Liú Dàxià, the Minister of War, argued
that Měng's family had been notoriously wicked for generations,
and he should not be returned to his old administration.
He requested that regular officials be established in both prefectures,
and Měng be demoted to a Commander of a Thousand Households,
and exiled to Fújiàn.
The Emperor agreed.
In the first month of the first year of the Zhèngdé era, he was summoned to be Minister of Justice of Nánjīng.
A year later,
he retired.
Initially,
when Fān left Guǎngdōng and Guǎngxī,
Cén Měng occupied Tiánzhōu and refused to move.
Xiè Hú, the Prefect, fearing Měng's ferocity,
also procrastinated.
When the matter was reported,
Hú was arrested and imprisoned in the imperial prison.
Hú blamed Fān, Wéi Jīng, and Máo Ruì.
Jīng, in turn, blamed Minister Dàxià.
Liú Jǐn happened to dislike Dàxià,
so all four were arrested.
Dàxià was charged with not following Fān's advice,
and Fān was also charged with failing to appease Měng.
Both were banished to Sùzhōu.
This was in the ninth month of the third year.
Later, Jǐn, following the suggestion of Zhuāng●, an official from the Ministry of Revenue,
sent the eunuch Wéi Yùn to audit the Guangdong treasury.
He reported that many of the goods to be remitted for corruption and fines were rotten and damaged,
and over 600,000 taels of silver for salt profits and military rewards stored in Wúzhōu were not remitted in time.
Fān, along with the former Grand Coordinator Dàxià, former Left Administration Commissioner Rén Hé Shěn Ruì, and 899 others, were arrested and interrogated,
and fined grain to be delivered to the border.
Ruì was incorruptible and upright.
He had already been promoted to Right Vice Minister of Justice of Nánjīng,
and had requested retirement.
At this point, he was stripped of his office.
After Jǐn was executed,
Fān retired with his original official rank.
Over six years later,
he died.
Ruì was not reinstated and allowed to retire until the early Jiājìng era.
When Fān was dismissed from office and returned home,
he had no house,
so he rented another person's residence.
When drinking with his fellow villagers,
he would sit openly under the flowers,
and when drunk, he would go wherever he pleased.
Such was his demeanor.
Hú Fù,
courtesy name Yǒngnián,
was from Jìxī.
He passed the imperial examination in the fourteenth year of Chénghuà.
He was appointed Judicial Reviewer of the Grand Court of Judicial Review of Nánjīng.
In the early Hóngzhì era,
he successively served as Assistant Surveillance Commissioner of Fújiàn.
In Fúníng, there were over 200 prisoners.
Fù settled all their cases in one interrogation,
and the prisons were emptied at once.
He left due to mourning,
was reinstated and reassigned to Shāndōng,
then promoted to Vice Surveillance Commissioner of Guǎngdōng.
When the Yáo people of Sìhuì revolted,
he suppressed and captured over 500 people.
The Yáo of Lóngshuǐ appeared and disappeared unpredictably.
Fù estimated the land they passed through,
and obtained over 3,000 qīng of barren land,
where he recruited tenant households to cultivate and herd.
The Yáo feared the tenants and dared not raid,
and the residents were able to farm.
When Fú Nánshé besieged Dānzhōu,
Fù and Councillor Liú Xìn went to scout.
The bandits suddenly attacked,
killing Xìn.
Fù personally cut down one notorious bandit,
and the bandits retreated.
He returned with additional troops and pacified them.
He successively served as Left and Right Administration Commissioner of Shǎnxī.
In the early Zhèngdé era,
he entered court as Prefect of Shùntiān Prefecture.
In the third year, he was promoted to Minister of the Grand Court of Judicial Review of Nánjīng,
and then moved to Right Vice Minister of Revenue.
In the first month of the fifth year, he was forced to retire due to slow handling of cases during his time at the Grand Court of Judicial Review,
which was also Jǐn's intention.
After Jǐn's defeat,
he was reinstated to his former office.
In the seventh year, he was appointed Minister of this ministry.
The granaries in Nánjīng only had enough provisions for one year.
Fù served in the ministry for three years,
and accumulated six years' worth of provisions.
He submitted over ten proposals,
most of which were inconvenient for powerful officials and nobles,
and were not implemented,
so he requested retirement due to age.
He died in the first year of Jiājìng.
He was posthumously granted Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
and given the posthumous title Kānghuì.
Zhāng Tài,
courtesy name Shúhēng,
was from Shùndé, Guǎngdōng.
He passed the imperial examination in the second year of Chénghuà.
He was appointed Magistrate of Shāxiàn.
At that time, after the rebellion of Dèng Màoqī,
Tài pacified and recruited the people,
and all the displaced returned.
He entered court as a Censor,
and together with fellow officials, he remonstrated against Noble Consort Wàn's interference in government,
and was flogged at court to the brink of death.
He was sent out to supervise schools in the capital region,
then left due to mourning,
and lived at home for over ten years.
In the fifth year of Hóngzhì, he was reinstated to his former office,
and inspected Yúnnán.
Sīdié, a native chieftain of Mèngmì, stirred up rebellion,
and used troops to block Hǎn Wàfǎ, the Pacification Commissioner of Mùbāng, at Mèngnǎi Fort.
The local officials tried to appease him,
but he refused to listen.
Tài, along with Circuit Inspector Zhāng Gào, assembled troops and showed their determination to suppress him.
Sīdié feared them,
and only then ceased hostilities.
When Lake Diānchí overflowed,
causing disaster for the people,
Tài built dikes to mitigate the problem.
Upon returning to court,
he requested the dismissal of court eunuchs in charge of textile production,
a reduction in taxes for imperial estates and noble family estates affected by disaster,
and the provision of oxen and seeds to disaster victims in the capital provinces.
An imperial decree only allowed the provision of oxen and seeds,
the rest was not implemented.
When bandits entered Yǒngchāng,
Lǔ Lín, a guerrilla commander in Gānsù, blamed Vice Grand General Táo Zhēn,
while Grand General Liú Níng memorialized that the local officials were not harmonious.
An imperial decree ordered Tài to investigate.
Tài reported that the garrison eunuch Fù Dé and the former Grand General Zhōu Yù had seized and occupied military farms,
and Circuit Inspector Féng Xù had reduced military rations,
so bandits repeatedly invaded without being resisted,
and over 600 soldiers, 20,000 horses, camels, cattle, and sheep were lost, none of which was reported.
The Emperor was enraged,
and handed them over to officials.
Dé was demoted to an inner servant,
imprisoned in Nánjīng,
and Xù was banished outside the Great Wall as a commoner.
Tài further stated that the fertile lands of Gānzhōu were all occupied by eunuchs and military officials,
who still demanded military taxes;
the Caohú (Grass Lake) north of the city, which provided pasture for garrison soldiers' horses,
was now also occupied.
He requested that all be returned to the military,
and that this policy be extended to the two garrisons of Yán and Níng.
The imperial decree approved all of this.
He was promoted to Vice Minister of the Imperial Stud, then transferred to the Grand Court of Judicial Review.
Initially,
in Jìzhōu (薊州), much of the civilian land had been encroached upon by pastureland for horses,
and it also encroached upon the Imperial Horse Stables and the Shenjī Camp's (神機營) pastureland and imperial estates.
The poor lost their livelihoods,
and the pastureland also fell short of its original quota.
Xiàozōng (孝宗) repeatedly dispatched Supervising Secretary Zhōu Xuán (周旋),
Vice Ministers Gù Zuǒ (顧佐) and Xióng Chōng (熊翀) and others to investigate,
but none could resolve it.
At this point, Tàiyǒu (泰) was ordered to accompany Imperial Guard officials to join Patrol Censor Zhōu Jìlín (周季麟) in a renewed investigation.
Tài (泰) secretly obtained old records from the Yǒnglè (永樂) era,
compared and examined them,
and found that over 930 qǐng (頃) of land should be returned to the people,
while the pastures of the Capital Garrisons and the Imperial Horse Stables did not lose their original quotas.
When the memorial was submitted,
it was twice rejected by those who debated against it.
Minister Hán Wén (韓文) strongly upheld it,
but it was kept by the emperor and not issued.
When Wǔzōng (武宗) succeeded to the throne,
Hán Wén (文) requested it again,
and only then was Tàiyǒu's (泰) memorial released,
allowing all those who had been displaced to return to their occupations.
Soon after, he was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief to oversee grain transport in Nánjīng (南京).
He submitted a memorial proposing twelve reforms,
most of which were approved.
In the second year of Zhèngdé (正德), he was summoned to serve as Right Vice Minister of Works,
and the following year, he was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief of Nánjīng (南京).
Tàiyǒu (泰) was honest and cautious.
When Liú Jǐn (劉瑾) held exclusive power,
the imperial nobility scrambled to offer bribes.
When Tàiyǒu's (泰) memorials and reports reached the capital,
he only sent local ramie cloth as gifts,
which Liú Jǐn (瑾) resented.
In the tenth month of that year, Liú Jǐn (瑾) ordered him to retire as Minister of Revenue of Nánjīng (南京).
In the seventh month of the following year, he died,
and for other offenses, he was fined several hundred shí (石) of rice.
After Liú Jǐn (瑾) was executed,
Tàiyǒu (泰) was granted a burial and sacrifice according to regulations.
Wú Wéndù (吳文度),
courtesy name Xiànzhī (憲之),
was from Jìnwāng (晉尪).
He followed his father as a sojourner in Jiāngníng (江寧),
and consequently settled there.
He passed the imperial examination in the eighth year of Chénghuà (成化),
and was appointed Magistrate of Lóngquán (龍泉).
He was recruited to serve as a Nánjīng (南京) Censor.
Together with fellow official Sūn Xū (孫需) and others, he impeached the demonic monk Jìxiǎo (繼曉),
and was subjected to a beating with the court stick.
Soon after, he was promoted to Prefect of Tīngzhōu (汀州).
The Yáo (瑤) people were not pacified,
so he implemented strategies to soothe and appease them,
and the Yáo (瑤) paid taxes like regular residents.
During the Hóngzhì (弘治) era, he successively served as Left Administration Vice Commissioner of Jiāngxī (江西),
and Left and Right Administration Commissioners of Shānxī (山西) and Hénán (河南).
In the first year of Zhèngdé (正德), he was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief,
and served as Patrol Censor of Yúnnán (雲南).
When the bandits Ā Běn (阿本) and others revolted in Shīzōngzhōu (師宗州),
his admonitions were not heeded.
So he dispatched Vice Commissioner Chén Yījīng (陳一經) and others to lead an army of twenty thousand to attack them,
and separately sent troops to cut off Pánjiāng (盤江),
occupying the rear of the bandit stronghold,
capturing and beheading a thousand people in total.
He then served as Vice Minister of Revenue.
In the winter of the third year, he was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief of Nánjīng (南京).
When Wéndù (文度) was recalled from Yúnnán (雲南),
