Liú Jǐn (劉瑾), coveting the gold and treasures produced in the region,
repeatedly demanded bribes.
Wéndù (文度) had nothing to offer,
and Liú Jǐn (瑾) held a deep grudge against him.
Coincidentally, when Minister of Works Lǐ Suì (李鐩) retired,
the court nominated Wéndù (文度) and Nánjīng (南京) Vice Minister of Revenue Wáng Héng (王珩).
Consequently, Wéndù (文度) was made Nánjīng (南京) Minister of Revenue,
and both he and Héng (珩) were ordered to retire.
When the decree was issued,
the entire court was shocked.
After returning home,
his residence consisted of only a few rooms.
After Liú Jǐn (瑾) was executed,
Wéndù (文度) died before he could be reappointed.
Héng (珩)
was from Zhào (趙).
He began his career as a *jìnshì* (進士),
and was also known for his integrity.
Zhāng Nài (張鼐),
courtesy name Yònghé (用和),
was from Lìchéng (歷城).
He passed the imperial examination in the eleventh year of Chénghuà (成化).
He was appointed Magistrate of Xiānglíng (襄陵),
and later served as a Censor.
In the final years of Xiànzōng's (憲宗) reign, he frequently flogged censorial officials,
and Nài (鼐) strongly remonstrated.
He also once impeached the demonic monk Jìxiǎo (繼曉) and the Daoist practitioner Dèng Cháng'ēn (鄧常恩) and others.
The emperor deeply disliked him.
He was sent out to inspect Jiāngxī (江西).
Many bandits were tenants and servants of powerful clans,
and Nài (鼐) and Patrol Censor Mǐn Guī (閔珪) jointly memorialized on the matter.
Yǐn Zhí (尹直) and others framed them,
so Guī (珪) was demoted, and Nài (鼐) was implicated as a member of Yǐn Mín's (尹旻) faction,
and demoted to Assistant Magistrate of Chénzhōu (郴州).
In the early Hóngzhì (弘治) era,
he was promoted to Assistant Surveillance Commissioner of Hénán (河南), then to Vice Commissioner,
and moved to Vice Surveillance Commissioner for his successful management of the Huánglíng Gāng (黃陵岡) area.
In the fifteenth year, he was promoted to Surveillance Commissioner.
Nài (鼐) served in Hénán (河南) for a long time,
and repeatedly suffered from river disasters.
He effectively supervised the management,
and the people built shrines for him.
In the autumn of that year, he was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief and Patrol Censor of Liáodōng (遼東).
At that time, military administration had long been lax,
and it was also permitted for surplus households to pay money to assist in courier services,
and be granted official caps and belts,
and have their status restored,
causing border residents to compete to use this precedent to avoid service.
Nài (鼐) argued against it,
and then submitted several proposals: to fix the horse regulations,
verify garrison grain, clarify hidden land occupations, audit tenant households, and reduce the number of military escorts,
all of which were approved and implemented.
Soon after, he impeached the corrupt and tyrannical eunuch Liú Gōng (劉恭) who was guarding a sector,
and built a border wall from Shānhǎiguān (山海關) to Kāiyuán (開原) and Àiyángbǎo (靉陽堡), spanning over a thousand *lǐ* (里).
After Xú Guàn (徐貫), the Patrol Censors of Liáo (遼) —
Zhāng Xiù (張岫), Zhāng Yù (張玉), Chén Yáo (陳瑤), and Hán Chóng (韓重) —
were mostly dismissed due to offenses,
until Nài (鼐) was praised for his ability.
When Wǔzōng (武宗) ascended the throne,
he was transferred to serve as Patrol Censor of Xuānfǔ (宣府).
In the first year of Zhèngdé (正德),
he was recalled,
and soon after, promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief to manage the Censorate.
There was a magistrate who committed embezzlement and deserved to be dismissed,
and a soldier who committed murder and deserved to be executed.
Liú Jǐn (劉瑾) received heavy bribes
and wanted to pardon them.
Nài (鼐) insisted on no pardon,
and was sent out as Right Censor-in-Chief of Nánjīng (南京).
Jiāo Fāng's (焦芳) son, Huángzhōng (黃中), wanted to forcibly purchase Nài's (鼐) residence,
and gave it to Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review Wèi Nà (魏訥).
Nài (鼐) refused,
and the Fāng (芳) father and son also resented him.
At this time, Liú Jǐn (瑾) sent Supervising Secretary Wáng Yì (王翊) and others to audit military provisions in Liáodōng (遼東).
Upon their return, they reported that much of the fodder and grain had rotted,
and this was attributed as a crime of the defending officials.
Nài (鼐) and his successors Patrol Censor Mǎ Zhōngxī (馬中錫) and Dèng Zhāng (鄧章),
former Vice Administration Commissioner Mào Zhèng (冒政),
Vice Commissioner Fāng Jǔ (方矩),
and Department Directors Wáng Jìn (王藎) and Liú Yì (劉繹)
were arrested and imprisoned in the imperial prison,
and their families were ordered to transport rice to Liáodōng (遼東).
Nài (鼐) was ordered to transport two thousand *shí* (石),
and being unable to do so,
was imprisoned in Liáodōng (遼東).
After a long time,
General-in-chief Máo Lún (毛倫) and others fully reported the suffering of these individuals,
requesting that they be allowed to pay a discounted price,
which Liú Jǐn (瑾) reluctantly agreed to.
The matter was only concluded after three years,
and all were dismissed as commoners.
After Liú Jǐn (瑾) was executed,
they were reinstated to their offices.
Nài (鼐) died earlier,
and in the early years of Shìzōng's (世宗) reign, he was granted a posthumous allowance.
Mào Zhèng (冒政),
from Tàizhōu (泰州).
He was a *jìnshì* (進士) in the same year as Nài (鼐),
and successively served as Right Vice Censor-in-Chief,
and Patrol Censor of Níngxià (寧夏).
He was an honest official,
and Liú Jǐn (劉瑾) coveted bribes but could not get them.
So he used the Liáodōng (遼東) incident as a pretext to arrest him,
and fined him up to three thousand *shí* (石) of rice.
After Liú Jǐn (瑾) was executed,
he was reinstated to his post and then retired.
After some time,
he died.
Wáng Jǐng (王璟),
courtesy name Tíngcǎi (廷采),
was from Yí (沂).
He passed the imperial examination in the eighth year of Chénghuà (成化).
He served as Magistrate of Dēngfēng (登封).
He successively served as Censor in both capitals.
In the fourteenth year of Hóngzhì (弘ì), as Nánjīng (南京) Court of State Ceremonial Minister, he was appointed Right Assistant Censor-in-Chief,
managing the salt administration of the Two Zhè (兩浙).
He relieved famine in Zhèjiāng (浙江),
and memorialized to implement ten famine relief policies,
saving many lives.
In the winter of the seventeenth year, he served as Patrol Censor of Bǎodìng (保定).
When Wǔzōng (武宗) ascended the throne,
Eunuch Xià Shòu (夏綬) requested an annual increase in reed marsh taxes in the various prefectures of Zhēndìng (真定),
Junior Eunuch Fù Zhuó (傅琢) requested to survey and verify the fields in Jìnghǎi (靜海), Yǒngqīng (永清), and Lóngpíng (隆平) counties,
and Eunuch Zhāng Jùn (張峻) wanted to tax passing goods and passengers on the Xiǎohé (小河) in Níngjìn (寧晉).
The emperor's edicts granted all these requests.
Also, due to imperial estates,
eunuch guards were sent to arrest over two hundred people, including Rǔ Táng (魯堂),
causing unrest in Jīnán (畿南).
Wáng Jǐng (璟) strongly remonstrated with a memorial,
and Minister Hán Wén (韓文) and others vigorously supported him,
so the eunuchs managing the estates were slightly recalled.
In the first year of Zhèngdé (1506), fourth month, Jǐng retired due to illness,
and was ordered to return home by post-chaise.
In the third year, he was implicated in a case, stripped of his office, and made to reside at home.
In the sixth year, he was reinstated as Grand Coordinator of Shānxī.
He manufactured over ten thousand firearms,
each containing six hidden arrows,
all coated with poison,
to defend against bandits.
The bandits dared not move west.
He was successively promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief.
Later,
he was promoted to Left Censor-in-Chief,
and Zhāng Lún was appointed Right Censor-in-Chief to replace him.
Afterward, Chén Jīn, as Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent and Left Censor-in-Chief, entered the court,
ranking above Jǐng,
so people called Jǐng
"Middle Censor-in-Chief."
At that time, small-minded individuals held power,
and many high officials fawned over them,
but Jǐng alone maintained his former principles.
He was again promoted to Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he retired,
and after his death, was posthumously granted Junior Guardian,
with the posthumous title Gōngjìng.
Initially,
after Jǐng returned from his Grand Coordinatorship of Bǎodìng,
Gāo Fāng, an investigating censor in the Ministry of War, inspected the pasturelands in Cāngzhōu and Yánshān.
He impeached sixty-one people,
including Jǐng and the former Grand Coordinator and Censor-in-Chief Gāo Quán,
Quán being Fāng's father.
An imperial edict stated that those dismissed from office would not be further questioned,
and Jǐng and Quán were both spared.
Quán,
a native of Jiāngdū,
had successively served as Minister of Revenue in Nánjīng.
In the second year of Zhèngdé, he was nominated by the court for Left Censor-in-Chief,
but Jǐn forced him to retire.
Soon after, he was arrested and imprisoned for an offense,
and then stripped of his name for a matter concerning the hereditary peerage of the Marquis of Lóngpíng,
and fined five hundred *shí* of rice.
Later, Jǐn became increasingly overbearing and severe.
Whenever he dispatched envoys for investigation,
they often acted harshly and urgently to please Jǐn,
so Fāng impeached both Quán and others.
Fāng later rose to the rank of Junior Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments,
but was despised by others for impeaching his father.
When Jǐn was executed,
Quán was reinstated and retired,
then passed away.
He was posthumously granted Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
Zhū Qīn,
courtesy name Màogōng,
was a native of Shàowǔ.
He studied under Wú Yǔbì,
and was renowned for his scholarship and conduct.
He passed the imperial examination in the eighth year of Chénghuà (1472) as a *jìnshì*,
and was appointed Judicial Commissioner of Níngbō.
His administration was excellent,
and he was summoned to serve as Censor.
He was dispatched to supervise grain transport,
inspect Hénán,
and pacify the military in Guǎngxī,
everywhere demonstrating integrity and rectitude.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
he was promoted to Vice Commissioner of Shāndōng,
and subsequently served as Surveillance Commissioner of Zhèjiāng.
In the fifteenth year, he came for an imperial audience.
The Ministry of Personnel nominated six people across the empire who excelled in governance and conduct,
and Qīn was among them.
Then Lín Jùn, the Assistant Censor-in-Chief, also recommended Qīn to succeed him,
so Qīn was gradually promoted to Left Administration Commissioner of Húguǎng.
When Wǔzōng ascended the throne,
Qīn was appointed Right Vice Censor-in-Chief and Grand Coordinator of Shāndōng.
The eunuch Wáng Yuè was banished,
and died en route.
Qīn submitted a memorial stating:
"Yuè was banished to guard the imperial tombs;
his crimes were not fully exposed,
and he was granted death on the road,
which does not satisfy public sentiment.
Your subject knows that Yuè was hated by Liú Jǐn and his ilk,
and it must be Jǐn's slander that led to this.
I hope Your Majesty will discern Yuè's innocence,
and punish Jǐn's treachery."
When the memorial arrived,
Jǐn concealed it and did not present it,
holding a grudge.
Qīn, finding the customs in Shāndōng to be lewd and prone to excessive drinking,
strictly prohibited alcohol sales in the market,
and ordered Zhāng Yuánkuí, the Judicial Commissioner of Jǐnán, to investigate,
with offenders' neighbors also being penalized.
Later, someone, fearing punishment, hanged himself.
His mother wanted to appeal,
but Yuánkuí and the Prefect Zhào Huáng bribed her to stop.
Jǐn dispatched investigating *xiaowèi* to expose this,
and all were arrested and imprisoned in the imperial dungeons.
Qīn was forced to retire,
Huáng was stripped of his name,
and Yuánkuí was banished to a frontier garrison.
Jǐn's resentment towards Qīn was not yet satisfied,
so he unearthed a minor incident from Qīn's time in Húguǎng,
and ordered the investigating censor to arrest and interrogate him.
Soon after, he was dismissed as a commoner for a land investigation matter in Shāndōng.
He was also penalized for an excess in the accounts for the renovation of the Sage Confucius Temple in Qūfù,
fined six hundred *shí* of rice to be transported to the frontier.
Moreover, while he was Grand Coordinator of Shāndōng,
he had provided common laborers to the household of Minister Qín Hóng,
and was again arrested and interrogated by the investigating censor.
After Jǐn was executed,
he was reinstated to office.
In the fifteenth year (of Zhèngdé, 1520), he died,
at the age of seventy-seven.
Among Wú Yǔbì's disciples who distinguished themselves in officialdom and scholarship,
Qīn was considered the foremost.
The encomium states: In the early years of Wǔzōng,
Liú and Xiè received the testament to assist in governance,
Hán Wén, Zhāng Fūhuá, and others served as high-ranking ministers.
Many upright individuals held positions of power,
and the nation's affairs had hope.
The "Eight Tigers"
lurked on the left and right,
and though they dared not openly challenge the court officials,
they were indeed maggots in the very heart of the state.
Indeed, to attack from the outside in
is extremely difficult.
Moreover, the Prime Minister's authority was diminished,
far different from previous dynasties;
even if one possessed the loyalty of Hán Qí,
one initially held no power of issuing decrees.
To merely contend for victory through words and debate,
this requires a firm and discerning ruler who is hard to come by,
and to expect it from Wǔzōng,
how could it possibly succeed?
If the first strike fails,
the counterattack is bound to be poisonous,
and the tide of waxing and waning
leaves no room for error.
The calamity brought by the eunuchs was severe,
alas, how dreadful!
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 75: Hé Jiàn, Mǎ Zhōngxī, Lù Wán, Hóng Zhōng (Chén Hào, Jiǎng Shēng), Chén Jīn, Yú Jiàn, Zhōu Nán (Sūn Lù), Mǎ Hào.
Hé Jiàn,
courtesy name Shìguāng,
was a native of Xīnchāng, Zhèjiāng.
He passed the imperial examination in the fifth year of Chénghuà (1469) as a *jìnshì*.
He was appointed Magistrate of Yíxīng.
He was summoned to serve as Censor,
and inspected Xuānfǔ and Dàtóng.
He impeached dozens of officials, including Grand Coordinator Zhèng Níng, for dereliction of duty,
and prosecuted military officers such as Mèng Xǐ for crimes.
He returned to inspect Tàicāng.
When a eunuch in charge of transport violated the law,
he arrested and prosecuted him,
but was then framed by the eunuch,
and imprisoned in the Jǐnyīwèi prison.
After his release,
he again inspected Jiāngběi.
Fèngyáng, where the imperial tombs were located,
had a law that anyone who took even an inch of wood near the border would be executed,
and the tomb guards often abused the populace, relying on this prohibition.
Jiàn requested that the mountain foothills be designated as the boundary,
and that other wood-gathering not be prohibited,
which then became a regulation.
He was dispatched as Prefect of Hénán.
He relieved the famine of several years,
and promulgated ten measures for famine relief.
He successively served as Left and Right Administration Commissioner of Sìchuān.
In the sixth year of Hóngzhì (1493), he was appointed Right Vice Censor-in-Chief and Grand Coordinator of Jiāngnán,
also overseeing the tax grain of the three prefectures of Hángzhōu, Jiāxīng, and Húzhōu.
When Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng suffered from floods,
he expediently issued one hundred and fifty thousand *shí* of transported grain for relief.
Together with Vice Minister Xú Guàn, he dredged the Wúsōng, Báimáo, and other canals,
draining water into the sea,
thereby eliminating the flood menace.
He then served as Grand Coordinator of Shāndōng again,
and was promoted to Vice Minister of Justice.
He left office due to mourning for his mother.
In the eighteenth year, he returned to court.
At that time, there had been a long period of peace,
and the population was growing daily.
Xiàozōng reviewed the national household registration numbers and found they had decreased compared to the early Ming dynasty,
blaming the responsible officials for negligence,
and wishing to rectify it.
He ordered Jiàn, in his former capacity and concurrently as Assistant Left Censor-in-Chief, to go to Hénán, Húguǎng, and Shǎnxī to verify the actual households and population.
He found two hundred thirty-five thousand odd households,
and seven hundred thirty-nine thousand odd people,
and then submitted ten proposals for post-disaster relief and the advantages and disadvantages for the military and civilians.
At that time, Xiàozōng had already died,
but Wǔzōng adopted all of his proposals.
In the second year of Zhengdé [正德], he was appointed Minister of War [Bīngbù Shàngshū 兵部尚shū] of Nánjīng [南京] and participated in state affairs [cānzàn jīwù 參贊機務].
Previously, when he served as the Grand Coordinator [fǔ 撫] of Jiāngnán [江南],
he once investigated the crime of the chiliarch Zhāng Wénmiǎn [張文冕].
Zhāng Wénmiǎn [張文冕] fled.
By this time, Zhāng Wénmiǎn [張文冕] conspired with Liú Jǐn [劉瑾] to frame Jìan [鑑],
and Liú Jǐn [劉瑾] was also displeased with Jìan [鑑] for not being in communication with him.
Consequently, Jìan [鑑] was implicated in the matter and fined rice.
Being poor, he could not pay.
He submitted a memorial to appeal and was pardoned.
In the sixth year, in the first month, he was summoned to serve as Minister of Justice [Xíngbù Shàngshū 刑部尚書].
At that time, major bandits rose in rebellion.
Liú Chǒng [劉寵], Liú Chén [劉宸], Yáng Hǔ [楊虎], Liú Huì [劉惠], Qí Yànmíng [齊彥名], Zhū Liàng [朱諒] and others caused unrest in Jīfǔ [畿輔].
Fāng Sì [方四], Cáo Fǔ [曹甫], Lán Tíngruì [藍廷瑞], Yān Běnshù [鄢本恕] and others rampaged through Sìchuān [四川].
Wāng Chéng Èr [汪澄二], Luó Guāngquán [羅光權], Wáng Hào Bā [王浩八], Wáng Yù Wǔ [王鈺五] and others disturbed Jiāngxī [江西].
All of them proclaimed themselves kings,
and there was not a single day without urgent reports from all directions.
The Minister of War [Bīngbù Shàngshū 兵部尚書] Wáng Chǎng [王敞] was unable to deal with the bandits.
The emperor had already ordered Hóng Zhōng [洪鍾], Chén Jīn [陳金], and Mǎ Zhōngxī [馬中錫] to lead armies and suppress them separately.
In the fifth month of that year,
Wáng Chǎng [王敞] was dismissed,
and Jìan [鑑] replaced him.
Jìan [鑑] then selected generals and trained soldiers,
recruiting skilled warriors from among the common people.
He ordered all villages and settlements to erect stockades and dig deep moats,
forming groups to assist each other.
Troops from Hénán [河南] and Shānxī [山西] guarded the Yellow River [Huánghé 黃河],
blocking the Tàiháng [太行] Mountains.
Imperial garrison troops [jīngcāo bānjūn 京操班軍]
remained to guard their respective cities and towns.
Each transport boat crew member was stationed along the riverbanks,
to protect the transport routes [yùndào 運道]
and facilitate travelers.
He requested an imperial decree to severely punish civil and military high officials who failed to contain the bandits,
and
to commend county magistrates who were capable of defeating the bandits.
Considering Mǎ Zhōngxī [馬中錫] to be treating the bandits lightly,
he memorialized to dispatch Lù Wán [陸完] to replace him and return,
and transfer border generals to assist Lù Wán [陸完] in suppressing the bandits.
The bandits were repeatedly defeated by the border armies,
and scattered in all directions.
At that time, the palace eunuch Gǔ Dàyòng [谷大用] and the Earl of Fúqiáng [Fúqiáng Bó 伏羌伯] Máo Ruì [毛銳] led troops stationed in Línqīng [臨清].
The bandits then planned to ambush the emperor when he went to perform the sacrificial rites to the southern suburbs [nánjiāo 南郊] on the first day of the twelfth month.
They intended to seize the opportunity to attack the imperial carriage,
and marched towards Bàzhōu [霸州] one day in advance.
Jìan [鑑] immediately reported this in a memorial,
and preparations were made overnight.
The next morning,
the emperor summoned and questioned Jìan [鑑].
Jìan [鑑] requested an early departure to reassure the people,
and so the ceremony was completed before the emperor returned.
The bandits, knowing that preparations had been made,
plundered the various prefectures and counties of Bǎodìng [保定] to the west and then departed.
The Grand Coordinator [Xúnfǔ 巡撫] of Hénán [河南], Dèng Zhāng [鄧璋], requested reinforcements.
Jìan [鑑] said:
“The bandits in Shāndōng [山東] are fewer than ten thousand,
how could the government troops be less than ten times their number?
It is because influential individuals use their private connections to fill the positions of commanders,
disrupting regulations and seizing功 [gōng 功], thereby
losing the hearts of the officers and soldiers.
I request that all such individuals be sent back.
Any commander below the rank of Grand Coordinator [Dū Zhǐhuī 都指揮] who commits an error [shīshì 失事]
should be immediately executed at the front.
Furthermore, deploy more border troops to assist Dèng Zhāng [鄧璋].”
The emperor followed all his advice.
Soon after, with repeated reports of victories,
Jìan [鑑] was promoted to Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent [Tàizǐ Shàobǎo 太子少保].
In the first month of the following year,
the bandits suddenly attacked Bàzhōu [霸州],
and the capital was put on alert.
Jìan [鑑] ordered the border troops to quickly intercept the bandits,
who then fled.
Bandit leaders Yáng Hǔ [楊虎] and Zhū Liàng [朱諒] died,
and their followers dispersed to harass Shāndōng [山東] and Hénán [河南].
Jìan [鑑] held the border generals Xǔ Tài [許泰], Xì Yǒng [郤永], Liú Huī [劉暉], and Lǐ Hóng [李鋐] responsible for the Shāndōng [山東] bandits Liú Chǒng [劉寵], Liú Chén [劉宸], Qí Yànmíng [齊彥名] and others;
and for the Hénán [河南] bandits Liú Huì [劉惠], Zhào Suì [趙鐩], Xíng Lǎohǔ [邢老虎] and others, he held the border generals Féng Zhēn [馮禎], Shí Yuán [時源], Shén Zhōu [神周], and Jīn Fǔ [金輔] responsible.
Before long,
Máo Ruì [毛銳] suffered a defeat,
and both he and Gǔ Dàyòng [谷大用] were recalled.
Jìan [鑑] then requested the employment of Péng Zé [彭澤],
to work with Chóu Yuè [仇鉞] to deal with the Hénán [河南] bandits,
while entrusting the Shāndōng [山東] bandits entirely to Lù Wán [陸完].
In the fifth month,
the Hénán [河南] bandits were pacified.
In the seventh month,
the remaining Shāndōng [山東] bandits were also pacified.
Chén Jīn [陳金] and Hóng Zhōng [洪鍾] also successively pacified the bandits in Jiāngxī [江西] and Sìchuān [四川].
The emperor was pleased,
and promoted Jìan [鑑] to Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent [Tàizǐ Tàibǎo 太子太保],
and bestowed hereditary centurion [shì bǎihù 世百戶] rank in the Imperial Bodyguard [Jǐnyīwèi 錦衣衛] upon his son.
Jìan [鑑] then submitted a memorial, stating:
“Now that the bandits have been pacified,
the people have suffered from war for a long time.
I beg that land taxes be reduced proportionally,
and various means be employed to provide relief.
Dismiss corrupt and cruel officials,
and suspend non-urgent public works.
Return the people to their former occupations,
lend them cattle and seeds,
and exempt them from taxes for three years.
Those who expose past misdeeds or are persistent evildoers
should all be brought to justice.”
The emperor approved all of it.
Prior to this,
in mid-seventh month,
Jìan [鑑], believing that the bandits were not entirely eliminated,
requested that border general Liú Huī [劉暉] be stationed in Shāndōng [山東],
Shí Yuán [時源] in Hénán [河南],
Xì Yǒng [郤永] in Jīfǔ [畿輔],
and Lǐ Hóng [李鋐] in Huái [淮] and Yáng [揚].
Each was to be granted the acting title of Commander-in-Chief [Zǒngbīng 總兵],
and dismissed only when peace was restored.
Chóu Yuè [仇鉞] stated that
the border troops had been long-suffering,
unaccustomed to the local climate,
and both men and horses were ill.
Now that the bandits were gradually pacified,
he requested that one-third be retained to suppress the remaining bandits,
and the rest be sent back.
The court deliberated,
and considered both proposals valid.
They requested that each of the four generals be allowed to retain one thousand men to maintain order,
while other generals like Xǔ Tài [許泰], Shén Zhōu [神周], Jīn Fǔ [金輔], and Wēn Gōng [溫恭] should all lead their respective units back to the border garrisons.
The emperor agreed,
ordering the troops from Yánsuí [延綏] to return directly,
and those from Liáodōng [遼東], Xuānfǔ [宣府], and Dàtóng [大同] to pass through the capital for commendation and rewards.
The emperor at this time enjoyed military displays.
The favored cronies said
that the border troops were far more robust and capable than the capital troops,
and ought to be kept in the capital garrisons.
The emperor agreed.
By the eleventh month,
troops from all three garrisons had arrived,
and so he ordered them to stay,
with the capital troops sent to replace them at the borders.
Jìan [鑑] strongly argued against this,
and the court officials gathered to deliberate,
again emphasizing its harms,
but the emperor ultimately did not comply.
From then on,
the border troops drilled inside the Forbidden City [dà nèi 大內],
and were called
“The Outer Four Families’ Army” [Wài Sì Jiā Jūn 外四家軍],
and Jiāng Bīn [江彬] gained favor.
In the eighth year,
Xuānfǔ [宣府] sent defectors from beyond the northern frontier, Tuōtuō Tài [脫脫太] and others, to the capital.
They were ordered to serve as brave warriors in the Imperial Stables Directorate [Yùmǎ Jiān 禦馬監].
Jìan [鑑] and others memorialized, stating:
“During the Hàn [漢] and Wèi [魏] dynasties, the Dī [氐] and Qiāng [羌] were relocated to Guānzhōng [關中].
Guō Qīn [郭欽] and Jiāng Tǒng [江統] both advised Emperor Wǔ [Wǔ Dì 武帝] of Jìn [晉] to eliminate this source of future chaos early.
Fú Jiān [苻堅] settled the Xiānbēi [鮮卑] in Hánnán [漢南],
and Fú Róng [苻融] also worried that they would probe for weaknesses.
Now, if we allow these defectors to freely enter and exit the forbidden palace,
granting them excessive favor, it will only lead to arrogance and disrespect.
Should the northern invaders hear of this,
and secretly send cunning bandits to feign surrender [wěi jiàng 偽降]
to act as spies,
would this not create future trouble?”
The emperor did not listen.
The Prince of Níng [Níng Wáng 寧王], Chén Háo [宸濠], plotted to restore his guards,
but Jìan [鑑] vigorously suppressed him.
Grand Commandant [Dūdū 都督] Bái Yù [白玉] was dismissed for misconduct.
He heavily bribed the favored eunuchs of the Leopard Chamber [Bàofáng 豹房] to seek reinstatement,
but Jìan [鑑] refused to comply.
The favored eunuchs instigated informers to expose Jìan's [鑑] household servants for accepting money from generals and officers.
Consequently, censors [yánguān 言官] jointly submitted memorials impeaching Jìan [鑑],
who then retired from office.
He died nine years later,
at the age of eighty.
Mǎ Zhōngxī [馬中錫],
courtesy name Tiānlù [天祿],
was from Gùchéng [故城].
His father, Wěi [偉],
served as the Chief Clerk [Zhǎngshǐ 長史] of the Prince of Táng's [Táng Fǔ 唐府] establishment.
He displeased the prince with his straightforward advice [zhí jiàn 直諫],
and was arrested and sent to the capital,
while all his family members were also imprisoned.
Mǎ Zhōngxī [馬中錫] was spared due to his young age,
and fled to appeal to the Investigating Censor [Xún'àn Yùshǐ 巡按御史].
The censor spoke to the prince,
and his family was released.
He then took his mother and went to the capital to appeal their case,
and his father was eventually exonerated,
ending his career as the Prefect [Zhīfǔ 知府] of Chǔzhōu [處州].
Mǎ Zhōngxī [馬中錫] achieved first place in the provincial examination [xiāngshì 鄉試] in the tenth year of Chénghuà [成化],
and became a successful candidate in the imperial examination [jìnshì 進士] the following year.
He was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Justice [Xíng Kē Jǐshìzhōng 刑科給事中].
Wàn Guìfēi's [萬貴妃] brother, Tōng [通], was arrogant and tyrannical.
Mǎ Zhōngxī [馬中錫] submitted two memorials condemning him,
and was flogged twice.
When a princess encroached upon farmland within the capital region [jī nèi 畿內],
he investigated and returned it to the people.
He also once impeached Wāng Zhí [汪直] for his transgressions and abuses.
He successively served as Surveillance Vice Commissioner for Education [Dūxué Fùshǐ 督學副使] in Shǎnxī [陝西].
In the fifth year of the Hóngzhì reign (1492), he was summoned to serve as Right Vice Minister of the Dá Lǐ Sì (Court of Judicial Review).
The Nánjīng Garrison Eunuch, Jiǎng Cóng, and the Minister of War's Director, Lóu Xìng, along with Commander Shí Wéntōng, mutually accused each other,
involving hundreds of people.
Officials were dispatched to investigate,
but they were not appeased.
Zhōng Xī, accompanied by Palace Eunuch Zhào Zhōng and others, went
and, with one inquiry, established the facts.
Xìng was dismissed from office,
and Cóng was imprisoned and punished.
He was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief
and made Grand Coordinator of Xuānfǔ.
He impeached and dismissed the corrupt and senile Commander-in-Chief, Mǎ Yí,
and abolished the private conscription of soldiers by garrison commanders and below,
registering them in the official records.
When invaders once breached the border,
he led the army to defeat them.
He retired due to illness,
but was widely recommended by officials both inside and outside the court.
Upon Wǔzōng's ascension to the throne,
he was recalled to be Grand Coordinator of Liáodōng.
He returned the garrison farmlands to the army
and impeached the Garrison Eunuch Zhū Xiù for offenses such as establishing official taverns and illicit horse markets.
In the first year of the Zhèngdé reign (1506), he entered the capital to serve successively as Left and Right Vice Ministers of War.
Liú Jǐn had just gained power,
and his associate Zhū Yíng falsely claimed military merits on the frontier for hundreds of people.
Minister Yán Zhòngyǔ was inclined to permit it,
but Zhōng Xī firmly opposed it.
Jǐn was greatly enraged
and, by imperial decree, transferred him to the Ministry of Works in Nánjīng.
The following year, he was forced into retirement.
That winter,
he was arrested and imprisoned in the imperial prison,
then chained and sent to Liáodōng
to compensate for the spoiled grain he had received.
After more than a year, the matter concluded,
and he was stripped of his status as a commoner.
After Jǐn was executed,
he was reinstated as Grand Coordinator of Dàtóng.
Zhōng Xī was an incorruptible official;
wherever he served, he abolished malpractices and incurred resentment,
which is why he was famous.
In the third month of the sixth year (1511),
bandits Liú Liù and others rose up.
Minister of Personnel Yáng Yīqīng suggested sending a high official to command the various provincial forces.
Zhōng Xī was then recommended as Right Censor-in-Chief to supervise military affairs,
and he, along with the Earl of Huì'ān, Zhāng Wěi, commanded the imperial army in the southern campaign.
Liú Liù's given name was Chǒng,
and his younger brother's given name was Chén.
They were from Wén'ān,
both fierce and skilled in archery and horsemanship.
Previously,
the authorities, troubled by bandits, had summoned Chǒng, Chén, and their associates Yáng Hǔ, Qí Yánmíng, and others to assist in their capture,
and they frequently achieved success.
It happened that Liú Jǐn's servant Liáng Hóng attempted to extort bribes from Chǒng and others but failed,
so he falsely accused them of being bandits.
Níng Gǎo and Liǔ Shàngyì were dispatched to draw their likenesses and capture them,
destroying their homes.
Chǒng and others then joined the great bandit Zhāng Mào.
Mào's house had high towers and multiple stories,
hidden walls and deep cellars,
and he traditionally harbored fugitives as a refuge leader.
Eunuch Zhāng Zhōng was his neighbor,
and Mào became his sworn brother.
Through Yǒngchéng Mǎ, Dàyòng Gǔ, and Jīng Yú and others, he gained access to the Bàofáng (Leopard Chamber)
and attended the emperor in playing cùjú (a ball game),
while continuing his banditry in between times.
Later, he was repeatedly defeated by Hékàn Brigadier Yuán Biāo.
Mào, in a desperate situation,
sought help from Zhōng.
Zhōng hosted a banquet at his private residence,
inviting Mào and Biāo to sit on the east and west sides.
As the wine flowed,
he raised his cup and enjoined Biāo, referring to Mào, saying:
"Yànshí is my brother.
From now on, do not make trouble for each other."
He then raised his cup again and enjoined Mào, saying:
"Master Yuán treats you well;
you must be careful not to offend Hékàn."
Biāo feared Zhōng and merely assented repeatedly.
Soon after,
Mào was captured by Níng Gǎo.
Chǒng and others then went to the capital to consider surrendering.
Zhōng and Yǒngchéng pleaded for them with the emperor,
and said:
"They must offer ten thousand taels of gold to be pardoned."
Chǒng and Chén could not manage it
and fled.
After Jǐn was executed,
an imperial decree permitted surrender.
Chǒng and others then emerged and went to the officials.
The Ministry of War memorialized for their pardon
and ordered them to capture other bandits to prove their loyalty.
Chǒng and others, wary of constraints,
rebelled again not long after.
Their followers grew daily,
and wherever they went, they captured cities and killed generals and officials.
Zhōng Xī and others received their orders and set out with the army,
defeating the bandits at Zhāngdé,
and then again at Hékàn,
whereupon he was promoted to Left Censor-in-Chief.
However, the bandits were then rampant,
and the generals were mostly cowardly, daring not to face their vanguard,
or even colluded with them.
Brigadier Sāng Yù once encountered the bandits in Wén'ān village.
Chǒng and Chén were in dire straits,
leaping onto the upper floor of a civilian house,
intending to commit suicide.
However, Yù had long received bribes from the bandits,
so he delayed.
After a moment,
Yánmíng arrived with a large saber,
killing and wounding dozens of people,
and shouted loudly from below the building.
Chǒng and Chén, knowing help had arrived,
came out
and shot several people dead.
Yù was utterly defeated.
Brigadier Sòng Zhèn defended against the bandits at Zǎojiàng,
but did not fire a single arrow.
The city was subsequently captured,
and seven thousand people died.
At this time,
Chǒng, Chén, and others advanced from the capital region to Shāndōng and Hénán,
then south to Húguǎng,
reaching Jiāngxī.
They then turned from south to north,
directly threatening Bàzhōu.
Yáng Hǔ and others entered Shānxī from Hébĕi,
then turned east to Wén'ān,
joining Chǒng and others,
capturing over a hundred towns,
ranging thousands of *lǐ* (li) without hindrance,
as if passing through an unpopulated land.
Although Zhōng Xī had some reputation at the time,
he was not skilled in military matters.
Wěi was also a pampered young man.
Seeing the bandits' strength
and the generals' timidity,
he estimated that the bandits could not be defeated,
and thus proposed pacification.
He argued that the bandits were originally good people,
provoked by cruel officials like Níng Gǎo and corrupt eunuchs.
If they were treated with sincerity,
they could surrender without battle.
So he issued an order: do not pursue bandits wherever they are,
do not intercept them when they pass,
feed and drink them when they are hungry and thirsty,
and grant life to those who surrender.
When the bandits heard this,
they wished to accept pacification,
admonishing each other not to burn and plunder,
but they remained hesitant.
Meanwhile, the court, considering the weakness of the capital army,
discussed deploying frontier troops.
If Zhōng Xī wished to fight,
the troops were not yet assembled;
if he wished to pacify,
the bandits' allegiance was wavering,
so he could not grasp the essential point.
Having initially proposed pacification,
he could not change course.
It happened that Chǒng and others heard that frontier troops were approaching
and retreated to encamp at Sāngyuán in Dézhōu.
Zhōng Xī entered their camp in a sedan chair,
offering them wine and food,
and sincerely comforting and persuading them.
The multitude bowed and wept,
offering a horse as a gift for his longevity.
Chǒng nobly offered to surrender.
Chén then sighed to the heavens, saying:
"One cannot dismount after riding a tiger.
Now, the eunuchs hold state power,
as everyone knows.
Can Grand Censor Mǎ decide this on his own?"
Thereupon, the meeting concluded.
At this time, an imperial edict was being issued offering a reward for the capture of the bandits.
Chǒng and others, upon detecting this,
became even more suspicious and fearful,
and left directly,
burning and plundering as before.
Only when they reached their hometown did they warn each other not to harm Grand Censor Mǎ's family.
As a result,
strong criticism of Zhōng Xī arose,
accusing him of intentionally letting the bandits go because of his family.
Censors jointly impeached him,
and an imperial edict severely reprimanded him.
Zhōng Xī still stubbornly insisted on his argument and petitioned.
Minister of War Hé Jiàn said that if the bandits truly laid down their arms, they would be pardoned,
but if not,
they should not be deceived by them.
Eventually, Chǒng and others still did not surrender,
so Vice Minister Lù Wán was sent to supervise the army,
and Zhōng Xī and Wěi were recalled.
Initially,
Mǎ Zhōngxī received orders to suppress the rebels.
Grand Secretary Yáng Tínghé said to Yáng Yīqīng:
“He is but a literatus,
unfit for such a task.”
Ultimately, he achieved no success,
and along with Zhāng Wěi, was imprisoned and sentenced to death.
Mǎ Zhōngxī died in prison;
Zhāng Wěi was stripped of his title.
In the eleventh year,
Censor Lú Yǒng appealed the injustice suffered by Mǎ Zhōngxī,
stating:
“The rebels were actually amenable to surrender.
Assistant Surveillance Commissioner Xǔ Chéngfāng, out of jealousy,
secretly requested additional troops,
creating suspicion in the rebels’ minds.
When the rebels accepted the agreement a second time,
just as they arrived at the army gate,
the prisoner carts had already set out.”
The imperial court then reinstated Mǎ Zhōngxī's office,
granted a sacrificial ceremony,
and conferred hereditary privilege.
Lù Wán,
courtesy name Quánqīng,
was a native of Chángzhōu.
He was a scholar.
When the eunuch Wáng Jìng arrived in Sūzhōu,
he dragged the scholars into court over some matter.
The scholars rose up to attack him,
but Lù Wán did not participate.
Those who disliked Lù Wán implicated him,
and Wáng Jìng promptly listed Lù Wán's name first in his report to the throne.
Governor Wáng Shù severely criticized Wáng Jìng's transgression,
and Lù Wán was thus spared.
He passed the imperial examination in the twenty-third year of Chénghuà.
When he went for official selection,
Wáng Shù was serving as Minister of Personnel
and said:
“This is the one who once attacked the eunuch;
he should be a Censor.”
Upon entering the Censorate,
he indeed gained a reputation.
In the early years of Zhèngdé,
he successively served as Jiangxi Surveillance Commissioner.
Prince Níng Chén Háo held him in high regard,
often inviting him to private banquets
and gifting him a golden wine vessel.
In the winter of the third year,
he was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief
and appointed Governor of Xuānfǔ.
Liú Jǐn disliked Lù Wán for being late in reporting to the capital,
and ordered him to assume his duties as an acting official.
The following summer,
he was reassigned to the Southern Censorate
to oversee the river defense forces.
Lù Wán, fearing that serving as an acting Censor-in-Chief was unprecedented,
was very apprehensive,
and bribed Liú Jǐn,
who then summoned him to serve as Left Vice Censor-in-Chief.
In the spring of the fifth year,
he was appointed Vice Minister of War.
When Liú Jǐn was defeated,
officials impeached Lù Wán for being a partisan,
but the emperor did not pursue the matter.
The following year,
rebels Liú Liù and Liú Qī from Bàzhōu rose up,
proclaiming Yáng Hǔ as their leader.
Earl Huì'ān Zhāng Wěi and Right Censor-in-Chief Mǎ Zhōngxī campaigned without success,
and were arrested, imprisoned, and sentenced to death.
In the eighth month,
an imperial edict appointed Lù Wán concurrently as Right Vice Censor-in-Chief and Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs,
to lead the Capital Garrisons, Xuānfǔ, and Yánsuí armies to suppress them.
When he reached Zhuōzhōu,
a report suddenly came that the rebels were approaching the capital,
and he was ordered to return with his army to defend it.
It so happened that Vice General Xǔ Tài and Guerrilla Commander Xì Yǒng and others defeated Yáng Hǔ and his forces at Bàzhōu,
and the rebels fled south,
whereupon the capital was relieved of its emergency status.
Commander Hè Yǒng and others again defeated the rebels at Xìn'ān,
and Vice General Féng Zhēn utterly routed them at Fùchéng,
then divided his troops to pursue them.
The rebels turned east and besieged Cāngzhōu.
As Liú Liù and Liú Qī were hit by stray arrows,
they lifted the siege and headed south,
capturing twenty counties in Shāndōng.
Yáng Hǔ's forces also ravaged Wēixiàn and Xīnhé to the north.
Thereupon, Lù Wán repeatedly requested reinforcements.
Additional troops from Liaodong and various garrisons in Shānxī were dispatched to pursue the rebels.
The rebels continued south,
besieging Jìníng,
burning transport boats,
and then attacking Cáozhōu.
Féng Zhēn, Xǔ Tài, and Xì Yǒng engaged them, slaying over two thousand men
and capturing their leader, Zhū Liàng.
In recognition of their merits,
Lù Wán was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief,
and all generals received increased ranks.
Eunuchs Gǔ Dàyòng and Zhāng Zhōng, believing the rebels would soon be pacified,
requested to personally oversee the army.
An imperial edict appointed Gǔ Dàyòng as Supreme Commander of Military Affairs,
Earl Fúqiáng Máo Ruì as Commander-in-Chief,
and Zhāng Zhōng as supervisor of firearms,
leading five thousand imperial troops
to join Lù Wán in suppressing the rebels.
At this time, Liú Liù and others roamed freely between Yí and Jǔ,
while Yáng Hǔ captured Sùqiān,
seizing Liú Xiáng, Prefect of Huái'ān, and Chén Bó'ān, Magistrate of Língbì,
and successively capturing Hóngxiàn, Yǒngchéng, Yúchéng, Xiàyì, and Guīdé Prefecture.
Border troops pursued and caught up,
and the rebels retreated to the ford of the Xiǎohuánghé River.
Centurion Xià Shí set an ambush and pressed them,
and Yáng Hǔ drowned.
The remaining rebels fled to Hénán,
electing Liú Huì as their leader,
and utterly defeated Vice General Bái Yù's army,
capturing Shěnqiū,
killing Commander Wáng Bǎo,
seizing Commander Pān Chōng,
and then capturing Lùyì to the north.
There was a man named Chén Hàn,
who conspired with Níng Lóng to proclaim Liú Huì as the Grand Marshal of the Punitive Expedition by Imperial Decree,
with Zhào Suì as his deputy.
Qū Zì was made Chief Scribe of the Marshal's Residence, responsible for military and state affairs,
and together with Níng Lóng, established eastern and western offices to manage affairs.
They divided their army into twenty-eight camps,
corresponding to the constellations,
each camp having a governor-general,
and gathered a multitude of up to one hundred and thirty thousand.
Wishing to tie down the government forces,
Liú Huì and Zhào Suì harassed Hénán,
while Liú Liù and Qí Yànmíng and others harassed Shāndōng,
thus their forces were divided into two.
Soon after, Liú Liù again turned north,
and Xì Yǒng defeated him at Wéixiàn.
Returning to Bàzhōu,
the emperor was about to go to the suburbs to offer sacrifices,
but upon hearing this, was frightened,
and urgently summoned Lù Wán for reinforcement.
Lù Wán attacked and routed them at Wén'ān.
The rebels headed south to Tāngyīn,
and Lù Wán again supervised his generals in pursuing and defeating them,
capturing and beheading a thousand men in total.
At this time,
Liú Liù's forces numbered tens of thousands,
but many were coerced,
and the elite troops did not exceed a thousand men.
Since the Ministry of War issued the order for rewards for heads,
when government troops pursued the rebels,
the rebels would drive innocent civilians forward,
and in an emergency, would abandon their plunder and escape.
All those killed by the government troops were innocent civilians,
which is why victory reports were frequently submitted,
yet the rebel strength did not wane.
In the first month of the following year,
Liú Liù and others again raided Bàzhōu,
and the capital was put on alert.
An edict ordered Lù Wán, Gǔ Dàyòng, and Máo Ruì to return and defend the vicinity of the capital.
The rebels then plundered Bóyě to the west,
and attacked Líxiàn and Línchéng.
Gǔ Dàyòng and Máo Ruì encountered them at Chángyuán
and suffered a great defeat.
The court deliberated and recalled the two,
separately ordering Censor-in-Chief Péng Zé, along with Earl Xiánníng Qiú Yuè, to deal with the Hénán rebels,
and entrusting Lù Wán with the rebels in the capital region and Shāndōng.
Lù Wán sent Xì Yǒng to pursue and defeat Liú Liù at Sòngjiāzhuāng.
The rebels attacked Téngxiàn to the south,
and Vice General Liú Huī utterly defeated them,
whereupon the rebels fled to the coastal area of Dēngzhōu and Láizhōu.
Lù Wán's army halted at Píngdù,
and he issued a dispatch ordering Xì Yǒng, Bái Yù, and Guerrilla Commander Wēn Gōng to advance in three columns,
and commanded Vice Generals Zhāng Jùn, Lǐ Hóng, Xǔ Tài, and Liú Huī to divide their forces to intercept their escape.
The rebels fled,
and were greatly defeated in successive battles.
The rebels then changed their clothes and horses and fled,
with a total of two thousand six hundred people captured and killed.
Only three hundred rebels fled north,
gathering recruits along the way,
and their power surged again.
They plundered Xiānghé, Bǎodí, and Yùtián,
then attacked Wǔqīng.
Guerrilla Commander Wáng Gǎo was defeated and killed,
and Governor Níng Gǎo's army was also defeated,
causing the capital region to be shaken again.
The rebels then turned south to Guānxiàn,
where Liú Huī launched a surprise attack and defeated them,
and Commander Zhāng Xūn again defeated them at Píngyuán.
The rebels fled south to Pīzhōu,
crossed the river, and reached Gùshǐ.
At this point, the Hénán rebels had already been pacified,
and the strength of Liú Liù and others further waned,
so they fled to Húguǎng.
They seized boats and reached Xiàkǒu,
where they encountered Censor-in-Chief Mǎ Bǐngrán
and killed him.
They then landed again,
burned Hànkǒu,
and were pursued by Commander Mǎn Bì and others.
Liú Liù was hit by a stray arrow,
and along with his son Zhònghuái, threw himself into the water and drowned.
Liú Qī and Qí Yànmíng led five hundred men by boat,
sailing downstream from Huángzhōu to Zhènjiāng.
Nánjīng sent an urgent report,
so Wán swiftly hastened south.
The Emperor ordered Péng Zé and Chóu Yuè to join Wán's army for a joint suppression campaign.
When the grand army had fully assembled south and north of the Jiāngnán,
the bandits still took advantage of the tides to plunder up and down.
Zhào Hóngzé, the Earl Wǔjìng who oversaw the Jiāng, and Chén Shìliáng, the Grand Censor, encountered them,
suffered a defeat,
and countless people died.
In the seventh month,
the bandits prepared their boats in Mèngdú.
Wán and others arrived at Zhènjiāng,
leaving Yuè to guard it,
ordering Gōng to station his cavalry north of the river,
Huī and Yǒng to go by boat to Jiāngyīn,
and Wán himself to lead the Grand Commanders Sūn Wén and Fù Kǎi to Fúshāngǎng.
The bandits, in fear,
fled to Tōngzhōu.
A hurricane arose,
and they abandoned their boats and fled to secure Lángshān.
Wán ordered the Assistant Prefect Luó Wěi to guide the army up the mountain at night to press them from the south.
Yànmíng died from a spear wound,
and Qī, hit by an arrow, also plunged into the water and died.
The remaining bandits were all pacified.
Upon returning to court,
Wán was promoted to Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent and Left Grand Censor,
and his son was enfeoffed as a hereditary centurion of the Jǐnyī Wèi.
In the following year, he replaced Hé Jiàn as Minister of War.
Wán was talented and intelligent,
eager for fame and fortune,
and skilled at cultivating powerful connections.
Liú Huī, Xǔ Tài, and Jiāng Bīn were all his subordinates,
and later all enjoyed favor and wielded power,
whereupon Wán benefited from their influence.
At that time, Chén Háo had already begun to harbor rebellious intentions.
Hearing that Wán was the Minister of War,
he sent a letter extensively detailing their old friendship,
wishing to restore the guard units and military colonies.
Wán replied,
telling him to use the ancestral system as an excuse.
Chén Háo then sent people to transport millions in gold and silk,
storing them at the home of Zāng Xián, a director of the imperial music bureau whom he knew well,
and distributing them widely to influential dignitaries,
entrusting Qián Níng to manage affairs internally.
When the memorial was submitted,
Wán then made a counter-request,
assigning the military colonies to the Ministry of Revenue,
and asking for it to be deliberated by the court.
The Grand Secretariat drafted the imperial edict and presented it,
and both requests were granted.
The entire court was in an uproar.
Gāo Fāng, a supervising secretary of the Six Bureaus, and Wāng Cì and other censors of the Thirteen Circuits, strenuously argued against it.
Their memorials were all sent to the ministry,
but were not answered for a long time.
Xú Wénpǔ, a supervising secretary in Nánjīng, then spoke up,
whereupon Wán requested to accept the censors' advice,
but the Emperor ultimately did not permit it.
In the tenth year, he was transferred to Minister of Personnel.
When Chén Háo rebelled,
Wán was apprehended.
The palace eunuch Zhāng Yǒng arrived in Nánchāng,
searched Chén Háo's records,
and found Wán's communications with him from ordinary days,
which he reported to the Emperor.
The Emperor was furious.
Upon returning to Tōngzhōu,
he had Wán arrested,
and seized his mother, wife, and children,
sealing and marking his house.
When they returned to the capital,
Wán was bound backwards to a pole,
his name displayed above his head,
mixed among the captured prisoners,
and paraded at the front of the triumphal procession as they entered,
intending to execute him.
It happened that Wǔzōng died,
and Shìzōng ascended the throne.
The judicial authorities reported that Wán had communicated with an outer vassal and did not reject the gold offered,
and that while stationed in the guard units, his memorials were not firm,
and thus he deserved to be beheaded.
Wán again pleaded for mercy,
and the matter was sent down for re-deliberation by court officials.
Because of his meritorious service in pacifying the bandits,
he was included in the Eight Deliberations (exemptions from punishment),
and thus was spared death,
being exiled to the Jìnghǎiwèi in Fújiàn.
His mother, over ninety years old,
eventually died in prison.
Initially,
Wán once dreamed of going to a mountain called
"Dàwǔ."
When he reached his place of exile,
there was a mountain with that very name,
and he sighed,
"My exile was long ago determined;
where can I escape?"
He eventually died in exile.
Hóng Zhōng,
courtesy name Xuānzhī,
was from Qiántáng.
He passed the imperial examination in the eleventh year of Chénghuà.
He served as a Principal of the Ministry of Justice,
then was promoted to Bureau Director,
and was ordered to pacify and settle the displaced people of Jiāngxī and Fújiàn.
Upon returning, he reported that Wǔpíng, Shàngháng, Qīngliú, Yǒngdìng in Fújiàn,
Ānyuǎn, Lóngnán in Jiāngxī,
and Chéngxiāng in Guǎngdōng were all places where displaced people were mixed,
prone to fighting and disputes,
and easily rebellious.
He suggested that during peacetime, officials should establish village and community schools
to teach them poetry, classics, rites, and deference.
At the beginning of Hóngzhì's reign,
he was again promoted to Surveillance Commissioner of Sìchuān.
The native prefect Ān Áo of Mǎhú was tyrannical and lewd,
and the literati resented him to the bone,
but officials, coveting his gold, ignored the matter,
dragging it on for twenty years.
The Assistant Surveillance Commissioner Qǔ Ruì requested the Inspecting Censor Zhāng Luán to investigate,
and Zhōng supported this decision,
arresting Áo and sending him to the capital,
where he was executed.
The Ān clan had held Mǎhú since the Táng dynasty,
but at this point, it was changed to an appointed official,
and the region finally became peaceful.
He successively served as Left and Right Administration Commissioner of Jiāngxī and Fújiàn.
In the eleventh year, he was promoted to Right Vice Grand Censor,
and became Grand Coordinator of Shùntiān.
He rectified the border defenses of Jìzhōu,
and proposed reinforcing and extending the frontier wall.
From Shānhǎiguān northwest to Gǔběikǒu and Huánghuāzhèn in Mìyún, straight to Jūyōng,
stretching over a thousand li,
he repaired and restored two hundred seventy castles,
and walled all the border counties.
Consequently, he memorialized to reduce the autumn defense troops by six thousand men,
saving tens of thousands in transport and reward expenses annually.
The Cháohé Chuān in his jurisdiction, two hundred li from the capital,
located between two mountains,
over a hundred zhàng wide,
would become a vast flood when the water rose,
but a flat plain when the water receded,
allowing invaders to drive straight in.
Zhōng said:
"About three li east of the pass,
the mountain is high on the outside and low on the inside,
about two zhàng remaining.
Two channels can be dug to
divert and diminish the water's force,
and a stone dam can be built diagonally outside the opening to constrict the water.
A pass can be placed inside the dam,
guarded by a hundred men,
preventing invaders from rushing through,
thus eliminating the capital's concern about the north,
and also allowing cultivation of the riverside land."
Mǎ Wénshēng, the Minister of War, and others requested to follow his advice.
When construction began,
the mountain rock collapsed during excavation,
crushing several hundred people to death.
The Censor Yì Fú, Supervising Secretary Mǎ Yǔcōng, and others impeached Zhōng.
Grand Coordinator Zhāng Xuān and others requested to stop the project,
but it was not heeded.
Soon after,
the project was completed.
Secretary Zhāng Dá, accompanied by a eunuch from the Directorate of Ceremonial, went to inspect it.
Upon returning, they reported that the rock tunnel only discharged a small amount of water,
and the land near the border wall was mostly sandy and rocky,
unfavorable for cultivation.
Supervising Secretary Qū Shēn and others impeached Zhōng for three counts of deception and falsehood.
All the censors and the Ministry of War all requested Zhōng's arrest.
The Emperor deemed that Zhōng was fortifying the border for the nation
and should not be punished,
suspending his salary for three months.
In the first year of Zhèngdé, he was recalled from Grand Coordinator of Guìzhōu to oversee grain transport and concurrently Grand Coordinator of the area north of the river.
The next year, he was promoted to Right Grand Censor.
Grain transport boats from Sūzhōu, Sōngjiāng, and Zhèjiāng would travel via Xiàgǎngkǒu and the Mèngdú River, ascending the great river to reach Guāzhōu,
a journey of over two hundred eighty li,
often encountering storms.
Zhōng said:
"Opposite Mèngdú on the river is a channel,
which can reach the mouth of the Báitǎ River.
It previously had four sluices,
a direct route of forty li.
Proceeding to Yílíngzhèn, then turning north again,
it directly reaches the Yángzhōu Grand Canal.
Opening and dredging it would be convenient."
This was adopted.
He was then transferred to administer the Nánjīng Censorate,
and then promoted to Minister of Justice.
In the winter of the fourth year,
he was given the additional title of Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent and concurrently Left Grand Censor,
administering the Censorate's affairs.
In the fifth year, spring,
Húguǎng suffered famine and banditry erupted.
Zhōng was ordered to take charge of military affairs as Grand Coordinator (zǒngzhì) with his existing official post.
Shǎnxī, Hénán, and Sìchuān were also under his command.
Bandits Yáng Qīng and Qiū Rén from Miǎnyáng presumptuously styled themselves Heavenly King (tiānwáng) and General (jiāngjūn),
appearing and disappearing around Dòngtíng.
They besieged Yuèzhōu,
and captured Línxiāng.
The government troops repeatedly suffered defeats.
Zhōng, along with Commander-in-chief (zǒngbīngguān) Máo Lún, dispatched orders to Regional Commanders (dūzhīhuī) Pān Xūn and Chái Kuí,
and Administration Commissioner (bùzhèngshǐ) Chén Hào,
and Surveillance Vice Commissioner (fùshǐ) Jiǎng Shēng, to attack and defeat them at Máhún Tān.
Over 740 people were captured and executed,
and the bandits were then pacified.
Initially,
Zhōng was in charge of the Grand Court of Revision (yuànshì).
Liú Jǐn was then at the height of his power.
When Jǐn was executed,
censor-officials impeached Zhōng for colluding with Jǐn and flogging censors.
The court deliberated, and considering Zhōng's efforts in suppressing the bandits,
decided not to prosecute him.
At that time, Lán Tíngruì, a bandit from Bǎoníng, styled himself King Shùntiān (shùntiānwáng);
Yān Běnshù styled himself King Guādì (guādìwáng);
and their accomplice Liáo Huì styled himself King Sǎodì (sǎodìwáng).
Their force numbered over 100,000,
with forty-eight Grand Controllers (zǒngguǎn) appointed,
spreading across the borders of Shǎnxī and Húguǎng.
Tíngruì and Huì plotted to seize Bǎoníng,
while Běnshù planned to take Hànzhōng,
and then capture Yúnyáng,
thence moving eastward down through Jīng and Xiāng.
Patrolling Censor (xúnfǔ) Lín Jùn was still discussing how to block the Tōngjiāng,
when Huì arrived
and attacked and captured the city,
killing Senior Secretary (cānyì) Huáng Zàn.
Investigating Censor (qiānshì) Qián Cháofèng and others fled.
Just then, government troops returning from another prefecture arrived,
and the bandits, suspecting reinforcements,
also fled.
Jùn further dispatched Luó, Huí, and Shízhù native troops to assist Cháofèng in launching a suppression campaign.
Senior Secretary Gōng Miǎnrén also joined.
The Lóngtán River swelled,
and when the bandits were halfway across,
the Luó and Huí troops fiercely attacked them,
capturing and executing over eight hundred people.
Many fell off cliffs and drowned.
Jùn again sent Prefects (zhīfǔ) Zhāng Mǐn and Hé Shān, among others, to pursue them,
and captured Huì.
The remaining bandits fled to Xīxiāng in Shǎnxī.
Zhōng then issued an order to offer amnesty and enlistment,
and over ten thousand people surrendered.
Soon after, the bandits gathered their scattered remnants,
captured Yíngshān,
killed Investigating Censor Wáng Yuán,
and plundered Péng and Jiàn prefectures.
Zhōng went to Sìchuān,
but his discussions with Jùn often conflicted,
which hampered military operations,
and the bandits grew stronger.
Eventually,
he issued orders for troops from Shǎnxī, Húguǎng, and Hénán to advance along separate routes.
The Húguǎng troops first caught up with them in Shíquán, Shǎnxī.
Tíngruì fled to Hànzhōng,
where Regional Commander Jīn Miǎn besieged him.
Shǎnxī Patrolling Censor Lán Zhāng was then stationed in Hànzhōng.
Tíngruì sent his accomplice Hé Hǔ to Zhāng,
requesting to return to Chuān to surrender.
Zhāng considered that Tíngruì was originally a Chuān bandit,
and feared that pressuring him too much would lead to a desperate fight,
which would also harm Shǎn.
He therefore ordered Miǎn to escort him out of the border.
Once Tíngruì entered Chuān,
he sought to surrender.
Zhōng and others ordered him to go to Dōngxiāng to await pacification.
The bandits intended to delay the army,
procrastinating for months,
establishing camps in the mountains,
and playfully demanding to settle their forces in Yíngshān County or Línjiāng City,
sending officials as hostages.
Zhōng ordered Hànzhōng Assistant Prefect (tōngpàn) Luó Xián to enter their camp.
Běnshù came to pay respects,
and an agreement was settled.
However, as it happened, government troops killed some of their woodcutters,
and the bandits became suspicious and fearful again,
so they killed Xián
and plundered as before.
The government troops built seven forts to guard them,
preventing the bandits from escaping,
and their accomplices gradually dispersed.
Tíngruì fraudulently presented a captured woman as his own daughter,
and arranged a marriage with Péng Shìlín, a native chieftain (tǔshè) from Yǒngshùn,
hoping to use this opportunity to escape.
Shìlín secretly informed Zhōng,
who provided strategies to deal with the situation.
When the appointed time came,
Tíngruì, Běnshù, and their accomplices Wáng Jīnzhū and twenty-eight others all came to the meeting.
The ambush was sprung, and they were all captured.
Only Liáo Mázi managed to escape.
When his followers heard of the change,
they scattered in panic and crossed the river.
Zhōng dispatched troops to pursue and attack them,
capturing and executing over seven hundred people.
For his merit, he was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent (tàizǐtàibǎo).
Not long after,
Liáo Mázi and his accomplice Cáo Fǔ plundered Yíngshān and Péngzhōu.
In the seventh year,
Commander-in-chief Yáng Hóng,
along with Surveillance Vice Commissioners Zhāng Mǐn, Mǎ Hào, and Hé Shān, jointly attacked them.
The bandits' situation became dire,
so Zhōng then proposed an amnesty and enlistment.
Mǐn went alone on horseback to Fǔ's camp.
Fǔ obeyed the order
and went to the army gate to submit to discipline,
then returned to disperse his followers.
However, Mázi resented Fǔ for betraying him,
so he killed him
and took over his followers,
then moved to plunder eastern Chuān.
Government troops dared not attack,
instead secretly trailing the bandits,
beheading good citizens for merit.
The native troops were particularly abusive.
At that time, there was a saying:
"Bandits are like a comb,
soldiers are like a fine-toothed comb,
and native troops are like a lice-comb."
Circuit Censor (xún'àn yùshǐ) Wáng Lún and Merit-Recording Censor (jìgōng yùshǐ) Wāng Jǐngfāng impeached Zhōng for letting his troops run wild.
Lún further reported that Zhōng indulged in drinking and pleasure trips,
leading to the bandits crossing the river from Hézhōu and capturing prefectures and counties.
An imperial edict recalled Zhōng,
and Péng Zé replaced him.
Zhōng then requested to return home.
He died in the third year of Jiājìng (1524),
and was posthumously named Xiānghuì.
Chén Hào was
a native of Kuàijī.
He passed the imperial examination in the 23rd year of Chénghuà (1487).
After pacifying the bandits,
he was promoted to Right Vice Grand Censor-in-chief (yòufù dūyùshǐ),
and Patrolling Censor of Húguǎng.
Jiǎng Shēng was
a native of Qíyáng,
and passed the imperial examination in the same year as Hào.
Chén Jīn,
courtesy name Rǔlì,
was a native of Yìngchéng,
who moved to Wǔchāng.
His grandfather Tǎn was
the Prefect of Kuízhōu.
His father Lín was
a Surveillance Investigating Censor of Guǎngxī.
Jīn passed the imperial examination in the eighth year of Chénghuà (1472),
was appointed Magistrate of Wùyuán,
and then promoted to Nanjing Censor (Nánjīng yùshǐ).
In the early years of Hóngzhì,
he was sent out to inspect Zhèjiāng.
Upon his return, due to natural disasters, he impeached nineteen high-ranking civil and military officials,
including Vice Minister (shìláng) Dīng Yǒngzhōng, Nanjing Grand Judge (Nánjīng dàlǐqīng) Wú Dàohóng, and Earl (bó) Máo Wén of Nánníng, many of whom were dismissed.
Soon after, he was transferred to Surveillance Vice Commissioner of Shānxī,
then served as Left Administration Commissioner of Yúnnán,
where he suppressed the rebellious Miáo of Zhúzǐ Qìng.
In the 13th year, he was appointed Right Vice Grand Censor-in-chief,
and Patrolling Censor of that region.
The chieftain Sī Lù of Mèngyǎng and the chieftain Sī Dié of Mèngmì had been at war for many years.
Jīn, by imperial edict, mobilized troops from Miàndiàn, Gānyá, Lǒngchuān, Nándiàn and other tribes,
amassing 120,000 units of grain
for a punitive expedition,
and sent Senior Secretary Guō Xù to pacify them.
Sī Lù was frightened,
and consequently ceased hostilities and offered tribute.
Jīn was rewarded with silver and silk for his achievements.
The Guìzhōu army defeated the female bandit Mǐ Lù.
Mǐ Lù retreated to attack Píngyí Guard and the forts of Dàhé and Èlè.
Jīn dispatched troops and repeatedly defeated her,
receiving a promotion in salary of one grade,
and was recalled to serve as Right Vice Minister of the Ministry of Revenue (hùbù yòushìláng) in Nanjing.
In the sixth year of Zhèngdé, [Jìan] was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief.
He managed water control in Sūzhōu, Hángzhōu, and other prefectures,
repairing and constructing dikes and ponds.
The people benefited from his work.
Soon after, he was promoted to Right Assistant Censor-in-Chief [sic, should be Right Vice Censor-in-Chief]
and appointed Grand Coordinator of River Operations (Tídū Cāojiāng).
In the spring of the eighth year,
the bandit Wáng Hàobā rebelled in Yáoyuán.
An imperial edict ordered Jiàn to replace Chén Jīn to supervise the armies of Jiāngxī, Zhèjiāng, and Fújiàn to suppress them.
At that time, Hàobā had over ten thousand followers,
encamped in Kāihuà, Zhèjiāng.
They were defeated by Assistant Prefect Wǔ Wéndìng and others,
and fled back to Déxīng, Jiāngxī.
Using the captured Regional Commanders Bái Hóng and Jiāng Hóng as hostages,
they sought surrender from Surveillance Commissioner Wáng Zhì.
Zhì accepted their surrender
and relayed it to Yáoyuán.
Hàobā then fled to and occupied Pèiyuánshān in Guìxī.
His remaining followers reassembled,
forming camps ten *lǐ* long.
Jiàn ordered Zhì, along with Surveillance Vice Commissioner Hú Shìníng and Administration Vice Commissioner Wú Tíngjǔ, to station troops at strategic points
to block their retreat.
He himself, along with Regional Commander Lǐ Hóng, advanced secretly overnight in the rain,
achieving a great victory.
Several thousand people were captured or beheaded,
and Hàobā was finally captured.
His followers scattered and fled to Yùshān.
Jiàn, along with Grand Coordinator of Nángàn Zhōu Nán and Grand Coordinator of Jiāngxī Rèn Hàn, attacked again, beheading over seven hundred people.
The remaining bandits fled to Yáoyuán.
Jiàn commanded Tíngjǔ and others to advance and suppress them,
forcing their capture.
Jiàn, learning from Chén Jīn’s failure,
was resolute in using military force.
Rèn Hàn, however, was timid.
Having previously served as Administration Commissioner,
he had advocated for Chén Jīn to accept surrender.
Although he reported initial victories promptly,
his pursuit of the bandits was slow,
and the remaining factions resurfaced.
Previously,
the Dōngxiāng bandits, defeated by Chén Jīn, had begged for surrender
and were assigned to Shìníng,
dubbed "new troops."
But they plundered as before.
Fearing punishment, they rebelled again.
Brigade General Guì Yǒng and others were dispatched to suppress and capture them.
Although Wànnián county was established,
bandits were still numerous.
Many yamen runners and clerks were bandit sympathizers,
and knew of every movement of the government.
Surveillance Vice Commissioner Lǐ Qíng governed with severity and urgency.
The populace wanted to rebel,
but feared Lǐ Hóng, who was in Yúgān, and dared not act.
When Lǐ Hóng died,
Wáng Chuíqī, Hú Niàn’èr, and others then revolted.
They killed Lǐ Qíng, along with Ráozhōu Assistant Prefect Chén Dá and Qín Bì,
Regional Commander Xíng Shìchén, and others,
and burned the public buildings.
Jiàn dispatched troops to capture them,
and the rebellion was quelled.
Censors impeached Jiàn, along with Rèn Hàn and Zhōu Nán.
The Ministry of War requested that Rèn Hàn be recalled,
and Jiàn was ordered to concurrently hold the post of Grand Coordinator.
The following year, he attacked the Línchuān bandits,
beheading their leader.
He dispatched Brigade General Lǐ Lóng to attack the Xīngàn bandits.
The bandits occupied the mountains,
usurping the title of "king" for eight years.
Lǐ Lóng and others advanced deep into their territory,
capturing them all.
Over seventeen hundred people were captured or beheaded.
In recognition of his achievements,
Jiàn was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief,
retaining his post as Grand Coordinator.
The notorious bandit Xú Jiǔlíng,
who initially gathered followers in Jiànchāng and Lǐyuán,
later
appeared and disappeared between Jiāng and Hú,
for thirty years.
Huángzhōu, Dé'ān, Jiǔjiāng, Ānqìng, Chízhōu, and Tàipíng were all afflicted by his depredations.
Jiàn suppressed and beheaded him,
and all the bandits were pacified.
Prince Níng, Chén Háo, instigated Censor Zhāng Áoshan to impeach Jiàn.
In the eleventh year, he was recalled,
and subsequently requested retirement.
In the first year of Jiājìng,
he was reinstated to his former official position based on recommendations,
and appointed Grand Coordinator of Grain Transport (Zǒngdū Cáoyùn).
The Qīngzhōu mine bandits, led by Wáng Táng and others, arose in Yánshénzhèn,
and plundered Dōngchāng, Yǎnzhōu, and Jǐnán.
Regional Commander Yáng Jì and Commander Yáng Hào and others attacked them.
Yáng Hào died,
and Yáng Jì barely escaped.
An imperial edict held the generals and officials of Shāndōng responsible.
Thereupon, various officials divided their forces to pursue the bandits.
The bandits no longer
concentrated their forces, but plundered between Jīnxiāng and Yútái.
They attacked Cáozhōu,
attempted to cross the river but failed,
then plundered Kǎochéng and the western bank of the river,
reaching Dōngmíng and Chángyuán.
The defending officials of Hénán and Bǎodìng all reported emergencies.
Bandit leaders Wáng Yǒuxián and others plundered Xiángfú and Fēngqiū,
reaching Xúzhōu in the south.
The court discussed that the authority of the various Grand Coordinators was equal,
so Jiàn and Regional Commander Lǔ Gāng were jointly appointed Grand Coordinator of Military Affairs for the Two Capitals (Liǎng Jī), Shāndōng, and Hénán,
with discretionary power to command the armies of various circuits to suppress them.
The bandits again moved to Kǎochéng.
Just as the government troops were about to attack,
Zhāng Jìn, a surrendered Hénán bandit, arrived with three hundred cavalry.
The Central Capital Garrison Commander Yán Kǎi advanced with him.
While fighting,
Zhāng Jìn suddenly waved his banner three times and retreated first.
The bandits took advantage of this,
and the government forces were routed.
Over eight hundred officers and soldiers died.
Jiàn and others advanced with continuous camps,
and the bandits were finally annihilated.
That autumn,
he was recalled to take charge of the Censorate.
He died in office the following year.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
and given the posthumous name Zhuāngxiāng.
Zhōu Nán,
courtesy name Wénhuà,
was from Jìnyún.
He obtained his *jìnshì* degree in the fourteenth year of Chénghuà.
He was appointed Magistrate of Liùhé,
then promoted to Censor,
and sent to inspect the metropolitan region (Jīfǔ).
In the early years of Hóngzhì,
he was again sent to inspect Guǎngdōng,
where he impeached General-in-Chief Liǔ Jǐng.
He successively served as Right Administration Commissioner of Jiāngxī,
and was promoted to Right Assistant Censor-in-Chief,
serving as Grand Coordinator of Dàtóng.
In the early years of Wǔzōng's reign,
invaders entered Xuānfǔ.
Brigade General Chén Xióng and others intercepted and attacked them,
defeating them.
In recognition of his merit,
Zhōu Nán's salary was increased by one rank.
He returned home for his mother's funeral.
In the third year of Zhèngdé,
Liú Jǐn monopolized power.
Because some grain in the Dàtóng granary was mildewed,
Zhōu Nán and Supervising Secretary of Grain Affairs Sūn Lù were arrested and imprisoned,
then shackled and sent to Dàtóng,
and ordered to pay double the amount.
At a general amnesty,
General-in-Chief of Dàtóng Yè Chūn and others pleaded on their behalf,
and the double payment was waived.
After payment,
they were released as commoners.
After Liú Jǐn's execution,
Zhōu Nán was reinstated to his former official post as Grand Coordinator of Xuānfǔ, but did not accept,
citing illness and returning home.
The following year, he was appointed Grand Coordinator of Military Affairs for Nán and Gàn.
The establishment of the Grand Coordinator of Nángàn
began with Zhōu Nán.
Bandits Zhāng Shíwàng, Huáng Yōng, Liú Lóng, Lǐ Sìzǎi, and others from Dàmàoshān in Tíngzhōu gathered followers and proclaimed themselves kings,
attacking and plundering cities and towns,
extending into the borders of Jiāngxī and Guǎngdōng.
For several years, there was no peace,
and government troops were repeatedly defeated when attacking them.
Investigating Censor Mò Zhòngzhāo, Magistrate Jiǎng Jī, Commander Yáng Zé, and others were captured,
and the bandit power grew even stronger.
Zhōu Nán gathered troops from various circuits and attacked them at Lóngyá,
capturing Zhāng Shíwàng.
The righteous civilian Lín Fù separately attacked and beheaded Huáng Yōng at Tiěkēng.
Other bandit strongholds were broken by Commander Sūn Táng and others.
Surveillance Vice Commissioner Yáng Zhāng and Assistant Surveillance Commissioner Líng Xiàng also attacked Liú Lóng and Lǐ Sìzǎi,
capturing them.
In total, five thousand people were captured or beheaded,
and Mò Zhòngzhāo and others escaped and returned.
When the victory was reported,
an imperial edict was issued to commend and reward them.
Zhōu Nán then moved his troops to join Grand Coordinator Chén Jīn,
and together they pacified the bandits of Yáoyuán,
bringing peace to the region.
In the spring of the ninth year, he was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief,
and appointed Grand Coordinator of Military Affairs for the Two Guǎng regions.
He requested to return home the following year,
and died.
He was posthumously granted the title of Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
Sūn Lù,
was from Qīxiá.
He obtained his *jìnshì* degree in the ninth year of Hóngzhì.
He successively served as Section Chief (Zhǔshì) and Supervising Secretary (Lángzhōng) in the Ministry of Revenue.
After Liú Jǐn's defeat,
he was reinstated to his former official post,
and successively promoted to Prefect of Yìngtiān.
Mǎ Hào,
whose original surname was Zōu,
courtesy name Zōngdà,
was a native of Níngxià.
He obtained his *jìnshì* degree in the twelfth year of Hóngzhì (1499).
He was selected from a *xíngrén* to be a Censor.
At the beginning of Zhèngdé (1506),
he was promoted to Surveillance Commissioner of Shāndōng,
but was demoted to Judicial Commissioner of Zhēndìng due to involvement in a culpability.
Bandits frequently appeared within the territory.
Mǎ Hào taught his officers and soldiers archery,
and extensively set up strategies.
When bandits appeared, they were immediately captured.
He was again implicated in a culpability,
and demoted to Magistrate of Kāizhōu.
The officials and common people of Zhēndìng prostrated at the imperial court, requesting that he be retained,
and thus he was spared the demotion.
He was then promoted to Surveillance Commissioner of Sìchuān.
Mǎ Hào was tall and agile,
skilled in horsemanship and archery,
and understood military affairs.
The great bandits Fāng Sì and Cáo Fǔ and others were rampant,
and Hóng Zhōng had been suppressing them for a long time without success.
When Mǎ Hào arrived,
he reviewed his department,
and laughed, saying:
"If a general does not understand military strategy,
how can he fight?"
Thereupon, he selected a thousand strong soldiers and divided them into several teams.
Each team appointed a leader,
and he trained them.
Coincidentally, Cáo Fǔ was about to attack Jiāngjīn.
Mǎ Hào, following the Grand Coordinator Lín Jùn, annihilated the bandits,
and severely defeated them,
capturing, beheading, and burning over two thousand people to death.
The next year,
Fāng Sì captured Jiāngjīn,
broke through Qíjiāng,
and threatened Chóngqìng.
Mǎ Hào led out a hundred cavalry at night,
lit fires and attacked the bandits.
The bandits were startled and scattered.
Taking advantage of this,
he captured and beheaded many.
Then he joined the Luó and Huí native troops to fight the bandits.
The bandits arrayed on the left and set up an ambush on the right.
Mǎ Hào faced the left with his main force,
and personally led a hundred cavalry to assault their ambush.
The ambush broke,
and fled to the left,
where the left also broke.
Fāng Sì fled to Wùchuān,
and fought with Cáo Fǔ,
and their followers then dispersed.
Fāng Sì changed his name and fled,
and was captured by another general.
Mǎ Hào was again commended,
promoted to Assistant Surveillance Commissioner,
and together with Commander-in-Chief Yáng Hóng, defeated Cáo Fǔ.
Cáo Fǔ surrendered,
but his confederate Liào Mázi gathered his followers,
and successively captured Tóngliáng and Róngchāng.
Mǎ Hào was stripped of his official cap and belt due to culpability.
At this time, Hóng Zhōng had already been recalled,
and the Grand Coordinator Gāo Chóngxī was timid and fearful,
and again advocated for pacification.
Liào Mázi and others feigned acceptance of the agreement.
Gāo Chóngxī hastily disbanded all the troops,
and ordered Assistant Surveillance Commissioner Zhāng Mǐn to relocate the citizens of Línjiāng market in Kāixiàn,
vacating the area to accommodate the bandits,
promising tax exemption for three years,
and requesting this from the court.
Mǎ Hào strenuously argued,
saying that Línjiāng market was the throat of Shǔ,
reaching up to Chóng[qìng] and [Kāixiàn],
and down to Hú[guǎng] and Xiāng[tán],
with rich and fertile land.
Why abandon it to aid the bandits,
and bring trouble upon ourselves?
Gāo Chóngxī did not heed him.
Mǎ Hào then further trained his troops and observed the changes.
The next year,
the bandits indeed seized Zhāng Mǐn and rebelled.
An imperial edict ordered the arrest of Gāo Chóngxī,
and promoted Mǎ Hào to Vice Censor-in-Chief on the Right to replace him.
The bandits besieged Zhōngjiāng,
and were about to advance on Chéngdū.
Mǎ Hào, with five thousand cavalry, and Governor-General Péng Zé, defeated them.
The mobile corps commander Yán Xūn pursued and beheaded Liào Mázi in Jiànzhōu.
The remaining followers fled,
and elected their confederate Yù Sīfèng as their leader.
Commander-in-Chief Chén Xún pursued them to Fùcūn,
where the bandits feigned surrender.
Then they crossed the river northward,
ambushed and killed Commander Yáo Zhèn,
and turned into their old lair in Bāshān.
Soon after, they came out and fled to Dà'ānzhèn,
but Chén Xún dared not advance.
And the Shǎnxī troops were defeated by the bandits,
who then crossed Níngqiāng and attacked Lüèyáng.
Chén Xún's army made a clamor with drums,
and the bandits fled during the night,
crossing Guǎngyuán.
They were intercepted by the government forces,
and returned to Tōng[jiāng] and Bā[zhōng] to gather their remaining followers.
All the generals claimed illness and did not attack the bandits.
An imperial edict ordered the arrest of Chén Xún,
and also rebuked Mǎ Hào.
Mǎ Hào then, with Péng Zé, supervised the various armies and captured Yù Sīfèng in the mountains of Xīxiāng.
Again with Péng Zé, he pacified the Nèijiāng bandit Luò Sōngxiáng,
and all the bandits were quelled.
For his merits,
he was promoted to Vice Censor-in-Chief.
In the tenth year (1515),
Yìbùlà raided Sōngpān.
The indigenous people, such as Móràng Liùshǎo, took the opportunity to rebel,
serving as guides for them,
causing great consternation in the western lands.
Mǎ Hào recruited native tribesmen as spies,
and dispatched troops to ambush them.
Commander Zhāng Lún and others led the pacified tribesmen at night to attack and defeat the bandits,
capturing Móràng Liùshǎo,
and Yìbùlà fled.
Mǎ Hào, considering the treacherous terrain of Sōngpān,
where the indigenous people often waylaid and plundered provisions,
then supervised Assistant Commander Zhāng Jié and others in building walls and palisades,
from Sānshèbǎo to Fēngdòngguān,
a total of fifty *lǐ*.
He was awarded an imperial edict of commendation.
The two prefectures of Wūméng and Mángbù adjoined Jūnlián and Gǒngxiàn,
stretching for a thousand *lǐ*,
with deep and rugged mountains and forests,
where various Mán, Bó Rénzǐ, Yìzǐ, Zhōngjiāzǐ, Miáozǐ, Luǒ, Gè, and other groups lived mixed together.
There was a Bó Rénzǐ named Pǔ Fǎ'è,
