who understood Chinese,
and was knowledgeable in talismans and incantations.
He falsely claimed that Maitreya Buddha had appeared in the world,
called himself the King of the Mán,
and incited various barbarians to rebellion.
The vagrants Xiè Wénlǐ and Xiè Wényì responded to him.
Commander Dù Cóng was defeated,
and Xiè Wényì seized his helmet.
In the twelfth year (1517),
Mǎ Hào supervised Commander Cáo Yù in launching an attack.
Pǔ Fǎ'è was defeated,
and fled to hold Qīngshānzhài.
Mǎ Hào divided his forces to occupy the water sources,
cutting off their supply route,
and leaving the southern side open to besiege them.
The bandits, suffering from lack of water and thirst,
charged the southern encirclement.
The government forces intercepted and attacked them.
Pǔ Fǎ'è was hit by a stray arrow and died,
and the various Mán greatly scattered.
For his merits,
he was again promoted to Censor-in-Chief on the Right,
and his son was granted a hereditary position as a Centurion in the Jǐnyī Wèi.
Hào had talent and spirit,
was adaptable,
and enjoyed being extravagant;
wherever he went, he achieved success.
However, he governed in Chuānzhōng for a long time,
grew accustomed to its customs,
and was keen on achieving fame and merit,
which ultimately led to his downfall.
Previously,
after Yìbùlà had fled,
Hào moved his troops to attack the Fān stockades on Xiǎodōnglù, but failed to capture them.
The various barbarians of Màozhōu feared being invaded,
and so gathered the Shēngmiáo to besiege the fortresses.
Cānjìang Ruì Xī and others attacked them,
but their army was defeated,
and Zhǐhuī Páng Shēng and others all died.
He also once dispatched Fùzǒngbīng Zhāng Jié and Fùshǐ Wú Lǐ to attack the Fān people of Sōngpān's northern and southern routes;
they were unsuccessful,
losing over three thousand soldiers,
and he concealed this, not reporting it.
When the Bómán were pacified,
he did not establish garrisons,
but hastily returned his army.
He requested to change Gāoxiàn to a zhōu,
and establish long-term officials,
and increase the land tax of Gāo, Gǒng, and Jūnlián by 1,800 shí,
ordering Zhǐhuī Wèi Wǔ to measure the land and seize the property of the surrendered people to give to the military and civilians.
The Zhīxiàn of Gǒngxiàn, Bù Liáng, divined Hào's intent
and enticed and killed the surrendered Ā Shàng.
Dù Cóng, due to a lost noble lineage,
resented Wén Yì,
and secretly sent someone to purchase his head.
Thereupon, Wén Yì took advantage of the resentment of the various barbarians,
instigated them,
and thus a great rebellion broke out,
attacking Gāo and Qìngfú counties,
and breaking their walls.
Cóng led troops to resist them,
but was again defeated,
with seven hundred dead and wounded.
From Líyǎ westward,
the Tiānquán Liùfān all rebelled one after another.
Nánjīng Jǐshìzhōng Sūn Mào, along with Xún'àn Yùshǐ Lú Yōng and Lí Lóng, successively impeached Hào.
In the fourteenth year, an official was dispatched to arrest Hào.
When he reached Hénán,
he memorialized, claiming severe illness,
and remained at home.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was finally arrested,
and soon stripped of his official status and returned home.
Yáng Yīqīng and Hú Shìníng recommended him,
but he was rejected by Guì È and stopped.
After a long time,
he died.
The encomium says: Hé Jiàn commanded the Zhōngshū.
He was able to appoint various generals to suppress rebels,
probably because at that time Yáng Tínghé was in the Zhèngfǔ,
and the cabinet and ministries were of one mind,
thus they were able to achieve results.
Mǎ Zhōngxī had a good reputation at the time,
but military affairs were not his strength,
and he consequently suffered defeat.
However, observing Liú Chén's words opposing surrender,
one can also understand the affairs of the court.
Lù Wán's crime of forming factions outweighed his initial merit,
and he was allowed to be considered under the Bāyì,
thus receiving a mitigated punishment.
Hóng Zhōng and Chén Jīn's military prowess was very evident,
but the rumors among the native soldiers,
hearing them makes one feel sad;
this is something those who command armies should pay attention to.
Collation Notes

Biographies Seventy-six: Liú Biāo (Lǚ Chōng, Ài Hóng, Gé Sōng), Zhào Yòu (Zhū Tíngshēng et al.), Dài Xiǎn (Lǐ Guānghàn et al.), Lù Kūn (Báo Yànhuī et al.), Jiǎng Qīn, Zhōu Xǐ (Tú Zhēn), Tāng Lǐjìng (Wáng Huàn, Hé Shàozhèng), Xǔ Tiānxī (Zhōu Yuè et al.), Xú Wénpǔ (Zhái Táng, Wáng Luán), Zhāng Shìlóng, Zhāng Wénmíng (Chén Dǐng et al.), Fàn Lù, Zhāng Qīn, Zhōu Guǎng (Cáo Hǔ), Shí Tiānzhù
Liú Biāo,
courtesy name Wéixīn,
a native of Fúzhōu.
He became a *jìnshì* in the twelfth year of Hóngzhì.
He was appointed Hùkē Jǐshìzhōng.
He impeached Hùbù Shàngshū Pān Zhōng for allowing his son to accept bribes,
criticized the families of the imperial relatives Qìngyún Hóu and Shòuníng Hóu for exploiting merchant profits
and disrupting salt regulations,
and also criticized Wénxuǎnláng Zhāng Cǎi for subverting appointment policies.
He had a reputation for integrity.
When Wǔzōng ascended the throne,
within a few months,
he gradually began to change Xiàozōng's policies.
Biāo memorialized, remonstrating:
"When the late emperor was gravely ill,
he summoned the Grand Secretaries Liú Jiàn, Lǐ Dōngyáng, and Xiè Qiān to his bedside,
entrusting Your Majesty to them.
Now, the imperial coffin has not yet been buried,
and his virtuous pronouncements still resonate,
yet many government affairs are amiss,
and edicts are not trusted.
Zhāng Yú and Liú Wéntài were careless with their medicines,
leading to the late emperor's passing,
but they were not immediately executed;
instead, they were allowed to present their defense.
The palace eunuch Liú Láng caused harm in Hénán,
and should have been investigated,
but was merely transferred to Jìzhōu.
The Hùbù requested to eliminate redundant officials,
and the Bīngbù requested to abolish 'transmission by imperial favor' appointments,
but both memorials were rejected.
The late emperor left Jiàn and others to assist Your Majesty,
yet recently, in the replies to memorials,
favor has encroached upon law,
and private interests have obscured public good,
meaning that the Grand Secretaries are not permitted to be heard,
while those close to you on the left and right secretly interfere.
May Your Majesty follow the last will.
Trust the experienced elders;
whether policies are great or small,
consult the Nèigé in all matters,
so that affairs will not be obstructed
and power will not be usurped."
The report was acknowledged.
In the first year of Zhèngdé,
Lìbù Shàngshū Mǎ Wénshēng retired,
and the court deliberated on a replacement.
Yùshǐ Wáng Shízhōng argued that Mǐn Guī and Liú Dàxià should not be among those nominated.
Biāo feared that worthy elders would become increasingly alienated,
and submitted a memorial strongly refuting his error.
The memorial was sent down to the relevant department,
and it was Biāo's words
that prompted an imperial edict to admonish remonstrating officials not to make arbitrary memorials driven by private interests.
When Xiàozōng was on the throne,
he was deeply aware of the harm caused by palace eunuchs being appointed to govern regions,
and those he dispatched were carefully selected.
When Liú Jǐn usurped power,
he recalled all of them,
and replaced them with his own partisans.
Biāo said:
"Using new people is not as good as using old people,
just as raising hungry tigers is not as good as raising fed tigers."
This was not heeded.
Soon after, he and Jǐshìzhōng Zhāng Wén and others strongly pointed out five shortcomings in the current administration,
which displeased the emperor,
and he was deprived of his salary for three months.
When Liú Jiàn and Xiè Qiān left their positions,
Biāo and Xíngkē Jǐshìzhōng Lǚ Chōng each submitted memorials pleading for them to be retained,
and their words infringed upon Jǐn.
Prior to this,
Bīngkē Dōujǐshìzhōng Ài Hóng had impeached the palace eunuch Gāo Fèng's nephew Lín Yíng for managing the Jǐnyīwèi.
These memorials were transmitted to Nánjīng Garrison Commander Wǔjìng Bó Zhào Chéngqìng,
and Yìngtiān Yǐn Lù Héng recorded them and showed them to his colleagues,
and Bīngbù Shàngshū Lín Hàn sighed deeply upon hearing of them.
Thereupon, Jǐshìzhōng Dài Xiǎn, Yùshǐ Báo Yànhuī, and others
each rushed memorials with strong remonstrances,
requesting to retain Jiàn and Qiān.
Jǐn and others were furious,
falsified an imperial edict to arrest Xiǎn, Yànhuī, and others,
and sent them to the imperial prison for interrogation;
Biāo, Chōng, and Hóng were all given court floggings and stripped of their official status;
Chéngqìng's salary was halved and he was idled;
Hàn and Héng were demoted and retired.
Afterward, Jiàn, Qiān, and fifty-three others were listed as "treacherous partisans,"
and Biāo, Chōng, and Hóng were also included.
When Jǐn was defeated,
Biāo was reinstated as Jīnhuá Zhīfǔ,
and his governance was noted as outstanding,
but before he could be promoted, he requested to retire.
In the early Jiājìng era,
he was reinstated as Zhīfǔ of Chángshā,
then promoted to Jiāngxī Fùshǐ, where he died.
Yùshǐ Fàn Yǒngkuí pleaded his case to the court,
and he was specially granted sacrificial rites and burial.
Lǚ Chōng,
a native of Yǒngfēng, Guǎngxìn.
He became a *jìnshì* in the twelfth year of Hóngzhì (1499).
His request to retain Jiàn and Qiān stated:
"There are five reasons why these two ministers should not be allowed to leave.
Confucius praised Mèng Zhuāngzǐ's filial piety,
considering it difficult not to change his father's ministers.
These two ministers were both selected by the late Emperor and entrusted to Your Majesty;
now, the soil on the tomb is not yet dry,
and to dismiss them without cause,
how can it comfort the spirits in heaven?
This is the first reason why it is unacceptable.
Although the two ministers pleaded old age and illness,
they in fact departed because their words went against policies, their plans were thwarted,
and they could not hold their positions.
If Your Majesty allows them to leave,
it would also be because they were not good at yielding and complying,
not truly because you intended to show deference to the elderly.
While it might be a matter of choosing to leave for the two ministers,
for Your Majesty, there is the suspicion of abandoning experienced elders.
This is the second reason why it is unacceptable.
Currently, the people are impoverished and resources are exhausted,
the treasuries are empty.
Floods, droughts, bandits, celestial phenomena, and changes in flora and fauna are appearing repeatedly and concurrently.
Should an unforeseen disaster arise,
and the country lacks experienced elders,
who will share the burden?
This is the third reason why it is unacceptable.
Since ancient times, upright and resolute individuals have been hard to tolerate,
while pliant and compliant ones are easily accepted.
Once these two ministers depart,
then pliant and compliant individuals will surely advance,
and they will simply defer to whatever Your Majesty does,
which is not a blessing for the state.
This is the fourth reason why it is unacceptable.
The *Shū* says,
'Do not abandon the aged and infirm.'
Jiàn and others are well-practiced and experienced,
not comparable to newly advanced officials.
Now, if they leave the country on the same day,
the world and future generations will say that Your Majesty prefers new advancements and dislikes old acquaintances.
This is the fifth reason why it is unacceptable."
After his name was struck from the register, he returned home,
and was later appointed Acting Section Chief (*qiānshì*) of Yúnnán.
He was promoted to Vice Commissioner (*fùshǐ*) of Sìchuān,
where he repaired the Chéngdū Jiāng Yàn (Dujiangyan Irrigation System) to provide irrigation,
greatly promoting water conservancy.
He died in the early Jiājìng period.
Ài Hóng,
a native of Bīnzhōu.
He became a *jìnshì* in the ninth year of Hóngzhì (1496).
He was appointed Supervising Secretary (*gěishìzhōng*) of the Ministry of War.
Upon Wǔzōng's ascension,
an edict ordered a thorough investigation of the Tengxiáng Guards and the seventy-two Guards in the capital.
Supervising Secretary Gé Sōng meticulously investigated without showing favoritism,
finding over 7,500 individuals who had occupied military service in various directorates and bureaus,
and an imperial decree ordered them to be sent to various garrisons for training.
Subsequently, court eunuchs Wèi Xīng, Xiāo Shòu, and others interfered,
blocking its implementation.
Hóng, leading his colleagues, argued strenuously.
Ultimately, they could not prevail.
He also impeached Duke Yīngguó Zhāng Mào, Marquis Huáiníng Sūn Yìngjué, Earl Xīnníng Tán Yòu, and Earl Péngchéng Zhāng Xìn,
and requested the dismissal of the Shǎnxī Garrison Supervisor Liú Yún and Jìzhōu Garrison Supervisor Liú Láng.
His requests were not granted.
Yún was soon transferred to Nanjing Defense Commissioner (*shǒubèi*),
and sought to have his adopted son Wěi appointed Commander of the Imperial Guard (*Jǐnyī Qiānhù*).
Hóng again led his colleagues to impeach him,
and the matter was dropped.
Hóng served long in the Ministry of War,
and many of his remonstrances were commendable.
After his name was struck from the register,
he was further fined 200 *dàn* of rice to be transported to Xuānfǔ.
Later, he was reappointed to office,
and ended his career as Assistant Administrative Commissioner (*zuǒcānzhèng*) of Fújiàn.
Gé Sōng,
courtesy name Zhōngfǔ,
a native of Wúxī.
He became a *jìnshì* in the twelfth year of Hóngzhì (1499).
He was promoted from Messenger (*xíngrén*) to Supervising Secretary (*gěishìzhōng*) of the Ministry of Rites,
inspected military provisions in Jìzhōu,
and investigated lands encroached upon by powerful relatives,
returning them to the people.
In the early Zhèngdé period,
he vigorously opposed powerful favorites by rectifying abuses in the garrisons.
He requested the release of the late Emperor's palace women,
and remonstrated against hunting,
subsequently impeaching Duke Wèiguó Xú Fǔ.
He also joined the Nine Ministers in requesting the execution of Liú Jǐn.
Jǐn, enraged,
denounced him as a traitorous partisan,
and dismissed him to return home.
Zhào Yòu,
courtesy name Rǔyì,
a native of Shuāngliú.
He became a *jìnshì* in the twelfth year of Hóngzhì (1499).
He was summoned from Magistrate (*zhīxiàn*) of Fánchāng to serve as Censor (*yùshǐ*).
In the sixth month of the first year of Zhèngdé (1506),
due to celestial anomalies and requests for criticism,
Yòu submitted a memorial stating:
"Eunuchs Liú Jǐn, Qiū Jù, Mǎ Yǒngchéng and their ilk daily offer hawks and dogs,
and encourage horseback archery.
Should there be an unforeseen accident involving a fall,
would it not cause worry for the two palaces?
The resident eunuchs Dèng Yuán and Mài Xiù are rather quiet and reserved,
yet Liú Jǐng and Liáng Yù have pushed them aside and replaced them.
The Ministry of Revenue discussed having the people rent and cultivate the horse pastures and fodder fields,
but Níng Jǐn himself secretly memorialized to stop it.
Lǐ Xīng unauthorizedly cut down timber from the imperial tombs,
already sentenced to capital punishment,
yet he sought to bribe those around him to gain clemency.
Others include Nanjing Defense Commissioner Liú Yún.
Granary Supervisors Zhào Zhōng, Wéi Jùn, Duàn Xún,
were all additionally appointed through illicit connections.
I request that Jǐn and his associates be brought to justice,
that Jǐng and Yù be dismissed and not dispatched,
and that superfluous and extra officials be eliminated.
From now on, state affairs must consult with senior ministers and censors,
and not be swayed by close attendants,
then disasters will naturally be averted."
When the memorial was presented,
the eunuchs were greatly resentful.
The Emperor was about to marry,
and an edict ordered 400,000 *liǎng* of silver from Tàicāng.
Yòu stated:
"Those around you use the wedding ceremony as an excuse
to indulge in insatiable desires.
Fiscal ministers fear calamity and dare not object,
and cabinet ministers avoid resentment and dare not argue.
Expenditures are like sand and mud,
leading to the depletion of the nation.
Should unfortunately military campaigns arise,
or famine be encountered,
what will be the plan then?"
In the ninth month,
plum blossoms bloomed profusely outside Wǎnpíng,
Yòu stated:
"This is the Yin usurping the Yang's authority,
not an accidental occurrence."
The Emperor accepted none of it.
At that time,
the eunuchs became increasingly arrogant,
and Yòu, along with his colleagues Zhū Tíngshēng and Xú Yù, repeatedly submitted memorials vigorously arguing against them.
The memorials were sent to the Grand Secretariat for deliberation,
intending to severely punish the eunuchs.
The situation suddenly changed,
and Liú Jiàn and Xiè Qiān left their positions.
Jǐn then extensively purged court officials who had offended him,
designating Yòu, Tíngshēng, Yù, and Chén Lín, Pān Táng, and others as a traitorous faction,
and forced their dismissal.
After Jǐn was executed,
Yòu was recommended for the position of Acting Section Chief (*qiānshì*) of Shānxī, where he died.
Zhū Tíngshēng, courtesy name Kèxié,
a native of Jìnxián.
He became a *jìnshì* in the twelfth year of Hóngzhì (1499).
During the Jiājìng period,
he ended his career as Vice Minister (*yòushìláng*) of the Ministry of Justice.
Xú Yù, courtesy name Yònglì,
a native of Jiāngxià.
He became a *jìnshì* in the ninth year of Hóngzhì (1496),
and ended his career as Left Administrative Commissioner (*zuǒbùzhèngshǐ*) of Sìchuān.
Chén Lín, courtesy name Yùchóu,
a native of Pútián.
He became a *jìnshì* in the ninth year of Hóngzhì (1496).
From *shùjíshì*, he was appointed Censor (*yùshǐ*),
and submitted fifteen proposals for "Rectifying the Fundamentals and Reforming Governance."
He was dispatched to supervise education in the Southern Metropolitan Region (*Nánjī*).
When Liú Jǐn purged Jiàn and Qiān,
and arrested Dài Xiǎn, Lù Kūn, and others,
Lín submitted a strong memorial stating:
"In Nánjīng, there was thunder in deep winter and a solar eclipse on New Year's Day.
It is precisely the time to cultivate virtue to avert disasters,
to entrust matters to senior officials,
and to broadly seek loyal counsel.
How can one abandon one's trusted aides
and block one's ears and eyes?"
Jǐn was greatly enraged,
and demoted him to Assistant Magistrate (*chéng*) of Jiēyáng.
After Jǐn's downfall,
he was promoted to Prefectural Judge (*tóngzhī*) of Jiāxīng.
During the Shìzōng period,
he ended his career as Vice Minister (*yòushìláng*) of the Nanjing Ministry of War.
Pān Táng, courtesy name Zōngjié,
a native of Liù'ān.
He became a *jìnshì* in the ninth year of Hóngzhì (1496).
He was known for his filial conduct.
He served as Magistrate (*zhīxiàn*) of Mǎnchéng,
and returned home due to mourning.
He subsequently served as Magistrate (*zhīxiàn*) of Huáxiàn,
and was promoted to Censor (*yùshǐ*),
where he presented four major proposals for current affairs.
Xiàozōng graciously accepted them.
In the early Zhèngdé period,
because of his criticism of Gāo Fèng, he was disliked by the eunuchs,
and an imperial decree stated that Táng was a partisan of Eunuch Wáng Yuè,
and his name was struck from the register.
In the eighth year, he was reappointed Acting Section Chief (*qiānshì*) of Guǎngdōng,
but resigned due to illness.
Dài Xiǎn,
courtesy name Bǎozhī,
was a native of Wùyuán.
He became a *jìnshì* in the ninth year of the Hóngzhì reign (1496),
and was made a *shùjíshì*.
He was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of War (*Bīngkē Jǐshìzhōng*),
and frequently offered proposals.
After a long time,
for the sake of supporting his parents, he was transferred to Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Revenue (*Hùkē Jǐshìzhōng*) in Nánjīng.
When Wǔzōng ascended the throne,

he and his colleagues requested that the Six Offices of Scrutiny be instructed to review all major policies enacted during the Hóngzhì reign—such as advancing the worthy, dismissing the wicked, economizing funds, training troops, revering sacrifices, cautious application of punishments, disaster relief, and aiding the distressed—
and prepare a detailed record for imperial perusal,
to serve as a standard for all future decisions on important matters.
This was reported to the emperor.
A month later,
he stated that the annual tributes from the four quarters often consisted of non-local products,
leading to excessive labor and expenditure,
and suggested that items not indigenous to the area should be exempted.
He also requested diligent attendance at the imperial lectures (*jīngyán*),
to allow high-ranking ministers to present their views at leisure.

Subsequently, he and Supervising Secretaries Lǐ Guānghàn, Xú Fān, Mù Xiāng, Rèn Huì, Xú Xiān, and Censor Bó Yànhuī, among others, jointly submitted memorials requesting that Liú Jiàn and Xiè Qiān be retained,
and impeaching the eunuch Gāo Fèng.
The emperor was enraged,
and they were arrested and imprisoned in the imperial jail,
then beaten with a staff in court and stripped of their official titles.
Dài Xiǎn was severely injured
and consequently died.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was posthumously granted the title of Junior Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments (*Guānglù Shàoqīng*).
Lǐ Guānghàn
was a native of Xīnxiāng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the twelfth year of the Hóngzhì reign (1499).
He was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Revenue in Nánjīng.
When the Zhèngdé reign began,
due to natural disasters, requests for candid advice were issued.
Lǐ Guānghàn and his colleagues submitted a memorial impeaching the eunuchs Miáo Kuí, Gāo Fèng, Lǐ Róng, and the Duke of Bǎoguó, Zhū Huī.
They also stated that the Grand Secretaries Liú Jiàn and others had submitted memorials regarding salt policies,
which were held back and not acted upon,
thereby making the elder ministers uneasy in their positions.
The emperor did not heed their advice.
He was later stripped of his position and returned home.
Later, he was appointed Prefect of Táizhōu,
and was praised alongside Xú Fān for his outstanding governance.
He died shortly thereafter.
Xú Fān
was a native of Táizhōu.
He became a *jìnshì* in the sixth year of the Hóngzhì reign (1493).
He was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Rites (*Lǐkē Jǐshìzhōng*) in Nánjīng.
When Wǔzōng ascended the throne,
he restored various superfluous expenses that had been eliminated by the previous dynasty.
Xú Fān and others strongly argued against this,
but their advice was not accepted.
Later, he was appointed Provincial Councillor of Jiāngxī,
and joined Grand Censor Chén Jīn in suppressing the bandits in Dōngxiāng.
During the Jiājìng era,
he was successively promoted to Vice Minister of the Right of the Ministry of Works (*Gōngbù Yòushìláng*).
Mù Xiāng
was a native of Yúyáo.
He became a *jìnshì* in the twelfth year of the Hóngzhì reign (1499).
He was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of War in Nánjīng.
He argued for the rescue of Grand Censor Yōng Tài of Xuānfǔ,
and also publicly memorialized to request the dismissal of Minister of Rites Cuī Zhìduān and others,
but none of these requests were granted.
In the first year of the Zhèngdé reign (1506), he was ordered to investigate the Imperial Stud (*Yùmǎ Jiān*) with Censor Lǚ Táng,
and consequently reported on the abuses of excessive labor and expenditure,
as well as the crime of eunuch Lǐ Táng obstructing imperial decrees for personal gain.
At this time,
he returned home after receiving the staff punishment,
and supported his mother by teaching students.
He was later reinstated to office
and promoted to Provincial Councillor of Guǎngxī.
When the order was issued,
Mù Xiāng had already died.
Rèn Huì
was a native of Luánzhōu.
He became a *jìnshì* in the ninth year of the Hóngzhì reign (1496).
From Messenger (*Xíngrén*), he was promoted to Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Personnel (*Lìkē Jǐshìzhōng*) in Nánjīng.
In the ninth month of the first year of the Zhèngdé reign (1506), he and his colleagues remonstrated against the emperor's idleness and pleasure-seeking,
speaking with directness and earnestness.
Later, he was appointed Assistant Surveillance Commissioner (*Qiānshì*) of Shāndōng,
but died before taking office.
Xú Xiān
was a native of Lìchéng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the fifteenth year of the Hóngzhì reign (1502).
When Wǔzōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Works (*Gōngkē Jǐshìzhōng*) in Nánjīng.
When the Zhèngdé reign began,
due to natural disasters, he submitted a memorial on seven matters,
and also requested the dismissal of Duke of Yīngguó Zhāng Mào and Minister Zhāng Shēng, among others,
the removal of all newly appointed eunuchs,
the clear punishment of Zhāng Yú and Liú Wéntài for improper medicinal treatment that harmed the late emperor,
as well as the crimes of eunuch Lǐ Xīng for unauthorized felling of trees at the imperial tombs,
and the Earl of Xīnníng Tán Yòu and Vice Minister Lǐ Suì for their failure to act on these matters.
The emperor forwarded the memorial to the relevant authorities.
Later, he was appointed Assistant Surveillance Commissioner of Shānxī,
and then promoted to Vice Surveillance Commissioner (*Fùshǐ*).
He pacified the great bandit Hùn Tiānwáng,
for which the people praised him.
He died in office.
Lù Kūn,
courtesy name Rúyù,
was a native of Guī'ān.
He became a *jìnshì* in the ninth year of the Hóngzhì reign (1496).
He was appointed Magistrate of Qīngfēng.
Due to his integrity and capability, he was summoned
and promoted to Censor of Nánjīng.
When Wǔzōng ascended the throne,
he submitted a memorial listing eight matters for strengthening discipline: One,
to reward candid speech.
In ancient times,
if a subject failed to remonstrate,
the punishment was tattooing.
Under the Sòng system,
if a Censor entered the Censorate
and remained silent for more than ten decades,
he was punished for disgracing the Censorate.
Today, when officials of the various bureaus offer advice,
such as Lǐ Mèngyáng and Yáng Zǐqì,
they should be visibly commended and promoted,
and the performance evaluation of censors
should be based on the number, quality, and appropriateness of their memorials.
Two,
to restore face-to-face impeachment.
According to the old system,
when a Censor presented himself at court,
the impeached party would step out to await punishment,
which was in the spirit of the Táng practice of reading impeachment documents before the accused.
Recently, memorials are often sealed and presented in writing,
and before an imperial reply is issued,
cover-ups often preempt them.
I request that the old practice of face-to-face presentation be followed,
and immediate imperial decisions be made.
Three,
to distinguish between the virtuous and the corrupt.
Ministers Liú Dàxià and Wáng Shì requested retirement due to illness,
while Vice Ministers Zhāng Yuánzhēn and Chén Qīng, though repeatedly impeached, remained in office.
This reversal of the worthy and the unworthy
is truly crucial to the rise and fall of governance.
It is fitting to urge the former two to stay
and dismiss Zhāng Yuánzhēn and others to their homes.
Four,
to verify imperial decrees.
Recently, advice that inconvenienced those around the emperor
was frequently held back.
Matters involving personal interests
were readily approved as imperial decrees.
I request that all memorials from various bureaus be numbered and sent to the Grand Secretariat,
so that those already enacted can be reviewed,
and those not yet acted upon can be easily resubmitted.
Five,
to cultivate keen spirit.
Censors and Grand Censors
are by custom authorized to mutually supervise each other,
and their actions should not be constrained.
Six,
to equalize assignments.
Censors are restricted by north and south,
clearly indicating differences in importance.
From now on, except for巡按 (*xún'àn*) who receive direct imperial appointments,
all other assignments and promotion qualifications
should be uniformly proposed for imperial approval,
to demonstrate impartiality.
Seven,
to delegate authority specifically.
The Henán Circuit has the responsibility of evaluation,
and I request that a dedicated person be selected for this task.
Eight,
to encourage all officials.
Secretaries Tián Yán, Yáo Tīng, Zhāng Xiàn,
Assistant Secretaries Lǐ Chéngxūn, Hú Shìníng, Zhāng Dǐng, Gù Lín, and twenty others,
should all be conspicuously promoted.
The memorial was sent to the relevant authorities.
He also impeached eunuchs Gāo Fèng, Miáo Kuí, and the Duke of Bǎoguó Zhū Huī,
and consequently requested the dismissal of newly appointed defense eunuchs in Nánjīng,
the broad opening of channels for advice,
and the absolute prohibition of banquets, leisure outings, and equestrian activities.
The emperor was unable to comply.
At that
time, the
“Eight Tigers” [bā dǎng]
held power, and the

imperial government daily degenerated. Kūn [kūn] and the thirteen supervising censors, Bó Yànhuī [bó yànhuī], Gě Hào [gě hào], Gòng Ānfǔ [gòng ānfǔ], Wáng Fān [wáng fān], Shǐ Liángzuǒ [shǐ liángzuǒ], Lǐ Xī [lǐ xī], Rèn Nuò [rèn nuò], Yáo Xuélǐ [yáo xuélǐ], Zhāng Míngfèng [zhāng míngfèng], Jiǎng Qīn [jiǎng qīn], Cáo [cáo], Huáng Zhāodào [huáng zhāodào], Wáng Hóng [wáng hóng], Xiāo Qiányuán [xiāo qiányuán], and others,
submitted a memorial with urgent remonstrance, saying:
“From ancient times, treacherous ministers who wished to usurp imperial power
would first corrupt the emperor’s mind and will.
For example, Zhào Gāo [zhào gāo] persuaded the Second Emperor to be cruel and indulge his desires
to the utmost of his sensory pleasures;
Hé Shìkāi [hé shìkāi] advised Wǔchéng [wǔchéng] not to exert himself or be frugal,
but to enjoy himself while young and strong;
Qiú Shìliáng [qiú shìliáng] taught his faction to guide the ruler with extravagance and luxury,
and not to let him get close to Confucian scholars
who knew the causes of the rise and fall of previous dynasties.
When their rulers were misled,
they all eventually suffered disaster.
Since Your Majesty ascended the throne,
the world has eagerly hoped for good governance.
But not long after, favored eunuchs and palace attendants
overturned established laws.
Grand Eunuchs Mǎ Yǒngchéng [mǎ yǒngchéng], Wèi Bīn [wèi bīn], Liú Jǐn [liú jǐn], Chuán Xìng [chuán xìng], Luó Xiáng [luó xiáng], Gǔ Dàyòng [gǔ dàyòng], and their ilk together engaged in deception,
spending their days in banquets and amusement.
This offends Heaven’s harmony,
as disasters and omens are repeatedly reported,
and court officials have repeatedly remonstrated,
but have not been heeded.
These people must think that enjoying themselves in the palace
has nothing to do with order or chaos.
This is precisely the old trick of treacherous people deceiving the sovereign.
Your Majesty, in your vast halls with fine carpets,
how can you know that ordinary people in their humble homes with dilapidated roofs are not sheltered from wind and rain?
Dressed in brocade and eating fine food,
how can you know that ordinary people cannot endure extreme cold and hot rain, or hunger and cold?
Riding and feasting,
how can you know that ordinary people, with aching heads and furrowed brows, have no way to appeal their grievances?
Yesterday, thunder struck the suburban altar;
a comet appeared in the Purple Enclosure;
there was severe drought in summer and autumn;
rice prices in Jiāngnán [jiāngnán] soared;
and bandits ran rampant in the capital city.
Can Your Majesty still indulge in pleasure and desire
without a single thought for this?
The Grand Secretaries, entrusted with the dying emperor’s mandate,
should rectify matters as they arise,
and greatly assist in overcoming difficulties.
If their words are not heard,
they must prostrate themselves before the palace gate and remonstrate unto death,
to awaken the sacred will.
But instead, they are negligent and compliant,
submissive and evasive.
If they are only looking out for themselves, then that is fine.
But what about the late emperor’s entrustment and the world’s expectations?
We humbly hope that Your Majesty will reflect on your conduct,
promptly dismiss Yǒngchéng [yǒngchéng] and his kind to cut off the source of disaster,
entrust important officials,
and diligently learn to govern personally,
to restore perfect order.”
When the memorial arrived,
court affairs had already changed.
Liú Jiàn [liú jiàn] and Xiè Qiān [xiè qiān] had both been banished.
Thereupon, Yànhuī [yànhuī], as the leader,
again submitted a public memorial,
requesting the retention of Jiàn [jiàn] and Qiān [qiān],
and the punishment of Yǒngchéng [yǒngchéng], Jǐn [jǐn], and others.
Jǐn [jǐn] was enraged
and had them all arrested and imprisoned in the imperial prison.
Each received thirty strokes of the cane
and was dismissed from office.
Zhāodào [zhāodào], Hóng [hóng], and Qiányuán [qiányuán] had not yet arrived for arrest,
so they were ordered to be caned immediately outside the palace gate in Nánjīng [nánjīng].
Wáng Liángchén [wáng liángchén], the supervising censor for military affairs in Jiāngxī [jiāngxī], heard that Kūn [kūn] and others had been arrested,
rushed to submit a memorial to save them,
and was also arrested and imprisoned in the imperial prison,
received thirty strokes of the cane,
and was stripped of his status as a commoner.
Later, Kūn [kūn], Yànhuī [yànhuī], and others were listed among the fifty-three treacherous partisans.
When Jǐn [jǐn] was executed,
Kūn [kūn] was restored to office and then retired.
In the early years of Shìzōng’s [shìzōng] reign,
he was reactivated,
but died before taking office.
Bó Yànhuī [bó yànhuī] was
a native of Yángqǔ [yángqǔ].
He passed the imperial examination in the 9th year of Hóngzhì [hóngzhì].
He was appointed supervising censor of Sìchuān [sìchuān] Circuit.
He once impeached Cuī Zhìduān [cuī zhìduān] for disgracing the Ministry of Personnel with a Daoist priest,
and had a reputation for integrity.
By this time,
he was caned and returned home,
and died before he could be reactivated.
Gě Hào [gě hào],
courtesy name Tiānhóng [tiānhóng],
was a native of Shàngyú [shàngyú].
He passed the imperial examination in the 9th year of Hóngzhì [hóngzhì].
He was promoted from magistrate of Wǔhé [wǔhé] to supervising censor.
He frequently pointed out deficiencies in current governance,
and Xiàozōng [xiàozōng] often adopted his suggestions.
In the 1st year of Zhèngdé [zhèngdé],
the Emperor granted the request of Gāo Fèng [gāo fèng], a eunuch of the Directorate of Ceremonial,
to have his nephew, Délín [délín], manage the affairs of the Imperial Bodyguard.
Hào [hào] and others argued against this,
saying:
“The late emperor decreed that all Imperial Bodyguard officials should be recommended by the Ministry of War,
and Your Majesty also dismissed all officials appointed by imperial decree without examination.
Now, Délín [délín] is appointed by imperial decree,
without involving the Ministry of War,
nullifying the late emperor’s order,
destroying the law of selection,
and rendering Your Majesty’s decree void.
This single act results in three faults,
caused by Fèng [fèng].
We request punishment for Fèng [fèng]
and the dismissal of Délín [délín].”
Supervising Censor Pān Táng [pān táng] also said:
“If Fèng [fèng] and Délín [délín] control major powers both inside and outside the court,
and other eunuchs follow their example,
where will the abuses end?”
The Emperor ignored them all.
After Hào [hào] was stripped of his official status,
Jǐn’s [jǐn] resentment had not dissipated.
Hào [hào] was again implicated for a previous impeachment of Chén Huì [chén huì], the Prefect of Wǔchāng [wǔchāng], which was deemed unsubstantiated.
He, along with Ānfǔ [ānfǔ], Fān [fān], Xī [xī], Xuélǐ [xuélǐ], and Kūn [kūn], a total of six people,
were arrested and caned outside the palace gate.
When Jǐn [jǐn] was executed,
Hào [hào] was reinstated as Prefect of Shàowǔ [shàowǔ].
When he had an audience,
he presented five proposals regarding advantages and disadvantages,
all of which were implemented.
During the Jiājìng [jiājìng] reign,
he successively served as Grand Judge of the Two Capitals.
When the Emperor was performing a suburban sacrifice,
someone violated the imperial procession.
The judicial authorities intended to impose a heavy sentence,
but Hào [hào] argued against it,
and the person was spared death.
In the summer of the 10th year,
after a lightning strike at the Wǔmén [wǔmén],
he impeached himself and retired,
dying at the age of ninety-two.
Gòng Ānfǔ [gòng ānfǔ],
courtesy name Kèrén [kèrén],
was a native of Jiāngyīn [jiāngyīn].
He passed the imperial examination in the 9th year of Hóngzhì [hóngzhì].
He was appointed magistrate of Chángyuán [chángyuán].
During Xiàozōng’s [xiàozōng] reign,
he was promoted to supervising censor
and once impeached Zhāng Hèlǐng [zhāng hèlǐng], Marquis of Shòuníng [shòuníng], in a memorial.
In the early Zhèngdé [zhèngdé] reign,
Yáng Zǐqì [yáng zǐqì], an officer of the Ministry of Personnel, was imprisoned in the imperial prison for matters concerning imperial tombs.
Ānfǔ [ānfǔ] strongly argued for his release in a memorial.
Liú Dàxià [liú dàxià], Minister of War, resigned due to illness after being obstructed by eunuchs.
Chén Qīng [chén qīng], Vice Minister of Revenue, was transferred to be Minister of Works in Nánjīng [nánjīng].
Ānfǔ [ānfǔ], leading the supervising censors, requested the return of Dàxià [dàxià] and the dismissal of Qīng [qīng].
The news was reported.
Yànhuī’s [yànhuī] public memorial
was penned by Ānfǔ [ānfǔ].
Jǐn [jǐn] knew this,
so he listed Ānfǔ [ānfǔ] as the head of the Southern supervising censors among the treacherous partisans.
He lived at home for ten years,
not entering the city for an entire year.
Later, he was reactivated as an assistant surveillance commissioner in Shāndōng [shāndōng],
but after only three months,
he resigned due to illness.
Shǐ Liángzuǒ [shǐ liángzuǒ],
courtesy name Yǔchén [yǔchén],
was also a native of Jiāngyīn [jiāngyīn].
He passed the imperial examination in the 12th year of Hóngzhì [hóngzhì].
He was promoted from an official of the Ministry of Rites to supervising censor.
Later, he was reactivated as a Vice Commissioner of Yúnnán [yúnnán].
He pacified the eighteen Miao [miáo] villages
and was bestowed with white gold and brocade.
He dredged the estuary,
irrigating a thousand *qǐng* [qǐng] of fields,
for which the people of Diān [diān] praised him.
Lǐ Xī,
a native of Shàngyuán.
He became a *jìnshì* in the ninth year of Hóngzhì.
He was promoted from magistrate of Jiānglè to censor.
In the eighteenth year,
the villains Xú Jùn and others spread rumors.
The Emperor sent officials with imperial warrants to Nánjīng
to arrest and prosecute certain individuals.
Later, it was found to be groundless.
Lǐ Xī publicly memorialized, saying:
"Your Majesty, your prestige and sagacity have been somewhat diminished by this matter.
If villains should imitate this [behavior],
and maliciously use slander to harm virtuous people,
the damage would be incalculable."
The matter was referred to the judicial authorities,
who also strongly stated the harm of the imperial warrants.
The Emperor accepted this.
In the ninth month of the first year of Zhèngdé,
due to natural disasters,
he again, with other censors, presented ten matters [in a memorial].
When Liú Jǐn was executed,
those who had suffered harm were all reinstated,
but Lǐ Xī alone remained dismissed.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was first reinstated as the prefect of Ráozhōu,
then promoted to Vice Commissioner of Zhèjiāng,
and was renowned for his integrity.
Yáo Xuélǐ,
a native of Bā,
had his home in the capital.
He became a *jìnshì* in the sixth year of Hóngzhì.
In the first year of Zhèngdé,
he publicly memorialized, advising against excessive excursions,
but it was not accepted.
Later, he was reinstated as Assistant Surveillance Commissioner of Yúnnán,
and eventually ended his career as a Councilor.
Zhāng Míngfèng,
a native of Qīngpíng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the ninth year of Hóngzhì,
and served as the magistrate of Yǒngkāng.
He had notable administrative achievements
and was promoted to censor.
Later, he was reinstated as Assistant Surveillance Commissioner of Húguǎng,
promoted to Vice Commissioner.
He returned home due to his mother's mourning,
and passed away.
Jiǎng Qīn was flogged to death;
his biography is elsewhere.
Cáo Mǐn,
a native of Shànghǎi.
He became a *jìnshì* in the ninth year of Hóngzhì,
and served as the magistrate of Shāxiàn.
When he was summoned for another appointment,
the people wept and clung to him,
preventing him from leaving for several days.
Later, he and Kūn were implicated together.
Though he was to be reinstated,
he declined due to caring for his mother.
After his mother passed away,
he slept on an earthen pillow [during mourning],
contracted a cold illness, and died.
Huáng Zhāodào,
a native of Píngjiāng,
became a *jìnshì* in the twelfth year of Hóngzhì.
Later, he was reinstated as Assistant Surveillance Commissioner of Guǎngxī,
and then promoted to Administration Councilor of Yúnnán.
He achieved merit in pacifying Mùbāng and Mèngmì.
He ended his career as Left Administration Commissioner.
Wáng Hóng,
a native of Liùhé,
became a *jìnshì* in the sixth year of Hóngzhì.
Xiāo Qiányuán,
a native of Wàn'ān,
became a *jìnshì* in the twelfth year of Hóngzhì.
When Wáng Fán and Rèn Nuò conducted their investigations,
they did not participate in the interrogations,
so they are not worthy of record.
Wáng Liángchén,
a native of Chénzhōu.
He became a *jìnshì* in the sixth year of Hóngzhì.
He served as a censor in Nánjīng.
When Liú Jǐn was executed,
he was reinstated as Vice Commissioner of Shāndōng,
and eventually ended his career as a Surveillance Commissioner.
Jiǎng Qīn,
courtesy name Zǐxiū,
a native of Chángshú.
He became a *jìnshì* in the ninth year of Hóngzhì.
He was appointed as Judicial Assessor of Wèihuī.
He was summoned and promoted to Censor of Nánjīng,
and frequently submitted memorials.
In the first year of Zhèngdé,
when Liú Jǐn expelled Grand Secretaries Liú Jiàn and Xiè Qiān,
Jiǎng Qīn, along with fellow officials Bó Yànhuī and others, earnestly remonstrated.
Liú Jǐn was furious,
arrested them, imprisoned them in the imperial prison,
and had them publicly flogged and demoted to commoners.
Three days later,
Jiǎng Qīn alone submitted a memorial, saying:
"Liú Jǐn
is merely a small eunuch.
Your Majesty personally treats him as a trusted confidant,
relies on him as eyes and ears,
and regards him as limbs and backbone;
yet you are utterly unaware that Liú Jǐn is a rebellious villain,
a thief who corrupts the nation.
He resented that your ministers memorialized to retain the two Grand Secretaries [Liú Jiàn and Xiè Qiān],
to curb the powerful traitors,
and thus falsely issued an edict to arrest and interrogate them,
flog them, and strip them of their offices.
However, your minister reflects that even in the fields, one does not forget the ruler,
much less when awaiting orders by the mat,
witnessing the current abuses;
how can I bear not to speak?
Yesterday, Liú Jǐn extorted bribes from the officials of the Three Bureaus nationwide,
a thousand gold pieces from each person,
some even up to five thousand gold pieces.
Those who did not give were demoted or dismissed,
while those who gave were promoted.
The whole country is chilled with fear,
yet Your Majesty alone employs him by your side.
This is not knowing that there is a thief by your side,
but treating a thief as a trusted confidant.
Censor Liú Mǒu pointed out that Your Majesty is dim in employing people
and muddled in handling affairs,
yet Liú Jǐn stripped him of his rank
and humiliated him with a beating.
He falsely issued an edict prohibiting all remonstrating officials
from making presumptuous criticisms.
If we do not speak, we fail by passively watching;
if we speak, we are cruelly punished unlawfully.
The whole country is chilled with fear,
yet Your Majesty alone employs him before and behind you.
This is not knowing that there is a thief before and behind you,
but treating a thief as eyes, ears, limbs, and backbone.
One thief wields power,
and the myriad people are disappointed;
the sound of their sorrow and lament reaches heaven and earth.
Yet Your Majesty remains oblivious and unheard,
allowing him to ruin national affairs
and disrupt ancestral laws.
How then can Your Majesty sustain yourself?
Please heed your minister's words,
and immediately execute Liú Jǐn to apologize to the nation,
and then execute your minister to apologize to Liú Jǐn.
If the imperial court is rectified,
ten thousand evils cannot enter;
if the ruler's heart is rectified,
ten thousand desires cannot invade.
This is your minister's wish.
Today's nation
is the nation of our ancestors.
If Your Majesty values the nation of our ancestors,
then heed your minister's memorial.
If you disregard it,
then let Liú Jǐn deceive you."
The memorial was submitted,
and he was flogged another thirty times
and imprisoned.
Three days later,
he again prepared a memorial, saying:
"Your servant and the traitor Lǐ Jǐn cannot coexist.
The traitor Lǐ Jǐn has harbored evil for more than a day;
taking advantage of opportunities to stir up trouble
is his fundamental ambition.
Your Majesty plays and amuses yourself with him daily,
completely unaware and unenlightened.
Officials and commoners, both inside and outside the court,
are as if in an icy abyss.
Yesterday, your servant was beaten after submitting a second memorial,
his flesh and blood dripping.
Lying on a pillow in prison,
it is still difficult for me to remain silent.
I wish to borrow the imperial sword to cut him down.
Who was Zhū Yún?
Would your servant yield even slightly to him?
Your Majesty, please compare your servant with Lǐ Jǐn:
Is Lǐ Jǐn loyal,
or is your servant loyal?
Loyalty or disloyalty,
the whole world knows it,
and Your Majesty also knows it clearly.
What enmity do you hold against your servant
that you trust this rebellious traitor?
Your servant's bones and flesh are all wasting away,
tears and snot flowing together.
This seventy-two-year-old father
no longer cares for his own sustenance.
What a pity is your servant's death?
But the calamity of Your Majesty's overthrowing the country and losing your family will arise in an instant;
this is indeed a great pity!
If Your Majesty sincerely kills Lǐ Jǐn and displays his head at the Wǔmén,
it would let the world know that your servant Qīn has the courage to speak out directly,
and that Your Majesty has the wisdom to punish traitors.
If Your Majesty does not kill this traitor,
you should first kill your servant,
so that your servant may roam underground with Lóng Fēng and Bǐ Gān.
Your servant truly does not wish to live alongside this traitor."
After the memorial was submitted,
he was again flogged thirty times.
When Fāng Qīn was drafting the memorial,
he faintly heard ghostly voices under the lamp.
Qīn thought, "If I submit this memorial, I will certainly incur great disaster.
This must be the spirit of my ancestors wishing me to abandon this奏章 (memorial)."
He then straightened his clothes and hat and said,
"If it is truly my ancestors,
why not speak louder to inform me?"
Before he had finished speaking,
a sound came from the wall,
even more mournful.
Qīn sighed, saying,
"I have already committed myself;
it is my duty not to consider private matters.
To remain silent and betray the country would be a disgrace to my ancestors.
What could be more unfilial than that!"
He sat down again
and wrote with renewed vigor, saying,
"Death is death;
this resolve cannot be changed!"
The sound then stopped.
Three days after the flogging,
he died in prison,
aged forty-nine.
After Lǐ Jǐn was executed,
he was posthumously granted the title of Guānglù Shàoqīng.
During the Jiājìng reign,
he was granted a sacrificial burial,
and one of his sons was admitted to the Guózi Jiàn.
Zhōu Xǐ,
courtesy name Tiānzhāng,
was from the Lúzhōu Guard.
He became a Jìnshì in the ninth year of Hóngzhì.
He was appointed Shìkē Jǐshìzhōng.
After three promotions, he became Lǐkē Dōu Jǐshìzhōng.
He was forthright and loved to speak on affairs of state.
When Wǔzōng first ascended the throne,
he requested the destruction of newly built temples and monasteries,
the expulsion of Fǎwáng and Zhēnrén,
the cessation of Jiàoshì rituals,
and also accused the former eunuch Qí Xuán of squandering money on alchemy.
Soon after,
due to prolonged rain,
he impeached Attendant Minister Lǐ Wēn and Grand Eunuch Miáo Kuí with his colleagues.
In September,
due to an anomalous celestial phenomenon,
he again impeached Wēn and Ministers Cuī Zhìduān, Xióng Chōng, Jiǎ Bīn,
and Censors-in-Chief Jīn Zé, Xú Yuán, and others.
Chōng, Wēn, and Zé were dismissed as a result.
The emperor sent the eunuch Wéi Xīng to guard Yún Yáng,
but Xǐ strongly argued against it.
Soon after, he and his colleagues again stated:
"Recently, the imperial sagacity has been obscured,
and imperial benevolence has not been bestowed.
Scholarly study is 'one day's warmth and ten days' cold,'
and imperial edicts are changed morning and evening.
Superfluous officials, just abolished, are retained again;
garrison eunuchs, recalled, are dispatched again.
Tax households are distressed by collection and delivery;
salt administration is corrupted by requests for favors.
The imperial relatives are favored, and summons are frequently issued;
personal favorites are close, and the imperial treasury is not scrutinized.
These must be promptly rectified."
This was not heeded.
In the first year of Zhèngdé, he again responded to an imperial edict by presenting eight matters,
which included impeaching eleven grand officials such as Jiǎ Bīn,
three eunuchs such as Lǐ Xīng,
seven imperial relatives and nobility such as Zhāng Mào,
and three border generals such as Zhū Tíng, Xiè Duān, and Lǐ Jī.
Not long after,
he stated:
"Since Your Majesty ascended the throne,
your fondness for hawks and dogs
has caused daily increasing extravagance.
If this continues unchecked,
then drinking, lust, and pleasure trips,
sycophancy and wickedness,
anything that can please the ears and eyes and corrupt the mind
will be indulged without limit.
The provisions supplied by Guānglù Sì [Board of Imperial Feasts]
have increased by seven or eight tenths compared to before.
If the new administration is already like this,
how can it be brought to a successful conclusion?"
Censor Hé Tiānqú and others also spoke similarly.
The memorial was sent to the Ministry of Rites,
and Minister Zhāng Shēng requested that it be followed.
Although the emperor did not censure him,
he could not act on it.
The next year, he was promoted to Shùntiān Fǔchéng.
Xǐ's remonstrances were profound and incisive,
and often clashed with the eunuchs,
so Lǐu Jǐn and others found him increasingly unbearable.
At this point,
Xǐ was ordered, along with Prison Registrar Zhāng Huái, Attendant Minister Zhāng Jìn, Censor-in-Chief Zhāng Luán, and Jǐnyīwèi Commander Yáng Yù, to investigate imperial estates in nearby counties.
Yù was
a member of Jǐn's faction,
and all three were subordinate to him.
Xǐ showed no pretense in his words and demeanor,
and in official correspondence with Yù, he only exchanged formal documents.
Yù reported Xǐ for insulting the imperial envoy,
and Jǐn immediately forged an imperial edict to arrest and imprison him in the imperial prison,
where he was beaten to death.
After Jǐn was executed,
an imperial edict restored his official position and granted a sacrifice,
and his family was compensated.
In the early Jiājìng reign,
one of his sons was recorded.
Also, Censor Tú Zhēn
was from Xīngàn.
He became a Jìnshì in the twelfth year of Hóngzhì.
He first served as the Magistrate of Jiāngyīn.
In the early Zhèngdé reign,
he was responsible for salt inspection in Chánglú.
Jǐn allowed his cronies to engage in salt dealings,
and also ordered his accomplice Bì Zhēn to exploit the collection of seafood,
infringing upon merchant profits.
Zhēn dealt with all of these according to the law.
When he returned to court,
he merely bowed to Jǐn.
Jǐn was enraged and
forged an imperial edict to imprison him in the imperial prison.
The people of Jiāngyīn who were in the capital
planned to raise money to bribe Jǐn for his release,
but Zhēn refused,
sighing deeply and saying,
"Death it is.
How can I defile the elders?"
He was then flogged thirty times
and sentenced to military exile in Sùzhōu,
but his severe injuries led to his death in prison.
Jǐn's anger had not subsided,
so he conscripted Zhēn's son Pǔ into military service.
After Jǐn was executed,
Pǔ was able to return,
and Zhēn's official position was restored and a sacrifice granted.
Tāng Lǐjìng,
courtesy name Rénfǔ,
was from Dāntú.
He became a Jìnshì in the ninth year of Hóngzhì.
He was appointed Xíngrén and then promoted to Xíngkē Jǐshìzhōng.
Early in the Zhèngdé reign,
he reported:
"Since Your Majesty ascended the throne,
Heaven has repeatedly shown signs of disaster and warnings.
Instead of heeding the warnings of Heaven,
Your Majesty has only indulged in horse racing and hunting,
and recreation without restraint.
Recently, in mid-fourth month,
there was thunder, lightning, rain, and hail.
At a time when the six yang energies should be dominant,
yin energy contended with it.
This is a manifestation of favored officials usurping power
and loyal, upright men being estranged."
Later,
he again discussed the regional inspector of Guǎngdōng and Guǎngxī, Wéi Jīng,
and then, together with the Nine Ministers, knelt before the palace to request the execution of
"the Eight Tigers."
Liú Jǐn bore a grudge against him.
Soon after, on the day when his request regarding the trial, memorialization, imprisonment, and execution of cases
where complaints of injustice had been screened out and not reported was to be reviewed,
he was accused of altering ancestral institutions
and was demoted to Judge of Jìzhōu.
Later, when the sixteen Censorate officials listed as a treacherous faction were announced,
Lǐ Jìng's name was at the top.
He was dismissed and returned home.
He died not long after.
Liú Jǐn detested censors who critically admonished current policies and often criticized him personally,
so he would often use other pretexts to incriminate them.
After Lǐ Jìng was found guilty,
there were Wáng Huàn and Hé Shàozhèng.
Wáng Huàn,
courtesy name Shílín,
was from Xiàngshān.
He passed the imperial examination in the ninth year of Hóngzhì.
From Magistrate of Chánglè, he was summoned to be appointed Censor.
In the first year of Zhèngdé,
in response to an imperial edict, he submitted five important principles for responding to Heaven,
much of which criticized eunuchs.
The following year, he was assigned to inspect the Shānhǎi passes and other areas,
but due to illness, he declined the duty and did not go.
Bandits broke out in his jurisdiction.
Grand Censor Liú Yǔ, following Liú Jǐn's directive, impeached Wáng Huàn for failing to report it.
He was arrested and imprisoned in the imperial prison,
caned,
and dismissed as a commoner.
When Liú Jǐn fell,
he was reinstated and retired.
Hé Shàozhèng
was from Chún'ān.
He passed the imperial examination in the fifteenth year of Hóngzhì.
He was appointed as a Messenger.
In the third year of Zhèngdé, he was promoted to Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Personnel.
When the palace eunuch Liáo Táng was stationed in Hénán,
he memorialized to recommend several regional officials,
and also presumptuously proposed their transfers and appointments.
Minister of Personnel Xǔ Jìn and others could not object,
but Hé Shàozhèng impeached him.
Liú Jǐn, having no choice, ordered Liáo Táng to make a self-report,
but secretly bore a deep grudge against Hé Shàozhèng.
In winter,
he was accused of an impropriety during the calendar distribution and escorting of the imperial carriage,
caned below the palace gate,
and demoted to Judge of Hǎizhōu.
He was successively promoted to Prefect of Chízhōu,
where he built over fifty embankments in Tónglíng to guard against drought and flood.
When Chén Háo rebelled
and attacked Ānqìng,
the people of Chí were terrified,
but Hé Shàozhèng ascended the city wall and held it firmly.
After the rebellion was quelled,
his salary was increased by one grade,
and he was promoted to Provincial Administration Commissioner of Jiāngxī and then retired.
The people of Chí built a temple for him,
worshipping him alongside Bāo Zhěng of the Sòng dynasty.
Xǔ Tiānxī,
courtesy name Qǐzhōng,
was from Mǐnxiàn.
He passed the imperial examination in the sixth year of Hóngzhì.
He was redesignated as a Shu-jí-shì.
He fell ill from longing for his parents
and submitted a petition requesting leave.
Emperor Xiàozōng granted him an imperial pass for his journey.
Upon returning to court,
he was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Personnel.
At that time, Censorate officials Hé Tiānqú and Ní Tiānmíng, along with Xǔ Tiānxī, all enjoyed contemporary renown,
and the people of the capital referred to them as
"The Three Tians of the Censorate and Ministries."
In the twelfth year,
the library in Jiàn'ān caught fire.
Xǔ Tiānxī said:
"Last year, the Temple of Confucius in Quēlǐ suffered a disaster by fire,
and this year, Jiàn'ān has again caught fire,
with ancient and modern printed books reduced to ashes.
Quēlǐ
is where the Dao originates;
the library
is where literature gathers.
In the Spring and Autumn Annals, it is recorded that the Xuānxiè Pavilion caught fire,
and commentators said: 'The pavilion
is where musical instruments are stored.
Heaven's will seems to say: if one cannot govern,
what use are rituals and music?
If rituals and music are not practiced,
Heaven therefore burned their repository as a warning.'
Currently, scholar-officials neglect their duties,
and correct teachings are not cultivated.
What is valued by those above is superficiality,
and what is practiced by those below are trivialities.
This series of disasters
seems intended to purge accumulated filth from the scholarly community.
It is fitting to dispatch officials to inspect the situation
and edit and publish beneficial classical and historical texts.
As for the empty rhetoric of the late Sòng,
such as 'Discussions on Fan,' 'Discussions on Grass,' 'Strategies,' 'Oceans of Strategies,' 'Literary Balances,' 'Literary Essences,' 'Main Ideas,' and 'Lecture Notes,'
all should be banned from printing.
This will be of no small benefit
to cultivating talent."
The relevant departments deliberated and followed his advice,
ordering the education officials to review and correct the texts.
When there was a mishap in Dàtóng,
Xǔ Tiānxī went to investigate,
fully ascertaining the facts,
and Governor Hóng Hàn, palace eunuch Liú Yún, Commander-in-chief Wáng Xǐ, and others were all punished.
The palace attendant Liú Xióng was angered by the Magistrate of Yízhēn, Xú Huái, for not maintaining the imperial kitchen properly,
and reported him to the palace eunuch commanding the Nánjīng garrison, who relayed the message,
leading to Xú Huái's arrest and imprisonment in the imperial prison.
Xǔ Tiānxī and Censor Féng Yǔnzhōng argued for his rescue,
and Xú Huái was eventually transferred to a border county.
When Censors Wén Sēn, Zhāng Jīn, and Zēng Dàyǒu were handed over to officials for speaking out,
and Cuī Zhìduān was promoted from a Daoist priest to Minister,
Xǔ Tiānxī strenuously argued against all of these.
In the fifth month of the seventeenth year,
with celestial anomalies occurring, an appeal for advice was made.
He submitted a memorial saying:
"The three-year evaluation system for external officials,
along with the supervision of Circuit Censors and Grand Coordinators,
and the impeachment by Supervising Secretaries and Censors,
is already as perfect as can be.
However, high-ranking officials in the two capitals are not subject to routine evaluation.
And although there is a ten-year evaluation rule for officials below the fifth rank,
they usually serve for a limited nine years,
or are transferred due to age and service,
or are reassigned after mourning leave,
so they cannot complete the term.
I now request that the term be set at six years,
and that a universal evaluation be carried out.
For high-ranking officials who have been impeached,
they should all be ordered to make self-reports and be dismissed,
as a warning to those in positions of authority.
In ancient times,
disasters and anomalies led to the dismissal of the Three Ducal Ministers,
and continuous rain would prompt the ruler to vacate his position.
Now, ministers do not acknowledge their faults,
and Your Majesty does not dismiss them.
It is appropriate to temporarily abolish the titles of Duke and Grand Guardian,
and restore them to their positions
once Heaven's will has returned.
Our ancestors governed palace eunuchs
without indiscriminately bestowing favors,
and without lightly pardoning legal transgressions.
The twenty-four directorates and bureaus of the imperial household and those managing affairs outside
all had regular staff.
In recent years, the number of seal-holders and assistant directors in various directorates and bureaus has reached thirty or forty,
with countless other managers;
the same applies to the auxiliary capital.
They are arrogant, extravagant, and tyrannical,
corrupting the people's wealth,
with mansions reaching the clouds
and fields spread across the countryside,
fine food satiating even servants,
and embroidered silk covering dogs and horses.
All such instances
are sufficient to invite calamity.
I beg that the Directorate of Ceremonial be ordered to collaborate with the Grand Secretariat to conduct a strict evaluation,
to determine who stays and who leaves.
Thereafter,
this should be carried out every three or five years,
established as a permanent system."
The emperor approved.
Thereupon, he ordered all officials of the fourth rank and above in the two capitals to make self-reports and await orders,
and officials below the fifth rank to undergo evaluation every six years,
which then became law.
However, the proposals to strip ministers of their ducal and grand guardian titles and to evaluate palace eunuchs
were obstructed and not implemented.
Soon after, together with Censor Hé Shēn, he investigated the imperial stables,
and submitted fourteen beneficial proposals,
saving over five hundred thousand in fodder expenses annually.
In the seventh month of Wǔzōng's (武宗) enthronement,
he submitted a memorial due to calamities and strange phenomena,
requesting a thorough self-examination and reform,
and widespread solicitation of candid advice.
He was promoted to Zǔ Gěishìzhōng (左給事中) of the Gōngkē (工科).
In the first year of Zhèngdé (正德),
he was sent as an envoy to enfeoff Ānnán (安南).
En route, he was promoted to Dū Gěishìzhōng (都給事中).
In the spring of the third year,
he completed his mission and returned to court.
Observing the great changes in court affairs,
where those who dared to speak were all demoted or exiled,
and Liú Jǐn's (劉瑾) tyranny became even more severe,
Xǔ Tiānxī (許天錫) was greatly indignant.
On the first day of the sixth month,
he audited the imperial treasury,
and discovered dozens of cases of Liú Jǐn's (劉瑾) embezzlement and concealment.
Knowing that submitting a memorial would certainly lead to disaster,
he secretly prepared a petition for the Dēngwéngǔ (登聞鼓) that night,
intending to offer remonstrance with his life,
and instructed his family to submit it after his death.
Then he hanged himself.
At that time, his wife and children were not with him;
only a servant boy was by his side,
who hid the petition and fled.
Some say that Liú Jǐn (劉瑾), fearing Xǔ Tiānxī (許天錫) would expose his crimes,
sent people at night to strangle him.
The truth could not be ascertained.
At that time, there was an imperial edict ordering the Jǐnyīwèi (錦衣衞) to check the attendance of the Gěishìzhōng (給事中) of the Six Divisions,
and to impeach those who were absent.
The commander of the Jǐnyīwèi (錦衣衞) impeached Xǔ Tiānxī (許天錫) for three days of absence.
When questioned,
he was already dead.
Those who heard of it mourned him.
When Liú Jǐn (劉瑾) was in power,
he was exceedingly arrogant,
and particularly detested remonstrating officials.
Those who feared disaster often committed suicide.
Zhōu Yuè (周鑰) from Hǎiyáng (海陽),
a *Jìnshì* (進士) of Hóngzhì (弘治) fifteenth year,
served as Gěishìzhōng (給事中) of the Bīngkē (兵科).
While investigating a matter in Huái'ān (淮安),
he became good friends with Zhīfǔ (知府) Zhào Jùn (趙俊).
Zhào Jùn (趙俊) promised him a loan of a thousand pieces of gold,
but later did not give it.
At that time, Liú Jǐn (劉瑾) demanded heavy bribes from
all who returned from imperial missions.
Zhōu Yuè (周鑰) saw no way out,
and when his boat reached Táoyuán (桃源),
he committed suicide by slitting his throat.
His attendants rescued him,
but he was already unable to speak.
He took a piece of paper and wrote
"Zhào Zhīfǔ (趙知府) has wronged me,"
and then died.
When the incident was reported,
Zhào Jùn (趙俊) was arrested and brought to the capital,
and questioned about Zhōu Yuè's (周鑰) death.
Ultimately, Zhào Jùn (趙俊) was convicted.
Xī Kuí (郗夔) from Píngdìng (平定),
a *Jìnshì* (進士) of Hóngzhì (弘治) fifteenth year,
served as Gěishìzhōng (給事中) of the Lǐkē (禮科).
In the fifth year of Zhèngdé (正德),
he was sent out to audit military achievements in Yánsuí (延綏).
Liú Jǐn (劉瑾) made requests through his confidants.
Xī Kuí (郗夔) realized that following them would violate national laws,
but not following them would bring disaster.
So he hanged himself.
Féng Yǒng (馮顒) from Qióngshān (瓊山),
a *Jìnshì* (進士) of Hóngzhì (弘治) ninth year,
served as Yùshǐ (御史).
He once offended Liú Jǐn (劉瑾) over a matter,
was slandered by him,
and committed suicide by hanging.
Féng Yǒng (馮顒) initially served as Zhǔshì (主事).
When the imperial army had long failed to suppress the rebellious Lí Fúnánshé (黎符南蛇),
Féng Yǒng (馮顒) detailed the causes of the unrest,
and proposed to recruit the descendants of deposed native officials,
to mobilize their former soldiers
and use barbarians to fight barbarians.
If they achieved success, they would be restored to their former positions.
Shàngshū (尚書) Liú Dàxià (劉大夏) highly praised this,
and memorialized to implement his strategy.
In the early Zhèngdé (正德) period,
he accompanied the eunuch Gāo Jīn (高金) to investigate the land requested by Jīngwáng (涇王) for estates,
and successfully recovered over two thousand seven hundred *qǐng* (頃).
However, he met an untimely death,
which everyone lamented.
After Liú Jǐn (劉瑾) was executed,
Xǔ Tiānxī (許天錫), Zhōu Yuè (周鑰), Xī Kuí (郗夔), and Féng Yǒng (馮顒) were all posthumously restored to their official ranks and granted sacrificial rites,
and their families were provided for.
During the Jiājìng (嘉靖) reign,
Xǔ Tiānxī's (許天錫) son, Xǔ Chūn (許春), appealed his father's wrongful death,
and his father was again granted sacrificial rites and burial.
When Liú Jǐn (劉瑾) fell,
Yuánwàiláng (員外郎) Sù Jìn (宿進) from Jiājíang (夾江) submitted a memorial outlining six matters,
stating:
"Those who died opposing Liú Jǐn (劉瑾),
such as eunuchs Wáng Yuè (王岳) and Fàn Hēng (范亨),
and remonstrating officials such as Xǔ Tiānxī (許天錫) and Zhōu Yuè (周鑰),
should all be granted posthumous pensions and honors.
Furthermore, high officials who colluded with Liú Jǐn (劉瑾),
such as Bīngbù Shàngshū (兵部尚書) Wáng Chǎng (王敞) and others, as well as the remaining faction of eunuchs,
should all be dismissed."
When the memorial was submitted,
the Emperor was enraged and intended to personally interrogate him,
ordering Zhāng Yǒng (張永) to summon Grand Secretary Lǐ Dōngyáng (李東陽).
Lǐ Dōngyáng (李東陽) said to Zhāng Yǒng (張永):
"This young man is arrogant,
and it is late, not the time to see the Emperor.
Please grant him some leniency."
Zhāng Yǒng (張永) went in,
and shortly after, Sù Jìn (宿進) was seized and brought to Wǔmén (午門),
given fifty strokes of the rod,
stripped of his official status, and sent home.
He died not long after.
In the early Shìzōng (世宗) reign,
he was posthumously granted the title of Guānglù Shàogīng (光祿少卿).
Xú Wénpǔ (徐文溥),
courtesy name Kědà (可大),
was from Kāihuà (開化).
He was a *Jìnshì* (進士) in the sixth year of Zhèngdé (正德).
He was appointed Nánjīng Lǐkē Gěishìzhōng (南京禮科給事中).
He impeached Shàngshū (尚書) Liú Yīng (劉櫻), Dū Yùshǐ (都御史) Lǐ Shìshí (李士實), Shìláng (侍郎) Lǚ Xiàn (呂獻), and Dàlǐ Qīng (大理卿) Máo Qīn (茆欽),
and requested the recall of retired Shàngshū (尚書) Sūn Jiāo (孫交) and Fù Guī (傅珪).
Contemporary opinion considered this appropriate.
When Níngwáng (寧王) Chén Háo (宸濠) sought to restore his guards,
Xú Wénpǔ (徐文溥) remonstrated, saying:
"Previously, due to the unrest in the Níng (寧) principality,
Emperor Yīng (英) abolished its guards and *túntián* (屯田).
When the traitor Liú Jǐn (劉瑾) disturbed the government,
he tried to restore them with heavy bribes.
Since Liú Jǐn (劉瑾) has been executed,
Your Majesty has again abolished them,
precisely to control them with righteousness and ensure their safety.
Yet it is said, 'There is a shortage of people to command.'
But living in deep seclusion,
without the toil of expeditions,
and enjoying honor and glory,
without the responsibility of defense,
for what purpose is there a shortage of people?
Furthermore, the King's tyrannical acts are widely known: he oppresses merchants and common people,
coerces officials,
entices scoundrels,
and widely engages in plunder,
causing shipping to cease
and towns and villages to become desolate,
making all the people gnash their teeth.
Even if we stop him now,
we still fear it might be too late.
How can we allow him to indulge further,
giving wings to a tiger?
Contributions originally had fixed regulations,
yet he senselessly deploys swift horsemen,
entering and exiting the capital,
spying on movements.
Moreover, the nation is currently facing many troubles,
and heavenly anomalies have not ceased.
Unexpected dangers are truly hard to predict.
It is appropriate to restrain him with great righteousness,
and not to indulge private feelings.
Punish those who offered him counsel,
and expel his spying envoys.
This would be a great fortune for the imperial ancestral temple and the state."
At that time, Chén Háo (宸濠) had many powerful supporters,
so when the memorial was submitted,
everyone considered Xú Wénpǔ (徐文溥) to be in danger,
but the Emperor merely blamed him for speaking presumptuously.
He also requested the selection of an heir apparent,
but received no reply.
When he went out to inspect Fèngyáng,
the palace eunuch Shǐ Xuān, who oversaw the Imperial Silk Factories, displayed two yellow cudgels in front of his retinue.
They were called
“賜棍” (Cìgùn, bestowed cudgels),
and he would use them to beat people,
some even to death.
From the Grand Censor down, none dared to question him.
Shìlóng impeached him in a memorial.
He also impeached Liào Kǎi, a chiliarch of the Embroidered Uniform Guard, for engaging in corrupt practices for profit,
and further stated:
“Kǎi's oppression in Shǎnxī
is merely a continuation of his father Péng's old habits of oppression in Hénán.
Hénán was embroiled in chaos due to Péng,
and Kǎi now wishes to cause chaos in Shǎnxī.
I beg that Kǎi and his father be brought to justice,
and that Liào Luán also be recalled
to appease the anger of the people of Shǎnxī.”
Luán
was Kǎi's subordinate, garrisoned in Shǎnxī.
Qián Níng had always been close to Kǎi,
and upon seeing the impeachment, he harbored great hatred.
He then used Shìlóng's investigation of Xuē Fèngmíng's case to frame him.
Fèngmíng,
a native of Bǎodí,
had formerly been a censor,
but was stripped of his position for a crime.
He ingratiated himself with various treacherous favorites,
and was particularly close to Níng.
He had a grudge against his younger cousin Fèngxiáng,
and incited the investigators to expose Fèngxiáng's private affairs,
leading to his arrest and sentencing to death.
The Ministry of Justice suspected an injustice,
and also arrested and interrogated Fèngmíng.
Fèngmíng, in fear,
had his concubine complain of injustice,
and then he himself cut his throat outside the Cháng'ānmén gate.
His testimony implicated Zhōu Zài, the magistrate of Bǎodí, and dozens of people he had always held grudges against,
all of whom were arrested and handed over to the judicial authorities.
Fèngmíng, however, was released.
Shìlóng and Censor Xǔ Wán successively investigated the case,
re-arrested Fèngmíng for questioning,
and released Zài, restoring him to his post.
Níng was enraged
and ordered Fèngmíng's daughter to accuse Shìlóng and Wán of partiality and injustice in handling the case.
Consequently, they were imprisoned by imperial decree,
and Shìlóng was demoted to judicial sub-prefect of Jìnzhōu.
After a long time,
he was promoted to prefect.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
an imperial decree restored him to his former office,
and he was sent out as Vice Commissioner of Shǎnxī.
The bandits Wáng Dà and others in Hánzhōng hid in influential families
and colluded with Huíhuí (Muslims) to cause unrest.
Shìlóng issued an order that
those who harbored bandits would be punished with their wives and children, without mercy.
The bandits had nowhere to hide
and were subsequently captured and annihilated.
He built dikes to irrigate a thousand qīng (mu) of fields,
which benefited the people.
He died in office.
Zhāng Wénmíng,
courtesy name Yìngkuí,
was a native of Yángqǔ.
He passed the imperial examination in the sixth year of Zhèngdé (1511).
He was appointed an envoy (xíngrén)
and then promoted to censor,
patrolling Liáodōng,
and soon after, Shǎnxī.
The garrison eunuch Liào Táng was greedy and tyrannical.
Wénmíng arrested and punished twenty-four of his henchmen,
which greatly angered Táng.
In the thirteenth year (1518),
the imperial chariot visited Yánsuī.
Wénmíng swiftly presented a memorial of remonstrance,
detailing the calamities and unusual phenomena,
and further stating that Jiāng Bīn indulged in evil and led the emperor astray,
and should be executed immediately.
He also stated that court officials who failed to provide corrective advice
should likewise be punished.
The emperor ignored it.
Later, Wénmíng attended the emperor's traveling court.
He restrained the powerful favorites who accompanied the emperor,
and many of their demands were not met.
The eunuchs of the Directorate of Ceremonial, Zhāng Zhōng and others, slandered him to the emperor,
saying that students beat flag-soldiers,
and Wénmíng deliberately failed to punish them.
The emperor was enraged
and ordered him shackled and sent to the capital,
where he was imprisoned by imperial decree.
In the spring of the following year,
officials repeatedly memorialized requesting his pardon,
but received no reply.
When the imperial chariot returned,
he was ordered to be brought to the Leopard Chamber,
where the emperor intended to personally interrogate him.
Wénmíng believed he would surely die.
However, upon seeing the emperor,
he was ordered to be released
and demoted to judicial sub-prefect of Diànbái.
At that time,
although Liú Jǐn had been executed,
the treacherous favorites were still rampant,
and countless remonstrating officials, both inside and outside the court, suffered misfortune.
Wénmíng's mere demotion
was considered fortunate by people.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was recalled and restored to his former office,
and soon after, was sent out as Prefect of Sōngjiāng.
He died
shortly after arriving at his post.
Patrolling Censor Mǎ Lù praised his loyalty,
and an imperial decree posthumously granted him the title of Junior Supervisor of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
Chén Dǐng,
courtesy name Dàqì,
was originally from Xuānchéng.
His great-great-grandfather, Minister Dí,
died during the disaster of Emperor Huìdì.
His descendants were assigned to guard Dēngzhōu Garrison,
and thus settled there.
Dǐng passed the imperial examination in the eighteenth year of Hóngzhì (1505).
In the fourth year of Zhèngdé (1509), he was appointed acting investigating censor of the Ministry of Rites.
The garrison eunuch Liào Táng in Hénán,
a native of Fújiàn,
had his nephew Kǎi (son of his brother Péng) fraudulently register for the Hénán provincial examination.
Public opinion was in an uproar,
but fearing Táng, no one dared to challenge him.
Dǐng submitted a memorial exposing the matter,
and Kǎi was consequently dismissed.
Táng and Péng harbored great hatred.
When roving bandits arose,
Dǐng proposed strategies for suppressing them.
Táng instructed the powerful favorites to extract phrases from Dǐng's memorial to provoke the emperor's anger,
and Dǐng was imprisoned by imperial decree and tortured.
They accused Dǐng of previously registering the assets of Píngjiāng Bó
and colluding with Liú Jǐn to inflate prices,
suspecting embezzlement.
Minister Yáng Yīqīng saved him,
and he was then released as a commoner.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was restored to his former office
and promoted to Provincial Administrator of Hénán.
When the cult leader Mǎ Lóng and others caused unrest,
Dǐng commanded troops to suppress them.
He was transferred to Vice Commissioner of Shǎnxī,
and then promoted to Provincial Surveillance Commissioner of Zhèjiāng.
He was honest, incorruptible, and upright,
and would not entertain private requests.
He was recalled to serve as Prefect of Yìngtiān Fǔ,
but died before taking office.
Hè Tài,
courtesy name Zhìtóng,
was a native of Wúxiàn.
He passed the imperial examination in the twelfth year of Hóngzhì (1499).
He served as a judicial sub-prefect of Qúzhōu Prefecture before being appointed censor.
Emperor Wǔzōng recruited ruffians from the capital and eunuch servants as adopted sons.
One day, one hundred and twenty-seven people were bestowed the imperial surname.
Tài outspokenly criticized this as wrong.
These people incited the emperor's anger,
and he was demoted to judicial sub-prefect of Qúzhōu.
He ended his career as a Provincial Administrator of Guǎngdōng.
Zhāng Pú,
courtesy name Zhōngshàn,
was a native of Jiāngxià.
He passed the imperial examination in the eighteenth year of Hóngzhì (1505).
He was appointed magistrate of Guī'ān County and then recalled to serve as censor.
In the eighth year of Zhèngdé (1513), he was sent out to patrol Yúnnán.
The garrison eunuch Liáng Yù was corrupt and tyrannical,
and Pú curbed him.
He was then slandered by Yù,
arrested and sent to an imperial prison,
where he died.
When Shìzōng succeeded to the throne,
he was posthumously granted the title of Junior Supervisor of the Court of the Imperial Stud
and given imperial sacrifices and burial.
Chéng Wén,
a native of Shānyīn, Dàtóng.
He passed the imperial examination in the fifteenth year of Hóngzhì (1502).
He was promoted from magistrate to censor.
During the Zhèngdé reign,
Ā'ěrtūshī and Yìbùlà, after being defeated in battle by the Little Prince,
led their部 (bù, tribes/followers) to encamp outside the Great Wall in Gānsù.
They frequently raided
and captured fifty-three forts and strongholds.
Governor Zhāng Yì and garrison eunuch Zhū Bīn and others, however, falsely claimed credit for over nineteen hundred enemy heads,
and eleven of them submitted reports of victory.
Wén went on an inspection tour
and exposed all their deceptions.
Yì and others bribed palace intermediaries to turn the tide against Wén.
At that time, Wén had impeached Assistant Surveillance Commissioner Zhào Yìnglóng,
who in turn exposed trivial matters about Wén,
leading to Wén's arrest
and dismissal as a commoner.
During the Jiājìng reign, he was reappointed,
and successively served as Vice Minister of War and Grand Censor, patrolling Liáodōng.
He retired,
and then died.
Lǐ Hànchén,
a native of Dàtóng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the third year of Zhèngdé (1508).
He served as a Censor,
touring Shāndōng.
When Liáng Gǔ, a director in the Ministry of Personnel, falsely accused Prince Guīshàn, Dānghù, of plotting rebellion,
Hànchén impeached Gǔ for acting out of personal spite.
However, favored courtiers, eager to claim merit,
accused Hànchén of covering up for a rebel.
