He was arrested and imprisoned in the imperial prison,
then demoted to assistant magistrate of Dézhōu.
He eventually served as Shāndōng Vice Surveillance Commissioner.
Zhāng Jīng,
a native of Xīngzhōu Zuǒwèi.
He became a *jìnshì* in the sixth year of Zhèngdé (1511).
He served as a Censor.
He was dispatched to tour Xuānfǔ,
where he impeached Yú Xǐ, the guarding eunuch, for his greed and wantonness.
He was impeached in turn by Xǐ,
arrested and imprisoned in the imperial prison,
then demoted to records keeper of Héxī, Yúnnán.
He died shortly after.
At the beginning of Shìzōng's reign,
he was granted posthumous honors and sacrifices, similar to Zhāng Pú.
Máo Sīyì,
a native of Yángxìn.
He became a *jìnshì* in the fifteenth year of Hóngzhì (1502).
He served as Prefect of Yǒngpíng.
In the thirteenth year of Zhèngdé (1518), when the emperor made a trip to Chāngpíng,
women in the populace were startled and fled.
Sīyì issued an order stating:
"With the great mourning not yet performed,
the imperial carriage will certainly not travel far.
Without official documents,
anyone who falsely claims the emperor has arrived and disturbs the people
will be punished according to the law."
Guō Yuán, the guarding eunuch, who had a grudge against Sīyì,
reported this.
Sīyì was immediately arrested and thrown into the imperial prison,
where he was held for half a year,
then demoted to Prefect of Ānníng, Yúnnán.
During the Jiājìng era,
he was successively promoted to Vice Censor-in-chief and Grand Coordinator of Yìngtiān.
Hú Wénbì,
a native of Léiyáng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the twelfth year of Hóngzhì (1499).
At the beginning of the Zhèngdé era,
he was transferred from a director in the Ministry of Revenue to a Censor.
He was dispatched to govern Fèngyáng,
then promoted to Tianjin Vice Surveillance Commissioner.
Zhāng Zhōng, a eunuch, supervised the imperial estates in Zhígū,
allowing his associates to profit unscrupulously.
Wénbì arrested and prosecuted them.
He was framed by them,
arrested, shackled, and imprisoned in the imperial prison,
then demoted to records manager of Yán'ān Prefecture.
At the beginning of the Jiājìng era,
he was successively promoted to Sichuan Surveillance Commissioner.
Wáng Xiàng,
a native of Guāngshān.
He became a *jìnshì* in the third year of Zhèngdé (1508).
He served as a Censor.
In the twelfth year (1517), he toured Shāndōng.
Lí Jiàn, the guarding eunuch, used the pretext of tribute collection to extort excessively.
Xiàng ordered the prefectures and counties not to comply.
Jiàn was enraged
and falsely reported him to the court.
He was arrested and imprisoned in the imperial prison,
then demoted to assistant magistrate of Gāoyóu.
He died not long after.
At the beginning of the Jiājìng era,
he was posthumously granted the title of Junior Steward of the Court of Imperial Entertainments.
Dǒng Xiàng,
a native of Sōngxiàn.
He became a *jìnshì* in the sixth year of Zhèngdé (1511).
He served as a Censor.
He inspected the various passes of Jūyōng.
When Jiāng Bīn sent his junior officer Mǐ Yīng to arrest people in Pínggǔ,
Mǐ Yīng relied on his power and behaved extremely arrogantly.
Xiàng arrested him and beat him,
intending to report the matter.
Bīn immediately slandered him to the emperor,
and Xiàng was arrested, shackled, and imprisoned in the imperial prison,
then demoted to assistant magistrate of Xúzhōu.
At the beginning of the Jiājìng era,
he was recalled to his former office.
He eventually served as Shāndōng Vice Surveillance Commissioner.
Liú Shìyuán,
a native of Péngxiàn.
He became a *jìnshì* in the sixth year of Zhèngdé (1511).
He served as a Censor,
touring the Gīfǔ.
In the thirteenth year (1518),
when the emperor hunted at Gǔběikǒu,
intending to invite Huā Dāng and Bǎ’érsūn of the Duǒyán Guard to a banquet,
Shìyuán presented four reasons why this should not be done.
Previously,
when the emperor visited Héxīwù,
commander Huáng Xūn had exploited his position as an imperial attendant to disturb the people.
Shìyuán investigated him.
Xūn, fearing,
fled to the imperial encampment
and, through favored courtiers, slandered Shìyuán to the emperor,
claiming that Shìyuán, upon hearing of the emperor's arrival,
ordered the populace to marry off all their daughters
and hide their women.
The emperor was enraged
and ordered him to be stripped, bound, and interrogated face-to-face.
As there were no cudgels in the field,
forty strokes were inflicted on him with a fresh willow branch,
nearly killing him.
He was then rushed into the capital in a cage cart.
Along with him, more than ten people, including County Magistrate Cáo Jùn,
were arrested and imprisoned in the imperial prison.
Wáng Jǐng, the Censor-in-chief, and Chen Zhān, Niú Tiānlín, and others from the Censorate submitted memorials to plead for him,
but received no response.
He was demoted to postmaster of Líshān.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was restored to his former office,
and dispatched to serve as Prefect of Húzhōu,
then promoted to Huguǎng Vice Surveillance Commissioner.
He managed relief efforts for famine,
accumulating over a million *shi* of grain.
When this was reported,
he was commended and rewarded.
In the ninth year of Jiājìng (1530), he was successively promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-chief,
and Grand Coordinator of Guìzhōu.
After three years, he was dismissed.
Fàn Lù,
courtesy name Yǐzài,
a native of Guìyáng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the sixth year of Zhèngdé (1511).
He was appointed an Usher,
then made Nanjing Censor.
As Wǔzōng had no heir for a long time,
Lù, together with his colleagues, requested that a worthy member of the imperial clan be chosen and raised in the palace,
following the precedent of Sòng Rénzōng,
but this was not adopted.
He successively impeached the eunuchs Lí Ān and Liú Láng, and the guard officials Jiǎn Wén and Wáng Zhōng, for their crimes.
He also argued that since Lady Mǎ was pregnant,
she should not enter the palace.
His words were all sharp and direct.
Soon after, he was ordered to pacify Jiāngxī.
When Prince Níng, Chénháo, ordered all officials to see him in court robes,
Lù objected.
He memorialized, saying:
"When Gāo Dì established the system,
subordinates of princely establishments were referred to as 'officials' (*guān*).
Later, they were called 'subjects' (*chén*).
Other civil and military officials, and capital officials on imperial missions, were all referred to as 'officials' (*guān*),
and imperial envoys met in informal attire.
Today, the ceremonial regulations for princely establishments throughout the empire
are not clearly defined.
Your subject believes that there cannot be two supreme authorities,
and therefore, all who do not refer to themselves as 'subjects' (*chén*)
should not wear court robes,
to strictly maintain the great distinction."
The memorial was sent to the ritual officials for deliberation.
Chénháo immediately submitted a memorial to dispute it,
but the court deliberation requested to follow Lù's words.
When Qín Róng, Chénháo's entertainer, acted presumptuously and extravagantly,
Lù impeached and prosecuted him.
He also impeached Bì Zhēn, the guarding eunuch, for fifteen acts of greed and cruelty,
but the memorial was held back and not acted upon.
Zhēn then fabricated other charges to falsely accuse him,
and he was subsequently arrested and imprisoned in the imperial prison.
As the emperor was on an imperial tour,
he was detained for a year.
It was not until the fourth month of the fourteenth year (1519) that he was demoted to Administrator of the Lóngzhōu Pacification Commission.
Not long after,
Chénháo and Zhēn were executed for their rebellion,
and Censors Xiè Yuán, Wǔ Xīrú, and others submitted memorials recommending Lù.
Before he could be recalled,
Shìzōng ascended the throne,
and he was restored to his former office.
He was promoted to Fujian Assistant Surveillance Commissioner,
then transferred to Jiangxi Vice Surveillance Commissioner,
and retired to his hometown.
He was later recommended by Hú Shìníng
and appointed Military Preparations Vice Surveillance Commissioner of Mìyún.
He had meritorious service in suppressing mining bandits,
and successively served as Jiangxi and Fujian Left and Right Administration Commissioner.
He died in office.
Zhāng Qīn,
courtesy name Jìngzhī,
a native of Tōngzhōu, Shùntiān.
He became a *jìnshì* in the sixth year of Zhèngdé (1511).
He was appointed an Usher, then made Censor,
inspecting the various passes of Jūyōng.
In the seventh month of the twelfth year,
the emperor listened to Jiāng Bīn's words,
and intended to leave the pass and visit Xuānfǔ.
Qīn submitted a memorial, remonstrating thus:
"I have heard that enlightened rulers do not detest straightforward criticism to embrace loyalty,
and valiant gentlemen do not fear the punishment of death to remonstrate to the utmost.
Recently,
rumors have been rife,
saying that the imperial carriage desires to cross Jūyōng
and travel far to the frontier.
I estimate that Your Majesty does not wish to wander idly,
but rather intends to personally lead an expedition against the northern barbarians.
Yet, I am unaware that the northern barbarians, though rampant,
can only be dealt with by dispatching generals for a punitive expedition;
how can Your Majesty, the Lord of Ten Thousand Chariots, personally toil?
Emperor Yīngzōng did not listen to the words of his grand ministers,
and the six armies marched far,
resulting in the incident of Jǐsì.
Moreover, even a common man does not make light of himself,
how can Your Majesty, whose person is tied to the ancestral temples and the altars of grain and soil, venture into unforeseen dangers?
Currently, internally there is no imperial prince overseeing the state,
nor is there a crown prince presiding over the court.
Externally, Gānsù suffers from the trouble of the native Tibetans,
Jiāngyòu has the disturbance of bandits,
Huáinán has the difficulty of grain transport,
and Bāshǔ has the hardship of procurement.
The various prefectures of the capital region had a poor harvest of summer wheat,
and autumn floods brought calamity.
Yet Your Majesty, without foreseeing disaster,
wishes to loose the reins and drive far,
displaying troops beyond the desolate frontier;
I am secretly concerned about this."
Later,
hearing that the emperor did not accept any of the fervent remonstrances from court officials,
he again submitted a memorial, stating:
"Your humble servant foolishly believes there are three reasons why the imperial carriage must not leave: the people's hearts are agitated,
and provisions are vast and burdensome,
this is one;
traveling far over dangerous obstacles,
the two empresses are worried,
this is two;
the northern barbarians are currently strong,
and it is difficult to contend with them,
this is three.
As your servant holds the office of censor,
and has been commanded to patrol the passes,
it is my duty to devote myself to death,
and I dare not spare my life and fail Your Majesty."
The memorial was submitted,
but not responded to.
On the first day of the eighth month,
the emperor traveled incognito to Chāngpíng,
and the news of his urgent departure from the pass was transmitted.
Qīn ordered Commander Sūn Xǐ to close the pass,
and put the gate key away.
The eunuch in charge of the defense, Liú Sōng, wanted to go to Chāngpíng to pay respects,
but Qīn stopped him, saying:
"The imperial carriage is about to leave the pass;
this is a moment of life and death for you and me today.
If the pass is not opened,
the imperial carriage cannot leave,
and disobeying the Son of Heaven's command
means death.
If the pass is opened,
and the imperial carriage leaves,
the state of affairs in the realm is unknowable.
Should there be an event like 'Tǔmù',
you and I will also die.
Better to die for not opening the pass;
such a death will be immortal."
A short while later,
the emperor summoned Xǐ.
Xǐ said:
"The censor is present,
your servant dares not leave without authorization."
So, Sōng was summoned instead.
Sōng said to Qīn:
"I am a servant of the emperor's household;
how dare I not go?"
Qīn then carried the imperial seal and, with sword in hand, sat by the pass gate, saying:
"Anyone who dares speak of opening the pass
shall be executed."
That night, he drafted a memorial, stating:
"I have heard that when the Son of Heaven is about to personally lead an expedition,
he must first issue an edict in advance to convene a discussion with court officials.
When he proceeds,
the six armies guard him,
and a hundred officials follow,
and only then are there sounds of carriages and horses,
and the splendor of feathers and banners.
Now, there is utter silence, not a word heard,
yet it is suddenly said 'the imperial carriage will pass through the gate today'.
This must be someone using Your Majesty's name to go beyond the frontier and collude with barbarians;
I request to capture this person
and punish him according to the law.
If Your Majesty truly wishes to leave the pass,
then both empresses must affix their seals;
only then will your servant dare to open it.
Otherwise, I will die ten thousand times rather than obey the edict."
Before the memorial reached him,
an envoy came again.
Qīn drew his sword and shouted at him, saying:
"This is a deception!"
The envoy, terrified, returned
and told the emperor
that "Censor Zhāng almost killed your servant."
The emperor was furious,
and turned to Zhū Níng:
"Go quickly and apprehend and kill the censor for me."
At that time, Liáng Chǔ, Jiǎng Miǎn, and others had pursued him to Shāhé,
and pleaded with the emperor to return to the capital.
The emperor hesitated, undecided,
but Qīn's memorial also arrived,
and many other court officials also remonstrated,
so the emperor had no choice but to return from Chāngpíng,
his displeasure lingering.
About twenty more days later,
Qīn was inspecting Báiyángkǒu.
The emperor, in disguise, departed from Déshèngmén,
spent the night in a civilian house in Yángfáng,
and then sped out of the pass,
repeatedly asking where the censor was.
Qīn heard about it,
pursued him,
but was already too late.
He wished to submit another memorial,
but the emperor had sent the eunuch Gǔ Dàyòng to guard the pass,
forbidding anyone from leaving.
Qīn, filled with indignation,
wept bitterly, looking west.
Thus, in the capital, the story of Censor Zhāng closing the pass with three memorials became widespread.
The following year,
the emperor returned from Xuānfǔ.
Upon reaching the pass,
he smiled and said,
"Previously, the censor obstructed me,
but now I have returned,"
yet he did not punish him.
When Emperor Shìzōng succeeded to the throne,
Qīn was appointed Prefect of Hànzhōng.
He successively held the post of Grand Minister of the Imperial Stud.
In the seventeenth year of Jiājìng, he was made Vice Censor-in-Chief on the Right, inspecting Sìchuān.
He was summoned to be Left Vice Minister of Works,
but was criticized and dismissed.
Qīn's original surname was Lǐ.
After he became prominent,
he resumed his original surname.
He was filial to his parents.
If they were displeased,
he would kneel long and plead,
stopping only when they were appeased.
Zhōu Guǎng,
courtesy name Kèzhī,
was a native of Kūnshān.
He became a *jìnshì* in the eighteenth year of Hóngzhì.
He successively served as Magistrate of Pútián and Jíshuǐ counties.
During the Zhèngdé reign,
he was summoned for his excellent governance and appointed Censor.
He submitted a memorial outlining four matters,
briefly stating: "Before the Three Dynasties,
there was no Buddhist doctrine.
Moreover, Tibetan Lamas are even despised by Buddhist teachings.
With copper rings piercing their ears,
and wearing ochre robes,
they violate rites and laws,
and
indulge in immorality and depravity.
They ought to be banished to the four distant borders
to guard against evil spirits;
how can they be allowed near the sovereign,
providing a pretext for bandits to raise troops?
In ancient times, Yǔ warned Shùn, saying:
'Do not be like Dānzhū, arrogant,
who only loved idle wandering.'
Duke of Zhōu warned King Chéng, saying:
'Do not be like King Zhòu of Shāng, confused and disordered,
indulging
in the vice of wine.'
Today's actors
are those who aid idle wandering and confusion.
Emperor Zhuāngzōng of Táng dallied with actors,
and when one man cried out in the night,
he fled in haste and panic.
Your servant
believes that musicians should be expelled
and no longer registered within the palace,
this is how to ban the music of Zhèng.
Your Majesty inherits the lineage of your ancestors,
yet petty individuals offer flattery and bewitch you,
causing the three palaces to harbor resentment,
and the orchid hall to be without issue.
Although Your Majesty is in the prime of life,
do you
not consider the plan for ten thousand generations?
Even common people with some assets
still keep concubines to ensure succession.
There has never been one who exclusively raised adopted sons,
disregarding the continuation of the ancestral line."
also.
The adopted son, Qián Níng 錢寧, was originally a palace eunuch’s attendant,
and had been excessively favored.
He then extorted and seized bribes,
and lightly disregarded royal decrees.
He even presented his calling card to people,
calling himself
a royal illegitimate son.
The crime of his usurpation was unbearable to speak of.
“Why does Your Majesty not carefully select worthy members of the imperial clan,
place them by your side,
to await the birth of an imperial heir?
All
the adopted sons and foster children should have their titles and ranks revoked.
This is how to keep sycophants at a distance.
Recently, the censors in the two capitals who have discussed ministers being derelict in their duty to resist bandits,
Your Majesty has generally treated with leniency,
even pardoning military generals who violated discipline rather than executing them.
Therefore, military morale is not
high,
and success is not in sight.
The plains and riverbanks are covered with white bones,
piled up like hills.
Sending out an army of 100,000
costs 1,000 gold pieces daily.
Now the empire is so exhausted that its bones are visible and its flesh
has wasted away.
Should generals in command, such as Chén Jīn 陳金 and Lù Wán 陸完 and their ilk, be allowed to leisurely play at resisting bandits,
without being severely reprimanded?
I request that a deadline be set for them to achieve success,
in order
to atone for their past faults.”
When Níng 寧 saw the memorial, he was furious,
and held it without issuing an order.
He then issued an imperial decree to demote Guǎng 廣 to the Postmaster of Huáiyuǎn 懷遠驛 in Guǎngdōng 廣東.
Principal Scribe Cáo Hǔ 曹琥 interceded for him,
and was also demoted.
Níng 寧’s anger did not subside,
and he sent people to block the road and assassinate Guǎng 廣.
Guǎng 廣 knew of this,
changed his name,
disguised himself,
and traveled secretly for over 400 *lǐ* before escaping.
The Marquis of Wǔdìng 武定, Guō Xūn 郭勛, who was stationed in Guǎngdōng 廣東,
acted on Níng 寧’s implied instruction by testing Guǎng 廣 with 100 pieces of silver.
Guǎng 廣 refused to accept it.
When Guǎng 廣 paid a visit to the censor,
Guō Xūn 郭勛 seized him and brought him to the army headquarters,
where he was flogged and tied up, almost to death.
The censor interceded for him, and he was finally released.
Two years later,
he was promoted to Magistrate of Jiànchāng 建昌,
and governed effectively.
Níng 寧 forged an imperial decree to demote him again to Postmaster of Zhúzhài 竹寨.
When Shìzōng 世宗 ascended the throne,
he was restored to his former post,
and successively served as Vice Commissioner of Jiāngxī 江西,
and concurrently Supervisor of Schools.
In the second year of Jiājìng 嘉靖 (1523), he was recommended for his outstanding administrative achievements,
and promoted to Provincial Surveillance Commissioner of Fújiàn 福建.
The eunuch who was stationed there as garrison commander sent him 100 gold pieces.
Guǎng 廣 stored it in the treasury,
intending to impeach him.
The eunuch was afraid,
apologized,
and from then on dared not interfere.
In the sixth year (1527), he became Assistant Censor-in-Chief on circuit in Jiāngxī 江西,
and corrupt officials fled at the mere mention of his name.
He intended to set limits on the land held by powerful gentry,
but it was not carried out.
The following year, he was appointed Vice Minister of Justice in Nánjīng 南京.
He served for two years,
then died suddenly of a severe illness.
At the end of Jiājìng 嘉靖,
he was posthumously appointed Censor-in-Chief.
Guǎng 廣 first entered the Imperial Academy through a provincial recommendation,
and studied under Zhāng Mào 章懋.
In his hometown,
he was good friends with Wèi Xiào 魏校.
Throughout his life, he was stern and serious, without a smile.
As an official, he was upright and resolute,
and did not accept requests or favors.
Scholars and officials alike all feared him.
Cáo Hǔ 曹琥,
courtesy name Ruìqīng 瑞卿,
was a native of Cháo 巢.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the eighteenth year of Hóngzhì 弘治 (1505).
He was appointed Principal Scribe of the Ministry of Works in Nánjīng 南jīng,
then transferred to the Ministry of Revenue.
After he submitted a memorial to save Guǎng 廣,
the Ministry of Personnel proposed transferring him to be an Assistant Prefect of Hénán 河南.
Níng 寧 wanted to exile him further,
so he was instead transferred to Xúndiàn 尋甸,
and then promoted to Assistant Prefect of Guǎngxìn 廣信.
Prince Níng 寧 and the eunuchs stationed as garrison commanders requested contributions,
and frequently imposed levies.
Hǔ 琥, acting as prefect,
adamantly refused to give,
and the gentry and common people were grateful to him.
He was promoted to Prefect of Gǒngchāng 鞏昌,
but died before taking office.
In the early Jiājìng 嘉靖 period,
he was posthumously appointed Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments.
Shí Tiānzhù 石天柱,
courtesy name Jìzhān 季瞻,
was a native of Yuèchí 岳池.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the third year of Zhèngdé 正德 (1508).
When he was to be appointed Investigating Censor,
Lǐ Xiàn 李憲 of the Ministry of Personnel requested that, following the precedent for censors,
he serve a probationary year,
and was appointed probationary Investigating Censor of the Ministry of Revenue.
When the Qiánqīng Gōng 乾清宮 caught fire,
he memorialized:
“Today, outside there are imperial shops,
and inside liquor establishments are set up.
Tibetan monks are favored,
and their ghostly religion is followed.
Border soldiers are recruited,
and their attire is imitated.
Even more, they form brotherhoods,
with no distinction of rank.
You frequently leave the deep palace,
and gallop in the suburbs.
Memorials are placed on high shelves,
and court audiences are held only two or three times a month.
Experienced elders are regarded as superfluous,
while adopted sons are treated as confidants.
Seasonal sacrifices are not personally attended,
and the empress dowager is rarely visited.
You do not consider that the star indicating a new heir has not yet shone,
and the heir apparent’s position has long been vacant.
Since you neither regularly reside in the palace,
nor pre-select a member of the imperial clan,
how can you eliminate the root of disaster,
and plan for the long term?”
He was successively promoted to Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Works.
In the eleventh year (1516),
Grand Coordinator Mǎ Áng 馬昂 presented his younger sister,
who was already pregnant.
The emperor favored her.
Tiānzhù 天柱, leading his colleagues, jointly remonstrated,
but received no reply.
He then submitted another memorial saying:
“Your subjects requested the pregnant woman be sent out,
but have not yet received a reply.
I suspect that Your Majesty intends to establish her child as your own?
Qín 秦 fell because Lǚ Bùwéi 呂不韋 substituted Yíng Zhèng 嬴政 for his own son, and Yíng 秦 perished.
Jìn 晉 fell because Niú Jī 牛繼 substituted the child of Mǎ 氏 for his own, and Mǎ 晉 was extinguished.
Those two rulers only unknowingly [fell victim to]
a treacherous scheme.
Do you mean to say that Your Majesty would also do such a thing?
The imperial throne is supreme,
a descendant of divine intelligence.
Even for such, it is not easy to bear the responsibility,
let alone the child of an unknown.
Even if, by Your Majesty’s power, it succeeds for a time,
in the future, would the princes and imperial clan willingly sit by and watch the ancestral foundation be given to another?
Would the internal and external ministers willingly bow their heads and stand in his court?
We hope that she will be urgently sent out,
to purify the palace,
and dispel the doubts of the empire.”
Still, there was no reply.
There was a temple to Bìxiá Yuánjūn 碧霞元君 on Tài Shān 泰山.
The eunuch Lí Jiàn 黎鑑 requested to collect incense money for repair expenses.
Tiānzhù 天柱 said that the sacrificial rites only recognized the god of Dōng Yuè 東嶽,
and there was no such thing as Bìxiá Yuánjūn 碧霞元君.
Such irregular sacrifices were contrary to propriety
and should not be permitted.
In the fourth month of the twelfth year (1517), an edict ordered the demolition of civilian residences in the Míngyù 鳴玉 and Jìqìng 積慶 two arches outside Xi'ān Mén 西安門,
for construction.
Tiānzhù 天柱 and others memorialized requesting its cessation.
The emperor ignored all of them.
That year,
the Emperor first toured beyond the frontier,
establishing the Zhènguófǔ in Xuānfǔ.
Tiānzhù, leading his colleagues, remonstrated strongly.
When Xiàozhēnchún Huánghòu was to be buried,
the Emperor used "breaking ground" as a pretext,
desiring to resume his tours.
Tiānzhù, considering the Emperor's excessive indulgence in travel,
and though court officials remonstrated,
the Emperor's will was unmoved.
Thinking of a way to move him,
he pricked his finger and wrote a memorial in blood,
which read:
"Your servant humbly reflects that
those who gave birth to your servant's body
are your servant's parents.
Those who enabled your servant's rise
are the favors of successive reigns.
The desire to repay Your Majesty for the favor of enabling my rise
is your servant's heart.
Therefore, I prick my blood
to express my heart,
to make clear my foolish loyalty,
hoping Your Majesty will pity and observe it.
For several years now,
there have been celestial anomalies and earthquakes,
great floods and strange famines.
Calamities and abnormalities are countless,
yet Your Majesty has not awakened,
and disaster has extended to the Tàihuángtàihòu.
Heaven's intention
is for Your Majesty to be in mourning attire,
to repent and renew yourself,
so as to preserve the great enterprise.
If you still do not awaken,
Heaven's will may almost cease.
Mourning rites are a great matter,
which a child ought to carry out fully.
If Your Majesty cannot fully show filial piety to the Tàihuángtàihòu,
then your officials will certainly not be able to be fully loyal to Your Majesty.
Disloyalty
will lead to all sorts of extremes.
Should an unexpected calamity occur,
people's hearts will scatter.
The great position
is watched by villains.
In the past, Tàikāng hunted at the Luò and Ruì rivers,
and Yángdì toured Jiāngdū;
both led to defeat.
Should this not be a warning!
At present, the court is empty,
cities are empty,
granaries are empty,
the frontiers are empty.
Everyone under Heaven knows the calamity of peril and ruin,
only Your Majesty does not know.
Order or chaos, security or danger,
lie in this action or inaction.
This is what grieves your servant's heart and what I regret for Your Majesty,
and again, defying death, I speak it for Your Majesty."
It contained several thousand words.
When Tiānzhù pricked his blood,
fearing obstruction from his family,
he secluded himself in a secret room,
even his wife and children did not know.
After submitting it,
he immediately changed into common clothes to await punishment.
All who heard were moved to sadness,
but the Emperor did not awaken.
After a month,
Bīngbù Shàngshū Wáng Qióng wanted to kill Dū Yùshǐ Péng Zé over the Hāmì affair.
Court officials gathered to deliberate;
Wáng Qióng waited with an arrogant air,
and the assembly dared not speak.
Tiānzhù and his colleague Wáng Kuàng strenuously declared Péng Zé innocent,
whereupon Péng Zé was dismissed and became a commoner.
Wáng Qióng was enraged,
and obtained an imperial decree to send both men out to provincial posts.
Tiānzhù received the post of Lín'ān Tuīguān.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was summoned back to his old post.
He was promoted to Dàlǐchéng,
and died not long after.
A long time later,
his son requested a posthumous grant,
and a special sacrifice was granted.
An eulogy states: The duty of a remonstrating official
lies in correcting wrongdoings and assisting against deviations.
The various officials cautioned against excessive travel,
denounced powerful favorites,
and contended strongly for righteousness,
not shaming their positions.
Although Emperor Wǔzōng's virtue as a ruler was desolate,
yet civilized men were only banished far away.
When Zhāng Qīn entered the pass, he was not punished.
His natural disposition was certainly not comparable to that of a cruel and tyrannical person.
However, adopted sons and eunuchs
stirred up trouble and committed evil.
Stocks and cangues crisscrossed the palace courtyard;
the loyal and upright suffered pain in prison cells.
Those who "brushed the dragon's scales" could still escape with their lives,
but those who "threw at the rat" were sure to fall into deadly peril.
The fundamental vitality daily dwindled,
the court and the populace were alarmed.
The dynasty's lifespan was not extended,
and the succession almost broke.
The admonition about errors in customs,
is it not truly urgent as a warning?
Collation Notes

Lièzhuàn Seventy-Seven: Lǐ Wénxiáng, Sūn Pán (Xú Guī), Hú Guàn (Zhōu Shícóng, Wáng Xióng), Luó Qiáo, Yè Zhāo (Liú Tiānqí), Dài Guān, Huáng Gǒng, Lù Zhèn, Xià Liángshèng (Wàn Cháo et al.), Hé Zūn (Liú Xiào et al.).
Lǐ Wénxiáng,
courtesy name Tiānruì,
was from Máchéng.
His grandfather, Zhèngfāng,
was a Shānxī Bùzhèngshǐ.
His father, [missing character],
was a Shǎnxī Cānzhèng.
Wénxiáng was remarkably talented from a young age.
At twenty, he passed the provincial examination,
and at the end of the Chénghuà era, he passed the Jìnshì examination.
When Wàn Ān was in power,
he esteemed Wénxiáng's talent.
Because Sūn Hóngbì was on the same examination roster,
Wàn Ān entertained him at his home,
but Wénxiáng was not pleased by this.
Wénxiáng was tasked to write an inscription for a painting of doves,
and his words contained a subtle jab,
which Wàn Ān deeply resented.
Not long after,
when Xiàozōng succeeded to the throne,
Wénxiáng immediately submitted a memorial,
which stated: "The ancestors established the Nèigé and the Liùbù
to assist in myriad affairs
and manage government matters;
their duties are extremely important.
Recently,
many unworthy individuals have been in office,
and power has shifted to the inner attendants.
Rewards
and punishments are determined by their whims,
and fortune and misfortune are swayed by them.
They view Yánguān as enemies,
and openly accept bribes.
Flatter them, and you are quickly promoted through connections;
oppose them, and you are cleverly slandered and banished
far away.
The court and populace are disheartened,
and people on the roads look askance.
We hope Your Majesty will secretly investigate the ringleaders,
clearly uphold the state laws,
and select diligent and upright individuals for service.
Furthermore, extensively select eminent
ministers,
consult with them on governance,
and entrust them wholeheartedly,
without further suspicion,
only then will the proper order be established and favored retainers not dare to act recklessly.
The ancestors established laws,
with appropriate degrees of severity.
Recently, the Fǎsī have exclusively pursued their private interests,
disregarding state statutes.
The powerful, though their crimes be grave, are certainly pardoned;
the poor and weak, though their offenses be
minor, are certainly punished.
Favors are extended to villains,
fostering a contemptuous attitude among the populace.
Moreover, the prevailing customs are extravagant and luxurious,
and the rites and regulations are completely abandoned.
Wealthy commoners usurp the residences of kings;
rich families imitate
the attire of dukes and marquises.
Strange and excessive crafts and skills
are rampant from top to bottom.
We hope Your Majesty will reassert the old statutes,
so that judicial officials abide by the laws and ordinances,
and officials and commoners alike maintain their respective ranks.
Only
then will ritual and law be clear, and people will not dare to be contemptuous.
However, if the state lacks the right people,
with whom can it be governed?
The retired Shàngshū Wáng Shù and Wáng Hóng
are self-professed loyal and solitary figures,
whose vigor has not yet waned;
Nánjīng Zhǔshì Lín
Jùn and Sīnán Tōngpàn Wáng Chún
are firm and upright in character,
and possess both talent and integrity.
We hope Your Majesty will summon them to court,
utilize their deliberations,
and they will certainly be beneficial,
able to assist
in these enlightened times.
Moreover, talented individuals are hard to come by,
which has been true since ancient times.
Customs influence people,
and even heroes are not immune.
However, among these officials and commoners,
not all are mediocre and foolish.
They are able to understand their own
To feel shame
means one belongs to the renowned;
to delight in others' misfortune
marks one as vulgar.
I wish Your Majesty would clearly discern all people,
dismiss those who deceive superiors, pursue selfish gain, defy Heaven, and harm the common good,
and
then encourage the rest to reform themselves.
Once the path to correction is opened,
there will surely be many who turn to good.
Your servant observed the enthronement edict,
which disallowed reporting matters based on hearsay.
Ancient sagely kings hung drums and set up wooden posts,
actively seeking criticism.
Even if what is said is not entirely factual,
listeners
can still take it as a warning.
How does it harm the state
that you so hastily wish to punish them?
In the past, Lǐ Línfǔ used this to bring disaster to the Táng [dynasty],
Wáng Ānshí used this to bring disaster to the Sòng [dynasty].
People far and near,
hearing this suddenly,
were all alarmed.
I wish Your Majesty would again issue a clear edict,
widely seeking frank advice,
so as not to fall into treacherous schemes,
and to fully display your sagely virtue.
Generally, the words of a gentleman
are definitely not to the advantage of petty individuals.
If consulted,
they will surely engage in slander.
If there is any doubt,
please try a face-to-face confrontation.
When the memorial was submitted,
the eunuchs and high officials Wàn Ān, Liú Jí, Yǐn Zhí, etc., all detested it,
and it was not acted upon for several days.
Suddenly an imperial decree ordered (him) to the Zuǒshùnmén,
because the memorial contained the phrase
"restoration and rebuilding"
and a message was conveyed to interrogate and reprimand him.
Wénxiáng calmly explained and departed.
He was demoted to Shǎnxī's Xiánníng County Magistrate.
Nánjīng Secretariat Supervisor Xià Chóngwén argued for his rescue,
but it was not accepted.
Ministry of Works Secretariat Supervisor from Pútián, Lín Yí, again requested to summon Wénxiáng and Tāng Nài,
to accept Chóngwén's words,
and moreover, to summon Chén Xiànzhāng, Xiè Duó, and others.
At that time, Ān had already left;
Jí and Zhí provoked the emperor's anger,
and a stern edict severely reprimanded them.
Many court officials recommended Wénxiáng,
but they were largely thwarted by Jí and Zhí.
In the second year of Hóngzhì, he was recommended by Wáng Shù to be summoned as a Ministry of War Secretariat Supervisor.
He accepted no gifts from surveillance commissioners downwards.
Less than a month after arriving at his post,
he was again imprisoned due to Jí's interference,
and demoted to Xīnglóngwèi Patrol Commissioner in Guìzhōu.
Censor-in-Chief Dèng Tíngzàn campaigned against the Miáo,
consulted him on military matters,
found him greatly extraordinary,
and wished to recommend him as a Surveillance Commissioner.
Wénxiáng said:
"In the past, I was dismissed for speaking out;
now to advance due to military merit
is not acceptable."
He firmly declined but could not get permission (to resign),
so he requested to carry a memorial to the capital,
firmly begging to retire.
His memorial was submitted again,
but not approved.
Returning via Shāngchéng,
he fell through ice while crossing,
and died there,
at just thirty years of age.
Sūn Pán,
a native of Liáoyáng.
He passed the imperial examination in the ninth year of Hóngzhì.
While serving as an apprentice official in a ministry,
Xú Guī, a clerk in the Ministry of Justice, impeached the eunuch Yáng Péng over the Mǎncāng'ér affair and incurred displeasure.
Pán submitted a memorial saying:
"Recently, remonstrating officials have treated speaking out as taboo,
while those who oppose favored individuals and challenge powerful traitors are found among clerks and low-ranking officials.
Your servant is secretly ashamed of this.
I request that those who submit proposals be categorized into four ranks:
The highest are those who do not shun harm,
openly impeaching the powerful and influential.
Next are those who promote the pure and suppress the corrupt,
able to make up for deficiencies and retrieve what has been overlooked.
Third are those who
propose current policies
beneficial to the military and the state.
All should be promoted accordingly.
As for those who merely embellish official documents and remain silent,
they should be dismissed.
This way, the remonstrating officials will know to be vigilant,
and not neglect their duties."
At the time, his proposal was not adopted.
Xú Guī
was from Yìngchéng.
Previously,
Qīanhù Wú Néng entrusted his daughter, Mǎn Cāng'ér, to a matchmaker to be sold to the entertainer Zhāng,
deceiving her by saying:
"She is a relative of the Zhōu imperial family."
Later, she was resold to the musician Yuán Lín.
After Néng died,
his wife Niè found her.
The daughter resented her mother for selling her
and falsely claimed that Niè was not her mother.
Niè and her son abducted the daughter home.
Lín sued at the Xíngbù,
where Lángzhōng Dīng Zhé and Yuánwàiláng Wáng Jué interrogated them and discovered the truth.
Lín spoke disrespectfully,
so Zhé flogged Lín,
who died a few days later.
Yùshǐ Chén Yù and Zhǔshì Kǒng Qí inspected Lín's corpse
and buried him.
The eunuch Yáng Péng, from the Dōngchǎng, whose nephew had previously committed illicit acts with the daughter,
instructed Lín's wife to appeal her grievance to Péng and had Zhāng point to the daughter as her sister,
and also instructed Jiǎ xiàowèi to have the daughter repeat Zhāng's statement.
The matchmaker then said that Niè's daughter had previously been sold to a relative of the Zhōu imperial family.
The memorial was sent down to the Zhènfǔ Sī,
who charged Zhé, Jué, and others.
It was then sent down again to the Fǎ Sī and Jǐnyī Wèi for review.
They searched the home of the imperial relative Zhōu Yù for the daughter,
but she was not there.
The Fǔbù ministers, Jǐshì, and Yùshǐ were again ordered to conduct a public interrogation in court.
Zhāng and the daughter then finally revealed the truth.
The Dūcháyuàn memorialized,
stating that Zhé, by flogging someone to death in the line of duty,
deserved the punishment of penal servitude.
Jué, Yù, Qí, and Niè's mother and daughter deserved flogging.
When the case was submitted,
Guī was indignant
and submitted a memorial stating:
"The case of Niè's daughter,
Zhé judged it correctly.
Péng tortured Niè to force a false confession,
and the Zhènfǔ Sī collectively covered up the deception.
When Your Majesty ordered the Fǎ Sī and Jǐnyī to jointly inquire,
they feared the Dōngchǎng and dared not be clear,
until the interrogation in the imperial court, where it could not be hidden.
Yet the daughter, who falsely accused her mother, is only sentenced to flogging,
while Zhé and others, who are innocent, are instead subjected to penal servitude.
Such a reversal of light and heavy punishments
is all caused by the intimidation of the Dōngchǎng.
I have been in the Xíngbù for three years
and have seen interrogations of bandits,
most of whom were arrested by the Dōngchǎng and Zhènfǔ Sī.
Some claimed to have been framed by xiàowèi,
some claimed xiàowèi retaliated for others,
and some claimed xiàowèi accepted bribes from the chief culprit and made them accessories, forcing innocent people to take the blame.
The judicial officials clearly saw the truth
but dared not change a single word.
This offends heavenly harmony,
and disasters and anomalies appear repeatedly.
I wish Your Majesty would abolish the Dōngchǎng,
execute Péng's uncle and nephew, along with Jiǎ xiàowèi and this daughter in the marketplace,
banish the Zhènfǔ Sī officials to the furthest frontiers,
promote Zhé, Jué, Qí, and Yù each by one rank,
to clear their names.
Then the will of Heaven can be restored,
and peace can be achieved.
If the Dōngchǎng is not abolished,
then at least select prudent and magnanimous eunuchs like Chén Kuān and Wéi Tài to lead it,
and also appoint a grand minister to manage it jointly.
The Zhènfǔ Sī handling of criminal cases should also not exclusively use Jǐnyī officials.
I humbly request that one or two officials from each of the imperial guards in the capital and one Xíngbù Zhǔshì
be selected to jointly oversee these matters.
If they are replaced every three or six years,
then the patrol officers and xiàowèi
will surely not commit wrongful acts and abuse their authority,
or falsely accuse the innocent.
I am but a humble individual.
All around me are people from the Dōngchǎng and Zhènfǔ Sī,
and disaster is inevitable.
But rather than dying at the hands of these people,
how much better to die at court.
I wish for my head to be cut off
to implement my words,
and for my wife and children to be given my remains to take home.
Even if I die, I will have no regrets."
The Emperor was enraged
and sent the matter to the Dūcháyuàn for investigation and interrogation.
Dūyùshǐ Mǐn Guī and others charged them with presenting inaccurate memorials,
punishing them with penal servitude redeemable by payment, then returning them to their duties.
The Emperor demanded full statements,
and they all submitted memorials admitting their guilt,
their salaries were docked to varying degrees.
After Guī completed his penal servitude,
he was dismissed as a commoner.
Later, Jǐshìzhōng Páng Pàn and others stated that more than three months had passed since the review of the court documents for Zhé and others' case,
and thirty-eight people were imprisoned.
They requested their early release.
So, Mǎn Cāng'ér was flogged
and sent to the Huànyī Jú;
Zhé was given funds for Lín's burial
and dismissed as a commoner.
Jué, Qí, and Yù all redeemed their flogging and were restored to their posts.
This was in the twelfth month of the ninth year of Hóngzhì.
Pàn was soon promoted to Lìbù Zhǔshì.
In the first year of Zhèngdé,
eunuchs gradually gained power,
and Pàn again submitted a memorial saying:
"Today's malpractices,
none are worse than inner officials commanding troops.
Indeed, officials referred to as 'inner' should not meddle in external affairs at all,
how much less should they wield military power!
In prosperous eras of previous dynasties,
this never happened.
It was only in the late stages of the Táng and Sòng dynasties that eunuchs were appointed as military supervisors,
and their states consequently did not last long.
Now, the various inner officials serving as garrison commanders and spear supervisors in the Nine Frontiers
rely on their power to act arbitrarily
and extort in a hundred ways.
When there is an alert, they gather elite soldiers for their own protection;
when an enemy is defeated, they allow their subordinates to claim credit.
Military officers use them for advancement,
and censorate officials dare not impeach them.
The family members and henchmen they bring with them
are mostly unruly youths and scoundrels.
They devour and snatch,
like wolves and tigers in their dominance,
causing the morale of the three armies to sink
and all officials to lose heart.
I humbly request that they all be recalled to the capital,
and military commanders be solely responsible for frontier affairs.
This is the essential task for governance and defense today."
This was not adopted.
When Liú Jǐn gained power,
he denounced Pàn as a "treacherous partisan"
and forced him to return home.
After Jǐn was executed,
Pàn was appointed Hénán Qiānshì,
but was dismissed due to implication in a case.
Guī was recommended by Xíngbù Zhǔshì Chén Fèngwú
and appointed Tóngxiāng Chéng.
During the Zhèngdé era,
he successively served as Gànzhōu Tōngpàn.
He persuaded the bandit leader Hé Jīyù to surrender.
Soon after,
Hé Jīyù rebelled again,
and Guī was imprisoned,
but was soon released.
Later, for his meritorious service in suppressing bandits,
he was promoted to Zhīzhōu.
Hú Guàn,
courtesy name Zhòngguāng,
was from Wúhú.
He obtained the *jìnshì* degree in the sixth year of Hóngzhì.
He was appointed a *shùjíshì*
and then Hùbù Zhǔshì.
In the third month of the tenth year,
due to disasters and anomalies, requests for advice were issued.
Guàn responded to the imperial edict,
memorializing that
"the eunuchs Lǐ Guǎng and Yáng Péng introduce heterodox figures like Liú Liángfǔ to mislead Your Majesty,
excessively establishing rituals and sacrifices,
thus depleting the national treasury.
Meanwhile, unworthy scholar-officials beg for favors at their doors in their declining years,
engaging in communication and illicit requests.
With the *yīn* ascendant and *yáng* diminished,
how can disasters be averted?"
He then vehemently denounced the harms caused by imperial relatives by marriage, Daoist priests, and redundant officials appointed by imperial decree.
The memorial was withheld from publication.
Not long after,
Lǐ Guǎng died,
so Guàn escaped punishment.
During the Chénghuà era,
eunuchs held great power.
Although Xiàozōng occasionally dismissed some after ascending the throne,
their accumulated power was too great to be reversed quickly.
Those who opposed them were inevitably framed by factions,
and the persecution would not cease until they were defeated.
Among the various officials previously and subsequently framed for opposing eunuchs,

for instance, in the first year of Hóngzhì, Hùbù Yuánwàiláng Zhōu Shícóng memorialized requesting severe punishment for the former dynasty's treacherous remnants like Wāng Zhí, Qián Néng, and Cài Yòng,
and to investigate the eunuchs serving as garrison commanders in both capitals and the four directions.
The various eunuchs picked out the character
"Zōngshè"
in his memorial for not being indented,
and ordered the Fǎ Sī to arrest and prosecute him.
He was later released.
In the autumn of the thirteenth year,
there was an alert in Dàtóng,
and Bǎoguó Gōng Zhū Huī was ordered to lead the defense.
Xíngrén Yǒngqīng Wáng Xióng strongly argued that Zhū Huī was not competent
and also requested the dismissal of eunuch supervisors
to enhance the authority of generals.
Miáo Kuí, who was then supervising Zhū Huī's army,
claimed Wáng Xióng was obstructing military efforts,
so Wáng Xióng was imprisoned by imperial decree
and banished to Yúnnán Làngqióng Chéng.
Luó Qiáo,
courtesy name Wéishēng,
was a native of Jíshuǐ.
His nature was pure and tranquil,
with few desires.
He studied under Zhāng Yuánzhēn
and lectured in his hometown.
He passed the imperial examination as a *jìnshì* in the 12th year of Hóngzhì (1499),
and was appointed Magistrate of Xīnhuì County,
where he was benevolent and loved.
In the early Jiàodé reign,
he entered the capital as a Right Reviewer of the Dàlǐ Temple.
In the 4th month of the 5th year (1510),
when the capital was afflicted by drought and haze,
he submitted a memorial saying:
“Your servant has heard that when human affairs are in order, yin and yang are harmonious;
when governance fails, disasters arise.
Recently, due to the prolonged drought in the capital,
Your Majesty specifically issued a virtuous decree,
releasing prisoners in arrears for military service,
and relaxing the prohibitions on guilt by association.
Yet, after fasting and prayers for more than ten days,
the rain still delays.
Your servant humbly believes that Heaven’s benevolent heart has not yet been fully satisfied.
Your Majesty holds court
sometimes until late in the day,
but also indulges in familiarity with petty people,
shouting and carousing until dawn.
How can this be in harmony with Heaven’s will and lay the foundation for a great undertaking?
The legal net grows tighter daily,
exactions are severe and urgent,
robbers kill people in broad daylight,
and the common people migrate along the roads,
their vital energy utterly exhausted.
The Censors and Investigating Censors know this but dare not speak,
and the Grand Secretariat speaks but dares not speak fully.
This is the great peril of obstruction and concealment.
In ancient times, the advancement or dismissal of high officials
was always done with decorum,
and crimes of tattooing and nose-cutting were not applied to Grand Masters.
Recently, high officials and ministers leave without propriety.
Loyal and trustworthy ministers of the former court, such as Liú Dàxià,
were banished to distant borders,
and three years have already passed.
Your Majesty leaves him unquestioned,
which is not the way to treat elders and respect ministers.
The laws and statutes of our dynasty
were compiled with reference to ancient and modern times,
sufficient to punish villains and prevent crimes.
Recently, the judicial authorities, in anticipation of the sovereign's implied wishes,
cleverly framed good people.
The *Yì* says: ‘If rewards are excessive, they extend to the immoral;
if punishments are excessive, they extend to the good.
Should one err,
it is better to be excessive in rewards than in punishments.’
Today’s punishments
are excessively severe.
I wish Your Majesty would be cautious in leisurely pursuits,
discard favorite trifles,
dismiss petty people,
recall old virtues (worthy officials),
and together with the officials in court,
work tirelessly for good governance,
and also order the judicial authorities to carefully uphold existing laws.
Even if there are cases where the law is light but the circumstances are serious,
they must still be reported for imperial judgment and decision,
without arbitrary alteration of severity or leniency.
Then, Heaven’s changes (disasters) can be stopped above,
and the people’s hearts can be won below.”
At that time, court officials had long considered speech taboo.
When Luó Qiáo's memorial was submitted,
he surmised that he would surely die,
and awaited his fate with a coffin (prepared).
Liú Jǐn was furious,
falsely issued an imperial edict severely rebuking him for several hundred words,
and ordered court officials to deliberate his punishment.
Grand Secretary Lǐ Dōngyáng strongly intervened,
and he was allowed to be reassigned to a teaching post in his native place.
That autumn,
Liú Jǐn was defeated,
and Luó Qiáo was soon recalled and reinstated,
but he claimed illness and left.
When Chén Háo rebelled,
Wáng Shǒurén raised an army in Jí'ān,
and Luó Qiáo was the first to answer the call of duty.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was directly appointed Prefect of Táizhōu from his home.
He built a Shrine of Loyalty and Fidelity
to venerate Fāng Xiàorú.
He invited the commoner Zhāng Chǐ
to inquire about the people's suffering.
Periodically, he traversed the fields,
inspected agriculture and sericulture,
and explained the rites of capping, marriage, funerals, and sacrifices.
The prefecture was greatly well-governed.
In the 2nd year of Jiājìng (1523), he was recommended as outstanding.
Censor-in-Chief Yáo Mò submitted a memorial defending Luó Qiáo, saying:
“For a minister to offend the imperial dignity with remonstrance
has been difficult since ancient times.
In the past, the ‘Eight Tigers’
usurped power,
and the traitor Jǐn disrupted governance.
Court officials remained silent,
preserving their lives.
But Censor Liú Mào and Reviewer Luó Qiáo sacrificed themselves for the country,
exposing the ills of the time,
and fortunately survived with their remaining breath.
Encountering a sagely dynasty,
they ought to be openly commended and promoted,
to encourage serving officials.
Yet Luó Qiáo is Prefect of Táizhōu,
and Liú Mào is Prefect of Chángshā,
causing officials of loyalty and utmost devotion to languish in ordinary posts.
Your servant humbly regrets this for the court.”
The Emperor accepted his words
and promoted Luó Qiáo to Left Administration Commissioner of Guǎngdōng,
but Luó Qiáo declined.
The ministry's dispatches urged him,
and he reluctantly took up the post.
After more than a year,
he finally pleaded illness and returned home.
Luó Qiáo upheld moral conduct,
and his actions were like those of the ancients.
When Luó Hóngxiān was in mourning,
he did not cease lecturing,
which Luó Qiáo deemed improper,
and he sent a letter of reproof.
Such was his stern straightforwardness.
Yè Zhāo,
courtesy name Shímǐan,
was a native of Fēngchéng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the 15th year of Hóngzhì (1502).
He was appointed Principal of the Ministry of Justice in Nánjīng.
Prisoners who had been long detained
were all released according to the law.
When the eunuch supervising the garrison encroached upon the reed marshes,
he ruled that it should be returned to the people.
When various prefectures in Yìngtiān suffered disaster,
he submitted four proposals for famine relief.
Soon after, he was promoted to Assistant Minister.
When Wǔzōng ascended the throne,
he responded to the imperial summons by presenting eight proposals,
which included:
“Xuān and Dà were invaded by bandits,
killing almost a thousand soldiers.
The supervising eunuch Miáo Kuí falsely reported merit for killing the enemy,
and should be recalled for investigation.
Eunuchs commanding troops
is unprecedented in antiquity.
The Táng dynasty first employed them,
and its ancestral altars became ruins;
our Zhèngtǒng reign employed them,
and the imperial carriage was captured in the north.
From now on, no supervising officials should be dispatched for military affairs,
and those guarding the borders should also be recalled.
Moreover, in the early days of the dynasty, eunuchs were all subordinate to the Ministry of Rites,
their rank no higher than fourth grade,
their duties no more than sweeping.
Now I request that they be returned to the ministry,
and the Directorate of Ceremonial be replaced,
so that they perform miscellaneous duties.
Abolish the Eastern Depot,
and move it to another department.
Only then can those close to the emperor not usurp power,
and then the empire can be at peace.”
He also requested the recall of Liú Dàxià
and the pardoning of remonstrating officials such as Dài Xiǎn.
Liú Jǐn was enraged,
accused him of mishandling legal cases and causing wrongful convictions,
arrested him and imprisoned him in the imperial prison,
and stripped him of his official status, sending him home.
He lectured in Xījiāng.
When Liú Jǐn was executed,
he was reinstated as Assistant Minister of the Ministry of Rites,
but died before hearing the order.
Scholars worshipped him at Shígǔ Academy.
At that time, there was also Liú Tiānqí, a Principal of the Ministry of Works,
a native of Línkuì,
and a *jìnshì* of the same year as Yè Zhāo.
He was in charge of the Lüliáng section.
When a eunuch passed through without showing proper respect,
the eunuch complained to Liú Jǐn.
Liú Tiānqí was arrested and imprisoned in the imperial prison,
and demoted to Postmaster of Ānzhuāng in Guìzhōu, where he died.
In the early Jiājìng reign,
he was posthumously reinstated and given funeral offerings.
Distribute funds from the imperial treasury to relieve the suffering in Jiānghuái,
disband border troops, sending soldiers back to their homes.
Rectify past misguided actions,
and regain the lost hearts of the people.
If these things are done,
then it is still
possible.
Fifth,
remove petty individuals (xiǎorén).
Since ancient times, there has never been a situation where petty individuals held power
without the nation perishing and its ruler being destroyed.
Today, those petty individuals who manipulate power and authority, and are insatiably greedy for wealth and nobility,
are
indeed numerous.
As for those who first instigated border conflicts,
treating warfare as a game,
causing Your Majesty to exhaust the strength of the entire realm,
deplete the wealth of the four seas,
and wound the hearts of the
people,
that is the doing of Jiāng Bīn.
Bīn is
a common soldier,
fierce, cruel, arrogant, and disrespectful,
without the manners of a subject.
Your servant only sees that he has crimes deserving of execution,
and has not
heard of any merits deserving of reward.
Yet now, he is bestowed with the imperial surname,
enfeoffed as an earl,
entrusted with Your Majesty's confidence,
and given the heavy responsibility of commanding the capital garrisons,
allowing him to wield military
power externally,
and harbor rebellious schemes internally,
thus creating an unstoppable momentum (like riding a tiger and being unable to dismount).
This is assuredly the path to chaos.
The people of the realm gnash their teeth in anger and curses,
all wishing to devour Bīn's flesh.
Why does Your Majesty
cherish one Bīn so much
as not to sacrifice him to appease the realm?
Sixth,
establish an heir apparent.
Your Majesty's age is gradually advancing,
but the auspicious star (referring to an heir) has not yet shone.
The trust placed in the ancestral temple and the state is precarious and without an anchor.
Yet Your Majesty is far away engaging in pleasure
tours,
repeatedly encountering unforeseen dangers,
adopting foster sons,
filling the entourage with them.
How can Your Majesty not proactively establish a virtuous close relative to inherit the great enterprise?
Your servant believes Your Majesty has put the cart before the horse.
I humbly hope that Your Majesty will report to the ancestral temple,
seek the command of the Empress Dowager,
and widely consult with the great ministers,
to select one virtuous close relative from the imperial clan to be raised in the palace,
thereby securing the hopes of the entire realm.
Should
a prince be born another day,
he can still be sent to a princely domain.
This would truly be boundless good fortune for the imperial clan and the state.
Assistant Minister Lù Zhèn drafted a memorial intending to remonstrate,
but upon seeing Gǒng's memorial and praising it,
he then destroyed his own [draft]
and submitted it jointly with Gǒng.
The Emperor was furious,
and sent both men to the imperial prison,
then had them kneel at the Wǔmén Gate.
The crowd thought the Emperor was about to emerge,
but Gǒng said:
"If the Emperor emerges,
I shall grab his robe and die."
They knelt for five days,
and when the period expired,
they were still imprisoned.
More than twenty days later,
they were given fifty strokes of the court staff
and dismissed as commoners.
Bīn sent men to assassinate Gǒng along the way.
A Supervising Secretary, Yǒu Hóng, knew of this and hid him,
allowing him to escape through hidden paths.
After returning home,
he devoted himself to writing.
Sometimes, with no rice left,
he would not cook even by midday,
yet remained calm.
He once sighed, saying:
"A person can reach the rank of high official and attain wealth and nobility,
but it lasts no more than thirty or forty years.
Only by establishing oneself and following the Way can one achieve immortality for a thousand years.
Yet people often
exchange this for that,
why is this?"
When Emperor Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was summoned to be Assistant Minister of the Court of Judicial Review in Nánjīng.
He memorialized, requesting to study ancient teachings and rectify scholarship,
revere Heaven and diligently serve the people,
take Yáo and Shùn as models,
preserve upright individuals,
and distinguish petty individuals.
The following year, he came to the capital to offer congratulations
and died in the capital.
Censor Zhāng Yuè pleaded for his upright integrity,
and he was posthumously granted the title of Junior Assistant Minister of the Court of Judicial Review,
and awarded sacrifices and a state funeral.
In the early Tiānqǐ era,
he was posthumously given the谥号 (shìhào) Zhōngyù.
Lù Zhèn,
courtesy name Rǔhēng,
was from Lánxī.
He studied under Zhāng Mào from the same county
and was known for his learning and conduct.
He became a *jìnshì* in the third year of Zhèngdé (1508).
He was appointed Magistrate of Tàihé.
At that time, Liú Jǐn wielded tyrannical power.
When hundreds of local residents were held responsible for arrears in salt tax,
Zhèn strenuously argued on their behalf to his superiors,
and they were exempted.
The eunuch guarding the region annually levied tribute ramie, and he reduced its quota.
He expanded and rebuilt school dormitories for the students,
and destroyed inappropriate shrines, instead
worshipping loyal and virtuous figures.
When irregular taxes burdened the people,
he investigated the tax registers,
and found fifteen thousand *shí* of falsely registered or hidden grain to compensate for the burden.
He built a granary to the west of the county seat
to store grain for relief.
He personally visited villages
to encourage agriculture and sericulture.
He established the *bǎowǔ* system (mutual guarantee system)
to enable the people to guard against bandits.
He built a brick city wall seven *lǐ* long,
and surrounded it with an outer earthen wall ten *lǐ* in circumference.
At that time, "wolf soldiers" (Lángbīng) were frequently dispatched to suppress rebels,
causing disturbances wherever they went.
Zhèn spoke to the governor-general,
ordering that they not be allowed to moor boats indiscriminately,
that officials provide their provisions,
and that their food be supplied in sequence,
so the army's movement was orderly.
He supervised the suppression of bandits in Yǒngfēng and Xīngàn
and was rewarded for his accomplishments.
He was jointly recommended by the Grand Coordinators and Grand Censors
and summoned to serve as a Supervising Secretary in the Ministry of War.
The people of Tàihé erected a living shrine for him.
While at the Ministry,
he was in charge of the memorials from various departments,
and he clashed with eunuchs,
so he was transferred to inspect the various passes at Zǐjīng.
He also angered Minister Wáng Qióng and Lù Wán
by arguing that Grand Censor Péng Zé and Vice Censor Hú Shìníng were innocent.
After Empress Xiàozhēn died,
Emperor Wǔzōng returned from Xuānfǔ.
After the funeral rites had begun for several days,
he again wanted to head north.
Zhèn submitted a strong memorial, saying:
"Recently,
Heaven was unmerciful,
and a great sorrow descended.
When the imperial carriage was on a hunting trip,
the public was in a state of alarm.
When Your Majesty returned to the palace alone, riding through the snow,
all officials and functionaries were deeply moved and saddened,
believing that Your Majesty, who was previously obscured, was now enlightened.
Yet, while the imperial coffin is still awaiting burial,
You are hastily planning a pleasure tour.
Your servant knows that Your Majesty's heart must be uneasy and distressed.
Moreover, Your Majesty has been on the throne for twelve years.
Ten marks the end of the *gān* cycle,
and twelve marks the end of the *zhī* cycle.
It is a time when cosmic forces converge,
a time for cultivating virtue and renewing oneself.
Yet, Your Majesty has chosen to build Xuānfǔ as a residence
and indulge in riding and archery for pleasure.
This is what Your servant deeply fears.
While ancient rulers sometimes had a fondness for chariots, horses, hunting, and touring,
it was
never to the extent of making the outside world their home
and their own home a temporary lodging,
entrusting the great instruments of the state and the great power of rewards and punishments to others,
and remaining completely unconcerned and indifferent.
This is unprecedented in history.
I humbly hope that Your Majesty will diligently complete the mourning rituals
and deeply guard against excessive pleasure tours."
There was no reply.
He was promoted to Wǔxuǎn Yuánwàiláng.
Later,
he and Huáng Gǒng admonished against the southern tour,
and consequently, he was thrown into the imperial prison.
In prison, he discussed the nine hexagrams of the Yì Jīng with Gǒng,
clarifying the way of sorrow and suffering.
Those imprisoned with them mostly arranged their affairs for after their deaths,
but Zhèn alone said nothing.
After being caned,
his wounds were severe.
He wrote a letter to his sons, saying:
"Although I die,
you all must strive to be loyal and filial.
My brush is messy,
but my spirit is not messy,"
and then he died.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was posthumously granted the title of Tàicháng Shàoqīng
and an imperial sacrifice.
When Fāng Zhèn and others were imprisoned,
Jiāng Bīn was determined to have them killed,
cutting off their food and drink.
Zhèn's youngest son, Tǐrén,
then fifteen years old,
disguised himself as a relative of another prisoner
and regularly delivered thin gruel.
Later, an imperial edict allowed one son to be appointed to office.
His elder brothers yielded to Tǐrén,
who became the Tōngpàn of Zhāngzhōu
and had a reputation for good governance.
His grandson, Kějiào,
became Nánjīng Lǐbù Shìláng after passing the Jìnshì examination.
Xià Liángshèng,
courtesy name Yúzhōng,
was a native of Nánchéng.
When he was young, he was recognized by Cài Qīng, the Dūxué Fùshǐ,
who said,
"You will certainly become an excellent minister in the future,
and no one will surpass you."
Thus, he was named Liángshèng (meaning "excellent and superior").
In the second year of Zhèngdé, he passed the provincial examination in first place.
The following year,
he became a Jìnshì
and was appointed Xíngbù Zhǔshì.
He was transferred to the Lìbù
and promoted to Kǎogōng Yuánwàiláng.
When the edict for the southern tour was issued,
Liángshèng prepared a memorial,
which he co-signed with Lǐbù Zhǔshì Wàn Cháo and Tàicháng Bóshì Chén Jiǔchuān, and submitted it,
stating:
"Currently, the disaster in the southeast
is not limited to Jiāng and Huái;
the worry in the northwest
is close to the imperial carriage.
The vacant position for ancestral sacrifices
cannot remain empty for long;
the filial care for the Sacred Mother
cannot be neglected.
The auspicious pregnancy in the palace
should be planned for early;
the heavy and complex state affairs
cannot be entirely entrusted to others.
The title of 'Zhènguó'
is heard throughout the land,
which may give rise to ambitions;
the border generals
are brought close to the forbidden inner court,
how can one forget the danger close at hand?
If the imperial tour continues,
your ministers will not know where they will die."
At this time, the memorials from Shū Fēn, Huáng Gǒng, and Lù Zhèn had already been submitted.
Lìbù Lángzhōng Zhāng Yǎnruì and fourteen others, and Xíngbù Lángzhōng Lù Fèng and fifty-three others followed.
Lǐbù Lángzhōng Jiāng Lóng and sixteen others, and Bīngbù Lángzhōng Sūn Fèng and sixteen others also followed.
Moreover, the physician Xú Ào also advised using his medical knowledge,
briefly stating:
"The way of nurturing one's health
is like placing a candle.
If the room is closed, it remains steady;
if exposed to wind, it will drip tears (melt quickly).
Your Majesty lightly regards the imperial carriage,
indulges in amusements,
leaps on horses, draws bows,
catches fish, and plays with animals.
Recently, you have not hesitated to travel far,
braving cold and heat,
crossing passes and rivers,
with irregular meals and drinks,
and indiscriminate food.
This is truly not the way of preserving health.
Furthermore, the south is low and damp,
making it especially easy to get sick.
I beg you to consider the importance of the ancestral temples and the state,
not to engage in horsemanship,
not to overindulge in drink and food,
let joy not harm the heart,
anger not harm the liver,
desire not harm the kidneys,
and labor not harm the spleen.
Seek the security of a secluded chamber,
and avoid the calamity of violent winds.
Your minister cannot express my deepest wishes enough."
After these memorials were submitted,
the emperor and his favored ministers were all greatly enraged.
Consequently, Liángshèng, Cháo, Jiǔchuān, Gǒng, Zhèn, and Ào were thrown into the imperial prison.
Fēn and Yǎnruì along with one hundred and seven others were punished by kneeling outside the Wǔmén for five days.
Meanwhile, Dàlǐsì Zhèng Zhōu and ten others,
Xíngrén Sī Fù Yú Tíngzàn and twenty others,
Gōngbù Zhǔshì Lín Dàlù, Hé Zūn, and Jiǎng Shānqīng submitted a jointly signed memorial one after another.
The emperor grew even angrier
and imprisoned them all in the imperial prison.
Soon after, Lì, Tíngzàn, Dàlù and others,
along with Liángshèng and the other six,
were all made to kneel beneath the imperial palace for five days,
and were additionally put in cangues and handcuffs.
In the evening,
they were still imprisoned.
The officials entered in the morning and left in the evening,
chained like severe criminals,
and onlookers along the road all shed tears.
And among the court officials, apart from Grand Secretary Yáng Tínghé and Hùbù Shàngshū Shí Jiè who submitted memorials to intercede,
no one else dared to speak.
The gentry and common people were all indignant,
throwing bricks and tiles and shouting curses.
All the grand ministers were afraid,
and entered court before daybreak,
requesting an imperial edict to forbid speaking on state affairs.
The Tōngzhèngsī then refused to accept any memorials.
At this time,
the sky was continuously overcast and dark during the day.
In the Nánhǎizi of the forbidden garden, the water rose over four feet,
and the seven iron pillars under the bridge all broke as if severed.
Jīnwúwèi Dūzhīhuī Qiānshì Zhāng Yīng said:
"This is an omen of change;
the emperor's departure will certainly be unfavorable."
Then, baring his chest and holding a blade to it,
with several sheng of earth in a bag,
he held an admonishing memorial and knelt weeping in the imperial path,
then stabbed himself in the chest,
and blood flowed all over the ground.
The guards seized his blade
and bound him, sending him to the imperial prison.
When asked what the earth in the bag was for,
he said:
"I feared defiling the imperial court, so I sprinkled earth to cover the blood."
An imperial edict ordered him to be caned eighty times,
and he died.
Fēn and the one hundred and seven others,
after their kneeling was completed,
each received thirty strokes of the cane.
Fēn, Yǎnruì, Fèng, Lóng, and Fèng were considered the instigators
and were demoted to outer posts;
the rest had half a year's salary docked.
Liángshèng and the six others, as well as Lì, Tíngzàn, and Dàlù, each received fifty strokes,
the other thirty people received forty.
Gǒng, Zhèn, Liángshèng, Cháo, and Jiǔchuān were dismissed from office,
others were demoted with varying degrees of punishment,
and Ào was exiled to the border.
And the imperial carriage no longer left the capital.
After Liángshèng returned,
he taught students.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was recalled to his former office.
Shàngshū Qiáo Yǔ considered him worthy
and recommended him as Wénxuǎn Lángzhōng.
He was public-spirited and honest, helping many to advance.
When the "Great Rites"
debate arose,
he repeatedly argued forcefully with his colleagues.
And when Xí Shū, Zhāng Cōng, Guì È, and Fāng Xiànfū were exceptionally promoted by imperial decree,
he again insisted it was unacceptable.
Because of this, he was bitterly resented by those who supported the ritual changes.
After long service, he was promoted to Nánjīng Tàicháng Shàoqīng,
but before taking up the post,
he was transferred to an outer position.
Gěishìzhōng Chén Guāng submitted a memorial,
aligning with the arguments of Zhāng Cōng and others,
accusing Liángshèng and Shàngshū Yǔ and others of forming a clique,
and pushing others out at will.
Consequently, Liángshèng was demoted to Zhīzhōu of Chálíng.
When the Dàdiǎn for establishing proper moral relations was completed,
an imperial edict blamed the former Lángzhōng Liángshèng for coercing other officials,
and causing especially deep trouble,
and he was dismissed from office and reduced to commoner status.
Initially,
Liángshèng had compiled the memorials from his department,
naming the collection Quánsī Cúnyà,
which contained all the memorials concerning the ritual debate.
This was discovered by his enemies,
and he was imprisoned again.
He was sentenced to be caned, but allowed to redeem the punishment,
however, by special imperial decree, he was demoted and exiled to Sānwànwèi in Liáodōng.
Over five years later,
he died in exile.
When Mùzōng ascended the throne,
he was posthumously granted the title of Tàicháng Qīng.
Shū Fēn and others have their own biographies.
Wàn Cháo,
courtesy name Rǔxìn,
was from Jìnxián.
He became a *jìnshì* in the 6th year of Zhèngdé.
From being the Judicial Commissioner of Níngguó, he was promoted to Supervising Secretary of the Bureau of Rites,
and with Fēn, Liángshèng, and Jiǔchuān, he was known as
"The Four Admonishers of Jiāngxī."
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was reinstated to his former office,
and successively served as Education Intendant of Zhèjiāng.
After a long time, he was promoted to Provincial Administration Commissioner,
and due to offending powerful magnates, he was transferred to Guǎngxī.
He was repeatedly promoted to Left Administration Commissioner of Shǎnxī, and Right Vice Censor-in-Chief and Grand Coordinator of Yánsūi,
and wherever he went, he made a name for himself.
Chén Jiǔchuān,
courtesy name Wéijùn,
was from Línchuān.
He became a *jìnshì* in the 9th year of Zhèngdé.
He studied under Wáng Shǒurén.
Soon after, he was appointed Erudite of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
After being stripped of his office,
he again completed his studies under Shǒurén.
When Shìzōng succeeded to the throne,
he was recalled and reinstated to his former office,
and again promoted to Director of the Bureau of Receptions.
He rectified the tribute items and names,
and saved tens of thousands in expenses for the tribute envoys' rewards.
At that time, the state of Tiānfāng offered jade and stones as tribute.
Jiǔchuān selected out the unusable ones.
When they requested python robes,
he did not present their request,
and moreover angrily cursed the interpreter Hú Shìshēn and others.
Shìshēn resented this,
and, fabricating words from the foreigners, impeached Jiǔchuān and Chén Bāngchēng, the Director of the Huìtóng Hostel.
The Emperor was enraged,
and sent the two to the imperial prison.
At this time, Zhāng Cōng and Guì È desired to overthrow Fèi Hóng and seize his position,
so they instructed Shìshēn to again impeach Jiǔchuān for stealing tribute jade to provide to Hóng for making belts.
The accusation implicated Zhāng Xiǎng, a Director in the Ministry of War, and Zhāng Cháo, a Commander of the Imperial Bodyguard, and others.
The Emperor was even more enraged,
and sent Xiǎng and the others to the imperial prison as well.
Commander Luò Ān requested to arrest Shìshēn for questioning,
and Supervising Secretary Xiè Yīguàn and others also spoke up about it,
but the Emperor did not allow it.
When the trial concluded,
Jiǔchuān was exiled to Zhènhǎi Guard,
and Bāngchēng and others were stripped of their offices with varying degrees of punishment.
After a long time,
they were released by a general amnesty and returned,
and he died.
Zhāng Yǎnrùi,
courtesy name Yuánchéng,
was from Jí.
He became a *jìnshì* in the 18th year of Hóngzhì.
He served as Magistrate of Qīngfēng.
Due to upholding the law, he offended Líu Jǐn,
was arrested and sent to the imperial prison,
and nearly died.
When Jǐn was executed,
he was released,
and became Director of the Bureau of Civil Appointments in the Ministry of Personnel.
After being flogged,
he was demoted to Assistant Prefect of Píngyáng.
In the early Jiājìng era,
he was recalled,
and promoted to Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
He died soon after,
and was posthumously granted the title of Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud.
Jiāng Lóng,
from Tàicāng,
is mentioned in the biography of his father Āng.
Sūn Fèng,
was from Luòyáng.
Lù Fèng,
was from Wúxiàn.
Zhōu,
was from Jiǔxī Guard.
Lín Dàlù,
was from Pútián.
Jiǎng Shānqīng,
was from Yízhēn.
All were *jìnshì*.
Shānqīng studied under Gù Lín,
and was famous at the time for his poetry.
After being flogged,
Fèng and Fèng were both demoted to Assistant Prefects of prefectures,
County Commissioners,
Dàlù to Departmental Judge,
and Shānqīng to former Prefectural Staff Administrator.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
all were recalled and reinstated to their former offices.
Fèng eventually became Vice Commissioner,
Fèng became Prefect,
then Minister of Works,
Dàlù became Right Vice Censor-in-Chief and Grand Coordinator of Húguǎng,
and Shānqīng became Provincial Administration Commissioner of Guǎngxī.
Xú Áo,
from Jiādìng,
was originally a son of the Gāo family.
He was orphaned young,
and relied on his maternal uncle in the capital.
He assumed the surname Xú,
followed his uncle's profession as a physician,
and served in the inner palace.
After being flogged,
he was demoted and exiled to Wūsā.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was recalled,
and soon promoted to Imperial Physician.
Áo was upright and unyielding.
At that time, many court officials were new nobles,
unaware of Áo's past.
Áo also did not speak of his past,
and held the same office for nearly thirty years without transfer.
At the age of seventy,
he requested to retire.
It happened that Xú Xuémó, from the same county, was a Director in the Ministry of Rites,
and introduced him to Minister Wú Shān.
Shān reviewed his dossier,
which included his remonstrance regarding the Southern Tour,
and was startled, saying:
"Is this Mr. Xú from Wǔmiào's time?
Why has he been neglected?"
The two Vice Ministers disliked his age,
but Xuémó firmly stated:
"Although Áo is old,
he suffered together with the Senior Wrangler Shū when young,
which makes him worthy of respect."
After a further long period,
he was finally promoted to Court Physician.
He retired voluntarily,
and died at the age of eighty-three.
Those who were flogged at the same time included:
Yáo Jìyán from the Ministry of Personnel;
Táo Zī, Bā Sīmíng, Lǐ Xī, Gù Kějiǔ, Dèng Xiǎnqí, Xióng Róng, Yáng Qín,
Wáng Mào, Huáng Guóyòng, Lǐ Yǎn, Pān Ruì, Líu Fú, Zhāng Yuè from the Office of the Bearer;
and Jīn Léi, the Judicial Commissioner of the Court of Judicial Review;
Mèng Tíngkē, Zhāng Shìgǎo, Hǎo Fèngshēng, Fù Shàngwén, Guō Wǔcháng, the Assistant Commissioners of the Court;
and Yáo Rúgāo, Cài Shí, the Judicial Assessors.
All were demoted.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
they were recalled.
Zhāng Yīng also received a posthumous official title and funeral sacrifices,
and his younger brother Xióng was granted the title of Assistant Commander.
Yáo Jìyán,
from Nántōng Prefecture,
was in the same *jìnshì* cohort as Zhāng Yǎnrùi.
When he was about to be promoted to Director of the Bureau of Civil Appointments,
he yielded the position to Yǎnrùi.
In the early Jiājìng era,
he successively served as Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
and knelt before the palace gate to dispute
"the Great Rites."
He embraced poverty and simplicity,
and kept away from powerful figures.
When he died,
his family could not afford a funeral.
Hé Zūn,
courtesy name Mèngxún,
was from Jiāngníng.
His family was poor,
and his father ordered him to engage in trade,
but he was unwilling,
and left to become a scholar.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the 9th year of Zhèngdé.
Lù Wán, Minister of Personnel, heard of his reputation,
and sent his sons and nephews to study under him.
When it came time to select censors,
Zūn pleaded illness, saying:
"One cannot advance due to others."
