He was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Works,
and oversaw timber taxation in Jīngzhōu.
He ordered that taxes below one hundred *jīn* be reduced by one-third,
and those who suffered losses due to storms and floods were exempted.
Those subject to taxation personally recorded their numbers,
which were stored in the prefectural treasury,
and the revenue was accounted for every few days.
When he left,
he did not take a single coin for himself.
The Emperor was about to make a southern tour,
using the excuse of offering incense at Dōngyuè.
Zūn remonstrated:
"Idolatrous temples bring no blessings.
Should a prince of the imperial clan use the pretext of welcoming you,
and secretly harbor rebellious intentions,
then blessings will not have descended, but disaster will have already followed."
This referred to Chén Háoháo.
The powerful favorites, seeing the memorial,
intercepted it and prevented its submission.
At that time, Huáng Gǒng and others had already been punished.
Zūn, together with his colleagues Lín Dàlù and Jiǎng Shānqīng, again submitted a memorial begging the Emperor to stop the southern tour,
strongly stating that Jiāng Bīn was abusing his power and instigating chaos,
and that Gǒng and others were innocent.
They wished for them to be pardoned,
so that later generations would not say the Emperor killed remonstrating officials.
The Emperor was enraged,
and had them imprisoned
and flogged forty times in court.
The wounds were severe,
their limbs were completely torn,
and he died two days later,
aged thirty-four.
His family was poor,
so his colleagues and friends helped with his burial.
When Zūn was drafting the memorial,
a family servant came forward,
embraced him, and cried, saying:
"Even if master doesn't consider himself,
does he not think of his elderly parents and young children?"
Zūn calmly held his brush and said:
"Tell my parents that it is enough if my sons do not abandon their studies."
On the day of his death,
his father was returning with the family after visiting the graves.
They heard a bird crying mournfully,
and felt it was unusual.
Someone spread the rumor that an official in the Ministry of Works had been punished for his words.
His father wailed loudly:
"Zūn is dead!"
And indeed, it was so.
At that time, those who died from flogging before Zūn were
Liú Xiào of Yǎnchéng, Principal of the Ministry of Justice, and Liú Yù of Jí, Superintendent of Seals.
Those who died under the rod with Zūn,
besides Lù Zhèn,
were Lín Gōngfǔ of Chánglè, Grand Judge of the Court of Judicial Review;
Yú Tíngzàn of Póyáng, Vice Commissioner of the Office of the Bearer of Credentials;
the Bearers of Credentials Lǐ Shàoxián of Xūyí, Méng Yáng of Zézhōu, Zhān Shì of Yùshān, Liú Gài of Ānlù, and Lǐ Huì of Xiángfú.
Liú Xiào,
courtesy name Zōngdào.
He was extremely filial.
His mother Hú was strict in educating her son.
If she was displeased,
he would kneel for a long time begging for forgiveness,
and would only rise when his mother was pleased.
In the sixth year of Zhèngdé, he passed the Imperial Examination with Zhān Shì and Liú Gài,
and was appointed Principal of the Ministry of Justice.
He went to welcome his father to live with him,
but his father died on the way.
Xiào rushed to him,
embraced the corpse, and wept so bitterly he almost fainted.
His face had dust on it,
which he licked off with his tongue.
When he resumed his official duties,
the Emperor was about to make a southern tour.
The memorial of remonstrance from the Ministry of Justice
was drafted by Xiào.
As he was dying from the flogging,
he cried out loudly:
"I have no regrets,
my only regret is not seeing my old mother!"
His son Yuánlóu,
eleven years old,
cried beside him.
Xiào said:
"You haven't read much,
but don't you understand the righteousness of dedicating oneself to serving the sovereign?
Serve your grandmothers and mother well,
and do not shame your father."
Then he expired.
Liú Yù
was a tribute student.
Lín Gōngfǔ,
courtesy name Zhìfū.
During the mourning period for his parents,
he ate only vegetables and gruel for three years,
and did not enter the inner quarters.
In the twelfth year of Zhèngdé, he passed the Imperial Examination with Lǐ Shàoxián and Lǐ Huì.
All the officials from various ministries who remonstrated against the southern tour
were punished by kneeling before the palace gate.
The treacherous villains also intimidated them daily with threatening words,
making all who heard them fearful.
Because of this,
the Ministry of Revenue dared not submit a memorial,
and only three officials from the Ministry of Works remonstrated.
Only the entire staff of the Court of Judicial Review remonstrated,
which made the Emperor's anger even greater.
Gōngfǔ drafted the memorial at night,
and though he heard weeping and sighing in the dark,
he paid it no mind.
When he was imprisoned,
Huáng Gǒng spoke with him,
and sighed:
"I have sought friends all over the world,
but only recently discovered Zhìfū.
The ancients said one should not be alarmed in danger,
is this not such a person?"
Gōngfǔ was frail,
and ultimately could not withstand the flogging and died.
Yú Tíngzàn,
courtesy name Bóxiàn.
Both he and Méng Yáng were imperial scholars in the ninth year of Zhèngdé.
When the Ministries of Rites and War submitted their remonstrances,
Tíngzàn also led his colleagues to list ten reasons why the tour was improper,
but the Office of Transmission alone withheld it.
After several days,
the various officials had already been punished by kneeling,
and only then was his memorial submitted.
The Emperor became even more enraged,
and the floggings and interrogations were particularly severe.
Lǐ Shàoxián,
courtesy name Chóngdé.
He once delivered an imperial edict to Xúzhōu.
The eunuch supervisor of the granary sat at the head of the席 (seat/mat),
but Shàoxián immediately ordered his席 to be removed.
The eunuch supervisor was astonished and left.
When he was arrested and imprisoned,
he still regarded the eunuchs as servants.
Méng Yáng,
courtesy name Zǐqián.
He was the son of Méng Chūn, Vice Minister of Personnel.
As a Bearer of Credentials,
he was not promoted for a long time.
Someone hinted that he should visit those in power,
but Yáng refused.
At this time,
he told his colleagues:
"This action concerns the safety of the state,
and even a low-ranking official should be concerned.
Why should only censors be willing to die?"
His father Chūn
had previously served as Governor of Xuānfǔ.
He had military accomplishments,
but offended the eunuch Zhāng Yǒng and was dismissed and returned home.
When he heard that his son died in remonstrance,
he mourned him with a poem,
the words were very tragic and heroic,
and people widely circulated it.
Zhān Shì,
courtesy name Jìngzhī.
He was open-minded, straightforward,
and good at discussion.
His cousin Hàn,
courtesy name Rǔyuē,
passed the Imperial Examination with Gōngfǔ.
At that time, he was serving as Principal of the Ministry of Justice
and was also flogged for remonstrance.
When Shì died,
he managed his funeral and brought his body home.
During the Jiājìng era,
Hàn contended
over the "Great Rites",
and was flogged again.
Whenever it was rainy and his old wounds ached,
he would say:
"I have no shame before Jìngzhī in the underworld,
that is enough."
He eventually rose to the position of Vice Minister of Justice.
Liú Gài,
courtesy name Píngfǔ.
Lǐ Huì,
courtesy name Déqīng,
son of Minister Yuè.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he posthumously appointed Zūn and Xiào as Imperial Seal Commissioners,
Yù as Principal of the Ministry of Justice,
Gōngfǔ and Tíngzàn as Assistant Ministers of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
and Shàoxián as Censor.
Each was granted sacrificial rites,
and one son was admitted to the National Academy.
Those who died from their wounds somewhat later were
Féng Jīng of Cíxī, Supernumerary Official of the Ministry of Rites;
Wáng Luán of Wújiāng, Director of the Bureau of Scrutiny and Evaluation;
and Wáng Hàn of Chānglí, Bearer of Credentials.
Féng Jīng,
courtesy name Bóqīng,
and Hàn both passed the Imperial Examination in the ninth year of Zhèngdé.
Jīng was known for his filial piety and fraternal love.
After his death,
his family was too poor to transport his body home.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
the Ministry of Personnel reported his situation,
and he was granted twenty *hú* of rice,
and the authorities were ordered to provide generous relief to his family.
Wáng Luán,
courtesy name Rǔhé.
He became a *jìnshì* in the sixth year of Zhèngdé (1511).
He served as a probationer official in the Ministry of Personnel,
and was recognized by Minister Yáng Yīqīng,
who promoted him to Principal of the Bureau of Selection.
He kept his door shut day and night,
and people rarely saw him.
He was twice promoted to Director of the Bureau of Scrutiny of Appointments.
He was wounded,
and died the following year.
Wáng Hàn had also died earlier.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was posthumously granted the title of Censor
and bestowed sacrificial rites.
When officials from various bureaus repeatedly presented memorials,
Jiāng Bīn was extremely angry.
He secretly ordered those in charge of the imperial prison to increase the severity of their floggings,
which is why many officials died.
Cries of lamentation reached the imperial palace,
and the Emperor was also moved by them.
He finally cancelled the southern tour;
this was due to the efforts of the various officials.
In the early Jiājìng era,
Principal Wǔ Yú submitted a memorial, saying:
"During the Zhèngdé period,
supervising secretaries and censors, presuming on their power, rode roughshod over others,
chasing power and choosing convenience.
Regarding major shortcomings of the imperial court
and great wickedness among officials,
they kept silent.
At that time, those who dared to admonish despite offending the emperor,
and faced death as if returning home,
were either flogged to death in the imperial court
or banished to the frontier.
These were all directors, assistant directors, principals, reviewers, emissaries, copyists, and probationary academicians,
not those with the specific duty of speaking out.
Zhāng Yīng, originally a military man,
spoke out defiantly and faced death,
causing sorrow among passers-by.
Now, fortunately, the sagely emperor reigns,
praising and showing compassion to the loyal and upright.
What face do those supervising secretaries and censors have to stand again in this clear and enlightened court?
I request that they be punished and dismissed
to serve as a warning and deterrent."
The memorial was sent down to the Ministry of Personnel.
Wǔ Yú later died by flogging for disputing
the "Great Rites";
his biography is elsewhere.
A eulogy states: Lǐ Wénxiáng and Sūn Pánfǔ began their careers as probationers,
and were not yet ranked in minor positions.
From Hú Guàn downwards, the various directors and high-ranking officials of the various bureaus,
some were dismissed to lowly positions.
Although not responsible for judicial review,
they were in the position to speak out,
and regarded remonstrance as fulfilling their duty.
They spoke out strongly and debated intensely;
banishments and exiles followed one after another,
yet more and more came forward.
They died piled upon each other,
yet rushed forward, fearing to be last.
Their opposition to powerful favorites
and their direct criticism of the emperor
were all crucial to the ultimate strategies for stability and danger.
As for Zhāng Yīng, who exposed his chest to enlighten the emperor,
and Xú Ào, who used a trick to offer subtle admonition,
their sincerity stemmed from loyalty and love;
indeed, these were even more difficult for others to achieve.
Collation Notes
Biography 78: Yáng Tínghé, Liáng Chǔ, Jiǎng Miǎn, Máo Jì, Shí Bǎo (elder brother Jiè)
Yáng Tínghé,
courtesy name Jièfū,
was from Xīndū.
His father, Chūn,
was an Assistant Surveillance Commissioner for Education in Húguǎng.
Tínghé passed the provincial examination at the age of twelve.
In the fourteenth year of Chénghuà (1478),
at the age of nineteen,
he became a *jìnshì* before his father.
He was appointed a probationary academician,
then took leave to get married,
and upon returning to court, was appointed an editor.
Tínghé was a man of handsome demeanor,
with a calm and meticulous nature.
His writings were concise, clear, and well-structured.
He enjoyed studying historical precedents, the suffering of the people, border affairs, and all legalistic theories,
and was full of the promise of a chief minister.
In the second year of Hóngzhì (1489), he was promoted to compiler.
When the *Veritable Records of Xìanzōng* was completed,
he was promoted to lecturing academician for his participation in its compilation.
He was transferred to Junior Supervisor of the Left in the Left Supervising Office of the Heir Apparent,
and attended the crown prince's lectures.
When the *Comprehensive Institutions* was completed,
he was exceptionally promoted to Grand Academician of the Left Supervising Office of the Heir Apparent
and served as a daily lecturer.
In the second year of Zhèngdé (1507), he entered the East Cabinet from the Grand Secretariat,
specializing in handling imperial edicts.
Due to his criticism of treacherous favorites during the imperial lectures,
he offended Liú Jǐn.
An imperial edict ordered him transferred to Assistant Minister of Personnel in Nánjīng.
In the fifth month, he was promoted to Minister of Revenue in Nánjīng.
Three months later, he was recalled
and promoted to Grand Academician of Wényuān Cabinet,
participating in state affairs.
The following year, he was granted the titles of Junior Protector and Junior Mentor of the Heir Apparent.
Jǐn found minor errors in the *Comprehensive Institutions*,
and deprived Tínghé and Grand Academician Lǐ Dōngyáng and others of two ranks of their salaries.
Soon after, this was restored due to their merit in completing the *Veritable Records of Xiàozōng*.
The following year, he was granted the titles of Grand Master of Glorious Happiness and Pillar of the State,
and transferred to Minister of Personnel and Grand Academician of Wǔyīng Hall.
At this time, Jǐn's arrogance grew even greater,
while Jiāo Fāng and Zhāng Cǎi colluded with him both inside and outside the court.
Tínghé and Dōngyáng maneuvered cautiously,
managing only small interventions and rescue efforts.
When Prince Ānhuà, Zhìfān, rebelled,
using the excuse of executing Jǐn,
Tínghé and others drafted a pardon edict
and requested the promotion of frontier general Qiú Yuè
to split the rebel faction.
Yuè indeed captured Zhìfān.
Just then, Zhāng Yǒng exposed Jǐn's crimes,
and Jǐn was executed.
Tínghé and others were then again rewarded for their merits, advancing to Junior Tutor and Junior Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent, Grand Academician of Jǐnshēn Hall,
and one of his sons was granted the position of Secretarial Official.
When the bandits Liú Liù, Liú Qī, and Qí Yànmíng rebelled,
Yáng Yīqīng recommended Mǎ Zhōngxī to suppress them.
Tínghé said:
"Zhōngxī
is a scholar,
not fit for this task."
By then, he had already been dispatched,
and indeed could not pacify the bandits.
Tínghé requested that Zhōngxī be arrested and imprisoned,
and replaced by Lù Wán,
and that Commander Sāng Yù, who had previously accepted bribes and let bandits escape, be executed.
Later,
acting on the advice of Academician Chén Jì,
he mobilized frontier troops to suppress the Hénán bandits Zhào Suì and others,
and recommended Péng Zé as overall commander.
After the bandits were pacified, in recognition of his merits,
one of Tínghé's sons was recorded as a Commander in the Imperial Guard.
He declined,
and was specially promoted to Senior Tutor, Grand Mentor of the Heir Apparent, and Grand Academician of Huágài Hall.
When Dōngyáng retired from office,
Tínghé thus became the chief grand academician.
Zhāng Yǒng, having removed Jǐn, became arrogant.
He captured a man with a dragon tattoo on his arm, claiming it as a great achievement,
and, citing the precedent of the late eunuch Liú Yǒngchéng,
hoped to be enfeoffed as a marquis.
Tínghé stated:
"Yǒngchéng's adopted son Jù was enfeoffed as an earl based on his own military merits,
and moreover, it was not Yǒngchéng himself who received it,"
and so the matter was dropped.
Péng Zé, about to lead an expedition west to suppress Yān Běnshù,
asked Tínghé for advice.
Tínghé said:
"With your talent,
the bandits are not difficult to pacify;
what you must be wary of is returning too early."
Zé later defeated and executed Běnshù and others and immediately returned to court,
but the remaining factions rose up again like swarming hedgehogs and could not be controlled.
After Zé had set out, he then stayed,
and sighed, saying:
"Master Yáng's foresight
is beyond me."
When the Palace of Heavenly Purity caught fire,
Tínghé requested the Emperor to vacate the palace,
issue an edict blaming himself,
and seek honest advice.
He then, with his colleagues, submitted a memorial,
urging the Emperor to hold court early and retire late,
personally attend the sacrifices at the nine ancestral temples,
show filial piety to the two empress dowagers,
and diligently attend daily lectures.
He further memorialized in person to open avenues for remonstrance,
understand the sentiments of the people,
recall frontier troops,
abolish palace markets,
dismantle imperial shops,
expel Western monks,
reduce construction projects,
and curtail weaving and manufacturing;
there were more than ten such items,
all critical and timely.
The Emperor did not heed them.
Soon after, he requested leave to attend his father's funeral,
but was refused.
After three requests, he was finally granted leave
and an imperial eunuch was dispatched to escort him.
He was soon recalled,
but after three memorials declining,
it was finally permitted.
Tínghé was the first Grand Academician
who was allowed to complete his parents' mourning period.
Tínghé oversaw the imperial government for nearly forty days.
Xīng Shìzǐ arrived in the capital and immediately ascended the throne.
Tínghé drafted the imperial edict for the ascension.
Officials from the document office suddenly came to the閣 (Grand Secretariat),
saying they wished to remove several inconvenient points from the edict.
Tínghé said:
"In the past, when things went awry,
it was always attributed to the emperor's will.
Is this also the new emperor's intention?
After we congratulate him on his ascension,
we should present our memorial directly to him
and ask who wished to amend the drafted edict."
Miǎn and Jì also successively voiced strong objections,
and the person was speechless.
Soon after, the edict was issued,
and the corrupt policies of the Zhèngdé era were almost entirely rectified.
The number of demoted or dismissed officials, including those from the Jǐnyī Zhū Wèi (Brocade-Clad Guards), palace eunuchs, banner escorts, and laborers, amounted to 148,700.
The grain tax was reduced by over 1,532,000 dàn.

Among them, the majority of those who obtained official positions through favoritism, such as the贵 (eunuchs' adopted sons), 義子 (eunuchs' adopted sons), 傳陞 (hereditary promotions), and 乞陞 (begged promotions), were dismissed.
Both within and outside the court, the new emperor was praised as a sagely ruler,
and Tínghé's accomplishments were lauded.
However, those who had lost their positions resented Tínghé to the core,
and there were even those who lay in wait with drawn swords beside Tínghé's sedan chair when he entered court.
When the matter was reported,
an edict ordered one hundred营卒 (camp soldiers) to guard him during his comings and goings.
The emperor held the Jīngyán (imperial lectures),
and Tínghé was in charge of the Jīngyán affairs.
He oversaw the compilation of the Wǔzōng Shílù (Veritable Records of Emperor Wǔzōng),
serving as the chief editor.
Tínghé had already been promoted to Tèjìn,
had served for nine full years as a First Rank official,
and also received the salary of a Dàxuéshì (Grand Secretary),
with an imperial edict commending him.
At this time, he was further promoted to Zuǒ Zhùguó.
The emperor summoned him for audiences three times,
offering utmost comfort and praise.
Tínghé became even more determined to express his views,
recommending upright individuals
and placing them in positions of authority.
Gěishì (supervising secretaries) and Yùshǐ (censors) submitted multiple memorials denouncing Wáng Qióng's crimes,
leading to his imprisonment.
Qióng, pressed,
submitted a memorial slandering Tínghé to clear himself.
The law court sentenced Qióng to death under the law for traitorous factions,
but Qióng strongly defended himself
and had his sentence reduced to exile to the frontier.
Some suspected the law court was acting under Tínghé's instruction.
At this time, Shí Bǎo, who had been Lǐbù Shàngshū (Minister of Rites), took charge of the Zhānshì Fǔ (Court of Imperial Clan Affairs).
He was then transferred to the Lìbù (Ministry of Personnel).
Tínghé again memorialized to have him transferred back to oversee the drafting of edicts in the Zhānshì Sī.
Some people said Tínghé was too overbearing.
However, Tínghé believed that although the emperor was young,
his nature was intelligent and sensitive,
and he was confident that he could assist in achieving great peace,
thus he debated and remonstrated on every matter.
Although Qián Níng and Jiāng Bīn had been executed,
the cases of Zhāng Ruì, Zhāng Zhōng, Yú Jīng, Xǔ Tài, and others had long remained unresolved.
Tínghé and others said:
"If these individuals are not punished,
then the national laws will not be just,
public justice will not be clear,
the spirits of the nine ancestral temples will not rest in peace,
the hearts of the myriad people will not be satisfied,
the seeds of disaster and rebellion will not be extinguished,
and the governance of great peace will not be achieved."
The emperor then confiscated their property.
Tínghé again memorialized, requesting the emperor to revere Heaven's warnings,
follow ancestral instructions,
promote filial piety,
protect his sacred person,
attend to the people's welfare,
diligently pursue learning,
be cautious in issuing commands,
be clear in rewards and punishments,
delegate responsibilities with trust,
accept remonstrances,
befriend good people,
and be frugal with expenditures.
His words were mostly earnest and incisive,
and all were approved with generous imperial edicts.
When discussing
"Dàlǐ" (the Great Rites Controversy),
Tínghé's arguments became even more unyielding,
and he ultimately offended the emperor's will with this.
Prior to this,
when Wǔzōng died,
Tínghé drafted the dying edict.
It stated that the eldest son of Xīng Xiàn Wáng, the biological brother of Huángkǎo Xiàozōng Jìng Huángdì (the deceased Emperor Xiàozōng),
was next in line according to lineage.
Following the ancestral instruction of "elder brother dying, younger brother succeeding,"
it was announced to the ancestral temples,
requested of Císhòu Huáng Tàihòu (Empress Dowager Císhòu),
and the heir was welcomed to the imperial throne.
Then, he ordered ritual officials to submit a memorial outlining the ceremonial procedures,
requesting that the emperor enter through the Dōng'ān Mén (East Peace Gate) and reside in the Wénhuá Diàn (Hall of Literary Glory).
The next day,
the hundred officials submitted three memorials urging the emperor to ascend,
awaiting the imperial decree for approval,
and then choosing a day for the enthronement.
The memorials all followed the precedents for a crown prince succeeding to the throne.
Shìzōng (the Jiajing Emperor) read the memorial from the Ministry of Rites
and said:
"The dying edict states that I am to succeed to the imperial throne,
not as a crown prince."
Upon arriving in the capital,
he stopped outside the city.
Tínghé firmly requested that he follow the rites outlined by the Ministry of Rites,
but Shìzōng did not comply.
Instead, he received the memorials in his temporary residence,
entered directly through the Dàmíng Mén (Great Bright Gate),
made offerings to the late emperor's temporary shrine,
and ascended the throne at noon.
The drafted edict stated,
"By imperial brother's dying edict, I enter to succeed to the imperial lineage."
The emperor hesitated for a long time
before finally approving it.
Three days later,
an official was dispatched to welcome the emperor's mother, Xīngxiàn Fēi (Consort of Xīngxiàn).
Soon after,
ritual officials were ordered to discuss the title for the ancestral worship of Xīng Xiàn Wáng.
Tínghé consulted the cases of Dìngtáo Wáng of Han and Pú Wáng of Song and handed them to Shàngshū Máo Chéng, saying:
"These are sufficient precedents.
It is proper to honor Xiàozōng as Huángkǎo (Deceased Emperor),
and refer to Xiànwáng as Huángshūkǎo Xīngguó Dàwáng (Imperial Uncle-Father, Great King of Xīngguó),
and his consort as Huángshúmǔ Xīngguó Tàifēi (Imperial Aunt-Mother, Great Consort of Xīngguó).
The emperor should refer to himself by his name as Zhí Huángdì (Nephew Emperor).
The second son of Yìwáng, Chóngrén Wáng, should be separately established as Xīng Wáng
to offer sacrifices to Xiànwáng.
Anyone with a differing opinion is treacherous
and should be executed."
Jìnshì Zhāng Cōng and Shìláng Wáng Zàn stated
that the emperor inherited the imperial lineage, not as an adopted heir.
Zàn spoke of this discreetly,
but Tínghé, fearing it would disrupt the discussion,
transferred Zàn to Nánjīng.
In the fifth month,
Chéng convened the court officials for discussion and memorialized,
following Tínghé's words.
The emperor was displeased.
However, whenever he summoned Tínghé, he would casually bestow tea and comfort him,
wishing to make some changes.
But Tínghé ultimately refused to comply with the emperor's wishes.
So, he ordered the court officials to discuss it again.
Tínghé, along with Jiǎng Miǎn and Máo Jì, memorialized, saying:
"In previous dynasties, rulers who succeeded as adopted heirs
and posthumously honored their birth parents
all went against ritual norms.
Only the Song Confucian scholar Chéng Yí's Pú Yì (discussion on the Pú Wáng case) captured the true essence of principle and reason,
and can serve as a model for all generations.
Regarding the sacrifices to Xīng Xiàn Wáng,
although Chóngrén Wáng is in charge,
in the future, when imperial descendants proliferate,
the second son will still succeed Xīng Xiàn Wáng,
and Chóngrén Wáng will be re-enfeoffed as a Qīnwáng (Prince of the First Rank).
This way, the principles of Heaven and human sentiment
will both be perfectly preserved without loss."
The emperor was even more displeased
and ordered a thorough study of ancient rituals
to seek the most appropriate solution.
Tínghé, Miǎn, and Jì again said:
"Before the Three Dynasties,
none was more sagely than Shùn,
yet we have not heard of him posthumously honoring his birth father Gǔsǒu.
After the Three Dynasties,
none was more virtuous than Hàn Guāngwǔ (Emperor Guāngwǔ of Han),
yet we have not heard of him posthumously honoring his birth father Nándùn Jūn.
If Your Majesty follows the example of these two rulers,
then your sagely virtue will be unblemished,
and your sagely filial piety will shine."
Chéng and others also repeatedly insisted on their stance.
The emperor kept their memorials and did not issue a decree.
In the seventh month,
Zhāng Cōng submitted a memorial arguing that the emperor succeeded to the lineage,
not as an adopted heir.
The emperor sent a Sīlǐ Tàijiàn (Director of Ceremonial Eunuchs) to show it to Tínghé,
saying that this proposal followed ancestral instructions
and was based on ancient rituals,
and should be adopted.
Tínghé said,
"How can a mere scholar understand matters of state?"
and took the memorial back.
Not long after,
the emperor went to the Wénhuá Diàn
and summoned Tínghé, Miǎn, and Jì,
handing them a personal edict
ordering them to honor his birth parents as emperor and empress.
Tínghé withdrew and memorialized, saying:
"Rituals state that those for whom one is an adopted heir are considered parents,
while one's birth parents are considered paternal uncles and aunts.
This not only lowers their mourning attire but also differentiates their titles.
Your subject dares not flatter or comply with the imperial will."
He then returned the personal edict.
All the officials also upheld the previous consensus.
The emperor did not listen.
By the ninth month,
the Imperial Mother Consort arrived in the capital.
The Emperor himself decreed that she enter through the central gate,
perform obeisance at the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
and then reiterated his desire to bestow the title of Emperor and Empress upon Xìngxiàn Dì and Hòu.
Yáng Tínghé said:
"Emperor Xuān of Hàn, succeeding Emperor Zhāo,
posthumously honored Shǐ Huángsūn and Lady Wáng as Dàokǎo and Dàohòu.
Emperor Guāngwǔ, succeeding Emperor Yuán,
established temples at Zhānglíng for Jùlù and Nándùn Jūn and above.
None of them ever posthumously bestowed the title 'Emperor.'
If the character 'Huáng' (Imperial) is added now,
placing them on par with Xiàomiào and Císhòu,
this would be forgetting the one succeeded and prioritizing the birth parents,
indulging private affection and abandoning great righteousness.
We, your ministers, cannot shirk this responsibility."
Thereupon, he requested his own dismissal.
Over a hundred court officials remonstrated.
The Emperor had no choice
but to issue an edict in the first year of Jiājìng, referring to Xiàozōng as Huángkǎo,
Empress Dowager Císhòu as Shèngmǔ,
and Xìngxiàn Dì and Hòu as Běnshēng Fùmǔ,
without using the title 'Huáng.'
At that time,
Tínghé had returned imperial rescripts four times and
submitted nearly thirty memorials of remonstrance.
The Emperor often harbored a vague sense of resentment.
His attendants, seizing the opportunity, spoke of Tínghé's insolence and lack of respect due to a minister.
Censors Shǐ Dào and Cáo Jiā then jointly impeached Tínghé.
The Emperor mildly demoted Dào and Jiā to appease Tínghé,
but his intention had already shifted.
Soon after, in recognition of his merit in determining the succession,
Tínghé, Miǎn, and Jì were enfeoffed as Earls,
with an annual stipend of a thousand *shí* of grain.
Tínghé firmly declined.
He was then offered a hereditary position as a Commander in the Jǐnyī Wèi,
which he also declined.
The Emperor, considering the reward too light,
added a hereditary fourth-rank capital office.
He declined again.
Having completed four evaluations,
he was promoted to Grand Tutor,
but declined four more times before ceasing.
The Emperor specially bestowed an imperial edict commending him,
and granted him a banquet at the Ministry of Rites,
with all nine chief ministers attending.
The Emperor was somewhat devoted to Daoist rituals.
Tínghé strongly argued against it,
citing Emperors Wǔ of Liáng and Huī of Sòng as examples,
and the Emperor acknowledged his advice with a gracious decree.
The Jiangnan region suffered from poor harvests for several years in a row.
Eunuchs requested that officials be dispatched to supervise weaving and manufacturing.
The Ministry of Works, Supervising Secretaries, and Censors spoke against it,
but all were ignored,
and the Grand Secretariat was urged to draft the edict.
Tínghé and others did not comply,
and instead strongly argued that the people were suffering and resources depleted,
requesting that no officials be dispatched.
The Emperor's urgency grew,
and he warned against further vexation and obstinacy.
Tínghé vigorously contended,
saying:
"Your ministers, along with all court officials and censors, speak, but are not listened to.
Instead, the words of two or three wicked and sycophantic individuals are heeded.
Can Your Majesty rule the ancestral realm alone with these two or three wicked and sycophantic individuals?
Furthermore, Your Majesty considers weaving and manufacturing an old practice of previous dynasties,
but does not know that it was never practiced since Hóngwǔ,
but only originated in Chénghuà and Hóngzhì.
Emperors Xiànzōng and Xiàozōng had many excellent policies demonstrating love for the people and frugality with resources.
Why does Your Majesty not follow their good examples,
but only emulate their bad ones?
What is the reason?
With the first edict of your ascension,
the paths of favoritism for eunuchs were almost entirely curtailed.
The world was praising your sagely virtue.
Now, suddenly, this happens.
How can trust be maintained?"
He then requested an investigation into who drafted the decree,
suspecting someone was using a false imperial rescript for private gain.
The Emperor apologized for his oversight,
and merely instructed the dispatched officials not to be reckless,
but could not stop the practice.
Tínghé had previously submitted many memorials requesting retirement,
and afterwards requested it with even greater urgency.
He also expressed his displeasure in a memorial regarding his disagreement on the discussion of honoring Xìngxiàn Dì.
The language of his memorial revealed his discontent.
In the first month of the third year,
the Emperor permitted his departure.
He was admonished for attributing fault due to his resignation,
which was not the way of a great minister.
However, he was still granted an imperial letter,
and provided with a carriage, provisions, and postal escort as per regulations,
reaffirming the previous order to enfeoff his son as a Commander in the Jǐnyī Wèi.
Supervising Secretaries and Censors requested that Tínghé be retained,
but all were ignored.
After Tínghé left,
the proposal to refer to Xiàozōng as Huángbǎokǎo was finally discussed.
Thereupon,
Tínghé's son, Shèn, a compiler, led a group of officials to prostrate themselves before the palace gate, weeping and protesting,
and was beaten and demoted to Yúnnán.

Later, Wáng Bāngqí falsely accused Tínghé and his second son, Dùn, a Ministry of War secretary, his son-in-law Jīn Chéngxūn, a compiler, and his fellow townsman Yè Guìzhāng, a court academician, as well as Péng Zé's younger brother Chōng, of illicit dealings and seeking favors,
and all were arrested and imprisoned in the imperial jail.
The investigation found no evidence,
and they were acquitted.
In the seventh year,
the *Mínglún Dàdiǎn* was completed,
and an edict determined the punishment for the ministers who had discussed the rites.
It stated that Tínghé had erroneously led the Pú discussion,
boasting of being the Son of Heaven's disciple and a state elder who determined the succession.
The law dictated that he should be executed in the marketplace,
but he was merely stripped of his office and reduced to a commoner.
He died in the sixth month of the following year,
aged seventy-one.
After a long time,
the Emperor asked Grand Secretary Lǐ Shí how much was accumulated in the Tàicāng granary.
Shí replied:
"It can sustain us for several years.
This is due to Your Majesty's edict in the early years to cut down on redundant officials and expenses."
The Emperor sighed with emotion, saying:
"This is the achievement of Yáng Tínghé,
and it must not be forgotten."
In the early years of Lóngqìng,
he was reinstated to office,
posthumously granted the title of Grand Preceptor,
and given the posthumous name Wénzhōng.
Originally,
when Tínghé entered the Grand Secretariat,
Wáng Yángmíng said to him:
"In terms of literary skill,
I might have a slight advantage,
but matters of statecraft must be left to Jièfū."
When Emperor Wǔzōng died,
it was Tínghé's efforts
that ultimately stabilized the state.
People regarded Wáng Yángmíng as having spoken wisely.
His younger brother, Tíngyí,
was the Right Vice Minister of War.
His sons, Shèn and Dùn,
and grandson, Yǒurén,
were all successful candidates in the imperial examinations.
A separate biography exists for Shèn.
Liáng Chú,
courtesy name Shúhòu,
was from Shùndé, Guǎngdōng.
He studied under Chén Xiànzhāng.
He placed first in the metropolitan examination of the fourteenth year of Chénghuà,
was selected as a *shùjíshì*,
appointed a compiler,
and soon also served as a proofreader in the Directorate of Education.
In the fourth year of Hóngzhì, he was promoted to Lecturer.
He was transferred to Royal Tutor,
attending Emperor Wǔzōng in the Eastern Palace.
He was sent to enfeoff Annan,
and refused their bribes.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Grand Academician of the Hanlin Academy,
jointly compiling the *Huìdiǎn*,
then moved to Junior Supervisor,
and appointed Right Vice Minister of Personnel.
In the early years of Zhèngdé,
he was transferred to Left Vice Minister,
promoted to Minister,
exclusively in charge of imperial edicts,
and oversaw the Zhanfu.
Liú Jǐn pinpointed minor flaws in the *Huìdiǎn*,
and Chú was demoted to Right Vice Minister.
After the *Shí Lù* of Emperor Xiàozōng was completed,
he was reinstated as Minister,
soon after promoted to Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
and transferred to the Ministry of Personnel in Nanjing.
After Jǐn was executed,
he served as Minister of Personnel concurrently with Grand Academician of the Wènyuān Pavilion,
participating in crucial state affairs.
He was repeatedly promoted to Junior Preceptor, Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent,
and advanced to the Jìnjí Hall.
In the tenth year,
Yáng Tínghé left due to mourning,
and Chú became the Senior Grand Secretary.
He was promoted to Junior Mentor, Grand Mentor of the Heir Apparent, and Grand Academician of the Huágài Hall.
At that time, the Qiánqīng and Kūnníng Palaces were being built,
and the Tàisù Hall, Swan Chambers, and boat docks were also under construction.
Chú, along with his colleagues Jìn Guì and Yáng Yīqīng, strongly remonstrated.
In the spring of the following year,
as the imperial succession was not yet settled,
he requested that worthy members of the imperial clan be chosen to reside in the capital,
to be prepared as candidates for the heir.
All his requests were ignored.
In the autumn of that year,
Yīqīng was dismissed,
and Jiǎng Miǎn replaced him.
By the next year,
Guì was also dismissed,
and Máo Jì entered the Grand Secretariat.
The Emperor enjoyed incognito excursions.
He once left through Xī'ānmén
and returned after a night.
Chú and others remonstrated,
but he did not listen,
though he still worried that the outer court would know.
That spring,
he commanded his favored attendants to summon all officials to Zuǒshùnmén,
openly announcing that after the suburban sacrifices, he would proceed to Nánhǎizǐ for a hunt.
Chú and others, as well as court ministers, remonstrated,
but he accepted none of it.
On the first day of the eighth month,
he rode in plain clothes with several tens of cavalry to Chāngpíng.
The next day,
Chú, Miǎn, and Jǐ only just realized,
pursued him to Shāhé but did not catch up.
They repeatedly submitted memorials requesting his return,
and he only turned back after thirteen days.
Chú and others, believing that the country had no heir apparent,
and that the Emperor was indulging in ceaseless pleasure-seeking,
causing apprehension and doubt both inside and outside the court,
strenuously reiterated their request for the establishment of an heir apparent,
but again received no reply.
In the ninth month,
the Emperor galloped out through Jūyōngguān,
visited Xuānfǔ,
and ordered Gǔ Dàyòng to guard the pass,
preventing any court officials from leaving.
He then proceeded from Xuānfǔ to Dàtóng,
encountered bandits at Yìngzhōu,
and was almost killed.
Chú and others were anxious and fearful,
and their requests for his return became even more urgent.
Over ten memorials were submitted,
but the Emperor remained unmoved,
and spent the New Year's Eve stationed at Xuānfǔ.
At this time,
the Emperor's lack of virtue became increasingly severe.
Petty individuals usurped power,
corrupting and disrupting the court administration,
and people's hearts were filled with fear.
Chú feared he could not handle the responsibility,
and as Tínghé's mourning period had ended,
he repeatedly requested his recall.
When Tínghé returned to court,
Chú then yielded and served under him.

The Palace Eunuch Qīu Dé, who was the Defense Commander of Fèngyáng, and the Palace Eunuchs who were the Defense Commanders of Yánsuī, Níngxià, Dàtóng, and Xuānfǔ, all petitioned for new imperial edicts allowing them to concurrently manage civil affairs,
and the Emperor granted it.
Chú and others strongly argued against it,
but were not listened to.
In the seventh month of the thirteenth year,
the Emperor, acting on Jiāng Bīn's advice,
decided to tour extensively beyond the Great Wall.
Under the pretext of frequent border alarms,
he ordered the Grand Coordinator of Military Affairs, Grand General of Might and Valor, and Commander-in-Chief Zhū Shòu, to lead six armies on a punitive expedition,
and commanded the Grand Secretariat to draft the edict.
The Grand Secretaries disapproved,
so the Emperor again assembled all officials at Zuǒshùnmén to personally instruct them.
Tínghé and Miǎn were on leave,
Chú and Jǐ remonstrated tearfully,
and the crowd also wept,
but the Emperor's will could not be swayed.
Soon after, Jǐ also claimed illness,
leaving Chú alone to contend with the Emperor for several days,
but the Emperor ultimately did not listen.
More than a month later,
the Emperor, believing that Grand General Shòu had pacified the border,
ordered him to be enfeoffed as Zhènguógōng.
Chú and Jǐ submitted a memorial stating:
"Although a Duke is noble,
he is still a subject.
Your Majesty inherited the ancestral legacy
and is the ruler of the entire realm.
How can you mistakenly devalue yourself?
If he is enfeoffed as a Duke,
then he will be granted a patent of nobility and his ancestors for three generations will be posthumously enfeoffed.
Will the spirits of the ancestors in Heaven also be willing to be devalued like Your Majesty?
Moreover, the iron certificate of privilege must contain a clause granting immunity from death.
Your Majesty's longevity and fortune are boundless;
why should you willingly demean yourself
and accept such inauspicious words?
If the name is not proper,
the words will naturally not be smooth.
We, your subjects, absolutely dare not flatter your intentions and blindly comply,
bringing upon ourselves the disaster of being executed and having our families destroyed in the future."
There was no reply.
The Emperor then passed through Xuānfǔ and Dàtóng,
proceeding directly to Yánsuī.
Chú and others submitted several tens of memorials,
all of which were ignored and unexamined.
The Prince of Qín requested idle land in Guānzhōng for pasture,
and Jiāng Bīn, Qián Níng, Zhāng Zhōng, and others all pleaded on his behalf.
The Emperor, overriding all dissenting opinions, granted it,
and ordered the Grand Secretaries to draft the imperial decree.
Tínghé and Miǎn claimed illness,
and the Emperor was extremely angry.
Chú, realizing that further argument was futile,
then submitted the draft decree, saying:
"Emperor Gāohuang of the Tàizǔ era explicitly decreed
that this land should not be granted to princely fiefs.
This was not out of stinginess,
but because he considered that if princely fiefs obtained such vast and fertile land,
they would accumulate many soldiers and horses,
become wealthy and arrogant,
and be instigated by treacherous individuals to rebel,
which would be detrimental to the imperial ancestral altars.
Now that the Prince has obtained the land,
he should be even more circumspect.
He must not gather treacherous individuals,
must not accumulate many soldiers and horses,
must not listen to madmen plotting rebellion,
which would shake the border regions
and endanger our nation.
At such a time,
even wishing to protect relatives would be impossible."
The Emperor was startled and said:
"Is it really so perilous?"
The matter was then dropped.
The next year,
the Emperor planned a southern tour.
Censors prostrated themselves at the palace gate to remonstrate,
and Chú, Miǎn, and Jǐ also spoke against it.
As many officials from various departments also remonstrated,
the plan was halted.
When Prince Níng Chén Háo rebelled,
the Emperor launched a southern expedition,
with Chú and Miǎn escorting him.
En route, upon hearing that the rebellion was quelled,
they repeatedly submitted memorials requesting the imperial carriage to return.
Arriving at Yángzhōu,
the Emperor discussed holding a suburban sacrifice in Nánjīng.
Chú and Miǎn calculated that if this plan proceeded,
the return to the capital would be even further delayed.
They strongly argued against it,
and only after submitting three memorials was their request granted.
As Chén Háo was about to be brought in chains,
the Emperor asked for suitable ways to deal with him.
Chú and others requested to follow the precedent of Emperor Xuānzōng's campaign against Gāo Xù:
once the criminal was captured,
the army should return immediately.
They also requested the return of the imperial carriage due to the change in the date for the suburban sacrifices,
various disasters and anomalies in all directions,
and border alarms.
Eight or nine memorials were submitted,
but the Emperor showed no intention of returning.
That autumn,
at the temporary imperial residence,
an object resembling a pig's head fell before the Emperor,
its color green.
Later, in the chamber of the imperial concubine,
something appeared like a hanging human head,
increasing public alarm.
Chú and Miǎn remonstrated with grave words,
and the Emperor's heart was somewhat moved.
However, the petty individuals still wanted to lead the Emperor to tour western Zhèjiāng,
and to travel by boat on the Jiāng and Hàn rivers.
Chú and Miǎn became even more afraid,
and knelt at the gate of the temporary palace with handwritten memorials, weeping,
from 1 p.m. to 7 p.m.
The Emperor sent someone to take their memorials and bring them in,
and ordered them to rise.
They kowtowed and said:
"Unless we receive your gracious permission,
we dare not rise."
The Emperor, left with no choice,
promised to return to the capital in a few days,
whereupon they kowtowed and left.
Upon the Emperor's death,
Yáng Tínghé and others decided to welcome the Heir Apparent of Xīng.
According to precedent, one Grand Secretary was to go with high-ranking eunuchs, noble relatives, and ritual officials.
Tínghé wanted to keep Jiǎng Miǎn to assist himself,
but feared that Chú, being old, might be reluctant to go.
So he feigned concern for Chú's old age and fatigue,
and tried to prevent him from going.
Chú bravely said:
"What matter could be greater than this? How dare I decline due to fatigue!"
Thus, he, along with Duke Dìngguó Xú Guāngzuò and others, welcomed the Heir Apparent at his residence in Ānlù.
After the new Emperor's enthronement,
Supervising Secretary Zhāng Jǐu and others impeached Chú for colluding with powerful traitors,
and for clinging to his salary and position.
Chú submitted three memorials requesting to resign,
but the Emperor ordered him to be granted an imperial edict, dispatched a relay carriage,
sent an official from the Bureau of Diplomatic Receptions to escort him,
and provided annual grain and servants according to regulations.
Upon his death,
his son Jūn submitted a memorial requesting a posthumous title.
Vice Minister of Personnel Guì È and others stated
that Chú's conduct in office and his role in government
had violated public opinion,
and they then presented impeachment memorials from censors in both capitals.
The Emperor, remembering his former minister from the previous reign,
specially granted him the posthumous title of Grand Tutor,
and his posthumous name was Wénkāng.
Previously,
Chǔ Zǐ Cìchū was a Centurion (Bǎihù) in the Imperial Bodyguard (Jǐnyīwèi).
While living at home, he contended with the wealthy man Yáng Duān over common land.
Duān killed the landowner,
and Cìchū then annihilated Yáng Duān's family, over two hundred people.
When the incident came to light,
Wǔzōng, for Chǔ Cìchū's sake,
merely had him sent to the border garrisons to earn merit.
Later, he was restored to his post,
and through accumulating false merits, he rose to Assistant Regional Military Commissioner (Dūzhīhuī Qiānshì) of Guǎngdōng.
Jiǎng Miǎn,
courtesy name Jìngzhī,
was from Quánzhōu.
His elder brother, Shēng,
was Minister of Revenue (Hùbù Shàngshū) in Nánjīng,
and was known for his caution and sincerity.
Jiǎng Miǎn passed the imperial examination in the 23rd year of Chénghuà (1487),
was selected as a Shùjíshì,
and appointed Compiler (Biānxiū).
In the 13th year of Hóngzhì (1500),
when the Crown Prince came of age,
Jiǎng Miǎn concurrently served as an editor (Jiàoshū) in the Bureau of Classical Studies (Sījīng Jú).
During the Zhèngdé reign,
he successively rose to Senior Vice Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Zuǒ Shìláng),
was then appointed to manage the Court of Imperial Accouterments (Zhānshì Fǔ),
and was in charge of imperial edicts and pronouncements.
He was promoted to Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū),
still managing the affairs of the Court of Imperial Accouterments.
Jiǎng Miǎn was upright and discreet, with good judgment and insight,
and was highly respected at the time.
In the 11th year (1516), he was ordered to concurrently serve as Grand Secretary of the Wényuān Pavilion (Wényuángé Dàxuéshì),
participating in state affairs.
The following year, he was transferred to the Wǔyīng Hall,
and given the added title of Grand Mentor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàifù).
When favorites claimed border merits,
and great promotions and rewards were distributed,
Jiǎng Miǎn and Liáng Chǔ were also granted hereditary centurionships in the Imperial Bodyguard (Jǐnyīwèi Shì Qiānhù).
Both men adamantly declined,
so it was changed to a civil hereditary privilege.
When the Emperor traveled to the border as the Grand General of Awe-inspiring Might (Wēiwǔ Dàjiāngjūn),
Jiǎng Miǎn was ill and on leave.
He submitted a memorial admonishing:
"Your Majesty diminishes your own prestige
and descends to the level of a subject.
If the princes in the places you pass through were to pay respects to you with the rites due a Grand General,
how would Your Majesty excuse yourself from blaming them?
In the past, Emperor Ruì (Yíngzōng) campaigned in the north.
With nearly 300,000 officers and men in the six armies,
he still fell into calamity at Tǔmù.
Now, with the palace guard thin and weak,
traveling through the border regions,
how can one not feel apprehension?
I request that those who guided Your Majesty's entourage be punished."
There was no reply.
In the 14th year (1519), upon returning from accompanying the Emperor's southern campaign,

he was given the added titles of Junior Mentor (Shàofù) concurrently Grand Mentor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàifù), Minister of Revenue (Hùbù Shàngshū), and Grand Secretary of the Jǐnshēn Hall (Jǐnshēndiàn Dàxuéshì).
When the Emperor died,
he cooperated with Yáng Tínghé in executing Jiāng Bīn.
Upon Shìzōng's accession,
when the merits for establishing the new emperor were discussed,
he was offered the title of Earl (Bójué),
but he firmly declined.
It was changed to an hereditary Imperial Bodyguard Commander (Jǐnyīwèi Shì Zhīhuī),
which he also declined.
Then he was granted a hereditary civil post of the fifth rank,
and still advanced one step.
Censor Zhāng Péng submitted a memorial evaluating the worthiness of ministers
and requested Jiǎng Miǎn's dismissal.
Censor Zhào Yǒnghēng criticized Shí Bǎo, saying he was unfit to manage personnel appointments.
Jiǎng Miǎn and Shí Bǎo then requested to resign.
The court deliberated and found this unfair;
all the Supervising Secretaries (Gěishì) and Censors (Yùshǐ) stated that they should not be allowed to leave.
The Emperor then ordered the Grand Herald (Hónglú) to convey a message for them to stay,
and issued two further gracious edicts,
only then did they resume their duties.
In the 3rd year of Jiājìng (1524), officials were dispatched to oversee weaving in Jiāngnán,
and Jiǎng Miǎn was ordered to draft the imperial edict.
Jiǎng Miǎn, considering Jiāngnán had suffered disaster,
submitted a detailed memorial requesting the cessation of the order,
but the Emperor did not comply,
and the edict was also not submitted for a long time.
The Emperor reprimanded him for his defiance and slowness,
and Jiǎng Miǎn acknowledged his fault and ceased the draft.
When the "Great Rites" (Dàlǐ) debate arose,
Jiǎng Miǎn firmly adhered to the argument of being an adopted heir,
and strongly contended with Yáng Tínghé and others.
At first, the Emperor gently admonished,
then rebuked,
but Jiǎng Miǎn held to his argument and would not yield.
When Yáng Tínghé was dismissed from politics,
and Jiǎng Miǎn was in charge of the government,
the Emperor became even more desirous of honoring his birth parents.
He dismissed Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū) Wāng Jùn to intimidate Jiǎng Miǎn,
and appointed Xí Shū to replace him,
and also summoned Zhāng Cōng and Guì È.
Public sentiment was greatly agitated,
so Jiǎng Miǎn submitted a memorial offering the strongest possible admonition, saying:
"Your Majesty's succession to the great foundation
is indeed due to the established order of lineage.
However, without the sagely decree of the Holy Empress Dowager (Zhāoshèng Huángtàihòu)
and the last will of Emperor Wǔzōng,
there would have been no mandate to receive.
Since you have received the mandate from Wǔzōng,
you naturally ought to be Wǔzōng's heir.
It is merely that the name of 'brother' cannot be confused.
Therefore, you simply refer to Wǔzōng as 'elder brother,'
Xiàozōng as 'father,'
and Zhāoshèng as 'mother,'
and to the temples of Xiàozōng and Wǔzōng, you both refer to yourself as 'successor emperor,'
'subject,'
and by your personal name,
to demonstrate the meaning of continuing the succession and ancestral worship.
Now, you wish to establish a temple for your birth parents beside the Fèngxiān Hall.
Even though I am extremely foolish,
I resolutely know this to be impossible.
Since ancient times, a monarch's succession to the throne is called 'inheriting the lineage and ascending the imperial seat,'
all referring to ancestral worship.
The rites for an adopted heir are solely for the senior lineage (Dàzōng),
because the senior lineage is the尊 (zūn) of the succession,
and also refers to ancestral temple sacrifices.
From the Hàn dynasty until now,
there has been no one who established a temple for their birth parents within the inner palace.
Emperor Xuān of Hàn, as the heir to his grand-uncle Emperor Zhāo,
only established a temple for his birth father at his burial site.
Guāngwǔ Zhongxīng, although not succeeding Emperor Píng,
only established four kinship temples at Zhānglíng.
Emperor Yīngzōng of Sòng's father, Prince Pú Ānyì,
also only established a temple at his garden.
Your Majesty previously issued an edict
to establish a temple in Ānlù,
which is exactly in line with previous dynasties and
is appropriate.
How can one, having already observed the rites for the senior lineage,
also observe the rites for the junior lineage?
If affection is given more to one's birth parents,
then loyalty will not be solely devoted to one's adopted lineage.
Where then will the spirits of the two temples of Xiào and Wǔ find repose?
I secretly fear that the spirit of Xiàndì will also not be at peace,
and even Your Majesty's own heart will not be at peace.
Recently, you further approved Wāng Jùn's departure
and hastened the arrival of Zhāng Cōng and Guì È,
which has further alarmed people.
On that day, during the court discussion about establishing the temple,
the sky was originally clear,
but suddenly turned overcast,
and by evening, strong winds and thunder erupted.
Such is the will of Heaven;
how can Your Majesty not consider changing your plan?"
He then vehemently requested to resign.
The Emperor was displeased upon receiving the memorial,
yet, due to his status as a high-ranking minister,
he replied with a gracious edict.
Not long after,
he again requested the cessation of the temple establishment discussion,
and also begged for retirement,
mentioning the celestial phenomena again in his memorial.
The Emperor was even more displeased,
and thus ordered him to return home by imperial carriage,
providing a monthly stipend and annual labor service as per regulations.
During the late Zhèngdé reign,
when the ruler was dim and government chaotic,
Jiǎng Miǎn upheld rectitude without yielding,
and had the merit of assisting and correcting.
In the early Shìzōng reign,
although the court administration was new,
the conflict between upper and lower echelons was even more intense,
but Jiǎng Miǎn maintained his principles.
He served as Chief Grand Secretary (Shǒufǔ) for merely two months after Yáng Tínghé,
and ultimately left due to disagreement.
Commentators said he possessed the demeanor of ancient great ministers.
When the "Great Canon on Human Relations" (Mínglún Dàdiǎn) was completed,
he was dismissed from his post and lived in idleness,
and died after a long time.
In the early Lóngqìng reign, his official title was restored,
and he was posthumously granted the name Wéndìng.
Máo Jì,
courtesy name Wéizhī,
was from Yèxiàn.
At the end of the Chénghuà reign,
he placed first in the provincial examination,
passed the imperial examination,
and was selected as a Shùjíshì.
In the early Hóngzhì reign,
he was appointed Compiler (Jiǎntǎo),
promoted to Reviser (Xiūzhuàn),
and served as a lecturer in the Imperial Lectures (Jīngyán Jiǎngguān),
and was specially chosen to attend and lecture to the Crown Prince (Dōnggōng).
When the "Collected Statutes" (Huìdiǎn) was completed,
he was promoted to Imperial Diarist (Shìdú).
Upon Wǔzōng's accession,
he was reappointed as Left Remonstrator (Zuǒ Yùdé),
but for a minor error in the "Collected Statutes,"
he was demoted to Imperial Diarist (Shìdú).
When the "Veritable Records of Emperor Xiàozōng" (Xiàozōng Shílù) was completed,
he was promoted to Lecturer-Academician (Shìjiǎng Xuéshì),
and served as a lecturer.
In the fifth year of the Zhèngdé reign, he was promoted to Grand Academician,
then transferred to Vice Minister of Revenue of the Right.
In the tenth year, he was appointed Minister of Rites from Vice Minister of Personnel of the Left.
When Wū Sī Zàng sent tribute,
its envoy said there was a living Buddha who could foretell fortune and misfortune.
The Emperor dispatched the eunuch Liú Yǔn to welcome him,
carrying 130 officials in brocade robes,
and several thousand guards, private servants, and attendants.
The cost of fodder, grain, boats, and carriages amounted to millions.
Jì and others submitted a memorial, saying:
"From the capital to Wū Sī Zàng is over 20,000 *lǐ*.
Public and private expenses,
are innumerable.
Moreover, from Yǎzhōu, Sìchuān, one exits the border,
traveling west across long rivers for several months before arriving.
There are no postal stations or markets.
All expenses
must be procured from Sìchuān.
Sìchuān has been at war for consecutive years;
roving bandits have just been pacified,
and barbarian invaders have risen again.
After enduring exhaustion,
to add this burden
may cause unexpected disturbances."
The memorial was submitted a second time.
Liáng Chǔ, Jìn Guì, and Yáng Yīqīng of the Grand Secretariat all earnestly remonstrated,
but received no reply.
After the suburban sacrifices were completed, he requested diligence in court lectures.
He also
requested that since no heir had been established,
a grand plan be decided early,
but this was also not heeded.
Soon after, he was reassigned to manage edicts and appointments
and oversee the Zhan-shì Fǔ.
In the twelfth year, he concurrently served as Grand Academician of the Dōnggé and participated in state affairs.
That autumn, he was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince
and reassigned to the Wényuān Gé.
When the Emperor campaigned in the south,
Jì assisted Yáng Tínghé in guarding the capital.
Upon the imperial return,
he was promoted to Junior Protector, Minister of Revenue, and Grand Academician of the Wǔyīng Diàn.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
his功 (meritorious service) in establishing the new reign was recognized,
and he was granted an earldom.
He submitted two memorials declining it.
In the early Jiājìng reign,
the Emperor wished to posthumously honor Emperor Xīngxiàn.
The Grand Secretariat officials insisted on their remonstrance,
disobeying the imperial decree.
In the third year,
Tínghé and Miǎn successively left court.
Jì became the Senior Grand Secretary,
and again held fast to his original stance.
The Emperor wished to remove the term "birth father" (bĕnshēng zhī chēng),
and Jì and Shí Bǎo jointly memorialized to dispute this.
The Emperor summoned him to the Píngtái,
and tried to persuade him with gentle words,
but Jì ultimately did not comply.
When court officials knelt at the palace gate weeping in protest,
they were all arrested and imprisoned.
Jì submitted a memorial pleading for their release.
The Emperor was enraged,
and issued an edict accusing Jì of colluding with wicked elements
and betraying the sovereign for private gain.
Jì then submitted a memorial, saying:
"Formerly, I received a sacred edict,
that matters of state should be discussed to ascertain their feasibility,
and then implemented.
This is indeed the duty of the Grand Secretariat.
I, in my foolishness, cannot live up to your brilliant command.
Recently, regarding the deliberation on the Grand Rites,
there were summonings to Píngtái,
and edicts conveyed by the Sīlǐ (Directorate of Ceremonial);
I do not know how many times there seemed to be discussion,
yet all decisions were made by Your Sacred Heart,
and were not approved.
What feasibility was there?
As for the flogging of court officials,
reaching several hundreds,
this is unprecedented since our ancestors,
and these too all came from imperial edicts from within the palace,
which we ministers were not allowed to hear.
Summoning us was merely a futile effort,
as our obstruction remained.
Though reassurance and retention were earnest,
reproaches were subsequently added.
Although I have a heart for the nation,
I cannot fully express myself.
Sīmǎ Guāng of the Sòng Dynasty told Shénzōng: 'Your Majesty employs me
presumably because you perceive my bluntness,
hoping it might be beneficial to the state.
If you merely honor me with office and salary but do not heed my words,
then you have improperly assigned an official to a position.
If I honor myself with office and salary,
but cannot correct wrongs,
then I am merely usurping titles and positions for personal gain.'
I, your minister, dare to present this to Your Majesty.
As for colluding with wicked elements
and betraying the sovereign for private gain,
these are precisely what I, your minister, have always vehemently deplored and deeply hated.
If I were guilty of any of these,
my crime would be more than mere dismissal.
Now that Your Majesty suspects me of these,
how can I shamelessly remain at court even for a single day?
I beg to be granted leave to return to my hometown,
to complete my life's journey with integrity.
Moreover, I earnestly hope Your Majesty will emulate the ancestral precedents in learning,
appoint worthy individuals, heed remonstrance,
discern right from wrong,
and distinguish loyalty from treachery,
to foster the blessings of peace and harmony."
The Emperor resented Jì's bluntness,
but permitted him to leave,
dispatching an imperial post station to provide servants and provisions as per custom.
Jì possessed scholarship
and was honest, quiet, simple, and serious in office.
Together with Tínghé and Miǎn, he stood firm and upright in court,
and was relied upon by the literati and officials.
His tenure replacing Miǎn was only three months.
Later, after the Grand Ceremony of Clarifying Human Relations was completed,
his dismissal from office was retrospectively confirmed.
After a long time,
Tínghé and Miǎn both perished.
Jì was reinstated by an imperial edict of grace,
and the Emperor had also largely forgotten him.
In the twenty-first year,
he was eighty years old.
The Provincial Grand Coordinator and Inspector reported this.
An edict was issued to send an official to inquire after him,
and again bestow servants and provisions.
He died three years later.
He was posthumously granted Grand Protector
and given the posthumous title Wénjiǎn.
His son, Qú,
was a *jìnshì*
and Grand Minister of the Imperial Stud.
Shí Bǎo,
courtesy name Bāngyàn,
was a native of Gǎochéng.
His father, Yù,
was Provincial Surveillance Commissioner of Shāndōng.
Bǎo and his elder brother Jiè both passed the *jìnshì* examination at the end of the Chénghuà reign.
He was appointed a *shùjíshì*,
then awarded Compiler,
and on several occasions excused himself due to illness to stay at home.
At the end of the Xiàozōng reign,
he was finally promoted to Reviser.
In the first year of Zhèngdé,
he was promoted to Academician-in-waiting of the Nánjīng Hanlin Academy.
He served as Libationer in both capitals,
then was transferred to Vice Minister of Personnel of the Right in Nánjīng.
He was summoned to be reassigned to the Ministry of Rites
and promoted to Vice Minister of the Left.
When Wǔzōng first traveled to Xuānfǔ,
Bǎo submitted a memorial earnestly remonstrating,
but received no reply.
He was reassigned to oversee the Hànlín Yuàn.
When court officials remonstrated against the Southern Tour,
fearing unforeseen calamities,
Bǎo memorialized in their defense.
In the sixteenth year, he was appointed Minister of Rites
and oversaw the Zhan-shì Fǔ.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he replaced Wáng Qióng as Minister of Personnel.
Since petty individuals usurped power,
personnel administration had become chaotic.
Bǎo was upright and resolute,
declining requests and favors.
Many who violated public integrity were dismissed,
and he gained great public respect.
However, Yáng Tínghé of the Grand Secretariat was displeased.
After only two months,
he was again reassigned to oversee the Zhan-shì Fǔ
and manage edicts and appointments.
In the first year of Jiājìng, he was dispatched to offer sacrifices at Quèlǐ and the Eastern Peak.
After completing the task, he returned home
and repeatedly requested retirement.
Censors, noting Bǎo's high standing,
jointly memorialized requesting his retention,
so he was recalled to duty.
In the fifth month of the third year, an edict appointed him Minister of Personnel concurrently Grand Academician of the Wényuān Gé to participate in state affairs.
The emperor wished to build a separate chamber beside the Fèngxiān Diàn to sacrifice to Emperor Xiànzōng.
Yáng Bǎo submitted a memorial strongly protesting that this was not in accordance with ritual.
When court officials knelt before the palace gate, weeping and contending,
Yáng Bǎo and Máo Jì assisted them.
Before long,
the "Grand Rites"
debate was settled,
and Máo Jì left his post.
Yáng Bǎo again remonstrated, saying:
"The matter of the Grand Rites has already received the imperial decision,
and there is nothing more to say.
However, as your servant repeatedly reflects on it,
there is still something that makes me uneasy.
If I do not speak what makes my heart uneasy,
and if I dare not speak fully for fear of offending,
then what use will Your Majesty have for your servant?
And how can your servant repay the sovereign and father?
Emperor Xiàozōng and Empress Dowager Zhāoshèng
are Your Majesty's closest blood relatives.
Now, mean and slanderous petty individuals are allowed to sow discord,
only knowing how to curry favor and seek advancement,
without considering Your Majesty's discernment.
As the winter solstice sacrifice is approaching,
when Your Majesty ascends to offer the sacrifice,
as if seeing them in person,
will you not be moved to some extent?
Indeed, one should serve the deceased as if they were alive.
Your Majesty inherits the lineage of the successive emperors,
presiding over all deities
and ruling over all lands.
How can you not exercise extreme caution,
and heed the words of petty individuals,
thus infringing upon an immutable canon?"
The emperor received the memorial with displeasure,
and ordered him not to speak of it again.
The next year, a ancestral temple was built to the east of the Tàimiào.
The emperor wished to follow Hé Yuān's advice
to demolish the shéngōngjiān (Spiritual Palace Superintendent's office)
and fell trees
to clear a path for the imperial carriage.
Attending Censor Hán Kǎi,
Censors Yáng Qín and Yè Zhōng and others repeatedly remonstrated,
offending the imperial will and having their salaries docked.
Attending Censor Wèi Dào subsequently spoke,
and was demoted and transferred to an external post.
Yáng Bǎo again submitted a strongly worded memorial,
emphasizing its impossibility,
but was not heeded.
When the ancestral temple was completed,
the emperor wished to escort Empress Dowager Zhāngshèng to pay respects.
Zhāng Cōng and Guì È strongly advocated for it.
Ritual officials Liú Lóng and others contended but failed.
The grand secretaries spoke on their behalf,
but the emperor did not reply,
hastening the preparations for the ceremony.
Yáng Bǎo then submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your Majesty wishes to escort the Empress Dowager to pay respects at the ancestral temple.
Your servant humbly believes that compliance is indeed filial,
but there is a greater filial piety than mere compliance.
Your servant truly dares not flatter to mislead the sovereign.
I humbly reflect that according to the ancestral family law,
once empresses and concubines enter the palace,
there has never been a case of them leaving without cause.
Moreover, the Tàimiào is solemn and venerable;
unless it is for seasonal or grand combined sacrifices,
even the Son of Heaven does not enter lightly,
let alone empresses and concubines?
The 'miao-jian' (temple visit) ritual cited by Cōng and his ilk
is now performed at the Fèngxiān Diàn.
Holy Ancestor and Divine Ancestor (Shèngzǔ Shénzōng) practiced this for 150 years,
and it has become a fixed custom.
During this period, empresses and concubines were received countless times,
yet no one dared to discuss this matter.
Why is this idea suddenly proposed today?
Do those sycophantic and treacherous officials possess true loyalty and love,
that Your Majesty would listen to them?
Furthermore, Yin and Yang have fixed positions
and cannot be transgressed.
Your Majesty, as the master of Heaven, Earth, and all deities,
to cause the Empress Dowager to enter and exit the Tàimiào gate without cause,
is for the female principle (kūn) to perform male principle (qián) duties,
Yin invading Yang's position,
which is the greatest impropriety.
How could your servant not know that imperial commands should be obeyed?
However, I fear it would tarnish the imperial virtue (shèngdé),
and therefore I dare not follow the decree obediently
to complete the fault of the sovereign and father,
and thus betray the virtue of Heaven and Earth."
When the memorial was submitted,
the emperor was greatly enraged.
Yáng Bǎo was a person of integrity, uprightness, and brilliance,
diligently serving the country.
He frequently spoke to the emperor about implementing the kingly way,
clearing the mind and examining affairs,
distinguishing loyal from treacherous,
fostering magnanimity,
and not pursuing immediate results.
The emperor regarded his words as impractical and broad,
and did not approve.
During the
"Grand Rites"
debate,
the emperor wished to draw him in to support himself,
but Yáng Bǎo argued based on ritual,
maintaining his position firmly.
This displeased the emperor,
and Cōng and È's faction were also unhappy.
Cōng and È conspired day and night to assist in governance,
attacking Fèi Hóng relentlessly.
Because Yáng Bǎo's conduct was lofty,
they could not harm him.
By the spring of the next year,
the treacherous man Wáng Bāngqí impeached Yáng Tínghé,
and falsely accused Yáng Bǎo and Fèi Hóng of being a treacherous faction.
The two then requested to retire.
The emperor permitted Fèi Hóng to use a relay post for his return,
but rebuked Yáng Bǎo for blaming the court
and losing the dignity of a grand minister.
All favors were denied.
His returning luggage consisted of only a single cart of bedding.
The capital residents sighed in admiration,
saying that among all prime ministers who had left the court,
none compared to Yáng Bǎo.
From Yáng Bǎo and Yáng Tínghé, Jiǎng Miǎn, Máo Jì, who were dismissed for their strong remonstrances,
until the end of the Jiājìng era,
there were no inner court ministers who dared to offer unpalatable advice.
Yáng Bǎo's official title was elevated,
from Prince Tutor (Tàizǐ Tàibǎo) to Junior Guardian (Shàobǎo).
He died in the winter of the seventh year (of Jiājìng),
and was posthumously named Wényǐn.
In the early Lóngqìng era,
his posthumous name was changed to Wénjiè.
Lǚ Jiè,
courtesy name Bāngxiù.
During the Hóngzhì era,
he was summoned from his post as Prefect of Fànshuǐ to become a Censor.
He was sent out to verify military supplies in Dàtóng,
and inspected Gānsù and Shǎnxī.
The frontier matters he reported
were all pertinent,
and he was entrusted by the Grand Censor Dài Shān.
Once, due to natural disasters,
he impeached 27 people, including Zhái Xuān, Minister of Justice in Nánjīng.
During the Zhèngdé era,
he successively held the post of Right Vice Grand Censor,
Patrolling Governor of Dàtóng,
and was summoned to be appointed Right Vice Minister of War.
As the Hải Xī tribes repeatedly infringed on the border,
and the Sān Wèi of Tàiníng were attacking other tribes,
tribute trade had been suspended for a long time.
Lǚ Jiè was dispatched as Left Vice Minister (of War) concurrently Acting Grand Censor (qiān dūyùshǐ) to inspect Liáodōng.
He went beyond the pass to pacify and persuade,
and all submitted to regulation.
The emperor was greatly pleased,
and sent an imperial letter of commendation and reward,
recalling him.
When Grand Censor Lù Wán was promoted,
the court nominated his replacement.
Three nominations were all rejected.
Finally, Lǚ Jiè was nominated,
and he was appointed Right Grand Censor in charge of the Censorate (zhǎng yuànshì).
Censor Lǐ Yǐn impeached Lǚ Jiè for illicit connections,
but it was not reported.
In the tenth year, he was appointed Minister of Revenue.
Eunuch Shǐ Dà, stationed in Yúnnán,
requested sole control of the silver mines.
Dù Fǔ, stationed in Húguǎng,
requested to borrow salt boat tax silver for tribute funds.
Liú Dé, guarding Liángzhōu,
requested to carry 600 'yǐn' of tea rations.
Lǚ Jiè refused all of these.
A Western Buddhist monk (Chǎn Jiàowáng) requested 300 boats to transport salt,
and Lǚ Jiè vehemently explained its harm.
When the emperor first left Jūyōng,
Lǚ Jiè earnestly remonstrated.
When he was in Xuānfǔ,
and required one million taels of silver,
Lǚ Jiè firmly refused.
The emperor did not comply,
but then offered half of the amount.
Wáng Qióng wished to harm Péng Zé over the Hāmì affair,
but Lǚ Jiè alone publicly praised him.
Treacherous commoners who wished to profit from salt bribed Zhū Níng to make requests,
but Lǚ Jiè refused,
submitting repeated memorials.
When court officials knelt before the palace gate to remonstrate against the Southern Tour,
most grand ministers dared not speak,
but Lǚ Jiè alone argued for their defense.
The petty faction incited the emperor's wrath,
and a stern decree ordered him to make a self-statement.
He then claimed illness and retired.
He was granted an imperial edict and imperial carriage, and provided with provisions and servants as per custom.
He died two years later at home,
and was posthumously granted Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shàofù).
Wáng Jiè possessed integrity.
When in office, he also maintained rectitude.
When he was Censor-in-Chief,
Hú Shìníng criticized Prince Níng,
and Wáng Jiè and Lǐ Shìshí requested that Hú Shìníng be punished,
for which he was ridiculed by others.
The encomium states: Towards the end of Wǔzōng's reign,
the imperial virtue daily declined,
and favored sycophants entrenched themselves around him.
Yáng Tínghé served as Grand Secretary;
though he was unable to change the emperor's virtue,
yet when roving bandits were rampant, there was no fear of complete collapse,
and when imperial princes rebelled, there was no disaster of total disintegration;
this truly relied on the court having far-sighted strategies for governance.
As for his execution of great villains,
making major decisions,
supporting the imperiled and stabilizing the tottering,
his merit lay with the nation;
even Zhōu Bó and Hán Qí could scarcely have surpassed him.
Although Liáng Chǔ incurred public criticism,
his fundamental integrity remained unstained.
Jiǎng Miǎn, Máo Jì, and Shí Bǎo
were pure, loyal, upright, and honest,
all outstandingly possessing the demeanor of ancient great ministers.
From that time onward,
the government increasingly undermined itself with power struggles.
Some were obsequious and spineless,
clinging to their emoluments to secure their own positions.
To find people like those (ministers),
how could they be often found?
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 79: Máo Chéng, Wāng Jùn (brother Wěi), Wú Yīpéng, Zhū Xīzhōu, Hé Mèngchūn, Fēng Xī (son Fāng), Xú Wénhuá, Xuē Huì (Hú Shì, Wáng Lù, Hóu Tíngxùn)
Máo Chéng,
courtesy name Xiànqīng,
was a native of Kūnshān.
He placed first in the metropolitan examination in the 6th year of Hóngzhì.
He was appointed Compiler.
After participating in the completion of the Collected Statutes,
he was promoted to Right Supervising Secretary,
and personally lectured the Crown Prince.
When Wǔzōng was Crown Prince,
the (then) Emperor praised Máo Chéng for his clear and lucid lectures.
The Emperor was greatly pleased.
At that moment, a banquet was being held on an autumn night,
and the emperor immediately had the dishes removed from his table and bestowed upon him.
When Wǔzōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Left Supervising Secretary,
and served as lecturer in the imperial lectures.
He returned home due to mourning for his mother.
In the 4th year of Zhèngdé,
Liú Jǐn found minor flaws in the Collected Statutes and demoted all the compilers,
and Máo Chéng was made Reader-in-Waiting.
After the mourning period ended, he returned to court,
and was promoted to Academician Expositor-in-Waiting.
He was again promoted to Academician,
and was in charge of the academy's affairs.
He successively held the post of Vice Minister of Rites.
In the 6th month of the 12th year, he was appointed Minister (of Rites).
On the first day of the 8th month of that same year,
the Emperor traveled incognito.
Máo Chéng, leading Vice Ministers Wáng Zàn, Gù Qīng, and others, submitted a memorial requesting his return to the palace.
Subsequently, he again went out of Jūyōng Pass,
visited Xuānfǔ,
and stayed for a long time without returning.
Máo Chéng and others frequently submitted memorials to remonstrate,
but all were ignored.
In the 1st month of the following year,
the imperial carriage returned,
and he ordered all officials to wear military attire and greet him in the suburbs.
Máo Chéng and others requested to wear ordinary court attire,
but this was not permitted.
In the 7th month,
the Emperor declared himself Zhū Shòu, Grand General of Military Might,
commanded the imperial army, and toured the borders.
He then visited Xuānfǔ,
reached Dàtóng,
passed through Shānxī, and went as far as Yúlín.
Máo Chéng and others repeatedly submitted memorials to urgently remonstrate.
By the 12th month,
they again, together with other court officials, submitted a memorial, saying:
"Since the 1st month of last year,
the imperial carriage has traveled frequently,
without having time for peaceful dwelling.
This present journey
has already lasted half a year.
The sacrificial rites to the ancestral temples and the altars of soil and grain have all been performed by proxies,
and the court greeting ceremonies for the imperial birthday, New Year's Day, and Winter Solstice have all been simplified.
The inspection of sacrificial animals on the first day of the 12th month
has been omitted and not performed,
for two years now.
The year is about to turn,
and the auspicious date for the suburban sacrifices has already been divined.
Our imperial ancestor's instruction says: 'For all sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
