if there is sincerity and devotion, they will be accepted by the spirits;
if there is negligence and disrespect, calamity will arise.'
Now the imperial carriage is traveling far afield,
with no fixed date for return.
Should ice and snow obstruct and hinder (the way),
and the roads be blocked,
and Your Majesty be unable to personally hold the jade and silk before the Lord on High on the principal New Year's Day,
how can Your Majesty be at ease?
Furthermore, the border regions are desolate and cold,
and deep winter makes it even worse.
Your ministers, residing in the capital,
and enjoying generous emoluments,
reverently think of Your Majesty's fatigued and weary body,
and the foundation (of the state) being empty and neglected.
Gazing from afar at Your Majesty's distant presence,
our hearts are heavy as if drunk with worry.
We humbly pray that the imperial carriage hasten its return,
and personally perform the anointing and sacrificial rites;
the ancestral temples, the state, and the ministers and people will be most fortunate."
It was ignored.
In the 2nd month of the 14th year,
the imperial carriage had just returned to the capital,
when an edict was immediately issued to the Ministry of Rites:
"Zhū Shòu, Grand General of Military Might Supervising All Military Affairs, Commander-in-Chief, Grand Tutor, and Duke Protector of the State, is to be sent to the Two Capital Regions,
to respectfully visit Mount Tài,
to respectfully install sacred images,
and pray for blessings and peace for the people."
Máo Chéng and others were startled and astonished,
and again, together with court officials, submitted a statement:
"Your Majesty, as the Son of Heaven and Earth,
inheriting the legacy of your ancestors,
the whole empire knows only that Your Majesty holds the title of Emperor.
Now, this 'Grand General of Military Might Supervising All Military Affairs, Grand Tutor, Duke Protector of the State'
your ministers do not know to whom it refers.
Indeed, the one who issued this edict
is Your Majesty.
The one who conferred this title
is Your Majesty.
We do not know what person received this title.
If it is because an imperial heir has not yet been established,
and you desire to announce this throughout the famous mountains and great rivers,
to pray for silent assistance,
then sending envoys bearing gifts
would be sufficient to show respect.
Why must Your Majesty personally carry divine images,
and offer precious incense,
like the practices of Buddhists and Taoists?"
Thereupon, they enumerated five reasons why it was impermissible.
This also was ignored.
When Zhū Chénáo rebelled in Jiāngxī,
the Emperor went on a southern expedition to display his military might.
He resided in the auxiliary capital for over a year.
Máo Chéng repeatedly requested for the imperial carriage to return.
When the imperial carriage returned to Tōngzhōu,
following the advice of Jiāng Bīn,
he was about to immediately bestow death upon Zhū Chénáo.
Máo Chéng, based on the precedent of the Han commoner,
requested that the emperor return to the capital to make announcements to the suburban altars and ancestral temples,
present the captives, and then carry out the execution.
This was not followed.
When the eunuch official Wáng Táng governed Zhèjiāng,
he requested to build a shrine for a living person (for himself),
and the envoy of the Prince Chǎnhuà of Xīfān begged for an additional bestowal of 90,000 catties of tea.
Máo Chéng vigorously opposed both.
He was not heeded.
When Wáng Qióng wanted to frame Péng Zé,
Máo Chéng alone pleaded his innocence.
When Emperor Wǔzōng passed away,
Máo Chéng, together with Grand Secretary Liáng Chǔ, Marquis of Shòuníng Zhāng Hèlǐng, Imperial Son-in-Law Cuī Yuán, Grand Eunuch Wéi Mìn, and others, welcomed Emperor Shìzōng in Ānlù.
Upon his arrival,
when he was about to have an audience,
some proposed to use the rites for the Son of Heaven.
Máo Chéng said:
"If we do so now,
what can be added later?
Surely the rites of urging ascension to the throne and deferring (to the emperor),
should then be abolished?"
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was transferred to be the Right Vice Minister of War in Nánjīng.
Halfway there, he was summoned back to be the Right Vice Minister of Personnel.
At that time, Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng prefectures suffered successive droughts and floods,
and the waters of the Jiāng and Huái rivers overflowed greatly in the north,
sweeping away countless fields, dwellings, people, and livestock.
Mèngchūn, following the example of the Han and Wei ministers, presented a memorial with eight proposals,
which the Emperor graciously accepted.
Soon after, he was promoted to Left Vice Minister.
When Shàngshū Qiáo Yǔ was dismissed,
he temporarily took charge of the ministry's affairs.
Before this,
the "Great Rites"
controversy had arisen.
Mèngchūn, hearing of it in Yúnnán,
submitted a memorial stating: "Your subject has perused the court gazettes
and seen the memorial by scholar Qū Rú requesting that the Holy Father be honored as
'Imperial Uncle-Father Xīngxiàn the Great King' and
the Holy Mother as
'Imperial Aunt-Mother Xīngxiàn
the Great King Consort.'
The imperial decree was sent down to the ministry,
and I know that an imperial command has not yet been issued.
Your subject observes that among emperors of previous dynasties,
those who ascended to the great lineage from a collateral branch,
and sought to honor their birth parents,
have their successes and failures fully recorded in historical annals.
Emperor Xuān did not dare to add a title to the Imperial Grandson Shǐ,
Emperor Guāngwǔ did not dare to add a title to Lord Nándùn,
Emperor Yuán of Jìn did not dare to add
a title to Prince Gōng;
they suppressed their emotions and upheld the rites.
This is what Sīmǎ Guāng of Sòng called 'praised by their contemporaries
and extolled by later generations.'
However, Emperors Āi, Ān, Huán, and Líng posthumously
honored their fathers and grandfathers,
thereby violating righteousness and infringing upon rites.
This is what Sīmǎ Guāng called 'ridiculed by their contemporaries
and disapproved of by later generations.'
The 'Yílǐ' commentary on 'Mourning Garments'
states, 'For one who is adopted as heir,'
the commentary says,
'Why is it three years?
One who receives a heavy responsibility
must wear the mourning garment of the highest rank for them.'
'For one who is adopted as heir,
they mourn for their birth parents for a period,'
the commentary says,
'Why
is it one year?
One does not wear two qī (three-year) mourning garments,'
'one who prioritizes the great lineage
lowers the status of their small lineage.'
Indeed, there is none higher in the world than parents.
Yet, when one succeeds to the great lineage,
one
reduces the mourning for them
and shifts it to the relatives one is adopted into,
for indeed, a name cannot have two masters.
One who is adopted as heir becomes a son to the adopted parents,
and dare not again regard private relatives.
The Sages established the rites so that
there are no two superiors;
if the heart of reverence is divided towards the other,
then it cannot be solely dedicated to this one.
Now, the court ministers have deliberated in detail,
but the matter is
still undecided.
Is it not that the designation 'Imperial Uncle-Father' is inappropriate?
Even your humble subject cannot but have doubts.
According to the rites,
while alive they are called 'parents' (fùmǔ),
after death they are called 'father' (kǎo) and 'mother' (bǐ).
There are texts for
'paternal relatives' (shìfùmǔ) and 'paternal uncles and aunts' (shúfùmǔ),
but no mention of 'paternal uncle-father' (shìshúkǎo) or 'paternal uncle-mother' (shìshúbǐ).
Now, to wish to call Prince Xīngxiàn 'Imperial Uncle-Father,'
what classical precedent is there?
During
Emperor Yīngzōng of Sòng's time, there was a request to add 'Imperial Elder-Father' to Prince Pú,
which Sòng Mǐnqíu strongly refuted as erroneous.
Therefore, how can the designation 'Imperial Uncle-Father'
be applied to Prince Xīngxiàn?
Even
calling him 'Imperial Uncle' (huángshúfù) is not proper according to righteousness.
The classics refer to 'elder uncle' (bófù) and 'younger uncle' (shúfù) as terms used while alive.
After their death,
there is never a general
term for blood relatives placed before a noble title.
Therefore, how can the designation 'Imperial Uncle'
be added to a Prince who has already been given a posthumous title by the previous dynasty?
Your subject humbly observes the previous imperial edict,
wherein Your Majesty referred to the late Emperor as 'Imperial Elder Brother,'
and indeed, referring to Prince Xīng as 'Imperial Uncle,'
as Wáng Guī and Sīmǎ Guāng of Sòng stated,
is already satisfactory.
However, the debaters
sometimes
disagree.
Why is this?
The empire
is the empire of Tàizǔ.
From Tàizǔ it was passed to Xiàozōng,
and Xiàozōng passed it to the late Emperor,
who specially selected Your Majesty
to bestow upon you this great enterprise.
Although Prince Xīng is Your Majesty's beloved birth relative,
the reason for your glorious ascension to the throne
and your possession of the entire realm,
with your descendants ruling for ten thousand generations,
is all due to
the virtue of the late Emperor
and the legacy of Xiàozōng.
Therefore, your subject wishes to take Emperors Xuān of Han, Guāngwǔ, and Yuán of Jin as models.
If it is not an ancient name
or a correct title,
it is not what your subject desires for Your Majesty."
By the time Mèngchūn became a Personnel official,
the birth parents had already been honored as Emperor Xīngxiàn and Empress Xīngguó,
and subsequently changed to Birth Imperial Father Gōngmù Xīngxiàn Emperor and Birth Holy Mother Zhāngshèng Imperial Empress Dowager.
Mèngchūn submitted three memorials requesting to follow the initial edict,
but none were heeded.
Thereupon, the Emperor further accepted the words of Zhāng Cōng, Guì È and others,
and again wished to remove the two characters 'birth' (běnshēng).
Zhāng Cōng was then at the height of his power,
and listed thirteen instances of deception and absurdity by the ritual officials,
further denouncing them as a faction.
Mèngchūn, along with the Nine Ministers Qín Jīn and others, submitted a joint memorial,
which roughly stated:
"Yī Yǐn said, 'If words are contrary to the heart,
one must seek them in the Way.
If words are submissive to the will,
one must seek them in the non-Way.'
Recently,
in the debate on the Great Rites,
the righteous and the perverse differed.
If the remonstrances of the various ministers,
accumulating to tens of thousands of words,
are what is called 'words contrary to the heart,'
has Your Majesty ever sought them in the Way?
A few humble individuals,
daring to use the pretext of compliance,
recruit idle, unlearned, and shameless individuals,
confusing the imperial ear.
These are what are called 'words submissive to the will.'
Has Your Majesty ever sought them in the non-Way?
Why are their words so easily accepted,
while these words are so difficult to enter?"
He then presented thirteen difficulties to refute Zhāng Cōng,
but the memorial was held up and not acted upon.
Once Zhāng Cōng and his associates gained influence,
they jointly petitioned to pardon officials who had been banished to military garrisons.
All of them first mentioned Xī,
but the emperor did not approve.
Finally, the Jǐnshēn Diàn suffered a fire,
and Xī was almost seventy.
The Supervising Secretary Tián Rú again requested leniency,
but it was ultimately not granted.
Thirteen years later,
he eventually died at his place of exile.
At the beginning of the Lóngqìng reign,
he was posthumously granted official titles and a pension.
His son, Fáng,
courtesy name Cúnlǐ,
placed first in the provincial examination.
In the second year of the Jiājìng reign, he became a *jìnshì*.
He was appointed as a Supervising Secretary of Merit Rating in the Nanjing Ministry of Personnel.
Soon after, he was demoted to Assistant Prefect of Tōngzhōu.
He was subsequently dismissed and returned home.
Fáng was learned and skilled in writing,
and also proficient in calligraphy,
but his nature was wild and unconventional.
After Xī died,
Fáng's family became impoverished.
He thought of imitating Zhāng Cōng and Xià Yán, who gained prominence with a single word.
In the seventeenth year, he went to the capital to present a memorial,
discussing the construction of the Míngtáng.
He also suggested that the posthumous title of the Xiàn Emperor should include *zōng* (宗),
to match Shàngdì.
Shìzōng was greatly pleased.
Not long after,
the Xiàn Emperor's title was advanced to Ruìzōng,
and he was enshrined in the Xuánjí Diàn.
This proposal originated with Fáng,
and people commonly disliked Fáng for "betraying his father."
The following year, he again presented a chapter of the elegant poem "Qīngyún,"
which an imperial edict ordered to be deposited in the Imperial Academy of History.
He waited a long time for an appointment,
but ultimately received no promotion,
and returned home to die in dejection.
In his later years, he changed his name to Dàoshēng.
He separately composed textual commentaries for the Thirteen Classics,
most of which contained far-fetched interpretations.
Some say that the "Zǐgòng Shīzhuàn" (子貢詩傳) circulated in the world
was also a forgery by Fáng.
Xú Wénhuá,
courtesy name Yòngguāng,
was a native of Jiādìng Zhōu.
He became a *jìnshì* in the third year of the Zhèngdé reign.
He was appointed Grand Judge of the Ministry of Justice.
He was promoted to Censor,
and then Circuit Censor for Guìzhōu.
When the Miáo leader Āzá and others in Kuīxī stirred up rebellion,
he joined Governor Wèi Yīng in suppressing them,
destroying six hundred and thirty stockades.
He received an imperial commendation and reward.
When Hú Shìníng, the Vice Commissioner of Jiāngxī, was imprisoned in the Imperial Guard's prison for criticizing Prince Níng Chénháo,
Wénhuá submitted a remonstrance, saying:
"Shìníng, on behalf of the sagely court above
and the imperial clan below,
exhausted his sincerity and gave vent to his indignation.
No sooner had his words left his mouth
than misfortune followed.
This is truly lamentable.
Prince Níng's power and influence grow daily,
and the hidden danger deepens daily.
If we do not suppress it now,
it may become boundless.
Yet you further subject Shìníng to severe punishment,
stopping the mouths of all beneath Heaven,
crushing the spirit of loyal and upright officials,
weakening the authority of the court,
inciting the ambitions of the imperial relatives,
and inviting unforeseen calamities.
All of this begins today."
It was not accepted.
When the emperor dispatched the eunuch Liú Yǔn to welcome Buddhist relics from Wūsīzàng,
Wénhuá strenuously remonstrated.
There was no response.
When Mǎ Áng presented his pregnant sister to the emperor,
Wénhuá again memorialized, remonstrating:
"Even a family of commoners would not take a woman who has remarried.
Your Majesty, the most revered of ten thousand chariots,
has made such a move.
If you reflect upon it, your heart will be uneasy;
if you proclaim it, it will be unseemly;
if it is passed down to all under Heaven and to future generations, it will be shameful.
Who presented this to Your Majesty?
Their crime deserves extermination of their clan.
Should guarding against breaches be lax,
and by misfortune, someone like Lǐ Yuán or Lǚ Bùwéi seize an opportunity,
would that be a minor matter?
Now, Áng's brothers, sons, and nephews enter and exit the Forbidden City,
and Your Majesty lowers your rank and status,
allowing them to mix their attire and sit together,
or even sleep and rise together.
There is no greater violation of the ancestral laws than this.
With Lady Mǎ monopolizing favor within,
and Áng and his associates manipulating power without,
the seeds of disaster are secretly sown,
and the consequences are beyond words.
I beg you to execute them early to cut off the source of calamity."
This also received no response.
Since Wénhuá had repeatedly offered forthright advice,
the emperor and his close favorites all harbored resentment.
It happened that Wénhuá enumerated five matters regarding ancestral temple rituals:
the ancestral temple,
the *dìxiá* sacrifice, special offerings, moving spirit tablets, and placing them in the ancestral temple.
All five matters
were based on classical texts and could be implemented.
The emperor was enraged,
accusing him of overstepping his authority and speaking recklessly.
The memorial was sent to the relevant department.
The officials of the Ministry of Rites were ignorant of classical scholarship
and also sought to please the emperor,
so they reported that Wénhuá's words were incorrect.
He was ordered to be imprisoned in the Imperial Guard's prison
and demoted to commoner.
This was in the tenth month of the eleventh year of Zhèngdé.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was reinstated to his former office,
and successively served as Vice Surveillance Commissioner of Hénán.
In the second year of Jiājìng, he was commended for his outstanding administration
and entered the court as Right Junior Minister of the Grand Court of Judicial Review,
soon after transferring to Left Junior Minister.
At that time, the "Grand Rites" for the Xīngxiàn Emperor
were being deliberated,
and Wénhuá, along with other high officials, repeatedly argued strongly against them.
In the seventh month of the following year,
he again led court officials to kneel before the palace gate and weep in remonstrance,
for which he was suspended from salary for four months.
Later,
Xí Shū, Zhāng Cōng, Guì È, and Fāng Xiànfū met with court officials for a major deliberation.
Wénhuá, along with Wāng Wěi and Zhèng Yuè, still argued strongly.
Marquis Wǔdìng Guō Xūn suddenly said:
"The ancestral instructions are thus,
and ancient rites are thus.
Cōng and his associates' words are appropriate.
The *Shūjīng* says that a minister serving his ruler
should follow and accommodate his virtues."
Thus, the decision was made.
When the ancestral tablet titles were to be changed,
Wénhuá remonstrated, saying:
"Xiàozōng has the virtue of an ancestor,
and cannot be referred to as 'elder paternal cousin'.
Wǔzōng has the virtue of a father,
and cannot be referred to as 'elder brother'.
It would be better to directly call them 'Emperor Xiàozōng Jìnghuángdì' and 'Emperor Wǔzōng Yìhuángdì',
which would preserve both without harm."
Upon receiving the memorial,
an order was given to again deduct his salary.
In the autumn of the sixth year,
the case of Lǐ Fúdá arose.
The chief judges, Cōng, È, and Xiànfū,
held a grudge against Wénhuá and others due to the ritual debate,
so they completely overturned the original verdict,
and imprisoned Wénhuá and the other judicial officials.
When the case was concluded,
Wénhuá was accused of colluding with a censor in killing,
and sent to exile in Liáoyáng.
He died on the way
before an amnesty was granted.
At the beginning of the Lóngqìng reign,
he was posthumously granted the title of Left Vice Censor-in-Chief.
After Grand Secretary Máo Jì and Vice Minister Hé Mèngchūn left office,
among the ministers who previously argued for
the "Grand Rites,"
some ambiguously complied with the imperial will,
but Wénhuá firmly adhered to his previous opinion unchanged.
His condemnation was not due to any crime,
and scholars deeply regretted it.
Xuē Huì,
courtesy name Jūncǎi,
was a native of Bózhōu.
At the age of twelve, he could compose poetry.
He became a *jìnshì* in the ninth year of Zhèngdé,
and was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Justice.
He remonstrated against Wǔzōng's southern tour,
and was flogged and had his salary deducted.
Soon after, he resigned due to illness.
He was reinstated to his former office,
transferred to the Ministry of Personnel,
and successively served as Director of Merit Rating.
In the second year of Jiājìng,
court officials repeatedly argued about
the "Grand Rites,"
and were at an impasse with Zhāng Cōng, Guì È, and others.
〔一三〕Huì wrote "Wèi Rén Hòu Jiě" (為人後解), "Wèi Rén Hòu Biàn" (為人後辨), and "Biàn Cōng È Suǒ Lùn Qī Shì" (辨璁、萼所論七事),
totaling tens of thousands of words, and submitted them to the court.
The "Jiě" had two parts, upper and lower,
expounding the meaning of the great lineage.
His "Biàn" stated: Your Majesty inherits the ancestral body and succeeds to the direct lineage,
which conforms to the principle of being a successor,
clearly without doubt.
Yet there are two or three ministers
who distort the classics and betray rites,
and above
Sī was young and impetuous.
He often pointed out the faults of others in a crowd.
He later regretted this
and restrained himself, becoming reserved and taciturn.
When he was demoted,
he departed calmly.
One night, passing Guīlóngshuǐ,
his boat drifted onto a large rock.
He sat on the rock and sang loudly.
His family arrived later,
heard his singing, and then moored their boat to cross.
Wáng Shǒurén was lecturing in Gànzhōu,
and Sī joined him.
When Shǒurén was campaigning against Chén Háo,
he summoned Sī to assist in military discussions.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
Sī was recalled to his former office,
and his stipend was further increased by one grade.
Sī declined in a memorial,
and moreover said:
"If Your Majesty wishes to foster a spirit of bold speech
to prevent the wickedness of obstruction and deception,
it is better to diligently examine memorials,
summon ministers for audience,
and not allow the words of perverse flattery to bewitch the sacred ear.
Then the governance of Yáo and Shùn can be achieved.
Otherwise,
even if grace is extended to those ministers criticized in the previous reign,
it would be but a trivial matter."
The Emperor did not approve,
and thus decreed that those whose stipends had recently been increased
were all not permitted to decline.
Soon after, he was appointed as a lecturer in the Imperial Lecture Hall (Jīngyán Jiǎngguān).
In Jiājìng’s third year, he repeatedly argued with his colleagues
over the "Great Rites" (Dàlǐ),
but was not heeded.
At that time, Zhāng Cōng, Guì È, and Fāng Xiànfū were academicians.
Sī was ashamed to be in the same rank as them
and submitted a memorial requesting to resign and return home.
It was not permitted.
In July of that year,
he and other court officials knelt at the Zuǒshùn Mén and wept in remonstrance.
The Emperor was greatly angered
and imprisoned him in the imperial prison (Zhàoyù),
giving him thirty strokes of the cane.
More than ten days later,
he was caned again.
Sī and his colleague Wáng Xiàng,
Supervising Censors (Jǐshìzhōng) Zhāng Yuán, Máo Yù, Péi Shàozōng,
Censors (Yùshǐ) Zhāng Yuètāo, Hú Qióng,
Secretaries (Lángzhōng) Yáng Huái, Hú Lián,
Assistant Secretaries (Yuánwàiláng) Shēn Liáng, Zhāng Càn,
Department Directors (Zhǔshì) Ān Xǐ, Wǔ Yú, Zāng Yīngkuí, Yú Zhēn, Yīn Chéngxù,
Document Secretaries (Sīwù) Lǐ Kědēng,
a total of seventeen people,
all died successively from their wounds.
In the early Lóngqìng reign,
each was granted patronage for one son,
and posthumous official titles varied.
Sī was posthumously granted the title of Right Remonstrance Official (Yòu Yùdé).
Sī's aspirations and conduct surpassed common customs.
He was close to Lǐ Zhōng and Zōu Shǒuyì.
Lǚ Nán of Gāolíng often praised him,
once saying:
"Happy to hear of one's faults like Jìlù,
desiring little but unable to achieve it like Bóyù—
that is Gǎizhāi."
Gǎizhāi
was Sī's courtesy name (biéhào).
Wáng Xiàng,
courtesy name Màoqīng,
was from Yín.
He became a *jìnshì* in Zhèngdé’s sixteenth year.
From *shùjíshì*, he was appointed Compiler (Biānxiū).
He was magnanimous and valued integrity.
He served his parents with profound filial piety.
Though his family was often poor and empty-handed,
he remained content.
He died after only four years in office.
Zhāng Chōng,
courtesy name Xízhī,
was from Tóngchuān.
He became a *jìnshì* in Zhèngdé’s sixth year.
He was selected as a *shùjíshì*,
then transferred to Supervising Censor of the Ministry of Justice (Xíngkē Jǐshìzhōng).
He resigned due to illness and returned home,
then was recalled to the Supervising Censor of the Ministry of Revenue (Hùkē).
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
an edict abolished all extraordinary contributions nationwide.
The following year, Zhāng Yáng, a eunuch garrison commander of the Middle Capital (Zhōngdū Zhènshǒu Nèiguān), again presented new tea as tribute.
The Ministry of Rites requested compliance with the edict’s prohibition,
but it was not granted.
Chōng said:
"Your Majesty’s edict ink is not yet dry,
yet you immediately go back on your word.
People will speculate about the court
and trifle with government decrees.
Moreover, Yáng's 'tribute tea'
is actually mixed with other items.
If the four quarters follow suit,
where will it end?
I wish that the former edict be upheld,
so as not to fall into cunning schemes."
This was not heeded.
Níngxià’s annual tribute of safflower
greatly harmed the military and common people.
Internal and external garrison officials, upon taking office,
usually offered horses as tribute to express gratitude.
Chōng requested the abolition of all these.
Though the Emperor agreed with his words,
he could not act on them.
Soon after, he said:
"Eunuchs serving as garrison commanders
was not an old system of Tàizǔ and Tàizōng.
Jǐngdì, facing many national crises,
only occasionally adopted it.
It was said that eunuchs were the court's household members,
and if there were urgent matters,
they were ordered to report.
Yet in past years, when Chén Háo plotted rebellion,
the garrison eunuch Wáng Hóng instead aided the rebellion.
Can eunuchs truly be relied upon?
In times of peace, they idly enjoy honor and prestige,
poisoning the common people;
in times of change, they harbor doubts and look on,
showing no concern for the borders.
They must be promptly dismissed."
Later, when Zhāng Fújìng became prime minister,
all garrison eunuchs were indeed abolished,
and this proposal originally came from Chōng.
He was repeatedly promoted to Supervising Censor of the Ministry of Rites (Lǐkē Dū Jǐshìzhōng).
He further stated:
"Recently, I heard that within the Forbidden City (Zǐjìn zhī Nèi),
prayers and sacrificial rites are flourishing.
In the Qiánqīng Gōng, a dozen eunuchs
are diligently studying classics,
chanting and reciting rituals.
Their rewards are excessive,
and their favor grows daily.
This is due to remnants of criminals from the previous reign, such as eunuch Cuī Wén and his ilk,
who employ evil arts as a trial scheme.
Your Majesty is being fooled by them,
and they have already been able to fully indulge their deceitful tricks.
They interfere with government affairs,
draw in various evils,
harm the foundation of great peace,
and lose the hopes of the four seas.
I surmise that Your Majesty would rather distance yourself from upright gentlemen than bear to rebuke their followers,
and would rather abandon frank counsel than wish to go against their teachings,
believing also that this can prolong your life and cure illnesses.
I have also heard that recently, imperial consorts and female attendants (bīnyù nǚyè)
fill the inner chambers,
and one or two clever and charming ones are particularly enchanting.
As a result,
daily lectures are neglected,
audiences are rare,
government decrees are often biased,
and daily routines are out of order.
Petty individuals, seeing this틈,
then use heterodox ways to bewitch.
To rely on Daoist rituals (zhāijiào) while indulging desires in the inner palace,
to consider licentiousness harmless while seeking blessings through邪妄之術 perverse and deceitful arts,
is far from the ancient emperors' way of seeking blessings without deviation."
In the fourth month of the second year of Jiājìng,
due to disasters and anomalies,
he, along with officials from the Six Offices, submitted a memorial, stating:
"In ancient times, Chéngtāng blamed himself with six matters, saying: 'Are government policies unrestrained?
Have the people lost their proper occupations?
Are the imperial palaces too extravagant?
Are female attendants overly influential?
Are bribes widespread?
Are slanderers flourishing?'
Now, let us truly compare this with recent events.
The fast ships were just reduced, yet Dài Bǎo's memorial to add them was immediately approved;
the garrison troops were just cut, yet Zhào Róng was further permitted to divide and guard.
An imperial edict ordered the examination of the imperial stables,
but it was immediately blocked by Yán Hóng's single word;
an imperial edict ordered the dismissal of military artisans,
but it was soon overturned by the clamor of the gate guards.
This cannot be called restrained governance.
Trivial crafts compete in ingenuity,
and idlers constitute half the populace.
Farming and sericulture are often neglected,
lacking the means for daily sustenance;
moral education is unheard of,
leading to a habit of idleness and deceit.
This cannot be said that the people have not lost their proper occupations.
The construction of the two palaces
involved arduous collection and transportation.
Sometimes, a single piece of wood required tens of thousands of laborers,
or a single rafter wasted hundreds of units of wealth.
The sight of deaths piled up,
and the sounds of groans and sighs,
Your Majesty cannot see or hear.
This cannot be said that the imperial palaces are not extravagant.
Following Fèngshèng and Bǎoshèng,
female favorites were prioritized over the Empress;
the names Zhuāngfèng and Sùfèng
conferred special titles upon wet nurses.
Some, having received favor, gradually became like Fēiyàn,
while others, being clever and astute, were no less than Wǎn'ér,
internally shifting the Emperor's temperament,
and externally creating a reliance among close attendants.
This cannot be said that female attendants are not overly influential.
The sharp and dominant among the utterly treacherous,
publicly offer bribes and escape the laws of confiscation;
the utterly wicked Pěng and Kǎi,
secretly engage in solicitations and evade a three-year punishment.
Money works its magic, and Wáng Yīng's inquiry was transferred to the Jǐnyī;
connections are established, and Yú Xǐ ultimately slipped through the imperial net.
This cannot be said that bribes are not widespread.
Regarding the ancestral temple rites,
the proposals of the various ministries were disregarded,
and the flattering and sycophantic schemes of Wáng Huái were adopted.
The replies to memorials from high-ranking officials
lacked proper decorum,
and were influenced by the divisive opinions of petty individuals.
Some slanders originated from within,
secretly spreading poison;
others, slanders circulated externally,
openly engaging in exclusion.
Above, they confuse right and wrong in the imperial court;
below, they disrupt the uprightness of individuals.
This cannot be said that slanderers are not flourishing.
All these,
which Chéngtāng did not have,
are present today.
Therefore, we do not shrink from the punishment of the axe,
but adhere to the principle of difficult remonstrance.
We hope Your Majesty will accept it."
In the winter of that year,
the Emperor ordered eunuchs to supervise the silk weaving in Sūzhōu and Hángzhōu,
which the entire court resisted but could not prevent.
Chōng, again with fellow officials like Zhāng Yuán, forcefully argued against it.
At that time, Shìzōng was in the early stages of his reign,
and Yáng Tínghé and others were in the Grand Secretariat.
Although petty individuals were already gaining influence,
righteous opinions still prevailed,
and Chōng pointed out faults without reservation both before and after.
Although the Emperor did not adopt his suggestions,
he did report them,
and did not punish him.
By the third month of the following year,
the Emperor, based on Guì È's words,
was eager to honor Xiàn Dì,
and also wanted to build a temple within the Forbidden City.
Chōng again, with his fellow officials, forcefully remonstrated.
The Emperor then accused them of factional speech disturbing governance,
and ordered their salaries to be withheld.
Later, he again assisted Minister Qiáo Yǔ and others in a second memorial arguing against the proposal to build rooms in the inner palace,
and was severely reprimanded by imperial edict.
Lǚ Nán and Zōu Shǒuyì were imprisoned,
and Chōng and others submitted a memorial to rescue them.
When Zhāng Cōng and Guì È were summoned,
Chōng and over thirty supervising secretaries submitted a joint memorial stating:
"These two men are inherently treacherous and
malevolent in their intentions,
disrupting the ancestral temples,
sowing discord in the imperial harem,
denouncing imperial edicts,
and harming good people.
We hope they will be immediately expelled,
as a warning against disloyal ministers."
None of these were accepted.
The Emperor grew more determined to honor Xiàn Dì,
changing Xiàozōng to Bó Kǎo.
Chōng and others were worried about this.
Coincidentally, Supervising Secretary Zhāng Hànqīng impeached Xí Shū for unlawful conduct in famine relief,
and Minister of Revenue Qín Jīn requested that an official be dispatched to investigate,
which the Emperor approved.
Chōng and others then took the memorials from court officials impeaching È and others,
sent them to the Ministry of Justice, ordering them to submit a request to the Emperor,
and privately discussed among themselves:
"If the Emperor also says 'yes' to this,
then we will beat them to death."
Cōng and others reported their words.
The Emperor withheld the memorial without responding,
and instead blamed Minister of Justice Zhào Jiàn and others for colluding with evil and harming the upright,
and Chōng and others for betraying righteousness and being disloyal,
and promoted Cōng and È to Academicians.
The court officials looked at each other in shock and dismay.
The various offices then each drafted a memorial,
forcefully stating that Xiàozōng could not be called Bó Kǎo,
with over two hundred and twenty signatories.
The Emperor kept all of them and did not reply.
On the Wùyín day of the seventh month,
the officials collectively knelt at the Zuǒshùnmén to plead.
The Emperor sent eunuchs twice to instruct them to withdraw, but they did not,
whereupon he became furious.
He first arrested the eight leading officials from the various offices and sent them to the imperial prison,
and Chōng was among them.
Soon after, they were flogged in court
and banished to garrison duty at Qútáng Wèi.
Meanwhile, Cōng and È's favor became even greater.
Chōng stayed in exile for over ten years
and was released due to the kindness shown during the enthronement of the Crown Prince,
then died.
Liú Jì,
courtesy name Rǔjí,
was from Téngxiáng Wèi.
He passed the imperial examination in the sixth year of Zhèngdé.
From a Shùjíshì, he was appointed Investigating Censor of the Ministry of Personnel.
Lǐ Yuè, the Governor of Shānxī, impeached the left and right administration commissioners, Ní Tiānmín and Chén Dá.
The Ministry of Personnel requested their dismissal,
but the Emperor disallowed it.
Jì submitted a memorial arguing,
but it was not heeded.
When the Emperor visited Xuānfǔ and Yúlín,
Jì both submitted memorials requesting his return.
An edict ennobled Xǔ Tài and Jiāng Bīn as earls,
and he again, with other supervising secretaries, strongly argued against it,
but none were reported.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was sent out to inspect border provisions in Gānsù.
He memorialized to abolish the supervising eunuch guarding Liángzhōu and the newly added patrolling soldiers in Yǒngchāng.
He was twice promoted to Left Investigating Censor of the Ministry of Works.
In the first year of the Jiājìng reign,
he was promoted to Investigating Censor (dū gěishìzhōng) of the Bureau of Punishments.
When Secretary Chén Jiāyán was imprisoned for a certain matter,
Jì memorialized to rescue him,
but this was not permitted.
Liào Péng's father and son, and Wáng Qīn and others of the Qián Níng faction,
were all sentenced to death for their complicity in rebellion.
Péng and the others, by currying favor with eunuchs, hoped to escape death.
Jì presented a memorial, saying:
"Since ancient times, when death row inmates were about to be executed,
even as the drums beat, complaints were still received,
and after memorializing and awaiting a reply,
it would already be late in the day.
If they were to request a second time before carrying out the execution,
it would already be twilight.
This is quite contrary to the intention of discarding them among the multitude.
I beg that after three requests,
no more complaints be received under the drums.
The crimes of Péng, Qīn, and the others are most fittingly punished;
I hope Your Majesty will not doubt this."
An imperial edict then stipulated that from now on, executions should be carried out during the shēn (3-5 PM) or yǒu (5-7 PM) hours.
Péng and the others were eventually granted a delayed execution,
and Qīn later received a secret imperial order (zhōngzhǐ) to be spared from death.
Jì vigorously argued against this,
but was not heeded.
According to custom,
when the Embroidered Uniform Guard (chǎngwèi) made an arrest,
they had to send the original memorial detailing the circumstances to the Bureau of Punishments to issue an arrest warrant (jiàtiē).
When Commander (qiānhù) Bái Shòu brought a warrant,
Jì demanded the original memorial.
Shòu did not provide it,
and Jì refused to issue the warrant.
Both men presented their cases to the Emperor.
The Emperor initially sided with Shòu,
and ultimately overruled Jì's proposal.
The eunuchs Cuī Wénpú and Lǐ Yángfèng were found guilty,
and had already been sent to the Ministry of Punishments.
The Emperor received a memorial from Wénsuò
and transferred them to the Detention Bureau of the Embroidered Uniform Guard (zhènfǔ).
Jì, leading the Six Bureaus of Scrutiny, argued against this,
but was not heard.
Grand Commandant (dūdū) Liú Huī was sentenced to military exile (shù) as a traitorous partisan,
but an edict restored him to office.
Lǐ Lóng, the Regional Commander (zǒngbīngguān) of Gānsù, incited mutineers to kill Governor (xúnfǔ) Xǔ Míng,
and was arrested and brought to the capital,
but conspired to avoid trial.
Jì strongly stated that these actions were unacceptable,
and the Emperor followed his advice.
Huī was stripped of his office,
and Lóng was interrogated and executed.
Xú Guāngzuò, the Duke of Dìngguó, unlawfully occupied commoners' land,
and incited the people of Luánzhōu to accuse Guō Jiǔgāo, the former Prefect (zhīfǔ) of Yǒngpíng.
The eunuch Ruì Jǐngxián presided over this,
and the Imperial Guards (tíqí) made arrests for interrogation.
Jì requested that Guāngzuò also be prosecuted,
and the memorial was sent to the relevant department.
Investigating Censor Liú Zuì was transferred to an outside post for impeaching the eunuch Cuī Wén.
Jǐngxián again impeached him for violating prohibitions,
and he and Censor Huáng Guóyòng were both arrested and sent to the Imperial Prison (zhàoyù).
Zuì was exiled as a soldier, and Guóyòng was demoted.
The judicial authorities argued against this without success.
Jì stated:
"The state established the Three Judicial Offices (sānfǎsī)
specifically to handle criminal cases,
some responsible for establishing guilt,
others for rectifying miscarriages of justice.
Powerful officials should not use personal favor or resentment to determine outcomes,
nor should the Son of Heaven use joy or anger to decide severity.
Since the officials of the Embroidered Uniform Guard's Detention Bureau (jǐnyī zhènfǔ) took exclusive charge of imperial prisons,
the judicial offices have almost become a mere formality.
For offenses as minor as Zuì's,
to be entrapped through informers,
and tried by the Imperial Prison,
with edicts issued from within the palace,
of which high officials are initially unaware—
this causes no small detriment to imperial governance.
Furthermore, Lǐ Hóng and Chén Xuān committed crimes as serious as murder,
yet were only demoted.
Wáng Qīn and his brothers colluded with traitors and disrupted governance,
yet were only banished as soldiers.
Compared to Zuì and the others,
the disparity is vast,
yet their punishments are similar.
How can this be shown to the world?"
The Emperor was enraged,
and docked Jì's salary for one month.
The Empress's father, Chén Wànyán's slave, Hé Xǐ, beat a person to death.
The Emperor ordered his release.
Jì upheld the edict, saying:
"Wànyán allowing his slave to commit murder and then escaping punishment is fortunate enough;
to also release Xǐ and others means the law does not apply to the slaves of imperial relatives."
Jì had been in the Censorate for a long time;
his outspoken opinions
often clashed with powerful and favored individuals.
His reputation for integrity was profound,
and the Emperor increasingly could not tolerate it.
When the "Great Rites" (dàlǐ) debate arose,
many court officials who argued against it were punished.
Jì memorialized to rescue Reviser (xiūzhuàn) Lǚ Nán,
Compiler (biānxiū) Zōu Shǒuyì,
Investigating Censor Dèng Jìzēng,
Censors Mǎ Mínghéng, Zhū Zhé, Chén Hòu, Jì Běn,
and Department Director (lángzhōng) Lín Yìngcōng,
but was not heard.
Subsequently, he blocked the court officials at Jīnshuǐqiáo,
and wept prostrate outside Zuǒshùnmén,
receiving a caning in the imperial court.
Twelve days later, he was caned again
and banished to Liáodōng.
In the sixteenth year, when the Crown Prince was enthroned,
those banished as soldiers were pardoned,
but Jì was not included,
and died in exile.
At the beginning of the Lóngqìng reign, he was posthumously restored to office
and granted the title of Junior Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (tàicháng shàoqīng).
Ān Pán,
courtesy name Gōngshí,
was from Jiādìngzhōu.
He obtained his *jìnshì* degree in the eighteenth year of Hóngzhì.
He was later made a probationary Hanlin academician (shùjíshì).
During the Zhèngdé era,
he successively served as Investigating Censor for the Bureaus of Personnel and War,
and then requested leave to depart.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was recalled to his former post.
The Emperor issued a handwritten edict intending to bestow an imperial title upon Emperor Xìngxiàn.
Pán stated:
"Xìng,
being a princely state,
cannot be placed above an imperial title.
Xiàn,
being a posthumous epithet,
cannot be applied to a living mother.
The birth parents and adoptive parents
cannot both be honored equally.
Great righteousness and private sentiment
naturally have their respective weights."
At this time, many court officials strongly argued,
and the matter was temporarily halted.
In the first year of Jiājìng,
Secretary Huò Tāo stated that
it was highly disrespectful for officials of the Censorate and circuit supervisors to receive imperial edicts in informal attire.
Pán, together with his colleagues, argued that Tāo had previously offended orthodox teachings by his discussions on rituals,
and fearing that censors would expose his treachery,
he therefore picked on minor issues,
intending to undermine them.
The Emperor disregarded this.
Soon after, in connection with another matter, he stated:
"The great traitors, both inside and outside the court, of the previous reign,
such as Zhāng Zhōng, Liú Yǎng, Wéi Mín, Wèi Bīn, Wáng Qióng, Níng Gǎo, etc.,
slipped through the net and escaped with their heads.
Their bribes could reach the heavens,
and they never ceased to curry favor, hoping for reappointment.
It is advisable to strictly investigate and prevent this,
so that such individuals do not again ruin affairs of state."
The Emperor accepted his words
and ordered Embroidered Uniform Guard officials to secretly investigate and apprehend them.
Lǐ Xián, a retainer of the eunuch Zhāng Qīn,
was granted by the Emperor the position of Commander (zhǐhuī) of the Embroidered Uniform Guard.
Pán strongly argued against this,
but was not heard.
Commander Zhāng Yí of the Embroidered Uniform Guard was dismissed for his attachment to the eunuch Zhāng Ruì.
Censor Yáng Bǎizhī suddenly pleaded his innocence,
saying:
"When Chén Háo's rebellion was plotted,
Yí was the first to advocate for great righteousness,
persuading Ruì to refuse his gifts.
Now that Ruì has been spared death because of this,
Yí's meritorious service is not recorded.
There is no way to show gratitude."
Pán memorialized, stating:
"Bǎizhī is cunning and treacherous;
he outwardly speaks for Yí,
but secretly colludes with Ruì,
paving the way for Ruì's return to power."
Bǎizhī's true intentions were discovered,
so he falsely accused Pán of harboring private resentment and slandering him because his personal requests were not granted.
Minister of Personnel (lìbù shàngshū) Qiáo Yǔ and others proposed dismissing Bǎizhī,
while the Ministry of Punishments stated that the facts were unclear
and that both should be arrested and tried.
The Emperor pardoned both of them,
docking Bǎizhī's salary for three months
and Pán's for one month.
The emperor frequently organized fasting rituals and Daoist sacrificial ceremonies.
Pán again spoke out firmly:
"Previously, Wǔzōng was misled by his attendants,
ordering the Tibetan monk Suǒnán Chuòjí to enter and exit the 'Leopard Chamber,'
and the eunuch Liú Yǔn to welcome Buddhist relics from the Western Regions.
Over a decade, vast sums were wasted from the imperial treasury,
and rumors spread on the streets.
After Liú Yǔn was dismissed,
and Suǒnán was imprisoned,
expenditures decreased,
and the petty officials submitted.
How is it that scarcely two years have passed
before the old habits are suddenly revived?
If not fasting, then performing ceremonies;
not a single day in the month is empty.
How can this be His Majesty's original intention?
It is actually the eunuchs Cuī Wén and others who are doing this.
Wén, a drum-beating servant,
improperly climbed the ranks through illicit means.
Having already been demoted and dismissed,
he now seeks to recover his position.
He leads Your Majesty to this point,
making you subject to ridicule by the world and future generations.
Wén deserves to be beheaded.
Wén tests Your Majesty:
if you wish to go on an incense procession, he follows;
if you wish to ascend the altar, he follows;
if you wish to offer a memorial, he again follows.
If there is no end to it, he will lead you to pleasure excursions and construction projects,
lead you to military campaigns.
He is poised to present a continuous stream of such things,
waiting for an opportune moment to act on them.
Therefore, I say Wén deserves to be beheaded."
The memorial was submitted
and reported to the emperor.
Luó Hóngzài, a secretary in the Ministry of Revenue, caused Zhāng Jǐn, a centurion of the Imperial Guard, to be beaten with a staff and imprisoned by imperial decree.
Pán, along with his colleagues Zhāng Hànqīng, Zhāng Kuí, and Gě Gāng, requested that they be handed over to the judicial authorities.
The emperor did not comply.
When Princess Yǒngfú was to be married,
the wedding date was chosen for late July.
Pán stated:
"Princess Cháng, as the unmarried granddaughter of Empress Dowager Xiàohuì,
has not yet completed the mourning period.
It would be appropriate to change the date.
According to old customs,
the imperial son-in-law performs two prostrations before the princess,
and the princess remains seated to receive them,
which violates the proper relationship between husband and wife.
This also ought to be rectified."
The emperor overruled him with an imperial edict,
and the meeting ceremony remained as before.
Wáng Bāngqí, a demoted officer of the Imperial Guard, repeatedly begged for reinstatement.
Pán stated:
"During the Zhèngdé era, Bāngqí and his like
were greedy and rapacious,
like tigers and wolves.
When they captured bandits and thieves,
they might implicate over ten people for one individual,
or several dozens of households for one family,
fabricating judicial evidence
and submitting it to the Ministry of Justice,
calling it 'casting copper plates.'
When they investigated seditious speech,
they might send barbarian agents to search for strange books among the common people,
or buy off deceitful monks to secretly induce the common people into the Maitreya cult.
Then they would ambush them,
with no chance of escape,
calling it 'sowing seditious speech.'
For several decades,
the dead filled the prisons,
and the living cried out in injustice.
Now, if their crimes are not corrected,
allowing them to keep their heads,
that is already fortunate enough.
How dare they act with such brazen impunity,
repeatedly disturbing the emperor's ears?
What are they trying to achieve?
Moreover, Your Majesty gathers the dispersed hearts of the people
and establishes the nation's precarious foundation,
truly through the single edict upon your ascension.
If these types are allowed to flex their arms and destroy it in a single day,
then treacherous people will rise up everywhere like insects,
and the defenses will collapse,
reaching an uncontrollable extent.
It is imperative to severely investigate and punish them
to cut off the source of disaster."
The emperor could not comply.
Later, Bāngqí indeed became a great scourge, just as Pán had predicted.
The emperor urgently summoned Xí Shū and Guì È and others.
Pán requested that they be dismissed to apologize to the world,
and also stated:
"Now, to establish a separate temple within the Inner Court
is to clearly admit that Gōngmù cannot be admitted into the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
If Xiàozōng cannot be a 'father-emperor,'
and Gōngmù cannot be admitted,
then there is no 'father-emperor.'
How can there be an Imperial Ancestral Temple without a 'father-emperor' in the world?
This argument contradicts itself."
The emperor did not listen.
He successively served as Supervising Secretary in the Ministry of War.
For leading a crowd to prostrate themselves at the palace gate and being beaten a second time,
he was stripped of his official title and reduced to a commoner.
He died at home.
Zhāng Hànqīng,
courtesy name Yuánjié,
was from Yífēng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the sixth year of Zhèngdé.
He was appointed Magistrate of Wèixiàn,
then summoned and appointed Supervising Secretary in the Ministry of Justice.
He once presented three proposals: curb opportunism, expand reserves, and be cautious in administering justice.
These were deeply pertinent to the problems of the time,
but were not acted upon.
When Wǔzōng was about to make a southern tour, he and his colleagues knelt at the palace gate to remonstrate.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
following the suggestion of Governor Lǐ Duó,
he allocated 200,000 *tài* of silver from the imperial treasury to provide generous relief to the soldiers and civilians of Xuānfǔ.
Based on Hànqīng's words,
an additional 130,000 *tài* were allocated to Dàtóng.
He was repeatedly promoted to Supervising Secretary in the Ministry of Revenue.
In the winter of the first year of Jiājìng,
he and his colleagues submitted a memorial stating:
"Your Majesty is concerned about the harm caused by manorial estates in the capital region
and has dispatched officials to conduct investigations.
An edict was issued that all lands presented after Zhèngdé or encroached upon beyond their quota
should be returned to the people.
When this imperial decree was issued,
who in the world did not praise Your Majesty's benevolence?
However, Supervising Secretary Xià Yán, Censor Fán Jìzǔ, and Secretary Zhāng Xīyǐn investigated and reported on the perfume factory in Zhuōzhōu and the hunting ground and fodder field in Ānzhōu,
and an imperial decree ordered them to be retained for imperial use.
The relevant authorities insisted on their original recommendation,
but the emperor ultimately refused to comply.
This is not how to fully uphold great trust and demonstrate ultimate impartiality.
The perfume factory originated with Mǎ Yǒngchéng,
and the hunting ground was established by Gǔ Dàyòng,
both seizing the people's livelihoods to create them.
Now, Mǎ Jùn and Zhào Píng, relying on old favors from the imperial residence,
presumptuously seek to avoid their abolition.
This is following the old path of Yǒngchéng and Dàyòng again.
We beg that these be entirely returned to the people,
and that Jùn and Píng be severely punished as a warning against deception."
The empress's father, Chén Wànyán, requested permission to build a new residence,
and then again requested manorial estates.
Eunuchs Wú Xūn and others requested to supervise the silk weaving in Sūzhōu.
Hànqīng remonstrated strongly against all of these.
They were not accepted.
There was a severe drought in the prefectures of Yìngtiān.
The emperor planned to sell surplus salt from Huái and Zhè and confiscated properties
to exchange for silver to provide relief.
Hànqīng said:
"Exchanging for silver is slow;
it must be done by issuing silver from the imperial treasury."
The emperor then issued 150,000 *tài* of silver.
Not long after,
he again, with his colleagues, stated:
"The annual revenue of the empire today
is insufficient for its annual expenditures.
Added to this are frequent floods and droughts,
exhausting the nation's resources.
Your Majesty is currently practicing frugality,
yet the eunuchs Liáng Dòng and others reported a shortage of pearls and jewels for construction,
which is an attempt to deplete the silver of the Ministry of Revenue.
Liáng Zhèng and others also, under the pretext of exempting one-third of the taxes,
wish to carry out transfers from the capital granaries,
which is an attempt to exhaust the grain of the Imperial Granary.
If the Inner Treasury is insufficient,
it draws from the Ministry of Revenue.
If the Ministry of Revenue is insufficient,
it draws from the common people of the prefectures and counties.
From where will the common people of the prefectures and counties draw?
Today, the southeast is suffering from successive famines,
and people are even resorting to cannibalism,
yet orders for requisitions and levies are frequently issued.
We humbly believe this is unacceptable."
This was reported to the emperor.
Later,
he impeached Xí Shū for his improper methods of relief
and requested that an official be sent to investigate
and correct his crimes of deception.
The emperor was very fond of Shū at the time,
urgently summoning him to be Minister of Rites,
and did not punish him.
Initially,
when there was a discussion of adding imperial titles for Emperor Xīngxiàn,
Hànqīng strongly opposed it.
By this time, he again led the crowd to prostrate themselves at the palace gate.
He was beaten twice
and dismissed as a commoner.
Twenty years later,
Censors Xíng Rúmò, Jiǎ Zhǔn, and others jointly recommended worthy individuals who had been overlooked by the empire,
including Hànqīng,
but he was ultimately not summoned.
Zhāng Yuán,
courtesy name Shìyuán,
was from Sānyuán.
He became a *jìnshì* in the ninth year of Zhèngdé.
He was appointed Investigating Censor of the Ministry of Personnel (*Lìkē Gěishìzhōng*).

He submitted a memorial proposing six measures: eliminating superfluous officials, acting cautiously in undertakings, prohibiting contributions, clarifying rewards and punishments, broadening channels for remonstrance, and promoting virtue and learning.
He said therein:
"The realm spans ten thousand *lǐ*,
yet whenever an undertaking is proposed, the financial ministers immediately declare a shortage;
this is because the people are poor.
Why are the people poor?
The extortions of local officials and
the contributions of inner court officials
are the cause.
In recent years, military provisions and miscellaneous levies have been ten times the previous regulations,
all managed by local officials.
Local officials use this as an opportunity to enrich themselves,
adding ten times more than what is submitted to the emperor.
The people are already distressed,
yet contributors invent clever new pretexts,
vying for novelty and uniqueness,
calling them 'filial piety and obedience.'
What is taken from the people is ten or a hundredfold,
but what reaches the emperor is only one or two.
Why does the court find joy in this and accept it?
A ruler governs subordinates solely by reward and punishment.
Lately, incompetent individuals and household servants are all ennobled as marquises and wear jade girdles.
Some receive rewards without leaving their homes,
or are credited with merits without ever stepping onto the battlefield.
Those who repel enemies often receive no favor,
while those who lead armies to defeat often escape punishment.
This is why the soldiers are demoralized."
When the memorial was submitted,
the powerful favorites resented it,
and an imperial decree demoted him to stationmaster of Xīntiān驿 (Xīntiān Yìchéng).
In the early Jiājìng era,
he was recalled to resume his post in the Ministry of War (*Bīngkē*),
and his salary was increased by one grade.
When Nánníng Bó Máo Liáng killed his son,
and Zhū Zhèn, Commander of the Imperial Bodyguard (*Jǐnyī Zhǎngyìn Zhǐhuī*) and others extensively connived,
Yuán impeached them repeatedly,
and they were all dismissed from their positions and retired.
The emperor promoted Zhāng Hèlǐng to Chāngguó Gōng,
enfeoffed Chén Wànyán as Tàihé Bó,
with hereditary succession,
and appointed Wànyán's son Shào Zǔ as Seal Office Supervisor (*Shàngbǎo Chéng*).
He also appointed five relatives by marriage, including Jiǎng Tài, as Imperial Bodyguard commanders of a thousand or a hundred households (*Jǐnyī Qiān/Bǎihù*).
Yuán vigorously remonstrated against this,
requesting to curtail them.
Soon after,
he impeached Jiànchāng Hóu Zhāng Yánlíng for forcibly occupying commoners' land,
and the son of Dìngguó Gōng Xú Guāngzuò, and the relatives by marriage Yùtián Bó Jiǎng Lún and Chānghuà Bó Shào Huì's household members for abusing their power.
Although these matters were not fully implemented,
the powerful and noble were all intimidated.
He was promoted to Investigating Censor of the Ministry of Revenue (*Hùkē Yòugěishìzhōng*).
He rattled the palace gate and wept,
was again beaten with the rod,
and died from severe injuries.
He was too poor to be buried in his hometown.
After a long time,
the Censor-in-Chief (*Dūyùshǐ*) Chén Hóngmó fully detailed the plight of Yuán and Máo Yù, Péi Shàozōng, Wáng Sī, Wáng Xiàng, and Hú Qióng's wives and children, who were scattered and displaced,
requesting imperial compassion.
This was not granted.
In the first year of Lóngqìng, he was posthumously granted the title of Junior Supervisor of Imperial Banquets (*Guānglù Shàogīng*).
Máo Yù,
courtesy name Guózhēn,
later changed to Yòngchéng,
was the son of a military family from Yúnnán Right Guard (*Yúnnán Yòuwèi*);
his ancestors were from Liángxiāng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the eighteenth year of Hóngzhì.
In the fifth year of Zhèngdé,
he was promoted from Messenger (*Xíngrén*) to Investigating Censor of the Ministry of Personnel of Nanjing (*Nánjīng Lìkē Gěishìzhōng*).
After Liú Jǐn's downfall,
great bandits rose up.
Yù stated that Grand Academicians (*Dàxuéshì*) Jiāo Fāng and Liú Yǔ had truly brought chaos to the realm,
requesting their public execution
to appease the myriad commoners.
When the bandits disturbed Shāndōng and Hénán,
Yù requested preparations for the secondary capital.
Soon after, the bandits did cross the river,
but dared not transgress due to strict defenses.
After his father's mourning period,
he was reappointed to the Ministry of War in Nanjing (*Nánjīng Bīngkē*).
When Censor Lín Yǒunián was imprisoned for remonstrating against welcoming the Buddha from Wūsīzàng,
Yù strongly memorialized to save him,
and Yǒunián received a light punishment.
He then left office again due to his stepmother's mourning period.
After the mourning period ended,
he was appointed to the Ministry of Personnel (*Lìkē*).
More than a year after Shìzōng ascended the throne,
the inner eunuchs from the Xīng Palace, emboldened by the emperor's favor,
gradually became arrogant and dissolute.
Moreover, former eunuchs Gǔ Dàyòng and Wèi Bīn and others successively plotted to resume their positions,
and signs of this were emerging.
Yù immediately submitted a memorial recounting the events during Wǔzōng's reign,
urging the emperor to curb his desires,
prevent personal requests,
to close the door to opportunism,
and block the channels for seduction.
The emperor praised and accepted it.
Censor Cáo Jiā was always impetuous and devious.
Imitating Sòng Fàn Zhòngyān's "Chart of One Hundred Officials" (*Bǎiguān Tú*),
he divided court officials into four ranks,
and assigned them ratings.
Investigating Censor Ān Pán submitted a memorial refuting this,
stating that Táng Wáng Guī's assessment of Fáng Xuánlíng and others,
and the current dynasty's Jiě Jìn's assessment of Huáng Fú and others,
were all done under imperial command to appraise them,
and there had never been anyone who wantonly indulged his tongue,
like Jiā.
Yù further stated that Jiā had defied established laws
and disrupted national policy,
requesting his dismissal.
The emperor followed his advice
and demoted Jiā to an outer post.
Censor Xǔ Zōnglǔ pleaded for Jiā,
requesting Yù's dismissal,
and his colleague Lún, by connivance, also spoke on Jiā's behalf.
Investigating Censor Zhāng Yuán stated that the common officials' collective dispute
was causing many problems for the court,
severely damaging the national prestige,
and requested to be the first to be dismissed.
Yù also submitted a memorial requesting to leave,
saying:
"Zōnglǔ and others prioritize personal friendships
and disregard the larger interests of the court.
My personal involvement is extremely minor,
but the public discussion is of great importance;
I request my dismissal to appease the censors."
The emperor comforted and kept them both.
At that time, hundreds of Chén Háo's relatives were implicated and arrested;
Yù was ordered to interrogate them,
saving many lives.
He also stated that Chén Háo's rebellion
was caused by the greed and bribery of those around him.
He then impeached the local officials who did not die for their duty,
and prohibited all officials in the realm from communicating with princely establishments.
The emperor followed all of this.
He was again promoted to Senior Investigating Censor (*Zuǒ Gěishìzhōng*).
Soon after, he prostrated himself before the palace gate to remonstrate on the
"Great Rites" controversy,
was imprisoned and beaten with the rod,
and ultimately died.
Later, he was posthumously granted the title of Junior Supervisor of Imperial Banquets (*Guānglù Shàogīng*).
Péi Shàozōng,
courtesy name Bóxiū,
was from Wèinán.
He became a *jìnshì* in the twelfth year of Zhèngdé.
He was appointed Magistrate of Hǎimén (*Hǎimén Zhīxiàn*).
When Wǔzōng made his southern tour,
he received an order to temporarily manage Jiāngdū affairs.
The powerful favorites feared him,
greatly reducing provisions.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was summoned to serve as Investigating Censor of the Ministry of War (*Bīngkē Gěishìzhōng*).
He immediately submitted a memorial requesting adherence to ancestral laws and established regulations,
saying:
"Tàizǔ's legacy of planning was perfect.
Such as valuing great ministers,
diligently attending court,
personally visiting fields,
wearing washed clothes,
growing vegetables in the palace,
destroying gilded beds,
breaking crystal clepsydras,
building the 'Pavilion for Observing the Heart' (*Guānxīn Tíng*),
and displaying the *Dàxué Yǎnyì* (Elaboration of the Great Learning) and similar texts—
these are what Your Majesty should ponder and emulate.
And the two or three great ministers should particularly offer admonitions day and night
to assist in nurturing Your Majesty's virtue.
If Your Majesty daily attends court in the private hall (*Biàndiàn*),
befriends Confucian scholars,
so that your ears and eyes are not obscured by immorality and wickedness,
and your attendants are not misled by dangerous sycophants,
then the ruler's will will be firm,
and governing achievements can be accomplished."
The emperor praised and accepted it.
When the emperor wished to bestow an imperial title upon Xīngxiàn Dì,
Shàozōng strongly remonstrated against it.
In the winter of the second year of Jiājìng,
due to frequent disasters and anomalies,
the emperor wished to cancel the celebratory banquet for the suburban sacrifices (*Jiāosì Qìngchéng Yàn*) for the following year.
Shàozōng said:
"Among sacrificial rites, none is more important than the suburban altars,
and the sentiments between ruler and ministers must be conveyed through banquets.
Previously, a great rite was abolished due to imperial relatives;
now that it is auspicious,
it should be held immediately.
How can it be canceled again due to disasters?"
Compiler (*Xiūzhuàn*) Táng Gāo also spoke similarly.
It was eventually held according to ritual.
The following year,
he died after being beaten with the rod for prostrating himself before the palace gate.
He received the same posthumous official title as Máo Yù.
Zhāng Yuè Tāo,
courtesy name Xízhēn,
was a native of Pútián.
In the twelfth year of the Zhèngdé reign (1517), he became a *jìnshì*.
He was appointed Judicial Reviser of Chángzhōu Prefecture.
When Emperor Wǔzōng made his southern tour,
Jiāng Bīn let his cronies run rampant in the prefectures and counties.
When they were about to arrive in Chángzhōu,
the people scrambled to flee and hide.
At that time, both the Prefect and the Magistrate of Wǔjìn had gone to court for an audience.
Yuè Tāo concurrently held the seals of both the prefecture and the county.
He summoned the elders and made an agreement, saying:
"When Bīn's partisans arrive,
you must unite your strength to resist them."
He also released the prisoners
and ordered them and the beggars to each prepare瓦 (tiles) and stones to await them.
Soon after,
Bīn's partisans indeed came in a large cavalry detachment.
The elders directly blocked them at the border,
saying:
"Chángzhōu has suffered disasters for several years,
and its material resources are greatly exhausted.
There is nothing to feed you.
In the prefecture, there is only one Judicial Reviser Zhāng,
not a single coin enters his pocket.
Even if we wanted to prepare fodder,
there would be no way to manage it."
After they had spoken,
Bīn's partisans suspected some other stratagem,
so they gradually retreated
and sent a rider to inform Bīn.
Yuè Tāo immediately submitted a memorial to the Imperial Censor on circuit, reporting the situation.
When the Censor, Dōngjiāo, was inspecting his department and passed through Chángzhōu,
he said:
"The situation is urgent.
Bīn will try to arrest you on some other pretext."
He ordered Yuè Tāo to board his boat and depart first,
while he himself followed in a small boat.
Bīn's partisans indeed arrived in great numbers,
seeking Yuè Tāo,
and mistakenly intercepted the Censor's boat.
Dōngjiāo ordered a strict arrest of those who intercepted the boat,
but secretly instructed that it be delayed.
His partisans, fearing that the Censor would report them to the emperor,
all dispersed,
and Yuè Tāo thus escaped.
Bīn also warned his partisans not to cause trouble,
and from then on, the prefectures south of the Cháng (Jiāng) River enjoyed peace.
When Emperor Shìzōng ascended the throne,
Yuè Tāo was summoned to serve as an Imperial Censor.
When Yáng Tínghé and others were disputing the issue of textile manufacturing,
Yuè Tāo also submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your Majesty has already stated that the cabinet ministers' memorials are solely out of love for the ruler and concern for the people.
This clearly indicates that Your Majesty knows the harm of textile manufacturing.
Since Your Majesty knows it,
yet still does not stop it,
it is truly because Your Majesty's trust in senior ministers is not exclusive,
and instead, minor figures are managing state affairs.
From ancient times, there has never been a situation where minor figures created obfuscation internally
while senior ministers could fully demonstrate loyalty externally.
Cui Wén and other two or three petty individuals once corrupted and disordered the previous court;
now they again mislead the sacred heart,
secretly wielding authority and power.
How can Your Majesty allow them to indulge their private interests
without expelling them early?
Your humble servant has heard that the official position for textile manufacturing
requires tens of thousands in bribes to obtain.
Since it is sought with heavy wealth,
to expect them not to seek repayment from the populace
is an impossible matter."
The Emperor could not adopt his advice.
When Xí Shū was appointed Minister by imperial edict,
Yuè Tāo and his colleague Hú Qióng each forcefully remonstrated in a memorial.
After being subjected to flogging,
he still submitted a memorial impeaching the villain Chén Guāng for his crimes.
Not long after,
he died.
In the early years of the Lóngqìng reign,
he was posthumously granted the title of Junior Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
Hú Qióng,
courtesy name Guóhuá,
was a native of Nánpíng.
In the sixth year of the Zhèngdé reign (1511), he became a *jìnshì*.
He served as Magistrate of Cíxī, then was appointed Imperial Censor.
He gained renown during his successive inspections of Guìzhōu and Zhèjiāng.
He made a tearful remonstrance,
was subjected to flogging, and died.
Later, his official titles were posthumously granted, similar to Yuè Tāo.
Yáng Huái,
courtesy name Dōngchuān,
was a native of Wúxī.
In the twelfth year of the Zhèngdé reign (1517), he became a *jìnshì*.
He was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Revenue,
and then promoted to Director.
He first supervised the Capital Granary,
eliminating almost all accumulated malpractices of clerks and attendants.
Later, he supervised the Huái and Tōng Granaries,
abolished the supply of tea and fruit to eunuchs,
and removed fees for granary foundations and extra matting and straw.
Finally, he supervised the Imperial Treasury,
where eunuchs customarily received provisions.
Huái completely stopped these.
He was diligent, honest, and cautious,
and highly regarded by Ministers Sūn Jiāo and Qín Jīn.
He was flogged at the palace gate
and died more than a month later.
There was nothing in his purse,
and his family sold their house to pay for his funeral.
Jīn and Huái were from the same village,
and Jīn managed the return of his coffin.
Later, he was posthumously granted the title of Junior Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
Shēn Liáng,
courtesy name Yánxián,
was a native of Gāopíng.
He passed the provincial examination
and was appointed Magistrate of Zhāoyuǎn.
When bandits rose in Shāndōng,
Liáng prepared defenses and combat provisions in advance.
When the bandits arrived,
he pursued and attacked them as far as Huángxiàn,
capturing and beheading several hundred people.
Later,
they returned,
and he again defeated and routed them.
He successively served as Magistrate of Zhūchéng and Liángxiāng.
When powerful dignitaries came and made demands,
Liáng rejected them all.
He was promoted to Prefect of Ānjí.
When Yè Qióng of the Imperial Guards, relying on Qián Níng's influence, seized commoners' land,
Liáng adjudicated and returned it to the people.
Qióng then instigated villains to falsely accuse Liáng,
but the matter was eventually clarified.
He was gradually promoted to Assistant Prefect of Chángzhōu,
and then served as an Assistant Director in the Ministry of Revenue.
He and Huái both died from flogging.
He was posthumously granted the title of Junior Vice Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud.
The people of Zhāoyuǎn cherished his administration
and painted his portrait to worship him.
Zhāng Càn,
courtesy name Jǐngchuān,
was a native of Shùndé, Guǎngdōng.
His grandfather, Shàn Zhāo,
was an Assistant Surveillance Commissioner of Sìchuān,
and was demoted to Assistant Prefect of Línjiāng.
Previously,
more than eighty relatives and associates of Liàn Zǐníng had been exiled to Línjiāng.
Shàn Zhāo submitted a memorial, saying:
"Zǐníng's loyalty pierced the sun and moon.
Emperor Tàizōng said, 'If Zǐníng were alive,
I would certainly employ him.'
Emperor Rénzōng also called Fāng Xiàorú and others 'loyal ministers.'
Since they were loyal,
why are their distant relatives and minor associates
still punished as traitors and villains,
unforgiven for a hundred years?"
Although the memorial was not acted upon,
both inside and outside the court, all admired his bravery.
Càn became a *jìnshì* in the ninth year of the Zhèngdé reign (1514)
and was appointed Magistrate of Jiànpíng.
He offended the Imperial Censor on circuit, Hè Hóng,
and was transferred to Guǎngchāng.
He denounced Hóng's crimes,
and Hóng was removed from office.
Càn was transferred from Guǎngchāng to Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Rites,
supervising the Huìtóng Hostel.
Minister Wáng Qióng had a grudge against Censor-in-Chief Péng Zé,
and used Zé's envoy to Tǔlǔfān, who promised gold and silk to redeem the seal of Hāmì city, as Zé's crime.
He incited the foreigners in the hostel to expose Zé's misconduct,
and tempted Càn to sign a document,
saying:
"Zé's actions
are a repeat of the Southern Sòng's blunders.
If this matter succeeds, you will be prominently promoted."
Càn forcefully refused, saying:
"Lord Wáng, you are mistaken.
Zé's dispatches with Tǔlǔfān are all preserved;
how can they be compared to the Sòng's appeasement of barbarians?
In the past, Fàn Zhòngyān also wrote letters to Yuánhào;
Zé is not alone in this."
He refused to sign.
Soon after, he was promoted to Assistant Director
and died from flogging.
Wǔ Yú,
courtesy name Zhōngfù,
was a native of Púqí.
His father, Shēn, was a Supervising Secretary in the Ministry of Works.
Yú showed ambition and integrity from a young age.
In the twelfth year of the Zhèngdé reign (1517), he began his official career,
but immediately resigned due to illness.
He was later reinstated as Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Rites,
but again resigned due to illness.
When Emperor Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was reinstated to his former office.

He submitted a memorial outlining ten matters: diligently studying the classics, strengthening familial bonds, opening channels for speech, respecting senior ministers, selecting upright officials, removing Buddhist practices, relieving the distressed and poor, valuing local officials, improving military preparedness, and cultivating talent.
Soon after,
he died under flogging.
Zāng Yìngkuí,
courtesy name Xiánzhēng,
was a native of Chángxīng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the twelfth year of Zhèngdé (1517).
He was appointed Principal of the Bureau of Equipages (Chējià Zhǔshì) in Nánjīng.
When palace eunuchs (gòng zhōngguān) requisitioned boats exceeding the quota,
he strenuously cut down the excess.
The eunuchs sent soldiers to cause a commotion in the bureau,
but he shouted at his attendants to seize them.
They fled.
When his birth mother (fù suǒ shēng mǔ) passed away,
it was not permissible by law for him to bear the main burden of mourning (chéngzhòng),
but he privately observed three years of mourning.
He was appointed Principal of the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù Zhǔshì),
but was soon beaten to death with a staff.
Yìngkuí studied under Zhàn Ruòshuǐ,
and aspired to be a sage or worthy.
Once, passing by the Confucius Temple (Wénmiào),
he emotionally said to his friend,
"When we die,
we too should be offered sacrifices there,"
such was his ambition.
Hu Lián, a director (Lángzhōng),
courtesy name Zhòngqì,
was a native of Xīnyù.
He became a *jìnshì* in the sixth year of Zhèngdé (1511),
and served in the Ministry of Punishments (Xíngbù).
He was once beaten with a staff for remonstrating against Wǔzōng's southern tour.
Yú Zhēn, a principal (Zhǔshì),
courtesy name Xīngbāng,
was a native of Fèngxīn.
He became a *jìnshì* in the ninth year of Zhèngdé (1514).
Lǐ Kědēng, a service secretary (Sīwù),
courtesy name Sīshàn,
was a native of Huīxiàn.
He passed the provincial examination (xiāngjiàn) at the end of Hóngzhì.
All served in the Ministry of War (Bīngbù).
Kědēng was always magnanimous,
and considered himself loyal and righteous,
and indeed lived up to his ambition.
Ān Xǐ, a principal of the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù Zhǔshì),
was a native of Wǎnpíng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the sixteenth year of Zhèngdé (1521).
Yīn Chéng, a principal of the Ministry of Punishments (Xíngbù Zhǔshì),
was a native of Jiāngxià.
He became a *jìnshì* in the ninth year of Zhèngdé (1514).
When Mùzōng ascended the throne,
Lián was posthumously granted the title of Junior Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Shàocīng),
Càn that of Junior Vice Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud (Tàipú Shàocīng),
Yú, Yìngkuí, Chéng, Xǐ, and Zhēn that of Junior Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Guānglù Shàocīng),
and Kědēng that of Administrator of a Grand Court (Sìchéng).
Guō Nán,
courtesy name Shìzhòng,
was a native of Jìnjiāng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the ninth year of Zhèngdé (1514).
He was appointed Magistrate of Pújiāng County.
His administration was ranked excellent (kè zuì),
and he was promoted to Censor (Yùshǐ).
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he requested the recall of honest officials such as Shū Fēn, Wáng Sī, Huáng Gǒng, and Zhāng Yǎnruì.
This was granted.
In the first year of Jiājìng (1522),
he audited military provisions in Guǎngdōng and Guǎngxī.
He impeached the Commander-in-Chief (Zǒngbīngguān) Marquiss of Fúníng, Zhū Qí, for greed and cowardice,
and an imperial edict was issued to reprimand him.
Soon after, he submitted a memorial,
requesting that the emperor meet with senior ministers during his leisure time after court,
following the precedents of the imperial ancestors.
He also stated that
Principal Chén Jiāyán had offended a palace eunuch,
and it was improper to arrest and imprison him.
The emperor was enraged
and deprived him of his salary.
When the officials knelt at the palace gate to dispute
"the Grand Rites (Dàlǐ),"
all were punished.
Nán was then inspecting Yúnnán,
and urgently sent a memorial stating:
"When a subject serves his sovereign,
those who merely flatter may not be loyal, and
those who boldly remonstrate may not be rebellious.
Now, officials are kneeling at the palace gate, crying out,
some beaten to death,
others exiled to distant garrisons.
It is unexpected that in the reign of a sagacious and enlightened emperor,
loyal and good men should be punished like this.
I beg that those still living have their posts restored,
and that the families of the deceased be commiserated with,
so as to win the hearts of the people,
and uphold the righteousness between sovereign and subject."
The emperor was furious,
and dispatched imperial guards (Tíqí) to arrest and try him.
The remonstrating officials' pleas for his rescue were all rejected.
Upon his arrival,
he was imprisoned and tortured in the Commander of Guards' (Zhènfǔ) prison,
then publicly flogged,
and stripped of his status.
Before this,
after several people had died,
no court official dared to report it.
Later, Yú Jìng, an administrator of the Prefectural Administration (Fǔjīnglì), memorialized:
"Academicians Fēng Xī and others, having brazenly offended His Imperial Majesty,
are imprisoned and interrogated.
Although these officials' actions may seem wild and defiant,
their hearts are truly loyal.
Now, we hear that Grand Secretaries Péi Shàozōng, Compilers Wáng Xiàng, Principals Yú Zhēn, and others have already died,
and those like Xī who are in prison are also on the verge of death.
As for those groaning on their beds,
too gravely injured to rise,
their number is unknown.
I humbly submit that since the spirit tablet of the late Emperor Xiànzōng has been reverently welcomed into the temple,
it is fitting to pardon past offenses and forgive crimes,
thereby manifesting great filial piety throughout the realm.
I hope Your Majesty will quell the thunderous wrath,
and bestow the grace of rain and dew.
Commiserate with the descendants of the deceased,
and pardon those on the verge of death,
so that subjects no longer deem speech a taboo,
which would be a blessing to the imperial altars."
Lǐ Jìxiān, an administrator of the Office of Transmission (Tōngzhèngsī Jīnglì), also memorialized:
