"Your Majesty's posthumous conferral of a revered title
is the ultimate filial sentiment of a son,
and indeed cannot be refrained from.
However, the officials, in a moment, recklessly offended the imperial majesty,
and suffered severe condemnation,
resulting in more than ten deaths.
Senior ministers have departed their posts one after another,
while junior officials tacitly preserve themselves.
Today, there is an alert in Dàtóng,
yet not a single person has submitted a memorial or proposed a strategy.
Thus, it is evident that both senior and junior officials
lack spirit and courage.
I beg that the deceased be recorded and commiserated with,
those exiled to garrisons be pardoned and returned,
and the officials who left the country be reinstated,
while those in office be entrusted with authority and treated leniently,
so that each may present border strategies.
Your foolish subject cannot but express his earnest concern."
The emperor disregarded all.
In March of the following year,
Censor Wáng Mào stated:
"Seventeen court officials died by flogging during the discussion of the rites.
Their parents, wives, and children are in pitiful distress.
I beg Your Majesty to grant them generous commiseration,
posthumous official titles, and hereditary privileges for their descendants."
The emperor was greatly enraged
and demoted Mào to a records clerk (Diǎnshǐ) in Gāoxiàn, Sìchuān.
A few days later,
Nán's memorial arrived.
The emperor was even more enraged,
and consequently ordered his arrest, trial, and stripping of status.
In the spring of the sixth year (1527),
due to natural disasters, the emperor reflected and reformed.
Following the Ministry of Personnel's recommendation, Nán was granted a post,
becoming an instructor (Jiàoyù) in Jíshuǐ.
He eventually served as Prefect of Nánníng.
A eulogy states:
The dispute over "the Grand Rites (Dàlǐ)"
led officials to shake the palace gate and weep bitterly;
this was indeed overly zealous and foolish.
However, to be flogged twice at court,
some dying, some dismissed,
and imprisoned for life,
how tragic was that?
Yáng Shèn was learned and well-informed,
and excelled in literature.
Wáng Sī, Zhāng Chōng, and others,
some offered remonstrance during Wǔzōng's reign,
others argued against Shìzōng's early policies,
speaking candidly and clearly,
dying for their principles while in office.
This was not merely a temporary outburst of passion.
Collation Notes

Biographies, Volume 81. Fèi Hóng (younger brother Cǎi; nephew Màozhōng; son Màoxián; paternal uncle Xuān). Zhái Luán. Lǐ Shí. Gù Dǐngchén. Yán Nà (Yuán Wěi). Lǐ Chūnfāng (grandson Sīchéng et al.). Chén Yǐqín. Zhào Zhēnjí (Yīn Shìdān). Gāo Yí.
Fèi Hóng,
courtesy name Zǐchōng,
was a native of Qiānshān.
Soon after reaching adulthood,
he was ranked first in the *jìnshì* examination in the twenty-third year of Chénghuà (1487),
and appointed Compiler (Xiūzhuàn).
During the Hóngzhì reign,
he was promoted to Left Expositor (Zuǒ Zànshàn),
lectured to the Crown Prince (Dōnggōng),
and advanced to Left Tutor (Zuǒ Yùdé).
When Wǔzōng was enthroned,
he was promoted to Tàicháng Shàoqīng,
and concurrently served as Shìjiǎngdú.
He participated in compiling the *Xiàozōng Shílù*.
He was appointed Rìjiǎng Guān.
In the second year of Zhèngdé, he was appointed Lǐbù Yòushìláng,
and soon after transferred to Zuǒshìláng.
In the fifth year, he was promoted to Shàngshū.
The emperor indulged in pleasure and ease,
and the early morning court audiences and daily lectures were both abolished.
Fèi Hóng requested diligence in governance, dedication to learning, and acceptance of remonstrance,
which was reported.
The Zōupíng prince, Zhū Dāngyì (朱當潩), of the Lǔ Fǔ (魯府), was supposed to inherit his father's title,
but it had been usurped by his younger brother, Zhū Dāngliáng (朱當涼), for several years.
Fèi Hóng, based on Dāngyì's plea and defense,
upheld justice according to the law.
Dāngliáng became enraged,
falsely accused Fèi Hóng of accepting bribes,
but Fèi Hóng was unmoved.
In the twelfth month of winter of the following year, Fèi Hóng was ordered to concurrently serve as Wényuángé Dàxuéshì, participating in crucial state affairs.
Soon after, he was granted the titles of Tàizǐ Tàibǎo and Wǔyīngdiàn Dàxuéshì,
and promoted to Hùbù Shàngshū.
The favored minister Qián Níng (錢寧) secretly sided with Chén Háo (宸濠),
and wished to curry favor with Fèi Hóng,
sending him silks, money, and other precious curios.
Fèi Hóng rejected them,
and Qián Níng felt ashamed and resentful.
Chén Háo plotted to restore the guard units and military colonies,
and transported tens of thousands of ounces of silver,
bribing many court dignitaries.
Qián Níng and Bīngbù Shàngshū Lù Wán (陸完) were in charge of this.
Fèi Hóng's cousin, editor Fèi Cǎi (費寀),
whose wife was related to Háo's wife
(they were sisters),
learned of this and informed Fèi Hóng.
When Fèi Hóng came to court,
Lù Wán greeted him and asked:
"Níng Wáng (寧王) seeks to restore his guard units;
is this permissible?"
Fèi Hóng replied:
"I do not know why they were abolished in the first place."
Lù Wán said:
"Now, I fear it may be impossible not to grant it."
Fèi Hóng sternly refused.
When a eunuch brought the memorial to the Grand Secretariat,
Fèi Hóng strongly argued against granting it,
but the imperial edict ultimately granted it.
Thus, Chén Háo allied with Qián Níng,
and resented Fèi Hóng.
Qián Níng frequently investigated Fèi Hóng's affairs but found nothing.
He then used the fact that Censor Yú Shān (余珊) had impeached Fèi Cǎi for improperly remaining in the Hanlin Academy,
and designated it as Fèi Hóng's offense.
An imperial edict ordered Fèi Hóng to submit a statement of explanation,
and Fèi Hóng requested retirement.
An order commanded both he and Fèi Cǎi to retire.
Qián Níng sent cavalry to follow Fèi Hóng,
and upon reaching Línqīng,
they burned his boat,
destroying all his luggage and possessions.
After Fèi Hóng returned home,
he closed his doors and refused visitors.
Chén Háo again sought to communicate with him,
but Fèi Hóng politely declined,
which further angered Chén Háo.
At that time, Fèi Hóng's clansmen were involved in a lawsuit with local villains, Lǐ Zhèn (李鎮) and others.
Chén Háo secretly ordered Lǐ Zhèn to raid Fèi Hóng.
Lǐ Zhèn and his group then occupied a strategic position and started a rebellion,
leading their followers to attack the Fèi family.
They couldn't find Fèi Hóng,
so they seized those involved in the lawsuit with them and dismembered them,
exhumed Fèi Hóng's ancestors' graves,
destroyed his home,
and looted far and wide,
their numbers reaching three thousand.
Fèi Hóng quickly sent an envoy to appeal to the court.
The court ordered Circuit Censor Sūn Suì (孫燧) to investigate the situation,
and only then dispatched troops to suppress them.
When Chén Háo was defeated,
memorialists vied to request Fèi Hóng's recall.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he sent an imperial envoy to Fèi Hóng's home to summon him,
granted him the title of Shàobǎo,
and had him join the government as an assistant.
Fèi Hóng was cautious and understood the larger picture,
and was well-versed in national precedents.
He worked in harmony with Yáng Tínghé (楊廷和), Jiǎng Miǎn (蔣冕), and Máo Jì (毛紀) to assist the emperor,
and repeatedly advised the emperor to reform the corrupt policies of Wǔzōng.
Regarding the "Grand Rites"
debate,
the ministers strongly argued with the emperor,
who could not tolerate it.
Fèi Hóng somewhat discerned the emperor's intentions,
only signing his name to public memorials,
and never remonstrated specifically,
for which the emperor favored him.
When Yáng Tínghé and others left their posts,
Fèi Hóng became the chief grand secretary.
He was granted the titles of Shàoshī, concurrently Tàizǐ Tàishī, Lìbù Shàngshū, and Jǐnshēndiàn Dàxuéshì,
and his trust and responsibility were profound.
The Hùbù proposed collecting outstanding taxes from the Zhèngdé period.
Fèi Hóng, along with Shí Bǎo (石珤) and Jiǎ Yǒng (賈詠), requested that it only apply to taxes from ten years ago onwards.
The emperor agreed.
Due to disasters and unusual phenomena in the four directions,
the emperor decreed that his officials should cultivate self-reflection and be diligent.
Fèi Hóng and others then stated:
"Your Majesty's expenditures are without moderation,
and public works never cease.
Half of the land in the capital region has become imperial estates,
and the demands for internal treasury revenue have more than doubled.
The grand granary lacks three years' worth of reserves, yet superfluous expenses increase daily,
and the capital garrisons do not have a hundred thousand soldiers, yet they are constantly deployed for labor.
Upright officials who committed offenses have not been pardoned,
yet censors who performed their duties are questioned.
Those who should have been punished by law have repeatedly been reviewed but not executed,
while those whose crimes are undeniable are suddenly pardoned by imperial decree.
Causing resentment and inviting grievances
is not a singular issue."
The emperor acknowledged his faults and responded with praise,
but he did not implement their advice.
During the military mutiny in Dàtóng,
Zhāng Cōng (張璁) requested its suppression.
Fèi Hóng said:
"If we suppress it and win,
both good and bad will be destroyed;
if we do not win,
they will occupy and defend the city,
which will greatly harm our prestige.
It is better to observe the situation and plan slowly."
The matter indeed settled quickly.
Hóng ěr was a kind and easygoing person,
fond of promoting junior scholars.
Regarding
the "Grand Rites,"
he could not offer strong remonstrances,
but neither did he ever blindly follow.
At this time, Xí Shū, Zhāng Cōng, and Guì È were in power.
Shū's younger brother, jiǎntǎo Chūn,
was therefore transferred from another department to serve.
When the Veritable Records of Emperor Wǔzōng were completed,
Hóng ěr suggested that Shū be appointed as a qiānshì (assistant prefect).
Shū resented Hóng ěr because of this.
Cōng and È entered the Hanlin Academy from a minor official position,
and swiftly rose to the position of zhānshì (Supervisor of the Imperial Household).
The entire court detested them,
but Hóng ěr always showed restraint.
Cōng and È also greatly resented him.
The Emperor once visited Píngtái,
and specially bestowed a chapter of seven-character regulated verse of his own composition,
ordering the compilation of a collection of matching poems.
He signed Hóng ěr's title as
"First Minister of the Cabinet, Overseeing Confidential Matters and Advising."
The respect and honor shown to him
were unprecedented.
Cōng and È became increasingly jealous of Hóng ěr's favor.
È said:
"Poetry and prose are minor skills,
unworthy of troubling Your Majesty's heart,
and they allow Hóng ěr to take advantage of imperial favor,
intimidating and oppressing court officials."
The Emperor ignored it.
È then conspired with Cōng to slander Hóng ěr to the Emperor,
saying that Hóng ěr had received a contribution of jade from Tiānfāng (Arabia) stolen by lángzhōng Chén Jiǔchuān,
and had accepted a bribe from shàngshū Dèng Zhāng in exchange for plotting his reappointment,
and also mentioned matters concerning his time in his hometown.
Hóng ěr submitted a memorial requesting retirement,
stating briefly:
"È and Cōng have repeatedly harbored private grudges against your servant.
They resented not being appointed as lecturers for the imperial lectures,
resented not being involved in compiling the Veritable Records of the Deceased Emperor,
resented not being examiners for the provincial examinations in both capitals,
and resented not being instructors.
È and Cōng suspect that matters of the Grand Secretariat are manipulated by your servant,
but they do not know that your servant merely gathers public opinion
and reports it for Your Majesty's sacred decision;
it cannot be monopolized.
È and Cōng daily roll up their sleeves and clench their fists,
coveting your servant's position.
How can your servant contend with petty men?
I beg for the return of my bones (permission to retire)."
This was not granted.
When Cōng was in the Ministry of War,
Hóng ěr wanted to appoint Xīnníng Bó Tán Lún to command the Fènwǔ Camp.
Cōng then impeached Hóng ěr for coercing a ministry.
Soon after,
again because Hóng ěr's son, Màoliáng, was convicted and imprisoned,
Cōng attacked him even more vigorously,
and resubmitted all previous impeachment memorials.
Failing to get his way,
he strongly demanded Hóng ěr's dismissal,
denouncing him even more sharply,
submitting memorials numerous times.
Hóng ěr also repeatedly submitted memorials requesting retirement,
and the Emperor always issued gracious edicts to comfort and retain him,
but ultimately did not condemn Cōng or È.
Thereupon, the wicked person Wáng Bāngqí, following the instructions of Cōng and È,
submitted a memorial slandering the deceased Grand Secretary Tínghé and others,
and also falsely accused Hóng ěr.
Hóng ěr consequently retired from office.
This was in the second month of the sixth year [of Jiājìng].
In the tenth month,
Cōng then entered the Grand Secretariat as shàngshū and Grand Secretary.
A year later, È also entered.
In the fourteenth year,
È had already died,
and Cōng had also left office.
The Emperor then began to remember Hóng ěr.
In the fourth month, he again dispatched a xíngrén (court usher) to his home to reinstate him to his former office.
In the seventh month, he arrived in the capital.
The Emperor sent an imperial envoy to console him with fine imperial cuisine,
and personally instructed him, saying:
"It has been a long time since we parted.
You are healthy and well.
You should wholeheartedly assist and advise, fulfilling Our expectations."
Hóng ěr bowed in thanks.
From then on, the favor and treatment became even more generous.
He was summoned with Lǐ Shí into the Wúyì Hall,
and together they toured the palace halls,
chatting and laughing casually.
After some time, they left.
He was bestowed with a silver seal inscribed
"Former Senior Grand Secretary and Meritorious Minister."
The Emperor frequently sought his advice,
and Hóng ěr also gave his utmost sincerity without reservation.
After the harsh and oppressive administration of Cōng and È,
he replaced it with leniency and harmony,
and all court officials admired and rejoiced in him.
He died not long after,
at the age of sixty-eight.
The Emperor sighed and mourned,
increasing his funeral expenses and posthumous grants,
and posthumously awarded him the title of tàibǎo,
with the posthumous name Wénxiàn.
Hóng ěr entered the Grand Secretariat three times,
serving two reigns for nearly ten years.
In between, he suffered from slander and conspiracy,
but ultimately ended his career with honor.
When he first entered as shàobǎo,
his younger brother, Cǎi, was a zànshàn,
and his nephew, Màozhōng, had passed the jinshì examination and become a biānxiū.
Hóng ěr's eldest son, Màoxián, had just been appointed as a shùjíshì (probationary compiler).
Father, sons, and brothers were all serving near the imperial court.
Cǎi's highest office was shàobǎo and Minister of Rites,
with the posthumous name Wéntōng.
Màozhōng ended his career as Vice Commissioner of Education for Húguǎng.
Màoxián served successively as lángzhōng in the Ministry of War.
Hóng ěr's cousin, Xuān,
passed the jinshì examination in the eleventh year of Chénghuà.
During the Hóngzhì reign, he served as yuánwàiláng in the Ministry of War.
Xìe Mù, the governor of Guìzhōu, and Wú Jīng, the commander-in-chief, and others reported that the Làntǔ Miáo had rebelled,
usurping the title of king,
and requested the dispatch of a large army for suppression.
Upon the request of Mǎ Wénshēng, the Minister of War,
Xuān was ordered to investigate with Yùshǐ Dèng Xiáng.
The Bái Miáo showed no signs of rebellion,
and were pacified.
Xuān impeached Mù, Jīng, and Zhāng Chéng, the eunuch in charge of the garrison, for their crimes.
He was promoted to Cānyì of Guìzhōu, where he ended his career.
Zhái Luán,
courtesy name Zhòngmíng,
was originally from Zhūchéng.
His great-grandfather was a xiàowèi (lieutenant) in the Imperial Bodyguard,
and thus his family settled in the capital.
He passed the jinshì examination in the eighteenth year of Hóngzhì,
and was appointed as a shùjíshì.
In the early Jiāzhèng reign,
he was appointed as a biānxiū.
Liú Jǐn transferred Hanlin officials to other departments,
appointing Luán as a zhǔshì in the Ministry of Justice.
He was soon reinstated,
and promoted to shìdú (reader).
During the Jiājìng reign,
he was successively promoted to Right Vice Minister of Rites.
In the spring of the sixth year,
cabinet ministers were recommended by the court.
The Emperor intended to appoint Zhāng Fújìng,
but he was not among the recommendations.
The Emperor ordered a second recommendation,
and then Luán was included.
Many influential eunuchs praised Luán,
so the Emperor appointed him out of order.
Yáng Yīqīng argued that Luán's reputation was too light,
and requested the appointment of Wú Yīpéng or Luó Qīnshùn.
The Emperor did not agree,
and ordered Luán, as Left Vice Minister of Personnel, concurrently a Grand Secretary, to serve in the Wènyuān Pavilion.
Soon after, he was bestowed with a silver seal inscribed
"Pure and Careful Grand Secretary."
When Luán first entered the cabinet,
Yīqīng and Xiè Qiān were assisting in governance.
Later, Fújìng and Guì È entered,
and Luán respectfully served them all.
Fújìng and È both sealed their memorials with the bestowed silver seals when presenting them,
but Luán alone offered no memorials.
When questioned,
he bowed his head and replied:
"Your Majesty is wise and sagacious;
your servant has barely enough time to comply and follow,
what criticisms or suggestions could there be?"
The Emperor cherished him in his heart.
Yīqīng, È, and Fújìng were dismissed one after another,
and Luán remained to govern alone for two months.
After that, Lǐ Shí and Fāng Xiànfū entered,
both holding positions superior to Luán,
but Luán showed no displeasure.
The Emperor frequently summoned Shí and Luán for audiences,
once asking:
"The Censorate proposes confiscating the assets of Gǔ Dàyòng.
Is this appropriate?"
Both Shí and Luán were northerners,
and aligned with the influential eunuchs.
Shí said:
"The proposal does not conform to the law."
Luán said:
"According to the law,
confiscation is limited to three categories:
rebellion, treason, and factionalism.
If it does not align with the law,
how can one gain the trust of the empire?"
The Emperor said:
"Dàyòng disturbed the government in the previous reign;
he is indeed a factionalist."
Luán said:
"Your Majesty
is heaven itself.
To give life in spring and take it in autumn,
what is there that cannot be done?"
The Emperor ultimately followed the more severe proposal.
In the twelfth year,
Zhāng Fú Jìng (張孚敬) returned to court.
Luán (鑾) left due to sorrow,
and Xiàn Fū (獻夫) retired from office.
Shí (時) then followed Fú Jìng (孚敬),
merely bowing and assenting,
which made Fú Jìng (孚敬) feel at ease.
When Fú Jìng (孚敬) resigned from government,
Fèi Hóng (費宏) re-entered court,
but died soon after.
Shí (時) then became the sole Grand Secretary.
Shí (時) had always been lenient and peaceful;
by this time, he became even more composed and tranquil.
The emperor also summoned him for an audience in the private hall,
sitting knee-to-knee to consult with him.
Although Shí (時) offered no great corrections or remedies,
his discussions were sincere and magnanimous,
and the court universally considered Shí (時) virtuous.
A guest star appeared near Tiān Bàng (天棓).
The emperor asked what events it portended.
He replied:
“The theory of portents originated with Jīng Fáng (京房) of the Hàn (漢) capital,
and not all of it necessarily holds true.
The only way is for the ruler to cultivate virtue to avert such omens.”
The emperor praised this.
Accompanying the imperial carriage on a visit to the imperial tombs,
they passed Shā Hé (沙河).
The emperor saw the residents were desolate
and said with sorrow:
“The Seven Mausoleums are here,
and should be specially protected.”
Shí (時) replied:
“Formerly, Qiū Jùn (丘濬) suggested that
the capital should have four auxiliary garrisons:
Lín Qīng (臨清) to the south,
Chāng Píng (昌平) to the north,
and Jì Zhōu (薊州) and Bǎo Dìng (保定) to the east and west,
each garrisoned by ten to twenty thousand troops.
If a Grand General (總兵) were now added at Chāng Píng (昌平),
they could defend the capital to the south
and protect the imperial tombs to the north.”
The emperor then ordered court officials to investigate and deliberate,
and ordered the construction of Gǒng Huá Chéng (鞏華城) at Shā Hé (沙河)
to establish a garrison there.
He was repeatedly promoted to Junior Tutor (少傅), Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (太子太師), Minister of Personnel (吏部尚書), and Grand Secretary of the Huá Gài (華蓋) Hall.
When Xià Yán (夏言) entered the Grand Secretariat,
Shí (時) did not contend with him,
deferring to Yán (言) in every matter,
and Yán (言) too felt at ease with him.
The emperor did not treat Shí (時) as well as Fú Jìng (孚敬) or Yán (言),
but he was rarely blamed or humiliated,
and remained in office from beginning to end,
which Fú Jìng (孚敬) and Yán (言) dared not hope for.
In the twelfth month of the seventeenth year, he died in office,
and was posthumously granted the title of Grand Tutor (太傅)
and the posthumous name Wén Kāng (文康).
Gù Dǐng Chén (顧鼎臣),
courtesy name Jiǔ Hé (九和),
was a native of Kūn Shān (崑山).
In the eighteenth year of Hóng Zhì (弘治), he came first in the imperial examinations.
He was appointed Compiler (修撰).
At the beginning of Zhèng Dé (正德),
he was again promoted to Junior Expositor of the Left (左諭德).
At the beginning of Jiā Jìng (嘉靖),
he was assigned to the Imperial Lectures (經筵).
He lectured on Fàn Jùn’s (范浚) “Heart Admonition” (心箴),
expounding it with precision and relevance.
The emperor was pleased,
and personally annotated it,
and Dǐng Chén (鼎臣) received special favor.
He successively held the posts of Chamberlain (詹事). Censors Liú Shì Yáng (劉世揚) and Lǐ Rén (李仁) impeached Dǐng Chén (鼎臣) for being corrupt and sycophantic.
The emperor imprisoned Shì Yáng (世揚) and others,
and due to Dǐng Chén’s (鼎臣) intercession,
they received only a light reprimand.
He was appointed Right Vice Minister of Rites (禮部右侍郎).
The emperor was fond of longevity techniques,
and held Daoist rituals (齋醮) in the inner palace.
Dǐng Chén (鼎臣) presented seven chapters of “Incantations of Stepping into Emptiness” (步虛詞),
and also listed the procedures to be followed on the altar.
The emperor responded with a gracious edict of praise,
and followed all his suggestions.
It was Dǐng Chén (鼎臣) who initiated the practice of officials gaining the emperor’s favor through composing “blue-paper memorials” (青詞).
He was reassigned as Left Vice Minister of Personnel (吏部左侍郎),
and managed the Chamberlain’s Office (詹事府).
He requested that the descendants of Zēng Zǐ (曾子) be appointed Erudites of the Five Classics (五經博士),
on par with the descendants of the Three Sages (三氏),
which was granted.
During the Dà Tóng (大同) military mutiny, Zhāng Fú Jìng (張孚敬) advocated military action,
but Dǐng Chén (鼎臣) argued against it,
and the emperor graciously accepted his advice.
In the first month of winter in the thirteenth year,
during the ancestral temple sacrifice,
Dǐng Chén (鼎臣) and Vice Minister Huò Tāo (霍韜) were ordered to carry the ancestral tablets.
Both men were in mourning for close relatives (期功服),
and should have declined.
They then submitted a memorial stating:
“According to ancient rites,
feudal lords were exempt from mourning periods.
Today’s high officials are like the ancient feudal lords,
so we request permission not to avoid this duty.”
Minister of Rites Xià Yán (夏言) vehemently criticized their impropriety,
and the matter was dropped.
Soon after, he was promoted to Minister of Rites (禮部尚書),
still overseeing the Chamberlain’s Office.
There were continuous rains in the capital,
and many floods in the four directions.
Dǐng Chén (鼎臣) requested famine relief and bandit suppression,
which was approved.
In the eighth month of the seventeenth year,
he was appointed Grand Secretary of the Wén Yuān Gé (文淵閣) concurrently with his current office,
to participate in national affairs.
Soon after, he was granted the titles of Junior Protector (少保), Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (太子太傅), and promoted to the Wǔ Yīng Diàn (武英殿).
Initially,
Lǐ Shí (李時) was the Senior Grand Secretary,
Xià Yán (夏言) was second,
and Dǐng Chén (鼎臣) was third.
After Shí (時) died,
Yán (言) dominated the government excessively.
Dǐng Chén (鼎臣), being inherently soft and obsequious,
was unable to achieve anything significant,
merely filling the position.
When the emperor was about to make a southern tour
and establish the Crown Prince,
he ordered Yán (言) to accompany him,
and Dǐng Chén (鼎臣) to assist the Crown Prince in overseeing the state.
Censor Xiāo Xiáng Yào (蕭祥曜) impeached Vice Minister of Personnel Zhāng Cháo (張潮) for accepting Dǐng Chén’s (鼎臣) instructions
to transfer Bureau Director Lù Kūn (陸崑) from the Ministry of Punishments to the Ministry of Personnel.
Cháo (潮) said:
“Bureau Director Mǎ Chéng Xué (馬承學) of the Ministry of War relied on his connection with Dǐng Chén (鼎臣)
and boasted that he would certainly obtain a position in personnel selection,
so I suppressed Chéng Xué (承學) and appointed Kūn (崑) instead.”
The emperor imprisoned Chéng Xué (承學) in the imperial prison,
but Dǐng Chén (鼎臣) was not questioned.
In the tenth month of the nineteenth year, he died in office
at the age of sixty-eight.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Protector (太保)
and the posthumous name Wén Kāng (文康).
When Dǐng Chén (鼎臣) was an attendant official,
he was concerned about the unequal distribution of taxes and labor in the southeast,
and repeatedly reported its abuses.
The emperor therefore instructed the governors and censors.
Governor Ōu Yáng Duó (歐陽鐸) rectified it.
Kūn Shān (崑山) had no city wall,
and he spoke to the authorities to have one built.
Later, when the Wō (倭) raiders arose,
Kūn Shān (崑山) was preserved,
and the local people erected a shrine to worship him.
Yán Nà (嚴訥),
courtesy name Mǐn Qīng (敏卿),
was a native of Cháng Shú (常熟).
He passed the provincial examination,
but because the examination supervisor’s record touched upon a taboo,
no one on that list was allowed to sit for the metropolitan examination.
In the twentieth year of Jiā Jìng (嘉靖), he became a *jìnshì*,
was made a *shùjíshì* (庶吉士),
appointed Compiler (編修),
and promoted to Reader (侍讀).
The Three Wú (三吳) region suffered frequent Wō (倭) raids,
and that year there was also a great famine,
with almost half the population dying or migrating.
The officials’ levies became even more urgent.
Nà (訥) submitted a memorial detailing the people’s distress,
requesting tax exemptions and loans.
The emperor was moved upon receiving the memorial
and approved his request.
Soon after, he and Lǐ Chūn Fāng (李春芳) were assigned to the Western Garden (西苑).
He composed blue-paper memorials (青詞),
and was exceptionally promoted to Academician of the Hàn Lín (翰林) Academy.
He successively held the posts of Junior Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (太常少卿),
Left and Right Vice Minister of Rites (禮部左、右侍郎),
then transferred to the Ministry of Personnel (吏部),
all concurrently holding the title of Academician,
and still serving in the Western Garden.
All the blue-paper memorials he composed pleased the emperor.
When Minister of Rites Guō Pú (郭朴) was transferred to the Ministry of Personnel,
Nà (訥) was appointed to replace him.
When Pú (朴) suffered the loss of his father,
Nà (訥) again replaced him as Minister of Personnel.
When Yán Sōng (嚴嵩) was in power,
the administration of personnel was corrupt and disordered.
After Sōng (嵩) fell,
Pú (朴) still could not completely reform the personnel selection system.
Nà (訥) conscientiously rectified himself,
and Xú Jiē (徐階) also fully trusted him with responsibility.
Nà (訥) then made an agreement with court officials that
all matters should be reported in the court office,
and private visits to residences should be avoided.
He carefully selected officials for the personnel bureau,
worked to suppress illicit competition,
and promoted those who were stagnating.
Furthermore, he believed that adhering too strictly to qualifications
prevented the full utilization of talent,
so he adopted the former dynasty’s "three paths" method,
where county and prefectural officials with outstanding political achievements were exceptionally promoted,
thus revitalizing personnel administration.
Soon after, in recognition of his service in the imperial presence,
he was granted the title of Grand Protector of the Crown Prince (太子太保).
In the forty-fourth year,
Yuán Wěi was dismissed,
and Nà was appointed concurrently as a Grand Secretary of Wǔyīngdiàn to participate in state affairs.
As his replacement, Guō Pǔ, had not yet arrived,
he continued to manage personnel selection.
The emperor resided in reclusion in the Xīyuàn,
and the residences of the attendant officials were all within the garden.
Nà would go out in the morning to handle affairs at the Ministry,
and at dusk, he would return to his residence to stay overnight,
offering "blue essays."
He was careful and reverent,
to the point of falling ill for a long time without recovering.
In the eleventh month of the winter of that year,
he requested to return home.
The following year,
Shìzōng passed away,
and he never again emerged from retirement.
After Nà returned to his hometown,
both his parents were still alive.
He diligently provided for them morning and evening with clean meals, showing filial piety,
which people regarded as an honor.
Nà once told someone:
"Personnel ministers and grand secretaries must be of one mind to be effective.
I managed personnel selection for two years,
just as Huátíng was in power,
and no affairs were obstructed.
Moreover, the chosen officials were virtuous,
and no one was misplaced."
Huátíng referred to Xú Jiē,
and the chosen official was Lù Guāngzǔ.
He lived at home for twenty years before he died,
at the age of seventy-four.
He was posthumously granted Shàobǎo [Junior Protector]
and given the posthumous title Wénjìng.
Yuán Wěi,
courtesy name Màozhōng,
was a native of Cíxī.
In the seventeenth year of Jiājìng, he placed first in the metropolitan examination
and third in the palace examination,
and was appointed compiling editor.
Wěi's character and conduct were unrestrained,
and he was impeached by Censor Bāo Xiào,
but the emperor pardoned him without punishment.
He was promoted to reader-in-waiting.
After a long time,
he was selected to serve in the Xīyuàn.
He composed "blue essays"
that were most pleasing to the emperor.
In the thirty-fifth year,
the grand secretaries nominated compiling editor Quán Yuánlì to take charge of the Nánjīng Hànlín Yuàn,
but the emperor specifically appointed Wěi.
Wěi submitted a memorial declining,
wishing to serve with his former rank.
The emperor was greatly pleased
and immediately promoted Wěi to Bachelor of the Hànlín Academy.
Barely two months later,
an imperial decree appointed him Vice Minister of Rítuál, Right.
The following year,
he was promoted to Tutor to the Heir Apparent concurrently with Bachelor,
and granted a first-rank official's attire.
In the thirty-ninth year,
due to his service in composing "blue essays," his salary was again increased by two grades,
and shortly after, he was promoted to Vice Minister, Left.
In the second month of the following year, he was transferred to the Ministry of Personnel,
continuing his concurrent duty of composing "blue essays" as before.
A month later, he was transferred to Minister of Rítuál,
and promoted to Junior Protector of the Heir Apparent,
and still ordered to serve in the palace.
From his service in composing "blue essays" onwards,
Wěi advanced to Grand Tutor and Minister in six years,
which was unprecedented.
Earlier, on the first day of the second month,
there was a slight solar eclipse,
and Wěi said that no rescue rituals were necessary.
Minister of Rítuál Wú Shān disagreed
and was censured and dismissed.
The emperor heard Wěi's words and approved of them,
so he replaced Shān with Wěi.
By the first day of the seventh month,
there was another solar eclipse.
Calendar officials said the eclipse was only one part and five minutes
and that rescue rituals were exempt by precedent.
Wěi then flattered the emperor by submitting a memorial saying:
"Your Majesty serves Heaven as a father
and the sun as an elder brother;
all darkness retreats and submits,
and all phenomena shine brilliantly.
Therefore, the sun is crystal clear,
and baleful influences are dissipated,
the eclipse is only one part,
which is equivalent to no eclipse at all.
Your subjects cannot but rejoice."
When the memorial was submitted,
the emperor was even more pleased.
That winter,
he was then appointed Minister of Revenue concurrently as Grand Secretary of Wǔyīngdiàn, joining the Grand Secretariat to manage state affairs.
He was successively promoted to Junior Tutor concurrently as Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent and Grand Secretary of Jiànjídian.
In the spring of the forty-fourth year,
he fell gravely ill,
requested leave to return home,
and died on the way,
at the age of fifty-eight.
He was posthumously granted Grand Tutor
and given the posthumous title Wénróng.
Wěi's talent and quick wit were exceptional.
If the emperor issued a slip of paper in the middle of the night,
ordering him to compose a "blue essay,"
he would pick up his brush and finish it immediately.
Whenever auspicious omens were reported from inside or outside the capital,
he would lavish praise with the most elaborate words.
Once, a cat kept by the emperor died,
and he ordered the literati officials to compose an eulogy for a ritual.
Wěi's essay contained
the phrase "turning a lion into a dragon,"
and the emperor was greatly delighted.
His deceptive words and flattery of the emperor were mostly like this.
Because of this, the emperor urgently employed him,
and his generous rewards were frequent and abundant,
which others could not hope for.
From the middle of the Jiājìng era,
the emperor devoted himself to Taoist rituals and self-cultivation,
and literati officials generally composed "blue essays."
Those who excelled were immediately promoted exceptionally,
eventually entering the Grand Secretariat.
At that time, Lǐ Chūnfāng, Yán Nà, Guō Pǔ, and Wěi were called
"Blue Essay Grand Secretaries."
However, Wěi was arrogant and rarely humble,
and although he came from Xú Jiē's school,
he directly insulted him with his haughtiness.
When he and Jiē jointly supervised the compilation of the *Chéngtiān Dàzhì*,
when the academicians submitted their drafts,
Wěi altered almost everything,
without deferring to Jiē.
The academicians were indignant,
but Jiē merely said, "Just let him do it."
Later, after Wěi died,
Jiē also altered all of his work.
Wěi prided himself on his literary skill.
When he saw others' compositions,
if they were slightly not to his liking,
he would openly criticize and ridicule them.
Those academicians who were his protégés
were especially subjected to intolerable reproach and humiliation,
which is why everyone feared and disliked him.
Lǐ Chūnfāng,
courtesy name Zǐshí,
was a native of Xīnghuà, Yángzhōu.
In the twenty-sixth year of Jiājìng, he placed first in the *jìnshì* examination,
and was appointed compiling editor.
He was selected to enter the Xīyuàn to compose "blue essays,"
and was greatly favored by the emperor,
and was exceptionally promoted to Bachelor of the Hànlín Academy along with Reader-in-waiting Yán Nà.
Soon after, he was transferred to Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
appointed Vice Minister of Rítuál, Right,
both concurrently as Bachelor,
and continued to serve in the Xīyuàn as before.
He assisted in the affairs of the Ministry,
was promoted to Vice Minister, Left,
transferred to the Ministry of Personnel,
and replaced Nà as Minister of Rítuál.
At that time, the imperial clan had proliferated,
and their annual stipends were difficult to sustain.
Chūnfāng researched precedents
and compiled a book which he submitted to the emperor.
He strictly established regulations for all major auspicious and inauspicious rituals and for seasonal grants and gifts.
The emperor praised him
and named it *Zōngfān Tiáolì* [Regulations for the Imperial Clan].
Soon after, he was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent.
In the forty-fourth year,
he was appointed concurrently as Grand Secretary of Wǔyīngdiàn,
and participated in state affairs along with Nà.
Shìzōng was generous towards the attendant officials,
and all their promotions and dismissals came from special imperial decrees.
From Bachelor to holding power,
Chūnfāng had six promotions,
none of which came through court deliberation.
Chūnfāng was respectful and cautious,
and did not use his power to oppress others.
While in government, his judgments were fair,
and he did not act harshly or arbitrarily;
people at the time compared him to Lǐ Shí;
though his talent and ability were not as great,
he surpassed him in integrity.
At that time, Xú Jiē was the Senior Grand Secretary
and was highly favored by the emperor.
Chūnfāng always deferred to Jiē in every matter,
and Jiē also held him in high regard.
In the spring of the first year of Lóngqìng,
an imperial edict ordered the repair of the Xiángfènglóu.
Chūnfāng said:
"The emperor has just ascended the throne,
and to immediately undertake construction projects,
is that appropriate?"
The matter was then halted.
When Qí Kāng impeached Xú Jiē,
his words implicated Chūn Fāng.
Chūn Fāng submitted a memorial defending himself and requesting to leave,
but the emperor consoled him and asked him to stay.
When he later replaced Jiē as Senior Grand Secretary,
he became even more devoted to maintaining peace and quiet,
which pleased the emperor.
At that time, his colleagues were Chén Yǐqín and Zhāng Jūzhèng.
Yǐqín was upright and cautious,
whereas Jūzhèng relied on his talent to treat others disdainfully,
regarding Chūn Fāng as nothing.
Initially, when Jiē was dismissed due to public opinion,
Chūn Fāng sighed, saying:
“Even Grand Secretary Xú suffers such a fate,
how can I remain long?
I shall beg to retire within a day or two.”
Jūzhèng immediately said:
“If so,
you might preserve your good name.”
Chūn Fāng was startled,
and submitted three memorials requesting retirement,
but the emperor did not grant it.
Soon after, Zhào Zhēnjí entered to replace Yǐqín,
being rigid and temperamental.
When Gāo Gǒng re-entered the Grand Secretariat,
he overshadowed Chūn Fāng,
and Chūn Fāng could not contend with him,
only discreetly admonishing himself.
When Āndá sought peace and a title at the frontier,
Chūn Fāng, along with Gǒng and Jūzhèng, decided the matter before the emperor.
At that time, Zhēnjí was driven out by Gǒng,
and Gǒng became even more overbearing,
reviving his old grievances with Jiē.
Chūn Fāng once calmly tried to mediate for Jiē,
which displeased Gǒng even more.
By then, Chūn Fāng had accumulated titles such as Junior Tutor and Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince,
and was promoted to Minister of Personnel,
then transferred to the Zhōngjí Hall.
Sensing that Gǒng and his faction would ultimately not tolerate him,
he submitted two memorials requesting to return home to care for his parents,
but these were not granted.
Wáng Zhēn, a Supervising Secretary from Nánjīng, curried favor with Gǒng
and submitted a memorial slandering Chūn Fāng,
making Chūn Fāng even more resolute in his request to leave.
He was granted an imperial edict, an official carriage,
and an escorting officer;
local officials provided laborers and provisions as per custom.
After a year,
Gǒng was again ousted by Jūzhèng,
barely escaping harm.
But Chūn Fāng, upon returning home,
found his parents still well,
and enjoyed banquets and feasts with them morning and evening,
which was admired by his fellow villagers.
He passed away several years after his parents,
at the age of seventy-five.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Tutor
and the posthumous name Wéndìng.
His grandson, Sīchéng,
served as Minister of Rites in the sixth year of Tiānqǐ,
but was soon dismissed.
In the early years of Chóngzhēn,
he was suspended from office for praising the eunuch faction.
Sīchéng’s grandson, Qīng,
courtesy name Yìngbì.
He became a *jìnshì* in the fourth year of Chóngzhēn.
He was promoted from Níngbō Prefectural Judge to Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Justice.
When Xióng Wéncàn pacified Zhāng Xiànzhōng,
Qīng criticized his poor strategy.
Due to a long drought, he requested leniency in punishments,
which displeased the emperor,
and he was demoted to Assistant Reviewer of the Zhèjiāng Surveillance Bureau.
He had not yet taken up the post
when he returned home due to mourning.
He was later appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Personnel.
Soon after, he was sent out to invest the Huái principality,
but due to a national crisis, he did not get the position.
During Fú Wáng’s reign,
he requested posthumous titles for founding meritorious officials and loyal remonstrating officials from the Wǔ and Xī reigns.
Consequently, Lǐ Shàncháng and fourteen others,
Lù Zhèn and fourteen others,
Zuǒ Guāngdǒu and nine others,
all received posthumous titles.
Chūn Fāng’s great-grandson, Xìn,
was the Magistrate of Pínghé, Guǎngdōng.
When the city fell,
he died with his two sons, Hóngyuǎn and Shūyuǎn.
Chén Yǐqín,
courtesy name Yìfǔ,
was a native of Nánchōng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the twentieth year of Jiājìng.
He was selected as a *shùjíshì* and
appointed Compiler.
After a long time,
he served as a lecturer for Yù Wáng,
was promoted to Reviser,
and then advanced to Literary Chancellor.
At that time, the position of Crown Prince had not yet been settled,
and many petty individuals stirred up trouble.
Shìzōng had always been distant from his son,
and the prince was not allowed to meet him at festivals or during the year.
Besides his regular stipend,
there were customary gifts,
but the prince dared not request them.
After three years,
the princely residence was in dire straits.
The prince’s attendants bribed Yán Shìfān with a thousand gold pieces;
Shìfān was pleased
and instructed the Ministry of Revenue,
resulting in the combined allocation of three years’ worth of funds.
However, Shìfān was always suspicious.
One day, he dismissed his attendants and said to Yǐqín and Gāo Gǒng:
“I hear His Highness has recently been perplexed,
what does he say about my father?”
Gǒng deliberately made a jesting remark,
but Yǐqín sternly said:
“The foundation of the state has been silently settled for a long time.
Born and named,
following the characters '后' (hòu, empress) and '土' (tǔ, earth),
pre-eminent in the nine regions –
this is the emperor’s intention.
Traditionally,
lecturers for princes were only Compilers;
now Revisers are also used,
making this residence uniquely different from others –
this is the Grand Secretary’s intention.
His Highness always calls the Senior Grand Secretary a minister vital to the state;
from whom did you hear such words?”
Shìfān left in silence,
and the Yù princely residence was then secure.
He served as lecturer for nine years,
rendering services akin to providing wings,
yet deeply concealed himself.
The prince once wrote
the two characters “忠貞” (zhōngzhēn, loyal and steadfast)
and bestowed them upon him.
After completing mourning for his father,
he returned as Academician Expositor-in-waiting,
presiding over the Hànlín Academy.
He was promoted to Grand Master of Ceremonies,
and concurrently led the National Academy.
He was elevated to Vice Minister of Rites (Right),
then soon transferred to Vice Minister (Left),
then transferred to the Ministry of Personnel,
presiding over the Zhānshìfu.
Upon Mùzōng’s ascension,
Yǐqín, considering himself an old minister from the former princely residence,
submitted ten articles on "beginning with caution,"

namely: establishing resolve, safeguarding position, revering Heaven, emulating ancestors, loving the people, promoting frugality, grasping authority, employing talent, engaging with subordinates, and listening to counsel.
His words on grasping authority and listening to counsel were particularly poignant,
and an imperial edict praised his loyalty and earnestness.
In the spring of the first year of Lóngqìng,
he was promoted to Minister of Rites and concurrently Grand Academician of the Wènyuān Pavilion,
entering to participate in state affairs.
He was successively granted the titles of Junior Tutor and Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince,
and transferred to the Wǔyīng Hall.
During Mùzōng’s reign, imperial lectures were rare,
and political decisions were not made.
Many favored individuals received generous imperial favors through inner edicts.
Yǐqín requested the emperor to exert himself and reform governance.
The emperor was moved,
intending to take action,
but was ultimately hindered by the inner eunuchs,
and his memorial was also shelved.
In the fourth year,
he submitted articles on the current abuses of procrastination,
requesting careful selection and appointment of officials,
consideration of long-term tenure,
punishment of corrupt officials,
broadening the use of talent,
training of civilian militias,
and emphasizing agriculture and grain.
The emperor praised him
and submitted his proposals to relevant departments for discussion.
Gāo Gǒng, who headed the Ministry of Personnel,
disliked that these suggestions encroached upon his authority,
and shelved the memorial,
with only the Censorate’s proposal regarding corrupt officials being implemented.
Initially,
when Yǐ Qín entered the Grand Secretariat,
Xú Jiē was the Senior Grand Secretary,
and Gǒng was just being promoted,
so the court officials each had their own factions,
attacking each other.
Yǐ Qín remained neutral, taking no side,
nor did he have any personal retainers.
Eventually, when Jiē and Gǒng departed,
no one spoke ill of him.
When Gǒng re-entered the Grand Secretariat,
he clashed with Zhào Zhēnjí,
and Zhāng Jūzhèng again stirred up trouble between them.
Yǐ Qín was an old colleague of Gǒng,
Zhēnjí was his fellow townsman,
and Jūzhèng was a scholar he had recommended.
Estimating that he could not mediate,
and fearing that he would ultimately not be tolerated by these men,
he strenuously pleaded illness and sought to resign.
Thereupon, he was promoted to concurrent Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince and Minister of Personnel,
granted an imperial edict, and sent home by express messenger,
with an imperial decree for his son, compiler Yú Bì, to accompany him.
Two years later,
Gǒng was expelled
and left the capital gate in a hurry,
sighing:
"Nánchōng
is a wise man!"
Yǐ Qín had been home for ten years,
aged seventy.
Again, imperial silver and silk were bestowed upon him,
and Yú Bì was ordered to return by express messenger to present them,
and officials were further commanded to inquire after his well-being.
Six more years later, he passed away.
He was posthumously granted Grand Guardian
and given the posthumous name Wénduān.
Yú Bì has a separate biography.
Zhào Zhēnjí,
courtesy name Mèngjìng,
was from Nèijiāng.
At six years old, he recited a scroll of text daily.
As he grew up,
he became famous for his extensive knowledge.
He was most skilled in Wáng Shǒurén's teachings.
He passed the imperial examination in the 14th year of Jiājìng,
was selected as a *shùjíshì* (probationary Hanlin academician),
and appointed compiler.
At that time, Daoist priests were just beginning to be favored,
and Zhēnjí requested true Confucian scholars to assist in the great enterprise.
The powerful officials were displeased,
so he requested leave on urgent grounds and returned home.
Upon returning to court, he was promoted to *zhōngyǔn* (expositor-in-waiting),
and oversaw the affairs of the *sīyè* (assistant director of studies).
When Āndá approached the capital city,
sending an insulting letter requesting tribute,
the emperor ordered all officials to deliberate in court.
Zhēnjí threw back his sleeves and spoke loudly, saying:
"The *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals) considered a treaty under the city walls a disgrace.
If tribute is promised, then they will certainly enter the city.
What if their demands are endless?
Xú Jiē said:
"You must have a good strategy."
Zhēnjí said:
"For the present situation,
I request His Majesty to quickly ascend the main hall,
issue an edict acknowledging fault,
record Zhōu Shàngwén's merits to encourage border generals,
release Shěn Shù from prison to open up avenues for criticism,
lighten orders that diminish the army,
and heavily reward those who achieve merit.
Send officials to proclaim these decrees to the generals
and supervise them in fierce combat.
To repel the enemy will be easy."
At that time, the emperor had sent eunuchs to secretly observe the court officials.
Though it was midday, no one had uttered a word.
Upon hearing Zhēnjí's words,
the emperor was invigorated.
He instructed Yán Sōng:
"Zhēnjí's words are right,
except that he should not have mentioned Zhōu Shàngwén and Shěn Shù."
He summoned Zhēnjí to the Left Shun Gate
and ordered him to draft a memorial on expedient measures.
He was immediately promoted to Left Remonstrance Official and concurrent Censor,
and ordered to carry an imperial edict to proclaim the decrees to the various armies.
He was given fifty thousand taels of silver
to use as he deemed fit for rewards.
Initially,
after Zhēnjí's court deliberation,
he arrogantly went to visit Yán Sōng.
Sōng declined to see him,
and Zhēnjí angrily shouted at the gatekeepers.
Just then, Zhào Wénhuá arrived,
and Zhēnjí again shouted at him.
Sōng greatly resented this.
When the imperial edict was drafted,
it did not instruct him to supervise the battle,
to diminish his authority,
nor was he given a single soldier for protection.
At that time, enemy cavalry were rampant.
Zhēnjí galloped into the various generals' camps,
distributed silver to reward the soldiers,
and proclaimed the emperor's benevolent intentions.
The next day, he returned to report.
The emperor was furious,
believing Zhēnjí had no plan,
but merely advocated for Shàngwén and Shù.
He was sent to the imperial prison,
flogged in court,
and demoted to judicial clerk of Lìbō.
He was gradually promoted to *tōngpàn* (assistant prefect) of Huīzhōu,
and then to principal of the Nanjing Ministry of Personnel.
In the 40th year, he was promoted to Vice Minister of the Ministry of Revenue.
The court deliberated sending a high minister to Jìzhōu to oversee provisions and train soldiers.
Sōng wanted to use Zhēnjí,
so he invited him to drink to show his intention.
Zhēnjí said:
"The one overseeing provisions,
is he overseeing imperial transport
or civil transport?
If these two transports already have their designated officials,
adding an official will only cause more trouble.
Moreover, the failure to train soldiers,
the fault should not lie there.
Even if ten Vice Ministers of Revenue were dispatched,
what good would it do for training soldiers?"
Sōng angrily dismissed him.
Soon, Sōng requested leave,
and the Ministry of Personnel appointed Lín Yìngliàng, Vice Minister of Granaries.
When Sōng returned,
he was even more enraged.
He ordered the Supervising Secretary Zhāng Yì to impeach Yìngliàng,
transferring him to Nanjing,
and appointed the Censor-in-chief Huò Jì instead.
Yì again said:
"Overseeing provisions is the exclusive duty of the Ministry of Revenue.
Now, Zhēnjí and Left Vice Minister Liú Dàbīn were not considered in the court selection,
which means they are remiss in their duties
and should be dismissed."
Thus, both men were stripped of their official positions.
At the beginning of Lóngqìng,
he was appointed Left Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites,
and took charge of the Zhan Shi Fu (Office of the Imperial Household).
When Mùzōng visited the Imperial Academy,
the Chancellor Hú Jié had just been dismissed,
so Zhēnjí was appointed to act in his stead.
His lecture on the *Dà Yǔ Mó* (Counsel of Great Yǔ) pleased the emperor,
and he was appointed daily lecturer.
Zhēnjí was over sixty,
yet his discussions were straightforward and upright,
and his deportment was always proper.
The emperor paid close attention to him.
Soon after, he was transferred to Minister of Rites of Nanjing.
After he had departed,
the emperor missed him
and retained him as a lecturer.
In the autumn of the third year,
he was ordered to concurrently serve as Grand Secretary of the Wényuān Pavilion and participate in state affairs.
Zhēnjí entered to express his gratitude,
memorializing:
"Court administration and border affairs are all neglected and in disarray.
I wish to sacrifice myself to serve,
but Your Majesty must preside over it."
The emperor was even more pleased.
Coincidentally, invaders entered Dàtóng,
and the Commander-in-chief Zhào Kě failed in his duty,
but the Governor-General Chén Qíxué instead reported a victory,
which was exposed by the Censor Yàn Rúhuàn.
Zhēnjí wanted to impose severe punishment,
but the Minister of War, Huò Jì, only proposed a demotion in rank.
Zhēnjí debated with his colleagues but failed to prevail,
so he submitted a memorial, saying:
"For border generals who fail to uphold discipline,
the ancestral laws are clear.
Now, those in charge bend the law to accommodate individuals.
What about public opinion?
I am old,
and have no means to show my loyalty.
I beg to be dismissed."
This was not granted.
Soon, he was promoted to Grand Guardian of the Crown Prince.
Zhēn Jí had earlier listed the imperial army as three great camps.
Each camp had its own commander.
Now, one person was to command all three camps,
wielding a power that would be difficult to control.
Therefore, he vehemently spoke of its disadvantages,
requesting that the camps be divided into five,
each commanded by a great general,
thus somewhat restoring the old system of the ancestors.
The Emperor approved of this,
ordering the Ministry of War to convene a discussion with court officials.
The Minister Hùo Jì had previously disagreed with Zhēn Jí,
and was quite disapproving of his words.
Many court officials also believed that a strong army lay in selecting good generals,
not in changing laws.
So, Jì and others presented a memorial arguing that the three great camps should remain as they were,
but that one person serving as grand coordinator,
whose power was too great,
should be replaced by each of the three camps establishing a great general,
and the grand coordinator position abolished,
with a civil official appointed as grand manager.
This was approved.
Previously,
the Supervising Secretary Yáng Róng had impeached Jì for greed and incompetence.
The Emperor had already retained Jì,
but Jì, knowing that Róng and Zhēn Jí were from the same district,
suspected that it was Zhēn Jí's idea.
He submitted a memorial defending himself and requesting dismissal,
and also slandered Zhēn Jí.
Zhēn Jí also submitted a memorial defending himself and asking to leave.
An imperial edict retained Zhēn Jí
and stripped Jì of his office.
Afterwards, the camp system was repeatedly changed,
but within less than a year, it reverted to its old form,
and Zhēn Jí could not contend against it either.
As Āndá sought peace at the frontier and requested enfeoffment,
Zhēn Jí strongly supported this proposal.
Prior to this,
Gāo Gǒng had rejoined the Grand Secretariat and immediately took charge of the Ministry of Personnel.
Zhēn Jí spoke to Lǐ Chūnfāng
and also gained charge of the Censorate.
Gǒng, out of personal resentment, wished to review and evaluate the Censorate officials.
Zhēn Jí and his colleagues memorialized, saying:
"Recently, due to Censor Yè Mèngxióng's words displeasing Your Majesty,
Your Majesty issued a stern decree to review and evaluate censors,
including those promoted and residing at home.
Nearly two hundred people are to be evaluated,
among whom there must be loyal and outspoken officials who dare to speak truth to their lord.
Now, to condemn them all as presumptuous and treacherous,
We fear that the responsible departments may act excessively,
failing to distinguish between loyalty and treachery,
thereby blocking the path of remonstrance
and disheartening the gentry,
which would not be a blessing for the state."
The Emperor did not comply.
Gǒng, realizing that Zhēn Jí knew his intentions,
resented him deeply.
During the evaluation,
Gǒng wanted to remove those whom Zhēn Jí favored,
while Zhēn Jí also held back those whom Gǒng favored in return.
Consequently, twenty-seven people were dismissed,
and all those Gǒng disliked were among them.
Gǒng still felt resentful,
and instigated his student, Supervising Secretary Hán Jí, to impeach Zhēn Jí for incompetence and arrogance,
and for showing favoritism during the evaluation.
Zhēn Jí submitted a memorial defending himself and requesting retirement,
and furthermore said:
"Since I took charge of the Censorate's affairs,
I have only differed with Gǒng on the matter of the evaluation.
As for other acts of disrupting the selection laws,
and indulging in treachery,
which are obvious to all,
I have remained silent and could not say a word,
failing in my assigned duty.
I am truly an incompetent official.
As for Gǒng,
he can truly be called arrogant.
After I am dismissed and return home,
I hope that Gǒng will still be returned to the Grand Secretariat,
and not be allowed to monopolize great power for long
and widely cultivate factions."
After the memorial was submitted,
Zhēn Jí was indeed granted permission to leave,
while Gǒng retained his power over the Ministry of Personnel as before.
Zhēn Jí was erudite and highly talented.
However, he was strong-willed and temperamental,
often clashing with others.
He would sometimes address high-ranking ministers by their personal names,
and people therefore harbored much resentment towards him.
Gāo Gǒng and Zhāng Jūzhèng, though his juniors,
were promoted earlier.
All were talented and competitive, unwilling to yield to each other,
and ultimately clashed and departed.
He died in the tenth year of Wànlì (1582),
and was posthumously granted the title of Junior Guardian
and the諡shì title Wénsù.
Yīn Shìdān,
courtesy name Zhèngfǔ,
was a native of Lìchéng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the twenty-sixth year of Jiājìng (1547).
He was selected as a *shùjíshì* and
appointed as a compiler.
After a long time,
he served as an instructor to Prince Yù.
Regarding matters of imperial virtue and governance,
he would often speak with grave and impassioned arguments,
which moved the Prince.
He was promoted to Right Grand Master of Remonstrance,
then to Assistant to the Heir Apparent,
continuing his direct remonstrance as before.
In the first year of Lóngqìng (1567), he was promoted to Academician of the Hanlin Academy with the title of Reader,
overseeing the affairs of the Hanlin Academy,
and then advanced to Right Vice Minister of Rites,
and soon after transferred to the Ministry of Personnel.
In the spring of the following year,
he was appointed Minister of Rites,
and oversaw the affairs of the Supervisorate of Imperial Instruction.
In the winter of that year,
he resumed his duties at the Ministry.
In the first day of the first month and the fifteenth day of the first month of the fourth year,
there were eclipses of both the sun and the moon.
Shìdān memorialized, requesting the Emperor to spread virtue, mitigate punishments, accept remonstrance, and economize expenditures,
and to instruct all officials, both inside and outside the court, to investigate the suffering of the people.
The report was heard.
Due to his past favors,
he was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
At that time, lectures were suspended in both hot and cold seasons.
Shìdān requested that, as in the old practice,
lectures should not cease throughout the four seasons,
and furthermore suggested lecturing on the *Zǔxùn*, *Dàxué Yǎnyì*, and *Zhēnguān Zhèngyào*.
The Emperor commended and accepted his suggestions.
Initially, Shìzōng had established regulations for the imperial princes, stating that
if a prince had no heir,
a brother or a brother's son should succeed,
and no collateral line should be allowed to inherit.
In the late Jiājìng period,
Prince Sùhuái died
without a son.
His grandmother, Princess Dìng, requested that General Fǔguó Jìn[móu] succeed him.
The Ministry of Rites argued that Jìn[móu] was actually Prince Huái's paternal cousin once removed,
and thus could not inherit the main line.
An imperial edict permitted the general to temporarily oversee the prince's household affairs.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
the Princess Dowager again petitioned,
but former Minister Gāo Yí strongly opposed it.
Jìn[móu] heavily bribed eunuchs
and instructed members of the imperial clan to memorialize on his behalf,
praying for success.
Shìdān strongly maintained his opposition.
The Emperor, considering that the Sù princely domain was located in a distant frontier,
and that without a prince, it could not be stabilized,
thus permitted Jìn[móu] to succeed.
Shìdān argued, saying:
"The Sù princely household moved from Gānzhōu to Lánzhōu,
which is actually in the interior.
Moreover, I request that a worthy *jùnwáng* be selected to manage the princely household affairs,
and not to grant this private request,
which would destroy the regulations."
But the Emperor's will was firm and could not be swayed.
Shìdān then requested that he be enfeoffed as a *jùnwáng*,
so that all imperial kinsmen would follow this precedent.
The Emperor ultimately did not allow it.
According to old customs,
after the suburban sacrifice,
a celebratory banquet was held.
Since Shìzōng grew weary of his duties,
this ceremony had long been abolished.
Three years after the Emperor's ascension,
it had still not been held.
Shìdān began to research and establish the old rites and implement them.
In the eleventh month, he was ordered to concurrently serve as a Grand Secretary of Wényuāngé in his current official capacity and handle affairs in the Grand Secretariat.
Soon after, the matter of Āndá's enfeoffment was concluded,
and he was promoted to Junior Guardian
and transferred to Wǔyīngdiàn.
Shǐ Shìdān (士儋) initially served as a staff member in the household of Prince Yù (裕) alongside Chén Yǐqín (陳以勤), Gāo Gǒng (高拱), and Zhāng Jūzhèng (張居正).
The latter three all attained positions of power,
while Shìdān (士儋) remained a Minister,
and could not but feel disappointed.
Gǒng (拱) had always been on good terms with Zhāng Sìwéi (張四維),
and wished to bring him into the government.
However, he disliked Shìdān (士儋) for not being close to him,
and did not help him.
Shìdān (士儋) then leveraged the power of Grand Eunuch Chén Hóng (陳洪),
and obtained an imperial edict to join the Grand Secretariat,
which caused him to resent Gǒng (拱) and Sìwéi (四維).
Sìwéi’s (四維) father monopolized salt profits,
and was impeached by Censor Gào Yǒngchūn (郜永春).
The matter had already been resolved,
but other censors brought it up again.
Gǒng (拱) and Sìwéi (四維) suspected this was instigated by Shìdān (士儋),
and their animosity intensified.
Censor Zhào Yìnglóng (趙應龍) then impeached Shìdān (士儋), stating that his advancement was due to Chén Hóng (陳洪),
and thus he was unfit to participate in major political affairs.
Shìdān (士儋) again made his case and requested to resign,
but it was not granted.
Meanwhile, Gǒng’s (拱) protégé, Supervising Secretary Hán Jí (韓楫), again openly threatened him,
and Shìdān (士儋) also suspected this was Gǒng’s (拱) doing.
According to custom,
supervising secretaries were to enter the Grand Secretariat for a collective bow on the first and fifteenth day of the lunar month.
Shìdān (士儋) questioned Jí (楫) directly, saying:
“I hear you have a grievance against me.
A grievance is fine,
but do not be used by others.”
Gǒng (拱) said:
“This is improper.”
Shìdān (士儋) rose in anger,
and cursed Gǒng (拱), saying:
“You drove away Lord Chén (陳公),
drove away Lord Zhào (趙公),
and then drove away Lord Lǐ (李公).
Now you are trying to drive me away for Sìwéi (四維).
Do you think you can always keep this seat?”
He raised his arm, intending to strike him.
Jūzhèng (居正) mediated from the side,
and also retorted sharply.
Censor Hóu Jūliáng (侯居良) again impeached Shìdān (士儋), stating his initial advancement was improper,
and his request to resign was not courageous.
Shìdān (士儋) submitted a memorial again, requesting more strongly,
and was then granted travel expenses,
and returned home by imperial post-horse.
Officials provided his living allowance and servants according to custom.
He lived at home for eleven years before he died.
At that time, Jūzhèng (居正) was near death,
and Sìwéi (四維) was in power.
Resenting Shìdān (士儋),
he posthumously granted him the title of Grand Tutor,
with the posthumous name Wéntōng (文通).
After some time,
it was changed to Wénzhuāng (文莊).
Gāo Yí (高儀),
courtesy name Zǐxiàng (子象),
was from Qiántáng (錢塘).
He obtained his *jinshì* degree in the 20th year of Jiājìng (嘉靖) (1541).
He was selected as a *shùjíshì* (庶吉士)
and appointed Compiler.
He successively served as Lecturer of the Hanlin Academy,
and took charge of the Nánjīng (南京) Hanlin Academy.
He was summoned to serve as Grand Master of Ceremonies,
managing the affairs of the Guózǐjiàn (國子監) (Imperial Academy).
He was promoted to Right Vice Minister of Rites,
then transferred to the Ministry of Personnel,
and instructed *shùjíshì*.
In the 45th year of Jiājìng (嘉靖) (1566), he replaced Gāo Gǒng (高拱) as Minister of Rites.
When Mùzōng (穆宗) ascended the throne,
all major ceremonial regulations were determined by Yí (儀).
Shìzōng’s (世宗) dying wishes stipulated
that the rituals for suburban sacrifices, ancestral temple enshrinement, and accompanying burials
should all be revised according to ancestral regulations.
Yí (儀) then convened court officials to discuss: the separate sacrifices to Heaven and Earth did not need to be changed;
after sacrificing to the God of Agriculture,
it was improper to again pray for grain at the Western Garden;
the sacrifices to the Gods of Soil and Grain, the Imperial Ancestor, the Imperial Mingtang with Heaven, and the exclusive worship at Yùzhīgōng (玉芝宮)
should be abolished;
Empress Xiàojié (孝潔) should be enshrined in the ancestral temple,
while Empress Xiàoliè (孝烈) should be worshipped elsewhere.
The emperor approved all.
Later, eunuch Lǐ Fāng (李芳) again requested the joint sacrifice to Heaven and Earth according to the Hóngwǔ (洪武) system,
and Censor Zhāng Jiǎ (張檟) requested to change the names of the Huángjí (皇極) halls,
restoring them completely to their old names. Yí (儀) opposed both.
Four months after the emperor ascended the throne,
he had not yet summoned ministers for an audience,
and Yí (儀) repeatedly requested it.
In the first month of Lóngqìng (隆慶) 2 (1568), during the sacrifice at the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
the emperor intended to send a substitute.
Yí (儀), along with his colleagues, remonstrated,
and the Grand Secretaries also spoke on the matter,
whereupon the emperor personally performed the sacrifice as prescribed by ritual.
Jìnqì (縉𢒞), a General of the State Guard of the Qìng (慶) Prince's household, requested to inherit the princely title.
Yí (儀) firmly refused.
When the Crown Prince was seven years old,
Yí (儀) memorialized requesting he move out of the inner chambers.
The emperor ordered it be done when he reached ten years old.
An edict requested 200,000 *liǎng* of silver from the Ministry of Imperial Entertainments,
which Yí (儀) strongly opposed.
Initially,
Shìzōng (世宗) revered Daoism,
and the Grand Court of Imperial Sacrifices had many superfluous officials.
Yí (儀) memorialized to dismiss forty-eight people.
Minister Chén Qìng (陳慶) reported a shortage of staff,
but Yí (儀) firmly disagreed.
He managed the Ministry of Rites for four years,
and at the end of each year, he would report on omens and disasters from the four directions.
He handled affairs with礼 (ritual) and followed the law,
and was highly commended in his position.
He submitted six memorials requesting retirement due to illness,
but was retained.
At that time, Censor Fù Chǒng (傅寵) impeached Yí (儀) for an incident during the previous emperor's reign concerning writing an essay for a ritual altar.
Yí (儀) submitted four memorials requesting to leave,
and was then granted the additional title of Junior Guardian of the Crown Prince and returned home by imperial post-horse.
Two years after his return,
recommended by Gāo Gǒng (高拱),
he was appointed to his former post to instruct the Crown Prince in reading,
and managed the詹事府 (Zhan Shi Fu) (Court of Imperial Sacrifices).

In the fourth month of the sixth year of Lóngqìng (隆慶) (1572), an imperial edict commanded him to concurrently serve as Grand Secretary of the Wényuāngé (文淵閣) and enter the Grand Secretariat to handle affairs.
A month later,
the emperor passed away,
and he was among those entrusted with the deathbed instructions.
When Gǒng (拱) was driven out by Zhāng Jūzhèng (張居正),
Yí (儀) was already ill,
and could only sigh deeply.
He died not long after.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince,
with the posthumous name Wénduān (文端).
Yí (儀) was naturally simple and quiet,
with few desires,
and no concubines in his household.
His old residence was destroyed by fire,
and he spent his life borrowing lodgings from others.
When he died,
there was almost nothing for his burial.
A eulogy says: Fèi Hóng (費宏) and others all started their careers in literature,
and rose to the position of Grand Secretary.
Hóng (宏) refused Qián Níng (錢寧),
resisted Chén Háo (宸濠),
and offended Zhāng (張) and Guì (桂).
He was obstructed and rose again twice,
but ultimately his clear reputation was not harmed.
Lǐ Shí (李時) and Zhái Luán (翟鑾) both had talent and prestige,
but Luán (鑾) failed to maintain his integrity in his later years.
Zhēn Jí (貞吉) was proud and self-important,
but in a situation of intense rivalry,
even if he had been more accommodating,
how could he have avoided trouble?
Gù Dǐngchén (顧鼎臣) and others, dignified in court,
can be said to have reached the height of their good fortune.
And Chén Yǐqín (陳以勤), with sincere dedication,
offered many good suggestions.
Later wise men emulated them,
and succeeded to the position of Grand Secretary.
Throughout the Ming Dynasty,
those who were compared to Wéi (韋) and Píng (平)
often included Yǐqín (以勤) and his son.
How profound was Heaven's reward to them!
Collation Notes

Biographies Eighty-Two: Qiáo Yǔ (喬宇), Sūn Jiāo (孫交) (courtesy name Yuán (元)), Lín Jùn (林俊) (courtesy name Dá (達), Zhāng Fú (張黻)), Jīn Xiànmín (金獻民), Qín Jīn (秦金) (grandson Zhù (柱)), Zhào Huáng (趙璜), Zōu Wénshèng (鄒文盛), Liáng Cái (梁材), Liú Lín (劉麟), Jiǎng Yáo (蔣瑤), Wáng Tíngxiàng (王廷相).
Qiáo Yǔ (喬宇),
courtesy name Xīdà (希大),
was from Lèpíng (樂平), Shānxī (山西).
His grandfather, Yì (毅),
was Left Vice Minister of Works.
His father, Fèng (鳳),
was Director of the Ministry of War.
Both were known for their integrity.
Yǔ (宇) obtained his *jinshì* degree in the 20th year of Chénghuà (成化) (1484),
and was appointed Principal of the Ministry of Rites.
At the beginning of Hóngzhì (弘治),
when Wáng Shù (王恕) was at the Ministry of Personnel,
he transferred Yǔ (宇) to the Bureau of Selection,
and he was promoted three times to Director.
No private visitors came to his gate.
He was promoted to Grand Master of Ceremonies.
Wǔzōng 嗣位,
遣祀中鎮、西海.
還朝,
條上道中所見軍民困苦六事.
巳,
遷光祿卿,
歷戶部左、右侍郎.
劉瑾敗,
大臣多以黨附見劾,
宇獨無所染.
拜南京禮部尚書.
乾清宮災,
率同列言視朝不勤,
經筵久輟,
國本未建,
義子猥多,
番僧處禁寺,
優伶侍起居,
立皇店,
留邊兵,
習戰鬬,
土木繁興,
織造不息,
凡十事.
帝不省.
久之,
改兵部,
參贊機務.
以帝遠遊塞上,
而監國無人,
請早建儲貳.
帝將自擊寇,
宇復率同列諫.
皆不報.
未幾,
寧王宸濠反,
揚言旦夕下南京.
宇嚴為警備,
而談笑自如.
時攜客燕城外,
密察地險易,
置戍守.
綜理周密,
內外宴然.
指揮楊銳有才略,
署為安慶守備.
鎮守中官劉瑯與濠通,
為預伏死士.
宇刺得其情,
詰瑯用事者,
瑯懼不敢動,
宇乃大索城中,
斬所伏壯士三百人,
懸首江上.
宸濠失內應,
且知有備,
不敢東.
攻安慶,
銳固守不得下.
未幾敗.
帝至南京,
詔百官戎服朝明年正旦.
宇不可,
率諸臣朝服賀.
江彬索城門諸鑰,
都督府問宇.
宇曰:
「守備者,
所以謹非常.
禁門鎖鑰,
孰敢索,
亦孰敢予,
雖天子詔不可得. 」
都督府以宇言復,
乃已.
彬矯旨有所求,
日數十至,
宇必廷白之,
彬亦稍稍止.
彬欲譖去宇.
守備太監王偉者,
初為帝伴讀,
帝信之,
每從中調護,
故彬謀不行.
帝駐南京九月,
宇倡諸臣三請回鑾,
又自伏闕請.
駕旋,
扈至揚州.
明年加太子太保.
論保障功,
復加少保.
世宗即位,
召為吏部尚書.
宇自為選郎,
有人倫鑒,
及是銓政一清.
帝求治銳甚.
宇與林俊、彭澤、孫交,
皆海內重望,
帝亦委任之.
凡為權倖所黜者,
皆起列庶位,
天下欣欣望治.
帝性剛,
好自用,
宇所執漸不見聽.
興府需次官六十三人,
乞遷.
宇言此輩虛隸名籍,
與見供事者不同.
黜罰之有差,
皆怨宇.
帝欲封駙馬都尉崔元為侯,
外戚蔣輪、邵喜為伯,
宇不可.
無何,
詔進壽寧侯張鶴齡為公,
封后父陳萬言為伯,
授萬言子紹祖尚寶丞.
宇言:
「累朝太后戚屬無生封公者,
張巒亦歿後贈,
今奈何以父贈為子封.
萬言封伯視巒更驟,
而子授尚寶非制.
願陛下守典章,
以垂萬世. 」
帝並不從.
史道訐楊廷和,
宇言道挾私,
遂下之詔獄.
曹嘉助道劾宇,
宇求罷,
帝命鴻臚趨視事.
宇遇事不可,
無不力爭,
而爭
「大禮」
尤切.
帝欲加興獻帝皇號,
宇言加皇於本生之親,
則干正統,
非所以重宗廟,
正名分.
及禮官請稱獻帝為本生考,
帝改稱本生皇考,
又詔建獻帝廟於大內,
宇等復連章諫.
特旨用席書為禮部尚書,
宇又偕九卿言:
「陛下罷汪俊,
用席書,
謫馬明衡、季本、陳逅,
召張璁、桂萼、霍韜,
舉措乖違,
人心駭愕.
夫以一二人邪說,
廢天下萬世公議,
內離骨肉,
外間君臣,
名為効忠,
實累聖德.
且書不繇廷推,
特出內降,
此祖宗來所未有.
乞令俊與書各仍舊職,
宥明衡等,
止璁、萼毋召. 」
尋復請罷璁、萼、書,
而出爭
「大禮」
者呂柟、鄒守益於獄.
Huì Cōng and È arrived at the capital.
An edict ordered them both to serve as Grand Secretaries.
Yǔ and others again said:
“Imperial grants of favor
were, in previous reigns, typically bestowed upon sycophantic small men.
If a scholar-official once participated in such,
he would immediately not be countenanced by upright public opinion.
Moreover, Grand Secretaries are of the purest and most distinguished rank,
yet you allow È and others to occupy these positions.
Who would still be willing to be their colleagues?”
The emperor was angered,
and severely rebuked them.
Yǔ then requested retirement,
which was granted.
He was given a rapid carriage and an allowance for sustenance,
just as in previous cases.
Censors Xǔ Zhōng, Liú Yú, and others requested Yǔ be retained,
but the emperor said:
“It is not that I do not want to use Yǔ;
Yǔ himself requested to leave due to illness.”
Later, after the Dà Diǎn of Mínglún was completed,
the previous discussion was re-evaluated,
and his official position was revoked.
When Yáng Yīqīng died,
Yǔ crossed the river to mourn him.
The elders of Nándū all came out to welcome him,
raising their hands to their foreheads and saying:
“It is you, our lord,
who saved us.”
When Yǔ was young, he followed his father to the capital,
and studied under Yáng Yīqīng.
After passing the imperial examination as a *jìnshì*,
he again associated with Lǐ Dōngyáng.
His poetry and prose were powerful and outstanding;
he was also skilled in seal and large seal script.
He had a fondness for mountains and waters,
and once climbed to the summit of Mount Huà.
He encountered a tiger,
and his servants all screamed and fell,
but Yǔ sat upright and did not move.
The tiger slowly tucked its tail and left.
His home life was simple and unadorned;
his clothes and possessions were like those of a poor scholar.
After his death,
his two concubines, Liú and Xǔ, both committed suicide to follow him.
When Mùzōng ascended the throne,
his official position was restored,
and he was posthumously granted Grand Tutor,
with the posthumous name Zhuāngjiǎn.
Sūn Jiāo,
courtesy name Zhìtóng,
was from Ānlù.
He became a *jìnshì* in the 17th year of Chénghuà.
He was appointed Principal of the Nanjing Ministry of War,
and was recognized by Minister Wáng Shù.
In the early Hóngzhì reign,
when Shù entered the Ministry of Personnel,
he recommended Jiāo for appointment as Director of the Bureau of Merits,
and he successively served as Secretary of the Bureau of Selection.
He served in the Ministry of Personnel for fourteen years,
and greatly promoted and supported virtuous individuals.
He was promoted to Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
and supervised the Sìmǎ Quǎn.
When there was an alert in Dàtóng,
he was ordered to dispatch Commissioner Huáng Huā to garrison the border regions.
He increased the walls and moats,
expanded cultivation,
and restrained enemy cavalry charges.
During the Yǒnglè reign,
troops from the Lóngqìng and other garrisons were sent annually to collect firewood and charcoal.
Later, this was abolished,
and they were ordered to annually pay twenty thousand taels of silver,
which greatly burdened the military.
Jiāo memorialized to have it exempted.
In the early Zhèngdé reign,
he was promoted to Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments.
In the third year, he advanced to Right Vice Minister of the Ministry of Revenue,
and supervised the granaries.
He was then transferred to the Ministry of Personnel.
Minister Zhāng Cǎi attached himself to Liú Jǐn,
and Jiāo frequently admonished him.
Cǎi was angered,
and transferred him to Nánjīng.
When Jǐn was defeated,
he was summoned and appointed Minister of Revenue.
At that time, there were campaigns against roving bandits,
and logistics were busy and urgent.
Moreover, it was a year of famine,
and regular taxes were insufficient,
but Jiāo’s planning was appropriate.
When famine was reported in various regions,
he would request tax exemptions and famine relief,
and thus the people did not suffer excessively,
but those small men in power all found this inconvenient.
The emperor wanted to bestow the Tàipíng granary upon the favored minister Péi Dé;
the eunuch supervising Yúnnán, Zhāng Lún, requested to mine for silver;
the eunuch supervising Nanjing weaving, Wú Jīng, reported a shortage of funds.
Jiāo vigorously argued against all of these.
In the sixth month of the eighth year,
an imperial decree ordered him and Minister of Rites Fù Guī to retire.
Many censors requested their retention,
but there was no reply.
Shìzōng had known Jiāo’s reputation when he was still in the princely residence.
Immediately upon his accession,
he summoned him to resume his former office.
He first requested that the emperor read the ancestral instructions daily,
that all his words and actions should be based on these principles,
and that daily lectures in the imperial study should not cease, regardless of season.
The emperor praised and accepted this.
Someone proposed moving the Xiǎnlíng mausoleum to Tiānshòu Mountain,
but Jiāo said:
“Matters concerning imperial mausoleums are grave.
Tàizǔ once wished to move Rénzǔ to Zhōng Mountain,
but fearing the dispersion of spiritual energy, he stopped.
This is fully recorded on the Imperial Mausoleum Stele.”
The matter was then dropped.
After the extravagance and wastefulness of Wǔzōng,
the imperial treasury was depleted.
Jiāo cut down on redundant expenses,
and established regular systems,
thereby clearing up long-standing abuses.
However, regarding matters involving eunuchs,
the emperor could not entirely follow his advice.
He once convened court officials to discuss releasing funds from the inner treasury for military provisions and official salaries,
which had already been approved,
but was obstructed by the eunuchs Liáng Jiàn and others.
Jiāo said:
“If the palace and the government differ,
and orders are issued only to be reversed,
this is not conducive to a new administration.”
He was not listened to.
Initially, there were only a few eunuchs supervising the granaries;
in the Zhèngdé reign, their number increased to fifty-five.
At Jiāo’s suggestion, more than half were dismissed,
but later they gradually increased again.
The emperor had already dismissed thirty-seven people,
and Jiāo wanted to remove all of them,
including those at the Línqīng, Xú, and Huái granaries,
and not to send any personnel there at all.
The emperor merely ordered that no more should be added from now on.
Regarding the eunuchs guarding the pearl fisheries,
an edict had stipulated that they should not interfere with local governance,
but Ān Chuān used his connections to revert to the old ways.
Jiāo impeached Chuān,
and an order was issued in accordance with the previous edict.
During the Zhèngdé reign,
the number of eunuchs in the Shànglín Garden reached ninety-nine,
who seized countless public and private lands.
Upon the emperor’s accession,
he ordered eighteen people to be retained,
as was the case during the Hóngzhì reign.
Soon, imperial orders again increased the number to sixty-two.
Jiāo requested their dismissal as before,
and also that all seized land be returned.
This was granted.
He also argued that the eunuchs of the Imperial Stables should adhere to ancestral regulations,
and should not supervise the collection of fodder and beans,
