and that the Ministry of Revenue should be informed of the number of horses,
to prevent embezzlement.
This was not followed.
Zhāng Jǐn, a centurion of the Embroidered Uniform Guard, led his subalterns to draw salaries from the granaries,
and extorted unscrupulously.
Principal Luó Hóngzài wanted to investigate him.
Jǐn deceptively requested to receive a caning,
and then memorialized that Hóngzài had arbitrarily flogged a forbidden guard official.
The emperor was angered,
arrested him, imprisoned him in the imperial prison, and exiled him.
Jiāo, along with Lín Jùn and Qiáo Yǔ, successively argued for his rescue,
but it was not accepted.
Yán Hóng, a eunuch of the Imperial Stables, requested land outside the Leopard Chamber.
Jiāo said:
“The previous emperor, due to the Leopard Chamber,
brought forth endless misfortune.
Hóng and others want to repair it to initiate a new round of hunting,
which we ministers dare not hear of.”
An edict granted ten *qǐng* of land to the Leopard Chamber,
and ordered the remaining land to be leased by centurion Zhào Kǎi and others as before.
He was ordered to report the number of imperial manor fields for each palace,
which differed from the old records.
The emperor questioned the reason.
Jiāo said:
“Many of the old records were based on memorialized requests and presented lands,
so the numbers were often falsely reported.
The new records show fewer,
because they were cleared and verified by imperial command,
and many fields were removed and exempted.”
The emperor’s anger somewhat subsided,
and he ordered an investigation of the records from the Chénghuà and Hóngzhì reigns to be reported.
Jiāo was already seventy years old,
and repeatedly submitted memorials requesting to retire.
The emperor consistently comforted him and urged him to stay,
sending doctors to examine and treat him.
He asked to work even harder,
and then he was granted permission.
He received an imperial edict adding the title of Tàizǐ Tàibǎo,
and was given a courier post-horse.
His son, a compiler, was ordered to accompany him,
and officials were to inquire after him regularly,
providing him with provisions, rice, carriages, and servants.
He was also granted travel expenses.
He died at the age of eighty,
and was granted the posthumous title Róngxī.
Jiāo's speech and discussions were always sincere and humble,
never arrogant towards others due to his position or power.
He was pure, cautious, tranquil, and content,
consistent from beginning to end.
When he was initially in Nánjīng,
his colleagues, finding their duties simple and having much leisure,
would gather to chat, drink, and play chess for enjoyment.
Jiāo would silently stay in his room,
reading books without interruption.
Someone once commented on this,
and Jiāo said:
"Conversing with sages and worthies,
is that not better than with guests, wives, and concubines?"
Xìngxiàn Wáng had always esteemed and valued Jiāo,
and once allotted him a piece of land to the east of the Yángchūntái to enlarge his residence.
Later, a eunuch spoke of Grand Secretary Sūn encroaching on the land,
and Shìzōng said:
"This was bestowed by the late emperor;
how dare I take it away?"
Yuán,
a *jìnshì*,
ended his career as the Sichuan Fùshǐ.
He was cautious and honest, possessing his father's demeanor.
Lín Jùn,
courtesy name Dàiyòng,
was from Pútián.
He became a *jìnshì* in the fourteenth year of Chénghuà.
He was appointed as a *zhǔshì* in the Ministry of Justice,
and promoted to *yuánwàiláng*.
His nature was forthright and honest,
and he did not drift with popular customs.
When matters involved powerful nobles,
Minister Lín Cōng would often assign Jùn to handle them.
He submitted a memorial requesting the execution of the demonic monk Jìxiǎo and the punishment of the powerful eunuch Liáng Fāng.
The emperor was furious
and ordered him to be imprisoned and interrogated.
Later, Zhāng Fú, an experience officer of the prefectural administration, saved him
and was also imprisoned.
Grand Eunuch Huái Ēn strongly interceded,
and Jùn was demoted to Yaózhōu Pànguān,
while Fú became Zhīzhōu of Shīzōng.
At that time, freedom of speech had long been suppressed,
and their forthright reputations shook the capital,
giving rise to the saying:
"The censor is in the Ministry of Justice,
the yellow gate is out of the rear office."
Soon after, due to a celestial anomaly on the first day of the first lunar month,
the emperor became enlightened,
restored Jùn's office,
and transferred him to Nánjīng.
In the first year of Hóngzhì, he was recommended and promoted to Yúnnán Fùshǐ.
At the Xuánhuà Temple in Hèqìng, there was said to be a living Buddha.
Every year, tens of thousands of men and women would gather,
vying to apply gold to its face.
Jùn ordered it to be burned,
and all the gold obtained was used to compensate the people's debts.
He also destroyed three hundred and sixty illicit shrines,
all their materials being removed to repair school buildings.
Dāo Pàyù, the *tǔshě* of Gānyá, wanted to seize the position of *xuānfǔguān* from his cousin,
and had held his seal for several years.
Jùn issued a directive to him,
and he returned the seal.
He was promoted to Ànchásǐ.
Five years later, he was transferred to Húguǎng.
Due to snow and ice disasters, he submitted a memorial discussing the gains and losses of current governance.
He also stated that the construction of princely mansions in Dé'ān and Ānlù and the expansion of the Jí Mansion
involved a vast number of laborers,
and expenses of tens of millions,
which the people could not bear.
He requested that, following the precedents of the Níng, Xiāng, and Dé prefectures,
everything should be simplified and economical,
without using glazed tiles and white stone carved railings,
and asked for this to be established as a rule.
This was not followed.
In the ninth year, he cited illness
and returned home without waiting for a reply.
After a long time,
he was recommended and appointed as Guǎngdōng Yòubùzhèngshǐ,
but he did not accept the appointment.
He was then appointed as Nánjīng Yòuqīandūyùshǐ,
supervising the river defenses.
On the first day of the first lunar month in the fourteenth year,
Shaǎnxī and Shānxī experienced earthquakes and rising waters.
He memorialized, recounting the disasters caused by inner palace affairs, imperial relatives, eunuchs, and powerful officials,
and requested the abolition of Daoist rituals,
reduction of weaving output,
cleansing of illicit occupations,
elimination of redundant officials,
halting of construction projects,
economizing of supplies,
restricting of rewards,
warning against excessive desires,
keeping away from flattering favorites,
and drawing close to virtuous people.
He also requested early education for the imperial heir,
and then recommended Vice Minister Xiè Duó,
Junior Ministers Chú Guàn and Yáng Lián,
retired Vice Envoy Cáo Shízhōng,
and recluse Liú Mǐn to assist in guidance.
This was reported.
Afterward,
he repeatedly submitted memorials requesting retirement,
recommending Shízhōng to replace himself.
This was not granted.
The commoner Wáng Wǔ from Xīnchāng, Jiāngxī, became a bandit.
Governor Hán Bāngwèn could not pacify him,
so Jùn was ordered to inspect the situation.
He personally entered Wǔ's lair,
and Wǔ requested to demonstrate his loyalty,
capturing all his bandit associates.
An imperial edict immediately appointed Jùn to replace Bāngwèn.
Jùn cited the examples of Zhū Xī replacing Táng Zhòngyǒu and Bāo Zhěng replacing Sòng Qí,
and strongly declined.
It was not granted.
He then revised the agreements,
and all public affairs were renewed.
The princely estates levied annual stipends,
often collecting double from the people.
Due to Jùn's words, this was greatly reduced.
Níng Wáng Chénháo was avaricious and tyrannical,
and Jùn repeatedly curbed him.
The prince requested to replace the glazed tiles,
which would cost twenty thousand.
Jùn said it should remain as it was,
and not involve the demands of Shū Duàn's capital borders,
or the bestowal of a staff by Wú Wáng.
The prince was angry,
and sought for his mistakes,
but found none.
When Jùn inspected the department during the imperial birthday festival,
he then impeached and reported it,
and his salary was suspended for three months.
Soon after, he returned home due to his mother's mourning.
When Wǔzōng 武宗 ascended the throne,
the remonstrating officials universally recommended him,
and the Jiāngxī 江西 people at court jointly submitted a memorial requesting the return of Jùn 俊.
He was then promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief [yòu fù dū yù shǐ 右副都御史],
and was to once again govern Jiāngxī 江西,
but due to his father’s mourning, this did not materialize.
In the fourth year of Zhèngdé 正德 (1509), he was appointed to govern Sìchuān 四川.
Liú Liè 劉烈, a native of Méizhōu 眉州, initiated a rebellion,
was defeated and fled.
Various unruly individuals then used his name to plunder.
Jùn 俊 had his image drawn and sought his capture,
but could not apprehend him.
At that time, the bandits Lán Tíngruì 藍廷瑞, Yān Běnshù 鄢本恕, Liáo Huì 廖惠, and others from Bǎoníng 保寧 subsequently rose up,
their power growing,
and they turned to raid Bāzhōu 巴州.
He suddenly encountered them at Huálǒng 華壟,
and traveled in a single palanquin to their camp,
explaining the advantages and disadvantages.
The bandits bowed down in rows and agreed to surrender.
Due to continuous rain, they missed the deadline,
rebelled again and fled,
attacking and capturing Tōngjiāng 通江.
Jùn 俊 defeated them at Lóngtānhé 龍灘河,
and sent Prefect Zhāng Mǐn 張敏 and others to pursue and defeat them at Ménzhènzi 門鎮子,
thus capturing Liáo Huì 廖惠.
However, Tíngruì 廷瑞 fled to Xīxiāng 西鄉 in Shǎnxī 陝西,
crossed the Thirty-Six Peaks of Hànzhōng 漢中,
and reached Dàbāshān 大巴山.
The government troops pursued and caught up,
and inflicted another great defeat upon them.
He then moved his forces to attack the Lúzhōu 瀘州 bandit Cáo Fǔ 曹甫,
and also sent people to invite and persuade them to submit.
Fǔ 甫 feigned compliance,
and had his younger brother Guǎn 琯 continue plundering as before.
Commander Lǐ Yìn 李蔭 beheaded Guǎn 琯,
whereupon the bandits moved to Jiāngjīn 江津,
divided into seven camps,
and were about to attack Chóngqìng 重慶.
Jùn 俊 dispatched native troops from Yǒuyáng 酉陽 and Bōzhōu 播州 to assist Yìn 蔭,
and on New Year's Day, they launched a surprise attack and destroyed four of their camps.
The bandits fled into civilian houses,
which were then burned, killing all of them.
Taking advantage of the victory, they attacked the main camp.
Commander Wāng Yáng 汪洋 and others fell into an ambush and died.
Yìn 蔭 advanced again,
fifteen lǐ from the bandits.
Fǔ 甫 came out with dozens of cavalry,
encountered Yìn's 蔭 troops,
and fled in defeat.
The government troops pursued the victory and surrounded them,
capturing or burning to death over two thousand.
Later,
Běnshù 本恕 and Tíngruì 廷瑞 were captured by Péng Shìlín 彭世麟, a native headman of Yǒngshùn 永順.
Jùn 俊 was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief [yòu dū yù shǐ 右都御史] for his merits.
Fǔ's 甫 accomplice Fāng Sì 方四, a fugitive, fled to Sīnán 思南,
and again attacked Nánchuān 南川 and Qíjiāng 綦江,
to threaten Lúzhōu 瀘州.
Jùn 俊 dispatched even more native troops,
ordering Vice Commissioners Hé Shān 何珊, Lǐ Yuè 李鉞, and others to defeat them and drive them away.
When the victory was reported,
an imperial decree bestowed praise and encouragement.
While Jùn 俊 was in the army,
he often disagreed with Grand Coordinator Hóng Zhōng 洪鍾.
He invariably prohibited the sons and younger brothers of favored eunuchs from falsely claiming military achievements.
Censor Yú Zī 俞緇 fled from the bandits,
while Vice Commissioner Wú Jǐng 吳景 died in battle.
Zī 緇 was ashamed,
and wanted to shift the blame to Jùn 俊,
so he impeached Jùn 俊 for repeatedly reporting head counts,
while the bandits were never completely eradicated;
and for ordering the digging of wells, destroying temples,
expelling monks,
and forcing them to become bandits.
Consequently, Jùn 俊 was severely reprimanded multiple times.
When Fāng Sì 方四 was defeated,
and the bandits were almost eradicated,
Jùn 俊 declined the promotion and rewards,
requesting to retire to his home with his old position.
An imperial edict forbade him from declining the rank,
but allowed him to retire.
Remonstrating officials repeatedly requested that he be kept,
but this was not granted.
When Jùn 俊 returned home,
the scholars and common people wept and saw him off.
This was in the eleventh month of the sixth year of Zhèngdé 正德 (1511).
When Shìzōng 世宗 ascended the throne,
he was appointed Minister of Works [gōngbù shàngshū 工部尚書],
and then transferred to Minister of Justice [xíngbù 刑部].
While on the way, he repeatedly cited illness,
but was not permitted to decline.
He then requested the emperor to draw close to scholarly officials,
rectify his heart to issue decrees,
and use simplicity as an example for the world.
He asked that what had been initially abolished by edict
should not be changed to undermine public opinion.
Upon arriving in the capital,
it happened that the summer lectures at the Classics Mat were suspended.
He cited the diligent study of the ancestors as a historical precedent to admonish the emperor.
Jùn 俊 was already seventy years old at this time,
and stayed in the imperial waiting room,
showing no intention of staying long.
He repeatedly spoke to the emperor about being close to high officials,
diligently studying the sagely teachings,
distinguishing heresies,
and economizing on expenses.
Whenever there was a major state policy,
he would always speak out frankly and boldly,
and people inside and outside the court admired his demeanor.
When the corruption of eunuch Gě Jǐng 葛景 and others came to light,
and they were impeached by remonstrating officials,
an imperial edict ordered the Directorate of Ceremonial [sīlǐ jiàn 司禮監] to investigate.
Jùn 俊 stated that if an inner court official violated the law,
and the judicial authorities could not interrogate him,
this would mean that the palace and the government were separate entities.
He requested that the case be handed over to the judicial authorities for public interrogation,
to demonstrate a fair and just rule.
When Grand Commissioner Liú Huī 劉暉 was imprisoned,
Jùn 俊 argued that according to the law on forming factions and cliques,
he was guilty of the same crime as Xǔ Tài 許泰,
and requested his execution to apologize to the world.
Liáo Péng 廖鵬, Liáo Kǎi 廖鎧, Qí Zuǒ 齊佐, and Wáng Huán 王瓛 were sentenced to death,
and repeated imperial edicts postponed their execution.
Jùn 俊 requested that they be executed immediately.
He also impeached Gǔ Dàyòng 谷大用 for occupying over ten thousand qǐng 頃 of civilian land.
None of these requests were granted.
Lǐ Yángfèng 李陽鳳, a family member of eunuch Cuī Wén 崔文, demanded a bribe from artisan Sòng Yù 宋鈺 but failed to get it,
and incited Wén 文 to beat him almost to death.
The case was sent to the Ministry of Justice for trial, but before a decision,
an imperial decree transferred it to the Commander of the Imperial Guard [zhènfǔ sī 鎮撫司].
Jùn 俊 detained the prisoner and refused to release him,
arguing strenuously but not being heeded.
The next day, he presented another memorial,
and the emperor angrily demanded an explanation.
Jùn 俊 said:
"The ancestors entrusted criminal cases to the judicial authorities,
and the apprehension of traitors and thieves to the Commander of the Imperial Guard.
Even after interrogation and conviction,
the case must still be handed over to the judicial authorities to determine the punishment.
There has never been a case where an undecided prisoner was taken away
and instead handed over to the interrogators.
Wén 文 had leaked secrets in the previous reign,
a crime for which execution is insufficient,
and now he again interferes with internal decrees.
I cannot bear to see the hundred and fifty years of the court's discipline
destroyed by such people."
The emperor, intimidated by his direct words,
then did not pursue the matter.
Jùn 俊, a venerable and virtuous man rising from the countryside,
maintained righteousness without avoiding suspicion.
After being repeatedly rebuffed,
he finally requested to retire.
An edict added the title Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent [tàizǐ tàibǎo 太子太保] to him,
and granted him post horses and attendants as per regulations.
Jùn frequently debated
the “Grand Rites” (dàlǐ),
and sided with Yáng Tínghé.
He once memorialized, stating that honoring one’s biological parents was an inescapable sentiment,
and an unalterable rite.
Consequently, he compiled ten items concerning events from Yáo and Shùn down to Sòng Lǐzōng,
and presented them.
When
the “Grand Rites”
were finally decided,
those who had offended were sometimes beaten to death.
In the autumn of the fourth year,
Jùn, from his sickbed, submitted a memorial stating:
“In ancient times, the punishment of flogging
was merely to inflict humiliation,
not to mutilate the body and cause death.
Nor was it applied to scholar-officials.
During the Chénghuà reign,
your servant still witnessed two or three officials being flogged in court.
They typically wore thick cotton-padded clothing,
with many layers of thick cloth wrapped around them.
Yet, they still lay critically ill,
recovering only after a long time.
During the Zhèngdé reign,
when the traitor Liú Jǐn usurped power,
he first ordered the removal of clothing,
leading to many deaths by flogging in the later years.
Your servant also observed that during the Chénghuà and Hóngzhì reigns,
only rebels, those spreading seditious rumors, and robbers were sent to the imperial prison (zhàoyù),
and only then were ordered to be beaten and questioned.
Other offenders were merely referred for questioning.
Now, to indiscriminately beat and question all is also not according to established practice.
Since last year, old officials have been dismissed and expelled almost entirely,
leaving the court offices empty.
I beg Your Sagely Majesty to take heed.
Those who have left should be recalled with courtesy,
and those who have not yet left should be comforted and retained.
Eminent virtues and respected figures like Luó Qīnshùn, Wáng Shǒurén, Lǚ Nán, and Lǔ Duó,
should be arranged to be placed by your side.
Your servant is old and sick, awaiting death,
with no other aspirations.
I dare to emulate the spirit of ancient valedictory memorials,
and respectfully express my humble devotion.”
The emperor merely referred it to the relevant department.
The next year,
when his illness became critical,
he again submitted a memorial urging the emperor to promote learning and filial piety,
appoint the worthy and accept remonstrance,
protect his body and guide harmony,
and also preemptively declined any posthumous honors.
He then died.
He was seventy-six years old.
One year later,
when the “Grand Canon of Human Relations” (Mínglún Dàdiǎn) was completed,
Jùn was posthumously implicated for having supported Yáng Tínghé,
his official post was stripped,
and his son Dá buried him with the rites of a scholar.
Jùn served four reigns,
offering strong remonstrance and daring to admonish,
advancing and retreating according to propriety,
maintaining his integrity from beginning to end.
In the early Lóngqìng reign,
his official post was restored,
he was granted the posthumous title of Junior Guardian (shàobǎo),
and posthumously named Zhēnsù.
Dá
was a successful candidate in the imperial examination in the ninth year of Zhèngdé.
He rose to the position of Nanjing Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Lángzhōng).
He was skilled in seal script (zhuànzhòu)
and capable of ancient prose.
Zhāng Fú
was from Jíshuǐ.
He was a successful candidate in the imperial examination in the eighth year of Chénghuà.
He successively served as Prefect of Fúzhōu and Sùzhōu,
known for his independence and fearlessness towards powerful officials.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
Jùn received a prominent promotion,
while Fú, being old, was not employed.
Wáng Shù pleaded on his behalf,
and he was specially granted a patent of appointment.
Jīn Xiànmín,
courtesy name Shùnjǔ,
was from Miánzhōu.
He was a successful candidate in the imperial examination in the twentieth year of Chénghuà.
He was appointed as an official for transmitting imperial decrees (xíngrén).
In the early Hóngzhì reign,
he was selected and appointed as a Censor (yùshǐ),
inspecting Yúnnán and Shùntiān,
and in both places, his integrity was notable.
He was dispatched as Vice Prefect of Tiānjīn,
and successively served as Provincial Surveillance Commissioner (ànchásǐ) of Húguǎng.
In the early Zhèngdé reign,
when Liú Jǐn was disturbing the government,
Xiànmín was retroactively accused of an inaccurate investigation of Tiānjīn land,
and, along with Governor Liǔ Yìngchén and others, was shackled and imprisoned in the imperial prison (zhàoyù),
then dismissed as a commoner.
Soon after,
he was again implicated in a Húguǎng matter,
imprisoned a second time,
and, after paying a ransom, returned home.
A year later,
he was again penalized for an inaccurate verdict in the case of Liú Dàolóng from Liúyáng,
and fined grain to be transported to the border.
After Liú Jǐn was executed,
he was reinstated as Provincial Surveillance Commissioner (ànchásǐ) of Guìzhōu.
He was promoted to Assistant Censor-in-Chief (qiāndū yùshǐ),
Governor (xúnfǔ) of Yánsuí,
and successively served as Nanjing Minister of Justice (Xíngbù Shàngshū).
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was summoned to be Left Censor-in-Chief (zuǒdū yùshǐ).
Lǐ Fèngyáng was sent to the Ministry of Justice,
Chéng Guì to the Censorate,
but both cases were changed to the imperial prison (zhàoyù).
Xiànmín strongly contended against this.
Afterward,
he was promoted to Minister of Justice (Xíngbù Shàngshū).
He insisted that the treacherous faction members Wáng Qīn and Wáng Quán should not be spared death.
None of his pleas were accepted.
Soon, he replaced Péng Zé as Minister of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū).
When five planets gathered in the constellation Yíngshì,
this omen indicated military matters.
Xiànmín therefore requested that imperial edicts be issued to all frontier defense officials to prepare for battle,
and also requested the appointment of worthy individuals, acceptance of remonstrance,
cessation of construction projects (tǔmù),
and removal of frivolous luxuries.
The emperor largely adopted his suggestions.
Xiànmín was upright and resolute by nature,
and held firm to his convictions.
Even if the emperor could not follow his advice,
he never yielded.
When the emperor first ascended the throne,
he dismissed all officials appointed through irregular channels from the previous reign.
Later,
after the eunuchs Qiū Fú and Pān Jié died,
an edict ordered that their younger brothers and nephews be appointed as Jin Yīwèi officials.
When the Grand Secretary of the Directorate of Ceremonial (sǐlǐ tàijiān) Zhāng Qīn died,
his household retainer Lǐ Xián was granted an inherited office.
When Xián died, the emperor again wanted to appoint his son Rú.
Xiànmín memorialized repeatedly,
but the emperor did not comply.
When Sultan Manṣūr of Turfan (Tǔlǔfān Sùtán Mǎnsù'ér) raided Sùzhōu,
Xiànmín was ordered to concurrently hold the position of Right Censor-in-Chief (yòudū yùshǐ) and be Commander-in-Chief of military affairs in the four garrisons of Shǎnxī.
By the time he reached Lánzhōu,
Governor Chén Jiǔchóu had already defeated the enemy.
Xiànmín again reported the victory.
Upon returning to the capital,
he resumed his departmental duties.
For his merits,
his family was granted an inherited Jin Yīwèi hundred-household position for generations.
Yú Xián,
a Jin Yīwèi hundred-household,
was the adopted son of the eunuch Tàihuáng.
He managed affairs through an imperial decree,
which the censorial officials disputed.
Xiànmín said:
“The ancestors had established precedents,
Emperor Xiào had prohibitions,
and Your Majesty had clear edicts upon ascending the throne.
Xián has no public service merit,
nor is he a son or relative of Tàihuáng.
To presumptuously usurp high office as a servant
violates and destroys the established institutions,
which is the greatest impropriety.
It is proper to heed the words of the censorial officials.”
This was not listened to.
Lǐ Quán and Wáng Bāngqí,
Jin Yīwèi deputy thousand-households, had been removed for abuses and excesses.
At this point, they endlessly petitioned to argue their case, which was sent to the ministry for re-deliberation.
Xiànmín said:
“Quán and others did not set foot on the battlefield but claimed top military honors,
and were not part of the public service but rapidly ascended to high ranks.
When Your Majesty ascended the throne,
over three hundred people were dismissed,
and the people rejoiced.
If, by any chance, an opening for undue favoritism reopens,
then all previous edicts will be meaningless,
and what limit will there be to future petitions?”
The emperor ultimately appointed Quán and others as probationary hundred-households.
Xiànmín again memorialized, saying:
“An order issued should be followed, not reversed.
Now, because of the petitions of petty men,
over ninety people are reinstated overnight,
pandering to private interests of those around you,
and undermining the laws of the ancestors.
I secretly regret this for Your Majesty.
Clear edicts forbade illicit connections for managing affairs,
yet vying for influence has already become a trend;
they forbade petitions based on similar precedents,
yet disturbances through petitions have already followed.
Who started this calamity
that continues to obstruct us to this day?
I hope that Quán and others will still be dismissed,
to quell public criticism
and avert heavenly omens.”
Censor Rèn Luò and others also made similar statements,
but were not heeded.
At that time, the General-in-chief (zǒngbīngguān) of Níngxià, Zhǒng Xūn (Zhǒng Xūn), bribed officials in the capital (Jīngshī).
Investigators caught his register,
and Xiàn Mín (Xiàn Mín)'s name was on it.
Attendant Cài Jīng (Cài Jīng) and Censor Gāo Shìkuí (Gāo Shìkuí) and others jointly impeached him,
so Xiàn Mín (Xiàn Mín) feigned illness and retired.
Two years later,
Bāng Qí (Bāng Qí) impeached former Minister (shàngshū) Péng Zé (Péng Zé),
and the charges implicated Xiàn Mín (Xiàn Mín).
He was arrested and imprisoned in the Ministry of Punishments (Xíngbù).
The judicial authorities impeached Xiàn Mín (Xiàn Mín) for being commanded to lead an expedition,
but before reaching the location,
he fabricated accomplishments and reported falsely,
losing the decorum of a high minister.
He ought to be stripped of his office and remain idle,
and his hereditary emolument should be abolished.
The emperor approved the decree.
Initially,
when the "Great Rites" (Dà Lǐ)
debate arose,
Xiàn Mín (Xiàn Mín) repeatedly joined court officials in submitting memorials to dispute it.
When they wept and remonstrated at the Zuǒshùnmén Gate,
he also joined Xú Wénhuá (Xú Wénhuá) in initiating it.
The emperor was displeased by this,
and he eventually incurred disfavor.
In the early Longqìng (Lóngqìng) reign,
he was posthumously honored and given a pension according to regulations.
Qín Jīn (Qín Jīn),
courtesy name Guóshēng (Guóshēng),
was a native of Wúxī (Wúxī).
He became a jinshì (jìnshì) in the sixth year of Hongzhi (Hóngzhì).
He was appointed as a Secretary (zhǔshì) in the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù),
and later became a Director (lángzhōng).
In the early Zhengde (Zhèngdé) reign,
he was promoted to Vice Provincial Education Commissioner (tíxué fùshǐ) of Henan (Hénán),
and then transferred to Right Administration Vice Commissioner (yòu cānzhèng).
While guarding Kāifēng (Kāifēng),
he defeated Zhào Suì (Zhào Suì) at Chénqiáo (Chénqiáo).
He successively served as Left and Right Provincial Administration Commissioner (zuǒ, yòu bùzhèngshǐ) of Shandong (Shāndōng).
After the devastation caused by bandits,
he and Governor (xúnfǔ) Zhào Huáng (Zhào Huáng) together consoled and cared for the people,
and the ravaged areas began to recover.
In the ninth year, he was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-chief (yòu fù dūyùshǐ)
and became Governor of Huguang (Húguǎng).
He memorialized to return all mountains, fields, lakes, and marshes occupied by the imperial princes' estates
to the government.
The surrendered bandits Hè Zhāng (Hè Zhāng) and Luó Dàhóng (Luó Dàhóng) rebelled again,
and he pacified them.
In Chēnzhōu (Chēnzhōu) and Guìyáng (Guìyáng), the Yao (Yáo) leader Gōng Fúquán (Gōng Fúquán) proclaimed himself king.
Qín Jīn (Qín Jīn) successively captured over eighty strongholds,
beheaded two thousand people,
and captured Gōng Fúquán (Gōng Fúquán) and his associates such as Liú Fúxīng (Liú Fúxīng).
For his merits,
his salary was increased by one grade,
and his son was granted a hereditary position as a Centurion (shì bǎihù) in the Imperial Bodyguard (Jǐnyīwèi),
but he firmly declined and his request was granted.
He entered the capital as Right Vice Minister of Revenue (Hùbù Yòushìláng).
When Shìzōng (Shìzōng) ascended the throne,
he was transferred to the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù).
Censors (yánguān) criticized Qín Jīn (Qín Jīn) for lacking discernment in judging people,
so he was again transferred to the Ministry of Revenue,
then moved to Left Vice Minister (zuǒ shìláng),
and oversaw ministry affairs.
The imperial relative by marriage, Shào Xǐ (Shào Xǐ), requested manors and fields.
Qín Jīn (Qín Jīn) cited ancestral regulations
and requested an investigation.
The emperor pardoned Shào Xǐ (Shào Xǐ)
and ordered the Censorate (Dūcháyuàn) to forbid such acts as per regulations.
An imperial edict from within the palace ordered that each imperial palace retain imperial estates (huángzhuāng),
and dispatched eunuchs (guānjiào) to oversee them.
Qín Jīn (Qín Jīn) said:
"During the flourishing period of the Western Han (Xīhàn) dynasty, imperial gardens and parks were distributed to the poor,
how can we now exploit the people to enrich the imperial family?
I beg to investigate those who illegally encroached upon land during the Zhengde (Zhèngdé) reign,
return all of it to its original owners,
and completely dismiss those who manage the estates."
The emperor praised his words
and immediately followed his suggestion.
In the second year of Jiajing (Jiājìng), he was promoted to Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū) of Nanjing (Nánjīng),
and led the officials in submitting a memorial which stated:
"Since Your Majesty's (Bìxià) succession to the throne,
you have illuminated virtue and curbed transgressions,
diligently strived for good governance,
and made no improper moves.
You ought to summon heavenly harmony,
yet disasters and misfortunes are frequently reported.
Why is this?
The Odes (Shī) say: 'There are few who have a good end,
though all have a good beginning.'
Upon Your Majesty's (Bìxià) enthronement, a single edict
established all regulations firmly,
and the empire eagerly anticipated perfect governance.
Recently, many things contradict the edicts,
all government departments fail to comply,
and the myriad people lose respect.
This shows that imperial edicts cannot be like the beginning.
At the beginning of your reign,
you dismissed the mediocre and the vacillating,
and appointed the experienced and venerable.
Recently, when the Grand Secretariat (Nèigé) drafts edicts, they are often altered from within,
and even when memorials are submitted,
only gentle words are returned.
This shows that appointing the worthy cannot be like the beginning.
At the beginning of your reign,
you listened to advice readily,
with requests made in the morning being answered by evening.
Recently, when matters concern imperial relatives by marriage or eunuchs (huànsì),
even if the Nine Ministers (Jiǔ Qīng) submit remonstrances,
and Censors (Kēdào) jointly memorialize,
it is always said, 'an imperial decree has already been issued.'
This shows that listening to advice cannot be like the beginning.
At the beginning of your reign,
all officials who were promoted through imperial favor or by requesting promotion in previous reigns
were thoroughly reformed.
Recently, imperial favors have been excessively lavish,
and enfeoffments and appointments frequently made.
This shows that cherishing official titles cannot be like the beginning.
At the beginning of your reign,
all treacherous factions and heinous criminals were handed over to the Three Judicial Offices (Sān Fǎ Sī).
Recently, they are often sent to the Garrison (Zhènfǔ).
This shows that upholding national laws cannot be like the beginning.
At the beginning of your reign,
you first ordered the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù) to reduce horse stable rations by half,
and also ordered Censors (Kēdào guān) to thoroughly audit the number of horses.
However, due to the words of eunuchs such as Yán Hóng (Yán Hóng),
the previous edict was suspended.
This shows that caring for the people's suffering cannot be like the beginning.
At the beginning of your reign,
you banished and expelled dharma kings (fǎwáng), sons of Buddha (fózǐ), national preceptors (guóshī), and Zen masters (chánshī).
Recently, fasts and rituals (zhāijiào) have been established in forbidden areas.
This shows that honoring the orthodox way cannot be like the beginning.
At the beginning of your reign,
your wisdom and vitality were abundant.
Recently, Your Sacred Person (Shènggōng) has not been well,
and your imperial countenance has not recovered.
This shows that conserving your spirit cannot be like the beginning.
The reason why early governance was clear and bright
was that policies originated from the public court,
and those close to the emperor did not interfere.
The reason why governance is now confused and muddied
is that policies reside with those close to the emperor,
and the outer court is unaware.
Indeed, governance cannot be absent from the court for a single day,
and power cannot be transferred to those close to the emperor for a single day.
What is meant by 'governance resides in the court'
does not necessarily mean that everything is decided solely by the emperor.
With trustworthy ministers as arms and legs,
and reliable officials as eyes and ears,
then the imperial prestige will be heavier than the Nine Tripods (Jiǔ Dǐng),
and the nation's stability more secure than Mount Tai (Tàishān).
Throughout history, emperors have controlled the empire
using only this method.
Otherwise, the power of the inner palace and outer government will be separated, leading to biased trust,
and the closeness of imperial women and eunuchs will obscure judgment,
superficially called 'total control,'
but the hilt of the great sword (Tài'ē) will have truly shifted downwards."
The memorial was sent to the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù).
Minister (shàngshū) Wāng Jùn (Wāng Jùn) strongly urged the emperor to adopt it,
and it was reported.
Soon after, he was transferred to the Ministry of War (Bīngbù).
When Sūn Jiāo (Sūn Jiāo) left,
Qín Jīn (Qín Jīn) was summoned to be Minister of Revenue (Hùbù Shàngshū).
The emperor wished to bestow an honorific title on his biological father, Emperor Xìan (Xìan Dì).
Qín Jīn (Qín Jīn) and other court officials knelt before the palace gate to remonstrate,
and also, with Hé Mèngchūn (Hé Mèngchūn) and others, enumerated the errors in Zhāng Cōng (Zhāng Cōng)'s suggestions.
When the imperial mother's册 (cè) was to be conferred,
Qín Jīn (Qín Jīn) and Zhào Huáng (Zhào Huáng) again did not attend,
and the emperor repeatedly questioned and reprimanded them.
Qín Jīn (Qín Jīn) was an easygoing person.
When he served as an official,
he consistently maintained integrity and honesty.
In the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù),
he was especially diligent for the nation.
Princess Yǒngfú (Yǒngfú Chánggōngzhǔ) requested land in Bǎodǐ (Bǎodǐ) and Wǔqīng (Wǔqīng),
which was somewhat reduced due to Qín Jīn (Qín Jīn)'s words.
The land in Fǔníng (Fǔníng) and Shānhǎi (Shānhǎi) that was granted to Duke Wèi (Wèi Guógōng) Xú Dá (Xú Dá)
returned to the government upon Xú Dá (Xú Dá)'s death.
Duke Dìngguó (Dìngguó Gōng) Guāng Zuò (Guāng Zuò) requested it,
but Qín Jīn (Qín Jīn) firmly refused.
Attendant (gěishìzhōng) Huáng Zhòng (Huáng Zhòng) and Censor (yùshǐ) Zhāng Héng (Zhāng Héng) and others argued in succession,
and Qín Jīn (Qín Jīn) and others again spoke out,
and only then was the request granted.
There were several thousand artisans and soldiers in the various imperial workshops and bureaus.
Eunuch Liáng Jiàn (Liáng Jiàn) requested that they be sent to ministries to mine for gold, jade, pearls, and stones,
but Qín Jīn (Qín Jīn) firmly remonstrated against it
and was not listened to.
Treacherous individuals like Lù Jùn (Lù Jùn) requested three hundred thousand salt licenses from the two Huai (Huái) regions.
The emperor granted it.
Qín Jīn (Qín Jīn) strongly argued against it,
repeatedly incurring the emperor's displeasure.
In the sixth year, in spring, he requested to retire on the grounds of an inspection,
and was granted a relay post and provisions as per regulations.
Five years after his return,
recommendations for him did not cease,
so he was appointed to the Ministry of Revenue in Nánjīng.
He submitted a memorial detailing six measures beneficial to the people.
Soon after, he was summoned to serve as Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shàngshū)
and was given the additional title of Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shǎobǎo).
The Emperor, along with ministers such as Zhāng Fújìng and Lǐ Shí píng,
considered Jīn worthy,
but somewhat disliked his old age.
After several months in office,
he was given the additional title of Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Tàibǎo)
and transferred to the Ministry of War (Bīngbù) in Nánjīng.
A year later, he retired and returned home.
In the twenty-third year, he died,
aged seventy-eight.
He was posthumously granted the title of Junior Guardian (Shǎobǎo)
and given the posthumous name Duānmǐn.
His grandson, Zhù,
was appointed to the Secretariat Drafter (Zhōngshū Shèrén) from among the students (zhūshēng).
When Grand Secretary (Dàxuéshì) Gāo Gǒng incurred the Emperor's displeasure
and hastily left the capital (Jīngshī),
all his protégés avoided him,
but Zhù alone saw him off more than a hundred *lǐ* away.
When Wú Zhōngxíng memorialized against Zhāng Jūzhèng for "usurping affection" (duóqíng),
he was beaten with a staff and imprisoned in the imperial prison.
Zhù brought a physician to attend to his medicine,
thereby offending Jūzhèng,
and was transferred to be a Judge (Shěnlǐ) in the Lǔ Princely Establishment.
Soon after, he was dismissed after a "faux inspection."
Zhào Huáng,
courtesy name Tíngshí,
was from Ānfú.
When he was young, he accompanied his father to his official post,
and fell into a river but did not die.
As he grew older,
while walking on the road,
he found some lost gold
and returned it all to its owner.
He passed the imperial examination as a *jìnshì* in the third year of Hóngzhì (1490),
and was appointed Secretary (Zhǔshì) in the Ministry of Works.
He was transferred to the Ministry of War,
and successively served as Assistant Director (Yuánwàiláng).
He was sent out to be Prefect (Zhīfǔ) of Jǐnán.
Corrupt officials manipulated documents
and had been a long-standing bane for years.
Huáng selected honest commoners and taught them laws and regulations,
finding over twenty competent individuals,
and then expelled the corrupt officials and replaced them with these people.
The commoners' pastures of Hán had long been registered as official land;
he recruited people to tenant them.
The Dé Princely Establishment requested them by memorial,
but Huáng investigated and returned them to the commoners.
After seven years,
his administrative achievements were widely recognized.
In the early years of Zhèngdé,
he was promoted to Vice Prefect (Fǔchéng) of Shùntiān Prefecture.
Before he could take office,
Liú Jǐn, who disliked Huáng,
implicated him in the case of Circuit Inspector (Xúnfǔ) Zhū Qīn,
arrested and imprisoned him in the imperial prison,
and stripped him of his rank.
When Jǐn was executed,
he was reinstated.
He was promoted to Vice Censor-in-Chief (Yòu Qiāndū Yùshǐ)
and served as Circuit Inspector of Xuānfǔ.
Soon after, he was transferred to Shāndōng.
There were hundreds of *lǐ* of riverbed land;
he encouraged migrant people to cultivate it and exempted them from rent.
Tibetan monks requested to levy taxes on it to fund their vegetarian meals (zhāiliáng),
and the Emperor permitted it,
but Huáng strenuously argued for exemption and succeeded.
Qǔfù was destroyed by bandits,
and the Quèlǐ temple-forest was in the wilderness.
Huáng requested to move the county seat to Quèlǐ,
and it was granted.
He was promoted to Right Vice Minister of Works (Gōngbù Yòu Shìláng)
and oversaw river administration.
Due to border alarms, he was transferred to manage military preparations in the capital region (Jīfǔ).
After the situation settled,
he was ordered to provide famine relief to the prefectures of Shùntiān,
and then returned to assist in the ministry.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Left Vice Minister (Zuǒ Shìláng)
and took charge of the ministry.
He cut down on eunuch burial expenses and the material costs for the Directorate of Imperial Accoutrements (Yùyòng Jiān),
and abolished the annual levy of iron and brick fees from the imperial wine, vinegar, and noodle bureaus, which amounted to tens of thousands of silver taels annually.
In the first year of Jiājìng (1522), he was promoted to Minister (Shàngshū).
Liú Jǐn had established the Xuánmíng Palace,
squandering hundreds of thousands of funds.
After Jǐn's death,
unscrupulous individuals offered it to be an imperial estate (huángzhuāng).
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
he ordered it to be given to the people,
but later an imperial decree from within the palace ordered it to be restored to its former status.
Huáng stated that an edict issued several months ago was suddenly changed,
showing untrustworthiness to the world;
the Emperor immediately approved his report.
At that time, the Rénshòu and Qīngníng Palaces were being renovated,
and funds were insufficient.
Huáng then requested that these, along with various houses at Shíjǐngshān, be sold off to provide funds,
thus avoiding burdening the people,
and the Emperor approved it.
Censor (Gěishìzhōng) Xú Jǐngsōng and others argued that the imperial edict had allowed it to be returned to the people,
and that officials should not sell it themselves,
and impeached Huáng.
Huáng submitted a memorial to defend himself,
and also exposed other misdeeds of Jǐngsōng.
Censor (Yùshǐ) Zhāng Pénghàn said that Huáng was slandering censorial officials,
which was unbecoming of a grand minister.
The Emperor reprimanded Pénghàn for taking Jǐngsōng's side,
and he was eventually dismissed.
His colleague Chén Jiāng was also reprimanded for impeaching Huáng
and sought to resign.
Censor (Gěishìzhōng) Zhāng Qiáo said that Huáng's single action led to the dismissal of two censorial officials,
which greatly harmed the national prestige.
Minister (Shàngshū) Péng Zé again memorialized that Qiáo was mistaken,
and Qiáo defended himself a second time;
the Emperor mediated between them twice.
An edict ordered the construction of a residence for the Empress's father, Chén Wànyán,
estimated to cost 600,000 *liǎng*.
Huáng delayed it.
Wànyán complained to the Emperor,
who imprisoned two officials, a Director (Lángzhōng) and an Assistant Director (Yuánwàiláng), in the imperial prison.
Huáng stated:
"These two officials are not involved,
please punish your servant instead."
The Emperor did not listen.
Afterward, arguments for their release came one after another,
and Wànyán felt uneasy,
and again requested their pardon.
The two were released,
and the construction cost was also greatly reduced.
In the third year,
the eunuch in charge of incense at the Xiǎnlíng mausoleum said that its design was too small
and requested to rebuild it
to match the other mausoleums at Tiānshòushān.
Huáng stated that the mausoleum's design corresponded to the mountains and waters,
making it difficult to generalize;
the Emperor accepted his words.
Later,
the Emperor wanted to relocate Xiǎnlíng,
but Huáng opposed it,
so it was dropped.
An edict ordered the construction of the Yùdé Palace
and the Jǐngfú and Ānxǐ Palaces.
Huáng requested to wait until the Rénshòu Palace was completed
before discussing these matters,
but the Emperor did not permit it.
Soon after,
due to portents of disaster, he reiterated his previous request,
and the Emperor finally yielded to him,
and also halted the Rénshòu construction project.
A Realized Person's Mansion (Zhēnrénfǔ) was to be built in Jiāngxī,
and manufacturing was to be supervised in Shǎnxī;
both involved dispatching imperial envoys (zhōngshǐ),
and Huáng memorialized against both.
When the Imperial Ancestral Temple (Shìmiào) was being constructed,
the Ministry of Revenue significantly cut down on the materials allocated by the eunuchs.
The Emperor questioned Huáng about this,
and Huáng stated that the accumulated surplus funds from the previous construction of the Qiánqīng and Kūnníng Palaces
were sufficient for the new project,
and the Emperor then approved.
Huáng served as Minister for six years,
during which time the Emperor was in the early years of his reign,
eager to rectify and prune,
and eunuchs dared not interfere;
thus, he was able to carry out his duties effectively.
Later, his persistent arguments
led to many powerful favorites envying him,
and the Emperor's favor also gradually waned.
Huáng had always been renowned alongside Qín Jīn.
He requested to retire on the grounds of an inspection,
and retired together with Jīn.
Court officials requested that he be retained,
but it was not permitted,
and he was granted a relay post and provisions as per custom.
Huáng was capable and decisive,
and full of wisdom and foresight.
When matters were complicated and entangled,
others would stare at each other in astonishment,
but Huáng would resolve them immediately.
After he left,
people vied to recommend him.
In the eleventh year, he was summoned to resume his former office,
but died before taking it up.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Tàibǎo)
and given the posthumous name Zhuāngjìng.
Zōu Wénshèng,
courtesy name Shímíng,
was from Gōng'ān.
He became a *jìnshì* in the 6th year of Hóngzhì.
He was appointed as a Supervising Secretary in the Office of Personnel.
Hán Chóng, the Grand Coordinator of Liáodōng, impeached the Resident Eunuch Liáo Qǐ.
Wénshèng, along with Director Yáng Màorén, investigated and confirmed his crimes,
and he was demoted to an incense attendant at Chánglíng.
When the Wūyán Sān Wèi repeatedly harassed the border,
Wénshèng returned and presented six strategies for their control.
Minister Liú Dàxià greatly approved of them,
and they were passed down to the border officials.
Soon after, he was sent out to audit the grain reserves in Liǎngguǎng.
When Cén Jùn, the native official of Sī'ēn, clashed with Cén Měng of Tiánzhōu,
Wénshèng stated:
"Tiánzhōu is a screen for Guǎngxī,
and Lǐ Mán is a bulwark for Tiánzhōu.
Assistant Administration Commissioner Wǔ Qīng, having received heavy bribes from Jùn,
used a scheme to kill Mán, brewing trouble and disorder.
Cén Yè, a consultant serving in the Secretariat of Edicts,
is a close relative of Jùn,
and he mediated for him,
leaking our secret plans.
I request that these two be executed first,
before proceeding with the punitive expedition."
Yè had internal support,
and the emperor did not heed the advice.
Qīng was soon dismissed due to a performance review.
At the beginning of Zhèngdé,
he successively served as a Supervising Secretary in the Office of Revenue,
then was appointed Prefect of Báodìng,
and subsequently promoted to Administration Commissioner of Fújiàn on the left.
In the 11th year, he was appointed Vice Censor-in-Chief on the right to patrol Guìzhōu.
The Miáo leaders Āpáng, Ājiē, and Āgé of Qīngpíng declared themselves kings.
Grand Coordinator Cáo Xiáng mobilized native troops from Yǒngshùn and Báojìng to suppress them,
but was soon impeached and dismissed.
Āpáng and others occupied Mount Xiānglú,
and various guards such as Xīnglóng, Piānqiáo, Píngyuè, Xīntiān, and Lónglǐ all suffered from their depredations.
When Wénshèng arrived,
he dispatched orders for troops from Chuān and Hú to assist in the suppression,
and used Guìzhōu troops to assault the Pàomù stockade,
capturing Āgé.
When the Chuān and Hú troops arrived,
they reached the foot of the mountain.
The mountain walls were sheer,
with only five small paths,
and the rebels had erected barricades everywhere.
They could not overcome them with an uphill assault,
so they constructed siege towers as high as the cliffs.
Under cover of night rain, they climbed the cliffs,
dismantled the barricades, and burned the houses.
The rebels fled to the rear mountain,
occupying the absolute summit.
The government troops seized the opportunity, using ladders and vines to ascend,
and thus captured Āpáng,
and all the remaining rebels were pacified.
He then moved his forces to suppress the Black Miáo in various stockades such as Lóngtóu, Dūlí, Dūlán, Dūpéng, Mìxī, Dàzhī, and Mǎluó,
killing and receiving surrenders in countless numbers.
For his merits,
his salary was increased by one grade,
and his son was granted the hereditary position of a Hundred-Household in the Imperial Bodyguard,
but he firmly declined.
When Chén Cōng and others of Mángbù rebelled,
he suppressed and defeated them.
Féng Lún of Zhòng'ān, a native official in Sìchuān, had a grudge against Yáng Hóng of Kǎilǐ.
When Hóng died,
Lún incited residual Miáo to engage in revenge killings,
encroaching into Guìzhōu territory.
Wénshèng dispatched Consultant Cài Cháo to Bōzhōu
to supervise Pacification Commissioner Yáng Bīn in pacifying the situation.
He requested the re-establishment of the Ānníng Pacification Office,
with Hóng's son succeeding to the post,
and also recognized Cháo's merits.
Minister Wáng Qióng deemed Cháo's actions an abuse of power,
and rejected it.
Shortly thereafter,
Wénshèng was transferred to serve in the Nánjīng Censorate.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was summoned to serve as Vice Minister of Revenue (Left and Right),
then promoted to Censor-in-Chief of Nánjīng on the right,
and soon after changed to Minister of Revenue.
In the 6th year of Jiājìng,
when Minister of Revenue Qín Jīn was dismissed,
Wénshèng was summoned to replace him.
His first memorial proposed eleven matters concerning salt administration and currency law.
Wénshèng was known for his integrity and caution,
appearing as if incapable.
He, Sūn Jiāo, Qín Jīn, and Zhào Huáng were all praised as virtuous elders.
After more than a year,
due to his age,
he submitted another memorial requesting retirement.
Upon his death, he was posthumously granted the title of Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent
and given the posthumous name Zhuāngjiǎn.
Liáng Cái,
courtesy name Dàyòng,
was from the Right Guard of Jīnwú in Nánjīng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the 12th year of Hóngzhì.
He was appointed Magistrate of Déqīng,
where he was diligent and astute, achieving remarkable administrative feats.
At the beginning of Zhèngdé,
he was promoted to Principal of the Ministry of Justice,
then changed to Censor.
He was appointed Prefect of Jiāxīng,
and then transferred to Hángzhōu.
As land taxes varied conventionally,
Cái adjusted them, making them lighter or heavier as appropriate,
and established a uniform system.
He was promoted to Assistant Administration Commissioner of Zhèjiāng on the right,
then advanced to Surveillance Commissioner.
When Resident Eunuch Bì Zhēn conspired with Chén Háo,
intending to surrender the entire city to him,
Cái and Inspecting Censor Zhāng Jìn seized Zhēn,
depriving him of his troops and guards.
He soon left due to mourning.
At the beginning of Jiājìng,
he was reinstated and appointed to Yúnnán.
When native officials had been feuding and killing each other for years,
Cái summoned their chieftains and said:
"Your crime deserves death.
But I will spare you now,
and you shall atone with cattle and sheep."
A Censor was surprised by the leniency,
but Cái said:
"This is sufficient.
If we press too hard, rebellion will ensue."
The chieftains, who had been wearing armor and awaiting an uprising,
stopped when they heard there would be no further demands.
He successively served as Administration Commissioner of Guìzhōu, and Administration Commissioner of Guǎngdōng (Left and Right).
When officials and people paid taxes, he ordered them to weigh and measure themselves,
and officials were not allowed to interfere.
At that time, among all Administration Commissioners in the empire,
two were most renowned for their integrity:
Cái and Yáo Mò.
In the 6th year, he was appointed Vice Censor-in-Chief on the right,
to patrol Jiāngxī.
After only two months,
he was summoned to serve as Vice Minister of Justice on the left.
Soon after, he was transferred to the Ministry of Revenue,
and then replaced Zōu Wénshèng as Minister.
From a local official to a high-ranking minister,
it took less than two years.
He felt deeply indebted for the favors received,
and became even more dedicated to his duties.
He reported to the emperor:
"Your subject estimates that last year's revenue was only 1.3 million *liǎng*,
while expenditures amounted to 2.4 million.
Furthermore, tax collection is stagnant,
border expenses are without limit,
and many exemptions are granted due to famine.
How can the national finances be managed?
Upon detailed examination of the malpractices: first, imperial relatives;
second, military officials;
third, redundant officials;
fourth, redundant expenses;
fifth, arrears.
I request that court officials be convened to plan and propose measures."
Consequently, three matters were proposed for imperial relatives and military officials respectively,
and all other expenditures were strictly curtailed.
The emperor approved all of them.
Only the proposal to suspend half the salary for military officials living in idleness
was not accepted by the emperor.
Expenses were greatly reduced,
and national resources became abundant.
When Eunuch Mài Fú requested full collection of rent from pasture lands,
Cái disagreed.
Vice Minister Wáng Yuè investigated the estates of meritorious relatives and imperial in-laws,
stating that limits should be set according to their ranks.
Cái memorialized:
"In the Chéng Zhōu era, officials were granted salaries and land,
with salaries derived from the land,
not having additional land beyond their regular salaries.
Currently, the salaries of meritorious relatives and imperial in-laws already exceed their due,
and their requests for land often reach tens of millions [of *mǔ*].
I request that this be strictly prohibited.
Except for special grants,
one-third of their land should be retained [by the state] for sacrificial rites."
The emperor ordered that even previously granted lands be investigated,
and all illegally encroached extra lands be returned to the people.
Thus, powerful families no longer dared to make extravagant requests.
For garrison farms in the capital region,
Censors were in charge of supervision.
During the Zhèngtǒng era, Assistant Surveillance Commissioners replaced them,
whose authority was weaker,
and the administration of garrison farms gradually declined.
Cái requested that Censors be reinstated.
Censor Guō Hónghuà stated that the amount of land in the empire had halved compared to the early days of the dynasty,
and a general cadastral survey should be conducted.
Cái feared disturbance,
and requested that the responsible authorities merely be ordered to clarify records,
and only those whose records were difficult to verify should have their land measured *mǔ* by *mǔ*.
The emperor approved all of these.
His mother died, and he left office.
When the mourning period ended,
he returned to his former post.
When Fán Jìzǔ (樊繼祖), the Grand Coordinator of Dàtóng (大同), requested additional military provisions,
Cái (材) said:
"The annual provisions for Dàtóng are seventy-seven myriad and odd taels of silver,
with additional emergency disbursements totaling tens of thousands,
already several times more than in the past.
With daily increases and monthly expansions,
the silver in the imperial granary is insufficient to supply even one garrison,
let alone the Nine Frontiers."
Jìzǔ repeatedly requested but was denied.
A proposal was made to establish new regulations (kāi shìlì 開事例),
which were then submitted to the Boards of Revenue and War for implementation.
At this time, the two palaces and seven imperial tombs were being constructed,
employing seventy thousand京jīng troops.
Guō Xūn (郭勛) requested monthly rations and winter clothes for them.
Cái said this was not according to custom,
and if granted,
would cost forty-five myriad taels of silver annually.
Moreover, winter clothes were customarily taken from the imperial treasury,
not a matter for the Board.
Xūn was angered,
and impeached Cái for impeding public affairs.
The Emperor reprimanded Cái,
and ultimately complied with Xūn's memorial.
Xūn then proposed three more matters:
requesting to open mines to assist the construction,
that all surplus salt be transported to the border,
and that grain transport soldiers be allowed to carry goods.
Cái deliberated,
but did not implement them all,
which further angered Xūn.
When Cái first served in the Board of Revenue,
the Emperor was diligent in governance,
and worked hard to eliminate long-standing abuses,
often adopting Cái's suggestions.
But by this time, he repeatedly clashed with powerful favorites,
and was not content,
so he requested a transfer to the south.
He was impeached by Investigating Censor Zhōu Gǒng (周珫),
and handed over to the Board of Civil Office.
Minister Xǔ Zàn (許讚) and others requested to retain him.
The Emperor was displeased,
and ordered them to jointly submit a statement with Cái.
Cái admitted his guilt and was pardoned,
but Zàn and others were punished with salary deductions.
Cái thereby lost the Emperor's favor.
After six years as Minister,
he was ordered to retire.
Earlier,
the Prince of Huī (徽王), who held a manor, had a lawsuit with his tenants.
Cái requested to abolish the manor-holder system,
ordering the officials to collect rent for the Prince,
which was approved.
The Prince memorialized that it was inconvenient,
and the Emperor again agreed with him.
Cái had already left,
but Vice Minister Táng Zhòu (唐冑) and others insisted on the initial edict.
The Emperor was greatly angered,
and also blamed Cái.
He was ordered to reside at home as a Right Vice Minister without duties,
while Zhòu's salary was docked,
and junior officials were sent to the imperial prison.
The next year,
Lǐ Tíngxiāng (李廷相), Minister of the Board of Revenue, was dismissed.
The Emperor remembered Cái's integrity and diligence,
and many high officials also recommended him,
so he was recalled to his former post,
and granted the additional title of Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent.
He thrice managed the national finances,
maintaining his integrity and public spirit as before,
and the Emperor's affection for him was also very deep.
That autumn,
when metropolitan officials were being reviewed,
he was specially appointed to supervise the process.
When there were major cases that could not be decided,
he was also ordered to concurrently manage the affairs of the Board of Punishments.
The Emperor sighed, saying:
"If I had twelve Ministers like Cái,
I would have no worries about the empire."
Major construction projects frequently arose,
employing forty-six thousand soldiers from outer garrisons and rotating service units.
Guō Xūn recorded those who did not arrive,
and compelled them to pay silver to hire workers,
whose provisions were the same as the rotating service units.
Tíngxiāng had previously measured and distributed some,
but Cái firmly refused to grant more.
Xūn impeached Cái,
and the Emperor ordered the provisions to be supplied.
Xūn then claimed the army was insufficient,
and registered runaway soldiers' cloth and cotton to be converted into silver for recruiting workers.
Cái said:
"There are now over forty thousand metropolitan rotating service soldiers,
which is already sufficient.
There is no need to use this as an excuse to deplete the national treasury."
The Emperor agreed with his memorial.
Xūn was further angered,
and impeached Cái for altering old regulations.
Earlier,
dragon's saliva incense was required for sacrificial altars,
but Cái did not present it in time,
which the Emperor held against him.
Consequently, Cái was accused of seeking fame and hindering affairs,
and dismissed from his post to reside at home without duties.
He returned home,
and soon died,
at the age of seventy-one.
In the early Lóngqìng (隆慶) era,
he was posthumously granted the title of Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent,
and given the posthumous name Duānsù (端肅).
In the middle years of the Jiājìng (嘉靖) era,
while other high officials might flatter the emperor to gain favor,
Cái alone remained unyielding,
and for this reason was ultimately not tolerated.
After Cái left,
border provisions and national expenditures became severely distressed.
Shìzōng (世宗) then sighed, saying:
"If Cái were here,
it would not have come to this."
Liú Lín (劉麟),
courtesy name Yuánruì (元瑞),
was originally from Ānrén (安仁).
His family had for generations served as Assistant Company Commanders of the Guǎngyáng (廣洋) Guard in Nánjīng (南京),
and thus settled there.
He was learned and skilled in writing,
and along with Gù Lín (顧璘) and Xú Zhēnqīng (徐禎卿), was called
"the Three Talents of Jiāngdōng (江東)."
He became a *jìnshì* in the ninth year of Hóngzhì (弘治).
When Censor Páng Pàn (龐泮) and others were imprisoned,
Lín, along with his fellow *jìnshì* Lù Kūn (陸崑), submitted a memorial to save them.
He was appointed Principal of the Board of Punishments,
and promoted to Supernumerary Director.
He reviewed prisoners in the capital region,
and reversed three hundred ninety-odd wrongful convictions.
In the early Zhèngdé (正德) era,
he was promoted to Director,
and then served as Prefect of Shàoxīng (紹興) Prefecture.
Liú Jǐn (劉瑾) resented Lín for not paying him respects,
and after only five months,
he fabricated minor pretexts from Lín's previous prisoner reviews,
and dismissed him to commoner status.
The gentry and common people collected money for him, but he refused it.
They built a Small Liú Shrine for him, pairing him with Liú Chǒng (劉寵) of the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
and he consequently lived in Húzhōu (湖州).
He, Wú Wǎn (吳琬), Shī Kǎn (施侃), Sūn Yīyuán (孫一元), and Lóng Ní (龍霓) were known as
"the Five Hermits of Húnán (湖南)."
When Jǐn was executed,
Lín was reinstated and appointed to Xī'ān (西安).
Upon the death of his father,
he enjoyed the mountains and waters of Wúxīng (吳興),
and brought his father's coffin there for burial,
thus residing in Húzhōu.
He was appointed Left Administration Vice Commissioner of Shǎnxī (陝西),
supervising grain storage.
When Grand Censor Dèng Zhāng (鄧璋) commanded the army,
he proposed increasing taxes to fund provisions,
but Lín strongly opposed it.
It happened that the people of Shǎnxī went to the imperial court to complain,
and the proposal was dropped.
Soon after, he was transferred to Judicial Commissioner of Yúnnán (雲南), but pleaded illness and returned home.
In the early years of the Jiājìng reign,
he was summoned and appointed Tàipú Qīng.
He was promoted to Yòufù Dūyùshǐ,
and was made governor of the six prefectures of Báodìng.
The eunuch Gěng Zhōng, who was garrison commander at Zǐjīng, frequently acted with impunity.
Lín impeached and memorialized against him.
He requested the exemption of the tax on the military agricultural colonies of the three garrisons of Tiānjīn,
and to disburse funds from the treasury to provide monthly stipends for the troops of the three garrisons of Héjiān.
The outstanding taxes were to be collected to repay this,
and all these requests were granted.
The emperor then issued an edict to the Hùbù,
stating that any unpaid military stipends, both within the capital and in the provinces,
should all be made up.
He again resigned due to illness.
He was recalled as Dàlǐ Qīng,
and appointed Gōngbù Shàngshū.
When the imperial guards lacked uniforms and footwear,
Luò Ān, the commander of the Jǐnyīwèi, requested that they be provided according to the precedent of the Hóngkuī Army.
Lín firmly opposed it.
An imperial decree ordered that silver be distributed for them to make their own,
and thereafter, a regular provision would be made every five years.
All funds and goods of the Four Bureaus were stored in the large vault in the back hall.
Bureau officials often embezzled when making disbursements and receipts.
Lín requested that a special bureaucrat (lángguān) be appointed to oversee it.
The emperor praised this idea,
and subsequently named it
"Jiéshèn Kù" (Thrifty and Prudent Vault).
Later,
he presented fourteen measures for saving money,
and eliminated the fraudulent expenditure of funds by the various bureaus and offices of the Imperial Household Department.
The powerful eunuchs greatly resented this.
When the Xiǎnlíng mausoleum project was completed,
all who had served in it hoped for official appointments.
Lín merely proposed rewards,
which further increased the resentment of the petty officials.
At that time, the emperor heeded the words of remonstrating officials
and suspended various levies and labor services inside and outside the capital.
Lín, by official letter, suspended the weaving projects in Zhèjiāng, Sūzhōu, and Sōngjiāng,
and the imperial robes and clothing were included in the suspension.
The eunuch Wú Xūn reported this,
and Lín was then forced to retire.
After a long time,
the Xiǎnlíng palace halls leaked due to rain.
Lín was retroactively censured
and stripped of his office.
Lín was pure, upright, and unyielding in his integrity.
When in office, he did not compromise.
While serving in the Gōngbù,
he saved money and was prudent with expenses for the court,
serving for barely over a year before being dismissed.
He resided in Nántǎn, in the suburbs,
composing poetry for his own amusement.
The prefect built a platform for him,
and ordered a hall to be constructed,
where he finally had a place to rest and wander.
He remained at home for over thirty years,
and court officials frequently recommended him.
In his later years, he liked living in a multi-story building,
but lacked the means to construct one.
He hung a basket sedan chair from a beam,
and would recline in it,
calling it the "Shénlóu" (Divine Chamber).
Wén Zhēngmíng painted a picture and presented it to him.
He died at the age of eighty-seven.
He was posthumously granted Tàizǐ Shàobǎo
and given the posthumous name Qīnghuì.
Jiǎng Yáo,
courtesy name Cuìqīng,
was from Guī'ān.
He passed the imperial examination in the twelfth year of Hóngzhì (1499).
He was appointed Xíngrén.
During the Zhèngdé reign,
he served successively as Yùshǐ in both capitals.
He presented seven articles on current abuses,
among which he said:
"The Imperial Arsenal Bureau has six thousand military artisans,
supervised by two eunuchs.
Now the number has increased to over sixty,
each occupying thirty artisans.
Other bureaus are similar,
how then can the ranks of the army not be depleted?"
He also said:
"The officials appointed by imperial decree (chuánfèng guān) and the excessively recruited junior officers (jiàowèi) and brave soldiers (yǒngshì) should all be reformed.
Although Liú Jǐn has been executed,
power still rests with the eunuchs."
An imperial decree ordered an inquiry,
and also stated:
"From now on, anyone who agrees with Yáo's proposals
need not submit another memorial."
Soon after, he was dispatched to serve as Zhīfǔ of Jīngzhōu.
He built the Huángtán embankment.
He was transferred to Yángzhōu.
When Wǔzōng made his southern tour and arrived in Yángzhōu,
Yáo merely provided imperial supplies and necessities,
offering no gifts.
All the favored courtiers were enraged.
Jiāng Bīn wished to seize the residence of a wealthy citizen to make it his Wēiwǔ Fùjiàngjūn's mansion.
Yáo firmly refused.
Bīn confined Yáo in an empty house to humiliate him,
and threatened him with the bronze mace bestowed by the emperor,
but Yáo was not intimidated.
It happened that the emperor caught a large fish while fishing,
and jokingly said it was worth five hundred gold.
Bīn immediately handed it to Yáo and demanded its value.
Yáo presented his wife's hairpins, earrings, and dresses,
saying:
"The treasury has no money;
this is all your servant possesses."
The emperor smiled and dismissed him.
The prefecture originally had the Qiónghuā Temple,
and an edict ordered the acquisition of the Qiónghuā (瓊花, Viburnum macrocephalum).
Yáo stated that since Sòng Huīzōng and Qīnzōng were taken north,
this flower had become extinct,
and there was nothing to offer now.
Another imperial decree ordered the collection of rare exotic objects.
Yáo fully explained that they were not products of Yángzhōu.
The emperor said:
"Is ramie white cloth
also not a product of Yángzhōu?"
Yáo had no choice
but to present five hundred bolts.
At that time,
the powerful favorites, seeing Yángzhōu's prosperity,
made all sorts of outrageous demands.
Were it not for Yáo,
the people would have been even more severely distressed.
When the imperial retinue returned,
Yáo escorted them to Báoyìng.
The eunuch Qiū Dé used iron chains to bind Yáo;
he was released only after several days,
and ultimately escorted the retinue to Línqīng before returning.
When the people of Yángzhōu saw Yáo,
they were all moved to tears.
Upon his transfer to Shǎnxī Cāncèng,
people vied to contribute funds to build a shrine and worship him,
and his reputation greatly soared thereafter.
In the early Jiājìng reign,
he successively served as Húguǎng, Jiāngxī Zuǒ, and Yòu Bùzhèngshǐ,
and as Yòufù Dūyùshǐ, he governed Hénán.
The emperor ordered Guì È and others to review the retention or dismissal of governors,
and Yáo was ordered to return home and await new deployment.
Later,
he was successively promoted to Gōngbù Shàngshū.
When the projects in the four suburbs were completed,
he was granted the additional title of Tàizǐ Shàobǎo.
When the Western Park palaces were completed,
the emperor held a banquet.
Seeing Yáo and Wáng Shízhōng seated outside,
he ordered them moved inside the hall,
and moved the imperial relatives to the right of the hall to make way for Yáo,
saying:
"Favoring relatives is not as good as honoring the worthy."
Such was his high regard for Yáo.
At that time, construction projects were frequent,
with annual expenses amounting to millions.
Yáo's plans always pleased the emperor,
and he frequently received rewards.
He left office due to mourning.
After a long time,
he was recalled from Nánjīng Gōngbù Shàngshū
to serve in the capital's ministry (Běibù).
When the emperor traveled to Chéngtiān,
Yáo accompanied him.
In the capital's construction projects,
the labor force consisted of capital troops,
many of whom were secretly taken by powerful families.
By this time, major construction projects were frequent,
and commoners were recruited annually for labor,
costing over two million.
Yáo spoke about this,
and requested the suspension of non-urgent projects.
The troops hidden by powerful families were all brought out,
and the cost of recruitment was greatly reduced.
He retired due to old age.
Yáo was upright, clear-minded, and incorruptible.
After returning,
he lived secluded in a humble alley.
He formed a literary and wine society with Grand Secretaries Liú Lín and Gù Yìngxiáng,
wandering among the Xiànshān mountains.
He died at the age of eighty-nine.
He was posthumously granted Tàizǐ Tàibǎo
and given the posthumous name Gōngjìng.
Wáng Tíngxiāng,
courtesy name Zǐhéng,
was from Yífēng.
He was known for his literary talent from a young age.
He passed the imperial examination in the fifteenth year of Hóngzhì (1502),
was selected as a Shùjíshì,
and appointed Bīngkē Jǐshìzhōng.
He left office due to mourning.
In the early Zhèngdé reign,
after completing his mourning period, he arrived in the capital.
Liú Jǐn charged him with a crime,
and he was demoted to Pànguān of Bózhōu,
then transferred to Zhīxiàn of Gāochún.
Zhào was appointed Censor.
He submitted a memorial stating:
"Great bandits have risen everywhere,
and the generals are unable to pacify them.
This is because the generals' authority is too light,
they cannot resist the enemy,
military movements are disorganized,
and they cannot hold strategic passes.
Wherever the bandits go,
the villagers offer oxen and wine,
and some even actively assist them.
Bandits have the power of life and death,
while the generals do not;
hence, the soldiers do not fight with their lives.
It is advisable to grant them discretionary power,
and those who retreat must be beheaded.
The Hénán region is flat and vast,
making it easy for bandits to flee.
The Shānxī region is rugged and dangerous,
yet they are allowed to penetrate deeply;
this is the fault of the generals.
If troops are stationed at the fords of the Yellow River,
preventing them from moving west,
and Jǐngxíng and Tiānjǐng are held in divisions,
preventing them from moving east,
and the commander-in-chief presses them with a large army,
then the bandits will be trapped in both advance and retreat,
and can be captured without a fight."
The Emperor severely reprimanded the governors and other officials,
and fully adopted Zhào's proposals.
Later,
he was sent out to inspect Shǎnxī.
He curbed and suppressed the eunuch defender Liáo Táng.
He was falsely accused.
At that time, he had already been appointed Supervisor of Schools in the capital region,
but was arrested and imprisoned in the imperial prison,
then demoted to Assistant Magistrate of Gànyú.
He was repeatedly promoted to Surveillance Commissioner of Sìchuān,
then Vice Envoy of Shāndōng,
always in charge of supervising schools.
In the second year of Jiājìng, he was commended for his outstanding administration,
and again promoted to Right Administration Commissioner of Shāndōng.
As Right Vice Censor-in-Chief, he pacified Sìchuān,
and suppressed the Mángbù bandit Shā Bǎo.
Soon after, he was summoned to manage the Censorate.
He successively served as Left and Right Vice Ministers of War,
then promoted to Minister of War of Nánjīng,
participating in military affairs.
Initially, there was an imperial edict
to reduce the number of express boats for tribute.
The defending eunuch Lài Yì again requested an increase.
Tíngxiàng requested that the number of boats be determined by the weight and importance of the items,
and greatly reduced those ordered by imperial decree after Xuāndé that were not based on ancestral institutions.
The officials guarding the five passes of Lóngjiāng, Dàshèng, Xīnjiāng, Púzi, and Jiānghuái, profited by inspecting and taxing.
Those in Ānqìng and Jiǔjiāng extorted bribes during spring and autumn inspections.
Tíngxiàng requested to abolish all of these.
The hayfields and reed tax silver were largely encroached upon by eunuchs Yáng Qí and Bǔ Chūn, and the Duke of Wèi Xú Péngjǔ.
At Tíngxiàng's request,
Qí and Chūn were arrested and interrogated,
and Péngjǔ's stipend was confiscated.
In the third month, he was appointed Left Censor-in-Chief.
He submitted a memorial stating that the defending authority of Nánjīng was too great,
and should not be held by the hereditary office of the Duke of Wèi.
The Supervising Secretary Zēng Biàn also stated this,
so Péngjǔ's military command was removed.
After two years,
he was promoted to Minister of War concurrently with his former office,
and became Supervisor of the Training Divisions,
still managing the Censorate.
After two full terms,
he was promoted to Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
When commoners in the capital region stole trees from the Tiānshòushān Imperial Tombs,
the Circuit Censor Yáng Shàofāng applied the law for stealing items for the great sacrifice to the gods, which prescribed beheading.
Tíngxiàng stated:
"Items for the great sacrifice to the gods
refer to sacrificial vessels and curtains used within the sacred space.
The law for stealing tomb trees
only prescribes one hundred blows with the heavy stick
and three years of penal servitude.
To disregard the specific law
is not just punishment."
This displeased the Emperor,
and he was fined one month's salary.
When the Emperor was about to visit Chéngtiān,
Tíngxiàng and other high officials admonished him,
but he did not accept it.
Upon returning from accompanying the Emperor,
as nine years had passed,
he was promoted to Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
When lightning struck the Fèngxiān Hall,
Tíngxiàng stated:
"Only after human affairs are rectified can the ways of Heaven be harmonious;
only after senior officials set an example can junior officials be honest.
Now, integrity is not upheld,
bribery is rampant.
In previous reigns, there were still secret night bribes,
but now they are openly seized in broad daylight.
If senior officials are corrupt, junior officials will all imitate them.
If capital officials are greedy, external officials will have no fear.
My duty is to uphold the imperial discipline,
but I cannot eradicate these evils.
I beg to be dismissed first."
He used this to criticize ministers Yán Sōng and Zhāng Zàn and their ilk.
The Emperor merely instructed him to remain.
Initially,
Tíngxiàng requested that censors be evaluated and recalled based on six articles.
The Emperor ordered him to elaborate on what was incomplete,
and compile it into a disciplinary code.
He then took what Zhāng Fúqìng and Wāng Hóng had presented,
and newly decided a total of fifteen articles to submit,
all of which were approved for implementation.
When the nine ancestral temples suffered a disaster,
an imperial edict was issued for self-reflection and reform.
The Emperor then commanded Tíngxiàng, saying:
"The duty of a circuit censor is very important.
You have been the Chief Censor for many years.
Since establishing the six articles,
not a single person has been evaluated or dismissed.
Now, you should earnestly reflect and reform."
Tíngxiàng responded with fear and gratitude.
Tíngxiàng held the position of Chief Censor for the longest time,
possessing great prestige and authority.
As Supervisor of the Training Divisions,
he worked with Guō Xūn,
but hesitated in his dealings,
unable to make any significant rectifications.
The Supervising Secretary Lǐ Fènglái and others criticized powerful nobles for seizing commoners' profits.
The memorial was sent to the Censorate.
Tíngxiàng ordered the censors of the five city districts to verify the facts,
but they delayed for over forty days.
The Supervising Secretary Zhāng Yǔnxián then impeached Tíngxiàng for favoritism and disrespect towards the Emperor.
While the Emperor was questioning and reprimanding him,
Tíngxiàng reported what the censors had verified,
that Guō Xūn's encroachments were the most extensive.
The Emperor ordered Xūn to make his own report,
whereupon a multitude of people impeached Xūn.
Xūn again incurred the Emperor's wrath by delaying in receiving an imperial order,
and was imprisoned.
Tíngxiàng was accused of forming factions and flattering,
and was dismissed as a commoner.
He died three years later.
Tíngxiàng was learned and fond of discussion,
known for his classical scholarship.
Regarding astrology, cartography, music theory, the Hétú and Luòshū, and the writings of Zhōu Dùn-yí, Shào Yǒng, Chéng Hào/Yí, and Zhāng Zài,
he offered arguments and refutations,
but his views were often eccentric.
In the early years of Lóngqìng,
his official position was restored,
and he was posthumously granted Junior Guardian,
with the posthumous title Sùmǐn.
The encomium states:
"Qiáo Yǔ, guarding Nánjīng,
was calm and composed,
yet strictly vigilant internally;
he can be said to have been capable of handling great affairs.
Observing Yǔ and Sūn Jiāo and others upholding integrity and public duty,
earnestly admonishing the court,
their intention was to block avenues for favoritism,
and benefit the nation's governance.
