Although they obtained imperial trust and exercised administration,
they could not compare to Jiǎn Yì and Xià Yuánjí.
Yet their purity, strictness, and incorruptibility,
and faultless conduct,
did not yield much to their predecessors.
Jiǎng Yáo, as Minister,
his achievements were diminished by his governorship.
Wáng Tíngxiàng, managing the Censorate,
his vigor was not fully manifested.
Perhaps this was due to the times."
Collation Notes:
Biographies, Volume 83: Wáng Shǒurén (Jì Yuánhēng)
Wáng Shǒurén,
courtesy name Bó'ān,
a native of Yúyáo.
His father, Huá,
whose courtesy name was Déhuī,
became a *jìnshì* as the first-place graduate in the 17th year of the Chénghuà reign (1481).
He was appointed Compiler.
During the Hóngzhì reign,
he successively rose to Grand Secretary and Junior Supervising Secretary.
Huá possessed a dignified bearing,
and served in the lecture hall the longest,
receiving much favor from Emperor Xiàozōng.
When Lǐ Guǎng was in high favor,
Huá lectured on the *Dàxué Yǎnyì*,
and when he reached the section about Lǐ Fǔguó and Empress Zhāng of Tang gaining power by manipulating the emperor,
he made his points very incisively.
The Emperor ordered a palace eunuch to bestow food upon him as a reward.
In the early years of the Zhèngdé reign,
he was promoted to Left Vice Minister of Personnel.
Because Shǒurén offended Liú Jǐn,
he was sent out as Minister of Personnel of Nánjīng,
but was dismissed from office due to an incident.
Shortly after, due to a minor error in the *Huìdiǎn*,
he was demoted to Right Vice Minister.
When Jǐn was defeated,
he was restored to his former position,
but passed away not long after.
Huá was filial by nature.
His mother, Cén, passed away at over a hundred years old.
Huá was already over seventy,
yet still slept on straw and ate only vegetables,
which scholars greatly praised.
Shǒurén was born after fourteen months in the womb.
His grandmother dreamt that a divine being descended from the clouds, carrying a child,
and so he was named Yún.
At five, he could not speak.
A strange person caressed him,
and renamed him Shǒurén,
whereupon he began to speak.
At fifteen,
he visited Jūyōng and Shānhǎiguān.
At that time, he ventured beyond the frontier,
freely observing the strategic terrain of mountains and rivers.
At twenty, he passed the provincial examination,
and his learning greatly advanced.
He became increasingly fond of discussing military matters,
and was also skilled in archery.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the twelfth year of the Hóngzhì reign (1499).
He was dispatched to supervise the funeral of the former Earl Wáng Yuè of Wēiníng.
Upon his return, the court was urgently debating the northwest frontier,
and Shǒurén submitted eight proposals.
Soon after, he was appointed Director of the Bureau of Punishments.
He judged prisoners north of the Jiāng River,
but returned home pleading illness.
He was reappointed Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs.
In the winter of the first year of Zhèngdé (1506),
Liú Jǐn arrested Dài Xiǎn and over twenty other Investigating Censors from Nánjīng.
Shǒurén bravely submitted a memorial to save them.
Jǐn was enraged,
and Shǒurén was flogged forty times in court
and demoted to Postmaster of Lóngcháng in Guìzhōu.
Lóngcháng was a place of dense mountains and thickets,
inhabited by a mix of Miáo and Liáo people.
Shǒurén adapted to their customs and guided them with his teachings.
The indigenous people rejoiced,
and together they cut down trees to build a house
to shelter Shǒurén.
When Jǐn was executed,
Shǒurén was moderately transferred to be Magistrate of Lúlíng.
He had an audience with the emperor,
and was promoted to Director of the Bureau of Punishments of Nánjīng.
Minister of Personnel Yáng Yīqīng changed his position to Director of the Bureau of Scrutiny and Review.
He was repeatedly promoted to Department Director of the Bureau of Evaluation,
then elevated to Junior Minister of the Grand Court of Imperial Sacrifices of Nánjīng,
and subsequently transferred to Minister of the Court of State Ceremonials.
Minister of Military Affairs Wáng Qióng had long admired Shǒurén's talent.
In the eighth month of the eleventh year (1516), he was promoted to Vice Censor-in-Chief on the Right,
and appointed Grand Coordinator of Nán and Gàn.
At this time,
bandits were rising like swarms of bees in the southern regions.
Xiè Zhìshān occupied Héngshuǐ, Zuǒxī, and Tǒnggāng,
while Chí Zhòngróng occupied Líntóu.
They all proclaimed themselves kings,
and together with Chén Yuènóng from Dàyǔ, Gāo Kuàimǎ from Lèchāng, Gōng Fúquán from Chēnzhōu, and others,
they plundered prefectures and counties.
And the bandits Zhān Shīfù and others from Dàmào Mountain in Fújiàn also rose up.
The former Grand Coordinator Wén Sēn feigned illness and fled.
Zhìshān joined with the Lèchāng bandits to plunder Dàyǔ,
and attacked Nánkāng and Gànzhōu.
Wú Bīn, the Sub-prefectural Magistrate of Gàn County, died in battle.
When Shǒurén arrived,
he knew that many of his subordinates were informants for the bandits.
So he called an old, cunning clerk and questioned him.
The clerk trembled and dared not conceal anything,
so Shǒurén pardoned his crime
and ordered him to spy on the bandits,
so that no movement of the bandits went unknown.
Thereupon, he sent despatches to Fújiàn and Guǎngdōng to assemble troops,
and first attacked the Dàmào Mountain bandits.
In the first month of the following year (1517),
he commanded Vice Commissioner Yáng Zhāng and others to defeat the bandits at Chángfù Village,
forcing them to Xiànghú Mountain.
Commander Tán Huán and County Sub-magistrate Jǐ Yōng died in battle.
Shǒurén personally led elite troops to camp at Shàngháng.
He feigned a retreat,
then unexpectedly struck,
breaking over forty strongholds in succession,
capturing and beheading over seven thousand.
Commander Wáng Kǎi and others captured Shīfù.
He submitted a memorial stating that his authority was too light
to command his officers and soldiers effectively,
and requested to be granted a banner and tally,
to supervise military affairs,
and to act expediently.
Minister Wáng Qióng memorialized to approve his request.
Thereupon, he reformed the military system: twenty-five men formed a *wǔ* (squad),
with a junior corporal in each *wǔ*;
two *wǔ* formed a *duì* (platoon),
with a chief corporal in each *duì*;
four *duì* formed a *shào* (company),
with a chief in each *shào*,
assisted by two auxiliary chiefs;
two *shào* formed a *yíng* (battalion),
with an officer in each *yíng*,
assisted by two staff advisors;
three *yíng* formed a *zhèn* (division),
with a partial general;
two *zhèn* formed a *jūn* (army),
with a vice general.
All were appointed as needed on the field,
not by imperial decree;
vice generals and below
could mutually punish and manage.
In the seventh month of that year, he advanced his troops to Dàyǔ.
Zhìshān seized the opportunity to launch an urgent attack on Nán'ān.
Prefect Jì Xué defeated him.
Vice Commissioner Yáng Zhāng and others also captured Yuènóng alive and returned.
Then a campaign was planned to attack Héngshuǐ and Zuǒxī.
In the tenth month,
Grand Commander Xǔ Qīng, Prefect Xíng Xún of Gànzhōu, and Magistrate Wáng Tiānyǔ of Níngdū each led a force to converge on Héngshuǐ.
Xuè, together with Garrison Commander Jiá Wén, Prefect Táng Chún of Tíngzhōu, and County Sub-magistrate Shū Fù, each led a force to converge on Zuǒxī.
Prefect Wǔ Wéndìng of Jí'ān and Magistrate Zhāng Jiǎn of Chéngxiāng blocked their escape.
Shǒurén himself was stationed at Nánkāng,
thirty *lǐ* from Héngshuǐ.
He first dispatched four hundred men to ambush the bandit lair's vicinity,
then advanced his main force to press them.
As the bandits were engaging in battle,
banners were raised on both mountains.
The bandits were greatly alarmed,
believing that the government troops had already razed their lair,
and thus scattered.
Seizing the victory, they captured Héngshuǐ.
Zhìshān and his confederate Xiāo Guìmó and others all fled to Tǒnggāng.
Zuǒxī was also broken.
Shǒurén, seeing Tǒnggāng's dangerous fortifications,
moved his camp to nearby ground,
and issued a proclamation explaining the consequences of resistance or surrender.
Bandit leaders Lán Tíngfèng and others were terrified.
Seeing the envoy arrive, they were greatly pleased,
and set a date for surrender on the first day of the second winter month.
However, Xún and Wéndìng had already braved the rain and stormed the dangerous passes.
The bandits formed a battle line obstructed by water.
Xún charged forward and fought,
while Wéndìng and Jiǎn emerged from the right.
The bandits were suddenly defeated and fled,
only to be defeated again by Chún's troops.
All the armies broke Tǒnggāng.
Zhìshān, Guìmó, and Tíngfèng surrendered, bound by their own hands.
In total, eighty-four strongholds were broken,
and over six thousand were captured or beheaded.
At that time, Grand Coordinator Qín Jīn of Húguǎng also defeated Fúquán.
A thousand of his confederates suddenly arrived,
but the various generals captured and executed them.
Thereupon, Chóngyì County was established at Héngshuǐ
to control the various Yáo groups.
Returning to Gànzhōu, they planned to attack the Líntóu bandits.
Initially,
when Wáng Shǒurén suppressed Shīfù,
the bandits Lú Kē, Zhèng Zhìgāo, and Chén Yīng from Lóngchuān all requested to surrender.
When he later campaigned against Héngshuǐ,
the bandit leader Huáng Jīncháo from Lìtóu also surrendered with five hundred men,
but Zhòngróng alone had not yet submitted.
After Héngshuǐ was defeated,
Zhòngróng finally sent his younger brother Zhòng’ān to submit,
but he strictly prepared for battle and defense.
He deceitfully claimed that Kē and Zhìgāo
were his enemies
and were planning to attack him,
hence his preparations.
Wáng Shǒurén pretended to tie up Kē and others with a staff,
but secretly sent Kē’s younger brother to gather troops and wait,
and then ordered his own troops to disperse.
At the beginning of the year, he extensively displayed lanterns and music.
Zhòngróng was both trusting and suspicious.
Wáng Shǒurén bestowed upon him seasonal gifts
and enticed him to enter and express gratitude.
Zhòngróng led ninety-three men to encamp on the training ground,
and he himself, with a few men, entered to pay respects.
Wáng Shǒurén reprimanded them, saying:
“Are you not all my people?
Encamping outside,
do you suspect me?”
He led them all into the Xiángfú Temple
and generously provided them with food and drink.
The bandits were overjoyed and surprised,
feeling even more secure.
Wáng Shǒurén kept Zhòngróng to watch the lanterns and music.
On the third day of the first lunar month, a grand banquet was held.
Armored soldiers were ambushed at the gate.
When the bandits entered,
they were successively captured and executed.
Wáng Shǒurén himself led his troops to the bandit strongholds,
successively breaking the upper, middle, and lower Lì settlements,
beheading and capturing over two thousand.
The remaining bandits fled to Jiǔlián Mountain.
The mountain range stretched for several hundred *lǐ*,
steep and impossible to attack.
So, he selected seven hundred brave men to wear bandit clothing
and rush to the foot of the cliff,
where the bandits invited them up.
The government troops advanced and attacked,
striking from both inside and outside,
capturing and slaying all without exception.
He then established Hépíng County in Xiàlì,
stationed a garrison, and returned.
From then on, the region was greatly pacified.
Initially,
the court deliberated that the bandit forces were strong
and dispatched troops from Guǎngdōng and Húguǎng to jointly suppress them.
Wáng Shǒurén submitted a memorial to stop this,
but it was too late.
After Tǒnggāng was destroyed,
the Húguǎng troops finally arrived.
And when Lìtóu was pacified,
Guǎngdōng had not yet received the official dispatch.
Wáng Shǒurén’s troops were all civil officials and minor officers and commanders,
yet he pacified major bandits of several decades,
astonishing those near and far, who regarded him as a god.
He was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief (Yòu Fù Dū Yùshǐ),
and granted a hereditary position as a Hundred-Household Commander (Bǎihù) of the Jǐnyī Guard (Jǐnyīwèi),
and then further promoted to Vice Thousand-Household Commander (Fù Qiānhù).
In the sixth month of the fourteenth year, he was ordered to investigate the rebellious army in Fújiàn.
While traveling to Fēngchéng, Prince Níng Chén Háo rebelled.
The county magistrate, Gù Bì, informed him.
Wáng Shǒurén immediately hastened to Jí’ān,
and with Wǔ Wéndìng, conscripted soldiers and provisions,
prepared weapons and boats,
issued a communiqué exposing Chén Háo’s crimes,
ordering magistrates and prefects to lead their officials and soldiers to serve the emperor.
Censor-in-Chief (Dū Yùshǐ) Wáng Màozhōng,
Compiler (Biānxiū) Zōu Shǒuyì,
Vice Commissioners (Fùshǐ) Luó Xún and Luó Qīndé,
Director (Lángzhōng) Zēng Zhí,
Censors (Yùshǐ) Zhāng Áosān and Zhōu Lǔ,
Reviewing Secretary (Píngshì) Luó Qiáo,
Assistant Prefect (Tóngzhī) Guō Xiángpéng,
Jìnshì scholar Guō Chípíng,
and demoted Post Station Masters (Yìchéng) Wáng Sī and Lǐ Zhōng,
all joined Wáng Shǒurén’s army.
Censors (Yùshǐ) Xiè Yuán and Wǔ Xīrú returned from Guǎngdōng,
and Wáng Shǒurén kept them to record merits.
He then gathered the crowd and deliberated, saying:
“If the bandits exit the Yangtze River and sail eastward downstream,
then the Southern Capital (Nándū) cannot be preserved.
I wish to delay them with a scheme,
and then there will be no trouble for another ten days or so.”
So he sent many
spies, and issued communiqués to prefectures and counties, stating:
“Grand Coordinators (Dūdū) Xǔ Tài and Xì Yǒng will lead border troops,
and Grand Coordinators (Dūdū) Liú Huī and Guì Yǒng will lead capital troops,
each with forty thousand,
advancing by both land and water.
Wáng Shǒurén of Nángàn, Qín Jīn of Húguǎng, and Yáng Dàn of Liǎngguǎng will each lead their respective forces, totaling one hundred and sixty thousand,
to directly attack Nánchāng.
Any local officials failing to provide supplies wherever they go
will be judged by military law.”
He also sent a sealed letter in wax to the false chancellors Lǐ Shìshí and Liú Yǎngzhèng,
expressing their sincerity in returning to the country,
and ordering them to incite Chén Háo to dispatch his troops eastward early,
and then let spies leak this information.
Chén Háo indeed became suspicious.
He consulted with Lǐ Shìshí and Liú Yǎngzhèng,
who both urged him to swiftly advance to Nánjīng to claim the throne.
Chén Háo became even more suspicious.
After more than ten days, he scouted and learned that no troops from inside or outside the capital had arrived,
and then realized that Wáng Shǒurén had deceived him.
On the first day of the seventh month, Rénchén (壬辰), he left Prince Yíchūn Gǒngchén (拱●) to guard the rear,
and coerced sixty thousand of his followers,
attacking and capturing Jiǔjiāng and Nánkāng,
exiting into the Great River,
and approaching Ānqìng.
Wáng Shǒurén was greatly pleased to hear that Nánchāng had few troops
and hurried to Zhāngshù Town.
Prefects Dài Dérú of Línjiāng, Xú Lián of Yuánzhōu, Xíng Xún of Gànzhōu,
Commander-in-Chief (Dū Zhǐhuī) Yú ēn,
Assistant Prefects (Tōngpàn) Hú Yáoyuán and Tóng Qí of Ruìzhōu, Zōu Hǔ of Fúzhōu, Tán Chú of Ānjí,
Judicial Commissioners (Tuīguān) Wáng Wěi and Xú Wényīng,
Magistrates (Zhīxiàn) Lǐ Měi of Xīngàn, Lǐ Jí of Tàihé, Wáng Miǎn of Wàn’ān, Wáng Tiānyǔ of Níngdū,
each came with troops to rendezvous,
totaling eighty thousand men,
and declared as three hundred thousand.
Some requested to save Ānqìng,
but Wáng Shǒurén said:
“Not so.
Now Jiǔjiāng and Nánkāng are already guarded by the bandits.
If we go beyond Nánchāng to confront them on the river,
the troops from these two prefectures will cut off our retreat,
which means we will be attacked from front and rear.
It is better to directly attack Nánchāng.
The bandits’ elite forces have all gone out,
leaving its defenses weak.
Our army is newly assembled and high in morale,
and will surely break through in attack.
When the bandits hear that Nánchāng has fallen,
they will certainly lift the siege to save it.
If we ambush them in the lake,
there will be no victory we cannot achieve.”
The crowd said,
“Excellent.”
On Jǐyǒu (己酉), they reached Fēngchéng,
with Wǔ Wéndìng as vanguard,
first sending the Magistrate of Fèngxīn, Liú Shǒuxù, to attack their hidden troops.
In the middle of the night on Gēngxū (庚戌),
Wǔ Wéndìng’s troops reached Guǎngrùn Gate,
and the defending soldiers were startled and dispersed.
At dawn on Xīnhài (辛亥),
all the armies climbed with ladders and ropes,
captured Gǒngchén (拱●) and others,
and many palace women burned themselves to death.
The soldiers somewhat engaged in killing and looting.
Wáng Shǒurén executed over ten violators of military orders,
pardoned those who were coerced,
pacified the officials and common people,
and comforted the imperial clan members,
whereupon the people’s hearts were pleased.
After two days,
Wáng Wéndìng, Xún, Lián, and Dérú were dispatched, each leading elite troops to advance by separate routes,
while Yáo Yuán and others were ordered to set up ambushes.
Zhū Chénháo indeed returned his troops from Ānqìng.
On the Yǐmǎo day, they met at Huángjiādù.
Wáng Wéndìng engaged their vanguard,
and the rebels pressed forward, seeking advantage.
Xún circled around to the rebels' rear and pierced through their center.
Wáng Wéndìng and Ēn capitalized on this.
Lián and Dérú spread out as two wings, dividing the rebel forces,
and Yáo Yuán's ambush was sprung.
The rebels were utterly routed,
retreating to defend Bāzìnǎo.
Zhū Chénháo was terrified,
and deployed all troops from Nánkāng and Jiǔjiāng.
Wáng Shǒurén dispatched the Prefects of Fúzhōu, Chén Huái, and Ráozhōu, Lín Chéng, to take Jiǔjiāng,
and Zēng Yú of Jiànchāng, and Zhōu Cháozǔo of Guǎngxìn, to take Nánkāng.
On the Bǐngchén day, they fought again,
and the government troops retreated.
Wáng Shǒurén beheaded those who retreated first.
All the armies fought to the death,
and the rebels were again greatly defeated,
retreating to defend Qiáoshè,
where they linked boats into a square formation,
and brought out all their gold and treasures to reward the soldiers.
The next day,
as Zhū Chénháo was holding court with his ministers in the morning,
the government troops arrived unexpectedly.
They loaded small boats with firewood,
and, taking advantage of the wind, set them ablaze,
burning his auxiliary boats.
Zhū Chénháo's consort, the Lóu氏, and others all drowned themselves in the water.
Zhū Chénháo's boat ran aground in the shallows;
in haste, he switched boats and fled.
The troops under Wáng Miǎn pursued and captured him.
Shì Shí, Yǎng Zhèng, and the surrendered investigating censor, Yáng Zhāng, among others, were all taken captive.
Nánkāng and Jiǔjiāng also fell.
In total, it took thirty-five days to pacify the rebels.
When news of the revolt reached the capital,
the high ministers were shocked and fearful.
Wáng Qióng declared loudly:
"Wáng Bó'ān resides upstream from Nánchāng;
he will surely capture the rebel."
By this time,
a report of victory indeed arrived.
The Emperor had already personally led an expedition,
styling himself as the "Mighty and Martial Grand General" (Wēiwǔ Dà Jiāngjūn),
leading tens of thousands of valiant soldiers from the capital and border southwards.
He appointed Hǔ Tái, Earl of Ānbiān, as Deputy General,
who, together with the Grand Eunuch Zhāng Zhōng, Supervising Military Affairs, and the General for Pacifying Rebels, Left Censor-in-Chief Liú Huī, commanded several thousand Imperial troops,
ascending the river
to Nánchāng.
The Emperor's favorite eunuchs had previously colluded with Zhū Chénháo.
When Wáng Shǒurén first submitted the memorial about Zhū Chénháo's rebellion,
he stated:
"Those who covet the throne are not only Níng Wáng alone;
I request that treacherous sycophants be dismissed to win back the hearts of the heroes of the realm."
All the favored eunuchs resented this.
After Zhū Chénháo was pacified,
they mutually envied Wáng Shǒurén's achievement.
Moreover, fearing that Wáng Shǒurén would expose their crimes to the Emperor,
they competed to spread rumors,
claiming that Wáng Shǒurén had initially colluded with Zhū Chénháo,
and, fearing the enterprise would fail,
only then raised an army.
They also wanted him to release Zhū Chénháo into the lake,
to await the Emperor's personal capture.
Wáng Shǒurén, before Zhāng Zhōng and Hǔ Tái arrived,
first captured Zhū Chénháo
and set off from Nánchāng.
Zhāng Zhōng and Hǔ Tái, using the Imperial Edict of the Mighty and Martial Grand General, intercepted him at Guǎngxìn.
Wáng Shǒurén did not comply,
but took a shortcut to Yùshān,
submitting a memorial requesting to present the captive
and asking the Emperor to stop his southern expedition.
The Emperor did not permit it.
Upon reaching Qiántáng, he met Grand Eunuch Zhāng Yǒng.
Zhāng Yǒng was in charge of supervising and advising on secret military affairs,
ranking above Zhāng Zhōng and Hǔ Tái,
and had previously been on good terms with Yáng Yīqīng;
he had eliminated Liú Jǐn,
for which he was praised by the realm.
Wáng Shǒurén met Zhāng Yǒng at night,
lauding his wisdom,
and then eloquently spoke of Jiāngxī's exhaustion and distress,
unable to bear the disruption of the imperial army.
Zhāng Yǒng deeply agreed,
saying:
"My coming here
is to protect His Sacred Majesty,
not to seek personal glory.
Your great achievement,
I know it,
but things cannot be handled straightforwardly."
Wáng Shǒurén then entrusted Zhū Chénháo to Zhāng Yǒng,
and personally went to Jīngkǒu,
intending to pay respects at the imperial encampment.
Upon hearing the order to be巡撫 Jiāngxī,
he returned to Nánchāng.
Zhāng Zhōng and Hǔ Tái had already arrived first,
resenting the loss of Zhū Chénháo.
Thus, they allowed the imperial troops to offend Wáng Shǒurén,
some calling him by name and insulting him.
Wáng Shǒurén was not moved,
but treated them with even greater kindness.
He gave medicine to the sick,
coffins to the dead,
and when he encountered a funeral procession on the road,
he would always stop his carriage to console them for a long time before leaving.
The imperial troops said, "Director-General Wáng loves us,"
and no one offended him again.
Zhāng Zhōng and Hǔ Tái said:
"The Níng princely establishment was the richest in the realm;
where are its current stores?"
Wáng Shǒurén replied:
"Zhū Chénháo at that time gave all of it to important people in the capital,
promising internal support;
the records can be checked."
Zhāng Zhōng and Hǔ Tái had previously accepted bribes from Zhū Chénháo,
and were intimidated, not daring to speak further.
Later,
they looked down upon Wáng Shǒurén as a mere scholar,
and pressured him to shoot arrows.
He slowly rose,
fired three shots, and hit the target three times.
The imperial troops all cheered,
and Zhāng Zhōng and Hǔ Tái became even more disheartened.
It happened to be the Winter Solstice.
Wáng Shǒurén ordered residents to offer sacrifices in their alleys,
and then
to visit graves and weep.
At that time, due to the recent chaos,
wails of sorrow shook the wilderness.
The imperial troops had been away from home for a long time,
and upon hearing this, none could help but weep and long to return home.
Zhāng Zhōng and Hǔ Tái had no choice but to withdraw their forces.
When they saw the Emperor,
together with the Recorder of Merits Censor Zhù Xù and Censor Zhāng Lún, they slandered Wáng Shǒurén in a hundred ways,
only Zhāng Yǒng consistently protected him.
Zhāng Zhōng openly declared before the Emperor:
"Wáng Shǒurén will surely rebel;
try summoning him,
and he will surely not come."
Zhāng Zhōng and Hǔ Tái repeatedly fabricated imperial decrees to summon Wáng Shǒurén.
Wáng Shǒurén received a secret letter from Zhāng Yǒng
and did not go.
When he learned that it was the Emperor's intention,
he immediately rushed there.
Zhāng Zhōng and Hǔ Tái's plan failed,
and they did not allow him to see the Emperor.
Wáng Shǒurén then entered Jiǔhuá Shān,
sitting in meditation in a Buddhist temple all day.
The Emperor secretly learned of this and
said:
"Wáng Shǒurén is a man of the Dao;
he came immediately upon being summoned.
How can you say he will rebel?"
He then ordered him to return to his post,
and to resubmit a report of victory.
Wáng Shǒurén then changed his previous memorial,
stating that he had pacified the rebellion following the strategy of the Mighty and Martial Grand General,
and included the names of all the favored eunuchs.
Jiāng Bīn and others then had nothing to say.
At that time,
calumny and wickedness incited unrest,
and disaster and upheaval were unpredictable.
But for Wáng Shǒurén,
the situation in the southeast would have been almost lost.
Shìzōng deeply understood this.
Immediately upon his ascension,
he urgently summoned Wáng Shǒurén to court to receive enfeoffment.
However, Grand Secretary Yáng Tínghé and Wáng Qióng were not on good terms.
Wáng Shǒurén, after repeatedly pacifying rebels,
attributed all the credit to Wáng Qióng,
which Yáng Tínghé disliked,
and many high officials were also jealous of his achievements.
There were those who argued that as the national mourning was not yet over,
it was inappropriate to hold banquets and confer rewards.
Therefore, Wáng Shǒurén was appointed Nánjīng Minister of War.
Wáng Shǒurén did not accept the post,
requesting leave to return home to visit his parents.
Later,
for his merits, he was enfeoffed as a Grand Master of the Imperial Household with Special Advancement, Pillar of the State, and Earl of Xīnjiàn,
a hereditary title,
with an annual stipend of one thousand *shí* of grain.
However, he was not granted an iron certificate,
nor was the annual stipend provided.
Among his colleagues who had distinguished themselves,
only Wǔ Wéndìng, the Prefect of Jí'ān, reached high office
and received the highest award.
The others were nominally promoted,
but secretly demoted,
or dismissed and no longer employed.
Wáng Shǒurén was deeply angered.
At that time, he was observing mourning for his father,
and repeatedly submitted memorials declining the peerage,
and begging for his subordinates' merits to be recorded,
but all were suppressed.
After his mourning period ended,
he was not summoned either.
After a long time,
his friend Xí Shū and disciples Fāng Xiànfū and Huáng Wǎn gained favor through their discussions on rites,
and spoke to Zhāng Cōng and Guì È,
intending to summon and employ him.
However, Fèi Hóng, who bore an old grudge against Wáng Shǒurén,
again thwarted it.
He was repeatedly nominated for Minister of War,
Supreme Commander of the Three Borders,
and Commander of the Training Camps,
but none ever materialized.
In the sixth year of Jiājìng,
the indigenous chiefs Lú Sū and Wáng Shòu of Sī'ēn and Tiánzhōu rebelled.
The Supreme Commander Yáo Mò could not quell them,
so an edict ordered Wáng Shǒurén, with his original rank, to concurrently hold the title of Left Censor-in-Chief
and be Supreme Commander of Liǎngguǎng and concurrently Provincial Governor.
Huáng Wǎn then submitted a memorial praising Wáng Shǒurén's achievements,
requesting the grant of an iron certificate and annual stipend,
and also for the other officials who participated in quelling the rebels to be rewarded.
The emperor approved all.
On his way, Wáng Shǒurén
submitted a memorial outlining the disadvantages of military action,
and stated:
"Sī'ēn has not yet established a regular official administration,
and its indigenous chiefs annually provide three thousand troops,
subject to official deployment.
Once regular officials are established,
we will instead have to dispatch several thousand troops annually for defense.
Thus, the establishment of regular officials
is clearly of no benefit.
Moreover, Tiánzhōu borders Jiāozhǐ,
with deep mountains and remote valleys,
all occupied by the Yáo and Zhuàng peoples.
It is essential to re-establish indigenous officials,
so that their military strength can be leveraged as a屏障.
If indigenous rule is replaced by regular official administration,
then the border troubles
will fall upon us,
and there will surely be future regrets."
The memorial was sent to the Ministry of War.
Minister Wáng Shízhōng listed five points of disagreement,
and the emperor ordered Wáng Shǒurén to reconsider.
In the twelfth month,
Wáng Shǒurén arrived at Xúnzhōu,
and together with the Imperial Inspector Shí Jīn, devised a plan for pacification through inducement.
He dismissed all the armies,
retaining several thousand indigenous troops from Yǒngshùn and Bǎojìng,
who were disarmed and rested.
Lú Sū and Wáng Shòu had initially sought pacification but were denied;
hearing of Wáng Shǒurén's arrival, they were even more fearful,
but now they were overjoyed.
Wáng Shǒurén proceeded to Nánníng,
and the two dispatched envoys to beg for surrender.
Wáng Shǒurén ordered them to present themselves at the military gate.
The two secretly discussed, saying:
"Earl Wáng is notoriously cunning;
we fear he might deceive us."
They entered for an audience with their troops deployed.
Wáng Shǒurén enumerated their crimes,
then flogged and released them.
He personally entered their camp
and appeased their seventy thousand followers.
He reported this to the court,
outlining ten disadvantages of military action
and ten benefits of pacification through inducement.
He then requested the re-establishment of regular officials,
to appropriate a portion of Tiánzhōu land,
and establish a separate prefecture,
appointing Cén Měng's second son, Bāngxiàng, as a registrar,
to oversee prefectural affairs,
and promote him to Prefect upon achieving merit.
And in Tiánzhōu, nineteen patrol posts were established,
with Lú Sū and Wáng Shòu appointed to them,
all subject to the authority of the regular official prefect.
The emperor agreed to all.
The Yáo rebels of Duànféng Xiá
were connected to the Eight Villages above.
Below, they communicated with the barbarians of Xiāntái, Huāxiàng, and other caves,
spanning over three hundred *lǐ*,
having afflicted prefectures and counties for decades.
Wáng Shǒurén wished to suppress them,
and thus remained in Nánníng.
He dismissed the Húguǎng troops,
indicating they would not be used again.
Waiting for the rebels to be unprepared,
he advanced on more than ten stockades like Niúcháng and Liùsì,
and all the gorge rebels were pacified.
Then he followed the Héngshí Jiāng downstream,
attacking and conquering the rebels of Xiāntái, Huāxiàng, Báizhú,
Gǔtáo, and Luófèng.
He ordered the Provincial Administration Commissioner Lín Fù to lead Lú Sū and Wáng Shòu's troops directly to the Eight Villages,
breaking through Shímén.
Deputy General Shěn Xīyí intercepted and cut down the fleeing rebels,
completely pacifying the Eight Villages.
Initially,
the emperor, regarding the pacification of Lú Sū and Wáng Shòu,
dispatched an attendant to convey an imperial letter of praise and commendation.
However, upon receiving the report of victory at Duànféng Xiá,
he inquired of Grand Secretaries Yáng Yīqīng and others with a handwritten edict,
stating that Wáng Shǒurén was boasting,
and also questioning his lifelong scholarship.
Yáng Yīqīng and others did not know how to respond.
Wáng Shǒurén's appointment was due to the recommendation of Zhāng Cōng and Guì È.
Guì È had never been fond of Wáng Shǒurén,
acting upon Zhāng Cōng's insistence.
Later, Guì È became the head of the Ministry of Personnel,
and Zhāng Cōng entered the Grand Secretariat;
they accumulated animosity towards each other.
Guì È, who had suddenly risen in power and sought fame,
hinted to Wáng Shǒurén to conquer Jiāozhǐ,
but Wáng Shǒurén declined.
Yáng Yīqīng was well-acquainted with Wáng Shǒurén,
but Huáng Wǎn had once submitted a memorial proposing Wáng Shǒurén assist the emperor,
criticizing Yáng Yīqīng,
so Yáng Yīqīng could not be without lingering resentment.
Guì È then openly denounced Wáng Shǒurén for failing in both military campaigns and pacification,
and for not implementing the reward system.
Fāng Xiànfū and Huò Tāo felt this was unjust,
and submitted a memorial arguing against it,
stating:
"The various Yáo people have been a scourge for years.
Initially, hundreds of thousands of troops were used,
only securing one Tiánzhōu,
which soon again invited rebels.
Wáng Shǒurén, with a single word of instruction,
brought Sī'ēn and Tiánzhōu to submission.
As for the rebels of the Eight Villages and Duànféng Xiá,
who were entrenched in deep cliffs and precipitous ridges,
no one since the founding of the dynasty had lightly discussed their suppression,
yet now, with a single campaign, they have been completely pacified,
as if pulling out decayed wood.
The critics, however, say that Wáng Shǒurén was ordered to campaign against Sī'ēn and Tiánzhōu,
but not to campaign against the Eight Villages.
Indeed, when a high official is dispatched beyond the borders,
if there is something that can bring peace to the state
and benefit the altars of soil and grain,
he may act on his own authority.
Moreover, Wáng Shǒurén was indeed acting under an imperial edict that allowed him to proceed as he saw fit, wasn't he?
When Wáng Shǒurén suppressed the rebellious prince,
those who were jealous slandered him, first by accusing him of conspiring with the rebel,
and then by accusing him of transporting gold and silk.
At that time, high officials Yáng Tínghé and Qiáo Yǔ fabricated the matter,
which remains unclarified to this day.
A loyal man like Wáng Shǒurén,
with achievements like Wáng Shǒurén,
was once humiliated in Jiāngxī,
and again humiliated in Liǎngguǎng.
Your subject fears that weary officials will lose heart,
and soldiers and officers will become dispirited.
After this, if there are troubles at the borders,
who will again take responsibility for Your Majesty!"
The emperor merely acknowledged the report.
Wáng Shǒurén was already severely ill,
and submitted a memorial requesting to retire,
recommending Lín Fù, the Provincial Governor of Yúnnán, to replace him,
and returned home without waiting for the imperial decree.
He died while traveling to Nán'ān,
at the age of fifty-seven.
When his funeral procession passed through Jiāngxī,
the soldiers and common people all wore white mourning clothes and wept as they saw him off.
Wáng Shǒurén had an extraordinarily keen natural talent.
At seventeen, he visited Lóu Liàng in Shàngráo,
and discussed with him Zhū Zǐ's main points on "investigation of things."
Upon returning home,
he sat upright daily,
lecturing and reading the Five Classics,
never speaking lightly or laughing casually.
After a trip to Jiǔhuá, he returned and
built a house in the Yángmíng Cave.
He dabbled widely in the teachings of Buddhism and Daoism,
but gained nothing for several years.
When he was banished to Lóngchǎng,
a desolate wilderness without books,
he daily reviewed his old knowledge.
Suddenly, he realized that "investigation of things and extension of knowledge"
should be sought within one's own mind,
not in external affairs and things.
He sighed and said,
"The Dao is here!"
Thereupon, he firmly believed and had no doubts.
His teachings
were primarily based on "extending innate knowledge."
He said that after the two Sòng scholars Zhōu Dūnyí and Chéng Hào,
only Lù Jiǔyuān of Xiàngshān was simple and direct,
and thus continued the tradition of Mèng Kē.
As for Zhū Zǐ's Collected Commentaries, or Inquiries, and similar works,
these were theories from his middle age that had not yet been finalized.
Scholars eagerly followed him,
and so the world came to have
"Yángmíng Studies."
After Shǒurén died,
Guì È memorialized that he had arbitrarily left his post.
The Emperor was greatly angered,
and ordered court officials to deliberate.
Guì È and others said:
"Shǒurén's actions did not follow ancient models,
and his words did not invoke his teachers.
Wishing to be unique and superior,
he therefore rejected Zhū Xī's theory of 'investigation of things and extension of knowledge';
knowing that public opinion would not support this,
he then claimed it was Zhū Xī's revised theory from his later years.
He summoned disciples,
who mutually advocated and echoed his views.
Those with talent and beauty enjoyed his freedom,
while the mediocre and vulgar borrowed his empty prestige.
His teachings spread and became distorted,
the deviations becoming increasingly severe.
However, his suppression of bandits
and capture of rebel princes
are merits worth recording.
It is fitting to exempt him from the posthumous forfeiture of his earldom to demonstrate great trustworthiness,
and to ban heterodox theories to rectify the hearts of the people."
The Emperor then issued an edict suspending the hereditary title,
and all posthumous honors were withheld.
At the beginning of the Lóngqìng reign,
many court officials praised his accomplishments.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him the title of Xīnjiàn Hóu,
and the posthumous name Wénchéng.
In the second year, the hereditary earldom was restored.
Later, there was another request to have Shǒurén, Xuē Xuān, and Chén Xiànzhāng all enshrined together in the Confucian Temple.
The Emperor only approved the proposal of the Minister of Rites
to enshrine Xuē Xuān.
Then, in the twelfth year of Wànlì,
Censor Zhān Shìjiǎng reiterated the previous request.
Grand Secretary Shēn Shíxíng and others stated:
"Shǒurén's 'extension of knowledge' comes from the Great Learning,
and 'innate knowledge' comes from Mencius.
Chén Xiànzhāng's emphasis on tranquility follows the Sòng Confucians Zhōu Dūnyí and Chéng Hào.
Moreover, their filial piety and fraternity, and their conduct in public and private life, like Chén Xiànzhāng,
and their integrity, literary skill, and achievements, like Shǒurén,
cannot be called Chan [Buddhism].
They truly deserve to be highly honored."
They also stated that Hú Jūfén's pure heart and earnest practice,
to which public opinion converged,
should also be jointly enshrined.
The Emperor followed all their suggestions.
Throughout the Míng dynasty,
only Shǒurén and these three others were enshrined.
Initially, Shǒurén had no sons,
so he adopted his disciple Zhèngxiàn as his heir.
In his later years,
he had a son, Zhèngyì,
who was orphaned at two years old.
When he grew up,
he inherited the position of vice-commander of the Imperial Bodyguard.
At the beginning of the Lóngqìng reign,
he inherited the title of Xīnjiàn Bó.
He died in the fifth year of Wànlì.
His son Chéngxūn succeeded him
and supervised grain transport for twenty years.
Chéngxūn's son Xiānjìn had
no sons,
and planned to adopt his brother Xiāndá's son Yèhóng as his heir.
Xiāndá's wife said:
"The Earl has no son,
so the title will naturally pass to my husband.
From father to son,
where would the title go?"
Xiānjìn was angered,
and consequently adopted a clan nephew, Yèxún, as his heir.
When Chéngxūn died,
Xiānjìn died before he could inherit the title.
Yèxún, considering himself not the direct heir,
believed the title would eventually revert to Xiāndá,
and also feared a dispute.
Thus, he slandered Xiāndá as having been adopted by begging,
and separately put forward Chéngxūn's nephew Xiāntōng as the rightful heir.
They repeatedly contested this at court,
which remained unresolved for decades.
During the Chóngzhēn reign,
Xiāndá's son Yèhóng again memorialized to argue against Xiāntōng.
At that time, Yèxún's elder brother Yèhào was a Governor-General,
and the responsible officials, fearing to offend Yèhào,
eventually ruled in favor of Xiāntōng.
Yèhóng, in indignation,
held his memorial and went to the Forbidden Gate to appeal.
He attempted to commit suicide by slitting his throat but failed,
was arrested and imprisoned,
and later released.
Xiāntōng held the earldom for four years
before the rebel army captured the capital,
and he was killed.
Shǒurén had disciples all over the empire;
those who carried on his tradition are not recorded here.
Only Jì Yuánhēng once shared hardships with Shǒurén.
Jì Yuánhēng,
courtesy name Wéiqían,
was a native of Wǔlíng.
He firmly believed in Shǒurén's teachings.
He passed the provincial examination in the eleventh year of Zhèngdé.
He followed Shǒurén to Gànzhōu,
where Shǒurén entrusted him with teaching his son.
Chén Háo harbored rebellious intentions,
but outwardly sought a reputation for high learning,
so he sent a letter to Shǒurén asking about his studies.
Shǒurén sent Yuánhēng to him.
Chén Háo tried to provoke him with his words,
but Yuánhēng pretended not to understand,
and only discussed scholarship with him.
Chén Háo regarded him as foolish.
Another day, when they discussed the "Western Inscription,"
Yuánhēng repeatedly explained the principles of loyalty between ruler and minister in great detail.
Chén Háo was also impressed,
gave him generous gifts and sent him away.
Yuánhēng returned the gifts to the officials.
Soon after,
Chén Háo was defeated.
Zhāng Zhōng and Xǔ Tài falsely accused Shǒurén of being in communication with him.
When Chén Háo was questioned,
he said there was no such thing.
When Zhāng Zhōng and the others pressed him further,
he said:
"I only once sent Jì Yuánhēng to discuss scholarship."
Zhāng Zhōng and the others were overjoyed,
flogged Yuánhēng,
and tortured him with branding irons,
but he never confessed.
He was shackled and imprisoned in the imperial prison in the capital.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
memorialists repeatedly cleared his name,
and he died five days after being released from prison.
While in prison, Yuánhēng
treated all the prisoners kindly, like brothers,
and all the prisoners were moved to tears.
When he was arrested,
the authorities arrested his wife, Lǐ.
Lǐ showed no fear,
saying:
"My husband respects his teacher and delights in goodness;
how could he have other worries?"
In prison, she and her two daughters diligently worked on hemp and ramie without stopping.
When the case was about to be cleared,
the jailers wanted to release her.
She said:
"Without seeing my husband,
where would I go if I left?"
The wives of the surveillance commissioners heard of her virtue
and summoned her,
but she declined to go.
When she finally did meet them,
she appeared in her prisoner's clothes,
her hands never letting go of the hemp and ramie.
When asked about her husband's studies,
she said:
"My husband's learning
does not go beyond the private matters of the inner chamber and the bed."
Those who heard her were awestruck.
The eulogy states: Wáng Shǒurén (王守rén) first became known for his upright integrity.
Later, when he took charge of border affairs,
leading weak troops,
he swept away long-standing banditry with a group of scholars,
and pacified rebellious vassals.
Throughout the Míng (明) dynasty,
there was no civil official who employed military force and achieved victory
like Shǒurén (守rén).
In times of danger and uncertainty,
his spirit and resolve became even firmer,
his wisdom and foresight flawless.
Though this was due to his high natural talent,
it must also have been something he gained internally.
Yet, he prided himself on his original insights,
setting himself apart from earlier Confucian scholars,
and was eventually criticized by other scholars.
Shǒurén (守rén) once told Hú Shìníng (胡世níng) that he lectured too little,
to which Shìníng (世níng) replied:
“My regret is that you, sir, lecture too much.”
Although Guì È (桂萼)’s propositions stemmed from private jealousy,
the harmful consequences were indeed real,
and could not be dismissed simply because of his great accomplishments.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 84: Zhāng Cōng (張璁) (Hú Duó (胡鐸)), Guì È (桂萼), Fāng Xiànfū (方獻夫), Xià Yán (夏言)
Zhāng Cōng (張璁),
courtesy name Bǐngyòng (秉用),
was from Yǒngjiā (永嘉).
He passed the provincial examination,
but failed seven times in the metropolitan examination.
As he was about to seek an alternative appointment,
the censor Xiāo Míngfèng (蕭鳴鳳), who was skilled in astrology,
told him:
“In three years from now, you will become a *jìnshì* (進士),
and in another three years, you will suddenly rise to prominence.”
Cōng (璁) then returned home.
He passed the examination in the 16th year of Zhèngdé (正德) (1521),
when he was forty-seven years old.
When Shìzōng (世宗) first ascended the throne,
there was a discussion about posthumously honoring his birth father, Xīngxiàn Wáng (興獻王).
The court officials resisted,
and the proposal was submitted three times and rejected three times.
Cōng (璁), who was then observing government affairs in a ministry,
submitted a memorial in the seventh month of that year, stating:
“Of the utmost devotion of a filial son,
none is greater than honoring one’s parents.
Of the utmost honoring of one’s parents,
none is greater than supporting them with all under heaven.
Your Majesty, having ascended to the great throne,
immediately proposed posthumously honoring your august father to rectify his title,
and welcoming your august mother to provide for her care;
this is truly great filial piety.
The court discussion insists on the precedents of Emperor Āi (哀) of Hàn (漢) (originally Prince of Dìngtáo (定陶)) and Prince Pú (濮) of Sòng (宋),
stating that one who becomes the successor to another is their son,
and must not consider their private parents.
But how can there be a country without parents in the world?
The *Lìjì* (禮記) says: ‘Rites are not descended from heaven,
nor produced from the earth;
they are simply human sentiment.’
Emperor Āi (哀) of Hàn (漢) and Emperor Yīng (英) of Sòng (宋) were indeed the sons of the Prince of Dìngtáo (定陶) and Prince Pú (濮) respectively,
but Emperor Chéng (成) and Emperor Rén (仁) both designated them as heirs beforehand,
raising them in the palace;
their status as successors was very clear.
Therefore, the arguments of Shī Dān (師丹) and Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光) were appropriate for that particular time.
Now, Wǔzōng (武宗) had no heir,
and the high officials, following the ancestral instruction,
welcomed Your Majesty to the throne because of your proper lineage.
The imperial edict simply stated ‘the eldest son of Xīngxiàn Wáng (興獻王),’
and never declared the principle of being a successor.
Thus, Your Majesty’s rise
is truly to inherit the lineage of the ancestors,
which is distinctly different from those designated as heirs beforehand and raised in the palace.
The debaters say that Emperor Xiào (孝)’s virtue and grace were upon the people,
and he could not be without an heir.
Supposing Your August Father were still alive and ascended the throne today,
it is likely that a younger brother would not have the duty to be heir to an elder brother.
Moreover, to welcome and care for your august mother
is because she is your mother.
To call her imperial aunt
would mean meeting her with the etiquette of ruler and subject;
it is feared that a son has no duty to act as a subject to his mother.
The *Lǐjì* (禮記) states: ‘An eldest son cannot become the successor of another.’
Your August Father only bore Your Majesty.
To benefit the empire by becoming a successor,
it is feared that a son has no duty to disown his own parents.
Therefore, for Your Majesty, to say that you succeeded to the ancestral line
and thus were able not to abandon your venerated parents is acceptable;
to say that you became a successor and thereby disowned your own parents is unacceptable.
Indeed, lineage (*tǒng*) and succession (*sì*) are different;
it is not necessarily that a father dies and a son succeeds.
Emperor Wén (文) of Hàn (漢) succeeded Emperor Huì (惠),
thus a younger brother succeeded;
Emperor Xuān (宣) of Hàn (漢) succeeded Emperor Zhāo (昭),
thus an elder brother’s grandson succeeded.
If one must usurp this parent-child relationship
and establish that parent-child title,
and only then call it inheriting the lineage,
then those of antiquity who were called *gāobózǔ* (高伯祖) (great-granduncle) or *huángbókǎo* (皇伯考) (imperial granduncle)
would all not be considered as having inherited the lineage?
I humbly suggest that the rites of today
should establish a separate temple for Your August Father in the capital,
thereby allowing for the profound filial piety of honoring one’s parents,
and also allowing the mother to be honored through her son,
her status equal to the father’s.
Then Your August Father would not lose his status as father,
and Your August Mother would not lose her status as mother.”
The Emperor was then struggling against the court’s opposition,
and upon receiving Cōng (璁)’s memorial, was greatly pleased,
saying:
“With this argument,
my father and I are saved.”
He strongly urged the court officials to deliberate.
The court officials were greatly shocked and disturbed,
and rose up to attack him.
The ritual officials, including Máo Chéng (毛澄), held to their original stance.
At this time, the Princess Consort of Xīngxiàn Wáng (興獻王) arrived at Tōngzhōu (通州),
and hearing that the honorific title had not yet been settled,
she stopped and refused to enter.
The Emperor heard of this and wept,
wishing to abdicate and return to his fiefdom.
Cōng (璁) then authored “Questions on the Great Rites” and submitted it,
whereupon the Emperor repeatedly refuted the ritual officials’ memorials.
The court officials, having no other choice,
collectively agreed to honor Emperor Xiàozōng (孝宗) as ‘Imperial Father’ (*huángkǎo*)
and Xīngxiàn Wáng (興獻王) as
‘Birth Father Emperor Xīngxiàn’ (*běnshēng fù Xīngxiàn Dì*).
Cōng (璁) was also appointed Assistant Minister of Justice in Nánjīng (南京) and departed,
and the discussion on posthumous honors was temporarily shelved.
By the first month of the third year of Jiājìng (嘉靖) (1524),
the Emperor was moved by Guì È (桂萼)’s memorial,
and again put the matter before the court.
Wāng Jùn (汪俊) replaced Máo Chéng (毛澄) as Minister of Rites
and held to Chéng (澄)’s stance.
Cōng (璁) then submitted another memorial, stating:
“Your Majesty, following the instruction of ‘when an elder brother dies, a younger brother succeeds,’
was rightly established in the proper lineage.
The ritual officials do not consider that Your Majesty is truly the sovereign who succeeded to the great lineage,
but forcefully compare you to the example of one who becomes a successor to another,
thereby severing the natural affection for Emperor Xīngxiàn (興獻),
disregarding the lineage transmitted by Wǔzōng (武宗),
and causing the names and realities of Your Majesty’s father-son, uncle-nephew, and brotherly relationships to be all disordered.
Rather than displease the Son of Heaven,
they dare not offend powerful ministers;
what kind of heart is this?
I humbly observe the imperial edict stating:
‘Xīngxiàn Wáng (興獻王) bore me alone;
if I cannot inherit his line,
nor can he receive an honorable title,
how can his boundless grace be repaid?’
The powerful ministers, observing the imperial mind,
saw the importance of exalted veneration.
Thus, today they contend over the character ‘Dì’ (帝) (Emperor),
tomorrow they contend over the character ‘Huáng’ (皇) (Imperial),
and Your Majesty’s heart also daily feels inadequate for not having the title ‘Dì’ or ‘Huáng.’
Eventually, they added the title ‘Dì,’
thinking that Your Majesty’s heart would then be appeased.
Therefore, they left out the character ‘Huáng’ to test Your Majesty’s future lingering desires,
and thus dared to call Emperor Xiàozōng (孝宗) ‘Imperial Father’ (*huángkǎo*)
and Emperor Xīngxiàn (興獻) ‘Birth Father’ (*běnshēngfù*).
Since the father-son titles have been changed,
where is the meaning of exaltation?
Then they hastily issued an edict to announce it to the world,
taking advantage of Your Majesty’s unawareness
to trap you in unfilial conduct.
The *Lǐjì* (禮記) says: ‘A gentleman does not usurp another’s parents,
nor should his own parents be usurped.’
Your Majesty, being honored as the Lord of Ten Thousand Chariots,
can the parent-child relationship
be usurped by others,
and can you tolerate others usurping it?
Therefore, the rites of today are not about ‘Imperial’ or not ‘Imperial,’
but solely about ‘Father’ (*kǎo*) or not ‘Father.’
If one merely contends over the character ‘Huáng,’
and Your Majesty will temporarily use this to satisfy your heart today.
I fear that those in the world who understand the rites
will certainly laugh at this endlessly.”
This was submitted concurrently with Guì È (桂萼)’s second memorial.
The Emperor was even more pleased,
and immediately summoned the two men to the capital.
Before the order reached them,
the two men, along with Huáng Zōngmíng (黃宗明) and Huáng Wǎn (黃綰),
jointly submitted another memorial, arguing forcefully.
When Emperor Xiàn decided to change the posthumous title of his biological father,
the Grand Secretaries, deeming the honorific title already settled,
requested to suspend the summons.
The Emperor reluctantly agreed.
The two (Guì É and Zhāng Cōng) were already on their way,
and then hastily sent another memorial stating:
"The ritual officials, fearing that we would confront them face-to-face,
therefore resorted to this tactic first,
seeking to fulfill their private desires.
If the appellation of 'biological father' is not immediately removed,
the world and future generations will ultimately consider Your Majesty to be the son of Xiàozōng,
falling into the deception and cover-up of the ritual officials."
The Emperor's heart was further stirred,
and he quickly summoned the two.
They arrived in the capital in the fifth month,
and again presented seven articles.
The crowd was furious,
wanting to beat them to death.
Guì É was afraid
and dared not come out.
Zhāng Cōng only held court after several days.
Censors Zhāng Chōng and Zhèng Běngōng, among others, repeatedly attacked them in memorials,
which further displeased the Emperor.
He specially appointed the two as Hanlin Academicians.
The two strongly declined,
and further requested to confront the court officials directly regarding their wrongs.
Censors Lǐ Xuézéng and Jí Táng, among others, said:
"Zhāng Cōng and Guì É pervert learning to pander to the age,
which must be punished in a sagely era.
To appoint them as Academicians by imperial decree without consultation slightly tarnishes the sagely virtue."
Censors Duàn Xù and Chén Xiāng also specially memorialized to criticize them,
and also included Xí Shū.
The Emperor rebuked Lǐ Xuézéng and others, ordering them to respond to the allegations,
and sent Duàn Xù and Chén Xiāng to imperial prison.
Zhào Jiàn, Minister of Personnel, also requested to subject Zhāng Cōng and Guì É to judicial process,
telling people:
"If I get imperial approval,
I will beat them to death."
The Emperor accused him of collusion
and also ordered him to respond to the allegations.
Zhāng Cōng and Guì É then again listed thirteen instances of deception and trickery,
forcefully refuting the court officials.
When the court officials prostrated themselves before the palace gates and wept in protest,
all were imprisoned and flogged in imperial prison.
More than ten people died under the杖 (flogging),
and banishments followed one after another,
whereupon Zhāng Cōng and his faction's influence greatly expanded.
In the ninth month of that year, their proposal for settling the honorific title was adopted.
The Emperor increasingly doted on and relied on Zhāng Cōng and Guì É,
who in turn increasingly relied on imperial favor to take revenge on court officials,
and all officials and literati in the court gnashed their teeth at these few individuals.
In the winter of the fourth year (of Jiājìng's reign),
the Grand Rites deliberations were completed,
and he was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent兼 (concurrently) Hanlin Academician.
Later, when discussing the divine path of the Shìmiào, temple music, martial dances, and the Empress Dowager's visit to the temple,
the Emperor consistently relied on Zhāng Cōng's words for decisions.
Zhāng Cōng embellished the classics,
skillfully conforming to the Emperor's wishes,
and the Emperor valued him even more.
Zhāng Cōng was eager to gain power,
but was suppressed by Grand Secretary Fèi Hóng,
so he and Guì É jointly attacked Fèi Hóng in memorials.
The Emperor also knew their intentions,
and kept Fèi Hóng, not immediately dismissing him.
In the seventh month of the fifth year,
Zhāng Cōng requested to visit his ancestral tomb.
After taking leave from court,
the Emperor again appointed him as Vice Minister of War (Right),
with his concurrent posts remaining as before.
Censors Dù Tóng, Yáng Yán, and Zhào Tíngruì jointly attacked him in memorials,
and also impeached Liào Jì, Minister of Personnel, for appointing wicked individuals.
The Emperor was enraged,
and severely reprimanded them.
Censors Xiè Yīguàn, Zhāng Lù
Fāng Jìdá, Dài Jìxiān, and others from both capitals again jointly memorialized incessantly,
but all were ignored.
Soon after, Zhāng Cōng was promoted to Vice Minister (Left),
and again attacked Fèi Hóng with Guì É.
In the second month of the following year, the Xìngwáng Bāngqí case arose,
which implicated Yáng Tínghé and others,
and Fèi Hóng and Shí Bǎo were dismissed on the same day.
Péng Zé, a director in the Ministry of Personnel, was dismissed for being frivolous,
but Zhāng Cōng said:
"When the rites were deliberated previously,
Péng Zé advised me to present the 'Grand Rites Questions and Answers,'
which attracted general animosity.
Now that the various officials are removing him,
they will successively remove us."
Péng Zé was then allowed to stay.
Three days later,
he again said:
"I have resisted the entire court for four or five years;
the entire court has attacked me in over a hundred memorials.
Now that the complete book on the Grand Rites is being compiled,
the chief culprits are chilled to the bone,
and the various scoundrels watch askance.
Therefore, as soon as the outline is presented,
slander and calumny proliferate.
If the complete book is finished,
the false accusations and entrapment will be even worse."
He then claimed illness and sought retirement to pressure the Emperor,
who issued a gracious decree to comfort and retain him.
The Ministry of Personnel had a vacancy for Minister,
and former Ministers Qiáo Yǔ and Yáng Dàn were recommended;
the Ministry of Rites also had a vacancy for Minister,
and Vice Ministers Liú Lóng and Wēn Rénhé were recommended.
Wēn Rénhé contended based on his seniority in俸 (salary/rank).
Zhāng Cōng said that Qiáo Yǔ and Yáng Dàn were members of Yáng Tínghé's faction,
and that Wēn Rénhé should not promote himself.
The Emperor ordered that retired high officials,
unless specially summoned by imperial decree, were not to be recommended,
and thus Qiáo Yǔ and others were discarded.
Zhāng Cōng harbored resentment towards the court officials,
and daily plotted revenge.
Coincidentally, Mǎ Lù, the Provincial Surveillance Commissioner of Shānxī, was handling the case of the rebel Lǐ Fúdá,
which implicated Guō Xūn, Marquis of Wǔdìng.
The judicial authorities ruled as Mǎ Lù had suggested.
Zhāng Cōng slandered them to the Emperor,
saying that the court officials were framing Guō Xūn because of the rites debate.
The Emperor indeed suspected the various officials of collusion,
and then ordered Zhāng Cōng to serve as acting Censor-in-Chief of the Censorate,
Guì É as acting Minister of Justice,
and Fāng Xiànfū as acting Minister of the Grand Court of Judicial Review,
to review the case.
They overturned the entire case,
and implicated all those who disagreed with them.
Senior officials like Yán Yíshòu and Niè Xián were all flogged,
and Mǎ Lù and others were convicted and banished afar.
The Emperor regarded them as even more capable,
and rewarded them in the privy palace,
bestowing official robes of the second rank,
and imperial patents of enfeoffment for three generations.
During the capital review and mutual impeachment among censors,
thirteen censors had already been dismissed.
Zhāng Cōng, in charge of the Censorate,
again requested to assess and dismiss twelve more.
He also proposed seven articles for the constitutional綱 (guiding principles),
which restricted the Provincial Surveillance Commissioners.
In the winter of that year,
he was appointed Minister of Rites兼 (concurrently) Grand Academician of the Wényuāngé to participate in government affairs,
only six years after shedding his green robes (starting his official career).
Yáng Yīqīng was the Senior Grand Secretary,
and Zhái Luán was also in the Grand Secretariat,
but the Emperor treated them not as he treated Zhāng Cōng.
He once admonished Zhāng Cōng:
"I have secret decrees that must not be divulged;
I and you will personally write the correspondence."
Zhāng Cōng then referenced Emperor Rénzōng bestowing silver seals upon Yáng Shìqí and others,
and the Emperor bestowed two seals upon Zhāng Cōng,
with the inscriptions:
"Loyal, virtuous, and upright,"
and
"Correcting errors and assisting in wrongs,"
and then included Yáng Yīqīng and others.
When Zhāng Cōng was first appointed Academician,
the Hanlin academicians were ashamed
and refused to rank alongside him,
which Zhāng Cōng deeply resented.
When Lecturer Wāng Diàn lectured on the Great Plan and did not meet the Emperor's approval,
the Emperor ordered him to be transferred to an outside post.
Zhāng Cōng then requested that from lecturers downwards, officials be assigned to outside posts according to their talent,
and twenty-two people were reassigned or dismissed.
All imperial students were appointed as ministry subordinates or county magistrates,
thus emptying the Hanlin Academy.
In the first month of the seventh year,
the Emperor held court,
and saw Zhāng Cōng and Guì É ranked below Lǐ Chéngxūn, Minister of War,
which displeased him.
Yáng Yīqīng then requested to add honorary titles,
and so the Emperor personally decreed to add Grand Preceptor of the Heir Apparent to the two.
Zhāng Cōng declined, saying that the Crown Prince had not yet been established, and the office should not be set up,
so he was further appointed Junior Guardian兼 (concurrently) Grand Preceptor of the Heir Apparent.
When the 'Grand Canon on Human Relationships' was completed,
he was again promoted to Junior Tutor兼 (concurrently) Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent, Minister of Personnel, and Grand Academician of the Jǐnshēndiàn.
Yīqīng's second appointment as grand secretary
was largely due to the efforts of Sōng and È.
He was devoted to these two men.
However, Sōng eventually overshadowed Yīqīng,
and as he could not have his way completely,
they clashed.
The commander Niè Néngqiān impeached Sōng,
and Sōng wanted to put him to death.
Yīqīng drafted a more lenient edict,
which made Sōng hate him even more,
denouncing Yīqīng as a treacherous and vulgar man.
Yīqīng submitted a second memorial requesting retirement,
and moreover hinted at Sōng's hidden misconduct.
The emperor personally issued an edict to console and retain him,
and then spoke at length about Sōng's self-aggrandizement,
and how he relied on imperial favor without yielding,
which was truly regrettable.
Sōng, seeing the emperor suddenly expose his flaws,
was quite ashamed and dejected.
In the autumn of the eighth year,
Supervising Secretary Sūn Yìngkuí impeached Yīqīng and È, and also Sōng.
His colleague Wáng Zhǔn further impeached Sōng for privately consulting with Garrison Commander Chén Fán,
and said he should be dismissed.
Sōng requested leave to retire twice,
his memorials containing many veiled criticisms of Yīqīng.
The emperor then praised and mollified Sōng.
But Supervising Secretary Lù Càn again impeached him for arbitrarily wielding power and authority,
and for retaliating for past grievances and favors.
The emperor was greatly enlightened,
and immediately dismissed Sōng.
Shortly thereafter,
his partisan Huò Tāo vigorously attacked Yīqīng,
subtly vindicating Sōng.
Sōng traveled as far as Tiānjīn,
when the emperor ordered an imperial messenger to carry a personal edict summoning him back.
Yīqīng was then dismissed,
and Sōng became the senior grand secretary.
The emperor, having personally overruled court discussions to establish
the "Grand Rites,"
thenceforth took it upon himself to formulate rituals and music.
As Xià Yán began to gain influence,
he proposed the empress's personal sericulture,
the pairing of Gōulóng and Qì with the altars of Soil and Grain,
the separate sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
the abolition of Tàizōng's supplementary sacrifice,
the establishment of separate eastern and western suburbs for the morning and evening sacrifices to the sun and moon,
the sacrifice to Gāoméi,
the placement of spirit tablets in the Wénmiào and the revised list of accompanying Confucian scholars,
the removal of Dézǔ's tablet to ensure Tàizǔ faced south,
the sacrifice for bountiful harvests,
the grand Dì sacrifice,
and the Imperial altars of Soil and Grain.
All these memorials had to be submitted to Sōng for deliberation.
However, the emperor preferred to make his own decisions,
and Sōng's opinions were not always adopted.
His remonstrance against removing Tàizōng from the supplementary sacrifice to Heaven
went back and forth three or four times,
but he ultimately could not prevent it.
In the second month of the tenth year,
Sōng requested a change of name because his name conflicted with the emperor's taboo name.
He was then granted the name Fújìng,
with the courtesy name Mòugōng,
and the emperor personally wrote four large characters to bestow upon him.
Xià Yán, relying on imperial favor,
frequently used affairs to expose Fújìng's shortcomings.
Fújìng bore a grudge,
but had no opportunity to act.
He adopted Péng Zé's suggestion to frame the Director of the Office of Imperial Messengers, Xuē Kǎn,
and then used Kǎn to harm Yán.
During the court interrogation, the plot was exposed,
and an edict denounced his malicious deceit.
Censors Tán Zuǎn, Duān Tíngshè, and Táng Yùxián jointly impeached him in multiple memorials.
The emperor ordered the Ministry of Justice to instruct him to retire,
and Fújìng left in great shame.
Not long after,
the emperor dispatched an imperial messenger with an edict to summon him.
He returned to court in the third month of the following year.
Yán had already been promoted to Minister of Rites
and was even more influential.
Lǐ Shí and Zhái Luán were in the Grand Secretariat,
and Fāng Xiànfū subsequently joined them,
so Fújìng could no longer act as arbitrarily as before.
In the eighth month,
a comet appeared in Dōngjǐng.
The emperor suspected that his high officials were wielding excessive power,
and Fújìng thereupon requested to retire.
The Supervising Secretary of the Capital, Wèi Liángbì, slandered Fújìng as treacherous,
to which Fújìng responded:
"Liángbì was deprived of his salary for濫舉京營官,
and because I drafted the edict,
he is taking private revenge."
Supervising Secretary Qín Áo impeached Fújìng for sophistically defending his treachery,
saying that when remonstrating officials presented their arguments, he would always find fault with them,
and that he would disclose the content of draft edicts,
attributing them to himself,
clearly showing to both the court and the outside world
that the emperor's power was in his grasp.
The emperor agreed with Áo's words,
ordered Fújìng to submit a self-statement,
and allowed him to retire.
Lǐ Shí requested that he be granted provisions and attendants, and an imperial edict,
but this was not allowed.
After a second request,
he was granted permission to return home by post-horse.
In the first month of the twelfth year,
the emperor thought of him again,
and dispatched a Honglu Temple officer with an edict to summon him.
He returned to court in the fourth month.
In the sixth month,
a comet reappeared between Bì and Mǎo.
He requested to abdicate his position,
but this was not allowed.
The following year, he was promoted to Junior Preceptor concurrent with Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince and Grand Secretary of the Huágài Hall.
Initially,
when Chén Qīng rebelled in Lùzhōu,
Fújìng advocated for military action,
and the rebels were ultimately crushed.
When Dàtóng rebelled again,
he also advocated for military action,
recommending Liú Yuánqīng as governor-general,
but the campaign was protracted and unsuccessful.
After the rebellion was suppressed,
the Prince of Dài requested that a high official be sent to pacify the region.
Xià Yán then strongly criticized the errors in military strategy,
requesting that the prince's words be heeded,
his words often infringing upon Fújìng.
Fújìng was angry and
held back the prince's memorial.
The emperor instructed him to be on good terms with Yán,
and dispatched Huáng Wǎn to Dàtóng,
to act according to the circumstances.
Fújìng, because his proposal was not adopted,
claimed illness and requested to retire,
submitting three memorials.
Later, his son died,
and he requested even more strongly.
The emperor replied:
"You are not ill,
you merely doubt Us."
Fújìng submitted another memorial,
not acknowledging any fault,
and moreover criticized È, Xiànfū, Tāo, Wǎn, and others who had discussed the rites with him.
The emperor questioned and reprimanded him,
whereupon he resumed his duties.
The emperor built the Jiǔwǔzhāi and Gōngmòshì behind the Wénhuá Hall as his vegetarian quarters,
and ordered his grand secretaries to compose poems.
Fújìng and Shí each wrote four or more poems.
Afterwards,
he was frequently summoned to the private chambers,
to leisurely discuss state affairs.
In the spring of the fourteenth year, he fell ill.
The emperor sent eunuchs to bestow wine and meat,
and spoke with Shí,
mentioning Fújìng's stubbornness,
and how he did not value talented people, thus accumulating resentment.
He also sent eunuchs to bestow medicine,
with a personal edict saying:
"In ancient times, there were those who cut off their beards to cure a high official's illness.
We now bestow upon you what We Ourselves take."
Fújìng was fortunate to receive such a warm edict,
and so repeatedly submitted memorials requesting leave to retire due to old age.
He was ordered to return home under the escort of an imperial messenger and imperial physicians,
and the appropriate authorities provided him with provisions and attendants according to regulations.
In the fifth month of the following year,
the emperor again dispatched an Imperial Guard officer with a personal edict to check on his illness,
urging him to return.
When he reached Jīnhuá,
his illness worsened greatly,
and he returned home.
He died in the second month of the eighteenth year.
The emperor, while in Chéngtiān,
heard of it and grieved deeply.
Fú Jìng was earnest, respectful, firm, bright, and decisive,
not avoiding suspicion or resentment.
Once he met the emperor,
he often offered frank advice.
The emperor wished to accuse Zhāng Yánlíng of rebellion
and exterminate his family.
Fú Jìng remonstrated, saying:
"Yánlíng
is merely a miserly wretch;
how could he rebel?"
He was interrogated several times,
but his answers remained the same.
When the autumn ended and the case was due for judgment,
Fú Jìng submitted a memorial stating:
"Zhāoshèng Huáng Tàihòu is advanced in age;
if she suddenly hears of Yánlíng's death,
and by some chance refuses to eat
or suffers some other misfortune,
how will we comfort the spirit of Jìng Huángdì in heaven?"
The emperor was enraged
and rebuked Fú Jìng:
"Throughout history, there have been many powerful officials who coerced their sovereigns.
Now, you champion a condemned prisoner and coerce your sovereign.
Perhaps you regret not having followed Tínghé in serving Jìng Huángdì?"
The emperor deliberately used harsh words to deter Fú Jìng,
but Fú Jìng's resolve did not waver.
For this reason, Zhāng Yánlíng was kept in long detention
until the end of Zhāoshèng Huáng Tàihòu's life.
Other matters, such as purifying the noble families' estates,
and dismissing all garrisoning eunuchs in the realm,
were almost entirely completed one after another,
all due to his efforts.
He maintained strict integrity,
detested corrupt officials,
and for a time, bribery was completely eradicated.
However, he was fiercely stubborn,
and sought vengeance,
failing to protect good people.
He desired to forcibly dismantle factions among officials,
yet he himself became a faction leader.
The "Great Rites"
controversy and its severe punishments
brought him much criticism that followed him even after his death.
Yet, the emperor cherished and treated him with reverence from beginning to end,
and no other court official could compare with him.
The emperor often referred to him as Shàoshī Luóshān, not by his personal name.
When he died,
the Ministry of Rites requested a posthumous title.
The emperor, drawing upon the meaning of "endangering oneself to serve the emperor,"
specially granted him the posthumous title Wénzhōng
and posthumously appointed him Tàishī.
At that time, there was a man named Hú Duó,
courtesy name Shízhèn,
from Yúyáo.
He became a *jìnshì* at the end of Hóngzhì's reign.
During the Zhèngdé era,
he served as Fújiàn Tíxué Fùshǐ.
In the early Jiājìng era,
he was promoted to Húguǎng Cāncèng,
and eventually to Nánjīng Tàipú Qīng.
Duó and Cōng passed the provincial examination together.
When the "Great Rites"
debate arose,
Duó also supported the view that Xiàn Wáng should be honored
and agreed with Cōng.
Cōng urged him to co-sign a memorial,
but Duó said:
"The emperor's natural filial piety is indeed unalterable,
but the common sentiments of the people in the realm cannot be disregarded either.
If honoring Xiàn Wáng is not enough, then he becomes Zōng (ancestor);
if Zōng is not enough, then he enters the ancestral temple;
if he enters the temple, then there should be a *tiáo* (remote ancestor).
To make a ruler of an imperial prince with an empty title,
and thereby depose the Zōng who reigned over the world,
is certainly not righteous.
If he enters the temple, he will have a position.
Will his position be above Wǔzōng,
or below Wǔzōng?
Living, I was his subject;
dead, I cannot be placed above my sovereign.
However, Lǔ once placed Xīgōng in the position of a remote ancestor.
I fear that in the future, there will be no shortage of people like Xiàfǔ."
Cōng's proposal was then submitted.
He was soon summoned to court.
Duó was just completing his mourning period and proceeding to the capital,
and Cōng again urged him to co-sign a memorial.
Duó wrote back, declining
and arguing with him about the meaning of succession.
After the "Great Rites"
were settled,
Duó again sent a letter advising Cōng to recall the officials involved in the rites debate,
to foster peace and blessings.
Cōng could not comply.
Duó was from the same locality as Wáng Shǒurén,
but did not follow his teachings.
He agreed with Cōng that honoring Xiàn Wáng was correct,
but did not join him in his advancements.
However, his argument about succession,
that when the imperial lineage is broken, the establishment of a ruler implicitly means establishing a worthy person,
was utterly mistaken.
Guì È,
courtesy name Zǐshí,
was from Ānrén.
He became a *jìnshì* in the sixth year of Zhèngdé.
He was appointed Zhīxiàn of Dāntú.
He was stubborn and given to temper,
repeatedly offending his superiors,
and refused a transfer to Qīngtián.
He was later recommended and appointed Zhīxiàn of Wǔkāng,
but again offended his superiors and was imprisoned.
In the early Jiājìng era,
he was transferred from Zhīxiàn of Chéng'ān to Nánjīng Xíngbù Zhǔshì.
Shìzōng wished to honor his birth parents,
but court officials vigorously opposed it.
He had already referred to Xīngxiàn Wáng as emperor
and his consort as Xīngguó Tàihòu,
and issued edicts to the realm for two years.
È and Zhāng Cōng were colleagues;
then, in the eleventh month of the second year, he submitted a memorial saying:
"Your servant hears that when an emperor is filial to his father,
he is clear in serving Heaven;
when filial to his mother,
he is discerning in serving Earth.
I have never heard of one who disregards the fundamental human relationship of father and son,
yet is able to serve Heaven and Earth and preside over all spirits.
Now, the officials of rites have failed to consult the ancient regulations,
obstructing Your Majesty's pure filial heart,
leading Your Majesty into the error of being a successor to another,
thereby extinguishing the lineage of Wǔzōng,
and usurping the Zōng of Xiàn Dì.
Moreover, they make Xīngguó Tàihòu subservient to Císhòu Tàihòu.
The rites are not fully observed,
and the Three Cardinal Guides are utterly abandoned.
This is an extraordinary change!
Since Zhāng Cōng and Huò Tāo presented their proposals,
critics have labeled them as seeking advancement,
silencing people,
causing those who understand the rites to dare not refute them.
I sincerely believe that Your Majesty, attending to Xīngguó Tàihòu,
has lamented for Xīngxiàn Dì not being honored
for three years now,
clutching your heart and shedding tears
countless times.
I beg Your Majesty to swiftly issue a clear edict,
referring to Xiàozōng as Huáng Bókǎo (Imperial Elder Uncle-Father)
and Xīngxiàn Dì as Huángkǎo (Imperial Father),
establishing a separate temple in the Grand Palace,
rectifying the rites for Xīngguó Tàihòu,
and formally designating her as Shèngmǔ (Holy Mother).
This would accord with the Way of serving Heaven and Earth.
As for what the court officials uphold, it is merely the Song court's debate on Pú Wáng.
According to Fàn Chúnrén of Song, who reported to Yīngzōng, 'Your Majesty previously received an edict from Rénzōng,
personally promising to be his son.
Regarding titles and ranks, all followed the precedents for imperial princes,
which is different from a ruler who succeeds by adoption.'
Thus, the arguments of the Song officials
also had their distinctions.
Now, Your Majesty, following ancestral instructions, has succeeded to the great lineage,
and has never received an edict from Xiàozōng to be his son.
Therefore, it is abundantly clear that Your Majesty is not a successor by adoption,
but a ruler who has succeeded to the lineage.
As for honoring Xīngxiàn Dì
and his mother Xīngguó Tàihòu,
what doubt can there be?
Your servant hears that only the Son of Heaven may deliberate on rites;
when the Way prevails in the realm,
rites and music originate from the Son of Heaven.
Your servant has long wished to request this;
recently, I have also received two memorials from Xí Shū and Fāng Xiànfū.
I humbly hope Your Majesty will resolutely make a judgment,
and transmit my memorial along with those of the other two officials to the Ministry of Rites,
allowing your servants to debate in person."
The emperor was greatly pleased,
and in the first month of the following year, he personally annotated and ordered it to be implemented.
In the third month,
Guì È again submitted a memorial, saying:
“Since ancient times, when emperors passed down their rule,
the succession of the imperial line was considered weighty,
while the individual heir was deemed lighter.
Therefore, Gāo Huángdì emulated earlier kings
and laid down the instruction that a brother succeeds upon the death of an elder brother.
Your Majesty inherited the great succession of the ancestors,
and is precisely following Gāo Huángdì’s system.
Yet the执政 (zhízhèng) [ministers] without cause indulge their private interests,
and betray the ancestral instructions.
How unrighteous this is,
can it still be spoken of?
Your servant hears it said on the streets
that the zhízhèng (zhízhèng) spy on Your Majesty’s deepest feelings incessantly,
merely to add a ‘Huáng’ (皇) character.
Indeed, Your Majesty’s filial piety towards your parents
does not lie in whether there is a ‘Huáng’ (皇) or not,
but solely in whether there is a ‘Kǎo’ (考) or not.
If the intention to treat Xiàn Dì (獻帝) as ‘Kǎo’ (考) can be swayed,
even adding a thousand or a hundred honorific characters
would be of no benefit to filial piety.
Your Majesty would then spend your entire life as a person without a father.
Such a violation of ethics and betrayal of righteousness,
can it still be allowed to participate in this discussion? ”
This memorial was submitted along with Cōng’s.
The Emperor was even more delighted,
and summoned him to the capital.
Initially,
among the officials debating the rites, none dared strongly criticize the zhízhèng (zhízhèng).
