It was Guì È who explicitly denounced them as unrighteous,
and even wished to prevent them from participating in the discussion.
His words were unrestrained and fearless;
the court officials particularly detested him.
When the summons was issued,
the multitude was even more startled and aghast,
and they rose en masse to attack and denounce him,
but the Emperor was unmoved.
Guì È then, together with Zhāng Cōng, continued to argue endlessly,
and was subsequently summoned to be a Hànlín Xuéshì (翰林學士).
Eventually, his words were adopted.
From then on, Guì È was exceptionally trusted and appreciated.
In the spring of the fourth year,
the Gěishìzhōng (給事中) Kē Wéixióng (柯維熊) said:
“Your Majesty associates with noble persons, yet noble persons are not tolerated,
as seen in the departure of Lín Jùn (林俊), Sūn Jiāo (孫交), and Péng Zé (彭澤).
You distance yourself from petty persons, yet petty persons remain,
as seen in the employment of Zhāng Cōng (張璁) and Guì È (桂萼).
Furthermore, many officials who submitted memorials to the throne have died or been banished,
and the Yùshǐ (御史) Wáng Mào (王懋) and Guō Nán (郭楠) have again been demoted and reprimanded.
I humbly believe the punishments are too severe.”
Guì È and Zhāng Cōng then sought to resign,
but the Emperor issued a gracious edict to console and retain them.
Soon after, they were promoted to Zhānshì (詹事) concurrently with Hànlín Xuéshì (翰林學士).
When debating the spirit way for the Shìmiào (世廟) and the empress dowager’s temple visit rites,
they again opposed the court’s consensus,
hoping to align with the Emperor’s will.
The Emperor increasingly regarded them as wise,
and the two men’s influence grew.
However, the cabinet ministers suppressed them,
not allowing them to be on par with the other Hànlín (翰林) scholars.
The two then jointly submitted memorials attacking Fèi Hóng (費宏) and Shí Bǎo (石珤),
and bitched them out of office.
When Gěishìzhōng (給事中) Chén Guāng (陳洸) committed a grave offense,
Guì È and Shàngshū (尚書) Zhào Jiàn (趙鑑) strongly argued,
and were impeached by the Nánjīng Gěishìzhōng (南京給事中),
but the matter was not pursued.
He often presented proposals on current governance,
requesting to prematurely exempt six years of land tax,
to rectify the long-standing abuses from the beginning of the reign,
to relax the restrictions on the Dēngwén Gǔ (登聞鼓) [lit. drum for presenting grievances],
to restore the Kāizhōng (開中) system on the frontier,
to punish wicked individuals who obstruct relief agencies,
to allow poor people to cultivate vacant land along city walls,
to suspend the practice of external officials going to the ministries for performance reviews,
to uphold imperial reverence,
and to expand imperial filial piety,
among several other matters.
Many of these proposals were put into practice.
In the third month of the sixth year, he was promoted to Lǐbù Yòu Shìláng (禮部右侍郎),
with his concurrent posts remaining as before.
At this time, a capital review (Jīngchá) was underway,
and Nánjīng (南京) censorial officials pointed out errors concerning Guì È.
Guì È submitted a memorial saying:
“The former Grand Secretary Yáng Tínghé (楊廷和) extensively cultivated his private faction,
obscuring the Emperor’s sagely judgment for six years.
Now they are being progressively dismissed,
but lingering remnants of their wickedness remain in the censorial system.
In the early years of Xiànzōng’s (憲宗) reign,
after he ordered the Censorate and Supervising Secretaries to report errors,
they impeached each other,
and the censorial system was thus cleared.
I request that this system be implemented as per regulations.”
The memorial was sent down to the Lìbù (吏部) [Ministry of Personnel],
where Shìláng (侍郎) Mèng Chūn (孟春) and others said:
“Xiànzōng (憲宗) issued no such edict.
Guì È is being criticized, and this is his retaliation,
which will not satisfy the public.”
Guì È said:
“The edict is found in Xiànzōng’s (憲宗) collected works.
Mèng Chūn (孟春) seeks to flatter the censorial officials;
he should also be investigated.”
The memorial was sent down for further deliberation by the ministry.

Mèng Chūn (孟春) and others then stated that during the Chénghuà (成化) era, some officials in the Censorate and Supervising Secretaries who were exceptionally promoted to巡撫 (xúnfǔ) [provincial governors] proved incompetent.
Xiànzōng (憲宗) then ordered them to impeach each other,
and seven individuals were dismissed.
This was not comparable to the Jīngchá (京察) [capital review] or the practice of reporting errors.
The Emperor, however, ultimately approved Guì È’s words,
urging prompt implementation.
The Gěishì (給事) and Yùshǐ (御史) argued against it,
and were all deprived of their salaries.
Mèng Chūn (孟春) and others then submitted the names of four Yùshǐ (御史), including Chǔ Liángcái (儲良才).
The Emperor exclusively dismissed Chǔ Liángcái (儲良才),
and by special decree dismissed Gěishìzhōng (給事中) Zhèng Zìbì (鄭自璧) and Mèng Qí (孟奇).
Moreover, he ordered the ministries and Censorate to re-examine the cases,
again dismissing four Gěishìzhōng (給事zhong) including Yú Jīng (余經),
and several Nánjīng Gěishìzhōng (南京給事中) including Gù Zhēn (顧溱),
before the matter finally concluded.
In the ninth month of that year, he was transferred to Lìbù Zuǒ Shìláng (吏部左侍郎).
In the same month, he was appointed Lǐbù Shàngshū (禮部尚書),
concurrently Hànlín Xuéshì (翰林學士).
According to established practice,
Shàngshū (尚shū) did not concurrently hold the title of Xuéshì (學士);
this began with Guì È.
Barely a month later,
he was promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書),
and bestowed two silver seals,
inscribed
“Loyal, Sincere, Serene, and Prudent,”
and
“Rectifying Faults, Correcting Deviations,”
ordering him to submit sealed memorials on state affairs, equal in status to a Grand Secretary.
In the first month of the seventh year,
an imperial handwritten edict added the title of Tàizǐ Tàibǎo (太子太保).
When the Dàdiǎn (大典) [Grand Ceremony] on clarifying proper relationships (Mínglún) was completed,
he was promoted to Shàobǎo (少保) concurrently with Tàizǐ Tàifù (太子太傅).
Having achieved his ambitions, Guì È
daily made it his business to seek revenge.
In the cases of Chén Jiǔchóu (陳九疇), Lǐ Fúdá (李福達), and Chén Guāng (陳洸),
many people, including Péng Zé (彭澤), Mǎ Lù (馬錄), and Yè Yìngcōng (葉應驄), were implicated successively,
some being framed and banished to military garrisons.
No court official failed to fear his fierce power.
However, he alone memorialized recommending Dèng Jìzēng (鄧繼曾) and Jì Běn (季本), who had been punished for their remonstrances,
and Huáng Guóyòng (黃國用), Liú Bǐngjiàn (劉秉鑑), and others who had been demoted and banished due to various incidents,
allowing these individuals to be transferred to less remote posts.
The world also somewhat esteemed Guì È for this.
However, when Wáng Shǒurén (王守仁) was appointed,
Guì È had indeed recommended him.
Later,
harboring resentment for Wáng Shǒurén (王守仁) not aligning with him,
he vigorously attacked and reviled him.
After Wáng Shǒurén (王守仁) died,
he vehemently slandered him,
depriving him of his hereditary enfeoffment,
and all posthumous honors were withheld.
In the second month of the eighth year, he was ordered to concurrently hold the office of Grand Secretary of the Wǔyīngdiàn and participate in state affairs.
Initially,
È and Cōng had been summoned to court,
and the court officials, wishing to emulate the precedent of Mǎ Shùn in the previous dynasty,
intended to beat them to death at the Zuǒshùnmén.
They fled to the house of Guō Xūn, Marquis of Wǔdìng, and thus escaped.
Xūn then became deeply allied with him,
and also received imperial favor, being entrusted with command of the palace guards.
After a long time,
Xūn's treachery was fully exposed.
Cōng and Huò Tāo vigorously protected Xūn.
È, knowing the emperor already disliked Xūn,
alone memorialized on several of Xūn's violent, greedy, and cunning acts,
whereupon Xūn was punished.
Yáng Yīqīng, as Senior Grand Secretary, maintained a serious demeanor,
while È and Cōng liked to cause changes and disputes,
and also resented his dominance over them,
so they were unable to get along.
The Supervising Secretary Sūn Yìngkuí requested an assessment of the virtues and flaws of the three ministers,
and was most critical of È.
The emperor already suspected È,
and ordered him to clear up his past misdeeds,
to preserve the integrity of the relationship between ruler and minister from beginning to end.
È was then greatly alarmed,
memorialized in his defense,
and also claimed illness to request retirement.
The emperor replied,
"You, esteemed minister, must strive to act in accordance with public opinion,
so as not to betray your previous loyalty."
È became even more frightened.
The Supervising Secretary Wáng Zhǔn then impeached È for privately appointing Lǐ Mènghè as an imperial physician.
An edict was sent to the Ministry of Personnel,
stating that Mènghè's selection through examination was impartial.
The emperor remained suspicious,
and ordered the Imperial Academy of Medicine to re-examine him.
The censors, knowing the emperor's intention had shifted,
the Supervising Secretary Lù Càn vehemently denounced È's crimes,
and also mentioned Mènghè's bribery through È's family members, Wú Cóngzhōu and Xùbān Guìlín.
When the memorial was submitted,
the emperor was greatly enlightened,
and immediately stripped È of his office,
allowing him to retire as a Minister.
Cōng was also dismissed from government.
The emperor then again listed the crimes of the two men in an edict to court officials,
stating briefly:
"Their self-serving and reckless behavior,
betraying their ruler and their country,
their actions are clear for all to see,
and È is particularly egregious.
Legally, they deserve criminal punishment,
but they are specially pardoned."
He then sent Mènghè and others to the judicial authorities,
who all confessed.
Not long after,
Huò Tāo submitted two memorials in defense of È,
stating that Yīqīng and the judicial authorities had conspired to fabricate È's embezzlement charges.
Yīqīng then left office,
Zhōu Lún, Minister of Justice, was transferred to Nánjīng,
and the Langzhong and Yuánwàiláng were all stripped of their posts.
The emperor ordered the judicial authorities to re-examine the case with the Jǐnyī Wèi commander.
It was then declared that Mènghè and others had engaged in private dealings under false pretenses,
and that È was not involved.
An edict stripped Mènghè and Lín of their scholar status,
Cóngzhōu was sentenced,
and È was reinstated to a titular office.
At this time, Cōng had already been recalled.
Cài Qí, a scholar at the Historiography Academy, knowing the emperor would definitely restore È,
memorialized praising È's achievements,
and requested his recall.
The emperor then bestowed an imperial decree,
ordering the regional inspectors and surveillance commissioners to hasten him on his way.
Before È arrived,
Qián Cháo and other students of the Guózǐjiàn again requested È's hastened arrival.
The emperor angrily said,
"How dare you interfere with the advancement and retirement of great ministers?!"
And he sent Qí to the authorities.
In the fourth month of the following year, he returned to court,
all his stripped offices were restored,
and he again participated in state affairs.
È initially was keen on achieving fame and merit,
boldly undertook tasks,
and disregarded public opinion.
Suddenly suppressed and curtailed,
his spirit was intimidated,
and he dared not act recklessly again.
He remained in office for several months,
repeatedly claiming illness,
and the emperor always issued gracious edicts to comfort and retain him.
In the first month of the tenth year, he received permission to return home,
and died at his residence.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Tutor,
and given the posthumous name Wénxiāng.
È's memorials and treatises,
such as the *Lùn Dìwáng Xīnxué*, *Huángjí Lùn*, *Yì Fù Guà*, *Lǐ Yuèlìng*, and his presentation of the *Yǔ Gòng Tú* and *Yúdì Túshuō*,
all benefited the emperor's virtue and contemporary governance.
He was naturally suspicious and cruel,
and fond of rejecting those who differed from him,
which is why he was not tolerated by public opinion.
Initially, he and Cōng were extremely congenial,
but when they served together in the government,
they eventually fell out.
Fāng Xiànfū,
courtesy name Shūxián,
was a native of Nánhǎi.
He was orphaned early.
At twenty, he passed the imperial examination in the eighteenth year of Hóngzhì,
and was appointed a Shùjíshì.
He requested to return home to care for his mother,
and then observed mourning for his mother's death.
During the Zhèngdé reign,
he was appointed a Ministry of Rites Section Chief,
transferred to the Ministry of Personnel,
and promoted to Assistant Director.
He discussed philosophy with Section Chief Wáng Shǒurén,
was delighted by him,
and then asked to become his disciple.
Soon after, he resigned due to illness and returned home,
studying in Xīqiáo Mountain for ten years.
In the summer of the first year of Jiājìng, he returned to court,
and on the way heard
that the "Great Rites"
debate was undecided.
He drafted a memorial saying: The ritual systems of the Former Kings
were originally based on human emotions.
When gentlemen discuss affairs,
they should investigate names and realities.
I humbly observe that the recent discussions of the ritual officials
contain points that do not accord with human emotions,
and are not appropriate to names and realities,
one adhering to the words of the ritual classics,
the other following the theories of Song Confucians.
I alone hold this to be incorrect.
According to the *Sāngfú Zhuàn* of the *Lǐjīng*
it states,
"How can one become an heir?
A collateral son is acceptable."
It also states,
"Who becomes an heir for others?
One becomes heir for the main lineage."
"The main lineage
is the lineage of honor
and cannot be cut off.
Therefore, a collateral son from the clan becomes heir for the main lineage.
A legitimate son cannot become heir for the main lineage."
The purpose of this ritual
is that only if there is a collateral son
can one become an heir for others;
there has never been a case of cutting off another's lineage to become an heir for others.
Now, Emperor Xīngxiàn had only Your Majesty as a son,
with no other collateral sons.
To make him cut off his own lineage to become heir to Emperor Xiàozōng,
how can this be human emotion?!
Moreover, for one to be an heir,
the father must have established him as a son,
and the son must have served him as a father,
and thus upon death
wear his mourning clothes.
Now, Emperor Xiàozōng already had Emperor Wǔzōng,
and never considered Your Majesty his son.
Your Majesty never wore three years of mourning for Emperor Xiàozōng,
which truly means
you never became heir to Emperor Xiàozōng.
To forcibly call him "father"
how can this accord with names and realities?!
Those who make this argument
have not shown it to be in accord with the words of the ritual classics.
Furthermore, according to Chéng Yí's Púyì, it states
"Since Emperor Yīngzōng already considered Emperor Rénzōng as his father,
he should not consider King Pú as his kin."
This is not to say that the theory of the Song Confucians is bad,
but rather
that today's circumstances are different.
Emperor Rénzōng did raise Emperor Yīngzōng in the palace,
so they were truly father and son.
Emperor Xiàozōng never raised Your Majesty in the palace;
this is one difference.
Emperor Xiàozōng had Emperor Wǔzōng as a son,
whereas Emperor Rénzōng never had a son;
this is the second difference.
King Pú had other sons, so his lineage would not be cut off,
whereas Emperor Xīngxiàn had no other sons;
this is the third difference.
How can the affair of King Pú be compared to today's affair?
Those who make this argument
have not shown themselves to have correctly
articulated the theory of the Song Confucians.
If it is argued that Emperor Xiàozōng cannot be without an heir,
and therefore Your Majesty must be his son,
this is even more a failure to comprehend the Great Way.
Tracing the mind of Emperor Xiàozōng,
the reason
he would wish to have an heir
lies in not severing the ancestral sacrifices,
and not losing the importance of the altars of soil and grain, that is all.
Why must one be so constrained by the appellation of father and son,
and only then have
later!
Xiàozōng had Wǔzōng,
Wǔzōng had Your Majesty.
This means that the ancestral sacrifices are not cut off,
and the importance of the altars of earth and grain of the empire is not lost.
This is truly having an heir.
Furthermore,
Wǔzōng reigned over the empire for sixteen years.
If you cannot bear Xiàozōng being without an heir,
how can you bear Wǔzōng being without an heir?
This is an even more illogical argument.
Indeed,
Xīngxiàn Dì ought to be recognized as father,
but is not.
Xiàozōng ought not to be recognized as father,
but is forcibly called father.
Wǔzōng ought to be succeeded,
but is not
succeeded.
This is three errors in one move,
your servant has not seen how this can be acceptable.
Moreover, there has never been a country without a father.
When Gǔsǒu killed,
Shùn secretly carried him away and fled.
Now, if Your Majesty were to abandon your father and possess the empire,
what would be in Your Majesty's heart?
Your servant knows Your Majesty's pure filial heart,
that you would rather not possess the empire
than endure not recognizing your father as father.
The proponents of the other view also say that Xīng
xiàn Dì should not be called emperor.
This shows even less understanding of the Great Way.
Mencius said,
"Of the utmost acts of filial piety,
none is greater than honoring one's parents."
Zhōu Gōng posthumously ennobled Tài
wáng and Wáng Jì,
and Zǐsī considered it perfect filial piety.
How can a son be the Son of Heaven,
yet his father not be allowed to be called emperor?
Regarding the current matter,
your servant has previously put forward this argument: Your Majesty's succession to the two emperors
should be a succession to the imperial lineage (tǒng) but not to the family line (sì).
The distinction of Xīngxiàn's ancestral temple from the other temples
lies in calling
him Dì (Emperor) but not Zōng (Ancestor).
Indeed, the nature of emperors and kings
is different from that of scholars and commoners.
Succession to the imperial lineage (jìtǒng)
is a public matter of the empire,
the way of the Three Kings.
Succession to the family line (jìsì)
is a private matter
of an individual,
a practice of later generations.
Xīngxiàn's right to be called emperor
is because Your Majesty is the Son of Heaven.
His not being called Zōng
is because he never actually held
the throne.
I humbly beg that you make this known to your court officials,
and again refer to Xiàozōng as Huángbó (Imperial Uncle),
and Xīngxiàn Dì as Huángkǎo (Imperial Deceased Father),
and establish a separate temple for his sacrifices.
Only then will it be in accord with human
sentiment,
and match the name and reality.
Not only will this achieve the intention of the ancient kings' establishment of rites,
but it will also fulfill Your Majesty's pure filial heart.
When the memorial was prepared,
seeing that the court officials were strongly opposing and dissenting,
he feared to submit it.
It was seen by Guì È,
and together with Xí Shū's memorial, it was presented to the emperor.
The emperor was greatly pleased,
and immediately convened a court discussion.
The court officials then regarded Xiànfū as a wicked person,
to the point of not associating with him.
Xiànfū then shut his door and requested leave,
but since his request was not granted,
he presented "The Great Rites, Upper and Lower Treatises,"
which explained his arguments in even more detail.
At that time, Zhāng Cōng and Guì È had already been summoned from Nánjīng;
upon their arrival, they were immediately appointed as Hànlín Xuéshì,
and Xiànfū was appointed as Shìjiǎng Xuéshì.
Attacks arose from all quarters,
and Xiànfū also strongly declined.
The emperor ultimately adopted the proposal of these individuals and settled
"the Great Rites."
From then on, he enjoyed the emperor's favor on par with Cōng and È.
In the winter of the fourth year, he was promoted to Shào Zhānshì.
Xiànfū eventually felt uneasy
and resigned due to illness, returning home.
In the sixth year, he was summoned to compile the Mínglún Dàdiǎn.
Xiànfū and Huò Tāo were from the same district;
they became close friends due to their discussions on rites,
and also went to the summons together.
They then jointly submitted a memorial stating:
"Since ancient times, among those who strongly advocated for the argument of being an heir,
none was more prominent than Sīmǎ Guāng in the Sòng dynasty,
and none was more prominent than Wáng Mǎng in the Hàn dynasty.
Sīmǎ Guāng was the leader in advocating for the Pú discussion,
with Lǚ Huì, Fàn Chúnrén, and Lǚ Dàfáng supporting him,
and Guāng's argument was the most misleading.
Wáng Mǎng was the leader in advocating for Emperor Āi's discussion,
with Shī Dān, Zhēn Hán, and Liú Xīn supporting him,
and Mǎng's argument had the deepest pernicious influence.
Sòng Confucians adopted Wáng Mǎng's arguments to mislead myriad generations
and deceive later students.
Your servants have carefully consulted the Hàn Shū, Wèi Zhì, and Sòng Shǐ,
briefly collecting the memorials of Wáng Mǎng, Shī Dān, and Zhēn Hán,
along with the beginning and end of their affairs,
as well as the edicts of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
and the Pú Garden discussion,
to critically analyze them and append them to this.
We beg that it be submitted to the compilation officials,
for mutual reference and verification,
so that all officials and subjects under heaven may know that the argument for being an heir indeed originated from Mǎng,
and that the Sòng Confucians' arguments indeed came from Mǎng.
This will clarify all doubts below
and manifest the sacred filial piety above."
An imperial edict ordered his book to be sent to the Imperial Historiography Institute.
Soon after returning to court,
he was ordered to take charge of the Dàlǐ Sì affairs,
and, together with Cōng and È, to review the case of Lǐ Fúdá.
While È and others advocated for Mǎ Lù's execution,
Xiànfū strenuously argued,
and he was spared from death.
In September of that year, he was appointed Rìbù Yòu Shìláng,
concurrently holding the position of Xuéshì,
and lectured daily in the imperial lectures.
Soon after, he replaced È as Lìbù Zuǒ Shìláng,
and then replaced him again as Lǐbù Shàngshū.
When the Mínglún Dàdiǎn was completed,
he was promoted to Tàizǐ Tàibǎo.
Xiànfū, compared to Cōng and È, had a more broad and balanced temperament.
On occasion, he also held his ground on matters,
not entirely going along with them.
When È sought to reverse the case of Chén Guāng,
and requested the arrest and interrogation of all officials involved, such as Yè Yìngcōng,
many were spared arrest due to Xiànfū's words.
When Sī'ēn and Tiánzhōu suffered disturbances for consecutive years,
Xiànfū requested that Wáng Shǒurén be given sole responsibility,
and that the supervising eunuch Zhèng Rùn and the commander-in-chief Zhū Qí be dismissed.
The emperor then recalled Rùn and Qí.
After Sī and Tián were pacified,
Shǒurén proposed building cities and establishing prefectures.
È vehemently criticized this.
Xiànfū extensively recounted Shǒurén's achievements,
and the city construction was not stopped.
Cōng and È conspired against Yáng Yīqīng.
Xiànfū took advantage of ominous natural phenomena to propose a doctrine of harmony and moderation,
and also requested the recall of those banished, exiled, or stripped of their positions, such as Yú Kuān and Mǎ Mínghéng,
and that the number of successful candidates in the imperial examinations be doubled.
The emperor replied with a gracious edict,
but Kuān and others were ultimately not reinstated.
Xiànfū, considering that Buddhist nuns and Taoist priestesses harmed public morality,
requested that they be forced to marry.
The emperor agreed.
Also, following Huò Tāo's suggestion,
all unlicensed monks and Taoists were removed, and privately built temples and monasteries were destroyed.
When the emperor wished to minimize the funeral rites for Empress Chén,
Xiànfū strongly argued based on ritual principles.
Soon after, he again replaced È as Lìbù Shàngshū.
When È and Cōng were dismissed from power,
an edict ordered the Ministry of Personnel to investigate their private factions.
Xiànfū said:
"Among the hundred or so people impeached by Lù Càn and others,
not a few were falsely accused.
In the past, those who attacked Cōng and È
were removed because they were considered a faction.
Now, those who adhered to Cōng and È
are again removed because they are considered a faction.
When will the disaster for the gentry cease?"
He then memorialized to retain Huáng Wǎn and twenty-three others,
and to dismiss Chǔ Liángcái and twelve others.
Liángcái,
who was initially an imperial censor,
had been dismissed during an evaluation.
He had submitted a memorial denouncing Yáng Tínghé,
and identifying Lìbù Shìláng Mèng Chūn and others as a wicked faction.
È had then requested his reinstatement.
Now, he was dismissed,
and contemporary opinion applauded this.
When Ānchāng Bó Qián Wéiqí died,
his elder half-brother Wéiyuán requested to inherit the爵.
Xiànfū argued that the enfeoffment of imperial relatives by marriage should not be hereditary,
citing historical precedents from the Hàn, Táng, and Sòng dynasties as evidence.
The emperor approved his words
and submitted them for court discussion,
and hereditary enfeoffment for imperial relatives by marriage was subsequently abolished permanently.
Cōng, È having been recalled,
Yǔlín Commander Liú Yǒngchāng impeached Governor Guì Yǒng,
and the language implicated È and Minister of War Lǐ Chéngxūn.
He also impeached Censor Liáo Zìxiǎn,
and Zìxiǎn was arrested and jailed.
Afterwards,
he again denounced Ministry of War Director Lú Xiāng and others.
Xiànfū requested an investigation into Yǒngchāng,
so that wicked people would not use slanderous words to harm good people,
but the emperor did not agree.
Xiànfū then requested to retire,
which the emperor also did not permit.
Grand Secretary Sūn Yìngkuí impeached Xiànfū for favoring his relatives and old friends, Dali Shaoqing Xǐ Guāng and Taichang Qing Péng Zé,
but the emperor did not listen.
Supervising Secretary Xià Yán also impeached Xiànfū for corrupting the selection process,
relocating Zhāng Cōng's disliked Zhejiang Cánzhèng Huáng Qīng to Shǎnxī,
and appointing Cōng's favored partisans in their place.
The corrupt Péng Zé was promoted beyond his rank to Taichang,
and other people he favored
also showed evidence [of impropriety].
Suspecting Xiànfū of collusion and bribery,
the memorial was submitted,
and the emperor ordered Qīng and others to return to their former posts.
Xiànfū and Cōng memorialized their defense,
and subsequently requested to withdraw.
The emperor was reluctant to go against the wishes of the two men,
and again ordered Qīng and others to be as previously proposed.
Shortly thereafter,
Grand Secretary Xuē Jiǎ said:
"Liú Yǒngchāng, a military man, impeached a prime minister;
Zhāng Lán, a military supernumerary, impeached a meritorious official.
The low transcend the high,
and there is no knowing where it will stop.
I wish to preserve the principle of 'integrity and distance from the high,'
so that petty individuals may not freely attack and denounce."
The memorial was sent to the Ministry of Personnel.
Xiànfū and others requested to follow Jiǎ's words,
and the emperor ordered the Censorate to strictly forbid officials and commoners
from fabricating and disrupting governance,
and also instructed the Grand Secretaries and Censors of the two capitals and all provincial surveillance officials to discuss matters
by prioritizing the general good and not dwelling on minor flaws.
At that time,
the emperor was eager to broaden his insights
and fully understand the true feelings of all officials.
He was displeased with Xiànfū's proposal
and dismissed it.
Thereupon, Grand Secretary Ráo Xiù impeached Jiǎ for being sycophantic:
"Since Liú Yǒngchāng,
officials of the remonstrance office have not been heard to discuss high officials,
only Xià Yán, Sūn Yìngkuí, and Zhào Hàn have discussed Cōng and Xiànfū.
Hàn has already been reprimanded,
and Yán and Yìngkuí's memorials all concerned errors in personnel appointments and administration.
Jiǎ, however, points to these as trivial matters
and endlessly praises high officials.
Even a corrupt and unrestrained person like Guō Xūn
does not want people to speak ill of him.
If high officials are allowed to act arbitrarily,
and all other officials remain silent,
what if there is a traitor among them?
How dreadful!"
The memorial was submitted,
and the emperor inwardly approved of his words.
He sent it to the Ministry of Personnel for reconsideration.
Jiǎ submitted a detailed memorial explaining himself,
but the emperor disliked his not waiting for the Ministry's report,
and ordered him stripped of two ranks and banished.
The Ministry stated that Jiǎ had already been punished
and would not be discussed further.
The emperor ordered them to provide a response,
suspended Xiànfū's salary for one month,
and doubled it for the directors.
Xiànfū was uncomfortable
and twice memorialized, citing illness.
The emperor immediately granted his request,
but still kept the position vacant, awaiting him.
In the autumn of the tenth year, an imperial edict summoned him back.
Xiànfū memorialized his refusal,
recommending Liáng Cái, Wāng Hóng, and Wáng Tíngxiàng to replace him.
The emperor personally issued an edict of praise and reply,
and dispatched messenger Cài Ài to hasten him.
Ài arrived at his gate,
but Xiànfū secretly went into Xīqiáo,
using illness as an excuse to decline.
After a while, the imperial envoy arrived again,
saying he would be appointed to a different position,
so he set out.
The following May, he arrived in the capital,
and was ordered to serve in his former post, concurrently as Wǔyīngdiàn Dàxuéshì, entering the Grand Secretariat to assist in governance.
Earlier,
Xiànfū had been granted a silver seal inscribed with
"Zhōngchéng Zhíliàng" (Loyalty, Sincerity, Uprightness, Magnanimity),
with instructions to seal and report matters to the throne.
Xiànfū returned [home],
and presented it to the court;
now it was again granted as before.
When Minister of Personnel Wáng Qióng died,
Xiànfū was ordered to take charge.
Xiànfū, when at home,
held himself in high esteem;
when provincial surveillance officials came to visit, he would always claim illness and not receive them.
His family and in-laws acted arrogantly in the prefecture,
and local people repeatedly denounced them.
Cánshì Gōng Dàrěn listened to them.
When Xiànfū returned to court,
he entrusted Dàrěn with something.
It so happened that Dàrěn lost his post due to an incident,
suspected Xiànfū was behind it,
and thus memorialized several illegal acts,
with words involving Huò Tāo.
Xiànfū memorialized his defense,
and the emperor, who favored Xiànfū,
had Dàrěn arrested and stripped of his official status.
In October, a comet appeared in Dōngjǐng.
Censor Féng Ēn criticized Xiànfū as being cunning and adept at specious arguments,
manipulating power and influence,
which would be detrimental to the state,
hence the comet appeared when Xiànfū took charge of the Ministry of Personnel.
The emperor was enraged
and imprisoned him.
Xiànfū also cited illness and requested retirement,
but the emperor's gracious edict did not permit it.
Xiànfū feigned a reputation for tranquility and modesty,
but was repeatedly impeached,
causing him inner distress.
Although he held great power,
his spirit was low and despondent.
Only when the emperor wanted to kill Zhāng Yánlíng
did he constantly argue vigorously.
At that time, Guì È had already died.
Zhāng Cōng was most favored,
and had been dismissed from premiership many times.
Whenever Huò Tāo and Huáng Zōngmíng's statements were inappropriate,
they were immediately sent to the officials.
Xiànfū saw that the emperor's favor and authority were unpredictable,
and after holding office for two years,
he thrice memorialized, citing illness.
The emperor graciously permitted him,
ordered him to use post-carriages,
and granted him travel expenses.
He lived at home for ten years and then died.
He had previously been granted Zhùguó and Shàobǎo,
and was posthumously granted Tàibǎo
and the posthumous name Wénxiāng.
Xiànfū rapidly gained prominence due to the Great Rites controversy.
When working with Cōng and È,
his arguments were rather fair and lenient,
so people did not detest him greatly.
Xià Yán,
courtesy name Gōngjǐn,
was a native of Guìxī.
His father, Dǐng,
was the Prefect of Línqīng.
Yán passed the imperial examination in the twelfth year of Zhèngdé,
was appointed Xíngrén,
and promoted to Bīngkē Jǐshìzhōng.
He was intelligent and quick-witted,
and skilled in writing.
When he held the remonstrance post,
he prided himself on speaking frankly and fearlessly.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he memorialized:
"Since Zhèngdé,
obstruction has reached its extreme.
Now that Your Majesty is reforming various policies,
I request that after the morning court,
you go to the Wénhuádiàn to review memorials,
and summon Grand Secretaries for direct decisions.
Or, if a matter involves great benefit or harm,
then send it down for deliberation by court officials.
It is inappropriate to consult with close retainers
and directly issue imperial edicts from within the palace.
Whatever the emperor grants or rejects
must also be sent to the Grand Secretariat for deliberation before implementation,
thereby eliminating the abuses of obstruction and deceit."
The emperor praised and accepted his words.
He received an edict to, along with Censor Zhèng Běngōng and Bureau Secretary Wāng Wénshèng,
investigate redundant personnel in the imperial guards and capital garrisons.
They reduced 3,200 people
and submitted nine reform articles.
The capital was made orderly and clean.
In the early years of the Jiājìng reign,
Yán went with Censor Fán Jìzǔ and others to investigate crown lands,
and succeeded in restoring all the seized property to the people.
He impeached the eunuch Zhào Yún and the Marquis of Jiànchāng, Zhāng Yánlíng,
submitting seven memorials in total.
He requested that the crown lands adjacent to the palace, which were originally private imperial property, be converted into a silkworm farm and a public mulberry orchard,

and that all requests for land from imperial relatives and powerful families, as well as offerings of commoners' fields to princely estates by unscrupulous individuals from Hénán and Shāndōng, be forbidden.
He rescued Guō Jiǔgāo, the Prefect of Yǒngpíng, who had been arrested.
When Xíng Fúhǎi, brother of Concubine Zhuāngfèng, and Gù Fú, brother of Concubine Sùfèng,
received imperial decrees appointing them hereditary battalion commanders in the Imperial Bodyguard,
Yán vehemently argued against it.
His memorials were generally forthright and
were widely circulated.
He was repeatedly promoted to Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of War.
He investigated the merits and faults in suppressing bandits at Qīngyángshān,
and his reports and recommendations were all found to be sound.
When Vice Commissioner Niú Luán obtained a list of names of those collaborating with the bandits,
Yán suggested destroying it to reassure the public.
In the Xiàozōng emperor's reign,

it was ordered that the Ministries of Personnel and War should quarterly submit the résumés of high-ranking officials in the two capitals and civil and military officials in the provinces to the emperor for review.
This practice gradually fell into disuse after the Zhèngdé reign,
and Yán requested its revival.
In the seventh year [of Jiājìng],
he was transferred to the Ministry of Personnel.
At this time,
the emperor was keenly focused on matters of ritual and ceremony.
Believing that the joint worship of Heaven and Earth was improper,
he wished to establish separate altars for them,
making them four alongside the altars for the Sun and Moon.
Grand Secretary Zhāng Fújìng dared not make a decision,
and the emperor's divination to Grand Ancestor Tàizǔ was also inauspicious,
so the discussion was temporarily shelved.
Coincidentally, Yán submitted a memorial requesting the emperor to personally plough at the Southern Altar,
and the empress to personally tend silkworms at the Northern Altar,
to set an example for the empire.
The emperor, seeing the idea of Northern and Southern Altars
as aligning with his proposal for separate altars,
ordered Fújìng to convey his command,
and Yán then requested separate worship for Heaven and Earth.
Court officials objected,
and Fújìng also found it difficult,
with Grand Secretary Huò Tāo being particularly forceful in his condemnation.
The emperor was furious,
and imprisoned Tāo.
He issued an imperial decree commending Yán,
granted him a fourth-rank official's robes and salary,
and ultimately adopted his request.
He also supported the proposal for subsidiary deities to be worshipped at the two altars,
details of which are found in the Ritual Records.
From then on, Yán received great imperial favor.
When construction began on the altars,
Yán was immediately appointed to supervise it.
When Yánsuí experienced famine,
Yán recommended Assistant Censor-in-Chief Lǐ Rúguī as Governor.
The Ministry of Personnel nominated a replacement for Rúguī,
but the emperor rejected it,
and then nominated Yán himself.
Censor Xióng Jué accused Yán of recommending Rúguī for his own benefit,
even comparing him to Zhāng Cǎi.
The emperor severely reprimanded Jué
and ordered Yán not to respond.
But Yán was indignant,
accused Jué, and declined the new appointment,
whereupon the emperor desisted.
Fújìng directed all officials with a nod,
and none dared to resist him.
Yán, confident in the emperor's favor,
alone refused to defer to him.
Fújìng then became deeply jealous of Yán's favor,
and Yán also resented Fújìng for swiftly appointing Péng Zé as Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices without favoring him.
Thus, a rift formed between the two.
Yán submitted a strong memorial impeaching Fújìng and Minister of Personnel Fāng Xiànfū.
Fújìng and Xiànfū both memorialized in their defense, requesting to resign.
The emperor was deeply fond of all of them
and reconciled the two parties.
Having risen to prominence,
Yán confronted Fújìng, Xiànfū, and Tāo,
and further solidified his reputation for being strong and upright.
The emperor wished to compile the suburban rituals into a comprehensive book,
and promoted Yán to Academician Expositor,
appointed him a Compiler,
and assigned him to the daily lectures at the imperial study,
while retaining his concurrent post as Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Personnel.
Yán also supported the emperor in revising the sacrificial rites at the Temple of Confucius and the Grand Dì Sacrifice,
which pleased the emperor even more.
In the third month of the tenth year, he was promoted to Junior Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent,
concurrently Academician of the Hànlín Academy,
in charge of academy affairs,
and his lecturing duties continued as before.
Yán had clear, bright eyes and eyebrows,
a beautiful beard,
and spoke with a clear and eloquent voice,
without a provincial accent.
Whenever he lectured,
the emperor would fix his gaze on him,
intending to give him a major appointment.
Fújìng's jealousy intensified,
and he then conspired with Péng Zé to orchestrate the case of Xuē Kǎn,
which led to Yán being handed over to the judicial authorities.
Later,
the emperor realized Fújìng's unfairness,
dismissed Fújìng, and released Yán.
In the eighth month,
when the construction of the four altars was completed,
Yán was promoted to Left Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites,
still in charge of academy affairs.
A month later,
he replaced Lǐ Shí as Minister of the Ministry.
To become a Minister of one of the Six Ministries less than a year after leaving the Censorate
was unprecedented.
At that time, scholar-officials still disliked Fújìng
and relied on Yán to resist him.
Yán, having gained the emperor's favor through his astuteness,
also humbled himself before scholars.
Censors Yù Xīlǐ and Shí Jīn requested clemency for
the officials who had been implicated in the
"Grand Rites" major purge.
The emperor was furious
and ordered Yán to impeach them.
Yán stated that Xīlǐ and Jīn had no ulterior motives
and requested the emperor to pardon them.
The emperor rebuked Yán for his response,
arrested the two and imprisoned them in the imperial prison,
and exiled them far away,
and Yán accepted his fault, whereupon the matter ceased.
Because of this, he gained great renown among the high officials.
Many of the emperor's creations of rites and music
were based on Yán's proposals when he was Minister,
while Grand Secretaries Lǐ Shí and Zhái Luán merely filled their positions.
Whenever the emperor composed poetry,
he would bestow it upon Yán,
who would always compose a reply and engrave it on stone to present to the emperor,
which pleased the emperor even more.
He would reply to imperial inquiries and compose pieces as ordered,
completing them instantly when expected.
He was frequently summoned for audiences,
where he was consulted on state affairs,
and was skilled at discerning the emperor's intentions,
often making suitable connections.
He was given a silver seal,
allowing him to submit sealed memorials,
with the inscription
"Profound Learning and Superior Talent."
He was successively granted robes with embroidered pythons, flying fish, and qílín, jade belts, double-gilt items, fine wines, rare delicacies, and seasonal gifts every month without fail.
Fújìng and Xiànfū subsequently returned to assist in government.
Knowing the emperor's deep affection for Yán,
they also dared not contend with him.
Later, they both retired from office,
and among the proponents of ritual reform, only Huò Tāo remained,
who relentlessly sought revenge against Yán.
In the fifteenth year, regarding the matter of Liú Shúxiàng, Prefect of Shùntiān Prefecture,
Tāo and Yán attacked and denounced each other.
Tāo ultimately lost,
the details of which are in Tāo's biography.
Yán's arrogance grew from then on.
When Bureau Directors Zhāng Yuánxiào and Lǐ Suì had a minor disagreement with him,
he immediately memorialized for their demotion.
When the imperial prince was born,
the emperor bestowed lavish gifts upon Yán.
He was initially given the title of Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
and then promoted to Junior Mentor and concurrently Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent.
In the intercalary twelfth month, he concurrently became Grand Secretary of Wǔyīng Hall, participating in important state affairs.
During an imperial visit to the imperial tombs,
upon returning to Shāhé,
a fire broke out in Yán's kitchen,
extending to the tents of Guō Xūn and Lǐ Shí,
and six of Yán's memorials entrusted to the emperor were also burned.
Yán should have solely taken the blame,
but he apologized jointly with Xūn and others,
and was consequently reprimanded.
At this time, Lǐ Shí was the Senior Grand Secretary,
but most policies originated from Yán.
When Gù Dǐngchén joined the cabinet,
relying on his seniority and age, he somewhat wished to have a say.
Yán was displeased,
so Dǐngchén dared not contend with him.
That winter,
Shí passed away,
and Yán became the Senior Grand Secretary.
In the eighteenth year,
for presenting the memorial and tablet for the ritual of venerating Huangtian Shangdi,
he was granted the titles of Junior Preceptor, Grand Master of Glorious Happiness, and Pillar of State.
No subject in the Ming dynasty had ever been granted the title of Pillar of State;
Yán had proposed it for himself.
Wǔdìng Hóu Guō Xūn 郭勛 gained favor,
and spoke ill of Yán Sōng 言嵩.
And Lǐbù Shàngshū Yán Sōng 嚴嵩 also secretly envied Yán 言.
Yán 言 and Sōng 嵩 accompanied the emperor's carriage to Chéngtiān 承天.
When the emperor finished his visit to Xiǎnlíng 顯陵,
Sōng 嵩 again requested to present a congratulatory memorial.
Yán 言 begged to wait until they returned to the capital.
The emperor dismissed it,
feeling greatly displeased.
Sōng 嵩 understood the emperor's intention,
and insisted on requesting it.
The emperor then said:
"It is permissible for rites and music to originate from the Son of Heaven."
He ordered a congratulatory memorial,
and from then on, the emperor was displeased with Yán 言.
When the emperor visited Dàyù Shān 大峪山,
Yán 言 was slightly late in submitting the edict for overseeing the capital.
The emperor reproached him,
and Yán 言, fearing, asked for punishment.
The emperor was furious and said:
"Yán 言, originally of low office,
advanced due to his sincerity in discussing the suburban sacrifices,
yet now he is negligent and disrespectful,
submitting secret memorials without using the bestowed seal.
Return all the hand-written edicts that have been accumulated and bestowed."
Yán 言 became even more afraid and
submitted a memorial of apology.
He requested exemption from the retrieval of the silver seal and hand-written edicts,
for the glory of his descendants for a hundred generations,
the words were very sorrowful.
The emperor's anger did not subside,
suspecting Yán 言 of damaging or destroying them,
and ordered the Lǐbù 禮部 to retrieve them.
His rank of Shǎoshī 少師 and honorary title were stripped,
and he was made to retire as Shǎobǎo Shàngshū Dàxuéshì 少保尚書大學士.
Yán 言 then submitted over four hundred hand-written edicts
along with the silver seal.
After several days,
the anger subsided,
and an order was given to halt the proceedings.
He was reinstated as Shǎofù 少傅 and Tàizǐ Tàifù 太子太傅 to enter court duty.
Yán 言 submitted a memorial of apology.
The emperor was pleased,
and instructed him to be diligent in his initial loyalty,
to uphold justice and impartiality,
and avoid public resentment.
Yán 言 knew in his heart that "public resentment"
referred to Guō Xūn 郭勛 and his ilk,
and submitted another memorial of apology.
He stated that he dared not place himself behind others,
was single-minded and independent,
and thus resented by the masses.
The emperor was again displeased
and questioned and reprimanded him.
He apologized in fear and trembling,
and then it stopped.
Not long after,
lightning struck the Fèntiān Diàn 奉天殿.
Yán 言 and Dǐngchén 鼎臣 were summoned but
did not arrive in time.
The emperor again questioned and reproached them,
ordering the Lǐbù 禮部 to impeach them.
Yán 言 and others sought punishment,
and the emperor again reproached Yán 言 for his arrogance,
and also criticized Dǐngchén 鼎臣.
Afterward,
the retrieved silver seal and imperial writings were returned.
When good news came from Shǎnxī 陝西,
he was reinstated as Shǎoshī 少師 and Tàizǐ Tàishī 太子太師,
promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū 吏部尚書,
and Wúyīng Diàn Dàxuéshì 武英殿大學士.
When the bandits in Jiāng-Huái 江淮 were pacified,
he received an imperial letter of commendation,
bestowed with gold and silk,
and also granted the full salary of a Dàxuéshì 大學士.
Dǐngchén 鼎臣 had already passed away,
and Zhái Luán 翟鑾 re-entered the court,
behaving deferentially as if he were a subordinate official,
not daring to show any discord.
However, Huò Tāo 霍韜 entered to take charge of the Zhānshì Fǔ 詹事府,
and repeatedly sought to settle grievances.
Knowing that Guō Xūn 郭勛 and Yán 言 had a rift,
he allied with Xūn 勛 to assist himself,
and the three daily plotted against each other.
Eventually, Tāo 韜 died,
and Yán 言 and Xūn 勛 continued their animosity as before.
When the Nine Temples suffered a disaster,
Yán 言 was on leave due to illness,
and begged to be dismissed,
but it was not granted.
When Zhāoshèng Tàihòu 昭聖太后 passed away,
an imperial edict inquired about the mourning attire for the Crown Prince,
and Yán 言's reported memorial contained a mistaken character.
The emperor severely reprimanded Yán 言,
who apologized and begged to return home to treat his illness.
The emperor became even angrier,
and ordered him to retire as Shǎobǎo Shàngshū Dàxuéshì 少保尚書大學士.
When Yán 言 first heard of the emperor's anger,
he submitted fourteen strategies for border defense,
hoping to resolve the situation.
The emperor said:
"Since Yán 言 possesses loyal strategies,
why does he so stubbornly cherish himself and
betray my trust and reliance?
Let us not question it for now."
Initially,
Yán 言's composition of Daoist prayer texts and other writings
most pleased the emperor.
When Yán 言 was dismissed,
only Zhái Luán 翟鑾 remained,
who was not urgently needed by the emperor.
When Yán 言 was about to leave the capital,
he went to the Xīyuàn Zhāigōng 西苑齋宮 to prostrate himself in gratitude.
The emperor heard of it and pitied him,
especially bestowing wine and food,
ordering him to return to his private residence to treat his illness,
and await further orders.
At this time, Guō Xūn 郭勛 was heavily impeached by censors,
and also took leave due to illness.
Jīngshān Hóu Cuī Yuán 京山侯崔元, newly favored,
was on duty in the Nèiyuàn 內苑,
and was jealous of Xūn 勛.
The emperor casually asked Yuán 元:
"Yán 言 and Xūn 勛 are both my trusted aides,
why do they envy each other?"
Yuán 元 did not answer.
The emperor asked when Yán 言 would return,
and he said:
"He will only dare to request it
after Your Majesty's birthday."
He then asked what illness Xūn 勛 had,
and he said:
"Xūn 勛 has no illness;
he will come out as soon as Yán 言 returns."
The emperor nodded.
The censors, knowing that the emperor favored Yán 言 and disliked Xūn 勛,
then jointly impeached Xūn 勛.
Xūn 勛's defense was rebellious and abusive,
the emperor was angry,
and stripped Xūn 勛's colleague Wáng Tíngxiàng 王廷相 from his register.
Gěishìzhōng Gāo Shí 給事中高時,
who was close to Yán 言,
exposed more than ten cases of Xūn 勛's corruption, recklessness, and unlawfulness.
Thereupon, Xūn 勛 was imprisoned,
and Yán 言 was reinstated as Shǎofù 少傅, Tàizǐ Tàishī 太子太師, Lǐbù Shàngshū 禮部尚書, and Wǔyīngdiàn Dàxuéshì 武英殿大學士.
When his illness was cured, he returned to court duty.
Even though Yán 言 was on leave,
many cabinet affairs were decided by him.
The handling of Xūn 勛's imprisonment
was entirely under his instruction.
In the spring of the twenty-first year,
after nine years in the first rank,
a eunuch was dispatched to bestow silver and silk, precious paper money, sheep, wine, and imperial cuisine,
fully restoring his official ranks.
An imperial letter praised him,
and a banquet was given at the Lǐbù 禮部,
with the Shàngshū 尚書, Shìláng 侍郎, and Dū Yùshǐ 都御史 accompanying him.
At this time,
although the emperor treated Yán 言 with courtesy,
his favor and affection were not as strong as before.
When the two empress dowagers Cíqìng 慈慶 and Cíníng 慈寧 passed away,
Xūn 勛 had once requested to convert one of their palaces for the Crown Prince.
Yán 言 disagreed,
which pleased the emperor.
Now, the emperor suddenly asked where the Crown Prince should reside.
Yán 言 forgot his previous words,
and, considering the troublesome expense of new construction,
replied according to Xūn 勛's suggestion.
The emperor was displeased.
He also suspected that the censors' impeachment of Xūn 勛 originated from Yán 言's intention.
When the Dàxiǎng Diàn 大享殿 was being built,
the emperor ordered the eunuch Gāo Zhōng 高忠 to supervise it,
but Yán 言 did not submit the edict.
The emperor allowed all officials on duty in the Xīyuàn 西苑 to ride horses,
and also bestowed fragrant leaf hair ties
and shoes made of leather and silk.
Yán 言 considered these not to be the proper attire for imperial subjects,
did not accept them,
and also rode only in a waist sedan chair.
The emperor had accumulated several grievances and wanted to dismiss Yán 言,
and Yán Sōng 嚴嵩 thereby found an opportunity to instigate against him.
Yán Sōng was from the same hometown as Yán Shìfán,
whom he addressed as his elder and superior,
serving him with great deference.
When Yán Shìfán entered the Grand Secretariat, he promoted Sōng to take his place,
treating him like a retainer.
Sōng felt deeply resentful.
After Yán Shìfán lost the emperor's favor,
Sōng gained increasing imperial寵 due to his submissive flattery.
Yán Shìfán feared being dismissed,
so he called Sōng to consult with him.
However, Sōng had already secretly visited the residence of Táo Zhòngwén
to plot against Yán Shìfán and take his position.
Yán Shìfán knew this and was very angry,
so he hinted to the censors to repeatedly impeach Sōng.
But the emperor, who favored Sōng at the time, did not listen.
The two then had a major falling out.
In the sixth month,
Sōng had a private audience,
bowing his head and weeping profusely,
accusing Yán Shìfán of insulting him.
The emperor ordered him to fully enumerate Yán Shìfán's offenses.
Sōng then fiercely exposed his shortcomings.
The emperor was furious
and personally issued an imperial edict to the Ministry of Rites,
listing Yán Shìfán's many crimes,
and further stating:
"Guō Xūn has already been imprisoned,
yet there are still countless schemes.
The censors are the eyes and ears of the court,
but they listen only to Yán Shìfán's commands.
If I do not hold court early,
Yán Shìfán also does not enter the Grand Secretariat.
Important military and state affairs
are decided in his private residence.
Crucial imperial decrees
are treated as mere playthings.
The censors do not utter a single word
but only deceive and slander the sovereign,
provoking the wrath of gods and spirits,
causing heavy rains that damage crops."
Yán Shìfán was greatly terrified
and pleaded for punishment.
After more than ten days,
on the anniversary of Xiàndì's passing,
he was still summoned to pay respects
and wait at the Western Garden.
Yán Shìfán then expressed his gratitude and requested to retire,
speaking with extreme sorrow.
His memorial was held for eight days.
Then, on the first day of the seventh month, there was a total solar eclipse.
An imperial edict was issued stating:
"The excessive solar eclipse
is precisely due to the fault of subordinates disrespecting superiors.
Therefore, Yán Shìfán is to be dismissed from all his posts and live in seclusion."
The emperor also personally cited three of his own faults
and announced them to the world.
Censor Qiáo Yòu, Supervising Secretary Shěn Liángcái, and others all submitted memorials condemning Yán Shìfán
and requesting punishment.
The emperor was greatly angered
and demoted thirteen people.
Gāo Shí, due to his impeachment of Xūn,
was uniquely banished to a distant frontier.
Thus, Yán Sōng then replaced Yán Shìfán in the Grand Secretariat.
Yán Shìfán had been powerful for a long time,
his family was wealthy and prosperous,
his attire and possessions were extravagant,
and he frequently exchanged gifts and greetings.
After a long time without being summoned,
the surveillance commissioners, prefects, and county magistrates also gradually became lax and disrespectful towards him,
making him melancholic and unhappy.
On New Year's Day and the emperor's birthday, he would always submit memorials of congratulations,
calling himself a "subject of the grass and earth."
The emperor gradually took pity on him,
restoring him as Minister of Rites and Grand Secretary.
By the twenty-fourth year,
the emperor vaguely sensed Sōng's greed and arrogance,
and again thought of Yán Shìfán.
He dispatched an official with an imperial edict to summon him back,
restoring all his official ranks, including Junior Mentor.
Sōng was also granted the title of Junior Mentor,
as if to be on par with Yán Shìfán.
When Yán Shìfán arrived,
he directly overshadowed Sōng.
Whatever he approved or replied to,
he hardly considered Sōng.
Sōng was so intimidated he dared not utter a single word.
Regarding his personal protégés,
Yán Shìfán dismissed and banished them,
and Sōng dared not save them,
hating him to the core.
Scholars and officials nationwide, who resented Sōng's greed and malice,
believed that Yán Shìfán could suppress Sōng and control his fate,
and were deeply pleased.
However, because Yán Shìfán had been out of power for a long time,
he strove to assert his authority.
The banishment of Gāo Jiǎn, the Director of the Bureau of Personnel,
the dismissal of Táng Lóng, Xǔ Chéngmíng, Cuī Tóng, Wáng Yòngbīn, and Huáng Zuǒ,
and the imprisonments of Wáng Gǎo, Wáng Wěi, and Sūn Jìlǔ
were all instigated by Yán Shìfán.
Wáng Xuéyì, the Governor of Guìzhōu, and Hé Áo, the Governor of Shāndōng, were impeached by censors at his instigation,
and he would draft edicts for their arrest and interrogation.
Táng Lóng was formerly close to Sōng.
The case of Wáng Wěi involved Yán Shìfán's son Yán Shìfān.
Other condemnations and banishments were not entirely just,
making court officials wary.
Finally, Censor Chén Qíxué impeached Cuī Yuán and the Imperial Guard Commander Lù Bǐng regarding salt administration.
Yán Shìfán drafted an edict ordering them to present their cases.
Both went to Yán Shìfán to plead for their lives.
Lù Bǐng knelt for a long time before he was spared.
These two were allied with Sōng and framed Yán Shìfán,
but Yán Shìfán did not realize it.
The emperor frequently sent junior eunuchs to Yán Shìfán's residence.
Yán Shìfán, proud and aloof,
treated them like servants.
Sōng, however, would always invite them to sit
and personally place gold and money into their sleeves.
Because of this, they daily praised Sōng and spoke ill of Yán Shìfán.
Yán Shìfán's petitions (qīngcí) often failed to meet the emperor's intentions.
Sōng, hearing this, became even more meticulous in handling his own.
Before long,
the discussion about the Hétáo region arose.
Yán Shìfán had always prided himself on his strategic and economic capabilities,
desiring to achieve extraordinary accomplishments.
Thus, when Zēng Xiǎn, the Governor-General of Shǎnxī, requested to reclaim the Hétáo,
he enthusiastically supported it.
Sōng, along with Yuán and Bǐng, slandered him in the midst of this,
and he ultimately failed because of it.
Sū Gāng of Jiāngdū
was Yán Shìfán's stepfather-in-law,
and was very close to Zēng Xiǎn.
As Zēng Xiǎn was requesting to reclaim the Hétáo,
Sū Gāng urgently recommended him to Yán Shìfán.
Yán Shìfán, relying on Zēng Xiǎn's ability to handle the matter,
secretly memorialized to recommend him,
stating that no other official was as loyal as Zēng Xiǎn.
The emperor ordered Yán Shìfán to draft an edict,
twice generously commending Zēng Xiǎn.
Zēng Xiǎn was pleased,
and became even more determined to launch an expedition.
Suddenly, the emperor issued an edict of reprimand,
in very stern language.
Sōng guessed the emperor's intentions
and vigorously argued that the Hétáo could not be reclaimed,
his words implicating Yán Shìfán.
Yán Shìfán was greatly terrified and apologized,
also stating that Sōng had never held a differing opinion,
but was now shifting all blame onto him.
The emperor accused Yán Shìfán of coercing the sovereign and intimidating the public.
Sōng again submitted a memorial attacking Yán Shìfán,
who also vigorously defended himself.
But the emperor had already fallen for Sōng's slander
and was irreconcilably angry.
In the first month of the twenty-seventh year, all of Yán Shìfán's official ranks were revoked,
and he was made to retire as Minister of Rites.
The emperor still had no intention of killing him.
However, there were rumors circulating in the forbidden palace
that Yán Shìfán was resentful and slandering the emperor when he left.
Sōng again drafted a memorial on behalf of Chóu Luán, denouncing Yán Shìfán for accepting gold from Zēng Xiǎn
and engaging in illicit profiteering.
The matter implicated Sū Gāng,
leading to Zēng Xiǎn and Sū Gāng being sent to the imperial prison.
Sōng, along with Yuán and Bǐng, conspired
to have Zēng Xiǎn executed for "colluding with close attendants,"
and Sū Gāng banished to the frontier.
Officials were dispatched to arrest Yán Shìfán.
When Yán Shìfán reached Tōngzhōu,
he heard of Zēng Xiǎn's sentence,
and was so shocked that he fell from his carriage, exclaiming:
"Alas!
I am doomed!"
He again submitted a memorial of appeal,
stating:
"Chóu Luán was just apprehended,
and the emperor's edict was issued less than two days ago.
How could Chóu Luán have known the emperor's words,
and how could he have known Sōng's memorial and attached himself to it like this?
It is Sōng and Cuī Yuán and their ilk who falsely fabricated this to ruin me.
Sōng, with his calm demeanor and common transgressions, resembles Gònggōng;
his humility and deference to scholars resemble Wáng Mǎng;
his cunning manipulation of power and his father-son monopoly on power resemble Sīmǎ Yì.
Inside, all officials are entrapped by him,
knowing Sōng but not knowing Your Majesty.
Outside, all officials are controlled by him,
also knowing Sōng but not knowing Your Majesty.
My life and death are in Sōng's grasp.
I only entrust myself to Your Sacred Mercy,
and beg for your preservation."
The emperor did not heed him.
When the trial was concluded,
Yù Màojiān, Minister of Justice, and Tú Qiáo, Censor-in-Chief on the Left, argued that Yán Shìfán deserved death,
but also cited the "deliberation on nobility and ability" clause to commute the sentence.
The emperor did not agree,
severely reprimanding Yù Màojiān and others,
and stripping them of their salaries,
even bringing up Yán Shìfán's previous offense of not wearing the incense crown.
In the tenth month of that year, Yán Shìfán was finally executed in the marketplace.
His wife, Sū, was exiled to Guǎngxī.
His cousin's son, Kèchéng, an attendant secretary, and his cousin's grandson, Cháoqìng, an assistant minister of the Imperial Seal,
were stripped of their official status and made commoners.
Yán Shìfán was sixty-seven years old when he died.
Yán was bold and eloquent with outstanding talent,
debating with a broad and profound range,
and no one could refute him.
Having received special favor,
he deduced that the emperor did not wish his subjects to form factions,
so he daily contended with the noble officials who were discussing the rites.
The emperor, believing he was not partisan,
treated him with even greater kindness.
However, he was ultimately ousted by Yán Sōng.
After Yán's death,
Sōng's calamity spread throughout the realm,
and only much later did many regret Yán's demise.
The Xú Jiē whom Yán had recommended
later managed to remove Sōng and became a famous prime minister.
In the early Lóngqìng reign,
his family submitted a petition to clear his name,
and an imperial edict restored his official position,
granted him sacrificial offerings and burial,
and posthumously named him Wénmǐn.
Yán initially had no sons.
His concubine became pregnant,
but his wife, out of jealousy, married her off,
and she bore a son.
After Yán's death,
his wife brought the son back,
and his appearance greatly resembled Yán's.
He had even obtained an official position,
but suddenly fell ill and died.
Yán ultimately had no descendants.
A eulogy says: Cōng, È, and Xiànfū's proposal to elevate Xìngxiàn Dì's status
was based on a son's deepest emotions,
hence their arguments were easily accepted.
Initially, their proposals were never out of line with human sentiment and ritual propriety,
but then, having encountered a favorable time and gained the emperor's trust,
they consistently invoked discussions of rites to secure their own positions,
eager to indulge in favors and revenge.
Thus, one realizes that the intention behind their proposals
was not a genuine and earnest loyalty and love,
seeking to guide their sovereign onto the proper path.
The rituals and ceremonies that Yán proposed and settled
also contained much that was commendable.
However, his arrogance and excessive ambition
ultimately led to his ousting by Sōng.
Upon a comprehensive review of these individuals' conduct and the right and wrong of their statements,
it is indeed clear that the two aspects do not obscure each other.
Collation Notes
Biographies 85: Xí Shū (Dìchūn, Zhuàn) Huò Tāo (Zǐyǔxiá) Xióng Jiá Huáng Zōngmíng Huáng Wǎn (Lù Chéng)
Xí Shū,
courtesy name Wéntóng,
a native of Suíníng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the third year of Hóngzhì.
He was appointed Magistrate of Tánchéng.
He entered the capital as a Principal in the Ministry of Works,
then transferred to the Ministry of Revenue,
and was promoted to Supernumerary Assistant Minister.
In the sixteenth year,
there was a daytime eclipse and an earthquake in Yúnnán,
and Vice Minister Fán Yíng was ordered to inspect the area,
resulting in the impeachment of over three hundred officials, from Surveillance Commissioners downwards.
Shū submitted a memorial saying:
"Calamities are related to the imperial court,
not to Yúnnán.
It is like when a person's vital energy is damaged internally,
and then sores erupt on the four limbs.
The imperial court
is the vital energy.
Yúnnán
is the four limbs.
How can one abandon the source of the poison
and exclusively treat the extremities?
Currently, the inner treasury's provisions are several times those of previous years,
there are thousands of redundant officials,
tens of thousands of enrolled *xiàowèi*,
sacrificial rituals and temples are active daily,
weaving is frequently commissioned,
and rewards exceed proper limits;
imperial relatives seize people's land,
and eunuchs are endlessly dispatched;
in major judicial cases, those accused dare not defend themselves based on their confessions,
and judicial officials dare not uphold justice;
wise high-ranking officials are not appointed,
and junior officials who spoke out and were demoted are not reinstated;
civil and military officials are promoted by rotation,
leading to a great abuse of official titles.
The warning of calamities
happens to manifest in Yúnnán,
and one wishes to make distant provincial officials bear the responsibility—
what logic is this?
The Hàn dynasty sent eight envoys to tour the empire,
and Zhāng Gāng alone said: 'When jackals and wolves block the road,
why ask about foxes?'
Now Fán Yíng's duty is to inspect,
but he cannot impeach imperial relatives and high-ranking officials,
only examining and dismissing Yúnnán officials,
addressing the symptoms but not the root cause.
I beg Your Majesty to rectify
all the malpractices I have mentioned.
Other great harms that should be eliminated
and major policies that should be implemented
should all be ordered for relevant departments to propose and reform."
At the time, this advice was not adopted.
During the reign of Wǔzōng,
he successively served as Surveillance Commissioner of Hénán and Provincial Education Vice Commissioner of Guìzhōu.
At that time, Wáng Shǒurén was exiled as the stationmaster of Lóngcháng Station,
and Shū selected promising students from prefectures and counties,
inviting Shǒurén to teach them,
whereupon scholars began to seek learning.
He was repeatedly promoted to Left Administration Commissioner of Fújiàn.
When Prince Chén Háo of Níng rebelled,
he urgently recruited twenty thousand soldiers to suppress him.
Upon arrival, the rebels had already been pacified,
so he returned.
Soon after, he was appointed Vice Censor-in-Chief and Grand Coordinator of Húguǎng.
Eunuchs Lǐ Zhèn and Zhāng Yáng, under the guise of tribute and imperial salt, extorted over 100,000 *liǎng*,
which Shū exposed in a memorial.
In the first year of Jiājìng, he was transferred to Right Vice Minister of War in Nánjīng.
A great famine struck the areas north and south of the Jiāng River,
and he was ordered to provide relief in the area north of the Jiāng River.
He ordered prefectures and counties to set up relief stations every ten *lǐ*,
to cook gruel and feed the people,
saving countless lives.
Previously,
when Shū was in Húguǎng,
he observed that the central court's discussion
on the "Great Rites"
had not yet been settled.
Sensing the emperor's inclination towards Zhāng Cōng and Huò Tāo,
he offered a proposal, stating:
"In the past, Sòng Yīngzōng, the thirteenth son of Prince Pú, was adopted as an heir;
today, His Majesty, the eldest son of Xìngxiàn Wáng, has succeeded to the imperial throne.
Yīngzōng's adoption occurred when he was already on the throne wearing the imperial robes,
whereas His Majesty's succession came after the imperial carriage had already passed away.
Those who argue that Your Majesty succeeded Wǔzōng,
while remaining the son of Xìngxiàn Dì,
and establishing a separate ancestral temple,
the proposals of Zhāng Cōng and Huò Tāo are not incorrect.
However, there cannot be two emperors.
In relation to Wǔzōng, Your Majesty is a brother by kinship,
and a subject by status.
Since Xiàozōng has been enshrined as the principal ancestor in the ancestral temple,
can there be any other designation?
It is fitting to refer to him as 'Imperial Father Xìngxiàn Wáng,'
this being an unalterable principle for all ages.
The persistent appeals of three or four ritual officials
were not misguided.
However, rites are rooted in human sentiment,
and for Your Majesty, exalted as the Son of Heaven,
if the Benevolent Mother has no honorific title,
would that be acceptable?
Therefore, honoring one's birth mother as empress dowager,
to comfort the benevolent mother,
this is an emotion that cannot be suppressed.
For the current discussion,
it is appropriate to designate him as 'Imperial Father Xìngxiàn Dì.'
A separate temple should be established within the imperial palace,
and after performing sacrifices at the Imperial Ancestral Temple annually,
he should still be worshipped with the rites of an emperor;
this might be a viable path.
For establishing a separate temple ensures the legitimacy of the imperial succession and orderly generations,
and conferring a special honorific ensures profound filial love and the preservation of the direct lineage,
thus honoring the honorable and loving one's kin can proceed without conflict.
As for the Benevolent Mother, she should be titled 'Imperial Mother Empress [surname],'
and the title 'Xìngxiàn' should not be added.
'Xiàn'
is a posthumous title;
how can it be added today?"
Once the proposal was complete,
officials in the imperial court contended fiercely, slandering Zhāng Cōng as having heretical views.
Shū, fearing, dared not submit it,
but secretly showed it to Guì È.
È approved of its argument.
In the first month of the third year,
È formally submitted a memorial along with it.
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
and immediately summoned Shū for an audience.
Soon after,
an edict was issued changing the designation of Xiàn Dì to “Běng Shēng Huáng Kǎo” (biological imperial father),
and the summons was subsequently dropped.
At the time, Wāng Jùn, Minister of Rítuál, had resigned due to his opposition to the establishment of the temple,
and a special imperial decree appointed Shū to replace him.
By custom,
the high-ranking officials of the Ministry of Rítuál were usually chosen from the Hànlín Academy.
At this time, court officials were even more strenuously opposing dissenting opinions.
Shū's promotion also did not follow the usual court recommendations,
so they submitted numerous memorials slandering Shū,
even accusing him of mishandling disaster relief
and engaging in much corruption.
Shū also repeatedly declined the new appointment,
and submitted the records of the "Great Rítuál" deliberations,
further requesting that officials be sent to investigate the state of disaster relief.
The Emperor sent eunuchs from the Directorate of Ceremonial,
Assistant Ministers from the Ministries of Revenue and Justice,
and a Jǐnyī Commander to investigate,
while pressing Shū to come to court with increasing urgency.
By the time Shū reached Dézhōu,
court officials had already prostrated themselves at the palace gate, weeping and contending,
and all had been imprisoned in the imperial jail.
Shū swiftly submitted a memorial saying:
“Deliberations on rites
are like a public debate.
When two arguments are held,
one must be correct.
Your Majesty should choose the correct one,
and need not deeply scrutinize the incorrect one.
I beg you to pardon their transgressions and mistakes,
allowing them to reform.”
This was not granted.
In the eighth month of that year, Shū came to court,
and the Emperor showed him exceptional comfort and praise.
More than a month later, a grand deliberation was held with court officials,
and Shū presented a memorial which stated: "According to the laws of the Three Dynasties,
when a father dies, his son succeeds;
when an elder brother dies, his younger brother succeeds.
From the Xià dynasty through the Hàn dynasty, for two thousand years,
there was no instance of adopting a nephew as an imperial son.
Hàn Chéng Dì,
out of personal preference, established the King of Dìngtáo,
thereby first破坏ing the traditional rites of the Three Dynasties.
Sòng Rén Zōng established the son of Prince Pú,
and after Yīng Zōng ascended the throne,
he never referred to Prince Pú
as his 'uncle.'
Now, Your Majesty was born two years after Xiào Zōng's death,
and therefore did not succeed to Wǔ Zōng's great line of succession.
To retroactively consider Xiào Zōng your father over sixteen years
is indeed a deviation from the great principle of natural human relationships.
Furthermore, [Your Majesty] was never established as an imperial son,
which differs from the Hàn and Sòng cases.
Since ancient times, emperors have had no 'great lineage' or 'minor lineage,'
nor 'those born [to them]' or 'those adopted [as heirs].'
The rites recorded in the ritual classics
pertain to officials and scholars,
and cannot be applied to emperors.
The relationships of paternal uncle, son, and nephew are all eternal and natural principles,
and cannot be altered.
Now,
to take an uncle as a father,
and a father as a paternal uncle,
is to invert human relationships,
which is a great change.
The meaning derived from the tradition of the Three Dynasties,
far exceeding the private successions of Hàn and Táng,
is best found in the Ancestral Instructions.
The Ancestral Instructions state:
'If the court has no imperial son,
then the elder brother's position
shall be succeeded by the younger brother.'
Thus, the one who inherits the throne
truly inherits the lineage,
not the position of a son.
The paternal uncle should naturally be called 'Huáng Bó Kǎo' (Imperial Paternal Uncle Father),
the father should naturally be called 'Huáng Kǎo' (Imperial Father),
and the elder brother should naturally be called
'Huáng Xiōng' (Imperial Elder Brother).
Now Your Majesty has already removed the "Běng Shēng" (biological) designation from Xiàn Dì and Zhāng Shèng,
and has again convened us ministers for a grand deliberation.
We, your ministers Shū, Cōng, È, Xiànfū,
and all other civil and military officials, all contend:
There are no two ways in the world,
and no two origins for a person.
Emperor Xiào Zōng
is a paternal uncle,
and should be called 'Huáng Bó Kǎo' (Imperial Paternal Uncle Father).
Empress Dowager Zhāo Shèng
is a paternal aunt,
and should be called 'Huáng Bó Mǔ' (Imperial Paternal Aunt Mother).
Emperor Xiàn
is the father,
and should be called 'Huáng Kǎo' (Imperial Father).
Empress Dowager Zhāng Shèng
is the mother,
and should be called 'Shèng Mǔ' (Holy Mother).
Wǔ Zōng
should still be called 'Huáng Xiōng' (Imperial Elder Brother),
and Empress Zhuāng Sù should be called 'Huáng Sǎo' (Imperial Elder Sister-in-law).
We especially wish that Your Majesty would look up to the benevolent and sagely virtue of Xiào Zōng,
and remember the supportive efforts of Zhāo Shèng,
so that your filial piety
and reverence may grow ever stronger,
without end from beginning to end,
thus ensuring both the great human relationships and the great succession are properly settled.
To enshrine the spirit tablet and establish a separate ancestral temple,
without discarding the closest relatives;
to bestow a lofty title but
not enter the Tàimiào (Grand Ancestral Temple),
without interfering with the legitimate succession—
thus reverence for parents and legitimate succession will not be at odds.
To follow the Ancestral Instructions completely,
and align with the sacred classics;
to restore the ritual codes
that were unclear for thousands of years since the Three Dynasties,
and cleanse the bad practices of Hàn and Sòng
that violated classics and rites—
who but a sage could accomplish this?"
Upon the submission of the proposal,
an edict was proclaimed throughout the empire,
and the honorific titles were thus settled.
After the Emperor had greatly elevated his biological parents,
eulogies and petitions from within and without the court, seeking favor, came in droves.
The Jǐnyī hundred-householder Suí Quán and Guānglù Record-Keeper Qián Zǐxūn, having been stripped of their positions for crimes,
sought to curry favor by requesting the relocation of Xiàn Dì's Xiǎnlíng (Mausoleum) and its coffin for burial north in Tiānshòu Shān.
Zhào Huáng, Minister of Works, and others denounced their error,
and the Emperor again submitted it for court deliberation.
Shū then convened court officials and submitted a memorial saying:
“Xiǎnlíng
is where the late Emperor's remains are interred;
it must not be lightly disturbed.
In the past, Gāo Huángdì did not relocate his ancestral mausoleum,
nor did Wén Huángdì relocate Xiàolíng.
Suí and the others are sycophantic rascals,
making presumptuous suggestions about the imperial mausoleum;
they should be sent to the judicial authorities for interrogation.”
The Emperor replied:
“The late Emperor's mausoleum is far away,
and I think of it day and night,
overwhelmed with sorrow.
Discuss this again in detail and report.”
Shū again gathered collective opinions,
strongly arguing against it,
and then it stopped.
Shū believed
that with the "Great Rítuál"
successfully concluded,
something should be done to respond to the expectations of the empire.
Thus, he presented twelve items of new policy,
and the Emperor replied with a favorable decree.
During the military mutiny in Dàtóng,
the mutineers killed the Provincial Governor Zhāng Wénjǐn,
burned the seal of the Commander-in-Chief Jiāng Huán,
released the former commander Zhū Zhèn from prison,
and ordered him to replace Huán.
The Emperor consequently appointed him,
instructing the Ministry of Rítuál to cast a new seal.
Shū held that this was unacceptable,
and requested punitive action,
thus clashing with the government.
At that time, the leading officials were Fèi Hóng, Shí Bǎo, and Jiǎ Yǒng,
and Shū did not think highly of them.
Thus, he strongly recommended Yáng Yīqīng and Wáng Shǒurén for cabinet positions,
further stating:
“Currently, all the great ministers are of mediocre talent;
none are fit to plan affairs of the empire.
To quell chaos and rescue the times,
none but Shǒurén can do it.”
The Emperor said:
“As a great minister, Shū
should express his strategic views
and collectively address the difficulties of the time.
Why does he excuse himself with 'mediocre talent'?”
Shǒurén ultimately did not gain power.
Four years later,
Hé Yuān (何淵), a Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, requested the establishment of a Shìshì (世室) [ancestral temple],
to venerate Xiàn Huángdì (獻皇帝) in the Tàimiào (太廟) [Imperial Ancestral Temple].
The emperor ordered the ritual officials to convene a discussion.
Shū (書) and others submitted their deliberations:
"According to the royal regulations,
'The Son of Heaven has seven ancestral temples,
three zhāo (昭) and three mù (穆).'
The Zhōu (周) dynasty, because of Wén (文) and Wǔ (武)'s great achievements and virtues,
established Shìshì (世室),
which, along with Hòujì Miào (后稷廟), would remain un-moved for a hundred generations.
Our Tàizǔ (太祖) established four temples for his close relatives.
Dézǔ (德祖) resided in the north,
but later this was changed to the same hall, different rooms.
Regarding giāo (祧) [transferring ancestral tablets], Tàizǔ (太祖) can be likened to Wén (文) in the Shìshì (世室),
and Tàizōng (太宗) to Wǔ (武) in the Shìshì (世室).
Now, Xiàn Huángdì (獻皇帝) was posthumously honored with the imperial title as a princely king.
Hé Yuān (何淵) now wishes to compare him to Tàizǔ (太祖) and Tàizōng (太宗),
and establish a Shìshì (世室) in the Tàimiào (太廟).
This is utterly baseless."
The request was not granted.
A short while later,
