Zhāng Cōng (張璁) made a special memorial,
strongly arguing against it.
Shū (書) also submitted three memorials, consistent with Cōng's (璁) view.
The emperor sent a eunuch to his home to convey his message,
but Shū (書) again secretly submitted a strong remonstrance.
The emperor was displeased,
accusing him of fearing the multitude and feigning uprightness.
Thus, the discussion turned to establishing a separate Mímiào (禰廟) [memorial temple],
and the proposal for Shìshì (世室) was ultimately dropped.
In the autumn of the fifth year,
Zhāngshèng Tàihòu (章聖太后) was about to visit the Shìmiào (世廟),
but the ritual officials could not agree.
Shū (書), on leave due to an eye ailment,
memorialized:
"A mother empress visiting the temple
is an unprecedented event.
The ritual officials indeed have no basis [for it];
only the sagely wisdom can decide.
Furthermore, since the Shìmiào (世廟) is now complete,
there should be a ceremony of general pardon.
I request the reinstatement of all officials who were banished for debating the rites.
This is what is meant by 'uniting the joy of all nations to sacrifice to the former kings,'
this is the great filial piety of the Son of Heaven."
The emperor acknowledged the memorial.
Shū (書), having gained the emperor's favor through his discussions on the rites,
was relied upon as a trusted minister.
Initially, upon his advancement in the Grand Rites deliberations,
he was promoted to Tàizǐ Tàibǎo (太子太保).
Soon after, with the completion of the Veritable Records of Xiàn Dì (獻帝),
he was promoted to Shàobǎo (少保).
The emperor's favor and distinction were great;
even the grand secretaries dared not aspire to it.
However, Shū (書) fell ill and could not attend to his duties,
repeatedly submitting memorials requesting retirement,
and recommending Luó Qīnshùn (羅欽順) to replace him.
The emperor always consoled him and refused to grant it.
Later, when his illness became critical,
he requested to exert himself further.
An edict promoted him to Wǔyīngdiàn Dàxuéshì (武英殿大學士),
granted him a residence in the capital,
and continued his salary as before.
He died shortly after hearing the command.
He was posthumously granted Tàifù (太傅) [Grand Tutor],
and given the posthumous name Wénxiāng (文襄).
One of his sons was appointed Shàngbǎo Chéng (尚寶丞) [Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Seal],
an exceptional favor.
Shū (書) was daring in his actions and
quite obstinate by nature.
Initially,
Lǐ Jiàn (李鑑) from Chángshā (長沙) became a bandit,
and Prefect Sòng Qīng (宋卿) sentenced him to death.
Shū (書) was then inspecting and pacifying Húguǎng (湖廣),
and uncovered Qīng's (卿) corruption.
He then impeached Qīng (卿) for framing Jiàn (鑑).
The emperor sent a high official to investigate,
who found it was not as Shū (書) had stated.
However, Shū (書) was already in favor at the time,
so the emperor ordered Jiàn (鑑) to be arrested and brought to the capital for a second interrogation.
Shū (書) then stated:
"I incurred public anger by debating the rites,
therefore the judicial officials sided with Qīng (卿) and exaggerated Jiàn's (鑑) crime.
I request an imperial edict for the Ministry of Justice to clarify and vindicate."
When the Ministry of Justice submitted its verdict with no dissenting opinion,
the emperor, reluctant to go against Shū's (書) wishes,
specifically commuted Jiàn's (鑑) death sentence to banishment.
Other instances include his protection of Chén Guāng (陳洸)
and his opposition to Fèi Hóng (費宏),
all of which showed his arbitrary and self-serving conduct,
for which he was criticized by contemporary opinion.
His brothers were Chūn (春) and Zhuàn (篆).
Chūn (春), starting as a Shùjíshì (庶吉士) [probationary bachelor], was appointed Censor,
and went on an inspection tour to Yúnnán (雲南).
Because his brother was a Dūyùshǐ (都御史) [Censor-in-Chief],
he was reassigned as a Hànlín Jiǎntǎo (翰林檢討) [Compiler in the Hanlin Academy].
He participated in the compilation of the Veritable Records of Wǔzōng (武宗), which was completed,
and was due for promotion.
The Grand Secretary Fèi Hóng (費宏) in the Grand Secretariat, seeing that Chūn (春) came from another official post,
proposed that he and Jiǎntǎo (檢討) Liú Kuí (劉夔) both be appointed Ànchá Qiānshì (按察僉事) [Assistant Surveillance Commissioner].
Kuí (夔) was also a former Censor,
who had been reassigned to avoid his brother, Attendant Censor Lóng (龍).
Shū (書) was furious,
and memorialized:
"According to precedent,
there is no instance of someone who completed the compilation of records
being sent out as an external official."
The emperor, for Shū's (書) sake, kept Chūn (春) in the capital,
and promoted him to Xiūzhuàn (修撰) [Compiler].
Kuí (夔) was also kept,
and promoted to Biānxiū (編修) [Compiler].
Shū (書) resented Hóng (宏) from then on,
frequently criticizing him.
When Shū (書) died,
the emperor, remembering his contributions to the rites debate,
repeatedly promoted Chūn (春) to Hànlín Xuéshì (翰林學士) [Academician of the Hanlin Academy].
In the twelfth year of Jiājìng (嘉靖), he was transferred from Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites to the Ministry of Personnel.
An edict called for the recommendation of suitable Hanlin scholars.
Chūn (春) wanted to recall former Hanlin scholars Yáng Wéicōng (楊惟聰) and Chén Yí (陳沂),
but Minister Wāng Hóng (汪鋐) disagreed,
creating a rift between them.
Later, when Hóng (鋐) made some recommendations,
he did not consult Chūn (春).
Chūn (春) angrily abused Hóng (鋐).
Hóng (鋐) then accused Chūn (春) of previously colluding with Yáng Tínghé (楊廷和) to oppose the officials who debated the rites,
and Chūn (春) was subsequently dismissed from office.
He died at home.
Zhuàn (篆) was a Household Censor.
The Duke of Qiánguó (黔國公) Mù Kūn (沐崑) impeached Surveillance Commissioner Shěn Ēn (沈恩) and others.
Zhuàn (篆) and his colleague Lǐ Cháng (李長) privately told Kūn (崑) that many accusations in his memorial were false.
Cháng (長) immediately impeached Kūn (崑).
Wǔzōng (武宗) reprimanded Cháng (長) for slandering a high official
and sent him to imperial prison.
The testimonies implicated Zhuàn (篆),
who was also arrested, tried, and demoted to an external post.
Zhuàn (篆) became the Magistrate of Yílíng (夷陵).
When Shìzōng (世宗) succeeded to the throne,
he was reinstated to his former office,
but died before taking up the post.
He was given a funeral sacrifice
and posthumously granted Shàonáo Lù (少卿) [Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices].
Huò Tāo (霍韜),
courtesy name Wèixiān (渭先),
was from Nánhǎi (南海).
He ranked first in the metropolitan examination of the ninth year of Zhèngdé (正德).
After visiting home for marriage,
he studied on Mount Xīqiáo (西樵山),
becoming deeply conversant in classics and history.
When Shìzōng (世宗) ascended the throne,
he was appointed Zhífāng Zhǔshì (職方主事) [Secretary of the Bureau of Military Provisions].
Yáng Tínghé (楊廷和) was then in power.
Tāo (韜) memorialized:
"The Grand Secretaries' duty is to participate in state affairs;
now they only draft proposals,
while decisions are made by favored attendants.
The auxiliary ministers lose their power to advise,
and favored attendants begin to interfere in government.
From now on, for memorials,
I request that high officials be summoned to make decisions face-to-face,
and that lecturers and censors
stand in their ranks to the left and right,
allowing public discussion and open criticism.
Thus, the prime minister can gain the reputation for choosing what is good,
and eunuchs can avoid the criticism of usurping power."
He then stated that the Jǐnyīwèi (錦衣衛) [Embroidered Uniform Guard] should not administer prisons,
the Dōngchǎng (東廠) [Eastern Depot] should not participate in court deliberations,
inspection and pacification officials with military command should not be granted ranks or hereditary privileges based on military merit,
and the guards from Xīngfǔ (興府) should not all be brought into the capital and generally granted official positions.
Censors Xiè Yuán (謝源) and Wǔ Xīrú (伍希儒), who had rendered meritorious service during the rebellion, should not be dismissed,
and honors for suppressing the rebel prince,
beyond Ānqìng (安慶) and Nánchāng (南昌), should not be indiscriminately bestowed.
The emperor praised and accepted his suggestions.
When
the "Grand Rites"
debate arose,
Máo Chéng (毛澄), Minister of Rites, strongly advocated honoring Xiàozōng (孝宗) as father.
Tāo (韜) privately refuted this with arguments for the Grand Rites.
Chéng (澄) sent a letter to debate him,
and Tāo (韜) submitted three memorials strongly refuting his errors.
Eventually,
realizing Chéng's (澄) intent was unchangeable,
he submitted a memorial in the tenth month of that year, saying: "The court's deliberation states that Your Majesty should regard Xiàozōng (孝宗) as father,
and Xìngxiàn Wáng (興獻王) as uncle,
and choose a prince from Chóngrén (崇仁) to be the heir to Xiàn Wáng (獻王).
Examined against ancient rites,
this is incompatible.
Measured against the way of sages and worthies, this is unintelligible.
Judged by the circumstances of today, this is improper.
The chapter on mourning attire in the Yílǐ (儀禮) states
that 'one wears zhaàncuī (斬衰) for the one whose heir one is.'
It also states
that 'one who is an heir
gives mourning in return for one's parents.'
This means that for the one whose heir one is,
there is
no mention of calling them parents,
nor is there any mention of changing one's biological parents to paternal uncles or aunts.
Hàn (漢) scholars did not understand its meaning,
and thus erroneously propagated false theories."
said:
“He who becomes the successor to someone is that person’s son.”
If it were truly as he said,
then Hàn Xuānzōng (漢宣宗) should have been the successor to Zhāodì (昭帝).
However, Zhāodì (昭帝) was his grand-uncle,
and Xuāndì (宣帝) was his grand-nephew.
A grand-nephew calling his grand-uncle father,
is that permissible?
Táng Xuānzōng (唐宣宗) should have been the successor to Wǔzōng (武宗).
However, Wǔzōng (武宗) was his nephew,
and Xuānzōng (宣宗) was his uncle.
An uncle in turn calling his nephew
father,
is that permissible?
Among the four brothers of Wú (吳) Zhū Fán (諸樊), the state was passed between them.
They presumably took turns being successors to each other.
This would mean brothers inherently acted as each other's great-grandfathers, grandfathers, and fathers,
and is that
permissible?
Therefore, I say that examining ancient rites, it is not in accord.
The empire
is the empire of all,
not something one person can possess privately.
The Sòng (宋) people, in addressing their sovereign, said:
“Rénzōng (仁宗), from among the imperial clan, specially selected a sage
and wise person,
and entrusted him with the great enterprise.
Your Majesty, your ability to sit facing the screen and wearing the imperial crown,
to possess the four seas,
and for your descendants to succeed for ten thousand generations,
all comes from the virtue of the former emperor.”
This presumably means that Rénzōng (仁宗)
bestowed the empire upon Yīngzōng (英宗),
and therefore Yīngzōng (英宗) should set aside his birth parents and take Rénzōng (仁宗) as his parents.
Your subject, viewing this through the Way of the Sages and Worthies,
Mèngzǐ (孟子) said that when Shùn (舜) was the Son of Heaven,
Gǔsǒu (瞽瞍) committed murder,
and Gāoyáo (皐陶) apprehended him.
Shùn (舜) then secretly carried his father and fled.
This shows that parents are weighty and the empire is light.
If we follow the Sòng (宋) Confucians’ view,
then the empire
would be weighty and parents light.
Therefore, I say that seeking it in the Way of the Sages and Worthies, it is not comprehensible.
Wǔzōng (武宗) succeeded Xiàozōng (孝宗) for sixteen years.
Xiàozōng (孝宗) was not without an heir.
Now, to forcefully demand that Your Majesty again become Xiàozōng’s (孝宗) heir,
for what purpose is this?
Indeed, if Your Majesty becomes Xiàozōng’s (孝宗) son,
who will be Wǔzōng’s (武宗) son?
Xiàozōng (孝宗) would have two heirs,
while Wǔzōng (武宗) alone would have no heir,
is that permissible?
The duty of a subject to
his sovereign and father is one and the same.
If you cannot bear for Xiàozōng (孝宗) to be without an heir,
how can you alone bear for Wǔzōng (武宗) to be without an heir?
If it is said that Wǔzōng (武宗), as an elder brother,
naturally deserves to enjoy the sacrifices of his younger brother,
then
Xiàozōng (孝宗), as an elder uncle,
should he alone not enjoy the sacrifices of his nephew?
Since it is permissible to bypass Wǔzōng (武宗) and directly succeed Xiàozōng (孝宗),
is it alone not permissible to bypass both Xiàozōng (孝宗) and directly succeed Xiànzōng (憲宗)?
Wǔzōng (武宗) had no heir,
and there was nothing that could be done.
Xiàozōng (孝宗) had an heir.
To forcefully succeed his heir,
and sever the line of Xīngxiàn (興獻),
is this not of no
benefit to Xiàozōng (孝宗),
but a great loss to Xīngxiàn (興獻)?
Therefore, I say that measuring it against today's situation, it is not appropriate.
However, the reasons for your subjects making this proposal are
three: first, being bound by precedents of former dynasties;
second, not forgetting the virtue of Xiàozōng (孝宗);
and third, avoiding the suspicion of
pandering.
Now that Your Majesty has honored Xiàozōng (孝宗) [as your father],
and conferred imperial titles upon Xīngxiàn Wáng (興獻王),
will it simply end there?
Your subject humbly believes that the succession of emperors
is merely the continuation of their lineage.
One should not be particular about the appellation of father and son.
By merely continuing the lineage,
not only will the lineage of Xiàozōng (孝宗) not be severed,
but also the lineage of Wǔzōng (武宗) will not be severed.
So, how can this be achieved?
Only if Your Majesty can establish the proper appellation of father and son with Xīngxiàn Wáng (興獻王),
so as not to sever the natural
bond.
Regarding the reception of the empress dowager,
the rites for the mother of the Son of Heaven should be properly observed.
Furthermore, if Zhāoshèng Tàihòu (昭聖太后) and Wǔzōng Huánghòu (武宗皇后) are treated with due respect,
and served
with utmost sincerity,
then both respecting the exalted and loving one’s kin will not be violated.
The emperor received the memorial and was very pleased,
but due to pressure from the general opinion, he did not immediately implement it.
However, the court officials all pointed to Tāo (韜) as promoting heterodox views.
Tāo (韜) felt disheartened
and soon resigned due to illness.
In the third year of Jiājìng (嘉靖) (1524),
the emperor's desire to honor his birth parents grew more urgent,
and he issued two edicts summoning Tāo (韜).
Tāo (韜) declined, citing illness,
and hastily submitted a memorial stating: "The current debate on the great rites
has only two aspects.
One is to uphold the great principle of legitimate succession,
the other is to rectify the great principle of human relations.
Solely upholding legitimate succession
leads to the defect of benefiting the empire at the expense of abandoning parents.
Solely emphasizing human relations
leads to the defect of the lesser usurping the greater and the humble surpassing the exalted.
Therefore, your subject suggests that Your Majesty should address Xiàozōng (孝宗)
as Huángbókǎo (皇伯考), (Imperial Uncle-Father),
and Xiàndì (獻帝) as Huángkǎo (皇考), (Imperial Father).
This is what must be clearly distinguished in human relations.
The debate on honoring them,
should for now be postponed.
This is what must be upheld concerning the great lineage.
However, the court debate wishes Your Majesty to honor Xiàozōng (孝宗) as your father,
and also simultaneously honor Xiàndì (獻帝) as your father.
This is the Han people's error of 'two lineages.'
Once the origin is mistaken,
the more the debate, the more
erroneous it becomes.
Your subject's humble opinion
is that Your Majesty should prevent future errors,
and not heap up future regrets.
Initially, Your Majesty honored Zhāoshèng Huángtàihòu (昭聖皇太后) as your mother.
Although this was not entirely in accordance with ritual,
the inner palace has since been at peace.
Now, suddenly changing the appellation
is greatly beyond what human emotions can bear.
Your subject requests that Your Majesty, in light of
the sentiments of us, your subjects, in making this suggestion,
approach the Empress Dowager
so that she will undoubtedly be pleased in her heart and free from any suspicion or doubt.
Should she by any chance not understand,
you can attribute the fault to us, your subjects,
and bestow upon us the punishment of execution
and banishment.
Thereafter, you can apply with tact and earnestness
to ensure her happiness.
All the efforts Your Majesty makes day and night to cater to her wishes
and relieve her worries
should be employed to their
fullest extent.
Thus, names and duties may be rectified, suspicions and doubts dispelled,
and the world will have nothing to criticize for ten thousand generations.
This is one of your subject's humble thoughts.
The legitimate heir of Zhāoshèng (昭聖) was Wǔzōng (武宗) alone.
Wǔzōng (武宗) had no heir,
which was the expectation of Zhuāngsù Huánghòu (莊肅皇后).
Your subject believes that Your Majesty's service to Zhāoshèng (昭聖),
although the ritual status is extremely exalted,
its actual influence daily diminishes.
Your Majesty's service to your Sacred Mother,
though the honorific may not yet be perfect,
its actual influence daily increases.
Therefore, today
the court officials earnestly request to uphold the great lineage
and to make Zhāoshèng (昭聖) your mother,
presumably to prevent Your Majesty's future errors
and to repay the duty to Xiàozōng (孝宗).
Your subject
has humbly read the clear edict,
and the great principle of legitimate succession
dares not be violated.
Knowing that Your Majesty honors Zhāoshèng (昭聖)
and respects Zhuāngsù (莊肅),
this heart can be vouched for by Heaven and Earth above,
and trusted by officials and commoners below.
But I fear that those around you do not comprehend your sacred intent,
and might groundlessly create doubts and discord,
or through trivial matters and minor details,
thereby create a rift between the two palaces.
This must not be disregarded
but prevented early.
Your subject requests that Your Majesty, in light of the sentiments of us, your subjects, in making this suggestion,
approach your Sacred Mother and say:
“Zhāoshèng Huángtàihòu (昭聖皇太后) is indeed the legitimate senior of the great lineage,
most exalted and without
equal.
I humbly wish that my Sacred Mother would at times humble herself,
showing sincere respect.
Zhuāngsù Huánghòu (莊肅皇后) has been a model mother to the empire for sixteen years.
The manner in which my Sacred Mother receives her
must not..."
Liú Shūxiāng (劉淑相), Prefect of Shùntiān Fǔ (順天府), was impeached for accepting bribes on behalf of his relatives.
He suspected that Xià Yán (夏言), Minister of Personnel, and Fèi Wán (費完), a circuit intendant who was Xià Yán's in-law, had framed him,
and then he publicly accused Xià Yán of seeking patronage.
The Emperor was enraged,
and sent Liú Shūxiāng to the imperial prison.
Liú Shūxiāng and (Hán) Tāo (韓韜) were on good terms,
so Xià Yán also suspected Hán Tāo of instigating it.
He then accused Hán Tāo of being grossly disrespectful for accompanying the Emperor on a visit to the imperial mausoleums
and then making a distant excursion to Yínshān Sì (銀山寺).
(Hán) Tāo defended himself
and then criticized Xià Yán, saying:
"He requested a posthumous title of Wénxiàn (文憲) for the late Junior Guardian Fèi Hóng (費宏),
even though Fèi Hóng was repeatedly impeached.
According to the law,
those who add to or subtract from crucial facts should be beheaded.
Moreover, 'xiàn' (憲)
is the temple name of a pure emperor.
How can a subject use it?"
At this time, Zēng Jūn (曾鈞), a supervising censor from Nánjīng (南京), rode his horse
and failed to yield to the sedan chairs of Ministers Liú Lóng (劉龍) and Pān Zhēn (潘珍).
Liú Lóng and Zēng Jūn mutually impeached each other in memorials.
(Hán) Tāo impeached Zēng Jūn
and requested a ban on junior officials riding in sedan chairs.
Li Chōngzhuó (李充濁), Cáo Mài (曹邁), and other supervising censors submitted memorials in quick succession,
stating that attendant officials should not have to avoid the road,
and cited examples of public gatherings and banquets where they were allowed to sit with ministers to prove their point,
their words somewhat criticizing (Hán) Tāo.
(Hán) Tāo suspected Li Chōngzhuó was relying on Xià Yán as his internal backer,
and accused Li Chōngzhuó of being a treacherous partisan,
further picking apart other matters concerning Xià Yán.
Xià Yán grew more enraged
and memorialized over ten major offenses of (Hán) Tāo.
He also stated that Péng Shí (彭時) and Sòng Lián (宋濂) were both posthumously titled Wénxiàn during the Zhèngdé (正德) era,
without avoiding temple names,
and that (Hán) Tāo was ignorant of such precedents.
The Emperor was already unfavorably disposed towards (Hán) Tāo,
and Liú Shūxiāng again extracted other matters concerning Xià Yán from prison.
The Emperor grew even angrier
and interrogated him.
He confessed that (Hán) Tāo was the instigator.
Thus, Liú Shūxiāng was dismissed as a commoner,
and (Hán) Tāo's salary was demoted by one rank.
When the matter of riding sedan chairs was deliberated,
Xià Yán was not involved in the impeachment.

Wáng Tíngxiàng (王廷相), Censor-in-Chief, together with Huáng Zōngmíng (黃宗明) and Zhāng Bì (張璧), Vice Ministers of Rites, requested to prohibit and discipline junior officials as (Hán) Tāo had memorialized,
but the supervising censors and censors in Nánjīng continued as usual.
(Hán) Tāo believed this was Xià Yán's doing,
and the Emperor reiterated his admonition,
causing general discontent.
Cáo Mài and his colleagues Yǐn Xiāng (尹相) and others then quarreled fiercely with (Hán) Tāo.
Yǐn Xiāng impeached (Hán) Tāo for complaining and being resentful about his transfer to the Southern Capital;
for unauthorizedly taking fish from the Imperial Pond (Hǎizi),
and drinking in groups with villagers under the pines at the suburban altar;
and for forcing Vice Minister Yuán Zōngrú (袁宗儒) to present a memorial during his mourning period, which was inappropriate.
(Hán) Tāo submitted a memorial defending himself.
The matter was sent for court deliberation.
The Emperor suspended (Hán) Tāo's salary for four months,
and Yǐn Xiāng and others also had theirs suspended for two months.
Since (Hán) Tāo had fallen out with Xià Yán,
whenever Xià Yán held power,
(Hán) Tāo frequently sought to frame him through various incidents.
He memorialized:
"Recently, the Ministry of Personnel selected Liú Wénguāng (劉文光) and others as supervising censors,
but they were suddenly dismissed.
Everyone said it was the Grand Secretaries who suppressed them.
Li Hèmíng (李鶴鳴), a supervising censor, was demoted after an evaluation
but soon restored to his original post.
Everyone said it was through bribery.
It is advisable to instruct the Ministry of Personnel not to accept directives from those in power,
so that the world knows that authority and power emanate from the court,
and ministers like Lǐ Línfǔ (李林甫) and Qín Huì (秦檜)
cannot manipulate affairs around the Emperor."
His intention was to target Xià Yán.
Thereupon, Li Hèmíng submitted a memorial to clear his name
and also exposed various unlawful acts (Hán) Tāo committed in his hometown.
The Emperor set both matters aside.
Shortly after,
(Hán) Tāo impeached Gōng Shí (龔湜) and Guō Běn (郭本), censors from Nánjīng.
Gōng Shí and others defended themselves
and also impeached (Hán) Tāo.
The Emperor set both aside without inquiry.
In the eighteenth year
he was appointed to fill a vacancy as a palace official.
The Emperor ordered (Hán) Tāo, as太子少保 Tàizǐ Shàobǎo (Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent) and Minister of Rites, to concurrently manage the affairs of the Zhānshì Fǔ (詹事府).
He submitted a memorial declining the additional rank,
and also criticized ministers for accepting emoluments without humility
and accepting promotions without declining,
and for some engaging in corrupt scheming
to secretly solidify their favor and power,
stating that the grievances they caused invited disaster
and had a real origin.
His intention was also to target Xià Yán.
After repeatedly attacking Xià Yán without success,
he finally saw that Guō Xūn (郭勛) had a rift with Xià Yán,
so he secretly allied with Guō Xūn
to jointly denigrate Xià Yán.
At that time, there was a rumor inside and outside the court that the Emperor would again make a southern tour.
(Hán) Tāo, capitalizing on this, openly praised Guō Xūn,
saying:
"When the Emperor last toured the south,
many officials accepted bribes and acted unlawfully.
Among civil officials, only Yuán Zōngrú,
and among military officials, only Guō Xūn, did not accept gifts.
Now, false rumors are spreading again;
measures should be taken to prohibit and curb them."
The Emperor had already issued an edict to calm public sentiment,
and then questioned (Hán) Tāo, saying:
"When I last toured the south,
you were not in attendance.
From whom did you hear about the bribery?
Report the facts truthfully."
(Hán) Tāo replied,
asking to consult Guō Xūn.
The Emperor chastised him for evading the issue
and insisted that he point out the facts.
(Hán) Tāo was in a predicament,
and then said:
"Among the accompanying officials, none did not accept gifts or extort labor from subordinates for payment.
Just ask Xià Yán;
let him tell you himself.
As for the actual instances of officials taking bribes,
Guō Xūn knows all the details from beginning to end
and will surely not deceive.
If Your Majesty insists that I speak,
please grant me the authority of a censor;
I will investigate along the way
and then present a complete report."
The memorial was sent to the relevant department.
(Hán) Tāo feared he had not pleased the Emperor,
and soon traveled to the capital,
listing the corrupt and tyrannical acts of the eunuchs on the ships delivering fresh provisions.
The Emperor also did not question him.
The following year, in the tenth month, he died in office
at the age of fifty-four.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tàizǐ Tàibǎo (太子太保, Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent)
and the posthumous name Wénmǐn (文敏).
(Hán) Tāo was broadly learned and highly talented,
but narrow-minded,
and wherever he went, he competed with others.
The Emperor was quite displeased with him
and thus did not employ him in major roles.
He made many proposals before and after,
and these often involved major state policies.
He also once recommended
officials who were punished in the "Great Rites" (Dàlǐ, 大禮) case,
as well as the dismissed Lǐ Mèngyáng (李夢陽) and Kāng Hǎi (康海).
In Nán Dū (南都, Southern Capital),
he prohibited feasting at funerals,
forbade women from entering temples and Taoist monasteries,
punished brothel owners for purchasing daughters of respectable families,
destroyed illicit shrines,
established community schools,
dispersed monks and nuns,
and honored loyal and virtuous individuals.
After he left,
the scholars and common people missed him.
Initially, he allied with Cōng (璁) and È (萼),
and later with Guō Xūn.
He passed the imperial examination and was a disciple of Máozhèng (毛澄).
He always treated Máozhèng with the respect due to a teacher,
but when they disagreed on the rites,
he no longer referred to him as his examiner.
When he presided over the Jǐchǒu (己丑) metropolitan examination,
he likewise did not consider Táng Shùnzhī (唐順之) and others as his students.
During his deliberation on rites,
he criticized Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光).
Later, when deliberating on Xuē Xuān's (薛瑄) enshrinement,
he went so far as to argue that Sīmǎ Guāng should not be enshrined in the Confucius Temple.
Such was his disregard for public opinion.
His son, (Hán) Yǔxiá (韓與瑕),
passed the imperial examination
and was appointed Magistrate of Cíxī (慈谿).
When Yān Màoxīng (鄢懋卿) toured the salt administration,
(Hán) Yǔxiá showed him no respect
and was impeached and dismissed by him.
He was later appointed Magistrate of Yínxiàn (鄞縣)
and eventually served as a Qian事 (Qiānshì, Assistant Surveillance Commissioner) in Guǎngxī (廣西).
Xióng Jiá,
courtesy name Yuèzhī,
was a native of Nánchāng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the ninth year of Zhèngdé (1514).
He was appointed Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Rites.
When Prince Chénháo of Níng was about to rebel,
Xióng Jiá and the Censor Xióng Lán, from the same prefecture, drafted a memorial.
They entrusted it to Censor Xiāo Huái to submit.
Chénháo hastily launched his rebellion
and was ultimately defeated.
This was thanks to the early efforts of these two men.
Xióng Jiá was dispatched to audit the border provisions at Sōngpān.
Vice-commander Zhāng Jié, relying on Jiāng Bīn's influence,
had embezzled colossal sums,
enticed and killed "tamed" *fān* (ethnic minorities) to claim merits, thereby instigating border conflicts,
and had flogged to death up to five hundred people, including commanders of a thousand households and below.
He had also once led his household retainers to ambush and attack Vice-commissioner Hú Lǐ.
The governors and investigating censors dared not speak out.
Upon Xióng Jiá's arrival,
he exposed all of Zhāng Jié's misdeeds,
and Zhāng Jié was subsequently stripped of his position.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
the court's deliberation on the posthumous honors for the emperor's parents remained undecided.
Xióng Jiá swiftly submitted a memorial, stating:
"Your Majesty rose from a princely vassalage
to ascend the great throne.
If one must insist on the theory of 'being adopted as heir,'
to consider Xiàozōng as the father and Císhòu as the mother,
then Your Majesty's birth mother, the Consort of Xīngxiàn, would have to be demoted to the title of aunt or uncle.
I do not know whether, when Your Majesty enjoyed the affection in the inner court,
You would retain the old address,
or change it to conform to the current address?
If You were to retain the old address,
yet could not honor her as empress,
then for Císhòu, it would merely be an empty formality of 'being adopted as heir,'
while for Your birth mother, it would lack the great ceremony of 'being honored,'
neither of which is acceptable.
Your humble servant believes that the Prince of Xīngxiàn should be honored with an imperial title,
and a separate temple should be built for him,
to show that he is not dared to be placed among the former emperors.
His consort, Your birth mother, should be honored as Empress Dowager,
but with a slightly reduced honorific title,
to show that she is not dared to be equated with Císhòu.
This would not impede the great imperial succession,
and the affection of natural kinship would also be fully expressed."
When the memorial arrived,
it so happened that the Prince of Xīng and his consort had already been referred to as Emperor and Empress,
so the matter was passed to the officials of rites.
In the early Jiājìng period (1522-1566),
he was transferred from Supervising Secretary of the Right to Provincial Surveillance Vice Commissioner of Hénán.
He returned home for mourning.
In the sixth year (1527),
after the mourning period ended,
he was summoned to compile the *Mínglún Dàdiǎn* (Great Canon of Human Relationships).
He was exceptionally promoted to Right Censor-in-chief,
assisting in court affairs.
In the following year, in the fourth month, he was transferred to Minister of the Dali Temple,
and soon after, to Right Vice Censor-in-chief.
After the *Dàdiǎn* was completed,
he was promoted to Left.
In the second month of the eighth year (1529), he was then promoted to Right Censor-in-chief,
presiding over court affairs.
A commoner in the capital, Zhāng Fú, accused his fellow villager, Zhāng Zhù, of murdering his mother.
The Eastern Depot reported this,
and the Ministry of Justice sentenced Zhāng Zhù to death.
Zhāng Zhù did not submit.
Zhāng Fú's sister also tearfully complained to the officials,
claiming their mother had committed suicide,
and the testimony of their neighbors also supported this.
An imperial edict ordered Department Director Wèi Yìngzhāo to re-examine the case,
and he changed the verdict to implicate Zhāng Fú.
The Eastern Depot memorialized that the judicial authorities had wantonly released the guilty,
the emperor was enraged,
and ordered Wèi Yìngzhāo to be imprisoned in the imperial prison.
Xióng Jiá agreed with Wèi Yìngzhāo's deliberation
and maintained the original conclusion.
The emperor became even more furious,
and stripped Xióng Jiá of his position.
Supervising Secretaries Lù Càn and Liú Xījiǎn argued against this,
the emperor was greatly angered,
and imprisoned both men in the imperial prison.
Vice-minister Xǔ Zàn and others then upheld Zhāng Zhù's death sentence,
while Wèi Yìngzhāo and the neighbors were exiled,
and Zhāng Fú's sister was flogged a hundred times.
People considered this an injustice.
At that time,
the emperor deeply resented the families of the Empresses of Xiào Zōng and Wǔ Zōng.
Zhāng Zhù was indeed a servant of the Xià family, Empress of Wǔ Zōng,
thus the emperor was determined to have him killed.
Xióng Jiá remained at home for ten years.
When the emperor visited Chéngtiān and discussed former officials with his close attendants,
he was then summoned to be Minister of Rites of Nánjīng,
then transferred to Minister of War,
participating in policy deliberations.
In the twenty-first year (1542), he was summoned to be Minister of War,
and concurrently presided over the Censorate.
After two years,
he replaced Xǔ Zàn as Minister of Personnel.
The emperor built an altar for spirit-mediums in the Forbidden City,
occasionally using their words to decide punishments and rewards.
Xióng Jiá argued against its absurdity.
The emperor was greatly angered
and wanted to punish him,
but because of his previous role in the rites deliberation, he was not immediately dismissed.
After serving six years in a second-rank position,
he was given the honorary title of Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent,
but was twice stripped of his salary due to various matters.
Xióng Jiá knew that the emperor's displeasure would never abate,
so he feigned illness and requested retirement.
The emperor was greatly angered
and stripped him of his position, reducing him to a commoner.
He died ten years later.
Xióng Jiá had lofty ambitions and integrity in his youth,
and maintained strict self-discipline.
Although he gained prominence through the rites deliberation,
he was not excessively partisan
and particularly cherished talented individuals.
Therefore, when he left the Ministry of Personnel,
many upright people missed him.
In the early Lóngqìng period (1567-1572),
he was reinstated to his official position,
granted sacrificial honors and a burial,
and given the posthumous name Gōngsù.
Huáng Zōngmíng,
courtesy name Chéngfǔ,
was a native of Yín.
He became a *jìnshì* in the ninth year of Zhèngdé (1514).
He was appointed Principal of the Ministry of War in Nánjīng,
and then promoted to Assistant Minister.
He once discussed scholarship with Wáng Shǒurén.
When Prince Chénháo of Níng rebelled,
he submitted three strategies for river defense.
When Wǔzōng marched south,
he strongly memorialized against it,
and soon after requested leave to return home.
In the second year of Jiājìng, he became a Director in the Ministry of Punishments in Nánjīng.
When Zhāng Cōng and Guì È debated
the "Grand Rites,"
he was summoned to the capital from Nánjīng,
but had not yet arrived.
In the fourth month of the third year,
Cōng, È, Huáng Wǎn, and Zōng Míng submitted a joint memorial, stating:
"Today's discussion on showing respect,
which considers Your Majesty to be an adopted heir,
is the private agreement of the ceremonial officials.
The argument that Your Majesty is the successor to the great succession
is the conclusion reached by us, your ministers, through examining the classics.
Some say
that the two arguments are at an impasse,
with an imbalance in magnitude and numbers.
We, your ministers, however, say
that only principle matters.
How great was Shùn as a ruler!
He viewed the whole world's joy and allegiance to him
as mere trifles,
but if he failed to be filial to his parents,
he would be like a destitute person with no place to return.
Now, those who speak out are pursuing their private interests and forming factions,
disregarding the deprivation of the Emperor's parents.
How can Your Majesty feel at ease in your position for even a single day without addressing this?
When the sacred decree ordered the court officials to convene for discussion,
they merely looked at each other all day, none daring to speak first.
This was because they were suppressed by power
and forced to yield to unreason.
We, your ministers, greatly fear that deceit and procrastination
will ultimately prevent the accomplishment of great filial piety.
Why does Your Majesty not personally preside over the court,
and question the officials, saying: 'I am the grandson of Emperor Xiànzōng,
the nephew of Emperor Xiàozōng,
and the son of Emperor Xīngxiàn.
Following the text of Tàizǔ regarding succession from an elder brother to a younger brother,
and complying with Emperor Wǔzōng's edict on the proper order of succession,
I have inherited the great succession,
and am not an adopted heir.
Previously, without detailed investigation,
an edict was hastily issued to the empire,
honoring Emperor Xiàozōng as Huángkǎo (Imperial Father)
and Empress Dowager Zhāoshèng as Shèngmǔ (Holy Mother),
while Emperor Xīngxiàn and his Empress were separately given the title of their birth parents.
I deeply regret this.
Now, we must clarify the great human bond of father and son,
and the great principle of succession.
I should rename Xiàozōng as Huáng Bókǎo (Imperial Uncle Father),
and Zhāoshèng as Huáng Bómǔ (Imperial Uncle Mother),
and remove the title of birth parents.
The titles should be Huángkǎo Gōngmù Xiàn Huángdì (Imperial Father Gongmu Xian Emperor)
and Shèngmǔ Zhāngshèng Huáng Tàihòu (Holy Mother Zhangsheng Empress Dowager).
This is a universal ritual for all ages.
You, civil and military court officials, should remember the affection between father and son,
and the righteousness between ruler and minister,
and together with me clarify this great human bond for all under Heaven.'
If this were done,
would there be any officials at court who would not be moved to tears and obey the edict?
Moreover, if this were announced to the myriad people under Heaven,
would there be any who would not be moved to tears and obey the edict?
This is the essence of the 'Rites of Zhōu' in questioning the officials and questioning the myriad people."
Upon receiving the memorial,
the Emperor was greatly pleased,
and ultimately acted according to their words.
Zōng Míng also subsequently received the Emperor's favor.
The following year, he was appointed Prefect of Jí'ān,
and then promoted to Salt Transport Commissioner of Fújiàn.
In the sixth year, he was summoned to participate in the compilation of the Mínglún Dàdiǎn (Grand Ceremony of Clarifying Human Relations),
but returned home due to his mother's mourning.
After the mourning period,
he was summoned and appointed Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Guānglù Qīng).
In the eleventh year, he was promoted to Right Vice Minister of War (Bīngbù Yòu Shìláng).
That winter,
compiling editor Yáng Míng was imprisoned by imperial edict for impeaching Wāng Hóng,
and the charges implicated his colleague Chéng Wéndé,
who was also arrested.
The imperial edict pressed harder for the masterminds.
Zōng Míng submitted a memorial to protest and plead for them,
and moreover stated:
"Collective punishment is not good governance.
Now, for one person's reckless words, it is insisted that the instigator be investigated;
which court official would not be afraid?
Moreover, Míng has been severely tortured,
and may die from the cold in this severe winter,
which would become a stain on Your Majesty's benevolence and wisdom."
The Emperor was furious,
deeming Zōng Míng to be the instigator,
and imprisoned him by imperial edict,
demoting him to Right Surveillance Commissioner (Yòu Cāncèng) of Fújiàn.
The Emperor, however, still remembered Zōng Míng's contributions to the debate on rites,
and the following year summoned and appointed him Right Vice Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Yòu Shìláng).
When a mutiny occurred in Liáodōng,
the soldiers beat and humiliated the巡抚 (Circuit Inspector) Lǚ Jīng.
But the Emperor was intent on leniency,
and accepted the words of the garrison eunuch Wáng Chún and others,
planning to arrest Jīng.
Zōng Míng stated:
"The previous mutiny in Liáoyáng
arose from provocation.
Now, the heavy taxes and harsh levies have all been rectified,
so who provoked the renewed mutiny in Guǎngníng?
The law should not grant another pardon.
I request that the new Circuit Inspector, Hán Bāngqí, lead troops to the border,
declare an expedition to punish the guilty,
capture the ringleaders,
and thus assert national prestige,
without resorting solely to leniency."
The Emperor did not comply,
and Jīng was ultimately arrested.
Zōng Míng was soon transferred to Left Vice Minister,
and died in office.
Initially,
the officials who debated the rites,
relying on the Emperor's favor,
acted with arrogance and power,
indulging their own opinions.
Although Zōng Míng rose rapidly because of this,
his arguments were quite balanced,
and among those people,
he alone was not feared or disliked.
Huáng Wǎn,
courtesy name Zōngxián,
was from Huángyán,
and was the grandson of the Vice Minister Kǒng Zhāosūn.
He inherited an ancestral yin privilege and became a Section Chief in the Rear Guard (Hòufǔ Dūshì).
He once studied under Xiè Duó and Wáng Shǒurén.
At the beginning of Jiājìng's reign,
he was a Recording Secretary in the Nánjīng Censorate.
When Zhāng Cōng and Guì È debated
the "Grand Rites,"
the Emperor's heart inclined towards them.
In the second month of the third year,
Wǎn also submitted a memorial, stating:
"Emperor Wǔzōng held the succession of Emperor Xiàozōng for sixteen years.
Now, if Your Majesty is again considered the son of Emperor Xiàozōng,
inheriting the succession of Emperor Xiàozōng,
then Emperor Wǔzōng should not have a temple.
This would prevent Emperor Xiàozōng from having Emperor Wǔzōng as his son,
which is to sever Xiàozōng's lineage.
Consequently,
this would prevent Emperor Xīngxiàn from having Your Majesty as his son,
which is to sever Emperor Xīngxiàn's lineage.
Would this not lead to the collapse of the Three Bonds
and the destruction of the Nine Laws?"
Upon receiving the memorial,
the Emperor was greatly pleased,
and passed it to the relevant department.
That month,
he submitted another memorial to elaborate on his previous argument.
Soon after hearing that the Emperor had issued an edict referring to his birth father as Huángkǎo (Imperial Father),
he again submitted a strong memorial to argue against it.
He also joined Cōng, È, and Huáng Zōng Míng in a joint memorial to debate,
and the "Grand Rites"
were finally settled.
From then on, Wǎn was greatly favored by the Emperor.
The following year,
when Hé Yuān requested the establishment of a "perpetual temple,"
Wǎn and Zōng Míng denounced its absurdity.
He was soon promoted to Assistant Minister of the Ministry of Punishments in Nánjīng,
but later retired due to illness again.
The Emperor remembered his contributions to the debate on rites,
and in the sixth month of the sixth year, summoned and promoted him to Junior Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Guānglù Shàogīng),
and he participated in the compilation of the Mínglún Dàdiǎn.
Wáng Shǒurén, despite being enfeoffed as a Count,
did not receive his patent of nobility, certificates, or annual emoluments due to envious individuals;
many other meritorious officials, such as Prefects Xíng Xún, Xú Lián, and Chén Huái,
and Censors Wǔ Xīrú and Xiè Yuán,
were dismissed after performance reviews.
Wǎn pleaded for them at court,
and also requested that Shǒurén be summoned to assist in governance.
Shǒurén then received his grants as prescribed,
and Xún and the others were also recorded.
Wǎn was soon promoted to Junior Minister of the Dali Temple (Dàlǐ Zuǒ Shàogīng).
In the tenth month of that year,
Cōng and È expelled many Hanlin academicians,
and appointed their own favored individuals to fill the vacancies,
thus Wǎn was appointed Assistant Supervisor of Instruction (Shàozhànshì) concurrently Grand Academician of the Lecture Hall (Shìjiǎng Xuéshì),
and served in the Imperial Lecture (Jīngyán).
It was unprecedented for a son to be appointed to the Hanlin Academy through this means.
The next year,
the great ceremony was completed,
and he was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent (Zhānshì).
Niè Néngqiān, a vice commander (qiānshì) of the Brocade-Clad Guard (Jǐnyī),
had initially attached himself to Qián Níng to gain office,
but according to the precedent of the emperor's enthronement edict, he was reverted to a centurion (bǎihù).
Later, he attached himself to Cōng and È in discussing
the "Grand Rites,"
and also colluded with the palace eunuch Cuī Wén,
regaining his former position.
When the great ceremony was completed,
all those involved were promoted in rank,
but Néngqiān alone was not included,
which greatly enraged him.
He instructed Wēng Hóng, an official who had been dismissed from a minor post, to draft a memorial,
slandering Wáng Shǒurén for bribing Xí Shū to gain employment,
and the charges also implicated Wǎn and Cōng.
Wǎn submitted a memorial to clarify,
and also requested to withdraw.
The emperor issued a gracious decree to retain him,
but sent Néngqiān to the judicial authorities,
and exiled him to the frontier.
Hóng was also banished to his native place as a commoner.
Wǎn and Cōng and their ilk were on very good terms.
Cōng wanted to appoint him as Vice Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shìláng),
and also assign him to preside over the provincial examinations in Nánjīng.
However, both proposals were suppressed by Yáng Yīqīng,
and because of his southern accent, he was not allowed to participate in the Imperial Lectures (Jīngyán).
Wǎn was greatly resentful,
and submitted a memorial slandering Yīqīng without explicitly naming him.
The emperor knew in his heart that it was directed at Yīqīng,
and rebuked him for his empty words.
In the tenth month of that year, he was sent out as Vice Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Yòushìláng) of Nánjīng,
concurrently taking charge of the seals of various ministries.
In the twelfth year, he was summoned to be appointed Vice Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Zuǒshìláng).
Initially,
Wǎn and Cōng were closely connected.
By this time,
Xià Yán was leading the Ministry of Rites,
and the emperor was favoring him,
so Wǎn secretly attached himself to him,
going against Cōng.
When he assisted at the Nánjīng Ministry of Rites,
Zhōu Shǒuyì, a director (lángzhōng), feigned illness.
The emperor decreed that Wǎn should investigate the truth.
He did not report for a long time,
and Shǒuyì eventually left.
Wāng Hóng, Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū), seeking to please Cōng, submitted a memorial revealing the matter,
and the emperor decreed the dismissal of Shǒuyì.
He ordered Hóng to reinvestigate,
and Hóng then impeached Wǎn for deception and concealment.
Cōng manipulated the decree to strip him of three ranks and send him out.
At that time, the Ministry of Rites requested officials for the prayer for grain and accompanying ceremonies.
The emperor retained Wǎn to attend to the duties.
Hóng then submitted another memorial attacking Wǎn,
and also brought up other matters.
The emperor again ordered him to be transferred out.
Wǎn submitted a memorial defending himself,
and thereby slandered Hóng as Cōng's hawk,
requesting to be dismissed to avoid disaster.
The emperor, however, still remembered Wǎn's contributions in discussing the rites,
and retained him in his position as before.
From then on, Wǎn openly opposed Cōng.
Previously,
in Dàtóng, there was a military mutiny,
in which the commander-in-chief (zǒngbīngguān) Lǐ Jǐn was killed,
and the city was occupied and defended.
The Grand Coordinator (zǒngzhì) and Vice Minister (shìláng) Liú Yuánqīng, and the Commander (tídu) Xì Yǒng, proposed to massacre them.
The people in the city were terrified,
and sought assistance from the Mongols outside,
causing a great shock at the frontier.
The Provincial Governor (xúnfǔ) Pān Fǎng urgently requested to stop the military action.
Yuánqīng was enraged,
and swiftly submitted a memorial strongly slandering Fǎng.
Cōng and the court discussions both favored Yuánqīng,
but Wǎn alone said it was not a good strategy.
When Yuánqīng was dismissed,
Vice Minister Zhāng Zàn went to replace him.
Before he arrived,
Director Zhān Róng and others had already quelled the rebellion.
Not all the rebellious soldiers had been captured,
and the military and civilians were severely wounded.
The Prince of Dài requested to send a high-ranking official to pacify and soothe them.
The memorial was sent down to the Ministry of Rites.
Xià Yán thought it should be granted,
but strongly criticized the folly of the previous military action,
his words implicating Cōng.
Cōng was angry,
and strongly insisted on not sending anyone.
The emperor tactfully explained and resolved it,
then specifically assigned Wǎn to the task,
and also ordered him to investigate the military situation,
examine merits and faults,
and act as he saw fit.
Wǎn rushed to Dàtóng.
The imperial clansmen, soldiers, and civilians submitted hundreds of petitions complaining about the atrocities of the official army,
but none reported on the rebel army.
Wǎn questioned nothing,
to pacify their hearts.
There was someone who had sent Mongols back for the rebel army.
Wǎn seized and executed him,
which again incited those who were wavering.
Wǎn gathered a large number of soldiers and civilians,
and enlightened them on the consequences.
Those who had suffered presented petitions.
Wǎn feigned not to ask,
but secretly handed the petitions to the relief officials,
who verified them house by house,
and in one day arrested dozens of ringleaders.
A soldier named Qīn had killed three people of one family,
and feared he could not escape.
At night, he beat a gong to instigate a rebellion,
but no one responded,
and he was then captured.
Wǎn also issued wanted posters for several ringleaders,
and the soldiers and civilians no longer worried about being falsely implicated.
He then ordered the local officials to erect wooden palisades,
set up a baojia system in the four corners,
established community schools (shèxué),
and educated the children of soldiers and civilians.
The city became greatly peaceful.
Upon returning to court,
he listed the merits and faults of the civil and military generals and officials,
strongly criticizing Yuánqīng and Yǒng.
Wǎn was rewarded with a promotion of one rank for his efforts,
but Cōng and the Ministry of War protected Yuánqīng,
secretly suppressing Wǎn.
Wǎn repeatedly submitted memorials on the matter.
The emperor also favored him,
and Yuánqīng and Yǒng were eventually arrested.
Wǎn soon returned home due to his mother's mourning.
In the eighteenth year,
the officials of rites, due to the reverent bestowal of the grand title "August Sovereign Emperor of Heaven" (Huáng Tiān Shàngdì) and the posthumous title of the imperial ancestor,
requested to send an official to issue an edict to Cháoxiǎn (Korea).
At that time, the emperor was discussing a punitive expedition against Ānnán (Vietnam),
and wished to use this opportunity to spy on them.
So he said:
"Ānnán is also a tributary state;
it cannot be excluded from hearing this
just because of its recent rebellions and submissions.
Choose a high-ranking official with learning and knowledge to go."
The court officials repeatedly submitted names,
but none were accepted.
The emperor specifically appointed Wǎn as Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū) concurrently Grand Academician of the Hànlín Academy (Hànlín Xuéshì) as the chief envoy,
with Zhāng Zhì, a Tutor of the Heir Apparent (Yùdé), as his deputy.
The emperor was then at Chéngtiān,
urging Wǎn to go to the temporary imperial residence (xíngzài) to receive the commission.
Wǎn was reluctant to go.
Upon reaching Xúzhōu, he first sent an urgent messenger to memorialize that he was ill and could not proceed,
thus missing the deadline.
The emperor rebuked Wǎn for not rushing to the imperial residence,
but instead taking a boat to the capital, deeming it a great disrespect.
He ordered him to state his case,
but later released him.
Wǎn repeatedly presented proposals for expediency,
requesting to be given authority over the high officials of Liǎngguǎng (Guǎngdōng and Guǎngxī), Yúnnán, and Guìzhōu,
to dispatch supervising secretaries (gěishì) and censors (yùshǐ) to work with him,
and to have two directors from the Ministries of Personnel, Rites, and War selected to be at his disposal.
The emperor granted all of them.
Finally, he requested posthumous honors for his parents,
and also, citing the precedent of the grace for the establishment of the heir, requested imperial patents (gàomìng) be granted commensurate with his official rank.
The emperor was enraged,
stripped him of his new appointment as Minister (shàngshū),
ordered him to be relieved of duty as Vice Minister (shìláng),
and the envoy mission was also cancelled.
After a long time, he died at home.
Wǎn rose from a hereditary appointee (rènzǐ)
to the position of a minister or vice minister.
He initially attached himself to Zhāng Cōng,
but in his later years, he turned against Cōng and attached himself to Xià Yán.
At the time, everyone regarded him as cunning and treacherous.
When
the "Great Rites"
arose,
the first to submit a memorial after Cōng was Yòu-sī (祐楒), Prince of Zǎo-yáng (棗陽) from the Xiāng (襄) princely household.
He said:
"Emperor Xiào-zōng (孝宗) should only be referred to as 'Imperial Eldest Uncle' (皇伯考),
and the Holy Father (聖父) should be referred to as 'Imperial Deceased Father Grand Prince Xīng-xiàn' (皇考興獻大王).
The imperial ancestral temple and sacrifices in Xīng-guó (興國) should use the rites and music of the Son of Heaven,
and the emperor should be addressed as 'Filial Son Emperor [name]'.
The Holy Mother (聖母) should be granted the honorific title of Grand Consort (太妃),
and welcomed into the palace to be cared for.
Thus, the path of succession will not be lost,
and the affection of natural kinship will not be extinguished."
This was in the eighth month of Shì-zōng's (世宗) accession year.
From that time onwards,
all those who hoped for favor and sought advancement
arose in a clamor.
Displaced military officers and idle petty officials also rolled up their sleeves and glared,
debating imperial policies.
Even Cōng (璁) and È (萼) felt ashamed to be associated with them,
and refused to be counted among them.
Therefore, apart from the eight individuals including Cōng,
most received no special promotion.
As for the retired instructional supervisor Wáng Jià (王价),
he even requested that the various officials be subjected to demotion, banishment, or execution,
as punishment for the crime of forming factions and deceiving the emperor.
The most unseemly among them was Lù Chéng (陸澄) of Guī-ān (歸安), an adjudicator in the Ministry of Justice in Nán-jīng (南京).
Initially, he vehemently argued against the legitimacy of the posthumous enthronement.
Upon completing his mourning period and arriving in the capital,
the Grand Rites of Clarifying Relationships (明倫大典) had already been settled,
and Cōng and È were wielding great power.
Chéng then claimed he had initially been misled by others,
and after consulting his teacher Wáng Shǒu-rén (王守仁), he deeply regretted his earlier stance.
È was pleased by his words
and requested his appointment as an adjudicator in the Ministry of Rites.
However, the emperor, having seen Chéng's previous memorial, was displeased with him,
and banished him as an assistant prefect of Gāo-zhōu (高州).
In the seventh month of the fourth year of Jiā-jìng (嘉靖) (1525),
Xí Shū (席書) was compiling the collected discussions on the Great Rites,
and thus stated:
"Recent petitions for publication
mostly concern suggestions made more than three years ago.
If we consider my writings and those of Cōng, È, Xiàn-fū (獻夫), and Tāo (韜),
only five individuals are primarily selected.

Apart from Xióng Jiá (熊浹), Right Supervising Secretary of the Bureau of Rites, Huáng Zōng-míng (黃宗明), department director in the Ministry of Justice in Nán-jīng, Huáng Wǎn (黃綰), recorder in the Censorate, Jīn Shù (金述), recorder in the Office of Transmission, Chén Yún-zhāng (陳雲章), imperial student, Zhāng Shào-lián (張少連), scholar, and the two imperial clansmen, Prince of Chǔ (楚) and Prince of Zǎo-yáng,
only six individuals are additionally selected.
There were simultaneous suggestions,
such as those from imperial student Hé Yuān (何淵), adjudicator Wáng Guó-guāng (王國光), assistant prefect Mǎ Shí-zhōng (馬時中), and patrol inspector Fáng Jùn (房濬).
Their statements were perhaps not pure,
and their principles mostly incorrect,
so they were also not selected.
Other retired and idle individuals
who made suggestions after Cōng and È were summoned for employment,
all hoped for imperial favor by following the trend,
having ulterior motives,
and were likewise entirely excluded.

Niè Néng-qiān (聶能遷), a commander of the Embroidered Uniform Guard, and Wáng Jià (王价), a retired instructional supervisor of Chāng-píng (昌平), made suggestions in the second and third months of the third year,
which were not previously adopted.
Now these two officials request to have their names included,
which should be granted."
The emperor agreed.
Subsequently, an edict declared
that the "Great Rites"
were settled,
and that from then on, anyone making false statements or petitions
would be punished without leniency.
In the first month of the twelfth year (1533),
Qín Táng (秦鏜), a student from Pú-zhōu (蒲州), knelt before the palace to submit a memorial,
stating:
"The lineage of Emperor Xiào-zōng (孝宗) ended with Emperor Wǔ-zōng (武宗).
Therefore, Emperor Xiàn-huáng-dì (獻皇帝) was truly a case of a younger brother succeeding an elder brother to Emperor Xiào-zōng.
Your Majesty inherited the lineage of Emperor Xiàn-huáng-dì,
and should enshrine him in the Supreme Ancestral Temple (太廟).
However, Zhāng Fú-jìng (張孚敬), in deliberating the rites,
instead created a separate World Temple (世廟) to worship him,
preventing him from participating in the order of generations (昭穆之次).
This is to relegate him to obscurity."
He also said:
"Dividing the sacrifices to Heaven, Earth, Sun, and Moon among the four suburbs
loses the order of seniority and importance.
Removing the imperial title from the Former Teacher,
removing his statues,
and diminishing his rites and music,
and increasing the Shrine of the Enlightened Sage,
are all contrary to the intentions of the Holy Ancestors.
I request that they be restored to their original state."
Upon receiving the memorial, the emperor
was greatly angered.
He accused Qín Táng of irreverence for slandering his superiors,
and ordered him to be interrogated severely in the imperial prison,
demanding that he confess to the mastermind.
Qín Táng admitted to recklessly discussing to seek favor,
and that there was truly no instigator.
He was then sentenced to death under the law against heretical speech,
and imprisoned.
Later, following the request of Fēng Fāng (豐坊),
Emperor Xiàn-huáng-dì was enshrined in the temple with the title Zōng (宗, Ancestor)
to be matched with the Supreme Lord.
By then, Cōng and his group had already died
and could not witness it.
A eulogy states: Xí Shū (席書) and others also gained recognition through their discussions on the rites,
and their arguments were relatively balanced.
However, events were brought about by agitation,
and the later developments varied greatly.
By the time of enshrinement in the temple with the title Zōng,
it was no longer the original intention of those who initiated the discussions.
Shū (書) and Tāo (韜) achieved quite a bit in office,
and Jiá (浹) and Zōng-míng (宗明) were able to restrain themselves,
which was considered superior by contemporary opinion.
As for Wǎn's (綰) cunning and treachery,
it is not worth mentioning.
Biographies, Volume 86: Yáng Yī-qīng (楊一清), Wáng Qióng (王瓊), Péng Zé (彭澤), Máo Bó-wēn (毛伯溫) (Wāng Wén-shèng (汪文盛), Bāo Xiàng-xián (鮑象賢)), Wēng Wàn-dá (翁萬達)
Yáng Yī-qīng (楊一清),
courtesy name Yìng-níng (應寧), his ancestors were from Ān-níng (安寧), Yún-nán (雲南).
His father Jǐng (景) retired as an assistant prefect of Huà-zhōu (化州)
and brought Yī-qīng to live in Bā-líng (巴陵).
In his youth, he was skilled in writing,
and was recommended as a Hanlin scholar (翰林秀才) for his extraordinary talent as a child.
Emperor Xiàn-zōng (憲宗) ordered the Grand Secretariat to select a tutor for him.
At fourteen, he passed the provincial examination
and became a successful candidate in the imperial examination (進士) in the eighth year of Chéng-huà (成化) (1472).
His father was buried in Dān-tú (丹徒),
and he consequently made it his home.
After the mourning period,
he was appointed a Grand Secretary (中書舍人).
After a long time,
he was promoted to Assistant Surveillance Commissioner of Shān-xī (山西),
and then as Surveillance Vice Commissioner supervised education in Shǎn-xī (陝西).
Yī-qīng was physically unassuming but alert and intelligent,
and enjoyed discussing grand strategies for governance and economy.
During his eight years in Shǎn-xī,
he extensively researched border affairs in his spare time.
He entered the central government as a Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (太常寺少卿),
and was promoted to Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices in Nán-jīng (南京太常寺卿).
In the fifteenth year of Hóng-zhì (弘治) (1502), upon the recommendation of Liú Dà-xià (劉大夏),
he was promoted to Left Vice Censor-in-Chief of the Censorate (都察院左副都御史),
and supervised horse administration in Shǎn-xī.
The Western barbarians (西番) were originally rich in horses,
but relied on Chinese tea to cure illnesses.
Emperor Tài-zǔ (太祖) established a regulation
to exchange Shǔ (蜀) tea for barbarian horses for military use.
Over time, this gradually slackened,
and many dishonest individuals smuggled private tea for profit,
so barbarian horses did not arrive on time.
Yī-qīng strictly prohibited this,
bringing all tea profits under government control
to appease the various barbarian tribes,
and barbarian horses gathered in great numbers.
At that time, invaders made a large incursion into Huā-mǎ-chí (花馬池),
and the emperor ordered Yī-qīng to serve as Governor of Shǎn-xī,
while continuing to supervise horse administration.
He had barely taken up the post
when the invaders retreated.
He then selected and trained soldiers,
established the two cities of Píng-lǔ (平虜) and Hóng-gǔ (紅古) to reinforce Gù-yuán (固原),
built walls along the river to defend Jìng-lǔ (靖虜),
impeached and dismissed the corrupt and mediocre Grand Commander (總兵) Zhèng Hóng (鄭宏), Marquis Wǔ-ān (武安侯),
and reduced redundant expenses of the garrison eunuchs (鎮守中官),
bringing military discipline into order.
When Emperor Wǔ-zōng (武宗) first ascended the throne,
tens of thousands of invaders reached Gù-yuán (固原).
Grand Commander Cáo Xióng's (曹雄) army was cut off and could not communicate.
Yī-qīng led light cavalry from Píng-liáng (平涼), traveling day and night,
reached Cáo Xióng's army and directed their movements.
He extensively deployed suspicious troops to intimidate the invaders,
who then moved to attack Lóng-dé (隆德).
Yī-qīng fired signal cannons at night,
their sounds echoing in the valleys.
The invaders suspected that a large army had arrived
and fled beyond the frontier.
Yī-qīng worried that Yán-suī (延綏), Níng-xià (寧夏), and Gān-sù (甘肅) did not support each other when under alert,
and lacked overall command.
He requested that a high minister be dispatched to take overall charge.
Dà-xià (大夏) requested that Yī-qīng be immediately appointed Supreme Commander of the military affairs of the three garrisons.
Soon after, he was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief (右都御史).
Yī-qīng then proposed to reinforce the borders,
the main points being: Among the various borders of Shǎn-xī,
Yán-suī occupies a strategic position,
Níng-xià and Gān-sù control the river and mountains.
Only the area from Huā-mǎ-chí (花馬池) to Líng-zhōu (靈州) is wide and expansive,
and the fortresses are sparsely distributed.
If invaders
destroy the walls and enter,
then Gù-yuán (固原), Qìng-yáng (慶陽), Píng-liáng (平涼), and Gǒng-chāng (鞏昌) would all suffer.
In the early Chéng-huà (成化) period,
Xú Tíng-zhāng (徐廷璋), the Governor of Níng-xià,
built a border wall extending over two hundred *li*.
The one in Yán-suī was very solidly repaired by Yú Zǐ-jùn (余子俊).
Because of this,
invaders did not enter the bend of the Yellow River (套) for more than twenty years.
Later, border defenses slackened, and walls and trenches were flattened day by day.
Yīqīng was most proficient in current political affairs,
but his nature was magnanimous.
He loved and cherished worthy scholar-officials,
and shared achievements and fame with them.
All those who were framed and entrapped by Jǐn
were generally seen to be rehabilitated and promoted.
If something became known in the morning court,
he would recommend it that very evening.
His protégés were spread throughout the empire.
He once twice commanded Guānzhōng,
and those who rose from junior officers to great generals and marquises
were numerous and continuous.
Whatever gifts and thanks he received
he immediately dispersed by hand.
When great bandits ravaged the Central Plains,
Yīqīng submitted memorials requesting generals and troops.
He did so several times,
and all were approved.
When the bandits were pacified,
he was promoted to Shàobǎo and Tàizǐ Tàibǎo,
and his family was granted hereditary Jinwèi Bǎihù status.
He was again nominated for the Grand Secretariat,
but was not appointed.
Instead, Minister Jìn Guì was appointed,
while Yīqīng was promoted to Shàofù and Tàizǐ Tàifù.
Investigating Censor Wáng Áng discussed the malpractices of the selection system,
pointing out that Yīqīng was establishing a private faction.
The emperor demoted Áng for this.
Yīqīng further interceded for him,
and the emperor responded with a gracious edict.
When the Qiánqīnggōng was damaged by fire,
an edict sought frank words.
Yīqīng submitted a memorial stating that the court audiences were too late,
the imperial sacrifices too slow,
that Buddhist temples were being constructed in the Xīnèi,
border troops were stationed in the Forbidden City,
and he spoke of the harm of imperial shops in the jīnéi,
and the disturbances caused by textile manufacturing in Jiāngnán.
He then pleaded illness and requested to retire,
but the emperor comforted and retained him.
When Grand Secretary Yáng Tínghé worriedly left,
Yīqīng was ordered to concurrently hold the position of Grand Secretary of the Wǔyīngdiàn and participate in government affairs.
Zhāng Yǒng was soon disgraced and dismissed,
and his adopted son Qián Níng gained power.
Níng was formerly on good terms with Yīqīng,
but those who sought to frame Yīqīng then harbored resentment.
At a time of calamities and unusual phenomena,
Yīqīng impeached himself,
and severely criticized current political affairs.
Within his memorial were
words like "wild words confuse the sacred ear,
common men shake the nation's foundation,
the Forbidden City is mixed with armed men,
and the capital has no protective barrier."
These remarks
were sharp criticisms of the close favorites,
but the emperor did not heed them.
Níng and others like Jiāng Bīn heard of this
and were greatly angered.
They made performers spread rumors before the emperor,
satirizing and criticizing Yīqīng.
At this time, there were officials dismissed during performance reviews.
They instigated the military student Zhū Dàzhōu to denounce Yīqīng's private affairs,
with Níng as the internal instigator.
Investigating Censors Zhōu Jīn and Chén Shì, among others, submitted joint memorials impeaching Dàzhōu for false accusations
and requesting an investigation into the instigator,
but the emperor refused.
Yīqīng then forcefully requested to resign,
and was granted an imperial edict of commendation,
with provisions for transport and sustenance as per regulations.
When the emperor campaigned in the south,
he visited Yīqīng's residence,
drinking joyfully for two days and nights,
and composing dozens of poems in harmony.
Yīqīng gently admonished him to stop,
and the emperor consequently did not proceed to Jiāngnán and Zhèjiāng.
When Shìzōng was a princely heir,
King Xiàn once said that Chǔ had three outstanding figures:
Liú Dàxià, Lǐ Dōngyáng, and Yīqīng.
He remembered this in his heart.
Upon his ascension,
court officials jointly recommended Yīqīng.
An official was then dispatched to bestow gold and silk and inquire about him,
informing him of the summons date,
and urging him to speak.
Yīqīng expressed his gratitude,
and his son was specially granted the position of Zhōngshū Shèrén.
In the twelfth month of the third year of Jiājìng (戊午 day), an edict ordered Yīqīng, as Shàofù and Tàizǐ Tàifù, to be changed to Minister of War and Censor-in-Chief of the Left,
to concurrently command the military affairs of the three borders of Shǎnxī.
Former Grand Secretaries commanding border regions
began with Yīqīng.
A gentle edict praised him,
comparing him to Guō Zǐyí.
By this time, Yīqīng had been a grand coordinator three times,
and all his troops were overjoyed.
When Yìbùlà fled to Xīhǎi,
causing harm in Xīníng and Táohé,
Jīn Xiànmín suggested appeasement,
but only Yīqīng requested extermination.
When Tǔlǔfān sought tribute,
Chén Jiǔchóu wished to refuse it,
but Yīqīng requested appeasement.
At that time, he trained his generals in military formations,
often saying:
"In times of peace, one should be on guard as if there were trouble;
in times of trouble, one should remain calm as if there were peace."
At this juncture, Zhāng Cōng and others strongly opposed Fèi Hóng,
and Censor Jí Táng then requested Yīqīng's return to the Grand Secretariat.
Investigating Censor Zhāng Qiáo and Censor Hóu Zhì, among others, argued against this.
The emperor demoted Zhì,
and summoned Yīqīng to be Minister of Personnel and Grand Secretary of the Wǔyīngdiàn.
Upon his arrival for an audience,
he was promoted to Shàoshī,
and still concurrently held Tàizǐ Tàifù,
which was not according to precedent.
Not long after,
when the Veritable Records of the Xiàn Emperor were completed,
he was promoted to Tàizǐ Tàishī and Grand Secretary of the Jǐnshēndiàn.
Yīqīng declined, stating he was not involved in the compilation,
but he was not allowed.
When Wáng Xiàn reported a victory,
Yīqīng was credited with merit,
and promoted to Tèjìn Zuǒ Zhùguó and Grand Secretary of the Huágàidiàn.
With Fèi Hóng already gone,
Yīqīng thus became the Senior Grand Secretary.
The emperor bestowed two silver seals,
one saying
"Aged Virtue and Loyalty,"
the other saying
"Correcting Errors and Rectifying Transgressions,"
ordering him to speak frankly in sealed memorials.
He discussed Zhāng Yǒng's past merits with Zhāng Cōng,
and Zhāng Yǒng was reinstated as Commander of the Training Regiments.
Investigating Censor Lù Càn requested to reinforce and extend the border walls,
promoting Yīqīng's past proposals,
and Yīqīng then strongly encouraged this.
The emperor allocated treasury funds for it,
and ordered Vice Minister Wáng Tíngxiàng to go,
but after a long time, it was eventually stopped.
When the Dàmíng Lúnliè (Great Rites) were completed,
he was given the stipend of a first-rank official.
Initially,
when the "Grand Rites"
controversy arose,
Yīqīng was at home.
Upon seeing Zhāng Cōng's memorial,
he wrote to his disciple Qiáo Yǔ, saying:
"This proposal by Zhāng,
even if a sage were to rise again,
could not be changed."
He also urged Xí Shū to quickly respond to the summons
to settle the grand debate.
Once Cōng and others quickly rose to prominence,
they largely drew Yīqīng in.
The emperor also regarded Yīqīng as an old minister,
and his favor and courtesy were exceptionally generous.
He was exempted from attending the daily court lectures,
and for the new moon and full moon audiences,
he was permitted to enter the Grand Secretariat to attend to affairs only at dawn.
Imperial writings, harmonious poems, and gifts of gold, silk, and wine
were exceptionally generous. Whatever he spoke about concerning border affairs and state finances,
large or small, was heard attentively.
Zhāng Cōng and Guì È, having overthrown Fèi Hóng,
believed that Yī Qīng would surely support them.
However, Yī Qīng instead requested that Xiè Qiān be summoned,
which caused resentment in them.
Before Xiè Qiān arrived,
Zhāng Cōng had already entered the Grand Secretariat
and made many changes and proposals.
Yī Qīng, citing precedents, somewhat restrained him,
and Zhāng Cōng's faction grew increasingly displeased.
Niè Néngqiān of the Embroidered Uniform Guard impeached Zhāng Cōng,
and Zhāng Cōng wished to put him to death,
but Yī Qīng disagreed.
Enraged, Zhāng Cōng
submitted a memorial covertly criticizing Yī Qīng,
and also instigated Huáng Wǎn to strongly oppose him.
Yī Qīng submitted a memorial in rebuttal,
stating that Zhāng Cōng opposed him because of Niè Néngqiān,
and also touched upon other matters concerning Zhāng Cōng.
He then requested to retire.
The Emperor mediated between the two.
Yī Qīng then, because of an inauspicious omen, requested that all officials be admonished to act in harmony,
and again begged for pardon for the officials involved in the Rites Controversy.
Zhāng Cōng resented him even more.
Guì È entered the Grand Secretariat,
and also could not get along with Yī Qīng.
Yī Qīng repeatedly requested to leave,
saying:
"Those who currently hold views are still engaging in constant change,
while I alone advocate for tranquility;
they are still harsh and exacting,
while I alone advocate for leniency and fairness.
Because of this, there are many disagreements,
and I wish to make way for the worthy."
The Emperor again issued a warm edict praising him.
However, Supervising Secretaries Wáng Zhǔn and Lù Càn exposed Zhāng Cōng and Guì È for abusing power and accepting bribes.
The Emperor immediately dismissed Zhāng Cōng and Guì È,
and revealed their crimes.
Their partisan Huò Tāo rolled up his sleeves and said:
"Zhāng and Guì are gone;
soon it will be my turn."
He then submitted a memorial vehemently attacking Yī Qīng,
alleging that he had accepted bribes from Zhāng Yǒng and Xiāo Jìng.
Yī Qīng again submitted a memorial in rebuttal,
requesting to be dismissed.
Although the Emperor comforted him and urged him to stay,
Zhāng Cōng was recalled,
and Huò Tāo intensified his attacks,
further alleging that the judicial authorities, following Yī Qīng's instructions,
had fabricated Guì È's crimes.
The Emperor was indeed angered,
and ordered the judicial authorities to convene court officials for a joint deliberation.
Zhōu Lún, the Minister of Justice, was sent to Nánjīng,
and Vice Minister Xǔ Zàn was appointed to replace him.
Xǔ Zàn then confirmed Huò Tāo's words,
and requested that Yī Qīng be stripped of his official status.
The Emperor ordered Yī Qīng to present his own case.
Zhāng Cōng then submitted three secret memorials,
citing Yī Qīng's merits in supporting the rites,
and requesting leniency for him,
but in reality, he intended to solidify the Emperor's resolve to dismiss him.
The Emperor indeed granted Yī Qīng's retirement,
and he returned home by post-horse,
still receiving gifts of gold and silk.
The following year,
Zhāng Cōng and others fabricated the case of Zhū Jìzōng,
implicating Yī Qīng for receiving money from Zhāng Yǒng's younger brother Róng,
writing a tomb inscription for Zhāng Yǒng,
and appointing Róng as a hereditary Embroidered Uniform Guard commander,
thus stripping him of his office and forcing him into retirement.
Yī Qīng expressed great hatred, saying:
"I am old,
yet I am betrayed by these youngsters!"
He died of a carbuncle on his back.
His last memorial stated that he had been slandered and disgraced,
and would not rest in peace even in death.
The Emperor ordered that the bribery charges be dropped.
Several years later, he was reinstated to his former office.
After a long time,
he was posthumously granted the title of Grand Tutor (Tàibǎo)
and the posthumous name Wénxiāng.
Yī Qīng was born with a hidden deformity (cryptorchidism),
and his appearance resembled that of a eunuch,
and he had no sons.
He was learned and skilled in adapting to circumstances,
and particularly well-versed in frontier affairs.
When urgent military despatches arrived one after another,
he would draft ten memorials in one night,
all hitting the mark.
If someone slandered him,
he would instead recommend and promote them.
However, in his later years, he differed from Zhāng Cōng and Guì È,
and was pushed out by them,
thus failing to end his career with grace and honor.
Nevertheless, his talent was unmatched at the time,
and some compared him to Yáo Chóng.
Wáng Qióng,
courtesy name Déhuá,
was a native of Tàiyuán.
He passed the imperial examination in the 20th year of Chénghuà (1484).
He was appointed as a Section Chief (zhǔshì) in the Ministry of Works,
and later promoted to Director (lángzhōng).
He was sent out to manage the Grand Canal for three years,
and recorded its affairs in a detailed gazetteer.
His successors, when examining his records,
found no discrepancies whatsoever,
and from then on, he was known for his astuteness and competence.
He was transferred to the Ministry of Revenue,
and successively served as Surveillance Vice Commissioner (yòu bùzhèngshǐ) of Hénán.
In the 1st year of Zhèngdé (1506), he was promoted to Vice Censor-in-Chief (yòu fù dūyùshǐ) to supervise grain transport.
The following year, he entered the court as Vice Minister (yòu shìláng) of the Ministry of Revenue.
The Prince of Héng's domain had land granted to it,
which was overgrown and unsuitable for cultivation,
but the people were coerced into paying rent as a regular practice.
Wáng Qióng, however, falsely accused the people such as Zhào Xián of encroaching upon and occupying it.
When Wáng Qióng went to investigate,
he confiscated land from neighboring commoners and gave it to the Prince,
and Zhào Xián and others were banished to the frontier,
causing widespread resentment among the people.
In the spring of the 3rd year (1508),
the court nominated six candidates for Vice Minister of Personnel,
all of whom were rejected by the Emperor.
Finally, Wáng Qióng's name was submitted,
and approved.
He was impeached for outstanding loans from the Tàicāng treasury to frontier officials during his tenure at the Ministry of Revenue;
because the department concerned delayed its report,
Minister Gù Zuǒ had his salary withheld,
while Wáng Qióng was transferred to Nánjīng.
Soon after,
he was again transferred to the Ministry of Revenue.
In the 8th year (1513), he was promoted to Minister.
Wáng Qióng was a calculating man,
skilled in auditing.
When he was a Director, he meticulously recorded old documents and regulations,
thoroughly understanding the state of income, expenditure, surplus, and deficit.
By the time he became Minister, he was even more proficient in national finances.
When frontier commanders requested fodder,
he would calculate on his fingers how much grain and fodder were stored in certain granaries and depots,
how much was transported annually by various prefectures, and how much autumn harvest frontier soldiers collected annually,
saying:
"That is sufficient.
To demand more is irrational."
People increasingly regarded Wáng Qióng as talented.
In the 10th year (1515), he succeeded Lù Wán as Minister of War.
At that time, bandits rose up everywhere,
and generals and soldiers were promoted based on presenting heads.
Wáng Qióng said:
"This is a harmful policy from the Qín dynasty.
While it might be acceptable in frontier regions,
there is no precedent for counting heads in the interior.
Currently, in Jiāngxī and Sìchuān, countless innocent civilians are wantonly killed,
leading to bandits running rampant and causing disaster,
all due to this policy.
From now on, during campaigns in the interior,
success will only be measured by the complete pacification of rebels,
not by counting heads."
