This was adopted.
At that time, the Emperor was traveling far beyond the Great Wall,
and did not return for over a year,
causing increased banditry near the capital.
Wáng Qióng requested that a Grand General (zǒngbīng) be stationed in Héjiān,
and a Vice Surveillance Commissioner (bīngbèi fùshǐ) for military affairs in each of Dàmíng and Wǔdìng,
holding them responsible for pacifying bandits.
He also issued orders to the two Grand Coordinators (xúnfǔ) of Shùntiān and Bǎodìng,
to strictly guard key strategic points as an outer defense,
and to gather soldiers and horses from Liáodōng and Yánsuí at the Emperor's temporary residence,
to protect the imperial carriage.
Both the court and the provinces relied on him and felt secure.
When the Xiàofēng bandit Tāng Májiǔ rebelled,
officials requested to send troops to suppress him.
Wáng Qióng suggested secretly ordering the Censor-in-Chief (dūyùshǐ) Xǔ Tíngguāng to investigate and arrest him unexpectedly,
and not a single one escaped.
Victorious reports from all directions arrived,
often attributing success to Wáng Qióng.
He received numerous imperial favors and rewards,
accumulating promotions to Junior Tutor (shàoshī) and Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent (tàizǐ tàishī),
and his son was granted a hereditary position as a chiliarch (qiānhù) in the Embroidered Uniform Guard.
When the Qiánqīng Palace was being constructed,
he was again granted two hereditary chiliarch positions in the Embroidered Uniform Guard for others,
enjoying the highest favor among all ministers.
In the fourteenth year [of the Zhèngdé reign (1519)],
Prince Níng, Chén Háo, rebelled.

Qióng requested an imperial edict for the Earl of Nánhé, Fāng Shòuxiáng, to oversee the training of the Jiāng army to defend the Southern Capital. X Nángàn Governor Wáng Shǒurén and Húguǎng Governor Qín Jīn were each to lead their respective units to Nánchāng.
Yìngtiān Governor Lǐ Chōngsì was to garrison Jīngkǒu.
Huáiyáng Governor Cóng Lán was to guard Yízhēn.
The memorial was submitted.
The emperor desired to personally lead the campaign,
and withheld a decision for three days.
Grand Secretary Yáng Tínghé urged him.
Eventually, an imperial edict for a personal campaign was issued,
ordering Qióng and Tínghé, among others, to remain and guard the capital.
Previously,
Qióng had appointed Wáng Shǒurén as Governor of Nán and Gàn,
granting him discretionary authority to oversee military affairs.
When Chén Háo rebelled,
and the news reached the court,
the entire court was anxious.
Qióng said,
"Gentlemen, do not worry.
I appointed Wáng Bó'ān in Gànzhōu
precisely for this day.
The rebel will be captured in no time."
Not long after,
it happened just as he had said.
Qióng was highly talented
and skilled at forming connections.
He cultivated a close relationship with Qián Níng, Jiāng Bīn, and others,
thus gaining opportunities to advance himself.
His requests were always granted.
His ability to achieve success in the Ministry of War
was also due to the influence of Bīn and others.
When Lù Wán was defeated,
he replaced him as Minister of Personnel.
Qióng was jealous of Péng Zé, who had pacified the roving bandits,
and whose reputation surpassed his own.
He conspired with Qián Níng
and implicated Zé in a dangerous legal case.
He also imprisoned Yúnnán Governor Fàn Yǒng, Gānsù Governor Lǐ Kūn, and Vice Commissioner Chén Jiǔchóu.
Many officials, both inside and outside the court, feared Qióng.
However, Grand Secretary Tínghé was also unable to tolerate
that Qióng's rewards and punishments
were often based on imperial decrees issued without consulting the Grand Secretariat.
The following year,
Emperor Shìzōng ascended the throne.
Censors impeached Qióng in unison,
and he was imprisoned in the Censorate's jail.
Qióng fiercely exposed Tínghé.
The emperor increasingly considered Qióng in the wrong
and sent the matter to be deliberated by court officials.
He was sentenced to death for colluding with close attendants,
but was ordered to be exiled to Zhuānglàng.
Qióng again pleaded old age,
and his exile was changed to Suídé.
Zhāng Cōng, Guì È, and Huò Tāo rose to power.
Considering Qióng an enemy of Tínghé,
they initially recommended him,
but he was not accepted.
Then, in the sixth year of Jiājìng (1527), there was a border alarm.
È strongly urged using Qióng,
but it did not happen.
The emperor, pitying Qióng's old age and illness,
ordered him to return to his hometown as a commoner.
Censor Hú Sōng then impeached È, leading to È's demotion and transfer to an outer post.
His colleague, Zhōu Zài, requested clemency for Sōng,
and both were sent to the imperial prison.
È again stated that Qióng had previously attacked Tínghé,
which was why court officials had collectively opposed him.
The emperor then ordered Qióng to be reinstated as Minister, awaiting appointment.
The following year, he was appointed Minister of War and concurrently Censor-in-Chief of the Right, replacing Wáng Xiàn to oversee military affairs in the Three Garrisons of Shǎnxī.
Turpan had occupied Hāmì,
and the court had debated closing the passes and ceasing tribute for four years.
By this time,
its general Yámùlán was suspected by the chieftain Sùtán Mǎnsù'ér.
He led over two thousand people to seek allegiance with China.
The Fān people of Shāzhōu, Tiēmùgē and Tǔbā,
who had long been subjected to Turpan's service,
suffered from their demands,
and also led over five thousand people to join.
The Fān people launched raids,
but were repeatedly defeated by Assistant Commander Yún Chāng and others.
Those who instigated the Wǎlà to raid Sùzhōu
were repelled by Vanguard Commander Péng Jùn.
As the rebels had lost their allies
and suffered several defeats,
they offered to return Hāmì,
requested to resume tribute,
and begged for the return of their detained envoys,
but their language was often rude.
Qióng memorialized, requesting to pacify and accept them.
The emperor followed the advice of Minister of War Wáng Shízhōng
and granted Qióng's request.
Huò Tāo found it difficult to agree.
Qióng again memorialized, requesting an imperial edict to return the Fān envoys
and resume tribute as before.
From then on, the Western Regions were pacified again,
but the northern raiders frequently became a border problem.
Initially, they invaded Zhuānglàng.
Qióng's generals intercepted and attacked them,
beheading dozens.
Soon after, they entered through Hóngchéngzǐ,
killing the provisions clerk Zhāng Wénmíng.
The following year, tens of thousands of cavalry raided Níngxià.
Later, they attacked Língzhōu.
Qióng commanded Vanguard Commander Liáng Zhèn and others to intercept and kill over seventy people.
That autumn,
he assembled thirty thousand elite soldiers from various routes
and inspected the border.
When the raiders heard,
they moved their camps and fled far away.
The armies dispersed and advanced on separate routes,
set fire to the wilderness,
displayed their military might, and returned.
Previously,
Nánjīng Supervising Secretary Qiū Jiǔrèn impeached Qióng.
The emperor comforted and retained him.
When Cōng and È were dismissed from government,
all those who impeached Cōng and È's faction first accused Qióng,
so he was ordered to retire.
Soon after, the previous edict was annulled,
and an envoy was sent to convey imperial comfort.
At that time, the Fān extensively plundered Líntáo.
Qióng gathered troops to attack the Ruòlóng and Bǎn'ěr tribes,
burned their nests,
beheaded three hundred sixty,
and pacified and accepted the surrender of over seventy tribes.
In recognition of his achievements,
he was promoted to Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
While Qióng was at the border,
military preparations were very strict.
Raiders once invaded Shānxī and gained spoils.
The next year, they again hunted on the border,
feigning a desire to go east.
Qióng ordered preparations in the west.
The raiders indeed entered there
and were soundly defeated.
All the Fān were pacified,
and the western frontier became more stable.
The military and civilians of Gānsù had long suffered from Turpan's incursions and violence.
Fearing Qióng's departure,
they collectively requested the defending officials to memorialize for his retention.
Thereupon, Governor Táng Zé and Investigating Censor Hú Míngshàn fully presented his accomplishments
and requested to grant the wishes of the military and civilians.
An especially gracious edict commended him.
Initially,
the emperor disliked Yáng Tínghé
and suspected all court officials were his partisans.
Therefore, he successively appointed Guì È and Fāng Xiànfū as Ministers of Personnel.
When Xiànfū left,
the emperor did not want to appoint anyone else,
and the position remained vacant for a long time.
Then, in the winter of the tenth year (1531),
an envoy was sent with an imperial edict to summon Qióng as Minister of Personnel.
Nánjīng Censor Mǎ Yáng and ten others fiercely denounced Qióng as a lingering villain from the previous reign.
The emperor was furious
and had Yáng and others arrested and imprisoned in the imperial prison,
while comforting Qióng.
Not long after,
Yáng and others were also reinstated.
There was an alarm at Huāmǎchí.
Minister of War Wáng Xiàn requested to dispatch troops.
Qióng said that the defenses at Huāmǎchí were strict,
and the raiders could not enter.
When a large army arrived,
they would retreat first,
only wasting China's resources.
Xiàn nonetheless dispatched six thousand men.
By the time they reached Zhāngdé,
the raiders had indeed fled.
He died in office the following autumn.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Preceptor
and the posthumous name Gōngxiāng.
That year,
Péng Zé had already died earlier.
During the Zhèngdé and Jiājìng eras,
Zé and Qióng both possessed talent and strategy.
They constantly harmed each other,
and their advancements and retreats alternated.
However, Qióng was cunning and malicious,
and public opinion was particularly against him.
Nevertheless, he achieved much while serving in the Ministry of War.
And when he oversaw the Three Garrisons,
people compared him to Yáng Yīqīng.
Péng Zé,
courtesy name Jìwù,
was a native of Lánzhōu.
As a child, he studied with his maternal grandfather, Duàn Jiān,
and had a strong character and integrity.
After completing the second session of the metropolitan examination,
he heard his mother was ill,
and immediately returned home.
His mother's illness had already passed.
He passed the imperial examination in the third year of Hóngzhì (1490),
and was appointed as a Master of the Bureau of Works (Gōngbù Zhǔshì),
later rising to Director (Lángzhōng) in the Ministry of Justice (Xíngbù).
When a powerful gentry killed someone,
Zé sentenced him to execution.
An influential eunuch pleaded for clemency,
but Zé firmly refused to listen.
He was sent out to serve as the Prefect of Huīzhōu.
Zé was about to marry off his daughter,
and had dozens of lacquerware items made,
ordering a clerk to send them to his home.
Zé’s father was furious,
and ordered them burned.
He then traveled on foot to Huīzhōu.
Zé was surprised and came out to greet him,
instructing the clerk to carry his father’s luggage.
His father angrily said:
"I carried this several thousand *lǐ*,
can you not carry it a few steps?"
Upon entering,
he flogged Zé in the hall.
After the flogging,
he took his luggage and left directly.
Zé subsequently applied himself even more diligently.
His administration was excellent,
and people compared him to the former prefect, Sūn Yù.
Yù is found in the 'Biography of Conscientious Officials' (Xúnlì Zhuàn).
He returned home for his father's mourning.
At the beginning of Zhèngdé (1506),
he was appointed Prefect of Zhēndìng.
When eunuchs repeatedly interfered with prohibitions,
Zé prepared a coffin in the administrative hall,
frightening them with the threat of death,
and they dared not act presumptuously.
He was promoted to Vice Surveillance Commissioner (Fùshǐ) of Zhèjiāng,
and then Surveillance Commissioner (Ànchásǐ) of Hénán.
Wherever he went, he was known for his sternness and power.
He was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief (Yòumiǎn Dūyùshǐ),
and appointed Grand Coordinator (Xúnfǔ) of Liáodōng.
He was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief (Yòufù Dūyùshǐ),
and transferred to Bǎodìng.
Before he could take up his post,
Liú Huì, Zhào Suì, and others rebelled in Hénán.
Zé was ordered to serve as Supreme Commander (Tídū Jūnwù) to suppress them, along with the Earl of Xiánníng, Chóu Yuè.
He presented eleven practical measures,
emphasizing generous rewards and severe punishments,
to motivate his officers and soldiers.
Zé was tall and stout,
with a waist measuring twelve spans (wéi),
and a loud voice,
sounding like a roar when speaking to people.
Upon his arrival,
he made a grand display of military might,
and summoned the generals and officers,
reprimanding them that timidity and shrinking back would result in death.
The generals and officers trembled and admitted their guilt,
and only after a long while were they released.
He then issued an order to advance with drums beating and press the rebels,
fighting dozens of battles, large and small,
and repeatedly defeating them.
In just four months,
the rebels were completely pacified.
The details are found in Yuè's biography.
For his merits,
he was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief (Yòudū Yùshǐ) and Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shàobǎo),
and his son was granted an inherited position as a company commander (Bǎihù) in the Imperial Bodyguard (Jǐnyīwèi).
Soon after, he replaced Hóng Zhōng as Supreme Commander of the forces in Sìchuān and Shǎnxī,
to suppress the rebels in Sìchuān.
At that time, Yān Běnshù, Lán Tíngruì, Liáo Huì, and Cáo Fǔ had already been pacified,
but only Liáo Mázi and Yù Sīfèng were still rampant.
Zé, accompanied by the Commander-in-Chief (Zǒngbīngguān) Shí Yuán, repeatedly defeated the rebels,
and his subordinate General Yán Xūn pursued and captured Mázi in Jiànzhōu.
Sīfèng fled between Tōng and Bā,
and his power revived.
Zé led his armies to surround him,
and he was eventually captured.
Zé then moved to Hànzhōng,
and requested to return the army.
Before a reply was received,
rebels in Nèijiāng and Róngchāng flared up again.
Zé again moved his forces to suppress and pacify them,
and also pacified the mutinous soldiers in Chéngdū who had seized the Prefect (Zhīzhōu) and Commander (Zhǐhuī).
He requested to return the army even more earnestly,
and an imperial edict ordered him to temporarily remain in Bǎoníng to maintain order.
He was promoted to Left Censor-in-Chief (Zuǒdū Yùshǐ) and Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Tàibǎo),
and his son was granted an inherited position as before.
Zé again requested to return twice more,
and was finally recalled.
Before he could depart,
Turfan occupied Hāmì,
captured King Zhōngshùn, Sùtán Bàiyáláng,
took his seal,
and sent insolent letters to Gānsù,
demanding gold and silk.
Grand Coordinator Dèng Zhāng and Gānsù Grand Coordinator Zhào Jiàn reported this,
and requested that a high minister be dispatched to deal with the situation.
Grand Secretary Yáng Tínghé and others jointly recommended Zé.
Zé had been in military service for a long time,
and was weary of it.
He declined on the grounds of his hometown,
and also claimed illness,
recommending Zhāng and Marquis of Xiánníng, Yuè, as suitable.
The Emperor issued a gracious edict to console and encourage him,
and he then departed.
Zé was capable in military matters and understood warfare,
but he was naturally careless and arrogant.
His handling of the Hāmì affair was quite inappropriate,
and Qián Níng, Wáng Qióng, and others repeatedly slandered him,
and he was consequently punished for it.
When Zé arrived at Gānzhōu,
Turfan was raiding the garrisons (wèi) of Chìjīn and Kǔyù.
They sent an envoy to demand gold and silk,
and requested the return of Hāmì.
Zé believed that the barbarians could be enticed with profit,
and conspired with Jiàn to
send Hāmì Commander (Dūdū) Xiěyì Hǔxiān with two thousand in currency and a silver wine pitcher as a bribe,
ordering him to return the Hāmì city seal.
Before receiving a reply,
he rashly reported that the matter was settled,
and requested to retire due to old age.
He was recalled to manage affairs in the Censorate (yuànshì).
The Supervising Censor (Xún'àn Yùshǐ) Féng Shíyōng said that the city had not been returned,
and Zé should not be recalled so hastily.
This was not accepted.
Initially,
there was a vacancy for the Minister of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū).
All the court officials jointly recommended Zé,
but Wáng Qióng obtained the position,
and secretly obstructed Zé.
Many censors impeached Qióng,
and from this, a rift formed.
Zé also often used alcohol to insult Qióng,
and Qióng increasingly desired to ruin him.
Zé sometimes cursed Qián Níng,
and Qióng told Níng about it,
but Níng did not believe him at first.
Qióng then invited Zé to drink,
hid Níng's confidant behind a screen,
and provoked Zé into a drunken rant so that the confidant would hear it.
Níng was indeed furious.
Coincidentally, a large force of invaders entered Xuānfǔ.
The court deliberated appointing Xǔ Tài as a general,
and Zé as Supreme Commander (Zǒngzhì) of the eastern and western armies.
However, when the edict was issued,
Xǔ Tài was dismissed and not sent,
and Zé was not appointed Supreme Commander.
He was only ordered to lead two vanguard (yóují) forces of six thousand men.
The intention was to put Zé in a difficult position.
Zé said:
"Your servant is a civil official;
breaking enemy lines and charging into battle is not something your servant can undertake alone."
Qióng then requested that the Duke of Chéng, Zhū Fǔ, be sent.
Coincidentally, the invaders fled,
and Zé returned to manage affairs in the Censorate.
In the winter of the fifteenth year,
an imperial heir was born.
An edict was to be issued to foreign countries.
Shàngshū of the Ministry of Rites, Xià Yán, believing that Ānnán had long neglected its tributary duties,
held that it was inappropriate to send envoys,
and requested to subjugate it.
Thus, Bó Wēn was appointed Yòudū Yùshǐ,
and with Xiánníng Hóu Qiú Luán, they were to prepare troops and await orders.
He declined due to his father's mourning,
but it was not permitted.
He arrived in the capital in the fifth month of the following year.
The emperor then outlined six strategies.
At this time, the heir apparent of Ānnán, Lí Níng, sent his attendant Zhèng Wéiliáo and others to accuse Mò Dēngyōng of regicide and usurpation,
requesting military intervention for revenge.
The emperor, doubting the veracity of the claim,
ordered a temporary halt to military action,
and commanded the provincial governors of Liǎngguǎng and Yúnnán to investigate and report.
Bó Wēn was ordered to assist in managing the affairs of the Censorate.
Censor Hé Wéibǎi requested that Bó Wēn be allowed to complete his mourning period,
but this was not granted.
Bó Wēn feigned illness and did not appear,
only returning to his duties after the completion of the mourning period.
That winter, he was promoted to Gōngbù Shàngshū.
In the spring of the seventeenth year,
Qiánguó Gōng Mù Cháofǔ and others arrived with Dēngyōng's surrender memorial,
requesting pardon and permission to offer tribute.
Earlier,
Yúnnán Patrol-Inspector Wāng Wénshèng reported that Dēngyōng, hearing of the impending military expedition,
had sent spies.
The emperor had already ordered to proceed with the invasion as per the previous edict.
Wénshèng also adopted the strategy of Wǔ Wènyuān, an Ānnán defector,
who fully explained how Dēngyōng could be defeated,
and then issued a proclamation to Ānnán ordering them to present a memorial and surrender territory.
Now,
Mù Cháofǔ's memorial was submitted for court deliberation,
and all agreed it should not be granted.
So, Bó Wēn was reappointed Bīngbù Shàngshū concurrently Yòudū Yùshǐ,
with a set date for departure.
The emperor, considering the gravity of military action,
did not necessarily intend to attack,
but particularly wished to intimidate and subdue them.
However, Bīngbù Shàngshū Zhāng Zàn offered no plans,
deferring to the emperor's wishes.
Court opinion largely favored not raising an army,
but dared not openly remonstrate.
Several months after the edict was issued,
the Governor-General of Liǎngguǎng, Shìláng Zhāng Jīng, submitted a military strategy,
and stated that thirty thousand troops
and one million six hundred thousand shí of provisions would be needed.
Qīnzhōu Zhīzhōu Lín Xīyuán, on the other hand, vehemently argued that Dēngyōng was easy to take,
and requested immediate deployment.
Zhāng Zàn dared not make a decision,
and again requested court deliberation.
No definitive plan emerged from the deliberation,
and the emperor was displeased.
He reprimanded Zhāng Zàn,
and the expedition was again halted.
Bó Wēn was ordered to continue assisting in managing the affairs of the Censorate.
In the second month of the following year,
the emperor visited Chéngtiān.
Bó Wēn was appointed Governor-General of military affairs for Xuān, Dà, and Shānxī.
Soon after, court officials were selected,
and he was additionally granted the title of Tàizǐ Bīnkè.
The five forts under Dàtóng, namely Zhènbiān, Zhènchuān, Hóngcì, Zhènhé, and Zhènlǔ,
were separated by over two hundred lǐ,
on the extreme frontier and close to enemy camps.
Since Patrol-Inspector Zhāng Wénjǐn caused rebellion by building forts,
no one dared to propose their repair.
Bó Wēn said:
"The chaos arose
from the appointment of inappropriate people,
not from a flawed proposal."
He ultimately oversaw their construction.
Three thousand soldiers were recruited for defense,
given vacant land,
and permanently exempted from taxes.
Border defense relied on this.
For his achievements,
he was promoted to Tàizǐ Shàobǎo.
At this time, Dēngyōng, fearing an invasion,
repeatedly submitted memorials begging for surrender.
The emperor also wished to pacify him,
and sent Shìláng Huáng Wǎn to offer a conciliatory proclamation.
Huáng Wǎn made many demands,
which angered the emperor,
and Huáng Wǎn was dismissed.
The matter was again submitted for court deliberation,
and all agreed that an attack was necessary.
The emperor assented.
In the intercalary seventh month, Bó Wēn and Qiú Luán were ordered to lead the southern expedition.
Those civil and military officials of the third rank and below who disobeyed orders
were to be dealt with according to military law.
Bó Wēn and others arrived in Guǎngxī,
and met with Governor-General Zhāng Jīng,
General-in-chief Ānyuǎn Hóu Liǔ Xún,
Councilor Wēng Wàndá, Zhāng Yuè, and others to deliberate.
They conscripted a total of one hundred twenty-five thousand indigenous and regular troops from Liǎngguǎng, Fújiàn, and Húguǎng,
divided into three vanguards,
to enter from Píngxiáng, Lóngdòng, and Sīlíngzhōu,
with two additional surprise forces as backup.
A proclamation was sent to Yúnnán Patrol-Inspector Wāng Wénshèng to lead troops and station them at Liánhuātān,
also advancing in three routes.
With the deployment set,
Qiú Luán was recalled due to an offense,
and Liǔ Xún immediately replaced him.
In the autumn of the nineteenth year,
Bó Wēn and others advanced to Nánníng,
and issued a proclamation to the officials and common people of Ānnán,
explaining the Heavenly Court's principle of supporting the fallen and restoring the broken,
that the guilt was limited to Dēngyōng and his son,
and that those counties and prefectures that surrendered would be granted their land.
A heavy reward was offered for Dēngyōng and his son,
while also proclaiming that if Dēngyōng registered his land and people and submitted tribute,
he would be pardoned as per the imperial edict.
Dēngyōng was greatly frightened,
and sent an envoy to Wēng Wàndá to beg for surrender,
with very mournful words.
Wàndá sent him to Bó Wēn.
Bó Wēn, acting on imperial authority, permitted it,
proclaimed the emperor's benevolence and majesty,
accepted their maps and registers,
along with the returned land of the four caves of Qīnzhōu.
He provisionally allowed them to return to their country to await further orders.
He swiftly submitted a memorial reporting this,
and the emperor was greatly pleased.
An edict was issued changing the state of Ānnán to the Ānnán Dūtǒngshǐ Division,
with Dēngyōng as Dūtǒngshǐ,
hereditary,
and establishing thirteen Xuānfǔ Divisions,
allowing him to appoint their officials.
Bó Wēn held his commission for over a year,
without firing a single arrow,
and Ānnán was pacified.
This was because the emperor fundamentally did not wish to use military force.
For his achievements,
he was promoted to Tàizǐ Tàibǎo.
In the first month of the twenty-first year, he returned to court,
and again managed the affairs of the Censorate.
The border regions frequently reported alarms.
Bó Wēn requested to build an outer wall for the capital.
The emperor had already approved it,
but Supervising Secretary Liú Yǎngzhí argued
that as temple construction was underway,
resources would be difficult to sustain.
Thus, it was ordered to temporarily halt.
In the tenth month of that year,
Zhāng Zàn died,
and Bó Wēn replaced him as Bīngbù Shàngshū.
Zhāng Zàn was corrupt and greedy.
During his eight years in the ministry,
all military preparations had fallen into disrepair.
Bó Wēn met with court officials to discuss and submit twenty-four measures for border defense,
and military regulations were completely renewed.
Censors proposed
to verify the actual numbers of new troops, capital troops, and palace guards, artisans,
to enrich the national treasury.
Bó Wēn then submitted over twenty articles on abuses that should be abolished,
including the Jǐnyī and Téngxiáng Guards,
and the御馬, Palace Affairs, and Imperial Kitchen Directorates,
which had long been controlled by powerful eunuchs,
all were subject to reform.
The emperor praised this as good,
and immediately ordered purification and elimination.
Many long-standing abuses were rectified,
but many close attendants were displeased.
In the autumn of the twenty-third year,
Shùntiān Patrol-Inspector Zhū Fāng requested the withdrawal of guest troops after the autumn defense was completed.
Soon after,
invaders greatly entered,
directly threatening the capital region.
The emperor was furious,
and had Governor-General Zhái Péng shackled and exiled,
and Zhū Fāng beaten to death.
Censor Shū Tīng said
that Zhū Fāng had only proposed withdrawing the Jì troops,
but it was Bó Wēn and Zhífāng Láng Hán Zuì who had also withdrawn those from Xuān and Dà.
The emperor then stripped Bó Wēn of his official status,
beat Hán Zuì eighty times,
and exiled him to the extreme frontier.
Bó Wēn returned home,
developed a carbuncle on his back, and died.
Upon Mùzōng's ascension,
he was reinstated to office
and granted posthumous compassion.
In the early Tiānqǐ era,
he was posthumously given the epithet Xiāngmào.
Bó Wēn was profound and resolute in character,
eating and drinking like ten men.
When facing critical decisions,
he remained calm and collected.
During the Ānnán campaign,
Wēng Wàndá and Zhāng Yuè contributed many strategies.
Bó Wēn strongly recommended them to the court,
and the two were subsequently appointed.
Wāng Wénshèng,
courtesy name Xīzhōu,
was a native of Chóngyáng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the sixth year of Zhèngdé.
He was appointed Judicial Commissioner of Ráozhōu.
A man named Gù Sōng
entered the residence of Prince Huái, Yòu Qǐ, with a blade.
He was apprehended
and falsely accused Wénshèng of instigating the assassination of the prince.
Wénshèng was imprisoned and interrogated.
After a long time, he was cleared
and reinstated to his office.
The details of this incident are found in the biography of the Prince of Huái.
He was appointed Principal of the Ministry of War.
Together with other officials, he remonstrated against Emperor Wǔzōng's southern tour,
and was caned outside the palace gate.
In the early Jiājìng era,
he successively served as Prefect of Fúzhōu,
then was promoted to Vice Commissioner of Zhèjiāng and Shǎnxī,
in both capacities overseeing schools.
He was promoted to Surveillance Commissioner of Yúnnán.
In the winter of the fifteenth year,
the court deliberated on a campaign to chastise Ānnán.
Given Wénshèng's talent,
he was immediately appointed Assistant Censor-in-Chief
and Grand Coordinator of that region.
As the Duke of Qiánguó, Mù Cháofǔ, was young,
all military matters were decided by Wénshèng.
Vice Commissioner Bào Xiàngxián suggested conciliation was better than suppression,
and Wénshèng agreed.
At that time, they heard that Mò Dēngyǒng had already usurped the throne,
and the former Ānnán officials were disaffected,
many occupying territories and raising armies.
A man named Wǔ Wényuān
occupied Xuānkuāng
and surrendered with his force of ten thousand men.
He presented maps for advancing troops,
and also stated that former officials such as Ruǎn Rénlián and Lí Jǐngmín were all occupying various regions and resisting Dēngyǒng.
When the heavenly troops arrived,
they would call upon righteous warriors across the country,
and with forces rising from all sides,
Dēngyǒng could be captured.
Wénshèng reported this.
Wényuān was granted official robes of the fourth rank,
and his sons and younger brothers were given hats and belts.
Wénshèng also rallied neighboring countries of Ānnán to assist in the campaign,
and they all obeyed.
He then submitted a memorial stating:
"Láowō has a vast territory and numerous soldiers,
and can be tasked with one front.
Bābǎi, Chēli, and Mènggèn have many soldiers and elephants,
and can be mobilized.
Their chieftains have not yet been confirmed in their hereditary posts.
I request that their vetting be waived,
and they be granted official titles first.
They will surely fight bravely for us."
The emperor followed all his suggestions.
Wénshèng then issued a proclamation stating that those of Ānnán's subordinates who returned their lands
would retain their former positions,
and also urged Dēngyǒng to surrender.
They attacked and breached Zhènshǒu Camp,
and Fāng Yíng's attempt to relieve it failed.
Many of Dēngyǒng's followers came to defect.
Wénshèng established camps and built fences at Liánhuātān to settle them.
Liánhuātān
was in Méngzì County,
a strategic land and water thoroughfare between Jiāo and Guǎng,
and the vital heartland of Ānnán.
Dēngyǒng grew more fearful
and requested to surrender,
offering to resume tribute.
He then claimed that Lí Níng was a descendant of the Ruǎn clan,
and the seal he held was also fake.
Wénshèng reported this,
but the court initially disallowed it.
Later, Máo Bówēn arrived in Nánníng
and accepted Dēngyǒng's surrender as Wénshèng had proposed,
and Ānnán was thus pacified.
In this campaign,
the success was attributed to Bówēn,
but in strategy and achieving victory,
Wénshèng's contribution was greater.
When merits were discussed,
Bówēn and the Grand Coordinators and Grand Commanders of Liǎngguǎng were all promoted in rank,
while Wénshèng merely received silver and silk.
The treacherous man Táng Bì requested to open the silver mines in Dàlǐ,
and the emperor granted it.
Wénshèng denounced it as absurd
and handed him over to the authorities.
He was summoned to serve as Minister of the Court of Judicial Review.
When the Nine Imperial Temples suffered a fire,
he fell ill on the road
and memorialized that he had been slow in his duties,
and was permitted to retire.
He died
and was granted posthumous benefits according to regulations.
His nephew Zōngyī,
courtesy name Zǐhéng,
succeeded Wénshèng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the seventeenth year of Jiājìng.
He was appointed Magistrate of Fúliáng
and successively served as Director of the Ministry of War.
When Yáng Jìshèng impeached Yán Sōng and his grandson Hú for falsely claiming merits,
Zōngyī's deliberations remained unyielding.
He offended Sōng
and resigned and returned home.
In the early Lóngqìng era,
he was reinstated as Director of the Ministry of Personnel in Nánjīng,
and successively served as Prefect of Yìngtiān.
He reduced expenditures for various bureaus,
saving tens of thousands in public funds annually.
In the early Wànlì era,
he was promoted to Minister of the Court of Judicial Review in Nánjīng.
After three promotions, he became Minister of the Ministry of Revenue, overseeing the granaries,
then retired,
and died.
In the early Tiānqǐ era,
he was posthumously granted the honorific Gōnghuì.
Bào Xiàngxián,
a native of Shè.
He became an Imperial Censor through the *jìnshì* examination,
and successively served as Vice Commissioner of Yúnnán.
Máo Bówēn dispatched Wénshèng to join forces,
with Xiàngxián leading the central vanguard.
He was repeatedly promoted to Assistant Censor-in-Chief,
Grand Coordinator of Shǎnxī,
and replaced Shí Jiǎn as Grand Coordinator of Yúnnán.
Initially,
the native chieftain Nà Jiàn of Yuánjiāng killed Prefect Nà Xiàn and rebelled.
Provincial Administration Commissioner Xú Yuè went to offer amnesty but was killed.
Jiǎn attacked but failed to subdue him,
and was dismissed due to the Yuè incident,
whereupon Xiàngxián replaced him.
He assembled 70,000 native and Han troops to chastise them.
Jiàn, in fear,
committed suicide by poison.
A successor from the Nà clan was chosen and enthroned.
Xiàngxián was promoted to Right Vice Minister of War,
overseeing military affairs of Liǎngguǎng.
The bandit leaders Xú Quán and others colluded with Japanese pirates, causing havoc along the coast.
He dispatched Vice Commissioner Wāng Bǎi and others to attack and kill them.
The Guangxi bandits under Huáng Fùjiāng and others harassed Qìngyuǎn.
He raided their stronghold
and achieved a great victory.
Xiàngxián was granted an official post for one of his sons.
He entered to assist the Ministry of War in Nánjīng.
He was impeached
and returned to his hometown for investigation.
After ten years at home,
he was reinstated as Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud.
He again served as Assistant Censor-in-Chief, Grand Coordinator of Shāndōng.
He was summoned and appointed Left Vice Minister of War.
Due to old age, he resigned.
He died in the early Lóngqìng era.
Wēng Wàndá,
courtesy name Rénfū,
was a native of Jiēyáng.
He became a *jìnshì* in the fifth year of the Jiājìng reign (1526).
He was appointed a Secretariat Director (*zhǔshì*) in the Ministry of Revenue (*Hùbù*).
He was later promoted to Department Director (*lángzhōng*),
then sent out as Prefect of Wúzhōu.
When the Marquis of Xiánníng, Qiú Luán, was stationed in Liǎngguǎng,
his soldiers were allowed to act cruelly.
Wàndá captured the most unruly ones
and flogged them.
After four years,
his reputation and achievements were greatly manifest.
At that time, the court deliberated on punitive action against Ānnán,
and Wàndá was promoted to Vice-Commissioner (*fùshǐ*) of Guǎngxī,
specifically to handle the Ānnán affair.
Wàndá requested of Governor-General Zhāng Jīng, saying:
“Mò Dēngyǒng boasted, ‘If the Central Kingdom cannot correct the crimes of local officials murdering and rebelling,
how can it question me?’
Now, Lǐ Huán, a local headman of Píngxiáng Prefecture, murdered his local official Zhēn;
Lú Huí, a local chieftain of Sī'ēn Prefecture, incited rebellion among the Nine Departments;
Zhào Kǎi, a local headman of Lóngzhōu, killed his nephews Suì and Nuǎn;
and then colluded with Wéi Yīng from Tiánzhōu to kill Suì’s younger brother Bǎo;
and Hóu Gōngdīng, a Yao chieftain of Duànféngxiá, remained defiant in his stronghold.
These individuals are united in their wickedness,
and should they conspire to act as internal collaborators,
we would not even be able to protect ourselves.
First capturing and punishing these few individuals
will make Ānnán easy to subjugate.”
Jīng replied,
“Indeed.
You may act as you see fit.”
Thereupon, Huán and Yīng were executed,
Huí was captured,
the Nine Departments were pacified,
Kǎi was lured and killed,
Gōngdīng was deceived by pretending to imprison those who sued him,
then seized in a meeting,
and his stronghold was destroyed by two armies.
He also proposed to annex the Four Dong (*dòng*) to Nánníng
and brought down the Dong chieftain Huáng Xiánsxiāng.
Dēngyǒng finally became fearful.
Wàndá was promoted to Right Policy Advisor (*Yòu cānzhèng*) of Zhèjiāng.
Jīng, believing that the campaign against Ānnán could not succeed without Wàndá,
memorialized to retain him,
and he was consequently ordered to oversee Guǎngxī as a Policy Advisor.
Later, when Máo Bówēn assembled troops for a punitive expedition,
Wàndá submitted a letter to Bówēn,
stating:
“To achieve success through peaceful persuasion
is the best strategy.
To intimidate them into submission
is the middle strategy.
To eradicate them completely
is ultimately the worst strategy.”
Bówēn agreed with him.
When an Ānnán spy, Dīng Nánjié, was captured,
Wàndá untied him,
treated him generously,
and sent him away,
frightening him with the might of the Celestial Court’s army.
Dēngyǒng became greatly afraid,
and so went to Bówēn to beg for surrender.
In this campaign,
Wàndá’s contribution was the greatest,
but his rewards did not exceed the usual standard.
However, the emperor knew his capabilities
and promoted him to Surveillance Commissioner (*ànchásǐ*) of Sìchuān.
He subsequently served as Left and Right Administrative Commissioner (*bùzhèngshǐ*) of Shǎnxī.
In the twenty-third year (1544), he was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief (*Yòu fùdūyùshǐ*)
and served as Grand Coordinator (*xúnfǔ*) of Shǎnxī.
Soon after, he was advanced to Right Vice Minister of War (*Bīngbù Yòu shìláng*) concurrently Right Assistant Censor-in-Chief (*Yòu qiāndūyùshǐ*),
replacing Zhái Péng as Governor-General (*zǒngdū*) of the military affairs of Xuān, Dà, Shānxī, and Bǎodìng.
He impeached and dismissed the Grand Commander (*zǒngbīngguān*) of Xuānfǔ, Xì Yǒng, and the Vice Commander (*fùzǒngbīng*) Jiāng Shì,
and recommended Hé Qīng, Zhào Qīng, and Shěn Xīyí.
Zhào Qīng then replaced Yǒng.
Wàndá meticulously conducted reconnaissance
and clearly distinguished rewards and punishments.
Every time autumn defense was due,
he dispatched soldiers to man the barriers,
and secretly sent soldiers to pour vermilion pigment into oil,
marking the locations of those who left their posts.
Upon their return, the soldiers were immediately tied up,
and no one dared to leave their posts again.
He strictly prohibited killing surrendered individuals,
punishing violators with death.
When captives were taken,
he treated them like close relatives,
thus gaining more knowledge of the enemy’s situation.
Tens of thousands of enemy cavalry invaded the Central Route of Dàtóng,
entering Tiěguǒmén,
where the former Grand Commander Zhāng Dá fought hard and repelled them.
They then attacked Bógé Gǔ,
where Assistant Commander (*cānjiàng*) Zhāng Fèng and scholar Wáng Bāngzhí, among others, died in battle.
Wàndá and Grand Commander Zhōu Shàngwén prepared defenses at Yánghé,
while dispatching cavalry in all directions to intercept and attack,
achieving considerable kills and captures.
The enemy ascended a mountain
and, seeing a large gathering of government troops,
then withdrew.
When the matter was reported,
an imperial edict was issued, praising and rewarding him.
He repeatedly memorialized to request the repair and construction of border walls.
The proposal was to build from Yánghékǒu on the eastern route of Dàtóng to Xīyánghé in Xuānfǔ,
requiring 290,000 *liǎng* of silver.
The emperor had already agreed,
but the Ministry of War obstructed the proposal,
arguing that Dàtóng already had two borders
and should not build another wall within the border.
The emperor did not listen.
Consequently, walls were built for 128 *lǐ* at Tiānchéng, Yánghé, Kāishānkǒu, and other locations on the eastern route of Dàtóng,
with seven forts
and 154 beacon towers;
and walls were built for 64 *lǐ* at Xīyánghé, Xǐmǎlín, Zhāngjiākǒu, and other locations on the western route of Xuānfǔ,
with ten watchtowers.
Cliffs were cut and slopes leveled for 50 *lǐ*.
The work was completed in over 50 days.
He was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief (*Yòu dūyùshǐ*).
He uncovered the rebellion plot by the imperial clan member Chōng Zhuó and others from Dàifǔ,
and was promoted to Left Censor-in-Chief (*Zuǒ dūyùshǐ*).
Later,
he convened officials from Xuān, Dà, and Shānxī to discuss border defense and garrison matters,
summarized as follows: Shānxī starts from the Yellow River bank at Bǎodé Zhōu,
passes through Piāntóu,
and reaches Lǎoyíng,
a total of 254 *lǐ*.
The western route of Dàtóng starts from Yākǒushān,
passes through the Central
and Northern Two Routes,
and extends east to Dōngyánghé Zhènkǒu Tái,
a total of 647 *lǐ*.
Xuānfǔ starts from Xīyánghé,
passes through the Central and Northern Two Routes,
and extends east to Yǒngníng Sì
Hǎiyě,
a total of 1023 *lǐ*.
All 1924 *lǐ*
are directly facing major invaders,
with dangers on the outside,
known as the "extreme border."
From Lǎoyíng Fort in Shānxī,
it turns south and then east,
passing through Níngwǔ and Yànmén,
to Píngxíng Guān, 800 *lǐ*.
Then turning south and east again,
passing through Lóngquán, Dàomǎ, Wúwáng
kǒu of Zǐjīng, Chājiàn Lǐng, and Fútú Yù,
to Yánhékǒu, over 1070 *lǐ*.
Then northeast,
passing through Gāoyá and Báiyáng,
to Jūyōng Guān, over 180
*lǐ*.
All over 2050 *lǐ*
are steep mountains and layered ridges,
with dangers on the inside,
known as the "secondary border."
Of the outer border,
Dàtóng is the most difficult to defend,
followed by
Xuānfǔ,
then Piān and Lǎo of Shānxī.
The most difficult part of Dàtóng to defend

and again received an inherited Jǐnyī Guard position for his merits.
When Emperor Wǔzōng campaigned in the south,
he was ordered to lead one bureau director from each of the Ministries of Revenue, War, and Works to supervise military provisions.
When the imperial carriage returned,
he was appointed Minister of War by imperial decree, replacing Wáng Qióng.
When Emperor Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was impeached and dismissed by the supervising secretary Shǐ Dào.
In the fourth year of Jiājìng,
the court recommended Dèng Zhāng and Xiàn to be Supreme Commanders of the Three Borders,
but the remonstrating officials held that it was unacceptable.
The Emperor ultimately used Xiàn.
His subordinate generals Wáng Zǎi and Shǐ Jīng repeatedly defeated the invaders,
and imperial letters praised and commended them.
Jínáng, with tens of thousands of cavalry, crossed the river and deeply penetrated from Shíjiùdūn.
Xiàn commanded the regional commanders Zhèng Qīng, Háng Xióng, Zhào Yīng, and others to divide and hold strategic points to attack them.
Commander Bǔ Yún cut off their retreat.
When the invaders reached Qīngyánglǐng,
they were utterly defeated and fled.
In five days, there were four victories,
over three hundred heads were taken,
and countless horses and weapons were captured.
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
added the title Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent to Xiàn,
and again granted him one son an inherited position.
By this point, he had received three inherited Jǐnyī Guard centurion positions.
When eunuchs wove velvet in Shǎn (Shǎnxī),
Xiàn requested its cessation.
Also, when the Nine Temples were completed,
he requested the release of those who had been punished for debating rites,
which was widely praised by scholars and officials.
Zhāng Cōng and Guì È wanted to use Wáng Qióng as Supreme Commander,
so they reassigned Xiàn as Nanjing Minister of War.
Later,
he entered court as Censor-in-Chief on the Left.
When Shuòzhōu declared an emergency,
the court recommended Xiàn to be Supreme Commander of Xuān and Dà (Xuānhuà and Dàtóng).
Xiàn refused to go,
saying:
"I have just entered the Central Censorate;
why am I being hastily driven out?"
Supervising secretaries Xià Yán and Zhào Tíngruì impeached Xiàn for feigning illness to avoid difficulties,
and he was again dismissed and returned home.
Not long after,
the Emperor, recalling Xiàn,
recalled him to be Minister of War.
When Xiǎowángzǐ invaded,
he memorialized on matters concerning pacifying the barbarians and various border defenses.
He also requested the establishment of a system for dividing and training the capital garrisons,
so that generals could not use service in the Imperial Household Bureau
as an excuse to evade camp training.
The Emperor praised and accepted all of them.
The old system
for evaluating military merits
included categories such as live capture, decapitation, being first, bringing up the rear, extraordinary merit, and first merit,
but later, abuses and false claims became increasingly common.
Xiàn established regulations for inheriting and replacing military merits,
from Yǒnglè to Zhèngdé,
weighing the differences in their severity and magnitude,
and itemized them for imperial review.
An imperial edict ordered them to be included in the Collected Statutes as a permanent regulation.
Soon after, he concurrently supervised the regiment and encampment.
More than a hundred rulers from various states of the Western Fan came to pay tribute,
claiming kingly titles.
Xiàn and the ritual officials Xià Yán and others requested that, following the precedents of the Chénghuà and Hóngzhì eras,
only the king of the state should receive a reply edict,
and that tribute periods and numbers of envoys should still be limited.
The deliberation was then settled.
When the Dàtóng military mutiny occurred,
Xiàn initially stated that the ringleaders should be executed,
and the rest dispersed.
However, Grand Secretary Zhāng Fúqìng and Supreme Commander Liú Yuánqīng strongly advocated for military action,
so Xiàn did not dare to firmly adhere to his former proposal.
Yuánqīng was unable to take the city,
and northern invaders again encroached.
He requested that another high official be dispatched to repel the northern invaders,
so that he could focus solely on attacking the city.
Xiàn also agreed with his memorial,
and many commentators criticized Xiàn.
It happened that the Emperor realized Dàtóng was an important strategic stronghold
and should not be destroyed,
so he shelved the matter,
and the rebellion soon subsided.
Yuánqīng was eventually punished and dismissed.
After several years,
Xiàn retired due to age,
and died.
He was posthumously granted the title of Junior Guardian
and the posthumous name Kāngyì.
His son Rǔxiào
was a Vice Censor-in-Chief.
See the biography of Dīng Rǔkuí.
Hú Shìníng,
courtesy name Yǒngqīng,
was from Rénhé.
He became a *jìnshì* in the sixth year of Hóngzhì.
He was by nature upright and firm,
not fearing the powerful,
and also knowledgeable in military affairs.
He was appointed Judicial Commissioner of Dé'ān.
When the Prince of Qí first took up his fiefdom,
his retinue was arrogant,
and Shìníng curtailed them.
Later, when the prince again requested lake fields,
Shìníng held that it was unacceptable.
He was transferred to Section Chief of the Ministry of Punishments in Nanjing.
In response to an imperial request, he presented ten strategies for border defense,
and further submitted a memorial strongly criticizing the deficiencies in current government policies.
At that time, Emperor Xiàozōng was already unwell,
but still nodded in agreement.
He was again promoted to Bureau Director.
He was on good terms with Lǐ Chéngxūn, Wèi Xiào, and Yú Yǒushàn,
and at that time they were called
"the Four Gentlemen of the Southern Capital."
He was transferred to be the Prefect of Táipíng [太平] in Guǎngxī [廣西].
The Táipíng [太平] Subprefect, Lǐ Jùn [李濬], had repeatedly killed and plundered officials and common people.
Shìníng [世寧] secretly sent a dispatch to Zhào Yuányáo [趙元瑤], the Zhīzhōu [知州] of Lóngyīng [龍英], to capture him.
The rebellious clan of Sīmíng [思明], led by Huáng Wénchāng [黃文昌], had for four generations killed prefects,
occupying three subprefectures and twenty-seven villages.
Vice Regional Commander Kāng Tài [康泰] accompanied Shìníng [世寧] into Sīmíng [思明]
and seized Wénchāng [文昌]'s three brothers.
However, Tài [泰], fearing Wénchāng [文昌], fled by night,
leaving Shìníng [世寧] in an empty city,
in great danger.
The various local chieftains, having esteemed Shìníng [世寧],
sent troops to assist him,
and he was thus able to return.
Wénchāng [文昌], fearful,
returned the encroached land and surrendered.
When local officials inherited their positions,
the chief magistrates often demanded bribes and delayed submitting reports,
which caused the various chieftains to resent and rebel.
Shìníng [世寧] issued an order:
"When a son is born, immediately report it to the prefecture.
Those who are to inherit positions,
if they are ten years of age or older,
shall visit the prefecture on the first and fifteenth day of each month.
If a father or elder brother has an issue,
a request for an official appointment shall be made to the court based on the register."
The local officials were greatly pleased.
He returned home for his mother's mourning.
After the mourning period, he went to the capital.
Passing through Cāngzhōu [滄州],
the roving bandits were urgently attacking the city.
Shìníng [世寧] immediately galloped into the city
and drew up a defense plan.
The bandits attacked for seven days and nights
but could not take it,
so they withdrew.
He was again appointed Prefect of Bǎoqìng [寶慶].
Both Prince Mín [岷王] and the supervising eunuch, Wáng Rùn [王潤], greatly feared and respected him.
He was promoted to Jiangxi Vice Commissioner.
He collaborated with the Censor-in-Chief Yú Jiàn [俞諫] in strategizing to capture bandits
and suppress Wáng Hàobā [王浩八].
At his leisure, he fortified Guǎngchāng [廣昌], Nánfēng [南豐], and Xīnchéng [新城].
At that time,
Prince Níng [寧王] Chénháo [宸濠] was arrogant, oppressive, and had rebellious intentions,
but no one dared to speak of it.
Shìníng [世寧] was deeply indignant.
In the third month of the ninth year of Zhèngdé [正德] (1514), he submitted a memorial, saying:
"Regarding the bandits in Jiāngxī [江西],
the two opinions of suppression and pacification are at a stalemate.
Your humble servant believes it is not difficult to decide.
Those already pacified shall not be executed;
those who rebel again shall not be pardoned;
those who rise initially shall be quickly suppressed—
that is all.
However, Jiāngxī's [江西] problem is not bandits.
The prestige of the Níng [寧] household grows daily;
undesirable elements gather in groups and are led to illegal activities;
all levels of officials above and below serve excessively.
They frequently use fires as pretexts to seize people's houses and land;
their purchasing activities disturb neighboring prefectures;
their oppression spreads throughout poor villages.
Your humble servant fears that good people will not be at peace
and will all rise up as bandits.
Subordinates, fearing calamity,
harbor many disloyal thoughts,
and the rites, music, punishments, and governance gradually no longer originate from the court.
I request that either Censor-in-Chief Yú Jiàn [俞諫] or Rèn Hànzhōng [任漢中] be solely entrusted,
or that another loyal and upright high official be selected to garrison and pacify.
An imperial edict should command the prince to merely govern his state,
and not interfere with officials,
to pacify the source of chaos
and eliminate unexpected changes."
The memorial was sent down to the Ministry of War.
Minister Lù Wán [陸完] deliberated,
ordering Jiàn [諫] to go and assess the bandit situation and the suitability of pacification and suppression.
As for the statement about violating regulations and disturbing the populace,
he suspected it was a fabrication,
and it was appropriate to order the prince to restrain himself.
The imperial decree approved this.
Chénháo [宸濠], upon hearing this,
was furious.
He listed Shìníng's [世寧] crimes,
bribed powerful favorites everywhere,
and was determined to kill Shìníng [世寧].
The memorial was sent down to the Censorate.
The Right Censor-in-Chief, Lǐ Shìshí [李士實],
a partisan of Chénháo [宸濠], along with the Left Censor-in-Chief Shí Jiè [石玠] and others, memorialized, saying
Shìníng [世寧] was reckless and ought to be punished.
Before the order was issued,
Chénháo's [宸濠] memorial arrived again,
accusing Shìníng [世寧] of seditious speech.
An order was then issued for Jin Yīwèi [錦衣衛] officers to arrest Shìníng [世寧].
Shìníng [世寧] had already been promoted to Fujian Surveillance Commissioner [福建按察使]
and was taking the road back to his hometown.
Chénháo [宸濠] then falsely accused Shìníng [世寧] of escaping,
and dispatched an envoy to order Zhèjiāng [浙江]巡按 Pān Péng [潘鵬] to arrest and send him to Jiāngxī [江西].
Péng [鵬] imprisoned all of Shìníng's [世寧] family
and urgently sought him.
Lǐ Chéngxūn [李承勛], as Surveillance Commissioner,
protected him.
Shìníng [世寧] then fled to the capital
and surrendered himself to the Jin Yīwèi [錦衣衛] prison.
While in prison, he submitted three memorials detailing Chénháo's [宸濠] rebellious acts,
but they were ultimately ignored.
After being imprisoned for more than a year,
Censors Chéng Qǐchōng [程啟充], Xú Wénhuá [徐文華], Xiāo Míngfèng [蕭鳴鳳], Xíng Huán [邢寰] and others repeatedly memorialized to save him.
Yáng Yīqīng [楊一清] further moved Qián Níng [錢寧] with urgent warnings,
and he was then banished to Shěnyáng [瀋陽] for military service.
Four years later,
Chénháo [宸濠] indeed rebelled.
Shìníng [世寧] was recalled from his exile for military service to be Húguǎng Surveillance Commissioner [湖廣按察使].
Soon after, he was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief [右僉都御史] and Circuit Governor of Sìchuān [四川].
On his way, he heard that Shìzōng [世宗] had ascended the throne
and submitted a memorial with Sīmǎ Guāng's [司馬光] three words: benevolence, enlightenment, and martial valor.
He then recommended Wèi Xiào [魏校], Hé Táng [何瑭], and Shào Ruì [邵銳] as suitable lecturers,
Lín Jùn [林俊], Yáng Yīqīng [楊一清], Liú Zhōng [劉忠], and Lín Tíngyù [林廷玉] as suitable advisors,
and Prefects Liú Lì [劉蒞] and Xú Yù [徐鈺], who had previously served as Censors with reputations for integrity, as suitable for promotion.
At the time, his words were praised.
The pacified barbarians [熟番] in the Sōngpān [松潘] commandery
had long been beyond the control of the generals and officials,
who often paid goods to secure passage.
If the barbarians killed government soldiers,
they dared not investigate.
If government soldiers killed barbarians,
they were always punished.
Shìníng [世寧] presented a strategy,
requesting the selection of generals, the increase of troops,
the establishment of clear reward and punishment regulations,
strict prohibitions against concealment,
the repair of signal fires,
and regular patrols
to boost military prestige
and open roads.
An imperial edict ordered all these measures to be implemented.
He also impeached and dismissed Vice Regional Commander Zhāng Jié [張傑] and eunuch Zhào Qīn [趙欽].
Just two months later,
he was summoned to be Right Vice Minister of Personnel.
Before he could assume the post,
he returned home due to his father's mourning.
After the period of mourning ended and he was at home,
the court was debating
the "Great Rites" [大禮],
and many who disagreed were punished.
Shìníng [世寧]'s view was consistent with Zhāng Cōng [張璁] and others.
He submitted a memorial requesting an early decision on honoring
the "Great Rites" [大禮].
Before it was submitted,
the news reached the capital.
There was already a proposal to move Xiǎnlíng [顯陵] to be interred with Tiānshòushān [天壽山].
Shìníng [世寧] strongly argued against it
and then submitted both memorials together.
The emperor greatly praised him.
Soon after,
he heard that court officials were kneeling at the palace gate to protest,
and some had been beaten to death.
He quickly submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your humble servant previously presented the three words: benevolence, enlightenment, and martial valor.
However, benevolence is particularly fundamental.
Benevolence [仁]
is the virtue of creation and nurturing;
enlightenment [明]
is like the sun and moon shining down.
Neither can be absent for a single day.
Martial valor [武], however, is the might of thunder,
but it can only strike once.
Now, court officials have displeased Your Majesty,
and Your Majesty has vehemently displayed power,
humiliating them with floggings,
causing the frail ones to perish.
This will be spread throughout the empire,
and recorded in historical annals,
saying that whipping was conducted in the palace halls,
and punishment and humiliation extended to scholars and officials. This
is not how to glorify Your Sacred Virtue.
Newcomers whose words happen to agree [with Your Majesty]
are not guaranteed to be correct later.
Old, virtuous, and seasoned officials whose actions happen to displease [Your Majesty]
may not necessarily always be wrong later.
I hope Your Majesty, with a heart of three impartialities,
will illuminate [from above],
and not first harbor favoritism or aversion within."
Although the emperor could not follow this,
he also did not take offense.
Soon after, he was summoned to serve as Vice Minister of War, Left Assistant.
He itemized twenty-five or more matters concerning the dangers and advantages of the strategic points he observed while garrisoning the border.
He also requested that His Majesty's sacred person be well-protected,
and that he not lightly partake of medicinal drugs.
He presented lectures on the chapters of Dàxué (大學) and Qínshì (秦誓),
as well as the 'Wéi Pì Wēifú' (惟辟威福) section of Hóngfàn (洪範),
and the first line of the Xìcí (繫辭) chapter.
He begged that these be retained in the palace.
Supervising Secretary Yú Jīng (余經) then impeached Shìníng (世寧) for initiating the precedent of secret petitions.
Shìníng requested dismissal,
but it was not granted.
When the 'Great Rites'
were concluded,
he was promoted one rank.
He again presented twenty matters concerning the employment of personnel.
Fifty-four artisans, including Zhào Kuí (趙奎), were, at the request of the eunuchs,
all granted official posts.
Shìníng said the rewards were excessive,
but it was not accepted.
He repeatedly submitted memorials citing illness.
He was reassigned to the Ministry of Personnel in Nánjīng (南京),
and then promoted to Minister of Works.
Later,
he was again summoned to be Censor-in-Chief of the Left,
and given the added title of Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
He declined the court title,
and it was permitted.
Shìníng had always been upright and strict.
When he took charge of the Censorate,
he strove to maintain overall principles.
He itemized over ten articles concerning the Censorate's regulations,
concluding with the words:
"Recently, scholars have developed a habit of jealousy and spite.
Once slandered,
they are abandoned for life.
Assistant Reviewer Péng Qí (彭祺) exposed the crimes of powerful tyrants,
suffered slander, and was stripped of his office.
In such cases,
ministers should be allowed to appeal for justice."
The Emperor adopted his words,
but only the report on Qí was shelved.
Executive officials requested a ban on private visits,
but Shìníng said:
"My office is named for its 'scrutiny'.
Without meeting a person and
hearing their words,
there is no way to fully understand their talent and conduct."
The Emperor agreed,
and so did not implement the ban.
Soon after, he was reassigned as Minister of Justice.
Whenever there was a serious criminal case,
he would clearly explain it to the Emperor,
and the Emperor would often understand and be moved.
The eunuch Gāng Cōng (剛聰) falsely accused a grain transport soldier of looting imperial robes,
implicating two thousand people.
Shìníng impeached him for his fabrication.
Later,
Cōng's true crimes were exposed, and he was punished,
and the Emperor then trusted Shìníng even more.
Wáng Qióng (王瓊) revised Xià Chén Jiǔchóu (郤陳九疇),
intending to condemn him to death.
Due to Shìníng's intervention,
he was exiled.
When Minister of War Wáng Shízhōng (王時中) was dismissed,
Shìníng replaced him,
and was given the added title of Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
He declined a second time but was not granted permission,
so he presented ten matters concerning military administration,

saying: define military strategies, uphold the duties of censors, emphasize the authority of generals, increase military preparedness, revise rewards and punishments, control border tribes, sufficiently provision border defenses, eliminate sources of corruption, correct errors, and cherish talent.
What he said often broke conventional rules,
and the Emperor responded with a gracious decree.
The tribute envoys from Tǔlǔfān (土魯番) requested the return of Hāmì (哈密) city,
and to exchange the surrendered man Yámùlán (牙木蘭).
Wáng Qióng submitted a memorial on the matter.
Shìníng said:
"The previous dynasty did not hesitate to abandon Dàníng (大寧) and Jiāozhǐ (交阯),
so what is Hāmì to us?
Moreover, Zhōngshùn (忠順) was initially enfeoffed as our external vassal,
but since Hǎnshèn (罕慎), he has been captured three times by Tǔlǔfān,
thus allowing them to become familiar with the barbarians,
exhausting our Middle Kingdom,
wasting wealth, and wearying our soldiers,
while the barbarians use this to demand concessions.
I believe this is no different from the Yuán (元) remnants Hèshùn (和順), Níngshùn (寧順), and Āndìng (安定), who were enfeoffed at the beginning of the dynasty.
Āndìng is within Hāmì,
near Gānsù (甘肅), and its current status is unknown;
we ask nothing about it,
so why do we alone value Hāmì?
It is appropriate to focus solely on guarding Hexī (河西) and severing ties with Hāmì.
Yámùlán was originally from Qǔxiān Wèi (曲先衞),
he rejoined and submitted,
which is not the same as surrendering,
so how can they demand him?
The matter of Táng Xīdámóu (唐悉怛謀) serves as a warning."
Zhāng Cōng (張璁) and others all supported Qióng's proposal,
which was blocked and not adopted,
and only Yámùlán was kept and not sent back.
After three months in the Ministry of War, he requested to leave,
but the Emperor refused,
exempting him from court attendance.
Shìníng again submitted three matters concerning border defense.
He persistently claimed severe illness,
and was then allowed to return home by post-chaise,
granted a sword and attendants as prescribed.
A few months after his return,
he was again appointed Minister of War in Nánjīng,
but he firmly declined the appointment.
He died in the autumn of the ninth year.
He was posthumously granted Junior Guardian,
and given the posthumous title Duānmǐn (端敏).
Shìníng's character was austere and upright,
and he was incorruptible in office.
He hated evil as if it were an enemy,
and recommended worthy scholars as if he could not do so quickly enough.
Censor-in-Chief Mǎ Hào (馬昊) and Chén Jiǔchóu (陳九疇) were implicated and dismissed,
Vice Commissioner Shī Rú (施儒) and Yáng Bìjìn (楊必進) were removed after evaluation,
and Censor Lǐ Rùn (李潤) and Vice Commissioner Fàn Lù (范輅) were suppressed by the times.
He repeatedly memorialized to recommend them.
When speaking to people,
he was hesitant and inarticulate.
But when composing memorials,
he would draw upon ancient and modern precedents,
hitting the mark precisely.
He was on good terms with Lǐ Chéngxūn (李承勛),
but his discussions were never compromised.
Chéngxūn wanted to grant Lǒng Shèng (隴勝) an official post
and restore the former territory of the Máng (芒) people.
Shìníng said that Shèng was not a son of the Lǒng clan,
and the Máng clan should not be restored.
Initially, he agreed with Zhāng Cōng and Guì È (桂萼) on the discussions of rites.
Cōng and È appreciated this,
and wanted to draw him in to help themselves.
Shìníng refused to be complaisant,
and his opinions on matters often clashed with theirs.
È proposed demobilizing the army,
but Shìníng strongly refuted him.
The Earl of Chānghuà (昌化) was claiming the title by falsely using a child of another family;
this was submitted to court deliberation.
Shìníng said, "We must not, due to heavy bribes,
deceive the imperial court,"
and È's expression changed.
È was then serving in the Ministry of Personnel,
and Níng cited illness,
saying:
"Heaven's changes and people's destitution,
with bandits rising everywhere,
are due to the Ministries of Personnel, Revenue, and War lacking capable people.
The Ministry of War is especially crucial,
I request to step aside for a worthy person."
Also, concerning the Hāmì discussion,
his words encroached upon Cōng,
and all the high ministers became wary of him.
The Emperor consistently treated him with exceptional courtesy and did not replace him.
His sons were Chún (純) and Jì (繼).
Chún, by virtue of his father's office, served as Prefect of Zhàoqìng (肇慶) Prefecture,
and was talented and virtuous.
Jì was young and not intelligent,
and not known to Shìníng.
When Shìníng was in Jiāngxī (江西) on an expedition against bandits,
his subordinate general came to see Jì.
Jì then pointed out battle formations,
explaining advances, retreats, separations, and combinations in great detail,
for a total of three days.
When Shìníng returned and reviewed them,
he was greatly surprised.
Knowing the reason,
he sighed:
"I have a son and I did not recognize him,
why is this?"
From then on, when attacking bandits,
he would always let Jì accompany him,
and discuss strategies.
Shìníng was successful seven out of ten times,
while Jì was successful nine out of ten times.
When Shìníng was drafting a memorial discussing Chén Háo (宸濠),
Jì pleaded:
"This will surely lead to grave misfortune."
Shìníng replied:
"I have already pledged myself to the country,
why should I worry about other things?"
When Shìníng was imprisoned,
Jì, grieving for his father,
died of illness.
Lǐ Chéngxūn,
courtesy name Lìqīng (立卿),
was from Jiāyú (嘉魚).
His father, Tián (田),
was a *jìnshì*,
and served as Right Assistant Censor-in-Chief,
inspecting and pacifying Shùntiān (順天).
He had integrity and was not harsh in his governance.
Chéngxūn passed the *jìnshì* examination in the sixth year of Hóngzhì.
From Magistrate of Tàihú (太湖), he was promoted to Principal of the Ministry of Justice in Nánjīng.
He successively served as Director in the Ministry of Works, and then promoted to Prefect of Nánchāng (南昌).
In the sixth year of Zhèngdé
bandits from Gànzhōu attacked Xīngàn,
capturing Counselor Zhào Shìxián.
Bandits from Jìng'ān occupied Yuèwánglǐng Mǎnǎonàn,
and Wáalín bandits also seized Ruìzhōu.
All the provincial troops dared not advance.
Chéngxūn led the militia to suppress them,
achieving several successes.
The Wáalín bandits killed Vice Envoy Zhōu Xiàn,
and Zhōu Xiàn's army suffered a great defeat.
Chéngxūn rode alone into Zhōu Xiàn's camp,
and only then did the troops reassemble.
Grand Censor Chén Jīn immediately ordered Chéngxūn to suppress them.
The bandit leader Wáng Qí agreed to surrender.
Chéngxūn searched him and found a dagger hidden in his clothes,
but still allowed him to return.
Wáng Qí was moved to tears,
swearing to repay him with his life.
Chéngxūn ordered Wáng Qí to secretly enter the stronghold,
persuade his comrades to surrender and act as an internal應,
while he personally led his troops up the mountain.
Wáng Qí pulled down the palisade at night,
the government troops advanced bravely,
and those who had surrendered emerged from within,
causing the bandits to scatter.
Afterwards,
Chéngxūn followed Chén Jīn to execute the bandit leaders Luó Guāngquán and Hú Xuě'èr,
and the Wáalín bandits were pacified.
The palace eunuch in charge of defense, Lí Ān, falsely accused Chéngxūn of unauthorized alteration of the prison confession of the bandit leader Wáng Hàobā,
leading to his arrest.
Grand Justice Yàn Zhōng immediately investigated,
and Chéngxūn was cleared.
He was recommended for outstanding governance,
and was promoted exceptionally to Circuit Inspector of Zhèjiāng.
He successively served as Right and Left Administration Commissioner of Shǎnxī and Hénán,
and as Right Vice Grand Censor to patrol Liáodōng.
The border defenses had long been neglected,
especially in Kāiyuán.
There were only twelve soldiers and horses,
and the walls, forts, and signal towers were almost completely dilapidated.
The generals and soldiers relied on the city moats for self-defense,
and several hundred *lǐ* outside the city were all hunting grounds for various tribes.
Chéngxūn memorialized asking for repairs and construction.
It happened that Shìzōng ascended the throne,
and issued over 400,000 *liǎng* of silver from the imperial treasury.
Chéngxūn ordered four infantry generals, each with an army, to guard strategic points,
and personally carried baskets and spades, leading his soldiers.
In total, he constructed city walls and moats extending over 91,400 *zhàng*,
and 181 forts.
He recruited 3,200 fugitives,
and opened 1,500 *qǐng* of military farms.
He also fortified Chéngzhōnggù and Tiělǐng,
cutting off the intersection of Yīnshān and Liáohé,
and fortified Púhé and Fǔshùn,
holding strategic passes,
making the border defenses very strong.
For his merits,
he was promoted one rank.
He also repeatedly presented the advantages and disadvantages for the military and civilians,
all of which were approved.
He returned due to illness.
He was reinstated to his former office,
taking charge of the Southern Court.
He was promoted three times to Minister of Justice,
and given the additional title of Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
The Emperor, seeing many abuses in the capital garrisons,
wanted to rectify them.
So he added the title Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent to Chéngxūn,
changed his position to Minister of War and concurrently Left Grand Censor,
specifically overseeing the military camps.
Soon after, he also took charge of the Censorate.
Due to illness,
he submitted three memorials requesting retirement,
and also stated:
"The bandits of Lùchéng in Shānxī were attacked by four routes of troops,
but they were not under one commander,
hence there was no success.
The arrangements for the campaign against the Máng Tribe in Sìchuān and Guìzhōu were inappropriate,
resulting in repeated victories followed by repeated rebellions.
Wǔ Wéndìng should be ordered to make thorough plans,
and not rely solely on military force.
For the river works in Fēng and Pèi,
the minister in charge was changed three times in two years,
and the work was not completed.
Those familiar with water conservancy should be ordered to present their respective views,
and Vice Minister Pān Xīcéng should assess their feasibility.
The most crucial thing
is to resolve the problem of obstruction.
Following the precedents of the Táng and Sòng dynasties for face-to-face and secondary discussions,
ministers should be summoned for audience irregularly."
The Emperor did not approve his resignation,
but submitted his proposals to the relevant departments.
At that time, Qín, Jìn, Chǔ, and Shǔ suffered from successive famines,
and an edict exempted them from land taxes.
Chéngxūn said:
"Officials usually begin collecting taxes in the tenth month.
It is now the ninth month,
and I fear that officials might press for collection
and secretly appropriate funds.
It is advisable, before collection begins,
to dispatch officials to swiftly announce the amount exempted.
In remote mountain areas,
ensure every household is informed.
Those officials who fail to convey the Emperor's benevolent decree
should be punished.
Governors and inspectors who fail to report such instances
should also be punished."
The Emperor praised and accepted his words.
He memorialized for the dismissal of Tāng Qīng, a *bǎzǒng* of the capital garrisons.
Guō Xūn sought his reinstatement,
and his words offended Chéngxūn.
Chéngxūn then requested to resign,
and Censor Wáng Zhǔn and others impeached Guō Xūn for his arrogance.
An imperial edict then reprimanded Guō Xūn,
and handed Tāng Qīng over to the judicial authorities.
When Minister of War Hú Shìníng retired,
an imperial edict ordered Chéngxūn to return to the ministry and replace him.
He memorialized, saying:
"When the court has major policies or the recommendation of civil and military ministers,
it must be submitted for court discussion.
However, those participating in discussions often look at each other and do not speak,
merely acquiescing.
It is advisable, before the discussion,
to prepare a detailed list of items to be discussed,
and announce it to the participants,
allowing them to first understand the matter,
and then calmly deliberate and express their full opinions.
If the opinions do not agree,
they should be allowed to submit separate memorials.
This would ensure that all ministers' views are fully heard,
and the decisions made are impartial."
The Emperor agreed with his words
and issued an edict to reiterate this.
Soon after, he was ordered to concurrently oversee the military camps.
Censors attacked Zhāng Cōng and Guì È's faction,
and Chéngxūn was also implicated.
Chéngxūn repeatedly memorialized to request retirement,
but the Emperor again replied with a gracious decree.
Eunuchs dispatched to guard various regions
were often tyrannical.
Following the suggestions of Censor Lǐ Fèngmáo and others,
Chéngxūn successively dismissed twenty-seven individuals,
and also abolished 500 Jǐnyī Wèi officials,
and several thousand people falsely listed as workers in supervisory bureaus.
Only the Imperial Stud Directorate had not been reduced,
so following a memorial from Censor Tián Qiū,
many more were cut.
He then requested to place the four Téngxiāng guards under the Ministry of War,
to investigate false claims,
and this was approved.
Eunuchs said that in the past, at Zhāngyìmén, Yěxiān was defeated,
and Cáo's rebels were suppressed at Dōngshì,
both being achievements of the four guards,
and because they were directly internal, they were easy to assemble,
so being under the Ministry of War would be inconvenient.
Chéngxūn said:
"The battle of Zhāngyìmén
was caused by Wáng Zhèn.
The rebellion at Dōngshì
was by Cáo Jíxiáng himself."
The Emperor finally followed Chéngxūn's suggestion
and placed them under the Ministry of War.
When invaders attacked Dàtóng,
a discussion was held to dispatch a minister to oversee the troops.
Everyone nominated Grand Censor Wáng Xiàn,
but Wáng Xiàn refused to go.
Censor Xià Yán said to Chéngxūn:
"The situation is urgent,
you should request to go."
Chéngxūn ultimately did not request it.
Censor Zhào Tíngruì impeached both of them.
Coincidentally, the invaders retreated,
and the matter was dismissed.
In the tenth year, spring,
a great wind obscured the day.
The Emperor was anxious about border affairs.
Chéng Xūn said:
“Last year, when the rivers froze,
enemy cavalry completely entered the Hétào.
Tíng, Níng, and Gùyuán all ought to be on alert.
The military provisions for Gānsù solely rely on Hédōng.
It is advisable to purchase and store grain at Lánzhōu,
to be prepared for emergencies.
Previously, Hexī suffered from Tǔlǔfān;
now, Yìbǔlā has deeply penetrated again.
With two bandit groups causing turmoil like clouds,
our isolation and peril are ever greater.
The Hétào bandits frequently come and go,
passing through Zhuānglàng.
It is urgent to repair the fortresses, establish strategic defenses,
cut off their arms and sever their heels,
so that they cannot unite.
The Wùliánghā are closest to the capital.
If not properly appeased,
they will become bandits at our very doorstep.
The rebellion of Ānfèng in Yúnnán
has exhausted both soldiers and civilians,
and bandits have resurfaced in Lín'ān and Méngzì.
If this drags on for too long,
I fear it will brew into a great disaster.
The crown prince of Jiāozhǐ lives as an exile in Lǎowō.
Should he return to pledge allegiance and request aid in the future,
or occupy territory and seek enfeoffment,
all are unpredictable.
The only urgent task is to employ capable people and manage finances,
to ensure there are no worries in the border regions.”
The Emperor praised and accepted his advice.
Chéng Xūn was resolute and possessed grand strategies.
Among those the Emperor trusted,
apart from the Grand Secretaries,
only Chéng Xūn and Hú Shìníng
were frequently consulted on major affairs.
The two also diligently served the state,
speaking everything they knew.
Six months after Shìníng's death,
Chéng Xūn also died,
and the Emperor deeply lamented him.
He was posthumously granted the title of Shàobǎo [Junior Protector]
and the posthumous name Kānghuì.
As for the gifts bestowed,
beyond the usual customs,
he was specially given silver, colored silks, rice, vegetables, and other items.
Chéng Xūn served in office for forty years,
but his family had no surplus wealth.
His discussions
on the "Great Rites"
were also in agreement with Shìníng.
Wáng Yǐqí,
courtesy name Shìzhāo,
was a native of Jiāngníng.
He obtained the *jìnshì* degree in the sixth year of Zhèngdé.
He was appointed Magistrate of Shànggāo County.
When the Huálín bandits were rampant,
Yǐqí trained local militia to resist them,
and the bandits dared not trespass.
He was summoned and appointed Censor,
and then sent to inspect Hénán.
When Chén Háo rebelled,
the supervising eunuch Liú Jǐng initiated a proposal to suspend the provincial examinations.
Yǐqí argued that Hénán was far from Jiāngxī,
and there was no valid reason to cancel the examinations.
So it was stopped.
Jǐng again said that
since the Emperor was personally leading an expedition
and his route would pass through Biàn,
he requested a牒 for forty thousand *liǎng* of silver for provisions.
The Provincial Governor considered granting it,
but Yǐqí insisted on not granting it.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he wanted to confer an imperial title upon Emperor Xìngxiàn.
Yǐqí strongly argued against it.
Later,
on the important task of averting disaster,
he stated:
“The Directorate of Ceremonial, through an imperial decree, exempted Zhāng Hàn from a bribery penalty.
Your subject was not informed of this.
This opens the door to deceit and falsehood.”
The Emperor did not heed him.
He was successively promoted to Vice Minister of War, Right.
When the two Hóng rivers, Xú and Lǚ, dried up,
the grain transport boats were stranded.
He was ordered to concurrently hold the position of Right Vice Censor-in-Chief and oversee river transport.
After more than a year,
the main canal was open,
and he was promoted one rank.
Soon after, he was appointed Right Censor-in-Chief of Nánjīng.
He was recalled to serve as Minister of Works,
then transferred to Left Censor-in-Chief,
and replaced Chén Jīng as Minister of War, concurrently supervising the training camps.
Zēng Xiǎn, the Grand Governor of the Three Borders, proposed recovering the Hétào,
and Grand Secretary Xià Yán supported him.
Several times, favorable imperial decrees praised Zēng Xiǎn,
ordering Yǐqí to convene court officials for deliberation.
Yǐqí and others strongly supported Zēng Xiǎn's proposal.
After the proposal was submitted,
the Emperor's attitude suddenly changed.
A stern decree blamed Zēng Xiǎn,
ordering a re-evaluation.
Yǐqí and others were terrified
and completely reversed their previous statements.
The Emperor arrested Zēng Xiǎn
and ordered Yǐqí to replace him.
The Hétào bandits returned from Xīhǎi
and plundered Yǒngchāng.
Wáng Jìzǔ, the Commander-in-Chief of Zhènqiāng, repelled them.
Later,
they attacked again,
extending to Zhènfān and Shāndān.
His subordinate generals Cài Xūn and Mǎ Zōng assisted, and won all three battles.
In total, over one hundred and forty heads were cut off.
For these achievements,
Yǐqí was granted the privilege of having one son inherit office.
Soon after, tens of thousands of bandits again encamped outside the Níngxià fortress,
planning a major incursion.
The government troops attacked them,
beheading over sixty,
and the bandits fled during the night.
Mǎ markets were opened in Yánsuī and Níngxià,
and the two garrisons traded five thousand horses.
Their leaders, such as Hěntáijí, restrained their subordinates,
and there was no disturbance throughout the market.
Yǐqí reported this.
An imperial edict greatly rewarded the civil and military officials and officers of the two garrisons,
and Yǐqí was again bestowed with gold and silks.
In recognition of the Yánsuī generals and soldiers'功 in defeating the enemy,
he was again granted the privilege of having one son inherit office.
He served as governor of the garrisons for six years,
repairing over four thousand five hundred fortresses and walls in Yánsuī,
and also building border walls in Lánzhōu.
