He was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
When he died,
the military and common people ceased business for him.
He was posthumously granted the title of Shàobǎo,
and the posthumous name Xiāngmǐn,
and again one son was granted an official post.
Fàn Cōng,
courtesy name Píngfǔ,
was originally from Lèpíng, Jiāngxī,
then moved to Shěnyáng.
Cōng obtained the *jìnshì* degree in the twelfth year of Zhèngdé,
and was appointed Secretary in the Ministry of Works,
then promoted to Assistant Secretary.
In the third year of Jiājìng, he prostrated himself before the palace gate to argue for
the "Great Rites,"
and was imprisoned and beaten with the rod in court.
From Secretary in the Ministry of Revenue, he was reassigned as Assistant Administrator of the Chánglú Salt Transport Commissioner's Office,
then promoted to Prefect of Hénán.
There was a great famine that year.
The Provincial Governor, Censor-in-Chief Pān Xūn, rejected all requests for relief documents,
waiting for verification before distribution.
Cōng, without waiting for a reply,
opened the granaries and distributed relief,
saving over a hundred thousand lives.
The people universally praised Cōng,
and the news reached the Forbidden City.
The Emperor reprimanded the Ministry of Revenue, Xūn, and the Surveillance Censor for concealing reports of the disaster.
Xūn blamed Cōng to exculpate himself,
but was impeached and dismissed.
Cōng's name became prominent from this.
He was promoted to Salt Transport Commissioner of Liǎnghuái,
and submitted ten important points on salt administration.
He successively served as Surveillance Vice Commissioner of Sìchuān,
Surveillance Commissioner of Húguǎng,
and Left and Right Administration Commissioners of Zhèjiāng and Hénán.
In the twentieth year, he was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief
and became Provincial Governor of Níngxià.
Cōng was a cautious man
with strategic ability.
Having taken charge of this important border town,
he did not boast of initial victories.
He focused on training infantry and cavalry,
accumulating provisions,
and repairing passes and watchtowers.
The bandits therefore moved far away,
and five hundred captives returned.
He submitted a memorial saying:
“Border generals each have their regular salaries;
there is no system for granting them land.
Since Wǔdìng Hóu Guō Xūn proposed using military surplus land for cultivation to be given to generals,
and appointed treacherous soldiers as estate managers,
the harm has been immense.
It is advisable to return the land to the soldiers and common people,
allowing them to cultivate it freely.”
The Emperor granted his request.
After a few years,
he returned home, claiming illness.
He was appointed to his old post,
governing Hénán.
Soon after, he was summoned to be Assistant Minister of War on the Right (Bīngbù Yòu Shìláng),
then transferred to the Left.
When Minister Wáng Yǐqí went out to supervise the Three Borders,
Cōng was put in charge of the ministry's affairs.
A short while later,
he was ordered to take overall charge of the border passes and strategic choke points.
He submitted a memorial on the overall strategy for Cháohé Chuān, Jūyōng Guān, and other areas,
proposing to add a watchtower outside the Gǔdào Mén at Fēngwō Lǐng as an outer screen,
dredge the moats, and set up bridges,
to prevent incursions.
At the point where the southwest and northwest mountains of the river meet,
he proposed to set up enemy towers,
to control the middle stream,
and divide the garrisoned soldiers into shifts to guard critical points.
He also proposed that watchtowers should be set up at Wǔlǐ Duǒ, Huáchē, Zāoliánkǒu,
Mùtiángǔ, and other places in Jìzhèn.
Watchtowers should be set up.
At Ègǔ, Hóngtǔgǔ,
Xiānglúshí, and other places,
cliffs should be cut and ditches dug.
The various passes outside Jūyōng Guān,
which were inland from Xuānfǔ,
but on the border from Jūyōng,
should be ordered to be repaired by the civil and military officials of the East-Central Route.
The Superintendent of Cháohé Chuān should be promoted to Garrison Commander (Shǒubèi),
and an additional Vice General (Fùjiàng) should be stationed at Jūyōng Guān,
to command Tiānshòu Shān and Huánghuā Zhèn.
The Hēnglǐng Garrison Commander
should block the Huáilái road.
Over two thousand new troops should be added
to supplement the militia.
He also discussed the overall strategy for Zǐjīng, Dàomǎ, Lóngquán, and other passes, as well as Shānhǎi Guān and Gǔběi Kǒu,
proposing to build city walls at Sānggǔ of Zǐjīng,
Zhōngyáoguāngù of Dàomǎ,
and Dǒushílǐng of Lóngquán, and other critical points,
and add enemy towers and barracks.
The four routes under Jìzhōu: Yànhé, Tàipíng, Mǎlán, and Mìyún,
whose repairs were unfinished,
should be completed with redemption funds from various departments.
And Fútú Yù and Chājiàn Lǐng were particularly vital to the two passes of Zǐjīng and Dàomǎ,
so an Assistant General (Cāncāng) should be relocated to Dùjiā Zhuāng at Shímén,
while the Bǎodìng Regional Commander (Zǒngbīng) should be stationed at Zǐjīng.
Jì and Liáo were separated by a thousand *lǐ*,
so the patrol commander (Yóujī) of Jiànchāng Camp should be moved to Shānhǎi Guān.
The shortage of troops in Sāntún and other camps
should be remedied quickly by recruitment,
and those lacking horses should be replenished.
The permanent garrison soldiers who lacked complete armor
should be supplied with an appropriate amount of armor and weapons,
and those on rotation duty
should all be given travel rations,
so that they would not carry halberds with empty stomachs.
He further said:
"Among the various routes,
the Mìyún defense sector is the most critical.
Among all the crucial passes,
the area west of Mìyún is the most important.
Cold Pass (Lěngkǒu) of Yànhé,
Huángyá of Mǎlán,
Yúmùlǐng and Cāyázi of Tàipíng,
are all urgent matters.
It should be ordered that the governors and regional commanders supervise all generals
to divide their various camp's soldiers and horses,
and also the secretly stationed nearby troops, to take turns in battle and defense."
The Ministry of War said:
"Soldiers have been stationed there for a long time
and are attached to their land.
A sudden relocation
might cause other problems.
It would be better to add one capable general at Shānhǎi Guān,
recruit three thousand troops to be stationed there,
and let the governors of Jì and Liáo deploy them
to reinforce Yànhé."
The rest of Cōng's proposals were followed,
and they were sent to the defending officials for discussion.
The emperor greatly appreciated Cōng's talent.
At that time, Minister of War Zhào Tíngruì was dismissed,
and Cōng was immediately ordered to replace him.
Cōng declined due to old age,
and also said that he was accustomed to adapting to circumstances
and lacked the proper demeanor for compliance.
The emperor was angry,
accused Cōng of disrespect,
and stripped him of his official status.
At that time, Yán Sōng was in power,
and Cōng had originally been recommended by Xú Jiē.
The world regarded him as a man of integrity,
and regretted his departure without fault.
However, after Cōng's dismissal,
the emperor summoned Wēng Wàndá,
but he left due to mourning as soon as he arrived.
Dīng Rúkuí replaced him.
The following year,
Āndá threatened the capital city,
and Rúkuí was subsequently executed.
Cōng, having been retired for a long time, then passed away.
In the first year of Lóngqìng, his official status was reinstated posthumously.
Wáng Bāngruì,
courtesy name Wéixián,
was from Yíyáng.
He showed great capability and discernment early on.
While he was a scholar (zhūshēng),
when bandits rose in Shāndōng,
he submitted fourteen strategies for suppressing the bandits to the prefect.
In the twelfth year of Zhèngdé, he became a successful candidate in the imperial examination (Jìnshì).
He was appointed as a Bachelor (Shùjíshì).
Having connections with a princely establishment,
he was appointed as Prefect (Zhīzhōu) of Guǎngdé.
At the beginning of Jiājìng,
he left due to mourning for his grandfather.
He was reappointed to Chúzhōu.
He was repeatedly promoted to Director (Lángzhōng) in the Ministry of Personnel of Nánjīng,
then appointed as Surveillance Commissioner for Education (Tíxué Qiānshì) in Shǎnxī.
Because fewer than five annual tribute scholars (suìgòng) from his jurisdiction passed the examinations,
he was demoted to Prefect of Bīnzhōu.
He was again promoted to Assistant Military Intendant (Bīngbèi Fùshǐ) of Gùyuán.
He suppressed Lǐ Mèngchūn, a major bandit from Jīng and Bīn,
who had been raiding Hédōng and Héxī.
He suppressed and pacified them.
He left due to mourning for his grandmother.
After the mourning period,
he was reappointed as Surveillance Commissioner for Education in Shǎnxī,
then promoted to Administration Commissioner (Cānzhèng).
He was dismissed due to mourning for his mother.
He was subsequently appointed and promoted to Assistant Censor-in-Chief on the Right (Yòu Qiān Dū Yùshǐ),
and then Pacifying Commissioner (Xúnfǔ) of Níngxià.
When the enemy invaded by crossing the ice,
he set up an ambush and defeated them.
He was transferred to be Chief Justice (Dàlǐ Qīng) of Nánjīng.
Before taking office,
he was summoned to be Assistant Minister of War on the Right (Bīngbù Yòu Shìláng).
He was transferred to the Ministry of Personnel,
then promoted to the Left.
When Āndá attacked the capital city,
Bāngruì was ordered to take overall command of the nine gates.
Bāngruì stationed the imperial guards outside the city wall,
and deployed the patrol army camps along the East and West Cháng'ān streets,
opening the city gates wide
to admit those from the four suburbs fleeing the bandits.
Minister of War Dīng Rúkuí was imprisoned,
and Bāngruì was ordered to temporarily take charge of his duties,
and also supervise the training battalions (tuányíng).
After the enemy retreated,
he requested to evaluate the merits and faults of the various generals,
and also to dredge the moats of the nine gates.
All his proposals were approved.
Bāngruì saw that the military system had long been lax,
and thoroughly pointed out its shortcomings.
Consequently, the twelve training battalions were abolished,
and all were merged into the three main camps,
under the command of Marquis of Xiánníng, Qiú Luán.
Bāngruì was also transferred to be Assistant Minister of War on the Left (Bīngbù Zuǒ Shìláng),
specifically to supervise camp affairs.
He then submitted six proposals for reform.
Among them, he stated that eunuchs commanding troops
was a great disaster throughout history,
and requested to withdraw all supervisors of firearms.
The emperor approved his request.
He also recommended former Compiler Zhào Shíchūn and Ministry of Works official Shēn Mǔ as skilled in military affairs,
and both were transferred to the Ministry of War
to manage the capital's camps.
Not long after,
the emperor summoned Minister of War Wēng Wàndá, but he had not yet arrived,
and because of the delay,
Bāngruì was ordered to take his place.
He submitted twelve proposals for pacification and defense.
Chóu Luán (仇鸞) framed Bāngruì (邦瑞) before the emperor.
The emperor's favor gradually shifted.
At that time, Luán (鸞) petitioned to remove Lǐ Fèngmíng (李鳳míng) as the Grand General of Jìzhōu (薊州) and Wáng Rèn (王任) as the Grand General of Dàtóng (大同).
He recommended Chéng Xūn (成勳), Vice General of the Capital Garrisons, to replace Fèngmíng (鳳鳴),
and Xú Rén (徐仁), Vice General of Mìyún (密雲), to replace Wáng Rèn (王任).
The imperial decree was issued accordingly.
Bāngruì (邦瑞) said:
"When the court replaces generals and commanders,
it must consult the high officials
and then make a decision from the imperial heart,
to carefully guard against potential problems
and show that subjects dare not act unilaterally.
Furthermore, a grand general of the Capital Garrisons is not in command of the generals of the border towns.
How can someone from the Capital Garrisons
demote or promote generals in other garrisons?
If we now bend to Luán's (鸞) request,
I fear that all the generals of the Nine Frontiers will rush to seek his patronage,
which is not a blessing for the country."
The emperor was displeased,
and issued a decree to reprimand him.
Luán (鸞) also wanted to control the border generals
and stop the construction of the Jìzhèn (薊鎮) border wall.
Bāngruì (邦瑞) deemed both unacceptable.
Luán (鸞) harbored great resentment
and intensified his slanders.
When Bāngruì (邦瑞) again presented a grand strategy for peace and security,
a stern imperial decree stripped him of his office,
though he was allowed to handle affairs with his official attire.
After several days,
his grand strategy was again presented personally.
Ultimately, he was expunged from the rolls,
and Zhào Jǐn (趙錦) was appointed to replace him.
After Bāngruì (邦瑞) left,
Luán (鸞) became even more overbearing.
The following year, Luán (鸞) was executed.
Jǐn (錦) was also implicated in a faction and banished to the frontier.
It was then that the emperor gradually remembered Bāngruì (邦瑞).
More than ten years later,
there was a shortage of personnel in the Capital Garrisons.
The emperor said:
"Only Bāngruì (邦瑞) will do."
So, he reinstated him to his former office.
Upon arrival,
he submitted several proposals for expedient measures,
all of which were approved and implemented.
He died the following year.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
with the posthumous name Xiāngyì (襄毅).
An imperial messenger was dispatched to escort his coffin home for burial.
Bāngruì (邦瑞) was stern, resolute, and perceptive.
He served in office for forty years,
distinguished by his integrity and rectitude.
His son, Zhèngguó (正國), was Assistant Minister of Justice in Nánjīng (南京).
Zhèng Xiǎo (鄭曉),
courtesy name Zhìfǔ (窒甫),
was from Hǎiyán (海鹽).
In the first year of Jiājìng (嘉靖), he came first in the provincial examination.
The following year, he passed the imperial examination,
and was appointed as Director of the Bureau of Military Appointments.
He spent his days poring over old documents,
gaining complete knowledge of all strategic passes in the realm,
and the strengths and weaknesses of its soldiers and horses.
Minister Jīn Xiànmín (金獻民) instructed him to compile a gazetteer of the Nine Frontiers,
which people eagerly copied and circulated.
For his involvement in the
"Great Rites"
dispute,
he was subjected to court flogging.
When a military mutiny occurred in Dàtóng (大同),
he submitted a memorial vehemently arguing that they should not be pardoned.
When Zhāng Fújìng (張孚敬) held power,
he admired Xiǎo (曉)
and wished to transfer him to the Hanlin Academy or the censorate,
but Xiǎo (曉) declined all offers.
He returned home for his father's mourning
and did not return to office for a long time.
When Xǔ Zàn (許讚) became Minister of Personnel,
he transferred Xiǎo (曉) to the Ministry of Personnel.
He successively served as Director of the Bureau of Merit Evaluation.
When Xià Yán (夏言) was dismissed as Grand Secretary,
the emperor was angry that the censors had not impeached him
and ordered an investigation into their retention or dismissal.
Grand Secretary Yán Sōng (嚴嵩) seized this opportunity to remove those he disliked.
Xiǎo (曉) removed Qíao Yòu (喬佑) and thirteen others,
many of whom were favored by Sōng (嵩).
Sōng (嵩) greatly resented Xiǎo (曉)
and transferred him to the Bureau of Selection.
Sōng (嵩) wanted to appoint Zhào Wénhuá (趙文華) as Director of Merit Evaluation.
Xiǎo (曉) said to Zàn (讚):
"In the past, when Huáng Zhēn (黃禎) was Director of Selection,
he transferred Lǐ Kāixiān (李開先) to Merit Evaluation.
Both were from Shāndōng (山東),
but the imperial decree did not permit it.
Now, if Wénhuá (文華) is transferred,
I will simply have to vacate my position."
Zàn (讚) conveyed this to Sōng (嵩).
Sōng (嵩) wanted to appoint his son, Shìfān (世蕃), as Supervisor of the Imperial Seal.
Xiǎo (曉) said:
"It is customary for a Judicial Commissioner to be promoted to Prefect.
However,
there is no precedent for promotion to Supervisor of the Imperial Seal."
Sōng (嵩) grew even angrier.
On the grounds of demoting officials like Zhōu Fú (周鈇) who had been exiled,
he had Xiǎo (曉) demoted to Assistant Prefect of Hézhōu (和州).
He was later promoted to Vice Minister of the Imperial Stud,
then successively served as Grand Minister of the Imperial Sacrifices in Nánjīng (南京).
He was recalled and appointed Assistant Minister of Justice.
Shortly after, he was transferred to the Ministry of War
and concurrently served as Assistant Censor-in-Chief supervising grain transport.
Both sides of the Grand River were plagued by Wōkòu (倭寇),
and grain transport vessels were almost blocked.
Xiǎo (曉) requested the release of several hundred thousand taels of silver from the treasury
to build warships,
construct fortresses,
train soldiers and generals,
and accumulate fodder and provisions.
The emperor approved the decree.
Corrupt Chinese citizens, coveting Wōkòu (倭寇) bribes,
often colluded with them.
Gù Biǎo (顧表) from Tōngzhōu (通州) was particularly cunning and treacherous,
acting as a guide for the Wōkòu (倭寇).
Because of this, all their camps and fortifications occupied strategic points,
and they knew all the strengths and weaknesses of the government troops.
Xiǎo (曉) offered generous rewards to capture and kill him.
He recruited brave and fierce salt smugglers as soldiers,
established an additional Vice Defense Commissioner for Maritime Affairs in Tàizhōu (泰州),
built Guāzhōu (瓜洲) city,
and increased troops and watchtowers at the maritime inlets of Miàowān (廟灣), Máyáng (麻洋), and Yúntī (雲梯).
Consequently, he defeated the Wōkòu (倭寇) at Tōngzhōu (通州),
then repeatedly defeated them at Rúgāo (如皐) and Hǎimén (海門),
attacked their forces at Lǚsì (呂泗),
and besieged them at Lángshān (狼山),
killing over nine hundred in total.
The bandits then scattered and fled.
In recognition of his achievements,
his rank was increased again,
and he was thrice rewarded with silver and silk.
At that time, many bandits were Chinese.
Xiǎo (曉) said:
"Those who are skilled and resourceful,
but have no outlet for their talents,
willingly turn to banditry.
Unless the state widely recruits them
and provides them with a path to advancement,
I fear that people like Sūn Ēn (孫恩) and Lú Xún (盧循) will emerge among them,
and the disaster will be greatly magnified.
During the Hóngwǔ (洪武) era, Wōkòu (倭寇) raided coastal prefectures.
Despite Emperor Gāo Huángdì's (高皇帝) mighty prestige,
and the presence of wise advisors and veteran generals,
it still took several years of building cities and training troops
to restore peace.
Eventually, fishermen, islanders, salt smugglers, and Tànhù (蜑戶) were conscripted into the navy, reaching tens of thousands.
Emissaries were also sent overseas to proclaim imperial might and virtue.
After a long time,
the Wōkòu (倭寇) ceased to be a problem.
Although the area north of the river is now pacified,
sails appear and disappear,
traveling thousands of miles in a flash.
The Wōkòu (倭寇) rely on Chinese people as their eyes and ears,
and the Chinese people use the Wōkòu (倭寇) as their claws and teeth.
Unless detailed plans are made,
future troubles will not be easily suppressed."
The emperor largely adopted his suggestions.
He was soon recalled to serve as Assistant Minister of Personnel,
then promoted to Minister of Personnel in Nánjīng (南京).
The emperor, knowing Xiǎo (曉) was skilled in military affairs,
transferred him to Censor-in-Chief (Right) to assist in military administration.
Soon after, he was appointed Minister of Justice.
When Āndá (俺答) urgently besieged the Right Guard of Dàtóng (大同),
the emperor ordered Minister of War Yáng Bó (楊博) to supervise the grand army,
and Xiǎo (曉) temporarily took charge of the Ministry of War.
Xiǎo (曉) said:
"Now that military affairs are critical,
the thirty-five thousand imperial troops selected for expedition
are being ordered to perform labor work.
How can they be prepared for battle and defense?
I beg that they be returned to their military camps."
The emperor immediately complied.
He soon returned to oversee affairs at the Ministry of Justice.
Yán Sōng's (嚴嵩) influence grew stronger.
Xiǎo (曉) had always been at odds with Sōng (嵩).
At that time, in major cases such as Governor Wáng Yù (王裕) for losing control
and Compiler Guō Xīyán (郭希顏) for speaking out,
Xiǎo (曉) consistently recommended lighter sentences,
while Sōng (嵩) imposed severe penalties.
When mutinous soldiers like Zhōu Shān (周山) in Nándū (南都) killed Assistant Minister Huáng Màoguān (黃懋官),
and pirate Wāng Zhí (汪直) colluded with the Wōkòu (倭寇) to cause rebellion,
Xiǎo (曉) imposed severe penalties,
while Sōng (嵩) deliberately showed leniency.
However, in the cases of Provincial Governor Ruǎn È (阮鶚), Governor-General Yáng Shùn (楊順), and Censor Lù Kǎi (路楷),
because Sōng (嵩) offered biased protection,
Xiǎo (曉) could not fully enforce the law.
Critics remarked that he failed to secure convictions.
In the early years of the Zhèngdé reign,
he was promoted to Prefect of Xīnghuà.
Zhāng Yòu (張祐), Marquis of Lóngpíng, had no son.
His younger brother, Lù (祿), disputed the succession with other clan members,
filing a complaint with the Nánjīng judicial authorities.
The case remained undecided for a long time,
so they appealed again to Jīngshī.
Liú Jǐn (劉瑾) was then in power,
and consequently, Grand Secretary Fán Yíng (樊瑩) and Censor-in-Chief Gāo Quán (高銓) were stripped of their positions.
Suì (嵿) was ordered to investigate as a director,
but was dismissed to commoner status.
After Jǐn (瑾) was defeated,
he was reinstated as Prefect of Nánxióng.
He was promoted to Administration Commissioner of Jiāngxī,
then advanced to Right Provincial Administration Commissioner.
Recognized for his outstanding governance,
he was transferred to Left Provincial Administration Commissioner.
Níng Wáng Chén Háo (寧王宸濠) wanted to expand his territory and enlarge his residence,
but Suì (嵿) steadfastly refused.
Chén Háo (宸濠) was greatly enraged,
and sent people to present gifts to him.
Suì (嵿) opened and examined them,
finding dates, pears, ginger, and mustard,
which were all allegorical allusions.
Not long after,
he was summoned to serve as Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments.
As Vice Censor-in-Chief, he was appointed Grand Coordinator of Bǎodìng and other prefectures.
Offending a palace eunuch,
he resigned due to illness and returned home.
When Shìzōng (世宗) ascended the throne,
he was ordered to oversee military affairs in Liǎngguǎng as Right Censor-in-Chief.
The bandit Huáng Liú (黃鏐) from Shàngsī Zhōu in Guǎngxī gathered aboriginal soldiers to plunder prefectures and counties.
Suì (嵿) led an expedition and captured him.
Bandits Cài Měngsān (蔡猛三) and others in Xīnníng and Ēnpíng in Guǎngdōng engaged in widespread plunder,
their numbers reaching tens of thousands.
Suì (嵿) assembled over thirty thousand troops to attack the bandits in Xīnníng,
destroying two hundred of their strongholds,
capturing and executing over fourteen thousand people,
and taking over five thousand nine hundred of their followers prisoner.
Měngsān (猛三) and others were all beheaded.
Among all military campaigns in Língnán,
none had achieved such a victory of the few over the many.
Upon hearing of the victory,
he was rewarded and commended.
Bandits Liáng Bāchǐ (梁八尺) and others in Chéngxiāng corresponded with roving bandits from Shàngháng in Fújiàn.
He dispatched Commander Lǐ Gāo (李臯) and others to join forces with Fújiàn government troops in a pincer attack,
capturing and executing over five hundred people.
In Guīshàn, Lǐ Wénjī (李文積) gathered villains and resisted arrest.
An expedition was sent to suppress him,
but it was unsuccessful for a long time.
Suì (嵿) dispatched Administration Commissioner Xú Dù (徐度) and others to suppress him,
capturing and executing over a thousand people.
People from the nation of Fólángjī, Bìdūlú (別都盧) and others, plundered Mǎlājiā and other nations.
They then led their subordinates, Shūshìlì (疎世利) and others, with five ships, to raid the nation of Bāxī,
and subsequently invaded Xīnhuì.
Suì (嵿) sent generals to sea to capture them,
seizing two of their ships,
whereupon the pirates fled.
Soon after, he was summoned to oversee the Nánjīng Censorate,
and then appointed Minister of Works.
In the sixth year, during the grand evaluation of capital officials,
he was impeached for errors and dismissed.
He retired.
He died several years later.
Wǔ Wéndìng (伍文定),
courtesy name Shítài (時泰),
was from Sōngzī.
His father, Xiù (琇),
was an Administration Vice Commissioner in Guìzhōu.
Wéndìng (文定) passed the imperial examination in the twelfth year of Hóngzhì.
He possessed great physical strength,
was skilled in archery and horsemanship,
and his discussions were passionate.
He was appointed Judicial Commissioner of Chángzhōu.
He was sharp, quick-witted, and adept at judging cases,
earning him a reputation as a strong official.
Xú Fǔ (徐俌), Duke of Wèi, disputed land with a commoner,
and Wéndìng (文定) investigated and returned it to the commoner.
Liú Jǐn (劉瑾) accepted a heavy bribe from Fǔ (俌),
initiating a major case.
Grand Coordinator Ài Pú (艾樸) and fourteen others were all arrested.
Wéndìng (文定) had already been promoted to Assistant Prefect of Chéngdū,
but was also imprisoned in the imperial prison,
and dismissed to commoner status.
After Jǐn (瑾) was defeated,
he was reinstated and reassigned to Jiāxīng.
Bandits Wáng Hào Bā (王浩八) and others from Yáoyuán in Jiāngxī raided Kāihuà in Zhèjiāng.
Censor-in-Chief Yú Jiàn (俞諫) ordered Wéndìng (文定) to join forces with Regional Commander Lǐ Lóng (李隆), Commander Jiāng Hóng (江洪), and Surveillance Commissioner Chǔ Shān (儲珊) to suppress them.
They encamped at Huápù.
However, Commander Bái Hóng (白弘) and Zhīfǔ Huáng Zhōng (黃衷) of Húzhōu set up a separate camp at Mǎjīn.
Bandit leader Liú Chāngsān (劉昌三) defeated and captured Hóng (弘),
and the government army suffered a major defeat.
Hào Bā (浩八) suddenly attacked Huápù,
but Hóng (洪) and Wéndìng (文定) defeated him,
pursuing him to Kǒngpù.
Lóng (隆) and Shān (珊) also pursued to Chíhuái,
destroying their stronghold,
and advanced to attack Yíntán.
Hóng (洪) penetrated deep with a surprise attack,
fell into a bandit trap,
and was captured along with Commander Zhāng Lín (張琳) and others.
Wéndìng (文定) and others covered the rear and managed to return,
while the bandits also fled back to Jiāngxī.
Jiàn (諫) and others reported Wéndìng's (文定) loyalty and bravery,
and an imperial edict ordered the relevant authorities to reward and commend him.
He was promoted to Prefect of Hénán,
where he successfully plotted the capture of formidable bandits Zhāng Yǒng (張勇) and Lǐ Wénjiǎn (李文簡).
Known for his talent in managing difficult situations,
he was transferred to Jí'ān.
He successfully pacified the bandits of Yǒngfēng and Dàmáo Shān.
Subsequently,
he assisted Grand Coordinator Wáng Shǒurén (王守仁) in pacifying Tǒnggāng and Héngshuǐ.
When Chén Háo (宸濠) rebelled,
the gentry and commoners of Jí'ān scrambled to flee and hide.
Wéndìng (文定) executed one person who fled,
and the populace was then settled.
He then welcomed Shǒurén (守仁) into the city.
Prefects Xíng Xún (邢珣), Xú Lián (徐璉), Dài Dérú (戴德孺), and others arrived successively,
and together they suppressed the bandits.
Wéndìng (文定) served as the supreme commander.
During the battle of Bǐngchén,
he personally faced arrows and stones,
and his beard was singed by fire, yet he remained unshaken.
When the rebellion was suppressed,
he was the most meritorious,
and was promoted to Provincial Surveillance Commissioner of Jiāngxī.
Zhāng Zhōng (張忠) and Xǔ Tài (許泰) arrived in Nánchāng,
wishing to claim his achievements,
but Shǒurén (守仁) had already taken Chén Háo (宸濠) captive to Zhèjiāng.
Zhōng (忠) and others were disappointed
and greatly resentful.
When Wéndìng (文定) came out to pay respects,
they immediately bound him.
Wéndìng (文定) cursed, saying:
“I disregarded my entire clan to pacify a great bandit for the nation,
what crime have I committed?
You are the trusted confidants of the emperor,
yet you humiliate loyalty and righteousness,
and avenge the rebel.
By law, you should be executed.”
Zhōng (忠) grew even angrier,
and beat Wéndìng (文定) to the ground.
Wéndìng (文定) requested to resign,
but received no reply.
Soon after, he was promoted to Right Provincial Administration Commissioner of Guǎngdōng.
Before he could depart,
Shìzōng (世宗) ascended the throne.
He reported the crimes of Zhōng (忠) and others,
and also said:
“Previously, Zhōng (忠), Tài (泰), and Liú Huī (劉暉) came to Jiāngxī.
Zhōng (忠) called himself the emperor's younger brother,
Huī (暉) called himself the emperor's son,
and Tài (泰) called himself Vice General-in-Chief Wēiwǔ,
an equal to the emperor.
They humiliated appointed officials,
falsely accused good commoners,
demanded countless things,
and preyed for over a million (taels),
leading to starvation everywhere,
and rampant banditry.
Even if these three men were cut into a thousand pieces,
it would not be enough to apologize to the people of Jiāngxī.
Now, the great villains Jiāng Bīn (江彬) and Qián Níng (錢寧) have both been executed.
These three were truly their associates.
I beg that the imperial execution be swiftly carried out,
to manifest the national laws.”
He also requested that Chén Háo's (宸濠) wealth be confiscated
and returned to Jiāngxī,
to be used for expenses;
and that the innocent people framed by Zhōng (忠) and Tài (泰), as well as members of the Níng (寧) princely clan not involved in the conspiracy, be pardoned,
to clear up the unjust cases.
The emperor graciously accepted all of it.
Based on his merits,
he was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief,
and appointed Grand Coordinator of the Yangtze River Patrol.
In the third year of Jiājìng, he suppressed and captured over two hundred sea pirates, including Dǒng Xiào (董效),
and was awarded an imperial edict of commendation.
Soon after, he resigned due to illness and returned home.
In the sixth year, he was summoned and appointed Right Vice Minister of War.
That winter, he was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief,
succeeding Hú Shìníng (胡世寧) in overseeing the Censorate.
It was merely humiliation.
Universally resented and widely envied,
people only sought to find fault and gather evidence to satisfy themselves,
never had there been anyone to speak out against the injustice or redress the wrongs endured by him.
Your servant secretly
grieves over this.
The memorial was submitted,
but ultimately shelved and not acted upon.
Cài Tiānyòu,
courtesy name Chéngzhī,
was a native of Suīzhōu.
His father, Shèng,
was the Prefect of Jǐnán,
known for his integrity and benevolence.
Tiānyòu passed the imperial examination in the 18th year of Hóngzhì (1505),
was appointed a *shùjíshì*,
and then granted the post of Supervising Secretary in the Ministry of Personnel.
He was later assigned out as an Assistant Surveillance Commissioner of Fújiàn.
He successively rose to Assistant Administration Commissioner of Shāndōng,
patrolling Liáoyáng.
In a year of famine,
he saved over ten thousand starving people.
He reclaimed tens of thousands of *qǐng* of polder fields along the coast,
which the people named
"Cài Gōng Tián" (Master Cài's Fields).
He was successively promoted to Surveillance Commissioner of Shānxī.
In the 3rd year of Jiājìng (1524),
a military rebellion broke out in Dàtóng,
and Governor Zhāng Wénjǐn was killed.
An imperial edict granted a partial amnesty to the rebellious soldiers,
and Lǐ Duó, the Governor and Censor-in-Chief of Xuānfǔ, was ordered to pacify them.
Duó did not arrive due to his mother's mourning,
so Tiānyòu was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief,
to govern Dàtóng.
Tiānyòu rode into the city with a few cavalrymen,
and ordered the soldiers to surrender the ringleaders,
and the hearts of the multitude gradually settled.
At that time, Minister Jīn Xiànmín and Commander-in-Chief Háng Xióng led troops to Gānsù,
passing through Dàtóng,
the rebellious soldiers suspected they were to be suppressed,
and again raised a clamor.
Tiānyòu, fearful,
urgently requested another amnesty.
The Ministry of War stated that if the prime offenders were not eliminated, there would be no warning for the future,
and requested that a high minister be specially dispatched to oversee military affairs in Xuānfǔ and Dàtóng,
to control the situation.
So Hú Zàn, Minister of Revenue, was ordered to go with Commander Lǔ Gāng, leading three thousand imperial troops.
Before Zàn and the others departed, Scholar Lǐ Zhī arrived with military provisions.
The rebellious soldiers said,
"This is to carry out a secret edict to kill all Dàtóng people
for military犒 [meat rations]."
Fire broke out in the night,
they surrounded Zhī's lodging,
but dispersed only after his official document was shown to them.
Soon after, they again killed Magistrate Wáng Wénchāng,
surrounded the palace of the Prince of Dài,
and threatened the Prince to memorialize for an amnesty.
The Prince hastily took two princes of the commandery and fled to Xuānfǔ.
Surveillance Censor Wáng Guān stated:
"The rebellious soldiers are rampant,
and a large army pressing on the border
will only incite them to rebel.
I request that the imperial army be stopped immediately,
and allow your servant to secretly plan."
Thus, Zàn was ordered to station his troops in Xuānfǔ.
After a while,
Tiānyòu reported that Commander-in-Chief Guì Yǒng had already captured fifty-four people,
and requested that the imperial army be stopped and not dispatched.
The Emperor reproached him for obstruction,
ordering that the ringleaders Guō Jiàn and others must be captured.
Subsequently, when Zàn reached Yánghé,
Yǒng and Tiānyòu ordered Battalion Commander Miáo Dēng to capture and execute Jiàn and eleven others,
send their heads in boxes to Zàn,
and requested the army to return.
Just two days later,
Jiàn's father, Guō Bāzǐ, again rallied Xú Bīnr and others to kill Yǒng's family members by night,
and also burned Miáo Dēng's house.
Zàn stated that unless they were all exterminated, it would be impossible.
The Emperor then severely reprimanded Tiānyòu,
recalled Yǒng to the capital,
replacing him with the former Commander-in-Chief Zhū Zhèn,
and ordered Zàn to remain stationed in Xuānfǔ.
Not long after,
Tiānyòu captured and executed Xú Bīnr and others,
and Zàn and the others then returned to the capital.
In the first month of the following year,
Ministers Lǐ Kūn and Mèng Chūn,
and Commander-in-Chief Mǎ Yǒng jointly memorialized that Bāzǐ had secretly fled beyond the Great Wall,
and would certainly become a future menace.
The Emperor was about to send an envoy to investigate,
but Zàn returned to the capital and stated that the escaped soldiers were not to be feared,
so the Emperor dismissed the investigative official and did not dispatch him.
Bāzǐ then secretly re-entered the city,
and burned Zhèn's residence.
The next morning,
Tiānyòu closed the city gates and conducted a widespread search.
Bāzǐ and thirty-four of his associates were captured,
all were executed and displayed.
Those who were coerced were completely pardoned,
and the people's hearts were then greatly settled.
When the matter was reported,
he was rewarded with silver and silk.
Afterwards,
he was promoted to Vice Censor-in-Chief,
continuing as governor.
Soon after, he was further promoted to Right Vice Minister of War.
After a long time,
he was recalled to the ministry.
Tiānyòu, seeing that the provincial salaries had long been deficient,
and that it was the year for repairing the border walls,
expediently increased the price of Huái salt certificates,
adding five thousand silver taels for every ten thousand certificates,
and was impeached.
The Emperor pardoned him.
At this point,
Censor Lǐ Zōngshū again brought up the old matter,
and Tiānyòu thereupon resigned due to illness.
Two years later,
he was summoned by imperial edict to resume his post.
Before he reached the capital,
he fell ill, announced his return home, and died.
He was ninety-five years old.
Tiānyòu possessed talent and wisdom.
During the military mutiny,
those around him were all informants for the rebels,
and all movements in the governor's office were known to them.
Tiānyòu widely recruited astrologers and fortune-tellers to frequent the army,
thereby gaining full knowledge of the situation,
and ultimately relied on this to achieve success.
He was stationed in the commandery for seven years,
and his prestige and virtue were greatly renowned,
and the elders erected a shrine of peace and pacification for him.
Hú Zàn,
courtesy name Bóhéng,
was a native of Yǒngpíng.
He was a *jìnshì*.
His highest official post was Minister of Works in Nánjīng.
Zhāng Wénjǐn
was a native of Ānqíu.
He passed the imperial examination in the 12th year of Hóngzhì (1499),
and was appointed a Secretary in the Ministry of Revenue.
In the early years of Zhèngdé,
he was implicated by Liú Jǐn,
arrested and imprisoned in the imperial prison,
and dismissed as a commoner.
After Jǐn was executed,
he was restored to his former office.
He was twice promoted to Department Director.
While supervising taxation in Shǎnxī,
he presented ten proposals for border defense and enriching the people.
He was promoted to Prefect of Ānqìng.
Realizing that Prince Níng Chén Háo would certainly rebel,
he planned defensive preparations with Commander Yáng Ruì.
Chén Háo indeed rebelled,
and sailed down the river.
Wénjǐn and others feared he would attack Nándū,
and ordered soldiers to ascend the city walls and insult him.
Chén Háo then stayed to attack,
but ultimately could not conquer it.
The details are found in the biography of Yáng Ruì.
He received imperial commendation,
and was promoted to Junior Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud.
In the first year of Jiājìng, he was appointed Right Vice Censor-in-Chief [yòu fù dū Yùshǐ],
and pacified Dàtóng.
Wén Jǐn's nature was unyielding.
He gained a great reputation by repelling invaders,
and thus became determined to revitalize and reorganize.
His methods were often harsh and without order.
To the north of Dàtóng, the four cardinal directions were flat and open,
and when the invaders arrived, there was nothing to defend against them.
Wén Jǐn said:
"When invaders attack Xuānfǔ, they cannot approach the garrison city [zhènchéng]
because of the outer screens provided by fortresses like Gégǔ and Báiyáng.
Now, the area outside our city is a battlefield;
how can we show its importance?"
He proposed to build five additional fortresses
ninety *lǐ* outside the city to the north,
named Shuǐkǒu, Xuānníng, Zhǐhé, Liǔgōu, and Huàgōu.
Assistant General Jiǎ Jiàn supervised the work with severity,
and the soldiers grew resentful.
When the fortresses were completed,
he wanted to move 2,500 families of garrison soldiers to garrison them.
The troops were reluctant to go,
and requested new recruits be enlisted.
His subordinates all echoed this sentiment.
Wén Jǐn angrily said:
"If this is the case,
then orders will not be obeyed!
The garrison's imperial guard [qīn bīng] will go first;
who would dare to lag behind!"
The imperial guard were usually idle and had families.
Hearing they were to be dispatched,
they were greatly frightened.
They requested to go alone,
and to serve in turns.
But this was not granted,
and he sternly urged them on.
Jiàn, following his lead,
caned their captains.
The border soldiers from the Five Guards of Gānzhōu had killed the Provincial Governor Xǔ Míng,
and the court's handling of the matter was lenient,
so they were quite fearless.
At this point,
soldiers Guō Jiàn, Liǔ Zhōng, and others, seizing on the popular anger,
incited a rebellion.
They killed Jiǎ Jiàn,
dismembered his corpse,
fled beyond the pass,
and encamped at Jiāoshāndūn.
Wén Jǐn feared they would collude with outside invaders,
so he ordered Vice General Shí Chén and others to invite them back into the city,
and then immediately demanded the leaders of the rebellion be punished.
Guō Jiàn and others were greatly alarmed,
and again gathered to rebel.
They burned the gate of Dàtóng Prefecture,
entered the Temporary Provincial Military Commission [xíng dū sī], released prisoners,
and then burned the gate of the Censor-in-Chief's [dū Yùshǐ] residence.
Wén Jǐn climbed over a wall and fled,
hiding in the residence of Bóyě Prince.
The rebellious soldiers wanted to burn the princely palace.
The Prince was frightened,
and handed Wén Jǐn over.
Guō Jiàn and others killed him,
also dismembering his corpse,
and then burned the office of the Garrison Commander [zhènshǒu zǒngbīng].
They released the former Commander Zhū Zhèn from prison,
and coerced him to be their commander.
This was in the eighth month of the third year of Jiājìng.
When the matter was reported,
the emperor ordered Assistant Minister Lǐ Kūn to pardon the rebellious soldiers.
Kūn petitioned for a special commendation for Wén Jǐn,
but received no reply.
After a long time,
Wén Jǐn's father, Zhèng, sued over his son's merits in defending Ānqìng,
and the Ministry of Rites petitioned on his behalf,
but it was ultimately not granted.
Wén Jǐn's wife, Lǐ Shì, again submitted a mournful petition.
The emperor was angered,
and ordered the person who delivered the petition to be arrested and punished.
Vice Censor-in-Chief Chén Hóngmó said:
"Wén Jǐn botched the affair;
the court could have executed him.
But to use soldiers to do it, and let it be spread everywhere,
harms the national prestige not a little."
A decree of reprimand was again issued.
From then on,
court officials
dared not speak of it.
In the middle of the Wànlì reign,
he was finally posthumously granted the title of Right Censor-in-Chief [yòu dū Yùshǐ].
In the early Tiānqǐ reign,
he was posthumously given the posthumous name Zhōngmǐn.
Zhān Róng,
courtesy name Rénfǔ,
was a native of Shānhǎi Guard.
He became a *jìnshì* in the fifth year of Jiājìng.
He was appointed Principal of the Ministry of Revenue [hùbù zhǔshì],
and later became a Department Director [lángzhōng].
While supervising grain transport in Dàtóng,
he encountered a military mutiny
that killed the Garrison Commander Lǐ Jǐn.
Grand Coordinator Liú Yuánqīng led troops to besiege the city,
but it did not fall for a long time.
Róng had always possessed wisdom and strategy,
and was good at adapting to changes.
Rebel soldiers plundered the city,
but none harmed Róng.
As the outer siege grew tighter,
Róng secretly allied with Commander Jǐ Zhèn, Guerrilla General Dài Lián, and Garrison Commander Wáng Níng to suppress the rebels.
He observed that rebel soldiers Mǎ Shēng and Yáng Lín had no rebellious intentions,
so he overtly ordered Níng to carry the petition of officials and commoners to Yuánqīng,
to beg for pardon for the rebels,
but secretly informed him of Róng's plan,
requesting that Shēng and Lín be spared death,
and be given 3,000 *jīn* of gold,
to recruit suiciders to serve.
It happened that Yuánqīng had already been dismissed,
so Provincial Governor Fán Jìzǔ granted it.
Shēng and Lín then gathered their trusted men,
captured and executed nine ringleaders, including Huáng Zhèn.
Róng then opened the city gates,
invited Jìzǔ in,
and subsequently arrested and beheaded twenty-six more people.
For his merits,
he was promoted to Junior Supervisor of the Court of Imperial Entertainments [Guānglùsì Shǎoqīng],
then again transferred to Junior Supervisor of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices [Tàichángsì Shǎoqīng].
In the twenty-second year,
he was made Assistant Censor-in-Chief [yòu qiān dū Yùshǐ] and pacified Gānsù.
There were over ninety Lǔmí tribute envoys detained in Gānzhōu;
Garrison Commander Yáng Xìn drove them to resist invaders,
and one-tenth of them died.
Róng said:
"They came in friendship,
yet were used on the battlefield,
losing the hearts of people from afar,
and moreover showing China's weakness."
An imperial edict stripped Xìn of his office,
and sent the coffins of the dead back to their homeland.
The Tibetans were moved and pleased.
In the *kuì* year (1543),
because Dàtóng Provincial Governor Zhào Jǐn and Garrison Commander Zhōu Shàngwén were not compatible,
an edict ordered Róng to swap positions with Jǐn.
Andá led tens of thousands of cavalry to plunder,
and Róng and Shàngwén defeated them north of Hēishān,
and he was promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief.
The invaders again launched a large-scale attack on the central route,
and Assistant General Zhāng Fèng and others died in battle.
Róng, Shàngwén, and Grand Coordinator Wēng Wàndá strictly defended Yánghé,
and dispatched cavalry to intercept and attack them,
inflicting many casualties,
whereupon the invaders retreated.
Fèngguó General Chōng Zhuó of the Dài Princely Establishment engaged in plunder;
Róng memorialized to strip him of his emoluments.
Chōng Zhuó and others conspired with the Little Prince to invade,
plotting to seize Dàtóng.
Róng informed Shàngwén, who captured them,
and all were executed.
As Dàtóng had no natural defenses,
Róng built a border wall 138 *lǐ* long on the eastern route,
with seven fortresses,
and 154 beacon towers.
Furthermore, believing that border defense required grain reserves,
and that the thirty-one fortresses near the border, such as Hóngcì,
extended over 500 *lǐ*,
he opened them up and cultivated them into fertile land,
which could yield hundreds of thousands of *qǐng* (acres).
He then memorialized to recruit military colonists for farming,
exempting them from rent and corvée,
and using Dàtóng's annual horse-purchasing funds to purchase cattle for them.
In autumn and winter, they would gather to repel invaders.
The emperor immediately agreed.
When invaders attacked,
he and Shàngwén defeated them at Mítuóshān,
beheading a tribal chief.
Róng had previously been promoted to Right Assistant Minister of War [Bīngbù Yòu Shìláng] for his merits in pacifying the rebellion,
and was repeatedly rewarded for repairing the border and defeating the enemy.
He was recalled to manage the ministry's affairs,
and promoted to Left Assistant Minister [zuǒ].
When Minister Zhào Tíngruì was dismissed,
Róng took charge of the ministry's affairs,
and memorialized for ten measures for autumn defense to be implemented.
Later, Wēng Wàndá became Minister,
but then suffered the loss of his mother,
and Róng was again to take charge of the ministry's affairs,
but he declined due to illness and requested retirement.
The emperor was angered,
and stripped him of his office and put him into idle residence.
He died two years later.
When Róng [Róng] was governing Dàtóng [Dàtóng],
Wàn Dá [Wàn Dá] was the Grand Coordinator,
and Shàng Wén [Shàng Wén] was the Grand Defender.
All three had talent and strategy,
and the invaders repeatedly entered but could not achieve their objectives.
From then on, their successors were incompetent,
and the invaders trampled the border yearly.
People increasingly missed Róng [Róng] and the others.
The following year,
Āndá [Āndá] approached the capital,
but Wàn Dá [Wàn Dá] and Róng [Róng] had already left.
Commentators said that if the two had been present,
the invaders would not necessarily have reached this point.
During the Wànlì [Wànlì] reign,
Róng's [Róng] grandson Yán [Yán] became the Shùntiān [Shùntiān] Subprefect [Tōngpàn],
and he submitted a memorial advocating for Róng's [Róng] merits.
Róng [Róng] was posthumously granted the title of Minister of Works [Gōngbù Shàngshū],
and given a pension according to regulations.
Liú Yuánqīng [Liú Yuánqīng],
courtesy name Rǔchéng [Rǔchéng],
was from Dōngpíng [Dōngpíng].
He became a *jìnshì* in the ninth year of Zhèngdé [Zhèngdé].
He was appointed Magistrate of Jìnxián [Jìnxián].
When Chén Háo [Chén Háo] rebelled,
Yuánqīng [Yuánqīng] piled firewood around his house,
and instructed his family, saying:
"If the situation becomes critical,
burn our house."
One servant tried to escape,
and he personally slew him to make an example.
All the wicked youths in the county who colluded with the rebels
were flogged to death.
Chén Háo's [Chén Háo] consort's younger brother Lóu Bóguī [Lóu Bóguī] went to Shàngráo [Shàngráo] to recruit soldiers,
but Yuánqīng [Yuánqīng] intercepted and killed him.
When a rebel dispatch arrived,
he immediately beheaded its envoy.
At this time, Mǎ Jīn [Mǎ Jīn], Magistrate of Yúgàn [Yúgàn], and Sūn Tiānyòu [Sūn Tiānyòu], Postmaster of Lóngjīn [Lóngjīn], also raised troops to resist the rebels.
A rebel leader, the "Seven Princes" [Qī Diànxià],
seized transport boats at Lóngjīn [Lóngjīn].
Tiānyòu [Tiānyòu] fought him,
killing several people.
When a rebel party recruiting soldiers passed Lóngjīn [Lóngjīn],
Tiānyòu [Tiānyòu] pursued and killed them,
and burned their boats.
The Lóu [Lóu] clan's retainers were moving west,
but were also intercepted by Tiānyòu [Tiānyòu],
who captured over seventy people.
The fact that the rebel army did not dare to pass through Húdōng [Húdōng] to spy on the two Zhè [Zhè] prefectures
was due to the efforts of these three men.
When the rebellion was pacified,
Yuánqīng [Yuánqīng] was summoned to serve as a Censor [Yùshǐ].
In the first year of Jiājìng [Jiājìng],
Jīn [Jīn] also entered service as a Censor.
Jīn [Jīn]
was from Chúzhōu [Chúzhōu].
He eventually became Vice Commissioner of Fújiàn [Fújiàn].
Yuánqīng [Yuánqīng] was soon promoted to Assistant Minister of the Court of Judicial Review [Dàlǐchéng],
but he resigned due to illness and returned home.
In the summer of the sixth year,
he was appointed Assistant Censor-in-Chief [Yòu Qiāndū Yùshǐ] to pacify Xuānfǔ [Xuānfǔ].
Guō Chūn [Guō Chūn], a bandit from Dīshuǐyá [Dīshuǐyá], occupied the city and rebelled,
proclaiming himself king.
Yuánqīng [Yuánqīng] dispatched soldiers to capture him,
but they were discovered.
Vice Grand Defender Liú Yuān [Liú Yuān] issued an order, saying:
"Only capture the principal culprit,"
and he rode around the city with banners, shouting.
His followers all dispersed,
and Chūn [Chūn] and his group committed suicide.
The Grand Defender Xì Yǒng [Xì Yǒng] oppressed his subordinates,
and Yuánqīng [Yuánqīng] impeached and dismissed him.
He was promoted to Vice Censor-in-Chief [Fù Dū Yùshǐ].
In the twelfth year,
due to border alerts, he was transferred to Assistant Minister of War [Bīngbù Zuǒ Shìláng],
and appointed Supreme Commander [Zǒngzhì] of military affairs for the garrisons of Xuān [Xuān], Dà [Dà], Shānxī [Shānxī], and Bǎodìng [Bǎodìng].
Lǐ Jǐn [Lǐ Jǐn], Grand Defender of Dàtóng [Dàtóng], excavated a forty *lǐ* long moat from the left side of Tiānchéng [Tiānchéng] at Gūdian [Gūdian],
rushing the work.
Soldiers Wáng Fúshèng [Wáng Fúshèng] and others burned and killed Jǐn [Jǐn],
and then burned the office of Grand Coordinator Pān Fǎng [Pān Fǎng].
Fǎng [Fǎng] memorialized that Jǐn [Jǐn] had provoked the mutiny,
and the emperor ordered Yuánqīng [Yuánqīng] to quell it with Grand Defender Xì Yǒng [Xì Yǒng].
Yuánqīng [Yuánqīng] posted notices ordering disbandment.
However, the notices mentioned that the mutiny at Wǔbǎo [Wǔbǎo]
was handled too leniently,
which greatly frightened the remaining remnants of Wǔbǎo [Wǔbǎo].
When the army reached Yánghé [Yánghé],
Fǎng [Fǎng] and others secretly arrested and flogged more than ten mutinous soldiers to death,
and imprisoned over seventy rebel leaders, including Wáng Bǎo [Wáng Bǎo], to offer as a submission,
requesting the army to return.
Yuánqīng [Yuánqīng], remembering the previous affair of Hú Zàn [Hú Zàn],
did not wish to stop,
and entrusted the prisoners to Censor Sū Yòu [Sū Yòu].
The prisoners falsely claimed that former Grand Defender Zhū Zhèn [Zhū Zhèn] was derelict in his duties and initiated the rebellion,
and also implicated many innocent people.
He met with Assistant Remonstrance Official Sūn Yǔnzhōng [Sūn Yǔnzhōng] who had come from Yuánqīng's [Yuánqīng] location,
and Yǔnzhōng [Yǔnzhōng] conveyed Yuánqīng's [Yuánqīng] intent,
only then were they appeased and settled.
Zhèn [Zhèn] had previously been coerced by the mutinous soldiers,
and had not actually rebelled.
He went to Yuánqīng [Yuánqīng] to explain himself.
Unable to clear his name,
he committed suicide out of indignation.
Yǒng's [Yǒng] troops arrived outside the city and plundered extensively,
whereupon the remnants of Wǔbǎo [Wǔbǎo] all rebelled again.
They engaged in battle,
killing Mobile Corps Commander [Yóují] Cáo Ān [Cáo Ān].
The government forces attacked and occupied the four gates,
besieging them day and night.
The mutinous soldiers released former Battalion Commander [Cāncéng] Huáng Zhèn [Huáng Zhèn] and others from prison,
and enthroned them as their commander,
holding the city desperately.
Fǎng [Fǎng] and the Duke-Defender General [Zhènguó Jiāngjūn] Jùn [Jùn] ● [●] and others ascended the city walls,
ordering no attack.
Jùn [Jùn] ● [●] went out to see Yǒng [Yǒng] and requested a ceasefire,
but neither was listened to.
Yǔnzhōng [Yǔnzhōng] lowered himself from the city wall and left,
reporting the situation of the generals and soldiers killing indiscriminately.
Yuánqīng [Yuánqīng] shouted:
"Are you a lobbyist for the rebels?!"
He wanted to imprison him.
Yǔnzhōng [Yǔnzhōng] did not dare to return.
Yuánqīng [Yuánqīng] then set up many patrols,
blocking memorials from the imperial princely establishment [Wángfǔ] and various officials and common people,
and requested an additional fifty thousand troops.
The emperor ordered Assistant Minister Qián Rújīng [Qián Rújīng] and Grand Commissioner Jiāng Huán [Jiāng Huán] to lead eight thousand capital troops there.
However, he suddenly realized,
and cancelled the dispatch,
solely tasking Yuánqīng [Yuánqīng] and Yǒng [Yǒng] with quelling the rebels.
Fǎng [Fǎng] urgently memorialized, stating
that the generals and soldiers had provoked the mutiny by killing indiscriminately,
and if they quickly returned the army,
the rebellion could be stopped.
Yuánqīng [Yuánqīng] also denounced Fǎng [Fǎng] as flattering the rebels.
Zhāng Fúfujìng [Zhāng Fúfujìng] supported Yuánqīng [Yuánqīng],
while Assistant Ministers Gù Dǐngchén [Gù Dǐngchén] and Huáng Wǎn [Huáng Wǎn] argued that the military action was mistaken,
and the emperor could not decide.
The city had been besieged for a long time and was in great distress,
destroying the imperial princely establishment [Wángfǔ] and various official residences to provide fuel.
The Ministry of War [Bīngbù] again issued an order for pacification,
and Yuánqīng [Yuánqīng] also erected banners to invite surrender,
and the rebellious soldiers gradually surrendered themselves.
The principal culprits, Huáng Zhèn [Huáng Zhèn] and others, also came out on different days,
begging for the firewood and foraging paths to be opened,
and Yǒng [Yǒng] assented.
The next day, when the firewood collectors came out,
Yǒng [Yǒng] seized them all.
The people in the city became even more frightened,
and the rebellious soldiers rebelled again,
colluding with foreign invaders for assistance.
Yǒng [Yǒng] encountered them,
suffered a great defeat, and fled.
The rebellious soldiers then led more than ten foreign cavalry into the city,
pointing to the imperial princely establishment of Dài [Dài] [Dàifǔ] and saying:
"Let this be the residence of the Nayán [Nayán]."
"Nayán" [Nayán]
means
"great person" in Chinese.
Upon hearing this, the people in the city
all wept in the streets.
The next day,
the foreign invaders attacked the two gates, east and south,
and the rebellious soldiers attacked from another direction,
while the government forces fought desperately,
with mutual casualties.
The invaders, knowing the rebellious soldiers were unreliable,
turned their weapons against them,
cursed loudly, and departed.
At this time,
the foreign cavalry ranged south, plundering as far as Shuò [Shuò] and Yìng [Yìng].
Yuánqīng [Yuánqīng] requested to recruit soldiers from the Nine Frontiers,
and increase the number of Supreme Commanders to defend against them,
so he could concentrate on attacking the city,
but the emperor did not allow it.
Yuánqīng [Yuánqīng] then attacked from a hundred directions,
tunneling into the city.
Those who were suffocated by poisonous smoke were piled up.
He again requested to block the water and flood it.
The emperor was greatly displeased,
stripped him of his office and sent him to live in idleness,
replacing him with Assistant Minister of War [Bīngbù Shìláng] Zhāng Zàn [Zhāng Zàn].
Before Zàn [Zàn] arrived,
Director [Lángzhōng] Zhān Róng [Zhān Róng] and others had already captured all the principal culprits.
Huáng Wǎn (黃綰) investigated merits and crimes.
He said Yuán Qīng (源清) and Yǒng Shí (永實) were the chief culprits,
and impeached them for their immeasurable greed and bribery.
Zēng Biàn (曾忭) and others from the Ministry of War stated
that during the Chén Háo (宸濠) rebellion,
Yuán Qīng (源清) had rendered service in defending the region,
and should be granted leniency under the Eight Deliberations.
The emperor was enraged,
and sent Zēng Biàn (曾忭) and the others to the imperial prison.
Yuán Qīng (源清) was arrested for trial.
The case remained unresolved for a long time.
Huáng Wǎn (黃綰) worried about his departure
and thus had Yuán Qīng's (源清) death sentence commuted, banishing him as a commoner.
When Ān Dá (俺答) threatened the capital,
he was recalled from his home,
but died before arriving.
In the early Lóngqìng (隆慶) reign,
he was posthumously appointed Minister of War.
Liú Tiānhé (劉天和),
courtesy name Yǎnghé (養和),
was from Máchéng (麻城).
He became a *jìnshì* in the third year of Zhèngdé (正德).
He was appointed Principal of the Nanjing Ministry of Rites.
When Liú Jǐn (劉瑾) dismissed eighteen censors,
and transferred twenty-four others to different departments to fill the vacancies,
Liú Tiānhé (劉天和) was among them.
He was sent out to inspect Shǎnxī (陝西).
The eunuch guarding the region, Liáo Táng (廖堂), was ordered to procure imperial provisions in Lánzhōu (蘭州).
Liú Tiānhé (劉天he) deemed it outside his jurisdiction
and declined to go.
Liáo Táng (廖堂) reported Liú Tiānhé (劉天和) for disobeying orders,
and an imperial decree ordered his arrest.
Ten thousand local people wept as they saw him off.
He was imprisoned in the imperial dungeon for a long time without release.
Yáng Yīqīng (楊一清), Minister of Personnel, submitted a memorial to save him.
The judicial authorities proposed that he should pay a fine in lieu of a caning and be reinstated to his post.
An imperial directive demoted him to Magistrate of Jīntán (金壇).
Sūn Jìfāng (孫繼芳), Principal of the Ministry of Justice, submitted an opposing memorial to save him,
but it was not acknowledged.
He was repeatedly promoted to Prefect of Húzhōu (湖州),
where he implemented many beneficial policies.
In the early Jiājìng (嘉靖) reign,
he was promoted to Vice-Commissioner of Education for Shānxī (山西).
He was successively promoted to Assistant Minister of the Nanjing Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
He was appointed Right Vice-Censor-in-Chief to oversee military farming policies in Gānsù (甘肅).
He requested that able-bodied men from Sùzhōu (肅州) and displaced people from Shān (山) and Shǎn (陝) be settled near the border for farming and herding,
and that this policy be extended to all borders.
Soon after, he submitted ten proposals for reforms,
which greatly increased land productivity.
He was transferred to be Governor of Shǎnxī (陝西).
He requested the removal of eunuchs guarding the region and the abolition of over thirty practices that harmed the people,
all of which the emperor approved.
Forty-two indigenous tribes in Táo (洮) and Mín (岷) stirred up trouble.
Liú Tiānhé (劉天和) executed those who disobeyed.
He also suppressed major bandits in Húdīan (湖店) and rebellious sorcerers in Hànzhōng (漢中),
and was promoted to Right Vice-Censor-in-Chief.
After the mourning period for his mother,
he resumed his former post to oversee river conservancy.
The Yellow River shifted south,
overflowing its banks in Jǐ (濟) and Xú (徐).
Liú Tiānhé (劉天和) dredged the Biàn (汴) River,
from Zhūxiān Zhèn (朱仙鎮) to Fēiyún Qiáo (飛雲橋) in Pèi (沛),
to reduce its lower flow.
He also dredged the seventy-two springs in Shāndōng (山東),
from Yí (沂) and Ní (尼) mountains to the Nánwàng (南旺) River,
deepening their lower reaches.
With twenty thousand laborers,
the work was completed in less than three months.
He was promoted to Right Vice Minister of Works.
According to custom,
the eight prefectures of Hénán (河南) annually conscripted people for river management.
Those who did not participate paid three *liǎng* of silver.
Liú Tiānhé (劉天和), due to a famine that year,
requested to exempt all those living along the river from the labor tax,
and halve it for those living further from the river who were not conscripted.
The imperial decree approved this.
In the fifteenth year, he was transferred to Left Vice Minister of War,
and appointed Supreme Commander of the three border military regions.
The existing war chariots had double wheels,
required twenty men,
and became stuck in dangerous terrain. Moreover, they were slow and impractical.
Liú Tiānhé (劉天和) requested to emulate the single-wheeled chariots of former Grand Coordinator Qín Hóng (秦紘),
which carried cannons, firearms, axes, and halberds.
In front, a *suānní* (狻猊) shield was erected,
and tiger shields on the left and right.
Two chariots linked together could protect thirty to forty men.
One man pulled it,
with two pushing and two flanking.
In battle,
the chariots protected the cavalry within.
If the enemy was far, firearms were deployed.
If somewhat closer, bows and crossbows were fired.
If even closer, short weapons were used.
If the enemy fled,
the cavalry pursued.
He also devised small tents to be carried with the chariots,
so that soldiers would not have to sleep exposed.
He also poisoned crossbow bolts
and repaired border walls and moats.
All these proposals were adopted.
Jí Náng (吉囊) led a force of one hundred thousand to camp behind Hèlán Shān (賀蘭山),
and sent a separate detachment to raid Liángzhōu (涼州).
Vice General Wáng Fǔ (王輔) pursued and captured their standard.
They raided Zhuānglàng (莊浪),
where Grand General Jiāng Shì (姜奭) repeatedly defeated them.
Liú Tiānhé (劉天和) was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief.
The enemy again amassed a large force, preparing to invade.
Liú Tiānhé (劉天和) predicted that if the enemy saw the west was prepared, they would turn east.
He secretly ordered Bai Jué (白爵), Vice General of Yánsuí (延綏), to march by night
and join with Staff Officer Wú Yīng (吳瑛).
The enemy indeed entered Hēihé Dūn (黑河墩) in the east,
where they encountered Bai Jué's (白爵) ambush,
suffered heavy losses, and withdrew.
Later, they entered Jílír Chuān (蒺藜川),
where Bai Jué (白爵) attacked their rear,
killing many of them.
Soon after, they raided Jiājiàn (家澗) and Zhāngjiātǎ (張家塔),
but were defeated by Bai Jué (白爵) and Wú Yīng (吳瑛).
Those who encroached upon Níngxià (寧夏)
were again defeated by Grand General Wáng Xiào (王效).
The emperor was greatly pleased,
and promoted Liú Tiānhé (劉天和) to Left Censor-in-Chief.
When Jí Náng (吉囊) invaded Héxī (河西),
Liú Tiānhé (劉天和) defended and repelled him,
and was promoted to Minister of War.
When the enemy was about to enter Pínglǔ Chéng (平虜城),
Liú Tiānhé (劉天和) set an ambush at Huāmǎ Chí (花馬池).
The enemy lost the battle
and fled to the river,
where they encountered another ambush
and many drowned.
Jí Náng (吉囊) seized the opportunity to raid Gùyuán (固原),
looting until satisfied.
It happened to be during continuous heavy rains,
rendering bows and arrows useless,
and they had no will to fight.
Many generals were timid,
so Liú Tiānhé (劉天和) executed two commanders
and summoned former Grand General Zhōu Shàngwén (周尚文) to make achievements.
At that time, Wèi Shík (魏時恪), Grand General of Shǎnxī (陝西), engaged the enemy at Hēishuǐ Yuàn (黑水苑).
Zhōu Shàngwén (周尚文) led his elite troops in a pincer attack,
killing Jí Náng's (吉囊) son, Xiǎo Shí Wáng (小十王).
The enemy retreated to Níngxià (寧夏),
where Governor Yáng Shǒulǐ (楊守禮) and Grand General Rèn Jié (任傑) again intercepted them,
defeating them at Tiězhù Quán (鐵柱泉),
killing and capturing a total of over four hundred and forty heads.
For his merits,
Liú Tiānhé (劉天和) was awarded Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince,
and one of his sons was granted the hereditary position of Commander of a Thousand Households in the Imperial Guard.
He was rewarded with silver and silk ten times before and after.
He was transferred to Minister of Revenue of Nanjing,
then recalled to serve as Minister of War to supervise the training camps.
Censors argued that Liú Tiānhé (劉天和) was old and frail,
so he requested to retire and returned home.
He died three years later at home.
He was posthumously awarded Junior Guardian
and given the posthumous title Zhuāngxiāng (莊襄).
When Liú Tiānhé (劉天和) first passed the *jìnshì* examination,
Liú Jǐn (劉瑾) wanted to claim kinship with him,
but he politely refused.
In his later years, when he was summoned to the capital,
Táo Zhòngwén (陶仲文) greeted him with a calling card,
claiming to be a relative.
Liú Tiānhé (劉天和) returned the card, saying:
"You are mistaken.
I have no such relative by marriage or blood."
Táo Zhòngwén (陶仲文) was resentful,
and played a part in his dismissal from office.
Yáng Shǒulǐ (楊守禮),
courtesy name Bǐngjié (秉節),
was from Púzhōu (蒲州).
He became a *jìnshì* in the sixth year of Zhèngdé (正德).
He was appointed Principal of the Ministry of Revenue.
In the early Jiājìng (嘉靖) reign,
he was repeatedly promoted to Surveillance Commissioner of Húguǎng (湖廣).
He cleverly captured the chief bandit of Gōng'ān (公安).
For an offense, he was demoted to Assistant Prefect of Zhōu (州).
He was successively promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief,
and Governor of Sìchuān (四川).
He, with Vice General Hé Qīng (何卿), suppressed rebellions by various tribes,
and was rewarded with silver and silk.
Earlier,
when Yáng Shǒulǐ (楊守禮) was demoted to Zhōu (州),
he was humiliated by Surveillance Commissioner Zhāng Wénkuí (張文奎).
Now,
Zhāng Wénkuí (張文kuí) was promoted to Provincial Censor of Sìchuān (四川),
and fearing Yáng Shǒulǐ (楊Shǒulǐ) would retaliate,
he preemptively memorialized with a list of alleged offenses.
An imperial decree ordered both men to resign and return home.
Shǒu Lǐ’s talent and capacity were keen and accomplished;
officials at court and in the provinces considered him capable.
He had been at home for a short time
when Qín Jīn (秦金), Minister of Works, and others jointly recommended him,
and he was recalled to serve as Henan Provincial Administration Commissioner.
He was successively promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief
and then Grand Coordinator of Níngxià.
When the rebels attacked Gùyuán,
they were defeated by Grand Superintendent Liú Tiānhé (劉天和).
Desiring to leave Níngxià,
Shǒu Lǐ, together with Commander-in-Chief Rèn Jié (任傑) and others, intercepted and defeated them.
At this time, Tiānhé was recalled,
and Shǒu Lǐ was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief and Grand Superintendent of Military Affairs, replacing him.
For his previous merits,
he was promoted to Minister of War.
Commanders-in-Chief Lǐ Yì (李義) and Yáng Xìn (楊信) successively repelled Jí Náng (吉囊),
and he was thrice granted imperial letters and silver currency.
Soon after, he submitted a memorial requesting retirement.
The emperor, displeased by his apparent avoidance of difficulty,
demoted his salary by two ranks.
That autumn,
three myriad cavalry of rebels reached Suídé.
Guerrilla Commander Zhāng Péng (張鵬) repelled them,
and Commanders-in-Chief Wú Yīng (吳英) and others pursued them beyond the frontier.
Zhōu Wén (周文), Regional Commander of the eastern route, also arrived with his troops.
They jointly attacked and defeated the rebels.
Investigating Censor Yīn Xué (殷學) stated
that the rebels had penetrated five hundred *lǐ* into the interior,
and requested punishment for the generals.
The Ministry deliberated: the mobile troops of Yánsuí were all transferred to Xuān and Dà (宣、大),
and the rebels avoided the strong points to attack the weak.
Yet, we were able to overcome the many with the few,
so their merits should be recorded.
Consequently, Shǒu Lǐ was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent,
while Xué was demoted and posted outside the capital.
Shǒu Lǐ soon left due to mourning.
When Āndá (俺答) approached the capital city,
court officials first recommended Shǒu Lǐ.
An imperial edict ordered him to hasten to the road.
When the rebels retreated,
he stopped and did not proceed.
After a long time, he died.
Zhāng Yuè (張岳),
courtesy name Wéiqiáo (維喬),
was a native of Huì’ān.
From a young age, he was fond of learning,
and aspired to be a great Confucian scholar.
He passed the imperial examination in the eleventh year of the Zhèngdé (正德) reign (1516) as a *jìnshì*,
and was appointed Executive Secretary.
When Wǔzōng (武宗) was ill in the Leopard Quarter,
he requested that senior officials attend him,
and censors take turns to report on his daily life,
monitor his medicines,
and prevent unforeseen incidents.
This was not reported.
Together with fellow officials, he remonstrated against the southern tour,
was flogged beneath the palace gate,
and demoted to Rector of the Nanjing National Academy.
When Shìzōng (世宗) succeeded to the throne,
he was restored to his former office,
and promoted to Vice Director of the Right Bureau.
His mother being old, he requested to be near her for care,
and was reassigned as a Supernumerary Assistant Director of the Nanjing Ministry of War, Bureau of Personnel.
He successively served as Director of the Bureau of Guests.
At that time, the grand *dàdì* (大禘) ritual was being discussed.
Zhāng Cōng (張璁) sought to identify the actual progenitor from whom the imperial lineage originated,
and the ritual officials all assented.
Yuè spoke to Minister Lǐ Shí (李時) saying:
“It would be better to establish a tablet for the Imperial First Ancestor,
without identifying him as a specific person.”
Shí was greatly pleased,
and informed Cōng.
Cōng did not agree,
and submitted the initial proposal.
The emperor ultimately ordered that a tablet for the Imperial First Ancestor be inscribed,
as Yuè had suggested.
Cōng bore a grudge,
and Yuè was appointed Guangxi Education Supervisor Assistant.
When he toured Liǔzhōu,
the troops mutinied loudly due to a shortage of rations,
and the city gates were closed for five days.
Yuè ordered the city defenders to open the gates,
summoned and questioned the mutineers, gave them rations, and sent them away.
Soon after, he used a stratagem to capture the ringleaders,
and brought them to justice.
Upon returning to court to offer congratulations,
he was reassigned as Jiangxi Education Supervisor.
He did not express gratitude to Cōng,
so Cōng dismissed seven Guangxi tribute students,
and demoted Yuè to Guangdong Salt Tax Supervisor.
He was promoted to Prefect of Liánzhōu.
He supervised the people in reclaiming abandoned land,
and taught them to use well-sweeps to draw water.
Many people in Lián (廉) illegally plundered pearl beds.
Yuè served there for four years,
and never took a single pearl.
When the emperor sent an envoy to Ānnán to interrogate Mò Dēngyōng (莫登庸) for killing his sovereign,
Yuè spoke to Grand Superintendent Zhāng Jīng (張經) saying:
“The Mò (莫) clan usurped the Lí (黎) dynasty;
this can be known without investigation.
If the envoy goes, he will receive deceitful words and disgrace the nation.
I request that the envoy be detained and not proceed.”
Jīng disagreed.
Lín Xīyuán (林希元), Prefect of Qīnzhōu, submitted a memorial requesting a decision to attack the Mò clan.
Yuè sent a letter to stop him,
and again itemized six reasons why an attack was not advisable.
He wrote a letter to the senior ministers, saying:
“According to reports from border residents,
Lí Zhōu (黎賙) was invested with the title but had no heir,
so he adopted his elder brother’s son, Huì (譓), as his own.
When Chén Gǎo (陳暠) rebelled,
Zhōu was killed,
and Gǎo usurped the throne.
Not long after, the people of the country enthroned Huì,
and Gǎo fled to Liàngshān.
Huì reigned for seven years and was pressured by Mò Dēngyōng,
and moved out to live in Shēnghuá.
Dēngyōng enthroned Huì’s young brother, Xiàn (●), and became his regent.
Eventually, he murdered Xiàn and established himself,
and the country was divided into three parts.
The Lí were in the south,
the Mò were in the center,
and the Chén were in the northwest.
Later, Liàngshān was also taken by Dēngyōng,
and the Chén line ended.
The territory occupied by the Lí was the ancient Rìnán (日南) land,
bordering Zhànchéng (占城),
separated by a vast sea.
Dēngyōng could not cross south of it,
hence both coexisted.
Recently, Dēngyōng again gave Jiāozhōu (交州) to his grandson, Fúhǎi (福海),
while he himself established a residence in Hǎidōng Fǔ (海東府) land, where he resided.
Among the prefectures of Ānnán,
Hǎidōng (海東) was the largest,
which is also known as Wángshān Jùn (王山郡).
This rebel, bearing the name of usurper,
constantly trains troops to guard against us,
and occasionally declares his desire to offer tribute.
Border people, knowing he is not the former king,
dare not report it.
I believe that since their internal strife has not involved any incursions,
we can leave it aside for now,
and wait until their chaos settles before accepting tribute.
If military action is insisted upon,
the outcome, whether victory or defeat, advantage or disadvantage, is not something I dare to predict.”
The senior ministers received the letter but could not decide.
Later,
Máo Bówēn (毛伯溫) came to inspect the troops,
and Zhāng Jīng entrusted all military affairs to Yuè.
He also, recognizing Wēng Wàndá’s (翁萬達) talent,
recommended both to Bówēn.
Yuè spoke with Bówēn for several days,
and Bówēn said:
“The affairs of Jiāo (交) are now entrusted to you, sir.”
He permitted Dēngyōng to offer tribute as Yuè had advised.
At this time, Yuè was promoted to Zhejiang Education Vice Commissioner,
and then again to Provincial Administration Commissioner.
Bówēn hastened to memorialize to retain him,
so he was reassigned as Guangdong Provincial Administration Commissioner,
stationed to guard Hǎiběi.
When Dēngyōng surrendered,
Yuè’s salary was increased by one rank,
and he was granted silver currency.
Soon after, for his merits in quelling the rebellion of Lí (黎) in Qióngzhōu,
his salary increase and grants were repeated.
Many incidents occurred at the frontier,
and censors recommended Yuè as skilled in frontier affairs.
Bówēn said:
“Yuè is suitable for the south,
and Wēng Wàndá is suitable for the north.”
Consequently, Yuè was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief,
and Grand Coordinator of Yún Yáng.
He was then transferred to Grand Coordinator of Jiangxi,
promoted to Right Vice Censor-in-Chief,
and concurrently Grand Superintendent of Military Affairs for both Guǎngdōng and Guǎngxī, and Grand Coordinator.
He attacked and defeated Su Gōnglè (蘇公樂) and others, the *Tóng* (僮) rebels in Fēngchuān, Guǎngdōng,
and was promoted to Right Vice Minister of War.
He pacified the Yáo (瑤) rebels in various counties of Mápíng, Guǎngxī.
He successively captured and beheaded four thousand,
and pacified over twenty thousand people.
He executed the rebel leaders Wéi Jīntián (韋金田) and others,
and his salary was increased by one rank.
He was summoned to serve as Right Vice Minister of Justice,
but by the advice of Censor Xú Nánjīn (徐南金), he was ordered to remain in his post.
The Lánshān (連山) rebel Lǐ Jīn (李金) and the Hèxiàn (賀縣) rebel Ní Zhòngliàng (倪仲亮) and others
had been appearing and disappearing in Héng (衡), Yǒng (永), Chēn (郴), and Guì (桂) for thirty years,
and could not be pacified.
Yuè gathered a large army, attacked, and captured them.
He served as commander for four years,
and all major rebels were pacified.
He was summoned and appointed Left Vice Minister of War.
Between Húguì, there was a mountain called Là’ěr,
where various Miáo groups resided.
To the east, it belonged to the Gānzǐpíng Sub-Prefecture of Zhènxī Thousand-Household Guard,
under Húguǎng;
to the west, it belonged to the Tóngrén and Píngtóu two Sub-Prefectures,
under Guìzhōu;
to the north, it bordered Yǒuyáng, Sìchuān.
Its vastness stretched for hundreds of *lǐ*.
The various Miáo groups repeatedly rebelled,
and the government troops could not control them.
Vice Minister Wàn Táng campaigned against them,
but failed for four years.
He then conferred a cap and sash upon their leader, Lóng Xǔbǎo.
The Hú Miáo temporarily ceased,
but the Guì Miáo continued to rebel as before.
Wàn Táng’s army returned,
and Lóng Xǔbǎo and his associate Wú Hēimiáo rebelled again.
Guìzhōu Grand Coordinator Lǐ Yìzhuàng reported the alarm,
so Yuè was ordered to oversee military affairs in Húguǎng, Guìzhōu, and Sìchuān,
and suppress them.
He was promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief.
Lǐ Yìzhuàng adhered to Wàn Táng’s proposal to pacify them,
but Yuè impeached him for obstructing the military,
and dismissed him.
Before Lǐ Yìzhuàng, the one who pacified Guìzhōu was
Assistant Censor-in-Chief Wáng Xuéyì, who, allied with Wàn Táng and attached to Yán Sōng,
advocated for pacification,
and repeatedly interfered with Yuè from the inside.
Yuè held his ground even more firmly.
Xǔbǎo ambushed and captured Xú Wénbó, the Magistrate of Yìnjiāng, and Dèng Běnzhōng, the Judicial Commissioner of Shíqiān, and took them away.
Yuè was disciplined by having his salary suspended.
He then sent Commander-in-Chief Shěn Xīyí, Assistant General Shí Bāngxiàn, and others to advance along separate routes,
while he personally entered Tóngrén to supervise them.
Fifty-three bandit leaders were successively executed,
but Xǔbǎo and Hēimiáo alone escaped.
Yuè reported the victory,
stating that the Guì Miáo were gradually pacified and
the Hú Miáo had submitted to pacification.
He requested that the local troops be sent back to farming,
which the imperial court agreed to.
Not long after,
Rǎn Yuán, the Pacification Commissioner of Yǒuyáng, incited Xǔbǎo and Hēimiáo to raid Sīzhōu,
and abducted Lǐ Yǔnjiǎn, the Prefect.
Shí Bāngxiàn’s troops intercepted them and rescued Lǐ Yǔnjiǎn,
but Lǐ Yǔnjiǎn eventually died.
Yán Sōng and his son, who held an old grudge against Yuè,
wanted to arrest and punish him,
but Xú Jiē argued against it.
Yuè was then stripped of his title as Right Censor-in-Chief,
and appointed Vice Minister of War to supervise the army.
Shí Bāngxiàn and others soon defeated the bandits.
Yuè searched the mountain thickets,
and the remaining bandits offered the Sīzhōu seal and Xǔbǎo.
Húguǎng troops also broke through and captured the chief culprit Lǐ Tōnghǎi and others.
As Hēimiáo was not yet captured,
Yuè dared not report his achievements.
Later, Rǎn Yuán’s plot was exposed,
and Yuè uncovered his treachery.
Rǎn Yuán bribed Yán Shìfān to accuse Yuè of cutting off the Miáo factions.
Shí Bāngxiàn finally captured Hēimiáo and presented him,
and the Miáo troubles then ceased.
Yuè died in Yuánzhōu.
When his coffin was returned,
the people of Yuánzhōu welcomed and wept for him in endless streams.
Afterwards,
for his achievements,
he was reinstated as Right Censor-in-Chief,
posthumously granted Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
and given the posthumous title Xiānghuì.
Yuè was widely read and skilled in writing.
His understanding of classical learning was profound,
and he disliked Wáng Shǒurén’s scholarship,
taking Chéng and Zhū as his doctrinal masters.
Lǐ Yǔnjiǎn was
a native of Róngxiàn.
He rose from being a *jǔrén*.
As there were many bandits in the prefecture,
he sent his family away,
living alone with his grandson Bǐngwén.
Both grandfather and grandson were captured,
and Xǔbǎo held them hostage for a large ransom.
Lǐ Yǔnjiǎn, however, sent a message to Shí Bāngxiàn, ordering him to advance his troops quickly.
While among the bandits, he threw himself off a high cliff.
The bandits dragged him out
and abandoned him on the road.
The people of Sīzhōu carried him back,
but he died at Qīnglàng Guard.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him Vice Commissioner of Guìzhōu,
bestowed sacrifices and burial,
and conferred an official position upon one of his sons.
Guō Zōnggāo,
courtesy name Jūnbì,
was a native of Fúshān,
and a *jìnshì* in the eighth year of Jiājìng.
He was selected as a *shùjíshì*.
Soon an imperial edict decreed that all those selected were to be reassigned,
and he obtained the position of Principal of the Ministry of Justice.
He was promoted to Censor.
