In the tenth month of the twelfth year,
stars fell like rain.
Not long after,
Crown Prince Āichōng passed away,
and Dàtóng suffered military unrest.
Guō Zōnggāo advised the Emperor to cultivate benevolence and generosity,
to heed and accept loyal counsel,
and not to govern solely with strictness and clarity.
The Emperor was greatly angered,
had him imprisoned by imperial decree,
and released him after forty strokes of the杖.
He successively served as investigating censor in Sūzhōu, Sōngjiāng, and Shùntiān.
When touring his circuit, he rode on horseback,
not in a shoulder palanquin.
At that time, the court nominated Liú Kuí, Grand Coordinator of Bǎodìng, to return and manage affairs in the Censorate,
but Guō Zōnggāo argued that Liú Kuí had once recommended the son of Grand Secretary Lǐ Shí,
accusing him of flattery and moral impropriety,
and unsuitability for maintaining discipline.
He was disciplined by having his salary deducted for two months.
Soon after, he was dispatched as Vice Commissioner for Military Preparedness of Yànmén,
then transferred to Provincial Administration Commissioner of Shǎnxī,
and promoted to Junior Minister of the Grand Court of Revision.
In the tenth month of the twenty-third year,
raiders entered Wànquán Right Guard,
reached Guǎngchāng,
and set up camps stretching forty *lǐ*.
Zhū Fāng, Grand Coordinator of Shùntiān, was imprisoned,
and Guō Zōnggāo was promoted to Right Assistant Censor-in-Chief to replace him,
but the raiders had already left.
Guō Zōnggāo said:
"Mìyún is the most critical strategic point,
and heavy troops should be stationed there.
I request an order for the three garrisons of Mǎlán, Tàipíng, and Yànhé to dispatch a thousand men annually,
to proceed to Mìyún in the fifth month.
If there is an alarm, the Commander-in-Chief will personally lead troops to reinforce.
Jūyōng and Báiyáng,
though strategically important, have weak forces.
If an alarm occurs, they must await an imperial report,
which will be too late.
I request a pre-arranged method for borrowing and dispatching troops,
ordering the troops from the three garrisons of Jiànchāng,
to assist Mìyún in peacetime,
and to be relocated to Jūyōng in case of an alarm."
All were approved.
After a long time,
Guō Zōnggāo heard that forty thousand enemy cavalry intended to invade by separate routes,
and memorialized to dispatch troops from the Metropolitan Army, Shāndōng, and Hénán for reinforcement.
However, this turned out to be baseless,
and he was disciplined by having his salary deducted for one year.
According to custom,
the Metropolitan Army dispatched five divisions annually to Jìzhèn for autumn defense.
Guō Zōnggāo requested to dismiss three divisions,
using their犒軍 silver to fund the recruitment of soldiers in the local garrison.
He also requested to use the surplus silver from border repairs
to expand and build Yànhé Camp and Gǔběikǒu.
The Emperor suspected embezzlement,
and ordered him to return home for investigation.
Later, the matter was clarified,
and he was reinstated to his former office,
as Grand Coordinator of Dàtóng,
exchanging posts with Lǐ Rén, Grand Coordinator of Xuānfǔ.
Soon after, he was promoted to Right Vice Minister of War,
overseeing military affairs in Xuānfǔ, Dàtóng, and Shānxī.
Āndá’s thirty thousand cavalry attacked Wànquán Left Guard,
and Commander-in-Chief Chén Fèng and Assistant Commander Lín Chūn fought them at Yào’ér Lǐng.
Casualties were even,
and Guō Zōnggāo was disciplined by having his salary deducted.
The following year, they attacked Dàtóng again,
and Commander-in-Chief Zhāng Dá and Lín Chūn both died in battle.
Guō Zōnggāo and Grand Coordinator Chén Yào were disciplined by having their salaries deducted.
Supervising Secretary Táng Yǔ memorialized further on the circumstances of the deaths,
stating that the entire army was annihilated,
which was the greatest defeat in decades.
The Emperor then arrested Guō Zōnggāo and Chén Yào,
each receiving one hundred strokes of the杖.
Chén Yào subsequently died,
and Guō Zōnggāo was exiled to Jìnglǔ Guard in Shǎnxī.
In the first year of Lóngqìng,
he was recalled from his place of exile as Right Vice Minister of Justice,
then transferred to the Ministry of War,
assisting in military administration.
He was soon promoted to Right Censor-in-Chief of Nánjīng,
then immediately transferred to Minister of War to participate in military councils.
Supervising Secretary Zhuāng Guózhēn impeached Guō Zōnggāo for being old and incompetent,
and Guō Zōnggāo also requested to retire due to old age,
which the emperor allowed by imperial decree.
During the Wànlì era,
he was twice inquired after and provided with
an annual stipend and servants.
In the sixteenth year,
Guō Zōnggāo was ninety years old,
and an emissary was again sent to inquire after him.
He died that year.
He was posthumously granted Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
and given the posthumous title Kāngjiè.
Zhào Shíchūn,
courtesy name Jǐngrén,
was a native of Píngliáng.
As a child, when playing with other boys,
he would always arrange banners and flags,
and deploy them according to military strategy.
At fourteen, he passed the provincial examination.
Four years later, in the fifth year of Jiājìng,
he came first in the metropolitan examination.
He was selected as a Shùjíshì.
Due to Zhāng Cōng's recommendation, he was reassigned
and became a Hùbù Zhǔshì.
Soon after, he was transferred to the Bīngbù.
In the seventh month of the ninth year, he submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your Majesty has been seeking advice on calamities and strange phenomena for a month now,
but officials, great and small, merely offer empty words and flattery.
Ever since the Zhīxiàn of Língbǎo spoke of the Yellow River becoming clear and was rewarded,
Dū Yùshǐ Wāng Hóng subsequently presented sweet dew.
Now, Fù Dū Yùshǐ Xú Zàn and Xùndǎo Fàn Zhòngbīn have presented auspicious wheat,
Zhǐhuī Zhāng Jí presented auspicious grain,
Wāng Hóng and Yùshǐ Yáng Dōng again presented 'salt blossoms,'
and Lǐbù Shàngshū Lǐ Shí further requested to present a congratulatory memorial.
Fàn Zhòngbīn and others are not worth mentioning,
but Wāng Hóng and Xú Zàn oversee discipline,
and Lǐ Shí presides over the three rites.
Yet they deceive the emperor
and corrupt the customs and harm the government."
The emperor reprimanded him for his presumptuous words,
and ordered him to present honest advice and good strategies.
Zhào Shíchūn, in fear, accepted the blame and did not respond immediately.
The emperor urged him,
so Zhào Shíchūn then submitted a memorial stating: "Among the current most important tasks, there are four;
among the most urgent, there are three.
The most important ones are:
First, to uphold the foundation of governance.
The ruler's joys and angers,
from which rewards and punishments originate,
should not be provoked by acts that go against one's wishes.
Then rewards and punishments will be greatly impartial, and the
empire will be well-governed.
Second, to be trustworthy in decrees.
Do not believe the words of one person alone,
but consult public opinion.
Do not be accustomed to temporary benefits,
but always consider the long-term.
If a measure benefits ten
but harms one, then the benefit should not necessarily be pursued;
if it achieves a hundred merits but costs half as much, then the merit should not necessarily be undertaken.
If this is done, the empire will enjoy the blessing of peace and tranquility.
Third, to extensively seek advice.
It is advisable to imitate the ancients' system of rotational audiences and our dynasty's system of imperial summons,
allowing high officials, censors, and attendants to present their views between the palace halls,
and summoning
other officials to inquire about their duties.
Fourth, to encourage integrity and shame.
High officials should be treated with courtesy,
their major virtues appreciated, and minor faults overlooked.
For censors, if their words are correct, use them;
if incorrect, show leniency.
Then
officials will have self-respect
and will not dare to neglect integrity.
The most urgent ones are:
First, to cherish talent.
For all officials who have been punished,
whose talents should not be discarded,
and whose faults may be pardonable,
an imperial decree should be issued
to recall
them to their former posts.
Furthermore, taking advantage of the completion of the Southern Sacrifice,
their banishment and military exile should be abolished,
and they should be given a new beginning.
Second, to strengthen border defenses.
The regulations for defeated armies should be strict.
Those who retreat in battle:
junior generals may execute soldiers;
major generals may execute junior generals;
and the supreme commander may execute major generals.
Then people's hearts will be awestruck,
and they will obey commands wherever they go.
Third, to rectify governance and education.
I request the restoration of ancient capping, marriage, mourning, and sacrificial rites,
and the abolition of Daoist rituals,
prayers, and offerings.
Any Buddhist or Daoist practitioners who falsely invoke talismans,
rely on scriptures for repentance, transmute yellow into white, or ascend to distant realms to seek imperial favor and emoluments
should be immediately dismissed and banished.
Then the righteous path will be illuminated, and the people's will will be stabilized."
The emperor, upon reading it,
grew even angrier,
imprisoned him in the imperial jail for torture and interrogation,
and demoted him to commoner status.
After a long time,
when officials for the Eastern Palace were being selected,
he was appointed as a Hànlín Biānxiū concurrent with Xiàoshū in the Sījīng Bureau.
When the emperor fell ill,
Zhào Shíchūn, along with Luó Hóngxiān and Táng Shùnzhī, memorialized requesting the crown prince to take his place in the palace
and receive the New Year's Day congratulations from all officials.
The emperor was furious
and again demoted him to commoner status.
When the capital was attacked by invaders,
the court considered Zhào Shíchūn knowledgeable in military affairs,
and appointed him as Bīngbù Zhǔshì
to assist in managing the capital's camps
and training civilian militias.
When Grand General Qiú Luán proposed horse trading,
Zhào Shíchūn indignantly said:
"This is a continuation of Qín Huì!
As a grand general,
to act like a market hawker,
is this acceptable?"
He offended Qiú Luán,
who then framed him,
and he nearly incurred severe punishment again.
He was gradually promoted to Shāndōng Qiānshì,
then to Fùshǐ.
In the thirty-second year, he was promoted to Qiān Dū Yùshǐ,
and served as Xúnfǔ of Shānxī.
Zhào Shíchūn was generous and possessed an extraordinary spirit,
and was skilled in horsemanship and archery.
He lamented that invaders roamed freely,
and generals were not capable of fighting.
He often said to people:
"If I were given command of five thousand elite soldiers,
Āndá and Qiū Fú would not be difficult to pacify."
He wrote 'Yù Kòu Lùn' (Discourse on Resisting Invaders),
discussing battle and defense in great detail.
Once he held military authority,
he was even more eager to distinguish himself through military achievements.
In the ninth month of that year,
invaders entered various forts like Shénchí and Lìmín.
Zhào Shíchūn led cavalry and infantry to resist them.
Upon reaching Guǎngwǔ,
all the generals assembled.
Spies reported that there were over two thousand enemy cavalry,
two shè away.
Zhào Shíchūn donned his armor and wanted to charge,
but Grand General Lǐ Lái firmly stopped him.
Zhào Shíchūn loudly declared:
"The enemy, knowing of my arrival, will surely flee.
If we pursue slowly, we will not catch them."
He then spurred his horse forward.
When they reached Dàchónglǐng,
ambush troops rose from all sides,
and they suffered a defeat.
In a panic, he threw himself into a fortified mound,
and the defending soldiers lowered ropes to him, thus he escaped.
Lǐ Lái's army was completely routed.
He was impeached,
relieved of his office, and awaited reassignment.
Zhào Shíchūn loved to discuss military strategy,
but on this one battle, he was defeated.
However, at that time, generals usually avoided the invaders and did not attack.
Governors and regional commanders lived securely in fortified cities,
remotely directing military affairs,
with none personally engaging the enemy.
Although Zhào Shíchūn's efforts did not succeed,
everyone admired his spirit.
Zhào Shíchūn was good at memorization from his studies,
and his prose was bold and unrestrained,
ranking him alongside Táng Shùnzhī and Wáng Shènzhōng.
His poetry
was unrestrained and self-pleasing, similar to his personality.
Eulogy says: Yáo Mò and others effectively proclaimed their plans for the border regions,
and their strategies for military affairs were well-executed,
leaving memorable achievements.
Wǔ Wéndìng, following Wáng Shǒurén, pacified the rebellion of Chén Háo,
his merit being the most outstanding.
Zhào Shíchūn considered himself a military strategist,
but suffered setbacks every time he went into battle.
Indeed, those who are truly skilled in military affairs do not praise dangerous endeavors lightly.
